RFC1.title: Host Software
RFC1.summary: RFC 1 is Steve Crocker's 1969 note on initial ARPANET host-to-host software: it summarizes IMP messages, links and error checking, proposes connection establishment over link 0, TTY-like and file-like connections, and the DEL console-control language, and outlines initial experiments.

ARPANET.why: The whole document specifies early ARPANET host software and IMP behaviour (messages, links, RFNMs, connection establishment over link 0), which is the ARPANET topic in its own right.
ARPANET.quote: The software for the ARPA Network exists partly in the IMPs and partly in the respective HOSTs.

NCP.why: It sketches the earliest host-host protocol (connection setup and teardown primitives, link selection, priority on simultaneous requests) that became NCP, though it does not name it.
NCP.quote: it has been decided to reserve link 0 for communication between HOST operating systems.

rejected.why: It describes TTY-like remote-terminal connections, but this is not the Telnet protocol and no Telnet options are specified.
It proposes a 16-bit end-around-carry checksum for host-to-host checks, but this is a minor part of the document.
The 24-bit cyclic checksum is an IMP hardware detail mentioned only in passing.
It is a primary-source working note and not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: DEL (console control language)
gaps.why: The document proposes DEL, a language sent to the local host to run the front end of remote programs for terminal control. The taxonomy has no tag for early network graphics or terminal-control languages other than the ARPANET-subtree 'network graphics', which is not a clean fit.

RFC2.title: Host software
RFC2.summary: RFC 2 (1969) is an early ARPANET host-software specification describing control, primary and auxiliary links between HOSTs, link setup protocol, checksum error checking, monitor functions and executive primitives.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies host-to-host software, links and monitor behaviour for the early ARPANET with IMPs and RFNMs.
ARPANET.quote: Logical link 0 will be a control link between any two HOSTs on the network

checksum.why: A substantial section defines an end-around-carry folding checksum for message integrity.
checksum.quote: A checksum will be associated with each message, which is order dependent.

rejected.why: The document describes link management that anticipates host-host protocol, but does not define NCP by name; the general ARPANET tag is safer.
It only mandates 8-bit ASCII as the transmission character set in one line; not the subject.
It is a historical document but not a retrospective about history.

RFC3.title: Documentation conventions
RFC3.summary: RFC 3 describes the documentation conventions for the early Network Working Group's notes (the RFC series): their informal content, required form, and distribution.

RFC series.why: The document defines the format, content expectations, numbering and distribution of the Request for Comments notes, so it is about the RFC series itself.
RFC series.quote: Documentation of the NWG's effort is through notes such as this.  Notes may be produced at any site by anybody and included in this series.

ARPANET.why: It describes the early ARPANET working group and its HOST software work, and lists planned notes on the network timetable and NIL. This is background on the group and not the protocols.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Working Group (NWG) is concerned with the HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and initial experiments with the network.

rejected.why: It describes an informal note-writing convention of the pre-IETF Network Working Group, not an IETF standards process.
It is a historical document, but it is not a retrospective. Its subject is the conventions it sets.

RFC4.title: Network timetable
RFC4.summary: RFC 4 is a 1969 plan by SRI's Elmer Shapiro laying out a timetable for installing, checking out, and testing the first ARPANET nodes (SRI, UCLA, UCSB, Utah), including IMP installation, host-IMP interface debugging, test messages, and simple terminal usage.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note scheduling the checkout of the early ARPANET: IMP installation, host-IMP interface debugging, and inter-site test messages between the first four nodes.
ARPANET.quote: Test messages between UCLA-SRI 10/15/69

rejected.why: Protocols are only mentioned as items to be established (9f 'Establish protocols'); NCP is not specified or discussed.
Simple TTY and typewriter systems are planned for testing, but Telnet is not defined or named in the document.
'Move files' and 'File storage and retrieval' are only brief timetable items, with no file transfer protocol described.
The document is a primary-source working note of the ARPANET rather than a history or retrospective, so the ARPANET tag fits better.

RFC5.title: Decode Encode Language (DEL)
RFC5.summary: RFC 5 describes the Decode-Encode Language (DEL), a machine-independent language and Network Standard Translator approach for running interactive display consoles across the early ARPANET, with its syntax and semantics.

ARPANET.why: An early ARPANET working-group document defining a host-level language and translator library for running interactive programs across the network.
ARPANET.quote: The initial ARPA network working group met at SRI on October 25-26, 1968.

rejected.why: DEL covers echo tables and terminal emulation but is a distinct language, not the Telnet protocol.
Considered because DEL defines display buffers and a logical screen; the document is mainly a general encode/decode language, so the parent ARPANET tag is safer.
A historical document, but not a retrospective about history.

gaps.name: Decode-Encode Language (DEL) / Network Standard Translator
gaps.why: A host-independent programming language for remote console interaction has no matching tag in the taxonomy.

RFC6.title: Conversation with Bob Kahn
RFC6.summary: A 1969 ARPANET working note recording a conversation with BBN's Bob Kahn about IMP character-code conversion, HOST-IMP control messages, and HOST software.

ARPANET.why: The note discusses early ARPANET IMP behaviour, HOST-IMP messages (RFNM, master link clear, status) and character conversion in the IMPs; it is an ARPANET working note.
ARPANET.quote: With respect to HOST-IMP communication, we now have a five bit link field and a bit to indicate conversion.

rejected.why: ASCII is only the target of the IMP code conversion; the note is not about ASCII itself.
Conversion of 6-9 bit host codes is mentioned, but this is a minor part of an IMP interface discussion, not character set registration or use.
HOST software is mentioned but NCP is not specified or discussed.

RFC7.title: Host-IMP interface
RFC7.summary: RFC 7 outlines the preliminary software design for the Host-IMP interface on a Sigma 7 host in the early ARPANET, splitting it into a Network program and a Handler program that share buffers and an interface table.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies host-side software for connecting a host to the ARPANET IMP, including the message header, link numbers and message size limits. This is early ARPANET host and network protocol work.
ARPANET.quote: Arpa Network - Specification Outlines for Host-IMP (HI) Interface Programs.

rejected.why: The document covers the Host-IMP interface, not the host-host protocol. It only asks in passing whether a host-host control procedure is needed.
EBCDIC-to-ASCII transcoding is mentioned only as one step in output processing. The document is not about the character set.
EBCDIC is mentioned only as the source encoding that the Network program transcodes. It is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Host-IMP interface
gaps.why: The document is about the Host-IMP interface, with its message header, buffering and handler design. The taxonomy has no tag below ARPANET for it, so the ARPANET topic is the closest fit.

RFC8.title: ARPA Network Functional Specifications
review: not tagged by the model: awaiting a tagger run, or no text in the corpus

RFC9.title: Host Software
review: not tagged by the model: awaiting a tagger run, or no text in the corpus

RFC10.title: Documentation conventions
RFC10.summary: RFC 10 (Crocker, 1969) revises RFC 3 to set out the content, form and distribution conventions for Network Working Group notes (the Request for Comments series), and lists member addresses.

RFC series.why: The document defines how notes in the RFC series are written, formatted, numbered and distributed, so it is about the format and publication conventions of the RFC series.
RFC series.quote: Documentation of the NWG's effort is through notes such as this. Notes may be produced at any site by anybody and included in this series.

ARPANET.why: It describes the early ARPANET Network Working Group, its members and its working notes, which readers of ARPANET history and working notes would want.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Working Group (NWG) is concerned with the HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and initial experience with the network.

rejected.why: It is a primary-source document from the era, not a retrospective or history of the Internet.
It predates the IETF. It describes the NWG's note conventions, not the IETF standards process.

RFC11.title: Implementation of the Host - Host Software Procedures in GORDO
RFC11.summary: RFC 11 describes the ARPANET HOST-HOST procedures (connections, links, message structure, control messages) and how they were implemented in the GORDO operating system on the UCLA Sigma 7 host.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies early ARPANET host-to-host procedures (control, primary and auxiliary connections, control messages) and a host implementation. This is a 1969 ARPANET working note, and no more specific tag fits.
ARPANET.quote: This technical note concentrates upon (1) the HOST-HOST procedures and (2) the implementation of the corresponding programs in GORDO

checksum.why: The document gives a detailed host-level checksum algorithm with rotated segment sums to detect packet transposition. This is a substantial part of the message-structure section.
checksum.quote: A checksum (16 bits). Its purpose is to check, at the HOST level, the right transmission of a message.

rejected.why: The HOST-HOST protocol described is the precursor to NCP, but the document doesn't name NCP. It is also an early draft of the control procedures, so the general ARPANET tag is safer.
It is a contemporaneous technical note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC12.title: IMP-Host interface flow diagrams
RFC12.summary: RFC 12 presents flow diagrams of the hardware logic sequences for IMP-to-Host and Host-to-IMP message transfer in the ARPANET IMP-Host interface, extracted from BBN Report No. 1822.

ARPANET.why: The document describes the ARPANET IMP-Host hardware interface logic from BBN Report 1822. It is an early ARPANET working note, and no more specific ARPANET technology tag fits.
ARPANET.quote: These diagrams indicate the logical sequence of hardware operations which occur within the IMP-HOST interface.

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host protocol layered above the IMP-Host interface. This document covers only the hardware interface logic, not NCP.
The document is a technical working note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC13.title: Zero Text Length EOF Message
RFC13.summary: A 1969 ARPANET note by Vint Cerf proposing a zero-length message as the end-of-file marker for file transmissions over auxiliary host-host connections.

ARPANET.why: The document proposes an EOF message format for early ARPANET host-to-host connections, a working note on the network's host protocols.
ARPANET.quote: file transmissions over auxiliary connections will require some mechanism to specify "END-OF-FILE."  It is proposed that a length 0 (zero) message be used for this purpose.

rejected.why: The message format relates to the host-host protocol era, but the text never names NCP or specifies it, so the general ARPANET tag fits better.
It is a historical artifact, but it is a protocol working note and not a retrospective.

RFC15.title: Network subsystem for time sharing hosts
RFC15.summary: RFC 15 proposes "Telnet", a simple subsystem program on time-sharing hosts that wraps the network primitives so a local terminal can act as a terminal on a remote serving host, with an example PDP-10 to SDS 940 session.

Telnet.why: The document is the early proposal for the Telnet subsystem, describing its commands (ESCAPE, CONNECT, LOGOUT, COPY FILE) and behaviour.
Telnet.quote: A sub-system called "Telnet" is proposed which is a shell program around the network system primitives, allowing a teletype or similar terminal at a remote host to function as a teletype

NCP.why: Describes the host-level primitives (open primary/auxiliary connection, transmit, close) of the early ARPANET host-host layer that Telnet is built upon.
NCP.quote: A set of network primitives has been defined (Network Working Group Note 11) for inclusion in the monitor systems of the respective HOSTS.

rejected.why: The ARPANET parent topic is implied by the NCP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The COPY FILE command moves files over auxiliary connections, but this is a minor feature of Telnet, not a file transfer protocol specification.

RFC16.title: M.I.T
RFC16.summary: A 1969 administrative note announcing that M.I.T. (Abhai Bhushan, Project MAC) is now to receive all Network Working Group memos, with the mailing address.

ARPANET.why: The memo is a working note of the ARPANET Network Working Group about where its memos are distributed. It fits the ARPANET topic's 'working notes' scope, though it has no technical content.
ARPANET.quote: M.I.T. is now to receive all Network Working Group memos.

rejected.why: It concerns distribution of NWG memos, but it is a one-off mailing-address notice and not about the format, style, editor role or publication of the RFC series.

RFC17.title: Some questions re: Host-IMP Protocol
RFC17.summary: RFC 17 poses questions about the BBN 1822 Host-IMP protocol (link deletion, RFNM generation, NOP messages, arbitrary delays), and the appended RFC 17a is BBN's reply clarifying IMP behaviour.

ARPANET.why: The document discusses ARPANET Host-IMP protocol details (links, RFNMs, NOP messages, IMP link tables) and is an early network working note.
ARPANET.quote: The deletion of a link entry from an IMP's link table will, in general, have no effect upon a Host transmission

rejected.why: The document concerns the Host-IMP interface (BBN 1822), not the host-to-host NCP protocol.

gaps.name: Host-IMP protocol (BBN 1822)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about the ARPANET Host-IMP interface, RFNMs and link tables. The taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the general ARPANET topic.

RFC18.title: IMP-IMP and HOST-HOST Control Links
RFC18.summary: RFC 18 suggests using ARPANET link 1 for the HOST-HOST control link and link 0 for IMP-IMP control to reduce interference and delay.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note assigning link numbers for IMP-IMP and HOST-HOST control traffic.
ARPANET.quote: It is suggested that link 1 be used for the HOST-HOST control link and link 0 be used for IMP-IMP control.

NCP.why: The HOST-HOST control link is the control channel of the ARPANET host-host protocol (NCP), so NCP readers would want this link assignment.
NCP.quote: It is suggested that link 1 be used for the HOST-HOST control link

RFC19.title: Two protocol suggestions to reduce congestion at swap bound nodes
RFC19.summary: 1969 ARPANET note proposing two protocol changes (HOST-controlled ordering of IMP-to-HOST message delivery, and core-to-core locked-memory file transfers between HOSTs) to reduce congestion at swap-bound nodes.

ARPANET.why: The document proposes changes to the ARPANET IMP-HOST protocol and a HOST-HOST protocol, which is early ARPANET host and network protocol working notes.
ARPANET.quote: There is a wide variance in swap rates between core and auxiliary store among the HOST systems to be nodes in the ARPA IMP network.

rejected.why: The HOST-HOST protocol is mentioned only as a suggested new protocol for file transfers. The document does not specify or extend NCP itself.
The document discusses multi-message file transfer only in terms of locking programs in core. It does not specify or discuss FTP.
The document is about reducing congestion at swap-bound nodes through host-level ordering and locking. It is not about transport-layer congestion control.

RFC20.title: ASCII format for network interchange
RFC20.summary: RFC 20 specifies 7-bit ASCII, embedded in 8-bit bytes with the high bit 0, as the standard character code for ARPANET host-to-host interchange, and reproduces the USASCII code table, control character definitions and usage notes.

ASCII.why: The whole document defines and reproduces the ASCII code set, its table, control characters and notation for network interchange.
ASCII.quote: we suggest the use of standard 7-bit ASCII embedded in an 8 bit byte whose high order bit is always 0.

HTTP.why: PLACEHOLDER
HTTP.quote: This code will be used over HOST-HOST primary connections.

rejected.why: HOST-HOST connections are mentioned only as where the code is used; the RFC does not specify NCP.
ASCII is the more specific child tag and already covers this.
Only a passing reference to HOST-HOST connections and SRI/UCLA end-of-line choices; the document is about the character code, not ARPANET operations.

RFC21.title: Network meeting
RFC21.summary: Minutes of an October 1969 ARPANET network meeting at UCLA discussing revisions to BBN Report 1822 (IMP-Host interface), obsoleting RFC 11, and a forthcoming RFC on multiple control messages.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note on the IMP-Host interface, link tables, and message types, plus coordination of other network RFCs.
ARPANET.quote: The IMP program can handle up to 63 active transmit links and 63 active receive links at a time.

rejected.why: Control messages and links are mentioned, but the document is not about the host-host protocol itself; it only references forthcoming RFCs on it.
It is a contemporaneous working note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC22.title: Host-host control message formats
RFC22.summary: RFC 22 defines the 8-bit binary format of ARPANET Host-Host control messages (connection establishment, cease, close, uncease) and their header embedding.

NCP.why: The document specifies control message formats for the ARPANET Host-Host protocol, which is the historic NCP. Readers of the NCP page would want it.
NCP.quote: All Host-Host control messages consist of sequences of 8-bit bytes of the form: <control byte> <parameter byte l> ... <parameter byte n>

rejected.why: The NCP tag is more specific and sits under ARPANET, so the parent is implied.
The message diagram shows a checksum field, but the document does not specify the checksum.

RFC23.title: Transmission of Multiple Control Messages
RFC23.summary: RFC 23 (1969) advises that ARPANET network programs must send and receive multiple control messages in a single control communication, batching messages queued while the control link awaits RFNM.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET host-level working note about handling control messages and the control link with RFNM blocking. No narrower ARPANET tag (NCP etc.) is explicitly named, so the parent topic is used.
ARPANET.quote: The network program at a site must be prepared to send or receive more than one control message in a single control communication.

rejected.why: The document concerns control messages and control links, which are NCP concepts, but NCP is never named, so the broader ARPANET tag is safer.

RFC24.title: Documentation Conventions
RFC24.summary: RFC 24 revises the early ARPANET Network Working Group note conventions, defining what NWG notes may contain, their required header form, and their distribution list and addresses.

RFC series.why: The document defines the format, numbering, content expectations and distribution of the Request for Comments note series, which is the RFC series' own format and publication conventions.
RFC series.quote: Every NWG note should bear the following information:

ARPANET.why: It is a working note of the ARPANET Network Working Group, describing the group, its HOST software concerns and its participating sites.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Working Group consists of interested people from existing or potential ARPA network sites.

rejected.why: The document is itself a historical artefact but is not a history or retrospective of the Internet.
It describes the NWG note conventions, predating the IETF, rather than IETF standards process.

RFC25.title: No High Link Numbers
RFC25.summary: A 1969 ARPANET note proposing that host-host link numbers above 63 not be used, reserving some for instrumentation, with UCLA sizing its tables accordingly.

NCP.why: Link numbers are part of the ARPANET host-host protocol (NCP). The note constrains the link number space used by that protocol.
NCP.quote: we suggest that no link number over 63 be used. At UCLA, we will implement our tables to take advantage of this limitation.

rejected.why: NCP is the more specific child tag and already covers the ARPANET host-host protocol, so the parent is implied.

RFC27.title: Documentation Conventions
RFC27.summary: RFC 27 revises earlier notes to set the conventions for ARPANET Network Working Group notes: their informal content, required header form, and distribution list with addresses.

ARPANET.why: The note describes the ARPANET Network Working Group and its documentation practices, which are the working notes of the early ARPANET.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Working Group (NWG) is concerned with the HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and initial experience with the network.

RFC series.why: It defines the format, numbering, authorship and distribution of the Request for Comments series, so readers of the RFC series page would want it.
RFC series.quote: Every NWG note should bear the following information:

rejected.why: It is a primary-source convention document, not a history or retrospective.
It predates the IETF and describes NWG note conventions, not IETF standards procedures.

RFC28.title: Time Standards
RFC28.summary: A 1970 ARPANET note from Bill English (SRI) asking for comments on network time standards, such as for delay measurement, before installing a real-time clock.

time synchronization.why: The note solicits network-wide time standards and clock accuracy for delay measurement, which is a time synchronization matter.
time synchronization.quote: I would like any comments relative to Network time standards for such things as delay measurement so we can decide how good our clock should be.

ARPANET.why: It is an early ARPANET working note, distributed to the ARPANET sites, about network-wide clock needs.
ARPANET.quote: We are about to install a relatively accurate real-time clock on our system.

rejected.why: NTP did not exist in 1970, and the note does not specify or discuss any protocol.
Delay measurement is mentioned only as the motivation for the clock, and the note has no measurement methods.

RFC29.title: Response to RFC 28
RFC29.summary: A 1970 ARPANET note from Robert Kahn replying to RFC 28, saying a millisecond clock suffices for network measurements and describing the IMP's 100-microsecond hardware clock and 25.6 ms software clock.

ARPANET.why: The note is about timing and clock resolution in ARPANET IMPs for network measurements, an ARPANET working note.
ARPANET.quote: The IMP contains a 16-bit hardware clock which is incremented every 100 microseconds to allow for timing of internal events within the IMP

rejected.why: The note concerns clock resolution for measuring transit times, not synchronizing clocks across a network.
It mentions network measurements and round-trip times, but only to justify clock granularity. It does not define metrics or methods.

RFC30.title: Documentation Conventions
RFC30.summary: RFC 30 is an early ARPANET Network Working Group note that defines the conventions for writing, numbering, formatting and distributing NWG notes (Requests for Comments), with a distribution list and contact addresses.

RFC series.why: The document defines the form, content, numbering and distribution of the RFC series notes, so it is about RFC series format and publication.
RFC series.quote: Every NWG note should bear the following information: "Network Working Group" "Request for Comments: X" (X underscored) where X is a serial number.

ARPANET.why: It documents the working practices and membership of the ARPANET Network Working Group and its sites, so ARPANET readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Working Group (NWG) is concerned with the HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and initial experience with the network.

rejected.why: It describes the early NWG's note conventions, not the IETF's standards process or procedures.
It is a primary-source document from the period, not a history or retrospective.

RFC31.title: Binary Message Forms in Computer
RFC31.summary: RFC 31 proposes a symbolic, BNF-like notation for describing the structure of binary messages exchanged between networked computers, covering fields, concatenation, repetition, and conditional fields, with bit sizes declared last.

ABNF.why: The whole document defines a formal syntax notation, modelled on BNF, for describing binary message formats. This is the closest taxonomy fit, a formal syntax notation for protocol data.
ABNF.quote: a message description language would be useful as a standard vehicle for defining message formats.

rejected.why: ASN.1 serves a similar purpose, but this RFC defines its own ad hoc notation and does not mention ASN.1.
ASCII appears only in passing, as the expected low-level message protocol. The document is not about it.
The document concerns computer networks generally and does not specify an ARPANET protocol.
It is an early document, but it is a technical proposal rather than a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Binary message description language
gaps.why: This is a notation for describing binary message layouts. ABNF is the nearest tag, but it is aimed at text syntax, so a dedicated tag for data description or binary format notations would fit better.

RFC32.title: Some Thoughts on SRI's Proposed Real Time Clock
RFC32.summary: A 1970 ARPANET working note from UCLA commenting on SRI's proposed host real-time clock (RFCs 28 and 29), covering its use for message delay measurement and a suggested resolution, accuracy and range.

performance measurement.why: The document's purpose is to discuss how a host clock would enable measuring HOST-to-HOST message delays, including internal host delays, by extending UCLA's "Trace" facilities.
performance measurement.quote: it (or they) would allow user-oriented message delay measurements

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET Network Working Group note on host hardware and network measurement, responding to other working notes (RFCs 28 and 29).
ARPANET.quote: The addition of a clock in one or more of the network HOST's seems to be very desireable

time synchronization.why: It discusses when clocks at source and destination need synchronization, and sets accuracy (1 part in 10E7) so two clocks keep reasonable relative accuracy.
time synchronization.quote: require synchronization of the two clocks

rejected.why: The note concerns measuring live network message delays, not benchmarking methodology for devices.
Clock synchronization is discussed only at the level of hardware clock specs, not a time protocol.

RFC33.title: New Host-Host Protocol
RFC33.summary: RFC 33 presents the 1970 ARPANET HOST-HOST protocol (NCP): links, RFNMs, sockets, connections, control commands, login, and a TELNET subsystem sketch, revised after the December 1969 meeting.

NCP.why: The document specifies the HOST-HOST protocol implemented by the NCP: connections, sockets, system calls and control commands (RFC, CLS, CEASE, RESUME).
NCP.quote: Processes within a HOST communicate with the network through a Network Control Program (NCP).

ARPANET.why: It also describes the ARPANET itself: IMPs, message leaders, links and RFNMs, HOST/IMP interfacing, and the initial four-site network.
ARPANET.quote: The Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) Computer Network (hereafter referred to as the "ARPA network") is one of the most ambitious computer networks attempted to date.

Telnet.why: A substantial section walks through the TELNET subsystem and a sample dialog. This is an early precursor of the Telnet protocol.
Telnet.quote: An example of a network-related subsystem is TELNET, which will allow users at the University of Utah to connect to Stanford Research Institute

rejected.why: It is a contemporary protocol design paper, not a retrospective.
Graphics and consoles are mentioned only as motivation for the proposed NIL language, which is not specified.
The document describes one specific host protocol rather than general architectural principles.

RFC34.title: Some Brief Preliminary Notes on the Augmentation Research Center Clock
RFC34.summary: A 1970 note describing the SRI Augmentation Research Center's hardware clock, which writes absolute (date/time) and relative (24-bit accumulator) time values into XDS 940 core memory, with their formats and accuracy.

time synchronization.why: The whole document specifies a time reference, its absolute and relative formats, and its accuracy and drift against WWV. It is a local clock, not a network protocol, so the fit is loose, but it is the nearest subject.
time synchronization.quote: The ARC clock system provides a time reference that is written into the core memory of the XDS 940 Computer.

rejected.why: The note was issued in the Network Working Group series, but it says nothing about ARPANET hosts, protocols or operations. It only describes a local hardware clock.
It defines a bit layout for date and time in memory words. That is not an Internet timestamp format like RFC 3339.
There is no network time protocol here. The clock is set locally against WWV.

gaps.name: Hardware clock / local time reference
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for local host clock hardware. Its time synchronization tag covers clock synchronization over networks, so this fits only loosely.

RFC35.title: Network Meeting
RFC35.summary: Crocker announces a March 17, 1970 meeting at UCLA to present the new ARPANET host-host network protocol outlined in RFC 33, with logistics for attendance.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET Network Working Group note announcing a meeting to present the new network protocol, which falls under ARPANET working notes.
ARPANET.quote: we will host a network meeting on Tuesday, March 17, at UCLA at 9:00 a.m.

NCP.why: The meeting presents the new host-host protocol outlined in RFC 33, which is the NCP. The RFC never names it, so the tag is secondary.
NCP.quote: a detailed presentation of the network protocol, suitable for implementing unless major flaws are discovered.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous meeting announcement, not a history or retrospective.

RFC36.title: Protocol Notes
RFC36.summary: RFC 36 is Crocker's 1970 note describing the ARPANET host-host (NCP) protocol: connection establishment via RFC commands, flow control via RFNM modification and RSM/SPD, and dynamic reconnection, with data structures and control command formats.

NCP.why: The document specifies the historic ARPANET host-host protocol run by the Network Control Program, including its control commands (RFC, CLS, RSM, SPD, FND, END, RDY, ASG), connection tables and reconnection scheme.
NCP.quote: The network protocol provides three facilities: 1. Connection establishment 2. Flow control 3. Reconnection

rejected.why: NCP is the more specific child tag under ARPANET and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
The flow control here is per-link RFNM-based stop/resume between hosts in the host-host protocol, not congestion control across transports.
The protocol is host-to-host, but the specific historic technology tag NCP fits better than the general transport topic.

RFC37.title: Network Meeting Epilogue, etc
RFC37.summary: Crocker's report on the March 1970 UCLA Network meeting, covering reception of the socket/connection-based host-host protocol with dynamic reconnection, the definition of process, and suggestions for reconnection, link decoupling and reserved protocol expansion space.

NCP.why: The document discusses the design of the ARPANET host-host protocol (sockets, connections, links, dynamic reconnection, RFNMs, NCP behaviour), which is the historic NCP.
NCP.quote: The protocol based on sockets and undistinguished simplex connections is quite different from the previous protocol as documented in NWG/RFC #11.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous working note, not a retrospective history of the Internet.
Implied as the parent of NCP; NCP is the more specific tag.

RFC38.title: Comments on Network Protocol from NWG/RFC #36

The note is a contemporary working-group memo, not a history or retrospective.

RFC74.title: Specifications for Network Use of the UCSB On-Line System
RFC74.summary: RFC 74 specifies how ARPANET users connect to and communicate with UCSB's On-Line System (Culler-Fried) through an Interface process, defining the login socket sequence, input key stream, and output record formats for alphameric, curvilinear and special-character displays.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note specifying how a host site exposes a service to network users via sockets, the NCP and Host-Host protocol, including the login and connection procedure.
ARPANET.quote: The interface conducts all Network transactions through the NCP, which operates under the Host-Host protocol of 3 August 70.

network graphics.why: A substantial part defines graphics display output records (line segments, dots, vector moves in sixteen directions) sent to remote display terminals, an early network graphics format.
network graphics.quote: The data field contains a list of X-Y display coordinates as depicted below:

rejected.why: The Interface uses the NCP as substrate; the document does not specify or extend NCP itself.
The service is a remote interactive session with a custom key-code and display protocol, not Telnet, and Telnet is not mentioned.
Figure 2 defines a custom EBCDIC-like alphameric code set specific to OLS, not ASCII.

RFC75.title: Network Meeting
RFC75.summary: RFC 75 is a 1970 announcement by Steve Crocker of a Network Working Group meeting at FJCC in Houston to discuss practical use of the ARPANET network.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET working note announcing a Network Working Group meeting on the practical use of the early network, which is the kind of material the ARPANET page collects.
ARPANET.quote: I have scheduled a meeting of the Network Working Group

rejected.why: Person-to-person message sending is only one agenda item in a meeting notice, and the document specifies nothing about it.
The document is a contemporaneous working note, not a history or retrospective. ARPANET fits better.
It announces a meeting and does not report on one.

RFC76.title: Connection by name: User oriented protocol
RFC76.summary: RFC 76 proposes extending the ARPANET host-host protocol with a request/response (RFSNL/AORP/AORN) that maps symbolic labels to socket numbers, plus an example user session and a PDP-11 terminal control language.

ARPANET.why: The document extends the ARPANET host-host protocol with name-to-socket lookup and describes ARPANET node usage, so it belongs under ARPANET.
ARPANET.quote: We propose facilities, by extension of the current protocol, that will allow users to use the network on a connection-by-name basis

rejected.why: The extensions are built on NCP socket and link exchange, but the document proposes new control messages and a user language, not a specification of NCP itself. Tagging ARPANET alone is the safer choice.
Mapping labels to socket numbers is a form of name resolution. It is specific to ARPANET sockets, though, and the historic 'telephone book' idea is not a general naming system.
The document only says its character set is the one proposed in RFC 66, i.e. ASCII. That is incidental.
The terminal user control language is for attaching to remote hosts, but it is not the Telnet protocol or one of its options.

RFC77.title: Network meeting report
RFC77.summary: Report by Jon Postel on three ARPANET Network Working Group meetings at the 1970 Fall Joint Computer Conference, covering NCP testing, Host-Host protocol rework, TELNET, console interaction types, file transmission, the NIC, and the RFC editor role.

ARPANET.why: The whole report concerns early ARPANET host protocols, NCP implementation, NIC and working-group coordination, which is what the ARPANET topic covers.
ARPANET.quote: Some people are interested in the network as an object of study. In particular UCLA-Computer Science, and BBN wish to perform measurements on the network.

NCP.why: Substantial discussion of NCP testing, Host-Host protocol rework, and command link transaction sizes.
NCP.quote: As NCP's are implemented they should be subjected to comprehensive testing by an independent group.

Telnet.why: The need for TELNET and the long half/full duplex and line vs character oriented console interaction discussion are about the design of remote terminal access.
Telnet.quote: The immediate need for specification of TELNET, the third level program which allows people to pass through their local hosts and use remote hosts.

rejected.why: The meeting names an RFC editor role, but only as a minor item, not the subject of the document.
A graphics protocol is mentioned as a topic but deferred; no graphics protocol is defined.
File transmission and end-of-file marking are discussed, but FTP is not specified and the discussion is exploratory.
It is a contemporaneous meeting report, not a retrospective.

RFC78.title: NCP Status Report: UCSB/Rand
RFC78.summary: A 1970 status report from UCSB and RAND on validating their ARPANET NCP implementations against the Document #1 host-host protocol via console-to-console tests.

NCP.why: The report is about checking out and validating the UCSB and RAND NCP implementations against the host-host protocol specification.
NCP.quote: The exercise was simply to verify that the NCPs behaved according to Document #1 protocol.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the setting, but the NCP tag is the more specific child that fits; the parent is implied.
RAND's video graphics consoles and its Network Services Program are mentioned, but only as the interface used in the test, not as a graphics protocol the document specifies.

RFC79.title: Logger Protocol error
RFC79.summary: RFC 79 points out that the logger protocol proposed in RFC 66 conflicts with the NCP rule that an ALL allocate command may only be sent on an open connection, and recommends changing the logger protocol to match NCP.

NCP.why: The document is about a conflict with the NCP host-host protocol's ALL command rules, and about keeping NCP unchanged. NCP is the specific technology it concerns.
NCP.quote: This conflicts with the restriction stated in Protocol Document 1 that an ALL command can be given only for an "open" connection.

rejected.why: NCP is the more specific tag and sits under ARPANET, so the parent is implied.
The logger protocol is the initial connection and login procedure for network hosts. It is not Telnet, and the document does not discuss Telnet.

gaps.name: Logger Protocol
gaps.why: The document is partly about the ARPANET logger (initial connection) protocol from RFC 66, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. It is a minor point because NCP covers the main subject.

RFC80.title: Protocols and Data Formats
RFC80.summary: RFC 80 restates and proposes a variant of the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol from RFC 66, and describes Rand's adaptable Form Machine (data format translation) and Protocol Manager (canned NCP command sequences) for the Network Services Program.

NCP.why: The document restates and varies the Initial Connection Protocol, built from NCP commands (RTS, STR, ALL, CLS) over host-host connections, and the Protocol Manager operates on NCP command sequences.
NCP.quote: Protocols are sequences of "system calls" that correspond to (and result in NCP's issuance of) NCP commands.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note on host protocols, data formats and Rand's Network Services Program, which falls under the ARPANET topic beyond the NCP specifics.
ARPANET.quote: We view the Network as an amalgamation of a) Hosts that provide services; b) parasite Hosts that interface terminals to the services

rejected.why: Graphics terminal descriptions are only mentioned as a planned future feature of the Form Machine, not as the document's subject.
Character code translation (ASCII, EBCDIC) is just one listed feature of the Form Machine, so the document is not about character sets.
The Form Machine notation resembles regular expressions, but it is a Rand-specific tool whose syntax the document says is unimportant. It is not a formal syntax notation standard.

RFC81.title: Request for Reference Information
RFC81.summary: A 1970 ARPANET-era note from J. Bouknight asking Technical Liaison Contacts to send references on data communications and communications theory to the University of Illinois Center for Advanced Computation.

ARPANET.why: An early ARPANET Network Working Group note, circulated through the Technical Liaison Contacts of the ARPANET sites. It is a working note, so the ARPANET topic fits.
ARPANET.quote: Please ask your Technical Liaison Contact if he will send me as many references as he can in the subject areas of data communications

rejected.why: The note is a contemporary working request. It is not a history or retrospective.
It is a request for references. It is not an introductory guide.

RFC82.title: Network Meeting Notes
RFC82.summary: Notes from three ARPANET meetings at the 1970 FJCC in Houston, covering NCP changes, the Network Information Center, logger/Telnet console protocol (half vs full duplex, line vs character), graphics consoles, accounting, and file transfer formats.

ARPANET.why: The document records ARPANET community meeting discussions on host protocols, site status, IMPs, NIC and network coordination, which is working-note material about the ARPANET.
ARPANET.quote: Reworking of NCP protocol. Some issues could be solved better: (a) error control, (b) flow control, (c) overloading

NCP.why: Substantial discussion of NCP changes, flow control, IMP message boundaries, and NCP statistics and accounting additions.
NCP.quote: Reworking of NCP protocol.

Telnet.why: Much of the Tuesday and Wednesday meetings debate the console/logger protocol: half vs full duplex, line vs character transmission, echoing. This is the precursor to Telnet.
Telnet.quote: Telnet system console interaction, or logger protocol. How to get into the system and how to get help when in trouble.

rejected.why: File transmission formats and end-of-file methods were discussed, but only as exploratory ideas, not as a protocol specification.
Graphics consoles and a planned graphics meeting were mentioned, but only briefly and no formats were discussed in substance.
The notes are a contemporaneous working record, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Network Information Center (NIC)
gaps.why: A substantial part of the notes covers Engelbart's NIC documentation service, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC83.title: Language-machine for data reconfiguration
RFC83.summary: RFC 83 proposes the "Form Machine", a syntax-driven interpreter over ordered replacement rules for reconfiguring data between RAND consoles (EBCDIC) and network (binary) formats, and suggests using it to simplify a Protocol Manager for ARPANET connection protocols.

ARPANET.why: Early ARPANET-era note on data reconfiguration between consoles and the network, and on representing host-host connection protocol sequences (INIT, ALLOCATE, CLOSE) with the Form Machine.
ARPANET.quote: the connection protocol in NWG/RFC #66 could be represented by passing the following form to a protocol manager
ARPANET.section: Application of the Form Machine to Program Protocols

EBCDIC.why: Much of the proposed data reconfiguration is conversion between ASCII, EBCDIC and binary, with truncation/padding rules for each.
EBCDIC.quote: The consoles generate and accept EBCDIC character strings and the Network transmits binary digits.
EBCDIC.section: Two System Forms to Handle Protocol Statements

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the connection protocol example (RFC 66 logger); the document is not about NCP itself.
ASCII is a data type in the rules, but the document is not about the character set.
The replacement-rule notation is a data transformation language, not a formal syntax notation like ABNF.
Remote Job System on the UCLA 360/91 is only the motivating context for the examples.

gaps.name: Form Machine / data reconfiguration language
gaps.why: The core subject is a rule-based data translation language and interpreter. The taxonomy has no tag for data-transformation languages or protocol-description languages.

RFC84.title: List of NWG/RFC's 1-80
RFC84.summary: RFC 84 is an index listing RFCs 1-80 of the early ARPANET Network Working Group with dates, NIC numbers, titles and authors.

ARPANET.why: The document catalogs the earliest ARPANET Network Working Group notes on host protocols and IMP interfaces, so ARPANET readers would want this index.
ARPANET.quote: ARPA Network Functional Specifications

RFC series.why: It is a bibliographic index of the first 80 RFCs, noting never-issued numbers, which is relevant to RFC series history and publication.
RFC series.quote: LIST OF NWG/RFC's 1-80

rejected.why: NCP appears only in a few listed titles; the document is an index, not about the protocol.
It is a historical artifact but not a retrospective or history; ARPANET and RFC series fit better.
RFC 20 'ASCII Format for Network Interchange' is just one list entry.

RFC85.title: Network Working Group meeting
RFC85.summary: Announcement by Steve Crocker that the ARPANET Network Working Group will meet roughly quarterly, with the next meeting on February 17-19, 1971 at the University of Illinois.

ARPANET.why: This is an early ARPANET Network Working Group working note announcing meeting schedule and logistics, which fits the ARPANET topic of working notes.
ARPANET.quote: we will hold general Network Working Group meetings approximately every three months

rejected.why: The document is a meeting announcement for the pre-IETF Network Working Group, not a description of IETF standards process or procedures.
It is a historical artifact but not a retrospective or history of the Internet; ARPANET fits better.

RFC86.title: Proposal for a Network Standard Format for a Data Stream to Control Graphics Display
RFC86.summary: RFC 86 proposes an illustrative network-standard data stream format, display list, and screen model for controlling remote refresh graphics displays on the early ARPANET.

network graphics.why: The whole document defines an early network standard graphics data stream (NGDS), display list, and Erase/Replace commands for refresh displays.
network graphics.quote: specifying the form of the output stream for the case that the output portion of the console is a typical refresh display with point, vector and character drawing capability

ARPANET.why: It is an early ARPANET-era Network Working Group proposal about Host-to-console interaction. It is only a general ARPANET working note, so this tag is secondary.
ARPANET.quote: Information entered by the user is transmitted to the remote Host, and output from the remote Host is transmitted back to the local user.

rejected.why: The NGLI character set is ASCII, but only as the character encoding for drawn text. The document is not about ASCII.
The document concerns remote console interaction, but it defines a graphics output stream rather than Telnet-style terminal handling.
The document is a period technical proposal, not a history or retrospective.

RFC87.title: Topic for Discussion at the Next Network Working Group Meeting
RFC87.summary: A 1971 note from Project MAC proposing that the February Urbana Network Working Group meeting discuss the length, format and content of a planned April network graphics meeting.

network graphics.why: The whole document is about organizing a meeting on network graphics, including proposals for network graphic protocols and facilities, which is the subject of the early network graphics tag.
network graphics.quote: Project MAC is planning a network graphics meeting to be held in April.

rejected.why: The parent topic of network graphics is implied; the document doesn't address ARPANET protocols or operations beyond the graphics meeting.
It is only meeting logistics for the Network Working Group, not a standards process or procedure document.

RFC88.title: NETRJS: A third level protocol for Remote Job Entry
RFC88.summary: RFC 88 specifies NETRJS, a third-level ARPANET protocol letting remote hosts submit jobs to and receive printer/punch output from CCN's RJS remote batch subsystem, using separate network connections per simulated unit-record device, with block formats and error checks.

RJE.why: The document defines a remote job entry protocol for the early ARPANET: job submission via simulated card reader, output via printer and punch channels.
RJE.quote: NETRJS is the name for a message protocol and set of control conventions which will allow users at remote Hosts to access the RJS

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the substrate and context; the subject-specific RJE tag is a child of it and fits better, so the parent is implied.
The protocol relies on NCP mechanisms (RFC connections, sockets, ALL flow control, initial connection protocol), but only uses them rather than specifying them.
The protocol uses EBCDIC as its character code, but this is incidental and not a subject of the document.

RFC89.title: Some historic moments in networking
RFC89.summary: 1971 report on early ARPANET experiments at MIT-DG connecting terminals to Multics and Harvard's PDP-10 and running a remote graphics program exchange, using an interim NCP over the IMP-Host interface.

ARPANET.why: The document reports early ARPANET host experiments (IMP interface, RFNMs, Multics and Harvard connections, network ASCII messages). That is working-note content for the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: we were able to achieve a number of 'historic moments in networking' worthy of some comment.

internet history.why: It is a contemporaneous account of firsts in early networking, so history readers would want it. It is a primary source and not a retrospective.
internet history.quote: we were able to achieve a number of 'historic moments in networking' worthy of some comment.

rejected.why: The document discusses an interim stand-in for the NCP and does not specify the NCP itself.
Terminal connections to remote hosts are described informally, with no Telnet protocol involved.
'Network ASCII messages' are mentioned as a message convention, but the document is not about the ASCII character set.
Remote graphics execution is the demo case, but the document does not define a graphics protocol or format.

RFC90.title: CCN as a Network Service Center
RFC90.summary: RFC 90 describes UCLA's Campus Computing Network IBM 360/91 hardware, software and planned ARPANET service-center offerings, including the planned NETRJS, NETCRT, NETTRANS and NETTYPE third-level protocols.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note describing a host joining the network and the services it will offer to other hosts.
ARPANET.quote: CCN, the Campus Computing network of UCLA, will shortly be connected to the ARPA Network as a host of the "Service Center" type.

RJE.why: A substantial part covers remote job service (RJS) and NETRJS, remote batch job entry over the network, which fits the remote job entry subject.
RJE.quote: NETRJS is the name of the third level protocol by which a user process in a remote host will simulate a remote batch terminal connected to CCN's RJS system.

rejected.why: The host-host protocol is not discussed; only third-level protocols layered above it are mentioned.
NETCRT simulates an alphanumeric display console, not a graphics protocol.
NETCRT and NETTYPE are terminal-style protocols, but Telnet is not discussed.

RFC91.title: Proposed User-User Protocol
RFC91.summary: 1970 proposal for an ARPANET USER-USER protocol layered above HOST-HOST, defining record-oriented flags (RS, GS, FS, SIZE, EOM, CONTROL, STATUS, etc.) and a PDP-10 UUO implementation for file transfer between hosts.

ARPANET.why: The document proposes a user-level protocol layered over the ARPANET IMP-IMP and HOST-HOST protocols and NCP, with Harvard's PDP-10 implementation. It is an early ARPANET host-level protocol working note.
ARPANET.quote: The present IMP-IMP and HOST-HOST protocols are unaffected by this proposal.

rejected.why: The document builds on the HOST-HOST protocol and NCP but does not specify or modify them. It says they are unaffected.
It describes a file transmission sequence over the proposed protocol, but it is a general user-user protocol and not FTP. FTP was a separate specification.
The ASCII flag is only one of several block flags. The document is not about the ASCII character set.

RFC93.title: Initial Connection Protocol
RFC93.summary: RFC 93 clarifies the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) by recommending that the 32-bit number sent from Server socket #1 be preceded by a message data type code of zero, resolving an ambiguity in the Host-Host Protocol and amending RFCs 66 and 80.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol, an early host-level protocol, and its relationship to the Host-Host Protocol. No more specific tag fits: NCP covers the Host-Host protocol itself, but this document only clarifies the ICP message format.
ARPANET.quote: A review of the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) first described in RFC #66 and restated in RFC #80 has revealed an area of ambiguity

rejected.why: The document clarifies an ambiguity in the Host-Host Protocol, which NCP implements, but its subject is the ICP's initial message format rather than NCP itself. It only touches NCP's message data type code in passing.
The document is a contemporary technical note, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Initial Connection Protocol (ICP)
gaps.why: The ARPANET ICP, used to establish initial connections to server sockets, has no dedicated tag. The ARPANET topic is the closest fit.

RFC94.title: Some thoughts on Network Graphics
RFC94.summary: 1971 ARPANET working note commenting on RFC 86's proposal for network graphics, arguing for broader display-language capabilities, define-then-instantiate graphics, and a data reconfiguration service using a high-level standard macro format.

network graphics.why: The whole note critiques and extends an early ARPANET network graphics proposal (RFC 86), proposing display languages, data structures and a reconfiguration service for network graphics.
network graphics.quote: The proposal in Note 86 should be broadened to include the description of more complex entities and it should be raised to a level of describing more general things.

rejected.why: Parent of network graphics and implied; the document is specifically about graphics, not general ARPANET operations.
Proposes an architecture for a reconfiguration service but only for graphics, which the network graphics tag already covers.

RFC95.title: Distribution of NWG/RFC's through the NIC
RFC95.summary: A 1971 administrative note from Steve Crocker changing distribution of Network Working Group RFCs to go through the Network Information Center's Technical Liaison Contacts, with a list of contacts at ARPANET sites.

ARPANET.why: The document sets out working procedures and lists site liaison contacts for the ARPANET Network Working Group. It is an operational working note for the early network community.
ARPANET.quote: NWG notes will be sent only to Technical Liaison Contacts and to those on the current mailing list who are not at a site.

RFC series.why: It describes how RFCs are numbered and distributed, which is part of the publication process of the RFC series.
RFC series.quote: RFC numbers and NIC numbers will continue to be assigned by Jeanne North at SRI

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous administrative notice, not a history or retrospective.
The NWG predates the IETF, and the document concerns mailing distribution rather than a standards process.

RFC96.title: An Interactive Network Experiment to Study Modes of Access the Network Information Center
RFC96.summary: RFC 96 outlines an experiment to study three ways remote ARPANET sites could access the SRI-ARC Network Information Center's NLS(T) online system via Telnet-style programs, front ends, and monitor-resident Telnet, measuring response times for different terminal modes.

Telnet.why: The document compares Telnet program designs (user program vs monitor-resident) and character/line, half/full duplex handling for remote terminal access, which is core Telnet usage.
Telnet.quote: There are three basic approaches to allowing remote sites to connect to the NIC through the network, which we can call User Program Telnet, NLS(T) Front End, Monitor Telnet.

ARPANET.why: It is an early ARPANET working note on remote host access to the NIC and the interactive characteristics of host-network-host communication.
ARPANET.quote: This experiment will also provide useful information about the interactive characteristics of the network, and guidelines for designers of other interactive systems to be used with the network.

rejected.why: The experiment collects response time statistics, but this is a user-access study of one service, not a measurement methodology or metrics document.
Telnet converts terminal codes to ASCII, which is only incidental.

gaps.name: NLS / Network Information Center (NIC)
gaps.why: The document is about access to SRI-ARC's NLS online system and the NIC service, which has no tag in the taxonomy.

RFC97.title: First Cut at a Proposed Telnet Protocol
RFC97.summary: RFC 97 is an early proposal for a Telnet protocol that lets a user-site terminal act as a terminal on a remote ARPANET server, covering echo control, format characters, end-of-stream and interrupts, with an appendix for access to SRI's NLS(NIC).

Telnet.why: The document proposes the Telnet protocol conventions: echo control, character set, CR/LF handling, and interrupt/escape.
Telnet.quote: The function of the Telnet process is to make a terminal at a user site appear over the network as logically equivalent to a terminal "directly" connected to the server site.

ARPANET.why: Written for the ARPANET and built on NCP connections (RTS/STR/CLS, sockets, links) with a connection protocol to the NIC.
ARPANET.quote: allows him to utilize a typewriter-like terminal to gain interactive service from a remote server site over the ARPA Network.

rejected.why: NCP is the substrate over which Telnet runs. The document only specifies connection setup to NIC using it, not NCP itself.
The 128-character ASCII set is assumed as the character set, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
It is an historic document, but it is a protocol proposal and not a retrospective.

RFC98.title: Logger Protocol Proposal
RFC98.summary: RFC 98 proposes a Logger Protocol for logging in to a remote ARPANET host from a console over the network, endorsing the RFC 80 initial connection protocol over NCP and defining an ASCII transaction-block format for the login dialog.

ARPANET.why: The document is a 1971 ARPANET host-level protocol proposal for remote login, specifying the initial connection over NCP control messages and a login dialog format. It is a working note on the early network's host protocols.
ARPANET.quote: The term "logger" has been commonly used to indicate the basic mechanism to gain access (to "login") to a system from a console.

NCP.why: A substantial part of the document restates the Initial Connection Protocol, giving the RTS/STR/CLS control message sequences and socket conventions on top of the Host-to-Host NCP protocol.
NCP.quote: It is a two-step process utilizing the NCP control messages to effect a connection between the logger and the console of a potential user.

ASCII.why: The proposal mandates ASCII as the login character set. It addresses line-ending conventions and escape sequences for characters that ASCII lacks.
ASCII.quote: The character set used in conducting the login dialog is standard ASCII as documented in "American National Standard Code for Information Interchange"

rejected.why: The document explicitly excludes general console communication after login; it covers only the login mechanism. Telnet came later.
The login dialog is discussed, but each host defines its own sequence, so the document specifies no authentication mechanism.
The document is a contemporaneous protocol proposal, not a retrospective.

gaps.name: Remote login / Logger Protocol (Initial Connection Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for remote login or the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol, apart from the Telnet and rlogin technologies, which are later and different protocols.

RFC99.title: Network Meeting
RFC99.summary: A 1971 announcement of the next Network Working Group meeting in Atlantic City, giving hotel and reservation logistics.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note from the ARPANET-era Network Working Group announcing its meeting. A reader browsing ARPANET working notes would expect to find it.
ARPANET.quote: The next meeting of the Network Working Group will be held in Atlantic City, New Jersey coincident with the SJCC.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous meeting notice, not a history or retrospective, so the ARPANET tag fits better.
It only gives meeting logistics for a precursor group. It does not describe any standards process or procedure.

RFC100.title: Categorization and guide to NWG/RFCs
RFC100.summary: RFC 100 is an early guide that categorizes the first ~102 NWG/RFCs on the ARPANET (Host/IMP, Host/Host/NCP, logger, console, TELNET, graphics, etc.), summarizing each and marking which are current.

ARPANET.why: The whole document is a guide to ARPANET Network Working Group notes covering Host/IMP and Host/Host protocols, NCP implementations, site documentation and measurement.
ARPANET.quote: The NWG/RFC Guide categorizes the NWG/RFC notes, identifies topics under discussion and the relevant NWG/RFCs

NCP.why: A large part of the guide summarizes the NCP Host/Host protocol: connection establishment, flow control, interrupts, error control and NCP implementations.
NCP.quote: The software which implements the protocol within each Host is called the Network Control Program (NCP).

Telnet.why: The guide has a dedicated section summarizing the early TELNET proposals and related logger and console protocols.
Telnet.quote: TELNET is a subsystem permitting a teletype-like terminal at a remote Host for function as a teletype at the serving Host.

RFC series.why: It indexes and categorizes the RFC series itself, and discusses numbering, documentation conventions and distribution.
RFC series.quote: The NWG/RFC Guide is an attempt to introduce some order into the NWG/RFC series, which now numbers 102.

internet history.why: It records the early development history of ARPANET protocols and the debates behind them.
internet history.quote: For historical reasons and for readers interested in tracing through the stages of development of a topic, a brief summary is given for each NWG/RFC

rejected.why: Graphics protocols are only one subcategory (D.6) summarized in the guide, and the document is not about them.
The 7-bit ASCII standard for the console is mentioned only in passing in the summaries.
Network clocks for delay measurement appear only as a short subcategory (E.2).
NETRJS is cited only as one logger implementation, so the document is not about remote job entry.

RFC101.title: Notes on the Network Working Group meeting, Urbana, Illinois, February 17, 1971
RFC101.summary: Notes from the February 1971 Network Working Group meeting at Urbana, covering site NCP status reports, the logger protocol decision, host-host protocol problems, committee formation, and NIC services on the early ARPANET.

ARPANET.why: The document records ARPANET site status, NCP implementations, IMP/TIMP plans, and NWG organisation, which is early ARPANET working-group business.
ARPANET.quote: There are currently 15 IMPs connected to the network.

NCP.why: Much of the meeting covers NCP implementation status at each site and a committee to evaluate and revise the host-host protocol.
NCP.quote: The UCSB NCP is about 39K bytes and runs in a 60K byte partition.
NCP.section: Network Working Group meeting notes (UCSB report)

rejected.why: It is a primary-source meeting record from the period, not a retrospective or history.
File transfer by name is only discussed as a future RFC topic (Grossman), with no protocol content.
The typewriter connection protocol committee is a precursor, but only its problems are listed and no protocol is specified.
RAND's use of the UCSB 360/75 remote job entry facility is only mentioned in passing.

RFC102.title: Output of the Host-Host Protocol glitch cleaning committee
RFC102.summary: 1971 committee report recommending changes to the ARPANET Host/Host protocol (NCP): command sizes, reset commands, message format, flow-control allocation, and unresolved alternatives.

NCP.why: The document proposes changes to the Host/Host protocol implemented by the NCP, including new commands, message format, and allocation changes.
NCP.quote: A new pair of one byte commands RST (reset) and RRP (reset reply) should be added.

rejected.why: The NCP tag sits under ARPANET and is more specific, so the parent is implied.
The console interrupt discussion is about third-level protocol use of INS, not the Telnet protocol itself.

RFC103.title: Implementation of Interrupt Keys
RFC103.summary: RFC 103 points out a flaw in the ARPANET NCP's handling of interrupt keys, where the INS/INR control messages cannot say where in the data stream input switches to the supervisory process, and proposes an in-band interrupt sync character (octal 200) to fix it.

NCP.why: The document critiques the NCP's INS/INR interrupt mechanism and proposes a patch to the NCP protocol, so it is about NCP.
NCP.quote: The current NCP protocol implements only half this function.
