RFC165.summary: RFC 165 specifies the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol family, by which a user process connects to a server process (e.g. Telnet to Logger) via a well-known socket, at both the user and NCP command levels.

NCP.why: The document defines the Initial Connection Protocol atop the ARPANET Host-Host protocol, specifying NCP control commands (STR, RTS, ALL, CLS) and socket usage at the second level.
NCP.quote: Init (local = S, Foreign = U+3, size Bu)

Telnet.why: The document specifies the ICP parameter values for connecting Telnet user processes to Logger server processes, the main use case.
Telnet.quote: For connecting Telnet and Logger processes, the ICP parameters are L=1, Bu, _s2_, and Bs = _s3_ = 8.

rejected.why: The NCP tag sits beneath ARPANET and fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.

RFC166.title: Data Reconfiguration Service: An implementation specification
RFC166.summary: RFC 166 specifies the experimental ARPANET Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS), which reformats network data streams using stored "forms" interpreted by a Form Machine, controlled over a TELNET-based control connection.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies an experimental ARPANET host-level service, with connection protocols (ICP, sockets, NCP interface) and a form language. No narrower tag fits, so the ARPANET topic applies.
ARPANET.quote: The DRS experiment involves a software mechanism to reformat Network data streams.
ARPANET.section: I. INTRODUCTION - Purpose of this RFC

rejected.why: TELNET is only used for the control connection message format and as the user's access path. The document does not specify or extend it.
The using and serving processes need only an NCP interface. NCP is the substrate and is not specified here.
Forms convert between EBCDIC and ASCII, but this is a data-transform feature of the Form Machine, not character set registration or use as such.
Network ASCII is just one data type in the form language, not the subject.
EBCDIC to ASCII translation appears in the examples, but the RFC is about a general reformatting service, not EBCDIC.
BNF is used to describe the Form Machine syntax, but the document is not about the notation itself.

gaps.name: Data Reconfiguration Service / Form Machine (data stream reformatting language)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for network data transformation services or their form-description languages. The document is mainly about this, and only the broad ARPANET topic fits.

RFC167.title: Socket conventions reconsidered
RFC167.summary: RFC 167 recommends setting aside two proposals for network-wide conventions on the 32-bit NCP socket number (user-number field for accounting, zero high-order 16 bits), and discusses how hosts should allocate unique, repeatable socket numbers pending a major NCP overhaul.

NCP.why: The whole document concerns socket-number conventions in the ARPANET NCP host-host protocol, including allocation, uniqueness and CLOSE semantics, and a possible NCP overhaul.
NCP.quote: The current NCP Protocol says nothing about how hosts should assign socket numbers to process ports, except that the low-order bit is to specify socket gender

rejected.why: It is the parent of NCP and is implied by the NCP tag, so it is not listed separately.
This is about NCP socket numbers (process port identifiers), not IP address architecture.
Accounting and access control are mentioned only as motivations for a proposal that the document recommends setting aside. They are not its subject.

RFC168.title: ARPA Network mailing lists
RFC168.summary: RFC 168 gives the three ARPANET postal distribution lists (initial distribution to Network Liaisons, NIC distribution, and NIC Station Agents) for circulating Network documents and RFCs, superseding RFC 95 and RFC 155.

ARPANET.why: The document is an administrative working note listing ARPANET site liaisons, participants and station agents, and how NIC and sites distribute documents to them. This is ARPANET operations material.
ARPANET.quote: The following three lists are those to be used for distribution of Network documents.

rejected.why: This tag covers email mailing list protocols and headers. These lists are physical postal address lists, and the document says to use Air Mail.
The document covers distribution of RFCs and other Network documents, but only as ARPANET-era postal logistics. It does not address RFC format, style or publication.
No electronic mail is involved. The mailing is by postal mail.

RFC169.title: COMPUTER NETWORKS
RFC169.summary: An announcement and call for participation for the IEEE Computer Society Workshop on Computer Networks at Lake Arrowhead (September 1971), with a tentative agenda and general information on IEEE workshops.

ARPANET.why: The announcement is an early ARPA-era network community notice from the Network Working Group, co-chaired by an ARPA official, about the then-emerging computer networks. It is the closest fit for a 1971 notice, though it is not about ARPANET protocols specifically.
ARPANET.quote: Presentations are invited on all aspects of computer networks, particularly including user communities, inter-node protocols, terminal and switching equipments, and communications technology.

rejected.why: Remote job entry protocols are only one listed topic for Session III, not what the document is about.
It is a contemporary workshop announcement, not a history or retrospective.
It announces a workshop and reports no results; the organizers state that no proceedings will be published.

RFC170.title: RFC List by Number
RFC170.summary: RFC 170 is an index listing early ARPANET Network Working Group RFCs 1-170 by number with authors, titles, dates and NIC numbers.

ARPANET.why: The document catalogs the early ARPANET Network Working Group notes (host-host protocol, IMP interface, NCP, meetings), so ARPANET readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: ARPA Network Functional Specifications

RFC series.why: It is an index of the early RFC series itself, listing RFC numbers, NIC numbers, authors and dates.
RFC series.quote: RFC brief List -- Title or Partial Title

rejected.why: NCP appears only as an entry title among many in the list; the document does not specify or discuss it.
Telnet proposals appear only as list entries; the document is not about the protocol.
A file transfer protocol RFC is merely listed; the document does not address it.
It is a catalog of early documents rather than a history or retrospective; ARPANET and RFC series fit better.

RFC171.title: The Data Transfer Protocol
RFC171.summary: RFC 171 specifies the ARPANET Data Transfer Protocol (DTP), a low-level mechanism over NCP connections for delimiting transactions (bit stream, DLE-transparent, and count modes), mode handshake, separators, errors and aborts, for use by file transfer, RJE and other applications.

ARPANET.why: The document is a 1971 ARPANET host-level protocol working note defining a data transfer mechanism over NCP connections. No more specific tag fits, since the ARPANET children (NCP, SUPDUP, RJE, network graphics) are not the subject.
ARPANET.quote: DTP serves three basic functions. It provides for convenient separation of NCP messages into "logical" blocks (transactions, units, records, groups, and files)

rejected.why: DTP runs over NCP connections but does not specify or extend NCP; NCP is only the substrate.
The companion RFC 172 defines file transfer; this document explicitly separates data transfer from FTP and only mentions it as a user of DTP.
Remote job entry is cited only as one application that may use DTP; the document does not define RJE.
Telnet is mentioned only to note that transaction type codes avoid conflicts and keep ASCII integrity.
The DLE/ETX convention borrows from ASCII but the document is not about the character set.

RFC172.title: The File Transfer Protocol
RFC172.summary: RFC 172 specifies the original ARPANET File Transfer Protocol (FTP), a user-level protocol with opcodes, data types, and transaction ordering for retrieving, storing, appending, deleting and renaming files over the RFC 171 data transfer protocol.

FTP.why: The entire document defines FTP: its op codes, data types, requests, error codes, order of transactions and initial connection.
FTP.quote: The file transfer protocol (FTP) is a user-level protocol for file transfer between host computers (including terminal IMP's), on the ARPA computer network.

rejected.why: The protocol runs on the ARPANET, but the document specifies an application protocol (FTP), not ARPANET infrastructure; FTP is the better fit.
NCP is used for connection establishment and CLS, but only as substrate.
Network ASCII is referenced from TELNET only for pathname encoding; the document is not about Telnet.
Network ASCII is mentioned as a data type, but only as one minor element of FTP.

RFC173.title: Network Data Management Committee Meeting Announcement
RFC173.summary: 1971 announcement of an ARPANET Network Data Management Committee meeting at CCA, soliciting position papers on network data sharing, data description languages, and a network data directory.

ARPANET.why: This is an early ARPANET Network Working Group working note about organizing a committee and meeting on network data sharing. It fits the ARPANET topic of working notes. No narrower tag applies.
ARPANET.quote: The data management discussions at the recent NWG meeting resulted in the formation of a Network Data Management Committee

rejected.why: A network data directory is only one suggested position paper topic. The document does not specify or discuss directory services.
The file transfer committee is mentioned only as a scheduling overlap, and the document does not address FTP.
The network graphics meeting (RFC 87) is cited only as a model for the meeting format. This document is not about graphics.
This is an announcement of an upcoming meeting, not a report from a workshop. The taxonomy entry covers IAB, IRTF and community workshops.

gaps.name: Network data management / data sharing (data computer, data description languages)
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is data sharing across the early network. The taxonomy has no tag for distributed data management, so only the ARPANET topic fits.

RFC174.title: UCLA - Computer Science Graphics Overview
RFC174.summary: A 1971 UCLA note describing its computer graphics hardware (Imlac PDS-1, DEC 340), software (SMOG library, MOSAIC, FISHEYE, MOVIE), and future plans.

network graphics.why: The document surveys a site's graphics consoles and graphics software on the early ARPANET, which is what the network graphics subject covers.
network graphics.quote: We have 2 PDS-1 graphics consoles each with 8K 16 bit words of memory.

rejected.why: Only the broader parent topic; network graphics is the more specific fit, and the document does not discuss ARPANET protocols or operations.
It is a contemporaneous site description, not a history or retrospective.

RFC175.title: Comments on "Socket Conventions Reconsidered"
RFC175.summary: 1971 ARPANET note commenting on RFC 167 socket conventions, proposing Rand's 32-bit socket name layout (16 zero high-order bits, administratively assigned field, dynamic field, gender bit) and endorsing an NCP overhaul.

NCP.why: The document discusses socket naming conventions in the ARPANET host-host protocol (NCP) and argues for an NCP overhaul.
NCP.quote: especially the necessity for a major NCP overhaul.

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET working note about site conventions (Rand, UCSB, UCLA/CCN, TIP) for socket assignment.
ARPANET.quote: Since there is an apparently serious TIP storage consideration, Rand- assigned sockets will have the high-order 16 bits zero.

rejected.why: Socket names here are NCP host-host port identifiers, not naming or name resolution in the sense of that subject.

RFC176.title: Comments on "Byte size for connections"
RFC176.summary: RFC 176 comments on the three views of byte size for ARPANET host-host connections, argues that user processes (3rd level) should choose byte size, and suggests deferring the bit-stream vs byte-stream question until a Host-Host Protocol overhaul.

NCP.why: The document debates the byte size semantics of the ARPANET Host-Host Protocol as implemented by NCPs, and what NCP implementors should do. Readers of NCP history would want it.
NCP.quote: it is imperative that corresponding 3rd level processes be able to specify (and impose) a particular byte size to the NCP.

rejected.why: Telnet is only cited as an example of a 3rd level protocol that needs a fixed 8-bit byte size. The document is not about Telnet.
This is the parent of NCP, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC177.title: Device independent graphical display description
RFC177.summary: RFC 177 (1971) defines a device-independent graphical display description for the ARPANET: a stream of commands, display lists, image areas, and interaction messages that a using host can render on varied refresh displays.

network graphics.why: The document specifies an early network graphics protocol and format (NGDS, display lists, image areas, interaction messages) for ARPANET hosts. This matches the network graphics tag directly.
network graphics.quote: To attempt to facilitate the transmission of graphical information over the network, a device independent description of a display is described.

rejected.why: The network is the setting, but the document's subject is the graphics description. The more specific child tag network graphics already sits under ARPANET.
ASCII is only the character encoding used for display strings. The document does not specify or analyse it.
The character handling in display strings is a minor detail of the graphics format and not a subject in its own right.

RFC178.title: Network graphic attention handling
RFC178.summary: RFC 178 (1971) discusses graphic attention handling for early ARPANET network graphics, surveying input devices and sketching a device/data-identification/data attention protocol from terminal to serving host.

network graphics.why: The document proposes guidelines for a network standard attention protocol complementing the graphic display data stream (NGDS/NGDL), which is an early network graphics protocol.
network graphics.quote: The process of attention handling is briefly described, various graphic configurations are discussed, input devices are surveyed to identify the types of data which they produce, and an attention protocol is suggested.

rejected.why: Parent of network graphics, which is implied; the document is about the graphics protocol, not ARPANET operations generally.
Discusses configurations of graphics systems on a network, but not Internet architectural principles.

RFC179.title: Link Number Assignments
RFC179.summary: RFC 179 announces the ARPANET Host-Host Protocol link number assignments: link 0 is the control link, 2-71 are for connections, 191 is for measurement, and 192-255 are for private experiments.

NCP.why: The document assigns link numbers within the ARPANET Host-Host Protocol, which is the NCP. It updates RFC 107 and is meant for the Host-Host Protocol Document.
NCP.quote: link numbers 2-71 (decimal), inclusive, are to be valid for use in connections

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note about the network's host protocol. It also refers to the Network Measurement Center at UCLA.
ARPANET.quote: measurement work under the direction of the Network Measurement Center at UCLA

rejected.why: The document is a link number assignment table, but it is not about IANA registries. IANA did not exist as a body in this period.

RFC180.title: File system questionnaire
RFC180.summary: RFC 180 is a 1971 questionnaire from Alex McKenzie soliciting descriptions of Host file system conventions (naming, access control, directories, commands, internal representation) to inform the NWG file transfer protocol subcommittee.

ARPANET.why: This is an early ARPANET Network Working Group working note collecting Host file system information to support network file transfer standardization.
ARPANET.quote: a subcommittee of the NWG, under the chairmanship of Abhay Bhushan, is currently generating proposals for a "data transfer protocol" and a "file transfer protocol"

FTP.why: The questionnaire exists to gather input for the early file transfer protocol work, which later became FTP. Readers of FTP history would want it.
FTP.quote: the file transfer protocol should provide standard methods for requesting the transfer of a file but should not, at this time, attempt to standardize file naming conventions

rejected.why: The 'directories' here are file system directories, not networked directory services such as LDAP or X.500.
It concerns file naming and conventions on Hosts for transfer, not network storage access protocols.
Access control is one questionnaire item among several, not the subject of the document.

RFC181.title: Modifications to RFC 177
RFC181.summary: A 1971 ARPANET note by John McConnell modifying RFC 177's proposed device-independent network graphics display list: redefines coordinate areas and image spaces, EXECUTE/COPY LIST parameters, adds mode-stack push/pop items, and changes DEFINE LIST.

network graphics.why: The document modifies the network standard graphics screen and display list (NGDL) proposal, an early network graphics protocol/format, so it belongs under early network graphics protocols.
network graphics.quote: This RFC is intended to modifiy the proposal for a device independent graphical display description discussed in RFC #177.

rejected.why: Written in the ARPANET era, but the subject is the graphics display description, which the more specific network graphics tag covers (the parent is implied).
The display list is a data representation, but the specific network graphics tag fits better, and no general data-format topic is addressed.

RFC182.title: Compilation of list of relevant site reports
RFC182.summary: 1971 NIC note announcing it is compiling a list of Site-produced reports on ARPANET-related work and offering to handle requests for them.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET Network Information Center working note about collecting and referring Site reports for ARPANET participants.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Information Center is working to compile a list of all Site-produced reports which are of interest to Network participants.

rejected.why: The document concerns site reports and bibliographies, not the format or publication of RFCs.
It is a contemporary administrative note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC183.title: EBCDIC Codes and Their Mapping to ASCII
RFC183.summary: RFC 183 defines the EBCDIC code set (controls and graphics) and proposes mappings between ASCII and EBCDIC for ARPA Network hosts, including suggested EBCDIC codes for Telnet control functions, and solicits site feedback.

EBCDIC.why: The document defines the EBCDIC code set and its mapping to ASCII, which is exactly what the EBCDIC tag covers.
EBCDIC.quote: this RFC describes and defines the IBM Standard Extended BCD Interchanged Code.

ASCII.why: A substantial part of the document works out how each ASCII control and graphic maps onto EBCDIC, so readers of ASCII would want it.
ASCII.quote: It is desirable to uniquely map the ASCII codes into corresponding EBCDIC codes in a consistent manner throughout the ARPA network.

Telnet.why: It proposes EBCDIC codes for Telnet control functions such as sync, break, NOP and echo, which is a Telnet-specific proposal.
Telnet.quote: For those sites who may wish to provide our use TELNET services that communicate using an EBCDIC code, a standard code must be specified.

rejected.why: This is the parent of EBCDIC and ASCII, which are chosen instead, so the parent is implied.
The document is aimed at ARPA Network hosts, but its subject is character code mapping, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
This is the parent of character sets and not what the document is about; it covers code tables for 1971 hosts, not internationalized text.

RFC184.title: Proposed graphic display modes
RFC184.summary: RFC 184 proposes a set of graphic display modes (points, lines, vectors, character streams, grey-scale raster modes such as GRIDAREA, MATRIXAREA, SCANLINE, SCANPOINT) for inclusion in the ARPANET Network Graphics Protocol.

network graphics.why: The whole document outlines display modes that the early ARPANET Network Graphics Protocol should include, so it belongs under early network graphics protocols and formats.
network graphics.quote: we are eager to ensure that our system data structures, files, etc., be as nearly compatible the Network Graphics Protocol as is practicable.

rejected.why: The network is the setting, but the subject is the graphics protocol. The child tag network graphics already sits under ARPANET and covers it.
It is a 1971 document, but it is a technical proposal, not a retrospective or history.

RFC185.title: NIC distribution of manuals and handbooks
RFC185.summary: A 1971 ARPANET NIC request that Network participants supply 100 copies of manuals and handbooks they produce so the NIC can distribute them to Station Agents, Liaisons and outside participants.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET Network Information Center working note about document distribution among Network participants, so it fits the ARPANET operations and working notes subject.
ARPANET.quote: NIC now plans to distribute such documents to all Station Agents for use as reference copies, to Liaisons for their own use

rejected.why: The document concerns distribution of manuals and handbooks by the NIC, not the format, style or publication of RFCs.
It is about distributing manuals, not an introductory guide itself, and it is not in the FYI series.

RFC186.title: Network graphics loader
RFC186.summary: RFC 186 specifies a network graphics loader on the Project MAC PDP-10 that lets remote ARPANET users send display programs for the Evans and Sutherland LDS-1, execute them, and receive the visible line-segment output (raw or ARDS format) over the network.

network graphics.why: The document defines an early network graphics protocol (SETUP, EXECUTE, TRANSMIT, UPDATE, FLUSH, MODESET requests) for remote display program loading and output return.
network graphics.quote: The facility described herein will permit remote users on the ARPA network to obtain graphics output from programs they write for the Evans and Sutherland Line Drawing System

rejected.why: The ARPANET is only the network the loader runs over. The document does not specify a host or network protocol of the ARPANET itself. Its subject is graphics, which the child tag network graphics covers.

RFC187.title: Network/440 Protocol Concept
RFC187.summary: RFC 187 is an informational description of IBM's Network/440 research network protocol concepts, covering transmission block headers, a store-and-forward Express Exchange, a Net Controller for job and file transfer control, and interactive use.

internet architecture.why: The document conveys the philosophy and architectural concepts of a logical network machine and a configuration-independent protocol design, which fits architectural principles rather than any specific Internet protocol.
internet architecture.quote: The main theme is to treat all systems involved in the network as a part of a single (large) multiprocessor system.

rejected.why: It is a contemporary design description from 1971, not a retrospective or history of the Internet.
The NC file transmission protocol is a proprietary IBM job and file transfer scheme, not FTP.
The network described is IBM's own Network/440, not the ARPANET, though it was circulated as an RFC.
The interactive terminal connection support is part of the IBM protocol and does not specify or extend Telnet.

gaps.name: Network/440 (IBM proprietary network protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about a specific non-IETF experimental network protocol, covering block headers, Express Exchange store-and-forward, and Net Controller job and file control. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC188.title: Data management meeting announcement
RFC188.summary: A 1971 announcement of the first Network Data Management meeting, giving its logistics and agenda of talks on data sharing, data definition languages and the "Data Computer" for the early ARPANET community.

ARPANET.why: This is a Network Working Group note from the ARPANET era. It announces a meeting to form a data management working group for the network and cites related ARPANET RFCs. It fits the ARPANET working-notes category, though no specific protocol is involved.
ARPANET.quote: The first Network Data Management meeting will take place on Monday and Tuesday, August 2nd and 3rd

rejected.why: The document is a contemporary meeting notice, not a history or retrospective.
Data management and data definition languages are discussed only as agenda items. The document does not cover directory access or synchronization.
The agenda covers data sharing on networks, but the document does not specify any storage access protocol.

gaps.name: Network data management / distributed data sharing (DDL, Data Computer, CODASYL)
gaps.why: The meeting's subject is data management and data definition languages on a network. The taxonomy has no tag for databases or distributed data management.

RFC189.title: Interim NETRJS specifications
RFC189.summary: Interim specification of NETRJS, the ARPANET remote job entry protocol to UCLA/CCN's IBM 360/91, covering sessions, Telnet console, data transfer channels, record formats and RJS commands.

RJE.why: The whole document specifies the NETRJS remote job entry protocol on the early ARPANET: job input via virtual card reader, output via printer and punch, and RJS commands.
RJE.quote: NETRJS is the protocol for the remote job entry service to the 360 Model 91 at the UCLA Campus Computing Network (CCN).

rejected.why: Telnet is used only for the operator console connection (RFC 158). It is a substrate here, and Appendix B only profiles character mappings for the console.
The NCP and ICP are used for connection setup, but the document does not specify them.
The parent of RJE, so it is implied by the RJE tag and not listed separately.
ASCII/EBCDIC translation is a small part of the protocol and is not the subject of the document.
The ASCII-to-EBCDIC mapping rules are a minor detail of this protocol, not its subject.

RFC190.title: DEC PDP-10-IMLAC communications system
RFC190.summary: RFC 190 describes an operational system for sending textual display information between a TENEX PDP-10 and a remote IMLAC PDS-1 display terminal. It covers the display facilities, the JSYS calls, the message formats and how the work is divided between the two machines.

ARPANET.why: This is an early ARPANET-era working note defining a host-to-terminal display protocol and its system calls. The taxonomy has no narrower tag for it, so the ARPANET topic is the closest fit.
ARPANET.quote: This report describes an operational system for communicating textual display information between a main-site computer and a remote-display processor.

rejected.why: The document covers text-string display on a remote terminal, not network graphics protocols. Vectors are only mentioned as a possible later addition.
The document uses ASCII-compatible escape codes but is not about ASCII.
The document includes teletype simulation, but the protocol is a custom display protocol and not Telnet.

gaps.name: Remote display terminal protocol (TENEX/IMLAC)
gaps.why: The document defines a host-to-display-terminal command protocol and its system calls. No taxonomy tag covers early display or terminal protocols other than SUPDUP, which is a different protocol.

RFC191.title: Graphics implementation and conceptualization at Augmentation Research Center
RFC191.summary: 1971 ARC description of the conceptual display model (rectangular display areas, string identifiers, teletype/display modes) for textual display in NLS/TENEX, plus new NLS commands for splitting file-viewing areas to edit across multiple files.

ARPANET.why: An early ARPANET-era working note from SRI's Augmentation Research Center describing NLS/TENEX display use, including over network teletype lines. It is a fit for the ARPANET working-notes subject, as a Legacy-stream document from 1971.
ARPANET.quote: RFC 190 includes a functional description of the implementation of the interface to our displays

rejected.why: Considered since it concerns displays, but the document explicitly covers only textual display, not a network graphics protocol or format.
Teletype lines and the network are mentioned as carriers of Display NLS, but the document does not specify or extend Telnet.
7-bit ASCII is only an assumption of the display formatters, not a subject of the document.
It is a display protocol for the ARPANET, but this document does not describe or relate to SUPDUP.

gaps.name: NLS (oN-Line System) display and editing
gaps.why: The document is about NLS display areas and multi-file editing commands, and the taxonomy has no tag for NLS or for user-interface and display design.

RFC192.title: Some factors which a Network Graphics Protocol must consider
RFC192.summary: 1971 ARPANET-era note arguing that a network graphics protocol must support picture structure (node/branch subpicture graphs), structural light-pen hits, attention handling and naming for interactive graphics terminals on timesharing systems.

network graphics.why: The whole document lists factors a network graphics protocol must address (picture structure, structural hits, attention handling, coordinate systems), which is the subject of the early network graphics protocols tag.
network graphics.quote: many are not providing general enough mechanisms to handle attention handling, picture structure, and other higher level processes involved in interactive graphics.

rejected.why: It is a network working group note, but it addresses graphics terminal design, not ARPANET host or network protocols directly. The child tag network graphics covers it.

RFC193.title: NETWORK CHECKOUT
RFC193.summary: A 1971 status report from Rand listing which ARPANET sites had been verified for NCP, ICP, Telnet, log-on and service access, with notes on per-site quirks.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on checking out ARPANET host software at the connected sites. It covers NCP, ICP and Telnet interoperability.
ARPANET.quote: The matrix indicates the elements of Network software we have verified at each site.

Telnet.quote: The Telnet-like protocol differs from Telnet in that lines are terminated by X'OD' rather than X'ODOA'.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous status report, not a retrospective.
EBCDIC is mentioned once in passing, in a note about LL-67. The document is not about it.

RFC194.title: The Data Reconfiguration Service -- Compiler/Interpreter Implementation Notes
RFC194.summary: Implementation notes for the ARPANET Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS): new form-language features and syntax, plus the stack-based form interpreter, its instruction set and an example compilation.

ARPANET.why: The document is a 1971 ARPANET-era working note by network-site authors on implementing the Data Reconfiguration Service. It is a host-level network service, and the ARPANET topic is the closest fit.
ARPANET.quote: The interpreter is a simple minded machine having the virtue of helping the compiler writer

rejected.why: EBCDIC and ASCII appear only as data types in the form language. The document is not about those encodings.

The syntax section uses BNF only to define the DRS language. The document is not about the notation.

gaps.name: Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the DRS form language, compiler or interpreter, or for data translation services on the early network.

RFC195.title: Data computers-data descriptions and access language
RFC195.summary: 1971 ARPANET-era discussion paper proposing that Network "data computers" store self-describing files (using EL1-style data descriptions), offer a data reconfiguration service, and provide a representation-independent access language.

rejected.why: The paper is about file data description and access for network data computers, but the storage tag covers modern storage protocols over IP such as NFS and iSCSI. This is a conceptual 1971 proposal, not one of those.
The paper concerns data access and representation conversion, but it never specifies or extends FTP.
The document is a period working note, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Network data management / data description and access languages
gaps.why: The paper is about self-describing data files, data reconfiguration services and an access language for network data computers. The taxonomy has no tag for data management or data description languages.

RFC196.title: Mail Box Protocol
RFC196.summary: RFC 196 specifies an early ARPANET Mail Box Protocol that lets a site receive sequential files (messages and documents) into numbered mail boxes for printing or storage, using NCP, the Initial Connection Protocol and the Data Transfer Protocol.

ARPANET.why: This is a 1971 ARPANET host-level protocol for delivering messages and documents between sites. It builds on the ARPANET's NCP, ICP and Data Transfer conventions.
ARPANET.quote: The Mail Box Protocol will use established network conventions, specifically the Network Control Program, Initial Connection Protocol, and Data Transfer Protocol

messaging.why: The protocol is a store-and-forward mail delivery mechanism with mail boxes. It predates SMTP, and the general messaging topic fits better than the email technology tag.
messaging.quote: to deliver messages and documents to remote sites, and to be able to receive documents for cataloging, redistribution, and other purposes

rejected.why: The protocol is an early mail-box file-delivery mechanism. It has no Internet email architecture, headers or addressing, and it is aimed at printing and clerk distribution, so the general messaging tag is safer.
NCP is only the substrate the protocol runs over. The document defines nothing new about NCP.
Telnet is mentioned only for the newline convention and as a possible host program for the sender. The document is not about it.
7-bit ASCII is the default transmission code, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
The protocol transfers files, but it is a separate mail-box mechanism and not FTP.

RFC197.title: Initial Connection Protocol - Reviewed
RFC197.summary: 1971 ARPANET note proposing a revised Initial Connection Protocol with new Host-Host commands (ISC/ASC/RSC, IDC/ADC/RDC) and a minimal ACC modification, plus suggested REJ/REF commands replacing overloaded CLS.

NCP.why: The document proposes new commands for the NCP Host-Host protocol to redesign the Initial Connection Protocol, and comments on CLS and new REJ/REF commands.
NCP.quote: To establish a regular connection one party can issue an INIT (NCP sends RTS or STR commands)

rejected.why: Parent of NCP and implied by it; the more specific NCP tag fits the Host-Host protocol content.
It is a contemporary working note proposing a design, not a retrospective.

gaps.name: Initial Connection Protocol (ICP)
gaps.why: The ARPANET ICP for establishing connections to server sockets has no dedicated tag; NCP is the closest fit.

RFC198.title: Site Certification - Lincoln Labs 360/67
RFC198.summary: A 1971 site certification note from Rand reporting that the Lincoln Labs 360/67 ARPANET host's NCP, ICP, ASCII Telnet, login, CMS access and operator communication all conform to current specifications.

NCP.why: The document certifies the Lincoln Labs host's NCP implementation, the historic ARPANET host-host protocol, as conforming to specifications.
NCP.quote: We have exercised Lincoln Labs Network software as follows: NCP, ICP, ASCII Telnet (user and server), login procedure

Telnet.why: The Telnet implementation, user and server, was tested and found to conform, so Telnet readers may want this.
Telnet.quote: ASCII Telnet (user and server)

rejected.why: The site is an ARPANET host, but NCP is the more specific child tag and already covers it, so the parent is implied.

RFC199.title: Suggestions for a Network Data-Tablet Graphics Protocol
RFC199.summary: 1971 ARPANET RFC from SDC proposing a network graphics protocol for data-tablet input (single-shot, raw asynchronous/synchronous, preprocessed stroke formats) plus character generation messages.

network graphics.why: The document proposes binary message formats for data-tablet graphics input and character generation as part of the early ARPANET network graphics protocol discussion.
network graphics.quote: The purpose of this document is to add SDC's comments to the discussion of a protocol for network graphics within the ARPA Network community.

rejected.why: Parent of network graphics and implied; the document is about the specific graphics protocol, so the child tag suffices.
The character set and generation section concerns displayable glyphs and size messages for graphics output, not character set registration or encoding in Internet protocols.

RFC200.title: RFC list by number
RFC200.summary: RFC 200 is the NIC's August 1971 index of RFCs 1 through 200, giving author, title, date and NIC number for each early Network Working Group note.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a catalogue of the RFC series. It lists every RFC issued so far, and notes the numbers never issued.
RFC series.quote: RFC List by Number

ARPANET.why: The listed RFCs are almost all ARPANET Network Working Group notes on host protocols, IMP interfaces, NCP, Telnet and file transfer. A reader of the ARPANET subject would want this index.
ARPANET.quote: ARPA Network Functional Specifications

rejected.why: The list is a primary-source index, not a history or retrospective. The RFC series and ARPANET tags cover it.
Several listed titles mention the NCP, but the document does not specify or discuss it.
Telnet RFCs appear only as titles in the list.
File transfer RFCs appear only as titles in the list.

RFC202.title: Possible Deadlock in ICP
RFC202.summary: 1971 ARPANET note identifying a possible deadlock in the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) when both hosts wait for RFC matches, and recommending the order in which the server and user issue RTS/STR requests.

ARPANET.why: The document analyses the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol, a host-host connection establishment procedure, and gives operational recommendations. The ARPANET topic covers its host and network protocols and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: We have noticed a possible deadlock situation which may arise using the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) specified in Document #2

rejected.why: The ICP runs over the Host-Host Protocol (NCP) using RTS/STR/CLS, but the document is about ICP's ordering, not the NCP specification. The parent ARPANET tag fits better.

gaps.name: Initial Connection Protocol (ICP)
gaps.why: The ARPANET ICP has no dedicated tag. It is the main subject of this document, so the broader ARPANET tag is the closest fit.

RFC203.title: Achieving reliable communication
RFC203.summary: RFC 203 proposes a non-standard stop-and-wait / sliding-window retransmission protocol with sequence numbers, timeouts and start/stop rules to achieve reliable communication over the ARPANET.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note proposing a host-level reliability protocol for the ARPA network, so readers of the ARPANET subject would want it.
ARPANET.quote: Over a message switching facility, such as the ARPA network, all transmission errors can be divided into two classes

transport.why: It specifies generic transport-layer reliability mechanisms: sequencing, acknowledgements, retransmission timers and windowing (L outstanding messages). No more specific transport tech tag fits, since it is a non-standard protocol.
transport.quote: Channel throughput can be increased by several techniques, the first of which would be to disassemble the data stream into several ( eg. four or eight ) streams

rejected.why: The document mentions parity bits and checksums only in passing and explicitly declines to discuss internal error detection further.
The protocol is a proposed non-standard second/third level protocol, not the ARPANET host-host NCP.
BCH error-correcting codes are mentioned briefly, but the document's focus is retransmission-based recovery, not forward error correction.
The sliding-window and retransmission ideas are TCP-like, but this predates TCP and does not specify or discuss it.

RFC204.title: Sockets in use
RFC204.summary: A 1971 ARPANET request from Jon Postel to collect information on which socket numbers host programs listen on for standard services (e.g. Telnet loggers on socket 1), proposing socket 5 for the mailbox protocol and asking how to assign sockets.

ARPANET.why: An ARPANET working note about host-level socket number assignment for standard services under the NCP-era network, so the ARPANET subject page is the right home.
ARPANET.quote: I would like to collect information on the use of socket numbers for "standard" service programs.

IANA.why: It raises the question of how to assign and reserve well-known socket numbers, which is an early form of a protocol number registry, the subject of IANA registries.
IANA.quote: Are there any suggestions for a method of assigning sockets to standard programs? Should a subset of the socket numbers be reserved

rejected.why: Telnet loggers listening on socket 1 are only an example of a standard service. The document does not specify or extend Telnet.
Sockets belong to the NCP host-host protocol, but the document never discusses NCP and only asks about socket usage.
The proposed mailbox protocol on socket 5 (RFC 196) is mentioned in passing, and the document is not about it.

gaps.name: well-known port/socket assignments
gaps.why: The document is about assigning socket numbers to standard services. That is the origin of well-known port numbers, and the taxonomy has no tag for port or socket number assignment.

RFC205.title: NETCRT - a character display protocol
RFC205.summary: RFC 205 specifies NETCRT, a third-level ARPANET protocol defining a virtual character display terminal so remote hosts can use CCN's display-based URSA conversational remote job entry system, including commands, states, message formats and break synchronization.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET host-level protocol specification, using ICP, NCP connections, INS and allocation, and is a Network Working Group working note from that era.
ARPANET.quote: This document defines a third-level protocol called NETCRT which allows a Network user in a remote Host to look like a CCI console to URSA.

rejected.why: The document explicitly contrasts NETCRT with TELNET as inadequate for display editing; it is not a Telnet specification or option.
NETCRT runs over NCP connections, ICP and INS, but only as a substrate and does not specify NCP.
URSA is a conversational remote job entry system and NETRJS is mentioned, but NETCRT itself is a display protocol, not a job entry protocol.
The document mentions that it may inform later full graphical display protocols, but NETCRT is a character display protocol, not a graphics protocol.

gaps.name: virtual character display terminal protocol
gaps.why: The document's subject is a virtual terminal/character display protocol (VCD). The taxonomy has no remote terminal or virtual terminal tag outside Telnet, SUPDUP and network graphics.

RFC206.title: A User TELNET Description of an Initial Implementation
RFC206.summary: RFC 206 describes UCSB's initial User TELNET implementation in the Online System, covering how OLS keyboard keys map to the 7-bit ASCII virtual teletype, connection handling, and error codes.

Telnet.why: The document describes a User TELNET implementation, its virtual teletype character mapping, connection to Server TELNETs and error handling.
Telnet.quote: The TELNET protocol is based upon the notion of a virtual teletype, employing a 7-bit ASCII character set.

rejected.why: User and Server TELNETs use NCP only as the network access substrate; the document does not specify NCP.
The 7-bit ASCII set is the virtual teletype's character set, but the document is about the TELNET mapping of keyboard keys, not ASCII itself.
The network sites list and NCP context are background; the subject is the TELNET program, which the Telnet tag covers more specifically.

RFC207.title: September Network Working Group meeting
RFC207.summary: Announcement of the September 1971 Network Working Group meeting at MIT Project MAC, describing its three phases: system programmers workshop, use workshops, and plenary session.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note of the ARPANET Network Working Group, announcing a meeting on host-to-host protocol implementation and Network use.
ARPANET.quote: The next meeting of the Network Working Group will be hosted by M.I.T.'s Project MAC in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

rejected.why: It is a contemporary meeting announcement, not a history or retrospective.
It announces a meeting of the NWG, a predecessor body, but does not describe IETF process or procedures.
Host-to-host protocol implementation is only mentioned as a workshop topic; the document does not address NCP.

RFC208.title: Address tables
RFC208.summary: RFC 208 circulates a revised BBN Report 1822 Appendix A table of ARPANET IMP/Host network addresses, including scheduled sites, and urges hosts' NCPs not to reject messages from addresses missing in local tables.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note listing IMP and host addresses and scheduled site installations.
ARPANET.quote: The table below gives the decimal values of IMP number, Host number, and network address for each Host currently connected to the ARPA Network

NCP.why: It gives guidance on NCP behaviour regarding local address tables, which NCP readers would want.
NCP.quote: it seems almost as irrational for an NCP to prevent a local user from trying to communicate with a remote site

rejected.why: The table maps sites and hosts to numeric network addresses and is not about host naming conventions or host tables as a naming scheme.
The addresses are ARPANET IMP/host addresses, not IP address architecture. The ARPANET tag covers them.

RFC209.title: Host/IMP interface documentation
RFC209.summary: 1971 BBN note announcing IMP system version 2500 and its 30-second Host-refusal delay, urging Hosts to rely only on BBN Report 1822's documented Host/IMP interface and not code around undocumented behaviour.

ARPANET.why: The document concerns the ARPANET IMP system, its Host/IMP interface (BBN Report 1822), and operational changes affecting NCPs. It fits the ARPANET topic directly.
ARPANET.quote: the IMP/Host interface should be well documented, well understood and invariant.

rejected.why: NCPs are mentioned only as hosts that were affected by the IMP timing change. The document does not specify or discuss the NCP protocol itself.
The document is a contemporary working note, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Host/IMP interface (BBN Report 1822)
gaps.why: The document is about the ARPANET Host-to-IMP protocol specification. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it, so only the ARPANET topic fits.

RFC210.title: Improvement of Flow Control
RFC210.summary: RFC 210 proposes changes to the ARPANET host-host flow control commands (give back, return, allocate), making return report remaining allocation, requiring give back to be answered by return, and removing fractions from give back.

NCP.why: The document revises allocate/give back/return flow control commands of the ARPANET host-host protocol (NCP), including RFNM handling on links.
NCP.quote: A "give back" must be answered by a "return" and no more "give backs" can be issued until that "return" is received.

rejected.why: The document concerns host-host buffer allocation flow control in the ARPANET, not congestion control across transports.
The more specific NCP tag fits, so the ARPANET parent is implied.

RFC211.title: ARPA Network Mailing Lists
RFC211.summary: RFC 211 is a 1971 list of postal mailing addresses for ARPANET liaisons, non-site participants and station agents, used for physical distribution of Network documents (RFCs) by sites and the NIC.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note listing network sites, liaisons and NIC station agents for distributing Network documents. It is about ARPANET administration, so the ARPANET topic fits.
ARPANET.quote: List A should be used by sites when they distribute their own documents, to get RFC's to Liaisons as quickly as possible.

rejected.why: The 'mailing lists' are postal (Air Mail) distribution lists of street addresses, not electronic mail.
This tag covers mailing list protocols, headers and management for email. These are physical paper distribution lists.
The document concerns distribution of RFCs and other Network documents, but it is an address list. It does not address RFC format, style or publication.

RFC212.title: NWG meeting on network usage
RFC212.summary: Announcement of the October 1971 Network Working Group meeting at MIT Project MAC, themed on network usage, with its schedule of workshops, protocol review, NIC course, and TIP session.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note about the ARPANET community's Network Working Group meeting, its theme of network usage, TIP access, NIC, and host system development.
ARPANET.quote: implementation efforts have been substantially completed and usage of the Network has emerged as a primary concern

rejected.why: This is a meeting announcement, not a report from a workshop.
It only schedules a meeting of the NWG and does not describe process or procedures.
It is a contemporaneous announcement, not a history or retrospective.

RFC213.title: IMP System change notification
RFC213.summary: A 1971 BBN notice announcing a new IMP system version (2505) that raises supported hosts from three to four and changes the statistics gathered and reported to the NCC.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on the ARPANET IMP software, covering host handling, statistics reporting to NCC and host-count changes.
ARPANET.quote: we installed a new version of the IMP system, version 2505

rejected.why: The NCP host-host protocol is not discussed; the change concerns IMP internals and statistics.
The statistics are reported to the NCC, but the note is an IMP release notice and does not specify a management protocol or practice.

RFC214.title: Network checkpoint
RFC214.summary: 1971 ARPANET status report listing which sites had been verified for NCP, ICP, Telnet and Logger function, with comments on failures.

NCP.why: The checkout table verifies host NCP implementations (RESET handling, ICP) at ARPANET sites, so it is about NCP conformance.
NCP.quote: It only indicates that the NCP in question functioned to the extent required to respond to a RESET

Telnet.why: User and server Telnet are checked per host, and comments describe Telnet message-processing problems.
Telnet.quote: User Server Telnet Telnet Logger Access Service

rejected.why: The ARPANET topic fits, but NCP is a child of it, so the ancestor is implied and not listed separately.
No FTP checkout is in the table.

gaps.name: ICP (Initial Connection Protocol) / network checkout
gaps.why: The document reports ICP-156 and Logger verification, but the taxonomy has no tag for ICP or for early ARPANET host-testing.

review: Telnet: quote not found in the text

notes: Telnet: quote not found in the text

RFC215.title: NCP, ICP, and Telnet: The Terminal IMP implementation
RFC215.summary: RFC 215 describes the Terminal IMP's implementation of the ARPANET NCP, ICP and TELNET protocols, documenting design choices and deviations from the protocols caused by memory limits.

NCP.why: The bulk of the document details how the Terminal IMP implements and deviates from NCP control commands (ECO, RFC, CLS, RET, GVB, allocation), and ICP socket handling.
NCP.quote: the Terminal IMP does not guarantee correct response to ECO commands.

Telnet.why: TELNET is one of the three implemented protocols and the Terminal IMP provides terminal access via it, though few details are discussed.
Telnet.quote: The Terminal IMP program currently implements only the NCP, the ICP, and the TELNET protocol

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about Terminal IMP host-access hardware and its implementation choices.
ARPANET.quote: By early December there will be six Terminal IMPs incorporated into the network

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous implementation note, not a retrospective.
It uses protocol command names but does not define terminology.

RFC216.title: Telnet Access to UCSB's On-Line System
RFC216.summary: RFC 216 describes a Telnet-based front-end (NETOLS) to UCSB's Online System, defining how a Telnet user simulates the OLS double keyboard and how OLS display output is mapped to the Telnet character set.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Server Telnet implementation for OLS, including key mappings, echo/duplex modes, and instructions for User Telnet. Readers of Telnet history would want it.
Telnet.quote: A teletype-compatible interface to UCSB's Online System (OLS) has been implemented in accordance with the Telnet protocol adopted by the NWG.

ARPANET.why: It is an early ARPANET host service note (NWG, NIC, Station Agent, socket numbers, NCP) describing network access to a host at UCSB.
ARPANET.quote: This Server Telnet is responsive to connection requests directed by User Telnet's to socket number 1, host address 3.

rejected.why: NCP is mentioned only as the substrate that UCSB's NET subsystem interacts with; the document does not specify it.
Character mapping is to the Telnet character set, but the document is about the OLS keyboard mapping, not ASCII itself.
The document notes that OLS graphical display is disregarded in the Telnet implementation; it does not define a graphics protocol.
Remote job entry appears only as a usage example (Section X.C), not as the subject of the document.

RFC217.title: Specifications changes for OLS, RJE/RJOR, and SMFS
RFC217.summary: 1971 UCSB note revising specifications for its On-Line System, Remote Job Entry/Output Retrieval and Simple-Minded File System on the ARPANET: obsoletes RFC 74, drops message type, and changes sockets to use standard ICP.

RJE.why: The document mainly revises the UCSB Remote Job Entry and Remote Job Output Retrieval network specifications, including socket numbers and connection types.
RJE.quote: the notion of 'message type' has been dropped from the specifications for RJE and RJOR, RFC 105

rejected.why: The document refers to Host-Host protocol changes and ICP only as the context for the revisions. It does not specify NCP.
The parent is implied by the RJE tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC218.title: Changing the IMP status reporting facility
RFC218.summary: BBN announces that the IMP status reporting facility will change: text status reports are removed in favour of binary reports sent to the NCC, and the remaining statistics reports on fake host 3 will no longer be affected by PARAMETER CHANGE parameters.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about IMP operations and the Network Control Center's status reporting, which falls under the ARPANET topic.
ARPANET.quote: we will be changing the status reporting facility of the IMP.

rejected.why: The NCC's status reporting is a form of network operations. However, this is a 1971 ARPANET-specific note, and the ARPANET tag fits it more directly.
The document does not concern the host-host protocol, only IMP status reporting.

RFC219.title: User's View of the Datacomputer
RFC219.summary: A 1971 memo describing the datacomputer, a specialized ARPA network node for managing a very large shared database, covering its data model, streams, operations and intended applications.

ARPANET.why: The document describes a service node on the early ARPANET and its user-facing design, fitting the ARPANET working-notes topic.
ARPANET.quote: The datacomputer is a specialized node of the ARPA network that is dedicated to the management of a large, shared database.

rejected.why: The memo mentions system file directories, but these are internal catalog files of the database, not a directory access service like LDAP or X.500.
The datacomputer is a database/file store, but the taxonomy's storage topic covers block/file protocols over IP (NFS, iSCSI), which this memo does not specify.
The memo refers to data transfer protocol transactions only in passing; it does not specify or extend any file transfer protocol.
NCP is the presumed substrate for network access, but the memo does not discuss it.

gaps.name: Datacomputer / data language (DCAM-1)
gaps.why: The document is about a shared network database service and its data description language, a database-management subject the taxonomy has no tag for.

RFC221.title: Mail Box Protocol: Version 2
RFC221.summary: RFC 221 proposes version 2 of the Mail Box Protocol, an early ARPANET mechanism for delivering messages and documents to a standard write-only mailbox file at remote sites. It is built as a subset of FTP's Append request.

email.why: The document defines an early network mail delivery mechanism with numbered mailboxes and a message address header. It is a precursor to later email transport.
email.quote: The purpose of a mail box protocol is to provide at each site a standard mechanism to receive sequential files for immediate or deferred printing or other uses.

FTP.why: The protocol is defined as a profile of FTP. It uses the Append request, a NETMAIL# pathname, FTP's standard socket, and FTP's data types and error codes.
FTP.quote: Given agreement on a standard mail box pathname, then the Mail Box Protocol can utilize a subset of the File Transfer Protocol conventions

ARPANET.why: This is an early ARPANET host-level protocol working note. It is based on NCP, ICP and the NIC protocol set, and it comes from the NIC's own delivery needs.
ARPANET.quote: The Mail Box Protocol will use established network conventions, specifically the Network Control Program, Initial Connection Protocol, Data Transfer Protocol, and File Transfer Protocol

rejected.why: NCP is only the underlying host-host substrate. The document does not specify or change it.
Telnet is cited only for the CRLF newline convention and as a possible host for the sending program. The document is not about Telnet.
Network ASCII is the default data type, but the document only uses it. It does not define or discuss ASCII as a subject.
The address string at the head of a message is only a loose human-readable convention, not a defined internet message format.

RFC222.title: Subject: System programmer's workshop
RFC222.summary: Announcement for a hands-on system programmers' workshop at MIT Project MAC (Oct 1971) to exercise TELNET connections among ARPANET hosts ahead of the NWG meeting.

Telnet.why: The workshop's purpose is to establish and exercise all possible TELNET connections between hosts and fix TELNET implementation problems.
Telnet.quote: teams of workshop participants will hit the ARPA network from MAC consoles in an intensive effort to study its operational characteristics

ARPANET.why: It is a working note about ARPANET operations, testing and protocol and implementation review among sites.
ARPANET.quote: the next meeting of the ARPA Computer Network Working Group (NWG) will be held at MIT Project MAC

rejected.why: NCP is only mentioned as something participants should know about. The document does not specify or analyse it.
It is a contemporaneous meeting announcement, not a history or retrospective.

RFC223.title: Network Information Center schedule for network users
RFC223.summary: RFC 223 announces the SRI-ARC Network Information Center's weekday service hours for ARPANET users starting October 1971, with login conventions and a list of site idents and support phone numbers.

ARPANET.why: An early ARPANET working note on the operations of the NIC host: availability schedule, login procedure and site contacts for ARPANET sites.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Information Center has planned to provide service for network users on a regular basis Monday through Friday.

rejected.why: Telnet is only the means of connecting to the NIC; the document specifies nothing about the protocol.
NCP is mentioned only as a support contact area for connection problems; the document does not address the protocol.
It is a period operational notice, not a history or retrospective.

RFC224.title: Comments on Mailbox Protocol
RFC224.summary: 1971 BBN comment noting the Terminal IMP cannot implement the proposed ARPANET mailbox protocol directly, and proposing that Terminal IMP sites rent mailboxes at a larger host (e.g. the NIC) and read them via TELNET.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about Terminal IMP limitations and how Terminal IMP sites can take part in the network mailbox scheme.
ARPANET.quote: the Terminal IMP will be unable to directly implement the currently-proposed mailbox protocol

email.why: It discusses early network mail delivery and mailbox storage, including rented mailboxes versus dedicated printers. This is a comment on the mailbox protocol, an early email precursor.
email.quote: a message destined for a Terminal IMP user would be shipped to the site of the "rented" mailbox according to protocol and stored there

rejected.why: TELNET is only the access method used to examine a rented mailbox, and the document does not specify or extend it.
The document only notes that the Terminal IMP is unlikely to support FTP, which is not what it is about.

gaps.name: Terminal IMP / ARPANET mailbox protocol
gaps.why: The document is about the early ARPANET mailbox protocol (RFC 221 and RFC 215) and Terminal IMP capabilities. The taxonomy has only the generic ARPANET and email tags for this.

RFC225.title: Rand/UCSB network graphics experiment
RFC225.summary: 1971 report on an experiment in which Rand's Video-Graphics System consoles accessed the UCSB On-Line System (OLS) over the ARPANET via the Network Services Program, with sample display figures.

network graphics.why: The document describes an early network graphics experiment: remote graphic consoles using a graphics-oriented on-line system over the network.
network graphics.quote: During the Network Graphics Meeting in July, several experiments were outlined to explore graphics over the Network.

rejected.why: NCP and ICP are mentioned only as the protocols the implementation conforms to, not specified or analysed here.
UCSB RJE and UCLA RJS are mentioned only as other services reachable from NSP.
The OLS input is described as an EBCDIC-like byte stream in passing, but the document is not about the character encoding.

RFC226.title: Standardization of host mnemonics
RFC226.summary: RFC 226 proposes a standard list of six-character host mnemonics (designators) for ARPANET hosts, to replace each site's own Telnet host-name list.

hostnames.why: The document standardizes host naming conventions, mapping ARPANET host numbers to standard mnemonics, which is what a host table does.
hostnames.quote: THE FOLLOWING LIST OF SIX CHARACTER DESIGNATORS IS PROPOSED AS THE STANDARD LIST.

ARPANET.why: The list covers ARPANET hosts by number and site, and is an early network working note. A reader of ARPANET history would want it.
ARPANET.quote: HOST # DESIGNATOR 1 UCLA 65 UCLA36 2 SRIARC

rejected.why: Telnet is only the application in which the host mnemonics are entered. The document does not specify or extend the protocol.

RFC227.title: Data transfer rates (Rand/UCLA)
RFC227.summary: 1971 ARPANET working note reporting measured data transfer rates between Rand and UCLA CCN when using remote job service (RJS), showing the effect of blocking and factors that slowed transfers.

ARPANET.why: Early ARPANET working note reporting host-to-host transfer timings, NCP priority and interrupt handling effects between Rand and UCLA.
ARPANET.quote: Here are some of the transmission rates I have noted over the network between Rand and UCLA.

RJE.why: The measurements concern remote job service use (sending card images and receiving output), which falls under remote job entry on the early network.
RJE.quote: The attached memo indicates data rates typical of our use of RJS at UCLA CCN.

rejected.why: NCP is only mentioned as a factor in scheduling priority; the document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
Modern network performance metrics topic; this is an ad hoc timing report on an ARPANET site, better covered by ARPANET.

RFC228.title: Clarification
RFC228.summary: A one-line 1971 erratum correcting a statement in a FORTRAN program on page 7 of RFC 70 to read N=1.

rejected.why: Published as an ARPANET-era Network Working Group note, but the body only corrects a FORTRAN statement in RFC 70 and says nothing about ARPANET protocols or operations.

RFC229.title: Standard host names
RFC229.summary: RFC 229 proposes standardized 8-character host names, with alternate names, for the ARPANET sites and their numeric host addresses.

hostnames.why: The whole document proposes a naming convention and a table of standard host names mapped to site numbers. This is the host naming and host table subject.
hostnames.quote: I suggest 8 character names and the following list:

rejected.why: The hosts listed are ARPANET sites, but the document is about naming them, not about ARPANET protocols or operations. The hostnames tag is the better fit.
DNS did not exist in 1971. This is a flat host-name list, not DNS.

RFC230.title: Toward reliable operation of minicomputer-based terminals on a TIP
RFC230.summary: 1971 note arguing that the ARPANET TIP-terminal protocol lacks error control and block transmission, which minicomputer-based terminals need, and proposing block-oriented error control layered on it, ending in either the TIP or the serving host.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on the ARPANET TIP terminal-attachment protocol. It proposes error-controlled block transmission between terminals and the TIP or serving host.
ARPANET.quote: The present protocol for communication between a TIP and attached terminals requires character-oriented transmission and provides for no error control.

rejected.why: Remote batch terminals are mentioned only as one motivating case. The document does not specify remote job entry.
Host-host communication is mentioned only briefly. The document is about the TIP-terminal protocol, not NCP.

hostnames.why: The whole document proposes a host naming convention for hosts on the network, which is what the hostnames tag covers.
hostnames.quote: Each host will have a formal name of the form: <Institution Mnemonic> "-" <Host or NIC Station Mnemonic> and an optional nickname

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET working note about naming its hosts, IMPs, TIPs and NIC stations, and it asks liaisons to submit names.
ARPANET.quote: Recognize the expanding character of the Network, with the potential eventually of several hundred sites.

rejected.why: The more specific hostnames tag fits, so the parent is not needed.
The document only recommends that Telnets recognise both the formal name and the nickname. This is a side remark, not about the Telnet protocol.
This predates DNS. It covers naming conventions only, with no resolution protocol.

RFC274.title: Establishing a local guide for network usage
RFC274.summary: 1971 ARPANET-era note in which MITRE proposes a local, NLS-based Guide to Network Usage supplementing the NIC Resources Notebook, with an outline of site files covering accounts, login procedures, documentation and usage comments.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note of the early ARPANET community about documenting and accessing network host resources (TENEX, NLS, NIC), so the ARPANET topic page fits.
ARPANET.quote: MITRE, to facilitate local user access to network resources, is planning to establish a local GUIDE TO NETWORK USAGE to supplement the Resources Notebook

rejected.why: This taxonomy tag is for FYI-series introductory guides to Internet users. This RFC proposes a local MITRE guide and outlines its file structure; it is not itself such a guide.
The resource locator file lists sites and subsystems for people. It is a human documentation index, not a network service discovery mechanism.
The NIC Locator-style files are informal NLS documents, not a directory service protocol or access method.
The document is a contemporaneous working note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC276.title: NIC course
RFC276.summary: Announcement of a NIC training course at SRI on Nov. 29-30, 1971, on using the NLS online system and Journal, aimed at station agents and secretaries.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET-era working note about the Network Information Center and its NLS service, which fits the ARPANET topic, since no narrower tag applies.

rejected.why: This is a course announcement, not an introductory guide for Internet users, and it is not an FYI document.
The document is a course notice, not about the RFC series' format, style or publication.

gaps.name: Network Information Center (NIC) / NLS online system
gaps.why: The document is about NIC services and training on NLS, but the taxonomy has no tag for the NIC or NLS.

RFC278.title: Revision of the Mail Box Protocol
RFC278.summary: RFC 278 revises the ARPANET Mail Box Protocol, specifying that mail is delivered as network-ASCII line-printer text via an FTP "Append With Create" command to a standard MAIL path, with printer control codes.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET host-level protocol working note defining mail delivery over NCP, ICP, Data Transfer and File Transfer protocols.
ARPANET.quote: The Mail Box Protocol will use established network conventions, specifically the Network Control Program, Initial Connection Protocol, Data Transfer Protocol, and File Transfer Protocol

FTP.why: The document extends the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol with a new command and uses FTP transactions as the mail delivery mechanism.
FTP.quote: A new command is to be added to the File Transfer Protocol called "Append With Create" which appends to a file if the file exists

email.why: The document specifies how mail items are delivered to a mailbox at a remote host, an early email transport mechanism.
email.quote: The Mail Box Protocol is only to allow ASCII stings of text formatted for a network standard line printer

rejected.why: NCP is only the underlying host-host substrate the protocol runs over; the document does not define anything about it.
Telnet is mentioned for TIP delivery and newline convention, but the document is not about Telnet.
Network ASCII is the data encoding used, not the subject of the document.
This is a precursor mail mechanism built on FTP, not SMTP itself.

RFC280.title: A Draft of Host Names
RFC280.summary: A 1971 ARPANET draft list assigning formal host names, nicknames and network addresses to the hosts then on the network, to be made official after feedback.

hostnames.quote: The enclosed list of host names is a draft.

ARPANET.why: The hosts listed are ARPANET hosts (IMPs, TIPs, host numbers). The list is an early network working note, so ARPANET readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: Formal Name                    Nickname         Network Address

rejected.why: This is a pre-DNS flat host table. It has no domain hierarchy or resolution protocol.
It is a historical artefact, but it is an operational ARPANET working note and not a retrospective.

RFC281.title: Suggested addition to File Transfer Protocol
RFC281.summary: RFC 281 proposes adding restart opcodes (append/retrieve at sequence number, resume retrieve, use sequence number) to the early ARPANET File Transfer Protocol so long file transfers, such as remote job service output, can resume after a path failure.

FTP.why: The document proposes new FTP opcodes and exchanges for restarting interrupted file transfers, so it extends FTP.
FTP.quote: it would seem that the FTP should include (perhaps as an option which interactive-user oriented systems could ignore) a method of "restarting" a long file transfer

rejected.why: Remote Job Service motivates the restart proposal, but the document only suggests an FTP addition. The RJS report is explicitly deferred to another RFC.
The document is set on the early network and its Data Transfer Protocol, but its subject is the FTP restart mechanism, which the FTP tag covers more specifically.
The document does not discuss the host-host protocol.

RFC282.title: Graphics meeting report
RFC282.summary: Report of the second Network Graphics Group meeting (Nov 1971) covering experiments connecting graphics consoles over the ARPANET, talks, committees, and a first-pass output graphics protocol with assumptions and low-level operators.

network graphics.why: The whole report concerns early network graphics protocols: the Standard Graphics Stream, virtual screen, operators (move, draw, text), and connection protocol for graphics consoles.
network graphics.quote: specification of a "first-pass" graphics protocol

ARPANET.why: Discussion of ARPANET host reliability, NCP overhead, TIPs and Resource Notebook documentation is part of the report, within ARPANET working notes.
ARPANET.quote: whether the Network as a whole is as yet sufficiently reliable to support graphics work

rejected.why: Telnet is proposed as the carrier for device-specific graphics codes with new control codes, but only as a proposal in discussion; the document is not about Telnet itself.
NCP is mentioned only as overhead and a bug source in experiments, not as a subject.
Network ASCII is only used for text output in the graphics operators.

RFC283.title: NETRJT: Remote Job Service Protocol for TIPS
RFC283.summary: RFC 283 specifies NETRJT, a modification of the NETRJS remote job entry protocol that lets ARPANET TIP terminals submit card/print/punch jobs to a server host using TELNET-like record formats and server-initiated data connections.

RJE.quote: NETRJT, a modification of CCN's NETRJS protocol specifically to provide remote job entry service to TIP's

rejected.why: TELNET is used for the operator connection and as a record format model, but the document specifies RJE, not TELNET itself.
Mentioned only as something TIPs cannot support; not specified here.
Parent topic of RJE and implied by the chosen tag.
Code selection (ASCII/EBCDIC) is a minor command option, not a subject of the document.
Only an option for the CODE command; the document is not about the encoding.

RFC285.title: Network graphics
RFC285.summary: RFC 285 surveys early ARPANET graphics proposals (network standard graphics language, attention handling, LDS-1 Graphics Loader, tablet input, NETCRT) and proposes a general model of process, input/output routines and display drivers exchanging standard graphics and attention messages.

network graphics.why: The whole document reviews and proposes a model for early network graphics protocols, including drawing messages, attention handling and display drivers.
network graphics.quote: This paper is therefore aimed at bringing together the present state of graphics on the NET for the newcomer

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the network graphics tag, so it is not listed separately.
It is a contemporary working paper, not a retrospective.

RFC286.title: Network Library Information System
RFC286.summary: A 1971 request from MITRE soliciting interest in sharing a library retrieval system with Georgetown University or designing a Network Library Information System for querying library holdings across the ARPA network.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET community working note proposing a network-wide library query system and a working group to set up its protocols.
ARPANET.quote: the ARPA community might undertake to design a Network Library Information System.

rejected.why: The proposal is about querying library holdings, not directory access or synchronization protocols; no directory service is specified.

gaps.name: Network Library Information System / library retrieval and inter-library loan

RFC287.title: Status of Network Hosts

ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from December 6 to December 18.

rejected.why: The document mentions ICP and CLS connection responses only as test outcomes. It does not specify or analyse the host-host protocol.

RFC288.title: Network host status
RFC288.summary: A 1972 BBN report on the availability status of ARPANET hosts (open, dead, timed out) during December 1971 testing from the Terminal IMP, listing which hosts are servers or user-only.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational status report on ARPANET hosts, their addresses, server/user roles and daily availability testing.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from December 20 to December 30.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in passing as a future service; the document does not specify or analyse Telnet.
Connection opening and ICP are used by the test but the document is not about NCP.
It is a contemporary working note about the ARPANET rather than a retrospective history.

RFC289.title: What we hope is an official list of host names
RFC289.summary: RFC 289 publishes an official list of ARPANET host formal names, nicknames and network addresses, reviewing the earlier proposals (RFC 226, 247, 273, 280) that led to it.

hostnames.why: The document's whole purpose is a standard list of host names and nicknames mapped to network addresses, which is host naming conventions and host tables.
hostnames.quote: The enclosed is what we hope will be accepted as a list of official formal host names and nicknames.

ARPANET.why: The list covers ARPANET hosts and their network addresses, and is an NWG working note on early network operations.
ARPANET.quote: The need for some standard set of names recognized by NCP's and Telnets and usable on hardcopy to designate a persons affiliation

rejected.why: NCP is mentioned only as a consumer of the host names; the document does not specify or discuss the protocol.
Telnet is mentioned only as a user of the names; the document is not about the protocol.
DNS did not exist in 1971; this is a flat host table, which the hostnames tag covers.

RFC290.title: Computer networks and data sharing: A bibliography
RFC290.summary: A 1972 bibliography on computer networks and data sharing, organised into seven areas (data structures, description, conversion, management, security, transmission, network design) with an author index; it specifies no protocol.

ARPANET.quote: Host-Host Communication Protocol in the ARPA Network," 1970 Spring Joint Computer Conf.

rejected.why: It is a bibliography of period literature, not a history or retrospective.
The data security section lists access control and privacy papers, but it is a small part and no mechanism is specified.
Data description and conversion entries are cited, but the document defines no format or encoding.
It cites the host-host protocol paper in one entry only; the document does not specify NCP.

gaps.name: Bibliographies of networking and data-sharing literature
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for reference lists or bibliographies. This RFC is entirely one, covering computer network design and data sharing.

RFC291.title: Data Management Meeting Announcement
RFC291.summary: 1972 announcement of a Mitre-hosted ARPANET Network Data Management Meeting to discuss network data applications and a proposed network data management protocol, with a speaker list.
