ARPANET.quote: Mitre will host a Network Data Management Meeting, February 23, 24.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous meeting notice, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Network data management protocol (data sharing facility, RFC-146 stage 2)
gaps.why: The meeting aims to specify a 'network data management protocol' for sharing data across the ARPANET. The taxonomy has no tag for early data management or data-sharing protocols, so ARPANET is the closest fit.

RFC292.title: Graphics Protocol: Level 0 only
RFC292.summary: RFC 292 specifies Level 0 of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol for ARPANET: an 8-bit byte-stream command set (move, draw, dot, text, erase, escape) sent from a serving host to a display at a using host.

network graphics.why: The document defines an early network graphics protocol and its output byte stream commands, which is exactly the subject of this tag.
network graphics.quote: It describes part of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol for transmitting graphics data within the ARPA network.

rejected.why: The protocol runs on the ARPANET, but the child tag network graphics is more specific and already implies its ancestor.
Network ASCII is only used to encode text strings; the document is not about ASCII.
The appendix uses BNF to describe the byte stream, but this is only a notation, not the subject.

RFC293.title: Network Host Status
RFC293.summary: A 1972 ARPANET status report from BBN listing which network hosts were up, down, or excluded from daily testing between January 3 and 15, with predictions of when servers would become available.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational working note on ARPANET host availability, with per-host status tables from Terminal IMP testing.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from January 3 to January 15.

rejected.why: The tests use ICP and connections, but the document does not specify or discuss NCP itself.
Telnet is mentioned only as a future service for some hosts, and the document is not about the protocol.
The daily host-availability probing is operational status reporting, not a performance metrics methodology.
NETRJS at UCLA is mentioned only in a footnote about what the test could not cover.

RFC294.title: The Use of "Set Data Type" Transaction in File Transfer Protocol
RFC294.summary: RFC 294 clarifies how the FTP 'set data type' transaction (opcode 00 in RFC 265) should be used to request Network ASCII or other data conversion on retrieve operations, with example exchanges.

FTP.why: The document clarifies the use of the 'set data type' transaction in the early File Transfer Protocol, updating RFC 265, with store and retrieve examples.
FTP.quote: it would be useful for a user to be able to instruct the Multics server to convert data into Network ASCII in retrieve operations

rejected.why: Network ASCII and EBCDIC appear only as data types negotiated in the FTP transaction. The document is not about the character sets themselves.
This is an early ARPANET-era document, but it specifies an application protocol, so FTP is the more specific fit.
EBCDIC appears only as one example data type code in the transaction sequence.

RFC295.title: Report of the Protocol Workshop, 12 October 1971
RFC295.summary: Jon Postel's report of the October 1971 protocol workshop, recording decisions on the ARPANET IMP-Host, Host-Host (NCP), Initial Connection and Telnet protocols.

NCP.why: Most of the report sets out recommendations on Host-Host protocol commands (GVB/RET, ECO/ERP, RST/RRP, CLS, ERR, STR/RTS). This is the historic ARPANET NCP.
NCP.quote: The Host-Host Protocol was discussed and several problems were brought to light, among them were the following listed together with the group's recommendations.

Telnet.why: A substantial section lists Telnet clarifications (end-of-line, Synch, Break, Network Virtual Terminal) and the agreements reached.
Telnet.quote: The Telnet committee has been reactivated to consider the following problems:

ARPANET.why: The document covers ARPANET protocols and working-group business, including the IMP-Host protocol, which has no child tag. It was also a Network Working Group meeting.
ARPANET.quote: The workshop addressed itself to protocols of four types: IMP-Host, Host-Host, Initial Connection, and Process-Process.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous working report, not a retrospective or history.
It is an NWG workshop report. It does not describe a standards process.

gaps.name: Initial Connection Protocol (ICP)

RFC296.title: DS-1 Display System
RFC296.summary: RFC 296 describes the proposed DS-1 display terminal, which pairs a 512x512 plasma display/memory panel with a minicomputer and modem for use as an intelligent or passive network terminal.

rejected.why: The DS-1 is a graphics terminal and mentions vector generation and ARDS 100A simulation, but the document describes hardware (plasma panel, processor, instruction set), not a network graphics protocol or format.
It is an ARPANET-era RFC and mentions TIP connectivity, but the content is a terminal hardware description, not ARPANET host or network protocols.
The terminal acts as a network terminal, but no Telnet protocol or options are specified.
ASCII keyboard and command encoding are only mentioned in passing, and the document is not about the character set.

gaps.name: Display terminal hardware (DS-1 plasma display system)
gaps.why: The RFC is a hardware and instruction-set description of a graphics/alphanumeric terminal. The taxonomy has no tag for terminal or display hardware, and the closest ARPANET tags do not fit.

RFC297.title: TIP Message Buffers
RFC297.summary: A 1972 BBN note describing the sizes of the ARPANET TIP's per-device message buffers for traffic to and from Hosts, how users can tune them, and why buffers are not allocated dynamically.

ARPANET.why: The document describes buffer sizes and allocation behaviour of the ARPANET Terminal IMP, an ARPANET network operations and working note.
ARPANET.quote: The TIP double buffers its terminal output. Thus, when a TIP terminal makes a connection to a Host, the TIP sends off an allocation

rejected.why: The document concerns TIP buffer sizing for terminal traffic, not the Telnet protocol or its options.
It is a buffer-size explanation for users, not about network management or operational practice in general.

RFC298.title: Network host status
RFC298.summary: RFC 298 reports the availability status of ARPANET hosts as probed from the BBN Terminal IMP between 17 and 28 January 1972, with tables of host states and who supplied status predictions.

ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from January 17 to January 28.

rejected.why: The document mentions ICP and CLS connection behaviour only as the way host status is probed. It does not specify or discuss NCP.
NETRJS at UCLA is mentioned only in a footnote about what the tester could not check. The document is not about remote job entry.
Telnet appears only in a status table entry, 'Telnet in April', which says when a service is expected. The document is not about the Telnet protocol.
The probing is a simple up/down availability survey of hosts, not network performance metrics or measurement methods.

RFC299.title: Information Management System
RFC299.summary: A 1972 announcement by the University of Illinois that it plans to build an Information Management and Statistical System for the ILLIAC IV, with datacomputer archival storage, and inviting contacts from interested researchers.

The document describes a database and statistics system, not directory access or synchronization.
The document is a contemporaneous working note, not a retrospective or history of the Internet.

gaps.name: Datacomputer / ILLIAC IV information systems
gaps.why: The document is about an ARPANET-era data management system for the ILLIAC IV and the Datacomputer. The taxonomy has no specific tag for early network database or computing resources, so the general ARPANET tag is used.

RFC300.title: ARPA Network mailing lists
RFC300.summary: RFC 300 lists the postal mailing addresses of ARPANET site liaisons, other participants, and station agents for physical distribution of Network documents (RFCs) by sites and the NIC.

ARPANET.quote: List A should be used by sites when they distribute their own documents, to get RFC's to Liaisons as quickly as possible.

RFC301.title: BBN IMP (#5) and NCC Schedule March 4, 1971
RFC301.summary: A 1972 ARPANET operational notice announcing that BBN's IMP #5 will be offline on March 4 for an equipment move, and that a new PDP-1D host, BBN-1D (address 197), will join the network for NCC functions.

RFC302.title: Exercising The ARPANET
RFC302.summary: A 1972 UCSB report describing a graduate-student test group's effort to learn and exercise ARPANET server sites, with initial questions and user-experience findings.

RFC303.title: ARPA Network mailing lists
RFC303.summary: RFC 303 is a 1972 list of ARPANET site liaisons, non-site participants and NIC station agents, with addresses and phone numbers, used for physical distribution of Network documents (RFCs).

RFC306.title: Network host status
RFC306.summary: RFC 306 is a 1972 status report from BBN on the availability of ARPANET hosts, listing which hosts are servers or user-only and tabulating results of daily connection tests from the BBN Terminal IMP.

ASCII is mentioned only as an option for the FTP command language, not as a subject.
It is a contemporaneous workshop announcement, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Data Transfer Protocol (DTP)
gaps.why: The workshop covers the ARPANET DTP (RFC 264) alongside FTP, but the taxonomy has no tag for it. It is only partly covered by the ARPANET topic.

RFC310.title: Another Look at Data and File Transfer Protocols
RFC310.summary: A 1972 ARPANET discussion paper proposing revisions to the Data Transfer Protocol (DTP) and File Transfer Protocol (FTP) to suit TIPs, the Datacomputer and Remote Job Service, covering transfer modes, ASCII commands, data types, and restart/error recovery.

FTP.why: The document critiques and proposes changes to FTP (commands as ASCII strings, restart procedure, negotiation of data type/structure/mode) and the companion DTP.
FTP.quote: This paper suggests some specific changes in DTP and FTP that should make them more useful and/or simplify implementation.

ARPANET.why: Set entirely in the early ARPANET context: NCP, ICP, TIPs, TENEX CPYNET, Datacomputer and RJS. It is a working note from the ARPANET protocol effort.
ARPANET.quote: A number of ad hoc techniques of transmitting data and files across the ARPANET already exist.

rejected.why: TELNET is discussed only as an ad hoc channel for ASCII file transfer and as a possible place to put DTP modes. It is not the subject.
NCP is mentioned for transmission rates and interrupts, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
Remote Job Service (NETRJS/NETRJT) is cited as a requirement driver, but the document is not about it.
Network ASCII is proposed as a default data type, but the document is not about the character set.

gaps.name: Data Transfer Protocol (DTP)
gaps.why: The document revises DTP, a historic ARPANET data transfer framing protocol, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. FTP and ARPANET are the closest fits.

RFC311.title: New Console Attachments to the USCB Host
RFC311.summary: 1972 note from UCSB describing its MLC/360M multiplexor-channel interface unit and two new graphics consoles (Tektronix 4002A, NIH GPGT) attached to its 360-75 host on the ARPANET.

ARPANET.why: An early ARPANET working note about host console attachments and their use on the network; fits the ARPANET topic of host operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: The Tektronix terminal can now be operated on the ARPANET and will provide our users with upper and lower case ASCII

rejected.why: ASCII is mentioned only as a capability of the Tektronix terminal, not as a subject of the document.
The document describes graphics display terminals as hardware attachments. It does not define a network graphics protocol or format.
This is a contemporaneous working note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC312.title: Proposed Change in IMP-to-Host Protocol
RFC312.summary: 1972 BBN note proposing redefinition of ARPANET IMP-to-Host error message types 1 and 8 and adding new types 10-13 to help Hosts choose recovery actions.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies changes to the ARPANET IMP-to-Host protocol error messages, an ARPANET host/network protocol working note.
ARPANET.quote: We are currently considering a redefinition of the IMP-to-Host error message types (type 1 and type 8) and the creation of additional IMP-to-Host error message types.

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host protocol; this document concerns the IMP-to-Host interface, a lower layer, not NCP itself.
Error messages are reported to Hosts but the document is not about OAM mechanisms in the general sense.

RFC313.title: Computer based instruction
RFC313.summary: A 1972 discussion paper proposing that ARPANET general-purpose network resources (communications, centralized storage, language processors, dialogue tools) be applied to Computer Based Instruction, soliciting comments.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the network whose resources are discussed, but the document is about applying them to computer based instruction, not about ARPANET protocols, operations or working notes themselves.
It is a period position paper, not a history or retrospective of the Internet or its protocols.
Centralized data storage and NIC dialogue support are mentioned only in passing; no directory service is specified.

gaps.name: Computer Based Instruction (CBI/CAI/CMI)
gaps.why: The whole document is about computer-based education applications over a general-purpose network, and the taxonomy has no tag for educational or application-area uses of networks.

RFC314.title: Network Graphics Working Group Meeting
RFC314.summary: A 1972 announcement of the next Network Graphics Working Group meeting, April 16-18 at Mitre in McLean, Virginia, with logistics for attendance, lodging and equipment.

network graphics.why: The document is a meeting notice for the Network Graphics Working Group, the body working on early network graphics protocols; readers of that subject would want to find it.
network graphics.quote: The next network graphics working group meeting has definitely been scheduled for April 16-18 at The Mitre Corporation, McLean, Virginia.

rejected.why: The document mentions a TIP (ARPANET terminal processor) only as available equipment at the meeting site. It is not about ARPANET protocols or operations, and network graphics already sits under ARPANET.

RFC315.title: Network Host Status
RFC315.summary: A 1972 ARPANET status report listing which network hosts were up, servers or user-only, and daily test results from the BBN Terminal IMP for Feb 14-25.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational status report on ARPANET hosts, their availability as servers or users, and daily connection testing. It belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from February 14 to February 25.

rejected.why: The tests open connections using ICP and CLS, but the document does not specify or analyse NCP.
Telnet and NETRJS are mentioned only as services hosts offer. The document does not cover the protocols.
Host status monitoring is operational, but it is specific to the ARPANET and has no fitting child tag. ARPANET is the better fit.

RFC316.title: ARPA Network Data Management Working Group
RFC316.summary: Minutes of the February 1972 ARPA Network Data Management Working Group meeting, covering network data-sharing applications, data directories and a common data language, and staged development plans for a network data facility.

ARPANET.why: This is a working note from the ARPANET community about organizing a data management committee and staging a network data facility for ARPA Network nodes.
ARPANET.quote: The second phase of the meeting was a working meeting to try and organize the committee and try and set up an active working interest group.

directory services.why: A substantial part of the document covers data directories and catalogs: centralized, distributed and replicated designs, plus the location and description catalogs of the staged plan.
directory services.quote: The directory can be centralized (all at one location), distributed (split into pieces but where each piece resides at one location)

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous meeting report, not a retrospective history.
The subject is data management and data sharing across nodes. It does not cover storage access protocols over IP.

gaps.name: network data management / distributed databases
gaps.why: The document is mainly about data sharing across a network, including a common data language and data conversion. The taxonomy has no tag for distributed data management.

RFC317.title: Official Host-Host Protocol Modification: Assigned Link Numbers
RFC317.summary: A 1972 ARPANET note modifying the Host-Host Protocol's link assignment table, reserving link numbers for the Message Switching Protocol experiment and for network measurement work under the Network Measurement Center.

NCP.why: It amends the official ARPANET Host-Host Protocol (NCP) link number assignment table, so it belongs with NCP.
NCP.quote: On page 28 of NIC 8246 the link assignment table should read:

rejected.why: The document is a link number assignment list, but IANA registries did not exist in this context. The document is not about IANA guidance or stewardship.
NCP is the more specific tag and already sits under ARPANET, so the parent is implied.

RFC318.title: Telnet Protocols
RFC318.summary: Jon Postel's 1972 RFC describes the ad hoc ARPANET Telnet protocol: the Network Virtual Terminal, control signals (BREAK, SYNCH, ECHO, etc.), end-of-line convention, minimum implementations, and proposed changes.

Telnet.why: The whole document specifies and discusses the Telnet protocol, its NVT, control signals and proposed changes.
Telnet.quote: The purpose of Telnet Protocol is to provide a standard method of interfacing terminals devices at one site to processes at another site.

rejected.why: The Network Control Program and its INS signal are used by SYNCH, but only as the host-to-host substrate, not the subject.
Telnet runs on the ARPANET, but the document is about the application protocol itself, which the Telnet tag covers.
ASCII is the NVT's character code, but the document does not specify ASCII. It only uses it.

RFC319.title: Network Host Status
RFC319.summary: A 1972 ARPANET status report from BBN summarizing the availability of Network hosts (via daily Telnet connection tests from the BBN Terminal IMP) between February 28 and March 10, including host tables and test result codes.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note reporting host availability, addresses, sites and testing results for the early network.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from February 28 to March 10.

rejected.why: Telnet connection attempts are used as the test method, but the document does not specify or extend the Telnet protocol.
The report is a status/availability survey of hosts, not about network management architecture or protocols; the ARPANET tag fits better.
Daily up/down testing of hosts is a simple status log, not a metrics or measurement methodology.
Connection opening/ICP is mentioned only as part of the test result definitions, not as the subject.

RFC320.title: Workshop on Hard Copy Line Graphics
RFC320.summary: Announcement of a one-day CMU workshop on the XCRIBL document-generation system and its PDP-11-driven Xerox Graphic Printer interface for hard copy line graphics, with agenda and a sample printout describing the XGP.

network graphics.why: The document is about hard copy line graphics and gray scale output on the Xerox Graphic Printer via the XCRIBL system, which fits early network graphics. It is a loose fit, since it concerns a local printing system rather than a network protocol.
network graphics.quote: The XGP is also capable of drawing lines and gray scale images.

rejected.why: The RFC was distributed via the ARPANET RFC series, but it does not discuss ARPANET protocols or operations.
The workshop agenda and printout mention character set design for the printer's dot patterns, not Internet character set registration or use.
The document describes a printer interface, not the Line Printer Daemon protocol.

gaps.name: Hard copy printing / document generation (XCRIBL, Xerox Graphic Printer)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for printing hardware or document-preparation systems, which is the main subject of this RFC.

RFC321.title: CBI Networking Activity at MITRE
RFC321.summary: A 1972 MITRE status report excerpt describing IR&D work using ARPANET resources (Culler-Fried graphics, SCHOLAR, LOGO) to augment the TICCIT computer-assisted instruction system, in response to a call for comments on computer-based instruction.

ARPANET.why: The document reports on MITRE's use of and experiments with ARPANET resources, including a low-level graphics protocol for an IMLAC terminal, so ARPANET working notes readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: MITRE/Washington became a node in the ARPA computer network in September 1971 when a Terminal Interface Message Processor (TIP) was installed.

rejected.why: Telnet is only the means used to reach the Culler-Fried system; the document does not specify or extend it.
Considered because a low-level graphics protocol for the IMLAC is mentioned, but it is not specified here, only referred to in passing.
NCP is mentioned only as not yet implemented at MIT/AI; the document is not about it.
Computer-based instruction is education, not accessibility of communications.

gaps.name: Computer-Based/Assisted Instruction (CBI/CAI)
gaps.why: The document's subject is using network resources for computer-based instruction (TICCIT, SCHOLAR, LOGO), and the taxonomy has no education or CAI tag.

RFC322.title: Well known socket numbers
RFC322.summary: 1972 ARPANET note asking hosts to report their well-known socket numbers for network services (noting socket 1 is the Network Logger for ICP) so a catalog can be built and a standard Discard service socket established.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about host socket assignments for standard network services, which is host-level protocol administration on the early network.
ARPANET.quote: At all HOSTs which permit login for services, socket 1 is the Network Logger on which ICP may be performed.

small services.why: It proposes a standard socket for a Discard service, an ancestor of the Discard small service. It is only a proposal, so this is a secondary tag.
small services.quote: The Network Measurement Group would like to establish a network standard socket number for a Process Discard service

rejected.why: Sockets are an NCP concept, but the document does not specify or discuss NCP itself.
It is an early catalog of well-known socket numbers, a precursor to port assignment. However, it does not describe IANA registries or guidance.

RFC323.title: Formation of Network Measurement Group (NMG)
RFC323.summary: RFC 323 announces the formation of the ARPANET Network Measurement Group and sets out its plans: reserved measurement links, discard services, NCP statistics collection and format, host surveys, and artificial traffic generators.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about measuring network and host behavior, including link allocations and host surveys.
ARPANET.quote: discuss plans to perform measurement experiments on the ARPANET

NCP.why: A substantial part defines NCP instrumentation, statistics, and a report format. It also covers link 0 control message distributions and discard links in NCPs.
NCP.quote: The NWG agreed to implement a minimal NCP instrumentation procedure which would gather by HOST for some standard 24 hour period

performance measurement.why: The document is about network performance measurement: statistics gathering, delay and throughput, host availability surveys, and traffic generators for loading the network.
performance measurement.quote: The purpose of the meeting was to discuss existing and planned measurements of network and HOST behavior.

rejected.why: Telnet is mentioned only as the way local users' connections are instrumented and as a model for starting traffic generators. The document is not about it.
The document is historically interesting, but it is a contemporaneous working note, not a retrospective. ARPANET is the better fit.
The discard services are related, but this taxonomy tag covers the TCP/UDP small services, not NCP-era link and process discard.

RFC324.title: RJE Protocol meeting
RFC324.summary: Announcement of a 21 April 1972 meeting at UCLA to discuss Remote Job Entry (RJE) protocols for the ARPA Network.

RJE.why: The whole document announces a meeting on ARPANET RJE protocols, so it belongs on the RJE page.
RJE.quote: There will be a meeting to discuss Remote Job Entry (RJE) protocols in the ARPA Network on Friday 21 April 72.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the setting, and RJE already sits under it. The document is about the RJE protocols, not the ARPANET in general.
It is an early meeting notice, but it is not a history or retrospective.

RFC325.title: Network Remote Job Entry program - NETRJS
RFC325.summary: Describes NETRJS, a TENEX program at Utah that submits batch jobs to the UCLA 360/91 Remote Job Service over the ARPANET and retrieves printed/punched output, with its commands and a sample session.

RJE.why: The whole document describes a remote job entry client for submitting batch jobs and retrieving output over the early network, which is exactly what the RJE tag covers.
RJE.quote: To use NETRJS the user creates a job file under the Tenex system. He then requests NETRJS to send that file to the UCLA RJS (Remote Job Service System).

rejected.why: NETRJS borrowed the TELNET command interpreter code and runs alongside Telnet, but the document specifies the job entry program, not the Telnet protocol or its options.
The parent of RJE is implied; the ARPANET is just the carrier network and the document is not about the network itself.

RFC326.title: Network Host Status
RFC326.summary: A 1972 ARPANET status report listing the availability of network hosts (servers vs. user-only) and results of daily connection tests from the BBN Terminal IMP between March 13 and 24.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational working note on ARPANET host availability, with host tables and daily test results, which is the ARPANET topic.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from March 13 to March 24.

rejected.why: Telnet is only mentioned as a service planned at one site, and the document doesn't specify or analyse it.
The report is host availability monitoring for the ARPANET, which is better covered by the ARPANET tag. It isn't about network management as a subject.
NETRJS is mentioned only as the one service at UCLA-360/91. The document is not about remote job entry.

RFC327.title: Data and File Transfer workshop notes
RFC327.summary: Notes from the April 1972 ARPANET Data and File Transfer Workshop, recording discussions and decisions that shaped the new File Transfer Protocol (separate control/data connections, Telnet control channel, data representations, transfer modes, restart).

FTP.why: The workshop's decisions define the design of the new file transfer protocol: commands, data representations, transfer modes and restart. This is the origin of FTP.
FTP.quote: Separate connections are to be used for data and control information.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET working-group meeting report. It covers TIP, NCP, RJE and Datacomputer user needs on the early network.
ARPANET.quote: satisfies the needs of ARPANET users including Maxi-HOSTs, Mini-HOSTs, TIPs, Datacomputer, RJE, and Mailbox users.

rejected.why: The control connection is to be a Telnet (NVT-ASCII) connection, but Telnet is only the substrate for the FTP control channel here.
The NETRJS/RJS protocol is presented only as a talk with usage statistics. The protocol is to be defined in a separate document.
NCP is mentioned as a parameter and as the layer that handles lost or scrambled bits. It is not the subject of the notes.

gaps.name: Datacomputer / Datalanguage
gaps.why: A substantial part of the notes describes the Datacomputer and its Datalanguage file-transfer commands. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC328.title: Suggested Telnet Protocol Changes
RFC328.summary: Jon Postel proposes three changes to the Telnet protocol: drop minimal implementations in favour of a single standard one, remove the DATA TYPE signals, and remove the HIDE YOUR INPUT signal.

Telnet.why: The whole document proposes changes to the Telnet protocol's implementation requirements and signals, so readers of the Telnet subject would expect it.
Telnet.quote: I hereby propose the following changes to the Telnet protocol.

rejected.why: ASCII is mentioned only as the code set the DATA TYPE signals would switch away from. The document is not about ASCII.
Telnet ran over the ARPANET host-host protocol, but the document does not discuss it.
This is a Telnet protocol change proposal. The ARPANET is only the background.

RFC329.title: ARPA Network Mailing Lists
RFC329.summary: RFC 329 is a 1972 directory of ARPANET site liaisons, NIC distribution recipients and station agents, used to mail Network documents such as RFCs.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational working note for the ARPANET. It lists the Network's sites, liaisons and station agents and says how the NIC distributes documents to them.
ARPANET.quote: List A should be used by sites when they distribute their own documents, to get RFC's to Liaisons as quickly as possible.

rejected.why: This tag covers electronic mailing list protocols and headers. These are postal mailing lists of people and addresses, so the match is only in the word 'mailing'.
The lists are used to send out RFCs, but the document does not address RFC format, style or publication. It is only a recipient directory.
The document is a historical artefact. It is not a history or retrospective, and the ARPANET tag already covers its subject.

RFC330.title: Network Host Status
RFC330.summary: A 1972 BBN status report on the availability of ARPANET hosts (servers, user-only hosts, Terminal IMPs) based on daily connection tests from the BBN Terminal IMP, March 27 to April 7.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational status report on ARPANET hosts, Terminal IMPs and the Network Control Center, so it belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from March 27 to April 7.

rejected.why: It is a contemporary operational report, not a history or retrospective, even though it is now of historical interest.
Connections and ICP are mentioned only as the test mechanism. The document does not specify or discuss the protocol.
Telnet is mentioned only as a future service at UCLA. The document is not about the protocol.

RFC331.title: IMP System Change Notification
RFC331.summary: 1972 BBN notice announcing the May 15, 1972 release of IMPSYS 2600, a major IMP program change on the ARPANET, asking sites to help load the new IMPLOD tape and to avoid scheduling production traffic during the switchover.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational working note about a change to the ARPANET IMP system software, including site cutover procedures and the Very Distant Host option.
ARPANET.quote: We are planning to release IMPSYS 2600 on May 15, 1972, be- tween 12 noon and 3 p.m. E.D.T.

rejected.why: The note says Host leader formats and message types are unchanged. It does not discuss the host-host protocol.
It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.

RFC332.title: Network Host Status
RFC332.summary: RFC 332 reports the status of ARPANET hosts (availability, server/user-only roles, daily test results) for April 10-21, 1972, including new hosts and Terminal IMPs.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational status report on ARPANET hosts, their addresses, Terminal IMPs and daily testing results, so it belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from April 10 to April 21.

rejected.why: Telnet is mentioned only as a planned service at UCLA and the test probes use ICP connections. The document is not about the Telnet protocol.
NETRJS is mentioned as a service at the UCLA 360/91, but only as a status entry. The document does not specify or discuss remote job entry.
The test table refers to CLS and ICP in passing. The document does not address the NCP protocol itself.

RFC333.title: Proposed experiment with a Message Switching Protocol
RFC333.summary: RFC 333 proposes an experimental ARPANET host-to-host Message Switching Protocol (MSP) based on SEND/RECEIVE rendezvous of IN/OUT messages, with a header format, an information operator for process naming, unique port allocation, and port protection.

ARPANET.why: The document proposes an experimental alternative to the ARPANET NCP host-host protocol, using reserved ARPANET links 192-195 and IMP message formats. It is an ARPANET working note on host protocols.
ARPANET.quote: sketch how one would organize the lowest level host-host protocol in the ARPANET around MSPs

rejected.why: The document critiques the NCP and proposes a different protocol to run alongside it. It does not specify or extend NCP.
Telnet appears only in a brief sketch of how it might run over MSP. The Telnet page is explicitly slated for replacement.
The information operator maps symbolic process names to port IDs, but this is a small part of a message-switching proposal. The ARPANET tag is the better fit.
MSP is a host-host interprocess communication layer. It is better covered by the ARPANET tag than by the general transport topic.

gaps.name: Interprocess communication / message switching host-host protocol
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for early interprocess communication or host-host protocol experiments beyond NCP.

RFC334.title: Network Use on May 8
RFC334.summary: A 1972 BBN announcement that UCLA heavy-traffic performance experiments on the ARPANET scheduled for May 8 might lock up the network, advising sites to avoid important work that day.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note announcing a scheduled measurement experiment and the risk of network lockup before new IMP software is installed.
ARPANET.quote: we suggest that sites do not schedule important network work for Monday, May 8

rejected.why: The experiments measure network performance, but the document only announces scheduling and the lockup risk; it specifies no metrics or methods.

RFC335.title: New Interface - IMP/360
RFC335.summary: A 1972 ARPANET note from UCSB announcing that its 360-75 host's network interface to the IMP was replaced by a new production controller that went into operation on 1 May 1972.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about a host-to-IMP interface change at UCSB. It asks network users to report any problems.
ARPANET.quote: The former interface to the network for our 360-75 was replaced by a production unit similar to the NASA- AMES and USC versions.

rejected.why: The note covers only the hardware interface and says nothing about the host-host protocol.
It is a brief operational announcement, not a history or retrospective.

RFC336.title: Level 0 Graphic Input Protocol
RFC336.summary: RFC 336 defines the Level 0 Graphic Input Protocol for the ARPANET Network Graphics working group, specifying text and simple position input messages tagged by type, device and length.

network graphics.why: The document specifies an early network graphics input protocol, with text and position input formats and device codes, which is the subject of the network graphics tag.
network graphics.quote: Only two types of input are defined at Level 0: text and simple position.

rejected.why: Text strings are carried in network ASCII, but this is only the character encoding the protocol uses, not the subject of the document.
The parent tag is implied by network graphics, so it is not listed separately.

RFC338.title: EBCDIC/ASCII Mapping for Network RJE
RFC338.summary: RFC 338 describes the revised EBCDIC/ASCII character mapping used by CCN's NETRJS remote job entry protocol, adds a TTY terminal mapping, and notes that servers need multiple translation tables.

EBCDIC.why: The document's core is the EBCDIC-to-ASCII character translation tables (basic 89 graphics, maverick characters, TTY mapping), which matches the EBCDIC tag.
EBCDIC.quote: EBCDIC consists of a standard ("basic") set of characters, combined with a number of overlapping ad-hoc character happenings.

RJE.why: The mapping is defined in the context of NETRJS remote job entry, including a new TTY virtual terminal type and its socket/command selection, so RJE readers would want it.
RJE.quote: Under NETRJS [1], CCN's Network rje protocol [2], a virtual remote batch terminal may be either EBCDIC or ASCII.

rejected.why: ASCII is the other side of the mapping, but the document is about the translation to EBCDIC; EBCDIC is the more specific subject. ASCII is a possible secondary tag but the mapping is the focus.
The parent of EBCDIC is implied by the more specific tag.
Parent of RJE; implied by the more specific tag.

RFC339.title: MLTNET: A "Multi Telnet" Subsystem for Tenex
RFC339.summary: RFC 339 describes MLTNET, a TENEX subsystem that multiplexes a user's console among several remote ARPANET host connections in a TELNET-like fashion, with local-mode and remote-mode commands.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a TELNET-like multi-connection remote terminal program, so readers of Telnet history would want it.
Telnet.quote: MLTNET is a TELNET-like facility for TENEX which enables a user to control a number of jobs, running on different ARPANET hosts.

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET host-level tool and working note that uses the initial connection protocol and reports network status.
ARPANET.quote: MLTNET goes through the ARPANET initial connection protocol with the remote site in order to establish a duplex connection with it.

rejected.why: The initial connection protocol is only mentioned in passing as the means of connecting; the document does not specify NCP.
Another ARPANET display protocol, but this document is about a Telnet-like tool, not SUPDUP.

RFC340.title: Proposed Telnet Changes
RFC340.summary: A 1972 comment on proposed TELNET protocol changes, arguing to keep the Data Types and Hide Your Input options while accepting a single standard protocol without minimum implementation.

Telnet.why: The whole document discusses proposed changes to the Telnet protocol and argues for keeping the Data Types and Hide Your Input features.
Telnet.quote: The proposed change to the TELNET protocol calling for one standard protocol and dropping the idea of minimum implementation seems reasonable at this time.

rejected.why: The document is written in an ARPANET context, but it is about the Telnet protocol itself, so the Telnet tag covers it and the ARPANET topic adds nothing.
ASCII is mentioned as the default code that data types switch away from and return to. The document is not about ASCII itself.

RFC342.title: Network Host Status
RFC342.summary: A 1972 ARPANET report from BBN's Network Control Center on the daily-tested availability status of network hosts (April 24 to May 5), with a table of which hosts are servers, users only, or excluded from testing.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note reporting the status of hosts, IMPs, Terminal IMPs and the Network Control Center. It fits the ARPANET topic directly, and no child tag such as NCP, SUPDUP, RJE or network graphics applies.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from April 24 to May 5.

rejected.why: The report is a manual host-availability survey, not a management protocol or architecture. The ARPANET tag covers it better.
NETRJS is mentioned only as the one service the UCLA 360/91 offers. The document is not about remote job entry.
The test connections go through Telnet and ICP, but they are only the probing mechanism. The document does not specify or discuss the Telnet protocol.
Connection opens and closes (CLS) are used as test outcomes, but the document says nothing about the NCP protocol itself.

RFC343.title: IMP System change notification
RFC343.summary: 1972 notice from BBN about the failed May 15 release of IMPSYS 2600 on the ARPANET IMPs, setting switch positions, and scheduling further release attempts.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational working note about releasing new IMP system software across the ARPANET, asking sites to set IMP switches and schedule release attempts.
ARPANET.quote: our attempt to release IMPSYS 2600 on May 15 (as discussed in RFC #331) was unsuccessful

rejected.why: It is a software release coordination notice for the ARPANET IMPs, not about network management protocols or practice in the modern sense. The ARPANET tag fits better.
It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.

RFC344.title: Network Host Status
RFC344.summary: A 1972 ARPANET status report summarizing which network hosts were up, servers, or user-only, based on daily connection tests from the BBN Terminal IMP between May 8 and May 19.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational status report on ARPANET hosts, their server/user roles and daily test results, which is the kind of host and network working note this subject covers.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC reports on the status of most Network Hosts from May 8 to May 19.

rejected.why: The tests open connections and mention ICP and CLS, but the document does not specify or analyse the host-host protocol. It only reports test outcomes.
Telnet is mentioned as a planned service, and the tests check user access. The document is not about the Telnet protocol.
It is host availability monitoring, but it is an ARPANET working note and the specific ARPANET tag fits better.

RFC345.title: Interest in Mixed Integer Programming (MPSX on NIC 360/91 at CCN)
RFC345.summary: A 1972 ARPANET-era notice seeking other network users to share the monthly rental cost of installing IBM's MPSX mixed integer programming package on the CCN 360/91.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note soliciting resource sharing among network sites for a software package on a network host. The ARPANET topic is the closest fit, although it describes no network protocol.
ARPANET.quote: We are looking for any other users from the Network who may need this software in order to prorate the cost between several installations.

rejected.why: It is a period document, but it is not a history or retrospective of the Internet or its protocols.

gaps.name: Mixed integer programming / shared computing resources (MPSX)
gaps.why: The document is about cost-sharing for an optimization software package on a remote host. The taxonomy has no tag for network resource sharing or host software services.

RFC346.title: Satellite Considerations
RFC346.summary: 1972 note by Postel warning that satellite links in the ARPANET would add large delay, harming character-at-a-time remote echo and small-buffer servers, and proposing renewed discussion of echo plex and buffering measures.

ARPANET.why: The document discusses how satellite delay would affect ARPANET hosts, interactive servers and buffer allocation. It is an ARPANET working note.
ARPANET.quote: The consideration of using space satellite transmission links in the ARPANET should be cause for some thought by the parties making use of the network.

satellite.why: It analyses the delay of satellite transmission links, which is the central concern. The satellite tag is a link-layer technology tag, so it fits the networking-over-satellite subject.
satellite.quote: if the satellite is in synchronous orbit about 22,000 miles above the earth, the path length is about 44,000 miles

rejected.why: The echo plex and remote echo issues relate to interactive terminal use, but the document never mentions or specifies Telnet.
It is a period document, but it is a technical consideration and not a retrospective.

gaps.name: Echo plex
gaps.why: The document is about echo plex techniques for remote echo over high-delay paths. The taxonomy has no tag for echo handling or terminal echo negotiation.

RFC347.title: Echo process
RFC347.summary: RFC 347 proposes that ARPANET hosts implement an "Echo" process, reached via the Initial Connection Protocol, that returns received data unmodified for debugging and measurement.

small services.why: The document specifies the Echo service, the ancestor of the Echo small service, which echoes received data bit for bit.
small services.quote: those hosts which are willing implement an "Echo" process.

ARPANET.why: The process is defined for ARPANET hosts and uses the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol to set up connections, with BBN-TENEX as an existing implementation.
ARPANET.quote: execute the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) as specified in NIC 7104 the "Current Network Protocols" notebook.

rejected.why: The ICP runs over NCP connections, but the document does not specify or extend NCP. It only relies on it as a substrate.
Measurement is named as one purpose of the echo process, but the document defines no metrics or methods.
The echo service is a debugging aid, but the document is not about path discovery tools.

RFC348.title: Discard Process
RFC348.summary: RFC 348 proposes that ARPANET hosts implement a "Discard" process that accepts a connection via the Initial Connection Protocol and silently discards all received data, for debugging and measurement.

small services.why: The RFC defines the Discard service, one of the TCP/UDP small services (Echo, Discard, Chargen, etc.), in its original ARPANET form.
small services.quote: those hosts which are willing implement a "Discard" process

NCP.why: The Discard process runs over the ARPANET NCP-era host-host protocol, using ICP to establish connections. The tag fits the historic ARPANET context, though the RFC does not specify NCP itself.
NCP.quote: execute the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) as specified in NIC 7104 the "Current Network Protocols" notebook

rejected.why: This is the parent topic of NCP, so it is implied by that tag. The NCP tag already covers the ARPANET context.
The RFC mentions measurement purposes, but it does not describe benchmarking methodology.

RFC349.title: Proposed Standard Socket Numbers
RFC349.summary: RFC 349 proposes a central authority ("czar") to assign official ARPANET socket numbers for standard protocols, with an initial allocation of ranges and specific well-known sockets for Telnet, File Transfer, Remote Job Entry, Echo and Discard.

ARPANET.why: The document defines socket number assignment for the ARPANET host-host environment, using the Initial Connection Protocol, which is an early network working note.
ARPANET.quote: I propose that there be a czar (me ?) who hands out official socket numbers for use by standard protocols.

IANA.why: It proposes the first central registry of protocol number assignments, the precursor of IANA port number registries.
IANA.quote: This czar should also keep track of and publish a list of those socket numbers where host specific services can be obtained.

Telnet.why: It assigns the standard socket for Telnet, one of the specific well-known services listed.
Telnet.quote: 1            Telnet

small services.why: It assigns the Echo and Discard sockets, which later became part of the TCP/UDP small services.

FTP.why: It assigns the standard socket for File Transfer, the ancestor of FTP.
FTP.quote: 3            File Transfer

rejected.why: Remote Job Entry is only assigned a socket number here. The document does not specify the RJE protocol.
The ICP and the network protocols are referenced only as the context in which the socket numbers are used. The document does not specify them.

RFC350.title: User Accounts for UCSB On-Line System

RFC351.title: Graphics information form for the ARPANET graphics resources notebook
RFC351.summary: A 1972 questionnaire form asking ARPANET sites to describe their graphics hardware, capabilities, network access and demo opportunities, to compile an ARPANET Graphics Resources Notebook for the Graphics Protocol Committee.

RFC352.title: TIP Site Information Form
RFC352.summary: A 1972 request from David Crocker (UCLA) asking ARPANET TIP sites to complete a form with contact, operator, hardware option and port information for TIP users.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note collecting operational information about ARPANET TIP (Terminal IMP) sites. The general ARPANET topic fits; no more specific child applies.
ARPANET.quote: We are attempting to provide additional information for TIP users of the NET.

RFC353.summary: A 1972 ARPANET status report listing which hosts were up, new Terminal IMP installations, and daily test results from the BBN Terminal IMP for May 22 to June 2.

The host availability monitoring is ARPANET operational reporting. It does not address network management as a subject or any management protocol.

RFC354.title: File Transfer Protocol
RFC354.summary: RFC 354 specifies the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol (FTP): its model, data connection, representation types, transfer modes, restart, commands, and replies, obsoleting RFCs 264 and 265.

ASCII is used as the command and data representation and one transfer type, but the document is not about the character set.
EBCDIC appears only as one print-file representation type, a minor detail.

RFC355.title: Response to NWG/RFC 346
RFC355.summary: 1972 response to RFC 346 on satellite delay effects, discussing partitioned local/remote echoing for interactive terminals on the ARPANET, based on BCC 500 experience, with the University of Hawaii's planned satellite link.

satellite.why: Satellite-induced delay on the ARPANET link to Hawaii is the motivating problem and is addressed throughout.
satellite.quote: Long transmission delays such as those inherent in satellite communication are most certainly a cause for concern among users of remote interactive systems.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the setting, but the document's subject is echoing and satellite delay, and Telnet is the more specific tag.
It is a period document, but it is not a history or retrospective.

RFC356.title: ARPA Network Control Center
RFC356.summary: 1972 BBN notice announcing that the ARPANET Network Control Center is staffed 24/7, giving its new phone number and mailing address.

RFC357.title: Echoing strategy for satellite links
RFC357.summary: RFC 357 proposes Remote Controlled Echoing, a TELNET option set where the server controls echoing performed locally by the User TELNET/TIP, to hide satellite-link delay for full-duplex terminals.

satellite.why: The motivation and title concern satellite link delay, and the scheme is designed to hide it. Satellite is a stated category, though the mechanism itself is a Telnet echo strategy.
satellite.quote: those interactive systems which provide echoing for full-duplex terminals over the ARPANET become more awkward to use as transmission delays increase.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the setting, and the TIP is an ARPANET terminal interface, but the document is about the Telnet echo strategy and not ARPANET operations.

RFC359.title: Status of the Release of the New IMP System (2600)

ARPANET.quote: We have still not managed to get the new IMP system up.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous operational status note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC360.title: Proposed Remote Job Entry Protocol
RFC360.summary: RFC 360 proposes an ARPANET Remote Job Entry protocol in which a user controls a batch server over a TELNET connection, with the server using FTP to fetch job input and deliver output, and defines the command language and reply codes.

RFC364.title: Serving remote users on the ARPANET
RFC364.summary: RFC 364 proposes a standard questionnaire-style outline of administrative, documentation, user-assistance, technical and operational information that ARPANET service hosts should provide to remote users, supplementing the resource notebook (NIC 6801).

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note about serving remote users of ARPANET service hosts and the resource notebook/NIC documentation, which falls under the ARPANET topic.

Non-printing ASCII characters appear in one questionnaire item; the document is not about ASCII.

RFC365.title: Letter to All TIP Users
RFC365.summary: A 1972 letter from BBN's David Walden to ARPANET TIP users announcing new TIP commands, listing the eleven TIPs on the network, and describing status notices, buffer limits, echo-mode changes and planned fixes.

Telnet.quote: When the Telnet ECHO (code 132) (=virtual fullduplex) or Telnet NO ECHO (code 131) (=virtual half- duplex) characters are received by the TIP

rejected.why: The letter mentions ICP to a socket, but only in passing. It does not discuss the host-host protocol.

gaps.name: TIP (Terminal IMP)

RFC366.title: Network Host Status
RFC366.summary: A 1972 BBN status report on ARPANET host availability, with daily test results from the BBN Terminal IMP and a table of host servers and predicted availability.

The document is host availability monitoring on the ARPANET. The ARPANET tag covers it more specifically, and the taxonomy's network management tags describe modern practice.

RFC367.title: Network host status
RFC367.summary: A 1972 ARPANET status report from BBN listing the availability of network hosts as probed from the BBN Terminal IMP between July 3 and 14, with a table of each host's server/user-only status.

RFC370.title: Network Host Status

rejected.why: This is not an FYI-series introductory guide, though it is user-oriented; the ARPANET tag fits better.
It is a contemporary operational note, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: IBM TSO (Time Sharing Option) at CCN
gaps.why: The document is mainly about a specific host time-sharing service, with no dedicated tag in the taxonomy; ARPANET is the closest fit.

RFC381.title: Three aids to improved network operation

rejected.why: The document tells hosts to modify their NCPs to handle the new IMP-to-Host messages. The messages belong to the IMP-Host interface, not the host-host NCP protocol, so NCP is not what the document is about.
The scheduled maintenance and the IMP-Going-Down notices are operational, but this is early ARPANET operations and not modern network management architecture. ARPANET fits better.

RFC382.title: Mathematical Software on the ARPA Network
RFC382.summary: A 1972 ARPANET note soliciting information exchange on mathematical and statistical software libraries (Bell Labs, IMSL, NATS) and announcing plans to host the NATS library on network IBM/360-370 and PDP-10 hosts.

gaps.name: Mathematical and statistical software libraries (NATS, IMSL, Bell Labs library)

RFC384.title: Official site idents for organizations in the ARPA Network
RFC384.summary: RFC 384 lists official site identifiers and network addresses for organizations connected to the ARPANET, in alphabetical and numeric order, obsoleting RFC 289.

It is a contemporaneous working list, not a history or retrospective.

RFC385.title: Comments on the File Transfer Protocol
RFC385.summary: RFC 385 gives errata, clarifications, and additions to the 1972 File Transfer Protocol (RFC 354), including minimum server requirements, print file types, mode clarifications, new reply codes, and new MLFL, MAIL and ACCT commands.

rejected.why: The MAIL command is sent over the TELNET control connection, but Telnet is only the substrate and is not specified or changed here.
NCP is mentioned for data connection close and listen behaviour, but only as the underlying transport.
MLFL and MAIL send mail files via FTP, but this is a small FTP extension and not about mail architecture or transport as a subject.
The protocol runs on the ARPANET, but the document is about FTP and not ARPANET operations.

RFC386.title: Letter to TIP users-2
RFC386.summary: A 1972 BBN letter to ARPANET TIP users announcing command changes (@LOGIN, @HOST, @TRANSMIT), new TIP messages, and explaining DEAD/lost-allocate problems and the TIP logger's behaviour.

NCP.quote: What is maybe needed is a Host/Host protocol command to reset the Host's connections with a particular user (TIP) socket

rejected.why: The TIP terminal commands are TIP-specific, not the Telnet protocol or its options.

gaps.name: TIP (Terminal IMP) user interface
gaps.why: The document is mainly about the TIP's user command language and logger, which has no dedicated tag; it falls under ARPANET only generally.

RFC387.title: Some experiences in implementing Network Graphics Protocol Level 0
RFC387.summary: Implementation experience report on Network Graphics Protocol Level 0 (NGP-0): clarifies the two's complement coordinate format for absolute and relative coordinates, discusses handling the TEXTR command on a Computek display via software beam registers, and appends conversion of NGP fractions to PDP-10 floating point.

network graphics.why: The whole document is about implementing the early Network Graphics Protocol Level 0, clarifying its coordinate number system and TEXTR command behavior.
network graphics.quote: We are in the process of implementing NGP-0 at several hosts.

rejected.why: Network graphics sits under ARPANET, but the child tag fits more specifically, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
It is a period implementation note, not a retrospective on history.

RFC388.title: NCP statistics
RFC388.summary: RFC 388 announces UCLA-NMC's automated daily collection of ARPANET NCP traffic statistics from hosts, specifying the data format sent over socket 241 and which counts (bits, messages, RFNM delay, link 0 control message distribution) to report.

NCP.why: The document defines NCP-level statistics gathering, including per-host message/bit counts and link 0 control message distributions, on the ARPANET host-host protocol.
NCP.quote: UCLA-NMC is prepared to gather your NCP statistics automatically on a daily basis.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET Network Measurement Note defining measurement data from ARPANET hosts (RFNM delay, host numbers, links).
ARPANET.quote: Average Round Trip delay on send connections to HOST

rejected.why: The document is about measurement of NCP traffic, but it is an ARPANET-era note. The NCP and ARPANET tags fit better and the generic topic adds little.

RFC389.title: UCLA Campus Computing Network Liaison Staff for ARPA Network
RFC389.summary: RFC 389 lists the UCLA Campus Computing Network contacts and phone numbers for ARPA Network users, by type of problem (administrative, network technical, programming, operations).

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note giving the liaison staff at UCLA CCN, a network host site, for ARPANET users.
ARPANET.quote: The ARPA Network contacts at CCN are:

rejected.why: It is a contact list for one site, not an introductory FYI guide for Internet users.

RFC390.title: TSO Scenario
RFC390.summary: A 1972 terminal-session transcript showing a user on the TSO time-sharing system at UCLA/CCN editing a Fortran source, submitting it for batch compile/link, inspecting output, and running the load module in the foreground.

ARPANET.why: A working note from the early ARPANET-era Network Working Group describing use of a host (TSO at CCN) for network users; no better taxonomy tag fits this early-network host usage documentation.
ARPANET.quote: UID LOGON IN PROGRESS AT 09:59:18 ON AUGUST 28, 1972

rejected.why: It is a usage scenario, but not an FYI-series introductory guide for Internet users.
The session is presumably accessed via a terminal connection, but no Telnet protocol content appears in the document.
It is a historical artifact but not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: TSO (IBM Time Sharing Option) / remote host job entry usage
gaps.why: The document is entirely about using IBM OS/360 TSO, EDIT, and batch job submission on a network host; the taxonomy has no tag for specific host operating systems or time-sharing systems (RJE covers only early remote job entry).

RFC391.title: Traffic statistics (August 1972)
RFC391.summary: Monthly ARPANET traffic statistics report for August 1972, tabulating internode and intranode traffic per host at each network site.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note reporting per-site, per-host traffic counts, which is what the ARPANET topic covers.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the network traffic statistics for the month of August 1972.

rejected.why: The document only reports raw traffic counts. It defines no metrics or measurement methods.
It is a statistics report, not a management protocol or operational practice document.

RFC392.title: Measurement of host costs for transmitting network data
RFC392.summary: 1972 report from Utah measuring the CPU and real-time cost on a TENEX host of sending and receiving data over the ARPANET (via the NETRJS remote job entry program to UCLA's RJS), finding costs far above predicted and suggesting host and protocol changes.

ARPANET.why: The document measures host-side costs of using the ARPANET and recommends changes to host network interfaces and NCP protocols; this is early ARPANET operations and working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: much work is needed on host machines and network protocols rather than on further refinements of the communication devices involved.

RJE.why: The measured program is NETRJS, a remote job entry client, and the measurements characterise its transmission cost and suggest changes to the RJS-UCLA protocol.
RJE.quote: we developed a program[1] to use the Remote Job Service System (RJS) at UCLA-CCN.
RJE.section: Background for the UTAH Timing Experiments

rejected.why: NCP is mentioned only in passing as a place where changes may be required; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The measurements are host CPU cost accounting for one program on one host, not network performance metrics or methods; the authors explicitly say they are not measuring network transmission rates.

RFC393.title: Comments on Telnet Protocol Changes
RFC393.summary: Winett objects to two of three proposed TELNET protocol changes from RFC 328 (Hide-your-input byte count, alternate data types such as EBCDIC) and proposes interpreting the TELNET Break code as an end-of-message code when sent from server to user.

Telnet.why: The whole document comments on proposed changes to the Telnet protocol and its control codes (Hide-your-input, Echo, Break, SYNC).
Telnet.quote: I am registering my objection to two of the three suggestions for changing the TELNET protocol as described in RFC 328

rejected.why: EBCDIC is discussed only briefly as an example of an alternate character code a Telnet server might support; the document is not about EBCDIC itself.
NVT ASCII is the baseline for Telnet control codes, but the document is not about ASCII as a character set.
The document is intended for ARPA network use, but it concerns the Telnet protocol rather than ARPANET operations in general.

RFC394.title: Two Proposed Changes to the IMP-Host Protocol
RFC394.summary: 1972 BBN proposal to change the ARPANET IMP-Host protocol by declaring unresponsive Hosts dead to the network and adding a 15-second timeout with a new "Resources Unavailable" message for Host-to-IMP messages.

ARPANET.why: The document changes the ARPANET IMP-Host interface protocol, including timeouts and control messages. It is an early ARPANET working note, so it belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: This note describes two changes to the IMP-Host communication protocol described in BBN Report 1822 and revised in RFC 381.

rejected.why: NCP is mentioned only in passing, as software that is not running when a Host is in breakpoint mode. The document is about the IMP-Host interface, not the host-host protocol.
It is a contemporaneous protocol proposal, not a history or retrospective.

RFC395.title: Switch Settings on IMPs and TIPs
RFC395.summary: A 1972 BBN note listing the correct front-panel switch settings on 516 IMPs and 316 IMPs/TIPs so ARPANET site personnel and field engineers keep the network software running correctly.

ARPANET.why: The document is operational guidance for ARPANET IMP and TIP hardware, giving switch settings for site personnel. This is ARPANET working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: important to the correct operation of the network software

rejected.why: The switches concern correct operation and maintenance, not security practice.
It is a hardware checklist for front-panel switches, not a network management architecture or protocol.

RFC396.title: Network Graphics Working Group Meeting - Second Iteration
RFC396.summary: A 1973 ARPANET-era note by Steve Bunch rescheduling the Network Graphics Working Group meeting to July 16, 1973 after feedback on the earlier proposal in RFC 474.

network graphics.why: The document is entirely about scheduling and organizing the Network Graphics Working Group meeting, so readers of the early network graphics subject would expect to find it.
network graphics.quote: I propose July 16, 1973 as the new meeting date.

rejected.why: The document is an ARPANET-era RFC, but its subject is the graphics working group meeting. The more specific child tag network graphics covers it, and it describes no ARPANET protocol or operations.
It is a historical artifact, but it is a meeting-logistics note and not a history or retrospective.

RFC398.title: UCSB Online Graphics
RFC398.summary: 1972 note from UCSB listing ICP sockets through which ARPANET users can reach UCSB online graphics from IMLAC and Tektronix terminals or via the level 0 graphics protocol, with notes on display-formatting limits.

network graphics.why: The document describes early network graphics access: terminal types, sockets and the level 0 graphics protocol at UCSB. This is the early network graphics subject.
network graphics.quote: users with TEKTRONIX or IMLAC terminals or with systems that support the proposed level 0 graphics protocol can access UCSB graphics

rejected.why: Telnet is only mentioned in passing, as the 'TELNET-like connection' used for alphanumerics. The document does not specify or extend it.
The ARPANET parent is implied by the network graphics tag, so I did not list it separately.

RFC399.title: SMFS Login and Logout
RFC399.summary: RFC 399 adds two commands, Login (LGI) and Logout (LGO), to UCSB's Simple Minded File System (SMFS) so users can identify themselves and an account number for future billing and usage statistics.

rejected.why: SMFS was an ARPANET-era file service and the RFC mentions the ICP (Initial Connection Protocol). The document specifies only SMFS login/logout commands, not ARPANET host or network protocols, so it is not about the ARPANET as a subject.
SMFS is a file system service at UCSB, not FTP. The RFC does not specify or extend FTP.
LGI and LGO carry user name and account number for accounting. But they are a trivial, unenforced, application-specific login with no authentication or authorization, not an AAA framework.
The ICP, which depends on NCP, is mentioned only in passing as the step before LGI. The document is not about NCP.

gaps.name: Simple Minded File System (SMFS)
gaps.why: The document is about the UCSB SMFS file service and its commands. The taxonomy has no tag for early ARPANET file systems or file services. ARPANET and FTP are too broad or wrong, so no tag fits.

RFC400.title: Traffic Statistics (September 1972)
RFC400.summary: A 1972 BBN report giving ARPANET host throughput statistics (packet counts per host and node) for September 1972.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational traffic report for the ARPANET listing per-host and per-node packet throughput at sites like UCLA, SRI, BBN and MIT.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the network traffic statistics for the month of September 1972.

rejected.why: The document only reports raw traffic counts; it does not define metrics or measurement methods.
It is a contemporary operational report, not a history or retrospective.

RFC401.title: Conversion of NGP-0 Coordinates to Device Specific Coordinates
RFC401.summary: RFC 401 describes an integer-arithmetic procedure (multiply, shift, add) for converting NGP-0 fractional graphics coordinates to device-specific integer screen coordinates, updating RFC 387.

network graphics.why: The document is about the NGP-0 early network graphics protocol's coordinate format and how to convert it to device coordinates, which belongs on the early network graphics page.
network graphics.quote: a means is described to convert NGP coordi- nates to integer coordinates in the range zero to M, where M is the maximum address of the device screen

rejected.why: Parent of network graphics and implied by the child tag. The document is about graphics coordinates rather than general ARPANET operations.
The NGP coordinate format is described, but the document is about arithmetic conversion to device coordinates. It does not define a general data encoding.

gaps.name: NGP-0 (Network Graphics Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about the NGP-0 graphics protocol's coordinate conversion. The closest tag is network graphics, which covers it adequately, so no new tag is needed.

RFC402.title: ARPA Network Mailing Lists
RFC402.summary: RFC 402 gives three postal distribution lists (Network Liaisons, NIC direct recipients, and NIC Station Agents) of ARPANET site contacts, used to send out Network documents such as RFCs.

ARPANET.why: The document is administrative working material of the ARPANET community. It lists ARPANET sites, liaisons and station agents and how the NIC distributes documents to them.
ARPANET.quote: The following are three lists to be used for distribution of Network documents.

RFC series.why: The lists exist to distribute RFCs and other formal documents to participants by physical mail. This is a matter of RFC publication and distribution.
RFC series.quote: List A should be used by sites when they distribute their own documents, to get RFC's to Liaisons as quickly as possible.

rejected.why: This tag covers email mailing list protocols, headers and management. These are postal address lists with Air Mail instructions, not electronic lists.
Nothing here concerns electronic mail. The distribution is by postal mail.
The document is a contemporary administrative list, not a history or retrospective, although it is of historical interest.

RFC403.title: Desirability of a Network 1108 Service
RFC403.summary: A 1973 request for comments from the University of Utah on whether to make its Univac 1108 (EXEC 8) computing service available to ARPANET users, with a description of facilities, pricing and priority schedules.

This concerns IP address architecture, and the ARPANET addresses here predate IP. The ARPANET tag covers them.
NCP is not mentioned or specified. The document only notes address changes.

ARPANET.quote: This week the RAND IMP was temporarily removed from the Network and a new IMP was installed at ISI.

rejected.why: Concerns ARPANET IMP/host numbers, not IP address architecture.
It is an operational note of the era, not a history or retrospective.

RFC406.title: Scheduled IMP Software Releases
RFC406.summary: 1972 BBN note reminding ARPANET sites of the Tuesday 7-8 a.m. IMP software reload window and defining the format of the IMP-Going-Down message sent to Hosts.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational note on IMP software maintenance scheduling and the IMP-Going-Down host message format, which fits the ARPANET topic directly.

rejected.why: The document covers maintenance scheduling, but it is a working note on ARPANET IMP operations. The ARPANET topic fits it better than modern network management.
The IMP-Going-Down message is an IMP-to-Host message. The document does not specify or extend the host-host protocol.

RFC407.title: Remote Job Entry Protocol
RFC407.summary: RFC 407 specifies the ARPANET Remote Job Entry protocol, in which a user controls a remote batch server over a TELNET connection while the server uses FTP to fetch job input and deliver output.

RJE is a child of ARPANET and is implied by the more specific tag.
Mentions of ICP and sockets are incidental; the document does not specify NCP.

RFC408.title: NETBANK
RFC408.summary: 1972 proposal for NETBANK, a single network-wide billing and account creation/validation service so a project manager can authorize users and get one bill across server hosts.

RFC412.title: User FTP Documentation
RFC412.summary: RFC 412 reproduces the HELP file for the Utah-10 user-side FTP process, documenting its command language, transfer modes/types/structures, and a sample session over the ARPANET.

ARPANET.quote: HOST THROUGHPUT SUMMARY (PACKETS OUTPUT)

ARPANET.quote: I WROTE A SIMPLE TENEX PROGRAM THAT SENT ITSELF STRINGS OVER THE NET.

RFC416.title: ARC System Will Be Unavailable for Use During Thanksgiving Week

RFC417.summary: A 1972 note by Postel and Kline stating that TENEX systems use link numbers outside the range allowed by the official ARPANET HOST-HOST protocol, causing connection problems, and urging conformance.

NCP.why: The document is about link number usage in the ARPANET HOST-HOST protocol, which is the NCP host-host protocol, and urges conformance to it.
NCP.quote: TENEX systems use link numbers outside the allowed range.  This is a violation of the official HOST-HOST protocol.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the NCP tag, so I did not list it separately.

RFC418.title: Server File Transfer Under TSS/360 At NASA-Ames Research Center
review: not tagged by the model: awaiting a tagger run, or no text in the corpus

RFC419.title: To: Network liaisons and station agents
RFC419.summary: A 1972 notice from MIT-MAC that its PDP-10 (Dynamic Modeling System) will be offline for about 10 days to three weeks over the holidays while a paging system is installed.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET-era working note from an ARPANET host site to network liaisons and station agents. It announces the downtime of a network host. The ARPANET topic covers operations and working notes like this.
ARPANET.quote: The PDP-10 at Project MAC, affectionately known as the Dynamic Modeling System, will, during the holiday season, take a short vacation from all activities including networking.

rejected.why: The document is a contemporaneous operational notice. It is not a history or retrospective.
The 'vacation' wording is lighthearted, but this is a genuine outage notice and not a humorous RFC.

RFC420.title: CCA ICCC weather demo
RFC420.summary: 1973 announcement of the CCA weather demo, in which a LISP natural-language program queries a remote Datacomputer over the ARPANET via Datalanguage, with usage notes, sample requests and file descriptions.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note about a network demo that runs across two hosts, with host numbers, FTP transfer and SNDMSG instructions. It fits the ARPANET topic, which has no narrower tag that applies.
ARPANET.quote: THE TWO PROGRAMS COMMUNICATE VIA DATALANGUAGE USING THE NET.

rejected.why: FTP is mentioned only as the way to copy the save file, with a byte-size hint. The document does not specify or extend FTP.
The Datacomputer is a data management system, not a directory service. The document does not describe directory access or synchronization.
The note mentions the host table fix (CCA missing, now host 37), but only in passing. It does not discuss naming conventions.
SNDMSG is mentioned only as the way to report problems. The document is not about mail.

gaps.name: Datacomputer / Datalanguage
gaps.why: The document is mainly about the CCA Datacomputer network data management service and its Datalanguage query protocol. The taxonomy has no tag for early network databases or remote data services.

gaps.name: Natural language question answering
gaps.why: The LISP program answers English questions about weather. The taxonomy has no tag for AI or natural language applications.

RFC421.title: Software Consulting Service for Network Users
RFC421.summary: RFC 421 announces an experimental software consulting service at the ARPANET Network Control Center to help network users with server systems and report host software difficulties.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note announcing a user-support service run by the Network Control Center, so the ARPANET subject page is the right place for it.
ARPANET.quote: BBN recently aided a "software consultant", Nancy Neigus, to the Networtk Control Center staff.

rejected.why: This is an announcement of a human consulting service, not an introductory guide or FYI document for Internet users.
The service is user support, not network operations or management protocols, even though it is hosted at the NCC.

RFC422.title: Traffic statistics (November 1972)
RFC422.summary: A BBN report giving ARPANET per-Host packet throughput statistics (internode, intranode, daily averages) for November 1972.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operations working note reporting monthly packet traffic per Host and node.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the Host traffic statistics for the month of November 1972.

rejected.why: The tables are simple ARPANET traffic counts, not a metrics or measurement method; the ARPANET tag fits better.
It is a contemporary operational report, not a history or retrospective.

RFC423.title: UCLA Campus Computing Network Liaison Staff for ARPANET
RFC423.summary: A 1972 notice listing UCLA Campus Computing Network staff contacts for ARPANET users (administrative, technical, consulting, operations); it specifies no protocol or technical subject.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note about the UCLA-CCN ARPANET node's liaison and contact staff, which falls under the ARPANET subject area of operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: The ARPA Network contacts at CCN are:

rejected.why: It is a contact list for network users, not an introductory FYI-style guide to Internet use.
Network protocol problems are mentioned only as a topic for the technical liaison; the NCP is not described.

RFC425.title: "But my NCP costs $500 a day"
RFC425.summary: 1972 ARPANET note announcing that MIT-DMCG and UCLA-NMC will serve as "Official Surveyors" providing a standard host-survey data format at a standard socket, to reduce wasteful per-site host polling.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note about host survey traffic, NCP costs and network etiquette between sites. It belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: MIT-DMCG and UCLA-NMC, who have both been doing surveys for some time, have agreed upon a standard format for host survey data

rejected.why: NCP appears only in the title as a cost. The document does not specify or analyse the protocol, so ARPANET is the better fit.
The host survey is a kind of status monitoring. The document is a short announcement about reducing polling overhead, not a management architecture or protocol.
The surveys find out which hosts are up, but the document doesn't define a discovery mechanism. The format and socket are left to a later note.

RFC426.title: Reconnection Protocol
