RFC426.summary: RFC 426 proposes a reconnection mechanism (RRQ/ROK/RNO/RDO commands) for moving one end of a communication path between hosts, and recommends adding it to TELNET as an option (RCP/RCS/RCW) instead of changing the ARPANET Host-Host protocol.

Telnet.why: The document's recommended outcome is a TELNET option, with new commands RCP, RCS and RCW defined using DO/WILL/WON'T/DON'T. Telnet readers would want it.
Telnet.quote: I recommend that the reconnection mechanism be included in TELNET as an "option" in the spirit of RFC #435.

NCP.why: A substantial section specifies how the reconnection commands would extend the ARPANET Host-Host protocol (NCP), interacting with its STR/RTS/CLS messages. The document also discusses why NCP changes are unlikely.
NCP.quote: The four reconnect commands could be included directly in Host-Host protocol as follows:
NCP.section: 3. Adding the Reconnection Mechanism to Host-Host Protocol

rejected.why: The document is set on the ARPANET, but the NCP and Telnet tags are more specific. The parent is implied by NCP.
Authentication hand-off is only one motivating example (Example B), not the subject of the document.

RFC429.title: Character Generator Process
RFC429.summary: RFC 429 proposes a standard Character Generator process on ARPANET hosts that, after the Initial Connection Protocol, sends characters continuously without regard to input, as the converse of the discard process.

small services.why: The document proposes the Character Generator (Chargen) service, one of the TCP/UDP small services, in its original ARPANET form. Readers of the small services subject would want it.
small services.quote: a standard process implemented on whatever hosts desire which generates character data with out any regard to input

ARPANET.why: The process is defined for ARPANET hosts and uses the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol, so it belongs with the ARPANET host protocols.
ARPANET.quote: execute the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) as specified in NIC 7104 the "Current Network Protocols" notebook

rejected.why: The ICP runs over NCP connections, but the document only relies on it as the connection mechanism and does not specify NCP.
The process is mentioned as a terminal testing tool (TTYTST), but the document does not address network management or testing as a subject.

RFC430.title: Comments on File Transfer Protocol
RFC430.summary: 1973 comments from a UCLA meeting on the File Transfer Protocol, covering objections to RFCs 354/385/414, TYPE parameter encoding, server-server transfers (RFC 438), and site-dependent parameters for IBM hosts.

FTP.why: The whole document comments on and proposes changes to FTP: TYPE encoding, block mode, PASS, STOR, GETSocket/SOCK commands, and site-dependent parameters.
FTP.quote: This RFC generally reports the consensus of that meeting on the following issues: server-server transfers

rejected.why: The host-host protocol and RFC exchange are discussed as the underlying context for server-server sockets, but the document is about FTP, not NCP itself.
Telnet is used for the FTP control connection and its control characters are mentioned for text mode, but it is only the substrate.
The ARPANET is the environment for the discussion, but the document's subject is FTP.
EBCDIC is discussed only as an FTP type and its limits in text mode, not as a subject in its own right.

RFC431.title: Update on SMFS Login and Logout
RFC431.summary: RFC 431 restates and completes the definition of the Login (LGI) and Logout (LGO) commands for UCSB's Simple Minded File System (SMFS), including command formats, op codes and completion codes.

rejected.why: SMFS was an ARPANET-era file service at UCSB, but the document concerns only its login/logout commands and says nothing about ARPANET itself or its host/network protocols. The ICP mention is incidental.
SMFS is a file system access protocol, not FTP. The document does not specify, extend or relate to FTP.
LGI identifies the user for billing and statistics, and no credentials are verified. It is accounting identification, not authentication.
LGI is meant for billing and accounting, but only as an optional, unbilled identification command. There is no AAA framework, so it is too thin for the tag.

gaps.name: Simple Minded File System (SMFS)
gaps.why: This is an early ARPANET-era network file service at UCSB. The document is entirely about its login and logout commands, and the taxonomy has no tag for early network file access protocols.

RFC432.title: Network logical map
RFC432.summary: RFC 432 transmits BBN's logical map of the ARPANET as of December 1972, showing which host computers connect to each IMP, and asks for notification of changes.

ARPANET.why: The document is a snapshot of ARPANET topology: IMPs and their connected hosts. It is a working note about the ARPANET's operation, so the ARPANET topic fits.
ARPANET.quote: Attached is the logical map of the network as of December 30, 1972.

rejected.why: The map is a historical artifact, but the document is an operational working note and not a retrospective. The ARPANET tag is the better fit.
Hosts on the map used NCP, but the document does not discuss the protocol.

RFC433.title: Socket number list
RFC433.summary: RFC 433 is a 1972 list of ARPANET socket number assignments for public network functions (Telnet, File Transfer, RJE, Echo, Discard, etc.) and a per-host tabulation of the services offered.

ARPANET.why: The document defines the ARPANET socket number structure and assignments and lists per-host services. This is ARPANET host-level protocol administration.
ARPANET.quote: The czar of socket numbers [Jon Postel] has established the following assignments for socket numbers used for public functions.

small services.why: It assigns well-known sockets for Echo, Discard and Character Generator, the precursors of the small services, and cites the RFCs that specify them.

rejected.why: Telnet appears only as an assigned socket (1) and in the host list. The document does not specify or extend it.
File Transfer is only listed as socket 3 with references to other RFCs. It is not the subject of this document.
Sockets are NCP concepts, but the document is an assignment list. It does not specify the NCP protocol.
This is an early assignment registry, but the document is ARPANET-specific and the ARPANET tag fits it better.

RFC434.title: IMP/TIP memory retrofit schedule
RFC434.summary: A 1973 BBN announcement of the schedule for retrofitting ARPANET IMPs and TIPs with additional core memory, listing per-site dates and resulting memory sizes.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note about IMP/TIP hardware upgrades and the per-site maintenance schedule.
ARPANET.quote: During the first several months of 1973 we will be retrofitting each IMP and TIP with additional core memory.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.
It concerns hardware upgrade scheduling for specific machines, not a network management protocol or practice in general.

RFC435.title: Telnet issues
RFC435.summary: 1973 BBN note proposing a symmetric, negotiated echo-mode scheme for the TELNET protocol and generalizing it into negotiated options with WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T-style command prefixes.

Telnet.why: The whole document proposes changes to TELNET echo negotiation, option negotiation principles, and command format, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: We will describe a method wherein both parties can initiate a change of echo mode and show that the method does not loop.

rejected.why: The document concerns TELNET over the ARPANET and mentions the TIP, but it is about the Telnet protocol itself, so Telnet is the more specific fit.
Negotiating EBCDIC or ASCII is mentioned only as one suggested option, not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC436.title: Announcement of RJS at UCSB
RFC436.summary: Announces a UCSB server implementing a subset of the Remote Job Entry Protocol (RFC 407) on socket 5, describing login, supported modes, commands, and TENEX FTP account extensions.

RJE.why: The document announces and describes a UCSB RJE server (RJS) implementation, its supported commands, modes and dispositions.
RJE.quote: a server program which supports a subset of the Remote Job Entry Protocol of RFC #407

rejected.why: FTP account commands (ACCT) are mentioned only as the file transfer mechanism RJS uses and for TENEX server accommodation; the document is about RJE, not FTP itself.
TELNET-like carriage control is just a transmission mode name; Telnet is not specified or extended.
Parent of RJE, implied by the RJE tag; not chosen separately.

RFC437.title: Data Reconfiguration Service at UCSB
RFC437.summary: RFC 437 announces the Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS) at UCSB, an ARPANET experiment for reformatting data streams between processes, and documents the DRS Time Sharing System command syntax accessed via Telnet.

ARPANET.why: The document describes an ARPANET host service, with socket-based connections and Network host numbers, and its operating commands. It is an early network working note.
ARPANET.quote: The DRS is an experiment in a flexible means for reformatting Network data streams.

rejected.why: Telnet is only the access path to DRS/TSS. The document does not specify or extend the protocol.
The document uses sockets and connection initiation (SICP, UICP, RFC) but does not specify NCP itself.

gaps.name: Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS)
gaps.why: This is a data stream reformatting service with its own form language and compiler. The taxonomy has no tag for it or for early network application services in general.

RFC438.title: FTP server-server interaction
RFC438.summary: RFC 438 proposes an extension to the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol (new LSTN command and modified SOCK/RETR/STOR/APPE) so an FTP user process can arrange direct server-to-server data transfers.

FTP.why: The document specifies an extension to FTP, adding the LSTN command and modifying SOCK, APPE, RETR and STOR to support server-server data connections.
FTP.quote: This RFC suggests a simple extension to FTP which would allow an FTP user process at one site to arrange for FTP server processes at other sites

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the setting for the protocol. The document's subject is the FTP extension, not ARPANET operations or host protocols in general.
The data connections and sockets are NCP-era mechanisms, but the document does not discuss NCP itself.

RFC439.title: PARRY encounters the DOCTOR
RFC439.summary: A humorous transcript of a 1972 conversation between the PARRY paranoid-patient chatbot and the DOCTOR (ELIZA) therapist program, relayed over the ARPANET for entertainment.

humor.why: The RFC is a whimsical, entertaining transcript of two chatbots conversing, with wry editorial comments, not a technical specification.
humor.quote: is herewith reproduced for your entertainment.

rejected.why: The programs were accessed over the network (SAIL, BBN Tenex, UCLA), but the document is about the conversation, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
It is a historical curiosity, but not a history or retrospective of Internet protocols.
Remote terminal access was presumably the means of reaching the hosts, but the document doesn't discuss it.

gaps.name: conversational agents / chatbots (PARRY, ELIZA/DOCTOR)
gaps.why: The document's subject is an AI dialogue between two early chatbot programs, and the taxonomy has no AI or natural-language-processing subject.

RFC440.title: Scheduled network software maintenance
RFC440.summary: Announces that BBN's weekly scheduled IMP software maintenance window on Tuesday mornings is extended from one hour to two hours (7-9am Eastern) because the ARPANET has grown to about forty IMPs.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operations notice about the IMP software release schedule and the IMP-to-Host message announcing maintenance, which falls under the ARPANET topic.
ARPANET.quote: we are extending our scheduled software maintenance period to two hours from 7am until 9am eastern time every Tuesday morning

rejected.why: It concerns scheduled maintenance of the ARPANET IMP software, but it defines no management protocol or architecture. The ARPANET topic is the more specific fit for this historic operations note.
It is a period document but not a history or retrospective.

RFC441.title: Inter-Entity Communication - an experiment
RFC441.summary: 1973 status report on an experiment in inter-host user-to-user communication (WHO, WHERE, LINK, CONNECT) via ports and the RSEXEC interim protocol on socket 245/365 octal, with ICP and command protocol details.

ARPANET.why: The document describes an early ARPANET host-level experiment and protocol (RSEXEC, ICP, socket assignments, TENEX/ITS hosts), a working note of the ARPANET era.
ARPANET.quote: The server and user programs complete the ICP by opening two 36 bit "working" connections

rejected.why: The design philosophy is said to parallel TELNET with server and user programs, but the document does not specify or extend Telnet.
It is user-to-user console conversation, but it is pre-email/IM-era terminal linking and not the instant messaging and presence protocol the tag covers.
The protocol runs over ARPANET host-host connections and sockets, but NCP itself is not specified or discussed.
WHO/USINF/SSTAT resemble finger-like user information lookups, but this is a different, experimental protocol.

gaps.name: Inter-Entity Communication / RSEXEC
gaps.why: Early ARPANET inter-host terminal linking and conferencing protocol; no taxonomy tag exists for it beyond the general ARPANET topic.

RFC442.title: Current flow-control scheme for IMPSYS
RFC442.summary: Cerf's 1973 note describes the ARPANET IMP operating system's flow-control scheme: source-to-destination IMP buffer reservation (REQ/ALL/RFNM), message ordering, and per-channel ACK bits.

ARPANET.why: The document describes the IMP subnet's internal flow-control, reassembly buffer allocation, message ordering and acknowledgment mechanisms, which are ARPANET host and network operations.
ARPANET.quote: The essential goal is to eliminate unnecessary retransmissions when the load is heavy, eliminate the retransmission time-out period when the load is light

rejected.why: The scheme is flow and congestion control, but it is specific to the ARPANET IMP subnet. The ARPANET tag is the better fit than the general transport-layer congestion control topic.
The document covers IMP-to-IMP protocols, not the host-host NCP protocol.
It is a technical description of a mechanism, not a retrospective.

RFC443.title: Traffic statistics (December 1972)
RFC443.summary: Monthly ARPANET host traffic statistics report from BBN for December 1972, tabulating packets output per host and node.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operations report giving per-host and per-node packet throughput figures, which fits the ARPANET topic's operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the Host traffic statistics for the month of December 1972.

rejected.why: The document is a tabulation of traffic counts for one network, not a metrics definition or measurement method.
It is a contemporary operational report, not a history or retrospective.

RFC445.title: IMP/TIP preventive maintenance schedule
RFC445.summary: A 1973 ARPANET note from BBN listing the monthly preventive maintenance schedule for each site's IMP and TIP.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operations working note scheduling maintenance of IMPs and TIPs at ARPANET sites, so it belongs under the ARPANET topic.
ARPANET.quote: This note presents the current IMP/TIP Preventive Maintenance schedule.

rejected.why: It is a maintenance calendar, not a network management protocol or practice specification; the ARPANET tag fits its historical operational nature better.
It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.

RFC446.title: Proposal to consider a network program resource notebook
RFC446.summary: A 1973 ARPANET note proposing that the NIC serve as a repository for a catalog of network program resources, and raising questions about the ARPANET's role as a service network versus a research experiment.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET community working note proposing a NIC resource catalog and discussing the ARPANET's purpose and obligations to outside agencies.
ARPANET.quote: the confusion between the ARPANET as a service network and the ARPANET as an experiment in the line of network research

rejected.why: The proposal is a catalog of programs and documentation kept at the NIC. It is not about discovering services on a network by protocol.
The document is a contemporary opinion piece, not a history or retrospective.

RFC447.title: IMP/TIP memory retrofit schedule
RFC447.summary: A 1973 ARPANET operational notice from BBN giving the revised schedule for retrofitting IMPs and TIPs with additional core memory, updating RFC 434.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on ARPANET IMP/TIP hardware operations, giving the site-by-site memory retrofit schedule.
ARPANET.quote: During the first several month of 1973 we will be retrofitting each IMP and TIP with additional core memory.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.
It is a hardware maintenance schedule, not a management protocol or operational guidance for network management.

RFC448.title: Print files in FTP
RFC448.summary: RFC 448 reviews the problem of how FTP's "print file" format relates to vertical format control cases (none, ASCII effectors, ASA) and the implications of the RJE protocol's interpretation, proposing either record structure as default or three FTP formats.

FTP.why: The document analyses the FTP print file format, its FORMat and STRUcture attributes, and proposes changes to FTP.
FTP.quote: This RFC is intended to review the problem of print files in preparation for the forthcoming FTP meeting.

rejected.why: The taxonomy's RJE tag covers remote job entry on the early network. RJE is discussed only for how its protocol forces an interpretation of FTP print files, so FTP is the subject, not RJE itself.
This is an ARPANET-era document, but the parent topic is implied by no chosen tag and the document addresses an FTP issue rather than ARPANET operations generally.
Telnet-like ASCII format effectors (CR, LF, FF) are mentioned only as one of the VFC cases, not as a Telnet subject.
ASCII controls are mentioned as one VFC case; the document is not about the character set.

RFC449.title: Current flow-control scheme for IMPSYS
RFC449.summary: A short 1973 note from BBN pointing readers to the authoritative publications (AFIPS paper and BBN Report 1822) on the ARPANET IMP flow-control scheme, updating RFC 442.

ARPANET.why: The document concerns flow control and inter-IMP acknowledgement in the ARPANET IMP subnet and the Host-IMP interface, relevant to NCP programmers and Very Distant Hosts.
ARPANET.quote: The Current Flow-control Scheme for IMPSYS.

rejected.why: NCP programmers are mentioned as readers, but the document is about IMP-level flow control, not the host-host protocol.
Flow control is the subject, but the document describes no mechanism itself and it is specific to the ARPANET IMP subnet, so the ARPANET tag fits better.

RFC450.title: MULTICS sampling timeout change
RFC450.summary: A 1973 ARPANET-era note announcing that the timeout for anonymous sampling use of MIT's Multics system via the Net was raised from 1 to 5 CPU minutes.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET working note about operating a host's network-accessible service (Multics sampling access), which falls under the ARPANET topic's host operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: the timeout on sampling ("anonymous") use of Multics via the Net has been increased to 5 cpu minutes

rejected.why: It is a historical document, but it is an operational notice and not a history or retrospective.
It concerns a host's access timeout policy, not network management protocols or practice.

RFC451.title: Tentative proposal for a Unified User Level Protocol
RFC451.summary: Padlipsky proposes replacing multiple contact sockets in the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol with a unified user-level protocol built on new Telnet Control Codes (e.g. "Network Generic Function Follows") so FTP, RJE and other protocols are reached through Telnet.

Telnet.why: The proposal extends Telnet with new control codes (NGF, Unimplemented Generic Function, Begin/End Protocol) to multiplex user-level protocols.
Telnet.quote: why not simply put hooks in Telnet to indicate that a Network Generic Function is wanted instead of a Host-specific one

NCP.why: A large part of the document critiques the ARPANET Initial Connection Protocol and its multiple contact socket approach, part of the NCP-era host-host protocol suite.
NCP.quote: even though the ICP gives us the ability to define a "family" of ICPlets by varying the contact socket

rejected.why: FTP is discussed as an example of a protocol that would be reached through the UULP, but it is not specified or extended here.
The remote job entry protocol is mentioned only as an example of a user-level protocol with its own contact socket.
The Network Graphics Protocol is mentioned only in passing as another user-level protocol.
The ARPANET is the context. The ARPANET topic is implied by the NCP tag, so I did not add it separately.

RFC452.title: TELNET Command at Host LL
RFC452.summary: Documents the TELNET command at Host LL (CP/CMS on an IBM 2741 terminal): its options, ASCII/EBCDIC mappings, control-character conventions, local control commands and a host table for ARPA network Telnet access.

Telnet.why: The document describes a Telnet client implementation, including NVT mapping, Telnet control codes (break, data mark, echo, hide-your-input) and local control commands.
Telnet.quote: The attached writeup documents the use of the TELNET command at Host LL for uses under the CP/CMS time-sharing system.

EBCDIC.why: A substantial part of the document defines EBCDIC-to-network-ASCII translation and a transparent EBCDIC mode, with mapping tables.
EBCDIC.quote: The complete mapping between 8-bit EBCDIC codes and 8-bit network ASCII codes is shown in Figure 4.

rejected.why: Network ASCII is the NVT code the client translates to and from. The document's focus is the EBCDIC mapping and the Telnet client, so ASCII is a secondary aspect.
The document is set in the ARPA network and lists serving hosts. It is about a Telnet client rather than the ARPANET itself, and the Telnet tag covers it better.
The file input and output controls give only a rudimentary file transfer facility, not FTP.
The READER, PRINTER and PUNCH controls support RJS job submission at UCLA CCN. This is a minor part of the document.

RFC453.title: Meeting announcement to discuss a network mail system
RFC453.summary: 1973 announcement of an SRI-ARC meeting to discuss designing a network-wide mail system on the ARPANET, using FTP for mail delivery, uniform user/site identification, and NIC services.

email.why: The document is about coordinating and extending network mail subsystems, covering mail origination, distribution, identification and TIP user mail. This is early email architecture.
email.quote: The purpose of this RFC is to announce a meeting at SRI-ARC on the Network Mail problem

ARPANET.why: It concerns ARPANET host-level operations, including TIPs, the NIC and Network Working Group coordination, so readers of ARPANET working notes would want it.
ARPANET.quote: There are already several subsystems existing on the Network whose function is to send and receive mail.

rejected.why: FTP is proposed as the mechanism for mail delivery, but the document does not specify or extend it. It is only the substrate.
It is a period document, but not a retrospective or history.

RFC454.title: File Transfer Protocol - meeting announcement and a new proposed document
RFC454.summary: RFC 454 announces a March 1973 meeting and presents a proposed revised File Transfer Protocol specification for the ARPANET, updating RFC 354, covering data connections, representation types, transfer modes, commands, and reply codes.

FTP.why: The document is a full proposed specification of FTP: commands, replies, data transfer modes, representation types and restart procedure.
FTP.quote: The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) is a protocol for file transfer between HOSTs (including terminal IMPs), on the ARPA Computer Network (ARPANET).

rejected.why: FTP uses TELNET connections for its control channel, but the document only relies on it as a substrate and does not specify or extend TELNET.
The protocol runs on the ARPANET, but the document is about FTP itself rather than ARPANET operations; the FTP tag is more specific.
ASCII and EBCDIC are used as data representation types, but the document is not about the character sets themselves.
NCP and the Host-Host protocol are assumed as the underlying layer and only mentioned in passing.
The MAIL and MLFL commands carry mail, but this is a minor part of the document.

RFC455.title: Traffic statistics (January 1973)
RFC455.summary: BBN's monthly report of ARPANET Host throughput statistics (packets output, internode and intranode) for January 1973.

ARPANET.why: The document is a table of per-Host packet traffic on the ARPANET, an operational working note of the network.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the Host traffic statistics for the month of January 1973.

rejected.why: The statistics are traffic counts for the ARPANET, not a metrics or methods document; the ARPANET tag fits better.
It is a contemporary data report, not a retrospective or history.

RFC456.title: Memorandum: Date change of mail meeting
RFC456.summary: A 1973 meeting announcement revising the date and time of the Network Mail meeting discussed in RFC 453, to be held at SRI-ARC.

rejected.why: The document only announces a meeting time and place about a network mail system; it specifies nothing about email architecture, transport or formats.
Though a historic ARPANET-era note, its content is a meeting logistics notice and not about ARPANET protocols or operations.

RFC457.title: TIPUG
RFC457.summary: A 1973 note asking TIP users who are not receiving TIP User's Guide updates or TIP User's Group Notes to send their name, TIP and Host to Dave Walden to be added to a distribution list.

rejected.why: TIPs (Terminal IMPs) are ARPANET devices, but the document is only a mailing-list administrative notice. It specifies or discusses no ARPANET protocol, operation or technical content.

gaps.name: TIP (Terminal IMP) User's Guide / TIP User's Group
gaps.why: The document concerns distribution of TIP documentation and user group notes. The taxonomy has no tag for TIP or ARPANET terminal access documentation, and the document has no technical content to tag.

RFC458.title: Mail retrieval via FTP
RFC458.summary: 1973 proposal to add two FTP commands, RDMF and RDML, letting users retrieve their mail from server sites via FTP, symmetric with the existing MLFL and MAIL commands.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with new commands and reply codes (RDMF, RDML, reply 152), so it is about FTP.
FTP.quote: We propose two new FTP commands called ReaDMailFile and ReaDMail.

email.why: The commands exist to retrieve network mail, and the document discusses a mail repository for each user. Mail retrieval is a substantial part of the subject.
email.quote: They would allow a user to read his mail at one or more sites without incurring the overhead of logging in

rejected.why: The Telnet connection only carries FTP replies and mail text. It is the substrate, not the subject.
The document is set in the early network, but it specifies an FTP extension and not an ARPANET host or network protocol as such.
The proposal is an early mail retrieval mechanism, but it is not POP3 and predates it.

RFC459.title: Network questionnaires
RFC459.summary: A 1973 complaint from an ARPANET site about the proliferation of network questionnaires, particularly the seven-page NCP questionnaire in RFC 460, and the burden they place on sites.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note within the ARPANET community about administrative burdens (questionnaires) on network sites. It is an ARPANET community/operations working note, so the ARPANET topic fits.
ARPANET.quote: The arrival of the seven-page NCP questionnaire (RFC 460) has pushed the annoyance level over the top.

rejected.why: The NCP questionnaire is only mentioned as the trigger for the complaint; the document does not specify or analyse NCP itself.
The tone is irritated and sardonic, but it is a sincere complaint rather than a humorous or April 1st RFC.

RFC460.title: NCP survey
RFC460.summary: A 1973 UCLA questionnaire asking ARPANET sites about their implementations of the Network Control Program (NCP), the host-to-host protocol, covering size, coding effort, IMP interface, buffers, queuing, timeouts and measurements.

NCP.why: The whole survey is about implementations of the ARPANET host-host Network Control Program: connection establishment, allocation, giveback, and IMP handling.
NCP.quote: An NCP is that part of the system which performs the tasks necessary for host to host protocol as specified by document NIC 7104

rejected.why: NCP is the more specific child tag and already implies ARPANET; the document is about NCP implementations, not the ARPANET generally.
Mentioned only as a future survey topic and in a measurement question; not what this RFC is about.
Only named as a future survey subject.

RFC461.title: Telnet Protocol meeting announcement
RFC461.summary: A 1973 announcement by Alex McKenzie of a meeting at UCLA to reach consensus on an official TELNET protocol, listing prior RFCs attendees should know.

Telnet.why: The whole document concerns convening a meeting to define an official TELNET protocol and its options, including echo-control conventions.
Telnet.quote: I hereby announce a TELNET Protocol meeting to be held at UCLA on Monday, March 5.

rejected.why: The document is set in the ARPANET community, but it is about the Telnet protocol meeting, not ARPANET operations or protocols in general.
It is a historical artifact, but it is a meeting announcement rather than a retrospective on the Internet or its protocols.

RFC462.title: Responding to user needs
RFC462.summary: RFC 462 supports forming a NIC working group on user information and services for the ARPANET, and proposes that server sites maintain a distributed, extensible network database of host service and access information.

ARPANET.why: The whole document is about getting ARPANET host service and access information to a growing user base. It covers the Resources Notebook, the NIC and the proposed working group, all of which are ARPANET operational matters.
ARPANET.quote: The ARPANET is currently undergoing a transition to an environment in which network resources will be made available to a larger user base.

rejected.why: The proposal is for a distributed information database, but it is a loose idea about user documentation. It does not describe directory access or synchronization.
The topic is user information, but the RFC is not an FYI or introductory guide. It is a proposal about how to collect and maintain that information.

RFC463.title: FTP comments and response to RFC 430
RFC463.summary: A 1973 response by Abhay Bhushan to Bob Braden's RFC 430 comments on the draft FTP specification, covering FTP parameter commands, the 255 socket reply and GSOC command, the 300 greeting, single-line parameter commands, and MAIL/MAIL.file handling.

FTP.why: The whole document discusses revisions to the FTP specification: commands, replies, data transfer parameters, and security checking of data connections.
FTP.quote: Most of the comments in RFC 430 by Bob Braden are useful suggestions which should be included in the forthcoming official FTP specification.

rejected.why: MAIL and MAIL.file commands are discussed in the further comments, but only as FTP commands. This is a minor part of an FTP-focused document, so email is not tagged.
NCP is mentioned only in passing, in the requirement that NCPs provide a socket-number reply. The document is not about NCP.
The document sits in the ARPANET era, but it is about the FTP specification, not the network itself.

RFC464.title: Resource notebook framework
RFC464.summary: A 1973 ARPANET-era RFC proposing a framework in which the Network Information Center coordinates, with regional data collectors, the collection, verification and dissemination of "resource notebook" information about network resources.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about how the NIC and network sites gather and share information on network resources. The ARPANET topic is the best fit for it.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Information Center will coordinate the task of collecting, verifying, and disseminating information of a "resource notebook" nature.

rejected.why: The resource notebook is a human-maintained catalogue of network resources collected by surveys. It does not describe a protocol for discovering services on a network.
The document mentions the notebook's history only by pointing to a companion document (NIC 14514). It is a contemporary proposal, not a retrospective.

gaps.name: Network Information Center (NIC) / resource notebook
gaps.why: The document is about NIC information services and the resource notebook data collection. The taxonomy has no tag for network information services or documentation, so ARPANET is the closest fit.

RFC466.title: Telnet logger/server for host LL-67
RFC466.summary: Describes the Lincoln Laboratory CP/CMS TELNET logger/server on host LL-67, including login handling, ASCII/EBCDIC translation, and mapping of TELNET controls (hide-your-input, noecho, break, sync) to EBCDIC codes.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet server implementation and how it maps Telnet controls (break, sync, NOP, echo/noecho, hide-your-input, data mark) to CP/CMS behaviour.
Telnet.quote: The attached writeup documents the TELNET LOGGER/SERVER for the CP/CMS system on the Lincoln Laboratory 360>67 (host 10).

EBCDIC.why: A substantial part of the document is the ASCII/EBCDIC mapping (Figure 1) and the choice of ASCII or EBCDIC operation, which is relevant to readers of EBCDIC translation.
EBCDIC.quote: Since the CP/CMS system operates with EBCDIC codes, ASCII codes must be translated into EBCDIC before being sent to a virtual machine.

rejected.why: The document is an ARPANET-era host implementation note, but its subject is Telnet and character mapping, and the Telnet and EBCDIC tags fit better.
The ICP connection setup runs over NCP sockets, but this is substrate and not the subject of the document.
ASCII is only one side of the translation table. The document is about mapping to EBCDIC for CP/CMS, not about ASCII itself.

gaps.name: ICP (Initial Connection Protocol)
gaps.why: The document follows ICP to set up its socket pair, but the taxonomy has no tag for this ARPANET connection protocol.

RFC467.title: Proposed change to Host-Host Protocol: Resynchronization of connection status
RFC467.summary: RFC 467 proposes adding RCS and RCR commands to the ARPANET Host-Host protocol to resynchronize per-connection allocation state, and redefines RTS, STR and ERR semantics to resolve half-closed connections.

ARPANET.why: The document proposes a change to the ARPANET Host-Host protocol as implemented by NCPs, with RFNM and subnet behaviour; this is ARPANET protocol working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: The current Host-Host protocol (NIC #8246) contains no provisions for resynchronizing the status information kept at the two ends of each connection.

NCP.why: The Host-Host protocol is implemented by the NCP. The RFC specifies new NCP commands (RCS/RCR) and state handling for connections.
NCP.quote: the NCP's at the two ends stay "confused" forever.

rejected.why: Telnet is not a tag id; TIP and TELNET users are only mentioned as examples of manual resync triggers, so Telnet is not a subject.
Mentioned only in passing as a user of connections; the document is not about the Telnet protocol.
The document concerns the historic NCP Host-Host protocol, not TCP, although it has similar connection-state concerns.

RFC468.title: FTP data compression
RFC468.summary: RFC 468 proposes a compressed transmission mode for FTP, adapting HASP's run-length encoding (byte strings, replicated bytes, filler strings) to reduce bandwidth for large file transfers, with an appendix describing HASP Multileaving.

FTP.why: The document defines the compressed transmission mode for the File Transfer Protocol, so FTP readers would want it.
FTP.quote: Therefore, our proposal for compressed mode of FTP is only an adaptation of the HASP compression scheme.

compression.why: It specifies a run-length style lossless compression encoding and analyses its CPU versus bandwidth economics.
compression.quote: A simple linear scheme could detect repeated single characters, for example.

rejected.why: RJE (remote job entry on the early network) is discussed as background (NETRJS, HASP RJE) but the document does not specify it.
The document is set in the ARPANET era, but its subject is the FTP compression mode, not ARPANET operations.

RFC469.title: Network mail meeting summary
RFC469.summary: A 1973 summary from the NIC's viewpoint of the Network Mail Meeting, which decided on new FTP mail subcommands (TO, FROM, AUTHOR, TITLE, ACKNOWLEDGEMENT, RECORDED, TYPE, TEXT/FILE/CITATION), user@host addressing, and NIC ident translation and recording of mail.

FTP.why: The document's core content is the set of new FTP mail command subcommands for carrying network mail over FTP.
FTP.quote: Additional FTP mail requirements were decided upon.  These would be implemented as a new mail command, with the following subcommands

email.why: It covers early network mail architecture: addressing, delivery responsibility, acknowledgement of delivery, undeliverable notices, recorded mail, and cost allocation for mail handling.
email.quote: The standard form of the address is:  user@host

rejected.why: It defines FTP subcommands for mail fields rather than an internet message header format, so the message format tag does not fit.
It mentions the NIC ident translation and query service, but only as a supporting facility for mail addressing and not as a directory protocol.
It is a period document, but it is a meeting summary on a specific design and not a retrospective on history.

RFC470.title: Change in socket for TIP news facility
RFC470.summary: 1973 ARPANET notice that the TIP News Facility at BBN-TENEX moved to socket 367 (octal), with the old socket kept until April 15, 1973.

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET host-level working note about a socket number assignment for a TIP service. The ARPANET topic fits it better than any technology tag.
ARPANET.quote: The Socket which supports the TIP News Facility has been changed to socket 367 (Octal) at BBN-TENEX.

rejected.why: User TELNET programs are mentioned only as clients with a 'news' command that must switch to the new socket. The document does not specify Telnet or its options.
Sockets and ICP belong to NCP, but the document only announces a number change. It says nothing about NCP itself.

gaps.name: Socket numbers
gaps.why: The document is categorised 'Socket Numbers', an ARPANET-era port and socket assignment. The taxonomy has no tag for early socket or port assignments.

RFC471.title: Workshop on multi-site executive programs
RFC471.summary: 1973 announcement of a tentative workshop on multi-site executive programs (an ARPANET Executive), covering standardizing server interfaces, protocols, user language, and single login across hosts, and mentioning the RSEXEC experimental service.

ARPANET.why: The document concerns an ARPANET-era resource-sharing facility (ARPANET Executive, RSEXEC on TENEX/TIP) and a workshop about it, so it belongs under ARPANET working notes.
ARPANET.quote: making resources on the ARPANET available to the user via a standard, conversational facility which one might call an ARPANET Executive

rejected.why: User TELNET is mentioned only as the way to reach the RSEXEC at socket 367; the document is not about Telnet.
Single login and accounting across hosts is listed as one discussion question, but it is not a substantial part of the document.
Locating a logged-in user by name is a brief example of what the executive could do, not the document's subject.

RFC472.title: Illinois' reply to Maxwell's request for graphics information (NIC 14925)
RFC472.summary: A 1973 ARPANET-era reply from Illinois (Steve Bunch) to a UCLA-NMC request for graphics information, describing local NGP0-based beam graphics support, grey-scale work, and plans for an interactive graphics system with simple commands (MOVE, DRAW, TEXT, UNDO).

network graphics.why: The document is about early ARPANET network graphics practice: NGP0 output, grey-scale work, and proposed interactive graphics commands and standardization philosophies.
network graphics.quote: our policy for supporting this type of graphics has been to emulate as closely as possible the CALCOMP plotter support package on the host machine, but with NGP0 output

rejected.why: Process-controlled FTP is mentioned only as a non-graphics hurdle, not as a subject of the document.
The parent is implied by the network graphics tag; the document is specifically about graphics, not general ARPANET operations.

RFC473.title: MIX and MIXAL?
RFC473.summary: A brief 1973 query asking whether any ARPANET host offers an interpreter for Knuth's MIX computer and a MIXAL assembler, and requesting one be made available.

rejected.why: The document only asks whether an ARPANET host offers a MIX interpreter and MIXAL assembler. It does not address ARPANET protocols, operations, or working notes.
It is a period artifact, but it is not a history or retrospective of the Internet or its protocols.

gaps.name: MIX/MIXAL (Knuth's hypothetical computer and assembly language)
gaps.why: The whole document is about obtaining a MIX interpreter and MIXAL assembler. The taxonomy has no tag for programming languages, assemblers, or software tools, so no tag fits.

RFC474.title: Announcement of NGWG meeting: Call for papers
RFC474.summary: A 1973 announcement by Steve Bunch of the next Network Graphics Working Group meeting at the University of Illinois, with a call for RFCs on higher-level graphics protocols.

network graphics.why: The document announces a Network Graphics Working Group meeting and solicits RFCs on higher-level graphics protocols, which is the early network graphics subject.
network graphics.quote: If you have ideas, comments, suggestions, or even derision for higher-level graphics protocols, please air your opinions via RFC sometime before the meeting

rejected.why: The document is distributed on the ARPANET community, but it is about graphics protocol work, not ARPANET operations. The more specific network graphics tag already sits under ARPANET.

RFC475.title: FTP and Network Mail System
RFC475.summary: 1973 ARPANET note describing the Network Mail System meeting outcome and proposing new FTP commands (MLTO, FROM, MTYP, RECO, etc.) to support network mail within FTP.

FTP.why: The document proposes new FTP commands and reply codes for mail and discusses the existing MAIL and MLFL commands, so it is about extending FTP.
FTP.quote: There was general agreement at the meeting that network mail function should be within FTP.

email.why: It defines mailbox addressing and the functions of a network mail system (creating, locating, sending, storing, recording, reading) and models for its use.
email.quote: The network mail system should provide a facility whereby users can conveniently send messages to other network users who have "mailboxes"

rejected.why: The TELNET connection is only used as the channel for the MAIL command, so it is a substrate and not the subject.
The setting is the ARPANET, but the document is about mail over FTP and not ARPANET operations. The more specific FTP and email tags cover it.
The document does not specify message header syntax. It only mentions a standard FROM address form.

RFC476.title: IMP/TIP memory retrofit schedule (rev 2)
RFC476.summary: A 1973 ARPANET working note giving the revised schedule for upgrading core memory in IMPs and TIPs at sites such as SRI, UCLA and SDC.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operations note about hardware retrofits of IMPs and TIPs at network sites, which falls under ARPANET operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: During the first several months of 1973 we will be retrofitting each IMP and TIP with additional core memory.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous operational schedule, not a history or retrospective.
It covers hardware maintenance scheduling, not network management protocols or operational practice.

RFC477.title: Remote Job Service at UCSB
RFC477.summary: RFC 477 documents UCSB's Remote Job Service, an ARPANET RJE implementation giving users a HASP virtual RJE terminal on an IBM 360/75, with its commands, local syntax, file transfer attributes and reply codes.

RJE.why: The document restates the official RJE protocol (RFC 407) and details UCSB's remote job entry service implementation.
RJE.quote: documents in detail UCSB's implementation of it.

rejected.why: FTP is used to move source and output files, and the document lists the FTP commands RJS issues. It is a substrate, not the subject.
Telnet carries the RJS command connection, but the document does not specify or extend Telnet.
The parent topic is implied by the RJE tag, so I did not list it separately.

gaps.name: HASP spooling system
gaps.why: The appendix describes HASP, the IBM job spooling system, and its operator commands. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC478.title: FTP server-server interaction - II
RFC478.summary: RFC 478 proposes the PASV and SOCK commands for FTP so a user can direct a third-party data transfer between two FTP servers without each having to queue RFCs for non-existent local sockets.

FTP.why: The document specifies the PASV and SOCK commands for FTP server-to-server transfers, extending the FTP protocol.
FTP.quote: Third party connections would be established using the SOCK command, which says "Be prepared to use socket S at Host H to establish your data connection"

rejected.why: The document uses ARPANET-era mechanisms (RFC socket connections, Telnet control) but is about the FTP protocol, not ARPANET operations in general.
Telnet is only the control-connection substrate between the user process and each server; nothing new is specified about it.
The 'RFC' (request for connection) and socket mechanics belong to NCP, but the document does not specify or discuss NCP itself, only how FTP uses it.

RFC479.title: Use of FTP by the NIC Journal
RFC479.summary: 1973 ARPANET-era RFC proposing new FTP MAIL sub-commands (TITLE, ADDRESSEES-ARE, RECORD, etc.) so the NIC Journal can receive and deliver mail via FTP's MLFL mechanism.

FTP.why: The document proposes new FTP sub-commands under a MAIL command for mail submission and delivery, so it is an extension of FTP.
FTP.quote: it was preferable to modify FTP in such a way that all required parameters could be explicitly declared

ARPANET.why: It is an early ARPANET working note about the NIC (SRI-ARC) Journal service and network mail handling between hosts.
ARPANET.quote: At the Network Mail Meeting (see -- 14317,) the NIC outlined it's requirements for implementing FTP Journal delivery and submission.

rejected.why: The mail is carried over FTP, and the document is about FTP commands. It is not about email architecture or email formats, so FTP is the better fit.
NCP is the underlying ARPANET host protocol and the document does not discuss it.

RFC480.title: Host-dependent FTP parameters
RFC480.summary: RFC 480 proposes embedding host-dependent parameters (a program name and parameters) in the pathname of FTP STOR/RETR commands so SRI-ARC's NIC can serve sequential views of NLS files without modifying FTP.

FTP.why: The memo proposes a pathname-extension convention for FTP STOR/RETR commands to pass site-dependent parameters, so it is about using and extending FTP.
FTP.quote: require the user to embed this information in the pathname of FTP's STOR and RETR commands by appending to a standard TENEX filename, a field of the form

rejected.why: The memo is set on the ARPANET, but it addresses an FTP usage convention and not ARPANET protocols or operations.

RFC482.title: Traffic statistics (February 1973)
RFC482.summary: Monthly ARPANET statistics report listing packets output per Host/IMP site for February 1973, with totals and averages.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note reporting host throughput by site (UCLA, SRI, BBN, etc.), so the ARPANET topic fits.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the Host traffic statistics for the month of February 1973.

rejected.why: The document presents raw traffic counts for one network rather than defining performance metrics or measurement methods.
It is a contemporary operational report, not a retrospective or history.

RFC483.title: Cancellation of the resource notebook framework meeting
RFC483.summary: A short 1973 ARPANET-era notice from the NIC announcing cancellation of the tentatively scheduled Resource Notebook Framework meeting, referring to RFC 464 for background.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET Network Working Group administrative note from the NIC about a meeting concerning the Resource Notebook. It fits the ARPANET working-notes category.
ARPANET.quote: announce a cancellation of the Resource Notebook Framework meeting that had tentatively been scheduled for March 19, 1973.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous meeting notice, not a history or retrospective.
It is not about the format, style or publication of the RFC series. The machine-readable note is document-format apparatus.

RFC485.title: MIX and MIXAL at UCSB
RFC485.summary: A 1973 note from a UCSB graduate student replying to a query about MIX, describing his SNOBOL4 MIXAL assembler and partially debugged 360-assembler MIX simulator and offering them to others.

rejected.why: Although it is an ARPANET-era Network Working Group note, it concerns a Knuth MIX assembler and simulator, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
It is a period document but not a history or retrospective of Internet protocols.

gaps.name: MIX/MIXAL assembler and simulator
gaps.why: The document is about Knuth's MIX computer, its MIXAL assembly language, and a simulator implementation. The taxonomy has no tag for programming tools or computer architecture simulation.

RFC486.title: Data transfer revisited
RFC486.summary: 1973 proposal to merge the RJE and FTP protocols into a single "data transfer" protocol with a shared control/data connection and command sets for system, parameter, data control, file and job execution operations.

FTP.why: The document proposes restructuring FTP, splitting it into a general data transfer layer and file transfer commands, and merging it with RJE.
FTP.quote: A possible course of action, then, would be to take the "official FTP" resulting from the 16 March meeting at BBN and divide the commands into data transfer and file transfer components.

RJE.why: The proposal merges the RJE protocol with FTP and leaves RJE as a job submission and execution command subset, so it concerns remote job entry on the early network.
RJE.quote: The RJE documents can then be revised or rewritten such that the "new" data transfer protocol will also have an RJE subset.

rejected.why: Telnet connections are mentioned only as something the merge would save. The document is not about Telnet.
This is the parent topic of RJE. The more specific RJE tag is the one that applies.

RFC487.title: Free file transfer
RFC487.summary: RFC 487 proposes that FTP servers allow anonymous file retrieval (and append-based storage) without a user name and password for files marked as accessible to everyone, with BBN TENEX implementing it.

FTP.why: The document proposes a change to FTP server behaviour to permit anonymous, no-password transfers, which is the origin of anonymous FTP.
FTP.quote: If a user connects to an FTP server and makes a file request without supplying a user name-password, the server should then examine the file access parameters.

rejected.why: The document concerns relaxing login requirements for public files in FTP, not an authentication mechanism in its own right.
It touches on access levels (user, group, everyone), but this serves the FTP proposal and is not a general treatment of access control.
The document is set on the ARPANET, but it is about FTP service behaviour, not ARPANET operations or protocols generally.

RFC488.title: NLS classes at network sites
RFC488.summary: RFC 488 solicits Network community comments on holding NLS (oN-Line System) training classes at network sites rather than at SRI-ARC, and outlines the course contents and logistics.

ARPANET.why: This is an early ARPANET working note about NLS, a network-accessed application, and about training at ARPANET sites. It is the closest fit in the taxonomy for this 1973 network-community notice.
ARPANET.quote: Network users have expressed interest in holding NLS classes at sites on the Network, instead of at SRI-ARC.

rejected.why: This is a proposal for on-site classes with a course outline. It is not an introductory guide for Internet users, and it is not part of the FYI series.
The class covers using NLS over the Network via TENEX/NLS interfaces, but the document does not specify or discuss the Telnet protocol.
The document is a contemporary working note, not a history or retrospective, so the ARPANET tag covers it.

gaps.name: NLS (oN-Line System)
gaps.why: NLS is Engelbart's hypertext and collaboration system at SRI-ARC. It is the subject of this RFC, and the taxonomy has no tag for it or for early online collaboration tools.

RFC489.title: Comment on resynchronization of connection status proposal
RFC489.summary: Postel endorses the Burchfiel/Tomlinson proposal (RFC 467) for resynchronizing connection status in the ARPANET host-to-host protocol, renaming the commands RAS/RAR and giving a sender/receiver step table.

NCP.why: The document comments on a resynchronization procedure for the ARPANET host-to-host protocol (NCP), defining RAS/RAR commands and the allocation reset sequence.
NCP.quote: a procedure in the host-to host protocol for resynchronization of connection status

rejected.why: NCP is the more specific child tag covering the host-to-host protocol; the parent is implied.

RFC490.title: Surrogate RJS for UCLA-CCN
RFC490.summary: RFC 490 describes how UCSB's Remote Job Server can be used as a surrogate to submit jobs to and retrieve output from UCLA-CCN's IBM 360/91 RJS over the ARPANET, including JCL commands, DD cards, and error handling.

RJE.why: The document is about remote job entry/submission on the early network: a surrogate RJS that submits jobs and retrieves print and punch output across hosts.
RJE.quote: By using UCSB's Network Standard RJS* users can now gain access to UCLA-CCN's RJS without converting to the UCLA protocol.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the network the service runs over. The document is about the RJS procedure, and the more specific RJE tag under ARPANET already covers it.
Connections are made over the ARPANET, but the document never specifies or discusses NCP.

RFC491.title: What is "Free"?
RFC491.summary: Padlipsky argues that FTP network mail should be "free" via a standard explicit login (USER NETML / PASS NETML) rather than a loginless mechanism, proposing an FTP FREE command if NETML is unacceptable to some hosts.

FTP.why: The document debates how FTP's USER/PASS login and the MAIL command should work for free mail, and proposes a new FTP FREE command. It is about FTP's design.
FTP.quote: USER NETML / PASS NETML should be made to work everywhere for free mail.

ARPANET.why: It is an early ARPANET Network Working Group note about host-protocol conventions, including Server FTP, per-Host login environments and socket 3.
ARPANET.quote: Network protocols should not implicitly legislate "unnatural" implementations for participating Hosts if it is conveniently avoidable

rejected.why: Mail is the use case, but the document is about FTP login and access-control semantics, not mail architecture or formats.
Login and authentication are discussed only as they bear on FTP mail, so this is not a separate subject.

RFC492.title: Response to RFC 467
RFC492.summary: A 1973 response to RFC 467 opposing its proposed ARPANET Host-Host protocol control messages (RCS/RCR) for lost-allocate and half-closed connections, and offering alternative GVB/RET changes and NCP principles.

NCP.why: The document critiques and proposes changes to the ARPANET Host-Host protocol implemented by NCPs: allocation control messages, half-closed connections, RST/ERR handling. This is the core subject.
NCP.quote: A proposed interim solution which modifies the existing GVB and RET commands and which has the additional feature of simplifying them somewhat is outlined below.

rejected.why: The child tag NCP fits more specifically, and its ancestor ARPANET is implied.
Allocation messages are flow control for the Host-Host protocol, not congestion control across transports.
TCP is a later protocol. This document concerns the earlier NCP Host-Host protocol.
Telnet is mentioned only as an example of a connection affected by lost messages. The document is not about it.

RFC493.title: GRAPHICS PROTOCOL
RFC493.summary: RFC 493 proposes part of a Network Standard Graphics Protocol for the ARPANET, defining a leveled 8-bit byte-stream command set (moves, lines, dots, text, subpictures, viewports) sent from a serving host to a display package at a using host.

network graphics.why: The whole document specifies an early network graphics protocol and its output byte stream, commands, levels and coordinate system.
network graphics.quote: It describes part of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol for transmitting graphics data within the ARPA network.

rejected.why: Parent of network graphics, which is the more specific tag and already implies it; the document is about the graphics protocol, not the ARPANET in general.
Network ASCII is only used to encode text strings in the commands; the document is not about ASCII.
Appendix 1 gives a BNF for the byte stream, but this is just a notation used to describe the protocol, not the subject.
Not discussed; connection establishment is explicitly left to a separate Connection Committee.

RFC494.title: Availability of MIX and MIXAL in the Network
RFC494.summary: A 1973 ARPANET note summarizing responses on which network hosts offer assemblers and interpreters for Knuth's hypothetical MIX computer.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET working note about software available to network users on specific hosts such as UCSB, UCSD, UCLA and Stanford. It is not about any particular protocol.
ARPANET.quote: MIX and an assembler for MIX are available for network use on the UCLA 360/91.

gaps.name: MIX/MIXAL (Knuth's hypothetical computer) software availability
gaps.why: The document is about the availability of MIX assemblers and interpreters. The taxonomy has no tag for programming tools or host software resources.

RFC495.title: Telnet Protocol specifications
RFC495.summary: Cover note announcing the 1973 TELNET Protocol Specification and TELNET Option Specifications from a UCLA meeting, with a phase-in schedule for the new command forms and a list of options to be specified.

Telnet.why: The document announces the official TELNET protocol specification and option specifications, and sets the transition dates for the new command forms.
Telnet.quote: an open meeting was held at UCLA on 5 March to formulate a new specification for the TELNET Protocol

rejected.why: TELNET was an ARPANET protocol, but the document is about the TELNET specification itself, and Telnet is the more specific tag.
An EBCDIC option is only mentioned as a possible future option, not addressed in this document.
The NVT character mapping appears only in a list of options to be specified later, so the document is not about ASCII.

RFC496.title: TNLS quick reference card is available
RFC496.summary: A 1973 announcement that SRI-ARC has produced a TNLS (Typewriter NLS) quick reference card covering basic commands, TIP settings, TENEX commands and VIEWSPECS codes.

ARPANET.why: An early ARPANET working note about user documentation for accessing the SRI-ARC NLS service via a TIP. The ARPANET topic is the closest fit.
ARPANET.quote: It includes TIP settings for connecting to SRI-ARC, basic TENEX/EXECUTIVE commands, and a complete of set of VIEWSPECS codes for TNLS usage.

rejected.why: The FYI user-guide series is for introductory guides to Internet users. This is a 1973 announcement of a card for one host's editing system, not an FYI guide.
TIP settings for connecting are mentioned, but the document does not specify or discuss the Telnet protocol.

gaps.name: NLS / TNLS (oN-Line System) text editing system
gaps.why: The document is about a specific early online system's user reference card. The taxonomy has no tag for NLS or early collaborative editing systems.

RFC497.title: Traffic Statistics (March 1973)
RFC497.summary: Monthly ARPANET Host traffic statistics report for March 1973, giving per-host packet counts (internode and intranode), daily averages and a packets-per-message ratio.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note reporting per-Host packet throughput for ARPANET nodes (UCLA, SRI, BBN, etc.), which is the ARPANET topic.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the Host traffic statistics for the month of March 1973.

rejected.why: The document is a data table of traffic counts, not a metrics definition or measurement method; it fits the ARPANET operations notes better.
It is a historical artifact but not a retrospective about the Internet; the ARPANET tag covers it more specifically.

RFC498.title: On mail service to CCN
RFC498.summary: 1973 note by Braden describing how CCN receives and prints ARPANET mail via SNDMSG and the FTP MAIL command, and proposing an extension of MAIL/MLFL user-name syntax for printing options.

email.why: The document is about mail delivery service at one host: receiving, printing and distributing network mail and proposing a mail-delivery extension.
email.quote: CCN has no plans to provide post-office services; we expect to receive mail only for the staff of CCN.

FTP.why: The proposal extends the FTP MAIL and MLFL commands' user and pathname fields and describes SNDMSG delivering mail via FTP MAIL.
FTP.quote: Dave Crocker of NMC has suggested an extension to the MAIL and MLFL (Mail File) commands in CCN's FTP

rejected.why: The document is set on the ARPANET, but it is about mail service at one host rather than ARPANET operations in general. The email and FTP tags cover its subject.
This predates SMTP. The mail is carried by FTP MAIL commands, not by SMTP.

RFC499.title: Harvard's network RJE
RFC499.summary: RFC 499 describes Harvard's PDP-10 remote job entry (RJE) program, which lets ARPANET users submit batch jobs to UCLA's IBM 360/91 via RJS and retrieve printed output, with local and remote command descriptions.

RJE.why: The whole document specifies and documents the usage of a remote job entry program on the early ARPANET.
RJE.quote: RJE was designed to provide network users with the facility of submitting jobs to remote servers via the ARPA net and retrieving results using Harvard's PDP-10.

rejected.why: FTP is used to move files to Harvard's PDP-10 before using RJE, but it is a supporting tool and not the subject.
Telnet is only the connection used to carry commands and error messages; the document defines nothing new about it.
The parent topic is implied by the RJE tag, so I did not list it separately.

RFC500.title: Integration of data management systems on a computer network
review: not tagged by the model: awaiting a tagger run, or no text in the corpus

RFC501.title: Un-muddling "free file transfer"
RFC501.summary: A 1973 ARPANET note critiquing RFC 487/467 proposals for "free" (login-less) FTP server access, separating access control, user authentication and accounting, and discussing whose principal identifier and account an FTP server process should use.

FTP.why: The whole document discusses how File Transfer Server (FTP server) implementations should handle authentication, access control and charging for login-less transfers.
FTP.quote: Whose principal identifier does a File Transfer Server process use?

authentication.why: A substantial part of the document untangles user authentication from file access control and accounting in server implementations.
authentication.quote: the notions of access controls on files (examples of protection mechanisms), and control of access to the system (user authentication) are thoroughly muddled

rejected.why: File access control is discussed, but mainly as a conceptual contrast to authentication and accounting. The document is not about an authorization mechanism, so authentication fits better.
The document is set on the ARPANET, but its subject is FTP server access and accounting, not ARPANET operations in general.
Mail transmission is the motivating use case, but the document does not address email protocols.

gaps.name: accounting / charging for network resource use
gaps.why: The document largely concerns who should be billed for free file transfers. The taxonomy has no tag for accounting, apart from AAA, which is a poor fit for this early host-level discussion.

RFC503.title: Socket number list
RFC503.summary: RFC 503 is an ARPANET socket number list assigning well-known sockets for standard network functions (Telnet, FTP, Echo, Discard, etc.) and tabulating which services each host offers.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note assigning host-host socket numbers for network-wide and host-specific services and listing per-host services.
ARPANET.quote: Following are the current assignments for socket numbers used for public functions.

small services.why: Assigns the Echo, Discard, Character Generator, Systat and Date-Time sockets, the precursors of the small services, and cites RFCs 347, 348 and 429.

IANA.why: It is a registry of assigned socket numbers, an early precursor of IANA port number assignment.
IANA.quote: 0 - 63              Network Wide Standard Functions

rejected.why: Sockets are used by NCP, but the document only lists assignments. It mentions NCP Measurement only as one entry.
Telnet is only listed as a socket assignment and the document does not specify it.
File Transfer is listed only as a socket assignment, with no protocol content.
Remote Job Entry and NETRJS appear only as socket entries, not as the subject.

gaps.name: Socket number / port number assignments
gaps.why: The document is a registry of well-known socket numbers. The taxonomy has no tag for port or socket assignment registries apart from the generic IANA topic.

RFC504.title: Distributed resources workshop announcement
RFC504.summary: 1973 announcement of a BBN workshop on automating resource sharing across ARPANET hosts, listing discussion topics such as remote access, accounting, security, and process-oriented protocols.

ARPANET.why: The whole document is a working-note announcement about ARPANET resource sharing, its hosts, protocols and services, so the ARPANET topic page fits.
ARPANET.quote: What steps can be taken to automate access to the distributed resources on the ARPANET?

rejected.why: The agenda touches on dynamically locating resources on several hosts, but this is one discussion item and not the document's subject.
Network-wide accounts and third-party password validation are listed as discussion items, but only briefly. The document is not about authentication.
The new TELNET protocol is mentioned in passing as one of the existing protocols, and the document does not address it.
This announces a workshop and is not a report from one. The tag is for reports from IAB, IRTF and community workshops.

RFC505.title: Two solutions to a file transfer access problem
RFC505.summary: 1973 ARPANET note by Padlipsky proposing two ways to send an FTP file to a user without knowing their password: recipient-initiated pull, or a new FTP POOL command that places the file in a pool directory and notifies the recipient.

FTP.why: The document proposes an extension to FTP (the POOL command, a free-account USER NETML/PASS NETML convention, and an access id argument to STOR) to solve an access problem in file transfer.
FTP.quote: I propose the addition of a new FTP "POOL" command, which does what the last paragraph described.

rejected.why: The document is set in the ARPANET community (NWG, Multics host), but the subject is the FTP access problem, not ARPANET operations. The FTP tag is the better fit.
Mail is mentioned only as a use case for pooled files, and for MAIL as a notification mechanism. It is not what the document is about.
Access control is the motivating problem, but the document is about extending FTP. FTP is the more specific tag.

RFC506.title: FTP command naming problem
RFC506.summary: RFC 506 proposes adding PUSH/PULL (or GIVE/TAKE, SEND) as synonyms for the confusingly named FTP commands STOR and RETR.

FTP.why: The whole document is a proposal to change command naming in the File Transfer Protocol, so it is about FTP.
FTP.quote: I propose that PUSH and PULL be added to the FTP as synonyms for RETR and STOR, respectively

rejected.why: It was written in the ARPANET era, but the document is about FTP command names, not ARPANET protocols or operations in general.

RFC508.title: Real-time data transmission on the ARPANET
RFC508.summary: 1973 experiment report measuring whether the ARPANET could carry real-time (simulated speech) data at various bit-rates and buffer sizes from a UCSB SEL 810-B through hosts to a UCLA discard socket, finding gaps mostly due to hosts.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET performance experiment measuring throughput and delay for real-time data across IMPs and hosts; it fits the ARPANET topic directly.
ARPANET.quote: an experiment was conducted with real-time data being sent from the UCSB SEL810-B computer, by way of the UCSB IBM 360 host, onto the ARPA Network

rejected.why: The motivation is audio/video conferencing, but the experiment sends simulated data to a discard socket and doesn't specify real-time communication protocols or media.
Standard NCP software was used only as the substrate; the document doesn't specify or analyse NCP.

It is a measurement experiment, but the taxonomy topic is about network performance metrics and methods for the modern Internet; the measurement here is a one-off ARPANET experiment and ARPANET covers it.
The UCLA discard socket was used merely as a data sink, and the document is not about the Discard service.

RFC509.title: Traffic statistics (April 1973)
RFC509.summary: A monthly ARPANET report giving per-host and per-node packet throughput statistics (internode, intranode, totals, daily averages) for April 1973.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operations working note reporting host packet throughput for ARPANET nodes (UCLA, SRI, BBN, etc.), which is what the ARPANET subject page covers.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the Host traffic statistics for the month of April 1973.

rejected.why: The document is a table of traffic counts, but it defines no metrics or measurement methods. It is better placed under ARPANET operations.
The statistics are operational reporting, but the document does not address management architecture or practice.

RFC510.title: Request for network mailbox addresses
RFC510.summary: 1973 request from the NIC asking host liaisons to supply users' NIC Idents, delivery modes, and host/FTP-mailbox details so Network Journal articles can be delivered as FTP mail.

email.why: The memo sets up delivery of Journal items to users' network mailboxes and collects mailbox addresses. This is early network mail delivery.
email.quote: NETWORK delivery to his on-line mailbox at his home host.

FTP.why: Delivery uses FTP mail commands, and FTP is also used to retrieve long messages by pathname. The memo does not specify FTP itself, but it describes a notable use of its mail function.
FTP.quote: using the mail command(s) defined by the File Transfer Protocol.

rejected.why: The memo is set in the ARPANET and addressed to its liaisons, but it is about Journal mail delivery, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
The NIC Ident file stores users' delivery parameters, but the memo does not define a directory service.
It mentions a header with the author's Ident, date and title, but gives no format specification.

RFC511.title: Enterprise phone service to NIC from ARPANET sites
RFC511.summary: 1973 NIC notice listing Enterprise/Zenith toll-free phone numbers that ARPANET sites can use to call the Network Information Center, with cost comparison against an 800 number and an answering service note.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about NIC telephone access arrangements for ARPANET sites, listing host sites by ident.
ARPANET.quote: NIC arranged for all Sites then on the Network to have phone service to NIC with all tolls billed to NIC.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.
It lists phone numbers rather than being an introductory guide for Internet users.

RFC512.title: More on lost message detection
RFC512.summary: RFC 512 proposes a per-link Sequence Control Byte in the ARPANET NCP level 2 message leader to detect lost messages, as an alternative to proposals in RFC 467.

NCP.why: The document proposes an extension to the NCP host-host protocol (message leader, ALL, RST, ERR messages) for lost message detection, so it belongs under NCP.
NCP.quote: I propose that one of the two unused eight-bit bytes in the level 2 message leader be designated the "Sequence Control Byte" (SCB).

rejected.why: The more specific NCP tag fits; ARPANET is implied as its parent.
It is a working note on a protocol proposal, not a history or retrospective.

RFC513.title: Comments on the new Telnet specifications
RFC513.summary: Comments on the proposed new TELNET protocol and option specifications, objecting to subnegotiation parsing, the loosely defined "interesting" things in the synch mechanism, tab handling, and several editorial points.

Telnet.why: The whole document critiques the new Telnet protocol and option specifications, covering subnegotiation, synch, DM, AO, EC, EL, GA and CR NUL handling.
Telnet.quote: I would like to make the following comments on the proposed new TELNET Protocol Specification (NIC # 15372) and TELNET Option Specification (NIC 15373).

rejected.why: File Transfer Protocol is mentioned only in passing, as a reference to how user-generated signals are sent after a synch.
The document concerns Telnet specifics. The NCP is mentioned only as the receiving host component, and the document is not about ARPANET operations.
The NCP is mentioned only as the component that scans input on a synch, not as the subject.

RFC514.title: Network make-work
RFC514.summary: A 1973 complaint by W. Kantrowitz of TX-2 protesting bureaucratic make-work requests on ARPANET sites, especially a proposed central repository of program listings and documentation.

ARPANET.why: The whole document is a working note about ARPANET community administration: the host charts, the Resource Notebook, and a central software repository request to ARPANET sites.
ARPANET.quote: The ARPA Network seems to have developed the proclivity of dragging compulsive collectors and organizers out of the woodwork

rejected.why: It is satirical in tone, but it is a sincere protest in the regular RFC series, not an April 1st or whimsical-series document.
It mentions the mid-1960s TX-2/SDC network prototype only in passing; it is not a history or retrospective.
It is an RFC about network community practice, not about the format, style or publication of the RFC series.

RFC515.title: Specifications for Datalanguage, Version 0/9
RFC515.summary: RFC 515 specifies Datalanguage Version 0/9, the data description and request language (containers, directory, CREATE/OPEN/FOR/assignment, BNF syntax) processed by the ARPANET Datacomputer data utility.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies an early ARPANET network service's language, including network port connections to hosts and sockets. It is an ARPANET-era working note, and no other taxonomy tag fits the Datacomputer.
ARPANET.quote: Datalanguage is the language processed by the Datacomputer, a data utility system being developed for the Arpanet.

rejected.why: The character set section (7-bit/8-bit ASCII conversion) is a minor part of the document, not its subject.
The document gives its grammar in plain BNF in section 11. That is only the notation for the spec, not what the document is about.
The Datacomputer directory is an internal tree of container names, not a directory service in the X.500/LDAP sense.
The Datacomputer is a data storage utility, but the taxonomy's storage topic covers modern block/file protocols over IP. This is a data language, so the fit is poor.

gaps.name: Datalanguage / Datacomputer (data management language)
gaps.why: The document is a database-style data description and query language for a network data utility. The taxonomy has no tag for database or data-management languages.

RFC516.title: Lost message detection
RFC516.summary: Postel's 1973 note proposes three ways for ARPANET hosts to detect lost messages: retransmission on IMP replies, host-to-host message sequence numbers, and host-to-host acknowledgements.

ARPANET.why: The document proposes host-level procedures using ARPANET IMP responses (RFNM, INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSION, DESTINATION DEAD) and host-to-host headers. It is an ARPANET working note about host and network protocol operation.
ARPANET.quote: I have three suggestions for detecting the loss of messages by the communications subsystem.

rejected.why: The host-to-host protocol context is NCP and its reset commands are mentioned, but NCP is never named. The note proposes additions at the host level rather than specifying or extending NCP.
Retransmission, sequence numbers and acknowledgements are transport-style reliability ideas. The document is specific to ARPANET message handling rather than a transport protocol.

RFC518.title: ARPANET accounts
RFC518.summary: A 1973 directory of ARPANET host sites listing contacts and how to obtain experimental or paid computer accounts at each site.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note listing host sites and how to get accounts on them, which is squarely ARPANET operations information.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC is being issued in response to numerous requests for information on opening an account at a given site on the ARPAnet.

rejected.why: It is a contemporary operational directory, not a history or retrospective.
Accounts are mentioned only administratively (who to contact); no authentication mechanism is discussed.
It is a printed list of sites and contacts, not a directory service protocol.

RFC519.title: Resource Evaluation
RFC519.summary: 1973 report by UCSB on a test group evaluating ARPANET resources (APL, BASIC, TSO, MACSYMA, IMLAC graphics) and proposing MINIMAN concise user manual formats.
