ARPANET.why: The document evaluates resources available on the ARPANET and proposes user manuals for them. It is an ARPANET working note about host resources and their usage.
ARPANET.quote: a new test group was organized at UCSB to take a detailed look at specific network resources and develop initial site dependent and function dependent MINIMAN's

rejected.why: The MINIMAN user manuals are discussed, but this is not an FYI-series user guide. It is a report on resource evaluation.
IMLAC graphics access is only one of seven projects, and no graphics protocol or format is specified.
Telnet settings are mentioned only as a heading in the proposed manual format. The document is not about the protocol.
FTP is mentioned once, as the way a program was moved between sites. It is only incidental.
This is a contemporaneous working note, not a retrospective.

RFC520.title: Memo to FTP group: Proposal for File Access Protocol
RFC520.summary: RFC 520 proposes the File Access Protocol (FAP), an extension to FTP adding OPEN, CLOS, SETP, GETP, READ and WRIT commands and a file pointer for random access to remote files, plus new reply codes.

FTP.why: The document specifies new commands, a file pointer, and reply codes extending FTP so that parts of remote files can be read or written without transferring the whole file.
FTP.quote: FAP is an extension to FTP.

rejected.why: The document is an ARPANET-era Network Working Group note, but its subject is the FTP extension. FTP is the more specific tag.
FAP gives access to remote files, but it is an FTP extension and not a storage protocol such as NFS. The FTP tag covers it.

RFC521.title: Restricted use of IMP DDT
RFC521.summary: RFC 521 announces that access to the ARPANET IMP's DDT debugging mechanism will be restricted (sense switch four or BBN-enabled override) to improve security and let the NCC coordinate its own use.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note about operating and access-controlling IMP DDT, the debugger on ARPANET IMPs, and about the Network Control Center's use of it.
ARPANET.quote: we will soon modify the IMP system so that any access to IMP DDT will require the same enabling actions

rejected.why: The document is about controlling access to a debugging tool, which touches on security. But it is a 1973 ARPANET IMP working note, and the ARPANET tag fits it better.
It restricts who may use DDT, but it describes a hardware switch and override flag for one system, not authorization mechanisms in general.

RFC522.title: Traffic Statistics (May 1973)
RFC522.summary: A monthly report of ARPANET per-host packet throughput statistics for May 1973, listing internode and intranode packet counts for each host.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational traffic report giving per-host and per-node packet counts for May 1973, so it belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: HOST THROUGHPUT SUMMARY (PACKETS OUTPUT)

rejected.why: The document is a traffic count table. It defines no metrics or measurement methods, and it is a historic ARPANET operations note.
The document is a raw statistics report. It is not a history or retrospective, so the ARPANET tag fits better.

RFC523.title: SURVEY is in operation again
RFC523.summary: 1973 announcement that MIT-DMCG's SURVEY host-monitoring program is running again, polling ARPANET hosts every 20 minutes via ICP/Telnet connections, and offering a NETSTATUS service on socket 15.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on an ARPANET host-surveying and status service, listing surveyed hosts and the NETSTATUS output format.
ARPANET.quote: We are also providing a NETSTATUS service on socket 15. (decimal).

rejected.why: Telnet connections are only used as the probe mechanism to measure response time. The document does not specify or extend Telnet.
The survey does measure host response times. But it is a brief operational notice about one tool, not a document on measurement methods or metrics.
The ICP and socket usage depend on NCP. NCP is not discussed in the document.

RFC524.title: Proposed Mail Protocol
RFC524.summary: RFC 524 proposes a Mail Protocol (MP), a subsystem of FTP commands for recording, delivering, distributing, forwarding, and retrieving citations of network mail, with acknowledgments, access lists, and formal command syntax.

email.why: The whole document specifies a network mail system: delivery, distribution agents, acknowledgments, forwarding and recording of mail. Early precursor of Internet email.
email.quote: It's a proposed specification for handling mail in the Network -- a Mail Protocol.

FTP.why: MP is defined as an FTP subsystem, replacing/extending the FTP MAIL and MLFL commands, borrowing FTP data transfer commands and reply conventions. Readers of FTP history would want it.
FTP.quote: MP is implemented as a set of commands accessible from within the FTP command space.

rejected.why: This predates SMTP and is not SMTP; it is an FTP-based mail protocol, so the generic email tag fits better.
The document mostly defines commands and functions, not a message header format.
Telnet NVT and Go Ahead are used as substrate for command syntax; the document is not about Telnet.
Network context is the ARPANET but the document does not address ARPANET operations or host protocols as such beyond mail; email/FTP tags are more specific.

RFC525.title: MIT-MATHLAB meets UCSB-OLS -an example of resource sharing
RFC525.summary: RFC 525 describes an early ARPANET resource-sharing experiment in which symbolic expressions from MIT's MATHLAB/MACSYMA are transferred by batch job to UCSB's OLS system and turned into OLS user programs for numeric and graphic work.

ARPANET.why: It is a working note about an application of resource sharing between two ARPANET hosts (MIT-ML PDP-10 and UCSB 360/75), including the sockets and access routes used. It fits the ARPANET topic's scope of host-level operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: Non-trivial resource sharing among dissimilar system is a much discussed concept which, to date, has seen only a few real applications.
ARPANET.section: I. Introduction, A. Resource Sharing, A Comment

rejected.why: TELNET is only the access path used to reach MATHLAB. The document does not specify or extend it.
The UCSB batch job submission is part of the tool's implementation, not a remote job entry protocol. The document does not define or discuss one.
The document is a contemporary technical note on an experiment, not a retrospective or history.

gaps.name: Network resource sharing applications (MATHLAB/MACSYMA to OLS data transfer)
gaps.why: The document is about an application-level cooperative use of remote computing resources. The taxonomy has no tag for early network applications or resource sharing apart from the generic ARPANET topic.

RFC526.title: Technical meeting: Digital image processing software systems
RFC526.summary: Announcement and agenda for a July 1973 USC technical meeting on digital image processing software systems and facilities for large-scale image processing over the ARPANET.

ARPANET.why: The meeting concerns using ARPANET-connected computing facilities for image processing, and it is an ARPANET community working note/announcement.
ARPANET.quote: existing hardware facilities and software systems suitable for large scale image processing operations over the ARPANET

rejected.why: This tag covers early network graphics protocols and formats. The document is a meeting agenda about image processing software and defines no protocol or format.
The document announces an upcoming meeting and gives its agenda. It is not a report from a workshop.

gaps.name: Digital image processing
gaps.why: The meeting is about image processing software systems (VICAR, LARSYS, PAZ II, etc.), and the taxonomy has no tag for this application domain.

RFC527.title: ARPAWOCKY
RFC527.summary: A humorous 1973 parody of Lewis Carroll's "Jabberwocky" recast around ARPANET protocols and components (FTP, RJE, NCP, IMPs, RFNM, NIC).

humor.why: The whole document is a poem parodying Jabberwocky with ARPANET jargon, which is the whimsical content the humor tag covers.
humor.quote: Twas brillig, and the Protocols Did USER-SERVER in the wabe.

ARPANET.why: The poem's subject matter is the ARPANET, including its IMPs, host-to-IMP links, RFNMs and NCP. Readers of the ARPANET page would want this period piece.
ARPANET.quote: Beware the ARPANET, my son; The bits that byte, the heads that scratch;

rejected.why: NCP is only named in passing as a joke. The poem does not specify or discuss the protocol.
FTP is mentioned only as a rhyme element. The document has no content about the protocol.
RJE appears only in the refrain of the poem. The document has no substantive content about remote job entry.
The poem is a contemporary parody, not a history or retrospective.

RFC528.title: Software checksumming in the IMP and network reliability
RFC528.summary: 1973 BBN note describing software checksums added to the ARPANET IMP and TIP programs for packets and routing messages to improve network reliability and diagnose hardware faults, plus TIP retransmission changes and future plans.

ARPANET.why: The document describes ARPANET IMP/TIP software changes, operations experience and Host-IMP reliability issues, which belong in the ARPANET subject.
ARPANET.quote: This note describes some modifications that have recently been made to the IMP and TIP programs in this regard.

checksum.why: The core subject is software checksumming of packets and routing messages for error detection, including the add checksum and the planned hardware CRC.
checksum.quote: The technique we chose to use was generating a software checksum on all packets as they are sent out over a line.
checksum.section: 1. A Changing View of Network Reliability

rejected.why: The CRC is mentioned only as the existing hardware circuit check and a future plan, not the subject of the document.
Routing message checksumming is covered, but it is a reliability measure, not routing architecture or protocol design.
The reliability and fault-diagnosis focus is not about security practices.
Host-Host protocol is mentioned only in passing as affected by lost messages.

RFC529.title: Note on protocol synch sequences
RFC529.summary: 1973 note arguing that the TELNET SYNCH sequence (INS plus Data Mark) should not be redefined, and that higher-level protocols such as FTP built on TELNET should define their own synch sequences using TELNET IP and a protocol-specific data mark.

Telnet.why: The document is a response to RFC 513 about the interpretation of the TELNET SYNCH sequence, Data Mark, IP and sub-negotiation handling, so it is about the Telnet protocol itself.
Telnet.quote: For the TELNET protocol the "out of band" signal is the INS of Host-Host Protocol and the "in band" marker is the TELNET Data Mark character (DM).

FTP.why: FTP is the main example of a higher-level protocol misusing TELNET SYNCH. The note proposes an FTP abort procedure and an FTP data mark, which makes it substantive for FTP readers.
FTP.quote: As an example, consider the case of the File Transfer Protocol (RFC 454) and the problem of aborting a file transfer in progress.

rejected.why: The Host-Host Protocol INS signal is used as the out-of-band mechanism, but the note does not specify or analyse NCP. It only mentions it as a layering analogy.
The document is set in the ARPANET but is about Telnet and FTP protocol design, not ARPANET operations.
The note touches on protocol layering discipline, but only in the narrow context of Telnet synch handling. The Telnet and FTP tags cover it better.

RFC606.title: Host names on-line
RFC606.summary: RFC 606 proposes that the NIC maintain a central, machine-readable on-line file of official ARPANET host names, addresses and attributes (property-list format) to replace each site's divergent host tables.

hostnames.why: The document proposes a single official on-line host table mapping host names to addresses, with attributes, which is the host-table naming convention subject.
hostnames.quote: each site on the network must maintain a different, generally out-of-date, host list for the use of its own operating system or user programs

ARPANET.why: The proposal is specific to ARPANET hosts, NIC, TIPs, NCPs and TENEX sites, and is a working note on ARPANET operations.
ARPANET.quote: The function of the host vis-a-vis the network ( user, server, TIP, etc.). This may aid NCPs in deciding whether to poll the host

rejected.why: Predates DNS; it is a flat host table file, not a DNS protocol or resource record.
FTP byte sizes are merely an attribute to be listed; the document does not specify or extend FTP.
Telnet echo mode is just one attribute in the proposed file; the document does not address Telnet itself.
NCPs are mentioned as consumers of the host list, not the subject of the document.
A BNF grammar is used to describe the file syntax but the document is not about the notation.

RFC607.title: Comments on the File Transfer Protocol
RFC607.summary: RFC 607 lists thirteen easily fixed problems in the 1970s File Transfer Protocol (command verbs, reply codes, handshaking order, length limits, blocked-mode EOR handling) and proposes a fix for each.

FTP.why: The whole document critiques FTP and proposes specific changes to its commands, reply codes and handshaking, so it belongs on the FTP page.
FTP.quote: There are several aspects of the File Transfer Protocol that constitute serious drawbacks.

rejected.why: The document mentions TELNET lines only as part of FTP's command-line length limits. It is not about Telnet.
FTP here is an ARPANET-era protocol, but the document is about FTP's design and not about the ARPANET as a network.

RFC608.title: Host names on-line
RFC608.summary: RFC 608 proposes that the NIC maintain an online ASCII file of official host names, addresses and status attributes (HOSTS.TXT), defining its syntax, host name constraints, and FTP retrieval location.

hostnames.why: The document specifies the official host name format and the host table file (HOSTS.TXT) with its syntax and attributes, which is exactly host naming conventions and host tables.
hostnames.quote: the NIC maintain an online ASCII text file of Host names, addresses, and attributes

rejected.why: FTP is only the means to retrieve the file and FTP byte size is a proposed attribute; the document does not specify or extend FTP.
The hosts are ARPANET hosts, but the document is about host naming, which has a more specific tag; ARPANET is context.
The file is ASCII text, but ASCII is merely the encoding and not the subject.
A BNF grammar is used to describe the file syntax, but the document is not about the notation.

RFC609.title: Statement of upcoming move of NIC/NLS service
RFC609.summary: A 1974 ARPANET notice from SRI-ARC announcing the move of NIC/NLS computer services for ROME, ARPA and NIC users to a new OFFICE-1 system at TYMSHARE in Cupertino.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note about moving the Network Information Center service host, including its site numbers for TELNET and TIP access.
ARPANET.quote: we will be transferring computer services for our ROME, ARPA, and NIC users from the ARC/NIC system to a new system we are installing at TYMSHARE

rejected.why: Telnet is mentioned only as the way to address the site number (53 octal); the document does not specify or discuss the protocol.

RFC610.title: Further datalanguage design concepts
RFC610.summary: RFC 610 presents preliminary design concepts and a semantic model for Datalanguage, the request language of the ARPANET Datacomputer data-management utility, covering data description, sharing, integrity, privacy, sets, control and extensibility.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET-era working paper on the Datacomputer, a network data-management node, and its language. The ARPANET topic is the closest fit for such a document.
ARPANET.quote: The Arpanet, for which the datacomputer is being developed, is an international network which has over 60 nodes.

rejected.why: FTP is only mentioned as a possible way to give file-level access to the datacomputer. The document does not specify or extend it.
Datalanguage directories are data aggregates in a data-management language, not a directory service such as LDAP or X.500.
Network standard ASCII is only the character transport for datalanguage requests, so it is a substrate.
The Datacomputer is a data-management utility, not a storage access protocol like NFS or iSCSI. This is a weak fit, and the language and data model are the real subject.

gaps.name: Datalanguage / Datacomputer data management language and database system
gaps.why: The whole document is about a database query and data description language and a data utility. The taxonomy has no tag for databases or data-management languages, so only ARPANET fits.

RFC611.title: Two changes to the IMP/Host Protocol to improve user/network communications
RFC611.summary: RFC 611 modifies the ARPANET IMP/Host protocol by expanding the Host-Going-Down message with return time and reason fields and adding a new Dead Host Status IMP-to-Host message.

ARPANET.why: The document changes the ARPANET IMP/Host interface protocol (BBN Report 1822), adding message fields and a new message type. It is an ARPANET host and network protocol working note.
ARPANET.quote: An additional IMP to Host message is therefore being added which provides status information on the dead Host.
ARPANET.section: 3. Addition of the Dead Host Status Message

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host protocol. This document changes the IMP/Host interface below it, not NCP.
The messages report host status to users, but the document specifies an IMP/Host protocol change, not network management.

RFC612.title: Traffic statistics (December 1973)
RFC612.summary: RFC 612 is a monthly ARPANET statistics report giving per-Host packet throughput (internode and intranode) for December 1973.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note reporting packet traffic by Host and node, so the ARPANET topic page is where readers would look for it.
ARPANET.quote: Attached are the Host traffic statistics for the month of December 1973.

rejected.why: The tables are traffic counts, but they are a historical ARPANET operations report. They do not define metrics or measurement methods.
The data is historically interesting, but the document is a contemporary working note, not a history or retrospective.

RFC613.title: Network connectivity: A response to RFC 603
RFC613.summary: A 1974 note from BBN responding to RFC 603 on ARPANET topology, arguing that node connectivity after failures matters more than per-node degree and that circuits should be added to break up long IMP chains.

ARPANET.why: The document discusses the ARPANET's topology, circuits, IMPs and expansion, which is network operations and planning working-note content.
ARPANET.quote: The weaknesses are not the three-connected and four-connected nodes but rather the ONE-connected (Hawaii, London) and two-connected nodes.

rejected.why: The document is about physical circuit topology and connectivity planning, not routing design or scalability.
It is a contemporaneous working note, not a retrospective history.

RFC614.title: Response to RFC 607: "Comments on the File Transfer Protocol"
RFC614.summary: A 1974 response to RFC 607 that comments point by point on proposed changes to the File Transfer Protocol, covering ACTV/PASV modes, command length, handshake order, multi-line replies, reply codes, and mail transmission via MAIL vs MLFL.

FTP.why: The whole document discusses and proposes changes to FTP commands, replies, data connection handshaking and mail handling, so readers of FTP would want it.
FTP.quote: Mark Krilanovich and George Gregg have pointed out a number of "sticky" issues in the current File Transfer Protocol.

rejected.why: The FTP control connection runs over Telnet, but the document is about FTP, not Telnet itself; Telnet is only the substrate.
The MAIL/MLFL discussion concerns how FTP carries mail, a small part of the document, not email architecture.
Context is the ARPANET, but the document specifically addresses FTP rather than ARPANET operations in general.

RFC615.title: Proposed Network Standard Data Pathname syntax
RFC615.summary: RFC 615 proposes a standardized syntax (NSDP) for naming file/data locations across ARPANET hosts, with network, host, peripheral, directory, file, type and site-specific fields.

ARPANET.why: The document defines a pathname syntax for ARPANET hosts (NETWORK currently only ARPA), with examples at ISI, UCLA-CCN, MIT-Multics and the NIC. It is an early ARPANET working note.
ARPANET.quote: a standardized means of referring to a specific location for/of a collection of bits somewhere on the Network.

rejected.why: This is about file pathnames, not name resolution or host/domain naming.
It is a precursor to resource-naming syntax, but it is not a URI scheme and predates URIs.
File transfer is the likely consumer of the pathname syntax, but the document does not specify FTP.
The BNF is only the notation used to state the syntax, not the subject.

gaps.name: Network Standard Data Pathname (virtual file pathnames)
gaps.why: There is no tag for file naming or pathname syntax for network file access, which is the document's actual subject.

RFC616.title: LATEST NETWORK MAPS
RFC616.summary: RFC 616 distributes the January 1974 geographic and logical maps of the ARPA Network (illustrations only, not reproduced in text).

ARPANET.why: The document consists solely of maps of the ARPANET topology, an ARPANET working note.
ARPANET.quote: ARPA Network, Logical Map, January 1974

RFC617.title: Note on socket number assignment
RFC617.summary: 1974 note arguing that ARPANET protocol designers (FTP, Network Graphics) should not assume fixed socket number relationships relative to the Telnet socket, and should negotiate additional connections over Telnet instead.

ARPANET.why: The document is about socket number assignment conventions in the ARPANET Host-Host protocol and the NCP implementation, an early network working note.
ARPANET.quote: the Host-Host Protocol (NIC #8246) quite explicitly places no interpretations or constraints on host assignment of socket numbers, except for the use of the low-order bit

NCP.why: A substantial part describes the PDP-10 NCP implementation's socket assignment and how fixed socket requirements conflict with it.
NCP.quote: The NCP allows a (non-privileged) user program to specify the low-order 8 bits of the socket number of any connection which it opens

FTP.why: The FTP fixed data socket requirement and its server implementation difficulties are a main case study.
FTP.quote: specifies that the default data transfer sockets are S+2, S+3, U+4, and U+5

Telnet.why: Socket assignment relative to the Telnet connection is central, and the conclusion recommends negotiating extra connections over Telnet.
Telnet.quote: any other necessary connections should be established by negotiation over the Telnet connection

rejected.why: The Network Graphics Protocol is discussed only as a second example of fixed socket assumptions, not specified or extended.

RFC618.title: Few observations on NCP statistics
RFC618.summary: A 1974 note by Edward Taft sharing observations from NCP operating statistics at Harvard/CMU hosts, covering delayed RFNMs, allocate strategies, and excess NOPs on the ARPANET.

NCP.why: The document analyses NCP operating behaviour: RFNM timeouts, allocation strategies, and NOP traffic. Readers of the NCP page would want it.
NCP.quote: The NCP in use at HARV-10, CMU-10A, and CMU-10B collects a number of operating and error statistics

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the setting, and NCP is the more specific tag. The parent is implied by NCP.
A Telnet session is only used to display the statistics. Single-character Telnet messages come up in the allocation discussion, but the document is not about the Telnet protocol.
FTP data connections are mentioned only as an example in the allocation discussion.
The statistics are NCP-specific host counters, not a network performance measurement methodology.

RFC619.title: Mean round-trip times in the ARPANET
RFC619.summary: RFC 619 reports mean round-trip delays measured in the ARPANET during week-long periods in August and December 1973, defining RTT as seen by IMP statistics and tabulating by hop count, source, destination, and site pair.

ARPANET.why: The document is a measurement report on ARPANET IMP/host behaviour: RFNMs, IMP buffers, routing messages, and per-site delays. This is ARPANET operations and working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: In this RFC we want to report the mean round-trip times (or delays) that were observed during these week-long measurements

performance measurement.why: A substantial part defines a delay metric and presents measured data and analysis of the factors affecting it. This is network performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: The round trip time (RTT) is now defined as the time interval T(6)-T(2).

rejected.why: It is a contemporary measurement report, not a retrospective or history.
The NCP appears only as a source of host processing delay and is excluded from the RTT. The document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
The hop-count tables come from IMP statistics, not from path-discovery tools.

RFC620.title: Request for monitor host table updates
RFC620.summary: A 1974 ARPANET notice asking all sites to update their monitor HOST tables and nicknames so that NIC refers to OFFICE-1 (site 53) and ARC refers to SRI-ARC (site 2).

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET operational working note about host table entries and nicknames for ARPANET sites (TENEX hosts, TIP). The ARPANET topic fits.
ARPANET.quote: we would like all sites to change their monitor HOST tables, effective Friday, March 8, 1974.

hostnames.why: The document is about host table entries, host names and nicknames mapped to site numbers, which matches the hostnames tag on host naming conventions and host tables.
hostnames.quote: The actual host name section should contain the following entries (they may already be present).

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.
The hostnames tag is more specific and already covers the host-table naming content.

RFC621.title: NIC user directories at SRI ARC
RFC621.summary: A 1974 ARPANET notice that NIC user directories at SRI-ARC will be deleted and the hostname "NIC" will point to OFFICE-1, so network mail to nicusername@SRI-ARC will no longer be accepted.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET operational working note about host naming changes and mail delivery for NIC users between SRI-ARC and OFFICE-1.
ARPANET.quote: Network mail sent to NIC users in the form "nicusername@NIC" will be delivered to OFFICE-1, as it should.

rejected.why: Mail delivery is affected, but the document is an operational notice about directory deletion and a host name change. It does not specify or discuss email architecture or protocols.
The hostname NIC is remapped to OFFICE-1, but the details are in RFC 620. This notice covers only the effect on mail and user directories, not host naming conventions or host tables.

RFC622.title: Scheduling IMP/TIP down time
RFC622.summary: 1974 ARPANET operational note announcing a policy for scheduling IMP/TIP down time via primary and secondary site contacts, with a list of primary contacts per site.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operations working note about scheduling downtime of IMPs/TIPs and notifying site contacts. It fits the ARPANET topic directly.
ARPANET.quote: From time to time it is necessary for an IMP or TIP to be taken down other than during its scheduled Preventive Maintenance period.

rejected.why: The note is about administrative scheduling and contact procedures, not network management protocols or architecture. It is better covered by the ARPANET tag.
No security practices are discussed.

RFC623.title: Comments on on-line host name service
RFC623.summary: Comments on proposals RFC 606 and 608 for an NIC-maintained online host name and address database, suggesting a secondary mirror host at UCSB, a binary format, and a dedicated socket service instead of FTP.

hostnames.why: The whole document discusses how to maintain and distribute the official host name/address table, which is the hostnames subject (host tables).
hostnames.quote: having a single host maintain a data base containing official host names and host addresses

rejected.why: FTP is the proposed retrieval mechanism in RFC 608 that the author argues against, but the document does not specify or extend FTP.
The context is the ARPANET and NIC, but the subject is host naming, which has a more specific tag. The ARPANET topic is a plausible parent but not needed.
This is a pre-DNS centralized host table service, not the DNS.

RFC624.title: Comments on the File Transfer Protocol
RFC624.summary: RFC 624 (replacing RFC 607) lists twelve easily fixed problems in the RFC 542 File Transfer Protocol, such as command verb length, reply code consistency, multi-line replies and handshake ordering, and proposes a fix for each.

FTP.why: The whole document critiques the FTP specification in RFC 542 and proposes changes to its commands and reply codes, so readers of the FTP subject would want it.
FTP.quote: There are several aspects of the File Transfer Protocol of RFC 542 that constitute serious drawbacks.

rejected.why: The document mentions the TELNET control connection and proposes maximum line lengths for it. It treats TELNET only as the substrate for FTP commands and replies and proposes no change to Telnet itself.
The document is from the ARPANET era and refers to Network mail and ICP. It is about FTP rather than the ARPANET in general.

RFC625.title: On-line hostnames service
RFC625.summary: A 1974 response to RFC 623 agreeing that multiple hosts should mirror the NIC's Hostnames database, but arguing the file should be fetched via FTP in ASCII rather than through a new server process.

hostnames.why: The document is about how the official Hostnames database is maintained, mirrored and made available online, which is the host naming and host tables subject.
hostnames.quote: more than one Host should be responsible for maintaining a copy of the Hostnames data base

FTP.why: A large part of the document defends FTP as the way to retrieve the Hostnames file and discusses common login parameters for FTP servers.
FTP.quote: The file in question is a sequential file and it seems to us that FTP is entirely appropriate for this need.

rejected.why: The setting is the ARPANET and its NIC, but the document is about the hostnames service and FTP rather than ARPANET operations in general. The more specific tags cover it.
The document says it prefers to keep the file in ASCII for easier debugging. That is a brief remark, not a substantial subject.

RFC626.title: On a possible lockup condition in IMP subnet due to message sequencing
RFC626.summary: RFC 626 analyses a possible reassembly-buffer deadlock in the ARPANET IMP subnet caused by IMP-to-IMP message sequencing combined with piggy-backed ALLOCATEs on RFNMs, and proposes reserving a buffer for single-packet messages.

ARPANET.why: The document analyses the IMP subnet's flow control, sequencing and buffer allocation, which are ARPANET host and network protocol operations, and proposes a fix to the IMPSYS.
ARPANET.quote: In this RFC we comment on a possible deadlock condition in the IMP subnet which, to our knowledge, has not yet occurred

rejected.why: The topic is reassembly buffer deadlock and flow control in the IMP subnet, not congestion control across transports. The taxonomy's congestion control tag is about modern transport mechanisms.
NCP is the host-host protocol. This document concerns the IMP-to-IMP subnet, not NCP. ICP is mentioned only in passing.
The document is a contemporary technical note, not a history or retrospective. ARPANET already covers it.

RFC627.title: ASCII text file of hostnames
RFC627.summary: RFC 627 announces the NIC's online ASCII file of official ARPANET hostnames (HOSTS.TXT), its contents, maintenance, nickname registration, and retrieval via FTP.

hostnames.why: The document announces the official host table file (HOSTS.TXT) with hostnames, addresses, status and nickname policy, which is exactly host naming conventions and host tables.
hostnames.quote: The online ASCII text file of official hostnames as defined in RFCs 606 and 608 is now available

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET working note on NIC administration of the host table for ARPANET hosts, which readers of ARPANET history and operations would want.
ARPANET.quote: Each network host will be responsible for accessing this file via FTP for new information.

rejected.why: FTP is only the means of retrieving the file; the document does not specify or extend it.
This predates DNS; it is a flat host table, not the Domain Name System.

RFC628.title: Status of RFC numbers and a note on pre-assigned journal numbers
RFC628.summary: A 1974 SRI-ARC announcement that RFC numbers can now be obtained on-line through NLS at OFFICE-1 rather than SRI-ARC, with a note on pre-assigned journal numbers.

ARPANET.why: This is an ARPANET-era Network Working Group administrative working note from the NIC about RFC number assignment via NLS, the early network's online system.
ARPANET.quote: RFC numbers can now be obtained on-line through NLS at OFFICE-1; they can no longer be obtained on-line at SRI-ARC.

rejected.why: The note concerns how RFC numbers are obtained, which touches on RFC series administration. It is an operational notice about NIC/NLS tooling, not about the format, style or publication of the series, so a reader of that subject page would find little of use.
Number assignment here means RFC and journal document numbers from the NIC, not protocol parameter registries.

gaps.name: NLS (oNLine System) / NIC services
gaps.why: The document is about NLS journal and RFC number assignment at the Network Information Center, but the taxonomy has no tag for NLS or NIC document services.

RFC629.title: Scenario for using the Network Journal
RFC629.summary: A 1974 ARPANET note giving step-by-step scenarios for sending mail through the NIC Network Journal using SNDMSG, TELNET or FTP, and retrieving journalized files via FTP.

email.why: The document is a usage scenario for sending and receiving network mail via the NIC Network Journal, including SNDMSG and FTP MAIL commands.
email.quote: Network users may send mail to individuals and to groups, input as messages or entire files, through the Network Journal, using SNDMSG

FTP.why: A substantial part shows FTP sessions to retrieve journal files and to submit mail via the FTP MAIL command to the NIC server.
FTP.quote: [*] GET <SP> <journal>number.NLS;xnls <CR>
FTP.section: Retrieving the file from Network Journal

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET working note about NIC services (Network Journal), so it belongs under ARPANET.
ARPANET.quote: See ARPANET Directory for NIC idents and Network addresses.
ARPANET.section: Sending the message or file by Telex SNDMSG

rejected.why: TELNET is used only as the access path to reach the NIC FTP server; the document does not specify or extend it.
This predates SMTP; mail is submitted via SNDMSG and FTP MAIL, not SMTP.
Group addressing is mentioned briefly, but the document is not about list management.

gaps.name: Network Journal (NIC/NLS)
gaps.why: The document is about the SRI-ARC NIC Network Journal document-distribution service, which has no specific tag in the taxonomy.

RFC630.title: FTP error code usage for more reliable mail service
RFC630.summary: 1974 note defining how TENEX FTP servers and mailing processes will use FTP 450-454 error codes in MAIL and MLFL commands to distinguish permanent from temporary mail delivery failures.

FTP.why: The document specifies how FTP error reply codes for the MAIL and MLFL commands are used and interpreted, so it is about FTP.
FTP.quote: The purpose of this RFC is to inform all sites of how TENEX sites will use and interpret the codes

email.why: The goal is reliable mail delivery: mailing processes decide whether to retry or give up based on the codes. Readers of email history would want it.
email.quote: A major hindrance to providing reliable mail service is the lack of well-defined FTP error replies

rejected.why: Telnet is mentioned only as the connection carrying mail lines in examples; the document is not about it.
This predates SMTP. Mail is sent through FTP MAIL/MLFL commands, so SMTP does not apply.
The setting is the early ARPANET, but the document concerns FTP mail error codes rather than ARPANET operations in general.

RFC631.title: International meeting on minicomputers and data communication: Call for papers
RFC631.summary: A 1974 call for papers for a Liège meeting (January 1975) on mini-computers and data communication, covering topics such as protocol definition, packet switching and computer networks.

rejected.why: The document is a conference announcement distributed as an RFC. It does not describe the ARPANET, its protocols or its operations.
It is a historical artefact, but it contains no history or retrospective of the Internet or its protocols.
It announces a meeting and is not a report from one. The meeting is also not an IAB or IRTF event.

gaps.name: Conference/meeting announcements (call for papers)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for external conference calls or event announcements. Readers looking for packet-switching and mini-computer networking events of the era would find this RFC there.

gaps.name: Packet switching
gaps.why: The call lists it as a topic, but only in a bullet list of solicited paper subjects. The RFC says nothing substantive about it, so it does not justify a tag.

RFC632.title: Throughput degradations for single packet messages
RFC632.summary: 1974 ARPANET note analysing why single-packet message throughput through IMPs drops to about a quarter of expected, due to out-of-order arrival triggering reassembly-buffer ALLOCATE/retransmission cycles, and proposing two flow-control modifications.

ARPANET.why: The document analyses IMP subnet flow control (RFNM, ALLOCATE, reassembly buffers) and proposes changes to it, which is ARPANET network operations and protocol working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: the observed throughput for single-packet messages is in many cases only about one fourth of what one would expect

rejected.why: The problem is IMP-to-IMP flow control and reassembly buffer allocation in the ARPANET subnet, not congestion control across transports.
The experiment with the IMP message generator is only used to expose the flow-control flaw. The document is not about measurement methods.
Digitized speech is the motivating application, but the document does not address real-time media protocols.

RFC633.title: IMP/TIP preventive maintenance schedule
RFC633.summary: A 1974 BBN note listing the monthly preventive maintenance schedule for ARPANET IMPs and TIPs at each site, with reserved Tuesday-morning software maintenance windows.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational working note for the ARPANET's IMP and TIP nodes, giving their maintenance schedule by site. It fits the ARPANET topic's scope of operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: This note presents the current IMP/TIP Preventive Maintenance schedule.

rejected.why: The note is a maintenance calendar for ARPANET nodes. It doesn't describe a network management architecture or any operational practice that applies beyond that network.
It is a historical artefact, but it isn't a history or retrospective. The ARPANET tag already covers it.

RFC634.title: Change in network address for Haskins Lab
RFC634.summary: A 1974 ARPANET notice that the Haskins Laboratory Very Distant Host connection will move from BBN (IMP #5) to Harvard (IMP #9), changing its network address from 197 to 201.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note about a host's IMP attachment and network address change, which falls squarely under the ARPANET topic.
ARPANET.quote: the Haskins Laboratory "Very Distant Host" connection will be moved from BBN (IMP #5) to Harvard (IMP #9)

rejected.why: The 'Network Address' here is an ARPANET IMP/host address, not IP address architecture; the ARPANET topic covers it.
It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.

RFC635.title: Assessment of ARPANET protocols
RFC635.summary: Cerf's 1974 assessment of the ARPANET Host/Host, IMP/IMP and Host/IMP protocols, analysing throughput, multipacket messages, ordering lockups, and proposing Host-level retransmission, sequencing, windowed flow control, full-duplex connections and in-header control.

ARPANET.why: The whole document critiques and proposes redesign of ARPANET host and IMP protocols, so it belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: This paper deals with the motivations for the redesign of the HOST-to-HOST, IMP-to-IMP, and HOST/IMP communication protocols in the ARPANET.

NCP.why: It analyses the Host/Host protocol (NCP): flow control, simplex connections, the control connection and ICP, and proposes replacements.
NCP.quote: The current Host/Host protocol uses control messages sent on a special control connection to establish new connections,.

congestion control.why: The document discusses flow control, windowing and congestion strategies for the network, and a sliding-window scheme that foreshadows TCP.
congestion control.quote: the IMP subnet must have a way of combating congestion which may result from too rapid influx of data from a source Host

rejected.why: Telnet is mentioned only briefly, in connection with the interrupt signal synchronization issue.
The document is a technical assessment rather than a history or retrospective, though it has some historical context.
It sketches the sequence-number and window scheme that became TCP, but it does not specify TCP.

RFC636.title: TIP/Tenex reliability improvements
RFC636.summary: RFC 636 describes BBN's plan to improve TIP/TENEX connection reliability on the ARPANET, including host-down status reporting, surviving TENEX halts, and ad hoc Host-Host protocol additions (RAR, RAS, RAP, NXR, NXS) to resynchronize allocation and close half-closed connections.

NCP.why: The appendix specifies new NCP Host-Host protocol commands (RAR, RAS, RAP, NXR, NXS) and procedures for resynchronizing allocations and closing half-closed connections.
NCP.quote: A slight addiition to the Host/Host protocol to allow connection allocates to be resynchronized has been designed and implemented for both the TIP and TENEX.

ARPANET.why: Covers ARPANET operations: TIP and IMP behaviour, host-down reporting, and service interruption handling on the early network.
ARPANET.quote: improvement in the reliability of users' connections between TENEXs and TIPs would have major impact on the appearance of overall network reliability

rejected.why: Host status reporting and reliability are operational, but the document is mainly protocol and ARPANET host software work, not network management architecture.

RFC637.title: Change of network address for SU-DSL
RFC637.summary: A 1974 ARPANET notice that the Stanford Electronics Research Lab host (SU-DSL) on the SRI IMP changes its network address from IMP 2 Host 2 to IMP 2 Host 3 (address 130 to 194).

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET operational working note announcing a host address change on an IMP, which is the ARPANET topic.
ARPANET.quote: has its address changed from IMP 2, Host 2, to IMP 2 Host 3.  Thus its "Network Address" is changed from 130 to 194.

rejected.why: The note concerns numeric ARPANET host/IMP addresses, not host naming conventions or host tables.
This is IP address architecture; the document covers a pre-IP ARPANET host address, with no allocation or architecture discussion.
NCP is not mentioned or specified; the document only changes a host's network address.

RFC638.title: IMP/TIP preventive maintenance schedule
RFC638.summary: RFC 638 publishes the monthly preventive maintenance schedule for ARPANET IMPs and TIPs at each site, correcting RFC 633.

ARPANET.why: The document is an operational working note on ARPANET IMP/TIP maintenance times at each network site, which is what the ARPANET subject page covers.
ARPANET.quote: This note presents the current IMP/TIP Preventive Maintenance schedule.

rejected.why: It is a maintenance downtime schedule for specific machines, not a network management architecture or practice. The ARPANET tag fits better.
Nothing in it concerns security practices.

RFC640.title: Revised FTP reply codes
RFC640.summary: RFC 640 (1974) revises the FTP reply code scheme, defining three-digit reply code semantics, multi-line replies, command-reply sequences and state diagrams for the File Transfer Protocol.

FTP.why: The whole document specifies FTP reply codes, their meanings, per-command reply sequences and state diagrams, a modification of the FTP protocol of RFC 542.
FTP.quote: This document describes a revised set of reply codes for the File Transfer Protocol.

rejected.why: FTP replies are carried on the TELNET control connection and end with the TELNET end-of-line code, but Telnet is only the substrate here and is not specified or extended.
The document is from the ARPANET era, but it addresses FTP itself rather than ARPANET network operations or protocols in general.

RFC642.title: Ready line philosophy and implementation
RFC642.summary: RFC 642 gives recommendations for implementing the ready-line handling and resynchronization logic in a host interface to an ARPANET IMP, including error flops, driver process logic and the 1/2 second stabilization delay.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on the ARPANET Host-IMP interface, specifying how hosts should operate the ready lines and resynchronize with the IMP.
ARPANET.quote: BBN Report #1822, Specifications for the Interconnection of a Host and an IMP, gives a complete specification of the Host-IMP interface.

rejected.why: The NCP is mentioned only to say that ready-line resynchronization should be invisible to it. The document is not about NCP.
The host-IMP hardware interface is loosely link-level, but the document is specific to the ARPANET and the taxonomy's link-layer tags cover IP over named media. The ARPANET tag fits better.

gaps.name: Host-IMP interface (BBN Report 1822)
gaps.why: The document is about the hardware and driver interface between a host and an IMP. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it beyond the general ARPANET topic.

RFC643.title: Network Debugging Protocol
RFC643.summary: RFC 643 proposes a level-2 ARPANET protocol, bypassing HOST-HOST, for PDP-11 network bootstrap and cross-network debugging, with commands for examining and depositing memory, breakpoints, single-stepping, and process control.

ARPANET.why: This is an early ARPANET host-level protocol that sends messages directly to and from the IMP on a dedicated link. It is a working note on ARPANET protocols, so the ARPANET topic page fits.
ARPANET.quote: The protocol is a level 2 protocol, which bypasses the ARPANET HOST-HOST protocol.

rejected.why: The protocol explicitly bypasses the HOST-HOST protocol (NCP). It does not specify or extend NCP.
Not relevant. The document covers debugging commands, not graphics.

gaps.name: Remote/network debugging protocol
gaps.why: The document defines a cross-network debugger protocol with breakpoints, single-stepping and memory examine/deposit. The taxonomy has no tag for debugging or bootstrap services.

RFC644.title: On the problem of signature authentication for network mail
RFC644.summary: 1974 note proposing that network mail receivers mark a sender's signature as authenticated by checking that the ARPANET connection originates from a reserved, host-controlled socket, avoiding passwords, with a planned TENEX experiment.

email.why: The whole document addresses authenticating the sender of network mail, and how the mail sending and receiving processes (via FTP) interact. This is email architecture and transport, and it is not a specific email authentication standard like SPF or DKIM.
email.quote: How can the recipient of a network mail message be "certain" that the signature (e.g., the name in the "FROM" field) is authentic

authentication.why: It proposes a process-authentication mechanism based on reserved sockets rather than passwords, and discusses why passwords are impractical. This is authentication across hosts and messages.
authentication.quote: a mechanism is required which will allow a properly authorized (by the sending host) mail sending process to identify itself as such to the mail receiving process

ARPANET.why: The proposal depends on ARPANET host-socket conventions, ICP, and reserved socket assignments, and it includes a planned TENEX experiment with specific socket numbers.
ARPANET.quote: In the ARPANET, a communication path is uniquely identified by its two ends: the send host-socket pair and the receive host-socket pair.

rejected.why: FTP servers are only the receiving process in the mail model. The note does not specify or extend FTP itself.
NCP socket and ICP mechanics are used as the substrate. The note does not define anything about NCP.
This tag covers domain-level anti-spoofing such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC. This 1974 note is a host-socket scheme that predates them, and the plain authentication tag fits better.
The FROM field is mentioned only as the signature being authenticated. The note does not specify headers or message formats.

RFC645.title: Network Standard Data Specification syntax
RFC645.summary: RFC 645 defines the basic syntax of a Network Standard Data Specification (NSDS) for specifying attributes of a collection of bits, with a complete pathname (file location) syntax in semi-structured (human) and highly-structured (machine) modes for ARPANET hosts.

ARPANET.why: This 1974 ARPANET working note specifies a network-wide file pathname syntax (network, host, peripheral, directory, file) for ARPANET hosts. No more specific tag fits, so the topic tag applies directly.
ARPANET.quote: A NSDS is intended to provide a mechanism for specifying all the attributes of a collection of bits.

rejected.why: The pathname syntax could be used by file transfer, but the document does not specify FTP or any transfer protocol.
The document uses BNF to describe its syntax but is not about the notation.
Directory fields here are file-system directories in pathnames, not a directory service.
The NSDS pathname is a precursor of resource naming but is not a URI scheme.

gaps.name: Network file naming / pathname syntax
gaps.why: The document defines a standard syntax for naming files and data across network hosts. The taxonomy has no tag for file naming or data specification outside the ARPANET topic.

RFC647.title: Proposed protocol for connecting host computers to ARPA-like networks via front end processors
RFC647.summary: RFC 647 proposes the Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP), a compact protocol between a host and a directly-connected front-end processor that handles the ARPANET NCP, and argues for it over known-device simulation, with an appendix of opinions on implementers.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies a host-to-front-end protocol for attaching new hosts to the ARPANET. It covers NCP offloading, IMP-Host functions and ARPANET working practice.
ARPANET.quote: the flexible front-end approach is no more than an updating of these 1971 ideas

NCP.why: The whole design aims to shield hosts from implementing the NCP. The front end performs the Host-Host protocol functions, including socket states and connection management.
NCP.quote: let the front-end processor handle the NCP; define an extremely compact protocol for the Host and front-end to follow (the H-FP)

rejected.why: Telnet is handled by the front end and discussed, but the document does not specify or extend it.
FTP is handled via socket 3 and discussed, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Appendix 2 tells anecdotes, but the document is a protocol proposal rather than a retrospective.

gaps.name: Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for host-to-front-end or host-to-IMP interface protocols. These are specific to early networking.

RFC651.title: Revised Telnet status option
RFC651.summary: RFC 651 revises the Telnet STATUS option so that WILL/DO only negotiate permission and actual option-state information is exchanged in SB STATUS SEND/IS subnegotiations.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a revision of a Telnet option (STATUS), including its commands, defaults and subnegotiation format, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This option allows a user/process to verify the current status of Telnet options (e.g., echoing) as viewed by the person/process on the other end

rejected.why: It is an ARPANET-era document, but it specifies a Telnet option and not ARPANET host or network protocols as such.

RFC652.title: Telnet output carriage-return disposition option
RFC652.summary: RFC 652 defines the historic Telnet option NAOCRD, which lets the data sender and receiver negotiate which party handles output carriage-returns and how (delay, discard, etc.).

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet option with its commands, subnegotiation and default, so it belongs under the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: NAOCRD     10   (Negotiate About Output Carriage-Return Disposition)

rejected.why: It is an ARPANET-era document, but it specifies a Telnet option rather than an ARPANET host or network protocol as such.
It deals with carriage-return and NUL characters, but only as parts of the option semantics, not as a character-set topic.

RFC653.title: Telnet output horizontal tabstops option
RFC653.summary: Defines the historic Telnet NAOHTS option (code 11), which lets the data sender and receiver negotiate who handles output horizontal tabstops and at which columns.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its commands, subnegotiation and default behaviour.
Telnet.quote: NAOHTS 11 (Negotiate About Output Horizontal Tabstops)

rejected.why: The RFC dates from the ARPANET era, but it specifies a Telnet option and not an ARPANET host or network protocol as such.
Tabstops are a terminal formatting concern. The document does not specify a character set.

RFC654.title: Telnet output horizontal tab disposition option
RFC654.summary: Defines the historic Telnet option NAOHTD, which lets the data sender and receiver negotiate which party handles output horizontal tab characters and how (delay, replace with space, discard, simulate).

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, with its commands, subnegotiation values and defaults, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: Negotiate About Output Horizontal Tab Disposition

rejected.why: The horizontal tab is an ASCII control character, but the document is about negotiating how it is handled, not about the character set.
The option comes from the ARPANET era, but the document does not address ARPANET protocols or operations as a subject.

RFC655.title: Telnet output formfeed disposition option
RFC655.summary: Defines the historic Telnet option NAOFFD (code 13) for negotiating which party handles output formfeeds and how (delays, CR/LF replacement, discard, simulation).

Telnet.why: The RFC specifies a new Telnet option with its commands, subnegotiation and default, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: The data sender requests or agrees to negotiate about output formfeed disposition with the data receiver.

rejected.why: The document dates from the ARPANET era, but it specifies a Telnet option, not an ARPANET-specific protocol or working note.
It mentions the formfeed character, but it is not about the character set itself.

RFC656.title: Telnet output vertical tabstops option
RFC656.summary: RFC 656 defines the historic Telnet Output Vertical Tabstops option (NAOVTS, code 14), which lets the data sender and data receiver negotiate which party handles vertical tabstops and which stop positions to use.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet option, including its negotiation commands, subnegotiation values, defaults and rules. It belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: The data sender requests or agrees to negotiate about output vertical tabstops with the data receiver.

rejected.why: It dates from the ARPANET era, but it specifies a Telnet option rather than an ARPANET-specific host or network protocol or its operations.
It has a command-name section but is not about terminology or glossaries.

RFC657.title: Telnet output vertical tab disposition option
RFC657.summary: Defines a Telnet option (NAOVTD) letting the data sender and receiver negotiate which party handles output vertical tab characters and how (delay, CR/LF replacement, discard, simulation).

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet option with its negotiation commands, subnegotiation and default behaviour, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: IAC DO NAOVTD The data sender requests or agrees to negotiate about output vertical tab character disposition with the data receiver.

RFC658.title: Telnet output linefeed disposition
RFC658.summary: Defines the historic Telnet option NAOLFD (code 16) for negotiating which party handles output linefeeds and how (delay, discard, simulate), including the DO/WILL/SB commands and the rules for who decides.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option with its negotiation commands, subnegotiation values, defaults and rules, so it belongs under the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: NAOLFD 16 (Negotiate About Output Linefeed Disposition)

rejected.why: It dates from the ARPANET era and refers to NIC numbering, but its subject is a Telnet option rather than ARPANET operations or host protocols.
It handles linefeed and carriage-return characters but does not specify the character set.

RFC659.title: Announcing additional Telnet options
RFC659.summary: A 1974 announcement that the Telnet Options in RFCs 651-658 (a revised Status option and new options controlling format effectors CR, HT, FF, VT, LF) are official and belong in the Protocol Notebook, also pointing to RFC 645.

Telnet.why: The document announces new and revised Telnet options, so readers of the Telnet subject would want it.
Telnet.quote: the set of Telnet Options defined in Request For Comments 651 through 658 (NIC 31154 through 31161) are part of the official Telnet Options

rejected.why: The document is set in the ARPANET era and mentions the NIC, but its subject is Telnet options, not the ARPANET itself.
It describes how RFCs are distributed, but only as incidental administrative detail.

RFC660.title: Some changes to the IMP and the IMP/Host interface
RFC660.summary: A 1974 BBN note announcing changes to the ARPANET IMP software and IMP/Host interface: decoupled per-Host-pair message number sequences, Host/Host access control, a larger message window (four to eight), and a special unsequenced message type.

ARPANET.why: The whole document specifies changes to ARPANET IMPs and the IMP/Host protocol, an ARPANET host and network protocol working note.
ARPANET.quote: several changes will be made to the IMP software including changes to the IMP/Host software interface as specified in BBN Report No. 1822

rejected.why: The changes concern the IMP/Host and IMP/IMP layer, not the Host-Host NCP protocol, which is not specified here.
The message window and resource handling are touched on, but the document is not about congestion control.
It is a contemporaneous technical notice, not a retrospective.

RFC661.title: Protocol information
RFC661.summary: A 1974 compendium by Jon Postel of the status, contacts and documents for the various ARPANET protocols (IMP-Host, NCP, TCP, NVP, Telnet, FTP, mail, RJE, graphics, NSW procedure call protocol, etc.).

ARPANET.why: The whole document is a catalogue of ARPANET host and network protocols, their contacts, documents and status.
ARPANET.quote: This file contains information on the various protocols in the ARPA Network.

NCP.why: Dedicated entries list the NCP host-to-host protocol specifications, link numbers and reliability extensions.
NCP.quote: ncp - standard host-to-host [Official]

Telnet.why: A substantial section lists old and new Telnet and a long set of Telnet option documents with recent developments.
Telnet.quote: NIC 18639 "TELNET Protocol Specifications" AUG 73

FTP.why: A section covers old and new FTP, reply codes, pathnames and file access.
FTP.quote: Neigus, N. "File Transfer Protocol," NIC 17759 RFC 542 12-July-73.

TCP.why: Entry reports TCP specification status, changes in addressing and sequencing, and implementation schedule.
TCP.quote: tcp - Transmission Control Protocol

RJE.why: Entries on RJE and RJS/NETRJS protocols and documents.
RJE.quote: RJE - Remote Job Entry

email.why: Current and proposed mail protocol entries with mail header and FTP-based mail documents.
email.quote: Concern over the authentication of the author of network messages has led to the concept of an authorized mail sending process

network graphics.why: Lists the network graphics protocol and its contacts.
network graphics.quote: Sproull, R, and E. Thomas. "A Networks Graphics Protocol," NIC 24308, 16-Aug-74.

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous status file, not a retrospective history.
It references RFCs as documentation but is not about the RFC series itself.
Not relevant; IMP-Host interface is not an internet layer protocol here.
Packet radio and satellite entries are empty placeholders and no tag fits well.

gaps.name: National Software Works Procedure Call Protocol (PCP/NSW)
gaps.why: A substantial section describes the PCP and its packages, with no taxonomy tag covering RPC-like distributed procedure calls on the early network.

gaps.name: IMP-Host interface (BBN 1822)
gaps.why: Documents the IMP-IMP and IMP-Host protocols; no tag besides the generic ARPANET topic.

gaps.name: Network Voice Protocol
gaps.why: The NVP is listed but there is no tag for early packet voice.

RFC662.title: Performance improvement in ARPANET file transfers from Multics
RFC662.summary: RFC 662 reports an experiment in which enlarging the Multics IMP DIM output buffers to send multi-packet messages raised ARPANET file transfer throughput between two Multics systems from about 6.8 to 27.6 kbit/s.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on ARPANET host-IMP behaviour (RFNMs, message sizes, IMP DIM buffering) and measured file transfer performance on the ARPANET.
ARPANET.quote: Performance improvement in ARPANET file transfers from Multics

rejected.why: The experiment uses the ARPANET File Transfer protocol (BYTE-SIZE and MODE parameters), but the document does not specify or extend FTP. It changes host-IMP buffering, and FTP is only the workload used to measure throughput.
RFNM and allocation handling are mentioned. The focus is the IMP-to-Host interface buffering in Multics, not the host-host NCP protocol.
The document reports throughput measurements, but they are an experiment on one implementation change. It does not propose measurement methods or metrics.

RFC663.title: Lost message detection and recovery protocol
RFC663.summary: RFC 663 proposes an extension to the ARPANET Host-to-Host (NCP) protocol that uses message sequence numbers and link resynch numbers to detect lost messages and recover from them, with new control commands (LMR, LMS, LMA, CLS2, ECLS, RSS, SFR, etc.).

NCP.why: The document amends the ARPANET Host-to-Host protocol implemented by the NCP, adding sequence numbers, resynch numbers and new control commands for loss detection and recovery.
NCP.quote: we propose an extension to the Host-to-Host protocol that will allow detection of lost messages and an orderly recovery from this situation.

rejected.why: NCP is the more specific child tag and already implies ARPANET; the document is about the host-host protocol rather than the network generally.
TCP is a later protocol; this memo concerns the earlier NCP host-to-host protocol, though it addresses similar reliability goals.
The document handles loss detection and retransmission, not forward error correction or network coding.
The memo notes data error detection is not covered and only expects recovery procedures to apply if it is added.

RFC666.title: Specification of the Unified User-Level Protocol
RFC666.summary: RFC 666 specifies the Unified User-Level Protocol, a common command language (login, mail, who, concom, file commands, call, help) offered as a Telnet negotiated option so users can issue generic commands on any ARPANET Server Host.

ARPANET.why: The document is an early ARPANET host-level user protocol proposal: a common command language for Server Hosts, TIPs and mini-Hosts. It is a working note for ARPANET resource sharing.
ARPANET.quote: the UULP is initially to be a Telnet Protocol "negotiated option".  When the option is enabled, the Server Host will furnish a command environment

Telnet.why: The UULP is defined as a Telnet negotiated option. It also covers Telnet erase, kill, eol and newline handling and the Hide Your Input option, which makes it an extension of Telnet.
Telnet.quote: the UULP is initially to be a Telnet Protocol "negotiated option".

rejected.why: FTP is referenced as an environment the UULP can enter and as a tool for file copy. The document does not specify or extend it.
The UULP includes mail and readmail commands, but a separate mail protocol is acknowledged, and these are only generic user commands.
Appendix 1 is described as a first-pass users' manual, but the document is a protocol specification, not an FYI-style guide.
Generic login and accounting are discussed as one motivation, but they are not the main subject.

gaps.name: Common command language / user-level host protocol
gaps.why: The ARPANET-era unified command language for remote hosts has no dedicated tag. ARPANET and Telnet are the closest fits.

RFC667.title: Host Ports
RFC667.summary: A 1974 BBN note describing the approved assignment of host numbers and IMP ports connecting BBN's PDP-10 and PDP-11 hosts and TIPs to the ARPANET.

ARPANET.why: The document is an ARPANET working note assigning host numbers and IMP connections for BBN hosts, so it belongs on the ARPANET page.
ARPANET.quote: The following is the approved scheme to connect our computers to the network.

rejected.why: The ICP to a logger socket is mentioned in passing, but the document does not specify or discuss the host-host protocol.
The host numbers are ARPANET host addresses, not IP address architecture, so the ARPANET tag covers them.
The document is an operational note from the period, not a history or retrospective.

RFC669.title: November, 1974, survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers
RFC669.summary: A 1974 survey of ARPANET server hosts reporting which support the New-Protocol TELNET (with option support) versus the old protocol, with a status table.

Telnet.why: The whole document surveys which hosts implement the new Telnet protocol and which Telnet options (Echo, Suppress-Go-Ahead, Timing-Mark, Transmit-Binary) they support.
Telnet.quote: Survey of New-Protocol TELNET Servers

ARPANET.why: It tracks ARPANET server hosts by host number and name, and records host status as operational notes. This is early ARPANET working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: SDC-LAB (10) is back on the net and the list;

rejected.why: The document refers to sockets 1 and 27 of the ARPANET host-host protocol, but only as the places where Telnet servers listen. It says nothing about NCP itself.

RFC671.title: Note on Reconnection Protocol
RFC671.summary: 1974 note documenting an experimental, modified Telnet RECONNECT option implemented in BBN-TENEX/RSEXEC, covering the protocol, race resolution, implementation advice and TENEX problems.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a modified version of the Telnet reconnection option, including negotiation, subnegotiation and race handling.
Telnet.quote: A process initiates the reconnection of two of its Telnet connections by sending (or requesting its "system" to send) the <IAC><DO><RECONNECT> Telnet command sequence
Telnet.section: I. PROTOCOL for RECONNECTING TELNET COMMUNICATION PATHS

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET working note that uses RFC-socket connections, NCP and TIPs, and discusses host-host protocol placement.
ARPANET.quote: This document deals with reconnection in terms of its current ARPANET definition as a Telnet protocol option.

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host substrate whose RFC/socket mechanism is used, and it appears in the Aside, but the document is not about specifying NCP.
RSEXEC is a resource sharing executive, not a network management system; it is not the subject here.

RFC672.title: Multi-site data collection facility
RFC672.summary: RFC 672 describes a multi-site data collection protocol (request, echo, go-ahead/discard) used by ARPANET TIPs to deliver accounting data reliably to one of several TENEX accounting servers without duplication.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies a protocol among ARPANET TIPs and TENEX hosts using host-host links, RFNMs and IMPs, and is an ARPANET working note on TIP accounting.
ARPANET.quote: The IMP subnet appends the signature (address) of the sending host to all of its messages, so there can be no forging.
ARPANET.section: Section II, Further Clarification of the Protocol, point 8

rejected.why: TIP accounting is a form of network operations, but the document's focus is a general reliable multi-server data collection protocol, not a management framework.
The protocol runs over host-host links, but it is only the substrate and the document does not specify NCP.
It discusses distributed computation and resource duplication, but it is a specific protocol design rather than architectural principles.

gaps.name: Distributed accounting / multi-server reliable data collection
gaps.why: The document's main subject is a duplicate-free, load-leveling data collection protocol across replicated servers, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC674.title: Procedure call documents: Version 2
RFC674.summary: Announcement of Version 2 of the National Software Works (NSW) Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) document set, listing and describing each document (PCP, packages, formats, host protocol) and suggesting reading order.

ARPANET.why: The document set is for the ARPANET-based NSW: a host-level protocol constraining the ARPANET host-host protocol, plus ARPANET inter-host IPC implementations. An ARPANET working-note announcement.
ARPANET.quote: The protocol is a slightly constrained version of the standard ARPANET host to host protocol.

RJE.why: The set includes an NSW Remote Job Entry model and a Batch Job Package, a notable part of the announced specs.
RJE.quote: This document discusses the process of utilizing a batch processing facility to complete a programming task in the NSW environment.

rejected.why: FTP is only the means to retrieve the documents, not a subject.
The host protocol is mentioned as a constrained ARPANET host-to-host protocol, but the announcement does not specify NCP itself.
PCP is a remote procedure call mechanism, but it is a different, unrelated system; ONC RPC is not discussed.
The announcement concerns documents distributed outside the RFC series; it is not about RFC format or publication.

gaps.name: Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) / National Software Works (NSW)
gaps.why: The document is about a remote procedure call protocol and distributed software environment with no fitting taxonomy tag; the closest are ONC RPC (unrelated) and ARPANET.

RFC675.title: Specification of Internet Transmission Control Program
RFC675.summary: The December 1974 specification of the Internet Transmission Control Program (an early TCP), defining its user interface, packet format, connection management (three-way handshake, ISN selection), flow control, implementation structure and measurement plans.

TCP.why: The whole document specifies an early version of TCP: user calls, packet header, connection state machine, three-way handshake, windows, retransmission and implementation structure.
TCP.quote: This document describes the functions to be performed by the internetwork Transmission Control Program [TCP] and its interface to programs or users that require its services.

rejected.why: ARPANET is the environment and source of terminology (sockets, well-known ports), but the document specifies an internetwork protocol, not ARPANET itself.
Buffer and window allocation is discussed as flow control for TCP, not congestion control in its own right.
It is a protocol specification, not a history or retrospective, even though it is historic.
Gateways and internetwork packets are covered, but only as part of TCP's design, not as a separate IP specification.
A checksum field is mentioned but not defined or specified; it is merely a TCP header field.

RFC677.title: Maintenance of duplicate databases
RFC677.summary: 1975 working paper describing a timestamp-based scheme for keeping duplicate (selector,value) databases consistent across ARPANET sites, with deletion flags and garbage collection of deleted entries, designed for the TIP user identification database.

ARPANET.why: The document addresses distributed database maintenance in the ARPANET environment, drawn from the TIP login and accounting system design. It is an ARPANET-era working note, so the ARPANET page is the closest fit.
ARPANET.quote: a working paper on the problem of maintaining duplicated databases in an ARPA-like network

rejected.why: The paper is about replicated (selector,value) databases in general, not directory access or synchronization protocols such as LDAP or X.500.
The TIP user authentication and accounting database is only the motivating example. The paper does not specify an AAA framework.
Timestamps are used for ordering updates, but the paper does not define clock synchronization. It only notes that a network time standard would help.
The paper makes a general distributed-systems argument, but it is not about Internet architectural principles.

gaps.name: distributed/replicated databases
gaps.why: The core subject is replica consistency, timestamp ordering and deletion garbage collection in distributed databases. The taxonomy has no tag for distributed systems or data replication.

RFC678.title: Standard file formats
RFC678.summary: RFC 678 defines six standard plain-text file formats (page length/width, ASCII format effectors, overstriking, end-of-line conventions) for online documents to be printed on line printers and terminals.

ASCII.why: The document fixes the character code of document files as NVT ASCII and specifies how ASCII format effectors (FF, CR, LF, HT, VT, BS) control printing; this is the core of the formats defined.
ASCII.quote: that is ASCII in an eight bit byte with the high order bit zero.

ARPANET.why: An early ARPANET-era working note on the format of online network documents, tied to NVT, Telnet and FTP conventions of the time.
ARPANET.quote: In an attempt to provide online documents to the network community we have had many problems with the physical format of the final documents.

rejected.why: The document explicitly says the formats are not additional FTP data types/modes/structures; FTP is only the transfer context.
Only the NVT code and Telnet end-of-line convention are borrowed; the document does not specify Telnet.
Motivated by online documents (NIC documents) but defines generic print file formats rather than RFC format and style specifically.
ASCII is a child tag and more specific; the document does not register or discuss character sets generally.

gaps.name: Plain-text document file formats / print formatting (format effectors, logical page)
gaps.why: The document's main subject is standard text file layout for printing, which has no matching tag beyond ASCII.

RFC679.title: February, 1975, survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers
RFC679.summary: A February 1975 survey tabulating which ARPANET hosts run Old- or New-Protocol Telnet servers on sockets 1 and 27, with the Telnet options each implements.

Telnet.why: The whole document surveys Telnet server implementations and the new-protocol Telnet options (Echo, Suppress-Go-Ahead, Timing-Mark, Transmit-Binary) they support.
Telnet.quote: The following is the latest version* of the summary and tabulation of server-host Telnet servers.

ARPANET.why: The survey covers ARPANET hosts, with host numbers and names and their server status. It is working-note material about the early network.
ARPANET.quote: progress" toward an all-new-protocol network has been even slower than previously.

rejected.why: It is a status survey, not a retrospective on the history of the protocols.
The socket-based connections rely on NCP, but the document is not about NCP.

RFC680.title: Message Transmission Protocol
RFC680.summary: RFC 680 defines ARPANET standard syntax and semantics for additional message header fields (FROM, SENDER, AUTHENTICATION, MESSAGE-ID, IN-REPLY-TO, REFERENCES, TO/CC/BCC, PRECEDENCE, MESSAGE-CLASS, SPECIAL-HANDLING), building on the RFC 561 message format.

message format.why: The document specifies the header syntax (BNF) and semantics of message header fields, which is Internet message format.
message format.quote: This document defines a number of message fields beyond those discussed in RFC 561.

email.why: It is an early ARPANET electronic mail message standard dealing with message servers, creation and reception processes, so email in general is a fitting broader subject.
email.quote: The purpose of this document is to establish ARPANET standards with regard to the syntax and semantics for these additional fields.

rejected.why: The document runs on the ARPANET but is about message fields, not ARPANET host or network protocols as such.
It uses a BNF-like notation only to describe the syntax, not to specify the notation.
FTP is mentioned only as a possible place where authentication fields get created.

RFC681.title: Network UNIX
RFC681.summary: RFC 681 describes Network UNIX, an implementation of the ARPANET NCP integrated into the UNIX kernel with network connections as special files, plus a Telnet user program, hardware requirements, availability and future plans.

NCP.why: The core of the document is how NCP, the ARPANET host-host protocol, is implemented in UNIX as a kernel part plus an NCP daemon, with connections exposed as special files.
NCP.quote: THE NETWORK CONTROL PROGRAM (NCP), IS INTEGRATED WITHIN THE UNIX FILE SYSTEM.

Telnet.why: A full section describes the UNIX Telnet user program, including IAC handling and CR/LF translation, so Telnet readers would want it.
Telnet.quote: THE USER THEN RUNS A PROGRAM, TELNET, WHICH AFTER ANNOUNCING ITSELF LEAVES HIM WITH SEVERAL OPTIONS.

rejected.why: FTP is mentioned only as a planned future user program, not specified or discussed in substance.
Network RJE is named only as a future implementation item.
The parent topic is implied by the NCP tag, so I did not list it separately.
This is a 1975 implementation note, not a history or retrospective of the Internet.

gaps.name: UNIX operating system network implementation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for operating-system implementations of network stacks, such as UNIX special-file network I/O and kernel/daemon structure.

RFC683.title: FTPSRV - Tenex extension for paged files
