RFC683.summary: RFC 683 describes a TENEX extension to the old FTP protocol, a new TYPE "XTP", that transfers TENEX paged, holey disk files in checksummed, sequence-numbered chunks.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with a new experimental TYPE (XTP) for paged files and discusses FTP MODE, TYPE and STRU design. Readers of FTP would want it.
FTP.quote: TYPE XTP is only implemented for STRU F, BYTE 36, and MODE S.

rejected.why: The chunk checksum is only a feature of the XTP type. The document is not about the Internet checksum in general.
The document is from the ARPANET era and mentions net transfers. Its subject is FTP, not ARPANET protocols or operations.

gaps.name: TENEX paged file transfer
gaps.why: The document is largely about the TENEX file system and how to represent paged, holey files. The taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC684.title: Commentary on procedure calling as a network protocol
RFC684.summary: A 1975 critique of the Procedure Call Protocol (RFC 674) arguing that procedure calling is the wrong basis for distributed computing and that message-passing/IPC models are better suited to networks.

rejected.why: The document critiques remote procedure calling conceptually (PCP, RFC 674), but ONC RPC is a specific, unrelated Sun protocol and is never discussed.
It discusses architectural philosophy for distributed computing systems (procedure call vs message passing), but not Internet architecture principles; the match is loose.
Context is ARPANET-era (TENEX, TIP, NSW), but the document is not about ARPANET host or network protocols and operations.
Only a very generic fit; PCP is a distributed-computation programming model, not an application protocol in the taxonomy's sense.
It is a historical artifact but not a history or retrospective of the Internet.

gaps.name: Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) / distributed computing models
gaps.why: The document is a commentary on RPC-style distributed computation (PCP, NSW) versus message-passing IPC; the taxonomy has no tag for distributed computing, remote procedure call in general, or early network operating systems.

RFC685.title: Response time in cross network debugging
RFC685.summary: RFC 685 reports measured response times of the BBN X-NET cross-network debugger, which runs a PDP-10 front end against a PDP-11 over the ARPANET, locally and across about nine IMPs, and concludes the network delay is tolerable.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on ARPANET use. It measures how ARPANET communication, including multi-IMP paths, affects the response time of a remote debugging application.
ARPANET.quote: Here we wish to discuss the contribution of communicating over the ARPA network to response time.

rejected.why: It reports response-time measurements, but of a debugger application. It does not define network performance metrics or methods, and it explicitly declines to break down network delay causes.
TELNET is mentioned only as one existing way to log into a remote machine to run a debugger. The document is not about the protocol.
Debugging a remote program is not network operations or management. The X-NET debugger is an application tool.

gaps.name: Cross-network debugging (X-NET remote debugger)
gaps.why: The document is about remote program debugging across a network. The taxonomy has no tag for debuggers or distributed debugging tools.

RFC686.title: Leaving well enough alone
RFC686.summary: Brian Harvey argues against waiting for FTP-2 and proposes specific changes to FTP-1 reply codes, HELP/STAT handling, experimental reply codes, and print-file TYPEs.

FTP.why: The whole document discusses FTP-1 versus FTP-2 and proposes concrete changes to FTP reply codes, TYPEs and commands such as HELP and STAT.
FTP.quote: it seems to me that the existence on paper of an unused protocol should not stand in the way of maintaining the current one

rejected.why: Telnet is the control connection FTP runs over. TELNET-2 is mentioned only as a reason for FTP-2, and the document does not propose changes to Telnet.
The MAIL and MLFL reply codes and the mailer are mentioned only as FTP uses. The document is not about mail.
The document is about network hosts on the ARPAnet, but its subject is FTP, not the ARPANET itself.
EBCDIC appears only as a TYPE E and TYPE F detail of FTP file transfer, not as a subject of its own.

RFC687.title: IMP/Host and Host/IMP Protocol changes
RFC687.summary: RFC 687 sketches an expansion of the ARPANET IMP/Host protocol (BBN Report 1822) with a larger leader, 24-bit addressing, message length and handling type fields, and backward compatibility.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies changes to the ARPANET host-to-IMP protocol, including leader format, addressing and NOP messages. It is an ARPANET working note and has no more specific tag.
ARPANET.quote: expansion to the IMP/host and host/IMP protocol which will include among other things the possibility of addressing hosts on more than 63 IMPs

rejected.why: The address field expansion is for ARPANET IMP/host addresses. It is not about IP address architecture.
The document covers the IMP/host interface below NCP's host-host layer. NCP is not discussed.

RFC688.title: Tentative schedule for the new Telnet implementation for the TIP
RFC688.summary: A 1975 BBN note giving the tentative implementation schedule for the new TELNET protocol with option negotiation on the ARPANET TIP.

Telnet.why: The whole document is a schedule for implementing the Telnet protocol and its options (Binary Transmission, Echo, Suppress Go-Ahead, Timing Mark, RCTE) on the TIP.
Telnet.quote: Implementation of the New TELNET Protocol has now become the top priority item on the TIP development queue.

ARPANET.why: The TIP is the ARPANET terminal interface processor, and the schedule is a working note on its development and its effect on hosts.
ARPANET.quote: Because what is done in the TIP potentially affects what is done at a number of hosts

RFC689.title: Tenex NCP finite state machine for connections
RFC689.summary: Describes the finite state machine used in TENEX 1.33 to implement ARPANET Host-to-Host protocol connections, listing states, events and actions.

NCP.why: The document specifies the connection state machine of an NCP (ARPANET Host-to-Host protocol) implementation: RFC/CLS handling, RFNM, allocation, and link tables.
NCP.quote: The attached figure describes the finite state machine used in TENEX version 1.33 to implement the ARPANET Host to Host protocol.

rejected.why: Parent of NCP, so it is implied; the document is about the NCP specifically.
Mentioned nowhere; this is the historic NCP, not TCP.

gaps.name: TENEX operating system implementation
gaps.why: The document is about a specific OS (TENEX) implementation, but the taxonomy has no tag for host operating system implementations.

RFC690.title: Comments on the proposed Host/IMP Protocol changes
RFC690.summary: Jon Postel's 1975 comments on Dave Walden's RFC 687 proposal to change the ARPANET Host/IMP protocol (leader size, address field, message length, handling types, non-blocking interface, backward compatibility).

ARPANET.why: The whole document discusses changes to the ARPANET Host/IMP interface protocol, including leader format, host addressing and IMP behaviour.
ARPANET.quote: This is a set of comments on Dave Walden's RFC 687 suggesting a set of changes to the host--imp protocol.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a concern about host-host protocol and network control programs; the document is about the Host/IMP protocol, not NCP.
The address field expansion is ARPANET host/IMP addressing, not IP address architecture.

gaps.name: Host/IMP protocol (BBN Report 1822)
gaps.why: The document is about the ARPANET host-to-IMP interface protocol, which has no specific tag; the ARPANET topic is the nearest fit.

RFC691.title: One more try on the FTP
RFC691.summary: Brian Harvey argues for keeping and incrementally fixing FTP version 1 rather than moving to FTP-2, and proposes specific changes to FTP-1 reply codes, HELP/STAT replies, print-file handling via the SRVR command, and a renumbering of replies.

FTP.why: The whole document discusses FTP-1 versus FTP-2 and proposes concrete changes to FTP reply codes, commands (HELP, STAT, SRVR, TYPE) and print file handling.
FTP.quote: it seems to me that the existence on paper of an unused protocol should not stand in the way of maintaining the current one

rejected.why: Telnet is the control-connection substrate for FTP; TELNET-2 is mentioned only as a difference in FTP-2, not specified or changed here.
The network is the context for the protocol; the document is about FTP, not ARPANET operations.
MAIL/MLFL reply codes and the mailer are mentioned only as consumers of FTP reply codes.
EBCDIC/ASCII TYPE parameters are discussed only as FTP transfer types, not as a character-set subject.

RFC692.title: Comments on IMP/Host Protocol changes (RFCs 687 and 690)
RFC692.summary: A 1975 comment on proposed ARPANET IMP/Host protocol changes (RFCs 687 and 690), proposing a 104-bit new IMP leader instead of 80 bits to avoid changing host leader length, and suggesting an IMP-to-Host message carrying a host name/address table.

ARPANET.why: The document is about changes to the ARPANET IMP/Host protocol, specifically the leader format between hosts and IMPs, and an added IMP-to-Host message type.
ARPANET.quote: The better solution is to change the length of the new proposed IMP leader. I suggest 104 bits instead of 80 bits.

rejected.why: The suggested IMP-to-Host table of host names and addresses is a minor side proposal, not a discussion of host naming conventions or host tables as such.
The document concerns the IMP/Host interface leader, not the host-to-host NCP protocol, which is mentioned only as the host-to-host leader.

RFC694.title: Protocol information
RFC694.summary: RFC 694 is Jon Postel's 1975 compendium of ARPANET protocol information, listing protocols (IMP-Host, NCP, TCP, Telnet, FTP, mail, RJE, NSW, etc.) with contacts, documents, status, and link/socket assignments.

ARPANET.why: The whole document catalogs ARPANET host and network protocols, their status, people, and assigned links/sockets.
ARPANET.quote: This file contains information on the various protocols in the ARPA Network.

NCP.why: Several entries cover the ARPANET host-host protocol and its experimental extensions (RFC 636, RFC 663).
NCP.quote: ncp - standard host-to-host [Official]

Telnet.why: A large section lists Telnet specifications, the full option list, and server status.
Telnet.quote: New Telnet [Official]

FTP.why: A substantial section tracks old and new FTP, reply codes, pathnames, and file formats.
FTP.quote: Old File Transfer

TCP.why: A detailed entry tracks TCP specification changes, implementations, and test plans in 1974-75.
TCP.quote: tcp - Transmission Control Protocol

RJE.why: Covers RJE and NETRJS protocol entries and their documents.
RJE.quote: RJE - Remote Job Entry

internet history.why: It is a dated snapshot of protocol development activity in 1975, of historical interest.
internet history.quote: Recent international agreements indicate that a form of TCP with a simpler header (144 bits instead of 256 bits)

rejected.why: The mail entries are a small part of the compendium, not a main subject.
Only a one-entry mention of a graphics protocol, with no substantive content.
The link and socket assignment tables are brief and part of a catalog, not a registry-guidance document.
The document points to RFCs and the NIC but is not about RFC series format or publication.

gaps.name: National Software Works / Distributed Programming System (PCP)
gaps.why: A sizable section covers NSW protocols, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC695.title: Official change in Host-Host Protocol
RFC695.summary: RFC 695 is an official change to the ARPANET Host-Host Protocol that splits the ambiguous ERR error code 5 into separate codes for a request on a non-open socket and a message on an unknown link, and adds a new code for an invalid host header.

NCP.why: The Host-Host Protocol is the ARPANET NCP protocol. The document amends its ERR command error codes.
NCP.quote: This is an official change to the Host to Host protocol

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the more specific NCP tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC696.title: Comments on the IMP/Host and Host/IMP Protocol changes
RFC696.summary: Vint Cerf comments on the 1975 proposed IMP/Host and Host/IMP protocol changes, relating them to an IFIP WG 6.1 proposed CCITT standard packet (datagram) header and discussing how it could fit the ARPANET message leader and NCP header.

ARPANET.why: The document comments on proposed changes to the ARPANET IMP/Host and Host/IMP protocol and how the message leader would be adapted, which is ARPANET host/network protocol working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: With reference to RFC's 687, 690, and 692 (NIC's 32564, 32699, and 32734, respectively) by D.C. Walden, J. Postel, and S. Wolfe

NCP.why: A substantial part of the document discusses fitting the 40-bit Host-to-Host (NCP) header together with the proposed packet header and the required NCP program modifications.
NCP.quote: A temporary fix (until we can introduce a new NCP design) might be to squeeze out the reserved 16-bit fields

rejected.why: The proposed datagram header and addressing fields foreshadow IP, but the document is about the ARPANET IMP/Host interface, not the IP layer in general.
The 96-bit address fields are discussed, but only as part of a header proposal for the ARPANET interface, not as an addressing architecture.
The document is a contemporaneous technical comment, not a history or retrospective.

RFC697.title: CWD command of FTP
RFC697.summary: RFC 697 proposes changing FTP so users can gain owner access to Tenex "files only" directories, either by removing the login restriction or by adding an optional password argument to the CWD command.

FTP.why: The document proposes a change to the FTP protocol's CWD command and to FTP login behaviour, so it is about FTP.
FTP.quote: Add an optional argument to the CWD (Change Working Directory) command to specify the password string for the directory.

rejected.why: It dates from the ARPANET era and concerns a Tenex host, but it specifies an FTP change, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
Directory ownership and password-based access come up, but only as the reason for the FTP command change. The document is not about authorization generally.

RFC698.title: Telnet extended ASCII option
RFC698.summary: Defines a Telnet option (EXTEND-ASCII, code 17) that lets peers transmit extended ASCII characters with extra CONTROL and META bits as two-byte subnegotiated sequences, motivated by SU-AI and MIT-AI keyboards.

Telnet.why: The RFC specifies a new Telnet option with its WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T meanings, subnegotiation format, and default, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This option is to allow the transmission of extended ASCII.

rejected.why: ASCII is the character set being extended, but the document is about a Telnet option for transmitting extra bits, not about ASCII itself. The Stanford character set is only described for reference.
The Stanford extended graphic set is listed only as a reference example and is explicitly not required by the option, so the document is not about character set registration or use.

RFC699.title: Request For Comments summary notes: 600-699
RFC699.summary: An annotated index of RFCs 600 through 699, listing each RFC's author, date, title and a short note, mostly covering ARPANET protocols, IMP/Host changes, Telnet and FTP options, and NIC and operations notices.

RFC series.why: The document exists to catalogue and summarise a block of RFCs, with issued and not-issued numbers and cross-references. That is RFC series bookkeeping.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 600 through RFC 699.

ARPANET.why: Most of the catalogued RFCs are ARPANET working notes (IMP/Host protocol, NCP, host names, network statistics, TIP maintenance). Readers of the ARPANET subject would want this overview of 1973-75 notes.
ARPANET.quote: References to documents and contacts concerning the various protocols used in the ARPANET, as well as recent developments

rejected.why: Many entries describe Telnet options, but this document only lists them and does not specify or analyse Telnet.
Several entries cover FTP revisions and reply codes, but the summary itself is not about FTP. It only lists the RFCs.
NCP appears in a few entries (RFCs 689, 618), but only as one item in a list.
It is a status list of RFCs rather than a history or retrospective. The RFC series and ARPANET tags cover it better.

RFC700.title: Protocol experiment
RFC700.summary: An early report on an experiment using a sliding-window, acknowledgement-based reliable transport protocol (derived from Cerf and Kahn's INWG Note 39) between a BBN TENEX host and a PDP-11 line printer over the ARPANET, covering association setup problems, throughput calculations and sequence number sizing.

TCP.why: The document specifies and tests a precursor of TCP: sliding window, sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmission timeout, SYN-like FRST flag and connection release. Readers of TCP history and design would want it.
TCP.quote: A dropped ACK will cause the sender's LEFT

rejected.why: The experiment ran over the ARPANET, but the network is only the substrate. The document is about the end-to-end protocol.
It briefly criticises the eight-bit checksum and recommends a better one, but this is a minor implementation note.
It is historically interesting, but it is an experiment report, not a history or retrospective.
It covers window sizing and throughput as W/2T, but not congestion control. Window size control was not implemented.

RFC701.title: August, 1974, survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers
RFC701.summary: A 1974 survey of ARPANET server hosts reporting which implement the new-protocol Telnet (sockets 1 and 27) and which Telnet options they support.

Telnet.why: The document surveys implementation status of the new Telnet protocol and its options (ECHO, SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD, TIMING MARK, TRANSMIT-BINARY) across servers.
Telnet.quote: MONTHLY REPORTS ON THE STATUS OF THE NEW-PROTOCOL TELNET IMPLEMENTAIONS ON THE SERVER HOSTS ON THE ARPA NETWORK

ARPANET.why: It is an operational working note about ARPANET hosts, tabulating each host's server status.
ARPANET.quote: SERVER HOSTS ON THE ARPA NETWORK

rejected.why: Sockets are used for Telnet connections, but the document is not about the host-host protocol.
It is a contemporaneous status report, not a retrospective.

RFC702.title: September, 1974, survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers
RFC702.summary: A September 1974 survey of ARPANET hosts' Telnet servers, tabulating which implement the new Telnet protocol (socket 1 vs 27) and which Telnet options (binary, echo, suppress-go-ahead, timing-mark) they support.

Telnet.why: The whole document surveys the status of new-protocol Telnet server implementations and their options across hosts, so it is about Telnet and its options.
Telnet.quote: SURVEY OF NEW-PROTOCOL TELNET SERVERS

ARPANET.why: It is an operational working note about ARPANET hosts (BBN, UCLA, SRI, MIT, etc.) and their server status, so ARPANET readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: TABULATION OF SERVER STATUS FOR ALL SERVER SITES

rejected.why: Hosts and sockets are NCP-era concepts, but the document does not discuss NCP itself.
It is a dated status report rather than a history or retrospective.

RFC703.title: July, 1975, survey of New-Protocol Telnet Servers
RFC703.summary: A July 1975 survey tabulating which ARPANET server hosts implement the New-Protocol TELNET (sockets 1 and 27) and which TELNET options (Echo, Suppress-Go-Ahead, Timing-Mark, Transmit-Binary) each supports.

Telnet.why: The whole document surveys server implementations of the New-Protocol TELNET and its options, so Telnet readers would want it.
Telnet.quote: Tabulation of server status for all server sites

ARPANET.why: It reports on ARPANET server hosts by site and socket number, an operational working note on the early network.
ARPANET.quote: In the nearly five months since the last report several new server sites have joined the network

rejected.why: The socket-based connections rely on NCP, but the document is not about NCP.
It is a period status report, not a history or retrospective.

RFC704.title: IMP/Host and Host/IMP Protocol change
RFC704.summary: RFC 704 sketches an expansion of the ARPANET IMP/Host and Host/IMP protocol (BBN Report 1822) with a larger leader, 16-bit IMP addressing beyond 63 IMPs, message length and handling type fields, and backward compatibility.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies changes to the ARPANET host-to-IMP interface protocol, including leader format, addressing and handling types.
ARPANET.quote: an expansion to the IMP/host and host/IMP protocol which will include among other things the possibility of addressing hosts on more than 63 IMPs

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host protocol; this document concerns the IMP/host interface beneath it, not NCP itself.
The address field expansion is specific to ARPANET IMP/host addressing, not IP address architecture.

RFC705.title: Front-end Protocol B6700 version
RFC705.summary: RFC 705 specifies a working-draft Front-End Protocol by which a Burroughs B6700 host offloads ARPANET NCP, ICP and TELNET/FTP network functions to a PDP-11 front-end processor using BEGIN, LISTEN, RESPONSE, MESSAGE, INTERRUPT, END and REPLY commands.

ARPANET.why: The document defines a host-to-front-end protocol for attaching a host to the ARPANET, covering sockets, ICP, NCP, IMP and RFNM handling in the front end. It is an ARPANET working note.
ARPANET.quote: specification and guideline for design of a Burroughs B6700 attachment to an ARPA-Style network

rejected.why: The front end implements the NCP, but the document specifies the host-to-FE protocol, not the NCP itself.
TELNET appears only as a scenario for using BEGIN and LISTEN; the document does not specify Telnet.
FTP appears only in a scenario of control and data paths; the document does not specify FTP.
TRANS-TYPE translation between EBCDIC, ASCII and others is a minor feature, not the subject.

gaps.name: Front-end processor / host-to-front-end protocol
gaps.why: The core subject is a protocol between a host and its network front-end processor. No taxonomy tag covers it except the general ARPANET topic.

RFC706.title: On the junk mail problem
RFC706.summary: A 1975 note by Jon Postel proposing that the ARPANET Host/IMP interface let a Host tell its IMP to refuse messages from a named source Host, to counter denial of service from malfunctioning Hosts sending "junk mail".

ARPANET.why: The whole document concerns an extension to the ARPANET Host/IMP interface protocol, i.e. an ARPANET host-network protocol working note.
ARPANET.quote: In the ARPA Network Host/IMP interface protocol there is no mechanism for the Host to selectively refuse messages.

rejected.why: 'Junk mail' here means unwanted network-level messages between Hosts and IMPs, not unsolicited bulk email.
The messages are Host/IMP-level packets, not electronic mail; the title is a metaphor.
It describes denial of service from a malfunctioning Host, but the subject is a Host/IMP refusal mechanism on the ARPANET, not DDoS mitigation as such.
Concerns a protocol mechanism proposal, not operational security practices.

RFC707.title: High-level framework for network-based resource sharing
RFC707.summary: RFC 707 (James White, SRI-ARC, 1976) proposes factoring the application-independent command/response discipline of ARPANET function-oriented protocols into a separate procedure call protocol (an early RPC) with typed data encodings and a run-time environment, forming a distributed programming framework.

ARPANET.why: The paper critiques ARPANET protocol strategy (Host-Host, TELNET, FTP, RJE) and proposes an alternative for ARPANET resource sharing. It is an ARPANET-era working paper.
ARPANET.quote: The principal goal of all resource-sharing computer networks, including the now international ARPA Network (the ARPANET), is to usefully interconnect geographically distributed hardware, software, and human resources

ONC RPC.why: It defines a remote procedure call protocol with CALL/RETURN messages and typed argument encodings. This is an early precursor to RPC and fits the nearest RPC/XDR-style tag, though not ONC RPC itself.
ONC RPC.quote: the Protocol might aptly be designated a "procedure call protocol (PCP)"
ONC RPC.section: 4b Modeling Resources As Collections of Procedures

rejected.why: FTP is used as an example of the command/response discipline, not specified or extended.
TELNET is discussed as a limitation of hands-on resource sharing, not specified or extended.
RJE is only mentioned as an example protocol in the family.
The Host-Host Protocol is only assumed as the IPC substrate; the paper explicitly sets it aside.
The framework is about application-layer distributed programming, not Internet architectural principles.

gaps.name: Distributed programming system / remote procedure call (PCP)
gaps.why: The core subject is a general remote procedure call protocol and distributed programming framework. The taxonomy only has ONC RPC, which is a different, later protocol.

RFC708.title: Elements of a Distributed Programming System
RFC708.summary: RFC 708 proposes extensions to the Procedure Call Protocol of a distributed programming system (DPS), adding remote process creation, introductions, packages, variables, parameter routing, and coroutine/signal/help/event/abort control transfers, as an early remote procedure call framework on the ARPANET.

rejected.why: ONC RPC and XDR is a specific later Sun system; this document describes a different, earlier RPC framework (PCP/DPS), not ONC RPC.
The ARPANET is only the environment where the IPC facility runs; the document is about a programming-system protocol, not ARPANET host or network protocols.
The document concerns a process-level distributed programming model, not architectural principles of the Internet.
No child tag fits and the document is a general distributed programming framework rather than a specific application protocol; the parent alone is too generic to be useful.

gaps.name: Remote procedure call / distributed programming system (Procedure Call Protocol, DPS)
gaps.why: The whole document is about an RPC-style protocol and model (PCP, run-time environment, system procedures). The taxonomy has no general RPC tag; the only one is ONC RPC, which is a different system.

RFC712.title: Distributed Capability Computing System (DCCS)
RFC712.summary: A 1976 preprint defining the DCCS protocol, which extends capability-list operating-system invocation across a network of hosts through message types such as Invoke, Return, Give, ACK and Delete. It also presents applications for single-copy data access and network resource optimization.

ARPANET.why: The document defines an experimental host-to-host protocol for the ARPA network. It is an early Network Working Group note, and a reader of the ARPANET subject would expect to find it.
ARPANET.quote: currently being implemented on a Digital Equipment Corporation PDP-11/45 computer for use as an experimental protocol on the ARPA computer network

authorization.why: The design is built on capability-based access control. It uses protected capability lists and per-host validation bit vectors, and it has no secret passwords. A substantial part of the paper covers extending this protection model across a network.
authorization.quote: neither host need trust the other host with anything more than the capabilities that it has been rightfully granted

rejected.why: The paper describes an operating-system and distributed-computing design, not architectural principles of the Internet.
It is a period technical proposal, not a retrospective or history of the Internet.
The hosts are peers, but the paper is about remote capability invocation, not peer-to-peer overlays.

gaps.name: Capability-based distributed operating systems / remote capability invocation
gaps.why: The core subject is distributed computing with capability lists. The taxonomy has no tag for distributed operating systems or remote object invocation.

RFC713.title: MSDTP-Message Services Data Transmission Protocol
RFC713.summary: RFC 713 defines MSDTP, a byte-stream encoding for transferring typed data items (integers, strings, structures, semantic items) between message servers, and sketches a general data transfer scheme.

messaging.why: The protocol is designed for message servers exchanging message-related data. No narrower email or message-format tag fits, since it is a generic data transfer layer used by message services.
messaging.quote: A mechanism is defined for use by message servers in transferring data between hosts.

rejected.why: It is a comparable abstract-to-byte-stream encoding, but the document does not use or specify ASN.1.
The binary encoding is a data format, but it is a bespoke historic one. Messaging is the better primary fit, so I did not add a general data-formats tag.
The document is aimed at message servers. It does not specify email transport, access, or formats, and it only references mail systems.
The protocol was written in the ARPANET era. Its content is a generic byte-stream encoding, not an ARPANET host or network protocol.

gaps.name: Data serialization / binary encoding of typed items (MSDTP)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about a binary encoding of abstract data types. The taxonomy has no general serialization tag apart from specific formats such as ASN.1, CBOR and JSON.

RFC714.title: Host-Host Protocol for an ARPANET-Type Network
RFC714.summary: RFC 714 proposes a revised Host/Host protocol for an ARPANET-type network using unmodified IMPs, adapting the ARPANET NCP protocol with IFIP-style full-duplex connections, windowed credit flow control, and a compact control command set.

NCP.why: The document specifies a Host/Host protocol derived from and replacing the ARPANET NCP protocol, with control commands like RFC, CLS, ACK, and RST.
NCP.quote: Processes within a Host are envisioned as communicating with the rest of the network through a network control program (NCP) resident in that Host, which implements the Host/Host protocol.

ARPANET.why: Designed for an ARPANET-type network built on IMPs, drawing on ARPANET Host/Host protocol experience and BBN Report 1822.
ARPANET.quote: would use ARPANET IMPs without modification, but would allow re-specification of Host/Host (and higher level) Protocol.

rejected.why: The protocol has transport-like features (windowing, sequence numbers, retransmission), but it is a host-host protocol for ARPANET-type networks, not TCP or an extension of it.
Credit-based flow control is described, but it is receiver window flow control within the protocol, not congestion control as a subject.

RFC716.title: Interim Revision to Appendix F of BBN 1822
RFC716.summary: An interim update to Appendix F of BBN Report 1822 clarifying how a Very Distant Host (VDH) connects to an IMP, covering out-of-order packet handling between RTPs, channel sequencing, and recommended retransmission delays.

ARPANET.why: The document revises the BBN 1822 Host-IMP interface specification for ARPANET Very Distant Host connections, an ARPANET host/network protocol working note. No narrower tag fits.
ARPANET.quote: some confusion as to how to operate a Host connected to an IMP as a Very Distant Host (or VDH)

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host protocol. This document covers the Host-IMP VDH interface, which is a lower layer.
It is a period technical specification update, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: BBN 1822 Host-IMP interface / Very Distant Host (VDH)
gaps.why: The document is about the IMP-Host interface and the VDH reliable transmission protocol. The taxonomy has no tag for them below ARPANET.

RFC717.title: Assigned Network Numbers
RFC717.summary: 1976 note by Jon Postel listing numbers assigned to networks for internetwork protocol experiments, and reproducing the then-current internetwork and TCP header formats.

addressing.why: The document is a registry of network numbers (BBNRCCnet, SanFranPRnet, ARPANET, BostonPRnet) that form the network part of internet addresses.
addressing.quote: This note specifies the numbers assigned to identify networks for use in the inter-network protocol experiments.

TCP.why: A substantial part of the document reproduces the TCP and short TCP header layouts, with field widths and format codes.
TCP.quote: For convenience the current Internetwork protocol header and TCP headers are reproduced here:

rejected.why: This is an early number-assignment list, but the IANA tag covers registries guidance and stewardship. The document gives no registry procedures.
ARPANET appears only as one entry in the list of assigned network numbers. The document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
The header is a pre-IPv4 internetwork header. The document does not specify IPv4 or its address lifecycle.

RFC718.title: Comments on RCTE from the Tenex Implementation Experience
RFC718.summary: A 1976 memo relaying TENEX implementation experience with the TELNET RCTE (Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing) option, describing problems with spontaneous output, interrupt characters, and cleared input buffers, and the solutions adopted.

Telnet.why: The whole memo analyses the TELNET RCTE option, its implementation problems, and a use of WILL RCTE to clear the input buffer. Readers of Telnet options would want it.
Telnet.quote: The code to implement the RCTE option of the new TELNET protocol for TENEX has been completed.

rejected.why: The memo is set in the ARPANET era, but it concerns a Telnet option and not the ARPANET network or its host protocols as such.

RFC719.title: Discussion on RCTE
RFC719.summary: A 1976 discussion thread following RFC 718 on the Telnet RCTE (Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing) option, debating a "clear input, reset counters" function via Synch/Data Mark and Abort Output, and interactions with GO-AHEAD, ECHO and BINARY options.

Telnet.why: The whole document discusses the RCTE Telnet option, its negotiation (WILL/DO), Synch/Data Mark, AO, and interactions with other Telnet options such as GO-AHEAD, ECHO and BINARY.
Telnet.quote: the RCTE option would have to explicitly require that this function reset the counters and cause a "clear your input buffer (of data)"

rejected.why: The Telnet work happened on the ARPANET (TENEX hosts), but the document concerns the Telnet option, not ARPANET operations or protocols generally.
Telnet's Synch mechanism is mentioned only implicitly and no TCP behaviour is discussed.

RFC720.title: Address Specification Syntax for Network Mail
RFC720.summary: RFC 720 proposes an extended syntax for address fields in ARPANET network mail, separating personal names from addresses, allowing group lists to be referenced by pathname, and supporting secondary mailboxes, with a modified BNF replacing parts of RFC 680.

message format.why: The document defines the syntax of address fields in mail messages (names, mailboxes, groups), which is Internet message format addressing.
message format.quote: the following general syntax is proposed to augment the existing syntax specified in RFC 680, for address fields specified by the user

ARPANET.why: It is an early ARPANET-era mail working note, so readers of ARPANET history and operations would want it.
ARPANET.quote: Experience with processing mail on the Arpanet has pointed up many addressing issues

rejected.why: The more specific child tag message format fits, because the document covers address syntax and not mail transport or access.
It uses a modified BNF only to express the address grammar. It does not define or discuss the notation.
It addresses group names and long lists inside address fields, but only as address syntax. It does not specify list protocols, headers or management.

RFC721.title: Out-of-Band Control Signals in a Host-to-Host Protocol
RFC721.summary: RFC 721 discusses requirements and design for a reliable out-of-band interrupt signal in a host-to-host protocol, focusing on TCP's lack of one, with a separate interrupt channel and sequence-number coupling.

TCP.why: The document analyses the early TCP's single-channel design and proposes how to add a reliable separate interrupt channel with its own sequence number handling, including acceptability tests and resynchronization.
TCP.quote: such a satisfactory mechanism does not exist in the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) of Cerf et. al.

rejected.why: The ARPANET host-to-host protocol is cited only as a comparison for its separate interrupt channel; the document is not about ARPANET operations.
The ARPANET host-to-host protocol (NCP) is mentioned only as an example of a separate control channel, not specified or analysed in its own right.
Flow control is discussed only as something interrupts must be independent of; the document is not about congestion control.

RFC722.title: Thoughts on Interactions in Distributed Services
RFC722.summary: 1976 paper by Haverty presenting a request-reply model for interactions between programs in distributed network services, and motivating the RRP interaction protocol (data precision, synchronization, extensibility).

ARPANET.why: The document draws on ARPANET protocol experience (mail, file transfer, Datacomputer, RJE) to design an interaction mechanism for ARPANET services; it is an early network working note on host-level service protocols.
ARPANET.quote: The ideas presented are derived mainly from experience with various service protocols [Reference 1] on the ARPANET.

rejected.why: FTP-based mail is only cited as an example of lost data semantics, not the subject.
The model derives from a mail-handling proposal but the paper is about generic service interactions.
Mentioned only as an example of protocol evolution problems.
Concerns application-level service interaction design rather than Internet architecture principles.
Remote job entry is only listed as an experience source.
Considered as a general application-protocol topic, but ARPANET fits the document's context better and applications is a very broad parent.

gaps.name: Request-reply process interaction protocol (RRP) / distributed service design
gaps.why: The document is about a general request-reply interaction discipline and the RRP for programs, which the taxonomy has no tag for (closest is ONC RPC, which is a different system).

RFC724.title: Proposed official standard for the format of ARPA Network messages
RFC724.summary: A 1977 CAHCOM proposal for an official standard format of ARPANET mail message headers (From, Sender, Reply-To, To, cc, Date, etc.), with formal syntax, address groups and semantics, superseding RFC 561 and RFC 680.

message format.why: The document defines the syntax and semantics of message headers, address fields, dates and folding, which is the internet message format subject.
message format.quote: Proposed Official Standard for the Format of ARPA Network Messages

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET-era standard for host-to-host mail, with historical discussion of the ARPANET mail service and its FTP-based delivery.
ARPANET.quote: wishes to promulgate an official standard for the format of ARPA Network mail headers

rejected.why: FTP MAIL/MLFL commands are only the interim delivery substrate; the document specifies message format, not FTP.
TELNET ASCII is used only as the character definition and the extension analogy.
The BNF is merely the notation used to specify the syntax.
The more specific child message format covers the subject; the document explicitly is not a transmission protocol.
ASCII is used as the character set for the format, not the subject.

RFC725.title: RJE protocol for a resource sharing network
RFC725.summary: RFC 725 proposes a revised NETRJE remote job entry protocol for the ARPANET offering three implementation levels (Telnet only, Telnet plus data transfer, Telnet plus FTP), with commands, FTP-style reply codes and protocol measurement.

RJE.why: The whole document defines an RJE protocol (NETRJE) with SCHED, OUTPUT, STATUS commands and reply codes for submitting jobs and retrieving output.
RJE.quote: The RJE protocol proposed here tries to mitigate the implementation problems and security problems.

rejected.why: FTP is used as one of the data transfer models and its reply codes are borrowed, but the document specifies RJE, not FTP.
Telnet is the control connection substrate for the RJE commands; the document defines nothing new about Telnet.
The protocol is described in ARPANET terms, but it is an RJE protocol and not about the ARPANET itself.

RFC726.title: Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing Telnet option
RFC726.summary: RFC 726 defines the Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing (RCTE) Telnet option, which lets a serving host control echoing and transmission buffering at the user's terminal to cut echo delay and network traffic.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, with its negotiation commands, subcommands, defaults, and interaction with the Echo and Suppress Go-Ahead options.
Telnet.quote: IAC SB RCTE <cmd> [BC1 BC2] [TC1 TC2] IAC SE

rejected.why: The document is set in the ARPANET era and mentions TENEX hosts, but it specifies a Telnet option rather than an ARPANET-specific protocol or operations.
Satellite echo delay is the motivation for the option, but the document is not about networking over satellite links.

RFC727.title: Telnet logout option
RFC727.summary: Defines the TELNET LOGOUT option (code 18), which lets one side ask the server to forcibly log off the user process instead of detaching it, and lets a server warn of impending auto-logout.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its command codes, negotiation semantics, defaults and sample use, so it belongs under the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: The sender of this command REQUESTS that the receiver forcibly log off the user process at the receiver's end

rejected.why: It is an ARPANET-era document, but it is about a Telnet option and not ARPANET host or network protocols in general.

RFC728.title: Minor pitfall in the Telnet Protocol
RFC728.summary: RFC 728 warns designers of Telnet options that a Telnet sync sequence can flush data after a subnegotiation, so the subnegotiation's effect lands on the wrong data. It proposes two workarounds.

Telnet.why: The whole document analyses a protocol pitfall in Telnet: the interaction of the sync sequence with option subnegotiation. It gives guidance to designers of Telnet options.
Telnet.quote: The Telnet sync sequence causes all data to be deleted from the data stream until a data mark is encountered.

RFC729.title: Telnet byte macro option
RFC729.summary: RFC 729 defines a Telnet option (Byte Macro, option code 19) that lets a sender define single-byte macros standing for longer strings, as a simple data compression technique to reduce subcommand overhead.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its negotiation commands (WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T BM) and subcommands, so it belongs under the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: The BM option is intended as a simple data compression technique, to remove this overhead from the communication channel.

rejected.why: The option is described as a simple data compression technique, but it is a Telnet-specific macro mechanism. It is not a lossless compression format, so the Telnet tag fits better.
The text mentions Telnet ASCII characters only as the content of expansion strings. The document is not about ASCII.

RFC730.title: Extensible field addressing
RFC730.summary: Postel proposes writing ARPANET host addresses as named, delimiter-separated fields (NET/IMP/HOST/MESSAGE-ID) that can grow on the left, on the right and in field size, prompted by the new Host-IMP interface and by multinetwork and multiprocessor hosts.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note on ARPANET host and IMP addressing, driven by the Host-IMP interface change and its effect on protocols such as TIP open, Telnet, FTP and MAIL.
ARPANET.quote: The revised Host-IMP interface provides for a larger address space for hosts and IMPs

addressing.why: It defines an extensible, hierarchical address syntax (Network/IMP/Host/Message-Identifier) and the ways it can grow, which makes it a study of address architecture. It anticipates internetwork addressing.
addressing.quote: we adopt a field based extensible address scheme where each field is separated from its neighbors by a delimiter character and each field has a name

rejected.why: The document deals with numeric host addresses and notation, not host naming conventions. It mentions the NIC host list only in passing.
It touches on multinetwork growth, but the subject is the address format, not architectural principles.
The NCP protocol is not specified or discussed. The document only refers to higher-level protocols affected by address changes.

RFC731.title: Telnet Data Entry Terminal option
RFC731.summary: RFC 731 defines the Telnet Data Entry Terminal (DET) option, which specifies a Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal using subnegotiation subcommands for cursor control, formatting, erasure, and transmission, plus facility negotiation.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option (DET, code 20) with its subnegotiation subcommands, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: The sender of this command REQUESTS or AGREES to send and receive subcommands to control the Data Entry Terminal.

rejected.why: ASCII is only the character set that the keyboard generates and the data stream carries. The document is not about ASCII.
The document is of ARPANET-era origin and cites NIC documents, but it specifies a Telnet option rather than ARPANET host or network protocols.
The IBM 3270 appears only as a reference for terminal capabilities. The option defines a generic virtual data entry terminal, not 3270 emulation.

RFC732.title: Telnet Data Entry Terminal option
RFC732.summary: Defines the Telnet Data Entry Terminal (DET) option, a Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal controlled through Telnet subnegotiation subcommands for cursor movement, formatting, protection, erasure and transmission.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option (code 20) with its negotiation, subcommands, defaults and minimal implementation.
Telnet.quote: The sender of this command REQUESTS or AGREES to send and receive subcommands to control the Data Entry Terminal.

rejected.why: ASCII is only the character set the virtual keyboard generates; the document is not about ASCII.
It is a different terminal/display protocol, so it does not fit. The document only defines a character-cell screen model.

gaps.name: Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal (NVDET)
gaps.why: The document is about a virtual terminal model for forms-based data entry. The taxonomy has no tag for virtual terminals or terminal protocols beyond Telnet itself.

RFC733.title: Standard for the format of ARPA network text messages
RFC733.summary: RFC 733 specifies the syntax and semantics of ARPANET text message (email) headers, including address, originator, date and reference fields, obsoleting RFCs 561 and 680.

message format.why: The document defines the Internet message format: header fields, addressing, dates, folding and the message body structure. This is the ancestor of RFC 822 and the later message-format specifications.
message format.quote: This standard specifies a syntax for text messages which are passed between computer users within the framework of "electronic mail".

ARPANET.why: The standard is written specifically for ARPANET mail. It refers to NIC-maintained host names, ARPANET FTP mail servers and TELNET NVT conventions.
ARPANET.quote: It is intended strictly as a definition of what is to be passed between hosts on the ARPANET.

rejected.why: FTP mail servers are the delivery mechanism the standard assumes. The document does not specify FTP.
TELNET ASCII is only the character set convention the syntax relies on.
It uses an augmented BNF, but only as the notation for its own syntax. ABNF itself is not the subject.
The parent tag is implied by message format, which is the more specific tag that fits.
The document defines a date and time syntax for headers. That is a small part of the header format, not a standalone subject, and the tag is for RFC 3339-style timestamps.

RFC734.title: SUPDUP Protocol
RFC734.summary: RFC 734 specifies the SUPDUP protocol, a device-independent display Telnet-like protocol (originating at MIT ITS) defining a virtual display terminal, its initialization, input encoding, and %TD output codes.

SUPDUP.why: The entire document specifies the SUPDUP protocol: initialization, TTYOPT bits, input protocol, and %TD display codes.
SUPDUP.quote: This document describes  the SUPDUP protocol,  a highly efficient  display telnet protocol.

rejected.why: SUPDUP is explicitly independent of TELNET and not an option to it; Telnet is only a comparison point.
The protocol ran over the ARPANET (ICP, socket 137) but the document is about the SUPDUP protocol; the child tag SUPDUP already sits under it.
The Stanford/ITS extended ASCII set is described, but as part of the SUPDUP terminal definition rather than as a character set registration.

RFC735.title: Revised Telnet byte macro option
RFC735.summary: Defines the Telnet Byte Macro (BM) option, which lets a sender define single-byte macros that expand to replacement strings as a simple data compression technique for the Telnet data stream.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet option (BM, code 19) with its negotiation commands and subnegotiations, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: The BM option is intended as a simple data compression technique, to remove this overhead from the communication channel.

rejected.why: The option is described as simple data compression, but it is a Telnet-specific macro mechanism and not a lossless compression format. Telnet is the better fit.
NVT ASCII characters appear only as the content of replacement strings. The document is not about ASCII.

RFC736.title: Telnet SUPDUP option
RFC736.summary: RFC 736 defines a Telnet option (code 21) that lets a host offer the SUPDUP display protocol on the normal Telnet socket, with negotiation then continuing as in RFC 734.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its command codes, defaults and negotiation behaviour, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This option allows a host to provide SUPDUP service on the normal TELNET socket (27 octal) instead of 137 (octal)

SUPDUP.why: The option exists to start the SUPDUP display protocol over Telnet. Once the option is accepted, SUPDUP negotiation proceeds as in RFC 734.
SUPDUP.quote: The sender of this command  REQUESTS permission to, or  confirms that it will, use the SUPDUP display protocol

rejected.why: The document sits in the ARPANET-era context, but its subject is the Telnet option and SUPDUP, which are already tagged. The ARPANET topic tag is the parent of SUPDUP, so it is implied.
The document does not address TCP. It refers only to the older ICP socket numbers.

RFC737.title: FTP extension: XSEN
RFC737.summary: RFC 737 defines three FTP commands (XSEN, XSEM, XMAS) for sending a message directly to a logged-in user's terminal and/or mailing it, with their special reply codes.

FTP.why: The document specifies new FTP commands (XSEN, XSEM, XMAS) and their replies, extending the FTP protocol.
FTP.quote: This note describes an extension to the File Transfer Protocol which provides for "sending" a message to a logged-in user

rejected.why: Mailing is a fallback in XSEM/XMAS, but the document is about FTP command extensions for terminal sending, not email architecture.
Written in the ARPANET era and mentions network sites, but the subject is an FTP extension, not ARPANET operations.

RFC738.title: Time server
RFC738.summary: RFC 738 specifies the Time Server protocol, in which a host listens on socket 37 and sends a 32-bit count of seconds since 1900 GMT to a connecting client, then closes the connection.

time synchronization.why: The whole document defines a network service for obtaining a machine-readable time so hosts can check or correct their clocks. That is clock synchronization over a network.
time synchronization.quote: The use of time-servers makes it possible to quickly confirm or correct a system's idea of the time, by making a brief poll of several independent sites

rejected.why: NTP is a different, later protocol. This document defines a simple time-of-day service and does not specify or analyse NTP.
The protocol uses ARPANET-era sockets and mentions ICP, but it only relies on that host-host layer and does not specify it.
The service runs on ARPANET-era hosts, but the document is about the time protocol itself and not ARPANET operations. A reader of the ARPANET page would only find it marginally relevant.
It resembles the Echo/Daytime-style small services, but those are separate protocols and the taxonomy entry does not list a Time service.

RFC739.title: Assigned numbers
RFC739.summary: A 1977 snapshot of the assigned-numbers registry for early ARPANET and internet protocols. It lists link numbers, socket numbers, network numbers, and internet message versions, formats and types.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned protocol numbers maintained by Jon Postel, the direct ancestor of the IANA registries.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

ARPANET.why: Link and socket assignments are for ARPANET host-to-host protocol (AHHP) services such as Telnet, FTP, RJE and SUPDUP, and the network number list is ARPANET-era. Readers of ARPANET history would want it.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: The document is a registry, not a retrospective. The ARPANET tag already captures its era.
The network number list is only a small registry table, not a treatment of address architecture.
FTP, Telnet and other services appear only as entries in the socket table, not as subjects the document specifies.
TCP-2 and TCP-3 appear only as version and format values in tables, with no specification of the protocol.

RFC740.title: NETRJS Protocol
RFC740.summary: RFC 740 specifies NETRJS, UCLA-CCN's ARPANET remote job entry protocol, covering virtual card reader/printer/punch channels, a Telnet operator console, a data transfer protocol and operator commands; it obsoletes RFC 189 and RFC 599.

RJE.why: The document defines the NETRJS remote job entry protocol.
RJE.quote: NETRJS, a private protocol for remote job entry service, was defined and implemented by the UCLA Campus Computing Network (CCN) for batch job submission

rejected.why: Telnet is used for the operator console as a substrate; Appendix B only lists conventions for that use.
NCP is the underlying host-host protocol the document relies on, not its subject.
The document is ARPANET-era, but the protocol is a private CCN service and the parent topic is implied by the child tag RJE.
Character translation is an appendix detail, not the main subject.

gaps.name: RJE (Remote Job Entry) / NETRJS
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists 'RJE' as a child of ARPANET, but I used the id 'RJE' as written. Its description says 'Remote job entry on the early network', so it fits.

RFC741.title: Specifications for the Network Voice Protocol (NVP)
RFC741.summary: RFC 741 specifies the ARPANET Network Voice Protocol (NVP): a control protocol for call setup and parameter negotiation, a data message header, and LPC vocoder data formats with coding tables, plus implementation recommendations.

ARPANET.why: NVP is an ARPANET-era host-level protocol using ARPANET links, IMP leaders and BBN 1822 message types; it is a historic working-note protocol of that network.
ARPANET.quote: The Network Voice Protocol (NVP), implemented first in December 1973, and has been in use since then for local and transnet real-time voice communication over the ARPANET

real-time communications.why: The document defines call control, negotiation and voice data transport for real-time interactive voice, which is the general subject of real-time voice communication; no more specific tag fits (not SIP, RTP, or SDP).
real-time communications.quote: there is a growing need for communication of real-time interactive voice over computer networks, new communication discipline must be developed.

codecs.why: A substantial part defines LPC and CVSD vocoding parameters, the LPC parcel data format and the quantization tables in Appendix 1.
codecs.quote: Version 1 (V1) is defined as: 1-1 LPC 2-150 150 microseconds sampling

rejected.why: The document is about voice over a packet network, with no interworking with the telephone network.
NVP predates RTP and is a separate protocol; sequence/timestamp header similarities do not make it about RTP.
The document says the ARPANET host-to-host protocol was unsuitable and NVP bypasses it, so it is not about NCP.
NVP's call setup resembles signalling but is unrelated to SIP.

gaps.name: Network Voice Protocol / packet voice (LPC vocoding)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for historic packet voice protocols or speech vocoding like LPC and CVSD; the closest tags are broad.

RFC742.title: NAME/FINGER Protocol
RFC742.summary: RFC 742 describes the Name/Finger protocol, a simple query protocol on socket 79 that returns a human-readable report of the users on a host or the status of a named user, with examples from ITS, SAIL and TOPS-20 sites.

Finger.why: The whole document specifies the Finger user information protocol: the command line, the default listing and the name listing with plans.
Finger.quote: This note describes the Name/Finger protocol. This is a simple protocol which provides an interface to the Name and Finger programs at several network sites.

rejected.why: Telnet is only mentioned as a possible client. The note says to filter IAC option negotiation, but it does not specify or extend Telnet.
FTP is mentioned only as the way to fetch the documentation files.
The protocol runs on ARPANET hosts, but the document is about the Finger application and not ARPANET operations or protocols.

RFC743.title: FTP extension: XRSQ/XRCP
RFC743.summary: RFC 743 extends FTP with XRSQ and XRCP commands so a user can mail one message text to multiple recipients at an ITS FTP server, using either a recipients-first or text-first scheme.

FTP.why: The document defines new FTP commands (XRSQ, XRCP) and their reply codes and interaction with MAIL/MLFL, so it is an FTP extension.
FTP.quote: This RFC describes an extension to FTP which allows the user of an ITS FTP server

email.why: The purpose is efficient multi-recipient mail delivery via FTP's MAIL/MLFL commands and handoff to a mailer, so email readers would want it.
email.quote: to mail the text of a message to several recipients simultaneously; such message transmission is far more efficient

rejected.why: The mail transfer happens via FTP MAIL/MLFL commands, not SMTP, which is not mentioned.
Written in the ARPANET era but the document is about an FTP extension, not ARPANET protocols or operations as such.

RFC744.title: MARS - a Message Archiving and Retrieval Service
RFC744.summary: RFC 744 describes MARS, a Datacomputer-based service at CCA that archives ARPANET mail messages sent to a Filer mailbox and retrieves them by indexed header and text fields through mailed retrieval requests.

email.why: The document specifies a mail-driven archive and retrieval service for ARPANET email messages, indexing header fields and bodies. Readers interested in email applications and services would look for it.
email.quote: A message is designated for archiving by sending it to MARS-Filer @ CCA using one of the usual message-mailing tools such as SNDMSG.

ARPANET.why: It is an ARPANET-era working service note, with Tenex, DFTP and ARPANET host addressing, so the ARPANET subject page fits.
ARPANET.quote: The Service is available, primarily, to groups for storage of teleconferencing transcripts. Is is also available, upon request, to individual ARPANET correspondents.

rejected.why: It relies on RFC 733 message formats and parses headers for indexing, but it does not define or extend the message format.
The Datacomputer is a database utility, not a directory service; the document is about archiving and retrieval, not directory access.
DFTP is mentioned only as the way to fetch the RR program, which is incidental.
It archives group teleconferencing transcripts from lists such as MsgGroup, but it does not specify list protocols, headers or management.

gaps.name: Message archiving and retrieval / database-backed indexing
gaps.why: The core subject is archiving and full-text, field-indexed retrieval of messages on the Datacomputer. The taxonomy has no tag for information retrieval or archival services.

RFC745.title: JANUS interface specifications
RFC745.summary: RFC 745 specifies the JANUS interface, a symmetrical 1822-like hardware interface for connecting devices (originally for Packet Radio), clarifying low-level protocol and electrical requirements relative to BBN Report 1822 for the ARPANET.

ARPANET.why: The document respecifies the ARPANET host-IMP 1822 interface in symmetrical form, covering its handshake, timing and electrical details, and interoperability with 1822 interfaces.
ARPANET.quote: The ARPANET employs a network of switching nodes, called IMPs, to provide interconnection among user equipment, called hosts.

rejected.why: The document is a hardware/electrical host interface specification, and no link-layer tag fits it better than the ARPANET topic.
It is a historical document, but it is a technical specification rather than a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Hardware/electrical interface specifications (1822, JANUS, RS-422)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for physical-layer or electrical host interface specifications. The ARPANET topic is the closest fit.

RFC746.title: SUPDUP graphics extension
RFC746.summary: RFC 746 proposes a graphics extension to the SUPDUP terminal protocol, defining a graphics mode, coordinate system, draw/erase commands, sets, blinking, XOR/rectangles, graphics input, and SMARTS capability bits.

SUPDUP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the SUPDUP display protocol, so it belongs on the SUPDUP page.
SUPDUP.quote: extends SUPDUP to permit the display of drawings on the screen of the terminal, as well as text.

network graphics.why: It defines an early network graphics command language (lines, points, rectangles, sets, graphic input) for terminals, which is what the network graphics page covers.
network graphics.quote: Those interested in network graphics should read about the Multics Graphics System, whose fundamental purpose is the same

rejected.why: The document says the extension 'has nothing really to do with the network'. The ARPANET parent is also implied by the SUPDUP tag.
SUPDUP is a separate protocol. Telnet is not specified or extended here.
Graphics commands use ASCII characters 0-177 only as the encoding. The document is not about ASCII.

RFC747.title: Recent extensions to the SUPDUP Protocol
RFC747.summary: RFC 747 updates RFC 734 by describing new SUPDUP initial-negotiation variables (SMARTS, ISPEED, OSPEED) and a new TTYOPT bit (%TPPRN) for swapping parentheses and square brackets.

SUPDUP.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the SUPDUP display protocol: new negotiation variables and a TTYOPT bit.
SUPDUP.quote: Recently, some extensions have been made to the SUPDUP protocol.

rejected.why: SUPDUP is an ARPANET-era protocol, but the parent topic is implied by the SUPDUP tag. The document itself is not about the ARPANET more broadly.
RFC 746 covers the graphics extension in detail. This RFC only mentions the SMARTS variable and excludes the graphics detail.
The document does not discuss Telnet or its options.

RFC748.title: Telnet randomly-lose option
RFC748.summary: An April 1st parody RFC defining a Telnet option, RANDOMLY-LOSE, that lets a server request or be granted permission to randomly crash, lose data or misbehave.

humor.why: The document is dated 1 April and is a whimsical parody proposing an option to permit random system lossage, with 100% reliable uptime as the joke.
humor.quote: Several hosts appear to provide random lossage, such as system crashes, lost data, incorrectly functioning programs, etc., as part of their services.

Telnet.why: It defines a new Telnet option (code 256) with WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T negotiation semantics, so Telnet option readers would look for it.
Telnet.quote: Since this is implemented as a TELNET option, it is expected that servers which do not implement this option will not randomly lose

RFC749.title: Telnet SUPDUP-Output option
RFC749.summary: Defines a Telnet option (SUPDUP-OUTPUT, code 22) that lets a server-side program send SUPDUP display-control codes to the user's terminal inside Telnet subnegotiation blocks, while normal Telnet stays in effect.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option with its negotiation commands, subnegotiation formats and defaults.
Telnet.quote: The SUPDUP-OUTPUT protocol provides a means to access the virtual display support provided by the SUPDUP protocol (see RFC 734) within the context of a standard TELNET connection.

SUPDUP.why: The option carries SUPDUP display output (TDCODEs) and terminal parameters inside Telnet. It reuses the SUPDUP display repertoire, so SUPDUP readers would want it.
SUPDUP.quote: The %TDCODEs and printing characters of SUPDUP output of RFC 734.

rejected.why: The RFC mentions graphics capability parameters only in passing. It does not define a graphics protocol.
The RFC only operates in the ARPANET era context. It does not address NCP.

RFC750.title: Assigned numbers
RFC750.summary: RFC 750 is a 1978 Assigned Numbers list documenting ARPANET link, socket, network, and internet message version, format, and type number assignments maintained by Jon Postel.

ARPANET.why: The document lists ARPANET link numbers, socket numbers for AHHP, and network numbers, which are host and network protocol working notes for the ARPANET.
ARPANET.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

IANA.why: It is an early number-assignment registry and describes the assignment process, the precursor to IANA registries.
IANA.quote: If you are developing a protocol or application that will require the use of a link, socket, etc. please contact Jon to receive a number assignment.

rejected.why: TCP versions are only listed as values in message format and type tables; the document does not specify TCP.
Internet protocol versions appear as version number assignments but the document is not about the IP protocol itself.
The AHHP host-host protocol is referenced as context for links and sockets, but NCP is not specified here.
Telnet, FTP, Finger, and others appear only as entries in the socket list.

RFC751.title: Survey of FTP mail and MLFL
RFC751.summary: A 1978 survey of ARPANET server hosts' FTP server responses to MAIL for an unknown recipient and to the MLFL mail-file command, listing which hosts support or reject each.

FTP.why: The survey examines FTP server behaviour for the MAIL and MLFL commands and the reply codes returned, so it is about FTP and its mail commands.
FTP.quote: The intent was to determine the response of the host's Server FTP program to: (a) An attempt to mail to an unknown recipient at that host.

ARPANET.why: The document surveys named ARPANET hosts using the old-FTP socket 3 and ICP, which is early ARPANET operational material.
ARPANET.quote: Two surveys of Arpanet Server hosts were run between September 20, 1978 and December 11, 1978.

rejected.why: Mail is the subject of the test, but the document is about FTP server command responses, not email architecture or formats.
ICP and socket-based connections rely on NCP, but the document does not specify or discuss NCP.
SMTP does not appear; mail is sent via FTP commands.

RFC752.title: Universal host table
RFC752.summary: RFC 752 describes the MIT/Stanford (ITS/SAIL) universal host table text format, a compiled 36-bit binary file format for it, and includes the host table itself, proposed as a replacement for the NIC host table.

hostnames.why: The document specifies a host table format (host names, nicknames, addresses, OS, machine type) and a binary form for lookups, which is exactly host naming conventions and host tables.
hostnames.quote: The network host table in use at MIT and Stanford is described. This host table is superior to the NIC and Tenex host tables in several ways.

rejected.why: The ARPANET host/IMP addressing appears as table content, but the document is about the host table format, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
The more specific hostnames tag covers it; parent is implied.
It is a period document but not a retrospective or history of the Internet.
Network and host address notation is part of the table format, but the document is not about IP address architecture or allocation.

RFC753.title: Internet Message Protocol
RFC753.summary: RFC 753 specifies the Internet Message Protocol, an early internetwork message system in which Message Processing Modules exchange structured binary-encoded messages (command, document header and body) over a reliable transport such as TCP.

email.why: The document defines a complete store-and-forward internetwork mail system, with message formats, delivery and acknowledgment commands, relaying and routing. It is an early email architecture and transport protocol.
email.quote: This document describes an internetwork message system. The system is designed to transmit messages between message processing modules

rejected.why: It defines its own binary list/proplist encoding and only recommends RFC 733 header fields. It is not the text Internet message format, so the delivery protocol is the main subject.
TCP is only the assumed reliable transport, used as a model. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
SMTP did not exist yet. The document specifies a different delivery protocol, so the email tag covers it.
It is the parent of email, which fits more specifically.
Appendix B borrows the ARPANET FTP compression scheme for shipping message bags. This is a minor mechanism, not the subject.

RFC754.title: Out-of-net host addresses for mail
RFC754.summary: RFC 754 compares four schemes (single mailbox, global names inside, global names outside, structured names) for addressing ARPANET mail to users on other networks such as NSW via a forwarding host, and recommends structured names.

email.why: The document is about mail addressing and forwarding between the ARPANET message environment and other networks. That is email architecture and transport.
email.quote: This memo discusses some possible alternatives for computer mail addressing for hosts outside the ARPANET in the short term.

ARPANET.why: It describes ARPANET mail mechanisms and a transition scheme specific to ARPANET hosts. These include Tenex mailbox naming, host tables and FTP-server mail delivery.
ARPANET.quote: a mechanism to support the interaction of the several already existing NSW-like message environments with the ARPANET message environment

rejected.why: The FTP server and its MAIL/MLFL commands are only the delivery substrate. The document does not specify or extend FTP.
The inside header lines such as To, CC and NSW-User are discussed. The document is about address routing, and it recommends relying on outside information instead.
SMTP did not exist yet, and the memo describes FTP-based mail delivery.

RFC755.title: Assigned numbers
RFC755.summary: RFC 755 is a 1979 snapshot of assigned numbers for ARPANET and early internet protocols (link, socket, network, internet version, protocol and message type numbers), maintained by Jon Postel.

IANA.why: The document is an assigned-numbers registry, the historic precursor of IANA registries, listing and administering number assignments.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

ARPANET.why: Link and socket assignments concern the ARPANET host-host protocol (AHHP) and its services and network numbers, so ARPANET readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: TCP versions appear only as entries in the protocol number list, not specified or analysed.
The AHHP/NCP is referenced as context for link and socket numbers but is not specified here.
Internet protocol versions are listed only as number values in a registry.
Telnet appears only as a socket assignment row.
FTP appears only as a socket assignment row.
It is a historic document, but it is a registry rather than a retrospective.

RFC756.title: NIC name server - a datagram-based information utility
RFC756.summary: 1979 SRI paper describing the provisional NIC Name Server, a datagram-based host name/address lookup service for the ARPANET and Internet, plus proposed extensions (query syntax, service queries, options, MORE DATA, dynamic updates) and distributed architecture ideas.

naming.why: The document is about a name server for host name to address resolution, with query syntax and distribution architecture. It predates DNS, so the DNS tag is not appropriate; the general naming topic fits.
naming.quote: a new method for distributing and updating host name/address information in large computer networks is described

ARPANET.why: The service is built on the ARPANET NIC host database and deployed on ARPANET DEC-10 hosts, so ARPANET readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: the Arpanet Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI International has maintained, administered, and distributed the host addressing data base to Arpanet hosts since 1972

service discovery.why: A substantial section proposes service queries to find hosts offering a service such as LoaderServer, which is service discovery.
service discovery.quote: Service descriptors consist of an official name, a list of alias names, and a network-dependent address.

rejected.why: The paper predates DNS and describes a different, centralized name server (IEN 89); it is not about DNS protocol or records.
It touches on host tables, but the focus is a query/response name service, not host naming conventions or host table format.
Datagrams (UDP/IP) are only the substrate for the query/response service.
Mentions user identification servers only as future work; the document is about host name binding.

RFC757.title: Suggested solution to the naming, addressing, and delivery problem for ARPANET message systems
RFC757.summary: A 1979 request-for-comments proposal to separate recipient identity (unique ID) from address in ARPAnet mail, using a distributed network "netmail" database for directory lookup, bulk/bundled delivery, and internetwork compatibility with RFC 753.

email.why: The document redesigns ARPAnet mail naming, addressing and delivery (bulk/bundled mail, forwarding, mail rooms). Readers of email architecture would want it.
email.quote: A network database supports a directory service which supplies correct address information for all recipients.

naming.why: A central theme is separating names (unique IDs) from addresses and resolving IDs via a distributed database, including birthplace-based ID resolution. This is general naming, not DNS.
naming.quote: The solution proposed here calls for a total break between the way a recipient is named or identified and the way in which his location is specified.

ARPANET.why: The proposal is specific to ARPAnet mail practice, the TIP login database, and the ARPANET/PRnet/SATNET catenet.
ARPANET.quote: The current ARPAnet message handling scheme has evolved from rather informal, decentralized beginnings.

rejected.why: It discusses RFC 733 address syntax only as a critique. The focus is naming and delivery, not header format.
It criticises the FTP-based mail delivery but does not specify or extend an SMTP-style protocol. SMTP did not exist yet.
FTP is mentioned only as the substrate of the current mail delivery system.
The network database acts as a directory service, but the document proposes it only conceptually and does not specify LDAP or X.500 style access. The taxonomy's directory tag is not a good fit.
The document is a contemporary proposal, not a retrospective, though it is historically interesting.

RFC758.title: Assigned numbers
RFC758.summary: RFC 758 is a 1979 snapshot of the protocol number registries kept by Jon Postel. It lists assigned network numbers, IP versions, IP protocol numbers, port/socket numbers and ARPANET link numbers.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned numbers, with a contact for requesting assignments. It is a direct ancestor of the IANA registries.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

ARPANET.why: A substantial part covers ARPANET-specific numbering: link numbers, AHHP sockets, the ICP, and ARPANET service contact sockets. Readers of ARPANET history would want it.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: It lists IP version and protocol number values but does not specify IP. The IP specification is IEN 111.
TCP versions and ports appear only as entries in the number lists. The document does not specify TCP.
NCP and AHHP are mentioned only as context for the link and socket numbers.
Echo, Discard and Chargen appear only as entries in the socket list.
The document is a historic artefact but is not a history or retrospective.

RFC759.title: Internet Message Protocol
RFC759.summary: RFC 759 specifies the Internet Message Protocol, an early (1980) internetwork message system in which Message Processing Modules exchange structured, typed-element messages (DELIVER, ACKNOWLEDGE, PROBE, etc.) over TCP, a precursor to Internet email.

email.why: The document specifies a complete store-and-forward internetwork mail system (MPMs, relaying, delivery acknowledgment, mailboxes, routing), which is electronic mail architecture and transport.
email.quote: This document describes an internetwork message system. The system is designed to transmit messages between message processing modules

ARPANET.why: The document is positioned against ARPANET message protocols and the ARPA internet hierarchy, with ARPANET addressing used throughout. This is a modest secondary link, since the protocol is intended for internetwork use.
ARPANET.quote: In the old ARPANET system, message transmission was part of the file transfer protocol.

rejected.why: TCP is only the assumed reliable transport for MPM connections. The document does not define anything new about TCP.
Defines its own binary structured message encoding, not the RFC 822-style Internet message format of headers and addressing. The document body is delegated to RFC 767.
This is a different, competing protocol. It is not SMTP or mail relaying and submission as defined by SMTP.
Not a taxonomy id. The ENCRYPT element is a minor section that merely mentions DES and public-key schemes, so the cryptography tags do not apply.
