The ISO-based timestamp used in handling-stamps is a small supporting object, not a subject of the document.

RFC760.title: DoD standard Internet Protocol
RFC760.summary: RFC 760 is the DoD Standard Internet Protocol (IPv4 predecessor to RFC 791), specifying the datagram header format, addressing, fragmentation and reassembly, type of service, time to live, options and header checksum.

IPv4.why: The document is the specification of Internet Protocol version 4 ("This document describes version 4"), covering header, 32-bit addressing, fragmentation, options and service interface.
IPv4.quote: The internet protocol provides for transmitting blocks of data called datagrams from sources to destinations, where sources and destinations are hosts identified by fixed length addresses.

rejected.why: TCP is only cited as an example upper-layer user of IP; it is not specified here.
The header checksum is a field of IP, described briefly; the document is not about checksums as a subject.
Addressing is a core function but the IPv4 tag already covers it; the document does not treat address architecture separately.
ARPANET is mentioned as an example local network and in mappings, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols.
Type of Service is a header field within IP, not a QoS architecture document.
It is a protocol specification, not a historical retrospective, even though it is an early edition.

RFC761.title: DoD standard Transmission Control Protocol
RFC761.summary: RFC 761 is the January 1980 DoD Standard specification of the Transmission Control Protocol, covering header format, sequence numbers, connection establishment/closing, data communication, the user/TCP interface and event processing, with precedence and security.

TCP.why: The entire document is the specification of TCP: header, state machine, three-way handshake, flow control, user interface and event processing.
TCP.quote: The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is intended for use as a highly reliable host-to-host protocol between hosts in packet-switched computer communication networks

rejected.why: IP is only the lower-layer protocol TCP runs over; it is specified in RFC 760, not here.
The TCP checksum is described only as one header field, not as a subject in its own right.
ARPANET is mentioned as an example network and in the glossary, but the document is not about it.
Telnet and FTP appear only as example higher-level users of TCP.
Precedence and security fields are a minor feature of TCP, not a QoS architecture.

RFC762.title: Assigned numbers
RFC762.summary: RFC 762 (IEN 127) lists the currently assigned values for network numbers, IP versions, IP protocol numbers, port/socket numbers and ARPANET link numbers, maintained by Jon Postel.

IANA.why: The document is an assigned-numbers registry, the forerunner of the IANA registries. It also says Postel handles number assignment.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

ARPANET.why: Large parts of the registry cover ARPANET-specific namespaces: link numbers, AHHP sockets and the ARPANET network number. It also lists early host services such as RJE, SUPDUP and NETRJS.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: Ports and TCP versions appear only as entries in the registry. The document does not specify TCP.
IP version and protocol numbers are listed, but the document does not specify IP.
It is historic in nature, but it is a registry and not a retrospective.

RFC763.title: Role mailboxes
RFC763.summary: RFC 763 proposes that systems install role-based mail address synonyms (e.g., SYSTEMS, MANAGEMENT, LIAISON) so mail reaches the current incumbent of an official position, and suggests standardizing a set of such names.

email.why: The document is about mail addressing practice: role-based mailbox aliases to ensure email delivery. No more specific email child tag (e.g. message format, SMTP) fits, since it concerns mailbox naming conventions in general.
email.quote: created MAIL address synonyms such as SYSTEMS, MANAGEMENT, and LIAISON to ensure that mail is correctly delivered no matter who the incumbent happens to be

rejected.why: The document concerns mailbox alias names, not header syntax or message format specifics.
No transfer protocol is specified or discussed; it only suggests local address synonyms.
Role mailbox names are email addresses, not name resolution; email is the more fitting subject.

RFC764.title: Telnet Protocol specification
RFC764.summary: RFC 764 specifies the TELNET protocol: the Network Virtual Terminal, option negotiation (DO/DON'T/WILL/WON'T), standard control functions, the Synch signal, command structure and connection establishment over TCP port 23.

Telnet.why: The whole document is the specification of the Telnet protocol, including NVT, option negotiation, commands and port assignment.
Telnet.quote: The purpose of the TELNET Protocol is to provide a fairly general, bi-directional, eight-bit byte oriented communications facility.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport; the document uses the Urgent notification for Synch but does not specify or extend TCP.
The NVT uses seven-bit USASCII as its code set, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
Written in the ARPA Internet context, but it specifies an application protocol over TCP, not ARPANET host or network protocols.

RFC765.title: File Transfer Protocol specification
RFC765.summary: RFC 765 (IEN 149) is the 1980 specification of the File Transfer Protocol, defining its model, data representation types, transmission modes, commands, replies, and a mail-over-FTP appendix.

FTP.why: The whole document specifies FTP: model, data connections, modes, commands, replies and state diagrams.
FTP.quote: The objectives of FTP are 1) to promote sharing of files (computer programs and/or data)

rejected.why: The control connection uses the TELNET protocol as substrate; FTP only follows its conventions and defines nothing new about Telnet.
TCP is only the transport underneath FTP; the document does not specify or extend it.
The MAIL/MLFL/MRCP commands and the mail appendix are a minor part of the FTP command set, not a document about email.
ASCII and EBCDIC are used as FTP representation types, but the document does not address the character sets themselves.

RFC766.title: Internet Protocol Handbook: Table of contents
RFC766.summary: RFC 766 announces the planned Internet Protocol Handbook, intended to replace the old ARPANET protocol handbook, and gives its draft table of contents listing gateway, host and application level protocol documents (RFCs and IENs).

internet history.why: The document records the 1980 transition from ARPANET protocols to the internet protocol family and catalogs the early protocol documents, making it a historical artifact of the protocol suite.
internet history.quote: it is appropriate for the internet family of protocols to replace the old ARPANET protocols

ARPANET.why: The handbook is framed as a successor to the ARPANET Protocol Handbook, and the ARPANET research program and NIC document distribution are the context. It is not about ARPANET protocols themselves.
ARPANET.quote: Internet Protocol Handbook will closely parallel the old ARPANET Protocol Handbook

rejected.why: TCP appears only as one entry in the table of contents; the document does not specify or discuss it.
FTP is listed as a handbook entry, and is also the means to retrieve files, but the document is not about it.
The Internet Datagram Protocol is only listed, not discussed.
It is a table of contents of RFCs and IENs, not about RFC format, style or publication.
Only listed as a handbook entry.
Only listed as a handbook entry.

RFC767.title: Structured format for transmission of multi-media documents
RFC767.summary: RFC 767 specifies a structured property-list format for multimedia documents (text, voice, facsimile, graphics) with header fields and sequential/simultaneous/independent presentation ordering, carried as the Document in the Internet Message Protocol's messages.

messaging.why: The document defines the document format (fields like DATE, FROM, TO, SUBJECT, BODY, mailbox objects) for an internetwork message delivery system. It is general store-and-forward messaging and predates the Internet mail standards, so the generic messaging topic fits better than the email tags.
messaging.quote: This document describes a format for transmitting structured data representations of multimedia documents.

rejected.why: The format is for the Internet Message Protocol's message system and mentions computer mail, but it is a distinct predecessor structure, not Internet email architecture or the RFC 822 message format.
Header fields resemble RFC 733/822 headers, but this defines a different property-list encoding, not the Internet message format.
It is a conceptual precursor for multimedia mail bodies, but it does not specify MIME or its encodings.
The document is set in the ARPANET environment and references NVP and NLS, but it is not about ARPANET protocols or operations themselves.

gaps.name: Multimedia document format
gaps.why: The core subject is a structured multimedia document and message body format with presentation ordering. The taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC768.title: User Datagram Protocol
RFC768.summary: RFC 768 specifies the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), a minimal connectionless datagram transport over IP with ports, length and a pseudo-header checksum.

UDP.why: The document is the UDP specification itself, defining header format, checksum, user interface and protocol number.
UDP.quote: This User Datagram  Protocol  (UDP)  is  defined  to  make  available  a datagram   mode  of  packet-switched   computer   communication

rejected.why: The checksum is defined only as a field within UDP, not as a general Internet checksum topic.
TCP is mentioned only as the alternative for reliable stream delivery.
IP is only the underlying protocol UDP runs over; the document does not specify it.
TFTP is cited only as an example use of UDP.
The Internet Name Server is cited only as an example use of UDP.

RFC769.title: Rapicom 450 facsimile file format
RFC769.summary: RFC 769 documents the record and block file format used to store Rapicom 450 facsimile machine data so that organizations can exchange fax files via file transfer.

fax.why: The whole document specifies a stored file format for facsimile data from Rapicom 450 fax machines, so it belongs on the fax subject page.
fax.quote: The purpose  of this note is to document  the  format used for  these  files  so  that  other  organizations  with  compatible facsimile devices can join

rejected.why: The note says fax files can be exchanged via file transfer, but it does not specify or extend FTP. It only describes the file contents.
It is a binary record format, but the subject is specifically facsimile data. The fax tag fits better.

RFC770.title: Assigned numbers
RFC770.summary: RFC 770 is a 1980 Assigned Numbers list documenting values for ARPANET/internet network numbers, IP versions, IP protocol numbers, ports/sockets, and link numbers.

ARPANET.why: Much of the document lists ARPANET-specific assignments: link numbers, AHHP sockets, and the ARPANET host-level service sockets. It is a historic ARPANET-era working note.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

IANA.why: It is the Assigned Numbers registry snapshot, maintained by Jon Postel, and is the ancestor of the IANA registries. It covers network numbers, protocol numbers, ports and link numbers.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations.

IPv4.why: A substantial part of the document assigns IP version values and IP protocol numbers, and the 8-bit network number space used by the internet address.
IPv4.quote: In the Internet Protocol (IP) there is a field to identify the version of the internetwork general protocol.

rejected.why: TCP is referenced only as an entry in the protocol number and port lists. The document does not specify or extend it.
It is a historic document, but it is a registry snapshot and not a history or retrospective.
FTP and the other services (Telnet, Echo and so on) appear only as rows in the port list.
The network number list is an address-space assignment, but the document does not discuss IP address architecture. IANA and IPv4 cover it better.

RFC771.title: Mail transition plan
RFC771.summary: RFC 771 is a 1980 plan for transitioning ARPANET text mail from NCP/FTP-based delivery to TCP-based Internet mail, using relay servers, expanded host tables and a separate mail transfer protocol.

email.why: The whole document is about the architecture and transport of computer mail, including mailer programs, relay servers, mailbox addressing and the NCP-to-TCP mail transition.
email.quote: The principal aim of the mail service transition plan is to provide orderly support for computer mail service during the period of transition

SMTP.why: It specifies the separate mail transfer protocol (the SMTP precursor) and relay behaviour between hosts, including multiple-recipient commands and error reporting. Mail relaying is the core of the plan.
SMTP.quote: the relay server will use a distinct mail transfer protocol, separate from the file transfer protocol.

rejected.why: NCP is the old transport being transitioned away from. The document is about mail, not NCP itself.
FTP is the legacy mail transfer mechanism (MAIL/MLFL commands) being replaced. The document does not specify or extend it.
TCP is the new transport substrate for mail. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document discusses host tables and compound host names, but only in support of mail routing. It is not mainly about host naming.
ARPANET is the environment of the transition. It was considered as a topic tag, but the subject is the mail service, and email is the more specific fit.

RFC772.title: Mail Transfer Protocol
RFC772.summary: RFC 772 is a 1980 first-draft specification of the Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP), an FTP/Telnet-derived command/reply protocol for transferring mail between hosts, including multi-recipient MRSQ/MRCP schemes, reply codes, and source routing.

SMTP.why: MTP is the direct precursor of SMTP, defining MAIL, MRCP commands, reply codes and relaying via path sequences. Readers of the SMTP page would want it.
SMTP.quote: The objective of Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently.

rejected.why: Telnet is only the substrate for the control connection and NVT-ASCII; the document defines nothing new about Telnet.
FTP is the historical origin and its terminology is borrowed, but the document does not specify or extend FTP.
NCP is only one of the transports the control connection may run over.
TCP is only the transport substrate.
NVT-ASCII is used as the data representation, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
The more specific SMTP tag covers the mail transfer protocol; no broader email architecture is addressed.

RFC773.title: Comments on NCP/TCP mail service transition strategy
RFC773.summary: RFC 773 reviews the plan for moving ARPANET electronic mail from NCP-based FTP mail to TCP-based mail. It proposes NCP/TCP forwarders (implicit and explicit), host-name tables with NCP/TCP capability bits, and a transition schedule.

email.why: The whole document is about transitioning ARPANET electronic mail transport and addressing to internet-based operation, including forwarders and mailbox naming.
email.quote: the principal aim of the plan is to provide for the orderly support of the most commonly used network service (mail) during the period of transition

NCP.why: The transition is from the historic ARPANET NCP host-host protocol to TCP. NCP-based mail servers, sockets and forwarders are a substantial part of the design.
NCP.quote: This paper addresses only the first of the transitions from NCP-based text mail to TCP-based multimedia mail.

rejected.why: The ARPANET topic is the parent of NCP, so it is implied by the NCP tag. The mail transition is the document's focus, not the ARPANET in general.
The document describes the FTP MAIL and MLFL commands as the old transport. It does not specify or extend FTP.
TCP is the target transport for the transition, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
This RFC predates SMTP and only refers to the Mail Transfer Protocol work in RFC 772. It does not define the protocol.
RFC 733 headers are mentioned only as a constraint on mailbox naming. The document does not specify a message format.
Host-name tables are discussed as part of the mail mapping. The document is not about host naming conventions.

RFC774.title: Internet Protocol Handbook: Table of contents
RFC774.summary: RFC 774 is a 1980 draft table of contents for the planned Internet Protocol Handbook. It lists the existing RFCs and IENs, grouped by gateway, host and application level and appendices, that the NIC would collect as the internet protocols replaced the ARPANET ones.

internet history.why: The document is a period catalogue of the early internet protocol suite and its documents, a snapshot of the 1980 transition from ARPANET protocols. Readers of history would want it.
internet history.quote: The internet family of protocols is replacing the old ARPANET protocols.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is mentioned only as the set of old protocols being replaced. The handbook lists internet-level protocols, not ARPANET host or network protocols.
The handbook is compiled from RFCs and IENs. The document is about a handbook's contents, not RFC format, style or publication.
TCP appears only as one line in the contents list. The document does not specify or discuss it.
The Internet Protocol (RFC 760) is only a listed item, not discussed.
FTP, Telnet, TFTP and the mail protocols are only entries in the contents list and are not discussed.
The handbook is a collection of specifications. It is not an introductory guide, and this document is only its table of contents.

gaps.name: Internet Protocol Handbook / protocol document catalogue
gaps.why: The document is an index of protocol specifications, and the taxonomy has no tag for protocol catalogues or document indexes. The closest fit is internet history.

RFC775.title: Directory oriented FTP commands
RFC775.summary: RFC 775 proposes four directory-oriented FTP commands (XMKD, XRMD, XPWD, XCUP) and associated reply codes, including the 257 reply returning the absolute pathname, for FTP servers on hosts with tree-structured file systems.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with new directory commands XMKD, XRMD, XPWD and XCUP and defines their reply codes.
FTP.quote: we have added four commands to our server

RFC776.title: Assigned numbers
RFC776.summary: RFC 776 is a 1981 snapshot of the assigned numbers for network numbers, IP version numbers, IP protocol numbers, ports and sockets, and ARPANET link numbers. It also gives the people responsible for each assignment.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of number assignments maintained by Jon Postel, the early IANA function. A reader browsing IANA registries would expect to find it.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

ARPANET.why: The link-number and socket assignments cover ARPANET Host/Host protocol (AHHP) usage, ICP, and the ARPANET network entry. This is a substantial part of the content.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: The document lists the IP version, protocol and network number fields. It does not specify IP.
TCP appears only as a protocol number and as the user of port numbers. The document does not specify it.
The document is a historical snapshot, but it is a registry and not a retrospective.
UDP appears only as an entry in the protocol number list.

RFC777.title: Internet Control Message Protocol
RFC777.summary: RFC 777 specifies the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), the IP-integrated control and error-reporting messages (destination unreachable, time exceeded, parameter problem, source quench, redirect, echo, timestamp) sent by gateways and hosts.

ICMP.why: The document defines ICMP in full: message formats, type and code values, and when each message is sent.
ICMP.quote: this protocol, the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), is used.

rejected.why: ICMP is described as integral to IP, but the document specifies ICMP, not IP itself; IP is the substrate.
Source Quench is a rate-reduction request, but it is one message among many and the document is not about congestion control.
Timestamp messages are defined, but only cite Mills' clock service as one use; the document is not about time synchronization.
Time Exceeded and Echo messages support such tools, but the document does not describe path discovery.

RFC778.title: DCNET Internet Clock Service
RFC778.summary: Describes the DCNET Internet Clock Service, which uses ICMP Timestamp and GGP Echo datagrams to give clock synchronization and one-way/roundtrip delay measurements against DCNET hosts, with timestamps referenced to a WWVB radio clock.

time synchronization.why: The document specifies a clock service for synchronizing host clocks, including timestamp format and offset corrections against a radio clock. It predates NTP, so the general topic tag fits better than NTP.
time synchronization.quote: The service, intended primarily for clock synchronization and one-way delay measurements with cooperating internet hosts

ICMP.why: The service is defined as a use of the ICMP Timestamp and Timestamp Reply messages, including their datagram format and type codes. Readers of ICMP would want it.
ICMP.quote: is provided using the Timestamp and Timestamp Reply messages of the proposed Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP)

performance measurement.why: A substantial section gives the method for computing one-way and roundtrip delay from the four timestamps.
performance measurement.quote: Delay measurements can be made with any DCNET host by simply sending an ICS datagram in the above format to it and processing the reply.

rejected.why: The document is an early precursor of NTP, but it does not describe NTP. Tagging NTP would be anachronistic.
Telnet is only used to read the offset table from the COMSAT-GAT host. It is a substrate, not the subject.
The roundtrip delay measurement is not path discovery.

gaps.name: GGP (Gateway-Gateway Protocol)
gaps.why: The service is also carried over GGP Echo messages, and the taxonomy has no tag for GGP.

RFC779.title: Telnet send-location option
RFC779.summary: Defines the Telnet SEND-LOCATION option (code 23), letting a user Telnet client send the user's location string to the server Telnet via subnegotiation so it can be shown in finger-style user listings.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T meanings, defaults and subnegotiation format.
Telnet.quote: The sender specifies the user's location to the other side via a SEND-LOCATION subnegotiation.

rejected.why: The NAME/FINGER protocol is mentioned only as motivation; the document does not specify or extend Finger.
SUPDUP is cited only as an existing protocol with similar functionality; the document is not about it.
The location is a sequence of ASCII printable characters, but this is only an encoding detail.
The location is a free-form text string for physically finding the user, not a geolocation format or conveyance mechanism.

RFC780.title: Mail Transfer Protocol
RFC780.summary: RFC 780 specifies the Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP), an early ARPANET-era predecessor of SMTP, defining commands, replies, relaying via source routes, multi-recipient schemes, and transport bindings.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a mail transfer and relaying protocol (MAIL, MRCP, reply codes, source routing), the direct precursor of SMTP, so it belongs on the SMTP/mail relaying page.
SMTP.quote: The objective of Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently.

rejected.why: TCP is only one of several transport substrates described in an appendix; the document defines nothing new about TCP itself.
NCP is only one of the transport bindings in Appendix B, not the subject of the document.
The protocol was designed for the ARPA Internet environment, but the document is about mail transfer, not ARPANET protocols as such.
X.25 appears only in an appendix that says it is too error prone to use directly as a transport.
Message text format is only referenced (RFC 733); this document specifies the transfer protocol, not headers or addressing formats.
ASCII is only used as the character set for commands and data, not the subject.

RFC781.title: Specification of the Internet Protocol (IP) timestamp option
RFC781.summary: RFC 781 specifies the format and semantics of the IP timestamp option (type 68), used to record per-gateway timestamps in IP headers for measuring catenet delays.

IPv4.why: The document defines an IPv4 header option (type 68, length, offset, overflow, flags, fragmentation behaviour). It extends the IP protocol of the era, which is IPv4.
IPv4.quote: a specification of the timestamp option format for IP is presented.

performance measurement.why: The option exists to measure one-way and per-network delays. Delay measurement is a substantial motivation and use of the document.
performance measurement.quote: An effective way to measure catenet delays is by means of packet header timestamping.

rejected.why: Clock synchronization is only assumed as a prerequisite (WWVB clocks, RFC 778). The document does not specify it.
The document does not discuss ICMP, including ICMP timestamp messages. It only defines an IP header option.
A more specific technology tag, IPv4, already fits. The broader topic is implied by it.

RFC782.title: Virtual Terminal management model
RFC782.summary: RFC 782 presents a virtual terminal management model in which a virtual terminal is an n-way, class-based shared device with virtual keys, controller and display, plus a workstation model with adaptation units and an executive, for windowed multi-conversation personal workstations.

network graphics.why: The model includes graphics virtual terminals and graphics virtual displays, windows and viewports. This is a weak fit with early network graphics, so it is a secondary tag.
network graphics.quote: using high-resolution graphics objects for output (e.g., line drawings, raster blocks and images, possibly intermixed with text)

rejected.why: Telnet options appear only in the references. The document describes a virtual terminal model, not the Telnet protocol or its options.
The document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations. It is a general model prepared for the Defense Communications Agency.
The document covers workstation and terminal architecture, not the architecture of the Internet.

gaps.name: Virtual terminal protocols / virtual terminal management
gaps.why: The whole document is about the virtual terminal abstraction (virtual keys, controller, display, adaptation units, windowing). The taxonomy has no tag for virtual terminals, and Telnet is the nearest tag but does not fit.

RFC783.title: TFTP Protocol (revision 2)
RFC783.summary: RFC 783 specifies TFTP revision 2, a simple lock-step file transfer protocol over UDP with RRQ/WRQ/DATA/ACK/ERROR packets, transfer modes, TIDs and termination rules.

TFTP.why: The document is the specification of the TFTP protocol, its packet formats, connection setup, and termination.
TFTP.quote: TFTP is a simple protocol to transfer files, and therefore was named the Trivial File Transfer Protocol or TFTP.

rejected.why: TFTP runs on UDP as substrate; the document only reproduces the UDP header for convenience and defines nothing new about UDP.
FTP is mentioned only for comparison (TFTP lacks most of its features); the document is not about FTP.
netascii is used as the text mode and footnoted, but the document does not address ASCII itself.
Mail mode is a minor transfer mode; the document is not about email.

RFC784.title: Mail Transfer Protocol: ISI TOPS20 implementation
RFC784.summary: Describes ISI's TOPS20 implementation of the Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP), including its sender/receiver programs over TCP and NCP, a dispatcher, control/data mail files, and host capability tables.

email.why: The document describes the architecture of a mail transfer implementation: receivers, dispatcher, senders, mailbox files. It is about email transport, and MTP is the predecessor of SMTP, which has no dedicated tag here.
email.quote: This implementation supports the MTP user and server functions using both TCP and NCP transport services, and provides interfaces to other mail delivery mechanisms.

rejected.why: MTP is the predecessor of SMTP, but this document does not specify SMTP or mail relaying and submission as defined by that tag.
NCP is only one of the transports the MTP programs run over. The document does not specify or change NCP.
TCP is only a transport used by the MTP sender and receiver programs.
FTP on NCP is mentioned only as the old mail delivery method in the dispatcher's host table. The document does not cover FTP.
RFC 733 headers are mentioned only in passing. The document does not discuss message format.

gaps.name: MTP (Mail Transfer Protocol)
gaps.why: The historic predecessor of SMTP has no dedicated tag. This implementation note would belong on such a page.

RFC785.title: Mail Transfer Protocol: ISI TOPS20 file definitions
RFC785.summary: RFC 785 defines the ISI TOPS20 file-based interface (a control file plus a mail text file) between mail creation systems and the Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) for relaying mail.

email.why: The document specifies how mail is handed from a mail creation system to the MTP transfer agent via control and text files, which is email architecture and transport. No more specific child tag fits, since it is not SMTP and MTP is the predecessor protocol.
email.quote: defines the ISI TOPS20s interface between the Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) and a mail creation system (e.g., MM, HERMES, etc.) in terms of the files

message format.why: The mail text file must be an RFC 733 message with header and body, and the example shows header fields. This is a minor part, though, since the document does not define the format itself.
message format.quote: It is mail which conforms to the standard described in RFC 733, "Standard for the Format of ARPA Network Text Messages".

rejected.why: The document concerns MTP (RFC 780), the predecessor of SMTP. It does not describe SMTP itself.
The files reside on a TOPS20 file system and MTP is related to FTP, but the document does not address FTP.

gaps.name: Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) / TOPS20 interface
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the historic MTP (RFC 780) or for TOPS20 operating-system-specific interfaces. The email tag is the closest fit.

RFC786.title: Mail Transfer Protocol: ISI TOPS20 MTP-NIMAIL interface
RFC786.summary: Defines the file-based interface at ISI TOPS20 between the Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) and NIMAIL, including file format and address transformations between source-route and percent-hack forms.

email.why: The document specifies how mail is handed between two mail transfer systems (MTP and NIMAIL), including address transformation and file formats. This is email transport architecture.
email.quote: MTP will present mail for processing by NIMAIL in files of the following form

rejected.why: MTP is the predecessor of SMTP, but this document defines a local file interface rather than SMTP or mail relaying/submission protocol itself.
The document shows a Via header line and a header/body layout, but only as part of the hand-off file format. It does not define Internet message format.
NIFTP is only mentioned in a reference title for NIMAIL, and the document does not address file transfer.

RFC787.title: Connectionless data transmission survey/tutorial
RFC787.summary: A 1981 working paper surveying connectionless data transmission versus connection-oriented transfer, arguing that the OSI Reference Model should incorporate connectionless service at its layers.

internet architecture.why: The paper is an architectural argument about layered communication models, connection-oriented versus connectionless service, and where each fits in the OSI layers.
internet architecture.quote: a complementary concept - connectionless data transmission - is an essential part of the Open Systems Interconnection architecture

OSI.why: It discusses connectionless service at the OSI network layer and the Reference Model's treatment of it. The OSI tag covers network-layer protocols, so this is a partial fit.
OSI.quote: Connectionless network service is useful for many of the same reasons that were identified in the previous discussion of network interconnection

rejected.why: UDP is only named as one example of a connectionless network-layer protocol, not specified or analysed.
The DoD Standard Internet Protocol is cited as an example of connectionless internetworking, but the paper is not about it.
Ethernet and IEEE 802 LANs appear as examples of where connectionless data link service is useful, not as the subject.
The paper is a standards-position tutorial from 1981, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: OSI Reference Model / connectionless data transmission (CDT)
gaps.why: The paper's central subject is the OSI Reference Model and connectionless versus connection-oriented service. The taxonomy has only the narrower OSI network-layer tag and the generic internet architecture tag.

RFC788.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
RFC788.summary: RFC 788 is the 1981 specification of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, defining its model, commands, reply codes, relaying, and transport bindings.

SMTP.why: The document is the specification of SMTP itself: commands, replies, relaying, transaction procedure and state diagrams.
SMTP.quote: The objective of Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently.

rejected.why: TCP is only one of several transport substrates described in an appendix; the document does not specify TCP.
NCP is an alternative transport in an appendix, not the subject of the document.
Message headers are only referenced via RFC 733; the document defines only the time stamp and return path lines.
X.25 is mentioned briefly in an appendix as a possible but unreliable transport.
ASCII is used as the character set for commands and data, not the subject.
ARPANET and NCP appear as transport context only.

RFC789.title: Vulnerabilities of network control protocols: An example
RFC789.summary: A 1981 case study of the October 1980 ARPANET outage, in which corrupted sequence numbers on routing updates (dropped bits) cycled through the IMPs' flooding-based update protocol and consumed their resources, with lessons on the vulnerabilities of network control protocols.

ARPANET.why: The whole document is an account of an ARPANET network-wide outage, its IMP routing update protocol and the ARPANET's response. The ARPANET page is where readers would look for it.
ARPANET.quote: On October 27, 1980, there was an unusual occurrence on the ARPANET.

routing architecture.why: A large part of the paper explains the ARPANET link-state routing update flooding scheme: sequence numbers, the LATER comparison and retransmission. It then analyses how this design fails and makes general points about robustness and design principles.
routing architecture.quote: Each routing update is broadcast (or flooded) to all IMPs, not just to immediate neighbors of the IMP which generated the update

rejected.why: The more specific routing architecture tag already covers the routing discussion, and the parent is implied.
Checksumming of update packets and tables is discussed only as a gap in the protection against dropped bits. It is not the subject of the paper.
The NCC's remote control and patching of IMPs is described as part of the narrative. It is not a management protocol or practice that the paper specifies.
The outage was caused by a hardware fault and not by an attack, and the paper is not about securing infrastructure.

gaps.name: Network robustness / failure analysis (control-protocol vulnerabilities)
gaps.why: The paper's main theme is how a hardware fault and a protocol design weakness cause network-wide failure, and the need for resource-use alarms. The taxonomy has no tag for network failure case studies or resilience.

RFC790.title: Assigned numbers
RFC790.summary: RFC 790 is the September 1981 Assigned Numbers list, which records values for IP network numbers, version numbers, protocol numbers, TCP/UDP port and socket numbers, and ARPANET link numbers.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned numbers (networks, protocols, ports, links) maintained by Postel, the early IANA function.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations.

addressing.why: A substantial part describes class A/B/C address formats and lists assigned network numbers.
addressing.quote: The Internet Protocol (IP) uses a 32 bit address and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

ARPANET.why: It covers ARPANET link numbers, AHHP sockets and the ICP, which are ARPANET host protocol matters.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: The IP address classes and protocol numbers are only listed as registry values. The document does not specify IP.
TCP ports are assigned here, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
It is a historic document, but it is a registry rather than a retrospective.

RFC791.title: Internet Protocol
RFC791.summary: RFC 791 is the original specification of IPv4, defining the datagram header, addressing (classful), fragmentation and reassembly, options, TTL, type of service, header checksum, and the user/IP interface.

IPv4.why: The document is the IPv4 specification itself: header format, addresses, fragmentation, options, and the module interface.
IPv4.quote: The internet protocol implements two basic functions:  addressing and fragmentation.

rejected.why: ICMP is only referenced for error reporting; it is specified in RFC 792.
TCP is only an example upper-layer user of IP.
Classful addressing is covered, but as part of the IPv4 spec, so the IPv4 tag covers it.
The header checksum is defined here but only as one IP header field, not a subject of its own.
The Type of Service field is later redefined by Diffserv, but this document does not address Diffserv.
ARPANET appears only as an example local network and in the glossary.

RFC792.title: Internet Control Message Protocol
RFC792.summary: RFC 792 specifies the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), the IP-integral protocol for error reporting and diagnostic messages (destination unreachable, time exceeded, redirect, echo, timestamp, etc.).

ICMP.why: The document is the core specification of ICMP, defining all message types, codes, and formats.
ICMP.quote: this protocol, the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), is used.

rejected.why: ICMP is an integral part of IP and runs over IPv4, but the document specifies ICMP, not IPv4 itself; IP is the substrate.
It defines the checksum field used in ICMP messages, but only as a message field using the standard Internet checksum, not as a subject in its own right.
Source Quench is a rate-reduction request, but it is one minor message type and the document is not about congestion control.
Timestamp messages exist, but they are a small part of the document and do not make it about time synchronization.
Time Exceeded messages are the basis of traceroute, but traceroute is not discussed in this document.

RFC793.title: Transmission Control Protocol
RFC793.summary: RFC 793 is the original DARPA standard specification of TCP, defining its header format, sequence numbers, connection establishment and closing state machine, flow control, urgent/push, user interface, and event processing.

TCP.why: The whole document is the base specification of TCP: header, three-way handshake, state machine, windowing, and event processing.
TCP.quote: The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is intended for use as a highly reliable host-to-host protocol between hosts in packet-switched computer communication networks

rejected.why: IP is only the assumed lower layer; the document specifies TCP, not IP (which is RFC 791).
The TCP checksum and pseudo header are described, but only as one header field of TCP, not as a subject in itself.
The document covers window-based flow control and a retransmission timeout example, not congestion control as such.
It is a protocol specification, not a history or retrospective, despite its age.

RFC794.title: Pre-emption
RFC794.summary: RFC 794 discusses how precedence-based pre-emption of resources can be supported in AUTODIN II over TCP by having terminal and server processes keep an extra LISTEN pending to accept high-precedence connection requests, and by local resource pre-emption at the initiating host.

TCP.why: The document's core proposal is how TCP connections with precedence are pre-empted using an extra pending LISTEN and exposing precedence of incoming connection requests to processes. It is about TCP usage and implementation behaviour.
TCP.quote: This capability can be realized in AUTODIN II without adding any new mechanisms to TCP (except to make precedence of incoming connection requests visible to the processes which use TCP).

QoS.why: The document discusses precedence and pre-emption as a means of allocating resources among users of differing priority, a QoS-style concern across circuit, message and packet switching.
QoS.quote: In general, precedence is a tool for deciding how to allocate resources when systems are saturated.

rejected.why: FTP is used only as an example of an application process that leaves a LISTEN pending; the document does not specify or extend FTP.
TELNET is mentioned as an example of a multi-connection user program; the document is not about the Telnet protocol.
Precedence here is a general resource-allocation idea for TCP connections, not the Differentiated Services architecture.
Saturation is the motivation, but the document addresses access priority and pre-emption, not congestion control mechanisms.

RFC795.title: Service mappings
RFC795.summary: RFC 795 maps the IP Type of Service field (precedence, delay, throughput, reliability) to the service parameters of AUTODIN II, ARPANET, PRNET and SATNET.

QoS.why: The document maps IP Type of Service (precedence, delay, throughput, reliability) onto network-specific service choices. That is QoS service-class mapping. No more specific QoS technology tag fits, since this predates Diffserv.
QoS.quote: This memo describes the relationship between the Internet Protocol (IP) [1] Type of Service and the service parameters of specific networks.

ARPANET.why: A substantial section covers ARPANET message types and priority and how they map to IP TOS. Readers of ARPANET material would want it.
ARPANET.quote: The service choices are in quite limited. There is one priority bit that can be mapped to the high order bit of the IP TOS precedence.

rejected.why: The document uses the IPv4 TOS field but does not specify or extend IP. It only maps network service parameters onto it.
Diffserv later redefined the TOS octet, but this 1981 memo predates it and does not discuss DSCPs.
The IP layer is the context. The subject is service mapping, which QoS covers more precisely.

RFC796.title: Address mappings
RFC796.summary: RFC 796 describes how 32-bit IP addresses (class A/B/C) map to local address formats of specific 1981 networks such as ARPANET, AUTODIN II, PRNET, SATNET, and WBCNET, and lists their network numbers.

addressing.why: The document defines the IP address classes and how local addresses and network numbers are assigned and mapped for specific networks, which is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: This memo describes the relationship between address fields used in the Internet Protocol (IP) [1] and several specific networks.

ARPANET.why: A substantial part covers the ARPANET host/logical host/IMP address mapping and its network number 10, which is of interest to readers of ARPANET material.
ARPANET.quote: The ARPANET (with 96 bit leaders) has 24 bit addresses. The 24 bits are assigned to host, logical host, and IMP leader fields
ARPANET.section: Internet to Local Net Address Mappings

rejected.why: The document is about address mapping to local networks. It does not specify IPv4 itself, and RFC 791 is only referenced. The addressing tag fits better.
SATNET and WBCNET are satellite networks, but the document covers only their address formats, not networking over satellite links.
The document is of historical interest, but it is a technical specification and not a retrospective.

RFC797.title: Format for Bitmap files
RFC797.summary: RFC 797 proposes a simple file format for one-bit-per-pixel bitmaps, with a 10-octet header (width, length, x and y increments) followed by row-scanned pixel data.

rejected.why: This tag covers early network graphics protocols and formats, and it sits under ARPANET. The document describes a local bitmap file format for passing data between closely coupled programs. It is not a network protocol and it does not appear in ARPANET context, so I did not tag it.
The RAPICOM 450 fax device is mentioned only as an example source of bitmaps. The document defines no fax protocol or transport over mail or IP.

gaps.name: Bitmap image file format
gaps.why: The document is about a raster image file format (1-bit-per-pixel bitmaps). The taxonomy has no tag for image or graphics file formats. The closest, network graphics, covers early network graphics protocols and doesn't fit.

RFC798.title: Decoding facsimile data from the Rapicom 450
RFC798.summary: RFC 798 describes a program that decodes Rapicom 450 fax machine data (a two-dimensional run-length encoding, sent in 585-bit blocks) into an ordinary bitmap, and it documents the block header, setup block and decoding algorithm.

fax.why: The whole document is about the Rapicom 450 facsimile data format and how to decode it. Fax is the closest fitting tag, even though the document predates fax over Internet mail and IP.
fax.quote: decode facsimile data from the Rapicom 450 facsimile (fax) machine into an ordinary bitmap

rejected.why: The 12-bit CRC polynomial is mentioned only as one field of the block layout. The document is not about CRC choice or error detection.
The run-length encoding is the fax machine's own scan-line encoding, not a general lossless compression format.
The document mentions displaying the decoded bitmaps on an HP graphics terminal. Its subject is decoding the fax data, not a network graphics protocol.
The work was done at ISI on TOPS20 and NLS. The document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.

gaps.name: Rapicom 450 facsimile data format / run-length bitmap decoding
gaps.why: The taxonomy's fax tag is aimed at fax over Internet mail and IP. It has no tag for legacy fax machine encodings or for related RFC 769, the Rapicom file format.

RFC799.title: Internet name domains
RFC799.summary: RFC 799 proposes a hierarchical name-domain scheme (<user>.<host>@<domain>) for internet hosts and mailboxes, with mail forwarders per domain and routing rules for the MTP/MRCP mail system.

naming.why: The document proposes partitioning the host name space into name domains to replace flat name-address tables. This is general naming and predates DNS, so the generic naming tag fits better than the DNS tag.
naming.quote: Some sort of hierarchical name-space partitioning can easily be devised to deal with this problem

email.why: A large part of the document covers mailbox naming, mail forwarders and relays, and source and return routing in the MTP/RFC-780 mail system. That makes it relevant to email readers.
email.quote: In its most general form, a standard internet mailbox name has the syntax <user>.<host>@<domain>

rejected.why: This is a precursor to the DNS. It does not specify DNS, and it describes forwarder tables rather than DNS servers or resource records.
The HOSTS.TXT host tables are mentioned, but only as the source of the ARPA forwarder's table. The document is about domains, not host naming conventions.
The document discusses MTP and MRCP commands from RFC 780 only to define routing rules. It does not specify or extend a mail transfer protocol.
Section 7 covers editing RFC-733 headers, but only as a side effect of the naming scheme. The document is not about the message format.

RFC800.title: Request For Comments summary notes: 700-799
RFC800.summary: RFC 800 is an annotated index and status summary of RFCs 700-799 (1974-1981), covering early ARPANET/Internet protocols such as TCP, IP, ICMP, UDP, Telnet, FTP, mail, and SUPDUP.

internet history.why: The document is a retrospective status listing of an early block of RFCs, so readers of Internet history would want it.
internet history.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 700 through RFC 799.  This is a kind of status report on these RFCs.

ARPANET.why: Many entries cover ARPANET host/IMP protocols, 1822 interfaces, NCP transition and ARPANET message systems. The catalogue as a whole is ARPANET-era working notes.
ARPANET.quote: A description of an outage in ARPANET service and the process of determining the cause

RFC series.why: It is a catalogue of RFC documents that tracks which ones replace or obsolete others. It is part of the RFC series' own bookkeeping.
RFC series.quote: Requests For Comments Summary Notes: 700-799

rejected.why: TCP is listed only as one entry (RFC 793); the document does not specify or analyse it.
Many Telnet option RFCs are listed, but only as one-line summaries in an index. The document itself is not about Telnet.
Many mail-related RFCs are listed, but only as index entries. Mail is not the document's subject.
Assigned Numbers appears only as list entries that supersede each other.
FTP appears only in a few index entries and is not the subject of this document.
IP (RFC 791) is listed as one entry. The document does not specify the protocol.

RFC801.title: NCP/TCP transition plan
RFC801.summary: RFC 801 is Postel's plan for transitioning ARPANET hosts from NCP to IP/TCP by 1 January 1983, covering relay hosts for Telnet, FTP and mail, milestones, implementation issues and implementation status.

NCP.why: The document is the plan for retiring NCP, the historic ARPANET host-host protocol, and replacing it with TCP/IP. Readers of NCP history would want it.
NCP.quote: The goal is to make a complete switch over from the NCP to IP/TCP by 1 January 1983.

TCP.why: Adopting TCP is the goal of the transition. The document also lists TCP implementation shortcuts and deficiencies to avoid, and surveys implementation status.
TCP.quote: TCP: This is specified in RFC793. Implementations exist for several machines and operating systems.

ARPANET.why: The document concerns an operational change to the ARPANET, including its hosts, relay services and milestones. It is an ARPANET working note.
ARPANET.quote: The time has come to put these protocols into use in the operational ARPANET

rejected.why: Telnet is covered only as a service to be moved to TCP, with relay scenarios. The document does not specify or extend it.
FTP appears as a service to be ported and relayed. The document does not specify it.
SMTP mail relaying between NCP and TCP hosts is described as part of the plan, but the protocol is specified in RFC 788, not here.
IP is mentioned as part of the IP/TCP base. The document is about the migration, not the protocol.
It is a contemporary plan and not a retrospective, so the more specific ARPANET and NCP tags fit better.
The name tables discussion is a minor implementation note, not a main subject.

RFC802.title: ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol
RFC802.summary: RFC 802 proposes the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, adding logical host addressing (names) and a short-blocking feature to the ARPANET 1822 host-IMP interface, with new leader formats.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies an ARPANET host-IMP access protocol, including leader formats, NDM messages, blocking behaviour and host-IMP initialization. This is core ARPANET protocol material.
ARPANET.quote: The new host access protocol is known as the ARPANET  1822L (for Logical) Host Access Protocol, and it represents an addition to the current ARPANET 1822 Host Access Protocol

rejected.why: NCP is mentioned only as a user of messages requiring sequential delivery, so the short-blocking feature cannot be used with it. The document does not specify NCP.
TCP is mentioned only in passing as a protocol for which short-blocking is recommended. The document is not about TCP.
The logical host names are ARPANET-specific 16-bit names, not IP address architecture. The ARPANET tag is the better fit.
Congestion control appears only as one reason a message may be rejected under short-blocking. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC803.title: Dacom 450/500 facsimile data transcoding
RFC803.summary: Describes the Dacom 450 two-dimensional run-length compression algorithm and Dacom 500 T.4 facsimile coding, with PDP-11 encoder/decoder programs, frame formats, file formats and transcoding times.

fax.why: The whole document is about transcoding facsimile data between Dacom machine formats, T.4, run-length and bit-map formats.
fax.quote: software modules to encode and decode facsimile data for the Dacom 450 and 500 models Computerfax facsimile machines have been constructed

rejected.why: Compression algorithms are described, but they are fax image coding specific to the machines, not general lossless data compression formats.
A CRC polynomial is used for frame checksums, but only as a minor detail.
Written for the DARPA Internet program, but the content is not about ARPANET protocols.

RFC804.title: CCITT draft recommendation T.4
RFC804.summary: RFC 804 reproduces CCITT Draft Recommendation T.4, which standardizes Group 3 facsimile apparatus: scan geometry, line timing, one-dimensional run-length coding with code tables, and modulation choices for transmitting documents over telephone circuits.

fax.why: The whole document specifies Group 3 facsimile: scanning, resolution, run-length coding tables, EOL/RTC signals and modulation. Facsimile readers would expect it on this page.
fax.quote: STANDARDIZATION OF GROUP 3 FACSIMILE APPARATUS FOR DOCUMENT TRANSMISSION

rejected.why: The run-length coding is a image coding scheme for fax lines, not a general lossless data compression format.
The document concerns telephone-circuit transmission, but it is about fax apparatus rather than Internet/PSTN interworking or gateway signalling.
The code tables are encoding details internal to fax, which the fax tag already covers.

RFC805.title: Computer mail meeting notes
RFC805.summary: Meeting notes from a January 1982 gathering at ISI that concluded the ARPA Internet mailbox format should extend from user@host to user@host.domain with hierarchical domains, and discussed name server functions and action items.

DNS.why: The notes establish hierarchical domain names and the name server functions (location-id to address, recursive queries to domain name servers) that led to the DNS.
DNS.quote: the current "user@host" mailbox identifier should be extended to "user@host.domain" where "domain" could be a hierarchy of domains.

email.why: The meeting is about mail addressing and relaying, plus the mailbox format and the SMTP and RFC 733 revisions needed. No narrower email tag fits as well as the general one.
email.quote: issues of addressing are of major concern as we develop an internet in which mail relaying is a common occurance.

rejected.why: The notes touch on the host table and host name server. The main subject is hierarchical domain naming, not host naming conventions or host tables.
SMTP is only mentioned as something to revise to handle domain names. The document does not specify or analyse it.
The RFC 733 grammar change for host indicators is a small part of the document. Mail addressing is the main subject.
The "white pages" service is mentioned briefly and was not pursued.

RFC806.title: Proposed Federal Information Processing Standard: Specification for message format for computer based message systems
RFC806.summary: A proposed NBS/FIPS specification defining the semantics (fields) and a binary TLV syntax (data elements) for the format of messages exchanged between computer-based message systems.

message format.why: The whole document defines the format of messages, with fields such as From, To, Reply-To, Message-ID and Subject. It is an early counterpart to the Internet message format.
message format.quote: The message format specification defines the form and meaning of message contents and their components as they pass from one CBMS to another

email.why: It describes the architecture of store-and-forward electronic mail systems, with User Agents and a Message Transfer System, as a framework for the format.
email.quote: CBMS message transfer facilities are store-and-forward.
email.section: 2. A SIMPLE MODEL OF A CBMS ENVIRONMENT

rejected.why: It uses the IFIP WG 6.5 and CCITT message handling model, but it does not specify or interwork with X.400.
The tagged length-value encoding resembles BER, but the document defines its own encoding and does not use or cite ASN.1.
Message transfer protocols and envelopes are explicitly out of scope.
The Date element uses FIPS 4, 58 and 59 formats, which the document only references. It does not define an Internet timestamp format.

RFC807.title: Multimedia mail meeting notes
RFC807.summary: Notes from a January 1982 meeting of multimedia mail projects (CMU, ISI, MIT, COMSAT, BBN, UCL, SRI) agreeing on CCITT T.4 bitmap encoding, listing open issues, and defining a bitmap-text document exchange experiment based on RFC 759/767.

email.why: The whole document concerns multimedia computer mail: message formats, negotiation, delivery, mailbox addressing, and interfacing to text-only mail systems. No more specific email tag fits this early architecture discussion.
email.quote: A meeting was held at USC Information Sciences Institute on the 12th of January 1982 to discuss multimedia mail issues and experiments.

fax.why: Fax encoding (CCITT T.4, Rapicom) and a FAX-TEXT document exchange demonstration are a substantial part of the experiments and decisions.
fax.quote: We agree to use the encoding specified in the CCITT T.4 recommendation for the exchange of black and white bitmap data.

rejected.why: MIME did not exist in 1982. The memo discusses multimedia message body structure only in a pre-MIME context, and it defines no MIME mechanism.
It mentions the RFC 759/767 message formats and a 'Multimedia Virtual Message Format', but only as items for further study. The memo does not specify or analyse a format.
File transfer is only the means of moving data in the experiment, and CFTP is mentioned in passing.
This is an informal working meeting's notes. It is not an IAB/IRTF/community workshop report in the usual sense.

gaps.name: Multimedia mail
gaps.why: The document is about multimedia (voice, bitmap, fax) mail, but the taxonomy has no multimedia or voice-mail tag apart from the narrower VPIM. The general email tag is the nearest fit.

RFC808.title: Summary of computer mail services meeting held at BBN on 10 January 1979
RFC808.summary: Minutes of a January 1979 meeting at BBN on the state and future of ARPANET computer mail, recording problems with existing mail systems, discussion of multimedia/structured mail, and conclusions freezing the existing mail service (RFC 733 based).

email.why: The whole document is about ARPANET mail services, their problems, and rules for existing and next-generation mail systems.
email.quote: to discuss the state of computer mail in the ARPA community and to reach some conclusions to guide the further development of computer mail systems

ARPANET.why: The meeting concerns mail systems across ARPANET hosts, including a list of ARPANET mail systems, so ARPANET readers would want it.
ARPANET.quote: to discuss Message Service support on the ARPANET

internet history.why: A retrospective record of a historic meeting, with a list of early mail systems and attendees.
internet history.quote: This note is a very belated attempt to document a meeting that was held three years ago

rejected.why: RFC 733 format is mentioned, but the document does not specify or analyse message format; it only decides to limit its features.
MAIL/MLFL FTP reply codes are mentioned briefly as the transport, not the subject.
Multimedia mail is discussed as a future idea, but there is no MIME specification here.

RFC809.title: UCL facsimile system
RFC809.summary: Describes the UCL computerised facsimile system: an LSI-11 with a DACOM fax machine, bit-map display and floppy disks, attached to ARPANET/SATNET, covering fax transfer over networks, format conversion, image enhancement and editing, and a multi-process task architecture.

fax.why: The whole document describes a facsimile system that sends fax images over computer networks and interworks different fax machines. It is the closest taxonomy fit.
fax.quote: the computerised facsimile system developed in the Department of Computer Science at UCL

rejected.why: The system is attached to the ARPANET/SATNET and used for experiments, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
TCP is only the underlying transport for NIFTP and is not specified or extended here.
A CRC routine for DACOM blocks is mentioned, but this is a minor implementation detail.
Fax image compression (run-length, CCITT T.4) is discussed, but these are image-coding schemes rather than the lossless data compression formats in this tag.
The system moves fax image files with NIFTP file transfer, not through Internet mail.

gaps.name: Image processing / facsimile image coding (CCITT T.4, DACOM)
gaps.why: The document covers fax image scaling, cleaning, editing and compression, and the taxonomy has no tag for image processing or fax coding.

gaps.name: NIFTP (Network Independent File Transfer Protocol)
gaps.why: It is the file transfer protocol used to move fax data, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC810.title: DoD Internet host table specification
RFC810.summary: RFC 810 specifies the DoD Internet host table format (HOSTS.TXT) mapping network, gateway and host names to addresses, with machine type, OS and protocol info, replacing RFC 608.

hostnames.why: The document defines the host table file format and host/gateway/net naming conventions, which is exactly the hostnames subject (host naming conventions and host tables).
hostnames.quote: This paper specifies a new host table format applicable to both ARPANET and Internet needs.

rejected.why: The host table predates DNS and the document does not specify DNS; it is the flat-file precursor.
Describes address classes only as background for table entries; the document is about the table format, not IP addressing.
Context for the table, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations; its subject is the host table.
Address class description is incidental to specifying how addresses are written in the table.
Only mentioned as the way to retrieve the file and as a protocol option in the list.
Appears only in the protocol-name lists in the appendices.

RFC811.title: Hostnames Server
RFC811.summary: RFC 811 specifies the NIC Internet Hostnames Server, a simple text query/response protocol (TCP port 101 / NCP socket 101) for looking up host, gateway and network name/address entries from the central DoD Internet host table.

hostnames.why: The document defines a protocol for querying the central host name/address table (the successor of Hosts.txt), which is host naming and host-table subject matter.
hostnames.quote: The function of this particular server is to deliver machine-readable name/address information describing networks, gateways, hosts, and eventually domains

rejected.why: The document only mentions a future decentralized name service as an interim-solution remark; it does not describe DNS.
TCP is merely the transport the server listens on (port 101); nothing new is specified about TCP.
The more specific hostnames tag already covers this and implies the parent.
NCP is only an alternative transport (socket 101) for the server, and not the subject of the document.

RFC812.title: NICNAME/WHOIS
RFC812.summary: RFC 812 describes the NICNAME/WHOIS server at SRI-NIC, a TCP/NCP query/response directory service on port 43 that returns names, addresses, phone numbers and mailboxes for ARPANET users, along with its protocol and client programs.

WHOIS.why: The document specifies the original NICNAME/WHOIS directory protocol, its query format, and example responses. It is the legacy WHOIS service itself.
WHOIS.quote: The NICNAME protocol is similar to the NAME/FINGER protocol (RFC 742). To access the server: Connect to the service host (SRI-NIC) TCP: service port 43 decimal

rejected.why: The protocol is described as similar to NAME/FINGER, but the document specifies NICNAME, not Finger.
TCP is only the transport the service runs over, on port 43. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
The service runs on the ARPANET and serves its users, but the document is about the directory service, not ARPANET protocols or operations in general. NCP is likewise only a transport here.
The service is a directory lookup, but the WHOIS tag is the more specific fit and sits under domain registration. The X.500 and LDAP tags do not apply.

RFC813.title: Window and Acknowledgement Strategy in TCP
RFC813.summary: RFC 813 describes TCP implementation strategies for window management and acknowledgement, defining Silly Window Syndrome and sender/receiver algorithms (and delayed acknowledgement) to avoid it and reduce CPU overhead.

TCP.why: The whole document gives implementation guidance for TCP's window and acknowledgement mechanisms, including SWS avoidance and delayed ACKs.
TCP.quote: it is possible, while complying with the specification, to produce implementations which yield very bad performance.

rejected.why: The document deals with flow control windows and ACK efficiency, and it explicitly ignores gateway buffer overflow. It is not about congestion control.
IP is only the substrate here. The document discusses nothing at the IP layer.

RFC814.title: Name, addresses, ports, and routes
RFC814.summary: RFC 814 gives implementation guidance for host tables and algorithms handling names, addresses, ports and routes in TCP/IP, covering name caches/name servers, address-to-route translation with ICMP redirects, source routes, and port dispatching.

addressing.why: The document is largely about how hosts manage addresses and the address-to-route translation tables, including gateway selection by network number and address size tradeoffs.
addressing.quote: Host names are translated into network "addresses", 32-bit values that identify the network to which a host is attached, and the location of the host on that net.

naming.why: A substantial section covers host name to address translation, host tables versus name servers and caching, which is general naming guidance predating DNS.
naming.quote: the internet is moving from its current position in which a single name table is maintained by the NIC and distributed to all hosts, to a distributed approach

internet architecture.why: Section 6 discusses architectural rationale for the IP/TCP layering, why ports are not in IP, and the 32-bit address compromise.
internet architecture.quote: IP contained exactly those functions that the gateways must understand.

rejected.why: ICMP redirects are used for route table updates but the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
Ports are discussed as a dispatching concept, but TCP is not specified or extended here.
Host table handling is discussed in passing as part of general naming, not host naming conventions.
Gateway selection is host-side address-to-route lookup, not routing protocols or systems.
UDP is mentioned only as a case of port dispatching.

RFC815.title: IP datagram reassembly algorithms
RFC815.summary: RFC 815 describes a simple hole-descriptor-list algorithm for reassembling fragmented IP datagrams at the receiving host, including handling of options, buffer lookup and reassembly timeouts.

IPv4.why: The document specifies an implementation algorithm for IP (IPv4) fragment reassembly, using IPv4 header fields such as identification, more fragments, options and time to live.
IPv4.quote: One of the mechanisms of IP is fragmentation and reassembly.

rejected.why: The document is about IPv4 specifically, so the child tag IPv4 fits better than the parent.
The document predates IPv6 and concerns IPv4 header fields and options only.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation and reassembly
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IP fragmentation and reassembly. IPv4 is the closest fit, but readers looking for fragmentation topics would benefit from a dedicated tag.

RFC816.title: Fault isolation and recovery
RFC816.summary: RFC 816 describes the host's role in Internet fault isolation and recovery: detecting dead first-hop gateways, using ICMP redirect/unreachable advice, and how TCP and higher layers should handle timeouts and errors.

ICMP.why: The host's fault recovery relies on interpreting ICMP redirect, destination unreachable, echo and parameter problem messages. The document discusses how hosts should act on them, so ICMP readers would want it.
ICMP.quote: The ICMP "redirect" message indicates that the gateway to which the host sent the datagram is not longer the best gateway to reach the net in question.

TCP.why: A substantial part covers TCP timeout behaviour, the two modes of operation (abandon vs. report upward), and when TCP should give up on error messages.
TCP.quote: TCP has a single fault recovery action; it repeatedly retransmits a segment until either it gets an acknowledgement or its connection timer expires.

routing architecture.why: The document discusses the host/gateway division of responsibility for routing fault recovery and convergence after failures. No narrower routing tag fits.
routing architecture.quote: Gateways collectively implement an algorithm which identifies the best route between all pairs of networks.

rejected.why: SMTP is only used as an example of an application-level timeout problem. The document does not specify or extend it.
Server telnet is used only as an example of failure detection above TCP. The document does not specify Telnet.
The ICMP tag already sits under this topic. The document is about gateway fault handling, not the IP layer in general.
The Arpanet's 'host dead' message is mentioned briefly as one detection method. The document is not about the ARPANET.

RFC817.title: Modularity and efficiency in protocol implementation
RFC817.summary: RFC 817 discusses how modular structure and operating-system integration of protocol implementations (kernel vs. process vs. front-end, layering, TCP/IP processing costs) affect performance, and offers implementation efficiency guidance.

TCP.why: Much of the document gives TCP implementation efficiency advice: checksum cost, optimizing the expected-case packet path, retransmission queue organization, data copying, and per-connection TCP structuring.
TCP.quote: TCP is a more complex protocol, and presents many more opportunities for getting things wrong.

internet architecture.why: A substantial part of the document argues about protocol layering, modularity and layer boundaries versus efficiency, which is an architectural principle discussion.
internet architecture.quote: layering is a mixed blessing.

rejected.why: The checksum computation cost is discussed, but only as one performance bottleneck within TCP implementation, not as the subject.
Server telnet is used as a recurring example of kernel placement and packet combining, but the document does not specify or extend Telnet.
IP table lookup and fragmentation cost are mentioned briefly; the document is not about IP itself.
No relation; the discussion of caching hints in IP lookup is not web caching.

gaps.name: Protocol implementation performance and structuring
gaps.why: The document is about implementation architecture and performance engineering of protocol stacks in operating systems. No taxonomy tag covers implementation guidance in general.

RFC818.title: Remote User Telnet service
RFC818.summary: RFC 818 designates well-known port 107 for a Remote User Telnet service, where a connection to that port reaches a user Telnet on a host, using the Telnet protocol, with a BBN TC68K terminal concentrator example.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet-based service on a well-known port and gives a concrete Telnet deployment example (user Telnet back to back with server Telnet). Readers of the Telnet subject would want it.
Telnet.quote: This memo specifies that the specific service of User Telnet may be accessed (on hosts that choose to provide it) by opening a connection to port 107 (153 octal).

rejected.why: TCP and NCP are only the substrate whose well-known ports identify the service; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
NCP and ARPANET are mentioned only as background for the well-known socket concept; the document is not about the ARPANET itself.
Assigning port 107 is the substance of the memo, but it is a service definition rather than a discussion of registry policy or stewardship.

RFC819.title: The Domain Naming Convention for Internet User Applications
RFC819.summary: RFC 819 describes the hierarchical Internet domain naming convention (domains, simple names, absolute vs relative naming), name service/name servers (iterative vs recursive), naming authority, and its application to mail and host naming.

DNS.why: The document defines the hierarchical domain naming convention and name server behaviour (iterative and recursive), which is the origin of DNS. Readers of the DNS subject would expect it.
DNS.quote: Name service is a network service providing name-to-address translation.

hostnames.why: Covers the transition from flat ARPANET host names to domain-style host names such as USC-ISIF.ARPA and the allowed name syntax.
hostnames.quote: To be compatible with ARPANET naming convention, a host can be treated as an endpoint domain.

rejected.why: Mail addressing and relaying are used as the main application example, but the document is about naming, not mail transport.
UUCP is discussed only as an example of relative naming and a foreign naming environment, not as mail interchange.
Parent of DNS, which is implied by the more specific tag.
The BNF mailbox syntax in Appendix A is for the domain part of addresses, and the document does not specify the message format.
ARPANET naming is the starting context, but the document is about the new internet-wide convention.

RFC820.title: Assigned numbers
RFC820.summary: RFC 820 is a 1983 snapshot of the Assigned Numbers registry. It lists assigned network, IP version, IP protocol, port, autonomous system, ARPANET link and Ethernet type numbers, and Appendix A gives the DARPA/DDN allocation policy.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of protocol number assignments, with a named coordinator and an allocation policy. That is the predecessor of the IANA registries.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

addressing.why: A large part of the document explains the class A/B/C address formats and lists assigned network numbers. Appendix A sets how they are allocated among R&D, DoD and commercial users.
addressing.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

ARPANET.why: The document registers ARPANET link numbers and covers the Host/IMP interface and the NCP/TCP transition. Readers of ARPANET history would want it.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: IP addresses and protocol numbers are registered here, but the document does not specify IP itself.
TCP port numbers are listed. TCP is only the context for the registry and is not specified or extended.
Autonomous system numbers are assigned for EGP, but the protocol is only referenced.
A short table of Ethernet type numbers is included. It is incidental to the registry.

RFC821.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
RFC821.summary: RFC 821 is the original specification of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, defining its model, commands, reply codes, relaying, and transport bindings for reliable mail transfer.

SMTP.why: The whole document specifies SMTP: its commands, reply codes, relaying, and state diagrams.
SMTP.quote: The objective of Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently.

rejected.why: TCP is only one of several transport substrates described in an appendix; nothing new is specified about TCP.
The message format is defined by RFC 822. This document only adds Received and Return-Path trace lines, which are a minor part.
NCP is an alternative transport described in a short appendix and is not the subject of the document.
X.25 gets a brief appendix as a possible transport and is not the document's subject.
ASCII is only the character set used for commands and data, so it is a substrate here.
SMTP is the more specific tag and it implies the email parent.

RFC822.title: STANDARD FOR THE FORMAT OF ARPA INTERNET TEXT MESSAGES
RFC822.summary: RFC 822 specifies the syntax of Internet text message (email) headers and bodies, including header fields, address syntax, and date-time format, obsoleting RFC 733.

message format.why: The whole document defines the Internet message format: header fields, folding, structured fields, address and date syntax, and the message body separation.
message format.quote: This standard specifies a syntax for text messages that are sent among computer users, within the framework of "electronic mail".

rejected.why: Only referenced as a transport (RFC 821) and in Received 'with' values; the document defines content format, not the envelope or transfer protocol.
Uses an augmented BNF notation (Section 2) as a tool to specify the syntax, but the document is not about the notation itself.
Section 5 defines a date-time syntax, but it is a small part solely serving the Date header field.
Messages are ASCII text, but ASCII is only the substrate here.
Domain syntax in addresses is covered, but it is mail address syntax rather than host naming conventions.

RFC823.title: DARPA Internet gateway
RFC823.summary: Status report describing the BBN DARPA Internet gateway as of September 1982: datagram forwarding, GGP shortest-path routing, supported monitoring/debugging protocols, EGP overview, and software structure.

routing architecture.why: The document describes a gateway system's forwarding procedure, routing table, and dynamic shortest-path routing design, which is routing architecture in general. GGP has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy, so this is the closest fit.
