routing architecture.quote: The gateway's primary purpose is to route internet datagrams to their destination networks.

EGP.why: A section summarizes EGP's elements: neighbor acquisition, neighbor up/down, reachability information, and gateway going down.
EGP.quote: The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) is used to permit other gateways and gateway systems to pass routing information to the DARPA Internet gateways.

ICMP.why: The gateway's generation of ICMP errors and redirects is described in the forwarding section and in a dedicated section on supported ICMP messages.
ICMP.quote: The gateway will generate the following ICMP messages under appropriate circumstances as defined by the ICMP specification

rejected.why: IP is the datagram format being forwarded. The document describes the gateway's handling of it and does not specify or extend IP itself.
It is a historic design snapshot, but it is a technical status report and not a retrospective.
The ARPANET is only one of several networks the gateway attaches to, and the document does not cover ARPANET protocols.
The Host Monitoring Protocol and the XNET debugging protocol are described only briefly as protocols the gateway supports.

gaps.name: Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol (GGP)
gaps.why: The main protocol described, including message formats, the distance-vector algorithm and the sequence-numbered reliable updates. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

gaps.name: Host Monitoring Protocol (HMP) / XNET
gaps.why: Historic monitoring and debugging protocols for gateways. They have no tag, and network management is too broad to cover them.

RFC824.title: CRONUS Virtual Local Network
RFC824.summary: Describes the Cronus Virtual Local Network, a datagram-transport abstraction over a physical LAN that is IP-compatible, with VLN addressing (specific/broadcast/multicast) and an Ethernet implementation that dynamically maps internet addresses to 48-bit Ethernet addresses.

Ethernet.why: Section 4 specifies IP-over-Ethernet encapsulation, address mapping via multicast host addresses and dynamic mapping updates, and multicast/broadcast handling on Ethernet controllers.
Ethernet.quote: An internet datagram is encapsulated in an Ethernet frame by placing the internet datagram in the Ethernet frame data field, and setting the Ethernet type field to "DoD IP".

addressing.why: The note centrally defines how the local address field of internet addresses encodes specific, broadcast and multicast modes, plus Ethernet address assignment.
addressing.quote: VLN addresses, in contrast, may refer to all hosts (broadcast) or groups of hosts (multicast) in a Cronus cluster

rejected.why: The VLN-to-Ethernet mapping is a different, custom mechanism (VPMap with multicast fallback and Mapping Update frames), not ARP itself, though it serves the same purpose.
The VLN multicast is a link-level service over Ethernet, not IP multicast routing or group membership protocols such as IGMP.
IP is the layer the VLN carries and remains compatible with; the document does not specify or extend IP.
The ARPANET is mentioned only as a contrasting network and as the connection for the prototype.
The note concerns the layer below IP, so ethernet and addressing are more specific fits.

RFC825.title: Request for comments on Requests For Comments
RFC825.summary: RFC 825 specifies the purpose statements, distribution method and plain-text format rules (ASCII, 58-line pages, 72-character lines) that authors must follow when writing RFCs.

RFC series.why: The document is a specification for RFCs: required intent statements, online distribution and format constraints. This is the RFC series topic.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is intended to clarify the status of RFCs and to provide some guidance for the authors of RFCs in the future.

rejected.why: ASCII is only one of the format rules, as the required character code. The document is not about ASCII itself.
It covers RFC document conventions, not IETF standards process or administration.
The sample intent paragraphs are not glossary or requirements-language definitions.

RFC826.title: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol: Or Converting Network Protocol Addresses to 48.bit Ethernet Address for Transmission on Ethernet Hardware
RFC826.summary: RFC 826 specifies ARP, a protocol for dynamically mapping network-layer protocol addresses (e.g., IP) to 48-bit Ethernet hardware addresses, including packet format, request/reply processing, and table handling.

ARP.why: The document defines the Address Resolution Protocol itself: packet format, generation, reception algorithm, and translation table behaviour.
ARP.quote: Presented here is a protocol that allows dynamic distribution of the information needed to build tables to translate an address A in protocol P's address space into a 48.bit Ethernet address.

rejected.why: Ethernet is the hardware medium the protocol runs over; the document specifies address resolution, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM generally.
IP is used as the main example protocol being resolved, but the document is not about IP itself.
The document covers hardware-to-protocol address mapping, which ARP covers more specifically; no IP address architecture or allocation is addressed.

RFC827.title: Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP)
RFC827.summary: RFC 827 specifies the original Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), which lets gateways in different autonomous systems acquire neighbors, check neighbor reachability, and exchange network reachability messages.

EGP.why: The whole document defines EGP: neighbor acquisition, neighbor reachability, NR polling and messages, stub gateways, and message formats. EGP is the specific historic inter-domain protocol tag.
EGP.quote: The purpose of the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) is to enable one or more autonomous systems to be used as transport media

rejected.why: The document does discuss autonomous systems and a core/stub structure. But it is about the specific protocol, and EGP already covers it.
The stub gateway is required to implement ICMP alongside EGP. This is a minor dependency, not the subject of the document.
ARPANET and SATNET are only the example environment (the DARPA core gateways). The document does not address ARPANET protocols.
The EGP messages use the Internet one's complement checksum. It is only a field definition in the message formats.
BGP's successor role is not mentioned in the text. It is a later protocol, and EGP is the more specific tag here.

RFC828.title: Data communications: IFIP's international "network" of experts
RFC828.summary: An IFIP-authored report describing the activities of Technical Committee 6 (Data Communications) and its working groups on local networks, computer messaging, protocols and human factors, distributed to inform the ARPA Internet community.

messaging.why: A substantial section covers WG 6.5's work on international computer message systems, including the message transfer agent/user agent model and policy recommendations. It is general messaging, not any specific email protocol.
messaging.quote: International computer message systems and services form another rapidly developing topic

workshop reports.why: The document reports on the workshops, symposia and conferences run by IFIP TC 6 and its working groups, and on their programme. It is closest to a community activity report.
workshop reports.quote: These "state of the art" or review conferences are an important part of the TC 6 programme.

rejected.why: Ethernet and local networks are discussed as a subject of WG 6.4 interest, but the document does not specify or analyse IP over Ethernet.
The CCITT message-handling standards effort is mentioned only briefly and is not named as X.400.
ISDN is mentioned only as a future development, with no access or IP specifics.
Satellite systems are discussed as a possible future subgroup topic, not as a subject the document addresses in depth.
It mentions the ARPANET origins of WG 6.1 and early messaging, but it is not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Standards-body and liaison activity reports (IFIP TC 6)
gaps.why: The document describes the activities of an external standards organization, and the taxonomy has no tag for liaison or external organization reports.

RFC829.title: Packet satellite technology reference sources
RFC829.summary: RFC 829 briefly describes DARPA's packet satellite technology (ALOHA lineage, the Atlantic Packet Satellite Experiment SATNET, MATNET) and supplies a bibliography of reference papers on it.

satellite.why: The whole document describes packet satellite networking (SATNET, MATNET, shared satellite channels, channel assignment strategies) and lists references on it, so readers of the satellite subject would want it.
satellite.quote: the packet satellite technology developed by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and several other participating organizations in the U.K. and Norway

rejected.why: The ARPANET is mentioned only as a contrast to ALOHA and satellite multiaccess channels. The document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
It has some historical flavour, but it is a technology reference list for satellite packet networking, not a history or retrospective of the Internet.
Interconnection of packet networks appears only as cited references [28-29], not as a substantial part of the body.

gaps.name: Packet radio / multiaccess channel protocols (ALOHA, PODA, CPODA)
gaps.why: The document covers multiaccess channel sharing and demand assignment (ALOHA, PODA, CPODA) and packet radio. The taxonomy has no tag for this, only amateur radio and satellite.

RFC830.title: Distributed system for Internet name service
RFC830.summary: RFC 830 proposes SINS, a distributed Internet name service architecture combining domain name servers for hierarchical domain resolution with an application interface for service negotiation, and defines a binary command protocol between components.

DNS.why: The document is an early design for the domain name service: hierarchical domain resolution via cooperating domain name servers, name-to-address databases, caching, and a request/response protocol. It is a precursor to DNS.
DNS.quote: we propose an architecture for a distributed System for Internet Name Service (SINS)

service discovery.why: A substantial part of the design is the application interface, which negotiates available transport and application services and returns addresses and ports. This is service discovery and negotiation.
service discovery.quote: The application interface provides a "what-can-you-do-for-me" negotiation capability between the source and destination endpoint domains.

rejected.why: The NCP-to-TCP transition section touches on host tables, but the document is about a distributed name service, not host naming conventions.
UDP is only discussed as a possible transport for the name service commands. The document does not specify or extend UDP.
TCP is only a transport option and a source of port assignments. The document is not about TCP.
SMTP appears only in examples of services to be resolved and negotiated.
The ARPANET naming convention and the NCP transition are context. The document proposes an internet-wide name service rather than ARPANET working notes.

RFC831.title: Backup access to the European side of SATNET
RFC831.summary: Braden proposes a backup path for reaching the European side of a partitioned SATNET, using a multi-homed "header munger" host at UCL and the IP Source Routing option via the VAN gateway's X.25 IP tunnels.

IPv4.why: The proposal is built on the IPv4 Source Routing option and header address rewriting at a multi-homed host. It is the only fitting tag for this IP-layer mechanism.
IPv4.quote: using the source routing option of IP

satellite.why: The problem is backup access when the SATNET satellite network is partitioned. Readers interested in networking over satellite links would want it.
satellite.quote: access the European side of SATNET indirectly via the VAN Gateway, when direct SATNET connectivity has been lost

rejected.why: X.25 virtual circuits only carry the IP tunnels between the VAN gateway and UCL hosts. The document is not about IP over X.25.
Source routing here is a one-off backup mechanism at the IP layer. The document does not address routing systems or protocols.
The IP tunnels over X.25 are the existing substrate. The document does not define or specify a tunnelling mechanism.
ICMP unreachable messages are mentioned only in passing.
The ARPANET appears only as the US-side network where host H sits. The document does not cover its protocols or operations.

RFC832.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC832.summary: A 1982 survey reporting which ARPANET hosts claiming TCP, Telnet, FTP or SMTP service actually accepted, refused, or were dead/unreachable when probed, with per-host result tables.

TCP.why: The survey measures which hosts actually accept TCP connections for services, compared with claims in the NIC host table; it is about TCP deployment.
TCP.quote: Who Talks TCP?

ARPANET.why: It documents the state of hosts on the ARPANET at the time, as an operational working note of the early network.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 2-Dec-82.

rejected.why: Telnet is only one of the services probed for reachability; the document does not specify or analyse the protocol itself.
FTP is probed as a service (including anonymous login), but the protocol is not the subject.
SMTP acceptance is measured as one column of results; the document is not about the protocol.
The NIC host table is the source of claims, but the document is not about host naming conventions or host tables.

RFC833.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC833.summary: A December 1982 survey report listing ARPANET hosts and whether each accepted TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, compared against claims in the NIC host table.

TCP.why: The document surveys which hosts actually accept TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, i.e. TCP deployment/availability.
TCP.quote: Who Talks TCP?

ARPANET.why: It is an operational working note on ARPANET hosts (10.x.x.x addresses) and their service availability.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 2-Dec-82.

rejected.why: Telnet is only one of the probed services; the document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
FTP is a probed service with anonymous login results, but the document is not about the protocol itself.
SMTP is just one tested service in the survey.
The NIC host table is the data source, but the document is a connectivity survey, not about host naming conventions.
A dated snapshot, but not a retrospective or history.

RFC834.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC834.summary: A December 1982 survey of ARPANET hosts listed in the NIC host table, reporting which ones accepted TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, with summary tables and per-host results.

ARPANET.why: The document is a survey of ARPANET hosts and their TCP service availability, an operational working note on the early network.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 2-Dec-82.

TCP.quote: Claims are taken from the NIC host table: T = tcp (no particular services mentioned)

Telnet.why: One of three services tested, with its own summary table and per-host results.
Telnet.quote: Telnet Result no telnet unreachable refused dead accepted

FTP.why: FTP availability and anonymous login were tested and tabulated per host.
FTP.quote: accepted+ (FTP allowed user anonymous, password guest)

SMTP.why: SMTP acceptance was surveyed with its own summary table and per-host results.
SMTP.quote: SMTP Result no tcp/smtp unreachable refused dead accepted

rejected.why: The document draws its host list from the NIC host table but is about service availability, not naming conventions or host tables themselves.
It is a dated snapshot, but not a retrospective or history of the Internet.

RFC835.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC835.summary: A 1982 survey report listing ARPANET hosts and whether each accepted TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, compared against claims in the NIC host table.

TCP.why: The document is a survey of which hosts actually accept TCP connections for services, measuring TCP deployment on the network.
TCP.quote: Who Talks TCP?

Telnet.why: Telnet connectivity is one of three services tested, with its own summary table of results per host.
Telnet.quote: t = tcp/telnet

FTP.why: FTP acceptance, including anonymous login, is tested and tabulated for each host.
FTP.quote: accepted+ (FTP allowed user anonymous, password guest)

SMTP.why: SMTP availability is the third service tested, with its own summary table.
SMTP.quote: s = tcp/smtp

rejected.why: The host list comes from the NIC host table, but the document is about service availability, not naming conventions or host tables.
The hosts are ARPANET hosts, but the document does not address ARPANET protocols or operations as such; it surveys TCP services.
It is a period survey, but not a history or retrospective.

RFC836.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC836.summary: A January 1983 survey of ARPANET hosts listed in the NIC host table, reporting which ones accept TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, set against what the table claims.

TCP.why: The survey measures TCP deployment across hosts at the time of the ARPANET TCP transition, and records which hosts respond to TCP connections.
TCP.quote: Claims are taken from the NIC host table: T = tcp (no particular services mentioned)

ARPANET.why: It is an operational survey of ARPANET-era hosts (10.x.x.x addresses, BBN, ISI, MIT and others). It reads as a working note on the state of the network.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 20-Dec-82.

rejected.why: Telnet is only one of the services probed for reachability. The document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
FTP is probed for acceptance, including anonymous login. The protocol itself is not discussed.
SMTP is only probed for connection acceptance. The document does not address mail relaying behaviour.
The host table is the data source for the survey. The document is not about host naming conventions.

RFC837.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC837.summary: A 1983 survey of ARPANET hosts reporting which accepted TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP (including anonymous FTP), compared against the NIC host table's claimed services.

ARPANET.why: The document is a working note surveying ARPANET hosts and their service availability, which fits the ARPANET operations and working notes subject.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 31-Dec-82.

Telnet.why: Telnet connectivity is one of three services tested, with its own summary table and per-host results.
Telnet.quote: t = tcp/telnet

FTP.why: FTP acceptance and anonymous access are tested and summarized in a dedicated table.
FTP.quote: accepted+ (FTP allowed user anonymous, password guest)

SMTP.why: SMTP acceptance is tested for each host and summarized in its own table.
SMTP.quote: s = tcp/smtp

hostnames.why: The survey compares the NIC host table's claimed services against actual behaviour and lists results in host table order.
hostnames.quote: Claims are taken from the NIC host table:

rejected.why: TCP is the transport being probed, but the document does not specify or analyse the protocol itself; it only tests which hosts accept connections.

RFC838.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC838.summary: A January 1983 survey of NIC host-table hosts testing which actually accept TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, with summary tables and per-host results.

TCP.why: The survey measures which hosts really support TCP-based services, so it is a deployment census of TCP, and readers of the TCP subject would want it.
TCP.quote: T = tcp (no particular services mentioned)

Telnet.why: One of three services probed, with its own summary table and per-host Telnet results.
Telnet.quote: t = tcp/telnet

FTP.why: FTP is probed on every host, including whether anonymous login (user anonymous, password guest) is allowed.
FTP.quote: f = tcp/ftp

SMTP.why: SMTP availability is tested on every host and summarised in its own table.
SMTP.quote: s = tcp/smtp

rejected.why: The host list comes from the NIC hostname table, but the document reports service availability and does not address host naming or host tables.
The hosts are ARPANET-era, but the document never discusses the ARPANET or its protocols as a subject.

RFC839.title: Who talks TCP?
RFC839.summary: A January 1983 survey of which hosts in the NIC host table actually accepted TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, compared against the services each host claimed, with summary tables and per-host results.

TCP.why: The survey measures TCP deployment: which hosts claim and actually support TCP-based services. Readers interested in early TCP adoption would want this RFC.
TCP.quote: Claims are taken from the NIC host table:

rejected.why: Telnet is one of three services probed. The RFC reports connection results and does not specify or analyse the protocol.
FTP is only probed for acceptance, including anonymous login. The protocol itself is not discussed.
SMTP is only probed for connection acceptance. The RFC says nothing about the protocol.
The NIC host table supplies the host list and the claimed services. The RFC does not address host naming conventions or the table format.
The hosts are ARPANET/Internet hosts, but the document is about TCP service availability, not ARPANET operations or protocols.

RFC840.title: Official protocols
RFC840.summary: RFC 840 is a 1983 catalogue of the official Internet protocols. For each protocol it gives status, specification, comments, references, dependencies and a contact.

internet history.why: The document is a snapshot of the protocol suite as it stood in 1983, with its handbooks and planned revisions. Readers of Internet history would want it.
internet history.quote: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet.  Annotations identify any revisions or changes planned.

TCP.why: The TCP entry is long. It discusses the push, maximum segment size, idle connections, out-of-order segments and user time-out.
TCP.quote: Idle connections are ok, and should not be closed.
TCP.section: Network Level / Host Level: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

FTP.why: The FTP entry gives extended guidance on data connection management, the PORT and PASV commands, and transfer modes.
FTP.quote: All FTP implementations must support use of the default data connection ports, and only the User-PI may initiate the use of non-default ports.

Telnet.why: The document has a Telnet entry and a table of Telnet options with their usage status. It recommends a subset of the options.
Telnet.quote: The following are recommended:  Binary Transmission, Echo, Suppress Go Ahead, Status, Timing Mark, and Extended Options List.

rejected.why: It cites the ARPANET Protocol Handbook and the old NCP FTP. The document is about the Internet protocol suite, not ARPANET operations.
It points to Assigned Numbers (RFC 820) as an appendix entry. That is a pointer only, not the subject.
SMTP has a short entry, mostly about revision status. It is one of about 40 entries.
The IP entry notes a few problems in RFC 791. It is not enough to make this document about IPv4.
The Catenet Model entry only gives a reference to IEN 48.
The document catalogues protocol specifications. It is not about the RFC series itself.

gaps.name: Official protocol / standards status list
gaps.why: The document's main purpose is to list protocols with a status of required, recommended, elective or experimental. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol standards catalogues or status lists.

RFC841.title: Specification for message format for Computer Based Message Systems
RFC841.summary: FIPS PUB 98 (NBS) specifies the semantics and a binary TLV-style syntax for the content of messages exchanged between computer-based message systems (CBMS), covering fields, data elements, and message processing functions, but not transfer protocols or envelopes.

message format.why: The whole document defines a message format with fields such as From, To, Reply-To, Message-ID, In-Reply-To and Date. It is an early counterpart of RFC 733/822 Internet message format.
message format.quote: The purpose of this message format specification is to present the semantics and syntax to be used for messages being exchanged between CBMSs.
message format.section: 1.3 The Scope of the Message Format Specification

rejected.why: The document is about CBMS message content generally and explicitly excludes transfer protocols and envelopes. The more specific message format tag covers it.
ASCII-String is the main primitive data element, but ASCII is only a building block here, not the subject.
The document mentions the CCITT message handling model as a related effort and shares its User Agent/MTS model, but it is not about X.400.
The identifier/length/contents encoding resembles ASN.1 BER but never references it, and the document defines its own encoding.
The Date data element uses FIPS 4/58/59 formats, but this is a minor part of the document.

gaps.name: Computer Based Message Systems (CBMS) message format / FIPS 98 binary message encoding
gaps.why: The binary TLV data-element encoding (identifier octet, length code, qualifier, property-list) has no matching tag. The message format tag captures the semantics but not this encoding.

RFC842.title: Who talks TCP? - survey of 1 February 83
RFC842.summary: A February 1983 survey of ARPANET hosts reporting which ones accept TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, with summary tables and per-host results.

TCP.why: The survey measures which hosts actually accept TCP connections for services, i.e. TCP deployment/adoption on the ARPANET.
TCP.quote: Who Talks TCP? - Survey of 1 February 83

Telnet.why: Telnet service availability is one of three surveyed services, with its own summary table and per-host results.
Telnet.quote: t = tcp/telnet

FTP.why: FTP availability, including anonymous login, is tested and tabulated.
FTP.quote: accepted+ (FTP allowed user anonymous, password guest)

SMTP.why: SMTP service availability is surveyed with its own summary table.
SMTP.quote: s = tcp/smtp

ARPANET.why: The document surveys ARPANET hosts and their operational status.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 28-Jan-83.

rejected.why: The NIC host table is only the source of the host list; the document is not about host naming.
It is a dated survey, not a history or retrospective.

RFC843.title: Who talks TCP? - survey of 8 February 83
RFC843.summary: A 1983 survey of ARPANET hosts reporting which ones accepted TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, compared against the claims in the NIC host table.

ARPANET.why: The document is a survey of ARPANET hosts and their TCP service availability, which is operational ARPANET working-note material.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 3-Feb-83.

TCP.why: The survey tests which hosts actually accept TCP connections, so it is about TCP deployment, though it specifies no protocol.
TCP.quote: Claims are taken from the NIC host table: T = tcp (no particular services mentioned)

Telnet.why: One of the three services surveyed, with its own results table.
Telnet.quote: Telnet Result no telnet unreachable refused dead accepted

FTP.why: FTP availability and anonymous login are surveyed with a dedicated table.
FTP.quote: accepted+ (FTP allowed user anonymous, password guest)

SMTP.why: SMTP availability is the third surveyed service and has its own results table.

hostnames.why: The survey compares the NIC host table's claims with observed behaviour, and the body is mostly a host-name listing.
hostnames.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 3-Feb-83.

rejected.why: It is a dated snapshot, not a history or retrospective.
It is a one-off survey, not a management or operations mechanism.

RFC844.title: Who talks ICMP, too? - Survey of 18 February 1983
RFC844.summary: A 1983 survey reporting which ARPANET hosts accepting TELNET could be reached from a class C site host that speaks ICMP redirects, with per-host results.

ICMP.why: The survey tests whether hosts handle ICMP-based gateway routing (redirects) and class C addressing. This is a minor part of the document, but it is the point of the title and the test.
ICMP.quote: This requires, in addition to IP and TCP, participation in gateway routing via ICMP and handling of class C addresses.

Telnet.why: The survey measures TELNET connectivity to hosts. Telnet connection attempts are the test method and the result being reported.
Telnet.quote: A survey was undertaken to determine how many hosts are able to respond to TELNET connections from a user at a class C site.

ARPANET.why: The hosts surveyed are ARPANET (net 10) and other internet hosts. The document is an operational survey of that network.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from RFC843, extracting only those hosts which are listed there as accepting TELNET connections.

rejected.why: IP and class C addressing are the setting for the survey. The document does not specify or analyse IPv4.
TCP is only the substrate under Telnet. Nothing about it is specified or analysed.
The document is a dated survey. It is not a history or retrospective, even though it is now historical.

RFC845.title: Who talks TCP? - survey of 15 February 1983
RFC845.summary: A 1983 survey that probes ARPANET hosts listed in the NIC host table to see which accept TCP connections for Telnet, FTP and SMTP, and reports the results per host.

TCP.why: The survey measures which hosts actually run TCP services compared with what they claim, so it documents TCP deployment.
TCP.quote: Who Talks TCP? -- Survey of 15 February 1983

Telnet.why: Telnet is one of three services tested, with its own result table and per-host column.
Telnet.quote: t = tcp/telnet

FTP.why: FTP is tested on every host, including whether anonymous login with password guest is allowed.
FTP.quote: f = tcp/ftp

SMTP.why: SMTP acceptance is tested for each host and summarised in its own table.
SMTP.quote: s = tcp/smtp

rejected.why: The NIC host table is only the source of the host list. The document does not discuss host naming.
The surveyed hosts are ARPANET hosts, but the document is about TCP service adoption and not ARPANET operations.

RFC846.title: Who talks TCP? - survey of 22 February 1983
RFC846.summary: A 1983 survey of ARPANET hosts that probed which hosts actually accepted TCP Telnet, FTP and SMTP connections, compared against claims in the NIC host table, with summary tables and per-host results.

TCP.why: The survey measures which hosts accept TCP connections for services, so it is about TCP deployment. It does not specify TCP itself, but readers of TCP history would look for it.
TCP.quote: Who Talks TCP? -- Survey of 22 February 1983

ARPANET.why: The document surveys ARPANET hosts, addresses (10.x.x.x) and the NIC host table, so it is a working note on the early network.
ARPANET.quote: The list of hosts was taken from the NIC hostname table of 18-Feb-83.

rejected.why: Telnet is only one of three services probed. The RFC reports acceptance rates and does not specify the protocol.
FTP is probed as a service, including anonymous login. The document is not about the protocol.

RFC847.title: Summary of Smallberg surveys
RFC847.summary: A 1983 summary table of David Smallberg's weekly surveys of how many ARPANET hosts accepted connections to their Telnet, FTP and SMTP servers, compared with total hosts.

ARPANET.why: The memo is a working note on the early ARPANET/Internet, reporting host counts and server availability across the network in 1982-83. Fits the ARPANET topic's operations and working notes.
ARPANET.quote: surveys of Telnet, FTP and Mail (SMTP) servers conducted by David Smallberg in December 1982 and January and February 1983

Telnet.why: A full table reports Telnet server acceptance rates per survey, so readers of Telnet history would want it.
Telnet.quote: extracts the number of hosts that accepted the connection to their server for each of Telnet, FTP, and SMTP

FTP.why: A full table reports FTP server acceptance rates per survey.
FTP.quote: extracts the number of hosts that accepted the connection to their server for each of Telnet, FTP, and SMTP

SMTP.why: A full table reports SMTP server acceptance rates per survey.
SMTP.quote: surveys of Telnet, FTP and Mail (SMTP) servers

rejected.why: It is a contemporaneous data summary, not a retrospective, so ARPANET fits better.
SMTP is only one of three services surveyed, so the more specific SMTP tag covers it.

RFC848.title: Who provides the "little" TCP services?
RFC848.summary: A 1983 survey listing which ARPANET hosts offered the "little" TCP services (Echo, Discard, Active Users, Daytime, Netstat, QOTD, Chargen, Time, Finger), based on tests from ISI-VAXA.

small services.why: The whole document is a per-host census of the small TCP services (Echo, Discard, Chargen, Daytime, Active Users, QOTD), so readers of that subject would want it.
small services.quote: This report lists those hosts which provide any of these "little" TCP services

Finger.why: Finger is one of the surveyed services, and the document includes a table of 35 hosts providing it. It is only one of nine services, so this is secondary.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport the services run over. The document says nothing new about the protocol.
The hosts are ARPANET hosts and the data comes from the NIC hostname table, but the document is about the services and not the network itself. I considered it a weak fit.
The document uses the NIC host table as its input list. It does not address host naming conventions.

RFC849.title: Suggestions for improved host table distribution
RFC849.summary: RFC 849 is a 1983 request for comments proposing improved ways to distribute and update the SRI-NIC HOSTS.TXT host table to Internet hosts, via NIC push updates, version polling, or mail.

hostnames.why: The document is about the distribution and updating of the host table (HOSTS.TXT), the central artifact of host naming at the time, and proposes protocols for its update.
hostnames.quote: Each site is expected to individually maintain a copy of the [SRI-NIC]<NETINFO>HOSTS.TXT file

rejected.why: DNS is not mentioned; the document predates it and proposes improving host table distribution, not a domain name system.
Considered as the parent topic, but the hostnames tag fits the host table subject more specifically.
FTP is only mentioned as the means of retrieving HOSTS.TXT (anonymous FTP); it is not specified or extended here.
Mail distribution of the table is one rejected option among the suggestions; the document is not about email.

RFC850.title: Standard for interchange of USENET messages
RFC850.summary: RFC 850 defines the USENET news article format (an RFC 822-based header set), control messages, transmission methods (remote execution, mail, batching) and the news propagation algorithm.

Netnews.why: The whole document specifies the netnews article format, control messages and propagation, which is exactly the Netnews subject.
Netnews.quote: This document defines the standard format for interchange of Network News articles among USENET sites.

UUCP.why: UUCP is a main transmission method for news, and senduuname exists to build UUCP mail routing maps. The document is not a UUCP specification, so this is only secondary.
UUCP.quote: news would be sent over a UUCP link with the command "uux - remote!rnews"

rejected.why: Articles must be valid RFC 822 messages and the document profiles the headers. The document is about news articles, not the general Internet message format, so the Netnews tag covers it.
Mail is used only as one possible transfer method (section 4.2) and as the base format. The document is not about email.
NNTP is not mentioned. The transmission methods here are UUCP, remote execution and mail.

RFC851.title: ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol
RFC851.summary: RFC 851 specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, a successor to 1822 that lets hosts address each other by logical names through new Host-IMP leader formats, name declaration, and an IMP name server.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies a host-to-IMP access protocol for the ARPANET, including leader formats, NOP handshakes, and IMP behaviour. This is ARPANET host and network protocol work.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, which will allow hosts to use logical addressing

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host protocol. This document covers the host-IMP interface below it and only mentions host-to-host protocols in passing.
1822L names are logical addresses at the IMP level. They are not name resolution in the general naming sense, and the closest fit is the ARPANET tag.
The addressing is ARPANET-specific host-IMP addressing, not IP address architecture.

gaps.name: 1822 / 1822L host-IMP interface
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the ARPANET host-to-IMP access protocol (BBN Report 1822). The ARPANET topic is the nearest fit.

RFC852.title: ARPANET short blocking feature
RFC852.summary: RFC 852 specifies the ARPANET Short Blocking Feature, an addition to the 1822 and 1822L host-IMP access protocols that lets hosts request a two-second maximum IMP blocking time via new Type 0 subtypes and new Type 9 Incomplete Transmission subtypes.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies an ARPANET host-IMP interface feature (1822/1822L host access protocols, IMP blocking, message subtypes), which is squarely ARPANET protocol work.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC specifies the ARPANET Short Blocking Feature, which will allow a host to shorten the amount of time that it may be blocked by its IMP

rejected.why: NCP is the host-host protocol; this document concerns the host-IMP interface (1822), not NCP.
Congestion control is only one of several listed reasons for message rejection; the document is about host blocking timers, not congestion control mechanisms.
It is a historic protocol spec but not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: 1822 / 1822L Host Access Protocol (IMP host interface)
gaps.why: The document extends the ARPANET host-IMP access protocols; the taxonomy has no specific tag for them beyond the general ARPANET topic.

RFC854.title: Telnet Protocol Specification
RFC854.summary: RFC 854 is the Internet Standard specification of the Telnet protocol, defining the Network Virtual Terminal, option negotiation (DO/DON'T/WILL/WON'T), control functions, the Synch signal and the command structure.

Telnet.why: The whole document specifies the Telnet protocol: NVT, option negotiation, commands, and port assignment.
Telnet.quote: The purpose of the TELNET Protocol is to provide a fairly general, bi-directional, eight-bit byte oriented communications facility.

rejected.why: Telnet runs over TCP and uses Urgent for Synch, but the document does not specify or extend TCP; it is only the substrate.
The NVT uses seven-bit USASCII, but this is a dependency rather than a subject of the document.

RFC855.title: Telnet Option Specifications
RFC855.summary: RFC 855 specifies how Telnet options are documented and assigned option codes, and describes the subnegotiation mechanism (IAC SB ... IAC SE) used by options needing parameters.

Telnet.why: The document is a specification of the Telnet protocol's option mechanism: required documentation sections for options and the subnegotiation procedure using DO/WILL/SB/SE.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies a method of option code assignment and standards for documentation of options.

rejected.why: Option code assignment by Postel is described, but it is a small part of a document that is really about Telnet option documentation and subnegotiation, not the IANA registry in general.
The document sets documentation standards for options, but this is protocol-specific, not general IETF process.

RFC856.title: Telnet Binary Transmission
RFC856.summary: RFC 856 specifies the Telnet Binary Transmission option, which lets two Telnet peers negotiate 8-bit binary data transmission, per direction, in place of NVT ASCII.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option, TRANSMIT-BINARY, with its commands, defaults and negotiation rules. It belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: the sender of this command REQUESTS permission to begin transmitting, or confirms that it will now begin transmitting characters which are to be interpreted as 8 bits of binary data

rejected.why: NVT ASCII is mentioned only as the default mode that binary mode reverts to. The document is not about ASCII.
EBCDIC appears only as an example of another mode that implementations may refuse while binary mode is active.
FTP is mentioned only as a higher-level alternative for binary transfer.

RFC857.title: Telnet Echo Option
RFC857.summary: RFC 857 specifies the Telnet ECHO option, which lets the two ends of a Telnet connection negotiate which side echoes data characters, with its commands, default, modes and a sample implementation.

Telnet.why: The document defines the ECHO option of the Telnet protocol, including its commands (WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T ECHO), defaults and negotiation behaviour.
Telnet.quote: it is necessary that there be a TELNET option to allow the parties at the two ends of the TELNET connection to agree that characters typed on an NVT keyboard are to be echoed

rejected.why: The Echo service of the small services is a separate TCP/UDP service; this document is about a Telnet option, not that service.
Telnet runs over TCP, but TCP is only the substrate and the document specifies nothing about it.
ASCII is mentioned only incidentally (ESC character echo) and is not a subject of the document.

RFC858.title: Telnet Suppress Go Ahead Option
RFC858.summary: Specifies the Telnet SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD option (option code 3), which lets Telnet parties agree to stop sending the GA character on full-duplex connections.

Telnet.why: The whole document defines a Telnet option, including its command codes, defaults and semantics, so it belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: it is desirable to have a TELNET option with which parties involved can agree that one or the other or both should suppress transmission of GO AHEADS

rejected.why: The Telnet tech tag sits under it and already covers the document, so the parent topic is not given separately.
Telnet usually runs over TCP, but the document says nothing about TCP. It is only the implied substrate.

RFC859.title: Telnet Status Option
RFC859.summary: RFC 859 specifies the Telnet STATUS option, which lets one Telnet peer ask for and report the other's view of the current state of Telnet options through SB subnegotiation.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option, including its command codes, subcommands (SEND and IS) and negotiation behaviour, so it belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: This option allows a user/process to verify the current status of TELNET options (e.g., echoing) as viewed by the person/process on the other end

RFC860.title: Telnet Timing Mark Option
RFC860.summary: RFC 860 specifies the Telnet Timing Mark option, which lets one end of a Telnet connection synchronize with the other by inserting a mark in the data stream. Uses include flushing type-ahead input and measuring round-trip delay.

Telnet.why: The document defines the TIMING-MARK option (code 6) for Telnet, including its DO/WILL/WON'T/DON'T semantics. This is a Telnet option specification.
Telnet.quote: It is sometimes useful for a user or process at one end of a TELNET connection to be sure that previously transmitted data has been completely processed

rejected.why: Telnet normally runs over TCP, but the document says nothing about TCP. It is only the substrate.
Measuring round-trip delay is listed as one example application. The document is not about performance measurement methods.

RFC861.title: Telnet Extended Options: List Option
RFC861.summary: Defines the Telnet Extended Options-List option (code 255), which reserves a way to negotiate a 257th and later Telnet options through subnegotiation.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet option (EXOPL), its commands, defaults and subnegotiation format, so it belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: Eventually, a 257th TELNET option will be needed. This option will extend the option list for another 256 options

RFC862.title: Echo Protocol
RFC862.summary: RFC 862 specifies the Echo Protocol, a debugging and measurement service that returns any received data to the sender, over TCP port 7 and UDP port 7.

small services.why: The document defines the Echo service, one of the TCP/UDP small services. The whole document is about it.
small services.quote: An echo service simply sends back to the originating source any data it receives.

rejected.why: TCP is only a transport for one variant of the service. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only a transport for the datagram variant. The document defines nothing new about UDP usage.
The document calls echo a measurement tool, but it specifies only the echo service and no measurement metrics or methods.

RFC863.title: Discard Protocol
RFC863.summary: RFC 863 specifies the Discard Protocol, a debugging and measurement service that throws away any data received, over TCP port 9 and UDP port 9.

small services.why: The document defines the Discard service, one of the TCP/UDP small services, so it belongs on that subject's page.
small services.quote: A useful debugging and measurement tool is a discard service. A discard service simply throws away any data it receives.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport for one variant of the service. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only the transport for the datagram variant. The document adds nothing about UDP itself.

RFC864.title: Character Generator Protocol
RFC864.summary: Specifies the Character Generator Protocol, a debugging and measurement service on TCP and UDP port 19 that sends arbitrary character data, with a recommended rotating 72-character ASCII pattern.

small services.why: The RFC defines the Chargen service, one of the TCP/UDP small services, on port 19 over both TCP and UDP.
small services.quote: A useful debugging and measurement tool is a character generator service. A character generator service simply sends data without regard to the input.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate for the connection-based variant; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only the transport for the datagram variant; the document adds nothing about UDP itself.
The recommended test pattern uses the ASCII printing characters, but the document is not about the ASCII character set.

RFC865.title: Quote of the Day Protocol
RFC865.summary: RFC 865 specifies the Quote of the Day Protocol, a simple TCP and UDP service on port 17 that returns a short quote and ignores any input, for debugging and measurement.

small services.why: The document defines the Quote of the Day (QOTD) service, one of the TCP/UDP small services, on port 17 over both TCP and UDP.
small services.quote: A useful debugging and measurement tool is a quote of the day service.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport the service runs over; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only a transport for the datagram variant; the document does not specify or extend UDP.
The quote syntax only recommends ASCII printing characters; the document is not about ASCII.

RFC866.title: Active users
RFC866.summary: RFC 866 specifies the Active Users service, a debugging and measurement service on TCP and UDP port 11 that returns a list of currently logged-in users.

small services.why: The document specifies the Active Users service, one of the TCP/UDP small services (Echo, Discard, Chargen, QOTD, Daytime, Active Users), on port 11 over both TCP and UDP.
small services.quote: A useful debugging and measurement tool is an active users service.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport the service runs over. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only a transport for the datagram variant. The document does not specify or extend UDP.
Finger also reports user information, but this is a different protocol. SYSTAT and WHO are mentioned only to define what an active user is.

RFC867.title: Daytime Protocol
RFC867.summary: RFC 867 specifies the Daytime Protocol, a simple TCP and UDP service on port 13 that returns the current date and time as an ASCII string, intended for debugging and measurement.

small services.why: Daytime is one of the TCP/UDP small services (Echo, Discard, Chargen, QOTD, Daytime, Active Users), and this RFC is its specification.
small services.quote: A server listens for TCP connections on TCP port 13.  Once a connection is established the current date and time is sent out the connection

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport the service runs over; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only the alternative transport; nothing about UDP itself is specified.
The service gives a human-readable time string for debugging. It is not about clock synchronization, and the note points to the Time Protocol for machine-usable time.
ASCII is just the encoding of the returned string; the document is not about the character set.
SMTP is mentioned only as the source of one example date syntax.

RFC868.title: Time Protocol
RFC868.summary: RFC 868 specifies the Time Protocol, a simple service on port 37 over TCP or UDP that returns the current time as a 32-bit count of seconds since 1900-01-01 GMT.

time synchronization.why: The protocol exists so hosts can obtain machine-readable network time to check or correct their clocks. This is clock synchronization over a network, and no more specific technology tag (NTP, PTP) fits.
time synchronization.quote: makes it possible to quickly confirm or correct a system's idea of the time

rejected.why: The Time Protocol is a separate, much simpler service. It does not specify, extend or analyse NTP.

The Time service is similar to Echo, Discard and Daytime, but this tag lists specific services (Echo, Discard, Chargen, QOTD, Daytime, Active Users) and the Time Protocol is not among them. The document itself does not describe it as one of them.
TCP is only one of two transports the service runs over. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only a transport substrate here. The document defines nothing new about how UDP is used.
The 32-bit seconds-since-1900 value is a time representation. However, the tag is about Internet timestamp formats such as RFC 3339, and the document's focus is the service that delivers the time.

gaps.name: Time Protocol (port 37)
gaps.why: There is no tag for this specific protocol, which is a standalone network time service. It is only partly covered by the general time synchronization topic.

RFC869.title: Host Monitoring Protocol
RFC869.summary: Specifies the Host Monitoring Protocol (HMP), a connectionless polling-based transport protocol (IP protocol 20) used by a monitoring center to collect traps, status and throughput statistics from IMPs, TACs and gateways, with appendices defining message formats.

ARPANET.why: HMP is an early ARPANET-era monitoring protocol, with appendices defining IMP and TAC monitoring messages and 1822 statistics. It is a host/network operations protocol of that network.
ARPANET.quote: The Host Monitoring Protocol (HMP) is used to collect information from hosts in various networks.

network management.why: The protocol is for monitoring and managing hosts, gateways and packet switches, with traps, polling, status, statistics and parameter setting. This makes it an early network management protocol.
network management.quote: HMP is used to collect three different classes of data: Spontaneous Events (or Traps), Current status, Statistical data collected over time

rejected.why: The document calls HMP a transport protocol, but it is a monitoring application protocol with a simple transaction mechanism. It is not about transport in general.
HMP rides on IPv4 (protocol number 20), which is only the substrate.
The one's complement checksum is just a header field and not the subject of the document.
The gateway appendix mentions EGP only as a measurement flag, so the document is not about EGP.
SNMP is a later and unrelated management protocol, and this document does not cover it.

RFC870.title: Assigned numbers
RFC870.summary: RFC 870 is the 1983 Assigned Numbers list, a registry of network numbers, IP version and protocol numbers, port numbers, AS numbers, ARPANET link numbers, Ethernet types and X.121 mappings, plus the allocation policy.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned protocol numbers and the policy for assigning them. This is the predecessor of the IANA registries.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations.

IPv4.why: A large part of the document defines class A/B/C IPv4 addressing and lists assigned network numbers. It also covers the IP version and protocol number fields and the allocation of address space.
IPv4.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

rejected.why: The ARPANET link number list is a small section. The document is a general number registry, not about the ARPANET.
IPv4 is the more specific fit for the address-class and network-number content.
Port numbers are listed for TCP/UDP use, but the document does not specify TCP.
The document only registers autonomous system numbers for EGP. It does not specify the protocol.

RFC871.title: Perspective on the ARPANET reference model
RFC871.summary: Padlipsky's 1982 paper articulates the ARPANET Reference Model (axioms of resource sharing, IPC, logical connections, layering, common intermediate representations), the design goals of TCP/IP and gateways, and contrasts the ARM with the ISO OSI reference model.

internet architecture.why: The document is an architectural reference model: layering, axioms, gateways, and a comparison with ISORM. Fits the architectural principles subject.
internet architecture.quote: the conceptual framework in which the ARPANET intercomputer networking protocol suite, including the DoD standard Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and Internet Protocol (IP), were designed

ARPANET.why: It describes the ARPANET Network Working Group's conceptual model and protocol suite, and the history of its concepts.
ARPANET.quote: the designers of the ARPANET protocol suite have had a reference model of their own all the long

internet history.why: A retrospective by a participant on the origins of layering, virtualization and logical connections.
internet history.quote: many now widely-accepted, fundamental concepts of intercomputer networking were original to the ARPANET Network Working Group

TCP.why: A substantial section explains the design goals and constraints of TCP, including reliability and replacing the original host-host protocol.
TCP.quote: the first discernible goal of what was to become TCP/IP was to develop a protocol to achieve "internetting"

rejected.why: IP is discussed only as part of the architectural design rationale, not specified or extended.
The NVT is cited as an example of a common intermediate representation, not specified.
FTP is used as an example of virtualization and the equity principle, not the subject.
X.25 is criticized in the OSI comparison but the document does not address it as a subject in its own right.
The OSI tag covers network-layer protocols and coexistence with IP; this paper compares reference models rather than addressing those protocols.
The original host-host protocol is mentioned only as background for TCP's design goals.

RFC872.title: TCP-on-a-LAN
RFC872.summary: Padlipsky argues that the fear that TCP/IP is inappropriate for use on a local area network is unfounded, explaining LANs, TCP, IP and UDP layering and noting the TCP checksum costs only about 12% of per-transmission processing.

TCP.why: The whole paper defends the use of TCP on local networks, covering its properties, checksum overhead and measured performance.
TCP.quote: fearing "TCP-on-a-LAN" is a Woozle which needs slaying.

internet layer.why: A substantial part explains IP's role, separation from TCP, gateways, fragmentation and the catenet, which is general IP-layer matter.
internet layer.quote: IP handles internet routing, whereas TCP (or some other Host-Host  protocol) handles only internet addressing.

internet architecture.why: The paper argues from the ARPANET Reference Model and the Principle of Layering, which are architectural principles.
internet architecture.quote: in ARPANET-style layering, layers aren't monoliths.

rejected.why: UDP is mentioned only briefly as an alternative for applications like packetized speech, not the subject.
The TCP checksum overhead is a supporting point, not a main subject.
The ARPANET reference model is context only; the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
LANs are the environment discussed, but the document is about TCP/IP use over them, not link-layer technology.

RFC873.title: Illusion of vendor support
RFC873.summary: Padlipsky argues that waiting for vendor-supported ISO Reference Model (OSI) protocols is a fallacy compared with procuring the existing ARPANET Reference Model protocols (TCP/IP, Telnet, FTP), citing timeliness, ambiguity, design process and efficiency.

internet architecture.why: The paper compares the ISO and ARPANET reference models and their layering principles, and argues for the ARPANET approach. That is architectural argument.
internet architecture.quote: The sometimes-held position that "vendor supplied" intercomputer networking protocols based upon the International Standards Organization's Reference Model for Open System Interconnection are worth waiting for

rejected.why: The OSI tag covers OSI network-layer protocols and their coexistence with IP. This paper critiques the OSI reference model and standards process in general and does not specify or analyse those protocols.
TCP is only named as an example ARPANET protocol and as a point of contrast, so the paper is not about TCP.
X.25 comes up as part of the ISO suite, but the document does not analyse it as a subject. It uses X.25 ambiguities as examples.
The paper is a 1982 position piece with some anecdotes about ARPANET design. It is not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: OSI vs ARPANET reference model / protocol standards politics
gaps.why: The paper's core subject is the comparison of ISO and ARPANET reference models and the procurement of standards. Only the broad internet architecture tag fits.

RFC874.title: Critique of X.25
RFC874.summary: Padlipsky's critique of the CCITT X.25 network interface protocol and the ISO Reference Model, arguing X.25 is poorly layered, ambiguous, space-time inefficient, unsuited to DoD security and survivability needs, and inferior to the ARPANET IP/TCP approach.

X.25.why: The whole document analyses X.25's conceptual model, personality problems, internetting via X.75, physical interface constraints and security, concluding it is not good.
X.25.quote: The widely touted network interface protocol, "X.25", and its attendant conceptual framework, the International Standards Organization's Reference Model for Open System Interconnection (ISORM), are analyzed and found wanting.

rejected.why: The OSI tag covers network-layer protocols and coexistence with IP. The ISO Reference Model is discussed mainly as the framework around X.25, not the OSI network-layer protocols, so X.25 is the better fit.
The paper compares layering and architectural principles such as the ARPANET Reference Model against the ISORM. Its subject is a critique of X.25, so the architecture tag is only secondary at most.
IP is mentioned as an alternative internetting approach that could run over X.25 subnets, but the document does not specify or analyse IP.
TCP is cited for comparison, for example the Well-Known Socket concept and the claim that X.25 needs a protocol as strong as TCP beneath it. The document is not about TCP.

RFC875.title: Gateways, architectures, and heffalumps
RFC875.summary: Padlipsky's essay argues that translating/mapping gateways between networks with differing protocol suites (e.g., NCP vs TCP/IP) suffer addressing, flow-control, out-of-band signalling and state problems, and that a protocol-compatible internet with IP gateways is preferable.

internet architecture.why: The document is an architectural argument against protocol-translating gateways and for a protocol-compatible internet, which is about internet architectural principles.
internet architecture.quote: the implications and shortcomings of gateways which must translate or map between differing protocol suites are not widely understood

ARPANET.why: A substantial part of the analysis uses ARPANET NCP, 1822 Host-IMP addressing and RFNMs as the worked example of mismatch against TCP/IP.
ARPANET.quote: the original ARPANET "NCP" -- which consists, strictly speaking, of the unnamed original ARPANET Host-Host Protocol and the unfortunately named "1822"

humor.why: The essay is satirical in tone and builds its conclusion on a Winnie-the-Pooh Heffalump parable, making it a whimsical document.
humor.quote: Gateways are Heffalumps

rejected.why: NCP is used as an example of a mismatched protocol set, not specified or analysed in its own right.
TCP is only one side of the NCP/TCP mismatch example, not the subject.
IP gateways are discussed, but the focus is the architectural argument against protocol translation, better captured by internet architecture.
SMTP is mentioned only in passing as a complex workaround for mail addressing.

RFC876.title: Survey of SMTP implementations
RFC876.summary: A 1983 survey of SMTP server implementations on the Internet, testing connectivity from the Arpanet and ISI-Net, VRFY/RCPT behaviour for postmaster and nonexistent users, and noting deviations from RFC 821.

SMTP.why: The whole document reports on the status and conformance of SMTP server implementations against RFC 821, including reply code bugs and VRFY/RSET behaviour.
SMTP.quote: I tested SMTP servers on the Internet to see whether they accepted connections from the Arpanet (a Class A network) and ISI-Net

rejected.why: The Arpanet is only the network from which tests were run and hosts are grouped by; the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
Covered by the more specific SMTP tag, which is implied as a child of email.
The NIC host table is only the source of host names and SMTP-support claims, not a subject of the document.

RFC877.title: Standard for the transmission of IP datagrams over public data networks
RFC877.summary: RFC 877 specifies how IP datagrams are carried over X.25 virtual circuits on public data networks, including protocol demultiplexing via Call User Data, packet sequencing, maximum datagram size, and virtual circuit management.

X.25.why: The whole document defines the mapping of IP datagrams onto X.25 virtual circuits (call user data, M bit, packet sizes, circuit closing). This is IP over public data networks, which X.25 covers.
X.25.quote: This RFC specifies a standard adopted by CSNET, the VAN gateway, and other organizations for the transmission of IP datagrams over the X.25-based public data networks.

rejected.why: IP is the payload carried over X.25. The document specifies the link-layer mapping, not IP itself.
The document only notes that protocols above IP, such as TCP, do not affect the standard.
This is a network-layer-over-link mapping, and the X.25 tag is more specific and fits better.

RFC878.title: ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol
RFC878.summary: Specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, a successor to 1822 that lets hosts address each other by logical names via new host-IMP leader formats, name declaration and translation, and a name server, and includes an appendix mapping 1822L names to IP addresses.

ARPANET.why: The whole document defines a host-to-IMP access protocol for the ARPANET, including leader formats, name declaration, and IMP behaviour. It belongs on the ARPANET subject page.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, which will allow hosts to use logical addressing

rejected.why: The logical addressing here is ARPANET host-IMP addressing, not IP address architecture. The IP mapping appendix is a minor part of the document.
1822L names are 16-bit logical host identifiers that the IMP translates to physical ports. This is a link-level access protocol feature, not a general naming or name resolution system.
The appendix maps 1822L names into IPv4 address fields, but IPv4 is not the subject of the document.
The document concerns the host-IMP interface, not the host-host NCP protocol.

RFC879.title: The TCP Maximum Segment Size and Related Topics
RFC879.summary: RFC 879 clarifies the TCP Maximum Segment Size option, defining MSS as the IP maximum datagram size minus 40 (default 536 for 576), and discusses TCP/IP layering, fragmentation and MTU handling.

TCP.why: The document exists to clarify the TCP MSS option and its calculation, a clarification to the TCP specification.
TCP.quote: THE TCP MAXIMUM SEGMENT SIZE IS THE IP MAXIMUM DATAGRAM SIZE MINUS FORTY.

IPv4.why: A substantial part covers IP datagram size limits, the 576-octet rule, source and gateway fragmentation, and TCP/IP inter-layer interaction.
IPv4.quote: Hosts are not required to reassemble infinitely large IP datagrams.  The maximum size datagram that all hosts are required to accept or reassemble from fragments is 576 octets.

rejected.why: The memo predates path MTU discovery and only discusses MTU, default sizes and fragmentation, not discovery of the path MTU.
ICMP is mentioned only in passing (Echo, Redirect, Destination Unreachable); it is not the subject.
The layering discussion is brief and supports the MSS clarification; it is not an architectural treatment in its own right.

RFC880.title: Official protocols
RFC880.summary: RFC 880 is a 1983 catalogue of the official Internet protocols. For each protocol it gives status (required, recommended, elective or experimental), the specification, comments on known problems, related references, dependencies and a contact.

internet history.why: It is a snapshot of the 1983 Internet protocol suite and its planned revisions. Readers of Internet history would want it as a period document.
internet history.quote: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet.

TCP.why: The TCP entry carries extended commentary on the specification. It covers maximum segment size, push, idle connections, out-of-order segments and user time-out.
TCP.quote: Idle connections are ok, and should not be closed.

FTP.why: The FTP entry has a long clarification of data connection management, transfer modes and LIST/NLST, and notes that the mail commands are not to be used.
FTP.quote: All FTP implementations must support use of the default data connection ports

Telnet.why: The Telnet and Telnet Options entries include a full table of options with their RFC numbers and a recommendation of which to implement.
Telnet.quote: The protocol for remote terminal access.

rejected.why: IP gets a short comment on route options and reassembly, but the document is a catalogue and does not specify IP.
SMTP is one entry among many, with only brief comments.
Echo, Discard, Chargen, QOTD, Daytime and Active Users are one-line entries, not a substantial part of the document.
Mentions the ARPANET Protocol Handbook and the old NCP, but the document is about Internet protocols, not the ARPANET itself.
Only a short entry listing status and contact.
Assigned Numbers appears only as an appendix pointer to another RFC.

gaps.name: Official protocol list / protocol status
gaps.why: The document's main subject is the standardisation status of Internet protocols (required, recommended, elective, experimental). The taxonomy has no tag for protocol standards status catalogues.

RFC881.title: Domain names plan and schedule
RFC881.summary: RFC 881 lays out the plan and schedule for introducing domain-style names (the ARPA and DDN domains), domain servers and resolvers, and the evolution of the HOSTS.TXT host table across the ARPA/DDN Internet in 1983-84.

DNS.why: The document is the deployment plan and schedule for the original Domain Name System, covering domain servers, resolvers, domain requirements, mailbox binding and rollout milestones.
DNS.quote: Domain names will be supported in the long run by a system of special servers called "domain servers" which will be used to translate names to addresses.

hostnames.why: A substantial part covers evolving the HOSTS.TXT host table to domain-style names (DHOSTS.TXT, DOMAINS.TXT) and the dot-in-host-name issue.
hostnames.quote: Nearly all the hosts in the Internet now use some form of host table based on the master file "HOSTS.TXT" maintained by the Network Information Center (NIC).

rejected.why: Mailbox binding and agent binding are discussed, but only as a feature of the domain servers, not as email specification.
The requirements for registering a domain with a central authority are described, but as part of the DNS rollout, not registry or registrar operations.
The ARPA/DDN communities are the setting for the rollout, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations as such.
It is a contemporary plan, not a retrospective or history.

RFC882.title: Domain names: Concepts and facilities
RFC882.summary: RFC 882 introduces the Domain Name System's concepts: the tree-structured name space, resource records, name servers, zones, authority, resolvers, caching, and the preferred name syntax, used for ARPA Internet host and mail addressing.

DNS.why: The whole document defines the original DNS architecture: name space, resource records, name servers, zones, resolvers, queries and caching.
DNS.quote: The DOMAIN NAME SPACE, which is a specification for a tree structured name space.

rejected.why: It motivates replacing the HOSTS.TXT host table and gives label syntax, but the document is about the distributed DNS rather than host naming conventions or host tables.
MD/MF mail records and mail forwarding are used as examples of DNS resource data, but the document does not specify mail transport or formats.
The more specific DNS tag applies, so the general naming parent is implied.
TCP and UDP are only mentioned as possible transports (datagrams and virtual circuits) and are not the subject.

RFC883.title: Domain names: Implementation specification
RFC883.summary: RFC 883 is the original Domain Name System implementation specification, defining name server and resolver behaviour, message formats, resource records, zone maintenance and transfer, master file format, mail support RRs, and the IN-ADDR domain.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies the DNS protocol: message format, resource records, name server and resolver algorithms, zone transfer, and IN-ADDR.
DNS.quote: This memo discusses the implementation of domain name servers and resolvers, specifies the format of transactions

email.why: A substantial section defines MAILA/MAILB queries and MD, MF, MB, MG, MR and MINFO records for mail routing, which email readers would want.
email.quote: The domain system encodes the global part of a mail destination as a domain name

rejected.why: Host naming syntax appears in Appendix 1, but the document is about the DNS, not host tables or naming conventions.
TCP and UDP are only transports for DNS messages and are not specified or extended here.
SMTP is mentioned only as an example delivery protocol for mail records.
MG and MINFO records support mail groups, but this is a minor part of the mail section and not mailing list protocol work.
The more specific DNS tag already covers this.
WHOIS appears only in the references.

RFC884.title: Telnet terminal type option
RFC884.summary: RFC 884 defines the Telnet TERMINAL-TYPE option (code 24), which lets a Telnet server learn the terminal type of the user's Telnet client through sub-negotiation, and it lists suggested terminal type names.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet option, including its commands, negotiation rules and sub-negotiation. Readers of the Telnet subject would expect to find it.
Telnet.quote: This option allows a telnet server to determine the type of terminal connected to a user telnet program.

rejected.why: Terminal type strings are NVT ASCII, but this is only an encoding detail and the document is not about ASCII.
IBM 3270-family terminal names appear in the suggested type list, but the document does not specify 3270 emulation.
The document refers to the Assigned Numbers RFC for the list of terminal types. This is a pointer to a registry and not the subject of the document.

RFC885.title: Telnet end of record option
RFC885.summary: Specifies the Telnet END-OF-RECORD option (code 25), which lets Telnet peers negotiate transmission of an IAC EOR marker (239) to delimit record boundaries in the data stream.

Telnet.why: The whole document defines a Telnet option, including its WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T negotiation semantics, default state and the IAC EOR code. Readers of the Telnet subject would expect it there.
Telnet.quote: This Telnet option provides a means of communicating the end of data unit in a standard way.

rejected.why: This is the parent topic of Telnet. The Telnet tag is more specific, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The document is addressed to the ARPA Internet community, but it is about a Telnet option and not ARPANET protocols or operations as a subject.

RFC886.title: Proposed standard for message header munging
RFC886.summary: RFC 886 proposes policies and conceptual rules for "message munging" agents that transform mail headers (fields, addresses, dates) between RFC 822 and other mail formats such as USENET, covering canonical forms, information preservation, error recovery via Illegal-Field/Illegal-Object headers, and Received header insertion.

message format.why: The whole document is about transforming Internet message headers (fields, addresses, dates) between formats, defining new reserved header fields and rules for the Received header. It is a header-level message format matter.
message format.quote: This memo describes the rules that are to be used when mail is transformed from one standard format to another.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the more specific message format tag; the document is about header transformation, not email architecture or transport broadly.
SMTP appears only in an example Received header ('with SMTP'); the document does not address SMTP.
UUCP and USENET are used only as illustrative examples of a non-822 network; the memo explicitly says it does not specify that munging.
USENET message format is used only as an example; the memo disclaims specifying USENET munging.
The CSnet example mentions host tables and address rewriting, but the document is not about host naming.

RFC887.title: Resource Location Protocol
RFC887.summary: RFC 887 specifies the Resource Location Protocol (RLP), a UDP-based request/reply protocol by which hosts broadcast or unicast queries to find hosts providing a given network service or resource (e.g., gateways, name servers).

service discovery.why: RLP exists to locate hosts providing services or resources, which is the service discovery subject in its own right. No more specific technology tag fits, since SLP and DNS-SD are different protocols.
service discovery.quote: Internet hosts are faced with the problem of determining where on the Internet some particular network service or resource is being provided.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport RLP is encapsulated in. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
A domain name server is used only as an example of a resource to locate. The document does not specify DNS.
TFTP crash dump service appears only in a sample usage scenario.
SLP is a different, later protocol. RLP is its own protocol and not SLP.
The document uses broadcast addressing but is not about IP address architecture.
The document is an ARPA Internet protocol, but it is not about the ARPANET network itself or its working notes.

gaps.name: Resource Location Protocol (RLP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for this specific historic protocol. The generic service discovery topic is the closest fit.

RFC888.title: "STUB" Exterior Gateway Protocol
RFC888.summary: RFC 888 specifies the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) used by stub gateways to acquire neighbors, check reachability, and exchange network reachability information with core gateways of an autonomous system.

EGP.why: The document is the specification of EGP itself: neighbor acquisition, neighbor reachability, NR messages, and message formats.
EGP.quote: This note describes the Exterior Gateway Protocol used to connect Stub Gateways to an Autonomous System of core Gateways.

rejected.why: The document touches on autonomous systems and core/stub structure, but the EGP tag covers it and is more specific.
ICMP is mentioned only as something stub gateways must also implement. It is not the subject of the document.
The EGP checksum is described only as a message field. The document is not about the Internet checksum.
EGP runs over IP as protocol 8. IP is only the substrate here.

RFC889.title: Internet Delay Experiments
RFC889.summary: Reports ICMP-echo measurements of Internet delay versus packet length and simulates the TCP retransmission-timeout (RSRE) algorithm on measured paths, proposing a two-weight smoothing improvement for TCP implementers.

TCP.why: The memo evaluates the TCP retransmission-timeout algorithm and recommends changes (F1=15/16, F2=3/4, G=2) as advice to TCP implementers.
TCP.quote: suggests some possible improvements to the TCP retransmission timeout calculation

performance measurement.why: A large part of the memo is active measurement of round-trip delay, loss and delay variation across ARPANET, MILNET, SATNET and other paths using ICMP Echo.
performance measurement.quote: One series of experiments was designed to determine the network delays with respect to packet length

rejected.why: ICMP Echo/Reply is only the probe mechanism used for measurement; the memo does not specify or extend ICMP.
ARPANET is one of the networks measured, but the memo is not about its protocols or operations.
Superfluous retransmissions and congestion are mentioned, but the memo is about timeout estimation, not congestion control mechanisms.
SATNET paths appear among the measured paths, but the memo is not about satellite networking itself.

RFC890.title: Exterior Gateway Protocol implementation schedule
RFC890.summary: A 1984 ICCB/DARPA policy statement setting an implementation schedule that requires all Internet gateways to become members of autonomous systems and to use the Exterior Gateway Protocol with the core system after 1-Aug-84.

EGP.why: The document is a policy and transition schedule for deploying EGP, including the stub EGP subset, the core autonomous system, and implementation help. EGP readers would want it.
EGP.quote: Some gateway of each autonomous system must exchange routing information with some gateway of the core autonomous system using the Exterior Gateway Protocol.
