rejected.why: It does discuss splitting gateways into autonomous systems. But EGP is the specific technology that covers this, so the parent topic is not added.
It is a historical document, but it is a contemporaneous policy memo and not a retrospective.
It is an ICCB/DARPA deployment policy statement, not an IETF standards process document.

RFC891.title: DCN Local-Network Protocols
RFC891.summary: Describes the DCN (Fuzzball) local-network HELLO protocol for connectivity, minimum-delay routing and clock synchronization, with a formal specification and link-level framing appendix.

time synchronization.why: The HELLO protocol maintains logical-clock offsets and synchronizes clocks to a master clock, and the spec includes a full CLOCK process. This is a substantial part of the document.
time synchronization.quote: provide connectivity, routing and timekeeping functions for a set of randomly connected personal computers and service hosts

routing architecture.why: It specifies a self-configuring, delay-based routing scheme with Host and Net Tables, hold-down and loop suppression. It is a local-net routing design that fits no specific routing protocol tag.
routing architecture.quote: they organize themselves into a network with routing based on minimum delay

rejected.why: The protocol carries IP datagrams and uses IP addressing, but it does not specify IP itself.
The HELLO clock sync is a precursor to NTP, but the document does not define NTP.
GGP/EGP is mentioned only as an optional gateway process maintaining the Net Table. It is not specified here.
Ethernet framing appears only as one of several link encodings in the appendix.
The appendix link framings (DDCMP, HDLC, X.25 LAPB, 1822) are only substrate and are not about PPP.

gaps.name: DCN / Fuzzball HELLO protocol
gaps.why: No tag covers this historic local-net HELLO routing and timekeeping protocol, or the Fuzzball system.

RFC892.title: ISO Transport Protocol specification
RFC892.summary: Republication of the ISO OSI Transport Protocol specification, defining five connection-oriented transport protocol classes (0-4), their mechanisms (flow control, error recovery, multiplexing, checksum, expedited data), TPDU encoding and conformance rules.

OSI.why: The document is the OSI transport layer protocol specification (classes 0-4, TPDUs), an OSI protocol. The OSI tag is the closest fit, though it is defined for network-layer protocols.
OSI.quote: The Transport Protocol Standard is positioned with respect to other related standards by the layers defined in the Reference Model for Open Systems Interconnection (ISO 7498).

transport.why: The document specifies a general transport protocol with connection establishment, segmenting, multiplexing, flow control, error recovery and release. These are transport-layer matters not tied to TCP or another listed protocol.
transport.quote: The functions in the transport layer are concerned with the enhancement of quality of service, including all aspects of cost optimization.

rejected.why: The document is the ISO transport protocol, not TCP. It is related only as an alternative transport protocol.
It defines a Fletcher-style checksum for TPDUs (6.18), but only as one mechanism within the protocol. It is not the document's main subject.
The credit-based flow control is end-to-end window management, not a congestion control subject.
The document assumes a connection-oriented network service and does not cover CLNP.

gaps.name: ISO/OSI Transport Protocol (TP0-TP4)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no OSI transport-layer tag. OSI covers only network-layer protocols, so this RFC fits it imperfectly.

RFC893.title: Trailer encapsulations
RFC893.summary: Informational RFC describing the trailer encapsulation, a link-level packet format (used by 4.2BSD) that moves variable-length protocol headers after the data to enable page-aligned receive and avoid copies, with formats for experimental Ethernet, 10 Mb/s Ethernet and V2LNI.

Ethernet.why: The document specifies a link-level encapsulation and its Ethernet type-field values (1001-1010 hex) for Ethernet framing. Ethernet is the best-fitting tag for a link-level frame format on Ethernet.
Ethernet.quote: the link level packet formats used on the 3 Mb/s Experimental Ethernet, and 10 Mb/s Ethernet networks as well as the 10 Mb/s V2LNI ring network

rejected.why: ARP is mentioned only as a possible vehicle for future per-host negotiation of trailers; it is not specified or extended here.
TCP/IP headers are used only as an example of the variable-length headers that get moved to the trailer; the document does not address TCP.
IP is cited only as an example header being relocated; the document is not about IP.
This is the parent of Ethernet, which is already tagged, so it is implied. The document's formats are tied to Ethernet-type media.

gaps.name: Trailer encapsulation (link-level packet format for zero-copy receive)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for generic link-level encapsulation formats, or for host performance optimizations such as page-aligned buffer receipt.

RFC894.title: A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks
RFC894.summary: Specifies the standard encapsulation of IP datagrams in 10-Mbit Ethernet frames (type 0x0800), including padding, MTU, address mapping via ARP, broadcast mapping and optional trailer formats.

Ethernet.why: The whole document defines how IP is carried over Ethernet: frame type, padding, maximum length, broadcast mapping. This is the core IP-over-Ethernet standard.
Ethernet.quote: IP datagrams are transmitted in standard Ethernet frames.  The type field of the Ethernet frame must contain the value hexadecimal 0800.

ARP.why: A substantial section covers mapping IP to Ethernet addresses and recommends ARP, with requirements on hosts to respond to and use ARP.
ARP.quote: The use of the ARP dynamic discovery procedure is strongly recommended.

rejected.why: IP is the payload being encapsulated, not specified or extended here; the document is about the Ethernet link-layer binding.
TCP MSS option is mentioned only as a way to discourage full-length packets; not a subject of the document.
The more specific Ethernet tag applies.

RFC895.title: Standard for the transmission of IP datagrams over experimental Ethernet networks
RFC895.summary: Standard specifying how IP datagrams are encapsulated in Experimental Ethernet (3 Mb/s, 8-bit address) frames, including type field, maximum length, address mapping, broadcast, trailers and byte order.

Ethernet.why: The whole document defines IP encapsulation over (Experimental) Ethernet, which is exactly what the Ethernet tag covers.
Ethernet.quote: IP datagrams are transmitted in standard Experimental Ethernet frames.  The type field of the Ethernet frame must contain the value 513 (1001 octal).

rejected.why: IP is the payload being carried; the document specifies only the link-layer encapsulation, not IP itself.
Address mapping is done by taking the low 8 bits of the host number; ARP appears only in the references.
The TCP Maximum Segment Size option is mentioned only as a way to discourage full-length packets.
Fragmentation and maximum datagram size are discussed, but not Path MTU Discovery.

RFC896.title: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks
RFC896.summary: Nagle's 1984 memo describes congestion collapse in IP/TCP internetworks and proposes the small-packet fix (the Nagle algorithm), host handling of ICMP Source Quench, and gateway self-defense packet-drop strategies.

TCP.why: The core contribution is a change to TCP sender behaviour (the Nagle algorithm) plus TCP handling of Source Quench, so it is TCP implementation guidance.
TCP.quote: The solution is to inhibit the sending of new TCP segments when new outgoing data arrives from the user if any previously transmitted data on the connection remains unacknowledged.
TCP.section: The solution to the small-packet problem

congestion control.why: The memo defines congestion collapse and proposes host and gateway mechanisms to prevent it. No more specific congestion child fits, since ICMP Source Quench is not a child tag.
congestion control.quote: In particular, IP gateways are vulnerable to a phenomenon we call "congestion collapse"

ICMP.why: A substantial part of the memo covers when gateways should send Source Quench and how hosts should react to it.
ICMP.quote: the only mechanism available to us under the IP standard was the ICMP Source Quench message.

rejected.why: Character-at-a-time Telnet is the motivating example for the small-packet problem, but the memo is not about the Telnet protocol.
ARPANET and IMP behaviour is background for why the problem went unnoticed, not the subject of the memo.
IP gateways are the setting, but the memo does not specify or extend IP itself.
The gateway packet-drop and early-quench suggestions anticipate queue management, but the memo does not describe an AQM algorithm.

review: ICMP: quote not found in the text

notes: ICMP: quote not found in the text

RFC897.title: Domain name system implementation schedule
RFC897.summary: A 1984 ICCB/DARPA policy memo setting the schedule and transition plan for moving Internet hosts from flat host-table names to hierarchical domain-style names served by distributed name servers.

DNS.why: The memo schedules the deployment of the Domain Name System: domain-style names, name servers for the ARPA domain, a top-level domain table and new domains.
DNS.quote: change from using central tables to using name servers.

hostnames.why: A large part covers host naming: flat names, the centrally maintained host table (HOSTS.TXT), primary names and nicknames, and the change from old names to domain-style names.
hostnames.quote: Hosts in the ARPA research and DDN operational communities are currently assigned names in a flat or global name space of character strings.

rejected.why: Mail relaying and addressing are discussed only as an example of how domain names affect mail. The memo does not specify SMTP.
Mail address changes appear as an impact of renaming hosts, but the memo is not about email systems.
This is the parent of DNS and hostnames, which are already tagged.

RFC898.title: Gateway special interest group meeting notes
RFC898.summary: Report on the February 1984 Gateway Special Interest Group meeting at ISI, summarizing talks on Internet gateway implementations, EGP, SPF routing, type-of-service routing, ST, and congestion control.

routing architecture.why: Many talks cover routing design for gateways: SPF vs GGP, multiple-constraint/TOS routing, subnet routing, exit-gateway model, and scalability.
routing architecture.quote: SPF routing -- BBN - Seamonson

EGP.why: Substantial coverage of EGP design, an EGP user-process implementation under 4.2 Unix, and autonomous-system loop-free topology.
EGP.quote: EGP has three major aspects, neighbor acquisition, neighbor reachability, and network reachability.

congestion control.why: Two talks and discussion address congestion control in gateways and TCP, including RFC 896 policies and source quench.
congestion control.quote: When a gateway nears overload, before starting to drop packets, send a Source Quench.

ST-II.why: Describes the Lincoln gateways implementing the ST stream protocol for voice. ST-II is the closest tag for the ST family.
ST-II.quote: The gateway implements both the regular IP, and the ST protocol which permits resource reservations

rejected.why: TCP is discussed only in the context of congestion and small-packet fixes; the document is not about TCP itself.
Source quench and redirects are mentioned in passing, not as the subject.
A single talk covers a LAN-to-X.25 bridge; not a substantial subject of the report.
It is a meeting record, but it is not a retrospective on Internet history.

gaps.name: GGP (Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol) / gateway design
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for GGP or Internet gateway implementations, which are central to this report.

RFC899.title: Request For Comments summary notes: 800-899
RFC899.summary: A 1984 index of RFCs 800 through 899 that gives each RFC's number, author, date, title and a short annotation of its status.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a catalogue of a hundred consecutive RFCs, so it is about the RFC series itself. It includes RFC 825 on the status of RFCs, but its purpose is to list and annotate the series.
RFC series.quote: This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: The summaries of RFCs 881-883, 897 and others only describe the domain name documents. This memo does not specify or analyse DNS.
Many entries summarise Telnet option RFCs, but the memo only lists them.
Entries such as RFC 821 are listed and annotated, but the memo does not address SMTP itself.
This is a contemporaneous status listing, not a retrospective or history of the Internet.
The ARPANET 1822L entries are only items in the list. The memo is not about the ARPANET.

RFC900.title: Assigned Numbers
RFC900.summary: RFC 900 is the June 1984 Assigned Numbers memo, a registry listing assigned network numbers, IP version and protocol numbers, ports, AS numbers, ARPANET link numbers, Ethernet types, Telnet options, and official names for ARPA-Internet protocols.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned numbers (ports, protocol numbers, AS numbers, network numbers) and the coordinator's assignment process, which is the subject of IANA registries.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

addressing.why: Substantial part of the document describes class A/B/C address allocation, dotted decimal notation, and lists of assigned network numbers.
addressing.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

ARPANET.why: Includes ARPANET link numbers and logical addresses, historic ARPANET-specific assignments.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: Port numbers are used with TCP, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Lists Telnet option numbers and terminal types only as registry entries, not specifying the protocol.
Only lists ARP parameter values briefly; ARP is not the document's subject.
Covers IP version numbers and address classes as registry values; IPv4 itself is not specified, and addressing already captures the address allocation.
Lists official machine and system names for the host table, but only as a short registry list.

RFC901.title: Official ARPA-Internet protocols
RFC901.summary: RFC 901 is a June 1984 status report listing the official ARPA-Internet protocols, with each entry's status, specification documents, known problems, dependencies and contact.

ARPANET.why: The whole document catalogues the protocols of the ARPA-Internet, including the old ARPANET Protocol Handbook items. Readers of the ARPANET subject would want it.
ARPANET.quote: This memo is an official status report on the protocols used in the ARPA-Internet community.

internet history.why: It is a snapshot of the protocol suite in 1984. It records what was required, experimental or obsolete during the NCP-to-TCP/IP era, which is useful as a historical record.
internet history.quote: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet.

rejected.why: TCP is one entry among about 50. The document gives it only brief comments and does not specify it.
IP, ICMP and the network-mapping entries are individual line items. The document is not about the IP layer as a subject.
The required, recommended and elective status labels are a form of standards classification. The document is not about the standards process itself.
SMTP, POP and MPM are entries in a long list. Mail is not the focus.
The Catenet Model entry only points to IEN 48 and does not discuss architecture.
Echo, Discard, Chargen, QOTD, Daytime and Users are listed, but only as short entries within the survey.

gaps.name: Official Internet protocol standards list / protocol status catalog
gaps.why: Many RFCs periodically list official protocols and their standardization status. The taxonomy has no tag for this kind of document.

RFC902.title: ARPA Internet Protocol policy
RFC902.summary: RFC 902 is a 1984 policy statement from the ICCB and DARPA explaining how protocols become official standards for the ARPA-Internet and DARPA research community, who holds authority, and how this relates to the DDN community.

internet history.why: The document describes the early Internet's governing bodies (DARPA, ICCB, DDN-PMO) and their relationships in 1984. It is a historical record of how the early Internet was run. Readers of Internet history would want it.
internet history.quote: In 1981 DARPA established the Internet Configuration Control Board (ICCB) to help manage the DARPA Internet Program.

ARPANET.why: The document covers the ARPA-Internet and ARPANET-era administration, including MILNET and the DDN. Its main subject is the standards process for that network community. Readers of ARPANET operations and working notes would find it relevant.
ARPANET.quote: In this way, DARPA developed the ARPANET, SATNET, Packet Radio Networks, and the Internet.

IETF process.why: It sets out the standards process: drafts, RFC Editor review, test implementations, and official status. It also sets out who has authority at each step. This is an early precursor of the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: The purpose of this memo is to explain how protocol standards are adopted for the ARPA-Internet and the DARPA research community.

rejected.why: TCP appears only as an example of two parallel specifications (RFC 793 and MIL-STD-1778). The document does not specify or analyse it.
The RFC Editor and the 'Official Protocols' memo are described only as steps in the standards process. The document is not about RFC format or publication.
The DAYTIME protocol is mentioned once as an example of a higher-level protocol that gets less scrutiny. The document is not about it.

RFC903.title: A Reverse Address Resolution Protocol
RFC903.summary: RFC 903 specifies RARP, a data-link-level protocol using the ARP packet format with new opcodes so diskless hosts can discover their protocol (IP) address from their hardware address via a server.

ARP.why: RARP is the reverse of ARP, defined on ARP's packet format with new opcodes 3 and 4. It is the ARP-family address resolution protocol, so readers of the ARP subject would expect it.
ARP.quote: RARP uses the same packet format that is used by ARP

rejected.why: Ethernet is only the example broadcast medium; the protocol is specified generically at the data-link level.
DHCP later solved the same bootstrapping problem, but this document does not specify or discuss it.
IP addresses are the example protocol address being discovered, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.

RFC904.title: Exterior Gateway Protocol formal specification
RFC904.summary: RFC 904 is the formal specification of the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), defining its state machine, neighbor acquisition and reachability procedures, Update-based net-reachability exchange, and message formats.

EGP.why: The whole document is the formal specification of EGP: state machine, timers, neighbor reachability algorithm, Update messages and message formats.
EGP.quote: EGP exists in order to convey net-reachability information between neighboring gateways, possibly in different autonomous systems.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in passing as a requirement that gateways support ICMP Redirect and Destination Unreachable; not specified here.
The EGP header checksum is defined using the standard one's complement sum, but this is a small part of a message format, not the document's subject.
The document explicitly excludes background and architecture discussion, deferring to RFC 827 and RFC 888.
ARPANET is cited as deployment context and influence on design, but the document is about EGP, not ARPANET operations.

RFC905.title: ISO Transport Protocol specification ISO DP 8073
RFC905.summary: RFC 905 reproduces the ISO DP 8073 OSI Transport Protocol specification, defining five transport classes (0-4), procedures, TPDU encodings, negotiation, flow control, and conformance.

OSI.why: The document is the OSI Transport Protocol standard (ISO 8073), an OSI-layer protocol, so the OSI subject page is the natural home.
OSI.quote: It also uses and makes reference to the Network Service Standard (DP 8348), whose provisions it assumes in order to accomplish the transport protocol's aims.

checksum.why: Defines a Class 4 checksum algorithm (Fletcher-style, modulo 255) with an annex on generating and checking it.
checksum.quote: The checksum procedure is used to detect corruption of TPDUs by the NS-provider.

rejected.why: Parent topic of the transport tags. No specific child fits, because the document is OSI TP4, not TCP or another listed protocol. The OSI tech tag is the better fit.
Mentioned nowhere. The OSI transport classes are a different protocol, not TCP.
The credit-based flow control in Classes 2-4 is flow control, not congestion control in the Internet sense.
The document assumes a connection-oriented network service (DP 8348), not CLNP.

gaps.name: OSI Transport Protocol (ISO 8073 / TP0-TP4)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the OSI network-layer tag, with CLNP beneath it. There is no OSI transport tag, so the document's main subject has no exact fit.

RFC906.title: Bootstrap loading using TFTP
RFC906.summary: RFC 906 proposes using TFTP as the standard protocol for bootstrap loading of diskless systems over a network, describing the booter's use of RARP/ARP and an Ethernet ROM implementation.

TFTP.why: The document specifies how a booting system uses TFTP read requests, DATA, ACK and ERROR packets to load its code file, so it belongs on the TFTP page.
TFTP.quote: We propose that TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) [6] be used as a standard protocol for bootstrap loading.

ARP.why: A substantial part of the document describes how the booter uses RARP and ARP to learn its own address and the server's hardware address before sending the TFTP request.
ARP.quote: RARP is used to determine a higher-level protocol address, given a known hardware address.
ARP.section: Network Protocols used by the Booting System

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport beneath TFTP. The document notes its datagram size implications but does not specify or extend UDP.
Ethernet is used only in the example ROM implementation. The proposal says it does not presuppose any particular data-link architecture.
IP is the substrate. The only IP-specific content is a brief note on broadcast addresses, which is not the document's subject.
The RARP-based address discovery is a precursor of DHCP, but the document does not cover DHCP.

gaps.name: Network bootstrap loading (diskless boot)
gaps.why: The document's main subject is booting diskless systems over a network. The taxonomy has no tag for network booting, so TFTP is the nearest fit.

RFC907.title: Host Access Protocol specification
RFC907.summary: Specifies the Host Access Protocol (HAP), the network-access protocol between a host and a Satellite IMP on packet-satellite networks (Wideband, SATNET, MATNET), covering datagram and stream messages, A/R flow control, stream and group setup, link monitoring, initialization and loopback.

satellite.why: The whole document defines the host-to-satellite-network access protocol, so a reader of satellite networking would look for it.
satellite.quote: HAP specifies the network-access level communication between an arbitrary computer, called a host, and a packet-switched satellite network.

ARPANET.why: HAP is an ARPANET-era host-to-IMP style protocol and is related to ARPANET 1822/VDH; it is a modest secondary fit as the ARPANET topic covers host and network protocols of the era.
ARPANET.quote: The term "Interface Message Processor" originates in the ARPANET, where it refers to the ARPANET's packet-switching nodes.

rejected.why: Group addressing is a satellite-network feature for conferencing, not IP multicast routing.
Priority and reliability levels exist but are local access-link parameters, not a QoS architecture.
FEC reliability levels are only mentioned as a service option; the document does not specify FEC.
Covered more specifically by the satellite tag; HAP sits above the link-level protocols (HDLC, 1822, VDH), which are only assumed.

RFC908.title: Reliable Data Protocol
RFC908.summary: RFC 908 specifies the Reliable Data Protocol (RDP), a simple connection-oriented transport protocol over IP offering reliable message delivery with optional sequenced delivery and out-of-order acknowledgements, aimed at bulk loading/dumping and remote debugging.

RDP.why: The entire document specifies RDP: connection management, segment formats, acknowledgement, flow control and event processing.
RDP.quote: The Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) is designed  to  provide  a  reliable  data  transport  service  for packet-based applications such as remote loading and debugging.

rejected.why: TCP is only discussed as a comparison and motivation for why RDP was designed; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
RDP defines its own 32-bit checksum, but this is a minor part of the protocol specification, not about Internet checksums generally.
IP is only the substrate carrying RDP segments.

RFC909.title: Loader Debugger Protocol
RFC909.summary: RFC 909 specifies the Loader-Debugger Protocol (LDP), an application-layer protocol for loading, dumping and debugging target machines (PSNs, PADs, gateways) from hosts over a network, normally carried on RDP or TCP.

rejected.why: RDP (RFC 908) is only the recommended transport beneath LDP; this document does not specify or extend it.
TCP is mentioned only as a less efficient alternative transport.
LDP is an application-layer protocol, but the parent topic is for application protocols in general and has no specific fit; no listed child matches loading/debugging.
LDP targets BBN network equipment of the ARPA Internet era, but the document is not about ARPANET host protocols or operations.
Remote loading and debugging of network nodes is loosely related to operations, but the document defines a debugger protocol, not network management architecture or practice.

gaps.name: Loader Debugger Protocol (LDP) / remote boot loading, dumping and debugging
gaps.why: The document is about remote loading, dumping and debugging of target machines. The taxonomy has no tag for remote debugging, bootstrapping or target-machine loading protocols, so no tag fits.

RFC910.title: Multimedia mail meeting notes
RFC910.summary: Report of a July 1984 meeting among BBN, ISI, SRI and Linkabit on the experimental multimedia mail system, recording status, agreements on syntax, graphics, document presentation, new media types, and the Multimedia Package Mail (MPM) transport.

email.why: The whole document is about experimental multimedia mail systems (Diamond, SRI MMH, MPM transport), their syntax, media types and message transport, so it belongs under email in general.
email.quote: A meeting was held at Bolt Beranek and Newman on 23-24 July 1984 to discuss recent progress by groups who are building multimedia mail systems

MIME.why: Substantial parts cover multimedia message body structure: media types (text, graphics, voice, spreadsheet, forms), handling unknown types, and a Caption property. This is a precursor to MIME body structure.
MIME.quote: we agreed that all of our systems should be prepared to accept (and possibly ignore) media types that are not currently implemented

rejected.why: SMTP is mentioned only as the text-only mail that MPMs should translate to and from. The document does not specify or extend it.
The Internet Domain system (RFCs 882 and 883) is mentioned briefly as a possible answer to the directory needs. The document is not about it.
WhoIs is mentioned in one sentence as limited to text mailbox information.
FTP is mentioned only as the way to fetch the MMM notes, and TFTP only as the way to move messages from the 1108. Both are substrate.
Section 3.4 raises the need for a directory service but only points to the Domain system and WhoIs. It is a short discussion, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Multimedia mail / compound documents and graphics representation (MMGraphics1, Diamond, MPM)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is multimedia mail and compound document presentation semantics. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it, so only email and MIME approximate it.

RFC911.title: EGP Gateway under Berkeley UNIX 4.2
RFC911.summary: Describes an experimental user-process implementation of the Exterior Gateway Protocol under Berkeley UNIX 4.2 BSD, covering its design, testing, enhancements and local topology/backup-gateway issues at ISI.

EGP.why: The whole document is about implementing and operating EGP: neighbor acquisition, reachability, updates, sequence numbers, and deviations from the EGP specification.
EGP.quote: This report describes an implementation of the Exterior Gateway Protocol that runs under the Unix 4.2 BSD operating system.

routing architecture.why: A substantial part discusses autonomous system topology restrictions, routing loops, the core/stub model and the EGP topological model, which are routing architecture design issues.
routing architecture.quote: The initial proposal was to prevent routing loops by restricting the topology of AS's to a tree structure so that there are no multiple routes via alternate AS's.

rejected.why: ICMP redirects and echo are used by the gateway and the backup scheme, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
Mentioned only in passing about idle connection closure during route updates.
The routed daemon is only the basis for the route management code, and RIP is not the subject.
A UDP socket is mentioned only as a possible vehicle for the proposed backup-gateway messages.

RFC912.title: Authentication service
RFC912.summary: RFC 912 specifies a simple TCP-based Authentication Service (on port 113) that, given a TCP port pair, returns the user identifier owning that connection; the precursor of the Ident protocol.

Ident.why: The document defines the connection-owner identification protocol on TCP port 113, the early form of Ident, so it belongs on the Ident page.
Ident.quote: The Authentication Server provides a means to determine the identity of a user of a particular TCP connection.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document defines no TCP extension or behaviour.
FTP is only a suggested use case, not what the document specifies.
The Ident tag already covers this subject and sits under authentication, so the parent is implied.

RFC913.title: Simple File Transfer Protocol
RFC913.summary: RFC 913 specifies SFTP, a simple TCP-based file transfer protocol with user login, directory listing/changing, rename, delete, retrieve and store commands, positioned between TFTP and FTP in complexity.

FTP.why: The document defines a file transfer protocol (SFTP) as a simpler alternative to FTP; readers browsing file transfer protocols would expect it under FTP, the closest fit in the taxonomy.
FTP.quote: SFTP is a simple file transfer protocol.  It fills the need of people wanting a protocol that is more useful than TFTP but easier to implement

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a comparison point; SFTP is a different protocol over TCP.
TCP is only the transport that SFTP is specified over; the document does not define anything new about TCP.
Referenced only for NETASCII end-of-line conventions in ASCII type.
The ASCII type is a transfer mode and the commands use ASCII text, but the document is not about the character set.

RFC914.title: Thinwire protocol for connecting personal computers to the Internet
RFC914.summary: RFC 914 proposes three "Thinwire" approaches (two header-compression schemes for TCP/IP and a gateway-based multiplexing protocol) for connecting personal computers to the Internet over slow serial lines, with an appendix specifying a reliable serial line protocol (SLIP).

header compression.why: Thinwire I and II compress TCP/IP headers over low-speed serial links using templates and updates; this is the core of the document.
header compression.quote: Thinwire I is a simple robust compressor, which will reduce the 41 byte minimum TCP/IP Telnet packets to a series of 17 byte update packets.

SLIP.why: Appendix D specifies a reliable serial-line framing/ARQ protocol called SLIP, used beneath Thinwire. It is a different protocol from the later well-known SLIP, but the taxonomy's SLIP tag is the closest fit for serial line IP carriage.
SLIP.quote: the Serial Line Interface Protocol (SLIP) maintains an attitude toward the world that includes both a mistrust of serial lines
SLIP.section: Appendix D -- Serial Line Interface Protocol (SLIP)

rejected.why: TCP headers are compressed and TCP connections are proxied, but TCP itself is not specified or extended.
Telnet packets are only the example traffic for the compression calculations.
IP headers appear in the examples, but the document is not about IPv4.
This is an early, unrelated compression scheme; ROHC is a later, distinct protocol.
IPHC (RFC 2507) is a later, separate scheme; Thinwire is not it.

RFC915.title: Network mail path service
RFC915.summary: RFC 915 proposes a TCP/TELNET-accessible network mail path service (port 117) that translates user@host.world names into relay-based mailbox addresses for non-ARPA-Internet mail networks such as UUCP, CSNET, BITNET and MAILNET.

email.why: The service exists to supply mail routing/relay addresses for sending mail across gatewayed mail networks, so it is about email addressing and relaying.
email.quote: determine mailbox addresses for hosts that are not part of the ARPA-Internet but can be reached by one or more relay hosts

service discovery.why: A network lookup service that discovers the path/address for reaching a host is a form of resource discovery on a network, though not general service discovery.
service discovery.quote: given a host and an optional addressing system or communication protocol or some other piece of information, supplies the mailbox address format for sending mail to that host

rejected.why: Telnet/TCP is only the access substrate; the document defines no new Telnet behaviour beyond refusing options.
TCP is only the transport for the service on port 117.
The DNS is mentioned as the long-term replacement; this service is explicitly a stop-gap and not about DNS.
SMTP is referenced for reply-code style and address syntax, not specified or extended.
UUCP is one of the mail worlds addressed, but the document is not about UUCP mail interchange itself.
Considered since it maps host names to mail paths, but it is mail routing address translation rather than general naming; email fits better.

RFC916.title: Reliable Asynchronous Transfer Protocol (RATP)
RFC916.summary: RFC 916 specifies RATP, a simple stop-and-wait reliable transfer protocol for full-duplex point-to-point links such as RS-232, with checksums, a three-way handshake, a state machine, and 4/8 packing for 7-bit links.

RATP.why: The document defines RATP itself: packet format, handshake, state machine, timers and error handling.
RATP.quote: This paper proposes and specifies a protocol which allows two programs to reliably communicate over a communication link.

rejected.why: RATP borrows TCP's state names, checksum style and handshake ideas, but it is a separate protocol and TCP is only a model and reference.
The document defines RATP's own 8-bit header and 16-bit data checksums. It does not address the Internet checksum as a subject.
RATP is a link-level alternative for serial lines, but PPP is not specified or discussed. Only DDCMP, XMODEM and KERMIT appear in the survey.
SLIP is not mentioned. RATP covers asynchronous serial links but is not IP framing.

RFC917.title: Internet subnets
RFC917.summary: RFC 917 proposes Internet subnetting: a three-level interpretation of IP addresses with a variable-width subnet field and bit mask, broadcast handling for subnets, a new ICMP Address Format Request/Reply to discover the subnet mask, routing and ARP-based subnetting approaches, and case studies.

addressing.why: The core of the document is how to divide the local address part into subnet and host fields, with masks and subnet broadcast addresses. This is IP address architecture.
addressing.quote: Interpretation of Internet Addresses

ICMP.why: It defines new ICMP message types for discovering the subnet field width and gives their format in Appendix I.
ICMP.quote: We propose to extend the ICMP protocol [9] by adding a new pair of ICMP message types, "Address Format Request" and "Address Format Reply"
ICMP.section: 2.4. Determining the Width of the Subnet Field

ARP.why: It describes ARP-based subnetting, in which gateways answer ARP for subnet targets, and compares it with ARP-based bridges.
ARP.quote: one can modify the ARP server module in a subnet gateway so that when it receives an ARP request, it checks the target Internet address

rejected.why: Routing is discussed, but only the host's local-versus-gateway decision. Routing exchange protocols are explicitly out of scope.
The document modifies IP addressing, but addressing is the more specific fit.
Broadcast to subnets is covered, but this is broadcast, not multicast.
LANs and bridges appear only as background and in the case studies.

gaps.name: IP subnetting / subnet masks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for subnetting. The addressing topic is the closest fit but does not name the subnet mask mechanism.

RFC918.title: Post Office Protocol
RFC918.summary: RFC 918 specifies the original Post Office Protocol (POP), a simple TCP-based command/response protocol letting a workstation read and optionally delete mail from a mailbox server.

POP3.why: The document defines the first version of POP, the ancestor of POP3, with its USER/PASS/RETR/RDEL commands. Readers of the POP3 subject page would want it.
POP3.quote: The intent of the Post Office Protocol (POP) is to allow a user's workstation to access mail from a mailbox server.

rejected.why: SMTP is only mentioned as the way mail is posted from the workstation to the server. The document does not specify or extend it.
TCP is only the transport the protocol depends on. The document adds nothing new about TCP.
RFC 822 is cited as a reference only. The document does not define message format.
The parent tag is implied by the more specific POP3 tag.

RFC919.title: Broadcasting Internet Datagrams
RFC919.summary: RFC 919 proposes rules for IP broadcast datagrams on local networks: broadcast address conventions (all-ones host number, 255.255.255.255), directed broadcasts, gateway forwarding and loop avoidance, and ARP server handling of broadcast addresses.

addressing.why: The core of the document defines the IP broadcast address conventions (all-ones host number, limited and directed broadcast addresses, zero-field notation), which is IP address architecture.
addressing.quote: The address 255.255.255.255 denotes a broadcast on a local hardware network, which must not be forwarded.

internet layer.why: The document specifies network-layer datagram broadcast behaviour for hosts and gateways. That includes receive-side address matching, directed broadcasts and loop avoidance. No narrower tag covers IP-layer broadcast in general.
internet layer.quote: Since broadcasting is not covered in the basic IP specification [13], there is no agreed-upon way to do it

ARP.why: A dedicated subsection gives a normative rule for how ARP must handle broadcast addresses, to avoid forwarding loops.
ARP.quote: An ARP server should never respond to a request whose target is a broadcast address.

rejected.why: Multicast is mentioned only as a concept that broadcast imperfectly substitutes for. The document is about broadcast, not IP multicast routing or group membership.
IPv4 is the protocol being extended, but the document is about broadcast addressing and forwarding rules. The addressing and internet layer tags cover that better than the IPv4 address lifecycle tag.
Ethernet is cited only as an example of a link layer that supports broadcast. The document assumes the link layer handles it.
Gateway forwarding of broadcasts is covered, but it is a loop-avoidance rule and not a routing protocol or routing architecture.

gaps.name: IP broadcast (limited and directed broadcast)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IP-layer broadcast datagrams. The closest fits are the addressing and internet layer topics.

RFC920.title: Domain requirements
RFC920.summary: RFC 920 is a 1984 IAB/DARPA policy statement setting requirements for establishing domains in the ARPA-Internet, defining the initial top-level domains (ARPA, GOV, EDU, COM, MIL, ORG, country codes) and the NIC registrar's registration procedure.

domain registration.why: The document sets out the registrar and administrator roles, registration requirements and the questionnaire for establishing a domain, which is domain registry and registrar operation.
domain registration.quote: the domain must be registered with the central domain administrator (the Network Information Center (NIC) Domain Registrar)

DNS.why: It describes the DNS namespace hierarchy, domain server redundancy requirements and zones, and the initial top-level domain set, giving DNS administration policy.
DNS.quote: The domain system is a tree-structured global name space that has a few top level domains.

rejected.why: It touches on host naming and the HOSTS.TXT file, but the main subject is domain administration and registration, not host naming conventions.
The more specific DNS and domain registration tags cover the document, so the general parent is not needed.
It is a historical policy document, but it is not a retrospective about Internet history.
The ARPA-Internet and ARPA domain appear as context, but the document is about domain policy, not ARPANET protocols or operations.

RFC921.title: Domain name system implementation schedule - revised
RFC921.summary: A 1984 IAB/DARPA policy memo giving the revised schedule for transitioning the Internet from flat host names and the centrally maintained HOSTS.TXT table to hierarchical domain names and distributed DNS name servers and resolvers.

DNS.why: The whole memo is the implementation schedule for the Domain Name System: servers, resolvers, domain registration, and the move from host tables to distributed name servers.
DNS.quote: There are three major phases to the implementation of the domain names system: (1) putting the machinery in place (servers, resolvers), (2) getting the data base installed

hostnames.why: Substantial discussion of host naming conventions, flat versus hierarchical names, HOSTS.TXT host table, primary names and nicknames, and the effects of hosts changing names.
hostnames.quote: The names are being changed from simple names, or globally unique strings, to structured names, where each component name is unique only with respect to the superior component name.

rejected.why: Mail addressing and delivery to the SMTP port are used only as examples of how domain names are used; the memo does not specify SMTP.
Mail relay and addressing to other systems appear as illustrative context for naming, not as the subject of the document.
The more specific DNS and hostnames tags apply, so the general parent is not needed.
It is a contemporaneous policy and schedule memo, not a retrospective, even though it is now of historical interest.

RFC922.title: Broadcasting Internet datagrams in the presence of subnets
RFC922.summary: RFC 922 specifies conventions for IP broadcast addressing (all-ones host and subnet fields, 255.255.255.255), broadcast classes, and gateway forwarding rules using Reverse Path Forwarding in the presence of subnets.

addressing.why: The document defines broadcast address conventions (all-ones host/subnet numbers, 255.255.255.255) in subnetted IP networks, which is IP address architecture and use.
addressing.quote: The "all subnets" number is also all ones; this means that a host wishing to broadcast to all hosts on a remote IP network need not know

multicast.why: Gateway one-to-many datagram forwarding via RPF is closely related to multicast/broadcast routing, and the document frames broadcast as a substitute for multicasting. Taxonomy has no broadcast tag, so this is the nearest fit.
multicast.quote: it must use the Reverse Path Forwarding algorithm to decide what to do. The method is simple: the gateway should forward copies of the datagram along all connected links

ARP.why: A dedicated subsection gives a normative rule for ARP behaviour with broadcast addresses to avoid forwarding loops.
ARP.quote: An ARP server should never respond to a request whose target is a broadcast address.

rejected.why: IPv4 is the substrate the document extends with conventions, but the document is about broadcast addressing, which fits addressing better.
The gateway forwarding algorithm is routing behaviour for broadcasts, but it is narrow and more naturally covered by the multicast/addressing tags.
ICMP is mentioned only in passing as a possible user of an all-zeros source address.
Ethernet is only an example of a link layer that supports broadcast.

gaps.name: IP broadcast / directed broadcast / subnet broadcast
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IP broadcasting or Reverse Path Forwarding broadcast; the document's central subject is closest to addressing and multicast but not exactly covered.

RFC923.title: Assigned numbers
RFC923.summary: RFC 923 is the October 1984 Assigned Numbers memo, a registry listing of assigned network, protocol, port, version, AS, link, Ethernet, ARP, Telnet option, and naming values for the ARPA-Internet.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned numbers (ports, protocol numbers, network numbers, etc.) maintained by the number coordinator, which is the IANA function's precursor.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

addressing.why: A large part of the document describes address classes A/B/C, dotted decimal notation, special addresses and lists network number assignments.
addressing.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

ARPANET.why: Includes ARPANET logical addresses and link numbers registries and ARPANET network assignments.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: Port numbers are listed for TCP/UDP, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Lists Telnet option numbers as one registry table; the protocol itself is not specified.
Only lists ARP parameter values in a short section; the protocol is not the subject.
AS numbers are registered for EGP use, but EGP is not specified here.
Lists official machine and system names from the host table; this is a registry list, not host naming conventions.

RFC924.title: Official ARPA-Internet protocols for connecting personal computers to the Internet
RFC924.summary: RFC 924 is a 1984 status report cataloguing the official ARPA-Internet protocols, giving each one's status (required, recommended, elective, experimental), specification, known problems, dependencies and contact.

internet history.why: The document is a snapshot of the 1984 ARPA-Internet protocol suite and its status. It is mainly of historical interest, including the NCP-to-TCP and HOSTS.TXT-to-DOMAIN transitions.
internet history.quote: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet.  Comments indicate any revisions or changes planned.

TCP.why: The TCP entry has a long list of clarifications to RFC 793. These cover push, urgent, MSS, idle connections and user timeout, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: Urgent:  Page 17 is wrong.  The urgent pointer points to the last octet of urgent data

FTP.why: The FTP entry has an extended discussion of data connection ports, PORT/PASV, stream versus block mode, and why NCP FTP did not have the same problem.
FTP.quote: Data Connection Management:

rejected.why: IP and ICMP get short entries. This is a catalogue of many protocols, not a specification or analysis of IP.
SMTP and the other mail protocols appear only as brief list entries.
The Domain Name Protocol is listed as experimental with no comments. It is one entry among many.
Telnet and its options table is a modest entry, not the focus of the document.
The ARPA-Internet is the subject, and ARPANET-specific material appears only incidentally.

gaps.name: Internet protocol suite status catalogue / official protocol standards list
gaps.why: This RFC belongs to the series of 'Official Internet Protocols' status lists. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol standardization status listings, only the broader IETF process and internet history tags.

RFC925.title: Multi-LAN address resolution
RFC925.summary: RFC 925 proposes "transparent subnets" for multi-LAN networks, extending ARP so that ARP-based bridge "boxes" relay ARP queries across LANs and proxy for remote hosts, as an alternative to explicit subnets.

ARP.why: The whole document specifies a multi-LAN extension of ARP, including BOX caches, search lists, timeouts and proxy replies.
ARP.quote: The idea in this memo is to extend the ARP to work in an environment of multiple interconnected LANs.

rejected.why: Datagram TTL handling and address classes are mentioned, but only as context for the ARP-based scheme. The document does not specify IPv4.
It compares explicit and transparent subnets and discusses address structure. The main subject is address resolution, so ARP is the better tag.
LANs are discussed generically. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet interworking.
The document explicitly avoids proposing a routing procedure or BOX-to-BOX protocol.

RFC926.title: Protocol for providing the connectionless mode network services
RFC926.summary: RFC 926 retypes ISO DIS 8473, specifying the OSI connectionless-mode Network Layer protocol (ISO IP): PDU formats, segmentation/reassembly, lifetime, error reports, header checksum, and a formal state-machine description.

CLNP.why: The whole document specifies ISO 8473, the Connectionless Network Protocol, including PDU encoding, functions, and formal description.
CLNP.quote: Protocol for Providing the Connectionless-Mode Network Services

checksum.why: A substantial part covers the header checksum algorithm, its error-detection power (Annex A.3) and computation algorithms (Annex C).
checksum.quote: The function is realized by a checksum computed on the PDU header. The checksum is verified at each point at which the PDU header is processed.

rejected.why: Parent of CLNP, implied by the more specific tag.
Only an informal analogue ('ISO IP'); the document specifies the OSI protocol, not IPv4.
CLNP is the more specific fitting tag under it.
The Error Report PDU is part of CLNP itself, not ICMP.
Routing is only an assumed function (Route PDU, Annex B management discussion); no routing protocol is specified.

RFC927.title: TACACS user identification Telnet option
RFC927.summary: Defines a Telnet option (TUID, code 26) letting a TAC or host pass an already-authenticated user's 32-bit UUID to a target host to avoid double login under TACACS.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its command code, negotiation, defaults and subnegotiation format.
Telnet.quote: The following is the description of a TELNET option designed to facilitate double login avoidance.

TACACS+.why: The option exists to pass along TACACS-authenticated identity. The taxonomy's TACACS entry covers TACACS and TACACS+, so readers of that subject would want this RFC.
TACACS+.quote: Under TACACS (the TAC Access Control System) a user must be authenticated (give a correct name/password pair) to a TAC before he can connect to a host

rejected.why: The option conveys an already-proven identity, but the TACACS tag is the more specific fit for the authentication aspect.
The UUID here is a 32-bit user identifier, not the Universally Unique Identifier standard.
The document does not describe a general AAA framework. TACACS+ is the more specific tag.

RFC928.title: Introduction to proposed DoD standard H-FP
RFC928.summary: Introduces the proposed DoD standard Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP), explaining the outboard processing (NFE/OPE) rationale, its three-layer structure (Link, Channel, ASCII-command layer), open issues, and host integration with examples from Multics NCP and Telnet.

ARPANET.why: Substantial historical and integration material on ARPANET NCP, IMPs, Well-Known Sockets and Host-Host protocol, and ARPANET Reference Model layers; the H-FP descends from ARPANET network front-ends.
ARPANET.quote: the author was presenting a status report on whether the Multics ARPANET implementation would be ready by the July 1 deadline

internet architecture.why: Document argues architecturally for outboard processing environments, layering, and the ARPANET Reference Model as the basis for attaching hosts to networks.
internet architecture.quote: the only protocols "seen" beyond the Comm Subnet Processor are the common intercomputer networking protocols

rejected.why: TCP is discussed as a protocol that could be offloaded, but the document is not about TCP itself.
Telnet integration is used as an example in the host integration note, not the subject of the document.
X.25 is considered as a possible Link/Channel mechanism but is not specified or profiled here.
The NCP is discussed as an analogue and integration example, not specified here; ARPANET covers it adequately.
Mentioned only briefly as an offloadable protocol and for its response-code style.
Security labeling is discussed only to say it is outside the standard H-FP.

gaps.name: Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP) / outboard processing
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers host-to-front-end/offload protocols, which is the central subject of this document and its companion RFC 929.

RFC929.title: Proposed Host-Front End Protocol
RFC929.summary: Proposes a Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP) with a small command set (Begin, Transmit, Signal, Condition, Status, End, No-op) letting a Host process drive protocol interpreters offloaded to an outboard front-end processor, with appendices mapping it onto TCP and Telnet.

TCP.why: Appendix 1 specifies how each H-FP command maps onto the MIL-STD 1778 TCP interface (open, send, urgent, push, close, abort, status) for an offloaded TCP.
TCP.quote: an interface between a Host process and an off-loaded interpreter of the DoD's Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

Telnet.why: Appendix 2 defines Telnet offloading: mediation levels, option negotiation via Condition, Go Ahead, Interrupt Process/Abort Output signals and Are You There.
Telnet.quote: an interface between a Host process and an off-loaded interpreter of the Telnet protocol

rejected.why: Only listed as a protocol that could be offloaded; the FTP appendix is marked TBS.
Mail offloading is only named in the protocol table and left TBS.
IP appears only as an example of an offloadable datagram protocol, with no IP-specific specification.
The document targets the ARPA-Internet community but is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
Commands are coded in ASCII, but that is only the encoding the protocol uses.
Mentioned once as an example Channel-layer protocol, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP) / outboard protocol processing
gaps.why: The document's main subject is the offloading of network protocol interpreters to a front-end processor and the Host-to-front-end command interface. No taxonomy tag covers it. The closest are internet architecture or transport mapping, and neither fits well.

RFC930.title: Telnet terminal type option
RFC930.summary: RFC 930 specifies the Telnet TERMINAL-TYPE option (code 24), letting a Telnet server query the client's terminal type via SB SEND/IS subnegotiation, superseding RFC 884.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option, including its commands, negotiation rules and subnegotiation exchange, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This option allows a telnet server to determine the type of terminal connected to a user telnet program.

rejected.why: Terminal type names are NVT ASCII strings, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
It refers to the Assigned Numbers RFC for terminal type names, but this is a minor reference and not the subject of the document.

RFC931.title: Authentication server
RFC931.summary: RFC 931 specifies the Authentication Server protocol (later known as Ident), in which a server on TCP port 113 returns the identity of the owner of a given TCP connection.

Ident.why: The document defines the protocol that became Ident (port 113, query/response of port pairs returning USERID or ERROR). This is the Identification Protocol's predecessor specification.
Ident.quote: The Authentication Server Protocol provides a means to determine the identity of a user of a particular TCP connection.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The protocol uses TCP port 113 and queries TCP port pairs, but it does not specify or extend TCP.
FTP automatic authentication is one suggested application, with a short paragraph. The document is not about FTP itself.
A Telnet option for eliminating double login is mentioned only in passing, and nothing is specified.
The Ident tag is more specific and covers the subject.

RFC932.title: Subnetwork addressing scheme
RFC932.summary: RFC 932 proposes a subnet addressing scheme in which subnets are numbered with reserved Class C addresses that distant gateways collapse into Class B ("B 1/2") addresses, requiring changes to gateways but not hosts.

addressing.why: The whole document is a proposal for IP subnet address structure and how gateways aggregate/collapse addresses (Class C to Class B), which is IP address architecture.
addressing.quote: the individual subnets of a network are numbered using Class C addresses.

rejected.why: The scheme aggregates classful addresses (C to B) for routing, but CIDR is classless aggregation, which postdates this document and is not what is specified.
The document concerns IPv4 addressing, but its subject is subnet addressing architecture, which the addressing topic covers more specifically; it does not specify IPv4 itself.
Gateways store collapsed routing information, but the document is about address structure rather than routing design principles.

gaps.name: Subnetting (Internet subnets)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about IP subnet addressing (cf. RFC 917); the taxonomy has no subnetting tag, so the broader addressing topic is used.

RFC933.title: Output marking Telnet option
RFC933.summary: RFC 933 proposes a Telnet option (OUTMRK, code 27) letting a Server-Telnet send a security banner to User-Telnet, which displays it on the screen independently of the application, to support labeling of human-readable output.

Telnet.why: The document defines a new Telnet option with its commands, negotiation and subnegotiation format, so it belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: This RFC proposes a new option for Telnet for the ARPA-Internet community

rejected.why: The motivation is displaying security-level banners (TCSEC labeling of human-readable output), but the document specifies a display-banner Telnet option, not a security label framework like CIPSO.
Banner data and control octets are ASCII, but this is just encoding used by the option, not the subject.

RFC934.title: Proposed standard for message encapsulation
RFC934.summary: RFC 934 proposes a standard for encapsulating forwarded messages inside another message (with dash-based encapsulation boundaries and character stuffing) so that bursting agents can extract them, including for digests and blind carbon copies.

message format.why: The document defines how messages are encapsulated within the body of an RFC-822 style message, including boundaries, header requirements for encapsulated messages and character stuffing. This is Internet message format.
message format.quote: two agents act on behalf of the user, a forwarding agent, which composes the message draft prior to posting, and a bursting agent which decomposes the message after delivery.

mailing lists.why: A major motivation is giving interest group digests an unambiguous standard so they can be burst. The document also discusses redistribution by discussion group moderators.
mailing lists.quote: In the case of an interest group digest, a bursting capability is especially useful.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the more specific message format tag, so it is not listed separately.
RFC 821 is referenced only for the Return-Path header. The document does not specify or extend SMTP.
This memo predates MIME. It defines a simpler encapsulation scheme and not MIME body structure.
X.400 is cited only as a standard that discourages direct redistribution. The document is not about X.400 or interworking with it.

RFC935.title: Reliable link layer protocols
RFC935.summary: RFC 935 compares character-oriented, bit-oriented (HDLC/LAPB) and DDCMP link layer protocols against RATP and Thinwire for reliable asynchronous serial links, and recommends character-oriented framing with a 16-bit CRC and LAPB control procedures.

link layer.why: The whole document compares data-link framing, error detection, sequencing and addressing for serial links and proposes a link layer protocol. No more specific link-layer tag fits, since SLIP and PPP are not discussed.
link layer.quote: The stated need is reliable communication between two programs over a full-duplex, point-to-point communication link

CRC.why: A substantial section argues for CRC over additive or XOR checks and recommends CRC-16 or the CCITT CRC polynomial.
CRC.quote: I would support the use of a CRC type of error check because of the far greater level of protection it affords.

RATP.why: RATP (RFC 916) is analysed and compared throughout, and the document argues that standard protocols are preferable to it.
RATP.quote: RATP does not represent a significant savings compared to other widely-used protocols.

X.25.why: The proposal adopts X.25 LAPB control procedures and CRC. The postscript discusses X.25 and X.32 access for PCs.
X.25.quote: I would recommend use of LAPB, since this is the most widely known of the family.

rejected.why: TCP and IP checksums are mentioned only as context for the link-layer error check, and the document does not specify or analyse TCP.
The document does not discuss SLIP. It compares link-layer protocol families for serial lines.
Thinwire's template compression is mentioned as an aside, but the document does not specify or propose header compression.
ASCII appears only as a reference and as the character set of the control characters. It is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: HDLC/ADCCP and DDCMP serial data link protocols
gaps.why: The document is mainly a comparison of HDLC/ADCCP bit-oriented, character-oriented basic mode and DDCMP framing. The taxonomy has no tag for these generic serial link protocols.

RFC936.title: Another Internet subnet addressing scheme
RFC936.summary: RFC 936 proposes the Berkeley IP subnet addressing scheme, which encodes a subnet number in the host part of Class A/B addresses so several physical networks share one network number, and compares it with RFC 917, 925 and 932.

addressing.why: The document specifies a subnet addressing scheme: how IP addresses split into network, subnet and host fields. This is IP address architecture, and no narrower child tag (CIDR, multihoming, anycast, renumbering) fits.
addressing.quote: the Berkeley subnet addressing utilizes encoding of the host part of the Internet address. Hosts and gateways on the local network are able to determine the subnet number

rejected.why: The scheme operates on IPv4 Class A/B/C addresses, but the document is about a subnetting convention, not the IPv4 protocol or its address lifecycle. The addressing topic fits better.
ARP is mentioned only in discussing RFC-925's alternative approach, not specified or extended here.
A new ICMP request for dynamic subnet-mask discovery is mentioned only as a drawback of RFC-917.
The scheme uses fixed subnet field widths within classful addresses and does not do classless aggregation.
Routing is discussed for hosts and gateways, but the focus is on address encoding rather than routing design.

gaps.name: IP subnetting
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for subnetting. The closest fit, addressing, is broader than this RFC's subject.

RFC937.title: Post Office Protocol: Version 2
RFC937.summary: RFC 937 specifies POP2, a simple command/reply protocol letting a workstation retrieve mail from a mailbox server (HELO, FOLD, READ, RETR, ACKS/ACKD/NACK, QUIT); it obsoletes RFC 918 and is now historic.

POP3.why: The document specifies POP2, the predecessor of POP3, and no separate POP2 tag exists. The POP3 tag is the closest fit for the Post Office Protocol family, which readers browsing that subject would want to find here.
POP3.quote: The intent of the Post Office Protocol Version 2 (POP2) is to allow a user's workstation to access mail from a mailbox server.

rejected.why: SMTP is only mentioned as the way mail is posted to the server. The document does not specify or extend it.
Messages are transmitted in RFC 822 format, but the document does not define or discuss that format. It is only the payload.
The more specific POP3 tag covers mail access, so the general email tag is not needed.
TCP is only the reliable stream substrate, with POP2 on port 109. Nothing new is defined about TCP.
NVT-ASCII is mentioned only as the transmission encoding. The document is not about it.

gaps.name: POP2 (Post Office Protocol Version 2)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only a POP3 tag and no POP2 or generic Post Office Protocol tag. The POP3 tag is used as the nearest fit.

RFC938.title: Internet Reliable Transaction Protocol functional and interface specification
RFC938.summary: RFC 938 specifies IRTP, an experimental transport-level host-to-host protocol over IP providing reliable, sequenced delivery of transaction packets with port multiplexing, synchronization, acknowledgments and retransmission.

IRTP.why: The entire document is the functional and interface specification of IRTP: header format, synchronization, data transfer, acknowledgment and implementation issues.
IRTP.quote: The Internet Reliable Transaction Protocol (IRTP) is a full duplex, transaction oriented, host to host protocol which provides reliable sequenced delivery of packets of data

rejected.why: TCP is only a comparison point and the source of the 'quiet time' concept; the document does not specify or extend it.
UDP is mentioned only for comparison of complexity; not about it.
The checksum field uses the standard one's complement sum, but it is only a header field, not the subject of the document.
ICMP is only a substrate for unreachable and source quench notifications.
IP is the underlying layer IRTP runs over (protocol number 28); the document does not specify IP.

RFC939.title: Executive summary of the NRC report on transport protocols for Department of Defense data networks
RFC939.summary: Executive summary of the 1985 NRC report comparing DoD TCP/IP with ISO TP-4/ISO-IP and recommending that DoD adopt TP-4 as a costandard with TCP, with transition options.

TCP.why: The report's central subject is a comparison of TCP with ISO TP-4 and a policy recommendation on whether DoD should keep TCP or move to TP-4.
TCP.quote: A detailed comparison of the DOD Transmission Control Protocol and the ISO Transport Protocol indicates they are functionally equivalent and provide essentially similar services.

OSI.why: A substantial part covers ISO/OSI transport (TP-4) and internetwork protocol, their maturity, and transition and coexistence with the DoD IP/TCP suite.
OSI.quote: The ISO IP, based very strongly on the DOD IP, became a draft international standard in April 1984.

rejected.why: The ISO internetwork protocol is discussed only briefly as 'ISO IP', without detail, so the broader OSI tag is a better fit.
The ARPANET appears only as historical background for TCP's development.
Brief historical remarks exist, but the document is a policy comparison and recommendation, not a history.
The DoD IP is mentioned only in combination with TCP, and the document does not specify or analyse IP itself.

gaps.name: Transport protocol standardization policy (DoD TCP vs ISO TP-4)
gaps.why: The document is a policy and economic evaluation of protocol standards and transition. The taxonomy has no tag for standards policy or protocol migration strategy outside the OSI tag.

RFC940.title: Toward an Internet standard scheme for subnetting
RFC940.summary: RFC 940 from the GADS Task Force proposes a standard IP subnetting scheme: a subnet field taken from the host part of the address, with a 32-bit mask used by hosts to decide whether a destination is on the local subnet or must go via a gateway.

addressing.why: The document defines how IP addresses are divided into network, subnet and host fields, and how a mask determines whether a destination is on the local subnet. This is IP address architecture. No more specific child tag fits, since CIDR is a later aggregation scheme.
addressing.quote: This subnet scheme adds an optional 'subnet' layer and field.

rejected.why: The document concerns IPv4 addresses, but it is about the subnetting scheme within address architecture, not the IPv4 protocol or its address lifecycle.
CIDR is classless aggregation. This memo covers classful subnetting with a mask, which predates CIDR.
The routing decision is covered only as the host's on-link versus gateway test. The memo explicitly says it does not specify how routing is done.

gaps.name: IP subnetting / subnet masks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for subnetting, so it is covered by the broader addressing topic. A dedicated subnetting tag would help readers of this and related RFCs (917, 932, 936, 950).

RFC941.title: Addendum to the network service definition covering network layer addressing
RFC941.summary: RFC 941 retypes ISO DP 8348/DAD2, an addendum to the OSI Network Service Definition that defines the abstract syntax, semantics, allocation authorities and preferred concrete encodings of the Network Service Access Point (NSAP) address.

OSI.why: The whole document specifies the OSI NSAP address format (AFI, IDI, DSP), allocation hierarchy and concrete syntaxes for the OSI network layer.
OSI.quote: defines the abstract syntax and semantics of the Network Address (Network Service Access Point Address)

rejected.why: The addressing topic covers IP address architecture; this document covers OSI NSAP addressing, which the OSI tag already captures.
The addendum explicitly does not specify protocol encodings, and it does not define CLNP. It only mentions connectionless-mode service parameters.
X.121 is only one of the IDI formats, used as a numbering plan for allocating authorities. The document is not about X.25.

gaps.name: OSI NSAP addressing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no OSI-addressing-specific tag. The OSI tag covers it, but readers looking for OSI address structure would benefit from a more specific one.

RFC942.title: Transport protocols for Department of Defense data networks
RFC942.summary: National Research Council committee report comparing DoD TCP/IP with ISO TP-4/ISO-IP and recommending that DoD adopt TP-4 as a costandard and plan a managed transition.

TCP.why: The report compares TCP's services (flow control, addressing, closing, urgent data) with TP-4 and recommends a transition away from it. TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: The committee recommends that the DOD move toward adoption of TP-4 as costandard with TCP and toward exclusive use of TP-4.

OSI.why: Covers ISO TP-4 and the ISO connectionless internetwork protocol, including their status, addressing, packet format comparison and coexistence with DoD IP.
OSI.quote: The ISO IP, based very strongly on the DOD IP, became a draft international standard in April 1984.

internet layer.why: A substantial section compares DoD IP and ISO IP, with a header format table, addressing, ICMP and GGP.
internet layer.quote: The internet protocols of DOD and ISO are much more similar to one another than the transport protocols.
internet layer.section: III. Comparison of DOD and ISO Protocols

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by TCP. The report is about specific transport protocols, not transport in general.
The report mentions the ARPANET and its NCP-to-TCP cutover as background and as lessons learned. It is not about the ARPANET itself.
The ISO connectionless internetwork protocol (DP 8473) is discussed, but only under OSI. A CLNP tag would be too specific for this policy-level comparison.
The report has historical content, but it is a policy study and not a retrospective.
ICMP and GGP are mentioned only in passing when comparing the internet layers.

gaps.name: Protocol standardization policy / DoD-ISO transition
gaps.why: The report's core subject is government protocol-standards policy and migration strategy from TCP/IP to ISO protocols. No taxonomy tag covers it.

RFC943.title: Assigned numbers
RFC943.summary: RFC 943 is the April 1985 Assigned Numbers memo listing assigned IP network numbers, version and protocol numbers, TCP/UDP ports, EGP autonomous system numbers, ARPANET link and logical addresses, Ethernet types, ARP parameters, Telnet options, and official names.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned protocol parameters, i.e. the precursor to the IANA registries, with number assignment coordinated by Joyce Reynolds.
IANA.quote: This Network Working Group Request for Comments documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations.

addressing.why: A large part of the document covers class A/B/C address structure, dotted decimal notation, special addresses and the allocation of network numbers among research, defense, government and commercial users.
addressing.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

ARPANET.why: It records ARPANET logical addresses and link numbers (Host/IMP interface), which are ARPANET-specific working parameters.
ARPANET.quote: The ARPANET facility for "logical addressing" is described in RFC 878 [58].

rejected.why: IP is the protocol whose address classes and numbers are catalogued, but the document is a registry rather than a specification of IPv4 itself; addressing covers the content.
Port numbers are listed for TCP/UDP services, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Telnet options are listed in a table only; the protocol is not specified here.
Autonomous system numbers are assigned for EGP, not BGP; the list is a registry rather than routing protocol content.
ARP parameter values are listed briefly but ARP is not specified or extended.
EGP autonomous system numbers are registered, but the protocol itself is not specified here.

gaps.name: Protocol number and port number registries
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for assigned protocol numbers, port numbers or autonomous system numbers as such; only the general IANA topic fits.

RFC944.title: Official ARPA-Internet protocols
RFC944.summary: RFC 944 is a 1985 status report cataloguing the official ARPA-Internet protocols, giving each one's status, specification document, comments, dependencies and contact.

ARPANET.why: The whole document is a catalogue of the protocols of the ARPA-Internet community in 1985, including legacy ARPANET-era protocols from the ARPANET Protocol Handbook.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet.

FTP.why: The FTP entry has a long discussion of data connection management and the multiple 1xx reply issue, with a ruling. Readers of FTP history would want it.
FTP.quote: there should be only one 1xx response.

TCP.why: The TCP entry lists corrections and clarifications to RFC 793: urgent, push, MSS, idle connections and user timeout.
TCP.quote: The urgent pointer points to the last octet of urgent data

rejected.why: It is a contemporary status report, not a retrospective, so it does not fit well.
No such id in the taxonomy. IPv4 was considered, but its entry is only a brief comment and not a substantial part of the document.
The Telnet options table is a listing only; Telnet is one entry among many.
Assigned Numbers is only mentioned in an appendix entry.
The Domain Name Protocol entry is only a pointer to its specifications.
The SMTP entry is brief and one among dozens.

gaps.name: Official Internet protocol status list
gaps.why: The document is an index of protocol statuses (required, recommended, elective, experimental). It resembles the later STD / Official Internet Protocol Standards documents, and the taxonomy has no tag for that.

RFC945.title: DoD statement on the NRC report
RFC945.summary: Reproduces a 1985 DoD (ASDC3I) memo to DCA responding to the National Research Council report on transport protocols, declining immediate adoption of ISO TP-4 alongside TCP/IP and directing DCA to prepare requirements, monitoring, testing and transition planning.

OSI.why: The memo is about whether and how DoD should adopt the ISO/OSI transport and internetwork protocols alongside TCP/IP, and directs a transition strategy. OSI is the closest fit for this coexistence question.
OSI.quote: The report recommends that DoD immediately adopt the International Standards Organization Transport Protocol (TP-4) and Internetwork Protocol (IP) as a DoD co-standard

TCP.why: The DoD TCP/IP mandate and its relationship to a possible TP-4 replacement is the policy backdrop and substance of the memo. The memo does not specify TCP itself, so this is a secondary tag.
TCP.quote: the current DoD standard Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and IP and move ultimately toward exclusive use of TP-4.

rejected.why: The Context section recounts earlier TCP/IP mandates, but the document is a policy letter and not a retrospective.
IP is mentioned only as part of the TCP/IP standard and is not the subject.
It deals with protocol standardization policy, not architectural principles.
The memo names the ISO Internetwork Protocol only in passing, so the broader OSI tag fits better.
It is a DoD policy memo, not an IETF procedure.

gaps.name: DoD protocol standardization policy (TCP/IP mandate vs ISO standards)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about government protocol-standards policy. The taxonomy has no tag for it beyond OSI coexistence.

RFC946.title: Telnet terminal location number option
RFC946.summary: RFC 946 defines a Telnet option (TTYLOC, code 28) that lets a client send a 64-bit terminal location number (host address plus terminal number) to a Telnet server.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its option code, WILL/WON'T/DO/DON'T negotiation, and subnegotiation format.
Telnet.quote: IAC SB TTYLOC <format> <TTYLOC number with IAC doubling> IAC SE

rejected.why: Finger and WHOIS are mentioned only as consumers of the location information, not specified or extended.
Mentioned only in passing as a mechanism that could use the location data; the document is not about it.
