The 32-bit host address is just a component of the TTYLOC number; the document does not address IPv4 itself.
TCP is only the substrate the option runs over, with no new TCP behaviour defined.
The terminal location here is a host and terminal-line identifier for physically locating users, not a geolocation format or conveyance mechanism.

RFC947.title: Multi-network broadcasting within the Internet
RFC947.summary: Describes a broadcast repeater that extends a LAN's UDP broadcast domain across multiple networks via forwarder and repeater processes, developed for the Cronus distributed operating system, with alternatives considered and implementation experience.

internet layer.why: The document is about network-layer broadcast delivery across multiple physical networks in the Internet. No more specific tag fits, so the general internet layer topic is used.
internet layer.quote: extension of a network's broadcast domain to include more than one physical network through the use of a broadcast packet repeater

rejected.why: The document notes multicast would be more appropriate but was unavailable. It deals with broadcast relaying, not multicast routing or group membership.
The repeater filters and forwards UDP broadcast packets, but UDP is the thing being relayed, not something the document specifies or extends.
TCP is only the transport used between forwarder and repeater, so it is substrate.
Ethernets are the example LANs in the test configuration. The document is not about Ethernet itself.

gaps.name: Broadcast forwarding / broadcast repeater across networks
gaps.why: The document's core subject is extending link-level broadcast domains across networks, and the taxonomy has no tag for broadcast.

RFC948.title: Two methods for the transmission of IP datagrams over IEEE 802.3 networks
RFC948.summary: RFC 948 specifies two methods for encapsulating IP datagrams on IEEE 802.3 networks: an Ethernet-compatible method using type values above 1500, and an IEEE 802.2/802.3 LLC Type 1 method with SAP 96. It also covers address mapping via ARP and the transition between the two.

Ethernet.why: The document specifies how IP is carried over IEEE 802.3 and Ethernet, covering both the Ethernet-compatible and 802.2/802.3 encapsulations. The Ethernet tag is the best fit.
Ethernet.quote: IP datagrams are transmitted in standard 802.2/802.3 LLC Type 1 Unnumbered Information format with the DSAP and SSAP fields of the 802.2 header set to 96

ARP.why: A substantial section covers address mapping and strongly recommends ARP for 802.3 address resolution.
ARP.quote: Mappings between 32-bit Internet addresses and 802.3 addresses could be accomplished through a protocol similar to the Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)

rejected.why: IP is the payload being encapsulated. The document defines nothing new about IP itself.
The Ethernet tag is more specific and already covers this.
TCP is mentioned only for the Maximum Segment Size option, as advice on datagram sizing.

RFC949.title: FTP unique-named store command
RFC949.summary: RFC 949 proposes adding a new FTP command, STOU, which stores a file under a name unique to the current directory and returns the generated name in the 250 response.

FTP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the File Transfer Protocol, a new unique-named store command.
FTP.quote: Add a new command, STOU, to FTP, which behaves like STOR except that the resultant file is to be created in the current directory under a name unique to that directory.

rejected.why: The FTP technology tag is more specific and already covers this document, so the parent topic is not added.

RFC950.title: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure
RFC950.summary: RFC 950 specifies the standard IP subnetting procedure: address-mask interpretation of the local address part, host software changes, and new ICMP Address Mask Request/Reply messages for discovering the mask.

addressing.why: The core of the document is how IP addresses are interpreted with a subnet field and address mask, and how hosts decide local versus gateway delivery. That is IP address architecture, and no more specific child tag fits (CIDR is a different subject).
addressing.quote: This memo specifies procedures for the use of subnets.

ICMP.why: The document defines new ICMP message types (17 and 18), with their format, usage and examples in Appendices I, II and IV. This is a substantial extension of ICMP.
ICMP.quote: the ICMP protocol [5] is extended by adding a new pair of ICMP message types, "Address Mask Request" and "Address Mask Reply"

rejected.why: The document is about IPv4 addressing, but its specific subject is subnetting, so the addressing tag is the better fit.
ARP and RARP are mentioned only as background for discovering a host's address or as an alternative approach. The document does not specify them.
RFC 950 predates CIDR. It describes subnet masks inside classful networks, not classless aggregation.
BOOTP/RFC 951 is only cited as another way to obtain the mask. It is not discussed in the document's main body.

RFC951.title: Bootstrap Protocol
RFC951.summary: RFC 951 specifies BOOTP, an IP/UDP bootstrap protocol letting diskless clients discover their IP address, a server address and a boot filename, including relaying through gateways.

DHCP.why: BOOTP is the direct predecessor of DHCP and the taxonomy has no separate BOOTP tag. The document specifies the packet format, client/server processing and relay (giaddr) behaviour that DHCP builds on, so DHCP readers would want it.
DHCP.quote: an IP/UDP bootstrap protocol (BOOTP) which allows a diskless client machine to discover its own IP address, the address of a server host

rejected.why: TFTP is the phase-two file transfer that follows BOOTP. The document only mentions it as the next step and does not specify it.
ARP is used for client/server address resolution (Chicken/Egg issues, Client Use of ARP). It is a supporting mechanism, not what the document is about.
UDP is only the transport, with reserved ports 67 and 68. Nothing new is defined about UDP itself.
The document uses IPv4 addressing and broadcast only as a substrate.
FTP is mentioned only as an alternative second-phase file transfer protocol.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no BOOTP tag. DHCP is the closest fit, but BOOTP is a distinct historic protocol with its own subject page.

RFC952.title: DoD Internet host table specification
RFC952.summary: RFC 952 is the official specification of the DoD Internet Host Table format, defining hostname syntax, entry fields and grammar for the HOSTS.TXT file maintained by the NIC.

hostnames.why: The document specifies host naming conventions and the host table format, which is exactly the hostnames subject (host naming conventions and host tables).
hostnames.quote: A "name" (Net, Host, Gateway, or Domain name) is a text string up to 24 characters drawn from the alphabet (A-Z), digits (0-9), minus sign (-)

rejected.why: DNS is only mentioned as background (RFC 921, domain-style names); the document specifies a flat host table, not DNS.
ARPANET and MILNET addresses are used in examples, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
The IP address classes are described only to explain the table's address field, not as the subject.
FTP is only mentioned as a way to retrieve the file.

RFC953.title: Hostname Server
RFC953.summary: RFC 953 specifies the NIC Hostname Server protocol, a TCP service on port 101 that returns host, gateway, network and domain table entries from the DoD Internet Host Table via simple text queries.

hostnames.why: The document defines a protocol for querying the host table by hostname or address (HNAME, HADDR, ALL). That is host naming and host-table lookup, which the hostnames tag covers.
hostnames.quote: deliver machine-readable name/address information describing networks, gateways, hosts, and eventually domains, within the internet environment

rejected.why: The document only mentions the Domain Name System as a future development (RFC-921). It does not specify DNS.
TCP is only the transport for the server on port 101. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
Both are NIC information services. This one serves host table data, not registration data directory lookups.

RFC954.title: NICNAME/WHOIS
RFC954.summary: RFC 954 is the official specification of the NICNAME/WHOIS protocol, a TCP query/response directory service on port 43 run by the SRI NIC for looking up DDN users, hosts, and organizations.

WHOIS.why: The document is the official specification of the NICNAME/WHOIS protocol and service, the legacy directory service for registration data lookup.
WHOIS.quote: Connect to the SRI-NIC service host at TCP service port 43 (decimal).

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport the WHOIS service runs over; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
WHOIS has a more specific tag under domain registration, and it is not an X.500 or LDAP-style directory; the WHOIS tag covers it.
RFC 742 NAME/FINGER is only cited in the bibliography as a predecessor; the document does not specify Finger.
ASCII CR/LF is mentioned only as the line terminator, not as a subject of the document.

RFC955.title: Towards a transport service for transaction processing applications
RFC955.summary: A 1985 discussion memo arguing that transaction-processing applications (name servers, distributed operating systems) fall in the gap between TCP and UDP, and outlining objectives for a new connectionless reliable transaction-oriented transport protocol.

transport.why: The whole memo defines service requirements for a new transport-level protocol for transactions, sitting between TCP and UDP. No specific transport technology tag fits, so the general topic applies.
transport.quote: We suggest that the solution should be a new transaction-oriented transport protocol with the following features:

rejected.why: TCP is only contrasted as the virtual-circuit alternative with high setup cost. The memo does not specify or extend it.
UDP is critiqued as inadequate for transactions (unreliable, size limit). The memo is not about UDP usage.
Name servers are used as a motivating example of a transaction application. The memo does not specify DNS behaviour.
RFC 938 (IRTP) is only cited as one existing transaction protocol. This memo is a general requirements discussion.
Multicast capability is mentioned as one desired feature in a single bullet. It is not a substantial subject.

gaps.name: Transaction-oriented / request-response transport (reliable datagram)
gaps.why: The memo's main subject is a transaction transport service. The taxonomy has only the generic transport topic for it.

RFC956.title: Algorithms for synchronizing network clocks
RFC956.summary: Mills proposes maximum-likelihood majority-subset and clustering algorithms for selecting a good clock offset estimate from mutually suspicious network clocks, with experimental data on Internet host clock accuracy using UDP Time and ICMP Timestamp.

time synchronization.why: The whole document is about algorithms for synchronizing network clocks and measuring host clock offsets, and it motivates a new time protocol that became NTP.
time synchronization.quote: The recent interest within the Internet community in determining accurate time from a set of mutually suspicious network clocks

rejected.why: NTP is only mentioned as a proposed protocol in RFC 958. This document covers estimation algorithms, not the NTP specification.
ICMP Timestamp messages are the measurement mechanism used in the experiments. The document does not specify or extend ICMP.
The UDP Time protocol is used as a data source, and UDP is only suggested as a base for a future protocol. The document is not about UDP.
ARPANET paths are the experimental environment. The document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.

RFC957.title: Experiments in network clock synchronization
RFC957.summary: Reports experiments validating Mills' DCnet clock synchronization algorithms and Hello-message protocol, comparing power-grid, radio (WWVB, GOES, WWV) and network-link clocks, leap-second handling, and ARPANET ICMP timestamp measurements.

time synchronization.why: The whole document is about designing and experimentally evaluating network clock synchronization algorithms. NTP is only referenced as a separate proposal (RFC 958), so the general topic tag fits better than NTP.
time synchronization.quote: This RFC discusses some experiments in clock synchronization in the ARPA-Internet community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

rejected.why: NTP is only cited as a separately proposed protocol (RFC 958). This document describes DCnet Hello-based synchronization experiments, not NTP.
ICMP Timestamp messages are used for the ARPANET measurements, but only as a measurement tool, not as the subject.
ARPANET paths are measured in a minor section; the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
Measurements serve to validate clock accuracy and are not a network performance metrics methodology.

RFC958.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP)
RFC958.summary: RFC 958 specifies the original Network Time Protocol (NTP), defining its UDP-based message format, timestamp representation, client/server and symmetric modes, and offset/delay calculation for synchronizing network clocks.

NTP.why: The whole document specifies NTP: its data formats, protocol modes, message processing and the roundtrip delay and clock offset calculation.
NTP.quote: This document describes the Network Time Protocol (NTP), a protocol for synchronizing a set of network clocks using a set of distributed clients and servers.

rejected.why: NTP runs over UDP and the appendix shows the UDP header only for completeness. UDP is the substrate, not the subject.
ICMP Timestamp is mentioned only as a predecessor that NTP can replace. The document does not specify or extend ICMP.
This is the parent topic of NTP, so it is implied by the NTP tag and not listed separately.
The document only notes that data integrity relies on the IP and UDP checksums. It says nothing new about checksums.

RFC959.title: File Transfer Protocol
RFC959.summary: RFC 959 is the official specification of the File Transfer Protocol (FTP), defining its model, data representation types, structures, transmission modes, commands, reply codes, and state diagrams.

FTP.why: The document exists to specify FTP, including its commands, replies, data types, and transfer modes.
FTP.quote: This memo is the official specification of the File Transfer Protocol (FTP).

rejected.why: FTP uses Telnet only for the control connection conventions; the document does not specify or extend Telnet.
TCP is only the underlying transport for the control and data connections.
NVT-ASCII is a data type FTP supports, not the subject of the document.
EBCDIC is one of the representation types FTP defines, a minor part of the document.

RFC960.title: Assigned numbers
RFC960.summary: RFC 960 is the 1985 ARPA-Internet Assigned Numbers registry listing network numbers, IP version and protocol numbers, TCP/UDP ports, AS numbers, ARPANET link numbers, Ethernet types, ARP parameters, Telnet options and official names.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned protocol parameter values, with Joyce Reynolds as the assignment coordinator. This is the ancestor of the IANA registries.
IANA.quote: This Network Working Group Request for Comments documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations.

ARPANET.why: The document has sections on ARPANET link numbers and logical addresses, and a large part of the network number list covers ARPANET and MILNET networks.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

addressing.why: A major part of the document defines the class A/B/C address formats, dotted decimal notation, special addresses, and the allocation of network numbers among Research, Defense, Government and Commercial users.
addressing.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

rejected.why: TCP and UDP port numbers are listed only as registry entries. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
The Telnet option numbers are only a registry table. The Telnet protocol itself is not specified.
The document registers IP version and protocol numbers, but it does not specify IPv4. Addressing covers the address-class content.
ARP hardware type and opcode values are listed only as a short registry table.
AS numbers are registered for EGP use, but the document is not about EGP itself.

RFC961.title: Official ARPA-Internet protocols
RFC961.summary: RFC 961 is a December 1985 status report that catalogues the official ARPA-Internet protocols. For each protocol it gives status, specification, comments, dependencies and a contact.

ARPANET.why: The document is a census of the ARPA-Internet protocols, with the specification, status and dependencies of each. Readers of the ARPANET subject would want it.
ARPANET.quote: This memo is an official status report on the protocols used in the ARPA-Internet community.

internet history.why: It is a snapshot of the state of the Internet protocol suite in 1985, including the revisions made to it and the protocols that were abandoned. That makes it a useful historical record.
internet history.quote: To first order, the official protocols are those in the "Internet Protocol Transition Workbook" (IPTW) dated March 1982.

rejected.why: TCP is one entry among about seventy. The document is a catalogue, not a specification or analysis of TCP.
IP is one entry in the catalogue and is not the subject of the document.
DOMAIN is only one entry. Tagging every protocol in the catalogue would be too diffuse.
The document defines a few status terms (required, recommended and so on), but this is not a glossary.
The Assigned Numbers appendix is a brief reference to RFC 960 and is not a substantive treatment.

gaps.name: Internet Official Protocol Standards / protocol status catalogue
gaps.why: This is the start of the recurring series of standards-status lists. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol standardization status lists, only the loosely related IETF process tag.

RFC962.title: TCP-4 prime
RFC962.summary: Padlipsky's informal memo responds to RFC 955's call for a transaction-oriented transport by proposing TCP be modified with NYS (no-way handshake) and NIF (graceless close) commands, with ISN handling tweaks, to avoid connection set-up and tear-down cost.

TCP.why: The whole memo proposes extending TCP with handshake-less open and close commands, including ISN handling, to support transaction-style use.
TCP.quote: why not add NYS (no-way handshake) and NIF (graceless close) commands to TCP and leave everything else as was

rejected.why: The memo is about TCP specifically, so the TCP tag is more specific and its parent topic is implied.
The memo continues the discussion of a transaction-oriented protocol from RFC 955, but it proposes modifying TCP rather than specifying or discussing IRTP.

RFC963.title: Some problems with the specification of the Military Standard Internet Protocol
RFC963.summary: RFC 963 identifies and proposes fixes for errors in the MIL-STD-1777 Internet Protocol specification, mainly in fragmentation and reassembly logic, header padding, and Ada syntax.

IPv4.why: MIL-STD-1777 is the DoD standard IPv4 specification. The document analyses its fragmentation, reassembly and header handling and proposes corrections, so IPv4 readers would want it.
IPv4.quote: This paper points out several significant problems in the specification of the Military Standard Internet Protocol (MIL-STD-1777, dated August 1983 [MILS83a]).

rejected.why: ICMP messages appear only as a case in the reassembly decision table (a missing row for fragmented ICMP). The document is not about ICMP itself.
TCP is mentioned only as the layer above IP that supplies reliability. It is not analysed here.
IPv4 is the more specific tag and already covers this.

RFC964.title: Some problems with the specification of the Military Standard Transmission Control Protocol
RFC964.summary: RFC 964 identifies three specification errors in MIL-STD-1778 (Military Standard TCP) involving SYN data acceptance, missing SYN retransmission timer, and data reception in ESTAB state, and proposes fixes.

TCP.why: The whole document analyses the TCP specification (three-way handshake, retransmission, ESTAB data handling) and proposes corrections, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: This note points out three errors with the specification of the Military Standard Transmission Control Protocol (MIL-STD-1778, dated August 1983 [MILS83]).

rejected.why: The TCP technology tag sits under it and already covers the document.
It is a 1985 document, but it is a technical errata analysis, not a history or retrospective.
NBS TP4 is mentioned only in the introduction as earlier work by the authors; it is not the subject.

RFC965.title: Format for a graphical communication protocol
RFC965.summary: RFC 965 proposes an Interactive Graphical Communication Format (PIGCF) built on the GKSM session metafile as the data format for on-line vector-graphics exchange, mainly for multimedia conferencing, with a processing architecture and example.

network graphics.why: The whole document specifies a graphics format and protocol basis for networked vector graphics exchange, matching the early network graphics tag.
network graphics.quote: A graphical communication protocol is needed to exchange interactive vector graphics information, possibly in conjunction with other information media like voice, text, and video.

rejected.why: Conferencing is the key application and an architecture is sketched, but the document is about a graphics data format, not a conferencing framework or control.
The ARPANET topic is a parent of network graphics and is implied. The document does not discuss ARPANET itself.
It defines a graphics metafile format, but the more specific network graphics tag covers it. The generic data formats tag adds nothing.
Audio-graphics conferencing is mentioned as an example, but the document does not address real-time media transport or signalling.

gaps.name: GKS/GKSM computer graphics metafile
gaps.why: The document centres on the Graphical Kernel System session metafile and its extension. The taxonomy has no tag for computer graphics standards other than the early network graphics tag.

RFC966.title: Host groups: A multicast extension to the Internet Protocol
RFC966.summary: RFC 966 defines the host group model of IP multicast, proposes extensions to IP (group addresses, distance control, delivery), sketches gateway implementation, and specifies an early Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) in an appendix.

multicast.why: The whole document defines the host group multicast model, group addressing, multicast delivery and routing between gateways. No more specific multicast tech tag covers this.
multicast.quote: This RFC defines a model of service for Internet multicasting and proposes an extension to the Internet Protocol (IP) to support such a multicast service.

IGMP.why: Appendix I specifies the original IGMP with message formats for create, join and leave group. This is a substantial part of the document.
IGMP.quote: The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used between IP hosts and their immediate neighbour multicast agents to support the allocation of temporary group addresses

rejected.why: The document extends IP but is about multicast. IPv4 is the base protocol being extended, not the subject.
ICMP is only used as a stylistic and implementation model for IGMP, and Echo is mentioned in a note.
Group address allocation (Class D) is part of the multicast model. The multicast tag already covers it.
Gateway multicast routing is discussed, but only as part of multicast implementation, so the multicast tag covers it.

RFC967.title: All victims together
RFC967.summary: Padlipsky observes that OS vendors resist changes needed for networking, and proposes a new RFC subseries of essays on how network protocol code (host-host, subnet drivers, Telnet, FTP) was integrated into various operating systems.

internet architecture.why: The document argues a principle about how network protocol implementations fit into host operating system architecture, and solicits essays on that integration.
internet architecture.quote: To us, it's axiomatic that networking code is system code when it has to be.

rejected.why: It proposes a new subseries of RFCs, but the subject is OS integration of networking, not RFC format, style or publication.
Telnet is only named as one component each essay should cover; the document does not specify or analyse it.
FTP is mentioned only as an item for the proposed essays to address.
The tone is wry, but it is a serious proposal and not part of the April 1st or parody series.
Context is the ARPANET-era community, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.

gaps.name: Operating system integration of network protocol code
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is how host OSs are modified to support networking. The taxonomy has no host-implementation or OS-integration tag, so the closest fit is internet architecture.

RFC968.title: Twas the night before start-up
RFC968.summary: A humorous poem by Vint Cerf parodying 'Twas the Night Before Christmas, about debugging a new network at start-up, ending with an off-by-one index bug.

humor.why: The whole document is a whimsical parody poem, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs subject.
humor.quote: Twas the night before start-up and all through the net, not a packet was moving; no bit nor octet.

rejected.why: TCP is only named in a list of protocols in a joke line; the document does not specify or discuss it.
X.25 appears only in the parodic reindeer-call line, not as a subject of the document.
The ARPANET hacker is a character in the poem; the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
SNA is merely name-dropped in a list of protocols in the poem.
OSI is only mentioned in a joke list, with no substantive treatment.

RFC969.title: NETBLT: A bulk data transfer protocol
RFC969.summary: RFC 969 specifies NETBLT, a transport-level bulk data transfer protocol over IP that uses large buffers, rate-based flow control, timers, and selective retransmission for high throughput.

NETBLT.why: The document is the specification of the NETBLT protocol itself, covering buffers, rate control, reliability, and packet formats.
NETBLT.quote: NETBLT (Network Block Transfer) is a transport level protocol intended for the rapid transfer of a large quantity of data between computers.

rejected.why: NETBLT uses the TCP checksum algorithm as a negotiated option, but the document is not about the Internet checksum.
Mentioned only as the source of the checksum algorithm and as a contrast (window flow control); not specified or extended.
Rate control is flow control for hosts and gateways, not a congestion control scheme in the modern sense; it is covered by the NETBLT tag.

RFC970.title: On Packet Switches With Infinite Storage
RFC970.summary: RFC 970 analyses congestion in datagram networks by considering packet switches with infinite storage, shows FIFO queuing with finite TTL drops all packets under overload, and proposes fair per-source round-robin queuing with Source Quench feedback.

congestion control.why: The whole document analyses congestion in datagram networks and proposes fair queuing with Source Quench feedback and well-behaved transport behaviour as remedies.
congestion control.quote: We demonstrate the unexpected result that a datagram network with infinite storage, first-in-first-out queuing, at least two packet switches, and a finite packet lifetime will, under overload, drop all packets.

rejected.why: The paper is about queue scheduling (per-source fair round-robin) and buffer exhaustion, not active queue management or early drop/marking.
TCP behaviour is discussed only by reference to an earlier paper and as the transport used in an experiment; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Source Quench is mentioned as the advisory feedback mechanism, but ICMP is not specified or extended here.
Fairness among sources is discussed, but not QoS architectures or signalling.
Congestion in datagram internetworks is the focus; it is not a general architecture-principles document.

gaps.name: fair queuing
gaps.why: The document introduces per-source round-robin fair queuing for packet switches; the taxonomy has no tag for queue scheduling or fairness, only congestion control as a parent.

RFC971.title: Survey of data representation standards
RFC971.summary: A 1986 survey comparing the data representation (presentation transfer syntax) standards CCITT X.409, NBS CBMS, DARPA Multimedia Mail, Xerox Courier and Sun RPC/XDR, concluding that explicit-type X.409 suits heterogeneous Internet applications.

ASN.1.why: X.409 is the notation and encoding (identifier/length/contents) that ASN.1 and BER grew from. The survey's main comparison and its conclusion centre on it.
ASN.1.quote: The CCITT recommendation X.409 defines the notation and the representational technique

ONC RPC.why: The survey covers Sun RPC and its XDR data representation as one of the compared standards, including implicit typing and its type table.
ONC RPC.quote: The SUN Remote Procedure Call package includes routines which

rejected.why: X.409 is part of the X.400 MHS series, but the document compares data encodings, not message handling.
NBS CBMS and Multimedia Mail are discussed only for their data element encodings, not as Internet message formats.
Mail systems are the context for some surveyed standards, but the subject is data representation.

gaps.name: Courier RPC / data representation standards
gaps.why: Xerox Courier, NBS CBMS and DARPA Multimedia Mail data encodings, and the implicit versus explicit typing comparison, have no specific tag. The data formats parent is implied by the ASN.1 tag.

RFC972.title: Password Generator Protocol
RFC972.summary: RFC 972 specifies PWDGEN, a simple TCP/UDP service on port 129 that returns six randomly generated, reasonably pronounceable eight-character words that users can pick from as login passwords.

authentication.why: The service exists to help hosts give users stronger, memorable login passwords. Password-based user authentication is the subject area it falls under, and the taxonomy has no narrower tag for it.
authentication.quote: user-selected login passwords are too easy to guess for even casual penetration attempts

rejected.why: The document says seed quality matters for the generated words. But it only gives short guidance on seeds and does not specify randomness requirements or generation, so it is not about this subject.
TCP is only the transport for one variant of the service, on port 129. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only the transport for the datagram variant of the service. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
The service has a similar shape to Echo, Discard and the other small services: no dialog, and the server closes the connection. It is not one of the listed services, though.
The document covers generating passwords, not hashing or key-stretching them.
The generated words are candidate permanent passwords for users to choose from. They are not one-time passwords.

gaps.name: Password generation / PWDGEN
gaps.why: The document defines a dedicated password-generation service, and the taxonomy has no tag for password generation or password policy. The nearest tags, authentication and randomness, only partly cover it.

RFC973.title: Domain system changes and observations
RFC973.summary: RFC 973 documents updates to the original DNS specifications (RFC 882/883), including 32-bit TTLs, the MX record, wildcard semantics, and IN-ADDR.ARPA, and gives operational guidelines, observed problems, and open issues.

DNS.why: The whole document concerns DNS protocol changes (TTL, CNAME, wildcards, MX, zone transfer), zone delegation operations, and implementation experiences.
DNS.quote: This RFC documents updates to Domain Name System specifications RFC-882 [1] and RFC-883 [2], suggests some operational guidelines

rejected.why: UDP checksum and address behaviour is mentioned only as an implementation pitfall for DNS servers; the document does not address UDP itself.
MX replaces MD/MF for mail routing, but this is a DNS record type change; mail routing is detailed in RFC 974, not here.
The document is about DNS domain names and zones, not host naming conventions or host tables.

RFC974.title: Mail routing and the domain system
RFC974.summary: RFC 974 specifies how mailers use DNS MX resource records (with CNAME and WKS handling) to decide where to route Internet mail, including preference ordering, loop avoidance, wildcards and examples.

email.why: The document defines mail routing behaviour for mailers on the Internet, which is email architecture and transport. It is not specific to SMTP message transfer, which it explicitly leaves out of scope.
email.quote: The purpose of this memo is to explain how mailers are to decide how to route a message addressed to a given Internet domain name.

DNS.why: The document specifies the MX resource record and how resolvers and mailers query and interpret DNS responses. That covers handling of CNAME, truncation, error codes, wildcards and caching.
DNS.quote: The first step for the mailer at LOCAL is to issue a query for MX RRs for REMOTE.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the example delivery mechanism. The memo says the mechanics of transferring the message are outside its scope.
The memo does not deal with message headers or addressing syntax. It covers routing by domain name only.
Host names appear only as the data in MX RRs. The memo is not about host naming conventions.

RFC975.title: Autonomous confederations
RFC975.summary: RFC 975 proposes enhancements to EGP that interpret the Update message distance field as a three-level metric (system, confederation, universe) to support multi-level routing among autonomous confederations.

EGP.why: The document extends EGP by giving the distance field of the EGP Update message a three-level interpretation, and discusses EGP restrictions and compatibility.
EGP.quote: This RFC proposes certain enhancements of the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) to support a simple, multiple-level routing capability

rejected.why: The multi-level hierarchy has an architectural flavour, but the document is specifically an EGP enhancement, so the EGP tag is the more specific fit.
Inter-domain routing is the same general space, but the document does not describe policy routing.
BGP does not exist yet in this document; it concerns EGP only.

RFC976.title: UUCP mail interchange format standard
RFC976.summary: RFC 976 defines the standard format for transmitting mail between UUCP hosts, adopting RFC-822 and RFC-920 conventions, specifying rmail invocation forms, From_ envelope lines, hybrid address handling, batch SMTP, and domain-based routing.

UUCP.why: The whole document specifies UUCP mail interchange: rmail invocation, From_ envelope lines, bang-path and domain addressing, and routing classes.
UUCP.quote: This document defines the standard format for the transmission of mail messages between machines in the UUCP Project.

SMTP.why: A section defines how to carry SMTP commands in batch form over UUCP, including the b-smtp alias and # line prefix convention.
SMTP.quote: Standard conforming implementations may optionally support a protocol called "Batch SMTP".

rejected.why: RFC-822 is adopted as the header format but not defined here; the document only profiles how addresses and envelope are used.
The parent is implied by the UUCP tag, which sits under messaging/email-related UUCP mail interchange.
Discusses 6-letter UUCP names versus domain names, but only as part of addressing and routing, not host naming conventions as a subject.
RFC-920 domain names are used for addressing, but no DNS protocol or resolution is involved; routing uses local tables.

RFC977.title: Network News Transfer Protocol
RFC977.summary: RFC 977 specifies NNTP, a stream-based (TCP) client-server protocol for distributing, querying, retrieving and posting Usenet-style news articles, with commands, response codes and sample sessions.

NNTP.why: The document is the original NNTP specification, defining its commands (ARTICLE, GROUP, IHAVE, NEWNEWS, POST, etc.) and response codes.
NNTP.quote: NNTP specifies a protocol for the distribution, inquiry, retrieval, and posting of news articles using a reliable stream (such as TCP) server-client model.

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable stream transport on port 119. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
Mailing lists are discussed only as motivation. SMTP-like commands are used as a style model, and the document is not about email.
UUCP is mentioned only as the traditional transport that NNTP is compared with.
NNTP is already a child of Netnews, so the more specific NNTP tag is used. The article format itself comes from RFC 850 and is not defined here.
The document only says commands and replies use ASCII. That is incidental to the protocol.

RFC978.title: Voice File Interchange Protocol (VFIP)
RFC978.summary: RFC 978 defines an 18-byte header (VFIP) that describes stored speech files (version, length, DTMF mask, recording rate, duration, encoding method) so voice recordings can be exchanged between different systems.

codecs.why: The document defines a container header for speech files that identifies the encoding/recording method and rate. This is the closest fit for audio codec and container definitions.
codecs.quote: The Voice File Interchange Protocol defines a header to describe the voice data.

rejected.why: Multimedia Mail is only cited as motivation. The document defines no mail transport or format.
The document predates MIME and defines a standalone file header, not a MIME body structure or encoding.
VFIP describes stored files, not real-time packet payloads.
NVP is listed only as one possible encoding method. The document does not cover ARPANET protocols or operations.
The document concerns file interchange of recorded speech, not real-time voice communication.

gaps.name: Voice file interchange format
gaps.why: The document defines an audio file header, which the taxonomy covers only loosely under codecs and containers. No tag exists for general audio or voice file formats.

RFC979.title: PSN End-to-End functional specification
RFC979.summary: Functional specification of the BBN PSN (IMP) end-to-end protocol and module in PSN Release 7.0, covering AHIP and X.25 host services, DDN Standard X.25 interoperability, addressing, peer protocol ACKs and performance goals.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies the end-to-end protocol of the ARPANET/MILNET packet switch nodes (IMPs), including AHIP (1822) host interface. This is ARPANET host and network protocol material.
ARPANET.quote: This memo contains the functional specification for the new BBNCC PSN End-to-End (EE) protocol and module (PSN stands for Packet Switch node, and has previously been known as the IMP).

X.25.why: A substantial part covers X.25 host service, DDN Standard X.25 interoperability with AHIP, and X.25 features like the D bit, hunt groups, and reset/interrupt.
X.25.quote: The new EE provides both DDN Standard and Basic X.25 service

rejected.why: TCP/IP is mentioned only as traffic carried over the PSN network, not specified here.
The optional 32-bit end-to-end checksum is a minor feature within the spec, not the subject.
NCP is mentioned only as a historical protocol above AHIP; the document does not specify it.
Precedence levels and resource fairness are features of the EE, but not the document's focus.

gaps.name: AHIP / 1822 host-IMP interface
gaps.why: The ARPANET Host-IMP Protocol is a major subject of the document, but the taxonomy has no tag for it apart from the general ARPANET topic.

RFC980.title: Protocol document order information
RFC980.summary: RFC 980 explains how to order DARPA/DDN protocol documents (RFCs, the 1985 DDN Protocol Handbook, MIL-STDs, ISO and CCITT documents) and lists the Handbook's table of contents.

RFC series.why: The document explains how RFCs are distributed (FTP from the NIC, hardcopy ordering, charges). Readers of the RFC series subject would want this.
RFC series.quote: RFCs are the working memos of the DARPA research community.
RFC series.section: DOD INTERNET PROTOCOL DOCUMENTS: How to get the Requests for Comments (RFCs)

rejected.why: It mentions the IPTW and the NCP-to-TCP transition only as background to the Handbook, not as a history.
FTP is only the means of retrieving RFCs and appears as a Handbook table-of-contents entry. The document does not specify it.
The ARPANET is mentioned in the Handbook contents and background, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
Assigned Numbers appears only as one Handbook table-of-contents entry.
It is an ordering guide for documents, not an introductory guide for Internet users in the FYI sense.

RFC981.title: Experimental multiple-path routing algorithm
RFC981.summary: RFC 981 describes the experimental Wiretap algorithm, a passive-monitoring, shortest-path-style multiple-path routing algorithm with a node/link cache for the AX.25 amateur packet-radio channel, with a prototype implementation and test results.

amateur radio.why: The whole document designs and tests a routing algorithm for the AX.25 amateur packet-radio channel, with digipeaters, callsigns and TNC firmware.
amateur radio.quote: a dynamic routing algorithm for the AX.25 packet-radio channel

routing architecture.why: It presents a class of routing algorithms: Viterbi/SPF-style multi-path computation, factors and weights, and pruning for limited resources. This is a general routing design topic, not a specific routing protocol.
routing architecture.quote: constructs a set of candidate paths on the network graph from the destination to the source in increasing number of hops

rejected.why: The channel has hidden stations and is ad hoc, but the document is about AX.25 digipeater routing, not MANET routing protocols like OLSR, AODV or DSR.
EGP is cited only as inspiration for the reachability shift-register mechanism.
The driver carries IP/TCP over AX.25, but TCP is only a substrate and is not specified or changed.
The ARPANET SPF algorithm is referenced as a comparison; the document is not about the ARPANET.
SPF is mentioned as similar prior art, but OSPF is not specified or analysed.

gaps.name: AX.25 packet radio source routing / Wiretap algorithm
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only a broad amateur radio tag and a general routing architecture tag. It has no tag for passive-monitoring or multipath routing on packet-radio channels.

RFC982.title: Guidelines for the specification of the structure of the Domain Specific Part (DSP) of the ISO standard NSAP address
RFC982.summary: An ANSI working draft, republished as an RFC, that gives guidelines for structuring the Domain Specific Part (DSP) of ISO NSAP addresses (subnetwork ID, subnetwork address, NSAP selector) for each IDI format (X.121, ISO DCC, F.69, E.163, E.164, ISO 6523-ICD).

OSI.why: The document is about the structure of OSI network-layer (NSAP) addresses under ISO 8348/DAD2. This is OSI network-layer addressing, so the OSI tag fits.
OSI.quote: This Technical Report specifies a recommended syntax and interpretation for the Domain Specific Part of an NSAP address.

rejected.why: The RFC says NSAP addressing is a prerequisite for CLNS coexistence with IP. It does not specify CLNP itself.
This is OSI NSAP addressing, not IP address architecture. The OSI tag is more specific and fits better.
X.121 is mentioned only as one IDI numbering authority, and the document does not cover X.25.
E.164 is mentioned only as an IDI format, and the document does not cover ISDN access.

RFC983.title: ISO transport arrives on top of the TCP
RFC983.summary: RFC 983 specifies how to offer the ISO transport service (TSAP, ISO 8072) on top of TCP using TPKT packets over TCP port 102, with a second TCP connection for expedited data, to allow ISO higher-layer protocols to run in the ARPA Internet.

transport mapping.why: The document defines a binding of the ISO transport service onto TCP, including TPKT framing, port 102 and expedited data handling. This is a transport mapping.
transport mapping.quote: we will base the internals of this TSAP on TCP/IP (as defined in [RFC-793,RFC791]), not on the ISO/CCITT transport and network protocols.

OSI.why: The document is about supporting OSI transport service (ISO 8072/8073) and higher-layer OSI entities in the Internet, and about migration from TCP/IP to ISO protocols.
OSI.quote: The ISO transport service definition describes the services offered by the TS-provider (transport service) and the interfaces used to access those services.

rejected.why: TCP is the substrate the ISO transport service is carried over. The document does not extend or specify TCP.
The memo explicitly avoids ISO network-layer gatewaying. It does not cover CLNP.
MHS appears only as one entry in the reserved TSAP ID table in the appendix.
The port 102 reservation and the TSAP ID list are incidental to the protocol and are not a registry-guidance topic.

RFC984.title: PCMAIL: A distributed mail system for personal computers
RFC984.summary: RFC 984 describes Pcmail, a distributed mail system for personal computers, with a central repository and PC clients synchronizing mail state via the Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP).

email.why: The document specifies a mail system architecture (repository, clients, mail state synchronization) and its client-repository access protocol DMSP, with mail delivery to the Internet via SMTP and RFC-822 address translation.
email.quote: Pcmail is a distributed mail system that provides mail service to an arbitrary number of users, each of which owns one or more personal computers (PCs).

rejected.why: The repository only hands outgoing Internet mail to a local SMTP server; SMTP is not specified or extended.
RFC-822 headers are used and descriptors copy header fields, but the document does not define message format.
Functionally similar remote mailbox access, but IMAP is not discussed or used; DMSP is a separate protocol.
Not referenced; the document is about a different client-repository protocol.

gaps.name: DMSP (Distributed Mail System Protocol) / Pcmail
gaps.why: A historic mail access protocol with disconnected-client synchronization has no specific tag; it is covered only by the general email tag.

RFC985.title: Requirements for Internet gateways - draft
RFC985.summary: Draft NSF NTAG requirements for Internet gateways: the protocols (IP, ICMP, EGP, ARP), subnetting, local-network interfaces, routing algorithm features, and operation/maintenance a vendor's gateway must support.

routing architecture.why: Core of the document is gateway/router requirements, including routing algorithm features (loop avoidance, scalability, default gateway discouragement, reachability). No tag for router requirements specifically, so routing architecture fits best.
routing architecture.quote: the routing mechanism, whether static or dynamic, is the single most important engineering issue in network design

EGP.why: Substantial section analyses EGP's gaps (no core procedures, no authentication, polling parameters) and requires EGP interoperability as the demarcation point.
EGP.quote: This is the basic protocol used to exchange information between gateway systems of the Internet and is described in RFC-904

ICMP.why: Gives specific guidance on ICMP unreachable, redirect, source quench and address mask messages, with Appendix A detail on redirect handling.
ICMP.quote: It is recommended that use of the ICMP Destination Network Unreachable messages be avoided.

IPv4.why: Specifies which IP options gateways must handle, reassembly, and Class-D/E address handling.
IPv4.quote: With respect to current gateway requirements the following can be ignored, although they may be required in future: Type of Service field

ARP.why: Appendix A specifies ARP behaviour for hosts and gateways on Ethernet, including subnet-related issues.
ARP.quote: An ARP reply is generated only if the destination protocol IP address is reachable from the local host

Ethernet.why: Ethernet is the mandated interoperability demarcation point for gateways (Section 4.4, Appendix A, B.1).
Ethernet.quote: Datagrams are encapsulated as Ethernet packets with 48-bit source and destination address fields and a 16-bit type field.

CIDR.why: Section on subnetting and address masks per RFC 950 (subnet masks, ICMP Address Mask). CIDR is not subnetting, so this is only a weak fit; addressing parent would be more apt.
CIDR.quote: The concept of subnets was introduced in order to allow arbitrary complexity of interconnected LAN structures within an organization

rejected.why: Subnetting (RFC 950) is not classless inter-domain routing; weak fit, better covered by addressing, which is also marginal.
Mentioned as one of several local network interface options (4.1, 4.3) but only briefly; not a main subject.
Mentioned as the transport that should generally not be required for gateway monitoring; not specified here.
The document recommends UDP or HMP for monitoring but specifies no management protocol; Section 7 is only operational requirements.
Section 7 covers operation and maintenance requirements but it is a minor part of the document.
1822 and DDN interfaces are described only as attachment options for gateways.

gaps.name: Internet gateway/router requirements
gaps.why: The document is a requirements specification for IP gateways (routers) as a whole. The taxonomy has no tag for router requirements, only the routing architecture catch-all.

RFC986.title: Guidelines for the use of Internet-IP addresses in the ISO Connectionless-Mode Network Protocol
RFC986.summary: RFC 986 proposes how to encode DoD Internet IP addresses and the IP protocol field as ISO NSAP addresses (AFI 47, ICD 0006) for use in CLNP, plus an X.121-based format for hosts and LANs attached via public data networks.

CLNP.why: The whole document specifies NSAP address formats for CLNP in the DoD Internet, so CLNP is the central subject.
CLNP.quote: This RFC suggests a method to allow the existing IP addressing, including the IP protocol field, to be used for the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP).

rejected.why: CLNP is the more specific child under OSI, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The document is about addressing, but the CLNP tag already covers it, and the taxonomy's addressing topic concerns IP address architecture.
IPv4 addresses are embedded in the NSAP format but are not what the document specifies or extends.
X.121 addresses are used for PDN-attached systems, but the document does not cover X.25 or IP over X.25.

RFC987.title: Mapping between X.400 and RFC 822
RFC987.summary: RFC 987 specifies gateway mappings between X.400 (1984) Interpersonal Messaging and RFC 822 mail, covering service elements, O/R name and address mapping, and protocol element conversion.

X.400.why: The whole document defines how X.400 P1/P2 elements and O/R names map to and from RFC 822, i.e. X.400 interworking gateways.
X.400.quote: enable interworking between systems operating the CCITT X.400 (1984) series of protocols [CCITT84a], and systems using the RFC 822 mail protocol

message format.why: Much of the document maps RFC 822 header fields and addresses to X.400 elements, and defines new RFC 822 extended header fields (e.g. P1-Message-ID, Expiry-Date, Importance).
message format.quote: RFC 822 message consists of a header, and content which is uninterpreted ASCII text.

rejected.why: SMTP is only one of several 822-P1 transports; Appendix C is brief and the document does not specify SMTP.
UUCP is mentioned as a network and in Appendix E for addressing, but the document is not about UUCP mail interchange.
The parent is implied by the more specific X.400 tag.
ASCII/IA5/PrintableString mapping is a small supporting section, not the subject.
Domain names are used for O/R name association, but the document does not specify DNS.

RFC988.title: Host extensions for IP multicasting
RFC988.summary: RFC 988 specifies host-side extensions to IP for multicasting (class D host group addresses, send/receive/membership services, Ethernet mapping) and defines the original IGMP version 0 in an appendix.

multicast.why: The whole document specifies IP multicast host behaviour: host group addresses, sending and receiving multicast datagrams, and group membership management.
multicast.quote: This memo specifies the extensions required of a host implementation of the Internet Protocol (IP) to support internetwork multicasting.

IGMP.why: Appendix I defines the IGMP message formats, codes, timers and rules. This is the original IGMP specification, and level 2 conformance requires it.
IGMP.quote: The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used between IP hosts and their immediate neighbor multicast agents to support the creation of transient groups
IGMP.section: APPENDIX I. INTERNET GROUP MANAGEMENT PROTOCOL (IGMP)

rejected.why: The Ethernet multicast address mapping is an example local network module. The document is not about IP over Ethernet in its own right.
The document extends IP, but its subject is multicast. IPv4 is the base protocol, and the class D addressing is a multicast matter.
ICMP is mentioned only for rules on not generating errors for multicast destinations. It is not a subject of the document.
ARP appears only as an example of IP-to-local address mapping in the host model.
Class D host group addresses are covered, but they are part of the multicast specification. The multicast tag covers them.

RFC989.title: Privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail: Part I: Message encipherment and authentication procedures
RFC989.summary: RFC 989 defines the original Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) procedures for end-to-end encryption, authentication and integrity of Internet email at the user-agent level, using DES-CBC, a canonical text encoding, a printable Base64-like encoding, encapsulation boundaries, and a DEK/interchange-key hierarchy.

PEM.why: The document is the original PEM specification, defining message encipherment, authentication, header fields and encapsulation for secure email.
PEM.quote: This RFC defines message encipherment and authentication procedures, as the initial phase of an effort to provide privacy enhancement services for electronic mail transfer in the Internet.

key management.why: A substantial part (Section 5) covers Data Encrypting Keys, Interchange Keys, IK IDs and Issuing Authorities.
key management.quote: A two-level keying hierarchy is used to support privacy-enhanced message transmission

DES.why: The document mandates DES (DEA-1) in CBC and ECB modes for text encryption, MAC computation and key encryption.
DES.quote: the Block Cipher Algorithm DEA-1, defined in ISO draft international standard DIS 8227 [1] shall be used for encryption of message text

email.why: The document specifies end-to-end security for email, including canonical encoding for SMTP transparency and encapsulation per RFC934.
email.quote: The mechanisms defined in this RFC are not restricted to a particular host or operating system

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport constraint the encoding must survive; the document does not specify or extend it.
The printable encoding is defined here and is a precursor of Base64, but it is a component of PEM and not a standalone encoding specification.
The document adds encapsulated header fields, but they are explicitly disjoint from RFC 822 headers and are part of PEM.
X.400 is cited only for terminology, and interoperability with it is listed as future work.
Sender authentication is a PEM service, already covered by the PEM tag.

RFC990.title: Assigned numbers
RFC990.summary: RFC 990 is the November 1986 Assigned Numbers memo, a registry listing of IP network numbers, protocol numbers, port numbers, AS numbers, Telnet options, ARP parameters, Ethernet/IEEE 802 type numbers, and official host/system/terminal names, maintained by Joyce Reynolds.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned numbers (ports, protocols, networks, AS numbers) and the assignment process run by Joyce Reynolds, the precursor of IANA registries.
IANA.quote: This Network Working Group Request for Comments documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations.

addressing.why: A large part of the document lists class A/B/C network assignments, address classes, special addresses and allocation by category (Appendix A).
addressing.quote: The network numbers listed here are used as internet addresses by the Internet Protocol (IP) [46,101].

ARPANET.why: Includes ARPANET logical address and link number assignments, with references to 1822 Host/IMP interface.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: Port numbers are listed for use with TCP/UDP but the document does not specify TCP.
Telnet option numbers are only listed as a registry table, not specified.
ARP parameter values are registered, but the protocol is only referenced; a small registry section.
Ethernet type numbers and 802 SAP/SNAP assignments are listed as registry entries, a minor part of the document.
Official machine and system names are listed for the host table, but as a name registry; the host naming conventions are in RFC 952.
AS numbers are registered for EGP, not BGP, and as a simple table.

RFC991.title: Official ARPA-Internet protocols
RFC991.summary: RFC 991 is a November 1986 status report cataloguing the official ARPA-Internet protocols, with each entry giving status, specification, comments, references, dependencies and contact.

internet history.why: The document is a snapshot of the state of the 1986 ARPA-Internet protocol suite, which makes it a historical record that readers of Internet history would want.
internet history.quote: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet.  Comments indicate any revisions or changes planned.

TCP.why: The TCP entry is one of the longest. It lists corrections and clarifications on push, urgent, MSS, idle connections and out-of-order segments.
TCP.quote: Provides reliable end-to-end data stream service.

Telnet.why: The Telnet entry includes a full table of Telnet options with RFC numbers and usage status, plus recommendations on which options to keep.
Telnet.quote: The protocol for remote terminal access.

small services.why: It catalogues the Echo, Discard, Chargen, Quote of the Day, Active Users and Daytime services, which are the TCP/UDP small services.
small services.quote: Debugging protocol, sends back whatever you send it.

rejected.why: The document covers the ARPA-Internet suite as a whole. The ARPANET appears only in the IP-over-ARPANET entry.
It is a protocol catalogue, not a statement of architectural principles. It only points to the Catenet Model as a reference.
IP gets one entry among many, so it is not a main subject of the document.
The Domain Name Protocol entry is brief and lists only references, so the document is not about DNS.
Assigned Numbers is mentioned only as a pointer to RFC 990.

gaps.name: Protocol status catalogue (Official Internet Protocol Standards)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for protocol-status or standards-track lists. The closest fits are internet history and the IETF process.

RFC992.title: On communication support for fault tolerant process groups
RFC992.summary: RFC 992 describes the ISIS project's GBCAST, ABCAST and CBCAST reliable, ordered multicast primitives, which are integrated with failure and recovery handling to support fault-tolerant process groups, and it contrasts them with best-effort IP host groups.

reliable multicast.why: The whole memo specifies reliable multicast with atomic delivery and ordering guarantees (GBCAST, ABCAST, CBCAST) under changing group membership. Readers of reliable multicast would want it.
reliable multicast.quote: a collection of multicast communication primitives integrated with a mechanism for handling process failure and recovery

rejected.why: The memo contrasts itself with IP host-group multicast (RFC 966/988) but does not specify IP multicast routing or group membership.
TCP is mentioned only as one possible substrate for the site-to-site acknowledgement layer.
The memo is about distributed-systems communication primitives, not Internet architectural principles.
It describes group communication semantics layered above unreliable datagrams, not a transport protocol or transport service in general.

gaps.name: fault-tolerant process groups / atomic and causal broadcast (virtual synchrony)
gaps.why: The central subject is distributed-systems group communication: process group membership views, failure detection, and causal/atomic ordering. The taxonomy has no distributed computing or group communication tag, so reliable multicast is only the closest fit.

RFC993.title: PCMAIL: A distributed mail system for personal computers
RFC993.summary: RFC 993 describes Pcmail, a distributed workstation-based mail system with a central repository and multiple clients that synchronize mail state using the Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP) over USP.

email.why: The document specifies a mail storage and access architecture and its client-repository protocol (DMSP), including mailboxes, bboards, message send and retrieval. This is email architecture and access, comparable to IMAP/POP-style remote mail access.
email.quote: Pcmail is a distributed mail system providing mail service to an arbitrary number of users, each of whom owns one or more workstations.

rejected.why: The repository hands outgoing Internet mail to a local SMTP server, but SMTP is only used as a substrate and is not specified here.
Messages carry RFC-822 headers and descriptors extract some fields, but the document does not define or extend the message format.
DMSP is functionally similar to IMAP (remote mailbox access with synchronization), but it is a distinct protocol and the document does not concern IMAP.
Bulletin board mailboxes are shared read-only mail stores with subscriptions, but they are a repository feature and not mailing list protocols or headers.

RFC994.title: Final text of DIS 8473, Protocol for Providing the Connectionless-mode Network Service
RFC994.summary: RFC 994 reproduces the final text of ISO DIS 8473, specifying the Connectionless-mode Network Protocol (CLNP): its functions, PDU formats, segmentation, error reporting, and options.

CLNP.why: The whole document is the specification of CLNP (ISO 8473): its protocol functions, PDU structure and encoding, and conformance.
CLNP.quote: This International Standard specifies a protocol which is used to provide the Connectionless-mode Network Service

rejected.why: Parent of CLNP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The PDU header checksum is a minor function of CLNP, not the subject of the document.
QoS maintenance and priority are options within CLNP, not a QoS architecture.
The Error Report PDU is a CLNP-internal mechanism, not ICMP.

RFC995.title: End System to Intermediate System Routing Exchange Protocol for use in conjunction with ISO 8473
RFC995.summary: RFC 995 reproduces the ISO 9542 draft that specifies the OSI End System to Intermediate System (ES-IS) routing exchange protocol, with ESH, ISH and RD PDUs, for use with the ISO 8473 connectionless network protocol (CLNP).

CLNP.why: The protocol is the ES-IS companion to ISO 8473 (CLNP). It is used by CLNP network entities, and its PDU encoding is compatible with CLNP's. CLNP is the most specific fit for this OSI network-layer protocol.
CLNP.quote: This protocol is also designed to operate in close conjunction with the Protocol for the Provision of the Connectionless-mode Network Service (ISO 8473).

OSI.why: It is an OSI network-layer routing exchange protocol. It covers NSAP addressing, Network Entity Titles and the ISO 7498 and DIS 8648 architecture, so OSI readers would want it.
OSI.quote: it is a protocol of the Network Layer. This protocol permits End Systems and Intermediate Systems to exchange configuration and routing information

rejected.why: The document does specify routing exchange. But it covers only ES-IS exchange on a subnetwork and explicitly excludes IS-IS routing, so the OSI and CLNP tags fit better.
The Query Configuration function resembles address resolution, mapping an NSAP to an SNPA. However, the document is a full ES-IS protocol, not an ARP specification.
It defines a header checksum with a Fletcher-style formula. This is a minor function inside the protocol, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: ES-IS (ISO 9542) End System to Intermediate System routing exchange
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OSI ES-IS routing. The document is about this protocol, and it is covered here only by the CLNP and OSI tags.

RFC996.title: Statistics server
RFC996.summary: RFC 996 specifies the Statistics Server (STATSRV) protocol, a lightweight request/response service on port 133 over UDP or TCP that returns host or gateway statistics as ASCII text for casual remote monitoring and debugging.

network management.why: The document defines a remote statistics monitoring protocol for hosts and gateways. No specific management technology tag such as SNMP fits, so the topic tag applies directly.
network management.quote: Hosts and gateways on the DARPA Internet that choose to implement a remote statistics monitoring facility may use this protocol to send statistics data upon request

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport the protocol is usually run over. The document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
TCP is mentioned only as a possible transport. The document does not specify or extend it.
Finger is cited only as an example of a lightweight service with no authentication. The document is not about it.
The document does not cover the Echo, Discard, Chargen or similar small services. It describes a different statistics service.
The document predates SNMP and does not cover it. It says it is not a full-function monitoring protocol.
ASCII is only the text encoding of commands and responses. The document is not about the character set.

RFC997.title: Internet numbers
RFC997.summary: RFC 997 is the March 1987 "Internet Numbers" status report that lists assigned IP network numbers (classes A, B, C), reserved addresses, and EGP autonomous system numbers, with contacts.

addressing.why: The document is a registry of IP network number assignments and describes address classes, special addresses and allocation among categories. This is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: The network numbers listed here are used as internet addresses by the Internet Protocol (IP)

IPv4.why: It describes the IPv4 32-bit address format, classes A-E, dotted decimal notation, loopback and all-ones addresses.
IPv4.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

EGP.why: A substantial section registers the autonomous system numbers used in EGP's 16-bit field.
EGP.quote: The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) [25,27] specifies that groups of gateways may form autonomous systems.

IANA.why: It is an early number-assignment registry maintained by Hostmaster, a precursor of IANA registries.
IANA.quote: This Network Working Group Request for Comments documents the currently assigned network numbers and gateway autonomous systems.

rejected.why: The ARPANET appears only as one assigned network entry (net 10) among many, so the RFC is not about it.
Class D multicast addresses are mentioned briefly and only as reserved space, with no multicast routing content.
The document describes classful addressing, which CIDR later replaced. It says nothing about CIDR.

gaps.name: Assigned numbers registry (network and AS number assignments)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for number-assignment registries as such, apart from the generic IANA topic. This document's main content is a list of network and AS number assignments.

RFC998.title: NETBLT: A bulk data transfer protocol
RFC998.summary: RFC 998 specifies NETBLT, an experimental transport-level bulk data transfer protocol over IP using large buffers, rate-based flow control, and timer-driven reliability.

NETBLT.why: The document is the specification of the NETBLT protocol itself, including its packet formats, flow control, and connection management.
NETBLT.quote: NETBLT (NETwork BLock Transfer) is a transport level protocol intended for the rapid transfer of a large quantity of data between computers.

rejected.why: Rate control is used for flow control and congestion avoidance, but it is a feature of NETBLT and not a general treatment of congestion control.
NETBLT uses a 16-bit ones-complement checksum, but it is only one component of the protocol and not what the document is about.
NETBLT runs directly over IP as protocol 30, not UDP.
NETBLT is an alternative to TCP for bulk transfer, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.

RFC999.title: Requests For Comments summary notes: 900-999
RFC999.summary: RFC 999 is a slightly annotated index of the 100 RFCs numbered 900 through 999, giving author, date, title and abstract for each as a status report.

RFC series.why: The document exists to catalogue a block of the RFC series. A reader browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find this index there.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC-900 through RFC-999.

rejected.why: It is a contemporary status listing, not a history or retrospective. The era is incidental.
Many summarized RFCs concern the ARPA-Internet. The document itself is only an index and does not address the ARPANET.
The listing mentions the Assigned Numbers RFCs only as entries. The document is not about number registries.
The summarized RFCs cover many protocols (NETBLT, NTP, FTP, EGP and others). The document does not specify or analyse any of them, so none of those technologies is tagged.
The annotations are summaries of other documents, not definitions or glossaries.

RFC1000.title: Request For Comments reference guide
RFC1000.summary: RFC 1000 is a reference guide that categorizes and summarizes RFCs 1 through 999 (1969-1987), with a foreword by Steve Crocker on the origins of the RFC series.

RFC series.why: The document is an index and guide to the RFC series itself, including its origins and categories.
RFC series.quote: This RFC Reference Guide is intended to provide a historical account by categorizing and summarizing of the Request for Comments numbers 1 through 999

internet history.why: Crocker's essay is a retrospective on how the ARPANET protocols and the RFCs began, and the guide is framed as a historical account.
internet history.quote: The procurement of the ARPANET was initiated in the summer of 1968
internet history.section: THE ORIGINS OF RFCS - by Stephen D. Crocker

rejected.why: The ARPANET is a major subject of the RFCs summarized, but the document is an index of RFCs. It does not specify ARPANET protocols.
Many summarized RFCs are about Telnet. This guide only lists them and does not address the protocol.
Many FTP RFCs are listed in the catalogue. The guide itself is not about FTP.
DNS RFCs appear as catalogue entries. The guide does not address DNS.
Assigned Numbers RFCs are listed only as entries in the catalogue.

RFC1001.title: Protocol standard for a NetBIOS service on a TCP/UDP transport: Concepts and methods
RFC1001.summary: RFC 1001 specifies the concepts and methods for providing NetBIOS name, session and datagram services over TCP and UDP, defining B/P/M node types and NBNS/NBDD support servers.

NetBIOS.why: The whole document defines NetBIOS name, session and datagram services over TCP/UDP, including node types and servers.
NetBIOS.quote: This RFC defines a proposed standard protocol to support NetBIOS services in a TCP/IP environment.

rejected.why: NetBIOS names are encoded to be DNS-compatible and the NBNS mimics DNS styles, but the document does not specify DNS; it only notes DNS would need extensions.
TCP is only the substrate for the session service and large name responses.
UDP is the transport for name and datagram services, not the subject.
Appendix A only discusses optional use of IP group multicast to extend broadcast areas.
A NetBIOS name service is covered, but the NetBIOS tag is the specific fit, so the generic parent is not needed.

gaps.name: NetBIOS over TCP/UDP (NBT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a NetBIOS tag under applications, but I used an id that I could not verify as listed exactly; the taxonomy lists it as 'NetBIOS' under applications, so no real gap beyond that.

RFC1002.title: Protocol standard for a NetBIOS service on a TCP/UDP transport: Detailed specifications
RFC1002.summary: RFC 1002 gives the detailed packet formats and protocol procedures for NetBIOS-over-TCP/UDP: the name service, session service and datagram service, with B, P and M node behaviour and the NBNS and NBDD servers.

NetBIOS.why: The whole document specifies NetBIOS services over TCP/UDP: name, session and datagram packets and protocols.
NetBIOS.quote: This RFC contains the detailed packet formats and protocol specifications for NetBIOS-over-TCP.

rejected.why: The NetBIOS name service reuses DNS packet format and name compression, but the document specifies NetBIOS name registration and resolution, not DNS itself.
TCP carries the session service, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
UDP carries the name and datagram services, but the document does not specify or extend UDP.
NetBIOS names are not host naming conventions or host tables.

RFC1003.title: Issues in defining an equations representation standard
RFC1003.summary: RFC 1003 explores issues in defining a standard text-based representation for displayed mathematical equations so they can be exchanged in mail messages and between existing equation systems, and suggests an EQN-like language with added positioning.

data formats.why: The whole memo is about what an interchange representation for equations should contain and which form it should take (EQN-like text with positioning). No more specific data-format tag fits, so the general topic applies.
data formats.quote: A standard for the efficient representation of mathematical equations should be defined as soon as possible in order to allow the interchange of equations

rejected.why: Email is the motivating use case, but the memo specifies nothing about mail transport, access or formats. It is about the equation representation.
The memo does not discuss message headers or structure. It only says the equation text could be sent inside messages.
MIME did not exist yet. The memo mentions multimedia mail only as background, and defines no body type or encoding.
This is a different markup-based document interchange approach. The memo considers EQN, LaTeX and Troff directive systems, not SGML.

gaps.name: Mathematical equation representation / equation typesetting interchange (EQN, LaTeX)
gaps.why: The document is about representing displayed equations for interchange. The taxonomy has no tag for math notation or typesetting formats, so only the generic data formats topic fits.

RFC1004.title: Distributed-protocol authentication scheme
RFC1004.summary: RFC 1004 proposes a Needham-Schroeder-derived authentication scheme using a "Cookie Jar" key server and session keys to authenticate associations between peers running distributed protocols such as EGP and DGP.

authentication.why: The whole document defines a mediated authentication procedure with a key server, session keys and checksum-based message authentication against spoofing and replay. It is general across protocols, so the topic tag fits.
authentication.quote: suitable for those cases when an association is to be set up between multiple users belonging to different trust environments

EGP.why: A full section describes how to add the authentication fields to EGP Request/Confirm messages and how the EGP state machine, neighbor acquisition and Cease are affected.
EGP.quote: This scheme can be incorporated in the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) [2] and Dissimilar Gateway Protocol (DGP) [3] models

rejected.why: DES is only suggested as the natural encryption algorithm and then flagged for reconsideration. The document is not about it.
The Internet checksum is used as the integrity primitive, and its weaknesses get a brief discussion. The document does not define or specify it.
The Cookie Jar distributes session keys, but this is the means of authenticating associations. Authentication is the subject, and key management is not treated in its own right.
The scheme is aimed at EGP and DGP associations, but the document does not secure routing information or paths. It only authenticates the peer messages.

gaps.name: Dissimilar Gateway Protocol (DGP)
gaps.why: The document names this draft inter-gateway protocol as a co-target, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC1005.title: ARPANET AHIP-E Host Access Protocol (enhanced AHIP)
RFC1005.summary: RFC 1005 specifies AHIP-E, an enhancement of the ARPANET AHIP (1822) host-PSN access protocol that enlarges the PSN field to 10 bits, adds logical host names, type-of-service bits, per-connection congestion feedback, and precedence cutoff messages, and defines the new Class A IP address mapping.

ARPANET.why: The document specifies enhancements to the ARPANET host-to-PSN access protocol (AHIP/1822), including leader formats and message types. This is ARPANET host and network protocol work.
ARPANET.quote: This RFC is a proposed specification for the encoding of Class A IP addresses for use on ARPANET-style networks such as the Milnet and Arpanet

addressing.why: A substantial part of the document defines the new interpretation of Class A IP address fields and the mapping to physical addresses and logical names.
addressing.quote: This section discusses the changes to the mapping between Class A IP addresses [5] and subnet addresses.

rejected.why: IP is only the context. The document changes the address-to-subnet mapping, which belongs under addressing, not the IPv4 protocol itself.
Logical names here are PSN-level host identifiers resolved by the PSN, not a general naming or name-resolution system.
STOP/SLOW/GO feedback is a host-PSN flow-control mechanism within AHIP-E, not a transport congestion control topic.
X.25 is mentioned only as a compatibility constraint for the address mapping.

gaps.name: AHIP / BBN Report 1822 host access protocol
gaps.why: The host-to-IMP/PSN access interface is not covered by any specific tag. ARPANET is the closest fit.

RFC1006.title: ISO Transport Service on top of the TCP Version: 3
RFC1006.summary: RFC 1006 specifies how to run the ISO transport service (class 0 TPDUs, framed in TPKTs) over TCP port 102, so OSI upper-layer protocols can run on TCP/IP.

OSI.why: The document defines the ISO/OSI transport service over TCP, so OSI-to-TCP/IP coexistence and migration is its subject.
OSI.quote: we will in fact implement the ISO TP0 protocol on top of TCP/IP (as defined in [RFC793,RFC791]), not on top of the the ISO/CCITT network protocol
