transport mapping.why: It is a transport binding: it maps ISO TP0 onto TCP primitives and defines TPKT framing and port 102.
transport mapping.quote: The protocol defined in this memo encapsulates these TPDUs in discrete units called TPKTs.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The memo does not specify or extend TCP.
The memo explicitly avoids the ISO network protocol and uses TCP/IP instead, so CLNP is not what it covers.
The document works at the transport layer, not the IP layer.

gaps.name: ISO transport service / TP0 (OSI transport layer)
gaps.why: There is no OSI transport-protocol tag. The OSI tag covers only network-layer protocols.

RFC1007.title: Military supplement to the ISO Transport Protocol
RFC1007.summary: A 1987 draft DoD profile that supplements ISO Transport Service/Protocol (IS 8072/8073) by selecting classes, options, parameter values, reference-number conventions and crash-recovery guidance, mandating Class 4 over connectionless network service (IS 8473) for DoD packet networks.

OSI.why: The whole document profiles the OSI transport protocol (TP Class 2/4) and its use over OSI connectionless network service alongside DoD networks. It is the closest taxonomy fit for OSI protocols.
OSI.quote: This document supplements the Transport Service and Protocol of the International Standards Organization (ISO), IS 8072 and IS 8073

transport.why: The content is transport-layer: connection negotiation, flow control credit, checksums, TPDU sizes, acknowledgement strategy, and connection reference reuse. No technology tag covers ISO TP4, so the general transport topic applies.
transport.quote: The ISO protocol has five classes of service, named Class 0 through Class 4.

rejected.why: IS 8473 (CLNP) is mandated as the network substrate with Class 4, but the document does not specify or profile CLNP itself. It only discusses operating transport over a connectionless network service.
The document concerns the ISO transport protocol as an alternative, not TCP.
The Fletcher checksum usage is a minor option discussion within the transport profile, not the document's subject.
Quality of service parameters are only mentioned and recommended not to be used; they are not a substantial part.

gaps.name: ISO Transport Protocol (TP4, IS 8073)
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is the ISO/OSI transport protocol, Classes 2 and 4, and no taxonomy tag exists for it. The OSI tag is described as network-layer, so it is a loose fit.

RFC1008.title: Implementation guide for the ISO Transport Protocol
RFC1008.summary: An implementation guide for the ISO (OSI) Transport Protocol (IS 8073, Classes 0/2/4) that explains its Estelle formal description and gives advice on environment, buffers, timers, flow control, the Fletcher checksum, parameter selection and special options.

OSI.why: The whole document concerns implementing the OSI transport protocol (IS 8073, Class 2/4) over OSI and other network services. No more specific tag exists for OSI transport, so OSI is the best fit.
OSI.quote: IMPLEMENTATION GUIDE FOR THE ISO TRANSPORT PROTOCOL

checksum.why: Section 7 is devoted to an enhanced Fletcher checksum algorithm, with C and assembler code and performance analysis.
checksum.quote: straightforward implementation of the Fletcher checksum using the algorithm recommended in the ISO transport standard leads to severe reduction of transport throughput
checksum.section: 7.1 Effect of checksum on transport performance

rejected.why: It is mentioned only as a source of an adaptive retransmission timer idea; the document is about ISO transport.
Credit-based flow control and Jain's scheme are discussed, but the document is about OSI transport flow control and parameter selection, not congestion control across transports.
Not relevant; IP is mentioned only as a network service beneath transport.
DOD IP appears only as one network service over which Class 4 transport is run.

gaps.name: OSI Transport Protocol (IS 8073, TP4) / Estelle formal description
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the OSI transport layer or for the Estelle formal description technique. The document is chiefly about these, and OSI covers only part of it.

RFC1009.title: Requirements for Internet gateways
RFC1009.summary: RFC 1009 specifies requirements for Internet gateways (IP routers) in 1987, covering required protocols (IP, ICMP, EGP, ARP, IGPs), constituent network interfaces, routing and forwarding algorithms, operation and maintenance, and NSFNET-specific policy requirements.

routing architecture.why: The core of the document is requirements for gateway (router) routing algorithms, subnets and routing, default routes, redirects and reachability. This is routing design guidance, not one protocol.
routing architecture.quote: The routing mechanism is fundamental to Internet operation. In all but trivial network topologies, robust Internet service requires some degree of routing dynamics

EGP.why: A dedicated section gives requirements and guidance on EGP implementation, its coupling to the routing database, its limitations and its configuration parameters.
EGP.quote: EGP is the protocol used to exchange reachability information between Autonomous Systems of gateways, and is defined in RFC-904

ICMP.why: A long section gives per-message gateway requirements for Destination Unreachable, Redirect, Source Quench, Time Exceeded, Echo and others.
ICMP.quote: ICMP is an auxiliary protocol used to convey advice and error messages and is described in RFC-792

IPv4.why: Specifies gateway handling of IPv4 options, fragmentation, reassembly, address classes, special addresses, broadcasts and TTL.
IPv4.quote: IP is the basic datagram protocol used in the Internet system. It is described in RFC-791

RIP.why: RIP is described as a candidate IGP with hold-down and counting-to-infinity requirements; this is part of the IGP discussion.
RIP.quote: RIP is the name often used for a class of routing protocols based upon the Xerox PUP and XNS routing protocols.

rejected.why: The subnetting discussion is pre-CIDR and concerns subnet masks, so it does not fit.
ARP and proxy ARP get a short section, but only as a protocol the gateway implements. The document is not about ARP.
Section 5 covers gateway O&M, but it is one part of the document and states no specific management protocol. Routing and gateway requirements are the main subject.
SPF is mentioned only as a class of routing algorithms, not OSPF.
TCP is mentioned only as background and as a substrate for O&M.
X.25 appears only as one of the constituent network interfaces in Section 3.

gaps.name: Gateway / router requirements
gaps.why: The document is the early router requirements specification, a precursor to RFC 1812. The taxonomy has no tag for router requirements, so routing architecture is the closest fit.

RFC1010.title: Assigned numbers
RFC1010.summary: RFC 1010 is the 1987 Assigned Numbers memo listing IP version and protocol numbers, TCP/UDP well-known ports, ARPANET link and logical addresses, IEEE 802 SAPs, Ethernet types, ARP parameters, Telnet options and official machine, system, protocol and terminal names.

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry of assigned protocol numbers, ports and names, which is what IANA registries cover.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

ARPANET.why: It has dedicated sections on ARPANET link numbers and logical addresses, and many entries are ARPANET-era services.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

Telnet.why: It carries a full registry of Telnet option numbers, plus terminal type names for the Telnet terminal-type option.
Telnet.quote: The Telnet Protocol has a number of options that may be negotiated.

ARP.why: It lists the ARP operation codes and hardware types, and ARP's protocol type codes come from the Ethernet numbers table.
ARP.quote: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) specified in RFC 826 [64] has several parameters.

Ethernet.why: It has an Ethernet type registry and the IEEE 802 SAP/SNAP policy for carrying IP over 802 networks.
Ethernet.quote: These systems use a message "type" field in much the same way the ARPANET uses the "link" field.

rejected.why: Only the DNS CLASS values and port 53 are listed. The document does not specify the protocol.
Port numbers are assigned for TCP, but TCP itself is not specified or extended here.
The machine and system name lists come from the host table, but they are just value lists and not about host naming conventions.
IP version and protocol numbers appear only as registry entries.

RFC1011.title: Official Internet protocols
RFC1011.summary: RFC 1011 is a 1987 status report listing the official Internet protocols, with the status, specifying documents, comments, dependencies and contact for each, covering protocols from the network layer to the application layer, plus ISO/CCITT protocols.

IETF process.why: The document exists to record which protocols are official and what their status is (required, recommended, elective, experimental). That is standards-status administration, not the specification of any single protocol.
IETF process.quote: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet.

internet history.why: It is a snapshot of the 1987 protocol suite and the handbooks that preceded it. Readers of Internet history would want it.
internet history.quote: An even older collection is the "ARPANET Protocol Handbook" (APH) dated January 1978.

rejected.why: TCP is one entry among about 80 in the catalogue. The document does not specify or extend it, apart from brief comments.
IP is catalogued with errata comments, but the document is not about it.
The document lists protocol specifications, not the format, style or publication of RFCs.
The Catenet Model entry is only a pointer to IEN 48, not a discussion of architectural principles.
The Domain Name Protocol entry only lists the RFCs that specify it.
FTP is one catalogue entry, with a short note on new optional commands. The same applies to SMTP, Telnet and the other entries.

gaps.name: Official protocol status list / protocol standards catalogue
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for protocol status reports or catalogues such as the Official Internet Protocol Standards series. IETF process is the closest fit.

RFC1012.title: Bibliography of Request For Comments 1 through 999
RFC1012.summary: RFC 1012 is a bibliographic index listing author, title, RFC number, NIC number, organization and date for RFCs 1 through 999 (1969-1987); it specifies no protocol.

internet history.why: The document is a retrospective catalogue of the early RFC series, covering ARPANET-era documents. Readers browsing Internet history would want it.
internet history.quote: a bibliographic summary of the Request for Comments numbers 1 through 999 issued between the years 1969-1987

RFC series.why: It is an index of the RFC series itself, listing entries, authors, dates, and which RFCs were never issued or were superseded.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a reference guide for the Internet community which provides a bibliographic summary of the Request for Comments

rejected.why: Many listed RFCs concern the ARPANET, but this document only catalogues them and is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
Many Telnet RFCs appear as entries, but the document does not specify or discuss the protocol.
FTP RFCs appear as list entries only; the document is not about FTP.
Mail-related RFCs are listed as entries, but the document does not address email itself.
Domain name RFCs are listed as entries only.

RFC1013.title: X Window System Protocol, version 11: Alpha update April 1987
RFC1013.summary: RFC 1013 specifies the X Window System core protocol version 11 (alpha update): terminology, request/reply/error/event formats, connection setup, and the full set of window, graphics, input and colormap requests and events.

X Window System.why: The whole document is the specification of the X11 core protocol, covering its formats, requests, events and connection handling.
X Window System.quote: For remote clients, the X protocol can be built on top of any reliable byte stream.

rejected.why: TCP is only one possible byte-stream transport (display N on port 6000+N); the document does not specify or extend TCP.
ASCII is mentioned only for byte-order bytes and name encodings, which is incidental.
This tag is for early ARPANET-era graphics protocols; X11 has its own specific tag.

RFC1014.title: XDR: External Data Representation standard
RFC1014.summary: RFC 1014 specifies XDR, Sun's External Data Representation standard: a C-like language for describing data and a canonical big-endian 4-byte-unit encoding for its types, used by Sun RPC and NFS.

ONC RPC.why: The taxonomy's ONC RPC tag explicitly covers XDR. This document is the XDR specification: its data types, encodings and description language, which Sun RPC and NFS use.
ONC RPC.quote: XDR is a standard for the description and encoding of data.

rejected.why: The document compares XDR to X.409/ASN.1 as an analogous but different approach (implicit vs explicit typing). It does not specify ASN.1.
NFS is mentioned only as a protocol that uses XDR. It is not specified or analysed here.
Section 5 uses an extended BNF to define the XDR grammar. That is only a notation for the XDR language, not the subject.

gaps.name: XDR (External Data Representation)
gaps.why: XDR is a general data description and encoding standard. The only fitting tag is ONC RPC, which covers it only by mention. A standalone XDR tag under data formats would be more precise.

RFC1015.title: Implementation plan for interagency research Internet
RFC1015.summary: An idea paper proposing an Interagency Research Internet (IRI) that interconnects US federal agency research networks using TCP/IP, with a management structure, phased implementation plan, and budget.

internet architecture.why: The document proposes interconnecting heterogeneous agency networks via the internet model (IP gateways, virtual network) as the architecture for a research internet.
internet architecture.quote: The structure is based on the concept of a network of networks using standard networking protocols.

internet history.why: A substantial background section recounts the history of the Arpanet, CSNET, MFEnet, NSFnet and the internet technologies.
internet history.quote: The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) developed the concept of packet switching beginning in the mid 1960's.

rejected.why: Arpanet is mentioned only as historical background and as one of the interconnected networks, not specified or operated by this document.
TCP/IP is the assumed substrate for interconnection; the document does not specify or extend it.
IP is described only at a high level as the interconnection mechanism, not specified.
The IRIO, Policy Board, TAB and IRAB are a proposed federal management structure, not IETF process, though the IAB's evolution into the IRAB is mentioned.
Gateways and routing are mentioned only in passing, not as a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Research networking program planning and funding / national research network policy
gaps.why: The document is mainly an organisational, management and budget plan for interagency research networking, which the taxonomy has no tag for.

RFC1016.title: Something a Host Could Do with Source Quench: The Source Quench Introduced Delay (SQuID)
RFC1016.summary: RFC 1016 is a "crazy idea" memo proposing that a source host's IP module introduce an adaptive inter-datagram delay (SQuID) in response to ICMP Source Quench messages, with a gateway source-quench queue-threshold scheme and simulation results.

congestion control.why: The memo proposes an algorithm for hosts and gateways to react to congestion signals, increasing and decreasing delay between datagrams. This is general congestion control at the IP layer, not tied to one transport.
congestion control.quote: The source quench message is a request to the host to cut back the rate at which it is sending traffic to the Internet destination.

ICMP.why: The ICMP Source Quench message is the congestion signal the whole proposal is built around, including how gateways should generate it (SQK/SQT/SQLW levels) and how hosts should respond.
ICMP.quote: If a gateway discards a datagram, it may send a source quench message to the Internet source host of the datagram.

rejected.why: TCP is the simulated traffic source and interacts with the algorithm, but the memo explicitly puts TCP behaviour beyond its scope and specifies IP-layer behaviour.
The memo is about congestion response, not quality-of-service architecture or signalling.

The gateway queue-threshold source quench scheme resembles early-warning queue management, but it is a source quench generation policy rather than active queue management as the tag is defined. Congestion control covers it.
NETBLT is mentioned only as an example of a rate-based protocol that sends in bursts.
Appendix A passively measures minimum inter-datagram arrival time, but only as input to the delay parameter I, not as a measurement methodology in its own right.

RFC1017.title: Network requirements for scientific research: Internet task force on scientific computing
RFC1017.summary: A 1987 IAB task force idea paper listing near-term and long-term requirements that scientific research places on networks: connectivity, end-to-end specifications, and user services.

internet architecture.why: The paper sets out architectural requirements for interconnected networks (interoperability via IP, type-of-service routing, expressway routing, address administration, OSI transition). It fits the broad internet architecture subject.
internet architecture.quote: The purpose of this paper is to identify the range of requirements for networks that are to support scientific research.

RJE.why: A dedicated subsection gives requirements for remote job entry on the Internet for supercomputer access, so readers of RJE would want it.
RJE.quote: The capabilities of standard network RJE implementations are inadequate, and are implemented prolifically among major operating systems.

directory services.why: The user services section calls for white pages and yellow pages directory services as a main near-term requirement.
directory services.quote: The network needs to provide mechanisms for looking up names and addresses of people and hosts on the network.

rejected.why: Type-of-service routing and the trade-offs between delay, bandwidth and reliability are discussed only as general requirements. The paper has no QoS architecture or signalling.
The DARPA Name Domain system is mentioned once as a suitable name-to-address service. The document is not about DNS.
The Arpanet appears as one of several example networks and as an example of congestion. The paper is not about it.
Access control, privacy and accounting are listed as brief requirements, not as a substantial subject of the paper.
IP is recommended as the interoperability layer, but the paper does not specify or analyse it.

RFC1018.title: Some comments on SQuID
RFC1018.summary: A 1987 discussion memo commenting on RFC 1016 (Source Quench) that distinguishes "Funneling" from "Mismatch" gateway congestion and proposes gateway strategies for when to send ICMP Source Quench messages.

congestion control.why: The memo analyses causes of gateway congestion and proposes strategies for signalling senders to slow down, which is congestion control across hosts and gateways.
congestion control.quote: Funneling congestion and Mismatch congestion are qualitatively different, and it would not be surprising if different SQ-sending strategies were best for dealing with them.

ICMP.why: The document is about when gateways should send ICMP Source Quench messages, so ICMP readers would want it.
ICMP.quote: This is the basis for the "hint" in the ICMP specification that maybe an SQ should be sent only when a datagram is dropped.

rejected.why: It mentions architectural assumptions about bursty traffic, but the document is about congestion signalling, not architectural principles.
It concerns gateways and queues, but not routing protocols or path selection.
It discusses queue-length thresholds for sending Source Quench, but it does not describe queue management that drops or marks packets, so AQM is a poor fit.

gaps.name: Source Quench
gaps.why: The document is about ICMP Source Quench (SQ) generation and the SQuID algorithm of RFC 1016. The taxonomy has no Source Quench tag, so ICMP and congestion control are the nearest fits.

RFC1019.title: Report of the Workshop on Environments for Computational Mathematics
RFC1019.summary: Workshop report proposing an architecture for Standard Mathematical Systems in which editors, displayers, computation systems and document systems exchange mathematical expressions as a common "Abstract Syntax".

rejected.why: The Abstract Syntax is an expression interchange representation, which is loosely data-format related. But it is a Lisp/functional-notation tree for math, not a general Internet data format or encoding, so the broad topic fits poorly.
The report assumes ASCII for Abstract Syntax expressions, but only as a minor assumption, not as a subject of the document.
Multimedia electronic mail is named as one of the participating communities, but the document does not address email protocols or formats.
Document interchange is discussed in a general sense, but SGML is never mentioned or addressed.

gaps.name: Mathematical expression representation / computational mathematics environments
gaps.why: The whole document concerns interchange of mathematical expressions among editors, displayers, computer algebra systems and document systems. The taxonomy has no tag for this subject.

RFC1020.title: Internet numbers
RFC1020.summary: RFC 1020 is the 1987 official registry of assigned IP network numbers (class A/B/C) and EGP autonomous system numbers, with address class definitions, special addresses, and contact handles.

addressing.why: The document describes IP address classes, special addresses, and lists assignments of network numbers; this is IP address allocation and architecture.
addressing.quote: The network numbers listed here are used as internet addresses by the Internet Protocol (IP)

IANA.why: It is a number-assignment registry, including autonomous system numbers, maintained by a registry operator (the precursor of IANA registries).
IANA.quote: The responsibility for the assignment of IP numbers and ASNs has been assumed by Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center (NIC).

rejected.why: EGP is mentioned only as the reason AS numbers exist; the document does not specify or extend EGP.
Class D is mentioned in one paragraph only; not a substantial subject.
Considered; the document is about the address/number registry, and 'addressing' fits better, though IPv4 address lifecycle is close.
NIC WHOIS is mentioned only as a way to look up contact handles.
ARPANET appears only as an entry in the network list.

gaps.name: Autonomous system numbers
gaps.why: The registry of AS numbers is a substantial part of the document, but the taxonomy has no tag for AS number assignment (nearest are routing and IANA).

RFC1021.title: High-level Entity Management System (HEMS)
RFC1021.summary: RFC 1021 is an overview of the experimental High-Level Entity Management System (HEMS), an IP internetwork management system with a query processor, event generator, applications and the HEMP protocol, intended to lead to a management standard.

HEMS.why: The document is the overview of HEMS itself, describing its architecture, query processor, events and protocol.
HEMS.quote: The HEMS is made up of three parts: a query processor which can reside on any addressable entity, an event generator which also resides on entities

rejected.why: CMIP is discussed only as a compatibility consideration in one short section, not specified or profiled here.
HEMS uses ASN.1 as its data encoding, which makes it a substrate and not the subject of the document.
TCP and UDP are the transports HEMP runs over (specified in RFC 1022), not the subject of this overview.
SNMP is not mentioned; HEMS was a competing proposal, not an SNMP document.
The HEMS tag is more specific, and the parent is implied by it.

RFC1022.title: High-level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP)
RFC1022.summary: RFC 1022 specifies HEMP, the application-layer message encapsulation protocol of the High-Level Entity Management System (HEMS), providing ASN.1-encoded request/reply/event messages with optional encryption, authentication, and protocol error reporting for managing hosts and gateways.

HEMS.why: The document defines the HEMP protocol, a component of HEMS.
HEMS.quote: An application protocol for managing network entities such as hosts, gateways and front-end machines, is presented.

RFC1023.title: HEMS monitoring and control language
RFC1023.summary: RFC 1023 specifies the HEMS query language, a stack-based, ASN.1-encoded language for monitoring and controlling network entities through a hierarchical data model with GET, SET, and MATCH operators.

HEMS.why: The document defines the HEMS monitoring and control language itself, with its data model, opcodes, attributes, and error handling.
HEMS.quote: This RFC specifies the design of a general-purpose, yet efficient, monitoring and control language for managing network entities.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the encoding the language relies on. The document uses it but does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
SNMP is a contemporary management protocol but the document does not discuss it. HEMS is a separate system.
Data definitions are deferred to RFC-1024. This document only defines the query language and the hierarchical data model.

RFC1024.title: HEMS variable definitions
RFC1024.summary: RFC 1024 defines the HEMS (High-Level Entity Management System) object space: instruction codes, ASN.1 types, and the dictionaries of managed objects (system, events, interfaces, IP, routing, ICMP, IGMP, TCP, EGP, UDP) for monitoring and controlling network entities.

HEMS.why: The whole document is the HEMS variable (MIB-like) definitions: the object tree, types, and event formats.
HEMS.quote: This memo assigns instruction codes, defines object formats and object semantics for use with the High-Level Monitoring and Control Language

rejected.why: HEMS defines its own object space, not SNMP MIB modules/SMI.
Competing/alternative management system; SNMP is not specified or used here.
ASN.1 is the encoding substrate for the objects, not the subject.
TCP statistics objects are defined, but only as part of the management dictionary; the document is not about TCP.
EGP counters and parameters are management objects only; EGP itself is not specified.
IGMP objects are a small part of the dictionary; not about IGMP.
ICMP counters are just management objects.

RFC1025.title: TCP and IP bake off
RFC1025.summary: Describes the procedures, scoring and test list used in early TCP and IP interoperability "bake offs" (1978-1980), plus new mechanisms and performance tests for testing TCP/IP implementations.

TCP.why: The document is a test suite and scoring scheme for TCP implementations (connections, urgent data, sequence wraparound, zero window, half-open), so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: Each implementor of a TCP and IP is to perform the following tests and to report the results.

IPv4.why: A substantial section tests IPv4 host and gateway features: fragmentation, source route options, TTL handling, type of service, timestamp and security options.
IPv4.quote: 25 points for doing fragmentation and reassembly.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as one of several performance test possibilities; the document is not about NETBLT.
Used only as a throughput test vehicle, not specified or analysed.
Used as a tool to open connections for testing; not the subject.
Source quench and routing advice are scored items but only briefly mentioned; not a substantial focus.
Nagle, Van Jacobson and SQuID procedures are only listed as new mechanisms to check, with no substantive treatment.
It recounts the history of the bake offs, but its main purpose is the test procedures, not a retrospective.

gaps.name: protocol interoperability testing / bake offs
gaps.why: The document is about interoperability testing of implementations, and the taxonomy has no tag for conformance or interop testing.

RFC1026.title: Addendum to RFC 987: (Mapping between X.400 and RFC-822)
RFC1026.summary: Addendum to RFC 987 correcting errata and extending the X.400 to RFC-822 mapping with component ordering rules, explicit omitted-component handling, and a new Appendix F defining domain/X.400 address mapping table formats.

X.400.why: The document amends the mapping between X.400 O/R names and RFC-822 addresses, including ordering of OUs and domain-defined attributes and the address mapping table format.
X.400.quote: This document specifies a number of additions and corrections to RFC-987, aka Mailgroup Note 19.

rejected.why: RFC-822 mail is one side of the mapping, but the document's subject is X.400 interworking, which the X.400 tag covers specifically.
RFC-822 addresses are mentioned only as the mapping target; the document does not specify message header format.
Domain names are associated with X.400 attributes in mapping tables, but the document does not specify DNS itself, only a table syntax suitable for use with nameservers.

RFC1027.title: Using ARP to implement transparent subnet gateways
RFC1027.summary: Describes Proxy ARP: how subnet gateways answer ARP requests on behalf of hosts on other subnets so hosts without subnet support can communicate transparently, with sanity checks, broadcast handling and a 4.3BSD implementation.

ARP.why: The whole document specifies the Proxy ARP technique, an extension of ARP behaviour in gateways.
ARP.quote: the use of the Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) by subnet gateways to permit hosts on the connected subnets to communicate without being aware of the existence of subnets

addressing.why: Substantial portions cover IP subnetting, network masks and broadcast address conventions needed for transparent subnets.
addressing.quote: There are two kinds of IP broadcast addresses:  main IP directed network broadcast and subnet broadcast.

rejected.why: Ethernet is the medium where ARP is used, but the document is about ARP gateway behaviour, not IP over Ethernet itself.
Routing lookups are discussed only as part of the gateway's reply decision; the document is not about routing design.
IPv4 is the substrate; the document does not specify IPv4 itself.

gaps.name: IP subnetting (RFC 950 subnets)
gaps.why: The document is largely about hiding subnets from hosts; the taxonomy has no dedicated subnetting tag beyond the general addressing topic.

RFC1028.title: Simple Gateway Monitoring Protocol
RFC1028.summary: RFC 1028 defines the Simple Gateway Monitoring Protocol (SGMP), an interim UDP-based protocol with Get/Set/Trap messages and a variable namespace for inspecting and altering gateway state, a precursor to SNMP.

network management.why: The document specifies a gateway monitoring and management protocol, with get/set/trap operations and defined management variables. No SNMP-specific tag fits this pre-SNMP protocol, so the parent topic is used.
network management.quote: a simple application-layer protocol by which management information for a gateway may be inspected or altered by logically remote users

EGP.why: The document defines EGP-related variables and an EGP neighbor loss trap, so it covers monitoring of EGP. This is a modest part of the document.
EGP.quote: This section describes variables that represent information related to protocols and mechanisms of the EGP protocol [4].

rejected.why: SGMP is the direct ancestor of SNMP, but the document specifies SGMP, not SNMP or its framework.
The document defines variables with octet-string names rather than a MIB module in SMI form.
UDP is only the transport substrate, and the document defines nothing new about it.
The messages are described in X.409 notation, but that is only the encoding mechanism the document relies on.
The Ethernet counters appear in an implementation-specific appendix and the document is not about Ethernet itself.
A minimal session-layer authentication protocol is defined, but it is a placeholder with trivial functions and is not the main subject.

RFC1029.title: More fault tolerant approach to address resolution for a Multi-LAN system of Ethernets
RFC1029.summary: Proposes an extension to transparent Ethernet bridges and ARP for multi-LAN systems: bridges keep global translation caches, detect host hardware/protocol address changes ("reboots"), and multicast a REBOOT packet to update ARP caches.

ARP.why: The whole document is an extension of ARP address resolution for bridged multi-LAN Ethernets, with a new REBOOT packet to keep ARP translation caches current.
ARP.quote: A protocol is presented which allows dynamic distribution of the information required to build tables that translate a host's address in protocol P's address space into a 48 bit Ethernet address.

Ethernet.why: Concerns transparent bridges linking multiple Ethernet LANs, with the bridge's caches and behaviour central to the proposal. This is a substantial part of the subject matter.
Ethernet.quote: Executing a protocol P, a sending host S decides, through P's routing mechanism, that it wants to transmit to a target host T located somewhere on a connected piece of 10Mbit Ethernet cable

rejected.why: IP is used only as the example protocol (benchmark) for address resolution; the document is not about IPv4.
Subnetting (explicit vs transparent) is reviewed as background, but the document does not address IP address architecture itself.
Bridge forwarding and loop resolution are mentioned, but the focus is address cache consistency, not routing design.

RFC1030.title: On testing the NETBLT Protocol over divers networks
RFC1030.summary: Reports results of testing the NETBLT bulk-transfer protocol (RFC 998) over a Proteon token ring, an Ethernet, and the 3 Mbit/s Wideband satellite network, including implementation changes prompted by the tests and a Wideband bandwidth analysis.

NETBLT.why: The entire document is test and performance evidence for NETBLT, plus the implementation and timer changes it motivated.
NETBLT.quote: NETBLT (NETwork BLock Transfer) is a transport level protocol intended for the rapid transfer of a large quantity of data between computers.

rejected.why: The Wideband satellite network is a test environment and its bandwidth analysis is supporting detail. The document is about NETBLT's performance, not networking over satellite links in general.
Ethernet is only a test LAN and access path. The document does not cover IP over Ethernet.
The Proteon Token Ring is the reference test environment, not the subject.
This is an ad hoc test report on one protocol, not a benchmarking methodology for network devices.

RFC1031.title: MILNET name domain transition
RFC1031.summary: RFC 1031 describes the MILNET transition from the central NIC host table to the Domain Name System, with a three-stage migration path, timetable, pointers to DNS documentation, and a list of DNS server/resolver implementations.

DNS.why: The whole document is about moving MILNET hosts to the domain system, summarizing the DNS RFCs and listing DNS implementations (BIND, JEEVES, resolvers).
DNS.quote: The domain system uses a distributed database and software to perform the same functions as the host table.

hostnames.why: A substantial part concerns the host table and its replacement, including RFC 952 host table and RFC 953 Hostnames Server.
hostnames.quote: At the end of the conversion period, the NIC will stop maintaining an internet host table.

rejected.why: MILNET/ARPANET are the deployment context, but the subject is name resolution, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
Mail exchanger (MX) handling is mentioned only briefly as part of conversion; not the document's subject.
FTP is only the means of fetching the host table and software; not discussed in its own right.
Parent of DNS, which fits more specifically.

RFC1032.title: Domain administrators guide
RFC1032.summary: RFC 1032 is a guide for domain administrators on registering top-level and second-level domains with the DDN NIC, covering roles, naming policies, verification via WHOIS, and the registration questionnaire.

domain registration.why: The whole document covers registry procedures, registrar policy, and the application questionnaire for registering top-level and second-level domains.
domain registration.quote: This memo describes procedures for registering a domain with the Network Information Center (NIC) of Defense Data Network (DDN)

DNS.why: It gives guidance on administering domains, zones, name servers and root servers, with the roles of the DA and zone contact. This is DNS operations.
DNS.quote: The domain-naming system is distributed and hierarchical.

rejected.why: WHOIS is only used as a way to verify registration data, with one example. The document does not specify or extend it.
RFC 952 host naming conventions are referenced briefly. The document is about domain administration, not host tables.
FTP is only the means of retrieving the online NIC files and the questionnaire template.

RFC1033.title: Domain Administrators Operations Guide
RFC1033.summary: RFC 1033 is an operations guide for domain administrators describing zone files, resource record formats (SOA, NS, A, CNAME, HINFO, WKS, MX, PTR), TTL choices, IN-ADDR.ARPA reverse mapping, and example zone and BIND boot files.

DNS.why: The whole document is about operating DNS servers, zone files, resource records, delegation, glue and reverse mapping, so it belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: This RFC provides guidelines for domain administrators in operating a domain server and maintaining their portion of the hierarchical database.

rejected.why: It briefly recommends characters for host names, but the document is about DNS zone administration rather than host naming conventions.
The MX record is described, but only as a DNS resource record type and not as mail architecture or transport.
This is the parent of DNS, and the document is about DNS specifically, so the more specific tag is used.

RFC1034.title: Domain names - concepts and facilities
RFC1034.summary: RFC 1034 introduces the Domain Name System: the name space, resource records, name servers, zones, resolvers, caching and zone transfers, with worked examples.

DNS.why: The whole document defines DNS concepts: name space, RRs, name servers, resolvers, zones, queries and caching.
DNS.quote: This RFC is an introduction to the Domain Name System (DNS), and omits many details which can be found in a companion RFC

rejected.why: Preferred host name syntax and HOSTS.TXT history are discussed, but only as a small part of a document about DNS.
Mail addressing and MX records appear as examples of DNS use, not as the subject.
UDP and TCP are only the transports that carry queries.
The document is about DNS specifically, so the child tag DNS is used instead of this parent.

RFC1035.title: Domain names - implementation and specification
RFC1035.summary: RFC 1035 is the core DNS specification: it defines resource record formats, message format and compression, UDP/TCP transport, master files, and name server and resolver implementation guidance, plus mail-related RRs (MX, mailbox binding).

DNS.why: The document is the foundational DNS specification covering RRs, messages, master files, name servers and resolvers.
DNS.quote: This RFC describes the details of the domain system and protocol

rejected.why: Section 8 covers MX and mailbox binding in DNS, but this is a DNS feature and not about email itself.
The preferred name syntax follows host naming rules, but it is a small part of a document about DNS.
TCP and UDP are only transports for DNS messages here, with no new definition of how they work.
UDP is only the substrate for queries; the 512-octet limit and retransmission advice are DNS-specific.
MINFO and MG records touch on mailing lists, but only as experimental DNS RR types.

RFC1036.title: Standard for interchange of USENET messages
RFC1036.summary: RFC 1036 defines the USENET news message format (headers built on RFC-822), control messages, transmission and batching methods, and the news propagation algorithm, replacing RFC 850.

Netnews.why: The whole document specifies the USENET article format, control messages, batching and propagation, which is the Netnews article format and distribution.
Netnews.quote: This document defines the standard format for the interchange of network News messages among USENET hosts.

UUCP.why: UUCP is the main transport for news batches (uux rnews), discussed in the transmission methods section, though only as one substrate.
UUCP.quote: there is a high overhead to start sending a new message with UUCP

rejected.why: News messages are RFC-822 format, but the document is about the USENET profile rather than the Internet mail message format; Netnews is the more specific fit.
Mail is used as a transfer method for news (rnews by mail) and as the format basis, but the document is not about email.
NNTP is not mentioned or specified; transmission is via UUCP/batching.
Newsgroups are not mailing list protocols.

RFC1037.title: NFILE - a file access protocol
RFC1037.summary: RFC 1037 specifies NFILE, Symbolics' historic file access protocol, along with its underlying Token List Transport Layer and Byte Stream with Mark, covering commands, resynchronization after aborts, errors, and character translation.

applications.why: The document specifies a remote file access application protocol. The taxonomy has no NFILE-specific tag and no generic file access tag, so the general applications topic is the closest fit.
applications.quote: NFILE is a file access protocol that supports a large set of operations on files and directories on remote systems

rejected.why: TCP is only one of the byte-stream substrates (alongside Chaosnet) that NFILE runs over. It also gets a port number, but the document defines nothing new about TCP.
NFILE is a different file protocol, a replacement for QFILE. It is not FTP and does not extend it.
The NFILE character set extends ASCII, but the document is not about ASCII itself. It defines its own translation modes.
NFS is another remote file system protocol. NFILE is unrelated to it and does not use it.
Byte Stream with Mark is a layer over TCP and Chaosnet, but it is a purpose-built protocol layer. It is not an X-over-transport binding.

gaps.name: NFILE / remote file access protocols (and QFILE, Chaosnet)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for general file access or file transfer protocols other than FTP, TFTP and NFS. Historic or niche file protocols such as NFILE can only be placed under the generic applications topic.

RFC1038.title: Draft revised IP security option
RFC1038.summary: Draft revision of the DoD IP Basic and Extended Security Options, which carry classification level and protection-authority flags in IPv4 datagram headers, with host input/output rules and out-of-range handling.

security labels.why: The whole document specifies a label (classification level plus authority flags) carried on datagrams and the rules for hosts to validate and enforce it.
security labels.quote: The option identifies the U.S. security level to which the datagram is to be protected, and the accrediting authorities whose protection rules apply

IPv4.why: The options are IPv4 header options, and the document lists the IP option table and amends the IP specification, so IPv4 readers would want it.
IPv4.quote: This document will be published as a change to the MIL-STD 1777, "Internet Protocol".

rejected.why: ICMP parameter problem and destination unreachable messages are used only to report out-of-range options, not specified here.
The more specific security labels tag fits, so the general topic is not needed.

RFC1039.title: DoD statement on Open Systems Interconnection protocols
RFC1039.summary: A reproduced 1987 DoD memorandum adopting the OSI message handling and file transfer protocols (per GOSIP) as experimental co-standards alongside DoD protocols, with a plan for interoperation and transition.

OSI.why: The document is a policy statement on adopting OSI protocols and their coexistence and transition with the DoD (TCP/IP) protocol suite, which is what the OSI tag covers.
OSI.quote: The OSI message handling and file transfer protocols, together with their underlying protocols as defined in GOSIP, are adopted as experimental co-standards to the DoD protocols

rejected.why: OSI message handling is mentioned only as a capability covered by GOSIP, and X.400 is never named. The document is about policy, not the message handling protocol.
File transfer is referred to only generically, as the OSI and DoD file transfer capabilities. FTP itself is not specified or discussed.
It is a dated policy memo, not a history or retrospective.
The memo is DoD procurement and standardization policy, not IETF process.

RFC1040.title: Privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail: Part I: Message encipherment and authentication procedures
RFC1040.summary: RFC 1040 specifies Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) message encipherment and authentication procedures for Internet email: DES-based encryption, MIC computation, canonicalization, printable encoding, encapsulation headers, and a key-management framework.

PEM.why: The document is the specification of Privacy Enhanced Mail, the historic secure email scheme, covering encryption, MIC, encapsulation and header fields.
PEM.quote: This RFC defines message encipherment and authentication procedures, as the initial phase of an effort to provide privacy enhancement services for electronic mail transfer in the Internet.

DES.why: DES in CBC/ECB modes is the mandated cipher for message text and key encryption, and DES-based MACs are defined in Appendix A.
DES.quote: The DEA-1 is equivalent to the Data Encryption Standard (DES), as defined in FIPS PUB 46

Base64.why: Defines the 6-bit printable encoding with '=' padding, the ancestor of Base64, as a substantial part of the specification.
Base64.quote: The encoding process represents 24-bit groups of input bits as output strings of 4 encoded characters.

rejected.why: Email is the substrate; the PEM tag already captures the subject more specifically.
SMTP transparency constraints drive the encoding design, but SMTP is only the transport and is not specified or extended.
Certificates per X.509 are referenced as a recommended encoding for future key management, not specified here.
Encapsulated headers resemble RFC-822 fields but are explicitly a disjoint set; the RFC does not define the Internet message format.
Key management is deferred to a later RFC; only the DEK/IK framework is outlined, a minor part.
Predates MIME; encapsulation derives from RFC 934, not MIME body structure.

RFC1041.title: Telnet 3270 regime option
RFC1041.summary: Defines the Telnet 3270-REGIME option, letting a Telnet client and server negotiate a 3270 data stream (versus NVT ASCII) and select a terminal type in a single subnegotiation, replacing separate TERMINALTYPE, BINARY and EOR negotiations.

TN3270.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option for establishing a 3270 regime, which is the TN3270 terminal emulation negotiation.
TN3270.quote: This option allows a telnet server running VM or MVS to negotiate with the telnet client on the type of data stream (3270 or NVT ASCII)

Telnet.why: It defines a new Telnet option (code 29) with WILL/DO/SB negotiation, so it extends the Telnet protocol and its options; readers of Telnet options would want it.
Telnet.quote: The purpose of this memo is not to describe (or define) protocols which are used in 3270 Regime, but rather define a new option for the Telnet Protocol

rejected.why: 3270 is IBM terminal technology, but the document is about Telnet negotiation, not SNA interworking; TN3270 is the more specific fit.
NVT ASCII and binary data are mentioned only as regime properties, not as the subject.

RFC1042.title: Standard for the transmission of IP datagrams over IEEE 802 networks
RFC1042.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IP datagrams and ARP messages on IEEE 802.3, 802.4 and 802.5 networks using 802.2 LLC and SNAP headers, including MTU, address mapping, broadcast and token-ring source-routing details.

Ethernet.why: The document defines IP encapsulation over IEEE 802 LANs, including 802.3 Ethernet framing, MTU and interoperation with Ethernet. Ethernet is the closest fitting tag.
Ethernet.quote: IP datagrams are sent on IEEE 802 networks encapsulated within the 802.2 LLC and SNAP data link layers, and the 802.3, 802.4, or 802.5 physical networks layers.

token ring.why: A substantial section covers 802.5 token ring, including the source-routing RIF, broadcast types, MTU and priority handling.
token ring.quote: The current standard for token ring's, IEEE 802.5-1985, specifies the operation of single ring networks.

ARP.why: The document specifies ARP parameters for 802 networks (hardware type 6, address lengths) and ARP behaviour with RIFs on token ring.
ARP.quote: The mapping of 32-bit Internet addresses to 16-bit or 48-bit IEEE 802 addresses must be done via the dynamic discovery procedure of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)

rejected.why: IP is the payload being carried. The document specifies the link-layer encapsulation, not IP itself.
ICMP is only mentioned as one option for handling an address-not-recognized error.
A more specific child tag (Ethernet, token ring) fits, so the parent is not needed.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.4 token bus and IEEE 802.2 LLC/SNAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for token bus or for LLC/SNAP encapsulation, both of which the document specifies.

RFC1043.title: Telnet Data Entry Terminal option: DODIIS implementation
RFC1043.summary: Specifies the DODIIS implementation profile of the Telnet Data Entry Terminal (DET) option, defining subcommands, facility negotiation, form construction and response, function keys, and line discipline for full-screen forms over Telnet.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option (DET, code 20) with its subcommands and negotiation rules, so it is squarely about the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: DODIIS implementations of the DET option use the subcommands described in the remainder of Section 2.

rejected.why: TCP is only the underlying transport, mentioned in passing when discussing character-echo overhead.
Field data is restricted to ASCII codes 32-126, but this is a constraint on content, not the subject of the document.
ARPANET and DDN are mentioned as context for the network, but the document does not address ARPANET protocols as such.

gaps.name: Full-screen / forms-oriented terminal emulation (Data Entry Terminal)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is a block-mode forms terminal model (fields, attributes, function keys); the taxonomy has only Telnet and TN3270, with no generic terminal-emulation tag.

RFC1044.title: Internet Protocol on Network System's HYPERchannel: Protocol Specification
RFC1044.summary: Specifies how IP datagrams are encapsulated in Network Systems HYPERchannel messages (16-bit and 32-bit address formats), defines an ARP variant for HYPERchannel with MTU negotiation, and describes address resolution techniques.

ARP.why: A substantial part defines an ARP message format for HYPERchannel (hardware type 8), ARP servers and broadcast ARP, based on RFC 826.
ARP.quote: To define an Address Resolution Protocol for HYPERchannel and other NSC products.

link layer.why: The document is IP encapsulation over a specific proprietary link technology (HYPERchannel). No specific child tag fits, so the parent link layer topic is used.
link layer.quote: the protocols and techniques used to embed DoD standard Internet Protocol datagrams (and its associated higher level protocols) on Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel

rejected.why: IP datagrams are the payload carried; the document does not specify or extend IP itself.
The end-to-end CRC flag is a minor header feature, not a main subject.
This is link-layer encapsulation of IP, not IP-in-IP or generic tunnelling.
TCP is only mentioned as a higher-level protocol carried in IP datagrams.

gaps.name: HYPERchannel (Network Systems Corporation)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for HYPERchannel, the proprietary high-speed LAN technology that this document covers, so only the generic link layer topic could be used.

RFC1045.title: VMTP: Versatile Message Transaction Protocol: Protocol specification
RFC1045.summary: Specifies VMTP, an experimental transport protocol for request-response message transactions (RPC) with selective retransmission, rate control, optional security, multicast, real-time datagrams, streaming and forwarding, plus management procedures and a BSD socket interface.

transport.why: VMTP is a new general-purpose transport protocol for transaction-oriented communication, and it is neither TCP nor UDP, so the generic transport topic fits best.
transport.quote: a transport protocol specifically designed to support the transaction model of communication, as exemplified by remote procedure call (RPC)

rejected.why: VMTP is not ONC RPC. XDR is only mentioned in passing in the presentation appendix.
Used only as a comparison baseline in the motivation.
Multicast is one VMTP feature built on IP multicast (RFC 966/988). The document is not about multicast routing.
VMTP runs over IP (protocol number 81) as a substrate only.
The document defines a 32-bit VMTP checksum, but only as one part of the protocol.
Priority fields exist, but the document is not about QoS architectures.

gaps.name: Request-response / transaction transport (RPC transport)
gaps.why: VMTP is a transaction-oriented transport protocol. The taxonomy has only generic transport and ONC RPC, and nothing for transaction-style transports or RPC in general.

RFC1046.title: Queuing algorithm to provide type-of-service for IP links
RFC1046.summary: An idea paper proposing a per-link queuing algorithm (separate low-delay, high-reliability, high-throughput queues with service rates, chits and priority aging) to implement the IP Type-of-Service field.

QoS.why: The whole document proposes queuing and scheduling to provide differentiated service classes and priorities, which is a QoS mechanism.
QoS.quote: This memo is intended to explore how Type-of-Service might be implemented in the Internet. The proposal describes a method of queuing which can provide the different classes of service.

rejected.why: Source Quench is discussed as a signal, but the main subject is class-of-service queuing, not congestion control.
The queues use tail drop and size limits with early source quench. It is not a specific AQM algorithm, and QoS fits better.
The memo predates Diffserv and does not specify it. It only uses the IP TOS field.
The TOS field is in the IPv4 header, but the document is about queuing behaviour, not the IP protocol.
TCP RTT estimation is mentioned only as a possible benefit and a question.
Source Quench is mentioned only in passing as a flow-control signal.

RFC1047.title: Duplicate messages and SMTP
RFC1047.summary: RFC 1047 describes an SMTP synchronization gap after the final dot of message data that can cause duplicate message delivery, and recommends acknowledging the final dot quickly and using longer timeouts.

SMTP.why: The whole document analyses a protocol-level problem in SMTP's end-of-data handshake and gives operational guidance for sending and receiving mailers.
SMTP.quote: many duplicate messages are the result of a synchronization problem in SMTP.

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by SMTP, and the document concerns SMTP transfer behaviour rather than email in general.
The document is about delivery synchronization, not the structure of message headers or bodies.
Mailing list expansion is mentioned only as an example of slow processing after the final dot.

RFC1048.title: BOOTP vendor information extensions
RFC1048.summary: RFC 1048 defines a vendor-independent interpretation of the 64-octet vendor information field in BOOTP packets, specifying the magic cookie and tagged fields (subnet mask, gateways, time/name/log/print servers, hostname) for client configuration.

DHCP.why: BOOTP vendor extensions are the direct precursor of DHCP options. The taxonomy has no BOOTP tag, and DHCP is the closest fit for host configuration via BOOTP and its option fields.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a (potentially) vendor-independent interpretation of this resource information.

rejected.why: The extensions do convey server addresses, and the memo compares BOOTP with multicast location. But the document is about configuration data in BOOTP, not a discovery mechanism.
The Domain Name Server field only carries name server addresses, and DNS is just referenced.
The multicast comparison is a short discussion of alternatives, not the subject of the document.
BOOTP runs over UDP, which serves only as the substrate.
The LPR Server field only carries printer server addresses and does not specify LPD.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: The document extends BOOTP, which has no tag in the taxonomy. DHCP is the nearest tag, but a BOOTP tag would fit more precisely.

RFC1049.title: Content-type header field for Internet messages
RFC1049.summary: RFC 1049 proposes a Content-Type header field for RFC-822 mail messages so mail readers can identify structured ASCII bodies (PostScript, TeX, troff, SGML, etc.) and process them for display; it is the precursor to MIME's Content-Type.

message format.why: The document defines a new RFC-822 header field, its grammar and parameters (type, version, resource reference, comment). That is an extension of the Internet message format.
message format.quote: We propose that a new header field, "Content-type:" be recognized as the standard field for indicating the structure of the message body.

MIME.why: It is the historic predecessor of MIME's Content-Type. It labels the body type and registers type values, which readers of MIME history would want.
MIME.quote: Content-Type:= type [";" ver-num [";" 1#resource-ref]] [comment]

rejected.why: Too generic. The more specific message format tag fits the header-field definition.
SMTP is discussed only as one option for capability negotiation, which the document explicitly does not recommend or specify.
SGML is only one of the listed type values, not a subject of the document.
The document defines a small set of type values but no media type registry rules. It only says additional values are registered with the IANA coordinator.
The ASCII-only restriction on message bodies is a constraint, not what the document is about.

RFC1050.title: RPC: Remote Procedure Call Protocol specification
RFC1050.summary: Specifies Sun's ONC RPC version 2 message protocol (call/reply formats in XDR), its authentication flavors (NULL, UNIX, DES), TCP record marking, the RPC language, and the Port Mapper program.

ONC RPC.why: The whole document defines the ONC RPC message protocol, program numbering, record marking, the RPC language, and the Port Mapper service.
ONC RPC.quote: This document specifies a message protocol used in implementing Sun's Remote Procedure Call (RPC) package.

authentication.why: A substantial part of the document defines the RPC authentication framework and the AUTH_NULL, AUTH_UNIX and AUTH_DES flavors, including Diffie-Hellman key exchange and timestamp verifiers.
authentication.quote: The RPC protocol provides the fields necessary for a client to identify itself to a service and vice-versa.

rejected.why: TCP is only a transport RPC can run over. The record marking standard is a small part of the document and does not change TCP.
UDP is only a substrate transport for RPC.
DES is used as the cipher for AUTH_DES verifiers. The document is not about DES itself.
The Port Mapper binds program numbers to ports, but it is an appendix to RPC. ONC RPC already covers it.

gaps.name: XDR (External Data Representation)
gaps.why: The RPC messages are defined in XDR, but the taxonomy has no XDR tag. XDR is only referenced here, and the ONC RPC tag mentions it.

RFC1051.title: Standard for the transmission of IP datagrams and ARP packets over ARCNET networks
RFC1051.summary: Specifies how to encapsulate IP datagrams and ARP packets in ARCNET frames, including system codes, MTU and padding rules, address mapping, and broadcast address.

link layer.why: The document defines IP and ARP over ARCNET, a specific link technology. The taxonomy has no ARCNET tag, so the generic link layer topic is the closest fit.
link layer.quote: This RFC specifies a standard method of encapsulating Internet Protocol (IP) [1] and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [2] datagrams on an ARCNET [3].

ARP.why: The document defines ARP encapsulation (system code 241, hardware type 7) and ARP-based address mapping on ARCNET.
ARP.quote: Mappings between 32-bit Internet addresses and 8-bit ARCNET node ids could be accomplished through ARP.

rejected.why: IP is the payload being carried. The document defines the link encapsulation, not IP itself.
The frame's CRC-16 is part of the ARCNET format and is only mentioned in passing.
TCP's MSS option is mentioned only as a way to discourage fragmentation.

gaps.name: ARCNET
gaps.why: The document is about IP over ARCNET, and the taxonomy has no ARCNET tag. Only the generic link layer topic is available.

RFC1052.title: IAB recommendations for the development of Internet network management standards
RFC1052.summary: IAB policy memo with the Ad Hoc Network Management Review Committee report recommending SNMP as the short-term basis for Internet network management, CMIS/CMIP as the long-term basis, and a common MIB, with HEMS withdrawn.

SNMP.why: The central recommendation is adopting and extending SNMP (successor to SGMP) and chartering an SNMP working group to revise its specification.
SNMP.quote: The IAB recommends that the Simple Network Management Protocol be adopted as the BASIS for network management in the short-term.

CMIP.why: A major recommendation is to develop, deploy and test CMIS/CMIP over TCP/IP as the long-term system, with a transition path from SNMP.
CMIP.quote: The longer-term needs of the Internet community are to be met using the ISO CMIS/CMIP framework as a basis.

MIB.why: Creating a common TCP/IP MIB working group is one of four recommendations, with its output feeding both SNMP and CMIP.
MIB.quote: define an extended Management Information Base (MIB) for SNMP and TCP/IP CMIP to bring them into closer conformance with the MIB defined for the experimental HighLevel Entity Management System (HEMS).

HEMS.why: HEMS is reviewed and withdrawn in favour of SNMP and CMIS/CMIP, and its MIB is a starting input. This is a substantial part of the discussion.
HEMS.quote: The HEMS effort produced a very thorough and widely-discussed set of elements to monitor

rejected.why: The more specific technology tags (SNMP, CMIP, HEMS, MIB) fit, so the parent is implied.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as the common representation used by all the proposals, not as a subject of the memo.
The memo directs the IETF chairman to form working groups, but the subject is network management technology, not IETF procedure.
ISO management protocols are discussed, but the memo concerns management, not OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC1053.title: Telnet X.3 PAD option
RFC1053.summary: Proposes a Telnet option (X.3-PAD) that lets a host and user Telnet negotiate CCITT X.3 PAD terminal parameters, with extension sets, to support local character handling over a Telnet connection.

Telnet.why: The document defines a new Telnet option (code 30) with its negotiation commands, subnegotiation messages and parameters, so it is about the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: This RFC proposes that the Internet community adopt that solution to handle the same problems under Telnet.

X.25.why: The option is motivated by X.25/X.3 PAD interworking, and the parameters map X.25 Interrupt, Reset and Break messages to Telnet equivalents. It is a substantial secondary theme, though not an IP-over-X.25 specification.
X.25.quote: Telnet and X.3 PAD traffic will have to coexist on X.25 networks; there will be a consequential desire for effective interoperation at the virtual terminal level.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an existing alternative Telnet option, not specified or extended here.
The parameters use ASCII character codes, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
Telnet runs over TCP, which is only the substrate and is not discussed.

RFC1054.title: Host extensions for IP multicasting
RFC1054.summary: RFC 1054 specifies the host-side extensions to IP for multicasting (sending, receiving, Ethernet mapping) and defines IGMP version 1 for hosts to report group memberships to multicast routers, obsoleting RFC 988.

IGMP.why: The memo specifies IGMP version 1 in full: message format, query/report behaviour, timers and state machine.
IGMP.quote: The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used by IP hosts to report their host group memberships to any immediately-neighboring multicast routers.
IGMP.section: APPENDIX I. INTERNET GROUP MANAGEMENT PROTOCOL (IGMP)

multicast.why: The document defines IP multicasting for hosts: host group addresses, sending and receiving multicast datagrams, and the service interfaces. The general multicast tag fits because no child tag covers host-side IP multicast service.
multicast.quote: This memo specifies the extensions required of a host implementation of the Internet Protocol (IP) to support multicasting.

rejected.why: The Ethernet multicast address mapping is only an example local-network binding, not the subject of the document.
Class D host group addresses are covered, but only as part of the multicast specification. The multicast tag already captures this.
ICMP is only mentioned as part of the IP module and for rules on when errors are not generated.
The document extends IPv4 hosts, but its subject is multicast, not IPv4 in general.
Using group addresses as logical addresses for mobile hosts is mentioned only as background in an appendix.

RFC1055.title: Nonstandard for transmission of IP datagrams over serial lines: SLIP
RFC1055.summary: RFC 1055 describes SLIP, the de facto serial line framing protocol for IP datagrams using END/ESC byte stuffing, along with its history, deficiencies and C driver code.

SLIP.why: The document specifies the SLIP framing protocol, its byte-stuffing algorithm, maximum packet size, deficiencies and reference drivers.
SLIP.quote: SLIP defines a sequence of characters that frame IP packets on a serial line, and nothing more.

rejected.why: Only alluded to as an unnamed future successor to SLIP; the document is not about PPP.
Compression is listed as a SLIP deficiency, but the document does not specify any header compression mechanism.
IP packets are the payload being framed; the document does not specify IP itself.
Mentioned only as an example of a second protocol that SLIP cannot share a line with.

RFC1056.title: PCMAIL: A distributed mail system for personal computers
RFC1056.summary: RFC 1056 describes Pcmail, a distributed mail system for workstations and PCs with a central repository and clients, and specifies DMSP, a simple TCP-based request/response protocol (port 158) for mail state manipulation and synchronization.

email.why: The document specifies a mail storage and access architecture (repository, clients, DMSP) for personal computers, comparable to mail access protocols like POP/IMAP. It is a mail system in its own right, not a more specific child tag.
email.quote: Pcmail is a distributed mail system providing mail service to an arbitrary number of users, each of whom owns one or more workstations.

rejected.why: The repository only hands outgoing mail to a local SMTP server. DMSP is described as similar to SMTP in style, but SMTP itself is not specified or extended.
RFC-822 headers are used and descriptors summarize them, but the document does not define message format.
DMSP runs over TCP port 158 as a substrate only; nothing new is defined about TCP.
DMSP response codes are modeled on NNTP and bboards resemble netnews, but the document is not about NNTP or Netnews.
DMSP serves a similar purpose with synchronization of mail state, but IMAP is not discussed. It is a comparison for the reader, not the subject.

gaps.name: Mail client/server synchronization protocol (DMSP, Pcmail)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for mail access or synchronization protocols other than IMAP and POP3, so the email parent is the nearest fit for DMSP.

RFC1057.title: RPC: Remote Procedure Call Protocol specification: Version 2
RFC1057.summary: Specifies version 2 of Sun's ONC RPC message protocol (call/reply formats, authentication flavors including AUTH_UNIX and AUTH_DES, record marking, RPC language) and includes the Port Mapper program protocol in an appendix.

ONC RPC.why: The whole document defines the ONC RPC v2 message protocol, its authentication flavors, record marking, and the RPC language, plus the port mapper.
ONC RPC.quote: This document specifies version two of the message protocol used in Sun's Remote Procedure Call (RPC) package.

rejected.why: TCP is only one transport RPC runs over; the record marking standard is RPC-specific and does not extend TCP.
UDP is a substrate for RPC, not the subject of the document.
DES is used in the AUTH_DES flavor, but the document is not about the cipher itself.
Authentication flavors are a substantial part, but they are specific to RPC and are covered by the ONC RPC tag.
Mentioned only as a way to synchronize clocks for DES authentication.
The message format uses XDR, which is not in the taxonomy as its own tag; it is covered by the ONC RPC tag, which includes XDR.

gaps.name: XDR (External Data Representation) / Port Mapper
gaps.why: The RPC message protocol is specified in XDR and the appendix defines the Port Mapper. The taxonomy covers XDR only inside the ONC RPC tag, so there is no separate tag for either.

RFC1058.title: Routing Information Protocol
RFC1058.summary: RFC 1058 specifies RIP version 1, a UDP-based distance-vector interior gateway protocol, documenting the existing routed-derived protocol and adding stability improvements (split horizon, triggered updates).

RIP.why: The whole document specifies RIP: message formats, timers, input and output processing, and the distance vector algorithms behind it.
RIP.quote: The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) described here is loosely based on the program "routed", distributed with the 4.3 Berkeley Software Distribution.

rejected.why: EGP is mentioned only as the inter-AS protocol that RIP sits alongside. The document does not specify or analyse it.
RIP runs over UDP port 520. UDP is only the substrate here, and the document defines nothing new about UDP.
The document discusses autonomous systems and IGPs only as context. Its subject is the RIP protocol, so the specific RIP tag is more fitting.

RFC1059.title: Network Time Protocol (version 1) specification and implementation
RFC1059.summary: RFC 1059 specifies Network Time Protocol version 1: its architecture, packet format, state variables, event procedures, clock filter and selection algorithms, logical clock design, and experimental evaluation.

NTP.why: The whole document is the formal specification and implementation guidance for NTP version 1, including its packet format, modes, and algorithms.
NTP.quote: This document describes the Network Time Protocol (NTP), including the architectures, algorithms and protocols to synchronize local clocks in a set of distributed clients and servers.

rejected.why: NTP runs over UDP and Appendix A only reproduces the UDP header for completeness. The document says UDP is not part of the NTP specification.
The ICMP Timestamp message is compared with NTP in the related-technology section and in the Appendix C survey. It is not specified or extended here.
This is the parent topic of NTP. NTP is the specific technology tag, so the parent is implied.
Appendices C and D report experimental clock-offset and delay measurements. They serve to evaluate NTP filter algorithms, not to define measurement methods.

RFC1060.title: Assigned numbers
RFC1060.summary: RFC 1060 is the March 1990 Assigned Numbers memo from IANA, listing assigned protocol numbers, ports, multicast addresses, Ethernet types, SNMP enterprise codes, Telnet options, machine/system/terminal names and similar parameter values.

IANA.why: The document is the IANA registry of protocol parameters (protocol numbers, ports, types, options), the core subject of IANA registries.
IANA.quote: documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations

ARPANET.why: Substantial sections cover ARPANET/MILNET logical addresses, link numbers and X.25 address mappings.
ARPANET.quote: The word "link" here refers to a field in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader.

rejected.why: Port numbers are used with TCP, but the document only lists assignments; it does not specify TCP.
Telnet options are listed as a table, but the document is not about Telnet itself.
Ethernet types and vendor address prefixes are listed as registry data, not as IP over Ethernet specification.
It lists SMI enterprise number assignments only, not MIB modules.
Special addresses and protocol numbers are mentioned as registry context; the document does not specify IPv4.

RFC1062.title: Internet numbers
RFC1062.summary: RFC 1062 is the August 1988 status report listing assigned IP network numbers (Class A/B/C), reserved addresses, and EGP autonomous system numbers, with contact handles.

addressing.why: The document is a registry of IP network number assignments, address classes A-E, and special addresses, i.e. IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: documents the currently assigned network numbers and gateway autonomous systems

IPv4.why: Describes the IPv4 classful address format, dotted decimal notation, loopback and all-ones special addresses.
IPv4.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

EGP.why: Contains the registry of 16-bit autonomous system numbers used with EGP, a substantial part of the document.
EGP.quote: The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) [33,35] specifies that groups of gateways may form autonomous systems.

rejected.why: This is a number registry, but it is a historical list of assignments rather than IANA registry guidance or stewardship.
ARPANET appears as one entry among thousands of networks; the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
Class D multicast is mentioned only briefly as an address class.
NIC WHOIS is mentioned only as a way to look up contact handles.

gaps.name: Assigned numbers / network and AS number registry
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for protocol-number or AS-number registries, so the AS number list is only partly covered by EGP.

RFC1063.title: IP MTU discovery options
RFC1063.summary: RFC 1063 proposes two experimental IP options, Probe MTU and Reply MTU, that let hosts learn the minimum MTU along a path. It also covers implementation approaches and a sample implementation sketch.

PMTUD.why: The whole document defines a mechanism for discovering the path MTU, so it belongs on the Path MTU Discovery page.
PMTUD.quote: we propose two new IP options that, when used in conjunction will permit two peers to determine the MINMTU of the paths between them.

rejected.why: The options are IPv4 header options, but the document is about MTU discovery. IPv4 itself is only the substrate.
The document discusses how the TCP MSS option relates to MINMTU. That is a comparison, not a TCP extension.
ICMP Time Exceeded (fragmentation reassembly timeout) is mentioned only as a trigger for sending a probe.

RFC1064.title: Interactive Mail Access Protocol: Version 2
RFC1064.summary: RFC 1064 specifies IMAP2, a tagged command/response protocol letting workstation clients access and manage mail stored on a mailbox server, including server-side envelope parsing and searching.

IMAP.why: The document is the specification of IMAP version 2, defining its commands, responses, flags, envelope structure, and syntax.
IMAP.quote: The intent of the Interactive Mail Access Protocol, Version 2 (IMAP2) is to allow a workstation or similar small machine to access electronic mail from a mailbox server.

rejected.why: POP2 (RFC 937) is only used as a comparison model; the document does not specify POP3.
SMTP is mentioned only as the separate mail transfer protocol used for posting; IMAP2 covers access only.
RFC 822 headers are parsed into an envelope structure, but the document does not define the message format itself.
TCP is only the reliable stream substrate (port 143).
The formal syntax uses BNF notation, but the document is not about the notation.

RFC1065.title: Structure and identification of management information for TCP/IP-based internets
RFC1065.summary: RFC 1065 defines the Structure of Management Information (SMI) for TCP/IP internets: the OBJECT IDENTIFIER naming tree, permitted ASN.1 syntax, defined types (Counter, Gauge, etc.), and the OBJECT-TYPE macro for defining MIB objects.

MIB.why: The SMI is the foundation for defining MIB modules: it specifies object naming, syntax, the OBJECT-TYPE macro and rules for extending the MIB. Readers of the MIB/SMI subject would expect it.
MIB.quote: This memo describes the common structures and identification scheme for the definition of management information used in managing TCP/IP-based internets.

ASN.1.why: The memo profiles ASN.1: it restricts permitted constructs, defines application-wide types and a macro, and specifies the ASN.1 module RFC1065-SMI plus use of the basic encoding rules.
ASN.1.quote: Only the ASN.1 primitive types INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and NULL are permitted.

rejected.why: SNMP is only a companion protocol (RFC 1067) that the memo explicitly says it does not specify; it is not the subject here.
The parent topic is implied by the MIB tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC1066.title: Management Information Base for network management of TCP/IP-based internets
RFC1066.summary: Defines the initial MIB (RFC1066-MIB) of managed objects for TCP/IP network management: System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP and EGP groups, written in ASN.1 using the SMI.

MIB.why: The document is the first MIB module, defining managed object groups and their ASN.1 definitions for use with SNMP and related management protocols.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the list of managed objects.

rejected.why: SNMP is specified in a companion memo (RFC 1067); this document only defines the objects it manages, so MIB is the more specific fit.
Only ICMP counters are defined; the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
TCP group objects are instrumentation counters and state tables, not a specification of TCP.
EGP group objects are management counters for EGP, which the document does not specify or analyse.
ASN.1 is the notation used to write the definitions, a substrate rather than the subject.
MIB, a child tag, is more specific and already covers it.

RFC1067.title: Simple Network Management Protocol
