RFC1067.summary: RFC 1067 specifies SNMP version 1, the protocol (PDUs, community-based access policies, traps, instance naming) by which management information of network elements is inspected or altered, running over UDP.

SNMP.why: The document is the specification of the SNMP protocol itself: architecture, community/access policy, PDUs, error handling and traps.
SNMP.quote: This memo defines a simple protocol by which management information for a network element may be inspected or altered by logically remote users.

rejected.why: The MIB and SMI are defined in companion memos (RFC 1065/1066); this document only defines how instances are named and referenced, not MIB modules.
ASN.1 and BER are the encoding substrate used for messages, not the subject.
UDP is only the transport used; no new usage guidance beyond port assignments.
Community-string authentication is part of SNMP architecture, not a separate subject; the document defines only a trivial scheme and leaves the rest open.

RFC1068.title: Background File Transfer Program (BFTP)
RFC1068.summary: Describes BFTP, a background (asynchronous) file transfer service that queues requests and uses FTP third-party (server-to-server) transfers with retries and mail notification, plus its user interface and implementation experience.

FTP.why: The whole service is built on FTP's server-server transfer model, and the document discusses FTP commands, server quirks and interoperability problems encountered. Readers of FTP would want it.
FTP.quote: The BFTP makes use of the "third party" or "Server-Server" model incorporated in the Internet File Transfer Protocol [RFC-959].

rejected.why: Telnet is only used as the access method to the BFTP service on port 152; the document does not specify or extend Telnet.
Mail is only the channel for completion notifications; the document is not about email.
TCP is only mentioned as an analogy for retry and exponential backoff, and as the substrate.

gaps.name: Background (asynchronous) file transfer service
gaps.why: The document's main subject is a queued, retrying background file-transfer service built on FTP, and the taxonomy has no tag for this kind of application service beyond FTP.

RFC1069.title: Guidelines for the use of Internet-IP addresses in the ISO Connectionless-Mode Network Protocol
RFC1069.summary: RFC 1069 proposes an NSAP address format (AFI 47, ICD 0006, routing domain, IGP-specific part) for using ISO CLNP datagrams in the Internet, including embedding IP and ANSI-format addresses and migration toward future inter-domain routing.

CLNP.why: The whole document defines how CLNP source and destination NSAP addresses are structured for Internet use, so it belongs on the CLNP page.
CLNP.quote: This RFC suggests an addressing scheme for use with the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) in the Internet.

rejected.why: The document is about addressing, but only for CLNP NSAP addresses. The CLNP tag is more specific, and the generic IP address architecture parent is not the subject.
This is the parent of CLNP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Section 6 discusses migration to future inter-domain routing and routing domains. That discussion exists to justify the address design, and the document does not specify any routing protocol.
Section 4 embeds four-octet IP addresses in the IGP-specific part, but the document does not specify or extend IPv4.
EGP is mentioned only as a possible initial inter-domain protocol that would need a new version. The document does not address it.

RFC1070.title: Use of the Internet as a subnetwork for experimentation with the OSI network layer
RFC1070.summary: RFC 1070 proposes EON, an experimental OSI internet that encapsulates OSI CLNP/ES-IS/IS-IS PDUs in IP datagrams (or UDP in EON-UDP), with an NSAP address format, multicast simulation via an SNAcP sublayer, and IANA-maintained core system lists.

CLNP.why: The document specifies how ISO 8473 CLNP and related OSI network-layer PDUs are carried over the Internet, including NSAP address format and multicast simulation.
CLNP.quote: We do this by encapsulating OSI connectionless network layer protocol (ISO 8473) packets in IP datagrams

OSI.why: The wider subject is OSI network-layer coexistence with IP, including ES-IS and IS-IS routing exchange over the IP subnet. CLNP is the specific child, so OSI is added as a secondary tag for the ES-IS and IS-IS coverage.
OSI.quote: This RFC proposes a scenario for experimentation with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) network layer protocols over the Internet

tunneling.why: The core mechanism is encapsulating OSI PDUs in IP (protocol 80) or UDP (port 147), which is generic tunnelling.
tunneling.quote: The entire OSI network layer PDU, whether it be an ISO 8473 PDU, an ISO DP 9542 PDU, or an IS-IS PDU, will be placed in the data portion of an IP datagrams

rejected.why: UDP is used only as an alternative substrate (EON-UDP). The document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
IP is the subnetwork the OSI packets run over. The document does not specify IP.
ICMP error handling is only a small suggested-actions table for the SNAcP.
IS-IS is referenced as a carried protocol, but the document does not specify it.
The NSAP address format is OSI addressing embedding IPv4 addresses. That is part of the OSI encapsulation scheme and not the IP address architecture.

RFC1071.title: Computing the Internet checksum
RFC1071.summary: Informational memo describing techniques and example implementations for efficiently computing the Internet (1's complement) checksum used by IP, UDP and TCP, with Plummer's IEN-45 checksum design analysis as an appendix.

checksum.why: The whole document is about the Internet checksum algorithm, its mathematical properties, incremental update, and implementations, which is exactly the checksum subject page.
checksum.quote: This memo discusses methods for efficiently computing the Internet checksum that is used by the standard Internet protocols IP, UDP, and TCP.

rejected.why: TCP is only a consumer of the checksum; the memo does not specify or extend TCP, though IEN-45 is framed around the TCP checksum.
IEN-45 briefly compares CRCs with the Internet checksum, but CRC is not a substantial subject of the document.
UDP is only mentioned as a protocol using the checksum.
IP header TTL update is cited as an incremental-update example only; the memo is not about IP.

RFC1072.title: TCP extensions for long-delay paths
RFC1072.summary: RFC 1072 proposes TCP options (Window Scale, SACK-permitted and SACK, Echo and Echo Reply) to make TCP efficient over long-delay, high bandwidth-delay-product paths.

TCP.why: The whole document defines new TCP options (window scaling, selective acknowledgment, echo-based RTT timing) and how a TCP should implement them.
TCP.quote: This RFC proposes a set of TCP extensions for this purpose.

rejected.why: The RTT measurement discussion touches congestion collapse, but the document's subject is TCP options for LFN performance, not congestion control algorithms.
Cited only as an example of a protocol using selective acknowledgments.
Cited only as prior evidence for selective acknowledgments.
Satellite channels are given as an example of long fat networks, not the document's subject.

RFC1073.title: Telnet window size option
RFC1073.summary: RFC 1073 defines the Telnet NAWS (Negotiate About Window Size) option, letting a Telnet client tell the server its window width and height in characters.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option (NAWS, code 31), including its negotiation commands and subnegotiation syntax.
Telnet.quote: This memo specifies an option to send the window height and width in characters from a client to a server.

rejected.why: X is mentioned only as an example of a windowing environment in which a Telnet client might run. The document does not specify or extend the X protocol.
This is the parent topic. The specific Telnet tag fits better, so the parent is implied.
Telnet runs over TCP, but the document is not about TCP. It only uses it as the substrate.

RFC1074.title: NSFNET backbone SPF based Interior Gateway Protocol
RFC1074.summary: Describes how the NSFNET backbone adapts the ANSI IS-IS and ISO ES-IS protocols as its interior gateway protocol, carrying PDUs over IP (protocol 85), encoding IP addresses in NSAPs, and interworking with EGP under policy-based routing.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies how the IS-IS link-state protocol is adapted and implemented in the NSFNET backbone: Level 2 only, point-to-point links, IP address encapsulation in NSAPs, and timers.
IS-IS.quote: This ANSI IS-IS protocol is used as the interior gateway protocol (IGP) of the NSFNET backbone.

EGP.why: A substantial part describes how EGP-learned routes and administrative domains are mapped into IS-IS PDUs and passed back to EGP peers under policy.
EGP.quote: The reachability information obtained from regional networks via EGP is distributed within the backbone by End System PDUs.
EGP.section: 4. How the ANSI IS-IS protocol is adapted for the NSFNET backbone routing

rejected.why: The OSI network-layer protocols (ES-IS, NSAP addressing) are used, but the document is about IS-IS as an IGP running over IP; IS-IS is the more specific fit.
CLNP is only referenced via the ES-IS reference title. The PDUs are carried over IP, not CLNP.
Backbone routing architecture is mentioned, but the document is a protocol implementation description, so the IS-IS tag covers it.

gaps.name: ES-IS (End System to Intermediate System) routing exchange protocol
gaps.why: The document specifies its use (hello interval, hold time, NET construction), but the taxonomy has no ES-IS tag.

gaps.name: NSFNET backbone / policy based routing
gaps.why: The document is largely about NSFNET backbone routing and its Policy Based Routing Database. The taxonomy has no tag for this historic network or for policy routing.

RFC1075.title: Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol
RFC1075.summary: Specifies DVMRP, an experimental RIP-derived distance-vector interior routing protocol for IP multicast datagrams using Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting, carried in IGMP messages, with tunnels for traversing non-multicast gateways.

multicast.why: DVMRP is a multicast routing protocol with no dedicated child tag in the taxonomy; the document specifies multicast routing, forwarding (TRPB), pruning, and group membership tracking.
multicast.quote: This RFC describes a distance-vector-style routing protocol for routing multicast datagrams through an internet.

IGMP.why: DVMRP messages are defined as IGMP type 3 messages, and the document describes IGMP membership queries and report handling for local group membership (section 5.4).
IGMP.quote: DVMRP uses the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) to exchange routing datagrams [2].

rejected.why: DVMRP is derived from RIP but is a separate protocol; RIP is only the starting point and is not specified or extended here.
Tunnels via LSRR weak encapsulation are a section of the document, but they are a mechanism within DVMRP rather than a generic tunnelling specification.
The document is about a specific protocol, not routing architecture in general.
IP options and addressing are used as substrate; the document is not about IPv4 itself.

gaps.name: DVMRP (Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DVMRP tag under multicast; the document is the DVMRP specification and its readers would expect a dedicated entry.

RFC1076.title: HEMS monitoring and control language
RFC1076.summary: RFC 1076 specifies the HEMS query language, a stack-based ASN.1-encoded language for monitoring and controlling network entities via a hierarchical data tree, with operators like GET, SET, BEGIN, and filters.

HEMS.why: The document is the HEMS query language specification, the core of the High-Level Entity Monitoring System.
HEMS.quote: This RFC specifies the design of a general-purpose, yet efficient, monitoring and control language for managing network entities.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the encoding used for queries and responses, but the document defines a query language rather than ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
The filter design is derived from CMIP, but the document does not specify or analyse CMIP.
It is a competing management protocol and is not discussed in the document.
The tag HEMS already sits under network management, so the parent is implied.

RFC1077.title: Critical issues in high bandwidth networking
RFC1077.summary: Report of the Gigabit Working Group recommending research on gigabit-speed networking: architecture, high-speed switching, host interfaces, network management algorithms, and network services such as directories.

internet architecture.why: The core of the document is rethinking internetwork architecture (layering, switch technologies, administrative domains, management-first design) for gigabit speeds.
internet architecture.quote: The central thrust of new research must thus be to explore new network architectures that are consistent with these very different speed assumptions.

network management.why: Substantial sections cover network management, accounting, decentralized management and resource management algorithms for the gigabit network.
network management.quote: The GN management system should be expected to provide proactive problem and resource management capabilities.

QoS.why: Bandwidth reservation, service classes, priority and preemption, and latency control are discussed as research needs.
QoS.quote: In order to support multiple types of service, two things must happen, both a change from current practice.

X.500.why: Directory services based on and extending X.500 are discussed in their own sections (2.4 and 3.5.2).
X.500.quote: One approach toward implementing a distributed network directory would be to base it upon the CCITT X.500/ISO DIS 9594 standard.

rejected.why: Multicast is discussed in one subsection as a switching capability, but is not a main focus of the document.
TCP and TP4 are criticized as examples of protocols poorly suited to hardware, but are not the subject.
Security requirements are a short section (2.6) among many; not a substantial focus.
Flow control is a brief subsection, with no specific mechanism specified.
Naming and addressing strategies is one subsection of research issues, not the document's focus.

gaps.name: High-speed / gigabit networking research
gaps.why: The document is a research agenda for gigabit networks (switching, host interfaces, optical networks), which the taxonomy has no specific tag for.

RFC1078.title: TCP port service Multiplexer (TCPMUX)
RFC1078.summary: RFC 1078 defines TCPMUX, a protocol that lets multiple services be reached through TCP port 1 by sending a service name, so new services need no dedicated well-known port.

TCP.why: The document specifies a TCP-level service multiplexer on port 1 and addresses TCP port usage and service contact. TCP is the only fitting tag; there is no narrower child for port multiplexing.
TCP.quote: This RFC defines a protocol to contact multiple services on a single well-known TCP port using a service name instead of a well-known number.

rejected.why: TCPMUX is not one of the Echo/Discard/Chargen/QOTD/Daytime/Active Users services, though it is a similar simple port-based service.
Clients name a known service on a known port; the document does not describe discovering services on a network. The HELP name only lists supported services.
The document discusses well-known port assignments and reserved names only as background for the multiplexer, not as registry guidance.

RFC1079.title: Telnet terminal speed option
RFC1079.summary: Specifies the Telnet TERMINAL-SPEED option (code 32), letting Telnet hosts negotiate and exchange a terminal's transmit and receive bit rates via subnegotiation.

Telnet.why: The document defines a new Telnet option, including its negotiation commands and subnegotiation format, so it belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: The purpose of this option is to provide similar information for telnet connections.

rejected.why: The speed string is encoded as NVT ASCII, but that is only the encoding used. The document is not about ASCII.

RFC1080.title: Telnet remote flow control option
RFC1080.summary: RFC 1080 defines the Telnet TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL option (code 33), letting a host remotely enable or disable flow control in the user Telnet process attached to a terminal.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its command code, WILL/WONT/DO/DONT meanings, and subnegotiation. Readers of Telnet options would expect to find it.
Telnet.quote: This memo describes a method of remotely toggling flow control between a user telnet process and the attached terminal.

rejected.why: Telnet runs over TCP, but the document does not specify or extend TCP. It is only the substrate.
The document mentions XON/XOFF control characters and ASCII, but only as background. It is not about the character set.

RFC1081.title: Post Office Protocol: Version 3
RFC1081.summary: RFC 1081 specifies POP3, a simple protocol letting workstations retrieve mail from a maildrop on a server host, with its states, commands, and the split-UA model.

POP3.why: The whole document specifies POP3: its AUTHORIZATION, TRANSACTION and UPDATE states, its commands (USER, PASS, STAT, LIST, RETR, DELE, TOP, RPOP) and its responses.
POP3.quote: The Post Office Protocol - Version 3 (POP3) is intended to permit a workstation to dynamically access a maildrop on a server host

rejected.why: SMTP is only mentioned as the way a client posts mail. The memo says it does not specify how mail is entered into the transport system.
The memo only says that messages conform to RFC 822. It defines nothing about message format.
POP3 is the more specific tag, and the parent tag is implied by it.
TCP is only the transport, used on port 110, and the memo adds nothing new about TCP.

RFC1082.title: Post Office Protocol: Version 3: Extended service offerings
RFC1082.summary: RFC 1082 defines optional POP3 extensions (the XTND command with BBOARDS, ARCHIVE and X-BBOARDS) that let clients access discussion group mail kept in shared spool maildrops on a mailbox server.

POP3.why: The document extends POP3 with the XTND command and its subcommands, so it is about POP3.
POP3.quote: All the new facilities are introduced via a single POP3 command, XTND.

mailing lists.why: A substantial part of the document covers discussion group (mailing list) structure, exploders, request addresses and moderators, and access to their mail.
mailing lists.quote: This additional service permits a client host to access discussion group mail, which is often kept in a separate spool area

rejected.why: Implied as an ancestor of POP3; not chosen separately.
RFC 822 syntax is only used to describe parameter syntax; the document does not address message format.
BBoards resemble news, but the document is about mail-based discussion groups accessed via POP3, not Netnews distribution.
Mail transport is not specified or extended; the document only mentions delivery to the group maildrop.

RFC1083.title: IAB official protocol standards
RFC1083.summary: Quarterly IAB memo (December 1988) describing the Internet standards process, the RFC series, the state/status terminology, and listing protocols by standardization state with their governing RFCs.

IETF process.why: The memo's main purpose is describing how protocols advance through proposed, draft standard, and standard states, plus required/recommended/elective status, and the IAB's role in the process.
IETF process.quote: Protocols that are intended to become standards are first designated as "proposed" protocols.

RFC series.why: A whole section explains the RFC series, submission, review, and that RFCs are never reissued, and the memo serves as the reference for the current RFC for each protocol.
RFC series.quote: The documents called Request for Comments (or RFCs) are the working notes of the Internet research and development community.

rejected.why: The definitions of states and statuses are part of the standards process description, not a glossary as such; covered by IETF process.
IANA is only mentioned as a contact and as manager of the standards list, and Assigned Numbers is only referenced.
It is a snapshot of status in 1988, not a retrospective or history.
DNS and the many other protocols appear only as rows in the status lists and are not specified or analysed.
Protocols from the ARPANET era are only listed in tables, not addressed in their own right.
TCP and the other listed protocols are only table entries with their status.

RFC1084.title: BOOTP vendor information extensions
RFC1084.summary: Defines a vendor-independent set of tagged option fields (subnet mask, gateways, servers, hostname, boot file size) for the 64-octet vendor information area of BOOTP packets, obsoleting RFC 1048.

DHCP.why: BOOTP vendor extensions are the direct precursor of DHCP options. The taxonomy has no BOOTP tag, and DHCP is the closest fit for host configuration via BOOTP/DHCP option fields.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a (potentially) vendor-independent interpretation of this resource information.

rejected.why: The Domain Name Server option only carries server addresses. The document does not specify DNS itself.
BOOTP runs over UDP, which is only the substrate here.
The comparison section discusses multicast as an alternative to BOOTP, but the document is not about multicast.
The document compares ways of locating servers, but its main subject is the BOOTP option encoding.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: The document extends BOOTP, but the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag. DHCP is the nearest fit.

RFC1085.title: ISO presentation services on top of TCP/IP based internets
RFC1085.summary: RFC 1085 specifies a minimal "streamlined" emulation of the ISO presentation service (P-CONNECT, P-RELEASE, P-DATA, aborts) by serializing ASN.1 PDUs directly over TCP or UDP, for OSI applications using only ACSE and ROSE (e.g., CMIP) in TCP/IP internets.

OSI.why: The document specifies an OSI presentation service substitute carrying OSI application layer entities (ACSE/ROSE) over TCP/UDP, i.e., OSI coexistence with IP.
OSI.quote: This memo describes an approach for providing "stream-lined" support of OSI application services on top of TCP/IP-based internets for such constrained environments.

transport mapping.why: It defines how presentation PDUs are mapped to TCP streams or single UDP datagrams, selected via a transport-mapping QoS element.
transport mapping.quote: If the value is "tcp-based", then the presentation provider will use TCP as the underlying transport service.

CMIP.why: CMIP running over TCP/IP was the motivating use case, and the design is tailored to the ACSE/ROSE elements CMIP uses.
CMIP.quote: The motivation for this memo was initially derived from a requirement to run the ISO Common Management Information Protocol (CMIP) in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate carrying serialized ASN.1 PDUs; the memo does not extend or specify TCP.
UDP is used as an alternative low-quality substrate, not specified or extended.
ASN.1 and BER are used for the PDUs and appendix syntax, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
DNS is only mentioned briefly for resolving service names in the minimal directory element.
A minimal Directory Service Element is assumed in one section only, not a substantial subject of the memo.

gaps.name: OSI presentation/session/application layer services (ACSE, ROSE)
gaps.why: The document is about ISO presentation service emulation and OSI application service elements; the taxonomy only has OSI network-layer tags, so this is only approximated by the OSI tag.

RFC1086.title: ISO-TP0 bridge between TCP and X.25
RFC1086.summary: RFC 1086 specifies a registration protocol on TCP port 146 that lets a bridge host relay ISO TP0 transport packets between TCP/IP hosts (RFC 1006) and X.25 hosts (ISO 8878).

X.25.why: The bridge connects TCP hosts to X.25 networks, defining X.121 address encoding and call setup toward X.25 hosts. The document is about interworking IP with X.25 public data networks.
X.25.quote: This memo specifies a protocol that is used to bridge ISO TP0 packets between X.25 and TCP networks.

OSI.why: The document concerns ISO TP0 transport (class 0) and OSI/DDN interoperability, so readers of OSI coexistence with IP would want it.
OSI.quote: if one is running higher-layer ISO protocols in both networks (namely ISO TP0), then a TP0 bridge can be used to achieve connectivity.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate carrying TP0 via RFC 1006. The memo defines a bridge registration protocol on port 146 and does not specify or extend TCP.

Considered as a fit, since TP0 is carried over TCP and X.25. However, the memo mainly defines a bridge and registration protocol between two existing mappings, so the more specific tags are preferred.
IP addresses appear only as a field in the address encoding, not as a subject of the document.
The memo uses TP0 over X.25 and does not involve the connectionless network protocol.

gaps.name: ISO TP0 transport class 0 bridging
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OSI transport protocol (TP0/RFC 1006) or transport gateways. OSI is the closest fit but is described as network-layer protocols.

RFC1087.title: Ethics and the Internet
RFC1087.summary: IAB policy statement declaring unethical and unacceptable any use of the Internet that gains unauthorized access, disrupts use, wastes resources, destroys information integrity, or compromises user privacy.

internet governance.why: The document is an IAB policy statement on acceptable and ethical use of the Internet. That is governance of how the Internet is administered, and no more specific child tag fits (it is not IETF process, IPR, IANA or RFC series).
internet governance.quote: This memo is a statement of policy by the Internet Activities Board (IAB) concerning the proper use of the resources of the Internet.

security.why: It addresses abuse, unauthorized access, disruption and the resilience of the Internet. This is general security guidance and is not tied to any one mechanism.
security.quote: The IAB plans to take whatever actions it can, in concert with Federal agencies and other interested parties, to identify and to set up technical and procedural mechanisms

rejected.why: The memo gives no operational practices for securing infrastructure. It is a high-level ethics statement.
Compromising user privacy is listed as one unethical activity, but the document does not treat protocol privacy considerations.
It is a policy statement and not a retrospective, even though it comes from the early Internet.

gaps.name: Internet ethics and acceptable use policy
gaps.why: The document is about ethical and acceptable use of Internet resources. The taxonomy has no tag for acceptable use or ethics, so the closest fit is internet governance.

RFC1088.title: Standard for the transmission of IP datagrams over NetBIOS networks
RFC1088.summary: Specifies how to encapsulate IP datagrams in NetBIOS datagrams, including NetBIOS name mapping from IP addresses (IP.XX.XX.XX.XX), broadcast via group name, a 512-byte MTU, and host initialization steps.

NetBIOS.why: The whole document defines how IP runs over NetBIOS datagram services, including name mapping, broadcast group name, MTU and the NetBIOS calls a host must make.
NetBIOS.quote: IP.XX.XX.XX.XX is the NetBIOS name for any IP over NetBIOS host where XX represents the ascii hexadecimal representation of that byte of the internet address.

rejected.why: IP is the payload being encapsulated; the document specifies a link-style mapping, not IP itself.
Mentioned only to say no address resolution mechanism is needed because names are derived from IP addresses.
Mentioned only in passing regarding optional adapter status queries.
802.3 is mentioned only as an example of a data-link protocol used by a router, and RFC 1042 is merely referenced.
The document explicitly says IP multicast is not supported; it only maps broadcast to a group name.
This is encapsulation of IP over a NetBIOS network layer, which is better covered by the NetBIOS tag than by generic IP tunnelling.

RFC1089.title: SNMP over Ethernet
RFC1089.summary: Experimental spec for carrying SNMP messages directly in Ethernet frames using a newly assigned Ethernet Type (0x814C), for LAN devices lacking UDP/IP.

SNMP.why: The document defines a new way to carry SNMP messages (a new transport mapping), so SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) as specified in [1] can be used over Ethernet MAC layer framing [2] instead of the Internet UDP/IP protocol stack

Ethernet.why: It specifies Ethernet framing for SNMP, including an Ethernet Type value, so it is about Ethernet encapsulation and management of LAN devices.
Ethernet.quote: assignment (by XEROX) of 33100 (hexadecimal 814C) to the Ethernet Type field for SNMP. The data portion of the Ethernet frame would then be a standard SNMP message

rejected.why: UDP/IP is the stack SNMP is explicitly moved away from, not the subject.

Considered because it carries SNMP over a different lower layer, but SNMP is the more specific tag already chosen under which this fits, and the transport mapping topic is generic. Tagging only the specific technologies is sufficient.
No MIB modules or SMI are defined or discussed.

RFC1090.title: SMTP on X.25
RFC1090.summary: RFC 1090 specifies how to carry SMTP sessions directly over X.25 virtual circuits, covering call user data, packet streaming, resets, character code, closing and timeouts.

SMTP.why: The document defines how SMTP sessions operate over X.25, including session closing and timeout behaviour specific to SMTP, so it belongs on the SMTP page.
SMTP.quote: This memo proposes a standard for SMTP on the virtual circuit facility provided by the X.25 standard of the CCITT.

X.25.why: The document is a binding of SMTP to X.25 virtual circuits (call user data, Q bit, resets, facilities), so readers of X.25 and IP over public data networks would want it.
X.25.quote: An X.25 virtual circuit (VC) is opened for each SMTP session.  The full duplex channel provided by the VC is used for the session.

rejected.why: This topic fits a carry-X-over-Y binding, but the specific technology tags (SMTP, X.25) already cover the subject, so the topic is not given directly.
The parent of SMTP, implied by the SMTP tag.
The document only states that ASCII-8 is the character code on the circuit. This is a minor detail and not the subject of the document.
TCP is mentioned only as the transport that X.25 replaces for SMTP. The document does not specify or analyse it.

RFC1091.title: Telnet terminal-type option
RFC1091.summary: RFC 1091 specifies the Telnet TERMINAL-TYPE option, letting a Telnet client present a list of terminal emulation types to a server via SEND/IS subnegotiation, and obsoletes RFC 930 by permitting cycling through the list.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option (code 24) with its negotiation commands and subnegotiation, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: Willingness to exchange terminal-type information is agreed upon via conventional Telnet option negotiation.

rejected.why: IBM-3278-2 appears as an example terminal type, and the idea came from the tn3270 mailing list, but the document specifies a general Telnet option, not TN3270 emulation.
Terminal type strings are NVT ASCII, but this is just the encoding used, not a subject of the document.
The document points to Assigned Numbers for terminal type names, but that is incidental and not the document's subject.

RFC1092.title: EGP and policy based routing in the new NSFNET backbone
RFC1092.summary: Describes how the NSFNET backbone will use EGP to exchange reachability with regional networks, supplemented by a rudimentary policy-based routing scheme (bilateral agreements, a Routing Policy Data Base, fixed metrics) to handle EGP's shortcomings in a meshed topology.

EGP.why: The document specifies how EGP is used and extended with metric conventions, NR record handling and validation between the NSFNET backbone and regional networks, and analyses EGP's problems.
EGP.quote: The EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) routing method will be used to exchange reachability information between the NSFNET backbone and the regional networks.

routing architecture.why: A substantial part of the document covers policy-based routing design, including primary and secondary regional representatives, a policy database and backbone-versus-backdoor preference. This is routing architecture and policy rather than EGP mechanics alone.
routing architecture.quote: some kind of a rudimentary Policy Based Routing method becomes imperative.

rejected.why: IS-IS is only mentioned as the backbone's interior protocol that carries the learned information. The document does not specify or extend it.
The Routing Policy Data Base is an ad hoc operational database. It is not a policy specification language or an Internet routing registry.
BGP is not mentioned. EGP is described as an interim measure until better inter-AS protocols are deployed.

gaps.name: Policy-based routing / NSFNET
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for inter-domain routing policy as a subject, or for NSFNET history. Only routing architecture comes close.

RFC1093.title: NSFNET routing architecture
RFC1093.summary: Describes the NSFNET backbone routing architecture, using an IS-IS-derived IGP internally and EGP with policy filtering, metric reconstitution and AS-based controls at the interface to regional and peer networks.

EGP.why: The document specifies how EGP is used at the backbone/regional interface, gives EGP requirements for attached gateways, and includes gated EGP extensions in its appendix.
EGP.quote: The routing interface between the NSFNET core and regional backbones as well as peer networks utilizes the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP).

routing architecture.why: It is an architecture document covering routing policy, AS numbering, metric reconstitution, default routes and loop prevention across backbone, regional and peer networks.
routing architecture.quote: This document describes the routing architecture for the NSFNET centered around the new NSFNET Backbone

IS-IS.why: The backbone's internal routing protocol is an IS-IS adaptation, described here as part of the architecture. It gets only brief treatment, so the tag is secondary.
IS-IS.quote: The NSFNET core uses a SPF based internal routing protocol, adapted from the IS-IS protocol submitted by ANSI for standardization to the ISO.

rejected.why: RIP appears only in the gated.conf example and the metric conversion table, not as a subject of the document.
The document hopes for a future inter-AS protocol to replace EGP but does not specify BGP.
The ARPANET is mentioned as a peer network whose routes are handled by policy. The document is about NSFNET routing, not the ARPANET.
Proxy-ARP is mentioned in passing as a workaround for subnetting, which is not enough to tag ARP.

gaps.name: NSFNET
gaps.why: The document is about the NSFNET backbone's routing architecture and regional attachments. The taxonomy has no tag for NSFNET or for the history of the research and education backbone.

RFC1094.title: NFS: Network File System Protocol specification
RFC1094.summary: Specifies version 2 of Sun's NFS protocol for transparent remote file access over RPC/XDR, plus the companion mount protocol in an appendix.

NFS.why: The whole document defines NFS version 2 procedures, data types, and implementation issues, and the mount protocol that supports it.
NFS.quote: The Sun Network Filesystem (NFS) protocol provides transparent remote access to shared files across networks.

rejected.why: NFS is built on Sun RPC and XDR, but RFC 1094 only uses them as substrate; RPC itself is specified in RFC 1057 and XDR in RFC 1014.
UDP is the normal transport for NFS here, but the document does not specify UDP.
Parent of NFS; it is implied by the NFS tag.

RFC1095.title: Common Management Information Services and Protocol over TCP/IP (CMOT)
RFC1095.summary: RFC 1095 specifies CMOT, which carries ISO CMIS/CMIP network management (with ACSE and ROSE) over TCP/UDP using a lightweight presentation protocol, and maps the Internet SMI/MIB onto CMIP.
review: CMIP: quote not found in the text

notes: CMIP: quote not found in the text

RFC1096.title: Telnet X display location option
RFC1096.summary: Specifies a Telnet option (code 35, X-DISPLAY-LOCATION) that lets a Telnet client send its X display location string to the remote host via sub-negotiation.

Telnet.why: The document defines a new Telnet option with its command code, negotiation rules and sub-negotiation format, so readers of the Telnet subject need it.
Telnet.quote: Sender is willing to send the X display location in a subsequent sub-negotiation.

rejected.why: The X display location is only the data carried by the option. The document does not specify or extend the X protocol, so it is not about X itself.
The display string is NVT ASCII, but that is only an encoding detail.

RFC1097.title: Telnet subliminal-message option
RFC1097.summary: An April 1st joke RFC defining a Telnet option (SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE) that lets a server make a client flash subliminal messages at users to persuade them to upgrade.

humor.why: Dated 1 April and parodies a Telnet option, with subliminal messages like "Use VMS" and caps-lock LED morse code. It belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: These users need to be gently "persuaded".

Telnet.why: It defines a new Telnet option, with its WILL/WONT/DO/DONT meanings, subnegotiation syntax and defaults. Readers of Telnet options would look for it.
Telnet.quote: IAC WILL SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE

RFC1098.title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC1098.summary: RFC 1098 specifies the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) version 1: its architecture, community-based administrative model, PDUs (Get, GetNext, Set, Response, Trap), instance naming and ASN.1 definitions, re-releasing RFC 1067 with a changed status section.

SNMP.why: The document is the SNMP protocol specification itself, covering architecture, community/access policies, PDU procedures and traps.
SNMP.quote: This memo defines a simple protocol by which management information for a network element may be inspected or altered by logically remote users.

rejected.why: The MIB and SMI are defined in companion memos (RFC 1065/1066). This document only defines how instances are named and referenced in SNMP operations.
ASN.1 and BER are the encoding substrate for the PDUs. The document uses them but does not define or profile them.
UDP is only the transport on ports 161 and 162, and this document does not define anything new about UDP.
CMOT is mentioned only in the status section as the other IAB-designated protocol, and is not the subject of this document.
This is the parent of SNMP, which is already tagged and implies it.

RFC1099.title: Request for Comments Summary: RFC Numbers 1000-1099
RFC1099.summary: An annotated catalogue of RFCs 1000 through 1099, giving each RFC's author, date, title and a short status or abstract paragraph.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a bibliographic summary of a block of RFCs. It is a publication index within the RFC series, so readers browsing the RFC series would want it.
RFC series.quote: This memo is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1000 through RFCs 1099.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: It lists RFCs from a period, but it is a series index and status report, not a history or retrospective of the Internet.
SNMP RFCs (1067, 1098) are only summarized as entries in the list. The document does not specify or discuss SNMP itself.
RFCs 1031-1035 appear as list entries only. The document does not address DNS itself.
Several Telnet option RFCs are listed, but only as one-paragraph entries in the catalogue.
Assigned Numbers and Internet Numbers RFCs are listed as entries only. The document does not address IANA registries.
RFC 1005 (AHIP-E) is a single entry, so ARPANET is not a subject of the document.

RFC1100.title: IAB official protocol standards
RFC1100.summary: RFC 1100 is the IAB's quarterly memo describing the Internet standards process, the RFC series, the standardization states and statuses, and listing protocols by state (standard, draft, proposed, experimental, historic).

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards procedures, states (proposed, draft, standard, historic) and statuses (required, recommended, elective) and applies them to protocols.
IETF process.quote: This memo describes the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as determined by the Internet Activities Board (IAB).

RFC series.why: A full section describes the RFC series, how to submit, review, and obtain RFCs, and that RFCs are never revised.
RFC series.quote: The documents called Request for Comments (or RFCs) are the working notes of the Internet research and development community.

rejected.why: TCP, IP, DNS, FTP, SMTP and others are only entries in the status tables; the document does not specify or analyse them.
IANA is mentioned as a contact and for Assigned Numbers, but the document is not about registries.
Listed as a draft standard with CMOT; only a table entry plus a short note, not the subject.
It is a status snapshot of 1989, not a retrospective.

gaps.name: Internet standards status list / protocol standards index
gaps.why: The document is a catalogue of the standards-track state of all protocols; the taxonomy has only the general IETF process tag for this.

RFC1101.title: DNS encoding of network names and other types
RFC1101.summary: RFC 1101 specifies how to encode network names and network/subnet number mappings in the DNS using PTR and A RRs under IN-ADDR.ARPA, and sketches an experimental general "YP" scheme for mapping between identifiers such as TCP ports and numbers.

DNS.why: The document extends the DNS (updating RFC 1034/1035) with new conventions for PTR and A resource records in IN-ADDR.ARPA for network and subnet names, plus an experimental general mapping scheme in the DNS namespace.
DNS.quote: A specific method for entering and retrieving RRs which map between network names and numbers.

rejected.why: It touches IP network numbers and subnet masks, but the document is about encoding them in DNS records, not about address architecture or allocation.
Network name syntax is borrowed from the host name syntax in the Host Requirements RFC, but the document does not address host naming conventions or host tables themselves.
The YP-style mappings (e.g. TCP port to name) are identifier lookups, not discovery of services on a network.

RFC1102.title: Policy routing in Internet protocols
RFC1102.summary: Clark proposes an architecture for policy-based inter-domain routing: source-synthesized Policy Routes across Administrative Regions, verified by Policy Gateways against Policy Terms, with Policy Servers, billing/cost recovery, and soft-state flow setup.

routing architecture.why: The whole document is an architectural proposal for policy routing across administrative regions (source-specified routes, policy gateways, policy servers, route setup), which is routing architecture rather than a specific protocol.
routing architecture.quote: This document proposes an approach to integrating policy controls into the Internet.

rejected.why: EGP is discussed only as the closest existing mechanism and its topological restrictions are criticized; the document is not about EGP.
Type of service appears as a policy condition, but QoS architectures and signalling are not the subject.
The Security section covers sealing PRs against resource theft, but it is a minor part of the document and no specific mechanism is specified.
BGP is not mentioned; the policy routing here is a precursor concept but not about BGP.
The proposed IP PR option is a mechanism for IP packets, but the document is not about IP itself.

gaps.name: Inter-domain policy routing
gaps.why: The document describes policy-based inter-AS routing. The taxonomy has IDPR, but it is a specific protocol (RFC 1479) and this memo is an earlier discussion paper, so I used routing architecture instead.

RFC1103.title: Proposed standard for the transmission of IP datagrams over FDDI Networks
RFC1103.summary: RFC 1103 specifies encapsulation of IP datagrams and ARP requests/replies over FDDI networks using 802.2 LLC/SNAP, including MTU, address size, and MAC-layer handling.

FDDI.why: The whole document defines how IP runs over FDDI: packet format, MTU, MAC layer details and frame handling.
FDDI.quote: This RFC specifies a method of encapsulating the Internet Protocol (IP) [1] datagrams and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [2] requests and replies on Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) Networks.

rejected.why: ARP is used as specified in RFC 826 and only parameterized for FDDI (hardware type, address lengths). The document does not define or extend ARP itself.
IP is the payload being carried. The document does not specify IP itself.
ICMP destination unreachable is mentioned only as one error-handling option.
The document draws on the IEEE 802 encapsulation of RFC 1042, but it is about FDDI, not Ethernet.

RFC1104.title: Models of policy based routing
RFC1104.summary: RFC 1104 outlines and compares three models of policy based routing (policy-controlled distribution of routing information, packet filtering/forwarding, and dynamic resource allocation), drawing on NSFNET experience, and briefly discusses accounting.

routing architecture.why: The document is a comparative architectural discussion of policy routing models, their scaling, benefits and costs in a large internetwork, which fits routing architecture and scalability.
routing architecture.quote: The purpose of this RFC is to outline a variety of models for policy based routing.

QoS.why: One of the three models, covered in its own section, concerns policy-based allocation of bandwidth and queue precedence, which sits in the QoS area. No narrower QoS technology tag applies.
QoS.quote: Policy based dynamic allocation of network resources (e.g., bandwidth, buffers, etc.)

rejected.why: EGP is mentioned as the protocol the NSFNET uses to exchange routes. The document is about policy models, not about EGP itself.
BGP is not discussed. The routing-policy discussion concerns EGP and NSFNET, and BGP does not appear in the text.
Route authentication is touched on only as a policy example. The document is not about securing routing protocols.
The NSFNET Routing Policy Data Base is described as an example. The document does not specify a policy language or an IRR.
The scope is policy routing models. It does not address overall architectural principles of the Internet.

gaps.name: policy based routing
gaps.why: This is the document's central subject, and the taxonomy has no tag for routing policy as such. The closest fit is routing architecture. Policy routing, covering Administrative Domains, policy-controlled route distribution and accounting, would merit its own tag.

RFC1105.title: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
RFC1105.summary: RFC 1105 specifies the first version of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-1), an inter-autonomous-system routing protocol, including its message formats, finite state machine, and UPDATE handling with AS-path loop detection.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies BGP version 1: OPEN, UPDATE, NOTIFICATION and KEEPALIVE messages, the FSM, and route propagation rules.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol.

rejected.why: BGP only uses TCP port 179 as its reliable transport. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
EGP is mentioned as the predecessor and as a source of routes passed over BGP. The document is not about EGP itself.
The full-mesh requirement for internal BGP sessions is mentioned, but route reflection and confederations are not defined.

RFC1106.title: TCP big window and NAK options
RFC1106.summary: RFC 1106 describes two experimental TCP options, a NAK option for advisory retransmission requests and a Big Window option extending the window to 30 bits, to improve performance over high bandwidth*delay paths such as satellite links.

TCP.why: The document specifies two new TCP options (NAK and Big Window), plus discussion of slow start and duplicate ack handling in TCP implementations.
TCP.quote: Two extensions to the TCP protocol are described in this RFC in order to provide a more efficient operation over a network with a high bandwidth*delay product.

congestion control.why: A substantial section discusses slow start, congestion versus noise loss, and window opening rate, relevant to congestion control readers.
congestion control.quote: An issue that must be looked at when implementing both the NAKs and big window scheme together is in the area of congestion versus lost packets

satellite.why: The motivating environment and test results are a 580 ms round trip satellite channel, so satellite networking readers would want it.
satellite.quote: this document does describe the use of these options in the isolated satellite network environment

rejected.why: Only cited as an example of selective acknowledgement research; the document is not about NETBLT.
Source quench is mentioned briefly as a possible congestion signal but is not specified or analysed.
NAK-based loss recovery is related, but the taxonomy tag covers FEC/ARQ coding schemes for packet transport and this is a TCP option; TCP is the better fit.
Appendix results are throughput tests of the options, not a measurement methodology.

RFC1107.title: Plan for Internet directory services
RFC1107.summary: A 1989 plan, from a February 1989 meeting, for a three-stage program to build an Internet/NRN white pages directory service, with field trials of X.500 (Quipu), Profile and DNANS.

X.500.why: The plan centres on X.500 as the likely basis for the white pages service. It analyses X.500's gaps (access control, replication, caching, strict hierarchy) and proposes field trials of Quipu.
X.500.quote: Although it has clearcut drawbacks, X.500 was identified as the most likely candidate directory service.

directory services.why: The document is about requirements for and a plan to deploy directory (white pages and yellow pages) services, and compares several directory systems (X.500, Profile, DNANS, Clearinghouse).
directory services.quote: A "White Pages" service is one in which one can look up people in order to learn information about them for finding them.

rejected.why: DNS is described only as a pre-existing service and as a source of experience with caching and delegation. It is not what the plan is about.
Naming is the subject in a general sense, but the directory services tag is more specific and fits better.
It is mentioned only as the message handling system for which X.500 supplies naming.
The DECnet naming service (DNANS) is evaluated, but the tag covers DECnet protocols over IP infrastructure, which is not the subject.
OSI protocol stacks are named as the transport that X.500 runs on. The document is not about OSI network-layer protocols.

gaps.name: White pages / Yellow pages services (Profile, DNANS, Clearinghouse)
gaps.why: The document compares these non-X.500 naming and directory systems, and the taxonomy has no tag for them apart from the generic directory services topic.

RFC1108.title: U.S. Department of Defense Security Options for the Internet Protocol
RFC1108.summary: RFC 1108 defines the DoD Basic Security Option and the top-level Extended Security Option, IP header options carrying classification levels and protection authority flags, with configuration parameters, processing rules and ICMP error handling.

security labels.why: The document specifies IP-layer security label options (classification level, protection authority flags) and their processing, which is the subject of security labels for networked data.
security labels.quote: The focus of this RFC is the definition of formats and processing conventions to support security labels for data contained in IP datagrams

IPv4.why: It defines new IPv4 header options (types 130 and 133), copy-on-fragmentation behaviour and option processing, extending IP itself.
IPv4.quote: The following two internet protocol options are defined for use on Department of Defense (DoD) common user data networks

rejected.why: ICMP Parameter Problem and Destination Unreachable messages are used for error responses, but the document does not extend or specify ICMP itself.
It notes that routing protocols must be augmented to carry labels but defines no routing security mechanism.
The specific child tag security labels fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC1109.title: Report of the second Ad Hoc Network Management Review Group
RFC1109.summary: IAB report of the second Ad Hoc Network Management Review (June 1989) assessing SNMP, CMOT, and the common MIB/SMI, and recommending that SNMP and CMOT be allowed to evolve independently for 12 months while coexisting with OSI management.

SNMP.why: The report reviews SNMP status, its limitations, and recommends extending it for operational reasons; SNMP is a central subject.
SNMP.quote: two network management protocols now known respectively as Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and Common Management Information Protocol on TCP (CMOT) were selected for further work

CMIP.why: CMOT/CMIP status, its OSI alignment, and the recommendation to foster real CMOT/CMIP use are a major part of the report.
CMIP.quote: The present specification for CMOT is based on the ISO Draft International Standard version of Common Management Information Protocol (CMIP).

MIB.why: A full section covers the common Internet MIB and SMI: versioning, extension, experimental/private subtrees, and the recommendation to relax the common MIB/SMI binding.
MIB.quote: roughly 100 were agreed and defined as mandatory for Internet management.

rejected.why: OSI is discussed as the coexistence context, but the tag covers OSI network-layer protocols, not OSI management; CMIP is the better fit.
More specific technology tags (SNMP, CMIP, MIB) already fit, so the parent topic is implied.
TCP is mentioned only for TCB visibility and as CMOT's transport, not as the subject.
The report is about network management policy, not architectural principles.

RFC1110.title: Problem with the TCP big window option
RFC1110.summary: RFC 1110 argues that the TCP Big Window option of RFC 1106 is unsafe in the Internet because enlarging the window without enlarging the 32-bit sequence number space allows old duplicate or disordered packets to be accepted as new data.

TCP.why: The document analyses a proposed TCP option and shows that enlarging the window without enlarging the sequence number space breaks TCP's data integrity guarantees.
TCP.quote: The TCP Big Window option discussed in RFC 1106 will not work properly in an Internet environment which has both a high bandwidth * delay product

rejected.why: The document concerns window size and sequence number uniqueness, not congestion control; packet loss from congestion is mentioned only as an example.
The IP TTL and packet lifetime are discussed only as the bound that keeps sequence numbers effectively unique, not as a subject of the document.
Satellite paths appear only as examples of disordering and as the setting RFC 1106 seems to assume. The document is not about satellite networking.

RFC1111.title: Request for comments on Request for Comments: Instructions to RFC authors
RFC1111.summary: RFC 1111 gives instructions to RFC authors on RFC format (ASCII and PostScript), status and distribution statements, UPDATES/OBSOLETES relationships, the RFC Editor, and how RFCs are announced and obtained.

RFC series.why: The whole document is about RFC format, style, status statements, obsoletes/updates terminology, the RFC Editor and publication and distribution of RFCs.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor attempts to ensure a consistent RFC style. To do this the RFC Editor may choose reformat the RFC submitted.

rejected.why: ASCII is only the character encoding required for one of the two allowed submission formats; the document is not about ASCII itself.
FTP is only mentioned as a way to retrieve RFCs from the NIC; the document does not specify or discuss the protocol.
The document covers RFC publication format rather than the standards process. The status statements are RFC series apparatus, not process definitions.
Email is mentioned only as a submission and request channel for RFCs.

RFC1112.title: Host extensions for IP multicasting
RFC1112.summary: RFC 1112 specifies host-side extensions to IP for multicasting (levels of conformance, class D addresses, send/receive behaviour, Ethernet mapping) and defines IGMP version 1 in an appendix.

multicast.why: The whole document defines IP multicast host behaviour: host groups, class D addresses, sending and receiving multicast datagrams. No more specific multicast technology tag covers the host model.
multicast.quote: This memo specifies the extensions required of a host implementation of the Internet Protocol (IP) to support multicasting.

IGMP.why: Appendix I specifies IGMP version 1, including the message format, the report-delay suppression behaviour and the state machine. Level 2 conformance requires it.
IGMP.quote: The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used by IP hosts to report their host group memberships to any immediately-neighboring multicast routers.
IGMP.section: APPENDIX I. INTERNET GROUP MANAGEMENT PROTOCOL (IGMP)

rejected.why: The Ethernet multicast address mapping is a small example section, not the subject of the document.
IPv4 is the substrate being extended. The document is about multicast, not IPv4 in general.
ARP appears only in the host model diagram as an example of IP-to-local address mapping.
ICMP is mentioned only for when errors must not be generated for multicast datagrams.
Class D group addresses are covered, but as part of multicast rather than as general address architecture.

RFC1113.title: Privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail: Part I - message encipherment and authentication procedures
RFC1113.summary: RFC 1113 defines the original Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) procedures for end-to-end encipherment, MIC-based authentication, printable encoding and encapsulated header fields for Internet email, with DEK/IK key hierarchy.

PEM.why: The document is the core Privacy Enhanced Mail specification, defining message transformations, encapsulation headers and key hierarchy.
PEM.quote: This RFC defines message encipherment and authentication procedures, in order to provide privacy enhancement services for electronic mail transfer in the Internet.

DES.why: Message text encryption is specified as DES in CBC mode (DES-CBC, DES-ECB, DES-EDE for key wrapping), a substantive part of the procedures.
DES.quote: the Block Cipher Algorithm DEA-1, defined in ANSI X3.92-1981 [2] shall be used for encryption of message text.

key management.why: Defines DEKs and Interchange Keys, symmetric and asymmetric key management, and IK identification subfields (Section 5).
key management.quote: A two-level keying hierarchy is used to support privacy-enhanced message transmission:

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport whose constraints shape the encoding; the document does not specify or extend it.
Encapsulated headers resemble RFC 822 but form a disjoint set; the document does not define the Internet message format.
A more specific tag (PEM) covers the secure email subject; email is the substrate.
The printable encoding is a precursor to Base64 and is defined here, but the document is about PEM overall, and PEM covers it.
RSA is only referenced as an IK use algorithm identifier, defined in RFC 1115.
Certificates are deferred to RFC 1114; only carried in header fields here.

RFC1114.title: Privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail: Part II - certificate-based key management
RFC1114.summary: RFC 1114 defines a certificate-based public-key management architecture for Privacy Enhanced Mail, covering user/notary/CA roles, X.509-compatible certificate conventions, cross-certification and certificate revocation lists.

PEM.why: The document is Part II of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series, defining key management for PEM.
PEM.quote: This RFC defines a supporting key management architecture and infrastructure, based on public-key certificate techniques, to provide keying information to message originators and recipients.

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificates, covering naming, validity, validation paths and revocation lists, and defines a hierarchy that is a subset of X.509's.
X.509.quote: This RFC interprets the X.509 certificate mechanism to serve the needs of privacy-enhanced mail in the Internet environment.

PKI.why: A large part of the document sets out the CA hierarchy, organizational notaries, cross-certification and revocation, which is general PKI architecture.
PKI.quote: all certifying authorities must agree to "cross-certify" one another, i.e., each must be willing to sign a certificate in which the issuer is that certifying authority

rejected.why: RSA is the chosen algorithm, but the document is about key management infrastructure, not the algorithm. RFC 1115 specifies the algorithms.
Email is the application the key management supports. The document does not define mail transport or formats. RFC 1113 does that.
ASN.1 is used only to write down the certificate and revocation list syntax.
X.500 Distinguished Names are used in certificates, but the document is not about the directory service.
The more specific PKI, X.509 and PEM tags cover this, so the parent topic is not needed.

RFC1115.title: Privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail: Part III - algorithms, modes, and identifiers
RFC1115.summary: RFC 1115 defines the cryptographic algorithms, DES modes (ECB, EDE, CBC), RSA, MAC and RSA-MD2 and their string identifiers used by Privacy Enhanced Mail (RFC 1113/1114), including a reference MD2 implementation.

DES.why: A major part of the document specifies DES-ECB, DES-EDE and DES-CBC modes and their identifiers for PEM.
DES.quote: The string "DES-CBC" indicates use of the DES algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode.

RSA.why: Defines RSA use for DEK and MIC encryption, including padding rules and exponent recommendations.
RSA.quote: The string "RSA" indicates use of the RSA public-key encryption algorithm

MD5.why: Specifies the MD2 message digest with a full reference implementation; the MD5 tag covers MD2/MD4 digests.
MD5.quote: The RSA-MD2 message digest algorithm accepts as input a message of any length and produces as output a 16-byte quantity.

PEM.why: The document is Part III of the Privacy Enhanced Mail specification, defining its algorithm identifiers.
PEM.quote: algorithms, usage modes, and associated identifiers used in RFC-1113 and RFC-1114 in support of privacy-enhanced electronic mail

rejected.why: Email is the application context only; the document is about the cryptographic algorithms, not mail transport or format.
The MAC is a DES-based FIPS 113 CBC-MAC, not HMAC.
DEK and MIC encryption are mentioned, but key management itself is specified in RFC 1114, not here.
X.509 is only cited for RSA description and certificates; no profile is defined here.

RFC1116.title: Telnet Linemode option
RFC1116.summary: Defines the Telnet LINEMODE option, letting the client do local line editing and signal trapping, with MODE, FORWARDMASK and SLC suboptions and new control characters (ABORT, SUSP, EOF).

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option (LINEMODE) with suboptions and new Telnet commands, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: Linemode Telnet is a way of doing terminal character processing on the client side of a Telnet connection.

rejected.why: ASCII codes are used for the forward mask and special characters, but the document is not about ASCII.
TCP urgent data is mentioned only for the Synch mechanism, which is substrate.
The Telnet tag is more specific and already covers it.

RFC1117.title: Internet numbers
RFC1117.summary: RFC 1117 is the August 1989 status report listing assigned IP network numbers (class A/B/C), reserved addresses, and EGP autonomous system numbers with their contacts.

addressing.why: The document is chiefly a registry of IP address allocations, describing classes A-D, special addresses, and assigned network numbers.
addressing.quote: The network numbers listed here are used as internet addresses by the Internet Protocol (IP)

IPv4.why: It describes the IPv4 classful address format, dotted decimal notation, loopback and reserved ranges.
IPv4.quote: The IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides that address into a network part and a "rest" or local address part.

EGP.why: A substantial section registers autonomous system numbers used with EGP.
EGP.quote: The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) [41,43] specifies that groups of gateways may form autonomous systems.

IANA.why: It is an early number-assignment registry maintained by the NIC Hostmaster, a predecessor of IANA registries.
IANA.quote: This Network Working Group Request for Comments documents the currently assigned network numbers and gateway autonomous systems.

rejected.why: The NIC WHOIS service is mentioned only as a way to look up contacts.
Class D multicast addresses are mentioned only briefly in the address format description.
It is a historical artifact but a current registry report rather than a retrospective.
The document is classful and predates CIDR.

gaps.name: AS numbers / autonomous system number registry
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for autonomous system number assignment; EGP and IANA are the nearest fits.

RFC1118.title: Hitchhikers guide to the Internet
RFC1118.summary: An informational 1989 orientation guide for new Internet participants covering how the Internet is run and governed, the NIC, RFCs, address allocation, routing protocols (RIP, Hello, EGP, gated), DNS/BIND naming, and BSD Unix TCP/IP problems.

user guides.why: The document is an introductory guide for new Internet users, which is the purpose of the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: make available some "hints" which will allow new network participants to understand how the direction of the Internet is set, how to acquire online information

routing.why: A large section surveys routing protocols (static, RIP, Hello, GGP, EGP, gated) and the metric conversion problems between them. No single protocol is the subject, so the general routing tag fits.
routing.quote: Routing is the algorithm by which a network directs a packet from its source to its destination.

DNS.why: A substantial section explains domain names, resolvers, root servers, domain allocation and BIND.
DNS.quote: RFC-1034 and a number of others describe Domain Name Service (DNS), a distributed data base system for mapping names into addresses.

addressing.why: The Address Allocation section covers IP address classes, allocation through the NIC and subnetting.
addressing.quote: Before a local network can be connected to the Internet it must be allocated a unique IP address.

internet history.why: It gives a brief account of how the Internet grew from the ARPANET, and describes the organisations that ran it in 1989 (IAB, NIC, NOCs).
internet history.quote: In the beginning there was the ARPANET, a wide area experimental network connecting hosts and terminal servers together.

rejected.why: RIP is discussed as one of several routing protocols in a survey, not specified or analysed in depth.
EGP is only one entry in the routing survey, so it does not warrant its own tag.
The retransmission behaviour of BSD TCP is mentioned as one of several BSD problems, and the document is not about TCP.
The IAB, IETF and RFC process are described briefly, but the document is not about the process itself.
There is a short explanation of RFC categories and a list of major RFCs, but this is only a small part of the guide.
The document describes the Internet's structure and operation informally and does not set out architectural principles.

RFC1119.title: Network Time Protocol (version 2) specification and implementation
RFC1119.summary: RFC 1119 specifies Network Time Protocol version 2 and its implementation, but only a placeholder notice is available as text because the full document exists only as PostScript.

NTP.why: The document's title names the Network Time Protocol (NTP) version 2 specification. The text available is only a stub, so the subject comes from the title in the body. The title is unambiguous about the subject.
NTP.quote: Network Time Protocol (Version 2) Specification and Implementation

rejected.why: This is the parent of NTP, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC1120.title: Internet Activities Board
RFC1120.summary: Cerf's 1989 memo describes the history, structure, functions and 1989-90 agenda of the Internet Activities Board and its subsidiary task forces (IETF, IRTF).

IETF process.why: The document describes the IAB, IETF and IRTF organisation, the standards track (Proposed, Draft, Standard) and how decisions are made, which is the IETF standards process and administration.
IETF process.quote: The IAB performs the following functions: 1) Sets Internet Standards, 2) Manages the RFC publication process, 3) Reviews the operation of the IETF and IRTF

internet history.why: The introduction gives a history of packet switching, the ICCB and the origins of the IAB and the TCP/IP suite.
internet history.quote: In 1979, it was necessary to form an informal committee to guide the technical evolution of the protocol suite. This group was called the Internet Configuration Control Board

rejected.why: The RFC series and Internet-Draft process are described only briefly as part of IAB functions, not as a main subject.
The ARPANET and the NCP-to-TCP/IP transition are mentioned only as historical background.
X.500 appears only as one item in the near-term agenda (white pages), not as a subject of the document.
Privacy-enhanced mail and X.400/SMTP interoperation are only brief agenda items.
Scaling and architecture are listed only as agenda foci, not discussed in depth.

RFC1121.title: Act one - the poems
RFC1121.summary: A collection of humorous poems presented at the "Act One" symposium commemorating the 20th anniversary of the ARPANET, recounting ARPANET history and queueing theory in verse.

humor.why: The whole RFC is a set of whimsical poems and parodies (e.g. a Hamlet parody), which fits the humorous/whimsical documents category.
humor.quote: a few of the speakers could not resist the temptation to commit poetry

internet history.why: Several poems, especially The Big Bang!, recount the birth of the ARPANET and the first IMP installation, so the document works as a retrospective on early network history.
internet history.quote: commemorate the 20th anniversary of the installation of the first Interface Message Processor (IMP) on the ARPANET which took place at UCLA

rejected.why: The ARPANET is the subject of the poems' history, but the document specifies nothing about ARPANET protocols or operations. The history tag fits better.
It is tied to a symposium, but it is a collection of poems and not a report of the proceedings.

RFC1122.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers
RFC1122.summary: RFC 1122 is the Internet Standard Host Requirements document for the communication layers, specifying requirements and corrections for hosts' link layer (ARP, Ethernet encapsulation), Internet layer (IP, ICMP, IGMP, multihoming, routing, fragmentation) and transport layer (UDP, TCP).

TCP.why: About half the document is a detailed TCP walk-through and requirements: window management, SWS avoidance, Nagle, keep-alives, connection failures, and corrections to RFC 793.
TCP.quote: A host TCP MUST implement Karn's algorithm and Jacobson's algorithm for computing the retransmission timeout ("RTO").

IPv4.why: The Internet layer chapter specifies host IP behaviour: addressing, options, TTL, TOS, fragmentation and reassembly, source routing, and broadcast.
IPv4.quote: A host MUST verify the IP header checksum on every received datagram and silently discard every datagram that has a bad checksum.

ICMP.why: A full ICMP walk-through covers each message type, including new codes, rules on when errors must not be sent, and handling in the transport layer.
ICMP.quote: Every host MUST implement an ICMP Echo server function that receives Echo Requests and sends corresponding Echo Replies.

UDP.why: Section 4.1 gives UDP host requirements for ports, checksums, IP options, ICMP handling and multihoming.
UDP.quote: UDP is almost a null protocol; the only services it provides over IP are checksumming of data and multiplexing by port number.

ARP.why: Section 2.3.2 specifies ARP cache validation, flood prevention and packet queuing.
ARP.quote: An implementation of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [LINK:2] MUST provide a mechanism to flush out-of-date cache entries.

Ethernet.why: Covers IP encapsulation on Ethernet and IEEE 802 networks, plus the trailer protocol.
Ethernet.quote: Every Internet host connected to a 10Mbps Ethernet cable: MUST be able to send and receive packets using RFC-894 encapsulation

multihoming.why: A dedicated section covers local multihoming, source address selection and the Strong and Weak ES models.
multihoming.quote: A multihomed host has multiple IP addresses, which we may think of as "logical interfaces".

IGMP.why: Covers IGMP and host IP multicast support requirements (Section 3.3.7), though in short sections.
IGMP.quote: IGMP [IP:4] is a protocol used between hosts and gateways on a single network to establish hosts' membership in particular multicast groups.

rejected.why: The introduction discusses architectural assumptions, but the document is a host implementation requirements spec, not an architecture document.
Slow start, congestion avoidance and Source Quench handling are mandated, but only as part of the TCP requirements.
Only discusses MTU, MMS_S and fragmentation. Path MTU discovery is mentioned as a future mechanism.
Multicast is handled in short sections on IGMP and local IP multicasting, so IGMP is the better fit.
Covers host route cache, default gateways and dead-gateway detection, which is host-side forwarding. It is not about routing protocols.
A terminology subsection and requirement-level keywords are present, but they are apparatus and not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Host requirements
gaps.why: The document is the canonical Host Requirements specification, covering whole-host protocol implementation conformance across layers. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so individual protocol tags are the closest fit.

RFC1123.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Application and Support
RFC1123.summary: RFC 1123 is the Host Requirements companion for application and support protocols, correcting and clarifying requirements for Telnet, FTP, TFTP, SMTP/RFC-822 mail, DNS resolvers/servers, host initialization, and SNMP/CMOT management.

Telnet.why: A whole major section walks through the Telnet spec, options, end-of-line convention and user interface requirements.
Telnet.quote: Telnet is the standard Internet application protocol for remote login.

FTP.why: Large section correcting RFC-959 and defining a minimum implementation, restart mechanism and reply codes.
FTP.quote: The File Transfer Protocol FTP is the primary Internet standard for file transfer.

TFTP.why: Dedicated section with TFTP requirements including the Sorcerer's Apprentice fix and timeouts.
TFTP.quote: Implementations MUST contain the fix for this problem: the sender (i.e., the side originating the DATA packets) must never resend the current DATA packet

SMTP.why: Extensive SMTP requirements: commands, queueing, timeouts, relay, error notification, MX handling.
SMTP.quote: electronic mail in a format specified in RFC-822 [SMTP:2] is transmitted using the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)

message format.why: Sections 5.2.13-5.2.19 amend RFC-822 syntax: dates, mailbox, local-part, domain literals, source routes.
message format.quote: RFC-822 specifies the Internet standard format for electronic mail messages.

DNS.why: Section 6.1 gives detailed DNS resolver and server requirements: caching, transport, TTL, retransmission, search lists.
DNS.quote: Every host MUST implement a resolver for the Domain Name System (DNS)

hostnames.why: Amends RFC-952 host name syntax and discusses the local host table.
hostnames.quote: the restriction on the first character is relaxed to allow either a letter or a digit.

SNMP.why: Remote management section sets host requirements for SNMP agents and MIB interpretation.
SNMP.quote: An Internet host SHOULD include an agent for either SNMP or CMOT.

rejected.why: Host initialization section discusses BOOTP and RARP, not DHCP, which did not yet exist.
TCP is the transport substrate, covered by companion RFC 1122.
MIB interpretation for hosts is brief, within the management section; SNMP covers it.
CMOT is only mentioned as an alternative management agent.
RARP appears only in a list of dynamic configuration options.
Mailing list and alias expansion is a short subsection of SMTP requirements.

gaps.name: Host requirements
gaps.why: The document's overall subject is host implementation requirements, which fits no taxonomy tag (internet architecture is the closest).

gaps.name: BOOTP
gaps.why: Host bootstrap configuration is a suggested approach, but there is no BOOTP tag.

RFC1124.title: Policy issues in interconnecting networks
RFC1124.summary: The text available is only a placeholder saying RFC 1124 ("Policy Issues in Interconnecting Networks") exists only as PostScript (RFC1124.PS), so its substance can't be read.

rejected.why: The title hints at inter-network policy, but the body has no text showing the document is about routing architecture.
The title hints at it, but the body has no content to support the tag. A title is a hint, not proof.

gaps.name: Full text of RFC 1124 (PostScript only)
gaps.why: The plain-text body is a stub. The PostScript file would need to be read before the RFC can be tagged. Until then it has no tags, and the title suggests a likely fit with routing or internet architecture.

RFC1125.title: Policy requirements for inter Administrative Domain routing
RFC1125.summary: RFC 1125 articulates requirements for policy-based inter-Administrative Domain routing, including AD topology assumptions, a taxonomy of access and charging policies with example policy terms, problematic requirements, and a brief review of proposed mechanisms (EGP, BGP, RFC 1102).

routing architecture.why: The document is a requirements and design-principles memo for inter-AD policy routing, covering topology assumptions, scalability concerns and policy types. It is not a specification of any one protocol, so the architecture topic fits best.
routing architecture.quote: This document articulates the requirements for policy based routing and should be used as input to the functional specification and evaluation of proposed protocols.

rejected.why: BGP (RFC 1105) is only mentioned briefly in the review of earlier mechanisms. The document does not specify or analyse it in depth.
EGP is cited as a previous protocol with a limited notion of policy. The document is not about EGP.
