RFC 1102 policy routing is discussed as the mechanism that best matches the requirements, but this memo is a requirements document, not a specification of that architecture.
QOS/TOS appears only as one policy parameter in the access-policy taxonomy, not as a subject of the document.
Security is raised only as a problematic requirement in a short bullet, and the Security Considerations section is explicitly empty.

gaps.name: Policy-based inter-domain routing
gaps.why: The document's main subject is policy routing between administrative domains, including source and transit policies and charging policies. The taxonomy has no tag for it apart from the general routing architecture topic.

RFC1126.title: Goals and functional requirements for inter-autonomous system routing
RFC1126.summary: RFC 1126 sets out goals, functional requirements, and non-goals for a new inter-autonomous system routing architecture and protocol to replace EGP, with an appendix on policy, TOS, scale, and migration issues.

routing architecture.why: The document defines goals and requirements for an inter-AS routing architecture: scalability, policy, autonomy, firewalls, and independence of inter- and intra-AS routing. This is routing architecture and design principles, not a specific protocol.
routing architecture.quote: the functional requirements specified here are intended to define the features required of the inter-autonomous system routing environment

rejected.why: BGP is never mentioned. The document is a precursor requirements document for a new inter-AS protocol, not a specification or analysis of BGP.
EGP is mentioned only as the existing protocol to migrate from and as a model whose core restrictions are unacceptable. The document is not about EGP itself.
Type-of-service routing and multipath are discussed only briefly in the appendix, and load splitting is explicitly a non-goal.
The credible-environment goal is only a short general statement, and the Security Considerations section says security is not addressed.

gaps.name: Inter-autonomous system routing / policy routing requirements
gaps.why: The document is about inter-domain (inter-AS) routing requirements and policy-sensitive route synthesis. The taxonomy has no inter-domain routing topic apart from BGP and EGP, so the general routing architecture tag is the closest fit.

RFC1127.title: Perspective on the Host Requirements RFCs
RFC1127.summary: Informal summary by the Host Requirements working group chair of settled and open issues and future work from RFC 1122/1123, covering link, IP, transport and application layer host issues.

internet architecture.why: The document is a cross-layer perspective on requirements for Internet host implementations, with goals such as interoperability, extensibility and architectural purity. It is not specific to one protocol.
internet architecture.quote: to reconcile theoretical and architectural concerns with the sometimes conflicting imperatives of the real world

TCP.why: Substantial parts cover TCP performance, connection robustness, window shrinking, delayed ACKs, keep-alives, SWS avoidance and RST text, and call for a TCP performance RFC.
TCP.quote: Encourage (mandate!) implementation of known TCP performance enhancements.
TCP.section: 1.1 GOALS OF THE HOST REQUIREMENTS RFCs

IPv4.why: Many IP-layer issues are discussed: source routing, multihoming, reassembly timeout, TTL, fragmentation, IP options and address masks.
IPv4.quote: Require that Time-to-Live (TTL) be configurable.

ARP.why: ARP cache management, queueing, proxy ARP and stolen IP addresses appear as settled and open issues.
ARP.quote: Require a mechanism to flush out-of-date ARP cache entries.

FTP.why: FTP restart, proposed extensions (STOA, NDIR, compression), reply codes and bidirectional transfer are discussed at length.
FTP.quote: Enlarge the minimum FTP implementation.

DNS.why: DNS requirements are covered: UDP preference, negative caching, WKS records, search lists and replacing hosts.txt.
DNS.quote: Require that hosts implement the Domain Name System (DNS).

Telnet.why: Telnet end-of-line, Go-Aheads, SYNCH, 8-bit NVT data, flushing output and LineMode are discussed.
Telnet.quote: Include compatibility requirements for Telnet end-of-line.

SMTP.why: Robust mail delivery, source routing of mail, global addressing, the Received: line and SEND are covered.
SMTP.quote: Recommend the use of long timeouts and of alternative addresses for multihomed hosts, to obtain robust mail delivery.

ICMP.why: ICMP Address Mask replies, Echo to broadcast, error handling, new Destination Unreachable codes and gateway discovery messages are discussed.
ICMP.quote: Discourage gratuitous ICMP Address Mask Reply messages.

rejected.why: MTU discovery appears only as one future-work item (RFC 1063 probe options), not as a main subject.
IP multicasting is only a brief encouragement item.
RFC-822 header handling is mentioned only briefly, in the SMTP items.
The document is about host requirements content, not RFC series format or publication.
It preserves some history, but its main purpose is requirements issues and future work.

gaps.name: Host requirements
gaps.why: No tag exists for host software requirements documents (RFC 1122/1123). internet architecture is the closest fit.

RFC1128.title: Measured performance of the Network Time Protocol in the Internet system
RFC1128.summary: A stub notice saying RFC 1128, "Measured Performance of the Network Time Protocol in the Internet System", is available only as PostScript; the text itself is not included.

NTP.why: The only substantive content is the title, which says the RFC reports measured performance of NTP. A reader browsing NTP would expect this RFC. The tag rests on the title because the body is only a stub.
NTP.quote: Measured Performance of the Network Time Protocol in the Internet System

rejected.why: This is the parent of NTP and is implied by the NTP tag.
The subject is NTP's own performance, but the body has no content on measurement methodology, so I did not add this topic.

RFC1129.title: Internet Time Synchronization: The Network Time Protocol
RFC1129.summary: RFC 1129 is a 1989 informational document on Internet time synchronization using the Network Time Protocol, but only a notice that the text is available solely in PostScript/PDF is present, so the tag rests on the title.

NTP.why: The only body text restates the title, which names the Network Time Protocol as the subject. I couldn't read the full text, so this tag is based on the title and the RFC's known subject.
NTP.quote: Internet Time Synchronization: The Network Time Protocol

rejected.why: This is the parent of NTP, so it is implied and isn't listed separately.

RFC1130.title: IAB official protocol standards
RFC1130.summary: RFC 1130 is the October 1989 IAB quarterly memo listing the standardization state and status (standard, draft, proposed, experimental, historic) of Internet protocols, explaining the standards process and the RFC series, and giving contacts.

IETF process.why: The memo's main content is the standards procedure, the states and statuses of protocols, and how the IAB/IESG review and advance them.
IETF process.quote: This memo describes the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as determined by the Internet Activities Board (IAB).

RFC series.why: A substantial section explains the RFC series, how to submit RFCs, and how to obtain them, and the memo is the reference for finding the current RFC for each protocol.
RFC series.quote: The documents called Request for Comments (or RFCs) are the working notes of the Internet research and development community.

rejected.why: IANA is only mentioned as the manager of the standards list and as a contact; Assigned Numbers is a referenced document, not the subject.
It is a dated snapshot of protocol status, not a history or retrospective, though it is of historical interest.
DNS appears only as one row in the standards table among dozens of protocols, so it is not a subject of the memo.
Section 5 defines states and statuses, but these are process definitions, not a glossary.

RFC1131.title: OSPF specification
RFC1131.summary: The document is only a placeholder stub for RFC 1131, "The OSPF Specification", stating the full text is available only in PostScript and explaining how to retrieve it by mail server.

OSPF.why: The title identifies this RFC as the OSPF specification. The body text is only a stub, but the RFC is the specification of OSPF and belongs on that subject page.
OSPF.quote: RFC-1131 "The OSPF Specification"

rejected.why: Parent of OSPF, so it is implied. The document is about the specific protocol.

RFC1132.title: Standard for the transmission of 802.2 packets over IPX networks
RFC1132.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IEEE 802.2 packets (and thus IP, ARP, CLNP) inside Novell IPX datagrams, including MTU, address mapping, broadcast/unicast conventions and a reserved socket.

IPX.why: The whole document defines how to carry 802.2/IP traffic over IPX networks: MTU, address mapping, broadcast and unicast settings, reserved socket 0x8060. It is the IPX interworking specification.
IPX.quote: This document specifies a standard method of encapsulating 802.2 [1] packets on networks supporting Novell's Internet Packet Exchange Protocol [2] (IPX).

rejected.why: ARP is used to map IP addresses to 10-byte IPX addresses, but the document only applies it and does not specify or extend it.
IP datagrams are the main payload carried, but the document is about the IPX encapsulation, not IP itself.
CLNP is mentioned as one protocol that could be carried; it is not a subject of the document.
The encapsulation is link-layer-style carriage over IPX rather than generic IP tunnelling; the IPX tag is more specific.
The document refers to 802.2 LLC/SNAP and RFC 1042 conventions only as the framing it reuses, not Ethernet itself.

RFC1133.title: Routing between the NSFNET and the DDN
RFC1133.summary: Case study describing how routing between the NSFNET and the DDN (MILNET/ARPANET) was implemented using EGP sessions with DDN Mailbridges, including metric and AS number policy, and shortcomings of the interconnection.

EGP.why: The whole interconnection is built on EGP sessions between NSFNET NSSs and DDN Mailbridges, with AS numbers and metrics for inbound and outbound announcements described in detail.
EGP.quote: These routers exchanged network reachability information via the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) with the NSFNET nodes as well as with the DDN Mailbridges.

routing architecture.why: The document analyses inter-domain path selection, redundancy, load sharing and the limits of the core model architecture between peer networks.
routing architecture.quote: Shortcomings of the current NSFNET/DDN interconnection routing
routing architecture.section: 4. Shortcomings of the current NSFNET/DDN interconnection routing

ARPANET.why: The document covers how the ARPANET/MILNET and their Mailbridges and PSNs were connected to the NSFNET.
ARPANET.quote: Ethernet adapters were installed in two of the Mailbridges, which previously just connected the MILNET and the ARPANET

rejected.why: BGP is not discussed; the document is about EGP-based interconnection.
The distributed policy routing database is mentioned but only by reference to other RFCs, and it is not RPSL or an Internet routing registry.
It is a case study of a contemporary implementation, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: NSFNET / inter-domain policy routing between administrative domains
gaps.why: The document is mainly about interconnecting administrative domains with policy-based metrics, and the taxonomy has no tag for NSFNET or inter-AS policy routing apart from the EGP tag.

RFC1134.title: Point-to-Point Protocol: A proposal for multi-protocol transmission of datagrams over Point-to-Point links
RFC1134.summary: RFC 1134 specifies the original Point-to-Point Protocol: HDLC-based framing for serial links, the Link Control Protocol (LCP) with its state machine and packets, and the IP Control Protocol (IPCP) for carrying IP over PPP.

PPP.why: The whole document defines PPP: encapsulation, LCP automaton and packets, and the IP NCP (IPCP).
PPP.quote: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) provides a method for transmitting datagrams over serial point-to-point links.

rejected.why: IP is only the network protocol carried over PPP; Section 5 defines IPCP, a PPP control protocol, not IP itself.
Appendix B gives a table-driven FCS implementation, but it is a minor implementation aid and not the subject of the document.
Van Jacobson compressed TCP/IP appears only as a reserved protocol number, not specified.
X.25 LAPB is cited only as a framing reference (HDLC-based), not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only implicitly as a de facto encapsulation; not discussed.

gaps.name: HDLC framing
gaps.why: The document is built on HDLC framing and asynchronous HDLC (Appendix A), but the taxonomy has no HDLC tag.

RFC1135.title: Helminthiasis of the Internet
RFC1135.summary: An informational retrospective on the November 1988 Internet worm, covering how it infected hosts, the cure, its impact, ethics statements, media role, computer crime, future prevention, and reviews of four analyses.

rejected.why: The document is an incident retrospective and discussion of ethics, not guidance on operational security practices for network infrastructure.
It recounts how teams responded to the worm, but it does not define a mechanism, format or procedure for exchanging or coordinating incident response. It is a historical narrative.

It is a look back at an event in the life of the Internet, so this was the closest fit. I rejected it because the taxonomy describes the tag as histories and retrospectives of the Internet and its protocols. This memo covers a security incident and its ethics, not the history of the Internet or its protocols.
Fingerd's buffer overflow was one of the worm's attack vectors, but the document does not specify or analyse the Finger protocol itself.
The sendmail debug command was exploited, but the document is not about SMTP or mail relaying.
The memo concerns a security incident, but it does not address a security mechanism, threat model or guidance. It is a narrative, ethics and legal discussion, so I chose no tag.

gaps.name: Computer worm / Internet Worm incident (1988)
gaps.why: The whole document is about the Morris worm incident, including its ethics, legal and media aspects. The taxonomy has no tag for security incidents, malware, or computer ethics and crime.

RFC1136.title: Administrative Domains and Routing Domains: A model for routing in the Internet
RFC1136.summary: RFC 1136 proposes adapting the OSI Routeing Framework's Administrative Domain / Routing Domain model to describe and engineer routing structure in the Internet, replacing the "core" Autonomous System model.

routing architecture.why: The document is a conceptual model of routing structure: administrative domains, routing domains, common domains, and how intra- and inter-domain routing and policy relate. This is routing architecture and design principles.
routing architecture.quote: This RFC proposes a model for describing routing within the Internet.

rejected.why: The OSI Routeing Framework is the source of the model and its terminology is borrowed, but the document does not specify OSI network-layer protocols. It is about describing Internet routing.
EGP and the AS concept are referenced as the old 'core' model that the document critiques. The document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
BGP is never mentioned. Only the Autonomous System concept is discussed, at a model level.
The scope is routing structure specifically, so the more specific routing architecture tag fits better.

gaps.name: Administrative Domains and Routing Domains / Autonomous System model
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the AD/RD routing model and its relation to Autonomous Systems. No tag covers inter-domain routing structure or AS concepts beyond routing architecture.

RFC1137.title: Mapping between full RFC 822 and RFC 822 with restricted encoding
RFC1137.summary: Defines a symmetric encoding of RFC 822 local-parts (quoted-strings) into restricted atoms so full RFC 822 addresses can pass through restricted-character mail networks such as UUCP.

message format.why: The document specifies how RFC 822 address local-parts are encoded and decoded between full and restricted forms. That is Internet message format addressing.
message format.quote: This document describes a symmetrical mapping between full RFC 822 addressing, and a form for use on these networks.

UUCP.why: UUCP mail transfer is the main motivating case for the restricted encoding, and the memo updates RFC 976 (UUCP mail interchange). A reader of UUCP mail interchange would want it.
UUCP.quote: UUCP transfer of RFC 822 messages is an important case of this

rejected.why: The more specific child tag, message format, fits the address-syntax content, so the parent is not needed.
RFC 987 on X.400 mapping is only cited as the origin of the mapping. The document does not address X.400.
Transfer at the MTS level is mentioned only in passing. The document does not specify SMTP.

RFC1138.title: Mapping between X.400(1988) / ISO 10021 and RFC 822
RFC1138.summary: Specifies a gateway mapping between X.400(1988)/ISO 10021 interpersonal messaging and RFC 822 mail, covering service elements, O/R address mapping, headers, reports and notifications.

X.400.why: The whole document defines X.400(88) interworking with RFC 822, including O/R addresses, IPMS and MTS mappings.
X.400.quote: This document describes a set of mappings which will enable interworking between systems operating the CCITT X.400 (1988) Recommendations on Message Handling Systems

message format.why: Substantial parts define RFC 822 header mappings and new extended header fields for X.400 services.
message format.quote: A single RFC 822 message is generated from the incoming IP Message, Report, or IP Notification.

rejected.why: Parent of X.400 and message format; implied, so not listed separately.
Only one of the 822-MTS environments mentioned; not specified or extended here.
Appendix C only briefly covers UUCP addressing via RFC 976; not a main subject.
Used as notation for referring to X.400 elements; the document is not about ASN.1.
EBNF is used as notation only.

RFC1139.title: Echo function for ISO 8473
RFC1139.summary: Defines an echo (ping) function for the OSI connectionless network protocol ISO 8473, with a short-term mechanism using special NSAP selectors and a long-term mechanism using new ERQ/ERP PDU types.

CLNP.why: The whole document extends ISO 8473 (CLNP) with an echo request/reply function, including new PDU types and NSAP selector use.
CLNP.quote: This memo defines an echo function for the connection-less network layer protocol.

rejected.why: The echo function is analogous to ICMP echo but is for OSI CLNP, not ICMP.
Ping-style diagnostics are only loosely related; the document does not cover path discovery tools as such.
CLNP is the more specific child tag and is chosen instead of the parent.

RFC1140.title: IAB official protocol standards
RFC1140.summary: RFC 1140 is the IAB's quarterly list of official Internet protocol standards, explaining the standards process, protocol states and statuses, and listing each protocol's current standardization state and RFC.

IETF process.why: The memo describes the standards track, state/status definitions, minimum delays, and IESG/IAB roles, which is the standards process and its administration.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial section covers the RFC series, submission to the RFC Editor, the decision table for publication, and how to obtain RFCs.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: Assigned Numbers and the IANA contact are mentioned, but only as references and contacts, not as the subject.
It is a snapshot status document from 1990, not a history or retrospective, though it is of historical interest now.
It defines protocol state and status terms, but these are process definitions rather than a glossary, so they are covered by IETF process.
TCP and the other listed protocols (IP, SNMP, DNS, OSPF, etc.) appear only as entries in the status tables, not as subjects the document specifies.
SNMP, SMI and MIB are listed with their status, and the notes on management cover only recommendation level, not the protocols themselves.

RFC1141.title: Incremental updating of the Internet checksum
RFC1141.summary: RFC 1141 corrects and replaces the description of incremental updating of the Internet checksum in RFC 1071, giving the one's-complement update equation and C code for updating the IP TTL and header checksum.

checksum.why: The whole memo is about how to incrementally update the standard Internet checksum without full recomputation, with the corrected equation and example code.
checksum.quote: the equation above updates the checksum C, rather than the 1's complement of the checksum, ~C, which is the value stored in the checksum field

rejected.why: The example updates the IP header TTL and checksum, but the memo is about the checksum technique, not the IP protocol itself.
The Internet checksum is a one's-complement sum, not a CRC.

RFC1142.title: OSI IS-IS Intra-domain Routing Protocol
RFC1142.summary: RFC 1142 republishes ISO DP 10589, the OSI IS-IS intra-domain link-state routing protocol for CLNP networks. It covers the two-level hierarchy, the decision and update processes, PDU formats, and the management objects.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies the IS-IS link-state routing protocol: LSPs, hello PDUs, SPF decision process, levels and areas, and PDU encodings.
IS-IS.quote: This protocol permits Intermediate Systems within a routeing Domain to exchange configuration and routeing information to facilitate the operation of the routeing and relaying functions

OSI.why: It is an OSI network-layer routing protocol that works with ISO 8473 CLNP and ISO 9542 ES-IS, and it uses NSAP addressing. OSI readers would want it.
OSI.quote: it is a protocol of the Network Layer. The protocol is designed to operate in close conjunction with ISO 9542 and ISO 8473.

rejected.why: CLNP (ISO 8473) is the data protocol IS-IS runs alongside. This document does not specify it.
The GDMO managed objects are a management appendix for IS-IS, not a treatment of CMIP itself.
X.25 (ISO 8208) is one subnetwork type the protocol supports. It is not the subject.
The hierarchical areas are part of the IS-IS protocol itself, so the IS-IS tag covers them.

RFC1143.title: The Q Method of Implementing TELNET Option Negotiation
RFC1143.summary: RFC 1143 describes the Q Method, an experimental implementation approach and state machine for TELNET option negotiation that prevents negotiation loops, supplementing RFC 854.

Telnet.why: The whole document is about implementing Telnet option negotiation (WILL/WONT/DO/DONT) correctly, including loop examples and a state machine.
Telnet.quote: This RFC amplifies, supplements, and extends the RFC 854 [7] option negotiation rules and guidelines, which are insufficient to prevent all option negotiation loops.

rejected.why: The Telnet tech tag sits under it and is the more specific fit.
The document uses MUST/SHOULD requirement language but is not about terminology.

RFC1144.title: Compressing TCP/IP Headers for Low-Speed Serial Links
RFC1144.summary: Specifies Van Jacobson's differential compression of TCP/IP headers (CSLIP) for low-speed serial links, with error handling, tuning, performance data and sample C code.

header compression.why: The whole document defines a TCP/IP header compression scheme. No taxonomy child (ROHC, CRTP, IPHC) fits this specific VJ compression, so the parent topic is used.
header compression.quote: It describes a method for compressing the headers of TCP/IP datagrams to improve performance over low speed serial links.

TCP.why: The compression is tied to TCP header fields and semantics, and relies on TCP retransmission for error recovery. Readers of TCP extensions and implementation would want it.
TCP.quote: This compression is specific to TCP/IP datagrams.

SLIP.why: The scheme is designed for SLIP links (CSLIP), and Appendix B covers backward-compatible SLIP servers and framing hacks.
SLIP.quote: The networking system calls a SLIP output driver with an IP packet to be sent over the serial line.

rejected.why: PPP is mentioned as the framing that can negotiate compression, but the document does not specify PPP.
IPHC (RFC 2507) is a later scheme and is not described here.
ROHC is a later, different compression framework and is not covered here.
IP header fields are compressed, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
This topic covers lossless data compression formats. The document only discusses data compression as an interaction in section 5.3.

gaps.name: Van Jacobson (VJ) TCP/IP header compression / CSLIP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for this scheme under header compression, which is the most widely cited TCP/IP header compression specification.

review: SLIP: quote not found in the text

notes: SLIP: quote not found in the text

RFC1145.title: TCP alternate checksum options
RFC1145.summary: Experimental (now historic) RFC defining TCP Alternate Checksum Request and Data options to negotiate alternate checksums such as 8-bit and 16-bit Fletcher at connection setup.

TCP.why: The document defines two new TCP options and their negotiation during connection establishment, so it is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: The TCP Alternate Checksum Request Option may be sent in a SYN segment by a TCP to indicate that the TCP is prepared to both generate and receive checksums

checksum.why: A substantial part of the document specifies the Fletcher checksum algorithms as alternatives to the standard Internet checksum for packet integrity.
checksum.quote: The 8-bit Fletcher Checksum Algorithm is calculated over a sequence of data octets (call them D[1] through D[N]) by maintaining 2 unsigned 1's-complement 8-bit accumulators
checksum.section: APPENDIX I: The 8-bit Fletcher Checksum Algorithm

rejected.why: Fletcher checksums are arithmetic checksums, not CRC polynomial codes.
The pseudoheader and fragment remarks are incidental; the document is not about IP.
OSI Fletcher checksum is mentioned only for comparison.

RFC1146.title: TCP alternate checksum options
RFC1146.summary: RFC 1146 defines two experimental TCP options (Alternate Checksum Request and Alternate Checksum Data) to negotiate and carry alternate checksums such as 8-bit and 16-bit Fletcher in place of the standard TCP checksum.

TCP.why: The document specifies new TCP options and their negotiation during connection establishment, so it is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: This memo suggests a pair of TCP options to allow use of alternate data checksum algorithms in the TCP header.

checksum.why: A substantial part of the document defines alternative checksum algorithms (8-bit and 16-bit Fletcher) and compares them with the Internet checksum. Readers of the checksum subject would want it.
checksum.quote: The 8-bit Fletcher Checksum Algorithm is calculated over a sequence of data octets

rejected.why: Fletcher checksums are arithmetic checksums, not CRC polynomial codes.
The OSI Fletcher checksum is mentioned only for comparison; the document does not deal with OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC1147.title: FYI on a Network Management Tool Catalog: Tools for Monitoring and Debugging TCP/IP Internets and Interconnected Devices
RFC1147.summary: FYI catalog of network management and debugging tools for TCP/IP internets (SNMP managers, packet analyzers, ping/traceroute, benchmarks), with keyword index and a network management tutorial.

network management.why: The whole document is a catalog of network management tools plus a network management tutorial on monitoring, fault, performance, and configuration management.
network management.quote: This catalog contains descriptions of several tools available to assist network managers in debugging and maintaining TCP/IP internets and interconnected communications resources.

SNMP.why: A large share of the catalogued tools (snmpd, snmpask, XNETMON, NMC, etc.) are SNMP agents, managers and utilities.
SNMP.quote: a network management system or component based on SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol.

traceroute.why: Traceroute, hopcheck, snmpsrc and NPRV's trace route function are path discovery tools covered in the catalog and tutorial.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute is a tool that allows the route taken by packets from source to destination to be discovered.

packet capture.why: Many entries (tcpdump, etherfind, Sniffer, LANWatch, netwatch) are eavesdropping packet capture and analysis tools.
packet capture.quote: Tcpdump can interpret and print headers for the following protocols: ethernet, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, NFS, ND, ARP/RARP, AppleTalk.

rejected.why: It is an FYI-series document, but the subject index tag is about guides as a category; the content is network management tools.
Several tools are benchmarks (hammer, nhfsstone, SPIMS, TTCP), but this is only a minor part of the catalog.
CMIP Library and OSIMIS tools are listed but only as a few entries among many.
Ping and traceroute rely on ICMP, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
nslookup and DiG are catalogued, but they are individual entries and not a main subject.

RFC1148.title: Mapping between X.400(1988) / ISO 10021 and RFC 822
RFC1148.summary: Specifies a gateway mapping between X.400(1988)/ISO 10021 interpersonal messaging and RFC 822 mail, covering service elements, address mapping, headers, reports and notifications.

X.400.why: The whole document defines X.400(88) to RFC 822 gateway mappings, including O/R addresses, IPM, reports and probes.
X.400.quote: This document describes a set of mappings which will enable interworking between systems operating the CCITT X.400 (1988) Recommendations on Message Handling Systems

message format.why: Substantial parts define RFC 822 header mappings and new extension header fields (X400-Received, Importance, etc.) for the Internet message format.
message format.quote: RFC 822 is the current specification of the messaging standard on the Internet. ... It specifies an end to end message format.

rejected.why: SMTP is only one of several 822-MTS substrates mentioned; the document does not specify or extend it.
Parent of X.400 and message format; implied, not listed separately.
ASN.1 is used for notation and element reference only, not the subject.
Appendix C is a brief note on UUCP gatewaying via RFC 976; not a substantial subject of the document.
Domain names are used for address mapping tables but DNS itself is not specified or extended.
Predates MIME; body part mapping uses RFC 934 encapsulation, not MIME.

RFC1149.title: Standard for the transmission of IP datagrams on avian carriers
RFC1149.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC specifying encapsulation of IP datagrams on scrolls of paper wrapped around birds' legs as an experimental link technology.

humor.why: The document is a dated 1 April parody of a link-layer specification, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs subject.
humor.quote: Avian carriers can provide high delay, low throughput, and low altitude service.

rejected.why: IP datagrams are the payload being carried, but the document does not specify or analyse IP itself.
It parodies a link-layer encapsulation, but it is a joke, not a real link technology, so the humor tag fits better.
It mentions IP datagrams only as the thing being carried, and it says nothing about the IP layer itself.

RFC1150.title: FYI on FYI: Introduction to the FYI Notes
RFC1150.summary: RFC 1150 introduces the FYI sub-series of RFCs, explaining its purpose, why FYIs are part of the RFC series, format and status rules, relationships to other FYIs, submission and distribution.

user guides.why: The document introduces the FYI (For Your Information) series, which is the user-guide sub-series. It is the first FYI (FYI 1) and describes the series' purpose and procedures.
user guides.quote: The FYI series of notes is designed to provide Internet users with a central repository of information about any topics which relate to the Internet.

RFC series.why: A substantial part covers why FYIs belong to the RFC series, RFC format rules, status statements, and UPDATES/OBSOLETES relationships between documents.
RFC series.quote: Since the FYIs are a part of the RFC series, they must conform to RFC-1111 (Request for Comments on Request for Comments: Instructions to RFC Authors) with respect to format.

rejected.why: FTP is only mentioned as a way to obtain FYIs from the NIC. The document is not about the protocol.
The User Services Working Group review of FYIs is mentioned briefly, but the document is about the FYI series and not the IETF standards process.
Email addresses and mail-based request services appear only as logistics for submitting and obtaining FYIs.

RFC1151.title: Version 2 of the Reliable Data Protocol (RDP)
RFC1151.summary: RFC 1151 updates RFC 908 to RDP version 2: it changes the checksum to the TCP checksum, widens ports to 16 bits, bumps the version number, and corrects ambiguities in the original pseudo-code and window handling.

RDP.why: The whole document revises the RDP specification, changing its header and fixing errors in its state machine and window handling.
RDP.quote: This RFC suggests several updates to the specification of the Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) in RFC-908 based on experience with the protocol.

rejected.why: The document adopts the TCP checksum for RDP, but only as a header change within RDP. It does not address the Internet checksum in its own right.
TCP is only the source of the checksum algorithm RDP now reuses, and the document is not about TCP.

RFC1152.title: Workshop report: Internet research steering group workshop on very-high-speed networks
RFC1152.summary: Report on the 1990 IRSG workshop on very-high-speed (gigabit) networks, summarizing sessions on protocol implementation, applications, optics, ATM/phone system, distributed systems, host interfaces, congestion control, switch architectures and protocol architectures.

congestion control.why: A full session and a major recurring theme covers congestion control, rate vs window flow control, and drop policies in gigabit networks.
congestion control.quote: There was much discussion throughout the workshop of congestion control and flow control.

ATM.why: ATM switching, cell networks, B-ISDN and IP over ATM backbones are discussed across several sessions (switch architectures, host interfaces).
ATM.quote: Gitlin (AT&T Bell Labs) gave a talk on issues and opportunities in broadband telecommunications networks
ATM.section: Session 3: Lightwave Technology and its Implications

internet architecture.why: The protocol architectures session and the architectural discussion address how the Internet architecture should evolve for gigabit speeds.
internet architecture.quote: Guru Parulkar (Washington University, St. Louis) presented a broad view of an Internet architecture in which some portion of the system would operate at gigabit speeds.

workshop reports.why: The document is a workshop report from the IRSG.
workshop reports.quote: This memo is a report on a workshop sponsored by the Internet Research Steering Group.

rejected.why: TCP is mentioned as a high-speed protocol example, but the document is not about TCP itself.
Reservation and quality of service come up, but only as part of broader discussions, not a focus.
Forward error correction is mentioned briefly in a few talks, not a substantial part.
SONET appears in HPPI gateway and backbone discussion only in passing.

gaps.name: high-speed / gigabit networking
gaps.why: The document's central subject is very-high-speed networking research, including host interfaces, switch architectures and gigabit testbeds. The taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC1153.title: Digest message format
RFC1153.summary: Documents the de facto Digest Message Format for enclosing multiple email messages into one composite RFC 822 message for mailing list redistribution, with preamble, separators and trailer rules.

mailing lists.why: The whole document specifies how mailing list moderators build and separate digest messages, a mailing list message format convention.
mailing lists.quote: developed a digest message format to enclose several messages into one composite message for redistribution to the mailing list addressees

message format.why: It specifies the header/body structure of a digest message and which headers of enclosed messages are retained and in what order.
message format.quote: A digest message is a conventional message consisting of a header and body conforming to RFC 822 as clarified in RFC 1123.

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen tags; implied, not listed separately.
The format predates MIME and is a distinct encapsulation convention; MIME is not discussed.
Mail transport is only mentioned in passing (gateway size limits); the document is not about it.

RFC1154.title: Encoding header field for internet messages
RFC1154.summary: RFC 1154 proposes an experimental Encoding header field for RFC 822 mail that splits a message body into multiple parts, each with a keyword-defined encoding (text, message, hex, EVFU, EDI, X.400, uuencode, encrypted).

MIME.why: It defines a multi-part body structure and per-part encodings for mail, the precursor to MIME body structure and encodings, and updates the Content-Type header of RFC 1049.
MIME.quote: The Encoding header field permits the message body itself to be further broken up into parts, each part also separated from the next

message format.why: It defines a new Internet message header field and its syntax (counts, keywords, options, comments) as an extension to RFC 822 format.
message format.quote: RFC 822 [2] defines an electronic mail message to consist of two parts, the message header and the message body

X.400.why: A section defines the X.400 keyword for gateway conversion of unknown X.400 body parts, and the message encoding handles recursive X.400 P2 messages.
X.400.quote: The Encoding header field provides a mechanism for mapping multi-part messages between CCITT X.400 [1] and RFC 822.

EDI.why: It defines an EDI encoding keyword for carrying X12 business documents in mail parts.
EDI.quote: The EDI (Electronic Document Interchange) keyword indicates that the message or part is a business document, formatted according to ANSI X12

rejected.why: Too general; the more specific MIME and message format tags capture the subject.
Only referenced for an 'encrypted' keyword and as a suggested update; the document is not about Privacy Enhanced Mail.
ASCII/ISO 8859-1 is mentioned in the text encoding description, but the document is not about the character set.
Encoding keywords parallel Content-Type values, but the document doesn't set up a media type registry.

RFC1155.title: Structure and identification of management information for TCP/IP-based internets
RFC1155.summary: RFC 1155 specifies the Structure of Management Information (SMI) for TCP/IP networks: the OBJECT IDENTIFIER naming tree, permitted ASN.1 syntax, defined types (Counter, Gauge, etc.) and the OBJECT-TYPE macro used to define MIB objects.

MIB.why: The SMI defines how MIB objects are named, typed and described (OBJECT-TYPE macro, object identifier tree), which is the core of MIB/SMI material.
MIB.quote: This memo describes the common structures and identification scheme for the definition of management information used in managing TCP/IP-based internets.

ASN.1.why: The document restricts the ASN.1 subset usable for object syntax, defines application-wide ASN.1 types and an ASN.1 module (RFC1155-SMI), and specifies use of BER.
ASN.1.quote: Formal descriptions of the structure are given using Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1)

rejected.why: SNMP is a companion protocol; this memo explicitly says it does not specify the management protocol.
Delegation of OID subtrees to IANA is mentioned only as administrative policy, not the main subject.
The more specific MIB tag applies, so the parent topic is implied.

RFC1156.title: Management Information Base for network management of TCP/IP-based internets
RFC1156.summary: RFC 1156 defines the initial Internet MIB (MIB-I): the managed objects for system, interfaces, address translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP and EGP, specified in the SMI for use with SNMP.

MIB.why: The document is the MIB-I module definition itself, defining object groups and ASN.1 object types under the SMI.
MIB.quote: Management Information Base for Network Management of TCP/IP-based Internets, which describes the managed objects contained in the MIB as set forth in this memo

SNMP.why: The MIB is part of the SNMP management framework and is required for SNMP-managed implementations, though the protocol is defined elsewhere.
SNMP.quote: together with its companion memos which describe the structure of management information along with the initial network management protocol

rejected.why: ICMP group is only counters of ICMP messages; the document does not specify ICMP.
TCP group exposes TCP statistics and connection state; TCP itself is not specified or extended.
EGP counters and neighbor table are instrumented, but EGP protocol is not the subject.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to define objects.
Parent of MIB and SNMP, which are tagged directly, so it is implied.

RFC1157.title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC1157.summary: RFC 1157 specifies SNMP version 1, the application protocol for inspecting and altering management variables on network elements, including its architecture, PDUs (Get, GetNext, Set, Response, Trap), community-based administrative model and ASN.1 definitions.

SNMP.why: The document is the core SNMPv1 protocol specification, covering architecture, community model, PDU procedures and traps.
SNMP.quote: This memo defines a simple protocol by which management information for a network element may be inspected or altered by logically remote users.

rejected.why: The MIB and SMI are defined in the companion RFCs 1155 and 1156. This memo only references them and defines naming of object instances.
ASN.1 and BER are the notation and encoding used to define the PDUs. The document does not specify ASN.1 itself.
UDP is only the transport the messages are carried over, on ports 161 and 162. Nothing new is defined about UDP.
The community-name authentication scheme is only an architectural placeholder. It is part of the SNMP model and not a separate subject.

RFC1158.title: Management Information Base for network management of TCP/IP-based internets: MIB-II
RFC1158.summary: Defines MIB-II, the second version of the SNMP Management Information Base, specifying managed object groups (system, interfaces, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, EGP, SNMP) and instance naming for use with SNMP.

MIB.why: The whole document is a MIB module definition (RFC1158-MIB) with object groups and their SMI definitions.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the second version of the Management Information Base (MIB-II) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

SNMP.why: Defines SNMP instance naming and an SNMP statistics group (snmpInPkts etc.); it is the MIB for the SNMP framework.
SNMP.quote: Identification of OBJECT instances for use with the SNMP

rejected.why: ICMP counters are only managed objects in the MIB; the document does not specify ICMP.
TCP group objects are monitoring variables; TCP itself is not specified.
EGP group objects are monitoring variables; EGP is not specified.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for object definitions, not the subject.
IP group is a set of managed objects, not a specification of IP.

RFC1159.title: Message Send Protocol
RFC1159.summary: Experimental protocol for sending a short message to a user's terminal on a host, over TCP or UDP port 18, with a defined message syntax.

instant messaging.why: The protocol delivers short real-time messages to a user's terminal, similar to Unix write. Instant messaging is the closest taxonomy fit.
instant messaging.quote: The Message Send Protocol is used to send a short message to a given user on a given terminal on a given host.

rejected.why: TCP is only one of two transports for the service and the document does not extend or specify TCP.
UDP is a transport substrate here; the document defines nothing new about UDP.
SMTP's SEND command is mentioned only for comparison; the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
The two transport bindings are the service definition itself, not a mapping of another protocol onto a transport.

RFC1160.title: Internet Activities Board
RFC1160.summary: RFC 1160 (Cerf, 1990) describes the history, structure, functions and near-term agenda of the Internet Activities Board and its subsidiary IETF and IRTF task forces.

IETF process.why: The document describes how the IAB, IETF, IESG and IRTF are organised and how standards are set (Proposed, Draft, Standard). That is the standards process and its administration.
IETF process.quote: The IAB performs the following functions: 1) Sets Internet Standards, 2) Manages the RFC publication process, 3) Reviews the operation of the IETF and IRTF

internet history.why: The introduction is a history of packet switching, the TCP/IP suite, the ICCB and the IAB, and the government coordinating bodies that supported them.
internet history.quote: In 1979, it was necessary to form an informal committee to guide the technical evolution of the protocol suite. This group was called the Internet Configuration Control Board

rejected.why: The RFC series and its editor are described only briefly, as the IAB's publication vehicle. The document is not mainly about the series.
X.500 is mentioned once, as an example white pages facility in the agenda. It is not a subject of the document.
OSI coexistence is one of seven agenda items, mentioned briefly. The document does not address OSI protocols in depth.
The ARPANET and the NCP-to-TCP/IP conversion appear only as historical background.
X.400 and RFC 822 interoperation and privacy-enhanced mail appear only in a short agenda paragraph.
The agenda mentions scaling and architectural limits only in passing. The document is about organisation, not architectural principles.

gaps.name: Internet Activities Board (IAB) organisation and its history
gaps.why: The document is mostly about the IAB as a body and its subsidiary groups (IETF, IRTF, IESG, IRSG). The taxonomy has no IAB-specific tag, so IETF process is the closest fit.

RFC1161.title: SNMP over OSI
RFC1161.summary: Experimental memo defining how to run SNMP over OSI transport services (CLTS and COTS), including transport selector and addressing conventions for CLNP, TP4 and TP0/X.25.

SNMP.why: The document specifies how SNMP is mapped onto OSI transport services, so it is about SNMP's transport bindings.
SNMP.quote: This memo defines an experimental means for running the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) over OSI transports.

OSI.why: A substantial part concerns OSI transport services (CLNP, TP4, TP0/X.25) and selectors used to carry SNMP, so readers of OSI coexistence would want it.
OSI.quote: this memo describes mappings from the SNMP onto both the COTS and the CLTS.

transport mapping.why: The document is a binding of one protocol onto other transports, with addressing conventions.
transport mapping.quote: the mapping consists of establishing a transport connection, sending one or more SNMP messages on that connection, and then releasing the transport connection.

rejected.why: CLNP is only the network service underlying the transport; the document does not specify it.
X.25 is only an underlying service with a protocol-ID convention; the document is not about X.25 itself.
UDP is the reference baseline for comparison and addressing example, not specified here.
SMI and MIB are cited as companion standards but not addressed by this document.

RFC1162.title: Connectionless Network Protocol (ISO 8473) and End System to Intermediate System (ISO 9542) Management Information Base
RFC1162.summary: Defines an experimental SNMP MIB for managing ISO 8473 CLNP and ISO 9542 ES-IS, with objects for CLNP statistics, routing and address translation tables, error PDU counters, and ES-IS PDU counters.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define MIB objects (CLNS-MIB module) in SMI, with object definitions and instance naming for SNMP.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an experimental portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

CLNP.why: The MIB covers management of CLNP and ES-IS (forwarding, reassembly, routing table, error PDUs, ESH/ISH/RDU counters), so it belongs under CLNP.
CLNP.quote: These objects can be used when the ISO Connectionless-mode Network Protocol [9] and End System to Intermediate System [10] protocols are present.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines MIB objects, not SNMP itself (MIB is the more specific tag).
ASN.1 is only the notation used for the object definitions, not the subject.
CLNP is the more specific child tag under OSI; the OSI parent is implied.
The address translation tables are CLNP-to-physical mappings, not ARP.
is-is appears only as a clnpRouteProto enumeration value, not as a subject.

gaps.name: ES-IS (ISO 9542 End System to Intermediate System)
gaps.why: The document covers an ES-IS MIB group, but the taxonomy has no tag for the ES-IS protocol; it is only partly covered by the CLNP and OSI tags.

RFC1163.title: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
RFC1163.summary: RFC 1163 specifies BGP version 2, an inter-autonomous-system routing protocol, covering message formats, path attributes, error handling, version negotiation, the finite state machine, and update handling; it obsoletes RFC 1105.

BGP.why: The document is the BGP version 2 protocol specification: messages, path attributes, FSM, error handling and update processing.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport BGP runs over; Appendix 3 gives minor TCP option usage but the document is not about TCP.
EGP is mentioned only as predecessor experience; the document specifies BGP, not EGP.
Policy and hop-by-hop paradigm are discussed briefly, but the document is a protocol specification, with architecture left to the companion RFC 1164.

RFC1164.title: Application of the Border Gateway Protocol in the Internet
RFC1164.summary: RFC 1164 describes how BGP (version 1) is applied in the Internet: AS topology model, policy expression and path selection with a configuration language, interaction between BGP and IGPs, and implementation recommendations.

BGP.why: The whole document is about applying BGP: topology, policy, path selection, IGP interaction and implementation advice.
BGP.quote: This paper discusses the use of BGP in the Internet environment.

routing architecture.why: A substantial part covers inter-AS routing design: stub, multihomed and transit AS categories, and how BGP and an IGP interact within an AS.
routing architecture.quote: Ensuring consistency of routing information between BGP and an IGP within an AS is a significant issue and is discussed at length later in this paper.

rejected.why: RIP is only mentioned as an example of an IGP that cannot carry BGP information or tag routes, and as a contrast for path metrics.
EGP is mentioned as a protocol that stub and multihomed ASs may run and as a route origin type. The document is not about EGP.
Encapsulation to the exit gateway is one short method in Section 5.2.3. It is not a main subject.
TCP is only the transport BGP runs over. Section 6.3 gives stream-processing advice but specifies nothing new about TCP.
Internal BGP is discussed only in general terms. There is no route reflection or confederation.

RFC1165.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP) over the OSI Remote Operations Service
RFC1165.summary: Experimental spec for running NTP over the OSI Remote Operations Service (ROS) on OSI/X.25 stacks, with an ASN.1 definition of NTP operations and packet, and connection-based reachability optimisations.

NTP.why: The document specifies how NTP operates over ROS, including modified peer states and protocol simplifications, so NTP readers would want it.
NTP.quote: This document describes the Remote Operations and Abstract Syntax for the operation of the Network Time Protocol (NTP) over an ISO OSI stack.

ASN.1.why: The appendix gives a full ASN.1 module with ROS operations and data types for the NTP packet and clock info; this is a substantial part of the document.
ASN.1.quote: NTP DEFINITIONS ::=

rejected.why: X.25 is only the underlying network service over which ROS ran in the prototype; the document does not specify anything about it.
The OSI tag covers network-layer protocols and IP coexistence; this is an application-layer use of OSI upper layers, not about CLNP or the network layer.
Implied by the NTP tag as its parent, so not listed separately.
UDP-based NTP is mentioned only for interworking comparison; it is not what the document specifies.

gaps.name: OSI Remote Operations Service (ROS)
gaps.why: The document's transport substrate is ROS/ROSE with ASN.1 bindings; the taxonomy has no tag for OSI application-layer services such as ROS or ACSE.

RFC1166.title: Internet numbers
RFC1166.summary: RFC 1166 is a 1990 status report listing assigned IP network numbers (Class A/B/C) and autonomous system numbers, with the address class structure and special addresses, plus contact references.

addressing.why: The document is a registry of IP network number assignments, with explanation of address classes A-D, dotted decimal notation and special addresses. That is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: This Network Working Group Request for Comments documents the currently assigned network numbers and gateway autonomous systems.

rejected.why: The document leans on IPv4 addressing but is an assignment registry rather than a specification of the protocol; addressing is the better fit.
It is a precursor to IANA number registries, but it is a snapshot of assignments by the DDN NIC, not guidance on IANA registries or stewardship.
WHOIS/NICNAME is mentioned only as a way to look up contacts.
The autonomous system numbers are listed, but BGP itself is not discussed.
The document covers classful addressing, which predates CIDR.

gaps.name: Autonomous system numbers
gaps.why: The document lists AS number assignments, and the taxonomy has no tag for AS number registry or allocation. The closest is routing or BGP, which don't fit well.

RFC1167.title: Thoughts on the National Research and Education Network
RFC1167.summary: Vint Cerf's 1990 informational essay outlining factors shaping the U.S. National Research and Education Network, including its evolution from the Internet, constituencies, commercial service provision, and operations.

internet architecture.why: The document discusses architectural principles of the NREN evolving from the Internet: layered protocols, network types, multi-protocol support, and interconnection with other networks.
internet architecture.quote: The NREN in the U.S. will evolve from the existing Internet base.

internet history.why: A substantial part recounts the history of Internet service provision from ARPANET to NSFNET and intermediate-level networks, shaping the NREN's future.
internet history.quote: In its earliest stages, the Internet consisted solely of government-sponsored networks such as the Defense Department's ARPANET, Packet Radio Networks and Packet Satellite Networks.

rejected.why: ARPANET is mentioned only as historical context for the funding and service-provider model, not as the document's subject.
Operations, accounting and monitoring agreements are mentioned briefly as needs, but the document does not address network management mechanisms in depth.
OSI protocol stacks are noted as needing support alongside TCP/IP, but only in a single passing point.
The discussion of an operational forum and funding is about NREN policy and economics, not governance of Internet standards or administration.

gaps.name: National Research and Education Network (NREN) policy, funding and commercialization
gaps.why: The document is mainly about network policy, funding models (vouchers, subsidies) and commercial service provision, which the taxonomy has no tag for.

RFC1168.title: Intermail and Commercial Mail Relay services
RFC1168.summary: Informational RFC describing the history, design, operation and problems of ISI's Intermail and Commercial Mail Relay store-and-forward gateways between Internet mail and commercial mail systems (Telemail, MCI Mail, Dialcom).

email.why: The whole document is about mail relaying and gateway interoperation between Internet email and other mail systems, including addressing, forwarding headers and error handling.
email.quote: The Intermail and Commercial Mail Relay (CMR) services described in this paper were developed to provide a means for sending mail between the Internet and these commercial mail systems.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the substrate by which Internet mail reaches the relay; the document does not specify or extend it.
X.400 appears only briefly, in the Sprint X.400 address syntax translation and as a future addressing option. It is not a main subject.
DNS is mentioned in a problems paragraph, a future-directions suggestion and Appendix D as background, not as a subject of the document.
UUCP is described only in Appendix A as one of the networks connected via mail relays, not as a subject.
The Simple Forwarding Header is a body-level addressing convention, not Internet message header format. RFC 822 is only referenced.

RFC1169.title: Explaining the role of GOSIP
RFC1169.summary: IAB/FNC informational statement explaining the role, applicability, exclusivity, waivers and implementation of the U.S. Government OSI Profile (GOSIP, FIPS 146) and the roles of the IETF and agencies in integrating OSI with TCP/IP in the Internet.

OSI.why: The whole document explains GOSIP, a profile of OSI protocols, and how OSI is to be integrated and coexist with TCP/IP in the Internet. The OSI tag covers this OSI coexistence subject.
OSI.quote: The U.S. Government OSI Profile (GOSIP) is a necessary tool for planning OSI integration.

rejected.why: The document discusses government procurement policy and agency roles, but it is not about how Internet standards are governed or published. The IETF-role section is incidental.
ISO 8473 routing in the NSFnet backbone is mentioned once. The document is not about CLNP itself.
It is a 1990 policy statement, not a retrospective or history of the Internet.
FTP and FTAM are mentioned only as ways to download the GOSIP documents in the appendix. This is boilerplate-like and not the subject.

gaps.name: GOSIP (U.S. Government OSI Profile) / government procurement policy
gaps.why: The document is mainly about a government OSI profile and procurement mandates. The taxonomy has only OSI network-layer coexistence, so the policy and procurement angle has no dedicated tag.

RFC1170.title: Public key standards and licenses
RFC1170.summary: A statement by Public Key Partners listing the public-key patents it holds sublicensing rights to (Diffie-Hellman, Hellman-Merkle, RSA, Hellman-Pohlig) and promising reasonable, non-discriminatory licenses for RSA signatures in any adopted digital signature standard.

IPR.why: The whole memo is a patent licensing statement about public key cryptography patents and the availability of licenses, which is intellectual property rights content.
IPR.quote: Public Key Partners hereby gives its assurance that licenses to practice RSA signatures will be available under reasonable terms and conditions on a non-discriminatory basis.

RSA.why: RSA signatures and the RSA patent are the focus of the licensing assurance and the endorsement for a digital signature standard.
RSA.quote: Public Key Partners strongly endorses its incorporations in a digital signature standard.

rejected.why: The RSA tag is more specific; the memo does not specify algorithms or parameters, only licensing.
Public key technology is discussed only in terms of patents, not certificates or infrastructure.

RFC1171.title: Point-to-Point Protocol for the transmission of multi-protocol datagrams over Point-to-Point links
RFC1171.summary: Specifies the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP): HDLC-based framing for serial links, the Link Control Protocol automaton and packets, and the IP Control Protocol (IPCP) for carrying IP over PPP.

PPP.why: The whole document defines PPP encapsulation, LCP and the IP NCP (IPCP), so the PPP tag fits as the primary subject.
PPP.quote: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) provides a method for transmitting datagrams over serial point-to-point links.

rejected.why: Appendix B gives a fast table-driven FCS implementation, but it is a small implementation aid for PPP framing. The document is not about CRC polynomial choice.
IPCP and IP-over-PPP encapsulation are specified, but the document is about the link protocol and IP is only the first network protocol carried.
Nothing in the document is specific to ISDN. Only dial-up and serial circuits are mentioned.
X.25 LAPB is cited only as a related HDLC-based framing. It is not the subject.

gaps.name: HDLC framing
gaps.why: The document is built on HDLC framing, including asynchronous HDLC in Appendix A, and the taxonomy has no HDLC tag. PPP covers it adequately.

RFC1172.title: Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) initial configuration options
RFC1172.summary: Defines the initial PPP LCP and IPCP configuration options, the Link Quality Monitoring mechanism, and the simple Password Authentication Protocol (PAP).

PPP.why: The whole document specifies PPP LCP and IPCP options, Link Quality Monitoring and PAP, which are all parts of PPP and its control protocols.
PPP.quote: This document defines the intial options used by the LCP and IPCP. It also defines a method of Link Quality Monitoring and a simple authentication scheme.

rejected.why: PAP is defined in Section 4, but it is a PPP-specific authentication protocol. The PPP tag covers it, and the document is not about cross-protocol authentication.
Protocol-field and address/control-field compression are LCP options, and IPCP only negotiates a Van Jacobson compression type. The document does not specify any header compression scheme.
IPCP negotiates IP addresses, but only as PPP configuration options. The document is not about IPv4 itself.
Link Quality Monitoring counts packets and octets, but it is a PPP LCP mechanism and not a general measurement methodology.

RFC1173.title: Responsibilities of host and network managers: A summary of the "oral tradition" of the Internet
RFC1173.summary: Informational RFC summarizing the conventions for Internet host and network managers: accessibility, contact registration, postmaster mailboxes, problem escalation, and security awareness.

operational security.why: A substantial part of the document covers operational security practices for managers: accepting other sites' security issues, avoiding open accounts and terminal servers, and each manager's responsibility for host security.
operational security.quote: Every host and network manager MUST be aware that the Internet as presently constituted is NOT secure.

network management.why: The document sets out the operational responsibilities and accessibility requirements of network and host managers. It is about the practice of running networks, not management protocols.
network management.quote: One or more individuals are responsible for every IP net or subnet which is connected to the Internet.

rejected.why: The postmaster mailbox is a section of the document, but the document is about manager responsibilities and does not specify or extend email.
The document is a policy-like statement of conventions, but it is not about how standards are governed or published. The RFC Editor's note only says it may inform future policy.
It mentions the decentralized structure of the Internet only briefly, as motivation. It does not discuss architectural principles.

gaps.name: Host and network manager responsibilities / site operational conventions
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the human operational responsibilities of site and network administrators. 'network management' and 'operational security' cover it only approximately.

RFC1174.title: IAB recommended policy on distributing internet identifier assignment and IAB recommended policy change to internet "connected" status
RFC1174.summary: IAB recommendations to the FNC to distribute Internet network and AS number assignment via delegated registries under the IANA/IR, and to replace "connected" status with recorded acceptable-use/transit policies, allowing any registered network into the DNS.

IANA.why: The first recommendation is about how the IANA and Internet Registry allocate and delegate assignment of numeric identifiers (network and AS numbers).
IANA.quote: the IR would also allocate to organizations approved by the Coordinating Committee for Intercontinental Research Networking (CCIRN) blocks of network and autonomous system numbers

addressing.why: Concerns the allocation, registration policy and registry administration of IP network number space, including the connected-status policy for registered networks.
addressing.quote: It is also essential to take into consideration that such identifiers, particularly network identifiers of class A and B type, will become an increasingly scarce commodity

rejected.why: DNS is discussed in Attachment 2 only as a policy point (registration in the DNS should not depend on connected status); the document does not specify or extend DNS.
Policy-based routing is mentioned in the discussion as motivation, but the document is about registry policy, not routing mechanisms.
Parent of IANA; the more specific IANA tag fits, so the parent is not listed.
Autonomous system numbers are mentioned only as identifiers to be registered, not BGP protocol or operations.

RFC1175.title: FYI on where to start: A bibliography of internetworking information
RFC1175.summary: FYI 3 is a user-oriented annotated bibliography of introductory internetworking resources (articles, books, guides, newsletters, reports, and key RFC abstracts) for beginner and intermediate Internet users.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory guide for Internet users, a starting-point bibliography prepared by the User Services Working Group.
user guides.quote: The intent of this bibliography is to offer a representative collection of resources of information that will help the reader become familiar with the concepts of internetworking.

rejected.why: The RFC series section describes how RFCs are obtained and published, but it is only one section of a general bibliography, so the document is not about the series itself.
Anonymous FTP is explained only as a way to retrieve the listed files. The document does not specify or analyse FTP.
DNS appears only as a book entry and as RFC 1034/1035 abstracts in a list of references. The document is not about DNS.
A glossaries section lists glossary resources, but the document is not itself a glossary or definition set.
TCP is mentioned throughout as part of the TCP/IP suite. It is only a bibliography entry and a one-line RFC abstract.
Some entries are historical, such as the worm report and NSFNET, but the document is a bibliography, not a history.

RFC1176.title: Interactive Mail Access Protocol: Version 2
RFC1176.summary: RFC 1176 specifies IMAP2, an experimental protocol letting clients access and manage mail on a remote mailbox server, with tagged commands, unsolicited responses, server-side search and envelope parsing; it obsoletes RFC 1064.

IMAP.why: The whole document is the specification of IMAP2, including commands, responses, formal syntax and implementation notes.
IMAP.quote: The intent of the Interactive Mail Access Protocol, Version 2 (IMAP2) is to allow a workstation, personal computer, or similar small machine to access electronic mail from a mailbox server.

rejected.why: POP is only discussed as a comparison point; the document specifies IMAP2, not POP.
SMTP is mentioned only as the separate mail posting mechanism; IMAP2 does not handle submission.
RFC 822 headers are parsed into envelopes, but the document does not define the message format itself.
TCP is only the reliable stream substrate (port 143).
Mentioned in passing as an alternative way to establish identity, not a subject of the document.

RFC1177.title: FYI on Questions and Answers: Answers to commonly asked "new internet user" questions
RFC1177.summary: FYI 4 is a new-user Q&A guide covering the Internet, TCP/IP, RFCs, Internet organizations (IAB, IETF, IRTF, IANA, NIC, IR), services such as WHOIS, X.500 white pages, Usenet and anonymous FTP, mailing lists, and a condensed glossary.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory guide for new Internet users, which is exactly what the user guides subject covers.
user guides.quote: New users joining the Internet community for the first time have had the same questions as did everyone else who has ever joined.

terminology.why: The glossary takes up roughly a third of the document and defines networking terms and acronyms.
terminology.quote: Below is a condensed glossary to assist in making some sense of the Internet world.

RFC series.why: A full section explains what RFCs are, how to submit them, how to obtain them and which ones are standards.
RFC series.quote: The Request for Comments documents (RFCs) are working notes of the Internet research and development community.

IETF process.why: The document describes the IAB, IETF, IESG, IRTF and their roles, and gives mailing list subscription details.
IETF process.quote: The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) ... To help coordinate the operation, management and evolution of the Internet, the IAB established the Internet Engineering Task Force
IETF process.section: 6. Questions about Internet Organizations and Contacts

WHOIS.why: Several Q&As explain how to use and register in the WHOIS database.
WHOIS.quote: How do I use the WHOIS program at the DDN NIC?

rejected.why: The document has a short Q&A about IANA, but it is one of many topics and is not a substantial treatment of IANA registries.
The PSI White Pages pilot, which is based on X.500, is only mentioned briefly.
Anonymous FTP is used as the way to retrieve RFCs and gets a short Q&A, but the document is not about the protocol.
The glossary has historical entries such as ARPANET and BBN, but the document is not a retrospective.
Usenet gets only two short Q&As of general description.
The TCP/IP overview is basic, and the document does not discuss architectural principles.

RFC1178.title: Choosing a name for your computer
RFC1178.summary: FYI 5 (republished CACM essay) giving guidelines on what to do and not do when choosing a hostname for a computer, covering ambiguity, length, spelling, character set, case, and domain-like names.

hostnames.why: The whole document is a set of guidelines for choosing host names, including length, characters, case, digits and reuse of hostnames.
hostnames.quote: This essay is only concerned with choosing a "good" name.

user guides.why: It is an FYI-series introductory guide for Internet users and administrators, so readers of the user guides subject would expect it.
user guides.quote: This FYI RFC is a republication of a Communications of the ACM article on guidelines on what to do and what not to do

rejected.why: The essay assumes basic DNS knowledge and touches on domain-qualified names, but does not specify or analyse DNS protocol or operations.
Parent of hostnames; the more specific hostnames tag fits, so the ancestor is implied.
Mail addresses appear only as examples of where a host name is used.

RFC1179.title: Line printer daemon protocol
RFC1179.summary: Informational RFC describing the existing Berkeley Unix Line Printer Daemon (LPR/LPD) protocol: TCP port 515 daemon commands, receive-job subcommands, and control file line formats.

LPD.why: The whole document specifies the LPD protocol: daemon commands, receive-job subcommands, and control file formats.
LPD.quote: This RFC describes the protocols with which a line printer daemon client may control printing.

rejected.why: LPR runs over TCP port 515 but TCP is only the substrate; the document specifies nothing new about TCP.
IPP is a different printing protocol; this document does not discuss it.
ASCII is used for commands and control files but is only the encoding, not the subject.

RFC1180.title: TCP/IP tutorial
RFC1180.summary: A 1991 informational tutorial on the TCP/IP protocol suite, explaining layering, Ethernet, ARP, IP routing with route tables, UDP, TCP and common applications.

internet layer.why: The core of the tutorial is IP datagram forwarding, direct and indirect routing, addressing and route tables, and the overall protocol suite structure, which is the general internet-layer subject.
internet layer.quote: The IP module is central to internet technology and the essence of IP is its route table.

ARP.why: A full section explains the ARP table, request/response exchange and queuing of outgoing packets.
ARP.quote: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is used to translate IP addresses to Ethernet addresses.

TCP.why: A dedicated section describes TCP's service, ports, virtual circuit and sliding window.
TCP.quote: TCP offers a connection-oriented byte stream, instead of a connectionless datagram delivery service.

UDP.why: A dedicated section covers UDP ports, message boundaries and checksum.
UDP.quote: UDP is a connectionless datagram delivery service that does not guarantee delivery.

Ethernet.why: The tutorial uses Ethernet as the example medium and includes a section reviewing Ethernet frames, addresses and CSMA/CD.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet uses CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense and Multiple Access with Collision Detection).

rejected.why: Only briefly described as an example UDP application, not a subject of the document.
Brief application description only.
Brief application description only.
One-paragraph application example.
Class C addressing and network numbers are explained only as part of routing.
Mentioned only in passing as a solution to hosts-file maintenance.

RFC1181.title: RIPE Terms of Reference
RFC1181.summary: Describes the Terms of Reference of RIPE, the European IP network coordination body, covering its objectives of administrative and technical coordination, forum role, and interconnection promotion.

internet governance.why: The document defines the charter of a coordinating organisation for European IP networks, which is a matter of how Internet administration is organised.
internet governance.quote: The objective of RIPE is to ensure the necessary administrative and technical coordination to allow the operation and expansion of a pan-European IP network.

rejected.why: The terms mention agreement on common network management practices, but only as one objective. The document does not specify any management protocol or practice.
RIPE is not part of the IETF, and the document describes no IETF procedures.
Interconnection of networks is mentioned only as an objective. No routing content is given.

gaps.name: Regional coordination bodies / RIPE
gaps.why: The document is the charter of a regional Internet coordination organisation (RIPE). The taxonomy has no tag for regional registries or operator coordination groups, so only the broad internet governance topic fits.

RFC1183.title: New DNS RR Definitions
RFC1183.summary: RFC 1183 defines five experimental DNS resource record types: AFSDB (AFS/DCE cell database server location), RP (responsible person), X25, ISDN, and RT (route-through binding).

DNS.why: The document specifies new DNS resource record types (AFSDB, RP, X25, ISDN, RT), including their formats and additional section processing.
DNS.quote: This RFC defines the format of new Resource Records (RRs) for the Domain Name System (DNS), and reserves corresponding DNS type mnemonics and numerical codes.

AFS.why: A whole section defines the AFSDB RR for locating AFS cell database servers, and the taxonomy's AFS tag covers DNS-based service discovery for AFS cells.
AFS.quote: The AFS (originally the Andrew File System) system uses the DNS to map from a domain name to the name of an AFS cell database server.

rejected.why: X.25 addresses are only stored in the new X25 RR. The document does not specify X.25 itself or IP over X.25.
The ISDN RR just holds E.164 numbers in the DNS. The document is not about ISDN access.
AFSDB does locate servers, but the AFS tag already covers that and sits under storage, so the generic topic adds nothing.
MX is not in the taxonomy. It is only a model for the RT and AFSDB record encodings.

RFC1184.title: Telnet Linemode Option
RFC1184.summary: Specifies the Telnet LINEMODE option, which lets the client do local line editing and signal trapping, with MODE, FORWARDMASK and SLC (special character) suboptions and new IAC ABORT/SUSP/EOF commands.

Telnet.why: The whole document defines a Telnet option, its suboptions, new Telnet commands and implementation rules, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: Linemode Telnet is a way of doing terminal character processing on the client side of a Telnet connection.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The urgent-data use for Synch is mentioned in passing and nothing new is defined for TCP.
ASCII codes are used for the character and mask definitions, but the document is not about the character set.
The SLC names and codes are protocol definitions, not a glossary.

RFC1185.title: TCP Extension for High-Speed Paths
RFC1185.summary: RFC 1185 specifies an experimental TCP extension that uses sender timestamps (the RFC 1072 Echo option) to reject old duplicate segments, which protects against sequence number wrap-around on high-speed paths and against segments from earlier connection incarnations.

TCP.why: The document extends TCP with timestamp-based old-duplicate rejection (PAWS). It also covers TCP sequence numbers, MSL, TIME-WAIT and header prediction, so TCP is the subject.
TCP.quote: This memo describes a small extension to TCP to support reliable operation over very high-speed paths, using sender timestamps transmitted using the TCP Echo option

rejected.why: The document is about reliability under sequence wrap-around. It does not address congestion control. RTT measurement is mentioned only as a side benefit of the timestamps.
The IP TTL field is mentioned only as the mechanism that enforces MSL. The document does not specify anything about IPv4.
FDDI appears only as an example speed in the Twrap table and a worked example. The document is not about IP over FDDI.

RFC1186.title: MD4 Message Digest Algorithm
RFC1186.summary: Specifies the MD4 message digest algorithm (128-bit hash), with an optional 256-bit extension and a C reference implementation, as an informational memo.

MD5.why: The whole document specifies MD4. The MD5 tag covers the MD2/MD4/MD5 message digests, and no narrower tag exists for MD4.
