MD5.quote: This note describes the MD4 message digest algorithm. The algorithm takes as input an input message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit "fingerprint"

rejected.why: RSA is mentioned only as the signature scheme MD4 would be used with. The document does not specify or analyse RSA.
SHA is a different hash family and is not discussed.
The document defines a plain digest, not a keyed MAC.

RFC1187.title: Bulk Table Retrieval with the SNMP
RFC1187.summary: Experimental memo describing pipelined and parallel algorithms that let an SNMP management station retrieve whole tables efficiently using multiple outstanding get-next requests, with adaptive thread counts and timeouts.

SNMP.why: The whole document is about how to use SNMP's get-next operator efficiently for table retrieval, including observations on incorrect agent implementations.
SNMP.quote: This memo reports an interesting family of algorithms for bulk table retrieval using the Simple Network Management Protocol

rejected.why: Tables such as ipRoutingTable are used only as examples; the document does not define or discuss MIB modules or the SMI.
Only acknowledged as inspiration for the adaptive timer approach; SNMP here runs over UDP and TCP is not the subject.
Throughput figures are reported for the algorithms, but the document is not about measuring network performance.

RFC1188.title: Proposed Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over FDDI Networks
RFC1188.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IP datagrams and ARP over FDDI networks using 802.2 LLC/SNAP, including ARP parameters, multicast mapping, MTU of 4352, and MAC/LLC details.

FDDI.why: The whole document defines IP over FDDI: encapsulation, MTU, MAC and LLC details.
FDDI.quote: This document specifies a method for the use of IP and ARP on FDDI networks.

rejected.why: ARP is used with FDDI-specific parameters, but the document does not define or extend ARP itself. It only profiles it for FDDI, which the FDDI tag covers.
The multicast address mapping is a short section applying RFC 1112 to FDDI, not a main subject.
The document mentions IEEE 802.5 only as a related MAC standard. It is about FDDI.
Ethernet is mentioned only for bridged-environment interoperability, such as the ARP hardware type code.

RFC1189.title: Common Management Information Services and Protocols for the Internet (CMOT and CMIP)
RFC1189.summary: RFC 1189 specifies the CMOT/CMIP profile: implementor agreements for using ISO CMIS/CMIP network management over TCP/UDP/IP (via the Lightweight Presentation Protocol) and over OSI stacks, including association negotiation and conformance requirements.

CMIP.why: The whole document profiles CMIS/CMIP, defining CMOT (CMIP over TCP/IP) and CMIP over OSI, association types, application context names and implementation agreements.
CMIP.quote: This memo defines a network management architecture that uses the International Organization for Standardization's (ISO) Common Management Information Services/Common Management Information Protocol (CMIS/CMIP) in the Internet.

rejected.why: Only cited in references as the alternative; the document is not about SNMP.
OSI network-layer protocols are not the subject; OSI upper layers are only the stack CMIP runs on.
Required background standard and used for application context names, but not specified or extended here.
The Internet MIB is referenced as the information carried, but MIB semantics were explicitly removed from this document.
Substrate for the lightweight presentation protocol only.
Substrate for the lightweight presentation protocol only.

RFC1190.title: Experimental Internet Stream Protocol: Version 2 (ST-II)
RFC1190.summary: Specifies ST-II, the experimental Internet Stream Protocol version 2: an IP-layer, stream-oriented protocol with resource reservation, the SCMP control protocol, HID negotiation, failure recovery and multicast support for real-time applications.

ST-II.why: The whole document is the ST-II protocol specification, including SCMP, PDUs, options and recovery.
ST-II.quote: This memo defines the Internet Stream Protocol, Version 2 (ST-II), an IP-layer protocol that provides end-to-end guaranteed service across an internet.

rejected.why: Multicast is used for efficient forwarding and HID negotiation, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership in its own right.
FlowSpec and resource reservation are central, but ST-II is the specific technology and is tagged directly.
ST is a sibling protocol to IP and is encapsulated in IP, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
TCP is only cited as a higher layer protocol and for retransmission timer algorithms.
IP encapsulation of ST is a minor subsection, not the main subject.

RFC1191.title: Path MTU discovery
RFC1191.summary: RFC 1191 specifies Path MTU Discovery for IPv4, using the DF bit and a modified ICMP "fragmentation needed" message carrying the Next-Hop MTU, with host and router behaviour and implementation guidance.

PMTUD.why: The whole document specifies Path MTU Discovery: host and router behaviour, PMTU caching, aging, and plateau tables.
PMTUD.quote: This memo describes a technique for dynamically discovering the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of an arbitrary internet path.

ICMP.why: The document changes the ICMP Destination Unreachable (code 4, fragmentation needed) message format to add the Next-Hop MTU field, and specifies how hosts process it.
ICMP.quote: the router MUST include the MTU of that next-hop network in the low-order 16 bits of the ICMP header field that is labelled "unused"

rejected.why: TCP MSS handling and TCP-layer actions are covered, but only as a consumer of PMTU information; the document is not about TCP itself.
The mechanism operates on IPv4 and its DF bit, but the document is about PMTU discovery, which has its own tag.
NFS is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that uses intentional fragmentation, with a short recommendation.
UDP is mentioned only as an example of a packetization layer.

RFC1192.title: Commercialization of the Internet summary report
RFC1192.summary: Workshop summary report on policy issues in commercializing and privatizing the Internet, NSFNET backbone subsidies, and the proposed NREN.

internet history.why: The report is a 1990 retrospective-style record of the Internet's transition from government-funded NSFNET/ARPANET to commercial service, covering NSFNET funding, regional networks, and the NREN. Readers of Internet history would want it.
internet history.quote: the workshop was designed to explore the issues involved in the commercialization of the Internet, including the envisioned National Research and Education Network (NREN).

rejected.why: The document addresses funding, policy and economics, not architectural principles, despite the figures on generalization of structure.
The ARPANET is mentioned only as a historical example of a government-underwritten network. The document does not cover its protocols or operations.
SMTP and NNTP appear only in a proposal to bar mail and news protocols from the backbone as a privatization measure. The document does not specify or analyse them.
X.400 is mentioned in passing as a possible improved mail functionality. It is not a subject of the document.
The document deals with funding and commercialization policy, not how the Internet or its standards are governed or developed.

gaps.name: Internet commercialization and funding policy (NSFNET, NREN)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about the economics, subsidy and policy of the Internet and the NREN. The taxonomy has no tag for Internet policy or economics, so only the history tag fits loosely.

RFC1193.title: Client requirements for real-time communication services
RFC1193.summary: Informational 1990 memo by Ferrari describing client requirements for real-time (performance-guaranteed) communication services: delay, jitter, throughput and reliability bounds, other properties, translation across protocol layers, and examples.

QoS.why: The whole document defines client-specified performance guarantees (delay, jitter, throughput, reliability bounds) and how to translate them across layers, which is quality of service requirements.
QoS.quote: A real-time communication service provides its clients with the ability to specify their performance requirements and to obtain guarantees about the satisfaction of those requirements.

rejected.why: The document is about performance guarantee requirements, not voice/video/media protocols. The QoS tag fits more specifically. Real-time here means guaranteed performance.
Congestion is mentioned only as a motivation. No congestion control mechanism is covered.
ATM cell sizes are used only as assumptions in the worked examples.
The document specifies requirements and bounds, not measurement methods or metrics.
Video and voice appear only as example applications of the requirements.

RFC1194.title: Finger User Information Protocol
RFC1194.summary: RFC 1194 specifies the Finger User Information Protocol, a TCP-based query protocol for remote user information programs (RUIP), including query formats, forwarding behaviour, and security recommendations; it obsoletes RFC 742.

Finger.why: The whole document is the specification of the Finger protocol: query grammar, RUIP behaviour, forwarding, responses and security guidance.
Finger.quote: This memo describes the Finger User Information Protocol. This is a simple protocol which provides an interface to a remote user information program (RUIP).

rejected.why: Finger only uses TCP port 79 as a substrate; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
Data format section requires ASCII with CRLF, but this is a minor requirement and not the subject of the document.
Security section is substantial, but it is specific to Finger's information disclosure and implementation, not general security guidance; the Finger tag covers it.
Mentioned only as a comparison for security perimeter scrutiny.

RFC1195.title: Use of OSI IS-IS for routing in TCP/IP and dual environments
RFC1195.summary: RFC 1195 specifies Integrated IS-IS, extending the OSI IS-IS intra-domain routing protocol with IP-specific TLVs so one link-state IGP can route IP, OSI, or both.

IS-IS.why: The whole document defines the IP extensions to IS-IS: new TLVs, reachability information, SPF changes, and route preference.
IS-IS.quote: This RFC specifies an integrated routing protocol, based on the OSI Intra-Domain IS-IS Routing Protocol, which may be used as an interior gateway protocol (IGP)

rejected.why: The document uses OSI CLNP addressing and dual routers, but its subject is the routing protocol, not OSI network-layer protocols themselves.
OSPF is mentioned only as a 'Ships in the Night' alternative for IP routing.
CLNP is the OSI data protocol routed alongside IP, not specified here.
IP is the protocol being routed. The document does not specify IP itself.
Management MIBs are deferred to a separate companion document.

RFC1196.title: Finger User Information Protocol
RFC1196.summary: RFC 1196 specifies the Finger user information protocol, a TCP-based query/response service for remote user information, its query grammar, forwarding behaviour, and security recommendations.

Finger.why: The whole document defines the Finger protocol: query specification, RUIP behaviour, responses and security.
Finger.quote: This memo describes the Finger User Information Protocol.  This is a simple protocol which provides an interface to a remote user information program (RUIP).

rejected.why: Finger only uses TCP port 79 as a transport substrate; nothing new is defined about TCP.
The data format section requires ASCII with CRLF line endings, but that is a minor constraint of the protocol rather than the subject.
Security sections discuss Finger-specific hardening and are part of the Finger protocol spec, not a general security topic.
Only mentioned as a comparison for security perimeter scrutiny.

RFC1197.title: Using ODA for translating multimedia information
RFC1197.summary: Informational memo pointing implementors to the EXPRES project's experiences using ISO 8613 ODA (Office Document Architecture) as an interchange format for multimedia documents sent by electronic mail.

rejected.why: The memo only notes that ODA has been specified for use in standards such as X.400. X.400 is not what the document addresses.
Email is the proposed transport for submitting proposals. The memo is about the document encoding format, not mail architecture or transport.
The memo mentions multimedia mail but says nothing about MIME body structure or encodings. It concerns ODA as an alternative interchange encoding.
ODA uses ASN.1-based encodings, but the memo does not discuss them.

gaps.name: ODA (ISO 8613 / CCITT T.410 Office Document Architecture)
gaps.why: The whole memo is about using ODA and document application profiles to interchange multimedia documents. The taxonomy has no tag for compound document or multimedia document interchange formats. The nearest tags, SGML and MIME, are different technologies.

RFC1198.title: FYI on the X window system
RFC1198.summary: FYI RFC listing the published standards and draft standards of the MIT X Consortium for the X Window System, and how to obtain the distribution.

X Window System.why: The whole document catalogues X Window System specifications (protocol, Xlib, Toolkit Intrinsics, ICCCM, extensions) and how to get them.
X Window System.quote: This FYI RFC provides pointers to the published standards of the MIT X Consortium.

rejected.why: Anonymous FTP is only mentioned as a distribution channel for the software, not specified or discussed.
It is an FYI-series document, but it is a pointer list for a specific system, so the specific X Window System tag fits better.

RFC1199.title: Request for Comments Summary Notes: 1100-1199
RFC1199.summary: RFC 1199 is an annotated index of the 100 RFCs numbered 1100 through 1199, giving each one's author, date, title, short abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The whole document catalogues a block of the RFC series with status notes, so readers browsing the RFC series subject would want it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1100 through RFCs 1199.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: It is a catalogue of documents from 1989-1991, not a history or retrospective of the Internet.
BGP RFCs 1105, 1163 and 1164 appear only as one-paragraph entries in the list.
RFC 1131 is one list entry, and the memo does not discuss the protocol itself.
The NTP RFCs are only list entries.
The SNMP and MIB RFCs are only list entries.
The PPP RFCs are only list entries.
The memo mentions standards-track status only as a label on entries and does not describe the process.

RFC1200.title: IAB official protocol standards
RFC1200.summary: RFC 1200 is the IAB's quarterly list of official Internet protocol standards, explaining the standardization process, protocol states and statuses, and listing protocols by maturity level.

IETF process.why: The document describes the IAB/IESG standards track, states, status levels, minimum delays and RFC processing decision table.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial section explains the RFC series, submission, and how to determine the current RFC for each protocol.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

internet history.why: As a 1991 snapshot of the state of all Internet protocols, including a list of historic ones, it is a historical record of the protocol suite.
internet history.quote: Some protocols have been superseded by better ones or are otherwise unused. Such protocols are still documented in this memorandum with the designation "historic".

rejected.why: IANA is only a contact and manager of the list; Assigned Numbers is referenced but not the subject.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but this is process vocabulary, not a glossary of the field.
The document catalogs protocols, not architectural principles.
TCP and many other protocols appear only as entries in the status lists, not as subjects of the document.

RFC1201.title: Transmitting IP traffic over ARCNET networks
RFC1201.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IP, ARP and RARP datagrams over ARCNET using the Novell/Datapoint packet header standard, including datalink fragmentation, address mapping, MTU and assigned protocol IDs; obsoletes RFC 1051.

link layer.why: The document defines IP-over-ARCNET, a specific link-layer medium. The taxonomy has no ARCNET tag, so the general link layer topic is the closest fit.
link layer.quote: This memo specifies a method of encapsulating Internet Protocol (IP) [1] and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [2] datagrams for transmission across ARCNET [3]

ARP.why: The document specifies how ARP and RARP are used on ARCNET: hardware type, address length and broadcast of requests. Readers of the ARP subject would want it.
ARP.quote: The hardware address length is 1 octet for ARP packets sent over ARCNET networks.  The ARP hardware type for ARCNET is 7.

rejected.why: IP is only the payload being encapsulated. The document does not specify or extend IPv4 itself.
TCP is mentioned only for an MSS suggestion to reduce fragmentation. It is incidental.
Ethernet is mentioned only as a contrast in the RARP discussion. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
MTU discovery is cited only as one way to announce a 504-octet MTU. The document is not about PMTUD.

gaps.name: ARCNET
gaps.why: The document is entirely about IP over ARCNET, a specific link technology. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so it is tagged only under the generic link layer topic.

RFC1202.title: Directory Assistance service
RFC1202.summary: Informational memo documenting the Directory Assistance (DA) protocol, a local TCP-based text interface (control and data connections) that lets lightweight clients access the OSI Directory (DAP) via a split-DUA "Directory Assistant".

X.500.why: The document specifies a simplified textual front-end to the X.500 Directory (DAP, DUA, DSA, DISH commands). Readers of X.500 would want it.
X.500.quote: The OSI Directory [1] provides a powerful infrastructure for the retrieval of information objects.

rejected.why: The X.500 tag is more specific and sits under directory services, so the parent is implied.
LDAP is not mentioned and is not the subject. The document is about DAP access.
TCP is only the transport for the control and data connections. Nothing new is defined about TCP.
NVT-ASCII is only borrowed as the text encoding. The Telnet protocol is not specified.
The 'fred' command is a white-pages front end, but Finger is not involved.

RFC1203.title: Interactive Mail Access Protocol: Version 3
RFC1203.summary: RFC 1203 specifies IMAP3, a revision of IMAP2 (RFC 1064) for workstations to access and manipulate mail on a remote mailbox server, with tagged solicited/unsolicited responses, version/feature negotiation, and extended search.

IMAP.why: The whole document defines the IMAP3 protocol: commands, responses, syntax and features for mailbox access.
IMAP.quote: The intent of the Interactive Mail Access Protocol, Version 3 (IMAP3) is to allow a (possibly unreliable) workstation or similar machine to access electronic mail

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the separate mail transfer protocol for posting mail; IMAP3 does not specify it.
RFC 822 is the message format the protocol exposes through envelopes and keys, but the document is not about the format itself.
POP2 is referenced only as a comparison model, not specified or extended.
TCP is only the assumed reliable transport; the document states it is network-protocol independent.
Multi-media mail is only anticipated as a future direction, with the ENCODING feature as a hook.

RFC1204.title: Message Posting Protocol (MPP)
RFC1204.summary: RFC 1204 specifies the experimental Message Posting Protocol (MPP), a TCP-based, SMTP/FTP-style command protocol on port 218 by which PC clients authenticate to a message posting server and submit mail for delivery.

email.why: The protocol is a mail submission protocol between a PC client and a posting server that hands mail to the delivery system. It fits the email architecture and submission scope. No more specific child fits, because it is a new protocol rather than SMTP itself.
email.quote: adding personal computers to an electronic mail network requires an agent (message posting server) to authenticate sender's identity and then submit mail to the message delivery system

rejected.why: MPP borrows SMTP's command and reply structure and the DATA dot-stuffing convention. It is a separate protocol, not an SMTP specification or extension.
Only the reply structure is borrowed, and FTP may be used for password checking. The document is not about FTP.
POP3 is only mentioned as one way the server can check passwords against an existing database.
USER/PASS authentication is a part of the protocol, but the document is about mail posting. Authentication is a feature of it, not the subject.
TCP is only the transport the protocol runs over.

RFC1205.title: 5250 Telnet interface
RFC1205.summary: Informational RFC documenting the interface for running the IBM 5250 work station data stream over Telnet, including option negotiation, record header format, data flow examples, and 5250 data stream corrections and enhancements.

Telnet.why: The document specifies how a Telnet client and server negotiate and carry the 5250 data stream, including the record header and EOR framing. It is a Telnet usage profile.
Telnet.quote: to enable 5250 mode, both the client and server must agree to at least support the Binary, End-Of-Record (EOR), and Terminal-Type Telnet options.

rejected.why: The header derives from SNA-based 5250 DSPT, but the document is about 5250 over Telnet, not SNA interworking. TN3270 is the analogous tag for 3270 and does not cover 5250.
5250 is the AS/400 counterpart of 3270 emulation, but this document is not about TN3270 itself.

gaps.name: TN5250 / IBM 5250 terminal emulation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has TN3270 under SNA but no tag for 5250 Telnet emulation. The 5250 work station data stream is the main subject of this RFC.

RFC1206.title: FYI on Questions and Answers: Answers to commonly asked "new Internet user" questions
RFC1206.summary: FYI 4 is a Q&A guide for new Internet users covering what the Internet and TCP/IP are, DNS basics, RFCs and Internet Drafts, Internet organizations (IAB, IANA, IETF, IRTF, NIC), directory and information services, mailing lists, Internet lore, and a glossary.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory guide for new Internet users, which is the definition of the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: The goal is to document the most commonly asked questions and answers in the Internet.

RFC series.why: A substantial section explains what RFCs are, how to submit and obtain them, the RFC index, and Internet Drafts.
RFC series.quote: The Request for Comments documents (RFCs) are working notes of the Internet research and development community.

terminology.why: The glossary of Internet terms and acronyms makes up roughly a third of the document.
terminology.quote: Below is a condensed glossary to assist in making some sense of the Internet world.

rejected.why: DNS gets only a two-question overview and a glossary entry. It is not specified or analysed.
The document explains how to use and register in the NIC WHOIS database, but only as one of many user services. This is a minor part of the whole.
IAB, IETF and IRTF are described briefly as organizations. The document does not cover the standards process.
IANA is described in one Q&A entry, which is not enough for the document to be about IANA registries.
TCP/IP is introduced at a very basic level in a single answer. The document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
The section covers how to find and join mailing lists for new users, not mailing list protocols or management.

RFC1207.title: FYI on Questions and Answers: Answers to commonly asked "experienced Internet user" questions
RFC1207.summary: FYI 7 is a collection of commonly asked questions and answers from mailing lists for experienced Internet users, covering NSFNET statistics, BITNET gateways, DNS, SNMP/MIB, SLIP/PPP, routing and miscellaneous protocol questions.

DNS.why: A full section of Q&A covers DNS query tools, BIND failures, name case and glue records.
DNS.quote: The model used by the DNS is that you get to control at a specific point in the name space, and are hence free to select case as you choose

MIB.why: Several Q&As cover SNMP MIB checking with MOSY, DisplayString and OCTET STRING handling, and defining private MIB objects.
MIB.quote: Can vendors make their enterprise-specific variables available to users through a standard distribution mechanism?

PPP.why: The SLIP/PPP section explains PPP and recommends it over SLIP. Its SLIP content is covered by the SLIP tag.
PPP.quote: PPP was designed to be useful for many protocols besides just IP.
PPP.section: 8. Questions about SLIP and PPP Implementations

SLIP.why: Questions cover SLIP line types, SCO Xenix support and NFS over SLIP needing UDP checksums.
SLIP.quote: SLIP is designed for async lines and is not a good fit on sync lines.
SLIP.section: 8. Questions about SLIP and PPP Implementations

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series Q&A guide, so it belongs with the user guides.
user guides.quote: The goal is to document the most commonly asked questions and answers in the Internet.

rejected.why: The SNMP questions are mainly about MIB definitions and tooling, so MIB fits better. The one question about SNMP authentication is minor.
Only a single Q&A about Ethernet type 80F3 mentions AppleTalk AARP.
The BITNET gateway answer mentions mail addressing, but only briefly and in the context of network interconnection.
FTP is only the means of retrieving files and is not the subject of any answer.

RFC1208.title: A Glossary of Networking Terms
RFC1208.summary: RFC 1208 is an informational glossary of networking terms and acronyms, adapted from the Interop Pocket Glossary, covering Internet and OSI terminology.

terminology.why: The whole document is a glossary defining networking terms and acronyms, which is what the terminology subject covers.
terminology.quote: This RFC is a glossary adapted from "The INTEROP Pocket Glossary of Networking Terms" distributed at Interop '90.

rejected.why: OSI protocols and layers are defined throughout, but each as one brief entry. The document is not about OSI network-layer protocols.
DNS has a one-line entry, and the document does not specify or analyse it.
It has a few historical entries such as ARPANET and MILNET, but the document is a glossary and not a history.
The ARPANET appears only as a short glossary entry, not as the subject of the document.
It is a reference glossary, not an FYI-style introductory user guide. The terminology tag fits better.

RFC1209.title: The Transmission of IP Datagrams over the SMDS Service
RFC1209.summary: Specifies encapsulation (LLC/SNAP), ARP address resolution, broadcast/multicast mapping and MTU for carrying IP datagrams over the SMDS service configured as a logical IP subnetwork.

SMDS.why: The whole document defines how IP runs over the SMDS service: LIS configuration, SIP/LLC-SNAP encapsulation, 9180-octet MTU and group-address use.
SMDS.quote: This memo defines a protocol for the transmission of IP and ARP packets over a Switched Multi-megabit Data Service Network configured as a logical IP subnetwork.

ARP.why: A substantial section profiles ARP for SMDS: hardware type 14, 8-octet addresses, and sending requests to smds$arp-req (the LIS group address).
ARP.quote: The dynamic mapping of 32-bit Internet addresses to SMDS addresses SHALL be done via the dynamic discovery procedure of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)

rejected.why: IP is the payload being carried; the document does not specify or extend IP itself.
Multicast is only addressed briefly, by mapping all IP multicast addresses to the LIS group address, which is too minor for a tag.
IEEE 802.2 LLC/SNAP framing is reused, but the document is not about Ethernet.
RFC 1188 is only a model for the text; the document is not about FDDI.

RFC1210.title: Network and infrastructure user requirements for transatlantic research collaboration: Brussels, July 16-18, and Washington July 24-25, 1990
RFC1210.summary: Workshop report from the Networks and Infrastructure Working Group summarising user requirements, one- and three-year targets and recommended actions for transatlantic US/European research collaboration (email, directories, login, file transfer, video conferencing, network management, multi-protocol support, links).

internet governance.quote: Convene an international research network operations, planning and management team to develop and apply procedural and technical recommendations for international network management

network management.why: A dedicated section sets targets for international network operations centres, fault management and automation, and CERTs.
network management.quote: Current network management technology and practice are not adequate to support large scale, international research networks.

email.why: Email is the first and most emphasised requirement: operations forum, gateway specifications, interoperability among X.400, UUCP, SMTP and BITNET.
email.quote: The current email services between the US and Europe suffer from gaps in connectivity, lack of reliability and poor responsiveness.

directory services.why: A dedicated section recommends US/European collaboration on directories, including X.500 and WHOIS access.
directory services.quote: White pages services to assist network users to find email addresses, computer services and other on-line facilities are, at best, only lightly deployed

OSI.why: Multi-protocol support and OSI/TCP-IP coexistence, including CLNP versus CONS, is a major theme.
OSI.quote: support campus-to-campus communication for a subset of coexisting protocol suites (at least OSI and TCP/IP) at a minimum of 64 Kb/s

rejected.why: Mentioned as an email protocol needing interoperability work, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
Named as a directory standard to work with, but only briefly and without technical content; the broader directory services tag covers it.
Video conferencing is a requirement section, but only at the needs level with no framework or protocol content.
Intercontinental X-windows support is a target, but only briefly and as an application requirement.
TCP/IP is mentioned as one of the protocol suites in use, not as a subject of the document.
RPC is mentioned only as a protocol to be agreed upon; no ONC RPC content.

gaps.name: Research networking policy and funding coordination (CCIRN, ESPRIT, NSF/DARPA)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about coordinating international research networks and funding. The taxonomy has no tag for research and education networking or international infrastructure planning.

RFC1211.title: Problems with the maintenance of large mailing lists
RFC1211.summary: Informational RFC from ISI describing operational problems in maintaining large mailing lists (the IETF list), especially misdirected error reports, sublists/exploders and owner- aliases, with an appendix of sample bounce messages.

mailing lists.why: The whole document is about the operational management of large mailing lists: sublists, exploders, list ownership, request mailboxes, and handling of list subscription changes.
mailing lists.quote: Maintaining large mailing lists, especially the processing of error reports, poses many problems.

email.why: Appendix F catalogues many mail delivery error and bounce messages from varied mail systems, and the body discusses SMTP error reporting, postmasters and VRFY/EXPN use, which is of interest to email operations readers.
email.quote: An additional problem is the creativity shown by mail program developers in inventing numerous different error reports.

rejected.why: SMTP VRFY/EXPN and error-return behaviour are used as investigative tools, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP; it is about list maintenance practice.
dig and MX records are used to diagnose problems, but DNS is only a diagnostic tool here, not a subject of the document.
Whois is used to find host administrators in examples; it is not the document's subject.
One appendix example shows an X.400 gateway non-delivery report, but only as a sample error message.
Mailing list management here concerns legitimate list errors, not unsolicited bulk email.

RFC1212.title: Concise MIB definitions
RFC1212.summary: RFC 1212 defines an extended OBJECT-TYPE ASN.1 macro (adding DESCRIPTION, REFERENCE, INDEX, DEFVAL clauses) for writing concise SNMP MIB modules, with guidance on conceptual rows and converting OSI MIBs.

MIB.why: The document specifies the format for writing MIB modules, including the OBJECT-TYPE macro and the INDEX, DEFVAL, and conceptual row conventions. This is the core SMI/MIB subject.
MIB.quote: This memo describes a straight-forward approach toward producing concise, yet descriptive, MIB modules.

rejected.why: SNMP operations are discussed to explain row creation and deletion, but the protocol itself is not specified or extended here. The document is about the MIB definition format.
The OBJECT-TYPE macro is written in ASN.1 macro notation, but ASN.1 is only the notation used. The document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
OSI management is mentioned only as the source of MIBs to de-osify, and the appendix does not define CMIP.

RFC1213.title: Management Information Base for Network Management of TCP/IP-based internets: MIB-II
RFC1213.summary: RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, the second version of the Management Information Base for SNMP-managed TCP/IP internets, with object groups for system, interfaces, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, EGP, transmission and SNMP.

MIB.why: The whole document is a MIB module (RFC1213-MIB) defining managed objects using the SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the second version of the Management Information Base (MIB-II) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

SNMP.why: It defines the SNMP group of statistics counters for SNMP entities and is a core part of the SNMP management framework.
SNMP.quote: snmp   OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { mib-2 11 }

rejected.why: The TCP group is only a set of management counters and state objects, not a specification or extension of TCP.
The ICMP group only holds message counters; ICMP is not specified or extended.
The EGP group provides monitoring objects only; EGP itself is not specified.
ASN.1 is the notation used to define the objects and is not the subject of the document.
The UDP group is monitoring counters and a listener table, not about UDP the protocol.
IP group objects are management counters and tables; the IP protocol is not specified.

RFC1214.title: OSI internet management: Management Information Base
RFC1214.summary: Defines an OSI-template (GDMO-style) version of MIB-II for use with CMIP/CMOT, recasting MIB-II groups as managed object classes with naming attributes, name bindings, and SNMP-derived notifications.

CMIP.why: The document is the managed object definitions and naming tree for CMIP-based management of TCP/IP internets; CMIP is the protocol it targets.
CMIP.quote: This RFC documents a MIB for use with CMIP, either over pure OSI stacks or with the CMIP over TCP specification.

MIB.why: It is a MIB module: MIB-II objects recast with additional attributes, events and containment naming.
MIB.quote: It redefines objects comprised by the second revision of the Management Information Base for Network Management of TCP/IP-based internets: MIB-II

rejected.why: SNMP events and instance naming are reused for compatibility, but the document specifies a CMIP/OSI MIB, not SNMP.
ASN.1 modules are the notation used, not the subject.
EGP objects are merely carried over from MIB-II as managed object classes.
TCP counters and table objects are recast MIB content; the document is not about TCP.
ICMP counters appear only as MIB attributes.
The OSI network layer (CLNP) is not the subject; OSI management templates are.

gaps.name: CMIP/CMOT, OSI Structure of Management Information (GDMO templates)
gaps.why: Management through OSI CMIP and GDMO managed object definitions has no tag in the taxonomy except the CMIP tech tag, which I used; GDMO as a template notation has none.

RFC1215.title: Convention for defining traps for use with the SNMP
RFC1215.summary: RFC 1215 defines the TRAP-TYPE macro, a convention for concisely defining SNMP traps in MIB modules, including examples for enterprise-specific and the standard generic traps.

MIB.why: The document defines an SMI macro extension for MIB modules to describe traps, with mapping rules and examples. This is MIB/SMI definition convention.
MIB.quote: The TRAP-TYPE macro is suggested for this purpose

SNMP.why: The macro maps directly onto SNMP Trap-PDU fields and defines the standard SNMP generic traps, so SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: the value of sysObjectID is placed in the enterprise field of the SNMP Trap-PDU

rejected.why: The macro is written in ASN.1 macro notation, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
egpNeighborLoss is only one of the example traps; the document is not about EGP.

RFC1216.title: Gigabit network economics and paradigm shifts
RFC1216.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing "Ultra Low Speed" (ULS) networking as an economic paradigm shift to counter gigabit network cost trends, joking about alternating-bit protocols and slow-start.

humor.why: The document is dated 1 April and is a whimsical parody of gigabit networking hype, proposing absurd ULS networking with Italian postal service and Congressional budget applications.
humor.quote: The road to Ultra Low Speed (ULS) technology is long, slow, and easy.

rejected.why: Low priority facsimile is mentioned only as a joke application of ULS, not a fax protocol.
Slow-start is mentioned satirically as a feature of ULS protocols; the document does not address congestion control.
Only passing references to sequence numbers and the alternating-bit protocol; no TCP content.
The economics and paradigm discussion is satire, not a real architectural treatment.

RFC1217.title: Memo from the Consortium for Slow Commotion Research (CSCR)
RFC1217.summary: An April 1 parody response from Vint Cerf's fictional "Consortium for Slow Commotion Research" to RFC 1216, proposing absurd ultra-low-speed networking designs (tanks, neutrinos, firefly cryptography, 49-layer OSI, Mashed Potato routing).

humor.why: The whole memo is an April 1 parody research proposal for deliberately slow, inefficient networks. It belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: CSCR looks forward to a protracted and fruitless discussion with you on this subject as soon as we can figure out how to transmit the proposal.
humor.section: 5. Options for Further Reducing Effective Throughput

rejected.why: The 'Slow Network Management Protocol (SNMP)' is a joke gag with MIBs in Serbo-Croatian. The memo does not specify or analyse SNMP.
The 49-layer recursive encapsulation of OSI is satirical and does not concern the OSI network-layer protocols.
ASN.1 appears only in a throwaway joke about a 32-bit-per-character set.
The 'Mashed Potato' and 'Airline Baggage' routing schemes are parody. The memo contains no real routing content.

RFC1218.title: Naming scheme for c=US
RFC1218.summary: RFC 1218 reproduces NADF-123, a proposed scheme for naming entries under c=US in the X.500 Directory Information Tree, using civil authority naming, optimized civil naming, organizational and application naming, with a schema.

X.500.why: The document defines how entries are named in the X.500 Directory Information Tree for the US, including DIT structure, object classes and RDNs. Readers of X.500 would want it.
X.500.quote: offer, or plan to offer, public Directory services in North America, based on the CCITT X.500 Recommendations

rejected.why: The naming here is X.500 Distinguished Name design, not general naming and name resolution; the X.500 tag is more specific.
Parent of X.500, so it is implied by the X.500 tag.
The appendix schema is written in ASN.1 macros, but only as notation, not as the subject.
The document concerns X.500 names, not the Domain Name System.

RFC1219.title: On the assignment of subnet numbers
RFC1219.summary: Informational memo describing a procedure for assigning IP subnet numbers and masks (mirror-image counting of subnet bits, growth bits) so subnets and hosts can grow without renumbering, requiring variable-length subnet mask support.

addressing.why: The whole document specifies an IP address assignment technique for subnets, including masks, s-bits, h-bits, and g-bits. It is about address architecture and allocation within a network, and no more specific child tag fits.
addressing.quote: This memo specifies a procedure for assigning subnet numbers that eliminates the need to estimate subnet size.

rejected.why: The memo covers subnetting within a single network using variable-length masks. It does not cover classless inter-domain aggregation.
OSPF is mentioned only as an example of a routing protocol that supports different subnet masks. The document is not about it.
RIP is cited only as a protocol that does not support variable masks.
The addresses are IPv4, but the document is about a subnet numbering procedure. The addressing tag is the better fit.
The procedure is designed to avoid renumbering hosts. It does not describe renumbering procedures.

gaps.name: Subnetting / subnet mask assignment
gaps.why: The document is about IP subnetting and subnet mask allocation. The taxonomy has no subnetting tag, so addressing is used as the nearest fit.

RFC1220.title: Point-to-Point Protocol extensions for bridging
RFC1220.summary: Defines the PPP Bridging Network Control Protocol (BNCP), frame formats and options for carrying IEEE 802.x transparent and source-routing bridged LAN traffic over PPP point-to-point links.

PPP.why: The document specifies a PPP network control protocol (BNCP), its protocol field values, options and frame formats for bridging.
PPP.quote: This document defines an extension of the Internet Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) described in RFC 1171, targeting the use of Point-to-Point lines for Remote Bridging.

Ethernet.why: Much of the document covers remote bridging of IEEE 802.3/Ethernet LANs, spanning tree BPDUs, and tinygram compression of Ethernet frames.
Ethernet.quote: There exist two basic sorts of bridges - ones that interconnect LANs directly, called Local Bridges, and ones that interconnect LANs via an intermediate medium

rejected.why: Source routing for 802.5 is covered, but as one of the bridged MAC types, not IP over token ring.
FDDI is only one MAC type carried in the frame format; the document is not about IP over FDDI.
LAN FCS preservation is a feature of the bridging encapsulation, not a topic about the Internet checksum.
Tinygram compression strips zero padding from small frames; it is a minor option, not header compression in the taxonomy's sense.

gaps.name: Remote bridging / transparent bridging / source routing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for LAN bridging (IEEE 802.1d spanning tree, source-route bridging), which is a central subject of this document.

RFC1221.title: Host Access Protocol (HAP) specification: Version 2
RFC1221.summary: Specifies version 2 of the Host Access Protocol (HAP), a network-layer host-to-packet-switch access protocol used in the Terrestrial Wideband Network, covering datagram and stream messages, multicast groups, a Service Agent for resource setup, link monitoring, and loopback.

satellite.why: HAP is the host access protocol for the Wideband Packet Satellite Network and its terrestrial successor. It is a network-layer access protocol for a satellite/wideband network, so the satellite page is the closest fit.
satellite.quote: first implemented about a decade ago for the DARPA/DCA sponsored Wideband Packet Satellite Network (WBNET), the precursor of the current Terrestrial Wideband Network (TWBNET)

QoS.why: A substantial part of the document covers streams with reserved bandwidth, precedence and priority classes, and reliability levels, which is resource reservation and QoS signalling.
QoS.quote: Stream service provides network bandwidth guarantees, but requires explicit setup and teardown operations to allocate and deallocate network resources.

multicast.why: Section 6.2 specifies group create, join, leave and delete operations with key authentication. This is network multicast group management.
multicast.quote: HAP supports multicast addressing via "groups".

rejected.why: The document only mentions that it is meant to simplify interaction with ST2 agents. It does not specify ST-II.
IP is only one of the upper-layer protocols HAP can carry, selected through the Protocol ID field.
ARPANET 1822 and VDH are only examples of link-level protocols HAP can run over. HAP is not an ARPANET protocol.
The 16-bit header checksum is a detail of the message formats. The document is not about checksums.
CLNP is mentioned only as an upper-layer protocol that HAP may carry.

gaps.name: Host Access Protocol (HAP) / Wideband Network host-to-switch access protocol
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for this historic network-layer access protocol. Satellite is the nearest fit, but the document is about a protocol for a specific wideband packet network.

RFC1222.title: Advancing the NSFNET routing architecture
RFC1222.summary: Informational memo recounting NSFNET Backbone routing history (Hello, EGP, T1/T3) and proposing a simpler attachment option in which two logical routing entities (subscriber IGP and backbone IGP) run in one physical router and exchange routes via EGP/BGP over loopback.

routing architecture.why: The document is about the NSFNET routing architecture: decoupling IGP domains, routing isolation, and where to place the demarcation between backbone and subscribers.
routing architecture.quote: The only essential requirement for routing isolation is the presence of two logical routing entities.

EGP.why: EGP's role in giving routing isolation, and its up/down-only signalling, is analysed as the basis of the Phase 2 architecture.
EGP.quote: The interface between the backbone network and its attached client was built by means of exterior routing, initially via the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP)

rejected.why: BGP is mentioned only as an alternative inter-domain session between the two logical entities. The memo does not specify or analyse it.
RIP is mentioned only as the mid-level networks' IGP, which is background.
PPP appears in one passing remark about its future evolution helping demarcation management.
The history of NSFNET phases is background for the proposal. The document's purpose is to suggest routing architecture changes.

gaps.name: NSFNET backbone
gaps.why: The document is about NSFNET Backbone routing and attachment, but the taxonomy has no tag for NSFNET or national backbone networks.

RFC1223.title: OSI CLNS and LLC1 protocols on Network Systems HYPERchannel
RFC1223.summary: Informational RFC specifying how OSI CLNS and other LLC1-based protocols are encapsulated over Network Systems Corporation HYPERchannel, including emulation of multicast for ES-IS and IS-IS.

CLNP.why: The document defines how CLNP/CLNS datagrams are carried over HYPERchannel (LLC1 SAP 0xFE, message type 0x0B01), and how ES-IS and IS-IS operate there. It is the OSI network-layer adaptation; CLNP is the most specific fitting tag.
CLNP.quote: To standardize the encapsulation of LLC1 packets over HYPERchannel. The format will be used for OSI CLNS and for any other protocols using LLC1 over HYPERchannel.

rejected.why: The IS-IS discussed is the OSI ISO 10589 protocol, and the document only describes how to emulate its multicast over HYPERchannel. It does not specify or extend the IS-IS routing protocol. The taxonomy's IS-IS tag is the IP-oriented one.
HYPERchannel is a different link technology, so the ATM tag does not apply. It was considered only as a neighbouring link-layer tag.
The parent of CLNP, so it is implied by the CLNP tag and not listed separately.
The document is about a specific medium, HYPERchannel, but no child tag exists for it. See gaps.

gaps.name: HYPERchannel
gaps.why: The whole document is about carrying LLC1/OSI traffic over NSC HYPERchannel, a link technology with no tag in the taxonomy. Readers browsing link-layer technologies would want it.

gaps.name: ES-IS
gaps.why: The document specifies ES-IS operation over HYPERchannel (ISO 9542): hello packets, SNARE address managers, and redirects. The taxonomy has no OSI routing protocol tag.

RFC1224.title: Techniques for managing asynchronously generated alerts
RFC1224.summary: RFC 1224 describes two techniques for managing asynchronously generated network management alerts, a feedback/pin sliding-window limit and polled, logged alerts, with experimental MIB objects and usage examples for SNMP and CMOT.

SNMP.why: The techniques are specified in terms of SNMP traps, GET/GET NEXT/SET and an experimental MIB subtree. Section 7 gives SNMP usage for both mechanisms.
SNMP.quote: To make any effective use of the alert mechanisms described in this memo, implementation of several MIB objects is required in the relevant managed systems.

MIB.why: The memo defines the alertMan experimental MIB objects (maxAlertsPerTime, windowTime, alertsEnabled, alertLog), which readers of MIB modules would want.
MIB.quote: All defined MIB objects used in this document reside under the mib subtree:

rejected.why: CMOT is mentioned as a second compatible protocol, but the memo only gives short usage examples and does not specify or analyse it.
The document is about network management, but the more specific SNMP and MIB tags already cover it, so the parent is implied.
The document concerns alert flow control, not OAM mechanisms.
UDP is only a transport assumption in the polling cost examples.

RFC1225.title: Post Office Protocol: Version 3
RFC1225.summary: RFC 1225 specifies POP3, a simple protocol with AUTHORIZATION, TRANSACTION and UPDATE states by which a workstation retrieves and deletes mail held in a maildrop on a server host.

POP3.why: The whole document specifies POP3: its commands, states, responses and optional commands such as TOP and RPOP.
POP3.quote: The Post Office Protocol - Version 3 (POP3) is intended to permit a workstation to dynamically access a maildrop on a server host

rejected.why: Only mentioned as the way a client posts mail into the transport system. The memo explicitly does not specify it.
Messages are assumed to conform to RFC 822, but the memo does not define or extend the format.
TCP port 110 is only the substrate for the protocol.
POP3 is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.

RFC1226.title: Internet protocol encapsulation of AX.25 frames
RFC1226.summary: Experimental memo specifying encapsulation of AX.25 amateur packet-radio frames, one per IP datagram, using IP protocol number 93.

amateur radio.why: The whole document defines how AX.25 amateur packet-radio frames are carried over IP, which is the subject of the amateur radio tag.
amateur radio.quote: Each AX.25 packet ("frame") is encapsulated in one IP datagram.
amateur radio.section: The AX.25 Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol

IP-in-IP.why: It is a generic-style encapsulation of link-layer frames in IP datagrams with an assigned protocol number. This is a looser fit, so it is listed as secondary.
IP-in-IP.quote: Each such IP datagram shall have a protocol number of 93.
IP-in-IP.section: The AX.25 Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied only if no child fits. Here the document is about AX.25 specifically, and IP-in-IP is a weak fit, so tunneling is not tagged on its own.
The CRC-CCITT FCS is only mentioned as being retained in the frame. The document does not address CRC itself.
This parent is implied by amateur radio, so it is not listed separately.

RFC1227.title: SNMP MUX protocol and MIB
RFC1227.summary: Defines the SMUX protocol, by which a local user process (SMUX peer) registers MIB subtrees with the host's SNMP agent over TCP port 199, plus a MIB module for SMUX peers and registered trees.

SNMP.why: The document specifies an SNMP agent extensibility protocol (peer registration, get/set/trap proxying, two-phase set) for implementing portions of the MIB.
SNMP.quote: a new protocol, the SNMP multiplexing (SMUX) protocol is introduced.

MIB.why: Section 4 defines SMUX-MIB with smuxPeerTable and smuxTreeTable, a substantial MIB module that the agent must implement.
MIB.quote: In addition to defining the SMUX protocol, this document defines a MIB for the SMUX.

rejected.why: AgentX is the later standardized subagent protocol, not defined here. SMUX is its predecessor, and this RFC does not cover AgentX.
TCP is only the transport (port 199 mapping), not the subject of the document.
ASN.1 and BER are used only to define and encode the PDUs, so they are substrate here.

RFC1228.title: SNMP-DPI: Simple Network Management Protocol Distributed Program Interface
RFC1228.summary: Experimental IBM protocol (SNMP-DPI) letting sub-agents register MIB variables with an SNMP agent over a stream connection, with packet formats and a C API, so agents can be extended without recompilation.

SNMP.why: The document specifies an extension to SNMP agents (agent/sub-agent protocol, GET/GET-NEXT/SET/TRAP handling), so it belongs under SNMP.
SNMP.quote: permits end-users to dynamically add, delete or replace management variables in the local Management Information Base without requiring recompilation of the SNMP agent

rejected.why: The document extends agents to host new MIB variables but does not define any MIB module or SMI content.
AgentX is the later standardized subagent protocol; this RFC is a different, earlier IBM protocol, and AgentX is not discussed in it.
TCP is only the stream transport for the DPI connection.
ASN.1/BER is only used for the bootstrap SNMP PDU. DPI exists to hide ASN.1 from sub-agent authors.
This is a parent of SNMP, so it is implied by the SNMP tag.

RFC1229.title: Extensions to the generic-interface MIB
RFC1229.summary: Defines experimental MIB objects extending the MIB-II generic interfaces table, adding an interface extension table, an interface test table, and a receive address table.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (RFC1229-MIB) defined in SMI, adding generic interface objects for network management.
MIB.quote: it defines managed object types as experimental extensions to the generic interfaces structure of MIB-II.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to access the objects, but the document defines only MIB objects, not the protocol or its framework. MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 and BER are only the notation the SMI uses to define the objects. The document does not specify them.
The objects apply to all interface types and are not specific to any link technology. The document is about management of interfaces, not the link layer itself.
The text mentions MAC addresses and token ring origins, but the objects are media-independent.

RFC1230.title: IEEE 802.4 Token Bus MIB
RFC1230.summary: Defines an experimental SNMP MIB module for managing IEEE 802.4 Token Bus interfaces, with operational, initialization and statistics tables plus test and chip-set identifiers.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SMI-defined objects, tables, OIDs) for 802.4 interfaces, so it belongs on the MIB page.
MIB.quote: this memo defines managed objects used for managing subnetworks which use the IEEE 802.4 Token Bus technology

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines a MIB module, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific child.
802.4 is token bus, not token ring, so the token ring tag does not fit; the text's mention of '802.5' is a typo.
802.4 is a different MAC technology from Ethernet; nothing here concerns Ethernet.
ASN.1 is only the notation in which the MIB objects are written, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.4 Token Bus
gaps.why: The document is about managing this link-layer technology, but the taxonomy has no tag for token bus. The nearest link-layer tags (token ring, Ethernet) are different technologies.

RFC1231.title: IEEE 802.5 Token Ring MIB
RFC1231.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module for managing IEEE 802.5 Token Ring interfaces, with interface, statistics and timer tables plus test and chip-set identifiers.

token ring.why: The MIB's subject is the 802.5 Token Ring link technology: ring state, MAC errors, timers and chip sets. Readers of the token ring subject would want it.
token ring.quote: managed objects used for managing subnetworks which use the IEEE 802.5 Token Ring technology

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defined with the SMI. It is meant for SNMP-based management of Token Ring interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines three tables: the 802.5 Interface Table, which contains state and parameter information which is specific to 802.5 interfaces

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with. The document defines objects, not protocol behaviour, so MIB is the more specific fit.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for the object definitions, not a subject of the document.
The more specific token ring tag already covers it.

RFC1232.title: Definitions of managed objects for the DS1 Interface type
RFC1232.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (experimental) of managed objects for DS1/T1/E1 physical interfaces and CSUs, including configuration, interval/current/total error statistics and fractional DS1 channel groups.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (RFC1232-MIB) using the SMI for DS1 interfaces, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: this memo defines MIB objects for representing DS1 physical interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines only a MIB module, not SNMP itself.
ASN.1 and the SMI are only the notation used to write the definitions.
DS1 is a telephony transmission interface, not ISDN access; no ISDN content.
Parent topic implied by the MIB tag, which is more specific.

gaps.name: DS1/T1/E1 transmission interfaces
gaps.why: The document is about managing DS1 (T1/E1) circuits and CSUs, with error-second statistics, loopbacks and fractional DS1. The taxonomy has no tag for T-carrier or digital transmission links.

RFC1233.title: Definitions of managed objects for the DS3 Interface type
RFC1233.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (experimental) for managing DS3 (44.736 Mbps) physical interfaces and CSUs, with configuration, 15-minute interval, current and 24-hour total error statistics groups.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition for DS3 interface objects, using SMI and OBJECT-TYPE macros; readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: this memo defines MIB objects for representing DS3 physical interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol framework the MIB is used with; the document defines objects, not the protocol itself. The MIB tag is the more specific fit.
ASN.1 is the notation used for the object definitions via the SMI, not a subject of the document.
DS3 is a PDH/T-carrier interface, not SONET/SDH; no SONET content.
Implied by the MIB tag as an ancestor, so not listed separately.

gaps.name: DS3 / T-carrier (PDH) transmission interfaces
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DS1/DS3 digital hierarchy transmission links or CSU/DSU equipment, which is the physical-layer subject of this MIB and its companion DS1 MIB.

RFC1234.title: Tunneling IPX traffic through IP networks
RFC1234.summary: RFC 1234 specifies encapsulating Novell IPX datagrams in UDP packets (port 213) so IPX traffic can be tunneled across IP internets, including address mapping and simulated broadcasts via peer lists.

IPX.why: The whole document defines how IPX is carried over IP, including IPX address mapping, broadcast simulation and MTU. The IPX tag covers IPX interworking and fits this document.
IPX.quote: a method of encapsulating IPX datagrams within UDP packets so that IPX traffic can travel across an IP internet

rejected.why: UDP is only the encapsulating substrate. The document defines no new UDP behaviour beyond a checksum recommendation and a port assignment.
The document is a tunnelling mechanism, but the more specific IPX tag already covers it. A generic tunnelling tag would add little.
IP is only the carrier network. The document does not specify or extend IPv4.
Multicast is mentioned only as a possible future replacement for the peer list. It is not the subject of the document.
The port 213 assignment is boilerplate in the Assigned Numbers section and does not make the document about IANA.

RFC1235.title: Coherent File Distribution Protocol
RFC1235.summary: RFC 1235 specifies the experimental Coherent File Distribution Protocol (CFDP), a UDP-based broadcast one-to-many file transfer protocol using tickets, block requests and NAK-style retransmission to serve many clients with a single transmission.

reliable multicast.why: CFDP is a one-to-many reliable file delivery protocol over broadcast (and potentially multicast) with client-driven loss recovery, so it belongs with reliable multicast transport.
reliable multicast.quote: designed to speed up one-to-many file transfer operations that exhibit traffic coherence on media with broadcast capability

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate on which CFDP runs; the document does not define anything new about UDP.
A TFTP-like front end (vtftp) is mentioned only as an example front end and is explicitly not part of CFDP.
BOOTP is mentioned as a possible ticket-server front end, not specified here; no DHCP/BOOTP tag fits the document's subject.
NETBLT is only cited as similar in buffer placement; the document is not about it.
CFDP is a file distribution protocol but not FTP; FTP is not discussed.
Multicast is mentioned only as a future delivery option; the protocol is built on broadcast and is covered better by the reliable multicast tag.

gaps.name: Broadcast file distribution / bulk file transfer protocols
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no general tag for one-to-many file distribution or bulk data transfer apart from specific protocols like FTP, TFTP and NETBLT.

RFC1236.title: IP to X.121 address mapping for DDN
RFC1236.summary: Informational memo defining a standard algorithm for mapping Class A, B and C IPv4 addresses to CCITT X.121 addresses for IP hosts on the DDN X.25 network.

X.25.why: The document specifies how IP addresses map to X.121 addresses used by DDN X.25 interfaces, i.e. IP over X.25 public data networks.
X.25.quote: This memo defines a standard way of converting IP addresses to CCITT X.121 addresses

IPv4.why: A substantial part of the document covers IPv4 Class A/B/C address structure and how its fields (network, host, REST) feed the mapping.
IPv4.quote: an IP address consists of the ASCII text string representation of four decimal numbers separated by periods

rejected.why: IPv4 is the more specific tag, and the document is about mapping IPv4 addresses to X.121, not about IP address architecture or allocation.
The DDN is related to the ARPANET lineage, but the document is about X.25 address mapping, not ARPANET protocols or operations.
The document is an algorithmic address mapping, not the ARP resolution protocol.

RFC1237.title: Guidelines for OSI NSAP Allocation in the Internet
RFC1237.summary: RFC 1237 gives guidelines for allocating OSI NSAP addresses in the Internet, structuring hierarchical addresses (GOSIP v2, ANSI DCC) so that CLNP routing with IS-IS and inter-domain routing can aggregate prefixes, including multi-homing and transition issues.

CLNP.why: The document is about NSAP address allocation for CLNP deployment in the Internet. CLNP is the network protocol these addresses serve, and the OSI node under internet layer is the closest fit.
CLNP.quote: This paper provides guidelines for allocating NSAPs in the Internet

addressing.why: Much of the document concerns address architecture, assignment authorities, hierarchical prefix allocation, multi-homing and address transition (renumbering).
addressing.quote: The ability of routing to scale is dependent upon the use of data abstraction based on hierarchical NSAP addresses.

IS-IS.why: Sections 3.2 and 3.3 describe DIS10589 operation and its constraints on NSAP structure, which drive the allocation guidelines.
IS-IS.quote: Arrangement of parts of the NSAP for efficient operation of the DIS10589IS-IS routing protocol;

rejected.why: The routing hierarchy and aggregation discussion is central, but it is mainly in service of address allocation, so addressing and CLNP cover it.
Section 5.4 covers multi-homed routing domains in depth, but only as one part of the allocation guidance, and the multihoming tag is geared to IPv6 and host multihoming.
Section 5.7 covers address transition briefly. It is a minor part and is explicitly said to be mostly out of scope.
BGP and IDRP are mentioned only as the expected inter-domain protocol, not specified or analysed.
The document concerns OSI CLNP addressing, not the IPng candidate protocols.

gaps.name: OSI NSAP addressing (ISO 8348/Add.2, GOSIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has CLNP under OSI but no tag specifically for OSI NSAP address formats and their registration authorities, which are the document's core subject.

RFC1238.title: CLNS MIB for use with Connectionless Network Protocol (ISO 8473) and End System to Intermediate System (ISO 9542)
RFC1238.summary: Defines an experimental SNMP MIB module for managing CLNP (ISO 8473) and ES-IS (ISO 9542) entities, with counters, address, routing, and address-translation tables and CLNP error PDU statistics.

CLNP.why: The MIB exists to manage CLNP entities: PDU counters, routing table, address tables, and CLNP error PDU counters. CLNP is the most specific tag for the protocol it manages.
CLNP.quote: The objects defined in this MIB module are be used when the ISO Connectionless-mode Network Protocol [10] and End System to

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module defined with the SMI and concise MIB conventions, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an experimental portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

OSI.why: A substantial portion covers the ES-IS (ISO 9542) group, with ESH, ISH and RDU PDU counters. ES-IS is an OSI network-layer protocol with no specific tag, so the OSI parent fits.
OSI.quote: esisESHins OBJECT-TYPE

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol the MIB is carried over; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
ASN.1 is just the notation used for the object definitions; the document does not address ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
The routing protocol enumerations (is-is, ospf, bgp) are only route-source values; no routing protocol is managed here.
The NetToMedia and MediaToNet tables resemble address translation, but they are CLNP-specific and not ARP.

RFC1239.title: Reassignment of experimental MIBs to standard MIBs
RFC1239.summary: Reassigns object identifier arcs for the Generic Interface extensions, Token Bus, Token Ring, DS1 and DS3 MIBs from the experimental subtree to the standard MIB and transmission subtrees, updating RFCs 1229-1233.

MIB.why: The document is entirely about OID assignments for MIB modules, moving them from the experimental to the standard MIB namespace.
MIB.quote: a preferable practice is to assign arcs in the standard MIB namespace at the earliest phase of standardization and to preserve these assignments

token ring.why: Reassigns the token ring MIB (RFC 1231) arc, though only as one entry in a table of reassignments.
token ring.section: SMI Network Management New Standard Codes

rejected.why: This is a registry-style assignment of OID arcs, but it concerns MIB namespace practice, not IANA registries or stewardship.
Not in the taxonomy as a tag; DS1/DS3 MIBs are only listed as reassigned arcs.
The MIBs are SNMP-related, but the document does not specify or discuss the SNMP framework.

gaps.name: DS1/DS3 interface MIBs (T1/T3 carrier objects)
gaps.why: Two of the five MIBs updated cover DS1 and DS3 transmission interface types, and the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC1240.title: OSI connectionless transport services on top of UDP: Version 1
RFC1240.summary: Specifies how to provide the OSI connectionless transport service (T-UNIT-DATA, ISO 8602) on top of UDP, including primitive mapping, UDP port 102, and the UD TPDU packet format.

OSI.why: The document specifies the OSI connectionless transport service (T-UNIT-DATA) and its mapping onto UDP/IP, supporting a transition from IP to OSI networks. OSI is the closest tag in the taxonomy.
OSI.quote: this memo specifies how to offer OSI connectionless transport service using the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) of the TCP/IP suite.

transport mapping.why: It is a binding of one protocol, the OSI connectionless transport protocol, over another transport, UDP. It defines the primitive and parameter mappings and the UD TPDU encapsulation.
transport mapping.quote: the OSI T-UNIT-DATA service will use UDP as its connectionless network service provider.

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate carrying the UD TPDUs. The document does not extend or analyse UDP, although it reserves port 102.
The document is about connectionless transport (ISO 8602), not the connectionless network protocol. It emulates the N-UNIT-DATA primitives with UDP instead of using CLNP.
The document covers transport-layer service mapping, not general IP-layer matters.

RFC1241.title: Scheme for an internet encapsulation protocol: Version 1
RFC1241.summary: Defines an experimental IP encapsulation (tunneling) protocol using Encapsulators, Decapsulators and Flow IDs, including header mapping, error messages, ICMP handling and virtual network construction.

tunneling.why: The whole document specifies a generic IP-in-IP style encapsulation (tunnel) protocol with its own header, flow mapping and decapsulation procedures.
tunneling.quote: A final alternative is to create a new IP encapsulation protocol which uses the current IP header format.

ICMP.why: A substantial appendix analyses how each ICMP message type interacts with encapsulation, and the protocol defines an error message that carries forwarded ICMP.
ICMP.quote: The most controversial aspect of encapsulation is the handling of ICMP messages.

rejected.why: The protocol defines its own Encapsulation Protocol Header with Flow ID rather than plain IP-in-IP, so the generic tunneling tag fits better.
IDPR Setup is only mentioned as an example of how Flow IDs might be managed; the document is not about IDPR.
Appendix D mentions virtual networks overlaid on routing topology, but this is a brief illustration, not the focus; the tag is for data-plane virtualization overlays like VXLAN.
The protocol operates over IPv4 headers but is not about IPv4 itself.
Fragmentation and DF handling are discussed, but not as a path MTU discovery mechanism.

RFC1242.title: Benchmarking Terminology for Network Interconnection Devices
RFC1242.summary: RFC 1242 defines terminology (throughput, latency, frame loss rate, back-to-back, etc.) for benchmarking network interconnection devices such as bridges and routers, as groundwork for later BMWG test methodology memos.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a benchmarking terminology for network devices (throughput, latency, frame loss rate, back-to-back), which is the benchmarking methodology subject.
benchmarking.quote: This memo discusses and defines a number of terms that are used in describing performance benchmarking tests and the results of such tests.

rejected.why: Benchmarking is the more specific child covering device benchmarking terminology; the document is not about network-path performance metrics.
It is a glossary, but of benchmarking terms; the benchmarking tag is the specific subject, not general glossaries or requirements language.
ARP is only mentioned as an example of overhead processing.
OSPF is mentioned only as an example of routing update processing load.

RFC1243.title: AppleTalk Management Information Base
RFC1243.summary: RFC 1243 defines an SNMP MIB module (mib-2 appletalk group) for managing AppleTalk networks, covering LLAP, AARP, ports, DDP, RTMP, KIP, ZIP, NBP and Echo.

AppleTalk.why: The managed objects are for the AppleTalk protocol suite (DDP, RTMP, ZIP, NBP, AARP, LLAP, KIP), so AppleTalk readers would want this.
AppleTalk.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing AppleTalk networks.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMI, placed under mib-2.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to access the objects; the document defines MIB objects, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1/SMI is only the notation used for the definitions.
AARP is one group among many and is AppleTalk-specific, not IP ARP.
KIP encapsulates AppleTalk in IP, but only as one managed group, not the document's subject.
RTMP and KIP routing tables are managed, but the document is about management objects, not routing protocol.

RFC1244.title: Site Security Handbook
RFC1244.summary: FYI 8 handbook guiding sites on setting computer security policies, preventive procedures, incident handling and post-incident follow-up, with resource lists and an annotated bibliography.

incident response.why: A large part of the handbook covers incident handling: evaluation, notification, containment, eradication, recovery, legal and documentation, and post-incident lessons. It also lists response teams such as CERT and CIAC.
incident response.quote: Section 5 discusses incident handling: what kinds of issues does a site face when someone violates the security policy.

operational security.why: The core subject is site security policy and operational procedures: risk assessment, monitoring, account and password management, configuration management, audits and backups.
operational security.quote: This handbook is a guide to setting computer security policies and procedures for sites that have systems on the Internet.

rejected.why: Considered as the general parent, but the more specific operational security and incident response tags fit better.
Passwords, Kerberos and smart cards are discussed only as site procedures or resources. The document does not specify or analyse them.
It gets a brief paragraph as one of the authentication systems a site might use. The document is not about the protocol.
Privacy Enhanced Mail is mentioned in a short subsection of encryption resources and is not a subject of the document.
Firewalls are covered in a short subsection and in some router filtering discussion, but only as one of many protective measures.
This is an FYI document, but the taxonomy tag is for introductory guides for Internet users, and this handbook's audience is system administrators and decision makers.

gaps.name: Site security policy and procedures
gaps.why: The handbook's main subject is organisational computer security policy, covering risk assessment, acceptable use and legal and ethical issues. The taxonomy has only operational security and incident response, which cover it only partly.

RFC1245.title: OSPF Protocol Analysis
RFC1245.summary: Informational analysis report on OSPF Version 2 summarizing its key features and analyzing its bandwidth, memory, CPU cost, scaling limits and suitable/unsuitable environments.

OSPF.why: The whole document is an analysis of OSPF v2 features, resource consumption and scaling, so it belongs on the OSPF page.
OSPF.quote: This report attempts to summarize the key features of OSPF V2. It also attempts to analyze how the protocol will perform and scale in the Internet.

rejected.why: RIP is only used as a comparison point for bandwidth, memory and CPU; the document is not about it.
Only generic EGP/policy-based exterior protocols are mentioned in passing, not BGP specifically.
Equal-cost multipath is listed as one OSPF feature, not a substantial subject of the document.
Scaling is discussed, but only for OSPF, so the OSPF tech tag is the more specific fit.

RFC1246.title: Experience with the OSPF Protocol
RFC1246.summary: Report on OSPF Version 2 experience (interoperability testing, operational deployments, simulation, MIB and authentication summaries) supporting advancement to Draft Standard.

OSPF.why: The whole document evaluates OSPF V2: implementations, interoperability rounds, deployments at NSI, BARRNet and OARnet, and simulation.
OSPF.quote: This report documents experience with OSPF V2. This includes reports on interoperability testing, field experience, simulations and the current state of OSPF implementations.

MIB.why: A section summarizes the OSPF MIB's groups, tables and object statistics.
MIB.quote: An OSPF Management Information Base has been published in RFC 1248 [3].

rejected.why: RIP is discussed only as an interchange partner and comparison baseline, not as the subject.
EGP appears as an exterior protocol whose routes are imported into OSPF, not as the subject.
SNMP is used only for trap collection at OARnet; the MIB section is covered by the MIB tag.
X.25 was only a test medium for OSPF non-broadcast networks.
The authentication section is a brief summary of OSPF's own mechanism, so it is covered by the OSPF tag.

RFC1247.title: OSPF Version 2
RFC1247.summary: RFC 1247 specifies OSPF version 2, a link-state interior gateway routing protocol with areas, flooding, Designated Router election, TOS routing, equal-cost multipath, and authentication, obsoleting RFC 1131.

OSPF.why: The whole document is the OSPF version 2 specification: packet formats, neighbor and interface state machines, flooding, and routing table calculation.
OSPF.quote: This memo documents version 2 of the OSPF protocol.  OSPF is a link-state based routing protocol.

rejected.why: Equal-cost multipath is one feature of OSPF handled within the protocol spec, not the subject of the document.
EGP appears only as a source of external routes that OSPF imports and advertises.
Mentioned only in the history section as a related SPF-based protocol.
OSPF uses IP multicast addresses (AllSPFRouters, AllDRouters) as a mechanism but does not specify multicast routing.
Mentioned only incidentally, such as destination unreachable messages.
OSPF runs over IP, which is a substrate here, and the document does not specify IP itself.

RFC1248.title: OSPF Version 2 Management Information Base
RFC1248.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module for managing OSPF Version 2, with tables for areas, link-state database, interfaces, virtual links and neighbors.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module in SMI/ASN.1 defining managed objects for OSPF, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing OSPF Version 2.

OSPF.why: All objects model OSPFv2 state and configuration: areas, LSAs, interfaces, neighbors, virtual links. OSPF readers would want this management specification.
