OSPF.quote: OSPF is a powerful routing protocol, equipped with features to handle virtually any configuration requirement

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it, and SNMP is an ancestor.
ASN.1 is used only as the SMI definition notation, not specified or extended.
IP addresses and TOS appear only as object syntax, not as the subject.

RFC1249.title: DIXIE Protocol Specification
RFC1249.summary: RFC 1249 specifies DIXIE, a lightweight UDP/TCP request-response protocol that lets small hosts access the OSI X.500 Directory without a full DAP/OSI stack.

X.500.why: DIXIE is a protocol translation front end to the X.500 Directory, with operations mirroring DAP read, search, list, modify, add, remove and bind.
X.500.quote: DIXIE offers both UDP and TCP access to The Directory.

rejected.why: DIXIE is a precursor with a similar goal, but the document does not specify or discuss LDAP.
The parent topic is implied by the X.500 tag, so it is not listed separately.
UDP is only the transport DIXIE runs over. The document does not define anything new about UDP.
TCP is only the transport DIXIE runs over. The document does not define anything new about TCP.
The OSI stack is what DIXIE avoids. The OSI tag covers network-layer protocols, which this document does not address.

RFC1250.title: IAB Official Protocol Standards
RFC1250.summary: RFC 1250 is the IAB's quarterly list of Internet protocol standards, explaining the standardization process, protocol states and statuses, and listing protocols by maturity level.

IETF process.why: The document describes the standards track, states, status levels, minimum delays, and IESG/IAB roles, i.e. the standards process.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: Substantial sections explain the RFC series, submission, the RFC Editor's decision table and how RFCs relate to standards.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned as contact and manager of the standards list, but the document is not about IANA registries.
It is a dated status snapshot, not a retrospective.
Defines states and statuses, but this is part of the process description rather than a glossary or requirements-language document.
Individual protocols (TCP, IP, DNS, OSPF, SNMP, etc.) are only listed in tables, not specified or analysed.
SNMP and MIBs appear only as list entries among many protocols.
Telnet options table is a list entry; the document is not about Telnet.

gaps.name: Internet standards status list / protocol maturity levels
gaps.why: The document is a catalogue of protocol standards status across the whole suite; no taxonomy tag captures standards-status roll-ups beyond IETF process.

RFC1251.title: Who's Who in the Internet: Biographies of IAB, IESG and IRSG Members
RFC1251.summary: An FYI RFC compiling biographies and personal views on Internet growth from 1991 members of the IAB, IESG and IRSG.

internet history.why: The memo is a retrospective collection of personal histories and reflections on how the Internet and its protocols grew, which fits histories and retrospectives.
internet history.quote: The ARPANET is 20 years old. The next meeting of the IETF in St. Louis this coming March will be the 20th plenary.

user guides.why: It is an FYI-series document written for the Internet community, so readers browsing FYI guides would expect it.
user guides.quote: This FYI RFC contains biographical information about members of the Internet Activities Board (IAB)

rejected.why: It describes the people who serve in IETF/IAB/IESG roles, not the standards process or procedures.
ARPANET is mentioned often in the biographies, but the document is not about the ARPANET's protocols or operations.
The RFC series and the FYI series are mentioned in passing, but the document is not about RFC format or publication.
Contributors comment on scaling and growth, but the document does not set out architectural principles.

gaps.name: Biographies of Internet leaders
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for people or biographical material, apart from the general internet history topic.

RFC1252.title: OSPF Version 2 Management Information Base
RFC1252.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module for managing OSPF Version 2 routers, with tables for areas, link-state database, interfaces, virtual links and neighbors.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (RFC1252-MIB) using SMI/concise MIB conventions, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

OSPF.why: The objects model OSPF areas, LSDB, interfaces, neighbors and virtual links, so it is a management extension for OSPF.
OSPF.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing OSPF Version 2.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to access the objects; the MIB module is the subject, and it is already covered by the MIB tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the objects and is not itself the subject.
IP addresses and TOS appear only as object syntax and metric context, and the document is not about IPv4.
The more specific MIB tag, which sits under SNMP, already covers it.

RFC1253.title: OSPF Version 2 Management Information Base
RFC1253.summary: RFC 1253 defines the SNMP MIB module for managing OSPF Version 2 routers, with tables for areas, link-state database, interfaces, virtual links and neighbors.

OSPF.why: The whole document is a management object model for OSPFv2: its areas, LSDB, interfaces, neighbors and virtual links, so OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing OSPF Version 2.

MIB.why: The document is an SMI MIB module definition (RFC1253-MIB) with textual conventions, conceptual tables and row creation rules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol used to reach the objects; the document defines MIB objects and does not extend or specify SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific child.
ASN.1 is just the notation the SMI uses for defining objects; the document is not about ASN.1.
Parent topic implied by OSPF; the OSPF tag fits more specifically.
IP addresses and TOS appear as object syntax only; the document is not about IPv4.

RFC1254.title: Gateway Congestion Control Survey
RFC1254.summary: A 1991 IETF Performance and Congestion Control WG survey of gateway congestion control policies (Source Quench, Random Drop, DEC-bit Congestion Indication, Fair Queueing) and the end-system responses such as Slow-start, with an appendix on X.25 SVC management.

congestion control.why: The whole document surveys gateway congestion control and avoidance policies and the end-system responses to them. The parent topic fits because the policies are cross-transport and no single child covers them.
congestion control.quote: The IETF Performance and Congestion Control Working Group surveyed and reviewed gateway congestion control and avoidance approaches.

AQM.why: Random Drop and queue-based gateway policies (Fair Queueing, Stochastic Fairness Queueing) are early active queue management. A substantial part of the survey covers them.
AQM.quote: Random Drop is a gateway congestion control policy intended to give feedback to users whose traffic congests the gateway by dropping packets on a statistical basis.

ECN.why: The DEC Bit Congestion Indication and Selective Feedback policies are the precursor of ECN, and the survey describes them in detail.
ECN.quote: the information is communicated in a single bit, the Congestion Experienced Bit, set in the network header of the packets already being forwarded by a gateway.

ICMP.why: Source Quench is analysed as a gateway congestion policy, including its drawbacks and the end-system response to it.
ICMP.quote: The method of gateway congestion control currently used in the Internet is the Source Quench message of the RFC-792 [Pos81a] Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP).

rejected.why: Slow-start and TCP retransmission timers are discussed as end-system responses. The document is about gateway policy, not TCP itself.
Only the appendix covers X.25 SVC management for IP gateways. That is a minor part of the document.
Fairness and resource allocation are discussed, but there is no QoS architecture or signalling.
Metrics such as power and measurement intervals are discussed only to support the congestion control policies.
The MIB objects for congestion evaluation are mentioned in one paragraph as a future need.

RFC1255.title: A Naming Scheme for c=US
RFC1255.summary: Informational copy of NADF-175 defining how entries in the public X.500 Directory under c=US are named, using civil naming authorities (states, counties, organizations, persons) to build Distinguished Names and listings.

X.500.why: The whole document defines the DIT structure, object classes and RDNs for the public X.500 Directory under c=US, so X.500 readers would want it.
X.500.quote: The NADF is a collection of organizations which offer, or plan to offer, public Directory services in North America, based on the CCITT X.500 Recommendations.

directory services.why: It also treats directory listing versus registration and right-to-use as general directory-service concepts, not only X.500 specifics.
directory services.quote: This publication stage is what the Directory Service is all about.

rejected.why: DNS appears only in a brief comparison of registration and publication in 3.2 and 3.3. The document is not about DNS.
It is about naming, but the specific X.500 tag fits better and the parent is implied only through DNS, which was rejected. The naming here is directory DN naming, not general name resolution.
LDAP is not mentioned. The document is about X.500 naming.

gaps.name: X.500 directory naming schemes / Distinguished Name structure
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for naming schemes within directories, such as DIT structure, RDNs and civil naming. X.500 is the closest fit.

RFC1256.title: ICMP Router Discovery Messages
RFC1256.summary: RFC 1256 specifies ICMP Router Advertisement and Router Solicitation messages, letting hosts on multicast/broadcast links dynamically discover neighboring routers, with router and host behaviour and configuration variables.

ICMP.why: The document defines new ICMP message types (9 and 10), Router Advertisement and Solicitation, so it extends ICMP and belongs on its subject page.
ICMP.quote: This document specifies an extension of the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) to enable hosts attached to multicast or broadcast networks to discover the IP addresses of their neighboring routers.

rejected.why: Advertisements and solicitations use the all-systems and all-routers multicast groups, but only as delivery. The document is not about multicast routing or group membership.
The document says the messages 'do not constitute a routing protocol'. They only discover first-hop routers.
The protocol runs over IPv4 and uses its addressing, but IPv4 is only the substrate.
BOOTP is mentioned only as a way for a host to learn its own address. It is not the subject here.
ARP appears only in the security discussion as a comparison.

RFC1257.title: Isochronous applications do not require jitter-controlled networks
RFC1257.summary: Informational memo arguing that networks supporting isochronous applications (voice, video) need only bound delay and provide bandwidth, not control jitter, because receivers can restore isochrony using timestamps and buffering.

performance measurement.why: The memo is about which delay, jitter and bandwidth properties a network must provide for real-time applications. The closest taxonomy fit is a performance topic, though it is a weak match.
performance measurement.quote: This memo argues that jitter control is not required for networks to support isochronous applications. A network providing bandwidth and bounds delay is sufficient.

rejected.why: NTP is cited only as evidence that a universal time source is feasible. The memo is not about it.
The memo discusses delay and bandwidth guarantees conceptually. It does not discuss QoS architectures or signalling, so QoS is only a possible fit.
The memo concerns voice and video applications, but it is about network service requirements, not real-time communication protocols. This is the closest general topic and a reasonable alternative.
It invokes the end-to-end principle in one passage, but architecture is not the main subject.

gaps.name: Isochronous/jitter-controlled networking (real-time service requirements)
gaps.why: The document is about delay, jitter and bandwidth requirements for multimedia networks. No taxonomy tag cleanly covers this, so the tagging is approximate.

RFC1258.title: BSD Rlogin
RFC1258.summary: Informational memo documenting the BSD rlogin protocol: a TCP-based remote login facility with connection setup, flow control, window size messages, urgent-data control bytes, and trust-related security cautions.

rlogin.why: The whole document specifies the BSD rlogin protocol: connection establishment, flow control, window size, control bytes, and closure.
rlogin.quote: The rlogin facility provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal with proper flushing of output.

rejected.why: rlogin only uses TCP as its transport (port 513, urgent data pointer); the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Mentioned only as a comparison; rlogin is a distinct protocol and Telnet is not specified here.
Mentioned in passing as a possible secure authentication extension, not covered by the document.
The trusted-host password bypass is discussed in the cautionary section, but it is a feature of rlogin and is covered by the rlogin tag rather than a general authentication subject.

RFC1259.title: Building the open road: The NREN as test-bed for the national public network
RFC1259.summary: Policy essay by Mitchell Kapor arguing that the NREN should serve as a test-bed for a future National Public Network, with recommendations on competition, open platforms, universal pricing, ease of use, standards, common carriage and privacy.

internet governance.why: The whole memo is a set of recommendations on how the national network should be governed and administered: carrier competition, common carriage, pricing and access policy. It is the closest taxonomy fit for a public-policy paper.
internet governance.quote: the NREN can serve as a working test-bed for new technologies, applications, and governing policies that will ultimately shape the larger national network.

rejected.why: The memo urges open, non-proprietary architecture and interoperability, but only as policy advocacy. It does not discuss Internet architectural principles in technical terms.
Section VII briefly urges public-key encryption and legal privacy protection. It is a short part of a policy paper, not a protocol privacy analysis.
It is a contemporary 1991 policy advocacy paper, not a retrospective.
ASCII is mentioned only as an example of an inadequate text standard.

gaps.name: Telecommunications and network policy (NREN, National Public Network, common carriage)
gaps.why: The memo is mainly about national communications and regulatory policy, including competition, universal service and common carriage. The taxonomy has no tag for telecom policy or law, so internet governance is only an approximate fit.

RFC1261.title: Transition of Nic Services
RFC1261.summary: Announces the 1 October 1991 transfer of the Network Information Center's registration, information and help desk services from SRI International to Government Systems Inc., with new contact details and a registration freeze during the move.

domain registration.why: The memo concerns the transfer of the registry operator for network numbers and top-level domain names, including suspension and resumption of registration actions and the HOSTMASTER/REGISTRAR contact points.
domain registration.quote: These services include network/user registration (i.e., network number and top level domain name assignment), on-line information services, and Help Desk operations.

rejected.why: The ID (WHOIS) database is mentioned only as the registration database being frozen and transferred. The memo says nothing about the WHOIS protocol or service.
It is a contemporaneous operational notice, not a history or retrospective.
The root domain server address is listed only as contact information. The memo does not cover DNS behaviour.

RFC1262.title: Guidelines for Internet Measurement Activities
RFC1262.summary: IAB guidance for researchers planning Internet measurement experiments, urging minimal impact on networks, privacy protection, and advance notification of providers and CERT.

performance measurement.why: The whole document is guidance on conducting network measurement activities: impact, passive vs. active, notification, and privacy.
performance measurement.quote: Measurement of the Internet is critical for future development, evolution and deployment planning.

rejected.why: Privacy of collected data is one of the listed conditions, but the document is about measurement ethics generally, not protocol privacy considerations.
It mentions informing CERT and avoiding the appearance of intrusion, but it does not address security practices for infrastructure.
CERT is mentioned only as a party to notify, not as an incident exchange subject.
Anonymous FTP is mentioned only as a way to publish study information.

gaps.name: Internet measurement ethics and etiquette
gaps.why: The document's focus is ethical and courteous conduct for measurement experiments. The nearest tag, performance measurement, covers metrics and methods rather than conduct guidelines.

RFC1263.title: TCP Extensions Considered Harmful
RFC1263.summary: An opinion piece arguing against backward-compatible TCP extensions (RFC 1072 and RFC 1185) and proposing protocol evolution with versioned TCP (via a VTCP version-selection protocol) and a new header format with larger fields, plus a separate RPC protocol for request-reply use.

TCP.why: The document critiques TCP extensions (window scaling, timestamps, SACK) and proposes an alternative evolved TCP with a new header format. Readers of TCP would want it.
TCP.quote: It is our intent to argue against acceptance of the various TCP extensions, most notably RFC's 1072 and 1185

rejected.why: Congestion control is mentioned only briefly as a future need for a TCP-independent scheme, not as a main subject.
The document criticizes the standardization process, but the discussion is incidental to its case study on TCP and does not address IETF procedures in detail.
RPC is mentioned only through VMTP and Sprite RPC as an alternative to misusing TCP, not ONC RPC.
The document discusses protocol evolution strategy, which is architecture-adjacent, but is primarily about TCP changes.

gaps.name: protocol evolution / extensibility strategy
gaps.why: The document's central theme is how to change protocols: creation vs backward-compatible extension vs evolution with versioned protocols. No taxonomy tag cleanly covers protocol extensibility and versioning.

RFC1264.title: Internet Engineering Task Force Internet Routing Protocol Standardization Criteria
RFC1264.summary: Informational RFC setting out the IAB/IESG criteria (specification, MIB, security, implementations, operational experience, reports) for advancing routing protocols through Proposed, Draft and full Internet Standard.

routing.why: The whole document is about what routing protocols must demonstrate to be standardized. It covers no single protocol, so the general routing topic fits.
routing.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide more specific guidance for the advancement of routing protocols.

IETF process.why: It defines the standards-track advancement requirements and the reports submitted to the IESG at each maturity level, which is IETF process.
IETF process.quote: The IAB and the IESG have evolved a three-stage Internet standardization process.

rejected.why: It requires an authentication mechanism for routing messages, but only as one checklist item. It does not address securing routing.
It requires a MIB for each routing protocol, but only as a requirement. It defines no MIB.
EGP is used as a generic class of exterior gateway protocols, not the historic EGP protocol.
RIP is only named as an existing protocol to compare against.

RFC1265.title: BGP Protocol Analysis
RFC1265.summary: RFC 1265 analyzes BGP's key features, bandwidth, CPU and memory scaling, and applicability, to document that BGP meets the Draft Standard requirements.

BGP.why: The whole document analyzes BGP's features, performance, scalability and applicability, so BGP is the subject.
BGP.quote: The purpose of this report is to document how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard have been satisfied by the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).

rejected.why: EGP is only a point of comparison for bandwidth and CPU use and for coexistence. The document does not specify or analyze it.
TCP is only the reliable transport BGP uses, so it is not a subject of the document.
The scalability discussion concerns BGP specifically. The BGP tag covers it, so this broader tag is not needed.

RFC1266.title: Experience with the BGP Protocol
RFC1266.summary: Report documenting how BGP (version 3) satisfies Draft Standard requirements, covering documentation, MIB, security, implementations, operational experience in CA*Net/NSFNET, and the use of TCP as BGP transport under congestion.

BGP.why: The whole document is about BGP: its versions, implementations, operational deployment and transport experience.
BGP.quote: The purpose of this memo is to document how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard have been satisfied by Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).

rejected.why: Section 9 discusses TCP as BGP's transport and convergence under congestion, but it defends the choice and defines nothing new about TCP. TCP is the substrate.
The BGP MIB is summarised in one short section (5), but the document is not about MIB modules. It only points to RFC 1269.
EGP appears only as a comparison point for bandwidth, CPU and convergence. The document is not about EGP.
Congestion is discussed as it affects routing convergence. The marking and priority measures are not congestion control mechanisms.

RFC1267.title: Border Gateway Protocol 3 (BGP-3)
RFC1267.summary: RFC 1267 specifies BGP version 3, the inter-autonomous-system routing protocol: message formats (OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION), path attributes, error handling, the finite state machine, and update processing, obsoleting RFCs 1105 and 1163.

BGP.why: The whole document is the specification of BGP-3: message formats, path attributes, FSM, error handling and update handling.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport BGP runs over (port 179); the appendix on TCP options is minor and not the document's subject.
EGP is mentioned only as historical background that BGP builds on, not specified or extended here.
Policy and hop-by-hop paradigm are discussed briefly, but the document is a protocol specification, so the BGP tag covers it.

RFC1268.title: Application of the Border Gateway Protocol in the Internet
RFC1268.summary: RFC 1268 describes how BGP-3 is applied in the Internet: the AS topological model, policy making, path selection, a recommended set of routing policies, and BGP/IGP interaction.

BGP.why: The whole document is about how BGP is used: topology, neighbor relationships, policy, path selection and IGP interaction.
BGP.quote: this document describes the usage of the BGP in the Internet.

rejected.why: Its topological model is specific to BGP, so the BGP tag covers it better than the general routing architecture tag.
EGP is mentioned only as a protocol that stub and multihomed ASes may keep running, not as a subject of the document.
RIP appears only as an example of a distance vector protocol and of an IGP that cannot tag routes.
Encapsulation is only one of several suggested BGP/IGP interaction methods in an appendix, and it is not specified in detail.
The multihomed AS is one category in the AS topological model. The document is not about multihoming architecture.

RFC1269.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Border Gateway Protocol: Version 3
RFC1269.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module for managing BGP-3 implementations, with a peer table, a received path attribute table, and two traps.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (RFC1269-MIB) defined with the SMI, with objects, tables and traps. MIB is the most specific tag under SNMP.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the Border Gateway Protocol [11,12].

BGP.why: The objects model BGP peer state, received path attributes (AS path, next hop, origin) and FSM transition traps. BGP readers would want this management specification.
BGP.quote: These objects are used to control and manage a BGP [11,12] implementation.

rejected.why: It is the management framework the MIB sits in. MIB is the more specific tag, and the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour.
ASN.1 is only the notation used by the SMI to define the objects. The document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
BGP runs over TCP and the MIB refers to the TCP connection table. The document does not specify anything about TCP.
The BGP tag covers the routing subject, so the parent tag is not needed.

RFC1270.title: SNMP Communications Services
RFC1270.summary: Informational memo discussing which communications services (UDP/IP, other transport/network stacks, or raw datalink; connectionless vs connection-oriented) an SNMP implementation should use, concluding UDP/IP is best in nearly all cases.

SNMP.why: The whole document analyses how SNMP messages should be carried (UDP/IP vs Ethernet, OSI, IPX) and recommends SNMP over UDP/IP.
SNMP.quote: This document discusses various issues to be considered when determining the underlying communications services to be used by an SNMP implementation.

transport mapping.why: The memo compares mappings of SNMP onto different transports and datalinks and the tradeoffs of each, which is the transport-mapping subject.
transport mapping.quote: documents specifying how to transport SNMP messages over protocols other than UDP/IP have been developed and published: SNMP Over Ethernet [3], SNMP Over OSI [2], and SNMP Over IPX [6]

rejected.why: TCP is discussed only as a rejected alternative and in the appendix packet-count illustration; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
UDP is the recommended substrate for SNMP, but the document is not about UDP itself or its usage guidelines.
The SMI and MIB RFCs are mentioned only as background of the management framework.
SNMP over IPX is mentioned as one of the alternative mappings, not the subject of the document.
SNMP over OSI is mentioned only as one alternative mapping.

RFC1271.title: Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base
RFC1271.summary: Defines the RMON MIB, SNMP managed objects for remote network monitoring probes (statistics, history, alarm, host, hostTopN, matrix, filter, packet capture, event groups), initially for Ethernet.

RMON.why: The document is the original RMON MIB specification, defining the monitoring groups and control semantics.
RMON.quote: it defines objects for managing remote network monitoring devices.

MIB.why: It is a MIB module in SMI/concise MIB format, including the OwnerString and EntryStatus textual conventions and row-creation semantics.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol the MIB is used with; the document defines objects, not protocol changes.
Ethernet statistics are the media-specific content, but the document is about monitoring, not IP over Ethernet.
The capture and filter groups are one part of the MIB, not a capture file format.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for object definitions.

RFC1272.title: Internet Accounting: Background
RFC1272.summary: Informational background document for the Internet Accounting Architecture, explaining motivations, policy context, meter placement, meter types, granularity and collection issues for IP-level usage reporting.

performance measurement.why: The document is about metering network usage: meters, flows, granularity, placement and collection of traffic counts. This fits performance measurement (traffic measurement methods) best of the available tags.
performance measurement.quote: A METER is a process which examines a stream of packets on a communications medium or between a pair of media.

rejected.why: SNMP is only mentioned as a possible collection framework to be investigated, not specified or extended here.
The parent is implied by the chosen tag; accounting management is the framing but measurement is the core.
IPFIX is a later flow export standard; this 1991 document is a precursor background but does not define it.
This is usage reporting, not authentication/authorization/accounting protocol frameworks; billing and enforcement are explicitly out of scope.
The document is about an accounting architecture, not general Internet architectural principles.

gaps.name: Internet accounting / usage reporting
gaps.why: The document is about accounting management (meters, collectors, usage reporting, cost allocation) and the taxonomy has no accounting tag, so the closest fit is performance measurement.

RFC1273.title: Measurement Study of Changes in Service-Level Reachability in the Global TCP/IP Internet: Goals, Experimental Design, Implementation, and Policy Considerations
RFC1273.summary: Informational memo describing a planned longitudinal measurement study that probes TCP service reachability (13 services) at ~12,700 domains, covering experimental design, load, control, and appropriate-use/privacy considerations.

performance measurement.why: The document is about an active Internet measurement study: its design, load considerations, and control of measurement collection.
performance measurement.quote: we have designed a study to measure changes in Internet service-level reachability over a period of one year

privacy.why: A substantial section addresses appropriate use, notification of probed sites, and privacy handling of the collected data.
privacy.quote: The data collected by this study is somewhat sensitive to privacy and security concerns, in the sense that it might be used as a "road map"
privacy.section: Network Appropriate Use and Privacy Issues

rejected.why: TCP connections are only the probing mechanism; the document specifies nothing about TCP itself.
Finger is used only to publish information about the study on the probing host.
DNS is used to select hosts and is one of the probed services, but the document is not about DNS.
The document explicitly states it is not a study of network security.
It is a contemporaneous measurement plan rather than a history or retrospective.

RFC1274.title: The COSINE and Internet X.500 Schema
RFC1274.summary: Defines the COSINE and Internet X.500 directory schema (pilot object classes, attribute types, syntaxes, OIDs) plus proformas and procedures for evolving the schema.

X.500.why: The whole document specifies object classes and attribute types for the X.500 Directory, and procedures for evolving that schema.
X.500.quote: This document suggests an X.500 Directory Schema, or Naming Architecture, for use in the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilots.

DNS.why: It defines the dNSDomain and domain object classes and the A, MX, NS, SOA and CNAME record attributes, which map DNS data into the directory.
DNS.quote: The DNS Domain (Domain NameServer) object class is used to define entries for DNS domains.

rejected.why: ASN.1 macros are the notation used to write the schema. The document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
The X.400 MHS object classes and attributes are reproduced only for completeness, and the document itself does not address X.400.
This is the parent of X.500, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
The rfc822Mailbox attribute only stores addresses. The document does not specify message format.
The proforma and registration process applies to the pilot schema's own OID subtree, not to IANA registries.

RFC1275.title: Replication Requirements to provide an Internet Directory using X.500
RFC1275.summary: RFC 1275 states requirements for knowledge and data replication, alternate DSA references, and scaling targets that must be met for a pilot Internet Directory built on the 1988 X.500 standard.

X.500.why: The whole document concerns X.500 deficiencies (DSAs, DIT, referrals) and the replication needed for an X.500-based Internet Directory.
X.500.quote: Knowledge information is critical to resolution of names, and performing searches. Knowledge information high up the tree needs to be widely available.

rejected.why: The X.500 tag is more specific and sits under it, so the parent is implied.
RFC 1006 transport over TCP/IP is mentioned only as the substrate for DSAs, and the document says nothing new about TCP.
LDAP is not mentioned or discussed in the document.

RFC1276.title: Replication and Distributed Operations extensions to provide an Internet Directory using X.500
RFC1276.summary: RFC 1276 specifies interim extensions to X.500(1988) for an Internet Directory: community-based distributed operations, knowledge representation, and an EDB-based replication protocol (GetEntryDataBlock).

X.500.why: The whole document extends the X.500 directory with replication, knowledge references and distributed operations extensions for DSAs and DUAs.
X.500.quote: This pulls an entire copy of the EDB.

rejected.why: The X.500 tag is more specific and already sits under directory services.
ASN.1 is only used to define the protocol and attributes. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
TCP/IP is mentioned only as one of the networks DSAs may run over.
LDAP is not mentioned and the document is not about it.

RFC1277.title: Encoding Network Addresses to Support Operation over Non-OSI Lower Layers
RFC1277.summary: Defines how OSI Network Addresses (X.121 form and a new Telex-AFI based DSP format) encode TCP/IP (RFC 1006) and X.25(80) addressing so OSI applications and the OSI Directory can run over non-OSI lower layers.

OSI.why: The whole document concerns OSI NSAP/Network Address encoding and how OSI applications coexist with non-OSI lower layers instead of a global OSI Network Service.
OSI.quote: This document defines a new network address format, and rules for using some existing network address formats.

X.25.why: A substantial part specifies how X.121 addresses and an X.25(80) DTE/PID/CUDF network-specific format are encoded in the address.
X.25.quote: The IDP/Prefix identifies an X.25(80) subnetwork.

addressing.why: Core content is address allocation and encoding (AFI/IDI/DSP structure, prefix assignments), an addressing matter in its own right.
addressing.quote: defines mechanisms to encode addressing information

rejected.why: The OSI Directory motivates the work, but the document specifies network address encoding, not the directory service.
RFC 1006 and X.25 transport mappings are assumed; the document only encodes addresses for them.
TCP/IP is just one network whose address (IP, port) is encoded; TCP itself is not specified.
The document explicitly excludes CLNS/CLNP use and refers to RFC 1237 for that.

RFC1278.title: A string encoding of Presentation Address
RFC1278.summary: Defines a human-readable string encoding for OSI Presentation Addresses (selectors plus network addresses), including a BNF, macros and examples, for use in ISODE/THORN.

OSI.why: The document specifies a string notation for OSI presentation addresses and network addresses (NSAPs), including RFC 1006 and X.25 forms, so it belongs with OSI addressing.
OSI.quote: OSI Application Entities use presentation addresses to address other Application Entities.

ABNF.why: A substantial part of the document is a formal BNF grammar defining the string syntax. However, this is the document's own grammar rather than a notation specification, so this tag is weak.
ABNF.quote: The BNF is given in figure 1.

rejected.why: A DNS domain name is allowed as input in the RFC 1006 form, but only as a convenience; the document does not specify DNS.
Presentation addresses are stored in the Directory, but the document is about a display string format, not the directory service.
The document has an X.25(80) network address form, but only as one encoding among several and not as IP over X.25.
The document is about OSI addresses, not IP address architecture. OSI is the more specific fit.

gaps.name: OSI presentation addresses / NSAP string encoding
gaps.why: The taxonomy has OSI and CLNP network-layer tags but none for OSI upper-layer naming and addressing, such as presentation addresses and selectors.

RFC1279.title: X.500 and Domains
RFC1279.summary: Experimental RFC proposing to represent DNS domain information (domain components, DNS records, networks, linkage to organisational names) in the X.500 Directory Information Tree, loosely coupled to organisational X.500 names.

X.500.why: The document defines X.500 object classes and attributes (Domain, DomainComponent, AssociatedName) for storing domain data in the DIT and linking to organisational X.500 entries.
X.500.quote: The basic model is that organisational X.500 is providing a layer of naming at the level above domain names.

DNS.why: A substantial part defines a text encoding of DNS resource records in the DIT, zone transfer between DSA and DNS server, and wildcard handling, so DNS readers would want it.
DNS.quote: DNS information can be associated with an entry in the DIT. It is important that this is done in a manner which is exactly equivalent

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which is already chosen and implies it.
Parent of DNS, implied; the document is about specific systems rather than naming in general.
RFC 822 mailbox mapping into the DIT is only an incidental use of domain components, not the subject.
Host naming conventions are not the subject; the document deals with domain names in the DIT.

RFC1280.title: IAB Official Protocol Standards
RFC1280.summary: RFC 1280 is the quarterly IAB list of Official Protocol Standards, explaining the standards process, maturity and requirement levels, and listing protocols by state, with contacts.

IETF process.why: The document describes the IAB/IESG standards track, maturity states, requirement levels and RFC processing decision table, which is IETF standards-process content.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial section explains the RFC series, submission to the RFC Editor, and the processing decision table for publication.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: Section 4 defines state and status terms, but this is part of the standards process, not a glossary.
IANA is only mentioned as a contact and manager of the list; the document is not about IANA registries.
TCP and many other protocols appear only as entries in the status lists; the document is not about any one of them.
It is a status snapshot of standards, not a history or retrospective.

RFC1281.title: Guidelines for the Secure Operation of the Internet
RFC1281.summary: An informational 1991 policy memo giving six guidelines on responsibilities of users, service providers and vendors for secure operation of the Internet, including incident cooperation and local security practices.

operational security.why: The document is a set of operational security guidelines for users, network operators and vendors, including Appendix A on local security practice (policy, controls, monitoring, incident response).
operational security.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide a set of guidelines to aid in the secure operation of the Internet.

incident response.why: A substantial part covers cooperation between sites on security incidents, security contacts, tracing violators and timely response to incidents.
incident response.quote: Each site is expected to notify other sites if it detects a penetration in progress at the other sites, and all sites are expected to help one another

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen tags; the document is about operational practice and incident handling, which have more specific children/topics.
Passwords and better authentication technology are mentioned only briefly as areas for improvement.
Privacy is mentioned as part of the definition of security and in log policy, but is not a main subject.
Voluntary rules of conduct are discussed, but the document is about security operations, not governance or standards administration.

RFC1282.title: BSD Rlogin
RFC1282.summary: Documents the BSD rlogin remote login protocol over TCP port 513, covering connection setup, flow control, window size messages, urgent-data control bytes, and security risks of trusted-host password bypass.

rlogin.why: The whole document specifies the BSD rlogin protocol: connection establishment, flow control, window size and urgent-data control bytes.
rlogin.quote: The rlogin facility provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal with proper flushing of output

rejected.why: Rlogin runs over TCP and uses the urgent pointer, but TCP is only the substrate and nothing new is defined for it.
Telnet is mentioned only as a comparison; the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned once as a possible secure authentication extension; not specified here.
The trusted-host password bypass is discussed as a security caveat, but the document is about the rlogin protocol and the rlogin tag covers it.

RFC1283.title: SNMP over OSI
RFC1283.summary: Defines mappings of SNMP onto OSI connectionless and connection-oriented transport services (CLNP, TP4, TP0/X.25), with addressing conventions and an OSI-specific Trap PDU.

SNMP.why: The document specifies how SNMP operates over OSI transports and defines an SNMP Trap PDU variant, so it is about SNMP.
SNMP.quote: This memo addresses these concerns by defining a framework for running the SNMP in an environment which supports the OSI transport services.

OSI.why: A substantial part covers OSI transport and network layer use (CLTS, COTS, TP4/CLNP, NSAP addressing), which readers of OSI coexistence would want.
OSI.quote: Unlike the Internet suite of protocols, OSI does not use well-known ports. Rather demultiplexing occurs on the basis of "selectors"

X.25.why: Defines SNMP addressing over TP0/X.25 using an X.25 protocol-ID and X.121 DTE addresses.
X.25.quote: When a COTS based on the TP0/X.25 is used to provide the transport backing for the SNMP

rejected.why: CLNP is the network substrate for the transport mapping; the document does not specify CLNP itself.
UDP is referenced only as the baseline Internet transport for comparison and addressing example.
The document imports a CLNS-MIB type and the SMI but defines no MIB module.
Considered as a topic, but the more specific SNMP and OSI tags already cover it.
The Trap PDU is written in ASN.1, but only as notation, not as the subject.

RFC1284.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types
RFC1284.summary: Defines a MIB module (dot3) of managed objects for Ethernet-like (IEEE 802.3) interfaces: generic control variables, error and collision statistics, collision histograms, tests (TDR, loopback), and chipset identifiers.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification defining dot3 objects with OBJECT-TYPE macros under the SMI, so it belongs on the MIB page.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

Ethernet.why: The managed objects are attributes of Ethernet-like (IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD) interfaces: MAC status, collisions, FCS and alignment errors, so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing ethernet-like objects.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access these objects; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, so the MIB tag is more specific.
ASN.1 is used only as the notation of the SMI to define objects; the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
Implied by the MIB tag as an ancestor; no need to list it separately.
The statistics counters are interface error and collision counts, not performance measurement methods or metrics.

RFC1285.title: FDDI Management Information Base
RFC1285.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module for managing FDDI devices (SMT, MAC, PATH, PORT, ATTACHMENT and chip set groups), derived from the ANSI X3T9.5 SMT standard.

FDDI.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing devices which implement the FDDI.

RFC1286.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges
RFC1286.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module (dot1dBridge) for managing IEEE 802.1d transparent and source-route bridges, including spanning tree, source routing, forwarding database, static filtering objects and traps.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition for bridges, specifying managed objects, tables and traps in SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP based internets.

Ethernet.why: Covers MAC bridging (transparent and source route) with forwarding database, filtering and spanning tree state; the closest taxonomy fit for LAN bridge management, though not strictly an Ethernet-only topic.
Ethernet.quote: In particular it defines objects for managing bridges based on the IEEE 802.1d draft standard between Local Area Network (LAN) segments.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access these objects; the document defines a MIB, not protocol changes, so the child MIB tag is more specific.
Source route bridging per IBM Token Ring is covered by the dot1dSr group, but the document is not about IP over token ring.
ASN.1 is just the notation used to write the MIB definitions.
Bridging is a link-layer subject, but the Ethernet tag was chosen as a more specific fit, so the parent is implied rather than listed.

gaps.name: MAC bridging / Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1d)
gaps.why: The document is about managing bridges and the spanning tree protocol, and the taxonomy has no tag for bridging or spanning tree.

RFC1287.title: Towards the Future Internet Architecture
RFC1287.summary: Report of the 1991 IAB/IESG architecture retreat that sets out directions for evolving the Internet architecture: routing and addressing, multi-protocol coexistence with OSI, security, traffic control and state, and advanced applications.

internet architecture.why: The whole document is about architectural principles and evolution of the Internet, so the broad architecture topic fits.
internet architecture.quote: This informational RFC discusses important directions for possible future evolution of the Internet architecture, and suggests steps towards the desired goals.

routing architecture.why: Section 2 covers the routing and addressing scalability problem, aggregation by ADs and policy routing, which is routing architecture and scalability.
routing architecture.quote: We must move to an addressing scheme in which network numbers are aggregated into larger units as the basis for routing.

IPv4.why: Address exhaustion of IPv4 and options for extended address formats is a major thread, though it is not a specification of a particular protocol.
IPv4.quote: The Internet will run out of the 32-bit IP address space altogether, as the space is currently subdivided and managed.

OSI.why: The multi-protocol architecture section addresses coexistence and migration between TCP/IP and OSI suites.
OSI.quote: The TCP/IP and OSI suites will coexist for a long time.

QoS.why: Section 5 discusses resource reservation and traffic control for real-time traffic, which is QoS architecture.
QoS.quote: This will require some "traffic control" mechanism in routers, controlled by additional state, to handle "real-time" traffic.

security.why: Section 4 is a general security architecture discussion, with perimeters, services and proposed actions, not tied to one mechanism.
security.quote: The principal themes for development of an Internet security architecture are simplicity, testability, trust, technology and security perimeter identification.

rejected.why: The document discusses next-generation address formats before IPv6 existed; no IPv6 specification is involved.
Privacy Enhanced Mail is mentioned as an example and a proposed action, but the document is not about PEM itself.
Multicast is mentioned as an assumption and a technical issue, but it is not a substantial subject of the document.
IDPR is cited as an example of routing on ADs and policy routing, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
The introduction and appendix give some background, but the document is forward-looking planning and not a retrospective.

RFC1288.title: The Finger User Information Protocol
RFC1288.summary: RFC 1288 specifies the Finger user information protocol, a TCP-based query/response interface to a remote user information program, including query syntax, forwarding behaviour, and security recommendations.

Finger.why: The whole document defines the Finger protocol: query specification, RUIP behaviour, expected responses and security guidance.
Finger.quote: This memo describes the Finger user information protocol. This is a simple protocol which provides an interface to a remote user information program (RUIP).

rejected.why: Finger only runs over TCP port 79 as a substrate; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
Data format section requires ASCII with CRLF, but this is a use of the encoding, not the subject.
Security section is specific to Finger's disclosure and forwarding risks, covered by the Finger tag.

RFC1289.title: DECnet Phase IV MIB Extensions
RFC1289.summary: Defines SNMP MIB objects (an extension to MIB-II) for managing DECnet Phase IV systems, covering system, end, routing, circuit, DDCMP, Ethernet, adjacency, line and area groups.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (RFC1289-phivMIB) written in SMI, defining managed objects for DECnet Phase IV. MIB is the best fit for readers browsing MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a set of DECnet Phase IV extensions that have been created for the Internet MIB.

DECnet.why: The managed objects cover DECnet Phase IV routing, end communication, circuits and adjacencies, so DECnet readers would expect this RFC.
DECnet.quote: DECnet Phase IV is one widely used protocol which often coexists in IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and the MIB tag already covers its place in the hierarchy.
The document has an Ethernet group and counters, but only as DECnet-specific parameters. It is not about IP over Ethernet.
ASN.1 and the SMI are only used as notation to write the MIB.

RFC1290.title: There's Gold in them thar Networks! or Searching for Treasure in all the Wrong Places
RFC1290.summary: FYI 10 is a user guide listing network information resources (anonymous FTP archives, CWIS systems, NICs, freenets, WHOIS servers, books, periodicals) and how to reach them.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide pointing end users to network information resources, so it belongs under user guides.
user guides.quote: This paper will present some of the "gold nuggets" of information and file repositories on the network that could of use to end users.

WHOIS.why: A whole section explains WHOIS and lists university WHOIS servers with usage examples. It describes how to use the directory service and does not specify the protocol.
WHOIS.quote: WHOIS is a program available on many workstation/mini/mainframe computers that can connect to another computer.

rejected.why: Anonymous FTP is the access method for most listed resources and the glossary explains it, but the document does not specify or extend FTP. It only uses FTP as a way to retrieve files.
Telnet is the means of reaching the CWIS and bulletin board systems, and the glossary describes it. The document is not about the protocol.
The WHOIS section describes people lookup, but WHOIS has its own tag and the document is not about directory services generally.
The document is a snapshot of 1991 resources, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Campus Wide Information Systems (CWIS) and network resource discovery
gaps.why: A large part of the document catalogues CWIS servers, Archie, freenets and resource guides. The taxonomy has no tag for information systems or resource directories. The nearest, service discovery, is about discovering network services.

RFC1291.title: Mid-Level Networks Potential Technical Services
RFC1291.summary: Informational memo proposing a set of technical services (DNS meta-domain server, software distribution pointers, NTP servers, Netnews feeds, mailing list exploders, testbeds, NIC and NOC contacts) that mid-level/regional networks could offer to their end sites and peers.

DNS.why: The DNS section and Appendix B propose a mid-level network nameserver that resolves queries for directly attached domains, with forwarders configuration and conventional service names in DNS. This is the most developed technical content.
DNS.quote: a robust DNS service is critical to any Internet site

NTP.why: A full section proposes placing NTP stratum-1 and stratum-2 servers in each mid-level network and naming them timekeeper-x. Readers interested in NTP deployment would want it.
NTP.quote: at least one stratum-1 and two stratum-2 servers be located within a mid-level network

Netnews.why: A section discusses Usenet news feed provision by mid-level networks, covering costs and the hub structure.
Netnews.quote: A mid-level network could alleviate such occurrences by being able to provide a newsfeed to any or all of its directly connected end sites.

mailing lists.why: A section proposes hierarchical mail exploders and bounce handling for mailing lists.
mailing lists.quote: mail exploders can be set up at the mid-level networks, each of which forwards the mail to exploders at the end sites

operational security.why: This is not really security. It is better covered by the network management tag below.
operational security.quote: The Network Operation Center's (NOC's) at the mid-level networks need to cooperate with each other to resolve network problems.

rejected.why: The document is about operational cooperation among NOCs, not security practices. Security Considerations says nothing.
FTP traffic and archive hosts are mentioned only as context for public software distribution, and the document does not specify FTP.
The White Pages pilot and X.500 appear only as examples of testbeds or in references.
Finger is mentioned only as an optional way to publish NOC contact info.

gaps.name: Mid-level / regional network services and NOC coordination
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about the role and services of regional networks and inter-NOC cooperation. The taxonomy has only the broad network management topic, which could be used but does not capture the regional network operations theme.

RFC1292.title: A Catalog of Available X.500 Implementations
RFC1292.summary: An FYI catalog of available commercial and free X.500 directory implementations (DSAs, DUAs, lightweight clients), with keyword indexes and per-implementation descriptions compiled by the DISI working group.

X.500.why: The whole document catalogs X.500 implementations (DSA, DUA, DAP/DSP support, conformance to the 1988 X.500 recommendations, pilot connectivity).
X.500.quote: The goal of this document is to provide information regarding the availability and capability of implementations of X.500.

rejected.why: LDAP is not described; DIXIE is a precursor lightweight gateway protocol but is not LDAP.
Parent of X.500, which already covers the subject; the specific tag is chosen instead.
Several DUAs use X Window System for their interface, but it is only a UI substrate, not the document's subject.
Mentioned only as a management interface for some DSAs, not a subject of the document.
Catalog is a listing of products, not about RFC format or publication.
Mentioned only in relation to some products' integration; not about messaging handling.

RFC1293.title: Inverse Address Resolution Protocol
RFC1293.summary: Specifies Inverse ARP (InARP), an extension of ARP that lets a station learn the protocol address of the peer at a known hardware address (e.g., a Frame Relay DLCI), with packet formats and Frame Relay operation.

ARP.why: The document defines InARP, an extension of ARP with new operation codes (8 and 9) and request/reply procedures.
ARP.quote: This memo describes additions to ARP that will allow a station to request a protocol address corresponding to a given hardware address.

frame relay.why: Frame Relay is the main motivating use case, with a dedicated section specifying InARP field values and operation over Frame Relay PVCs.
frame relay.quote: Specifically, this applies to Frame Relay stations that may have a Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI)

rejected.why: IP is used only as an example protocol address; the document does not specify IP itself.
The document is about a link-layer address resolution mechanism, not IP address architecture or allocation; ARP covers it.

RFC1294.title: Multiprotocol Interconnect over Frame Relay
RFC1294.summary: Specifies encapsulation of routed and bridged multiprotocol traffic (IP, CLNP, 802 LAN frames) over Frame Relay using NLPID/SNAP headers, with XID parameter negotiation, fragmentation, and ARP/Inverse ARP address resolution.

frame relay.why: The whole document defines how multiprotocol traffic is encapsulated, fragmented and negotiated over Frame Relay DTEs.
frame relay.quote: This memo describes an encapsulation method for carrying network interconnect traffic over a Frame Relay backbone.

ARP.why: A substantial section defines how ARP, RARP and Inverse ARP operate over Frame Relay, including DLCI-to-hardware-address handling.
ARP.quote: Address resolution may be accomplished using the standard Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [6] encapsulated within a SNAP encoded Frame Relay packet

rejected.why: IP is only one of the payloads carried; the document specifies the Frame Relay encapsulation, not IP itself.
CLNP is mentioned only as an example payload with an NLPID; the document does not specify it.
Bridged 802.3/Ethernet frames are one of several carried formats; the document is about Frame Relay, not Ethernet.
FDDI and other 802 media appear only as bridged-frame PID values.
The encapsulation is link-layer framing over Frame Relay, not IP-in-IP or generic IP tunnelling.

RFC1295.title: User Bill of Rights for entries and listings in the Public Directory
RFC1295.summary: The North American Directory Forum's User Bill of Rights lists seven rights (not to be listed, to be informed, examine, correct, remove entries, legal compliance, timeliness) for users' entries in the X.500-based Public Directory.

X.500.why: The document sets out user rights for entries and listings in a public directory service built on X.500, so readers of X.500 would want it.
X.500.quote: interconnecting electronic directories using a set of internationally developed standards known as the CCITT X.500 series
X.500.section: Scope of Intent - User Bill of Rights

privacy.why: The rights concern user control over personal information and compliance with privacy law, which are privacy policy concerns.
privacy.quote: To address significant security and privacy issues, the North American Directory Forum introduces the following "User Bill of Rights"

rejected.why: The X.500 child tag fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
The rights concern listing and data control, not access-control mechanisms. Security Considerations says nothing.

RFC1296.title: Internet Growth (1981-1991)
RFC1296.summary: RFC 1296 presents statistics on Internet growth from 1981 to 1991, counting hosts and domains using pre-DNS host tables and DNS data collected by the ZONE zone-transfer program.

internet history.why: A retrospective on a decade of Internet growth, with historical host and domain counts. A reader browsing Internet history would expect it.
internet history.quote: This document provides statistics on the growth of the Internet by examining the number of Internet hosts and domains over a 10-year period.

DNS.why: The study's method is a DNS zone-transfer walker (SOA, AXFR, NS, A, MX queries), and its results are DNS domain and host counts. It is about measuring the DNS, not specifying it.
DNS.quote: ZONE would "walk" the DNS tree and build a host table of all the information it collected.

rejected.why: Section N.5 tabulates common host names, and the host table is discussed, but the document does not define host naming conventions or host tables.
The measurement is of network size, not of network performance metrics.
The pre-DNS data come from SRI-NIC host tables, but the document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
The SRI-NIC Official Host Table registration is mentioned only as background for the host counts.

gaps.name: Internet growth statistics / size measurement
gaps.why: The document's main subject is counting Internet hosts and domains over time. No taxonomy tag covers Internet measurement or growth statistics apart from the history tag.

RFC1297.title: NOC Internal Integrated Trouble Ticket System Functional Specification Wishlist ("NOC TT REQUIREMENTS")
RFC1297.summary: An informational wishlist of functional requirements for an integrated trouble ticket system used by Network Operations Centers, covering ticket structure, fields, integration with alerts, email and databases, and statistical reporting.

network management.why: The whole document is about NOC operational tooling: trouble tickets, alert monitoring, escalation, and MTBF/MTTR reporting. No specific protocol tag fits, so the broader network operations topic applies.
network management.quote: Professional quality handling of network problems requires some kind of problem tracking system, herein referred to as a "trouble ticket" system.

rejected.why: The document never specifies SNMP or any management protocol. It only mentions an alert system and querying machines in general terms.
Email integration is one of many listed integration points (ticket creation from mail, emailed reports). The document is not about email itself.
The document is about operations tooling, not security practices. The security discussion is only a brief per-field access-control note and the boilerplate Security Considerations section.
The document describes human-operator ticketing workflow, not OAM mechanisms in the network.

gaps.name: Trouble ticket systems / NOC operations tooling
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for trouble ticketing, help desk or NOC problem tracking. The generic 'network management' topic is the nearest fit.

RFC1298.title: SNMP over IPX
RFC1298.summary: Informational memo defining how to carry SNMP messages over Novell IPX datagrams, including socket assignments, maximum packet length, trap agent-addr handling, and an IPX transport address textual convention.

SNMP.why: The document specifies a transport mapping for SNMP: socket numbers for requests and traps, packet size, and Trap-PDU agent-addr handling. SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: This memo defines a convention for encapsulating Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) [1] packets over the transport mechanism provided via the Internetwork Packet Exchange (IPX) protocol [2].

IPX.why: The document is about running a management protocol over IPX, covering the IPX packet type, socket assignments, maximum packet length and IPX address representation. It is relevant to IPX interworking.
IPX.quote: This memo addresses the use of SNMP over the IPX protocol, which has become quite widespread principally due to the popularity of Novell NetWare.

MIB.why: It defines a small MIB module (RFC1298-MIB) with the ipxTransportDomain OID and an IpxTransportAddress textual convention for use in other MIBs.
MIB.quote: IpxTransportAddress ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE (12))

rejected.why: UDP is only the common alternative transport that the memo compares against. The document does not specify or extend it.

This is the parent topic of what the document does. It was considered, but the SNMP and IPX tags already cover the subject, and the instructions say to give a topic tag directly only when no chosen technology tag sits under it.
It is the broad parent of SNMP, which is already tagged.

RFC1299.title: Summary of 1200-1299
RFC1299.summary: An annotated index of RFCs 1200 through 1299, giving each one's author, date, title, short abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The document catalogues a block of the RFC series. Readers browsing the RFC series subject would want this summary of one hundred RFCs.
RFC series.quote: a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1200

rejected.why: Many listed RFCs concern SNMP and MIBs, but this document only mentions them as entries in the list.
BGP-3 RFCs are listed as entries. The document does not specify or analyse BGP.
OSPF RFCs appear only as list entries.
The memo notes standards-track status for the listed RFCs. It does not describe the standards process itself.
Several listed RFCs concern X.500, but the memo only lists them.
It is a catalogue of RFCs, not a historical retrospective.

RFC1300.title: Remembrances of Things Past
RFC1300.summary: A humorous poem by Stanley Greenfield playing on the double meanings of computing and networking terms as they were used in the past.

humor.why: The whole document is a whimsical poem punning on computing jargon (modem, router, token ring, bauds), so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: When Shannon was a river and Turing was a car When Banyan was a tree and buses travelled far

rejected.why: It nostalgically riffs on old terms, but it is a joke poem, not a history or retrospective of Internet protocols.
It plays with word meanings but is not a glossary or definitions document.

RFC1301.title: Multicast Transport Protocol
RFC1301.summary: Specifies MTP, a reliable, flow-controlled, atomic multicast transport protocol using a master-issued transmit token, NAK-based retransmission, and an IP encapsulation (protocol 92) with 224.0.1.9 multicast.

reliable multicast.why: The whole document defines a reliable multicast transport protocol with NAK-based loss recovery, ordering and agreement. A reliable multicast subject page is the right place for it. No child tag fits, since it is not FLUTE, NORM, PGM, ALC or LCT.
reliable multicast.quote: This memo describes a protocol for reliable transport that utilizes the multicast capability of applicable lower layer networking architectures.

rejected.why: The document is about reliable multicast transport and does not cover multicast routing or group membership. The more specific reliable multicast tag covers it.
The appendix notes the MTP bridge protocol resembles UDP but deliberately does not use it. It defines its own IP protocol number.
RFC 1112 host-group multicast is only the substrate MTP uses for IP addressing. The document does not specify or extend IGMP.
TCP appears only as a reference. MTP is a different transport and is not an extension of TCP.
NETBLT is only cited as an influence on the retransmission mechanisms. The document is not about it.
The reliable multicast tag is more specific and fits the document, so the parent transport tag is implied.

gaps.name: atomic multicast / group communication ordering and agreement
gaps.why: The document's core is token-based total ordering of messages and agreement on acceptance across a web of members, even with partitions. The taxonomy has no tag for group communication or atomic broadcast.

RFC1302.title: Building a Network Information Services Infrastructure
RFC1302.summary: FYI RFC defining the role of Network Information Centers (NICs) in the Internet, four essential NIC functions, examples of existing NIC user-support services and delivery mechanisms, and database accuracy guidance.

user guides.why: This is an FYI document (FYI 12) about user support and information services for Internet users, which fits the user guides (FYI series) subject.
user guides.quote: The purpose of this document is to define the role of NICs in the Internet and establish guidelines for new and existing NICs regarding the user services they provide.

rejected.why: The history section mentions the ARPANET and SRI's role as the first NIC, but only as background.
FTP is listed as one delivery mechanism for NIC information, and the document does not specify or extend it.
Email is a delivery channel, and the NIC@domain help-desk address convention is a minor point.
Finger and whois appear only as rows in the delivery mechanism table.
White pages are mentioned only in passing as a NIC administrative service.

gaps.name: Network Information Centers / user support services
gaps.why: The document is about NIC organisation and user services. The taxonomy has no tag for user support or NIC operations beyond the FYI user guides tag.

RFC1303.title: A Convention for Describing SNMP-based Agents
RFC1303.summary: Informational memo defining the MODULE-CONFORMANCE macro, a convention for describing which MIB groups an SNMP agent implements and how it varies syntax, access, and row creation, bound to the agent's sysObjectID.

MIB.why: The document extends the SMI with a macro for stating MIB group conformance and variations of objects by SNMP agents. This is MIB/SMI material.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a new macro, MODULE-CONFORMANCE, which allows an agent implementor to describe the precise level of support which an agent claims in regards to a MIB group

SNMP.why: It is about describing SNMP agents' capabilities, including SMUX-based dynamic support and set-request row creation semantics, so SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: Practical experience has demonstrated a need for concisely describing the capabilities of an agent with regards to the MIB groups that it implements.

rejected.why: ASN.1 macro notation is used to define the macro, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
SMUX is mentioned only as an example of an agent that learns its objects dynamically. AgentX is a different protocol and is not discussed.

RFC1304.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the SIP Interface Type
RFC1304.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module for managing SMDS Interface Protocol (SIP) interfaces, covering Level 3, Level 2, DS1/DS3 PLCP, IP-over-SMDS addressing and an error log.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining managed objects for the SIP interface type (ifType sip(31)). MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing SIP (SMDS Interface Protocol) objects.

SMDS.why: The objects manage SMDS Interface Protocol levels 2 and 3, PLCP and IP-over-SMDS. The taxonomy has an SMDS tag, so the subject is SMDS.
SMDS.quote: The SIP (SMDS Interface Protocol) protocol stack is defined as follows in TR-TSV-000772

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the objects. The document defines no new SNMP behaviour, so MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is used only as the notation for the MIB definitions. The document does not specify ASN.1 itself.
The ipOverSMDS table mentions the addresses used for ARP requests, but ARP is not the subject.
The PLCP and DS1/DS3 framing is related to ATM, but the document covers only SMDS.

RFC1305.title: Network Time Protocol (Version 3) Specification, Implementation and Analysis
RFC1305.summary: RFC 1305 specifies NTP version 3, including the protocol, data formats, filtering/selection/clock-combining algorithms, local-clock discipline, control messages, authentication, timescale chronometry and error analysis.

NTP.why: The whole document is the NTP v3 specification and analysis.
NTP.quote: This document describes the Network Time Protocol (NTP), specifies its formal structure and summarizes information useful for its implementation.

rejected.why: NTP merely runs over UDP; the document does not define anything new about UDP.
DES is used only as the optional authentication cipher in Appendix C; it is a substrate.
Mentioned only as an alternative to the NTP control messages; the document does not specify SNMP.
The parent topic is implied by the NTP tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC1306.title: Experiences Supporting By-Request Circuit-Switched T3 Networks
RFC1306.summary: Informational memo from Cray Research describing experiences implementing by-request circuit-switched T3 network support, including switch control, kernel and user-program source-host implementations, and link selection via type-of-service and route aliases.

QoS.why: A substantial part of the memo covers selecting the switched link via IP type-of-service (high throughput) and routing table entries. This is the closest taxonomy fit for selecting service levels, though it is not specifically Diffserv.
QoS.quote: The first possibility is to use the type-of-service bits, which seemed natural to us.

routing architecture.why: The memo extends kernel routing lookups with switch-controller state and defines route aliases to steer traffic onto the switched link. This is host and router routing design for multiple links of differing service.
routing architecture.quote: We also derived a method we call route aliasing.

rejected.why: TCP changes (a separate timer for route setup delay, freeing the route in TIME_WAIT) are described, but only as a side effect of the kernel switch-control implementation. The memo is not about TCP.
FDDI is mentioned only as the backbone in the demo system, not as the subject.
The T3 circuit switch is not ATM, and no IP-over-ATM material appears.
Not relevant; the memo concerns on-demand circuit setup, not mobility.
The switch controller translates requests into switch protocol, but this predates and is not about software-defined networking.

gaps.name: Circuit-switched / by-request (dynamically switched) WAN links
gaps.why: The main subject, on-demand T3 circuit switching controlled from hosts, has no taxonomy tag. The companion protocol RFC 1307 (Dynamically Switched Link Control Protocol) would also fit such a tag.

RFC1307.title: Dynamically Switched Link Control Protocol
RFC1307.summary: Experimental protocol (DSLCP) by which a host's transport provider asks a link controller to set up or tear down downstream circuit-switched network links, with message format and a six-state machine.

rejected.why: DSLCP controls setup and teardown of external switched links, but it is a network-layer control protocol and not a specific link-layer technology or IP-over-medium mapping. The generic link layer topic is a weak fit.
DSLCP messages may be carried over UDP or IP, but UDP is only the substrate and the document does not specify or extend it.
TCP is mentioned only as a possible transport for DSLCP messages, so it is substrate and not a subject of the document.
The protocol reserves no resources and signals no QoS. It only brings a switched link up or down.
DSLCP is a control and signalling protocol for link setup, not a management, monitoring or operations framework. The fit is too loose.
The circuit-switched T3 services are not ATM, and the document is not about IP over ATM.

gaps.name: Dynamically Switched Link Control Protocol (DSLCP) / circuit-switched link control
gaps.why: The document is about host-initiated control of dynamically switched circuit-switched network links, such as T3 services. No taxonomy tag covers circuit-switched link setup and teardown signalling.

RFC1308.title: Executive Introduction to Directory Services Using the X.500 Protocol
RFC1308.summary: An FYI executive introduction to X.500 directory services, contrasting the limits of centralized WHOIS and DNS for directory uses with X.500's distributed, searchable global directory.

X.500.why: The whole document introduces X.500, its features, operational experience and limitations, so readers of the X.500 subject would expect it.
X.500.quote: X.500 is a CCITT protocol which is designed to build a distributed, global directory.

rejected.why: WHOIS is discussed only briefly as an example of a centralized directory with flaws. The document is not about specifying or operating it.
DNS is described only as a contrast to X.500, and the document is not about DNS itself.
This is the parent of X.500, so it is implied by the X.500 tag and not listed separately.
The document is an FYI, but the subject is X.500 directory services, so the more specific X.500 tag fits better.

RFC1309.title: Technical Overview of Directory Services Using the X.500 Protocol
RFC1309.summary: An FYI overview of the X.500 directory standard for newcomers, comparing it with finger, whois and DNS, describing its information and directory models, QUIPU extensions, limitations, and current uses.

X.500.why: The whole document is a technical overview of X.500: entries, object classes, the DIT, DUAs and DSAs, QUIPU, and the 1988 and 1992 standards.
X.500.quote: X.500 is a CCITT protocol which is designed to build a distributed, global directory.
X.500.section: 3: THE X.500 MODEL OF DIRECTORY SERVICE

rejected.why: Finger is described only as an existing directory service to compare against X.500, not specified or extended.
Whois is discussed as a comparison point with its centralized-database flaws; the document is not about it.
DNS is compared as a limited directory service; the document does not specify or analyse DNS itself.
This is the parent of X.500, so the specific X.500 tag implies it.
X.400 is mentioned only as an application that uses X.500 for mail addressing.

RFC1310.title: The Internet Standards Process
RFC1310.summary: RFC 1310 describes the 1992 Internet standards process: standards track maturity levels, RFC and Internet Draft publication, IANA parameter assignment, handling of external specifications, and IPR/patent disclosure policy.

IETF process.why: The whole document defines the standards track, maturity levels, review and approval by IESG/IAB, and advancement rules.
IETF process.quote: This memo documents the process currently used for the standardization of Internet protocols and procedures.

IPR.why: Sections 5 and 6 set out IPR disclosure and patent policy for standards, a substantial part of the document.
IPR.quote: all interested parties are required to disclose to the IAB the existence of any intellectual property right claims known to them

IANA.why: A dedicated section describes IANA's role in parameter assignment and its documentation requirements.
IANA.quote: The IAB has delegated to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) the task of assigning such protocol parameters for the Internet.
