RFC series.why: Covers RFC publication, Internet Drafts, STD subseries and non-standards-track RFC statuses (Experimental, Informational, Historic).
RFC series.quote: Each distinct version of a specification is published as part of the "Request for Comments" (RFC) document series.

rejected.why: Section 3 defines maturity and requirement level nomenclature, but this is part of the process description rather than a glossary or requirements-language document.
The document mentions the Internet's evolving, multi-protocol nature only in passing; it is about process, not architecture.
ASCII is mentioned only as an example of an externally incorporated standard.

RFC1311.title: Introduction to the STD Notes
RFC1311.summary: RFC 1311 introduces the STD sub-series of the RFC series, explaining how STD numbers are assigned to Internet standards, format rules for STD RFCs, and listing the grandfathered standards.

RFC series.why: The document defines a sub-series of the RFC series, its numbering, format rules, publication and distribution.
RFC series.quote: This RFC describes a new sub-series of RFCs, called STDs (Standards).

IETF process.why: It ties STD numbering to the standardization process and IAB designation of standards, including how maturity level and status are identified.
IETF process.quote: an STD number will be assigned to a specification when it reaches the Standard maturity level.

rejected.why: DNS is only used as an example of STD-13 spanning RFCs 1034 and 1035; the document is not about DNS.
Telnet options appear only as an example of multiple STD numbers and in the appendix list.
Assigned Numbers appears only as an entry in the appendix table; the document does not address IANA registries.
Explains the term STD but is not a glossary or definitions document.

RFC1312.title: Message Send Protocol 2
RFC1312.summary: Specifies Message Send Protocol version 2, a simple protocol for sending short text messages to a user's terminal on a host, over UDP and TCP port 18, with message syntax, acknowledgements and security advisories.

instant messaging.why: The RFC defines a protocol for delivering short messages directly to a user's terminal. That is the closest fit in the taxonomy, which has no narrower tag for terminal messaging.
instant messaging.quote: The Message Send Protocol is used to send a short message to a given user on a given terminal on a given host.

rejected.why: UDP is only one of two transports for the protocol (port 18). The document does not specify UDP itself.
TCP is only a transport binding on port 18. The document is not about TCP.
SMTP's SEND command is mentioned only to explain why a new protocol is needed. The document does not specify or extend SMTP.
The more specific child tag 'instant messaging' fits, so the parent is not used.
ISO 8859/1 is only used as the message character set and filtering rule. The document does not specify or register a character set.

gaps.name: Message Send Protocol (MSP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for terminal-write or message-send protocols. 'instant messaging' is only an approximate fit.

RFC1313.title: Today's Programming for KRFC AM 1313 Internet Talk Radio
RFC1313.summary: An April Fools' RFC presenting a parody radio programming schedule for KRFC Internet Talk Radio, featuring jokes about well-known Internet figures and networking topics.

humor.why: The document is a whimsical April 1st parody radio schedule poking fun at Internet personalities, so it belongs on the humorous RFCs page.
humor.quote: Hi and welcome to KRFC Internet Talk Radio, your place on the AM dial for lively talk and just-breaking news on internetworking.

rejected.why: OSPF is mentioned only in a joke about a guest on a radio show; the document is not about the protocol.
Anonymous FTP is mentioned only as a way to get transcripts; the document does not specify or discuss the protocol.
It mentions people and events of the era, but it is a parody rather than a history or retrospective.
DES appears only in a joke about a decryption contest; the document is not about the cipher.

RFC1314.title: A File Format for the Exchange of Images in the Internet
RFC1314.summary: RFC 1314 specifies TIFF-B (with MMR/MH/MR compression, one strip per page, standard resolutions) as the file format for exchanging black-and-white fax-like images across the Internet.

fax.why: The document defines an image file format for fax-like images, relates it to CCITT Group 3/4 fax encodings, and is a product of the Network Fax Working Group. Fax is the closest taxonomy subject.
fax.quote: This document defines a standard file format for the exchange of fax-like black and white images within the Internet.

rejected.why: FTP is mentioned only as one possible way to move image files; the document is about the file format, not the transfer protocol.
SMTP is mentioned only as a possible transport, with a note on its binary-data limits; it is not specified or extended here.
MIME appears only as a reference to a pending RFC on message body formats; the document defines no MIME type or encoding.
No media type registration is made; the document defines a file format only.

gaps.name: TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) / image file formats
gaps.why: The document is mostly a profile of TIFF-B for bilevel images (header, IFD, tags, resolutions). The taxonomy has no tag for image formats or TIFF, so only fax is a loose fit.

RFC1315.title: Management Information Base for Frame Relay DTEs
RFC1315.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module for managing Frame Relay DTE interfaces: DLCMI parameters, circuit table, error table, and a DLCI status-change trap.

frame relay.why: The MIB's subject matter is Frame Relay interfaces, DLCIs, virtual circuits, LMI, FECN/BECN and burst parameters.
frame relay.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing Frame Relay.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defined with the SMI, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through. The document defines objects and one trap, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the definitions. The document says nothing new about it.
This is an ancestor of MIB, so it is already implied.

RFC1316.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Character Stream Devices
RFC1316.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (Character MIB) for managing character stream ports (e.g. RS-232 terminal ports) and the sessions running over them.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is to define a MIB module (RFC1316-MIB) with port and session tables, which is the content MIB readers would look for.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to access the MIB, but the document only defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific fit.
Telnet is only listed as a well-known session protocol OID value, not specified or extended.
Only mentioned as a protocol OID value (protocolRlogin), not what the document is about.
ASN.1 is the notation the MIB is written in, so it is a substrate, not the subject.
PPP is mentioned only as a related MIB in the same family, not covered here.
SLIP is mentioned only as an example of a network protocol a character port might run.

gaps.name: Character stream devices / serial ports (terminal ports, RS-232, parallel printer ports)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for character-port or serial-device management beyond the generic MIB tag.

RFC1317.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for RS-232-like Hardware Devices
RFC1317.summary: Defines a MIB module for managing RS-232-like hardware ports (RS-232, RS-422, V.35), covering general, asynchronous and synchronous port parameters, error counters, and modem control signal tables.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (RFC1317-MIB) for RS-232-like hardware devices, written in SMI. It is a MIB specification.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the protocol used to access the objects. The document defines no SNMP behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is used only through SMI to define objects. The document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
The PPP MIB is mentioned only as a possible higher layer stacked above this MIB. The document does not specify PPP.
The objects describe physical serial ports, but the document is a management MIB and does not define link-layer protocol behaviour.

gaps.name: RS-232 / serial hardware port management
gaps.why: The document's subject is managing RS-232-like serial hardware ports and their modem control signals. The taxonomy has no tag for serial physical interfaces apart from SLIP, which is not a fit.

RFC1318.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Parallel-printer-like Hardware Devices
RFC1318.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module for managing parallel-printer-like (Centronics/Data Products) hardware ports, including port, input signal and output signal tables.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (RFC1318-MIB) defining managed objects for parallel-printer-like ports using the SMI. MIB is the most specific tag; SNMP is implied as the parent.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through. The document only defines objects and does not specify protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
The document concerns the physical parallel printer port hardware signals. It does not cover the Internet Printing Protocol.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the definitions. The document is not about ASN.1.
The document does not cover print spooling or the line printer protocol. It covers only hardware port signals.

RFC1319.title: The MD2 Message-Digest Algorithm
RFC1319.summary: RFC 1319 specifies the MD2 128-bit message-digest algorithm, with a C reference implementation and test suite, for use in digital signatures and Privacy-Enhanced Mail.

MD5.why: The document specifies the MD2 message digest. The MD5 tag also covers the MD2 and MD4 digests, so it is the closest fit in the taxonomy.
MD5.quote: This document describes the MD2 message-digest algorithm. The algorithm takes as input a message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit "fingerprint"

rejected.why: PEM is the intended application and the licensing context. The document specifies a hash algorithm, not PEM itself.
RSA is mentioned only as the public-key system used to sign the digest. The document does not specify it.
X.509 is mentioned only for the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters and the OID. This is incidental.
The object identifier is given only briefly and is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: MD2 message digest
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated MD2 tag. The MD5 tag covers MD2 and MD4 as well, so it is used as the closest fit.

RFC1320.title: The MD4 Message-Digest Algorithm
RFC1320.summary: RFC 1320 specifies the MD4 128-bit message-digest algorithm, with a C reference implementation and test suite, intended for digital signature use.

MD5.why: The document specifies the MD4 message digest algorithm. The MD5 tag's description covers the MD2/MD4 message digests, so it is the closest fit.
MD5.quote: This document describes the MD4 message-digest algorithm [1]. The algorithm takes as input a message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit "fingerprint"

rejected.why: RSA is mentioned only as an example public-key system that would encrypt the digest. The document does not specify it.
X.509 is cited only for the AlgorithmIdentifier type that carries MD4's parameters. The document is not about certificates.
SHA is a different hash family and is not discussed.
The MD4 object identifier is given in one passing line. That is not the subject of the document.

RFC1321.title: The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm
RFC1321.summary: RFC 1321 specifies the MD5 message-digest algorithm, which produces a 128-bit fingerprint of arbitrary-length input, and includes a C reference implementation and test suite.

MD5.why: The document exists to specify MD5, including its padding, round functions, and output, and lists its differences from MD4.
MD5.quote: This document describes the MD5 message-digest algorithm. The algorithm takes as input a message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit "fingerprint"

rejected.why: RSA is only mentioned as the public-key system that signs the digest. The document does not specify RSA.
X.509 is cited only for the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters type (NULL) and the OID. The document is not about certificates.
The OBJECT IDENTIFIER is a one-line mention, not a substantive part of the document.
The reference code is taken from RSAREF, a toolkit for Privacy-Enhanced Mail. The document itself does not address PEM.
The MD5 tag is the more specific child of cryptography, so the parent is implied.

RFC1322.title: A Unified Approach to Inter-Domain Routing
RFC1322.summary: Informational RFC proposing a unified inter-domain routing architecture combining hop-by-hop path-vector node routing (BGP/IDRP-style) with IDPR-style source-demand routing for scalability and policy/TOS support.

routing architecture.why: The document is an architecture and scalability design for inter-domain routing, covering aggregation, complexity and policy tradeoffs.
routing architecture.quote: our scalable inter-domain routing architecture consists of two major components: source-demand routing (SDR), and node routing (NR)

BGP.why: The NR component is based on path-vector as in BGP, with analysis of its storage, computation and policy properties and a transition plan replacing EGP with BGP.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) (see [BGP91]) and the Inter Domain Routing Protocol (IDRP) (see [IDRP91]) are examples of path vector (PV) protocols

IDPR.why: The source-demand routing component is built on IDPR mechanisms (route setup, route servers, link-state updates), which are discussed at length.
IDPR.quote: the SDR component employs an IDPR-like architecture in which link-state style updates are distributed with explicit policy terms
IDPR.section: 4.1 Path Vector vs. Link State for SDR

rejected.why: Link-state IGPs are only cited as comparison points for link-state vs path-vector.
Mentioned only as an example of a simple distance vector protocol that does not scale.
Mentioned as the protocol BGP would replace in the transition; not the subject.
One of the network layers the architecture should apply to; not discussed in its own right.
Mentioned as a network layer protocol the architecture must accommodate; not a subject.
Type-of-service routing is a policy criterion, but the document is about routing, not QoS mechanisms.

RFC1323.title: TCP Extensions for High Performance
RFC1323.summary: Specifies TCP window scale and timestamp options, with the RTTM round-trip measurement and PAWS sequence-wrap protection mechanisms, to improve TCP performance and reliability on high bandwidth*delay paths; obsoletes RFC 1072 and RFC 1185.

TCP.why: The whole document defines new TCP options (Window Scale, Timestamps) and the RTTM and PAWS mechanisms, modifying TCP event processing.
TCP.quote: This memo presents a set of TCP extensions to improve performance over large bandwidth*delay product paths and to provide reliable operation over very high-speed paths.

rejected.why: Fast retransmit/recovery and slow start are mentioned only as background; the document's subject is window scaling, RTT measurement and PAWS.
The TCP checksum is mentioned only in a probabilistic reliability argument.
NETBLT, RDP and VMTP appear only as examples of protocols with selective acknowledgments.
RDP is cited only as an example of selective acknowledgments in the introduction.

RFC1324.title: A Discussion on Computer Network Conferencing
RFC1324.summary: An informational discussion paper arguing for a common standard protocol for real-time computer network conferencing (IRC/BRC-style), outlining goals, server and client responsibilities, and design questions.

IRC.why: The memo is a discussion of relay-chat conferencing systems like IRC and the need for a unified protocol, drawing on IRC's network size, servers, channels and operation as its guide.
IRC.quote: there are some systems which have been around for some time (BRC - Bitnet Relay Chat and IRC - Internet Relay Chat)

rejected.why: The memo concerns multi-user real-time chat conferencing, which IRC fits more specifically; no presence or IM protocol is discussed.
That tag covers multiparty media conferencing frameworks (XCON, CLUE); this memo is about text chat relay systems, so IRC is the better fit.
TCP/IP is only the substrate on which the proposed protocol would be layered.
SMTP, NNTP and FTP are cited only as analogies for ASCII command/numeric reply design.

gaps.name: Network conferencing protocol (proposed NCP/ICP)
gaps.why: The memo calls for a general real-time text conferencing protocol; the taxonomy has only IRC for it, which the memo treats as one existing implementation.

RFC1325.title: FYI on Questions and Answers Answers to Commonly asked "New Internet User" Questions
RFC1325.summary: FYI 4 (RFC 1325) is a beginner-oriented Q&A guide for new Internet users covering the Internet, TCP/IP, DNS, RFC/FYI/STD documentation, Internet organizations, services such as WHOIS, archie, USENET, mailing lists, mail addressing, and a glossary.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide for new Internet users, which is exactly what the user guides subject covers.
user guides.quote: This FYI RFC is one of two FYI's called, "Questions and Answers" (Q/A), produced by the User Services Working Group

RFC series.why: A large section explains what RFCs, FYIs, STDs and Internet Drafts are and how to obtain and index them.
RFC series.quote: The Request for Comments documents (RFCs) are working notes of the Internet research and development community.

WHOIS.why: Several Q&As explain how to use and register in the WHOIS database, and the Knowbot meta-service queries it.
WHOIS.quote: How do I use the WHOIS program at the DDN NIC?

terminology.why: About 12 pages of glossary define Internet terms and acronyms.
terminology.quote: Below is a condensed glossary to assist in making some sense of the Internet world.

rejected.why: The DNS and FQDN are explained in only two short answers, which is too little to make DNS a subject of the document.
USENET and newsgroups get a few Q&As, but the document is not about the Netnews format or distribution.
The IAB, IETF, IRTF, ISOC and IANA are described, but only as background answers. user guides and RFC series fit better.
Anonymous FTP is used throughout as a way to fetch files and has one short Q&A. The document does not specify or analyse FTP.
The mailing list Q&As cover how to subscribe and the -request convention, not mailing list protocols or headers.
One short Q&A describes IANA assignments, which is not enough to make the document about IANA registries.

RFC1326.title: Mutual Encapsulation Considered Dangerous
RFC1326.summary: Informational memo describing a packet explosion and routing-loop problem when two protocols encapsulate each other (e.g., IP over AppleTalk and AppleTalk over IP), and discussing potential fixes such as hop-count preservation and header peeking.

tunneling.why: The whole document analyses generic encapsulation of one network protocol in another, the loops it can cause, and fixes. This is a generic tunnelling topic, not specific to GRE or IP-in-IP.
tunneling.quote: This memo describes a packet explosion problem that can occur with mutual encapsulation of protocols (A encapsulates B and B encapsulates A).

AppleTalk.why: AppleTalk is the concrete example of mutual encapsulation, and the memo discusses its hop count limit and the IP-over-AppleTalk draft. It is an illustration rather than the main subject, so it is secondary.
AppleTalk.quote: For example, there exists cases of both IP over AppleTalk and AppleTalk over IP.

rejected.why: The memo treats generic encapsulation among many protocols, not IP-in-IP specifically.
Routing loops are the trigger, but the memo is about encapsulation, not routing design.
Mentioned only in a list of internet protocols, not discussed.
Mentioned only in a list of internet protocols, not discussed.
Mentioned only in a list of internet protocols, not discussed.
IP is used only as one example protocol in the encapsulation discussion.

RFC1327.title: Mapping between X.400(1988) / ISO 10021 and RFC 822
RFC1327.summary: RFC 1327 specifies gateway mappings between X.400(1988)/ISO 10021 message handling and RFC 822 mail, covering service elements, O/R address to RFC 822 address mapping, headers, delivery reports and notifications.

X.400.why: The whole document defines how X.400 IPMS/MTS/MTA elements map to and from RFC 822, i.e. X.400 interworking.
X.400.quote: describes a set of mappings which will enable interworking between systems operating the CCITT X.400 1988) Recommendations on Message Handling Systems

message format.why: The RFC 822 side is mapped in detail, and it defines new RFC 822 header fields (X400-Received, Importance, etc.) and updates RFC 822.
message format.quote: RFC 822 evolved as a messaging standard on the DARPA (the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) Internet.

rejected.why: SMTP is only one of the 822-MTS transports. It has a short appendix (VRFY for probes) but is not the subject.
UUCP is covered only by a brief appendix noting that UUCP addresses are gatewayed via RFC 976 into RFC 822 first.
The more specific tags, X.400 and message format, already cover the document.
ASN.1 is only the notation for the X.400 elements being referenced, not a subject of the document.
MIME is not covered. Multipart handling uses RFC 934 encapsulation, and the document says MIME is future work.

RFC1328.title: X.400 1988 to 1984 downgrading
RFC1328.summary: Specifies rules for downgrading X.400(1988) messages to X.400(1984), extending X.419 Annexe B with O/R address handling (DDA X400-88, Common Name), IPM content type 22 to 2 downgrade, and body part conversion.

X.400.why: The whole document is about X.400 message handling interworking between the 1988 and 1984 versions, including gateway address and body part downgrading.
X.400.quote: This document considers issues of downgrading from X.400(1988) to X.400(1984)

rejected.why: RFC 822 is mentioned only briefly, with a pointer to RFC 1327. The document is about X.400 versions, not Internet message format.
The parent is implied by X.400. The document's subject is X.400 downgrading specifically.
Body part conversion here concerns X.400 body parts, not MIME.

RFC1329.title: Thoughts on Address Resolution for Dual MAC FDDI Networks
RFC1329.summary: Informational memo proposing a "load sharing layer" and a Dual MAC Address Resolution Protocol (DMARP) so IP and ARP work on mixed single-MAC/dual-MAC FDDI rings, letting dual MAC stations use both rings.

FDDI.why: The whole document concerns IP over FDDI dual-ring networks and a new layer for dual MAC stations.
FDDI.quote: how IP and ARP can be used on inhomogeneous FDDI networks (FDDI networks with single MAC and dual MAC stations)

ARP.why: DMARP is an ARP-like address resolution protocol that runs alongside ARP to exchange secondary MAC addresses, and ARP is kept transparent to dual MAC.
ARP.quote: the load sharing entities in dual MAC stations communicate with the Dual MAC Address Resolution Protocol (DMARP)
ARP.section: 7. Protocol Layers in Dual MAC Stations

rejected.why: Only transparent bridges and Ethernet hardware type codes are mentioned; the document is about FDDI.
IP is used as the client of the new layer but is not specified or extended.
Load splitting across two rings is similar in spirit, but the document is about FDDI dual MAC address resolution, not link aggregation (IEEE 802.1AX).

RFC1330.title: Recommendations for the Phase I Deployment of OSI Directory Services (X.500) and OSI Message Handling Services (X.400) within the ESNET Community
RFC1330.summary: ESnet task force whitepaper recommending Phase I deployment of X.500 directory (QUIPU, PSI White Pages Pilot, naming under c=US) and X.400 message handling (PRMD peering, MTA routing, gateways) plus OSI name registration procedures.

X.500.why: Half the document specifies how ESnet sites should deploy X.500 DSAs, DIT naming, white pages attributes and access methods.
X.500.quote: X.500 is a CCITT/ISO standard which defines a global solution for the distribution and retrieval of information (directory service).

X.400.why: The other half covers X.400 MHS deployment: PRMD/ADMD structure, O/R names, WEPs, MTA routing tables, SMTP gateways.
X.400.quote: a logical X.400 backbone must be established through out the entire ESnet backbone.

WHOIS.why: Describes WHOIS emulation as an access method to the directory, with usage examples, a modest but real part of the document.
WHOIS.quote: The Pilot Project software allows you to configure the X.500 Directory service to be made available via a network port offering an emulation of the SRI-NIC WHOIS service.

rejected.why: Considered as parent of X.400, but X.400 is the more specific tag and already covers the mail content.
Only mentioned as a gateway target (bidirectional SMTP-X.400 gateways) and local mail product, not the subject of the document.
DNS only appears in comparisons (X.400 routing vs DNS) and the glossary; DECdns/X.500 interaction is a future issue only.
Parent of X.500, which is already chosen.
RFC 1006 over TCP is only a transport stack option for QUIPU and MTAs, not the subject.
OSI is the context for X.500/X.400 and registration; the OSI network-layer protocols (CLNP) are only mentioned as stack options.
Finger interface to X.500 is mentioned briefly as an access method, not a substantial subject of the document.

gaps.name: OSI name registration (ANSI/GSA/DOE registration authorities)
gaps.why: Section 4 is a substantial part of the document on registering OSI organization names; no taxonomy tag covers OSI naming/registration authorities.

gaps.name: GOSIP (Government OSI Profile)
gaps.why: The deployment is shaped by U.S. GOSIP requirements, but no tag exists for GOSIP profiles.

RFC1331.title: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) for the Transmission of Multi-protocol Datagrams over Point-to-Point Links
RFC1331.summary: Specifies the Point-to-Point Protocol: HDLC-based framing/encapsulation for multi-protocol datagrams over serial links, the Link Control Protocol with its option negotiation automaton, packet formats and configuration options.

PPP.why: The whole document defines PPP encapsulation, LCP, the negotiation automaton and LCP options.
PPP.quote: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) provides a method for transmitting datagrams over serial point-to-point links.

rejected.why: Appendix B gives a fast FCS implementation, but it is a supporting detail of the framing, not the document's subject.
Protocol-field and address/control-field compression are LCP options within PPP, not a header compression subject in their own right.
Authentication is only negotiated here via the Authentication-Protocol option; PAP and CHAP are defined elsewhere.
HDLC and LAPB are referenced only as the basis of the framing.

gaps.name: HDLC framing
gaps.why: The document is built on HDLC framing, including async HDLC in Appendix A, and the taxonomy has no HDLC tag.

RFC1332.title: The PPP Internet Protocol Control Protocol (IPCP)
RFC1332.summary: RFC 1332 defines IPCP, the PPP Network Control Protocol for configuring IP over point-to-point links, including IP-Address negotiation and negotiation of Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression.

PPP.why: The document specifies IPCP, a PPP control protocol, including its packet encapsulation, codes, and configuration options.
PPP.quote: This document defines the NCP for establishing and configuring the Internet Protocol [2] over PPP

IPHC.why: A substantial part (IP-Compression-Protocol option and Section 4) defines negotiating VJ TCP/IP header compression over PPP. IPHC is the nearest taxonomy tag for IP header compression over PPP, though it formally covers RFC 2507.
IPHC.quote: a method to negotiate and use Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression [3] with PPP

rejected.why: IP is the network protocol being configured, not specified here. The IP-Address option only negotiates the link-end address.
TCP/IP headers are compressed, but TCP itself is not specified or extended.
The more specific tag IPHC is chosen instead of the parent.
Mentioned only in passing as a way to avoid fragmentation.
This is about TCP/IP compression, not RTP header compression.

gaps.name: Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression (RFC 1144)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for VJ TCP/IP header compression. IPHC is the closest fit, but it formally refers to RFC 2507.

RFC1333.title: PPP Link Quality Monitoring
RFC1333.summary: RFC 1333 defines the PPP Link Quality Monitoring protocol: the Link-Quality-Report packet, its LCP Quality-Protocol option, counters, and procedures for measuring packet and octet loss on a point-to-point link.

PPP.why: The document specifies a PPP quality protocol: an LCP Quality-Protocol configuration option and the LQR packet (protocol c025) carried in PPP frames.
PPP.quote: This document defines a protocol for generating Link-Quality-Reports.

rejected.why: The document uses the MIB-II interface counters as inputs but defines no MIB module.
SNMP counter types and MIB-II objects are only referenced as the source of the counters. SNMP itself is not specified or extended.
The document measures link loss, but it does so as a PPP mechanism on a single link. It is not about general network performance metrics or methodology.
LQR is link monitoring built into PPP. It is not a general OAM mechanism, so the PPP tag covers it.

RFC1334.title: PPP Authentication Protocols
RFC1334.summary: RFC 1334 defines the two PPP authentication protocols, PAP (two-way password handshake) and CHAP (three-way challenge-response using a one-way hash), including their option formats and packets.

PPP.why: The document specifies PPP authentication protocols (PAP and CHAP), their LCP Authentication-Protocol option formats and packet encapsulation in PPP frames. It is a PPP extension, so PPP readers need it.
PPP.quote: This document defines two protocols for Authentication: the Password Authentication Protocol and the Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol.

authentication.why: The document is about peer authentication mechanisms (password and challenge-response). Neither PAP nor CHAP has its own technology tag, so the authentication topic tag fits.
authentication.quote: The Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP) is used to periodically verify the identity of the peer using a 3-way handshake.

rejected.why: MD5 is only the hash algorithm CHAP uses (algorithm value 5). The document does not specify or analyse it.
The document covers link-level peer authentication only. It does not address a broader authentication, authorization and accounting framework.
PPP is the more specific tag and already sits under link layer.
SNMP Security Protocols are mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a possible way to distribute secrets.

gaps.name: PAP and CHAP (PPP authentication protocols)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for these specific protocols. The generic authentication topic is the closest fit, and PPP is tagged as the carrying protocol.

RFC1335.title: A Two-Tier Address Structure for the Internet: A Solution to the Problem of Address Space Exhaustion
RFC1335.summary: An informational idea paper proposing the Dual Network Addressing (DNA) scheme, a two-tier internal/external IPv4 address structure with a shared pool of external addresses managed by an External Address Sharing Service, to mitigate address space exhaustion.

addressing.why: The whole document proposes a new address structure with internal and external addresses to counter address exhaustion. It is about IP address architecture and allocation, and no more specific child tag fits.
addressing.quote: The "Dual Network Addressing (DNA)" scheme proposed here is based on a two-tier address structure and sharing of addresses.

IPv4.why: The problem is exhaustion of the IPv4 32-bit space and Class A/B/C network numbers, and the scheme works within the 32-bit space. This is substantial IPv4 address lifecycle discussion.
IPv4.quote: The current Internet address space is 32-bit. Each Internet address is divided into two parts: a network portion and a host portion.

rejected.why: The scheme resembles address sharing and translation, but it assigns temporary external addresses to hosts and does not translate addresses in packets. It only cites the NAT proposal in references.
DHCP is suggested as one way to implement the EASS server, but it is a passing mention and not what the document is about.
The DNS implications (returning internal or external addresses by source address, updating entries) are a brief side effect. The document does not specify DNS.
Supernetting and C-sharp are discussed only as competing short-term fixes. The document does not propose or analyse classless aggregation.
The document is a specific addressing proposal. It makes no broad architectural-principles argument.

RFC1336.title: Who's Who in the Internet: Biographies of IAB, IESG and IRSG Members
RFC1336.summary: An FYI RFC compiling biographies and opinions on Internet growth from 1992 members of the IAB, IESG and IRSG.

internet history.why: The memo records the careers and recollections of Internet leaders and their views on how the Internet grew. That makes it a retrospective on the Internet's people and history.
internet history.quote: The ARPANET is 20 years old. The next meeting of the IETF in St. Louis this coming March will be the 20th plenary.

user guides.why: It is an FYI-series document written for the wider Internet user community, and its stated aim is to let users know who runs the Internet.
user guides.quote: This FYI RFC contains biographical information about members of the Internet Activities Board (IAB), the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG)

rejected.why: It describes the people who sit on the IAB, IESG and IRSG. It does not describe IETF procedures.
The ARPANET comes up often in the biographies and recollections. The document is not about ARPANET protocols or operations.
The bios touch on scaling and architecture, but only in passing personal opinion. The document is not about architecture.

RFC1337.title: TIME-WAIT Assassination Hazards in TCP
RFC1337.summary: Informational memo describing TIME-WAIT Assassination hazards in TCP, where old duplicate segments or RSTs prematurely end TIME-WAIT, and proposing fixes such as ignoring RST in TIME-WAIT.

TCP.why: The whole document analyses a failure mode in TCP's TIME-WAIT state and proposes changes to TCP behaviour.
TCP.quote: Fix (F1), ignoring RST segments in TIME-WAIT state, seems like the best short-term solution.

rejected.why: Not about integrity checks; the topic is sequence numbers and connection state.
No congestion control content; the focus is connection-state failure from old duplicates.

RFC1338.title: Supernetting: an Address Assignment and Aggregation Strategy
RFC1338.summary: RFC 1338 proposes supernetting: hierarchical allocation of blocks of class-C addresses to service providers plus classless route aggregation rules in inter-domain routing to slow routing table growth and class-B exhaustion.

CIDR.why: The memo is the original supernetting proposal that led to CIDR: classless prefixes, provider-based address allocation, and route aggregation.
CIDR.quote: routing destinations are represented by network+mask pairs and that routing is done on a longest-match basis

routing architecture.why: A substantial part covers routing table scaling, aggregation rules (longest match, sink routes), multihoming effects, and growth projections for default-free routers.
routing architecture.quote: slow the growth of the routing table and the need for allocating new IP network numbers

rejected.why: Inter-domain protocols are discussed generically and EGP2 is mentioned; BGP is not specified or named.
OSPF is only cited as an example of an IGP that supports classless routes.
Multihoming is discussed as a limit on aggregation, but the document is about aggregation and address allocation, not multihoming architectures.
The parent topic is implied by the CIDR tag, which is more specific.
The document is about IPv4 address space allocation, but CIDR is the more specific fit.

RFC1339.title: Remote Mail Checking Protocol
RFC1339.summary: Defines an experimental UDP-based protocol (port 50) for a client to poll a server for whether a user's maildrop has new, old, or no mail, with optional cleartext-password authentication.

email.why: The protocol is a mail-access/notification service for checking maildrop status, used alongside remote mail servers such as POP. It fits the general email tag, since no child tag (POP3, IMAP) is specified.
email.quote: This RFC defines a simple, low-overhead protocol for checking the status of a maildrop on a host.

UDP.why: The protocol is defined as single-datagram UDP exchanges on a dedicated port, and the document specifies the datagram formats. However, UDP is mostly the substrate, so this tag is weaker.
UDP.quote: the Remote Mail Checking Protocol is based on the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), using UDP port 50 decimal (62 octal) for the server.

rejected.why: POP (RFC 1225) is mentioned only as the kind of remote mail server this protocol complements. The document does not specify or extend POP.
It has a simple cleartext-password authentication step, but this is a minor feature of the polling protocol and not the document's subject.
The Security Considerations discuss privacy of mail-arrival information, but that is boilerplate-level discussion and not the main body's subject.

RFC1340.title: Assigned Numbers
RFC1340.summary: RFC 1340 is the 1992 IANA Assigned Numbers registry snapshot, listing protocol numbers, port numbers, multicast addresses, Ethernet types, PPP fields, SNMP MIB OIDs, Telnet options, MIME types, character sets and name lists, now obsolete.

IANA.why: The whole document is the IANA registry of assigned parameter values (protocol numbers, ports, types), which is the subject of IANA registries.
IANA.quote: This Network Working Group Request for Comments documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations.

internet history.why: It is the 1992 snapshot in the long Assigned Numbers lineage, preserving many historic protocols and ARPANET-era assignments, useful to history readers.

rejected.why: MILNET logical addresses and link numbers are only a few registry tables, not the document's subject.
Port numbers are assigned for TCP/UDP services, but TCP itself is not specified or extended.
A character set name list is included, but it is one table among many and just reproduces RFC 1345 names.
A small MIME type table is included, but the document does not set media type registration rules.
PPP protocol and option number tables are one section of a general registry.
Management OID assignments are listed, but SNMP is not the subject of the document.

RFC1341.title: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions): Mechanisms for Specifying and Describing the Format of Internet Message Bodies
RFC1341.summary: RFC 1341 specifies the original MIME, defining the MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-ID and Content-Description header fields, the seven top-level content types (including multipart and message subtypes), quoted-printable and base64 encodings, and IANA registration procedures.

MIME.why: The whole document defines MIME: body structure, multipart/message types and the Content-Transfer-Encoding mechanisms (quoted-printable, base64).
MIME.quote: This document redefines the format of message bodies to allow multi-part textual and non-textual message bodies to be represented and exchanged without loss of information.

media types.why: It defines the top-level types and initial subtypes (text, image, audio, video, application, message, multipart) and the registration rules and templates for new types and subtypes.
media types.quote: New standard values must be documented, registered with, and approved by IANA, as described in Appendix F.

rejected.why: Parent of MIME in the taxonomy, so it is implied. The document covers message bodies, not mail transport or access.
SMTP's 7-bit limits motivate the encodings, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
RFC 822 headers are the substrate. MIME is orthogonal to RFC 822 and is tagged under MIME.
Base64 is defined here as a transfer encoding, but it is part of MIME and not a general encoding spec. MIME covers it.
The charset parameter is only one part of the document, and it is covered under MIME.
The registration appendix is boilerplate-like procedure for MIME values, so MIME and media types cover it.

RFC1342.title: Representation of Non-ASCII Text in Internet Message Headers
RFC1342.summary: RFC 1342 defines "encoded-words" (B and Q encodings with a charset label) that let non-ASCII text be carried in RFC 822 message headers, as a companion to MIME.

MIME.why: The document is a MIME extension (the RFC 1342 predecessor of RFC 2047) that defines encoded-word encodings (B = Base64, Q = quoted-printable variant) and charset labelling for header text.
MIME.quote: An "encoded-word" is a sequence of printable ASCII characters that begins with "=?", ends with "?=", and has two "?"s in between.

message format.why: It amends RFC 822 header grammar (phrase, comment) and specifies where encoded-words may appear in message headers.
message format.quote: to allow the encoding of non-ASCII text in various portions of a RFC 822 [2] message header

internationalization.why: The purpose is carrying non-ASCII text in headers, which is internationalization of text in protocols; no child tag fits.
internationalization.quote: to allow the representation of character sets other than ASCII in RFC 822 message headers

rejected.why: It uses charset names defined by RFC 1341 but does not register or define character sets.
The B encoding is simply Base64 as defined in RFC 1341; the document does not define it.
Implied by the more specific tags chosen (message format, MIME).
ASCII is the target encoding substrate, not the subject of the document.

RFC1343.title: A User Agent Configuration Mechanism for Multimedia Mail Format Information
RFC1343.summary: Informational memo defining the "mailcap" file format by which mail user agents find locally installed programs to view, compose, edit and print MIME-typed message bodies, with UNIX semantics in an appendix.

MIME.why: The mailcap file maps MIME content-types to local handler programs for viewing, composing, editing and printing body parts. It is a MIME-related facility for mail user agents, and the document is about it.
MIME.quote: when they need to display mail of an unfamiliar (non-text) type, they consult an external file for information on how to display that file

rejected.why: Mail is the context, but the document specifies a user-agent configuration file, not email architecture, transport or formats. MIME is the more specific fit.
Mailcap entries match on content-types, but the document does not register media types or define registry rules.
RFC 822 headers are only referenced. The document does not define message header syntax.

RFC1344.title: Implications of MIME for Internet Mail Gateways
RFC1344.summary: Informational memo describing how mail gateways can use MIME features (encapsulated rejection messages, message/partial fragmentation, external-body handling, image format conversion, and robust transfer encoding) to improve mail transport.

MIME.why: The whole memo is about applying MIME mechanisms (multipart, message/partial, message/external-body, Content-Transfer-Encoding) at gateways.
MIME.quote: MIME offers several features that should be of interest to those responsible for message transport services.

email.why: The memo addresses mail transport and gateway behaviour, including rejection notices and size limits, so email readers would want it.
email.quote: mail transport software is responsible for moving a message within a homogeneous electronic mail service network.
email.section: Mail Transport and Gateway Services: A Key Distinction

rejected.why: SMTP is mentioned only in passing (the SIZE extension and relays); the memo does not specify or extend it.
It uses existing MIME types such as message/partial and message/external-body but registers none and sets no registry rules.
Gateways are discussed generically, with no X.400 interworking.
Anonymous FTP appears only as an access type in external-body examples.
Header fields appear in examples, but the memo is not about the RFC 822 message format itself.

RFC1345.title: Character Mnemonics and Character Sets
RFC1345.summary: RFC 1345 tabulates character mnemonics and many coded character sets (ISO 8859, ISO 646 variants, EBCDIC, PC codepages), defines a table format and charset names, and defines "mnemonic" charsets for lossless conversion in text/mail.

character sets.why: The memo tabulates and names dozens of coded character sets, defines their table format and the registered charset names, which is the core of the document.
character sets.quote: The coded character sets are given names for easy reference.

internationalization.why: The mnemonic scheme and conversion without information loss between character sets address internationalized text in Internet protocols; this is the broader subject beyond the charset registry.
internationalization.quote: With the growing internationalization of the Internet, support for many coded character sets is required.

rejected.why: ASCII is one of many charsets tabulated and used as the default base for mnemonic charsets, but the document is not about ASCII specifically.
EBCDIC variants are tabulated as part of the broad set, but the document is not specifically about EBCDIC.
ISO 10646 codes are used only as character identifiers; the memo is not about Unicode usage.
Charset names are registered with IANA, but that is administrative boilerplate-level mention.
Mail transport is the motivating context and a Mnemonic-Intro header is mentioned, but the document does not specify email message format.

RFC1346.title: Resource Allocation, Control, and Accounting for the Use of Network Resources
RFC1346.summary: An informational 1992 discussion paper arguing that tools for allocating, controlling and accounting for shared network and link resources among user groups are lacking, and recommending further studies.

QoS.why: The paper is about guaranteeing minimum shares, imposing maximums and prioritising traffic on shared links, which is resource allocation and control of service quality. It is a general discussion, not tied to one protocol.
QoS.quote: the challenge of sharing network resources (and for example intercontinental link resources) between groups of users is neither well understood, nor well catered for

network management.why: The paper is written from the Network Manager and IT Service Manager viewpoint. It covers control tools and usage accounting for operating service networks.
network management.quote: There seems to be a lack of tools to enable the controlling and the sharing of networks and links.

rejected.why: The paper discusses contention for bandwidth, but as a matter of allocation policy and sharing between groups, not transport congestion mechanisms.
X.25(84) throughput class and transit delay are mentioned only as one example of a technology with some controls. The document is not about X.25.
It mentions marking traffic as high priority only in general terms. It does not discuss Diffserv.

gaps.name: Network resource accounting and usage charging
gaps.why: The title and content cover accounting and charging for shared network use. The taxonomy has no tag for accounting or resource-sharing policy outside AAA frameworks.

RFC1347.title: TCP and UDP with Bigger Addresses (TUBA), A Simple Proposal for Internet Addressing and Routing
RFC1347.summary: RFC 1347 proposes TUBA, a migration path from IPv4 to CLNP with NSAP addresses under TCP/UDP, using new DNS record types to signal updated hosts.

IPng.why: TUBA is one of the historic IPng candidate protocols, and the document is the proposal itself.
IPng.quote: This approach is known as "TUBA" (TCP & UDP with Bigger Addresses).

CLNP.why: The proposal replaces IP with CLNP and describes running TCP and UDP over it, including pseudo-header options.
CLNP.quote: an updated suite (based on the same Internet applications, running over TCP or UDP, running over CLNP

DNS.why: A substantial section defines new DNS resource records and the resolver and server behaviour for migration.
DNS.quote: TUBA requires that a new DNS resource record entry type ("long-address") be defined, to store longer Internet (i.e., NSAP) addresses.
DNS.section: 5 Updates to the Domain Name Service

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport run over CLNP. Only the pseudo-header question is touched, and the details are left for further study.
TUBA is an alternative candidate and does not specify IPv6.
NAT is mentioned only as a possible alternative technique and is explicitly out of scope.
CIDR is cited only as a short-term measure that postpones address exhaustion.
The migration is from IPv4 to CLNP, not IPv6, so this tag does not fit.

RFC1348.title: DNS NSAP RRs
RFC1348.summary: Experimental RFC defining two new DNS resource record types, NSAP and NSAP-PTR, for mapping DNS names to OSI NSAP addresses (targeted at CLNP/TUBA) and back via nsap-in-addr.arpa.

DNS.why: The document specifies new DNS resource record types (NSAP, type 22, and NSAP-PTR, type 23), including format, master file syntax and reverse mapping.
DNS.quote: This RFC defines the format of two new Resource Records (RRs) for the Domain Name System (DNS), and reserves corresponding DNS type mnemonic and numerical codes.

CLNP.why: The RRs exist to store NSAP addresses for CLNP-compliant hosts and routers. A substantial motivation, so CLNP readers would want it.
CLNP.quote: This format may be used with the any proposal that has variable length addresses, but is targeted for CLNP use.

rejected.why: The RRs are intended for use in the TUBA proposal, but the document only references it and does not specify or analyse it.
NSAP addressing follows RFC 1237 and OSI definitions, but the document is about DNS representation; CLNP is the more specific fit.
It records NSAP addresses in the DNS but does not address IP address architecture or allocation.
DNS is the more specific tag and already covers this.

gaps.name: NSAP addresses / OSI addressing in DNS
gaps.why: The document is about storing NSAP addresses in DNS. The taxonomy has CLNP and OSI under the internet layer but nothing specific to NSAP address formats.

RFC1349.title: Type of Service in the Internet Protocol Suite
RFC1349.summary: RFC 1349 redefines the IP Type of Service octet's TOS field as a four-bit enumerated value, adds a "minimize monetary cost" value, and specifies how hosts and routers use TOS in ICMP, routing and forwarding.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies the IP TOS octet semantics and its handling. This is the IP-layer service differentiation mechanism that Diffserv later replaced. The taxonomy has no separate TOS tag, so Diffserv is the closest fit, which also leaves QoS as its parent.
Diffserv.quote: This memo changes and clarifies some aspects of the semantics of the Type of Service octet in the Internet Protocol (IP) header.

IPv4.why: It updates RFC 791 by redefining the IPv4 header's Type of Service octet fields, so readers of IPv4 would want it.
IPv4.quote: While this memo is primarily an update to the IP protocol specification [11]

ICMP.why: A full section specifies the TOS-related ICMP Destination Unreachable codes and Redirect codes. It also sets the TOS values used for ICMP messages.
ICMP.quote: A router generates a code 11 or code 12 Destination Unreachable when an unreachable destination (network or host) would have been reachable had a different TOS value been specified.

rejected.why: The memo gives updated TOS encoding tables for OSPF LSAs and the OSPF MIB, but only as a peripheral appendix on compatibility.
Only a small appendix changes the Integrated IS-IS TOS-to-metric table. The document is not about IS-IS.
It covers TOS-based host routing and forwarding, but the subject is the TOS facility, not routing architecture in general.
The parent of Diffserv, so it is implied. The memo says TOS is advisory and not a service-guarantee mechanism.
TCP is mentioned only as one transport that uses TOS, with a short note on TOS for control segments.

gaps.name: IP Type of Service (TOS) field
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the IPv4 TOS octet itself. Diffserv is the nearest tag but is a later redefinition of the same field.

RFC1350.title: The TFTP Protocol (Revision 2)
RFC1350.summary: RFC 1350 specifies TFTP revision 2, a simple lock-step UDP-based file transfer protocol with RRQ/WRQ/DATA/ACK/ERROR packets, transfer modes, and TID-based connection setup.

TFTP.why: The document is the TFTP protocol specification itself, defining packets, modes, connection setup and termination.
TFTP.quote: TFTP is a simple protocol to transfer files, and therefore was named the Trivial File Transfer Protocol or TFTP.

rejected.why: TFTP is implemented on top of UDP, but UDP is only the substrate. The UDP header appears in the appendix for convenience only.
The document contrasts TFTP with FTP only to explain what TFTP lacks. It does not specify or extend FTP.
Netascii is one transfer mode defined by the document. The document is not about ASCII itself.
Telnet is cited only as the source of the netascii modifications. It is a reference, not the subject.

RFC1351.title: SNMP Administrative Model
RFC1351.summary: RFC 1351 elaborates the SNMP administrative model based on parties (identity, authentication, privacy, MIB view), access control policy, proxy parties, and procedures for processing messages, with example configurations.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the party-based administrative model for SNMP, including message formats, access control, proxy and processing procedures.
SNMP.quote: This model provides a unified conceptual basis for administering SNMP protocol entities to support authentication and integrity, privacy, access control

MIB.why: Substantial portions define MIB views and view subtree families as the basis of access control, with examples in section 4.5.
MIB.quote: A MIB view is a subset of the set of all instances of all object types defined according to the Internet-standard SMI

rejected.why: Access control and authentication are within SNMP's own administrative model, not a general AAA framework.
ASN.1 is only used to describe the message and party structures, as a notation, not the subject.
md5AuthProtocol appears only as an example authentication protocol in configurations; the algorithm is defined elsewhere (RFC 1352).
desPrivProtocol is only mentioned in example configurations; it is not specified here.
UDP is merely the transport used by the example transport domain.
The access control policy is specific to SNMP and is covered by the SNMP tag.

RFC1352.title: SNMP Security Protocols
RFC1352.summary: Defines the SNMP Digest Authentication Protocol (MD5-based) and Symmetric Privacy Protocol (DES-CBC) for SNMP parties, plus clock and secret distribution procedures, to provide integrity, origin authentication and confidentiality for SNMP management.

SNMP.why: The document specifies security protocols for SNMP within the SNMP administrative model, covering authentication, privacy, clock synchronization and secret distribution for SNMP parties.
SNMP.quote: this memo defines protocols to support the following three security services: data integrity, data origin authentication, and data confidentiality.

rejected.why: MD5 is only the chosen digest algorithm for the authentication protocol. The document is not about MD5 itself.
DES in CBC mode is only the chosen encryption algorithm. The document defines the privacy protocol around it, not DES.
The MIB for parties is a separate document (RFC 1353) and is only referenced here.
Clock synchronization is covered, but only as a mechanism internal to the SNMP security protocol, not as general time synchronization.
SNMP is the more specific tag for this SNMP-specific authentication protocol.
ASN.1 is only used to define message syntax and is not the subject.

RFC1353.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Administration of SNMP Parties
RFC1353.summary: Defines the SNMP party MIB module (party public, secrets, access control and MIB view tables) used to administer SNMP parties under the SNMP security framework.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition with four tables of managed objects, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: it describes a representation of the SNMP parties defined in [8] as objects defined according to the Internet Standard SMI [1]

SNMP.why: The MIB administers SNMP parties, their authentication and privacy protocols, access privileges and views, so it is part of the SNMP security framework.
SNMP.quote: All four of the groups are mandatory for those SNMP implementations that realize the security framework and mechanisms defined in [8] and [9].

rejected.why: md5AuthProtocol is only an identifier value for a party's authentication protocol; the document does not specify MD5.
desPrivProtocol is only an identifier for the privacy protocol; DES is not specified here.
ASN.1 is the notation used for the MIB definitions, not the subject of the document.
The access control table is part of the SNMP MIB and is covered by the SNMP tag. The document is not about authorization generally.
UDP only appears as the transport in the rfc1351Domain address format.

RFC1354.title: IP Forwarding Table MIB
RFC1354.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module (ipForwardTable) for managing IP routes, with multipath and policy-based routes and next-hop AS, intended to replace MIB-II's ipRouteTable.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMI/ASN.1 for the IP forwarding table, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines only a MIB module, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
The document manages routes through a MIB but does not address routing architecture or design principles.
ASN.1 is only the notation in which the objects are written.
The ipForwardPolicy object maps the IP TOS field to a policy code, but this is only an index and not a QoS architecture.
OSPF, BGP, RIP and others appear only as ipForwardProto enumeration values, not as subjects of the document.

RFC1355.title: Privacy and Accuracy Issues in Network Information Center Databases
RFC1355.summary: FYI 15 gives guidelines for operators of public Network Information Center databases on privacy policies and accuracy procedures for the personal and organizational data they hold.

privacy.why: The first half of the document recommends privacy policies for public NIC databases: what is stored, who sees it, and how entries are changed or removed. Readers of the privacy subject would want it.
privacy.quote: the responsible handling of the personal and organizational information maintained by NICs in publically accessible databases

user guides.why: It is FYI 15, a guidance document for NIC operators and users, not a protocol specification.
user guides.quote: This document provides a set of guidelines for the administration and operation of public Network Information Center (NIC) databases.

rejected.why: The document mentions overlap with public directories and RFC 1295, but it sets no directory protocol or service. It is about NIC database policy.
NIC databases are the kind of data WHOIS serves, but the document never mentions WHOIS or any particular service. It says it makes no recommendations for specific databases.
The document does not discuss registry or registrar operations. It only gives generic NIC database policy.

RFC1356.title: Multiprotocol Interconnect on X.25 and ISDN in the Packet Mode
RFC1356.summary: RFC 1356 specifies how IP and other network-layer protocols (CLNP, SNAP-encapsulated, multiplexed) are encapsulated over X.25 virtual circuits and ISDN packet mode, replacing RFC 877 and raising the IP MTU to 1600.

X.25.why: The whole document defines the use of X.25 virtual circuits, call user data, NLPIDs, packet sequences and facilities to carry network-layer protocols.
X.25.quote: This document specifies the encapsulation of IP and other network layer protocols over X.25 networks, in accordance and alignment with ISO/IEC and CCITT standards.

ISDN.why: The title and scope explicitly cover ISDN packet mode, where the X.25 encapsulation applies. Readers of the ISDN subject would want it.
ISDN.quote: This document also specifies the Internet encapsulation for protocols, including IP, on the packet mode of the ISDN.

rejected.why: IP is the main payload carried, but the document defines an X.25 encapsulation, not IP itself.
CLNP is only one of several NLPID values the encapsulation can carry. It is not specified or extended here.
RFC 1183 DNS records are mentioned once, as a possible aid to address resolution, and the document is not about them.
Frame relay (RFC 1294) is referenced only for its bridging PIDs. The document is not about frame relay.

RFC1357.title: A Format for E-mailing Bibliographic Records
RFC1357.summary: RFC 1357 defines a simple tagged plain-text record format (CS-TR) for e-mailing bibliographic records of computer science technical reports, listing the mandatory and optional fields.

rejected.why: E-mail is only the delivery substrate. The memo defines a bibliographic record format and says nothing about mail architecture, transport or access.
The tagged record is the body content of a message. It is not about Internet message headers or addressing as in the RFC 822 sense.
The memo restricts records to printable ASCII, but this is a minor constraint and the document is not about ASCII.
FTP appears only in example RETRIEVAL field text, so the document is not about FTP.
The memo only mentions possibly registering publisher-IDs with IANA. This is a brief side note and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Bibliographic records / technical report metadata (CS-TR)
gaps.why: The whole document is a metadata format for describing technical reports in library-style records (ID, AUTHOR, ABSTRACT, etc.). The taxonomy has no tag for bibliographic or library metadata.

RFC1358.title: Charter of the Internet Architecture Board (IAB)
RFC1358.summary: RFC 1358 is the charter of the Internet Architecture Board, defining its responsibilities, membership, appointment of the RFC Editor and IETF/IRTF chairs, and its relationship to the Internet Society.

internet governance.why: The document defines the governance structure of the IAB, its membership, appointments, and its role in standards-making and the Internet Society. No more specific child (IETF process, RFC series) captures the whole charter.
internet governance.quote: The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) shall be constituted and shall operate as a technical advisory group of the Internet Society.

RFC series.why: The charter makes RFC series editorial management an IAB responsibility and specifies how the RFC Editor is appointed and removed (Section 8).
RFC series.quote: The editorial management and publication of the Request for Comments (RFC) document series, which constitutes the archival publication series for Internet Standards

IETF process.why: The charter covers the IAB's role in the standards process and the appointment of the IETF chair, and it names the IETF and IRTF as the IAB's task forces.
IETF process.quote: The development, review, and approval of Internet Standards, according to a well-defined and documented set of "Procedures for Internet Standardization".

rejected.why: The document charters a body that oversees architecture. It does not itself discuss architectural principles.
It is a charter document from 1992, not a history or retrospective.

RFC1359.title: Connecting to the Internet - What Connecting Institutions Should Anticipate
RFC1359.summary: FYI 16 is an informational guide from the ACM SIGUCCS Networking Taskforce that tells institutions, mainly US academic ones, what to plan, budget for and evaluate when connecting a campus to the Internet.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide for institutions new to the Internet. It covers planning, costs, providers, support, training and evaluation.
user guides.quote: This FYI RFC outlines the major issues an institution should consider in the decision and implementation of a campus connection to the Internet.

rejected.why: Section 4.3 briefly covers obtaining an IP address and domain name, but it is only one step in the checklist and the document says a tutorial is out of scope.
The Security Considerations section and the acceptable use policy discussion touch on site security. They are boilerplate-level advice, not the subject of the document.
The introduction gives a short account of NSFNet's origins, but this is background and not what the document is about.
Section 5 mentions network operations in passing. The document concerns institutional planning, not network management practice.
The document only points to RFC 1178 on choosing a computer name. It has no content on host naming.

gaps.name: Internet connectivity planning / IP service providers and acceptable use policies
gaps.why: The document is about organisational decision-making for joining the Internet: provider selection, costs, NSFNet acceptable use policy and mid-level networks. The taxonomy has no tag for this beyond the generic user guides tag.

RFC1360.title: IAB Official Protocol Standards
RFC1360.summary: RFC 1360 is the quarterly IAB Official Protocol Standards memo (STD 1), which describes the Internet standardization process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and lists the state of every protocol, with recent changes.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity and requirement levels, and the RFC Editor's decision table. This is Internet standards process and administration.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A section describes the RFC series, how documents are submitted and published, and the RFC Editor's processing table.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

IANA.why: The memo points to Assigned Numbers and says the IANA manages protocol standards. This is a minor part of the document.
IANA.quote: The protocol standards are managed for the IAB by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority.

rejected.why: The IAB is the author, but the memo is about standards status and not architectural principles.
It is a snapshot of 1992 standards status, not a historical retrospective.
It defines state and status terms, but only as part of the process description.
TCP and the many other protocols (DNS, SNMP, Telnet, etc.) appear only as list entries. The document is not about any one of them.

RFC1361.title: Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP)
RFC1361.summary: RFC 1361 describes SNTP, a simplified stateless RPC-style client/server subset of NTP for clock synchronization where full NTP accuracy is not needed.

NTP.why: The document specifies SNTP, an adaptation of NTP, including message format, client and server operations. Readers of the NTP subject would want it.
NTP.quote: SNTP can be used when the ultimate performance of the full NTP implementation described in RFC-1305 is not needed or justified.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport; the document does not define anything new about UDP usage.
The parent topic is implied by the NTP tag, so it is not listed separately.
IP is only mentioned as the underlying layer for the message format.

RFC1362.title: Novell IPX over Various WAN Media (IPXWAN)
RFC1362.summary: Informational RFC from Novell describing the IPXWAN protocol, which exchanges router-to-router information (timer request/response, master/slave election, link delay, common network number) after WAN link establishment before IPX RIP/SAP routing, plus IPX operation over PPP, X.25 and frame relay.

IPX.why: The whole document specifies IPXWAN, the Novell IPX WAN link initialization protocol, with its packet formats and procedures.
IPX.quote: This document describes how Novell IPX operates over various WAN media.

rejected.why: PPP and IPXCP are only the link layer over which IPXWAN runs; the document just states IPXWAN starts after the IPX NCP is Open.
X.25 SVC/PVC is covered only as a media-dependent link establishment and encapsulation note, relying on RFC 1356; the document is not about X.25.
Frame relay gets a brief mention conforming to RFC 1294; not a substantial subject of the document.
The Telebit compression option is a minor option number entry, not a subject of the document.

RFC1363.title: A Proposed Flow Specification
RFC1363.summary: RFC 1363 (IRTF, informational) defines a flow specification data structure that hosts use to request QoS guarantees (token bucket rate/size, delay, loss, guarantee type) from an internetwork for real-time applications.

QoS.why: The whole document defines a data structure for requesting quality of service (bandwidth, delay, loss, guarantee level), a QoS signalling subject.
QoS.quote: A flow specification (or "flow spec") is a data structure used by internetwork hosts to request special services of the internetwork

Intserv.why: The flow spec's guaranteed and predicted service classes and token bucket traffic characterization anticipate the Integrated Services model. This is weak evidence, since the quote is a reference title, but the main body's content supports it.
Intserv.quote: Supporting Real-Time Applications in an Integrated Services Packet Network

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example of hop-by-hop flow setup; the document does not specify or extend ST-II.
Used only as an example flow spec; the document is not about the Telnet protocol.
Not mentioned; the setup mechanism is explicitly out of scope.
The document contrasts its parametric flow spec with the IP Type of Service field, but does not address Diffserv.
Only mentions IANA assigning version numbers and constants, which is boilerplate-level.

RFC1364.title: BGP OSPF Interaction
RFC1364.summary: RFC 1364 specifies design criteria for AS border routers running BGP externally and OSPF as the IGP, covering route exchange, identifier matching, OSPF tag encoding mapped to BGP ORIGIN/AS_PATH, and forwarding address/NEXT_HOP handling.

BGP.why: The document specifies how BGP attributes (INTER-AS METRIC, ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP) and route import/export are handled at an ASBR.
BGP.quote: define the various criteria to be used when designing Autonomous System Border Routers (ASBR) that will run BGP [RFC1267] with other ASBRs external to the AS

OSPF.why: The document defines how OSPF cost, type, tag and forwarding address are set when interacting with BGP, including the tag sub-field encoding.
OSPF.quote: The OSPF external route tag is a "32-bit field attached to each external route
OSPF.section: 4. Setting OSPF tags, BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes

rejected.why: EGP is mentioned as a source of imported routes and for the ORIGIN mapping, but the document is not about EGP.
RIP is mentioned only as an example IGP whose routes may be tagged on import.
The document cites route-leaking and next-hop papers but addresses a specific BGP/OSPF interaction rather than general routing architecture.
IBGP is mentioned as the carrier for path information, but route reflection is not discussed.

RFC1365.title: An IP Address Extension Proposal
RFC1365.summary: An informational 1992 proposal to extend IPv4 addressing beyond 32 bits by introducing a new class F whose address is split between the fixed header and a new IP option, to relieve address shortage.

IPv4.why: The document proposes extending IPv4 addressing (classes, header options) to address exhaustion of network numbers; it is about the IPv4 address lifecycle.
IPv4.quote: This RFC suggests an extension to the IP protocol to solve the shortage of IP address problem

addressing.why: Substantial part defines new address classes F-4 and F-8 with network/host splits, i.e. IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: A new class F is proposed with its six high order bits set to 111110.

rejected.why: The proposal modifies IPv4 via options and is not the IPv6 specification or an IPng candidate.
The proposal keeps classful addressing and extends it rather than introducing classless aggregation.
CLNP is only mentioned as an alternative that would take time to implement.
The proposal is an extension to IPv4, not one of the historic IPng candidates TUBA, PIP, SIPP or TP/IX.

RFC1366.title: Guidelines for Management of IP Address Space
RFC1366.summary: RFC 1366 gives guidelines for how the Internet Registry and regional registries should allocate and assign IPv4 class A, B and C network numbers. It divides the Class C space into regional blocks and sets criteria for assignments.

addressing.why: The whole document is about IP address architecture, allocation and assignment policy, including regional registries and block sizes. No more specific child tag fits, since CIDR is only a related aggregation concern.
addressing.quote: This document proposes a plan which will forward the implementation of RFC 1174 and which defines the allocation and assignment of the network number space.

rejected.why: The document is about IPv4 address space management policy. The IPv4 tag covers the protocol and its address lifecycle, but the more specific fit here is addressing, so I did not add IPv4.
It mentions aggregation-compatible allocation and contiguous Class C blocks, but it does not specify CIDR. The aggregation techniques it points to are in other documents.
IANA and the IR appear as the allocating bodies. The document is not about IANA registries or stewardship in general.

gaps.name: Regional Internet Registry / address registry policy
gaps.why: The document sets qualifications for delegated regional registries and rules for allocating address space. The taxonomy has no tag for RIR or address allocation policy beyond the general addressing tag.

RFC1367.title: Schedule for IP Address Space Management Guidelines
RFC1367.summary: RFC 1367 proposes a 1992 schedule for implementing the IP network number allocation plan of RFC 1366, phasing out Class A/B allocations in favour of blocks of Class C numbers ahead of an expected address aggregation mechanism.

addressing.why: The document is about the schedule for allocating IP network numbers (Class A/B/C, regional registries, blocks of Class C). This is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: This memo suggests a schedule for the implementation of the IP network number allocation plan described in RFC 1366.

CIDR.why: Allocating blocks of Class C numbers and deploying an address aggregation mechanism to limit router table growth is the precursor to CIDR aggregation.
CIDR.quote: The IR begins to allocate all networks according to the addressing plan in appropriately sized blocks of Class C numbers.

rejected.why: The document concerns allocation of IPv4 network numbers, but it does not specify or analyse the protocol. The more specific addressing tag fits better.
It mentions router forwarding table size as motivation only. It does not address routing design.
The IANA and IR are named as actors in the schedule. The document is not about IANA registries or stewardship.

RFC1368.title: Definition of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Repeater Devices
RFC1368.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module for managing IEEE 802.3 10 Mb/s baseband repeaters (hubs), with basic, monitor and address-tracking groups plus traps.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module (SNMP-REPEATER-MIB) defining managed objects, tables and traps for repeaters.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing IEEE 802.3 10 Mb/second baseband repeaters, sometimes referred to as "hubs."

Ethernet.why: The managed objects model IEEE 802.3 repeater units, ports, collisions and frame errors, which is Ethernet layer management.
Ethernet.quote: Instances of the object types defined in this memo represent attributes of an IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet-like) repeater

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with, but the document defines only managed objects, not the protocol. MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is used only as the SMI definition syntax, not as the subject.
This parent tag is implied by the MIB tag.

RFC1369.title: Implementation Notes and Experience for the Internet Ethernet MIB
RFC1369.summary: Informational report on vendor implementation experience with the Ethernet MIB (IEEE 802.3 managed objects), tabulating which MIB variables 11 implementations support and recording the working group's recommendations to deprecate or keep variables.

MIB.why: The whole document reports implementation experience with the Ethernet MIB variables and decisions on which objects to deprecate, so readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: Develop an implementation report on the Ethernet MIB.

Ethernet.why: Covers Ethernet interface chips and driver-level counters (collisions, FCS and alignment errors), so it is relevant to Ethernet interfaces and their management.
Ethernet.quote: This report shall cover MIB variables which are implemented in both Ethernet interface chips, and in software (i.e., drivers)

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism (noSuchName and badValue error codes appear in the table legend). The document is about the MIB objects, not the protocol.
The parent is implied by the MIB tag, and the document has no broader operational management content.

RFC1370.title: Applicability Statement for OSPF
RFC1370.summary: IAB Applicability Statement requiring IP routers that implement any routing protocol (other than static routes) to implement OSPF and the OSPF MIB, with TOS routing recommended.

OSPF.why: The whole document states when and how OSPF must be implemented by router vendors, so it belongs on the OSPF page.
OSPF.quote: An IP router that implements any routing protocol (other than static routes) is required to implement OSPF [1] and the OSPF MIB [2].

rejected.why: The OSPF MIB is mentioned as a required companion, but the document does not specify or discuss it beyond the requirement.
ICMP Router Discovery is cited only as the recommended host mechanism in place of wiretapping routing protocols; it is a passing reference.
