The document is about one protocol's applicability, not routing architecture in general.

RFC1371.title: Choosing a Common IGP for the IP Internet
RFC1371.summary: IESG recommendation to the IAB that OSPF be designated the "common IGP" for the IP Internet, with background on OSPF vs Integrated IS-IS and IP/CLNP integrated routing.

OSPF.why: The document's core purpose is recommending OSPF as the common IGP and requiring routers to implement it.
OSPF.quote: the IESG recommends that OSPF be designated as the common IGP for the IP portions of the Internet
OSPF.section: 7.1 Regarding the Common IGP for the IP Internet

IS-IS.why: Integrated IS-IS is the alternative IGP weighed against OSPF, and integrated IP/CLNP routing with it is a substantial discussion.
IS-IS.quote: the IESG wishes to encourage implementation of Integrated IS-IS so that a reasonable position can be determined based on operational experience

rejected.why: CLNP appears as context for the integrated routing discussion, but the document is about IGP choice rather than CLNP itself.
Exterior routing is explicitly out of scope; EGP and BGP are mentioned only to distinguish them from IGPs.
BGP is cited only as an example of an exterior protocol and is explicitly not considered.
OSI coexistence is background to the IP/CLNP routing discussion, not the subject of the memo.
The IGP choice is covered by the specific OSPF and IS-IS tags, so the broader routing architecture tag is not needed.

RFC1372.title: Telnet Remote Flow Control Option
RFC1372.summary: Specifies the Telnet Remote Flow Control Option (TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL), which lets a host remotely enable/disable software flow control in a user telnet process and set restart-on-any or restart-on-XON behaviour, obsoleting RFC 1080.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option with its negotiation, subnegotiation commands and defaults, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies an extended version of the Telnet Remote Flow Control Option, RFC 1080, with the addition of the RESTART-ANY and RESTART-XON suboptions.

rejected.why: XON/XOFF control characters are mentioned only as the flow-control signals; the document is not about the character set.
No glossary or definitions are the subject of the document.

RFC1373.title: Portable DUAs
RFC1373.summary: Informational guide for users and ISODE maintainers on building, installing and packaging portable X.500 Directory User Agents (WHOIS interface, de, dixie/ud, doog).

X.500.why: The whole document is about client programs (DUAs) accessing the X.500 Directory via DSAs, using ISODE/QUIPU. X.500 is the best-fitting tag.
X.500.quote: set up their own DUAs (Directory User Interfaces) to access the Directory

WHOIS.why: A substantial part covers the WHOIS emulation front-end to X.500, how to query it and how maintainers configure the whois service port.
WHOIS.quote: A WHOIS interface to X.500 may be available on any ISODE-resident machine which also runs a DSA

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which is already tagged, so it is implied.
Only used to fetch the tar files; it is a delivery mechanism, not the subject.
The WHOIS here is the legacy whois emulation, not the WHOIS++ architecture.
Not mentioned; dixie is a lightweight access mechanism but the document does not describe LDAP.

gaps.name: ISODE / QUIPU software distribution
gaps.why: The document is largely build and installation instructions for ISODE-based DUAs (de, ud, doog, dixie). The taxonomy has no tag for this software.

RFC1374.title: IP and ARP on HIPPI
RFC1374.summary: Specifies how IP datagrams and ARP are carried over HIPPI-SC switched LANs, covering packet encapsulation (HIPPI-FP/LE, LLC/SNAP), I-field usage, connection rules, MTU, ARP with switch address resolution, and self-address discovery.

ARP.why: A large part of the document defines ARP/RARP over HIPPI, piggybacked with HIPPI-LE address resolution, ARP agents and self-address discovery.
ARP.quote: The HIPPI ARP/RARP protocol uses the same packet format as ARP for Ethernet.

rejected.why: Only mentions path MTU discovery via RFC 1191 in passing.
A short section says RFC 1191 applies unchanged; not a substantive part of the document.
Ethernet/802 is referenced only as the conventional comparison, not the subject.
IP is the payload being encapsulated; the document is about the link layer, not IPv4 itself.

gaps.name: HIPPI (High-Performance Parallel Interface)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about IP over HIPPI switched LANs (encapsulation, I-field, connection rules, MTU). The link layer section has no HIPPI tag, so only the ARP part is covered.

RFC1375.title: Suggestion for New Classes of IP Addresses
RFC1375.summary: Informational memo proposing to carve new IP address classes F, G, H and K out of the Class C space to give small networks finer-grained address allocations and reduce wasted address space.

addressing.why: The whole document is about IP address architecture and allocation: redefining the Class C prefix and adding new classes with smaller local address fields to reduce wasted address space.
addressing.quote: This memo then proposes to add four new types of addresses, to be referred to as "Class F", "Class G", "Class H", and "Class K"
addressing.section: Suggestion for new IP address classes

rejected.why: The proposal modifies the IPv4 classful address format, but it is about address-space allocation in general. The addressing topic fits it better, though IPv4 and its address lifecycle was a close alternative.
The memo is about classful addressing with finer granularity, not classless aggregation or CIDR.
Class D multicast is mentioned only in passing to explain the existing class layout.
Telnet and FTP are mentioned only as examples of services BBSs might offer; the memo is not about them.

RFC1376.title: The PPP DECnet Phase IV Control Protocol (DNCP)
RFC1376.summary: Defines DNCP, the PPP Network Control Protocol for configuring and carrying DECnet Phase IV Routing packets over point-to-point links, including encapsulation, protocol field values and routing timer considerations.

DECnet.why: The document specifies how DECnet Phase IV Routing packets are encapsulated and carried over PPP, which is exactly the DECnet-over-IP-infrastructure subject.
DECnet.quote: This document defines the NCP for establishing and configuring Digital's DNA Phase IV Routing protocol (DECnet Phase IV) over PPP.

PPP.why: It defines a new PPP Network Control Protocol (DNCP) with its own protocol field values, code usage and negotiation behaviour.
PPP.quote: The DNA Phase IV Routing Control Protocol is exactly the same as the Link Control Protocol [1] with the following exceptions:

rejected.why: DNA Phase IV Routing uses distance-vector updates, but the document does not specify RIP; it only gives timer advice for DNA routing.
The overview mentions the DNA Naming Service (DNS), a different Digital system, and says it is out of scope; it is not the Internet DNS.
Packets use Ethernet format minus header, pad and FCS, but Ethernet is only the model for the encapsulation, not the subject.
The DNA Time Service is mentioned only in a list of out-of-scope protocols.

RFC1377.title: The PPP OSI Network Layer Control Protocol (OSINLCP)
RFC1377.summary: Defines the PPP Network Control Protocol for OSI network layer protocols (OSINLCP), including its packet encapsulation, NPDU alignment handling and the Align-NPDU configuration option.

PPP.why: The document specifies a PPP Network Control Protocol (OSINLCP) with its Align-NPDU option, so it belongs under PPP and its control protocols.
PPP.quote: This document defines the NCP for establishing and configuring OSI Network Layer Protocols.

OSI.why: It covers how OSI network layer protocols (CLNP, ES-IS, IS-IS, IDRP) are carried over PPP, NLPID use and NPDU alignment.
OSI.quote: OSI Network Layer protocols can be discriminated according to the first octet in each Network Protocol Data Unit

rejected.why: CLNP is discussed as one OSI protocol that runs over PPP, but the document is about the general OSI NCP, not CLNP itself; OSI covers it.
IS-IS behaviour over PPP is discussed only as an operational consideration, not specified or extended.
PPP header compression is only used to achieve alignment in the Align-NPDU option, not the subject.

RFC1378.title: The PPP AppleTalk Control Protocol (ATCP)
RFC1378.summary: Defines ATCP, the PPP Network Control Protocol for negotiating and configuring AppleTalk over point-to-point links, including its configuration options and operating modes.

AppleTalk.why: The document specifies AppleTalk configuration (addresses, routing protocol, zones, half-routers) over PPP, so readers of the AppleTalk subject would expect it.
AppleTalk.quote: This document defines the NCP for establishing and configuring the AppleTalk Protocol [3] over PPP.

PPP.why: ATCP is a PPP Network Control Protocol, defined as a variant of LCP with its own protocol field, codes and options.
PPP.quote: The AppleTalk Control Protocol is exactly the same as the Link Control Protocol [1] with the following exceptions:

rejected.why: Not a taxonomy tag. RTMP and AURP are only referenced as routing protocol values.
RTMP is AppleTalk's routing protocol, not RIP, and it is only mentioned as a default.
The AT-Compression-Protocol option is a negotiation hook, and no compression protocols are defined.
'AppleTalk ASCII' only refers to the character codes used for names.

RFC1379.title: Extending TCP for Transactions -- Concepts
RFC1379.summary: RFC 1379 describes concepts for extending TCP to support transaction-oriented service (T/TCP) by bypassing the 3-way handshake with TAO using cached connection counts, shortening TIME-WAIT, and adding new connection states.

TCP.why: The whole document proposes extensions to TCP: TAO, shortened TIME-WAIT, connection count option, and a modified state machine.
TCP.quote: extension of TCP to provide transaction-oriented service, without altering its virtual-circuit operation

rejected.why: UDP is mentioned only as the alternative that transaction applications currently use; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Mentioned only as a potential application in the conclusions.
The TCP tag is more specific and already covers the transport-layer subject.

gaps.name: Transaction TCP (T/TCP), TAO
gaps.why: The document is about transaction-oriented transport extensions to TCP; no taxonomy tag exists for transaction protocols, so TCP is the closest fit.

RFC1380.title: IESG Deliberations on Routing and Addressing
RFC1380.summary: IESG report summarizing Internet routing and addressing scaling problems (Class B exhaustion, routing table explosion, address exhaustion), the ROAD group, endorsement of CIDR, and the process and selection criteria for choosing a bigger-address IP successor.

CIDR.why: The IESG's main recommended action is to adopt CIDR, with a course of action for pursuing it in the IETF (BGP extensions, address assignment guidelines, deployment).
CIDR.quote: The IESG accepted ROAD's endorsement of CIDR [Fuller92].  CIDR solves the routing table explosion problem (for the current IP addressing scheme)
CIDR.section: 4.3 A Solution For Routing Table Explosion -- CIDR

addressing.why: The memo is about IP address exhaustion, address assignment policy, and aggregation. It is the broad addressing topic beyond CIDR alone.
addressing.quote: The Internet now faces three growth-related problems: Class B network number exhaustion - Routing table explosion - IP address space exhaustion

routing architecture.why: It covers routing table scalability, aggregation, and the criteria for choosing a new routing and addressing architecture.
routing architecture.quote: The IESG felt there needed to be an open and thorough evaluation of any proposed new routing and addressing architecture.

IPng.why: A substantial part of the memo reviews the candidate next-generation IP proposals (TUBA, PIP, SIP, IPAE) and sets the selection process and criteria.
IPng.quote: "Simple CLNP" [Callon92a], "IP Encaps"  [Hinden92], "CNAT" [Callon92b], and "Nimrod" [Chiappa91].

rejected.why: BGP4's CIDR extensions are mentioned as a work item, but the memo does not specify or analyse BGP itself.
IPv4 address exhaustion is the subject, but the memo frames it as general addressing and CIDR rather than IPv4 protocol specification.
It discusses IP architecture evolution, but the more specific routing and addressing tags fit better.
Nimrod is only one of several proposals listed, with no substantive coverage.
CLNP is mentioned only as the basis of the Simple CLNP and TUBA proposal.

RFC1381.title: SNMP MIB Extension for X.25 LAPB
RFC1381.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (admin, operational, flow and XID tables) for managing the X.25 LAPB link layer, used alongside MIB-II, the X.25 packet-layer MIB and the RS-232 MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module in SMI/concise MIB format defining lapbAdmnTable, lapbOperTable, lapbFlowTable and lapbXidTable. Readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the Link Layer of X.25, LAPB.

X.25.why: The managed objects instrument the X.25 LAPB link layer, covering its timers, window sizes, frame states, FRMR and XID. They are used alongside the X.25 packet layer MIB.
X.25.quote: The objects defined below are defined in the context of ISO 7776 [10] and ISO 8885 [11].

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB plugs into. The document defines objects only, not protocol behaviour. The MIB tag is the more specific fit.
ASN.1 is only the notation used by the SMI to write the object definitions. The document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
This is a general parent tag. The more specific X.25 tag fits, so the parent is implied.
LAPB is related to HDLC but the document is about X.25 LAPB only. It explicitly excludes LAPD and other HDLC flavours.

gaps.name: LAPB / HDLC link-layer procedures
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for LAPB or HDLC. The X.25 tag is the nearest, but LAPB readers would want a dedicated tag.

RFC1382.title: SNMP MIB Extension for the X.25 Packet Layer
RFC1382.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module for managing the X.25 Packet Layer (administration, operation, statistics, channel, circuit, cleared-circuit and call-parameter tables, plus traps), designed to work with MIB-II, the LAPB MIB and RS-232 MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining managed objects, tables and traps for the X.25 packet layer using SMI.
MIB.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing the Packet Layer of X.25.

X.25.why: The managed subject is the X.25 packet layer (PLE, circuits, facilities, timers, clearing causes), so readers of X.25 would want it.
X.25.quote: Instances of the objects defined below represent attributes of an X.25 Packet Layer interface.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol framework used; the document defines MIB objects, not protocol changes. MIB tag is more specific.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the objects.
Not related; X.25 is the subject, not ISDN access.

RFC1383.title: An Experiment in DNS Based IP Routing
RFC1383.summary: Experimental proposal to route IP packets for multihomed fringe domains by looking up MX-like "RX" records (carried in DNS TXT records under in-addr.arpa) to find access gateways, then using IP loose source routing to reach them.

routing architecture.why: The memo addresses routing table explosion and scalability for multihomed stubs, proposing a directory-based routing scheme complementary to hierarchical routing.
routing architecture.quote: The current proposal presents a scheme that allows for simple routing. It is complementary with the classic "hierarchical routing" approach

DNS.why: A new use of DNS: RX records (initially encoded as TXT records) under in-addr.arpa are used to obtain routing information, with a record format defined in section 5.1.
DNS.quote: it will query the DNS with the name build up from "Dx" in the "in-addr.arpa" domain, obtain the RX records

multihoming.why: Supporting multihomed stub domains without announcing extra routes is the main motivation, with gateway preference and selection discussed throughout.
multihoming.quote: allow to support multihomed domains without requiring additional overhead on routing and without requiring hosts to have explicit knowledge of multiple addresses.

rejected.why: CIDR is cited as the hierarchical alternative and rationale context, not specified or extended here.
MX records are only the analogy for the RX scheme; the document is not about mail routing.
IP source routing is used as the forwarding mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend IPv4 itself.
BGP is mentioned only as a source of routing-table load; the document does not address BGP.
ICMP unreachable messages are monitored as a trigger in the implementation, but the document is not about ICMP.

RFC1384.title: Naming Guidelines for Directory Pilots
RFC1384.summary: RFC 1384 gives naming guidelines for X.500 Directory pilots: DIT structure, naming of organisations, organisational units, people and application entities, multinational organisations, aliases and access control.

X.500.why: The whole document gives guidance on DIT structure and entry naming for X.500 directory pilots, including aliases, RDNs and multinational organisation models.
X.500.quote: A DIT structure is suggested in Annex B of X.521, and it is recommended that Directory Pilots should follow a slightly modified form of these guidelines.

rejected.why: Section 2.2 only notes that DNS is represented in the DIT under O=Internet per RFC 1279. This is a brief aside, not the subject of the document.
The document is about naming, but only within X.500. The specific X.500 tag already covers it, and the parent is implied.
This is the parent of X.500, so it is implied. The document is specific to X.500.
LDAP is not mentioned. The document predates it and addresses X.500 DIT naming only.

RFC1385.title: EIP: The Extended Internet Protocol
RFC1385.summary: RFC 1385 proposes EIP, an IPv4-compatible extended header that carries extra network-number addressing in an IP option, as a backward-compatible answer to address exhaustion and routing explosion, with a transition plan and an IP-option experiment.

IPv4.why: The document specifies an extension of IPv4 (header format, host/network numbers, translation, transition) to address IPv4 address exhaustion.
IPv4.quote: The Extended Internet Protocol (EIP) provides a framework for solving the problem of address space exhaustion with a new addressing and routing scheme, yet maintaining maximum backward compatibility with current IP.

IPng.why: EIP is itself an IP Next Generation-era candidate proposal, positioned against Pip, TUBA, SIP and IPAE, with an evolutionary transition plan.
IPng.quote: A number of proposals have been put forward: Pip[7], Nimrod [8], TUBA [6] and SIP [14].

rejected.why: Addressing is a topic covered by the IPv4 tag already chosen; the document's subject is the protocol extension as a whole.
Only a new RR type 'N' is mentioned briefly as a needed modification; the document is not about DNS.
The document merely states ARP/RARP need no modification.
ICMP is only mentioned as unaffected, and in comparison with IPAE; the document is not about it.
Nimrod is cited as an addressing scheme EIP could accommodate; the document does not specify or analyse it.
EIP predates IPv6 and is a different proposal; no IPv6 content.

RFC1386.title: The US Domain
RFC1386.summary: Informational RFC describing the .US top-level country domain: its geographic naming hierarchy, registration and delegation procedures, and the DNS zone and resource record practices used to run it.

DNS.why: The document specifies the operation of the .US DNS zone: naming structure, delegation of subdomains, name servers, zone files, and RR usage (A, CNAME, MX, HINFO, PTR, wildcards).
DNS.quote: The US Domain is an official top-level domain in the DNS of the Internet community.

domain registration.why: A large part covers registrar procedures, questionnaire, delegation requirements and procedures, and subdomain contacts.
domain registration.quote: There are two ways to be registered in the US Domain, directly, or by delegation.

rejected.why: UUCP hosts are discussed only as non-IP hosts that register via MX forwarders. The document is not about UUCP mail interchange.
MX records and mail forwarding appear as a DNS mechanism for non-IP hosts, but the document is about the naming and registration of a domain.
The document covers DNS domain naming, not host naming conventions or host tables, though HOSTS.TXT is mentioned as history.
The registrar role is domain administration, not IANA registry stewardship.

gaps.name: country-code top-level domain (ccTLD) administration
gaps.why: The document describes the policy and structure of the .US ccTLD, and the taxonomy has no tag for country-code domain policy beyond general DNS and domain registration.

RFC1387.title: RIP Version 2 Protocol Analysis
RFC1387.summary: Informational analysis of RIP version 2, as required by RFC 1264, summarizing its key features (domains, route tags, subnet masks, next hop, authentication, multicast), its MIB and implementation experience.

RIP.why: The whole document analyses RIP-2 features, MIB and implementations, so it belongs on the RIP page.
RIP.quote: this report documents the key features of the RIP-2 protocol and the current implementation experience.

rejected.why: The RIP-2 MIB gets one short section, but it is defined in RFC 1389. This document does not specify it.
CIDR is mentioned once as a motivation for subnet masks. The document is not about it.
Multicast delivery of RIP-2 packets is a brief feature note, not a multicast routing topic.
OSPF is only mentioned as the source of the authentication mechanism.

RFC1388.title: RIP Version 2 Carrying Additional Information
RFC1388.summary: RFC 1388 specifies RIP version 2, extending the RIP datagram format with authentication, routing domain, route tag, subnet mask, next hop and multicast fields, with backward compatibility to RIP-1.

RIP.why: The whole document defines RIP version 2, its packet format extensions, and compatibility with RIP-1.
RIP.quote: This document specifies an extension of the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), as defined in [1], to expand the amount of useful information carried in RIP packets

rejected.why: Multicast address 224.0.0.9 is used for RIP-2 updates, but this is a small part of the RIP spec, not about IP multicast routing.
Route Tag may carry AS numbers for EGP/BGP, but BGP is only mentioned in passing.
OSPF is mentioned only as a comparison and in the next hop example.
Simple password authentication is a feature of RIP-2 packets, covered by the RIP tag rather than a general authentication subject.

RFC1389.title: RIP Version 2 MIB Extensions
RFC1389.summary: RFC 1389 defines an SNMP MIB module (rip2, mib-2 23) for managing RIP Version 2, with global counters, interface status and configuration tables, and an optional peer table.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module definition in SMI/OBJECT-TYPE format, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

RIP.why: The managed objects cover RIP-2 interfaces, authentication, send/receive versions, and peers, so RIP readers would want this MIB.
RIP.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing RIP Version 2.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects. The document only defines a MIB module and does not extend or specify SNMP, so MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 and the SMI are only the notation used to write the definitions, not the subject.
Multicast is mentioned only in object descriptions for sending RIP-2 updates and is incidental.
This parent is implied by the MIB tag, and the document is about one MIB module, not general management.

RFC1390.title: Transmission of IP and ARP over FDDI Networks
RFC1390.summary: Standard specifying encapsulation of IP datagrams and ARP requests/replies on FDDI networks using 802.2 LLC/SNAP, including ARP parameters, multicast mapping, MTU, and MAC/LLC details.

FDDI.why: The whole document specifies IP over FDDI: packet format, MTU of 4352 octets, MAC-layer and LLC details, and multicast address mapping.
FDDI.quote: This memo defines a method of encapsulating the Internet Protocol (IP) datagrams and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) requests and replies on Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) Networks.

ARP.why: A substantial section profiles ARP for FDDI: hardware type code 1, canonical bit order for addresses, and field values. ARP is in the title.
ARP.quote: The mapping of 32-bit Internet addresses to 48-bit FDDI addresses shall be done via the dynamic discovery procedure of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)

rejected.why: IP is the payload being carried. The document does not specify IP itself.
Ethernet interoperability via translational bridges is a design constraint (ARP hardware type 1, trailing pad). The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
The multicast address mapping is a short subsection that follows RFC 1112. It does not make the document about multicast.
The document mentions IEEE 802 token ring only as a related standard. It does not cover IP over token ring.

RFC1391.title: The Tao of the IETF: A Guide for New Attendees of the Internet Engineering Task Force
RFC1391.summary: An FYI guide for newcomers to IETF meetings explaining the IETF's structure, mailing lists, registration, meeting etiquette, proceedings, and RFC/Internet-Draft series.

IETF process.why: The document explains IETF organization (IESG, IAB, Areas, Working Groups, BOFs), meeting procedures and working-group phases, which is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: The purpose of this For Your Information (FYI) RFC is to explain to the newcomers how the IETF works.

user guides.why: It is itself an FYI (FYI 17) introductory guide for newcomers, fitting the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: The For Your Information RFC sub-series was created to document overviews and things which are introductory.

RFC series.why: A section describes the history of RFCs, IENs, the FYI and STD sub-series, and Internet-Draft conventions.
RFC series.quote: there are now two special sub-series within the RFCs: FYIs and STDs.

internet history.why: Gives a short history of the IETF's early meetings and structural changes, such as the introduction of Working Groups.
internet history.quote: The first IETF meeting was held in January, 1986 at Linkabit in San Diego with 15 attendees.

rejected.why: The acronym list is reference apparatus, not the document's subject.
The mailing list section covers IETF participation lists, not mailing list protocols or headers.
Anonymous FTP and mail servers are only mentioned as ways to retrieve files.
Email is only a communication channel used by participants, not the subject of the document.
The tone is light, but it is a genuine informational guide rather than a humorous RFC.

gaps.name: IETF meetings and participation
gaps.why: The document is mainly about attending IETF meetings (registration, etiquette, agenda, proceedings), which the taxonomy only covers broadly under IETF process.

RFC1392.title: Internet Users' Glossary
RFC1392.summary: FYI 18 is a general glossary of Internet and networking terms and acronyms for users, covering protocols, organizations, and slang.

user guides.why: An FYI-series introductory glossary for Internet users. The taxonomy places user guides and FYI documents under this tag.
user guides.quote: There are many networking glossaries in existence. This glossary concentrates on terms which are specific to the Internet.

terminology.why: The whole document defines terms and acronyms, so it belongs on the terminology page.
terminology.quote: Naturally, there are entries for some basic terms and acronyms because other entries refer to them.

rejected.why: DNS, MX records and FQDN each get a short glossary entry. The document is not about DNS.
Email entries such as SMTP, POP, MIME and mail gateway are brief definitions only.
It defines historical terms like ARPANET and core gateway but is not a history.
TCP, UDP, IP and other protocols are defined in one-paragraph entries only.
Some entries are jokes, such as 'binary' and 'recursive', but the document is a serious glossary.

RFC1393.title: Traceroute Using an IP Option
RFC1393.summary: RFC 1393 defines an experimental IP option and ICMP Traceroute message (type 30) that let routers report the outbound and return path to the originator with n+1 packets instead of 2n.

traceroute.why: The whole document specifies an alternative traceroute mechanism for path discovery, so the traceroute tag fits.
traceroute.quote: This document specifies a new IP option and ICMP message type which duplicates the functionality of the existing traceroute method while generating fewer packets

ICMP.why: It defines a new ICMP message type (Type 30, Traceroute) with its own code values and format, which is new ICMP content.
ICMP.quote: The presence of this option in an ICMP Echo (or any other) packet

rejected.why: The IP option is defined for IPv4, but the document is about the traceroute function. It is not about IPv4 itself or its address lifecycle.
The message reports link speed and MTU, but the purpose is path tracing and debugging, not performance metrics.
The Output Link MTU field is incidental information. The document does not specify path MTU discovery.

RFC1394.title: Relationship of Telex Answerback Codes to Internet Domains
RFC1394.summary: Informational reference table mapping countries and areas to telephone codes, telex country codes, telex answerbacks and Internet country domain identifiers, plus major public email system domains.

naming.why: The document catalogues the mapping between Internet country domain names (and top-level domains) and telex and telephone codes. It is about names and identifiers in general, not DNS protocol behaviour, so the general naming topic fits best.
naming.quote: the conversion between specific country telex answerback codes and Internet country domain identifiers

rejected.why: The document lists domain identifiers but does not specify or analyse DNS protocol, records, or server behaviour.
It is a lookup table of existing domains, not about registry or registrar operations.
It lists telephone country codes beside domains but does not map E.164 numbers into the DNS.
UUCP and BITNET addressing appear only in a brief note on gateway routing, not as a subject of the document.
Public email system domains are listed as table entries, but the document does not address email architecture or transport.
Fax is mentioned as a use of the codes, but the document has no fax protocol content.

gaps.name: Telex answerback codes / country code cross-reference
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the telex and telephone country code correspondence to Internet country domains, and the taxonomy has no tag for telex or for country-code registries.

RFC1395.title: BOOTP Vendor Information Extensions
RFC1395.summary: RFC 1395 defines a vendor-independent interpretation of the BOOTP vendor information field, specifying the magic cookie and tagged options (subnet mask, gateways, servers, hostname, domain name, etc.) for host configuration.

DHCP.why: BOOTP vendor extensions are the direct ancestor of DHCP options. The taxonomy has no BOOTP tag, and DHCP is the closest fit for readers browsing host configuration protocols and option definitions.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a (potentially) vendor-independent interpretation of this resource information.

rejected.why: DNS appears only as the name server and domain name options' content, and the document is not about DNS itself.
RARP is mentioned only as background in the BOOTP overview, and the document does not specify it.
BOOTP runs over UDP/IP, so UDP is only the substrate.
The multicast discussion appears only as a short comparison of alternatives, not as the subject of the document.
The comparison section touches on locating servers, but the document is about configuration options, not service discovery.
The only IANA content is the registration contact for new tags, which is boilerplate-like and not the main body.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol) and vendor extensions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no BOOTP tag. The document is entirely about BOOTP vendor information tags, so readers would look for a BOOTP page. DHCP is only an approximate fit.

RFC1396.title: The Process for Organization of Internet Standards Working Group (POISED)
RFC1396.summary: A report by the POISED working group chair summarizing the 1992 events and deliberations that led to a new IAB/IESG selection process (nomination committee, recall) and a shift of standards-action decisions to the IESG.

IETF process.why: The document is about reorganizing IETF/IAB/IESG decision-making and leadership selection and recall procedures, which is IETF process.
IETF process.quote: IAB and IESG members would be selected by a nomination and recruiting committee.

NomCom.why: A substantial portion describes the origin of the nominating committee: its composition, volunteer selection by lot, terms and ratification.
NomCom.quote: The committee is to consist of seven members from the community, with non-voting representatives from the IAB and IESG

rejected.why: It is a retrospective of events, but its purpose is reporting a working group's process outcome rather than a general history of the Internet; IETF process fits better.
The IP address depletion and ROAD discussion is only background for the governance controversy.
Mentioned only as part of the technical controversy that triggered POISED; the document is not about it.
The IAB's role is discussed organizationally, not architectural principles.

RFC1397.title: Default Route Advertisement In BGP2 and BGP3 Version of The Border Gateway Protocol
RFC1397.summary: Specifies how a default route is advertised in BGP-2 and BGP-3 UPDATE messages using network 0.0.0.0, with NEXT_HOP, ORIGIN, AS_PATH and INTER-AS-METRIC attribute usage.

BGP.why: The whole document defines how BGP-2 and BGP-3 speakers advertise a default route in UPDATE messages, which is a BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: A default route is advertised in an UPDATE message that carries reachability information for network 0.0.0.0.

rejected.why: The document is about a specific BGP mechanism, not general routing architecture or scalability principles, even though it mentions routers unable to hold full tables.
The 0.0.0.0 address is just the encoding of the default route within BGP, not a subject of the document.

RFC1398.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-Like Interface Types
RFC1398.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module (dot3) for managing Ethernet-like interfaces, including statistics, collision histograms, tests (TDR, loopback) and chipset identifiers, obsoleting RFC 1284.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module definition (RFC1398-MIB) using the SMI and OBJECT-TYPE macro, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

Ethernet.why: The managed objects cover IEEE 802.3 Ethernet-like interface statistics, collisions, tests and MAC chipsets, so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing ethernet-like objects.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is accessed through; the document defines objects only, not protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 subset is used as the definition notation via the SMI, not the subject of the document.
Covered by the more specific Ethernet tag.

RFC1399.title: Summary of 1300-1399
RFC1399.summary: RFC 1399 is an annotated index and status report of the 100 RFCs numbered 1300 through 1399, giving each one's author, date, title and abstract.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a catalogue of a block of the RFC series. Readers browsing the RFC series subject would want this publication summary.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1300 through RFCs 1399.

rejected.why: Many summarised RFCs define MIB modules, but this document only lists them and does not define or discuss any MIB.
Several PPP RFCs appear as one-paragraph entries. The document is not about PPP.
It lists process RFCs such as 1310 and 1396, but it is a summary list and does not address the process itself.
SNMP security and administrative RFCs are listed only as entries, not specified or analysed here.
BGP default route and BGP/OSPF interaction RFCs are only listed, not discussed.
RFC 1300 is listed as a poem, but this document is not itself humorous.

RFC1400.title: Transition and Modernization of the Internet Registration Service
RFC1400.summary: Announces the March 1993 transition of non-DDN Internet registration services (IP, domain, ASN registration, WHOIS, root zone and root server) from the DDN NIC to the InterNIC Registration Service, and describes the new email-based automated registration process.

domain registration.why: The document is about the transfer of registry operations and the new automated registration (autoreg) template process for domains, IP addresses and ASNs.
domain registration.quote: non-DDN registration services will soon be transferred from the DDN NIC to the new Internet Registration Service, which is a part of an entity referred to as the InterNIC

WHOIS.why: A substantial part describes where WHOIS service will be offered at DDN NIC and InterNIC, what data each holds, and a sample WHOIS session.
WHOIS.quote: The WHOIS service available from whois.internic.net will contain all information on IP addresses, domains, and ASNs.

rejected.why: Root zone file and new root server ns.internic.net are mentioned only as operational relocation notes, not a DNS specification.
Finger is used only as a way to check ticket status, a substrate for the service rather than the subject.
Gopher and WAIS are listed only as services available on the rs.internic.net host.
Telnet is only the access method to the registration host.
The host.txt file is mentioned only in passing regarding which site will serve it.

gaps.name: InterNIC / NIC registration services transition
gaps.why: The document is about the administrative handover of Internet registration (NIC) services from DDN NIC to InterNIC; the closest tag, domain registration, covers it only partly.

RFC1401.title: Correspondence between the IAB and DISA on the use of DNS
RFC1401.summary: Reproduces IAB–DISA letters urging universal adoption of the Domain Name System and phasing out static hosts.txt host tables, especially on MILNET.

DNS.why: The whole correspondence advocates adopting DNS throughout the Internet instead of centrally maintained host tables, and mentions MX records as a DNS facility.
DNS.quote: the critical need for widespread adoption of a uniform Domain Name service is very apparent
DNS.section: 1. Letter from the IAB to DISA

rejected.why: hosts.txt host tables are discussed only as the legacy approach to be phased out. The memo is about adopting DNS, not about host naming conventions.
MX records are mentioned only as one benefit of DNS. The memo does not address mail transport.
The memo is a policy appeal about one service, not a statement of architectural principles.

RFC1402.title: There's Gold in them thar Networks! or Searching for Treasure in all the Wrong Places
RFC1402.summary: FYI 10 is a 1993 annotated guide to network information resources: lists of documents, anonymous FTP sites, archie, NICs, campus-wide information systems, Freenets, WAIS, Gopher, WWW and WHOIS servers, books and periodicals, intended for those who provide network information to users.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide that points network users and information providers to resources and explains how to get access.
user guides.quote: This paper will present some of the "gold nuggets" of information and file repositories on the network that could be useful.

WHOIS.why: A whole section describes WHOIS, how to query it, and lists university WHOIS servers for finding e-mail addresses.
WHOIS.quote: WHOIS is a program available on many workstation/mini/mainframe computers that can connect to another computer.

FTP.why: Anonymous FTP is the main access method used throughout. There is a section on FTP sites, a glossary entry with usage steps, and archie for searching FTP archives.
FTP.quote: A direct connection to the Internet also allows you to transfer a file from a remote computer.  This program is referred to as FTP

Gopher.why: Gopher is presented as an information-access system and as the replacement for CWISes. This is a short entry but it is substantive.
Gopher.quote: Gopher is a client server system that accesses information on the Internet.

rejected.why: Telnet is the access method for nearly every listed resource, but the document only uses it and gives a glossary entry. It does not specify or analyse the protocol.
WAIS gets only a brief pointer entry (8.95), a minor mention among many resources.
The World Wide Web entry mentions HTTP briefly as one resource among many. The document does not address HTTP in any depth.
The WHOIS and white-pages material is about finding e-mail addresses with existing tools. It does not address directory services in general, and WHOIS is already tagged.

gaps.name: Network information resource guides / archie / campus-wide information systems
gaps.why: The document is mainly a catalogue of resource-discovery tools and CWISes (archie, Hytelnet, Netfind, CWIS). The taxonomy has no tag for Internet resource discovery or information services other than the generic user guides tag.

RFC1403.title: BGP OSPF Interaction
RFC1403.summary: RFC 1403 specifies design criteria for ASBRs running BGP externally and OSPF as IGP, defining route exchange rules, identifier matching, OSPF tag encoding mapped to BGP ORIGIN/AS_PATH, and forwarding address/NEXT_HOP handling.

BGP.why: The document specifies how BGP attributes (ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, INTER-AS METRIC) are set and how routes are exchanged with BGP at an ASBR.
BGP.quote: define the various criteria to be used when designing an Autonomous System Border Routers (ASBR) that will run BGP [RFC1267] with other ASBRs external to the AS

OSPF.why: The document defines usage of the OSPF external route tag, cost, type and forwarding address when interacting with BGP.
OSPF.quote: The OSPF external route tag is a "32-bit field attached to each external route
OSPF.section: 4. Setting OSPF tags, BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes

rejected.why: EGP routes are mentioned as an import source mapped to tag settings, but the document is not about EGP.
RIP is only mentioned as an IGP for which tags may be configured per interface.
The document is protocol-interaction specific, covered by the BGP and OSPF tags rather than general architecture.

RFC1404.title: A Model for Common Operational Statistics
RFC1404.summary: RFC 1404 describes a model for common operational statistics at NOCs, recommending SNMP MIB-based metrics, polling periods, aggregation, a storage file format, and report formats to let networks compare traffic and utilization data.

performance measurement.why: The document defines a minimal set of utilization, performance, availability and stability metrics, polling and aggregation practices, and reports for network operational statistics. This is network performance measurement and its methods.
performance measurement.quote: It gives recommendations for metrics, measurements, polling periods, storage formats and presentation formats.

rejected.why: SNMP is the collection mechanism the model relies on. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document selects existing MIB-II variables such as ifInOctets to poll. It defines no MIB module, and its MIB-related ideas are only future considerations.
This is the parent topic of performance measurement, so it is implied by the chosen tag.
The document covers counter polling and aggregation, not flow export or packet sampling.

RFC1405.title: Mapping between X.400(1984/1988) and Mail-11 (DECnet mail)
RFC1405.summary: Experimental RFC defining mappings between X.400 (1984/1988) O/R addresses and service elements and Mail-11 (DECnet Phase IV mail) addresses, including triangular cases with RFC822 gateways.

X.400.why: The document specifies X.400 to Mail-11 gateway mappings of O/R addresses and service elements, so it is about X.400 interworking.
X.400.quote: enable inter working between systems operating the CCITT X.400 ( 1984 / 1988 ) Recommendations on Message Handling Systems, and systems running the Mail-11

DECnet.why: Mail-11 is DECnet mail, and the mappings are defined within DECnet Phase IV addressing and routing, including DECnet network names and node names.

message format.why: A substantial part covers RFC822 address mapping to and from Mail-11 (Chapter 6 and Appendix A) and RFC822-style headers in the mapping.
message format.quote: Any eventual RFC822-like text header in Mail-11 body part will be interpreted as specified into RFC1327 and its updates.

rejected.why: Parent tag; the more specific X.400 and message format tags fit instead.
SMTP is only mentioned as an RFC822 transport and is not specified or profiled here.
Addresses are described as ASCII strings, but only incidentally.

gaps.name: Mail-11 / DECnet mail
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the Mail-11 mail protocol itself, which is the main subject. The DECnet tag is the closest fit but is imprecise.

RFC1406.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the DS1 and E1 Interface Types
RFC1406.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module for managing DS1 (T1) and E1 interfaces, with configuration, current/interval/total error-performance tables, far-end statistics and a fractional channel table; it obsoletes RFC 1232.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining managed objects for DS1/E1 interfaces, using the SMI and the extended OBJECT-TYPE macro.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the objects. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, and the MIB tag is the more specific fit.
ISDN Primary Rate appears only in an example comment about channel allocation. The document is not about ISDN access.
The error-event and performance-parameter definitions (ES, SES, UAS) are part of the MIB objects. They are not a general measurement methodology, and the MIB tag covers them.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB definitions.

gaps.name: DS1/T1/E1 digital transmission interfaces
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for T1/E1 physical line interfaces, framing (ESF/D4/G.704) or transmission-layer error performance. The document is mainly about managing these.

RFC1407.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the DS3/E3 Interface Type
RFC1407.summary: RFC 1407 defines an SNMP MIB module for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces (configuration, near-end and far-end performance statistics, fractional channel mapping), obsoleting RFC 1233.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification: it defines managed object tables for DS3/E3 interface configuration, current/interval/total statistics, far-end data, and fractional channels.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing DS3 and E3 Interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects. The document defines only a MIB module and does not specify or extend the protocol; MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the object definitions.
DS3/E3 are PDH interfaces, not SONET/SDH. The tag's scope is IP and multi-access protocols over SONET/SDH, which doesn't fit.
The statistics are interface error counters in a MIB. This is not a performance measurement methodology or metric framework.

gaps.name: DS3/E3 (T3/E3) transmission interfaces
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PDH/T-carrier physical-layer interface types such as DS1/DS3/E3. Readers browsing that subject would need a dedicated tag, and the closest option, MIB, covers only the management aspect.

RFC1408.title: Telnet Environment Option
RFC1408.summary: Specifies the Telnet ENVIRON option (option 36), which lets a Telnet client and server exchange environment variables such as USER, ACCT, DISPLAY and user-defined variables via SEND/IS/INFO subnegotiation.

Telnet.why: The document defines a new Telnet option, including its commands, negotiation rules and well-known variables. This is the core subject.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies a mechanism for passing environment information between a telnet client and server.

rejected.why: The DISPLAY variable carries an X display location, but the document only mentions it and does not specify X.
FTP is referenced only because SYSTEMTYPE reuses the value of the FTP SYST command.
Quoted strings are described as ASCII values in passing, but the document is not about ASCII.
The short security section only warns about which variables are safe to set before login. It is boilerplate-level and not the subject of the document.

RFC1409.title: Telnet Authentication Option
RFC1409.summary: Defines the experimental Telnet AUTHENTICATION option (option 37), a framework for negotiating and carrying authentication information (e.g., Kerberos) within a Telnet session so passwords are not sent in clear text.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its commands, negotiation rules and suboptions, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: The purpose of the AUTHENTICATION option is to provide a framework for the passing of authentication information through the TELNET session.

authentication.why: A substantial part of the document defines one-way and mutual client/server authentication modes and a negotiation of authentication types. It is a generic framework, not tied to one mechanism.
authentication.quote: AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL: The client will send authentication information about the local user to the server

rejected.why: Kerberos V4 and V5 appear as authentication types and in the example, but the document does not specify Kerberos. It only carries its data.
The document uses TCP open semantics only to define client and server. TCP is the substrate, not the subject.
This is a separate Telnet-specific negotiation framework, not SASL.
RSA is listed only as an authentication type code, and the document does not specify it.

RFC1410.title: IAB Official Protocol Standards
RFC1410.summary: RFC 1410 is the quarterly IAB Official Protocol Standards memo (STD 1), describing the Internet standards track, maturity and requirement levels, and listing every protocol by standardization state.

IETF process.why: The document's main body explains the standards track, maturity states, requirement levels, IESG/IAB roles and RFC processing decisions.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial part describes the RFC series, how RFCs are submitted, published and never revised, and the RFC Editor processing table.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned as the contact managing the standards list and Assigned Numbers is cited, but the document is not about IANA registries.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but these are process definitions rather than a glossary or requirements-language document.
It is a point-in-time status list, not a retrospective, even though many entries are historic.
TCP and many other protocols appear only as list entries; the document is not about any individual protocol.
Written by the IAB, but it covers standards status rather than architectural principles.

RFC1411.title: Telnet Authentication: Kerberos Version 4
RFC1411.summary: Defines the Kerberos Version 4 authentication type for the Telnet Authentication option, including AUTH, ACCEPT, REJECT, CHALLENGE and RESPONSE suboption commands for one-way and mutual authentication.

Telnet.why: The document specifies Telnet authentication option suboption commands and negotiation sequences. It is an extension of the Telnet protocol.
Telnet.quote: IAC SB AUTHENTICATION IS <authentication-type-pair> AUTH <kerberos ticket and authenticator> IAC SE

Kerberos.why: It specifies how Kerberos V4 tickets, session keys and principals (rcmd.host@realm) are used for Telnet authentication.
Kerberos.quote: This is used to pass the Kerberos ticket to the remote side of the connection.

rejected.why: Kerberos is the more specific tag for the authentication mechanism, and this document is not about authentication across protocols in general.
The document does not use GSS-API. It defines a direct Kerberos V4 exchange.

RFC1412.title: Telnet Authentication: SPX
RFC1412.summary: Defines the SPX authentication type for the Telnet Authentication option, including suboption commands (AUTH, REJECT, ACCEPT), mutual/one-way modes, and an example exchange.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a Telnet authentication option type, with its suboption commands and negotiation rules, so it belongs with the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: IAC SB AUTHENTICATION IS <authentication-type-pair> AUTH <SPX authentication token> IAC SE

authentication.why: The document defines an authentication mechanism with one-way and mutual authentication and key establishment. No more specific tag fits, since SPX is not in the taxonomy.
authentication.quote: After an SPX authentication exchange, both sides have securely established a random 8-byte key to be used as the default key for the ENCRYPTION option.

rejected.why: SPX is a different (DEC) authentication system. The document does not describe Kerberos.
GSS-API is not mentioned, and the token syntax is deferred to a future document.
The document only notes that a session key is established. It does not specify any key management mechanism.

gaps.name: SPX (DEC Sphinx) authentication
gaps.why: The document defines the SPX authentication mechanism for Telnet, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC1413.title: Identification Protocol
RFC1413.summary: RFC 1413 specifies the Identification Protocol (Ident), a TCP service on port 113 that returns the user identity owning a given TCP connection, obsoleting RFC 931.

Ident.why: The entire document specifies the Ident protocol: its query/response format, response types, error codes, and formal syntax.
Ident.quote: The Identification Protocol (a.k.a., "ident", a.k.a., "the Ident Protocol") provides a means to determine the identity of a user of a particular TCP connection.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport the protocol runs over; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Finger is mentioned only as an analogy for the privacy and identifier format, not addressed by the document.
The protocol was formerly named Authentication Server Protocol, but the document says it is not an authorization or access control mechanism and only provides auditing information.
Character set identifiers are used in the USERID response but are defined by Assigned Numbers; the document does not address character sets in their own right.
A formal syntax is given, but it is just the notation used to define the protocol, not the subject.

RFC1414.title: Identification MIB
RFC1414.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (ident, mib-2 24) exposing user identity information (OS type, charset, userid, misc) for TCP connections, roughly equivalent to the Ident protocol of RFC 1413.

MIB.why: The document's sole content is a MIB module with an identTable and its objects, defined using the SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a MIB for use with identifying the users associated with TCP connections.

Ident.why: The MIB is an SNMP-based alternative to the Identification Protocol, providing user identification for TCP connections; readers of the Ident subject would want it.
Ident.quote: It provides functionality approximately equivalent to that provided by the protocol defined in RFC 1413

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour.
TCP connections are indexed by the MIB (via MIB-II tcpConn objects) but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Finger is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a privacy analogy.
ASN.1 is just the notation for the MIB definitions, not the subject.
Privacy is discussed only in Security Considerations, not the main body.

RFC1415.title: FTP-FTAM Gateway Specification
RFC1415.summary: Specifies an application-layer gateway that translates interactively between FTP and OSI FTAM, with command/primitive mappings, state machines, naming/addressing, and reply-code to FTAM diagnostic mappings.

FTP.why: The document maps every FTP command and reply code to FTAM primitives and back, so it is about FTP and its interworking.
FTP.quote: performs protocol translation, in an interactive environment, between the FTP and FTAM file transfer protocols

rejected.why: X.500 Directory is used only to resolve Distinguished Names to Presentation addresses; it is not specified or profiled here.
DNS is used for name lookup by the gateway but is not the subject of the document.
The taxonomy tag is for OSI network-layer protocols; FTAM is an application-layer protocol, so it does not fit.
Telnet is mentioned only as the service FTP uses for its control connection.
Section 3 on naming and addressing is a small part of the document, not a main subject.

gaps.name: FTAM (File Transfer, Access and Management, ISO 8571)
gaps.why: The OSI file transfer protocol is half of the gateway mapping, and the taxonomy has no tag for it or for OSI application-layer protocols.

RFC1416.title: Telnet Authentication Option
RFC1416.summary: Defines the Telnet AUTHENTICATION option (experimental), a framework for negotiating and carrying authentication exchanges (e.g., Kerberos) within a Telnet session so passwords are not sent in clear text.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, including its commands, suboptions, negotiation rules and defaults, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: The purpose of the AUTHENTICATION option is to provide a framework for the passing of authentication information through the TELNET session.

authentication.why: The option is a generic framework for client-to-server, server-to-client and mutual authentication, with a negotiated list of mechanism types. Readers interested in authentication would want it.
authentication.quote: It is intended that the AUTHENTICATION option be general enough that it can be used to pass information for any authentication system.

rejected.why: Kerberos V4 and V5 are only listed as authentication types and used in the example. The document does not specify Kerberos itself.
TCP is only the substrate. The client and server roles are defined by passive versus active open.
The only IANA content is a note that additions to the authentication type list must be registered, which is boilerplate-level.
This is a different mechanism-negotiation framework, and the document does not discuss SASL.

RFC1417.title: NADF Standing Documents: A Brief Overview
RFC1417.summary: An overview of the North American Directory Forum's Standing Document series (SD-0 to SD-12), which define agreements for a cooperative public X.500 Directory Service offered by competing providers, plus how to obtain the documents.

X.500.why: The whole memo summarizes NADF agreements on naming, schema, DIT mapping, security and service for a public X.500 directory, so it belongs on the X.500 subject page.
X.500.quote: plans to cooperatively offer a Public Directory Service in North America using the CCITT X.500 Recommendations

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the X.500 tag, so it is not listed separately.
Anonymous FTP is only named as one way to fetch the documents, so the memo is not about FTP.
Email is only listed as a way to request the documents, and the memo does not address it.
The standing documents SD-5 and SD-6 cover X.500 DIT naming, but this memo only summarizes them in a few sentences. The naming is specific to X.500 and is covered by the X.500 tag.

RFC1418.title: SNMP over OSI
RFC1418.summary: Defines how to run SNMP over the OSI connectionless-mode transport service (CLTS), specifying transport selectors, trap addressing, and minimum message size.

SNMP.why: The document specifies a mapping of SNMP onto a different transport, including selectors, trap handling and message size. SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: This memo addresses these concerns by defining a framework for running the SNMP in an environment which supports the OSI connectionless-mode transport service.

transport mapping.why: It is a transport mapping that carries one protocol over another transport (SNMP over the OSI CLTS).
transport mapping.quote: Mapping the SNMP onto the CLTS [7,8] is straight-forward. The elements of procedure are identical to that of using the UDP.

OSI.why: A substantial part of the document concerns OSI transport addressing, with selectors in place of ports, and CLNS/CONS realizations of the CLTS.
OSI.quote: it is necessary define four selectors for this purpose.

rejected.why: UDP is only the reference mapping that the document contrasts with. The document does not specify or extend it.
The MIB and SMI are only mentioned as companion standards. The document defines no MIB content.
The CLNS is mentioned as a preferred network service for realizing the CLTS. The document does not specify CLNP.

RFC1419.title: SNMP over AppleTalk
RFC1419.summary: Specifies how SNMP messages are carried in AppleTalk DDP datagrams (sockets 8 and 9, protocol type 8), with NBP-based agent/trap-handler advertisement and guidance on NBP name-to-address caching.

SNMP.why: The document defines a new transport mapping for SNMP requests, responses and traps, including agent and trap-handler advertisement and addressing rules.
SNMP.quote: the method by which the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) as specified in [1] can be used over AppleTalk protocols [2] instead of the Internet UDP/IP protocol stack

AppleTalk.why: The specification is built on AppleTalk DDP and NBP, and much of the document covers AppleTalk addressing, NBP naming and lookup caching.
AppleTalk.quote: SNMP REQUESTS encapsulated according to this standard will be sent to DDP socket number 8; they will contain a DDP protocol type of 8.

rejected.why: The document is a transport mapping, but the SNMP and AppleTalk tags are more specific. The topic tag is not needed alongside them.
The AppleTalk MIB (RFC 1243) is only referenced for the nbpEntry variables included in traps. The document defines no MIB.
UDP is mentioned only as the stack that this specification replaces. The document does not specify or analyse UDP.
NBP name binding is discussed as part of the AppleTalk mapping. It is not a general naming subject.

RFC1420.title: SNMP over IPX
RFC1420.summary: Defines how SNMP messages are encapsulated in Novell IPX datagrams, including packet type, socket assignments, trap handling and maximum message size.

SNMP.why: The document specifies a new transport mapping for SNMP, including socket assignments for requests and traps and trap agent-addr handling. SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: This document defines a convention for encapsulating Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) [1] packets over the transport mechanism provided via the Internetwork Packet Exchange (IPX) protocol [2].

IPX.why: The document specifies how IPX is used to carry SNMP: packet type 4, sockets 0x900F and 0x9010, and the 546-byte maximum message size. It is IPX interworking material.
IPX.quote: This specification describes the mapping of SNMP onto the Internetwork Packet Exchange (IPX) protocol [2] used in Novell NetWare environments.

rejected.why: This is a transport-mapping document, but the SNMP and IPX tags are more specific and already cover it. The generic topic is not needed.
UDP is only cited as the preferred SNMP mapping that this one parallels. The document does not specify or extend UDP.
The SMI and MIB are cited as companion standards only. The document defines no MIB module.

RFC1421.title: Privacy Enhancement for Internet Electronic Mail: Part I: Message Encryption and Authentication Procedures
RFC1421.summary: RFC 1421 specifies Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) message encryption and authentication procedures for RFC-822 email, including message transformations, encapsulation, header fields and key management constructs.

PEM.why: The document is the core specification of PEM: processing, encapsulation, header fields and key identifiers.
PEM.quote: This document defines message encryption and authentication procedures, in order to provide privacy-enhanced mail (PEM) services for electronic mail transfer in the Internet.

email.why: Defines end-to-end security processing for Internet mail at the UA level, including mailing list handling and canonicalization for SMTP transport.
email.quote: The current specification's scope is confined to PEM processing procedures for the RFC-822 textual mail environment

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport constraint the encoding works around; no SMTP changes are specified.
Certificates are used but defined in RFC 1422; this document only carries them in header fields.
A printable encoding is defined (Section 4.3.2.4), but as an internal step of PEM rather than a general data encoding specification.
Section 5 describes DEKs and IKs, but detailed key management is delegated to RFC 1422.
The encapsulated headers are PEM-specific and explicitly disjoint from RFC 822 header fields.
Algorithms are specified in RFC 1423, not here; DES appears only in examples.

RFC1422.title: Privacy Enhancement for Internet Electronic Mail: Part II: Certificate-Based Key Management
RFC1422.summary: RFC 1422 specifies the certificate-based key management architecture for Privacy Enhanced Mail, defining an X.509-compatible hierarchy (IPRA, PCAs, CAs), certificate and CRL formats, and validation procedures.

PEM.why: The document is part II of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series, defining the key management infrastructure that PEM relies on.
PEM.quote: This document defines a supporting key management architecture and infrastructure, based on public-key certificate techniques, to provide keying information to message originators and recipients.

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificates and CRLs for the Internet, including ASN.1 syntax, validity, and validation procedures.
X.509.quote: The key management architecture described in this document is compatible with the authentication framework described in CCITT 1988 X.509

PKI.why: It defines a certification hierarchy (IPRA, PCAs, CAs), registration, revocation, and validation: a full PKI architecture.
PKI.quote: The infrastructure specified in this document establishes a single root for all certification within the Internet, the Internet Policy Registration Authority (IPRA).

rejected.why: X.500 DNs and directories are used for naming and CRL storage but the document is not about the directory service itself.
RSA is mentioned as the anticipated signature algorithm and in licensing, but algorithms are specified in RFC 1423.
ASN.1 is only used to define certificate and CRL syntax in the appendix.
Email is the application context; the document is about key management, not mail transport or format.

RFC1423.title: Privacy Enhancement for Internet Electronic Mail: Part III: Algorithms, Modes, and Identifiers
RFC1423.summary: RFC 1423 specifies the cryptographic algorithms, modes (DES-CBC, DES-ECB, DES-EDE), message digests (MD2, MD5), RSA key and signature usage, and identifiers used by Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM).

PEM.why: The document is Part III of the PEM RFC set, defining algorithm identifiers and header-field parameters for PEM messages.
PEM.quote: definitions, formats, references, and citations for cryptographic algorithms, usage modes, and associated identifiers and parameters used in support of Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM)

DES.why: Substantial parts specify DES-CBC, DES-ECB and DES-EDE modes, padding, key parity and IV handling.
DES.quote: Message text and, if required, message signatures are encrypted using the Data Encryption Standard (DES) algorithm in the Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode of operation.

MD5.why: Defines MD5 and MD2 (RSA-MD2) as MIC algorithms with identifiers, OIDs and encoding for PEM.
MD5.quote: The RSA-MD5 message digest is computed using the algorithm defined in RFC 1321

RSA.why: Specifies RSA key constraints, RSAEncryption block formatting and md2WithRSAEncryption signatures for PEM.
RSA.quote: The RSAEncryption public-key encryption algorithm, defined in PKCS #1 [11], is used for DEK and MIC encryption when asymmetric key management is employed.

rejected.why: Certificates and the SIGNED macro are referenced for algorithm identifiers, but certificate profiling is in RFC 1422, not here.
Object identifiers and AlgorithmIdentifier are used for identification only; the document is not about ASN.1.
PEM is the more specific tag; this document concerns only algorithms, not mail transport or format.
Symmetric and asymmetric key management algorithms are defined, but only as algorithm choices for PEM, and RSA/DES tags cover them.
Certificate-based key management is in RFC 1422; this document only names signature algorithms for certificates and CRLs.

RFC1424.title: Privacy Enhancement for Internet Electronic Mail: Part IV: Key Certification and Related Services
RFC1424.summary: RFC 1424 specifies PEM key certification, CRL storage and CRL retrieval services, using email requests and replies in RFC 1421 privacy-enhanced message syntax.

PEM.why: The document is Part IV of the PEM specification suite. It defines certification and CRL services and the message syntax for them, all inside PEM.
PEM.quote: This document describes three types of service in support of Internet Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM) [1-3]: key certification, certificate-revocation list (CRL) storage, and CRL retrieval.

PKI.why: It covers certification authority services: certificate requests, certification paths, and CRL storage and retrieval. Readers of PKI would want it.
PKI.quote: The key-certification service signs a certificate containing a specified subject name and public key.

rejected.why: Certificates and CRLs are used, but the document does not specify or profile X.509. It defers to RFC 1422 for that.
Email only carries the requests and replies. The document does not define mail transport or formats.
The messages use RFC 1421 syntax with a new process type. That is PEM syntax, not the Internet message format of RFC 822.
RSA appears only in example MIC-Info fields and in the patent statement. The document is not about the algorithm.

RFC1425.title: SMTP Service Extensions
RFC1425.summary: RFC 1425 defines the SMTP service extension framework: the EHLO command, an IANA registry of extensions and EHLO keywords, optional parameters on MAIL FROM and RCPT TO, and the ESMTP Received clause.

SMTP.why: The whole document extends SMTP with the EHLO command, an extension registry and MAIL FROM/RCPT TO parameters. SMTP is the protocol being specified, so this is the primary tag.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines a framework for extending the SMTP service by defining a means whereby a server SMTP can inform a client SMTP as to the service extensions it supports.

rejected.why: RFC 822 headers and the Received: field annotation are mentioned, but only briefly. The document does not define message format.
MIME appears only as a reference for body structure, and the 8BITMIME keyword appears only in an example. The document does not specify either.
The IANA registry is part of the extension mechanism, but the document is about SMTP extensions and not IANA registry guidance in general.
The more specific SMTP tag applies, so the parent is not listed.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax definitions.

RFC1426.title: SMTP Service Extension for 8bit-MIMEtransport
RFC1426.summary: Defines the 8BITMIME SMTP service extension, which adds a BODY=7BIT/8BITMIME parameter to MAIL FROM so MIME messages with 8-bit octets can be relayed over SMTP.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension: the 8BITMIME EHLO keyword, the BODY parameter on MAIL FROM, and server/client behavior.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby an SMTP content body containing octets outside of the US ASCII octet range

MIME.why: The extension exists to transport 8-bit MIME bodies, and it constrains the downgrade conversion to valid 7bit MIME using transport encodings.
MIME.quote: a significant portion of the Internet community wishes to exchange messages in which the content body consists of a MIME message [3]

rejected.why: RFC 822 header and format rules are referenced only for context; the document changes transport behavior, not message format.
The US ASCII octet range is only the boundary for 7-bit versus 8-bit content. The document is not about ASCII itself.
ABNF is used only to write the body-value syntax, which is incidental notation.
SMTP is the more specific tag and already implies email.

RFC1427.title: SMTP Service Extension for Message Size Declaration
RFC1427.summary: Defines the SMTP SIZE service extension, letting a client declare message size in MAIL FROM and a server advertise its maximum size in EHLO so oversized messages can be refused before transfer.

SMTP.why: The whole document specifies an SMTP service extension: the SIZE EHLO keyword, the extended MAIL FROM parameter, and the related reply-code behaviour.
SMTP.quote: an extension to the SMTP service whereby an SMTP client and server may interact to give the server an opportunity to decline to accept a message

rejected.why: MIME is mentioned only as the motivation for larger messages. The document does not specify or extend MIME.
The message size definition refers to message content, but the document does not address header or addressing format.
TCP port 25 appears only in the example. TCP is just the substrate.

RFC1428.title: Transition of Internet Mail from Just-Send-8 to 8bit-SMTP/MIME
RFC1428.summary: Informational memo on transitioning from ad-hoc 8-bit SMTP mail to 8bit-ESMTP/MIME, describing gateway upgrade of non-MIME 8bit messages and defining the "unknown-8bit" charset label.

SMTP.why: The document is about transition between ad-hoc 8-bit SMTP and 8bit ESMTP, including gateway behaviour between the two.
SMTP.quote: Protocols for extending SMTP to pass 8bit characters have been defined [3] [4].

MIME.why: It specifies how gateways add MIME-Version, Content-Type and Content-Transfer-Encoding headers and defines the unknown-8bit charset parameter.
MIME.quote: A gateway which has been upgraded to support Extended SMTP may upgrade an 8bit message received to MIME.
MIME.section: 3. Upgrade Path from 8bit Transparent to ESMTP/MIME

character sets.why: It defines a new charset label and discusses handling of ISO 8859, ISO 646 and ISO 2022 character sets in mail.
character sets.quote: A special purpose character set called "unknown-8bit" is defined to be an unknown 8bit character set, encoded into a sequence of octets.

rejected.why: RFC 822 header encoding under RFC 1342 is mentioned only as part of the upgrade; the document is not about message format.
It is a general parent. The more specific SMTP and MIME tags fit better.
US-ASCII is the baseline limitation discussed, not the subject of the document.
This concerns 8-bit body content and charsets, not internationalized email addresses.

RFC1429.title: Listserv Distribute Protocol
RFC1429.summary: Informational RFC describing the BITNET LISTSERV DISTRIBUTE protocol, a job-card based request format that lets non-BITNET mailing list exploders hand a message and recipient list to a LISTSERV server for efficient bulk mail delivery.

mailing lists.why: The document specifies the DISTRIBUTE protocol used by LISTSERV to deliver mailing list traffic to large recipient sets, and how list exploders use it.
mailing lists.quote: a simple solution to the "sendmail" turnaround problem is to wrap the message and recipient list in a DISTRIBUTE envelope and pass it to a BITNET server for delivery

rejected.why: SMTP is only the convenient transport for submitting the request; the document does not specify or extend it.
RFC822 headers are required in the submitted message, but the document is not about the message format itself.
Parent of the more specific mailing lists tag; the document is specifically about bulk list distribution, so the child is chosen.

gaps.name: BITNET / LISTSERV
gaps.why: The document is about the BITNET LISTSERV bulk distribution service, but the taxonomy has no BITNET or LISTSERV tag; mailing lists is the closest fit.

RFC1430.title: A Strategic Plan for Deploying an Internet X.500 Directory Service
RFC1430.summary: Informational strategic plan for deploying a global Internet Directory Service based on OSI X.500, covering information framework, naming, infrastructure, data management, technical issues, security, and relation to DNS.

X.500.why: The whole document is a strategy for deploying an X.500-based directory service on the Internet, covering DSAs, DUAs, the DIT, schema, replication and naming.
X.500.quote: It is proposed to establish an Internet Directory Service based on X.500.

rejected.why: LDAP is mentioned only briefly as a lightweight protocol the OSI-DS WG is working on. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Section 9 only notes the relationship to DNS and RFC 1279's mapping of DNS information onto the Directory. DNS is not the subject.
PEM and X.509 certificate storage are discussed as an application of the directory's authentication role. The document is not about PEM.
X.509 strong authentication is discussed in Section 8.1 as a directory service. The certificate format and profile are not specified here.
This is the parent of X.500, so the more specific X.500 tag is used instead.

RFC1431.title: DUA Metrics (OSI-DS 33 (v2))
RFC1431.summary: RFC 1431 defines a questionnaire-style set of metrics, with point scores, for evaluating X.500 Directory user agent (DUA) user interfaces, especially white pages DUAs.

X.500.why: The whole document evaluates X.500 Directory user agents: DAP use, DIT structure, schema, DSA associations, referrals and query resolution. A reader browsing X.500 would want it.
X.500.quote: This document defines a set of criteria by which a DUA implementation, or more precisely a Directory user interface, may be judged.

rejected.why: LDAP is only listed as one option for how a DUA user interface talks to a DUA server. The document is not about it.
The parent is implied by X.500, so it is not listed separately.
The SearchStones measure counts operations used per query. It is a scoring questionnaire for user interfaces, not a benchmarking methodology for network devices.

RFC1432.title: Recent Internet Books
