RFC1432.summary: An annotated bibliography of recent books about using the Internet and other networks (user guides, standards, NREN policy, hacking/cracking, resource guides), reprinted from Matrix News.

user guides.why: The memo is a guide to introductory books and resources for Internet users, which fits the user guides subject. It is a bibliography for newcomers.
user guides.quote: Here is a list of books related to using the Internet, which is the global and exponentially growing network of more than a million computers

rejected.why: A few listed books are histories, but the memo is a book list and not a history.
It mentions two books that describe the IETF standards process. That is a minor part of a bibliography.
Anonymous FTP is only the way to retrieve further information. The memo is not about the protocol.
The hacking and cracking books are only listed. The memo does not address security practice.
Email is mentioned only as the service that connects the wider Matrix of networks.

RFC1433.title: Directed ARP
RFC1433.summary: Defines Directed ARP, an experimental procedure by which hosts and routers resolve next-hop IP addresses on foreign IP networks sharing the same link level network, using a router-supplied ARP Helper Address, and describes its use with ICMP Redirects, distance-vector and link-state routing.

ARP.why: The document specifies an extension of ARP, with request forwarding, helper addresses and filtering procedures.
ARP.quote: Directed ARP is a dynamic address resolution procedure that enables hosts and routers to resolve advertised potential next-hop IP addresses on foreign IP networks

ICMP.why: A substantial section extends the use of ICMP Redirects to foreign next-hops via Directed ARP.
ICMP.quote: If a router forwards a packet to a next-hop address that is on the same link level network as the host that originated the packet, the router may send an ICMP Redirect

rejected.why: SMDS is only an example link level network; the procedure is not specific to it.
BGP is cited as an example distance-vector protocol that can advertise foreign next-hops, but is not specified or extended.
OSPF is the example for link-state SPF modifications, but the document describes generic link-state handling rather than extending OSPF itself.
Routing interactions are discussed, but the core subject is address resolution, not routing architecture.

RFC1434.title: Data Link Switching: Switch-to-Switch Protocol
RFC1434.summary: Informational RFC documenting IBM's Data Link Switching Switch-to-Switch Protocol (SSP), which terminates LLC2/SDLC locally and multiplexes SNA and NetBIOS circuits over TCP between DLS routers, including frame formats, message types and state machines.

DLSw.why: The whole document specifies the DLS Switch-to-Switch Protocol: SSP frame formats, message types, circuit establishment and the DLS state machine.
DLSw.quote: Data Link Switching (DLS) is a forwarding mechanism for the IBM SNA and IBM NetBIOS protocols.

NetBIOS.why: A substantial part covers NetBIOS-specific SSP messages (NETBIOS_NQ, NETBIOS_NR, ANQ/ANR), name resolution and NetBIOS datagram handling (Section 4.3).
NetBIOS.quote: For NetBIOS systems, Data Link Switching uses the NetBIOS name to forward datagrams and to set up connections for NetBIOS sessions.

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable transport used between switches; the document defines nothing new about TCP beyond default port numbers.
DLSw is a child of SNA and is the more specific tag. SNA is the traffic being carried, so the parent is implied rather than listed separately.
Token-ring LANs are the attached media, but the document is not about IP over token ring.
Carrying LLC connections over TCP is implied by DLSw. The document is about the full switching protocol, not just a binding to TCP.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.2 LLC / SDLC data link control
gaps.why: The document centres on terminating LLC Type 2 and SDLC locally and spoofing acknowledgments, but the taxonomy has no tag for LLC or SDLC.

RFC1435.title: IESG Advice from Experience with Path MTU Discovery
RFC1435.summary: IESG advice that routers with ICMP suppression enabled should still send ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (fragmentation needed, DF set) so Path MTU Discovery works without harming older BSD hosts.

PMTUD.why: The whole memo is operational advice on deploying Path MTU Discovery, addressing a failure mode caused by suppressed ICMP messages.
PMTUD.quote: adjusting the routers to continue to send ICMP message Type 3 code 4 (destination unreachable, don't fragment (DF) bit sent and fragmentation required)
PMTUD.section: Advice on the Deployment of Path MTU Discovery Protocol

ICMP.why: The memo's recommendation concerns router generation of a specific ICMP message (Type 3 Code 4) and its suppression, which ICMP readers would want.
ICMP.quote: some vendors have added to their routers the ability to disable ICMP messages generated by the router
ICMP.section: Advice on the Deployment of Path MTU Discovery Protocol

rejected.why: Only the IPv4 DF bit and fragmentation are mentioned incidentally; the document is not about IPv4 itself.
The memo is an operational deployment note, not about security practices; Security Considerations says nothing.

RFC1436.title: The Internet Gopher Protocol (a distributed document search and retrieval protocol)
RFC1436.summary: RFC 1436 specifies the Internet Gopher protocol, a simple TCP-based client-server protocol for distributed document search and retrieval using hierarchical menus, selectors, and item types.

Gopher.why: The whole document specifies the Gopher protocol: its model, item types, transactions and grammar.
Gopher.quote: The Internet Gopher protocol is designed for distributed document search and retrieval.

rejected.why: TCP is only the assumed reliable transport for Gopher; the document specifies nothing new about TCP.
WAIS is mentioned only as a gateway target for search servers, not specified here.
X.500 and the CSO phonebook are mentioned only as services that item types can point to.
DNS CNAMEs are recommended for server naming, but this is a minor aside rather than a subject of the document.
Telnet is mentioned for debugging and as item type 8, not specified.
The appendix uses an informal BNF variant to describe the Gopher grammar. This only describes the protocol and is not about the notation.

RFC1437.title: The Extension of MIME Content-Types to a New Medium
RFC1437.summary: An April 1st parody RFC defining a MIME content-type, matter-transport/sentient-life-form, for emailing human beings as molecular readouts, with jokes about X.400 gateways and implementation hazards.

humor.why: A 1 April parody RFC whose whole premise is transporting living beings, including politicians, by email. Readers of the humor page would expect it.
humor.quote: This document defines one particular type of MIME data, the matter-transport/sentient-life-form type.

MIME.why: The joke is built as a new MIME top-level type and subtype. It has parameters and a content-transfer-encoding discussion, so MIME readers would find it relevant.
MIME.quote: this document defines a new MIME content-type, "matter-transport", and for an initial subtype, "sentient-life-form".

rejected.why: There is a short gateway-considerations section, but the document is not about X.400 or interworking with it.
The syntax is said to be SGML-compatible, but only as a passing design criterion.
It defines a fictional type but does not register it or deal with registry rules.
Email is only the transport for the joke. MIME is the more specific tag, and the document does not address email architecture.
Molecule formulas are rendered in ASCII, which is a minor incidental use.
NFS appears only in a joke in the implementation considerations.

RFC1438.title: Internet Engineering Task Force Statements Of Boredom (SOBs)
RFC1438.summary: An April Fools' RFC that parodies the IETF standards process by creating a fictitious subseries of "Statements Of Boredom" (SOBs) that carry no useful information.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody of the IETF standards process and the RFC series, so it belongs on the humorous RFCs page.
humor.quote: This document creates a new subseries of RFCs, entitled, IETF Statements Of Boredom (SOBs).

rejected.why: The document mocks the IETF process but specifies no real procedure. The humor tag fits better.
It satirically proposes a new RFC subseries, but it is a joke and not a real statement about RFC series format or publication.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as a joke, as a translation step in the fictitious review process.

RFC1439.title: The Uniqueness of Unique Identifiers
RFC1439.summary: Informational memo analysing how likely duplicate user identifiers are under common name-derived formats, using birthday-problem probabilities, plus notes on identifier reuse and privacy.

rejected.why: Email is the motivating use (predicting addresses from names), but the document is about user identifier uniqueness, not email architecture or transport.
Local-part naming is touched on, but the document does not specify headers or addressing syntax.
This is about account/user-name assignment for people, not naming and name resolution systems; considered but too loose a fit.
The appendix briefly notes misdelivered mail and reuse of identifiers, but this is a minor aside, not a privacy threat model or protocol privacy considerations.
Concerns unique identifiers in a general sense, but UUID is a specific format and the document deals with human-name-derived user names.

gaps.name: user names / account identifier assignment
gaps.why: The document's whole subject is choosing unique user or account identifiers for people and estimating collision probability. The taxonomy has no tag for user identifiers or account naming.

RFC1440.title: SIFT/UFT: Sender-Initiated/Unsolicited File Transfer
RFC1440.summary: Defines SIFT/UFT, an experimental TCP (port 608) protocol for sender-initiated, unsolicited file transfer with a command set, representation types, and an optional MIME-carried mode.

applications.why: The document specifies a new application-layer file transfer protocol. No specific file-transfer tag fits: FTP is only a contrast and reference, so the generic applications topic is the best match.
applications.quote: We define sender-initiated file transfer for IP as a TCP service as follows: a receiver program (the server or "daemon") listens on port 608

rejected.why: UFT is contrasted with traditional file transfer and FTP is only cited as a reference. The document does not specify or extend FTP.
MIME is an optional alternative transport, with UFT commands carried as Content-Type parameters. The document does not define MIME itself.
TCP is only the substrate the protocol runs over.
The document argues that email is unsuited to file transfer. Mail is only an optional envelope for UFT.
BASE64 is mentioned only as the encoding used when UFT is carried over mail.
The document uses application/octet-stream but does not register a media type.

gaps.name: file transfer
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an FTP tag but no general file-transfer tag. SIFT/UFT is a distinct file transfer protocol that readers browsing file transfer would expect to find.

RFC1441.title: Introduction to version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework
RFC1441.summary: Overview document for SNMPv2, the second version of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, describing its components: SMI, textual conventions, protocol operations, transport mappings, MIB instrumentation, administrative framework and conformance statements.

SNMP.why: The whole document introduces the SNMPv2 framework and its protocol, operations, transport mappings and administrative/security model, so the SNMP page is the right home.
SNMP.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide an overview of version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, termed the SNMP version 2 framework (SNMPv2).

MIB.why: A substantial part covers the SMI, textual conventions, MIB modules, protocol-instrumentation MIBs and conformance statements, which are MIB/SMI subject matter.
MIB.quote: Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects, residing in a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base (MIB).

rejected.why: MIB modules are written in a subset of ASN.1 and the SMI uses ASN.1 macros, but ASN.1 is only the notation substrate here, not the subject.
The document says the UDP mapping is preferred, but that is a passing mention of a transport; it does not specify or analyse UDP.
This is the parent topic of SNMP, so it is implied and should not be listed alongside the more specific tag.
Section 2.4 only summarises the separate Transport Mappings document in a short paragraph, so this is not a substantial part of the RFC.

RFC1442.title: Structure of Management Information for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1442.summary: RFC 1442 defines the SNMPv2 Structure of Management Information (SMI): the ASN.1 subset, macros (MODULE-IDENTITY, OBJECT-TYPE, NOTIFICATION-TYPE, OBJECT-IDENTITY), data types and rules for writing MIB modules.

MIB.why: The document is the SMI itself, defining how MIB modules and managed objects are written, including the macros, syntaxes, tables and naming rules.
MIB.quote: Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules.  These modules are written using a subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1)

SNMP.why: It is a core part of the SNMPv2 framework, covering notifications (traps/informs) and SNMPv2 agent behaviour at the SMI level.
SNMP.quote: The current framework is termed the SNMP version 2 framework (SNMPv2).

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation the SMI subsets and uses; the document is about management information structure, not ASN.1 modules or encoding rules generally.
Parent of the chosen tags, so it is implied.

RFC1443.title: Textual Conventions for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1443.summary: RFC 1443 defines the initial set of SNMPv2 textual conventions (DisplayString, RowStatus, TruthValue, DateAndTime, etc.) and the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION ASN.1 macro used by MIB modules.

MIB.why: The document defines the SNMPv2-TC MIB module and the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro, core SMI/MIB infrastructure that MIB authors use.
MIB.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules.

SNMP.why: Part of the SNMPv2 framework. RowStatus describes row creation and deletion semantics via SNMP set operations and error codes.
SNMP.quote: SNMPv2-TC DEFINITIONS ::= BEGIN

rejected.why: ASN.1 macro notation is the substrate for the definitions; the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules in general.
DateAndTime is one textual convention among many and is SNMP-specific, not a general timestamp format.
DisplayString references NVT ASCII only incidentally.
The more specific MIB and SNMP tags already cover it.

RFC1444.title: Conformance Statements for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1444.summary: Defines the SNMPv2-CONF ASN.1 macros (OBJECT-GROUP, MODULE-COMPLIANCE, AGENT-CAPABILITIES) used to write conformance groups, compliance statements and agent capability statements for SNMPv2 MIB modules.

MIB.why: The document defines SMI macros for conformance in MIB modules (object groups, compliance, agent capabilities). Readers of MIB/SMI would look for it.
MIB.quote: The MODULE-COMPLIANCE macro is used to convey a minimum set of requirements with respect to implementation of one or more MIB modules.

SNMP.why: It is part of the SNMPv2 framework and specifies how agents describe their implementation level, so SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: The AGENT-CAPABILITIES macro is used to convey the capabilities present in a SNMPv2 entity acting in an agent role.

rejected.why: ASN.1 macro notation is the substrate used to write the definitions; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Not related; this is SMIv2-era conformance, not YANG modelling.

RFC1445.title: Administrative Model for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1445.summary: RFC 1445 defines the SNMPv2 administrative model (parties, contexts, MIB views, proxy relationships, access control policy, and message processing procedures) with example configurations.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the SNMPv2 administrative framework: parties, contexts, access control, procedures for generating and processing SNMPv2 messages, and proxy configurations. This is SNMP framework and security content.
SNMP.quote: It is the purpose of this document, the Administrative Model for SNMPv2, to define how the administrative framework is applied to realize effective network management

rejected.why: MIB views and view subtrees are discussed, but the document defines no MIB module. The Party MIB is a separate RFC.
ASN.1 syntax is used only to describe the model's data structures, not as the subject.
Authentication and privacy protocols are referenced as pluggable parameters. They are specified in RFC 1446, and this document only places them in the party model.
UDP serves only as the transport in the examples.

RFC1446.title: Security Protocols for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1446.summary: Defines the SNMPv2 Digest Authentication Protocol (MD5-based) and Symmetric Privacy Protocol (DES-CBC), plus clock and secret distribution procedures, as the security protocols for the SNMPv2 party-based administrative model.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies security protocols for SNMPv2: message authentication, privacy, clock synchronization and secret distribution between agents and management stations.
SNMP.quote: It is the purpose of this document, Security Protocols for SNMPv2, to define one such authentication and one such privacy protocol.

MD5.why: The digest authentication protocol is specified with MD5 as the mandatory algorithm (v2md5AuthProtocol), including key and digest sizes.
MD5.quote: In support of data integrity, the use of the MD5 [3] message digest algorithm is chosen.

DES.why: The privacy protocol is specified with DES-CBC (desPrivProtocol), with key/IV layout and padding rules.
DES.quote: the use of the Data Encryption Standard (DES) in the Cipher Block Chaining mode of operation is chosen.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define message structures, not the subject.
Clock synchronization is a mechanism internal to the protocol and explicitly independent of NTP.
Secret distribution is described but as one part of the SNMPv2 security protocols, so SNMP covers it.
The generic topic is subsumed by the SNMP tag for this protocol-specific document.

RFC1447.title: Party MIB for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1447.summary: RFC 1447 defines the SNMPv2 Party MIB module, with managed objects for SNMPv2 parties, contexts, access control policy (ACL) and MIB views, plus initial default assignments and conformance statements.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SNMPv2-PARTY-MIB) defining tables for parties, contexts, ACLs and views using the SMI.
MIB.quote: It is the purpose of this document, the Party MIB for SNMPv2, to define managed objects which correspond to these properties.

SNMP.why: It specifies the SNMPv2 administrative framework objects: parties, authentication/privacy protocol assignments, access control and views, which are core to SNMPv2 security and administration.
SNMP.quote: The Administrative Model for SNMPv2 document [3] defines the properties associated with SNMPv2 parties, SNMPv2 contexts, and access control policies.

rejected.why: desPrivProtocol is only referenced as an identifier for a privacy protocol defined elsewhere (RFC 1446).
v2md5AuthProtocol is only an OID assignment; the algorithm is specified in another document.
ASN.1/SMI is merely the notation in which the MIB is written.
The ACL table is part of the SNMPv2 MIB, already covered by the SNMP tag; no separate general authorization subject is addressed.

RFC1448.title: Protocol Operations for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1448.summary: RFC 1448 specifies the protocol operations of SNMPv2: the PDU types (Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set, Response, Trap, Inform), their ASN.1 definitions and the elements of procedure for processing them.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies SNMPv2 PDU processing, including GetBulk, Set, Trap and Inform, so it belongs on the SNMP page. It defines the protocol itself, not a MIB module.
SNMP.quote: It is the purpose of this document, Protocol Operations for SNMPv2, to define the operations of the protocol with respect to the sending and receiving of the PDUs.

rejected.why: MIB modules and the SMI are mentioned and used in the table-traversal examples. The document does not define any MIB module.
The PDUs are defined in an ASN.1 module, but ASN.1 is only the notation used. The document is not about ASN.1.
UDP is named as the preferred transport mapping, but it is only the substrate. Transport mappings are specified in another document.

RFC1449.title: Transport Mappings for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1449.summary: Defines how SNMPv2 messages map onto UDP, OSI, AppleTalk DDP and IPX transports, with a proxy domain for SNMPv1 and BER serialization rules.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies SNMPv2 transport mappings, textual conventions and proxy to SNMPv1, so it belongs under SNMP.
SNMP.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define how the SNMPv2 maps onto an initial set of transport domains.

AppleTalk.why: A substantial section covers the DDP mapping and NBP name-to-address handling in AppleTalk.
AppleTalk.quote: SNMPv2 messages are sent using DDP protocol type 8.

IPX.why: Defines the IPX transport mapping, addresses and sockets for SNMPv2.
IPX.quote: SNMPv2 messages are sent using IPX packet type 4 (i.e., Packet Exchange Packet).

OSI.why: Defines the OSI CLTS/CONS mapping and OSI address format for SNMPv2.
OSI.quote: Each instance of a message is serialized onto a single TSDU [3,4] for the OSI Connectionless-mode Transport Service

rejected.why: UDP is the preferred substrate but the document defines no new UDP behaviour beyond ports and addressing.
BER serialization rules are given, but the document is about SNMPv2 transport, not ASN.1 itself.
The topic fits, but the SNMP tag covers it more specifically; the tech tags already chosen sit under other parents.
Contains a small SMI module of textual conventions, but the document is not about MIB content.

RFC1450.title: Management Information Base for version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1450.summary: Defines the SNMPv2-MIB module: managed objects for SNMPv2 entity statistics, SNMPv1 statistics, object resources, traps, and the set serialization lock, with conformance groups.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SNMPv2-MIB) written in the SMI, defining objects, notifications, compliance statements and groups for SNMPv2 entities.
MIB.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define managed objects which describe the behavior of a SNMPv2 entity.

SNMP.why: The objects instrument SNMPv2 protocol behaviour itself (packet counts, authentication failures, traps, set coordination), so SNMP readers would want it. The MIB tag is the more specific home, but this document is also about SNMPv2 operation.
SNMP.quote: The management protocol, SNMPv2 [3], provides for the exchange of messages which convey management information between the agents and the management stations.

rejected.why: The MIB module is written in an ASN.1 subset via the SMI, but ASN.1 is only the notation and not the subject.
The egpNeighborLoss trap and egpNeighAddr are imported or defined for completeness, but EGP is not the subject.
The more specific SNMP and MIB tags already sit beneath it.

RFC1451.title: Manager-to-Manager Management Information Base
RFC1451.summary: RFC 1451 defines the SNMPv2 Manager-to-Manager MIB module, with alarm, event and notification tables that let one management station request threshold monitoring and event reporting from another.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SNMPv2-M2M-MIB) defining alarm, event and notification tables in SMI. MIB is the most specific tag, and SNMP is its parent so it is implied.
MIB.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define managed objects which describe the behavior of a SNMPv2 entity acting in both a manager role and an agent role.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is the framework the MIB is written for. The more specific MIB tag already covers it, and SNMP is its ancestor.
The alarm and event configuration resembles management policy, but the document defines a MIB, not a policy information model.
The MIB is written in an ASN.1 subset (SMI). That is only the notation, and the document does not specify ASN.1.
The alarm table samples MIB variables against thresholds, but it does not define performance metrics or measurement methods.

RFC1452.title: Coexistence between version 1 and version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework
RFC1452.summary: RFC 1452 describes how SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 coexist, covering conversion of SMIv1 MIB modules, traps, compliance and capabilities statements to SMIv2, and proxy agent and bi-lingual manager behaviour.

SNMP.why: The document specifies how SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 protocol entities interoperate, including proxy PDU mapping (GetBulkRequest to GetNextRequest, Trap to SNMPv2-Trap) and bi-lingual managers.
SNMP.quote: the proxy behavior between a SNMPv2 entity and a SNMPv1 agent; and, the behavior of "bi-lingual" protocol entities acting in a manager role

MIB.why: A large part of the document lists the changes needed to convert SMIv1 MIB modules, trap definitions, compliance and capabilities statements to the SMIv2 notation.
MIB.quote: MIB modules defined using the current framework may continue to be used with the SNMPv2 framework. However, for the MIB modules to conform

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the basis of the descriptive notation. The document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
The parent topic is implied by the SNMP and MIB tags, so it is not listed separately.

RFC1453.title: A Comment on Packet Video Remote Conferencing and the Transport/Network Layers
RFC1453.summary: Informational comment promoting XTP (Xpress Transfer Protocol) as a unified transport protocol for packet video remote conferencing over ATM/FDDI networks, summarizing workshop requirements and XTP experiments.

conferencing.why: The document centres on remote conferencing requirements: session scheduling, control, multicast membership, and synchronization.
conferencing.quote: The remote-conferencing session needs a control subsystem that is either tightly controlled for an n-to-n connection for two to 15 participants

transport.why: It argues for a unified transport/network protocol (XTP) with priority, error control and rate control. XTP has no specific tag in the taxonomy, so the generic transport topic fits.
transport.quote: Another approach might be to unify the protocols. It is felt that this is one of the main goals of XTP

rejected.why: ATM is the motivating link layer, but the document is not about IP over ATM.
ST-II is mentioned in the architecture figures and as an alternative approach, but it is not the subject.
NETBLT is cited as an ancestor of XTP, not discussed in its own right.
RTP/RTCP appear only in a comparison figure of an emerging architecture.
QOS is discussed as an input to the transport layer, but there is no QoS architecture or signalling content.
Multicast needs are mentioned for conferencing, but there is no multicast routing or group membership content.

gaps.name: XTP (Xpress Transfer Protocol)
gaps.why: The document's main subject is XTP as a unified transport protocol, and the taxonomy has no XTP tag.

RFC1454.title: Comparison of Proposals for Next Version of IP
RFC1454.summary: A RARE report comparing the three main IPng candidate proposals (PIP, SIP, TUBA) to replace IPv4, covering shared features, gaps, differences and transition plans.

IPng.why: The document compares the historic IPng candidates PIP, SIP and TUBA, which is exactly what the IPng tag covers.
IPng.quote: TUBA is based on CLNP (ISO 8473) and the ES-IS (ISO 9542) control protocol.

IPv6 transition.why: A substantial section discusses dual stacks, translation and tunnelling for IPv4/IPng coexistence.
IPv6 transition.quote: The transition plans espoused by the various proposals are simply different combinations of the above.

rejected.why: TUBA is based on CLNP, but CLNP is discussed only as one candidate's basis, not specified or analysed in its own right.
IPv4 is the baseline being compared against and its inadequacy motivates the document, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
CIDR is mentioned only as a near-term remedy, not a subject of the document.
DNS changes for longer addresses get a short section, but this is not a substantial focus.
Address assignment is discussed, but as part of the IPng comparison rather than as a standalone subject.

RFC1455.title: Physical Link Security Type of Service
RFC1455.summary: Experimental RFC that defines a new IPv4 Type of Service value (15, 0xF) asking the network to route packets over the most physically secure links. The aim is to resist traffic analysis and add some confidentiality.

IPv4.why: The memo's core content is a new value for the IPv4 header TOS field, extending RFC 1349. IPv4 is the closest tag, since the taxonomy has no Type of Service tag.
IPv4.quote: The value 15 decimal (F hex) in the four-bit Type of Service IP header field requests routing the packet to minimize the chance of surreptitious observation

privacy.why: A large part of the memo is the motivation of resisting traffic analysis and improving confidentiality by choosing physically secure links.
privacy.quote: The purpose is protection against traffic analysis and as an additional possible level of data confidentiality.

rejected.why: OSPF is cited only as an example of a protocol that can do TOS-based routing by assigning link costs. The memo does not specify or extend it.
Diffserv later redefined the TOS octet. This 1993 memo concerns the older four-bit TOS semantics, not differentiated services.
The memo says it gives no guaranteed level of service and says guarantees would need resource reservation. It is a routing-preference hint, not a QoS architecture.
End-to-end encryption is mentioned only as context. The memo is about link-level physical security.

gaps.name: IP Type of Service (TOS)
gaps.why: The document defines a TOS value. The taxonomy has no tag for the IP TOS field or its registry, so IPv4 is the nearest fit.

review: no tag in common with RFC2474, which obsoletes it

RFC1456.title: Conventions for Encoding the Vietnamese Language  VISCII: VIetnamese Standard Code for Information Interchange VIQR: VIetnamese Quoted-Readable Specification
RFC1456.summary: Informational RFC describing VISCII, an 8-bit Vietnamese character encoding, and VIQR, a 7-bit ASCII mnemonic convention for Vietnamese text, including their MIME charset registrations.

character sets.why: The document defines two Vietnamese character encodings (VISCII 8-bit, VIQR 7-bit) and notes their charset registrations. It is about character set definition and use.
character sets.quote: the value "VISCII" has been registered as a charset with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority for the VISCII encoding convention

rejected.why: MIME is only the context for labelling the charset in a short section. The document does not specify or extend MIME.
VIQR uses 7-bit ASCII as its substrate, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
Unicode is mentioned only in passing, as a translation target in the tcs utility.
Email is a motivating use case, but the document does not specify email protocols or formats.
The parent topic is implied by character sets, so it is not listed separately.

RFC1457.title: Security Label Framework for the Internet
RFC1457.summary: RFC 1457 is an informational framework describing how security labels (integrity and sensitivity labels) can be placed and used across OSI layers, in end and intermediate systems, to guide protocol designers.

security labels.why: The whole document is a framework for security labels (integrity and sensitivity labels, explicit/implicit, connectionless/connection-oriented, and placement by layer), discussing IPSO, SP4 and X.400 labels.
security labels.quote: This memo presents a security labeling framework for the Internet.

rejected.why: The more specific security labels tag fits; the parent is implied.
The OSI reference model is only the structure used to present the discussion, not the subject itself.
X.400 message envelope labels are mentioned only as one example at the Application Layer.
IPSO is cited as an example of an explicit network-layer label but is not specified or extended here.
Access control decisions based on labels are discussed, but only as a use of labels, not as the subject.

RFC1458.title: Requirements for Multicast Protocols
RFC1458.summary: Informational memo reviewing IP multicast, XTP, ST-II and MTP against image-communication needs, and outlining a new reliable adaptive multicast transport (RAMP), a Multicast Group Authority for Class D address management, and QoS-aware multicast routing support.

multicast.why: The memo's core subject is multicast requirements: group address allocation, membership maintenance, and QoS-based multicast routing changes. No more specific multicast child fits (not PIM, IGMP spec, etc.).
multicast.quote: The Multicast Group Authority (MGA) provides services related to managing the multicast address space and high-level management support to existing multicast groups.

reliable multicast.why: It designs a reliable multicast transport with NAK-based selective retransmission, a multicast/unicast retransmission threshold and rate-based flow control, and reviews XTP and MTP as reliable multicast candidates.
reliable multicast.quote: RAMP is a transport-level protocol designed to provide reliable multicast service on top of a network protocol such as IP/Multicast

ST-II.why: A full subsection analyses ST-II's multicast set-up, bandwidth reservation and teardown against the requirements.
ST-II.quote: ST-II is another network protocol that provides support for multicast communications.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a reservation system the proposed suite should be compatible with, not specified or analysed.
Described briefly as part of how IP/Multicast works; the memo is not about IGMP itself.
RAMP's flow control is one piece of the design, but the document's focus is multicast; reliable multicast covers it.
The memo redefines QoS as image quality levels for multicast groups, rather than addressing QoS architectures or signalling.
Only an analogy for the hierarchical structure of the MGA.
The MGA does address allocation, but MADCAP/MALLOC are later specific protocols not discussed here.

RFC1459.title: Internet Relay Chat Protocol
RFC1459.summary: RFC 1459 specifies the original Internet Relay Chat (IRC) protocol: client-server and server-server architecture, channels, message format, commands, numeric replies and implementation notes.

IRC.why: The entire document specifies the IRC protocol: messages, channels, commands, replies and server behaviour.
IRC.quote: The IRC (Internet Relay Chat) protocol has been designed over a number of years for use with text based conferencing.

rejected.why: IRC runs over TCP, which is only the substrate; the document merely explains why TCP is used.
DNS lookups are mentioned only as an implementation detail for hostname resolution.
Ident is used as an optional authentication check, not specified here.
IRC is chat, but that tag covers instant messaging and presence systems such as XMPP and SIMPLE. IRC has its own tag, so I chose that one.
This tag is for multiparty real-time media conferencing frameworks. IRC is text chat and has no XCON or BFCP-style floor control.

gaps.name: Internet Relay Chat (IRC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IRC tag in the applications section, but it was not available among the tag ids I could use here. IRC chat protocols deserve their own subject page. I used the IRC id as given in the taxonomy.

RFC1460.title: Post Office Protocol - Version 3
RFC1460.summary: RFC 1460 specifies POP3 version 3, a simple TCP-based protocol letting a workstation retrieve mail from a server maildrop, with USER/PASS and optional APOP (MD5 digest) authentication and a TOP command.

POP3.why: The entire document specifies the POP3 protocol: states, commands, responses and the split-UA model.
POP3.quote: The Post Office Protocol - Version 3 (POP3) is intended to permit a workstation to dynamically access a maildrop on a server host

rejected.why: SMTP is only mentioned as the method for posting mail; the memo explicitly does not specify it.
MD5 is used only as the digest function in APOP; the document is not about the algorithm.
Messages are assumed to conform to RFC 822, but the document does not define message format.
TCP is merely the transport substrate on port 110.
APOP is a part of POP3 and is covered by the POP3 tag; no general authentication subject is addressed.

RFC1461.title: SNMP MIB extension for Multiprotocol Interconnect over X.25
RFC1461.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (MIOX25-MIB) for managing Multiprotocol Interconnect traffic (IP, CLNP, SNAP) carried over X.25 per RFC 1356, with PLE, peer and peer-encapsulation tables.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (MIOX25-MIB) using SMI, with three tables of managed objects.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing Multiprotocol Interconnect (including IP) traffic carried over X.25.

X.25.why: The managed objects concern X.25 circuits, X.121 addresses, call parameters and encapsulation of IP/CLNP/SNAP over X.25, so readers of X.25 would want this.
X.25.quote: Instances of the objects defined below provide management information for Multiprotocol Interconnect traffic on X.25 as defined in RFC 1356

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol framework this MIB is used with, not specified or extended here; MIB covers the subject.
CLNP is only one of the encapsulation types listed in an object's values; the document is not about CLNP.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB definitions.
RFC 1356 mentions ISDN, but this document only addresses X.25 interconnect.

RFC1462.title: FYI on "What is the Internet?"
RFC1462.summary: An informational FYI introducing "What is the Internet?", covering its definition, history from ARPANET and NSFNET, governance (ISOC, IAB, IETF), funding, and issues like OSI, commercialization and privatization.

internet history.why: A large part of the document narrates the Internet's origins from ARPANET through NSFNET, regional networks and Merit's upgrade.
internet history.quote: The Internet was born about 20 years ago, trying to connect together a U.S. Defense Department network called the ARPAnet and various other radio and satellite networks.
internet history.section: The Internet (excerpt from "The Whole Internet User's Guide and Catalog")

internet architecture.why: It explains the design philosophy of an unreliable network with end-to-end responsibility and peer communication, and defines the Internet as a network of networks.
internet architecture.quote: The communicating computers--not the network itself--were also given the responsibility to ensure that the communication was accomplished.
internet architecture.section: The Internet (excerpt from "The Whole Internet User's Guide and Catalog")

internet governance.why: A dedicated section covers how ISOC, the IAB and the IETF govern and standardize the Internet, plus who pays for it.
internet governance.quote: The ultimate authority for where the Internet is going rests with the Internet Society, or ISOC.

user guides.why: It is an FYI introductory guide for Internet users, from the User Services Working Group.
user guides.quote: This FYI RFC answers the question, "What is the Internet?" and is produced by the User Services Working Group

rejected.why: OSI is discussed only briefly as a possible future standard, not as the document's subject.
The IETF's working group process is described only in passing as part of the governance overview.
ARPANET appears as historical background, not as a document about its protocols or operations.
SNA is mentioned once as the commercial mainframe protocol suite, which does not make the document about it.

RFC1463.title: FYI on Introducing the Internet-- A Short Bibliography of Introductory Internetworking Readings
RFC1463.summary: FYI 19 is a short annotated-style bibliography of introductory readings, books, and on-line guides to help network novices learn about the Internet, its networks, resources, protocols and history.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory guide for Internet novices, intended as a handout for user services personnel, so it belongs on the user guides page.
user guides.quote: This bibliography offers a short list of recent information resources that will help the network novice become familiar with the Internet

rejected.why: History is mentioned as one topic the readings cover, but the document is a reading list, not a history.
It lists introductory protocol books but does not discuss architectural principles.
Anonymous FTP is only the means of retrieving the on-line files, not a subject of the document.
Email is only used to request the access guide, and the document is not about email.

RFC1464.title: Using the Domain Name System To Store Arbitrary String Attributes
RFC1464.summary: RFC 1464 defines an experimental convention for storing arbitrary attribute=value string data in DNS TXT resource records, including quoting and name matching rules, with no change to DNS implementations.

DNS.why: The document specifies a usage convention for DNS TXT resource records, including syntax, quoting and matching rules, so it belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: This paper proposes the use of the DNS TXT resource record (defined in STD 13, RFC 1035) to contain new types of information.

rejected.why: The values are ASCII text, but ASCII is only the character repertoire. The document is not about ASCII itself.
The attributes are generic key/value data. The document does not describe discovering services.
DNS-SD also uses TXT records for key/value data, but this document predates it and does not specify service discovery.

RFC1465.title: Routing Coordination for X.400 MHS Services Within a Multi Protocol / Multi Network Environment Table Format V3 for Static Routing
RFC1465.summary: Defines an experimental table format (V3) of COMMUNITY, RELAY-MTA, DOMAIN and PERSON documents plus routing rules for coordinating static X.400 MHS routing across multi-stack, multi-network environments until X.500-based routing is available.

X.400.why: The whole document specifies table-based routing coordination for X.400 MHS: RELAY-MTAs, MHS domains/subtrees, OR-address matching and routing rules.
X.400.quote: It proposes a strategy for maintaining and distributing routing information and shows how messages can travel over different networks by using multi stack MTAs as relays.

rejected.why: X.500 is mentioned as the future directory-based replacement and Distinguished Names may be used as keys, but the document specifies a static table format, not X.500.
Only mentioned as a placeholder 'Internet-SMTP' gateway keyword; not a subject of the document.
X.400 is the more specific tag and already covers this X.400 mail routing document.
Routing here is X.400 message routing, not IP routing; the X.400 tag fits more specifically and the routing subtree concerns IP routing.
FTP and FTAM are only listed as access methods for the file server hosting the documents.

RFC1466.title: Guidelines for Management of IP Address Space
RFC1466.summary: RFC 1466 gives guidelines for how the Internet Registry and regional registries allocate and assign IPv4 Class A, B and C network numbers, including geographic Class C blocks, to slow address space depletion and allow aggregation.

addressing.why: The whole document is about IP address architecture, allocation and assignment policy, including regional registry delegation and Class A/B/C criteria.
addressing.quote: This document proposes a plan which will forward the implementation of RFC 1174 and which defines the allocation and assignment of the network number space.

IPv4.why: The guidelines manage the classful IPv4 address space and its exhaustion. IPv4 address lifecycle is a substantial subject of the document.
IPv4.quote: The Class A portion of the number space represents 50% of the total IP host addresses; Class B is 25% of the total
IPv4.section: 3.0 Allocation of the Network Number Space by the Internet Registry

rejected.why: The document assigns contiguous Class C blocks to enable aggregation and mentions an 18-bit prefix. It does not specify CIDR itself and only cites RFC 1338 as related work.
The conclusion notes the growth in routing information, but only in passing.
IANA is mentioned as an authority over the address space. The document is not about IANA registries or stewardship in general.

gaps.name: Internet Registry / regional registry address allocation policy
gaps.why: The document is mainly about the policy and delegation structure of address registries (RIR precursors). The taxonomy has no registry-policy tag, so addressing is the closest fit.

RFC1467.title: Status of CIDR Deployment in the Internet
RFC1467.summary: Status report on CIDR deployment in 1993: milestones of the RFC 1367 address-management schedule, vendor BGP-4 implementation status, routing table growth, and router capacity of transit providers.

CIDR.why: The whole document reports on the development and deployment status of CIDR, including address allocation procedures, aggregation support in routers, and its expected impact on routing table growth.
CIDR.quote: there is consensus in the Internet community to use Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) [4]. CIDR is supported by BGP-4 and IDRP.
CIDR.section: 4. Current status of address aggregation mechanisms in commercial routers

BGP.why: A substantial section surveys vendor BGP-4 implementation status (aggregation and de-aggregation support), which is needed for CIDR deployment and is of interest to BGP readers.
BGP.quote: Most router vendors are working on BGP-4, first, and there is a consensus to use BGP-4 to support the initial deployment of CIDR in the Internet.
BGP.section: 4. Current status of address aggregation mechanisms in commercial routers

rejected.why: The address space exhaustion and Class A/B/C allocation are discussed, but the document's subject is CIDR aggregation deployment, which sits under addressing; CIDR is the more specific tag.
Routing table growth and scalability are discussed, but only as motivation and capacity data for CIDR deployment, not as architecture itself.
IANA and regional registries are mentioned in the allocation milestones, but the document is not about IANA registries or stewardship.

RFC1468.title: Japanese Character Encoding for Internet Messages
RFC1468.summary: Informational RFC defining ISO-2022-JP, the escape-sequence-based Japanese character encoding (ASCII, JIS X 0201 Roman, JIS X 0208) used in email and news messages, and its MIME charset name.

character sets.why: The document defines and names a character encoding (ISO-2022-JP) for use as a MIME charset, including escape sequences and formal syntax. This is character set specification and registration.
character sets.quote: The name given to this encoding is "ISO-2022-JP", which is intended to be used in the "charset" parameter field of MIME headers

rejected.why: MIME is the context for the charset parameter. The document only says how the charset name is used and does not specify MIME itself.
The encoding is for mail and news messages, but the document is about the character encoding, not email architecture or transport.
The encoding is based on JIS and ISO 2022, not Unicode.
ASCII is one of the character sets the encoding switches between. The document does not specify ASCII or its use in its own right.
Netnews is only mentioned as one place the encoding is used. The document does not address news article format or distribution.

gaps.name: Japanese text encoding / CJK character encodings (ISO 2022, JIS X 0208)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only generic character set tags. It has none for ISO 2022 code-extension encodings or for CJK encodings, which readers of this subject would look for.

RFC1469.title: IP Multicast over Token-Ring Local Area Networks
RFC1469.summary: Specifies how IP multicast datagrams are mapped to Token-Ring MAC addresses, mainly using a single assigned functional address (03-00-00-20-00-00), with the all-rings broadcast address as a fallback.

token ring.why: The whole document defines the mapping of IP multicast addresses to Token-Ring MAC and functional addresses. It belongs on the IP over token ring page.
token ring.quote: This document specifies a method for the transmission of IP multicast datagrams over Token-Ring Local Area Networks.

rejected.why: IP multicast is the subject being carried, but the document is about the Token-Ring link-layer mapping. The token ring tag fits more specifically, and it is not a multicast routing or group membership specification.
RFC 1112 is cited for group addresses, but IGMP itself is not specified or extended here.
Ethernet and FDDI mappings are mentioned only as comparisons.
RFC 1188 is cited only as a precedent for the mapping approach.

RFC1470.title: FYI on a Network Management Tool Catalog: Tools for Monitoring and Debugging TCP/IP Internets and Interconnected Devices
RFC1470.summary: FYI 2 catalog (obsoletes RFC 1147) of tools for monitoring and debugging TCP/IP internets: a keyword index plus standardized entries for network management, traffic analysis, benchmarking, and diagnostic tools (SNMP agents/managers, ping, traceroute, protocol analyzers).

network management.why: The whole document is a catalog of network management and monitoring tools with an indexing scheme, so it belongs on the network management page.
network management.quote: Tools for Monitoring and Debugging TCP/IP Internets and Interconnected Devices

SNMP.why: A large share of catalog entries are SNMP agents, managers, libraries and utilities, so SNMP readers would want this catalog.
SNMP.quote: a network management system or component based on SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol.

traceroute.why: It contains full entries for traceroute, hopcheck and related path-discovery tools.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute is a tool that allows the route taken by packets from source to destination to be discovered.

benchmarking.why: Several entries (hammer & anvil, ttcp, LADDIS, nhfsstone, SPIMS, spray) are benchmarking and traffic-generation tools.
benchmarking.quote: Hammer and Anvil are the benchmarking programs for IP routers.

packet capture.why: Many entries are packet capture and protocol analyzers (tcpdump, etherfind, Sniffer, LANWatch).
packet capture.quote: Tcpdump can interpret and print headers for the following protocols

rejected.why: CMIP-based tools (CMIP Library, CMOT agent, MIB Browser) appear only as a few catalog entries, not a substantial subject of the document.
DiG, nslookup, host and lamers are a few entries among many; DNS is not the document's subject.
MIB tools appear incidentally within SNMP product entries.
ping and traceroute use ICMP, but ICMP itself is not specified or analysed here.
It is an FYI document, but the FYI category is a series label. The content is a tool catalog, so network management is the better fit.

RFC1471.title: The Definitions of Managed Objects for the Link Control Protocol of the Point-to-Point Protocol
RFC1471.summary: Defines the PPP-LCP-MIB, SNMP managed objects for monitoring and configuring the PPP Link Control Protocol and Link Quality Monitoring on PPP interfaces, plus echo and discard tests.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (PPP-LCP-MIB) defined with the SMI, so readers browsing MIB modules would expect it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

PPP.why: The managed objects cover PPP LCP options (MRU, ACCM, magic number, FCS) and LQR, so the document is about managing PPP.
PPP.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the Link Control Protocol and Link Quality Monitoring on subnetwork interfaces that use the family of Point-to-Point Protocols

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the objects. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation the SMI uses to write the definitions, not the subject.
Not related. PPP's lower-layer interfaces are mentioned only as RS-232 or HDLC examples.
The FCS size objects are just one of the LCP option parameters, not a discussion of CRC polynomials.

RFC1472.title: The Definitions of Managed Objects for the Security Protocols of the Point-to-Point Protocol
RFC1472.summary: Defines a MIB module (PPP-SEC-MIB) with managed objects for configuring PPP authentication protocols (PAP, CHAP) and their ID/secret pairs per link.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (PPP-SEC-MIB) using the SMI, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: describes managed objects used for managing the Security Protocols on subnetwork interfaces using the family of Point-to-Point Protocols

PPP.why: The managed objects cover PPP authentication protocols (PAP, CHAP) configuration, preference order and secrets on PPP links, so it belongs under PPP.
PPP.quote: The PPP Security Group contains all configuration and control variables that apply to PPP security.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework used to access the objects. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour.
PAP and CHAP are only configured through the MIB. The document does not specify or analyse the authentication mechanisms themselves.
ASN.1 is only the notation the MIB definitions are written in.

RFC1473.title: The Definitions of Managed Objects for the IP Network Control Protocol of the Point-to-Point Protocol
RFC1473.summary: Defines a MIB module (PPP-IP-NCP-MIB) with managed objects for monitoring and configuring the IP Control Protocol (IPCP) of PPP on interfaces, including status, VJ header compression and admin control.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition with tables of objects for IPCP, so it belongs under MIB modules and SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

PPP.why: The managed subject is PPP's IP Control Protocol (IPCP), including its state machine, open/close control and option negotiation results.
PPP.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the IP Network Control Protocol on subnetwork interfaces using the family of Point-to-Point Protocols

rejected.why: SNMP is only the protocol used to access the objects. The document defines no SNMP behaviour, only a MIB module, so MIB is the more specific tag.
The MIB reports Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression as an IPCP option, but it does not specify the compression. That is a different mechanism from IPHC (RFC 2507).
ASN.1 is only the notation the SMI uses to define the objects.

RFC1474.title: The Definitions of Managed Objects for the Bridge Network Control Protocol of the Point-to-Point Protocol
RFC1474.summary: Defines a MIB module (PPP-BRIDGE-NCP-MIB) with managed objects for monitoring and configuring the Bridging Network Control Protocol (BNCP) on PPP links.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module in SMI format defining managed objects for the PPP bridge NCP.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

PPP.why: The objects manage BNCP, a PPP control protocol (RFC 1220), including its option negotiation and operational status, so PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the bridge Network Control Protocol [10] on subnetwork interfaces using the family of Point-to-Point Protocols.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines no SNMP behaviour itself.
ASN.1 is just the notation used by the SMI to define the objects, not a subject of the document.
The document mentions MAC bridging and 802.5 token ring options only as parameters of BNCP, not as a subject in its own right.
The 802.5 ring and line ID options are only a few configuration objects, not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC1475.title: TP/IX: The Next Internet
RFC1475.summary: RFC 1475 specifies TP/IX (IP version 7), a proposed next-generation IP with 64-bit addresses, a forward route identifier, expanded TCP/UDP fields, and stateless conversion between IPv4 and IPv7.

IPng.why: TP/IX is one of the historic IPng candidate protocols (TUBA, PIP, SIPP, TP/IX); the whole document specifies it.
IPng.quote: This memo presents the specification for version 7 of the Internet Protocol, as well as version 7 of the TCP and the user datagram protocol.

IPv4.why: A large part (Section 8) defines IPv4 interoperation, conversion procedures and a new IPv4 address extension option.
IPv4.quote: It must permit network layer state-free translation of datagrams between IPv4 and IPv7

TCP.why: Defines TCPv7 header, options, and conversion to and from TCPv4.
TCP.quote: Internet version 7 expands the sizes of the sequence and acknowledgement fields, the window, and the port numbers.

rejected.why: TP/IX is a competing proposal, not IPv6.
ICMP is adapted for IPv7 and a Conversion Failed message is defined, but only as a minor part of the document.
Section 7 gives brief notes on A and PTR records, a minor part of the document.
Conversion between IPv4 and IPv7 is a transition mechanism, but that tag covers IPv6, and IPng captures the document's subject.
UDP is expanded in a short section only.
Mobile hosts are discussed in a short subsection about forward route identifiers.

RFC1476.title: RAP: Internet Route Access Protocol
RFC1476.summary: Defines RAP, an experimental distance-vector routing protocol usable from LANs to inter-domain networks, with route add/purge commands, extensible metrics/options, and filtering/aggregation procedures.

routing architecture.why: The document specifies a new general-purpose routing protocol that does not split interior and exterior routing. No tag exists for RAP itself, and the routing architecture and design principles subject is the closest fit.
routing architecture.quote: RAP is a general protocol for distributing routing information at all levels of the Internet, from private LANs to the widest-flung international carrier networks.

rejected.why: RIP is only cited as a comparison and as a source of redistributed routes. RAP is not a RIP specification.
OSPF is mentioned only as a contrasting link-state protocol.
BGP is mentioned only as a possible source of imported route distances.
TCP port 38 is only the transport RAP runs over.
IPv7 (TP/IX) addressing is used internally, but this document is not about the IPng candidate protocols.
The document uses prefix masks and aggregation, but it does not address CIDR itself.
This is the parent topic. The more specific child, routing architecture, was chosen.

gaps.name: RAP (Route Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for this historic experimental distance-vector routing protocol. Only generic routing topics are available.

RFC1477.title: IDPR as a Proposed Standard
RFC1477.summary: Informational overview of Inter-Domain Policy Routing (IDPR): its policies, functions, entities, security, scaling, coexistence with BGP/EGP, and prototype and gated implementation experiments.

IDPR.why: The whole document describes IDPR: its functionality, entities, security, and implementation experiments.
IDPR.quote: The objective of IDPR is to construct and maintain routes between source and destination administrative domains, that provide user traffic with the services requested

rejected.why: BGP is mentioned only as a coexisting inter-domain routing procedure in section 6.
EGP is mentioned only alongside BGP as a coexisting procedure.
DNS is mentioned only as a place where the mapping server function could be integrated.
IDPR is the more specific tag and already covers the architecture discussion.
MD5 and RSA appear only as examples of recommended integrity/authentication algorithms.

RFC1478.title: An Architecture for Inter-Domain Policy Routing
RFC1478.summary: RFC 1478 describes the architecture for Inter-Domain Policy Routing (IDPR): link-state policy route generation, source-specified path-based forwarding, policy gateways, route servers, and mechanisms for scaling to tens of thousands of domains.

IDPR.why: The whole document specifies the IDPR architecture, its entities, functions, and scaling features.
IDPR.quote: We present an architecture for inter-domain policy routing (IDPR). The objective of IDPR is to construct and maintain routes, between source and destination administrative domains

rejected.why: BGP-3 and BGP-4 are only mentioned as related work and for a loop clarification; the document is not about BGP.
The IDPR tag is the more specific fit for this architecture.
DNS is only mentioned as a possible home for the mapping server function.
Section 3.3 covers authentication and integrity of control messages, but it is a small part of the document and is specific to IDPR.

RFC1479.title: Inter-Domain Policy Routing Protocol Specification: Version 1
RFC1479.summary: Specifies the Inter-Domain Policy Routing (IDPR) protocol suite: virtual gateway protocol, flooding of routing information, route server query protocol, route generation, path control and data forwarding, plus the CMTP transport.

IDPR.why: The whole document is the IDPR version 1 protocol specification.
IDPR.quote: We present the set of protocols and procedures that constitute Inter-Domain Policy Routing (IDPR).

rejected.why: IDPR is a specific protocol, so the child tag fits better.
IDPR is encapsulated in IP with protocol numbers 35 and 38, but IP is only the substrate.
Flooding is described as similar to OSPF and IS-IS, but these are only cited for comparison.
Mapping servers are to be integrated into DNS, but that is only mentioned in passing.
SNMP is mentioned only as a way to distribute configuration. Managed objects are in a separate document.
The RSA/MD5 integrity and authentication option is recommended, but it is a minor detail.

RFC1480.title: The US Domain
RFC1480.summary: Informational RFC describing the structure, naming conventions, registration procedures, delegation requirements and DNS database conventions of the US top-level country-code domain.

DNS.why: The document defines the namespace hierarchy, delegation of zones, name servers, zone files and resource records (A, CNAME, MX, HINFO, PTR, wildcards) for the US DNS top-level domain.
DNS.quote: The US Domain hierarchy is based on political geography. The basic name space under US is the state name space, then the "locality" name space

domain registration.why: A substantial part covers registry operations: registration templates, requirements for registrants, delegation requirements and procedures, and the registrar's role.
domain registration.quote: There are two types of registrations (1) Delegation, where a branch of the US Domain is delegated to an organization running name servers

rejected.why: MX records for UUCP forwarding are discussed, but only as DNS registration practice, not email specification.
UUCP hosts are registered via MX forwarders; the document is about domain registration, not UUCP mail interchange.
WHOIS is mentioned only briefly regarding which delegated names are listed.
Hostname conventions are touched on, but the document is about the DNS namespace structure rather than host tables or hostname conventions.

RFC1481.title: IAB Recommendation for an Intermediate Strategy to Address the Issue of Scaling
RFC1481.summary: IAB statement endorsing CIDR (supernetting) as an intermediate strategy to address Internet routing table growth and IPv4 address space exhaustion, and supporting IANA, InterNIC, vendor and operator implementation.

CIDR.why: The whole memo is the IAB's endorsement of Classless Inter-Domain Routing as the near-term answer to scaling, covering address allocation and route aggregation.
CIDR.quote: The IAB endorses the CIDR architecture and its implementation.

rejected.why: The memo concerns extending the life of the 32-bit address space via CIDR, but the specific subject is CIDR; IPv4 is the context.
Routing table growth and aggregation are discussed, but CIDR is the more specific tag and covers it.
Inter-domain routing protocols are only mentioned generically, with no BGP specifics.

RFC1482.title: Aggregation Support in the NSFNET Policy-Based Routing Database
RFC1482.summary: Describes how the NSFNET Policy-Based Routing Database will support CIDR route aggregation (accepting, proxy-generating and announcing aggregates with BGP-4 peers), proposes a CIDR Aggregate Registry, and assesses operational impact and routing table reduction.

CIDR.why: The document is about deploying CIDR aggregation on the NSFNET backbone, including aggregate configuration, the aggregate registry and the effect on routing table size.
CIDR.quote: This document describes plans for support of route aggregation, as specified in the descriptions of Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) [1] and the BGP-4 protocol [2]

BGP.why: Exchange of aggregates between backbone and regional peers over BGP-4, and the policy-based inbound/outbound announcement configuration, are a substantial part of the document.
BGP.quote: In this case the regional peer router is CIDR-capable (i.e., runs BGP-4) and the announcement comes into the backbone as an IP address prefix.

RPSL.why: The proposed CIDR Aggregate Registry is a routing-policy registry of aggregate announcements, comparable to routing registries, and is intended to be compatible with the RIPE database.
RPSL.quote: Note: This can be represented using the syntax used for objects in the RIPE-81 paper[9].

rejected.why: The document addresses aggregation support for a specific network and CIDR, not general routing architecture and scalability principles; CIDR is the more specific tag.
Address allocation is mentioned only as related policy; CIDR is the more specific tag.
Anonymous FTP is only mentioned as the way reports are distributed.
IDRP is only mentioned in passing as a later CIDR-capable protocol.

gaps.name: NSFNET Policy-Based Routing Database
gaps.why: The document is about the NSFNET backbone's routing policy database and its operations; the taxonomy has no tag for NSFNET or backbone routing policy configuration.

RFC1483.title: Multiprotocol Encapsulation over ATM Adaptation Layer 5
RFC1483.summary: RFC 1483 specifies two methods, LLC/SNAP encapsulation and VC-based multiplexing, for carrying routed and bridged network interconnect PDUs over ATM AAL5.

ATM.why: The whole document defines how multiprotocol traffic (IP, ISO, bridged LAN frames) is encapsulated over ATM AAL5, either with LLC/SNAP headers or by using a separate VC per protocol.
ATM.quote: This memo describes two encapsulations methods for carrying network interconnect traffic over ATM AAL5.

rejected.why: Frame Relay SSCS encapsulation appears only in an informational appendix, and RFC 1294 is cited for the details.
Bridged Ethernet/802.3 PDUs are one of several bridged media formats carried over ATM. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
CLNP is only an example of a routed ISO protocol, shown in the NLPID and FR-SSCS appendices.
IP is one of several carried protocols, and the document defines no IP-specific behaviour beyond its EtherType value.
The encapsulation is a link-layer adaptation over AAL5, not IP-in-IP or generic IP tunnelling.
RFC 1209 on SMDS is mentioned only as the earlier source of the LLC encapsulation subset.

RFC1484.title: Using the OSI Directory to achieve User Friendly Naming (OSI-DS 24 (v1.2))
RFC1484.summary: Experimental RFC defining User Friendly Names (UFNs) for the OSI/X.500 Directory: a human-oriented notation for purported names and a default algorithm for resolving them to distinguished names via directory searches.

X.500.why: The whole document specifies how to name and look up entries in the X.500 Directory using friendly names, with a matching algorithm built on directory search and read operations.
X.500.quote: The OSI Directory has user friendly naming as a goal. A simple minded usage of the directory does not achieve this.

rejected.why: The document is about naming, but the naming is specific to the X.500 directory, so the more specific X.500 tag fits better.
It is the parent of X.500, so it is implied and not listed separately.
ASN.1 appears only in the pseudo-code appendix and in passing as the form that names should not take, so it is not a subject of the document.
Names here are X.500 distinguished names, not DNS names.
LDAP is not mentioned. The document concerns X.500 DAP operations in the DUA.

RFC1485.title: A String Representation of Distinguished Names (OSI-DS 23 (v5))
RFC1485.summary: Defines a user-oriented string representation (BNF grammar, keywords, escape forms) for X.500 Distinguished Names, for use in mail messages, business cards and similar contexts outside directory protocols.

X.500.why: The whole document specifies a string format for X.500 Distinguished Names, covering RDNs, attribute types and X.520 keywords. Readers of the X.500 subject would expect to find it there.
X.500.quote: The OSI Directory uses distinguished names as the primary keys to entries in the directory.

rejected.why: X.500 is the more specific tag and already sits under directory services. The document defines a name notation and no directory access protocol.
LDAP is not mentioned. This memo is the precursor to the LDAP string DN format, but it describes none of the protocol.
The BNF grammar only defines the notation. It uses RFC 822 BNF as a tool and is not about the BNF notation itself.
Email is only mentioned as a context where DN strings may appear. The document does not specify mail headers or addressing.
ASN.1 is the encoding the string form replaces. The document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC1486.title: An Experiment in Remote Printing
RFC1486.summary: Experimental protocol for remote printing (to G3 fax devices) via Internet mail, using MIME application/remote-printing content, telephone-number-derived addresses under tpc.int, and DNS MX wildcard routing.

fax.why: The document specifies delivering Internet mail to G3-facsimile devices on the telephone network, i.e. fax over Internet mail.
fax.quote: the experiment in remote printing is about "outreach"; specifically, integrating the e-mail and facsimile communities.
fax.section: 1.1 The Advantage of a General-Purpose Infrastructure

media types.why: It registers the application/remote-printing and image/tiff media types with their syntax.
media types.quote:
MIME type name: application

   (2)  MIME subtype name: remote-printing

ENUM.why: Telephone numbers are mapped into the DNS under tpc.int with MX wildcards and per-country-code zones, a precursor of ENUM-style number mapping.
ENUM.quote: the domain-part is constructed by reversing the telephone number, converting each digit to a domain-label, and being placed under "tpc.int."

rejected.why: Mail is the substrate for the service; the document is about printing/fax delivery, so the more specific fax tag fits.
DNS MX records and zones are used for routing but no new DNS mechanism is defined; the ENUM-like mapping is captured by the ENUM tag.
MIME is used as a container, with only a new type registered, which the media types tag covers.
Only the transport substrate; nothing new is specified about SMTP.
The Internet Printing Protocol is a different, later printing protocol and is not discussed here.
No tel URI scheme is used; telephone numbers are encoded in domain names.

gaps.name: Remote printing / printing services
gaps.why: The document is primarily about remote printing, but the taxonomy has only LPD and IPP for printing, with no general printing tag.

RFC1487.title: X.500 Lightweight Directory Access Protocol
RFC1487.summary: RFC 1487 specifies version 2 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), a lightweight TCP-based alternative to X.500 DAP, covering its operations, ASN.1 definitions and BER encoding restrictions.

LDAP.why: The document defines the LDAP protocol itself: bind, search, modify, add, delete, modify RDN, compare and abandon operations.
LDAP.quote: The protocol described in this document is designed to provide access to the Directory while not incurring the resource requirements of the Directory Access Protocol (DAP).

rejected.why: X.500 is the directory service LDAP fronts, but the document specifies LDAP, not X.500. X.500 is only the backend and reference model.
ASN.1 and BER are the notation and encoding used to define LDAP messages. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Kerberos v4 is only one of the authentication options in the Bind request, mentioned in passing.
TCP is only the transport LDAP is mapped onto (port 389). The document defines nothing new about TCP.

RFC1488.title: The X.500 String Representation of Standard Attribute Syntaxes
RFC1488.summary: Defines the string encodings of the standard X.500 attribute syntaxes (strings, lists, telephone/fax numbers, certificates, etc.) for use as octet-string AttributeValues in LDAP.

LDAP.why: The document specifies how X.500 attribute syntaxes are rendered as strings for LDAP attribute values, a core part of LDAP's schema/encoding specification.
LDAP.quote: requires that the contents of AttributeValue fields in protocol elements be octet strings. This document defines the requirements that must be satisfied by encoding rules

X.500.why: The attribute syntaxes encoded are the standard X.500 Directory syntaxes (X.520 and COSINE/Internet X.500 schema), so X.500 readers would want it.
X.500.quote: define the encoding rules for the standard set of attribute syntaxes defined in [1,2] and [3].

rejected.why: Certificate and CRL syntaxes get string encodings, but the document is not about X.509 certificate profiles.
Syntaxes derive from ASN.1 types, but the document defines BNF string encodings, not ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
It uses BNF only as a notation to define encodings; it is not about the notation.
Facsimile number and Fax image syntaxes are encoded, but the document is not about fax transport.
Only mentioned incidentally in a CRLF definition.

RFC1489.title: Registration of a Cyrillic Character Set
RFC1489.summary: Registers the KOI8-R Cyrillic character set as a MIME charset name, giving its mapping table to Unicode/ISO 10646 and character descriptions for the upper half.

character sets.why: The document registers the koi8-r character set, with its coding table to Unicode and a description of every upper-half character.
character sets.quote: MIME character set name: koi8-r

rejected.why: MIME is only the context for the charset name. The document defines nothing about MIME body structure or encodings.
Unicode is used as the reference for the mapping table. The document is about registering koi8-r, not about how Unicode is used in protocols.
The lower half of the table coincides with ASCII. That is a passing remark, not the subject of the document.
The parent tag is implied by character sets, so it is not listed separately.

RFC1490.title: Multiprotocol Interconnect over Frame Relay
RFC1490.summary: Specifies encapsulation of routed and bridged multiprotocol traffic (IP, CLNP, IPX, ARP, Ethernet/802.x bridging) over Frame Relay, including fragmentation, XID parameter negotiation, and address resolution.

frame relay.why: The whole document defines how protocols are encapsulated over Frame Relay virtual circuits, including frame format, NLPID/SNAP, fragmentation and bridging.
frame relay.quote: This memo describes an encapsulation method for carrying network interconnect traffic over a Frame Relay backbone.

ARP.why: A substantial section specifies ARP, RARP and Inverse ARP operation over Frame Relay, including DLCI handling and hardware type assignment.
ARP.quote: Address resolution may be accomplished using the standard Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [6] encapsulated within a SNAP encoded Frame Relay packet

rejected.why: IP encapsulation is one of several protocols carried; the document is about the Frame Relay link layer, not IP itself.
CLNP is only an example of a protocol with an NLPID; not the subject.
IPX is mentioned briefly as an example of SNAP encapsulation.
Bridging of 802.3 frames is covered, but the focus is Frame Relay encapsulation, not IP over Ethernet.
Implied by the more specific frame relay tag.

RFC1491.title: A Survey of Advanced Usages of X.500
RFC1491.summary: An FYI survey collecting implementers' descriptions of advanced X.500 directory uses beyond white pages, such as EDI, security key distribution, network topology data, sendmail lookups, WHOIS front ends and X.400 routing tables.

X.500.why: The whole document surveys applications built on the X.500 directory, so readers of the X.500 page would want it.
X.500.quote: It is intended to show how various organizations are using X.500 in ways which extend the view of X.500 as a "White Pages" service.

user guides.why: It is an FYI-series (FYI 21) informational survey, not a specification, so the FYI/user guides subject fits.
user guides.quote: This memo provides information for the Internet community.  It does not specify an Internet standard.

rejected.why: One response (NASA Phone Book) fronts X.500 with the WHOIS protocol, but this is a minor part of the survey and the document does not specify or analyse WHOIS.
X.400 appears in the table-handling and ODA conversion responses, but only as a consumer of directory data. The document is not about X.400 itself.
Only one response uses the directory for EDI trading-partner and catalogue data. It is a small part of the survey.
The more specific X.500 tag already covers this parent topic.
Sendmail lookups and MHS routing are example applications, not the focus of the document.

RFC1492.title: An Access Control Protocol, Sometimes Called TACACS
RFC1492.summary: RFC 1492 documents the extended TACACS access control protocol used by Cisco terminal servers, specifying its request/response semantics, UDP and TCP encodings, and a University of Minnesota case study.

TACACS+.why: The whole document specifies the TACACS protocol (requests, packet formats, client/server behaviour). The taxonomy's TACACS+ tag covers TACACS and TACACS+, so it fits.
TACACS+.quote: This RFC documents the extended TACACS protocol use by the Cisco Systems terminal servers.

rejected.why: TACACS+ already sits under AAA, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
UDP is only one of two transport encodings for TACACS. The document does not define anything new about UDP itself.
SLIP connection requests (SLIPON, SLIPOFF) appear as TACACS message types, but the document is not about SLIP.
