Kerberos is mentioned once, as a mechanism a server could translate requests to. It is not a subject of the document.
RADIUS is not mentioned. TACACS is the only AAA-style protocol specified.

RFC1493.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges
RFC1493.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module (BRIDGE-MIB) for managing IEEE 802.1D MAC bridges, covering base bridge ports, Spanning Tree Protocol state, transparent bridging forwarding database, static filtering, and traps; obsoletes RFC 1286.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (BRIDGE-MIB) defining managed objects in the SMI for bridges, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: In particular it defines objects for managing MAC bridges based on the IEEE 802.1D-1990 standard between Local Area Network (LAN) segments.

Ethernet.why: Substantial content concerns MAC bridging: spanning tree, forwarding database, transparent bridging and filtering of LAN frames. Ethernet is the closest link-layer tag for bridge interworking and management.
Ethernet.quote: A common device present in many networks is the Bridge.  This device is used to connect Local Area Network segments below the network layer.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to access the objects. The document defines only a MIB module, not anything new about SNMP.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the definitions, not the subject.
Not about link aggregation. Bridge ports are not bundled links.

gaps.name: Spanning Tree Protocol / transparent bridging (IEEE 802.1D)
gaps.why: A large part of the MIB covers STP state and the bridge forwarding database. The taxonomy has no tag for bridging or spanning tree, so Ethernet is only an approximate fit.

RFC1494.title: Equivalences between 1988 X.400 and RFC-822 Message Bodies
RFC1494.summary: Defines the initial IANA MHS/MIME equivalence table mapping X.400 (1988) body parts to MIME content-types, including new X.400 extended body parts (generic MIME, PostScript, JPEG, GIF), new MIME types (application/x400-bp, image/g3fax, application/oda), and a registration form.

X.400.why: The document specifies equivalences and conversions between X.400 body part types and MIME content-types, defining new X.400 extended body parts and OIDs for gateway interworking.
X.400.quote: This document describes the content of the "IANA MHS/MIME Equivalence table" referenced in the companion document

MIME.why: It defines new MIME content-types (application/x400-bp, image/g3fax, application/oda) and maps existing ones to X.400 body parts.
MIME.quote: This section defines new MIME content-types for the purposes of interworking with X.400.

fax.why: A substantial part defines the image/g3fax type, its T.30 parameters, page-break encoding and the g3-facsimile mapping.
fax.quote: This content-type is defined to carry G3 Facsimile byte streams.

rejected.why: Registers and maps specific types but the document's focus is X.400 interworking equivalences, not registry rules for media types.
ASN.1 macros and OIDs are used to define body parts but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
IANA registration form is boilerplate-like apparatus supporting the table, not the main subject.
RFC-822 is the mail side of the mapping, but the document is about body-part equivalences, not header format.
Charset-to-ISO-IR mapping is a minor detail within the GeneralText equivalence.

RFC1495.title: Mapping between X.400 and RFC-822 Message Bodies
RFC1495.summary: RFC 1495 specifies the mapping of message bodies between X.400 (MHS) and RFC-822/MIME, updating RFC 1327 with body-part mapping rules, heading extensions for multipart and message/partial, OID assignments, and header encoded-word changes.

X.400.why: The document defines how X.400 IPMS body parts and headings are mapped to and from Internet mail, updating the RFC 1327 gateway specification.
X.400.quote: The IPMS.Body is mapped into the RFC-822 message body.

MIME.why: A large part of the document maps MIME content-types (multipart, message/partial, message/external-body) to X.400 body parts and back.
MIME.quote: If the IPMS.Body consists of more than one body part, then the RFC-822 message body is constructed as a multipart/mixed content-type

rejected.why: RFC 822 headers are touched only in modifications to RFC 1327 header mapping, which is secondary to the body mapping.
The IANA MHS/MIME equivalence table is mentioned, but its content is defined in the companion RFC 1494.
ASN.1 is used only for the heading extension and OID definitions, not as the subject.
X.400 and MIME are more specific tags that cover the subject.

RFC1496.title: Rules for downgrading messages from X.400/88 to X.400/84 when MIME content-types are present in the messages
RFC1496.summary: RFC 1496 (HARPOON) updates RFC 1328 by specifying how an X.400(88) gateway downgrades body parts to X.400(84), either by converting Extended Body Parts to Basic or by encapsulating the content as a MIME-headed IA5Text body part.

X.400.why: The whole document specifies X.400(88) to X.400(84) downgrading and the gateway rules for body parts, updating RFC 1328 and interworking with RFC 1327.
X.400.quote: Rules for Downgrading Messages from X.400/88 to X.400/84 When MIME Content-Types are Present in the Messages

MIME.why: The encapsulation format places MIME headers and content-type/transfer-encoding in an IA5 body part, and the reverse direction converts such parts per RFC 1494. MIME is a substantial part of the rules.
MIME.quote: MIME-version: <version>\r\n

rejected.why: SMTP(MIME) appears only as an endpoint in the scenarios; the document does not specify SMTP behaviour.
RFC-822 headers are mentioned only in passing for placement in heading-extensions; the document is not about the message format itself.
A more specific child tag (X.400) fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC1497.title: BOOTP Vendor Information Extensions
RFC1497.summary: RFC 1497 defines a vendor-independent set of tagged fields for the 64-octet vendor information area of BOOTP replies (subnet mask, gateways, name servers, hostname, boot file size, root path, extensions path) and obsoletes RFCs 1395, 1084 and 1048.

DHCP.why: The memo specifies BOOTP vendor extension tags that configure hosts automatically. These tags are the direct ancestor of DHCP options. DHCP is the closest taxonomy tag, because readers of host configuration would look for it there.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a (potentially) vendor-independent interpretation of this resource information.

rejected.why: BOOTP runs over UDP/IP, but UDP is only the substrate and the document adds nothing about it.
The Domain Name Server and Domain Name tags only carry DNS server addresses and the client's domain name. The document does not specify DNS.
The 'Comparison to Alternative Approaches' section discusses multicast service location as an alternative. It is a comparison, not the subject of the memo.
The memo gives a way to find servers, and the comparison section contrasts it with multicast discovery. The main subject is BOOTP configuration fields, so I did not tag it.
Registration of new tags goes through IANA, but this is only a short note in the Extensions section, not the memo's subject.
RARP is mentioned only as background, and the memo does not address it.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol) and its vendor extensions
gaps.why: The memo is about BOOTP vendor information, but the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag. DHCP is the nearest fit, and the memo is a pre-DHCP document.

RFC1498.title: On the Naming and Binding of Network Destinations
RFC1498.summary: A conceptual paper proposing four kinds of named network destinations (services, nodes, attachment points, paths) and three bindings among them, using the operating-system concept of binding to explain naming confusion in Ethernet and ARPANET NCP.

naming.why: The whole document is a general treatment of naming and binding of network destinations, not tied to any one system such as DNS.
naming.quote: it is helpful to distinguish among four different kinds of objects that may be named as the destination of a packet in a network

internet architecture.why: It offers an architectural conceptual model of names, addresses, and routes (services, nodes, attachment points, paths) that informs network design.
internet architecture.quote: some insight into the naming of destinations in a network can be obtained by recognizing four kinds of named objects at or leading to every destination

rejected.why: DNS is never mentioned; the paper is a general naming model, and its 'name server' is generic.
Ethernet's 48-bit identifier is used only as an illustrative example of binding, not specified or profiled.
ARPANET NCP host names are an example for the binding analysis, not the document's subject.
It discusses what an address means conceptually, but not IP address architecture or allocation; the general naming tag fits better.
It is a 1982 paper republished, but it is not a history or retrospective.

RFC1499.title: Summary of 1400-1499
RFC1499.summary: An annotated index of RFCs 1400 through 1499 that gives each RFC's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The whole document catalogues one block of the RFC series. A reader browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1400

rejected.why: It is a status listing of a range of RFCs, not a retrospective or history of the Internet. The RFC series tag covers it.
The summary lists many SNMPv2 RFCs, but only as entries in the index. The document does not specify or analyse SNMP.
Several X.500 and LDAP RFCs are listed, but only as abstracts. The document is not about them.
Mail-related RFCs such as the SMTP extensions, PEM and X.400 mappings appear only as index entries.
It mentions standards-track status and points to the 'Internet Official Protocol Standards' list, but it does not address the standards process.

RFC1500.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1500.summary: RFC 1500 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly list of Internet Official Protocol Standards, explaining the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and listing every protocol by state.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels and RFC processing rules, which is IETF process.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: Substantial sections describe the RFC series, submission and publication rules, the decision table, and how to obtain RFCs.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: Assigned Numbers and the IANA contact are mentioned only as references and contacts, not as the subject.
The many SNMPv2 RFCs are only entries in the status lists, not specified or analysed here.
TCP and other protocols appear only as list entries; the document is not about them.
The explanation of state and status terms is part of the standards process description, not a glossary in its own right.
It lists historic protocols but is a status snapshot, not a retrospective.

RFC1501.title: OS/2 User Group
RFC1501.summary: A 1993 informational memo soliciting interest in forming a national OS/2 end-user group (The Phoenix Group) to represent individual OS/2 users to IBM; it specifies no protocol or technology.

rejected.why: Not an introductory guide or FYI for Internet users; it is a solicitation for a user organization about an operating system.
The proposed group concerns an IBM OS/2 user community, not governance, administration, or development of the Internet or its standards.
Email addresses are given only as a contact point for responses; the document is not about email.

gaps.name: OS/2 user group / vendor user organizations
gaps.why: The document is about forming an end-user advocacy group for IBM's OS/2 operating system, a non-Internet-protocol community matter with no fitting taxonomy subject.

RFC1502.title: X.400 Use of Extended Character Sets
RFC1502.summary: RFC 1502 gives guidelines for using the X.400 GeneralText body part to carry ISO 8859, ISO 2022-switched and other extended character sets in X.400 mail, including generation, rendering and character-set selection rules.

X.400.why: The document specifies how the X.400 GeneralText body part should be used in X.400 messaging, so X.400 readers would want it.
X.400.quote: This RFC defines a suggested method of using "GeneralText" in order to harmonize as much as possible the usage of this body part.

character sets.why: A large part of the document recommends which registered character sets (ISO 8859 parts, ISO 6937, multi-byte sets) to designate and how to select them, which is character set registration and use.
character sets.quote: ISO 8859 defines a set of character sets, each suitable for use in some group of languages.

rejected.why: MIME is mentioned as the Internet counterpart and for gateways, but the document is about X.400 GeneralText, not MIME.
ISO 10646 is discussed only as a future character set, not as the subject of the document.
US-ASCII/IA5 is used as the G0 set in the recommendations, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
The GeneralText ASN.1 definition is quoted, but ASN.1 is only the notation, not the subject.
X.400 is the more specific tag for this mail system.

RFC1503.title: Algorithms for Automating Administration in SNMPv2 Managers
RFC1503.summary: Informational memo suggesting algorithms by which an SNMPv2 manager resolves textual context handles to parties/contexts and automatically maintains clock synchronization and secret update knowledge for authenticated communication.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies SNMPv2 manager behaviour: context resolution, party database use, access control entry selection, and automatic maintenance of authentication clock and secrets.
SNMP.quote: it may be desirable for the user to specify the minimum amount of information necessary to establish and maintain SNMPv2 communications.

rejected.why: Party MIB objects are referenced (partyAuthClock etc.) but the document defines no MIB module; it is about manager algorithms.
Parent of SNMP; the specific SNMP tag fits and implies it.
Clock sync and secret update support md5Auth, but the document is about SNMPv2 manager administration, not authentication mechanisms generally.
md5Auth is only a party attribute used in examples; MD5 itself is not discussed.
Domain names are resolved to IP addresses only as an input step in context resolution; not about DNS.

RFC1504.title: Appletalk Update-Based Routing Protocol: Enhanced Appletalk Routing
RFC1504.summary: Informational RFC documenting Apple's AppleTalk Update-based Routing Protocol (AURP), which tunnels AppleTalk over IP and point-to-point links, propagates routing information between exterior routers, and offers network hiding, remapping, clustering and loop detection.

AppleTalk.why: The whole document specifies AURP, an AppleTalk routing and tunnelling protocol, covering AppleTalk tunnelling, RTMP/ZIP replacement, NBP device hiding and DDP hop counts.
AppleTalk.quote: AURP provides wide area routing enhancements to the AppleTalk routing protocols and is fully compatible with AppleTalk Phase 2.

rejected.why: The tunnelling here is AppleTalk-specific (AURP over UDP port 387), not generic IP-in-IP. The AppleTalk tag covers it.
UDP is only the substrate for AURP-Tr packets on IP tunnels.
PPP and ATCP are mentioned as a point-to-point link option and defined in RFC 1378. This document does not specify them.
The SNMP MIB for AURP management is mentioned briefly and the MIB itself is not defined here.
The document specifies one protocol, AppleTalk routing, rather than general routing architecture.

gaps.name: AURP / AppleTalk Update-Based Routing Protocol (and RTMP/ZIP)
gaps.why: The AppleTalk tag listed in the tags does not exist in the taxonomy provided. The closest entry is AppleTalk under internet layer, which I cited from memory of the schema. Please verify that id. If it is absent, this document has no fitting tag: AppleTalk routing is not covered by the routing tags.

RFC1505.title: Encoding Header Field for Internet Messages
RFC1505.summary: RFC 1505 defines an experimental Encoding header field for Internet mail and news messages that divides a body into typed parts, plus the FS file-system encoding and the LZJU90 compressed text encoding.

message format.why: The document specifies a new Internet message header field and its syntax (count, keywords, nesting, comments), extending the RFC 822 message format.
message format.quote: The Encoding header field permits the message body itself to be further broken up into parts, each part also separated from the next by a blank line.

MIME.why: It is an experimental multi-part, multi-encoding body structure mechanism that competes with MIME, which is the standards-track alternative. Readers of MIME would want to find it.
MIME.quote: Note that a standards-track technology already exists in this area [11].

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by message format and MIME, so I did not list it separately.
LZJU90 is specified in detail, but it is one of the encodings defined for this header field. The document is not mainly about compression.
PEM and PGP appear only as encoding keywords. The document does not specify them.
PGP is only a keyword that labels a body part. The document does not define the PGP format.
PEM is only a keyword that labels a body part. The document does not specify PEM.
CRC-32 is used only as an integrity check inside LZJU90. The document does not address the CRC itself.
EDI-X12 and EDIFACT are only keywords for labelling parts. The document does not specify EDI transport.
The document mentions that the field is useful in news, but it is mainly about mail message structure.

gaps.name: file system object encoding (FS)
gaps.why: Section 4 defines a portable encoding of files, directories and their attributes, and the taxonomy has no tag for file archive or encoding formats.

gaps.name: LZJU90 compression/text encoding
gaps.why: Section 5 specifies an LZ77-variant compressor with a 6-bit text armouring, and the taxonomy has no tag for this format.

RFC1506.title: A Tutorial on Gatewaying between X.400 and Internet Mail
RFC1506.summary: An informational tutorial for gateway managers on mapping between X.400 and RFC 822 Internet mail per RFC 1327, covering service elements, address formats, and mapping tables.

X.400.why: The whole document explains X.400 (MHS, P1/P2/P3, O/R addresses) and its gatewaying to Internet mail via RFC 1327, including address mapping tables.
X.400.quote: A Tutorial on Gatewaying between X.400 and Internet Mail

message format.why: A substantial part covers RFC 822 headers, addresses and service element mappings (From/Sender/To etc.) to X.400 IPM headings.
message format.quote: STD 11, RFC 822 defines a standard for the format of Internet text messages.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the 822-MTS underlying transport mentioned in passing (MAIL FROM/RCPT TO mapping); the document is not about it.
Parent of the chosen tags; the more specific X.400 and message format tags fit.
DNS MX/A records are mentioned only as routing prerequisites for mapped domains.
Mentioned only as how X.400 addresses are defined; not a subject of the document.
UUCP and BITNET addresses are mentioned only as other 822-MTS environments reached via gateways.

RFC1507.title: DASS - Distributed Authentication Security Service
RFC1507.summary: Experimental RFC specifying DASS, a public-key (RSA/X.509-style certificate) distributed authentication architecture with delegation, a CA hierarchy tied to X.500 naming, a CDC certificate/credential distribution protocol, and GSSAPI support.

authentication.why: The whole document defines a strong mutual authentication service with tokens, credentials, delegation and login. It is a standalone authentication architecture, not tied to one existing protocol.
authentication.quote: DASS uses cryptographic mechanisms to provide "strong, mutual" authentication.

PKI.why: A large part of the document covers certification authorities, certificate types, cross-certification, tree-walk chain validation and revocation.
PKI.quote: DASS addresses this problem by creating a hierarchy of CAs.  The CA hierarchy is tied to the naming hierarchy.

GSS-API.why: Annex B defines a GSSAPI mechanism over DASS, with its mechanism OID and token wrapping. GSSAPI readers would want this.
GSS-API.quote: This annex explains how the GSSAPI can be implemented using the primitive services provided by DASS.
GSS-API.section: Annex B - Support of the GSSAPI

rejected.why: DASS certificates are defined in terms of X.509 and the ASN.1 is imported from it. The document is about DASS, not about X.509 certificates and profiles.
X.500 is used as the naming service and for principal names. DASS only depends on it for storage and name syntax.
RSA is the underlying cryptosystem the design uses. The document does not specify RSA itself.
Kerberos is mentioned only for comparison and interoperability. The document does not specify it.
ASN.1 is used only as the encoding for the messages.

RFC1508.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface
RFC1508.summary: RFC 1508 defines the mechanism-independent GSS-API: credentials, security contexts, tokens, per-message protection (sign/seal), naming and support calls, so applications can use varied security mechanisms portably.

GSS-API.why: The entire document specifies the GSS-API services and primitives, so it is the core GSS-API specification.
GSS-API.quote: This Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) definition provides security services to callers in a generic fashion, supportable with a range of underlying mechanisms

rejected.why: Kerberos V5 appears only as an example underlying mechanism in Section 3; the document does not specify it.
X.509 is used only as an example public-key mechanism scenario, not profiled or specified.
ASN.1/DER is used only for the optional token framing in Appendix B and does not make the document about ASN.1.
The parent topic is implied by the GSS-API tag, which is the more specific fit.

RFC1509.title: Generic Security Service API : C-bindings
RFC1509.summary: Specifies the C language bindings for the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API), defining data types, status codes, routine prototypes and the gssapi.h header for credentials, security contexts, per-message sign/seal services and names.

GSS-API.why: The whole document defines the C bindings of GSS-API: routines, types, status codes and header file.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies C language bindings for the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API)

rejected.why: Object identifiers are BER-encoded, but this is incidental to the C type definitions.
Only SPX is mentioned, as an example mechanism; Kerberos is not discussed.
GSS-API is the more specific tag and covers the authentication services provided.
SPX is mentioned only as an example mechanism OID, not specified.

RFC1510.title: The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)
RFC1510.summary: RFC 1510 specifies Version 5 of the Kerberos network authentication service: its tickets, AS/TGS/AP exchanges, KRB_SAFE/PRIV/CRED messages, ASN.1 message formats, DES-based encryption and checksum types, realm and principal naming, and interoperability requirements.

Kerberos.why: The whole document specifies the Kerberos V5 protocol, including its exchanges, message formats, database and interoperability requirements.
Kerberos.quote: This document gives an overview and specification of Version 5 of the protocol for the Kerberos network authentication system.

rejected.why: ASN.1 with Distinguished Encoding is only the encoding used for the Kerberos messages. The document does not define ASN.1 itself.
DES in CBC mode is the cipher used in the encryption types. It is a building block of Kerberos, and the document is not about DES.
MD4, MD5 and CRC-32 are used as checksums inside Kerberos encryption and checksum types. The document does not specify them.
This is the generic parent topic. The Kerberos tech tag is more specific and already implies it.
Kerberos does distribute session keys. The document is about the authentication service as a whole, and the Kerberos tag covers that.
KDC requests are sent over UDP port 88 (section 8.2.1). This is only transport, with no new UDP definition.

RFC1511.title: Common Authentication Technology Overview
RFC1511.summary: Informational overview of the IETF CAT working group's work: the GSS-API common security service interface and its C bindings, plus candidate underlying mechanisms (Kerberos V5 and DASS).

GSS-API.why: The document's central subject is the GSS-API as a mechanism-independent interface for security services, and its related RFCs (1508, 1509).
GSS-API.quote: the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface, or GSS-API), allowing callers to invoke security functions

Kerberos.why: Kerberos V5 is presented as one of the two candidate mechanisms realizing the GSS-API, so readers of Kerberos would want this overview.
Kerberos.quote: RFC-1510, a standards-track specification, documents the Kerberos Version 5 technology, based on secret-key cryptography

rejected.why: DASS is based on X.509 public-key technology, but this is mentioned only in passing and the document does not address X.509 certificates.
The document is about authentication, but the more specific GSS-API tag covers it, so the parent topic is not listed separately.
This is the general parent topic. It is implied by the specific tags and the document is not about general security guidance.

gaps.name: Distributed Authentication Security Service (DASS)
gaps.why: RFC 1507 is described as a candidate GSS-API mechanism based on X.509 public-key technology. The taxonomy has no tag for DASS.

RFC1512.title: FDDI Management Information Base
RFC1512.summary: RFC 1512 defines the SNMP MIB module (FDDI-SMT73-MIB) for managing FDDI devices based on ANSI FDDI SMT 7.3, with SMT, MAC, enhanced MAC counters, PATH and PORT groups, updating RFC 1285.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification defining managed objects for FDDI interfaces using the SMI. Readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

FDDI.why: The managed objects cover FDDI station management: SMT, MAC, PATH and PORT, ring state machines and link error monitoring. It belongs on the IP over FDDI page.
FDDI.quote: it defines objects for managing devices which implement the FDDI based on the ANSI FDDI SMT 7.3 draft standard

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol the MIB is designed for. The document defines objects only and does not specify or extend the protocol, so MIB is the more specific fit.
The MIB is written in the ASN.1 subset of the SMI, but that is only the notation used. The document is not about ASN.1.
The parent topic is implied by the MIB tag, and no separate broader subject is addressed.

RFC1513.title: Token Ring Extensions to the Remote Network Monitoring MIB
RFC1513.summary: Defines the Token Ring extensions to the RMON MIB (statistics, history, ring station, station order, station config and source routing groups) for monitoring 802.5 Token Ring networks.

RMON.why: The document extends RMON (RFC 1271) with Token Ring-specific statistics and history groups plus new monitoring groups.
RMON.quote: This memo defines extensions to the Remote Network Monitoring MIB for managing 802.5 Token Ring networks.

MIB.why: The bulk of the document is a MIB module in SMI with tables and objects for Token Ring monitoring.
MIB.quote: TOKEN-RING-RMON-MIB DEFINITIONS ::= BEGIN

token ring.why: The subject is managing IEEE 802.5 Token Ring LANs, including MAC-layer errors, ring stations and source routing.
token ring.quote: These are defined in the Ring Station Group, the Ring Station Order Group, the Ring Station Configuration Group, and the Source Routing Statistics Group.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol of the management framework; the document defines MIB objects, not SNMP itself.
ASN.1 is used only as the notation for the MIB definitions.

RFC1514.title: Host Resources MIB
RFC1514.summary: Defines the Host Resources MIB, an SNMP MIB module with objects for managing host computers: system, storage, devices, file systems, running and installed software.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (HOST-RESOURCES-MIB) written in SMI. Readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a MIB for use with managing host systems.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to access the objects. The document only defines a MIB module and does not specify or extend the protocol, so the more specific MIB tag fits.
ASN.1 is only the syntax notation underlying the SMI definitions, not the subject.
NFS and other file system types appear only as OID registrations for hrFSType values.
The storage group describes local host storage areas for monitoring. It does not cover storage access protocols over IP.

RFC1515.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs)
RFC1515.summary: Defines a MIB module of SNMP managed objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (repeater MAUs, interface MAUs and broadband MAUs), including MAU type identifiers and jabber traps.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (MAU-MIB) written in SMI, defining tables and traps for 802.3 MAUs. Readers browsing MIB modules would expect it.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs).

Ethernet.why: The managed objects describe IEEE 802.3 Ethernet physical attachment units (10BASE-T, 10BASE5, FOIRL and others). It is closely tied to the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB and the 802.3 Repeater MIB.
Ethernet.quote: These MAUs may be connected to IEEE 802.3 repeaters or to 802.3 (Ethernet-like) interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP and the SMI are the management framework the MIB is written for, and the document does not extend the protocol itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB, not a subject of the document.
The Ethernet tag is more specific, and the document is about management objects rather than the link layer in general.

RFC1516.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Repeater Devices
RFC1516.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module (SNMP-REPEATER-MIB) for managing IEEE 802.3 10 Mb/s baseband repeaters, with basic, monitor and address-tracking groups plus traps; obsoletes RFC 1368.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition, with managed objects, tables and traps for repeaters, written in SMI. MIB is the most specific tag.
MIB.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing IEEE 802.3 10 Mb/second baseband repeaters, sometimes referred to as "hubs."

Ethernet.why: The managed objects model IEEE 802.3 repeater units, ports, collisions, FCS errors and runts, so readers interested in Ethernet management would want this RFC.
Ethernet.quote: Instances of the object types defined in this memo represent attributes of an IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet-like) repeater

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects. The document defines a MIB, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag covers it.
The MIB is written in ASN.1 via the SMI, but ASN.1 is only the notation used and is not what the document is about.

RFC1517.title: Applicability Statement for the Implementation of Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)
RFC1517.summary: IESG applicability statement requiring backbone/transit IPv4 domains to implement CIDR to slow routing table growth and conserve address space, pointing to the CIDR architecture and address allocation documents.

CIDR.why: The whole document states when and by whom CIDR must be implemented, so it is about CIDR and aggregation.
CIDR.quote: The CIDR architecture is applicable to any group of connected domains that supports IP version 4

rejected.why: IPv4 is only the protocol CIDR applies to; the document does not specify or extend IPv4.
Inter-domain routing protocols are mentioned but the statement explicitly does not mandate any particular one.
CIDR is the more specific tag covering routing table scaling here.

RFC1518.title: An Architecture for IP Address Allocation with CIDR
RFC1518.summary: RFC 1518 describes an architecture for hierarchical, topology-based IP address allocation (CIDR) to enable route aggregation and scaling of inter-domain routing, including multi-homing, private links, and transition issues.

CIDR.why: The document is the CIDR address allocation architecture, assigning prefixes hierarchically along provider topology to permit aggregation.
CIDR.quote: This paper provides an architecture and a plan for allocating IP addresses in the Internet.

multihoming.why: A substantial section compares four addressing approaches for multi-homed domains, with their routing and policy tradeoffs.
multihoming.quote: There are additional considerations for routing domains which are attached to multiple providers. Such "multi-homed" routing domains

renumbering.why: Discusses changing addresses when topology or provider changes, and how longest-match routing eases the transition.
renumbering.quote: a gradual transition is required in which both the old and the new addresses will remain valid for a limited period of time

rejected.why: Routing scalability is the motivation, but the document is about address allocation, and CIDR is the more specific tag.
Inter-domain routing is discussed generically; no routing protocol is specified or analysed.
This is the parent of CIDR, which is already tagged.
The addresses are IPv4, but the document is about allocation and aggregation, not the protocol or its address lifecycle.

RFC1519.title: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR): an Address Assignment and Aggregation Strategy
RFC1519.summary: RFC 1519 specifies CIDR, a classless address assignment and route aggregation strategy that allocates blocks of addresses to service providers, with rules for inter-domain route advertisement and IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation changes.

CIDR.why: The whole document defines CIDR: classless prefix allocation to providers and aggregation of routes using network/mask pairs and longest-match.
CIDR.quote: The proposed solution is to topologically allocate future IP address assignment, by allocating segments of the IP address space to the transit routing domains.

rejected.why: Inter-domain routing protocol changes are discussed generically, with no BGP-specific specification.
Section 7 covers IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation on non-octet boundaries, but it is a secondary consequence of the allocation plan and not the document's subject.
Aggregation and routing table scaling are covered, but CIDR is the more specific tag.
Mentioned only as an example of an IGP that supports classless routes.
Multi-homed sites are discussed as a limit on aggregation, not as the subject.
The plan applies to the IPv4 address space, but CIDR captures the topic more specifically.

RFC1520.title: Exchanging Routing Information Across Provider Boundaries in the CIDR Environment
RFC1520.summary: Informational guidance on how CIDR-capable and CIDR-incapable service providers should exchange inter-domain routing information (default routes, aggregation, controlled de-aggregation) during the transition to CIDR, plus implications for interior routing.

CIDR.why: The whole document is about the transition to CIDR and how aggregation and de-aggregation of CIDR reachability information is handled between CIDR-capable and non-CIDR providers.
CIDR.quote: it describes various alternatives for exchanging inter-domain routing information across domain boundaries, where one of the peering domain is CIDR-capable and another is not.

BGP.why: The document addresses running CIDR-capable inter-domain protocols (BGP-4) across provider boundaries, including internal BGP and the ATOMIC_AGGREGATE attribute, so BGP readers would want it.
BGP.quote: all the providers that can't rely on using Default route(s) for inter-domain routing (Type 1 providers) are expected to deploy BGP-4 and transition to CIDR
BGP.section: 3. Assumptions on Deployment of CIDR in the Internet

rejected.why: IDRP is mentioned alongside BGP but is not in the taxonomy and is not a major focus.
OSPF is only named as one CIDR-capable IGP option in the interior routing section; no OSPF specification is provided.
The document is about operational transition arrangements between providers, which is covered by the more specific CIDR and BGP tags.
Mentioned only as an example CIDR-capable IGP.

RFC1521.title: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) Part One: Mechanisms for Specifying and Describing the Format of Internet Message Bodies
RFC1521.summary: RFC 1521 specifies MIME Part One: the MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-ID and Content-Description header fields, the seven top-level content types (text, multipart, message, application, image, audio, video), quoted-printable and base64 encodings, and the IANA registration procedures for new types.

MIME.why: The whole document defines MIME: header fields, content types, multipart structure and transfer encodings for Internet message bodies.
MIME.quote: This document redefines the format of message bodies to allow multi-part textual and non-textual message bodies to be represented and exchanged without loss of information.

media types.why: It defines the content-type/subtype model, the initial predefined types and the registration templates (Appendix E) for new type/subtype values.
media types.quote: New standard values must be documented, registered with, and approved by IANA, as described in Appendix E.

Base64.why: It specifies the base64 alphabet and encoding algorithm, which is the original definition of this encoding for mail. The Quoted-Printable encoding is specified alongside it.
Base64.quote: The Base64 Content-Transfer-Encoding is designed to represent arbitrary sequences of octets in a form that need not be humanly readable.

rejected.why: MIME is a mail body format, but the more specific MIME tag covers it. Message format and SMTP are the substrate.
The document is largely orthogonal to RFC 822 header format; it defines body structure, which MIME covers.
SMTP is only the transport whose 7-bit limits motivate the encodings. The document does not specify it.
The charset parameter and a few names are defined, but this is a small part of the document and not its subject.
The registration procedures in Appendix E are specific to MIME types and are covered by the media types tag.
FTP and TFTP appear only as access-types for message/external-body.

RFC1522.title: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) Part Two: Message Header Extensions for Non-ASCII Text
RFC1522.summary: RFC 1522 defines "encoded-words" (Q and B encodings with a charset label) that let non-ASCII text appear in RFC 822 message headers, and sets out how mail composers and readers handle them.

MIME.why: The document is Part Two of MIME. It extends MIME to message headers through encoded-words, the Q and B encodings, and charset labelling.
MIME.quote: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) Part Two: Message Header Extensions for Non-ASCII Text

message format.why: It amends the RFC 822 grammar for comment and phrase and says where in headers encoded-words may appear. That is a change to Internet message header format.
message format.quote: An encoded-word may replace a "text" token (as defined by RFC 822) in any Subject or Comments header field
message format.section: 5. Use of encoded-words in message headers

rejected.why: The B encoding is simply defined as identical to the RFC 1521 BASE64 encoding. The document only reuses it.
The document uses charset names as labels in encoded-words, and it does not register or define character sets.
The document does address non-ASCII text in headers. The more specific MIME and message format tags already cover it.
This is the parent of MIME and message format. The more specific tags are chosen instead.
ASCII is the target representation that encoded-words are built from. The document is not about ASCII itself.
ABNF is used only as notation for the grammar.

RFC1523.title: The text/enriched MIME Content-type
RFC1523.summary: Defines the text/enriched MIME subtype, a simple formatted-text markup (bold, italic, justification, indentation, verbatim, param) refining text/richtext, with parsing rules, conformance and a sample C converter.

media types.why: The document defines and specifies a new MIME text subtype, including its parameter and semantics, which is a media type definition.
media types.quote: This document defines a new MIME content-type, "text/enriched". The content-type line for this type may have one optional parameter, the "charset" parameter

MIME.why: It extends MIME with a new body format and discusses its use inside multipart/alternative and relation to text/richtext, so MIME readers would want it.
MIME.quote: MIME [RFC-1341, RFC-1521] defines a format and general framework for the representation of a wide variety of data types in Internet mail.

rejected.why: Email is the carrier for the content type, but the document specifies a body format, not mail transport or access.
text/enriched is a hypertext-like markup but not HTML or part of its family; it is a simple formatted text type for mail.
Charset handling for non-ASCII text is discussed briefly, but only as a subsidiary consideration.
The document only notes that SGML compatibility claims were dropped.
ASCII is the default character set and used for commands, not the subject.

gaps.name: text/enriched rich text markup
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers simple formatted-text markup formats for mail; media types is the closest fit.

RFC1524.title: A User Agent Configuration Mechanism For Multimedia Mail Format Information
RFC1524.summary: RFC 1524 defines the mailcap file format that lets multiple mail user agents find locally installed programs to view, compose, edit and print MIME body parts by content-type, with UNIX semantics in an appendix.

MIME.why: The mailcap mechanism maps MIME content-types to handler programs for body parts. The document is about handling MIME-typed mail content, including Content-Type parameters, compose and Content-Transfer-Encoding behaviour.
MIME.quote: they consult an external file for information on how to display that file. That file might say, for example, that if the content-type of a message is "foo"

email.why: It is a configuration mechanism for mail user agents (readers and composers), so it belongs under email architecture and user agent behaviour.
email.quote: This memo suggests a file format to be used to inform multiple mail reading user agent programs about the locally-installed facilities for handling mail

rejected.why: The document does not register media types or set registry rules. It only matches on existing types.
It refers to RFC 822 headers only incidentally. The subject is the local handler configuration file, not the message format.
It uses a modified BNF to define the mailcap syntax, but this is a tool for the spec and not the subject.
Mail transport is not addressed. The document only mentions RFC 821 as context.

RFC1525.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Source Routing Bridges
RFC1525.summary: Defines a SNMP MIB module (dot1dSr and dot1dPortPair groups) for managing source routing and source routing transparent bridges, obsoleting the SR portion of RFC 1286.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is a MIB module with managed objects for source routing bridges, defined in SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines objects needed for management of a source routing bridge, and is an extension to the SNMP Bridge MIB [6].

token ring.why: Source routing bridging is a token ring (IEEE 802.5) bridging technique, and the MIB covers its objects such as explorer frames and routing descriptors. This is a weaker fit than the MIB tag.
token ring.quote: Source route bridging has been defined by I.B.M. and is described in the Token Ring Architecture Reference [12]

rejected.why: SNMP is only the protocol used to access the objects. The document defines MIB objects, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB definitions.
The document covers source-route and transparent bridging, which is not specific to Ethernet. Bridging is only generally related.

gaps.name: Source routing bridges / MAC bridging (IEEE 802.1D, 802.5M SRT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for link-layer bridging or the Bridge MIB, which is the real subject domain of this document.

RFC1526.title: Assignment of System Identifiers for TUBA/CLNP Hosts
RFC1526.summary: Informational memo defining conventions for assigning 6-octet (and other length) system identifiers in RFC 1237 NSAP addresses for TUBA/CLNP, including embedding IP addresses in IEEE 802-compatible IDs, to support autoconfiguration.

CLNP.why: The document specifies how system identifiers in OSI NSAP addresses used by CLNP hosts are assigned and encoded, including autoconfiguration.
CLNP.quote: the system identifier portion of an RFC 1237 style NSAP address may be guaranteed uniqueness within a routing domain for the purpose of autoconfiguration in TUBA/CLNP internets

IPng.why: TUBA is one of the historic IPng candidates, and the memo supports TUBA addressing and autoconfiguration.
IPng.quote: autoconfiguration of NSAP addresses in TUBA/CLNP internets [2]

rejected.why: IS-IS is referenced for ID length rules and the ID/SEL structure, but the document does not specify or extend it.
The document is about addressing, but the more specific CLNP tag covers it. The embedded IP address is only a way to encode the ID.
CLNP is the more specific child tag. The document is about NSAP addresses for CLNP rather than OSI in general.
IEEE 802 addresses are used as a source of identifiers. The document does not cover IP over Ethernet.

RFC1527.title: What Should We Plan Given the Dilemma of the Network?
RFC1527.summary: An informational essay by Gordon Cook offering a policy framework for Congress on the NREN, covering regulation, access, commercialization, and a proposed Corporation for Public Networking.

rejected.why: It touches on Internet growth statistics and NSFnet commercialization, but it is a forward-looking policy proposal, not a history or retrospective.
The memo discusses governance, funding and access policy, not architectural principles of the Internet.
ATM and SONET are mentioned only in passing as possible future backbone technologies in a funding debate.
ISDN is mentioned once as an EFF proposal for affordable access. The document is not about it.

The taxonomy defines this as governance of the Internet and its standards development. This memo covers US federal funding and regulatory policy for the NREN. That is a loose fit, and no child tag applies.

gaps.name: Network policy / NREN public policy and regulation
gaps.why: The whole document is US national network policy: regulation, universal access, funding and governance of the NREN. The taxonomy has no tag for public policy or regulation.

RFC1528.title: Principles of Operation for the TPC.INT Subdomain: Remote Printing -- Technical Procedures
RFC1528.summary: RFC 1528 specifies a remote printing service in which MIME email is sent to addresses under the tpc.int DNS subdomain, derived from reversed telephone numbers, and relayed to G3 fax devices, including a cover-sheet content type and return receipts.

fax.why: The service delivers Internet mail to G3-facsimile devices via a remote printer server, with cover sheets and delivery receipts. Fax over Internet mail is the core subject.
fax.quote: this memo focuses on the case in which remote printers are connected to the international telephone network.

ENUM.why: Telephone numbers are mapped into the DNS by reversed-digit labels, with wildcard MX records for routing. This is a precursor to ENUM-style E.164 mapping, and readers of that subject would want it.
ENUM.quote: the domain-part is constructed by reversing the telephone number, converting each digit to a domain-label, and being placed under "tpc.int."

media types.why: The document registers the application/remote-printing and image/tiff media types in its appendices.
media types.quote: The "application/remote-printing" content-type contains originator and recipient information used when generating a cover-sheet.

rejected.why: Mail is the transport for the service. The document is not about mail architecture itself, and fax is the more specific tag.
The document uses multipart/mixed and defines two content types, but the MIME mechanisms themselves are only relied on. The media types tag covers the registrations.
MX records and wildcards are used for routing, but no new DNS behaviour is defined beyond the naming scheme, which is covered by ENUM.
Normal mail routing is used. Nothing about SMTP is specified or extended.
The document is about printing, but it uses email and fax. It has no relation to the Internet Printing Protocol.

gaps.name: Remote printing / TPC.INT subdomain
gaps.why: The document's main subject is Internet-mail-based remote printing via the tpc.int subdomain. The taxonomy has no remote printing tag. Only fax and ENUM approximate it.

RFC1529.title: Principles of Operation for the TPC.INT Subdomain: Remote Printing -- Administrative Policies
RFC1529.summary: RFC 1529 sets out administrative policies (resource-recovery models, audit logging and privacy, denial of access) for operators of remote printer servers that deliver email as G3 fax in the tpc.int subdomain.

fax.why: The document is about the policies for operating an email-to-G3-fax gateway service. Readers browsing fax over Internet mail would expect it.
fax.quote: The remote printing facility allows a user to image documents on a remote printer, defined as a G3-compatible facsimile device connected to the public telephone network.
fax.section: Overview of Remote Printing in the TPC.INT Subdomain

rejected.why: The Domain Name System is only the routing mechanism for the tpc.int subdomain. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
Email is the substrate used to submit requests. The document is about gateway administrative policy, not mail protocols.
The log-retention and privacy rules are part of the operator policy. They are not a protocol privacy analysis, so this is not a general privacy topic document.

gaps.name: TPC.INT remote printing administrative policy
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for operator policies or service administration of the tpc.int fax gateway, such as cost-recovery models, audit logging and denial of access.

RFC1530.title: Principles of Operation for the TPC.INT Subdomain: General Principles and Policy
RFC1530.summary: Informational RFC setting out the general principles and governance policy of the tpc.int DNS subdomain, a cooperative that maps telephone number prefixes to remote fax/printer gateways via MX records in the DNS.

fax.why: The tpc.int service exists to provide Internet-to-fax (remote printing) gateways over Internet mail. Readers browsing fax would expect it.
fax.quote: a remote printing service is defined which ties together G3-compatible facsimile devices on the telephone network with users of electronic mail in the Internet

ENUM.why: Maps telephone number prefixes to hosts via DNS names under tpc.int, a precursor of telephone numbers in the DNS. The document gives the MX record naming scheme with examples.
ENUM.quote: registers itself in the DNS as being willing to provide access to some portion of the telephone system numbering plan as registered by one or more MX records
ENUM.section: Operation of Name Service in the TPC.INT Subdomain

DNS.why: Defines an administered DNS subdomain with MX registration, record ordering rotation and small TTLs. Substantial DNS operational policy.
DNS.quote: the DNS MX resource record is used to register those Internet sites that provide access to the remote printing facility
DNS.section: Operation of Name Service in the TPC.INT Subdomain

rejected.why: Remote printing runs over Internet mail (RFC 822, MIME), but mail is the substrate, not the subject. The document specifies no mail behaviour.
Sites register in tpc.int, but this is cooperative policy for a service namespace, not registry or registrar operations or protocols.
Only cited as a base for the mail transport; not discussed.
The Board of Arbitration and Conciliation governs only this subdomain cooperative, not the Internet or IETF standards.
Considered, since the subdomain is a listing of services. It is better covered by the specific DNS and ENUM tags.

RFC1531.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
RFC1531.summary: RFC 1531 specifies the original Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, a BOOTP-based client-server protocol for delivering IP configuration parameters and dynamically allocating leased network addresses to hosts.

DHCP.why: The entire document defines DHCP: message format, client-server exchanges, lease handling, server and client behaviour and the client state machine.
DHCP.quote: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) provides a framework for passing configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network.

rejected.why: DHCP only uses UDP as its transport (ports 67/68); the document defines nothing new about UDP.
ARP is used only for address-in-use probing and announcements by the client, not specified or extended here.
Address allocation is handled through DHCP itself, so the DHCP tag is the more specific fit.
This is the IPv4 DHCP specification from 1993; DHCPv6 does not exist yet and is not covered.
TFTP is mentioned only as related work for boot image transfer.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol) and BOOTP relay agents
gaps.why: DHCP is built on BOOTP and captures relay agent behaviour, but the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag, so the DHCP tag covers this.

RFC1532.title: Clarifications and Extensions for the Bootstrap Protocol
RFC1532.summary: RFC 1532 clarifies and extends the BOOTP specification (RFC 951), defining the 'flags' BROADCAST bit, client, relay agent and server behaviour, and BOOTP over token ring.

DHCP.why: BOOTP is the predecessor of DHCP, and the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag. DHCP is the closest fit. The memo states its requirements also apply to DHCP, and DHC working group produced it. It specifies relay agent behaviour that DHCP relies on.
DHCP.quote: This memo attempts to clarify and strengthen the specification in these areas.

rejected.why: Section 2.4 gives token ring guidance for BOOTP, but it is a small part of the memo and not about IP over token ring generally.
BOOTP runs over UDP, which is only the substrate here.
ARP is used for hardware address handling, but the memo is not about ARP.
The memo concerns IPv4 BOOTP/DHCP only.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: The memo is about BOOTP, its relay agents, and its client and server behaviour. The taxonomy has no BOOTP tag, so DHCP is used as the nearest one.

RFC1533.title: DHCP Options and BOOTP Vendor Extensions
RFC1533.summary: RFC 1533 specifies the set of DHCP options (and BOOTP vendor extensions), defining the tag-length-value option format and each option's code, length and meaning.

DHCP.why: The whole document defines DHCP options, including DHCP-specific ones such as message type, lease time, and client identifier.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies the current set of DHCP options.

rejected.why: Domain name server and domain name options only carry DNS configuration; the document does not specify DNS.
NetBIOS name server, node type and scope options are just a few of many configuration options, not the subject.
The NTP servers option merely conveys server addresses.
Font server and display manager options only convey addresses of X services.
Section 10 on registering new options is brief and not the main subject.
This is DHCP for IPv4 only, not DHCPv6.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol) vendor extensions
gaps.why: The document obsoletes RFC 1497 and defines BOOTP vendor information extensions, but the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag.

RFC1534.title: Interoperation Between DHCP and BOOTP
RFC1534.summary: Specifies how DHCP servers and clients interoperate with BOOTP clients and servers, including address assignment, infinite leases and message formation.

DHCP.why: The whole document defines DHCP server and client behaviour when interacting with BOOTP participants, including automatic addresses, lease handling and BOOTREPLY formation.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies the ways in which DHCP and BOOTP participants may interoperate.

rejected.why: The document covers only DHCP for IPv4, not DHCPv6.
IPv4 addresses are what is assigned, but the document is about DHCP/BOOTP interoperation, not IPv4 itself.
Address allocation is discussed only as part of DHCP server behaviour toward BOOTP clients, and the DHCP tag already covers it.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is substantially about BOOTP interoperation, and the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag. DHCP is the closest fit.

RFC1535.title: A Security Problem and Proposed Correction With Widely Deployed DNS Software
RFC1535.summary: Informational memo describing a security flaw in BIND-derived DNS resolvers' implicit search-list heuristic for partial names, which allows spoofing via domains like edu.com, and recommending limiting search lists to locally administered domains.

DNS.why: The whole document concerns DNS resolver client behaviour (search list handling of partial names) and recommends changes to it, including the BIND 4.9.2 behaviour.
DNS.quote: At a minimum, DNS resolvers must honor the BOUNDARY between local and public administration, by limiting any search lists to locally-administered portions of the Domain Name space.

rejected.why: Partial hostnames are discussed, but the subject is resolver search behaviour in DNS, not host naming conventions or host tables.
The spoofing problem is a resolver search-list flaw, not about signing or validation; DNSSEC is not mentioned.
The DNS tag is more specific and ancestors are implied.
The security issue is specific to DNS resolver behaviour, which is already covered by the DNS tag; the document isn't about general operational security practice.

RFC1536.title: Common DNS Implementation Errors and Suggested Fixes
RFC1536.summary: Informational memo cataloguing common DNS resolver and name server implementation errors (fast retransmission, recursion loops, zero-answer, dead-server detection, cache leaks, name errors, format errors) with suggested fixes and BIND examples.

DNS.why: The whole document is about DNS resolver and server behaviour, including retransmission, caching, negative caching and search lists, and cites RFC 1034/1035 violations.
DNS.quote: This memo describes common errors seen in DNS implementations and suggests some fixes.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport DNS queries use; the document does not specify or analyse UDP itself.
NOTIFY/PUSH and incremental zone transfer are mentioned only briefly as a fix, not as dynamic update.
Backoff and retransmission are discussed for DNS clients to limit traffic, but the document is about DNS implementation bugs, not congestion control.

RFC1537.title: Common DNS Data File Configuration Errors
RFC1537.summary: Informational memo listing common mistakes in DNS zone data files (SOA timers, glue records, MX and wildcard records, hostnames, HINFO, localhost/in-addr.arpa zones) and giving advice on nameserver placement and naming-authority practice.

DNS.why: The whole document is operational guidance on DNS zone file configuration: SOA timers, glue, MX, HINFO, secondary servers and reverse zones.
DNS.quote: This memo describes errors often found in DNS data files. It points out common mistakes system administrators tend to make

rejected.why: Section 11 discusses naming authority and registrar conduct, but this is a minor part of a document focused on zone file errors.
Section 8 touches hostname syntax briefly, but the document is not about hostname conventions or host tables.
MX records are discussed only as DNS records and their zone file pitfalls, not mail architecture or transport.
Although it is operational advice, the subject is specifically DNS, which is the more specific tag.

RFC1538.title: Advanced SNA/IP : A Simple SNA Transport Protocol
RFC1538.summary: Informational RFC documenting Advanced SNA/IP, a McDATA/I/O Concepts protocol that carries SNA sessions over IP using UDP datagrams for XID-based connection setup and TCP for session data transfer.

SNA.why: The whole document specifies how SNA sessions between gateways and downstream nodes are transported over IP, so it belongs under IBM SNA interworking.
SNA.quote: a method for establishing and maintaining SNA sessions over an IP internet

DLSw.why: The document positions SNA/IP as an alternative to DLSw (RFC 1434) and discusses LLC-to-IP conversion and a data link switch function, so DLSw readers would want it. It is related but not the main subject.
DLSw.quote: an SNA/IP-based "subnet SNA gateway" application could do many of the things being discussed in the context of the DLSw specification

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable transport substrate for SNA data; the document does not extend or analyse TCP.
UDP datagrams carry the logical XID exchange, but this is a use of UDP as a substrate, not a UDP specification or usage guideline.
The I/O Concepts X-Direct TN3270 Server is mentioned only as one implementation; the document does not specify TN3270.
Carrying SNA over TCP/UDP is a transport mapping in a loose sense, but the more specific SNA tag already covers it.
Token-ring LLC is background motivation for the design; the document is not about IP over token ring.

RFC1539.title: The Tao of IETF - A Guide for New Attendees of the Internet Engineering Task Force
RFC1539.summary: FYI 17 (RFC 1539), an introductory guide for newcomers to IETF meetings, explaining IETF structure (ISOC, IAB, IESG, Areas, WGs), mailing lists, registration, meeting etiquette, proceedings, document archives, and the RFC/FYI/STD/I-D series.

user guides.why: This is an FYI introductory guide for newcomers to the IETF, which is exactly the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: The purpose of this For Your Information (FYI) RFC is to explain to the newcomers how the IETF works.

IETF process.why: It explains IETF organization, Areas, Working Groups, BOFs, IESG and the standards track, plus meeting procedures and how to participate.
IETF process.quote: A Working Group is a group of people who work under a charter to achieve a certain goal.

RFC series.why: A substantial section describes the RFC series, FYI, STD and RTR sub-series, and Internet-Drafts.
RFC series.quote: there are now two special sub-series within the RFCs: FYIs and STDs.

rejected.why: The 'Humble Beginnings' section gives a brief history of IETF meetings, but it is a small part of a how-to guide, not a history.
Anonymous FTP is only mentioned as a way to retrieve documents; the document is not about FTP.
The tag covers mailing list protocols and headers; this document only describes IETF mailing lists to join, not list protocols.
The tone is light, but it is a genuine guide and not a whimsical or April 1st RFC.

RFC1540.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1540.summary: RFC 1540 is the quarterly IAB list of Internet Official Protocol Standards (STD 1), explaining the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and listing protocols by state.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity states, requirement levels and RFC processing decision table, and lists the state of each protocol.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial section describes the RFC series, how to submit documents and the RFC Editor's processing table, and the memo is the reference for which RFC is current for each protocol.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: Assigned Numbers and the IANA contact are mentioned, but the document is not about IANA registries.
Issued by the IAB, but it catalogues protocol standards status rather than discussing architectural principles.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but this is process vocabulary within the standards-track description, not a glossary document.
TCP and many other protocols appear only as entries in the status lists; the document is not about any of them.

gaps.name: Internet standards status list / STD index
gaps.why: The document is the periodic roster of protocol standards and their maturity status. The taxonomy has no tag for standards status listings apart from the general IETF process tag.

RFC1541.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
RFC1541.summary: RFC 1541 specifies the original Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, a BOOTP-based client-server protocol for delivering host configuration parameters and dynamically allocating IP addresses with leases (reissue of RFC 1531).

DHCP.why: The whole document specifies DHCP: message format, client-server exchanges, lease allocation, server and client behavior and state machine.
DHCP.quote: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) provides a framework for passing configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network.

rejected.why: DHCP only uses UDP ports 67/68 as transport; nothing new is defined about UDP.
ARP is only used for address-in-use probing and announcements, not specified here.
Mentioned only in related work as a boot image transport.
DHCP allocates IPv4 addresses, but the document is about configuration protocol, not IP itself.
Document explicitly says DHCP does not address DNS registration.
Address allocation is part of DHCP, which is already tagged via the technology tag.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: DHCP is built on BOOTP message format and relay agent behavior; the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag.

RFC1542.title: Clarifications and Extensions for the Bootstrap Protocol
RFC1542.summary: RFC 1542 clarifies and extends the BOOTP specification, defining the 'flags' BROADCAST bit, client/server behaviour, relay agent rules, and BOOTP over token ring.

DHCP.why: BOOTP is the predecessor of DHCP and the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag; the document states its requirements also apply to DHCP and specifies relay agent and server behaviour that DHCP relies on. DHCP is the closest fitting tag.
DHCP.quote: The Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP) is a UDP/IP-based protocol which allows a booting host to configure itself dynamically and without user supervision.

token ring.why: A dedicated section specifies how BOOTP operates over token ring (RIF handling, chaddr bit ordering), which readers of IP over token ring would want.
token ring.quote: Special consideration of the client/server and client/relay agent interactions must be given to IEEE 802.5 networks because of non-transparent bridging.
token ring.section: 2.4 BOOTP Over IEEE 802.5 Token Ring Networks

rejected.why: BOOTP merely runs over UDP; the document does not specify UDP usage beyond port numbers and checksum recalculation.
ARP is referenced for chaddr bit ordering and cache entries, but the document is not about ARP.
Only mentioned in the 'silently discard' definition and router discovery reference.
Mentioned only as an example of a subsequent boot-file transfer.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about BOOTP, but the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag; DHCP is used as the nearest fit.

RFC1543.title: Instructions to RFC Authors
RFC1543.summary: RFC 1543 gives authors instructions for preparing RFCs: editorial policy, ASCII and PostScript format rules, headers, required sections, UPDATES/OBSOLETES terminology, and contact and distribution details.

RFC series.why: The whole document covers the format, style, editorial policy and publication of the RFC series, which is the subject of this tag.
RFC series.quote: This Request for Comments (RFC) provides information about the preparation of RFCs, and certain policies relating to the publication of RFCs.

rejected.why: The document requires ASCII as the RFC text format, but it is about RFC preparation, not the ASCII character set.
It mentions the IESG and IETF working groups as a source of RFCs, but only briefly. The document is about the RFC series, not the IETF standards process.
The appendix includes RFC 1149 as a sample memo. That is only an example of the nroff format, not the subject of the document.
The document has no IPR or copyright content.

RFC1544.title: The Content-MD5 Header Field
RFC1544.summary: Defines the optional Content-MD5 header field for MIME messages, carrying a base64-encoded MD5 digest of a leaf entity's decoded data as an accidental-modification integrity check.

MIME.why: The document defines a new MIME header field and how it is generated and processed for MIME entities, so MIME readers would want it.
MIME.quote: this memo defines the use of an optional header field, Content-MD5, which may be used as a message integrity check (MIC)

MD5.why: It specifies how the MD5 digest is computed over canonical data and encoded for use as an integrity check. The MD5 algorithm itself is defined elsewhere (RFC 1321), but the use of MD5 here is a substantial part of the document.
MD5.quote: This memo specifies how the algorithm may be used as an integrity check for MIME mail.

rejected.why: The field is carried in email, but the subject here is the MIME header field. MIME is the more specific tag.
It adds a header field, but within the MIME framework, not the base RFC 822 message format.
Privacy-Enhanced Mail is mentioned only as the alternative for secure integrity, not specified here.
Base64 is just the encoding for the digest value, so it is a substrate and not a subject of the document.

RFC1545.title: FTP Operation Over Big Address Records (FOOBAR)
RFC1545.summary: Experimental RFC defining the FTP LPRT and LPSV commands and reply codes 228 and 521, which allow long network and transport addresses in FTP data connections for IP next-generation alternatives and other protocol families.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with new LPRT and LPSV commands and new reply codes, so it is about FTP.
FTP.quote: This RFC specifies a method for assigning long addresses in the HOST-PORT specification for the data port to be used in establishing a data connection

IPng.why: The motivation and address-family values cover the IPng candidates (SIP, PIP, TUBA, TP/IX, ST), so IPng readers would want this RFC.
IPng.quote: To accommodate larger network addresses anticipated for all IP "next generation" alternatives, new commands and reply codes are needed for FTP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport for the FTP data connection and is not changed by this document.
The document predates IPv6 and addresses generic next-generation IP candidates, not IPv6 specifically.
The document defines how FTP carries long addresses, not IP address architecture or allocation.
AppleTalk is mentioned only as a possible future transport in the rationale.

RFC1546.title: Host Anycasting Service
RFC1546.summary: RFC 1546 (IRTF informational) defines the semantics of an IP anycast service, in which a datagram sent to an anycast address is delivered best-effort to at least one, and preferably only one, of the hosts serving that address. It covers anycast address allocation, how hosts and routers handle anycast datagrams, and how UDP and TCP use anycast.

anycast.why: The whole document defines anycast semantics, anycast address options, and host and router handling for IP anycast. It is the foundational anycast RFC.
anycast.quote: IP anycasting provides best effort delivery of an anycast datagram to one, but possibly more than one, of the hosts that serve the destination anycast address.

rejected.why: Multicast is only compared with anycast in a section of its own. The document is not about multicast routing.
The TCP-specific rule is that anycast addresses are allowed only as the remote address of a SYN. This is one section on how TCP uses anycast, not a TCP specification.
The address-class discussion is part of anycast, and the more specific anycast tag already covers it.
UDP is mentioned only to say it can treat anycast addresses like unicast addresses.
DNS server autoconfiguration is given as a motivating example, not as the document's subject.
ARP is one possible local delivery mechanism for anycast datagrams. It is not specified or extended.

RFC1547.title: Requirements for an Internet Standard Point-to-Point Protocol
RFC1547.summary: Informational requirements document (the design requirements that guided PPP, RFC 1134 onward) listing features required and not required of an Internet Standard point-to-point data link protocol and evaluating existing protocols (SLIP, HDLC, LAPB, RATP, etc.) against them.

PPP.why: The whole document is the requirements specification for what became PPP (framing, multiplexing, option negotiation, liveness, address and compression negotiation).
PPP.quote: This document discusses the evaluation criteria for an Internet Standard Data Link Layer protocol to be used with point-to-point links.

SLIP.why: SLIP is analysed in detail as the main de facto prior protocol and shown to fail most requirements (section 4.1.6), though it is not the document's focus.
SLIP.quote: SLIP provides only the most rudimentary support for sending IP datagrams over asynchronous serial lines

rejected.why: RATP is only one of the prior protocols reviewed briefly and rejected as the ISPPP; the document is not about it.
X.25 LAPB is reviewed only as a prior protocol that fails the requirements.
Header compression is mentioned only in describing Thinwire; data compression negotiation is a requirement but not header compression.
Error detection by checksum or CRC is a required feature but only discussed at requirement level, not as a subject in its own right.
ISDN is mentioned only as an example of switched media and LAPD is a reviewed protocol.

gaps.name: HDLC framing / data link protocols
gaps.why: The document evaluates HDLC (ISO 3309/6256), LAPB and LAPD as building blocks, but the taxonomy has no HDLC tag.

RFC1548.title: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP)
RFC1548.summary: RFC 1548 specifies the Point-to-Point Protocol: its multiprotocol encapsulation, link phases, the option negotiation automaton, and the Link Control Protocol with its packets and configuration options.

PPP.why: The document is the core PPP specification, defining encapsulation, LCP, the negotiation automaton and the link phases.
PPP.quote: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) provides a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links.

rejected.why: Protocol-Field-Compression and Address-and-Control-Field-Compression are small LCP options, not IP/UDP/RTP header compression.
The Authentication-Protocol option and phase only negotiate PAP/CHAP, which are defined in a companion document.
PPP is the more specific child tag and already covers the document.
The Protocol field value assignments are reference tables, not the subject of the document.

RFC1549.title: PPP in HDLC Framing
RFC1549.summary: Specifies how PPP packets are framed using HDLC over asynchronous, bit-synchronous and octet-synchronous links, including transparency, FCS computation and framing modifications.

PPP.why: The document is a PPP specification defining the link framing, escape mechanism and frame modifications negotiated by LCP for PPP.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of HDLC for framing PPP encapsulated packets.

CRC.why: Substantial part covers the 16-bit FCS (HDLC CRC polynomial x^16+x^12+x^5+1) and an appendix with a fast table-driven implementation and generator.
CRC.quote: PPP uses the HDLC Frame Check Sequence for error detection.

rejected.why: Octet-synchronous HDLC mentions SONET only as an example link type; the document is not about IP over SONET.
X.25 LAPB is only cited as being consistent with HDLC framing; not the subject.
ISDN B/H channels are mentioned only as an example of octet-synchronous links.
A more specific tag, PPP, applies.

gaps.name: HDLC framing
gaps.why: The document is about HDLC framing as used by PPP, but the taxonomy has no HDLC tag.

RFC1550.title: IP: Next Generation (IPng) White Paper Solicitation
RFC1550.summary: A call for white papers on IPng requirements and selection criteria, describing the review process, format rules, and a list of engineering topics (scaling, transition, security, mobility, flows, routing policy, etc.) for the IP Next Generation selection effort.

IPng.why: The whole document is part of the IPng selection process, soliciting requirements input for the next-generation IP candidates (TUBA, PIP, SIPP, TP/IX). It forms part of the historical record of IPng.
IPng.quote: The IP: next generation (IPng) area in the IETF is soliciting white papers on topics related to the IPng requirements and selection criteria.

rejected.why: IPv6 is not named or specified; the document concerns the selection process that preceded it, and IPng is the more specific fit.
It describes a review process for white papers, but only for the IPng area's selection, not general IETF procedures.
Appendix A reproduces RFC 1543 formatting rules, but this is boilerplate apparatus for submissions, not the document's subject.
Mobile hosts appear only as one of sixteen solicited topics, not a substantial part.
IPv4 is mentioned only as the baseline for comparison with IPng.

RFC1551.title: Novell IPX Over Various WAN Media (IPXWAN)
RFC1551.summary: Informational RFC describing Novell's IPXWAN protocol, which negotiates master/slave roles, routing type and link delay between IPX routers (and workstations) after WAN link establishment over PPP, X.25 and Frame Relay.

IPX.why: The whole document specifies IPXWAN, the Novell IPX WAN link negotiation protocol, including Unnumbered RIP and on-demand static routing.
IPX.quote: This document describes how Novell IPX operates over various WAN media.

rejected.why: PPP and IPXCP are only the link layer over which IPXWAN runs; the document just says IPXWAN starts after the IPX NCP is Open.
X.25 SVC/PVC use is a media-dependent encapsulation note, not the subject of the document.
Frame Relay is one of the underlying media, covered only briefly for link establishment and encapsulation.
IPX RIP is the routing protocol that IPXWAN negotiates, not Internet RIP, and the document does not specify RIP itself.
The Telebit IPX header compression option is only negotiated here; the compression method is defined in RFC 1553.

gaps.name: IPXWAN
gaps.why: The IPXWAN protocol is the subject of this document, but the taxonomy has no tag for it. The nearest tag, 'IPX' (Novell IPX interworking), is under 'internet layer' and is the one I would use, but the exact id 'IPX' does not appear in the taxonomy; the taxonomy lists 'IPX' as the id for Novell IPX interworking.

RFC1552.title: The PPP Internetworking Packet Exchange Control Protocol (IPXCP)
RFC1552.summary: Defines IPXCP, the PPP Network Control Protocol for negotiating and configuring Novell IPX over point-to-point links, including its configuration options and coexistence with IPX-WAN.
