IPX.why: The RFC specifies IPXCP, the NCP for IPX over PPP.
IPX.quote: This document defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring the IPX protocol over PPP.

RFC1553.title: Compressing IPX Headers Over WAN Media (CIPX)
RFC1553.summary: RFC 1553 specifies CIPX, a Van Jacobson-style header compression scheme for Novell IPX (and NCP/IPX) datagrams over low-speed WAN links, with negotiation via PPP IPXCP and IPXWAN.

IPX.why: The whole document defines compression of IPX headers, including NCP/IPX, packet formats, slots and IPXWAN negotiation, so readers of IPX interworking would look for it.
IPX.quote: This document describes a method for compressing the headers of IPX datagrams (CIPX).

header compression.why: The document is a header compression scheme (slots, compressed/initial/confirm packets) for constrained WAN links, with no more specific child tag fitting IPX.
header compression.quote: These header compression algorithms are based on those Van Jacobson described [2] for TCP/IP packets.

rejected.why: PPP is only one of the link types over which CIPX is negotiated via IPXCP; the document does not specify PPP itself.
X.25 is mentioned as a possible WAN medium only.
This is a header compression scheme for IPX, not for IP/UDP/RTP.
IPHC is IP header compression for IP/TCP/UDP; CIPX is unrelated apart from the Van Jacobson heritage.
TCP/IP header compression is cited only as the inspiration (RFC 1144).

gaps.name: IPXWAN / IPXCP negotiation
gaps.why: The document defines negotiation options for CIPX in IPXCP and IPXWAN, but the taxonomy has no specific tag beyond IPX and PPP.

RFC1554.title: ISO-2022-JP-2: Multilingual Extension of ISO-2022-JP
RFC1554.summary: Describes ISO-2022-JP-2, a 7-bit multilingual extension of the ISO-2022-JP character encoding (adding Korean, Chinese, Greek, Latin-1 and JIS X 0212) for email and news, with formal syntax and a MIME charset name.

character sets.why: The document defines a character encoding and the escape sequences and registered character sets it uses, and names it for use as a MIME charset value.
character sets.quote: This memo describes a text encoding scheme: "ISO-2022-JP-2"

media types.why: A short section covers how the charset name is used in MIME Content-Type and headers, but the document is not a media type registration.
media types.quote: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-jp-2

rejected.why: MIME is only the context in which the charset name is used; the document does not specify MIME mechanisms.
Email is the application the encoding is used in, not the subject.
Netnews is mentioned as a use case only.
The formal syntax uses RFC 822 notation only to describe the encoding.
The parent of character sets; the more specific child tag fits.
The document concerns message body charset encoding, not internationalized email addresses.

gaps.name: ISO 2022 code extension techniques / ISO-2022-JP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for ISO 2022 escape-sequence-based encodings; character sets is the closest fit.

RFC1555.title: Hebrew Character Encoding for Internet Messages
RFC1555.summary: Specifies that Hebrew email text be encoded in ISO-8859-8 and sent via MIME with Quoted-Printable or Base64, with default visual directionality, header guidance and Listserv caveats.

character sets.why: The document defines the use of the ISO-8859-8 Hebrew character set (with a code table comparing Hebrew encodings) for Internet messages, which is character set use and registration.
character sets.quote: All Hebrew text when transferred via e-mail must first be translated into ISO-8859-8, and then encoded using either Quoted-Printable (preferable) or Base64

MIME.why: Specifies the required MIME headers, charset parameter and content-transfer-encodings for Hebrew mail, plus Q-encoding of headers per RFC 1522.
MIME.quote: Content-type: text/plain; charset=ISO-8859-8

rejected.why: Email is the carrier; the document's subject is the character encoding and MIME labeling, which are covered by more specific tags.
Header encoding is only an optional pointer to RFC 1522; the document does not specify message format.
EBCDIC appears only as one column in a comparison table, not as a subject of the document.
ASCII is used only as a descriptive label in the table; the document is not about ASCII.
The more specific character sets tag covers this; a parent tag is not needed.
Base64 is merely one of two permitted transfer encodings, used as is from MIME.

RFC1556.title: Handling of Bi-directional Texts in MIME
RFC1556.summary: Informational memo defining new MIME charset suffixes (-i implicit, -e explicit; visual default) for ISO-8859-6 and ISO-8859-8 to label bi-directional Arabic/Hebrew text, based on ECMA TR/53.

character sets.why: The document defines new charset names (ISO-8859-6-e, -i, ISO-8859-8-e, -i) for bidirectional text, which is character set registration and use.
character sets.quote: a new character set is being defined which will indicate that the bi-directional message is either encoded in implicit mode or explicit mode

MIME.why: It extends MIME Content-type charset usage for bidirectional text, and visual mode is the MIME default.
MIME.quote: Content-type: text/plain; charset=ISO-8859-8-i

rejected.why: The child tag character sets fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
Email transport is only the substrate; the document is about charset labeling.
It does not register a media type; it only adds charset parameter values.

gaps.name: Bi-directional text handling
gaps.why: The document is about right-to-left and mixed-direction text display (implicit, explicit and visual modes), and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC1557.title: Korean Character Encoding for Internet Messages
RFC1557.summary: Informational RFC describing ISO-2022-KR, the encoding of Korean (KS C 5601 Hangul/Hanja) characters in Internet mail message bodies using SO/SI shifts, with the charset name for MIME and EUC-KR for RFC 1522 headers.

character sets.why: The document defines a Korean character encoding and registers its charset name for use in MIME. A reader browsing character set registration and use would expect to find it.
character sets.quote: The name to be used for the Hangul encoding scheme in the contents is "ISO-2022-KR".

MIME.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how the encoding is labelled in MIME Content-Type and used in RFC 1522 encoded headers (EUC-KR with B/Q encoding).
MIME.quote: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-kr

rejected.why: Mail is the context in which the encoding is used, but the document is about the character encoding rather than mail transport or architecture.
The document touches RFC 822 headers and bodies only as the place where the encoding is used. It does not specify the message format itself.
ASCII is only the base set that SI shifts back to. The document is not about ASCII.
This is a parent of character sets, so it is implied by the more specific tag.
The encoding is based on KS C 5601 and ISO 2022, not Unicode.

RFC1558.title: A String Representation of LDAP Search Filters
RFC1558.summary: Informational RFC defining a human-readable string format (prefix BNF) for representing LDAP search filters, with examples.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies a string representation of LDAP search filters, an extension of LDAP usage that LDAP readers would want.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a human-readable string format for representing LDAP search filters.

rejected.why: The ASN.1 filter definition and BER encoding are only quoted from LDAP as background; the document defines a string syntax, not ASN.1.
The BNF is merely the notation used to define the string format, not the subject.
Implied parent of LDAP, so not listed separately.

RFC1559.title: DECnet Phase IV MIB Extensions
RFC1559.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB (DECNET-PHIV-MIB) for managing DECnet Phase IV nodes, covering system, end, routing, circuit, DDCMP, Ethernet, adjacency, line and area objects, and obsoleting RFC 1289.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (DECNET-PHIV-MIB) written in SMI/OBJECT-TYPE form for SNMP management.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a set of DECnet Phase IV extensions that have been created for the Internet MIB.

DECnet.why: The subject being managed is DECnet Phase IV (routing, end communication, circuits, adjacencies), so readers of DECnet would expect it.
DECnet.quote: DECnet Phase IV is one widely used protocol which often coexists in IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines a MIB, not SNMP itself.
Ethernet link parameters and counters are one group within the MIB, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet.
ASN.1 subset is just the SMI notation used to write the definitions.
X.25 is only listed as a circuit type value.

RFC1560.title: The MultiProtocol Internet
RFC1560.summary: An IAB strawman position paper arguing that the IETF should stay focused on TCP/IP, select a single next-generation internet protocol (IPng) with an IPv4 transition path, and keep pursuing interoperability and resource sharing with other protocol suites.

internet architecture.why: The document is an IAB architectural position on the single-protocol-suite principle, the common IP layer and multiprotocol coexistence. This is the Internet architecture subject.
internet architecture.quote: Fundamental to this ability was the fact that the Internet was based on a single, common, virtual network service (IP) with a supporting administrative infrastructure.

IPng.why: A substantial section argues that a single next-generation internet protocol should be chosen and that IPv4 transition methods should be developed. The IPng tag covers this historic selection debate.
IPng.quote: Currently, there are several candidates for IPng, which raises the question of how to deal with multiple protocols at that level.

rejected.why: IPv6 is never named. The memo discusses selecting an IPng candidate in general terms and does not specify or analyse IPv6.
The memo only says transition mechanisms from IPv4 should be developed. It does not describe any.
The memo discusses the IETF/IESG/IAB's strategic role and focus, not its standards procedures or administration.
OSI is named only as one of several other protocol suites, alongside IPX and SNA. The memo does not address OSI network-layer protocols in any detail.
TCP/IP is mentioned as the primary protocol suite, but the memo does not discuss the TCP protocol itself.

gaps.name: multiprotocol Internet / protocol suite interoperability and resource sharing
gaps.why: The central subject is how the Internet should accommodate and interoperate with other protocol suites (IPX, OSI, SNA) and share resources with them. The taxonomy has no tag for this beyond the general internet architecture topic.

RFC1561.title: Use of ISO CLNP in TUBA Environments
RFC1561.summary: Experimental profile of ISO CLNP (ISO/IEC 8473) for carrying TCP and UDP in TUBA environments, mapping IP header fields, options, ICMP errors and pseudo-header onto CLNP with NSAP addresses.

CLNP.why: The whole document profiles CLNP header fields, options, error reports and addressing for use under TCP/UDP.
CLNP.quote: This memo specifies a profile of the ISO/IEC 8473 Connectionless-mode Network Layer Protocol (CLNP, [1]) for use in conjunction with RFC 1347

IPng.why: TUBA is one of the historic IPng candidates; this document is the CLNP network-layer profile for TUBA.
IPng.quote: RFC 1347, TCP/UDP over Bigger Addresses (TUBA, [2])

rejected.why: TCP is the client of CLNP; the document only defines the pseudo-header for it, not TCP itself.
UDP is only carried over CLNP; no UDP specification or usage guidance.
ICMP is compared with CLNP Error Reports, but the document specifies CLNP errors, not ICMP.
The Fletcher checksum appendix is part of the CLNP header definition, not a general checksum topic.
Parent of CLNP, so implied.
IPv4 is the reference for mapping semantics, not the subject.

RFC1562.title: Naming Guidelines for the AARNet X.500 Directory Service
RFC1562.summary: Informational AARNet engineering note giving naming guidelines for the Australian X.500 Directory Service, aligning DIT naming under c=AU with Standards Australia rather than RFC 1384.

X.500.why: The whole document defines how entries (DSAs, states, organisations, residential people) are named in the X.500 DIT under c=AU, so it belongs on the X.500 page.
X.500.quote: AARNet is a member network of the global Internet and participates in the global Internet X.500 based Directory Service.

rejected.why: This is X.500 directory naming (DIT/RDN), not general naming or name resolution. The X.500 tech tag is more specific.
This is the parent of X.500. The more specific X.500 tag fits, so the parent is implied.
DNS is not discussed. The naming here concerns X.500 distinguished names, not domain names.

RFC1563.title: The text/enriched MIME Content-type
RFC1563.summary: Defines the text/enriched MIME subtype, a simple formatted-text markup with a small set of formatting commands, obsoleting the text/richtext type of RFC 1341.

media types.why: The document defines and specifies a new MIME media type (text/enriched), including its parameters and syntax. Readers of media type pages would expect it.
media types.quote: This document defines a new MIME content-type, "text/enriched".

rejected.why: The document leans on MIME as a framework but defines a specific media type, so the more specific media types tag fits.
Intended for use in Internet mail, but mail is only the context. The document is about the content format.
A simple hypertext/markup format, but it is not HTML, and the document drops its SGML compatibility claims.
A short section covers non-ASCII charsets and the charset parameter, but this is a minor part of the document.
Appendix B mentions SGML compatibility claims being dropped, which is incidental.

RFC1564.title: DSA Metrics (OSI-DS 34 (v3))
RFC1564.summary: RFC 1564 defines a questionnaire and scoring metrics for evaluating X.500 Directory System Agent (DSA) implementations, covering standards conformance, schema, replication, access control, management, interoperability and performance benchmarking.

X.500.why: The whole document evaluates X.500 DSA implementations: conformance to X.519/X.520/X.521, DAP/DSP, schema, replication and access control. Readers of X.500 would want it.
X.500.quote: whilst an X.500 DSA must conform to the specification in the standard - this is a sine qua non - protocol conformance is not in itself the hallmark

benchmarking.why: A substantial section defines a benchmarking methodology (20000-entry database, cold/optimum timings, bind, list, search, read, add, modify) and result tables.
benchmarking.quote: A number of operations are timed in order to give a feel for the DSA's speed and throughput.

rejected.why: The document is about OSI X.500 DSAs and DAP/DSP; LDAP is not discussed.
Parent of X.500, which is already chosen and more specific.
CMIP is only mentioned as one possible monitoring interface in a single question.
SNMP is only mentioned as one possible monitoring interface in a single question.
OSI protocol stacks appear only as conformance questions about transport options for the DSA; the document is about the Directory, not OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC1565.title: Network Services Monitoring MIB
RFC1565.summary: RFC 1565 defines the SNMPv2 Application MIB module (applTable and assocTable) for monitoring common status and association information of network service applications such as MTAs and DSAs.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (APPLICATION-MIB) with tables, objects, and conformance groups for SNMP monitoring of network service applications.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB which contains the elements common to the monitoring of any network service application.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is built for, but the document defines only a MIB module; the more specific MIB tag covers it.
The directory is referenced via applDirectoryName as an external key, but the document is not about the directory service.
MTAs and X.400 are mentioned only as examples of monitored applications, not as the subject.
ASN.1 is just the notation used for the MIB definitions.
Section 3.3 discusses the relationship to directory services, but only as a linkage recommendation; the document is not about directory access.

RFC1566.title: Mail Monitoring MIB
RFC1566.summary: Defines the SNMP MIB module (MTA-MIB) for monitoring Message Transfer Agents, with counters and gauges for messages, volume, recipients, groups and associations, extending the Network Services Monitoring MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (MTA-MIB) defining managed objects, tables and conformance groups for monitoring MTAs.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

email.why: The managed subject is mail transfer agents and their message flow, so readers of email operations would want it. Email is the subject being monitored, not just a substrate.
email.quote: this memo extends the basic Network Services Monitoring MIB [5] to allow monitoring of Message Transfer Agents (MTAs).

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is the framework the MIB is written for, not something the document specifies or extends; MIB covers the module.
SMTP is only mentioned as an example of a protocol whose message volumes are counted; the document does not specify it.
X.400 is mentioned only as an example in volume counting and naming; the document does not address it.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB definitions.

RFC1567.title: X.500 Directory Monitoring MIB
RFC1567.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module (DSA-MIB) for monitoring X.500 Directory System Agents, with tables for operation counters, entry/cache statistics, and peer DSA interactions.

MIB.why: The document's core is a MIB module (DSA-MIB) written in SMIv2 with tables, object groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: It defines the MIB for monitoring Directory System Agents (DSA), a component of the OSI Directory.

X.500.why: The managed subject is the X.500 DSA: its operations (Read, Search, etc.), chaining, referrals, binds and cache. Readers of X.500 would want this monitoring MIB.
X.500.quote: The Directory System Agent [DSA], a component of the OSI-Directory [5] [9], is an application process.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is only the management framework the MIB plugs into; the MIB tag covers the document's actual content.
ASN.1 subset is only the notation used by the SMI to define the objects.
LDAP is not mentioned; the document concerns X.500 DSAs and their operations.
A parent of X.500, which is already tagged.

RFC1568.title: Simple Network Paging Protocol - Version 1(b)
RFC1568.summary: Informational RFC specifying SNPP, a simple command/response TCP protocol for delivering one-way alphanumeric and numeric pages to radio paging terminals via a gateway to TAP/IXO.

paging.why: The whole document defines SNPP, a protocol for delivering pages to paging terminals, with commands, responses and TAP/IXO gateway behaviour.
paging.quote: This RFC suggests a simple way for delivering both alphanumeric and numeric pages (one-way) to radio paging terminals.

rejected.why: Discussed only as an alternative SNPP was argued against; the document neither specifies nor extends SMTP.
Email is compared and contrasted in motivation and IETF review sections, but the document is not about email.
Mentioned only as a way to manually interact with the SNPP gateway; it is just a client convenience.
SMS is mobile short messaging; this document covers radio paging, which has its own tag.

RFC1569.title: Principles of Operation for the TPC.INT Subdomain: Radio Paging -- Technical Procedures
RFC1569.summary: Describes how to send radio pages via Internet mail by mapping telephone numbers to tpc.int domain names, routed with DNS wildcard MX records to radio pager servers, with SMTP MAIL/SEND semantics.

paging.why: The whole document specifies how radio pager servers receive mail and send pages to alphanumeric and numeric pagers.
paging.quote: this memo describes a technique for radio paging using the Internet mail infrastructure

ENUM.why: Maps E.164 telephone numbers into DNS names under tpc.int and uses wildcard MX records, an ENUM-like telephone-number-in-DNS technique.
ENUM.quote: where the domain-part is constructed by reversing the telephone number, converting each digit to a domain-label, and being placed under "tpc.int."

SMTP.why: Defines SMTP command semantics and reply-code meaning for paging servers, including latency implications.
SMTP.quote: The radio pager server MUST support the MAIL command, and MAY support any of the SEND, SOML, or SAML commands.

rejected.why: DNS wildcard MX records are used for routing, but the document defines no new DNS behaviour; the tpc.int naming is better covered by ENUM.
RFC 822 messages are the substrate; the document only constrains the local-part atom syntax.
A text/plain MIME example is shown, but MIME is not the subject.
The more specific tags SMTP and paging cover the mail aspects.

RFC1570.title: PPP LCP Extensions
RFC1570.summary: RFC 1570 extends the PPP Link Control Protocol with new Identification and Time-Remaining packets and the FCS-Alternatives, Self-Describing-Padding, Callback and Compound-Frames configuration options, and includes 32-bit FCS code.

PPP.why: The whole document specifies new LCP packets and options for PPP, so it belongs on the PPP page.
PPP.quote: This document defines several additional LCP features which have been suggested over the past few years.

rejected.why: The appendix gives 32-bit FCS code and FCS-Alternatives negotiates the FCS format. The document is about PPP LCP negotiation, not CRC polynomial selection.
The FCS is a frame check, but it is only one option among several and is not the document's subject.
The document does not mention PPP over Ethernet.
The Callback option applies to dial-up links in general. ISDN is not discussed.

RFC1571.title: Telnet Environment Option Interoperability Issues
RFC1571.summary: Informational RFC updating RFC 1408 that gives heuristics for Telnet clients and servers to detect whether the peer has VAR and VALUE definitions reversed in the Telnet Environment option, resolving an interoperability problem.

Telnet.why: The document addresses interoperability of the Telnet Environment option, a Telnet option, and specifies how client and server telnet parse SEND, IS and INFO suboptions.
Telnet.quote: providing a set of heuristics that can be used to help identify which definitions for VAR and VALUE are being used by the other side of the connection

RFC1572.title: Telnet Environment Option
RFC1572.summary: RFC 1572 specifies the Telnet NEW-ENVIRON option, which lets a Telnet client and server exchange environment variables (USER, DISPLAY, etc.) using subnegotiation commands, correcting errors in RFC 1408.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option (NEW-ENVIRON) with its commands, negotiation rules and well-known variables, so it belongs on the Telnet protocol and options page.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies a mechanism for passing environment information between a telnet client and server.

rejected.why: The DISPLAY variable carries an X display location, but this is only one well-known variable and the document is not about X.
SYSTEMTYPE reuses the FTP SYST value, which is only a reference.
The Security Concerns section is a brief note about which variables are safe to set before login, not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC1573.title: Evolution of the Interfaces Group of MIB-II
RFC1573.summary: Defines the updated IF-MIB (interfaces group of MIB-II) and IANAifType module, adding interface sub-layer stacking, 64-bit counters, ifName, ifHighSpeed, trap control, and guidance for media-specific MIB designers.

MIB.why: The document specifies the IF-MIB and IANAifType MIB modules, re-specifying the MIB-II interfaces group in SNMPv2 SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

SNMP.why: The MIB is written for SNMPv2, using SNMPv2 compliance statements, 64-bit counters, and linkUp/linkDown notifications; much of the design rationale concerns SNMP semantics.
SNMP.quote: The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework consists of four major components.

rejected.why: Interface sub-layers are modelled generically for management; no specific link-layer protocol is specified.
IANAifType registry is defined as a MIB textual convention, but the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
The MIB modules use ASN.1 / SMI only as notation.
Ethernet and other media appear only as examples of interface types and counter wrap times.

RFC1574.title: Essential Tools for the OSI Internet
RFC1574.summary: Specifies the minimum CLNP (ISO 8473) debugging toolset for OSI hosts and routers: ping via the CLNP echo function, traceroute using the Lifetime field, a routing table dump with CLNS MIB variables via SNMP, and an osi host.txt name-to-NSAP file format.

CLNP.why: The whole document defines echo, traceroute and table-dump tools for CLNP (ISO 8473), including the echo selector values and error codes used.
CLNP.quote: specify a standard ping, traceroute, and OSI routing table dumping mechanisms for use for the ISO 8473 (CLNP) protocol in the OSI Internet

traceroute.why: A substantial section specifies a CLNP traceroute function, including partial source routing and the information it must report.
traceroute.quote: The CLNP trace is similar to the ping utility except that it utilizes the "Lifetime" field in the ISO 8473 packet.

MIB.why: Section 3.4 requires the CLNS MIB variables clnpAddrTable and clnpRoutingTable and reproduces their ASN.1 syntax.
MIB.quote: Section 3.4 specifies the RFC 1238 MIB variables which MUST be available via SNMP.

rejected.why: CLNP is the more specific child tag. The document is about the CLNP tools, not OSI network-layer protocols in general.
SNMP is only the access mechanism for the CLNS MIB variables. The document specifies no new SNMP behaviour.
The CLNP echo function resembles ICMP echo, but ICMP is not specified or used here.
The osi host.txt format is a small part of the document. It maps names to NSAP addresses and is not a general hostname convention.
IS-IS is only listed as one source of routing table entries.

RFC1575.title: An Echo Function for CLNP (ISO 8473)
RFC1575.summary: Defines an echo (ping) function for CLNP (ISO 8473) with two new packet types, ERQ and ERP, for testing and debugging reachability at the OSI network layer; obsoletes RFC 1139.

CLNP.why: The whole document extends CLNP (ISO 8473) with echo-request and echo-response PDU types and specifies their construction and processing.
CLNP.quote: This memo defines an echo function for the connection-less network layer protocol.

rejected.why: The echo function is analogous to ICMP echo, but ICMP is never specified or discussed. This is a CLNP-native mechanism.
The document describes ping-like reachability probing, not path discovery tools.
CLNP is a child of OSI and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The echo function is a diagnostic mechanism, but it is specific to CLNP and the CLNP tag covers it. It is not a general OAM framework.

RFC1576.title: TN3270 Current Practices
RFC1576.summary: Informational RFC documenting current TN3270 practice: the Telnet options negotiated (Terminal-Type, Binary, EOR), 3270 data handling, structured fields, and ATTN/SYSREQ key mapping for 3270 terminal emulation over Telnet.

TN3270.why: The whole document describes TN3270 negotiation, data handling, and special key handling, so it belongs on the TN3270 page.
TN3270.quote: This document describes the existing implementation of transferring 3270 display terminal data using currently available telnet capabilities. The name traditionally associated with this implementation is TN3270.

Telnet.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how Telnet options (BINARY, TERMINAL-TYPE, EOR, ECHO, SGA, TIMING-MARK) and commands (BREAK, IP, NOP) are used, so Telnet readers would want it.
Telnet.quote: TN3270 makes use of existing Telnet options and does not define any additional options or commands.

rejected.why: SNA concepts (SSCP, LU, SYSREQ) are explained for context, but the document is about TN3270, which is classed as non-SNA. TN3270 is the more specific child tag.
EBCDIC is mentioned only as a difference from ASCII in the Motivation section. The document does not cover translation or the encoding itself.
TCP is only the transport, with a mention of port 23. The document does not define anything new about TCP.

RFC1577.title: Classical IP and ARP over ATM
RFC1577.summary: RFC 1577 specifies classical IP over ATM in a Logical IP Subnet, defining LLC/SNAP encapsulation, default MTU, and the ATMARP/InATMARP address resolution protocols with an ATMARP server.

ATM.why: The document defines how IP operates over ATM AAL5 in a Logical IP Subnet: encapsulation, MTU, VCs, and ATM address structures.
ATM.quote: transmitting IP datagrams and ATM Address Resolution Protocol (ATMARP) requests and replies over ATM Adaptation Layer 5 (AAL5)

ARP.why: A substantial part specifies ATMARP and InATMARP, including the ARP_NAK extension, server and client behaviour, table aging and packet format.
ARP.quote: ATMARP is the same protocol as the ARP protocol presented in [3] with extensions needed to support ARP in a unicast server ATM environment.

rejected.why: NHRP is a later NBMA resolution protocol. This memo only mentions that future work will address larger ATM networks.
The IP datagrams carried are IPv4, but the document is about the ATM link mapping and address resolution, not IPv4 itself.
Section 8 only says there is no mapping of IP multicast to ATM multicast service. It does not address multicast in any real depth.
The ATM address structures are used for ARP resolution. The document does not cover IP address architecture or allocation.
The default 9180-octet MTU is set in a short section. It is part of the ATM encapsulation rather than a separate subject, and PMTUD is not discussed.

RFC1578.title: FYI on Questions and Answers - Answers to Commonly Asked "Primary and Secondary School Internet User" Questions
RFC1578.summary: FYI 22 is a question-and-answer guide for K-12 educators and administrators on connecting to and using the Internet. It covers funding, equipment, security and ethics, and collaboration, and gives pointers to resources, mailing lists and servers.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide for a particular group of Internet users, so it belongs on the user guides page. It has no protocol content.
user guides.quote: to document the questions most commonly asked about the Internet by those in the primary and secondary school community, and to provide pointers to sources which answer those questions

rejected.why: UUCP appears only as a low-cost store-and-forward access option for schools (Q5.5). The document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
FTP is explained as a way to retrieve documents (Appendix B). It is a usage tutorial, not a specification or analysis of the protocol.
Gopher servers are listed as resources and Appendix B briefly explains the protocol. The document is not about Gopher itself.
Usenet newsgroups are listed as places to find help and collaborators. The document does not treat the article format or distribution.
The mailing lists are only resource contacts for educators, not mailing list protocols or management.
Section 6 gives brief advice on viruses, hackers and acceptable use policies. It is not operational security practice for network infrastructure.

gaps.name: Education / K-12 schools use of the Internet
gaps.why: The whole document concerns Internet use in primary and secondary education. The taxonomy has no education or user-community tag, so only the generic user guides tag fits.

RFC1579.title: Firewall-Friendly FTP
RFC1579.summary: Informational memo recommending that FTP clients use the PASV command instead of PORT so data connections are outbound and work through packet-filter firewalls, and sketching an optional APSV command.

FTP.why: The document is about changing FTP client behaviour (PASV vs PORT) and proposes an FTP extension (APSV, reply code 151).
FTP.quote: We recommend that vendors convert their FTP client programs (including FTP proxy agents such as Gopher daemons) to use PASV instead of PORT.

firewall.why: The motivation and much of the discussion concern packet-filter firewall traversal and the security tradeoffs of inbound vs outbound calls.
firewall.quote: this scheme does not work well with packet filter-based firewalls, which in general cannot permit incoming calls to random port numbers.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate; the memo mentions connection setup and TIMEWAIT but specifies nothing new about TCP.
Gopher proxies are mentioned only as an example of an FTP client; the memo is not about Gopher.

RFC1580.title: Guide to Network Resource Tools
RFC1580.summary: FYI 23 is an introductory user guide to network resource discovery and retrieval tools (Gopher, WWW, WAIS, Archie, WHOIS, X.500, Netfind, Trickle, BITFTP, LISTSERV, Netnews, and others), explaining what each is, how to reach it and how to use it.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide for network users, which is what the user guides subject covers.
user guides.quote: The purpose of this guide is to supply the basic information that anyone on the network needs to try out and begin using these tools.

Gopher.why: A full section describes Gopher usage, menus and Veronica search, so Gopher readers would want it.
Gopher.quote: The Internet Gopher, or simply Gopher, is a distributed document delivery service.

WAIS.why: A full section explains WAIS access, query steps and the e-mail interface.
WAIS.quote: WAIS, Wide Area Information Server,  is a distributed information retrieval system.

WHOIS.why: A full section covers WHOIS client, Telnet and e-mail usage plus the InterNIC database and WHOIS++ plans.
WHOIS.quote: WHOIS provides directory service to network users.

X.500.why: A full section covers X.500 directory concepts, DUAs, public access sites and e-mail access.
X.500.quote: X.500 is an OSI (Open System Information) based directory services protocol designed by the CCITT

Netnews.why: A full section describes Usenet newsgroups and news readers.
Netnews.quote: Netnews, or Usenet as it is more commonly called, is a message sharing system that exchanges messages electronically around the world

mailing lists.why: The long LISTSERV section covers list subscription, options and file server commands.
mailing lists.quote: LISTSERV is a distribution list management package.

IRC.why: A brief subsection describes IRC and how to reach it.
IRC.quote: IRC, Internet Relay Chat, is a real-time conversational system.

FTP.why: BITFTP, Trickle and Archie all provide access to anonymous FTP archives, so FTP readers would find these useful.
FTP.quote: BITFTP, BITNET FTP Server, allows users of EARN, Bitnet and associated networks to access FTP sites on the Internet.

rejected.why: The WWW section is a user-level introduction, but HTTP/HTML are not specified. The generic web tag would be a weak fit versus the guide focus.
Already covered more specifically by X.500 and WHOIS tags; Netfind is a white-pages tool but a minor part.
E-mail is only the access mechanism for many of the servers, not the subject.
Only mentioned as a means Netfind uses for searching.
Used as an access method only; the guide explicitly says describing it is out of scope.
Mentioned only as a forthcoming protocol in one paragraph.

gaps.name: Archie, Veronica, Netfind, Trickle, BITFTP, Prospero
gaps.why: Resource-discovery and file-retrieval tools with substantial coverage but no taxonomy tag; the closest generic subject would be resource discovery or information retrieval.

RFC1581.title: Protocol Analysis for Extensions to RIP to Support Demand Circuits
RFC1581.summary: Protocol analysis report documenting the key features, applicability, implementations and restrictions of Demand RIP, extensions to RIP for routing over demand circuits on WANs.

RIP.why: The whole document analyses the Demand RIP extensions to RIP and RIP-2: triggered updates, acknowledgements, and reachability handling on demand circuits.
RIP.quote: Extensions to RIP to Support Demand Circuits" [2] suggests an enhancement to the "Routing Internet Protocol" (RIP) [3] and "RIP-2" [4]

rejected.why: X.25 is only named as an example of a connection-oriented WAN where Demand RIP applies. The document is not about X.25.
ISDN is only mentioned as an example network and as a test environment, not as a subject of the document.
PPP link quality monitoring is only mentioned as one way to detect link failure. The document is not about PPP.
IPX RIP and SAP are supported by the implementation, but only in passing. The document doesn't specify or analyse them.

RFC1582.title: Extensions to RIP to Support Demand Circuits
RFC1582.summary: RFC 1582 extends distance-vector routing protocols (IP RIP v1/v2, Netware RIP, Netware SAP) with triggered updates, acknowledgements, retransmission and fragmentation so they work economically on demand circuits such as X.25 and ISDN WANs.

RIP.why: The document specifies extensions to RIP (v1 and v2 packet formats, new triggered request/response/acknowledgement commands) for demand circuits. It is the main subject.
RIP.quote: This memo defines a generalized modification which can be applied to Bellman-Ford (or distance vector) algorithm information broadcasting protocols, for example IP RIP, Netware RIP or Netware SAP

rejected.why: X.25 is the WAN medium the extension runs over. The document does not specify anything about X.25 itself.
ISDN is the example connection-oriented network. It is the use case, not the subject.
Netware RIP and SAP run over IPX, and the document defines packet-format changes for them. IPX itself is not specified, and the tag is about interworking.
IP RIP runs over UDP port 520. UDP is only the transport substrate.
The document addresses one family of protocols, not routing architecture in general.

gaps.name: Netware RIP / Netware SAP (Novell IPX routing and service advertising)
gaps.why: The document specifies triggered-update extensions for these Novell protocols. The taxonomy has no tag for them; IPX interworking is the closest.

gaps.name: Demand circuits / dial-on-demand routing
gaps.why: This is the central problem the document addresses. No taxonomy tag covers it.

RFC1583.title: OSPF Version 2
RFC1583.summary: RFC 1583 specifies OSPF version 2, a link-state interior gateway routing protocol with areas, flooding, designated routers, TOS-based routing, and authentication, obsoleting RFC 1247.

OSPF.why: The whole document is the OSPF v2 specification: packets, neighbor and interface state machines, LSAs, flooding, and routing table calculation.
OSPF.quote: This memo documents version 2 of the OSPF protocol.  OSPF is a link-state routing protocol.

rejected.why: Equal-cost multipath is a feature mentioned briefly within OSPF, not the subject of the document.
OSPF runs over IP (protocol 89) and handles subnetting, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
OSPF uses IP multicast addresses (AllSPFRouters) as a substrate; it only mentions MOSPF in passing.
EGP is only referenced as a source of external routes, not specified here.
IS-IS is cited only in the history section.
Supernetting support is mentioned as an implementation requirement, but the document is not about CIDR.

RFC1584.title: Multicast Extensions to OSPF
RFC1584.summary: Specifies MOSPF, backward-compatible extensions to OSPF Version 2 that route IP multicast datagrams using source/destination shortest-path trees, a new group-membership-LSA, and IGMP interaction, including inter-area and inter-AS multicasting.

MOSPF.why: The entire document defines MOSPF: the group-membership-LSA, datagram shortest-path trees, forwarding cache, and inter-area/inter-AS behaviour.
MOSPF.quote: This memo documents enhancements to the OSPF protocol enabling the routing of IP multicast datagrams.

rejected.why: MOSPF builds on OSPF v2, but the document is about the multicast extensions, which have their own tag; the base protocol is the substrate.
IGMP is used to learn local group membership but is specified in RFC 1112; the document only describes how MOSPF interacts with it.
Parent of MOSPF; implied by the more specific tag.
Not related; this is source/destination routing within an OSPF domain, not source-specific multicast.

RFC1585.title: MOSPF: Analysis and Experience
RFC1585.summary: Informational memo evaluating the MOSPF multicast extensions to OSPF against IETF routing protocol standardization criteria, covering features, implementation experience, testing, scaling analysis and known difficulties.

MOSPF.why: The whole document analyses MOSPF: its features, implementation, testing, scaling and difficulties.
MOSPF.quote: MOSPF is an enhancement of OSPF V2, enabling the routing of IP multicast datagrams.
MOSPF.section: 1. Summary of MOSPF features and algorithms

rejected.why: MOSPF is built on OSPF, but the document is about the multicast extensions. MOSPF is the more specific tag.
MOSPF uses IGMP to monitor group membership, but IGMP is not specified or analysed here.
Mentioned only as a link-layer encapsulation reference.
MIB support is covered in a brief section, and it is not a substantial part of the document.
The MOSPF tag sits under multicast, so the parent is implied.

RFC1586.title: Guidelines for Running OSPF Over Frame Relay Networks
RFC1586.summary: Informational guidelines for implementing and configuring OSPF over frame relay, using logical point-to-point and NBMA interfaces per VC so partial-mesh connectivity works without protocol changes.

OSPF.why: The document is about how OSPF interface types (point-to-point, NBMA) should be implemented and configured over frame relay.
OSPF.quote: This memo specifies guidelines for implementors and users of the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing protocol to bring about improvements in how the protocol runs over frame relay networks.

frame relay.why: The document covers frame relay VC and DLCI configuration, partial-mesh design and cost considerations for running IP routing over frame relay.
frame relay.quote: A frame relay (FR) network provides virtual circuits (VCs) to interconnect attached devices.

rejected.why: The interface MIB and OSPF MIB are only referenced for how entries (ifTable, ospfIfTable) are created; the document does not define or specify MIB modules.
Inverse ARP is mentioned only as an optional address-resolution mechanism for DLCI-to-IP bindings, not the subject.
Not relevant; listed only to rule out confusion, nothing in the document concerns mobility.

RFC1587.title: The OSPF NSSA Option
RFC1587.summary: RFC 1587 defines the OSPF "not-so-stubby area" (NSSA) option, adding the N-bit and type-7 LSAs so a stub-like area can import limited external routes, with translation of type-7 to type-5 LSAs at area border routers.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF v2 with a new area type, N-bit, type-7 LSAs, route calculation and translation rules. It is squarely an OSPF extension.
OSPF.quote: This document describes a new optional type of OSPF area, somewhat humorously referred to as a "not-so-stubby" area (or NSSA)

rejected.why: RIP appears only in the motivating example, where routes learned by RIP are imported into the area. The document does not specify or extend RIP.
The MC-bit is mentioned only in the options field appendix, referencing the multicast extensions to OSPF. It is incidental.
The 'not-so-stubby' name is a lighthearted pun, but the document is a serious technical specification.
The document specifies OSPF version 2 only. OSPFv3 is not covered.

RFC1588.title: White Pages Meeting Report
RFC1588.summary: Report of the November 1993 IETF white pages meeting assessing X.500, Whois++, Netfind and other approaches to an Internet white pages directory service, with recommendations for a "common ground" interoperation approach, index-servers, central X.500 management and certificate storage.

X.500.why: The report centrally evaluates X.500 deployment problems, quipu/ISODE, DSAs, naming and central management, and recommends supporting X.500 infrastructure.
X.500.quote: to discuss the viability of the X.500 directory as a practical approach to providing white pages service for the Internet in the near future

WHOIS++.why: Whois++ is reviewed in its own section as the main simpler alternative, including centroids and index servers, and is discussed throughout.
WHOIS++.quote: Simpler white pages services (such as Whois++) must be defined to promote multiple implementations.

directory services.why: The document is about white pages directory services in general: functions, searching, indexing, naming and deployment strategy across multiple technologies (X.500, Whois++, Netfind, LDAP).
directory services.quote: to discuss the future of and approaches to a white pages directory services for the Internet

rejected.why: LDAP is mentioned as a lightweight client-side access method for X.500, but it is not specified or analysed in depth.
Finger is described briefly as a lookup mechanism used by Netfind and judged inefficient for searching. This is not a substantial subject of the report.
Only the Gopher-to-X.500 gateway is mentioned as a deployment aid and a model for adoption.
PEM is mentioned as motivating storage of security certificates in the directory, but the document is not about PEM.
DNS is used as an analogy and as a place to store pointers, but it is not the subject.
The WHOIS tag covers legacy registration data directories, whereas the report concerns Whois++ for people white pages; the more specific WHOIS++ tag fits.

gaps.name: Netfind / white pages services
gaps.why: Netfind, archie and the general concept of Internet white pages services have no specific tag. The directory services topic is the closest fit.

RFC1589.title: A Kernel Model for Precision Timekeeping
RFC1589.summary: Describes a Unix kernel model for precision timekeeping (PLL/FLL clock discipline, PPS and external clock support, ntp_gettime/ntp_adjtime system calls, leap-second state machine) for use with NTP.

time synchronization.why: The whole document is about disciplining the system clock in time and frequency, including PPS/IRIG sources and leap seconds. NTP is only the client of the model, so the general topic fits better than the NTP tag.
time synchronization.quote: describes an engineering model which implements a precision time-of-day function for a generic operating system

rejected.why: The kernel model serves NTP daemons but does not specify or extend the NTP protocol. NTP is the example application, and the protocol itself is in RFC 1305.
Not related. The document concerns NTP-style discipline of a host clock, not PTP.

gaps.name: operating system kernel clock discipline (PLL/FLL, PPS)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is kernel clock discipline and its system-call API. The taxonomy only has the general time synchronization topic.

RFC1590.title: Media Type Registration Procedure
RFC1590.summary: RFC 1590 specifies the IANA administrative procedure and email template for registering MIME media types (content-type/subtypes), generalizing their use beyond mail.

media types.why: The whole document defines the registration procedure, review process and templates for media types, which is exactly the media type registry rules subject.
media types.quote: This document addresses these issues and specifies a procedure for the registration of new Media Types (content-type/subtypes).

IANA.why: The procedure is an IANA registration process: submission to IANA, OID assignment, and posting of registrations. Readers of IANA registry guidance would want it.
IANA.quote: MIME and other applications use the registration process for Media Types defined in this RFC which uses the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as a central registry

rejected.why: MIME is the context whose types are registered, but the document does not define MIME body structure or encodings; the registry-rule subject is covered by media types.
Mentioned only in passing for OID mapping to media types; not a substantive part of the document.
Mail is the original context, but the document generalizes media types beyond mail and does not address email itself.

RFC1591.title: Domain Name System Structure and Delegation
RFC1591.summary: RFC 1591 describes the structure of DNS top-level domains (generic and country-code) and sets out policy for delegating and administering domains, including the responsibilities of designated managers and the role of IANA and the Internet Registry.

DNS.why: The document is about DNS namespace structure, TLDs and delegation of zones to designated managers, including operating nameservers. It is about DNS administration rather than protocol mechanics.
DNS.quote: This memo provides some information on the structure of the names in the Domain Name System (DNS), specifically the top-level domain names; and on the administration of domains.

domain registration.why: A substantial part covers registry and registrar operations: the central IR, regional registries, designated manager requirements, transfer of delegations and rights to names.
domain registration.quote: Second level domains in COM, EDU, ORG, NET, and GOV are registered by the Internet Registry at the InterNIC.

rejected.why: The document only mentions using whois to find a TLD contact. That is a passing usage example, not a specification or analysis of WHOIS.
IANA's role in delegating TLDs is discussed, but the document is not about IANA registries or parameter-assignment guidance. The domain registration tag covers the delegation role.
A more specific child tag (DNS) fits, so the parent is implied.
The delegation policy has a governance flavour, but the subject is DNS delegation and registration, which the chosen tags cover more specifically.

gaps.name: TLD delegation policy / country-code TLD administration
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for top-level domain delegation, ccTLD management or domain-name dispute and trademark policy. The nearest tags are DNS and domain registration.

RFC1592.title: Simple Network Management Protocol Distributed Protocol Interface Version 2.0
RFC1592.summary: Experimental RFC specifying SNMP DPI version 2.0, a protocol between an SNMP agent and sub-agents that lets MIB sub-trees be dynamically registered and requests (GET, GETNEXT, GETBULK, SET/COMMIT/UNDO, TRAP) be passed to sub-agents, plus a small DPI20-MIB.

SNMP.why: The document specifies an agent/sub-agent extension protocol for SNMP agents, including how SNMP requests, sets and traps are distributed to sub-agents.
SNMP.quote: The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP [1]) Distributed Protocol Interface (DPI) is an extension to SNMP agents that permits end-users to dynamically add, delete or replace management variables

MIB.why: Defines a MIB module (dpiPortForTCP, dpiPortForUDP) and the protocol centres on registering MIB sub-trees with the agent.
MIB.quote: DPI20-MIB DEFINITION

rejected.why: ASN.1/BER only appears as the encoding of the SNMP PDUs used to query the DPI port; the DPI protocol itself is a custom binary format.
TCP and UDP are only transports (and a port number is discovered via SNMP); the document defines nothing new about them.
Character-set selection between native EBCDIC and ASCII is a minor detail of the protocol, not the subject.
AgentX is a later, different subagent protocol; this document does not discuss it (it references SMUX only).

RFC1593.title: SNA APPN Node MIB
RFC1593.summary: Defines IBM's enterprise SNMP MIB module for SNA APPN nodes, covering node, port, link station, topology, directory and class-of-service objects.

APPN.why: The whole MIB models APPN nodes, topology database, TGs, directory and COS, so it belongs on the APPN page.
APPN.quote: This RFC describes IBM's SNMP support for SNA Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking (APPN) nodes.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module in SMI format (OBJECT-TYPE tables and entries), which MIB readers would want.
MIB.quote: IBM-6611-APPN-MIB DEFINITIONS          ::= BEGIN

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines a MIB, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
DLS ports and link station tables appear, but only as DLC-specific objects; the document does not specify DLSw.
Token ring port and link station tables are just DLC-specific attributes; the document is not about IP over token ring.
Parent of APPN is implied, so it is not listed separately.
TCP/IP port and address objects are DLC-specific attributes for one link type; the document is not about TCP.
Class of Service tables are APPN route selection weights, a part of the APPN MIB rather than a general QoS architecture.

RFC1594.title: FYI on Questions and Answers - Answers to Commonly asked "New Internet User" Questions
RFC1594.summary: FYI 4 (RFC 1594) is a beginner-oriented Q&A guide for new Internet users covering the Internet, TCP/IP, DNS, RFCs/FYIs/STDs, Internet organizations (IAB, IETF, IANA, InterNIC), services (WHOIS, Knowbot, archie, gopher, WWW, Netnews, FTP, Telnet), mailing lists, and a glossary.

user guides.why: This is FYI 4, an introductory Q&A guide for new Internet users, which is exactly what the user guides (FYI series) subject covers.
user guides.quote: The goal is to document the most commonly asked questions and answers in the Internet.

terminology.why: A glossary of about 30 pages defines Internet terms and acronyms. This is a substantial part of the document.
terminology.quote: Below is a condensed glossary to assist in making some sense of the Internet world.

RFC series.why: Section 6 explains what RFCs, FYIs, STDs and Internet Drafts are and how to obtain them. Readers of the RFC series subject would want this.
RFC series.quote: FYI stands for For Your Information.  FYIs are a subset of the RFC series of online documents.

IETF process.why: Section 7 describes the IAB, IETF, IRTF, ISOC and IANA, plus Internet Drafts and the standards track. This gives a substantial overview of IETF organization.
IETF process.quote: The IETF is a large open community of network designers, operators, vendors, and researchers concerned with the Internet and the Internet protocol suite.

rejected.why: DNS gets only two short answers and a glossary entry. It is not a substantial subject of the document.
WHOIS usage is explained as one service among many for end users. The document does not specify or extend the protocol.
Gopher is described in one brief answer among many tools. It is not the subject of the document.
IANA is described in one Q&A with a list of assignment types. The document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
USENET and newsgroups are covered in a few short answers. Not the main subject.
The document mentions the ARPANET and early networks only in passing. It is not a history.

RFC1595.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the SONET/SDH Interface Type
RFC1595.summary: Defines the SONET/SDH MIB module (SNMPv2 SMI) with objects for medium, section, line, path and virtual tributary configuration and performance statistics, plus ifTable usage for SONET/SDH interfaces.

SONET.why: The document is entirely about managing SONET/SDH interfaces: section, line, path and VT layers, defects, and error counters, so the SONET tag fits.
SONET.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) objects.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition for SONET/SDH interfaces, using the SMI and interface group conventions.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework and substrate; the document defines a MIB module, covered by the MIB tag, not SNMP protocol itself.
ASN.1 is used only as the SMI notation for the definitions, not the subject of the document.
The error-second and coding-violation counters are SONET-specific MIB objects, not a general performance measurement methodology.
The AToM working group name does not make this document about ATM; it covers SONET/SDH only.

RFC1596.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Frame Relay Service
RFC1596.summary: Defines the FRNETSERV-MIB SNMPv2 module for Customer Network Management of a Frame Relay network service, covering logical ports, in-channel signalling parameters, PVC end-points and connections, accounting, and traps.

frame relay.why: The document is a MIB for Frame Relay service.
frame relay.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing the Frame Relay Service.

RFC1597.title: Address Allocation for Private Internets
RFC1597.summary: RFC 1597 reserves three IPv4 address blocks (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) for private internets that need no globally unique addresses, and gives operational guidance on their use, filtering, and DNS leakage.

addressing.why: The document defines private IP address space allocation and how enterprises use it versus globally unique addresses, which is IP address architecture and allocation. No more specific addressing child (CIDR, anycast, etc.) is the main subject.
addressing.quote: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has reserved the following three blocks of the IP address space for private networks

IPv4.why: The reserved blocks are IPv4 class A/B/C ranges, and the motivation is conserving the finite IPv4 address space. IPv4 address lifecycle is covered by this tag.
IPv4.quote: describes methods to preserve IP address space by not allocating globally unique IP addresses to hosts private to an enterprise

rejected.why: NAT is not described. The document relies on application-layer gateways and filtering, not address translation.
The split-nameserver advice to avoid leaking private addresses is a minor operational note, not the subject.
Renumbering is discussed as a drawback and tradeoff, but the document is not about renumbering procedures.
CIDR is mentioned only in passing as a reason renumbering will become more common.
Firewalls and application layer gateways are mentioned as examples of where private addresses are suitable, not specified.

gaps.name: private address space / special-use IP address blocks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for reserved or special-use IP address ranges (RFC 1918 style). The closest fit is addressing.

RFC1598.title: PPP in X.25
RFC1598.summary: Specifies how PPP-encapsulated packets are carried over X.25 virtual circuits, using X.25 framing, NLPID-based call setup, and LCP configuration constraints.

X.25.why: The whole document defines how PPP runs over X.25: frame format, call setup via the PPP NLPID in call user data, and X.25-specific configuration.
X.25.quote: This document describes the use of X.25 for framing PPP encapsulated packets.

PPP.why: It profiles PPP for X.25. It forbids Address-and-Control-Field-Compression, recommends Protocol-Field-Compression, sets the initial MRU, and covers LCP behaviour and authentication.
PPP.quote: The Link Control Protocol can negotiate modifications to the basic frame structure.

rejected.why: Frame Relay is mentioned only as a switch-to-switch protocol that can hide the X.25 header. The document is not about it.
ISDN appears only in the title of RFC 1356, which is cited as a reference. The document does not address it.
CLNP appears only as an example of an NLPID value that conformance does not require.
The document mentions VJ header compression and PPP field compression only in passing. It does not specify header compression.

RFC1599.title: Summary of 1500-1599
RFC1599.summary: RFC 1599 is an annotated index of RFCs 1500 through 1599, giving each RFC's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track marking.

RFC series.why: The document catalogues a block of RFC series publications and reports their status. It is series bookkeeping, so it belongs on the RFC series page.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1500 through RFCs 1599.

rejected.why: It is a status list of documents, not a history or retrospective, although it is a useful historical record.
A few listed RFCs concern DNS, such as 1591 and 1535-1537. This summary only mentions them and is not about DNS.
Several listed RFCs cover PPP, such as 1548 and 1549. The summary only lists them.
Several listed RFCs cover OSPF, such as 1583 and 1587. The summary only lists them.
Several listed RFCs cover MIME, such as 1521 and 1522. The summary only lists them.
It lists standards-track status markers but does not describe or discuss the standards process.

RFC1600.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1600.summary: RFC 1600 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly list of Internet Official Protocol Standards, explaining the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and listing protocols by state.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels and RFC processing decision table, and records each protocol's standardization state.
IETF process.quote: This memo describes the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as determined by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB).

RFC series.why: A substantial section describes the RFC series, submission and publication rules, and how RFCs are obtained.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: The Assigned Numbers document and the IANA contact are only mentioned as references and contacts, not as the subject of the document.
Section 4 defines maturity-level terms, but it is part of the standards-process explanation rather than a glossary.
The document is a status snapshot as of 1994, not a history or retrospective.
TCP and the many other protocols (DNS, SMTP, SNMP, BGP and so on) appear only as entries in the status lists, and none is specified or analysed.

gaps.name: Internet standards track / protocol status listing
gaps.why: The document is a catalogue of protocol standardization states across all areas. The closest taxonomy fit is IETF process, which does not capture the catalogue function.

RFC1601.title: Charter of the Internet Architecture Board (IAB)
RFC1601.summary: RFC 1601 is the 1994 charter of the Internet Architecture Board, defining its membership, selection, roles (IESG selection, architectural oversight, standards process appeal, RFC series and IANA oversight, liaison, advice to ISOC) and organization.

internet governance.why: The document is a governance charter for the IAB, covering how the body is composed, selected and what it oversees. This is the broad governance topic, with no more specific child fitting a general IAB charter.
internet governance.quote: This memo documents the composition, selection, roles, and organization of the Internet Architecture Board and its subsidiary organizations.

IETF process.why: A substantial part covers the IETF nomination committee, IESG appointment approval, and IAB appeals of the standards process.
IETF process.quote: The IAB provides oversight of the process used to create Internet Standards.

RFC series.why: The charter assigns the IAB responsibility for the RFC Editor and the RFC series, and makes the RFC Editor an ex-officio member.
RFC series.quote: The IAB shall select an RFC Editor, who shall be responsible for the editorial management and publication of the RFC series.

IANA.why: The charter makes the IAB responsible for designating IANA and administering assigned numbers.
IANA.quote: The IAB shall also designate an Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) to administer the assignment of Internet protocol numbers.

NomCom.why: The document describes NomCom composition and its role in nominating IAB and IESG members.
NomCom.quote: The IETF nomination committee is formed every year and consists of a non-voting chair designated by the Internet Society

rejected.why: The IAB's architectural oversight role is mentioned, but the document is about the organization, not architectural principles.
It is an organizational charter, not a retrospective, even though it is now historic.

RFC1602.title: The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 2
RFC1602.summary: RFC 1602 (Revision 2) describes the Internet Standards Process: the organizations involved, maturity levels, standards-track procedures, appeals, external standards, and intellectual property rights policy.

IETF process.why: The whole document defines the standards track, maturity levels, IESG review, advancement, revision, retirement and appeals procedures.
IETF process.quote: This memo documents the process currently used by the Internet community for the standardization of protocols and procedures.

IPR.why: Section 5 is a substantial, fully revised IPR policy covering contributions, copyright, patents, notices and assurances.
IPR.quote: ISOC will not propose, adopt, or continue to maintain any standards, including but not limited to standards labelled Proposed, Draft or Internet Standards

rejected.why: Section 1.4 describes IANA's role briefly, but it is a small part of a document about the standards process.
Section 1.3 describes RFCs and Internet Drafts, but only as publications related to the standards process.
The nominating committee is mentioned only in passing in the organizations section.
The IAB's architectural oversight role is mentioned, but the document does not address architectural principles.

RFC1603.title: IETF Working Group Guidelines and Procedures
RFC1603.summary: RFC 1603 describes the guidelines and procedures for forming, operating, and terminating IETF working groups, including charters, BOFs, roles of chairs and area directors, appeals, and WG document handling.

IETF process.why: The whole document defines IETF working group procedures: charters, BOFs, sessions, appeals, roles and document submission. This is the core IETF process subject.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the guidelines and procedures for formation and operation of IETF working groups.

rejected.why: RFCs and Internet-Drafts are covered only briefly in section 6 as the output of WGs. The document is not about RFC format or publication.
NomCom is not discussed anywhere in the document.
The mmusic charter in the appendix is only a sample charter. The document does not specify session control protocols.
FTP appears only as a way to access the meeting document archive. It is substrate, not subject.

RFC1604.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Frame Relay Service
RFC1604.summary: Defines the FRNETSERV-MIB SNMPv2 MIB module for customer network management of a Frame Relay network service, covering logical ports, signaling, PVC endpoints, connections, accounting and traps.

frame relay.why: The MIB's whole subject is Frame Relay service: UNI/NNI logical ports, PVC endpoints, DLCIs, CIR/Bc/Be and LMI signalling.
frame relay.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing the Frame Relay Service.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (FRNETSERV-MIB) in SMIv2, with compliance statements and interface table usage.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with; the document defines objects rather than the SNMP framework, and MIB is the more specific tag.
It provides counters and monitoring objects, but it is a service MIB, not a performance measurement methodology.
ATM appears only in the MIB stack figure as an adjacent layer.
The X.25 MIB is mentioned only in the MIB stack figure.

RFC1605.title: SONET to Sonnet Translation
RFC1605.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC proposing SONNET, a scheme that "compresses" SONET OC-1 frames by replacing them with English sonnets catalogued by Cerf number.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody dated 1 April 1994, with a poetry-based joke protocol. Readers of the humor page would expect it.
humor.quote: SONNET is a method for compressing 810-byte (9 lines by 90 bytes) SONET OC-1 frames into approximately 400-byte (fourteen line decasyllabic) English sonnets.

SONET.why: The joke is built on SONET framing, with OC-1 and OC-3 frames, interleaving and concatenation. It parodies SONET but does not specify real SONET behaviour, so this tag is secondary.
SONET.quote: For rates higher than OC-1, the OC-1 frames may either come interleaved or concatenated into larger frames.

rejected.why: The 'compression' is a parody and is not a real lossless data compression format.

RFC1606.title: A Historical Perspective On The Usage Of IP Version 9
RFC1606.summary: An April 1st parody RFC presenting a fictional retrospective on "IP version 9", describing absurd uses such as addressing light bulbs, blood-stream monitors, packaging and magazines, and intergalactic routing.

humor.why: The document is dated 1 April and is a whimsical parody of IP addressing and deployment, with fictional faster-than-light stacks and networked shoes. It belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: The take-up of the network protocol TCP/IPv9 has been phenomenal over the last few years.

rejected.why: It talks about address allocation and hierarchy, but only as satire about a fictional protocol. It gives no real addressing guidance.
IPv9 is a joke protocol, not IPv6. The document does not specify, analyse or discuss IPv6.
The 42-level routing hierarchy is a parody element. The document has no real routing content.
SNMPv9 traps are mentioned only in passing as part of the joke.

RFC1607.title: A VIEW FROM THE 21ST CENTURY
RFC1607.summary: Vint Cerf's April 1994 humorous RFC presenting fictional emails from 2023 between scientists on Mars, the Moon and Earth, which recount a retrospective history of the Internet (ARPANET, NSFNET, IPng, ATM, growth) and speculate on the future.

humor.why: This is an April 1st whimsical RFC with a fictional time-capsule premise, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: The letters below were discovered in September 1993 in a reverse time-capsule apparently sent from 2023.

internet history.why: Much of the body is a retrospective on Internet history: ARPANET, CYCLADES, TCP/IP adoption in 1983, NSFNET, commercialization and the IPng debate.
internet history.quote: Did you know that the original work on Internet was intended for military network use?

rejected.why: ARPANET appears only as part of a broad historical narrative. The document is not about its protocols or operations.
The 1991-1994 address-space debate is mentioned in passing, but the document does not discuss the candidate protocols TUBA, PIP, SIPP or TP/IX.
The new IP is alluded to only vaguely, with a joke about a 64-bit address space. The document does not specify or analyse IPv6.
ATM is mentioned only once, in a historical aside.
The letters are formatted as email, but the document is not about email as a technology.

RFC1608.title: Representing IP Information in the X.500 Directory
RFC1608.summary: Defines X.500 Directory object classes and namespace tree for representing IP networks, nodes, interfaces, Autonomous Systems, routing policy, and IP/AS number delegation and assignment information.

X.500.why: The whole document defines X.500 object classes, attributes, OIDs and a DIT layout for IP information, so it is about using the X.500 directory service.
X.500.quote: This document describes the objects necessary to include information about IP networks and IP numbers in the X.500 Directory.

addressing.why: A large part covers IP address and AS number assignment and delegation blocks, classless masks and registry hierarchy, so addressing readers would want it.
addressing.quote: Directory objects have been defined to represent IP and AS (Autonomous System) namespace in the Directory.

rejected.why: DNS is only referenced for mapping IP numbers to domain names via attributes like associatedDomain. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
This is the parent of X.500. The specific child tag X.500 fits, so the parent is implied.
AS routing policy attributes (asIn, asOut) align with the RIPE database, but the document does not specify RPSL itself.
Classless addressing is supported through masks and supernetting is cited, but CIDR itself is not the subject.
The IP network image holds data that a NIC-WHOIS server would reveal, but WHOIS is not specified.

RFC1609.title: Charting Networks in the X.500 Directory
RFC1609.summary: Experimental RFC defining an X.500 Directory schema (object classes for physical and logical/image network, node and network-interface objects) for representing communication network topology and related information in the DIT.

X.500.why: The document defines X.500 object classes and attributes and their placement in the Directory Information Tree, so it is about using the X.500 directory.
X.500.quote: This document presents a model in which a communication network with all its related details and descriptions can be represented in the X.500 Directory.

rejected.why: Motivated by network management and configuration information, but the document specifies a directory schema, not management protocols or practice.
Only cited as an example of piecemeal network information services, not the subject.
Only mentioned as a piecemeal prior effort; not specified or extended.
Parent of X.500; implied by the more specific X.500 tag.
Route management is listed as a possible use of the network map, but the document does not address routing itself.

RFC1610.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1610.summary: RFC 1610 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly list of Internet Official Protocol Standards, describing the standards process, maturity and requirement levels, and cataloguing protocols by standardization state.

IETF process.why: Core content explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels, and RFC processing decision table.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: Substantial section on the RFC series, submission, and the RFC Editor's processing table.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: IANA appears as a contact and manager of the list and Assigned Numbers is mentioned, but the document is not about IANA registries.
TCP and many other protocols are only entries in the status lists, not subjects of the document.
DNS appears only as list entries; the document does not address DNS itself.
SNMP and numerous MIBs are just listed in the tables.
It is a status catalogue of the time, not a history or retrospective.

RFC1611.title: DNS Server MIB Extensions
RFC1611.summary: RFC 1611 defines the DNS-SERVER-MIB SNMPv2 module, with configuration, counter, optional counter and zone groups, for managing DNS name server software via SNMP.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (DNS-SERVER-MIB) defined in SMIv2 with object groups and compliance statements; MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: it describes a set of extensions which instrument DNS name server functions.

DNS.why: The MIB models DNS name server operation: queries, responses, recursion, zones and zone transfers, so DNS readers would want it.
DNS.quote: A name server is a program (or piece thereof) that provides resource records to resolvers.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework used to carry the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol changes. MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 subset is only the notation used for the SMI definitions, not the subject.
Implied by the MIB parent; MIB tag is more specific.

RFC1612.title: DNS Resolver MIB Extensions
RFC1612.summary: Defines the SNMPv2 DNS Resolver MIB module, with managed objects for resolver configuration, counters, lame delegations, and positive and negative caches.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (DNS-RESOLVER-MIB) in SMIv2, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: it describes a set of extensions which instrument DNS resolver functions

DNS.why: The managed objects cover DNS resolver behaviour: sbelt servers, caching, negative caching, lame delegations, and query and response counters. DNS operators would want this.
DNS.quote: The MIB module for entities implementing the client (resolver) side of the Domain Name System (DNS) protocol.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document does not extend or specify the protocol, and the MIB tag already covers its place in that subject.
ASN.1 is only the notation used in the MIB definitions.
It is implied by the MIB tag, and the document does not address network management as a broader subject.

RFC1613.title: cisco Systems X.25 over TCP (XOT)
RFC1613.summary: Informational cisco specification for XOT, which carries X.25 packets over TCP (port 1998) using a 4-byte length header, covering virtual circuit setup, flow control, and PVC setup.

X.25.why: The whole document specifies how X.25 virtual circuits, call setup, flow control and PVCs are carried over TCP/IP, so X.25 and IP over public data networks is the subject.
X.25.quote: This memo documents a method of sending X.25 packets over IP internets by encapsulating the X.25 Packet Level in TCP packets.

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable byte-stream substrate; XOT adds a length header and uses port 1998 but defines nothing new about TCP itself.
The document is a binding of X.25 over TCP, which fits the topic, but the specific X.25 technology tag is the better fit and the topic would be redundant alongside it.
It is encapsulation of X.25 in TCP, not IP-in-IP or generic IP tunnelling.

RFC1614.title: Network Access to Multimedia Information
RFC1614.summary: A RARE report surveying user requirements for networked multimedia information access, evaluating Gopher, WAIS and WWW plus research hypermedia systems and standards, and recommending further work centred on the World-Wide Web.

Gopher.why: Gopher and Gopher+ are described in detail, including protocol, type IDs, attributes, publishing and limitations, as one of the three main systems evaluated.
Gopher.quote: The Internet Gopher is a distributed document delivery service.

WAIS.why: WAIS is examined in its own section covering the Z39.50-based protocol, publishing, non-text data and limitations.
WAIS.quote: The Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) system allows users to search for and retrieve information from databases anywhere on the Internet.

web.why: The report's central recommendation is to build multimedia support on the WWW. It examines WWW architecture, Mosaic and the gaps.
web.quote: it is recommended that RARE should select the World-Wide Web to concentrate its efforts on.

HTTP.why: The report describes HTTP and the proposed HTTP2 multimedia extensions (HEAD, format negotiation, charging, authorisation).
HTTP.quote: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the protocol employed between server and client.

HTML.why: HTML and the HTML2 multimedia enhancements such as IMG and link relations are discussed substantively.
