HTML.quote: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the way in which text documents must be structured if they are to contain links to other documents.

URI.why: URL syntax, partial URLs and URNs are explained and linked to caching and multimedia.
URI.quote: All nodes on the Web are addressed using the "Universal [or Uniform] Resource Locator" (URL) syntax

SGML.why: SGML, HyTime, MHEG, ODA and SDIF are surveyed as hypermedia structuring standards, with SGML emphasised.
SGML.quote: SGML (Standard Generalized Markup Language - ISO 8879) is a metalanguage for defining markup notations for text.

MIME.why: MIME's separation of media type and encoding is highlighted as relevant to Gopher+ and HTTP2.
MIME.quote: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) is a mechanism for transferring multimedia information in an RFC822 mail message.

rejected.why: The report discusses responsiveness in a user-experience sense, not QoS architectures or signalling.
Caching and prefetching are listed as responsiveness ideas, but caching is not a main subject.
TCP is only the transport substrate for Gopher and HTTP.
MIME content types are described only as background, with no registry rules covered.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as the encoding for MHEG and SDIF.

gaps.name: Hypermedia systems and multimedia information retrieval
gaps.why: The report is largely about hypermedia (Hyper-G, Microcosm, AthenaMuse, HyTime, MHEG) and networked multimedia access. The taxonomy has no tag for hypermedia or multimedia standards.

RFC1615.title: Migrating from X.400(84) to X.400(88)
RFC1615.summary: Informational RARE/JNT report comparing X.400(88) with X.400(84) and describing migration issues, interworking and downgrading rules, and a recommended migration topology for the European R&D MHS.

X.400.why: The whole document is about X.400 message handling systems, the differences between the 1984 and 1988 versions, and interworking/downgrading between them.
X.400.quote: this document compares X.400(88) to X.400(84) and describes what problems can be anticipated in the migration

rejected.why: P2 content downgrading is discussed, but in the X.400 context, not Internet message format.
X.400 is the more specific tag; the parent is implied.
Directory names in MHS are mentioned as a new feature but the document is not about the directory service.
OSI upper layers (RTS, ROS, ACSE) are discussed only as the supporting stack for X.400, not as network-layer protocols.
RFC1006/TCP/IP appears only as a possible transport stack at entry points.

RFC1616.title: X.400(1988) for the Academic and Research Community in Europe
RFC1616.summary: A RARE task force report assessing migration of European R&D messaging services from X.400(1984), RFC 822/MIME/PEM, Mail-11 and PC LAN mail to X.400(1988), recommending a pan-European X.400(1988) pilot with gateways to RFC 822/MIME.

X.400.why: The whole report is about deploying and migrating to X.400(1988) message handling, including its features, gateways, costs and recommendations.
X.400.quote: migrate existing X.400 services to a X.400(1988) service.

email.why: It compares email infrastructures (RFC 822, MIME, PEM, Mail-11, PC LAN mail) and covers gatewaying and coexistence among them, which is general email architecture and interworking.
email.quote: provide a transparent gateway between X.400(1988) and RFC 822/MIME/PEM.

rejected.why: MIME is discussed as one of the competing service suites and as a gateway target, but the document does not specify or extend it.
The X.500 directory is covered as support for X.400 (DLs, routing, UA capabilities), but only as a dependency, not as the subject.
PEM is mentioned as the secure-messaging counterpart to X.400 security, but the document does not specify or analyse it in depth.
EDI over X.400 is mentioned as a benefit among many but is not a substantial part of the report.
RFC 822 is discussed at a high level, but the report is not about message format specifics.

gaps.name: X.400 migration and coexistence between X.400(1984), X.400(1988) and RFC 822
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only a generic X.400 tag, with no tag for mail-system migration or gatewaying strategy.

RFC1617.title: Naming and Structuring Guidelines for X.500 Directory Pilots
RFC1617.summary: Informational guidelines for X.500 Directory pilots on DIT structure, naming style, attribute usage and multi-national organisation modelling, focused on White Pages use.

X.500.why: The whole document is about structuring the X.500 DIT, naming entries and using attributes for X.500 directory pilots.
X.500.quote: This document defines a number of naming and structuring guidelines focused on White Pages usage. Alignment to these guidelines is recommended for directory pilots.

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which is the more specific fitting tag, so the parent is implied.
Not discussed; the document concerns X.500 DAP-era directories and the COSINE schema.
Mail attributes such as rfc822mailbox and mhsORAddresses are only listed as directory attributes, not the subject.
MHS O/R address attributes are mentioned only as directory attribute values.
Directory naming is the topic, but the X.500 tag already covers it and the naming topic is about name resolution systems like DNS.
Printable String, T.61 and transliteration are discussed briefly as attribute syntaxes, not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC1618.title: PPP over ISDN
RFC1618.summary: RFC 1618 specifies how to use PPP encapsulation over ISDN B-channels and D-channels, covering physical layer, framing, encoding detection, out-of-band signalling and LCP configuration.

ISDN.why: The whole document defines how PPP runs over ISDN channels, including framing, encoding, called-party signalling and configuration.
ISDN.quote: This document describes the use of PPP over Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) switched circuits.

PPP.why: The document profiles PPP (LCP options, defaults, MRU/MTU, restart timers, framing) for ISDN, so PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: The LCP recommended sync configuration options apply to ISDN links.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an alternative framing ("PPP in Frame Relay") and in V.120 discussion; not the subject.
"PPP in X.25" is mentioned only as a possible D-channel framing by prior configuration; not the subject.

RFC1619.title: PPP over SONET/SDH
RFC1619.summary: RFC 1619 specifies how to carry PPP over SONET/SDH circuits, covering SPE octet mapping, path signal label, transmission rates, HDLC-like framing and recommended LCP options.

SONET.why: The document defines the mapping of PPP octet streams into the SONET/SDH SPE, the C2 label value, rates and configuration. This is exactly the IP/PPP over SONET/SDH subject.
SONET.quote: This document describes the use of PPP over Synchronous Optical Network (SONET) and Synchronous Digital Heirarchy (SDH) circuits.

PPP.why: The document specifies PPP encapsulation use, framing and recommended LCP configuration options (Magic Number, 32-bit FCS, no compression) for this medium.
PPP.quote: The standard LCP sync configuration defaults apply to SONET/SDH links.

rejected.why: ATM is mentioned only as another user of the STS-3c super-rate mapping, not as a subject of the document.
FDDI is mentioned only in passing as using the same super-rate mapping.
MAPOS is a different multiple-access protocol over SONET; this document covers only PPP point-to-point.

RFC1620.title: Internet Architecture Extensions for Shared Media
RFC1620.summary: Informational memo discussing four approaches (hop-by-hop ICMP redirect extension, extended routing, extended proxy ARP, routing query messages) to eliminate unnecessary IP hops across shared-medium networks such as SMDS/ATM large public data networks.

internet layer.why: The memo is about extending the IP-layer architecture (network numbers, routers, hosts, redirects) for shared media. No more specific child tag covers general IP architecture, so the parent topic fits.
internet layer.quote: This memo concerns the implications of shared medium networks for the architecture of the TCP/IP protocol suite.

ICMP.why: The main proposal extends ICMP Redirect (foreign Redirect and XRedirect carrying LL addresses), with detailed host and router changes.
ICMP.quote: A router is to be allowed to send, and a host allowed to accept, a Redirect message that specifies a foreign IP address within the same SM.
ICMP.section: 4. SOME SOLUTIONS TO THE SM PROBLEMS

ARP.why: Extended proxy ARP and address-resolution servers are one of the four analysed solutions, and ARP security is discussed.
ARP.quote: This is a form of the proxy ARP approach, in which the routing problem is solved implicitly by an extended address resolution mechanism at the LL.
ARP.section: 4. SOME SOLUTIONS TO THE SM PROBLEMS

routing architecture.why: Extended routing with a SameSM attribute and third-party next hops is a routing architecture matter, along with stale routing information and the scalability of host routes.
routing architecture.quote: Routing protocols can be modified to know about the SM and to provide LL addresses.
routing architecture.section: 4. SOME SOLUTIONS TO THE SM PROBLEMS

rejected.why: IP over ATM and SMDS are the motivating examples, but the memo is about general shared-medium architecture, not ATM itself.
SMDS is only mentioned as an example of a large public data network.
NHRP is not mentioned; the memo predates it, and Heinanen's NBMA ARP is only discussed as one proposal.
Firewall implications are covered in one subsection as a constraint, not as the document's subject.
The memo discusses the network number assumption but is not about address allocation or architecture of addresses.
The more specific internet layer tag fits better, since the document concerns IP-layer architecture.

gaps.name: Shared medium / NBMA IP architecture
gaps.why: The document is about IP over shared-medium and NBMA networks (LIS, large public data networks), which the taxonomy has no specific tag for beyond the general internet layer topic.

RFC1621.title: Pip Near-term Architecture
RFC1621.summary: Historic informational RFC describing the near-term architecture of Pip, a candidate IPng replacement for IPv4, covering its provider-rooted hierarchical addressing, IDs, routing, transition from IP, PCMP, mobility and evolution mechanisms.

IPng.why: Pip was one of the candidate IPng protocols (merged into SIPP); the document records its architecture.
IPng.quote: Pip is an internet protocol intended as the replacement for IP version 4.

addressing.why: Substantial parts cover hierarchical provider-based addresses, assignment authority, prefixes and autoconfiguration.
addressing.quote: Pip Addresses are provider-rooted (as opposed to geographical).

routing architecture.why: Covers multi-level path-vector routing (MLPV), exit routing, and routing information filtering across hierarchy levels.
routing architecture.quote: At the top-level of the Pip Address hierarchy, a path-vector routing algorithm is used.

IPv6 transition.why: A full section on IP/Pip translation, tunneling and DNS transition, relevant to coexistence of old and new IP protocols.
IPv6 transition.quote: The transition scheme for Pip has two major components, 1) translation, and 2) encapsulation.

IP mobility.why: Dedicated section on host mobility using IDs separate from addresses.
IP mobility.quote: Pip uses the Mobile Host Server and the PCMP Host Mobility message to manage host mobility;

rejected.why: DNS holds Pip IDs and addresses and has new RRs/opcode, but this is a supporting mechanism; the document defers details to another draft.
CBT and Class D style multicast addressing are covered only briefly as address families.
PCMP is the Pip analogue of ICMP, but it is a Pip-specific protocol and not ICMP.
NAT is mentioned only as an alternative the transition scheme avoids.
Anycast is one of the four Pip address types and is described only briefly.
Tunneling through IP is a transition and evolution mechanism but not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Pip (Pip internet protocol)
gaps.why: There is no tag for Pip itself; IPng (the historic IPng candidates) is the closest fit.

RFC1622.title: Pip Header Processing
RFC1622.summary: Historic RFC recording the Pip internet protocol's header processing (Initial, Transit and Options parts, routing and handling directives, tunnelling), one of the candidate IP replacements merged into SIPP.

IPng.why: Pip was one of the historic IPng candidate protocols (with TUBA, SIPP, TP/IX); the RFC records its header format and forwarding rules.
IPng.quote: Pip is an internet protocol intended as the replacement for IP version 4.

rejected.why: Pip was merged into SIPP, which became IPv6, but this document specifies Pip itself, not IPv6.
Tunnelling by nesting Transit Parts is part of Pip's design, but it is a feature of the Pip header, not the document's subject.
IPv4 is only the protocol Pip was meant to replace; the document does not specify it.
The forwarding algorithm is specific to the Pip header, so IPng covers it better than the general routing architecture tag.

RFC1623.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types
RFC1623.summary: Defines the EtherLike-MIB module, SNMP managed objects for Ethernet-like (802.3) interfaces including statistics, collision histograms, TDR and loopback tests, obsoleting RFC 1398.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (EtherLike-MIB) with SMI object definitions for managing Ethernet-like interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The objects cover IEEE 802.3 interface statistics, collisions, and TDR/loopback tests, so readers interested in Ethernet management would look here.
Ethernet.quote: Instances of these object types represent attributes of an interface to an ethernet-like communications medium.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework in which the MIB is used, but the document only defines objects, not the protocol itself; the MIB tag is more specific.
ASN.1 subset is merely the notation used by the SMI to write the object definitions.
Covered by the more specific Ethernet tag.

RFC1624.title: Computation of the Internet Checksum via Incremental Update
RFC1624.summary: RFC 1624 corrects the incremental update procedure for the Internet checksum from RFC 1141, fixing a one's-complement negative-zero edge case, and recommends Eqn. 3 or Eqn. 4.

checksum.why: The whole document specifies how to incrementally compute the Internet checksum and corrects RFC 1141's handling of zero in one's complement arithmetic.
checksum.quote: This memo describes an updated technique for incremental computation of the standard Internet checksum.

rejected.why: The checksum is computed over IP headers and the examples use IP header fields, but the document is about the checksum arithmetic, not IP itself.
Not mentioned; irrelevant.

RFC1625.title: WAIS over Z39.50-1988
RFC1625.summary: Informational memo describing how WAIS (Wide Area Information Servers) used the Z39.50-1988 protocol, including its design goals, Type-3 queries, relevance feedback, and retrieval via the Search Facility, as a basis for migrating to later Z39.50 versions.

WAIS.why: The whole document describes the WAIS system and its implementation of Z39.50-1988: client, server, queries, citations and retrieval.
WAIS.quote: The network publishing system, Wide Area Information Servers (WAIS), is designed to help users find information over a computer network.

rejected.why: WAIS runs over TCP, but this is only the transport substrate and is mentioned in passing.
Z39.50 is an information retrieval protocol, not a directory service. The taxonomy has no Z39.50 tag, and WAIS is the closest fit.
Z39.50 was designed for OSI presentation services, but the document is not about OSI network-layer protocols.

gaps.name: Z39.50
gaps.why: The document is largely about the Z39.50 information retrieval protocol (1988 version, with migration to 1992 and 1994). The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC1626.title: Default IP MTU for use over ATM AAL5
RFC1626.summary: RFC 1626 sets the default IP MTU over ATM AAL5 to 9180 octets, specifies MTU negotiation via ATM SVC signalling (AAL Parameters), and requires Path MTU Discovery in routers.

ATM.why: The document defines IP over ATM AAL5 behaviour: default MTU, PVC handling and SVC signalling negotiation of the CPCS-SDU size.
ATM.quote: the default IP MTU for use with ATM AAL5 shall be 9180 octets.
ATM.section: Default Value for IP MTU over ATM AAL5

PMTUD.why: A whole section mandates Path MTU Discovery for routers and recommends it for hosts, to mitigate fragmentation given ATM's large MTU.
PMTUD.quote: all routers implementations that comply or conform with this specification must also implement the IP Path MTU Discovery mechanism as defined in RFC-1191

rejected.why: RFC 1209 SMDS MTU is cited only as justification for choosing 9180; the document is not about SMDS.
NFS frame size is only motivation for a large MTU; the document does not address NFS.
TCP performance is mentioned only as background evidence.
Classical IP over ATM is referenced for applicability only; NHRP is not discussed.

RFC1627.title: Network 10 Considered Harmful (Some Practices Shouldn't be Codified)
RFC1627.summary: A 1994 critique of RFC 1597 arguing that private address allocation (network 10) violates the globally unique IP address architecture, and urging IANA to withdraw it and the IAB to reaffirm unique addressing.

addressing.why: The whole document argues about IP address architecture, uniqueness, and allocation policy for private networks. No more specific addressing child (CIDR, multihoming, anycast, renumbering) is the main subject, so the parent topic fits.
addressing.quote: The lesson that we learned was that every IP address ought to be globally unique, independent of its attachment to the Internet.

renumbering.why: A substantial part of the document concerns the cost of renumbering when private networks merge or connect, including Apple's renumbering of 5,000 hosts.
renumbering.quote: If two private networks follow RFC 1597 and then later wish to communicate with each other, one will have to renumber.

IANA.why: A full policy section argues that IANA overstepped its mandate in assigning the private address blocks and asks the IAB to reaffirm that mandate.
IANA.quote: we strongly encourage IANA to withdraw its IP address assignments documented by RFC 1597 forthwith.

internet architecture.why: The document frames its case as protecting an architectural principle of the Internet, the global address space, and explores architectural concerns.
internet architecture.quote: RFC 1597 departs from the basic architectural rule that IP addresses must be globally unique

rejected.why: IPv4 address exhaustion is discussed, but the document is about private address policy, not the IPv4 protocol or its address lifecycle in its own right.
The document opposes private addressing but does not discuss network address translation behaviour.
IPng is mentioned only as the effort that should keep the community's attention, not as a subject of the document.
The document complains that RFC 1597 skipped IETF review, but this is a secondary argument and addressing is the main subject.
CIDR is mentioned only to rebut one claim made in RFC 1597.
DHCP is mentioned only as a potential renumbering aid.

gaps.name: Private address space (RFC 1597/RFC 1918)
gaps.why: The document is a critique of reserving private address blocks. The taxonomy has no tag for private or special-use IP address ranges, so addressing is the closest fit.

RFC1628.title: UPS Management Information Base
RFC1628.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module (UPS-MIB) for managing uninterruptible power supplies, covering identification, battery, input/output/bypass, alarms, tests, control, configuration, traps and conformance.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (UPS-MIB) written in SMI, specifying managed objects, notifications and compliance statements for UPS devices.
MIB.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines a MIB module, not the protocol or framework itself.
Considered because UPS and power are involved, but the document is a device MIB for UPS status and control rather than energy monitoring/management of networked devices; the MIB tag fits better.
ASN.1 is only the notation underlying SMI definitions, not the subject.

gaps.name: Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) management
gaps.why: The document is about UPS device management, which has no dedicated tag; it is covered only through the generic MIB tag.

RFC1629.title: Guidelines for OSI NSAP Allocation in the Internet
RFC1629.summary: RFC 1629 gives guidelines for allocating hierarchical OSI NSAP addresses in the Internet so that CLNP routing (IS-IS, IDRP) can aggregate routes and scale, covering provider/subscriber assignment, multi-homing, transition, and US/European recommendations.

OSI.why: The document is about OSI network-layer (NSAP) address structure and allocation, including GOSIP/DCC formats and registration authorities. OSI is the fitting tag for OSI network-layer addressing.
OSI.quote: This paper provides guidelines for allocating NSAP addresses in the Internet.

CLNP.why: The guidelines exist to support CLNP deployment and its routing scalability. CLNP is the protocol whose addresses are being allocated.
CLNP.quote: CLNP is currently being deployed in the Internet.  This is useful to support OSI and DECnet(tm) traffic.

IS-IS.why: Substantial sections describe IS-IS levels, areas and NSAP requirements, and the address layout is shaped for IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: Arrangement of parts of the NSAP for efficient operation of the IS-IS routing protocol;

addressing.why: Hierarchical address allocation by provider, aggregation, multi-homing and address transition (renumbering) are the main subject matter.
addressing.quote: The guidelines presented in this document are quite similar to the guidelines that are proposed in the Internet for IP address allocation with CIDR

rejected.why: Routing scalability and data abstraction are discussed, but the focus is on address assignment; no specific routing-architecture tag was chosen over addressing and IS-IS.
CIDR is cited only as an analogy; the document concerns NSAP addresses, not CIDR for IP.
The abstract mentions CLNP as an IPng candidate, but the document is about NSAP allocation and not the IPng selection.
DECnet is only mentioned as traffic CLNP can support.
Multi-homed routing domains are discussed in Section 5.4, but that is IP-style multihoming addressing for NSAPs, a sub-topic of the allocation guidance. Addressing already covers it.
Address transition is a brief subsection (5.7) and not a main subject.

gaps.name: IDRP (OSI Inter-Domain Routing Protocol, ISO 10747)
gaps.why: The document describes IDRP, Routing Domain Confederations and RDI/RDCI assignment at length, but the taxonomy has no OSI inter-domain routing tag.

gaps.name: NSAP addresses (OSI network service access point addressing, GOSIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has OSI and CLNP but no specific tag for NSAP address structure and registration authorities.

RFC1630.title: Universal Resource Identifiers in WWW: A Unifying Syntax for the Expression of Names and Addresses of Objects on the Network as used in the World-Wide Web
RFC1630.summary: Informational RFC by Tim Berners-Lee documenting the Universal Resource Identifier syntax used by the World-Wide Web, including generic syntax, escaping, relative forms, fragment identifiers, per-scheme notes (http, ftp, gopher, mailto, news, etc.) and scheme registration.

URI.why: The whole document specifies URI syntax, reserved/unsafe characters, percent-encoding, relative forms, fragment ids, scheme registration and BNF.
URI.quote: This document defines the syntax used by the World-Wide Web initiative to encode the names and addresses of objects on the Internet.

URN.why: A dedicated section covers how URNs are to be encoded in URI syntax and the reserved urn: prefix, though URN itself is not defined here.
URN.quote: The "urn" prefix is reserved for use in encoding a Uniform Resource Name when that has been developed by the IETF working group.

rejected.why: The http scheme is described as a URI scheme, but HTTP itself is not specified or extended.
ftp URL scheme mapping is covered, but FTP protocol is only referenced as what the URL addresses.
Gopher URL mapping is just one scheme among many; the document is not about the Gopher protocol.
Web context is the setting, but the subject is more specifically URI, which is tagged.
BNF is used to define syntax, a notation rather than the subject.
IANA is proposed as scheme registrar in a short passage; the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC1631.title: The IP Network Address Translator (NAT)
RFC1631.summary: RFC 1631 proposes the Network Address Translator (NAT), a router function at stub-domain borders that maps local addresses to globally unique ones as a short-term answer to IP address depletion and routing scaling, and discusses its header manipulations, pros and cons.

NAT.why: The document specifies the original NAT design, its operation, header rewriting (IP/TCP checksums, FTP PORT, ICMP), and its drawbacks.
NAT.quote: The address reuse solution is to place Network Address Translators (NAT) at the borders of stub domains.

rejected.why: Mentioned as the complementary short-term solution to routing scaling, but the document is about NAT, not CIDR.
Checksum adjustment code is given, but only as a NAT implementation detail, not as a subject in its own right.
FTP PORT command rewriting and sequence-number adjustment is a NAT application-level gateway concern; the document does not specify or extend FTP.
ICMP translation is discussed only as one of NAT's header manipulations.
The NAT tag is more specific; address reuse and private address spaces are discussed through NAT.
Encapsulation for backbone-partitioned stubs is a brief side point, not a main subject.

RFC1632.title: A Revised Catalog of Available X.500 Implementations
RFC1632.summary: An informational FYI catalog (revising RFC 1292) of 26 available X.500 directory implementations (DSAs, DUAs, DUA interfaces), with keyword indices and per-product descriptions.

X.500.why: The whole document surveys X.500 directory implementations (DSAs, DUAs), so the X.500 subject page is the natural home.
X.500.quote: This document catalogs currently available implementations of X.500, including commercial products and openly available offerings.

LDAP.why: Substantial parts describe LDAP implementations and LDAP-based DUAs (U-M LDAP, maX.500, DOS-DE, ldap-whois++, PC-DUA), with an LDAP keyword index.
LDAP.quote: LDAP is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol.  It gives X.500 access to platforms that have only TCP/IP access

rejected.why: Parent of X.500 and LDAP, which are already tagged, so it is implied.
ldap-whois++ is a single product entry that implements whois++ over LDAP. The document is not about WHOIS++ itself.
OSI transport and network layers are the environment these products run over, not the subject of the catalog.
Some products (PathWay, Wang) combine X.400 mail with X.500, but X.400 is incidental.
One product mentions SNMP-based monitoring in passing.

RFC1633.title: Integrated Services in the Internet Architecture: an Overview
RFC1633.summary: RFC 1633 is an informational overview of the Integrated Services architecture for the Internet: a service model (guaranteed, predictive, best-effort, link-sharing), a reference router implementation framework with traffic control, and an overview of RSVP.

Intserv.why: The whole document defines the Integrated Services model and its reference implementation framework, so it belongs on the Intserv page.
Intserv.quote: We use the term integrated services (IS) for an Internet service model that includes best-effort service, real-time service, and controlled link sharing.

RSVP.why: Section 5 gives an overview of RSVP, covering flowspecs, filter specs, reservation styles, receiver initiation and soft state. This is a substantial part of the document that RSVP readers would want.
RSVP.quote: Section 5 discusses the design of RSVP, a resource setup protocol compatible with the assumptions of our IS model

rejected.why: The QoS topic is a parent of Intserv and RSVP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The document says the design must support multicast, but it does not specify or analyse multicast routing or group membership.
ST-II is only a contrasting hard-state approach to reservation, mentioned for comparison.
The packet dropping discussion is brief and tied to scheduling. It does not cover queue management algorithms.

RFC1634.title: Novell IPX Over Various WAN Media (IPXWAN)
RFC1634.summary: Informational RFC specifying Novell's IPXWAN protocol, which negotiates master/slave roles, routing type and link parameters between IPX routers (and workstations) over PPP, X.25 and Frame Relay links before IPX routing begins.

IPX.why: The whole document specifies IPXWAN, the Novell IPX WAN link-setup protocol, including packet formats, negotiation and routing types.
IPX.quote: This document describes how Novell IPX operates over various WAN media.

rejected.why: PPP is one of the media IPX runs over and IPXCP reaching Open triggers IPXWAN, but the document does not specify or extend PPP.
X.25 SVC/PVC operation is described only as a link-establishment and encapsulation substrate for IPX.
Frame Relay PVC activity is used only for link establishment and encapsulation; the document is not about frame relay.
Unnumbered RIP/SAP is a routing type negotiated by IPXWAN, but this is IPX RIP, not the RIP family tagged in the taxonomy.
The Telebit IPX header compression option is only negotiated here; the compression method is defined in another RFC.

RFC1635.title: How to Use Anonymous FTP
RFC1635.summary: An FYI guide for novice users explaining FTP, anonymous FTP and archive sites, with a sample session, file packaging/compression conventions (compress, tar, zip, gzip, uuencode etc.) and etiquette.

FTP.why: The whole document explains how to use FTP and anonymous FTP, including a sample session, commands, binary/ASCII modes and etiquette.
FTP.quote: Anonymous FTP is a means by which archive sites allow general access to their archives of information.

user guides.why: It is FYI 24, an introductory guide for Internet users, so it belongs on the user guides page.
user guides.quote: This document provides information for the novice Internet user about using the File Transfer Protocol (FTP).

compression.why: A substantial section surveys compression and bundling formats and file naming conventions (compress, zip, gzip, zoo, arc) used on archives.
compression.quote: "Compressing" (reducing the size of) the stored information makes more space available on the archive, and reduces the amount of data actually transferred
compression.section: The Packaging and Naming of Files

rejected.why: gzip is only one of thirteen utilities listed in the packaging survey; the document is not about the gzip format itself.
ASCII vs binary transfer modes are mentioned only as practical advice, not as a subject of the document.
uuencode's origin in UUCP is a passing mention only.
Not discussed; FTP session is shown without Telnet content.

RFC1636.title: Report of IAB Workshop on Security in the Internet Architecture - February 8-10, 1994
RFC1636.summary: Report of a 1994 IAB workshop on security in the Internet architecture, covering firewall architecture, secure QoS forwarding, an authentication service, multicast security, secure plug-and-play, and short/medium/long-term recommendations.

security.why: The whole report is a general, cross-mechanism treatment of Internet security architecture, threats and recommendations, not tied to one protocol.
security.quote: The workshop was intended to explore the interconnections between security and the rest of the Internet architecture

firewall.why: Section 3 is a substantial treatment of application-layer and IP-layer firewall architecture, policy control, source authentication and firewall-friendly applications.
firewall.quote: The workshop spent considerable time on the architecture of firewall routers.

QoS.why: Section 4 develops a model for securing QoS setup and classification (HLID/LLID), discussing RSVP and ST-II, a substantial part of the document.
QoS.quote: This section contains a conceptual model for these problems, which we may call secure QOS forwarding.

authentication.why: Section 5 discusses an Internet-wide authentication service, names, credentials and identity-based authorization across protocols.
authentication.quote: The purpose of an authentication service is simply to verify names, or more precisely to verify the origin of "messages".

rejected.why: PEM is discussed as context for slow adoption, but the document does not specify or analyse it in depth.
Section 6.1 covers multicast group privacy and authentication briefly, but it is a short subsection rather than a main subject.
Mentioned only as an existing mechanism and a short-term action to support.
DNS names for certificates are debated, but the document is not about DNS protocol or operation.
RSVP is referenced as a setup protocol example, not the subject.
The report is security-focused; architecture is the context, so the security tag fits better.

RFC1637.title: DNS NSAP Resource Records
RFC1637.summary: Defines the DNS NSAP resource record (type 22) for mapping domain names to OSI NSAP addresses, and the use of PTR records under NSAP.INT for reverse mapping, to support CLNP/TUBA.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record type (NSAP, type 22), its RDATA and master file format, additional section processing, and PTR-based reverse mapping under NSAP.INT.
DNS.quote: This document defines the format of one new Resource Record (RR) for the DNS for domain name-to-NSAP mapping.

CLNP.why: The motivation is supporting CLNP addressing (OSI NSAPs, TUBA) in the Internet. A substantial part of the document covers NSAP structure and CLNP use.
CLNP.quote: The reason for defining DNS mappings for NSAPs is to support CLNP in the Internet.

rejected.why: The parent of CLNP is implied by the CLNP tag, so it is not listed separately.
TUBA is mentioned as motivation and affects additional section processing, but the document is not about the IPng candidate proposals themselves.
NSAP structure is described, but only to define DNS mapping, not IP address architecture.
Hostnames appear only as the names mapped to NSAPs, and the document is not about host naming conventions.

gaps.name: NSAP addresses (OSI network-layer addressing)
gaps.why: The document's subject is mapping OSI NSAP addresses in the DNS. The taxonomy has no tag for NSAP addressing apart from CLNP and OSI.

RFC1638.title: PPP Bridging Control Protocol (BCP)
RFC1638.summary: Defines the PPP Bridging Control Protocol (BCP), a PPP Network Control Protocol that negotiates and configures remote MAC bridging (transparent and source-route) over point-to-point links, including frame formats for bridged LAN traffic and spanning tree BPDUs.

PPP.why: The RFC specifies BCP, a PPP NCP with its own configuration options, protocol numbers and encapsulation, so it belongs under PPP and its control protocols.
PPP.quote: This document defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring Remote Bridging for PPP links.

rejected.why: Ethernet/802.3 frames are carried as one of several bridged MAC types, but the document is about PPP bridging, not IP over Ethernet.
802.5 source routing is discussed and 802.5 frames are carried, but the document does not cover IP over token ring.
FDDI is only one of the MAC types bridged, not the subject.
LAN FCS preservation is a feature of the bridging encapsulation, not a document about checksums.
The more specific PPP tag already covers this document.

gaps.name: MAC bridging / spanning tree (remote bridges, source route bridging)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is remote transparent and source-route bridging and spanning tree BPDU carriage, but the taxonomy has no bridging tag.

RFC1639.title: FTP Operation Over Big Address Records (FOOBAR)
RFC1639.summary: Experimental RFC defining the FTP LPRT command and LPSV reply (with reply code 521) to carry long, variable-length network and port addresses and address-family identifiers, so FTP can operate over IPv6 candidates and non-IP network protocols.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with new LPRT and LPSV commands and a new 521 reply code, so it belongs on the FTP page.
FTP.quote: This RFC specifies a method for assigning addresses other than 32-bit IPv4 addresses to data ports through the specification of a "long Port (LPRT)" command

rejected.why: The IPng candidates (SIP, PIP, TUBA, TP/IX) are only listed as address-family values. The document is about FTP, not those protocols.
IPv6 is never named. The mechanism is generic across next-generation IP alternatives.
TCP is the transport FTP assumes. The document does not change TCP.
Novell IPX appears only as one assigned address-family value, not as a subject of the document.

RFC1640.title: The Process for Organization of Internet Standards Working Group (POISED)
RFC1640.summary: Crocker's report summarizing the 1992 POISED working group: events leading to its formation, deliberations on IETF/IAB/IESG structure, the nomination and recall committee selection process, and ISOC Trustee approval.

IETF process.why: The whole document narrates the reform of IETF standards-process decision making and IAB/IESG roles, so it belongs under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: it became clear that it was necessary to examine the decision process and the procedures for populating the IESG and IAB.
IETF process.section: Background and Formation of POISED Working Group

NomCom.why: A substantial part describes the nomination committee's composition, volunteer selection by lot, terms, ratification and recall, which is the origin of NomCom procedures.
NomCom.quote: IAB and IESG members would be selected by a nomination and recruiting committee.

rejected.why: It is a historical account, but of IETF governance events rather than Internet protocols or technology; the governance tags fit better.
The ROAD/IP-addressing debate is only background; the document is about process, not architectural principles.
CLNP is mentioned only in passing as part of the background controversy.
The address-depletion and routing-table concerns are context only; the document does not address IP evolution itself.

RFC1641.title: Using Unicode with MIME
RFC1641.summary: RFC 1641 specifies how to use the 16-bit Unicode (UCS-2) character set within MIME, defining the UNICODE-1-1 charset name, a naming pattern for Unicode variants, and base64 usage examples.

Unicode.why: The document defines the Unicode character set's octet serialization (UCS-2, big-endian) and charset naming for Internet use, so it is about Unicode usage in protocols.
Unicode.quote: This document specifies the usage of Unicode within MIME.

MIME.why: It registers a MIME charset identifier (UNICODE-1-1) and specifies content-transfer-encoding usage (Base64, B encoding) with MIME examples.
MIME.quote: all registrations of Unicode variants and versions for MIME usage should have MIME charset names which conform to one of the two following patterns
MIME.section: General Specification of Unicode Character Sets Within MIME

character sets.why: The document defines a charset name and a naming scheme for charset registrations, which fits character set registration and use.
character sets.quote: The MIME character set identifier is UNICODE-1-1.
character sets.section: Encoding Character Set Unicode Within MIME

rejected.why: Email is the motivating context but the document is specifically about charset usage in MIME, not mail architecture or transport.
RFC 822 headers are only mentioned in passing; no header format is defined.
UTF-8 appears only as a hypothetical charset naming example, not specified here.
Base64 is just the transfer encoding used in examples, not something the document defines.
US-ASCII is mentioned as the baseline limitation and for fallback advice, but the document is not about it.

RFC1642.title: UTF-7 - A Mail-Safe Transformation Format of Unicode
RFC1642.summary: RFC 1642 defines UTF-7, a transformation format that encodes 16-bit Unicode as 7-bit US-ASCII using a modified Base64 shift sequence, and specifies its use as a MIME charset (UNICODE-1-1-UTF-7) in mail headers and bodies.

Unicode.why: The document defines a new transformation format of Unicode and compares it with UTF-8 and UTF-1 for encoding Unicode characters for Internet transport.
Unicode.quote: UTF-7 encodes Unicode characters as US-ASCII, together with shift sequences to encode characters outside that range.

character sets.why: It specifies a MIME charset identifier (UNICODE-1-1-UTF-7) for use in Content-Type, so it is a character set definition.
character sets.quote: Character set UTF-7 is safe for mail transmission and therefore may be used with any content transfer encoding in MIME
character sets.section: Use of Character Set UTF-7 Within MIME

MIME.why: A substantial part of the document explains how UTF-7 is used with MIME content transfer encodings, headers (RFC 1522) and bodies, with examples.
MIME.quote: The MIME character set identifier is UNICODE-1-1-UTF-7.
MIME.section: Use of Character Set UTF-7 Within MIME

rejected.why: Modified Base64 is the encoding mechanism UTF-7 relies on, but the document is not about Base64 itself.
UTF-8 is discussed only as the alternative that UTF-7 is compared against; the document does not specify it.
Mail is the motivating transport, but the document specifies a character encoding rather than mail architecture or transport.
RFC 1522 header encoding is referenced as a constraint, but the document does not define message header formats.
It names a charset in text/plain, not a media type registration.

RFC1643.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types
RFC1643.summary: Defines the EtherLike-MIB, SNMP managed objects for Ethernet-like (IEEE 802.3) interfaces, including error and collision statistics, TDR and loopback tests, and chipset identifiers.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to specify a MIB module (EtherLike-MIB) with managed objects for Ethernet-like interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The objects instrument IEEE 802.3 interfaces (ethernet-csmacd, iso88023-csmacd, starLan), covering collisions, FCS errors, and TDR/loopback tests, so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: Instances of these object types represent attributes of an interface to an ethernet-like communications medium.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB lives in. The document only defines objects and does not specify or extend the protocol, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
ASN.1/SMI is only the notation used to write the object definitions, not the subject of the document.
Ethernet is the more specific tag for the medium covered, so the parent is not needed.

RFC1644.title: T/TCP -- TCP Extensions for Transactions Functional Specification
RFC1644.summary: RFC 1644 specifies T/TCP, an experimental backwards-compatible TCP extension for transaction-oriented request/response service, using connection-count options (CC, CC.NEW, CC.ECHO) to bypass the three-way handshake (TAO) and truncate TIME-WAIT state.

TCP.why: The whole document defines new TCP options, connection states, and processing rules extending TCP.
TCP.quote: This memo specifies T/TCP, an experimental TCP extension for efficient transaction-oriented (request/response) service.

rejected.why: UDP is only mentioned as the alternative that T/TCP aims to compete with and as an overhead lower bound; the document is not about it.
Congestion window caching and initial window are mentioned briefly but are not a substantial subject of the document.
DNS is only cited as an example of a request/response protocol.

RFC1645.title: Simple Network Paging Protocol - Version 2
RFC1645.summary: RFC 1645 specifies SNPP version 2, a simple text command/response protocol for delivering one-way alphanumeric and numeric pages to radio paging terminals over the Internet, as an alternative to email/SMTP.

paging.why: The document defines SNPP, a protocol for delivering pages to paging terminals (TAP/IXO, TME). This is squarely the paging subject.
paging.quote: This RFC suggests a simple way for delivering both alphanumeric and numeric pages (one-way) to radio paging terminals.

rejected.why: SMTP is discussed only as the alternative SNPP is compared against and its response codes are mirrored. The document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Email is the approach the IETF reviewers preferred and the document argues against. Email gateways are mentioned but are not the subject.
Manual telnet sessions are mentioned only as a way to use SNPP. Telnet is not specified or extended here.
SMS is mobile short messaging. This document is about radio paging terminals, not SMS.

RFC1646.title: TN3270 Extensions for LUname and Printer Selection
RFC1646.summary: Informational RFC extending TN3270 (TN3287) so a client can request a specific LU name and a 3287 printer device, and defining the printer status message sent from client to server over Telnet.

TN3270.why: The document extends TN3270 with LU name selection and 3287 printer support, including negotiation, status messages and error conditions.
TN3270.quote: The first defines a way by which a TN3270 client can request a specific device (LUname) from a TN3270 server.

rejected.why: Telnet options (TERMINAL-TYPE, BINARY, EOR) are the substrate the extension is built on, though the memo says it supplements RFC 854. The subject is TN3270, which is the tag chosen.
VTAM/SNA concepts (LUs, LUSTAT, BIND) are background. The subject is the TN3270 extension, and TN3270 already sits under SNA.
TCP is only the substrate for the Telnet connection.
The 3287 printer is an IBM host printer data stream, not the Internet Printing Protocol.
Printing here uses the 3270 data stream over Telnet, not the line printer daemon protocol.

RFC1647.title: TN3270 Enhancements
RFC1647.summary: Specifies TN3270E, a Telnet option that improves 3270 terminal and printer emulation with device-type/device-name negotiation, a function negotiation, a data-message header, SNA response handling, and ATTN/SYSREQ support.

TN3270.why: The whole document defines the TN3270E enhancement to tn3270 3270 terminal emulation, including negotiation, header and functions.
TN3270.quote: this document proposes a new Telnet Option - TN3270E.

Telnet.why: Defines a new Telnet option, with commands such as IAC SB TN3270E and use of the IP, AO and Timing Mark commands. However, there is no Telnet tag in the taxonomy; this entry is invalid.
Telnet.quote: This protocol would be negotiated and implemented under a new Telnet Option

rejected.why: SNA concepts (BIND, RUs, SSCP-LU) are used for interworking, but the document is about the Telnet-based tn3270 protocol, not SNA itself.
Commands are NVT ASCII strings only incidentally.

gaps.name: Telnet
gaps.why: The document defines a new Telnet option and uses other Telnet options and commands, but the taxonomy has a Telnet tech entry under applications that I could not tag correctly in this output; no, the Telnet tag exists as 'Telnet'.

RFC1648.title: Postmaster Convention for X.400 Operations
RFC1648.summary: Requires that X.400 domains with RFC 1327 mapping rules support the "postmaster" address (Surname=Postmaster, and CommonName=Postmaster in 1988), extending the RFC 822/RFC 1123 postmaster convention to mapped X.400 mail domains.

X.400.why: The document sets an operational convention for X.400 mail domains and their address elements, including interworking with RFC 822 via RFC 1327 mapping. Readers of X.400 and interworking material would want it.
X.400.quote: For every X.400 domain for which an RFC 1327 mapping rule exists, if any address of the form Surname=User; <Other X.400 Address Elements> is a valid address

rejected.why: The document is about the postmaster mailbox convention, which is mail operations. However, the specific focus is X.400 and its mapping to RFC 822, so the more specific X.400 tag fits better.
RFC 822 is the source of the postmaster convention and the addressing form. The document does not specify or extend message format, so it is not about it.
SMTP is not discussed. Only RFC 822-style addresses and X.400 are involved.

RFC1649.title: Operational Requirements for X.400 Management Domains in the GO-MHS Community
RFC1649.summary: Informational memo defining minimum operational requirements and policies for X.400 management domains in the GO-MHS community: architecture, RELAY-MTAs, O/R address registration, X.400/RFC-822 address mapping, routing documents, and accounting.

X.400.why: The whole document specifies operational requirements for X.400 management domains, MTAs, RELAY-MTAs, O/R address registration and routing policy within the GO-MHS community.
X.400.quote: Operational Requirements for X.400 Management Domains in the GO-MHS Community

email.why: A substantial part covers interworking and address mapping between X.400 and RFC-822/SMTP mail via RFC 1327 gateways. This is a general email architecture and interoperability concern.
email.quote: All GO-MHS Community end-users shall be reachable from all end-users in the RFC-822 mail service in the Internet (SMTP), and vice versa.

rejected.why: X.500 is mentioned as the preferred future routing directory. It is only a passing reference and not specified here, and the taxonomy tag X.500 sits under directory services.
SMTP is only the RFC-822 side of the interworking. The document does not specify or extend SMTP.
RFC-822 addresses appear only in the mapping to X.400 O/R addresses. The document does not define the message format.
RFC 952 is cited only for character rules on X.400 address components. The document is not about host naming.

RFC1650.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types using SMIv2
RFC1650.summary: Defines the EtherLike-MIB (SMIv2), a MIB module of managed objects for Ethernet-like interfaces (statistics, collision histograms, TDR and loopback tests), updating RFC 1398.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification in SMIv2 defining managed objects, so it belongs under MIB modules and SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The managed objects cover IEEE 802.3 Ethernet interface statistics, collisions and tests, so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing ethernet-like objects.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is the framework the MIB is used with; the document defines only objects, not the protocol, so MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB definitions, not a subject of the document.
The more specific Ethernet tag covers the link-layer subject.

RFC1651.title: SMTP Service Extensions
RFC1651.summary: RFC 1651 defines the SMTP service extension framework: the EHLO command, an IANA registry of extension keywords, and optional parameters on MAIL FROM and RCPT TO.

SMTP.why: The whole document specifies the EHLO command, the extension registry and the MAIL FROM/RCPT TO parameter syntax. These extend SMTP, so the SMTP page is where readers would look for it.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines a framework for extending the SMTP service by defining a means whereby a server SMTP can inform a client SMTP as to the service extensions it supports.

rejected.why: RFC 822 headers and the Received: field are mentioned (the 'with ESMTP' clause), but only in passing. The document is not about message format.
MIME is cited as the structure for message bodies, but it is background and not the subject.
The document creates an IANA registry of SMTP extensions, but the registry is part of the SMTP extension framework and not a general IANA subject. SMTP covers it.
This is the parent of SMTP, so it is implied by the SMTP tag.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the command syntax. It is not the subject.

RFC1652.title: SMTP Service Extension for 8bit-MIMEtransport
RFC1652.summary: Defines the 8BITMIME SMTP service extension, using EHLO keyword 8BITMIME and a BODY parameter on MAIL FROM, so MIME messages with 8-bit octets can be relayed over SMTP.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension (EHLO keyword 8BITMIME, BODY parameter on MAIL), so it belongs under SMTP.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby an SMTP content body consisting of text containing octets outside of the US-ASCII octet range

MIME.why: The extension exists to carry 8-bit MIME bodies, and it defines how 8BITMIME content relates to 7bit MIME conversion and the 8BIT content-transfer-encoding.
MIME.quote: a MIME message [3] containing arbitrary octet-aligned material

rejected.why: The more specific SMTP tag covers it, and the parent is implied.
US-ASCII is only the 7-bit boundary the extension goes beyond. The document is not about ASCII itself.
TCP port 25 appears only in the usage example, where TCP serves as the transport.
RFC 822 is cited only as a reference. The document does not define message headers or addressing.

RFC1653.title: SMTP Service Extension for Message Size Declaration
RFC1653.summary: RFC 1653 defines the SMTP "SIZE" service extension, letting a client declare a message's size in MAIL FROM and a server advertise its maximum message size in EHLO so oversized messages can be rejected before transfer.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an extension to SMTP: a new EHLO keyword, a SIZE parameter on MAIL FROM, and the client and server behaviour and reply codes (452, 552) that go with them.
SMTP.quote: the name of the SMTP service extension is "Message Size Declaration"; the EHLO keyword value associated with this extension is "SIZE"
SMTP.section: 2. Framework for the Size Declaration Extension

rejected.why: SMTP is the more specific child tag, and the document is about the transport extension rather than email in general.
MIME is cited in the Introduction as the motivation for larger messages, but the document does not specify or extend it.
The document only defines how message size is counted in octets for SMTP. It does not cover header or message format.
TCP port 25 appears only in the example as the underlying transport, and nothing in the document is about TCP.

RFC1654.title: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)
RFC1654.summary: Specifies BGP-4, the inter-autonomous-system routing protocol, including message formats, path attributes, error handling, finite state machine, decision process, and route aggregation with CIDR support.

BGP.why: The whole document is the BGP-4 protocol specification: messages, path attributes, FSM, decision process, and aggregation.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol.

rejected.why: BGP only uses TCP as its transport; the appendix on TCP options is minor and does not make the RFC about TCP.
BGP-4 supports classless prefixes and aggregation, but the document specifies BGP, not the CIDR addressing scheme itself.
EGP is mentioned only as historical background and as an ORIGIN value, not specified here.
The document specifies a protocol; architecture and usage are deferred to the companion document RFC 1655.

RFC1655.title: Application of the Border Gateway Protocol in the Internet
RFC1655.summary: RFC 1655 describes how BGP-4 is applied in the Internet: topology model, route aggregation requirements, policy and path selection, interaction with EGP2/BGP-3, operation over SVCs, and BGP/IGP interaction.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies usage guidelines for BGP-4: policy, path selection, aggregation, required policies, and operation over SVCs.
BGP.quote: This memo describes the use of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) [1] in the Internet environment.

CIDR.why: Section 4 sets requirements for route aggregation and de-aggregation of NLRI, which is CIDR-driven, and the introduction motivates BGP-4 with CIDR.
CIDR.quote: BGP-4 is an extension of BGP-3 that provides support for routing information aggregation and reduction based on the Classless inter-domain routing architecture (CIDR)

EGP.why: A section covers interoperation and migration between BGP-4 and EGP2, the historic exterior gateway protocol.
EGP.quote: This document suggests the following guidelines for exchanging routing information between BGP-4 and EGP2.

rejected.why: The document is about a specific protocol's application, not general routing architecture; BGP is the more specific tag.
TCP is only the substrate; the small TCP modification in Section 9 is minor and tied to BGP over SVCs.
SVC operation is discussed generically, not IP over ATM.
Encapsulation to exit gateways appears only as an optional method in an informational appendix.
Internal BGP is mentioned but route reflection is not discussed.

RFC1656.title: BGP-4 Protocol Document Roadmap and Implementation Experience
RFC1656.summary: Informational roadmap and implementation-experience report for BGP-4, describing implementations, testing, CIDR aggregation support, and conclusions about deaggregation and version negotiation.

BGP.why: The whole document is about BGP-4: its applicability, implementations, test experience, and operational conclusions on aggregation and version negotiation.
BGP.quote: BGP-4 is explicitly designed for carrying reachability information between Autonomous Systems.

CIDR.why: A substantial part covers CIDR prefix carriage, route aggregation and deaggregation as BGP-4's primary feature and its test results.
CIDR.quote: BGP-4 provides a new set of mechanisms for supporting classless inter-domain routing.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an IGP that BGP-4 is not intended to replace.
Only mentioned in the applicability statement as an interior protocol.
The BGP-4 MIB is only referenced as defined elsewhere (RFC 1657).
IP-over-IP tunnels are just used in the test network setup, not the subject.

RFC1657.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Fourth Version of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4) using SMIv2
RFC1657.summary: Defines the BGP4-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for managing BGP-4 implementations, with peer table, received path attribute tables and traps.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition (BGP4-MIB) with tables, objects and notifications, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

BGP.why: The managed objects model BGP-4 peers, FSM state, timers, path attributes and traps, so BGP readers would want it.
BGP.quote: These objects are used to control and manage a BGP-4 implementation.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried by; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Only referenced by the peer port objects as a substrate for BGP connections.
Implied by the more specific MIB tag, which is a descendant.

RFC1658.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Character Stream Devices using SMIv2
RFC1658.summary: Defines the SMIv2 Character MIB module for managing character stream ports (such as RS-232 terminal ports and parallel printer ports) and their sessions, obsoleting RFC 1316.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (CHARACTER-MIB) defined in SMIv2, with port and session tables and conformance groups for character stream devices.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document defines objects only and does not specify or extend the protocol, so the MIB tag is the better fit.
Telnet is only named as a typical session protocol and given an OID (protocolTelnet). The document says nothing about how Telnet works.
rlogin appears only as a protocol identifier OID in the list of well-known session protocols.
ASN.1 is the notation used to write the module. The document is not about ASN.1.

RFC1659.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for RS-232-like Hardware Devices using SMIv2
RFC1659.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module (RS-232-MIB) for managing RS-232-like serial hardware ports, covering port parameters, async/sync port tables, error counters and control signals; obsoletes RFC 1317.

MIB.why: The document's whole body is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables and conformance groups for RS-232-like ports, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: In particular, it defines objects for the management of RS-232-like devices.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is only the framework the MIB is written for. The document defines managed objects and does not extend the SNMP protocol, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
The MIB module is written in ASN.1 through the SMI, but that is only the notation. The document is not about ASN.1.
The PPP MIB is mentioned only as a higher layer that may sit above the RS-232-like physical layer.
The objects cover physical-layer serial ports, but the document is a management MIB and not a link-layer protocol specification.

gaps.name: RS-232 serial hardware interfaces
gaps.why: The document is about managing RS-232, RS-422, V.35 and X.21 serial ports and their modem control signals. The taxonomy has no tag for serial physical-layer interfaces.

RFC1660.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Parallel-printer-like Hardware Devices using SMIv2
RFC1660.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module (PARALLEL-MIB) for managing Parallel-printer-like (Centronics/Dataproducts) hardware ports, including port and input/output control signal tables, and obsoletes RFC 1318.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a MIB module (PARALLEL-MIB) written in SMIv2, defining managed objects for parallel-printer-like hardware ports.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for the management of Parallel-printer-like devices.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is only the framework the MIB is defined within; the document does not specify or extend the protocol itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 subset is used only as the SMI notation for object definitions, not the subject.
Concerns printer hardware port signals, not the Internet Printing Protocol.
No relation to the line printer daemon protocol; this is physical-layer port management.

RFC1661.title: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP)
RFC1661.summary: RFC 1661 is the core PPP specification, defining encapsulation of multi-protocol datagrams, link phases, the option negotiation automaton, and LCP packets and options.

PPP.why: The document is the PPP base specification, covering encapsulation, LCP, link phases and the negotiation state machine.
PPP.quote: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) provides a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links.

rejected.why: Authentication is only negotiated via an LCP option and a link phase; PAP and CHAP are defined elsewhere.
Protocol-Field and Address/Control-Field compression are minor LCP options, not header compression of network protocols.
No HDLC tag exists in the taxonomy and framing is deferred to companion documents.
Magic-Number guidance on choosing random values is incidental to loopback detection.

RFC1662.title: PPP in HDLC-like Framing
RFC1662.summary: RFC 1662 specifies HDLC-like framing for PPP packets over bit- and octet-synchronous and asynchronous links, including octet/bit stuffing, FCS-16/32, and the ACCM LCP option.

PPP.why: The whole document defines the PPP data link framing, the ACCM LCP option, and frame modifications such as address-and-control-field compression.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of HDLC-like framing for PPP encapsulated packets.

CRC.why: A substantial appendix specifies the 16- and 32-bit frame check sequence polynomials and table-driven implementations, which fits CRC error detection over frames.
CRC.quote: The FCS-16 generator polynomial: x**0 + x**5 + x**12 + x**16.

rejected.why: Bit-synchronous links are discussed generically, with no SONET/SDH-specific content.
ASCII control characters are mentioned only in the context of ACCM mapping, so the document is not about ASCII.
The FCS is a CRC, so the more specific CRC tag fits better than the parent.

RFC1663.title: PPP Reliable Transmission
RFC1663.summary: RFC 1663 defines an LCP Numbered-Mode configuration option and procedures for using ISO 7776 LAPB to provide reliable, sequenced delivery over PPP serial links, including multi-link addressing and LAPB parameter defaults.

PPP.why: The document extends PPP with a new LCP configuration option and operating mode for reliable transmission, so it belongs on the PPP page.
PPP.quote: This document defines a method for negotiating and using Numbered-Mode, as defined by ISO 7776 [2], to provide a reliable serial link.

rejected.why: ISO 7776 LAPB is the X.25 link-layer procedure, but it is only borrowed here as the reliable-link mechanism. The document is not about X.25 or IP over public data networks.
Van Jacobson header compression and data compression are mentioned as motivation and shown in the encapsulation order. The document does not specify any compression.

Inverse multiplexing and the ISO Multi-Link Procedure are discussed, but the document explicitly offers no standard for multilink. It only defines address negotiation for it, and defers to the PPP multilink procedure.

RFC1664.title: Using the Internet DNS to Distribute RFC1327 Mail Address Mapping Tables
RFC1664.summary: Defines the DNS PX resource record and an X42D name subtree under country TLDs to store RFC1327 X.400/RFC822 mail address mapping tables in the DNS instead of static tables.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS resource record type (PX), a new name subtree (X42D), and query procedures for gateways, so it extends DNS.
DNS.quote: This memo defines how to store in the Internet Domain Name System the mapping information needed by e-mail gateways and other tools

X.400.why: The document is about mapping between X.400 O/R addresses and RFC822 domains for X.400/Internet mail gateways per RFC1327, and defines a DNS name space for X.400 O/R names.
X.400.quote: map RFC822 domain names into X.400 O/R names and vice versa

email.why: It concerns email gateway address mapping between Internet mail and X.400 mail; this is the email interworking context readers would look for.
email.quote: The connectivity between the Internet SMTP mail and other mail services, including the Internet X.400 mail and the commercial X.400 service providers

rejected.why: X.500 is mentioned only briefly as an alternative distribution mechanism in the administration section, not the subject.
The document maps addresses only; message header and body conversion is RFC1327's scope and is expressly excluded here.
SMTP and MX records are mentioned as background; the document does not specify SMTP.

RFC1665.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for SNA NAUs using SMIv2
RFC1665.summary: Defines the SNA-NAU-MIB SMIv2 module for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of SNA Physical Units, Logical Units, LU-LU sessions and response time monitoring.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (SNA-NAU-MIB) with tables, traps and conformance groups for SNA nodes, LUs and sessions.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

SNA.why: The managed subject is SNA network addressable units (PU types 1.0, 2.0, 2.1; LU types 0-7), sessions, BIND/UNBIND and RTM. SNA interworking is the domain the MIB covers.
SNA.quote: it defines objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of Physical Units (PUs) and Logical Units (LUs) in an SNA environment.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is only the framework the MIB is written for. The document defines no new protocol behaviour. The MIB tag covers the subject.
The module is written in the SMI subset of ASN.1, which is only the notation.
The RTM response-time tables are a small optional group within an SNA-specific MIB, not a general performance measurement subject.

RFC1666.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for SNA NAUs using SMIv2
RFC1666.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module (SNA-NAU-MIB) for configuring, monitoring and controlling SNA Physical Units, Logical Units, LU-LU sessions and response-time monitoring, obsoleting RFC 1665.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module in SMIv2 with tables, traps and conformance groups for SNA NAUs, so it belongs on the MIB page.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of Physical Units (PUs) and Logical Units (LUs) in an SNA environment

SNA.why: The managed subject is SNA nodes, LUs and sessions, including BIND/UNBIND handling and RTM, so SNA readers would want it.
SNA.quote: This memo identifies managed objects for PU Type 1.0, 2.0 and Type 2.1 and LU Type 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is the framework the MIB plugs into. The document defines no new protocol behaviour, and the MIB tag sits under SNMP.
This is a parent of the chosen MIB tag, so it is implied.
The module is written in SMI, which is an ASN.1 subset, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The RTM table measures end-user response times, but that is a small SNA-specific part of the MIB.

RFC1667.title: Modeling and Simulation Requirements for IPng
RFC1667.summary: White paper submitted to the IPng area setting out the network-layer requirements (real-time response, multicast, resource reservation) of Defense Modeling and Simulation / Distributed Interactive Simulation applications for IPng.

multicast.why: A major part of the requirements is multicast: scalability to thousands of groups, dynamic join/leave in under a second, and sender- and receiver-initiated joining.
multicast.quote: M&S requires a multicasting capability and a capability for managing multicast group membership.

QoS.why: Resource reservation and real-time latency/jitter guarantees are one of the three requirement categories, with RSVP and ST2 discussed as candidate mechanisms.
QoS.quote: The M&S community requires performance guarantees in supporting networks. This implies that IPng must be compatible with a capability to reserve bandwidth

IPng.why: The document is a requirements submission to the IPng effort, in response to RFC 1550. It is not a specification of one of the candidate protocols.
IPng.quote: This paper is intended to serve as input to the IPng design effort by specifying the network-layer requirements of Defense Modeling and Simulation (M&S) applications.

rejected.why: RSVP is only mentioned as work in progress that is being watched for resource reservation. The document does not specify or analyse it.
ST2 is mentioned as what the M&S community currently uses for reservation and multicast. It is background only, not the subject.
ATM link-layer multicast is mentioned as an expectation. It is not a subject of the document.
The document addresses IPng as a design effort, not the IPv6 specification. IPng is the more fitting tag.
IGMP is named once as a possible companion protocol and is not examined.

gaps.name: Distributed Interactive Simulation (DIS) / Defense Modeling and Simulation
gaps.why: The document's application domain, real-time distributed military simulation and its PDU traffic profile, has no matching tag.

RFC1668.title: Unified Routing Requirements for IPng
RFC1668.summary: Submission to the IPng area listing requirements that the Unified Routing Architecture (RFC 1322) places on IPng: topologically significant hierarchical addressing, routing labels, and flexible source routing.

routing architecture.why: The document sets out routing architecture and scalability requirements (hierarchical aggregation, hop-by-hop forwarding, routing labels, source routing) that the network layer must support.
routing architecture.quote: To provide scalable routing, IPng addressing must provide support for topologically significant address assignment.

IPng.why: It is a requirements submission in response to the IPng call (RFC 1550), about what the next-generation IP addressing and packet header must provide.
IPng.quote: The following list provides requirements on the IPng from the perspective of the Unified Routing Architecture

rejected.why: The document gives requirements for the IPng effort in general. It does not specify or analyse IPv6 itself.
Addressing requirements are discussed only as they serve routing scalability, so the routing architecture tag fits better.
The Unified Routing Architecture and its source routing are related to policy routing, but IDPR is never named or specified.

RFC1669.title: Market Viability as a IPng Criteria
RFC1669.summary: A 1994 IPng white paper arguing that a next-generation IP must offer new functionality over IPv4 and transparent IPv4/IPng interworking to be viable in the marketplace, given migration costs and the likely rise of NAT devices.

IPng.why: The whole document evaluates IPng candidate protocols against a market viability criterion, in response to the IPng area call (RFC 1550).
IPng.quote: "Viability in the Marketplace" is an important requirement for any IPng candidate

IPv4.why: A substantial part of the analysis concerns IPv4's installed base, address depletion, and why sites would or would not migrate away from it.
IPv4.quote: Given the large installed base of IPv4 systems, computer system manufacturers will need to continue to provide IPv4 capabilities for the foreseeable future.

NAT.why: The paper argues NAT devices will emerge and compete with IPng, which is central to its conclusion about IPng's viability.
NAT.quote: The development of network address translation devices and subsequent services is highly likely under these market conditions.

rejected.why: The paper concerns the IPng selection process and generic candidates, not the specified IPv6 protocol. IPng is the more specific fit.
It is a market and adoption argument, not architectural principles.
It touches on IPv4/IPng coexistence, but only as a market requirement. It does not discuss transition mechanisms.

RFC1670.title: Input to IPng Engineering Considerations
RFC1670.summary: A CERN white paper responding to RFC 1550, offering opinions based on DECnet Phase V transition experience on how to break down IPng decisions, transition planning, and configuration/administration needs.

IPng.why: The document is an input to the IPng area's selection process, discussing engineering considerations, timescales and transition for the next-generation IP.
IPng.quote: This white paper expresses some personal opinions on IPng engineering considerations, based on experience with DECnet Phase V transition.

rejected.why: DECnet Phase V transition is only the experience the author draws on; the document does not specify or analyse DECnet.
The memo predates any IPv6 specification and discusses generic IPng considerations, not IPv6 itself.
Transition is discussed generically for IPng, not for IPv6/IPv4 coexistence mechanisms.
Automatic configuration is wished for in general terms but DHCP is not discussed.
DNS updates and name service changes are mentioned only in passing.

RFC1671.title: IPng White Paper on Transition and Other Considerations
RFC1671.summary: An IPng white paper by Brian Carpenter setting out requirements for IPv4-to-IPng transition (interworking, dual stack, no header translation, address mapping, DNS), plus remarks on multicast, ATM, policy routing/accounting and firewall security.

IPv6 transition.why: The core of the paper is requirements for stepwise IPv4/IPng coexistence: interworking, dual-stack hosts, address mapping, and avoiding header translation. It was written as an input to the IPv6 design.
IPv6 transition.quote: It identifies the following requirements for stepwise transition

rejected.why: The IPng tag covers the historic candidate protocols (TUBA, PIP, SIPP, TP/IX). This paper states general requirements for any IPng and does not discuss those candidates.
DNS is mentioned only as a requirement that it return both IPv4 and IPng addresses. That is a small part of the paper, not a subject it addresses in its own right.
The paper predates the IPv6 specification and is about transition requirements, which the transition tag covers.
ATM gets one brief paragraph saying IPng needs a model for running over ATM. That is too slight to make the paper about ATM.
The multicast remarks are a short architectural rule, not a substantial treatment.
The paper explicitly says it does not discuss NAT, and only distinguishes header translation from it.

RFC1672.title: Accounting Requirements for IPng
RFC1672.summary: White paper submitted to the IPng area recommending that all IPng packets carry variable-size accounting tags (a voucher identifying the responsible party, plus optional higher-layer accounting variables) for use by accounting meters and policy routing.

IPng.why: The document is a white paper in response to the IPng call (RFC 1550), stating accounting requirements for the next-generation IP; the IPng tag covers historic IPng-era input documents.
IPng.quote: It recommends that all IPng packets carry accounting tags, which would vary in size.

rejected.why: Meters are mentioned, but the document is about packet tags for accounting, not performance metrics or measurement methods.
IPng became IPv6, but the document does not specify or discuss IPv6 itself, only requirements for a generic next-generation IP.
Accounting is related to the Internet Accounting Model, but this is a short requirements paper on packet tags and not network management architecture or practice.
Policy-based routing and charging are mentioned in passing; the document does not address QoS architectures or signalling.

gaps.name: Internet accounting
gaps.why: The document is about accounting (usage metering and charging) and the Internet Accounting Model of RFC 1272. The taxonomy has no accounting tag; AAA is about authentication, authorization and accounting frameworks, not packet-level usage accounting.

RFC1673.title: Electric Power Research Institute Comments on IPng
RFC1673.summary: EPRI's informational submission to the IPng area (response to RFC 1550) arguing that the next-generation IP should be based on OSI protocols (CLNP-style dual network layer), with requirements for large address space, routing economy, transition, and mobility.

IPng.why: The document is a requirements and position statement submitted to the IPng selection process, stating what the next-generation IP must provide.
IPng.quote: This document was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550.

OSI.why: The core argument is that the next IP should be based on OSI protocols and standards, with an IP dual network layer strategy and OSI applications (MMS, TP) supported.
OSI.quote: Any solution must provide an evolutionary transition path using an OSI.
