rejected.why: The document predates any IPv6 specification and states general requirements for a next-generation IP; it is not about IPv6 itself.
CLNP is never named. The document only implies an OSI network layer, so the OSI tag is the better fit.
Address space requirements are discussed, but they are part of the IPng/OSI position rather than a standalone treatment of addressing.
The mobility item only asks for dynamic address learning by hosts and is too brief to count as IP mobility.

RFC1674.title: A Cellular Industry View of IPng
RFC1674.summary: A CDPD consortium white paper responding to RFC 1550, listing cellular-industry requirements for IPng: mobility, scale, addressing, security, accounting, route selection, data efficiency, and transition from IPv4.

IPng.why: The whole document is a white-paper input on requirements for the IP Next Generation effort, so the IPng page is where readers would look for it.
IPng.quote: This is a draft of the requirements for IPng as envisioned by representatives of the Cellular Digital Packet Data (CDPD) consortium of service providers.

IP mobility.why: Mobility is the stated primary requirement. The paper asks for native IP-layer mobility support, connectionless datagrams that allow redirection, and support for occasionally-connected hosts.
IP mobility.quote: we propose that native support for mobility be regarded as an explicit IPng requirement.

rejected.why: The paper comes from the cellular industry (CDPD), but it specifies no cellular interworking. It only states requirements for IPng, so cellular is context rather than subject.
Addressing requirements (hierarchical, variable-length, distributed administration) are one section of a general requirements list, not the focus of the document.
Packet prioritization and class and grade of service are mentioned only briefly under Data Efficiency.
The document predates any IPv6 specification and discusses IPng generically, not IPv6.
The Transition section is a short requirement that IPng interoperate with IPv4. It does not discuss transition mechanisms.

RFC1675.title: Security Concerns for IPng
RFC1675.summary: Informational 1994 memo to the IPng area outlining security concerns (firewalls, encryption, source routing and address-based authentication, accounting) that IPng candidates must address.

IPng.why: The memo evaluates the historic IPng candidates (TUBA, SIPP, IPAE) against security requirements, so it belongs on the IPng page.
IPng.quote: A number of the candidates for IPng have some features that are somewhat worrisome from a security perspective.

firewall.why: A major section sets out the requirements firewalls place on IPng: address structure, transport header access, and translators.
firewall.quote: For better or worse, firewalls are very much a feature of today's Internet.

security.why: The memo gives general security guidance covering encryption, authentication, source routing and accounting. It is not tied to one mechanism, so the general security topic fits.
security.quote: While it is not necessary that IPng be an improvement over IPv4, it is mandatory that it not make things worse.

rejected.why: The memo discusses IPng candidates in general, not the IPv6 specification, and IPv6 is not named.
IP-level encryption and authentication are mentioned only as things IPng must not hinder. No IPsec architecture is discussed.
Network-level translators for the transition are discussed only in terms of firewall deployment, not NAT behaviour.
Address-based authentication is discussed only as a casualty of source routing. This is a minor part of the document, and the general security tag already covers it.

RFC1676.title: INFN Requirements for an IPng
RFC1676.summary: INFN's white paper responding to RFC 1550 sets out its requirements for IPng: address exhaustion, flat addressing and routing, a CLNS/NSAP-based network layer, policy routing, multicast, and a dual-stack transition with a deadline.

IPng.why: The whole document is a submission to the IPng area stating requirements for the next-generation IP, which is what the IPng subject covers.
IPng.quote: The aim of IPng study should be to define a plan that solves all these problems as a whole and not each of them separately.

CLNP.why: The paper proposes CLNS and its 20-byte NSAP addressing as the basis for IPng, a substantial part of its argument. CLNP is the connectionless network protocol of CLNS.
CLNP.quote: CLNS could be a solution and a reliable starting point for the IPng.

IPv6 transition.why: A full section discusses dual stack, translation, tunnelling and a deadline for IPv4 backward compatibility, which are transition mechanisms.
IPv6 transition.quote: We think that a dual stack approach could simplify very much the transition, whereas a translation mechanism would need a widely and deep coordination

rejected.why: The paper makes routing requirements such as policy-based routing, hierarchical routing and NSAP aggregation, but they are brief remarks within an IPng requirements paper, not a main subject.
DECNET to DECNET/OSI migration is cited only as the authors' experience informing transition advice. The document is not about DECnet.
TCP is mentioned only to say it should keep the same interfaces and services. The document does not specify or extend it.
Multicast is mentioned in a single sentence as a feature IPng should support, which is not enough to make the document about it.

RFC1677.title: Tactical Radio Frequency Communication Requirements for IPng
RFC1677.summary: A US Navy submission to the IPng effort setting out tactical military RF network requirements for the next-generation IP: compact headers, address scaling, security, mobility, flow/resource reservation, multicast, QoS/priority, and support for heterogeneous low-rate media.

IPng.why: The whole document is a requirements input to the IPng selection effort responding to RFC 1550, so the IPng page is where readers would look for it.
IPng.quote: This paper describes requirements for Internet Protocol next generation (IPng) candidates with respect to their application to military tactical radio frequency (RF) communication networks.

QoS.why: A substantial part covers resource reservation, flow identification, RSVP flow specs, and datagram priority levels needed for QoS on limited-capacity links.
QoS.quote: Quality of service and policy based routing are of particular importance in a tactical environment with limited communication resources, limited bandwidth
QoS.section: Quality of Service and Policy-Based Routing

multicast.why: Multicast is one of the main requirements stressed, because RF media are broadcast and information must be disseminated efficiently.
multicast.quote: A multicast architecture is the general case for information flow in a tactical internetwork.

IP mobility.why: A dedicated section covers node and whole-subnetwork mobility, including platforms moving between RF networks and the resulting routing changes.
IP mobility.quote: in some cases, entire subnetworks may be moving.  An example of this is a Navy ship with multiple LANs on board

header compression.why: Compact headers for low-throughput RF links are a recurring requirement throughout the document.
header compression.quote: any mechanisms which facilitate compression of network headers can be considered highly valuable in an IPng candidate.

rejected.why: CLNP is the protocol used in the CSNI project, and the document cites its QoS and priority features as experience. The document is not about CLNP itself.
RSVP's Flow Specification is mentioned only as an example of a more general mechanism. The document does not specify or analyse RSVP.
Security is discussed as one requirement, but it is not the focus. The Security Considerations section only points back to the main text.
IPng is the generic next-generation IP effort, not specifically IPv6 as specified.
Address scaling is touched on briefly, but the document does not address addressing in its own right.

gaps.name: Tactical military RF networks
gaps.why: The document's central subject is military tactical radio networks, and the taxonomy has no tag for military or tactical networking.

RFC1678.title: IPng Requirements of Large Corporate Networks
RFC1678.summary: Informational IBM submission to the IPng area (response to RFC 1550) listing large corporate network requirements for the next-generation IP: IPv4 migration/coexistence, SLAs and service classes, security, multiprotocol support, mobility, and DNS/DHCP operations.

IPng.why: The document is a requirements submission to the IPng area, so it belongs on the IPng page.
IPng.quote: This draft summarizes some of the requirements of large corporate networks for the next generation of the Internet protcol suite.

IPv6 transition.why: Migration from and coexistence with IPv4 is the first major requirement and gets its own section.
IPv6 transition.quote: IPng must have a viable strategy for migration from, and coexistence with, IPv4.

QoS.why: Service levels, class of service, priority and resource reservation for isochronous traffic make up a substantial part of the requirements.
QoS.quote: Functions, such as class of service and priority, that let an enterprise control use of bandwidth also may help meet service level agreements.

rejected.why: The document predates IPv6 and states requirements for a generic IPng, not the IPv6 specification.
DHCP is mentioned only briefly, as a requirement for secure interaction with DNS.
Dynamic secure DNS updates are asked for in one sentence, which is too little to tag.
The mobile hosts section is short and states only general wireless and topology requirements.
CIDR is cited only as a way to postpone address exhaustion.
GSS-API is recommended for wider deployment but is not analysed in the document.

RFC1679.title: HPN Working Group Input to the IPng Requirements Solicitation
RFC1679.summary: The Navy HPN working group's input to the IPng requirements solicitation (RFC 1550), listing assumptions, general requirements (addressing, integrated services, mobility, multicast, rapid route reconfiguration) and additional considerations for a next-generation IP.

IPng.why: The whole document is a requirements submission to the IPng selection process, so the IPng subject page is the natural home.
IPng.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide what the HPN working group perceives as requirements for an IPng protocol set.

multicast.why: A dedicated section argues that multicast should be basic IPng functionality, with group addressing, scope control and scalable multicast routing. It is one of the three areas the group wants to help develop.
multicast.quote: Multicast transfer is a very critical IPng requirement for the Navy's mission critical systems.

QoS.why: The integrated services section asks for predictable traffic flow management, delivery deadlines and end-to-end importance or priority. This is a QoS architecture requirement.
QoS.quote: The HPN working group is looking for mechanisms in the IPng protocols to provide for both of these classes of problems in an integrated fashion.

rejected.why: The document gives requirements for a not-yet-chosen IPng. It does not specify or discuss IPv6 itself, so IPng is the better fit.
Section 4.1 covers address space size and structure, but it is one requirement among several. IPng covers it well enough.
Mobility is only a short requirement section (4.3) with no protocol content.
Section 5.4 is a brief additional consideration and does not make time synchronization a main subject.
IPsec is mentioned only as ongoing work that IPng should support. The document is not about it.
Rapid route reconfiguration and policy-based routing are short requirement items without architectural treatment.

RFC1680.title: IPng Support for ATM Services
RFC1680.summary: A white paper submitted in response to RFC 1550 describing what IPng must provide so IPng packets and applications' flows can be mapped to ATM services (addresses, QoS, connection management, virtual circuit identifier).

ATM.why: The whole document concerns mapping IP-layer packets to ATM virtual circuits, signalling, QoS and addressing, i.e. IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: This paper describes parameters that are needed to map IPng (or any protocol operating above the link level) to ATM services.

IPng.why: It is an IPng white paper stating requirements an IPng candidate should meet regarding link technologies.
IPng.quote: This white paper describes engineering considerations for IPng as solicited by RFC 1550

rejected.why: QoS mapping is discussed, but only as one ATM parameter; RSVP is cited as a possible source, not specified.
Only referenced as a potential source of QoS mappings; not the subject.
IPng is generic here, a candidate-agnostic requirements paper, not the IPv6 specification.
Classical IP over ATM ARP is only mentioned in passing in the addressing section.

RFC1681.title: On Many Addresses per Host
RFC1681.summary: An IPng-input memo arguing that hosts should have many IP addresses each (for service encoding, charging, per-user addressing, low-grade mobility, subnet merging) and recommending 2^6 to 2^8 extra addresses per host in the next-generation address space.

addressing.why: The whole memo is about IP address architecture and sizing: assigning multiple addresses per host and how many the address space must accommodate.
addressing.quote: I recommend that we allow for 2^6, and perhaps as many as 2^8, extra addresses per host, to leave room for the ideas presented here.
addressing.section: How Many Addresses Do We Need?

IPng.why: It is a requirements-style input to the IPng selection process, concerning address space size for the next-generation IP, but it does not discuss the candidate protocols TUBA, PIP, SIPP or TP/IX.
IPng.quote: This document was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550.

rejected.why: DNS is discussed only as an alternative (returning port numbers, MX records) and as something to avoid depending on; the memo does not specify or extend it.
Only a brief 'low-grade mobility' section on moving addresses within a subnet for load balancing; not about Mobile IP itself.
Firewall filtering by service address is mentioned as a side benefit, not a subject of the memo.
The memo addresses the generic IPng address-space question, not the IPv6 specification.
Multiple addresses per host here are for services and users, not for site or host multihoming across providers.

RFC1682.title: IPng BSD Host Implementation Analysis
RFC1682.summary: A 1994 IPng white paper analysing the changes a BSD TCP/IP host implementation (sockets, transport, network, link layers, APIs, transition software) would need to support a next-generation IP replacing IPv4.

IPng.why: The whole paper analyses host engineering considerations for the IPng candidate protocols during the IPng selection process.
IPng.quote: IPng will require changes to a hosts network software architecture.

sockets API.why: A substantial part covers socket address structure and network API changes needed on BSD hosts for larger addresses.
sockets API.quote: There will have to be enhancements to the network APIs that an application uses to retrieve BIND DNS records to differentiate between IPv4 and IPng address requests.

IPv6 transition.why: Section 5 lists the host transition software for IPv4/IPng coexistence, including dual network layers and no recompilation of IPv4 applications.
IPv6 transition.quote: Transition software on a host will be required to maintain compatibility between IPv4 and IPng, and to manage both the existing IPv4 and IPng environments

rejected.why: The paper predates the IPv6 specification and is about the generic IPng candidate set, not IPv6 itself; IPng is the fitting tag.
BIND DNS is mentioned as an application needing updates, but DNS is not the subject of the paper.
TCP/UDP are part of the reference architecture only, not analysed in their own right.
DHCP and BOOTP are briefly listed as autoconfiguration items needing IPng support, not a substantial part of the paper.

RFC1683.title: Multiprotocol Interoperability In IPng
RFC1683.summary: Informational IPng-area submission arguing that the next-generation IP should include features (flexible addressing, option handling, multiplexing, error feedback, MTU discovery, directory support) to operate in multiprotocol environments with tunneling, translation and multiprotocol end-systems.

IPng.why: The whole document is a requirements/position paper submitted to the IPng area (response to RFC 1550) on what IPng should include.
IPng.quote: The next generation Internet Protocol should have features that support its use with a variety of protocol architectures.

tunneling.why: Tunneling and conversion are two of the three core multiprotocol techniques discussed, and IPng features are motivated by them.
tunneling.quote: Encapsulation or tunneling is commonly used when two networks that support a common protocol must be connected using a third intermediate network

OSI.why: Coexistence and interworking with OSI (CLNP/TP4, RFC 1006, TUBA stacks) is the central worked example of multiprotocol systems.
OSI.quote: other protocols (e.g., IPX, AppleTalk, OSI) exist either natively or encapsulated as data within IP.

rejected.why: DNS is only mentioned as a mechanism the authors' earlier work uses to distribute protocol configuration; this document does not specify it.
MTU discovery is a feature discussed briefly as a desired IPng capability, not a specification of the mechanism.
ICMP is cited as a model for the desired error feedback mechanism, but the document is not about ICMP.
The document concerns requirements for IPng in general, before IPv6 was chosen; IPng tag fits better as the historic candidate selection context.
Considered since it discusses multiprotocol Internet design, but the IPng tag is more specific.

gaps.name: Multiprotocol interoperability / protocol determination
gaps.why: The document's main subject, multiprotocol networking and the Protocol Determination task, has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC1684.title: Introduction to White Pages Services based on X.500
RFC1684.summary: An informational introduction to X.500-based White Pages directory services for organisation managers, covering the directory and information models, benefits, organisational lessons from the Paradise pilot, and other X.500 applications.

X.500.why: The whole document introduces X.500: its directory model (DSAs, DUAs, DIT), information model, benefits and deployment experience.
X.500.quote: The X.500 standard describes a so-called 'Directory Service', which can be used for all types of electronic directories.

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which is the more specific tag and already implies it.
Only listed in the references (RFC 1487); the body does not discuss LDAP.
Mentioned briefly as a future application using X.500 for public key distribution, but not a substantial subject of the document.
Mentioned only as an application (X.400 routing via X.500); not the subject.
Email is context for why White Pages are needed, not the subject.

RFC1685.title: Writing X.400 O/R Names
RFC1685.summary: RARE recommendation on how humans should write X.400 O/R names, adopting the ITU/ISO F.401 Annex F labelled format (G=;I=;S=;O=;OU1=;...;C=) with semicolon delimiters and reproducing the annex text.

X.400.why: The whole document is about the textual representation of X.400 O/R addresses and the user-interface requirements for entering them.
X.400.quote: RARE recommends that the ISO standard be followed when writing O/R names.

rejected.why: O/R names are X.400 addresses written for humans, not Internet message header syntax.
Too general; the X.400 tag is the specific fit.
The text mentions printable string characters only in passing.

RFC1686.title: IPng Requirements: A Cable Television Industry Viewpoint
RFC1686.summary: A cable television industry viewpoint submitted in response to RFC 1550, describing cable network architecture and stating requirements (scaling, transition, security, flows/resource reservation, source routing, mobility, accounting) for the IP Next Generation (IPng) protocol.

IPng.why: The whole document is input on requirements and selection criteria for IPng, the next-generation IP effort, from one industry's perspective.
IPng.quote: This paper provides comments on topics related to the IPng requirements and selection criteria from a cable television industry viewpoint.

QoS.why: A substantial section argues for resource reservation, flows and quality-of-service parameters for real-time video and audio in IPng.
QoS.quote: IPng, if it aims to be a general protocol useful for interactive multimedia applications, will need to support some form of resource reservation or flows.

rejected.why: The document predates any chosen IPng design and sets out requirements for the candidate effort, not IPv6 itself. IPng is the more specific fit.
Mobile hosts get only a short paragraph (3.6), which is not enough to count as a substantial part of the document.
ATM appears only in describing the Orlando trial network, not as a subject of the document.
Multicast is mentioned as a need for video delivery but not discussed in depth.
The document describes cable plant architecture in general and does not cover DOCSIS.

RFC1687.title: A Large Corporate User's View of IPng
RFC1687.summary: A Boeing user-perspective position paper submitted in response to RFC 1550, explaining why large corporate users view IPng with disfavor and listing five user requirements (piecemeal transition, no hindrance to advances, OSI synergy, plug-and-play, better security) for any IPng solution.

IPng.why: The whole document is an input to the IPng selection effort, assessing deployment motivations and user requirements for the next-generation IP.
IPng.quote: The goal of this paper is to examine the implications of IPng from the point of view of Fortune 100 corporations

firewall.why: A substantial section defends firewalls/security islands and application-layer relays as shaping corporate IPng deployment.
firewall.quote: Another core philosophical difference between large end users and the IETF is concerning the importance of Security Islands (i.e., firewalls).

rejected.why: The document predates IPv6 specification and discusses the generic IPng candidate selection, not IPv6 itself; IPng tag fits better.
OSI convergence is discussed as a motivation and requirement, but the document is not about OSI network-layer protocols themselves.
IPv4 is the incumbent being compared against; the document is not about IPv4 specification or address lifecycle.
Mentioned once as a good beginning for self-defining networks; not a subject of the document.
Piecemeal transition and IPv4 coexistence are stated as requirements, but no transition mechanisms are discussed.

RFC1688.title: IPng Mobility Considerations
RFC1688.summary: Informational 1994 submission to the IPng area listing mobility-related criteria (addressing, communication, security, bandwidth, processing) for the design and selection of the next-generation IP.

IP mobility.why: The whole document sets out requirements for host mobility (Home-Address, Home Agent, Foreign Agent, roaming without losing transport connections) at the IP layer. Mobile IP is the generic IP mobility topic, and the document is not specific to Mobile IPv4 or Mobile IPv6.
IP mobility.quote: This RFC specifies criteria related to mobility for consideration in design and selection of the Next Generation of IP.

IPng.why: It is an IPng requirements submission on mobility for choosing the next-generation IP, so it belongs on the IPng page of historic candidate-protocol material.
IPng.quote: This document was submitted to the IPng Area in response to RFC 1550.

rejected.why: The document predates the selection of IPv6 and sets criteria for any IPng candidate. It does not specify or analyse IPv6.
It draws on the Mobile IP working group's work, but it is about requirements for IPng mobility, not the Mobile IPv4 protocol.
Van Jacobson header prediction is discussed only as a constraint on header design, not as the subject.
Section 2 on Home-Address properties is part of the mobility requirements, not a general treatment of address architecture.

RFC1689.title: A Status Report on Networked Information Retrieval: Tools and Groups
RFC1689.summary: FYI 25 status report from the NIR working group cataloguing networked information retrieval tools (Alex, archie, Gopher, Hytelnet, Netfind, Prospero, Veronica, WAIS, WHOIS, WWW, X.500) and the groups working on them, using standard templates.

Gopher.why: Gopher and Veronica get the most extensive coverage in the report, with many server and client entries.
Gopher.quote: The Internet Gopher protocol is a client/distributed-server document search and retrieval protocol originally developed at the University of Minnesota.

WAIS.why: WAIS and freeWAIS are a major covered tool with server and client listings.
WAIS.quote: WAIS - The Wide Area Information Servers system - is an electronic publishing software set which allows you to search out and retrieve multimedia information

WHOIS.why: WHOIS is a covered tool, and the WNILS group and WHOIS++ are described in the groups and appendix sections.
WHOIS.quote: NICNAME/WHOIS services is a TCP transaction based query/response server, running on a few specific central machines

X.500.why: X.500 White Pages is a covered tool, and the OSI-DS and IDS groups also relate to it.
X.500.quote: X.500 is an international standard designed to provide a distributed global directory service.

HTTP.why: The World-Wide Web, including HTTP servers and the Mosaic, Lynx and line-mode browsers, is a major covered tool. HTTP is the closest fitting tag in the taxonomy.
HTTP.quote: A simple protocol (" HTTP ") is used to allow a browser program to request a keyword search by a remote information server.

URI.why: The URI working group entry describes URLs, URNs and URCs, which are the group's subject matter.
URI.quote: Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), which specify a standardized method for encoding location and access information to resources across multiple information systems

directory services.why: The report groups WHOIS, X.500 and Netfind as directory services, and several groups (IDS, CNI directories) address them.
directory services.quote: Directory Service tools are intended to provide a lookup service for locating information about users (often referred to as White Pages)
directory services.section: 5. Overview of the types of NIR Tool

rejected.why: Anonymous FTP is the substrate that archie and Alex index and use. The report does not specify or analyse FTP.
Alex is implemented as a user-level NFS server, but NFS is only the substrate for it.
WHOIS++ appears only as a forthcoming item in Appendix D and as a WNILS goal. The visible text gives it no substantive coverage.
Prospero's authentication mechanisms mention Kerberos in passing. The document is not about it.
LDAP is mentioned only as a lightweight client access protocol for X.500.
The report is a status snapshot of tools and groups, not a history or retrospective.

gaps.name: Networked information retrieval / resource discovery (archie, Veronica, Prospero, Z39.50)
gaps.why: The central subject has no tag in the taxonomy. archie, Veronica, Prospero, Netfind and Z39.50 have no tags of their own. Only WAIS, Gopher and WHOIS have close fits.

RFC1690.title: Introducing the Internet Engineering and Planning Group (IEPG)
RFC1690.summary: An informational memo introducing the Internet Engineering and Planning Group (IEPG), an open forum of Internet service operators, giving its charter, mailing list and archive location.

network management.why: The IEPG is an operators' forum coordinating operational aspects of Internet services. Operational coordination fits the network management topic (operations and operational practice) best.
network management.quote: To facilitate the operations and management of Global Internet services
network management.section: 1. Charter of the Internet Engineering and Planning Group

rejected.why: The IEPG is an operators' coordination forum, not a body governing standards or administration. The memo is about its charter, not governance of the Internet.
The IEPG is not part of the IETF standards process and the memo describes no IETF procedures.
Security issues are explicitly not discussed in the memo.

RFC1691.title: The Document Architecture for the Cornell Digital Library
RFC1691.summary: Defines the Cornell Digital Library document architecture for storing and retrieving scanned books and images, with logical structure files, physical reference files, multiple views, and a UNIX file-system layout.

rejected.why: The referencing database for searching by author and title is bibliographic, not a directory access or synchronization protocol; Z39.50 is only a planned migration.
FTP and Gopher are mentioned only as standard data access methods the file naming should permit, not specified or extended.
Mentioned only as a way to access the file layout; the document does not specify anything about the Gopher protocol.
The Physical References and Logical Structure files are custom vertical-bar-delimited formats specific to this library, not a general data format or encoding subject in the taxonomy.
The architecture is a document storage architecture for one digital library, not Internet architectural principles.

gaps.name: Digital libraries / document storage and retrieval architecture
gaps.why: The whole document is about a digital library's document architecture (CLASS, logical structure, physical references, multiple views of scanned books), and the taxonomy has no tag for digital libraries or document management.

RFC1692.title: Transport Multiplexing Protocol (TMux)
RFC1692.summary: RFC 1692 specifies TMux, a protocol (IP protocol 18) that multiplexes multiple small transport segments from different sessions (mainly Telnet/Rlogin) into a single IP datagram using 4-octet mini-headers to reduce packet load.

TMux.why: The document defines the TMux protocol itself: header format, ENQ negotiation, message construction and implementation notes.
TMux.quote: TMux is a protocol which allows multiple short transport segments, independent of application type, to be combined between a server and host pair.

rejected.why: Telnet and Rlogin sessions are the motivating traffic, but the document does not specify or extend them.
TCP segments are carried as payload; TMux is transparent to the transport layer and does not change TCP.
UDP segments are only an example of multiplexed payload; the document does not specify UDP.
TMux is an IP protocol (number 18) running over IPv4, but the document does not define IPv4 itself.
Path MTU Discovery is only mentioned as an implementation suggestion for choosing the maximum TMux message size.
TMux reduces per-packet overhead by combining packets, which is multiplexing rather than compressing headers.

RFC1693.title: An Extension to TCP : Partial Order Service
RFC1693.summary: Experimental (now historic) proposal to extend TCP with a partial order, partial reliability service, using new POC-permitted and POC-service-profile options, object reliability classes, and modified receiver window and ACK handling.

TCP.why: The document extends TCP with new options, object-based delivery, modified windows and acknowledgments, so it belongs on the TCP page.
TCP.quote: A TCP implementation that provides a partial order service requires the use of two new TCP options.

rejected.why: QOS parameters are mentioned as the way to express the service level, but the document is about transport ordering and reliability, not QoS architectures or signalling.
Windows and acknowledgments are redesigned, but for ordering and reliability, not congestion avoidance.
UDP is only mentioned as the unordered-service contrast to TCP.
The TCP tag is more specific and covers the document, so the parent topic is not listed.

gaps.name: partial order / partial reliability transport service
gaps.why: The document's central idea is a transport service with partial ordering and partial reliability, which is not tied to TCP alone. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC1694.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for SMDS Interfaces using SMIv2
RFC1694.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module for managing SMDS access interfaces (SIP Level 3/2, PLCP, DXI, IP-over-SMDS, error log), replacing RFC 1304 and mapping many objects onto the MIB-II ifTable.

SMDS.why: The document exists to define managed objects for SMDS interfaces.
SMDS.quote: it defines objects for managing objects for SMDS access interfaces.

MIB.why: It specifies an SMIv2 MIB module (SIP-MIB) with object groups and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for, not the subject; the MIB tag covers it.
SIP/ATM access is mentioned only as an underlying layer; objects for ATM are defined in other documents.
SIP/FR is only an access method referenced; FR objects are defined elsewhere.
ipOverSMDS table mentions ARP request addresses but the document is not about ARP.
ASN.1 is just the notation for the MIB definitions.

RFC1695.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for ATM Management Version 8.0 using SMIv2
RFC1695.summary: Defines the SNMPv2 ATM-MIB module for managing ATM interfaces, virtual links (VPL/VCL), VP/VC cross-connects, traffic descriptors, and AAL5 entities and connections.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (ATM-MIB) defined in SMIv2, specifying managed objects, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: it describes objects used for managing ATM-based interfaces, devices, networks and services.

ATM.why: The subject matter is ATM management: VPLs/VCLs, cross-connects, traffic descriptors, QoS classes, AAL5, DS3 PLCP and TC sublayer.
ATM.quote: ATM management objects are used to manage ATM interfaces, ATM virtual links, ATM cross-connects, AAL5 entities and AAL5 connections

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is the framework the MIB is written for, but the document defines no protocol behaviour. The MIB tag already covers it.
The module is written in ASN.1-based SMI, but that is only the notation.
The TC sublayer and DS3 PLCP objects mention SONET/DS3 transport, but the document is about ATM, not IP over SONET.
SMDS is mentioned only as an example application and as a reference for AAL3/4 management.
The document defines ATM traffic descriptors and QoS class objects, but only as MIB parameters for ATM, not as a QoS architecture.

RFC1696.title: Modem Management Information Base (MIB) using SMIv2
RFC1696.summary: Defines the Modem MIB (SMIv2), a set of SNMP managed objects for monitoring and controlling dial-up modems: identity, line interface, DTE interface, call control, error control, compression, signal conversion and statistics.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module (Modem-MIB) defined in SMIv2, so readers of MIB modules would look for it. It is a specific MIB, the most specific fitting tag.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing dial-up modems and similar dial-up devices.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is defined for. The document specifies managed objects, not the protocol; the MIB tag sits under SNMP and is more specific.
The MIB is written in ASN.1-based SMI notation, but ASN.1 is only the definition syntax, not the subject.
It is implied by the MIB tag, which sits under SNMP and network management.
Dial-up modems run over analogue telephone lines, not ISDN.

gaps.name: Modem / dial-up device management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for modems or dial-up access hardware (V.xx modulation, MNP, V.42bis, V.58). The MIB tag covers the form of the document but not this subject.

RFC1697.title: Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) Management Information Base (MIB) using SMIv2
RFC1697.summary: Defines the RDBMS-MIB, an SNMPv2 MIB module for monitoring relational database installations, servers, parameters, limited resources, and database/server relations, extending the APPLICATION-MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (RDBMS-MIB) written in SMIv2, defining tables, objects, traps and conformance groups for managing relational databases.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is the framework the MIB is written for, but the document defines no protocol behaviour; the MIB tag covers it.
Relational databases are not directory services; the document only manages database servers.
The module uses ASN.1/SMI notation only as the definition language, not as a subject.
Some counters (reads, writes, transactions) are performance-related, but the document is a general management MIB, not about measurement methods.

gaps.name: Database management / RDBMS
gaps.why: The document is about managing relational database systems, which is an application-level subject with no fitting tag in the taxonomy.

RFC1698.title: Octet Sequences for Upper-Layer OSI to Support Basic Communications Applications
RFC1698.summary: Informational "cookbook" giving the exact octet sequences for the OSI Session, Presentation and ACSE upper-layer protocols so that thin implementations can support basic connection-oriented applications and interwork with full OSI stacks.

OSI.why: The whole document re-specifies parts of the OSI upper-layer protocols and how they interwork with full OSI implementations and run over RFC 1006 transport. OSI is the closest taxonomy tag, though it is described there as network-layer.
OSI.quote: This document states particular octet sequences that comprise the OSI upper-layer protocols (Session, Presentation and ACSE) when used to support applications with "basic communications requirements".

rejected.why: BER encoding rules are the substrate for the Presentation and ACSE PDUs. The document only summarises how to encode them and defines no ASN.1 modules or new encoding rules.
The Directory appears only as the source of AP-title and RDN naming forms and as an example application (DAP). The document is not about it.
Mentioned only as an example of a Group I migrant protocol.
X.400 P7 is cited only as an example Group IV application.
RFC 1006 transport over TCP is mentioned only as a possible way to carry the TSDU.

gaps.name: OSI upper layers (Session, Presentation, ACSE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy's OSI tag covers network-layer protocols, so there is no tag for the OSI session, presentation and application-association protocols that are this document's actual subject.

RFC1699.title: Summary of 1600-1699
RFC1699.summary: RFC 1699 is an annotated list giving the title, author, date, abstract and standards-track status of each of RFCs 1600 through 1699.

RFC series.why: The document is a periodic catalogue of RFC publications. Readers browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find this summary of the series.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1600 through RFCs 1699.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: It lists several process RFCs (1602, 1603, 1640), but it only summarizes them and does not address the process itself.
It is a status listing of a block of RFCs, not a history or retrospective, though it has some historical value.
Many listed RFCs are MIB definitions, but this document only lists them. The same holds for BGP, SMTP, PPP, X.400, X.500 and IPng, which appear as one-line entries.
Many listed entries are IPng white papers, but this document is not about IPng. It only catalogues them.

RFC1700.title: Assigned Numbers
RFC1700.summary: RFC 1700 is the October 1994 snapshot of IANA's Assigned Numbers registries: protocol numbers, port numbers, multicast addresses, IP/ICMP/TCP/Telnet options, DNS parameters, mail keywords, DHCP options, MIME media types, character sets, SNMP MIB/OID and enterprise numbers.

IANA.why: The whole document is the IANA registry of protocol parameters (numbers and keywords), so the IANA subject page is where readers would look for it.
IANA.quote: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) is the central coordinator for the assignment of unique parameter values for Internet protocols.

media types.why: It contains the MIME content type and subtype registry and the MIME/X.400 mapping tables, which is a substantial section.
media types.quote: [RFC1521] specifies that Content Types, Content Subtypes, Character Sets, Access Types, and Conversion values for MIME mail will be assigned and listed by the IANA.

character sets.why: It has a long registry of character set names and aliases, taking up roughly twenty pages.
character sets.quote: These are the official names for character sets that may be used in the Internet and may be referred to in Internet documentation.

MIB.why: It registers the MIB-II OID tree, ifType values, experimental MIB codes and private enterprise numbers, a large part of the document.
MIB.quote: The SMI includes the provision for panrameters or codes to indicate experimental or private data structures. These parameter assignments are listed here.

rejected.why: TCP option numbers are only one table among many, and the document specifies nothing about TCP.
It lists DNS class and type values, but this is a short registry table and the document is not about DNS.
It lists BOOTP/DHCP option codes in a single table, which is too small a part of the document to tag.
It lists Telnet option numbers, but only as one registry among many.
It lists multicast address assignments, but this is just one registry section.
ICMP type and code numbers are one registry table, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Port and protocol number registries
gaps.why: The core content is the well-known and registered port number list and the IP protocol number list. The taxonomy has no tag for port or protocol number assignments apart from the generic IANA tag.

RFC1701.title: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE)
RFC1701.summary: RFC 1701 specifies Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), a general header format for encapsulating an arbitrary network-layer payload protocol inside another network-layer delivery protocol, with optional checksum, key, sequence number and source routing fields.

GRE.why: The entire document defines the GRE header, its optional fields, forwarding behaviour and protocol type values. GRE is the specified technology.
GRE.quote: This document specifies a protocol for performing encapsulation of an arbitrary network layer protocol over another arbitrary network layer protocol.

rejected.why: It is the parent of GRE. The document is about GRE specifically, so the child tag is used and the parent is implied.
The introduction cites IP-over-IP encapsulation proposals as related work. GRE is a more general mechanism, and the IPv4 delivery binding is in RFC 1702.
The Checksum field uses the Internet checksum, but only as a header field. The document is not about checksums.
Policy routing and source routes are mentioned as motivation and in the optional routing field. The document does not specify IDPR.

RFC1702.title: Generic Routing Encapsulation over IPv4 networks
RFC1702.summary: Companion to RFC 1701 specifying how GRE is used over IPv4: IP protocol 47 as delivery, 0x800 payload type, IP-in-IP handling of TTL/TOS, and IP-address and AS-number source routes in GRE SREs.

GRE.why: The whole document defines how GRE operates over IPv4, including delivery protocol number, payload type, and source route entries. GRE readers would want it.
GRE.quote: GRE packets which are encapsulated within IP will use IP protocol type 47.

rejected.why: The document covers IP encapsulated in GRE within IP, not the separate IP-in-IP encapsulation protocol; only a short TTL/TOS paragraph touches this.
IPv4 is the delivery/payload substrate; the document is not about IPv4 itself.
Implied as the parent of GRE; GRE is the more specific tag.
AS numbers are used in AS source routes, but BGP is not specified or discussed.

RFC1703.title: Principles of Operation for the TPC.INT Subdomain: Radio Paging -- Technical Procedures
RFC1703.summary: Describes how radio pagers are addressed and reached via Internet mail by mapping telephone numbers to domain names under tpc.int, using MX routing, pager-specific local-parts, and SMTP MAIL/SEND semantics.

paging.why: The whole document specifies how to send pages to alpha-numeric and numeric radio pagers via email, so readers of paging would expect it.
paging.quote: this memo describes a technique for radio paging using the Internet mail infrastructure

SMTP.why: A substantial section defines how MAIL, SEND, SOML and SAML reply codes are interpreted by paging servers, and latency/direct SMTP-hop guidance.
SMTP.quote: An SMTP client communicating with a radio paging server may use attempt either the MAIL or SEND command.

rejected.why: It maps telephone numbers into the DNS in a similar way, but uses the tpc.int scheme, not E.164 ENUM (e164.arpa/NAPTR).
Wildcard MX records and CNAME synthesis are used for routing, but DNS is the substrate and nothing new is specified about the DNS protocol.
RFC 822 messages and atoms are used as the carrier and the local-part syntax is restricted, but the document is not about the message format itself.
A text/plain MIME example is shown, but MIME is only used as the content carrier.
The more specific tags (paging, SMTP) cover the email-based service; no general email architecture is addressed.

RFC1704.title: On Internet Authentication
RFC1704.summary: Informational overview of authentication technologies (passwords, non-disclosing schemes, Kerberos, SPX, cryptographic checksums, digital signatures), user-to-host and service authentication, and key distribution, with suggestions for protocol designers.

authentication.why: The whole memo surveys authentication classes, user-to-host and service authentication, and gives guidance across protocols, which is the general authentication topic.
authentication.quote: This document describes a spectrum of authentication technologies and provides suggestions to protocol developers on what kinds of authentication might be suitable

key management.why: A full section covers key distribution, key servers, public-key certificates and multicast key management scaling.
key management.quote: Key management is perhaps the hardest problem faced when seeking to provide authentication in large internetworks.

Kerberos.why: Kerberos is discussed repeatedly as the main example of symmetric, trusted-third-party authentication, with its strengths and limits.
Kerberos.quote: A well known system that addresses insecure open networks as a part of a computing environment is the Kerberos (TM) Authentication Service

rejected.why: S/Key and SecurID are mentioned as examples of non-disclosing passwords, but only briefly, not as the subject.
Privacy Enhanced Mail is cited as an example of certificate-based key management, not discussed in its own right.
Secure SNMP is used as an example of cryptographic checksum authentication, not the document's subject.
The more specific authentication tag fits better than the general security parent.
Key certificates and certifying authorities are touched on briefly, but PKI is not the focus.

RFC1705.title: Six Virtual Inches to the Left: The Problem with IPng
RFC1705.summary: An IPng-era position paper proposing a new TCP/UDP (TCPng) with a globally unique 64-bit Transport Address, decoupling transport from the network layer, with new headers, options, and transporter gateways.

TCP.why: The document specifies a new TCP header, options, 64-bit sequence numbers and compatibility behaviour, so it is about TCP extensions and redesign.
TCP.quote: This RFC suggests that a new version of TCP (TCPng), and UDP, be developed and deployed.

UDP.why: A modified UDP header with Transport Addresses is proposed alongside TCPng.
UDP.quote: Proposed UDP Header

IPng.why: The paper is a response to RFC 1550 and critiques and complements the IPng candidates, proposing transport independence from the network layer.
IPng.quote: The motivation for writing this paper resulted from research into the various Internet Protocol Next Generation (IPng) proposals

rejected.why: The paper is about IPng in general, not the IPv6 specification, and it proposes a transport change rather than IPv6 itself.
The Transport Address is a new identifier, but it is mainly a TCP/UDP redesign, so the TCP tag covers it.
Transition and coexistence are discussed, but via transport-layer gateways, not the transition mechanisms listed under this tag.
DNS is used to resolve TAs and a TA record is sketched in Appendix B, but DNS is not the subject.
CIDR appears only as background on address exhaustion.

RFC1706.title: DNS NSAP Resource Records
RFC1706.summary: Defines the DNS NSAP resource record (TYPE 22) for mapping domain names to OSI NSAP addresses, and describes using PTR RRs under NSAP.INT for NSAP-to-name reverse mapping.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS resource record type (NSAP, TYPE 22), its wire and master file formats, and PTR-based reverse mapping under NSAP.INT. It is a DNS RR specification.
DNS.quote: This document defines the format of one new Resource Record (RR) for the DNS for domain name-to-NSAP mapping.

CLNP.why: The RR exists to support CLNP deployment and debugging, and much of the body covers NSAP structure and the NSel. Readers of CLNP and OSI addressing would want it.
CLNP.quote: OSI lower layer protocols, comprising the connectionless network protocol (CLNP) and supporting routing protocols, are deployed in some parts of the global Internet.

rejected.why: CLNP is the more specific tag for the network-layer protocol that motivates the document. The OSI parent is implied.
The document mentions a hosts.txt-like file only as the problem being replaced. It is not about host naming conventions.
IPv4 appears only as an analogy (IN-ADDR.ARPA and A records). The document is not about IPv4.

gaps.name: NSAP (OSI network addresses)
gaps.why: The document is largely about NSAP address structure and its DNS representation. The taxonomy has no tag for OSI NSAP addressing, apart from the broad OSI and CLNP tags.

RFC1707.title: CATNIP: Common Architecture for the Internet
RFC1707.summary: CATNIP is an IPng proposal defining a common compressed network-layer packet format and NSAP-based addressing that integrates CLNP, IPv4, IPX and SIPP/IPv6 with stateless translation between them.

IPng.why: CATNIP is a historic candidate next-generation IP protocol submitted to the IPng area, with a new network-layer datagram format (IPv7).
IPng.quote: This document was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550

CLNP.why: A substantial part of the document defines translation between CLNP and CATNIP and uses NSAP addressing so CLNP addresses map directly.
CLNP.quote: The CATNIP integrates CLNP, IP, and IPX.

IPX.why: The document defines the mapping of IPX addresses and datagrams into the common format and interworking with IPX.
IPX.quote: An IPX address in the common form looks like:

rejected.why: SIPP/IPv6 is discussed only as a protocol to be integrated; the document does not specify it.
CLNP is the more specific tag; the OSI network-layer coexistence is covered through CLNP, and NSAP addressing is used as a mechanism.
IPv4 is mapped into the common address space, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
A short section describes NSAP RR use and a .NSAP.INT inverse zone, but it is a minor part of the document.
The compressed form is a network-layer format with cache handles, not link-level header compression.

RFC1708.title: NTP PICS PROFORMA - For the Network Time Protocol Version 3
RFC1708.summary: RFC 1708 provides an ISO 9646 PICS proforma, a conformance checklist, for implementations of NTP version 3 (RFC 1305). It lists data formats, state variables, procedures, algorithms, local clocks and control messages.

NTP.why: The whole document is a conformance statement proforma for NTP v3. It covers NTP's variables, procedures, clock filter and selection algorithms, packet format and control messages.
NTP.quote: This document provides the PICS proforma for the Network Time Protocol (NTP) in compliance with the relevant requirements

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the NTP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The document only mentions NTP port 123 in a parameter table. It says nothing about UDP itself.
Conformance testing is not benchmarking of device performance.

gaps.name: Protocol conformance / PICS proforma (ISO 9646)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for conformance testing or implementation conformance statements. They are the document's methodological subject.

RFC1709.title: K-12 Internetworking Guidelines
RFC1709.summary: FYI 26 gives K-12 schools and districts guidelines for building campus TCP/IP networks and connecting them to the Internet. It covers LAN design, wiring, links to district offices, and NOC/NIC support.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory and planning guide for a non-specialist audience (K-12 educators and administrators), not a protocol specification.
user guides.quote: is intended to bridge that gap and provides a recommended technical

network management.why: A substantial part of the document covers NOC and NIC organisation, network monitoring, address and name administration, and staffing for operations. This is operational practice, not a specific management protocol.
network management.quote: Internet technology network management consists primarily of

rejected.why: DNS is described as a district responsibility, but only at an introductory level. The document specifies nothing about DNS.
SNMP is mentioned as the monitoring tool but is not specified or analysed.
Frame Relay appears only as one circuit option in a cost comparison, so the document is not about it.
Ethernet is recommended as the LAN technology, but the document does not address IP over Ethernet itself.
The document is a practical deployment guide, not a statement of architectural principles.
TCP/IP is advocated as the school networking protocol suite in general terms. The document says nothing about TCP itself.

gaps.name: K-12 school networking / education networks
gaps.why: The whole document concerns campus and district networking for schools. The taxonomy has no education or campus-network topic, so only the generic user guides tag fits.

RFC1710.title: Simple Internet Protocol Plus White Paper
RFC1710.summary: A white paper by the SIPP working group giving an overview of the Simple Internet Protocol Plus, a candidate for IPng (the next IP), covering its history, header, addressing, routing, QoS flow labels, security options and IPAE transition mechanisms.

IPng.why: The document presents SIPP as a candidate IPng, submitted in response to RFC 1550, and describes the history of the IPAE, SIP and Pip efforts that merged. This matches the historic IPng candidates tag.
IPng.quote: one of the candidates being considered in the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) for the next version of the Internet Protocol

IPv6.why: SIPP became the basis of IPv6. The paper covers its header format, addressing (unicast, cluster, multicast), options and routing, which readers of IPv6 history would want.
IPv6.quote: SIPP is a new version of the Internet Protocol, designed as a successor to IP version 4 [IPV4].  SIPP is assigned IP version number 6.

IPv6 transition.why: A full section covers IPv4/SIPP coexistence: embedded IPv4 addresses, tunnelling SIPP in IPv4, and header translation. Transition is also a main theme of sections 2.2 and 6.
IPv6 transition.quote: The mechanisms and policies of the SIPP transition are called "IPAE".

rejected.why: The Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Header are only briefly described in section 4.6. They are not a main subject of the paper.
The flow label and drop priority are an early QoS capability, but they are a short subsection and not Diffserv.
Mobility is mentioned only as a use of the routing option and is not specified.
Addressing is a major section, but the IPv6 and IPng tags already cover it.
CIDR is mentioned only as the comparison point for routing and address assignment.

RFC1711.title: Classifications in E-mail Routing
RFC1711.summary: Informational RFC that classifies e-mail routing concepts (static/dynamic, direct/indirect, source routing, bulk routing, routing communities) and applies them to Internet mail, UUCP, EARN, X.400 GO-MHS and related services.

email.why: The whole document is about how MTAs route e-mail across Internet, X.400, UUCP and BITNET systems, which is e-mail architecture and transport.
email.quote: This paper presents a classification for e-mail routing issues.

X.400.why: X.400 MHS routing, RELAY-MTAs, ADMD/PRMD and GO-MHS and Long Bud are used throughout as the main examples and realisations.
X.400.quote: X.400 routing according to RFC 1465 [2] is clearly table based, but at the same time allows a fairly dynamic kind of mail routing

rejected.why: MX records and DNS-based routing rules are cited only as an example of a routing community's rules, and the document does not specify or extend DNS.
SMTP appears only incidentally, for envelope grouping. The document is about routing classification, not the protocol.
UUCP bang addressing and its routing are described as one realisation, but the document is not about UUCP mail interchange itself.
RFC 822 addressing, source routes and the %-hack are mentioned as examples of address forms. The document does not address message format.

RFC1712.title: DNS Encoding of Geographical Location
RFC1712.summary: Defines the experimental GPOS DNS resource record (type 27) that encodes a host's longitude, latitude and altitude as printable strings, so geographic location can be published in DNS.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record type (GPOS, type 27), its RDATA format and master file syntax. This is a DNS extension.
DNS.quote: This document defines the format of a new Resource Record (RR) for the Domain Naming System (DNS), and reserves a corresponding DNS type mnemonic and numerical code.

geolocation.why: The record's purpose is conveying host geographic location (longitude, latitude, altitude). Readers of geolocation formats would want it.
geolocation.quote: This definition deals with associating geographical host location mappings to host names within a domain.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in Background as an alternative (sysLocation) that was not chosen.
Mentioned only as a deferred alternative provider of location data.
Cited only as a tool that could be supplemented by location data; the document does not specify or extend it.
Named only as an existing tool that location data could supplement.

RFC1713.title: Tools for DNS debugging
RFC1713.summary: An informational FYI document surveying tools (host, dnswalk, lamers, DOC, DDT, Checker) that DNS administrators can use to detect and correct configuration anomalies such as lame delegations.

DNS.why: The whole document is about debugging and operating DNS: zone transfers, lame delegations, authority data, resource record checks and name server traffic.
DNS.quote: This document presents some tools available for domain administrators to detect and correct those anomalies.

rejected.why: The document is FYI 27, but the subject index tag should reflect its subject, which is DNS operations, not the FYI series itself.
The tools are operational, but the document is specifically about DNS and not general network management.
Mail is mentioned only as an application of DNS (MX records, lamers reports sent by mail), not as a subject.
Hostname checks occur only as part of DNS data validation, not as a discussion of host naming conventions.

RFC1714.title: Referral Whois Protocol (RWhois)
RFC1714.summary: RFC 1714 specifies version 1.0 of the Referral Whois (RWhois) client/server protocol, a hierarchical, referral-based distributed system for registration data lookup that stays backward compatible with RFC 954 whois.

RWhois.why: The whole document defines the RWhois protocol: directives, responses, referrals, authority areas (SOA), query reduction, and error codes.
RWhois.quote: This memo describes version 1.0 of the client/server interaction of RWhois. RWhois provides a distributed system for the display of hierarchical information.

rejected.why: RFC 954 whois is the legacy protocol RWhois must stay compatible with, but the RWhois tag sits under it and is more specific. The parent is implied.
Whois++ servers are mentioned only as possible referral targets and leaf nodes, not specified.
The SOA, TTL and refresh concepts resemble DNS, but the document does not specify or use DNS.
Mentioned only in the introduction as a rejected alternative.
MIME is cited as one possible display method only.

RFC1715.title: The H Ratio for Address Assignment Efficiency
RFC1715.summary: Informational IPng-era memo proposing the logarithmic H ratio as a measure of address assignment efficiency, deriving typical values from historical numbering plans and using it to argue that 128-bit addresses are sufficient.

addressing.why: The document defines a metric for address assignment efficiency and applies it to evaluate address sizes and plans, which is about address architecture and allocation in general.
addressing.quote: I propose to use a logarithmic scale for the efficiency ratio

IPng.why: It was submitted in response to the IPng area's call (RFC 1550) and argues about address size for the IPng candidates, so IPng readers would want it.
IPng.quote: A substantial part of the "IPng" debate was devoted to the choice of an address size.

rejected.why: The memo argues for 128-bit addresses during the IPng selection debate but does not specify or describe IPv6 itself.
IPv4's 32-bit space is used as one data point (about 3 million hosts, ratio 0.20), not as the subject.
DECnet Phase IV is only one example data point for the ratio, not a subject of the document.
The DNS is mentioned only as a source of host counts.

RFC1716.title: Towards Requirements for IP Routers
RFC1716.summary: A snapshot of the Router Requirements working group's draft specifying requirements for IPv4 routers: link layer, IP/ICMP/IGMP, forwarding algorithms, routing protocols (OSPF, RIP, BGP, EGP), SNMP management and operations.

routing.why: The whole document is cross-protocol router requirements, covering forwarding, next-hop selection and routing protocols; this is the general routing/router topic.
routing.quote: It defines and discusses requirements for devices which perform the network layer forwarding function of the Internet protocol suite.

ICMP.why: Extensive ICMP requirements for routers: message generation, rate limiting, redirects, unreachable codes including new codes 13-15.
ICMP.quote: A router MUST generate a Time Exceeded message Code 0 (In Transit) when it discards a packet due to an expired TTL field.

IPv4.why: Detailed IP protocol walk-through: options, fragmentation, addressing, broadcasts, TTL, TOS, header validation.
IPv4.quote: Routers MUST implement the IP protocol, as defined by [INTERNET:1].

OSPF.why: Requires OSPF and gives errata on virtual links and a new version.
OSPF.quote: A router which implements any routing protocol (other than static routes) MUST IMPLEMENT OSPF

RIP.why: RIP gets a protocol walk-through covering timeouts, split horizon, triggered updates and shutdown.
RIP.quote: An implementation of RIP MUST implement split horizon

BGP.why: BGP requirements and a walk-through are included as part of exterior routing protocols.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-AS routing protocol which exchanges network reachability information

EGP.why: Has an EGP section with a protocol walk-through.
EGP.quote: if a router does implement EGP it also MUST IMPLEMENT BGP.

PPP.why: Specific LCP/IPCP option requirements for routers using PPP.
PPP.quote: Routers which contain such general purpose serial interfaces MUST implement PPP.

multicast.why: Covers IP multicast forwarding, IGMP and multicast routing protocols (Appendix D).
multicast.quote: An IP router SHOULD support forwarding of IP multicast packets

congestion control.why: Discusses router discard policy, Random Drop and Source Quench.
congestion control.quote: Congestion in a network is loosely defined as a condition where demand for resources

SNMP.why: A chapter on router SNMP and MIB requirements.
SNMP.quote: The Simple Network Management Protocol - SNMP

Diffserv.why: IP Precedence and TOS handling is a QoS topic, but Diffserv is not an exact fit; QoS is a weaker choice, so skipped in favor of rejected.
Diffserv.quote: This section specifies requirements and guidelines for appropriate processing of the IP Precedence field in routers.

rejected.why: Precedence/TOS predates Diffserv and the document does not define Diffserv; tag removed from consideration.
Only substrate/host requirements incorporated by reference in a short chapter.
Short compliance section only.
BOOTP relay is a small section and DHCP is not the subject.
Only brief router-specific rules in the link layer chapter.
Only brief mentions of host and router parts of IGMP.

gaps.name: Router requirements
gaps.why: The document is a general IP router requirements profile; only the generic 'routing' tag fits, with no dedicated router-requirements subject.

RFC1717.title: The PPP Multilink Protocol (MP)
RFC1717.summary: Specifies the PPP Multilink Protocol (MP), which splits, sequences and recombines datagrams across multiple PPP links in a bundle, with new LCP options (MRRU, short sequence numbers, Endpoint Discriminator).

PPP.why: The document defines a new PPP protocol and LCP options for bundling multiple PPP links; it extends PPP directly.
PPP.quote: This document proposes a method for splitting, recombining and sequencing datagrams across multiple logical data links.

ISDN.why: ISDN bearer channel aggregation is the stated motivation, though the protocol applies to any PPP links.
ISDN.quote: This work was originally motivated by the desire to exploit multiple bearer channels in ISDN

rejected.why: This tag is for IEEE 802.1AX LAG; MP is PPP-specific and is covered by the PPP tag.
X.25 SVCs are mentioned only as an example of member links.
Mentioned only as an example of a multiplexed link type.
PPP authentication is relied on to join bundles securely but is not the subject.

RFC1718.title: The Tao of IETF - A Guide for New Attendees of the Internet Engineering Task Force
RFC1718.summary: FYI 17 guide for newcomers to IETF meetings, explaining IETF structure, history, mailing lists, registration, meeting etiquette, and where to find RFCs, Internet-Drafts and proceedings.

IETF process.why: The document explains IETF organization, working groups, BOFs, meeting practice and participation, which is the IETF process and its administration.
IETF process.quote: The purpose of this For Your Information (FYI) RFC is to explain to the newcomers how the IETF works.

user guides.why: It is itself an FYI introductory guide (FYI 17) for newcomers, fitting the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: The For Your Information RFC sub- series was created to document overviews and topics which are introductory.

RFC series.why: A substantial section describes RFC history, the FYI/STD/RTR sub-series, Internet-Drafts and how to retrieve RFCs.
RFC series.quote: there are now two special sub-series within the RFCs: FYIs and STDs.

rejected.why: The Humble Beginnings section gives brief IETF meeting history, but the document is a how-to guide, not a retrospective.
IETF mailing lists are discussed only as participation logistics, not mailing list protocols or headers.
Anonymous FTP is only a means of retrieving files, not the subject.
The nominating committee is mentioned only in passing in describing the hierarchy.

RFC1719.title: A Direction for IPng
RFC1719.summary: An IESG/IETF Director memo announcing a temporary IPng area with co-Area Directors and a Directorate, and setting out the scope and timeframe questions to resolve before recommending the next-generation IP.

IPng.why: The whole memo is about the process and direction for choosing the next-generation IP (IPng), including scope, timeframe and decision criteria for the candidate protocols.
IPng.quote: The IESG will establish a temporary, ad hoc, "area" to deal specifically with IPng  issues.

rejected.why: CIDR aggregation is discussed only as a factor in estimating address-exhaustion timeframe, not as the document's subject.
The memo describes an IESG organisational action, but it concerns the IPng effort specifically, which the IPng tag covers better.
The memo predates any selection and discusses IPng candidates in general, not IPv6 specifically.
Address assignment rates and policies are mentioned as inputs to the timeframe estimate, not as the main subject.

RFC1720.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1720.summary: RFC 1720 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly list of Internet Official Protocol Standards, describing the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and listing every protocol by standardization state.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels and the RFC processing decision table, which is IETF standards process content.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial part covers the RFC series: what RFCs are, how they are submitted and published, and how to obtain them.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: IANA is only a contact and the Assigned Numbers pointer, not the subject of the document.
TCP and the many other listed protocols appear only as entries in status tables; the document does not specify or analyse them.
The document is a status snapshot as of 1994, not a history or retrospective.
The IAB is the author, but the content is about standards status, not architectural principles.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but this is part of the standards process explanation, not a glossary.

RFC1721.title: RIP Version 2 Protocol Analysis
RFC1721.summary: Informational analysis report documenting the key features, MIB, implementations and operational experience of RIP-2, required to advance RIP-2 on the standards track.

RIP.why: The whole document analyses RIP version 2: its features (route tags, subnet masks, next hop, authentication, multicast), implementations and operational experience.
RIP.quote: this report documents the key features of the RIP-2 protocol and the current implementation experience.

rejected.why: The RIP-2 MIB is only summarised briefly in one short section; it is defined in RFC 1724, so the document is not substantially about MIB modules.
OSPF is mentioned only as the source of the extensible authentication mechanism.
CIDR is mentioned only in passing as a use case for subnet masks.
Multicasting of RIP-2 packets is a feature mention, not a multicast routing topic.

RFC1722.title: RIP Version 2 Protocol Applicability Statement
RFC1722.summary: Applicability statement for RIP-2, explaining in which environments its extensions (subnet masks, next hop, authentication, multicast) make it a suitable IGP relative to RIP-1 and OSPF.

RIP.why: The whole document analyses where RIP-2 is applicable and how each extension to RIP-1 is useful.
RIP.quote: this report defines the applicability of the RIP-2 protocol within the Internet.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the alternative for large autonomous systems that RIP-2 is not meant to replace; the document is not about OSPF.
Appears only as an example of what external routers might run in the Next Hop topology.
Mentioned only as background for why subnet masks are needed in RIP entries.
Section 3.4 notes RIP-2 uses multicast for advertisements, but it is a minor feature of RIP-2, not about multicast routing.
The RIP-2 MIB is only referenced as a companion document (RFC 1724).

RFC1723.title: RIP Version 2 - Carrying Additional Information
RFC1723.summary: RFC 1723 specifies RIP version 2, extending the RIP message format with route tags, subnet masks, next hop, multicast, and simple password authentication, with compatibility rules for RIP-1.

RIP.why: The whole document defines RIP-2: new message format fields, multicast, authentication, and RIP-1 compatibility.
RIP.quote: This document specifies an extension of the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), as defined in [1,2], to expand the amount of useful information carried in RIP messages

rejected.why: Multicast address 224.0.0.9 is only used for RIP-2 periodic updates; the document is not about multicast routing.
Simple password authentication is a part of RIP-2, not a cross-protocol subject; the RIP tag covers it.
OSPF is mentioned only as a comparison and in an example.
BGP appears only as a source of imported routes for the route tag.

RFC1724.title: RIP Version 2 MIB Extension
RFC1724.summary: RFC 1724 defines the RIPv2-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing RIP Version 2, with global counters, interface status and configuration tables, and a peer table, obsoleting RFC 1389.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (RIPv2-MIB) written in SMI, with object groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

RIP.why: The managed objects cover RIP-2 interface configuration, authentication type, send/receive versions, and peers. RIP readers would want this MIB.
RIP.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing RIP Version 2.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through. The document defines objects, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag is more specific.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for the SMI definitions, not the subject of the document.
Implied by the RIP tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC1725.title: Post Office Protocol - Version 3
RFC1725.summary: RFC 1725 specifies POP3 version 3, a protocol letting a workstation retrieve and manage mail held in a maildrop on a server, with its states, commands (including optional TOP, UIDL, APOP) and security notes.

POP3.why: The whole document defines the POP3 protocol: its authorization, transaction and update states, and its commands and responses.
POP3.quote: The Post Office Protocol - Version 3 (POP3) is intended to permit a workstation to dynamically access a maildrop on a server host in a useful fashion.

rejected.why: SMTP is mentioned only as the mail transport and as a suggested way for clients to submit mail; the memo does not specify it.
MD5 is only used to compute the APOP digest. The memo does not specify or analyse it.
Messages are assumed to follow RFC 822. This is a reference to that format, not a subject the memo addresses.
TCP port 110 is only the substrate the protocol runs over.
The APOP command is a small part of the protocol, and the POP3 tag already covers it. It is not a general authentication topic.

RFC1726.title: Technical Criteria for Choosing IP The Next Generation (IPng)
RFC1726.summary: An informational memo submitted to the IPng area defining technical criteria (scale, transition, security, multicast, mobility, extensibility, etc.) for evaluating candidate next-generation IP protocols.

IPng.why: The whole document sets out requirements for choosing among the IPng candidate protocols, which is the subject of the IPng tag.
IPng.quote: define a set of criteria to be used in evaluating the protocols being proposed for adoption as the next generation of IP

IPv6 transition.why: A full criterion covers IPv4-to-IPng coexistence, dual stacks and the lack of a flag day. This is the transition subject, though the document is about IPng generally and not IPv6 specifically.
IPv6 transition.quote: The protocol must have a straightforward transition plan from the current IPv4.

rejected.why: The document predates IPv6's specification and evaluates candidates generically without specifying or analysing IPv6.
Multicast is one criterion among seventeen, so it is not a substantial enough focus of the document.
Mobility is a single criterion (5.15) with only a general framework statement. The abstract mentions mobility, but the body does not treat it in depth.
Section 4 gives general architectural principles, but they serve the IPng criteria and are not an architecture document in their own right.
Addressing and scale appear as criteria, but the document is about the protocol choice as a whole, so IPng is the more specific tag.

RFC1727.title: A Vision of an Integrated Internet Information Service
RFC1727.summary: An informational vision paper proposing a four-layer architecture (resources with transponders, URN-to-URL mapping, resource discovery, information delivery tools) to integrate Gopher, WAIS, WWW, Archie and other Internet information services.

URN.why: The architecture centres on URNs and a URN-to-URL mapping level that maintains the URN space and resolves names to locators. This is the core naming mechanism of the proposal.
URN.quote: should have a Uniform Resource Name (URN) [Weider 94b] associated with it to uniquely identify its contents.
URN.section: 4. An architecture to provide interoperability and integration.

service discovery.why: A whole architectural level is a distributed resource discovery system that accepts search criteria and returns URNs. Publishing agents and transponders announce new resources to it.
service discovery.quote: The third level of the architecture is a resource discovery system.
service discovery.section: 4. An architecture to provide interoperability and integration.

rejected.why: Gopher is one of the services to be integrated and is used in the examples, but the document does not specify or extend it.
WAIS is mentioned as an example information service and index builder. The document is not about it.
The WWW is discussed only as one of the information networks to be interoperated with. No HTTP semantics are addressed.
Whois++ is suggested only as a possible basis for the discovery and mapping layers, in passing.
X.500 is mentioned briefly as a candidate for the URN-to-URL mapping level and is not the subject.
The paper proposes an architecture for information services specifically, not for the Internet as a whole.

gaps.name: Internet information services / resource discovery integration
gaps.why: The document's main subject is the integration of Gopher, WAIS, WWW and Archie into a resource discovery architecture. The taxonomy has no tag for information retrieval or resource discovery systems.

RFC1728.title: Resource Transponders
RFC1728.summary: An informational research paper proposing "resource transponders", meaning metainformation and an agent attached to each resource that automatically update resource location systems, with no protocol specified.

service discovery.why: The whole document is about keeping resource location and discovery systems (archie, Gopher, WAIS) up to date automatically. Service discovery is the closest fit in the taxonomy.
service discovery.quote: This paper describes an automatic mechanism, the resource transponder, for maintaining resource location information.
