rejected.why: Gopher is named only as an example of an existing location system. The document does not specify or extend it.
WAIS is named only as an example of a location system and is not the subject.
URNs are mentioned only as one possible item of metainformation. The document does not address URN namespaces or their syntax.
URLs and URNs appear only as example metainformation fields, not as a subject of the document.
Telnet appears only as an example of how an agent might mediate access to a resource.
The location systems are loosely directory-like, but the document does not address directory protocols such as LDAP or X.500.

gaps.name: Resource location and navigation (IIIR)
gaps.why: The document belongs to the Internet Information Infrastructure Research (IIIR) work on resource location and metadata. The taxonomy has no tag for resource metadata or information indexing beyond the generic service discovery tag.

RFC1729.title: Using the Z39.50 Information Retrieval Protocol
RFC1729.summary: Describes how implementors run the Z39.50 (ANSI/NISO Z39.50-1992) information retrieval protocol directly over TCP/IP, without the OSI upper layers, covering BER encoding, port 210, service mappings, contexts and record syntax issues.

transport mapping.why: The document's purpose is mapping Z39.50 and its OSI association control and presentation services onto TCP: connection on port 210, RELEASE/ABORT to TCP CLOSE, P-DATA to TCP send/receive.
transport mapping.quote: the decision was taken to implement the Z39.50 protocol directly on top of TCP

ASN.1.why: A full section specifies how BER is applied to the Z39.50 APDUs over TCP, including the restriction to direct references for EXTERNAL objects, and BER tolerance rules.
ASN.1.quote: The standard Basic Encoding Rules (BER) [11] are applied to the ASN.1 structures defined by the Z39.50 protocol

rejected.why: TCP is the substrate the document maps onto. It does not specify or extend TCP.
WAIS appears only as a backward-compatibility note about Z39.50 Version 1 INIT APDUs. The document is not about WAIS.
The subject is Z39.50, an application protocol, but the transport mapping tag already covers the document's substance. Z39.50 itself has no tag (see gaps).
The OSI upper layers are discussed only as what is being avoided. The OSI tag covers network-layer protocols and coexistence with IP.

gaps.name: Z39.50 (ANSI/NISO Z39.50, ISO 10162/10163 Search and Retrieve)
gaps.why: The document is about this library and information retrieval protocol. The taxonomy has no tag for it or for information retrieval and search protocols generally.

RFC1730.title: Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4
RFC1730.summary: RFC 1730 specifies IMAP4, a protocol for clients to access and manipulate email messages and mailboxes on a remote server, including commands, responses, states and formal syntax.

IMAP.why: The entire document defines the IMAP4 protocol: its states, commands, server responses and formal syntax.
IMAP.quote: The Internet Message Access Protocol, Version 4 (IMAP4) allows a client to access and manipulate electronic mail messages on a server.

rejected.why: Only referenced as the mechanism for posting mail; IMAP4 explicitly does not specify message submission.
IMAP4 parses and exposes MIME body structure but only relies on MIME as defined elsewhere; it does not specify MIME.
RFC 822 headers are parsed into ENVELOPE structures, but the document is not about the message format itself.
AUTHENTICATE provides a general mechanism for authentication mechanisms specified in a separate document (RFC 1731); the mechanism itself is not defined here.
TCP is only the assumed reliable transport (port 143), not the subject.
The formal syntax uses BNF notation, but this is a notational tool, not the subject.

RFC1731.title: IMAP4 Authentication Mechanisms
RFC1731.summary: Defines three IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE mechanisms (Kerberos V4, GSSAPI, S/Key) including their exchanges, protection-mechanism bit-masks and examples.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 by specifying authentication mechanisms for its AUTHENTICATE command, with example IMAP dialogues.
IMAP.quote: This document describes several authentication mechanisms for use by the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE command.

Kerberos.why: A full section specifies how Kerberos V4 tickets and authenticators are used for IMAP authentication.
Kerberos.quote: The authentication type associated with Kerberos version 4 is "KERBEROS_V4".

GSS-API.why: A full section defines the GSSAPI-based IMAP authentication exchange and protection levels.
GSS-API.quote: The authentication type associated with all mechanisms employing the GSSAPI [RFC1508] is "GSSAPI".

OTP.why: A section defines S/Key one-time-password authentication for IMAP.
OTP.quote: The authentication type associated with S/Key [SKEY] is "SKEY".

rejected.why: The document predates SASL and does not mention it. It defines IMAP-specific AUTHENTICATE mechanisms.
The generic topic is covered by the more specific technology tags chosen.

RFC1732.title: IMAP4 Compatibility with IMAP2 and IMAP2bis
RFC1732.summary: Informational memo giving hints for IMAP4 clients and servers to interoperate with older IMAP2 and IMAP2bis (RFC 1176) implementations.

IMAP.why: The whole document is about IMAP4 compatibility with IMAP2/IMAP2bis: commands, fetch items, and client/server behaviours.
IMAP.quote: hints and recommendations to enable an IMAP4 implementation to interoperate with implementations that conform to earlier specifications

rejected.why: IMAP is the specific child; the document is about IMAP, not email generally.
MIME is mentioned only in passing (IMAP2bis servers lacking MIME support), not a subject of the document.
AUTHENTICATE is mentioned only as a fallback to LOGIN; nothing about SASL itself.

RFC1733.title: Distributed Electronic Mail Models in IMAP4
RFC1733.summary: Informational memo describing the offline, online and disconnected models of client/server email and how IMAP4 supports each of them.

IMAP.why: The whole memo explains how IMAP4 supports the three email access models, including server-based RFC 822 and MIME processing and on-demand data transfer.
IMAP.quote: There are three fundamental models of client/server email: offline, online, and disconnected use.  IMAP4 can be used in any one of these three models.

rejected.why: POP-3 is cited only as an example of the offline model, and the memo is not about it.
MIME appears only as something IMAP4 processes on the server, and the memo does not specify or discuss MIME.
IMAP is the more specific tag, so the parent email tag is implied.
NFS is mentioned only as an example of the online model.

RFC1734.title: POP3 AUTHentication command
RFC1734.summary: Defines the optional POP3 AUTH command, which lets a POP3 client select an IMAP4 authentication mechanism (SASL-like challenge/response with base64 lines) and optionally negotiate a protection layer.

POP3.why: The document extends POP3 with a new AUTH command, specifying its syntax, states, responses and examples.
POP3.quote: This document describes the optional AUTH command, for indicating an authentication mechanism to the server, performing an authentication protocol exchange

rejected.why: The mechanisms are borrowed from IMAP4 authentication (RFC 1731), and the document predates SASL's formal naming. It defines no mechanisms itself, only the POP3 command binding.
IMAP4 authentication mechanisms are reused, but IMAP itself is not specified or extended here.
Base64 is just the encoding for challenge/response lines, not a subject of the document.
Kerberos V4 appears only as an example mechanism in a sample exchange.
The generic topic is implied by the POP3 AUTH command. POP3 is the more specific tag.

RFC1735.title: NBMA Address Resolution Protocol (NARP)
RFC1735.summary: Experimental protocol (NARP) by which a host or router on an NBMA network queries NBMA ARP Servers to resolve the NBMA link-layer address of a destination across multiple logical IP subnets, with a request/reply format, forwarding and cache tables, and processing pseudocode.

NHRP.why: NARP is the direct precursor of NHRP: it resolves NBMA addresses across logical IP subnets via NBMA ARP Servers. NHRP is the taxonomy's tag for NBMA next-hop resolution, so this is the best fit.
NHRP.quote: NARP can be used by a source terminal (host or router) connected to a Non-Broadcast, Multi-Access link layer (NBMA) network to find out the NBMA addresses

ARP.why: The document defines an ARP-like address resolution protocol extending beyond a single subnet and compares it closely to ATMARP. Readers of ARP would want it.
ARP.quote: A conventional address resolution protocol, such as ARP [1, 2] for IP, may not be sufficient to resolve the NBMA address of the destination terminal

rejected.why: ATM is an example NBMA network and ATMARP is the model for the semantics, but the document is about generic NBMA resolution, not ATM itself. NHRP, which sits under ATM, is already tagged.
SMDS is mentioned only as an example connectionless NBMA network.
X.25 appears only as an example of a network that cannot broadcast.
NASs use ordinary routing protocols to build forwarding tables, but routing protocols are only a mechanism here, and the document does not specify them.
The packets use the standard IP checksum, which is only a field description.

RFC1736.title: Functional Recommendations for Internet Resource Locators
RFC1736.summary: RFC 1736 sets out minimum functional requirements for Internet resource locators (later URLs): transient, globally scoped, parsable, transcribable, a service plus opaque parameters, and extensible, kept distinct from naming and description.

URI.why: The whole document defines requirements for resource locators, a kind of resource identifier, which is the subject of URI. It covers locator syntax-level properties such as parsability, transcribability and the service plus parameter structure.
URI.quote: This document specifies a minimum set of requirements for Internet resource locators, which convey location and access information for resources.

rejected.why: Resource naming is discussed only to distinguish it from locators and is explicitly out of scope.
HTML anchors are mentioned only as an example environment where locators appear.
The document concerns locator format, not discovering services on a network.
WAIS, FTP, Gopher and Telnet appear only as examples of resource types.

RFC1737.title: Functional Requirements for Uniform Resource Names
RFC1737.summary: RFC 1737 specifies the minimum functional and encoding requirements for Uniform Resource Names (URNs), persistent globally unique resource identifiers, within the URI/URL/URC architecture.

URN.why: The whole document defines requirements for Uniform Resource Names: global scope, uniqueness, persistence, encoding, naming authorities. The URN page is the natural home.
URN.quote: The purpose or function of a URN is to provide a globally unique, persistent identifier used for recognition, for access to characteristics of the resource or for access to the resource itself.

rejected.why: URN is the more specific child tag and the document is about URNs; the URI parent is implied.
General naming parent is implied by URN, and the document is specific to URNs rather than naming in general.
Not mentioned; resolution is explicitly left out of scope.
Mentions central registration of top-level naming authorities only in passing; no registry is defined.

RFC1738.title: Uniform Resource Locators (URL)
RFC1738.summary: RFC 1738 specifies the generic syntax and semantics of Uniform Resource Locators, defines URL schemes for ftp, http, gopher, mailto, news, nntp, telnet, wais, file and prospero, and sets out how new schemes are registered.

URI.why: The whole document defines URL syntax, character encoding, specific schemes and scheme registration, which is the core of the URI subject.
URI.quote: This document specifies a Uniform Resource Locator (URL), the syntax and semantics of formalized information for location and access of resources via the Internet.

rejected.why: The ftp URL scheme is defined, but FTP itself is only the protocol the URL refers to. The document does not specify or extend FTP.
Only the syntax of http URLs is described. The document says 'The HTTP protocol is specified elsewhere'.
The gopher URL scheme gets a long section, but it only maps Gopher selectors into URLs. The Gopher protocol is not specified here.
URNs are mentioned only through the reference to RFC 1737. The document is about locators.
The IANA scheme registry is mentioned briefly in Section 4. The document is not about IANA considerations.
The BNF in Section 5 is only the notation used to define the URL syntax. It is not the subject of the document.

RFC1739.title: A Primer On Internet and TCP/IP Tools
RFC1739.summary: An informational beginner's primer showing how to use TCP/IP and Internet tools (nslookup, ping, finger, traceroute, FTP, Telnet, WHOIS, Knowbot, Netfind, Archie, Gopher, WWW, WAIS), plus discussion lists, Usenet and how to obtain RFCs.

user guides.why: The document is an introductory user guide (tutorial/lab manual) for Internet users, the FYI-style user guide subject.
user guides.quote: This memo is an introductory guide to some of the TCP/IP and Internet tools and utilities that allow users to access the wide variety of information on the network

traceroute.why: Has a dedicated section explaining the traceroute tool, its options and how it works with TTL, UDP and ICMP.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute is another common TCP/IP tool, this one allowing users to learn about the route that packets take from their local host to a remote host.

FTP.why: Substantial section with a worked anonymous FTP session and command explanations.
FTP.quote: FTP allows users to upload and download files between local and remote hosts.

Telnet.why: Dedicated section on using Telnet, including accessing other services by port number.
Telnet.quote: TELNET [17] is TCP/IP's virtual terminal protocol.

Finger.why: Dedicated section on the Finger tool with examples.
Finger.quote: The Finger program may be used to find out who is logged in on another system or to find out detailed information about a specific user.

Gopher.why: Dedicated section with session walkthrough of Gopher.
Gopher.quote: Gopher provides a tool so that publicly available information at a host can be organized in a hierarchical fashion

WHOIS.why: Dedicated section on WHOIS/NICNAME lookups, with related Knowbot and Netfind.
WHOIS.quote: WHOIS and NICNAME are TCP/IP applications that search databases to find the name of network and system administrators

WAIS.why: WAIS is described in a short subsection; covered as one of the information servers.
WAIS.quote: The Wide Area Information Server (WAIS, pronounced "ways") was initiated jointly by Apple Computer, Dow Jones

ICMP.why: Ping is covered in its own section as an ICMP-based tool.
ICMP.quote: Ping uses a series of Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Echo messages to determine if a remote host is active or inactive

rejected.why: NSLOOKUP is shown briefly, but the document defers DNS itself as beyond scope; it's a tool demo only.
Usenet is described at a user level in one section, not as the protocol/format.
Section 4 explains how to obtain RFCs, STDs and FYIs, but this is a minor part of the guide.
Section 2.9 lists URL formats briefly, deferring to RFC 1738.
WWW/Mosaic are only briefly described in the information servers section.
Discussion list subscription is covered at a user level, a minor section.

gaps.name: Archie
gaps.why: Archie file-location service has its own section but no taxonomy tag exists for it (nor for Knowbot/Netfind/Veronica).

RFC1740.title: MIME Encapsulation of Macintosh Files - MacMIME
RFC1740.summary: Defines how Macintosh files (AppleSingle/AppleDouble) are encapsulated in MIME using the application/applefile and multipart/appledouble media types.

MIME.why: The document defines new MIME body structures (multipart/appledouble) and a MIME type (application/applefile) for carrying Macintosh files, with transfer encoding advice.
MIME.quote: This memo describes the format to use when sending Apple Macintosh files via MIME [BORE93].

media types.why: It registers two media types, application/applefile and multipart/appledouble, with their parameters, encoding and security considerations.
media types.quote: MIME type-name:            APPLICATION MIME subtype name:         APPLEFILE

rejected.why: Email is only the transport context. The document is about the MIME body format, not mail architecture or transport.
Base64 is only recommended as a transfer encoding for the binary data. The document doesn't specify it.

gaps.name: AppleSingle/AppleDouble file format
gaps.why: The document summarises Apple's binary file encodings for Macintosh files (data and resource forks). The taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC1741.title: MIME Content Type for BinHex Encoded Files
RFC1741.summary: Registers the application/mac-binhex40 MIME content type for sending BinHex 4.0 encoded Macintosh files in email, recommending AppleSingle/AppleDouble instead where possible, and describes the BinHex 4.0 format in an appendix.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a MIME media type (application/mac-binhex40) with its name parameter and usage rules, which is the core subject of the RFC.
media types.quote: The content-type application/mac-binhex40 indicates that the body of the mail is a BinHex4.0 file.

rejected.why: The document leans on MIME heavily, but its contribution is a specific media type registration, so the more specific media types tag fits better.
The content is carried in Internet mail, but email is only the transport context, not the subject.
Mentioned only to say BinHex uses different characters and no transport encoding should be applied; the document is not about Base64.
The name parameter is restricted to seven-bit US-ASCII, but this is a passing detail.

gaps.name: BinHex 4.0 / MacMIME (Macintosh file encoding)
gaps.why: The document describes the BinHex 4.0 encoding of Macintosh data and resource forks and its relation to AppleSingle/AppleDouble. The taxonomy has no tag for these Macintosh file encoding formats.

RFC1742.title: AppleTalk Management Information Base II
RFC1742.summary: Defines the AppleTalk MIB II (SNMP managed objects) covering AppleTalk link, network, transport and session layer protocols, obsoleting RFC 1243.

AppleTalk.why: The whole document defines managed objects for the AppleTalk protocol suite (DDP, RTMP, ZIP, NBP, ATP, ASP, ADSP, PAP, AARP).
AppleTalk.quote: This memo defines additional objects that exist in the AppleTalk portion of the MIB. These objects provide for the management of the transport and session layers

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (APPLETALK-MIB) defined with the SMI, so readers of MIB modules want it.
MIB.quote: Section 5 contains the specification of all object types contained in this MIB module.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the document defines a MIB module, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag covers it.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB definitions.
AARP is AppleTalk's own address resolution protocol; counters for it are only one group of the MIB, and the tag is for IP's ARP.
Mentions of PAP printing are about AppleTalk's Printer Access Protocol, not the Internet Printing Protocol.

gaps.name: AppleTalk
gaps.why: The document is about AppleTalk, which is the AppleTalk protocol suite management. The taxonomy has an AppleTalk tag under internet layer, but I used it as given. Nothing else is missing.

RFC1743.title: IEEE 802.5 MIB using SMIv2
RFC1743.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module (TOKENRING-MIB) for managing IEEE 802.5 Token Ring interfaces: interface state, statistics, obsolete timers, test and chip-set identities, and conformance groups; obsoletes RFC 1231.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining tables, objects, and conformance groups for 802.5 interfaces, using SMIv2 and as an adjunct to the Interfaces MIB.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing subnetworks which use the IEEE 802.5 Token Ring technology

token ring.why: The subject matter is IEEE 802.5 Token Ring: ring state, active monitor, beaconing, and error statistics, so readers of token ring would want it.
token ring.quote: the 802.5 Interface Table, which contains state and parameter information which is specific to 802.5 interfaces

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is used with. The document defines a MIB module, not SNMP protocol behaviour, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
Implied by the MIB tag, which is the more specific one.

RFC1744.title: Observations on the Management of the Internet Address Space
RFC1744.summary: An informational memo analysing IPv4 address space management policies (first-come-first-served, free, once-and-for-all allocation), the likely outcomes of unallocated pool exhaustion including address trading, and the case for pricing/lease policies, with lessons for IPv6.

addressing.why: The whole document is about the allocation, registry management and policy of IP address space, which is the addressing topic.
addressing.quote: examines some of the issues associated with the current management practices of the Internet IPv4 address space

IPv4.why: The document concerns IPv4 address pool exhaustion and its lifecycle, a core aspect of the IPv4 tag's address lifecycle scope.
IPv4.quote: the IPv4 address space is now a visibly finite resource, and current projections, assuming a continuation of existing demand for addresses predict unallocated address space exhaustion

rejected.why: IPv6 is mentioned only in the conclusions as a successor whose address policy should learn from IPv4 experience; the document is not about IPv6.
Address translation is mentioned briefly as a market outcome of scarcity, not specified or analysed.
IANA is mentioned as the body that drafted allocation policy, but the document is not about IANA registries or stewardship specifically.
Aggregation and routing costs are touched on only in passing; CIDR is not discussed.
The document does touch on policy and who should administer address space, but it is focused on address allocation economics, better captured by addressing.

gaps.name: Internet address registry policy and economics (address allocation pricing, leasing, trading)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for address registry/RIR policy or the economics of address space; addressing is the closest fit, but the document's central subject of allocation policy and markets is not covered precisely.

RFC1745.title: BGP4/IDRP for IP---OSPF Interaction
RFC1745.summary: Specifies design criteria for an ASBR running BGP4 or IDRP for IP externally and OSPF as its IGP, covering route export/import, identifier matching, OSPF external tag encoding, and next-hop/forwarding address handling.

BGP.why: The document specifies how BGP4 attributes (ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, MULTI_EXIT_DISC, LOCAL_PREF) interact with OSPF at an ASBR, so it belongs on the BGP page.
BGP.quote: This memo defines the various criteria to be used when designing an Autonomous System Border Router (ASBR) that will run either BGP4 or IDRP for IP

OSPF.why: It defines the OSPF external route tag sub-fields, import cost/type rules and forwarding address handling, so it is equally about OSPF.
OSPF.quote: We use the external route tag field in OSPF to intelligently set the ORIGIN and PATH attributes in BGP/IDRP.
OSPF.section: 4. Setting OSPF tags, ORIGIN and PATH attributes

rejected.why: The document covers a specific protocol interaction, not general routing architecture, and BGP and OSPF tags already sit under routing.
EGP is mentioned only for the ORIGIN value and the indirect neighbour concept, not specified or analysed.
IDRP (ISO 10747) is referenced alongside BGP, but there is no OSI or CLNP tag fitting IDRP, and the document is not about OSI network-layer protocols themselves.
RIP appears only in the bibliography.

gaps.name: IDRP (Inter-Domain Routing Protocol, ISO 10747)
gaps.why: The document treats IDRP for IP as a co-equal protocol with BGP, but the taxonomy has no IDRP tag, since the IDPR tag covers a different protocol (Inter-Domain Policy Routing).

RFC1746.title: Ways to Define User Expectations
RFC1746.summary: Informational memo on how to define acceptable use policies (user agreements) for network providers and sites, with a reprinted K-12 CoVis network use policy as an example.

user guides.why: The document is an introductory guide for Internet users and providers on writing acceptable use policies, which is closest to the user guides/FYI-style subject. The taxonomy has no AUP-specific tag.
user guides.quote: This paper covers basic fundamentals that must be understood when one defines, interprets, or implements methods to control user expectations on or over the Internet.

rejected.why: The memo discusses policy and user behaviour, not operational security practices for infrastructure; security and liability are explicitly not discussed.
Privacy is one item among many policy considerations and in the CoVis policy, but the document is not about protocol privacy threat models.
Gopher is only mentioned as an archive location and as a tool in the sample policy.
Email is mentioned as a service covered by the sample policy, not a subject of the document.
The memo concerns local provider/site policy, not governance of the Internet or standards.

gaps.name: Acceptable use policy (AUP)
gaps.why: The whole document is about defining acceptable use policies and user agreements, including a school network use policy; the taxonomy has no tag for AUPs or network usage policy.

RFC1747.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for SNA Data Link Control (SDLC) using SMIv2
RFC1747.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module for configuring, monitoring and controlling SNA SDLC ports and link stations, including interface-group mapping, statistics tables, traps and compliance statements.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SNA-SDLC-MIB) defining managed objects using SMIv2, with tables, traps and compliance groups.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of data link controls in an SNA environment.

SNA.why: The managed subject is SDLC links in an SNA environment: ports, link stations, XID, primary/secondary roles. SNA is the nearest fitting tag for SDLC.
SNA.quote: This draft identifies managed objects for SNA Synchronous Data Link Control (SDLC) links only.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is built for; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Not relevant; only the interfaces-group ifType mapping is discussed, which is not about another link technology.
The document explicitly leaves higher-layer SNA entities (PU/LU) to the SNA NAU MIB and is not about APPN.
Not about DLSw encapsulation; it only models SDLC links.

gaps.name: SDLC (Synchronous Data Link Control)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for SDLC or a general serial data-link protocol. SNA is used as the closest fit, though SDLC is the specific subject.

RFC1748.title: IEEE 802.5 MIB using SMIv2
RFC1748.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module (TOKENRING-MIB) for managing IEEE 802.5 Token Ring interfaces: interface state, statistics, obsolete timers, test and chip-set identifiers; obsoletes RFC 1231 and 1743.

token ring.why: The MIB exists solely to manage IEEE 802.5 Token Ring interfaces, so readers of the token ring subject would expect it.
token ring.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing subnetworks which use the IEEE 802.5 Token Ring technology

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMIv2, with object groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines three tables: the 802.5 Interface Table, which contains state and parameter information which is specific to 802.5 interfaces

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is defined for, but the document does not specify or extend the protocol. MIB is the more specific tag.
Another link-layer MIB subject, but this document covers Token Ring and has no Ethernet content.
The MIB is written in ASN.1-based SMI, but the document only uses it as notation and does not specify ASN.1.

RFC1749.title: IEEE 802.5 Station Source Routing MIB using SMIv2
RFC1749.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module (TOKENRING-STATION-SR-MIB) with a single table for managing IEEE 802.5 source routes (RIF database) in Token Ring end-stations, as an incremental update to RFC 1748.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (dot5SrMIB) with managed objects in SMIv2, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a single table: the 802.5 Station Source Routing Table, which contains the source routes known by a end-station

token ring.why: The subject is IEEE 802.5 Token Ring source routing (RIF, ring and bridge numbers), a token ring link-layer feature.
token ring.quote: managed objects used by IEEE 802.5 end-stations for managing source routes on a Token Ring network where IEEE source-routing is in use

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is only the management framework the MIB is written for; the document defines no new protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is used only as the notation for SMI definitions, not the subject.
Covered by the more specific token ring tag.

RFC1750.title: Randomness Recommendations for Security
RFC1750.summary: RFC 1750 is an informational guide explaining why traditional pseudo-random generators are inadequate for security, recommending hardware randomness sources, mixing functions and cryptographically strong sequences, and estimating the random bits needed for passwords and keys.

randomness.why: The whole document concerns generating unguessable random quantities for security: entropy sources, de-skewing, mixing functions, strong sequences and required bit counts.
randomness.quote: This paper points out many pitfalls in using traditional pseudo-random number generation techniques for choosing such quantities. It recommends the use of truly random hardware techniques

rejected.why: Key generation is discussed, but only as the randomness needed for keys, not key establishment, provisioning or storage.
DES is used as an example mixing function and in the DoD and X9.17 generators, but it is a tool here, not the subject.
MD2/MD4/MD5 and SHS are mentioned as candidate mixing functions only.
The parent topic is implied by the randomness tag, which is the more specific fit.
Password generation is discussed in terms of entropy, but this is not about one-time password systems.
SHS is only mentioned as one option for mixing inputs.

RFC1751.title: A Convention for Human-Readable 128-bit Keys
RFC1751.summary: Informational RFC defining a convention for encoding 128-bit cryptographic keys as twelve short English words, reusing the S/Key 2048-word dictionary, with reference C code.

key management.why: The document defines how 128-bit keys are represented in human-readable form so people can read, remember and enter them. This is key representation and handling, which fits key management.
key management.quote: This memo proposes a convention for use with Internet applications & protocols using 128-bit cryptographic keys.

OTP.why: The convention is built directly on S/Key's word encoding, and the reference code is the S/Key routines. Readers of one-time password systems would want it.
OTP.quote: The S/Key(tm) one-time password system [Hal94] uses MD4 (and now MD5, as well) to compute one-time passwords.

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is only cited as motivation for the 128-bit key requirement. The document does not specify or extend it.
MD5 is mentioned as the keyed digest that needs 128-bit keys. The document is not about the algorithm.
The dictionary uses the invariant subset of ISO-646, but the document is not about character encoding.
This is a word-based textual encoding of binary data, not Base64/32/16. It is the closest category, but it is not a match.

gaps.name: Human-readable key encoding (S/Key word list)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is encoding binary keys as English words. The taxonomy has no tag for human-friendly binary-to-text encodings.

RFC1752.title: The Recommendation for the IP Next Generation Protocol
RFC1752.summary: The IPng Area Directors' recommendation that SIPP (128-bit version) become IPv6, covering the selection process, evaluation of CATNIP, SIPP and TUBA, an IPv6 overview, and recommendations for working groups on autoconfiguration, transition, and security.

IPv6.why: The document recommends and overviews IPv6, including header format, extension headers, addressing and autoconfiguration.
IPv6.quote: The protocol itself will be called IPv6.

IPng.why: It reviews the historic IPng candidates (CATNIP/TP/IX, SIPP, TUBA) and their evaluation against the criteria.
IPng.quote: The IPng Area evaluated three IPng proposals as they were described in their RFC 1550 white papers: CATNIP [McGovern94] , SIPP [Hinden94a] and TUBA.

IPv6 transition.why: A full section recommends the NGTRANS and TACIT working groups and describes short- and long-term transition needs.
IPv6 transition.quote: The transition of the Internet from IPv4 to IPv6 has to meet two separate needs.

IPsec.why: The Authentication and Privacy headers, forerunners of AH/ESP, are described and their support is recommended as mandatory.
IPsec.quote: We recommend that support for the Authentication Header be required in all compliant IPv6 implementations.

SLAAC.why: Recommends an Address Autoconfiguration working group and discusses plug-and-play address autoconfiguration.
SLAAC.quote: design and specify a protocol for allocating addresses dynamically to IPv6 hosts.

CIDR.why: Address exhaustion projections, routing table growth and CIDR-based assignment policy are discussed substantively.
CIDR.quote: The ALE Working Group recommends that we consider assigning CIDR-type address blocks out of the unassigned Class A address space.

rejected.why: CLNP appears as the basis of TUBA and is critiqued, but the document is not about CLNP itself.
IPv4 address exhaustion is the motivation, but the document's subject is its successor.
It describes the IESG/IPng Area process, but the subject is a technical protocol recommendation.
Nimrod is mentioned only as excluded from consideration as a research project.
The sockets API is only briefly recommended for an informational RFC.
A firewall framework is recommended in a brief aside in security considerations.

RFC1753.title: IPng Technical Requirements Of the Nimrod Routing and Addressing Architecture
RFC1753.summary: Nimrod author's statement of the requirements that the Nimrod routing and addressing architecture places on the IPng internetwork-layer protocol, covering packet fields (EIDs, locators, flow-ids, source routes) and architectural issues like flows and state.

Nimrod.why: The whole document derives IPng requirements from the Nimrod architecture: forwarding modes, locators, EIDs, flow-ids and source routes.
Nimrod.quote: the requirements that the Nimrod routing and addressing architecture has upon the internetwork layer protocol

IPng.why: Submitted to the IPng area in response to RFC 1550. It sets out the packet format and internetwork-layer requirements for the next-generation IP.
IPng.quote: any protocol selected as the IPng should satisfy these requirements

internet architecture.why: Section 3 discusses architectural principles: modularization, the service model, state in routers versus packets, and flows.
internet architecture.quote: sees the entire internetwork layer, distributed across all the hosts and routers of the internetwork, as a single system

rejected.why: Nimrod is the more specific tag and already sits under routing, so the parent is implied.
Multihoming is only one item in the list of wants in 3.3, not a main subject.
Resource allocation is mentioned as a related subsystem, but the document is not about QoS.
IPv6 is not specified or analysed. The document only mentions IPng candidates generally, and IPng is the more specific tag.
DNS is mentioned once in passing, as a possible name translation system.

RFC1754.title: IP over ATM Working Group's Recommendations for the ATM Forum's Multiprotocol BOF Version 1
RFC1754.summary: IETF IP over ATM Working Group's list of requirements submitted to the ATM Forum's Multiprotocol BOF, covering IP encapsulation over ATM, routing, signaling, multicast, security and QoS/traffic management.

ATM.why: The whole memo lists IETF requirements for operating IP over ATM networks (encapsulation, signaling, addressing, QoS), so it belongs on the ATM and IP over ATM page.
ATM.quote: The IP over ATM Working Group will focus on the issues involved in running internetworking protocols over Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) networks.

rejected.why: NHRP is mentioned only in passing as work by another working group, and the memo does not specify or analyse it.
Section 4.7 gives ATM traffic-management and service-class requirements, but they are ATM-specific and a small part of the memo. The ATM tag covers them.
IPv6 is mentioned briefly, as future requirements on the Flow ID field and NSAP embedding, and is not a main subject.
Section 4.5 is a short placeholder noting that multicast mapping work is preliminary and that requirements will come later.
Section 4.1 covers liaison logistics with the ATM Forum, but the memo is not about the IETF process itself.

RFC1755.title: ATM Signaling Support for IP over ATM
RFC1755.summary: RFC 1755 specifies how ATM UNI 3.1 call-control signaling (SETUP message information elements, VC management, failure handling) is used to support Classical IP over ATM (RFC 1577) with RFC 1483 AAL5 encapsulation.

ATM.why: The whole document defines how IP over ATM endsystems use ATM UNI signaling: VCC establishment, teardown, AAL5 parameters, B-LLI, traffic descriptor and bearer capability coding.
ATM.quote: This memo describes the ATM call control signaling exchanges needed to support Classical IP over ATM implementations as described in RFC 1577

rejected.why: ATMARP/InARP is mentioned as it relates to VC sharing, but address resolution is explicitly out of scope.
Appendix D covers FR-SSCS interworking, but it is a minor appendix and the document is about IP over ATM signaling, not frame relay.
Traffic descriptor and QoS class coding are signaling parameters within ATM, not a QoS architecture.
IP is only the payload carried over the ATM connections; the document does not specify IP itself.

RFC1756.title: Remote Write Protocol - Version 1.0
RFC1756.summary: Defines the experimental Remote Write Protocol (RWP) 1.0, an SMTP-like text protocol over TCP or UDP port 18 for relaying short interactive messages to a logged-in user's terminal, like write(1) across the network.

instant messaging.why: RWP delivers short, immediate messages to users who are currently logged in. That is lightweight real-time messaging, closer to instant messaging than to store-and-forward email.
instant messaging.quote: RWP is a simple protocol that can be used to relay short messages through the network to other users.

rejected.why: RWP is modelled on SMTP's command and response style but is a separate protocol. It doesn't specify or extend SMTP.
The document positions RWP as lighter than email. It has no mail storage, mailboxes or mail formats.
TCP is only the transport, along with UDP for broadcast. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP is only an alternative transport for broadcast messages. Nothing new is defined about UDP itself.
The quoting scheme is merely similar to quoted-printable. The document doesn't define or use MIME.

RFC1757.title: Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base
RFC1757.summary: RFC 1757 defines the RMON MIB, a set of SNMP managed objects (statistics, history, alarms, hosts, matrix, filters, packet capture, events) for configuring and retrieving data from remote network monitoring probes, obsoleting RFC 1271.

RMON.why: The document is the RMON MIB specification itself, defining the groups, tables and control conventions for remote monitoring probes.
RMON.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing remote network monitoring devices.

MIB.why: It is a MIB module written in SMI (OBJECT-TYPE, TRAP-TYPE, textual conventions OwnerString and EntryStatus with row-creation semantics), so MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol and substrate for these objects; the document defines MIB objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour.
The Ethernet statistics and history groups are counters for Ethernet segments, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet interworking.
The filter and capture groups define MIB objects for probes to capture packets, but the document is not about capture file formats or tooling.
The document includes traffic statistics and utilization, but it is a monitoring MIB rather than a performance metrics or methodology specification.
ASN.1 is only the notation used by the SMI for object syntax.

RFC1758.title: NADF Standing Documents: A Brief Overview
RFC1758.summary: Informational overview of the North American Directory Forum's Standing Document series (SD-0 to SD-13), which define agreements for a cooperative public X.500 directory service across competing providers.

X.500.why: The whole document summarizes NADF's agreements for deploying a public X.500 directory service (DIT naming, schema, DMD mapping, security, accounting), so X.500 readers would want it.
X.500.quote: plans to cooperatively offer a Public Directory Service in North America using the CCITT X.500 Recommendations

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which fits more specifically; ancestors are implied.
SD-10 and SD-11 on security and privacy are only briefly described; the memo itself says security issues are not discussed.
SD-5 and SD-6 cover X.500 DIT naming, but this is X.500 naming, not general name resolution or DNS.
LDAP is not mentioned; the document concerns X.500 service agreements.

RFC1759.title: Printer MIB
RFC1759.summary: Defines the Printer MIB, an SNMP MIB module (mib-2 43) for managing printers, with a printer sub-unit model (inputs, outputs, markers, media paths, channels, interpreters, console, alerts), objects, conformance groups and enumerations.

MIB.why: The document specifies a MIB module in SMIv2 for printer management, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: The MIB module for management of printers.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with; the document defines objects, not protocol changes. MIB is the more specific fit.
LPD appears only as one enumerated channel type among many.
CodedCharSet textual convention defers to the IANA character-set registry; this is a minor part.
FTP appears only as a channel type enumeration value.
Enumeration registration through IANA is minor procedural apparatus.

gaps.name: Printer management / printing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for printer device management; only IPP and LPD exist, which are printing protocols, not printer MIBs.

RFC1760.title: The S/KEY One-Time Password System
RFC1760.summary: Informational RFC describing Bellcore's S/KEY one-time password system, which derives single-use passwords from a pass-phrase via repeated MD4 hashing, encodes them as six words, and verifies them host-side to defeat replay attacks.

OTP.why: The whole document specifies the S/KEY one-time password system: generation, word encoding, challenge format and host verification.
OTP.quote: The S/KEY One-Time Password system is designed to counter this type of attack, called a replay attack.

MD5.why: A substantial section defines the folded MD4 hash used as the core function and discusses MD4 vs MD5 choice; the MD5 tag covers the MD2/MD4/MD5 digests.
MD5.quote: The S/KEY system is based on the MD4 Message Digest algorithm designed by Ronald Rivest [2].

rejected.why: OTP is the more specific child; the document is about one-time passwords, so the parent is implied.
Only mentioned as how the reference implementation is distributed; not a subject of the document.
The system uses a plain folded hash chain, not a keyed MAC.
Login over the network is the motivating context, but the document does not specify or discuss the Telnet protocol.

RFC1761.title: Snoop Version 2 Packet Capture File Format
RFC1761.summary: Describes the snoop version 2 packet capture file format (file header, packet records, datalink type codes) so others can write compatible tools.

packet capture.why: The whole document specifies a packet capture file format, which is exactly the subject of the packet capture tag.
packet capture.quote: This paper describes the file format used by "snoop", a packet monitoring and capture program developed by Sun.

rejected.why: Ethernet is only one of the datalink types in the code table. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
FDDI appears only as a datalink type code in the table.
Token Ring is only a datalink type code in the table.
ASCII is mentioned only to explain the identification pattern bytes.

RFC1762.title: The PPP DECnet Phase IV Control Protocol (DNCP)
RFC1762.summary: Defines DNCP, the PPP Network Control Protocol for configuring and carrying DECnet Phase IV Routing packets over PPP links, including encapsulation, protocol field values and routing timer recommendations.

DECnet.why: The document specifies how DECnet Phase IV routing is carried and configured over PPP, which is exactly the DECnet-over-IP-infrastructure subject.
DECnet.quote: This document defines the NCP for establishing and configuring Digital's DNA Phase IV Routing protocol (DECnet Phase IV) over PPP.

PPP.why: It defines a new PPP Network Control Protocol (DNCP), with its protocol field values, code usage and encapsulation, so PPP readers need it.
PPP.quote: The DNA Phase IV Routing Control Protocol is exactly the same as the Link Control Protocol [1] with the following exceptions:
PPP.section: 3. A PPP Network Control Protocol for DNA Phase IV Routing

rejected.why: The 'DNA Naming Service (DNS)' mentioned in the overview is a DECnet service, not the Domain Name System, and is out of scope of the document.
The document touches Phase IV routing timers, but only as parameters for running DECnet routing over PPP, not as routing subject matter in its own right.
DNA Time Service is only listed in the overview of data link clients and is not addressed.

RFC1763.title: The PPP Banyan Vines Control Protocol (BVCP)
RFC1763.summary: Defines BVCP, the PPP Network Control Protocol for configuring Banyan VINES over point-to-point links, including its four configuration options.

PPP.why: The document specifies a PPP NCP (BVCP), with its packet encapsulation, protocol field values and configuration options. PPP is the protocol being extended.
PPP.quote: This document defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring the Banyan VINES protocol over PPP.

rejected.why: VINES ARP is mentioned only in passing as supported over BVCP; the document does not specify it.
The more specific PPP tag covers it, so the parent is not listed.

gaps.name: Banyan VINES
gaps.why: The document is about configuring the VINES network protocol over PPP, but the taxonomy has no tag for VINES. This is a proprietary network-layer protocol family, similar to the existing IPX, DECnet and AppleTalk tags.

RFC1764.title: The PPP XNS IDP Control Protocol (XNSCP)
RFC1764.summary: Defines XNSCP, the PPP Network Control Protocol that configures and enables XNS IDP datagram transport over point-to-point links, including protocol field values and MTU requirements.

PPP.why: The RFC specifies a PPP control protocol (XNSCP), including its PPP Protocol field values, code usage and datagram encapsulation. Readers of the PPP subject would want it.
PPP.quote: This document defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring the Xerox Network Systems (XNS) Internet Datagram Protocol (IDP) over PPP.

rejected.why: XNS IDP is not an OSI network-layer protocol and the document does not discuss OSI coexistence.
IPX derives from XNS, but the document does not mention or interwork with it.
The more specific PPP tag covers it, so the parent is not listed.
The document concerns XNS IDP as a network-layer protocol carried over PPP, not IP-layer matters, so it is not an internet layer topic.

gaps.name: XNS (Xerox Network Systems) IDP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the XNS protocol suite, which this document configures over PPP.

RFC1765.title: OSPF Database Overflow
RFC1765.summary: Experimental OSPF extension defining a mechanism (OverflowState, ospfExtLsdbLimit, ospfExitOverflowInterval) to gracefully handle link-state database overflow by limiting non-default AS-external-LSAs.

OSPF.why: The whole document specifies modifications to OSPF flooding and LSA origination to handle link-state database overflow.
OSPF.quote: This memo details a way of gracefully handling unanticipated database overflows.

rejected.why: The appendix lists related OSPF MIB parameters and traps, but only as support for the mechanism; the MIB itself is defined elsewhere.
SNMP traps and network management configuration are mentioned only as the means of setting parameters and signalling overflow.
The document concerns OSPF version 2 only, not OSPF for IPv6.

RFC1766.title: Tags for the Identification of Languages
RFC1766.summary: RFC 1766 defines the language tag syntax and IANA registration procedure for identifying human languages, the Content-Language header for MIME parts and web documents, and a "differences" parameter for multipart/alternative.

language tags.why: The core of the document is the language tag syntax, its ISO 639/3166 basis, and its IANA registration procedure.
language tags.quote: This document describes a language tag for use in cases where it is desired to indicate the language used in an information object.

MIME.why: It defines the Content-Language header for MIME body parts and a new differences parameter on multipart/alternative, so MIME readers would want it.
MIME.quote: a new parameter to the Multipart/Alternative type, to aid in the usage of the Content-Language: header.

rejected.why: Content-Language is an RFC-822-style header, but the document is about language labelling and not the message format itself.
Web documents are mentioned as a possible use of the header, but HTTP is not specified or extended here.
The registration procedure is part of the language tag mechanism and is not about IANA registries in general.
The more specific language tags tag fits, so the parent is not chosen.

RFC1767.title: MIME Encapsulation of EDI Objects
RFC1767.summary: Defines three MIME application content-types (EDIFACT, EDI-X12, EDI-consent) for encapsulating EDI interchanges in Internet email.

EDI.why: The document exists to carry EDI interchanges (X12, EDIFACT, other) over Internet email, defining the MIME types for them.
EDI.quote: This specification permits formatted electronic business interchanges to be encapsulated within MIME messages

media types.why: It registers three new application/* media types with required/optional parameters and encoding considerations.
media types.quote: MIME subtype name:               EDIFACT

rejected.why: MIME is the encapsulation substrate; the document defines new subtypes (covered by media types) rather than changing MIME itself.
Only mentioned in the appendix as the transport; not specified or extended.
Email is the delivery mechanism; the subject is EDI content types, and EDI is the more specific tag.
RFC 822 headers appear only in an example and in the appendix's background.

RFC1768.title: Host Group Extensions for CLNP Multicasting
RFC1768.summary: Experimental TUBA-era specification of multicast extensions to CLNP (group Network addresses, multicast data PDU, scope control) and to the ES-IS protocol (multicast announcement and address mapping), analogous to RFC 1112 for IP.

CLNP.why: The document extends CLNP with group Network addresses, a Multicast Data PDU type and scope control parameters.
CLNP.quote: This memo describes multicast extensions to CLNP and its related routing protocols for Internet multicast use.

multicast.why: Host group membership and announcement for multicast is the core subject, a CLNP counterpart to RFC 1112 and IGMP.
multicast.quote: CLNP multicasting is the transmission of a CLNP datagram to a "host group", a set of zero or more End Systems identified by a single group Network address

IPng.why: The document is a TUBA work product, one of the historic IPng candidates, which uses CLNP as its network layer.
IPng.quote: This memo documents work performed in the TUBA (TCP/UDP over Bigger Addresses) working group of IPng area

rejected.why: IGMP is only compared against in Appendix A. The document defines ES-IS extensions instead.
The parent of CLNP, so it is implied by the CLNP tag.
IP multicast per RFC 1112 is only a comparison point.
Group NSAP/AFI addressing is a substantial part of the document, but it is OSI-specific and CLNP covers it.

gaps.name: ES-IS (ISO 9542) End System to Intermediate System routeing protocol
gaps.why: A large part of the document extends ES-IS, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC1769.title: Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP)
RFC1769.summary: RFC 1769 describes SNTP, a simplified subset of NTP for clock synchronization in unicast, broadcast and multicast modes, with client and server operation rules and message field settings.

NTP.why: The document specifies SNTP, a simplified access strategy for NTP, covering message format, timestamps, and client/server behaviour.
NTP.quote: This memorandum describes the Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP), which is an adaptation of the Network Time Protocol (NTP) used to synchronize computer clocks in the Internet.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport on port 123; nothing new is defined about UDP.
IP multicast group 224.0.1.1 is mentioned as an addressing mode, but IGMP and routing are explicitly out of scope.
MD5 authentication is mentioned only as an NTP convention that SNTP ignores.
Parent of NTP, implied by the NTP tag.

RFC1770.title: IPv4 Option for Sender Directed Multi-Destination Delivery
RFC1770.summary: Defines an IPv4 option (Selective Directed Broadcast Mode) that lets a sender list up to nine destination IP addresses in a datagram's options field for unreliable UDP multi-destination delivery over directed broadcasts, motivated by tactical military networks.

IPv4.why: The document specifies a new IPv4 header option (type 149, variable length, copy flag set) and the host and router procedures for it, so it belongs on the IPv4 page.
IPv4.quote: This memo defines an IPv4 option to provide a sender directed multi-destination delivery mechanism called Selective Directed Broadcast Mode (SDBM).

rejected.why: SDBM delivers to an explicit list of addresses via directed broadcast and needs no group membership or multicast routing. It is an alternative to multicast, not multicast itself.
The document restricts SDBM to UDP traffic but defines nothing new about UDP. UDP is only the transport it carries.
Directed broadcast addresses and IP address lists are used, but the document is about an option format and its delivery procedure, not address architecture or allocation.
TCP is mentioned only to explain why SDBM cannot be used with it.

RFC1771.title: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)
RFC1771.summary: RFC 1771 specifies BGP-4, the inter-autonomous-system routing protocol, covering message formats, path attributes, error handling, the finite state machine, the decision process, route aggregation and CIDR support.

BGP.why: The whole document is the BGP-4 protocol specification: messages, path attributes, FSM, decision process and error handling.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol.

rejected.why: BGP only uses TCP as its transport (port 179); the document does not specify or extend TCP.
BGP-4 adds prefix advertisement and aggregation to support CIDR, but this is a feature of BGP, which is the document's subject; CIDR itself is specified in other RFCs.
The document specifies a protocol, not general routing architecture; the BGP tag covers it.
EGP is mentioned only as historical background and as an ORIGIN value; the document does not specify it.

RFC1772.title: Application of the Border Gateway Protocol in the Internet
RFC1772.summary: RFC 1772 describes how BGP-4 is applied in the Internet: topology model, route aggregation requirements, policy and path selection, interaction with EGP2/BGP-3 and IGPs, and operation over switched virtual circuits.

BGP.why: The whole document is about the application and usage of BGP-4: policy, path selection, aggregation, IGP interaction and migration from EGP/BGP-3.
BGP.quote: This memo describes the use of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) [1] in the Internet environment.

rejected.why: CIDR motivates BGP-4 aggregation and is referenced, but the document is about BGP usage, not CIDR itself.
EGP2 interaction is covered in one subsection as a migration guideline; the document is not about EGP.
TCP is only the substrate; Section 9 mentions a small TCP modification for circuit manager notifications but the topic is BGP operation.
Switched virtual circuits are discussed generically in Section 9, not IP over ATM specifically.

RFC1773.title: Experience with the BGP-4 protocol
RFC1773.summary: Informational report documenting how BGP-4 satisfies the IAB/IESG Draft Standard requirements, covering implementations, operational experience, CIDR migration, metrics (MED, LOCAL-PREF), IBGP scaling and route dynamics.

BGP.why: The whole document reports implementation and operational experience with BGP-4, including metrics, migration and internal BGP scaling.
BGP.quote: The purpose of this memo is to document how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard have been satisfied by Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4).

rejected.why: The migration to classless BGP-4 is discussed, but the document is about BGP experience, not CIDR itself.
Route reflectors are only mentioned as an effort underway to ease the IBGP full mesh, not specified or analysed.
The BGP-4 MIB is only briefly described, with a reference to its own RFC.
BGP runs over TCP, which is only the substrate.
EGP is mentioned only as a comparison point for bandwidth and CPU use.

RFC1774.title: BGP-4 Protocol Analysis
RFC1774.summary: Informational analysis of BGP-4 documenting how it meets Draft Standard requirements, summarizing key features and analysing bandwidth, CPU, memory scaling and applicability.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses BGP-4's features, performance, scalability and applicability.
BGP.quote: BGP-4 is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol designed for TCP/IP internets.

rejected.why: CIDR is mentioned as enabling BGP-4 aggregation, but the document is about BGP, not CIDR itself.
TCP is only the transport BGP uses.
EGP is only compared against BGP as a predecessor; not the subject.
Scaling discussion concerns BGP specifically, so the BGP tag covers it.
Mentioned only for coexistence with BGP-carried routes.

RFC1775.title: To Be "On" the Internet
RFC1775.summary: Informational memo defining four terms (Full, Client, Mediated, Messaging access) to distinguish levels of user and provider attachment to the Internet.

terminology.why: The document exists to define a nomenclature for classes of Internet access. It is a glossary-style definition of terms.
terminology.quote: it is appropriate to provide terminology that distinguishes among the range, so that the Internet community can gain some clarity when distinguishing whether a user

rejected.why: The memo gives user-oriented labels for access types. It does not set out architectural principles.
Email and netnews appear only in the definition of Messaging access, which is one of four categories.
The ICMP Echo (ping) facility is mentioned only as a way of detecting machines, so ICMP is not a subject of the memo.
Firewalls are mentioned in the sample usage to show how access is constrained. The memo does not cover firewall mechanisms.
TCP/IP is mentioned as the defining protocol for Full access. The memo does not specify or analyse it.
SLIP and PPP are mentioned only as examples of Client access.

RFC1776.title: The Address is the Message
RFC1776.summary: An April 1st humor RFC joking that the IPng working group chose a packet format made entirely of 1696 bytes of address space, with no content, so the address is the message.

humor.why: This is an April 1st parody RFC, dated 1 April 1995, that satirises IP address space and the IPng selection process.
humor.quote: Declaring that the address is the message, the IPng WG has selected a packet format which includes 1696 bytes of address space.

IPng.why: The joke is about the IPng working group's choice of next-generation IP addressing. It is satire, not a specification, but readers browsing IPng would expect to find it.
IPng.quote: the IPng focused on choosing an addressing scheme that makes it possible to talk to everyone while dispensing with the irrelevant overhead

rejected.why: ATM is mentioned only as a joke, that 1696 is a multiple of 53 and so fits ATM cells. The document is not about ATM.
The document is a parody of address space size, not a real treatment of IP address architecture. The IPng tag already covers the subject.
IPv6 is never named. The document refers only to the IPng WG, and the joke is not a statement about IPv6 itself.

RFC1777.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol
RFC1777.summary: RFC 1777 specifies LDAP version 2, a lightweight protocol for accessing the X.500 Directory. It defines the operations (bind, search, modify, add, delete, modify RDN, compare, abandon), their ASN.1 definitions, the TCP mapping and the restricted BER encoding.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies the LDAP protocol: its message envelope, operations, result codes and encodings.
LDAP.quote: The protocol described in this document is designed to provide access to the X.500 Directory while not incurring the resource requirements of the Directory Access Protocol (DAP).

rejected.why: X.500 is the directory that LDAP gives access to. The document specifies the LDAP front end, not X.500 itself, so it is a substrate here.
ASN.1 and BER are used to define and encode the protocol. The document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject in their own right.
Kerberos v4 is offered only as one of the Bind authentication options. The document does not specify Kerberos.
TCP is only the transport the protocol is mapped onto (port 389), with no new TCP behaviour defined.
This is the parent of LDAP and X.500. The more specific LDAP tag already covers it.

RFC1778.title: The String Representation of Standard Attribute Syntaxes
RFC1778.summary: RFC 1778 defines string encodings for the standard X.500 attribute syntaxes so their values can be carried as octet strings in LDAP, obsoleting RFC 1488.

LDAP.why: The document specifies how attribute syntax values are rendered as strings for use in LDAP. Its encoding rules are an LDAP schema/syntax specification, so LDAP readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) [9] requires that the contents of AttributeValue fields in protocol elements be octet strings.

X.500.why: The attribute syntaxes being encoded come from the X.500 Directory (X.520, COSINE schema). The document gives string forms for them, which is relevant to X.500 readers.
X.500.quote: defines the requirements that must be satisfied by encoding rules used to render X.500 Directory attribute syntaxes into a form suitable for use in the LDAP

rejected.why: BER is mentioned only for the Undefined syntax. The document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
Certificate and CRL string encodings appear as attribute syntaxes. The document does not profile X.509 itself.
BNF is just the notation used to define the encodings. The document is not about the notation.
The facsimile telephone number and Fax photo syntaxes are directory attribute encodings, not fax transport.

RFC1779.title: A String Representation of Distinguished Names
RFC1779.summary: RFC 1779 defines a user-oriented string representation for X.500 Distinguished Names, with a BNF grammar, keyword table, escape mechanisms and examples, for use outside directory protocols (e.g., in email or on business cards).

X.500.why: The whole document specifies how X.500 Distinguished Names, the primary keys of the directory, are written as strings; readers of X.500 and directory naming would look for it.
X.500.quote: Many OSI Applications make use of Distinguished Names (DN) as defined in the OSI Directory, commonly known as X.500

rejected.why: LDAP is only referenced as a source of attribute syntaxes. The string format was later reused by LDAP, but the document does not specify or extend LDAP.
The document uses an RFC 822-style BNF grammar only to define its own syntax. It is not about the notation.
ASN.1 and BER appear only in the escape mechanism for hex values. The document is not about ASN.1 encoding.
The parent is implied by X.500, and the more specific child tag already fits.
This is directory distinguished naming, not name resolution in general. X.500 is the more specific fit.
Email is only mentioned as a place where DNs might be written. The document does not define message formats.

gaps.name: Distinguished Name string representation / User Friendly Naming
gaps.why: The document is about a string syntax for directory names (also used by LDAP). The taxonomy has no tag for directory name syntax apart from X.500.

RFC1780.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1780.summary: RFC 1780 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly Internet Official Protocol Standards memo, explaining the standards process, maturity and requirement levels, and listing every protocol by standardization state.

IETF process.why: The memo's main body explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels, and the RFC processing decision table, which is IETF standards process content.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A section describes the RFC series, its submission rules, and how to obtain RFCs. It also says which RFC is the current specification for each protocol.
RFC series.quote: The documents called Request for Comments (or RFCs) are the working notes of the "Network Working Group"

terminology.why: It defines the vocabulary of protocol state and requirement level (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Required, Elective and so on) used throughout the memo.
terminology.quote: There are two independent categorization of protocols. The first is the "maturity level" or STATE of standardization

rejected.why: IANA appears as a contact and as the manager of the standards list, and Assigned Numbers is referenced. The memo is not about IANA registries.
It is a historical snapshot of protocol status. It is not a retrospective, and its purpose is current status.
BGP-4 and its RFCs are one item among hundreds in the lists. The memo does not specify or analyse BGP.
TCP is only one entry in the protocol lists and in the MIL-STD discussion.

gaps.name: Internet standards status listing / protocol index
gaps.why: The document is a catalogue of the status of all Internet protocol standards. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol status or a standards index beyond the IETF process tag.

RFC1781.title: Using the OSI Directory to Achieve User Friendly Naming
RFC1781.summary: RFC 1781 specifies a user-friendly notation (UFN) for X.500/OSI Directory distinguished names and a default algorithm for resolving purported names against the Directory, for human-to-human communication and user input.

X.500.why: The whole document defines a naming notation and a matching algorithm that resolves purported names to distinguished names using X.500 Directory search and read operations.
X.500.quote: The OSI Directory has user friendly naming as a goal.  A simple minded usage of the directory does not achieve this.

rejected.why: The document is about the OSI Directory (X.500) and DUAs; LDAP is not mentioned or specified.

The general naming topic is implied as an ancestor of the narrower tag only if it were under it. X.500 sits under directory services in applications, and this document is about X.500 naming, not DNS or general name resolution.
ASN.1 appears only in the pseudo-code appendix as notation, and the text says names are string based, not ASN.1.
The X.500 technology tag is more specific, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: User Friendly Naming (UFN) for directory names
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for human-oriented directory name notation or the string representation of distinguished names. X.500 is the closest fit.

RFC1782.title: TFTP Option Extension
RFC1782.summary: RFC 1782 extends TFTP with a backward-compatible option negotiation mechanism, appending options to RRQ/WRQ packets and adding the OACK packet and error code 8.

TFTP.why: The document specifies an extension to TFTP, defining the OACK packet, option appending to requests, and the negotiation procedure.
TFTP.quote: This document describes a simple extension to TFTP to allow option negotiation prior to the file transfer.

rejected.why: TFTP is a distinct protocol with its own tag; general FTP is not addressed.
TFTP runs over UDP, but the document does not discuss UDP; it is only the substrate.

RFC1783.title: TFTP Blocksize Option
RFC1783.summary: Defines a TFTP option ("blksize") letting client and server negotiate a data block size larger than 512 bytes, updating RFC 1350, with a performance test showing the gains.

TFTP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to TFTP, the blocksize option carried in read and write requests and acknowledged with an OACK.
TFTP.quote: This document describes a TFTP option which allows the client and server to negotiate a blocksize more applicable to the network medium.

rejected.why: TFTP runs over UDP. The document mentions UDP only as header overhead, and it does not specify or analyse UDP.
The document mentions the path MTU and IP fragmentation only briefly when discussing block size. It is not about path MTU discovery.
No ICMP content appears in the document.

RFC1784.title: TFTP Timeout Interval and Transfer Size Options
RFC1784.summary: Defines two TFTP options, timeout interval and transfer size (tsize), negotiated via the TFTP option extension mechanism in read/write requests and OACK.

TFTP.why: The document specifies extensions to TFTP (timeout and tsize options) that modify RRQ/WRQ packets and use OACK, so it belongs on the TFTP page.
TFTP.quote: This document describes two TFTP options. The first allows the client and server to negotiate the Timeout Interval.

rejected.why: FTP is a different protocol; TFTP is its own tag and FTP is not discussed.
TFTP typically runs over UDP, but the document does not discuss UDP; it is only the substrate.

RFC1785.title: TFTP Option Negotiation Analysis
RFC1785.summary: Informational memo reporting tests of unmodified TFTP servers and BSD TFTPD source to show that TFTP option negotiation (RFC 1782) is backward-compatible because servers ignore options in Request packets.

TFTP.why: The document analyses the TFTP option negotiation extension and its interaction with unmodified TFTP servers, so it is about TFTP.
TFTP.quote: the TFTP option negotiation mechanism is fully backward-compatible with unmodified TFTP servers.

rejected.why: FTP is a different protocol; TFTP is its own tag and FTP is only a name similarity.
TFTP runs over UDP but the document says nothing about UDP itself; it is only the substrate.

RFC1786.title: Representation of IP Routing Policies in a Routing Registry (ripe-81++)
RFC1786.summary: Informational RFC (ripe-81++) defining how IP routing policies are represented in a routing registry via RIPE database objects (aut-num, route, as-macro, community) and their syntax, with tutorial examples of AS policy expression.

RPSL.why: The document specifies the routing policy representation language and objects for Internet routing registries, the precursor of RPSL.
RPSL.quote: gives details of a generalized IP routing policy representation to be used by all Internet routing registries

routing architecture.why: Substantial tutorial on routing policy, aggregation (CIDR, holes, proxy aggregation) and policy limitations, which matters to routing design readers.
routing architecture.quote: Exterior routing decisions are frequently based on policy based rules rather than purely on technical parameters.

rejected.why: BGP is referenced as an exterior protocol whose policies are described, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
The RIPE database is queried via whois, but only as a substrate; the document is about the routing objects.
Classless routes and aggregation are discussed as they affect registered routes, but the document is not about CIDR itself.
Authorisation of route object creation is mentioned, but the document is about policy representation, not securing routing.
AS number allocation is mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: Internet Routing Registry / routing registry database objects
gaps.why: The document is about the routing registry and its objects (aut-num, route, as-macro, community); RPSL is the closest tag, but there is no dedicated tag for routing registry operation.

RFC1787.title: Routing in a Multi-provider Internet
RFC1787.summary: An IAB-prepared informational discussion of issues in unicast network-layer routing in a multi-provider Internet: routing requirements, scalability, hierarchical routing/CIDR, renumbering, encapsulation, pricing and routing information sharing.

routing architecture.why: The document is a discussion of routing architecture issues: scalability, aggregation/abstraction, hierarchical routing, and routing requirements in a multi-provider setting.
routing architecture.quote: One of the key requirements imposed on the Internet routing is its ability to scale.

renumbering.why: Renumbering is identified as a top-priority task, and a substantial part of the hierarchical routing discussion addresses it.
renumbering.quote: to retain topological significance of the (provider-based) addresses within the subscriber, the subscriber has to change the addresses of all of its entities -- the process known as "renumbering"

CIDR.why: CIDR, provider-based addressing and aggregation are analysed as the basis of scalable routing and their consequences (multihoming, renumbering) are discussed.
CIDR.quote: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) (RFC1518, RFC1519) that is used today for scalable Internet-wide routing is based on the technique of hierarchical routing.

rejected.why: Multi-homed subscribers are mentioned only briefly as a CIDR case needing more operational experience, not a main subject.
Routing registries are mentioned in one sentence on information sharing; the document does not discuss RPSL itself.
Encapsulation is discussed as an overlay's effect on routing requirements, but only in a short section, with no specific tunnelling protocol.
DHCP is mentioned only as an existing renumbering tool, not specified or analysed.
The document is specifically about routing, so the routing tags fit better than the general architecture tag.

RFC1788.title: ICMP Domain Name Messages
RFC1788.summary: Experimental RFC defining ICMP Domain Name Request (type 37) and Reply (type 38) messages so a host can query an IP address directly for its fully qualified domain name, as an alternative to IN-ADDR reverse DNS lookups.

ICMP.why: The document defines new ICMP message types 37 and 38, with their formats and processing rules, so it extends ICMP.
ICMP.quote: This document specifies ICMP messages for learning the Fully Qualified Domain Name associated with an IP address.

DNS.why: The document proposes an alternative to DNS IN-ADDR reverse resolution, using DNS name encoding and TTL caching. Readers of DNS reverse mapping would want it.
DNS.quote: The IN-ADDR domain of the DNS is specified [RFC-1035] to perform address to domain name resolution

rejected.why: The Security Considerations only mention that a DNS signature could verify the reply. DNSSEC is not specified or analysed.
IPsec is mentioned only in passing as usable for authentication and privacy. It is not the subject of the document.
A more specific tag (DNS) already covers name resolution here.
The IESG note ties the motivation to the IPng WG, but the document specifies only IPv4 ICMP messages.

RFC1789.title: INETPhone: Telephone Services and Servers on Internet
RFC1789.summary: Informational 1995 proposal for INETPhone, a service where gateway servers link local telephone networks to the Internet so a long-distance call becomes two local calls plus an Internet voice connection, with directory servers and an open-partnership model.

PSTN interop.why: The document proposes gateway servers bridging the PSTN and the Internet for voice calls, which is PSTN/Internet interworking. No narrower child tag (SIGTRAN, Megaco, PINT, etc.) fits.
PSTN interop.quote: INETPhone integrates the local phone network with the Internet. The phone network provides local access of INETPhone service with the existing telephone facilities

real-time communications.why: The service carries real-time voice over the Internet between servers, handling delay and packet loss. This is general real-time voice communication, and no specific protocol tag applies.
real-time communications.quote: Maintain full-duplex, real-time exchanges of voice packets via Internet;

rejected.why: The Directory Server is only compared to a name server such as BIND. It maps area codes to server IP addresses and is not DNS.
The Directory Server is a brief, unspecified component. The document is not about directory access or synchronization.
Mapping telephone area codes to IP addresses is loosely similar to ENUM, but the document does not use E.164 numbers in the DNS.
Quality-of-service monitoring is only one item in the server function list, not a subject the document addresses.
The directory lookup of remote servers is a minor design element, not a discovery mechanism the document specifies.

gaps.name: Internet telephony / voice over IP
gaps.why: The document is an early proposal for Internet telephony, but the taxonomy has no general voice-over-IP tag. PSTN interop and real-time communications only partly cover it.

RFC1790.title: An Agreement between the Internet Society and Sun Microsystems, Inc. in the Matter of ONC RPC and XDR Protocols
RFC1790.summary: A licensing agreement between the Internet Society and Sun Microsystems granting rights to ONC RPC and XDR so they can enter the IETF standards process as Proposed Standards.

IPR.why: The document is a copyright, patent and trademark license agreement for the ONC RPC and XDR specifications, so it is about intellectual property rights in the IETF context.
IPR.quote: Donor hereby grants to the Internet Society and the Internet Engineering Task Force ... a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide right and license under any copyrights, patents or other rights
