ONC RPC.why: ONC RPC and XDR are the subject of the agreement, and readers of that subject would want this record of the licence and change-control transfer. The document does not specify the protocols themselves.
ONC RPC.quote: Open Network Computing ("ONC") Remote Procedure Call ("RPC") and External Data Representation ("XDR") (together the "Technology"

rejected.why: The agreement mentions the Internet Standards Process and the move to Proposed Standard, but its main subject is the licence, not the process.
The parent topic is implied by IPR, and the document does not address governance more broadly.
RFC 1057 and RFC 1014 are incorporated by reference, but the document is not about RFC publication or format.

RFC1791.title: TCP And UDP Over IPX Networks With Fixed Path MTU
RFC1791.summary: Experimental spec for running TCP and UDP directly over Novell IPX networks, including a new IPXF fragmentation layer, socket assignments, pseudo-headers for checksums, and multiplexing when both IPX and IP are present.

IPX.why: The whole document defines how TCP and UDP are carried over IPX, including the IPXF fragmentation layer and IPX packet formats, so it belongs on the IPX interworking page.
IPX.quote: TCP/IPX allows TCP/IP applications to run over IPX networks by letting TCP and UDP run over IPX.

TCP.why: A substantial section specifies TCP operation over IPX: segment size, MSS, socket 0x9091, and the TCP/IPX pseudo header.
TCP.quote: Unlike UDP, TCP runs directly over IPX. Since IPX does not support fragmentation, no TCP segment sent over IPX can be larger than the path MTU

UDP.why: UDP over IPX is specified, including socket use, packet type, pseudo header and fragmentation via IPXF.
UDP.quote: UDP must send and receive the packets on IPX/IPXF socket 0x9092.

rejected.why: Path MTU is a constraint, but the document says discovery of the path MTU is outside its scope and only uses fixed or static values.
DLSw is mentioned only as a motivating example of a TCP application; the document does not specify it.
Checksum pseudo headers are defined, but they are a small adaptation of the TCP/UDP checksum and not the subject of the document.
Considered because the document carries TCP and UDP over another network layer. The more specific IPX, TCP and UDP tags already cover it.

RFC1792.title: TCP/IPX Connection Mib Specification
RFC1792.summary: Defines an experimental enterprise MIB (Novell) with tables describing TCP connections and UDP listeners running over IPX or an unspecified network layer, replacing RFC 1213's IP-only tcpConnTable and udpTable.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module (TCPIPX-MIB) in SMI format defining management objects and tables.
MIB.quote: New MIB objects, tcpIpxConnTable, udpIpxTable, tcpUnspecConnTable and udpUnspecTable are presented in this paper

IPX.why: The MIB defines an IPX address type and objects for TCP/UDP over IPX, so it belongs on the IPX interworking page.
IPX.quote: For TCP and UDP running over IPX, tcpConnTable and udpTable objects from RFC 1213 cannot be used since they define the address to be of type IpAddress.

TCP.why: Objects model TCP connection state (including deleteTCB), so TCP readers would find the management of TCP connections here.
TCP.quote: The TCP/IPX connection table contains information about this entity's existing TCP connections over IPX.

rejected.why: UDP listener tables are defined, but only as management objects; the document does not specify or extend UDP itself.
SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for, but the document does not specify or extend the protocol itself.

RFC1793.title: Extending OSPF to Support Demand Circuits
RFC1793.summary: RFC 1793 extends OSPF with demand-circuit support, adding the DC-bit and DoNotAge LS age semantics, Hello suppression and reduced flooding so ISDN, X.25 and dial-up data-link connections can be closed when idle.

OSPF.why: The whole document specifies extensions to OSPF: the DC-bit, DoNotAge LSAs, Hello suppression, flooding changes and neighbor/interface state machine modifications.
OSPF.quote: This memo defines enhancements to the OSPF protocol that allow efficient operation over "demand circuits".

rejected.why: ISDN is only an example of a demand circuit. The document does not specify IP over ISDN.
X.25 SVCs are only an example of a demand circuit. The document does not specify IP over X.25.
The RIP demand circuit extensions (RFC 1582) are referenced for comparison, but this document is not about RIP.
MOSPF is mentioned only as a backward-compatible extension, not as a subject of this document.
The document covers OSPF version 2 only, not OSPF for IPv6.

RFC1794.title: DNS Support for Load Balancing
RFC1794.summary: Informational memo describing how DNS load balancing can be supported without protocol changes, by modifying BIND to use an external zone transfer agent that regenerates volatile address records, with implementation and CPU performance results.

DNS.why: The whole document is about DNS server behaviour (zone transfers, TTLs, refresh rates, RR ordering, BIND modifications) to support load balancing.
DNS.quote: the changes could be implemented without changes to the protocol; if zone transfer behavior could be subtly changed, then the zone transfer process could accommodate the changing of various RR information

rejected.why: The document uses a custom zone transfer agent to refresh zone data, not the dynamic update protocol.
Load balancing here is done by ordering DNS address records, not by network-layer routing or ECMP.

RFC1795.title: Data Link Switching: Switch-to-Switch Protocol AIW DLSw RIG: DLSw Closed Pages, DLSw Standard Version 1
RFC1795.summary: RFC 1795 specifies version 1 of the DLSw Switch-to-Switch Protocol, which multiplexes SNA and NetBIOS data-link connections over TCP between data link switches. It obsoletes RFC 1434 and defines the frame formats, circuit state machines, capabilities exchange, priority and pacing/flow control.

DLSw.why: The whole document specifies the DLSw Switch-to-Switch Protocol, including its message formats, state machines, capabilities exchange and flow control.
DLSw.quote: Data Link Switching (DLSw) is a forwarding mechanism for the IBM SNA (Systems Network Architecture) and IBM NetBIOS (Network Basic Input Output Services) protocols.

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable transport that SSP runs over. The document defines no new TCP behaviour beyond default port numbers and connection counts.
NetBIOS name query and datagram handling is covered, but only as traffic that DLSw forwards. The document does not specify NetBIOS over TCP/IP.
SNA is the traffic being switched. DLSw is the child tag that fits, and the SNA parent is implied by it.
Token-Ring appears only as the LAN attachment and virtual-ring emulation. The document is not about IP over token ring.
The adaptive pacing here is SSP-specific flow control between switches, not general transport congestion control.

RFC1796.title: Not All RFCs are Standards
RFC1796.summary: An IAB memo clarifying that publication as an RFC does not make a document an Internet standard, explaining RFC status categories, the STD subseries, and why a single RFC archive is preferred.

RFC series.why: The document is about the RFC series itself: its statuses, the STD subseries, and the case for a single archival series versus subseries.
RFC series.quote: The "Request for Comments" (RFC) document series is the official publication channel for Internet standards documents and other publications of the IESG, IAB, and Internet community.

rejected.why: It mentions the standards track and maturity levels, but only to explain how RFC status differs from standardization. The subject is the RFC series, not the process.
It proposes publishing an html version of STD-1 using web hypertext, but this is a passing publicity suggestion, not a subject of the document.
The parent is implied by the RFC series tag, and the document doesn't address governance more broadly.

RFC1797.title: Class A Subnet Experiment
RFC1797.summary: Defines an experiment in which IANA temporarily uses class A network 39 as subnetted address space, allocating sub-blocks by AS number, with in-addr.arpa delegation, to test routing software handling of subnetted class A addresses.

addressing.why: The document is about IP address architecture and allocation: subnetting class A space, an allocation scheme for net 39, and address portability between providers.
addressing.quote: There appears to be some interest in experimenting with subnetting the class A addresses.

DNS.why: A substantial part covers forward A records and reverse PTR delegation in IN-ADDR.ARPA for the experimental address space.
DNS.quote: the 39.IN-ADDR.ARPA branch is delegated to the IANA to be managed at ISI.

rejected.why: The document concerns IPv4 address space, but it is about address allocation and subnetting, which the addressing tag covers more specifically.
The variable-prefix case hints at classless allocation, but the document does not specify CIDR or aggregation.
RWhois is mentioned only as the registry source for AS numbers, not specified or extended.
IANA is the author and allocator here, but the document is not about IANA registries or considerations guidance.
Routing software handling of subnetted class A is a motivation, but the document does not discuss routing design.

RFC1798.title: Connection-less Lightweight X.500 Directory Access Protocol
RFC1798.summary: Specifies CLDAP, a connectionless variant of LDAP carried over UDP for simple, fast single-entry lookups in the X.500 Directory.

LDAP.why: The document defines a connectionless adaptation of LDAP, with a restricted operation set and a new result code. It belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: CLDAP is based directly on LDAP [4] and inherits many of the key aspects of the LDAP protocol

X.500.why: It provides lightweight access to the X.500 Directory and compares itself with DAP, and it can be mapped to the Directory abstract service.
X.500.quote: designed to provide access to the Directory while not incurring the resource requirements of the Directory Access Protocol (DAP)

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport. The document maps CLDAP onto datagrams but does not specify UDP itself.
DNS is mentioned only as an analogy for lookup use and retry behaviour. The document is not about DNS.
ASN.1 is used only to define the message. It is not the subject.
The transport mapping section is brief and secondary to the LDAP variant. The LDAP tag covers the document.

RFC1799.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 1700-1799
RFC1799.summary: RFC 1799 is an annotated catalogue of the 100 RFCs numbered 1700-1799, giving each one's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track marker.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a publication-series index of RFCs, so readers browsing the RFC series would look for it. It is not about the subject matter of the listed RFCs.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1700 through RFCs 1799.

rejected.why: BGP-4 RFCs (1771-1774) are only entries in the list; the document does not address BGP.
Several listed RFCs concern IPng candidates, but they are only catalogue entries.
LDAP and X.500 RFCs appear as list items, but the document is not about them.
It mentions the standards track only as a marker on entries, not as a subject discussed.

RFC1800.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1800.summary: RFC 1800 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly list of Internet Official Protocol Standards, describing the standards process, maturity and requirement levels, and listing protocols by standardization state.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels and RFC submission processing, so it belongs under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial part describes the RFC series, RFC Editor processing decisions and how to obtain RFCs.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

terminology.why: Section 4 defines the state and status terms (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Required, Elective and so on) used for classifying protocols.
terminology.quote: There are two independent categorization of protocols. The first is the "maturity level" or STATE of standardization

rejected.why: Assigned Numbers and the IANA contact are mentioned only as references and contacts, not as the subject.
It is a point-in-time status list, not a retrospective, even though it now reads as historical.
TCP, IP, DNS, SNMP and the other protocols appear only as entries in the status tables, not as protocols specified or analysed.
The IAB authored it, but the content is about standards status, not architectural principles.

RFC1801.title: MHS use of the X.500 Directory to support MHS Routing
RFC1801.summary: Experimental RFC defining how X.400 MHS MTAs use the X.500 Directory (routing trees, routing information, MTA entries, bilateral agreements, policy) to perform global message routing.

X.400.why: The whole document specifies routing of X.400 messages between MTAs, including O/R addresses, P1/P3/P7, and X.400 versions.
X.400.quote: MHS Routing is the problem of controlling the path of a message as it traverses one or more MTAs to reach its destination recipients.

X.500.why: Routing information, MTA naming, and bilateral tables are all defined as X.500 DIT object classes and attributes, with read-based lookups and error handling.
X.500.quote: Each community is represented in the directory as a routing tree.

rejected.why: Parent of X.400 in taxonomy sense; X.400 is the more specific fit and the RFC 822 routing is only mentioned in companion documents.
Mentioned only as an alternative protocol an MTA might support; not specified here.
Used as notation for definitions in the appendix; it is only the encoding substrate, not the subject.
Parent of X.500; the more specific X.500 tag applies.
This is application-level mail routing, not network routing; the term is used in a different sense.
Not relevant; X.400 content types are not MIME.

RFC1802.title: Introducing Project Long Bud: Internet Pilot Project for the Deployment of X.500 Directory Information in Support of X.400 Routing
RFC1802.summary: Describes Project Long Bud, an Internet pilot to deploy X.500 Directory information to support dynamic, distributed X.400 MTA routing in the GO-MHS community, based on the MHS-DS specification.

X.400.why: The pilot's purpose is to improve X.400 MTA routing and to migrate the operational GO-MHS X.400 service from static tables to directory-based routing.
X.400.quote: The IETF MHS-DS Working Group has specified an approach for X.400 Message Handling Systems to perform message routing using OSI Directory Services.

X.500.why: The project deploys and populates the X.500 DIT and DSAs with routing information, including replication and core DSAs, so it is about operational use of X.500.
X.500.quote: The Long Bud pilot wishes to demonstrate that the X.500 Directory is able to provide a global-scale service to messaging applications.

rejected.why: LDAP is only mentioned as one permitted access protocol for the tools, alongside DAP.
The X.400 tag is more specific to the mail system in question, and the document is not about general email.
A route-display tool is described as being 'very much the same as the traceroute facility', but this is an analogy and not about traceroute.
This is the parent of X.500, which is implied by the X.500 tag.

gaps.name: MHS-DS (MHS use of X.500 for routing)
gaps.why: The document is about the MHS-DS approach to directory-based X.400 routing, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC1803.title: Recommendations for an X.500 Production Directory Service
RFC1803.summary: Informational RFC giving operational, personnel and software recommendations for running country-level master and shadow X.500 DSAs as a production directory service.

X.500.why: The whole document recommends how to operate X.500 DSAs (master, shadow, DMD, replication, schema) as a production service, so it belongs under the X.500 directory service.
X.500.quote: This document contains a set of basic recommendations for a country-level X.500 DSA.

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which is already chosen and implies it.
The document is about service availability and operations, not security. Its Security Considerations say security is not discussed.
Tim Howes is an author, but LDAP is not mentioned in the body.
The operational recommendations concern running a directory service, not network management protocols or architectures.

RFC1804.title: Schema Publishing in X.500 Directory
RFC1804.summary: Experimental RFC proposing a naming scheme (cn=subschema entries with oid= RDNs) and a meta-schema for publishing X.500 directory schema in the directory itself, plus an algorithmic procedure for retrieving unknown schema at runtime.

X.500.why: The whole document defines how schema objects are named, stored and retrieved in the X.500 Directory, including a meta-schema and a read-based resolution procedure.
X.500.quote: This document presents a solution to the schema distribution problem using the existing mechanisms of the directory.

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which is the more specific fitting tag; the ancestor is implied.
The meta-schema is written with ASN.1-style definitions, but it only uses the notation to define directory object classes and attributes; the document is not about ASN.1.
LDAP is not mentioned in the body; the document works with DAP/DSP-based X.500 operations.
The OID arc under experimental is used for the meta-schema but the document is not about registry management.

RFC1805.title: Location-Independent Data/Software Integrity Protocol
RFC1805.summary: RFC 1805 describes an ASCII-message protocol (as implemented in Betsi) in which a trusted third party certifies file hashes and times so authors can distribute files with location-independent integrity assurance.

trust management.why: The protocol is built around a trusted third party that registers authors, verifies identity, and signs certificates, with users deciding whether to trust its verification method. This is the closest fit for a trust-based integrity scheme.
trust management.quote: The three entities in the protocol are Authors (A), Users (U), and a Trusted third party (T).

rejected.why: The memo uses public keys, signed certificates and a CRL. However, it defines a bespoke ASCII certification protocol, not Internet PKI or X.509 infrastructure.
MD5 and SHA are only named as examples of hash functions the protocol can use. The protocol is algorithm independent.
Messages may be carried by e-mail, but e-mail is only one possible transport and the memo says 'or any other means'.
PGP is mentioned only as one signature scheme that could be used, and the memo notes its drawbacks.

Software distribution integrity is related. But this taxonomy tag is about modern supply chain transparency for digital artefacts, and a 1995 certification protocol is a weaker fit than the trust management tag.

gaps.name: Data/software integrity certification via trusted third party
gaps.why: The memo's main subject is file integrity and timestamp assurance. The taxonomy has no general tag for integrity or digital notarization, apart from the narrower LTANS and supply chain tags.

RFC1806.title: Communicating Presentation Information in Internet Messages: The Content-Disposition Header
RFC1806.summary: Defines the MIME Content-Disposition header (inline and attachment types, filename parameter, extension rules) so senders can convey presentation information for message parts.

MIME.why: The document extends MIME with a new body-part header field, its disposition types, filename parameter and IANA-based extension procedure, so it belongs under MIME.
MIME.quote: It specifies a new "Content-Disposition" header, optional and valid for any [RFC 1521] entity ("message" or "body part").

rejected.why: The header is used in mail, but the document's subject is the MIME body-part header. The MIME tag is more specific.
It touches RFC 822 header syntax, but it specifically extends MIME, not the base message format.
It does not register media types. It defines disposition types and parameters, which are separate from content types.
The BNF is only used to give the header's syntax. The document is not about the notation.

RFC1807.title: A Format for Bibliographic Records
RFC1807.summary: RFC 1807 defines a tagged, human-readable text format for bibliographic records of technical reports, used by Dienst and SIFT, obsoleting RFC 1357 and adding handle, other_access, keyword and withdraw fields.

handle system.why: A new HANDLE field is introduced, specifying how Handle System identifiers are carried in records. This is a substantial new element, though not the main subject.
handle system.quote: Handles are unique permanent identifiers that are used in the Handle Management System to retrieve location data.

rejected.why: OTHER_ACCESS carries URLs/URNs, but only as a field value. The document defines nothing about URI syntax or schemes.
URNs are mentioned only as a placeholder in OTHER_ACCESS. The document says nothing about URN namespaces.
Records may be sent by email, but the RFC defines the record format, not mail handling.
The record is restricted to printable ASCII, but this is a constraint on the format, not the subject.
A publisher-ID registration coordinated with IANA is mentioned in a closing note. It is peripheral.

gaps.name: Bibliographic records / digital libraries metadata
gaps.why: The whole document defines a bibliographic record format for technical reports (Dienst, SIFT, USMARC mapping, CS-TR). The taxonomy has no tag for library or metadata formats.

RFC1808.title: Relative Uniform Resource Locators
RFC1808.summary: RFC 1808 defines the syntax, base-URL establishment rules, and resolution algorithm for relative URLs, as a companion to RFC 1738.

URI.why: The whole document specifies relative URL syntax, parsing, base URL establishment and resolution to absolute form, which is core URI syntax and resolution.
URI.quote: This document defines the syntax and semantics for such Relative Uniform Resource Locators.

rejected.why: HTML BASE element appears only in a non-normative appendix example; the document is not about HTML.
http is just one of several example schemes used in resolution examples.
MIME composite types are mentioned only for base URL inheritance context, not specified.
The Base: header is a minor recommendation, not a substantial part of the document.
BNF is used as notation for the syntax, not the subject.

RFC1809.title: Using the Flow Label Field in IPv6
RFC1809.summary: Informational memo distilling End-to-End Research Group views on how IPv6 routers and sources should handle the 24-bit Flow Label: unknown labels, flushing stale state, and which datagrams carry labels.

IPv6.why: The whole memo is about how the IPv6 Flow Label header field should be used and handled, including its relation to the Priority field.
IPv6.quote: The current draft of the IPv6 specification states that every IPv6 header contains a 24-bit Flow Label.
IPv6.section: Brief Description of the Flow Label

rejected.why: RSVP Path messages are mentioned only as one possible way to refresh flow state, not specified or analysed.
TCP connections are discussed as candidates for flow labels, and ISN handling is an analogy, but the document is not about TCP.
Flows relate to special service, but the memo focuses on label state management, not QoS architecture or signalling.
ICMP is mentioned only as a rejected option for signalling unknown labels.

RFC1810.title: Report on MD5 Performance
RFC1810.summary: Informational report measuring software and hardware performance of MD5 as the proposed default IPv6 authentication algorithm, concluding it cannot keep up with high-speed networks and suggesting a parallel-chaining modification or alternatives.

MD5.why: The whole document benchmarks and analyses the MD5 algorithm's speed, and proposes a block-chaining modification to it.
MD5.quote: This RFC addresses how fast MD5 can be implemented in software and hardware, and whether it supports currently available IP bandwidth.

IPv6.why: The performance analysis is framed around IPv6's authentication digest, and it argues that MD5 should be reconsidered as the IPv6 default. Readers of IPv6 would want it.
IPv6.quote: MD5 is an authentication algorithm, which has been proposed as one authentication option in IPv6

rejected.why: The Internet checksum is mentioned only as a faster comparison point for IPv4, not as a subject of the document.
The IPv6 Authentication Header is cited only as the context. The document does not specify or analyse AH or IPsec.
The document measures MD5 on hosts. It does not cover benchmarking methodology for network devices.
Authentication is the use context, but the document is about the performance of the MD5 algorithm. The MD5 tag covers it.

RFC1811.title: U.S. Government Internet Domain Names
RFC1811.summary: Informational policy memo from the Federal Networking Council setting registration rules for the .GOV top-level domain, restricting registrations to federal agencies per FIPS 95-1 and phasing out multiple registrations.

domain registration.why: The whole document defines who may register under .GOV, naming rules, one-registration-per-agency, and a transition for existing registrations. This is registry policy, so it belongs under domain registration.
domain registration.quote: This document describes the registration policies for the top-level domain ".GOV".

rejected.why: The memo concerns registration policy for a TLD, not DNS protocol, record, or server behaviour.
The parent of domain registration is implied. The document is about registry policy for one domain, not naming in general.
.GOV is an ordinary delegated TLD, not a reserved or special-use name.
The document is an administrative policy for one TLD. It is not about governance of the Internet or of standards in general, and domain registration fits better.

RFC1812.title: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers
RFC1812.summary: RFC 1812 specifies requirements for IPv4 routers, covering link layer, IP/ICMP/IGMP, forwarding, routing protocol support, SNMP management, BOOTP relay, and operations/maintenance.

IPv4.why: The document is a walk-through of IPv4 header processing, options, fragmentation, addressing and forwarding requirements for routers.
IPv4.quote: This memo defines and discusses requirements for devices that perform the network layer forwarding function of the Internet protocol suite.

ICMP.why: Extensive router-specific ICMP requirements, including new Destination Unreachable codes 13-15, redirects, rate limiting.
ICMP.quote: ICMP is an auxiliary protocol, which provides routing, diagnostic and error functionality for IP.  It is described in [INTERNET:8].  A router MUST support ICMP.

CIDR.why: Requires CIDR and longest-match forwarding, variable length prefixes, and updates directed broadcast rules for CIDR.
CIDR.quote: Routers MUST use the most specific matching route (the longest matching network prefix) when forwarding traffic.

routing architecture.why: Defines the route lookup pruning rules, administrative preference, load splitting, route filtering and IGP redistribution, which are router and routing design matters.
routing architecture.quote: The goal of the next-hop selection process is to examine the entries in the router's Forwarding Information Base (FIB) and select the best route

OSPF.why: Mandates OSPF support for routers that run a dynamic routing protocol.
OSPF.quote: A router that implements any routing protocol (other than static routes) MUST IMPLEMENT OSPF

BGP.why: Specifies BGP-4 requirements for policy control and route selection in routers.
BGP.quote: if a router does implement EGP it also MUST IMPLEMENT BGP.

SNMP.why: A whole chapter on SNMP requirements, the community table and mandatory MIBs for routers.
SNMP.quote: Routers MUST be manageable by SNMP [MGT:3].  The SNMP MUST operate using UDP/IP as its transport

PPP.why: Gives LCP and IPCP option requirements for routers using PPP.
PPP.quote: Routers that implement point to point or general purpose serial interfaces MUST IMPLEMENT PPP.

Diffserv.why: IP Precedence and TOS handling and queue service are a substantial QoS part of the forwarding requirements. Diffserv is the closest fit; QoS is not specifically about Diffserv in this 1995 document, so a broader tag would apply.
Diffserv.quote: Routers SHOULD implement precedence-ordered queue service.

rejected.why: Only brief router-specific amendments to host requirements; not a main subject.
BOOTP relay agent is a short section; BOOTP is not a DHCP tag and the coverage is minor.
RIP is only discussed in a historical appendix, which is a minor part.
IGMP is mentioned briefly with a SHOULD to implement, and multicast routing is only a short appendix.
Only a few sentences of ARP requirements in the link layer chapter.
NHRP appears only as a short optional step in next-hop determination.
The congestion control section is short and discusses router discard policy generally.

gaps.name: IP router requirements
gaps.why: The document defines requirements for IPv4 routers as a whole, with no taxonomy tag for router or forwarding requirements, so the closest tags are IPv4 and routing architecture.

RFC1813.title: NFS Version 3 Protocol Specification
RFC1813.summary: Informational specification of the Sun NFS version 3 over-the-wire protocol (RPC procedures, data types, semantics), plus the MOUNT v3 protocol and the NLM v4 lock manager differences.

NFS.why: The whole document specifies NFS version 3, its procedures, semantics, and implementation issues, along with the MOUNT and NLM companion protocols.
NFS.quote: This paper describes the NFS version 3 protocol.  This paper is provided so that people can write compatible implementations.

rejected.why: NFS runs on Sun RPC/XDR, which are specified in other RFCs. This document only uses them as the substrate and defines no new RPC or XDR behaviour.
TCP and UDP are only mentioned as the transports NFS runs over.
UDP is only mentioned as a transport, with a note on duplicate request handling over it.
AUTH_KERB is mentioned only as one RPC authentication flavor, not specified here.
The document defers to RPC authentication flavors and defines nothing new about authentication.
This is the parent of NFS. The specific child tag NFS fits, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: NFS (Network File System)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no NFS technology tag. The `storage` topic mentions NFS in its description, and the id `NFS` used above is not a listed taxonomy id. The tag should be `NFS` under `storage`, and the id was written as shown in the taxonomy hierarchy (NFS appears as a child of storage).

RFC1814.title: Unique Addresses are Good
RFC1814.summary: IAB/IANA guidance to Internet registries on IP address allocation: private address space (RFC 1597) does not preclude obtaining globally unique addresses under RFC 1466, and organizations anticipating external connectivity should obtain unique addresses.

addressing.why: The document is guidance on IP address allocation and the choice between private and globally unique addresses, which is the addressing topic. No child tag (CIDR, multihoming, anycast, renumbering) is the main subject.
addressing.quote: any enterprise which anticipates external connectivity to the Internet should apply for a globally unique address from an Internet registry or service provider.

rejected.why: The memo concerns IPv4 address allocation policy, but it does not specify or analyse the protocol. The more general addressing topic fits better.
Private address use is discussed, but NAT is never mentioned or specified.
Renumbering is only mentioned in passing, as a condition some providers may impose.
IANA and the registries are the audience for the guidance. The document is about address allocation criteria, not IANA registries or stewardship.
Aggregation and provider-assigned blocks are touched on only implicitly, and CIDR is not discussed.

RFC1815.title: Character Sets ISO-10646 and ISO-10646-J-1
RFC1815.summary: Informational memo defining two profiled ISO 10646 (UCS) charsets, "ISO-10646" and "ISO-10646-J-1", with their character repertoires and MIME charset names, while discouraging their practical use.

character sets.why: The document defines and names two character sets, specifying repertoires, encoding form and directionality. This is character set definition and registration.
character sets.quote: this memo defines two variations of ISO 10646. They are "ISO-10646" as the minimal basic variation and "ISO-10646-J-1" as the variation which could be useful in Japan.

rejected.why: MIME is only the context in which the charset names are used. The short MIME Considerations section gives the Content-Type charset parameter and suggests Base64, but it defines nothing new about MIME.
ISO 10646 is the same repertoire as Unicode, but the document profiles ISO 10646 rather than discussing Unicode usage. The charset tag fits better.
Base64 is only suggested as a Content-Transfer-Encoding for the 16-bit text. The document is not about it.
The parent topic is implied by the character sets tag, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: ISO 10646 / UCS profiled charsets
gaps.why: The 'character sets' tag I used does not appear in the taxonomy. The closest ids are 'character sets' under internationalization, which does exist as 'character sets [tech]'. Check that I used the exact id.

RFC1816.title: U.S. Government Internet Domain Names
RFC1816.summary: RFC 1816 sets the registration policy for the .GOV top-level domain, limiting registrations to US federal entities listed in FIPS 95-1, allowing one registration per agency, and phasing out duplicates.

domain registration.why: The whole document defines who may register under .GOV, how duplicates are resolved, and how the registrar and registration authority behave. That is domain registry policy.
domain registration.quote: This document describes the registration policies for the top-level domain ".GOV".

rejected.why: DNS is the namespace being administered. The memo sets registration policy and does not specify protocol, record or server behaviour. The CNAME and query-routing FAQ answers are incidental.
.GOV is an ordinary delegated top-level domain, not a special-use or reserved name.
The more specific domain registration tag covers the subject, so the parent is not chosen.
The registration database is mentioned only in passing. The memo does not describe a directory service.

RFC1817.title: CIDR and Classful Routing
RFC1817.summary: IAB evaluation of the implications of CIDR deployment for sites still using classful routing technology (RIP, BGP-3, EGP, IGRP), noting reliance on default routes and the need to transition to CIDR-capable protocols.

CIDR.why: The whole document evaluates CIDR's implications for classful routing sites, including which protocols support CIDR and the allocation of former Class A space as variable-size blocks.
CIDR.quote: Deployment of CIDR has certain implications on the segments of the Internet that are still using routing technology that can not support CIDR.

rejected.why: BGP-4 and BGP-3 are mentioned only as examples of CIDR-capable or non-capable protocols; the document does not specify or analyse BGP.
RIP and RIP II are listed only in the enumeration of protocols that do or do not support CIDR.
OSPF is named only as a CIDR-capable interior protocol, not analysed.
The document concerns routing scalability, but CIDR is the more specific tag and is already chosen, so the parent topic is implied.
The discussion of the former Class A address space touches IPv4 addressing, but the subject is CIDR's routing impact, not the IPv4 address lifecycle.

RFC1818.title: Best Current Practices
RFC1818.summary: RFC 1818 creates the Best Current Practice (BCP) subseries of RFCs, documents carrying IESG/IETF technical endorsement but not on the standards track.

IETF process.why: The document defines a new IETF document track and its review process (IESG review, last call, approval and publication), which is an IETF process matter.
IETF process.quote: This document creates a new subseries of RFCs, entitled Best Current Practices BCPs).

RFC series.why: It establishes a new subseries within the RFC series and distinguishes it from standards track, informational and FYI RFCs, so readers of the RFC series subject would want it.
RFC series.quote: This document describes a new series of documents which describe best current practices for the Internet community.

rejected.why: OSPF and OSI NSAP allocation are only cited as possible examples of future BCPs, not addressed by the document.
The OSPF Applicability Statement is mentioned only as an example of a candidate BCP topic.
RFC 1149 is cited only as a reference for informational RFCs having no standing in the IETF process; the document itself is not humorous.

RFC1819.title: Internet Stream Protocol Version 2 (ST2) Protocol Specification - Version ST2+
RFC1819.summary: RFC 1819 specifies ST2+, the revised Internet Stream Protocol version 2: an experimental connection-oriented resource reservation protocol, with the ST data protocol, the SCMP control protocol and the ST2+ FlowSpec, for multicast real-time streams with guaranteed QoS.

ST-II.why: The whole document is the ST2+ protocol specification, covering ST, SCMP, the FlowSpec and the PDU formats.
ST-II.quote: ST2 is an experimental resource reservation protocol intended to provide end-to-end real-time guarantees over an internet.

rejected.why: The document is about QoS and resource reservation, but ST-II is the specific child tag, so the parent is implied and not listed.
The IESG note mentions alternative reservation approaches under development, but RSVP is not specified or discussed.
RFC 1633 is cited only as an example of an alternative architecture.
ST2 builds multicast stream trees and uses IP multicast addresses, but this is incidental to the stream protocol and is not IP multicast routing.
ST2 coexists with IP and can be encapsulated in it, but IP is only the substrate.
RTP is mentioned only as an example transport layer that can run above ST2.

RFC1820.title: Multimedia E-mail (MIME) User Agent Checklist
RFC1820.summary: Informational checklist for evaluating MIME-capable email user agents, plus a description of a MIME test-responder that returns sample messages of various content types.

MIME.why: The core of the document is a MIME support checklist (content types, encodings, multipart handling, charsets, MIME-Version) for user agents, plus test messages for each content type.
MIME.quote: This document presents a checklist that facilitates evaluation of MIME capable E-mail User Agents.

email.why: The checklist also covers general email user agent features: delivery and submission protocols, folders, filtering, header generation, and secure mail.
email.quote: Does the UA support native RFC 822/MIME or does it require a gateway?

rejected.why: It lists content types to test but does not register or define media types or registry rules.
SMTP/ESMTP appear only as checklist items for what a UA supports, not as the subject.
RFC 822 header generation is a minor checklist item, not the focus.
IMAP and POP are only listed as options in a checklist question.

RFC1821.title: Integration of Real-time Services in an IP-ATM Network Architecture
RFC1821.summary: Informational RFC outlining the issues in integrating IETF Integrated Services (RSVP, ST-II) real-time QoS with ATM service models, signalling, multicast and routing in IP-over-ATM networks.

ATM.why: The whole document concerns IP over ATM: mapping IP QoS onto ATM service classes, signalling (Q.2931), connections and MARS multicast.
ATM.quote: to provide a clear statement of what issues need to be addressed in interfacing the IP integrated services environment with an ATM service environment

RSVP.why: A major section analyses RSVP's soft-state, receiver-initiated model against ATM signalling and the problems for mapping RSVP onto ATM.
RSVP.quote: RSVP has been proposed to enable network resources to be reserved for a connectionless data stream.

ST-II.why: A dedicated section compares ST-II/ST2+ reservation with ATM and discusses mapping its flowspec to ATM.
ST-II.quote: ST-II [27] and ST2+ [12] (referred to generically as ST hereafter) have data distribution and resource reservation schemes that are similar to ATM

Intserv.why: Integrated services model (Tspec/Rspec, guaranteed, predictive, controlled-delay classes) and its mapping to ATM classes is central (section 3).
Intserv.quote: The IETF is currently developing an integrated service model which is designed to support real-time services on the Internet.

QoS.why: QoS characterisation, traffic and service class mapping and QoS routing are core topics.
QoS.quote: There are several significant differences between the ways in which IP and ATM will provide QoS.

multicast.why: Multicast over ATM, VC aggregation and multicast QoS routing are discussed as a significant part.
multicast.quote: In the MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) model [1], a server is designated for the Logical IP Subnet (LIS) to supply the ATM addresses

rejected.why: Mentioned only as background for best-effort delivery.
Section 6.3 on mobile routing is brief and about general mobile networking, not Mobile IP.
OSPF/MOSPF cited only as examples of routing protocols lacking QoS.
Security section only briefly points to authentication headers; not a substantial subject.
Appears only as a reference.
QoS routing is discussed but as one section; QoS and ATM tags cover it better.

RFC1822.title: A Grant of Rights to Use a Specific IBM patent with Photuris
RFC1822.summary: IBM records a patent non-assertion covenant for US Patent 5,148,479 covering implementations of the Photuris key management protocol and derivatives, with a termination clause if the implementer asserts a patent against IBM.

Photuris.why: The whole document concerns the licensing terms for implementing Photuris, so readers browsing Photuris would expect to find it.
Photuris.quote: an official public record of a grant by IBM Corporation for the use of a specific IBM patent in conjunction with the Photuris key management protocol

IPR.why: The document is a patent grant and covenant not to sue, which is an intellectual property rights statement.
IPR.quote: IBM hereby covenants that it will not assert its US Patent 5,148,479 or its non-US counterparts against any party that implements Photuris
IPR.section: A Grant of Rights to Use IBM US Patent 5,148,479

rejected.why: Photuris sits under IKE in the taxonomy, but this RFC does not specify or analyse IKE. The more specific Photuris tag covers it.
The document says nothing about IPsec architecture. It only says the grant applies when Photuris is used with any Internet Protocol.
The Photuris tag already sits under key management. The document does not address key management itself.

RFC1823.title: The LDAP Application Program Interface
RFC1823.summary: Informational RFC defining a C language application program interface (ldap_open, ldap_bind, ldap_search, etc.) for LDAP clients, with synchronous and asynchronous calls and sample code.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies the client API for LDAP: opening connections, binding, searching, modifying, adding and deleting entries, and parsing results.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a C language application program interface to the lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP).

rejected.why: X.500 is only mentioned as something LDAP can front; the API does not specify or extend it.
Kerberos v4 is offered as one bind method (ldap_kerberos_bind), but this is a minor parameter option, not what the document is about.
TCP is just the transport LDAP uses; the API only takes a port number.
This is an LDAP-specific library API, not a sockets API extension.

RFC1824.title: The Exponential Security System TESS: An Identity-Based Cryptographic Protocol for Authenticated Key-Exchange (E.I.S.S.-Report 1995/4)
RFC1824.summary: RFC 1824 describes TESS, an identity-based cryptographic system using ElGamal signatures and the KATHY protocol for authenticated key exchange, signatures, and hierarchical self-certified public key distribution.

key management.why: The document specifies key establishment (KATHY-based authenticated key exchange), key generation by SKIAs, regeneration and distribution of keys. No narrower tag fits the technology.
key management.quote: an identity based system for the secure authenticated exchange of cryptographic keys, the generation of signatures, and the authentic distribution of public keys

authentication.why: Substantial sections define zero-knowledge, unilateral and mutual authentication protocols between principals.
authentication.quote: The "Zero Knowledge Authentication" is used if Alice wants to authenticate herself to Bob without need for a session key.

rejected.why: The hierarchical SKIA scheme is a form of self-certified public key infrastructure, but it is not the Internet PKI (X.509) this tag covers, and the document is mainly about the cryptographic protocol.
DNS name space is used only as an example of a hierarchy for SKIAs in section 5.3. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
The document is about a specific protocol and key management. The parent tag is implied by key management, so it is not listed separately.
Elliptic curves are mentioned only in passing as an alternative group in 4.7.

gaps.name: Identity-based cryptography / ElGamal signatures / Diffie-Hellman key exchange
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for discrete-logarithm schemes, identity-based cryptography, or digital signature algorithms in general. These are the core of the document.

RFC1825.title: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
RFC1825.summary: RFC 1825 describes the IP-layer security architecture for IPv4 and IPv6, covering the Authentication Header, Encapsulating Security Payload, Security Associations, key management requirements and usage scenarios.

IPsec.why: This is the original IPsec architecture document, defining AH, ESP, Security Associations and their use.
IPsec.quote: This memo describes the security mechanisms for IP version 4 (IPv4) and IP version 6 (IPv6) and the services that they provide.

ESP.why: A substantial section covers ESP modes, usage, performance and mandatory DES-CBC.
ESP.quote: The IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) is designed to provide integrity, authentication, and confidentiality to IP datagrams

key management.why: Section 4 covers manual, automated, user- vs host-oriented and multicast keying plus requirements for implementations.
key management.quote: This document also describes key management requirements for systems implementing those security mechanisms.

rejected.why: Key management protocol is explicitly not specified; IKMP and Photuris are mentioned only as future options.
Multicast use of SAs and key distribution is discussed, but only as a usage consideration, not the subject.
Use with firewalls is one usage subsection, not the focus of the document.
DES-CBC is only the mandated default algorithm, specified in a separate document.
Keyed MD5 is only the default AH algorithm, specified elsewhere.
IPSO labels are discussed in MLS usage, but only as a minor part of the document.

gaps.name: IP Authentication Header (AH)
gaps.why: AH is a core mechanism described here, but the taxonomy has no AH tag, so IPsec covers it.

RFC1826.title: IP Authentication Header
RFC1826.summary: Specifies the IPv4/IPv6 Authentication Header (AH), which provides cryptographic integrity and authentication for IP datagrams, including header syntax, SPI use, and how authentication data is calculated.

IPsec.why: AH is a core IPsec protocol, and this RFC defines it. There is no narrower AH tag in the taxonomy, so the IPsec parent applies.
IPsec.quote: This document describes a mechanism for providing cryptographic authentication for IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams. An Authentication Header (AH) is normally inserted after an IP header

rejected.why: ESP is mentioned only as the option for confidentiality. This document does not specify it.
Key management is deliberately decoupled from AH and left to other documents. The only coupling is the SPI.
Keyed MD5 is the mandatory-to-implement algorithm, but it is defined in a companion RFC and is not the subject here.
The header is defined for both IPv4 and IPv6 and its placement is described for each, but the document is about IPsec authentication and not the IPv6 protocol.
Path MTU Discovery is required for intermediate authentication, but only as a supporting requirement.
Section 3.3 on sensitivity labeling is brief and secondary to the main subject.

RFC1827.title: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC1827.summary: RFC 1827 specifies the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), which provides confidentiality and integrity for IPv4/IPv6 datagrams in tunnel and transport modes, using an SPI to identify security associations.

ESP.why: The whole document defines the ESP header, its SPI field, tunnel and transport mode processing, and conformance requirements. ESP is the specific technology it specifies.
ESP.quote: ESP is a mechanism for providing integrity and confidentiality to IP datagrams.

rejected.why: ESP is a child of IPsec, so the parent is implied. The IPsec architecture is in a separate document (RFC 1825).
DES-CBC is only the mandatory transform, and it is defined in a separate document (RFC 1829). This RFC only requires support for it.
The document explicitly excludes a key management protocol and only couples to it through the SPI.
The mechanism works with both IPv4 and IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Section 3.2 briefly discusses implicit and explicit security labels. It is a minor point and not a substantial part of the document.

RFC1828.title: IP Authentication using Keyed MD5
RFC1828.summary: Specifies how keyed MD5 is used as the authentication transform for the IP Authentication Header, defining the key handling, data size, and digest calculation over the datagram.

IPsec.why: The document defines the keyed-MD5 transform for the IPsec Authentication Header, so it belongs with IPsec architecture (AH) documents.
IPsec.quote: The Authentication Header (AH) [RFC-1826] provides integrity and authentication for IP datagrams. This specification describes the AH use of keys with Message Digest 5 (MD5)

MD5.why: The document specifies a keyed MD5 construction (key, keyfill, datagram, key, MD5fill) and discusses MD5's strength and collision attacks.
MD5.quote: The 128-bit digest is calculated as described in [RFC-1321]. The specification of MD5 includes a portable 'C' programming language description of the MD5 algorithm.

rejected.why: The construction is the older keyed-MD5 envelope (key prefix and suffix), not HMAC.
The document concerns only the Authentication Header, not ESP.
Keys are only mentioned in terms of size and quality. The document specifies no key management mechanism.
IP datagrams are the substrate being authenticated, but the document is not about IPv4.

RFC1829.title: The ESP DES-CBC Transform
RFC1829.summary: Specifies the DES-CBC encryption transform for the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), covering keys, IV handling, payload format, padding, and encryption/decryption procedures.

DES.why: The whole document specifies how DES in CBC mode is used for ESP, including key format, IV and security analysis of DES weakness.
DES.quote: This document describes the DES-CBC security transform for the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

ESP.why: It defines the ESP payload format (SPI, IV, padding, pad length, payload type) and the mandatory-to-implement transform for ESP.
ESP.quote: The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) [RFC-1827] provides confidentiality for IP datagrams by encrypting the payload data to be protected.

rejected.why: Parent of ESP, so implied; the document is about the ESP transform, not the overall IPsec architecture.
Key management is only mentioned as the mechanism that indicates IV size; not specified here.
Mentioned only as the error message for an unrecognized payload type.
Only mentioned as Payload Type 4 for tunnel mode; not the subject.
IV selection notes briefly mention counters and PRNGs but this is incidental.

RFC1830.title: SMTP Service Extensions for Transmission of Large and Binary MIME Messages
RFC1830.summary: Experimental RFC defining two SMTP service extensions: CHUNKING (the BDAT command for sending large messages in length-prefixed chunks) and BINARYMIME (sending unencoded binary MIME bodies via BDAT).

SMTP.why: The document defines new SMTP service extensions (CHUNKING, BDAT, BINARYMIME), so it is about extending SMTP.
SMTP.quote: The first service enables a SMTP client and server to negotiate the use of an alternate DATA command "BDAT" for efficiently sending large MIME messages.

MIME.why: BINARYMIME defines transport of binary MIME bodies without base64/quoted-printable encoding, and constrains conversion to 7bit MIME. A substantial part concerns MIME transfer encoding.
MIME.quote: The second extension takes advantage of the BDAT command to permit the negotiated sending of unencoded binary data.

rejected.why: Parent of SMTP; the document is specifically about SMTP extensions, so the child tag is chosen.
The document does not define header or addressing formats; it concerns transport of message bodies.
Only the substrate (port 25 connection) appears in examples; not about TCP.

RFC1831.title: RPC: Remote Procedure Call Protocol Specification Version 2
RFC1831.summary: Specifies ONC RPC version 2, the message protocol (call/reply structures, authentication flavors, record marking, and the RPC language) defined in XDR for remote procedure calls.

ONC RPC.why: The entire document specifies the ONC RPC v2 message protocol, including call/reply formats, program numbers, AUTH_SYS authentication, record marking and the RPC language.
ONC RPC.quote: This document specifies version two of the message protocol used in ONC Remote Procedure Call (RPC).

rejected.why: TCP is only a transport RPC can run over; the record marking section adapts RPC to it but the document is not about TCP itself.
UDP is merely an alternative substrate for RPC; nothing new is specified about UDP.
Only appears in the references list; no Kerberos authentication flavor is defined in the body.
Authentication flavors (AUTH_NONE, AUTH_SYS) are part of the RPC specification, which is already captured by the ONC RPC tag; not a separate subject.
Program number and flavor number assignment through rpc@sun.com is a minor part, not a standalone IANA registry subject.

RFC1832.title: XDR: External Data Representation Standard
RFC1832.summary: RFC 1832 specifies XDR, the External Data Representation Standard: a language and canonical binary encoding for describing and transferring data between different machine architectures, as used by ONC RPC and NFS.

ONC RPC.why: The taxonomy groups XDR with ONC RPC ("ONC RPC and XDR"). This document is the XDR specification, produced by the oncrpc working group, so readers of that subject would expect it.
ONC RPC.quote: Protocols such as ONC RPC (Remote Procedure Call) and the NFS* (Network File System) use XDR to describe the format of their data.

rejected.why: The document compares XDR to ASN.1/X.409 only in passing (implicit vs explicit typing). It does not specify or extend ASN.1.
NFS is mentioned as a user of XDR, but the document does not specify NFS.
Section 5 uses an extended BNF to define the XDR language, but only as a notation for the grammar. It is not about BNF notations.
XDR is a data encoding, but the ONC RPC tech tag covers it, and the taxonomy places XDR under storage/ONC RPC. A separate generic data formats tag would add little.

gaps.name: XDR (External Data Representation)
gaps.why: XDR is a standalone data description language and encoding that is also used outside ONC RPC, for example in NFS and file formats. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag, only the combined ONC RPC and XDR tag.

RFC1833.title: Binding Protocols for ONC RPC Version 2
RFC1833.summary: Specifies the RPCBIND (versions 3 and 4) and Port Mapper (version 2) binding protocols that map ONC RPC program/version numbers to transport addresses via a well-known service on port 111.

ONC RPC.why: The whole document defines the RPCBIND and Port Mapper binding protocols, which are ONC RPC services for locating RPC servers. Readers of the ONC RPC subject would expect to find it.
ONC RPC.quote: This document specifies the binding protocols used in conjunction with ONC RPC Version 2.

rejected.why: RPCBIND does act as a lookup service for RPC programs. But the document is about ONC RPC binding specifically, and the ONC RPC tag covers it more precisely.
The protocols are reachable on port 111 over TCP and UDP. TCP is only the transport and the document defines nothing new about it.
UDP is only a substrate, and the port mapper uses it for callit. The document adds nothing about UDP itself.
XDR is the encoding used to define the protocol. It is a dependency and not the subject of this document.
The lookup service maps program numbers to addresses, but this is RPC binding and not name resolution in the naming sense.

RFC1834.title: Whois and Network Information Lookup Service, Whois++
RFC1834.summary: RFC 1834 describes the WNILS working group's Whois++ enhancements to WHOIS: client and server behavior, person/host/domain record fields, search options, help, and extensibility.

WHOIS++.why: The memo defines Whois++, the extended WHOIS service with new record types, search options, and extensibility. The WHOIS++ tag is the most specific fit. Its description mentions centroid indexing, which this memo does not cover. The memo is still the base Whois++ specification.
WHOIS++.quote: The purpose of the Whois and Network Information Lookup Service Working Group (WNILS) is to expand and define the standard for WHOIS types of services

rejected.why: This is the parent of WHOIS++, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The memo does not describe referral-following. It only mentions discovery of extended records.
DNS is mentioned only for the whois.domain nameserver naming convention and the QTYPE analogy. The memo is not about DNS.
WHOIS++ is a directory-style service. The more specific WHOIS++ tag already covers it, and the memo does not address LDAP or X.500.
The memo defines domain records, but its main subject is the lookup service. The WHOIS++ tag already sits under this branch.

RFC1835.title: Architecture of the WHOIS++ service
RFC1835.summary: RFC 1835 specifies the architecture and query protocol of WHOIS++, an extension of the trivial WHOIS service with structured templates, constraints, response formats and a distributed centroid-based indexing service.

WHOIS++.why: The document defines the WHOIS++ architecture, command set, constraints and response formats, plus the indexing (centroid) architecture. This is exactly what the WHOIS++ tag covers.
WHOIS++.quote: WHOIS++, an extension to the trivial WHOIS service described in RFC 954 to permit WHOIS-like servers to make available more structured information

rejected.why: WHOIS++ is the more specific child tag. The WHOIS parent is implied, so it is not listed separately.
WHOIS++ is framed as a white pages directory service, but the taxonomy has a specific tag for it. It is not about LDAP or X.500.
TCP is only the transport that WHOIS++ servers listen on, not something the document specifies.
RWhois is a different referral-based protocol. It is not described here.
WHOIS++ is a general information lookup service, not specifically domain registry data.

RFC1836.title: Representing the O/R Address hierarchy in the X.500 Directory Information Tree
RFC1836.summary: Defines how X.400 O/R Address components are represented as an X.500 Directory Information Tree hierarchy, with object classes, attributes, naming rules, and mappings between O/R Addresses and directory names.

X.500.why: The document defines X.500 schema (object classes, attributes, DIT structure) for O/R addresses, so readers of the X.500 subject would want it.
X.500.quote: An O/R Address hierarchy is represented in the X.500 directory by associating directory name components with O/R Address components.

X.400.why: The document represents X.400 O/R Address components in the directory and maps between X.400 addresses and directory names, supporting MHS routing and X.400/RFC 822 mapping.
X.400.quote: Support for X.400/RFC 822 address mappings [2, 5].

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the schema definitions; the document is not about ASN.1.
The more specific X.500 tag fits, and its parent is implied.
The document concerns O/R address representation in the directory, not RFC 822 message format. RFC 822 is mentioned only as a mapping target.
X.121 addressing for fax is mentioned only in passing.

RFC1837.title: Representing Tables and Subtrees in the X.500 Directory
RFC1837.summary: Defines X.500 Directory schema (object classes and attributes) for representing flat key-to-value tables and private subtrees, developed for MHS use of the Directory.

X.500.why: The whole document specifies X.500 Directory object classes, attributes and DIT placement for tables and subtrees, so it belongs under the X.500 directory service.
X.500.quote: This document defines techniques for representing two types of information mapping in the OSI Directory

rejected.why: MHS routing is the motivating use case, but the document defines only generic directory table and subtree representations.
Examples use MTA entries and X.400 names, but the document is not about message handling; it only references the MHS use in RFC 1801.
The schema is written in ASN.1 object-class notation, which is only the notation used, not the subject.
LDAP is not mentioned; the document is purely about the X.500 directory.

RFC1838.title: Use of the X.500 Directory to support mapping between X.400 and RFC 822 Addresses
RFC1838.summary: Experimental RFC defining X.500 directory object classes and DIT subtrees to hold the RFC 1327 mapping between X.400 O/R addresses and RFC 822 domains/mailboxes, with lookup algorithms.

X.500.why: The document defines X.500 object classes, attributes and DIT subtrees for storing the mapping, and the directory lookup procedures. It is about using the X.500 directory.
X.500.quote: This document defines how to use directory to support the mapping between X.400 O/R Addresses and mailboxes defined in RFC 1327

X.400.why: The subject is mapping X.400 O/R addresses to and from RFC 822 addresses, which is X.400/Internet mail interworking.
X.400.quote: RFC 1327 defines an algorithm for maintaining a global mapping between X.400 and RFC 822 addresses

rejected.why: The X.500 tag is more specific and already covers this. The parent is implied.
The document concerns address mapping between mail systems, but X.400 is the more specific tag for the interworking.
RFC 822 addresses are only one side of the mapping. The document does not specify message format.
The ASN.1 object class definitions are the notation used to express the schema. The document is not about ASN.1.
Domain hierarchies are represented in the DIT, not in DNS.

RFC1841.title: PPP Network Control Protocol for LAN Extension
RFC1841.summary: Informational Cisco RFC defining PPP-LEX, a PPP Network Control Protocol that lets a remote LAN extension interface unit tunnel MAC frames to a host router and be configured, monitored and software-updated by in-band remote commands.

PPP.why: The document specifies a new PPP NCP (protocol types 0x8041/0x0041), its startup option negotiation, control packets and data encapsulation, so it belongs under PPP.
PPP.quote: a new Network Control Protocol (NCP) for PPP exists. This NCP is called PPP-LEX.

rejected.why: Ethernet MAC frames are the payload carried, but the document defines a PPP NCP, not Ethernet interworking or OAM.
The more specific PPP tag already covers the link-layer subject.
The download data frame is only described as similar to TFTP; TFTP is not used or specified.
The download/flash commands update the unit's software, but this tag targets IoT firmware update architectures and manifests, which do not fit this document.
Statistics gathering is done via custom remote commands, not SNMP or MIBs.
The Set Priority command provides simple four-level queueing, a minor feature that is not a QoS architecture.

RFC1842.title: ASCII Printable Characters-Based Chinese Character Encoding for Internet Messages
RFC1842.summary: Informational RFC describing HZ-GB-2312, a 7-bit ASCII-printable encoding of GB 2312 Chinese text using ~{ and ~} escape sequences for email and Usenet messages, with its MIME charset name.

character sets.why: The document defines a Chinese character encoding (HZ) of GB 2312 and registers its charset name. This is a character set definition and use.
character sets.quote: The name given to this encoding is "HZ-GB-2312", which is intended to be used in the "charset" parameter field of MIME headers

rejected.why: Email and news are the carriers for the encoding. The document specifies a character encoding, not mail protocol behaviour.
It only names a charset for the Content-Type header, which is use of MIME rather than a MIME extension.
SMTP's 7-bit limitation motivates the design, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
The encoding uses printable ASCII as a substrate to carry GB codes. The document is not about ASCII itself.
Usenet is a testing ground and a use case, not the subject of the document.
The parent of character sets, so it is implied by the character sets tag. A broader tag is not needed.

RFC1843.title: HZ - A Data Format for Exchanging Files of Arbitrarily Mixed Chinese and ASCII characters
RFC1843.summary: Defines HZ, a 7-bit escape-based encoding for exchanging text mixing GB2312 Chinese characters and ASCII, e.g. through email.

character sets.why: The document specifies a character encoding scheme (HZ) that switches between ASCII and GB2312 modes using escape sequences. Readers of the character set subject would want it.
character sets.quote: HZ is a 7-bit data format proposed for arbitrarily mixed GB and ASCII text file exchange.

rejected.why: Email is only the motivating transport. The format is not specific to email and the document does not specify any mail behaviour.
ASCII is one of the two modes, but the document is about the mixed Chinese/ASCII encoding, not ASCII itself.
The document does not define MIME structure or encodings. It only mentions electronic mail as a reason to use a 7-bit format.
The document predates any Unicode use here and is about GB2312, not Unicode.

gaps.name: GB2312 / Chinese character encoding
gaps.why: The document is about encoding Chinese (GB2312-80) text, but the taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the generic character sets tag.

RFC1844.title: Multimedia E-mail (MIME) User Agent Checklist
RFC1844.summary: RFC 1844 provides a checklist for evaluating MIME-capable email user agents, plus a test-responder service that sends sample MIME messages of each content type.

MIME.why: The checklist is mostly about how user agents handle MIME content types, encodings, multipart structure, boundaries and charsets, so MIME readers would want it.
MIME.quote: This document presents a checklist that facilitates evaluation of MIME capable E-mail User Agents.

email.why: Large parts of the checklist cover general email user agent features: delivery and submission protocols, folders, filtering, sorting, and secure mail support.
email.quote: Does the UA support the following basic functionalities: List messages Read messages Delete messages Compose new messages

rejected.why: It lists media types to test, but it does not register them or set registry rules.
SMTP, ESMTP, POP and IMAP appear only as checklist options about which protocols the UA supports, and the document does not specify them.
Checking RFC 822 headers is a small part of the checklist, not its subject.
Charset support is a single checklist question (4.11), not a main topic.
PEM and PGP are mentioned only as options in one checklist item.

RFC1845.title: SMTP Service Extension for Checkpoint/Restart
RFC1845.summary: RFC 1845 defines an experimental SMTP service extension (CHECKPOINT EHLO keyword, TRANSID parameter on MAIL FROM, and a 355 reply carrying an octet offset) that lets an interrupted message transfer be resumed rather than retransmitted in full.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension: a new EHLO keyword, a MAIL FROM parameter and a new reply code. It belongs on the SMTP page.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby an interrupted SMTP transaction can be restarted at a later time

rejected.why: TCP is only the underlying connection that gets broken and re-established. The document defines nothing about TCP.
It only says to check DNS for the server's IP addresses, following RFC 974. That is a substrate use, not the subject.
The TRANSID syntax is designed to be a legal RFC822 msg-id, but the document does not specify message format.
This is the parent of SMTP. SMTP is the more specific tag and already implies email.

RFC1846.title: SMTP 521 Reply Code
RFC1846.summary: Defines a new SMTP reply code, 521, that a host or MX relay uses to indicate it does not accept incoming mail, with server and client behaviour rules.

SMTP.why: The document extends SMTP with a new reply code and specifies server, MX relay and client behaviour for it. SMTP is the protocol being extended.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines a new Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) [1] reply code, 521, which one may use to indicate that an Internet host does not accept incoming mail.

rejected.why: This is the parent of SMTP. The document is about one SMTP reply code, so the more specific child tag fits.
MX records are mentioned for relay and client behaviour. The document does not define or change anything about DNS.

RFC1847.title: Security Multiparts for MIME: Multipart/Signed and Multipart/Encrypted
RFC1847.summary: RFC 1847 defines the MIME multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted content types, a framework for applying security protocols (signatures and encryption) to MIME body parts via a protocol parameter and control-information body part.

MIME.why: The document defines two new multipart subtypes of MIME (signed and encrypted), including their parameters, structure and processing, so it extends MIME body structure.
MIME.quote: This document defines a framework within which security services may be applied to MIME body parts.
MIME.section: 3. Definition of Control Information Content Types

S/MIME.why: These security multiparts are the framework on which MIME-based secure email (S/MIME, PGP/MIME, MOSS) is built; readers of secure MIME email need it. The document itself defines no protocol, so this is a secondary tag.
S/MIME.quote: The new content types are subtypes of multipart: signed and encrypted.

rejected.why: PEM is mentioned only in acknowledgements as motivation; the document does not specify PEM.
Email is the setting, but the subject is the MIME body structure, which the more specific MIME tag covers.
The document defines two multipart subtypes, but it is not about media type registration rules in general.
No cryptographic message syntax is specified; the control information format is left to separate documents.
SMTP is mentioned only for its 7-bit constraint on transport of signed content; it is not the subject.
No OpenPGP content is defined here; protocols are left to other documents.

RFC1848.title: MIME Object Security Services
RFC1848.summary: RFC 1848 defines MIME Object Security Services (MOSS), which uses multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted to apply end-to-end digital signature and encryption to MIME objects, derived from PEM, with key identifiers and key-management content types.

MIME.why: The document defines MIME content types (application/moss-signature, moss-keys, mosskey-request, mosskey-data) and secure multipart body structures; it is a MIME security specification.
MIME.quote: MOSS, a protocol that uses the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted framework [7] to apply digital signature and encryption services to MIME objects

PEM.why: MOSS is a direct descendant of PEM, with a full section comparing it to PEM and reusing its header fields and grammar.
PEM.quote: MOSS is based in large part on the PEM protocol as defined by RFC 1421.

key management.why: Substantial parts define identifiers for public keys and the request/data content types for conveying keys, certificates and CRLs.
key management.quote: this document defines two key management content types: one for requesting cryptographic key material and one for sending cryptographic key material.

rejected.why: S/MIME is a different, competing specification based on CMS; MOSS is not S/MIME.
MOSS is carried in mail, but the child MIME and PEM tags fit more specifically.
Certificates and SubjectPublicKeyInfo are referenced, but MOSS does not profile X.509.
RSA-MD5 and DES-CBC are the algorithms used via RFC 1423, but the document does not specify them.
RFC 822 headers are the syntax of control information only; the document is not about message format.

RFC1849.title: "Son of 1036": News Article Format and Transmission
RFC1849.summary: Historic publication of Henry Spencer's 1994 "Son of 1036" draft, specifying the Usenet/Netnews article format, headers, control messages, batch transmission, propagation rules and gatewaying, superseded by RFC 5536/5537.

Netnews.why: The whole document specifies Netnews article format, headers, control messages, batches and propagation. It is the direct predecessor of the Netnews standards.
Netnews.quote: This Draft defines the format and procedures for interchange of network news articles.

rejected.why: NNTP is mentioned only as one possible transport; the draft explicitly does not specify transmission methods and says ihave/sendme have nothing to do with NNTP.
The article format is a subset of RFC 822 mail format, but the document is about news articles, not the Internet message format itself.
MIME is summarized in Appendix B and used for encodings, but it is a supporting mechanism rather than the subject.
UUCP is mentioned as an alternate transport for news batches, not specified or profiled here.
News-to-mail gatewaying is a section, but the document is not about email architecture or transport.
The draft defines ASCII-only article constraints, but this is incidental to the news format.

RFC1850.title: OSPF Version 2 Management Information Base
RFC1850.summary: Defines the SNMPv2 MIB modules (OSPF-MIB and OSPF-TRAP-MIB) for managing and monitoring OSPF Version 2 routers, obsoleting RFC 1253.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module with tables for areas, interfaces, neighbors, LSDB, plus traps, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing the Open Shortest Path First Routing Protocol.

OSPF.why: The managed objects model OSPF's areas, interfaces, neighbors, LSAs and virtual links, and the document includes OSPF traps. OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: The MIB module to describe the OSPF Version 2 Protocol

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document does not extend the protocol itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Only the ospfMulticastExtensions and ospfIfMulticastForwarding objects touch multicast, so it is not a substantial subject.
MOSPF is mentioned only through a couple of capability bits and is not specified or managed here.
ASN.1 is the notation used for the MIB definitions, not the subject.

RFC1851.title: The ESP Triple DES Transform
RFC1851.summary: Specifies the Triple DES-CBC (EDE) encryption transform for the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), covering keys, IV, payload format, padding, and encryption/decryption procedures.

DES.why: The document specifies Triple DES in CBC mode, including key structure, EDE algorithm and security analysis of 3DES versus DES.
DES.quote: This document describes the Triple DES-CBC security transform for the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

ESP.why: It defines the ESP payload format (SPI, IV, padding, pad length, payload type) and processing for the 3DES transform, so ESP readers would want it.
ESP.quote: The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) [RFC-1827] provides confidentiality for IP datagrams by encrypting the payload data to be protected.

rejected.why: It is the parent of ESP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
AES is not discussed; the document concerns DES/3DES only.
Key management is only mentioned as the mechanism that signals the IV size; it is not specified here.
The datagrams are IP, but IP is only the substrate and is not what the document is about.

RFC1852.title: IP Authentication using Keyed SHA
RFC1852.summary: Specifies how keyed SHA (SHA-1, FIPS-180-1) is used as the authentication transform for the IP Authentication Header, including key handling, padding, and the keyed digest calculation.

IPsec.why: The document defines an AH authentication transform, part of the IPsec architecture. No narrower AH tag exists, and ESP is not involved, so IPsec is the best fit.
IPsec.quote: This document describes the use of keyed SHA with the IP Authentication Header.

SHA.why: The body defines how the 160-bit SHA digest is computed over key, datagram and key, and compares SHA's performance and strength. Readers of the SHA subject would want it.
SHA.quote: This specification describes the AH use of keys with the Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) [FIPS-180-1].

rejected.why: MD5 is mentioned only in the performance comparison and the security discussion, not specified here.
The construction is an ad hoc keyed envelope (key, datagram, key), not HMAC.
The document concerns only the Authentication Header, not ESP.
DES hashing appears only as a performance comparison.

RFC1853.title: IP in IP Tunneling
RFC1853.summary: Informational memo describing IP-in-IP (protocol 4) encapsulation for tunneling: outer header field handling and tunnel soft-state management of ICMP errors, MTU discovery, congestion and routing failures.

IP-in-IP.why: The whole document specifies IP-in-IP encapsulation with protocol number 4, including how each outer header field is set.
IP-in-IP.quote: An outer IP header is added before the original IP header.

ICMP.why: A substantial part covers how encapsulators handle and relay ICMP errors (Datagram Too Big, Source Quench, Time Exceeded, Unreachable) using tunnel soft state.
ICMP.quote: the encapsulator can return accurate ICMP messages in most cases.

PMTUD.why: Defines a requirement for Path MTU Discovery inside tunnels, a dedicated subsection of the document.
PMTUD.quote: all implementations MUST support Path MTU Discovery [RFC-1191, RFC-1435] within their tunnels.

rejected.why: IP-in-IP is a more specific child tag that fits, so the parent is implied.
GRE is only mentioned as a later tunneling technique that differs from this one.
IP Security is mentioned as a use case and in the abstract, but the document does not specify IPsec.
Mobile IP is only mentioned as background and as a related effort; the document is not about mobility.
