The document applies to IPv4 only as the encapsulated protocol; it is about tunneling, not the IPv4 specification.

RFC1854.title: SMTP Service Extension for Command Pipelining
RFC1854.summary: Defines the SMTP Pipelining service extension (EHLO keyword PIPELINING) letting clients batch multiple SMTP commands in one TCP send, with client and server rules and examples.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension, including client and server behaviour for pipelined commands and responses.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby a server can indicate the extent of its ability to accept multiple commands in a single TCP send operation.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport; the document mentions send operations and window size but does not define anything new about TCP.
The parent of SMTP, so it is implied by the SMTP tag and not listed separately.

RFC1855.title: Netiquette Guidelines
RFC1855.summary: RFC 1855 (FYI 28) is a bulleted set of Netiquette guidelines for users, administrators and moderators covering email, talk, mailing lists, NetNews and information services.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory guide to acceptable behaviour for new Internet users and administrators. It is not a protocol specification.
user guides.quote: This document provides a minimum set of guidelines for Network Etiquette (Netiquette) which organizations may take and adapt for their own use.

email.why: A large part of the guide covers etiquette for email use and administration, including postmaster aliases, quoting, signatures and message size.
email.quote: One-to-one communication, which includes mail and talk; One-to-many communications, which includes mailing lists and NetNews

mailing lists.why: It has dedicated sections of user, administrator and moderator guidance for mailing lists, such as -request aliases, cross-posting and auto-replies.
mailing lists.quote: Send subscribe and unsubscribe messages to the appropriate address.

Netnews.why: It has dedicated sections on Usenet posting, cross-posting, cancellation, hierarchies and moderation etiquette.
Netnews.quote: NetNews is a globally distributed system which allows people to communicate on topics of specific interest.

rejected.why: IRC is mentioned only briefly among real-time interactive services (MUDs, MOOs). The document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
FTP appears only in conventions for README files, mirrors and dumping. The protocol itself is not addressed.
WWW is mentioned as one of several information services. The guidance on homepages and file extensions is generic and not about web architecture.
Privacy remarks (mail is like a postcard, delivery receipts) are incidental etiquette tips. The document is not about privacy threat models.

gaps.name: Netiquette / acceptable use
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for online conduct or acceptable-use guidance. 'user guides' is the closest fit, but a dedicated netiquette subject would suit this and related documents such as RFC 1087.

RFC1856.title: The Opstat Client-Server Model for Statistics Retrieval
RFC1856.summary: Defines a client-server protocol (LOGIN, SELECT, STATUS, LIST, GET, EXIT) for retrieving collected network performance statistics from a NOC/NSP server, as part of the Opstat operational statistics model.

performance measurement.why: The document defines a protocol for sharing and retrieving gathered network performance and utilization statistics between NOCs, NSPs and customers; this is performance data collection and retrieval.
performance measurement.quote: Network administrators gather data related to the performance, utilization, usability and growth of their data network.

network management.why: The protocol is part of the Opstat network management data model and is used by NOCs for operations and planning, with no narrower management tag fitting.
network management.quote: tools exist for the collection, storage, retrieval and presentation of network management data.

rejected.why: SNMP variables like ifInOctets are the data being retrieved, but the document specifies a separate retrieval protocol, not SNMP itself.
MIB variable names are referenced as data names, but no MIB module is defined.
TCP is only the assumed reliable transport substrate.
The LOGIN command has simple authentication types (password, S/Key), but this is a minor part of the document.
The protocol uses printable ASCII text, but only as an encoding substrate.

gaps.name: Operational Statistics (Opstat) model
gaps.why: The document is part of the Opstat statistics collection and retrieval framework (RFC 1404), which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC1857.title: A Model for Common Operational Statistics
RFC1857.summary: RFC 1857 describes a model for common operational statistics: a minimal set of SNMP-retrievable metrics, polling and aggregation recommendations, an interchange file format for storing the data, and report formats for sharing statistics between NOCs.

performance measurement.why: The document defines which network utilization, performance, availability and stability metrics to collect, how often to poll and aggregate them, and how to report them. That fits performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo describes a model for operational statistics in the Internet. It gives recommendations for metrics, measurements, polling periods and presentation formats

MIB.why: The recommended metrics are chosen from Internet Standard MIB variables such as ifInOctets and sysUpTime, and the memo proposes a future MIB subtree for statistics. MIB variables are central to metric selection, but the document does not define a MIB module.
MIB.quote: these metrics should be available as variables in the Internet Standard MIB.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the means of retrieving the variables. The memo does not specify or extend the protocol.
This is the parent topic of the performance measurement tag I chose, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The storage format is given in a BNF-like grammar, but the grammar is only how the format is written down. The document is not about the notation.
IPFIX is about flow export. This memo is about aggregate interface counters and a file format, not flow records.

gaps.name: Operational statistics interchange file format
gaps.why: The memo defines a label/device/data section file format for exchanging collected statistics between NOCs. No taxonomy tag covers this kind of network statistics data format.

RFC1858.title: Security Considerations for IP Fragment Filtering
RFC1858.summary: Informational memo describing two IP fragmentation attacks (tiny fragment and overlapping fragment) that evade router/host packet filters for TCP, and giving filtering rules to prevent them.

IPv4.why: The document is about IPv4 fragmentation and reassembly behaviour (RFC 791, RFC 815) and how its subtleties are exploited, with fragment-offset rules to counter it.
IPv4.quote: IP fragmentation can be used to disguise TCP packets from IP filters used in routers and hosts.

firewall.why: The core subject is packet filtering in routers and hosts and making filters robust against fragment-based evasion, which fits firewalls and middlebox security.
firewall.quote: IP packet filters on routers are designed with a user interface that hides packet fragmentation from the administrator

rejected.why: TCP headers are the target of the attacks, but the document does not specify or extend TCP; it is only the protocol whose fields get hidden.
Parent topic is implied by the firewall tag; the document is about a specific mechanism.
Considered since the advice targets router vendors and administrators, but the firewall tag already captures filtering and this is a protocol-level attack and remedy.
Parent of IPv4, implied by that tag.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation and reassembly
gaps.why: The document's central subject is IP fragmentation and overlapping-fragment reassembly; the taxonomy has no dedicated tag, so IPv4 is the nearest fit.

RFC1859.title: ISO Transport Class 2 Non-use of Explicit Flow Control over TCP RFC1006 extension
RFC1859.summary: Extends RFC 1006 to run ISO 8073 Transport Class 2 (non-use of explicit flow control) over TCP on port 399, with expedited data via split TCP connections, and describes its use for DECnet over TCP/IP.

OSI.why: The document specifies an OSI transport protocol (ISO 8073 Class 2) mapped onto TCP, extending RFC 1006. OSI is the closest tag for OSI protocols coexisting with IP.
OSI.quote: This memo defines how to implement ISO 8073 Transport Class 2 Non-use of Explicit Flow Control on top of TCP.

DECnet.why: A dedicated section describes how DECnet runs over TCP/IP using this extension, which is the motivating use case.
DECnet.quote: DECnet over TCP/IP is implemented using the DECnet Session Control layer over this RFC1006 extension protocol.

rejected.why: TCP is the substrate that carries the TPKTs. The memo does not extend or specify TCP itself.
The memo is a transport mapping (ISO transport over TCP). It is tagged with the more specific OSI tag, and the mapping tag is only a generic fallback.

RFC1860.title: Variable Length Subnet Table For IPv4
RFC1860.summary: Informational table listing IPv4 variable-length subnet masks /1 to /32 with hex, CIDR, decimal, address counts and classful equivalents, plus examples of subnet/host splits within /16 and /24 blocks.

CIDR.why: The whole document is a CIDR prefix-length table (/1 to /32) with masks, address counts and classful equivalents, so readers of CIDR and aggregation would want it.
CIDR.quote: The following table lists the variable length subnets from 1 to 32, the CIDR representation form and the Decmial equivalents.

rejected.why: The RFC is about IPv4 subnet masks, but the more specific CIDR/addressing tag fits better. The ancestor is implied by the child.
This is the parent topic of CIDR. A child tag already covers it, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: IPv4 subnetting / subnet masks
gaps.why: The document is mainly about subnet mask values and host/subnet partitioning. The taxonomy has no subnetting tag, so CIDR is the closest fit.

RFC1861.title: Simple Network Paging Protocol - Version 3 -Two-Way Enhanced
RFC1861.summary: Informational RFC specifying SNPP v3, a simple command/response protocol for submitting one-way and two-way (ReFLEX) pages from Internet clients to paging terminals, bridging to TAP/IXO and TME.

paging.why: The whole document defines SNPP, a network paging protocol with level 1, 2 and 3 (two-way) commands and response codes for delivering pages to paging terminals.
paging.quote: The intent of Simple Network Paging Protocol is to provide a standard whereby pages can be delivered to individual paging terminals.

rejected.why: SMTP is discussed only as an alternative that SNPP is argued to be better than, and as a model for response codes. The document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Email is compared against SNPP and is not the subject of the document. The email-based approach is mentioned only in the section on relationship to other IETF work.
SMS means mobile short text messages. SNPP targets radio pagers and paging terminals, not SMS.
Manual telnet sessions are mentioned only as a way to use SNPP. The document does not specify Telnet or its options.

RFC1862.title: Report of the IAB Workshop on Internet Information Infrastructure, October 12-14, 1994
RFC1862.summary: Report of an IAB workshop on Internet information infrastructure, covering caching/replication, an information architecture with URN resolution and naming, search/indexing, and security recommendations to the IESG.

internet architecture.why: The report's core is an architecture for the Internet's information layer (wholesale/retail/raw materials layers, core services). It is an architectural principles discussion.
internet architecture.quote: This document is a report on an Internet architecture workshop, initiated by the IAB and held at MCI on October 12-14, 1994.

workshop reports.why: The document is a report from an IAB workshop, matching the workshop reports subject.
workshop reports.quote: The reports are contained in this document, in addition to a set of specific recommendations to the IESG and IETF community.

HTTP caching.why: Group 1 devotes its whole report to a general caching and replication architecture and management interface for WWW/Gopher and other services.
HTTP caching.quote: Caching and replication are important pieces of Internet middleware, and solutions need to be found soon.

URN.why: URNs, location-independent identifiers and their resolution are a substantial part of both Group 2 reports.
URN.quote: URN resolution is a database lookup that returns the URLs associated with a URN.

rejected.why: DNS is only mentioned as an overloaded example of a replicated database and a precedent for query consistency; the document is not about DNS.
Mentioned once as a common security interface example; not a subject of the document.

Security recommendations appear (security model, guidelines for security considerations) but are one part among many; the security topic is not the document's primary focus, and the taxonomy fit is weaker than the chosen tags.
Search and indexing are discussed generically, not directory access protocols or synchronization.
Gopher and WWW are cited as example systems needing caching, not specified or analysed.
A recommendation that Assigned Numbers be available in an online database is brief, not a main subject.

gaps.name: Information infrastructure / resource discovery and indexing architecture
gaps.why: The workshop centres on an information-layer architecture (object retrieval, publication, resource discovery, search and index), which the taxonomy has no tag for.

RFC1863.title: A BGP/IDRP Route Server alternative to a full mesh routing
RFC1863.summary: Experimental RFC defining BGP/IDRP Route Servers that relay unmodified external routes between client routers as an alternative to a full mesh of peering sessions, adding the ADVERTISER and RCID_PATH attributes, a LIST message and intra-cluster coordination.

route server.why: The whole document specifies route server design for BGP/IDRP: route relaying, clusters, redundancy and new attributes. Route servers are the subject.
route server.quote: this paper proposes to use IDRP/BGP Route Servers which would relay external routes with all of their attributes between client routers.

BGP.why: It extends BGP-4 with new path attributes, an OPEN optional parameter, a LIST message type and new error codes.
BGP.quote: UPDATE messages sent by route servers have the same format and semantics as it respective BGP-4/IDRP counterparts but also carry the ADVERTISER path attribute

rejected.why: Route reflection and confederations are a related alternative for avoiding the iBGP full mesh. This document defines a different route server scheme, not route reflection.
ATM is only mentioned as an example of a switched fabric where a full mesh is impractical; the document is not about IP over ATM.
A more specific tag fits the document better.

gaps.name: IDRP (ISO Inter-Domain Routing Protocol)
gaps.why: The document covers IDRP alongside BGP, and the taxonomy has no IDRP tag. The existing IDPR tag is a different protocol.

RFC1864.title: The Content-MD5 Header Field
RFC1864.summary: Defines the optional Content-MD5 header field for MIME messages, carrying a base64-encoded MD5 digest of the canonical entity body as an end-to-end integrity check against accidental modification.

MIME.why: The document defines a new MIME header field, specifying how it is generated and processed relative to canonical form and content-transfer-encoding. Readers of MIME would expect it.
MIME.quote: this memo defines the use of an optional header field, Content-MD5, which may be used as a message integrity check (MIC)

MD5.why: The document specifies how MD5 is applied as an integrity check, including the digest encoding as 16 octets then base64. This is a profile of MD5 use, not the algorithm itself.
MD5.quote: the MD5 algorithm is computed on the canonical form of the MIME entity's object.

rejected.why: The header is MIME-specific; MIME is the more specific fit and email is implied as its ancestor.
Base64 is only used to encode the digest value; it is an encoding mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
PEM is only mentioned as a stronger alternative for secure integrity; the document is not about it.
It adds a header field, but the document is framed as a MIME extension rather than general Internet message header format.

RFC1865.title: EDI Meets the Internet Frequently Asked Questions about Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) on the Internet
RFC1865.summary: An informational FAQ introducing the EDI community to the Internet, covering how X12/EDIFACT EDI can be carried over Internet email (MIME) and FTP, the role of VANs and ISPs, US federal EDI policy, and EDI resources and security.

EDI.why: The whole document is about carrying X12/EDIFACT EDI over Internet transports, trading partner agreements, addressing and routing in ISA/GS segments, and EDI resources.
EDI.quote: attempts to answer frequently asked questions concerning the use of the Internet for Electronic Data Interchange (EDI)

email.why: A substantial part covers using SMTP, POP, UUCP and MIME email as the transport for EDI messages, including MIME/EDI body parts.
email.quote: The simplest and most widely supported means of exchanging messages is via internet email.

FTP.why: FTP is described as the second main way of exchanging EDI messages, including account and file naming conventions.
FTP.quote: To exchange EDI messages via FTP, some setup information must be included in the trading partner agreement.

rejected.why: MIME is mentioned as the wrapper for EDI body parts, but the 'EDI in MIME' spec is a separate work in progress, so this FAQ is not about MIME itself.
X.400/X.435 is compared with SMTP/MIME for EDI in 6.5, but only as a short policy comparison, not a main subject.
SMTP is described as the transport substrate for EDI mail, not specified or extended here.
Mailing lists are listed as resources and broadcast methods, but the document does not specify list protocols.
Digital signatures and PEM/PGP are discussed briefly in security Q&A, not as a major subject.
UUCP is described only as one connection option for store-and-forward mail.

gaps.name: Electronic commerce / EDI over Internet
gaps.why: The taxonomy has EDI only under messaging as 'EDI over Internet transports'. That fits, but the document's wider topics (VANs, US federal procurement policy, trading partner agreements) have no dedicated tag.

RFC1866.title: Hypertext Markup Language - 2.0
RFC1866.summary: RFC 1866 specifies HTML 2.0 as an SGML application, including its DTD, document structure, hyperlinks, forms, and the text/html media type.

HTML.why: The whole document defines HTML 2.0: elements, attributes, DTDs, forms, and user agent conformance.
HTML.quote: The HyperText Markup Language (HTML) is a simple data format used to create hypertext documents that are portable from one platform to another.

SGML.why: A substantial part defines HTML as an SGML application, including the SGML declaration, lexical syntax, DTDs and entity catalog.
SGML.quote: HTML is an application of ISO 8879:1986 -- Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML).
SGML.section: 3. HTML as an Application of SGML

media types.why: The document registers the text/html media type with its level and charset parameters, and defines the application/x-www-form-urlencoded encoding.
media types.quote: This specification defines the Internet Media Type [IMEDIA] (formerly referred to as the Content Type [MIME]) called `text/html'.

rejected.why: URIs are used for hyperlinks, but this document defines only how HTML uses them. The URI syntax comes from other RFCs.
HTTP is only the retrieval and form-submission substrate. META HTTP-EQUIV and POST are mentioned, but HTTP itself is not specified.
MIME is relied on for the content type mechanism, and the document does not extend MIME itself.
The HTML document character set (Latin-1, ISO 10646) is defined, but only as a supporting part of the HTML specification.
A more specific tag, HTML, already covers the document.

RFC1867.title: Form-based File Upload in HTML
RFC1867.summary: Experimental RFC extending HTML forms with INPUT TYPE=FILE and an ACCEPT attribute, and defining the multipart/form-data media type for returning form data and uploaded files, with a backward-compatibility strategy for old browsers.

HTML.why: The document extends HTML forms with a new INPUT type, an ACCEPT attribute and a DTD change, so it belongs under HTML.
HTML.quote: This proposal makes two changes to HTML: 1) Add a FILE option for the TYPE attribute of INPUT.

media types.why: It registers the multipart/form-data media type (Appendix A and Section 7) and specifies its structure and use.
media types.quote: it defines a new MIME media type, multipart/form-data, and specifies the behavior of HTML user agents

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport for the POST. The document defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
The document builds on multipart MIME rules, but its contribution is the registered media type, which is covered by media types.
Mail transport via mailto: ACTION is mentioned only as a side consideration.
The mailto: URL and the ACTION URL are mentioned in passing, not specified.

gaps.name: HTML forms / file upload
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for HTML form submission or file upload, which is the central subject of the document. HTML is the closest fit.

RFC1868.title: ARP Extension - UNARP
RFC1868.summary: RFC 1868 specifies UNARP, an experimental ARP extension in which a node or proxy-ARP server broadcasts an unsolicited ARP Reply with zero hardware address length so other nodes delete stale ARP cache entries when a host departs.

ARP.why: The document defines an extension to ARP: an UNARP packet (unsolicited ARP Reply) that causes receivers to remove cache entries, including for the Proxy ARP case.
ARP.quote: a trivial modification to the ARP mechanism, not the packet format, which allows a node to announce that it is leaving the network

rejected.why: UNARP carries IPv4 protocol addresses, but the document is about ARP cache maintenance, not IPv4 itself.
It touches on conserving address space with proxy ARP, but the subject is ARP cache invalidation, not address architecture or allocation.
Dial-in hosts connect via communication servers, but this is background for the proxy ARP scenario. The document says nothing about PPP.

RFC1869.title: SMTP Service Extensions
RFC1869.summary: Defines the SMTP service extension framework: the EHLO command, an IANA registry of extension keywords, and optional parameters on MAIL FROM and RCPT TO.

SMTP.why: The whole document specifies ESMTP: the EHLO command, extension keyword registry, and MAIL FROM/RCPT TO parameters. It extends SMTP directly.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines a framework for extending the SMTP service by defining a means whereby a server SMTP can inform a client SMTP as to the service extensions it supports.

rejected.why: RFC 822 headers are only mentioned as background. The only header change is the 'with ESMTP' Received: annotation, which is minor.
MIME is cited as background for message bodies and via the 8BITMIME example. The document does not specify it.
An extension registry is created, but only as part of the SMTP framework. The document is not about IANA registry guidance in general.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the command syntax.

RFC1870.title: SMTP Service Extension for Message Size Declaration
RFC1870.summary: Defines the SMTP "SIZE" service extension, letting a client declare a message's size in MAIL FROM and a server advertise its maximum size in EHLO so oversized or unstorable messages can be rejected before transfer.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension: the SIZE EHLO keyword, the SIZE parameter on MAIL FROM, and the related 452/552 reply code behaviour.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby an SMTP client and server may interact to give the server an opportunity to decline to accept a message

rejected.why: MIME is cited only as motivation for larger messages. The document does not specify or extend it.
The parent of SMTP, so it is implied. The document is specifically about SMTP.
The document covers message size in octets for transfer, not header or body format.

RFC1871.title: Addendum to RFC 1602 -- Variance Procedure
RFC1871.summary: RFC 1871 defines an interim variance procedure letting the IESG, on WG recommendation, enter or advance a specification on the standards track despite unmet RFC 1602 section 5 requirements, with extended Last Call and IAB appeal.

IETF process.why: The document modifies IETF standards-process procedures by adding a variance procedure involving the IESG, Last Call and IAB appeals.
IETF process.quote: allow an escape from a situation where the existing procedures are not working or do not seem to apply

rejected.why: The document is about standards-track process, not RFC format, style or publication; the RFC Editor is mentioned only in passing.
No glossary or requirements-language content.

RFC1872.title: The MIME Multipart/Related Content-type
RFC1872.summary: Defines the MIME Multipart/Related media type for compound objects made of inter-related body parts, with type, start and start-info parameters, user agent requirements and examples.

MIME.why: The document defines a new MIME multipart subtype, its parameters and user agent processing rules, so it belongs with MIME body structure.
MIME.quote: The Multipart/Related content-type provides a common mechanism for representing objects that are aggregates of related MIME body parts.

media types.why: It includes a media type registration form for multipart/related with its parameters. That is a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: Media Type name:           Multipart  Media subtype name:        Related

rejected.why: MIME is the subject. Email is only the context where it is used.
The document does not define MHTML. It is the generic mechanism that MHTML later builds on, and the HTML-like example is an invented markup language.
The document uses RFC 822 msg-id syntax for content-IDs but does not specify message headers or addressing.
The Text/X-Okie example is an invented HTML-like language and is only illustrative.

RFC1873.title: Message/External-Body Content-ID Access Type
RFC1873.summary: Defines a new MIME Message/External-Body access-type, content-id, letting one body part refer to another body part in the same multipart message to avoid duplicating data.

MIME.why: The document extends MIME by registering a new Message/External-Body access-type and specifying how a MUA constructs the resulting body part from the referring and referenced parts.
MIME.quote: The content-id header of the access-type=content-id MIME entity must match (be identical to) exactly one content-id in the same message

rejected.why: SGML documents are only the motivating example of structured objects encapsulated in MIME; the document does not specify anything about SGML.
It registers a MIME access-type parameter, not a media type or registry rules.
Email is only the carrier; the subject is MIME body-part structure, covered by the MIME tag.
The document does not concern RFC 822 headers or addressing beyond using Content-ID in MIME entities.

RFC1874.title: SGML Media Types
RFC1874.summary: Registers the Text/SGML and Application/SGML MIME media types for exchanging SGML entities, defining their optional parameters (charset, SGML-bctf, SGML-boot).

SGML.why: The document defines how SGML entities are carried, including SGML-specific parameters such as bit combination transformation format and boot attribute, so SGML readers would want it.
SGML.quote: This document proposes new media sub-types of Text/SGML and Application/SGML. These media types can be used in the exchange of SGML documents and their entities.

media types.why: The document is a media type registration with template fields (type name, subtype name, parameters, encoding and security considerations).
media types.quote: There are two media-types for SGML parsable entities, Text/SGML and Application/SGML. Both have the same optional parameters.

rejected.why: MIME is the framework in which the types are registered; the document does not extend MIME body structure or encodings, and the media types tag covers the registration.
The charset parameter and BCTF values touch character encodings, but only as parameters of the SGML types, not as a character set registration.
utf-8 appears only as one BCTF value in the appendix list.
SGML is the basis of HTML, but the document does not cover HTML or hypertext formats.

RFC1875.title: UNINETT PCA Policy Statements
RFC1875.summary: Informational policy statement of the UNINETT Policy Certification Authority describing its PEM-style certification hierarchy, security requirements, certification procedures, CRL handling and naming conventions.

PKI.why: The document is a PCA policy statement covering CAs, RAs, certificate issuance, validity, CRL management and naming, which is public key infrastructure policy.
PKI.quote: to evaluate the trust they can place in a certification path that includes a certificate issued by the UNINETT PCA

PEM.why: The certification hierarchy and procedures follow the PEM certificate-based key management documents, with RA modifications. PEM readers would want this policy profile.
PEM.quote: CAs are described in the PEM documents [1,2,3,4].

rejected.why: X.500 is used only as a repository for certificates and CRLs and for DN disambiguation. The document does not specify or extend it.
Certificates and CRLs are implied but X.509 is never named or profiled. The document is about policy.
RSA key lengths are mentioned only as security requirements, not as the subject.
DES is used only to encrypt keys in bulk certification, which is incidental.

RFC1876.title: A Means for Expressing Location Information in the Domain Name System
RFC1876.summary: Experimental RFC defining the DNS LOC resource record (type 29) for carrying latitude, longitude, altitude, size and precision of hosts, networks and subnets, with master file format and search algorithms.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record (LOC), its RDATA and master file formats, and DNS lookup algorithms for it, updating RFC 1034/1035.
DNS.quote: This memo defines a new DNS RR type for experimental purposes.

geolocation.why: The record's content is geographic location (WGS 84 latitude, longitude, altitude, precision), so readers interested in conveying location information would want it.
geolocation.quote: a mechanism to allow the DNS to carry location information about hosts, networks, and subnets

rejected.why: A visual traceroute is only mentioned as a suggested application of LOC RRs, not specified.
UUCP maps are mentioned only as the flat-file location source that LOC could replace; the document is not about UUCP.
The more specific DNS tag applies instead.

RFC1877.title: PPP Internet Protocol Control Protocol Extensions for Name Server Addresses
RFC1877.summary: Defines four new PPP IPCP configuration options (129-132) for negotiating primary and secondary DNS and NetBIOS name server addresses between PPP peers.

PPP.why: The RFC specifies new IPCP configuration options, extending PPP's Network Control Protocol for IP.
PPP.quote: This document extends the NCP for establishing and configuring the Internet Protocol over PPP [2], defining the negotiation of primary and secondary Domain Name System (DNS)

NetBIOS.why: Half of the defined options (130 and 132) carry NetBIOS Name Server addresses, so NetBIOS readers would want it.
NetBIOS.quote: provide a method of obtaining the addresses of Domain Name System (DNS) servers and (NetBIOS Name Server (NBNS) nodes on the remote network.

rejected.why: DNS server addresses are only configuration data delivered over PPP; the document does not specify or change DNS protocol behaviour.
The options resemble DHCP-style configuration, but the document never mentions DHCP and works only within IPCP.
Only conveys name server addresses; it is not about naming or name resolution itself.

RFC1878.title: Variable Length Subnet Table For IPv4
RFC1878.summary: An informational memo giving a table of IPv4 variable-length subnet masks (/1 to /32) with hex and decimal forms, address counts, classful equivalents, and per-subnet network, host range and broadcast addresses for Class B and C subnetting.

addressing.why: The document is about IPv4 subnetting and address block sizing, which is IP address architecture and use. No more specific technology tag fits, since CIDR is only referenced for notation.
addressing.quote: This memo clarifies issues surrounding subnetting IP networks by providing a standard subnet table.

rejected.why: CIDR is used only for the /xx notation and cited as a reference. The document does not specify or analyse CIDR aggregation.
The memo is about subnet tables, not the IPv4 protocol or its address lifecycle. The addressing topic fits better.
Routing is only touched on through the router requirements reference. The memo has no routing content.

gaps.name: IPv4 subnetting
gaps.why: The memo is specifically about subnet masks and subnet tables. The taxonomy has only the broader addressing topic for this.

RFC1879.title: Class A Subnet Experiment Results and Recommendations
RFC1879.summary: Reports results of the RFC 1797 experiment subnetting Class A address space (net 39), covering routing and operational problems (classful IGPs, cisco configuration) and recommending that Class A space can safely be carved up by the registries.

addressing.why: The document's central conclusion concerns allocation and delegation of subnets of old Class A address space by registries and IANA.
addressing.quote: We believe it safe to start carving up "Class A" space, if the spaces are delegated according to normal IR conventions

CIDR.why: Much of the body addresses classful versus classless routing and aggregation (ip classless, no auto-summary, supernet routes) when subnetting Class A space.
CIDR.quote: the promotion problem identified above, was manifest. The problem turned out to be that a classful IGP (RIPv1) was being used

RIP.why: RIPv1 is analysed as causing unintended aggregate announcements, and it is recommended to be considered historic.
RIP.quote: Equipment that depends on use of a classful routing protocol, such a RIPv1 are prone to misconfiguration.

rejected.why: DNS service (root server on subnetted space, classless in-addr.arpa delegation) was tested but is only a brief part of the experiment, not a main subject.
BGP appears only in cisco configuration examples for route redistribution; the document is not about BGP itself.
Traceroute/LSRR is mentioned as an operational troubleshooting aid, not a subject of the document.
The Internet Routing Registry is only mentioned in passing as a place to register aggregates.
The discussion is about specific configuration and classful behaviour, covered better by CIDR and RIP tags.

RFC1880.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1880.summary: RFC 1880 is the quarterly IAB-issued Internet Official Protocol Standards memo (STD 1), describing the standards process, maturity and requirement levels, and listing protocols by standardization state.

IETF process.why: The document's main body explains the standards track, maturity states, requirement levels and RFC processing decision table, which is IETF standards process content.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial section describes the RFC series, how RFCs are submitted and published by the RFC Editor, and how to obtain them.
RFC series.quote: The documents called Request for Comments (or RFCs) are the working notes of the "Network Working Group"

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned as a contact and for Assigned Numbers, but the document is not about IANA registries.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but these are process terms rather than a glossary; covered by IETF process.
The memo is a snapshot of current standards status, not a history, even though it is now historic.
Issued by the IAB, but it does not discuss architectural principles.
TCP and the many other protocols (SMTP, DNS, SNMP, BGP, PPP, etc.) appear only as entries in status lists, not as subjects of the document.

RFC1881.title: IPv6 Address Allocation Management
RFC1881.summary: IAB/IESG statement that the IANA will manage the IPv6 address space with advice from IAB and IESG, delegating allocation to regional registries, with revocation, fee, and anti-monopoly principles.

addressing.why: The document sets out the policy for allocating and delegating IPv6 address space via regional registries, which is about address allocation. It is not about IPv6 protocol mechanics, so the addressing topic fits better than the IPv6 tag.
addressing.quote: The IANA will delegate to regional (and other) registries the task of making specific address allocations to network service providers and other subregional registries.

IANA.why: It defines IANA's stewardship and delegation role over the IPv6 address space, including revocation and the plan for the initial allocation.
IANA.quote: The Internet community recognizes the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as the appropriate entity to have the responsibility for the management of the IPv6 address space.

rejected.why: The document is about governance of address allocation, not the IPv6 specification, addressing format, or deployment. The more specific addressing topic covers it.
The document does touch governance, but the IANA tag is the more specific child that fits.

gaps.name: Regional Internet registries (RIRs) and address allocation policy
gaps.why: The document is about delegation to regional registries and their fee and monopoly principles. The taxonomy has no tag for RIRs or address policy beyond the general addressing topic.

RFC1882.title: The 12-Days of Technology Before Christmas
RFC1882.summary: A humorous parody of "The Twelve Days of Christmas" listing frustrating IT operations problems (broken databases, transceiver failures, SCSI issues, SNMP alerts, licensing) in a corporate network.

humor.why: The whole memo is a whimsical parody of a Christmas carol, exactly the kind of April-1st-style humorous RFC the humor tag covers.
humor.quote: On the first day of Christmas, technology gave to me: A database with a broken b-tree (what the hell is a b-tree anyway?)

rejected.why: SNMP alerts and MIBs are mentioned only as punchlines; the document does not specify or discuss the protocol.
Operational woes are the joke's subject matter, but the document gives no actual management guidance.
Transceiver failures and SQE appear only as gags, not as technical content about Ethernet.
Mentions of modems as a security violation are jokes, not security guidance; the memo states security is not discussed.

RFC1883.title: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
RFC1883.summary: RFC 1883 specifies the original IPv6 protocol: base header format, extension headers (hop-by-hop, routing, fragment, destination options), packet size/MTU rules, flow labels, priority, and upper-layer protocol effects.

IPv6.why: The document is the core IPv6 specification, defining the header, extension headers, options, flow labels and priority.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6), also sometimes referred to as IP Next Generation or IPng.

rejected.why: ICMPv6 is specified separately in RFC 1885; this document only references ICMP errors and the pseudo-header checksum.
Path MTU Discovery is required/recommended but is specified elsewhere (RFC 1191); only IPv6-specific notes appear in one section.
AH and ESP are referenced as extension headers but specified in other RFCs.
The IPng tag covers historic candidate protocols; this is the chosen IPv6 spec, already covered by IPv6.
Address format and semantics are in RFC 1884, not this document.
TCP/UDP appear only as upper-layer examples (pseudo-header, MSS), not as subjects.

RFC1884.title: IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture
RFC1884.summary: RFC 1884 defines the IPv6 addressing architecture: the addressing model, text representations, unicast, anycast and multicast address formats, and the addresses a node must recognise.

IPv6.why: The whole document specifies IPv6 address formats, types, text forms and required node addresses, so it belongs on the IPv6 page.
IPv6.quote: This specification defines the addressing architecture of the IP Version 6 protocol.

addressing.why: A substantial part covers address architecture, including format prefixes, provider-based allocation and anycast address use and restrictions. The anycast and multicast sections are a major share of the text.
addressing.quote: There are three types of addresses:

rejected.why: Multicast addresses are defined here only as one part of the addressing architecture, not as multicast routing or group membership.
CIDR is cited only as an analogy for address assignment and aggregation and is not the subject.
IPv4-compatible and IPv4-mapped addresses appear only as address formats in a brief subsection.
Anycast is covered in its own section, but only as one of three address types in the architecture. The addressing tag covers it.
Autoconfiguration from a MAC-based interface ID gets a passing mention only.

RFC1885.title: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMPv6) for the Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6)
RFC1885.summary: Specifies ICMPv6, the IPv6 version of ICMP, defining its error messages (Destination Unreachable, Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem), Echo Request/Reply, and the group membership messages absorbed from IGMP.

ICMP.why: The document defines ICMPv6 message formats, source address selection, checksum and processing rules; this is the core ICMP specification for IPv6.
ICMP.quote: This document specifies a set of Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) messages for use with version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6).

IPv6.why: ICMPv6 is a mandatory component of IPv6, with IPv6-specific details such as Next Header 58, the pseudo-header checksum and extension header handling.
IPv6.quote: ICMPv6 is an integral part of IPv6 and MUST be fully implemented by every IPv6 node.

MLD.why: Defines the group membership Query, Report and Reduction messages, the IPv6 replacement for IGMP, which later became MLD.
MLD.quote: The ICMPv6 Group Membership messages are used to convey information about multicast group membership from nodes to their neighboring routers.

rejected.why: The Packet Too Big message supports Path MTU Discovery, but the document explicitly leaves the procedure to other documents.
IGMP is IPv4 only and is merely absorbed into ICMPv6 here; the IPv6 group membership messages fit MLD.
Neighbor Discovery is only mentioned as a separate document that adds ICMPv6 message types.
The checksum calculation is a small subsection of a message-format spec, not the subject of the document.
Time Exceeded and Echo messages are used by diagnostic tools, but the document does not describe traceroute.

RFC1886.title: DNS Extensions to support IP version 6
RFC1886.summary: Defines DNS extensions for IPv6: the AAAA resource record, the IP6.INT reverse-lookup domain, and updated additional-section processing for NS, MX and MB queries.

DNS.why: The RFC specifies a new DNS resource record type (AAAA), a new reverse-lookup domain, and revised query processing. It is a DNS protocol extension.
DNS.quote: This document defines the changes that need to be made to the Domain Name System to support hosts running IP version 6 (IPv6).

IPv6.why: The document is about storing and looking up IPv6 addresses in the DNS, so readers of IPv6 deployment material would want it.
IPv6.quote: A 128 bit IPv6 address is encoded in the data portion of an AAAA resource record in network byte order

rejected.why: Transition issues are explicitly deferred to another document; this RFC only defines the DNS record and domain.
The RFC uses the IPv6 address architecture (RFC 1884) for textual format but does not define addressing itself.
IP6.INT is a reverse-mapping domain, not a special-use name reservation in the sense of that tag.

RFC1887.title: An Architecture for IPv6 Unicast Address Allocation
RFC1887.summary: Informational architecture for allocating IPv6 unicast addresses hierarchically along provider/topological boundaries to enable route aggregation, covering multi-homed, zero-homed, private-link, continental aggregation and private address cases.

addressing.why: The whole document is about IP address allocation architecture: provider-based hierarchical prefix assignment, continental aggregation, private addresses, and allocation recommendations.
addressing.quote: This document provides an architecture for allocating IPv6 [1] unicast addresses in the Internet.

IPv6.why: The allocation architecture is specific to IPv6 addressing and its prefix structure, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 address prefixes will be represented as X/Y, where X is a prefix of an IPv6 address

multihoming.why: A substantial portion presents four alternative addressing solutions for multi-homed domains and their routing tradeoffs.
multihoming.quote: there are additional considerations for routing domains which are attached to multiple providers. Such `multi-homed' routing domains

routing architecture.why: The document's rationale is routing scalability via aggregation of reachability information in hierarchical routing domains.
routing architecture.quote: The objective behind the use of hierarchical routing is to achieve some level of routing data abstraction, or summarization

rejected.why: The aggregation concept is similar, but the document is IPv6-specific and does not discuss CIDR itself.
Only mentioned briefly (zero-homed domains changing addresses), not a substantive topic.
DNS split nameservers for private addresses are mentioned only in a short passage.
Inter-domain routing is discussed generically without BGP being specified or analysed.

RFC1888.title: OSI NSAPs and IPv6
RFC1888.summary: RFC 1888 recommends redesigning OSI NSAP addressing plans as native IPv6 plans, and defines elective mechanisms for mapping restricted or truncated NSAPs into IPv6 addresses, carrying full NSAPs in an IPv6 destination option, and embedding IPv6 addresses in NSAPs.

OSI.why: The document is about OSI network-layer addressing (NSAPs) and its coexistence with IPv6, including mapping and embedding between the two address formats.
OSI.quote: defines a set of mechanisms for the support of OSI NSAP addressing in an IPv6 network

IPv6.why: It defines IPv6 address formats (0x02/0x03 prefixes), a destination option, and addressing plan advice for IPv6 deployment.
IPv6.quote: This document also defines a mapping of IPv6 addresses within the OSI address format, should this be required.

rejected.why: CLNP is the OSI protocol whose addresses are being mapped, but the document is about NSAP addressing and IPv6, not specifying CLNP. The OSI tag covers it.
The document is about addressing, but the more specific IPv6 and OSI tags already cover it.
The document is about OSI-to-IPv6 address mapping, not IPv4/IPv6 coexistence. It explicitly excludes migration of routing protocols and infrastructure.
IS-IS and ES-IS are mentioned as the existing OSI routing context, but the document says it does not address migrating them.
ICMP Parameter Problem is only mentioned as an error response to an inconsistent option.
Truncated NSAPAs may be interpreted as anycast addresses, but this is a minor point.

RFC1889.title: RTP: A Transport Protocol for Real-Time Applications
RFC1889.summary: RFC 1889 specifies RTP, the real-time transport protocol for audio/video and similar data, together with its control protocol RTCP, translators and mixers, SSRC handling, and basic confidentiality.

RTP.why: The document is the core RTP specification: header format, sessions, SSRC/CSRC, translators and mixers, and profile framework.
RTP.quote: This memorandum specifies the real-time transport protocol (RTP), which provides end-to-end delivery services for data with real-time characteristics, such as interactive audio and video.

RTCP.why: A large part of the document specifies RTCP: SR/RR/SDES/BYE/APP packets, transmission interval algorithm, jitter and loss reporting.
RTCP.quote: the RTP control protocol (RTCP), to monitor the quality of service and to convey information about the participants in an on-going session.

rejected.why: UDP is only the typical underlying transport; the document does not specify it beyond port conventions.
Security is limited to a simple DES-CBC confidentiality option in RTP itself, not the later SRTP.
RTP is designed to work over multicast, but the document does not address multicast routing or group management.
DES is only the default encryption algorithm mentioned in a short subsection.
NTP timestamp format is used for wallclock time, but the protocol itself is not addressed.
Parent topic is implied by the RTP tag.

RFC1890.title: RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences with Minimal Control
RFC1890.summary: RFC 1890 defines the RTP audio/video conference profile: default static payload type mappings, audio and video encoding descriptions, and port assignment for RTP version 2 and RTCP.

RTP.why: The document is an RTP profile that interprets generic RTP fields, defines payload type mappings, timestamp rates, port assignment and security defaults for RTP.
RTP.quote: This memo describes a profile for the use of the real-time transport protocol (RTP), version 2, and the associated control protocol, RTCP

codecs.why: A large part of the document describes audio and video encodings (PCMU, DVI4, GSM, H261, JPEG, MPV and others) and their properties, with pointers to the specifications.
codecs.quote: It defines a set of standard encodings and their names when used within RTP.

rejected.why: The document defines the profile's static payload type table and describes encodings briefly, but the detailed payload formats are in separate work in progress. It is not a specification of a payload format for a particular codec.
RTCP is mentioned only as part of the profile, and the document defines no RTCP packet types or extensions.
The security section only describes a pass-phrase-to-key mapping for the RTP default encryption. It does not describe secure RTP.
UDP is only the underlying transport and the source of the port pair assignment. The document does not specify anything new about UDP.
PCMA and PCMU are mapped to G.711 in a short entry, but the document is not about G.711 itself.
H.264 is not mentioned. The video encodings in this document are H.261, JPEG and MPEG.

RFC1891.title: SMTP Service Extension for Delivery Status Notifications
RFC1891.summary: Defines the SMTP service extension (DSN) adding NOTIFY, ORCPT, RET and ENVID parameters to RCPT/MAIL so clients can control delivery status notifications, with MTA conformance rules and examples.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new ESMTP service extension with new MAIL and RCPT parameters and MTA relay behaviour, so it belongs under SMTP.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service, which allows an SMTP client to specify (a) that delivery status notifications (DSNs) should be generated

MIME.why: A substantial section covers how DSNs are structured as multipart/report with message/delivery-status parts. The formats are defined in companion RFCs, so this is secondary.
MIME.quote: A DSN is transmitted as a MIME message with a top-level content-type of multipart/report

rejected.why: The parent of SMTP, so it is implied by the more specific SMTP tag.
Mailing list handling of DSNs is covered in 6.2.7, but only as one case of forwarding behaviour, not the document's subject.
The DSN message format is defined in RFC 1894, not here. This document only references it.
DNS appears only as the 'dns' MTA-name-type in the appendix and is not a subject of the document.
IANA registration of address-types is mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: Delivery Status Notifications (DSN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DSNs or mail delivery reporting. The SMTP tag covers the extension but not the notification subject itself.

RFC1892.title: The Multipart/Report Content Type for the Reporting of Mail System Administrative Messages
RFC1892.summary: Defines the multipart/report MIME container type for mail system administrative reports (such as delivery status notifications) and the text/rfc822-headers type for returning only the headers of a failed message.

MIME.why: The document defines a new MIME multipart subtype and a new text subtype, specifying body part structure and parameters.
MIME.quote: The Multipart/Report MIME content-type is a general "family" or "container" type for electronic mail reports of any kind.

media types.why: It registers two media types (multipart/report and text/rfc822-headers) with their required parameters and encoding considerations.
media types.quote: MIME type name: Text MIME subtype name: RFC822-Headers Required parameters: None

rejected.why: Considered the general email tag, but the more specific MIME and media types tags fit the content. Email is only the setting for the reports.
The document refers to the SMTP DSN extension (RFC 1891) only as a reference for requesting return of content. It does not specify or extend SMTP.
It mentions RFC 822 headers, but only to label and return them. It does not define header fields or addressing.

RFC1893.title: Enhanced Mail System Status Codes
RFC1893.summary: RFC 1893 defines a structured, machine-readable set of enhanced status codes (class.subject.detail) for mail system conditions, intended for use in delivery status notifications.

email.why: The document specifies mail system status codes for reporting delivery success and failure in Internet mail. It is about email delivery reporting in general, so readers of email would look for it there.
email.quote: This document defines a new set of status codes to report mail system conditions.

rejected.why: SMTP reply codes are the motivation and the model for the new codes. The document does not specify or extend SMTP. It defines a separate code space for use in DSNs.
The DSN message format is defined in a separate document (RFC 1894). This RFC defines only the status code values.
DNS is mentioned only as an example of a directory server failure (X.4.3) and of an unable-to-route condition (X.4.4).
The document says new codes are added only by standards-track documents, but it has no IANA registry section or registration procedure.

gaps.name: Delivery status notifications (DSN) / enhanced status codes
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for mail delivery status notifications or their status code registry. The nearest fit is the generic email tag.

RFC1894.title: An Extensible Message Format for Delivery Status Notifications
RFC1894.summary: Defines the message/delivery-status MIME content-type (used within multipart/report) for machine-readable delivery status notifications issued by MTAs and gateways, with fields, gatewaying guidance, and IANA type registries.

email.why: The document specifies the format of email delivery status notifications issued by MTAs and gateways, an email architecture/transport matter. No narrower email child tag (SMTP, message format) fits as the primary subject.
email.quote: This memo defines a MIME content-type that may be used by a message transfer agent (MTA) or electronic mail gateway to report the result of an attempt to deliver a message

media types.why: Defines and registers the message/delivery-status media type with its parameters and encoding considerations, and report-type for multipart/report.
media types.quote: The message/delivery-status content-type is defined as follows:

mailing lists.why: A dedicated appendix gives guidelines for mailing list managers to process DSNs and maintain subscriber lists, which is a stated purpose of the protocol.
mailing lists.quote: DSNs are designed to be used by mailing list exploders to allow them to detect and automatically delete recipients for whom mail delivery fails repeatedly.

rejected.why: The SMTP extension for DSNs is a separate memo; this one only defines the notification format and uses SMTP as context (MAIL FROM:<>, reply codes).
MIME and multipart/report are the framework used; the document defines a new content-type but is not about MIME structure itself, so the media types tag fits better.
Fields use RFC 822 header syntax, but the document is about status notifications, not the Internet message format.
X.400 appears only as an example foreign system for gatewaying and tunneling, not as a subject of the document.
Registries and registration forms for address-, diagnostic- and MTA-name-types are boilerplate-like appendices, not the main subject.

gaps.name: Delivery Status Notifications (DSN)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is DSNs, and the taxonomy has no tag for them. The closest fit is the generic email tag.

RFC1895.title: The Application/CALS-1840 Content-type
RFC1895.summary: Defines and registers the Application/CALS-1840 MIME media type, with filename and version parameters and a Multipart/Mixed structure, for exchanging MIL-STD-1840 technical data by Internet email.

media types.why: The document's core content is registering a new MIME media type (Application/CALS-1840) with required parameters, which is what the media types subject covers.
media types.quote: This document defines a new media type and a MIME message structure for exchanging data in conformance with MIL-STD-1840.

MIME.why: It specifies how MIL-STD-1840 transfer units are structured as MIME multipart messages and encoded, including an example message. This is substantial MIME body-structure content.
MIME.quote: each transfer unit shall correspond to a Multipart/Mixed MIME entity.

rejected.why: Email is only the transport for the data. The document defines a MIME type, not mail architecture or transport.
The RFC 822 header format is used in the example but not specified or extended.
PEM and MOSS are mentioned only in the Security Considerations as recommended privacy mechanisms.
The registration form is part of the media type definition, not guidance on IANA registries.

RFC1896.title: The text/enriched MIME Content-type
RFC1896.summary: Defines the text/enriched MIME content-type, a simple formatted-text subtype for Internet mail, with its formatting commands, line-break rules, charset handling, and example C converters.

media types.why: The RFC specifies a MIME text subtype, its syntax, parameters and semantics, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document defines one particular type of MIME data, the text/enriched MIME type.

MIME.why: Defines a MIME content-type and discusses multipart, charset parameters and multipart/alternative usage.
MIME.quote: MIME [RFC-1521] defines a format and general framework for the representation of a wide variety of data types in Internet mail.

rejected.why: HTML is only compared against and a converter to HTML 2.0 is given in an appendix; the document is not about HTML.
Mentioned only as an alternative format.
Mail is the context of use, but the document specifies a body format, not mail architecture or transport.
Charset handling is discussed, but only as a constraint on text/enriched, not as the subject.
The lang command uses RFC 1766 tags, a minor dependency.

RFC1897.title: IPv6 Testing Address Allocation
RFC1897.summary: Defines a temporary allocation of IPv6 provider-based unicast addresses (Registry ID 11111) for testing IPv6 prototype software, derived from AS numbers and IPv4 network addresses.

IPv6.why: The whole document specifies an IPv6 address format and allocation plan for testing, so it belongs under IPv6 addressing and deployment.
IPv6.quote: This document describes an allocation plan for IPv6 addresses to be used in testing IPv6 prototype software.

rejected.why: The document is about IPv6 addresses specifically, and IPv6 is the more specific tag. It already covers IPv6 addressing.
DHCP for IPv6 is only mentioned as one way to assign the addresses. The document does not specify it.
Autoconfiguration is only mentioned as one assignment method, and the document does not cover it.
IANA reserves the Registry ID, but the document is an address allocation plan, not IANA registry guidance.

RFC1898.title: CyberCash Credit Card Protocol Version 0.8
RFC1898.summary: Describes CyberCash's version 0.8 credit card payment system: its text-based message wrapper, RSA signature and DES encryption approach, and the set of customer, merchant and server messages for registration, card binding, purchase, authorization/capture and utility functions.

CyberCash.why: The whole document specifies the CyberCash credit card payment protocol and its messages, so it belongs on the CyberCash page.
CyberCash.quote: CyberCash is developing a general payments system for use over the Internet. The structure and communications protocols of version 0.8 are described.

rejected.why: The CyberCash tag is the more specific child, so its parent is implied and not listed.
MD5 is only used for hashes and checksums in the message format, and the document is not about it.
RSA is used for signatures and key encryption but is not the subject of the document.
DES is the encryption mechanism the protocol relies on, not what the document is about.
The document mentions application/cybercash and base64 encoding, but only as supporting apparatus.
Base64 is used only to encode binary fields.

RFC1899.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 1800-1899
RFC1899.summary: An annotated index of RFCs 1800 through 1899 giving each RFC's author, date, title, short abstract and status.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a catalogue of a block of RFC Series publications with their status. A reader browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1800 through RFCs 1899.

rejected.why: It notes standards-track status and lists RFCs 1871 and 1818 as entries, but it does not describe or address IETF procedures.
Several IPv6 RFCs appear as one-paragraph entries, but the document is not about IPv6.
SMTP extension RFCs are listed as entries among many others. The document does not specify or analyse SMTP.
MIME RFCs are listed as entries among many others. The document does not specify or analyse MIME.
The IPsec RFCs (1825-1829) are only listed as entries. The document is not about IPsec.
The X.500 RFCs (1801-1804, 1836-1838) are only listed as entries.

RFC1900.title: Renumbering Needs Work
RFC1900.summary: IAB statement urging development and deployment of tools and practices (FQDNs over hardcoded IPs, DHCP, dynamic DNS update, documentation) to make IP renumbering easier, motivated by CIDR aggregation.

renumbering.why: The whole document is about renumbering: its causes, costs, and the need for tools, procedures and documented experience.
renumbering.quote: A change in such IP addressing information associated with a host or subnet is known as "renumbering".

DHCP.why: The IAB strongly encourages DHCP implementation and deployment as a core part of the renumbering toolkit.
DHCP.quote: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is clearly an essential part of such a toolkit.

DNS update.why: The document urges standardization of authenticated dynamic DNS update and its integration with DHCP. Section 2 also argues that DNS localizes the changes caused by renumbering.
DNS update.quote: Support for dynamic update capabilities to the Domain Name System (DNS) that could be done with sufficient authentication would further facilitate host renumbering.

rejected.why: DNS is discussed as the indirection that localizes renumbering changes. The document does not specify or extend it, and the more specific DNS update tag already covers the DNS-related content.
CIDR is cited only as the motivation for renumbering. The document is not about CIDR itself.
The renumbering tag is a child of addressing and fits more specifically, so the parent is not listed.
The IAB authored the document and it mentions architecture in passing, but its subject is renumbering rather than architectural principles.

RFC1901.title: Introduction to Community-based SNMPv2
RFC1901.summary: Defines the Community-based Administrative Framework (SNMPv2C) for SNMPv2, reusing the SNMPv1 community concept with a new message version number, and introduces the SNMPv2 framework components.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the community-based administrative framework and message wrapper for SNMPv2 and overviews the SNMP framework components.
SNMP.quote: The purpose of this document is to define the Community-based Administrative Framework for the SNMP version 2 framework (SNMPv2).

rejected.why: MIB and SMI are only described briefly as framework components defined in other documents (RFC 1902, 1907).
ASN.1 is used for the message wrapper definition and SMI, but is only the notation, not the subject.
UDP is mentioned only as the preferred transport mapping, which is defined in another document.

RFC1902.title: Structure of Management Information for Version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1902.summary: Defines the SMIv2 for SNMPv2: the ASN.1 subset, macros (MODULE-IDENTITY, OBJECT-TYPE, NOTIFICATION-TYPE, OBJECT-IDENTITY), base data types, conceptual tables, naming hierarchy and rules for writing and revising MIB modules.

MIB.why: The SMI defines how MIB modules and managed objects are written, including macros, types, tables and revision rules. This is the core MIB/SMI specification.
MIB.quote: Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules.  These modules are written using an adapted subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1)

SNMP.why: It is a core part of the SNMPv2 framework and covers notifications and SNMPv2 entity behaviour. Its main subject is the information structure, which MIB covers.
SNMP.quote: The current framework is termed the SNMP version 2 framework (SNMPv2).

rejected.why: The document uses and restricts an ASN.1 subset as the notation for MIBs. It does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules in general; ASN.1 is the substrate.
Not related; it is a later data modelling language.

RFC1903.title: Textual Conventions for Version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1903.summary: RFC 1903 defines the initial set of SNMPv2 textual conventions (DisplayString, RowStatus, TruthValue, DateAndTime, etc.) as an SNMPv2-TC MIB module, plus the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro and its DISPLAY-HINT mapping.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB/SMI-level module (SNMPv2-TC) defining reusable types for MIB modules, including RowStatus row-creation semantics and the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro.
MIB.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the conventions are used with; the document's content is MIB type definitions, so the more specific MIB tag is used and SNMP is its ancestor.
The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro is written in ASN.1 macro notation, but ASN.1 is just the notation substrate, not the subject.
DisplayString references NVT ASCII from RFC 854 only as a character set definition; the document is not about Telnet.
NVT ASCII is only referenced for DisplayString; the document is not about the character set.
DateAndTime is one of many conventions defined, an SNMP-specific octet string format and not a general date-time representation.

RFC1904.title: Conformance Statements for Version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1904.summary: RFC 1904 defines the SNMPv2-CONF macros (OBJECT-GROUP, NOTIFICATION-GROUP, MODULE-COMPLIANCE, AGENT-CAPABILITIES) used to write conformance and capability statements for MIB modules.

MIB.why: The document specifies the SMI-level macros for conformance groups, compliance statements and agent capabilities that accompany MIB modules. This is MIB/SMI authoring material.
MIB.quote: The MODULE-COMPLIANCE macro is used to convey a minimum set of requirements with respect to implementation of one or more MIB modules.

SNMP.why: It is part of the SNMPv2 framework suite. It defines how SNMPv2 agents declare implementation level, and how management stations use sysORID to adapt to agents.
SNMP.quote: The AGENT-CAPABILITIES macro is used to convey a set of capabilities present in a SNMPv2 entity acting in an agent role.

rejected.why: The macros are written in ASN.1 macro notation, but the document is about SNMP conformance semantics, not ASN.1 itself.
YANG is unrelated here. The document predates it and concerns SMIv2 only.

RFC1905.title: Protocol Operations for Version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1905.summary: Specifies the protocol operations of SNMPv2: the PDU types (Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set, Response, Trap, Inform), their ASN.1 definitions, and the processing rules for sending and receiving them.

SNMP.why: The document is the core SNMPv2 protocol operations specification, defining PDUs, elements of procedure, error handling and roles of manager and agent entities.
SNMP.quote: It is the purpose of this document, Protocol Operations for SNMPv2, to define the operations of the protocol with respect to the sending and receiving of the PDUs.

rejected.why: MIBs and the SMI are referenced as what is being accessed, but the document defines no MIB module; it specifies protocol operations.
The PDUs are defined in ASN.1, but that is the notation used, not the subject.
UDP is only the preferred transport mapping, specified elsewhere (RFC 1906).
Transport mappings are defined in a separate document; here they are only mentioned in passing.
Fragmentation and Path MTU are mentioned briefly to advise on GetBulk max-repetitions, not as a subject of the document.

RFC1906.title: Transport Mappings for Version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1906.summary: Defines how SNMPv2 messages map onto transport domains (UDP, OSI CLNS/CONS, AppleTalk DDP, IPX), including address textual conventions, well-known ports, BER serialization rules, and proxy to SNMPv1.

SNMP.why: The document specifies SNMPv2 transport mappings, domains, and serialization, which is part of the SNMP framework.
SNMP.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define how the SNMPv2 maps onto an initial set of transport domains.

transport mapping.why: The document's core content is binding SNMPv2 onto several underlying transports (UDP, OSI, DDP, IPX), which fits the transport mapping topic.
transport mapping.quote: Each instance of a message is serialized onto a single DDP datagram [5], using the algorithm specified in Section 8.

rejected.why: AppleTalk DDP/NBP is only one of the transports SNMPv2 is mapped onto. The document does not specify AppleTalk itself, although it does discuss NBP addressing.
IPX is just one of the transports used. The document does not specify IPX itself.
UDP is the substrate for the preferred mapping. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
BER is used as the serialization encoding. The document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules, only restrictions on how BER is applied.
The SNMPv2-TM module only defines a few object identities and textual conventions for transport addresses. The document is not about MIB modules in general.
OSI CLNS/CONS is only a substrate here, and the document does not specify OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC1907.title: Management Information Base for Version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv2)
RFC1907.summary: RFC 1907 defines the SNMPv2-MIB module, with the system group, SNMP group, trap/notification objects, set-serialization lock, and conformance statements for SNMPv2 entities. It obsoletes RFC 1450.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SNMPv2-MIB) written in SMI, defining managed objects for the system and snmp groups. MIB is the most specific tag.
MIB.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define managed objects which describe the behavior of a SNMPv2 entity.

SNMP.why: The MIB instruments the SNMPv2 protocol entity itself: message counters, authentication-failure traps, and the set-coordination lock. SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: The management protocol, SNMPv2 [3], provides for the exchange of messages which convey management information between the agents and the management stations.

rejected.why: The MIB is written using an ASN.1 subset (the SMI), but ASN.1 is only the notation, not the subject.
Traps and notifications are SNMP-specific and unrelated to syslog.

RFC1908.title: Coexistence between Version 1 and Version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework
RFC1908.summary: Describes coexistence between SNMPv1 and SNMPv2: how to convert SMIv1 MIB modules, traps, compliance and capabilities statements to SMIv2, and how proxy agents and bi-lingual managers map protocol operations.

SNMP.why: The document specifies proxy agent and bi-lingual manager behaviour mapping PDUs between SNMPv1 and SNMPv2, the core of the SNMP framework coexistence.
SNMP.quote: The purpose of this document is to describe coexistence between version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework

MIB.why: A large part of the document lists rules for converting SMIv1 MIB modules (objects, traps, compliance, capabilities) to the SMIv2 form.
MIB.quote: MIB modules defined using the current framework may continue to be used with the SNMPv2 protocol.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation underlying SMI; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Parent of SNMP; the more specific SNMP tag fits.
Transport mappings are only mentioned as references, not addressed.

RFC1909.title: An Administrative Infrastructure for SNMPv2
RFC1909.summary: RFC 1909 defines an experimental administrative framework for SNMPv2: contexts, MIB views and view subtree families, access control policy, security models, proxy semantics, and the Report-PDU, plus clarifications on Inform-Request senders.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the SNMPv2 administrative framework (contexts, views, access control, proxy, Report-PDU) and amends the SNMPv2 protocol definition on Inform-Requests, so it belongs on the SNMP page.
SNMP.quote: to define an administrative framework which realizes effective management in a variety of configurations and environments

rejected.why: MIB views and view subtrees are discussed, but the document defines no MIB module and is not about the MIB or SMI itself.
Access control and MIB views are central, but they are specific to SNMP and are covered by the SNMP tag.
OBJECT IDENTIFIERs are used for view subtree naming only; the document is not about ASN.1.
The parent of SNMP, so it is implied; the document is about SNMP specifically.
Authentication and privacy algorithms are mentioned only as parameters of security models. The document explicitly says security issues are not directly discussed.

RFC1910.title: User-based Security Model for SNMPv2
RFC1910.summary: Defines the User-based Security Model (USEC) for SNMPv2, providing MD5 digest authentication, optional DES privacy, time-window replay protection, message format, processing procedures, and a MIB module.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the security model for SNMPv2: message format, authentication, privacy, replay protection and processing procedures.
SNMP.quote: it is the purpose of this document, User-based Security Model for SNMPv2, to define the first, and, as of this writing, only, security model

MIB.why: Defines the USEC MIB module with agentID, agentBoots, agentTime and error statistics counters, with compliance statements.
MIB.quote: SNMPv2-USEC-MIB DEFINITIONS ::= BEGIN

rejected.why: MD5 is used as the digest algorithm but the document is not about MD5 itself.
DES in CBC mode is the optional privacy mechanism, relied on rather than specified.
Agent time/boots synchronization is internal replay protection, not network clock sync like NTP.
ASN.1 is just the message encoding substrate.
Authentication is covered by the specific SNMP security model; SNMP is the more specific tag.

RFC1911.title: Voice Profile for Internet Mail
RFC1911.summary: RFC 1911 defines the Voice Profile for Internet Mail, a profile of MIME and ESMTP for exchanging voice messages between voice messaging platforms, including a new Multipart/Voice-Message type and the Audio/32KADPCM type.

VPIM.why: The whole document is the voice profile for Internet mail, which is the definition of VPIM.
VPIM.quote: The following document is a profile of the Internet standard MIME and ESMTP protocols for use as a digital voice networking protocol.

MIME.why: It defines the new Multipart/Voice-Message and Audio/32KADPCM MIME types and profiles which content types and encodings voice systems must support.
MIME.quote: This new MIME multipart structure provides a mechanism for packaging the senders spoken name, a spoken subject and, the message.

SMTP.why: A substantial section profiles which ESMTP commands, keywords and parameters are required or optional for voice messaging.
SMTP.quote: Messages are transported between voice mail machines using the Internet Extended Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (ESMTP).

message format.why: It profiles RFC 822 header fields and addressing for voice messages.
message format.quote: The following header lines are permitted for use with voice messages.

rejected.why: It registers Audio/32KADPCM and Multipart/Voice-Message, but only as part of the profile. The document is not about media type registration rules.
Section 6 only recommends that SNMP and MIBs be supported. This is a minor point and the document does not specify any management protocol.
DNS is only used for host naming in addresses and is not specified or extended here.
G.721 ADPCM is the default audio encoding. It is not G.711, and the taxonomy has no G.721 tag.

gaps.name: Audio/32KADPCM (G.721 ADPCM) audio encoding
gaps.why: The document registers this audio MIME type for G.721 32 kb/s ADPCM. The taxonomy has no G.721 or ADPCM tag.

RFC1912.title: Common DNS Operational and Configuration Errors
RFC1912.summary: RFC 1912 is an informational guide to common errors in DNS zone data (PTR/A, SOA, CNAME, MX, NS, glue, wildcards) and in BIND nameserver operation, obsoleting RFC 1537.

DNS.why: The whole document is operational and configuration guidance for DNS: resource records, SOA timers, delegation, lame delegations, glue, and server operation.
DNS.quote: This memo describes errors often found in both the operation of Domain Name System (DNS) servers, and in the data that these DNS servers contain.

rejected.why: Host label character rules are discussed in one subsection, but only as part of DNS data correctness, not as the document's subject.
MX records and mail naming are discussed only as DNS data, not mail transport.
The UDP checksum advice is a brief server-issue note; UDP is only the substrate.
Mail addresses in SOA/RP and MX records appear only as DNS data content.

RFC1913.title: Architecture of the Whois++ Index Service
