RFC1913.summary: Describes the architecture of the WHOIS++ Index Service, a mesh of index servers exchanging centroids as forward knowledge to make distributed directory search feasible, with POLL, CENTROID-CHANGES, DATA-CHANGED and SERVER-TO-ASK syntax.

WHOIS++.why: The whole document specifies the WHOIS++ distributed directory index architecture, with centroids, mesh servers and the protocol messages. This matches the WHOIS++ tag definition exactly.
WHOIS++.quote: A whois++ index server collects and collates the centroids (or other forward knowledge) of either a number of whois++ servers or of a number of other index servers.

rejected.why: X.500 is discussed only as the hierarchical approach whose flaws motivate the design. The document does not specify or profile it.

The topic is relevant, but the WHOIS++ tech tag sits under domain registration rather than directory services. The document is about WHOIS++ specifically, so I chose that tag and did not add the generic topic.
WHOIS++ is the more specific tag and the parent is implied, so listing WHOIS separately would duplicate it.
The index service locates which servers hold matching records, but it is a directory search and referral mechanism, not service discovery in the usual sense.

gaps.name: Distributed directory indexing / forward knowledge (centroids)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is a general architecture for indexing distributed databases using directory meshes and centroids. The taxonomy only has WHOIS++, which sits under domain registration, and no tag for general distributed directory indexing.

RFC1914.title: How to Interact with a Whois++ Mesh
RFC1914.summary: RFC 1914 specifies how a WHOIS++ client should traverse a mesh of WHOIS++ servers: following referrals, detecting loops, expanding searches via polled-by/polled-for, using the Directory of Servers, and caching.

WHOIS++.why: The whole document defines client behaviour for interacting with the WHOIS++ distributed directory mesh, including referral resolution, loop detection, and the Directory of Servers. This is the WHOIS++ tag.
WHOIS++.quote: In the Whois++ architecture [Deutsch94],[Weider94], mesh traversal is done by the client, since each server 'refers' the client to the next appropriate server(s).

rejected.why: WHOIS++ is a child of WHOIS and is the more specific fit, so the parent is not listed.
RWhois is a different referral-based registration data protocol. This document is only about WHOIS++.
DNS is only used to resolve server hostnames in the caching algorithm and is not the subject.
A WHOIS++ technology tag already sits under domain registration, and this is not about LDAP or X.500 directories. It is not tagged as a separate topic.

RFC1915.title: Variance for The PPP Compression Control Protocol and The PPP Encryption Control Protocol
RFC1915.summary: A BCP documenting an IESG variance to the RFC 1602 patent-license procedures, allowing the PPP Compression Control Protocol and Encryption Control Protocol to advance despite Motorola's patent claims, on the basis of a licensing assurance.

IPR.why: The document is about a variance to the IETF's patent and licensing assurance rules (RFC 1602 section 5.6) and Motorola's patent license statement.
IPR.quote: the IESG grants a variance on behalf of the PPP Working Group, to the procedures of RFC 1602 to allow the IESG to adopt the CCP and ECP

IETF process.why: It applies the IETF variance procedure and discusses rough consensus and standards-track advancement rules.
IETF process.quote: Within the Variance Procedure (published as RFC 1871), the IESG grants a variance

PPP.why: The affected specifications are the PPP CCP and ECP control protocols, which the variance allows to be standardized. The document does not specify them, only their standardization status.
PPP.quote: the Compression Control Protocol (CCP)

rejected.why: CCP is only the subject of the patent dispute. The document defines no compression format.
ECP is PPP encryption control, not IPsec, and the document has no technical content on encryption.

RFC1916.title: Enterprise Renumbering: Experience and Information Solicitation
RFC1916.summary: A PIER working group solicitation asking sites for case studies, tool descriptions, and lists of problem applications from IPv4 enterprise network renumbering efforts, to feed planned renumbering guidance documents.

renumbering.why: The whole document is about site renumbering: collecting experience, tools and application issues for changing IP addresses of enterprise networks.
renumbering.quote: There are immediate and increasingly severe requirements to renumber both small and large-scale networks.

rejected.why: The document focuses on renumbering in IPv4 networks, but it does not specify or analyse IPv4 itself. IPv4 is only the setting for the renumbering.
DNS is listed only as one of many places that must be updated in a renumbering. It is not a subject of the document.
The more specific child tag renumbering fits, so the parent is not needed.
The formatting rules in Appendix A are only apparatus for submissions, not the subject of the document.

RFC1917.title: An Appeal to the Internet Community to Return Unused IP Networks (Prefixes) to the IANA
RFC1917.summary: BCP appeal asking sites and providers to return unused IPv4 address blocks to the IANA or registries to slow address exhaustion and routing table growth, in the context of CIDR.

addressing.why: The document is about the stewardship, reclamation and reallocation of IPv4 address space, including the history of Class A/B/C allocation and how to return blocks.
addressing.quote: an appeal to the Internet community to return unused address space, i.e. any block of consecutive IP prefixes, to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA)

CIDR.why: A substantial part explains CIDR, supernetting and aggregation, and urges providers to keep CIDR blocks intact to limit routing table growth.
CIDR.quote: CIDR blocks are allocated in a way which promotes hierarchical routing.

rejected.why: The document concerns IPv4 address space, but the focus is address allocation and return, which fits addressing better. IPv4 is only the address family it discusses.
IANA is the party that receives returned blocks, but the document does not concern IANA registries or considerations guidance in the sense of the tag.
Routing table growth is the motivation, but the document is an address-return policy appeal, not a routing architecture or design document.
BGP is mentioned only in passing, as the protocol the customer's router must speak.
NAT is mentioned only as a reason some sites will never announce their internal networks.

RFC1918.title: Address Allocation for Private Internets
RFC1918.summary: BCP defining three IANA-reserved private IPv4 address blocks (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) for enterprises not needing global connectivity, with guidance on usage, filtering, renumbering and DNS handling.

addressing.why: The document's core is allocation and use of private IP address space, an address architecture matter; the IPv4 tag is less apt as it concerns allocation policy rather than the protocol.
addressing.quote: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has reserved the following three blocks of the IP address space for private internets

renumbering.why: Renumbering costs and strategies when moving hosts between private and public space or merging private internets are a substantial discussion theme.
renumbering.quote: The cost of using private internet address space is the potentially costly effort to renumber hosts and networks between public and private.

rejected.why: Document is about address allocation policy rather than the IPv4 protocol itself; addressing covers it more specifically, though IPv4 address lifecycle is arguably relevant.
NAT is not discussed; the document predates and does not specify translation, only gateways and filtering.
CIDR is referenced only as motivation for aggregation; the document is not about it.
DNS split-horizon is mentioned briefly in operational considerations but is not a main subject.
Mentioned only as an example of renumbering tools.

RFC1919.title: Classical versus Transparent IP Proxies
RFC1919.summary: Informational RFC comparing classical (client-aware) and transparent (intercepting) application proxies used in firewalls, covering addressing, routing, DNS, address hiding, packet filtering and conflicting-network interconnection.

firewall.why: The whole document analyses proxy-based firewall technology, classical versus transparent proxies, and their security and operational trade-offs.
firewall.quote: Many modern IP security systems (also called "firewalls" in the trade) make use of proxy technology to achieve access control.

rejected.why: DNS requirements and isolation are discussed as a consequence of each proxy type, but the document is not about DNS itself.
FTP is only the running example session; the protocol is not specified or analysed.
SOCKS is mentioned briefly as an example of modified-client proxy software, not the subject.
Address hiding and conflicting networks are touched on, but the document is about application proxies, not NAT.
Transparent proxies need TCP stack modifications, but TCP is not the subject.

gaps.name: application proxies / transparent proxying
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for application-layer proxies in general; firewall is the closest fit.

RFC1920.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC1920.summary: RFC 1920 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly list of Internet Official Protocol Standards, explaining the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and listing protocols by standardization state.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels, and RFC Editor/IESG processing rules, which is the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial part describes the RFC series, its publication rules, RFC Editor decision table, and how to obtain RFCs.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned only as a contact and as the source of Assigned Numbers; the document is not about IANA registries.
Many SNMP RFCs appear in the lists, but only as entries in status tables; the document is not about SNMP.
DNS RFCs are listed as entries only, not specified or analysed.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but these are process definitions rather than a glossary; covered by IETF process.
Lists historic protocols but gives no historical narrative or retrospective.

RFC1921.title: TNVIP Protocol
RFC1921.summary: Informational RFC from Bull defining TNVIP, a Telnet profile (terminal-type, EOR, binary, SGA options) plus a message format for emulating block-mode VIP terminals (screen, printer, screen-copy flows) to reach Bull DSA hosts over TCP/IP.

Telnet.why: The document is a Telnet profile: it specifies use of Terminal-Type, End of Record, Binary Transmission and Suppress Go Ahead options and Telnet commands (AO, BRK, IP) for TNVIP.
Telnet.quote: The goal of this document specifies a Telnet profile to support VIP terminal emulation allowing the access to the BULL hosts applications through a TCP/IP network.

rejected.why: Similar block-mode terminal emulation over Telnet, but it is for IBM 3270, not Bull VIP terminals.
TN3270 and SNA are IBM-specific; the document concerns Bull DSA, not SNA.
TCP is only the transport substrate for the Telnet connection.
ASCII character sets are mentioned only as the terminal character set, not as the subject.

gaps.name: TNVIP / Bull VIP terminal emulation (DSA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Bull DSA or VIP block-mode terminals. Telnet is the closest fit, but the TNVIP message protocol itself is not covered.

RFC1922.title: Chinese Character Encoding for Internet Messages
RFC1922.summary: Informational RFC defining the ISO-2022-CN and ISO-2022-CN-EXT 7-bit encodings and the CN-GB and CN-Big5 8-bit MIME charsets for carrying Chinese text in Internet messages, plus two new MIME parameters (charset-edition, charset-extension).

character sets.why: The document specifies Chinese character encodings (ISO-2022-CN, CN-GB, CN-Big5) and registers them as charset names. Readers of the character sets page would expect it.
character sets.quote: This document describes two encodings, ISO-2022-CN and ISO-2022-CN-EXT.

MIME.why: It defines new MIME Content-Type parameters (charset-edition, charset-extension) with formal syntax, and defines the MIME charset names for the encodings.
MIME.quote: Here we define two new MIME parameters to be used with "charset" parameters.

rejected.why: Email is the main carrier, but the document is about the character encodings, not the mail protocol.
ISO/IEC 10646 and Unicode get only a brief mention, and the document explicitly gives no details on how to use them.
Section 6 has a short note on using the encodings in X.400 GeneralText. That is not a substantial part of the document.
The parent topic is implied by the character sets tag, so it is not listed separately.
The ASN.1 appears only as a short X.400 definition, so the document is not about ASN.1.
The formal syntax is used to define the encodings, but the document is not about the notation.

gaps.name: Chinese character encodings (GB, Big5, CNS 11643, ISO-2022-CN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CJK or Chinese-specific encodings. The closest fit is the generic character sets tag.

RFC1923.title: RIPv1 Applicability Statement for Historic Status
RFC1923.summary: Applicability statement explaining why RIPv1 is moved to Historic status, chiefly because it is classful and a simple distance-vector protocol, and recommending RIPv2 instead.

RIP.why: The whole document analyses RIPv1's limitations and its applicability, and recommends RIPv2. It is about the RIP protocol family.
RIP.quote: Chief among these is that it is a classful routing protocol.  RIP packets do not carry prefix masks.

rejected.why: CIDR and supernetting are mentioned only as the changes that make classful RIPv1 unsuitable. The document is not about CIDR.
The document discusses a specific protocol's applicability, not routing architecture in general.

RFC1924.title: A Compact Representation of IPv6 Addresses
RFC1924.summary: An April 1 1996 joke RFC proposing a base-85 text encoding of 128-bit IPv6 addresses in 20 characters, with a chosen character set and a conversion procedure.

humor.why: Published 1 April 1996 as a whimsical April Fools RFC, with tongue-in-cheek claims such as processor flaws and obscurity as a security feature.
humor.quote: The new standard way of writing IPv6 addresses is to treat them as a 128 bit integer, encode that in base 85 notation

IPv6.why: The whole document is about the textual representation of IPv6 addresses and compares it with the existing text forms.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies a more compact representation of IPv6 addresses, which permits encoding in a mere 20 bytes.

rejected.why: It is a base-85 encoding of addresses, not Base64/32/16/45, and the taxonomy tag covers those specific encodings.
IPv6 is the more specific tag for IPv6 address text representation; the document does not address allocation or architecture.
ASCII is only the source of the character set chosen, not the subject.

RFC1925.title: The Twelve Networking Truths
RFC1925.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC listing twelve whimsical "fundamental truths" of networking, such as "It Has To Work" and "One size never fits all".

humor.why: The document is an April 1 humorous RFC of witty aphorisms about networking, with whimsical corollaries about babies and pigs flying. It fits the humorous RFCs subject.
humor.quote: With sufficient thrust, pigs fly just fine. However, this is not necessarily a good idea.

rejected.why: The truths are general engineering aphorisms, not architectural principles of the Internet, and the document is satirical.
The document defines no terms or glossary and does not address requirements language.

RFC1926.title: An Experimental Encapsulation of IP Datagrams on Top of ATM
RFC1926.summary: An April 1st joke RFC that defines "IP over ATM" as IP datagrams sent as Morse code beeps over Acoustical Transmission Media (sound waves), with nibble-to-letter mapping and standard tone frequencies.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody that redefines ATM as Acoustical Transmission Media and encapsulates IP in Morse code beeps. It belongs on the humorous RFCs page.
humor.quote: This is a non-recommended standard. Distribution of this memo is unnecessary.

rejected.why: The title and abbreviation suggest Asynchronous Transfer Mode, but the document uses ATM to mean Acoustical Transmission Media. It has nothing to do with real ATM.
It nominally describes an IP encapsulation over a link medium, but the content is a joke and not a real link-layer specification.

RFC1927.title: Suggested Additional MIME Types for Associating Documents
RFC1927.summary: An April 1st joke RFC proposing new MIME types for electronic staples and paper clips to associate documents, with patents, recycling, sculpture and safety hazards.

humor.why: Dated 1 April 1996, this is a whimsical April Fools RFC that parodies MIME type proposals with electronic staples, paper clip sculpture and safety hazards.
humor.quote: electronic staples should be bought in boxes of 5000.
humor.section: 2) patents on the electronic staple and paper clip

media types.why: The document is framed as a proposal for new MIME types and their parameters, so readers browsing media type registrations might look for it. The proposal is a parody.
media types.quote: "color=" and "shape=" attributes in the MIME line should allow senders to customize the appearance of individual staples or paper clips.
media types.section: 4) custom-look electronic staples and paper clips

rejected.why: The document only borrows MIME type names as the frame for its joke. It does not specify body structure or encodings.
It mentions First Virtual charges per staple, but only as part of the parody, so the document is not about payment protocols.

RFC1928.title: SOCKS Protocol Version 5
RFC1928.summary: Specifies SOCKS version 5, a shim-layer protocol letting TCP and UDP client-server applications traverse a network firewall via a proxy server, with authentication method negotiation, CONNECT/BIND/UDP ASSOCIATE requests and replies.

SOCKS.why: The whole document defines the SOCKS v5 protocol: method negotiation, request/reply formats, and UDP relay.
SOCKS.quote: The protocol described here is designed to provide a framework for client-server applications in both the TCP and UDP domains to conveniently and securely use the services of a network firewall.

rejected.why: SOCKS is a child of firewall and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
TCP is only the transport the SOCKS client uses to reach the server; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
UDP datagrams are relayed, but the document specifies SOCKS's UDP relay header, not UDP itself.
GSSAPI is only named as a mandatory authentication method; its sub-negotiation is in separate memos.
Method negotiation is part of SOCKS, but the document defines no authentication mechanism of its own.
FTP is mentioned only as an example use of the BIND command.

RFC1929.title: Username/Password Authentication for SOCKS V5
RFC1929.summary: Specifies the username/password authentication subnegotiation for SOCKS Version 5, defining the request and response message formats exchanged during connection setup.

SOCKS.why: The document extends SOCKS V5 by defining one of its authentication subnegotiation methods, so readers of the SOCKS subject would expect it.
SOCKS.quote: This document describes one of those protocols, as it fits into the SOCKS Version 5 authentication "subnegotiation".

rejected.why: The SOCKS tag is more specific and the authentication here is a SOCKS subnegotiation. Tagging the generic topic as well would be redundant.
The subnegotiation is SOCKS-specific and does not use SASL.
Not related to HTTP. It is only a similar username/password scheme.
SOCKS runs over TCP, but the document says nothing about TCP itself.

RFC1930.title: Guidelines for creation, selection, and registration of an Autonomous System (AS)
RFC1930.summary: BCP giving operators guidelines on when to create, select and register an Autonomous System number, based on routing policy, multihoming, and prefix-to-AS mapping.

routing architecture.why: The document defines the AS as the unit of inter-domain routing policy and gives design guidance on when to create one, including multihoming and prefix aggregation. This is routing architecture and design principles.
routing architecture.quote: ASes are the unit of routing policy in the modern world of exterior routing

BGP.why: The guidance on AS use is framed around BGP as the recommended exterior protocol, and it covers BGP-specific aspects such as AS_SET and ATOMIC_AGGREGATE origin handling.
BGP.quote: This happens when aggregating using the AS_SET attribute in BGP, wherein the concept of origin is lost.

rejected.why: Multi-homed sites are the main sample case, but the document is about AS allocation criteria in general, not multihoming architectures.
CIDR prefixes are used as terminology and for aggregation advice, but the document is not about CIDR.
EGP is mentioned only as an example of a protocol the guidance applies to, and it is historic.
OSPF and IS-IS are cited only as examples of classless-capable IGPs in the IGP issues section.
The reserved private AS range is mentioned briefly, but the document is not about IANA registry policy.
WHOIS is mentioned only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

gaps.name: Autonomous System number allocation and registration
gaps.why: The document's core subject is the policy for assigning and registering AS numbers. The taxonomy has no tag for AS numbers or Internet number resource policy, so routing architecture is the closest fit.

RFC1931.title: Dynamic RARP Extensions for Automatic Network Address Acquisition
RFC1931.summary: Informational memo documenting Dynamic RARP (DRARP), Sun's extension of RARP that uses new opcodes to dynamically allocate temporary protocol addresses from an address authority, later superseded by DHCP.

ARP.why: DRARP extends RARP, part of the ARP family, with new opcodes (DRARP_REQUEST, DRARP_REPLY, DRARP_ERROR) in the same packet format. ARP is the closest taxonomy tag for this address-resolution protocol family.
ARP.quote: DRARP is used to acquire (or allocate) a protocol level address given the fixed hardware address for a host.

DHCP.why: The document performs automatic network address acquisition and allocation, the same role DHCP later took over. It also discusses an address authority, temporary bindings and lease-like recycling, so readers of DHCP history would want it.
DHCP.quote: The role of DRARP, and to some extent the configuration protocol used in conjunction with it, has subsequently been addressed by the DHCP protocol [9].

rejected.why: TFTP is only mentioned as the second phase of the RARP/TFTP boot model that DRARP extends. The document does not specify or change it.
Naming services (NIS, DNS domains) appear only as context for the surrounding administrative framework.
ONC RPC is mentioned only as the authentication and IPalloc substrate of the Sun framework. It is not what the document is about.
ICMP echo is mentioned once as a way to probe for duplicate addresses. That is incidental.

gaps.name: RARP (Reverse Address Resolution Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no RARP tag. DRARP is a direct extension of RARP, so a RARP or bootstrap tag would fit better than ARP.

RFC1932.title: IP over ATM: A Framework Document
RFC1932.summary: Informational framework document that classifies and compares the IP over ATM proposals (Classical IP, NHRP, Peer, Integrated, transition models), covering encapsulation, connection-oriented vs connectionless tradeoffs, and crossing IP subnet boundaries.

ATM.why: The whole document is a taxonomy of IP over ATM models, encapsulations (LLC/SNAP, TULIP, TUNIC), and ATM signalling/addressing issues.
ATM.quote: The IP over ATM Working Group of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is chartered to develop standards for routing and forwarding IP packets over ATM sub-networks.

NHRP.why: NHRP is described as the ROLC model, and its routing-loop limitations are analysed at length in Sections 7 and 8.2.
NHRP.quote: NHRP supports the establishment of direct connections across IP subnets in the ATM domain.
NHRP.section: 3. Parameters Common to IP Over ATM Proposals

rejected.why: ARP and address resolution are discussed throughout, and Appendix A covers ARP in ATM. The ARP server itself is specified in RFC 1577, so ARP is only a supporting topic here.
Section 5 mentions RSVP and QoS only to say they are outside the working group's scope.
Section 7 covers routing loops over NBMA networks, but this is a side issue of the ATM and NHRP discussion.
RFC 1626 and MTU discovery get a passing mention only.
IP multicast over ATM (IPMC) is mentioned briefly and is not a substantial part of the document.

RFC1933.title: Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 Hosts and Routers
RFC1933.summary: Specifies IPv6/IPv4 transition mechanisms: dual IP layer nodes, IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses, and configured and automatic IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling, including MTU, hop limit, ICMP handling and header construction.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document defines IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and transition mechanisms (dual stack, tunneling), which is exactly this topic.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document specifies IPv4 compatibility mechanisms that can be implemented by IPv6 hosts and routers.

tunneling.why: A major part of the document specifies configured and automatic IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation, decapsulation, MTU/fragmentation, hop limit and ICMP handling.
tunneling.quote: IPv6/IPv4 hosts and routers can tunnel IPv6 datagrams over regions of IPv4 routing topology by encapsulating them within IPv4 packets.

rejected.why: The more specific child IPv6 transition fits better; the document does not specify IPv6 itself, only coexistence with IPv4.
It specifies IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation (protocol 41), not generic IP-in-IP; the general tunneling topic suffices.
Section 3.2 only briefly covers A/AAAA record handling by resolvers; it is a minor part, not a subject of the document.
Path MTU Discovery is used to size the tunnel MTU but is not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only as one way to acquire an IPv4 address; not the subject.
ICMP error relaying across the tunnel is a supporting detail, not the document's subject.

RFC1934.title: Ascend's Multilink Protocol Plus (MP+)
RFC1934.summary: Defines Ascend's MP+, an extension to PPP Multilink that adds an in-band control channel with reliable delivery, messages and state machines for adding/removing channels, closing sessions and remote management, plus a new LCP option.

PPP.why: MP+ extends PPP Multilink, is negotiated via a new LCP option (type 22) and uses PPP framing and a PPP protocol ID. PPP is the closest taxonomy fit, as there is no multilink-specific tag.
PPP.quote: Multilink Protocol Plus (MP+) is a new control protocol for managing multiple data links that are bundled by MP.

rejected.why: This tag is about IEEE 802.1AX link aggregation of Ethernet links. MP+ bundles PPP channels, although the concept is similar.
Dial-up channels and phone numbers are used, but ISDN access is never specified or discussed.
The remote management feature is only a simple keystroke and character relay. It is not a management architecture or protocol in the sense of this tag.

gaps.name: PPP Multilink Protocol (MP) / bundling of multiple links
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for multilink bundling or inverse multiplexing over PPP. This is the central subject, and PPP is only the parent.

RFC1935.title: What is the Internet, Anyway?
RFC1935.summary: An informational essay (from Matrix News) defining what "the Internet" is, distinguishing the core Internet, consumer Internet, and the Matrix based on IP and interactive services versus asynchronous mail/news networks.

internet architecture.why: The document's whole purpose is to define what the Internet is and to layer it into core, consumer and Matrix categories. This is a conceptual question about the Internet's scope and architecture.
internet architecture.quote: We further choose to define the Internet as being those networks that use IP to permit users to use both the communication services

terminology.why: A large part of the document proposes and defends definitions such as core Internet, consumer Internet, the Matrix and enterprise IP network. A reader looking for glossary-style definitions would want it.
terminology.quote: Let's call the non-firewalled computers the core Internet, and the core plus the consumer-capable computers the consumer Internet.

rejected.why: Firewalls are used to distinguish supplier-capable from consumer-capable networks, but the memo does not specify or analyse firewall technology.
Mail is discussed as an asynchronous service that defines the Matrix, but the memo does not address email protocols or architecture.
It touches on earlier attempts to equate the Internet with the ARPANET, NSFNET and USENET, but this is a brief aside and not a retrospective.
USENET news is mentioned as an example of an asynchronous service, but the memo does not cover news formats or distribution.
DNS names are mentioned briefly to show they do not define Internet membership, and the memo does not address DNS itself.

RFC1936.title: Implementing the Internet Checksum in Hardware
RFC1936.summary: Informational memo describing a pipelined hardware design (with PLD source code) for computing the Internet Checksum at 1.26 Gbps in DMA/host-interface hardware, using a toroidal ones-complement carry-lookahead adder.

checksum.why: The whole document is about implementing the Internet Checksum: ones-complement summation, a toroidal lookahead adder, hardware and software interfaces, and PLD code.
checksum.quote: This memo presents a techniques for efficiently implementing the Internet Checksum in hardware.

rejected.why: The Internet checksum is a ones-complement sum, not a cyclic redundancy check.
TCP, UDP and IP are only cited as protocols that use the checksum; the memo does not specify or extend them.
UDP is only cited as a user of the checksum; the memo does not address UDP itself.
IP appears only as an example of a protocol with a header checksum; the memo does not address IP.

RFC1937.title: "Local/Remote" Forwarding Decision in Switched Data Link Subnetworks
RFC1937.summary: Informational memo arguing that the IP subnet "local/remote" forwarding decision should be decoupled from addressing on SVC-based data link subnetworks (ATM, Frame Relay, X.25), letting hosts choose direct SVCs, shortcuts or routers based on QoS and traffic needs.

ATM.why: The document's main running example and concern is IP over ATM SVC subnetworks (RFC1577 LIS model) and how to relax its constraints. ATM is the principal SVC technology addressed.
ATM.quote: A typical example of applying the IP subnet architecture to an SVC-based Data Link subnetwork is "Classical IP and ARP over ATM"

addressing.why: The document revisits the IP subnet addressing model, decoupling forwarding from address prefixes and proposing Local Addressing Groups with prefix assignment.
addressing.quote: To provide scalable routing each LAG should be given an IP address prefix, and elements within the LAG should be assigned addresses out of this prefix.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one possible mechanism for obtaining link layer addresses; the document does not specify or analyse it.
QoS requirements motivate the forwarding decision, but the document explicitly defines no QoS mechanism or signalling.
Named only as another example of an SVC technology; the discussion is generic and ATM-centred.
Mentioned only in passing as an SVC example, not addressed in its own right.
Referenced only as a way to resolve addresses in the traditional model; not the subject.

RFC1938.title: A One-Time Password System
RFC1938.summary: RFC 1938 specifies the S/KEY-derived One-Time Password (OTP) system, using iterated secure hashes of a pass-phrase and server seed to produce single-use passwords, with challenge syntax, six-word/hex encodings, reinitialization and race-attack protection.

OTP.why: The whole document specifies the OTP system: generation, challenge format, verification, and pass-phrase changes.
OTP.quote: This document describes a one-time password authentication system (OTP).

rejected.why: MD5 is a mandatory hash used as a building block, but the document is not about MD5 itself; it only defines the interface to it.
SHA is one of the supported hash functions; used as a substrate, not the subject.
Parent topic of OTP; the more specific OTP tag already covers it.
No HMAC is used; the construction is iterated plain hashing.

RFC1939.title: Post Office Protocol - Version 3
RFC1939.summary: RFC 1939 specifies POP3, the Post Office Protocol version 3, a simple protocol letting a workstation retrieve and delete mail from a server maildrop, with its states, commands, optional commands, and APOP authentication.

POP3.why: The whole document defines the POP3 protocol: states, commands, responses, optional commands, and operational considerations.
POP3.quote: The Post Office Protocol - Version 3 (POP3) is intended to permit a workstation to dynamically access a maildrop on a server host

rejected.why: Only mentioned as how mail enters the transport system and as the context for the maildrop; POP3 does not specify SMTP.
Mentioned as a more advanced alternative and compared in the scaling section, but the document is not about IMAP.
MD5 is only the digest used inside the APOP command; the document defines nothing new about MD5.
The Message Format section only covers octet counting and says messages conform to RFC 822; it does not define the format.
TCP is just the transport (port 110) the protocol runs over.

RFC1940.title: Source Demand Routing: Packet Format and Forwarding Specification (Version 1)
RFC1940.summary: Specifies the Source Demand Routing Protocol (SDRP) version 1 packet format, forwarding procedures, control packets, probing and MTU discovery for source-initiated inter-domain and intra-domain routes via IP encapsulation (protocol 42).

routing architecture.why: SDRP is a source-routing architecture and forwarding scheme complementing hop-by-hop routing; no specific protocol tag fits, so the routing architecture topic is the best match.
routing architecture.quote: The purpose of SDRP is to support source-initiated selection of routes to complement the route selection provided by existing routing protocols

rejected.why: BGP/IDRP only supply routing information for the D-FIB and loop prevention; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
ICMP messages are consumed for MTU discovery and error correlation, but the document does not define ICMP.
Section 9 describes SDRP-specific MTU discovery using ICMP and probes, a minor part of the document.
SDRP encapsulates IP in an SDRP header over IP protocol 42, but it is a source-routing protocol, not generic IP-in-IP encapsulation.
IPv4 is the substrate for delivery headers and addressing; the document is not about IPv4 itself.

gaps.name: Source Demand Routing Protocol (SDRP) / source routing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for source-routing or source-demand-routing protocols; the document specifies this protocol directly, so a dedicated tag would help.

RFC1941.title: Frequently Asked Questions for Schools
RFC1941.summary: FYI 22 is an introductory FAQ for primary and secondary school educators about getting connected to and using the Internet (costs, access types, services, projects, acceptable use and security), with resource lists and a glossary.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory guide aimed at Internet users (educators), which is the subject of the user guides topic.
user guides.quote: act as an introduction to the Internet for faculty, administration, and other school personnel in primary and secondary schools

rejected.why: Not a taxonomy id; the closest is 'web', but the Web is only explained at a lay level as one of several services, not specified or analysed.
The Web is explained in a few paragraphs for novices; the document is not about web architecture.
Email and mailing lists are described briefly as user services, not specified or analysed.
FTP, Telnet, Gopher and WAIS are only briefly described as user tools, not the subject of the document.
SLIP/PPP accounts are mentioned only as an access option and glossary entries.
Section 7 gives general advice on AUPs, filtering and viruses for schools, but it is a minor part and not operational security guidance for infrastructure.

gaps.name: Internet in education / K-12 school networking
gaps.why: The document is about getting schools online and educational use of the Internet, with no matching taxonomy subject beyond the generic user guides.

RFC1942.title: HTML Tables
RFC1942.summary: RFC 1942 specifies an experimental extension to HTML that adds a table model (TABLE, CAPTION, COLGROUP, COL, THEAD/TBODY/TFOOT, TR, TH/TD), with its DTD and recommended layout algorithms.

HTML.why: The whole document defines HTML table elements, attributes, DTD and layout behaviour, so it belongs on the HTML page.
HTML.quote: This specification extends HTML to support a wide variety of tables.

rejected.why: The DTD is written in SGML, but SGML is only the notation HTML is defined in. The document does not address SGML document interchange.
LANG and DIR attributes are described, but only as common attributes. They are a minor part of the document.
Speech and braille rendering are mentioned as motivations and supported by AXIS/AXES attributes, but this is not the document's main subject.
The LANG attribute refers to RFC 1766, but the document only uses language tags and does not specify them.

RFC1943.title: Building an X.500 Directory Service in the US
RFC1943.summary: Informational guide for US organizations planning to build an X.500 White Pages directory service, covering the X.500 directory and information models, legal and privacy issues, infrastructure, pilot projects, and recommendations.

X.500.why: The whole document is about building and operating an X.500 directory service: its directory model (DSA, DUA, DIT), information model, infrastructure (QUIPU, PSI pilot) and deployment recommendations.
X.500.quote: This document provides definition and recommends considerations that must be undertaken to operate a X.500 Directory Service in the United States.

LDAP.why: LDAP is described as the lightweight DUA access protocol to X.500 and its use at Michigan is noted. It is only a brief part of the document, so it is secondary.
LDAP.quote: The IETF has since defined and standardized the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) [11]; a protocol for accessing on-line Directory services

rejected.why: The legal and privacy sections (user rights, data integrity) are about directory policy rather than protocol privacy considerations. They are a supporting part of the X.500 deployment guidance.
Whois and finger are mentioned only as DUA access interfaces to X.500, not specified or analysed.
PEM is mentioned only as one application of X.500 key certificates.
This is the parent of X.500 and LDAP, so it is implied by the more specific tags.
Whois++ is mentioned only in passing as an alternative DUA interface and as a possible alternative to X.500.

RFC1944.title: Benchmarking Methodology for Network Interconnect Devices
RFC1944.summary: RFC 1944 defines a benchmarking methodology for network interconnect devices (routers, bridges): throughput, latency, frame loss, back-to-back, system recovery and reset tests, with setup, frame formats and reporting formats.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a benchmarking methodology for network devices: test setup, procedures and reporting formats.
benchmarking.quote: This document discusses and defines a number of tests that may be used to describe the performance characteristics of a network interconnecting device.

rejected.why: The document is about lab benchmarking of devices, which the more specific benchmarking tag covers.
RIP update frames are used only as test traffic in an appendix example.
SNMP queries are used only as a management-load modifier.
Ethernet, FDDI and token ring are test media and frame sizes, not the subject.
ARP is used only for learning frames in the test setup.
A UDP Echo Request is the test frame; UDP itself is not the subject.

RFC1945.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.0
RFC1945.summary: RFC 1945 specifies HTTP/1.0, the request/response application protocol of the World Wide Web, covering messages, methods, status codes, header fields, caching-related headers, and Basic access authentication.

HTTP.why: The document is the HTTP/1.0 specification itself, defining messages, methods, status codes and headers.
HTTP.quote: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is an application-level protocol with the lightness and speed necessary for distributed, collaborative, hypermedia information systems.

HTTP authentication.why: Section 11 defines the challenge-response framework and the Basic scheme (WWW-Authenticate, Authorization), which readers of HTTP authentication would want.
HTTP authentication.quote: HTTP provides a simple challenge-response authentication mechanism which may be used by a server to challenge a client request

rejected.why: Expires, If-Modified-Since, Pragma and Last-Modified are defined, but caching is only one part of the HTTP spec, not a focus of its own.
The document defines the http URL scheme and uses URI syntax, but the focus is HTTP itself and URI syntax is delegated to RFC 1738 and RFC 1808.
HTTP borrows MIME constructs and Appendix C compares the two, but the document is not about MIME.
Appendix A defines message/http, but this is incidental to the main subject.
The augmented BNF is only the notation used in the specification.
TCP is only the transport HTTP usually runs over.

RFC1946.title: Native ATM Support for ST2+
RFC1946.summary: Informational memo describing how to support native ATM virtual circuits for ST2/ST2+ reservations, covering signalling options over ATM (Q.2931), QoS mapping from ST flowspecs to ATM parameters, and implementation experience.

ST-II.why: The document describes how the ST2/ST2+ stream protocol and its SCMP signalling are mapped onto ATM, so it is about ST-II.
ST-II.quote: Both ST2 and ST2+ really consist of two protocols: SCMP and ST.

ATM.why: It covers native ATM circuits, Q.2931 signalling, multipoint VCs, AAL5 encapsulation and IP over ATM interworking.
ATM.quote: This memo describes a working implementation which enables applications to directly invoke ATM services

QoS.why: A substantial part of the document maps reservation flowspec QoS parameters (rate, delay, jitter) to ATM QoS parameters (PCR, CPCS-SDU size, transit delay).
QoS.quote: Mapping Reservation QoS to ATM QoS
QoS.section: 5.0 Mapping of Reservation QoS to ATM QoS

rejected.why: RSVP is discussed only as a comparison point and for its shortcomings over ATM. The document is about ST2+, not RSVP.
The document refers to IPv5 and to classical IP over ATM only as background and as a signalling substrate. It says nothing new about IPv4 itself.
Multicast mapping to ATM multipoint VCs is discussed, but it is part of ST2 over ATM and not IP multicast routing.
ATMARP is mentioned only as an address resolution aid and is not the subject of the document.

RFC1947.title: Greek Character Encoding for Electronic Mail Messages
RFC1947.summary: Informational RFC specifying how to encode Greek text in email using ISO 8859-7 with MIME Base64 or Quoted-Printable, with a character-set mapping table and warnings about common non-standard practices.

character sets.why: The document defines the use of the ISO 8859-7 Greek character set and maps many Greek code pages to it, so it belongs under character set registration and use.
character sets.quote: the text is first translated into the ISO 8859-7 character set, and then encoded using either the Base64

MIME.why: It profiles the MIME headers, charset parameter, transfer encodings (Base64, Quoted-Printable, 8BIT) and RFC 1522 header encoding for Greek email.
MIME.quote: Content-type: text/plain; charset=ISO-8859-7

rejected.why: Email is the application context, but the subject is the character encoding. MIME is the more specific tag for the email-specific content.
Base64 is only one of the transfer encodings used. The document does not define or specify it.
Header encoding is mentioned only briefly as an optional item, and the RFC 822 header format is not itself addressed.
The child tag character sets is the more specific fit for this document.
8-bit SMTP is mentioned only as a future possibility, and the document does not specify it.

RFC1948.title: Defending Against Sequence Number Attacks
RFC1948.summary: Informational RFC proposing a TCP implementation change that derives initial sequence numbers from a per-connection keyed hash (MD5 over the connection 4-tuple and a secret) plus the timer, to block sequence number guessing and IP spoofing attacks.

TCP.why: The document specifies a change to how TCP implementations choose initial sequence numbers and discusses a common TCP implementation bug (SYN-RCVD queue handling). Readers of TCP would want it.
TCP.quote: we propose a simple modification to TCP implementations that should be a very substantial block to the current wave of attacks.

randomness.why: A substantial part of the design concerns the secret and its generation, and requires random numbers to follow the randomness recommendations. The ISN scheme depends on unpredictability.
randomness.quote: The secret data can either be a true random number [10], or it can be the combination of some per-host secret and the boot time of the machine.

rejected.why: MD5 is only the suggested hash used inside function F, not something the document is about.
The topic is covered by the more specific TCP tag and the attack discussion. Nothing in the document is general security guidance beyond this attack.
Cryptographic authentication is mentioned only as the proper but slow-to-deploy solution; the document does not address it.
Telnet, rlogin and rsh are mentioned as victim protocols or context, not specified or analysed.
F is described as a hash of the connection-id and a secret, but HMAC is not specified or named.

gaps.name: TCP sequence number attacks / IP spoofing defence
gaps.why: The document is about defending against ISN prediction and spoofing; no taxonomy tag covers transport-layer attack defence, so TCP is used as the closest fit.

RFC1949.title: Scalable Multicast Key Distribution
RFC1949.summary: RFC 1949 proposes using the Core Based Tree (CBT) multicast protocol's secure join process to distribute group and sender-specific keys scalably, via group key distribution centres delegated to authenticated tree nodes, with IGMPv3 support suggested.

multicast security.why: The whole document is about distributing group session keys and sender-specific keys to multicast groups, plus secure joining and access control. This is group key management for multicast.
multicast security.quote: This memo provides a scalable solution to the multicast key distribution problem.

multicast.why: The scheme is built into the CBT multicast protocol's join and ack process. It also proposes secure-join extensions to IGMP (Appendix B). Readers of multicast routing would want it.
multicast.quote: CBT is a new architecture for local and wide-area IP multicasting, being unique in its utilization of just one shared delivery tree per group

rejected.why: IGMP is only the host-to-router mechanism the scheme relies on. Appendix B suggests a small extension for secure, non-suppressible reports, but that is a side proposal, not the document's subject.
The security architecture and Security Associations are the context for the scheme. The document does not specify or extend IPsec.
The more specific child multicast security fits better, so the parent is not listed.
PIM is mentioned only in comparison with CBT's hard state.
Photuris and ISAKMP are cited only as protocols for negotiating sender security parameters with the primary core. The document does not specify or extend them.
Public-key distribution via DNS is assumed, and X.509-like ACLs are suggested, but PKI is not the subject.

gaps.name: Core Based Trees (CBT) multicast protocol
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CBT tag. The document is closely tied to the CBT protocol, which readers would look for under multicast routing.

RFC1950.title: ZLIB Compressed Data Format Specification version 3.3
RFC1950.summary: RFC 1950 specifies the zlib compressed data format, a wrapper (header, optional preset dictionary ID, Adler-32 trailer) around DEFLATE-compressed data, and defines the Adler-32 checksum.

zlib.why: The whole document defines the zlib stream structure: CMF/FLG header, FDICT preset dictionary, compressed data and ADLER32 trailer.
zlib.quote: This specification defines a lossless compressed data format.

checksum.why: Adler-32 is defined, rationalised and given sample code; readers of checksum topics would want it.
checksum.quote: This specification also defines the ADLER-32 checksum (an extension and improvement of the Fletcher checksum), used for detection of data corruption

rejected.why: DEFLATE is the compression method carried inside zlib but is specified in a separate document (RFC 1951); here it is only referenced.
gzip is only mentioned as another user of deflate; it is not specified here.
The more specific zlib tag fits, so the parent topic is implied.
CRC32 is only mentioned in the rationale as a comparison to Adler-32.

RFC1951.title: DEFLATE Compressed Data Format Specification version 1.3
RFC1951.summary: Specifies the DEFLATE lossless compressed data format (LZ77 plus Huffman coding), its block structure, and the code tables, and is compatible with gzip and zlib.

DEFLATE.why: The whole document defines the DEFLATE format: block types, fixed and dynamic Huffman codes, and length/distance codes. It is the specification for that format.
DEFLATE.quote: This specification defines a lossless compressed data format that compresses data using a combination of the LZ77 algorithm and Huffman coding

rejected.why: The format is meant to be compatible with gzip output. The gzip file format and its wrapper are not specified here, only DEFLATE.
zlib is cited only as source code and a reference for integrity checking. The zlib wrapper format is defined elsewhere.
This is the parent topic. The more specific DEFLATE tag fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC1952.title: GZIP file format specification version 4.3
RFC1952.summary: Specifies the gzip lossless compressed file format (member header/trailer, flags, CRC-32, extra fields), which uses DEFLATE and is compatible with the gzip utility.

gzip.why: The entire document specifies the gzip file format: member structure, header fields, flags, trailer and compliance rules.
gzip.quote: This specification defines a lossless compressed data format that is compatible with the widely used GZIP utility.

rejected.why: DEFLATE is the compression method used (CM=8) but is documented elsewhere; this document only wraps it.
CRC-32 is used for integrity and sample code is given in an appendix, but the document is not about CRC polynomial choice.
CRC-32 is a component of the format, not the subject of the document.
The more specific gzip tag applies, so the parent is implied.
ISO 8859-1 is only mentioned for file name and comment fields.

RFC1953.title: Ipsilon Flow Management Protocol Specification for IPv4 Version 1.0
RFC1953.summary: Specifies the Ipsilon Flow Management Protocol (IFMP), a private protocol by which a node tells an adjacent node to attach a layer 2 label to an IPv4 flow so it can be switched rather than routed, including the adjacency and redirection sub-protocols.

ATM.why: IFMP is Ipsilon's IP switching protocol for flow-labelled IPv4 over ATM links, with labels switched at layer 2. The ATM encapsulation is in a companion document, so this is the closest taxonomy fit for IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: The specification for ATM data links is given in [ENCAP].

IPv4.why: The protocol is defined specifically for IPv4 flows. It uses IPv4 header fields as flow identifiers and runs as IP protocol 101.
IPv4.quote: This document specifies the IFMP protocol for IPv4 on a point-to-point link.

rejected.why: The document describes a flow-label switching scheme that predates MPLS, but it never mentions MPLS or its label distribution. Tagging it would overreach.
TCP appears only as an analogy for instance numbers (ISN) and as a source of port fields in flow types. The document is not about TCP.
The IFMP checksum uses the standard Internet checksum, but this is incidental to the protocol.
UDP ports appear only as flow identifier fields. The document does not address UDP itself.

gaps.name: IP switching / flow-labelled IP (Ipsilon IFMP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for pre-MPLS IP switching or flow-based label switching. A reader looking for IFMP and GSMP-era IP switching has no direct subject page.

RFC1954.title: Transmission of Flow Labelled IPv4 on ATM Data Links Ipsilon Version 1.0
RFC1954.summary: Specifies how IPv4 datagrams are encapsulated on ATM links (AAL-5 via RFC 1483), both by default (LLC/SNAP) and for Ipsilon IFMP flow types 0, 1 and 2 with compressed headers.

ATM.why: The whole document defines IPv4 encapsulation on ATM AAL-5, VPI/VCI labels and MTUs, so it belongs under IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: This document specifies the manner for transmitting IPv4 datagrams over an ATM data link, both in a default manner and in the presence of flow labelling

rejected.why: IPv4 is the payload being carried. The document defines nothing about IPv4 itself, only how to encapsulate it on ATM.
NHRP is a different mechanism for NBMA next-hop resolution and is not discussed here.
Flow labelling is used for per-flow switching, not QoS signalling, and IFMP is only referenced. No IFMP tag exists in the taxonomy.
The IP checksum is adjusted for the omitted TTL, but this is a minor detail and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Ipsilon Flow Management Protocol (IFMP) / IP switching
gaps.why: The document is companion to RFC 1953 (IFMP) and defines flow-labelled encapsulations. The taxonomy has no tag for IFMP or flow-labelled IP switching.

RFC1955.title: New Scheme for Internet Routing and Addressing (ENCAPS) for IPNG
RFC1955.summary: A 1992 proposal by Hinden, published as an informational IPng submission, for a medium-term routing and addressing fix in which border routers encapsulate datagrams in an IP header carrying autonomous-domain addresses looked up in the DNS, so inter-domain routing is done on ADs.

routing architecture.why: The document proposes a scheme to fix Internet routing scalability by separating inter-AD routing from intra-AD routing and shrinking routing tables.
routing architecture.quote: inter-domain routing be done by routing on autonomous domains (AD)

IP-in-IP.why: The core mechanism is IP-in-IP encapsulation with an AD-Header at entry border routers and decapsulation at exit border routers.
IP-in-IP.quote: the border routers to encapsulate the original IP datagrams with another IP header

addressing.why: The proposal reserves Class A/B network numbers as AD identifiers, organized into commonwealths, and addresses the addressing problem.
addressing.quote: The addresses I propose to use for the AD addresses are plain old IP addresses.

rejected.why: DNS is used for AD-address lookup and would need an extension, but this is a small part of the proposal rather than its subject.
BGP is mentioned as one option for routing between border routers, with OSPF or IS-IS as alternatives. No BGP specification is given.
The IPng tag is for the historic candidate protocols TUBA, PIP, SIPP and TP/IX. This is a medium-term stopgap submitted in response to RFC 1550, not one of those candidates.
NAT is only mentioned as needed if globally unique addresses were dropped, which is a side remark.
IP-in-IP is the more specific tag for the encapsulation described.

RFC1956.title: Registration in the MIL Domain
RFC1956.summary: Informational RFC setting the policy for registering second-level domains under the .MIL top-level domain, administered by the DoD NIC.

domain registration.why: The whole document is a registry policy: who may register under .MIL, naming rules, name server requirements and the registration template process.
domain registration.quote: This RFC describes the policy for the registration of second level domains under the ".MIL" domain.

rejected.why: Name server requirements (two servers, within .MIL) are registration conditions, not a specification or operation of DNS itself.
Anonymous FTP is only mentioned as a way to obtain the registration template.
No registration data directory service is described.
Registration is by emailed template, not a provisioning protocol.

RFC1957.title: Some Observations on Implementations of the Post Office Protocol (POP3)
RFC1957.summary: Informational note on POP3 implementation quirks: some clients expect a space after the status indicator, and Netscape and Eudora require the optional UIDL and TOP commands, while APOP adoption is limited.

POP3.why: The whole memo records how POP3 servers and clients behave in practice and updates RFC 1939. It covers the status indicator space, the UIDL and TOP commands, and APOP.
POP3.quote: POP3 servers and clients are no exception.

rejected.why: POP3 is the more specific tag and already sits under email. The memo does not address email in general.
APOP is mentioned only as an optional authentication command. The memo does not discuss SASL or any general authentication framework.

RFC1958.title: Architectural Principles of the Internet
RFC1958.summary: IAB informational memo recording a snapshot of the guiding principles of Internet architecture, such as end-to-end design, simplicity, naming and address rules, and security design guidance.

internet architecture.why: The whole document exists to state architectural principles of the Internet (end-to-end argument, fate-sharing, heterogeneity, scalability, simplicity).
internet architecture.quote: it nevertheless seems useful to record a snapshot of the current principles of the Internet architecture.

rejected.why: Section 6 gives brief security design principles, but they are a small part of a general architecture memo; not a substantial subject of the document.
Section 4 has a few naming and address rules, but only a short part of the document; DNS is mentioned only as an example.
Single Internet-level protocol is discussed as an architectural principle, not as the subject of the IP layer itself.
Mentioned only as an example of a circular dependency and case-independent names.
Mentions evolution since ARPANET but is a statement of principles, not a retrospective.

RFC1959.title: An LDAP URL Format
RFC1959.summary: Defines the "ldap" URL scheme and its grammar (host, DN, attributes, scope, filter) so clients can reference LDAP entries or searches directly.

LDAP.why: The URL format expresses LDAP operations (base/one/sub searches, attributes, filters) and is an LDAP-specific extension that LDAP readers need.
LDAP.quote: This document describes a format for an LDAP Uniform Resource Locator which will allow Internet clients to have direct access to the LDAP protocol.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URL scheme with its syntax, escaping rules and examples, which is the core subject of URI scheme definitions.
URI.quote: An LDAP URL begins with the protocol prefix "ldap" and is defined by the following grammar.

rejected.why: X.500 is the backend directory LDAP fronts; the document only notes that entries in the X.500 namespace are reachable, and does not specify anything about X.500.
Implied as an ancestor of LDAP; the LDAP tag is more specific.
Only mentioned as the default port 389 transport; not the subject.

RFC1960.title: A String Representation of LDAP Search Filters
RFC1960.summary: RFC 1960 defines a human-readable string representation (prefix grammar with &, |, !, and comparison operators) for LDAP search filters, replacing RFC 1558.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies a string notation for LDAP search filters, an extension to the LDAP protocol's usage. Readers of the LDAP subject would expect to find it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a human-readable string format for representing LDAP search filters.

rejected.why: The ASN.1 filter definition and BER encoding are quoted from LDAP as background. The document's own subject is the string grammar, not ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
The grammar is written in a BNF-like notation, but it is only the means of defining the format. The document is not about the notation.
This is the parent of LDAP, so it is implied by the LDAP tag and not listed separately.

RFC1961.title: GSS-API Authentication Method for SOCKS Version 5
RFC1961.summary: Specifies the GSS-API authentication method for SOCKS V5, covering GSS-API context establishment, protection-level subnegotiation, and per-message encapsulation of TCP/UDP traffic between SOCKS client and server.

SOCKS.why: The document extends SOCKS V5 with a new authentication method and message framing, so SOCKS readers would want it.
SOCKS.quote: This document provides the specification for the SOCKS V5 GSS-API authentication protocol, and defines a GSS-API-based encapsulation for provision of integrity, authentication and optional confidentiality.

GSS-API.why: It profiles how GSS-API calls are used for context establishment, protection levels and per-message wrap/unwrap.
GSS-API.quote: The approach for use of GSS-API in SOCKS V5 is to authenticate the client and server by successfully establishing a GSS-API security context

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an example mechanism for name format; the document is mechanism-independent.
TCP is only the carried traffic/transport; the document does not specify TCP.
UDP is only carried traffic that is encapsulated; nothing is specified about UDP itself.
A broad topic; the specific GSS-API and SOCKS tags already cover it.

RFC1962.title: The PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP)
RFC1962.summary: Defines the PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP), which negotiates, enables and resets data compression algorithms on PPP links, including Reset-Request/Reset-Ack and compression configuration options.

PPP.why: CCP is a PPP control protocol, modelled on LCP, with its own PPP protocol numbers, codes and options. Readers of PPP would expect it.
PPP.quote: The Compression Control Protocol (CCP) is responsible for configuring, enabling, and disabling data compression algorithms on both ends of the point-to-point link.

compression.why: The document is about negotiating data compression, including Predictor, LZS and V.42bis option types and compressed datagram handling. It does not define a compression format itself, but readers of compression would want it.
compression.quote: CCP Configuration Options allow negotiation of compression algorithms and their parameters.

rejected.why: LZS is only listed as one assigned option type (17). The document does not specify the algorithm.
CCP compresses the whole payload, not protocol headers.
The option and code values refer to Assigned Numbers, but this is boilerplate-level and not the subject.
CRC is mentioned only as one possible way to detect decompression failure.

RFC1963.title: PPP Serial Data Transport Protocol (SDTP)
RFC1963.summary: Informational RFC defining PPP Serial Data Transport Protocol (SDTP) and its control protocol (SDCP), which encapsulate synchronous HDLC-like and asynchronous serial data over PPP using a V.120-based header, to enable compression of serial data.

PPP.why: The document defines a new PPP network-layer protocol (protocol ID 0049) and its NCP-like control protocol SDCP with configuration options, so it is a PPP extension.
PPP.quote: provides encapsulation and an associated control protocol for transporting serial data streams over a PPP link

rejected.why: V.120 is an ISDN terminal adaptation standard, but only its header format is borrowed; the document is not about ISDN access.
Compression of synchronous data is the motivation, but the compression protocols are separate RFCs; this document only defines the transport and control protocol.
FCS-Type option merely selects the frame check sequence to regenerate; not about CRC polynomial choice.
Not about compressing protocol headers; it is about data compression and serial data encapsulation.

RFC1964.title: The Kerberos Version 5 GSS-API Mechanism
RFC1964.summary: Defines the Kerberos V5 mechanism for GSS-API: token formats for context establishment, per-message MIC/Wrap and context deletion, name types and OIDs, credentials handling, and parameter values.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies a GSS-API mechanism: tokens, name types, QOP values, minor status codes and credentials handling.
GSS-API.quote: This specification defines protocols, procedures, and conventions to be employed by peers implementing the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface

Kerberos.why: It profiles Kerberos V5 messages (AP-REQ, AP-REP, KRB-ERROR), tickets and credential caches for use under GSS-API.
Kerberos.quote: The innerContextToken of the initial context token will consist of a Kerberos V5 KRB_AP_REQ message

rejected.why: DES-CBC and DES MAC are used for per-message protection, but the document isn't about DES itself.
MD5 is used in checksums and channel binding hashes, but only as a building block.
ASN.1 syntax is used to describe the tokens, but the document isn't about ASN.1.
DNS is mentioned only for hostname canonicalization in the service name form.

RFC1965.title: Autonomous System Confederations for BGP
RFC1965.summary: Experimental extension to BGP defining AS confederations: new AS_CONFED_SET and AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE AS_PATH segment types and rules for AS_PATH modification so a group of member ASes appears as one AS externally.

route reflection.why: The document specifies BGP confederations, which the taxonomy groups under route reflection (route reflection and confederations). It defines segment types and AS_PATH rules for them.
route reflection.quote: create a confederation of autonomous systems which is represented as one single autonomous system to BGP peers external to the confederation

rejected.why: The child tag route reflection (which covers confederations) fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
BGP runs over TCP, but TCP is only the substrate here.
The document's concern is a specific BGP extension, not routing architecture in general.

RFC1966.title: BGP Route Reflection An alternative to full mesh IBGP
RFC1966.summary: Experimental RFC specifying BGP Route Reflection, a method letting IBGP speakers reflect routes via route reflectors and clusters (with ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST attributes) to avoid a full IBGP mesh.

route reflection.why: The whole document specifies BGP route reflection: RR roles, client/non-client peers, clusters, loop avoidance attributes ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST.
route reflection.quote: This document describes the use and design of a method known as "Route Reflection" to alleviate the the need for "full mesh" IBGP.

rejected.why: Route reflection is the more specific child tag; BGP is implied as its ancestor.
Scalability of IBGP is the motivation, but the document specifies a BGP mechanism, covered by the more specific route reflection tag.
BGP sessions run over TCP, but this is only the substrate and is not addressed by the document.

RFC1967.title: PPP LZS-DCP Compression Protocol (LZS-DCP)
RFC1967.summary: Specifies the PPP LZS-DCP compression protocol, which uses Stac LZS compression with a DCP header for PPP packets, including packet format, history and reset handling, and a CCP configuration option.

PPP.why: The document defines a PPP compression protocol: new PPP protocol field use (00FD/00FB), a CCP configuration option, and packet format over PPP. PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of the Stac LZS data compression algorithm for compressing PPP encapsulated packets, using a DCP header

LZS.why: The protocol is built around Stac LZS compression, covering its histories, anti-expansion behaviour, and compressed data format.
LZS.quote: The Stac LZS compression algorithm is Defined in ANSI X3.241-1994 [7]. The format of the compressed data is repeated here

rejected.why: IPComp compresses IP payloads, not PPP frames. This document is not about it.
The parent is implied by the LZS tag, and the document covers one specific scheme, not compression in general.
The compression applies to whole packet payloads, not protocol headers on constrained links.

RFC1968.title: The PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP)
RFC1968.summary: Defines the PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP), which negotiates data encryption algorithms (including proprietary OUI options and DESE) on PPP links, along with encrypted datagram encapsulation and Reset-Request/Reset-Ack.

PPP.why: ECP is a PPP control protocol, modelled on LCP, with its own protocol numbers, codes and options. The document specifies it in full, so it belongs on the PPP page.
PPP.quote: The Encryption Control Protocol (ECP) is responsible for configuring and enabling data encryption algorithms on both ends of the point-to-point link.

rejected.why: DESE is only referenced as the recommended option, and it is defined in a separate RFC (1969). This document does not specify DES.
The Compression Control Protocol is mentioned only for the order of operations (compress, then encrypt). The document is not about compression.
The document negotiates algorithms, not keys. No key establishment or provisioning is specified.
This is a specific PPP control protocol for negotiating encryption. The PPP tag is the more specific fit, and the Security Considerations section is boilerplate.
The option-number registry is mentioned only in passing. The IANA references are not the subject of the document.

RFC1969.title: The PPP DES Encryption Protocol (DESE)
RFC1969.summary: Specifies how to encrypt PPP packets with DES in CBC mode under the PPP Encryption Control Protocol, including the ECP DESE option, packet format, padding, and recovery after packet loss.

DES.why: The document defines how DES in CBC mode is applied to PPP packets, including IV derivation from a nonce and chaining across packets.
DES.quote: This document provides specific details for the use of the DES standard [5, 6] for encrypting PPP encapsulated packets.

PPP.why: It defines a PPP ECP configuration option and data protocol (protocol IDs 0x53/0x55), with padding, Multilink, ACFC/PFC and MRU considerations, so PPP readers need it.
PPP.quote: The ECP DESE Configuration Option indicates that the issuing implementation is offering to employ this specification for decrypting communications on the link

rejected.why: Encryption here is at the PPP link layer, not IP-layer security.
Key establishment is explicitly out of scope; the shared secret is configured outside this document.
The specific DES tag and the PPP tag cover the subject; the general security topic adds nothing.

gaps.name: PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP)
gaps.why: The document is a bearer-protocol specification for ECP (RFC 1968), but the taxonomy has no ECP tag; PPP is the nearest fit.

RFC1970.title: Neighbor Discovery for IP Version 6 (IPv6)
RFC1970.summary: Specifies the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol (router/prefix discovery, address resolution, neighbor unreachability detection, redirects) using ICMPv6 messages and options.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document defines the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol, its messages, options, host and router behaviour.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document specifies the Neighbor Discovery protocol for IP Version 6.

rejected.why: ND messages are carried as ICMPv6 types, but ICMP is only the carrier; the document does not specify ICMP itself.
Address autoconfiguration is delegated to a separate document (ADDRCONF); this RFC only supplies the prefix information and flags.
ARP is only compared with ND in the IPv4 comparison section; it is not specified here.
The more specific child tag neighbor discovery is chosen instead of the parent.
The Authentication Header is only mentioned as an optional protection for ND packets, in the Security Considerations.
TCP forward-progress hints for reachability are an implementation note in an appendix; TCP is not the subject.

RFC1971.title: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
RFC1971.summary: Specifies IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration: link-local address creation, Duplicate Address Detection, and forming site-local/global addresses from Router Advertisement prefixes plus interface tokens, with address lifetimes.

SLAAC.why: The whole document defines IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, including link-local generation, DAD and prefix-based address formation.
SLAAC.quote: the process for generating site-local and global addresses via stateless address autoconfiguration, and the Duplicate Address Detection procedure

renumbering.why: Renumbering is a stated design goal and has its own section covering preferred/deprecated lifetimes, though it is not the main subject.
renumbering.quote: Address leasing facilitates site renumbering by providing a mechanism to time-out addresses assigned to interfaces in hosts.

rejected.why: Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement and Router Advertisements are used as the mechanism, but they are specified in RFC 1970. This document only uses them for DAD.
Stateful autoconfiguration is referred to and coordinated with, but its details are specified elsewhere.
A more specific child tag, SLAAC, fits the document.
SLAAC is the more specific tag for this document's address autoconfiguration subject.

RFC1972.title: A Method for the Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Ethernet Networks
RFC1972.summary: Specifies IPv6 over Ethernet: frame format (type 86DD), MTU, link-local address formation from the IEEE 802 address, link-layer address option content for Neighbor Discovery, and multicast address mapping.

Ethernet.why: The whole document defines how IPv6 is carried over Ethernet: frame format, MTU, address token, and unicast and multicast address mapping.
Ethernet.quote: This memo specifies the frame format for transmission of IPv6 [IPV6] packets and the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses on Ethernet networks.

IPv6.why: The document specifies IPv6 addressing details (link-local address formation, autoconfiguration prefix length, multicast mapping) for this link type.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 Link-local address [AARCH] for an Ethernet interface is formed by appending the interface's IEEE 802 address to the 80-bit prefix FE80::.

rejected.why: The document only defines the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option for Ethernet. Neighbor Discovery itself is specified in RFC 1970, so this is a minor part.
It only specifies the address token and prefix length for Ethernet. The autoconfiguration protocol is defined elsewhere (RFC 1971).
The multicast address mapping is a small link-layer detail, not multicast routing or group membership.

RFC1973.title: PPP in Frame Relay
RFC1973.summary: Specifies how PPP packets are encapsulated and framed over point-to-point Frame Relay circuits using Q.922 headers and the NLPID 0xCF, including demultiplexing against RFC 1490 encapsulations and LCP configuration details.

frame relay.why: The whole document defines the Frame Relay framing for PPP: frame format, NLPID, physical layer requirements, MRU, and demultiplexing against other Frame Relay encapsulations.
frame relay.quote: This document describes the use of Frame Relay for framing PPP encapsulated packets.

PPP.why: It specifies how PPP works over Frame Relay, covering LCP negotiation, Address-and-Control-Field-Compression, Protocol-Field-Compression, NCP phases and MRU defaults.
PPP.quote: The Link Control Protocol can negotiate modifications to the basic frame structure.

rejected.why: X.25 is mentioned only as a comparison in the introduction. The document is not about it.
Inverse ARP is mentioned in one line, which says it is not required. That is not enough to tag ARP.

RFC1974.title: PPP Stac LZS Compression Protocol
RFC1974.summary: Describes using the Stac LZS compression algorithm, with single or multiple histories, to compress PPP packets, including CCP option negotiation, packet formats, check modes, history resynchronization and an extended mode.

LZS.why: The whole document specifies LZS compression for PPP: packet format, histories, check values, extended mode and CCP option.
LZS.quote: This document describes the use of the Stac LZS data compression algorithm, with single or multiple compression histories, for compressing PPP encapsulated packets.

PPP.why: Defines a PPP CCP configuration option (Type 17), protocol field values 00FD/00FB/4021 and Reset-Request/Reset-Ack use, so PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: The CCP Stac LZS Configuration Option negotiates the use of Stac LZS on the link.

rejected.why: The more specific LZS tag already applies, and its parent is implied.
The CRC is a minor check option (HDLC FCS-16 polynomial) within the document, not its subject.
LZS compresses whole packet payloads including the protocol field, not protocol headers on constrained links in the header-compression sense.
A different, IP-layer payload compression protocol; this document is PPP-specific.

RFC1975.title: PPP Magnalink Variable Resource Compression
RFC1975.summary: Informational RFC describing the Magnalink Variable Resource Compression Algorithm (MVRCA), a PPP compression method negotiated via a CCP option (type 24), with its packet encapsulation and configuration option format.

PPP.why: The document defines a PPP compression protocol: a CCP configuration option and a PPP encapsulation (protocol ID, CID, PIB). It extends PPP's Compression Control Protocol with a new algorithm.
PPP.quote: The CCP MVRCA Configuration Option negotiates the use of MVRCA on the link.

compression.why: The document specifies a data compression algorithm with history buffers, contexts, and handling of data expansion. Readers browsing compression would expect it.
compression.quote: The Magnalink variable resource compression algorithm defines a family of interoperable compression solutions with compression performance as a function of available CPU and memory resources.

rejected.why: MVRCA compresses packet payload data, including the PPP protocol field, with history buffers. It is not a header compression scheme.
The algorithm is proprietary and is not identified as LZS or tied to it in the text.
MVRCA runs over PPP via CCP and is not the IP Payload Compression Protocol.

RFC1976.title: PPP for Data Compression in Data Circuit-Terminating Equipment (DCE)
