RFC1976.summary: Informational RFC defining a PPP LCP extension (DCE-Identifier option) and a required parameter profile so DCE devices (DSU/CSUs) can compress synchronous serial data using PPP, CCP, LZS-DCP and PPP-SDTP, with Mode-0/1/2 handshake.

PPP.why: The document extends PPP LCP with a new DCE-Identifier option and profiles required PPP options and handshake behaviour for DCE devices.
PPP.quote: The use of PPP in Compression DCE requires the use of an additional LCP Configuration Option:

LZS.why: The profile mandates LZS-DCP as the default compression protocol and specifies its required configuration options.
LZS.quote: The Stacker-LZS algorithm from Stac Electronics was chosen as the default compression algorithm for DCE devices.

rejected.why: The compression here is of serial payload data, not protocol headers; Protocol-Field and Address/Control-Field compression are only incidental PPP options.
The generic compression topic is implied by the LZS child tag, so it is not listed separately.
HDLC-synchronous serial transport is not SONET/SDH.
V.120 is cited only as the basis of the SDTP terminal adaption header; ISDN access is not what the document is about.

gaps.name: PPP-SDTP / PPP Serial Data Transport Protocol
gaps.why: The document builds on carrying serial data in PPP, but the taxonomy has no tag for PPP-SDTP or the PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP).

RFC1977.title: PPP BSD Compression Protocol
RFC1977.summary: Informational RFC describing how to use the BSD Unix compress (LZW) algorithm as a PPP compression protocol negotiated via CCP, including packet format, configuration option, and reference C code.

PPP.why: The document defines a PPP compression protocol: packet format with PPP Protocol 0xFD/0xFB, CCP configuration option type 21, and reset/sequencing behaviour over PPP links.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of the Unix Compress compression protocol for compressing PPP encapsulated packets.

compression.why: The document specifies an LZW dictionary compression algorithm, with dictionary clearing, code width and expansion handling, and full reference code. Readers of lossless compression would want it.
compression.quote: UNIX compress as embodied in the freely and widely distributed BSD source has the following features:

rejected.why: This compresses whole PPP packet payloads with LZW, not protocol headers on constrained links.
LZS is a different Lempel-Ziv-Stac algorithm. This document uses BSD compress LZW.
IP payload compression is a different protocol. This one runs at the PPP layer and is negotiated through CCP.
The algorithm is LZW from BSD compress, not DEFLATE.

gaps.name: PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP)
gaps.why: The document is a CCP-negotiated compression method, but the taxonomy has no CCP tag, so PPP is the closest fit.

gaps.name: LZW / Unix compress
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for LZW or Unix compress, so the generic compression topic is used.

RFC1978.title: PPP Predictor Compression Protocol
RFC1978.summary: Informational RFC describing use of the Predictor compression algorithm to compress PPP packets under CCP, including the algorithm, reference code, and type 1/type 2 encapsulations.

PPP.why: The document defines a PPP compression method: encapsulation in PPP Information field with protocol 0x00FD, CCP interaction, and resynchronization behaviour.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of the Predictor data compression algorithm for compressing PPP encapsulated packets.

compression.why: A substantial part specifies the Predictor lossless compression algorithm with worked example and C code. No narrower compression tag fits.
compression.quote: Predictor works by filling a guess table with values, based on the hash of the previous characters seen.

rejected.why: Predictor compresses whole PPP packet payloads, not protocol headers.
CRC-16 is only used as a desynchronization check; the document is not about CRC polynomials.
LAPB is mentioned only as a reliable link assumption, not specified.

RFC1979.title: PPP Deflate Protocol
RFC1979.summary: Informational RFC defining the PPP Deflate compression protocol, which compresses PPP packets using the deflate format, negotiated via a CCP configuration option (type 26), with sequencing, reset and incompressible-data handling.

PPP.why: The document defines a PPP compression protocol with PPP protocol numbers 0xFD/0xFB and a CCP configuration option; PPP readers would look for it.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of the PPP Deflate compression protocol for compressing PPP encapsulated packets.

DEFLATE.why: The document specifies how deflate-compressed data is framed per packet (block boundaries, stripped trailing bytes, window size, zlib method), which is of interest to readers of deflate.
DEFLATE.quote: The basic format of the compressed data is precisely described by the 'Deflate' Compressed Data Format Specification[3].

rejected.why: Parent of DEFLATE, which already covers the lossless compression subject; no need to list the ancestor.
PPP Deflate compresses whole packets (payload and protocol field), not protocol headers on constrained links.
gzip is only mentioned as another user of deflate; the document is not about the gzip file format.

The zlib library is cited as the source of deflate and its licence is quoted, and the Method field uses the zlib method identifier. The document does not specify the zlib format; it is about deflate in PPP.
A different compression scheme; not discussed.

gaps.name: PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP)
gaps.why: The document defines a CCP configuration option and relies heavily on CCP Reset-Request/Reset-Ack. The taxonomy has no CCP tag beyond PPP.

RFC1980.title: A Proposed Extension to HTML : Client-Side Image Maps
RFC1980.summary: RFC 1980 specifies a proposed HTML/2.0 extension (USEMAP attribute, MAP and AREA elements) enabling client-side image maps, with DTD changes and fallback behaviour.

HTML.why: The whole document defines new HTML elements and attributes (USEMAP, MAP, AREA) and the corresponding DTD changes, so it belongs on the HTML page.
HTML.quote: This document specifies an extension to the HTML language, referred to as "Client-Side Image Maps," which resolves these limitations.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the limitation of server-side image maps; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
URIs are used as link destinations and USEMAP values, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
The map is expressed in SGML-compliant markup and the DTD is changed, but this is the substrate for HTML rather than the subject.

RFC1981.title: Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6
RFC1981.summary: Specifies Path MTU Discovery for IPv6, where a source node learns a path's MTU from ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages, with requirements and implementation guidance for caching, aging and transport-layer reactions.

PMTUD.why: The whole document specifies the PMTU discovery mechanism for IPv6, including requirements, PMTU caching, aging and transport-layer actions.
PMTUD.quote: This document describes Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6.

rejected.why: The document is about one mechanism that runs on IPv6, not the IPv6 specification or addressing. PMTUD is the more specific tag.
It relies on ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages, but ICMPv6 and the router behaviour are defined elsewhere.
Section 5.4 gives TCP-layer guidance, but it is one part of the implementation notes. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
NFS is mentioned briefly as an example of a transport user that should use PMTUD. The document is not about NFS.

RFC1982.title: Serial Number Arithmetic
RFC1982.summary: RFC 1982 defines serial number arithmetic (addition and comparison on wrapping unsigned integers) and applies it to the 32-bit DNS SOA serial number, updating RFC 1034/1035.

DNS.why: The document clarifies the SOA serial number comparison semantics for DNS zone consistency, updating RFC1034 and RFC1035. It gives guidance on incrementing the serial relative to SOA.expire for secondary servers.
DNS.quote: The serial number in the DNS SOA Resource Record is a Serial Number as defined above, with SERIAL_BITS being 32.

rejected.why: TCP sequence number arithmetic (RFC 793, IEN-74) is only cited as the origin of the idea. The document does not specify or extend TCP.

gaps.name: Serial number arithmetic
gaps.why: The general modular sequence-number comparison and addition rules have no dedicated tag. The document says they may be cited outside DNS, but the taxonomy only has DNS for this subject.

RFC1983.title: Internet Users' Glossary
RFC1983.summary: FYI 18 (obsoletes RFC 1392) is a glossary of Internet-specific terms and acronyms for users, covering protocols, organizations, networking concepts and net culture.

user guides.why: This is an FYI-series introductory glossary for Internet users, which fits the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: There are many networking glossaries in existence. This glossary concentrates on terms which are specific to the Internet.

terminology.why: The whole document is a set of definitions of Internet terms and acronyms, which is terminology in its own right.
terminology.quote: Naturally, there are entries for some basic terms and acronyms because other entries refer to them.

rejected.why: DNS is defined as one glossary entry among hundreds; the document is not about DNS.
The entries for RFC, STD, BCP and FYI are only a few of the definitions. The document does not address the series as a subject.
IETF, IESG, IAB and working groups are defined as glossary entries only. The process itself is not covered.
Entries for layers, routers and the Internet hierarchy are brief definitions, not an architectural treatment.
TCP and the other protocols are mentioned only as brief definitions.

RFC1984.title: IAB and IESG Statement on Cryptographic Technology and the Internet
RFC1984.summary: An IAB/IESG policy statement opposing government export controls, weak key-size limits, key escrow and usage bans on cryptography, with technical arguments for why strong, unescrowed cryptography is needed for Internet security.

cryptography.why: The whole document is about access to and policy for cryptographic technology: key sizes, key escrow, export controls. The general cryptography topic fits, since no specific algorithm is addressed.
cryptography.quote: Cryptography is the most powerful single tool that users can use to secure the Internet. Knowingly making that tool weaker threatens their ability to do so

key management.why: Much of the technical analysis concerns key escrow, private key custody, signature keys and data recovery, which are key management matters.
key management.quote: Key escrow implies that keys must be disclosed in some fashion, a flat-out contradiction of this principle.

internet architecture.why: This is an IAB/IESG architectural position on what the Internet needs in order to be trustworthy and grow.
internet architecture.quote: The Internet is becoming the predominant vehicle for electronic commerce and information exchange. It is essential that the support structure for these activities can be trusted.

rejected.why: The certification authority paragraph only distinguishes CAs from escrow centers. The document does not specify or analyse PKI.
Privacy is mentioned as a motivation, but the document does not address protocol privacy threat models.
The topic is covered more specifically by cryptography. The document is about cryptographic policy, not general security guidance.
Electronic commerce is cited as motivation, but no payment protocol is discussed.

gaps.name: Cryptographic policy / export controls / key escrow
gaps.why: The document's core subject is government policy on cryptography. The taxonomy has no tag for policy or legal matters.

RFC1985.title: SMTP Service Extension for Remote Message Queue Starting
RFC1985.summary: Defines the ETRN SMTP service extension, which lets a client ask a server to start processing its mail queue for the client's host, subdomain or named queue. It replaces the insecure TURN command.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension (the ETRN verb, EHLO keyword, and reply codes) for remote queue starting in mail relaying.
SMTP.quote: this memo introduces the ETRN command. This command uses the mechanism defined in [4] to define extensions to the SMTP service

rejected.why: DNS is only mentioned for the node name, which may be a CNAME or MX name. The document does not specify anything about DNS.
UUCP appears only in the example `ETRN #uucp` for flushing a queue. The document is not about UUCP mail interchange.
The more specific SMTP tag fits. The parent tag is implied.

RFC1986.title: Experiments with a Simple File Transfer Protocol for Radio Links using Enhanced Trivial File Transfer Protocol (ETFTP)
RFC1986.summary: Describes ETFTP, an experimental NETBLT-over-UDP file transfer application derived from TFTP source, with message formats, tunable parameters, timers and test results over half-duplex tactical UHF satellite radio links.

NETBLT.why: The document specifies NETBLT-based message types, modifications (T bit, R bit, radio delay field, renegotiated packet size), timers and flow control, and reports test results of NETBLT-derived transfer.
NETBLT.quote: This protocol is an experimental implementation of the NETwork BLock Transfer Protocol (NETBLT), RFC 998 [1], as a file transfer application program.

TFTP.why: ETFTP is an enhanced TFTP-derived file transfer program with a TFTP-like client command set and TFTP-like limitations (no authentication, no directory listing).
TFTP.quote: The original source files for TFTP, as downloaded from ftp.uu.net, were modified to implement the ETFTP/NETBLT protocol.

amateur radio.why: Tuning of AX.25 p-persistence, slot time, TX tail and TX delay over half-duplex radio links is a substantial part of the performance work.
amateur radio.quote: To reduce the number of channel accesses required, a number of AX.25 parameters were modified.

satellite.why: The experiments address file transfer throughput over slow, long-delay, high-BER UHF satellite links, including FEC and channel turnaround delays.
satellite.quote: This document will discuss results obtained from using ETFTP across a point-to-point LST-5C tactical SATellite COMmunications (SATCOM) link.

rejected.why: FTP is only used as the baseline that performed poorly; the document does not specify or extend it.
UDP is just the transport substrate on which ETFTP/NETBLT is layered.
TCP behaviour (slow start, backoff) is discussed only as a reason it performs poorly on these links, not as the subject.
A prototype link-layer FEC device is mentioned as a supporting piece of the testbed, not packet-level FEC schemes specified in the document.
SLIP is merely one link in the test network.
Backoff discussion is brief and tied to the transport timers of ETFTP rather than a congestion control subject.

gaps.name: NETBLT
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about an implementation of NETBLT (RFC 998), but the taxonomy has no NETBLT tag under transport as listed? It does list NETBLT under transport; no gap if available.

RFC1987.title: Ipsilon's General Switch Management Protocol Specification Version 1.1
RFC1987.summary: Specifies Ipsilon's GSMP v1.1, a master-slave protocol by which a controller sets up and releases ATM switch connections (including multicast branches), manages ports, queries configuration and statistics, receives events, and runs an adjacency protocol.

GSMP.why: The whole document is the GSMP specification: message formats, connection management, port management, statistics, configuration, events and the adjacency protocol.
GSMP.quote: The General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP), is a general purpose protocol to control an ATM switch.

rejected.why: GSMP runs over ATM links and controls ATM switches, but the document specifies a switch control protocol, not IP over ATM or ATM itself; ATM is the substrate.
Controller/switch separation is conceptually similar, but the document is an ATM switch control protocol and does not frame itself as SDN.
Only references the IANAifType values for the Port Type field; it defines no MIB.
A related separation of control and forwarding, but the document is not about ForCES.

RFC1988.title: Conditional Grant of Rights to Specific Hewlett-Packard Patents In Conjunction With the Internet Engineering Task Force's Internet-Standard Network Management Framework
RFC1988.summary: HP announces a conditional patent non-assertion grant covering US patents 5,293,635 and 5,421,024 (search address autotopology technology) for implementations of IETF standards-track MIB modules in the Internet-standard network management framework.

IPR.why: The whole document is a patent rights grant and its conditions (termination, confirmatory license), which is an IPR disclosure/licensing statement.
IPR.quote: HP hereby covenants that it will not assert any claims in US Patents 5,293,635, 5,421,024
IPR.section: A Grant of Rights to Hewlett-Packard US Patents 5,293,635 and 5,421,024

rejected.why: The document only mentions MIB modules as the context for the patent grant. It does not specify or analyse any MIB module.
The Internet-standard network management framework is the setting for the grant. The document says nothing about the protocol itself.

RFC1989.title: PPP Link Quality Monitoring
RFC1989.summary: RFC 1989 defines the PPP Link Quality Monitoring protocol: the Link-Quality-Report packet, counters, Quality-Protocol configuration option, and procedures for measuring packet/octet loss on each direction of a PPP link.

PPP.why: The document specifies an LCP Quality-Protocol (protocol field c025) for PPP, including its configuration option and packet format. It is a PPP extension and PPP readers would look for it.
PPP.quote: This document defines a protocol for generating Link-Quality-Reports.

rejected.why: The document uses SNMP MIB-II interface counters as the source for its counters. It does not define or extend a MIB module.
SNMP counters are only referenced as the definition for the counters. The document is not about SNMP.
The document measures link loss, but it does so as a PPP-specific mechanism. The PPP tag fits better, and the document is not about general network performance metrics.
This parent tag is implied by the PPP tag.

RFC1990.title: The PPP Multilink Protocol (MP)
RFC1990.summary: RFC 1990 specifies the PPP Multilink Protocol, which splits, sequences and recombines datagrams across multiple PPP links in a bundle, using new LCP options (MRRU, short sequence numbers, Endpoint Discriminator); it obsoletes RFC 1717.

PPP.why: The document defines the PPP Multilink Protocol with a new PPP protocol ID, fragment header and LCP options. It extends PPP and is about PPP.
PPP.quote: This document proposes a method for splitting, recombining and sequencing datagrams across multiple logical data links.

rejected.why: ISDN is only the motivating use case. The protocol applies to any set of PPP links, including async links.
Multilink bundles multiple links in a conceptually similar way, but that tag covers IEEE 802.1AX. This document is PPP-specific and is already covered by PPP.
X.25 SVCs are mentioned only as one kind of link that can be bundled.
Frame relay is mentioned only as an example of a multiplexed link that can be bundled.
Compression Control Protocol use on member links is mentioned only briefly. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC1991.title: PGP Message Exchange Formats
RFC1991.summary: RFC 1991 describes the PGP 2.x message exchange formats: packet types, signature and encryption services, compression, and ASCII armor (radix-64) encoding for encrypted and signed email and files.

OpenPGP.why: The document specifies the PGP message and packet formats, the predecessor of OpenPGP. Readers of the OpenPGP subject would expect to find it.
OpenPGP.quote: This document describes the format of "PGP files", i.e., messages that have been encrypted and/or signed with PGP.

Base64.why: A substantial part of the document defines the radix-64 ASCII Armor encoding, including its mapping table, headers and CRC checksum.
Base64.quote: The scheme used for this purpose is radix-64 conversion. Each group of three bytes of binary data is mapped into 4 ASCII characters.

rejected.why: Email is only the channel that ASCII armor is designed to survive. The document is about the PGP message format, not email architecture.
RSA is used as the public-key algorithm and its PKCS signature and DEK encodings appear, but the document does not specify RSA itself.
MD5 is the only message digest defined for signatures. It is a field value here, not the subject of the document.
The armor checksum uses a 24-bit CRC. This is a minor detail inside the armor definition, not a discussion of CRC polynomial choice.
S/MIME is a different secure email format. It is not discussed in this document.

RFC1992.title: The Nimrod Routing Architecture
RFC1992.summary: RFC 1992 describes the Nimrod scalable, hierarchical, map-based internetwork routing architecture, covering endpoints, nodes, maps, locators, connectivity specifications and forwarding modes.

Nimrod.why: The whole document specifies the Nimrod routing architecture: maps, locators, node attributes, and forwarding modes.
Nimrod.quote: Nimrod is a scalable routing architecture designed to accommodate a continually expanding and diversifying internetwork.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as sharing link-state distribution and path-oriented forwarding ideas with Nimrod; the document is not about IDPR.
Nimrod is a more specific tech tag under this topic, so the parent is implied.
Referenced only for comparison of source routing and hop-by-hop forwarding.
DNS names appear only in examples and as an analogy for endpoint labels.

RFC1993.title: PPP Gandalf FZA Compression Protocol
RFC1993.summary: Informational RFC describing use of the Gandalf FZA (and FZA+) LZ-derived compression algorithm for PPP packets, including packet format and the CCP Gandalf-FZA configuration option.

PPP.why: The document defines the PPP packet format, protocol field values, and the CCP configuration option for FZA, so it extends PPP and its Compression Control Protocol.
PPP.quote: the PPP Protocol field indicates type hex 00FB (link compressed datagram), or type hex 00FD (compressed datagram).

compression.why: FZA is a Lempel-Ziv-derived lossless compression algorithm, and the document specifies how it is applied to PPP payloads. This is the closest fit for general lossless compression.
compression.quote: This document describes the use of the Gandalf FZA data compression algorithm [3] for compressing PPP encapsulated packets.

rejected.why: FZA compresses whole PPP packets, not protocol headers, so this does not fit.
IPHC is a header compression scheme for PPP, not this payload compression algorithm.
LZS is a different Lempel-Ziv scheme. FZA is only LZ-derived and is not LZS.

gaps.name: PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP) / PPP compression algorithms
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PPP CCP or PPP payload compression algorithms such as FZA, so this RFC and its sibling PPP compression RFCs have no precise home.

RFC1994.title: PPP Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP)
RFC1994.summary: RFC 1994 specifies CHAP, a PPP authentication protocol using a 3-way challenge/response handshake with a hashed secret (MD5), including its option negotiation and packet formats.

PPP.why: CHAP is a PPP authentication protocol, negotiated via an LCP option and carried in PPP frames with protocol 0xc223. PPP readers would expect it.
PPP.quote: This document defines a method for Authentication using PPP, which uses a random Challenge, with a cryptographically hashed Response

rejected.why: MD5 is only the required hash algorithm used by CHAP. The document does not specify or analyse it.
CHAP is an authentication protocol, but the PPP tag is the more specific fit. The generic authentication topic is not needed as a separate tag.
The document only mentions that a central server may check challenge and response values. It does not define an AAA framework.
RADIUS is not mentioned. The central-server implementation note is generic.

RFC1995.title: Incremental Zone Transfer in DNS
RFC1995.summary: RFC 1995 specifies IXFR, an incremental zone transfer mechanism for DNS that transfers only changed portions of a zone, with query and response formats, purging, and condensation rules.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS query type (IXFR) and its server and client behaviour for zone transfers, updating RFC 1035.
DNS.quote: This document proposes extensions to the DNS protocols to provide an incremental zone transfer (IXFR) mechanism.

rejected.why: Dynamic updates are not specified; IXFR only propagates zone changes between servers.
TCP and UDP are only the transports for the query; nothing new is defined about their use.
UDP is used as the first-try transport and checksum is mentioned, but the document is not about UDP itself.

RFC1996.title: A Mechanism for Prompt Notification of Zone Changes (DNS NOTIFY)
RFC1996.summary: Defines the DNS NOTIFY opcode, by which a master server tells slave servers that a zone's SOA has changed so they can query for new data and start a zone transfer.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS opcode and message flow. It also defines master, slave and stealth server roles and refines zone refresh behaviour.
DNS.quote: This memo describes the NOTIFY opcode for DNS, by which a master server advises a set of slave servers that the master's data has been changed

rejected.why: UDP and TCP are only the transports NOTIFY runs over. The document defines nothing new about how UDP is used.
NOTIFY announces zone changes between servers. It is not the dynamic update protocol for modifying zone data.
NOTIFY uses the base DNS message format, with no EDNS options.

RFC1997.title: BGP Communities Attribute
RFC1997.summary: RFC 1997 defines the BGP COMMUNITIES optional transitive path attribute, which groups destinations for policy control, and specifies the well-known communities NO_EXPORT, NO_ADVERTISE and NO_EXPORT_SUBCONFED.

BGP communities.why: The whole document specifies the BGP COMMUNITIES attribute, its value encoding, well-known communities, operation and aggregation behaviour.
BGP communities.quote: This document creates the COMMUNITIES path attribute is an optional transitive attribute of variable length.

rejected.why: The more specific child BGP communities fits; BGP itself is only the protocol being extended, so the parent is implied.
Confederations are mentioned only in defining NO_EXPORT semantics. The document does not address route reflection or confederations in their own right.
Aggregation is mentioned briefly for how communities are combined on aggregates. The document is not about CIDR.

RFC1998.title: An Application of the BGP Community Attribute in Multi-home Routing
RFC1998.summary: Informational RFC showing how providers can use the BGP community attribute to map customer-tagged communities to LOCAL_PREF values, replacing AS-based per-customer configuration in multihomed routing, with an MCI example and cisco configurations.

BGP communities.why: The whole document is an application of the BGP community attribute to set LOCAL_PREF, with community-to-LOCAL_PREF mappings and configuration examples.
BGP communities.quote: the technique presented uses a community-based, rather than the common AS-based, configuration of the BGP "LOCAL_PREF"

rejected.why: BGP is the protocol being operated, but the more specific BGP communities tag covers the document; the parent is implied.
Multihoming is the motivating scenario, but the document is about the community-based policy technique, and the multihoming tag is under addressing, which concerns IP address architecture.
Not discussed; the document does not cover route reflection or confederations.

RFC1999.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 1900-1999
RFC1999.summary: RFC 1999 is a slightly annotated catalogue of RFCs 1900 through 1999, giving each one's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track marking.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a status report and index of a block of RFCs. Readers browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1900

rejected.why: RFC 1997 and RFC 1998 are listed as entries only. The document does not specify or analyse BGP communities.
Many PPP RFCs appear in the list, but each gets only a one-paragraph abstract. The document is not about PPP.
The SNMPv2 RFCs are listed as entries only. The document does not cover SNMP in any depth.
DNS NOTIFY, IXFR and other DNS RFCs are mentioned as list entries only.
It is a status listing of one block of RFCs, not a history or retrospective. RFC series fits better.

RFC2000.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2000.summary: RFC 2000 (STD 1) is the IAB's quarterly catalogue of Internet protocol standards, describing the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and listing protocols by state (standard, draft, proposed, experimental, informational, historic) with new RFCs and changes.

IETF process.why: Describes the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels and RFC processing rules, which is the process content of the document.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: Explains the RFC series, submission to the RFC Editor, the decision table and how to obtain RFCs.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: Assigned Numbers and the IANA contact are only mentioned as references and contacts.
The IAB is the author, but the document is a standards status list, not architectural principles.
Explains state and status terms, but this is process definition rather than a glossary.
The list is a snapshot of standards status, not a retrospective.

RFC2001.title: TCP Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Retransmit, and Fast Recovery Algorithms
RFC2001.summary: RFC 2001 documents the TCP slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery algorithms originally developed by Van Jacobson.

congestion control.why: The whole document specifies TCP congestion control algorithms (cwnd, ssthresh, loss response). Congestion control is the best-fitting subject, and readers of that page would expect this RFC.
congestion control.quote: four intertwined algorithms that have never been fully documented as Internet standards: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery

TCP.why: The document specifies sender-side behaviour that modern TCP implementations must follow, so it belongs on the TCP page.
TCP.quote: Slow start adds another window to the sender's TCP: the congestion window, called "cwnd".

rejected.why: NewReno is a later modification of fast recovery. This RFC describes the original Reno-era algorithms and does not define NewReno.
Loss is the only congestion signal discussed. Explicit congestion notification does not appear.

RFC2002.title: IP Mobility Support
RFC2002.summary: RFC 2002 specifies Mobile IPv4: agent discovery, registration of care-of addresses with a home agent, tunnelling of datagrams to mobile nodes, and related routing, ARP and authentication rules.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document defines the Mobile IPv4 protocol: home agents, foreign agents, care-of addresses, agent discovery, registration and tunnelling.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document specifies protocol enhancements that allow transparent routing of IP datagrams to mobile nodes in the Internet.

ARP.why: A substantial section specifies proxy and gratuitous ARP rules the home agent and mobile node must follow, which ARP readers would want.
ARP.quote: A Proxy ARP [18] is an ARP Reply sent by one node on behalf of another node which is either unable or unwilling to answer its own ARP Requests.

rejected.why: IP-in-IP, minimal and GRE encapsulation are only used and referenced (defined in RFC 2003/2004), not specified here.
ICMP Router Discovery is extended as the carrier for Agent Advertisements, but ICMP itself is a substrate.
Keyed MD5 is the default authentication algorithm but is only used as a mechanism, not specified.
UDP port 434 is only the transport for registration messages.
Section 4.4 covers multicast for mobile nodes briefly, but it is not a substantial subject of the document.
DHCP is mentioned only as one way to obtain a co-located care-of address, and its details are out of scope.

RFC2003.title: IP Encapsulation within IP
RFC2003.summary: RFC 2003 specifies IP-in-IP encapsulation (protocol 4): outer header field settings, TTL handling, ICMP relaying from within the tunnel, tunnel soft state and MTU discovery, and security considerations.

IP-in-IP.why: The whole document defines the IP-in-IP encapsulation method, including outer header fields, protocol number 4, and decapsulation behaviour.
IP-in-IP.quote: This document specifies a method by which an IP datagram may be encapsulated (carried as payload) within an IP datagram.

ICMP.why: Sections 4 and 5 specify in detail how the encapsulator handles and relays each ICMP message type from inside the tunnel.
ICMP.quote: After an encapsulated datagram has been sent, the encapsulator may receive an ICMP [9] message from any intermediate router within the tunnel
ICMP.section: 4. ICMP Messages from within the Tunnel

PMTUD.why: A full subsection covers tunnel MTU discovery and its interaction with the Don't Fragment bit and fragmentation.
PMTUD.quote: all encapsulator implementations MUST support Path MTU Discovery [5, 7] soft state within their tunnels.

rejected.why: Mobile IP is the motivating application, but the document defines a generic encapsulation method, not Mobile IP itself.
The IP Authentication Header and ESP are mentioned only in the security considerations as filtering and authentication aids.
IP-in-IP is the more specific child of tunneling, so the parent is implied and not listed.
The document operates on IPv4 headers, but it is about the encapsulation method, not IPv4 itself.
Source Quench and congestion handling get only brief treatment in 5.2.

RFC2004.title: Minimal Encapsulation within IP
RFC2004.summary: Specifies minimal encapsulation for IPv4 datagrams (protocol 55) using a small forwarding header inserted after the IP header, as a lower-overhead alternative to IP-in-IP tunnelling, motivated by Mobile IP.

tunneling.why: The whole document defines a new IP encapsulation/tunnelling method with its own header format and encapsulation/decapsulation rules. It is not IP-in-IP or GRE, so the generic tunneling topic is the right fit.
tunneling.quote: This document specifies a method by which an IP datagram may be encapsulated (carried as payload) within an IP datagram, with less overhead

Mobile IPv4.why: The mobileip working group produced it as an optional encapsulation for Mobile IPv4 home-agent tunnelling, so Mobile IP readers would want it. Mobility is the main motivation, but the mechanism is general.
Mobile IPv4.quote: delivery of a datagram to a mobile node using Mobile IP

rejected.why: The document contrasts itself with IP-in-IP (RFC 2003) and defers to it for ICMP and routing-loop handling, but it specifies a different mechanism.
It modifies IPv4 header fields, but IPv4 is the substrate and the document is not about the IP protocol itself.
Path MTU Discovery is mentioned only as a reason for the fragmentation restriction, a minor point.
The ICMP section only defers to RFC 2003.

RFC2005.title: Applicability Statement for IP Mobility Support
RFC2005.summary: Applicability statement for Mobile IP (RFC 2002), describing its key features, scope (macro mobility), security, MIB, implementations and interoperability evidence supporting advancement to Proposed Standard.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document discusses the applicability, features, security and interoperability of Mobile IP (IPv4, RFC 2002), which is the subject of the Mobile IPv4 tag.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Mobile IP provides an efficient, scalable mechanism for node mobility within the Internet.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as the recommended mechanism for protecting data packets; not what the document is about.
Tunneling is the mechanism Mobile IP relies on and is described briefly, but the document is not about tunneling itself.
Keyed MD5 is mentioned as the mandatory authentication algorithm in one sentence; not a subject of the document.
The Mobile IP MIB (RFC 2006) is only noted as existing, not specified here.
Parent of Mobile IPv4; the more specific child tag fits.

RFC2006.title: The Definitions of Managed Objects for IP Mobility Support using SMIv2
RFC2006.summary: Defines the SNMPv2 MIB module (MIP-MIB) for managing Mobile IP mobile nodes, foreign agents and home agents, including registration, agent advertisement, and security association/violation objects.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMIv2 with object groups, tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

Mobile IPv4.why: The MIB's subject is Mobile IP (RFC 2002) entities, covering agent discovery, registration, bindings and security associations. This is IPv4 Mobile IP, so Mobile IPv4 fits.
Mobile IPv4.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the Mobile Node, Foreign Agent and Home Agent of the Mobile IP Protocol.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework used to carry and access the MIB. The document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour; MIB is the more specific tag.
The security text mentions the IP Authentication Header and ESP only as optional ways to protect MIB access.
GRE appears only as an encapsulation-type value in objects. The document is not about GRE.
The RFC 1256 router discovery parameters are referenced for advertisement configuration objects. The document is not about ICMP.
Gratuitous and proxy ARP counters are mentioned only as statistics objects. The document is not about ARP.

RFC2007.title: Catalogue of Network Training Materials
RFC2007.summary: FYI 29 is a catalogue of Internet user and trainer training materials (guides, tutorials, videos, collections) compiled by the TRAINMAT working group, with the template used to submit entries.

user guides.why: The RFC is an FYI-series catalogue of introductory guides and training resources for Internet users and trainers, which is the subject the user guides tag covers.
user guides.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide a catalogue of quality Network Training Materials for use by Internet trainers.

rejected.why: FTP appears only as an access method for the listed materials, and one entry is a book about FTP. The RFC does not specify or analyse the protocol.
Gopher is only an access method and a topic in some of the listed guides. The RFC says nothing about the protocol itself.
The URL examples appear in the template field notes, but the RFC is not about URI syntax or schemes.
The Content-Type field of the template refers to MIME types, but this is only a field convention, not a media type registration.

gaps.name: Network training materials / user education
gaps.why: No tag covers training and education resources. The user guides tag is the nearest fit.

RFC2008.title: Implications of Various Address Allocation Policies for Internet Routing
RFC2008.summary: BCP 7 analyses how address allocation policies ("address ownership" vs "address lending") affect the scalability of Internet routing under CIDR aggregation, and recommends address lending, with renumbering, for organizations that cannot provide aggregation.

addressing.why: The document is about IP address allocation and management policies (ownership vs. lending) and their routing consequences, so it belongs under addressing.
addressing.quote: The purpose of this document is to articulate certain relevant fundamental technical issues that must be considered in formulating unicast address allocation and management policies

CIDR.why: Provider-based aggregation under CIDR is the core mechanism the policy analysis rests on, and a substantial part of the document discusses it.
CIDR.quote: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) [RFC1518, RFC1519] has been deployed since late 1992 in the Public Internet as the primary mechanism to contain the growth rate

renumbering.why: Renumbering is the direct consequence of address lending, and the document recommends it and discusses how to reduce its costs.
renumbering.quote: If a loan ends, the organization can no longer use the borrowed addresses, and therefore must get new addresses and renumber to use them.

routing architecture.why: The document discusses hierarchical routing, aggregation and the scaling limits of the routing system, which are routing architecture and scalability matters.
routing architecture.quote: Hierarchical routing requires that addresses be assigned to reflect the actual network topology.
routing architecture.section: 3 Hierarchical routing and its implication on address allocation

rejected.why: BGP is never discussed. The document covers route aggregation in general terms, not the protocol.
It is mentioned only once, as a tool that could ease renumbering. The document is not about it.
NATs and application gateways are mentioned briefly as an alternative to renumbering. This is not a substantial part of the document.
A single closing sentence says the recommendations also apply to IPv6. The document is about IPv4-era policy.
The document concerns allocation policy principles and registries only in passing. It does not address IANA registries or stewardship.

RFC2009.title: GPS-Based Addressing and Routing
RFC2009.summary: Experimental proposal for geographic (GPS-based) addressing and routing in IP, using GPS-mapped multicast groups or a geometric polygon-based router overlay, with last-mile filtering, a management protocol (IGPSMP), and a DNS-based application-layer variant.

multicast.why: The main routing scheme maps geographic partitions to multicast groups, builds multicast trees with designated routers, and uses multicast for last-mile delivery.
multicast.quote: Each partition and atom is mapped to a multicast address.

addressing.why: The document defines a new geographic addressing model (atoms, partitions, polygons) and how it maps into the IPv4 address space.
addressing.quote: By a geographic address we mean an IP address assigned to a geographic area or point of interest.

routing architecture.why: The GEO scheme defines a hierarchical router architecture with service-area tables, failover and optimizations, and a scalability design.
routing architecture.quote: a virtual network which uses GPS addresses for routing will be overlayed onto the current IP internetwork.

rejected.why: DNS is used to resolve postal-like geographic names and a 'geographic' domain is sketched, but this is a minor part, not a DNS specification.
GPSRouteD uses IP tunnels between routers, but as an implementation substrate, not a new tunneling mechanism.
GPScast messages are encapsulated in UDP datagrams, which is only a carrier.
Mobile hosts and base stations are assumed, but the document does not specify mobility management.
Considered because the document is built on GPS location. Its focus is addressing and routing, not conveying location information, so it fits less well than addressing and multicast.

gaps.name: geographic addressing/routing (GPScast)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for location-based or geocast routing. The document's core subject is delivering messages to geographic regions.

RFC2010.title: Operational Criteria for Root Name Servers
RFC2010.summary: RFC 2010 specifies operational requirements for DNS root name servers, covering software, hardware performance, network connectivity, physical environment, zone transfers, and reporting.

DNS.why: The whole document defines operational requirements for DNS root servers: recursion disabled, AXFR/IXFR/NOTIFY zone transfers, glue, NS RRsets, PTR records, and performance.
DNS.quote: This document specifies the operational requirements of root name servers, including host hardware capacities, name server software revisions, network connectivity, and physical environment.

rejected.why: NTP is only required for clock synchronization of the host in one short clause (2.4); the document is not about NTP.
The UDP checksum requirement (2.2) is a single item and UDP is the DNS transport here, not the subject.
Sections 2.3, 2.6 and 2.7 touch on host and physical security, but they are part of the DNS server requirements and not the main subject.
Outage reporting and response times are administrative requirements for DNS servers. The document does not address network management practice in general.
IANA is named as zone master for the root zone, but the document is not about IANA registries or stewardship.

RFC2011.title: SNMPv2 Management Information Base for the Internet Protocol using SMIv2
RFC2011.summary: Defines the SMIv2 IP-MIB module, with managed objects for IP and ICMP statistics, the IP address table and the address translation table, taken from MIB-II.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module written in SMIv2 that defines the IP and ICMP management objects, so it belongs on the MIB page.
MIB.quote: This document is the MIB module which defines managed objects for managing implementations of the Internet Protocol (IP) [3] and its associated Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) [4].

ICMP.why: A large part of the module is the ICMP group, with per-message-type in and out counters, so ICMP readers would want it.
ICMP.quote: icmpInDestUnreachs OBJECT-TYPE

IPv4.why: The IP group's counters, address table and forwarding controls manage IPv4 implementations, and the IESG note says the module is IPv4-only.
IPv4.quote: The IP, UDP, and TCP MIB modules currently support only IPv4.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is used with. The document defines no protocol behaviour, only objects.
ipNetToMediaTable is an address translation table, but the document doesn't specify ARP itself.
The module is written in ASN.1-based SMI, which is only the notation used.

RFC2012.title: SNMPv2 Management Information Base for the Transmission Control Protocol using SMIv2
RFC2012.summary: Defines the SNMPv2 (SMIv2) MIB module for managing TCP implementations, re-expressing the TCP group of MIB-II objects such as RTO parameters, connection counters and the TCP connection table.

MIB.why: The document's entire purpose is a MIB module (TCP-MIB) written in SMIv2, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This document is the MIB module which defines managed objects for managing implementations of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

TCP.why: The objects expose TCP internals (RTO algorithm, connection states, segment counters, TCB deletion), so readers interested in TCP would want this management view.
TCP.quote: The MIB module for managing TCP implementations.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects. The document defines a MIB module, not SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
The IESG note says the module supports only IPv4 addresses (IpAddress type). That is a limitation of the module, not a subject of the document.
The MIB is written in a subset of ASN.1 through the SMI. ASN.1 is only the notation used and is not the subject.

RFC2013.title: SNMPv2 Management Information Base for the User Datagram Protocol using SMIv2
RFC2013.summary: Defines the SMIv2 version of the UDP MIB module, with counters and a listener table for managing UDP implementations, updating the MIB-II UDP group (RFC 1213).

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (UDP-MIB) written in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules and SMI.
MIB.quote: This document is the MIB module which defines managed objects for managing implementations of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP)

UDP.why: The managed objects are UDP datagram counters and the UDP listener table, so readers interested in UDP operation and management would want it.
UDP.quote: The MIB module for managing UDP implementations.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is used with. The document defines objects only, not protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
The module is written in ASN.1-derived SMI notation, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The IESG note says the objects support only IPv4 addresses. The document is not about IPv4.

RFC2014.title: IRTF Research Group Guidelines and Procedures
RFC2014.summary: BCP 8 defines guidelines and procedures for forming, operating and terminating IRTF Research Groups, and describes the duties of the IRTF Chair, IRSG members and Research Group chairs.

IETF process.why: The document is a process BCP for the IRTF, the research sibling of the IETF, covering chartering, operation, termination, roles and publication of research group documents. IETF process is the closest governance tag for standards-organization procedures and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the guidelines and procedures for formation and operation of IRTF Research Groups.

rejected.why: Section 6.2 touches on publishing Research Group output as Informational or Experimental RFCs, but this is a small part of the document, not its subject.
The document covers appointment of the IRTF Chair and IRSG members, but not NomCom procedures.
The IAB's review of charters for architectural fit is mentioned, but the document is about organizational procedure, not architectural principles.

gaps.name: IRTF (Internet Research Task Force) / research group procedures
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the IRTF or for research group organization. It is closest to the IETF process tag, which only approximates it. A dedicated IRTF tag would help readers looking for IRTF governance.

RFC2015.title: MIME Security with Pretty Good Privacy (PGP)
RFC2015.summary: RFC 2015 defines how PGP encryption, signatures and public keys are carried in MIME using the RFC 1847 multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted security multiparts, and registers application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys.

OpenPGP.why: The document specifies the use of PGP-formatted encrypted, signed and key data in MIME messages (PGP/MIME), which is the OpenPGP usage subject.
OpenPGP.quote: This document describes how Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) can be used to provide privacy and authentication using the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME)

MIME.why: It defines new MIME content types and the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted structure, content-transfer-encoding restrictions and canonicalization rules for MIME bodies.
MIME.quote: This document defines three new content types for implementing security and privacy with PGP: application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys.

rejected.why: S/MIME is a different MIME security approach based on CMS. The document only mentions MOSS and RFC 1847 as related work.
Email is the substrate. The document is about MIME and PGP, and a more specific tag covers each.
MD5 and SHA-1 appear only as micalg values and are not the subject of the document.
The document registers content types, but this is incidental to the PGP/MIME specification and not about media type registry rules.

RFC2016.title: Uniform Resource Agents (URAs)
RFC2016.summary: RFC 2016 describes an experimental architecture for Uniform Resource Agents (URAs): objects that encapsulate high-level Internet information-access activities (targets as URLs/URNs, activation data, scripts, response filters) and are executed by a "URAgency", with a Tcl prototype in the Silk tool.

applications.why: The document specifies an application-level agent architecture and object structure for Internet information clients. It is not tied to any single protocol, so the general applications topic fits.
applications.quote: an experimental agent system architecture that provides sophisticated Internet information access and management

URI.why: The work was presented to the URI working group. Its targets are URLs/URNs, and it aims to identify classes of resources through activity specifications. Readers of the URI subject would want to find it, though it does not define URI syntax.
URI.quote: originally conceived as an extension to the family of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs): Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), Uniform Resource Characteristics (URCs)

rejected.why: URNs are only mentioned as possible targets, and the document does not address them.
URAs help with locating and accessing resources, but the document is about an agent object architecture, not a discovery protocol.
HTTP GET/POST is only the mechanism the sample URA uses to contact targets.
DNS is mentioned only in the introduction, as an example of layered encapsulation.

gaps.name: Software agents / mobile agent systems
gaps.why: The document defines an agent system architecture (URAs and URAgencies) and the taxonomy has no tag for agents.

review: applications: quote not found in the text

notes: applications: quote not found in the text

RFC2017.title: Definition of the URL MIME External-Body Access-Type
RFC2017.summary: Defines a new "URL" access-type for MIME message/external-body parts, letting a URL (carried in a mandatory URL parameter, split into 40-character words) specify how to retrieve the external data.

MIME.why: The document extends MIME's message/external-body media type with a new access-type and a new content-type parameter, including its syntax and use in MIME headers.
MIME.quote: This memo defines a new access-type for message/external-body MIME parts for Uniform Resource Locators (URLs).

URI.why: A substantial part concerns how URL strings are encoded and carried in a header parameter. This includes re-encoding unsafe characters and splitting the URL into words, so readers of URL material would want it.
URI.quote: Uniform Resource Locators, or URLs, also provide a means by which remote data can be retrieved automatically.

rejected.why: The document defines an access-type parameter within message/external-body, not a media type registration or registry rules.
MIME messages are the carrier, but the document is about the MIME external-body mechanism rather than mail architecture or transport.
The header syntax is a MIME content-type parameter, not RFC 822 message format work.
HTTP appears only as an example URL scheme; the document does not specify or extend it.

RFC2018.title: TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options
RFC2018.summary: RFC 2018 specifies the TCP SACK-permitted and SACK options, which let a receiver report non-contiguous received blocks so the sender can selectively retransmit, with receiver and sender behaviour rules.

TCP.why: The document defines new TCP options (SACK-permitted, Kind 4, and SACK, Kind 5) and the data sender and receiver behaviour for them. It is a TCP extension specification.
TCP.quote: The selective acknowledgment extension uses two TCP options. The first is an enabling option, "SACK-permitted"

rejected.why: Section 5.1 only says the existing de facto TCP congestion control algorithms must be preserved. It does not specify any congestion control algorithm.
Reno-style fast recovery is mentioned only in passing as existing behaviour. The document does not define NewReno.
RDP and NETBLT appear only as earlier transports that used selective acknowledgment. They are background in the introduction.
NETBLT is cited only as prior art for selective acknowledgment. The document is not about it.

RFC2019.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets Over FDDI
RFC2019.summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over FDDI: MTU, LLC/SNAP frame format, bridge interaction (adjacency detection), link-local address formation, and link-layer address options and multicast mapping.

FDDI.why: The whole document defines IPv6 over FDDI: MTU, framing, address formation and mapping.
FDDI.quote: This memo specifies the MTU and frame format for transmission of IPv6 [IPV6] packets on FDDI networks

rejected.why: IPv6 is the payload being carried; the document is about the FDDI link-layer binding, and the FDDI tag covers it.
Only the link-layer address option format used by Neighbor Discovery on FDDI is defined; ND itself is specified elsewhere.
It only defines the interface token and prefix length for FDDI; SLAAC itself is in another RFC.
Mentioned only as background for bridges; the document defines its own adjacency detection mechanism instead.

RFC2020.title: IEEE 802.12 Interface MIB
RFC2020.summary: Defines the DOT12-IF-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing IEEE 802.12 (100VG-AnyLAN, Demand Priority) interfaces, covering configuration, training, master/slave mode and priority counters, and its relation to the Interface MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (DOT12-IF-MIB) written in SMI, with objects, conformance groups and mapping to IF-MIB. It exists to define managed objects for 802.12 interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with; the document defines objects, not the protocol itself, so the more specific MIB tag fits.
802.12 can use Ethernet framing, but the document says Ethernet-like MIBs should not be implemented and it does not cover Ethernet.
Token ring framing mode is mentioned, along with the 802.5 MIBs, but only as a framing option; the document is not about token ring.
The subject is a link technology, but the MIB tag is the more specific home. There is no 802.12-specific tag in the taxonomy.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.12 / 100VG-AnyLAN (Demand Priority Access Method)
gaps.why: The document is about managing this LAN medium, and no taxonomy tag covers it. Readers browsing link-layer technologies would expect to find it.

RFC2021.title: Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base Version 2 using SMIv2
RFC2021.summary: Defines the RMON2 MIB module (RMON2-MIB) for remote network monitoring probes, adding protocol directory, protocol distribution, address mapping, network/application layer host and matrix, user history, probe configuration groups, and enhancements to the RMON1 tables.

RMON.why: The document is the RMON version 2 MIB, specifying managed objects for remote network monitoring probes.
RMON.quote: This document continues the architecture created in the RMON MIB [RFC 1757] by providing a major feature upgrade, primarily by providing RMON analysis up to the application layer.

MIB.why: It is a MIB module written in SMIv2, defining new textual conventions (TimeFilter, LastCreateTime, ZeroBasedCounter32) and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to access the MIB objects; the document defines MIB content, not SNMP itself.
Token Ring RMON tables are only augmented with dropped-frames and create-time objects; the document is not about IP over token ring.
TFTP is only used by the probe download objects; it is incidental.
Traffic statistics are collected, but the document is a management MIB rather than a performance metrics specification.

RFC2022.title: Support for Multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 based ATM Networks
RFC2022.summary: Defines the MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) architecture and endpoint behaviours for supporting IP (and other layer 3) multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 ATM point-to-multipoint VCs, using VC meshes or multicast servers.

ATM.why: The whole document specifies how IP multicast is carried over ATM VCs, including MARS control messages, LLC/SNAP encapsulation and VC management.
ATM.quote: Mapping the connectionless IP multicast service over the connection oriented ATM services provided by UNI 3.0/3.1 is a non-trivial task.

multicast.why: It defines group membership distribution and address resolution for multicast, plus multicast router behaviour (promiscuous joins, IGMP alternatives).
multicast.quote: ATM based IP hosts and routers use a Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) to support RFC 1112 style Level 2 IP multicast

rejected.why: IGMP is discussed as context and the MARS offers an alternative to its queries, but the document does not specify IGMP.
The MARS is an analog of the ATM ARP server (RFC 1577), not NHRP.
IPv4 is the example protocol, but the document is about multicast over ATM, not IPv4 itself.
The MARS extends the ATMARP server concept, but it is not ARP and it resolves multicast groups.
Multicast routing protocols such as DVMRP are explicitly out of scope.

RFC2023.title: IP Version 6 over PPP
RFC2023.summary: Defines how IPv6 packets are carried over PPP, the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP) with its Interface-Token and IPv6-Compression-Protocol options, and formation of IPv6 link-local addresses on PPP links.

PPP.why: The document specifies a new PPP NCP (IPV6CP), its options and encapsulation of IPv6 in PPP frames, so PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: This document defines the method for transmission of IP Version 6 [2] packets over PPP links as well as the Network Control Protocol (NCP)

IPv6.why: A substantial part covers IPv6 link-local address formation from the interface token and the autoconfiguration interaction (DupAddrDetectTransmits).
IPv6.quote: It also specifies the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses on PPP links.

rejected.why: Stateless autoconfiguration is referenced only for how the interface token is used and DAD is set to zero; the document does not specify SLAAC itself.
The IPv6-Compression-Protocol option only negotiates which compression protocol to use (value 004f); no compression scheme is defined.
Only listed as a reference; not addressed in the body.

RFC2024.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Data Link Switching using SMIv2
RFC2024.summary: Defines a SMIv2 MIB module for configuring, monitoring and controlling Data Link Switches (DLSw), covering transport connections, interfaces, directory caches, circuits, SDLC stations and traps.

DLSw.why: The whole document is the management object definitions for DLSw nodes, their partner transport connections, circuits and directories.
DLSw.quote: it defines objects for configuring, monitoring, and controlling Data Link Switches (DLSw)

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (DLSW-MIB) written in SMIv2, with compliance statements, groups and notifications.
MIB.quote: This specification defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with SNMP-based network management.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is used with. The document defines no new protocol behaviour, only a MIB module, which falls under the MIB tag.
TCP is only a transport for DLSw. The document defines a few TCP-specific config objects but is not about TCP.
NetBIOS names appear in the DLSw directory objects, but the document does not specify or extend NetBIOS.
SDLC link stations are mapped to DLSw, but the SDLC MIB is a separate RFC. The DLSw tag already sits under SNA.

RFC2025.title: The Simple Public-Key GSS-API Mechanism (SPKM)
RFC2025.summary: Specifies SPKM-1 and SPKM-2, public-key-based GSS-API mechanisms defining algorithms, context establishment, per-message and deletion tokens, QOP values and ASN.1 token formats.

GSS-API.why: The document defines a GSS-API mechanism (SPKM) with its tokens, status codes, QOP and support functions, so it belongs on the GSS-API page.
GSS-API.quote: This specification defines protocols, procedures, and conventions to be employed by peers implementing the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface

rejected.why: Certificates and the X.509 authentication exchanges are used as the basis for key management, but the document is not about X.509 itself.
Kerberos V5 GSS mechanism is a model for compatibility only, not the subject.
RSA is used as a mandatory algorithm, but the document is not about RSA.
ASN.1 is the encoding for tokens and an appendix module, i.e. substrate.
Relies on a public-key infrastructure but does not specify one.
Authentication is provided via the GSS-API mechanism, already covered by the more specific GSS-API tag.

RFC2026.title: The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3
RFC2026.summary: RFC 2026 (BCP 9) defines the IETF Internet Standards Process: maturity levels, standards actions, appeals, handling of external specifications, and IPR and copyright rules for contributions.

IETF process.why: The whole document specifies the IETF standards track, maturity levels, IESG review, Last Call, appeals and variance procedures.
IETF process.quote: This memo documents the process currently used by the Internet community for the standardization of protocols and procedures.

IPR.why: Section 10 is a substantial body of main-text policy on contributor licences, patent disclosure, RAND assurances and copyright notices. The abstract names it as a topic of the memo.
IPR.quote: In all matters of intellectual property rights and procedures, the intention is to benefit the Internet community and the public at large

rejected.why: It describes RFC publication, STD and BCP subseries and Internet-Drafts, but only as part of the standards process. The document is not about RFC format or editing.
Section 14 is a short glossary and the document is not about terminology.
Mentioned only in the glossary and in the definition of 'online'.
Mentioned only as an example of an external standard incorporated by reference.
IANA appears only in the acronym glossary.

RFC2027.title: IAB and IESG Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Operation of the Nominating and Recall Committees
RFC2027.summary: BCP 10 documents the process by which the IETF Nominating Committee selects candidates for IESG and IAB positions, how those candidates are confirmed, and how sitting members may be recalled.

NomCom.why: The whole document specifies NomCom selection, operation, confirmation and recall procedures, which is exactly the NomCom subject.
NomCom.quote: The principal function of the nominating committee is to recruit and nominate candidates for open IESG and IAB positions.

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child and fits the document; the parent is implied.
Implied by the NomCom tag via its ancestors; no broader governance subject is addressed.

gaps.name: IAB/IESG member recall process
gaps.why: The document also specifies the recall committee procedure for removing sitting IAB or IESG members, which has no dedicated tag; it is partly covered by the NomCom tag.

RFC2028.title: The Organizations Involved in the IETF Standards Process
RFC2028.summary: RFC 2028 (BCP 11) describes the individuals and organizations in the IETF standards process: RFC Editor, WG chairs, document editors, IETF, Secretariat, ISOC, IESG, IAB, IANA and IRTF.

IETF process.why: The whole document describes the roles and bodies (IESG, IAB, WGs, chairs, Secretariat) that operate the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the individuals and organizations involved in the IETF. This includes descriptions of the IESG, the IETF Working Groups

rejected.why: Nomcom is mentioned only briefly, with a pointer to RFC 2027 for its procedures; the document is not about it.
IANA is one short section describing its role; the document is not about registries or IANA guidance.
The RFC Editor is described in one short section; the document is not about RFC format or publication.
Only a single sentence on disclosure of intellectual property; not a substantial part.

RFC2029.title: RTP Payload Format of Sun's CellB Video Encoding
RFC2029.summary: Defines an RTP packetization scheme and payload header for Sun's CellB video encoding, including the CellB bytestream structure in an appendix.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for the CellB video codec, defining RTP timestamp/marker usage and a payload header.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes a packetization scheme for the CellB video encoding.

codecs.why: Appendix A describes the CellB bytestream (cell, skip and table codes). CellB has no dedicated child tag, so the generic codecs tag fits.
codecs.quote: The Cell image compression algorithm is a variable bit-rate video coding scheme.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the RTP payload format tag; the document does not extend RTP itself.
Not related; the H.261 reference is only a cited RFC and CellB is a different codec.

gaps.name: CellB video codec
gaps.why: CellB is the subject of the document, but the taxonomy has no specific tag for it. It is covered here only by the generic codecs tag.

RFC2030.title: Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) Version 4 for IPv4, IPv6 and OSI
RFC2030.summary: RFC 2030 specifies SNTP version 4, a simplified, stateless client/server profile of NTP for clock synchronization, with IPv6 and OSI header reinterpretation and an optional anycast mode.

NTP.why: The document defines SNTPv4, an adaptation of NTP: message format, timestamp format, and client and server operations for synchronizing clocks.
NTP.quote: SNTP can be used when the ultimate performance of the full NTP implementation described in RFC-1305 is not needed or justified.

rejected.why: Multicast and anycast modes are used by SNTP, but the document does not address multicast routing or group management. IGMP is only a requirement for participants.
UDP port 123 is only the transport substrate, and the document defines nothing new about UDP.
IPv6 is mentioned for the header reinterpretation of the Reference Identifier. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
OSI CLTS is mentioned as an alternative carrier for SNTP packets. The document is not about OSI network-layer protocols.
Anycast here is an SNTP operating mode, not anycast addressing and operation in general.

RFC2031.title: IETF-ISOC relationship
RFC2031.summary: Informational summary by the Poised WG chair of the proposed division of responsibilities between the IETF and the Internet Society, covering the legal umbrella and ISOC's roles in the standards process, to gauge consensus.

IETF process.why: The document defines how ISOC takes part in IETF standards process administration (nomcom chair, IAB approval, appeals, approval of process documents) and the boundary conditions for that involvement.
IETF process.quote: ISOC will assist the standards process by - appointing the nomcom chair - approving IAB candidates

IPR.why: A substantial part covers ISOC's legal umbrella: officer insurance, copyright protection of RFCs and protection in IPR disputes over standards.
IPR.quote: legal protection of the RFC series of documents; In such a way that these documents can be freely distributed, copied etc. but cannot be altered or misused.

rejected.why: The nomcom chair appointment is mentioned only briefly. The document is not about NomCom procedures, which are covered in separate Poised documents.
The parent is implied by the more specific IETF process tag.
RFC copyright protection is mentioned only as one item in the legal umbrella. The document is not about RFC format or publication.

review: IPR: quote not found in the text

notes: IPR: quote not found in the text

RFC2032.title: RTP Payload Format for H.261 Video Streams
RFC2032.summary: Specifies how to packetize H.261 video streams in RTP, defining the payload header fields, fragmentation at macroblock boundaries, and optional H.261-specific RTCP control packets (FIR and NACK) for loss recovery.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines an RTP payload format for H.261 video, including the payload header and packetization rules.
RTP payload format.quote: The purpose of this memo is to specify the RTP payload format for encapsulating H.261 video streams in RTP

codecs.why: The document covers the H.261 video codec's structure (GOBs, MBs, Huffman coding) and how to packetize it. The taxonomy has no H.261-specific tag, so this is the closest fit.
codecs.quote: The ITU-T recommendation H.261 [6] specifies the encodings used by ITU-T compliant video-conference codecs.

RTCP.why: A substantial section defines new RTCP packet types, FIR and NACK, for video refresh after packet loss.
RTCP.quote: This specification defines two H.261-specific RTCP control packets, "Full INTRA-frame Request" and "Negative Acknowledgement"
RTCP.section: 5.1. Use of optional H.261-specific control packets

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate. The more specific RTP payload format tag already covers the document, and its ancestors are implied.
UDP is mentioned only as the underlying transport. The document does not specify anything about UDP.
ISDN appears only as the original target of H.261. The document is about carrying H.261 over packet networks.
NACK-based reliable multicast protocols are mentioned only as a contrast. The document's own control packets are unicast and not reliable-multicast mechanisms.

gaps.name: H.261 video codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no H.261-specific tag, though other codecs such as H.264 and VP8 have their own. The codecs tag is only an approximate fit.

RFC2033.title: Local Mail Transfer Protocol
RFC2033.summary: RFC 2033 defines LMTP, a variant of SMTP/ESMTP for delivering mail into systems without a queue, returning one reply per recipient after DATA or BDAT LAST.

SMTP.why: LMTP is a modified SMTP/ESMTP variant, specifying the LHLO command and per-recipient replies to DATA and BDAT. It is a mail transfer protocol derived from SMTP and belongs on the SMTP page.
SMTP.quote: The LMTP protocol is identical to the SMTP protocol SMTP [SMTP] [HOST-REQ] with its service extensions [ESMTP], except as modified by this document.

rejected.why: SMTP is the more specific child tag and already covers the subject.
TCP is only the substrate. The document merely says LMTP must not use port 25.
BINARYMIME/CHUNKING is mentioned only for how BDAT LAST replies behave, not as MIME content.
The document is about transfer and reply semantics, not message headers or format.

RFC2034.title: SMTP Service Extension for Returning Enhanced Error Codes
RFC2034.summary: RFC 2034 defines an SMTP service extension (ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES) by which servers prefix 2xx/4xx/5xx reply text with RFC 1893 enhanced status codes, to aid delivery status notifications.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension, with an EHLO keyword and changes to server response behaviour. It is an extension of SMTP.
SMTP.quote: the name of the SMTP service extension defined here is Enhanced-Status-Codes
SMTP.section: 3. Framework for the Enhanced Error Statuses Extension

rejected.why: The delivery status notification format (RFC 1894) appears only in the usage example. This document does not define it.
The parent is implied by SMTP, and the document is about the SMTP extension in particular.
The multipart/report example is illustrative only.
ABNF is used only as notation for the status-code syntax.

RFC2035.title: RTP Payload Format for JPEG-compressed Video
RFC2035.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for carrying JPEG (Motion-JPEG) compressed video, including a 64-bit payload header, type codes, quantization table derivation from Q, restart marker handling, and fragmentation/reassembly.

RTP payload format.why: The whole document specifies how JPEG video frames are packetized in RTP, including header fields, fragmentation and restart markers.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes the RTP payload format for JPEG video streams.

codecs.why: It defines the JPEG video coding subset (sampling factors, Huffman and quantization tables, type codes) that the payload carries. The taxonomy has no JPEG-specific tag, so the codecs parent fits.
codecs.quote: Six type codes are currently defined.

rejected.why: The more specific child RTP payload format is chosen instead, so the parent is implied.
Session setup protocol for dynamic types is explicitly out of scope.
Not discussed.

gaps.name: JPEG / Motion-JPEG
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the JPEG image/video compression standard. Only the generic codecs tag is available.

RFC2036.title: Observations on the use of Components of the Class A Address Space within the Internet
RFC2036.summary: Informational commentary on allocating unallocated Class A address space as classless prefixes, analysing the implications for service providers and end networks and concluding that widespread classless routing deployment is needed.

addressing.why: The document is about IP address space allocation from the Class A pool and its operational guidelines, which is the addressing subject.
addressing.quote: commence allocation of the presently unallocated components of the Class A address space to registries, for deployment within the Internet as class-less address blocks

CIDR.why: Much of the body analyses classless prefixes, aggregation and the transition from class-full to classless routing, which is the CIDR subject.
CIDR.quote: Network Service Providers Must Use Class-less Routing
CIDR.section: Implications of Address Allocation from the Class A space

rejected.why: The routing implications are discussed, but the document's focus is address allocation and the CIDR transition, not routing architecture or scalability design in general.
The document concerns IPv4 address space, but the more specific addressing and CIDR tags already cover it.
Multihoming appears only as one constraint in the allocation guidelines, not as a main subject.

RFC2037.title: Entity MIB using SMIv2
RFC2037.summary: Defines the ENTITY-MIB SMIv2 module for representing multiple physical and logical entities managed by a single SNMP agent, with physical, logical, mapping, general and notification groups plus usage examples.

MIB.why: The RFC defines a new MIB module (ENTITY-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables, conformance groups and a notification, which is exactly what the MIB tag covers.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing multiple logical and physical entities managed by a single SNMP agent.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is carried over; the document defines a MIB module, not changes to SNMP. The MIB tag is the more specific child.
Implied as an ancestor of MIB, so it is not listed separately.
The SMI uses ASN.1 only as the definition notation for the module; the document is not about ASN.1.
The community-string and naming-scope discussion concerns how entities are addressed, not SNMP protocol specification.

RFC2038.title: RTP Payload Format for MPEG1/MPEG2 Video
RFC2038.summary: Defines two RTP packetization schemes for MPEG-1/MPEG-2: encapsulation of MPEG System/Transport/Program streams, and direct encapsulation of video and audio elementary streams with video- and audio-specific headers and error-recovery guidance.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for MPEG-1/2 video and audio, defining RTP header usage and payload-specific headers.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes a packetization scheme for MPEG video and audio streams.

codecs.why: MPEG-1/2 video and audio codecs have no dedicated tag in the taxonomy. The codecs parent fits as the subject of the payload format.
