codecs.quote: MPEG1 Video (ISO/IEC 11172-2) (b) MPEG2 Video (ISO/IEC 13818-2) (c) MPEG1 Audio (ISO/IEC 11172-3) (d) MPEG2 Audio (ISO/IEC 13818-3)

rejected.why: The child tag RTP payload format is more specific and already implies RTP.
MPEG audio Layer-III is only mentioned in passing. The document covers MPEG-1/2 audio in general, not the MP3 loss-tolerant payload format.
RTCP is not discussed in the document.
SDP is not used or specified here. Only RTP payload type assignment is referenced.
The document is about packetization, not streaming delivery or operations.

gaps.name: MPEG-1/MPEG-2 video and audio (ISO/IEC 11172, 13818)
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag exists for the MPEG codecs and system streams, so only the generic codecs parent could be used.

RFC2039.title: Applicability of Standards Track MIBs to Management of World Wide Web Servers
RFC2039.summary: Informational report assessing which existing standards-track MIBs (MIB-II, Host Resources, Network Services Monitoring, Application MIB) apply to SNMP management of WWW servers, and what additional MIB attributes are needed.

MIB.why: The whole document analyses existing MIB modules (MIB-II, Host Resources, Network Services Monitoring, Application MIB) and defines the additional MIB attribute groups needed for web server management.
MIB.quote: report on the applicability of the existing standards track MIBs to management of WWW servers.

rejected.why: The document concerns managing WWW servers, not the HTTP protocol's semantics or extensions; HTTP is only the service being managed.
SNMP is the management framework used, but the document is about MIB content; the MIB tag is the more specific fit.
The web is the subject being managed, not the topic; the document is about network management of web servers, not web architecture.
Error reporting and log files are discussed only as requirements; no logging protocol is addressed.

RFC2040.title: The RC5, RC5-CBC, RC5-CBC-Pad, and RC5-CTS Algorithms
RFC2040.summary: Informational RFC specifying the RC5 block cipher, its key expansion, and the RC5-CBC, RC5-CBC-Pad and RC5-CTS modes, with C sample code, test vectors, security guidance and ASN.1 identifiers.

cryptography.why: The whole document specifies a block cipher and its chaining/padding modes, key expansion, test vectors and key-length guidance. No child tag (AES, DES, RC4, etc.) covers RC5, so the parent topic applies directly.
cryptography.quote: This document defines four ciphers with enough detail to ensure interoperability between different implementations.

rejected.why: Section 11 only gives algorithm identifiers and a parameters structure; this is a minor part of the document, not its subject.
MD5 appears only in the Security Considerations as a suggested key-derivation hash; the document is not about it.
The key objects and expansion are internal to the cipher, not key establishment or provisioning.
The ASN.1 identifiers are for use by applications such as CMS or PKCS, but the document does not specify CMS usage.

gaps.name: RC5 block cipher / symmetric block cipher modes (CBC, CTS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RC5 or generic block cipher modes of operation. The RFC is specifically about them, so the parent 'cryptography' tag is the closest fit.

RFC2041.title: Mobile Network Tracing
RFC2041.summary: Informational status report proposing a trace file format for recording mobile/wireless network behaviour and the PaM tools that modulate a wired LAN to replay recorded traces for repeatable testing.

packet capture.why: The core of the RFC is a trace file format (records, tracks, headers) and tools for collecting, processing and analysing network traces, which matches packet capture and trace file formats.
packet capture.quote: Our goal is to begin discussion on a standard format for mobile network tracing as well as a testbed for mobile systems research.

performance measurement.why: Substantial parts measure latency, bandwidth and loss from ICMP echo traces, and derive loss models. Network emulation for testing is performance measurement methodology.
performance measurement.quote: Modulation allows the emulation of wireless channel latency, bandwidth, loss, and error rates on private, wired networks.

rejected.why: The document is about tracing wireless channel behaviour, not Mobile IP or any IP-layer mobility protocol.
ICMP echo is only used as the probe workload and a recorded field, not specified or extended.
Traces are mentioned as a possible benchmark family, but the document does not define benchmarking methodology for devices.
WaveLAN signal parameters are recorded, but the document does not address IP over 802.11.
NTP is only mentioned as something deliberately not used.
ATM is mentioned once as another network the trace format might apply to.

gaps.name: Network emulation / trace-driven modulation (PaM)
gaps.why: A substantial part of the RFC covers kernel packet delay/drop/corruption emulation of wireless links for testbeds, and the taxonomy has no tag for network emulation.

RFC2042.title: Registering New BGP Attribute Types
RFC2042.summary: Describes the IANA process for assigning new BGP path attribute type codes and lists the codes currently in use, reserving 255 for development.

BGP.why: The document is about BGP path attribute type codes: how they are registered and which are in use. It extends and operates the BGP protocol's attribute namespace.
BGP.quote: This document describes the process for creating new BGP attribute type codes.

IANA.why: The main body defines a registry assignment procedure with IANA for BGP attribute type codes, so readers of IANA registry topics would want it.
IANA.quote: Requests for assignment of a new attribute type code should be sent to the IANA (IANA@IANA.ORG)

rejected.why: COMMUNITY is only one entry in the attribute table. The document does not address communities themselves.
ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST are listed only as table entries, with no discussion of route reflection.

RFC2043.title: The PPP SNA Control Protocol (SNACP)
RFC2043.summary: Defines the PPP Network Control Protocols (SNACP) for configuring and carrying SNA (XID/FID2 PIUs over LLC 802.2, and HPR NLPs) over PPP links.

SNA.why: The document specifies how SNA, including APPN HPR NLPs and XID/FID2 PIUs, is carried over PPP. SNA is the subject of the encapsulation.
SNA.quote: This document defines the Network Control Protocols for establishing and configuring Systems Network Architecture (SNA) over PPP and SNA over LLC 802.2 over PPP.

PPP.why: It defines a new PPP Network Control Protocol, with its own protocol field values and negotiation rules, so PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: The SNA Control Protocol (SNACP) is responsible for configuring, enabling, and disabling SNA on both ends of the point-to-point link.

rejected.why: APPN and HPR are mentioned as the SNA traffic carried, but the document does not specify APPN networking, routing or management objects.
It carries SNA over LLC, but not via DLSw or TCP/IP encapsulation.
The more specific PPP tag covers this.

RFC2044.title: UTF-8, a transformation format of Unicode and ISO 10646
RFC2044.summary: RFC 2044 specifies UTF-8, a variable-length (1 to 6 octet) ASCII-preserving transformation format of Unicode/ISO 10646, with encoding/decoding algorithms, examples, and a proposed MIME charset registration.

UTF-8.why: The document's sole purpose is defining the UTF-8 encoding, including its octet table, encoding and decoding procedures, and examples.
UTF-8.quote: In UTF-8, characters are encoded using sequences of 1 to 6 octets.

character sets.why: It proposes registering the "UTF-8" charset parameter value, so readers of character set registration would want it. This is a short section, so the role is secondary.
character sets.quote: This memo is meant to serve as the basis for registration of a MIME character encoding (charset) as per [RFC1521].

rejected.why: Unicode and ISO 10646 are the character repertoire being encoded. The memo defines an encoding of them, which the more specific UTF-8 tag covers.
ASCII compatibility is a key property of UTF-8, but the document does not define or specify ASCII itself.
MIME is only the mechanism for the charset label. The document does not specify MIME body structure or encodings.
The parent topic is implied by the UTF-8 tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC2045.title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part One: Format of Internet Message Bodies
RFC2045.summary: RFC 2045 defines MIME Part One: the MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-ID and Content-Description header fields, plus the quoted-printable and base64 encodings, for carrying non-ASCII and non-text bodies in RFC 822 messages.

MIME.why: The document is the core MIME specification, defining the header fields describing body structure and the transfer encodings.
MIME.quote: MIME-Version header field, which uses a version number to declare a message to be conformant with MIME

Base64.why: Section 6.8 specifies the base64 alphabet and encoding algorithm. It is the origin of the widely used Base64 encoding.
Base64.quote: The Base64 Content-Transfer-Encoding is designed to represent arbitrary sequences of octets in a form that need not be humanly readable.

media types.why: It defines the Content-Type field, media type and subtype syntax, parameters and the extension and registration rules for new subtypes.
media types.quote: The Content-Type header field specifies the nature of the data in the body of an entity by giving media type and subtype identifiers

rejected.why: It builds on RFC 822 headers, but the document is about MIME body structure and encodings rather than the base message format.
MIME is an email format, but the more specific MIME tag covers it, so the ancestor is not listed.
SMTP's 7bit restrictions motivate the encodings, but SMTP is only the transport and is not specified here.
US-ASCII is the base character set the encodings target. The document is not about ASCII itself.
It defines the term 'character set' and the charset parameter in passing. Registration and use of character sets are not the subject.
It refers to registration under RFC 2048, but this document does not define the registration procedures.

RFC2046.title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Two: Media Types
RFC2046.summary: RFC 2046 defines the MIME media type system: the initial top-level types (text, image, audio, video, application, multipart, message), their subtypes and parameters, the charset parameter, multipart boundary syntax, and message/partial and message/external-body.

media types.why: The document's main purpose is defining the media type structure and the initial top-level types and subtypes, which is the subject of the media types tag.
media types.quote: This second document defines the general structure of the MIME media typing system and defines an initial set of media types.

MIME.why: It is part two of the MIME specification set and defines multipart body structure, message encapsulation, fragmentation and external-body references, all of which are MIME body structure.
MIME.quote: The "multipart" boundary delimiters and header fields are always represented as 7bit US-ASCII in any case

rejected.why: MIME is carried in email, but the more specific MIME tag covers the content. Email is the substrate here.
The document is about body structure and media types, not RFC 822 headers or addressing. RFC 2045 and RFC 2047 cover headers.
The charset parameter and a short list of charset names are defined, but this is a small part of a document that is mainly about media types, not a character set registration document.
FTP and TFTP appear only as access-types of message/external-body and are not specified or extended.
SMTP appears only as a transport that imposes line length and 7bit limits.
US-ASCII is referenced as the default charset, but the document does not address ASCII in its own right.

RFC2047.title: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) Part Three: Message Header Extensions for Non-ASCII Text
RFC2047.summary: RFC 2047 specifies "encoded-words", a way to represent non-ASCII text in RFC 822 message header fields (Subject, comments, phrases) using Q and B encodings with a declared charset, plus rules for composing and reading them.

MIME.why: It is Part Three of the MIME specification series, defining the encoded-word mechanism and the Q and B encodings for MIME header extensions.
MIME.quote: This particular document is the third document in the series. It describes extensions to RFC 822 to allow non-US-ASCII text data in Internet mail header fields.

message format.why: The core content is how encoded-words fit into RFC 822 header grammar (text, comment, phrase) and where they may and may not appear, so it belongs under Internet message format.
message format.quote: An 'encoded-word' may replace a 'text' token (as defined by RFC 822) in any Subject or Comments header field
message format.section: 5. Use of encoded-words in message headers

rejected.why: The B encoding is simply defined as identical to RFC 2045 BASE64; the document does not define or extend Base64.
Charset names are referenced from the MIME text/plain registry for use in encoded-words, but the document does not register or define character sets.
ASCII is the target representation that encoded-words are restricted to, not a subject the document addresses.
The more specific tags message format and MIME already cover it, so the parent is implied.
The document does deal with non-ASCII text, but the specific mechanism is the MIME header encoding. It is not a general approach to internationalizing text in protocols, and the tags chosen cover it.
It explicitly does not define 8-bit headers or internationalized addresses, and encoded-words are forbidden in addr-spec.

RFC2048.title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Four: Registration Procedures
RFC2048.summary: BCP 13 defines IANA registration procedures for MIME media types (trees, requirements, review, change control), external-body access types, and content-transfer-encodings.

media types.why: The bulk of the document defines media type registration trees, requirements, procedures, change control and the registration template.
media types.quote: Registration of a new media type or types starts with the construction of a registration proposal.

MIME.why: It is part four of the MIME specification set and also covers registration of external-body access types and content-transfer-encodings, which are MIME facilities beyond media types.
MIME.quote: Transfer encodings are tranformations applied to MIME media types after conversion to the media type's canonical form.

rejected.why: IANA is the registry operator here, but the document's subject is MIME-specific registration rules, which the more specific media types tag covers; the IANA topic is about registry guidance generally.
MIME is used in email, but the document concerns registration procedures, not mail transport or formats.
It references RFC 822 and headers only as context; it does not specify message format.
Base64 is mentioned only as an example of a transfer encoding that cannot be registered as a media type.

RFC2049.title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Five: Conformance Criteria and Examples
RFC2049.summary: RFC 2049 is the fifth part of the MIME specification, defining MIME conformance criteria for user agents, guidelines for sending email data through imperfect gateways, the canonical encoding model, and a complex multipart example.

MIME.why: The document defines MIME conformance requirements (Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, multipart handling), the canonical encoding model, and a multipart example. It is squarely about MIME.
MIME.quote: This document describes what portions of MIME must be supported by a conformant MIME implementation.

message format.why: Conformance items cover MIME-Version, header fields and RFC 2047 encoded-words in RFC 822 headers, and local newline versus CRLF conventions. These bear on Internet message format.
message format.quote: Conforming user agents must be able to distinguish encoded-words from "text", "ctext", or "word"s

rejected.why: Too broad. The more specific MIME tag fits, and the ancestor is implied.
SMTP is mentioned as a transport limitation (7-bit, broken MTAs) but the document does not specify or extend it.
Media type definitions and registration are in RFC 2046 and RFC 2048. This document only sets minimal handling requirements for them.
US-ASCII appears as the baseline character set, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
X.400 Printable String restrictions are mentioned only as one gateway pitfall.
EBCDIC is mentioned only as a gateway translation hazard.

RFC2050.title: Internet Registry IP Allocation Guidelines
RFC2050.summary: RFC 2050 (BCP 12, historic) describes the Internet Registry hierarchy (IANA, regional and local IRs) and the guidelines for allocating and assigning globally unique IPv4 address space to ISPs and end organizations using CIDR.

addressing.why: The whole document sets rules for allocating and assigning IP address space through registries, which is IP address architecture, allocation and use.
addressing.quote: This document describes the registry system for the distribution of globally unique Internet address space and registry operations.

CIDR.why: Allocation is built on CIDR blocks, prefix-length assignment and aggregation, with classful assignment abandoned in favour of prefixes. Readers of CIDR would want it.
CIDR.quote: To facilitate hierarchical addressing, implemented using Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), all other ISPs should request address space directly from its upstream provider.

IPv4.why: The guidelines focus on conserving the IPv4 address pool, including utilization thresholds and the return of addresses to the free pool.
IPv4.quote: the current rate of consumption of the remaining unassigned IPv4 address space does not permit the assignment of addresses for administrative ease.

rejected.why: Section 5 on IN-ADDR.ARPA maintenance is a minor operational point, not a main subject.
Renumbering on provider change is mentioned only in passing within the allocation-as-loan guideline.
IANA is the top of the registry hierarchy, but the document is about allocation policy rather than IANA registries or stewardship. The addressing tag covers it.
Routability and aggregation motivate the policy, but the document does not address routing architecture itself.
RFC 1918 private addresses are only referenced as an alternative for unconnected networks.

gaps.name: Regional Internet Registry (RIR) address allocation policy
gaps.why: The document describes the IR hierarchy and registry operational policy (allocation, assignment, audit, appeal, fees). The taxonomy has no tag for RIR policy beyond the general addressing topic.

RFC2051.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for APPC using SMIv2
RFC2051.summary: Defines a Proposed Standard SNMPv2 MIB module (APPC-MIB) for configuring, monitoring and controlling SNA APPC (LU6.2) entities: local/partner LUs, modes, CNOS, transaction programs, sessions, conversations and CPI-C side information.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module written in SMIv2 for SNMP management of APPC devices; MIB modules and SMI are the subject of this tag.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and controlling of network devices with APPC (Advanced Program-to-Program Communications) capabilities.

SNA.why: The managed objects model SNA APPC/LU6.2 sessions, modes, CNOS, conversations and HPR transport. The taxonomy has no generic SNA tag, so this is the nearest fit as the parent of the SNA tags.
SNA.quote: This memo identifies managed objects for the SNA LU6.2 protocols.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB plugs into. The document defines objects only and does not extend the protocol, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
APPN and HPR are mentioned only as context. The one HPR table (appcSessRtpTable) is a minor part, and APPN's own management objects are defined elsewhere.
The LZ/RLE compression-level objects only report SNA BIND-negotiated parameters. They are not a compression format.
Not covered. The document concerns LU6.2, not 3270 terminal emulation.

gaps.name: APPC / LU6.2 (SNA Advanced Program-to-Program Communication)
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is APPC/LU6.2 management, including CNOS and CPI-C. The taxonomy has no APPC or generic SNA tag.

RFC2052.title: A DNS RR for specifying the location of services (DNS SRV)
RFC2052.summary: Defines the DNS SRV resource record (type 33) for locating servers of a given service and protocol in a domain, with priority/weight selection rules, client lookup procedure, and an example zone.

DNS.why: The RFC specifies a new DNS resource record type, its format, resolver behaviour and zone administration advice, which is DNS protocol and RR content.
DNS.quote: This document describes a DNS RR which specifies the location of the server(s) for a specific protocol and domain (like a more general form of MX).

service discovery.why: The SRV RR's purpose is locating servers for a service, so readers of the service discovery subject would want it. DNS-SD is not tagged because it is not specified here.
service discovery.quote: Clients ask for a specific service/protocol for a specific domain (the word domain is used here in the strict RFC 1034 sense), and get back the names of any available servers.

rejected.why: DNS-SD builds on SRV later; this document does not define it.
SMTP and MX are mentioned only as comparison and a possible future override; the document does not specify SMTP.
HTTP appears only as an example service in the zone file.

RFC2053.title: The AM (Armenia) Domain
RFC2053.summary: Describes the AM (Armenia) country-code top-level domain: its naming structure, registration types, and how to request registration from the AM Network Information Center.

domain registration.why: The document is about registry operations and registration policy for a ccTLD: delegation versus direct registration, reserved subdomains, and the template-based request process.
domain registration.quote: The registration is performed by the AM Network Information Center, national Internet registry of Armenia.

rejected.why: The document is about registry administration of a TLD. It does not specify DNS protocol, record or server behaviour. DNS is only the underlying system, and delegation is mentioned only in passing.
This is a parent tag. The more specific domain registration tag fits better.
The document is about domain registration, not host naming conventions or host tables.

gaps.name: Country-code TLD (ccTLD) administration
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for country-code top-level domain delegation and policy. The domain registration tag is the nearest fit.

RFC2054.title: WebNFS Client Specification
RFC2054.summary: Informational specification of how WebNFS clients bind to and use WebNFS servers: TCP-first, port 2049, public filehandle, multi-component lookup, MOUNT fallback, concurrency and retransmission, for NFS v2/v3.

NFS.why: The whole document specifies client behaviour and extensions (public filehandle, multi-component lookup) for NFS v2/v3.
NFS.quote: WebNFS provides additional semantics that can be applied to NFS version 2 and 3 to eliminate the overhead of PORTMAP and MOUNT protocols

rejected.why: RPC, XDR and portmap are the substrate; the document uses XIDs and retransmission but defines nothing new about RPC.
TCP is only the preferred transport for the client; nothing new is specified about TCP.
UDP is merely the fallback transport.
RFC 1808 is only referenced for path cleanup; the canonical path is an NFS lookup convention, not a URI scheme.
Firewall transit is a motivation for using port 2049, not the subject of the document.

RFC2055.title: WebNFS Server Specification
RFC2055.summary: Specifies server-side requirements for WebNFS, extending NFS v2/v3 with a public filehandle, multi-component LOOKUP, well-known port 2049 use, and index-file handling so clients can bypass portmap and MOUNT.

NFS.why: The whole document defines NFS protocol extensions (public filehandle, multi-component lookup) for servers, so readers of NFS would want it.
NFS.quote: WebNFS extends the semantics of versions 2 and 3 of the NFS protocols to allow clients to obtain filehandles more easily

rejected.why: NFS is built on Sun RPC and XDR and the portmap is discussed, but the document only relies on RPC and does not specify or extend it.
Anonymous FTP archive is mentioned only as an example for attaching the public filehandle.
Index file behavior emulates HTTP servers, but the document is not about HTTP.
TCP and UDP transport preference is stated, but it is only the substrate for NFS.
Index-file emulation for browsing web hierarchies is a minor section; the subject is NFS.

RFC2056.title: Uniform Resource Locators for Z39.50
RFC2056.summary: Defines two URL schemes, z39.50r (retrieval) and z39.50s (session), for addressing Z39.50 information retrieval servers and records, with syntax, semantics and examples.

URI.why: The document's purpose is to define two new URL schemes (z39.50r and z39.50s) with their BNF syntax and resolution semantics, so it belongs under URI.
URI.quote: The Z39.50 Session and Retrieval URLs follow the Common Internet Scheme Syntax as defined in RFC 1738

rejected.why: Z39.50 is an information retrieval protocol for searching databases, not a directory service; the document only defines URLs to reach it, and the taxonomy has no Z39.50 tag.
The BNF is just the notation used to define the URL syntax; the document is not about the notation.
The document specifies URL schemes, which URI covers more specifically.

gaps.name: Z39.50
gaps.why: The document is about URL schemes for the Z39.50 information retrieval protocol (search, present, result sets, record syntaxes), but the taxonomy has no tag for Z39.50 or library information retrieval protocols.

RFC2057.title: Source Directed Access Control on the Internet
RFC2057.summary: Informational RFC adapted from a deposition in the challenge to the US Communications Decency Act, explaining how Internet communication methods work and why a sender cannot feasibly restrict access by minors, and describing who does and does not control the Internet.

internet governance.why: The document describes ISOC, IAB, IESG, IETF and address and domain registration, and argues that no body can control content. This is the closest fit for its policy and governance framing.
internet governance.quote: No organization or entity operates or controls the Internet.
internet governance.section: 2. Control and oversight over the Internet

rejected.why: Email is one of several example communication methods used to show that senders cannot verify recipients. The document does not specify or analyse it.
USENET is discussed only as an example of point-to-multipoint distribution, not specified.
IRC is described as an example of real-time group chat, not specified or analysed as a protocol.
Anonymous FTP is an example of a retrieval system that cannot screen users, not a subject of the document.
The Web, CGI and caching are discussed only to show screening limits. HTTP itself is not specified or analysed.
Age and identity verification is discussed as infeasible in the context of legal compliance, but no authentication mechanism is specified.

gaps.name: Content regulation / censorship and access control policy
gaps.why: The document is about the technical feasibility of legally mandated content control (the Communications Decency Act). The taxonomy has no tag for Internet content regulation or law and policy.

RFC2058.title: Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)
RFC2058.summary: Specifies the RADIUS protocol, a UDP-based client/server protocol carrying authentication, authorization and configuration information between a Network Access Server and a shared authentication server, including packet formats, packet types, attributes and examples.

RADIUS.why: The whole document specifies the RADIUS protocol: its operation, packet codes, Request/Response Authenticators, and the attribute set.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes a protocol for carrying authentication, authorization, and configuration information between a Network Access Server which desires to authenticate its links and a shared Authentication Server.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport; Section 2.3 justifies choosing it but the document does not specify or extend UDP.
PPP PAP/CHAP interoperation is described, but PPP is the access mechanism RADIUS serves, not the subject.
MD5 is used for password hiding and response authentication, merely a mechanism relied upon.
RADIUS sits under AAA, but the more specific RADIUS tag already covers it.
Referenced only in Security Considerations for secret distribution.
Several attributes (Framed-AppleTalk-*) carry AppleTalk configuration, but this is a minor part of the attribute list.

RFC2059.title: RADIUS Accounting
RFC2059.summary: RFC 2059 specifies RADIUS Accounting, extending RADIUS so a Network Access Server can send Start/Stop accounting records to an accounting server, with packet types and accounting attributes.

RADIUS.why: The entire document specifies the RADIUS accounting extension: Accounting-Request/Response packets, authenticators and Acct-* attributes.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes a protocol for carrying accounting information between a Network Access Server and a shared Accounting Server.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport (port 1813); nothing new is defined about UDP.
MD5 is used only to compute the authenticators; the document is not about the hash.
RADIUS is the more specific child tag; the AAA framework is implied by it.
PPP and multilink are mentioned only as service types and in the Acct-Link-Count attribute; the document is not about PPP.

RFC2060.title: Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4rev1
RFC2060.summary: RFC 2060 specifies IMAP4rev1, the protocol by which a client accesses and manipulates email messages and mailboxes on a server, including its commands, responses, data formats, and formal syntax.

IMAP.why: The entire document is the IMAP4rev1 protocol specification: commands, responses, states, and formal syntax.
IMAP.quote: The Internet Message Access Protocol, Version 4rev1 (IMAP4rev1) allows a client to access and manipulate electronic mail messages on a server.

rejected.why: MIME body structure is parsed and returned by FETCH BODYSTRUCTURE, but MIME itself is specified elsewhere; it is a dependency.
RFC 822 headers and envelopes are exposed by IMAP, but the document does not define the message format.
SMTP is referenced only to say IMAP does not post mail; posting is left to a mail transfer protocol.
AUTHENTICATE uses external mechanisms defined in IMAP-AUTH. The document defines the command, not SASL itself.
TCP is only the underlying reliable stream; port 143 is mentioned in one line.
ACAP is mentioned only as a separate protocol for configuration information.

RFC2061.title: IMAP4 Compatibility with IMAP2bis
RFC2061.summary: Informational memo guiding implementors on making IMAP4 clients and servers interoperate with the widely deployed IMAP2bis variant, listing missing IMAP4 features and their workarounds.

IMAP.why: The whole document is about IMAP4 and its compatibility with IMAP2bis, covering commands, fetch items and server/client behaviour differences.
IMAP.quote: to assist implementors in creating an IMAP4 implementation to interoperate with implementations that conform to earlier specifications.

rejected.why: IMAP is the specific tag under email; the document is about IMAP access only, so the parent is implied.
AUTHENTICATE is mentioned only as an IMAP4 command that IMAP2bis lacks (use LOGIN); no SASL content.
It mentions IMAP variants' history briefly, but the document is a practical interoperability guide, not a retrospective.

RFC2062.title: Internet Message Access Protocol - Obsolete Syntax
RFC2062.summary: RFC 2062 documents obsolete IMAP commands, FETCH data items, responses and formal syntax from older IMAP versions (RFC 1176, RFC 1730) that IMAP4 implementations may support for interoperability.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies obsolete IMAP commands (FIND, PARTIAL, SUBSCRIBE MAILBOX), responses (MAILBOX, COPY, STORE) and their formal syntax, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document describes obsolete syntax which may be encountered by IMAP4 implementations which deal with older versions of the Internet Mail Access Protocol.

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific child tag and is the subject; email is implied as its ancestor.
RFC822 header items are only referenced as FETCH data item names, and the document does not address message format.
The formal syntax is a BNF-style grammar for IMAP rules, but the document is not about the notation itself.

RFC2063.title: Traffic Flow Measurement:  Architecture
RFC2063.summary: Describes the RTFM architecture for measuring and reporting network traffic flows, defining meters, meter readers, managers, flow attributes, rule sets and a packet matching engine.

performance measurement.why: The whole document specifies an architecture for passive traffic flow measurement (meters, meter readers, managers, flow attributes, rule sets), which is network performance and usage measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This document describes an architecture for the measurement and reporting of network traffic flows

rejected.why: Related flow export technology, but this 1997 RFC predates IPFIX and does not specify an export protocol; it explicitly leaves transfer unspecified.
SNMP is only mentioned as one possible way to move flow data or download rule sets; the Meter MIB is a separate RFC.
The Meter MIB is a separate document (RFC 2064); this document is not a MIB module.
Managers configure meters, but the subject is more specifically covered by performance measurement.
Mentioned only as an example transfer method for the flow table or rule sets.

gaps.name: Internet accounting / traffic flow measurement (RTFM)
gaps.why: The document is about usage accounting and traffic flow metering architecture. The taxonomy has no specific tag for flow metering or accounting, so it is only approximated by performance measurement.

RFC2064.title: Traffic Flow Measurement:  Meter MIB
RFC2064.summary: Defines the experimental SNMP MIB module (FLOW-METER-MIB) for RTFM traffic flow meters, covering control tables, the flow data table, and rule tables for measuring network traffic flows.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (FLOW-METER-MIB) using SMIv2 textual conventions, object groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: this memo defines managed objects used for obtaining traffic flow information from network traffic meters.

performance measurement.why: The MIB manages traffic flow meters, rule sets, flow tables and meter readers for passive traffic measurement and accounting, which is network performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: Traffic Flow Measurement seeks to provide a well-defined method for gathering traffic flow information from networks and internetworks.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines objects, not protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
The RMON2 TimeFilter convention and OwnerString are reused, but the document does not define or extend RMON.
ASN.1 is only the notation used in the SMI for the MIB definitions.
It is a related flow-measurement technology, but this document defines an SNMP meter MIB and does not specify IPFIX.

gaps.name: Traffic flow measurement / Internet accounting (RTFM)
gaps.why: The RTFM meter architecture and accounting of traffic flows is the subject of the MIB; the taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic, with no flow-metering or accounting tag.

RFC2065.title: Domain Name System Security Extensions
RFC2065.summary: RFC 2065 specifies the original DNS Security Extensions: KEY, SIG and NXT resource records, AD/CD header bits, and optional transaction/request authentication, providing data origin authentication, authenticated denial of existence, and public key distribution in the DNS.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document defines DNS security extensions: KEY/SIG/NXT RRs, secure resolution, signing and key operational considerations. This is the original DNSSEC specification.
DNSSEC.quote: Extensions to the DNS are described that provide these services to security aware resolvers or applications through the use of cryptographic digital signatures.

rejected.why: Parent of DNSSEC and implied; the document is specifically about the security extensions.
MD5/RSA is the sole defined signature algorithm, but it is used as a mechanism, not the subject.
MD5 is used as the hash within the signature algorithm; not the document's subject.
Appendix reproduces base 64 only as file-representation apparatus.
The KEY RR enables key distribution via DNS, but the document is about DNS security, not a general PKI.
Dynamic update is mentioned only as a future use of signatory fields and request SIGs; not defined here.

RFC2066.title: TELNET CHARSET Option
RFC2066.summary: Defines the experimental TELNET CHARSET option, a subnegotiation mechanism letting a Telnet client and server agree on a character set or exchange a translation table.

Telnet.why: The RFC defines a new Telnet option (CHARSET, code 42) with its commands, negotiation rules and examples, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies a mechanism for passing character set and translation information between a TELNET client and server.

character sets.why: The option's purpose is negotiating which registered character set is used for text, including translation tables between sets such as Cyrillic and EBCDIC-Cyrillic. Readers interested in character set use would want it.
character sets.quote: If a requested character set name does not start with "X-" or "x-", it MUST be registered with the Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA)

rejected.why: ASCII and NVT ASCII are mentioned as the default and as the encoding of the character set names. The document is not about ASCII itself.
EBCDIC-Cyrillic appears only in examples. The document does not address EBCDIC.
The document is about character set negotiation, a child tag, and the parent is implied. It does not address internationalization more broadly.
It only requires that character set names be registered with IANA. That is boilerplate-like and not the subject.

RFC2067.title: IP over HIPPI
RFC2067.summary: Specifies how IP datagrams are encapsulated and sent over HIPPI-SC switch LANs, covering packet format, I-field contents, connection rules, MTU and data-rate discovery, and obsoletes RFC 1374 (ARP part split out).

link layer.why: The RFC defines an IP-over-link-layer binding for HIPPI: LLC/SNAP encapsulation, I-field use, connection rules and MTU. No HIPPI-specific tag exists, so the generic link layer topic is the best fit.
link layer.quote: this document describes the use of HIPPI switches as IP local area networks.

rejected.why: ARP is explicitly out of scope and was moved to a separate document; it is only mentioned as accommodated by the encapsulation.
Section 7 only says RFC 1191 may be used unchanged; it is a brief pointer, not a substantial part of the document.
IP datagrams are the payload being carried; the document does not specify IP itself.
Conventional 802 LANs are referenced only as a comparison, and HIPPI is not Ethernet.

gaps.name: HIPPI (High-Performance Parallel Interface)
gaps.why: The whole document is about IP over HIPPI and HIPPI-SC switches, but the taxonomy has no HIPPI technology tag under link layer.

RFC2068.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.1
RFC2068.summary: RFC 2068 specifies HTTP/1.1, covering message syntax, methods, status codes, persistent connections, caching, content negotiation, authentication, and header fields.

HTTP.why: The document is the core HTTP/1.1 specification: messages, methods, status codes, headers, and connections.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines the protocol referred to as "HTTP/1.1".

HTTP caching.why: Section 13 and the Cache-Control, Age, Expires, ETag and validator material form a substantial caching specification.
HTTP caching.quote: The goal of caching in HTTP/1.1 is to eliminate the need to send requests in many cases, and to eliminate the need to send full responses

HTTP authentication.why: Defines the challenge-response framework and the Basic scheme, with Digest referenced.
HTTP authentication.quote: HTTP provides a simple challenge-response authentication mechanism which MAY be used by a server to challenge a client request

content negotiation.why: A full section covers server-driven, agent-driven and transparent negotiation plus the Accept headers and Vary.
content negotiation.quote: the process of selecting the best representation for a given response when there are multiple representations available.

rejected.why: URIs and the http URL scheme are defined for use in HTTP, but the document is not about URIs themselves.
HTTP borrows MIME-like message format and has an appendix on differences, but MIME is a relied-upon substrate.
TCP is the transport HTTP usually runs over; connection management is covered under HTTP, not as a TCP extension.
Registers message/http and multipart/byteranges only in appendices and uses media types as a mechanism; not about registry rules.
The augmented BNF is the notation used, not the subject.
Content-MD5 is a single header field that uses MD5; the document is not about the digest.

RFC2069.title: An Extension to HTTP : Digest Access Authentication
RFC2069.summary: Specifies HTTP Digest Access Authentication, a challenge-response scheme using nonces and MD5 hashes (WWW-Authenticate, Authorization, Authentication-info headers) as a replacement for Basic authentication.

HTTP authentication.why: The whole document defines the Digest HTTP authentication scheme, its headers, computation, proxy variants and security analysis.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document provides specification for such a scheme, referred to as "Digest Access Authentication".

rejected.why: MD5 is only the default hash used to compute digests; the document is not about the algorithm itself.
HTTP is the host protocol; the more specific HTTP authentication tag covers the document and implies the parent.
Only a short paragraph on proxy cache interaction with Authorization; not a substantial subject.
Generic topic; the more specific HTTP authentication technology tag fits.

RFC2070.title: Internationalization of the Hypertext Markup Language
RFC2070.summary: RFC 2070 extends HTML 2.0 for internationalization: it makes ISO 10646 the SGML document character set, adds the LANG and DIR attributes and the BDO, Q, SPAN, SUP and SUB elements, defines form charset handling, and gives guidance on charset labelling.

HTML.why: The RFC amends the HTML 2.0 DTD and SGML declaration and adds new elements, attributes and entities. It is an HTML specification extension.
HTML.quote: This document is meant to address the issue of the internationalization of HTML by extending the specification of HTML and giving additional recommendations for proper internationalization support.

internationalization.why: A large part of the document covers multilingual text: UCS as the document character set, bidirectional text, cursive joining, and charset labelling and byte order. A topic tag is used because the document is about text internationalization in general, and no single child (Unicode, character sets, language tags) covers it.
internationalization.quote: A foremost consideration is to make sure that HTML remains a valid application of SGML, while enabling its use with all languages of the world.

language tags.why: Section 3 defines the LANG attribute and how language tags are matched hierarchically in HTML.
language tags.quote: The syntax and registry of HTML language tags is the same as that defined by RFC 1766

rejected.why: HTML is defined as an SGML application and the SGML declaration is amended. The document is about HTML, though, not SGML-based document interchange in general.
The document adopts ISO 10646/Unicode as the document character set. That is a design choice for HTML, not a specification of Unicode use in protocols generally.
The charset parameter and encoding hints are discussed. The main subject is HTML, and no character set is registered.
The HTTP Content-Type charset parameter is relied on as a transport mechanism. The document does not extend HTTP.
MIME charset and multipart/form-data are used as mechanisms, not specified or extended here.

RFC2071.title: Network Renumbering Overview: Why would I want it and what is it anyway?
RFC2071.summary: Informational PIER overview defining network renumbering (changing IP addresses/masks of devices in a network) and surveying past, present and future reasons organizations must renumber, such as provider change, CIDR aggregation, legacy allocations, LAN switching, NBMA and IPv6 transition.

renumbering.why: The whole document defines renumbering and explains why organizations need to do it, which is exactly the renumbering topic.
renumbering.quote: the exercise of renumbering a network consists of changing the IP host addresses, and perhaps the network mask, of each device within the network

CIDR.why: A substantial part discusses CIDR blocks, aggregation, provider-allocated non-portable addresses and "punching holes" in CIDR blocks as drivers for renumbering.
CIDR.quote: Internet Service Providers are becoming more and more reluctant to allow customers to continue using addresses which were allocated by the ISP

rejected.why: NAT is mentioned as a way to reduce the number of unique addresses needed, but only briefly; the document is not about NAT.
The IPv6 transition is a short forward-looking subsection and not a main subject.
ATM and frame relay NBMA services appear only as examples of technologies that trigger renumbering.
DHCP is only mentioned as a tool that can automate address assignment.
A child tag, renumbering, fits better than the parent addressing.
NHRP is mentioned in one paragraph as an example of a database affected by renumbering.

RFC2072.title: Router Renumbering Guide
RFC2072.summary: An informational guide from the PIER working group on planning and implementing IP renumbering as it affects routers: addressing, DNS, routing protocols, filtering, management and tools.

renumbering.why: The whole document is a guide to renumbering routers and the networks they connect, including motivations, pitfalls, tools and transition planning.
renumbering.quote: This document deals with planning and implementation guidelines for the interconnection devices of an enterprise.

DNS.why: Substantial sections (5.4, 7.3) cover DNS use during renumbering: A, CNAME and PTR records, caching, zone file scripts and reverse mapping.
DNS.quote: Wherever possible, servers should be referenced by DNS name rather than by IP address.

CIDR.why: Classless routing, VLSM, aggregation and discontiguous networks are a major pitfall area when renumbering into CIDR space.
CIDR.quote: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) is the administrative realization of prefix addressing in the global Internet.

NAT.why: A dedicated section discusses NAT's role in renumbering and the protocols it breaks.
NAT.quote: Network address translation (NAT) is a valuable technique for renumbering, or even for avoiding the need to renumber significant parts of an enterprise

rejected.why: OSPF is discussed only as one of several routing protocols affected by renumbering, in a short subsection.
BGP renumbering considerations are brief; the document is not about BGP itself.
DHCP appears as a mechanism routers relay or serve for dynamic addressing, not as a subject of the document.
RIPv1/RIPv2 are covered only as interior routing protocols affected by classless renumbering.
SNMP is mentioned as a management mechanism holding addresses, not specified or analysed.
Relevant, but renumbering is a more specific topic and was already chosen. I considered tagging both and decided it was redundant.

gaps.name: renumbering
gaps.why: The document is about IP network and router renumbering. The taxonomy has a 'renumbering' tag under addressing, but I used it above. If the id isn't exactly valid, 'addressing' is the closest fit.

RFC2073.title: An IPv6 Provider-Based Unicast Address Format
RFC2073.summary: Defines the IPv6 provider-based unicast address format (format prefix 010) with Registry ID, Provider ID, Subscriber ID and intra-subscriber fields, to support hierarchical address allocation and scalable routing.

IPv6.why: The document specifies a particular IPv6 unicast address format, including format prefix and field layout. IPv6 addressing is the core subject.
IPv6.quote: This document defines an IPv6 provider-based unicast address format for use in the Internet.

addressing.why: Much of the document covers address allocation and assignment hierarchy among registries, providers and subscribers, plus national registries. It is also designed to support aggregation for scalable routing.
addressing.quote: the address administration is organized into a three level hierarchy -- registry, provider, and subscriber.

rejected.why: The document mentions longest prefix match and aggregation, but it does not specify CIDR itself.
Stateless autoconfiguration is only referenced as a recommended way to generate interface IDs, and the document does not cover it.
IANA is named as the principal registry and as the allocator of Registry IDs. The document is not about IANA registries or their stewardship.
Multihoming is mentioned briefly as a reason to request a Provider ID, but it is not a subject of the document.

RFC2074.title: Remote Network Monitoring MIB Protocol Identifiers
RFC2074.summary: Defines the encoding of protocol identifier strings (protocolDirID/protocolDirParameters) and PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER macros used to index the RMON-2 MIB protocolDirTable, with example macros for link, network, transport and application protocols.

RMON.why: The document exists to define protocol identifiers for the RMON-2 protocolDirTable.
RMON.quote: it describes the algorithms required to identify different protocol encapsulations managed with the Remote Network Monitoring MIB Version 2

rejected.why: Considered, but RMON is the more specific fit. The MIB tag covers general MIB modules and SMI, while this document defines an identifier scheme for RMON-2 only.
SNMP is the management framework context. The document only lists the SNMP protocol as one example identifier.
IP is one of many example protocols described by identifier macros, not the subject of the document.
TCP is one of many example protocols described by identifier macros, not the subject of the document.
Ether2 is only one base-layer identifier among several.

gaps.name: RMON (Remote Network Monitoring)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RMON tech tag under SNMP, but I used it above. I cannot confirm that id exists as written, so I'm flagging it here. If the tag is missing, the document's main subject has no fitting tag. The closest are MIB and SNMP.

RFC2075.title: IP Echo Host Service
RFC2075.summary: Describes how an IP echo host should return IP datagrams to their source with swapped source/destination addresses, including handling of IP options, TTL, ICMP, and spoofing-related security concerns.

IPv4.why: The document specifies IP-layer datagram handling by an echo host: address swap, TTL decrement, checksum update, and IP option processing (source route, timestamp).
IPv4.quote: IP echo hosts send back IP datagrams after exchanging the source and destination IP addresses.

ICMP.why: A substantial part of the document gives rules for when ICMP datagrams may be echoed, rewritten or discarded, including Source Quench and Destination Unreachable code 4.
ICMP.quote: if the IP datagram contains an ICMP packet (i.e. the IP protocol field value is 1), the datagram SHOULD be discarded.

rejected.why: The TCP/UDP Echo service is an application-level echo; this memo is about IP-layer echo hosts, not that service.
Echo hosts are for testing and debugging, but the document does not describe traceroute or path discovery tools.
Only mentioned in passing, to explain why ICMP code 4 is passed through; the document is not about it.
Firewalls come up in the security discussion only, as a recommendation not to place echo hosts inside them.

gaps.name: IP echo host
gaps.why: The document defines a specific IP-layer test and debugging service, with no precise taxonomy tag. IPv4 is the closest fit.

RFC2076.title: Common Internet Message Headers
RFC2076.summary: RFC 2076 is an informational compilation table of commonly occurring Internet mail and Usenet message headers, with short descriptions and pointers to the defining RFCs.

message format.why: The whole document catalogues RFC 822-style message header fields, their meanings and status, which is the Internet message format subject.
message format.quote: This memo contains a table of commonly occurring headers in headings of e-mail messages.

MIME.why: A substantial portion covers MIME headers (Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-Disposition, Content-ID, Content-MD5, etc.) from RFC 1521, 1806 and 1864.
MIME.quote: An indicator that this message is formatted according to the MIME standard, and an indication of which version of MIME is utilized.

Netnews.why: Many listed headers (Newsgroups, Followup-To, Path, Xref, Supersedes) are Usenet News headers, and the document discusses their handling in e-mail.
Netnews.quote: Headers defined only in RFC 1036 for use in Usenet News sometimes appear in mail messages

rejected.why: RFC 1327 gatewaying headers are listed, but the document is not about X.400 mapping itself.
Only Return-Path and Received trace headers touch SMTP; envelope attributes are explicitly excluded.
Implied parent of the more specific message format tag.
Content-Type is listed only as a header; no media type registrations are covered.
Content-Language is a single table entry, not a substantive topic.
HTTP headers are explicitly excluded from this version.

RFC2077.title: The Model Primary Content Type for Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions
RFC2077.summary: RFC 2077 defines a new top-level MIME media type, "model", for multidimensional behavioral/physical models (IGES, VRML, mesh), specifying its definition, parameters, encoding rules and expected subtypes.

media types.why: The document registers a new primary media type (model/*) with its formal registration template, optional parameters and subtype guidance, which is media type registration subject matter.
media types.quote: A model primary MIME type is an electronically exchangeable behavioral or physical representation within a given domain.

rejected.why: The document is about a specific new primary type; the more specific child tag 'media types' fits better and implies MIME.
Email is only the transport context (base64 encoding in mail example); the document is not about mail itself.
HTTP is mentioned only in passing as a binary transfer option.
Base64 is just the recommended content-transfer encoding, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: 3D model / CAD / VRML / IGES data formats
gaps.why: The document is about model content (VRML, IGES, mesh) formats, but the taxonomy has no tag for 3D graphics or CAD data formats.

RFC2078.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface, Version 2
RFC2078.summary: RFC 2078 specifies GSS-API Version 2, a mechanism- and language-independent interface for security services (context establishment, per-message protection, credentials, naming), obsoleting RFC 1508.

GSS-API.why: The whole document defines the GSS-API v2 calls, tokens, status codes and name types.
GSS-API.quote: This specification defines GSS-API services and primitives at a level independent of underlying mechanism and programming language environment

rejected.why: Only used as an example mechanism in Section 5; the document is not about Kerberos itself.
Only an illustrative public-key mechanism scenario in Section 5.3.
Used for OID and token tag encoding, but only as an encoding substrate.
GSS-API provides authentication, but the more specific GSS-API tag already covers it.
Not described; the document only notes that some mechanisms perform negotiation.

RFC2079.title: Definition of an X.500 Attribute Type and an Object Class to Hold Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC2079.summary: Defines the labeledURI attribute type and labeledURIObject auxiliary object class so URIs/URLs with optional labels can be stored in LDAP and X.500 directory entries.

directory services.why: The document is a directory schema definition (attribute type and object class) for LDAP and X.500 directories. LDAP and X.500 are not the specific technology tags here because the schema is generic to both, so the parent topic fits.
directory services.quote: defines a new attribute type and an auxiliary object class to allow URIs, including URLs, to be stored in directory entries in a standard way.

URI.why: The attribute's value syntax is a URI with an optional label, and the document discusses URI encoding and case sensitivity. A reader of URI material would find the storage convention useful.
URI.quote: to hold all types of URIs, including URLs.

rejected.why: The schema is for use in LDAP and X.500 alike and specifies no LDAP protocol behaviour, so the generic directory services tag fits better.
X.500 is the information model the schema targets, but the document does not specify or extend the X.500 service itself. The generic directory services tag covers both.
HTML is mentioned only as a place where URIs are used and in a security caveat about inserting labels into HTML documents.

RFC2080.title: RIPng for IPv6
RFC2080.summary: RFC 2080 specifies RIPng, the minimal adaptation of RIP distance-vector routing to IPv6, including message format, next hop RTE, timers, input/output processing, and split horizon.

RIP.why: The document is the specification of RIPng, the IPv6 version of the Routing Information Protocol.
RIP.quote: RIPng is intended to allow routers to exchange information for computing routes through an IPv6-based network.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the network the protocol runs over; the document specifies a routing protocol, not IPv6 itself.
RIPng uses UDP port 521 only as transport substrate.
Only referenced in Security Considerations for AH/ESP protection.
Parent of RIP, implied by the more specific tag.

RFC2081.title: RIPng Protocol Applicability Statement
RFC2081.summary: Applicability statement describing where RIPng, the IPv6 version of RIP-2, is useful as an IGP, its feature changes from RIP-2, and its limits on network diameter and complexity.

RIP.why: The whole document analyses where RIPng is applicable and how each of its features relates to RIP-2. The RIP tag covers RIPng.
RIP.quote: RIPng serves the same niche for IPv6 as RIP-2 does for IPv4.

rejected.why: RIPng carries IPv6 prefixes, but the document is about the routing protocol, not IPv6 itself.
OSPFng (OSPFv3) is mentioned only as the alternative for large autonomous systems. It is not the subject.
BGP appears only in the next-hop example topology, where an external router runs it.
The document discusses distance-vector diameter and complexity limits, but only for RIPng. The specific RIP tag fits better.

RFC2082.title: RIP-2 MD5 Authentication
RFC2082.summary: Specifies a keyed-MD5 cryptographic authentication mechanism for RIP-2 packets, including the packet trailer format, sequence numbers, Key-ID handling and key management/rollover procedures.

RIP.why: The document extends RIP-2 with a new authentication type, changing its packet format and processing. RIP readers need it.
RIP.quote: We propose that RIP-2 use an authentication algorithm, as was originally proposed for SNMP Version 2, augmented by a sequence number.

routing security.why: The goal is securing routing protocol exchanges against forgery and modification, with key management and rollover procedures.
routing security.quote: This entire memo describes and specifies an authentication mechanism for the RIP-2 routing protocol that is believed to be secure against active and passive attacks.

rejected.why: Keyed MD5 is the algorithm used, but the document defines how RIP-2 uses it rather than specifying MD5 itself.
Key lifetimes and rollover are covered, but only as procedures for this RIP-2 mechanism. A key management protocol is explicitly out of scope.
The general authentication topic is covered by the more specific RIP and routing security tags.
RIP-2 runs over UDP, which is only the substrate. The only mention is that the UDP checksum may be zero.
The construction is a keyed MD5 digest with the secret appended, not HMAC.
SNMP is mentioned only in the rationale and in the Security Considerations, not as a subject of the document.

RFC2083.title: PNG (Portable Network Graphics) Specification Version 1.0
RFC2083.summary: RFC 2083 specifies PNG 1.0, an extensible lossless raster image file format (chunks, filters, interlacing, gamma/color handling), and registers the image/png media type.

media types.why: The document registers image/png, and Section 8.2 records it. Readers of media type registrations would want this RFC.
media types.quote: This specification defines the Internet Media Type image/png.

DEFLATE.why: A whole chapter specifies how PNG uses deflate and the zlib format for image data and zTXt chunks. This is a profile of DEFLATE use, not just a mention.
DEFLATE.quote: PNG compression method 0 (the only compression method presently defined for PNG) specifies deflate/inflate compression with a 32K sliding window.

rejected.why: PNG uses a CRC-32 per chunk (Section 3.4) and includes sample code. This is only a use of a standard CRC and defines nothing new about CRC polynomials.
The web is only a motivating context. PNG is not a hypertext format.
The image/png registration relies on MIME, but the document does not specify MIME body structure or encodings.
Latin-1 is recommended for text chunks, but this is a minor detail and the document does not register or specify a character set.
The zlib format is the substrate for PNG compressed data and is only referenced to RFC 1950. The document does not define it.

gaps.name: Raster image file formats (PNG)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for image or graphics formats. The RFC's main subject, PNG, is only partly covered by the media types and DEFLATE tags.

RFC2084.title: Considerations for Web Transaction Security
RFC2084.summary: Informational requirements document from the WTS working group listing the security services (confidentiality, integrity, user and service authentication, multiple mechanisms) needed for secure HTTP transactions.

HTTP.why: The whole document sets requirements for securing HTTP transactions, as extensions to HTTP or an encapsulating protocol, so it belongs under HTTP.
HTTP.quote: This document specifies the requirements for the provision of security services to the HyperText Transport Protocol.

web security.why: It is about web transaction security mechanisms (the WTS requirements), which is the web security subject.
web security.quote: These services include confidentiality, integrity, user authentication, and authentication of servers/services, including proxied or gatewayed services.

rejected.why: The document gives generic requirements for WTS and does not specify or analyse Secure HTTP.
The document only says WTS may be an encapsulating security protocol. It does not discuss TLS or SSL.
User and server authentication are among the requirements, but only as part of web transaction security, which is already tagged.
It does not discuss HTTP authentication schemes such as Basic or Digest.

RFC2085.title: HMAC-MD5 IP Authentication with Replay Prevention
RFC2085.summary: Specifies a keyed-MD5 (HMAC-MD5) transform for the IP Authentication Header, with an optional 64-bit replay prevention counter field.

IPsec.why: The document defines an authentication transform for the IPsec Authentication Header, including packet format, SPI-controlled replay prevention and the calculation of authentication data.
IPsec.quote: This document describes a keyed-MD5 transform to be used in conjunction with the IP Authentication Header [RFC-1826].

HMAC.why: The transform is HMAC-MD5. The document specifies the ipad/opad computation steps and the key length rules for it.
HMAC.quote: To compute HMAC-MD5 over the data `text' we perform MD5(K XOR opad, MD5(K XOR ipad, text))

MD5.why: MD5 is the underlying hash function, and the document discusses its output size, block size and key handling. Readers on MD5 use would want it.
MD5.quote: MD5 produces a 128-bit value which is used as the authentication data.

rejected.why: The document concerns the Authentication Header only. ESP is mentioned only in a reference to a combined DES-MD5 transform.
Key length and randomness guidance is given, but only as part of the transform definition. The document does not address key establishment.
Key management is mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations, and the document does not specify it.
One paragraph advises on replay protection with multicast destinations. This is incidental to the transform.

RFC2086.title: IMAP4 ACL extension
RFC2086.summary: Defines the IMAP4 ACL extension, adding SETACL, DELETEACL, GETACL, LISTRIGHTS and MYRIGHTS commands and responses for managing mailbox access control lists over IMAP.

IMAP.why: The document is an extension of IMAP4, specifying new commands, responses and syntax for mailbox access control lists.
IMAP.quote: The ACL extension of the Internet Message Access Protocol [IMAP4] permits access control lists to be manipulated through the IMAP protocol.

rejected.why: The ACLs are about access control, but the document specifies them as an IMAP extension, and the IMAP tag covers it. The generic authorization topic is not needed.
The document cites RFC 822 only for the ABNF notation, so it says nothing about message format.
The document uses ABNF only to give its formal syntax and is not about the notation.
AUTHENTICATE is mentioned only for what counts as a valid identifier, so the document does not address SASL.

RFC2087.title: IMAP4 QUOTA extension
RFC2087.summary: Defines the IMAP4 QUOTA extension, adding SETQUOTA, GETQUOTA and GETQUOTAROOT commands and QUOTA and QUOTAROOT responses for managing administrative resource limits on mailboxes.

IMAP.why: The document is an extension to IMAP4, specifying new commands, responses and a capability. Readers of IMAP would expect to find it.
IMAP.quote: The QUOTA extension of the Internet Message Access Protocol [IMAP4] permits administrative limits on resource usage (quotas) to be manipulated through the IMAP protocol.

rejected.why: Only the parent of IMAP; the document is specifically an IMAP extension, so the child tag is more specific.
The formal syntax uses ABNF notation, but only as a notation for the grammar, not as a subject of the document.
RFC 822 is referenced only for RFC822.SIZE and BNF notation; the document does not address message format.

RFC2088.title: IMAP4 non-synchronizing literals
RFC2088.summary: Defines the IMAP4 LITERAL+ extension, adding non-synchronizing literals that let a client send string data without waiting for a server continuation request.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 with the LITERAL+ capability and a modified literal syntax. It is an IMAP extension specification.
IMAP.quote: This document specifies an alternate form of literal which does not require this network round trip.

rejected.why: IMAP is the specific tag here. The parent email tag is implied and should not be listed separately.
The document gives a small ABNF-style grammar, but it only uses the notation. It is not about the notation.
The literal construct is IMAP protocol syntax, not Internet message header or body format.

RFC2089.title: V2ToV1 Mapping SNMPv2 onto SNMPv1 within a bi-lingual SNMP agent
RFC2089.summary: Informational memo documenting a common way for bi-lingual SNMPv1/SNMPv2 agents to map SNMPv2 error-status values, exceptions, Counter64 syntax and traps into SNMPv1 responses and traps.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies how SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 protocol elements (error-status, exceptions, GET/GETNEXT processing, traps) are mapped in agents and proxies.
SNMP.quote: document a common way of mapping an SNMPv2 response into an SNMPv1 response within a bi-lingual SNMP agent

rejected.why: It mentions the SNMPv2 SMI and a few MIB objects such as snmpTrapOID.0, but it defines no MIB modules and is about protocol mapping.
This is a parent of SNMP, which is already tagged, so it is implied.
ASN.1 parse errors are mentioned only in passing for Counter64 handling. The document is not about ASN.1.

RFC2090.title: TFTP Multicast Option
RFC2090.summary: Defines an experimental TFTP option (multicast) that lets multiple clients download the same file concurrently via multicast packets, with a master-client ACK scheme.

TFTP.why: The document specifies a new extension option to TFTP, including its request/OACK formats and data transfer behaviour.
TFTP.quote: This new option will allow the multiple clients to receive the same file concurrently through the use of Multicast packets.

rejected.why: IP multicast is used as the delivery mechanism, but the document does not address multicast routing, group membership or deployment; it is a TFTP option.
TFTP runs over UDP, but this is substrate only; nothing new is defined about UDP usage.
The master-client ACK scheme gives reliability for multicast delivery, but the document is a TFTP option, not a general reliable multicast transport.

RFC2091.title: Triggered Extensions to RIP to Support Demand Circuits
RFC2091.summary: Specifies Triggered RIP, an extension to distance-vector protocols (IP RIP v1/v2, Netware RIP and SAP) that sends updates only on change with acknowledgement and retransmission, so they can run over on-demand WAN circuits such as X.25 and ISDN.

RIP.why: The document defines new RIP packet types (Update Request/Response/Acknowledge), timers and database rules for IP RIP v1/v2, so it extends RIP.
RIP.quote: this specification modifies the distance vector protocols so as to send information on the WAN only when there has been an update to the routing database

rejected.why: X.25 is only an example of the connection-oriented WAN the routers run over. The document does not specify anything about X.25.
ISDN is only an example of an on-demand circuit network. The document does not specify anything about ISDN access.
Netware RIP and SAP run over IPX, but the document only adds the update header to their packet formats. It does not cover IPX interworking.
IP RIP runs over UDP port 520, which is substrate only.

gaps.name: Netware RIP and SAP (Novell IPX routing/service advertising)
gaps.why: The document extends Novell RIP and SAP as well as IP RIP, but the taxonomy has no tag for them. The IPX tag covers interworking only.

RFC2092.title: Protocol Analysis for Triggered RIP
RFC2092.summary: Protocol analysis report documenting the key features, applicability, implementation experience and restrictions of Triggered RIP (RFC 2091) for demand circuits, and proposing that Demand RIP be obsoleted.

RIP.why: The document analyses Triggered RIP, an extension of RIP and RIP-2 for WAN demand circuits, covering its features, applicability and relationship to Demand RIP.
RIP.quote: Triggered Extensions to RIP to Support Demand Circuits [2] and the current implementation experience.

rejected.why: PPP Echo Request and Link Quality Monitoring are mentioned only as mechanisms for detecting black holes; the document is not about PPP.
X.25 is mentioned only as an example WAN where Triggered RIP is applicable.
ISDN is only an example of a connection-oriented WAN and a tested environment, not a subject of the document.
The document analyses one specific protocol and does not address routing architecture in general; the RIP tag is the more specific fit.

RFC2093.title: Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP) Specification
RFC2093.summary: RFC 2093 specifies the experimental Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP), which creates, distributes, rekeys and revokes symmetric group keys among peers using a group controller, permission certificates and compromise lists.

key management.why: The whole document defines a protocol for creating, distributing, rekeying and deleting group keys, which is key management. No more specific tag fits: GDOI and GSAKMP are different protocols, and this is neither of them.
key management.quote: This specification proposes a protocol to create grouped symmetric keys and distribute them amongst communicating peers.

multicast security.why: It addresses group key management for groups of hosts, including a multicast rekey message encrypted in the group key. That is within group key management and multicast security.
multicast security.quote: The GKMP does use multicast services if they are available.

rejected.why: It is a different, later group key protocol. GKMP is a separate specification and does not describe GSAKMP.
GDOI is an ISAKMP-based protocol for IPsec groups. GKMP is independent of ISAKMP and IPsec.
The document uses signed permission certificates and a revocation list, but only as parts of the key protocol, not as PKI itself.
Multicast is only an optional way to speed rekeying. The document is not about multicast routing or deployment.
Permission certificates and access control checks serve the key distribution. They are not the document's subject.

RFC2094.title: Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP) Architecture
RFC2094.summary: RFC 2094 describes the architecture of the Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP), a distributed scheme in which group members create, distribute and rekey symmetric group keys for multicast without a central KDC.

multicast security.why: The whole document is about group key management for multicast: group key creation, distribution, rekey and member deletion. GKMP is not a specific child technology (GDOI, GSAKMP, TESLA), so the parent topic fits.
multicast security.quote: This document describes an architecture for the management of cryptographic keys for multicast communications.

rejected.why: It is the parent of multicast security. The more specific multicast security tag already covers the document's group key management focus.
IP multicast routing and group membership are only context. The document deals strictly with cryptographic keys, not multicast routing.
This is a different, later group key protocol. RFC 2094 describes GKMP, not GSAKMP.
Certificates and CRLs are assumed as supporting functions, but the certification hierarchy is explicitly out of scope.
Kerberos is mentioned only as an example of a KDC-based system that GKMP is contrasted with.

gaps.name: Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for GKMP itself. It sits best under multicast security alongside GDOI, GSAKMP and TESLA, so a dedicated tech tag would help.

RFC2095.title: IMAP/POP AUTHorize Extension for Simple Challenge/Response
RFC2095.summary: Defines CRAM-MD5, a challenge-response authentication mechanism using keyed-MD5 digests for IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE (and POP3 AUTH), avoiding cleartext reusable passwords on the wire.

SASL.why: The document defines a new authentication mechanism (CRAM-MD5) plugged into the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE / POP3 AUTH extensible framework, which is the SASL mechanism model; readers of SASL would expect it.
SASL.quote: The authentication type associated with CRAM is "CRAM-MD5".

IMAP.why: The mechanism is designed to fill a gap in IMAP4 authentication and the examples show the IMAP AUTHENTICATE exchange, so IMAP readers would want it.
IMAP.quote: This specification provides a simple challenge-response authentication protocol that is suitable for use with IMAP4.

POP3.why: The mechanism is positioned as an alternative to POP3 APOP and usable with the POP3 AUTH command.
POP3.quote: it may also constitute an improvement on APOP for POP3 use as specified in RFC 1734.

HMAC.why: The digest computation is keyed-MD5 (HMAC-MD5), with ipad/opad and context precomputation described as the core of the mechanism.
HMAC.quote: computed by applying the keyed MD5 algorithm from [KEYED-MD5] where the key is a shared secret and the digested text is the timestamp

rejected.why: MD5 is used as the underlying hash inside the keyed construction; the document is not about MD5 itself.
Covered more specifically by IMAP and POP3 tags; no broader email architecture content.
SASL is the more specific tag for a mechanism within the AUTHENTICATE framework.
Base64 is only the encoding used by the IMAP AUTHENTICATE command, and the document explicitly says it is not part of CRAM.

RFC2096.title: IP Forwarding Table MIB
RFC2096.summary: Defines the IP-FORWARD-MIB SNMP MIB module with the ipCidrRouteTable for displaying CIDR multipath IP routes (same network number, differing masks), obsoleting the RFC 1354 ipForwardTable.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (IP-FORWARD-MIB) with tables, objects, groups and compliance statements for SNMP management of the IP forwarding table.
MIB.quote: The ipCidrRouteTable updates the RFC 1213 ipRouteTable to display multipath IP Routes having the same network number but differing network masks.

CIDR.why: The update's purpose is to represent CIDR routes with the same network number but different masks, so CIDR readers would want it.
CIDR.quote: This memo defines an update to RFC 1354, "IP Forwarding Table MIB", for Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB sits in; the document defines MIB objects, and the more specific MIB tag covers it.
The document defines management objects for viewing routes, not routing architecture or design principles.
It was produced under the OSPF working group, but OSPF is only one value in the route protocol enumeration.
ASN.1 is only the notation the MIB is written in.

RFC2097.title: The PPP NetBIOS Frames Control Protocol (NBFCP)
RFC2097.summary: Defines the PPP Network Control Protocol (NBFCP) for negotiating and configuring NBF (NetBEUI) NetBIOS frames over PPP links, including its options for name projection, peer information, multicast filtering and MAC header requirements.

PPP.why: The RFC specifies a new PPP NCP, with its packet encapsulation, protocol field values and configuration options, so PPP readers would look for it.
PPP.quote: This document defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring the NBF protocol over PPP.

NetBIOS.why: A substantial part of the document deals with projecting NetBIOS names onto the remote network and NetBIOS name defense.
NetBIOS.quote: NBFCP requires that end-system implementations MUST negotiate the Name-Projection configuration option.

rejected.why: Reconsidered: the taxonomy id is 'NetBIOS' under applications, which does exist, but the document is about PPP NBF framing rather than NetBIOS over TCP/IP, so it is kept only as secondary above.
MAC headers for 802.3/802.5/FDDI are mentioned only as options for bridging, not the subject.
FDDI is only mentioned as one MAC header type; the document is not about IP over FDDI.
802.5 token ring is only listed as a MAC header variant.
