The Multicast-Filtering option concerns NetBIOS multicast frame forwarding rates on the link, not IP multicast routing.

gaps.name: NBF / NetBEUI (NetBIOS Frames protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about carrying NBF (formerly NetBEUI) over PPP, and the taxonomy has no tag for NBF itself.

RFC2098.title: Toshiba's Router Architecture Extensions for ATM : Overview
RFC2098.summary: Informational overview of Toshiba's Cell Switch Router (CSR) architecture, which adds ATM cell switching to IP routers to build bypass pipes across IP subnets and works with RSVP, and which discusses control-architecture alternatives.

ATM.why: The whole document is about an IP-over-ATM architecture: CSRs, Default-VCs, Dedicated-VCs and VC concatenation across ATM subnets.
ATM.quote: A concept of "Cell Switch Router (CSR)" is introduced as a new internetworking equipment, which has ATM cell switching capabilities in addition to conventional IP datagram forwarding.

RSVP.why: Interworking with RSVP resource reservation is a stated goal. It drives Bypass-pipe setup for QoS and bandwidth, and it motivates the control design.
RSVP.quote: since the CSR can handle RSVP messages which are transmitted in a hop-by-hop manner, it can provide Bypass-pipes which satisfy QoS requirements

rejected.why: NHRP is discussed as the competing model and compared with CSR. The document does not specify or extend it.
RSVP is a child of QoS and is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
Multicast Bypass-pipes are mentioned briefly, but they are not a main subject.
ST-II is only background, mentioned as an alternative reservation approach.
OSPF is only named as an example of IP routing used alongside ATM routing.

gaps.name: Cell Switch Router (CSR) / flow-based IP switching over ATM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IP switching or cut-through designs that bind IP flows to ATM VCs, such as CSR, IP Switching and tag switching. They are the precursors of MPLS.

RFC2099.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 2000-2099
RFC2099.summary: RFC 2099 is a slightly annotated status list of the 100 RFCs numbered 2000 through 2099, giving each one's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track marking.

RFC series.why: The document is a catalogue of a block of RFC numbers. It belongs on the RFC series page as a publication index.
RFC series.quote: a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2000

rejected.why: It mentions standards-track status and lists process RFCs such as 2026 and 2027, but it only catalogues them and does not describe the process.
Several IMAP RFCs appear as list entries. The memo is not about IMAP.
HTTP/1.1 and Digest authentication appear only as entries in the list.
Many MIB RFCs are listed, but this document defines no MIB.
The MIME RFC series is listed as entries only. The memo does not specify MIME.
DNS-related RFCs are listed as entries and none is treated in the body.

RFC2100.title: The Naming of Hosts
RFC2100.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC, a parody of T.S. Eliot's "The Naming of Cats" in verse, about choosing distinctive hostnames for computers and the nameserver knowing a host's address.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st poem parodying T.S. Eliot. It exists as whimsy, so the humor tag fits as its main subject.
humor.quote: The Naming of Hosts is a difficult matter,

hostnames.why: The verse is a commentary on choosing host names such as venus, athena and titan. A reader browsing hostname naming conventions would want to find it.
hostnames.quote: a host must have THREE DIFFERENT NAMES.

rejected.why: The nameserver appears only as a joke in the last verse. The memo specifies and analyses nothing about DNS.
The more specific hostnames tag covers the naming subject, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.

RFC2101.title: IPv4 Address Behaviour Today
RFC2101.summary: IAB informational note clarifying how IPv4 addresses are now interpreted as identifiers versus locators, given private realms, NATs/ALGs, CIDR, renumbering and dynamic allocation, with a short comparison to IPv6.

addressing.why: The document is about the meaning, uniqueness and lifetime of IP addresses (identifier vs locator), their allocation and renumbering; this is IP address architecture.
addressing.quote: clarify the current interpretation of the 32-bit IP version 4 address space, whose significance has changed substantially since it was originally defined

NAT.why: A substantial section compares NATs and ALGs, their limitations, and their impact on IPsec and DNS.
NAT.quote: we define a NAT as a device that just modifies the network and the transport layer headers, but does not understand the syntax/semantics of the application layer data stream
NAT.section: 4.1. Addresses are no longer globally unique locators

CIDR.why: The Annex describes CIDR, aggregator-based allocation and its implications for renumbering.
CIDR.quote: during 1992 - 1993 period the Internet adopted Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)
CIDR.section: ANNEX: Current Practices for IPv4 Address Allocation & Routing

rejected.why: Only a short section compares IPv6 addressing with IPv4; the document is mainly about IPv4.
Renumbering is discussed as a consequence of CIDR and dynamic allocation but is not treated in its own right; procedures are not covered.
IPv4 and its address lifecycle is plausible, but the more specific addressing tag fits the document's subject of address semantics.
DNS is mentioned only as a dependency for interconnecting realms, with no DNS specification.
IPsec is noted as broken by NAT/ALG boundaries, but only briefly.
DHCP and PPP are cited only as promoting dynamic address allocation.

gaps.name: identifier/locator separation
gaps.why: The document's central theme is splitting IP address roles into identifier and locator, which has no dedicated tag; ILNP and HIP are related but not fitting.

RFC2102.title: Multicast Support for Nimrod :  Requirements and Solution Approaches
RFC2102.summary: Informational memo stating the requirements Nimrod places on a multicast solution, comparing DVMRP, CBT, PIM, MOSPF and IDPR approaches, and outlining how PIM sparse-mode style multicast could be realised using Nimrod flow setup.

Nimrod.quote: Nimrod does not specify a particular solution for multicasting. Rather, Nimrod may use any of a number of emerging multicast techniques.

RFC2103.title: Mobility Support for Nimrod :  Challenges and Solution Approaches
RFC2103.summary: Informational memo on the requirements Nimrod places on a mobility solution, a classification of mobility approaches (centralized/distributed association, remapping at source/home/routers), and an outline of using Mobile-IP with Nimrod EIDs and locators.

Nimrod.why: The whole document concerns how the Nimrod routing architecture accommodates mobility, including effects on Nimrod topology maps and locators.
Nimrod.quote: Nimrod does require that the solution have certain characteristics.

IP mobility.why: The document compares mobility approaches (home agent, triangular routing, router-based state) and details Mobile-IP registration, agent discovery and forwarding adapted to Nimrod. Mobile IPv4 is the specific protocol, but the document is a general mobility analysis, so the parent topic fits.
IP mobility.quote: we outline how mobility can be implemented within Nimrod using the same mechanism and indeed, the same protocol headers defined in [Sim94].

rejected.why: The Mobile-IP scheme is adapted as one example in section 5 rather than specified or extended; the document's focus is a general approach comparison, so the broader IP mobility tag fits better.
Nimrod is the more specific tag for this routing architecture, and the document is about mobility within it.
Encapsulation from home agent to foreign agent is merely a mechanism within Mobile-IP, not a subject of the document.
ICMP Router Discovery is mentioned only in passing for agent discovery.

RFC2104.title: HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication
RFC2104.summary: RFC 2104 specifies HMAC, a keyed-hash message authentication mechanism built on any iterative cryptographic hash function such as MD5 or SHA-1, with key guidance, truncation, security discussion and sample code.

HMAC.why: The entire document defines and analyses the HMAC construction, its keys, truncation and security, so the HMAC tag is the direct fit.
HMAC.quote: This document describes HMAC, a mechanism for message authentication using cryptographic hash functions.

rejected.why: MD5 is used as an example hash and in the sample code, but the document is not about MD5 itself; it only notes MD5 can be used within HMAC.
SHA-1 is named as an example underlying hash function only; the document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
Section 3 gives key length and refresh guidance, but this is a small part of an HMAC specification rather than key establishment or provisioning.
The IPsec working group origin and the reference to the IP Authentication Header are incidental; the document does not specify IPsec.

RFC2105.title: Cisco Systems' Tag Switching Architecture Overview
RFC2105.summary: Informational overview of Cisco's tag switching architecture, a label-swapping forwarding paradigm with a routing-driven control component for tag binding and distribution, with applications to hierarchy of routing, multicast, explicit routes, ATM and QoS; a precursor to MPLS.

MPLS.why: Tag switching is the Cisco precursor to MPLS: label swapping forwarding, tag stacks, encapsulation and binding distribution. The whole document is the architecture overview.
MPLS.quote: Forwarding is accomplished using simple label-swapping techniques, while the existing network layer routing protocols plus mechanisms for binding and distributing tags are used for control.

ATM.why: A full section covers carrying tags in VCI/VPI fields, tag allocation for ATM switches and coexistence with the ATM control plane.
ATM.quote: tag switching technology can readily be applied to ATM switches by implementing the control component of tag switching.

rejected.why: The Tag Distribution Protocol (TDP) is only mentioned as a mechanism for distributing bindings and is not specified here.
BGP is cited as a routing protocol the tag switches participate in, plus a brief mention of a Tag Binding attribute. It is not a subject of the document.
Section 4.3 covers tags bound to multicast trees, but only briefly, as one application of the forwarding paradigm. PIM is only an example.
Section 6 is short and speculative about tags marking packet classes. It is not a substantial part of the document.
Explicit routes are discussed in one short subsection (4.4) as flexible routing, not as a traffic engineering architecture.
RSVP is only mentioned as an example of a flow a tag could be bound to.

gaps.name: Tag switching / label switching (pre-MPLS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for historic pre-standard label-switching proposals. MPLS is the closest fit.

RFC2106.title: Data Link Switching Remote Access Protocol
RFC2106.summary: Specifies DRAP, a client/server protocol between workstations and DLSw routers that carries SNA/NetBIOS traffic over TCP, with frame formats, dynamic MAC address assignment and capability exchange.

DLSw.why: The document defines a DLSw extension (DRAP) reusing the DLSw state machine and frame types for client-to-router use. DLSw readers would want it.
DLSw.quote: This memo describes the Data Link Switching Remote Access Protocol that is used between workstations and routers to transport SNA/ NetBIOS traffic over TCP sessions.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport (port 1973); nothing new is specified about TCP itself.
NetBIOS traffic is carried and a capability flag exists, but the document is not about NetBIOS services.
SNA is the traffic being carried. DLSw is the more specific tag, and it sits under SNA.
PPP appears only in the example topology diagrams as the access link.

RFC2107.title: Ascend Tunnel Management Protocol - ATMP
RFC2107.summary: Informational RFC describing Ascend's private ATMP protocol, which uses UDP registration/challenge messages between a NAS foreign agent and home agent and GRE tunnels to give dial-in users virtual presence on a home network (IP and IPX), with RADIUS attributes for configuration.

tunneling.why: The document specifies a tunnel management protocol (registration, deregistration, tunnel IDs, GRE encapsulation) for dial-in access to a home network. No more specific tunnelling tag fits as the protocol is ATMP itself.
tunneling.quote: A tunnel between the NAS and a special "Home Agent" (HA) located on the Home Network is used to carry data to and from the client.

GRE.why: ATMP uses GRE as its data tunnel protocol and defines how the Tunnel ID is carried in the GRE Key field, a substantive part of the specification.
GRE.quote: all data received from the MN will be encapsulated using GRE and sent to the HA with the assigned Tunnel ID included in the GRE Key field.

RADIUS.why: The appendix defines new RADIUS attributes (Home-Agent-IP-Addr, Home-Agent-Password, etc.) and the IPX attributes in Appendix B, so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: This appendix indicates the RADIUS attributes that have been added by Ascend to support ATMP for IP.

IP mobility.why: ATMP uses Mobile-IP-style home agent/foreign agent/mobility binding terminology and offers a subset of that functionality, so it is closely related to IP mobility.
IP mobility.quote: Unlike the mobile-IP protocol [3], ATMP assumes that a single NAS will provide the physical connection to a remote client

IPX.why: IPX tunnelling is a supported payload and Appendix B covers IPX network numbers and node addressing for it.
IPX.quote: ATMP specifies a mechanism which allows IPX clients to receive mobility services from a HA.

rejected.why: VPN access is mentioned as a use case, but the VPN tag covers provider-provisioned BGP/MPLS-style VPNs, which this is not.
UDP is only the transport for the ATMP messages and is not specified or extended here.
Standard PPP clients are assumed and PPP is not specified or extended by this document.
MD5 is used for the challenge/response hash but is only a security mechanism the protocol relies on.
L2TP is not mentioned in the body. The IESG note only alludes to a similar protocol in an IETF working group.

RFC2108.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Repeater Devices using SMIv2
RFC2108.summary: Defines the SNMPv2 MIB module for managing IEEE 802.3 10 and 100 Mb/s repeaters (basic, monitor, address tracking, TopN objects), obsoleting RFC 1516.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SNMP-REPEATER-MIB) defined with SMIv2 for repeater management, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing IEEE 802.3 10 and 100 Mb/second baseband repeaters based on IEEE Std 802.3 Section 30

Ethernet.why: The managed objects model IEEE 802.3 Ethernet repeaters, ports, collisions, and FCS errors, so readers of Ethernet management would want it.
Ethernet.quote: attributes of an IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet-like) repeater, as defined by Section 9, "Repeater Unit for 10 Mb/s Baseband Networks"

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework and protocol the MIB is carried over. The document defines objects, not protocol changes, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation underlying SMI.
The monitor counters are statistics objects, not a performance measurement methodology.

RFC2109.title: HTTP State Management Mechanism
RFC2109.summary: RFC 2109 specifies the original HTTP state management mechanism, defining the Cookie and Set-Cookie headers, their attributes, user agent and server behaviour, privacy controls, and compatibility with Netscape cookies.

cookies.why: The whole document specifies HTTP cookies: syntax, attributes, user agent and origin server rules, privacy and security.
cookies.quote: It describes two new headers, Cookie and Set-Cookie, which carry state information between participating origin servers and user agents.

HTTP caching.why: A dedicated section and the caching proxy role plus HTTP/1.0 caching issues address how Set-Cookie interacts with caches and Cache-Control directives.
HTTP caching.quote: An origin server must be cognizant of the effect of possible caching of both the returned resource and the Set-Cookie header.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate; the cookies tag is the more specific fit for the new headers.
Security and privacy considerations are part of cookie handling, not a separate web security mechanism in their own right.
Privacy section covers user control of cookies but the document is about the cookie mechanism, not a general privacy threat model.
Path and domain matching use URLs but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.

RFC2110.title: MIME E-mail Encapsulation of Aggregate Documents, such as HTML (MHTML)
RFC2110.summary: RFC 2110 specifies how to send HTML and other aggregate documents with linked objects in MIME email, using multipart/related and the new Content-Location and Content-Base headers, plus CID-based linking and URI resolution rules.

MHTML.why: The document is the MHTML specification itself: bundling an HTML document and its inline resources into one MIME message.
MHTML.quote: MIME E-mail Encapsulation of Aggregate Documents, such as HTML (MHTML)

MIME.why: It defines new MIME content headers and the use of multipart/related, character encoding and line-break rules for MIME body parts, which MIME readers would want.
MIME.quote: the document uses the MIME type multipart/related and specifies the MIME content-headers "Content-Location" and "Content-Base".

URI.why: A substantial part covers base URI resolution, matching relative and absolute URIs, and cid: URL linking between body parts.
URI.quote: Relative URIs inside contents of MIME body parts are resolved relative to a base URI.
URI.section: 5. Base URIs for resolution of relative URIs

rejected.why: HTML is the main example format being carried, but the document does not specify HTML; it specifies its email encapsulation, which MHTML covers.
The document is about email, but the more specific MHTML and MIME tags fit; it does not address email architecture or transport in general.
HTTP is mentioned only for comparison (caching, line breaks, base URI resolution), not specified or extended.
SMTP is only the transport substrate for the messages and is not specified here.
It uses multipart/related but does not register a media type or define registry rules; the type is defined in RFC 2112.
It adds content headers to MIME parts, but it is not about RFC 822 message format as such.

RFC2111.title: Content-ID and Message-ID Uniform Resource Locators
RFC2111.summary: Defines the "cid:" and "mid:" URL schemes for referring to MIME message body parts and email messages by Content-ID and Message-ID, e.g. for HTML in multipart/related messages to reference inline images.

URI.why: The document specifies two URL schemes, their syntax, and conversion to message headers, so it belongs under URI.
URI.quote: The Uniform Resource Locator (URL) schemes, "cid:" and "mid:" allow references to messages and the body parts of messages.

MHTML.why: Produced by the mhtml working group. It provides the cid: scheme that lets HTML parts in a MIME message reference inline resources, which is the core of MHTML aggregate documents.
MHTML.quote: The use of [MIME] within email to convey Web pages and their associated images requires a URL scheme to permit the HTML to refer to the images

rejected.why: MIME Content-ID headers and multipart/related are the substrate the URLs refer to. The document defines URL schemes, not MIME mechanisms.
The URLs map to the RFC 822 Message-ID header, but the document does not specify the header format itself.
HTML appears only as the example context where cid: URLs are used.
Email is the environment in which the URLs are used. The document is about the URL schemes, not email architecture.

RFC2112.title: The MIME Multipart/Related Content-type
RFC2112.summary: Defines the MIME Multipart/Related media type for compound objects made of inter-related body parts, with type, start and start-info parameters, Content-Disposition handling, user agent requirements and examples.

MIME.why: The RFC defines a new MIME multipart subtype, its parameters, root part selection and user agent processing rules, so it is about MIME body structure.
MIME.quote: The Multipart/Related content-type provides a common mechanism for representing objects that are aggregates of related MIME body parts.

rejected.why: It includes a media type registration form, but the document is mainly about the multipart structure and processing, not registry rules.
This is the base mechanism MHTML builds on, but the RFC does not itself define HTML aggregation.
It touches Content-ID and Content-Disposition headers, but only in service of the multipart type.
MIME user agents are the context, but the document does not address email architecture or transport.

RFC2113.title: IP Router Alert Option
RFC2113.summary: Defines the IP Router Alert option, a new IP option telling transit routers to examine a packet more closely, intended for protocols like RSVP and IGMP.

router alert.why: The document specifies the Router Alert IP option: its syntax, semantics and use. This is the exact subject of the tag.
router alert.quote: This memo describes a new IP Option type that alerts transit routers to more closely examine the contents of an IP packet.

rejected.why: RSVP is the motivating user of the option, but the document does not specify or extend it. It only mentions RSVP as a protocol that needs the option.
IGMP is named as a protocol that should use the option. The document says nothing about IGMP itself.
The option is defined for the IPv4 header, but the document is about the option and not about IPv4 in general. The router alert tag is the more specific fit.

RFC2114.title: Data Link Switching Client Access Protocol
RFC2114.summary: Specifies DCAP, a client/server protocol between workstations and DLSw routers that carries SNA/NetBIOS traffic over TCP, addressing DLSw scalability with dynamic MAC assignment, capability exchange, and optional UDP multicast discovery.

DLSw.why: DCAP is a client-to-router companion to DLSw (RFC 1795), reusing its state machine and frames; it is the document's whole subject.
DLSw.quote: This memo describes the Data Link Switching Client Access Protocol that is used between workstations and routers to transport SNA/ NetBIOS traffic over TCP sessions.

rejected.why: NetBIOS name query frames are carried as payload, but the document does not specify NetBIOS services; it only encapsulates them.
TCP (port 1973) is only the transport substrate for DCAP sessions.
SNA is the traffic being carried; DLSw is the more specific tag and the parent is implied.
Optional UDP multicast is used for discovery (224.0.1.49/50), but it is a minor part of a protocol that does not address multicast routing.
UDP is used only for optional multicast and unicast discovery frames, so it is substrate.

RFC2115.title: Management Information Base for Frame Relay DTEs Using SMIv2
RFC2115.summary: Defines the SMIv2 FRAME-RELAY-DTE-MIB module, obsoleting RFC 1315, with objects for managing Frame Relay interfaces on DTEs: DLCMI parameters, virtual circuits, errors and traps.

frame relay.why: The MIB's subject is Frame Relay interface management (DLCMI, DLCIs, circuits, errors), so readers of the frame relay page would want it.
frame relay.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing Frame Relay interfaces on DTEs.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition (FRAME-RELAY-DTE-MIB) with object groups, compliance statements and a notification.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP- based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB plugs into. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and the MIB tag covers its subject.
Not related to the document; it concerns Frame Relay only.
Q.922 and Q.933 are referenced as sources for the frame relay data link and management, but the document is not about ISDN.

RFC2116.title: X.500 Implementations Catalog-96
RFC2116.summary: An FYI catalog of 31 available X.500 directory implementations (DSAs, DUAs, DUA interfaces), with keyword definitions, an index, and vendor-supplied descriptions including conformance to X.500 and LDAP RFCs.

X.500.why: The whole document catalogs X.500 directory implementations (DSAs, DUAs), so the X.500 directory service page is the natural home.
X.500.quote: This document catalogs currently available implementations of X.500, including commercial products and openly available offerings.

LDAP.why: Many catalogued products are LDAP clients, servers or gateways (UM-LDAP, maX.500, DIR.D, ORG.D, Critical Angle Enabler), and LDAP RFC conformance is a catalog keyword.
LDAP.quote: UM-LDAP is an implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the specific X.500 and LDAP tags, so it is not listed separately.
RFC 1006 (ISO transport over TCP) appears only as the networking environment of these products, not as a subject of the document.
Some products offer SNMP monitoring or the directory monitoring MIB, but this is incidental to the catalog.
X.400 messaging integration is mentioned in a few product descriptions only.
It is only a keyword for product user interfaces, not a subject of the document.

RFC2117.title: Protocol Independent Multicast-Sparse Mode (PIM-SM): Protocol Specification
RFC2117.summary: Specifies PIM-SM, the experimental sparse-mode multicast routing protocol: RP-rooted shared trees, switching to source trees, Register, Join/Prune, Assert, Hello, Bootstrap/RP-set distribution, timers and packet formats.

PIM-SM.why: The whole document is the protocol specification of PIM Sparse Mode, covering its messages, state machines, timers and packet formats.
PIM-SM.quote: This document describes a protocol for efficiently routing to multicast groups that may span wide-area (and inter-domain) internets.

rejected.why: IGMP is only used by hosts to signal membership to the designated router; it is not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only briefly as an option to secure PIM control messages; the document is not about IPsec.
The more specific child PIM-SM applies, so the parent is implied.
The PIM header checksum is defined, but this is routine packet-format detail and not a subject of the document.

RFC2118.title: Microsoft Point-To-Point Compression (MPPC) Protocol
RFC2118.summary: Informational RFC describing the Microsoft Point-to-Point Compression (MPPC) protocol, an LZ-based sliding-window compression negotiated via PPP CCP, with its packet format, option, and encoding.

PPP.why: MPPC is a PPP compression method negotiated through CCP, with a PPP protocol number (00FD) and a CCP configuration option. PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of the Microsoft Point to Point Compression protocol (also referred to as MPPC in this document) for compressing PPP encapsulated packets.

compression.why: A large part of the document specifies the LZ-based compressor and its literal and copy-tuple encodings, which is lossless data compression.
compression.quote: The MPPC algorithm uses an LZ [3] based algorithm with a sliding window history buffer.

rejected.why: MPPC compresses whole PPP packets, including already header-compressed ones. It is not a header compression scheme.
The document mentions Van Jacobson compressed TCP/IP headers only as an example of input to MPPC.
The algorithm is Stac-licensed LZ-based, but the document does not define LZS itself or its use in PPP.

RFC2119.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels
RFC2119.summary: RFC 2119 (BCP 14) defines the requirement-level key words MUST, SHOULD, MAY and related terms for use in IETF documents, and gives guidance on using them sparingly.

terminology.why: The document is a glossary of normative requirements-language key words and how to interpret them, which is exactly what the terminology topic covers.
terminology.quote: This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents.

rejected.why: The document concerns wording conventions inside RFCs, but it is not about RFC format, style or publication processes as such; terminology fits better.
It is a BCP used by IETF authors, but it does not describe standards process or administration.

RFC2120.title: Managing the X.500 Root Naming Context
RFC2120.summary: Experimental RFC describing how to use 1993 X.500 shadowing (DISP) and hierarchical operational bindings (DOP) to manage the root naming context via a root DSA, with fast-track, slower-track and long-term solutions plus ISO defect reports.

X.500.why: The whole document specifies how X.500 DSAs shadow and manage the root naming context, using DISP and DOP, and proposes fixes to the X.500 standard.
X.500.quote: This document describes the use of 1993 ISO X.500 Standard protocols for managing the root context.

rejected.why: LDAP is mentioned only to say the root DSA will not support LDAP user operations. The document is not about it.
This is the parent of X.500. The more specific X.500 tag fits, so the parent is implied.
ASN.1 parameter settings appear, but only as the encoding the X.500 protocols use. The document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC2121.title: Issues affecting MARS Cluster Size
RFC2121.summary: Informational RFC giving a qualitative analysis of the factors limiting MARS Cluster size for IP multicast over ATM, including VC and leaf-node limits, signaling load, group change latency, and the effect of Mrouters, Cell Switch Routers and Multicast Servers.

ATM.why: The document analyses MARS clusters, pt-mpt SVCs, UNI signaling and VC limits in IP over ATM networks. ATM is the most specific fitting tag for this subject.
ATM.quote: IP multicast over ATM currently uses the MARS model [1] to manage the use of ATM pt-mpt SVCs for IP multicast packet forwarding.

multicast.why: It covers IP multicast group membership handling, VC Mesh versus MCS forwarding, and multicast routers (Mrouters) as ways to scale multicast deployment.
multicast.quote: Large scale IP multicasting over ATM requires a combination of Mrouters and appropriately sized MARS Clusters.

rejected.why: MADCAP and MALLOC concern multicast address allocation. MARS is address resolution and group membership for ATM, so this is not the same subject.
IPv4 Logical IP Subnets are mentioned only as the comparison for the cluster concept. The document is not about IPv4.
Host group membership is mentioned only in passing. The document discusses MARS_JOIN and MARS_LEAVE, not IGMP.
The document discusses VC consumption and signaling load, not quality of service.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server)
gaps.why: The document is about MARS clusters, but the taxonomy has no tag for MARS. It is covered only by the general ATM and multicast tags.

RFC2122.title: VEMMI URL Specification
RFC2122.summary: Defines the "vemmi" URL scheme for connecting VEMMI clients and terminals to VEMMI multimedia interactive services (ITU-T T.107 / ETS 300 709), including syntax, the service-selection dialog, and the application/vemmi media type registration.

URI.why: The document's main purpose is to define a new URI scheme, its syntax, defaults and parameters, so it belongs under URI.
URI.quote: A new URL scheme, "vemmi" is defined. It allows VEMMI client software and VEMMI terminals to connect to multimedia interactive services

media types.why: A substantial section registers the application/vemmi media type with its parameters, encoding, security and interoperability considerations.
media types.quote: The assignment of a MIME media type application/vemmi will allow this transport and exchange of VEMMI objects

rejected.why: HTTP is mentioned as an alternative way to carry VEMMI objects and for status code syntax, but the document explicitly says this use is not described here.
HTML documents contain vemmi links and VEMMI can display HTML, but the document does not specify HTML itself.
The service selection dialog is telnet or videotex compatible, but Telnet is not specified or extended.
MIME is used only for the media type registration, which is covered by media types. The document does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
Web browser integration is discussed, but the specific subject is the URI scheme, which is already tagged.

gaps.name: VEMMI (Videotex Enhanced Man-Machine Interface)
gaps.why: The document is about the VEMMI multimedia/videotex service protocol (ITU-T T.107, ETS 300 709, TCP port 575). The taxonomy has no tag for videotex or VEMMI.

RFC2123.title: Traffic Flow Measurement: Experiences with NeTraMet
RFC2123.summary: Informational memo recording experience implementing and using the Traffic Flow Measurement architecture and Meter MIB via NeTraMet (meter) and NeMaC (manager/meter reader), covering implementation, rule-set writing, flow data files and deployment.

performance measurement.why: The document is about traffic flow metering: meters, rule sets, flow data collection and analysis. This is network performance and usage measurement, and no more specific tag fits.
performance measurement.quote: This memo records experiences in implementing and using the Traffic Flow Measurement Architecture and Meter MIB.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document covers how the Traffic Meter MIB is implemented and used, including HighWaterMark, FloodMark, TimeFilter and the reader info table.
MIB.quote: The Meter MIB [2] specifies a more general table of meter reader information.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the meter. The document uses it, and the Opaque column-activity optimisation is a minor point, but the document is not about SNMP itself.
This is a predecessor flow-measurement effort (RTFM). It does not specify IPFIX or packet sampling.
TCP and UDP port numbers appear only as flow attributes in example rule sets.
Ethernet is only the capture medium for the PC meter.

gaps.name: Traffic flow measurement (RTFM)
gaps.why: The document is about the RTFM architecture and meter implementation. The taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic, and nothing specific to flow metering or accounting.

RFC2124.title: Cabletron's Light-weight Flow Admission Protocol Specification Version 1.0
RFC2124.summary: Informational Cabletron specification of LFAP, a TCP-based protocol between a switch's connection control entity and an external Flow Admission Service that decides flow admission, operating policy, redirection and accounting.

QoS.why: The protocol is about admission control for flows, including per-flow priority and bandwidth-related operating policies and signalling between switch and admission server. This fits the QoS admission/signalling area, and no more specific tag exists.
QoS.quote: allows an external Flow Admission Service (FAS) to manage flow admission at the switch

policy management.why: A central FAS supplies optional and mandatory operating policies (usage, routing, administrative) to switches, centralizing policy enforcement. The topic is only a loose fit, since the document defines a protocol and not an information model.
policy management.quote: define the parameters under which a given flow is to operate (operating policy)

rejected.why: LFAP resembles COPS in function, but the document does not specify or use COPS.
The FAS keeps flow records for billing and accounting, but this is secondary and the document does not frame itself as an AAA framework.
TCP is only the transport substrate used to reach the FAS, so it is not tagged.
ATM and LANE are mentioned only as ways to get IP reachability. The protocol is not specific to ATM.
Allowing or disallowing flows is a kind of authorization, but the QoS/admission framing fits better and the document does not present itself as access control.

gaps.name: Flow admission control / connection admission control
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for admission control of flows by an external server. It is the core subject of the document and is only approximated by QoS.

RFC2125.title: The PPP Bandwidth Allocation Protocol (BAP) / The PPP Bandwidth Allocation Control Protocol (BACP)
RFC2125.summary: Defines the PPP Bandwidth Allocation Protocol (BAP) and Bandwidth Allocation Control Protocol (BACP), which let peers negotiate adding and dropping links in a PPP multilink bundle for bandwidth on demand, plus a new LCP Link Discriminator option.

PPP.why: BAP and BACP are PPP control protocols (BACP reuses LCP mechanics, with its own PPP protocol field values) and the RFC adds an LCP Link Discriminator option. It is a PPP extension and the PPP subject page is where readers would look for it.
PPP.quote: BAP defines datagrams to co-ordinate adding and removing individual links in a multilink bundle

rejected.why: ISDN is only one of several link types named in the Link-Type option, and the document is not about ISDN access.
Multilink PPP bundles are conceptually similar, but the tag is defined as IEEE 802.1AX link bundling, which is a different mechanism.
X.25 appears only as one value in the Link-Type bit mask.
Bandwidth on demand adjusts link capacity. It is not a QoS architecture or a signalling protocol for QoS.

gaps.name: PPP Multilink Protocol / bandwidth on demand
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for multilink PPP bundles or bandwidth on demand. The PPP tag covers the protocol family but not this specific mechanism.

RFC2126.title: ISO Transport Service on top of TCP (ITOT)
RFC2126.summary: RFC 2126 (ITOT) revises RFC 1006 to specify ISO Transport Protocol classes 0 and 2 running over TCP on IPv4 or IPv6, using TPKT framing, new expedited-data options, and NSAP/address representations.

OSI.why: The document specifies ISO 8072/8073 transport service and protocol classes 0 and 2 over TCP, interworking OSI with the IP suite. OSI is the closest tag, as there is no OSI transport tag.
OSI.quote: This document defines a Transport Service which appears to be identical to the Services and Interfaces offered by the ISO Transport Service Definition [ISO8072]

TCP.why: The document defines how TCP is mapped as a connection-oriented network service provider, including TCP connection use for expedited data, port 102, keep-alive and Nagle guidance for implementers.
TCP.quote: The Transmission Control Protocol is used in place of the ISO 8348 to provide a CONS like service.

rejected.why: IPv6 is only an alternative network address family for TCP; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
Considered since this carries one protocol over another transport, but the OSI and TCP tags fit more specifically.
The document concerns the connection-oriented network service mapping to TCP, not the connectionless network protocol.
IPv4 is only the underlying substrate for TCP and is not itself addressed.

gaps.name: ISO Transport Protocol (ISO 8073) over TCP / RFC1006 / TPKT
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the ISO transport service and protocol itself. OSI network-layer protocols is the nearest fit but is imprecise, since this is a transport-layer mapping.

RFC2127.title: ISDN Management Information Base using SMIv2
RFC2127.summary: Defines the SMIv2 ISDN MIB module for SNMP management of ISDN basic/primary rate interfaces, B channels, D channel signaling and LAPD, terminal endpoints and directory numbers, with its relationship to the Interfaces MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (ISDN-MIB) in SMIv2, defining tables, groups, traps and compliance for ISDN interfaces.
MIB.quote: it defines a minimal set of managed objects for SNMP-based management of ISDN terminal interfaces

ISDN.why: The subject is ISDN access: BRI/PRI, B and D channels, LAPD, SPIDs, NFAS and D-channel backup, so readers of ISDN would want it.
ISDN.quote: This MIB controls all aspects of ISDN interfaces.  It consists of five groups.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for; the document defines no protocol change, so the MIB tag is more specific.
X.25 packet-mode service over B and D channels is mentioned only as an implementation hint, not a main subject.
PPP appears only as an example of an interface layered over B channels.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB definitions.

RFC2128.title: Dial Control Management Information Base using SMIv2
RFC2128.summary: Defines the DIAL-CONTROL-MIB SMIv2 module for managing demand access circuits (including ISDN): peer configuration and statistics, active calls, call history, and call notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (DIAL-CONTROL-MIB) with SMIv2 tables, groups, traps and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing demand access circuits, including ISDN.

ISDN.why: ISDN is the primary example medium, and many objects (B/D channels, Q.931 cause values, info types) are ISDN-specific, so ISDN readers would want it.
ISDN.quote: The low-level interfaces are either physical interfaces, e.g.  modem interfaces, or logical interfaces, e.g. ISDN B channels

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is defined for; the document specifies a MIB module, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation used in the SMI module definition, not a subject of the document.
PPP is only mentioned as an example encapsulation whose interface MIB defines ifEntry; the document doesn't specify it.
Implied by the MIB tag, which is more specific.

RFC2129.title: Toshiba's Flow Attribute Notification Protocol (FANP) Specification
RFC2129.summary: Describes Toshiba's FANP, a neighbor-to-neighbor protocol that maps IP packet flows to dedicated ATM virtual connections so Cell Switch Routers can cut-through forward packets without IP processing.

ATM.why: FANP manages flow-to-VC mappings on ATM networks (Dedicated-VCs, VPI/VCI, SVC/PVC/VP, ATM signaling) for IP over ATM cut-through forwarding. The document assumes an ATM datalink throughout.
ATM.quote: By using FANP, routers (e.g., CSR; Cell Switch Router) can forward incoming packets based on their datalink-level connection identifiers, bypassing usual IP packet processing.

rejected.why: NHRP also addresses shortcut paths over NBMA networks, but FANP is a distinct neighbor-to-neighbor protocol and does not use or specify NHRP.
Label-switching-like cut-through forwarding, but the document never mentions MPLS and defines its own protocol, so it is not about MPLS.
Frame Relay is named only as another connection-oriented datalink platform. The specification is written for ATM.
The PROPOSE message reuses the ATM ARP message format from RFC 1577 as an encoding. The document is not about ARP.
RSVP and QoS signaling are listed only as future enhancements, not covered in the body.

gaps.name: Cut-through / flow-based IP switching over ATM (FANP, Cell Switch Router)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IP switching or flow-attribute cut-through forwarding, which is the document's main subject. ATM is the closest fit.

RFC2130.title: The Report of the IAB Character Set Workshop held 29 February - 1 March, 1996
RFC2130.summary: Report of the 1996 IAB workshop on character sets, giving an architectural model (CCS, CES, TES), recommending MIME charset tagging, ISO 10646 and UTF-8 as defaults, language tagging, and registration guidelines for character sets.

character sets.why: The whole report is about character set handling, a framework of CCS/CES/TES, defaults, conversion and registration.
character sets.quote: recommends a default character set *without* stating that there is no need for other character sets

UTF-8.why: Recommends UTF-8 as default encoding for new protocols and recommends registering it with MIME.
UTF-8.quote: This report recommends the use of ISO 10646 as the default Coded Character Set, and UTF-8 as the default Character Encoding Scheme

language tags.why: Substantial discussion of language tagging, Han unification disambiguation, and a recommendation that new protocols tag text with language.
language tags.quote: To specify the language used in a particular block of text, we recommend that the MIME tag "Content-Language" be used.

MIME.why: Recommends MIME charset and content-transfer-encoding labels as the tagging mechanism and changes to MIME charset registration.
MIME.quote: we recommend that MIME registered values be used for all tagging of character sets and languages

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen tags; the more specific tags fit, so the parent is implied.

It is a workshop report, and the tag fits the genre. But the taxonomy describes IAB/IRTF/community workshop reports, and this one is arguably also covered; kept out in favour of subject tags. Reconsider if genre tagging is wanted.
Email is one of many protocols surveyed in Appendix A, not the focus.
Mentioned as an example and a legacy default, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
ISO 10646 is the default CCS, but the document addresses it as a character set rather than Unicode usage in protocols.
Recommends IANA charset registration procedures, but only as a minor part.

gaps.name: workshop reports
gaps.why: The taxonomy has this tag, but I excluded it from the tags above. Under the stated rules the document is arguably about it, so add it if genre tagging is wanted.

RFC2131.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
RFC2131.summary: RFC 2131 specifies DHCP, the client-server protocol for allocating IP addresses and delivering host configuration parameters, based on BOOTP message format and relay agent behaviour.

DHCP.why: The document is the core DHCP specification, defining message formats, client and server behaviour, state machine, leases and retransmission.
DHCP.quote: DHCP consists of two components: a protocol for delivering host-specific configuration parameters from a DHCP server to a host and a mechanism for allocation of network addresses to hosts.

rejected.why: DHCP only uses UDP ports 67/68 as its transport; the document specifies nothing new about UDP.
ARP is used only for address-in-use probing by the client; it is not the subject of the document.
ICMP echo is mentioned only as an optional probe of offered addresses.
TFTP appears only in related work and as a bootstrap service reference.
The document explicitly says DHCP does not address DNS registration; DNS names appear only as possible client identifiers.
Address allocation is done through DHCP, so the DHCP tag already covers it. The document does not address IP address architecture in general.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol)
gaps.why: DHCP is built on BOOTP message format and relay agent behaviour, and the document covers interoperation with BOOTP clients and relay agents. The taxonomy has no BOOTP tag.

RFC2132.title: DHCP Options and BOOTP Vendor Extensions
RFC2132.summary: RFC 2132 specifies the current set of DHCP options (and BOOTP vendor extensions), defining the tag-length-value option format and the IP, link, TCP, application and DHCP-specific options, and the procedure for defining new ones.

DHCP.why: The whole document defines DHCP option formats and codes, including DHCP-specific options such as message type, lease time and client-identifier.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies the current set of DHCP options.

rejected.why: Only IPv4 DHCP and BOOTP options are defined; DHCPv6 is not covered.
The domain name server and domain name options only configure DNS clients. They are two options among many, not a DNS specification.
The NetBIOS options are a few of the application options. NetBIOS itself is not specified here.
Section 10 describes how option numbers are allocated, but this is minor and the document is not about IANA registries.
The NTP servers option only conveys server addresses and does not specify NTP.

gaps.name: BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol) vendor extensions
gaps.why: The document also defines BOOTP vendor information extensions, and the taxonomy has no BOOTP tag.

RFC2133.title: Basic Socket Interface Extensions for IPv6
RFC2133.summary: Informational memo defining IPv6 extensions to the BSD sockets API: sockaddr_in6, AF_INET6, interface index functions, IPv6 socket options (hop limit, multicast), getaddrinfo/getnameinfo, gethostbyname2, and inet_pton/inet_ntop.

sockets API.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the sockets API for IPv6: address structures, socket options, interface functions and library functions.
sockets API.quote: changes are required to the sockets API to support IPv6 and this memo describes these changes.

IPv6.why: The API changes serve IPv6 deployment and cover IPv6 addresses, IPv4-mapped compatibility, hop limit and multicast options, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 interfaces are identified by 128-bit addresses.

rejected.why: Name lookup functions such as gethostbyname2 query AAAA/A/PTR records, but the document specifies a C library API, not DNS protocol or resolver behaviour.
Multicast socket options (IPV6_ADD_MEMBERSHIP etc.) are a small section of the API, not multicast routing or group membership protocols.
TCP and UDP sockets are only the transports that the API exposes; the document does not specify them.
The document uses IPv6 addresses and the IPv4-mapped format but does not define address architecture.
Hostname-to-address translation is done via library functions in the API; it is not about host naming conventions or host tables.

RFC2134.title: Articles of Incorporation of Internet Society
RFC2134.summary: RFC 2134 publishes the legal Articles of Incorporation of the Internet Society (ISOC), a District of Columbia non-profit, covering its purposes, board of trustees, internal governance and initial trustees.

internet governance.why: The document is the founding legal charter of ISOC, an organization that administers and supports the Internet and its standards development. It sets out ISOC's purposes, board structure and amendment rules, so readers of the governance subject would want it.
internet governance.quote: To facilitate and support the technical evolution of the Internet as a research and education infrastructure

rejected.why: The document concerns ISOC's corporate structure, not IETF standards procedures. The IETF is not mentioned in the body apart from the abstract's publication note.
The only legal content is corporate and tax-exempt status, not intellectual property, copyright or trust provisions.
It is a founding legal document rather than a history or retrospective of the Internet.

RFC2135.title: Internet Society By-Laws
RFC2135.summary: The Internet Society's by-laws (as amended June 1996), covering its offices, Board of Trustees, officers, membership classes, and amendment rules, published for information at the request of the poisson working group.

internet governance.why: The document is the governing charter of ISOC, the organization that administers and supports Internet standards development. No more specific child tag fits, because it is not IETF process, IPR, IANA or RFC series material, so the parent topic applies.
internet governance.quote: The affairs of the Society shall be directed by its Board of Trustees.

rejected.why: The by-laws govern ISOC, a separate corporate body. They do not define IETF standards procedures or IETF administration.
The Trustee election and appointment rules are ISOC's own. They are not IETF Nominating Committee procedures.

RFC2136.title: Dynamic Updates in the Domain Name System (DNS UPDATE)
RFC2136.summary: RFC 2136 specifies the DNS UPDATE opcode, which lets a requestor add or delete RRs and RRsets in a zone, subject to prerequisites, with atomic processing, server and forwarder behaviour, and SOA serial handling.

DNS update.why: The whole document defines the dynamic update mechanism for DNS: message format, prerequisites, update operations, server, requestor and forwarder behaviour.
DNS update.quote: Using this specification of the UPDATE opcode, it is possible to add or delete RRs or RRsets from a specified zone.

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by the more specific DNS update tag, so it is not listed separately.
Secure DNS Update (RFC 2137) is only referenced as the recommended security companion, and this document does not specify it.
UDP and TCP are only transport options for update messages (Section 2.1), not the subject of the document.
DHCP servers are mentioned once as likely sources of updates, but the document is not about DHCP.
IPsec is mentioned in Security Considerations as an alternative protection and is not otherwise discussed.

RFC2137.title: Secure Domain Name System Dynamic Update
RFC2137.summary: RFC 2137 specifies how to use DNSSEC SIG/KEY records to authenticate and authorize DNS dynamic updates, defining two zone modes (A and B), update key signatory bits, and request/data signatures.

DNS update.why: The document defines the security of DNS dynamic update: authorizing keys, update modes, and request/data signatures.
DNS update.quote: This memo describes how to use DNSSEC digital signatures covering requests and data to secure updates and restrict updates to those authorized to perform them

DNSSEC.why: It extends DNSSEC (SIG, KEY, NXT RRs, zone keys, signatory field) for update authentication, so DNSSEC readers would want it.
DNSSEC.quote: This memo proposes techniques based on the defined DNS security mechanisms to authenticate DNS updates.

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen tags and implied by them; no separate general DNS subject.
Authentication is achieved through the DNSSEC mechanism, which is already tagged; the document is not about authentication in general.
Update authorization is expressed through DNSSEC KEY signatory bits, which the DNS update and DNSSEC tags already cover.
Key rollover is only a side note to the update modes; the document does not address key management as a subject.

RFC2138.title: Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)
RFC2138.summary: RFC 2138 specifies the RADIUS protocol, a UDP-based client/server protocol carrying authentication, authorization and configuration information between a Network Access Server and a shared authentication server, including packet formats, attributes and examples.

RADIUS.why: The whole document defines the RADIUS protocol: packet types, the authenticator and password-hiding algorithms, and the attribute set.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes a protocol for carrying authentication, authorization, and configuration information between a Network Access Server which desires to authenticate its links and a shared Authentication Server.

rejected.why: PAP, CHAP and PPP framing are interoperated with and carried in attributes, but PPP itself is not specified or extended here.
UDP is only the transport. Section 2.3 justifies the choice but defines nothing new about UDP.
MD5 is used for password hiding and response authentication, but the document is not about the algorithm.
RADIUS is the more specific tag under AAA, so the parent is implied.
The document is about a specific protocol, which has its own tag, rather than authentication in general.
Telnet is only a Login-Service attribute value and appears in an example.

RFC2139.title: RADIUS Accounting
RFC2139.summary: RFC 2139 specifies the RADIUS Accounting protocol, which carries accounting records (Start/Stop, usage statistics, termination causes) from a Network Access Server to a shared accounting server, extending RADIUS over UDP port 1813.

RADIUS.why: The document defines the RADIUS Accounting packet types (Accounting-Request/Response), authenticators and accounting attributes 40-51, so it is about RADIUS.
RADIUS.quote: This memo extends the use of the RADIUS protocol to cover delivery of accounting information from the Network Access Server (NAS) to a RADIUS accounting server.

rejected.why: RADIUS is the more specific tag and already sits under AAA. The document does not discuss AAA frameworks in general.
UDP is only the transport for the packets (port 1813). The document defines nothing new about UDP.
MD5 is only used to compute the Request and Response Authenticators. The document is not about MD5.
PPP is mentioned only as a service type and in the multilink attributes. It is not the subject.

RFC2140.title: TCP Control Block Interdependence
RFC2140.summary: RFC 2140 argues for sharing TCP control block state (MSS, RTT, congestion window) across sequential and concurrent connections to the same host to improve transient performance.

TCP.why: The whole document proposes a change to TCP implementations: how the TCB is initialized and shared across connections. It is squarely about TCP implementation.
TCP.quote: This memo makes the case for interdependent TCP control blocks, where part of the TCP state is shared among similar concurrent connections

congestion control.why: A substantial part discusses sharing congestion window state and initial window options among concurrent connections, so congestion control readers would want it.
congestion control.quote: Congestion window size aggregation is more complicated in the concurrent case.

rejected.why: Web traffic and persistent HTTP are only motivating examples; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
IP is mentioned only as the layer where state might be shared; the document is not about IP itself.
The layering remark about per-path state at the network layer is a side implication, not the document's main subject.

RFC2141.title: URN Syntax
RFC2141.summary: RFC 2141 defines the canonical syntax of Uniform Resource Names (urn:<NID>:<NSS>), including character encoding, reserved characters, and lexical equivalence rules.

URN.why: The document exists to specify the canonical URN syntax, NID and NSS rules, and lexical equivalence. This is the core of the URN subject.
URN.quote: All URNs have the following syntax (phrases enclosed in quotes are REQUIRED): <URN> ::= "urn:" <NID> ":" <NSS>

rejected.why: URN is the more specific child tag and fits. The URI parent is implied, so it is not listed.
UTF-8 is only the mechanism used to percent-encode characters outside the URN character set. The document does not specify it.
The grammar is written in BNF notation, but the document is not about the notation.

RFC2142.title: Mailbox Names for Common Services, Roles and Functions
RFC2142.summary: RFC 2142 specifies well-known mailbox names (e.g., POSTMASTER, ABUSE, HOSTMASTER, LIST-REQUEST) that organizations must or should support for business, network operations, specific Internet services and mailing list administration.

email.why: The document defines standard email mailbox names and their handling by mail exchangers; it is about email addressing conventions and operations, with no narrower email tag fitting better.
email.quote: This specification enumerates and describes Internet mail addresses (mailbox name @ host reference) to be used when contacting personnel at an organization.

mailing lists.why: A dedicated section mandates LIST-REQUEST administrative mailbox names for mailing lists.
mailing lists.quote: Mailing lists have an administrative mailbox name to which add/drop requests and other meta-queries can be sent.

rejected.why: POSTMASTER is listed as the SMTP contact mailbox, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Mentions the SOA RR mailbox field and HOSTMASTER, but only briefly; DNS is not the subject.
Mailbox names are addresses, but the document does not address header or message format.
SECURITY and ABUSE mailboxes are listed, but only as contact addresses, not operational security practice.
USENET/NEWS mailbox is tied to NNTP, but NNTP is only referenced.
WEBMASTER is tied to HTTP, but HTTP is only referenced.

RFC2143.title: Encapsulating IP with the Small Computer System Interface
RFC2143.summary: Experimental memo defining how to carry IPv4 datagrams over a SCSI bus as a data link, using the SEND MESSAGE(10) command, and sketching address resolution and scaling for such networks.

link layer.why: The RFC specifies IP encapsulation over SCSI as a data-link medium (header fields, framing, address resolution). The taxonomy has no SCSI-specific tag, so the generic link layer topic fits best.
link layer.quote: This document outlines a protocol for connecting hosts running the TCP/IP protocol suite over a Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) bus.

rejected.why: Section 4 only adapts ARP-style resolution to a bus with no broadcast, by round-robin transmission. It defines no new ARP protocol. It also sits under link layer, which is already the right tag.
This topic covers storage protocols carried over IP, such as iSCSI. This RFC does the reverse and carries IP over SCSI, and it is not about storage access.
IPv4 is the payload being encapsulated, not the subject. The document only uses the IPv4 datagram length field to choose the SCSI header form.
The encapsulation is link-layer framing of IP in SCSI messages, not IP-in-IP or generic tunnelling.

gaps.name: SCSI (Small Computer System Interface) as an IP link medium
gaps.why: The document is about running IP over SCSI buses, but the taxonomy has no SCSI tag. Readers browsing link technologies like FireWire or InfiniBand would expect to find it there.

RFC2144.title: The CAST-128 Encryption Algorithm
RFC2144.summary: RFC 2144 describes the CAST-128 (CAST5) Feistel block cipher, including its key schedule, variable key sizes, s-boxes, OIDs and test vectors, as an unencumbered encryption algorithm for Internet use.

cryptography.why: The whole document specifies a symmetric block cipher, its key schedule, s-boxes and test vectors. No specific cipher tag in the taxonomy fits CAST-128, so the general cryptography topic is the right one.
cryptography.quote: This document describes the CAST-128 encryption algorithm, a DES-like Substitution-Permutation Network (SPN) cryptosystem

rejected.why: CAST-128 is only compared to DES as a similar Feistel cipher; the document is not about DES.
The OBJECT IDENTIFIER and Parameters definitions are a small apparatus within a cipher spec, not the subject.
CAST-128 is a different cipher and AES is not discussed.
The password-based encryption OID only references PKCS #5; the document does not specify password-based key derivation.

gaps.name: CAST-128 / CAST5 block cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for this specific cipher, so only the general cryptography topic can be used. Similar named ciphers such as Camellia and ARIA do have their own tags.

RFC2145.title: Use and Interpretation of HTTP Version Numbers
RFC2145.summary: Informational RFC clarifying the intended use and interpretation of HTTP major/minor version numbers, covering proxy behavior, compatibility between minor versions, and which version a client or server should send.

HTTP.why: The whole document specifies how HTTP version numbers are used and interpreted by clients, servers and proxies, so it is about HTTP semantics and interoperability.
HTTP.quote: The major version sent in a message MAY indicate the interpretation of other header fields. The minor version sent in a message MUST NOT indicate the interpretation of other header fields.

rejected.why: Cache-control is mentioned only as an example of a header sent to an HTTP/1.0 recipient. The document is not about caching.
The document covers version numbers in all HTTP versions (HTTP/1.0 and 1.1 are the ones discussed). It does not specify HTTP/2.
The RFC uses requirements language but is not a glossary or about requirements terminology.

RFC2146.title: U.S. Government Internet Domain Names
RFC2146.summary: Informational FNC memo updating RFC 1816 that sets registration policy for the .GOV (and FED.US) top-level domain, defining which US federal entities may register second-level names and how duplicates are resolved.

domain registration.why: The document is a registry policy for who may register names under .GOV and FED.US, covering eligibility, duplicate resolution, and registrar behaviour. This is domain registry and registrar operations.
domain registration.quote: This document describes the registration policies for the top-level domain ".GOV".

rejected.why: DNS is the namespace in which the names are registered. The document covers naming policy, not protocol or resolver behaviour. The FAQ on resolution and caching and the CNAME mention are minor.
WHOIS is mentioned only as a way to look up administrative contacts and check for conflicting names. The document does not specify or extend it.
The Security Considerations mention digital signatures on DNS data only in passing. This is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
The document concerns ordinary delegated TLDs (.GOV, .MIL, .US), not reserved or special-use names.

RFC2147.title: TCP and UDP over IPv6 Jumbograms
RFC2147.summary: Specifies how UDP (zero length field) and TCP (MSS of 65535 as infinity, Urgent Pointer handling) can carry IPv6 jumbograms larger than 65535 bytes.

UDP.why: The document changes UDP length-field handling so UDP can carry jumbograms, a protocol extension of UDP.
UDP.quote: a length of zero is used to indicate that it is to be ignored, and the length in the "pseudo-header" is to be used

TCP.why: Defines changes to TCP MSS and Urgent Pointer processing to support jumbograms.
TCP.quote: When an MSS value of 65535 is received, it is to be treated as infinity.

IPv6.why: The work is about using IPv6 Jumbo Payload packets with transports, and it updates the IPv6 specification (RFC 1883).
IPv6.quote: IPv6 supports datagrams larger than 65535 bytes long, often referred to as jumbograms, through use of the Jumbo Payload hop-by-hop option

rejected.why: Path MTU discovery is mentioned only to determine the actual MSS after an MSS of 65535 is received. The document does not specify it.
The UDP pseudo-header length used in the checksum is noted briefly, but the document is not about checksums.

RFC2148.title: Deployment of the Internet White Pages Service
RFC2148.summary: BCP recommending that organizations publish public white pages (people/address) information, preferably via X.500 with LDAP access and optionally Whois++, and covering data management, legal, and no-charge policy.

X.500.why: The document recommends X.500 as the directory protocol for the Internet White Pages Service, with sections on the global name space, DIT, DSAs and NameFLOW-Paradise.
X.500.quote: The currently preferable way for publishing the information is by using X.500 as its data structure and naming scheme

LDAP.why: LDAP access is a key recommendation and has its own section (Use LDAP). It is also discussed as the surviving access protocol.
LDAP.quote: The organization SHOULD make the published information available to LDAP clients, by allowing LDAP servers access to their data

WHOIS++.why: Whois++ is named as the second most popular IWPS protocol and an optional publication method. It is discussed only briefly, hence secondary.
WHOIS++.quote: The organization MAY additionally publish it using additional data structures such as whois++.

rejected.why: Its children X.500 and LDAP are tagged, so the parent is implied.
The legal and privacy section is about national law on publishing personal data, not protocol privacy considerations.
Email addresses are the data being published. The document does not address email protocols, apart from a recommendation that email vendors add LDAP lookup.
Character sets are mentioned only as an X.500 limitation.

gaps.name: Internet White Pages Service (IWPS)
gaps.why: The document is about white pages deployment practice and the common indexing and schema effort. The taxonomy has no white pages tag apart from the directory services parent.

RFC2149.title: Multicast Server Architectures for MARS-based ATM multicasting
RFC2149.summary: Informational RFC detailing the design of a Multicast Server (MCS) for MARS-based IP multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 ATM networks, including a HELLO-based mechanism for multiple MCSs per group for fault tolerance.

ATM.why: The document specifies an MCS architecture for IP multicasting over UNI 3.0/3.1 ATM networks, using point-to-multipoint VCs and the MARS. This is IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: This memo provides details on the design and implementation of an MCS, building on the core mechanisms defined in RFC 2022.

multicast.why: It addresses IP multicast group membership and delivery through a shared multicast server. It also covers the MCS control interactions with the MARS and fault-tolerant multi-MCS operation.
multicast.quote: Two basic approaches exist for the intra-subnet (intra-cluster) multicasting of IP packets.

rejected.why: The MARS is analogous to the ATM ARP server, but NHRP is not discussed.
The ATM ARP server is mentioned only as an analogy for the MARS, so the document is not about ARP.
The document deals with intra-cluster multicast forwarding and server failover, not reliable multicast transport protocols.
MARS and MCS handle group-to-ATM address resolution, not multicast address allocation.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) / MCS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ATM multicast address resolution or multicast servers. The closest fits are the ATM and multicast tags.

RFC2150.title: Humanities and Arts: Sharing Center Stage on the Internet
RFC2150.summary: FYI 31 is an introductory guide for artists and humanities scholars to the Internet: what it is, how the Web, email, news, IRC and multimedia work, how to create and publish content, and legal and security issues.

user guides.why: An FYI-series introductory guide for non-technical Internet users in the arts and humanities; this is the document's whole purpose.
user guides.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide members of the Arts and Humanities communities with an introduction to the Internet as a valuable tool

rejected.why: Explained only at an introductory level as the format for web pages; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Mentioned briefly as the Web's transfer protocol; not specified or extended.
One short subsection describes chat; the document is not about the protocol.
Briefly described as one forum among many.
URL structure is explained for novices only.
The Web is explained as one of many topics in a general guide; the document is not about web architecture.
Section 8.4 gives copyright and trademark advice to artists, but it is a small part of the document and not about IETF IPR provisions.

RFC2151.title: A Primer On Internet and TCP/IP Tools and Utilities
RFC2151.summary: FYI 30 is an introductory user guide to common TCP/IP and Internet tools (nslookup, ping, finger, traceroute, telnet, FTP, whois, Knowbot, archie, Gopher, WAIS, WWW, mailing lists, Usenet) and to obtaining RFCs and other Internet documentation.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory tutorial for Internet users, which is exactly the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: This memo is an introductory guide to many of the most commonly- available TCP/IP and Internet tools and utilities.

traceroute.why: A full section explains the traceroute tool, its options, how it works with TTL and ICMP, and a sample session.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute is another common TCP/IP tool, this one allowing users to learn about the route that packets take from their local host to a remote host.

FTP.why: A substantial section covers FTP use, commands, and a sample session.
FTP.quote: FTP allows users to upload and download files between local and remote hosts. Anonymous FTP, in particular, is commonly available at file archive sites

Telnet.why: A section covers Telnet use, including using port numbers to reach other services.
Telnet.quote: TELNET is TCP/IP's virtual terminal protocol. Using TELNET, a user connected to one host can login to another host

WHOIS.why: A section covers WHOIS/NICNAME usage with sample queries, and Knowbot builds on it.
WHOIS.quote: WHOIS and NICNAME are TCP/IP applications that search databases to find the name of network and system administrators

Gopher.why: Gopher gets its own section with a sample session, and VERONICA and JUGHEAD are described as adjuncts to it.
Gopher.quote: The Internet Gopher protocol was developed at the University of Minnesota's Microcenter in 1991, as a distributed information search and retrieval tool

WAIS.why: WAIS is described as an information server tool, in a short paragraph.
WAIS.quote: The Wide Area Information Server (WAIS, pronounced "ways") was initiated jointly by Apple Computer, Dow Jones, KMPG Peat Marwick

Finger.why: Finger has its own section with usage and sample sessions.
Finger.quote: The Finger program may be used to find out who is logged in on another system or to find out detailed information about a specific user.

web.why: A whole section introduces the WWW, browsers, HTTP, HTML, URLs, and web access to the other tools.
web.quote: The World Wide Web (WWW) is thought (erroneously) by many to be the same thing as the Internet.

ICMP.why: The ping section covers the ICMP-based tool, its options, and sample sessions.
ICMP.quote: Ping uses a series of Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) [22] Echo messages to determine if a remote host is active or inactive

Netnews.why: Usenet and its newsgroup hierarchies are described in their own subsection.
Netnews.quote: Usenet, also known as NETNEWS or Usenet news, is another information source with its own set of special interest mailing lists organized into newsgroups.

mailing lists.why: Section 8 covers discussion lists and the LISTSERV and Majordomo list servers, with their subscribe and unsubscribe conventions.
mailing lists.quote: A large set of discussion groups is maintained using a program called LISTSERV.

DNS.why: The nslookup section shows how to query DNS records (A, MX), though it is only an introduction.
DNS.quote: A user can use NSLOOKUP to examine entries in the Domain Name System (DNS) database that pertain to a particular host or domain

rejected.why: Section 9 explains RFCs, STDs, FYIs and BCPs and how to get them, but this is one part of a tools primer, and the user guides tag already covers the document's purpose.
Section 7.1 summarises URL formats briefly and refers to RFC 1738 for the full description, so it is not substantial enough to tag.
The document mentions ARPANET history in passing but does not cover ARPANET protocols or operations.
Mail is only the substrate for list servers and RFC-INFO requests, and the document does not address email itself.
HTTP appears only as the protocol browsers use, with no treatment of its semantics.

gaps.name: Network diagnostic tools (ping, nslookup, traceroute)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a traceroute tag but nothing for ping or general network troubleshooting utilities, which the document covers.

gaps.name: Archie, Veronica, Jughead and Knowbot Internet search tools
gaps.why: These early information-discovery and user-lookup tools have no fitting tag, and the closest, service discovery, is a poor fit.

RFC2152.title: UTF-7 A Mail-Safe Transformation Format of Unicode
RFC2152.summary: RFC 2152 specifies UTF-7, a 7-bit-safe transformation format of Unicode using modified Base64 shift sequences, and defines its use as the charset "UTF-7" in MIME mail.

Unicode.why: The document defines a transformation format of Unicode (UTF-7), its encoding rules, and compares it with UTF-8; it is about Unicode encoding for Internet protocols.
Unicode.quote: UTF-7 encodes Unicode characters as US-ASCII octets, together with shift sequences to encode characters outside that range.

MIME.why: A substantial section defines the MIME charset tag UTF-7 and its interaction with content transfer encodings (7bit, Q, Quoted-Printable) and header encoding.
MIME.quote: Character set UTF-7 is safe for mail transmission and therefore may be used with any content transfer encoding in MIME
MIME.section: Use of Character Set UTF-7 Within MIME

rejected.why: UTF-8 is discussed only as an alternative that UTF-7 is compared against; the document does not specify it.
Modified Base64 is used as a building block of UTF-7 but the document is not about Base64 itself.
Mail is the motivating context, but the document specifies a character encoding, not mail architecture or transport.
UTF-7 is registered as a MIME charset, but the document is mainly about the Unicode transformation format; Unicode and MIME fit better.
US-ASCII is the target repertoire for the encoding, not the subject of the document.

RFC2153.title: PPP Vendor Extensions
RFC2153.summary: RFC 2153 defines a general vendor-specific mechanism for PPP: an LCP/NCP Vendor Specific packet (Code 0) and a Vendor-Specific configuration option (Type 0), identified by IEEE OUIs, plus a PPP-specific OUI series (CF0000) from IANA.

PPP.why: The document extends PPP's LCP and NCPs with a new Vendor Specific packet code and a Vendor-Specific configuration option, updating RFC 1661 and RFC 1962.
PPP.quote: This document defines a general mechanism for proprietary vendor extensions.

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned for OUI registration, but the document is about the PPP extension mechanism, not IANA registry procedures.
The proprietary vendor mechanism is not about intellectual property rights or copyright provisions.
Not about PPP over Ethernet; the document only concerns generic PPP control protocols.

RFC2154.title: OSPF with Digital Signatures
RFC2154.summary: Experimental extension of OSPF v2 that adds per-LSA digital signatures, a new Router Public Key LSA, Trusted Entity certification of router keys, key replacement procedures, and coexistence with unsigned OSPF areas.

OSPF.why: The document specifies extensions to OSPF: signed LSAs, a new PKLSA type, and compatibility with OSPF V2.
OSPF.quote: This memo describes the extensions to OSPF required to add digital signature authentication to Link State data, and to provide a certification mechanism for router data.

routing security.why: The goal is securing routing protocol data end-to-end with signatures, certificates and key management, including a vulnerability analysis.
routing security.quote: The basic idea of this proposal is to add digital signatures to OSPF LSA data, distribute certified router information and keys

rejected.why: RSA-MD5 is the only signature algorithm, but it is used as a mechanism and its formats are taken from RFC 2065; the document is not about RSA.
MD5 appears as the hash inside RSA-MD5 and as keyed MD5 for neighbor authentication, which is only referenced.
Key replacement is covered, but it is specific to the routing-security design and sits under the routing security tag.
The Trusted Entity issues certificates, but this is a custom OSPF-specific certificate format, not Internet PKI or X.509.
IDPR is only cited as prior work recommending signatures.
RFC 2065 is referenced only for the signature and key formats.

RFC2155.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for APPN using SMIv2
RFC2155.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module for monitoring and controlling APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking) nodes, ports, link stations, topology, directory, class of service and intermediate sessions.

APPN.why: The whole document defines the managed objects for APPN nodes, ports, link stations, TGs, directory, COS and sessions; APPN is the subject and the child tag of SNA.
APPN.quote: it defines objects for monitoring and controlling network devices with APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking) capabilities.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module written in SMIv2 with textual conventions, conformance groups and a trap, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
