MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework carrying the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag covers it.
DLSw is mentioned only as a transport the APPN ports may use, with a separate MIB referenced.
APPN is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
The Rapid Transport Protocol of HPR is an SNA mechanism, unrelated to the Real-time Transport Protocol. Only a few objects refer to it.
Not related; DLC types are only referenced via IANAifType.

gaps.name: HPR (High-Performance Routing)
gaps.why: HPR objects appear in the MIB (ANR labels, RTP connections, option sets 1400-1402), but the taxonomy has no HPR tag and the full HPR MIB is a separate document.

RFC2156.title: MIXER (Mime Internet X.400 Enhanced Relay): Mapping between X.400 and RFC 822/MIME
RFC2156.summary: RFC 2156 (MIXER) specifies the gateway mapping between X.400 (1988/1992) Interpersonal Messaging and RFC 822/MIME Internet mail, covering service elements, addressing (OR addresses and MCGAMs), message IDs, headers, delivery reports and notifications.

X.400.why: The whole document defines how X.400 IPMS/MTS/MTA elements, OR addresses, reports and notifications map to Internet mail, so it is about X.400 and its interworking.
X.400.quote: X.400 defines an Interpersonal Messaging System (IPMS), making use of a store and forward Message Transfer System.

message format.why: A large part of the document defines new RFC 822 header fields (X400-Received, Supersedes, Importance, etc.) and header mappings, and updates RFC 822.
message format.quote: RFC 822 specifies an end to end message format, consisting of a header and an unstructured text body.

email.why: It is an Internet mail gateway specification covering addressing, delivery status notifications and probes, and Appendix A covers SMTP-specific mappings.
email.quote: There is a large community using RFC 822 based protocols for mail services, who will wish to communicate with users of the IPMS

rejected.why: SMTP is the 822-MTS service that the mapping uses, and Appendix A is only a short set of SMTP-specific mappings. The document does not specify or extend SMTP.
MIME body part mapping is defined in the companion RFC 2157. This document only maps headers and generates MIME messages.
ASN.1 is the notation of the X.400 side, used as a substrate. The ASN.1 module is a small appendix.
DNS distribution of MCGAMs is defined in RFC 2163. Here DNS is only mentioned as one lookup mechanism.
X.500 distribution of MCGAMs is defined in RFC 2164, so X.500 is only referenced here.

RFC2157.title: Mapping between X.400 and RFC-822/MIME Message Bodies
RFC2157.summary: Defines how X.400 message body parts are mapped to and from MIME entities by MIXER gateways, including encapsulation methods (FTBP, BP15, HARPOON/IA5, BP14), user conversion-control headers, and an equivalence registry.

X.400.why: The whole document specifies X.400 body part mapping and interworking with Internet mail, including encapsulation and gateway conformance.
X.400.quote: This document defines how to map body parts of X.400 messages into MIME entities and vice versa, including the handling of multipart messages and forwarded messages.

MIME.why: Defines new MIME content types (application/x400-bp, application/x-ftbp.*), multipart handling and the equivalence registry mapping MIME types to X.400 body parts.
MIME.quote: The content-type field is "application/x400-bp".
MIME.section: 3.2 Encapsulating X.400 Body Parts in MIME

rejected.why: RFC 822 header mapping is in the companion MIXER document; this one concerns bodies.
It registers equivalences, not media types per se; the x-ftbp type is explicitly unregistered.
ASN.1 is used to define body parts and OIDs but is the notation, not the subject.
Character set conversion (GeneralText, Teletex) is part of the mappings but not the main subject.
The more specific X.400 and MIME tags cover it.
The IANA registration for equivalences is boilerplate-like and minor.

gaps.name: MIXER (X.400/RFC 822 gateway mapping)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MIXER gateway interworking beyond X.400; X.400 covers it adequately.

RFC2158.title: X.400 Image Body Parts
RFC2158.summary: Defines X.400 Extended Body Parts for JPEG and GIF image data and documents equivalences between these and MIME image types, including FTAM EMA OIDs.

X.400.why: The document specifies new X.400 body parts for carrying JPEG and GIF images and maps them to MIME types, so it belongs on the X.400 page.
X.400.quote: The following Extended Body Part is defined for JPEG data streams.

MIME.why: A substantial part of the document defines equivalences between X.400 body parts and MIME image content types for gateway conversion. This is about MIME-to-X.400 mapping, not just use of MIME as a substrate.
MIME.quote: X.400 Body Part: Extended Body Part, OID jpeg-body-part MIME Content-Type: image/jpeg Conversion: None

rejected.why: Considered as the general subject area. The more specific X.400 tag already covers it.
The document maps existing MIME types to X.400 body parts but does not register media types or set registry rules.
JPEG and GIF are only the payload formats being carried. The document does not define or describe the image formats themselves.

RFC2159.title: A MIME Body Part for FAX
RFC2159.summary: Defines the image/g3fax MIME content-type for carrying CCITT G3 Fax byte streams, with its parameters, page-break encoding, and mapping to/from the X.400 g3-facsimile body part.

fax.why: The whole document specifies how to carry T.4/T.30 G3 facsimile data in Internet mail, including parameters, page delimiting and X.400 conversion.
fax.quote: This content-type is defined to carry G3 Facsimile byte streams.

media types.why: It defines a MIME media type (image/g3fax) with its parameters and content encoding, which readers of media type registrations would want.
media types.quote: The image/g3fax content-type

X.400.why: A substantial part specifies the mapping between the MIME body part and the X.400 g3-facsimile body part, including the bit-order and page conversion algorithm.
X.400.quote: how to carry CCITT G3Fax in MIME, and how to translate it to its X.400 representation.

rejected.why: MIME is the framework in which the new content-type is defined; the document does not specify MIME itself, and the more specific media types tag covers it.
Base64 is only the suggested content-transfer-encoding and is used for the DCS parameter; it is not what the document is about.
ASN.1 BIT STRING and SEQUENCE appear only in describing the X.400 conversion, not as a subject of the document.

RFC2160.title: Carrying PostScript in X.400 and MIME
RFC2160.summary: Defines how PostScript is carried in X.400 (Extended Body Part and FTAM body part) and MIME (application/postscript), with MIXER conversion rules and OID assignments.

X.400.why: Specifies X.400 body parts (Extended Body Part and FTBP) for PostScript and their mapping to MIME, which is X.400 interworking.
X.400.quote: This document describes methods for carrying PostScript information in the two standard mail systems MIME and X.400, and the conversion between them.

MIME.why: The document maps the application/postscript MIME content type to the X.400 body parts, so MIME body handling is a substantial part of it.
MIME.quote: In MIME, PostScript is carried in the body part "application/PostScript", which is defined in RFC 1521.

rejected.why: The document uses application/postscript but does not register it; it was defined in RFC 1521, so this is not a media type registration.
Contains a small ASN.1 module for OID assignments, but that is only apparatus for the X.400 mapping, not the subject.
The document is about email systems generally, but the more specific X.400 and MIME tags cover it.

RFC2161.title: A MIME Body Part for ODA
RFC2161.summary: Defines the application/oda MIME content-type (profile and class parameters) for carrying Office Document Architecture documents, and its mapping to and from the X.400 ODA body part.

media types.why: The document defines the application/oda media type and its parameters (profile, class), which is a media type registration.
media types.quote: The "ODA" subtype of application is used to indicate that  a body contains  information  encoded according to the Office Document Architecture

X.400.why: A substantial part specifies the mapping between the X.400 ODA body part and MIME, including defaulting rules and EIT handling for gateways.
X.400.quote: how to carry ODA in MIME, and how to translate it to its X.400 representation

rejected.why: The parent of media types; the document is about a specific media type registration, so the more specific child tag fits.
ASN.1 definitions appear only as an abbreviated excerpt of the X.400 body part, not as the subject.
It is only mentioned as the appropriate content-transfer-encoding; the document is not about it.
The parent of the chosen tags; the document is narrower than email in general.

gaps.name: ODA (Office Document Architecture)
gaps.why: The document format being carried has no tag in the taxonomy; readers interested in ODA would find no subject page for it.

RFC2162.title: MaXIM-11 - Mapping between X.400 / Internet mail and  Mail-11 mail
RFC2162.summary: RFC 2162 (MaXIM-11) specifies mappings between X.400 and Internet (RFC822/MIME) mail and DECnet Mail-11 mail, mainly addresses and service elements, obsoleting RFC 1405.

X.400.why: The document defines O/R address and service element mappings between X.400 MHS and Mail-11, including multi-gateway cases. It is an X.400 interworking specification.
X.400.quote: enable inter working between systems operating the ISO/IEC 10021 - CCITT (now ITU) X.400 Recommendations on Message Handling Systems, and systems running the Mail-11

message format.why: A substantial part maps Mail-11 addresses and header elements to and from RFC822 headers (From, To, Cc, Date, Subject) and addresses. Chapter 6 covers Mail-11/RFC822 address mapping.
message format.quote: Mail-11 to RFC822/MIME service elements.

rejected.why: MIME bodypart mapping is explicitly delegated to MIXER and MIME-MHS. This document only notes that MIME can be carried in Mail-11 text bodyparts.
The DECnet tag does not apply: its definition covers DECnet protocols over IP infrastructure. This document is about Mail-11 messaging and addressing, which has no tag in the taxonomy.
SMTP is mentioned only as one of the transports under RFC822, and the document does not specify SMTP.
A more specific child tag (X.400) fits. Email is implied as an ancestor.

gaps.name: Mail-11 (DECnet mail / VMSmail)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the Mail-11 protocol and its address mapping. The taxonomy has no tag for Mail-11 or DECnet mail.

gaps.name: MIXER (X.400 to RFC822/MIME mapping)
gaps.why: The document builds on the MIXER mapping rules, but no taxonomy tag covers X.400-to-Internet-mail gateways beyond X.400.

review: message format: quote not found in the text

notes: message format: quote not found in the text

RFC2163.title: Using the Internet DNS to Distribute MIXER Conformant Global Address Mapping (MCGAM)
RFC2163.summary: Specifies the DNS PX resource record and an X42D name subtree under country TLDs to store MIXER MCGAM mapping rules between RFC822 domains and X.400 O/R addresses for email gateways.

DNS.why: Defines a new DNS RR type (PX), its RDATA format, a new X42D name space branch, and how to query it.
DNS.quote: The definition of the new 'PX' DNS resource record is:
DNS.section: 4. The new DNS resource record for MIXER mapping rules: PX

X.400.why: The document is about mapping between X.400 O/R addresses and RFC822 domains for X.400/Internet mail gateways (MIXER), which is X.400 interworking.
X.400.quote: map RFC822 domain names into X.400 O/R names and vice versa

rejected.why: Covered more specifically by X.400 interworking; the document is about address mapping, not general email architecture.
Concerns address mapping, not Internet message header format.
X.500 is mentioned only as an alternative publication method for MCGAM; not specified here.
MX records and SMTP are background only.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a future mitigation.

RFC2164.title: Use of an X.500/LDAP directory to support MIXER address mapping
RFC2164.summary: Defines X.500/LDAP directory object classes and attributes for representing and looking up MIXER global X.400↔RFC 822 address mappings (MCGAMs), including omitted components and gateway selection of mapping tables.

X.500.why: The document defines DIT subtrees, object classes and attributes in the X.500 directory to hold address mappings.
X.500.quote: This specification defines how to represent and maintain these mappings (MIXER Conformant Global Address Mappings of MCGAMs) in an X.500 or LDAP directory.

X.400.why: The directory data drives X.400/Internet mail address translation at gateways, so it belongs on the X.400 interworking page.
X.400.quote: MIXER (RFC 2156) defines an algorithm for use of a set of global mapping between X.400 and RFC 822 addresses

LDAP.why: The mapping schema is explicitly intended for use via LDAP as well as X.500, and the title names LDAP.
LDAP.quote: in an X.500 or LDAP directory

rejected.why: Mail is the application context, but the document is about directory schema for address mapping. X.400 interworking is the more specific tag.
The schema is written in ASN.1 object-class notation, but only as a definition language. The document is not about ASN.1.
Domain hierarchies are represented as DomainComponent entries in the DIT, not in the DNS.
RFC 822 addresses are mapped, but the document does not specify message format.

gaps.name: MIXER (MIME Internet X.400 Enhanced Relay)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MIXER X.400/RFC 822 gateway address mapping, which is the document's central subject.

RFC2165.title: Service Location Protocol
RFC2165.summary: RFC 2165 specifies SLP version 1, a protocol for discovering and selecting network services using User, Service and Directory Agents, scopes, service: URLs, attributes, and optional authentication of registrations.

SLP.why: The entire document defines SLP: message formats, agents, scopes, multicast discovery and configuration.
SLP.quote: The Service Location Protocol provides a scalable framework for the discovery and selection of network services.

rejected.why: DHCP is only one way to learn a Directory Agent address (options 78/79); a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
The service: URL scheme is defined, but as part of SLP rather than as a general URI topic.
Multicast is used for discovery but the document is about service location, not multicast routing.
Implied by SLP's parent; SLP is the more specific tag.
RSA/MD5 are used for authentication blocks but only as a mechanism, not the subject.
IANA is the default naming authority, but the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC2166.title: APPN Implementer's Workshop Closed Pages Document DLSw v2.0 Enhancements
RFC2166.summary: RFC 2166 defines DLSw v2.0, a set of backward-compatible scalability enhancements to RFC 1795 (IP multicast/UDP address resolution, TCP connections on demand, single-session TCP setup, HALT reason codes) plus clarifications to RFC 1795.

DLSw.why: The whole document specifies DLSw v2.0 extensions and clarifications to the DLSw v1.0 standard, so it belongs on the DLSw page.
DLSw.quote: This document defines v2.0 of Data Link Switching (DLSw) in the form of a set of enhancements to RFC 1795.

rejected.why: IP multicast is used as the transport mechanism for DLSw address resolution, but the document does not specify multicast routing or group management itself.
TCP connection setup rules (ports 2065/2067, race conditions) are defined, but only as DLSw transport usage, not TCP protocol work.
UDP is used as the carrier for SSP messages; the document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
NetBIOS frames are carried and optimized by DLSw, but the document is not about NetBIOS services; it only handles NetBIOS UI frames as DLSw traffic.
SNA is the traffic DLSw carries; the document does not specify SNA, and the DLSw tag already sits under SNA.

RFC2167.title: Referral Whois (RWhois) Protocol V1.5
RFC2167.summary: Specifies RWhois v1.5, a hierarchical, referral-based distributed directory protocol and architecture (authority areas, query routing, replication, directives) for registration-style data such as domains and IP networks.

RWhois.why: The whole document defines the RWhois protocol and architecture: referrals, authority areas, directives, replication, and error codes.
RWhois.quote: This memo describes Version 1.5 of the client/server interaction of RWhois.

rejected.why: DNS concepts and SRV records are borrowed or used for server location, but the document is not about DNS.
RWhois is a child of WHOIS and the more specific RWhois tag fits, so the parent is implied.
RWhois is described as a directory protocol, but the specific RWhois tag already sits under the WHOIS branch and covers it.
TCP is only the default transport for the protocol.
X.500 is cited as an influence only.
Server location uses referrals and DNS SRV records, not SLP.

RFC2168.title: Resolution of Uniform Resource Identifiers using the Domain Name System
RFC2168.summary: Experimental RFC defining the DNS NAPTR resource record, whose regex/replacement rewrite rules map URIs (especially URNs) to domain names to discover resolvers, used with SRV records.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS resource record type (NAPTR, type 35), its format, flags, and client lookup procedure including SRV/A follow-up and additional-section handling.
DNS.quote: It is implemented by a new DNS Resource Record, NAPTR (Naming Authority PoinTeR), that provides rules for mapping parts of URIs to domain names.

URN.why: The record is a resolver discovery service for URNs, forming the foundation of URN resolution and grandfathering other naming systems; produced by the URN working group.
URN.quote: For URNs, the prefix is always "urn:" and we extract the following colon-delimited namespace identifier

URI.why: The document specifies how URIs, including existing URLs, are rewritten into domain names to locate resolvers, so URI resolution readers would want it.
URI.quote: The start of the URI is scanned to extract its colon-delimited prefix.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a security expectation that NAPTR records will be signed; not the subject.
SRV is used to find hosts, but the document's focus is the NAPTR record and URI resolver discovery; DNS tag covers it. Considered as a parent topic.
Only listed as one resolution protocol name in the service field.
Appears only as an example resolution protocol and in a sample URL.
hdl is just one listed protocol value in the service field.
Parent of DNS and URN, implied by the chosen tags.

RFC2169.title: A Trivial Convention for using HTTP in URN Resolution
RFC2169.summary: Defines THTTP, a trivial convention for encoding URN resolution service requests (N2L, N2R, N2C, etc.) and responses as HTTP/1.0 or 1.1 GET requests, plus the text/uri-list media type.

URN.why: The document specifies a URN resolution protocol (THTTP) with services mapping URNs to URLs, resources and URCs, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: The Uniform Resource Names Working Group (URN-WG) was formed to specify persistent, location-independent names for network accessible resources, as well as resolution mechanisms

HTTP.why: The document defines a convention for using HTTP GET, status codes (302/303), Location headers and Accept negotiation for a specific application, which HTTP readers would want.
HTTP.quote: a trivial convention for encoding resolution service requests and responses as HTTP 1.0 or 1.1 requests and responses

media types.why: Appendix A defines the text/uri-list media type used for resolver results.
media types.quote: The text/uri-list Internet Media Type is defined to provide a simple format for the automatic processing of such lists of URIs.

rejected.why: The NAPTR DNS record that locates resolvers is specified in RFC 2168. This document only references it.
URIs are the input and output of resolution, but the document is about URN resolution rather than URI syntax or schemes.
The text/uri-list format is a list of URIs and does not define typed link relations.
multipart/alternative is used only for the N2Rs response and is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: URN resolution
gaps.why: The URN tag covers URN namespaces generally. A narrower tag for URN resolution services and resolver discovery would fit this document better.

RFC2170.title: Application REQuested IP over ATM (AREQUIPA)
RFC2170.summary: Informational RFC defining AREQUIPA, a host-only method letting applications request dedicated end-to-end ATM connections with QoS for IP traffic, with IPv4 and IPv6 implementations and an HTTP example.

ATM.why: The whole document defines how hosts set up application-dedicated ATM SVCs for IP, using ATMARP and ATM signalling with a BHLI. It belongs on the IP over ATM page.
ATM.quote: set up end-to-end IP over ATM connections within the reachable ATM cloud, on request from applications, and for the exclusive use by the requesting applications

QoS.why: The motivation is QoS guarantees for applications. It also discusses mapping intserv service classes to ATM traffic descriptors.
QoS.quote: This allows the requesting applications to benefit in a straightforward way from ATM's inherent ability to guarantee the quality of service (QoS).

rejected.why: The IPv6 implementation (flow labels, neighbour cache) is one section. It is a variant of the ATM mechanism and not about IPv6 itself.
HTTP is used only as an illustrative example of how applications exchange ATM addresses and ports. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Intserv is mentioned only as a possible source of service specifications to map to ATM traffic descriptors. It is not specified here.
The IPv6 neighbour cache is extended conceptually, but this is not a neighbour discovery specification.
ATMARP is extended for socket-level associations. It is a mechanism within the ATM approach and does not make the document about ARP.
The firewall bypass concern appears only in Security Considerations.

RFC2171.title: MAPOS - Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH Version 1
RFC2171.summary: RFC 2171 specifies MAPOS version 1, a multiple-access protocol that sends HDLC-framed datagrams over SONET/SDH links through frame switches, defining addressing, frame format and octet-stuffing.

MAPOS.why: The document is the core specification of MAPOS version 1, covering its address format, HDLC frame format and octet-synchronous framing.
MAPOS.quote: This document describes the protocol MAPOS, Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH, for transmitting network-protocol datagrams over SONET/SDH.

rejected.why: MAPOS is the more specific child tag and already implies SONET. The document is about MAPOS, not SONET itself.
The framing is borrowed from RFC 1662 PPP-in-HDLC-like framing, but PPP is not specified or extended here.
IPv4 over MAPOS is covered in a separate RFC (RFC 2176) and is only referenced here.
The FCS is mentioned only as a frame field, with no discussion of polynomials or error detection.
Ethernet is mentioned only as an analogy for multiple access.

RFC2172.title: MAPOS Version 1 Assigned Numbers
RFC2172.summary: Informational RFC listing the protocol field value assignments (IPv4, ARP, NSP, SSP) for MAPOS version 1, a link-layer protocol for multiple access over SONET/SDH.

MAPOS.why: The whole document is the assigned-numbers table for MAPOS version 1 protocol field values, so it belongs on the MAPOS page.
MAPOS.quote: This document describes the protocol parameters used in the Multiple Access Over SONET/SDH (MAPOS) version 1.

rejected.why: SONET/SDH is only the underlying medium MAPOS runs over; the document defines MAPOS parameters, and MAPOS is the more specific child tag.
ARP appears only as one entry in the protocol number table (MAPOS Version 1 ARP); the document does not specify ARP.
IPv4 is just one encapsulated protocol with an assigned number; nothing about IPv4 itself is specified.
HDLC-like framing for PPP is mentioned only as the basis of the frame format, not the subject.
The document is an assigned-numbers list for one protocol, but it isn't about IANA registries or their guidance.

RFC2173.title: A MAPOS version 1 Extension - Node Switch Protocol
RFC2173.summary: Informational RFC defining the Node Switch Protocol (NSP), an extension to MAPOS version 1 by which a node requests and receives its HDLC address from the SONET/SDH switch it is attached to.

MAPOS.why: The document specifies an extension to MAPOS v1 (NSP), covering address format, packet format and special cases. MAPOS tag explicitly covers its extensions.
MAPOS.quote: This document describes a MAPOS extension, Node Switch Protocol, for automatic node address assignment.

rejected.why: SONET/SDH is the underlying medium; the document is about MAPOS, the child tag, which is more specific.
HDLC framing is used, but the document does not concern PPP.
NSP performs automatic address assignment analogous to DHCP, but at the HDLC link layer, not IP.

RFC2174.title: A MAPOS version 1 Extension - Switch-Switch Protocol
RFC2174.summary: Informational RFC defining SSP, a RIP-like distance-vector routing protocol between MAPOS version 1 SONET switches, providing unicast routing and VRPB spanning-tree broadcast/multicast forwarding.

MAPOS.why: The document specifies the SSP extension to MAPOS, the switch-to-switch protocol for MAPOS networks over SONET/SDH, so it belongs on the MAPOS page.
MAPOS.quote: This document describes a MAPOS version 1 extension, SSP (Switch Switch Protocol).

rejected.why: SSP's packet format is modelled on RIP and RIPv2, but RIP is only a design basis. SSP is a separate protocol.
The document covers broadcast/multicast forwarding via VRPB, but only inside MAPOS switch segments. It is not IP multicast routing, and the MAPOS tag already captures it.
SONET/SDH is the underlying medium. MAPOS is the more specific child tag and is the one that applies.
The document specifies a particular routing protocol, not general routing architecture principles.

gaps.name: SSP (Switch Switch Protocol) / VRPB
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for link-layer switch routing. MAPOS covers it, but a generic tag for distance-vector or spanning-tree switch routing would be useful.

RFC2175.title: MAPOS 16 - Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH with 16 Bit Addressing
RFC2175.summary: Informational RFC defining MAPOS 16, a variant of MAPOS that carries HDLC-framed datagrams over SONET/SDH with a 16-bit address field, including frame format, address layout, and IP multicast address mapping.

MAPOS.why: The document specifies MAPOS 16, the 16-bit addressing variant of MAPOS. It defines the frame and address formats and how the MAPOS protocol family (ARP, NSP, SSP) is affected.
MAPOS.quote: MAPOS 16, a multiple access protocol for transmission of network-protocol datagrams, encapsulated in HDLC frames with 16 bit addressing, over SONET/SDH.

rejected.why: The framing is based on RFC 1662 HDLC-like framing, but PPP is only referenced as the basis for the frame format. The document does not specify PPP.
SONET/SDH is the underlying medium. MAPOS is the more specific child tag, so SONET is implied and not listed separately.
MAPOS ARP is mentioned only to say it needs no change beyond placing the 16-bit address in its 32-bit field. The document is not about ARP.
Section 5 maps IP multicast addresses to MAPOS 16 addresses. This is a short framing detail, not a substantial treatment of multicast routing.
The FCS field is described only briefly as 16 or 32 bits. The document does not deal with CRC polynomials.

RFC2176.title: IPv4 over MAPOS Version 1
RFC2176.summary: Informational RFC specifying how IPv4 datagrams are encapsulated in MAPOS version 1 HDLC frames, including MAPOS ARP, UNARP, cache validation, and broadcast/multicast address mapping.

MAPOS.why: The whole document defines IPv4 over MAPOS v1: frame format, ARP, UNARP, and broadcast/multicast mapping. MAPOS is the specific technology covered.
MAPOS.quote: This document describes a protocol for transmission of IP datagrams over MAPOS version 1 [1]. It explains IP datagram encapsulation in HDLC frame of MAPOS

ARP.why: A substantial part of the document defines a MAPOS-specific ARP packet format, the UNARP mechanism and ARP cache validation.
ARP.quote: The MAPOS ARP is similar to that for ethernet.  Prior to sending an IP datagram, the node must know the destination HDLC address

rejected.why: MAPOS is the child tag under SONET and fits more specifically. SONET/SDH is only the underlying link.
The document only describes carrying IPv4 over a link layer. It does not specify IPv4 itself.
Path MTU discovery is mentioned only in passing as an option for dealing with the large MTU.
The IP multicast to HDLC address mapping is a short section on link-layer address mapping, not a multicast routing or deployment topic.
The HDLC-like framing of PPP is only the basis of the MAPOS frame format. The document does not specify PPP.

RFC2177.title: IMAP4 IDLE command
RFC2177.summary: Defines the IMAP4 IDLE command, which lets a client tell the server it is ready to receive real-time unsolicited mailbox updates instead of polling.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 with a new IDLE command, its capability, semantics and formal syntax, so readers of the IMAP subject need it.
IMAP.quote: This document specifies the syntax of an IDLE command, which will allow a client to tell the server that it's ready to accept such real-time updates.

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag; email is implied as its ancestor.
The formal syntax uses BNF notation only as a notation; the document is not about it.
Document concerns mailbox access protocol commands, not message headers or format.

RFC2178.title: OSPF Version 2
RFC2178.summary: RFC 2178 specifies OSPF version 2, a link-state interior gateway routing protocol with areas, flooding, DR election, LSAs, authentication, and routing table calculation, obsoleting RFC 1583.

OSPF.why: The entire document is the OSPFv2 protocol specification.
OSPF.quote: This memo documents version 2 of the OSPF protocol. OSPF is a link-state routing protocol.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a source of external routes; not specified here.
Equal-cost multipath is a brief feature of OSPF, not the document's subject.
This is OSPF for IPv4 (version 2), not the IPv6 version.
Mentioned only in the history section.
Mentioned only in passing as a multicast extension.

RFC2179.title: Network Security For Trade Shows
RFC2179.summary: An informational checklist of simple host, service and router packet-filtering security measures for exhibitors on trade show networks such as Networld+Interop.

operational security.why: The whole document is practical operational security guidance for hardening hosts, services and network edges at trade shows, which fits operational security practices.
operational security.quote: its purpose is to provide a checklist-style collection of frequently overlooked, simple ways to minimize the chance of a costly attack.

firewall.why: A substantial section gives an ordered packet-filter ruleset (anti-spoofing, deny-by-default, port rules) for a boundary router, which is firewall guidance.
firewall.quote: Many routers support basic packet filtering. If a router can be deployed between the local network and the show's network, general basic packet filtering should be employed.

rejected.why: SSH is recommended as one tool for encrypted access, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
Anonymous FTP hardening tips are only one of many checklist items; the document is not about FTP.
NFS export security is one checklist item, not a main subject.
Authentication tokens producing one-time passwords are recommended briefly, but the document does not address OTP systems in their own right.
BIND is mentioned only as software to keep updated and DNS ports appear in the filter rules.
The more specific operational security tag fits better than the general security parent.

RFC2180.title: IMAP4 Multi-Accessed Mailbox Practice
RFC2180.summary: Informational RFC documenting common IMAP4 server practice for handling deletion, renaming, expunging, fetching, storing, searching and copying when multiple clients access the same mailbox simultaneously.

IMAP.why: The whole document describes allowed IMAP4 server behaviours and client responsibilities for multi-accessed mailboxes (DELETE, RENAME, EXPUNGE, FETCH, STORE, COPY), so it is about IMAP.
IMAP.quote: By documenting common IMAP4 server practice for the case of simultaneous client access to a mailbox, we hope to ensure the widest amount of inter-operation

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag; the document concerns IMAP mailbox access behaviour, not email architecture generally.
FETCH response examples show envelope and RFC822 data, but the document does not address message format.

RFC2181.title: Clarifications to the DNS Specification
RFC2181.summary: RFC 2181 clarifies several ambiguous areas of the DNS specification: reply source address selection, RRSet and TTL rules, zone cuts, SOA details, TTL range, the TC bit, CNAME/canonical name issues and label syntax.

DNS.why: The whole document updates RFC 1034/1035 and clarifies core DNS protocol behaviour for servers, resolvers and resource records.
DNS.quote: This document considers some areas that have been identified as problems with the specification of the Domain Name System, and proposes remedies for the defects identified.

rejected.why: DNSSEC (SIG/NXT/KEY) is handled only as special cases in sections 5.3 and 6.2. The document says it is mostly orthogonal and not about security.
UDP source address and port selection is a DNS server behaviour, not a UDP specification.
TCP is mentioned only as the fallback after a truncated reply.
Section 11 on name syntax concerns DNS label rules, not host naming conventions.

RFC2182.title: Selection and Operation of Secondary DNS Servers
RFC2182.summary: BCP guidance on choosing, placing, counting and maintaining secondary DNS servers for a zone, including reachability of listed NS servers, stealth servers, and SOA serial number maintenance.

DNS.why: The whole document is operational guidance for DNS authoritative servers: secondary placement, number of NS records, stealth servers, unreachable servers and SOA serial number handling.
DNS.quote: The Domain Name System requires that multiple servers exist for every delegated domain (zone). This document discusses the selection of secondary servers for DNS zones.

rejected.why: NAT is mentioned only briefly as a problem case for listing unreachable servers; the document is not about NAT.
Firewalls appear as a cause of unreachable servers and split DNS setups, but only as a side issue within DNS operations.
Not mentioned; geographic and topological dispersion is achieved by separate servers, not anycast.
The document concerns reliability and availability of DNS service, not security practices; the Security Considerations is minimal.

RFC2183.title: Communicating Presentation Information in Internet Messages: The Content-Disposition Header Field
RFC2183.summary: Defines the MIME Content-Disposition header field (inline/attachment types and filename, date and size parameters) for conveying presentation information, with an IANA registration procedure for new values and parameters.

MIME.why: The document is an extension to MIME defining a new header field for MIME entities and body parts, and how it applies to multipart structures.
MIME.quote: It specifies the "Content-Disposition" header field, which is optional and valid for any MIME entity ("message" or "body part").

rejected.why: Content-Disposition is a header field, but the document is a MIME extension concerned with body-part presentation rather than RFC 822 message format in general.
Email is the substrate carrying MIME messages. The document is about MIME body-part presentation, not mail architecture or transport.
The document registers no media types. It only establishes a registry procedure for Content-Disposition parameters.
The registration section is boilerplate-like and covers only this header's parameters. It is not about IANA guidance in general.

RFC2184.title: MIME Parameter Value and Encoded Word Extensions: Character Sets, Languages, and Continuations
RFC2184.summary: RFC 2184 extends MIME Content-Type/Content-Disposition parameter values with character set, language, and continuation mechanisms, and extends RFC 2047 encoded words with language tags.

MIME.why: The document extends MIME parameter value syntax (RFC 2045/2183) with continuations and charset/language encoding, and updates MIME ABNF.
MIME.quote: a continuation mechanism for long parameter values to avoid problems with header line wrapping

message format.why: Extends RFC 2047 encoded words in message headers (e.g., From:) with language tags and addresses RFC 822 header folding issues.
message format.quote: This memo also defines an extension to the encoded words defined in RFC 2047 to allow the specification of the language

language tags.why: Defines how language tags are attached to parameter values and encoded words for display.
language tags.quote: suffixing the character set specification with an asterisk followed by the language tag

character sets.why: A core goal is carrying non-ASCII character sets in parameter values and encoded words, with charset labelling.
character sets.quote: a means to specify parameter values in character sets other than US-ASCII

rejected.why: Parent of the more specific MIME/message format tags; implied, not listed separately.
Only a one-sentence note that IMAP4 servers should decode continuations in BODYSTRUCTURE; not the document's subject.
The document concerns parameter syntax for media type parameters generally, not media type registration or registry rules.
Parent topic; the more specific language tags and character sets tags already cover it.
The document modifies ABNF for MIME but only as a notation for its own spec.

RFC2185.title: Routing Aspects of IPv6 Transition
RFC2185.summary: Informational overview of routing issues in IPv4-to-IPv6 transition: dual-IP-layer routing, manually configured tunnels, automatic tunneling, and route leaking between IPv4-only and IPv6 regions.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document addresses coexistence of IPv4 and IPv6 and the routing needed for dual-stack and tunnelling transition mechanisms.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document gives an overview of the routing aspects of IPv4 to IPv6 transition.

tunneling.why: A substantial part covers manual and automatic tunnels (host-to-host, host-to-router, router-to-host) and how routing must be consistent with encapsulation.
tunneling.quote: Static point-to-point tunnels may also be established between a host and a router, or between two hosts.

rejected.why: OSPF and RIP are mentioned only as examples of protocols that could run two instances; the document does not specify them.
The document is about transition routing specifically, which fits IPv6 transition better than general routing architecture.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag covers the subject; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
DNS support is only mentioned in passing and deferred to RFC 1933.

RFC2186.title: Internet Cache Protocol (ICP), version 2
RFC2186.summary: RFC 2186 specifies the message format, opcodes and option flags of ICPv2, a lightweight UDP-based protocol that Web caches use to query neighbor caches for hits and misses.

HTTP caching.why: The whole document defines ICP, the protocol Web proxy caches use to locate objects in neighbor caches and choose where to fetch them. This is web caching.
HTTP caching.quote: ICP is a lightweight message format used for communicating among Web caches.

rejected.why: ICP is implemented over UDP, but UDP is only the substrate. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
Caches use HTTP to transfer the object data, but the document specifies ICP messages, not HTTP semantics.
URLs appear in the payload, but the document does not address URI syntax or schemes.

RFC2187.title: Application of Internet Cache Protocol (ICP), version 2
RFC2187.summary: Informational RFC describing how ICPv2 is applied in Web cache hierarchies (Harvest/Squid): configuration, query/reply processing, firewalls, multicast, lessons learned, and security issues.

HTTP caching.why: ICP is a protocol among Web caches for locating cached objects in neighbor caches and building cache hierarchies; the whole document is about its application to Web caching.
HTTP caching.quote: ICP is a lightweight message format used for communicating among Web caches.

multicast.why: A dedicated section covers multicast ICP: unicast-only replies, TTL scoping, trust, and estimating the number of expected replies.
multicast.quote: a cache may deliver ICP queries to a multicast address, and neighbor caches may join the multicast group to receive such queries.

rejected.why: HTTP is the traffic whose objects are located; the document discusses differences from HTTP but does not specify or extend it.
UDP is only the transport for ICP; nothing new is defined about its use.
AH and ESP are mentioned only as a possible mitigation in the Security Considerations.
The firewall section covers cache behaviour behind firewalls, not firewall security or middlebox traversal.
The security analysis is boilerplate-level Security Considerations for ICP, not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Internet Cache Protocol (ICP)
gaps.why: The document is about ICP itself, but the taxonomy has no ICP tag. HTTP caching is the closest fit, though ICP is a separate inter-cache protocol.

RFC2188.title: AT&T/Neda's Efficient Short Remote Operations (ESRO) Protocol Specification Version 1.2
RFC2188.summary: Specifies ESRO, a lightweight remote-operation (RPC-like) service and protocol giving reliable connectionless operation delivery over UDP, with 2-way and 3-way handshake modes, segmentation/reassembly, concatenation, and an ASN.1-macro notation, designed for wireless networks such as CDPD.

transport.why: The document defines a new reliable, connectionless request/response transport-layer protocol with retransmission timers, handshakes, segmentation and multiplexing. No specific transport child tag fits, so the parent topic is used.
transport.quote: ESRO protocol provides reliable connectionless remote operation services on top of UDP (or any other non-reliable connectionless transport service) with minimum overhead.

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate (port 259) carrying ESRO PDUs. The document defines no new UDP usage guidance.
Only compared with ESRO in section 1.1.1. ESRO is a different protocol and is not an extension or profile of ONC RPC.
ASN.1 macros define the operation notation, and BER/PER are named as encoding tags. The document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules, and encoding is explicitly out of scope.
CDPD is the motivating wireless network, but the document is not about IP over cellular systems.
IRTP is a similar historic transaction protocol, but ESRO is a distinct protocol and not IRTP.

gaps.name: Remote Operations / Remote Procedure Call
gaps.why: ESRO is a remote operation service (ROSE/RPC-like), and the taxonomy has no generic RPC or remote-operations tag. Only ONC RPC exists, and it is specific to Sun RPC.

RFC2189.title: Core Based Trees (CBT version 2) Multicast Routing -- Protocol Specification --
RFC2189.summary: Specifies CBT version 2, a shared-tree multicast routing protocol with core routers, join/ack/quit/echo/flush control messages, DR election via HELLO, and core discovery via bootstrap or static configuration.

multicast.why: The document specifies a multicast routing protocol (CBT). No more specific multicast child tag (PIM, IGMP, etc.) covers CBT, so the parent topic is used.
multicast.quote: CBT builds a shared multicast distribution tree per group, and is suited to inter- and intra-domain multicast routing.

rejected.why: IGMP host membership reports only trigger CBT joins. The document does not specify or extend IGMP.
The PIM bootstrap mechanism is referenced for core discovery, but the document is not about PIM.
IP-in-IP encapsulation is used for non-member sending. It is only a mechanism here and is not defined or extended.
Multicast security is mentioned only in Security Considerations, which does not count as evidence.
The architecture is in a separate document (RFC 2201). This one is the protocol specification.

gaps.name: Core Based Trees (CBT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CBT tech tag under multicast, so the parent topic is used.

RFC2190.title: RTP Payload Format for H.263 Video Streams
RFC2190.summary: Specifies how an H.263 video bitstream is packetized in RTP, defining three payload header modes (A, B, C) for GOB- and macroblock-boundary fragmentation.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format for a specific video codec (H.263), defining payload header modes and RTP header field usage.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for encapsulating an H.263 bitstream in the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP).

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the child tag RTP payload format is the more specific fit and implies RTP.
H.263 is the codec carried, but the document does not define the codec; it only specifies its RTP packetization. No H.263 tag exists, and the RTP payload format tag covers it.
Different codec (H.264/AVC); H.263 is a predecessor and not covered by this tag.
UDP is only mentioned as underlying transport, not specified or extended.
Not addressed; only packet loss resilience in packetization design is discussed.

gaps.name: H.263 video codec
gaps.why: The document is about packetizing H.263 video, but the taxonomy has no H.263 tag under codecs; readers browsing for H.263 would expect to find it.

RFC2191.title: VENUS - Very Extensive Non-Unicast Service
RFC2191.summary: Informational memo analysing a hypothetical multicast shortcut service (VENUS) that would extend the MARS model for IP multicast over ATM across multiple clusters/LISes, showing its complexity and similarity to a large distributed MARS cluster.

ATM.why: The whole document concerns IP multicast over ATM: MARS clusters, pt-mpt SVCs, LIS boundaries and shortcut connections, so the ATM and IP over ATM subject is the best fit.
ATM.quote: The MARS model (RFC2022) provides a solution to intra-LIS IP multicasting over ATM, establishing and managing the use of ATM pt-mpt SVCs

multicast.why: The document examines IP multicast group membership, Mrouters, IDMR interaction and multicast forwarding trees in depth, so multicast readers would want it.
multicast.quote: A second problem is the impact that shortcut connections will have on IP level Inter Domain Multicast Routing (IDMR) protocols.

rejected.why: NHRP is cited only as the unicast analogy motivating a multicast equivalent; the document does not specify or extend it.
Inter-domain multicast routing impact is discussed, but it is deferred to future analysis and is covered better by multicast.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server)
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about extending the MARS model (RFC 2022) for IP multicast over ATM, and the taxonomy has no MARS tag.

RFC2192.title: IMAP URL Scheme
RFC2192.summary: Defines the imap URL scheme for referencing IMAP servers, mailbox lists, mailboxes, searches, messages and MIME parts, including authentication, relative URLs, and mailbox name encoding.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme (imap://), its syntax, ABNF and relative URL resolution.
URI.quote: This document defines a URL scheme for referencing objects on an IMAP server.

IMAP.why: The scheme maps URLs onto IMAP commands (SELECT, UID FETCH, SEARCH, LIST, LOGIN/AUTHENTICATE), so IMAP readers would want it.
IMAP.quote: The IMAP URL scheme is used to designate IMAP servers, mailboxes, messages, MIME bodies [MIME], and search programs on Internet hosts

rejected.why: MIME body parts are addressable, but MIME is only the object structure being referenced, not what the document specifies.
Mailbox names are converted from modified UTF-7 to UTF-8, but this is a small section and not the document's subject.
Authentication mechanisms are referenced via ;AUTH=, but the document does not specify SASL.
Content-Base/Content-Location are only cited for relative URL base determination.

RFC2193.title: IMAP4 Mailbox Referrals
RFC2193.summary: Defines the IMAP4 MAILBOX-REFERRALS extension, which lets a server return a REFERRAL response code containing IMAP URLs so clients can reach mailboxes on other servers, and adds the RLIST and RLSUB commands.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 with a capability, a REFERRAL response code, and the RLIST/RLSUB commands. It is squarely an IMAP extension.
IMAP.quote: IMAP4 servers that support this extension MUST list the keyword MAILBOX-REFERRALS in their CAPABILITY response.

rejected.why: The referrals carry IMAP URLs defined in RFC 2192, but this document defines no new URI scheme. URLs are only the payload of the referral.
IMAP is an email access protocol, but the more specific IMAP tag already covers this document.
Referrals resemble LDAP-style referrals, but the document is about mailbox access and not directory services.
The formal syntax uses ABNF, but only as notation. The document is not about ABNF.

RFC2194.title: Review of Roaming Implementations
RFC2194.summary: Informational review of existing ISP roaming implementations (GRIC, i-Pass, ChinaNet, Microsoft/MSN, Merit, FidoNet), describing phone book handling, distributed authentication, RADIUS/TACACS+ proxying, and accounting/settlement.

RADIUS.why: Most of the reviewed implementations (ChinaNet, Microsoft, Merit, i-Pass, GRIC) use RADIUS proxying with realm-based routing, and the document analyses attribute conflicts and accounting records. This is a substantial part of the review.
RADIUS.quote: The roaming system was developed by AsiaInfo, and is based on the RADIUS protocol.

AAA.why: The document reviews distributed authentication, NAS authorization and accounting/settlement among roaming ISPs. It is a survey of AAA architectures for roaming.
AAA.quote: Merit operates a set of Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) servers supporting the RADIUS protocol which are called core servers.

rejected.why: TACACS+ is supported by some products, but it is mentioned only as an alternative interface and is not analysed.
PPP and SLIP are the dial-up substrate for connection management and are not specified or analysed.
DNS SRV records are suggested only as a possible future scalability option, and the FidoNet DNS proposal is mentioned in passing.
HTTP GET is used only as the transport for phone book updates.
i-Pass uses SSL to protect transactions, but only as a security mechanism.
FTP is used for accounting record transfer and phone book download, only as a substrate.

gaps.name: roaming / ISP roaming (roamops)
gaps.why: The whole document is about dial-up roaming among ISPs, including phone book exchange, settlement and shared-use networks. The taxonomy has no roaming tag.

RFC2195.title: IMAP/POP AUTHorize Extension for Simple Challenge/Response
RFC2195.summary: Defines CRAM-MD5, a challenge-response authentication mechanism using keyed MD5 for IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE (and in principle POP3 AUTH), avoiding cleartext passwords on the network.

SASL.why: The document specifies a new SASL-style authentication mechanism (CRAM-MD5) plugged into the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE and POP3 AUTH extensible frameworks.
SASL.quote: The authentication type associated with CRAM is "CRAM-MD5".

IMAP.why: The mechanism is an extension to IMAP4 authentication, with examples using the IMAP AUTHENTICATE command; IMAP readers would want it.
IMAP.quote: This specification provides a simple challenge-response authentication protocol that is suitable for use with IMAP4.

POP3.why: Positioned as an alternative to POP3 APOP and usable with the POP3 AUTH command.
POP3.quote: it may also constitute an improvement on APOP for POP3 use as specified in RFC 1734.

rejected.why: Keyed-MD5 (HMAC) is the primitive used, but the document does not define or analyse it.
MD5 is the underlying digest; the document is about the authentication mechanism, not MD5 itself.
Parent topic; the more specific SASL tag fits.
Parent of IMAP/POP3, implied by the specific tags.

RFC2196.title: Site Security Handbook
RFC2196.summary: RFC 2196 (FYI 8) is a handbook guiding site administrators in developing security policies, architecture, security services and procedures, and security incident handling for Internet-connected sites.

operational security.why: The document is a practical guide to operational security practices for site infrastructure: network and service configuration, firewalls, modems, auditing, backups.
operational security.quote: The purpose of this handbook is to provide practical guidance to administrators trying to secure their information and services.

incident response.why: Chapter 5 is a substantial treatment of incident handling: preparation, notification, containment, eradication, recovery and follow-up.
incident response.quote: This chapter of the document will supply guidance to be used before, during, and after a computer security incident occurs

user guides.why: It is an FYI-series (FYI 8) introductory guide for administrators and decision makers rather than a protocol specification.
user guides.quote: This document provides guidance to system and network administrators on how to address security issues within the Internet community.

firewall.why: A dedicated section covers firewall architecture: filtering routers, bastion hosts, proxy servers and application layer gateways.
firewall.quote: A firewall is any one of several mechanisms used to control and watch access to and from a network for the purpose of protecting it.

rejected.why: The general security topic is the parent of the more specific tags chosen, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Section 4.1 covers passwords, one-time passwords and Kerberos, but only as one part of a broad handbook.
It is described briefly in one subsection as an authentication option; the document is not about Kerberos.
DNS appears only as one service whose security needs protecting, in a short paragraph.
Privacy comes up as a policy and legal consideration, not as protocol privacy analysis.
Although the document came from a working group, its content is not about IETF procedures.

gaps.name: Site security policy and risk assessment
gaps.why: Chapters 1 and 2 deal with security policy formation and risk analysis, which the taxonomy has no specific tag for beyond general security.

RFC2197.title: SMTP Service Extension for Command Pipelining
RFC2197.summary: RFC 2197 defines the SMTP PIPELINING service extension, letting a server advertise via EHLO that it accepts batched commands in a single TCP send, and specifies client and server rules for pipelining.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension (PIPELINING), including EHLO keyword, client batching rules and server requirements.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby a server can indicate the extent of its ability to accept multiple commands in a single TCP send operation.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate; the document mentions send operations and window size but does not extend or analyse TCP.
The parent tag is implied by the more specific SMTP tag.

RFC2198.title: RTP Payload for Redundant Audio Data
RFC2198.summary: Defines an RTP payload format ("red") that encapsulates a primary audio encoding plus one or more redundant encodings in a single packet, to recover from packet loss, with SDP bindings.

RTP payload format.why: The RFC specifies a new RTP payload format (block headers with PT, timestamp offset, length) for redundant audio, which is exactly the subject of RTP payload formats.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for the transmission of audio data encoded in such a redundant fashion.

FEC.why: The scheme is a loss-recovery mechanism using redundancy for packet audio, so readers interested in loss recovery schemes would want it.
FEC.quote: If a packet is lost then the missing information may be reconstructed at the receiver from the redundant data that arrives in the following packet(s)

SDP.why: A section defines how the redundancy format is signalled in SDP using rtpmap and a format-specific fmtp parameter list.
SDP.quote: SDP has a mechanism for binding a dynamic payload types to particular codec, sample rate, and number of channels using the "rtpmap" attribute.

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the more specific child RTP payload format is chosen and its ancestor is implied.
The document uses PCM, DVI and LPC as example encodings but does not define any codec.
Security considerations only mention generic encryption of RTP streams, which is boilerplate and not about SRTP.
Congestion effects of redundancy are mentioned only briefly in Security Considerations.

RFC2199.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 2100-2199
RFC2199.summary: An annotated index of the 100 RFCs numbered 2100 through 2199, giving each one's author, date, title, short abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The document is a catalog of a block of the RFC series and reports on the status of those RFCs. It is about the series itself, not about any protocol inside it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2100 through RFCs 2199.

rejected.why: DNS RFCs such as 2181, 2182 and 2136 appear only as one-paragraph entries in the list. The document does not address DNS.
Many mail-related RFCs (SMTP, IMAP, MIME, X.400) are listed. The memo is a summary of RFCs, not about email, and tagging each subject would turn this index into a catch-all.
The memo mentions standards-track status only to label the entries. It does not discuss the standards process.
Several MAPOS RFCs are listed among the 100 entries, but the document is not about MAPOS.

RFC2200.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2200.summary: RFC 2200 is the quarterly IAB snapshot (STD 1) of Internet standardization: it explains the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and lists every protocol RFC by state (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Informational, Historic).

IETF process.why: The document's main body explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels, IESG recommendation and minimum delays, i.e. the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: Describes the RFC series, how RFCs are submitted and published by the RFC Editor, and the RFC processing decision table. It also serves as the reference for the current RFC on each protocol.
RFC series.quote: The documents called Request for Comments (or RFCs) are the working notes of the "Network Working Group"

rejected.why: IANA is only a contact and a pointer to Assigned Numbers. The document is not about IANA registries.
Published by the IAB, but the content is standards status bookkeeping, not architectural principles.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but this is part of the standards-process explanation, not a glossary.
It is a point-in-time status list, not a history or retrospective, even though it now has historical value.
SNMP and many other protocols appear only as rows in the status lists. The document is not about any of them.

RFC2201.title: Core Based Trees (CBT) Multicast Routing Architecture
RFC2201.summary: Describes the Core Based Trees (CBT) shared-tree multicast routing architecture, motivating it against source-based tree algorithms (DVMRP, MOSPF) on scalability grounds and outlining its components, join/maintenance mechanisms, and core discovery.

multicast.why: The whole document is an architecture for IP multicast routing using shared trees, compared against source-based multicast algorithms. No more specific taxonomy tag covers CBT itself, so the parent multicast topic fits.
multicast.quote: CBT is a multicast routing architecture that builds a single delivery tree per group which is shared by all of the group's senders and receivers.

rejected.why: PIM-SM is referenced only as a comparison and for its bootstrap mechanism; the document is not about it.
IGMP is the host-to-router membership mechanism CBT relies on, not something the document specifies or extends.
Mentioned only as an example of a link-state source-based tree algorithm in the background discussion.
PIM-DM and PIM-SM are cited only as points of comparison.
The Security Considerations section only cites a few references and says security is not addressed, so the body is not about it.
IP-in-IP encapsulation is only the mechanism used to send non-member sender data to the core.

gaps.name: Core Based Trees (CBT)
gaps.why: No technology tag exists for CBT itself, the shared-tree multicast routing protocol and architecture, so it can only be placed under the generic multicast topic.

RFC2202.title: Test Cases for HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1
RFC2202.summary: Informational RFC providing conformance test vectors (keys, data, digests) and reference C code for HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 implementations.

HMAC.why: The whole document is test vectors and reference code for the HMAC construction with MD5 and SHA-1, so it belongs on the HMAC page.
HMAC.quote: The test cases and results provided in this document are meant to be used as a conformance test for HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 implementations.

rejected.why: MD5 is only the hash function used inside HMAC-MD5. The document gives no test vectors for MD5 itself.
SHA-1 is only the underlying hash in HMAC-SHA-1. The document does not specify or test SHA itself.
IPsec is mentioned only as a user of these constructs, in the Abstract and references. The document does not address IPsec.

RFC2203.title: RPCSEC_GSS Protocol Specification
RFC2203.summary: RFC 2203 specifies the RPCSEC_GSS ONC RPC security flavor, which lets RPC protocols use GSS-API for context setup, per-request authentication, integrity and privacy protection, and context destruction.

ONC RPC.why: The document defines a new ONC RPC security flavor (flavor 6), new auth_stat values, and the credential/verifier formats carried in RPC messages. It is an extension of ONC RPC.
ONC RPC.quote: This memo describes an ONC/RPC security flavor that allows RPC protocols to access the Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface

GSS-API.why: The protocol maps context creation, GetMIC/VerifyMIC and Wrap/Unwrap onto RPC exchanges, and it defines GSS-API major status code values in Appendix A. GSS-API readers would want it.
GSS-API.quote: The RPCSEC_GSS security flavor uses GSS-API interfaces to provide security services that are independent of the underlying security mechanism.

rejected.why: Kerberos V5 is mentioned only as an example mechanism. The protocol is mechanism-independent.
The more specific GSS-API tag covers the security content.
The topic is covered by the more specific GSS-API and ONC RPC tags.
A network filing protocol is mentioned only as a hypothetical example of an application that would reference RPCSEC_GSS.

RFC2204.title: ODETTE File Transfer Protocol
RFC2204.summary: Describes the ODETTE File Transfer Protocol (OFTP), an EDI-oriented file transfer protocol from the European motor industry, adapted to run over TCP with a Stream Transmission Header, including service primitives, commands, buffer formats and state machines.

EDI.why: The protocol exists to carry EDI between trading partners (direct or via clearing centres), and is specified in full over TCP/IP, so it belongs under EDI over Internet transports.
EDI.quote: This memo describes a file transfer protocol to facilitate electronic data interchange between trading partners.

FTP.why: It is a file transfer protocol with its own sessions, virtual files, restart and commands. It is a distinct protocol rather than the Internet FTP, but readers of file transfer protocols would want it.
FTP.quote: The ODETTE File Transfer Protocol (ODETTE-FTP) was defined in 1986 by working group four

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport substrate. The Stream Transmission Header is framing within ODETTE-FTP, not a TCP extension.
The original network service was X.25, but this memo specifies the TCP mapping and does not cover X.25 itself.
Section 2 and Section 7 map OFTP onto TCP, but this is a small part of a full protocol specification.
The protocol is modelled on OSI layers, but it does not concern OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC2205.title: Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) -- Version 1 Functional Specification
RFC2205.summary: RFC 2205 specifies RSVP version 1, a receiver-initiated resource reservation setup protocol for unicast and multicast flows in an integrated services Internet, covering messages, objects, soft state, merging, styles, errors and interfaces.

RSVP.why: The document is the functional specification of RSVP itself: message formats, objects, state handling, error codes, and UDP encapsulation.
RSVP.quote: This memo describes version 1 of RSVP, a resource reservation setup protocol designed for an integrated services Internet.

rejected.why: RSVP carries flowspecs, Tspecs and Adspecs opaquely; their contents are defined in the Integrated Services documents (RFC 2210), not here.
RSVP works alongside multicast routing and IGMP and handles merging across multicast trees, but it is not a multicast routing or group membership protocol.
Appendix C defines UDP encapsulation only for hosts without raw I/O; UDP is a substrate, not the subject.
RSVP uses the Router Alert IP option on some messages but does not define or extend it.
IPsec data flows are mentioned and deferred to RFC 2207; this document does not specify them.

RFC2206.title: RSVP Management Information Base using SMIv2
RFC2206.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module for managing RSVP (sessions, senders, reservations, interfaces, neighbors, and flow notifications), tied to the Integrated Services MIB.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module (RSVP-MIB) defined in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) within the interface attributes defined in the Integrated Services Model

RSVP.why: The MIB models RSVP protocol state (PATH/RESV state, refresh timers, neighbors, interfaces) for management of RSVP.
RSVP.quote: The MIB module to describe the RSVP Protocol

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through; the document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the more specific MIB tag.
The MIB cross-references and requires the Integrated Services MIB, but it specifies RSVP objects, not Integrated Services itself.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB module.
IPv6 sessions are mentioned only in object syntax and descriptions, not as a subject of the document.

RFC2207.title: RSVP Extensions for IPSEC Data Flows
RFC2207.summary: Extends RSVP v1 with new GPI SESSION, FILTER_SPEC and SENDER_TEMPLATE objects that use the IPsec SPI and a virtual destination port, so individual AH/ESP data flows can be reserved per flow.

RSVP.why: The document defines new RSVP objects (GPI SESSION, FILTER_SPEC, SENDER_TEMPLATE) and processing rules, extending RSVP.
RSVP.quote: These extensions permit support of individual data flows using RFC 1826, IP Authentication Header (AH) or RFC 1827, IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

ESP.why: The extension is built around identifying AH and ESP flows by SPI. This makes IPsec and ESP a substantial part of the subject, though the IPsec protocols themselves are unchanged.
ESP.quote: The data classifier will need to look for the four byte GPI at transport header offset +4 for AH, and at transport header offset +0 for ESP.

rejected.why: IPsec is the kind of traffic being classified. The document explicitly leaves RFC 1826/1827 unchanged, so ESP is the closer fit and IPsec is not tagged separately.
The extensions support both IPv4 and IPv6 objects, but IPv6 is not the subject.
RSVP sits under QoS and is the more specific tag.

RFC2208.title: Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) -- Version 1 Applicability Statement Some Guidelines on Deployment
RFC2208.summary: Applicability statement giving guidelines on deploying RSVP with the Integrated Services specifications, covering scalability, security, and policy control limits and recommending intranet/limited-ISP use.

RSVP.why: The whole document is about where RSVP is applicable and how to deploy it, including scalability, security and policy control.
RSVP.quote: RSVP [RFC 2205] is a unicast and multicast signalling protocol, designed to install and maintain reservation state information at each router along the path

Intserv.why: The document treats RSVP and the integrated services specifications together as one deployable package, so Intserv readers would want it.
Intserv.quote: The state handled by RSVP is defined by services [RFC 2211] and [RFC 2212] specified by the Integrated Services WG.

rejected.why: RFC 2207 on IPsec data flows is mentioned only briefly. The document is not about IPsec.
Hop-by-hop MD5 integrity is mentioned in passing as part of RSVP authentication, not as a subject of the document.
Policy control is discussed in general terms, and COPS is never mentioned.
A parent of RSVP and Intserv, so it is implied and not listed separately.
SNA/DLSw is named only as a likely beneficiary application, not as a subject.
The RSVP MIB (RFC 2206) is cited only for its newFlow trap, as a precaution against theft of service.

RFC2209.title: Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) -- Version 1 Message Processing Rules
RFC2209.summary: Informational memo giving an algorithmic description of RSVP version 1 message processing rules (PATH, RESV, teardown, error, confirm messages, state blocks, traffic control updates and refreshes) to clarify RFC 2205.

RSVP.why: The whole document specifies RSVP message processing rules, state blocks (PSB, RSB, TCSB, BSB), refresh and teardown sequences.
RSVP.quote: This memo contains an algorithmic description of the rules used by an RSVP implementation for processing messages.

rejected.why: The flowspecs and traffic control calls are Intserv-related, but the document is about RSVP processing, not Integrated Services models.
Implied as the parent of RSVP; the document is about the RSVP protocol itself, so the specific tag suffices.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations regarding future modifications for RFC 2207; boilerplate-level.
Multicast routing is referenced for route queries and shared-tree handling, but the document is not about multicast.

RFC2210.title: The Use of RSVP with IETF Integrated Services
RFC2210.summary: Specifies how RSVP carries Integrated Services data, defining the usage and wire formats of the SENDER_TSPEC, FLOWSPEC and ADSPEC objects for Controlled-Load and Guaranteed services, including path MTU negotiation.

RSVP.why: The document specifies how RSVP objects are used and formatted, an extension and profile of RSVP.
RSVP.quote: It defines the usage and contents of three RSVP protocol objects, the FLOWSPEC, ADSPEC, and SENDER_TSPEC

Intserv.why: It defines how the integrated services framework's Controlled-Load and Guaranteed services are invoked, including TSpec/RSpec and ADSPEC characterization parameters.
Intserv.quote: This note describes the use of the RSVP resource reservation protocol with the Controlled-Load and Guaranteed QoS control services.

rejected.why: Parent topic of RSVP and Intserv, which are the more specific tags chosen.
The MTU negotiation here is a scheme within RSVP ADSPEC, not the general Path MTU Discovery mechanism.
XDR is used only as an encoding for the object fields, so it is substrate rather than subject.

RFC2211.title: Specification of the Controlled-Load Network Element Service
RFC2211.summary: Specifies the network element behavior required to deliver Controlled-Load service, an Integrated Services QoS class approximating unloaded best-effort service through admission control, including TSpec, policing, and ordering/merging rules.

Intserv.why: The document is one of the Integrated Services service specifications, defining the Controlled-Load service, its TSpec, admission control and policing.
Intserv.quote: This memo specifies the network element behavior required to deliver Controlled-Load service in the Internet.

rejected.why: RSVP is only one possible invocation mechanism; its use with this service is specified in RFC 2210, and the document only references it in the appendix and in TSpec merging.
The more specific Intserv tag covers the QoS subject, so the ancestor is not listed.
RTP is mentioned only as an example protocol applications may use for timing recovery.
SNMP is mentioned only as one of several possible mechanisms to invoke the service.
RED is mentioned only briefly as a way to isolate excess traffic. The document is about the service, not queue management.

RFC2212.title: Specification of Guaranteed Quality of Service
RFC2212.summary: Specifies the Guaranteed Service of Integrated Services: network element behavior (fluid model, TSpec/RSpec, C and D error terms, policing/reshaping) that gives firm end-to-end queueing delay bounds and bandwidth.

Intserv.why: The document is an Integrated Services service specification (intserv WG) defining the Guaranteed Service, including TSpec, RSpec, exported parameters, and policing.
Intserv.quote: This memo describes the network element behavior required to deliver a guaranteed service (guaranteed delay and bandwidth) in the Internet.

rejected.why: RSVP is one possible setup mechanism; the spec is explicitly independent of setup mechanism and only references RSVP use in an appendix.
ATM appears only as an example subnetwork for computing C and D and header overhead.
Parent of Intserv; implied by the more specific Intserv tag.
Mentioned only as one possible way to configure a reservation.
RED is mentioned only in passing for best-effort treatment of non-conforming datagrams.

RFC2213.title: Integrated Services Management Information Base using SMIv2
RFC2213.summary: Defines the Integrated Services MIB module (SMIv2), with interface attribute and flow tables for managing RSVP/Intserv reservations on router interfaces.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (INTEGRATED-SERVICES-MIB) defined in SMIv2 with tables, textual conventions and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the the interface attributes defined in the Integrated Services Model.

Intserv.why: The managed objects describe Integrated Services reservations, flows, Controlled Load and Guaranteed services on interfaces, so Intserv readers would want it.
Intserv.quote: The MIB module to describe the Integrated Services Protocol

rejected.why: RSVP is referenced as the reservation protocol that installs flows, but the document specifies a MIB, not RSVP itself.
SNMP is the management framework used to access the MIB; the document does not extend or specify SNMP, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Intserv is the more specific tag under QoS and already covers the QoS subject.
ASN.1/SMI is only the notation the MIB module is written in.

RFC2214.title: Integrated Services Management Information Base Guaranteed Service Extensions using SMIv2
RFC2214.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module with objects for managing per-interface attributes (backlog, delay, slack) of the Integrated Services Guaranteed Service.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (INTEGRATED-SERVICES-GUARANTEED-MIB) defined in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the the interface attributes defined in the Guaranteed Service of the Integrated Services Model.

Intserv.why: The managed objects describe Guaranteed Service parameters (Backlog, Delay, Slack) of the Integrated Services model, so Intserv readers would want it.
Intserv.quote: The MIB module to describe the Guaranteed Service of the Integrated Services Protocol

rejected.why: RSVP is mentioned only in Security Considerations and as the usual reservation mechanism. The MIB does not specify or extend it.
SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried over. The MIB tag is more specific.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the MIB module, not the subject of the document.
ST-II appears only in a comment saying the interface attributes are shared with other reservation procedures.

RFC2215.title: General Characterization Parameters for Integrated Service Network Elements
RFC2215.summary: Defines the general control and characterization parameters (NON_IS_HOP, NUMBER_OF_IS_HOPS, AVAILABLE_PATH_BANDWIDTH, MINIMUM_PATH_LATENCY, PATH_MTU, TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC), their IDs and composition rules, shared by all integrated services QoS control services.

Intserv.why: The document specifies the parameters common to all Integrated Services QoS control services, so it belongs on the Intserv page.
Intserv.quote: This memo defines a set of general control and characterization parameters for network elements supporting the IETF integrated services QoS control framework.

rejected.why: RSVP is only the setup protocol that carries these parameters, and RFC 2210 defines that use. This document does not specify RSVP.
It mentions that parameter IDs can form the tail of a MIB object ID, but it defines no MIB module.
XDR is used only as the wire representation for the parameters. The document does not define XDR.
The parent tag is implied by Intserv, and the document is specific to integrated services.
PATH_MTU is defined as a QoS parameter that replaces existing MTU discovery mechanisms. The document does not specify or extend Path MTU Discovery.

RFC2216.title: Network Element Service Specification Template
RFC2216.summary: Defines the template that Integrated Services service specifications must follow, covering terminology, data formats, service/parameter naming, and required sections such as TSpec/RSpec, policing, and ordering/merging.

Intserv.why: The document is the Integrated Services template for specifying network element QoS services (TSpec, RSpec, characterization parameters, merging), so it belongs under Intserv.
Intserv.quote: This document defines a framework for specifying services provided by network elements, and available to applications, in an internetwork which offers multiple qualities of service.

rejected.why: RSVP is referenced as an example setup protocol and for merge semantics, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Parent of Intserv. The more specific Intserv tag already covers it.
Only cited as an example setup protocol.
Only mentions mapping service parameter numbers to MIB object names. The document defines no MIB module.

RFC2217.title: Telnet Com Port Control Option
RFC2217.summary: Defines an experimental Telnet option (COM-PORT-OPTION, 44) letting a client configure and monitor a serial com port and modem lines on an access server, with its own flow control commands.
