Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option, its negotiation and subnegotiation commands for baud rate, parity, modem state and flow control.
Telnet.quote: IAC WILL COM-PORT-OPTION The sender of this command is willing to send com port control option commands.
Telnet.section: 1. Negotiation of the Com Port Control Option Protocol

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport; the document mentions it only for acknowledgment of delivery.
Only referenced in Security Considerations as an available Telnet authentication method.
Authentication is only mentioned in boilerplate Security Considerations.

gaps.name: Serial port / modem control over IP
gaps.why: The document is about remote control of serial (RS-232/UART) ports and modem signals, which has no specific tag in the taxonomy; only the Telnet tag covers it.

RFC2218.title: A Common Schema for the Internet White Pages Service
RFC2218.summary: Defines a common minimum schema (core attributes of a Person information object) for the Internet White Pages Service, independent of any directory access protocol, and recommends publishing object templates.

directory services.why: The document defines a common white pages directory schema for people, which is the directory services subject. It is protocol-independent, so the generic topic fits better than LDAP or X.500.
directory services.quote: The IWPS Person Object specifies a limited set of recommended attributes that a White Pages Service must include.
directory services.section: 4.0 Syntax for Definition/Representation of Information Object Templates

rejected.why: Only the LDAP attribute syntax notation is borrowed. The document explicitly does not specify a directory access protocol.
Mentioned only as one technology that would publish a companion schema mapping. It is not specified here.
X.500 schema is mentioned only as a possible database structure that the document deliberately leaves out of scope.
Listed only as an example technology that would map the schema. The document does not define or profile vCard.
The Data Privacy section is short and defers to local law. The document is not about privacy considerations.

RFC2219.title: Use of DNS Aliases for Network Services
RFC2219.summary: BCP describing the convention of using standard DNS alias names (www, ftp, gopher, etc., typically CNAMEs) to locate network services in a domain, and how to configure them.

DNS.why: The document specifies DNS naming conventions and configuration of CNAME/A records for service aliases, including round-robin and mirror considerations.
DNS.quote: It has become a common practice to use symbolic names (usually CNAMEs) in the Domain Name Service

service discovery.why: The aliases serve as a heuristic service-discovery convention for finding which hosts offer services in a domain, compared with SRV and WKS.
service discovery.quote: a mechanism by which people or agents may programmatically discover that an organization runs, say, a World-Wide Web server

rejected.why: HTTP servers are only one example service named by the 'www' alias; the document is not about HTTP.
FTP is merely one of the listed services with an alias.
Mentioned in the alias table and limitations only; not the subject.
Only an entry in the alias table.
Document is about service alias names in DNS rather than host naming conventions or host tables; DNS is the more fitting tag.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as ongoing work.

RFC2220.title: The Application/MARC Content-type
RFC2220.summary: Registers the application/marc media type for files of MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) bibliographic records, specifying the harmonized USMARC/CANMARC format, encoding considerations and contact information.

media types.why: The document's sole purpose is registering the application/marc media type, with registration template fields, so it belongs on the media type registrations page.
media types.quote: this content-type/subtype refers to the harmonized USMARC/CANMARC specification

rejected.why: MIME is the framework used for the registration; the document only registers a type and does not define body structure or encodings. The more specific 'media types' tag covers it.
Base64 is merely recommended as the transfer encoding for email transmission; the document is not about it.
Email is mentioned only as a transmission context in the encoding considerations.

gaps.name: MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) bibliographic records
gaps.why: The document is about the MARC library cataloging format, which has no fitting tag in the taxonomy (nothing for library or bibliographic metadata formats).

RFC2221.title: IMAP4 Login Referrals
RFC2221.summary: RFC 2221 defines the IMAP4 LOGIN-REFERRALS capability and REFERRAL response code, which lets an IMAP server redirect a client to another IMAP server (via an IMAP URL) at login or connection startup.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 with a new capability, LOGIN-REFERRALS, and a new response code, amending the IMAP grammar. It is squarely an IMAP extension.
IMAP.quote: Login referrals allow clients to transparently connect to an alternate IMAP4 server, if their home IMAP4 server has changed.

rejected.why: The referral carries an IMAP URL, but the URL scheme is defined in another RFC (RFC 2192). This document only uses it as an argument.
ABNF is only the notation used for the one-line grammar amendment. The document is not about it.
GSSAPI appears only in an AUTHENTICATE example, so the document is not about it.
AUTHENTICATE and the AUTH= URL parameter are mentioned only in passing. The document does not specify or change any authentication mechanism.

RFC2222.title: Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL)
RFC2222.summary: Defines SASL, a framework for adding authentication and optional security layers to connection-based protocols, with a mechanism registration procedure and the KERBEROS_V4, GSSAPI, SKEY and EXTERNAL mechanisms.

SASL.why: The document specifies SASL itself: profiling requirements, the exchange model, the security layer, mechanism registration and initial mechanisms.
SASL.quote: The Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) is a method for adding authentication support to connection-based protocols.

GSS-API.why: A substantial section defines how the GSSAPI SASL mechanism uses GSS_Init_sec_context, GSS_Accept_sec_context and GSS_Wrap, so GSS-API readers would want it.
GSS-API.quote: The mechanism name associated with all mechanisms employing the GSSAPI [RFC 2078] is "GSSAPI".

Kerberos.why: Defines a complete Kerberos v4 SASL mechanism, including ticket/authenticator exchange and security layers.
Kerberos.quote: The mechanism name associated with Kerberos version 4 is "KERBEROS_V4".

OTP.why: Defines the SKEY one-time-password SASL mechanism with examples.
OTP.quote: The mechanism name associated with S/Key [RFC 1760] using the MD4 digest algorithm is "SKEY".

rejected.why: IMAP is used only for examples of the profile; the document is not about IMAP.
Only discussed in the appendix as a transport security service relative to SASL and via EXTERNAL; the document is not about TLS.
Mentioned only as a possible external authentication source for the EXTERNAL mechanism and in the appendix.
The mechanism registration procedure is a part of the SASL specification, not a document about IANA registries generally.
DES is used inside the Kerberos v4 mechanism but the document is not about the cipher.
A parent topic; SASL is the more specific tag and already implies it.

RFC2223.title: Instructions to RFC Authors
RFC2223.summary: RFC 2223 gives instructions to authors on preparing RFCs: editorial policy, ASCII and PostScript format rules, headers, status and copyright sections, and Updates/Obsoletes conventions.

RFC series.why: The whole document defines the format, style, editorial policy and publication process of the RFC series, so it belongs on the RFC series page.
RFC series.quote: This Request for Comments (RFC) provides information about the preparation of RFCs, and certain policies relating to the publication of RFCs.

rejected.why: ASCII is only the required character encoding for the RFC text. The document is about RFC preparation, not the ASCII character set.
The IESG and working group review path is mentioned only as context for submissions. The document is about RFC authoring and publication.
The copyright notice text is boilerplate that authors must include. It is not the subject of the document.
RFC 1149 appears only as a sample nroff memo in the appendix. The document itself is not humorous.
The sample memo describes IP datagrams on avian carriers, but it is only a formatting example.

RFC2224.title: NFS URL Scheme
RFC2224.summary: Defines the 'nfs' URL scheme for referring to files and directories on NFS servers, evaluated via WebNFS using the public filehandle and multi-component lookup, with fallback to the MOUNT protocol.

NFS.why: The document specifies how NFS servers are accessed via URLs: the public filehandle, multi-component LOOKUP, version fallback, and MOUNT protocol fallback. All of this is NFS protocol behaviour.
NFS.quote: It is used to refer to files and directories on NFS servers using the general URL syntax defined in RFC 1738

URI.why: It defines a new URL scheme with its syntax, a BNF, path encoding rules, and relative-URL resolution of symbolic links.
URI.quote: An NFS URL is based on the Common Internet Scheme Syntax described in section 3.1 of RFC 1738.

rejected.why: NFS is built on ONC RPC and XDR, but the document only uses them as the substrate. It defines nothing new about RPC.
The BNF in section 10 only gives the URL syntax. The document is not about the notation.
TCP and UDP are only the transports tried for the server connection (port 2049). Nothing new is specified about them.
The document requires US-ASCII in paths, but this is a minor constraint. It is not the subject.

RFC2225.title: Classical IP and ARP over ATM
RFC2225.summary: Specifies classical IP over ATM: LIS configuration, LLC/SNAP encapsulation, default 9180-octet MTU over AAL5, and ATMARP/InATMARP address resolution with a single ATMARP server, obsoleting RFC 1577 and RFC 1626.

ATM.why: The whole document defines how IP datagrams and address resolution run over ATM AAL5, including LIS configuration, MTU and encapsulation.
ATM.quote: This memo defines an initial application of classical IP and ARP in an Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) network environment configured as a Logical IP Subnetwork (LIS)

ARP.why: A substantial part of the document specifies ATMARP and InATMARP, extensions of ARP/InARP, including packet formats, server and client behaviour and table aging.
ARP.quote: ATMARP is the same protocol as the ARP protocol presented in [3] with extensions needed to support address resolution in a unicast server ATM environment.
ARP.section: 8.1 ATM-based ARP and InARP Equivalent Services

rejected.why: Next Hop Resolution Protocol is not specified here; the memo only notes future work on multi-LIS and global resolution.
Path MTU Discovery is required of routers (Section 7.3) but only referenced from RFC 1191, not specified here.
SMDS is mentioned only as the precedent for the 9180-octet default MTU.
IPv4 is the protocol carried, not the subject; the document is about the ATM mapping.
The MIB is defined in a separate document (RFC 2320); this memo only requires clients to implement it.

RFC2226.title: IP Broadcast over ATM Networks
RFC2226.summary: Specifies how IP broadcast (255.255.255.255 and CIDR-prefix directed broadcast) is emulated over ATM by treating it as a multicast group that all LIS members join via the MARS of RFC 2022, with host requirements for joining, transmitting and tearing down the broadcast channel.

ATM.why: The document defines how IP broadcast is carried over ATM networks using point-to-multipoint VCs within Logical IP Subnets, which is IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: This memo describes how the IP multicast service being developed by the IP over ATM working group may be used to support IP broadcast transmission.

rejected.why: Broadcast is treated as a special case of multicast using the MARS from RFC 2022, but the document does not specify multicast routing or group membership in its own right.
CIDR-prefix directed broadcast is discussed only as one of the two broadcast addresses; the document is not about CIDR aggregation.
The broadcast addresses are IPv4, but the document is about emulating broadcast over ATM, not about IPv4 itself.
The ATM ARP Server of RFC 1577 appears only as background and as a discarded alternative in Appendix A.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server)
gaps.why: The document builds entirely on the MARS of RFC 2022 for registration and group membership. The taxonomy has no tag for MARS or for IP multicast over ATM.

RFC2227.title: Simple Hit-Metering and Usage-Limiting for HTTP
RFC2227.summary: RFC 2227 defines an HTTP extension, the hop-by-hop Meter header, letting proxy caches report hit counts to origin servers and letting origin servers limit cached-response usage, as an alternative to cache-busting.

HTTP caching.why: The document specifies a Meter header and counting rules for proxy caches, plus usage-limiting of cached responses before revalidation. This is an HTTP caching extension.
HTTP caching.quote: permits a limited form of demographic information (colloquially called "hit-counts") to be reported by caches to origin servers, in a more efficient manner than the "cache-busting" techniques

rejected.why: HTTP is the extended protocol, but the more specific child HTTP caching fits, so the parent is implied and not listed.
Section 7 covers interaction with Vary and Transparent Content Negotiation. It is a minor part of the document and not its subject.
Privacy is discussed only as a non-goal and in Security Considerations. The document is not about privacy.
Proxy-Authorization is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to trust reporting proxies.

gaps.name: Hit-metering / web usage measurement
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for web analytics or usage counting. HTTP caching is the closest fit but does not cover the demographic reporting aspect.

RFC2228.title: FTP Security Extensions
RFC2228.summary: RFC 2228 extends FTP (RFC 959) with optional security commands (AUTH, ADAT, PBSZ, PROT, CCC, MIC, CONF, ENC) and protected 6yz replies, providing authentication, integrity and confidentiality on the control and data channels, with GSS-API and Kerberos v4 mechanism specifications.

FTP.why: The document specifies new FTP commands, reply codes and data channel encapsulation, updating RFC 959.
FTP.quote: This document defines extensions to the FTP specification STD 9, RFC 959, "FILE TRANSFER PROTOCOL (FTP)" (October 1985).

GSS-API.why: Appendix I specifies how the FTP security exchange maps onto GSS-API calls (GSS_Init_Sec_Context, GSS_Wrap), a substantial normative part.
GSS-API.quote: it is desirable that new mechanisms be implemented as GSSAPI mechanisms rather than as FTP security mechanisms.
GSS-API.section: Appendix I: Specification under the GSSAPI

Kerberos.why: Appendix II defines a full Kerberos v4 mechanism for FTP authentication, integrity and privacy.
Kerberos.quote: The security mechanism name (for the AUTH command) associated with Kerberos Version 4 is KERBEROS_V4.
Kerberos.section: Appendix II: Specification under Kerberos version 4

rejected.why: FTP control connection follows Telnet conventions and the document uses Telnet strings, but it is not about the Telnet protocol or its options.
Section 10 defines base 64 encoding for security data, but this is a supporting encoding borrowed from PEM, not the subject.
Authentication is central, but the specific FTP, GSS-API and Kerberos tags cover it more precisely.
PEM is cited only as prior practice and as the source of the base 64 definition.

RFC2229.title: A Dictionary Server Protocol
RFC2229.summary: Specifies the DICT protocol, a TCP query/response protocol for accessing dictionary definitions from multiple natural-language dictionary databases, including commands, response codes, authentication hooks, pipelining and a dict: URL scheme.

applications.why: DICT is a new application-layer protocol with no specific tech tag in the taxonomy, so the general applications topic is the best fit.
applications.quote: The Dictionary Server Protocol (DICT) is a TCP transaction based query/response protocol that allows a client to access dictionary definitions

URI.why: The document defines the dict: URL scheme with syntax for DEFINE and MATCH, which URI readers would want.
URI.quote: The DICT URL scheme is used to refer to definitions or word lists available using the DICT protocol

rejected.why: SASLAUTH reserves a hook for SASL, but the document only reserves commands and does not specify or extend SASL.
TCP is only the transport; the document just says it runs on port 2628.
OPTION MIME prefaces responses with MIME headers, but this only uses MIME as a mechanism and does not extend it.
UTF-8 is the required encoding for commands and text, used as a substrate rather than the subject.
AUTH uses an APOP-style MD5 scheme, but it is a small part of the protocol and not the main subject.
The dictionary databases are word lookups, not directory access or synchronization.

gaps.name: DICT (Dictionary Server Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the DICT protocol or for dictionary and lexical lookup services, so it falls back to the generic applications topic.

RFC2230.title: Key Exchange Delegation Record for the DNS
RFC2230.summary: Informational RFC defining the DNS KX (Key Exchanger) resource record, type 36, which lets a node delegate authorisation for another node to act as key exchanger, secured by Secure DNS and illustrated mainly with IPsec.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS RR type with syntax, RDATA format, and additional-section processing rules, so it belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: This document specifies a new kind of DNS Resource Record (RR), known as the Key Exchanger (KX) record.

DNSSEC.why: The mechanism is intended to be used only with Secure DNS. Signed KX records and authenticated lookups underpin the delegation, and unsigned or invalid KX records must be ignored.
DNSSEC.quote: KX records MUST always be signed using the method(s) defined by the DNS Security extensions specified in [RFC-2065].

IPsec.why: Section 2.1 walks through IPsec security association setup in subnet-to-subnet, subnet-to-host and host-to-subnet scenarios, which makes IPsec the main use case for the KX record.
IPsec.quote: a system seeking to use IP Security can use this mechanism to determine the set of authorised remote key exchanger systems for that destination.

rejected.why: Kerberos KDCs appear only in an illustrative example in section 2.2.1. The document is not about Kerberos.
ISAKMP and key management sessions are mentioned only generically as what happens after the KX lookup. The document does not specify or extend IKE.
Dynamic DNS Update is mentioned only as a risk if used without authentication, which is not a substantial part of the document.
The KX record is about locating and authorising key exchangers, but it does not specify key establishment itself. The DNS and IPsec tags cover it better.

review: IPsec: quote not found in the text

notes: IPsec: quote not found in the text

RFC2231.title: MIME Parameter Value and Encoded Word Extensions: Character Sets, Languages, and Continuations
RFC2231.summary: Extends MIME parameter values (Content-Type, Content-Disposition) with character set, language and continuation mechanisms, and extends RFC 2047 encoded words with language tags.

MIME.why: The document extends MIME parameter value syntax (RFC 2045) and RFC 2047 encoded words, including ABNF changes. It is squarely about MIME header mechanisms.
MIME.quote: a means to specify parameter values in character sets other than US-ASCII

language tags.why: A substantial part of the document adds language tagging to parameter values and encoded words, so readers of language tags would want it.
language tags.quote: suffixing the character set specification with an asterisk followed by the language tag

rejected.why: MIME headers appear in email, but the document defines MIME parameter encoding rather than email transport or architecture.
The encoded-word change touches RFC 822 headers. The focus is MIME parameters, which MIME already covers.
Character sets are used as labels in parameter values, but the document does not register or define any.
Only a one-sentence note that servers should decode continuations; not a substantial part of the document.

RFC2232.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for DLUR using SMIv2
RFC2232.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module (APPN-DLUR-MIB) for monitoring SNA Dependent LU Requester (DLUR) capabilities, supported PUs, and control sessions with Dependent LU Servers in APPN nodes.

APPN.why: DLUR is an APPN extension, and the MIB manages APPN nodes with DLUR capability. The taxonomy's APPN tag covers APPN management objects, so this is the closest fit.
APPN.quote: Dependent LU requester/server (DLUR/S) is an extension to the Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking (APPN) architecture that provides dependent LU services in APPN networks.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition with object groups, tables and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document defines no protocol behaviour of its own, so the MIB tag covers it.
APPN sits under SNA and is the more specific tag, so the SNA parent is implied and not listed separately.
The document does not mention DLSw or the encapsulation of SNA traffic over TCP/IP.
The parent topic is implied by the MIB and SNMP tags, and no technology tag beneath it needs the topic added.

gaps.name: DLUR (Dependent LU Requester)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for DLUR or DLUS. The APPN tag is the nearest fit, but DLUR is a distinct SNA function whose management objects readers might look for on their own.

RFC2233.title: The Interfaces Group MIB using SMIv2
RFC2233.summary: RFC 2233 specifies the IF-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for the interfaces group (ifTable, ifXTable, ifStackTable, ifRcvAddressTable) with the sub-layer model, 64-bit counters, and link traps, obsoleting RFC 1573.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define the Interfaces Group MIB module and the architectural model behind it, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

SNMP.why: The MIB is part of the SNMP framework. It defines linkUp/linkDown traps, 64-bit counters and SNMPv2 compliance statements, which matter to SNMP readers.
SNMP.quote: The SNMP Network Management Framework presently consists of three major components.

rejected.why: The MIB is written in SMI, which is a subset of ASN.1. That is only the definition notation, not the subject of the document.
Ethernet, PPP, ATM and other media appear only as examples of interface types. The document defines no media-specific MIB.
The IANAifType textual convention is mentioned, but it is defined in a separate document.
The document is about generic management objects for interface sub-layers, not about link-layer protocols themselves.

RFC2234.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF
RFC2234.summary: RFC 2234 defines Augmented BNF (ABNF), the metalanguage for specifying syntax in Internet specifications, with its operators, formal self-definition and a core set of rules.

ABNF.why: The whole document specifies the ABNF notation: rule naming, operators, terminal values, its own ABNF definition, and the core rules.
ABNF.quote: a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications.

rejected.why: ABNF strings and the core rules assume US-ASCII, but the document is about the syntax notation, not the ASCII character set.
ABNF descends from the RFC 733/822 email specifications, but this document only separates out the notation and does not define message formats.
It mentions external encodings and character mapping only briefly. It does not register or specify character sets.

RFC2235.title: Hobbes' Internet Timeline
RFC2235.summary: RFC 2235 (FYI 32) is a historical timeline of the Internet from 1957 to 1997 with growth statistics for hosts, networks, WWW and USENET.

internet history.why: The whole document is a retrospective chronology of the Internet and its protocols, which is exactly the internet history subject.
internet history.quote: This document presents a history of the Internet in timeline fashion, highlighting some of the key events and technologies which helped shape the Internet

rejected.why: ARPANET is covered extensively but only as one thread of a broader Internet timeline, not the document's subject.
It is an FYI-numbered document, but it is a history, not an introductory guide for users.
DNS introduction and the 1997 .com corruption are brief timeline entries, not a substantial treatment.
USENET is mentioned and has a growth table, but it is one item among many in the timeline.

RFC2236.title: Internet Group Management Protocol, Version 2
RFC2236.summary: RFC 2236 specifies IGMPv2, the protocol by which IP hosts report multicast group memberships to neighbouring routers, adding Leave Group, querier election, and IGMPv1 compatibility.

IGMP.why: The whole document specifies IGMPv2: message formats, host and router state machines, timers, and IGMPv1 compatibility.
IGMP.quote: This memo documents IGMPv2, used by IP hosts to report their multicast group memberships to routers.

rejected.why: The IP Router Alert option is only required in IGMP messages. The document doesn't define or extend it.
The Internet checksum is used in the message format but is not what the document is about.
This is the parent of IGMP and is implied by the IGMP tag. The document covers only host-router membership, not multicast routing.
ICMP is mentioned only as an analogy ('Like ICMP, IGMP is an integral part of IP').

RFC2237.title: Japanese Character Encoding for Internet Messages
RFC2237.summary: Informational RFC defining the ISO-2022-JP-1 Japanese character encoding (adding JIS X 0212 to ISO-2022-JP) for use in email and Netnews, with its escape sequences, formal syntax and MIME charset name.

character sets.why: The document defines a Japanese character set encoding, its escape sequences, and registers the charset name iso-2022-jp-1. This is character set definition and use.
character sets.quote: This memo defines an encoding scheme for the Japanese Characters, describes "ISO-2022-JP-1"

MIME.why: A dedicated section gives the MIME charset name and covers use with Content-Transfer-Encoding, Base64, Quoted-Printable and MIME headers.
MIME.quote: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-jp-1

rejected.why: Email is the use case for the encoding, but the document specifies a character encoding, not mail architecture or transport.
Unicode is mentioned only as context and as a recommended addition to the encoding. The document is not about Unicode.
Netnews is named only as a place the encoding is used, and the document does not specify anything about it.
The formal syntax is just the document's way of defining the encoding. The document is not about ABNF.
ASCII is the initial and default character set in the encoding. The document is about the Japanese encoding, not ASCII.

gaps.name: ISO-2022-JP / JIS X 0212 Japanese encoding
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for a specific CJK or ISO-2022 encoding. It is covered only by the generic character sets tag.

RFC2238.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for HPR using SMIv2
RFC2238.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module for monitoring HPR (High Performance Routing, an APPN enhancement) nodes, covering ANR routing, network connection endpoints, and Rapid Transport Protocol connections and path switches.

APPN.why: HPR is an APPN extension and the MIB manages HPR nodes and the HPR transport used by APPN. The APPN tag covers the peer-based SNA node networking, routing and management objects, so the subject's readers would want this MIB.
APPN.quote: HPR is an enhancement to the Advanced Peer-to-Peer Network (APPN) architecture that provides fast data routing and improved session reliability.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (HPR-MIB) defined with SMIv2 objects, tables and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is written for; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific fit.
The RTP here is the HPR Rapid Transport Protocol, not the IETF Real-time Transport Protocol, so this would be a false match.
The parent of APPN is implied by the APPN tag, so it is not listed separately.
ARB flow and congestion control is mentioned in the overview, but the document only exposes counters and rates and does not specify congestion control.

gaps.name: HPR (High Performance Routing)
gaps.why: The document is about HPR, including ANR routing and the Rapid Transport Protocol, but the taxonomy has no HPR tag. APPN is the closest fit.

RFC2239.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs) using SMIv2
RFC2239.summary: Defines a SMIv2 MIB module for managing IEEE 802.3 10/100 Mb/s Medium Attachment Units (repeater and interface MAUs), including auto-negotiation, jacks, broadband MAUs and jabber traps, superseding RFC 1515.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (MAU-MIB) with tables, object groups, notifications and compliance statements defined in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The managed subject is IEEE 802.3 Ethernet MAUs, including auto-negotiation and MAU types, so readers of Ethernet management would want it.
Ethernet.quote: it defines objects for managing 10 and 100 Mb/second Medium Attachment Units (MAUs) based on IEEE Std 802.3 Section 30

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework the MIB is defined within; the document specifies no protocol changes. The more specific MIB tag applies.
ASN.1 subset is used merely as the notation of the SMI for the module definitions.
Ethernet is the more specific fitting child, so the parent is not chosen.

RFC2240.title: A Legal Basis for Domain Name Allocation
RFC2240.summary: An informational memo proposing that country-code TLDs create second-level domains based on legal company designations (LTD.UK, INC.US, etc.) to reduce domain name exhaustion and disputes, rather than adding new gTLDs.

domain registration.why: The document is about domain name allocation policy by registries, including who decides name ownership (company registration authority vs. domain registry) and how disputes are avoided.
domain registration.quote: The registries for the appropriate top-level country domain should create and manage the sub-domains based on the laws for allocating company names in that particular country.

naming.why: It discusses the structure of the domain namespace and proposes new hierarchical structure under country TLDs. This is namespace design, not DNS protocol behaviour, so the general naming topic fits better than the DNS tag.
naming.quote: Presently the domain space is organised as a heirarchical tree-structured namespace with several top level domains (TLDs), and sub-domains beneath them.

rejected.why: The memo discusses the namespace hierarchy and allocation policy, not DNS protocol, records, or resolver/server behaviour.
Section 4.5 only notes that names are limited to ASCII per RFC 1035. It proposes no internationalization mechanism.
The memo touches on policy and registry practice, but it is about domain allocation, not governance of Internet standards or administration.

gaps.name: Domain name dispute / trademark policy
gaps.why: The memo's central concern is conflicts between organisations and trademark holders over domain names. The taxonomy has no tag for domain name allocation policy or dispute resolution beyond the general 'domain registration' topic.

RFC2241.title: DHCP Options for Novell Directory Services
RFC2241.summary: Defines three DHCP options (NDS Servers, NDS Tree Name, NDS Context) that deliver Novell Directory Services configuration to NDS clients.

DHCP.why: The document specifies new DHCP options (codes 85, 86, 87), extending DHCP, so it belongs on the DHCP page.
DHCP.quote: This document defines three new DHCP options for delivering configuration information to clients of the Novell Directory Services.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the encoding used for the tree name and context strings; the document does not define anything new about it.
NDS is the subject of the configuration, but the document only carries bootstrap information to clients in DHCP options. It does not specify the directory service or its access protocol.
IPX is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as NDS's native environment, which is boilerplate.
Unicode appears only as the character repertoire of NDS strings, with UTF-8 as the transport encoding.

gaps.name: Novell Directory Services (NDS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for NDS or a Novell directory service. The closest tag, directory services, covers LDAP and X.500 access and synchronization, which this document does not address.

RFC2242.title: NetWare/IP Domain Name and Information
RFC2242.summary: Defines two DHCP options (62 and 63) that carry the NetWare/IP domain name and NetWare/IP sub-options (DSS addresses, nearest server, retries, etc.) to DHCP clients.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCP by defining new options (62 and 63) with sub-options and their encoding, so it belongs on the DHCP page.
DHCP.quote: This document defines options that carry NetWare/IP domain name and NetWare/IP sub-options to DHCP clients.

IPX.why: The options configure NetWare/IP clients (Novell NetWare over IP), so readers interested in NetWare/IPX interworking would want it.
IPX.quote: If the value is 1, the client SHOULD perform a NetWare Nearest Server Query to find out its nearest NetWare/IP server.

rejected.why: The 'NetWare/IP domain name' is a NetWare/IP configuration string, not a DNS name or DNS feature.
NVT ASCII is only the string encoding used for the domain name; it is not the subject of the document.
RFC 854 is cited only for NVT ASCII; the document doesn't concern Telnet.

gaps.name: NetWare/IP
gaps.why: The document is about Novell NetWare/IP configuration, and the taxonomy has no specific tag for it. The nearest match is the IPX interworking tag.

RFC2243.title: OTP Extended Responses
RFC2243.summary: RFC 2243 specifies extended challenge/response formats for the One-Time Password (OTP) system, including explicit-encoding hex/word responses and init-hex/init-word responses for re-initializing an OTP sequence.

OTP.why: The whole document extends the One-Time Password system with extended challenges and responses and a re-initialization response, so it belongs on the OTP page.
OTP.quote: This document provides a specification for a type of response to an OTP [RFC 1938] challenge that carries explicit indication of the response's encoding.

rejected.why: The OTP technology tag already sits under this topic's subtree, and the document is specific to OTP, so the generic topic is not needed.
IPsec AH is only recommended in Security Considerations to guard against active attacks; the document is not about IPsec.
md4, md5 and sha1 are only algorithm names in the new-params syntax inherited from OTP; the document does not specify or analyse them.
sha1 appears only as an algorithm token in the init response parameters, not as a subject of the document.
Augmented BNF is only the notation used to describe the syntax, not the subject.

RFC2244.title: ACAP -- Application Configuration Access Protocol
RFC2244.summary: RFC 2244 specifies ACAP, an IMAP-style text protocol for remote storage and access of application configuration and preference data, with hierarchical datasets, inheritance, contexts, ACLs, quotas and an acap:// URL scheme.

ACAP.why: The document defines the ACAP protocol itself: data model, commands, responses, namespaces and registration procedures.
ACAP.quote: The Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) is designed to support remote storage and access of program option, configuration and preference information.

URI.why: It defines the acap:// URL scheme, including user name and authentication parameters and relative URL resolution, which URI readers would want.
URI.quote: ACAP URLs are used within the ACAP protocol for the "subdataset" attribute, referrals and inheritance.

rejected.why: ACAP is modelled on IMAP's framework and borrows its ACL and URL conventions, but it does not specify or extend IMAP.
AUTHENTICATE uses SASL, and CRAM-MD5 is mandatory. This is a use of SASL as a security mechanism. The document defines only an 'acap' service name, nothing new about SASL itself.
ACLs are a substantial part of the protocol, but they are ACAP-specific access control. They are not a general authorization topic.
UTF-8 is the encoding used for strings and names. It is a substrate here, not the subject.
The LANG command negotiates the language of error messages, but this is a minor feature. The document does not define language tags.
ACAP runs over TCP on port 674, and TCP is only the transport.

RFC2245.title: Anonymous SASL Mechanism
RFC2245.summary: Defines the ANONYMOUS SASL mechanism, a single client message carrying optional trace information, allowing anonymous login in SASL-based protocols without plaintext passwords.

SASL.why: The document specifies a new SASL mechanism named ANONYMOUS, including its message grammar and security considerations.
SASL.quote: a new way to provide anonymous login is needed within the context of the SASL [SASL] framework.

rejected.why: IMAP is used only as an example profile of SASL in the example section; the document does not specify or extend IMAP.
Parent topic of SASL; the SASL tag is more specific and implies it.
ABNF is only used as notation for the message grammar, not the subject.
Privacy of trace information is discussed in Security Considerations, but the document is not about privacy threat models.

RFC2246.title: The TLS Protocol Version 1.0
RFC2246.summary: RFC 2246 specifies TLS 1.0, a record and handshake protocol that provides privacy and integrity between client/server applications, including cipher suites, key derivation and SSL 3.0 backward compatibility.

TLS.why: The whole document defines the TLS 1.0 protocol: Record Protocol, Handshake Protocol, alerts, cipher suites and security analysis.
TLS.quote: This document specifies Version 1.0 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are used for peer authentication, but the document defers certificate profiles to PKIX and does not specify them.
HMAC and the PRF are built on HMAC, but the document only uses it as a building block, so it is not about HMAC.
RSA is used for key exchange and signatures, but only as a mechanism within TLS.
TCP is only the reliable transport TLS layers over.
DES and 3DES appear in cipher suites, but the document is not about those ciphers.
Certificate handling is a supporting mechanism; PKIX is referenced rather than specified.

RFC2247.title: Using Domains in LDAP/X.500 Distinguished Names
RFC2247.summary: Defines an algorithm mapping DNS domain names to LDAP/X.500 distinguished names using the DC (domainComponent) attribute, and defines the dc attribute type and the dcObject and domain object classes.

LDAP.why: The document specifies LDAP schema: the dc attribute type, the dcObject and domain object classes, and a DN structure for LDAP directory entries.
LDAP.quote: The algorithm for transforming a domain name is to begin with an empty distinguished name (DN) and then attach Relative Distinguished Names (RDNs)
LDAP.section: 3. Mapping Domain Names into Distinguished Names

DNS.why: The document maps DNS names into directory names, so DNS naming readers would want it. It does not specify DNS protocol behaviour, so this is secondary.
DNS.quote: This document defines an algorithm by which a name registered with the Internet Domain Name Service [2] can be represented as an LDAP distinguished name.

rejected.why: X.500 naming and schema are used and the DC attribute can be represented in X.500 servers, but the focus is on LDAP; LDAP is the more fitting tag.
Parent of LDAP, so it is implied by the LDAP tag.
A general naming tag is implied by DNS, and the document is about a specific mapping rather than naming in general.
The schema definitions use ASN.1-style object identifiers and syntax notation, but the document is not about ASN.1.

RFC2248.title: Network Services Monitoring MIB
RFC2248.summary: Defines the NETWORK-SERVICES-MIB, an SNMP MIB module with application and association tables for monitoring network service applications generically (obsoletes RFC 1565).

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (applTable, assocTable, conformance groups) in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB which contains the elements common to the monitoring of any network service application.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is defined within; the document defines only a MIB module, so the more specific MIB tag fits.
applDirectoryName merely links to an X.500 entry; the document is not about directory services.
Only referenced via a distinguished name key; not the subject.
MTAs are cited only as examples of monitored applications.
URLString textual convention is incidental.
ASN.1 is just the notation used for the MIB definitions.

RFC2249.title: Mail Monitoring MIB
RFC2249.summary: Defines the MTA-MIB, an SNMPv2 MIB module extending the Network Services Monitoring MIB to monitor Message Transfer Agents (message counts, volumes, groups, associations, errors), obsoleting RFC 1566.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (MTA-MIB) with tables, objects and compliance statements for monitoring MTAs.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

email.why: The subject being monitored is mail transfer agents, covering message flow, queues, and SMTP/X.400 errors, so email readers would want it.
email.quote: this memo extends the basic Network Services Monitoring MIB [8] to allow monitoring of Message Transfer Agents (MTAs).

rejected.why: SNMPv2 is only the framework in which the MIB is defined; the document does not specify or extend SNMP itself.
SMTP is mentioned only as an example of a mail transport protocol whose data volumes are counted; the document does not specify it.
X.400 is referenced only as an alternative MTA type in object descriptions, not as a subject of the document.

RFC2250.title: RTP Payload Format for MPEG1/MPEG2 Video
RFC2250.summary: Defines the RTP packetization for MPEG-1/MPEG-2 video and audio, covering encapsulation of MPEG System/Transport streams and elementary streams, with video- and audio-specific payload headers and loss-recovery guidance.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for MPEG1/MPEG2 video and audio, defining payload-specific headers and RTP header field usage.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes a packetization scheme for MPEG video and audio streams.

codecs.why: Specific codecs (MPEG-1/2 video and audio) have no dedicated tag, so the general codecs tag is used since the payload format is specific to them, including their picture/slice structure and the MPEG-2 header extension.
codecs.quote: MPEG1 Video (ISO/IEC 11172-2) (b) MPEG2 Video (ISO/IEC 13818-2) (c) MPEG1 Audio (ISO/IEC 11172-3) (d) MPEG2 Audio

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format is defined for; it is covered by the more specific RTP payload format tag, which implies RTP.
Layer-III audio is mentioned only as one of the MPEG audio layers carried; the document is not about MP3 loss-tolerant payloads.
Document is about packetization, not streaming delivery or operations.
IGMP/multicast is mentioned only in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: MPEG-1/MPEG-2 video and audio
gaps.why: No specific taxonomy tag exists for the MPEG video/audio codecs and transport/program streams; only the generic codecs tag fits.

RFC2251.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (v3)
RFC2251.summary: RFC 2251 specifies LDAPv3, a lightweight directory access protocol for X.500-model directories, defining its data model, operations (bind, search, modify, add, delete, modify DN, compare, abandon, extended), controls, referrals, and BER/TCP encoding.

LDAP.why: The document is the core LDAPv3 protocol specification, defining all operations, the message envelope, result codes and the ASN.1.
LDAP.quote: The protocol described in this document is designed to provide access to directories supporting the X.500 models, while not incurring the resource requirements of the X.500 Directory Access Protocol (DAP).

rejected.why: X.500 is the model LDAP accesses and maps onto, but the document specifies LDAP, not X.500 itself.
SASL is used for LDAP bind authentication, but the document only references it as a mechanism rather than specifying or extending it.
ASN.1 and BER are the notation and encoding used for the protocol, not the subject.
TCP is only the transport that LDAP messages are mapped onto.
UTF-8 is used for LDAPString encoding, as a substrate rather than the subject.
LDAP URLs are used in referrals but are defined in another RFC (RFC 2255).

RFC2252.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (v3): Attribute Syntax Definitions
RFC2252.summary: RFC 2252 defines the LDAPv3 attribute syntaxes, their string encodings, the schema description formats, and the standard operational attributes, object classes and matching rules that LDAP servers must or should support.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies LDAPv3 schema elements: attribute syntaxes, attribute types, object classes and matching rules. Readers of LDAP would expect to find it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a set of syntaxes for LDAPv3, and the rules by which attribute values of these syntaxes are represented as octet strings

rejected.why: The schema model comes from X.501/X.500, but the document specifies the LDAP representation, not X.500 itself.
BER/ASN.1 is only referenced for binary transfer of values. The document is not about ASN.1.
UTF-8 is used as the encoding for Directory String. It is a substrate, not the subject.
BNF is used as notation for the encodings. The document does not define the notation.
The more specific LDAP tag applies, so the parent is not listed separately.
Fax syntaxes (Group 3 images, facsimile telephone numbers) are defined only as attribute value encodings, not as fax transport.

RFC2253.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (v3): UTF-8 String Representation of Distinguished Names
RFC2253.summary: Defines the UTF-8 string format for LDAPv3 distinguished names, including conversion from ASN.1 DN structures, escaping rules, a parsing grammar, and compatibility with RFC 1779/LDAPv2.

LDAP.why: The document specifies how LDAPv3 represents distinguished names as strings, a core part of the LDAP specification family.
LDAP.quote: In the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, a string representation of distinguished names is transferred. This specification defines the string format for representing names

X.500.why: The DN model and ASN.1 structures come from X.500/X.501, and the document defines conversion from them. The directory data model is a substantial part of the content.
X.500.quote: The X.500 Directory uses distinguished names as the primary keys to entries in the directory.

rejected.why: ASN.1 DN structures are the input to the conversion, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
UTF-8 is the output encoding of the strings, but the document does not define or discuss UTF-8 itself.
A BNF grammar is given for parsing, but only as a notation and not as the subject.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an example where the DER form is needed.

gaps.name: Distinguished Names (string representation)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for directory names or DN syntax apart from the general LDAP and X.500 tags.

RFC2254.title: The String Representation of LDAP Search Filters
RFC2254.summary: RFC 2254 defines a human-readable string representation (grammar, escaping rules, examples) for LDAP version 3 search filters, replacing RFC 1960.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies how LDAPv3 search filters are written as strings, including extensible match filters. It is an LDAP specification.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a human-readable string format for representing LDAP search filters.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar. The document is not about ABNF.
The ASN.1 filter definition and BER encoding come from the LDAP spec and are only background for the string form.
UTF-8 is mentioned as the limit on LDAPString and in an escaping example. It is not a subject of the document.
LDAP is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.

RFC2255.title: The LDAP URL Format
RFC2255.summary: Defines the LDAP URL format (ldap:// scheme) that encodes an LDAP search operation, including an extension mechanism, the bindname extension, resolution procedure and examples; replaces RFC 1959.

LDAP.why: The document specifies how an LDAP search is represented as a URL and how clients resolve it, including a bindname extension for LDAP authentication. It belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: This document describes a format for an LDAP Uniform Resource Locator. The format describes an LDAP search operation to perform to retrieve information from an LDAP directory.

URI.why: It defines a new URL scheme, with grammar, escaping rules and an extension mechanism. Readers of URI schemes would want it.
URI.quote: An LDAP URL begins with the protocol prefix "ldap" and is defined by the following grammar.

rejected.why: TLS is only mentioned as an optional way to protect the connection when resolving a URL. The document defines nothing new about it.
The grammar is given in ABNF, but the document is not about the notation.
The LDAP tag is more specific, and it sits under this topic.
The bindname extension touches authentication, but only as a small part of the URL format. It is not a focus of the document.

RFC2256.title: A Summary of the X.500(96) User Schema for use with LDAPv3
RFC2256.summary: RFC 2256 summarizes the X.500(96) user schema (attribute types, syntaxes, object classes, matching rules) for use with LDAPv3 directories.

LDAP.why: The document defines the LDAPv3 schema (attributes, syntaxes, object classes) used by LDAP directories, so it belongs under LDAP.
LDAP.quote: This document provides an overview of the attribute types and object classes defined by the ISO and ITU-T committees in the X.500 documents

X.500.why: The schema is a summary of X.500(96) attribute types and object classes, so X.500 directory readers would want it.
X.500.quote: The schema definitions in this document are based on those found in X.500 [2],[3],[4],[5], and updates to these documents

rejected.why: Certificate and CRL attributes (userCertificate, cACertificate) are defined only as directory attributes; the document is not about certificate formats or profiles.
Syntaxes are given as LDAP string-encoding BNF, not ASN.1 modules.
Certificate-related attributes and object classes are a minor part of the schema; the document is not about PKI.
Parent of LDAP and X.500, which are tagged directly.

RFC2257.title: Agent Extensibility (AgentX) Protocol Version 1
RFC2257.summary: RFC 2257 specifies AgentX version 1, the protocol between SNMP master agents and subagents for extensible agents, including PDU formats, registration/dispatch procedures, and TCP/UNIX-socket transport mappings.

AgentX.why: The document is the AgentX protocol specification itself: PDUs, encodings, elements of procedure, and transport mappings.
AgentX.quote: This memo defines a standardized framework for extensible SNMP agents.  It defines processing entities called master agents and subagents, a protocol (AgentX)

rejected.why: The SNMP framework is the context AgentX extends and the document relies on it, but the document specifies AgentX, not SNMP; AgentX is a child of SNMP so the more specific tag covers it.
MIB regions and index allocation are handled, but the document defines no MIB modules; it only references the MIB tree for registration and dispatching.
TCP is only a transport binding in section 8 (port 705); nothing new is defined about TCP.
The transport mappings section is brief and subsidiary to the protocol definition, so the topic tag is not warranted.
AgentX explicitly does not use BER/ASN.1 encoding; ASN.1 is mentioned only in describing SMI.

RFC2258.title: Internet Nomenclator Project
RFC2258.summary: Informational overview of the Internet Nomenclator Project, which integrates hundreds of CCSO (ph/qi) white-pages servers into one cross-server query service using an active catalog, schema mapping and meta-data/data caching, and explains how to register servers and query it.

directory services.why: The document describes a white-pages directory integration and query system over CCSO name servers, with schema integration, catalogs and caching. No more specific directory technology tag (LDAP, X.500) is the subject, so the parent topic fits.
directory services.quote: The goal of the Internet Nomenclator Project is to integrate the hundreds of publicly available CCSO servers from around the world.

rejected.why: X.500 is mentioned only as the environment for one performance study, and the project is not about it.
The document says 'name service' but concerns people-search directories rather than name resolution, so directory services is the better fit.
CCSO is a white-pages service in a similar space, but the document is not about WHOIS or domain registration data.
The web interface is only an access method for the query service. The document is not about HTML.

gaps.name: CCSO/ph/qi nameserver
gaps.why: The document integrates CCSO name servers, but the taxonomy has no tag for the CCSO protocol.

RFC2259.title: Simple Nomenclator Query Protocol (SNQP)
RFC2259.summary: Defines SNQP, an ASCII request-reply protocol (in the style of SMTP) for querying a descriptive name/information service such as Nomenclator with SQL queries, cost advice and cache t-bounds.

directory services.why: SNQP is a query protocol for a white-pages-style name and information service. It searches distributed repositories such as CCSO and X.500 views and returns person entries.
directory services.quote: allows a client to communicate with a descriptive name service or other relational-style query service

naming.why: The protocol serves a descriptive name service that resolves attribute-based descriptions to entries. This is general naming, not tied to DNS or any other specific system.
naming.quote: SNQP was specifically designed for use with the Nomenclator name and information service

rejected.why: Only the reply-code conventions and dot-terminated blocks are borrowed. SNQP is not about mail.
X.500 is only one possible back-end, mentioned in passing.
Cited only as a reference for relational views of X.500. It is not specified or extended here.
TCP is the transport substrate only.
DNS appears only in the Security Considerations, as a dependency for locating servers.

gaps.name: Nomenclator / descriptive name service
gaps.why: The document is about querying a descriptive, attribute-based name service. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it beyond the generic directory services and naming tags.

RFC2260.title: Scalable Support for Multi-homed Multi-provider Connectivity
RFC2260.summary: Informational RFC describing addressing and routing strategies (address lending, auto route injection, non-direct EBGP) for multi-homed enterprises connected to multiple ISPs, aimed at limiting routing overhead in the default-free zone.

multihoming.why: The whole document is about multihoming architectures for enterprises with multiple ISPs, including address allocation and route advertisement strategies.
multihoming.quote: addressing and routing strategies for multi-homed enterprises attached to multiple Internet Service Providers (ISPs) that are intended to reduce the routing overhead

BGP.why: Auto route injection and non-direct EBGP peering are BGP-based mechanisms specified in substantial parts of the document.
BGP.quote: An enterprise border router would maintain EBGP peering not just with the directly connected border router of an ISP, but with the border router(s) in one or more ISPs

routing architecture.why: The document addresses routing scalability in the default-free zone and aggregation, a routing architecture concern.
routing architecture.quote: Scaling the Internet, and being able to support a growing number of such enterprises demands mechanism(s) to contain this overhead.

rejected.why: CIDR is discussed in the comparison section as the source of alternative allocation strategies, but the document is not about CIDR itself.
The Community attribute is only mentioned briefly as a way to constrain route propagation.
Renumbering is mentioned in the discussion as a consequence of address lending but is not a main subject.
Encapsulation is referenced only as the forwarding mechanism for non-direct peering routes.
NAT is explicitly declared out of scope.

RFC2261.title: An Architecture for Describing SNMP Management Frameworks
RFC2261.summary: RFC 2261 defines the SNMPv3 architecture: a modular SNMP engine (dispatcher, message processing, security and access control subsystems) plus applications, with its vocabulary, abstract service primitives, and the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies the SNMPv3 architecture: engine, subsystems, applications, naming and primitives. It is squarely about the SNMP framework.
SNMP.quote: This document describes an architecture for describing SNMP Management Frameworks.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB module (snmpEngineID, snmpEngineBoots, textual conventions), and Section 2 also discusses MIB documents and SMI. MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: Section 5 defines a collection of managed objects used to instrument SNMP entities within this architecture.

rejected.why: Access Control Subsystem is a conceptual component of the architecture, not the document's subject in its own right. Details live in the VACM RFC.
UTF-8 appears only in the SnmpAdminString textual convention as an encoding choice.
UDP and IPX are shown only as example transports in diagrams. Transport mappings are defined elsewhere.
Message-level security is treated abstractly as Security Subsystem and Security Models. No authentication mechanism is specified.

RFC2262.title: Message Processing and Dispatching for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC2262.summary: RFC 2262 specifies the SNMP Dispatcher and Message Processing Subsystem procedures, the SNMP-MPD-MIB module, and the SNMPv3 Message Processing Model (message format and elements of procedure).

SNMP.why: The document specifies SNMP engine message dispatching and the SNMPv3 message format and processing, which is the core of the SNMPv3 framework.
SNMP.quote: It defines the procedures for dispatching potentially multiple versions of SNMP messages to the proper SNMP Message Processing Models, and for dispatching PDUs to SNMP applications.

MIB.why: Section 5 defines the SNMP-MPD-MIB module with counters and compliance statements, which MIB readers would want.
MIB.quote: This document defines these managed objects, the MIB module which contains them, and how these managed objects might be used to provide useful management.

rejected.why: The SNMPv3 message syntax is written in ASN.1, but it is only the notation used to define the format. The document is not about ASN.1.
authFlag and privFlag and the security levels are described, but the actual security processing is delegated to Security Models defined elsewhere.
The document does not cover authentication, authorization and accounting frameworks. It only mentions access control as an interface to another subsystem.

RFC2263.title: SNMPv3 Applications
RFC2263.summary: RFC 2263 specifies five SNMPv3 application types (command generator, command responder, notification originator, notification receiver, proxy forwarder) and defines the SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB and SNMP-PROXY-MIB modules.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the procedures of SNMPv3 applications built on the SNMP engine architecture, which is core SNMP framework content.
SNMP.quote: This memo describes five types of SNMP applications which make use of an SNMP engine

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document (section 4) defines three MIB modules: SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB and SNMP-PROXY-MIB.
MIB.quote: This memo also defines MIB modules for specifying targets of management operations, for notification filtering, and for proxy forwarding.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the SNMP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The document mentions securityModel, securityName and access control, but only as parameters inherited from other SNMPv3 documents. It is not about AAA.
MIB modules are written in SMI/ASN.1-style syntax, but this is only the notation. The document is not about ASN.1.
Access control is applied through the isAccessAllowed interface, which is defined in the view-based access control model (RFC 2265) and only called here.

RFC2264.title: User-based Security Model (USM) for version 3 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv3)
RFC2264.summary: Specifies the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3, providing message-level authentication (HMAC-MD5-96, HMAC-SHA-96), privacy (CBC-DES), timeliness/replay protection, key localization, discovery, and a MIB for managing USM users.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the SNMPv3 security model, including its procedures and message security parameters. It is part of the SNMP framework and its security.
SNMP.quote: It defines the Elements of Procedure for providing SNMP message level security.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB module, with the usmUserTable, usmStats counters and the KeyChange textual convention.
MIB.quote: This document also includes a MIB for remotely monitoring/managing the configuration parameters for this Security Model.

authentication.why: A large part of the document covers user authentication and data origin authentication of messages, using HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96, plus replay protection.
authentication.quote: Provide for verification of the identity of the user on whose behalf a received SNMP message claims to have been generated.

key management.why: It covers key localization, password-to-key conversion and the KeyChange mechanism for remote key update.
key management.quote: A localized key is a secret key shared between a user U and one authoritative SNMP engine E.

rejected.why: CBC-DES is the privacy protocol used, but the document is about the SNMP security model. DES is only the cipher.
HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 apply HMAC as a mechanism. The document does not specify HMAC itself.
MD5 is used as the hash inside HMAC and in key derivation. It is not the subject.
SHA-1 is used as the hash inside HMAC. It is not the subject.
The ASN.1/BER encoding of the security parameters is only a supporting detail.
The engine boots/time synchronization exists only for replay protection. It is not clock synchronization as a networking topic.

RFC2265.title: View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC2265.summary: Specifies the View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for SNMP, defining the access-control elements of procedure (isAccessAllowed) and the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB for remotely configuring groups, contexts, access rights and MIB views.

SNMP.why: The document specifies an access control model within the SNMP framework (groups, views, isAccessAllowed procedure), so it belongs on the SNMP page.
SNMP.quote: This document describes the View-based Access Control Model for use in the SNMP architecture [RFC2261]. It defines the Elements of Procedure for controlling access to management information.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document is the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB module (vacmContextTable, vacmAccessTable, vacmViewTreeFamilyTable) with conformance statements.
MIB.quote: A MIB module, the View-based Access Control Model Configuration MIB, which defines these managed object types is included in this document.

authorization.why: VACM is an authorization/access control mechanism deciding who may read, write or receive notifications for which objects, and it assumes authentication was done elsewhere.
authorization.quote: The Access Control Subsystem of an SNMP engine has the responsibility for checking whether a specific type of access (read, write, notify) to a particular object (instance) is allowed.

rejected.why: VACM explicitly assumes the securityName is already authenticated and provides none of its own.
OBJECT IDENTIFIER subtrees are used to define views, but the document does not concern ASN.1 modules or encodings as a subject.
The more specific SNMP and MIB tags already cover this; no general operations topic is addressed.
Parent topic implied; the document is about a specific mechanism (access control), not general security guidance.

RFC2266.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.12 Repeater Devices
RFC2266.summary: Defines a SNMP MIB module (DOT12-RPTR-MIB) for managing IEEE 802.12 (100VG-AnyLAN, Demand Priority) repeaters, covering repeater/group/port configuration, monitoring counters, address tracking and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SMI object definitions, tables, conformance groups) for 802.12 repeaters, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing network repeaters based on IEEE 802.12.

rejected.why: SNMP and the SMI are only the framework the MIB is written in; the document defines objects rather than extending SNMP, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
802.12 repeaters can use 802.3 framing, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM. It mentions the 802.3 Repeater MIB only for a topology-mapping object group.
Token ring framing is only a configurable framing mode of the 802.12 repeater, not the subject of the document.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for the object definitions.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.12 / 100VG-AnyLAN (Demand Priority) repeaters
gaps.why: The document is about managing this LAN technology, but the link layer taxonomy has no tag for it. A reader browsing for 802.12 or 100VG-AnyLAN would have no subject page to find it on.

RFC2267.title: Network Ingress Filtering: Defeating Denial of Service Attacks which employ IP Source Address Spoofing
RFC2267.summary: Informational RFC (BCP 38 predecessor) recommending that ISPs apply ingress traffic filtering at customer-facing links to block packets with forged source addresses, thereby mitigating spoofed-source DoS attacks such as TCP SYN floods.

DDoS.why: The whole document is about mitigating denial of service attacks that rely on spoofed source addresses, via ingress filtering by providers.
DDoS.quote: using ingress traffic filtering to prohibit DoS attacks which use forged IP addresses to be propagated from 'behind' an Internet Service Provider's (ISP) aggregation point

operational security.why: The document is operational guidance to ISPs and network administrators on filtering practice at periphery routers, including logging and monitoring dropped packets.
operational security.quote: All providers of Internet connectivity are urged to implement filtering described in this document to prohibit attackers from using forged source addresses

rejected.why: SAVI concerns source address validation in the IPv6/link-local context; this RFC is about provider-edge ingress filtering by prefix, not the SAVI work.
TCP SYN flooding is the example attack, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Mobile IP is mentioned only as a liability (reverse tunneling), a minor paragraph.
Traffic filtering is at routers for source address validity, not firewall or middlebox traversal.
Only a brief note on interaction with ingress filtering; the document is not about Mobile IPv4.
Prefix-based filtering relies on advertised prefixes, but the document does not address address architecture or allocation.

gaps.name: ingress filtering / source address spoofing prevention
gaps.why: The document's core subject (BCP 38-style anti-spoofing filtering) has no dedicated tag; DDoS is the nearest fit.

RFC2268.title: A Description of the RC2(r) Encryption Algorithm
RFC2268.summary: Describes the RC2 variable-key-size 64-bit block cipher: key expansion, encryption, decryption, test vectors, and the ASN.1 object identifier and parameters for RC2-CBC.

cryptography.why: The document specifies the RC2 block cipher itself. No child tag fits RC2 (the RC4 tag is for a different cipher), so the parent cryptography topic is used.
cryptography.quote: This memo describes a conventional (secret-key) block encryption algorithm, called RC2, which may be considered as a proposal for a DES replacement.

rejected.why: RC4 is a different stream cipher; RC2 is a block cipher and not covered by that tag.
DES is only mentioned as the cipher RC2 might replace and as a speed comparison; the document is not about DES.
The ASN.1 OID and parameter structure in Section 6 is a small part used to identify RC2-CBC, not the subject of the document.
RC2-CBC is used in CMS and S/MIME, but this document does not mention or specify that use.

gaps.name: RC2 block cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for RC2, unlike RC4, DES, AES and Camellia, so the document is tagged at the cryptography parent.

RFC2269.title: Using the MARS Model in non-ATM NBMA Networks
RFC2269.summary: Informational memo explaining how the RFC 2022 MARS multicast model for IP over ATM applies unchanged to other NBMA networks that offer point-to-multipoint calls, generalising its terminology, address families and signalling primitives.

ATM.why: The document generalises the MARS model for IP multicast over ATM (UNI 3.0/3.1 point-to-multipoint VCs) to other NBMA networks. The ATM and IP-over-ATM tag is the closest fit.
ATM.quote: Any NBMA service that offers an equivalent to (or superset of) the ATM point to multipoint call service can use the MARS model directly.

multicast.why: MARS exists to support IP multicast over link layers with no group addressing. The memo discusses VC mesh versus multicast server modes and cluster sizing.
multicast.quote: Most network layer models, like the one described in STD 5, RFC 1112 [1] for IP multicasting, assume sources may send their packets to an abstract 'multicast group addresses'.

rejected.why: The memo cites NHRP only as precedent for using address family values to carry non-ATM NBMA addresses. It does not specify or analyse NHRP.
The document is about NBMA networks in general, but the ATM tag is the more specific fit. The memo names no other specific link technology.

gaps.name: NBMA / MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MARS or for generic NBMA multicast address resolution. The ATM tag only partly covers the document's non-ATM scope.

RFC2270.title: Using a Dedicated AS for Sites  Homed to a Single Provider
RFC2270.summary: Informational RFC proposing that BGP customers homed to a single ISP (including multi-homed to that one ISP) use a single dedicated, provider-specified (often private) AS number rather than obtaining a globally allocated AS, and discusses implications for routing tables, aggregation, and routing registries.

BGP.why: The document is about how BGP-4 customers and ISPs use AS numbers in BGP peering, including loop detection effects and private AS stripping. It is operational BGP practice.
BGP.quote: The solution we are proposing is that all BGP customers homed to the same single ISP use a single, dedicated AS specified by the ISP.

RPSL.why: A subsection covers how route objects in the Internet Routing Registry (origin, mntner and community attributes) must be used when many customers share one AS.
RPSL.quote: With multiple customers using the same AS, finer granularity will be necessary to generate the correct route filtering.

rejected.why: Aggregation of customer prefixes within the provider's CIDR block is mentioned in one short subsection, but it is not a main subject.
Multi-homing to a single provider is a motivating scenario, but the document is about AS numbering for BGP customers, not multihoming architectures.
The document touches on global routing system concerns, but BGP is the more specific fit.

gaps.name: Autonomous System numbers / private AS usage
gaps.why: The document is mainly about AS number assignment and use (private AS space, dedicated AS). The taxonomy has no tag for AS numbers, so BGP is the closest fit.

RFC2271.title: An Architecture for Describing SNMP Management Frameworks
RFC2271.summary: RFC 2271 defines the SNMPv3 architecture: the modular SNMP engine (dispatcher, message processing, security and access control subsystems), applications, naming vocabulary, abstract service primitives, and the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies the SNMP management framework architecture (SNMPv3), its entities, subsystems and interfaces.
SNMP.quote: This document describes an architecture for describing SNMP Management Frameworks.

MIB.why: Defines the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB module with textual conventions and the snmpEngine group; MIB module readers would want it.
MIB.quote: Section 5 defines a collection of managed objects used to instrument SNMP entities within this architecture.

rejected.why: Security models are described abstractly; no specific authentication mechanism is specified here (USM is in another RFC).
Access control subsystem is described only as an abstract framework with one primitive; the model itself is in RFC 2275.
Only referenced in the SnmpAdminString textual convention as an encoding.
Parent of SNMP, which is the more specific tag and is implied.

RFC2272.title: Message Processing and Dispatching for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC2272.summary: RFC 2272 specifies the SNMP Dispatcher procedures for routing messages to version-specific Message Processing Models and PDUs to applications, defines the SNMP-MPD-MIB, and defines the SNMPv3 message format and Message Processing Model (v3MP).

SNMP.why: The document specifies SNMP engine message dispatching and the SNMPv3 message processing model and message format, which is core SNMP framework content.
SNMP.quote: It defines the procedures for dispatching potentially multiple versions of SNMP messages to the proper SNMP Message Processing Models, and for dispatching PDUs to SNMP applications.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-MPD-MIB module, with counters such as snmpUnknownSecurityModels, snmpInvalidMsgs and snmpUnknownPDUHandlers. Readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: This document defines these managed objects, the MIB module which contains them, and how these managed objects might be used to provide useful management.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only used to notate the SNMPv3 message syntax and the MIB definitions. The document is not about ASN.1.
Authentication and privacy flags are handled here, but the actual security processing is delegated to Security Models defined elsewhere (e.g. the User-based Security Model in RFC 2274).
The parent is implied by the SNMP tag.

RFC2273.title: SNMPv3 Applications
RFC2273.summary: Specifies the five SNMPv3 application types (command generator, command responder, notification originator, notification receiver, proxy forwarder) and defines the SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB and SNMP-PROXY-MIB modules.

SNMP.why: The document specifies SNMPv3 application procedures (generators, responders, notification originators and receivers, proxy forwarders) within the SNMP architecture.
SNMP.quote: This memo describes five types of SNMP applications which make use of an SNMP engine as described in [RFC2271].

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document defines three MIB modules (SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB, SNMP-PROXY-MIB) in SMIv2, which MIB readers would want.
MIB.quote: This memo also defines MIB modules for specifying targets of management operations, for notification filtering, and for proxy forwarding.

rejected.why: Parent topic; implied by the SNMP tag, so not listed separately.
Notification filtering and target configuration are SNMP-specific, not policy information models.
Only referenced in textual convention descriptions as the encoding for tag values; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only for delimiter characters in tag lists; incidental.
No such tag exists; SNMP proxy forwarding is covered under SNMP.

RFC2274.title: User-based Security Model (USM) for version 3 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv3)
RFC2274.summary: Specifies the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3, providing message-level authentication (HMAC-MD5-96, HMAC-SHA-96), privacy (CBC-DES), timeliness/replay protection, key localization, discovery, and the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB.

SNMP.why: The document is the SNMPv3 security model, specifying how SNMP messages are authenticated, encrypted and checked for timeliness within the SNMP architecture.
SNMP.quote: It defines the Elements of Procedure for providing SNMP message level security.

MIB.why: Section 5 defines the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB module (usmUserTable, usmStats counters, KeyChange textual convention), a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: This document also includes a MIB for remotely monitoring/managing the configuration parameters for this Security Model.

HMAC.why: Sections 6 and 7 specify the HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 authentication protocols step by step, a substantial part of the document.
HMAC.quote: It uses MD5 hash-function which is described in [MD5], in HMAC mode described in [RFC2104], truncating the output to 96 bits.

DES.why: Section 8 specifies DES in CBC mode as the USM privacy protocol, including key and IV derivation and the salt.
DES.quote: This section describes the CBC-DES Symmetric Encryption Protocol. This protocol is the first privacy protocol defined for the User-based Security Model.

rejected.why: MD5 is used as the hash inside HMAC and for password-to-key; the document is not about MD5 itself.
SHA-1 is only the hash underlying HMAC-SHA-96 and key localization; the document does not specify it.
BER-encoded UsmSecurityParameters is only the message encoding used, not a subject of the document.
Key localization and KeyChange are part of USM and covered by the SNMP tag; not a general key management document.
Authentication is specific to SNMP USM, so the more specific SNMP tag fits better.
The time synchronization is a replay-protection mechanism internal to USM, not clock synchronization as a subject.
