RFC2275.title: View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC2275.summary: Defines the View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for SNMPv3, including its elements of procedure (isAccessAllowed) and the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB for remotely configuring groups, contexts, access rights and MIB views.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the SNMP access control subsystem model (VACM) within the SNMP architecture, so SNMP readers would expect it.
SNMP.quote: It defines the Elements of Procedure for controlling access to management information.

MIB.why: A substantial part is the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB module with its tables, conformance statements and initial configuration.
MIB.quote: This document also includes a MIB for remotely managing the configuration parameters for the View-based Access Control Model.

authorization.why: The document is about authorization and access control (who may read, write or be notified of which objects), a topic page readers would want it on.
authorization.quote: The Access Control Subsystem of an SNMP engine has the responsibility for checking whether a specific type of access (read, write, notify) to a particular object (instance) is allowed.

rejected.why: OBJECT IDENTIFIER naming and the SMI are used to define views, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
VACM explicitly assumes the securityName is already authenticated and provides none of its own.
Access control here is within SNMP engines, not an AAA framework.

RFC2276.title: Architectural Principles of Uniform Resource Name Resolution
RFC2276.summary: RFC 2276 lays out assumptions, guidelines (evolvability, usability, security/privacy) and a framework for Resolver Discovery Services that help find URN resolvers translating URNs to URLs/URCs.

URN.why: The whole document is about architecture and design principles for resolving Uniform Resource Names, so readers of the URN subject would expect it.
URN.quote: the engineering criteria for what we will call here a Resolver Discovery Service (RDS), a service to help in the learning about URN (Uniform Resource Name) resolvers

rejected.why: DNS is mentioned only as an example of a restricted-syntax namespace and as an analogy for volunteer operation; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The parent topic is implied by URN, which is the more specific tag; the document does not address naming in general beyond URNs.
The RDS discovers resolvers, but this is specific to URN resolution rather than general service discovery; URN covers it.
Security and privacy guidelines are one section of the design principles, but they are specific to RDS design and no security mechanism is specified.

gaps.name: URN resolution / Resolver Discovery Service (RDS)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about resolving URNs and discovering resolvers; the taxonomy's URN tag covers URNs generally but has no distinct subject for resolution architecture.

RFC2277.title: IETF Policy on Character Sets and Languages
RFC2277.summary: BCP 18 sets IETF/IESG policy requiring protocols to identify charsets, support UTF-8, carry language tags, support language negotiation and a default language, and document internationalization decisions.

internationalization.why: The whole document is policy on charsets, language tagging, language negotiation and locale for text in Internet protocols, which is internationalization of text in protocols.
internationalization.quote: Protocols MUST be able to use the UTF-8 charset

character sets.why: A substantial part defines 'charset', requires identification, and requires registration in the IANA charset registry.
character sets.quote: All protocols MUST identify, for all character data, which charset is in use.

UTF-8.why: The central requirement is that all protocols support UTF-8, so UTF-8 readers would want this policy.
UTF-8.quote: Protocols MUST be able to use the UTF-8 charset, which consists of the ISO 10646 coded character set combined with the UTF-8 character encoding scheme

language tags.why: Section 4 mandates language tagging with RFC 1766 tags, the i-default tag, and language negotiation.
language tags.quote: Protocols that transfer text MUST provide for carrying information about the language of that text.

rejected.why: The document is a policy applied during IETF standards processing, but its subject is character set and language handling, not process.
It mentions the IANA charset registry, but only as a requirement for registering charsets, not as registry guidance.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example where charsets can be negotiated.
The MIME charset= parameter is mentioned only as the source of the term 'charset'.
US-ASCII appears only in passing, in the discussion of names and of EBCDIC.

RFC2278.title: IANA Charset Registration Procedures
RFC2278.summary: BCP 19 defines the IANA procedure and requirements for registering charsets (names, MIBenum values, review by a charset reviewer) used to label character encodings in MIME and other protocols.

character sets.why: The whole document defines what a charset is and how charsets are registered and named, which is exactly character set registration.
character sets.quote: This registration procedure exists solely to associate a specific name or names with a given charset

IANA.why: It specifies an IANA registry procedure with reviewer, mailing list, and appeal steps, so readers of IANA registry procedures would want it.
IANA.quote: the IANA will register the charset, assign a MIBenum value, and make its registration available to the community.

rejected.why: MIME is the context in which charset names are used, but the document specifies a registration procedure, not MIME itself.
It concerns charset names, not media type registration; it even says things better thought of as media types cannot be registered as charsets.
The Printer MIB is cited only as the source of MIBenum values; the document defines no MIB module.
US-ASCII is mentioned only as an example of a coded character set.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as an example of a character encoding scheme.

RFC2279.title: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646
RFC2279.summary: RFC 2279 specifies UTF-8, the variable-length octet encoding of ISO 10646/UCS characters that preserves US-ASCII, and proposes the MIME charset labels "UTF-8" and "UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8".

UTF-8.why: The document defines the UTF-8 encoding, its octet sequence table, encoding and decoding algorithms, and examples.
UTF-8.quote: In UTF-8, characters are encoded using sequences of 1 to 6 octets.

character sets.why: A substantial section covers registering the UTF-8 and UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8 charset labels and the versioning rationale, which is character set registration and use.
character sets.quote: This memo is meant to serve as the basis for registration of a MIME character set parameter (charset) [CHARSET-REG].

rejected.why: Unicode and ISO 10646 are the repertoire being encoded, but the document specifies a transformation format, which is covered by UTF-8.
US-ASCII compatibility is a design property of UTF-8, not the subject of the document.
MIME is only the context for the charset label registration. The document does not specify MIME body structure or encodings.
The document registers charset parameter values, not media types or media type registry rules.

RFC2280.title: Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL)
RFC2280.summary: RFC 2280 specifies RPSL, an object-oriented language for registering Internet routing policies (aut-num, route, route-set, as-set, inet-rtr, dictionary classes) in the Internet Routing Registry, replacing RIPE-181.

RPSL.why: The document defines RPSL itself: its classes, import/export policy syntax, filters, dictionary and aggregate route specification for routing registries.
RPSL.quote: This memo is the reference document for the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL).

BGP.why: Much of the policy language operates on BGP attributes (MED, DPA, communities, AS-path, flap damping) and BGP peerings, so BGP policy readers would want it. BGP is the main protocol policy is expressed for.
BGP.quote: Most interAS policies are specified by specifying what route subsets can be imported or exported, and how the various BGP route attributes are set and used.

rejected.why: The community rp-attribute is defined in the RPSL dictionary, but the document does not specify BGP communities themselves.
Aggregate route specification relates to CIDR aggregation, but it is a policy-language feature, not about CIDR itself.
The aim of accurate registry data helps routing integrity, but the document does not specify a security mechanism.
OSPF appears only as a protocol name in the dictionary and in route injection examples.

RFC2281.title: Cisco Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP)
RFC2281.summary: Informational RFC specifying Cisco's Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP), in which multiple routers on a LAN present one virtual router to hosts and fail over between active and standby routers, including packet format, state machine, and MAC/ARP considerations.

HSRP.why: The whole document specifies HSRP: packet formats, states, timers, events, actions and state transitions.
HSRP.quote: The memo specifies the Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP).

rejected.why: The IESG note mentions an IETF standards-track effort on the same problem, but VRRP is not specified or discussed here.
Gratuitous ARP and proxy ARP interactions are covered, but only as supporting considerations for HSRP, not as the subject of the document.
HSRP runs over UDP port 1985, but UDP is only the substrate and nothing new is defined about its use.
ICMP redirects must be disabled while running HSRP, but this is a minor operational point and the document is not about ICMP.

RFC2282.title: IAB and IESG Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Operation of the Nominating and Recall Committees
RFC2282.summary: BCP 10 specifying how the IETF Nominating Committee selects, and confirming bodies confirm, IAB and IESG members, how the NomCom is formed and operates, and how members are recalled; obsoletes RFC 2027.

NomCom.why: The whole document specifies NomCom selection, operation, confirmation and recall procedures, which is exactly the NomCom subject.
NomCom.quote: The principal functions of the nominating committee are to review the open IESG and IAB positions and to either nominate its incumbent or recruit a superior candidate.

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child that fits, so the parent is implied and not listed.
MD5 is mentioned only as one possible way to derive randomness from lottery numbers; the document is not about it.
The random selection of volunteers is a small procedural rule, not a treatment of randomness generation.

gaps.name: IAB/IESG recall process
gaps.why: The document also specifies the recall committee for removing sitting IAB/IESG members. NomCom covers it only approximately, and no separate tag exists.

RFC2283.title: Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4
RFC2283.summary: Defines Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4 (MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes, AFI/SAFI) so BGP can carry routing information for multiple network layer protocols such as IPv6 and IPX, with unicast/multicast SAFIs.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies new BGP-4 path attributes (MP_REACH_NLRI, MP_UNREACH_NLRI), their encoding and the SAFI values; it is a core BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: This document defines extensions to BGP-4 to enable it to carry routing information for multiple Network Layer protocols (e.g., IPv6, IPX, etc...).

rejected.why: IPv6 is only named as an example of an additional network layer protocol; the document is not about IPv6.
SAFI values for multicast forwarding NLRI are defined, but the document does not address multicast routing or deployment beyond that.
SAFI assignment rules are a minor note, not the document's subject.
IPv4 is the baseline BGP-4 carried; the document is not about IPv4.

RFC2284.title: PPP Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)
RFC2284.summary: Defines the PPP Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), a general PPP authentication framework with Request/Response/Success/Failure packets and initial types (Identity, Notification, Nak, MD5-Challenge, OTP, Generic Token Card).

EAP.why: The document specifies EAP itself: its packet formats, codes, and initial method types.
EAP.quote: The PPP Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)  is a general protocol for PPP authentication which supports multiple authentication mechanisms.

PPP.why: Defines a new LCP Authentication-Protocol configuration option value and PPP encapsulation (protocol field C227), which is a substantial PPP extension that PPP readers need.
PPP.quote: C227 (Hex) for PPP Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)

rejected.why: The OTP type is only one of several EAP method types and merely refers to RFC 1938. The document does not specify the one-time password system.
A back-end server is mentioned only as a passthrough use case. The document does not address AAA frameworks.
The MD5-Challenge type reuses CHAP with MD5. The document is not about the MD5 algorithm.
The generic authentication topic is implied by the more specific EAP tag.

RFC2285.title: Benchmarking Terminology for LAN Switching Devices
RFC2285.summary: RFC 2285 defines benchmarking terminology for LAN switching devices (traffic orientation and distribution, loads, forwarding rates, congestion control, address handling, errored frames, broadcasts), extending RFCs 1242 and 1944.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a glossary of benchmarking terms for switching devices, extending the BMWG terminology in RFC 1242 and 1944.
benchmarking.quote: This document is intended to provide terminology for the benchmarking of local area network (LAN) switching devices.

Ethernet.why: Many definitions concern MAC-layer Ethernet switch behaviour such as back-off, jamming, flow control, inter-frame gap and MAC address learning. This is the closest fit among link-layer tags.
Ethernet.quote: Switches implementing full duplex Ethernet links may use IEEE 802.3x Flow Control for the same purpose.

rejected.why: Backpressure and forward pressure are defined here only as switch behaviours that affect measurement. The document is not about transport congestion control.
Benchmarking is the more specific tag, and the document gives terminology rather than active or passive measurement methods.
SNMP frames are mentioned only as modifiers of the frame count.
Address learning and caching here refers to MAC address tables in switches, not ARP.

RFC2286.title: Test Cases for HMAC-RIPEMD160 and HMAC-RIPEMD128
RFC2286.summary: Informational RFC giving conformance test vectors (key, data, digest) for HMAC-RIPEMD160 and HMAC-RIPEMD128, with C reference code.

HMAC.why: The whole document is test vectors and reference code for HMAC constructed with RIPEMD-160 and RIPEMD-128, so HMAC is the subject.
HMAC.quote: This document provides two sets of test cases for HMAC-RIPEMD160 and HMAC-RIPEMD128, respectively.

rejected.why: The document uses RIPEMD hashes, not SHA. SHA-1 appears only in a stale code comment.
HMAC-MD5 is only mentioned as having code elsewhere. The document is not about MD5.
HMAC-MD5 for IP authentication is cited in the references only. The document does not address IPsec.

gaps.name: RIPEMD-160 / RIPEMD-128 hash functions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the RIPEMD hash family. The document is about HMAC built on them, so HMAC is the closest fit.

RFC2287.title: Definitions of System-Level Managed Objects for Applications
RFC2287.summary: RFC 2287 defines the SYSAPPL-MIB, an SNMP MIB module giving a system-level view of installed and running applications (packages, elements, running and past-run processes, and a process-to-application map) on a host.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module (SYSAPPL-MIB) with tables and conformance groups for application management. MIB is the most specific tag; SNMP is its ancestor and is implied.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is defined within. The ancestor is implied by MIB, and the document does not extend the protocol itself.
UTF-8 appears only in the textual conventions Utf8String and LongUtf8String. It is a minor encoding choice for string objects, not a subject of the document.
ASN.1 is only the notation that the SMI uses to define the objects. The document does not address ASN.1 itself.
The DateAndTime textual convention is imported from SNMPv2-TC and used for timestamp objects. The document defines nothing new about date and time representation.
This is the parent of SNMP and MIB, so it is implied. The document is specific to a MIB module.

gaps.name: Application / host systems management (system application MIB)
gaps.why: The document is about managing installed and running applications on a host. The taxonomy has no tag for host or application management, so the MIB tag only covers the form of the specification, not the subject.

RFC2288.title: Using Existing Bibliographic Identifiers as Uniform Resource Names
RFC2288.summary: Informational memo showing how ISBN, ISSN and SICI bibliographic identifiers can be encoded as URNs within the URN syntax, covering encoding and lexical equivalence rules for each.

URN.why: The whole document defines how existing bibliographic identifiers map into URN namespaces (NIDs ISBN, ISSN, SICI), with encoding and equivalence rules.
URN.quote: This document discusses how three major bibliographic identifiers (the ISBN, ISSN and SICI) can be supported within the URN framework

rejected.why: URN is the more specific child and fits; the document is about URN namespaces, not general URI matters.
Parent of URN is implied; the document is specific to URNs.
Namespace identifier management is mentioned only as an open question, not addressed in the document.

RFC2289.title: A One-Time Password System
RFC2289.summary: RFC 2289 specifies the S/KEY-derived One-Time Password (OTP) system, in which a secret pass-phrase and server seed are hashed repeatedly to produce single-use passwords that resist replay attacks, including the challenge format, six-word encoding, and re-initialization.

OTP.why: The whole document specifies the OTP system: generation, challenge syntax, verification, pass-phrase changes and race protection. Readers of the one-time password subject would expect it.
OTP.quote: This document describes a one-time password authentication system (OTP).

rejected.why: MD5, MD4 and SHA are only the hash primitives used by OTP. The document defines their interfaces and folding but does not specify or analyse the algorithms.
SHA-1 is one of three hash options used as a substrate. The document is not about the SHA family.
The topic is implied by the more specific OTP tag, which sits under cryptography, not authentication. OTP covers the subject adequately.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended defence against session hijacking.

RFC2290.title: Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option for PPP IPCP
RFC2290.summary: Defines the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option for PPP's IPCP, letting a mobile node and its peer negotiate Mobile IP support (foreign agent care-of vs co-located address) during PPP link setup, updating RFC 2002.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document updates RFC 2002 Mobile IP behaviour over PPP, covering foreign agent care-of addresses, agent advertisements, registration and move detection.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Mobile IP [RFC 2002] defines media-independent procedures by which a Mobile Node can maintain existing transport and application-layer connections

PPP.why: It defines a new IPCP configuration option and the negotiation of it alongside the IP-Address option within PPP.
PPP.quote: defining the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option to the Internet Protocol Control Protocol (IPCP) [RFC 1332]

rejected.why: IPv4 addresses are negotiated, but the document is about Mobile IP and IPCP options, not IPv4 itself.
VJ header compression is mentioned only briefly regarding the V bit in registration requests.
DHCP is only mentioned as an alternative way to obtain a co-located care-of address.

RFC2291.title: Requirements for a Distributed Authoring and Versioning Protocol for the World Wide Web
RFC2291.summary: RFC 2291 lists the WebDAV working group's requirements for HTTP extensions supporting distributed authoring and versioning: properties, links, locking, reservations, partial write, namespace operations, collections, versioning, variants, security and internationalization.

WebDAV.why: The whole document is the requirements specification for WebDAV. It covers locking, properties, collections, namespace operations and versioning.
WebDAV.quote: This document presents a list of features in the form of requirements for a Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning protocol

rejected.why: HTTP is the base protocol being extended, and WebDAV is the child tag that fits this document. Tagging HTTP as well would be redundant.
HTML is mentioned only as an example of a resource type, and as a comparison for link support. The document is not about it.
URIs are referenced only as resource identifiers. The document does not address them.
Variants are briefly covered, but the detailed requirements are deferred to a separate document.
The internationalization section is only a short requirement to follow the IETF character set policy.

gaps.name: Versioning / configuration management for web resources
gaps.why: A substantial part of the document covers version graphs, check-out/check-in and versioning policies. No taxonomy tag covers versioning, so it can only be reached through WebDAV.

RFC2292.title: Advanced Sockets API for IPv6
RFC2292.summary: RFC 2292 specifies the advanced sockets API for IPv6: raw IPv6/ICMPv6 sockets, ancillary data for packet info, hop limit, Hop-by-Hop/Destination options and Routing header, plus header structures and helper functions.

sockets API.why: The whole document defines sockets API extensions (raw sockets, ancillary data, cmsghdr macros, inet6_option and inet6_rthdr functions) for IPv6 applications.
sockets API.quote: Specifications are in progress for changes to the sockets API to support IP version 6

IPv6.why: It gives API access to IPv6 header fields, extension headers (Hop-by-Hop, Destination, Routing), and interface and hop-limit control, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: There are other features of IPv6 that some applications will need to access: interface identification

ICMP.why: It defines ICMPv6 header structures, type and code constants, neighbor discovery message structures, raw ICMPv6 socket checksum semantics and type filtering.
ICMP.quote: Each ICMPv6 raw socket has an associated filter whose datatype is defined as

rejected.why: It defines ND message structures and constants for C headers only. It does not specify the protocol itself.
TCP appears only in the sticky-option semantics for the IPV6_PKTOPTIONS socket option, which is not a TCP extension.
UDP is used as an example transport for ancillary data and is not the subject.
AH and ESP are explicitly out of scope; the document only defines their protocol constants.
It mentions only that a router-alert Hop-by-Hop option proposal exists.

RFC2293.title: Representing Tables and Subtrees in the X.500 Directory
RFC2293.summary: Defines X.500 Directory schema (object classes and attributes) for representing key-to-value tables and private subtrees, developed for MHS use of the Directory.

X.500.why: The whole document defines X.500 Directory object classes, attributes and DIT structures for tables and subtrees, so readers of X.500 would want it.
X.500.quote: This document defines techniques for representing two types of information mapping in the OSI Directory [1].

rejected.why: Parent of X.500, which is the more specific fit, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The tables were developed for X.400 MHS routing, but this document only defines generic directory schema; the MHS use is in RFC 1801.
Mentioned only as the motivating use (MTA examples); the document is not about X.400 itself.
The schema is written in ASN.1 object class notation, but that is only the notation used, not the subject.

RFC2294.title: Representing the O/R Address hierarchy in the X.500 Directory Information Tree
RFC2294.summary: Defines an X.500 DIT schema (object classes, attributes, naming rules) representing the X.400 O/R Address hierarchy, with mappings between O/R addresses and directory names, to support MHS routing and X.400/RFC 822 address mapping.

X.500.why: The document specifies X.500 object classes, attributes and DIT structure for O/R addresses, so readers of the X.500 subject would want it.
X.500.quote: This document defines a representation of the O/R Address hierarchy in the Directory Information Tree

X.400.why: The subject matter is X.400 O/R addresses (ADMD, PRMD, DDA, etc.), their mapping to directory names, and support for MHS routing and X.400/RFC 822 mapping.
X.400.quote: An O/R Address hierarchy is represented in the X.500 directory by associating directory name components with O/R Address components.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to write the schema, not the subject.
LDAP appears only in the title of a referenced RFC, and the document is not about it.
The more specific X.500 tag already covers this parent.
The document concerns directory representation of addresses, not RFC 822 message format. The RFC 822 mapping is only referenced.

RFC2295.title: Transparent Content Negotiation in HTTP
RFC2295.summary: Experimental extension to HTTP defining transparent content negotiation: variant lists (Alternates), Negotiate/TCN/Accept-Features headers, feature tags, list/choice/adhoc responses, and cache validators for automatic selection of the best variant of a resource.

HTTP.why: The document specifies new HTTP headers (Alternates, Negotiate, TCN, Accept-Features, Variant-Vary), a new 506 status code, and caching extensions.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines transparent content negotiation as an extension on top of the HTTP/1.1 protocol

content negotiation.why: The whole document defines a media feature and content negotiation mechanism, including feature tags and predicates, variant selection algorithms and negotiation dimensions.
content negotiation.quote: Transparent content negotiation is an extensible negotiation mechanism for automatically and efficiently retrieving the best variant

HTTP caching.why: Substantial parts cover variant list validators, structured entity tags, elaborate Vary headers, proxy cache optimizations and choice response construction.
HTTP caching.quote: this specification extends the caching model of HTTP/1.1 [1] in various ways.

rejected.why: Media type is one negotiation dimension, but the document does not deal with type registration or registry rules.
MIME types are only an attribute of variants; the document is not about MIME body structure or encodings.
Language tags appear as a negotiation dimension but are not defined or specified here.
URIs identify variants but the document does not address URI syntax or schemes.

RFC2296.title: HTTP Remote Variant Selection Algorithm -- RVSA/1.0
RFC2296.summary: Defines RVSA/1.0, the remote variant selection algorithm by which an HTTP server computes overall quality values from Accept- headers to choose a variant for transparent content negotiation, plus guidance on short requests for user agents.

content negotiation.why: The whole document specifies an algorithm for transparent content negotiation, computing quality values over type, charset, language and features and deciding between choice and list responses.
content negotiation.quote: This document defines the remote variant selection algorithm with the version number 1.0.

HTTP.why: It is an HTTP extension working on Accept- headers, Alternates and the Negotiate header, so HTTP readers would want it.
HTTP.quote: A remote variant selection algorithm can be used by a HTTP server to choose a best variant on behalf of a negotiating user agent.

rejected.why: Proxy caches are mentioned only in passing when discussing unstable results; the document is not about caching.
Accept-Language is one input to the quality computation, but the document does not address language tags themselves.
Media types appear only as an Accept-header dimension and are not registered or specified here.

RFC2297.title: Ipsilon's General Switch Management Protocol Specification Version 2.0
RFC2297.summary: RFC 2297 specifies GSMP version 2.0, a master-slave protocol for a controller to manage an ATM switch (connections, ports, configuration, statistics, events, QoS messages, adjacency protocol), updating RFC 1987.

GSMP.why: The whole document is the GSMP v2.0 specification, including message formats, adjacency protocol and QoS extensions.
GSMP.quote: GSMP is a general purpose protocol to control an ATM switch.

ATM.why: The protocol controls ATM switches (VPI/VCI connections, cells, UPC/GCRA policing) and is carried over ATM links, so ATM readers would want it.
ATM.quote: GSMP packets are variable length and for an ATM data link layer they are encapsulated directly in an AAL-5 CPCS-PDU [I.363] with an LLC/SNAP header

rejected.why: The QoS messages (scheduler, classifier, policer) are a substantial part but are ATM switch-specific and part of GSMP; not about general QoS architectures or signalling.
Ethernet encapsulation is only an alternative transport for GSMP, not a subject of the document.
Mentions of IP switching and label ranges are incidental; the document does not specify MPLS.
Controller/switch separation is conceptually similar, but the document is not framed as SDN and GSMP is a specific tech tag.

RFC2298.title: An Extensible Message Format for Message Disposition Notifications
RFC2298.summary: RFC 2298 defines the message/disposition-notification MIME content type for Message Disposition Notifications (read receipts) and the mail headers (Disposition-Notification-To, Disposition-Notification-Options, Original-Recipient) used to request them, plus gateway guidance.

email.why: The document specifies an email feature: requesting and generating read-receipt style notifications between user agents, MTAs and gateways. No narrower email tag covers MDNs.
email.quote: Message disposition notifications are requested by including a Disposition-Notification-To header in the message.

message format.why: A substantial part defines new RFC 822 message headers (Disposition-Notification-To, -Options, Original-Recipient) with ABNF syntax and rules for their use.
message format.quote: Additional message headers are also defined to permit Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs) to be requested by the sender of a message.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new MIME media type, including its fields, and gives IANA registration forms for its extension names.
media types.quote: The message/disposition-notification content-type is defined as follows:

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport. The document mentions the ORCPT parameter and the null envelope sender, but it does not specify or extend SMTP.
MIME is the framework used, via multipart/report. The new content type is covered by media types, and the document does not define MIME body structure itself.
Mailing list exploder behaviour for MDNs is covered only briefly in the conformance section, so it is not a main subject.
X.400 is mentioned as a foreign system for gatewaying. The document does not specify X.400 interworking in detail.
The registration forms are boilerplate-like apparatus and do not make the document about IANA registries.

gaps.name: Message disposition notifications / read receipts
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no email tag for delivery or disposition notifications (MDN, DSN), so this RFC's core subject is covered only by the generic email tag.

RFC2299.title: Request for Comments Summary
RFC2299.summary: RFC 2299 is a slightly annotated status list of the 100 RFCs numbered 2200 through 2299, giving each RFC's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track marker.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a catalogue of a block of RFC-series publications. Readers of the RFC series subject would look for it as a series index and status report.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2200 through RFCs 2299.

rejected.why: Many SNMP RFCs are listed (2261-2275 and others), but the document only summarises them and specifies nothing about SNMP.
LDAPv3 RFCs 2247-2256 appear as entries in the list. The document is not about LDAP.
RSVP and Intserv RFCs 2205-2216 are listed. They are only entries in a catalogue.
The note on the standards track and the pointer to RFC 2200 are incidental. The document does not describe or change IETF procedures.
RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) is one listed entry among 100, so the document is not about TLS.

RFC2300.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2300.summary: RFC 2300 (STD 1) is the IAB's periodic catalogue of Internet protocol standards. It explains the standards process and maturity and requirement levels, then lists every protocol by state: Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Informational and Historic.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels and how the IESG and RFC Editor handle submissions, and uses that to catalogue protocol status.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: It describes the RFC series, how RFCs are submitted and published, and the RFC Editor decision table. It also serves as the reference for the current RFC for each protocol.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: IANA appears only as a contact and as the manager of the protocol standards. Assigned Numbers is mentioned only in passing, and the document is not about IANA registries.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but these are process labels and not a glossary or requirements-language document.
The document lists historic protocols, but it is a status catalogue and not a retrospective.
DNS RFCs are only entries in the lists. The same is true of OSPF, SNMP, TFTP, LDAP and the other protocols listed. The document is not about any of them.

gaps.name: Internet standards index / protocol status catalogue
gaps.why: The document is a cross-protocol list of the standardization state of all protocols, with no specific taxonomy tag. IETF process is the closest.

RFC2301.title: File Format for Internet Fax
RFC2301.summary: Defines TIFF-FX, the TIFF-based file format profiles (S, F, J, C, L, M) for black-and-white and colour Internet fax, with required TIFF fields and values and the image/tiff MIME application parameter values faxbw and faxcolor.

fax.why: The whole document specifies the file format for Internet fax: profiles of TIFF matching ITU-T Group 3 fax modes. Fax readers would expect it on the fax page.
fax.quote: This document describes the TIFF (Tag Image File Format) representation of image data specified by the ITU-T Recommendations for black-and-white and color facsimile.

media types.why: Section 9 and Annex B define new application parameter values (faxbw, faxcolor) for the image/tiff media type and register them with IANA.
media types.quote: an optional "application" parameter is defined for image/tiff to identify a particular application's subset of TIFF and TIFF extensions

rejected.why: MIME is only the transport wrapper for the image/tiff content; the document is about the file format and the media type parameter, not MIME body structure.
VPIM is mentioned only as an example use of TIFF-F in Section 4.6, not something the document specifies.
Store-and-forward messaging is the motivating context, but the document defines only a file format, not email transport or access.
MH/MR/MMR, JBIG and JPEG are referenced from ITU-T Recommendations and only mapped to TIFF fields. The document defines no codecs. The taxonomy's codec tags concern audio and video.

gaps.name: TIFF (Tag Image File Format) / image file formats
gaps.why: The document is chiefly a profile of TIFF, but the taxonomy has no tag for raster image formats such as TIFF, JBIG or JPEG.

RFC2302.title: Tag Image File Format (TIFF) - image/tiff MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC2302.summary: Registers the image/tiff MIME media type for TIFF 6.0 image data, redefining the earlier RFC 1528 registration and adding an optional "application" parameter.

media types.why: The document exists to register the image/tiff media type, including its new optional application parameter and registration form for new values.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type image/tiff.

rejected.why: The document came from the Internet Fax working group, but it only registers a media type. Fax-specific TIFF profiles are in other RFCs, such as RFC 2301 and RFC 2306.
MIME is the framework the registration sits in. The document is about a specific media type registration, so the more specific media types tag applies.
The IANA registration form is part of the media type registration process. The document does not address IANA registries or stewardship in its own right.
The document mentions messaging only as one use of the media type. It is not about email.

gaps.name: TIFF (Tag Image File Format)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for raster image formats such as TIFF. The document describes TIFF 6.0 scope and features as background for the media type registration.

RFC2303.title: Minimal PSTN address format in Internet Mail
RFC2303.summary: RFC 2303 defines a minimal encoding of PSTN addresses (service-selector=global-phone with /keyword=value qualifiers) in the local-part of Internet email addresses for email-to-PSTN gateways, with an extension mechanism.

email.why: The document specifies an email address format (pstn-email, addr-spec with local-part structure) for gateways to PSTN services. It is about email addressing generally, not SMTP or the header format specifically.
email.quote: This memo describes a simple method of encoding PSTN addresses in the local-part of Internet email addresses

fax.why: Fax is a main target service for the addressing scheme, shown in the examples, and this is the base spec for the companion fax address RFC 2304. The document is service-generic, so this is secondary.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport. The document constrains the address syntax, not mail relaying.
It refers to RFC 822 addr-spec but defines a local-part convention, not header or message format.
SMS appears only as one example service-selector; the document is not about SMS.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.
It encodes PSTN numbers in email addresses but specifies no signalling transport or gateway control. Gateway interworking is only the context.
DNS appears only in the Security Considerations, as boilerplate-level routing context.

RFC2304.title: Minimal FAX address format in Internet Mail
RFC2304.summary: RFC 2304 defines a minimal syntax for encoding PSTN fax numbers (FAX=+number/T33S=subaddr) in the local-part of Internet email addresses so email can be routed to email-to-fax gateways.

fax.why: The whole document specifies how fax device addresses are written as email addresses for fax-over-email gateways, which is the subject of the fax tag.
fax.quote: This memo describes the MINIMAL addressing method and standard extensions to encode FAX addresses in e-mail addresses

rejected.why: The address conforms to RFC 822 addr-spec but the document defines a local-part convention for fax numbers, not header or message format rules.
SMTP is only the transport over which the addresses are carried. The document does not specify or extend it.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the syntax definitions. The document is not about the notation.
DNS appears only in the Security Considerations on mail routing, which is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
Email is the carrier. The fax tag is the more specific fit, and the generic email tag adds nothing beyond it.

RFC2305.title: A Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail
RFC2305.summary: RFC 2305 specifies a "simple mode" of Internet facsimile as a profile of Internet mail, using MIME and TIFF-F images, with offramp gateways to G3Fax devices, addressing, error handling and security considerations.

fax.why: The whole document defines Internet fax as an email profile, covering IFax devices, onramp/offramp gateways, addressing and TIFF image format.
fax.quote: This specification provides for "simple mode" carriage of facsimile data over the Internet.

rejected.why: Internet mail is the substrate the fax profile is built on; the document profiles it for fax rather than specifying mail itself.
SMTP is only the relay mechanism used; nothing new is defined about it.
MIME is used to carry image/TIFF; the only MIME-specific content is a short appendix of exceptions, not the document's subject.
Mentioned only in security considerations as possible end-to-end protection.
Mentioned only as an optional mailbox access protocol for gateways.
Unsolicited bulk email causing outdials is noted only briefly within security considerations.

gaps.name: TIFF for Facsimile (TIFF-F, image/TIFF)
gaps.why: The image file format profile is central to the document, but the taxonomy has no tag for TIFF or image formats.

RFC2306.title: Tag Image File Format (TIFF) - F Profile for Facsimile
RFC2306.summary: Defines TIFF-F, the profile of TIFF 6.0 for storing and interchanging black-and-white facsimile images (T.4/T.6 compressed), including required fields, a minimum interoperable subset, and the image/tiff application=faxbw MIME parameter.

fax.why: The whole document defines a file format profile for facsimile images, covering T.4/T.6 encodings, page quality fields and fax resolutions.
fax.quote: This document references the Tag Image File Format (TIFF) to define the F profile of TIFF for facsimile (TIFF-F) as a file format

media types.why: Section 4 defines the application parameter for the image/tiff media type, a media type registration refinement that readers of that subject would want.
media types.quote: The "faxbw" application parameter is defined for black and white facsimile.
media types.section: 4.1 Refinement of MIME sub-type image/tiff for Application F

rejected.why: MIME is only the transport wrapper for the TIFF-F content; the document is not about MIME body structure.
VPIM is mentioned only as a secondary usage of TIFF-F in a short section; the document does not specify VPIM.
Email is only the transport context via MIME; not the subject of the document.
T.4/T.6 fax compression is used as specified elsewhere (ITU-T); this document does not define a general lossless compression format in the taxonomy's sense.

gaps.name: TIFF (Tag Image File Format)
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about a TIFF profile, an image file format, and the taxonomy has no tag for raster image file formats such as TIFF.

RFC2307.title: An Approach for Using LDAP as a Network Information Service
RFC2307.summary: Experimental RFC defining an LDAP/X.500 schema (attributes, object classes, syntaxes) and resolution guidelines so that UNIX/TCP/IP entities (users, groups, hosts, services, netgroups, NIS maps) can be looked up via LDAP as a nameservice replacing NIS.

LDAP.why: The document defines an LDAP schema and the rules for DUAs to interpret it, extending LDAP use as an organizational nameservice.
LDAP.quote: mapping entities related to TCP/IP and the UNIX system into X.500 [X500] entries so that they may be resolved with the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol

rejected.why: X.500 is the underlying data model, mentioned for compatibility, but the document is about LDAP usage and schema.
It uses the word nameservice, but the subject is a directory schema for NIS-style lookups, not naming systems like DNS.
DNS is only mentioned as an alternative nameservice and as a contrast to dNSRecord; the document does not specify DNS.
Only maps RPC program numbers to names in a directory class; it does not specify or extend ONC RPC.
Host entries are represented in the schema, but the document is not about host naming conventions or host tables.
ASN.1 syntax is given for X.500 representation incidentally; the document is not about ASN.1.

gaps.name: NIS (Network Information Service / YP)
gaps.why: The document is about replacing or emulating NIS and mapping NIS maps, netgroups and UNIX nameservice databases into LDAP, but the taxonomy has no tag for NIS or UNIX nameservices.

RFC2308.title: Negative Caching of DNS Queries (DNS NCACHE)
RFC2308.summary: RFC 2308 specifies negative caching of DNS responses (NXDOMAIN and NODATA), requiring authoritative servers to include the SOA in negative answers, redefining the SOA MINIMUM field as the negative-answer TTL, adding the $TTL master file directive, and replacing RFC 1034 section 4.3.4.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies DNS resolver and server behaviour for caching negative responses, SOA minimum semantics and the $TTL master file directive, updating RFC 1034/1035.
DNS.quote: Negative caching was an optional part of the DNS specification and deals with the caching of the non-existence of an RRset [RFC2181] or domain name.

rejected.why: NXT and SIG records (RFC 2065) are handled in the caching rules and the example, but the document is about negative caching, not about DNS security. Security is incidental.
Only the word 'caching' matches. This is DNS caching, not HTTP caching.

RFC2309.title: Recommendations on Queue Management and Congestion Avoidance in the Internet
RFC2309.summary: Informational memo recommending that routers deploy active queue management (RED by default) and urging research on mechanisms to control unresponsive or non-TCP-compatible flows to prevent congestion collapse.

AQM.why: The document's main recommendation is active queue management in routers, with RED as the default mechanism. Sections 2 and 3 are devoted to it.
AQM.quote: strong recommendation for testing, standardization, and widespread deployment of active queue management in routers

congestion control.why: Section 4 and Recommendation 2 cover congestion collapse, TCP-compatible flows and unresponsive flows. That is broader congestion control than AQM alone.
congestion control.quote: urges a concerted effort of research, measurement, and ultimate deployment of router mechanisms to protect the Internet from flows that are not sufficiently responsive to congestion notification

rejected.why: TCP congestion avoidance is background and the yardstick for 'TCP-compatible' flows. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
ECN is mentioned only as a possible future functionality that RED deployment would enable.
Integrated and differentiated services are explicitly out of scope. Fair Queueing and CBQ are mentioned only in passing.
UDP-based streaming applications are cited as examples of unresponsive flows. The document is not about UDP.
CoDel postdates this document and is not discussed.

RFC2310.title: The Safe Response Header Field
RFC2310.summary: Defines the HTTP response header field "Safe", which lets origin servers indicate that repeating a request (notably POST) is safe so user agents can skip the repost confirmation dialog.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a new HTTP header field extension and its semantics relative to HTTP/1.1 safe methods, so it belongs under HTTP.
HTTP.quote: This document defines a HTTP response header field called Safe, which can be used to indicate that repeating a HTTP request is safe.

rejected.why: Web forms are the motivating use case, but the document defines no HTML format; form-related RFCs are only referenced.
The header concerns user-agent retry behaviour for browser form submission, not conventions for building APIs on HTTP.
Nothing in the document concerns caching; it only governs request repetition.
Security Considerations is brief boilerplate-like discussion; the document is not about a web security mechanism.

RFC2311.title: S/MIME Version 2 Message Specification
RFC2311.summary: Historic informational RFC specifying S/MIME version 2: how to sign and/or encrypt MIME entities using PKCS #7, the application/pkcs7-mime, pkcs7-signature and pkcs10 MIME types, algorithm requirements, and compatibility with prior practice.

S/MIME.why: The whole document specifies S/MIME v2 message formats, signing, enveloping and processing requirements.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data.

media types.why: Defines and registers application/pkcs7-mime, application/pkcs7-signature and application/pkcs10 (Appendix D), plus smime-type parameter and file extensions.
media types.quote: This memo also defines the application/pkcs7-mime MIME type that can be used to transport those body parts.

rejected.why: MIME is the substrate being secured; the document adds security body parts rather than specifying MIME itself. S/MIME and media types cover the new content.
Relies on PKCS #7, the predecessor of CMS, but defers to PKCS #7 (RFC 2315) rather than specifying CMS.
RSA is mandated as the algorithm but is not specified or analysed here.
Certificate processing is explicitly out of scope; only certs-only messages and PKCS #10 request transport are covered.
Covered by the more specific S/MIME tag; the document also notes use with non-mail transports.
MD5 and SHA-1 are merely required digest algorithms, not the subject.

RFC2312.title: S/MIME Version 2 Certificate Handling
RFC2312.summary: Historic informational RFC specifying how S/MIME version 2 agents handle X.509 certificates, CRLs, chain validation, distinguished names with email addresses, and PKCS #10 certification requests.

S/MIME.why: The document is the certificate-handling companion to S/MIME v2, defining agent requirements for certificates, CRLs and certification requests in secure MIME email.
S/MIME.quote: This memo describes the mechanisms S/MIME uses to create and validate keys using certificates.

X.509.why: A substantial part profiles X.509 certificates: v3 extensions (basicConstraints, keyUsage, key identifiers), CRL handling, name attributes, and signature algorithms.
X.509.quote: Receiving agents MUST support X.509 v1 and X.509 v3 certificates.

rejected.why: PKCS #7 is the message format used, but the document profiles certificate handling rather than the message syntax, which is in RFC 2311.
RSA signature algorithms and key sizes are named for verification, but the document is not about RSA itself.
Internet mail addresses in certificates are covered, but the subject is certificate handling, not mail transport or format.
Distinguished Names originate in X.500, but the document explicitly requires no directory service.
ASN.1 definitions appear in the appendix as supporting syntax only.
X.509 is the more specific fit for the certificate profiling content.

RFC2313.title: PKCS #1: RSA Encryption Version 1.5
RFC2313.summary: RFC 2313 (PKCS #1 v1.5) specifies RSA encryption and decryption with block-formatting padding, RSA public and private key ASN.1 syntax, MD2/MD4/MD5-with-RSA signature algorithms, and the related object identifiers.

RSA.why: The whole document specifies RSA key generation, key syntax, encryption/decryption with padding block types, and RSA-based signature algorithms.
RSA.quote: This document describes a method for encrypting data using the RSA public-key cryptosystem.

rejected.why: ASN.1 and BER are used to define key syntax and DigestInfo, but only as the encoding substrate; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
MD2/MD4/MD5 are used as digest algorithms in the signature schemes and discussed briefly, but their definitions are in other RFCs; this document is about RSA.
Public-key syntax is compatible with X.509 and signs certificates, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
PKCS #7 is the intended application of the encryption, but this document does not specify CMS.
Certificates and CRL signing are mentioned as intended uses only; the document does not address PKI.

RFC2314.title: PKCS #10: Certification Request Syntax Version 1.5
RFC2314.summary: PKCS #10 v1.5 defines the ASN.1 syntax of a certification request (subject name, public key, attributes, signed by the requester) sent to a certification authority to obtain an X.509 certificate.

PKI.why: The document specifies the certification request format used to obtain public-key certificates from a CA, which is core PKI. No more specific PKI child fits, since it is not CMP, EST or ACME.
PKI.quote: A certification request consists of a distinguished name, a public key, and optionally a set of attributes, collectively signed by the entity requesting certification.

X.509.why: The request exists to produce X.509 certificates, and it reuses X.509 types such as Name and AlgorithmIdentifier. The document does not profile certificates themselves, so this tag is secondary.
X.509.quote: transforms the request to an X.509 public-key certificate, or a PKCS #6 extended certificate

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation and encoding used to define the types. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
RSA appears only as an example public-key and signature algorithm (rsaEncryption, md5WithRSAEncryption). The document does not specify RSA.
PKCS #7 is mentioned only as one possible way for the CA to return the certificate, and the document puts that outside its scope.
RFC 1424 is mentioned only to say this syntax is not compatible with it.

RFC2315.title: PKCS #7: Cryptographic Message Syntax Version 1.5
RFC2315.summary: RFC 2315 specifies PKCS #7 v1.5, a general ASN.1/BER syntax (ContentInfo) for data with cryptography applied, defining data, signed, enveloped, signed-and-enveloped, digested and encrypted content types, and a degenerate form for distributing certificates and CRLs.

CMS.why: PKCS #7 is the direct predecessor of Cryptographic Message Syntax; the whole document defines the signed, enveloped and digested content types that CMS inherits.
CMS.quote: This document describes a general syntax for data that may have cryptography applied to it, such as digital signatures and digital envelopes.

rejected.why: The document describes compatibility with PEM and says content can be converted to and from PEM messages. PEM is a compatibility target, not the subject.
ASN.1 and BER are the notation and encoding used to define the types. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
X.509 certificates and CRLs are carried and referenced by the syntax, but the document does not specify or profile them.
rsaEncryption from PKCS #1 appears only as an example digest-encryption and key-encryption algorithm.
MD2 and MD5 are named only as example digest algorithms.
The document does not mention S/MIME and is not about secure email over MIME.

RFC2316.title: Report of the IAB Security Architecture Workshop
RFC2316.summary: Report of the 1997 IAB workshop on Internet security architecture, which designates core security mechanisms, identifies missing pieces, lists documents to be written, and gives guidance on Security Considerations sections.

security.why: The document is a general security architecture workshop report covering philosophy, core mechanisms and missing pieces, not tied to one mechanism, so the broad security topic fits.
security.quote: The ultimate goal was to design a security architecture for the Internet.

workshop reports.why: It is a report of an IAB workshop, which belongs on the workshop reports page.
workshop reports.quote: On 3-5 March 1997, the IAB held a security architecture workshop at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, NJ.

IETF process.why: A substantial part covers IETF structure, working group charter language and guidelines for how RFCs must treat security, which concern IETF procedure.
IETF process.quote: Guidelines on writing Security Considerations in an RFC
IETF process.section: 9. Guidelines on writing Security Considerations in an RFC

rejected.why: IPsec is designated a core mechanism and discussed, but only as one item among many in a survey; the document is not about it.
Listed as a core mechanism and as signed keys in the DNS, but only briefly within the survey.
Mentioned in the secure email discussion and 'useful but not core' list; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned as 'not useful' and as a failed secure email attempt; just a passing survey item.
Firewall issues are a planned document, with only a short description here.
Route security is named as a missing piece in one short paragraph, not a substantial part of the document.

RFC2317.title: Classless IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation
RFC2317.summary: BCP describing how to delegate IN-ADDR.ARPA reverse DNS zones for address blocks smaller than 256 addresses using CNAME records in the parent zone and new child zones, plus operational guidance.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies a DNS zone delegation technique using NS, CNAME and PTR records in reverse zones, with operational advice on secondaries and CNAME handling.
DNS.quote: This document describes a way to do IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation on non-octet boundaries for address spaces covering fewer than 256 addresses.

CIDR.why: The motivation is classless address assignment with prefixes longer than /24, and keeping reverse-mapping delegation workable for such allocations.
CIDR.quote: With the proliferation of classless routing technology, it has become feasible to assign address space on non-octet boundaries.

rejected.why: IPv4 addresses are the subject of the reverse mappings, but the document is about DNS delegation rather than IPv4 itself.
The document briefly notes that '/' in labels is legal because these are not host names, but this is a minor aside, not a subject of the document.
Address allocation is the motivation; CIDR is the more specific fit and the document's content is DNS delegation.

RFC2318.title: The text/css Media Type
RFC2318.summary: Registers the text/css media type for Cascading Style Sheets, regularizing its use since 1995, with the registration template including charset parameter, encoding and security considerations.

media types.why: The document exists to register the text/css MIME media type, giving its parameters, encoding, security and interoperability considerations.
media types.quote: Registration of MIME media type text/css

rejected.why: HTTP is only mentioned as a context where the media type appears in Content-Type and Accept headers; the document specifies nothing about HTTP.
HTML is mentioned as a document type containing internal style sheets, but the document is not about HTML.
The more specific child tag media types applies, so the parent MIME is implied.
The charset parameter is only a brief part of the registration template, not a substantial subject of the document.

gaps.name: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)
gaps.why: The document describes the CSS style sheet language, but the taxonomy has no tag for CSS or web styling. Readers browsing a CSS subject page would expect to find this RFC.

RFC2319.title: Ukrainian Character Set KOI8-U
RFC2319.summary: RFC 2319 documents the KOI8-U Ukrainian Cyrillic character set, a KOI8-R-compatible 8-bit encoding adding four Ukrainian letters, with its full code table and MIME charset name koi8-u.

character sets.why: The document defines and registers a specific character set (MIME charset koi8-u), its code table and its differences from KOI8-R, which is exactly character set registration and use.
character sets.quote: This document provides information about character encoding KOI8-U (KOI8 Ukrainian) wich is a de-facto standard in Ukrainian Internet community.

rejected.why: The lower half of KOI8-U copies ASCII, but this is only a compatibility note; the document is about the Cyrillic upper half.
The code table maps characters to UCS code points, but Unicode is only a descriptive reference, not the subject.
The MIME charset name is mentioned briefly, but the document does not specify MIME mechanisms.
The parent topic is implied by the character sets tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC2320.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Classical IP and ARP Over ATM Using SMIv2 (IPOA-MIB)
RFC2320.summary: Defines the IPOA-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for managing Classical IP and ARP over ATM clients and ATMARP servers (LIS, remote server, VC, PVC config tables, and notifications).

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, notifications and conformance groups for managing IP over ATM entities.
MIB.quote: The purpose of this memo is to define the Management Information Base (MIB) for supporting Classical IP and ARP over ATM

ATM.why: The managed subject is Classical IP and ATMARP over ATM, including LIS, ATMARP servers and clients, SVCs and PVCs. Readers of the ATM subject would want it.
ATM.quote: extending the traditional MIBs supported by a TCP/IP implementation to support Classical IP and ARP over ATM

rejected.why: ATMARP and InATMARP are the managed protocols, but the document only defines counters and configuration for them. It does not specify ARP itself, so ATM is the better fit.
SNMPv2 and its SMI are the framework the MIB is written in. The document does not extend SNMP itself, and the MIB tag already covers it.
IP-MIB is a prerequisite that this MIB extends, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
The MIB is written in a subset of ASN.1 only as the SMI requires, so this is a substrate rather than the subject.

RFC2321.title: RITA -- The Reliable Internetwork Troubleshooting Agent
RFC2321.summary: An April 1st parody RFC describing RITA, a rubber-chicken-like "troubleshooting agent" used to diagnose and fix network problems by placing it on equipment or striking vendors with it.

humor.why: The document is a dated 1 April 1998 whimsical parody of network troubleshooting tools, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: A Description of the usage of Nondeterministic Troubleshooting and Diagnostic Methodologies as applied to today's complex nondeterministic networks and environments.

rejected.why: SNMP is only mentioned in passing as an existing tool, and a RITA MIB is just a joke in Further Work.
The 'RITA MIB under development' line is a gag, not a MIB specification.
RMON is only named in the introduction as an example of existing tools.
The document parodies troubleshooting but does not address network management seriously.

RFC2322.title: Management of IP numbers by peg-dhcp
RFC2322.summary: An April 1st joke RFC describing "peg-dhcp", a manual scheme where wooden clothes-pegs bearing IP numbers are handed out to assign addresses at field events, with a paper for netmask/gateway/proxy.

humor.why: This is an April 1st parody protocol for handing out IP numbers on clothes-pegs, with a joke extension using avian carriers. The humor page is where readers would look for it.
humor.quote: the idea came up of using wooden clothes-pegs.

rejected.why: The name is a pun. The document describes a manual peg-based process, not DHCP or its messages.
It is about handing out IP numbers, but only as a joke. The humor tag covers it, and the document says nothing real about address architecture.
The dotted-quad numbers are only the thing written on the pegs. The document says nothing about IPv4 itself.

RFC2323.title: IETF Identification and Security Guidelines
RFC2323.summary: An April 1st humor RFC offering tongue-in-cheek guidelines for avoiding mistaken identification of bearded men ("facial hairius extremis") at IETF conferences.

humor.why: The document is a dated 1 April parody with mock-Latin taxonomy, fake references and a joke security section, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: This memo provides entertainment for the Internet community. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, but is rather unstandard, actually.

rejected.why: The Security Considerations section and the 'security protocols' wording are jokes about recognising people by facial hair. No security mechanism is discussed.
It concerns social conduct at IETF meetings, not the standards process or its procedures.

RFC2324.title: Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)
RFC2324.summary: The April 1st joke RFC specifying HTCPCP, an HTTP-based protocol with new methods (BREW, WHEN), headers, return codes (418 I'm a teapot) and a coffee: URI scheme for controlling coffee pots.

humor.why: An April 1st parody protocol for networked coffee pots; this is the defining subject of the document.
humor.quote: This document describes HTCPCP, a protocol for controlling, monitoring, and diagnosing coffee pots.

HTTP.why: Defines HTTP extensions (BREW, WHEN methods, Accept-Additions header, 418 status code, Safe header extension), so readers of HTTP would look for it.
HTTP.quote: The HTCPCP protocol is built on top of HTTP, with the addition of a few new methods, header fields and return codes.

URI.why: Defines a new URI scheme (coffee:) with a full syntax and internationalized scheme names.
URI.quote: All coffee URL schemes are written with URL encoding of the UTF-8 encoding of the characters that spell the word for "coffee"

rejected.why: PROPFIND is borrowed from WebDAV for metadata, but the document does not specify or extend WebDAV.
Only recommends coffee pots synchronize clocks via NTP; a passing mention.
Mentioned in passing (toaster, Coffee Pot MIB reference); the document does not define a MIB.
Defines a message/coffeepot media type in a short section, but the document is not about media type registration rules.
The firewall discussion is jocular and only about heat; it is not about firewall traversal as a subject.

RFC2325.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Drip-Type Heated Beverage Hardware Devices using SMIv2
RFC2325.summary: An April 1st parody RFC defining a SNMP MIB module (COFFEE-POT-MIB) for managing drip-type coffee-brewing hardware, with objects for pot type, level, status, start time and temperature.

humor.why: Dated 1 April and specifies a MIB for coffee pots, a whimsical April 1st document, so the humor page is where readers would look for it.
humor.quote: it defines objects for the management of coffee-brewing and maintenance devices.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a SMIv2 MIB module definition (COFFEE-POT-MIB) with object types and its relationship to the Interface MIB.
MIB.quote: The COFFEE POT MIB applies to managed devices that brew, store, and deliver heated coffee beverages.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is written for, but the document only defines a MIB module. The more specific MIB tag covers it.
The MIB uses ASN.1-subset SMI syntax. That is only the notation, not the subject.

RFC2326.title: Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP)
RFC2326.summary: RFC 2326 specifies RTSP, an HTTP-like application-level protocol for controlling on-demand and live delivery of real-time media streams (methods SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE, RECORD, etc.), including its SDP usage and RTP interaction.

RTSP.why: The document defines RTSP in full: methods, headers, status codes, state machines, and examples.
RTSP.quote: The Real Time Streaming Protocol, or RTSP, is an application-level protocol for control over the delivery of data with real-time properties.

rejected.why: RTSP is modelled on HTTP/1.1 and reuses its syntax, headers and authentication, but the document specifies a distinct protocol rather than HTTP.
Appendix C describes using SDP for RTSP session descriptions, but SDP is a presentation description format used as input, not defined here.
RTP is the usual media transport; RTSP only controls it and carries RTP-Info and interleaving, and the document says it is not tied to RTP.
Section 13 and Cache-Control cover RTSP proxy caching of streams, but this is a small part of the RTSP specification, not HTTP caching.
TCP and UDP are only transports that RTSP can run over.
The rtsp and rtspu URL schemes are defined in Section 3.2, but only as a small part of the protocol definition.

RFC2327.title: SDP: Session Description Protocol
RFC2327.summary: RFC 2327 defines SDP, a textual format for describing multimedia sessions (name, timing, media, addresses, ports, formats, attributes) for announcement, invitation and other session initiation.

SDP.why: The document is the original SDP specification, defining its fields, attributes, grammar and IANA registration guidelines.
SDP.quote: This document defines the Session Description Protocol, SDP. SDP is intended for describing multimedia sessions for the purposes of session announcement, session invitation

rejected.why: RTP is referenced for payload types and rtpmap bindings but is only a described transport, not specified here.
SIP is named as one possible transport for SDP; this document does not specify SIP.
Multicast addresses and TTL appear in c= lines, but the document is about the description format, not multicast routing.
RTSP is only listed as a possible carrier of SDP.
The MIME type application/sdp and registration of format names are mentioned, but the main body is not about media type registry rules.
The Appendix A grammar is written in ABNF, but this only describes SDP's syntax; the document does not specify ABNF.

gaps.name: SAP (Session Announcement Protocol)
gaps.why: The document describes SDP being carried in SAP announcements for session directories, but the taxonomy has no tag for SAP or session announcement.

RFC2328.title: OSPF Version 2
RFC2328.summary: RFC 2328 specifies OSPF version 2, the link-state interior gateway routing protocol: areas, adjacencies, flooding, LSAs, SPF routing table calculation, and authentication.

OSPF.why: The whole document is the OSPFv2 protocol specification.
OSPF.quote: This document is a specification of the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) TCP/IP internet routing protocol.

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is the IPv6 version; this document specifies version 2 only.
Equal-cost multipath is described briefly as a feature of OSPF but is not the subject.
BGP is mentioned only as a source of external routes.
IS-IS is cited only in the history section.
OSPF runs over IPv4 as substrate; the document does not address IPv4 itself.
OSPF uses multicast addresses for packets but does not specify multicast routing.

RFC2329.title: OSPF Standardization Report
RFC2329.summary: RFC 2329 documents how OSPFv2 meets the criteria for advancing to Full Standard, covering changes since Draft Standard (Point-to-MultiPoint interface, cryptographic authentication), implementation/deployment survey data, and protocol security.

OSPF.why: The whole document is a standardization report on OSPFv2, covering its modifications, implementation and deployment experience, and security.
OSPF.quote: This memo documents how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Full Standard, set out in [Ref2], have been met for OSPFv2.

rejected.why: The OSPF MIB is mentioned only as being at Draft Standard; the document does not specify or analyse it.
MD5 is the digest used by OSPF cryptographic authentication but is only a mechanism the document relies on.
Equal-cost multipath appears as a feature in the survey table, not as a subject of the document.
OSPF cryptographic authentication is discussed as part of OSPF, and this document does not address authentication across protocols.
CIDR support is only listed as an OSPF feature in the introduction and survey table.
Section 4 covers OSPF protocol security, but only briefly and as a part of OSPF itself. The document is not about routing security in general.

RFC2330.title: Framework for IP Performance Metrics
RFC2330.summary: RFC 2330 defines the general framework for IETF IP Performance Metrics: criteria for metrics, path/cloud terminology, metric and methodology concepts, composition, clock and wire-time issues, singleton/sample/statistic definitions, Poisson sampling, and goodness-of-fit testing.

performance measurement.why: The whole document is a framework for defining and measuring IP performance metrics, covering methodology, sampling, errors, and statistics.
performance measurement.quote: The purpose of this memo is to define a general framework for particular metrics to be developed by the IETF's IP Performance Metrics effort

time synchronization.why: A substantial section defines clock offset, skew, drift, resolution and synchronization for measurement, and discusses the unsuitability of NTP for calibrating such measurements.
time synchronization.quote: we define a clock's "offset" at a particular moment as the difference between the time reported by the clock and the "true" time

rejected.why: NTP is discussed only as a source of terminology and as a caution against calibrating measurements. The document does not specify or extend it.
IPPM grew out of BMWG, but the document is about metrics for live Internet paths, not benchmarking methodology for devices.
Standard-formed packet criteria mention the IP header, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
The document defines measurement concepts, not OAM mechanisms.

RFC2331.title: ATM Signalling Support for IP over ATM - UNI Signalling 4.0 Update
RFC2331.summary: RFC 2331 updates RFC 1755 to describe how IP over ATM entities should use UNI Signalling 4.0 call setup procedures and information elements, including ABR, traffic parameter negotiation and frame discard.

ATM.why: The whole document specifies ATM SVC signalling (SETUP message IEs, traffic descriptors, ABR, frame discard) for carrying IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: This memo describes how to efficiently use the ATM call control signalling procedures defined in UNI Signalling 4.0 [SIG40] to support IP over ATM environments

rejected.why: NHRP (RFC 2332) is only cited as one of the IP over ATM environments this signalling supports; the document does not specify it.
RSVP is mentioned only for VC teardown context and explicitly out of scope, as the document excludes Integrated Services.
The document explicitly says it does not pertain to IP with Integrated Services.
The ATM traffic and QoS parameters are ATM-layer signalling details for best-effort IP, not an IP QoS architecture.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to secure IP over ATM.

RFC2332.title: NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP)
RFC2332.summary: RFC 2332 specifies NHRP, the protocol by which a station on an NBMA subnetwork resolves the internetwork-layer and NBMA addresses of the next hop toward a destination, including its packet formats, extensions, caching and operation.

NHRP.why: The whole document defines NHRP: its resolution, registration, purge and error messages, extensions, caching rules and deployment.
NHRP.quote: NHRP can be used by a source station (host or router) connected to a Non-Broadcast, Multi-Access (NBMA) subnetwork to determine the internetworking layer address and NBMA subnetwork addresses

rejected.why: NHRP is a functional superset of NARP and coexists with ARP, but the document does not specify ARP. ARP is only referenced.
ATM is a main example NBMA technology and encapsulation target. The protocol is media-independent, so ATM is substrate.
NHRP depends on routed paths and NHS placement, but it is an address resolution protocol, not a routing protocol.
HMAC-MD5 is only the default algorithm for the authentication extension, a mechanism the protocol relies on.
SMDS is only cited as an example NBMA subnetwork and encapsulation.

RFC2333.title: NHRP Protocol Applicability Statement
RFC2333.summary: Applicability statement for NHRP, describing its key features, appropriate use, scalability and limits (e.g. router-router loops) for resolving IP addresses to NBMA addresses over ATM, SMDS and X.25.

NHRP.why: The whole document discusses when and how NHRP applies, its features and scalability. NHRP is the subject.
NHRP.quote: this memo discusses the applicability of the Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP) in routing of IP datagrams over Non-Broadcast Multiple Access (NBMA) networks

rejected.why: ATM is an example NBMA technology and a QoS case. The document is about NHRP, which is technology-independent, not about IP over ATM.
It is mentioned only as an example NBMA network and a reference. The document does not address it.
It is listed only as an example NBMA network.
The document says NHRP is not a routing protocol. It discusses short-cut routing next to routing protocols, but the NHRP tag covers that.
QoS guarantees are mentioned as a benefit of short-cuts. They are not a subject of the document.

RFC2334.title: Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (SCSP)
RFC2334.summary: RFC 2334 specifies SCSP, an OSPF-like Hello, cache-alignment and flooding protocol that keeps the caches of distributed servers in a Server Group synchronized. It is aimed at NBMA servers such as NHRP and ATMARP, and each client/server protocol needs its own protocol-specific companion document.

NHRP.why: NHRP servers are the main worked example, and the NHRP-specific use is in the companion RFC 2335. Readers of NHRP and NBMA server redundancy would want this document. SCSP itself is generic, so the tag is only secondary.
NHRP.quote: SCSP synchronizes caches (or a portion of the caches) of a set of server entities of a particular protocol which are bound to a Server Group (SG)

rejected.why: SCSP borrows OSPF's hello, database synchronization and flooding procedures but is not a routing protocol and does not extend OSPF.
The protocol runs over ATM VCs with LLC/SNAP and NBMA is its context, but it is a server synchronization protocol, not IP-over-ATM specification. ATMARP is only one of several client protocols.
HMAC-MD5 is only the default MAC for the authentication extension, a minor supporting detail.
It uses the standard IP checksum in the fixed header, which is incidental.
The caches hold client binding state, but the document does not address directory access or synchronization as a directory service.

gaps.name: SCSP (Server Cache Synchronization Protocol) / cache synchronization
gaps.why: The document's own subject is a generic server cache replication and flooding protocol. The taxonomy has no tag for it, and NHRP only covers one of its client protocols.

RFC2335.title: A Distributed NHRP Service Using SCSP
RFC2335.summary: Specifies the NHRP-specific part of SCSP (CSA record format and field values) so that NHRP Servers within a LIS can synchronize their client databases.

NHRP.why: The document defines how NHRP servers are distributed and synchronized, including NHRP-specific CSA record fields and NHC leave/re-register behaviour. NHRP is the client/server protocol being served.
NHRP.quote: This method uses the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (SCSP) [2] to synchronize the client information databases held by NHRP Servers (NHSs) within a LIS.

rejected.why: ATMARP is mentioned only in a flag bit. NHRP is already the more specific tag under ATM, and the document is not about ATM itself.

gaps.name: SCSP (Server Cache Synchronization Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SCSP. This document is its NHRP-specific part, and RFC 2334 defines the protocol-independent part. Readers browsing a subject page for SCSP would want both.

RFC2336.title: Classical IP and ARP over ATM to NHRP Transition
RFC2336.summary: Informational RFC defining how NHRP servers must respond to ATMARP clients in a LIS so ATMARP and NHRP clients can coexist during transition from Classical IP and ARP over ATM to NHRP.
