NHRP.why: The document specifies NHS behaviour for NHRP servers serving ATMARP clients and how NHRP replies treat ATMARP-registered stations. NHRP is the central protocol being transitioned to.
NHRP.quote: NHSs will be required to respond to ATMARP Client queries in a fashion which will permit continued use of the ATMARP Client within the LIS

ATM.why: The document covers IP over ATM address resolution (ATMARP, LLC/SNAP, AAL5 SVC environments), so it belongs under ATM. NHRP sits under ATM in the taxonomy, but ATMARP is a distinct subject that the NHRP tag does not cover.
ATM.quote: describes methods and procedures for the graceful transition from an ATMARP LIS[1] to an NHRP LIS[2] network model over ATM.

rejected.why: ATMARP is ARP-like address resolution over ATM, but the document is about transition to NHRP in ATM LIS, not the generic ARP protocol.
IP is only the protocol layer being resolved; the document is not about IPv4 itself.

RFC2337.title: Intra-LIS IP multicast among routers over ATM using Sparse Mode PIM
RFC2337.summary: Experimental RFC describing how PIM-SM routers within a single ATM Logical IP Subnet can support intra-LIS IP multicast using shared and per-group point-to-multipoint VCs, driven by PIM joins/prunes, without needing MARS.

PIM-SM.why: The document specifies how PIM-SM routers use their join/prune messages and switch to source-rooted trees to build and manage ATM point-to-multipoint VCs. PIM-SM is the protocol being profiled over ATM.
PIM-SM.quote: The method described here is specific to Sparse Mode PIM [PIM-SM], and relies on the explicit join mechanism inherent in PIM-SM to notify routers

ATM.why: The document is about IP multicast over ATM, covering LISs, point-to-multipoint VCs, ATM/IP address mapping and encapsulation. It fits the IP over ATM subject.
ATM.quote: Each PIM router within a LIS is required to maintain a single (shared) point-to-multipoint distribution VC rooted at the router

rejected.why: IGMP reports are mentioned only as a trigger for adding leaves to VCs. The document does not specify or extend IGMP.
The parent topic is implied by the PIM-SM tag, and the document does not address multicast generally.
The document concerns MARS-style multicast address resolution only as a comparison. It does not specify MADCAP or MALLOC.
The security section is boilerplate-like general commentary on routing protocol security, mentioning GKMP and key management only in passing. The body is not about multicast security.
ARP server for IP-to-ATM mapping is mentioned only as one optional means of address mapping.

RFC2338.title: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol
RFC2338.summary: RFC 2338 specifies VRRP version 2, an election protocol that lets a group of IPv4 routers on a LAN share a virtual router address, with automatic failover of the default gateway.

VRRP.why: The document defines the VRRP protocol: packet format, state machine, Master election, virtual MAC and authentication.
VRRP.quote: VRRP specifies an election protocol that dynamically assigns responsibility for a virtual router to one of the VRRP routers on a LAN.

rejected.why: HSRP is mentioned only as a similar proprietary protocol that VRRP parallels. The document does not specify or analyse it.
ARP behaviour (gratuitous ARP, proxy ARP, virtual MAC replies) is used in operation, but the document is about VRRP, not ARP.
The IP Authentication Header is one optional authentication type, covered in a short subsection and not a main subject.
Section 9 gives operational notes on running VRRP over FDDI. That is only a small part of the document, so it is not an FDDI subject.
Section 9 describes VRRP operation over token ring using functional addresses. It is a secondary part of a VRRP document, not about IP over token ring.
VRRP advertisements use the link-local multicast address 224.0.0.18, but this is only the transport and is not a multicast routing topic.

RFC2339.title: An Agreement Between the Internet Society, the IETF, and Sun Microsystems, Inc. in the matter of NFS V.4 Protocols
RFC2339.summary: A record of the licence agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society that lets Sun's NFS v2/v3 specifications be used as the starting point for IETF standardisation of NFS version 4.

IPR.why: The document is a copyright and patent licence agreement. Its main body covers licence terms, warranty disclaimers and liability, so IPR readers would want it.
IPR.quote: Donor hereby grants to the Internet Society ("Licensees" ...) a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide right and license under any copyrights owned or otherwise licensable by Donor

NFS.why: The agreement concerns the NFS specifications (RFC 1094 and 1813) and control of the NFS version numbers for NFS v4 development. It does not specify the protocol itself, but NFS readers would look for it as part of its history.
NFS.quote: This Request for Comments records an agreement between Sun Microsystems, Inc. and the Internet Society to permit the flow of Sun's Network File System specifications

rejected.why: Exhibit A mentions XDR and ONC RPC only to exclude them from the licensed specification and to note a separate licence. The document is not about them.
The agreement mentions the Internet Standardization Process (RFC 2026) as the purpose of the licence. It does not define or change any process.

RFC2340.title: Nortel's Virtual Network Switching (VNS) Overview
RFC2340.summary: Informational overview of Nortel's Virtual Network Switching (VNS), a proprietary multiprotocol label-switching architecture with its own header, link-state routing, logical networks, multicast, load spreading and CoS over ATM/frame trunks.

MPLS.why: The document describes a label-switching architecture (header, label format, forwarding, label distribution) that is a precursor/alternative to MPLS; readers of MPLS history would look for it.
MPLS.quote: VNS is a CoS-sensitive multi-protocol label switching architecture that reduces or eliminates the number of layer 3 hops over the WAN by switching traffic based on labels.

ECMP.why: A dedicated section specifies equal-cost multipath forwarding with a load-spreading key carried in the VNS header.
ECMP.quote: Equal cost multipaths allows different streams (unique network layer source and destination address pairings) to be load spread between multiple relatively equal cost paths

rejected.why: ATM is only an underlying trunk technology VNS runs over, not the subject.
VNS routing is OSPF/PNNI-like but is its own link-state system; OSPF is only referenced for network-layer routing.
VPN/traffic segregation is a benefit of logical networks but not provider-provisioned VPN specification; MPLS covers the core subject.
VNS multicast is a brief forwarding mechanism within the logical network, not IP multicast routing as such.
Section 8 covers only load spreading, which is captured by ECMP.
CoS handling is a brief, VNS-specific mechanism, not Diffserv.

RFC2341.title: Cisco Layer Two Forwarding (Protocol) "L2F"
RFC2341.summary: Historic Cisco specification of L2F, a protocol that tunnels PPP/SLIP link-layer frames from an ISP NAS to a remote Home Gateway for virtual dial-up, including packet format, tunnel/client setup, and state tables.

L2TP.why: L2F is the Layer Two tunneling protocol that preceded and was merged into L2TP; the nearest taxonomy tag for a layer-2 dial-up tunneling protocol is L2TP, where readers of that subject would look for it.
L2TP.quote: This document describes the Layer Two Forwarding protocol (L2F) which permits the tunneling of the link layer (i.e., HDLC, async HDLC, or SLIP frames)

PPP.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how PPP (and SLIP) frames, LCP CONFACKs and CHAP/PAP authentication data are encapsulated and carried in the tunnel.
PPP.quote: Encapsulation of PPP packets within L2F. The ISP NAS and the Home gateway require a common understanding of the encapsulation protocol

rejected.why: SLIP is only one of the carried payloads; the document defines encapsulation of it but is not about SLIP itself.
UDP is merely the substrate (port 1701) in a short section; L2F is media-independent.
Generic tunneling parent is implied by the more specific L2TP tag.
RADIUS and TACACS+ are only mentioned as authentication options, not specified.
GRE is only cited as inspiration for the packet format in the acknowledgments.
Authentication and accounting are discussed as service-model issues, but the document does not specify an AAA framework.

gaps.name: Layer Two Forwarding (L2F) / virtual dial-up
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for L2F; L2TP is used as the closest fit, but L2F is a distinct predecessor protocol.

RFC2342.title: IMAP4 Namespace
RFC2342.summary: RFC 2342 defines the IMAP4 NAMESPACE command and untagged response, letting a client discover the prefixes and hierarchy delimiters of a server's personal, other users', and shared mailbox namespaces.

IMAP.why: The document specifies an extension to IMAP4: a new command, response, capability keyword and formal syntax. It belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document defines a NAMESPACE command that allows a client to discover the prefixes of namespaces used by a server for personal mailboxes

rejected.why: The 'namespace' here means mailbox name prefixes within IMAP. It is not general naming or name resolution.
This is implied as the parent of IMAP. The document is specifically about the IMAP extension.
The ABNF is used only to write the formal syntax. The document is not about the notation.
The IMAP URL is mentioned only in passing, as a reason to avoid the '#' prefix. The document does not specify URIs.

RFC2343.title: RTP Payload Format for Bundled MPEG
RFC2343.summary: Defines an experimental RTP payload format that bundles MPEG-2 video and audio into a single RTP stream, with a BMPEG-specific header and error recovery guidance.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies a new RTP payload format (BMPEG) for MPEG-2 audio/video, with RTP header field usage and a payload-specific header.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes a payload type for bundled, MPEG-2 encoded video and audio data that may be used with RTP, version 2.

rejected.why: RTP is the protocol the payload format plugs into; the document defines a payload format, which is covered by the more specific child tag.
MPEG-2 is packetized, not defined; no MPEG-2 codec tag exists and the document does not define the codec itself.
Path MTU is only mentioned in passing regarding fragmentation avoidance.
Mentioned only as an example of packet classification affected by fragmentation.

gaps.name: MPEG-2 video/audio
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPEG-1/MPEG-2 codecs and systems, though the RTP payload format tag fits the packetization aspect.

RFC2344.title: Reverse Tunneling for Mobile IP
RFC2344.summary: Extends Mobile IP registration (new 'T' bit, Encapsulating Delivery Style extension, new reply codes) so a foreign agent or mobile node can set up topologically correct reverse tunnels to the home agent, which works with ingress-filtering routers.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends the Mobile IPv4 (RFC 2002) registration and agent advertisement messages and defines mobile node, foreign agent and home agent behaviour for reverse tunnels.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document proposes backwards-compatible extensions to Mobile IP in order to support topologically correct reverse tunnels.

rejected.why: IP in IP encapsulation (RFC 2003) is the assumed encapsulation method. The document only relies on it and does not specify or extend it.
Reverse tunnels are the document's subject, but the Mobile IPv4 tag fits better because the tunnels are set up through Mobile IP registration. The generic tunneling parent is not needed.
AH and ESP are mentioned only as assumptions about firewalls. The document does not address them.
Multicast and broadcast support is mentioned briefly in Section 5.3. It is not a substantial focus.
The document explicitly says it does not try to solve the firewall traversal problem. Ingress filtering is only motivation.

RFC2345.title: Domain Names and Company Name Retrieval
RFC2345.summary: Experimental RFC proposing a company-name-to-URL lookup service built on the WHOIS protocol, defining query/response line formats, variation numbers (ASCII and UTF-8), and a demo client/server.

WHOIS.why: The document specifies a modified use of WHOIS (one company name per line, URL plus name responses, variation prefixes) and a demo WHOIS server and client.
WHOIS.quote: This document proposes a company name to URL mapping service based on the oldest and least complex of Internet directory protocols, whois

rejected.why: DNS naming conventions are the motivating problem, but the document proposes a directory lookup instead and specifies nothing about DNS.
Mentioned only as an alternative not chosen.
Only listed as an alternative directory protocol not used.
Only listed as an alternative directory protocol not used.
URLs are the returned data, but the document does not define or extend URL syntax, apart from the demo client's WHO:// moniker.
Variation 1 uses UTF-8, but this is a minor detail and not the subject of the document.

RFC2346.title: Making Postscript and PDF International
RFC2346.summary: Informational advice on setting margins (or print scaling) so PostScript and PDF documents print correctly on both North American Letter and ISO A4 paper.

rejected.why: The document names the application/postscript and application/pdf MIME types only to identify the formats. It does not register them or discuss registry rules.
MIME is cited only for the type names and, in the Security Considerations, for PostScript's known risks. The body is not about MIME body structure or encodings.
The document says it is not intended for HTML. It mentions HTML only in passing, for fixed-size graphics.
The 'international' in the title means paper-size portability. It does not mean text internationalization such as character sets or language tags.

gaps.name: PostScript and PDF document formats / paper sizes (Letter vs A4)
gaps.why: The whole document concerns page-layout formats and printable margins for PostScript and PDF. The taxonomy has no tag for page description or document formats, or for printing.

RFC2347.title: TFTP Option Extension
RFC2347.summary: RFC 2347 defines a backward-compatible option negotiation extension for TFTP, adding options to RRQ/WRQ packets, a new OACK packet, and error code 8.

TFTP.why: The document specifies the TFTP option negotiation mechanism, the OACK packet and error code 8, updating RFC 1350.
TFTP.quote: This document describes a simple extension to TFTP to allow option negotiation prior to the file transfer.

rejected.why: FTP is a different protocol; TFTP is the separate child-level tech here and the document is not about FTP.
TFTP runs over UDP but the document does not specify anything about UDP; it is only the substrate.
Option names and values are case-insensitive ASCII strings, merely an encoding detail rather than the subject.

RFC2348.title: TFTP Blocksize Option
RFC2348.summary: Defines the TFTP "blksize" option, which lets a client and server negotiate a data block size (8 to 65464 octets) instead of the fixed 512 octets, with performance measurements showing the benefit.

TFTP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to TFTP, modifying the read/write request packets and the OACK negotiation.
TFTP.quote: This document describes a TFTP option which allows the client and server to negotiate a blocksize more applicable to the network medium.

rejected.why: TFTP runs over UDP, but the document only mentions UDP header length in an example. UDP is the substrate and is not specified or extended here.
The document notes that a blocksize above the path MTU causes IP fragmentation. This is a passing remark and not about path MTU discovery.
TFTP is a different protocol from FTP, so this tag does not apply.

RFC2349.title: TFTP Timeout Interval and Transfer Size Options
RFC2349.summary: Defines two TFTP options, timeout interval negotiation and transfer size (tsize), carried in read/write requests and acknowledged via OACK.

TFTP.why: The document extends TFTP with the timeout and tsize options, modifying RRQ/WRQ packets and using OACK.
TFTP.quote: This document describes two TFTP options. The first allows the client and server to negotiate the Timeout Interval.

rejected.why: TFTP is a distinct protocol with its own tag; FTP is not discussed.
No IANA section in the body; the options are defined only in the protocol specification.

RFC2350.title: Expectations for Computer Security Incident Response
RFC2350.summary: BCP 21 describes the Internet community's expectations of Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) and gives a template, with a filled-in example, for CSIRTs to publish their policies, services, contacts and disclosure practices.

incident response.why: The whole document is about how CSIRTs operate, what services they offer, how they cooperate and disclose information, and how they describe this to constituents. Incident response is the subject page where it belongs.
incident response.quote: The purpose of this document is to express the general Internet community's expectations of Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs).

rejected.why: The document does not define an incident data format. It only mentions incident reporting forms such as the CERT/CC form.
The document covers organisation and policy of response teams, not operational security practices for network infrastructure. The Site Security Handbook it cites is a separate document.
PGP is recommended as a way to secure communications but only in passing, and the document explicitly says the technical details are out of scope.
The more specific child, incident response, fits. The document says it is not concerned with the security of protocols themselves.

RFC2351.title: Mapping of Airline Reservation, Ticketing, and Messaging Traffic over IP
RFC2351.summary: RFC 2351 (MATIP) defines how airline Type A (reservation/ticketing) and Type B (messaging) traffic is mapped over TCP ports 350/351, specifying session open/confirm/close commands and data packet formats.

transport mapping.why: The document specifies a shim layer mapping airline-specific protocols (P1024B, P1024C, Type B/BATAP) onto TCP connections, with session establishment and packet formats.
transport mapping.quote: The purpose of this RFC is to define the mapping of the airline traffic types over TCP/IP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate; the document defines a layer above it, plus port allocation, not TCP itself.
Mentioned only optionally in Security Considerations; boilerplate-level.
AX.25 is referenced for backward compatibility of field layout, but the document is not about X.25.
Type B is described as messaging akin to e-mail, but it uses IATA formats, not Internet email.
Port allocation is a single sentence; the document is not about IANA registries.

gaps.name: MATIP / airline reservation traffic (IATA Type A and Type B)
gaps.why: The document's specific subject is an industry-specific application protocol mapping for airline reservation, ticketing and messaging, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC2352.title: A Convention For Using Legal Names as Domain Names
RFC2352.summary: An independent-submission informational memo proposing that country-code domain registries create legal-name sub-domains (e.g. LTD.UK, INC.<state>.US, TM.INT) so company and trademark names map to domain names without conflicts or TLD exhaustion.

domain registration.why: The document proposes a registry allocation policy for domain names under country TLDs, tying registration to legal name registries and addressing name exhaustion and disputes.
domain registration.quote: The registry for the appropriate upper level country, state, province or locality domain should create entries in these sub-domains based on the laws for allocating such legal names

rejected.why: The document discusses the DNS namespace structure only as the setting for a registration/naming convention; it does not specify protocol, records or resolver behaviour.
Section 4.5 only notes that names are limited to ASCII per RFC 1035; it defines nothing about internationalized domain names.
Parent of domain registration, which fits more specifically.
The mention of the INT gTLD for international trademarks is a convention proposal, not about reserved or special-use names.

gaps.name: Domain name policy / trademark and legal-name disputes
gaps.why: The document is about the policy of allocating domain names by legal name and avoiding trademark disputes and TLD exhaustion, which the taxonomy covers only loosely under domain registration.

RFC2353.title: APPN/HPR in IP Networks APPN Implementers' Workshop Closed Pages Document
RFC2353.summary: Informational AIW Closed Pages document specifying a native IP data link control (HPR/IP) that lets APPN High Performance Routing nodes run over UDP/IP, including port and link activation, connection networks, XID changes, IP prioritization, and MIB rules.

APPN.why: The whole document specifies APPN/HPR over IP, covering APPN connection networks, transmission groups, XID negotiation and COS.
APPN.quote: This memo defines a method with which HPR nodes can use IP networks for communication, and the enhancements to APPN required by this method.

rejected.why: UDP is the transport substrate for the native IP DLC. Only the use of ports 12000-12004 is specified, and UDP itself is not extended.
IPv4 is the carrier network. Its header fields are used, but the document is not about IPv4.
DLSw is only mentioned as an existing integration technique that HPR/IP improves on.
RSVP is mentioned only as a possible future extension, not specified.
IP precedence mapping is described, but this is not Diffserv work.
Section 2.8 gives only a few rules for returning values in the existing APPN MIB, so the document is not about MIB modules.

gaps.name: APPN/HPR
gaps.why: The taxonomy has APPN only as a child of SNA. I used APPN, but the HPR and RTP specifics have no separate tag.

RFC2354.title: Options for Repair of Streaming Media
RFC2354.summary: Informational survey of sender-involved techniques for repairing packet loss in RTP/UDP continuous media streams: retransmission, forward error correction, redundancy and interleaving, with recommendations and TCP-friendly loss guidance.

FEC.why: The core of the document is loss-recovery schemes for packet streams: media-independent and media-specific FEC, retransmission and interleaving. This is what the FEC tag covers.
FEC.quote: The techniques discussed include redundant transmission, retransmission, interleaving and forward error correction.

RTP.why: The repair techniques are framed around RTP sequence numbers, timestamps and payload formats, including redundant audio and generic FEC payloads. The document does not specify RTP itself, but RTP readers would want it.
RTP.quote: The framework of RTP [18] is assumed.  This implies that packets have a sequence number and timestamp.

rejected.why: Section 5 discusses congestion control and a TCP-friendly loss rate formula. This is a side recommendation, not the main subject.
The document refers to payload formats for redundancy and FEC but does not define any.
UDP is only the unreliable transport whose losses motivate the document.
Reliable multicast schemes such as SRM are cited only as related work for retransmission.
RTCP reception reports are mentioned once, only to estimate round-trip time in an example.

RFC2355.title: TN3270 Enhancements
RFC2355.summary: RFC 2355 specifies the TN3270E Telnet option, which negotiates 3270 terminal and printer emulation, device-name selection, and extra functions (ATTN, SYSREQ, SNA responses, BIND image) over Telnet, replacing RFC 1647.

TN3270.why: The whole document specifies TN3270E, the enhanced Telnet 3270 emulation protocol, including device-type and function negotiation and the data message header.
TN3270.quote: This protocol is negotiated under the TN3270E Telnet Option

Telnet.why: TN3270E is defined as a new Telnet option with sub-negotiation, and it uses IAC commands such as IP and AO for ATTN and SYSREQ. Telnet readers would want it.
Telnet.quote: In order to address these issues, this document proposes a new Telnet Option - TN3270E.

rejected.why: The document covers SNA bind images, response handling and SYSREQ. SNA is the environment it interworks with, not a subject it defines, and TN3270 already sits under SNA.
TCP is only the substrate. TCP keepalive appears as one keep-alive option in the guidelines.
Device names are NVT ASCII strings. This is incidental use, not a subject of the document.

RFC2356.title: Sun's SKIP Firewall Traversal for Mobile IP
RFC2356.summary: Informational RFC from Sun describing how a Mobile IP mobile node traverses a SKIP-based firewall into its private home network, using SKIP/AH/ESP tunnelling and a new Traversal Extension for Registration Requests and Replies.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IP registration and data tunnelling with a new Traversal Extension (type 129) so mobile nodes and home agents can work through firewalls.
Mobile IPv4.quote: The mechanisms described in this document allow a mobile node out on a public sector of the network to negotiate access past a SKIP firewall

firewall.why: The central subject is firewall traversal: firewall requirements, nomadic access control entries, dynamic packet filtering and secure channel configurations at the firewall.
firewall.quote: The firewall imposes restrictions on packets entering or leaving the private network.

IPsec.why: Substantial parts specify how SKIP session-less IP security with AH/ESP is used and how the NSID/MKID fields support nomadic hosts, and compare secure channel configurations.
IPsec.quote: It encrypts it using SKIP combined with the ESP [6] protocol and possibly the AH [7] protocol.

rejected.why: SOCKS v5 is discussed only as an alternative that is rejected in favour of SKIP; the document does not specify it.
Mentioned only as a cleartext encapsulation option for one configuration.
Mentioned only as a way the mobile node obtains a temporary address.
SKIP key management is the mechanism relied on, but the document does not specify key management. It is covered under the IPsec tag.
ESP is used as a component of the SKIP packet formats, but the document does not specify or extend it.

gaps.name: SKIP (Simple Key-management for Internet Protocols)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SKIP, which is central to this document. It is covered here only indirectly through IPsec.

RFC2357.title: IETF Criteria for Evaluating Reliable Multicast Transport and Application Protocols
RFC2357.summary: TSV Area Directors set out the review process and technical criteria (scalability, congestion control, security, containment) that reliable multicast protocol Internet-Drafts must meet to be published as RFCs.

reliable multicast.why: The whole document defines evaluation criteria for reliable multicast transport protocols, including scalability, error recovery, and congestion issues. It is not a specific protocol, so the parent topic fits.
reliable multicast.quote: This memo describes the procedures and criteria for reviewing reliable multicast protocols within the Transport Area (TSV) of the IETF.

congestion control.why: Section 3.2 and criteria a, c and d focus on congestion control and the risk of congestion collapse. This is a substantial part of the review criteria.
congestion control.quote: reliable multicast protocols could do great damage through causing congestion disasters if they are widely used and do not provide adequate congestion control.

rejected.why: The document describes an AD review process, but that process is specific to reliable multicast drafts. The subject is the technical evaluation, not IETF process in general.
TCP is only a comparison point for congestion behaviour and reliable unicast. The document does not specify or analyse TCP.
Criterion 5.e asks for security and key management analysis. That is a short checklist item, not a substantial treatment of group key management.

RFC2358.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types
RFC2358.summary: Defines the EtherLike-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing Ethernet-like interfaces, obsoleting RFC 1650 and adding 100 Mb/s support (dot3StatsSymbolErrors, etherStats100MbsGroup), with Interfaces MIB mappings and IEEE 802.3 object mapping.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is an SMIv2 MIB module (EtherLike-MIB) with object definitions, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The managed subject is Ethernet interfaces (802.3 statistics, collisions, tests, ifType guidance, 100 Mb/s support), so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing ethernet-like interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for; the document defines objects, not protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is only the notation underlying the SMI used to write the module.
Parent of Ethernet; Ethernet is the specific fit.
Chipset OID registrations are mentioned, but IANA registry matters are not the subject.

RFC2359.title: IMAP4 UIDPLUS extension
RFC2359.summary: RFC 2359 defines the IMAP4 UIDPLUS extension, adding the UID EXPUNGE command and the APPENDUID and COPYUID response codes to reduce client work, mainly for disconnected-use clients.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to IMAP4: a new command (UID EXPUNGE) and new response codes (APPENDUID, COPYUID). Readers of the IMAP subject would want it.
IMAP.quote: The UIDPLUS extension of the Internet Message Access Protocol [IMAP4] provides a set of features intended to reduce the amount of time and resources used by some client operations.

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The formal syntax section only uses ABNF as a notation to define the new IMAP elements. The document is not about ABNF.
The example message uses RFC 822 headers, but only as sample APPEND data. The document does not address message format.

RFC2360.title: Guide for Internet Standards Writers
RFC2360.summary: BCP 22 guide for authors of Internet standards-track specifications, giving guidelines on clarity, security discussion, options, requirement levels, notation, packet diagrams, summary tables, state machines, and a document checklist.

IETF process.why: The document guides authors on preparing standards-track specifications, including IESG requirements and progression through Proposed, Draft and Full Standard. This is IETF standards process and procedure.
IETF process.quote: It offers guidelines on how to write a standards-track document with clarity, precision, and completeness.

RFC series.why: It is a companion to the RFC author instructions and covers how RFCs are written: format, change logs, packet diagrams, glossaries and checklists.
RFC series.quote: These guidelines are to be used with RFC 2223, "Instructions to RFC Authors".

terminology.why: It sets guidance on glossaries and requirement-level key words (RFC 2119), both of which fall under terminology.
terminology.quote: Every standards track RFC should have a glossary, as words can have many meanings.

rejected.why: Section 2.1 tells authors how to write security discussions, but it is only one guideline among many. The document defines no security mechanism.
Section 2.13 is a short note telling authors to coordinate with IANA. It is not a substantial focus.
Section 2.12 discusses formal syntax notations (BNF, ASN.1) generally, in one subsection only.
Section 2.14 only requires a MIB where relevant and does not define one.
RFC 1958 is cited only as a pointer, and the document gives no architectural principles of its own.

RFC2361.title: WAVE and AVI Codec Registries
RFC2361.summary: Informational RFC defining how codecs in Microsoft's WAVE and AVI registries are referenced via the audio/vnd.wave and video/vnd.avi media types with a codec parameter, mapping them to GUIDs, and listing the registered audio and video codecs.

media types.why: The document registers/defines vendor-tree media types audio/vnd.wave and video/vnd.avi with a required codec parameter, which is media type registration.
media types.quote: video/vnd.avi; codec=XXX identifies a specific video codec (i.e., XXX) within the AVI Registry.

codecs.why: The bulk of the document enumerates audio and video codec identifiers (WAVE Format IDs and FourCCs), a codec registry.
codecs.quote: Appendix A is an authoritative list of the complete set of audio codecs that have been registered (as of January 1998) within the WAVE Registry.

UUID.why: A section defines the mapping of codec IDs into GUID/UUID values for use in ASF.
UUID.quote: WAVE Format IDs are converted to GUIDs by inserting the hexadecimal value of the WAVE Format ID into the XXXXXXXX part of the following template
UUID.section: 4 Mapping Codec IDs to GUID Values

rejected.why: Codecs are named but no RTP payload formats are defined.
RTSP is only mentioned as an example application that could use the identifiers.
SDP is only cited as a protocol that might reference the codecs.
MPEG Layer 3 is just one registry entry (A.48), not the subject.
The document is about registry references via media types, not IANA registry stewardship or guidance.
H.264 appears only as one FourCC entry in the AVI list.

RFC2362.title: Protocol Independent Multicast-Sparse Mode (PIM-SM): Protocol Specification
RFC2362.summary: Specifies PIM-SM, the experimental sparse-mode multicast routing protocol using rendezvous points, shared and shortest-path trees, Join/Prune, Register, Assert, and Bootstrap/RP-set mechanisms, with packet formats and timers.

PIM-SM.why: The whole document is the protocol specification of PIM-SM: message types, state machines, timers, RP mapping, and packet formats.
PIM-SM.quote: This document describes a protocol for efficiently routing to multicast groups that may span wide-area (and inter-domain) internets.

rejected.why: IGMP is only used by hosts to signal membership to the DR; the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned only in brief security statements (2.12, 3.10) as an option for protecting control messages; not the subject.
The PIM header checksum is just one field in the packet formats; the document is not about checksums.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific PIM-SM tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC2363.title: PPP Over FUNI
RFC2363.summary: Specifies how PPP packets are framed over ATM FUNI virtual connections, using VC-multiplexed or LLC-encapsulated (RFC 1483-style) payloads, Q.2931 SVC signalling, and LCP option restrictions.

PPP.why: The document defines how PPP is carried over FUNI, including LCP option constraints, NCP behaviour and encapsulation-transition recovery.
PPP.quote: This document describes the use of ATM Frame User Network Interface (FUNI) for framing PPP encapsulated packets.

ATM.why: FUNI is an ATM access interface. The document covers VC multiplexing, LLC encapsulation over AAL5-style framing, and Q.2931 SVC setup with B-LLI encoding.
ATM.quote: When an ATM network is configured with point-to-point connections, PPP can use FUNI as a framing mechanism.

rejected.why: Frame Relay appears only through the FRF.8 interworking exemption and RFC 1973 as a model. The document is not about it.
Not a taxonomy tag. It is mentioned only as the usual PPP framing that FUNI replaces.

RFC2364.title: PPP Over AAL5
RFC2364.summary: RFC 2364 specifies how PPP is carried over ATM AAL5 virtual connections, using VC-multiplexed or LLC-encapsulated framing, SVC signalling via Q.2931 B-LLI, and LCP option restrictions.

ATM.why: The document defines how PPP maps onto AAL5 PVCs and SVCs, including encapsulation and Q.2931 signalling. This is IP-over-ATM material.
ATM.quote: This document describes the use of ATM Adaptation Layer 5 (AAL5) for framing PPP encapsulated packets.

PPP.why: It specifies PPP framing, LCP state machine interaction, LCP option restrictions (Magic Number, PFC, ACFC, ACCM, MRU) and recovery from encapsulation changes.
PPP.quote: The PPP layer treats the underlying ATM AAL5 layer service as a bit-synchronous point-to-point link.

rejected.why: RFC 1973 and FRF.8 interworking are mentioned only as a compatibility constraint, not the subject.
PAP/CHAP are mentioned only in Security Considerations as boilerplate-level context.
It is a child of ATM that concerns NBMA address resolution, which this document does not address.

RFC2365.title: Administratively Scoped IP Multicast
RFC2365.summary: RFC 2365 (BCP 23) defines the administratively scoped IPv4 multicast address space 239.0.0.0/8, the semantics of boundary routers, its local and organization-local scopes, and a mapping to IPv6 multicast scopes.

multicast.why: The document specifies administratively scoped IP multicast: address range, scope boundaries and boundary router behaviour, replacing TTL scoping. No narrower multicast child tag fits, so the parent topic applies.
multicast.quote: defines the "administratively scoped IPv4 multicast space" to be the range 239.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255

addressing.why: A substantial part of the document partitions the IPv4 multicast address space into scopes. It also sets relative assignment rules and maps IPv4 prefixes to IPv6 scope values.
addressing.quote: 239.192.0.0/14 is defined to be the IPv4 Organization Local Scope

rejected.why: PIM-SM is only mentioned for how a boundary router treats joins in the scoped range. The document does not specify or extend it.
The IPv6 address architecture is used only as a model for the scope structure and for a mapping table. The document is not about IPv6.
The relative assignment guidelines direct requests to IANA. This is a small procedural part of the document, not its main subject.
ESP and ISAKMP appear only in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.

RFC2366.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 based ATM Networks
RFC2366.summary: Defines the MARS MIB (IPATM-IPMC-MIB) with SNMP managed objects for MARS clients, MARS servers and multicast servers (MCS) used for IP multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 ATM networks.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (tables, objects, conformance groups) for managing MARS entities, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

ATM.why: The managed objects cover ATM addresses, VCs, VPI/VCI and MARS/MCS operation for IP over ATM multicast, so readers of IP over ATM would want it.
ATM.quote: it describes managed objects for IP hosts and routers that use a Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) to support IP multicast over ATM

rejected.why: The MIB manages MARS-based multicast address resolution over ATM, but it does not specify IP multicast routing or group membership protocols; the ATM tag fits better.
SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is written for. The MIB tag is the more specific fit.
The module is written in ASN.1 SMI, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.

RFC2367.title: PF_KEY Key Management API, Version 2
RFC2367.summary: Documents PF_KEY version 2, a socket-based API between key management daemons and the kernel's Security Association Database, used mainly for IPsec but also for OSPF, RIP and similar protocols.

key management.why: The whole document specifies an API for key management applications to add, update, acquire, expire and delete security associations in the kernel Key Engine.
key management.quote: A generic key management API that can be used not only for IP Security but also for other network security services is presented in this document.

IPsec.why: IPsec is the principal consumer of the SADB. The SA types (AH, ESP), SPI handling, tunnel and proxy examples and ACQUIRE flow are IPsec-centric, so IPsec readers would want it. IKE and ISAKMP daemons are the intended users.
IPsec.quote: PF_KEY is a new socket protocol family used by trusted privileged key management applications to communicate with an operating system's key management internals

rejected.why: ISAKMP/Oakley daemons are named as users of the API, but the document does not specify IKE.
ESP and AH are only SA types the API carries, not what the document specifies.
PF_KEY is a socket protocol family, but the focus is the key-management message interface, not general sockets API extensions. Considered, but it is less apt than key management.
OSPFv2 authentication is only an example consumer of SAs.
DES, 3DES, MD5-HMAC and SHA1-HMAC are only algorithm identifiers in the registry of types.
The Sensitivity extension carries labels, but this is a minor part of the document.

gaps.name: PF_KEY / Security Association Database API
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for kernel key-management APIs. The nearest fits are key management and IPsec.

RFC2368.title: The mailto URL scheme
RFC2368.summary: Defines the mailto URL scheme for designating email addresses, extended with header and body fields so a URL can prefill an RFC 822 message, and covers its encoding, semantics and security.

URI.why: The document specifies a URI scheme: its syntax, percent-encoding rules, and resolution semantics. It updates RFC 1738 and RFC 1808.
URI.quote: This document defines the format of Uniform Resource Locators (URL) for designating electronic mail addresses.

email.why: A substantial part of the document covers how mail clients build messages from the URL: headers, body, unsafe headers and user approval before sending. Readers on email would want it. It does not specify transport or message format itself, so a more specific email child is not warranted.
email.quote: the client creates a message to the designated address with the various header fields set as default.

rejected.why: The document uses RFC 822 mailbox and header syntax as the thing the URL encodes. It does not define the message format.
SMTP is mentioned only once, in a security note about setting the From address. The document does not specify or extend it.
MIME encoded words are permitted in header values and MIME headers are flagged as unsafe. The document is not about MIME.
The only HTML content is a note that '&' must be written '&' inside HTML. That is an incidental encoding point.

RFC2369.title: The Use of URLs as Meta-Syntax for Core Mail List Commands and their Transport through Message Header Fields
RFC2369.summary: Defines the List-Help, List-Subscribe, List-Unsubscribe, List-Post, List-Owner and List-Archive email header fields, which carry URLs (usually mailto) so mail clients can offer automated mailing list commands.

mailing lists.why: The whole document specifies mailing list headers and their handling by list servers, sublists and clients.
mailing lists.quote: The mailing list command specification header fields are a set of structured fields to be added to email messages sent by email distribution lists.

message format.why: It defines new structured Internet message header fields, their syntax and processing rules, which message format readers would want.
message format.quote: The list header fields are subject to the encoding and character restrictions for mail headers as described in [RFC822].

rejected.why: URLs, notably mailto, are used as the content syntax. The document defines no new URI scheme or URI syntax.
Covered by the more specific tags mailing lists and message format.
Only mail transport is assumed. Nothing about SMTP is specified.
MIME parts were considered and rejected in the appendix. They are not the subject of the document.

RFC2370.title: The OSPF Opaque LSA Option
RFC2370.summary: Defines OSPF Opaque LSAs (types 9, 10, 11) with link-local, area-local and AS-wide flooding scopes, the O-bit capability negotiation, neighbor state machine changes, and management considerations, as a generic extensibility mechanism for OSPF.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with a new LSA class, flooding scope rules, O-bit option, and changes to the neighbor state machine.
OSPF.quote: This memo defines enhancements to the OSPF protocol to support a new class of link-state advertisements (LSA) called Opaque LSAs.

rejected.why: Section 5 lists OSPF MIB objects needed for Opaque support but only as management considerations; no MIB module is defined.
Security Considerations restate existing OSPF authentication and are boilerplate; the document is not about routing security.
MOSPF is only mentioned in describing the MC-bit of the Options field.
The IANA section only sets the Opaque type allocation policy; it is boilerplate rather than the document's subject.

RFC2371.title: Transaction Internet Protocol Version 3.0
RFC2371.summary: Specifies TIP 3.0, a simple two-phase commit protocol letting transaction managers on different Internet nodes agree atomically on a transaction's outcome, with a tip: URL scheme and an optional TIP Multiplexing Protocol appendix.

TIP.why: The whole document defines the Transaction Internet Protocol: its commands, responses, connection states, and failure recovery.
TIP.quote: This memo proposes a very simple two-phase commit protocol.

rejected.why: TLS is only an optional security layer for TIP connections via the TLS command; nothing new is defined about TLS itself.
TCP is the substrate transport. TMP in Appendix A multiplexes over it but does not extend TCP.
The tip: URL scheme is defined, but it is a small part of the document and the scheme is not the main subject.
HTTP appears only in the shopping-basket example, not as a subject of the document.
UUIDs are only suggested as one way to ensure transaction identifier uniqueness.
URN-form transaction identifiers are referenced but not defined here.

gaps.name: two-phase commit / distributed transactions
gaps.why: The document is about atomic commitment among transaction managers, but the taxonomy has no transaction-processing topic besides the TIP tech tag.

RFC2372.title: Transaction Internet Protocol - Requirements and Supplemental Information
RFC2372.summary: Informational RFC describing usage scenarios, requirements and supplemental information (recovery, logging, example TM API) for the Transaction Internet Protocol (TIP), a two-phase commit protocol separate from the application protocol.

TIP.why: The whole document states the requirements for TIP and gives supplemental information (usage scenario, recovery, logging rules, example API) to help implement it.
TIP.quote: TIP is a 2-pc protocol which is intended to provide ubiquitous distributed transaction support, in a heterogeneous (networked) environment.

rejected.why: TLS is only the security mechanism TIP uses, mentioned briefly in Security Considerations and requirement 6. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
HTTP appears only as an example application protocol used alongside TIP in the travel agency scenario. TIP is deliberately independent of it.
TIP URLs are described as the transaction context format. They are a small part of the document, and the URL syntax belongs to the TIP specification (RFC 2371).
TCP is mentioned only as the transport, for example in the requirement of 1 to n transactions per TCP connection. It is not the subject of the document.
The scope section says TIP does not describe how business transactions or electronic commerce are conducted. Travel agency is only an example.

gaps.name: Distributed transactions / two-phase commit
gaps.why: The document is about two-phase commit distributed transaction processing (X/Open DTP, XA). The taxonomy has no general tag for it beyond the TIP protocol tag.

RFC2373.title: IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture
RFC2373.summary: RFC 2373 defines the IPv6 addressing architecture: address types (unicast, anycast, multicast), text representations, format prefixes, interface identifiers, and the addresses a node must recognize.

IPv6.why: The whole document specifies IPv6 addressing: unicast, anycast, multicast formats, text forms, and required node addresses.
IPv6.quote: This specification defines the addressing architecture of the IP Version 6 protocol.

rejected.why: The IPv6 tag is more specific and the document is about IPv6 addressing; the addressing parent is implied by IPv6 only as a sibling topic, so not added separately.
Anycast addresses are covered in one section (2.6) but the document is not primarily about anycast operation; IPv6 covers it.
Multicast address format is defined, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
CIDR is only referenced as a model for prefix notation and aggregation.
ABNF is merely used in an appendix to describe address text syntax.
Solicited-node multicast addresses support it, but ND is not specified here.

RFC2374.title: An IPv6 Aggregatable Global Unicast Address Format
RFC2374.summary: RFC 2374 defines the IPv6 aggregatable global unicast address format (FP 001, TLA, NLA, SLA, 64-bit EUI-64 interface ID) to support scalable provider- and exchange-based route aggregation, replacing RFC 2073.

IPv6.why: The document specifies an IPv6 unicast address format and its fields, which is IPv6 addressing specification.
IPv6.quote: This document defines an IPv6 aggregatable global unicast address format for use in the Internet.

addressing.why: A substantial part covers address hierarchy, allocation of TLA/NLA/SLA space and aggregation. This is IP address architecture and allocation beyond just the IPv6 spec.
addressing.quote: Aggregatable addresses are organized into a three level hierarchy: Public Topology, Site Topology, Interface Identifier
addressing.section: 3.0 IPv6 Aggregatable Global Unicast Address Format

rejected.why: Longest-prefix-match aggregation is assumed, but the document does not specify or discuss CIDR itself.
Multihoming and provider independence are mentioned as benefits, but the document explicitly says the mechanisms are out of scope.
Avoiding renumbering is a motivation, but no renumbering procedures are given.
Route aggregation is the motivation, but the document defines an address format and not routing design.

RFC2375.title: IPv6 Multicast Address Assignments
RFC2375.summary: Informational RFC listing the initial assignments of IPv6 multicast addresses (fixed-scope and all-scope groups), adapted from the IPv4 multicast assignments.

IPv6.why: The document is an IPv6 addressing companion that assigns specific IPv6 multicast addresses (FF01::1, FF02::2, etc.) per the IPv6 addressing architecture.
IPv6.quote: This document defines the initial assignment of IPv6 multicast addresses.

multicast.why: It catalogues well-known multicast groups (all nodes, all routers, PIM routers, OSPF, DHCP agents, etc.) that readers of IP multicast would look up.
multicast.quote: IPv6 multicast addresses which are only different in scope represent different groups.  Nodes must join each group individually.

rejected.why: Broadly relevant, but IPv6 and multicast already capture the subject; the document does not discuss address architecture or allocation policy itself.
The list later became a registry, but the document itself is an assignment list, not guidance on IANA registries or stewardship.
MADCAP covers dynamic multicast address allocation; this document only lists static permanent assignments.
OSPF, RIP, EIGRP, PIM, NTP, SLP and others appear only as entries in the assignment table, not as subjects of the document.

RFC2376.title: XML Media Types
RFC2376.summary: Registers the text/xml and application/xml MIME media types for XML entities, specifying the charset parameter, encoding considerations, BOM handling and examples.

media types.why: The document is a media type registration for text/xml and application/xml, with the registration templates for each.
media types.quote: This document introduces two new media types for XML entities, text/xml and application/xml.

XML.why: The media types label XML entities. The document covers how XML encoding declarations and the charset parameter interact, and the security issues of XML entity expansion.
XML.quote: for use in exchanging network entities which are conforming Extensible Markup Language (XML)

character sets.why: A large part of the document covers charset parameter semantics: defaults, UTF-8 and UTF-16 choices, BOM handling, and ISO-2022-KR examples.
character sets.quote: the use of the charset parameter is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED, since this information can be used by XML processors to determine authoritatively the charset

rejected.why: HTTP is only a transport that carries the XML entities. The document notes HTTP's exemption from the MIME text restrictions but does not specify or extend HTTP.
The document registers media types and relies on MIME conventions, but the media types tag fits more specifically.
SGML is mentioned only to justify why separate XML types are needed, not as a subject of the document.
WebDAV is cited only as a motivating user of XML. The document does not specify it.
UTF-8 is a recommended charset value, not the subject. The character sets tag covers the charset discussion.

RFC2377.title: Naming Plan for Internet Directory-Enabled Applications
RFC2377.summary: Informational RFC proposing a directory naming plan for LDAP/X.500-style directories that builds upper DN levels from DNS domain names (dc attributes) and names leaf objects with uid or cn, including schema and name form definitions.

LDAP.why: The plan defines how LDAP distinguished names are constructed, plus auxiliary object classes (uidObject) and name forms for LDAP/X.500 servers. It is about LDAP directory naming and schema.
LDAP.quote: The upper portions of the hierarchical directory tree should be constructed using the components of registered DNS names using the domain component attribute "dc".

X.500.why: The plan is positioned as an alternative or extension to X.500 naming. Section 2 analyses the X.500 and NADF naming problems in detail, and the schema and name forms extend X.500 constructs.
X.500.quote: Application of the conventional X.500 approach to naming has heretofore, in the experience of the authors, proven to be an obstacle

rejected.why: DNS names are reused as the basis for DNs, but the document does not specify or extend DNS. DNS is the source registry, not the subject.
The document is about naming, but the more specific directory tags (LDAP, X.500) fit. The generic naming topic is not also needed.
RFC822 mailbox identifiers are used as an example source for uid values, but the document is not about email.
This is the parent of LDAP and X.500, which are both tagged, so it is implied.

RFC2378.title: The CCSO Nameserver (Ph) Architecture
RFC2378.summary: Informational RFC formally defining the CCSO Nameserver (Ph) client-server protocol: its information model of fields, command language, response codes, and authentication options for a people/white-pages directory.

directory services.why: Ph is a white-pages directory service for information about people and objects; the RFC specifies its data model, commands and responses. No Ph-specific tag exists, so the directory services topic is the best fit.
directory services.quote: It is in short a nameserver for people and objects.

rejected.why: Despite the 'Nameserver' name, Ph is not the Domain Name System; DNS is only referenced for client hostname checks in email login.
Kerberos is one of several optional authentication methods listed for xlogin; it is not specified here.
Only listed as an authentication option and referenced; the document defines nothing about it.
Ph is a similar white-pages service, but it is a distinct protocol and does not fall under registration data directory services.
The login methods are a part of the protocol but not the main subject, so I did not tag this separately.
TCP is only the transport (port 105).

gaps.name: CCSO Nameserver (Ph/Qi)
gaps.why: The document specifies this specific white-pages protocol, and the taxonomy has no tech tag for it. Only the generic directory services topic applies.

RFC2379.title: RSVP over ATM Implementation Guidelines
RFC2379.summary: BCP giving implementation guidelines for running RSVP over ATM SVCs: RSVP message VC usage, aggregation, short-cuts, and VC management for heterogeneous multicast sessions.

RSVP.why: The document specifies how RSVP should be implemented and operated over ATM, including message VC usage and reservations per VC.
RSVP.quote: presents specific implementation guidelines for running RSVP over ATM switched virtual circuits (SVCs)

ATM.why: It covers IP over ATM SVCs, short-cuts across LIS boundaries and VC management, so ATM readers would want it.
ATM.quote: discusses running IP over ATM in an environment where SVCs are used to support QoS flows

rejected.why: NHRP is cited only as the definition of unicast short-cuts. The document is not about NHRP itself.
QoS is the context, but RSVP is the more specific tag and already sits under QoS.
Heterogeneous multicast VC handling is only one section. The document is about RSVP over ATM, not multicast routing or membership.
Integrated Services mappings are covered in a separate RFC (2381). This document only mentions them.

RFC2380.title: RSVP over ATM Implementation Requirements
RFC2380.summary: RFC 2380 specifies mandatory implementation requirements for running RSVP over ATM SVCs, covering VC initiation, teardown, dynamic QoS, encapsulation, and multicast handling, to ensure interoperability.

RSVP.why: The document specifies how RSVP reservations map onto ATM VCs, including receiver-oriented RESV handling, dynamic QoS changes and heterogeneous multicast receivers.
RSVP.quote: This memo presents specific implementation requirements for running RSVP over ATM switched virtual circuits (SVCs).

ATM.why: The requirements concern ATM SVC setup, teardown, inactivity timers, LLC encapsulation (RFC 1483) and point-to-multipoint VCs for IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: RSVP over ATM implementations MAY send data in the backwards direction on an RSVP initiated QoS point-to-point VC.

rejected.why: Integrated Services is the service model RSVP carries, but the ATM service mappings are in a separate document (RFC 2381). This document does not specify Intserv itself.
Multicast data distribution (mesh and server modes) is a substantial section. It is about multicast over ATM VCs, not IP multicast routing or group membership, so I did not tag it.
QoS is the goal, but RSVP is the more specific tag for the signalling architecture covered here.
IPv4 and IPv6 are mentioned only as an assumption, and the document requires neither.

RFC2381.title: Interoperation of Controlled-Load Service and Guaranteed Service with ATM
RFC2381.summary: Specifies how IP Integrated Services Guaranteed Service and Controlled-Load Service (and best effort) map onto ATM service categories, traffic descriptors, QoS parameters and UNI signalling for IP/ATM edge devices.

ATM.why: The whole document defines VC setup parameters, service categories and UNI signalling encodings for carrying IP integrated services over ATM subnetworks.
ATM.quote: This document provides guidelines for mapping service classes, and traffic management features and parameters between Internet and ATM technologies.

Intserv.why: It maps Guaranteed and Controlled-Load services, TSpec/RSpec and Adspec parameters to ATM, which is integrated services interoperation.
Intserv.quote: The IP services considered are Guaranteed Service (GS) [9] and Controlled Load Service (CLS) [10].

RSVP.why: RESV triggers the service mapping, and PATH Adspec/GCP handling and slack term use at ATM edges are covered substantially.
RSVP.quote: This document is intended to be consistent with the rsvp protocol [3] for IP-level resource reservation

rejected.why: The more specific children Intserv and RSVP are tagged, so the parent is implied.
TCP is mentioned only in connection with frame discard and ABR design, and is not a subject of the document.
IP is the carried protocol, but the document is about service mapping, not IP itself.

RFC2382.title: A Framework for Integrated Services and RSVP over ATM
RFC2382.summary: Informational framework document from the ISSLL ISATM subgroup outlining issues and approaches for running IP Integrated Services and RSVP over ATM, including VC management, QoS mapping, multicast heterogeneity and encapsulation.

RSVP.why: The document is about how RSVP signalling and reservations operate over ATM, including VC management for RSVP data and control messages.
RSVP.quote: This document outlines the issues and framework related to providing IP Integrated Services with RSVP over ATM.

Intserv.why: It frames mapping of IntServ models (Controlled Load, Guaranteed Service) to ATM QoS and service categories.
Intserv.quote: A key remaining issue for IP in an ATM environment is the integration of RSVP signalling and ATM signalling in support of the Internet Integrated Services (IIS) model.

ATM.why: Covers IP over ATM: UNI 3.x/4.0, PVCs/SVCs, point-to-multipoint VCs, Classical IP, MARS, LANE, and RFC1483 encapsulation.
ATM.quote: One of the important features of ATM technology is the ability to request a point-to-point Virtual Circuit (VC) with a specified Quality of Service (QoS).

rejected.why: Mentioned as a short-cut mechanism but only briefly discussed; not a main subject.
Multicast heterogeneity and MARS are discussed, but within the RSVP/ATM VC management context; ATM tag covers it.
Parent of RSVP and Intserv, which are already tagged.
Label switching only mentioned as a possible future interaction.

RFC2383.title: ST2+ over ATM Protocol Specification - UNI 3.1 Version
RFC2383.summary: Specifies how ST2+ (RFC 1819) streams run over ATM UNI 3.1, mapping one ST2+ hop to one ATM VC, with AAL5 encapsulation, FlowSpec-to-traffic-descriptor mapping, SCMP/UNI signalling interaction, and RFC 1819 errata.

ST-II.why: The document extends and revises RFC 1819 ST2+ (new SCMP element, reason codes, modified JOIN-REJECT processing, errata), so it is about ST2+.
ST-II.quote: This document specifies an ATM-based protocol for communication between ST2+ agents.

ATM.why: It defines IP-layer stream protocol interaction with ATM on the UNI: AAL5 encapsulation, SVC/PVC use, UNI 3.1 signalling and traffic descriptor coding.
ATM.quote: The ST2+ over ATM protocol supports the matching of one hop in an ST2+ tree-structure stream with one ATM connection.

Intserv.why: A substantial part defines the Controlled-Load FlowSpec format and its mapping to ATM VBR/UBR parameters.
Intserv.quote: The ST2+ over ATM protocol specifies the ST FlowSpec format for the Integrated Services.

rejected.why: Only listed as a protocol to coexist with; not specified or extended.
QoS mapping is covered, but the Intserv tag already fits more specifically.
RSVP appears only in a reference on Integrated Services; not the subject.
Only mentioned for coexistence with RFC 1483 IPv4 encapsulation.

RFC2384.title: POP URL Scheme
RFC2384.summary: Defines the "pop" URL scheme for referencing a POP3 mailbox, including optional user, authentication mechanism (SASL, APOP, extensions), host and port, with ABNF and examples.

URI.why: The document's purpose is to define a new URL scheme, with syntax, ABNF, relative-URL rules and encoding rules.
URI.quote: This memo defines a URL scheme for referencing a POP mailbox.

POP3.why: The scheme identifies POP3 mailboxes and maps URLs to POP3 commands (USER, APOP, AUTH). Readers of POP3 would want it.
POP3.quote: The POP URL scheme designates a POP server, and optionally a port number, authentication mechanism, authentication ID, and/or authorization ID.

rejected.why: SASL mechanisms are referenced for the auth parameter, but the document does not specify or extend SASL.
ABNF is only the notation used to describe the URL syntax.
IMAP and its URL scheme are mentioned only as an analogy and a model.
ACAP is cited only as a motivating use case.
UTF-8 is mentioned in a single sentence about URL encoding, which is not enough to make the document about it.

RFC2385.title: Protection of BGP Sessions via the TCP MD5 Signature Option
RFC2385.summary: Defines a new TCP option (kind 19) carrying an MD5 digest over the segment and a shared key, to protect BGP sessions against spoofed TCP segments such as resets.

TCP.why: The document specifies a new TCP option, its syntax, processing rules and implications for TCP (MSS, header size, resets), so it is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: It defines a new TCP option for carrying an MD5 [RFC1321] digest in a TCP segment.

BGP.why: The stated motivation and application is protecting BGP sessions, including operational effects on BGP recovery from peer crashes. Readers of BGP would want it.
BGP.quote: This memo describes a TCP extension to enhance security for BGP.

MD5.why: The option's digest is MD5 and the document discusses its suitability and weakness as a hashing algorithm for this use.
MD5.quote: the MD5 algorithm has been found to be vulnerable to collision search attacks [Dobb]

rejected.why: Concerns securing BGP sessions, but the more specific BGP and TCP tags cover it; the document is not about routing security mechanisms such as RPKI or BGPsec.
The digest is a keyed MD5 hash by appending the key, not HMAC.
It does provide segment authentication, but the TCP tag is more specific and no separate authentication subject is addressed.

RFC2386.title: A Framework for QoS-based Routing in the Internet
RFC2386.summary: Informational framework for QoS-based routing in the Internet, describing issues, intradomain requirements, an interdomain routing model, and QoS multicast routing, extending the intra/interdomain routing split to support QoS.

routing architecture.why: The document is an architectural framework for QoS routing: issues, intradomain requirements, interdomain model, scalability and aggregation. It fits routing architecture best.
routing architecture.quote: This framework is based on extending the current Internet routing model of intra and interdomain routing to support QoS.

QoS.why: QoS requirements, admission control, and the interaction with reservation protocols (RSVP, Integrated Services) are a substantial part of the document.
QoS.quote: QoS-based routing: A routing mechanism under which paths for flows are determined based on some knowledge of resource availability in the network as well as the QoS requirement of flows.

multicast.why: Section 6 and parts of Section 3 are devoted to QoS-based multicast routing, covering source routing versus receiver-oriented models and multicast admission control.
multicast.quote: QoS-based multicast routing is an important problem, especially if the notion of higher level admission control is included.

rejected.why: BGP-4 is mentioned only as a protocol that could be QoS-enhanced. The document does not specify or analyse BGP.
RSVP is discussed only in terms of its interaction with QoS routing, and the document says it does not specify that interface.
OSPF and QOSPF are cited as examples and related work, not specified or extended here.
The document is about QoS routing and resource-aware path selection but does not address MPLS-style traffic engineering.
Integrated Services is background for the QoS classes, not the subject of the document.
PNNI and ATM routing appear only in the related-work survey.

gaps.name: QoS-based routing
gaps.why: The document is about routing that selects paths using resource availability and flow QoS requirements. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for it. The closest fits are routing architecture and QoS.

RFC2387.title: The MIME Multipart/Related Content-type
RFC2387.summary: Defines the MIME Multipart/Related media type for compound objects made of inter-related body parts, with its type, start and start-info parameters, Content-Disposition handling, and user agent requirements.

MIME.why: The document defines a new MIME multipart subtype, its parameters, and how user agents must process body parts. That is MIME body structure.
MIME.quote: The Multipart/Related content-type provides a common mechanism for representing objects that are aggregates of related MIME body parts.

media types.why: It includes a media type registration for multipart/related with its required and optional parameters. The registration is a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: Media Type name:           Multipart

rejected.why: This RFC is the foundation MHTML builds on, but it does not specify HTML aggregation. The cid: URL use appears only as an example, and it says that use is not part of the specification.
MIME user agents are discussed, but the document is about the MIME body structure, not email architecture or transport.
It deals with MIME entity structure and Content-* headers, not RFC 822 headers or addressing.
The cid: scheme is mentioned only in an example and is explicitly outside the specification.

RFC2388.title: Returning Values from Forms: multipart/form-data
RFC2388.summary: Defines the multipart/form-data MIME media type for returning form field values, including per-part Content-Disposition names, filenames, charsets and encodings, and registers the type.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new MIME media type (Appendix A), so it belongs under media type registrations.
media types.quote: This specification defines an Internet Media Type, multipart/form-data, which can be used by a wide variety of applications

MIME.why: The body specifies a multipart MIME structure, using Content-Disposition, content-transfer-encoding and RFC 2047/2231 encodings of names and filenames.
MIME.quote: The media-type multipart/form-data follows the rules of all multipart MIME data streams as outlined in [RFC 2046].

rejected.why: HTTP is one transport for the form data, but the document defines the representation independently of it.
HTML forms are the originating use case, but the document explicitly defines the format independently of HTML.
Email is a possible transport, but the document is not about email.
The charset parameter and non-ASCII names are handled only briefly via existing MIME mechanisms.

RFC2389.title: Feature negotiation mechanism for the File Transfer Protocol
RFC2389.summary: RFC 2389 extends FTP with the FEAT command, which lets a client discover the extensions a server supports, and the OPTS command, which lets it set options for other commands.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with new commands (FEAT and OPTS) and defines their syntax and replies. A reader browsing FTP would expect to find it.
FTP.quote: This document amends the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) [1].  Two new commands are added: "FEAT" and "OPTS".

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to specify command and reply syntax. The document is not about it.
ASCII is mentioned only as the character set underlying the token definitions, not as a subject of the document.
The more specific FTP tag already covers this topic.

RFC2390.title: Inverse Address Resolution Protocol
RFC2390.summary: RFC 2390 specifies Inverse ARP (InARP), an extension of ARP letting a station learn the protocol address for a known hardware address (e.g., a Frame Relay DLCI), with Frame Relay encapsulation and procedures.

ARP.why: The document defines InARP, an extension of ARP with new opcodes and operation, so it belongs on the ARP page.
ARP.quote: This memo describes additions to ARP that will allow a station to request a protocol address corresponding to a given hardware address.

frame relay.why: Frame Relay is the principal motivating environment, with DLCI/Q.922 address handling and encapsulation detailed.
frame relay.quote: In a frame relay environment, InARP packets are encapsulated using the NLPID/SNAP format defined in [3] which indicates the ARP protocol.

rejected.why: IP is only used as an example protocol address type; the document is not about IPv4.
Mentioned nowhere; NHRP/ATM resolution is not addressed, only similar networks in general terms.

RFC2391.title: Load Sharing using IP Network Address Translation (LSNAT)
RFC2391.summary: Informational RFC extending NAT to load sharing (LSNAT and LS-NAPT), where a router binds inbound sessions to servers in a pool chosen by real-time load-share algorithms, with dead-host detection.

NAT.why: The whole document specifies a NAT variant (LSNAT/LS-NAPT) for load sharing, including session binding, translation and unbinding phases, and its interaction with Basic NAT and NAPT.
NAT.quote: we extend the use of NATs to offer Load share feature, where session load can be distributed across a pool of servers

rejected.why: DNS round-robin reordering is mentioned only as prior art that LSNAT improves on; the document is not about DNS.
TCP session start and end detection is discussed only as needed for NAT state; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Cost-based server selection consults RIP/OSPF routing tables, but this is peripheral to the document.
The document covers enterprise or server-pool NAT, not carrier-grade NAT.

gaps.name: Server load balancing
gaps.why: The document's main subject is distributing sessions across a server pool using load-share algorithms, and the taxonomy has no load-balancing tag. NAT is the closest fit.

RFC2392.title: Content-ID and Message-ID Uniform Resource Locators
RFC2392.summary: RFC 2392 defines the "cid:" and "mid:" URL schemes for referring to MIME message body parts by Content-ID and to messages by Message-ID, obsoleting RFC 2111.

URI.why: The document defines the syntax and semantics of two new URL schemes, including encoding rules and conversion to Content-ID/Message-ID headers.
URI.quote: The Uniform Resource Locator (URL) schemes, "cid:" and "mid:" allow references to messages and the body parts of messages.

MIME.why: The cid scheme addresses MIME body parts via Content-ID, with rules for multipart/alternate and multipart/related selection. Readers of MIME would want it.
MIME.quote: The "cid" scheme refers to a specific body part of a message; its use is generally limited to references to other body parts in the same message

rejected.why: The RFC was produced by the MHTML working group and supports HTML in mail, but it only defines URL schemes. Bundling HTML with inline resources is specified in other documents.
It relies on Message-ID and addr-spec from RFC 822 but does not specify or extend the message format.
HTML appears only as an example context for cid references; the document does not specify HTML.
Email is the environment in which the URLs are used, but the document is about the URL schemes, so the more specific tags fit better.

RFC2393.title: IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp)
RFC2393.summary: RFC 2393 specifies IPComp, a stateless lossless IP payload compression protocol with its header format, IPv4/IPv6 header modifications, non-expansion policy, and IPComp Association negotiation.

IPComp.why: The document is the specification of IPComp itself, so the IPComp tag is the exact fit.
IPComp.quote: This document defines the IP payload compression protocol (IPComp), the IPComp packet structure, the IPComp Association (IPCA), and several methods to negotiate the IPCA.

rejected.why: IPsec is only the context. IPComp is applied before IPsec processing and IPCA negotiation can use ISAKMP, but the document does not specify IPsec.
ISAKMP is only one way to negotiate the IPCA, and the document merely names the proposal and transform payloads. It defines nothing new about IKE.
IPv6 header handling is covered, but only as part of the IPComp encapsulation rules, so the document is not about IPv6 itself.
IPComp compresses payloads, not protocol headers, so it does not belong under header compression.
PPP CCP is mentioned only as a lower-layer compression example that encryption makes ineffective.

RFC2394.title: IP Payload Compression Using DEFLATE
RFC2394.summary: Informational RFC defining how the DEFLATE algorithm is used as a compression method within the IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp), including thresholds and the ISAKMP transform ID.

IPComp.why: The document specifies the DEFLATE transform for IPComp, covering compression and decompression, thresholds and the transform ID.
IPComp.quote: This document defines the application of the DEFLATE algorithm to the IP Payload Compression Protocol.

rejected.why: DEFLATE is the algorithm being applied, but the document defers to RFC 1951 for the format and does not specify it. It is used inside IPComp, so the more specific IPComp tag fits.
The document mentions the IPsec transform identifier and ISAKMP, but only to assign a transform ID. It is not about IPsec itself.
The zlib library is cited as an implementation source and for its licence, but the document is not about the zlib format.
gzip is mentioned only as an example of a compressor that uses DEFLATE.

RFC2395.title: IP Payload Compression Using LZS
RFC2395.summary: Informational RFC defining how the LZS lossless compression algorithm is applied as a compression method for the IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp), including history reset, encoding, decompression and ISAKMP/manual association parameters.

LZS.why: The document defines LZS compression of IP payloads, its encoding format and compression/decompression process; LZS is a named compression technology.
LZS.quote: This document specifies the application of LZS compression, a lossless compression algorithm, to IP datagram payloads.

IPComp.why: The document is a transform specification for IPComp, defining the IPCOMP_LZS transform ID, CPI use, and per-datagram history handling.
IPComp.quote: This document defines the application of the LZS algorithm to the IP Payload Compression Protocol [IPCOMP].

rejected.why: ISAKMP/IPsec DOI is only used to negotiate the transform; the document is not about IPsec itself.
Only mentions that ISAKMP MAY negotiate the LZS transform ID; no new IKE behaviour is defined beyond a transform ID reference.
RFC 1967 (LZS-DCP) is acknowledged as similar, but the document does not address PPP.
Different compression algorithm; not discussed.

RFC2396.title: Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI): Generic Syntax
RFC2396.summary: RFC 2396 defines the generic syntax of Uniform Resource Identifiers, including absolute and relative forms, character escaping, URI references with fragments, and relative reference resolution, replacing the generic parts of RFC 1738 and RFC 1808.

URI.why: The whole document specifies URI generic syntax: components, escaping, references, relative resolution, normalization. This is the core URI specification.
URI.quote: This document defines the generic syntax of URI, including both absolute and relative forms, and guidelines for their use

rejected.why: URNs are mentioned only to define the term and point to RFC 2141; the document does not specify URN syntax or namespaces.
http URLs are used as examples and in the security considerations, but HTTP itself is not specified or extended.
Appendix D shows embedding a BASE URI in HTML only as a descriptive, non-normative example.
The host component syntax follows RFC 1034/1123 hostnames, but the document merely reuses that syntax as part of the URI authority.
Non-ASCII characters are explicitly out of scope and deferred to a future document.
The BNF grammar is just the notation used to define URI syntax, not the subject of the document.

RFC2397.title: The "data" URL scheme
