RFC2397.summary: Defines the "data" URL scheme, which embeds small media-typed data items inline in a URL, with syntax, base64 option, examples, and security notes.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme, its syntax and semantics, so readers of URI schemes would expect it.
URI.quote: A new URL scheme, "data", is defined. It allows inclusion of small data items as "immediate" data, as if it had been included externally.

rejected.why: Base64 is only used as an encoding option within the scheme; the document does not define or extend it.
Media types are embedded in the URL but the document does not register or define media type rules.
MIME tokens and base64 are imported for syntax only; the document is not about MIME.
HTML appears only as an example context and for attribute length limits, not as the subject.
The document concerns URLs only, not internationalized identifiers.

RFC2398.title: Some Testing Tools for TCP Implementors
RFC2398.summary: RFC 2398 (FYI 33) catalogues available tools for testing TCP implementations, describing each tool's category, automation, availability and environment.

TCP.why: The whole document is about testing, evaluating and analysing TCP implementations (correctness, performance, stress), so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: Available tools for testing TCP implementations are catalogued by this memo.

benchmarking.why: Many of the catalogued tools (netperf, ttcp, TReno, dbs) are throughput and latency measurement and benchmarking tools, and the document gives a performance-test category for them.
benchmarking.quote: Performance tests how quickly a TCP implementation can send and receive data, etc.

rejected.why: Considered, but benchmarking fits better. The tools are mostly implementation test and load tools, not network performance metrics or methods.
Netperf, ttcp and TReno use UDP, but only as a test traffic type. The document is not about UDP.
The memo is FYI 33, but its subject is TCP testing tools, not a general introductory guide for users.
Several tools read tcpdump or snoop traces, but the document does not address capture formats or capture itself.

RFC2399.title: Request for Comments Summary
RFC2399.summary: RFC 2399 is a slightly annotated index of RFCs 2300 through 2399, giving each one's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a catalogue of a block of RFC series publications. It is a publication-series summary, so readers of the RFC series subject would expect it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2300 through RFCs 2399.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: It marks documents as [STANDARDS-TRACK] and points to the Official Protocol Standards list. That is only labelling. The document does not describe the process.
The list includes April 1 RFCs such as 2324 and 2325, but they are only entries. The document itself is not humorous.
Entries such as RFC 2396 and the mailto, data and cid URL scheme RFCs are only listed. The document is not about URIs.
Many ATM-related RFCs are listed, but only as index entries. The document does not address ATM.

RFC2400.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2400.summary: RFC 2400 (STD 1) is the IAB's periodic list of Internet official protocol standards, explaining the standards process, maturity levels and requirement levels, and listing protocols by standardization state.

IETF process.why: The document explains the standards track, maturity levels, requirement levels and the RFC processing decision table, and lists protocols by state. This is IETF standards process content.
IETF process.quote: Protocols which are to become standards in the Internet go through a series of states or maturity levels (proposed standard, draft standard, and standard)

RFC series.why: A substantial part covers how RFCs are submitted, reviewed and published, including the RFC Editor decision table and contacts for obtaining RFCs.
RFC series.quote: All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards.

rejected.why: IANA appears as a contact and as the source of Assigned Numbers. The document is not about IANA registries.
Section 4 defines state and status terms, but these are standards-process labels and not a glossary. They are covered by the IETF process tag.
It is a status snapshot of standards in 1998. It is not a history or retrospective.
TCP and the many other protocols are only entries in the status lists. The document does not specify any of them.

RFC2401.title: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
RFC2401.summary: RFC 2401 specifies the base IPsec security architecture: security associations, the SPD and SAD, selectors, AH/ESP tunnel and transport mode combinations, IP traffic processing, ICMP/PMTU handling, and MLS use.

IPsec.why: The whole document defines the IPsec architecture: SAs, SPD/SAD, selectors, modes, and processing rules.
IPsec.quote: This memo specifies the base architecture for IPsec compliant systems.

ESP.why: The document describes how AH and ESP are used within SAs, their services, ordering and header construction, though the protocol itself is specified elsewhere.
ESP.quote: The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol [KA98b] may provide confidentiality (encryption), and limited traffic flow confidentiality.

rejected.why: IKE is only named as the default automated key management protocol; it is specified in other RFCs.
Path MTU handling for IPsec is discussed in section 6 and Appendix B, but as part of IPsec processing rather than as a PMTUD specification.
ICMP processing is discussed only as it affects IPsec (error messages and the Appendix D categorization), so the document is not about ICMP itself.
Tunnel mode is a core IPsec mode, but the document is about IPsec, so the IPsec tag covers it.
Section 8 covers MLS and IPSO sensitivity labels as an IPsec selector, but it is a minor part of the document.
Section 4.6 covers SA and key management requirements, but only as a part of the IPsec architecture.

RFC2402.title: IP Authentication Header
RFC2402.summary: Specifies the IPsec IP Authentication Header (AH), which provides connectionless integrity, data origin authentication and optional anti-replay for IPv4/IPv6 datagrams, covering header format, processing, mutable-field handling, and auditing; obsoletes RFC 1826.

IPsec.why: The document defines AH, one of the core IPsec protocols, including transport and tunnel mode processing, SA lookup, and anti-replay. IPsec is the most specific fitting tag, since AH has no child tag of its own.
IPsec.quote: The IP Authentication Header (AH) is used to provide connectionless integrity and data origin authentication for IP datagrams

rejected.why: ESP is only compared with AH and mentioned as a combinable protocol. The document does not specify it.
IKE is only mentioned as a key management option. This document does not specify it.
HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 are named as mandatory-to-implement algorithms, but their specifications are in other RFCs.
IPv6 extension header handling is covered, but only as part of ICV computation for AH. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
IPv4 header and option mutability is covered only as it affects AH. The document is not about IPv4.
Tunnel mode is an AH operating mode here, not a generic tunnelling specification.

RFC2403.title: The Use of HMAC-MD5-96 within ESP and AH
RFC2403.summary: Specifies the use of HMAC combined with MD5, truncated to 96 bits, as the authentication algorithm within IPsec ESP and AH, including key length and truncation requirements.

HMAC.why: The document defines how HMAC is used with MD5, including truncation to 96 bits and fixed 128-bit keys, so it belongs on the HMAC page.
HMAC.quote: HMAC-MD5-96 produces a 128-bit authenticator value.  This 128-bit value can be truncated as described in RFC 2104.

MD5.why: MD5 is the hash function in the specified transform, and the Security Considerations discuss its collision-resistance weaknesses in this role.
MD5.quote: This memo specifies the use of MD5 [RFC-1321] combined with HMAC [RFC-2104] as a keyed authentication mechanism

ESP.why: The document specifies an authentication transform for ESP and AH, so readers of ESP would want it. AH has no separate tag; IPsec is implied by ESP.
ESP.quote: as a keyed authentication mechanism within the context of the Encapsulating Security Payload and the Authentication Header

rejected.why: It is implied as the parent of ESP. ESP is the more specific tag for this transform.
The key length and randomness requirements are brief and specific to the transform. The document does not address key establishment itself.
SHA-1 is mentioned only as an alternative hash that could replace MD5, so the document is not about it.
Security Association negotiation is mentioned only in passing. The document does not cover key exchange.

RFC2404.title: The Use of HMAC-SHA-1-96 within ESP and AH
RFC2404.summary: Specifies the use of HMAC with SHA-1, truncated to 96 bits with 160-bit keys, as the authentication algorithm within IPsec ESP and AH.

HMAC.why: The document defines HMAC-SHA-1-96: truncation to 96 bits, fixed 160-bit key length, and keying requirements. That makes it an HMAC profile.
HMAC.quote: describes the use of the HMAC algorithm [RFC-2104] in conjunction with the SHA-1 algorithm [FIPS-180-1] as an authentication mechanism

ESP.why: The document specifies an authentication transform for ESP and AH. Readers of IPsec ESP would want it, and it also covers AH.
ESP.quote: within the context of the Encapsulating Security Payload and the Authentication Header

SHA.why: SHA-1 is the underlying hash. The document covers its block size, padding and how it is used within HMAC.
SHA.quote: HMAC-SHA-1-96 produces a 160-bit authenticator value.

rejected.why: It is the parent of ESP, which is already tagged, so it is implied. The document does not address the IPsec architecture itself.
MD5 is mentioned only as an alternative hash that could replace SHA-1 in HMAC.
Keying requirements are discussed only briefly, in relation to the 160-bit key. The document is not about key management.
Security Association negotiation is only mentioned in passing.

RFC2405.title: The ESP DES-CBC Cipher Algorithm With Explicit IV
RFC2405.summary: Specifies use of DES in CBC mode with an explicit per-packet IV as the confidentiality cipher for IPsec ESP, covering IV, padding, key material, weak keys, key lifetime and security considerations.

DES.why: The whole document defines how DES-CBC is used, including IV, key size, weak keys and brute-force key lifetime analysis, which is exactly the DES subject.
DES.quote: This document describes the use of the DES Cipher algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining Mode as a confidentiality mechanism within the context of the Encapsulating Security Payload.

ESP.why: It defines the ESP payload layout, padding and keying for a cipher transform of ESP, so readers of ESP would want it.
ESP.quote: DES-CBC requires an explicit Initialization Vector (IV) of 8 octets (64 bits).  This IV immediately precedes the protected (encrypted) payload.

rejected.why: It is the parent of ESP, which is already tagged, so the ancestor is implied.
Authentication algorithms are mentioned only in passing in Section 5 and the document does not specify any.
Random IVs and a strong pseudo-random function for keys are required, but the document only cites RFC 1750 and is not about randomness generation.
AES is not discussed. The document covers DES, and the only other cipher it mentions is Triple DES, which falls under the DES tag.

RFC2406.title: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC2406.summary: RFC 2406 specifies the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP): packet format, transport and tunnel modes, and the outbound/inbound processing, anti-replay and auditing rules, for IPv4 and IPv6.

ESP.why: The whole document specifies the ESP header format, its fields, and how ESP packets are processed. ESP is the most specific tag that fits.
ESP.quote: The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) header is designed to provide a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6.

rejected.why: It is the parent of ESP, so it is implied. The IPsec architecture is defined in a separate document (RFC 2401).
IKE is mentioned only as one key management option. This document does not specify it.
DES-CBC is named as a mandatory-to-implement algorithm, but it is defined in a separate RFC. This document only references it.
HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 are listed as mandatory authentication algorithms, but they are specified elsewhere.
IPv6 is one of the two IP versions ESP runs over. It is used as context and is not the subject of the document.

RFC2407.title: The Internet IP Security Domain of Interpretation for ISAKMP
RFC2407.summary: Defines the IPsec Domain of Interpretation for ISAKMP, specifying the situation, protocol and transform identifiers, SA attributes, identification payload types and notify messages used when IKE negotiates IPsec security associations.

IPsec.why: The document specifies the IPsec DOI: the identifiers, attributes and payload formats for negotiating AH/ESP/IPComp SAs. It belongs on the IPsec page.
IPsec.quote: This document defines the Internet IP Security DOI (IPSEC DOI), which instantiates ISAKMP for use with IP when IP uses ISAKMP to negotiate security associations.

IKE.why: The DOI defines the IKE-related Phase I/II values, SA attributes, ID payloads and notify types, so IKE readers need it. It does not define the IKE exchanges themselves.
IKE.quote: This entire memo pertains to the Internet Key Exchange protocol ([IKE]), which combines ISAKMP ([ISAKMP]) and Oakley ([OAKLEY])

rejected.why: ESP transform identifiers are listed, but the document does not specify ESP itself; it only assigns numbers for negotiating it.
Section 6 gives IANA assignment rules for the DOI registries, but this is boilerplate-like registry guidance and not the main subject.
ESP_DES is mandatory-to-implement here and the IESG note comments on it, but the document does not define DES. It only assigns identifiers.
Not a taxonomy tag. IPCOMP transform identifiers are assigned, but the compression protocol is defined elsewhere.
Situation bits for labeled secrecy and integrity are defined, but they are a minor part of the document and not a CIPSO-style labeling framework.

gaps.name: ISAKMP (Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol)
gaps.why: The DOI instantiates ISAKMP, but the taxonomy has no ISAKMP tag. IKE and IPsec are the closest fits.

RFC2408.title: Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol (ISAKMP)
RFC2408.summary: RFC 2408 specifies ISAKMP, a framework of packet formats, payloads, exchange types and processing rules for negotiating, modifying and deleting Security Associations and establishing keys, used by IPsec (via IKE and the IPsec DOI).

IKE.why: ISAKMP is the SA negotiation and key management framework underlying IKE. The taxonomy has no separate ISAKMP tag, so IKE, under IPsec, is the closest fit for readers of this subject.
IKE.quote: ISAKMP defines procedures and packet formats to establish, negotiate, modify and delete Security Associations (SA).

key management.why: The document covers key establishment, key exchange properties and key exchange payloads. The IKE tag does not fully cover generic key management.
key management.quote: ISAKMP defines payloads for exchanging key generation and authentication data.

rejected.why: IPsec is the main consumer of ISAKMP, but the document is about the negotiation framework. IKE already sits under IPsec.
Certificate payloads and certificate authorities are discussed, but only as authentication inputs, not as PKI itself.
Authentication is a required component, but it is a facet of the SA exchange protocol, not the document's subject.
UDP port 500 is only the transport it runs over.
DNSSEC appears only as a possible source of certificates.
Photuris is cited only for the anti-clogging cookie idea.

gaps.name: ISAKMP (Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ISAKMP or Security Association negotiation. Only IKE and the generic key management topic come close.

RFC2409.title: The Internet Key Exchange (IKE)
RFC2409.summary: RFC 2409 specifies IKE, a hybrid of Oakley and SKEME within ISAKMP that authenticates peers and negotiates keying material and security associations for IPsec, with Phase 1/Phase 2 modes, Oakley DH groups and attribute definitions.

IKE.why: The document is the original IKE specification: Main, Aggressive, Quick and New Group modes, key derivation and authentication methods.
IKE.quote: This document describes a protocol using part of Oakley and part of SKEME in conjunction with ISAKMP to obtain authenticated keying material

key management.why: Substantial content on key derivation (SKEYID, KEYMAT), Diffie-Hellman groups, and perfect forward secrecy.
key management.quote: The purpose is to negotiate, and provide authenticated keying material for, security associations in a protected manner.

rejected.why: IKE is the child tag, which implies IPsec; AH/ESP SAs are only negotiated, not specified here.
DES is a mandatory-to-implement algorithm and weak keys are listed, but the document is not about DES.
EC2N groups 3 and 4 are defined, but only as a small part of the Oakley groups section.
HMAC is used as the prf but only as a building block.
RSA signatures and encryption are authentication options, not the subject.

gaps.name: ISAKMP / Oakley / Diffie-Hellman key exchange
gaps.why: The document is built on ISAKMP and Oakley groups. The taxonomy has no tag for ISAKMP or for Diffie-Hellman exchange, though IKE and key management cover most of it.

RFC2410.title: The NULL Encryption Algorithm and Its Use With IPsec
RFC2410.summary: Defines the NULL encryption algorithm (identity function) and its use as ESP_NULL within IPsec ESP to provide authentication and integrity without confidentiality.

ESP.why: The document specifies the NULL cipher as an ESP transform (ESP_NULL), with key size, IV size and padding requirements within ESP. ESP is the most specific fitting tag under IPsec.
ESP.quote: This memo defines the NULL encryption algorithm and its use with the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

rejected.why: IKE is mentioned only for key extraction (key size MUST be zero); the document does not specify or extend IKE.
NULL is technically an algorithm, but it provides no cryptography. It is defined only as an ESP option, so the ESP tag covers it.
This is the parent of ESP, which is implied by the more specific ESP tag.
Block cipher comparisons are incidental. The document does not cover AES or other real ciphers.
The text has jokes (Roman origins, test vector text), but it is a serious standards-track specification and not a humorous RFC.

RFC2411.title: IP Security Document Roadmap
RFC2411.summary: Informational roadmap describing how the IPsec documents (Architecture, ESP, AH, DOI, key management, and encryption/authentication algorithm documents) relate, and what new algorithm documents for ESP and AH should contain.

IPsec.why: The whole document is a roadmap of the IPsec suite (Architecture, ESP, AH, DOI, algorithm and key management documents) and guidance for adding algorithms to ESP and AH.
IPsec.quote: The interrelationship and organization of the various documents covering the IPsec protocol are discussed here.

rejected.why: ESP is covered as one box in the roadmap and as the context for algorithm documents, but the document does not specify ESP itself; IPsec is the better fit.
ISAKMP, Oakley and the key management box are only mentioned as references and in the keying material discussion; the document does not address IKE.
HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 are cited only as examples of authentication algorithm documents.
DES-CBC is cited only as an example of an encryption algorithm document.
There is a short section on keying material length and slicing, but it supports the roadmap rather than being a subject of its own.

RFC2412.title: The OAKLEY Key Determination Protocol
RFC2412.summary: RFC 2412 specifies OAKLEY, a Diffie-Hellman based key determination protocol with cookies, PFS, user-defined groups, quick mode key derivation, and ISAKMP compatibility, for establishing keying material for IPsec.

IKE.why: OAKLEY is a direct ancestor of IKE, specifying key exchange for IPsec SAs in ISAKMP/Oakley fashion. The document exists to define this key exchange protocol.
IKE.quote: This document describes a protocol, named OAKLEY, by which two authenticated parties can agree on secure and secret keying material.

key management.why: Substantial parts cover key derivation from old keys (quick mode), pre-distributed keys, and external key distribution, beyond a single exchange.
key management.quote: Once an OAKLEY session key and ancillary algorithms are established, the keying material and the "H" algorithm can be used to distribute an externally generated key

rejected.why: OAKLEY produces keys for AH/ESP, but the document is about key determination, not the IPsec architecture; IKE is the more specific fit.
Secure DNS KEY/SIG records are only one authentication source for public keys, not the subject.
Elliptic curve groups appear as Diffie-Hellman group options, but the document is not about ECC itself.
RSA is only one authentication algorithm option used for signatures and encryption in the exchanges.
Certificate fetching and validation are mentioned briefly, but defer to other standards.
Nonce and random number requirements are mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key exchange
gaps.why: The document's core mechanism, including well-known MODP/EC groups and private group definition, has no dedicated taxonomy tag; the closest is key management or IKE.

RFC2413.title: Dublin Core Metadata for Resource Discovery
RFC2413.summary: Informational RFC introducing the 15-element Dublin Core metadata element set for networked resource discovery and defining the semantics of each element.

rejected.why: Document is about resource-description metadata (bibliographic-style elements) for discovering web documents, not discovering network services or resources on a network.
Motivated by finding information on the Web, but the document defines a metadata element set, not web architecture or protocols.
HTML is mentioned only as an environment where elements may be embedded (case-sensitivity note); no HTML specification is given.
XML is mentioned only in passing regarding case sensitivity; the document does not specify XML usage.
Date element recommends an ISO 8601 profile by reference, but this is a minor detail, not the subject of the document.
Language element just points to RFC 1766; incidental.
URLs and URNs appear only as example identifier values.

gaps.name: Dublin Core metadata / resource description (digital library metadata)
gaps.why: The whole RFC defines a 15-element metadata set for resource discovery; the taxonomy has no tag for metadata schemas or library/resource description, so no existing tag fits.

RFC2414.title: Increasing TCP's Initial Window
RFC2414.summary: Experimental RFC that raises TCP's permitted initial congestion window from one segment to roughly 4K bytes (two to four segments), weighing the advantages and disadvantages and citing simulation and experimental results.

TCP.why: The document modifies TCP's slow-start initial window behaviour. It is a TCP protocol extension and implementation change.
TCP.quote: This document specifies an increase in the permitted upper bound for TCP's initial window from one segment to between two and four segments.

congestion control.why: Much of the document concerns slow start, cwnd, congestion collapse risk and drop rates. Readers of congestion control would want it. TCP is the only technology tag that fits, so the topic tag is added alongside it.
congestion control.quote: This upper bound for the initial window size represents a change from RFC 2001 [S97], which specifies that the congestion window be initialized to one segment.

rejected.why: Interaction with Path MTU Discovery is discussed in Implementation Issues, but only briefly. The document is not about PMTUD.
HTTP transfers are cited as a motivating workload, and the document warns about browsers opening multiple connections. HTTP is not specified or extended.
RED and active queue management are mentioned only as context for burst tolerance.
Satellite link experiments are cited as evidence of benefit. The document is not about networking over satellite links.

RFC2415.title: Simulation Studies of Increased Initial TCP Window Size
RFC2415.summary: Reports ns-2 simulation studies of raising TCP's initial window from one to three or four segments, measuring web and FTP performance, drop rates, and effects on IW=1 flows.

TCP.why: The document evaluates a proposed change to TCP's initial window and its effects on TCP connections, so it belongs on the TCP page.
TCP.quote: An increase in the permissible initial window size of a TCP connection, from one segment to three or four segments, has been under discussion

rejected.why: Congestion effects (drops, overload) are measured, but the subject is the TCP initial window; the TCP tag fits better.
RED is mentioned only briefly as unreported side experiments.
HTTP/1.0 and 1.1 are only traffic models for the workload, not specified or analysed as protocols.
This is a simulation study of TCP, not about network measurement methods or metrics.

RFC2416.title: When TCP Starts Up With Four Packets Into Only Three Buffers
RFC2416.summary: Reports a simulation experiment showing that a four-packet TCP initial window into a 3-buffer 9600 bps modem link performs no worse than normal one-packet slow start.

TCP.why: The document analyses a proposed change to TCP's initial window and slow start behaviour (tahoe, reno, sack, fack) via simulation, so it is about TCP protocol behaviour and extensions.
TCP.quote: in the case of a TCP receiver behind a 9600 bps modem link at the edge of a fast Internet

congestion control.why: It examines slow-start behaviour, packet loss at a small bottleneck queue, and whether a larger initial window is safe for the network, which is a congestion control question.
congestion control.quote: it remains (in the authors' opinions at this time) an open question whether or not the four-packet start would be safe for the network.

rejected.why: The simulations use tahoe, reno, sack and fack, but the document does not specify or analyse NewReno.
It is a one-off simulation experiment, not a benchmarking methodology for network devices.
Router buffer limits are part of the scenario, but the document does not address QoS architectures or signalling.

RFC2417.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 based ATM Networks
RFC2417.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (IPATM-IPMC-MIB) for managing MARS clients, MARS servers and multicast servers (MCS) used for IP multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 ATM networks; obsoletes RFC 2366.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition with tables, objects, and conformance groups for MARS entities.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

ATM.why: The managed objects cover ATM addresses, VCs, VPI/VCI and MARS operation for IP multicast over ATM networks.
ATM.quote: managed objects for IP hosts and routers that use a Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) to support IP multicast over ATM

multicast.why: The MIB manages IP multicast group address blocks, group membership mappings and multicast servers (MCS).
multicast.quote: This table contains a list of IP multicast address blocks associated with a MARS.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB, not what the document specifies. The MIB tag covers the SNMP-related content.
NHRP is a related NBMA address-resolution mechanism but is not discussed in the document.
IGMP is not mentioned. MARS is ATM-based multicast address resolution, not IP group membership signalling.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server)
gaps.why: The document is about managing MARS from RFC 2022, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC2418.title: IETF Working Group Guidelines and Procedures
RFC2418.summary: BCP 25 describes the guidelines and procedures for forming, operating, rechartering and terminating IETF working groups, including the roles of WG chairs, editors and Area Directors, and the handling of WG documents.

IETF process.why: The whole document defines IETF working group chartering, operation, rough consensus, roles and document review procedures, which is the IETF standards process and its administration.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the guidelines and procedures for formation and operation of IETF working groups.

rejected.why: Section 7.3 on RFCs and Internet-Drafts is only a small part of the document; the main subject is WG process, not RFC format or publication.
The sample charter in the appendix describes a Call Processing Syntax work item only as an example charter, so the document is not about CPL.
The appendix's Gateway Attribute Distribution Protocol is an example charter item, not a subject of the document.
The nominating committee is mentioned once and cited by reference; the document does not cover NomCom procedures.
IPR appears only as one formation criterion and in the boilerplate copyright text.

RFC2419.title: The PPP DES Encryption Protocol, Version 2 (DESE-bis)
RFC2419.summary: Specifies how DES in CBC mode is used to encrypt PPP packets under the PPP Encryption Control Protocol, defining the ECP DESE option, packet format, padding, and loss recovery (obsoletes RFC 1969).

DES.why: The document defines how DES in CBC mode generates and retrieves ciphertext for PPP packets; it is the core of the specification.
DES.quote: This document provides specific details for the use of the DES standard [5, 6] for encrypting PPP encapsulated packets.

PPP.why: It defines a PPP ECP configuration option, a PPP encryption data protocol with its own protocol IDs, and its interaction with ACFC, PFC, Multilink and LCP padding, so PPP readers need it.
PPP.quote: The ECP DESE Configuration Option indicates that the issuing implementation is offering to employ this specification for decrypting communications on the link

rejected.why: The DES tag is more specific and already implies the cryptography parent.
Key establishment is explicitly out of scope; the shared secret is assumed to be configured by other means.
The document is not about IPsec; it provides link-layer PPP encryption and does not use IPsec.
It is not about ESP; the encryption is applied at the PPP layer, not within IPsec.

gaps.name: PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP)
gaps.why: The document specifies a data protocol within ECP, but the taxonomy has no ECP tag. The PPP tag is the closest fit.

RFC2420.title: The PPP Triple-DES Encryption Protocol (3DESE)
RFC2420.summary: Specifies how to encrypt PPP packets with Triple-DES (DES-EDE3-CBC) under the PPP Encryption Control Protocol, covering the ECP option, packet format, padding and loss recovery.

PPP.why: The document defines an ECP configuration option and packet format for encrypting PPP frames, so it is a PPP extension. PPP's readers would want it.
PPP.quote: This document provides specific details for the use of the Triple-DES standard (3DES) [6] for encrypting PPP encapsulated packets.

DES.why: It specifies the Triple-DES (DES-EDE3-CBC) algorithm, its keys, weak-key handling and CBC chaining as applied to PPP. That is core DES/3DES content.
DES.quote: The variant used is the DES-EDE3-CBC, which is described in more detail in the text.

rejected.why: The document explicitly relies on external, unspecified methods for retrieving shared secrets, so key management is out of scope.
The ESP Triple DES transform is only referenced as the reason for choosing the variant. The document is not about IPsec.
ESP is cited only as a source of text and a precedent for the cipher choice. The document is not about ESP.

RFC2421.title: Voice Profile for Internet Mail - version 2
RFC2421.summary: RFC 2421 defines VPIM v2, a profile of Internet mail (MIME and ESMTP) for exchanging voice and fax messages between voice messaging systems, obsoleting RFC 1911.

VPIM.why: The document specifies the VPIM v2 profile itself: addressing, headers, content types, and transport restrictions for voice messaging over Internet mail.
VPIM.quote: The profile is referred to as VPIM (Voice Profile for Internet Mail) in this document.

MIME.why: A large part of the profile covers MIME body structure: multipart/voice-message, audio/32KADPCM, image/tiff, text/directory, multipart/report, and a new voice Content-Disposition parameter.
MIME.quote: Only the contents profiled subsequently can be sent within a VPIM voice message construct (i.e., the mulitpart/voice-message content type)

SMTP.why: Section 5 profiles which ESMTP commands, keywords and parameters are required or optional (DSN, SIZE, BINARYMIME, PIPELINING, downgrading).
SMTP.quote: Messages are transported between voice mail machines using the Internet Extended Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (ESMTP).

rejected.why: vCard is profiled for carrying originator info and a VPIM EMAIL type is registered. This is a supporting component, not the main subject.
The header field profile is a section of the document, but the document is about the voice messaging profile as a whole. The VPIM tag covers it.
Fax is supported through TIFF-F image/tiff content, but only as an attached content type, not as fax-over-email specification.
Section 7 only notes that IMAP/POP can retrieve VPIM messages without changes. It is not about IMAP.
The document registers a Content-Disposition parameter and a vCard EMAIL type, but media type registration is done in companion RFCs.
Network management gets only a brief optional mention of MIB-II.

RFC2422.title: Toll Quality Voice - 32 kbit/s ADPCM MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC2422.summary: Registers the MIME audio sub-type audio/32KADPCM for ITU-T G.726 32 kbit/s ADPCM audio with little-endian code word packing, primarily for VPIM voice messaging, refining RFC 1911.

media types.why: The document's purpose is a MIME media type registration with the IANA registration template, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type audio/32KADPCM for toll quality audio.

codecs.why: It defines how G.726 ADPCM audio is carried, including the bit packing of the 4-bit code words, which is an audio codec container definition. No narrower codec tag fits G.726.
codecs.quote: The MIME sub-type audio/32KADPCM is defined to hold binary audio data encoded in 32 kbit/s ADPCM exactly as defined by ITU-T Recommendation G.726.

VPIM.why: The type exists mainly for voice messaging, and the document states how it is used in VPIM and obsoletes the earlier VPIM-related registration in RFC 1911.
VPIM.quote: The audio/32KADPCM sub-type is a primary component of the VPIM specification [VPIM].

rejected.why: The document uses MIME only as the framework for the registration. The more specific media types tag covers it.
X.420 is cited only for the equivalent body part's bit ordering, which is a passing reference.
G.726 transcodes from 64 kbit/s PCM, but the document does not define or extend G.711.
G.722 is a different ITU-T wideband codec and is not mentioned. G.726 does not belong under it.
Base64 is only mentioned as a typical content transfer encoding.

gaps.name: G.726 ADPCM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for the ITU-T G.726 ADPCM speech codec, so the document is only covered by the generic codecs tag.

RFC2423.title: VPIM Voice Message MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC2423.summary: Registers the MIME sub-type multipart/voice-message, a multipart/mixed-equivalent wrapper with a required version parameter, for use by VPIM v2 voice messaging, replacing the RFC 1911 registration.

VPIM.why: The document defines the wrapper content type that every VPIM message must carry, including its version parameter and permitted contents. VPIM readers need it.
VPIM.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type multipart/voice-message for use with the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM).

media types.why: The document's main purpose is a media type registration, with required parameters, encoding and interoperability considerations. It belongs on the media type registrations page.
media types.quote:
MIME media type name: multipart

   MIME subtype name: voice-message

rejected.why: The document registers a sub-type under MIME but does not define MIME body structure or encodings. The more specific media types tag covers it.
VPIM is email-based, but the document is about one media type. The VPIM tag is the more specific fit.
The IANA registration template is the document's content, but the subject is a media type registration, not IANA registry stewardship or guidance.

RFC2424.title: Content Duration MIME Header Definition
RFC2424.summary: Defines the Content-Duration MIME header field, which gives the duration in seconds of time-varying media content (audio/video), and notes its required use in VPIM voice messages.

MIME.why: The RFC defines a new MIME header field for describing body content, which is a MIME extension.
MIME.quote: This document describes the MIME header Content-Duration that is intended for use with any time varying media content (typically audio/* or video/*).

VPIM.why: A section explains the header's use in VPIM voice messages, which makes the RFC relevant to VPIM readers. The VPIM link is the motivating use case.
VPIM.quote: All VPIM Messages MUST contain this sub-type to carry the audio of a voice message.

rejected.why: The header is a MIME content header, not a core RFC 822 message header. MIME covers it better.
The RFC defines a header field, not a media type registration or registry rules.
Email is only the substrate. The document is about a MIME header.

RFC2425.title: A MIME Content-Type for Directory Information
RFC2425.summary: Defines the text/directory MIME content-type, a general "type:value" framework for carrying directory information independent of any directory service, plus IANA registration procedures for profiles, types, parameters and value types.

media types.why: The document registers the text/directory media type using the MIME registration template. It also defines registration procedures for profiles, types, parameters and value types under it.
media types.quote: This document defines a MIME Content-Type for holding directory information.

MIME.why: It defines a new MIME content-type, with charset and encoding parameters and multipart/related usage. Part of the content concerns how MIME body parts carry directory data.
MIME.quote: The text/directory Content-Type can also be used as the root body part in a multipart/related Content-Type

directory services.why: It is a directory-information interchange format that is independent of any particular directory service. It refers to LDAP, X.500 and WHOIS++ as sources, with a SOURCE type to point to them.
directory services.quote: The framework is general enough to handle information from any number of end directory services, including LDAP

rejected.why: vCard is only the example profile and is defined in the companion RFC 2426. This document is the generic framework.
LDAP is mentioned only as a possible source of directory data and in URI examples. The document does not specify or extend it.
Email is the transport context. The document defines a content-type rather than mail behaviour.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax, not the subject of the document.
The registration procedures apply only to this content-type's profiles, types, parameters and value types. They are not general IANA guidance.

RFC2426.title: vCard MIME Directory Profile
RFC2426.summary: Defines the vCard 3.0 profile of the MIME Directory content type (text/directory), specifying the electronic business card types, parameters, value types and formal grammar for person/white-pages information.

vCard.why: The whole document specifies the vCard format (types FN, N, ADR, TEL, EMAIL, etc.), so it belongs on the vCard page.
vCard.quote: This memo defines the profile of the MIME Content-Type [MIME-DIR] for directory information for a white-pages person object, based on a vCard electronic business card.

media types.why: It registers a MIME profile of text/directory and many types using MIME registration templates, so media type readers would want it.
media types.quote: Subject: Registration of text/directory MIME profile VCARD
media types.section: 1. The vCard Mime Directory Profile Registration

rejected.why: MIME is the substrate; the document profiles a content type rather than defining MIME body structure or encodings.
The schema derives from X.500 person attributes, but the profile is explicitly independent of any directory service or protocol.
Only the X.520/X.521 attribute semantics are borrowed; the document does not specify or extend the X.500 service.
A formal grammar is given in ABNF but only as a syntax aid for the vCard format, not as a subject of the document.
The EMAIL and MAILER types hold address data but the document is not about email.
The GEO type holds latitude and longitude, but this is a minor property, not a main subject.

RFC2427.title: Multiprotocol Interconnect over Frame Relay
RFC2427.summary: Standards-track specification of multiprotocol encapsulation (NLPID/SNAP, routed and bridged frames) over Frame Relay, including XID parameter negotiation, ARP/RARP address resolution over PVCs, IP encapsulation, and remote bridging models; obsoletes RFC 1490.

frame relay.why: The whole document defines how routed and bridged protocols are encapsulated over Frame Relay (Q.922 frames, NLPID, SNAP, DLCIs).
frame relay.quote: This memo describes an encapsulation method for carrying network interconnect traffic over a Frame Relay backbone.

ARP.why: A substantial section specifies how ARP and RARP operate over Frame Relay PVCs, including DLCI-based hardware address substitution and gratuitous ARP.
ARP.quote: This may be accomplished using the standard Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [6] encapsulated within a SNAP encoded Frame Relay packet

rejected.why: Bridged 802.3 frames are one of several encapsulated media; the document is about Frame Relay, not IP over Ethernet.
IP encapsulation is one section, but IP is the payload carried rather than the subject of the document.
802.5 bridged frames are only one encapsulation format among several.
FDDI bridged frames are just one of the media formats encapsulated.
CLNP and ISO NLPIDs are mentioned as examples of payload protocols, not the document's subject.
Not discussed; only the 802.6 bridged format appears.

RFC2428.title: FTP Extensions for IPv6 and NATs
RFC2428.summary: Defines the FTP EPRT and EPSV commands (and reply code 522/229) so FTP can carry data-connection endpoint information for IPv6 and other network protocols, and so it works better through NATs and firewalls.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with new commands EPRT and EPSV and new reply codes, so it belongs on the FTP page.
FTP.quote: This paper specifies extensions to FTP that will allow the protocol to work over IPv4 and IPv6.

IPv6.why: The extensions exist so FTP can operate over IPv6 addresses during IPv4/IPv6 transition, with address family numbers and IPv6 address formats specified.
IPv6.quote: With the deployment of version 6 of the Internet Protocol [DH96] addresses will no longer be 32 bits long.

NAT.why: The title and Section 4 address NAT friendliness: EPSV avoids address rewriting, and EPSV ALL lets NATs use a fast path.
NAT.quote: using EPSV as defined in this document does not require NATs to change the network address in the traffic as it is forwarded.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport for the control and data connections; nothing new is specified about TCP.
The document addresses multi-protocol negotiation for FTP, not a transition mechanism such as tunnelling or translation.
Firewall-friendly passive mode is mentioned briefly, but the document does not specify firewall traversal mechanisms beyond the NAT discussion.
It only references IANA address family numbers; it does not address IANA registry matters.

RFC2429.title: RTP Payload Format for the 1998 Version of ITU-T Rec. H.263 Video (H.263+)
RFC2429.summary: Defines an RTP payload header and packetization rules for carrying H.263+ (1998 H.263) video, including picture-header copies for loss resilience and a Video Redundancy Coding header extension.

RTP payload format.why: The RFC defines a new RTP payload format for a specific video codec (H.263+), including header fields and packet types.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies an RTP payload header format applicable to the transmission of video streams generated based on the 1998 version of ITU-T Recommendation H.263

codecs.why: H.263/H.263+ has no specific child tag, so the codecs parent fits. Much of the text covers codec options such as slice mode, ISD, reference picture selection, scalability and VRC, and how they affect packetization.
codecs.quote: The 1998 version of ITU-T Recommendation H.263 added numerous coding options to improve codec performance over the 1996 version.

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format runs over. The RTP payload format tag is more specific, and the document only specifies header usage and the payload.
This is a different video codec. H.263 is a predecessor with no tag of its own in the taxonomy.
Security considerations only refer to RTP's security. The document defines nothing about secure RTP.
Mentioned only in passing in the Security Considerations, so it is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: H.263 / H.263+ video codec
gaps.why: There is no tag for the ITU-T H.263 codec or its RTP payload formats (RFC 2190 and RFC 2429). The codecs parent is the closest fit.

RFC2430.title: A Provider Architecture for Differentiated Services and Traffic Engineering (PASTE)
RFC2430.summary: Informational architecture (PASTE) for providing scalable differentiated services and traffic engineering in ISPs by aggregating flows into class-specific MPLS LSP trunks established with RSVP and explicit routes.

traffic engineering.why: Traffic engineering is a co-equal goal of the architecture; trunks are placed on explicit routes to avoid congestion and diverge from IGP shortest paths.
traffic engineering.quote: Traffic engineering is performed by directing trunks along explicit paths within the ISP's topology.

MPLS.why: The architecture is built on MPLS LSPs as aggregated traffic trunks, with label stacking, merging, and CoS bits discussed.
MPLS.quote: MPLS defines mechanisms to install label-based forwarding information along a series of Label Switching Routers (LSRs) to construct a Label Switched Path (LSP).

RSVP.why: A full section explains the extended use of RSVP (ERO, label binding, router-to-router sessions) to establish and maintain trunks.
RSVP.quote: RSVP is used in PASTE to install state that applies to a collection of flows that all share a common path and common pool of reserved resources.

Diffserv.why: The document defines a provider architecture for differentiated services with traffic classes, inter-provider SLAs, and shaping/policing.
Diffserv.quote: Providing differentiated services in ISPs is a challenge because the scaling problems presented by the sheer number of flows

rejected.why: RSVP is used here for aggregate trunk signalling rather than per-flow integrated services; the document argues against per-flow state.
The document describes RSVP with an explicit route object for LSP setup, a precursor of RSVP-TE, but it does not specify the extensions; they are only cited as work in progress.
VPNs are mentioned only as an example application of differentiated services, not as the subject.
BGP path information is mentioned only in passing for locating the destination ISP.
The document is about differentiated services in ISPs, which has its own more specific tag, so the broader QoS parent is not needed.

RFC2431.title: RTP Payload Format for BT.656 Video Encoding
RFC2431.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for carrying uncompressed ITU-R BT.656 studio-quality 4:2:2 video, one scan line (or fragment) per packet, with a four-octet payload header.

RTP payload format.why: The whole document defines a payload format for a specific video media type over RTP, including header fields, fragmentation and sample packing.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the RTP payload format for encapsulating ITU Recommendation BT.656-3 video streams in the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP).

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the document only defines a payload format and uses the RTP header fields, so the more specific child tag applies.
The video is uncompressed BT.656/BT.601 samples, not a codec definition; the payload format tag covers it.
Path MTU discovery is only recommended for choosing fragment size, not specified or analysed.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-level registry of the Type field and not the main subject.

gaps.name: BT.656 / BT.601 uncompressed studio video
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for raw digital video formats; the document's subject is packetizing uncompressed ITU-R BT.656 video, only partly captured by RTP payload format.

RFC2432.title: Terminology for IP Multicast Benchmarking
RFC2432.summary: Defines terminology and benchmark metrics (throughput, latency, join/leave delay, group capacity, burdened responses) for benchmarking IP multicast forwarding devices, extending RFC 1242 and RFC 2285.

benchmarking.why: The RFC is a BMWG benchmarking terminology document defining metrics for DUT/SUT testing.
benchmarking.quote: The purpose of this document is to define terminology specific to the benchmarking of multicast IP forwarding devices.

multicast.why: The metrics are specific to IP multicast forwarding (group join/leave delay, group capacity, aggregated multicast throughput), so multicast readers would want it.
multicast.quote: Network forwarding devices are being required to take a single frame and support delivery to a number of destinations having membership to a particular group.

rejected.why: IGMP join and leave messages are only the trigger events for the Group Join/Leave Delay metrics; the document does not specify or analyse IGMP.
The parent of the benchmarking tag's sibling area; the document is specifically device benchmarking, which has its own tag.
Encapsulation/decapsulation throughput metrics mention tunneling only generically as a benchmarked operation, not as a tunnelling mechanism.

RFC2433.title: Microsoft PPP CHAP Extensions
RFC2433.summary: Informational RFC describing Microsoft's MS-CHAP, a PPP CHAP dialect (algorithm 0x80) with its Response, Failure and Change Password packets, plus the hashing/encryption routines used to generate the fields.

PPP.why: MS-CHAP is a PPP authentication protocol negotiated via LCP option 3 and derived from PPP CHAP. The document specifies it, so readers of PPP would expect it.
PPP.quote: This document describes Microsoft's PPP CHAP dialect (MS-CHAP), which extends the user authentication functionality provided on Windows networks to remote workstations.

authentication.why: The document specifies a challenge-response user authentication scheme with retry, failure codes and password change. No more specific authentication tag fits.
authentication.quote: MS-CHAP provides authenticator-controlled authentication retry and password changing mechanisms.

rejected.why: DES is used as a primitive in the hash and response routines in the appendix. The document is not about DES itself.
MD5 is mentioned only as the standard CHAP algorithm that MS-CHAP replaces. MD4 is used for the NT hash, but MD4 is not a separate tag.
RC4 is used only to encrypt the password block in the Change Password packet. It is a building block, not the subject.
The document covers PPP peer authentication, not an AAA framework.
The cryptographic algorithms are only used as components, in the pseudocode appendix.

RFC2434.title: Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs
RFC2434.summary: BCP 26 gives guidelines to RFC authors for writing IANA Considerations sections, defining registration policies (Private Use, First Come First Served, Expert Review, Specification Required, IESG Approval, IETF Consensus, Standards Action) and registration maintenance.

IANA.why: The whole document is guidance on IANA registry policies and what IANA Considerations text must say.
IANA.quote: This document discusses issues that should be considered in formulating a policy for assigning values to a name space and provides guidelines to document authors

rejected.why: It touches designated experts, IESG approval and appeals, but only as part of registration policy, so the subject is IANA.
DHCP options are cited only as an example name space.
MIME type registration is used as an example, not the subject.
DNS is mentioned only as an example of hierarchical delegation.
It uses RFC 2119 keywords and defines 'name space' and 'registration', but that is incidental.

RFC2435.title: RTP Payload Format for JPEG-compressed Video
RFC2435.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for carrying JPEG (Motion-JPEG) compressed video, defining the RTP/JPEG header, type and Q fields, restart markers, and fragmentation/reassembly; obsoletes RFC 2035.

RTP payload format.why: The whole document defines how JPEG frames are packetized in RTP, with a header, fragmentation scheme and marker/timestamp rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes the RTP payload format for JPEG video streams.

codecs.why: The document covers the JPEG/Motion-JPEG video codec subset, its quantization tables, Huffman tables and sampling types. No specific JPEG tag exists, so the codecs parent fits.
codecs.quote: The Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) standard [1,2,3] defines a family of compression algorithms for continuous-tone, still images.

rejected.why: RTP payload format is the more specific child, so the parent is implied.
A session setup protocol is mentioned only as out of scope for dynamic types.
Not discussed; only RTP data packets are specified.
IGMP is mentioned only in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: JPEG / Motion-JPEG image compression
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no JPEG codec tag. The document is largely about the JPEG subset, quantization tables and JFIF parameters carried in RTP.

RFC2436.title: Collaboration between ISOC/IETF and ITU-T
RFC2436.summary: Informational RFC describing how ITU-T Study Groups and ISOC/IETF collaborate: contacts, representation, mailing lists, document sharing, and guidelines for ITU-T referencing of RFCs.

IETF process.why: The document defines procedures for how IETF working groups, area directors and the IESG interact with ITU-T, including new-work mailing lists, delegate recognition, Internet-Draft sharing and rules for referencing RFCs.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the collaboration process between the ITU-T and ISOC/IETF.

rejected.why: The Annex touches on IPR in referencing standards, but it is a minor part of the document and not its subject.
It mentions RFC formats and referencing RFCs, but only in the context of collaboration, not the RFC series itself.
The more specific child, IETF process, fits better, so the parent is implied and not listed.

RFC2437.title: PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.0
RFC2437.summary: PKCS #1 v2.0 specifies RSA cryptographic primitives, the RSAES-OAEP and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 encryption schemes, the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature scheme, encoding methods, and ASN.1 syntax for RSA keys and scheme identifiers.

RSA.why: The whole document specifies RSA primitives, encryption schemes, signature schemes and key syntax, so readers of the RSA subject would expect it.
RSA.quote: This document provides recommendations for the implementation of public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm [18]

ASN.1.why: Section 11 defines ASN.1 types and OIDs for RSA keys and schemes, a substantial part of the document.
ASN.1.quote: This section defines ASN.1 object identifiers for RSA public and private keys, and defines the types RSAPublicKey and RSAPrivateKey.

rejected.why: SHA-1 is only recommended as the hash used by the encoding methods and is not defined or specified here.
MD2, MD5 and MD4 are discussed only as hash options and their cryptanalysis status, not specified.
X.509 certificates are cited only as an intended application of the key and OID definitions.
PKCS #7 is mentioned only as an example context for the encryption schemes.
The patent statement is boilerplate and not the document's main subject.

gaps.name: RSA / PKCS #1 padding schemes (OAEP, PKCS1-v1_5)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no RSA tag shown. The `RSA` tag id above comes from the taxonomy under cryptography, so it fits. No gap beyond finer-grained OAEP/padding schemes, which have no dedicated tag.

RFC2438.title: Advancement of MIB specifications on the IETF Standards Track
RFC2438.summary: BCP describing the process the IESG uses to decide whether a MIB specification has the multiple interoperable implementations required to advance beyond Proposed Standard, with the rationale and alternative testing models.

MIB.why: The whole document is about how MIB specifications are evaluated for standards-track advancement, their nature, and how to test interoperability of MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This document specifies how the IESG has decided to judge "MIB specification interoperability" in the context of the IETF Standards Process.

IETF process.why: It is a standards-process BCP on advancement beyond Proposed Standard, implementation reports and Last-Call, so it belongs under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: This document specifies the process which the IESG will use to determine if a MIB specification document meets these requirements.

rejected.why: SNMP agents and managers appear only in the testing examples. The document is about MIB specifications, which have their own tag under SNMP.
The testing alternatives concern implementation interoperability evidence, not network device benchmarking methodology.

RFC2439.title: BGP Route Flap Damping
RFC2439.summary: Describes BGP route flap damping: a per-route exponentially decaying figure-of-merit with cutoff/reuse thresholds and reuse lists that suppress unstable EBGP routes to reduce routing load, with parameter guidance and implementation experience.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies a damping technique for BGP updates, including per-route state, processing of withdrawals/advertisements, and deployment guidance for operators.
BGP.quote: A usage of the BGP routing protocol is described which is capable of reducing the routing traffic passed on to routing peers

rejected.why: Concerns scalability but the document specifically specifies a BGP mechanism; the BGP tag is more specific.
Deployment advice exists but the subject is route instability damping, not security practice.
Security Considerations only note damping does not weaken security; not the document's subject.

gaps.name: route flap damping
gaps.why: The document's central subject is damping of unstable routes; the taxonomy has no specific tag, so BGP is the closest fit.

RFC2440.title: OpenPGP Message Format
RFC2440.summary: Specifies the OpenPGP message and key packet formats (signatures, session-key packets, key material, S2K, ASCII armor, cleartext signatures, algorithm constants) for encryption, signing and key management.

OpenPGP.why: The entire document defines the OpenPGP message format, packet types, key formats and algorithm usage.
OpenPGP.quote: publish all necessary information needed to develop interoperable applications based on the OpenPGP format

rejected.why: RSA is one of several public-key algorithms used by the format. It is not the subject of the document.
Radix-64/ASCII armor is a section of the document. It is an OpenPGP-specific encoding with a CRC-24, so the generic Base64 tag does not fit.
The document mentions OpenPGP-MIME (RFC 2015) only as a separate document.
Triple-DES is a mandatory-to-implement cipher but the document is not about it.
The web-of-trust certification model is part of OpenPGP and is covered by that tag. It is not X.509-style PKI.
Key formats and certification are covered by the OpenPGP tag.

RFC2441.title: Working with Jon, Tribute delivered at UCLA, October 30, 1998
RFC2441.summary: A personal tribute to Jon Postel, delivered at UCLA in 1998, recalling the author's work with him at ISI, his role as IANA and RFC editor, and the TCP/IP versus OSI contest.

internet history.why: The document is a retrospective on early ARPAnet and Internet work, Los-Nettos, InterMail and the TCP/IP versus OSI/GOSIP rivalry, told through Postel's career.
internet history.quote: The Internet, against all the conventional wisdom, grew without anyone being in charge, without central control, and without any central planning.

RFC series.why: A substantial part of the tribute covers Postel as RFC editor: his curation of the series, his insistence on plain ASCII format, and the funding of RFC editing and distribution.
RFC series.quote: he insisted on them being in ASCII, easy to e-mail, guaranteed to be readable anywhere in the world.

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned only in passing ('Jon was IANA'). The document is about Postel as a person, not IANA registries or stewardship.
The ARPAnet appears as background to the author's career. The document does not address its protocols or operations.
The OSI/GOSIP contest is recalled as history. The document does not cover OSI protocols themselves.
The InterMail mail-tunnel hack is a brief anecdote, not a subject the document specifies or analyses.

RFC2442.title: The Batch SMTP Media Type
RFC2442.summary: Defines the application/batch-SMTP MIME media type, a container for the client side of an SMTP/ESMTP transaction, so envelope information and multiple messages can be tunneled over any MIME-capable transport, with rules for generators and processors.

SMTP.why: The document specifies how SMTP/ESMTP transactions are captured, generated, and processed in batch form, including which SMTP extensions may be used and what processors must accept.
SMTP.quote: This document defines a MIME content type suitable for tunneling an ESMTP [RFC-821, RFC-1869] transaction through any MIME-capable transport.

media types.why: It registers a new MIME media type, with name, subtype, parameters, encoding and security considerations, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: The "application/batch-SMTP" MIME content type is a container for the client side of an SMTP or ESMTP transaction.

rejected.why: MIME is the framework in which the new type is defined. The more specific media types tag covers the registration.
It is only mentioned as an example transport that can carry the object.
This is an ancestor of SMTP, which is the more specific tag and already implies it.
This is IP-layer tunneling, whereas this document tunnels SMTP over MIME transports.

RFC2443.title: A Distributed MARS Service Using SCSP
RFC2443.summary: Defines the MARS-specific part of SCSP (PID 0x0003) so multiple MARS Servers in an ATM LIS can synchronize their multicast group membership databases, including CSA record formats and server failure handling.

ATM.why: The MARS service provides IP multicast address resolution and connection services over ATM LIS networks. The document distributes that service and uses ATM addresses and VCs throughout. ATM is the closest fit; the taxonomy has no MARS or SCSP tag.
ATM.quote: It provides the necessary connection and addressing services required by layer 3 multicast services over ATM.

multicast.why: The document synchronizes layer 3 multicast group membership across MARS servers, covering joins, leaves, MCS serve/unserve, and redistribution of membership information.
multicast.quote: there MUST be a method by which to synchronize multicast information across all MARS Servers within the LIS.

rejected.why: NHRP is only mentioned as a reserved version number value. SCSP is also used there, but this document is about MARS.
IPv4 addresses appear only as the example protocol type for MARS; the document is not about IPv4.
The document synchronizes server caches or databases, but these are not directory services such as LDAP or X.500.
The PID assignment is mentioned only in passing, so the document is not about IANA registries.

gaps.name: SCSP (Server Cache Synchronization Protocol) / MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server)
gaps.why: The document is about SCSP applied to MARS. The taxonomy has no tag for either, so the nearest tags are only approximate.

RFC2444.title: The One-Time-Password SASL Mechanism
RFC2444.summary: Defines the OTP SASL mechanism, profiling One-Time Password (RFC 2289) and extended responses for use in SASL-enabled protocols such as IMAP, ACAP, POP3 and LDAPv3, replacing the SKEY mechanism.

SASL.why: The document defines a new SASL mechanism named OTP, including its message exchange, profile rules, and IANA registration for it.
SASL.quote: This specification defines an OTP SASL [SASL] mechanism so it can be easily and formally integrated into many application protocols.

OTP.why: The document profiles OTP and its extended responses, specifying required response types, hash algorithms and dictionaries, so readers of the OTP subject need it.
OTP.quote: OTP [OTP] and OTP extended responses [OTP-EXT] offer a number of options. However, for authentication to succeed, the client and server need compatible option sets.

rejected.why: IMAP is only one of the protocols used in an example of the SASL profile; the document does not specify or extend IMAP.
ACAP is used in examples only and is not specified or extended by this document.
UTF-8 is only mentioned as a permitted encoding for identities, a minor detail rather than a subject of the document.
MD5 and SHA1 are only required hash algorithms within OTP; the document is not about the hash functions.
A more specific tag (SASL) and the OTP tag already cover this; the generic authentication topic adds nothing.

RFC2445.title: Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
RFC2445.summary: Defines iCalendar, the text/calendar MIME content type and format for exchanging calendaring and scheduling data (events, to-dos, journals, free/busy, time zones, alarms, recurrence rules).

iCalendar.why: The whole document specifies the iCalendar object format: components, properties, parameters, value types and recurrence rules.
iCalendar.quote: The Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification, or iCalendar, allows for the capture and exchange of information normally stored within a calendaring and scheduling application

media types.why: The memo is formatted as a media type registration for text/calendar, with parameters (method, component, optinfo), file extensions and a registration process for new properties.
media types.quote: The following text is intended to register this memo as the MIME content type "text/calendar".

rejected.why: MIME is the packaging for the content type; the document registers a media type rather than specifying MIME body structure or encodings.
This tag covers time zone data distribution. VTIMEZONE is one component of iCalendar, and the document defers a global time zone registry to future work.
SMTP and email are only one of several transports named for carrying iCalendar objects (IMIP/iTIP handle that).
vCard is only referenced as an alternate representation for location and contact; it is not specified here.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the grammar.
The date and time value types are based on ISO 8601 and serve iCalendar; they are not a general Internet timestamp format.

RFC2446.title: iCalendar Transport-Independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP) Scheduling Events, BusyTime, To-dos and Journal Entries
RFC2446.summary: RFC 2446 specifies iTIP, the transport-independent protocol by which calendaring systems use iCalendar objects to publish, request, reply to, counter and cancel scheduling of events, to-dos, journal entries and free/busy time.

calendaring.why: The whole document defines group calendaring and scheduling semantics (PUBLISH, REQUEST, REPLY, COUNTER and so on). That fits the calendaring topic.
calendaring.quote: This document specifies how calendaring systems use iCalendar objects to interoperate with other calendar systems.

iCalendar.why: It profiles iCalendar objects (VEVENT, VTODO, VJOURNAL, VFREEBUSY) with a METHOD property and restriction tables for each method. Readers of the iCalendar subject would want it.
iCalendar.quote: iTIP complements the iCalendar object specification by adding semantics for group scheduling methods commonly available in current calendar systems.

rejected.why: The iMIP companion binds iTIP to email. This document only mentions store-and-forward transport abstractly.
iTIP messages are text/calendar entities, but MIME is only the carrier here. The document defines nothing new about MIME.
Security is delegated to RFC 1847 security multiparts in the transport bindings. It appears only in the Security Considerations.
VTIMEZONE appears in restriction tables and examples. The document is not about time zone data distribution.
CalDAV is not mentioned. iTIP is transport-independent.

RFC2447.title: iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol (iMIP)
RFC2447.summary: RFC 2447 (iMIP) binds iCalendar scheduling messages (iTIP) to Internet email by defining the text/calendar MIME content type usage, addressing, security, and examples.

iCalendar.why: The document defines how iCalendar objects and iTIP scheduling methods are carried in messages, i.e. iCalendar interoperability.
iCalendar.quote: specifies a binding from the iCalendar Transport-independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP) to Internet email-based transports

email.why: It is an email transport binding for calendaring messages, covering addresses, headers and content handling.
email.quote: This section defines the message binding to the MIME electronic mail transport.

MIME.why: Substantial parts concern MIME content type parameters (method, charset, component), multipart/alternative, related and mixed structures, Content-Disposition and Content-ID usage.
MIME.quote: A MIME body part containing content information that conforms to this document MUST have an [RFC-2045] "Content-Type" value of "text/calendar".

rejected.why: Security uses RFC 1847 multipart/signed and encrypted, not S/MIME; security is a minor section.
RFC 822 addresses are discussed only as they relate to ATTENDEE/ORGANIZER; not about message format itself.
The text/calendar type is used but registered elsewhere (RFC 2445), not here.
Authentication guidance is brief and delegated to RFC 1847 mechanisms.

gaps.name: iTIP (iCalendar Transport-Independent Interoperability Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no iTIP tag, but the document is a binding of it. The iCalendar tag covers it only indirectly.

RFC2448.title: AT&T's Error Resilient Video Transmission Technique
RFC2448.summary: Informational RFC describing AT&T's techniques for packet-loss-resilient video transmission by reliably delivering high-priority bitstream segments (via TCP or reliable multicast, RTP-packetized, or out-of-band) over networks without prioritization.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines how HP video segments are packetized in RTP: payload type, M bit, timestamp and SSRC rules. Readers of RTP payload formats for video would want it.
RTP payload format.quote: HP segments can be packetized using RTP with the following definitions for the header fields:
RTP payload format.section: 3. Transmission of HP data using a reliable transport protocol

codecs.why: A substantial part of the document is about partitioning compressed video bitstreams (MPEG-2 data partitioning) into high- and low-priority segments. That is video coding, not just transport.
codecs.quote: It is impossible to segment a compressed video bitstream without knowing the syntax and the semantics of the encoding algorithm.

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable transport used to carry HP segments. The document specifies nothing new about TCP.
It is mentioned only as an option for multipoint delivery of HP segments, with a web page reference. The document does not specify or analyse it.
FEC is listed only as an alternative protection technique that the document does not adopt.
Reserved channels and differentiated services are mentioned only as alternatives that need network changes. The document is aimed at networks without prioritization.
RTCP BYE and SDES appear only in the SSRC handling rules, which is too minor to count as being about RTCP.
Path MTU is cited only to say how many HP segments fit in a packet.

RFC2449.title: POP3 Extension Mechanism
RFC2449.summary: RFC 2449 defines the POP3 extension mechanism: the CAPA command for advertising capabilities, an initial set of capabilities (TOP, USER, SASL, RESP-CODES, LOGIN-DELAY, PIPELINING, EXPIRE, UIDL, IMPLEMENTATION), extended response codes, and registries for both.

POP3.why: The document extends and updates POP3 with the CAPA command, capabilities, response codes and a grammar, so it is squarely about POP3.
POP3.quote: This memo updates RFC 1939 [POP3] to define a mechanism to announce support for optional commands, extensions, and unconditional server behavior.

rejected.why: The SASL capability only advertises the AUTH command and its mechanisms. SASL is specified elsewhere, so the document is not about SASL.
IMAP is mentioned only as the recommended alternative for richer mail access.
The ESMTP PIPELINING extension is mentioned only as a comparison for the POP3 PIPELINING capability.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the command and response grammar. The document is not about ABNF.
The IANA registries for POP3 capabilities and response codes are boilerplate-like and a minor part of the document.

RFC2450.title: Proposed TLA and NLA Assignment Rule
RFC2450.summary: Informational IPng WG proposal of rules for IANA and registries assigning IPv6 Top-Level and Next-Level Aggregation IDs (Sub-TLA/TLA/NLA) in the aggregatable global unicast address format.

IPv6.why: The document is about allocation and assignment of fields of the IPv6 aggregatable global unicast address format, which is IPv6 addressing.
IPv6.quote: This document proposes assignment rules for the TLA ID and NLA ID fields in the IPv6 Aggregatable Global Unicast Address Format.
IPv6.section: 3.0 IPv6 Aggregatable Global Unicast Address Format

addressing.why: A large part covers address allocation policy: IANA to registries to organizations, requirements, and NLA hierarchy design. This is address architecture, allocation and aggregation, not covered by an IPv6 child tag.
addressing.quote: TLA ID's are assigned to organizations providing transit topology. They are specifically not assigned to organizations only providing leaf topology.
addressing.section: 5.0 Proposed Rules for Assignment of Top-Level Aggregation ID's

rejected.why: IANA is the allocating authority, but the document sets address assignment policy and does not create or manage an IANA registry or give IANA considerations guidance.
CIDR is cited only as a precedent for 'slow start' allocation.
Routing table size motivates the rules, but the document is about address assignment.
Multihoming is mentioned only as a reason not to give leaf sites TLAs.

RFC2451.title: The ESP CBC-Mode Cipher Algorithms
RFC2451.summary: Specifies how CBC-mode block ciphers (CAST-128, RC5, IDEA, Blowfish, 3DES) are used with IPsec ESP, covering key sizes, weak keys, block size, padding, rounds and the IV/payload layout.

ESP.why: The document is a companion to the ESP specification. It defines the ESP payload format with IV and ciphertext, and the padding, keying material and IV rules for CBC ciphers in ESP.
ESP.quote: This document describes how to use CBC-mode cipher algorithms with the IPSec ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) Protocol.

cryptography.why: A large part of the document specifies cipher parameters for CAST-128, RC5, IDEA, Blowfish and 3DES. These include key sizes, weak keys, rounds and CBC mode. No specific cipher tag in the taxonomy fits, since DES covers only the 3DES part, so the parent topic is used.
cryptography.quote: All symmetric block cipher algorithms share common characteristics and variables. These include mode, key size, weak keys, block size, and rounds.

rejected.why: Only 3DES (DES-EDE3-CBC) is covered here, as one of five ciphers. The plain DES-CBC cipher is explicitly left to another document.
The document is specifically about ESP's cipher usage. ESP is the more specific tag and already sits under IPsec.
Key exchange is mentioned only in passing, in the keying material section.
The keying material section is only a brief note on how many bits to take from the key exchange. It is not a substantial subject of the document.

gaps.name: Block cipher modes (CBC) and generic block ciphers (CAST-128, RC5, IDEA, Blowfish)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tags for these ciphers or for cipher modes. Only AES, DES and a few others are listed, so the document falls back to the parent cryptography topic.

RFC2452.title: IP Version 6 Management Information Base for the Transmission Control Protocol
RFC2452.summary: Defines the IPV6-TCP-MIB module, an experimental SNMP MIB adding an ipv6TcpConnTable for TCP connections between IPv6 endpoints, and recommends that the rest of the RFC 2012 TCP MIB applies unchanged to IPv6.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (IPV6-TCP-MIB) defining a connection table, conformance groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: this document is the MIB module which defines managed objects for implementations of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) over IP Version 6 (IPv6).

TCP.why: The MIB manages TCP connections and states, and discusses how TCP is transparent to the IP version, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: The state of this TCP connection.

IPv6.why: It is part of the IPv6 MIB series. Its table uses IPv6 addresses and interface indexes, so IPv6 deployment and management readers would look for it.
IPv6.quote: This memo defines a new, separate table to represent only those TCP connections between IPv6 endpoints.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol the MIB is carried over. The document defines objects, not protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
The SMI is written in an ASN.1 subset, but ASN.1 is only the notation and the document is not about it.

RFC2453.title: RIP Version 2
RFC2453.summary: RFC 2453 specifies RIP version 2, the distance-vector IGP, extending RIP-1 messages with route tags, subnet masks, next hop, multicast and simple-password authentication, and covers compatibility with RIP-1.

RIP.why: The whole document specifies RIP-2: the distance-vector algorithm, message format, timers, input/output processing, extensions and compatibility with RIP-1.
RIP.quote: This document specifies an extension of the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), as defined in [1], to expand the amount of useful information carried in RIP messages
