rejected.why: RIP-2 uses multicast address 224.0.0.9 for updates, but that is a small part of the document and does not concern multicast routing.
RIP runs over UDP port 520, but UDP is only the substrate and nothing new is defined about it.
A simple plaintext password authentication entry is defined, but it is a minor extension within RIP. The stronger mechanism is in a separate document.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as the newer IGPs RIP is compared with, and the document does not specify them.
Distance-vector theory is explained, but it is in service of specifying RIP and is not general routing architecture.

RFC2454.title: IP Version 6 Management Information Base for the User Datagram Protocol
RFC2454.summary: Defines the IPV6-UDP-MIB module, a table of UDP listeners on IPv6 endpoints, and recommends that the RFC 2013 UDP MIB otherwise applies unchanged to UDP over IPv6.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (IPV6-UDP-MIB) defining ipv6UdpTable and conformance statements. MIB is the most specific tag for this.
MIB.quote: this document is the MIB module which defines managed objects for implementations of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) over IP Version 6 (IPv6).

UDP.why: The MIB manages UDP endpoints and discusses how UDP relates to IP versions, so UDP readers would want it. The subject is UDP management objects, not UDP's protocol behaviour, so this is secondary.
UDP.quote: The fact that UDP is carried over IPv6 as opposed to IPv4, is largely invisible to a UDP implementation.
UDP.section: 3. Transparency of IP versions to UDP

IPv6.why: The document is part of the IPv6 MIB series. It defines IPv6-specific managed objects, including IPv6 address and interface index handling for UDP listeners.
IPv6.quote: This memo defines a new, separate table to represent only those UDP endpoints that utilize an IPv6 addresses.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol the MIB is used with. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour. Its SNMPv3 security advice appears only in Security Considerations.
The MIB is written in SMI, an ASN.1 subset, but this is only the notation. The document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
ICMP is mentioned only in passing, in the Security Considerations.

RFC2455.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for APPN
RFC2455.summary: Defines an SNMPv2 MIB module for monitoring and controlling APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking) nodes, ports, link stations, topology, directory, class of service and intermediate sessions, obsoleting RFC 2155.

APPN.why: The whole document defines managed objects for APPN nodes, TGs, topology, directory and COS, so it belongs on the APPN page.
APPN.quote: It defines a MIB module for managing devices with Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking (APPN) capabilities.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module with textual conventions, tables, and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with. The document defines objects, not new SNMP protocol behaviour, so MIB is the fitting tag.
APPN is the SNA child tag and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
DLSw is mentioned only as a transport that APPN link stations can use, and is covered by a separate MIB.
The RTP here is the HPR Rapid Transport Protocol, not the IETF Real-time Transport Protocol. It appears only in a few HPR-related objects.

gaps.name: HPR (High Performance Routing)
gaps.why: The MIB includes HPR objects, but the taxonomy has no HPR tag. HPR is mostly covered by the separate RFC 2238.

RFC2456.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for APPN TRAPS
RFC2456.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (APPN-TRAP-MIB) of notifications and supporting objects for APPN and DLUR devices, reporting TG, port, link station, DLUR-DLUS session state changes and final intermediate-session accounting statistics.

APPN.why: The whole MIB module is for managing APPN/DLUR nodes, defining notifications on APPN local TG, port, link station and DLUR-DLUS session status.
APPN.quote: it defines objects for receiving notifications from network devices with APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Network) and DLUR (Dependent LU Requester) capabilities.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SMIv2) with notifications, objects, and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for; the document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the MIB tag, rather than specifying SNMP itself.
APPN is a child of SNA and is the more specific tag; SNA is implied as an ancestor.
Not discussed; the document concerns APPN and DLUR only.
Implied by the MIB tag's ancestry; no separate topic coverage needed.

gaps.name: DLUR (Dependent LU Requester)
gaps.why: The document covers DLUR-DLUS session state notifications, but the taxonomy has no DLUR tag; APPN is the closest fit.

RFC2457.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Extended Border Node
RFC2457.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module for managing APPN Extended Border Node (EBN) devices, covering subnet affiliation of LUs, intermediate session RSCV/COS, COS mapping, subnet routing lists and HPR EBN session info.

APPN.why: The whole document is about managing APPN Extended Border Nodes, which is the APPN technology under SNA. The managed objects extend the APPN MIB tables.
APPN.quote: it defines objects for monitoring and controlling network devices with APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Network) EBN (Extended Border Node) capabilities.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMIv2, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, so MIB is the better fit.
APPN is the more specific child of SNA, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
DLSw is a different SNA-over-IP technology. The document does not cover it.

RFC2458.title: Toward the PSTN/Internet Inter-Networking--Pre-PINT Implementations
RFC2458.summary: Informational survey of pre-PINT implementations (Lucent, Siemens, AT&T, Nortel) through which Internet applications request PSTN services such as click-to-dial-back and click-to-fax, with architecture, interfaces, security lessons and a SIP outlook.

PINT.why: The whole document describes PINT services, architecture and pre-PINT systems that the PINT WG was chartered to standardise.
PINT.quote: the arrangements through which Internet applications can request and enrich PSTN telecommunications services

SIP.why: Section 7 presents SIP as the emerging solution and shows how SIP INVITEs convey PSTN addresses for click-to-dial.
SIP.quote: SIP, the Session Initiation Protocol, is a simple signaling protocol for Internet conferencing and telephony.

PSTN interop.why: Internet/PSTN interworking via gateways, Service Nodes and IN components is the central theme, including a PSTN/IN tutorial appendix.
PSTN interop.quote: the Internet is used for non-voice interactions, while the voice (and fax) are carried entirely over the PSTN

rejected.why: SNMP is only used for the Lucent SMS interface and a small example MIB; not the subject.
Cookies are discussed as a mechanism in the Siemens system, but only incidentally.
HTTP/web is the request front-end substrate, not specified or extended here.
Finger is used as a notification trick in the Siemens system; not the subject.
SDP appears only in SIP examples.
Fax is a PINT service delivered over the PSTN, not Internet fax work.

gaps.name: Intelligent Network (IN) / Computer-Telephony Integration
gaps.why: The document covers IN architecture (SCP, SSP, SN, INAP) and CTI/call centers at length, but the taxonomy has no tag for them beyond PSTN interop.

RFC2459.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile
RFC2459.summary: RFC 2459 profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and v2 CRL for the Internet PKI, defining extensions, a certification path validation algorithm, algorithm identifiers/encodings, and ASN.1 modules.

X.509.why: The whole document is a profile of X.509 certificates and CRLs, including extensions and path validation.
X.509.quote: This memo profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and X.509 v2 CRL for use in the Internet.

ASN.1.why: Large appendices give normative ASN.1 modules (1988 and 1993 syntax) for certificates, CRLs and extensions.
ASN.1.quote: Finally, ASN.1 modules are provided in the appendices for all data structures defined or referenced.

rejected.why: RSA keys and signature OIDs are encoded in section 7, but the document is not about the RSA algorithm itself.
PEM's RFC 1422 hierarchy is discussed as background and compatibility, not the subject.
Only an authority information access OID for OCSP is referenced; no OCSP protocol is defined.
MD2/MD5/SHA-1 are listed as hash options for signatures; the document does not address them in their own right.
Not relevant; no DES content.
X.500 naming is used for DNs but the profile explicitly does not assume a Directory deployment.

RFC2460.title: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
RFC2460.summary: RFC 2460 specifies the core IPv6 protocol: the base header, extension headers (hop-by-hop, routing, fragment, destination options), packet size rules, flow labels, traffic classes, and upper-layer protocol issues.

IPv6.why: The document is the base IPv6 specification, defining the header format, extension headers, fragmentation and upper-layer rules.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6), also sometimes referred to as IP Next Generation or IPng.

rejected.why: ICMPv6 is specified separately in RFC 2463. This document only references ICMP error messages.
AH and ESP are specified in other RFCs. This document only names them in the extension header order and in the Security Considerations.
Path MTU Discovery is only recommended by reference to RFC 1981. It is not specified here.
The Traffic Class section only says the field is intended to allow similar functionality. The semantics are left to separate documents.
IPv6 address format and semantics are specified separately in the Addressing Architecture.
TCP and UDP appear only as upper-layer examples for the pseudo-header checksum and MSS computation.

RFC2461.title: Neighbor Discovery for IP Version 6 (IPv6)
RFC2461.summary: Specifies the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol (obsoleting RFC 1970): router and prefix discovery, address resolution, neighbor unreachability detection, and redirects, using five ICMPv6 message types and options.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document defines the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol: message formats, host and router behaviour, NUD, redirects, and options.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document specifies the Neighbor Discovery protocol for IP Version 6.

rejected.why: Address autoconfiguration is defined in RFC 2462 (ADDRCONF). This document only carries prefix information and the M/O flags for it.
ND messages are ICMPv6 types, but ICMPv6 is only the carrier here and is specified in RFC 2463.
ARP is mentioned only in the IPv4 comparison. ND replaces it for IPv6 and does not specify ARP.
Anycast handling is a small subsection (7.2.7) of ND behaviour, not the document's subject.
The neighbor discovery tag is the more specific fit and already implies IPv6.
The Authentication Header is only a SHOULD-level security mechanism mentioned in the message formats and Security Considerations.

RFC2462.title: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
RFC2462.summary: RFC 2462 specifies IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration: link-local address creation, Duplicate Address Detection, and forming global/site-local addresses from Router Advertisement prefixes, with address lifetimes and interplay with stateful configuration.

SLAAC.why: The whole document defines IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, including link-local generation, DAD, and prefix-based address formation.
SLAAC.quote: the process for generating site-local and global addresses via stateless address autoconfiguration, and the Duplicate Address Detection procedure

rejected.why: The document relies on Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement and Router Advertisements defined in RFC 2461, using them for DAD but not specifying Neighbor Discovery itself.
Stateful autoconfiguration is only referenced as being specified elsewhere; this document does not define it.
Site renumbering is a design goal with a short section (4.1), but the document is not about renumbering procedures.
SLAAC is the more specific child tag and already implies IPv6.

RFC2463.title: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMPv6) for the Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
RFC2463.summary: RFC 2463 specifies ICMPv6, the Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6, defining its general message format, processing rules, checksum, and the error (Destination Unreachable, Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem) and informational (Echo Request/Reply) messages.

ICMP.why: The whole document defines ICMPv6 message formats, source address selection, processing and rate-limiting rules, so it belongs on the ICMP page.
ICMP.quote: This document specifies a set of Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) messages for use with version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6).

rejected.why: ICMPv6 runs over IPv6 and is a required part of it, but the document specifies ICMP messages, not IPv6 itself.
The Packet Too Big message feeds Path MTU Discovery, but the document says the procedures are described elsewhere.
The ICMPv6 checksum and pseudo-header are covered only as one part of the message format, not as the subject of the document.
Neighbor Discovery is mentioned only as another user of ICMPv6 message types.
AH and ESP appear only in the Security Considerations as a way to authenticate ICMP messages.
Echo and Time Exceeded messages are used for diagnostics, but the document does not specify traceroute or path discovery tools.

RFC2464.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Ethernet Networks
RFC2464.summary: RFC 2464 specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over Ethernet: frame format, MTU, interface identifier and link-local address formation, link-layer address option format, and multicast address mapping.

Ethernet.why: The whole document defines IP over Ethernet: frame type 86DD, MTU, address mapping for unicast and multicast. This is the specific child tag for IPv6 over Ethernet.
Ethernet.quote: This document specifies the frame format for transmission of IPv6 packets and the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on Ethernet networks.

IPv6.why: It specifies IPv6 addressing details (EUI-64 interface identifiers, link-local addresses, multicast mapping) and the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option. Readers of IPv6 would want it.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 link-local address [AARCH] for an Ethernet interface is formed by appending the Interface Identifier, as defined above, to the prefix FE80::/64.

rejected.why: Only the 64-bit prefix length and interface identifier derivation for SLAAC are given. SLAAC itself is specified in RFC 2462.
Only the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option on Ethernet is specified. The Neighbor Discovery protocol itself is defined in RFC 2461.
The mapping of IPv6 multicast addresses to Ethernet multicast addresses is a link-layer detail, not multicast routing or group membership.
Interface identifier formation is covered by the IPv6 tag. The document is not about address architecture, allocation or use in general.

RFC2465.title: Management Information Base for IP Version 6: Textual Conventions and General Group
RFC2465.summary: Defines the IPv6 MIB textual conventions and the IPv6 General group (interfaces, interface statistics, address prefixes, addresses, routes, neighbor address translation) for SNMP-based management of IPv6 entities.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (IPV6-TC and IPV6-MIB) using SMI, so it belongs on the MIB page.
MIB.quote: Specifically, the IPv6 MIB textual conventions as well as the IPv6 MIB General group is defined in this document.

IPv6.why: The managed objects model IPv6 interfaces, addresses, prefixes, forwarding and fragmentation/reassembly counters, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: provides for the basic management of IPv6 entities and serve as the foundation for other IPv6 MIB definitions.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework and protocol the MIB is used with; the document defines MIB objects (covered by the MIB tag, a child of SNMP), not protocol operations.
The ipv6NetToMediaTable reflects Neighbor Discovery state, but the document does not specify or extend ND itself.
ASN.1/SMI is just the notation for the module, not the subject.
The route table objects are one part of an interface and general-management MIB; no routing protocol is specified.

RFC2466.title: Management Information Base for IP Version 6: ICMPv6 Group
RFC2466.summary: Defines the IPV6-ICMP-MIB module, an SNMP MIB group with per-interface ICMPv6 message statistics counters and conformance statements.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is to define a MIB module (IPV6-ICMP-MIB) in SMIv2 with objects, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the IPv6-based internets.

ICMP.why: The MIB's objects count ICMPv6 message types (destination unreachable, packet too big, neighbor solicitation, and so on). Readers of ICMPv6 would want this management view of the protocol.
ICMP.quote: ipv6IfIcmpInDestUnreachs OBJECT-TYPE

IPv6.why: It is part of the IPv6 MIB series, with per-IPv6-interface statistics that augment ipv6IfEntry.
IPv6.quote: This document is the one in the series of documents that define various MIB object groups for IPv6.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is used with. The document defines no new protocol behaviour, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
Neighbor and router solicit/advertise messages are only counted, and the document does not specify neighbor discovery.
The MIB is written in ASN.1-based SMI, but that is only the notation used.
Group membership message counters are included, but the document does not specify MLD.

RFC2467.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over FDDI Networks
RFC2467.summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are framed (LLC/SNAP), how MTU, interface identifiers, link-local addresses, and neighbor discovery link-layer address options and multicast mapping work over FDDI networks, replacing RFC 2019.

FDDI.why: The whole document defines IPv6 over FDDI: frame format, MTU, address mapping, so it belongs on the IP over FDDI page.
FDDI.quote: This document specifies the frame format for transmission of IPv6 packets and the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on FDDI networks.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the protocol being carried, but the document is about the FDDI link-layer binding. The FDDI tag is more specific and fits.
The Source/Target Link-layer Address option format for FDDI is defined, but neighbor discovery itself is only referenced from RFC 2461.
Interface identifier formation is defined for FDDI, but stateless autoconfiguration itself is specified elsewhere (RFC 2462).
Path MTU Discovery is mentioned only in the bridge discussion; it is not specified or extended here.
Ethernet appears only as a mixed-media bridging example and as the model for the sibling RFC 2464.

RFC2468.title: I REMEMBER IANA
RFC2468.summary: Vint Cerf's remembrance of Jon Postel, the long-time IANA, RFC editor and IAB founding member, recounting his career and legacy in the development of the ARPANET and Internet.

internet history.why: The memo is a retrospective on Postel's roles from the early ARPANET at UCLA through the IAB, the Internet Society and IANA. It is personal history of the Internet's formative decades.
internet history.quote: Beginning with the ARPANET, an endless stream of networks evolved, and ultimately were interlinked to become the Internet.

rejected.why: IANA is the title and Postel's role, but the memo is a eulogy. It says nothing about registries, procedures or stewardship that a reader of the IANA subject would need.
The ARPANET is mentioned as the setting for Postel's early work, but the memo does not cover its protocols or operations.
Postel's role as the first RFC editor is mentioned in passing. The memo is not about the format, style or publication of the series.

gaps.name: Obituary / biographical remembrance
gaps.why: The memo is a tribute to a person (Jonathan B. Postel) and the Postel Service Award. The taxonomy has no biography or obituary tag, so internet history is the closest fit.

RFC2469.title: A Caution On The Canonical Ordering Of Link-Layer Addresses
RFC2469.summary: Informational caution to implementors that link-layer addresses in ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery must be in canonical (LSB/Ethernet) bit order, and that Token Ring and some FDDI adaptors need bit swapping.

ARP.why: The document analyses how link-layer addresses are carried in ARP packets, including Token Ring practice and bridge bit-swapping of ARP address fields.
ARP.quote: Ethernet addresses that appear in ARP packets are in canonical order.

neighbor discovery.why: A full section addresses canonical ordering of link-layer address options in IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages.
neighbor discovery.quote: Implementors must insure that any addresses that appear in link-layer address options of Neighbor Discovery [DISCOVERY] messages are sent in canonical order

token ring.why: Token Ring's non-canonical MSB bit ordering is the main source of the problem, and the Token Ring/Ethernet bridging case is discussed.
token ring.quote: Token Ring (and some FDDI) hardware does not behave consistently with this definition

Ethernet.why: Ethernet canonical form defines the reference format, and bridging between Ethernet and Token Ring is covered.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet and 802.3 hardware behave consistently with this definition.

rejected.why: FDDI is only mentioned as having some adaptors that use non-canonical order. The document is not about IP over FDDI.
IPv6 matters only through Neighbor Discovery, which is the more specific tag.
This parent is implied by the specific tags chosen.

RFC2470.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Token Ring Networks
RFC2470.summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over IEEE 802.5 Token Ring: MTU, LLC/SNAP frame format, interface identifier and link-local address formation, and neighbor discovery link-layer address options and multicast mapping.

token ring.why: The whole document defines IPv6 over Token Ring: MTU, LLC/SNAP framing, source-route bridging RIF handling, and multicast functional address mapping.
token ring.quote: This memo specifies the MTU and frame format for transmission of IPv6 packets on Token Ring networks.

IPv6.why: Defines IPv6 interface identifier derivation from EUI-64, link-local address formation, and a 64-bit prefix requirement for stateless autoconfiguration on this link type.
IPv6.quote: It also specifies the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses on Token Ring networks

rejected.why: The document only defines the Source/Target Link-layer Address option format for Token Ring; the Neighbor Discovery protocol itself is specified elsewhere (RFC 2461).
Stateless autoconfiguration is referenced for interface identifier formation, but the procedure is defined in another RFC; this document only supplies link-specific details.
Ethernet is mentioned only for MTU compatibility and EtherType encoding; it is not the subject.

RFC2471.title: IPv6 Testing Address Allocation
RFC2471.summary: Defines the temporary IPv6 aggregatable global unicast address allocation (TLA 0x1FFE) used for 6bone testing of IPv6 prototype software, replacing RFC 1897.

addressing.why: The document is an address allocation plan: it defines the TLA/NLA/SLA field assignment of the test prefix. No more specific addressing child fits, so the addressing topic is used directly.
addressing.quote: This document describes an allocation plan for IPv6 addresses to be used in testing IPv6 prototype software.

IPv6.why: It specifies IPv6 addressing for the 6bone testbed and its temporary TLA, which is IPv6 addressing and deployment.
IPv6.quote: The addresses described in this document are consistent with the IPv6 Addressing Architecture [ARCH].

rejected.why: Only mentioned as one way addresses may be assigned; the document is not about DHCPv6.
Autoconfiguration is mentioned only as an assignment method, not specified here.
IANA assigned the TLA ID, but the document is an address plan, not about registry procedures.
6bone is a testbed, but the document does not define a transition mechanism.

gaps.name: 6bone testbed
gaps.why: The document is about addressing for the 6bone IPv6 testbed; the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC2472.title: IP Version 6 over PPP
RFC2472.summary: Defines how IPv6 packets are carried over PPP links, the IPV6CP network control protocol with its Interface-Identifier and IPv6-Compression-Protocol options, and formation of link-local addresses on PPP links.

PPP.why: The document specifies IPV6CP, a new PPP NCP, and IPv6 encapsulation over PPP, so it belongs on the PPP page.
PPP.quote: This document defines the method for transmission of IP Version 6 [2] packets over PPP links as well as the Network Control Protocol (NCP)

IPv6.why: A substantial part covers IPv6 interface identifier formation from EUI-64 and link-local addressing, which interests IPv6 readers.
IPv6.quote: It also specifies the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses on PPP links.

rejected.why: Stateless autoconfiguration is referenced only for the interface identifier and duplicate address detection settings; the document does not specify it.
The IPv6-Compression-Protocol option is only a negotiation placeholder with no values assigned, so the document does not cover compression.
The interface identifier and link-local address are specific to IPv6, so the IPv6 tag covers them.

RFC2473.title: Generic Packet Tunneling in IPv6 Specification
RFC2473.summary: Specifies generic tunneling of packets (IPv6, IPv4, others) inside IPv6: encapsulation/decapsulation, nested encapsulation limits via a Tunnel Encapsulation Limit destination option, tunnel header fields, MTU/fragmentation, and ICMP error relaying.

tunneling.why: The document defines generic IPv6 encapsulation tunneling, its nested encapsulation limits and tunnel state. No GRE or IP-in-IP child fits, so the parent topic tag applies.
tunneling.quote: This document specifies a method and generic mechanisms by which a packet is encapsulated and carried as payload within an IPv6 packet.

IPv6.why: It defines a new IPv6 destination option, plus tunnel header field rules, hop limit, flow label and fragmentation behaviour in IPv6. Readers of IPv6 would want it.
IPv6.quote: The Tunnel Encapsulation Limit option is carried in a Destination Options extension header

rejected.why: ICMP error relaying through tunnels is a section of the document, but ICMP is not the subject. The document uses it to report errors.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to secure the tunnel.
The document is IPv6-encapsulating generic tunneling, and mentions IPv4-in-IPv6 only as one case. RFC 1853 IP-in-IP is just referenced.
Path MTU discovery is used to set the tunnel MTU but is not specified here.

RFC2474.title: Definition of the Differentiated Services Field (DS Field) in the IPv4 and IPv6 Headers
RFC2474.summary: RFC 2474 defines the Differentiated Services (DS) field, redefining the IPv4 TOS octet and IPv6 Traffic Class octet as a 6-bit DSCP plus 2 unused bits. It also defines Class Selector codepoints, the Default PHB, and guidelines for standardizing per-hop behaviors.

Diffserv.why: The document is the core Diffserv specification: DS field layout, DSCP codepoints, PHB requirements, Class Selector codepoints and PHB standardization guidelines.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines the IP header field, called the DS (for differentiated services) field.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
The document redefines the IPv4 TOS octet, but only as the carrier of the DS field. The subject is Diffserv, not IPv4 itself.
The IPv6 Traffic Class octet is redefined the same way. The document is not about IPv6 specification or deployment.
Section 7.2 discusses IPsec and tunnel interactions, but only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate. The document is not about IPsec.
Section 6 divides the codepoint space into pools, but this is a registry allocation note for the document's own subject, not IANA guidance.

review: no tag in common with RFC1455, which it obsoletes

RFC2475.title: An Architecture for Differentiated Services
RFC2475.summary: RFC 2475 defines the Differentiated Services architecture: scalable service differentiation via DS-field packet marking, traffic classification and conditioning at domain boundaries, and per-hop behaviors in the core.

Diffserv.why: The entire document specifies the Diffserv architecture: DS domains, classifiers, traffic conditioners, PHBs, and PHB specification guidelines.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines an architecture for implementing scalable service differentiation in the Internet.

rejected.why: Section 6.2 discusses interaction of IPsec tunnels with the DS field, but this is a subsidiary consideration, not the document's subject.
RSVP/Intserv is only compared against Diffserv as an alternative model; not the subject.
Parent of Diffserv, which is implied by the more specific tag.
MPLS is mentioned only in the comparison with other approaches.
Tunnel/DS-field interaction is a minor section and mostly about IPsec; not the document's focus.
Section 5 is a short discussion of multicast considerations for provisioning, not substantial enough to warrant the tag.

RFC2476.title: Message Submission
RFC2476.summary: Specifies message submission as distinct from relay over SMTP: port 587, the Message Submission Agent's required, recommended and optional actions, SMTP extension usage, and permitted message modifications.

SMTP.why: The document defines the submission service on SMTP (ESMTP), including MSA behaviour, reply codes, and which SMTP extensions apply on the submit port. This is the core subject of SMTP submission and relaying.
SMTP.quote: Port 587 is reserved for email message submission as specified in this document. Messages received on this port are defined to be submissions.

rejected.why: SMTP is the more specific child tag and already implies email.
The MSA fixes headers like Date, Message-ID and Sender, but it only enforces conformance to RFC 822. It does not define the message format.
Spam and relay control are cited as motivations, but the document is not about spam filtering or reporting.
POP authentication before submission is mentioned only as one authorization method.
IPsec is mentioned only as one option for authorizing submission.
MIME transfer encoding is only an optional MSA modification mentioned in passing.
Fully-qualified domains and CNAME resolution are mentioned, but the document is not about DNS.

RFC2477.title: Criteria for Evaluating Roaming Protocols
RFC2477.summary: Informational requirements document listing criteria for evaluating dialup roaming protocols across phone book, authentication, and accounting subsystems, including RADIUS gateway support, PPP, tunneling, and security requirements.

AAA.why: The core of the document is requirements for authentication, authorization and accounting across roaming ISPs, including proxies, attribute editing and accounting record formats.
AAA.quote: A roaming standard MUST provide support for real-time accounting.

PPP.why: Connection management and authentication requirements are framed around PPP, with CHAP/PAP/EAP used in the PPP framework.
PPP.quote: a roaming standard MUST provide support for PPP and IP.

rejected.why: RADIUS is only required to be accommodated via gateways; the document does not specify or extend it.
EAP is only mentioned as a SHOULD-support authentication type, not a subject of the document.
Mobile IP is only mentioned as a layer 3 tunneling case that must not be precluded.
Layer 2 tunneling protocols are only mentioned as something proxies must not preclude.
IPsec is only mentioned as one possible way to provide hop-by-hop security.
The security requirements are a part of the AAA roaming requirements and not a standalone security subject.

gaps.name: Roaming (dialup ISP roaming, ROAMOPS)
gaps.why: The document is about roaming among dialup ISPs, including phone book updates and the Network Access Identifier, and no taxonomy tag covers this.

RFC2478.title: The Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation Mechanism
RFC2478.summary: RFC 2478 specifies SPNEGO, a GSS-API pseudo-mechanism that lets peers negotiate in-band a common security mechanism, with optimistic token piggybacking and MIC protection of the mechanism list.

SPNEGO.why: The document defines the SPNEGO mechanism itself: its negotiation model, NegTokenInit/NegTokenTarg tokens, mechListMIC processing and examples.
SPNEGO.quote: The Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation Mechanism defined here is a pseudo-security mechanism

rejected.why: SPNEGO is a child of GSS-API and the more specific tag fits; the parent is implied. The appendix GSS-API calls support negotiation and do not make the document about GSS-API in general.
The tokens are defined in ASN.1 with DER encoding, but that is only the encoding substrate, not the subject.
Negotiation selects a security mechanism but does not itself define authentication. SPNEGO under GSS-API covers it.

RFC2479.title: Independent Data Unit Protection Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (IDUP-GSS-API)
RFC2479.summary: RFC 2479 specifies IDUP-GSS-API, an extension of GSS-API that gives applications a mechanism-independent interface for protecting stand-alone data units (signing, encryption, non-repudiation evidence) without a live peer connection, for uses such as secure email.

GSS-API.why: The whole document defines an extension of GSS-API: environment, per-IDU protect/unprotect, evidence and support calls, replacing session-oriented GSS calls.
GSS-API.quote: The IDUP-GSS-API extends the GSS-API [RFC-2078] for applications requiring protection of a generic data unit (such as a file or message)

rejected.why: Secure email is only a motivating application, and the document does not specify S/MIME.
PEM is cited only as an example mechanism in Appendix B.
Kerberos is mentioned only in passing as a GSS mechanism for token framing.
Authentication is generic here and covered by the GSS-API tag.
Certificates and revocation appear only as supporting mechanism details, not as the subject.
The document is an API specification and defines no algorithms; QOP strength qualifiers are minor.

gaps.name: Non-repudiation evidence services
gaps.why: A substantial part of the document covers evidence generation and verification (proof of origin, delivery, receipt), but the taxonomy has no tag for non-repudiation.

RFC2480.title: Gateways and MIME Security Multiparts
RFC2480.summary: RFC 2480 defines requirements for gateways between MIME and non-MIME environments so that MIME security multiparts (multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted) can pass through safely, including tunnelling or disassembling them.

MIME.why: The document specifies gateway handling of MIME security multipart body structures and conversion of MIME objects to non-MIME formats. This is about MIME body structure.
MIME.quote: MUST provide the ability to tunnel multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted objects as monolithic entities if there is any chance whatsoever that MIME capabilities exist

email.why: It specifies mail gateway behaviour between MIME mail and non-MIME messaging environments such as voice messaging systems. Email readers would want it.
email.quote: Gateways that deal with MIME objects have to be able to convert them to non-MIME formats.

rejected.why: The document concerns the generic RFC 1847 security multiparts. It does not cover S/MIME or CMS.
The topic is security-related, but the document is about gateway behaviour for a specific MIME mechanism. The MIME and email tags cover it better.
OpenPGP is not mentioned. The document applies to any security multipart mechanism.

RFC2481.title: A Proposal to add Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to IP
RFC2481.summary: RFC 2481 proposes adding Explicit Congestion Notification to IP (ECT and CE bits in the TOS/Traffic Class octet) and to TCP (ECN-Echo and CWR flags, negotiation at setup), with discussion of RED, tunnels, IPsec, and non-compliance.

ECN.why: The whole document defines ECN: the ECT and CE bits in the IP header, router marking behaviour, and end-system response.
ECN.quote: Routers could instead set a Congestion Experienced (CE) bit in the packet header of packets from ECN-capable transport protocols.

TCP.why: A substantial part (Section 6.1) specifies TCP changes: ECN-Echo and CWR flags, SYN/SYN-ACK negotiation, sender and receiver behaviour.
TCP.quote: For TCP, ECN requires three new mechanisms: negotiation between the endpoints during setup to determine if they are both ECN-capable

rejected.why: RED and active queue management motivate ECN, but the document says it does not specify a particular active queue management mechanism.
Section 10.2 covers ECN interaction with IPsec tunnels, but this is a side consideration, not the document's subject.
Section 10.1 gives encapsulation rules for the ECN bits, but it is a minor part of the document.
The parent topic is implied by the ECN tag, and a more specific tag already fits.
The ECN field is placed in the IPv4 TOS octet and the checksum is discussed, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
The DS field is cited only for the history of bits 6 and 7, and the document does not address Diffserv.

RFC2482.title: Language Tagging in Unicode Plain Text
RFC2482.summary: Proposes Plane 14 Unicode tag characters (including a LANGUAGE TAG and CANCEL TAG character) for embedding RFC 1766 language tags in Unicode plain text, with syntax, scope and conformance rules.

Unicode.why: The document proposes new Unicode/ISO 10646 characters and their encoding, conformance and display behaviour, so it is about Unicode usage in Internet protocols.
Unicode.quote: A set of special-use tag characters on Plane 14 of [ISO10646] (accessible through UTF-8, UTF-16, and UCS-4 encoding forms) are proposed for encoding

language tags.why: The document defines how to embed RFC 1766 language tags in plain text, so it is about language tagging.
language tags.quote: a language tag identification character is proposed to identify a language tag string specifically; the language tag itself makes use of [RFC1766] language tag strings

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only one of three encoding forms in which the tag characters can be expressed. The document does not specify or extend UTF-8.
ACAP is named only as a protocol that motivates the proposal. The document does not specify or extend it.
HTML appears only as an example of heavyweight in-band markup that this proposal is an alternative to.
The document is about Unicode characters and does not register or specify character sets.
The document uses an extended BNF only to describe its own tag syntax, which is a formal-syntax apparatus and not the subject.

RFC2483.title: URI Resolution Services Necessary for URN Resolution
RFC2483.summary: Experimental RFC defining an initial set of URI resolution operations (I2L, I2Ls, I2R, I2Rs, I2C, I2N, I2Ns, I=I) for access services, guidelines for specifying new operations, and the text/uri-list media type.

URN.why: The document defines resolution services for URIs/URNs (URN to URL, URN to URN, equality), produced by the URN working group; readers of URN resolution would look for it.
URN.quote: Retrieving the resource identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) [1] is only one of the operations that can be performed on a URI.

media types.why: A substantial section registers the text/uri-list media type, including its format and registration template.
media types.quote: The text/uri-list Internet Media Type is defined to provide a simple format for the automatic processing of such lists of URIs.

rejected.why: URN is the more specific tag chosen; the document's resolution services target URNs primarily, and the parent URI is implied.
Only referenced via RFC 2168 as a related resolution approach; not specified here.
MIME multipart/alternative is used as output encoding for I2Rs only; the media type registration is covered by media types.
Mentioned only as an existing system that must not be harmed; not the subject.

gaps.name: URN resolution / Resolution Discovery Service (RDS)
gaps.why: The document is about resolution of URIs/URNs to locators, resources and descriptions; the taxonomy has no dedicated tag for URI/URN resolution services, only the URN tag and generic naming.

RFC2484.title: PPP LCP Internationalization Configuration Option
RFC2484.summary: Defines PPP LCP configuration option 28 (Internationalization) that lets peers negotiate the charset (MIBenum) and language tag used for human-readable messages.

PPP.why: The RFC extends PPP's Link Control Protocol with a new configuration option, so it belongs on the PPP page.
PPP.quote: This document defines an LCP configuration option for the negotiation of character set and language usage

internationalization.why: The option exists to negotiate charset and language for text in protocol messages, as RFC 2277 requires. No technology tag under internationalization fits better, since the language-tag and charset specs are only referenced.
internationalization.quote: both the language in which human-readable messages it sends should be composed and the charset in which that language should be represented

rejected.why: The option carries an RFC 1766 language tag, but the document does not define or specify tags. It only uses them as a field value.
The option carries a MIBenum from the IANA charset registry, but the document does not register or define charsets. It only references the registry.
UTF-8 is only the default charset value (MIBenum 106), not the subject of the document.
EAP is cited only as one source of human-readable text. The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC2485.title: DHCP Option for The Open Group's User Authentication Protocol
RFC2485.summary: Defines DHCP option 98, carrying a list of URLs pointing to User Authentication Protocol (UAP) servers for Open Group Network Computing Clients.

DHCP.why: The RFC's sole purpose is to define a new DHCP option (code 98) carrying a URL list, so it extends DHCP and belongs on the DHCP page.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a DHCP [1] option that contains a list of pointers to User Authentication Protocol servers

rejected.why: UAP basic authentication uses HTTP Basic, but the document only defines a DHCP option pointing to servers. It does not specify or extend the HTTP authentication scheme.
Secure authentication is Basic auth inside an SSLv3 session. SSL is only the substrate and nothing new is defined about it.
URLs are the data carried in the option. The document defines no URL syntax or scheme.
The document is about how clients discover UAP servers, not how authentication works. The authentication mechanisms belong to the Open Group standard.
HTTP 1.1 is only the protocol UAP servers speak. The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC2486.title: The Network Access Identifier
RFC2486.summary: Defines the syntax (user@realm) of the Network Access Identifier, the userID a client submits during PPP authentication, used to identify users and route authentication requests in dialup roaming and tunneling.

AAA.why: The NAI identifies the user and helps route authentication requests to the home authentication server in roaming. That is core AAA infrastructure, and the document standardizes the identifier it uses.
AAA.quote: the Network Access Identifier (NAI) is the userID submitted by the client during PPP authentication.

rejected.why: PPP authentication is the context in which the NAI is submitted. The document defines only the identifier syntax and does not specify or extend PPP.
RADIUS is cited as a protocol that carries the NAI in clear text, in the Security Considerations. The document does not specify or extend it.
The realm reuses FQDN syntax and the DNS namespace for administration. The document explicitly says it does not require DNS for locating servers.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammar.
The realm grammar is derived from the domain name BNF, but the document is about user identifiers, not host naming.
Tunneling protocols such as L2TP are mentioned only as a use case for the NAI.

gaps.name: Network Access Identifier / roaming
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for user identifier syntax or dialup roaming. AAA is the closest fit.

RFC2487.title: SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over TLS
RFC2487.summary: Defines the STARTTLS extension to SMTP, letting an SMTP client and server upgrade a connection to TLS for privacy and authentication.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension: the STARTTLS EHLO keyword and command, reply codes, and post-handshake protocol reset behaviour.
SMTP.quote: The STARTTLS extension to SMTP is laid out as follows

TLS.why: A substantial part covers how TLS is negotiated in-band on SMTP, how its results are evaluated, and how state is reset. This is a deployment profile for TLS readers, not just a substrate use.
TLS.quote: After the TLS handshake has been completed, both parties MUST immediately decide whether or not to continue based on the authentication and privacy achieved.

rejected.why: SASL is only mentioned in passing, as an example of an extension advertised after TLS and for the EXTERNAL mechanism. The document does not specify it.
The Security Considerations say STARTTLS is not suitable for authenticating the author of a message. It secures hop-to-hop transport, not the domain-authentication mechanisms in that subject.
TCP is only the underlying transport, on port 25. The document defines nothing about it.
SMTP is a more specific tag than email and fits the document better.

RFC2488.title: Enhancing TCP Over Satellite Channels using Standard Mechanisms
RFC2488.summary: BCP describing standard TCP mechanisms (congestion control, large windows, delayed ACKs, SACK) plus Path MTU Discovery and FEC that improve TCP performance over satellite channels.

TCP.why: The document recommends TCP mechanisms (slow start, fast retransmit/recovery, window scaling, PAWS, RTTM, SACK, delayed ACKs) for satellite paths.
TCP.quote: this document focuses on improving TCP in the satellite environment

satellite.why: It covers satellite link characteristics (delay, noise, asymmetry, intermittent connectivity) and how to run TCP over them.
satellite.quote: Satellite channels have several characteristics that differ from most terrestrial channels.  These characteristics may degrade the performance of TCP.

PMTUD.why: A dedicated section recommends Path MTU Discovery as a lower-level mitigation for satellite paths.
PMTUD.quote: Path MTU discovery [MD90] is used to determine the maximum packet size a connection can use on a given network path

congestion control.why: A substantial section explains the TCP congestion control algorithms and their impact over long-delay satellite links.
congestion control.quote: TCP employs four congestion control mechanisms [Jac88] [Jac90] [Ste97].  These algorithms are slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery.

FEC.why: A dedicated section recommends link-level FEC to avoid false congestion signals, though it is link-level coding rather than packet-level loss recovery.
FEC.quote: The use of forward error correction coding (FEC) on a satellite link should be used to improve the bit-error rate (BER) of the satellite channel.

rejected.why: ICMP is only the signalling mechanism Path MTU Discovery relies on, not something the document specifies.
The document discusses fast retransmit/recovery per RFC 2001 and SACK-based recovery, not the NewReno modification.
IP fragmentation and the DF bit are mentioned only within the PMTUD discussion.
No QoS architecture is addressed.

RFC2489.title: Procedure for Defining New DHCP Options
RFC2489.summary: A BCP describing the procedure for defining new DHCP options, under which option numbers are assigned by IANA only when the option specification is approved for publication as an RFC.

DHCP.why: The whole document concerns how DHCP options are defined, reviewed and numbered, so it belongs on the DHCP page.
DHCP.quote: This document describes the procedure for defining new DHCP options.

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document sets the policy for IANA registry assignment of DHCP option codes (Private Use vs Specification Required, IETF consensus).
IANA.quote: IANA is requested to assign DHCP option numbers only for options that have been approved for publication as RFCs

rejected.why: The review path (Internet Draft, DHC WG, IESG) is incidental to the option-number registry policy, so IANA is the better fit.
Only the standard copyright boilerplate is present, which is not evidence of the subject.

RFC2490.title: A Simulation Model for IP Multicast with RSVP
RFC2490.summary: Describes an OPNET discrete-event simulation model of IPv4 multicast (IGMP, MOSPF, DVMRP) with RSVP, made available to the community for studying resource-reserved multicasting.

RSVP.why: A large part of the model is RSVP process behaviour on hosts and routers (Path, Resv, tear, confirm handling), and the title names RSVP.
RSVP.quote: The current version of the RSVP model supports only fixed-filter reservation style.

multicast.why: The document models IP multicast group membership and multicast routing (IGMP, multicast routing table) and an interface for plugging in multicast routing protocols.
multicast.quote: This document describes a detailed model of IPv4 multicast with RSVP that has been developed using the OPNET simulation package

IGMP.why: The host and router IGMP process models (queries, responses, join/leave, group membership table) are described in detail.
IGMP.quote: The IGMP node implements the IGMP protocol as defined in RFC 1112.

MOSPF.why: A full section describes the MOSPF/OSPF simulation process model, including group-membership LSAs and the multicast SPF calculation.
MOSPF.quote: OSPF and MOSPF models [5] are implemented in the OSPF model containing fourteen states.

OSPF.why: The OSPF model (LSAs, SPF calculation, area border routers) is described as the underlying unicast routing for the model.
OSPF.quote: This state will create Router, Network, Summary Link State Advertisements and pack all of them into an Link State Update packet.

rejected.why: The document is a simulation model, not a benchmarking methodology for devices. Only a brief runtime table is given.
RSVP is the QoS mechanism and is tagged directly. The QoS parent is implied.
The addr_trans node performs IP-to-MAC translation, but this is only a minor part of the model.
FDDI and Ethernet appear as simulated subnet link types, not as the subject of IP-over-FDDI specification.
UDP is used only for the background best-effort traffic generator.

gaps.name: Network simulation models (OPNET)
gaps.why: The document is about a simulation model and environment, which is a subject readers would look for. The taxonomy has no tag for network simulation or modelling.

gaps.name: DVMRP
gaps.why: A full section models DVMRP (probe, report, prune, graft), which is a multicast routing protocol. The taxonomy has no DVMRP tag, so multicast is the nearest fit.

RFC2491.title: IPv6 over Non-Broadcast Multiple Access (NBMA) networks
RFC2491.summary: Defines a general architecture for running IPv6 over NBMA networks, using Logical Links, a MARS-based multicast emulation for Neighbor Discovery, and router-to-router NHRP to set up shortcut paths, with PVC operation also covered.

ATM.why: The ATM tag is the closest fit for IP over ATM/NBMA: the architecture is built on ATM-style SVCs/PVCs and MARS. The tag also covers the NHRP child; companion RFC 2492 is IPv6 over ATM.
ATM.quote: This document describes a general architecture for IPv6 over NBMA networks. It forms the basis for companion documents that provide details specific to various NBMA technologies

NHRP.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how NHRP is used between routers for shortcut discovery, including NHRP/ND translation rules and purge handling.
NHRP.quote: routers SHALL use NHRP in an NHS to NHS mode to establish the IPv6 to link level address mapping of a better first hop.

neighbor discovery.why: The document specifies ND operation over NBMA, including Redirects as shortcuts, host-triggered NS, a new Shortcut Limit option and link-layer address options.
neighbor discovery.quote: The IPv6 over NBMA architecture allows conventional host-side operation of the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol

IPv6.why: It defines IPv6 link-layer behaviour, with encapsulation, interface tokens and link-local addresses on NBMA links.
IPv6.quote: IPv6/NBMA interfaces utilize RFC 2022 (MARS) for general intra- Logical Link multicasting.

rejected.why: MARS multicast emulation is used, but the document is about IPv6 ND support, not general multicast routing.
It is mentioned only as an example NBMA technology; no SMDS details are specified.
It is only named as a future companion-document technology.
It appears only in the descriptive appendix on stateful address configuration.
Stateless autoconfiguration is described only in the non-normative appendix.
IGMPv6 is only discussed non-normatively in an appendix as working unmodified.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server, RFC 2022)
gaps.why: The document augments MARS for IPv6 ND message distribution, but the taxonomy has no MARS tag.

RFC2492.title: IPv6 over ATM Networks
RFC2492.summary: Companion to the IPv6-over-NBMA specification that defines how IPv6 runs over ATM PVCs and SVCs: LLC/SNAP and null encapsulations, MARS/NHRP/ND code points, MTU, and interface token generation.

ATM.why: The document specifies IPv6 over ATM: AAL5 encapsulation, PVC and SVC modes, UNI signalling and ATM address encoding in ND options.
ATM.quote: It provides specific details on how to apply the IPv6 over NBMA architecture to ATM networks.

IPv6.why: It defines IPv6 encapsulation, MTU and interface-token generation for a link type, which is IPv6 specification and deployment content.
IPv6.quote: IPv6/ATM drivers MAY also support null encapsulation as a configurable option.

NHRP.why: It specifies NHRP control message encapsulation and field values (ar$pro = 0x86DD) for IPv6 over ATM, and NHRP enables the shortcut paths.
NHRP.quote: The encapsulation of NHRP control messages remains the same as shown in RFC 2332 [4]

rejected.why: ND is used and its link-layer address option is encoded for ATM, but the ND protocol itself is not specified or extended here.
Path MTU Discovery is only mentioned in relation to MTU negotiation; the document does not specify or extend it.
PPP over AAL5 is explicitly out of scope.
Interface token formation is a part of the IPv6 over ATM specification, covered by the IPv6 tag, and does not constitute a separate addressing topic.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server)
gaps.why: The document specifies MARS control and multicast encapsulation for IPv6/ATM, but the taxonomy has no MARS tag.

RFC2493.title: Textual Conventions for MIB Modules Using Performance History Based on 15 Minute Intervals
RFC2493.summary: Defines a MIB module (PerfHist-TC-MIB) of SNMP textual conventions (PerfCurrentCount, PerfIntervalCount, PerfTotalCount) for performance history counters kept in 15-minute intervals, with notes on related objects.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining SMI textual conventions for use in other MIB modules, so readers of MIB/SMI material would look for it.
MIB.quote: This MIB Module provides Textual Conventions to be used by systems supporting 15 minute based performance history counts.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework the MIB module is written for. The document defines textual conventions, not SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
It covers history interval bookkeeping for counters in MIB objects, not performance metrics or measurement methods. The MIB tag fits better.
SONET/SDH MIBs are cited only as examples of users of these conventions.

RFC2494.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the DS0 and DS0 Bundle Interface Type
RFC2494.summary: Defines SMIv2 MIB modules (DS0-MIB and DS0BUNDLE-MIB) for managing DS0 and DS0 Bundle interfaces, including channel mapping, robbed bit signalling, and BONDing mode objects.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is to specify two MIB modules (DS0-MIB, DS0BUNDLE-MIB) for DS0 and DS0 Bundle interface types, using SMIv2 and the Interfaces MIB.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried over; the document defines only managed objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
BONDing (Nx56/64 kbit/s inverse multiplexing) is referenced for bonding modes, but the document does not address ISDN access or IP over ISDN.
Frame Relay appears only as an illustrative example of a service stacked on ds0Bundles in ifStackTable; the document is not about frame relay.

gaps.name: DS0/DS1/DS3 TDM transmission interfaces (T1/E1 trunks)
gaps.why: The document is about managing TDM channel and bundle interfaces (DS0, DS0 Bundle, BONDing), and the taxonomy has no tag for T-carrier or TDM transmission interfaces beyond the generic MIB tag.

RFC2495.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the DS1, E1, DS2 and E2 Interface Types
RFC2495.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module for managing DS1, E1, DS2 and E2 interfaces, including configuration, near/far-end performance statistics, line status, loopbacks, channelization and traps, obsoleting RFC 1406.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to specify a MIB module (DS1-MIB) with tables, groups, traps and compliance statements for DS1/E1/DS2/E2 interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document specifies a MIB module, and the MIB tag sits under SNMP.
The error-second and unavailable-second counters are part of the MIB objects, not a general performance measurement methodology; MIB tag covers it.
ISDN Primary Rate appears only in compliance statements for the line type and coding; the document is not about ISDN access.
SONET/SDH is mentioned only as a companion MIB in progress.

gaps.name: DS1/E1/DS2/E2 (T-carrier/PDH) transmission interfaces
gaps.why: The document is about managing these digital transmission line types, and the taxonomy has no tag for T1/E1 or PDH links, so only the generic MIB tag applies.

RFC2496.title: Definitions of Managed Object for the DS3/E3 Interface Type
RFC2496.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces, including configuration, loopbacks, line status, near-end and far-end performance statistics, and channelization usage guidance, obsoleting RFC 1407.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define the DS3-MIB module (SMIv2) for DS3/E3 interfaces, with tables, conformance groups and traps.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part defines performance parameters (errored seconds, unavailable seconds), interval handling, and a delay-line approach in Appendix B.
performance measurement.quote: All performance parameters are accumulated in fifteen minute intervals and up to 96 intervals (24 hours worth) are kept by an agent.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB runs under; the document defines objects, not protocol behavior.
Implied as an ancestor of MIB; the more specific MIB tag is used.
Only mentioned in passing for ifConnectorPresent; not a subject of the document.
Referenced only as a companion work in progress, not covered here.

gaps.name: DS3/E3 (T-carrier/E-carrier) transmission interfaces
gaps.why: The document's core subject is the physical DS3/E3 line interface (framing, line coding, loopbacks, channelization into DS2/DS1), and the taxonomy has no tag for T-carrier/E-carrier digital transmission links.

RFC2497.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over ARCnet Networks
RFC2497.summary: Specifies the frame format, MTU, interface identifier and link-local address formation, and Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option and multicast mapping for transmitting IPv6 packets over ARCnet.

IPv6.why: The document is an IPv6-over-link specification covering interface identifiers, link-local addresses, MTU and address mapping. No ARCnet-specific tag exists, so IPv6 is the best fit.
IPv6.quote: This memo specifies a frame format for transmission of IPv6 [IPV6] packets and the method of forming IPv6 link-local and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on ARCnet networks.

rejected.why: The document only defines the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option for ARCnet. It does not specify or extend Neighbor Discovery itself.
It defines how the interface identifier is formed for stateless autoconfiguration. That is a small part of the document, and it does not specify SLAAC itself.
The topic fits, but IPv6 is the more specific choice. ARCnet has no technology tag in the taxonomy.
RFC 2464 for Ethernet is only cited as a model for this memo. The document is not about Ethernet.

gaps.name: ARCnet
gaps.why: The document is about IP over ARCnet networks. The taxonomy has no tag for ARCnet, so the link-layer technology cannot be indexed.

RFC2498.title: IPPM Metrics for Measuring Connectivity
RFC2498.summary: Defines IPPM analytic metrics for IP connectivity between host pairs (instantaneous, interval, and temporal two-way), with sketched measurement methodologies including a TCP SYN-probe method.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines IPPM performance/connectivity metrics and methodologies for estimating them, which is the subject of performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a series of metrics for connectivity between a pair of Internet hosts.

rejected.why: TCP SYN probes are used only as one example measurement methodology; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
ICMP unreachable messages are interpreted as evidence in the TCP methodology, but ICMP is not the subject.
IP is the substrate being measured; the document does not specify or change IP.
The metrics are for measuring live Internet paths, not for benchmarking devices or functions.

RFC2499.title: Request for Comments Summary
RFC2499.summary: An annotated index of RFCs 2400 through 2499 (July 1999) giving each RFC's author, date, title, one-paragraph abstract and standards-track marking.

RFC series.why: The document is a periodic summary of a block of RFCs, a publication-catalogue item for the RFC series. Readers browsing the RFC series would look for it.
RFC series.quote: a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2400

rejected.why: Many summarised RFCs are IPv6 specifications, but this memo only lists them and specifies nothing about IPv6.
The IPsec, IKE and ESP RFCs appear as one-paragraph entries in the list. The memo is not about IPsec.
Several MIB RFCs are listed, but the memo defines no MIB modules.
It is a status listing of one block of RFCs, not a history or retrospective.
It mentions standards-track status only as a marking on list entries. The process itself is not the subject.

RFC2500.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2500.summary: RFC 2500 is the periodic Internet Official Protocol Standards summary (STD 1), listing the standards-track status of RFCs by maturity level plus non-standard and historic protocols.

RFC series.why: The document is a status catalogue of RFCs by standards-track maturity level, a publication of the RFC Editor. Readers of the RFC series page would want it.
RFC series.quote: This memo lists the level and status of the archival documents known as RFCs (Request for Comments) within the Internet standards process.

IETF process.why: It explains standards-track categories (Proposed, Draft, Standard, Experimental, Historic) and the STD/BCP labelling, so it is relevant to the standards process.
IETF process.quote: Specifications subject to the Internet Standards Process fall into one of two categories:  Technical Specification (TS) and Applicability Statement (AS).

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned only as a contact and in the Assigned Numbers list entry, so the document is not about IANA registries.
DNS RFCs appear as list entries only. The document specifies nothing about DNS.
IPv6 specifications are catalogued entries only, not subjects of the document.
Many SNMP and MIB entries appear in the lists, but the document does not address them.
The memo gives protocol nicknames but is not a glossary or definitions document.

RFC2501.title: Mobile Ad hoc Networking (MANET): Routing Protocol Performance Issues and Evaluation Considerations
RFC2501.summary: Informational memo describing MANET characteristics and proposing qualitative and quantitative metrics and context parameters for evaluating MANET routing protocol performance.

MANET.why: The whole document characterizes mobile ad hoc networks and sets out routing protocol properties and evaluation metrics for them. MANET is the most specific fitting tag.
MANET.quote: The following is a list of desirable qualitative properties of MANET routing protocols:

performance measurement.why: A substantial part of the document defines quantitative metrics (throughput, delay, route acquisition time, efficiency) and context parameters for evaluating routing protocol performance.
performance measurement.quote: The following is a list of quantitative metrics that can be used to assess the performance of any routing protocol.

rejected.why: The document contrasts mobile IP with ad hoc routing, but it is about MANET routing, not Mobile IP.
MANET is the more specific tag for this document's routing subject.
IP Security is mentioned only in passing as one way to meet the security property.
The document proposes evaluation metrics but not a benchmarking methodology for devices.

RFC2502.title: Limitations of Internet Protocol Suite for Distributed Simulation the Large Multicast Environment
RFC2502.summary: LSMA working group memo identifying services needed for large-scale distributed simulation (DIS/HLA) over multicast networks and the gaps in IP protocols: RSVP aggregation, ATM multicast, hybrid reliable/best-effort multicast, management, session control, security, naming, inter-domain multicast routing.

multicast.why: The whole memo concerns IP multicast requirements and shortcomings for large-scale multicast applications, including group scaling, ATM multicast and inter-domain routing.
multicast.quote: to produce documents aimed at a consensus based development of the Internet protocols to support large scale multicast applications including real-time distributed simulation

RSVP.why: Section 3.1 analyses RSVP scalability and aggregation limits for large shared networks, a substantial part of the document.
RSVP.quote: the current RSVP draft standard for LSMA does not support aggregation of reservation resources for groups of flows and therefore does not meet the needs of existing RTIs

reliable multicast.why: Section 3.3 discusses the need for hybrid best-effort and reliable multicast transport and the limits of existing reliable multicast protocols.
reliable multicast.quote: Recently the IETF has seen proposals for several reliable multicast transport protocols

rejected.why: IP multicast over ATM is discussed in 3.2 and in the dual-mode aggregation, but it is one limitation among many, not the document's subject.
Section 3.4 only suggests that SNMP and a simulation MIB could serve; it is a brief point.
Section 3.5 only suggests SIP could be used for session control; it is a brief mention.
Section 3.7 notes DNS latency is unsuitable for multicast naming; this is a short requirement, not a DNS specification.
Section 3.6 mentions IPv6 security only briefly.
Resource reservation is covered through RSVP; no separate QoS tag is needed.

gaps.name: Distributed Interactive Simulation (DIS) / High Level Architecture (HLA)
gaps.why: The document's driving application domain, distributed real-time simulation, has no taxonomy tag.

RFC2503.title: MIME Types for Use with the ISO ILL Protocol
RFC2503.summary: Registers two MIME media types (application/iso-10161-ill-1 and application/ill-ddi) for carrying BER-encoded ISO Interlibrary Loan protocol PDUs and Document Delivery Instructions in MIME messages, with parameters and Base64 encoding guidance.

media types.why: The document's sole purpose is registering two media types with their parameters, encoding and interoperability considerations.
media types.quote: This memorandum describes a set of MIME types for use with the ISO Interlibrary Loan Protocol (ISO 10160/10161). Two MIME types are specified below.

ASN.1.why: The media types carry BER-encoded ASN.1 PDUs, and the required transfer-encoding parameter identifies the ASN.1 encoding rules in use.
ASN.1.quote: The two protocols described in this RFC specify their APDU's using ASN.1 (ISO 8824:1990) and the most common way of encoding ASN.1 packets is to use the Basic Encoding Rules

rejected.why: The document registers media types, which is covered by the more specific media types tag. It does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
Base64 is only recommended as the transport encoding for binary BER data. The document does not define or extend it.
MIME/RFC822 email is only the transport substrate for the PDUs.

gaps.name: ISO ILL (Interlibrary Loan) protocol, ISO 10160/10161
gaps.why: The document is about carrying interlibrary loan protocol messages and document delivery instructions, and the taxonomy has no tag for library or ILL protocols.

RFC2504.title: Users' Security Handbook
RFC2504.summary: An informational FYI handbook giving end-users practical security advice (passwords, downloads, email, viruses, social engineering, home-system administration) with a glossary, companion to the Site Security Handbook.

security.why: The whole document is general security guidance for end-users, not tied to one mechanism, so the broad security topic fits.
security.quote: It is intended to provide users with the information they need to help keep their networks and systems secure.

user guides.why: It is an FYI-series (FYI 34) introductory guide for Internet users, including a glossary of security terms.
user guides.quote: This document provides guidance to the end-users of computer systems and networks about what they can do to keep their data and communication private

rejected.why: Secure Shell is only mentioned as an example of a secure login tool; the document does not specify or analyse it. 'SSH' in the working group name means Site Security Handbook.
SSL is mentioned only as a way to protect web traffic and verify pages, not specified or profiled.
One-time passwords are recommended in passing, not a substantial subject.
PGP is only named as an example of encryption software.
The document targets end-users rather than operational practice for network infrastructure; the general security tag fits better.
Password hygiene is one section among many, not a substantial focus warranting its own tag.

RFC2505.title: Anti-Spam Recommendations for SMTP MTAs
RFC2505.summary: BCP giving implementation recommendations for SMTP MTAs to resist spam: relay restriction, Received: tracing, logging, host/sender refusal, rate control, MAIL From verification, VRFY/EXPN/ETRN control, and return code choices.

spam.why: The whole document is about preventing and handling unsolicited bulk email at MTAs, which is the spam subject.
spam.quote: implementation recommendations for SMTP, [1], MTAs (Mail Transfer Agents, e.g. sendmail, [8]) to make them more capable of reducing the impact of spam

SMTP.why: It specifies MTA behaviour for SMTP relaying, MAIL From/RCPT To handling, VRFY, EXPN, ETRN and reply codes. This is operational guidance on SMTP and mail relaying.
SMTP.quote: MUST be able to restrict unauthorized use as Mail Relay.

rejected.why: DNS lookups are used to verify MAIL From domains and FQDNs, but the document does not specify DNS itself; DNS is only a supporting mechanism.
It mentions refusing by host or network lists, but does not define DNS-based blocklist conventions.
It covers Received: lines for traceability, but only as one anti-spam measure, not as a message format specification.
It gives MTA guidance rather than general network infrastructure security practice; the spam and SMTP tags cover the content.

RFC2506.title: Media Feature Tag Registration Procedure
RFC2506.summary: BCP defining the IANA registration procedure, trees, syntax, data types and template for media feature tags used in content/capability negotiation.

content negotiation.why: The document defines the registry and vocabulary of media feature tags that content/capability negotiation mechanisms use; this is the media feature negotiation subject.
content negotiation.quote: This has created a need for media feature descriptions and negotiation mechanisms in order to identify and reconcile the form of information

rejected.why: Media feature tags are explicitly distinct from MIME media types, which must not be re-registered as feature tags; the procedure is modelled on MIME registration but is not about media types.
It defines an IANA registry procedure, but the subject is the media feature tag registry itself; the IANA topic is for general IANA guidance and stewardship.
HTTP is only referenced for the token definition and as background for negotiation; the document does not specify HTTP.
The 'u.' tree embeds URIs in tags, but this is a minor part and the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Optional ASN.1 identifiers are mentioned briefly for gateway interoperability, not as ASN.1 modules or encoding.

gaps.name: Media feature tags
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for media feature tag registries; content negotiation is the closest fit.

RFC2507.title: IP Header Compression
RFC2507.summary: RFC 2507 specifies IP header compression for IPv6/IPv4, TCP and UDP headers (including tunneled and extension headers) per hop over point-to-point links, designed to tolerate packet loss, with full-header refresh, generations, and TCP context repair mechanisms.

IPHC.why: The document is the specification of IP Header Compression (RFC 2507) itself, defining packet types, context handling and subheader compression rules.
IPHC.quote: This document describes how to compress multiple IP headers and TCP and UDP headers per hop over point to point links.

rejected.why: Parent topic of IPHC; the more specific IPHC tag fits so the ancestor is implied.
TCP headers are compressed and Van Jacobson's repair is extended, but the document is about header compression, not TCP itself.
Only referenced as a hook for compressing RTP on top of UDP; CRTP is defined in a separate RFC.
Link-layer negotiation is delegated to a separate PPP document; only mentioned as an example.
IPv6 headers are compressed, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
UDP headers are compressed as a subheader; the document does not specify UDP usage.

RFC2508.title: Compressing IP/UDP/RTP Headers for Low-Speed Serial Links
RFC2508.summary: RFC 2508 specifies CRTP, a link-by-link compression scheme that reduces combined IP/UDP/RTP headers to 2-4 bytes on low-speed serial links such as dial-up modems, including its packet formats, delta encoding and error recovery.

CRTP.why: The whole document defines the IP/UDP/RTP header compression scheme over low-speed serial links, which is exactly what CRTP covers.
CRTP.quote: This document describes a method for compressing the headers of IP/UDP/RTP datagrams to reduce overhead on low-speed serial links.

rejected.why: RTP is the protocol whose headers are compressed, not something the document specifies or extends. The topic is header compression, so the CRTP tag covers it.
The document is designed to fit within the IPv6 header compression framework of RFC 2507. It defines a separate IP/UDP/RTP scheme and is not about IPHC itself.
PPP is the link layer assumed for packet type codes and negotiation. The document leaves PPP negotiation to be defined separately.
Section 3.4 only explains why RTCP is deliberately not compressed. It does not specify or extend RTCP.
UDP headers are compressed, but the document is not about UDP itself.

RFC2509.title: IP Header Compression over PPP
RFC2509.summary: RFC 2509 defines an IPCP/IPV6CP configuration option and PPP protocol field values for negotiating and demultiplexing IP header compression (IPHC and compressed RTP) over PPP links.

IPHC.why: The document specifies how IPHC is negotiated and carried over PPP, defining the option format and nine protocol field values for IPHC packet types.
IPHC.quote: This document describes an option for negotiating the use of header compression on IP datagrams transmitted over the Point-to-Point Protocol

PPP.why: It extends the PPP NCPs (IPCP and IPV6CP) with a new configuration option and defines new PPP Data Link Layer Protocol Field values.
PPP.quote: It defines extensions to the PPP Control Protocols for IPv4 and IPv6 [RFC1332, RFC2023].

CRTP.why: It defines the RTP-Compression suboption and PPP protocol values for the compressed RTP/UDP formats and the context state message of CRTP.
CRTP.quote: Enable use of Protocol Identifiers COMPRESSED_RTP, COMPRESSED_UDP and CONTEXT_STATE as specified in [CRTP].

rejected.why: ROHC is a different, later compression framework. This document covers IPHC and CRTP only.
IPv6 is only one of the packet types compressed and one of the NCPs involved. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
RTP headers are compressed under CRTP, but the document does not specify RTP.
TCP headers are compressed by IPHC, but the document does not specify TCP.

RFC2510.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Management Protocols
RFC2510.summary: RFC 2510 specifies the PKIX Certificate Management Protocol (CMP): PKI entities, message structures, operations (initialization, certification, key update, cross-certification, revocation, recovery), proof of possession, profiles, and transports (file, TCP, email, HTTP).

CMP.why: The whole document defines CMP messages, data structures, operations and profiles.
