CMP.quote: This document describes the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Certificate Management Protocols. Protocol messages are defined for all relevant aspects of certificate creation and management.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are the objects being managed, but the document defines a management protocol, not the certificate profile.
ASN.1 is the notation and DER the encoding used for messages; it is a substrate, not the subject.
HTTP is only one of several transports (with a short media type binding), not the subject.
It registers application/pkixcmp, but that is a small appendix item rather than a substantial subject of the document.
MIME is used only for the email transport binding, a minor part of the document.
CMP is a child of PKI and is implied by the more specific tag.

RFC2511.title: Internet X.509 Certificate Request Message Format
RFC2511.summary: Defines the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF), an ASN.1 syntax for requesting X.509 certificates from a CA/RA, including proof-of-possession methods, registration controls and regInfo.

X.509.why: The document specifies the message format for requesting X.509 certificates, including CertTemplate, proof of possession and controls. That is certificate management for X.509 PKI, and X.509 is the most specific fitting tag.
X.509.quote: This syntax is used to convey a request for a certificate to a Certification Authority (CA) (possibly via a Registration Authority (RA)) for the purposes of X.509 certificate production.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the structures. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
CMP is the protocol that carries CRMF. This document defines only the request message format and leaves the protocol to others.
HMAC is used for the password-based MAC and dhMAC computations. It is a mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
EnvelopedData from CMS is imported to carry encrypted private keys. CMS is a dependency here.
The parent of X.509 is already implied, and the document is specifically about X.509 certificate requests.

RFC2512.title: Accounting Information for ATM Networks
RFC2512.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module identifying ATM-specific per-connection accounting data items (connection type, VPI/VCI, parties, cell counts, traffic descriptors, CRC) that can be selected for collection into accounting files, complementing the generic accounting-control MIB.

MIB.why: The document's core is an SMIv2 MIB module (ATM-ACCOUNTING-INFORMATION-MIB) defining accounting objects, so MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

ATM.why: The objects describe ATM connections (VPI, VCI, service category, cells, traffic descriptors, SVC/PVC/SPVC), so it is about ATM management.
ATM.quote: This memo defines a set of ATM-specific accounting information which can be collected for connections on ATM networks.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework in which the MIB is defined; the objects are not-accessible and not read or written via SNMP.
The CRC-16 object is merely one accounting record field, not a document about CRC polynomials.
Cell counts are collected for accounting, not for performance measurement methodology.
Already covered by the more specific MIB tag, which implies this ancestor.

gaps.name: Accounting information collection
gaps.why: The document is about network accounting data (usage records for billing), and the taxonomy has no accounting tag; the closest fit is the generic network management topic.

RFC2513.title: Managed Objects for Controlling the Collection and Storage of Accounting Information for Connection-Oriented Networks
RFC2513.summary: Defines a SMIv2 MIB module (ACCOUNTING-CONTROL-MIB) for controlling selection, collection and file storage of accounting data for connection-oriented networks such as ATM, plus a BER-encoded accounting file format.

MIB.why: The document's core is a MIB module with tables, objects, notifications and conformance groups controlling accounting data collection.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for controlling the collection and storage of accounting information for connection- oriented networks such as ATM.

ATM.why: The MIB is aimed at ATM switches' connection accounting (SVCs, PVCs, SPVCs), though defined independently of network type; ATM readers would want it.
ATM.quote: This need exists for ATM networks, and may well exist for other connection-oriented networks, such as Frame Relay.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is built on and accessed through; the document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag is the better fit.
BER/ASN.1 is used to specify the accounting file format, but only as an encoding mechanism, not the subject.
File transfer is merely mentioned as the way collected files are retrieved; no file transfer protocol is specified.
Mentioned only as another possible connection-oriented network; no Frame Relay content.
Parent of MIB, implied by the MIB tag.

gaps.name: Network accounting / usage data collection
gaps.why: The document is about accounting data collection and storage for billing/usage, which has no dedicated taxonomy tag.

RFC2514.title: Definitions of Textual Conventions and OBJECT-IDENTITIES for ATM Management
RFC2514.summary: Defines the ATM-TC-MIB module, a set of SNMP textual conventions and OBJECT-IDENTITY traffic descriptor types for use by ATM management MIB modules.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (ATM-TC-MIB) defining textual conventions and object identities in SMI, for reuse by other ATM MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo describes Textual Conventions and OBJECT-IDENTITIES used for managing ATM-based interfaces, devices, networks and services.

ATM.why: The content is ATM-specific: addresses, connection kinds, VPI/VCI, service categories, interface signalling types and traffic descriptors. ATM readers would want it.
ATM.quote: AtmServiceCategory ::= TEXTUAL-CONVENTION

rejected.why: SNMP and its SMI are only the framework the MIB module is written in; the document defines no protocol behaviour.
Traffic descriptor types and service categories are ATM traffic parameters, defined here only as identifiers, not a QoS architecture.
Parent of MIB, which is already chosen and implies it.

RFC2515.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for ATM Management
RFC2515.summary: Defines the SMIv2 ATM-MIB module for managing ATM interfaces, virtual links (VPL/VCL), cross-connects, traffic descriptors and AAL5 connection statistics, replacing RFC 1695.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module (ATM-MIB) defining managed objects for ATM interfaces, VPLs/VCLs, cross-connects and AAL5 statistics.
MIB.quote: it describes objects used for managing ATM-based interfaces, devices, networks and services.

ATM.why: The whole subject is ATM management: virtual channels/paths, traffic parameters, service categories, ILMI, and AAL5, so readers of the ATM subject would want it.
ATM.quote: ATM management objects are used to manage ATM interfaces, ATM virtual links, ATM cross-connects, AAL5 entities and AAL5 connections

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol framework the MIB is written for; the document defines objects only, not the protocol, and MIB is the more specific tag.
DS3 PLCP and TC sublayer counters are mentioned, but the document is not about IP over SONET/SDH.
Traffic descriptors and service categories are objects within the ATM MIB, not a QoS architecture or signalling.

RFC2516.title: A Method for Transmitting PPP Over Ethernet (PPPoE)
RFC2516.summary: RFC 2516 specifies PPPoE, which has a Discovery stage (PADI/PADO/PADR/PADS/PADT) and a PPP session stage for carrying PPP frames over Ethernet between hosts and an Access Concentrator.

PPPoE.why: The whole document defines PPPoE: its discovery protocol, packet formats, tags and session stage.
PPPoE.quote: This document describes how to build PPP sessions and encapsulate PPP packets over Ethernet.

rejected.why: PPP is the payload being carried. The document adds LCP considerations (section 7) but does not extend PPP itself. PPPoE is the more specific tag.
Ethernet is only the substrate. The Ethernet framing is just the encapsulation PPPoE uses, and the document defines nothing new for Ethernet.
Broadband access such as ADSL is only mentioned as motivation and applicability. The document specifies no DSL mechanisms.
UTF-8 is just the string encoding used in tags, so it is not a subject of the document.
HMAC appears only as an example in the Security Considerations section for generating the AC-Cookie.

RFC2517.title: Building Directories from DNS: Experiences from WWWSeeker
RFC2517.summary: Informational memo sharing lessons from building the WWWSeeker/Netfind directory mapping organization names to domain names and web sites, populated from registry data via WHOIS, FTP, HTTP and Gopher rather than DNS tree walks.

WHOIS.why: The directory's back end was built mainly from WHOIS queries to domain registries, and the memo discusses the limits of WHOIS data and coverage. It is a main part of the experience reported.
WHOIS.quote: use an automated system that makes repeated queries using the WHOIS protocol to gather information about the organization that owns a domain

directory services.why: The memo is about how to build, populate, update and present an Internet directory that maps organization names to domain names. It uses no specific directory protocol such as LDAP or X.500, so the parent topic is the right tag.
directory services.quote: There has been much discussion and several documents written about the need for an Internet Directory.

DNS.why: The memo argues against DNS tree walks and DNS guessing as directory methods. It recommends bulk retrieval and DNS lookups to verify domains, so DNS usage as a directory is a substantial theme.
DNS.quote: Many people are using DNS as a directory today to find this type of information about a given company.

rejected.why: FTP is only one of several bulk-retrieval channels mentioned in passing for registry data.
Gopher is mentioned only as a way some registries publish domain data; the memo is not about it.
The memo consumes registry data but does not address registry or registrar operations or protocols. The WHOIS tag covers the relevant part.
The directory finds web sites for organizations, but this is not network service discovery in the taxonomy's sense.

RFC2518.title: HTTP Extensions for Distributed Authoring -- WEBDAV
RFC2518.summary: RFC 2518 specifies WebDAV, HTTP/1.1 extensions (new methods, headers, status codes, XML bodies) for remote web authoring: resource properties, collections, namespace copy/move, and write locking, including the opaquelocktoken URI scheme.

WebDAV.why: The document defines WebDAV itself: PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE, LOCK, UNLOCK, headers, properties and compliance classes.
WebDAV.quote: This document describes an extension to the HTTP/1.1 protocol that allows clients to perform remote web content authoring operations.

URI.why: It defines the opaquelocktoken URI scheme and DAV: namespace URIs, a substantial new URI scheme specification.
URI.quote: This specification provides a lock token URI scheme called opaquelocktoken that meets the uniqueness requirements.

rejected.why: WebDAV is a child of HTTP in the taxonomy, so HTTP is implied by the WebDAV tag and not listed separately.
XML is the encoding for request and response bodies and a substrate; the document does not define XML itself, only WebDAV elements.
The opaquelocktoken scheme uses UUIDs and gives a node-field generation method, but this is a minor supporting detail, not the subject.
Basic and Digest are mentioned only in the Security Considerations and examples; no new scheme is defined.
WebDAV link property elements are a property value type, not Web Linking link relations in the sense of that subject.
Only brief notes that results should not be cached; not a substantial part of the document.

RFC2519.title: A Framework for Inter-Domain Route Aggregation
RFC2519.summary: Informational framework for inter-domain route aggregation: aggregate at the originating AS and use the BGP no-export community toward upstream providers, with an example Cisco configuration.

BGP communities.why: The framework's central mechanism is tagging routes with the well-known no-export community toward upstream providers. Readers of BGP communities would want this document.
BGP communities.quote: strongly encourages the use of the "no-export" BGP community to balance the provider-subscriber need for more granular routing information

BGP.why: The document sets out BGP route announcement and aggregation policy, with provider/customer rules and sample router configuration. This is BGP operational practice.
BGP.quote: in its outbound route announcements, each AS aggregates the BGP routes originated by itself, by dedicated AS and by private-ASs

routing architecture.why: The document is about the scalability and design principles of the global routing system: aggregation by the source, a hierarchical recursion across tiers, and a smaller routing table.
routing architecture.quote: establish a clearly defined framework in which scaleable inter-domain route aggregation can be realized

rejected.why: CIDR is the background that makes aggregation possible. The document does not specify or analyse CIDR, and address allocation policy is explicitly out of scope.
Renumbering is mentioned only as relevant background and is explicitly not the focus of the document.
Multi-homed sites are a consideration that the framework accommodates. The document is not about multihoming architectures.

RFC2520.title: NHRP with Mobile NHCs
RFC2520.summary: Defines an NHRP Mobile NHC Authentication Extension giving end-to-end keyed-hash authentication (HMAC-MD5 default, SPI-based keying) for registration requests from mobile NHCs that attach via a non-serving NHS.

NHRP.why: The document specifies a new NHRP extension and its message processing for mobile NHCs registering with serving NHSs.
NHRP.quote: This document describes an extension to NHRP [1] which would allow Mobile NHCs to perform a registration with and attach to an NHS in their home LIS

rejected.why: HMAC-MD5-128 is only the default keyed-hash algorithm the extension uses; the document is not about HMAC.
Despite 'Mobile' in the title, this is NHC attachment and registration in an NBMA network, not Mobile IP. Mobile IP is cited only for end-to-end authentication.
The extension provides authentication, but it is specific to NHRP. The NHRP tag covers it.
The document uses MD5 only through HMAC-MD5 as the default algorithm.
VCs are mentioned, but the document does not address ATM itself.

gaps.name: NHRP (NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the tag NHRP only as a child of ATM, with the description 'NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol) for NBMA networks'. The id is exactly 'NHRP', so I used it, but it sits under ATM even though this document is not about ATM.

RFC2521.title: ICMP Security Failures Messages
RFC2521.summary: Defines ICMP Type 40 "Security Failures" messages with six codes (Bad SPI, Authentication Failed, Decompression Failed, Decryption Failed, Need Authentication, Need Authorization) that report failures when processing IPsec AH/ESP-protected datagrams.

ICMP.why: The document specifies a new ICMP message type (40) with codes, message format, and error-handling/rate-limiting procedures, so it extends ICMP.
ICMP.quote: This document specifies ICMP messages for indicating failures when using IP Security Protocols (AH and ESP).

IPsec.why: The messages report SPI, authentication and decryption failures for AH and ESP, and the document discusses their interaction with Security Associations and key management, so IPsec readers would want it.
IPsec.quote: These messages may also be used to trigger automated session-key management.

rejected.why: ESP is only one of the protocols whose failures are reported; the document does not specify or extend ESP itself, so the parent IPsec tag is more apt.
Automated key management is mentioned only as something these messages may trigger and a DoS concern; the document is not about IKE.
Photuris appears only as the mailing list for discussion (photuris@adk.gr), which is not evidence the document is about it.
Key management is discussed only in passing in the Security Considerations, not as a subject of the document.

RFC2522.title: Photuris: Session-Key Management Protocol
RFC2522.summary: RFC 2522 specifies Photuris, an experimental Diffie-Hellman based session-key management protocol for IPsec AH and ESP, defining its cookie, value, identity and SPI message exchanges, error messages, and basic schemes and attributes.

Photuris.why: The document defines the Photuris protocol itself: its phases, message formats, key computation, and basic schemes.
Photuris.quote: Photuris is a session-key management protocol intended for use with the IP Security Protocols (AH and ESP).

rejected.why: AH and ESP are the protocols Photuris supplies keys for; the document specifies key management, not IPsec itself. Photuris is already under IPsec.
Photuris is a competing key exchange protocol, not IKE. It is tagged only through its own Photuris tag.
UDP port 468 is only the transport substrate for Photuris messages.
MD5 is used as the key-generation and MAC function, but the document is not about MD5.
The more specific Photuris tag covers the key management subject.
ICMP Security Failures messages only trigger exchanges; they are specified in RFC 2521.

RFC2523.title: Photuris: Extended Schemes and Attributes
RFC2523.summary: RFC 2523 defines additional optional Exchange-Schemes, a SHA1 key-generation function, DES-based privacy methods, SHA1-IPMAC validity check, and extra AH/ESP authentication and encryption attributes for the Photuris session-key management protocol.

Photuris.why: The whole document extends Photuris with new exchange-schemes, key generation, privacy and validity methods, and attributes.
Photuris.quote: Photuris is a session-key management protocol. Extensible Exchange-Schemes are provided to enable future implementation changes without affecting the basic protocol.

rejected.why: DES-CBC and Triple-DES are used as privacy methods and ESP attributes, but only as components of Photuris; the document is not about the cipher.
SHA1 is used as a key-generation function and MAC hash, a building block rather than the subject.
Attributes are negotiated for use with ESP and AH, but the ESP transforms themselves are defined elsewhere.
Photuris supplies keys for IPsec, but this document extends Photuris, and the more specific Photuris tag covers it.
The IPMAC keyed-hash constructions (SHA1-IPMAC, RIPEMD-160-IPMAC) are not HMAC.
Photuris is a sibling key-management protocol, not IKE, so the parent tag is not chosen directly.

RFC2524.title: Neda's Efficient Mail Submission and Delivery (EMSD) Protocol Specification Version 1.3
RFC2524.summary: RFC 2524 specifies EMSD, a compact ASN.1/BER-encoded mail submission and delivery protocol over ESRO/UDP for short messages (e.g., two-way paging over wireless IP), with an IESG note limiting its deployment.

email.why: The document defines a mail submission and delivery protocol and a compact format for RFC-822 messages, a companion to SMTP/IMAP/POP. No more specific email child tag fits, because EMSD is its own protocol.
email.quote: EMSD is a messaging protocol that is highly optimized for submission and delivery of short Internet mail messages.

paging.why: Two-way paging over IP wireless networks is the main anticipated use and design driver, so readers of paging would want this RFC.
paging.quote: EMSD is anticipated to become an initial basis for convergence of Internet Mail and IP-based Two-Way Paging.

ASN.1.why: The protocol and format are defined entirely in ASN.1 modules (Appendices A and B) with mandatory BER restrictions, and the document explains why ASN.1 was chosen.
ASN.1.quote: This specification expresses information objects using ASN.1 [X.208].
ASN.1.section: 3 EFFICIENT MAIL SUBMISSION AND DELIVERY PROTOCOL

rejected.why: SMTP is the comparison point and gateway target, but EMSD is an alternative protocol and does not specify or extend SMTP.
UDP is only the substrate under ESRO; the document just specifies using port 642.
EMSD-FS is a compact binary encoding of RFC-822 messages, but it is part of the EMSD protocol rather than an Internet message format in its own right. The email tag covers it.
The body is structured using MIME and MIME fields are carried in the heading, but this is only a reuse of MIME.
EMSD is layered on ESRO/UDP, but the document defines an application protocol rather than a binding of another protocol to a transport.
IMAP appears only in the comparison table and as a complementary protocol.

gaps.name: ESRO (Efficient Short Remote Operations)
gaps.why: EMSD relies heavily on ESRO (RFC 2188), a reliable connectionless remote operations protocol over UDP. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC2525.title: Known TCP Implementation Problems
RFC2525.summary: Informational catalog of 18 known TCP implementation problems (slow start, keepalive, RTO backoff, ACK behaviour, RST handling, MSS calculation, etc.), each with traces, detection and fixes.

TCP.why: The whole document analyses TCP implementation bugs relative to the TCP specifications, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: This memo catalogs a number of known TCP implementation problems.

congestion control.why: Many problems are classified as congestion control (no slow start, uninitialized cwnd, extra additive constant, failure to back off RTO, window deflation), a substantial part of the document.
congestion control.quote: Entering slow start upon timeout forms one of the cornerstones of Internet congestion stability

rejected.why: Path MTU discovery appears only as context in the MSS calculation problem (2.18), not as a subject.
tcpdump traces are used as evidence, but the document is not about capture formats or tools.
Fast recovery is discussed only as implementation context, not NewReno itself.
Not discussed; only IP/TCP behaviour matters.

RFC2526.title: Reserved IPv6 Subnet Anycast Addresses
RFC2526.summary: Defines a set of reserved IPv6 anycast addresses within each subnet prefix (the highest 128 interface identifier values), their construction, and the initial allocation, including the Mobile IPv6 Home-Agents anycast.

anycast.why: The document's whole subject is reserved subnet anycast addresses: their format, reservation and allocation. This is the anycast addressing topic, and no more specific tag fits.
anycast.quote: This document defines a set of reserved anycast addresses within each subnet prefix, and lists the initial allocation of these reserved subnet anycast addresses.

IPv6.why: It specifies IPv6 address construction, covering EUI-64 interface identifiers, the universal/local bit and format prefixes. This is IPv6 addressing architecture, and IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: Within each subnet, the highest 128 interface identifier values are reserved for assignment as subnet anycast addresses.
IPv6.section: 2. Format of Reserved Subnet Anycast Addresses

rejected.why: The Home-Agents anycast ID is listed as one allocation, but the document is not about Mobile IPv6 itself. Mobile IPv6 is only a user of the reserved address.
The IANA Considerations section only says how new anycast IDs are assigned. That is boilerplate, and the main body is not about IANA registries.
This is the parent of anycast. The more specific anycast tag is chosen instead.

RFC2527.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Policy and Certification Practices Framework
RFC2527.summary: Informational PKIX framework listing the topics a certificate policy or certification practice statement (CPS) writer should cover for X.509-based public key infrastructures, with an outline of a set of provisions.

PKI.why: The whole document is about certificate policies and CPSs for CAs and PKIs: their relationship, contents and operational, security and administrative provisions.
PKI.quote: a framework to assist the writers of certificate policies or certification practice statements for certification authorities and public key infrastructures

X.509.why: A substantial part explains the X.509 v3 certificate policy extensions, policy qualifiers, and the certificate and CRL profile component. The framework is adaptable to other formats, so this is secondary.
X.509.quote: The following extension fields in an X.509 certificate are used to support certificate policies: Certificate Policies extension; Policy Mappings extension; and Policy Constraints extension.

rejected.why: RFC 1422 is cited only as the historical origin of the policy statement concept; the document is not about PEM.
Key pair generation, escrow, backup and activation data appear as checklist items within the provisions, but they are not the document's subject.
The document is about PKI certificate policy, which the more specific PKI tag covers; it is not general security guidance.
Identification and authentication of subjects is one component of the provisions checklist, not the document's focus.

gaps.name: Certificate policy / Certification Practice Statement (CP/CPS)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the CP/CPS framework for CAs. The taxonomy has no more specific tag than PKI, which covers it only broadly.

RFC2528.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Representation of Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) Keys in Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificates
RFC2528.summary: Profiles how Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) public keys are represented in X.509 v3 certificates, defining the algorithm OID, domain-identifier parameters, public key encoding, and keyUsage values, as an addendum to RFC 2459.

X.509.why: The document is a certificate profile for KEA keys in X.509 certificates, covering subjectPublicKeyInfo and keyUsage.
X.509.quote: This specification profiles the format and semantics of fields in X.509 V3 certificates containing KEA keys.

rejected.why: ASN.1 modules are included only as the definition apparatus for the OID and parameter types, so the document is not about ASN.1.
KEA is a key exchange algorithm, but the document only specifies how its keys are encoded in certificates. It does not specify key establishment or provisioning.
The parent tag is implied by X.509, and the document is specifically an X.509 certificate profile.
SHA-1 is used only to compute the domain identifier, and the document says nothing about SHA itself.

gaps.name: Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the classified KEA algorithm or for algorithm-specific certificate key encodings. X.509 is the closest fit.

RFC2529.title: Transmission of IPv6 over IPv4 Domains without Explicit Tunnels
RFC2529.summary: RFC 2529 specifies "6over4": transmission of IPv6 over an IPv4 multicast domain as a virtual link, defining the frame format (protocol 41), link-local address formation, link-layer address option contents for Neighbor Discovery, and IPv4 multicast address mapping, as a transition mechanism without explicit tunnels.

IPv6 transition.why: 6over4 is an IPv6/IPv4 coexistence mechanism that lets isolated IPv6 hosts function using an IPv4 multicast domain as a virtual link. No more specific child tag (6to4, ISATAP, etc.) fits it.
IPv6 transition.quote: The "IPv6 over IPv4" mechanism is intended to take its place in the range of options available for transition from IPv4 to IPv6.

neighbor discovery.why: A substantial part of the document defines how IPv6 Neighbor Discovery link-layer address options and multicast groups map onto IPv4 (Sections 5, 6 and Appendix A).
neighbor discovery.quote: specifies the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in the Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, and Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages

rejected.why: The document encapsulates IPv6 in IPv4 (protocol 41), but its point is avoiding explicit tunnels. It treats the IPv4 domain as a virtual link, so it is not about generic tunnelling.
IPv4 multicast is the substrate that provides the virtual link, and the document maps addresses onto administratively scoped groups. It does not specify multicast routing or deployment.
Section 4 defines the interface identifier and link-local address for autoconfiguration. This is a small part of the document and does not amount to a SLAAC specification.
The IPv6 parent tag is implied by the more specific transition and neighbor discovery tags.
ISATAP is a different automatic tunnelling mechanism. RFC 2529 predates it and does not describe it.

RFC2530.title: Indicating Supported Media Features Using Extensions to DSN and MDN
RFC2530.summary: Defines a Media-Accept-Features field for DSNs and MDNs so email/fax recipients can tell senders which media features they support, using media feature tag expressions.

email.why: The document extends Internet mail status notifications (DSN and MDN) with a new field, so it is an email-architecture extension.
email.quote: There is a need in Internet mail and Internet fax for a recipient to indicate the media features it supports

fax.why: Developed in the Internet Fax working group; the capability indication serves Internet fax senders and receivers.
fax.quote: There is a need in Internet mail and Internet fax for a recipient to indicate the media features it supports

content negotiation.why: The field conveys media feature sets (media feature tag expressions) so senders can match content to recipient capabilities.
content negotiation.quote: The <media-feature-tags> are defined in separate schema documents which MUST utilize the language described in [SYNTAX].
content negotiation.section: 3. Extensions for use by DSN and MDN

rejected.why: Only a recommendation to reject with status 5.6.1 is given; the document is not about SMTP itself.
DSN/MDN fields are extended, but this is not the core Internet message header format.
ABNF is only used as notation for the field syntax.

gaps.name: DSN/MDN (Delivery Status and Message Disposition Notifications)
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no dedicated tag; email is the nearest fit.

RFC2531.title: Content Feature Schema for Internet Fax
RFC2531.summary: Defines a schema of media feature tags (resolution, color, image coding, TIFF-FX file structure, MRC) for describing capabilities of extended Internet fax systems, and registers new feature tags.

fax.why: The whole document defines the feature vocabulary for describing Internet fax capabilities, with fax-specific examples and TIFF-FX mappings.
fax.quote: for use in performing capability identification between extended Internet fax systems [5]

content negotiation.why: It profiles the media feature tag registration and feature-set syntax used for capability matching, registers new feature tags, and shows sender/receiver feature matching.
content negotiation.quote: a profile of the media feature registration mechanisms [1,2,3]

rejected.why: Fax is carried over Internet mail, but the document is about capability feature tags, not MIME structure.
It registers media feature tags, not media types.
Only the transport context for extended Internet fax; no mail mechanisms are specified.
ASN.1 identifiers are only assigned to registrations; the document is not about ASN.1.
The IANA section is boilerplate-like registration; the document is not about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: TIFF-FX
gaps.why: The document relies on the TIFF-FX image file format profiles, but the taxonomy has no tag for image file formats.

RFC2532.title: Extended Facsimile Using Internet Mail
RFC2532.summary: RFC 2532 extends the simple-mode Internet fax over email by requiring DSN/MDN-based delivery and processing confirmation and by allowing richer TIFF document capabilities negotiated via capabilities returned in DSN/MDN.

fax.why: The whole document specifies extended facsimile over Internet mail: sender/recipient requirements, confirmation and higher-quality document capabilities.
fax.quote: This document describes extensions to "Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail" [RFC2305] and describes additional features, including transmission of enhanced document characteristics

email.why: A large part of the document sets requirements on senders, recipients and the mail infrastructure for DSN and MDN use, which is email architecture and transport behaviour.
email.quote: The confirmation of these two operations are supplied by two different standards-track mechanisms: Delivery Status Notifications (DSN) [RFC1891, RFC1894] and Message Disposition Notifications (MDN)

rejected.why: SMTP and its DSN extension are used and required of the infrastructure, but the document defines no new SMTP extension; it profiles mail-level use for fax.
Mentioned only as a way recipients retrieve mail, with a brief note on DSN behaviour.
Mentioned only as a way recipients retrieve mail; not the subject.
multipart/alternative is mentioned in passing; the document is not about MIME structure.
Capability feature tags are referenced from other RFCs (2531, 2533, 2530); this document only requires senders to use them, so it is not about negotiation itself.
Header fields like Disposition-Notification-To are used, but the document does not define message format.

RFC2533.title: A Syntax for Describing Media Feature Sets
RFC2533.summary: RFC 2533 defines an LDAP-filter-style syntax for describing media feature sets (combinations and relations of media features) used in content negotiation, plus an algorithm for matching feature sets.

content negotiation.why: The document specifies the feature-set syntax and matching algorithm that are the media-feature part of the content negotiation framework.
content negotiation.quote: This document introduces and describes a syntax that can be used to define feature sets which are formed from combinations and relations involving individual media features.

rejected.why: The syntax is modelled on LDAP search filters (RFC 2254), but LDAP is only the inspiration and the document does not specify or extend LDAP.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar. The document is not about ABNF.
Transparent Content Negotiation in HTTP and the q-value syntax are referenced as background. The document is protocol-independent.
Fax capabilities appear only as a worked example and a scoping note. The document is not about fax.

gaps.name: media feature sets
gaps.why: The document is about describing media feature sets, which is exactly what the content negotiation tag covers, but the taxonomy has no separate tag for media feature tags or the registration procedure.

RFC2534.title: Media Features for Display, Print, and Fax
RFC2534.summary: Defines and registers six media feature tags (pix-x, pix-y, dpi, ua-media, paper-size, color) that let a recipient describe display, print and fax capabilities so a sender can choose a suitable content variant.

content negotiation.why: The document registers media feature tags for the media feature and content negotiation framework, which is exactly what this tag covers.
content negotiation.quote: a recipient may inform a sender as to the characteristics of its message handling. The sender may then provide the variant of the message that is most suitable

rejected.why: Fax is only one of several application areas the features are intended for; the document does not specify fax protocols.
Web browsing motivated the work, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
The registrations are of feature tags under the separate [REG] procedure. The IANA section is boilerplate.
HTML pages are only mentioned as an example of content variants a server might choose between.
Mentioned only in passing as an interoperability consideration for ua-media.
ASN.1 identifiers are just OIDs assigned to the feature tags and are not the subject of the document.

RFC2535.title: Domain Name System Security Extensions
RFC2535.summary: RFC 2535 specifies the original DNS Security Extensions, defining the KEY, SIG and NXT resource records, AD/CD header bits, secure resolution and key distribution through the DNS, and obsoleting RFC 2065.

DNSSEC.why: The document is the core DNSSEC specification: SIG/KEY/NXT records, signing, validation chains, trust anchors (statically configured keys) and authenticated denial of existence.
DNSSEC.quote: Extensions to the Domain Name System (DNS) are described that provide data integrity and authentication to security aware resolvers and applications through the use of cryptographic digital signatures.

rejected.why: Secure dynamic update is mentioned as a use of SIG and signatory bits, but the document does not specify it; RFC 2136/2137 do.
KEY RRs distribute public keys, but this is DNS key distribution within DNSSEC, not general PKI; certificate storage is in a separate RFC.
Appendix A reproduces base64 only as presentation apparatus for the RR formats.
Implied as the parent of DNSSEC; the more specific child tag is chosen.
Mentioned only as a secure time source in Section 6.4; the document is not about NTP.
Referenced only as a protocol that may use KEY RRs (protocol octet value 4) and as a confidentiality option.

RFC2536.title: DSA KEYs and SIGs in the Domain Name System (DNS)
RFC2536.summary: Specifies how US Government DSA public keys and signatures are encoded in DNS KEY and SIG resource records (algorithm 3) for DNS security.

DNSSEC.why: The document defines the DSA algorithm's KEY and SIG RR formats for DNS Security Extensions, so DNSSEC readers need it.
DNSSEC.quote: DSA public keys are stored in the DNS as KEY RRs using algorithm number 3 [RFC 2535].

rejected.why: DSA is the algorithm involved, but there is no DSA tag and the document is about its DNS RR encoding, not the algorithm itself; DNSSEC is the better fit.
DNS is the substrate; the more specific DNSSEC tag covers the subject.
SHA-1 is only used as the hash within DSA signing, not the subject of the document.
RSA is mentioned only in a performance comparison; it is specified in a separate RFC.
Random number needs are mentioned only briefly in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DSA/DSS signatures, which would let readers find DSA usage across protocols.

RFC2537.title: RSA/MD5 KEYs and SIGs in the Domain Name System (DNS)
RFC2537.summary: Specifies how RSA public keys and RSA/MD5 signatures are encoded in DNS KEY and SIG resource records as part of DNS security extensions.

RSA.why: The document defines the RSA key format and RSA/MD5 signature computation, including exponent and modulus size limits and PKCS#1 padding.
RSA.quote: RSA public keys are stored in the DNS as KEY RRs using algorithm number 1

DNSSEC.why: It defines an algorithm-specific KEY and SIG record format for DNS security extensions, which readers of DNSSEC would want to find.
DNSSEC.quote: The DNS has been extended to include digital signatures and cryptographic keys as described in [RFC 2535].

MD5.why: MD5 is the hash used in the signature algorithm, and the document gives the MD5 DigestInfo prefix. This is a substantial part of the signature definition.
MD5.quote: hash = MD5 ( data )

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already covers the DNS KEY and SIG record usage.
The document is about key storage in DNS, not about PKI in general.
No certificates are used. PKCS#1 is only referenced for the signature format.

RFC2538.title: Storing Certificates in the Domain Name System (DNS)
RFC2538.summary: Defines the DNS CERT resource record (type 37) for storing X.509, SPKI, PGP and private-format certificates and CRLs in the DNS, with type values, text representation, and recommended owner names.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record type, its wire and text formats, and owner-name conventions, so it belongs under DNS.
DNS.quote: A CERT resource record (RR) is defined so that such certificates and related certificate revocation lists can be stored in the Domain Name System (DNS).

PKI.why: It concerns publishing certificates and CRLs (X.509, SPKI, PGP) in a distribution channel, which is a PKI matter. The tag is secondary because the RR is the main subject and the document does not define the PKI itself.
PKI.quote: Public keys are frequently published in the form of a certificate and their authenticity is commonly demonstrated by certificates and related certificate revocation lists (CRLs).

rejected.why: The document relies on the RFC 2535 KEY/SIG algorithm and key tag definitions. It states that CERT RRs are not used in securing DNS, so it is not about DNSSEC.
X.509 certificates are one payload type carried in the record. The document does not profile X.509 and only lists OIDs for the record's type prefix.
PGP certificates are only one carried type, referenced to RFC 2440. The document does not define the PGP format or its usage.
The SPKI certificate type is only a reserved value in the type table. The document does not specify SPKI.
DANE (TLSA records) did not exist when this was written. CERT RRs are a different mechanism and do not provide TLS certificate association.

RFC2539.title: Storage of Diffie-Hellman Keys in the Domain Name System (DNS)
RFC2539.summary: Defines how Diffie-Hellman public keys (prime, generator, public value) are stored in DNS KEY resource records using algorithm number 2, including well-known prime/generator groups.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies a new KEY RR algorithm format within the DNS Security Extensions (RFC 2535), a DNS key storage and distribution mechanism.
DNSSEC.quote: Diffie-Hellman keys are stored in the DNS as KEY RRs using algorithm number 2.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific fit, since the document is about KEY RRs from the security extensions, and its ancestors are implied.
Diffie-Hellman is the cryptographic basis, but the document only defines a DNS storage format for DH public keys. It does not define a key establishment protocol.
The document uses Diffie-Hellman and defines well-known prime groups, but its main subject is DNS record format, not a cryptographic algorithm.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and only allocates table entries.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key exchange
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Diffie-Hellman or finite-field DH groups. The document defines two well-known DH prime/generator groups (768-bit and 1024-bit) in its appendix.

RFC2540.title: Detached Domain Name System (DNS) Information
RFC2540.summary: Defines a standard binary and text format for storing detached DNS resource records (including DNSSEC KEY/SIG records) together with their retrieval time, for archival or offline use.

DNS.why: The document defines a format for storing DNS resource records outside the live DNS, including binary wire-format RRs and a zone-file-based text format with a new $DATE entry. Readers of DNS would want it.
DNS.quote: A standard format is defined for representing detached DNS information.

DNSSEC.why: The main motivating use is archiving DNSSEC KEY/SIG chains to later prove authenticity. The format also handles SIG expiration relative to retrieval time. The document is not itself a DNSSEC specification, so this is secondary.
DNSSEC.quote: preserve the KEY RR for that public key, the SIG RR signing that KEY RR, the KEY RR for the key used to authenticate that SIG

rejected.why: It defines a retrieval-time field and a YYYYMMDDHHMMSS text form, but only as part of the detached DNS format, not as a general date/time representation.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-level (reserved retrieval-time byte values) and the document's main body is not about IANA registries.

RFC2541.title: DNS Security Operational Considerations
RFC2541.summary: Informational RFC giving operational guidance on generation, lifetime, size and storage of keys and signatures used with DNS KEY and SIG records, with special attention to the root zone and a meta-root key.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is operational guidance for DNS Security Extensions keys and signatures, covering key rollover, key sizes, offline signing, and root zone and meta-root key handling.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes operational considerations for the generation, lifetime, size, and storage of DNS cryptographic keys and signatures for use in the KEY and SIG resource records

rejected.why: RSA key sizes are discussed only as a parameter choice for DNS zone keys. The document is not about RSA itself.
Key lifetime and storage are covered, but only as part of DNSSEC operations. The DNSSEC tag fits more specifically.
Secure dynamic update is mentioned only in passing, as a case where private keys must stay online.
The advice is operational security, but it is specific to DNSSEC keys, so the DNSSEC tag is the better fit.
DNS is the underlying system. The more specific DNSSEC tag applies, and its ancestors are implied.

RFC2542.title: Terminology and Goals for Internet Fax
RFC2542.summary: Informational RFC defining terminology and prioritized goals for Internet Fax, covering store-and-forward, session and real-time modes, gateway roles, interoperability, confirmation, addressing, security and capability exchange.

fax.why: The whole document defines Internet Fax terminology, roles, operational modes and goals against which fax protocols are judged.
fax.quote: This document defines a number of terms useful for the discussion of Internet Fax.

rejected.why: Internet mail is discussed as a store-and-forward transport and interoperability goal, but the document is about fax goals, not email itself.
MIME is mentioned only briefly as a minimum format set for interoperability; not a subject of the document.
Onramp/offramp gateways to the GSTN are defined as roles, but the document is about fax goals rather than PSTN interworking signalling or gateway control.
The document does define terms, but they are specific to Internet Fax, which the fax tag covers more precisely.
Addressing in email headers is mentioned only as a goal; no message format is specified.

RFC2543.title: SIP: Session Initiation Protocol
RFC2543.summary: RFC 2543 specifies the original Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), an application-layer signalling protocol for creating, modifying and terminating multimedia sessions, covering messages, methods, headers, proxy/redirect/registrar behaviour, reliability and security.

SIP.why: The document is the core SIP specification: methods, headers, status codes, proxy and registrar behaviour, and examples.
SIP.quote: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is an application-layer control (signaling) protocol for creating, modifying and terminating sessions with one or more participants.

rejected.why: SDP is the session description format carried in bodies; Appendix B only describes its usage with SIP. Substrate, not the subject.
Section 14 reuses HTTP Basic and Digest in SIP, but it is a small reuse of existing schemes rather than the document's subject.
Section 15 defines a PGP authentication and encryption scheme for SIP, but it is a minor part and the PGP format itself is not specified.
SIP borrows HTTP syntax and status codes but explicitly states it is not an extension of HTTP.
UDP and TCP are used as transports with SIP's own reliability, but the document does not define the transports.
The SIP URL is defined in Section 2, but it is part of the SIP specification and not a general URI document.

RFC2544.title: Benchmarking Methodology for Network Interconnect Devices
RFC2544.summary: RFC 2544 defines a benchmarking methodology (throughput, latency, frame loss, back-to-back, system recovery, reset tests) and reporting formats for network interconnect devices such as routers and bridges, obsoleting RFC 1944.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a benchmarking methodology for network devices, with test procedures and reporting formats.
benchmarking.quote: This document discusses and defines a number of tests that may be used to describe the performance characteristics of a network interconnecting device.

rejected.why: Benchmarking is the more specific child topic for lab testing of devices; this is not active or passive network measurement.
SNMP is only used as a management-query modifier frame in tests; the document does not specify or extend it.
RIP routing update frames are only used as test load; the protocol is not specified or analysed.
Ethernet, FDDI and token ring are only the media for frame sizes and rates in tests, not the subject.
A UDP Echo Request is only the test frame type, not a subject of the document.
Routers are the devices under test, but the document is about benchmarking, not routing.

RFC2545.title: Use of BGP-4 Multiprotocol Extensions for IPv6 Inter-Domain Routing
RFC2545.summary: Defines how BGP-4 multiprotocol extensions (MP_REACH_NLRI) carry IPv6 reachability, chiefly the rules for building the next hop field with global and link-local addresses, and notes on transport over IPv4 or IPv6.

BGP.why: The document specifies how BGP-4 is used to carry IPv6 routes, including next hop construction and peering transport. It is a BGP protocol extension/profile.
BGP.quote: This document defines how compliant systems should make use of those attributes for the purpose of conveying IPv6 routing information.

rejected.why: IPv6 address scopes are discussed only as they affect the BGP next hop. The document is about BGP, not IPv6 itself.
TCP is only the transport for BGP sessions, and nothing new is defined about it.
RIPng is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that uses link-local next hops.
The document covers one protocol's address-family usage, not general routing architecture.

RFC2546.title: 6Bone Routing Practice
RFC2546.summary: Informational RFC giving routing best-current-practice rules for 6Bone sites: which IPv6 prefixes may be advertised via IGPs/BGP4+, aggregation, peering policy, registry, and operations.

IPv6.why: The document is about operating the IPv6 6Bone testbed and handling of IPv6 address prefixes (link-local, site-local, IPv4-mapped, etc.) in routing.
IPv6.quote: The 6Bone is an environment supporting experimentation with the IPv6 protocols and products implementing it.

BGP.why: Specifies BGP4+ configuration and route advertisement/aggregation policy among 6Bone backbone sites.
BGP.quote: pTLA sites MUST use BGP4+ [RFC 2283] as the mandatory routing protocol for exchanging routing information among them.

routing architecture.why: Covers hierarchical topology, aggregation, default-free core and peering policy as routing design practice.
routing architecture.quote: The 6Bone is structured as a hierarchical network with pseudo Top Level Aggregator (pTLA) sites, pseudo Next Level Aggregator (pNLA) sites and leaf sites.

rejected.why: RIPng is only mentioned as an example IGP; the document does not specify it.
DNS server maintenance for joining sites is a minor requirement, not a subject of the document.
The RIPE-181 6Bone registry is described briefly, but the document is not about the policy language or routing registries in general.
Rules filter bogus routes, but the focus is routing practice rather than security practice.
Prefix handling is covered only in terms of what to advertise, not address architecture.

gaps.name: 6Bone
gaps.why: The IPv6 testbed network and its operational rules have no dedicated tag; IPv6 is the closest fit.

RFC2547.title: BGP/MPLS VPNs
RFC2547.summary: Describes the original BGP/MPLS IP VPN architecture, in which PE routers use BGP with VPN-IPv4 addresses, route distinguishers and target attributes, and a two-level MPLS label stack, to give customers VPN service across a provider backbone.

L3VPN.why: The document specifies the BGP/MPLS layer 3 VPN architecture: per-site forwarding tables, VPN-IPv4 routes, route distinguishers, target and origin attributes. This is the origin of L3VPN.
L3VPN.quote: a method by which a Service Provider with an IP backbone may provide VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) for its customers

BGP.why: It defines a new BGP address family and attributes, and covers PE-CE BGP peering, so BGP extensions are a substantial part of the document.
BGP.quote: The BGP Multiprotocol Extensions [3] allow BGP to carry routes from multiple "address families".  We introduce the notion of the "VPN-IPv4 address family".

MPLS.why: Forwarding across the backbone uses a two-level MPLS label stack, and keeping VPN routes out of P routers depends on it. The document discusses label distribution and the security of label acceptance.
MPLS.quote: This is done by means of MPLS with a two-level label stack.

rejected.why: Route reflectors are mentioned for scalability of VPN-IPv4 distribution, but the document does not specify or extend them.
Section 9 discusses using IPsec tunnel mode on top of the VPN as an option and speculates about multi-party security associations. It is an adjunct, not the main subject.
The target and origin attributes are said to be similar to communities and could be encoded as extended communities. This is a passing mention and no communities format is defined.
Section 10 is a brief note that existing QoS mechanisms apply and that it is not the focus of the paper.
The more specific child tag L3VPN fits, so the parent is not listed separately.

RFC2548.title: Microsoft Vendor-specific RADIUS Attributes
RFC2548.summary: Informational RFC defining Microsoft's vendor-specific RADIUS attributes (Vendor-ID 311) for MS-CHAP v1/v2, MPPE keys and policy, BAP, ARAP, and miscellaneous remote access features.

RADIUS.why: The whole document specifies vendor-specific attributes for RADIUS, their formats and which packet types may carry them.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes the set of Microsoft vendor-specific RADIUS attributes.

PPP.why: Many attributes carry PPP-related authentication (MS-CHAP), MPPE encryption, and BAP/multilink bandwidth control parameters for PPP links.
PPP.quote: designed to support the dynamic control of bandwidth allocation in multilink PPP [11]

rejected.why: EAP types are only reported in an accounting attribute; the document is not about EAP.
DNS server addresses are merely conveyed in attributes; the document does not specify DNS.
NBNS server addresses are passed as attributes only; NetBIOS is not specified here.
RC4 is the cipher used by MPPE, which is referenced rather than specified here.
RADIUS is the more specific tag and is already chosen.
MD5 is used only as a building block in key encryption.

gaps.name: MS-CHAP / MPPE (Microsoft PPP authentication and encryption)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CHAP, MS-CHAP or MPPE. The attributes are mostly about these Microsoft PPP protocols, and the nearest tag, PPP, covers them only loosely.

RFC2549.title: IP over Avian Carriers with Quality of Service
RFC2549.summary: An April 1st parody RFC amending RFC 1149 to add quality of service classes, queueing, multicast, and a mock MIB for IP datagrams carried by avian carriers.

humor.why: The document is a 1 April whimsical RFC parodying QoS, queueing, MIBs and NAT using birds as carriers. It belongs on the humor page.
humor.quote: The following quality of service levels are available: Concorde, First, Business, and Coach.

rejected.why: QoS is the joke's framing, but the document defines no real QoS architecture or signalling. The humor tag covers it.
The MIB section is a parody with bird taxonomy OIDs, not a real MIB module.
RED and WFQ are mentioned only as jokes (RED paint, scales), with no real queue management content.
NATs are mentioned only as a joke ('Avian Carriers MAY eat the NATs'). The document is not about NAT.
MPLS gets a one-line joke about the BOF and labels, with no substantive content.
Multicast gets a brief joke about clone devices and pruning, with no real multicast content.

RFC2550.title: Y10K and Beyond
RFC2550.summary: An April 1st RFC proposing a lexically sortable, arbitrary-length date format (Y10K) using letter and caret prefixes to encode year length, with BCE complement rules, ABNF, and a list of affected standards.

humor.why: Dated 1 April, category "Stinkards Track", with whimsical content about the end of the universe and Pentium MMDCLXVI. It belongs in the April 1st humorous series.
humor.quote: Unfortunately, the current fixes for Y2K lead inevitably to a crisis in the year 10,000 when the programs are again designed to fail.

date-time formats.why: The document defines a date and timestamp representation with year-length prefixes, BCE complement form and ABNF. That is squarely the subject of date and time representation.
date-time formats.quote: Every Y10K date MUST begin with a Y10K year. Following the year, there MAY be an arbitrary sequence of digits.

Y2K.why: The whole premise is the follow-on to the Y2K problem. It discusses year-field overflow and lists affected RFCs, so readers of Y2K readiness would look for it.
Y2K.quote: Early date formats reserved only two digits to represent the year portion of a date.  Programs that use this format make mistakes when dealing with dates after the year 2000.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to give the syntax of the date format. The document is not about ABNF itself.
ASCII ordering is relied on for lexical sorting, but the document does not specify or analyse ASCII.
TAI is mentioned as the time base, and the open issues touch on interplanetary time. The document does not address clock synchronization.
X.509 and many other RFCs appear only in the list of affected standards. They are not subjects of this document.

RFC2551.title: The Roman Standards Process -- Revision III
RFC2551.summary: An April 1st parody of RFC 2026 (the IETF Standards Process), rewritten with Roman numerals and "Roman" in place of "Internet", describing maturity levels, WCPs, appeals, external standards and IPR rules.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st whimsical parody: Roman numerals throughout, 'Roman' replacing 'Internet', and 'Worst Current Practice' replacing 'Best'.
humor.quote: This Worst Current Practice is dedicated to Steve Coya, whose inspirational e-mail suggestion of renumbering all RFC Page numbers with Roman Numerals was taken to heart by the RFC Editor.

IETF process.why: The body is a full parody of the IETF standards process: maturity levels, standards actions, last call, appeals, variance procedure.
IETF process.quote: This memo documents the process used by the Roman community for the standardization of protocols and procedures.

IPR.why: A substantial section covers IPR, contributor licensing, and copyright notices, as in the original.
IPR.quote: In all matters of intellectual property rights and procedures, the intention is to benefit the Roman community and the public at large

rejected.why: It describes RFC publication and sub-series, but the main subject is the standards process, not RFC format or editorial matters.
Only an acronym-glossary mention (RANA); the document is not about registries.
Mentioned only in definitions and as a retrieval means.
Mentioned only as an example of an incorporated external standard.

RFC2552.title: Architecture for the Information Brokerage in the ACTS Project GAIA
RFC2552.summary: Informational overview of the GAIA generic architecture for information brokerage, covering its reference model (Customer, Broker, Supplier, Helpers; Search, Locate, Order, Deliver), functional architecture, CORBA-based interfaces and protocol profiles.

e-commerce.why: The document defines a brokered trading architecture in which a Customer searches, locates, orders and pays for products from Suppliers. It includes a Payment Extension Module based on SET. Readers interested in e-commerce frameworks would want it.
e-commerce.quote: The GAIA brokerage system allows a customer to search for a particular "product" (information, content or services)

rejected.why: Search and Locate are part of the brokerage model. The document is about trading intermediaries as a whole and does not specify a network service discovery mechanism.
HTTP/1.1 and HTML 2.0 are only the user interface required by the Minimal profile, a substrate the document does not specify or extend.
FTP is listed in the Discrete Delivery module as a delivery protocol the broker must support. The document does not specify FTP.
Email (SMTP/RFC 822/MIME) is only named as a delivery and alerting channel in the extension modules.
RTP, RTCP and MPEG audio are listed as the Stream Delivery profile. The document is not about them.
A directory service and LDAP are mentioned only as a way to register and find brokers. The choice of protocol is explicitly left open.

gaps.name: Information brokerage architecture
gaps.why: The document describes brokerage systems built from Functional Units, Functional Unit Managers and a Kernel over CORBA. No taxonomy tag covers brokered information retrieval or Z39.50/ISO ILL-style library protocols.

RFC2553.title: Basic Socket Interface Extensions for IPv6
RFC2553.summary: Informational RFC defining the basic IPv6 extensions to the BSD sockets API: sockaddr_in6, in6_addr, interface-index functions, IPv6 unicast/multicast socket options, getipnodebyname/getaddrinfo/getnameinfo, and address conversion functions.

sockets API.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the sockets API (address structures, options, library functions) for IPv6.
sockets API.quote: changes are required to the sockets API to support IPv6 and this memo describes these changes

IPv6.why: The API adaptation covers IPv6 addressing, IPv4-mapped addresses, scope IDs and interoperability with IPv4 nodes, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 interfaces are identified by 128-bit addresses. The socket interface makes the size of an IP address quite visible to an application

rejected.why: getipnodebyname and getaddrinfo perform DNS lookups, but DNS is only the resolution substrate; no DNS protocol is specified.
The multicast socket options (join/leave, hop limit, loop) are a part of the API, but the document doesn't address multicast routing or group management.
TCP and UDP sockets are created through the API, but the transport protocols are only used, not specified.
IPv4-mapped addresses give application-level interoperability, but the document is not about transition mechanisms.

RFC2554.title: SMTP Service Extension for Authentication
RFC2554.summary: Defines the SMTP AUTH service extension, a SASL profile letting an SMTP client authenticate, optionally negotiate a security layer, and carry an AUTH parameter on MAIL FROM.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP extension: the AUTH EHLO keyword, the AUTH command, the AUTH parameter on MAIL FROM, and new reply codes.
SMTP.quote: This document defines an SMTP service extension [ESMTP] whereby an SMTP client may indicate an authentication mechanism to the server

SASL.why: It defines the SMTP profile of SASL, including the service name "smtp", the challenge/response framing, and how a security layer takes effect. Readers of SASL would want it.
SASL.quote: This extension is a profile of the Simple Authentication and Security Layer [SASL].

rejected.why: This is about authenticating the submitting client and its identity, not domain-based anti-spoofing like SPF, DKIM or DMARC.
Base64 is only used to encode challenges and responses; the document defines nothing new about it.
The SASL tag already covers the authentication subject, and the generic topic is not needed beyond it.
S/MIME is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a contrast, not as a subject of the document.
ABNF is only the notation for the formal syntax section.

RFC2555.title: 30 Years of RFCs
RFC2555.summary: A commemorative RFC marking 30 years of the RFC series, with recollections from Crocker, Cerf, Feinler, Reynolds and others about RFC 1, the early ARPANET Network Working Group, Jon Postel's editorship, and the evolution of the series.

internet history.why: The document is a retrospective on the origins and evolution of the RFC series, the ARPANET, the NWG and IETF; a history piece.
internet history.quote: Thirty years ago today, the first Request for Comments document, RFC 1, was published at UCLA

RFC series.why: It is about the RFC series itself: its numbering, editors, style, publication, and the Favorite RFCs project.
RFC series.quote: the transformation of the RFCs themselves from their earliest, tentative dialog form to today's much more structured character

ARPANET.why: Substantial discussion of ARPANET design, IMPs, NWG, NIC and early host software, with RFC 1 'Host Software' as the central subject.
ARPANET.quote: At the time RFC 1 was written, the ARPANET was still under design.

rejected.why: IETF evolution is mentioned only as part of the history; the document does not describe procedures.
April 1 RFCs are mentioned in passing, but the document itself is not humorous.
RFC 1 and host software are discussed historically; NCP is not specified or discussed by name.
RFCs 791 and 793 and the DoD TCP/IP mandate are mentioned only as history.

RFC2556.title: OSI connectionless transport services on top of UDP Applicability Statement for Historic Status
RFC2556.summary: Applicability statement recommending that RFC 1240 (OSI connectionless transport services over UDP) be reclassified Historic due to no implementations and congestion-control concerns.

OSI.why: The document is about the OSI transport-over-UDP technology of RFC 1240 and moves it to Historic. OSI network-layer protocols and their coexistence with IP is the closest fitting tag.
OSI.quote: RFC 1240, "OSI connectionless transport services on top of UDP", was published as a Proposed Standard in June 1991

UDP.why: A substantial part of the rationale concerns the risks of running transport protocols over UDP, which is what UDP usage guidelines cover.
UDP.quote: any UDP-based protocol is somewhat worrisome since quite frequently people who use UDP-based protocols invent their own reliability and congestion control functions

rejected.why: Congestion is cited as a reason for historic status and RFC 896 is referenced, but the document does not address congestion control itself.
RFC 2126 (ITOT, OSI over TCP) is mentioned only as the recommended alternative, not specified or analysed.
The document does reclassify an RFC to Historic, but that is the document's purpose and not a subject about IETF process.

RFC2557.title: MIME Encapsulation of Aggregate Documents, such as HTML (MHTML)
RFC2557.summary: RFC 2557 defines how to aggregate a text/html root resource and its subsidiary resources into a MIME multipart/related message, and defines the Content-Location header and URI resolution rules so links can reference other body parts.

MHTML.why: The document is the MHTML specification itself: bundling an HTML document and its inline resources into one MIME message.
MHTML.quote: defines the use of a MIME multipart/related structure to aggregate a text/html root resource and the subsidiary resources it references

MIME.why: It defines a new MIME content header, Content-Location, and rules for using multipart/related and Content-ID body-part references. MIME readers would want it.
MIME.quote: specifies a MIME content-header (Content-Location) that allow URIs in a multipart/related text/html root body part to reference subsidiary resources

rejected.why: Email transfer is the original motivation, but the document specifies MIME body structure and URI resolution, not mail transport or access.
HTML is the root resource being aggregated. The document does not specify or extend HTML. MHTML is the more specific tag under HTML.
It uses URI resolution (base URIs, thismessage:/) within a MIME structure but does not define URI syntax or schemes, so the URI tag is not warranted.
HTTP is mentioned only as an alternate transfer protocol and for comparing line-break handling. The document is not about it.
The document is about URI references between body parts, not typed web links or link relations.

RFC2558.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the SONET/SDH Interface Type
RFC2558.summary: Defines the SONET/SDH MIB module (SMIv2) for managing SONET/SDH interfaces: medium, section, line, path and VT/VC performance and status objects, use of the ifTable, and error-second terminology; obsoletes RFC 1595.

SONET.why: The whole document specifies management objects and performance-monitoring semantics for SONET/SDH sections, lines, paths and VTs, so readers of the SONET/SDH subject need it.
SONET.quote: it defines objects for managing Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) interfaces.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (SONET-MIB) with object groups, conformance and compliance statements, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document is about the MIB module, not SNMP itself. The framework section and security text are boilerplate.
Performance counters (ES, SES, CV, UAS) are central, but they are SONET-specific MIB objects, and the MIB tag covers them better.
Mentioned only in passing (Broadband ISDN FEBE); the document is not about ATM.

RFC2559.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Operational Protocols - LDAPv2
RFC2559.summary: RFC 2559 profiles LDAPv2 for the Internet X.509 PKI, defining the subsets of Bind, Search, Modify, Add, Delete and Unbind needed for reading, searching and modifying certificates and CRLs in a repository, and updating RFC 1778 attribute encodings for certificates and CRLs.

LDAP.why: The document is a profile of LDAPv2, specifying required operation subsets and the DER-based attribute value encoding for PKI data. It updates RFC 1778.
LDAP.quote: defining a profile of that protocol for use within the IPKI and updates encodings for certificates and revocation lists from RFC 1778

PKI.why: It is a PKIX operational protocol for retrieving and managing certificates and CRLs in PKI repositories, so it belongs on the PKI page.
PKI.quote: addresses requirements to provide access to Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) repositories for the purposes of retrieving PKI information and managing that same information

rejected.why: Certificates and CRLs are the data carried in the repository, but the document does not profile X.509 itself. It only specifies how to access and encode them over LDAP.
ASN.1 appears only as the notation for the LDAP message subsets and for DER encoding. The document is not about ASN.1.
TCP is only the required transport for LDAPv2 (Section 9). It is a substrate here.
X.500 attribute definitions are referenced for the encoding, but the document does not address the X.500 directory service.

RFC2560.title: X.509 Internet Public Key Infrastructure Online Certificate Status Protocol - OCSP
RFC2560.summary: RFC 2560 specifies the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP), which lets a client query a responder for the revocation status of an X.509 certificate without using CRLs. It defines the request and response formats, extensions, signing delegation, and an HTTP binding.

OCSP.why: The whole document defines OCSP: its request/response syntax, certificate status values, responder authorization, extensions and the HTTP transport.
OCSP.quote: The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) enables applications to determine the (revocation) state of an identified certificate.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates and the PKIX profile (RFC 2459) are the objects whose status is checked, but the document does not profile certificates. It only defines an extended key usage value and a few extensions for OCSP.
Appendix A binds OCSP to HTTP GET/POST, but HTTP is only the transport and the document adds nothing new to HTTP itself.
The messages are defined in ASN.1 with DER encoding, but that is only the encoding mechanism.
Appendix C registers application/ocsp-request and application/ocsp-response, but this is IANA-style boilerplate and not the main subject.
Covered by the more specific OCSP tag, so the parent is not listed separately.

RFC2561.title: Base Definitions of Managed Objects for TN3270E Using SMIv2
RFC2561.summary: Defines the SMIv2 TN3270E-MIB module for configuring and managing TN3270E servers (host and gateway), including server config, ports, statistics, client-group/resource-pool mappings, and per-session TCP connection tables.

TN3270.why: The MIB's whole subject is managing TN3270E servers, their sessions, and SNA resource mappings.
TN3270.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for configuring and managing TN3270E servers.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition with tables, textual conventions and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: Its purpose is to define a MIB module for support by a TCP/IP implementation for configuration and management of TN3270E servers.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is defined within; the document does not extend the protocol.
Telnet and its Timing Mark option are referenced for the managed server's behaviour, but the document is not about the Telnet protocol itself.
SNA concepts (SLU, PLU, SSCP) are used for resource name mappings, but the document manages TN3270E servers, not SNA interworking itself; TN3270 is the more specific fit.
The IANA-administered textual conventions module is a minor part of the document.
The TCP connection table is supplemented, but TCP is not specified or extended.

RFC2562.title: Definitions of Protocol and Managed Objects for TN3270E Response Time Collection Using SMIv2 (TN3270E-RT-MIB)
RFC2562.summary: Defines the TN3270E-RT-MIB, an SNMP MIB module and collection methodology for a TN3270E server to measure response times (averages, buckets, notifications) for TN3270 and TN3270E sessions.

MIB.why: The document's main deliverable is a MIB module (tn3270eRtCollCtlTable, tn3270eRtDataTable, notifications) defined in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the protocol and the Management Information Base (MIB) for performing response time data collection on TN3270 and TN3270E sessions by a TN3270E server.

TN3270.why: The MIB monitors TN3270/TN3270E sessions, using the RESPONSES function and the Telnet TIMING-MARK option to compute response times.
TN3270.quote: A TN3270E server connects a Telnet client performing 3270 emulation to a target SNA host over both a client-side network

performance measurement.why: Substantial parts cover response time methodology, timestamps, sliding-window averages and buckets for SLA monitoring.
performance measurement.quote: The response time data collected by a TN3270E server is structured to support both validation of service level agreements and performance monitoring

rejected.why: The SNMP framework is the substrate for the MIB; the document only recaps it in boilerplate and does not extend SNMP.
The Telnet TIMING-MARK option is used as a measurement mechanism but the document does not specify or extend Telnet itself.
SNA flows (DR, RUs) are background for the timestamping; the document is not about SNA interworking per se.

RFC2563.title: DHCP Option to Disable Stateless Auto-Configuration in IPv4 Clients
RFC2563.summary: Defines DHCP option 116 (Auto-Configure) letting DHCP servers tell IPv4 clients not to self-assign a link-local address when the server has no address to offer, and specifies client and server behaviour.

DHCP.why: The document defines a new DHCP option (code 116) and modifies client and server handling of DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPOFFER. This is an extension of DHCP for IPv4.
DHCP.quote: Clients that have auto-configuration capabilities MUST add the Auto-Configure option to the list of options included in its initial DHCPDISCOVER message.

rejected.why: The document concerns IPv4 link-local self-assignment, but its specification is entirely a DHCP option. It does not address IPv4 itself.
IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration is mentioned only in the introduction as a comparison. The document is about IPv4 clients.
Link-local address generation is the behaviour being controlled, but the document specifies a DHCP mechanism. The DHCP tag already covers it.
The document covers IPv4 DHCP only.

RFC2564.title: Application Management MIB
RFC2564.summary: Defines the Application Management MIB (SMIv2 module) with objects for service-level views, open/former I/O channels, transaction statistics, and status/control of running application elements, extending the System Application MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition for application management, so the MIB tag applies directly.
MIB.quote: it defines objects used for the management of applications. This MIB complements the System Application MIB

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried over; the document only defines objects, not SNMP protocol itself. MIB is the more specific child tag.
Only mentioned in Implementation Issues as a way to support subagents; not the subject.
Transaction and throughput counters are included, but the document is a general application management MIB, not a performance measurement methodology.
Mentioned only as an example of a service; not a subject of the document.

RFC2565.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.0: Encoding and Transport
RFC2565.summary: Defines the binary encoding of IPP/1.0 operations and attributes into the application/ipp media type and the mapping of that message body onto HTTP/1.1 POST requests, with examples and a media type registration.

IPP.why: The document specifies IPP/1.0's wire encoding and transport binding, so it is about IPP.
IPP.quote: This document defines the rules for encoding IPP operations and IPP attributes into a new Internet mime media type called "application/ipp".

media types.why: The document defines and registers the new application/ipp media type, with a full registration template.
media types.quote: The information following this paragraph will be forwarded to IANA to register application/ipp
media types.section: 10. Appendix C: Registration of MIME Media Type Information

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is only the transport. The document mandates POST and port 631 but does not extend HTTP.
Security considerations mention SSL3 and encourage TLS experiments, but the body does not specify TLS. SSL3 is only a mentioned substrate.
ABNF is used as a notation for the encoding syntax. The document is not about ABNF.
The target-URI duplication in operation attributes and the HTTP request line is a mapping detail, not a URI specification.
LPD is only referenced; the mapping between LPD and IPP is in a separate document.
Digest authentication is mentioned only in Security Considerations as boilerplate.

gaps.name: IPP (Internet Printing Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has IPP in the applications section but the tag list I used is IPP, which exists as 'IPP'. No gap in the taxonomy, but there is no general printing topic tag; none is needed.

RFC2566.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.0: Model and Semantics
RFC2566.summary: RFC 2566 specifies the abstract model and semantics of IPP/1.0: Printer and Job objects, their operations (Print-Job, Get-Jobs, Cancel-Job, etc.), attributes, attribute syntaxes, conformance, and internationalization and security considerations for distributed printing.

IPP.why: The whole document defines the IPP/1.0 object model, operations and attributes, so it belongs on the IPP page.
