IPP.quote: The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application level protocol that can be used for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is only the transport for IPP. The mapping is defined in the separate Encoding and Transport document (RFC 2565).
The IESG note encourages experiments with TLS and the security sections use SSL3, but TLS is only a security mechanism the document relies on. It is not specified here.
IPP objects are identified by URIs, but the document only uses URIs and defines the 'uri' attribute syntax. It does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Section 16 gives a generic directory schema for Printer entries, but this is an appendix and not the main subject.
The 'mimeMediaType' attribute syntax uses MIME types, but the document does not register or define media type rules.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IPP tag under applications; it is used above. The document also defines printing-specific semantics, such as job and printer state, which have no separate tag.

RFC2567.title: Design Goals for an Internet Printing Protocol
RFC2567.summary: RFC 2567 sets out the design goals, requirements and usage scenarios for the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP/1.0), covering end-user printing needs, with operator and administrator needs deferred.

IPP.why: The whole document defines the design goals, requirements and scenarios for IPP. It is the core subject.
IPP.quote: IPP is an application level protocol that can be used for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies.

LPD.why: A dedicated section covers the relationship and interoperability goals between IPP and LPD (RFC 1179). That is enough for readers of the LPD page to want it.
LPD.quote: a mapping of LPD functionality and IPP functionality shall be provided so as to enable a gateway between LPD and IPP.

rejected.why: IPP is mapped onto HTTP/1.1 in a separate document. This one only mentions web browsers and servers as optional context.
TLS appears only in the IESG note and SSL3 in the security goals. The document does not specify TLS use.
Printer discovery via a directory service is explicitly out of scope of IPP. Only a directory schema goal is noted.
HTTP Digest is mentioned only as an example of an existing security service.
Payment appears only in scenarios and is described as outside the scope of IPP.

gaps.name: Internet printing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has IPP and LPD tags but no general printing topic, which would cover the design goals for distributed printing independent of one protocol. The IPP tag covers this adequately.

RFC2568.title: Rationale for the Structure of the Model and Protocol for the Internet Printing Protocol
RFC2568.summary: Explains the high-level architecture of the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP/1.0), the roadmap of IPP documents, and the rationale for the model, the binary encoding, the choice of HTTP POST transport, the directory schema, and security.

IPP.why: The whole document describes IPP's structure and the rationale for its model, encoding and transport decisions, so it belongs on the IPP page.
IPP.quote: The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application level protocol that can be used for distributed printing on the Internet.

rejected.why: HTTP 1.1 POST is the transport for IPP and the document justifies that choice, but it proposes no changes to HTTP and does not specify or extend it. It is substrate.
The LPD/IPP mapping is only mentioned as a companion document in the roadmap, and this RFC does not cover it.
The directory schema is covered in a short section (5), but it is a subset of IPP model attributes. It is not a directory protocol and is better handled as part of IPP.
SNMP and the Printer MIB are mentioned only for model alignment and as the likely management interface of a printer.
The IESG note encourages experimenting with TLS, and the document names SSL3 as a security mechanism, but it does not specify or analyse either.
HTTP digest authentication is named as the access control mechanism, but only in passing within the security rationale.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no printing tag. The only printing-related tags are LPD and IPP, and I used IPP for this document, so I treated it as covered. Check that the taxonomy actually includes the IPP tag I used.

RFC2569.title: Mapping between LPD and IPP Protocols
RFC2569.summary: Experimental RFC giving implementers guidance for gateways between LPD (RFC 1179) and IPP/1.0, mapping LPD commands and control file functions to IPP operations and attributes and vice versa.

LPD.why: The document specifies how LPD commands, sub-commands and control file functions map to IPP, and the reverse. It is about LPD as much as IPP.
LPD.quote: This document describes the mapping between (1) the commands and operands of the 'Line Printer Daemon (LPD) Protocol' specified in RFC 1179

IPP.why: Maps IPP operations such as Print-Job, Create-Job, Cancel-Job and Get-Jobs, and their attributes, to LPD. It serves as a worked example of IPP semantics.
IPP.quote: the operations, operation attributes and job template attributes of the Internet Printing Protocol/1.0 (IPP)

rejected.why: IPP runs over HTTP, but this document never discusses HTTP. HTTP is only the substrate.
TLS appears only in the IESG note and is not part of this document's subject.
ABNF is used only as notation for the LPD command syntax and the appendices.
The Printer MIB is mentioned only in passing, in the context of registering document formats.
The document gives document-format values such as application/octet-stream, but it does not define or register any media types.

gaps.name: LPD (Line Printer Daemon protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has LPD under applications, but nothing for IPP. A subject page for Internet Printing Protocol would be needed for IPP/printing RFCs, and I tagged IPP and LPD as if both exist.

RFC2570.title: Introduction to Version 3 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework
RFC2570.summary: Informational roadmap and tutorial overview of the SNMPv3 Management Framework, its relation to SNMPv1/v2, and summaries of the documents that specify it.

SNMP.why: The whole document is an overview and roadmap of the SNMP framework, covering SNMPv1, v2 and v3 architecture, security (USM, VACM), and coexistence.
SNMP.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide an overview of the third version of the Internet-standard Management Framework, termed the SNMP version 3 Framework (SNMPv3).

MIB.why: A substantial part summarises SMIv2, textual conventions, conformance statements and MIB modules, which readers of the MIB subject would want.
MIB.quote: STD 58, RFCs 2578, 2579, 2580, together define the MIB module language, specify the base data types for objects

rejected.why: The SMI language borrows ASN.1 macros, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
USM's optional use of DES is mentioned only in a summary of another document.
MD5 and SHA appear only as algorithms used by USM, described in summary.
UDP is mentioned only as the preferred transport mapping, so it is substrate.
VACM access control is summarised briefly, but the document is about the SNMP framework overall, so the SNMP tag covers it.

RFC2571.title: An Architecture for Describing SNMP Management Frameworks
RFC2571.summary: RFC 2571 defines the modular SNMPv3 management architecture (SNMP engine, dispatcher, message processing, security and access control subsystems, applications), abstract service primitives, and the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies the architecture of the SNMP framework (SNMPv3), its subsystems, naming, and primitives.
SNMP.quote: This document describes an architecture for describing SNMP Management Frameworks.

MIB.why: Defines the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB module with textual conventions such as SnmpEngineID and SnmpAdminString, and the snmpEngine group.
MIB.quote: Section 5 defines a collection of managed objects used to instrument SNMP entities within this architecture.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the SNMP tag.
The Access Control Subsystem is described only as an abstract component. The access control model itself is specified elsewhere.
UTF-8 is used only as the encoding for the SnmpAdminString textual convention.
The IANA section only sets up number spaces for security models, message processing models and engine ID formats. That is boilerplate here.
Message-level security is treated architecturally, with the concrete model (USM) left to other documents.

RFC2572.title: Message Processing and Dispatching for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC2572.summary: RFC 2572 specifies the SNMP Dispatcher procedures for sending and receiving messages and dispatching PDUs to applications, defines the SNMP-MPD-MIB module, and defines the SNMPv3 Message Processing Model and message format.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the SNMP engine's Dispatcher and the SNMPv3 message format and processing model, which is core SNMP framework protocol.
SNMP.quote: It defines the procedures for dispatching potentially multiple versions of SNMP messages to the proper SNMP Message Processing Models, and for dispatching PDUs to SNMP applications.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-MPD-MIB module with counters such as snmpUnknownSecurityModels, snmpInvalidMsgs and snmpUnknownPDUHandlers, so readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: This document defines these managed objects, the MIB module which contains them, and how these managed objects might be used to provide useful management.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used only to define the SNMPv3 message syntax and the MIB module. It is the notation, not the subject.
authFlag, privFlag and securityLevel are handled, but the security models are defined in other documents. This RFC only calls them through abstract primitives.
Not rejected. See the accepted tag.

RFC2573.title: SNMP Applications
RFC2573.summary: RFC 2573 specifies five SNMP application types (command generators, command responders, notification originators, notification receivers, proxy forwarders) and defines the SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB and SNMP-PROXY-MIB modules.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the procedures of SNMP applications within the SNMPv3 architecture, including notification and proxy forwarding behaviour.
SNMP.quote: This memo describes five types of SNMP applications which make use of an SNMP engine

MIB.why: A large part of the document is the definition of three MIB modules (SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB, SNMP-PROXY-MIB) with their tables, compliance statements and usage.
MIB.quote: This memo also defines MIB modules for specifying targets of management operations, for notification filtering, and for proxy forwarding.

rejected.why: Implied by the SNMP tag; no need to list the ancestor.
MIB modules use SMIv2 syntax, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
Only mentioned in textual convention descriptions as the encoding for tag values; incidental.
Access control via isAccessAllowed is used by the applications but is defined in the VACM specification, not here.

RFC2574.title: User-based Security Model (USM) for version 3 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv3)
RFC2574.summary: RFC 2574 specifies the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3, defining message-level authentication, timeliness/replay protection, and privacy procedures (HMAC-MD5-96, HMAC-SHA-96, CBC-DES), key localization and change, plus the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the SNMPv3 security model within the SNMP architecture, including message processing, discovery and time synchronization.
SNMP.quote: It defines the Elements of Procedure for providing SNMP message level security.

MIB.why: Section 5 defines the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB module (usmUserTable, usmStats, KeyChange textual convention), a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: This document also includes a MIB for remotely monitoring/managing the configuration parameters for this Security Model.

rejected.why: CBC-DES is specified as the privacy protocol, but as one component of USM; the document is about the SNMP security model, not DES itself.
HMAC is used as the authentication mechanism (HMAC-MD5-96/SHA-96) but the document does not specify HMAC itself.
MD5 is the hash underlying one authentication protocol; it is a building block, not the subject.
SHA-1 is the hash underlying the other authentication protocol; only a building block.
Authentication is covered, but the specific SNMP tag captures it; a generic topic tag would be redundant.
ASN.1/BER is used only to encode msgSecurityParameters, as an encoding substrate.

RFC2575.title: View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC2575.summary: Specifies the View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for SNMP, defining the isAccessAllowed procedure, MIB views and view subtree families, and the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB for remotely configuring access control.

SNMP.why: VACM is the access control subsystem model of the SNMP architecture. The whole document specifies how SNMP engines decide read, write and notify access.
SNMP.quote: It defines the Elements of Procedure for controlling access to management information.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document is the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB module (vacmContextTable, vacmAccessTable, vacmViewTreeFamilyTable) with its compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This document also includes a MIB for remotely managing the configuration parameters for the View-based Access Control Model.

rejected.why: The document is about authorization, but the SNMP tag is more specific and the topic tag is not needed alongside it. Authorization is not a separate subject here.
The MIB module is written in SMIv2/ASN.1 notation and OBJECT IDENTIFIER subtrees are used for views, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Only a general parent topic. The document's subject is SNMP access control, which the SNMP tag covers more specifically.
A parent of SNMP and MIB, so it is implied by those tags and is not listed separately.

gaps.name: View-based Access Control Model (VACM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SNMP access control or the SNMPv3 architecture components. SNMP and MIB are the closest fits, so VACM readers would benefit from a dedicated tag.

RFC2576.title: Coexistence between Version 1, Version 2, and Version 3 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework
RFC2576.summary: Describes coexistence of SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3: SMIv1-to-SMIv2 MIB conversion, notification parameter translation, multi-lingual agent and proxy behaviour, and the v1/v2c message processing and community-based security models plus the SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB.

SNMP.why: The document specifies how SNMPv1, v2c and v3 entities interoperate: command responder, proxy and notification handling, error mappings, and v1/v2c message processing and security models.
SNMP.quote: describe coexistence between version 3 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, (SNMPv3), version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework (SNMPv2), and the original

MIB.why: Section 2 gives rules for converting MIB modules from SMIv1 to SMIv2 (objects, traps, compliance, capabilities), and the document defines the SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB module.
MIB.quote: MIB modules defined using the SMIv1 may continue to be used with protocol versions which use SNMPv2 PDUs.

rejected.why: SMI is based on an ASN.1 subset, but the document is about SMI conversion, not ASN.1 itself.
The community-based security model is mentioned, but it is part of the SNMP coexistence machinery and is covered by the SNMP tag.
VACM mapping of community names is mentioned, but VACM is defined elsewhere (RFC 2575).

RFC2577.title: FTP Security Considerations
RFC2577.summary: Informational RFC describing FTP security weaknesses (bounce attack, brute-force password guessing, username probing, port stealing, clear-text exchange) and giving recommendations to FTP server implementers and administrators.

FTP.why: The whole document analyses FTP's security problems and recommends server behaviours such as rejecting PORT to ports below 1024, limiting PASS attempts and always returning 331 to USER.
FTP.quote: The specification for the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) contains a number of mechanisms that can be used to compromise network security.

rejected.why: The document is about security, but it is specifically about FTP. The FTP tag is the more specific subject, and no general security threat-model content stands apart from it.
TCP is only the transport for FTP data connections. The port-number discussion is about FTP behaviour, not TCP.
The introduction explicitly puts FTP with IPsec out of scope.
The advice for administrators is tied to FTP servers specifically, so it does not make the document about operational security practice in general.
Clear-text passwords and stronger alternatives are mentioned, but they point to RFC 2228 and are not a substantial topic here.

RFC2578.title: Structure of Management Information Version 2 (SMIv2)
RFC2578.summary: RFC 2578 (STD 58) specifies SMIv2, the adapted ASN.1 subset and macros (MODULE-IDENTITY, OBJECT-TYPE, NOTIFICATION-TYPE, OBJECT-IDENTITY) used to write MIB modules, including base types, conceptual tables, and rules for extending modules.

MIB.why: The document defines the SMI, the language and macros for writing MIB modules, including object types, tables, and module revision rules. This is the core subject of the MIB tag.
MIB.quote: Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules.  These modules are written using an adapted subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol these MIB modules are managed through. The document defines the data definition language, not the protocol, so it only mentions SNMP in passing.
The document defines an adapted ASN.1 subset and macros for MIB definitions. It is about the SMI rather than ASN.1 modules and encoding rules in general, so ASN.1 is the substrate here.
The MIB tag is the more specific fit, so its parent is implied and not listed separately.
The OID naming hierarchy mentions IANA's administration of the subtree, but only in passing.

RFC2579.title: Textual Conventions for SMIv2
RFC2579.summary: RFC 2579 (STD 58) defines the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro for SMIv2 MIB modules and the initial set of textual conventions (DisplayString, RowStatus, TruthValue, DateAndTime, etc.), with rules for their mapping, sub-typing and revision.

MIB.why: The document defines the SNMPv2-TC MIB module of textual conventions used when writing MIB modules under SMIv2, which is core MIB/SMI material.
MIB.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol context; the document defines data-type conventions for MIB modules, not SNMP protocol behaviour (RowStatus semantics are expressed via set operations but remain MIB-level).
The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro is written in adapted ASN.1, but ASN.1 is the notation substrate, not the subject; the SMI is the subject.
Parent of MIB, which is implied and the more specific tag fits.
DisplayString references NVT ASCII but only as one definition; the document is not about ASCII.

gaps.name: SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2)
gaps.why: The document is part of the SMIv2 specification family; the MIB tag, which covers MIB modules and SMI, is the nearest fit.

RFC2580.title: Conformance Statements for SMIv2
RFC2580.summary: RFC 2580 (STD 58) defines the SMIv2 conformance macros OBJECT-GROUP, NOTIFICATION-GROUP, MODULE-COMPLIANCE and AGENT-CAPABILITIES, which MIB modules use to state compliance requirements and agent capabilities, and the rules for extending them.

MIB.why: The document specifies the SMIv2 notation for conformance groups, compliance statements and capabilities statements used in MIB modules. This is MIB/SMI material.
MIB.quote: Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules. These modules are written using an adapted subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol context. The document only references SNMP operations such as noSuchObject and sysORID and does not specify protocol behaviour. The MIB/SMI tag is the more specific fit.
The macros use ASN.1 macro notation, but the document defines conformance notation for management information and is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
It is implied as the ancestor of MIB, so it is not listed separately.

RFC2581.title: TCP Congestion Control
RFC2581.summary: RFC 2581 specifies TCP's four congestion control algorithms (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery), plus restart after idle periods and ACK generation rules.

TCP.why: The document is a Standards Track specification of TCP sender and receiver behaviour, including delayed ACK generation and idle restart, so it belongs under TCP.
TCP.quote: This document specifies four TCP [Pos81] congestion control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery.

congestion control.why: The core subject is congestion control: cwnd and ssthresh management, loss response and avoiding congestion collapse. No more specific child tag fits, since NewReno is only referenced, not specified here.
congestion control.quote: The slow start and congestion avoidance algorithms MUST be used by a TCP sender to control the amount of outstanding data being injected into the network.

rejected.why: NewReno is only mentioned as a proposed loss-recovery enhancement that this document explicitly does not standardize.
Path MTU discovery is mentioned only in the SMSS definition and the ACK discussion, and is not a subject of the document.
Persistent HTTP connections are cited only as an example of why the idle-detection test fails.
ECN is not discussed. Congestion is detected from loss only.

RFC2582.title: The NewReno Modification to TCP's Fast Recovery Algorithm
RFC2582.summary: Experimental RFC specifying the NewReno modification to TCP's Fast Recovery algorithm, which responds to partial acknowledgments when SACK is unavailable, with variants and a fix for avoiding multiple Fast Retransmits.

NewReno.why: The document defines the NewReno modification to TCP Fast Recovery, which is exactly what the NewReno tag covers.
NewReno.quote: This document describes a specific algorithm for responding to partial acknowledgments, referred to as NewReno.

rejected.why: NewReno is a TCP congestion control modification and the NewReno tag sits under congestion control. TCP is the substrate, and the document does not specify TCP generally.
This parent is implied by the NewReno tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC2583.title: Guidelines for Next Hop Client (NHC) Developers
RFC2583.summary: Informational guidelines for developers of NHRP clients (NHC) on ATM NBMA networks, covering local/remote decision, caching of ACK/NAK shortcut vs routed-path state, and socket options to override behaviour.

NHRP.why: The whole document is about NHC behaviour and state handling for NHRP.
NHRP.quote: This document provides guidelines for developers of the Next Hop Resolution Protocol Clients (NHC).

rejected.why: ATM is the underlying network; the document is about NHRP client behaviour, and NHRP is the more specific child tag under ATM.
TCP PCB is only discussed as a place to store state, not specified or extended.
UDP is mentioned only as a place to keep shortcut/routed state.
ICMP echo is mentioned briefly regarding ping/traceroute path selection; not a subject of the document.
A new socket option is proposed, but it is a minor part of the document focused on NHC state.

RFC2584.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for APPN/HPR in IP Networks
RFC2584.summary: Defines a SMIv2 MIB module (HPR-IP-MIB) for monitoring and configuring APPN/HPR nodes running over IP, counting UDP packets per APPN traffic type and mapping traffic types to IP TOS precedence bits.

APPN.why: The MIB manages APPN/HPR ports, link stations and connection networks when running over IP, so it belongs on the APPN page.
APPN.quote: HPR is an enhancement to the Advanced Peer-to-Peer Network (APPN) architecture that provides fast data routing and improved session reliability.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module definition (HPR-IP-MIB) with tables, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is defined for; the document specifies no new SNMP protocol behaviour.
TOS precedence bits are mapped and the DSCP redefinition is mentioned only in passing; the document is not about Diffserv.
UDP is the transport whose packets are counted, not something the document specifies or extends.
APPN is the more specific tag under SNA, so the SNA parent is implied and not listed separately.
The TOS-to-traffic-type mapping is a configuration detail of the MIB, not a QoS architecture or signalling document.

RFC2585.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Operational Protocols: FTP and HTTP
RFC2585.summary: Specifies conventions for retrieving and publishing X.509 certificates and CRLs in PKI repositories via FTP and HTTP (URI forms, file suffixes, DER encoding), and registers the application/pkix-cert and application/pkix-crl media types.

X.509.why: The document is part of the Internet X.509 PKI suite and defines how X.509 certificates and CRLs are distributed from repositories. X.509 is the most specific fitting tag, below PKI.
X.509.quote: specifies the conventions for using the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to obtain certificates and CRLs from PKI repositories

media types.why: It registers application/pkix-cert and application/pkix-crl, a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: Two MIME types are defined to support the transfer of certificates and CRLs.

FTP.why: It profiles FTP use for certificate and CRL retrieval, including URI forms and file naming, in a dedicated section.
FTP.quote: An IA5String describes the use of anonymous FTP to fetch certificate or CRL information.

HTTP.why: It specifies conventions for using HTTP to fetch and publish certificates and CRLs, in a dedicated section.
HTTP.quote: An IA5String describes the use of HTTP to fetch certificate or CRL information.

rejected.why: URIs are used to locate certificates, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
The document registers media types but does not address MIME body structure or encodings, so media types is the better fit.
Proxy caching appears only as a warning in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
X.509 is a child of PKI and fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.

RFC2586.title: The Audio/L16 MIME content type
RFC2586.summary: Registers the audio/L16 MIME media type, uncompressed 16-bit linear PCM audio with rate and channels parameters, based on the RTP L16 format.

media types.why: The document exists to define and register a new MIME media type (audio/L16), with an IANA registration form listing its parameters.
media types.quote: This document defines the audio/L16 MIME type, a reasonable quality audio format for use in Internet applications.

codecs.why: It defines an audio sample format, including sample rates and channel ordering. This is an audio encoding definition that readers of audio codecs would want.
codecs.quote: L16 denotes uncompressed audio data, using 16-bit signed representation in twos-complement notation and network byte order.

rejected.why: L16 comes from the RTP audio profile (RFC 1890), but this document defines a MIME type for files and transport, not an RTP payload format.
MIME is the framework this type is registered in. The document's focus is the specific media type registration, which the narrower media types tag covers.
Base64 is mentioned only as a suitable encoding for email transport in the registration form. The document is not about it.
RTP is referenced only as the origin of the L16 format definition.

RFC2587.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure LDAPv2 Schema
RFC2587.summary: Defines the minimal LDAPv2 schema (auxiliary object classes and attributes such as pkiUser, pkiCA, userCertificate, cACertificate, CRL attributes, cRLDistributionPoint, deltaCRL) for LDAP servers acting as PKIX repositories for certificates and CRLs.

PKI.why: The document defines how PKIX repositories store end-entity and CA certificates, cross-certificate pairs, CRLs, and delta CRLs, so it is about PKI repository infrastructure.
PKI.quote: The schema defined in this document is a minimal schema to support PKIX in an LDAPv2 environment

LDAP.why: It specifies LDAP object classes and attributes, a schema extension for LDAP servers, so LDAP readers would want it.
LDAP.quote: This specification defines the attributes and object classes to be used by LDAP servers acting as PKIX repositories

X.509.why: The schema carries X.509 certificates, CRLs and cross-certificate pairs, and adapts X.509-defined object classes to PKIX needs.
X.509.quote: Some object classes and attributes defined in X.509 are duplicated here for completeness.

rejected.why: The LDAP tag sits under it and is more specific, so the parent is implied.
The X.500-derived schema notation is used, but the document is about LDAP repositories, not the X.500 service.
Schema is written in ASN.1-style object class notation, but that is only the definition notation.
Mentioned only as an alternative repository access mechanism, not addressed.

RFC2588.title: IP Multicast and Firewalls
RFC2588.summary: Informational RFC discussing how IP multicast traffic can traverse an application-level firewall: security policy, determining when to relay groups, UDP-based tunnelling, multi-firewall setups, and why SOCKS is a poor fit for multicast.

firewall.why: The whole document is about firewall handling of multicast: policy, relaying and control of traffic across a security gateway.
firewall.quote: we discuss the issues surrounding the traversal of IP multicast traffic across a firewall, and describe possible ways in which a firewall can implement and control this traversal

multicast.why: Covers multicast group membership (IGMP, domain-wide reports), relaying, TTL and scoping, and multicast tunnelling across firewalls, so readers of multicast would want it.
multicast.quote: This document discusses how a firewall handles IP multicast [1] traffic.

SOCKS.why: A full section analyses SOCKS V5 and its proposed multicast extensions (MU-mode, MM-mode) and argues they are less appropriate.
SOCKS.quote: SOCKS [10] is a mechanism for transparently performing unicast communication across a firewall.
SOCKS.section: 10. Why SOCKS is Less Appropriate for Multicast

rejected.why: IGMP is mentioned as one way a firewall can learn group membership, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Section 8 discusses UDP-based tunnelling (UMTP) for relaying multicast, but it is a brief part of the document and not generic IP-in-IP or GRE tunnelling.
RTP is mentioned only as an example of a protocol designed with relaying in mind.
The SAP/SDP session directory is used only as an example source of candidate groups.
An RTSP proxy is mentioned in passing as one way to notify the firewall.

RFC2589.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (v3): Extensions for Dynamic Directory Services
RFC2589.summary: Defines LDAPv3 extensions for dynamic directory entries: a Refresh extended operation, the dynamicObject class, entryTtl and dynamicSubtrees attributes, and client/server rules for time-to-live based entries.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAPv3 with a Refresh extended operation, a new object class and operational attributes for dynamic entries, so LDAP readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines the requirements for dynamic directory services and specifies the format of request and response extended operations for supporting client-server interoperation

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used only to encode the request and response values, so it is a substrate.
The mapping to X.500/DAP Modify is a one-line mention and the document is not about X.500.
The LDAP tag sits under this topic and already covers it.
Presence-like use is mentioned only as an example of dynamic entries.

RFC2590.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Frame Relay Networks Specification
RFC2590.summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are transmitted over Frame Relay: NLPID encapsulation, MTU, interface identifier and link-local address formation, and ND/IND link-layer address option formats and multicast emulation.

frame relay.why: The whole document defines IPv6 over Frame Relay: frame format, MTU, DLCI-based interface identifiers, and address mapping.
frame relay.quote: This memo describes mechanisms for the transmission of IPv6 packets over Frame Relay networks.

neighbor discovery.why: Large parts define Frame Relay-specific ND/IND link-layer address option formats and the sending and receiving procedures.
neighbor discovery.quote: It also specifies the content of the Source/Target link-layer address option used in Neighbor Discovery [ND] and Inverse Neighbor Discovery [IND] messages

SLAAC.why: A full section defines how Frame Relay interface identifiers and link-local addresses are generated for stateless autoconfiguration.
SLAAC.quote: The Duplicate Address Detection specified in [AUTOCONF] is used repeatedly during the interface identifier and local-link address generation process

rejected.why: IPv6 is the parent of the tags chosen (neighbor discovery, SLAAC), so it is implied and not listed.
IPsec is referenced only in Security Considerations, as a mechanism protecting ND messages.
The related ATM and NBMA IPv6 documents are only cited as sibling specifications.
X.121 numbers are used only as a Frame Relay address format, and the document is not about X.25.

RFC2591.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Scheduling Management Operations
RFC2591.summary: Defines the DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for scheduling SNMP set operations periodically, by calendar, or one-shot, with usage examples.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB) defined in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules and SMI.
MIB.quote: it describes a set of managed objects that are used to schedule management operations periodically or at specified dates and times.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is defined for, but the document defines only a MIB module. MIB is the more specific tag.
The MIB deals with calendar and local-time scheduling, including DST transitions. It does not synchronize clocks.
The DST transition handling is incidental to scheduling and does not distribute time zone data.

RFC2592.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Delegation of Management Script
RFC2592.summary: RFC 2592 defines the Script MIB (DISMAN-SCRIPT-MIB), a set of SNMP managed objects for delegating management scripts to distributed managers: transferring, launching, controlling and monitoring them, with VACM access control examples.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a MIB module (DISMAN-SCRIPT-MIB) with tables, groups and compliance statements defined in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: it describes a set of managed objects that allow the delegation of management scripts to distributed managers

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol and framework the MIB is built on. The document defines objects, not new SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
URLs are used only as the pull-model script source. Nothing new is specified about URIs.
FTP is mentioned only as an example protocol for retrieving scripts.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example protocol for retrieving scripts.
VACM configuration examples appear, but they are usage illustrations. The document's subject is the MIB for script delegation.

gaps.name: Script MIB / management script delegation (DISMAN)
gaps.why: There is no tag for distributed management or script delegation. MIB covers the module form only.

RFC2593.title: Script MIB Extensibility Protocol Version 1.0
RFC2593.summary: Defines SMX, a lightweight text-based protocol over local TCP between a Script MIB SNMP agent and language-specific script runtime systems, with commands, replies and procedures for starting, controlling and monitoring scripts.

MIB.why: SMX is the extensibility protocol for the Script MIB implementation. It maps MIB objects such as smRunState, smRunExitCode and smLaunchStart to protocol commands and replies, so readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: The IETF Script MIB defines an interface for the delegation of management functions based on the Internet management framework.

rejected.why: The SNMP agent is one endpoint, but the document specifies SMX between agent and runtime, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific fit.
TCP is only the local transport for SMX and nothing new is defined about TCP.
ABNF is used only as the notation for message syntax.
The security profile discussion is part of the protocol design and is not general operational security guidance.

gaps.name: Management by delegation / Script MIB runtime protocol
gaps.why: The document is about delegating management scripts to runtime systems such as Java and Tcl, and the taxonomy has no tag for this beyond MIB.

RFC2594.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for WWW Services
RFC2594.summary: Defines the WWW-MIB SNMP module for managing WWW services (servers, clients, proxies), with service information, protocol statistics and document statistics based on an abstract document transfer protocol mapped to HTTP and FTP.

MIB.why: The document's core content is a SMIv2 MIB module (WWW-MIB) with tables and conformance groups for WWW services.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a set of objects for managing World Wide Web (WWW) services.

HTTP.why: Section 7.1 maps HTTP methods and status codes to the MIB's request and response types, and the MIB manages HTTP servers, clients and proxies. Readers of HTTP would want it.
HTTP.quote: The WorldWide Web protocol statistics defined in the WWW Service MIB are based on an abstract document transfer protocol (DTP). This memo also defines a mapping of the abstract DTP to HTTP and FTP.

rejected.why: The document also maps FTP commands and replies to the abstract DTP, but this is a smaller secondary mapping. The MIB is not about FTP itself.
SNMP is the management framework used. The document defines a MIB module, not SNMP protocol behaviour, so the more specific MIB tag applies.
Caching proxies are only a service type, and hit ratio is derivable from counters. The document defines no caching behaviour.
URIs are only referenced in the WwwDocName textual convention, so the document is not about URIs.

RFC2595.title: Using TLS with IMAP, POP3 and ACAP
RFC2595.summary: Defines the STARTTLS (IMAP, ACAP) and STLS (POP3) commands for negotiating TLS on existing connections, security requirements for them, the IMAP LOGINDISABLED capability, and the PLAIN SASL mechanism.

IMAP.why: Specifies the IMAP STARTTLS extension and the LOGINDISABLED capability, extending IMAP.
IMAP.quote: This extension adds a single command, "STARTTLS" to the IMAP protocol which is used to begin a TLS negotiation.

POP3.why: Defines the POP3 STLS command and capability, extending POP3.
POP3.quote: The POP3 STARTTLS extension adds the STLS command to POP3 servers.

ACAP.why: Defines the ACAP STARTTLS capability and command, extending ACAP.
ACAP.quote: When the TLS extension is present in ACAP, "STARTTLS" is listed as a capability in the ACAP greeting.

SASL.why: Defines a new SASL mechanism (PLAIN), a substantial part of the document.
SASL.quote: This defines the "PLAIN" SASL mechanism for use with ACAP and other protocols with no clear-text login command.

TLS.why: Gives TLS deployment requirements: mandatory cipher suite, server identity check, privacy mode and policy check.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as having a separate STARTTLS RFC; not specified here.

Used only as the encoding for PLAIN message fields.
Used only as notation for the syntax.

RFC2596.summary: Specifies how RFC 1766 language codes are carried as attribute description options in LDAPv3 and how servers interpret them in search, compare, add, modify and requested-attribute operations.

Only mentions that UTF-8 is always used for DirectoryString values; the language code has no effect on encoding.

Parent of LDAP, so implied by the LDAP tag and not listed separately.

RFC2597.title: Assured Forwarding PHB Group
RFC2597.summary: Defines the Assured Forwarding (AF) Differentiated Services per-hop-behavior group: four forwarding classes with three drop precedences each, queueing/discard requirements, and recommended codepoints.

Drop behavior responds to congestion, but the document is about a forwarding PHB, not a congestion control mechanism.
The DS field is carried in IPv4 and IPv6 headers, but that is only the substrate. The document is not about the IP protocols.
There is only a short section saying the tunneling packet's PHB must not reduce the AF assurance. The document is not about tunnelling.

RFC2598.title: An Expedited Forwarding PHB
RFC2598.summary: Defines the Expedited Forwarding (EF) per-hop behavior for Differentiated Services, giving its forwarding requirements, example implementation mechanisms, recommended codepoint 101110, and a Virtual Leased Line use with simulation results.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies a Diffserv PHB, its codepoint, mutability, tunneling and interaction with other PHBs, so it belongs on the Diffserv page.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific tag under QoS, and the parent is implied.
The document is about queueing and forwarding treatment, not congestion control. The TCP behaviour mentioned appears only in simulations.

SNMP traps are mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations.

RFC2599.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 2500-2599
RFC2599.summary: RFC 2599 is a slightly annotated status list of the 100 RFCs numbered 2500 through 2599, giving each one's author, date, title and abstract.

The listed IPP RFCs (2565-2569) are only entries in the catalogue; the memo does not address the protocol.

RFC2600.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2600.summary: RFC 2600 (STD 1) is the RFC Editor's periodic catalogue of Internet protocol standards, listing RFCs by maturity level (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Historic) with contact and retrieval information.

rejected.why: IANA appears only as a contact pointer and in the title of the Assigned Numbers entry; the document does not address IANA registries.
It lists protocols across the whole suite but does not discuss architectural principles.
DNS RFCs are entries in the catalogue. The document does not specify or discuss DNS.

FTP is mentioned only as a way to retrieve RFCs and as a list entry.

RFC2601.title: ILMI-Based Server Discovery for ATMARP
RFC2601.summary: Defines how ATMARP clients and servers use ILMI 4.0 Service Registry MIB (via SNMP GetNext sweeps) to dynamically discover ATMARP server ATM addresses, including the parameter string format, OID, and client/server behaviour.

ATM.why: The document is about IP over ATM operation: discovering ATMARP servers on ATM networks via ILMI. ATM is the most specific fitting tag, and ATMARP and ILMI have no own tags.
ATM.quote: ILMI-based Server Discovery, which provides a method for ATM-attached hosts and routers to dynamically determine the ATM addresses of servers, shall be used to locate ATMARP servers.

service discovery.quote: ILMI-based Server Discovery, hereafter referred to as "server discovery," provides a solution to these problems.

rejected.why: ATMARP is a variant of ARP over ATM, but this document only covers locating the servers, not the ARP protocol itself; ATM covers the setting.
ILMI is based on SNMPv1 and used as a substrate (GetNext sweeps), but the document does not specify or extend SNMP.
It uses the ATM Forum Service Registry MIB defined elsewhere; it does not define a new MIB module.
Sits under ATM but NHRP is not discussed; only ATMARP is.

gaps.name: ILMI / ATMARP
gaps.why: The document is about ATM Forum ILMI Service Registry and ATMARP server discovery, which the taxonomy has no specific tag for; ATM is the closest.

RFC2602.title: ILMI-Based Server Discovery for MARS
RFC2602.summary: Defines how ATM hosts and routers use ILMI 4.0 Service Registry MIB lookups to dynamically discover MARS server ATM addresses, including the parameter string format and client/server behaviour.

ATM.why: The document specifies how ATM-attached devices discover MARS servers via ILMI and the ATM Forum service registry, in the context of IP over ATM. No MARS-specific tag exists, so ATM is the best fit.
ATM.quote: provides a method for ATM-attached hosts and routers to dynamically determine the ATM addresses of servers, shall be used to locate MARS servers

service discovery.why: The core subject is dynamic discovery of servers, replacing static configuration, so the service discovery topic applies.
service discovery.quote: ILMI-based Server Discovery, hereafter referred to as "server discovery," provides a solution to these problems.

rejected.why: ILMI is based on SNMPv1 and uses GetNext to sweep the table, but SNMP is only the substrate. The document does not extend or specify SNMP.
It uses the ATM Forum Service Registry MIB and describes its row and parameter string. It defines no new MIB module, so this is mostly reference to an existing one.
MARS is a multicast address resolution server, but the document is about locating the server, not multicast routing or group membership.
IPv4 and IPv6 appear only as protocol type values in the parameter string.

gaps.name: MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) / ILMI
gaps.why: The document is about ILMI-based discovery of MARS servers. The taxonomy has no tag for MARS or ILMI, so the best available tags are only approximate.

RFC2603.title: ILMI-Based Server Discovery for NHRP
RFC2603.summary: Defines how ATM hosts and routers use ILMI-based Service Registry MIB server discovery to dynamically locate NHRP Next Hop Servers, including the NHRP service OID and parameter string format.

NHRP.quote: This memo defines how ILMI-based Server Discovery, which provides a method for ATM-attached hosts and routers to dynamically determine the ATM addresses of servers, shall be used to locate NHRP servers.

rejected.why: ILMI is based on SNMPv1, but SNMP is only the substrate. The document does not extend SNMP.
It uses the ATM Forum Service Registry MIB, which is defined elsewhere. It defines no new MIB module.
ATM is the link environment, but the document is about NHRP server discovery. NHRP sits under ATM in the taxonomy and is the more specific tag.

The document does discover servers, but the NHRP tag is the specific fit and a topic tag is not added when a technology tag already sits under it. NHRP is not a child of service discovery, so this was a close call.

gaps.name: ILMI (Integrated Local Management Interface) / ATM Forum service registry
gaps.why: The document is largely about ILMI-based server discovery, and the taxonomy has no tag for ILMI or ATM Forum service registry mechanisms.

RFC2604.title: Wireless Device Configuration (OTASP/OTAPA) via ACAP
RFC2604.summary: Informational paper proposing use of ACAP over IS-707 data services as a provisioning server protocol for over-the-air service provisioning (OTASP) and parameter administration (OTAPA) of CDMA handsets, as an alternative to IS-683A.

rejected.why: SASL and CRAM-MD5 are only the authentication mechanism ACAP uses; the document does not specify or extend them.
Parent of cdma2000; the more specific child tag was chosen.
Keyed-MD5 challenge-response is mentioned only as the baseline authentication mechanism, not the subject.
SMS is mentioned only as one option to trigger OTAPA calls, not a subject of the document.
DNS is only mentioned as a mobile requirement for locating the provisioning server.
TCP is just the transport used by ACAP and is not the subject.

gaps.name: OTASP/OTAPA over-the-air provisioning of wireless handsets
gaps.why: The document is about over-the-air service provisioning and parameter administration for mobile stations, which has no dedicated tag; cdma2000 covers it only partially.

RFC2605.summary: Defines the DIRECTORY-SERVER-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for monitoring directory servers (X.500 DSA, LDAP, CLDAP) with tables for server entries, per-protocol operation statistics and peer interaction; obsoletes RFC 1567.

SNMP is the management substrate; the framework section is boilerplate and the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour.

RFC2606.summary: RFC 2606 reserves the top-level domain names .test, .example, .invalid and .localhost, plus example.com/net/org second-level names, for testing and documentation examples.

Only used as the notation for the grammar.

AppleTalk appears only as an address family in the URL syntax.

RFC2610.summary: Defines two DHCP options (SLP Directory Agent, code 78, and SLP Service Scope, code 79) used to configure Service Location Protocol agents with Directory Agent addresses and scopes.

RFC2612.summary: RFC 2612 specifies the CAST-256 128-bit block cipher (variable key sizes 128-256 bits), including its quad-round structure, key schedule, s-boxes, naming, and test vectors.

RFC2613.summary: Defines the SMON MIB, an RMON extension for switched networks providing VLAN and priority statistics, extended data sources, and port copy configuration objects.

RFC2614.summary: Defines standardized C and Java APIs for the Service Location Protocol (SLP), plus portable configuration and serialized registration file formats for SLP agents.

RFC2617.summary: RFC 2617 specifies HTTP's challenge-response authentication framework, the Basic scheme, and the MD5-based Digest Access Authentication scheme, replacing RFC 2069.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document defines only a MIB module, which is covered by the MIB tag, and does not extend SNMP itself.
RADIUS is covered by its own tag, which sits under AAA. The document does not address AAA frameworks in general.

RFC2622.title: Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL)
RFC2622.summary: RFC 2622 specifies RPSL, an object-oriented language for describing routing policies (aut-num, route, set, inet-rtr and dictionary classes) stored in Internet Routing Registries, from which router configurations can be generated.

RPSL.why: The document defines RPSL itself: its classes, attributes, policy syntax, dictionary extensibility and grammar.
RPSL.quote: This memo is the reference document for the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL).

rejected.why: BGP attributes and communities are referenced in policy filters and actions, but the document specifies a policy language, not BGP.
The community rp-attribute is an example in the RPSL dictionary, not the subject of the document.
The mntner authentication model is a minor part, and security is delegated to a separate document.
Aggregate route specification refers to CIDR aggregation, but the document is about the policy language.
OSPF is only one of the protocol names listed in the dictionary.

RFC2623.title: NFS Version 2 and Version 3 Security Issues and the NFS Protocol's Use of RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos V5
RFC2623.summary: Clarifies NFS v2/v3 security issues (port monitoring, flavors, mount-time auth, negotiation) and specifies how NFS uses RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos V5 via pseudo flavors krb5, krb5i, krb5p.

NFS.why: The whole document concerns NFS v2/v3 security behaviour: port monitoring, mount-time authentication, export flavor binding, and flavor negotiation via MOUNT v3.
NFS.quote: clarifies various security issues involving the NFS protocol (Version 2 and Version 3 only)

GSS-API.why: Specifies how NFS uses RPCSEC_GSS/GSS-API: server principal naming, QOP and mechanism/service triples, pseudo flavors, and QOP handling for the Kerberos V5 mechanism.
GSS-API.quote: When using RPCSEC_GSS, the NFS server MUST identify itself in GSS-API via a GSS_C_NT_HOSTBASED_SERVICE name type.

Kerberos.why: Defines how NFS operates over Kerberos V5, including required integrity/privacy algorithms and the krb5/krb5i/krb5p pseudo flavor registrations.
Kerberos.quote: The NFS protocol uses Kerberos V5 security using the RPCSEC_GSS security flavor.

rejected.why: RPC and its security flavors are the substrate; the document specifies NFS's use of RPCSEC_GSS rather than RPC itself. Although ONC RPC is a sibling of NFS in the taxonomy, the document explicitly does not specify RPC.
IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like registration guidance for pseudo flavors; not the main subject.
DES MAC MD5 and 56-bit DES are mentioned as Kerberos V5 mechanism algorithms but the document is not about DES.
Authentication flavors are covered, but the more specific tags (GSS-API, Kerberos) fit better.

gaps.name: RPCSEC_GSS
gaps.why: The RPCSEC_GSS RPC security flavor is central to the document, but the taxonomy has no tag for it apart from the generic ONC RPC and GSS-API tags.

RFC2624.title: NFS Version 4 Design Considerations
RFC2624.summary: Informational design-considerations document for the NFS version 4 working group, laying out goals and investigation areas (extensibility, caching, ACLs, security via RPCSEC_GSS, locking, internationalization, Internet accessibility) for the new distributed file system protocol.

NFS.why: The whole document concerns the design goals and feature areas of NFS version 4, so it belongs on the NFS page.
NFS.quote: The main task of the NFS version 4 working group is to create a protocol definition for a distributed file system

ONC RPC.why: A substantial part discusses ONC RPC versioning, RPCSEC_GSS security flavors, transport independence and batching RPCs for NFSv4. These are design issues for ONC RPC readers.
ONC RPC.quote: NFS relies on the security mechanisms provided by the ONCRPC [RFC1831] protocol.

rejected.why: RPCSEC_GSS is recommended as the framework, but GSS-API itself is not specified or analysed here.
TLS is mentioned only as one candidate security mechanism in a list.
Section 9 proposes Unicode/UTF-8 for strings, but this is one design consideration among many, not the document's subject.
UTF-8 is mentioned as a possible wire encoding within a single section and is not the focus of the document.
The document says NFS must use TCP, but that is a transport choice, not a topic the document is about.
The NFS tag is more specific and already sits under storage.

RFC2625.title: IP and ARP over Fibre Channel
RFC2625.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IPv4 and ARP packets over Fibre Channel (LLC/SNAP, Network_Header, MTU, topologies) and defines FARP, an ELS-based protocol resolving WW_PN to Port_ID, plus optional InARP.

fibre channel.why: The whole document defines IP and ARP transport over Fibre Channel, including frame formats, FARP and login behaviour. Fibre Channel is the subject of the document, though the tag description is phrased for the opposite direction (FC over IP).
fibre channel.quote: The purpose of this document is to specify a way of encapsulating IP and Address Resolution Protocol(ARP) over Fibre Channel

ARP.why: A substantial part specifies ARP packet format, broadcast operation per FC topology, and InARP, mapping IP addresses to WW_PN.
ARP.quote: The ARP uses two packet types - Request and Reply - and each type of packet is 28 -bytes long in this specification.

rejected.why: IPv4 is the payload carried; the document defines encapsulation, not IPv4 itself.
iFCP carries FC over TCP/IP, the opposite direction from IP over FC.
Parent of fibre channel so implied; the document is about IP, not SCSI storage access.
Only an analogous link-layer encapsulation, not related.

gaps.name: IP over Fibre Channel / FARP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no link-layer tag for IP over Fibre Channel; the fibre channel tag sits under storage and is described as FC over IP, which fits poorly.

RFC2626.title: The Internet and the Millennium Problem (Year 2000)
RFC2626.summary: Informational report by the Year 2000 WG surveying RFCs 1–2128 for Y2K (two-digit year) and other time-rollover (2036, 2038) problems across protocol areas, with suggested fixes (fixed window, sliding window) and a methodology/appendix listing RFCs examined.

Y2K.why: The whole document is a Year 2000 readiness survey of Internet protocols, including period problems like 2038 rollover and suggested solutions.
Y2K.quote: The Year 2000 Working Group (WG) has conducted an investigation into the millennium problem as it regards Internet related protocols.

rejected.why: DNS serial-number and DNSSEC timestamp issues are only one short section among many protocol areas surveyed.
NTP is examined in one section as year-2000 compliant; the document is not about NTP.
Mail protocols are one surveyed area (two-digit years in RFC 822, IMAP); not the subject of the document.
NNTP's two-digit dates are noted as a problem but in a short subsection of a broad survey.
HTTP date formats are discussed briefly as one of many examples.

RFC2627.title: Key Management for Multicast: Issues and Architectures
RFC2627.summary: Informational report discussing multicast group key management issues and candidate architectures, recommending a hierarchical key tree approach for efficient, collusion-resistant rekeying after user compromise or removal.

multicast security.why: The whole document is about group key management for multicast: initializing the group net key and rekeying after compromise, which is the multicast security topic.
multicast security.quote: The Hierarchical Tree Approach is our recommended approach to address the multicast key management problem.

rejected.why: The document is about key management for multicast groups, not multicast routing or group membership. The more specific multicast security tag fits.
The document cites ISAKMP and GKMP and Ballardie's scheme. It does not specify GSAKMP.
This is the parent of multicast security in a different branch, but the document is about multicast key management specifically, so the multicast security tag fits better.
ISAKMP is mentioned only briefly in 5.4.2.6 as being compatible with the approach. The document does not specify it.

RFC2628.title: Simple Cryptographic Program Interface (Crypto API)
RFC2628.summary: Informational RFC defining a simple C-language Cryptographic Program Interface (Crypto API) that separates cryptographic libraries ("cryptoplugins") from applications and kernel-level drivers, covering encrypt/decrypt, sign/verify, compress, hash and random-number algorithm types.

cryptography.why: The whole document specifies an API for invoking cryptographic algorithms (encryption, signatures, hashes, random generation, key weakness checking) from separate crypto modules. No specific algorithm tag fits, so the general cryptography topic is correct.
cryptography.quote: This document describes a simple Application Program Interface to cryptographic functions.

rejected.why: IPsec, ISAKMP, IKE and TLS are cited only as example consumers of the API in the abstract. The document does not specify or extend them.
Mentioned only as a possible user of the API in the abstract and references, not specified or profiled.
Key handling here is limited to passing keys into contexts and a weak-key check. The document does not address key establishment or provisioning.
DES and Triple-DES appear only as entries in the algorithm ID list in Appendix A. The document is not about them.
Compress/uncompress is one algorithm type in the API, and DEFLATE and LZS are only listed IDs. It is a minor part of the interface, not the subject.
A random-number algorithm type exists in the API, but the document does not address randomness requirements or generation methods.

gaps.name: Cryptographic API / programming interface to crypto libraries
gaps.why: The document is about a software API for pluggable cryptographic modules. The taxonomy has only the general cryptography topic, and no tag for crypto APIs or library interfaces.

RFC2629.title: Writing I-Ds and RFCs using XML
RFC2629.summary: RFC 2629 describes an XML DTD and the xml2rfc tooling for writing Internet-Drafts and RFCs in XML as a source format, with element-by-element usage and the DTD itself.

RFCXML.why: This is the original specification of the RFC XML vocabulary (DTD) processed by xml2rfc, so it is the core subject of the document.
RFCXML.quote: This memo presents a technique for using XML (Extensible Markup Language) as a source format for documents in the Internet-Drafts (I-Ds) and Request for Comments (RFC) series.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document covers XML basics, DTD design, and XML tooling (validators, editors, XSL), so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: describe a simple XML Document Type Definition (DTD) that is powerful enough to handle the simple formatting requirements of RFC-like documents

rejected.why: The document is about the RFC series' source format, which RFCXML covers more specifically. The parent is implied by the child tag.
HTML output is only one of the formats the xml2rfc tool produces. The document does not specify or analyse HTML.
Only mentioned as the tooling background (sgml-mode in Emacs). The document is not about SGML-based interchange.
The ipr attribute and the RFC 2026 conformance text are a small part of the markup specification, not a subject of the document.
The eref element takes a URI target, but this is incidental use of URIs.

RFC2630.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax
RFC2630.summary: Specifies the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), an ASN.1/BER encapsulation syntax for digitally signing, digesting, authenticating, and encrypting arbitrary data, derived from PKCS #7, with mandatory algorithms and key wrap procedures.

CMS.why: The document is the core specification of CMS, defining ContentInfo and the signed-, enveloped-, digested-, encrypted- and authenticated-data content types.
CMS.quote: This document describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax.  This syntax is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt arbitrary messages.

rejected.why: S/MIME is only referenced as a user of CMS (RFC 2633, 2634); this document does not specify the mail-specific message format.
ASN.1 and BER/DER are the encoding the syntax is written in; the document defines CMS types, not ASN.1 itself.
Certificates and CRLs are imported from X.509 and carried in CMS but not profiled here.
Triple-DES is a mandatory content-encryption algorithm, but the document uses it rather than defining the cipher.
The key transport, agreement and KEK mechanisms are part of CMS structures, so CMS covers them; no separate generic tag is needed.
HMAC with SHA-1 is only a mandatory MAC algorithm for authenticated-data and is defined elsewhere (RFC 2104).

RFC2631.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement Method
RFC2631.summary: Standardizes the ANSI X9.42-based Diffie-Hellman key agreement variant (ephemeral-static and static-static modes), including ZZ computation, KEK derivation from ZZ via SHA-1, and group parameter generation and validation, for use with CMS.

key management.why: The document specifies a key agreement method and how to derive keying material (KEK) from the shared secret, plus parameter generation and validation. This is key establishment, and no more specific taxonomy tag fits Diffie-Hellman.
key management.quote: Diffie-Hellman is a key agreement algorithm used by two parties to agree on a shared secret.

rejected.why: CMS is the context in which the key agreement is used, with fields like RecipientIdentifier and UserKeyingMaterial. The document defines the DH method, not CMS itself.
SHA-1 is only the hash used in the KM derivation and in parameter generation. The document is not about the hash.
Recipient certificates and the PKIX DH key ASN.1 are referenced but not specified here.
The OtherInfo structure is defined in ASN.1 and DER-encoded, but this is only an encoding detail.
3DES and RC2 key lengths appear as examples of KEK sizes. The document is not about those ciphers.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key agreement
gaps.why: The document is entirely about Diffie-Hellman (X9.42 variant), but the taxonomy has no DH tag. Only the generic key management topic fits.

RFC2632.title: S/MIME Version 3 Certificate Handling
RFC2632.summary: Specifies S/MIME v3 requirements for handling PKIX X.509 certificates and CRLs: certificate/CRL formats, chain validation, email address binding, signing algorithms, and required certificate extensions.

S/MIME.why: The whole document defines certificate handling requirements for S/MIME agents, so readers of the S/MIME subject need it.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME agents MUST meet the certificate processing requirements documented in this document in addition to those stated in [KEYM].

X.509.why: It profiles X.509/PKIX certificate and CRL handling, covering required extensions (basicConstraints, keyUsage, subjectAltName), CRL support and chain validation.
X.509.quote: Receiving agents MUST support PKIX v1 and PKIX v3 certificates.

rejected.why: CMS is the message format the document builds on and uses data types from. The document adds certificate-handling rules and does not specify CMS.
Email addresses in certificates are covered, but the document is about certificate processing, not mail architecture or transport.
It checks the From/Sender header against the certificate address, but it does not define message format.
X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers the PKI content. The ancestor is implied.
X.500 is mentioned only as an example certificate retrieval mechanism.
RSA signature algorithms are listed only as verification requirements for certificates, which is not substantial coverage.

RFC2633.title: S/MIME Version 3 Message Specification
RFC2633.summary: Specifies S/MIME version 3: how to create CMS-based signed, enveloped and certs-only MIME body parts, the application/pkcs7-mime and application/pkcs7-signature types, algorithm requirements, and signed attributes.

S/MIME.why: The whole document is the S/MIME v3 message specification: message formats, MIME types, algorithm requirements and attributes.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data.

CMS.why: Section 2 profiles CMS options (SignedData, EnvelopedData, SignerInfo attributes, algorithms), a substantial part of the document for CMS readers.
CMS.quote: This memo defines how to create a MIME body part that has been cryptographically enhanced according to CMS [CMS]

media types.why: Defines application/pkcs7-mime (with smime-type parameter) and application/pkcs7-signature, and uses multipart/signed with protocol and micalg parameters.
media types.quote: This memo also defines the application/pkcs7-mime MIME type that can be used to transport those body parts.

rejected.why: MIME is the substrate being secured; the document defines new media types, which is covered by media types, not MIME body structure itself.
S/MIME applies to mail but is explicitly not restricted to it; the subject is covered better by S/MIME.
Certificate handling is deferred to a separate document (RFC 2632); only a few references to key-management certificates here.
Not mentioned; algorithms are tripleDES and RC2, with no dedicated tag for them in scope, and DES is only a mandated algorithm choice.
Appendix A gives an ASN.1 module but it is apparatus for the attributes, not the subject.

RFC2634.title: Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME
RFC2634.summary: Defines four optional S/MIME extensions (signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing list agents with expansion history, and signing certificate attribute) as CMS signed attributes and content types, plus triple-wrapping rules.

S/MIME.why: The whole document specifies extensions to S/MIME v3: signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing lists, and signing certificates, including triple-wrapped message formats.
S/MIME.quote: This document describes four optional security service extensions for S/MIME.

CMS.why: The services are defined as new CMS signed attributes and a Receipt content type carried in SignedData/SignerInfo. Readers of CMS would want these attribute definitions.
CMS.quote: some of the attributes described in this document are quite useful in other contexts and should be considered when extending S/MIME or other CMS applications.

mailing lists.why: A substantial section specifies MLA processing, the mlExpansionHistory attribute, loop detection, and receipt policy for secure mailing lists.
mailing lists.quote: Mail List Agents (MLAs) that can take a single message and perform the recipient-specific encryption for every recipient are often desired.

rejected.why: Section 5 binds certificates into signatures via the signingCertificate attribute, but the document defines a CMS attribute, not an X.509 profile.
The syntax is given in ASN.1, but that is only the notation used for the definitions.
MIME wrapping (multipart/signed, application/pkcs7-mime) is used for triple wrapping, but the document is not about MIME itself; the MIME framing belongs to S/MIME.
Security labels are a substantial topic here, but the taxonomy's security labels tag covers CIPSO/CALIPSO and frameworks for networked data, not S/MIME ESS labels. I did not tag it.
The signing certificate attack discussion touches on PKI, but the document is not about PKI as a subject.

RFC2635.title: DON'T SPEW A Set of Guidelines for Mass Unsolicited Mailings and Postings (spam*)
RFC2635.summary: FYI guidelines explaining why mass unsolicited email and Netnews postings (spam) are harmful and advising users, administrators, mailing list managers, news admins and ISPs how to respond and trace spammers.

spam.why: The whole document is about spam: its harms, user and admin responses, ISP policy, and tracing spammers.
spam.quote: This document explains why mass unsolicited electronic mail messages are harmful in the Internetworking community.

Netnews.why: A substantial section covers Usenet spam, cancelbots, the Breidbart Index, and news admin countermeasures.
Netnews.quote: Netnews is also subject to spamming.
Netnews.section: 4b. There's a Spam in My Group!

rejected.why: Mentions relaying and source routing abuse, but only as spam context; it does not specify or extend SMTP.
Header forgery and Received: headers are discussed for tracing, but the document is not about the message format.
NNTP servers are mentioned as abuse vectors, but the protocol is not the subject.
Gives some advice to list administrators, but it is only a part of the spam guidance, not about list protocols or headers.
Contains admin configuration advice, but the focus is spam abuse handling rather than general infrastructure security practice.
This is an FYI document, but the subject is spam, not a general introductory guide.

RFC2636.title: Wireless Device Configuration (OTASP/OTAPA) via ACAP
RFC2636.summary: Informational paper proposing ACAP (RFC 2244) as the protocol for over-the-air provisioning (OTASP/OTAPA) of CDMA handsets over IS-707 data services, defining the OTAP dataset layout and client/server flows, and comparing it with IS-683A-over-TCP and browser-form alternatives.

ACAP.why: The document profiles ACAP for handset provisioning, defining the OTAP dataset class, entries, attributes, inheritance and the mobile and administrative client behaviours.
ACAP.quote: This paper describes a viable and attractive means to provide OTASP/OTAPA via IS-707, using the ACAP [ACAP] protocol.

cdma2000.why: A substantial part concerns CDMA packet-data networks (IS-707, IS-683A OTASP/OTAPA, HLR, NAM provisioning), which fits the 3GPP2 cdma2000 subject.
cdma2000.quote: OTASP/OTAPA via data services require that the CDMA carrier have an IS-707 data services capable network.

rejected.why: SASL and CRAM-MD5 are only the authentication mechanism ACAP uses; the document defines nothing new about them.
SMS is mentioned only as one way to trigger OTAPA calls, not as a subject of the document.
The web and browser-based forms are discussed only as a rejected alternative.
TCP is only the transport substrate for ACAP.
A DNS lookup is only mentioned as a mobile requirement for finding the server.
Keyed-MD5 appears only inside CRAM-MD5 authentication.

gaps.name: OTASP/OTAPA over-the-air device provisioning
gaps.why: The document is about remote provisioning and configuration of wireless handsets, which has no dedicated tag. The nearest is cdma2000.

RFC2637.title: Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol (PPTP)
RFC2637.summary: Specifies PPTP, a vendor-developed protocol that tunnels PPP over IP using a TCP control connection and enhanced GRE data encapsulation with flow control, between PPTP access concentrators and network servers.

PPP.why: PPTP is a PPP tunneling protocol: it carries PPP sessions, handles call control for dial-in/out, and relates to PPP multilink and NCPs. Readers of PPP would want this RFC.
PPP.quote: This document specifies a protocol which allows the Point to Point Protocol (PPP) to be tunneled through an IP network.

GRE.why: Section 4 defines an enhanced GRE header (version 1, with acknowledgment number, key as call ID) that is new to how GRE is used.
GRE.quote: PPTP uses an enhanced GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) mechanism to provide a flow- and congestion-controlled encapsulated datagram service

VPN.why: The architecture is explicitly aimed at supporting VPNs for private networks via ISPs. The VPN tag is broader than the provider-provisioned scope, so this is a weaker fit.
VPN.quote: decouple functions which exist in current Network Access Servers (NAS) and support Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate for the control connection on port 1723; the document does not extend it.
L2TP is only mentioned in the IESG note as the Standards Track successor. This document does not specify it.
GRE is the more specific child tag, and the document is better described by PPP and GRE than by generic tunneling.
Section 4 suggests sliding-window and adaptive time-out algorithms, but these are tunnel-specific flow control and not a general congestion control subject.
The document uses ISDN and PSTN calls as the access it controls, but it does not address IP over ISDN.

RFC2638.title: A Two-bit Differentiated Services Architecture for the Internet
RFC2638.summary: Informational 1999 memo proposing a two-bit differentiated services architecture (Premium and Assured services), with forwarding-path mechanisms and a Bandwidth Broker framework for allocation, which preceded the Diffserv WG's RFCs 2474/2475.

Diffserv.why: The whole document defines a differentiated services architecture: Premium and Assured services, P-bit/A-bit marking, markers, profile meters and bandwidth brokers. It is a direct predecessor of the Diffserv WG work.
Diffserv.quote: This document presents a differentiated services architecture for the internet.

Intserv.why: Section 5 is devoted to how the architecture interoperates with int-serv (Controlled-Load and Guaranteed Service) and with RSVP signalling through bandwidth brokers.
Intserv.quote: the forwarding path mechanisms described in section 3 are general enough that they can also be used to provide the Controlled-Load service [8]

rejected.why: RSVP is discussed as a possible way to pass configuration and in the interoperability section, but the document does not specify or extend it.
RED/RIO queue management is used in the Assured service's output queue, but only as a mechanism. The document is not about AQM.
SNMP is mentioned only as one possible way to configure leaf routers.
The parent topic is implied by the Diffserv tag, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: Bandwidth Broker
gaps.why: The document's allocation framework is built on bandwidth brokers, and the taxonomy has no tag for them. Diffserv is the closest fit.

RFC2639.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.0: Implementer's Guide
RFC2639.summary: An informational implementer's guide for IPP/1.0 that supplements the Model and Semantics and Encoding and Transport specifications. It gives suggested request-processing and error-checking steps, status-code usage, clarifications on charsets and natural language, and notes on HTTP header and chunking use.

IPP.why: The whole document is guidance for implementing IPP/1.0 clients and IPP objects: operation attributes, validation steps, status codes, and clarifications of the IPP specifications.
IPP.quote: This document contains information that supplements the IPP Model and Semantics [RFC2566] and the IPP Transport and Encoding [RFC2565] documents.

rejected.why: IPP is carried over HTTP/1.1. Section 3 lists which HTTP headers IPP clients and servers use and warns about chunking, but this is IPP's use of the substrate, not a specification of HTTP itself.
Section 2.6 discusses UTF-8 and US-ASCII charset support in IPP. It is a small part of the IPP guidance, not a subject of the document.
Charset conversion is covered briefly in section 2.6 as an IPP matter. It is not the document's subject.
LPD appears only in the abstract's description of a companion document. This guide does not cover LPD.
Section 2.5 gives a short note on case sensitivity in URIs. It is not a main subject.

RFC2640.title: Internationalization of the File Transfer Protocol
RFC2640.summary: RFC 2640 extends FTP (updating RFC 959) for internationalization: UTF-8 pathnames, relaxed pathname syntax, a UTF8 FEAT feature, and a new LANG command for negotiating the language of server messages.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP: it changes pathname syntax, adds the UTF8 feature and defines the new LANG command, and it updates RFC 959.
FTP.quote: This document addresses the internationalization (I18n) of FTP, which includes supporting the multiple character sets and languages found throughout the Internet community.

UTF-8.why: Much of the document specifies UTF-8 as the transfer encoding for pathnames, with validity-check and conversion code in the annexes.
UTF-8.quote: For support of global compatibility it is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED that clients and servers use UTF-8 encoding when exchanging pathnames.

language tags.why: The LANG command negotiates the language of server responses using RFC 1766 language tags, and the document specifies the syntax and server matching behaviour.
language tags.quote: The parameter associated with the LANG command SHALL be one of the language tags defined in RFC 1766 [RFC1766].

rejected.why: Unicode and ISO 10646 are described as background, but the UTF-8 tag fits the actual encoding requirement more closely.
The document recommends a single character set, but it does not register or define character sets. The UTF-8 tag covers it.
This parent topic is implied by the UTF-8 and language tags I chose, so I did not list it directly.
Telnet is cited only for the CR-NUL padding convention. The document does not specify or extend Telnet.
ASCII is the legacy baseline the document moves beyond. It is not the subject.

RFC2641.title: Cabletron's VlanHello Protocol Specification Version 4
