RFC2641.summary: Informational specification of Cabletron's VlanHello protocol (Version 4), part of ISMP, by which SecureFast VLAN switches discover neighbouring switches over IEEE 802 frames and build the switch-fabric topology, including port states, topology events, and the Interswitch Keepalive message format.

link layer.why: The document defines a layer-2 neighbour discovery and topology protocol between switches, carried directly in IEEE 802 frames with a dedicated multicast MAC and ethertype. No narrower link-layer tag fits, so the general topic is used.
link layer.quote: Switches use the VlanHello protocol to discover their neighboring switches and establish the topology of the switch fabric.

rejected.why: The protocol uses IEEE 802 framing, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet, Ethernet interworking or Ethernet OAM. It is a vendor-specific switch-to-switch protocol.
The keepalives detect neighbour loss, but the document specifies topology discovery for a proprietary VLAN product, not a general OAM mechanism.
It builds a switch-fabric topology, but it is not an IP routing protocol or a routing design document.
The topology events and keepalives are internal control-plane signalling, not network management or operations practice.

gaps.name: VLAN switching / Cabletron SecureFast VLAN (ISMP)
gaps.why: The document is about a proprietary VLAN switch-fabric control protocol (InterSwitch Message Protocol). The taxonomy has no tag for VLANs or vendor switch fabric protocols.

RFC2642.title: Cabletron's VLS Protocol Specification
RFC2642.summary: Specifies Cabletron's Virtual LAN Link State Protocol (VLSP), an OSPF-derived link-state routing protocol running at the MAC layer among SecureFast VLAN switches, with neighbor discovery, database synchronization, flooding, and equal-cost best-path calculation.

routing architecture.why: The document specifies a link-state intradomain routing protocol for a switch fabric. It is not OSPF, so no OSPF tag fits. The routing-architecture tag is the closest fit for a proprietary link-state routing design.
routing architecture.quote: VLSP is used to determine and maintain a fully connected mesh topology graph of the switch fabric.

ECMP.why: The protocol computes and returns up to three equal-cost best paths. This is a stated feature of the protocol.
ECMP.quote: VLSP provides support for equal-cost multipath routing

rejected.why: VLSP is derived from OSPF and compared with it, but it is a distinct protocol that runs at the MAC layer. The document does not specify or extend OSPF.
VLSP packets are carried in 802 frames, but that is only the substrate. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
This is the parent topic, so it is implied by the more specific tag.

gaps.name: Cabletron VLSP / ISMP (proprietary VLAN switch link-state routing)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for proprietary link-state routing among Layer 2 VLAN switches or for the InterSwitch Message Protocol. The closest fits are generic routing tags.

RFC2643.title: Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN Operational Model
RFC2643.summary: Informational description of Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN switching product: its VLAN model, call-processing service centers, call tapping, and the Interswitch Message Protocol (ISMP) message formats used between switches.

link layer.why: The document specifies a proprietary MAC-layer switching and VLAN protocol (ISMP) with 802 frame encapsulation. No narrower link-layer tag fits, so the generic link layer topic applies.
link layer.quote: implements a distributed connection-oriented switching protocol that provides fast forwarding of data packets at the MAC layer

rejected.why: The product uses IEEE 802 frames and 802.1D spanning tree, but the document is about a proprietary VLAN switching fabric, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Broadcast ARP packets are intercepted and resolved, but only as one input to the resolve service; ARP itself is not specified or extended.
Path computation uses the VLS link-state protocol, but that is specified in another RFC. Here it is only referenced, and the switching is at MAC layer.

gaps.name: VLANs / MAC-layer switching (SecureFast VLAN, ISMP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for virtual LANs or layer-2 switching fabrics. This is the document's core subject, and the generic link layer topic is the nearest fit.

RFC2644.title: Changing the Default for Directed Broadcasts in Routers
RFC2644.summary: BCP that updates RFC 1812 so routers must, by default, not receive or forward network-prefix-directed broadcasts, to reduce Smurf amplification denial-of-service attacks.

operational security.why: The document is a best current practice on a safer default router configuration to mitigate Smurf amplification attacks, which is operational security guidance for network infrastructure.
operational security.quote: Network service providers and corporate network operators are urged to ensure their networks are not susceptible to directed broadcast packets originating outside their networks.

IPv4.why: It amends the IPv4 router requirements (RFC 1812) on directed broadcast addresses and forwarding behavior, so IPv4 readers would want it.
IPv4.quote: Router Requirements [1] is updated as follows:

rejected.why: The document is about Smurf-attack amplification, but it only changes a router default. It does not address DDoS mitigation or signalling mechanisms, so operational security fits better.
Mobile IP is mentioned only as a user of directed broadcasts in agent discovery, and the document suggests this language might be removed. The document is not about mobility.
The document concerns router packet-handling defaults, not routing architecture or scalability.
Directed broadcast addresses are discussed, but only as a forwarding behavior to disable, not as address architecture or allocation.

RFC2645.title: ON-DEMAND MAIL RELAY (ODMR) SMTP with Dynamic IP Addresses
RFC2645.summary: Specifies On-Demand Mail Relay (ODMR), an SMTP profile in which an intermittently connected customer with a dynamic IP authenticates (AUTH) and issues ATRN to reverse client/server roles so the provider can deliver queued mail.

SMTP.why: The document defines a new SMTP profile and the ATRN command, with state machine and response codes for mail relaying to intermittently connected hosts.
SMTP.quote: On-Demand Mail Relay is a restricted profile of SMTP [SMTP, ESMTP]. Port 366 is reserved for On-Demand Mail Relay.

rejected.why: AUTH uses SASL mechanisms (CRAM-MD5 mandatory) but the document defines nothing new about SASL; it is only the authentication mechanism relied on.
Parent of SMTP; implied, so not listed separately.
ABNF is used only to give the ATRN syntax, not the subject of the document.
Authentication is a minor part, delegated to SMTP AUTH/SASL, not a subject in its own right.

RFC2646.title: The Text/Plain Format Parameter
RFC2646.summary: RFC 2646 defines the "format=flowed" parameter for the text/plain media type, using trailing spaces as soft line breaks, plus space-stuffing and quoting rules so paragraph text can be reflowed while remaining plain text to legacy mail clients.

media types.why: The document defines a new parameter (Format=Fixed/Flowed) for the text/plain media type and asks IANA to update the registration. It belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: This document defines a new MIME parameter for use with Text/Plain:
media types.section: 4. The Format Parameter to the Text/Plain Media Type

email.why: The format addresses email display problems, including embarrassing line wrap in quoted replies, space-stuffing against From-munging, and soft line breaks on the wire. Mail user agent behaviour is a substantial part of the content.
email.quote: The Text/Plain media type is the lowest common denominator of Internet email, with lines of no more than 997 characters

rejected.why: The document extends MIME with a parameter, but media types is the more specific tag. MIME is the parent, so it is implied.
SMTP is cited only for line-length limits and dot-stuffing analogies. It is not the subject.
ABNF is used only as notation for the grammar. The document is not about ABNF.
The document concerns body text formatting, not Internet message headers or addressing.
HTML and text/enriched are mentioned only as earlier failed approaches that the document contrasts itself against.

RFC2647.title: Benchmarking Terminology for Firewall Performance
RFC2647.summary: RFC 2647 defines terminology for benchmarking firewall performance (e.g., allowed traffic, bit forwarding rate, concurrent connections, proxy types, rule set), extending the router and switch benchmarking terminology RFCs.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking terminology RFC from the BMWG, defining metrics such as bit forwarding rate, goodput, connection establishment time and concurrent connections for firewall DUT/SUTs.
benchmarking.quote: This document defines terms used in measuring the performance of firewalls. It extends the terminology already used for benchmarking routers and switches

firewall.why: The whole vocabulary is about firewalls: packet filtering, stateful filtering, application and circuit proxies, rule sets, DMZ and homing. Readers on the firewall subject page would want this.
firewall.quote: A device or group of devices that enforces an access control policy between networks.

rejected.why: Network address translation is defined as one term (3.21) but only as a factor that may affect forwarding rate; the document is not about NAT.
Closely related, but benchmarking is the more specific fit for device-level benchmarking terminology.
TCP is mentioned as an example of a connection-oriented protocol in connection definitions; it is not specified or analysed.
ATM appears only as an alternative connection type and UOT example.
The document is a glossary, but its subject is firewall benchmarking, which is covered by more specific tags.

RFC2648.title: A URN Namespace for IETF Documents
RFC2648.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "ietf" for RFCs, STDs, FYIs, BCPs, IETF meeting minutes and Internet-Drafts, specifying its syntax, uniqueness, persistence and resolution (with example Perl CGI resolvers).

URN.why: The document defines a new URN namespace with a specification template, NSS structure, assignment and resolution rules. Readers of the URN subject would want it.
URN.quote: this document proposes the "ietf" namespace. This namespace consists of the RFC family of documents (RFCs, STDs, FYIs, and BCPs) developed by the IETF

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the NSS syntax. The document is not about ABNF.
Resolution scripts run over HTTP CGI, but HTTP is only the substrate here.
The document names RFC series documents as the things being named, but it does not address the series' format, style or publication.
The scripts use content negotiation on Accept headers, but this is incidental to the namespace registration.

RFC2649.title: An LDAP Control and Schema for Holding Operation Signatures
RFC2649.summary: Defines LDAP v3 controls (SignedOperation, DemandSignedResult, SignedResult) and schema (signedAuditTrail, Changes, zombieObject) for carrying S/MIME signatures of directory operations to build a signed audit journal of entry changes.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAP v3 with new controls, object classes and attributes (signedAuditTrail, Changes, zombieObject, rootDSE attribute), so LDAP readers need it.
LDAP.quote: This document describes an LDAP message control which allows for the retrieval of digitally signed information.

rejected.why: S/MIME is only the format used to wrap signatures; the document does not specify or extend S/MIME.
TLS is mentioned only as the better way to protect connection integrity, not specified here.
Referenced via PKCS 7 for the signature format only; substrate.
Certificates and verification are used but not the subject of the document.
The MIME directory content-type is only referenced for the sequence-0 object representation.
The document is about signing operations for audit trails, and it expressly says it is not a mechanism guaranteeing origin and integrity of operations.

RFC2650.title: Using RPSL in Practice
RFC2650.summary: A tutorial on using RPSL to register routing policies (aut-num, route, as-set, route-set, mntner objects) in the Internet Routing Registry and to generate router configurations with RtConfig.

RPSL.why: The whole document explains how to write and register RPSL policies in the IRR and analyse them with tools such as RtConfig.
RPSL.quote: This document is a tutorial on using the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) to describe routing policies in the Internet Routing Registry (IRR).

rejected.why: BGP attributes (MED, LOCAL_PREF, communities) appear in the examples, but the document is about describing policy in RPSL, not about BGP.
One section expresses an RFC 1998 community-based multihoming policy in RPSL, but this is one example and not the document's subject.
The whois service is only used to query IRR objects and is not specified or extended here.
Route aggregation under CIDR is mentioned only in passing.

RFC2651.title: The Architecture of the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP)
RFC2651.summary: Describes the architecture of the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) version 3, which passes index objects between servers in a mesh to enable query routing, extracted and generalised from the Whois++ centroid indexing system.

WHOIS++.why: CIP is the generalised successor to Whois++ index passing (centroids, meshes, polling). The document reuses the Whois++ mesh traversal algorithm and POLLED-BY/POLLED-FOR. The WHOIS++ tag is the closest fit for a Whois++-derived indexing mesh.
WHOIS++.quote: CIP is an evolution and refinement of distributed indexing concepts first introduced in the Whois++ Directory Service

rejected.why: Directory services is one application domain CIP can serve, but the document is about general-purpose index passing and query routing, not directory access.
Mentioned as an example data access protocol and for cross-protocol mapping. The document does not specify or extend LDAP.
MIME is only the encoding for index objects. The object definitions are in a companion RFC.
CIP routes queries to datasets using indices. It is not about discovering services on a network.
The author's email address contains RWhois.net, but the body says nothing about RWhois.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) / query routing / index passing
gaps.why: The document's main subject is a distributed index-exchange protocol for query routing across databases. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so WHOIS++ is only the nearest match.

RFC2652.title: MIME Object Definitions for the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP)
RFC2652.summary: Defines the MIME media types (application/index.cmd, .response, .obj, .vnd) used for CIP commands, responses and index objects, plus requirements for defining new index types and the response codes.

media types.why: The document defines and registers the application/index media type tree and its facets, plus rules for registering new index types, so media type readers would want it.
media types.quote: Appendix A contains the actual MIME [RFC2046] registration templates sent to the IANA for registration [RFC2048].

directory services.why: CIP is a directory/indexing mesh protocol for referral-based query routing among servers (RWhois, LDAP, etc.). The taxonomy has no CIP tag, so the nearest topic is directory services.
directory services.quote: The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) is used to pass indexing information from server to server in order to facilitate query routing.

rejected.why: MIME is the encapsulation substrate; the document defines new media types, which fits media types more specifically, not MIME body structure itself.
RWhois appears only as an example access protocol for referrals and in an example, not as the subject.
Mentioned only as an example referral protocol in the referral generation discussion.
Only referenced for body termination style and response code conventions.
PGP/MIME is merely recommended in Security Considerations.
The DSI uses an OID encoded as ASCII, which is not ASN.1 specification.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP)
gaps.why: The document is about CIP index meshes and query routing, and the taxonomy has no CIP or indexing tag; directory services only approximates it.

RFC2653.title: CIP Transport Protocols
RFC2653.summary: Defines three transports (TCP stream, Internet mail, HTTP POST) for carrying Common Indexing Protocol requests, responses and index objects, including version negotiation and response codes.

transport mapping.why: The document's whole purpose is binding CIP messages to TCP, mail and HTTP transports, which is what the transport mapping topic covers.
transport mapping.quote: This document specifies three protocols for transporting CIP requests, responses and index objects, utilizing TCP, mail, and HTTP.

WHOIS++.why: CIP is the index mesh protocol of the WHOIS++ directory architecture. The stream transport is built to coexist with Whois++ servers, with version negotiation via an illegal Whois++ command.
WHOIS++.quote: In order to maintain backwards compatibility with existing Whois++ servers, CIPv3 sender-CIPs MUST first verify that the newer protocol is supported.

rejected.why: HTTP is only a carrier here (POST of CIP MIME objects); no new HTTP semantics are defined.
Internet mail is used as a transport substrate; only a CIP-Version header and a Reply-To rule are added.
CIP objects are MIME messages, but the object formats are defined in CIP-MIME, not here.
TCP is merely the underlying stream for the stream transport.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional protection.
The directory/index context is covered by WHOIS++, which fits better; this document only specifies transport.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP)
gaps.why: The document is about CIP index mesh transport, and the taxonomy has no CIP tag. WHOIS++ is the closest fit.

RFC2654.title: A Tagged Index Object for use in the Common Indexing Protocol
RFC2654.summary: Defines the Tagged Index Object, a CIP index format with tagged tokens, full and incremental updates, and aggregation, for exchanging index information among directory and information servers (LDAP, X.500, Whois++).

directory services.why: The document defines an index object for exchanging index information among directory servers (LDAP, X.500, Whois++). No specific CIP tag exists, so the directory services topic is the best fit.
directory services.quote: defines a mechanism by which information servers can exchange indices of information from their databases by making use of the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP)

LDAP.why: A substantial motivation is improving LDAP referrals. The index schema and examples use LDAP attributes, LDIF and LDAP URLs.
LDAP.quote: This specification defines a mechanism whereby LDAP server can exchange index information that will allow referrals to point towards a clearly accurate destination.

rejected.why: The Whois++ Centroid is the comparison point and the format is usable by Whois++ servers. The document does not specify or extend Whois++ itself.
X.500 DISP is only contrasted with this approach. The document does not specify X.500 behaviour.
The index object is carried as a MIME content type, so MIME is only the substrate.
Only listed as one of the security options in the agreement. The document does not define S/MIME.
A content type is named, but registration rules are not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP)
gaps.why: The document defines an index object format for CIP, but the taxonomy has no CIP or index-service tag. Only the generic directory services topic is available.

RFC2655.title: CIP Index Object Format for SOIF Objects
RFC2655.summary: Defines SOIF (Summary Object Interchange Format) as an index object type for the Common Indexing Protocol, specifying its MIME type, payload grammar, attribute matching semantics, and example template types.

media types.why: The document defines and names a new MIME media type for the SOIF index object, so readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: The index object described below will have the MIME type of application/index.obj.HARVEST-SOIF-1.

directory services.why: The document is about an index object format for CIP, a directory/index referral mesh. The taxonomy has no CIP tag, so the nearest fit is directory services (it compares itself to Rwhois). This is the best available fit, not an exact one.
directory services.quote: The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) allows servers to form a referral mesh for query handling by defining a mechanism by which cooperating servers exchange hints

rejected.why: MIME is only used to name the media type and for Base64 encoding. The document does not specify MIME body structure.
Base64 is only recommended as an encoding for SOIF objects. The document does not define it.
URLs serve as object identifiers, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Rwhois is mentioned only as a contrast to Web resources. The document is not about it.
The SOIF grammar is given in a BNF-like notation, but the document does not specify or discuss that notation.
The document concerns index objects for CIP, not WHOIS++ centroids. The mesh idea is similar but the document does not cover WHOIS++.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) / SOIF
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CIP, index meshes or query referral, or for SOIF and metadata summary formats. The RFC is mainly about these subjects.

RFC2656.title: Registration Procedures for SOIF Template Types
RFC2656.summary: Defines the IANA registration procedure for SOIF (Summary Object Interchange Format) template types, including identifier naming (IANA- prefix), attribute definitions, versioning relationships, and a registration form.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is a registry and registration procedure for SOIF template types run by IANA, so readers of IANA registry matters would want it.
IANA.quote: The initial registrar of SOIF template types will be the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

rejected.why: URLs are mentioned only as one SOIF object component that is explicitly not subject to registration.
SOIF and the Common Indexing Protocol relate to indexing and query referral, but this document only covers template type registration, not directory access or synchronization.
Template type registration resembles media type registration but is a different registry.
IAFA templates are only historical background for SOIF.

gaps.name: SOIF (Summary Object Interchange Format) / Harvest / CIP indexing
gaps.why: The document concerns SOIF template types and query referral in the Common Indexing Protocol, but the taxonomy has no tag for SOIF, resource indexing or metadata.

RFC2657.title: LDAPv2 Client vs. the Index Mesh
RFC2657.summary: Defines LDAP object classes and attribute types that present a Common Indexing Protocol Index Mesh as a DIT to LDAPv2 clients lacking referrals, and describes how such a client finds, searches and queries through the mesh.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAPv2 client behaviour and defines LDAP object classes and attribute types (cIPIndex, cIPDataSet) so clients can work with the Index Mesh.
LDAP.quote: LDAPv2 clients as implemented according to RFC 1777 [1] have no notion on referral.

WHOIS++.why: CIP index mesh (centroid/index-server architecture, successor of the WHOIS++ mesh) is the subject being integrated. It is the closest taxonomy fit for the distributed index mesh, though CIP itself has no tag.
WHOIS++.quote: an Index Mesh, as defined by the Common Indexing Protocol [2], heavily depends on referrals

rejected.why: X.500 DIT concepts are referenced only as the model for the tree structure; the document is not about the X.500 service.
Parent of LDAP; implied by the LDAP tag so not listed separately.
Attributes hold URIs (LDAP URI, mailto) but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
Schema definitions use LDAP attribute syntax BNF, not ASN.1 modules.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) / Index Mesh
gaps.why: The document is about integrating clients with the CIP Index Mesh, but the taxonomy has no CIP tag; WHOIS++ is only an approximate fit and may be a poor match.

RFC2658.title: RTP Payload Format for PureVoice(tm) Audio
RFC2658.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for Qualcomm PureVoice (QCELP) speech codec audio, including frame packing, bundling, and variable interleaving to mitigate packet loss.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies an RTP payload format for a specific codec (QCELP/PureVoice), with packet layout, bundling and interleaving rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes the RTP payload format for PureVoice(tm) Audio.

rejected.why: PureVoice/QCELP is the codec being packetized, but the document does not define the codec; it defines its RTP payload, and RTP payload format is the more specific fit.
RTP is the transport the payload runs over; the document does not extend RTP itself, and the payload format tag sits under RTP.
CDMA is mentioned only as background for where the IS-733 codec is standardized.
Interleaving mitigates loss but is not an FEC or loss-recovery coding scheme in the sense of that tag.

RFC2659.title: Security Extensions For HTML
RFC2659.summary: Defines HTML extensions (anchor attributes DN, NONCE, CRYPTOPTS and CERTS/CRYPTOPTS elements) for embedding S-HTTP negotiation parameters and certificates in HTML documents.

S-HTTP.why: The document exists to bind S-HTTP negotiation headers to HTML anchors, extending Secure HTTP; S-HTTP readers would want it.
S-HTTP.quote: This memo describes a syntax for embedding S-HTTP negotiation parameters in HTML documents.

HTML.why: It specifies new HTML attributes and elements (CERTS, CRYPTOPTS), so it is an extension of HTML.
HTML.quote: We define the following new anchor (and form submission) attributes:

rejected.why: Certificates are carried in CERTS elements but only as opaque advisory data; the document does not profile certificates.
Anchors use shttp:// URLs only as examples; the URI scheme is not defined here.
SGML quoting conventions are mentioned only as a detail of attribute syntax; the document is not about SGML-based interchange.
PEM certificate groups are only mentioned as one of two permitted certificate formats.

RFC2660.title: The Secure HyperText Transfer Protocol
RFC2660.summary: Specifies S-HTTP/1.4, a message-level security protocol for HTTP that wraps HTTP messages in CMS or MOSS encapsulation with negotiable signature, encryption and MAC enhancements.

S-HTTP.why: The document is the specification of Secure HTTP itself, which has its own tag.
S-HTTP.quote: Secure HTTP (S-HTTP) provides independently applicable security services for transaction confidentiality, authenticity/integrity and non-repudiability of origin.

rejected.why: S-HTTP wraps and extends HTTP, but the S-HTTP tag is the more specific fit and sits under web security. HTTP is the substrate here.
CMS is the main encapsulation format and is summarised in an appendix. The document uses it rather than specifying it, since RFC 2630 does that.
The MAC-Info construction is derived from HMAC, but it is a small part of the document.
MIME types and MOSS multiparts are used, and a message/s-http media type is registered. The document is not about MIME itself.
S-HTTP is compared with Digest authentication and offers MAC-based auth. It is not an HTTP authentication scheme specification.
This is the parent of S-HTTP, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC2661.title: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol "L2TP"
RFC2661.summary: RFC 2661 specifies L2TP version 2, a protocol for tunneling PPP frames between an L2TP access concentrator and network server, including its header, AVPs, control messages, state machines, reliable control channel, and UDP/IP binding.

L2TP.why: The document is the core specification of L2TP: header format, AVPs, control messages, state machines and operation.
L2TP.quote: L2TP facilitates the tunneling of PPP packets across an intervening network in a way that is as transparent as possible to both end-users and applications.

PPP.why: L2TP tunnels PPP sessions and includes substantial PPP-specific content: proxy LCP and authentication AVPs, ACCM, multilink PPP and PPP framing.
PPP.quote: L2TP extends the PPP model by allowing the L2 and PPP endpoints to reside on different devices interconnected by a packet-switched network.

rejected.why: IPsec is discussed only in the Security Considerations as a way to secure L2TP, not specified or profiled here.
UDP is just the transport for L2TP (port 1701). Section 8.1 is a binding, not new UDP usage guidance.
Section 8.1 is a short UDP/IP binding inside the L2TP specification. It is not the document's main subject.
Appendix A borrows TCP-style slow start for the control channel. It is a minor supporting detail.
MD5 is used only inside the AVP hiding mechanism and is not the subject of the document.
RADIUS appears only as an optional source of a Private Group ID and as the origin of the hiding method.

RFC2662.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the ADSL Lines
RFC2662.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (ADSL-LINE-MIB) for managing ADSL lines, covering both ATU-C and ATU-R ends: line, physical and channel status, performance counters and intervals, profiles, traps and conformance.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is to define a MIB module in SMIv2 with tables, objects, traps and conformance groups for ADSL line management.
MIB.quote: This document defines a standard SNMP MIB for ADSL lines based on the ADSL Forum standard data model [9].

DSL.why: The managed subject is the ADSL access line (ATU-C/ATU-R, fast and interleaved channels, rate adaptation, SNR margins), so DSL access networks readers would want it.
DSL.quote: The ADSL standard describes ATU-C and ATU-R as two sides of the ADSL line. This MIB covers both ATU-C and ATU-R agent's perspectives.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is defined for; the document defines a MIB module, and the more specific MIB tag covers it.
Access Node Control Protocol is a different protocol; this document only defines a line MIB.
SMIv2 uses an ASN.1 subset only as notation for the MIB definitions; the document is not about ASN.1.
The performance counters and interval buckets are part of the MIB's objects, not a measurement methodology.

RFC2663.title: IP Network Address Translator (NAT) Terminology and Considerations
RFC2663.summary: Informational RFC defining terminology for the flavors of NAT (traditional/Basic NAT, NAPT, bi-directional, twice, multihomed, RSIP), its operation, and its limitations including application and IPsec issues.

NAT.why: The whole document defines NAT terminology, flavors, operation, and limitations, so it belongs on the NAT page.
NAT.quote: Network Address Translation is a method by which IP addresses are mapped from one address realm to another, providing transparent routing to end hosts.

rejected.why: IPsec incompatibility with NAT is discussed, but only as a limitation of NAT, not as the subject.
A DNS-ALG is used for bi-directional and twice NAT, but DNS is not specified or extended here.
FTP ALG handling of PORT/PASV is an example of an application NAT must support, not the document's subject.
The document is a terminology document, but it is specific to NAT. The NAT tag fits better.
Tunnels are used in RSIP and VPN scenarios, but they are secondary to the NAT subject.
CGN is not discussed. The document covers general NAT only.

gaps.name: Realm Specific IP (RSIP)
gaps.why: Section 5 describes RSIP, RSA-IP and RSAP-IP as an alternative to NAT. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so it falls under NAT.

RFC2664.title: FYI on Questions and Answers - Answers to Commonly Asked "New Internet User" Questions
RFC2664.summary: FYI 4 is an introductory Q&A for new Internet users, explaining what the Internet is, common activities, addresses, netiquette, how it works, and who runs it.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide for unsophisticated Internet users, which is exactly what the user guides subject covers.
user guides.quote: This memo provides an overview to the new Internet User.

rejected.why: Email is explained only as a consumer activity and address format, with no protocol content.
URLs are explained informally to lay readers; the document does not specify or analyse URI syntax.
The 'how the Internet works' section is a simplified lay explanation, not an architectural-principles discussion.
The web is described only as a user activity (surfing), with nothing about the protocol.
FTP is mentioned once as a way to transfer files and is not the document's subject.
Spam is mentioned in passing as a mailing-list abuse and in the glossary, not as a substantial topic.

RFC2665.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types
RFC2665.summary: Defines the EtherLike-MIB SMIv2 module for managing Ethernet-like interfaces (statistics, collision histogram, MAC Control/PAUSE, duplex status), based on IEEE 802.3 Clause 30 and obsoleting RFC 2358.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (EtherLike-MIB) and its relationship to the Interfaces MIB and MAU MIB.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The managed objects cover Ethernet MAC statistics, collisions, duplex, and PAUSE flow control for 10/100/1000 Mb/s Ethernet per IEEE 802.3.
Ethernet.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol framework that the MIB is used with. The document only gives the standard framework boilerplate and does not specify SNMP itself. The MIB tag is more specific.
The data model is written in SMIv2, not YANG.
The more specific Ethernet tag already covers this.

RFC2666.title: Definitions of Object Identifiers for Identifying Ethernet Chip Sets
RFC2666.summary: Defines a MIB module of OBJECT IDENTIFIER registrations identifying Ethernet MAC chip sets, for use with the (now deprecated) dot3StatsEtherChipSet object in the EtherLike-MIB.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (ETHER-CHIPSET-MIB) whose content is OID registrations for chip sets, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines OBJECT IDENTIFIER values for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The OIDs identify Ethernet MAC hardware and complement the Ethernet-like interface MIB, so Ethernet readers would find it relevant.
Ethernet.quote: registered OID values for use with the dot3StatsEtherChipSet object in the EtherLike-MIB

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB belongs to; the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and the framework section is boilerplate.
The OID registrations are chipset identifiers, not an IANA registry or guidance on IANA considerations.

RFC2667.title: IP Tunnel MIB
RFC2667.summary: Defines the TUNNEL-MIB SMIv2 module for managing IP tunnels of any encapsulation type over IPv4, with a tunnel interface table and a config table for dynamic tunnel creation, tied to the Interfaces MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (TUNNEL-MIB) with tunnelIfTable and tunnelConfigTable, extending the Interfaces MIB via ifStack and ifType. This is its entire content.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 networks

tunneling.why: The MIB covers generic IP tunnel management (endpoints, encapsulation method, hop limit, TOS) across many encapsulations, so readers of the tunneling subject would want it. It does not specify any one tunnel protocol, so the generic tunneling tag fits better than GRE or IP-in-IP.
tunneling.quote: This document describes a Management Information Base (MIB) used for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 networks, including GRE [16,17], IP-in-IP [18]

rejected.why: GRE is only one of several encapsulation methods enumerated in tunnelIfEncapsMethod. The document does not specify or extend GRE.
IP-in-IP is only one listed encapsulation value. The document does not specify or extend it.
L2TP is only an enumerated encapsulation value, and the document does not manage L2TP-specific objects.
SNMP is the management framework the MIB runs under. The boilerplate framework section is not specific to this document, and the MIB tag already sits under SNMP.
IPsec appears only as a tunnelIfSecurity value, and a separate security MIB is expected to cover it.
IPv4 is the underlying network for the tunnels but is not itself the subject of the document.

RFC2668.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs)
RFC2668.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (MAU-MIB) for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units, obsoleting RFC 2239 and adding 1000 Mb/s MAU types, PAUSE/flow-control negotiation and remote fault objects.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (MAU-MIB) defining managed objects, tables, notifications and conformance groups in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs).

Ethernet.why: The managed objects cover Ethernet MAU types (10/100/1000 Mb/s), auto-negotiation, jabber, and link state, so readers of Ethernet management would look for it.
Ethernet.quote: This specification is intended to serve the same purpose: to provide for management of all types of Ethernet/802.3 MAUs.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol framework the MIB is used with; the document specifies no protocol behaviour, only a MIB module (the more specific MIB tag applies).
Implied as an ancestor of the MIB tag; no separate broader treatment.
The MIB is written in SMIv2/ASN.1 notation, which is only the definition language, not the subject.
Not related; PAUSE and flow control negotiation are only auto-negotiation capability bits.

RFC2669.title: DOCSIS Cable Device MIB Cable Device Management Information Base for DOCSIS compliant Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems
RFC2669.summary: Defines the DOCS-CABLE-DEVICE-MIB SMIv2 module for SNMP management of DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems and CMTSs, covering device status, software upgrade, event/trap throttling, LLC/IP filters and CPE anti-spoofing.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is a MIB module in SMIv2 for cable devices; MIB is the most specific tag for it.
MIB.quote: it defines a basic set of managed objects for SNMP-based management of DOCSIS 1.0 compliant Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems.

DOCSIS.why: The MIB is specific to managing DOCSIS cable access devices, so readers of DOCSIS would expect it.
DOCSIS.quote: This MIB provides a set of objects required for the management of DOCSIS compliant Cable Modems (CM) and Cable Modem Termination Systems (CMTS).

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with; the parent is implied by MIB and the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour.
Syslog is only a configurable event-reporting destination (docsDevEvSyslog); the document does not specify syslog.
TFTP is used for software download and provisioning, merely referenced by objects, not specified.
DHCP appears only in boot-state enumerations of the provisioning process.
The LLC/IP filters are packet classifiers for bridged traffic, but the document is not about firewalls or middlebox security.
TOS bit rewriting via policy table is a minor feature and not framed as Diffserv.

RFC2670.title: Radio Frequency (RF) Interface Management Information Base for MCNS/DOCSIS compliant RF interfaces
RFC2670.summary: Defines the DOCS-IF-MIB SMIv2 module for SNMP management of DOCSIS/MCNS cable modem and CMTS RF interfaces, including channel, modulation, QoS profile, signal quality and MAC status tables and their relation to the Interfaces MIB.

DOCSIS.why: The MIB manages DOCSIS cable modem and CMTS RF interfaces.
DOCSIS.quote: it defines a basic set of managed objects for SNMP-based management of MCNS/DOCSIS compliant Radio Frequency (RF) interfaces.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (DOCS-IF-MIB) with its ifEntry relationship to the Interfaces MIB.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module in a manner that is compliant to the SNMP SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with; the MIB tag is the more specific fit.
The QoS profile table is only one table of the MIB, which is not about QoS architectures or signalling.
DOCSIS is tagged via its specific child; the MIB covers interface layering but is not generic link-layer material.

RFC2671.title: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS0)
RFC2671.summary: Specifies EDNS0, a backward-compatible mechanism for extending the DNS wire protocol via the OPT pseudo-RR, extended RCODEs and flags, larger UDP payload size advertisement, and extended label types.

EDNS.why: The whole document defines EDNS(0): the OPT pseudo-RR, option format, version, extended RCODE and UDP size advertisement. This is the EDNS tag's subject.
EDNS.quote: One OPT pseudo-RR can be added to the additional data section of either a request or a response.

rejected.why: The parent of EDNS, so it is implied. The document is about the extension mechanism, not DNS in general.
The document raises UDP payload size limits, but UDP is only the transport here. It specifies nothing new about UDP itself.
The IANA Considerations section only requests registries and is boilerplate. The body is not about IANA.

RFC2672.title: Non-Terminal DNS Name Redirection
RFC2672.summary: Defines the DNAME DNS resource record (type 39), which redirects an entire subtree of the DNS namespace to another domain, and modifies server and resolver query-processing algorithms accordingly.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record and modifies the server and resolver name-resolution algorithms. DNS is the subject, and no more specific child tag fits.
DNS.quote: This document defines a new DNS Resource Record called "DNAME", which provides the capability to map an entire subtree of the DNS name space to another domain.

rejected.why: EDNS0 is only used to decide whether a client understands DNAME, so that the server knows whether to synthesize a CNAME. The document does not define or extend EDNS.
DNSSEC is mentioned only for optionally signing synthesized CNAMEs and in Security Considerations. The document does not specify anything new about DNSSEC.
Renumbering motivates DNAME and is the subject of one example, but the document is about the DNS record, not renumbering procedures.
The document refers to YXDOMAIN (from RFC 2136) only as an error code and does not deal with dynamic updates.

RFC2673.title: Binary Labels in the Domain Name System
RFC2673.summary: Defines the DNS Bit-String Label, an extended label type (ELT 000001) that compactly represents sequences of one-bit labels in domain names, with its wire encoding, textual form, canonical form and sort order.

DNS.why: The document extends DNS with a new label type, specifying its wire format, text representation, matching rules and canonical sort order.
DNS.quote: This document defines a "Bit-String Label" which may appear within domain names.

rejected.why: The Bit-String Label uses the extended label type space from EDNS0 (RFC 2671), but this document defines a label type, not an EDNS option or mechanism.
Canonical form and sort order are defined so DNSSEC signatures work, but this is a supporting part of the label definition, not DNSSEC itself.
ABNF is only the notation used for the textual syntax.
The IANA request is a single code point registration, which is boilerplate here.

RFC2674.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges with Traffic Classes, Multicast Filtering and Virtual LAN Extensions
RFC2674.summary: Defines the P-BRIDGE-MIB and Q-BRIDGE-MIB SNMP MIB modules for managing IEEE 802.1D-1998 traffic classes and multicast filtering (GARP/GMRP) and IEEE 802.1Q VLAN bridging, supplementing the original bridge MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a pair of SMIv2 MIB modules (P-BRIDGE-MIB and Q-BRIDGE-MIB) for bridge management; this is the specific technology tag for MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it defines two MIB modules for managing the new capabilities of MAC bridges defined by the IEEE 802.1D-1998 MAC Bridges and the IEEE 802.1Q-1998 Virtual LAN (VLAN) standards

Ethernet.why: The MIBs manage MAC bridging, VLANs, traffic classes, and filtering databases, which are Ethernet/LAN layer 2 matters. Readers of link-layer and Ethernet bridging would want this.
Ethernet.quote: This device is used to connect Local Area Network segments below the network layer. These devices are often known as 'layer 2 switches'.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol that carries the MIB, not the subject. The document defines MIB objects and does not extend or specify the protocol.
YANG is not used. The modules are written in SMIv2.
Traffic classes and user priority mapping are part of the MIB, but it is bridge management of 802.1D priority rather than a QoS architecture or signalling document.
Multicast filtering by GMRP is at the MAC layer within bridges. It is not IP multicast routing or group membership.
The more specific MIB tag already covers this document; the parent is implied.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.1 bridging / VLANs (802.1D, 802.1Q, GARP, GMRP, GVRP)
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about managing transparent bridges, VLANs and GARP-based registration protocols. The taxonomy has no tag for bridging or VLANs, so Ethernet is only an approximate fit.

RFC2675.title: IPv6 Jumbograms
RFC2675.summary: Specifies the IPv6 Jumbo Payload hop-by-hop option for packets over 65,535 octets and the TCP and UDP changes (UDP zero length, TCP MSS and Urgent Pointer handling) needed to use jumbograms.

IPv6.why: The document defines a new IPv6 hop-by-hop option and its processing and error rules, so it is about IPv6 specification.
IPv6.quote: This document describes the IPv6 Jumbo Payload option, which provides the means of specifying such large payload lengths.

TCP.why: A substantial part specifies TCP changes for MSS and the Urgent Pointer so TCP can use jumbograms.
TCP.quote: When an MSS value of 65,535 is received, it is to be treated as infinity.

UDP.why: The document modifies UDP length handling and checksum computation for jumbograms.
UDP.quote: UDP packets longer than 65,535 octets may be sent by setting the UDP Length field to zero

rejected.why: ICMPv6 Parameter Problem is only used to report format errors, not specified here.
Path MTU Discovery is referenced for deriving the TCP MSS but is not the subject.
Only notes the pseudo-header length computation and reduced accuracy; the checksum itself is not specified.

RFC2676.title: QoS Routing Mechanisms and OSPF Extensions
RFC2676.summary: Experimental RFC defining QoS routing extensions to OSPFv2: bandwidth/delay metrics encoded as extended TOS, a Bellman-Ford based pre-computation path selection algorithm, and a GateD implementation with performance measurements.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 with a Q-bit, extended-TOS encodings of bandwidth and delay in Router and Summary LSAs, and QoS path computation.
OSPF.quote: This memo describes extensions to the OSPF [Moy98] protocol to support QoS routes.

traffic engineering.why: QoS-constrained path selection on available bandwidth and hop count, with update-triggering policies, is a substantial part of the document and fits traffic engineering of paths. The QoS routing subject has no closer tag.
traffic engineering.quote: The focus of this document is on the algorithms used to compute QoS routes

rejected.why: RSVP is only the assumed mechanism for requesting QoS routes, and the document is about routing, not RSVP.
The QoS parent is not chosen because the document is about routing for QoS flows, not QoS architectures or signalling.
Diffserv is mentioned only as a data-path classification example, with no Diffserv content.
The Guaranteed Service proposal is cited only for a delay extension, and Intserv itself is not addressed.
The document is protocol-specific to OSPF rather than about routing architecture in general.

gaps.name: QoS routing
gaps.why: The document's central subject is QoS-based routing: constraint-based path selection on bandwidth and delay. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag, so traffic engineering is the nearest fit.

RFC2677.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP)
RFC2677.summary: Defines the NHRP-MIB SMIv2 module of managed objects (general, client and server groups: cache, purge, registration, NHS/NHC and statistics tables) for managing the NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol of RFC 2332.

NHRP.why: The whole document defines managed objects for NHRP clients and servers, so readers of NHRP would want it.
NHRP.quote: it describes managed objects for the Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP) as defined in RFC 2332

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module in SMIv2 with tables, objects, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document does not extend or specify SNMP itself, and the SNMP section is boilerplate.
ATM is only an example NBMA subnetwork for ifIndex layering. The MPOA MIB and Classical IP over ATM are referenced for complementarity but are not the subject.
The IANA section only mentions the address family numbers MIB it imports. It is boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC2678.title: IPPM Metrics for Measuring Connectivity
RFC2678.summary: Defines IPPM metrics for connectivity between a pair of Internet hosts (instantaneous, interval, and temporal one-way/two-way), with a sketched active-probe methodology including a TCP SYN-based one.

performance measurement.why: The document defines IPPM analytic metrics and active measurement methodologies for connectivity, which is the core of performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a series of metrics for connectivity between a pair of Internet hosts.

rejected.why: TCP SYN probing is only one example methodology for estimating connectivity; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
ICMP unreachable messages are interpreted as evidence in the methodology, but ICMP itself is not the subject.
The document measures reachability, not path discovery.
Security uses of connectivity testing are mentioned only in passing and in the boilerplate Security Considerations.

RFC2679.title: A One-way Delay Metric for IPPM
RFC2679.summary: Defines the Type-P-One-way-Delay singleton metric, its Poisson-stream sample, and derived statistics (percentile, median, minimum, inverse percentile) for IP performance measurement, with error, calibration and reporting guidance.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines an active network performance metric, its sampling, statistics, error analysis and calibration. This is the core of the performance measurement topic.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a metric for one-way delay of packets across Internet paths.

rejected.why: NTP is mentioned only as one way to synchronise clocks at source and destination. The document is not about NTP.
Clock synchronisation, accuracy and skew are discussed only as error sources for the delay measurement. The document does not specify synchronisation methods.
QoS appears only as a motivation for measuring in each direction. It is not a subject of the document.
The document defines active one-way delay metrics. It does not cover flow export or sampling of observed traffic.
The document defines metrics for Internet paths, not a methodology for benchmarking network devices.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metric definitions
gaps.why: The document is part of the IPPM metric family (framework, one-way delay and loss, connectivity). The taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic, with no specific IPPM tag.

RFC2680.title: A One-way Packet Loss Metric for IPPM
RFC2680.summary: Defines the Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss singleton metric, a Poisson-stream sample of it, and an average-loss statistic for IPPM active measurement of Internet paths.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines an active performance metric (singleton, Poisson sample, statistics), including methodology, errors and reporting. This is the IPPM metrics subject.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths.

rejected.why: Loss is discussed as it affects transport protocols, but the document does not address congestion control.
IP packets are the measured objects and RFC 791 is cited only for packet lifetime. The document is not about IPv4.
QoS is mentioned only as motivation for measuring each direction separately. The document does not address QoS mechanisms.
TCP appears only as an example of an application affected by loss and of biased loss sampling. It is not specified or extended here.
It is a later protocol for carrying such measurements. This document only defines the metric and explicitly leaves implementation techniques out of scope.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metrics
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for IPPM metric definitions. The generic 'performance measurement' topic is the nearest fit.

RFC2681.title: A Round-trip Delay Metric for IPPM
RFC2681.summary: Defines the IPPM round-trip delay metric (Type-P-Round-trip-Delay), its Poisson-stream sample, statistics, error/calibration analysis and reporting guidance.

performance measurement.why: The document defines an active network performance metric with singleton, sample and statistics, plus calibration and reporting. It is a core IPPM performance measurement document.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a metric for round-trip delay of packets across Internet paths.

rejected.why: NTP is only mentioned as a way to get clock accuracy; the document does not specify or profile it.
ICMP Echo/ping is only cited as an example measurement method, not specified.
Clock synchronization, accuracy, and skew are discussed only as error sources in measurement, not as the subject.
QoS appears only as a caveat about asymmetric provisioning, not as a subject.
Path reporting is mentioned briefly; no path discovery tool is specified.

RFC2682.title: Performance Issues in VC-Merge Capable ATM LSRs
RFC2682.summary: Informational analysis, by simulation, of the additional buffering and delay incurred by VC merging in ATM label switching routers (MPLS), compared with non-VC-merging switches.

MPLS.why: The document studies VC merging in ATM-based label switching routers (MPLS LSRs), analysing buffer and delay performance of a VC-merge capable MPLS switch architecture.
MPLS.quote: VC merging allows many routes to be mapped to the same VC label, thereby providing a scalable mapping method that can support thousands of edge routers.

ATM.why: The analysis is about ATM switches, AAL5 cell reassembly and VC/VP labels, i.e. IP over ATM, so ATM readers would want it.
ATM.quote: In this document, we will assume that layer 2 switching uses ATM technology. In this case, each IP packet may be segmented to multiple 53-byte cells

rejected.why: The document is a buffer and delay performance study, not about traffic engineering of networks, despite a reference mentioning ATM traffic engineering.
It is simulation-based switch performance analysis, not network performance metrics or measurement methods.
QoS is mentioned only in passing (partial merging per QoS, fair queueing), not as a subject of the document.
CIDR prefix is mentioned only as one granularity of destination.

RFC2683.title: IMAP4 Implementation Recommendations
RFC2683.summary: Informational RFC giving interoperability and implementation recommendations for IMAP4 (RFC 2060) client and server developers, covering connections, scaling, flood control, UIDs, LIST reference names, hierarchy delimiters and testing.

IMAP.why: The whole document is about implementing IMAP4 clients and servers interoperably, covering commands, UIDs, LIST, FETCH and so on.
IMAP.quote: This document attempts to outline these issues and to make recommendations in order to make the end products as interoperable as possible.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a contrast for IMAP's multiple-access and long-lived session design.
MIME parsing and BODYSTRUCTURE come up only as IMAP fetch behaviour, not as the subject.
Referenced only for the SEARCH CHARSET and the modified UTF-7 mailbox name encoding, which is incidental.
IMAP is the more specific tag and it already sits under email.

RFC2684.title: Multiprotocol Encapsulation over ATM Adaptation Layer 5
RFC2684.summary: RFC 2684 specifies two methods, LLC encapsulation and VC multiplexing, for carrying routed and bridged multiprotocol PDUs over ATM AAL5, plus an optional VPN encapsulation header, and obsoletes RFC 1483.

ATM.why: The whole document defines how routed and bridged PDUs are encapsulated over ATM AAL5, with LLC/SNAP and VC multiplexing formats.
ATM.quote: describes two encapsulations methods for carrying network interconnect traffic over AAL type 5 over  ATM

rejected.why: The VPN-Id header in section 8 is a small optional part, and it concerns provider VPN identification over ATM, not provider-provisioned L3VPN/L2VPN services.
Bridged Ethernet/802.3 PDU formats are carried over ATM, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The FR-SSCS/RFC 2427 encapsulation appears only in the informational Appendix A and is not recommended for most uses.
RFC 2364 (PPP over ATM) is only pointed to as an alternative and is not specified here.
CLNP is mentioned only as an NLPID example in the appendices.
NHRP is only listed in Appendix D as an application of the encapsulation.

RFC2685.title: Virtual Private Networks Identifier
RFC2685.summary: Defines a globally unique 7-octet VPN identifier format (3-octet IEEE OUI of the VPN authority plus a 4-octet VPN index) for referring to a VPN across providers and layers.

VPN.why: The whole document defines the VPN-ID format for provider-provisioned/IP VPNs, so readers browsing VPNs would want it.
VPN.quote: There is a requirement for the use of a globally unique VPN identifier in order to be able to refer to a particular VPN

rejected.why: The identifier is layer-agnostic and not specific to BGP/MPLS L3VPNs; it explicitly covers layer 2 and layer 3.
It mentions layer 2 VPN support as a requirement but does not define an L2VPN service.
ATM signalling and AAL5 encapsulation are only cited as example usage contexts.
A MIB is mentioned only as one place the VPN-ID might be used; no MIB is defined.
The VPN-ID scopes private IP addresses but the document defines a VPN identifier, not IP address architecture.

RFC2686.title: The Multi-Class Extension to Multi-Link PPP
RFC2686.summary: Defines the multi-class extension to PPP Multilink, adding class bits to fragment headers for multiple levels of suspension of real-time traffic over low-bitrate links, plus two new LCP options (Multilink Header Format and Prefix Elision).

PPP.why: The document extends PPP Multilink with class numbers in the fragment header and defines new LCP options. It is a PPP extension, and PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: This document defines two new LCP options: Multilink Header Format, Prefix Elision

header compression.why: Prefix elision removes common prefix bytes per class to cut overhead. This is a header-byte compression technique for low-speed links. It is not ROHC, CRTP or IPHC, so the parent topic fits.
header compression.quote: Prefix elision is not a replacement for header compression or data compression: it allows implementations to compress away prefixes
header compression.section: 5. Prefix elision: Compressing common header bytes

rejected.why: The motivation is integrated services and real-time priority over slow links. The document specifies only a PPP fragmentation and encapsulation mechanism, not a QoS architecture or signalling.
Compressed RTP/G.723.1 packets are mentioned only as an example of small high-priority packets. RTP is not specified or extended here.
The companion architecture document concerns integrated services. This document only provides the encapsulation format, so Intserv is background.
Multilink bundles multiple links, but this document is about fragment classes and suspension, not link bundling or aggregation.

gaps.name: PPP Multilink Protocol (MP) / real-time encapsulation over low-bitrate links
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PPP Multilink fragmentation or for real-time framing over slow links. PPP is the closest fit.

RFC2687.title: PPP in a Real-time Oriented HDLC-like Framing
RFC2687.summary: Defines a suspend/resume-oriented real-time encapsulation for PPP over HDLC-like links, using compact multilink fragment headers and a fragment suspend escape byte, plus new Multilink Header Format option codes.

PPP.why: The document extends PPP Multilink with compact fragment formats, an HDLC-like real-time frame format, and new LCP Multilink Header Format option codes. Readers of the PPP subject would want it.
PPP.quote: The general approach is to start from the PPP Multilink fragmentation protocol [2] and its multi-class extension [5] and add suspend/resume

header compression.why: The document is part of the low-bitrate integrated services architecture and works to reduce per-fragment overhead with compact headers and prefix elision. It is not itself a header compression scheme, so this tag is weak. I am not confident in it.
header compression.quote: A companion document describes an architecture for providing integrated services over low-bitrate links

rejected.why: The motivation is real-time and integrated services, but the document specifies only a link-layer framing format, not a QoS architecture or signalling.
The multilink fragment format is used, but the document is mainly about single-link operation, and multi-link use is explicitly a partial non-requirement.
ISDN B-channels are mentioned only as an example of low-bitrate links.

RFC2688.title: Integrated Services Mappings for Low Speed Networks
RFC2688.summary: Defines guidelines for mapping Integrated Services controlled load and guaranteed service onto low-speed PPP links using MCML/RTF classes, including admission control, error term (D) calculation, and scheduling.

Intserv.why: The document specifies how Intserv controlled load and guaranteed services are mapped to low-speed links, including admission control and C/D error term calculation.
Intserv.quote: This document defines the mapping of integrated services "controlled load" [5] and "guaranteed" [6] services on to low-bandwidth links.

PPP.why: A substantial part covers mapping flows to MCML/RTF PPP classes, fragmentation vs suspend/resume, prefix elision, and bit/byte stuffing effects on PPP links.
PPP.quote: Supporting integrated services over PPP links which implement MCML or RTF can be accomplished in several ways.
PPP.section: 3. Controlled Load and Guaranteed Service Class Mapping

rejected.why: RSVP is only mentioned as the assumed signaling protocol; the document does not specify or extend it.
Compression is discussed only as an input to admission control calculations; the compression schemes are defined in companion RFCs.
Casner-Jacobson compression is referenced for its effect on rate and MTU, not specified here.
Intserv is the more specific tag and already covers the QoS subject.

RFC2689.title: Providing Integrated Services over Low-bitrate Links
RFC2689.summary: Informational architecture document for carrying integrated-services real-time flows over low-bitrate links, combining real-time PPP encapsulation, RTP/UDP/IP header compression, RSVP-based announcement and PPP negotiation.

CRTP.why: A core component of the architecture is a header compression scheme optimized for real-time flows, i.e. compressing IP/UDP/RTP headers on low-speed serial links. The document explains why it is needed and how it fits.
CRTP.quote: the CRTP (compressed RTP) specification makes use of this relationship by encoding these fields only when the second order difference is non-zero [7]
CRTP.section: 5. Principles of Header Compression for Real-Time Flows

QoS.why: The document is about providing integrated services (admission control, reservations, flow identification) over low-bitrate links, an architecture-level QoS topic with no single protocol being specified.
QoS.quote: An important component of the integrated services architecture is the provision of reservations for real-time flows.

RSVP.why: The announcement mechanism relies on RSVP PATH state and proposes new RSVP objects to convey compression and encapsulation info to routers.
RSVP.quote: Additional RSVP objects could be defined that are included in PATH messages by those applications that desire good performance over low-bitrate links

PPP.why: The real-time encapsulation (multi-class multilink, real-time HDLC-like framing) and negotiation of compression are built on PPP; significant parts discuss PPP-level framing and negotiation.
PPP.quote: PPP options that can be negotiated at the link setup (LCP) phase are included in [8], [9], and [10].

rejected.why: RTP is the traffic being carried and compressed; the document does not specify or extend RTP.
The more specific CRTP tag is chosen instead; the parent is implied.
Not discussed; the compression schemes are IPHC and CRTP.
IP header compression is discussed as a baseline, but the document's focus is the combined architecture and RTP header compression.
Integrated services is the framing, but the document is about low-bitrate link support rather than the Intserv service specifications; QoS and RSVP cover it.
ISDN B-channels are only mentioned as example link types.

RFC2690.title: A Proposal for an MOU-Based ICANN Protocol Support Organization
RFC2690.summary: Scott Bradner's proposal, submitted to ICANN, for an MOU-based Protocol Support Organization (PSO) with a Protocol Council and General Assembly that nominates ICANN directors and advises on protocol parameter assignment.

internet governance.why: The whole document defines a governance body within ICANN, its council, director nominations, open meetings and SDO membership criteria. This is Internet governance, and no narrower child tag fits.
internet governance.quote: The Protocol Support Organization (PSO) will be a consensus-based advisory body within the ICANN framework.

IANA.why: The PSO's advisory role and policy development concern protocol parameter assignment and registration, which is the subject of the IANA registries. This is a substantial part of the proposal but not its main focus.
IANA.quote: only matters relating to the assignment of parameters for Internet protocols would be so referred.

rejected.why: The IETF poisson working group produced the proposal, but the document describes an ICANN/SDO body and not the IETF's own standards process or procedures.
The Protocol Council nominates ICANN directors, but this is not the IETF NomCom and does not describe its procedures.
The document is only published as an RFC. It says nothing about the RFC series itself.

gaps.name: ICANN / Protocol Support Organization (PSO) organizational structure
gaps.why: The document is about the structure of ICANN's supporting organizations and the relationship between ICANN and standards bodies. The taxonomy has no tag for ICANN or its supporting organizations, so the general internet governance tag is the nearest fit.

RFC2691.title: A Memorandum of Understanding for an ICANN Protocol Support Organization
RFC2691.summary: Text of the 1999 Memorandum of Understanding among ICANN, IETF, ITU-T, W3C and ETSI creating the Protocol Support Organization (PSO) with its Protocol Council, ICANN board appointments, and SDO membership criteria.

internet governance.why: The document is a governance instrument defining how ICANN and standards bodies organize the PSO, Protocol Council, board appointments and SDO membership criteria. No more specific child tag (IETF process, IANA, etc.) fits as well.
internet governance.quote: This MoU creates the Protocol Support Organization (PSO) within the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN).

rejected.why: The PSO advises ICANN on protocol parameter assignment policy, but the document is about the PSO's organizational structure, not IANA registries or their stewardship.
The IETF is one signatory appointing council members; the document does not describe IETF standards procedures.

RFC2692.title: SPKI Requirements
RFC2692.summary: RFC 2692 summarizes the requirements for the SPKI (Simple Public Key Infrastructure) certificate structure and operation. It centres on authorization certificates rather than name-key bindings, and it covers validity, CRLs and implementation simplicity (no ASN.1).

SPKI.why: The document states the requirements for SPKI, a certificate format and operating procedure. A reader browsing SPKI would expect to find it.
SPKI.quote: The main purpose of an SPKI certificate is to authorize some action, give permission, grant a capability, etc. to or for a keyholder.

rejected.why: SPKI is a child of PKI, so PKI is implied and not listed separately.
The document contrasts SPKI with traditional name-key certificates and rejects ASN.1. It does not cover X.509.
The abstract mentions trust management, and the SPKI authorization-certificate model fits it. The more specific SPKI tag was chosen. The trust management tag describes KeyNote and its successors.
Authorization certificates are central, but the SPKI tag already covers the subject. A separate topic tag would add little.
ASN.1 is explicitly excluded from the design, so the document is not about it.
LDAP is mentioned only as an example global repository that the keyholder may choose to use. It is not part of the requirements.

gaps.name: SPKI (Simple Public Key Infrastructure)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SPKI tag. It lists SPKI only as a child under PKI, with the label 'SPKI (Simple Public Key Infrastructure), historic'. I used that tag, but check that it exists exactly as 'SPKI'. It does appear in the taxonomy under PKI.

RFC2693.title: SPKI Certificate Theory
RFC2693.summary: Explains the theory behind SPKI certificates: SDSI local names, authorization over name binding, delegation, validity conditions (CRLs, revalidation), 5-tuple/4-tuple reduction for authorization decisions, and key management.

SPKI.why: The whole document is the theory of SPKI certificates, ACLs, delegation, validity and tuple reduction.
SPKI.quote: The SPKI Working Group has developed a standard form for digital certificates whose main purpose is authorization rather than authentication.

authorization.why: Authorization decisions from certificates and ACLs, delegation and tuple reduction are central.
authorization.quote: the application needs to know if the keyholder is authorized for some access.

key management.why: A full section covers key lifetimes, replacement, revocation services and threshold root keys.
key management.quote: Rather than define a mechanism for declaring a key to be bad or replaced, SPKI defines a mechanism for giving certificates limited lifetimes

rejected.why: Discussed and compared, and translated to tuples, but the document is not a profile of X.509.
Broader parent of SPKI; the more specific SPKI tag fits, and the document is about the alternative certificate model.
Online validity tests are discussed conceptually, not OCSP.
Mentioned only historically.

gaps.name: SPKI/SDSI certificates
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SPKI tag in the security hierarchy except the historic SPKI under PKI; I used 'SPKI' as listed. If it is absent in practice, PKI would be the nearest parent.

RFC2694.title: DNS extensions to Network Address Translators (DNS_ALG)
RFC2694.summary: Informational RFC describing a DNS Application Level Gateway (DNS_ALG) on NAT devices that rewrites addresses in DNS payloads (A, PTR records, in-addr.arpa queries) as they cross address realms, with Basic/bi-directional and Twice-NAT walkthroughs.

NAT.why: The document specifies NAT behaviour extensions (DNS_ALG, temporary/committed bindings, Bind-holdout timer) for Basic, bi-directional and Twice NAT.
NAT.quote: This document identifies the need for DNS extensions to NATs and outlines how a DNS Application Level Gateway (DNS_ALG) can meet the need.

DNS.why: Much of the body covers DNS payload handling: question and RR sections, PTR/A/AXFR handling, TTL changes, and zone transfer and dynamic update considerations.
DNS.quote: DNS_ALG modifies payload transparently to alter address mapping of hosts as DNS packets cross one address realm into another.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is discussed only as a limitation that breaks DNS_ALG, not specified or profiled.
Dynamic updates get one short subsection that recommends keeping zones within one realm. That is too minor for a tag.
UDP and TCP are only the transport of DNS packets that NAT rewrites.
The document handles IPv4 addresses, but its subject is NAT and DNS, not IPv4.

RFC2695.title: Authentication Mechanisms for ONC RPC
RFC2695.summary: Informational RFC documenting Sun's two ONC RPC authentication flavors, AUTH_DH (Diffie-Hellman) and AUTH_KERB4 (Kerberos v4), with their credential/verifier structures, nickname handling and status codes, and warning that they are weak.

ONC RPC.why: The document specifies authentication flavors (AUTH_DH, AUTH_KERB4) for ONC RPC, with XDR structures for credentials and verifiers. Readers of ONC RPC would want it.
ONC RPC.quote: two authentication mechanisms created by Sun Microsystems that are commonly used in conjunction with the ONC Remote Procedure Call (ONC RPC Version 2) protocol

Kerberos.why: A substantial section specifies an AUTH_KERB4 flavor using Kerberos v4 tickets, naming and error codes, so Kerberos readers would find it relevant.
Kerberos.quote: Kerberos-based authentication takes advantage of the fact that Kerberos tickets have encoded in them the client name and the conversation key

authentication.why: The AUTH_DH flavor is a non-Kerberos authentication mechanism using Diffie-Hellman key exchange and encrypted timestamps. No more specific technology tag fits it.
authentication.quote: DH authentication was created to address these problems.

rejected.why: DES is only the cipher used to encrypt timestamps and conversation keys, not the subject.
RPCSEC_GSS and GSS-API appear only in the warning and security considerations as recommended replacements.
NTP is mentioned only as a way to synchronize clocks.
NFS appears only as a Kerberos service-name example and in the security section.
The Diffie-Hellman exchange is part of the AUTH_DH mechanism and is not a general key management topic.

RFC2696.title: LDAP Control Extension for Simple Paged Results Manipulation
RFC2696.summary: Defines an LDAPv3 control extension (pagedResultsControl) letting a client retrieve search results in pages using a size and opaque cookie, with an example and X.500 mapping.

LDAP.why: The RFC specifies a new LDAP control extending the search operation, including its ASN.1 structure and client-server interaction.
LDAP.quote: This document describes an LDAPv3 control extension for simple paging of search results.

rejected.why: Section 5 only gives a brief mapping to X.511 PagedResultsRequest for LDAP front ends; the document is not about X.500.
ASN.1 and BER are only used to define the control's structure, not the subject of the document.

RFC2697.title: A Single Rate Three Color Marker
RFC2697.summary: Defines the Single Rate Three Color Marker (srTCM), a Diffserv meter/marker that uses CIR, CBS and EBS token buckets to mark packets green, yellow or red.

Diffserv.why: The srTCM is a metering and marking component of a Diffserv traffic conditioner, and its colors are coded in the DS field (e.g. AF drop precedence). Readers of Diffserv would want this RFC.
Diffserv.quote: defines a Single Rate Three Color Marker (srTCM), which can be used as component in a Diffserv traffic conditioner

rejected.why: It is the parent of Diffserv, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The marker operates on IP packets and the DS field, but the document is not about IP itself.
Token-bucket metering and marking is policing and conditioning, not congestion control in the sense of that subject.

RFC2698.title: A Two Rate Three Color Marker
RFC2698.summary: Defines the Two Rate Three Color Marker (trTCM), a token-bucket meter and marker that colors packets green, yellow or red based on peak and committed rates, for use in Diffserv traffic conditioners.

Diffserv.why: The trTCM is a metering and marking component of a Diffserv traffic conditioner. It codes color in the DS field, for example as AF drop precedence.
Diffserv.quote: can be used as a component in a Diffserv traffic conditioner

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS subject, so the parent is implied.
Drop precedence marking is mentioned, but the document is about metering and marking, not congestion control.
The marker operates on IP packets and the DS field, but the document says nothing specific about IPv4.

RFC2699.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 2600-2699
RFC2699.summary: RFC 2699 is a slightly annotated status list of the 100 RFCs numbered 2600 through 2699, with a one-paragraph abstract and standards-track marking for each.

RFC series.why: The document is a catalogue of a block of RFC numbers, published by the RFC Editor staff. It is about the RFC series itself, not about the subjects of the RFCs it lists.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2600 through RFCs 2699.

rejected.why: It marks entries as standards track and points to the Internet Official Protocol Standards list. It does not discuss the standards process itself.
It lists DNS RFCs (EDNS0, DNAME, binary labels, reserved TLDs) only as entries in the summary. The document is not about DNS.
Many of the listed RFCs are MIBs, but they appear only as one-line entries.
HTTP/1.1 and HTTP authentication are only entries in the list.
The Diffserv markers and architecture are only mentioned as listed items.
The S/MIME RFCs are mentioned only as listed entries.

RFC2700.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2700.summary: RFC 2700 (STD 1) is the RFC Editor's periodic catalogue of Internet protocol standards, listing RFCs by standardization stage (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Historic) rather than specifying any protocol itself.

IETF process.why: The document reports the standards-track maturity levels of RFCs under the IETF standards process (RFC 2026). Readers interested in standardization status would look for it.
IETF process.quote: This memo describes the current state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as determined by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

RFC series.why: It is an RFC Editor publication that indexes the RFC series. Its contacts section explains how to obtain RFCs and the RFC Editor's role.
RFC series.quote: This memo is published by the RFC Editor in accordance with Section 2.1 of "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", RFC 2026
