rejected.why: It only points to IANA as a contact and cites the Assigned Numbers RFC in a list; it is not about IANA registries.
It is a status snapshot, not a retrospective, even though many entries are historic.
DNS RFCs appear only as entries in the lists. The document does not address DNS.
Many SNMP and MIB entries are listed, but the document is not about them. The same applies to every other protocol in the lists, so none are tagged.

RFC2701.title: Nortel Networks Multi-link Multi-node PPP Bundle Discovery Protocol
RFC2701.summary: Informational Nortel RFC defining a UDP multicast discovery protocol by which Remote Access Servers locate the Multi-link PPP Bundle Head across nodes, and using L2TP to transfer PPP fragments to it.

PPP.why: The whole document extends Multi-link PPP so that links of one bundle can terminate on different RASes, specifying discovery of the Bundle Head and fragment handling.
PPP.quote: This document specifies a standard way for Multi-link PPP to operate across multiple nodes.

L2TP.why: Section 3 specifies L2TP as the transfer protocol for PPP fragments to the Bundle Head. It is a defined part of the solution, though brief and reuses an existing protocol.
L2TP.quote: The Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) [L2TP] will be used to transfer PPP fragments from a RAS containing a secondary link

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport for discovery messages, with a port assigned in IANA considerations. The document defines nothing new about UDP usage.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional authentication mechanism.
Discovery messages are sent to a multicast address, but the document is not about IP multicast routing or group membership.
The discovery here is specific to locating a PPP Bundle Head, and the PPP tag covers it. It is not general service discovery.

RFC2702.title: Requirements for Traffic Engineering Over MPLS
RFC2702.summary: Informational requirements document for traffic engineering over MPLS, defining traffic trunk and resource attributes and a constraint-based routing framework for efficient, reliable backbone operation.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document covers traffic engineering objectives, traffic trunk and resource attributes, and constraint-based path selection to optimize network resource utilization and traffic performance.
traffic engineering.quote: This document presents a set of requirements for Traffic Engineering over Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS).

MPLS.why: The requirements are specifically for MPLS: LSPs, traffic trunks, induced MPLS graph and the capabilities an MPLS implementation must provide. Readers of MPLS architecture would want it.
MPLS.quote: MPLS is strategically significant for Traffic Engineering because it can potentially provide most of the functionality available from the overlay model

rejected.why: OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as IGPs that could be extended for constraint-based routing; the document does not specify them.
QoS routing is mentioned only as another name for constraint-based routing; the document is not about QoS architectures or signalling.
Constraint-based routing is discussed, but the document's subject is traffic engineering over MPLS, which has its own more specific tag.
RSVP is referenced only through the PASTE architecture. No signalling protocol is specified.

RFC2703.title: Protocol-independent Content Negotiation Framework
RFC2703.summary: Informational memo setting out terminology, an abstract framework, goals and technical issues for protocol-independent content negotiation (media features, feature sets, negotiation metadata) across application protocols.

content negotiation.why: The whole document defines the terminology, abstract process, metadata model and goals for media feature and content negotiation.
content negotiation.quote: Content negotiation covers three elements:

rejected.why: HTTP and TCN are cited only as examples of negotiation; the framework is explicitly protocol-independent.
MIME media types are mentioned as the existing axis of variation, but the document is about other features.
Mentioned only as a possible third-party directory for negotiation metadata.
A possible metadata encoding is discussed briefly in one subsection, not a substantial part of the document.
Email and fax are used as example transports; not the document's subject.
The security section is boilerplate-style cataloguing of issues for negotiation protocols, not the document's subject.

RFC2704.title: The KeyNote Trust-Management System Version 2
RFC2704.summary: RFC 2704 specifies version 2 of the KeyNote trust-management system: its assertion language for policies and credentials, action attribute handling, query evaluation semantics, and application architecture.

trust management.why: The document defines the KeyNote trust-management system itself: assertion syntax, compliance checking and the trust-management architecture. This is the exact subject of the tag.
trust management.quote: This memo describes version 2 of the KeyNote trust-management system. It specifies the syntax and semantics of KeyNote `assertions'

rejected.why: KeyNote is about authorization, but the more specific trust management tag sits under security and fits the document better.
Credentials subsume the role of certificates, but KeyNote binds keys to authorizations rather than names and does not define a PKI.
X.509 is mentioned only as something that could be converted into KeyNote assertions.
RSA and DSA appear only as example key algorithms in principal identifiers. The document is not about them.
The assertion syntax is inspired by RFC822 headers, but it is not an email message format.

RFC2705.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Version 1.0
RFC2705.summary: RFC 2705 specifies MGCP 1.0, a text-based master/slave protocol by which external Call Agents control telephony media gateways (endpoints, connections, commands, event packages), carried over UDP and using SDP.

MGCP.why: The whole document defines MGCP: its model, commands, encoding, UDP transmission, failover and event packages.
MGCP.quote: an application programming interface and a corresponding protocol (MGCP) for controlling Voice over IP (VoIP) Gateways from external call control elements

SDP.why: The document specifies how SDP is used in MGCP for audio, network access, ATM and local connections, which readers of SDP would want.
SDP.quote: These descriptions will follow the conventions delineated in the Session Description Protocol which is now an IETF proposed standard, documented in RFC 2327.

rejected.why: RTP carries the media and is only referenced for connection statistics; it is not specified or extended here.
Discussed only as a related signalling protocol in the introduction.
Only a relationship section on interworking via the Call Agent; the document is not about H.323.
Mentioned only for signalling backhaul.
Used as the security mechanism for MGCP, not specified here.
Substrate transport for MGCP; the document defines no new UDP behaviour.

RFC2706.title: ECML v1: Field Names for E-Commerce
RFC2706.summary: RFC 2706 defines ECML v1, a standard set of HTML form field names (shipping, billing, card payment) so electronic wallets can auto-fill merchant checkout forms.

ECML.why: The document specifies ECML v1 field names for e-commerce forms, which is exactly this technology.
ECML.quote: A standard set of information fields is defined as the first version of an Electronic Commerce Modeling Language (ECML) so that this task can be more easily automated

rejected.why: HTML forms are only the delivery vehicle for the fields; the document adds no new HTML technology.
IOTP is mentioned only as a related standard and an alternative transmission method; ECML is not a replacement for it.
SSL/TLS is mentioned only in Relationship to Other Standards and Security Considerations as a suggested protection.
The parent topic is implied by the ECML tag, so it is not listed separately.
Privacy is touched on only briefly in Security Considerations, and the document defers privacy mechanisms to future versions.

RFC2707.title: Job Monitoring MIB - V1.0
RFC2707.summary: Defines the Job Monitoring MIB, a PWG-originated SNMP MIB module for monitoring print job status, resource requirements, consumption and accounting data in printers or print servers, published as Informational.

MIB.why: The document specifies a complete MIB module (tables, textual conventions, attributes, conformance groups) for job monitoring, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This document provides a printer industry standard SNMP MIB for (1) monitoring the status and progress of print jobs

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through; the document defines MIB content, not the SNMP framework itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Not in the taxonomy as a tag for printing; IPP is only referenced for compatible attribute values and the document does not specify it.
Registration considerations section describes PWG registration of enums, which is boilerplate-like apparatus rather than the main subject.
Internationalization of strings (UTF-8, jobCodedCharSet) is a small supporting part, not the document's subject.
Used only as the encoding for text objects in the MIB, a substrate.
Security considerations are minimal boilerplate stating objects are read-only.

gaps.name: Printing / Printer MIB / print job monitoring
gaps.why: The document is about printer job monitoring and the Printer Working Group's printing ecosystem (Printer MIB, IPP, DPA), but the taxonomy has no printing subject tag other than LPD and IPP technologies listed under applications.

RFC2708.title: Job Submission Protocol Mapping Recommendations for the Job Monitoring MIB
RFC2708.summary: Informational RFC recommending how attributes of popular print job submission protocols (LPR/LPD, AppleTalk, IPP, IPDS, DPA, NDPS, PJL, PostScript, NetWare, SMB, TIP/SI) map to objects in the Job Monitoring MIB, chiefly jmJobSubmissionID and jmJobIndex.

MIB.why: The document is a set of mappings into the Job Monitoring MIB objects and attributes, so it belongs with MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This document defines the recommended mapping for many currently popular Job submission protocols to objects and attributes in the Job Monitoring MIB.

LPD.why: A full section maps LPR/LPD data and control file fields to Job MIB objects, so readers of LPD would want it.
LPD.quote: The LPR/LPD printing protocol [LPD] is used with BSD UNIX systems in the client-server-printer configuration.

IPP.why: A substantial section maps IPP job attributes such as job-uri, job-id and job-state to Job MIB objects and attributes.
IPP.quote: The Internet Printing Protocol [IPP] supports printing using any one of the three possible configurations.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management substrate for the MIB. The document does not specify or extend SNMP itself.
AppleTalk gets a short section, and the document says it provides very little usable information. The document is not about AppleTalk.
SMB is one of many mapped protocols and the section is short. NetBIOS services are not the subject.
TIP/SI here is the IEEE 1284.1 printer interface. It is not the Transaction Internet Protocol.
The MIB tag already implies this parent. No broader network management topic is addressed.

gaps.name: Job Monitoring MIB / printing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no printing or print-monitoring tag. Only LPD and IPP exist, so the Job MIB, PJL, IPDS, DPA, NDPS and PostScript mappings have no fitting tag.

RFC2709.title: Security Model with Tunnel-mode IPsec for NAT Domains
RFC2709.summary: Informational RFC describing a security model in which NAT devices act as tunnel-mode IPsec endpoints (IPsec Policy Controlled NAT, IPC-NAT), including an IKE-ALG that translates security policies during IKE Quick Mode, and applications such as extranet and remote access.

NAT.why: The document defines IPC-NAT, a NAT variant whose translations are controlled by IPsec policy, and describes NAT device behaviour and mapping per security policy.
NAT.quote: All applications traversing a NAT device, irrespective of whether they require assistance of an ALG or not, can benefit from IPsec tunnel-mode security

IPsec.why: The core subject is tunnel-mode IPsec operation (policies, SAs, tunnel endpoints) on a NAT gateway.
IPsec.quote: This document describes a security model by which tunnel-mode IPsec security can be architected on NAT devices.

IKE.why: A full section describes how an IKE-ALG translates private-realm policies into external addressing during Quick Mode, an IKE extension of substance.
IKE.quote: we will focus on the operation of IKE in conjunction with tunnel mode IPsec on NAT devices.
IKE.section: 4. Operation of IKE protocol on IPC-NAT device.

rejected.why: Mobile-IP is only compared with the remote-access application and its binding is explicitly out of scope.
ESP and AH are referenced as part of the IPsec architecture but not specified or extended here.
IP-in-IP tunnels are the means of IPsec tunnel mode, not a subject of the document in their own right.
Only a passing mention of configuring an enterprise DNS server for remote users.

RFC2710.title: Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) for IPv6
RFC2710.summary: Specifies Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD), the ICMPv6-based protocol by which IPv6 routers discover multicast listeners on attached links, derived from IGMPv2.

MLD.why: The whole document defines MLD: message formats, querier election, node and router state machines, timers.
MLD.quote: This document specifies the protocol used by an IPv6 router to discover the presence of multicast listeners

rejected.why: MLD is derived from IGMPv2 but the document specifies the IPv6 protocol, not IGMP.
MLD messages are ICMPv6 types, but ICMPv6 is only the carrier and is not itself specified or extended.
IPv6 is the substrate for MLD; the document does not define IPv6 itself.
The Router Alert option is merely used on MLD messages and is specified in another RFC.
The more specific child tag MLD applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC2711.title: IPv6 Router Alert Option
RFC2711.summary: Defines the IPv6 Router Alert Hop-by-Hop option, which signals transit routers to examine datagrams (e.g., RSVP, MLD) more closely, and creates a value registry.

router alert.why: The document specifies the Router Alert option for IPv6: its syntax, semantics, and values. This is the core subject.
router alert.quote: This memo describes a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Option type that alerts transit routers to more closely examine the contents of an IP datagram.

rejected.why: RSVP is the motivating user of the option, and the RFC mandates the option for RSVP datagrams. The document does not specify or extend RSVP itself.
MLD is only one of the defined option values (value 0). The document does not specify MLD.
The option is an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop extension, but the router alert tag is the more specific fit, so the IPv6 parent is implied.
The value registry is only a short IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate.

RFC2712.title: Addition of Kerberos Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC2712.summary: Defines new Kerberos-based cipher suites for TLS 1.0, adding a KerberosWrapper option to ClientKeyExchange so Kerberos tickets provide mutual authentication and pre-master secret transport.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS with new cipher suites and a new ClientKeyExchange option, so it belongs on the TLS page.
TLS.quote: This document proposes the addition of new cipher suites to the TLS protocol [1] to support Kerberos-based authentication.

Kerberos.why: The document specifies how Kerberos tickets are used within TLS, including the service naming convention host/MachineName@Realm. Kerberos readers would want it.
Kerberos.quote: Kerberos credentials are used to achieve mutual authentication and to establish a master secret which is subsequently used to secure client-server communication.

rejected.why: The ticket and authenticator are ASN.1 encoded per RFC 1510, but that is only an encoding the document relies on.
RC4 cipher suites are listed among the new suites, but the document is not about RC4.
DES and 3DES suites are listed, but the document is not about those ciphers.
Authentication is the document's purpose, but the more specific Kerberos tag already covers it.

RFC2713.title: Schema for Representing Java(tm) Objects in an LDAP Directory
RFC2713.summary: Defines an LDAP schema (attribute types and object classes) for storing Java serialized objects, marshalled objects, remote objects and JNDI references in an LDAP directory.

LDAP.why: The RFC specifies LDAP schema elements (attribute types, object classes) for storing Java objects in LDAP directories, so readers of LDAP would expect it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines the schema for representing Java(tm) objects in an LDAP directory [LDAPv3].

rejected.why: Implied parent of LDAP; the more specific LDAP tag is chosen.
Syntax OIDs are referenced but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encodings.
Base64 is used only as an encoding detail inside javaReferenceAddress values.
URLs are used as codebase values but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
RMI/RPC-like mechanisms are described as background, not specified here.

gaps.name: Java object representation / JNDI / RMI
gaps.why: The document is about storing Java objects (serialized, marshalled, JNDI references, RMI remote objects) in a directory; the taxonomy has no Java or object-reference tag besides the generic LDAP tag.

RFC2714.title: Schema for Representing CORBA Object References in an LDAP Directory
RFC2714.summary: Defines an LDAP schema (attribute types corbaIor and corbaRepositoryId, and object classes corbaContainer, corbaObject, corbaObjectReference) for storing CORBA object references in an LDAP directory.

LDAP.why: The document specifies LDAP schema elements (attribute types and object classes) for CORBA object references, so LDAP readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines the schema for representing CORBA object references in an LDAP directory

rejected.why: LDAP is the more specific child tag and already covers this.
DCE-style repository ids contain a UUID, but this is a passing mention and the document is not about UUIDs.
The document cites X.500-derived schema and matching rules, but it only reuses them. It defines nothing about X.500.
Attribute values are encoded in UTF-8, but this is only the encoding used. The document says nothing new about UTF-8.
The document mentions the COS Naming service as the traditional alternative. Its subject is a directory schema, not naming or name resolution.

gaps.name: CORBA (Common Object Request Broker Architecture)
gaps.why: The schema is entirely about CORBA interoperable object references (IORs), but the taxonomy has no CORBA or distributed-object tag.

RFC2715.title: Interoperability Rules for Multicast Routing Protocols
RFC2715.summary: Defines interoperability rules for multicast border routers connecting independent multicast routing domains, with instantiations for DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM-DM, PIM-SM, CBT and IGMP-only links.

multicast.why: The whole document specifies rules for multicast border routers interconnecting multicast routing domains. It covers several protocols (DVMRP, CBT, MBR rules), so the general multicast topic fits better than any one child.
multicast.quote: The rules described in this document will allow efficient interoperation among multiple independent multicast routing domains.

PIM-SM.why: Section 4.4 specifies how the interop rules apply to PIM-SM: wildcard receiver behaviour, (*,*,RP) Joins, Border-bit Registers, and alert handling.
PIM-SM.quote: To achieve correct PIM-SM behavior within the domain, the PIM-SM domain MUST be convex so that Bootstrap messages reach all routers in the domain.

MOSPF.why: Section 4.2 gives a full instantiation of the rules for MOSPF, including group-membership-LSA handling.
MOSPF.quote: An MOSPF component acts as a wildcard receiver for internally-reached sources if and only if any other component is a wildcard receiver

IGMP.why: Section 4.6 defines how IGMP-only links take part in interoperation as a component, with Membership Report and Leave handling.
IGMP.quote: In this section we describe how the rules in section 2 apply to a link which is not within any routing domain

rejected.why: PIM-DM and PIM-SM are both covered, but only PIM-SM has a child tag worth choosing. PIM-DM gets less coverage, so the parent adds nothing.
BGMP is mentioned as an inter-domain protocol with its own dispatcher, but it is not BGP and the document is not about BGP.
The document touches domain topology, but the subject is multicast interoperation, which the multicast tag covers.

gaps.name: DVMRP and CBT (Core Based Trees)
gaps.why: The document gives full instantiations for DVMRP (4.1) and CBTv2 (4.5), but the taxonomy has no tags for either protocol. The parent multicast tag is the closest fit.

RFC2716.title: PPP EAP TLS Authentication Protocol
RFC2716.summary: Defines EAP-TLS, an EAP method that carries TLS handshake messages inside PPP EAP packets to provide mutual authentication, ciphersuite negotiation, key derivation for PPP encryption, and fragmentation/reassembly.

EAP.why: The document specifies a new EAP method (EAP-Type 13) with its packet formats, fragmentation, and key derivation.
EAP.quote: This document describes how EAP-TLS, which includes support for fragmentation and reassembly, provides for these TLS mechanisms within EAP.

PPP.why: EAP-TLS runs within PPP authentication phase and specifies interaction with LCP, ECP and CCP negotiation, so PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is a PPP extension that provides support for additional authentication methods within PPP.

TLS.why: The document defines how TLS handshake records are encapsulated and how keys are derived from the TLS master secret, which is a new use of TLS.
TLS.quote: The EAP protocol described in this document allows a PPP peer to take advantage of the protected ciphersuite negotiation, mutual authentication and key management capabilities of the TLS protocol

rejected.why: RADIUS is only mentioned as a possible backend to which the authenticator passes EAP packets; the RFC does not specify it.
Certificates are used for authentication, but the document specifies no certificate profile.
L2TP and PPTP appear only in security considerations as contexts where PPP encryption may be used.
Key derivation is part of the EAP-TLS method and is covered by the EAP tag; it is not a standalone key management subject.
The more specific EAP tag already covers authentication.

RFC2717.title: Registration Procedures for URL Scheme Names
RFC2717.summary: BCP defining the registration procedures, trees, change control and template for new URL scheme names, with an IETF tree and alternative trees.

URI.why: The whole document is about registering URI/URL scheme names, including syntax constraints on names, registration trees and the scheme documentation template.
URI.quote: This document defines the process by which new URL scheme names are registered.

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned only as one possible registration mechanism for alternative trees; the document is not about IANA registry stewardship.
It touches on IESG review and RFC publication paths, but only as part of the scheme registration process, not IETF process in general.
Character encoding is only briefly mentioned in the template; the document does not address IRIs.

RFC2718.title: Guidelines for new URL Schemes
RFC2718.summary: Informational guidelines for defining new URL schemes, covering syntactic compatibility with generic URI syntax, well-defined semantics, utility, and security considerations.

URI.why: The whole document is about how to define URI/URL schemes: syntax compatibility with RFC 2396, relative URLs, character encoding, and scheme semantics.
URI.quote: This document provides guidelines for the definition of new URL schemes.

rejected.why: HTTP appears only as an example scheme and as a gateway target for proxies, not as the subject.
Registration process is defined in RFC 2717; this document only gives design guidelines.
Recommended for character encoding in a single bullet; not a substantial subject.
Mentioned as an example scheme only.

RFC2719.title: Framework Architecture for Signaling Transport
RFC2719.summary: RFC 2719 defines the SIGTRAN framework architecture and functional/performance requirements for transporting SCN signaling (SS7, ISDN Q.931) over IP between Signaling Gateways, Media Gateway Controllers and Media Gateways.

SIGTRAN.why: The document is the SIGTRAN framework: it defines the SG/MGC/MG architecture, protocol stacks and requirements for carrying SS7 and ISDN signalling over IP.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document defines an architecture framework and functional requirements for transport of signaling information over IP.

rejected.why: The Media Gateway Controller and Media Gateway appear as entities, but gateway control protocols are not specified. The document is about signalling transport.
IPsec is only mentioned in Security Considerations as an available mechanism, which is boilerplate.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as an available security option.
This is the parent of SIGTRAN, which fits the document more specifically, so the parent is not listed.
The Common Signaling Transport Protocol is only a generic component in this framework. SCTP is not named.

RFC2720.title: Traffic Flow Measurement: Meter MIB
RFC2720.summary: Defines the SMIv2 Meter MIB for controlling an RTFM traffic flow meter (rule sets, readers, managers) and retrieving flow data via SNMP, including an efficient data-package retrieval table.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (FLOW_METER-MIB) defining managed objects for a traffic flow meter, so MIB modules and SMI is the fitting tag.
MIB.quote: This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for use in controlling an RTFM Traffic Meter, in particular for specifying the flows to be measured.

performance measurement.why: The MIB's subject is network traffic flow measurement (meters, meter readers, flow counters), which is network measurement of traffic. No more specific measurement technology tag applies.
performance measurement.quote: Traffic Flow Measurement seeks to provide a well-defined method for gathering traffic flow information from networks and internetworks.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB and flow data. The document defines no SNMP protocol changes, only managed objects, so MIB is the better fit.
IPFIX is a different flow export approach. This document is the RTFM meter MIB and does not specify or discuss IPFIX.
The MIB borrows the TimeFilter convention and the table style from RMON2, but it does not specify RMON.
BER encoding is used for the data package values, but only as an encoding mechanism. The document is not about ASN.1.

gaps.name: RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement) architecture
gaps.why: The document is about the RTFM traffic meter and its rule-based flow definition. The taxonomy has no tag for traffic flow metering or accounting.

RFC2721.title: RTFM: Applicability Statement
RFC2721.summary: Applicability statement for the RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement) system, summarising its component documents, uses, limitations, policy and security considerations, and implementation experience with NeTraMet and the Meter MIB.

performance measurement.why: RTFM is a traffic flow measurement system with meters, readers and managers. The document is about when and how to apply it and where it falls short, so performance measurement is the right topic.
performance measurement.quote: This document provides an overview covering all aspects of Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement, including its area of applicability and its limitations.

MIB.why: Appendix A is a working group report on the Meter MIB. It covers the TimeFilter, DataPackage and GetBulk conventions used to read the flow table, which is a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: meters are SNMP agents implementing the RTFM Meter MIB, and managers are SNMP clients using the Meter MIB to store and access the flow data.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management transport for the meter. The document describes the Meter MIB, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag covers it.
IPFIX is a later flow export protocol. RTFM is a different, earlier system and the document does not discuss IPFIX.
The Meter MIB is said to resemble RMON2 and borrows its TimeFilter convention. That is only a passing comparison.
The more specific MIB and performance measurement tags already cover this.

gaps.name: RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the RTFM architecture and its documents, such as the NeTraMet meter, SRL and flow accounting. Readers looking for traffic flow measurement and usage accounting have no dedicated subject page.

RFC2722.title: Traffic Flow Measurement: Architecture
RFC2722.summary: Informational RFC defining the RTFM architecture for network traffic flow measurement: meters, meter readers, managers, flows, rule sets and the packet matching engine, and how usage data is collected and reported.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines an architecture for measuring and reporting network traffic flows (meters, readers, managers, rule sets). No more specific tag (IPFIX, SNMP, etc.) fits, so the parent topic applies.
performance measurement.quote: This document provides a general framework for describing network traffic flows, presents an architecture for traffic flow measurement and reporting

rejected.why: The Meter MIB is only mentioned as one possible meter-to-reader transfer method; this document specifies no protocol.
The MIB is a separate document (RFC 2720); here it is only referenced.
IPFIX is a later flow export standard, and this RFC does not specify an export protocol. It is a predecessor architecture, but not about IPFIX.
Managers configure meters, but the document is specifically about flow measurement, which the more specific performance measurement tag covers.
This is about live traffic measurement, not benchmarking methodology for devices.

gaps.name: Traffic flow measurement / accounting (RTFM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for passive traffic flow metering and usage accounting. IPFIX is the nearest match, but it is a different protocol, so performance measurement is used as an approximation.

RFC2723.title: SRL: A Language for Describing Traffic Flows and Specifying Actions for Flow Groups
RFC2723.summary: Defines SRL, a procedural language for writing rulesets that configure RTFM traffic flow meters, specifying which flows are measured and what is stored per flow.

performance measurement.why: SRL configures RTFM traffic flow meters, which is network traffic measurement. The taxonomy has no RTFM tag, so the parent topic for performance measurement is the best fit.
performance measurement.quote: a language for specifying rulesets, i.e. configuration files which may be loaded into a traffic flow meter so as to specify which traffic flows are measured by the meter

rejected.why: The RTFM Meter MIB is only referenced as the definitive attribute specification. SRL itself is not a MIB module.
IPFIX is a later flow export standard. This document covers RTFM rulesets, not IPFIX.
IPv4 addresses and ports appear only as example attributes in rules, not as the subject.
The BNF grammar in the appendix just describes SRL's own syntax. It is not about the notation.
The more specific performance measurement topic fits better than the broader parent.

gaps.name: RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement)
gaps.why: The document, and its sibling RFCs for the RTFM architecture and meter MIB, concern RTFM meters and rulesets. The taxonomy has no tag for RTFM or traffic flow measurement.

RFC2724.title: RTFM: New Attributes for Traffic Flow Measurement
RFC2724.summary: Experimental RFC defining new flow attributes (distributions, short-term rates, turnaround times, QoS/IIS, AS numbers, DS code point) as extensions to the RTFM traffic flow measurement meter.

performance measurement.why: The document extends RTFM traffic meters with attributes for measuring throughput, loss, delay and jitter of flows; this is passive network traffic/performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: Performance attributes include throughput, packet loss, delays, jitter, and congestion measures.

QoS.why: A substantial part defines QoS/Integrated Services attributes (token bucket rate, slack term, etc.) for metering RSVP-reserved flows.
QoS.quote: QoSService: Service class for the flow (guaranteed, controlled load)

rejected.why: DSCodePoint is only one attribute added so the meter can serve as a Diffserv edge device; Diffserv is not the document's subject.
Integrated Services parameters are measured, but the document does not specify Intserv; QoS tag covers it more generally.
RSVP-reserved flows are metered, but RSVP itself is not specified or extended.
A companion document will define the MIB; this document does not define MIB modules.
SNMP data model is mentioned as a fit for attributes, but the document is not about SNMP.
Mentioned only as an existing implementation of packet traces.

gaps.name: RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement)
gaps.why: The document is about the RTFM traffic flow meter architecture and its attributes; the taxonomy has no tag for RTFM or flow measurement specifically, only the generic performance measurement topic.

RFC2725.title: Routing Policy System Security
RFC2725.summary: Defines an authentication and authorization model (maintainer objects, mnt-routes, mnt-lower, reclaim, referral-by, as-block) controlling who may add, modify or delete objects in RPSL-based Internet Routing Registries, to protect the integrity of routing policy data.

RPSL.why: The document extends the RIPE/RPSL schema (as-block, mnt-routes, mnt-lower, reclaim, referral-by) and specifies authorization rules for routing registry objects, which is the subject of RPSL and Internet routing registries.
RPSL.quote: This document addresses the need to assure integrity of the data by providing an authentication and authorization model.

routing security.why: The motivation is securing routing information against misconfiguration and denial of service by controlling who may register prefix/origin data, which readers of routing security would want.
routing security.quote: Routing protocols themselves provide no assurance that the origination of a route is legitimate and can actually reach the stated destination.

rejected.why: Not a taxonomy tag; OpenPGP is only mentioned as one authentication method, with details deferred to RFC 2726.
PGP authentication is only one of several 'auth' methods mentioned and is specified in a separate document (RFC 2726).
Considered the generic authorization topic, but the RPSL technology tag and routing security cover the subject more specifically.
RPKI is a different, later mechanism for origin validation; this document is about IRR registry object authorization.
BGP is only context for the route announcements being validated; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
CIDR's more-specific-prefix preference is the motivating context, not the subject.

gaps.name: Internet Routing Registry (IRR) / routing registry authorization
gaps.why: The taxonomy only has RPSL as a technology tag for routing registries; there is no dedicated tag for registry database integrity or for the RIPE database schema.

RFC2726.title: PGP Authentication for RIPE Database Updates
RFC2726.summary: Defines PGP-signature-based authentication for updates to the RIPE routing registry database, adding a key-cert object and a PGPKEY auth value to mntner objects.

RPSL.why: Extends the RIPE database (routing registry) object schema with a key-cert object and a new mntner auth value, which is RPSL/IRR-related work from the rps WG.
RPSL.quote: A new object type is defined below for the purpose of storing the key certificates of the maintainers

OpenPGP.why: The document specifies how PGP keys, certificates and signed messages are used for authentication, including key requirements.
OpenPGP.quote: The goal was to implement a digital signature mechanism based on a widely available and deployed technology. The first choice was PGP

rejected.why: Updates are sent by e-mail but the document does not specify email itself; it is only the substrate.
The generic authentication topic is implied by the more specific chosen tags; the document is specific to database updates using PGP.
Security Considerations mention routing policy information, but the document is about database maintainer authentication; authorization is in RFC 2725.
The RIPE database is queried via whois-like means but the document does not address the WHOIS protocol.

RFC2727.title: IAB and IESG Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Operation of the Nominating and Recall Committees
RFC2727.summary: BCP 10 specifies how the IETF Nominating Committee is selected and operates to choose IAB and IESG members, how they are confirmed, and how sitting members are recalled; it obsoletes RFC 2282.

NomCom.why: The whole document specifies NomCom selection, operation, confirmation and the parallel recall committee procedures.
NomCom.quote: The process by which the members of the IAB and IESG are selected, confirmed, and recalled is specified.

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child tag and fits the document exactly; the parent is implied.
Only boilerplate mentions; the document is not about IANA registries.
The random volunteer selection is only referenced to RFC 2777 and is a minor rule, not the subject.

RFC2728.title: The Transmission of IP Over the Vertical Blanking Interval of a Television Signal
RFC2728.summary: Specifies broadcasting IP datagrams unidirectionally over the TV vertical blanking interval using NABTS packets, a Reed-Solomon-style FEC, SLIP-style framing, and a UDP/IP header compression scheme with CRC-32.

header compression.why: Defines schema 0x00 compressing UDP/IP headers for unidirectional links (compression key, groups, only IP ID and UDP checksum sent). This is a major part of the spec and not under a more specific tag like ROHC/CRTP/IPHC.
header compression.quote: It includes a description for compressing IP headers on unidirectional networks

FEC.why: Defines the NABTS bundle FEC (GF(2^8) codewords, correction procedures) in section 3.3 and Appendix A.
FEC.quote: Due to the unidirectional nature of VBI data transport, Forward Error Correction (FEC) is needed to ensure the integrity of data at the receiver.

link layer.why: The core subject is a new link/medium for carrying IP: NABTS over the television VBI. The taxonomy has no specific tag for this medium, so the parent topic fits.
link layer.quote: This document describes a method for broadcasting IP data in a unidirectional manner using the vertical blanking interval of television signals.

SLIP.why: Specifies SLIP-style END/ESC framing for the serial stream, with a schema byte. It is a defined part of the stack, not only a reference.
SLIP.quote: A framing protocol identical to SLIP is proposed for encapsulating the packets

CRC.why: Specifies the CRC-32 generator polynomial and initial state, taken from MPEG-2, for the final integrity check.
CRC.quote: A 32-bit CRC has also been added to the end of every packet in this scheme to ensure data integrity.

rejected.why: UDP is only the payload carried with compressed headers, not the subject of the document.
The document handles IPv4 packets as payload, but IPv4 itself is not specified or extended.
DVB is a different broadcast medium (IP over MPEG-2). This document covers analog TV VBI.
Point-to-multipoint broadcast delivery is the motivation, but no IP multicast routing or group membership is specified.
The IANA section only sets up a schema registry. That is boilerplate.

gaps.name: NABTS / VBI television data broadcast (teletext)
gaps.why: The central subject is IP over the NABTS byte structure in the TV vertical blanking interval. The taxonomy has no tag for broadcast television or teletext carriage, so the link layer parent is the closest fit.

RFC2729.title: Taxonomy of Communication Requirements for Large-scale Multicast Applications
RFC2729.summary: Informational memo defining a taxonomy of communication parameters (reliability, ordering, timeliness, session control, topology, directory, security, charging) for describing requirements of large-scale multicast applications.

multicast.why: The whole document classifies requirements of large-scale multicast applications and sessions, so readers of the multicast subject would want it. No specific multicast protocol is addressed, so the general topic fits.
multicast.quote: define a classification system for the communication requirements of any large-scale multicast application (LSMA)

rejected.why: Latency, jitter and bandwidth parameters are listed, but as application requirements, not QoS architectures or signalling.
Security parameters such as collusion prevention and KEK sharing are listed, but the document does not address group key management mechanisms.
The security parameters are one section of a requirements checklist. The document is not about security as a whole.
Reliability is one parameter category, but no reliable multicast transport is specified or analysed.
The payment and charging parameters are only a short list of cost fields, not payment protocols.

gaps.name: application communication requirements taxonomy
gaps.why: The document classifies application-level communication requirements to help standardise APIs and protocol adaptation. The taxonomy has no tag for requirements frameworks.

RFC2730.title: Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol (MADCAP)
RFC2730.summary: RFC 2730 specifies MADCAP, a UDP-based client-server protocol by which hosts request, renew, and release leases on IP multicast addresses from multicast address allocation servers.

MADCAP.why: The whole document defines the MADCAP protocol: message formats, message types, options, lease handling, scopes and errors.
MADCAP.quote: a protocol that allows hosts to request multicast address allocation services from multicast address allocation servers

rejected.why: MADCAP was originally based on DHCP, but the document says it is completely separate with no dependencies.
IPsec is only recommended for protecting unicast messages in Security Considerations; the document does not specify it.
UDP is only the transport for MADCAP messages. Nothing new is defined about UDP.
Considered as the parent topic. MADCAP is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
NTP is cited only when discussing clock skew and timestamp conversion; the document is not about it.

RFC2731.title: Encoding Dublin Core Metadata in HTML
RFC2731.summary: Informational RFC explaining how to encode Dublin Core metadata elements in HTML using META and LINK tags, with per-element examples and Perl scripts for processing the metadata.

HTML.why: The whole document specifies conventions for embedding Dublin Core metadata in HTML via META and LINK tags, so readers of HTML topics would want it.
HTML.quote: This document explains how these elements are expressed using the META and LINK tags of HTML [HTML4.0].

rejected.why: XML and RDF are mentioned only as future, more expressive alternatives; the document is not about them.
RFC 1766 language codes appear only as values in the DC.Language examples and the lang attribute, not as a subject of the document.
MIME types appear only as example values for DC.Format; the document does not deal with media type registration.
URLs, URNs and URIs appear only as example identifier values and link targets.
ISO 8601 and W3C profile dates appear only as example values for DC.Date; the document says it is not about element semantics.

gaps.name: Dublin Core metadata
gaps.why: The document is about Dublin Core resource-description metadata and its HTML encoding. The taxonomy has no metadata or resource-description tag, so only HTML fits.

RFC2732.title: Format for Literal IPv6 Addresses in URL's
RFC2732.summary: Defines the bracketed syntax for literal IPv6 addresses in URLs and updates RFC 2396's generic URI syntax (host non-terminal, reserved/unwise character sets) accordingly.

URI.why: The document's core content is a change to URI generic syntax: adding IPv6reference to host and moving "[" and "]" into the reserved set.
URI.quote: This document updates the generic syntax for Uniform Resource Identifiers defined in RFC 2396 [URL].

IPv6.why: It specifies how IPv6 addresses are textually represented in URLs, an IPv6 deployment/addressing matter that IPv6 readers would want.
IPv6.quote: This document defines the format for literal IPv6 Addresses in URL's for implementation in World Wide Web browsers.

rejected.why: HTTP URLs are only used as examples; the document does not specify HTTP behaviour.
Mentioned only as an intended future user of the format; not specified here.
The IPv6 tag already covers the address-related content; the document does not address address architecture or allocation.
Grammar is given in the RFC 2396 notation, but the document is not about the notation.

RFC2733.title: An RTP Payload Format for Generic Forward Error Correction
RFC2733.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for generic XOR-parity forward error correction of RTP media, including FEC header, protection and recovery procedures, use with RFC 2198 redundancy, and SDP signalling.

FEC.why: The document defines parity-based FEC packets and recovery procedures for packet loss, which is the FEC subject.
FEC.quote: This document specifies a payload format for generic forward error correction of media encapsulated in RTP. It is engineered for FEC algorithms based on the exclusive-or (parity) operation.

RTP payload format.why: It is a new RTP payload format (parityfec) with its own header and SDP binding, so it belongs with RTP payload formats.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines a payload format for RTP [3] which allows for generic forward error correction of real time media.

SDP.why: A substantial section defines the parityfec rtpmap name and fmtp parameters for signalling FEC in SDP.
SDP.quote: This section describes how this can be accomplished using the Session Description Protocol (SDP), specified in RFC 2327 [6].

rejected.why: The more specific RTP payload format tag already covers it; the document does not extend RTP itself.
Only a short subsection (11.3) describes the fmtp line for RTSP control URLs; RTSP is not the subject.
This is an earlier, separate format and does not use the FEC Framework.
Only a brief note in Security Considerations warns against raising FEC as loss increases.

RFC2734.title: IPv4 over IEEE 1394
RFC2734.summary: Specifies transport of IPv4 datagrams over IEEE 1394 (Serial Bus), including link encapsulation and fragmentation, a 1394-specific ARP, and the MCAP multicast channel allocation protocol.

FireWire.why: The whole document defines IP over IEEE 1394: encapsulation, fragmentation, ARP, unicast/broadcast/multicast, configuration ROM.
FireWire.quote: This document specifies how to use IEEE Std 1394-1995, Standard for a High Performance Serial Bus (and its supplements), for the transport of Internet Protocol Version 4 (IPv4) datagrams.

ARP.why: A substantial section defines a 1394-specific address resolution protocol with its own packet format and field usage.
ARP.quote: 1394 ARP requests SHALL be transmitted by the same means as broadcast IP datagrams
ARP.section: 5. SERIAL BUS ADDRESS RESOLUTION PROTOCOL (1394 ARP)

rejected.why: IPv4 is the payload carried over the link; the document is about the link-layer mapping, not IPv4 itself.
MCAP is a 1394-specific channel allocation for IP multicast on one bus, not general multicast routing or group membership; it is part of the link mapping.
The IANA section creates a CSR Protocol Identifiers registry, but this is boilerplate-level relative to the main body.
Not a taxonomy tag; link-level fragmentation is part of the 1394 encapsulation.

gaps.name: MCAP (Multicast Channel Allocation Protocol)
gaps.why: A 1394-specific multicast channel management protocol with no matching tag; it is covered only under the FireWire link mapping.

RFC2735.title: NHRP Support for Virtual Private Networks
RFC2735.summary: Extends NHRP so it can resolve private VPN addresses on a shared NBMA network, defining a VPN LLC/SNAP encapsulation, a Device Capabilities extension, and new error codes.

NHRP.why: The document specifies extensions to NHRP: VPN-aware operation, a Device Capabilities extension, VPN encapsulation, and new error codes.
NHRP.quote: This document describes the enhancements necessary to enable NHRP to perform the same function for private internetworking layer addresses available within the framework of a Virtual Private Network

rejected.why: VPN here means provider-provisioned VPN services as the scope of NHRP resolution. The document extends NHRP, not L3VPN/L2VPN technologies, and NHRP is the more specific fit.
ATM is only the underlying NBMA network, and the encapsulation is referenced from RFC 2684. The document does not specify anything about IP over ATM.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional protection.
The LLC/SNAP VPN encapsulation is a per-PDU header, not generic IP tunnelling.

RFC2736.title: Guidelines for Writers of RTP Payload Format Specifications
RFC2736.summary: BCP giving guidelines to authors of RTP payload format specifications: ALF design, loss tolerance, packetisation on codec frame boundaries, avoiding IP fragmentation, header extensions and header compression considerations.

RTP payload format.why: The whole document is guidance on designing RTP payload formats for codecs and media, which is the subject of this tag.
RTP payload format.quote: general guidelines aimed at assisting the authors of RTP [9] Payload Format specifications in deciding on good formats

rejected.why: The more specific child RTP payload format fits. RTP itself is not being specified.
Section 4.2 only mentions header compression (RFC 2508) as a design consideration. That is too small a part of the document, and ROHC is also the wrong technology (CRTP would be the closer fit).
RFC 2508 is cited in one short section as a design consideration. The document is not about it.
FEC appears only as a consideration affecting packetisation and header-extension choices. The document does not address it substantively.
Codecs serve as examples. The document is about payload packetisation, not codec definitions.
The TCP throughput and loss-rate discussion only motivates the loss-tolerance requirement.

RFC2737.title: Entity MIB (Version 2)
RFC2737.summary: RFC 2737 defines the Entity MIB (version 2), an SMIv2 MIB module for representing the physical and logical entities managed by a single SNMP agent, with their containment, mappings and change notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define the ENTITY-MIB module (entPhysicalTable, entLogicalTable, mapping tables, notification) in SMIv2. MIB is the most specific fitting tag, under SNMP.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing multiple logical and physical entities managed by a single SNMP agent.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol the MIB is accessed with. The document defines a MIB module, so the more specific MIB tag covers it. SNMP contexts and community strings are discussed only as they relate to logical entities.
This is an ancestor of MIB and is implied by it.
The module is written in SMI/ASN.1-derived notation, but that is only the definition language and not what the document is about.
The usage examples model Ethernet and FDDI ports and repeaters, but only as sample hardware. The document is not about Ethernet.

RFC2738.title: Corrections to "A Syntax for Describing Media Feature Sets"
RFC2738.summary: RFC 2738 corrects two errors in RFC 2533 (media feature set syntax): an ABNF production for 'setentry' and a simplification rule for comparing feature predicates.

content negotiation.why: The document corrects the media feature set expression syntax and the feature set matching reduction rules of RFC 2533, which is the content negotiation/media feature specification.
content negotiation.quote: an expression format is presented for describing media feature capabilities using simple media feature tags

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to express the corrected production; the document is not about ABNF itself.
Media feature tags are related to but distinct from MIME media type registrations; the document does not address media type registry rules.
Message handling agents are mentioned only as context; the document is not about MIME body structure.

RFC2739.title: Calendar Attributes for vCard and LDAP
RFC2739.summary: Defines calendar and free/busy URI types and distributes them via new vCard properties (FBURL, CALURI, CAPURI, CALADRURI) and new LDAP schema attributes and object class (calEntry) so calendar users can be located.

vCard.why: The document extends vCard with new calendar URI properties and registers them, so it belongs on the vCard page.
vCard.quote: Inside a vCard object, four new properties are defined: "CALURI", "CAPURI", "CALADRURI", and "FBURL"

LDAP.why: It defines a new LDAP auxiliary object class and eight attributes for storing calendar URIs in a directory, which is an extension of LDAP.
LDAP.quote: In order to encode the calendaring URIs in the directory, the following are defined: One object class: calEntry

calendaring.why: The document is about locating calendar and free/busy data for scheduling. No calendaring technology tag fits it better, because iCalendar is only the format of the data the URIs point to.
calendaring.quote: a calendar user agent (CUA) needs a mechanism to locate (URI) individual user's calendar and free/busy time.

rejected.why: iCalendar objects are what the URIs point to, but the document does not specify or extend the iCalendar format.
The CAPURI semantics are deferred to a future Calendar Access Protocol. CalDAV is not defined or used here.
The document defines calendar URI semantics but is not about URI syntax, schemes or resolution.
The vCard property registrations are not media type registrations. The text/calendar type is only mentioned in passing.
FTP and HTTP are only mentioned as ways to retrieve the resources the URIs point to.

RFC2740.title: OSPF for IPv6
RFC2740.summary: RFC 2740 specifies OSPF version 3, the modifications to OSPF needed to route IPv6, including new LSA types, per-link operation, flooding scopes, and reliance on IPv6 AH/ESP for authentication.

OSPFv3.why: The whole document defines OSPF for IPv6 (OSPF version 3): packet formats, LSA types, flooding scope, and routing calculation changes.
OSPFv3.quote: This document describes the modifications to OSPF to support version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6).

rejected.why: IPv6 is the network layer OSPFv3 runs over; the document is not about IPv6 itself. OSPFv3 is the more specific tag.
AH and ESP are relied on for authentication in place of built-in OSPF authentication, but IPsec is not specified or extended here.
MOSPF is only mentioned as a supported option (MC-bit, group-membership-LSA); it is not specified here.
OSPF Hello-based neighbor discovery is part of OSPF itself, not IPv6 neighbor discovery.
BGP is mentioned only as a source of external routes and attributes.

RFC2741.title: Agent Extensibility (AgentX) Protocol Version 1
RFC2741.summary: RFC 2741 specifies AgentX version 1, a protocol and elements of procedure by which SNMP master agents and subagents communicate to form an extensible SNMP agent, including PDU encodings, registration, index allocation, and TCP/UNIX-socket transport mappings.

AgentX.why: The whole document defines the AgentX subagent protocol, so it is the primary subject.
AgentX.quote: It defines processing entities called master agents and subagents, a protocol (AgentX) used to communicate between them

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework AgentX extends and is processed by the master agent, but the document specifies AgentX, not SNMP itself. The AgentX tag sits under SNMP, so SNMP is implied.
MIB regions are registered and served, but the document defines no MIB modules or SMI; MIBs are only what the protocol dispatches over.
TCP is only a transport mapping (port 705) for AgentX, not something the document defines or extends.
Section 8 maps AgentX to TCP and UNIX sockets, but this is a small part of the document and not its main subject.
TLS is only mentioned in the Security Considerations as a way to protect subagent connections.

gaps.name: AgentX (SNMP agent extensibility)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for AgentX, so the nearest fit is SNMP. That tag does not appear in the taxonomy listing, though AgentX does.

RFC2742.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Extensible SNMP Agents
RFC2742.summary: Defines the AGENTX-MIB module, which lets managers inspect the master agent's AgentX connections, subagent sessions and MIB region registrations, and optionally close sessions.

AgentX.why: The whole document is a MIB module for managing AgentX master agents, covering connections, sessions and registrations. AgentX is the subject, and the MIB is how it is managed.
AgentX.quote: it describes objects managing SNMP agents that use the Agent Extensibility (AgentX) Protocol.

rejected.why: Considered because the document is a MIB module. AgentX is the more specific tag for this one and the task says to choose the most specific tag that fits, so I did not also list MIB.
SNMP is the management framework the MIB is accessed through. It is the substrate here, not the subject.

RFC2743.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface Version 2, Update 1
RFC2743.summary: RFC 2743 specifies GSS-API Version 2, Update 1, a mechanism-independent, language-independent interface for credentials, security contexts, per-message protection, and names, obsoleting RFC 2078.

GSS-API.why: The whole document defines the GSS-API calls, concepts, token formats and name types.
GSS-API.quote: The Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API), Version 2, as defined in [RFC-2078], provides security services to callers in a generic fashion

rejected.why: Kerberos V5 appears only as an example mechanism (Section 5) and a referenced mechanism spec, not as the subject.
ASN.1/DER is used only for the token tag format and OIDs; the document is not about ASN.1.
X.509 appears only in an illustrative example scenario.
The GSS-API tag is more specific; the generic authentication topic is not addressed separately.
GSS-API names are opaque security principal names, not DNS or general name resolution.

RFC2744.title: Generic Security Service API Version 2 : C-bindings
RFC2744.summary: RFC 2744 specifies the C-language bindings (routines, data types, status codes, header file) for GSS-API Version 2 Update 1, obsoleting RFC 1509.

GSS-API.why: The whole document defines the C API for GSS-API: routines, types, status codes and the gssapi.h header. It is the core GSS-API programming interface specification.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies C language bindings for Version 2, Update 1 of the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS- API)

rejected.why: ASN.1 BER encoding is mentioned only for how gss_OID values are represented; the document is not about ASN.1.
Not mentioned as a mechanism; the API is mechanism-independent.
GSS-API tag already covers this; authentication is a service the API offers, not a separate subject here.
Mechanism negotiation is not specified in this document.

RFC2745.title: RSVP Diagnostic Messages
RFC2745.summary: RFC 2745 specifies the RSVP diagnostic facility, adding DREQ and DREP messages and related objects so a client can collect RSVP path and reservation state hop-by-hop along a path.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with new message types (DREQ/DREP), objects and processing rules, so it belongs on the RSVP page.
RSVP.quote: This document specifies the RSVP diagnostic facility, which allows a user to collect information about the RSVP state along a path.

rejected.why: Traceroute and mtrace are mentioned as complementary tools for crossing legacy routers, but the document does not specify or extend them.
The facility is diagnostic in nature, but the RSVP tag is more specific and OAM was not chosen as a separate subject.
RSVP is used for Intserv reservations, but the document is about RSVP state diagnosis rather than Intserv service models.
The TUNNEL object is defined in another RFC and is only referenced here.

RFC2746.title: RSVP Operation Over IP Tunnels
RFC2746.summary: Specifies how RSVP reservations are made across IP-in-IP tunnels by recursively applying RSVP between tunnel endpoints, using UDP encapsulation, new SESSION_ASSOC and NODE_CHAR objects, and mapping end-to-end sessions to tunnel sessions.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with new objects (SESSION_ASSOC, NODE_CHAR) and defines message handling at tunnel endpoints.
RSVP.quote: This document describes an IP tunneling enhancement mechanism that allows RSVP to make reservations across all IP-in-IP tunnels.

IP-in-IP.why: The document is about making IP-in-IP tunnels RSVP-controllable links, including encapsulation changes (IP+UDP) for reserved packets. Tunneling is a substantial subject of the document.
IP-in-IP.quote: IP-in-IP "tunnels" have become a widespread mechanism to transport datagrams in the Internet.

rejected.why: Section 7 only briefly covers IPsec tunnels using SPI for classification; not a substantial part.
Integrated services framework (ADSPEC, Tspec composition) is referenced but the document is about RSVP over tunnels, not the Intserv specifications.
UDP is only used as an encapsulation substrate for port-based classification.
GRE is only mentioned as one of the existing tunneling protocols in the introduction.
RSVP is the more specific tag; QoS is implied as an ancestor.
MTU discovery gets only a brief mention in Section 6.3.

RFC2747.title: RSVP Cryptographic Authentication
RFC2747.summary: Defines the RSVP INTEGRITY object and procedures (keyed HMAC-MD5 digest, sequence numbers, integrity handshake, key management, optional Kerberos key generation) for hop-by-hop authentication and replay protection of RSVP messages.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with a new INTEGRITY object, new Integrity Challenge/Response message types and modified message processing rules. Readers of RSVP need it.
RSVP.quote: This document describes the format and use of RSVP's INTEGRITY object to provide hop-by-hop integrity and authentication of RSVP messages.

HMAC.why: HMAC-MD5 is the mandatory baseline algorithm for the keyed message digest, and the digest computation is specified in the processing steps.
HMAC.quote: the document describes the use of Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication using HMAC-MD5 [7]

key management.why: Sections 5 and 12 and Appendix 1 cover key lifetimes, smooth key rollover, manual key distribution requirements and a key management interface.
key management.quote: Each key has a lifetime associated with it that is recorded in all systems (sender and receivers) configured with that key.

rejected.why: Section 1.2 explains why IPsec AH was not used. The document specifies its own mechanism rather than being about IPsec.
Section 7 optionally uses Kerberos to generate keys. That is a small optional section, and Kerberos is a mechanism the document relies on rather than something it specifies.
MD5 is only the hash inside HMAC-MD5, so the HMAC tag already covers it.
NTP timestamps are only suggested as a source of sequence numbers, which is a minor use.
The more specific RSVP tag already covers this authentication mechanism, and the generic topic is not needed on top of it.
The document mentions integrated services only in passing, and its subject is the RSVP security mechanism.

RFC2748.title: The COPS (Common Open Policy Service) Protocol
RFC2748.summary: Specifies COPS, a TCP-based client/server query-and-response protocol by which policy enforcement points (e.g., RSVP routers) obtain policy decisions and configuration from policy decision points, including message formats, state synchronization, keep-alives and message-level integrity.

COPS.why: The document defines the COPS protocol itself: header, objects, messages, and operation.
COPS.quote: This document describes a simple query and response protocol that can be used to exchange policy information between a policy server (Policy Decision Point or PDP) and its clients

rejected.why: RSVP is the example policy client for admission control, not specified here; client-type usage is left to separate documents.
TCP is only the transport substrate.
HMAC-MD5-96 is used for the Integrity object but the document is not about HMAC.
TLS and IPsec are only mentioned as optional channel security.
IPsec is only mentioned as optional channel security.
COPS is a child of QoS, so the more specific COPS tag covers it.

RFC2749.title: COPS usage for RSVP
RFC2749.summary: Specifies how COPS is used for RSVP clients (PEPs) to outsource policy control decisions to PDPs, defining client-type, context, decision objects, operational rules and examples.

COPS.why: The document is the COPS client-type specification for RSVP, defining object values and operation, so it belongs on the COPS page.
COPS.quote: It provides specific usage directives for using COPS in outsourcing policy control decisions by RSVP clients (PEPs) to policy servers (PDPs).

RSVP.why: It details how RSVP messages (Path, Resv, PathErr, ResvErr), flows, admission control and error reporting map onto COPS policy control.
RSVP.quote: RSVP is COPS client-type 1

rejected.why: The topic is policy-based management information models; the document is about COPS/RSVP admission policy, and COPS already sits under QoS.
RSVP is the Intserv signalling protocol but this document does not address Intserv service models; RSVP tag covers it.
MD5 authentication is mentioned only in Security Considerations and a brief note on Tear messages; not the subject.
Only referenced as inter-router authentication for RSVP; not specified or analysed here.

RFC2750.title: RSVP Extensions for Policy Control
RFC2750.summary: RFC 2750 extends RSVP with a standard POLICY_DATA object format, options (including INTEGRITY and policy refresh timing), and processing and error rules so RSVP can support policy-based admission control.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with POLICY_DATA objects, options, processing rules and policy error codes. It updates RFC 2205.
RSVP.quote: This memo presents a set of extensions for supporting generic policy based admission control in RSVP.

rejected.why: COPS is only referenced as a policy protocol that can be used with these extensions. The document says it does not advocate particular policy control mechanisms.
The INTEGRITY option reuses RSVP cryptographic authentication (RFC 2747, MD5-based). That is a security mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
The document is about policy objects carried in RSVP messages, not about policy-based management information models.
RSVP is already a child of QoS, so the more specific RSVP tag is used.

RFC2751.title: Signaled Preemption Priority Policy Element
RFC2751.summary: Defines the PREEMPTION_PRI RSVP policy element, which carries preemption and defending priorities for signaled policy-based admission control, along with merge strategies and error handling, for use with RSVP and COPS.

RSVP.why: The document specifies a new RSVP policy element (P-Type 3) carried in Policy Data objects, including merging of reservations and error handling. It extends RSVP.
RSVP.quote: This document describes a preemption priority policy element for use by signaled policy based admission protocols (such as [RSVP] and [COPS]).

COPS.why: A section specifies how the element is carried in COPS as stateless policy data, and the PDP/PEP/LDP model is central. COPS is a secondary carrier of the element.
COPS.quote: when carried in COPS messages for the outsourcing of policy decisions, these objects are included as COPS Stateless Policy Data Decision objects

rejected.why: Parent of RSVP and COPS, which are tagged directly, so it is implied.
The document is about a signaled admission policy element rather than policy information models for management.
The IANA section only assigns P-Type 3, which is boilerplate.
Preemption of flows is admission control, not congestion control.

RFC2752.title: Identity Representation for RSVP
RFC2752.summary: Defines the AUTH_DATA policy element carried in RSVP POLICY_DATA objects to convey user and application identity (simple, Kerberos, public-key), with processing rules and error signalling for policy-based admission control.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with a new identity policy element, specifying encoding, message generation and reception rules, and error signalling for RSVP messages.
RSVP.quote: This document describes the representation of identity information in POLICY_DATA object [POL-EXT] for supporting policy based admission control in RSVP.

Kerberos.why: A substantial section defines how Kerberos tickets are carried as credentials and used operationally. This is a profile of Kerberos use in RSVP, not a Kerberos extension, so it is secondary.
Kerberos.quote: Kerberos [RFC 1510] authentication uses a trusted third party (the Kerberos Distribution Center - KDC) to provide for authentication of the user to a network server.

rejected.why: The PDP/PEP policy architecture is referenced, but COPS is not specified or used here.
X.509 certificates are only a credential subtype carried in the element; the document does not profile them.
Authentication is central, but the specific technology tags (RSVP, Kerberos) already cover it, so the generic topic is not added.
A parent of RSVP, which is implied by the RSVP tag.

gaps.name: RSVP policy control / policy-based admission control
gaps.why: The document is about identity elements for RSVP policy-based admission control. The taxonomy has no tag for RSVP policy elements or admission control, so RSVP is the closest fit.

RFC2753.title: A Framework for Policy-based Admission Control
RFC2753.summary: Informational framework describing PEP/PDP/LPDP architecture, requirements, example policies and PEP-PDP protocol requirements for policy-based control of admission decisions, using RSVP as the main example.

QoS.why: The document is a framework for policy control of QoS admission across signalling protocols (RSVP, Diff-Serv). No more specific QoS child fits the framework as a whole.
QoS.quote: This document is concerned with specifying a framework for providing policy-based control over admission control decisions.

RSVP.why: RSVP is the main worked example: RSVP router PEP interaction, policy objects in PATH/RESV, preemption priorities. A substantial part of the document addresses RSVP policy control.
RSVP.quote: it focuses on policy-based control over admission control using RSVP as an example of the QoS signaling mechanism.

COPS.why: Section 6 states the requirements for the PEP-PDP protocol that led to COPS, and the document is part of the COPS/policy framework. It specifies requirements for that protocol rather than COPS itself, so this is secondary.
COPS.quote: specifies the requirements for a client-server protocol for communication between a policy server (PDP) and its client (PEP)

rejected.why: The document is about policy control of admission, not policy information models. Policy schema is referenced externally and left out of scope.
LDAP is only mentioned as a possible way for the PDP to store policy information, and the document says it does not discuss it.
SNMP is mentioned in passing as one possible protocol for PDP external access.
IPsec appears only in the Security Considerations as the way to secure the PEP-PDP channel.
Diff-Serv is mentioned as a possible other QoS context, but the document's focus is RSVP and int-serv.
Authentication and accounting are listed as requirements but they are not the framework's subject.

gaps.name: Policy-based admission control framework (PEP/PDP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no policy framework tag, only policy management (information models) and COPS. The PEP/PDP architecture is the core subject and is only partly covered by QoS.

RFC2754.title: RPS IANA Issues
RFC2754.summary: Specifies the seed RPSL objects (maintainer, key-cert, repository, as-block, inetnum) that IANA must create and PGP-sign as the root of the hierarchical authorization model for the Routing Policy System, and the IANA operations needed to maintain it.

RPSL.why: The document defines the RPSL seed objects and the IANA operations on them in the Internet routing registry. The taxonomy has no RPSL id, so this tag is invalid and is dropped in favour of the valid tag below.
RPSL.quote: RPS Security [2] requires certain RPSL [1] objects in the IRR to be hierarchically delegated.

RFC2755.title: Security Negotiation for WebNFS
RFC2755.summary: Informational RFC specifying how a WebNFS client negotiates a security mechanism with a WebNFS server by overloading the multi-component LOOKUP request and the returned NFS v2/v3 filehandle, avoiding the need for MOUNT v3.

NFS.why: The document extends WebNFS/NFS v2 and v3 with a security negotiation using modified LOOKUP and overloaded filehandles. NFS readers would want it.
NFS.quote: a protocol for a WebNFS client [RFC2054] to negotiate the desired security mechanism with a WebNFS server [RFC2055]

rejected.why: RPC authentication flavors and RPCSEC_GSS are the security mechanisms negotiated, but the document does not specify or extend RPC itself.
RPCSEC_GSS flavors are only mentioned as possible mechanisms to be negotiated; the document is not about GSS-API.
WebNFS is an NFS extension for Internet access, not about the web (HTTP/HTML) architecture.
The negotiation is NFS-specific; the general security topic is too broad when a specific tech tag applies.

RFC2756.title: Hyper Text Caching Protocol (HTCP/0.0)
RFC2756.summary: Specifies HTCP/0.0, an experimental protocol for discovering HTTP caches and cached objects, managing cache sets, and monitoring cache activity using full HTTP headers, as a successor to ICP.

HTTP caching.why: The whole document defines a cache-to-cache protocol (TST, MON, SET, CLR operations and cache headers) for HTTP cache management, which is exactly the HTTP caching subject.
HTTP caching.quote: a protocol for discovering HTTP caches and cached data, managing sets of HTTP caches, and monitoring cache activity

rejected.why: HTTP is the protocol whose objects and headers are cached; HTCP is a separate cache-management protocol, and the more specific HTTP caching tag covers it.
UDP is only the transport (TCP optional) for HTCP messages; nothing new is defined about UDP usage.
HMAC-MD5 is used only for the optional AUTH signature; the document is not about HMAC.
MD5 appears only as the HMAC digest and in the Cache-MD5 header; it is not a subject of the document.

RFC2757.title: Long Thin Networks
RFC2757.summary: Informational survey of TCP and related optimizations for long thin networks (wireless WANs), with recommendations on which mechanisms to implement, including split TCP, Snoop, header compression, ECN and queue management.

TCP.why: The document reviews and recommends TCP extensions (initial window, fast retransmit, SACK, T/TCP, Snoop, M-TCP) for long thin networks.
TCP.quote: Our goal is to identify a TCP that works for all users, including users of long thin networks.

ECN.why: ECN is evaluated and recommended, with discussion of its interaction with IPsec and RED.
ECN.quote: Recommendation: Implement ECN. In spite of this, mechanisms for explicit corruption notification are still relevant and should be tracked.

AQM.why: A dedicated section covers active queue management (RED) with a recommendation.
AQM.quote: RED is currently being deployed in the Internet, and LTNs should follow suit. ECN deployment should complement RED's.

header compression.why: A section surveys and recommends TCP/IP header compression (VJ, IPHC, IPHC-PPP) for low-bandwidth wireless links.
header compression.quote: Recommendation: Implement [IPHC], in particular as it relates to IP-in-IP [RFC2003] and Minimal Encapsulation [RFC2004] for Mobile IP

cellular.why: The target environment is wireless WANs such as GSM/GPRS/CDMA, and their link characteristics frame the whole analysis.
cellular.quote: Mobile Wireless networks can be grouped in W-LANs (for example, 802.11 compliant networks) and W-WANs (for example, CDPD [CDPD], Ricochet, CDMA [CDMA], PHS, DoCoMo, GSM [GSM]

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an experimental alternative that is not recommended; SACK is preferred.
Payload compression gets one short section with an optional recommendation; it is not a main subject.
Discussed repeatedly as a constraint on Snoop and header compression, but not the subject.
One brief subsection recommends Path MTU discovery; too minor to tag.
Mobile IP is cited as a reason to prefer IP and TCP, not analysed.
The tcpsat work is used as a starting point, but the document explicitly scopes itself to long thin links rather than satellite networks.

gaps.name: Performance-enhancing proxies (PEPs) / split TCP / Snoop
gaps.why: A large part of the document covers split-connection and Snoop-style proxies for wireless links. The taxonomy has no tag for PEPs, so TCP is the closest fit.

RFC2758.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Service Level Agreements Performance Monitoring
RFC2758.summary: Defines the experimental SLAPM-MIB, an SNMP MIB module for monitoring performance statistics, thresholds and notifications of Service Level Agreements expressed as policy rules.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (SLAPM-MIB) with tables, objects, notifications and compliance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for performance monitoring of Service Level Agreements (SLAs) defined via policy definitions.

performance measurement.why: Substantial portion covers monitoring min/max rates and delay over intervals with thresholds and notifications, i.e. performance monitoring of SLAs.
performance measurement.quote: The slapmPRMonTable provides a method of monitoring the effect of SLA policy being used at a system.

policy management.why: The MIB reports statistics on policy rules from the Policy Framework schema, tying into policy-based management.
policy management.quote: The goal of the MIB defined within this document is to defined statistics related to a policy rule definition

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for; the document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the more specific MIB tag.
Policies relate to QoS but the document only monitors rate/delay statistics, not QoS architecture or signalling.
Only RSVP flow counters are mentioned incidentally.
TCP connection statistics are monitored but TCP is not specified or extended.
Policy directory is referenced only as background; no directory protocol is defined.
A textual convention mentions UTF-8 incidentally.

RFC2759.title: Microsoft PPP CHAP Extensions, Version 2
RFC2759.summary: Informational RFC specifying Microsoft's MS-CHAP-V2, a PPP CHAP dialect (algorithm 0x81) with mutual authentication, packet formats, change-password support, pseudocode and examples.
