PPP.why: The document specifies a CHAP authentication dialect for PPP, negotiated via LCP option 3, with its own Challenge, Response, Success, Failure and Change-Password packets.
PPP.quote: This document describes version two of Microsoft's PPP CHAP dialect (MS-CHAP-V2).

authentication.why: A challenge-response peer authentication protocol with mutual authentication and password-change handling. No more specific tag fits, since CHAP is not in the taxonomy.
authentication.quote: MS-CHAP-V2 provides mutual authentication between peers by piggybacking a peer challenge on the Response packet and an authenticator response on the Success packet.

rejected.why: DES is used only as a primitive in the response computation, and the document does not define or analyse it.
MD4 and SHA-1 are used as building blocks. The RFC does not specify or analyse them, and MD5 is mentioned only as the standard CHAP algorithm value.
RC4 only encrypts the password block in the change-password routine and is not the subject of the document.
SHA-1 is used in the pseudocode as a building block, and the document is not about it.
The document covers peer-to-authenticator link authentication over PPP and does not frame it as an AAA framework.

gaps.name: CHAP (Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol) / MS-CHAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CHAP or its Microsoft variants. Readers looking for PPP authentication protocols would want this RFC grouped with them.

RFC2760.title: Ongoing TCP Research Related to Satellites
RFC2760.summary: Informational survey of experimental TCP mitigations (larger initial window, byte counting, SACK/FACK loss recovery, ECN, header compression, ACK filtering, etc.) for improving TCP performance over satellite links.

TCP.why: The whole document surveys TCP enhancements: slow start, loss recovery, congestion avoidance, T/TCP, pacing, state sharing.
TCP.quote: This document outlines mechanisms that may help the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) [Pos81] better utilize the bandwidth provided by long-delay satellite environments.

satellite.why: Focus is on satellite network architectures and their effect on TCP performance.
satellite.quote: This document outlines possible TCP enhancements that may allow TCP to better utilize the available bandwidth provided by networks containing satellite links.

NewReno.why: A dedicated subsection covers NewReno partial-ACK fast recovery.
NewReno.quote: These sender-side algorithms, known as NewReno TCP, do not depend on the availability of selective acknowledgments (SACKs)

ECN.why: A dedicated section covers ECN, and ACK congestion control builds on it.
ECN.quote: Explicit congestion notification (ECN) allows routers to inform TCP senders about imminent congestion without dropping segments.

header compression.why: Section 3.7 covers TCP/IP header compression and the twice algorithm for lossy links.
header compression.quote: The TCP/IP header compression methods described in [DNP99,DENP97,Jac90] reduce the overhead of TCP sessions

rejected.why: The document is about congestion control, but the more specific TCP, NewReno and ECN tags already cover it.
RED is mentioned as a requirement for ECN and for marking ACKs, but AQM is not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only in passing, as a limit on ACK filtering.
Source Quench and corruption-experienced messages are mentioned as proposals, but ICMP is not specified or analysed here.
Mentioned briefly as a partial solution and deferred to RFC 2488.

RFC2761.title: Terminology for ATM Benchmarking
RFC2761.summary: RFC 2761 defines terminology and performance metrics for benchmarking ATM switching devices (cell relay, signaling, AAL5, SONET, ILMI), extending the BMWG terminology of RFCs 1242, 2285 and 2544, focused on IP/TCP performance over ATM.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking terminology document defining metrics such as CLR, CDV and connection establishment time.
benchmarking.quote: This memo discusses and defines terms associated with performance benchmarking tests and the results of these tests in the context of Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) based switching devices.

ATM.why: Nearly all definitions concern ATM: cells, AAL5, traffic management, UNI/PNNI signaling, and their effect on IP and TCP throughput.
ATM.quote: A transfer mode in which the information is organized into 53 octet PDUs called cells.

rejected.why: Only three SONET physical-layer metrics are defined (pointer movements, overhead error counts). This is a minor part of the document.
TCP RTT and throughput are discussed as the effects of ATM parameters. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
ILMI is described as using SNMPv1 over AAL5, and two ILMI timing metrics are defined. SNMP itself is not the subject.
ATM service categories and traffic contracts are defined only as ATM terms for benchmarking. The document is not about QoS architectures.
The benchmarking tag is more specific for this BMWG device-benchmarking terminology.

RFC2762.title: Sampling of the Group Membership in RTP
RFC2762.summary: Experimental RFC describing SSRC sampling mechanisms (corrective factors and binning) that let RTP participants estimate group size with a reduced membership table in large multicast sessions.

RTCP.why: The document addresses scalability of RTCP group-size estimation by sampling the SSRC membership table that RTCP interval computation depends on. RTCP is the most specific tag; RTP is implied.
RTCP.quote: RTCP packets be transmitted from each participant with a period roughly proportional to the group size.

rejected.why: Large multicast groups are the motivating setting, but the document is about the RTP/RTCP membership table, not multicast routing or group management.
MD5 is only suggested as a hash to randomize SSRCs; the document is not about it.
H.323 is mentioned only as an example of non-random SSRC assignment.
The IPR claim on the binning algorithm is a notice, not the subject of the document.

RFC2763.title: Dynamic Hostname Exchange Mechanism for IS-IS
RFC2763.summary: Defines a new IS-IS TLV (type 137) that lets routers flood their symbolic hostname to system ID mapping in LSPs, as an alternative to static tables or DNS lookups.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new Dynamic Hostname TLV carried in link-state PDUs, so it is about the IS-IS protocol.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines a new TLV which allows the IS-IS routers to flood their name to system ID mapping information across the IS-IS network.

rejected.why: DNS is discussed only as an alternative that the document decides against. The TLV value is a domain name, but the document does not specify DNS.
The TLV carries router names, but it is an IS-IS routing protocol extension. It is not about host naming conventions or host tables in general.
IS-IS is an OSI protocol and system IDs and NSAPs appear in the text. The document is about the IS-IS TLV, not OSI network-layer coexistence.

RFC2764.title: A Framework for IP Based Virtual Private Networks
RFC2764.summary: Informational framework describing types of IP-based VPNs (virtual leased lines, VPRNs, VPDNs, VPLS), their requirements, tunneling needs, and recommended mechanisms and protocol extensions.

VPN.why: The whole document is a framework for provider-based and CPE VPNs, including VPRN and VPLS types and membership/reachability mechanisms.
VPN.quote: This document describes a framework for Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) running across IP backbones.

tunneling.why: A substantial section compares IP tunneling protocols (IP/IP, GRE, L2TP, IPsec, MPLS) against VPN requirements.
tunneling.quote: An IP tunnel connecting two VPN endpoints is a basic building block from which a variety of different VPN services can be constructed.

L2TP.why: Section 6 analyses L2TP characteristics, compulsory and voluntary tunneling for virtual private dial networks.
L2TP.quote: The IETF have developed the Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) [8] which allows for the extension of of user PPP sessions
L2TP.section: 6.0 VPN Types: Virtual Private Dial Networks

IPsec.why: The document recommends IPsec/IKE extensions (VPN-ID, null/null, multiprotocol, sequencing) and discusses IPsec for voluntary tunnels.
IPsec.quote: IPSec is needed whenever there is a requirement for strong encryption or strong authentication.

rejected.why: MPLS is discussed as one tunneling option and related VPN proposals, but the document is not about MPLS itself.
The VPLS here is a conceptual VPN type in one section; the tag is a specific technology (later IETF VPLS), and the parent VPN covers it.
RFC 2547 BGP/MPLS VPNs are only cited as related work; the document is not about them.
BGP appears only as a piggybacking approach for membership dissemination.
PPP is the substrate carried by L2TP, not specified or extended here.

RFC2765.title: Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT)
RFC2765.summary: RFC 2765 specifies SIIT, a stateless algorithm for translating IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers and ICMP messages in translator boxes so IPv6-only hosts can communicate with IPv4-only hosts.

SIIT.why: The document is the SIIT specification itself, defining the header and ICMP translation rules in both directions.
SIIT.quote: The algorithm translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers (including ICMP headers) in separate translator "boxes" in the network without requiring any per-connection state

rejected.why: ICMP/ICMPv6 message translation is a substantial part, but it is part of SIIT's mechanism rather than a specification of ICMP; the SIIT tag covers it.
The document leans on IPv6 heavily, but its subject is the translation algorithm, which sits under IPv6 transition. The more specific SIIT tag covers it.
Path MTU handling across the translator is discussed, but only as one detail of translation.
AH and ESP traversal through the translator is discussed briefly as a limitation, not as a subject of the document.
This is the stateless predecessor algorithm. It does not specify stateful NAT64.

RFC2766.title: Network Address Translation - Protocol Translation (NAT-PT)
RFC2766.summary: RFC 2766 specifies NAT-PT, an IPv6-to-IPv4 transition mechanism combining address/port translation with SIIT-style protocol translation, plus a DNS-ALG and FTP-ALG.

NAT64.why: NAT-PT is the stateful IPv6-to-IPv4 translation mechanism, the predecessor of NAT64. It is the closest tag for stateful v6/v4 address and protocol translation.
NAT64.quote: This is achieved using a combination of Network Address Translation and Protocol Translation.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is explicitly a transition and coexistence mechanism, and its applicability statement discusses use at the edge of IPv6-only stub networks.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document specifies an IPv4-to-IPv6 transition mechanism, in addition to those already specified in [TRANS].

SIIT.why: Section 5 specifies how SIIT header translation is modified for NAT-PT, so SIIT readers would want this document.
SIIT.quote: Protocol translation details specified in [SIIT] would be used to extend address translation with protocol syntax/semantics translation.

DNS.why: A substantial section specifies DNS-ALG translation of A/AAAA/A6 queries and responses, including TTL handling, and discusses the DNSSEC conflict.
DNS.quote: The DNS-ALG on the NAT-PT device would modify DNS Queries for A records going into the V6 domain
DNS.section: 4. Use of DNS-ALG for Address Assignment

rejected.why: NAT-PT is a v6/v4 translator rather than ordinary IPv4 NAT. NAT64 is the more specific fit, and NAT is only the referenced background.
The FTP-ALG section covers PORT/PASV to EPRT/EPSV translation, but it is a supporting ALG, not the document's main subject.
Section 7.5 only notes that DNS translation is incompatible with DNSSEC. It is a limitation, not something the document specifies.
The DNS-ALG does synthesize AAAA records from A records, but DNS64 is a later, separate specification. The DNS tag covers this document's DNS-ALG.
Checksum update is a small part of the protocol translation details, with no new checksum mechanism defined.

RFC2767.title: Dual Stack Hosts using the "Bump-In-the-Stack" Technique (BIS)
RFC2767.summary: RFC 2767 proposes the Bump-in-the-Stack (BIS) mechanism, in which a dual stack host inserts a translator, an extension name resolver and an address mapper under its TCP/IPv4 stack so that existing IPv4 applications can talk to IPv6 hosts.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is a host-based IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and transition mechanism for the early stage of the move from IPv4 to IPv6. No more specific child tag fits the BIS mechanism itself.
IPv6 transition.quote: This memo proposes a mechanism of dual stack hosts using the technique called "Bump-in-the-Stack" in the IP security area.

SIIT.why: The BIS translator module is built on SIIT header translation, and a substantial part of the document describes how it is applied inside the host. It is not the main subject, though.
SIIT.quote: It translates IPv4 into IPv6 and vice versa using the IP conversion mechanism defined in [SIIT].

rejected.why: The extension name resolver snoops A/AAAA queries, but DNS is only a mechanism the host uses to trigger address mapping. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
The document compares IP conversion to NAT and to NAT-PT, and notes the shared problem of embedded addresses. It is not about NAT behaviour.
IPv6 is the subject of the transition, but the more specific IPv6 transition tag covers this document better.
This is a host-internal translator, not stateful NAT64 in the network, and it predates NAT64.

RFC2768.title: Network Policy and Services: A Report of a Workshop on Middleware
RFC2768.summary: Report of a 1998 ad hoc workshop on middleware that defines the term, surveys exemplary middleware components (policy, directories, resource management, AAA, QoS, information discovery, network management, multicast), and lists R&D needs.

policy management.why: Policy architecture (PDP/PEP, repository, information model) is a central theme tying together directories, resource management and QoS.
policy management.quote: The IETF Policy Framework working group is addressing a policy framework definition language, a policy architecture model, policy terminology

QoS.why: A substantial section discusses IntServ, DiffServ, bandwidth brokers and signalling of QoS needs by applications.
QoS.quote: The first IETF model was the Integrated Services (IntServ) model, which used RSVP as the signaling mechanism.

AAA.why: Dedicated sections cover AAA requirements for middleware, resource managers and policy.
AAA.quote: The IETF AAA (authentication, authorization, and accounting) effort is but one of many IETF security initiatives.

directory services.why: A full section on directories, CIM/DEN and LDAP mapping, and directory vs database.
directory services.quote: Directories are critical resource components that provide support to many other elements in the middleware environment, especially policy.

service discovery.why: Covers resource and information discovery, locators, resolvers and metadata services.
service discovery.quote: There are a wide range of middleware services broadly related to the discovery and retrieval of networked information.
service discovery.section: 10.0 Networked Information Discovery and Retrieval Services

internet architecture.why: The document defines middleware conceptually and its place in the architecture, with a framework for further work.
internet architecture.quote: Generally, in advanced networks, middleware consists of services and other resources located between both the applications and the underlying packet forwarding and routing infrastructure

workshop reports.why: The RFC is itself a workshop report.
workshop reports.quote: This document is a product of an ad hoc Middleware Workshop held on December 4-5 1998.

rejected.why: Discussed as an example within QoS, but not the subject; covered by the QoS tag.
Mentioned as a PDP-PEP protocol only; not specified or analysed in depth.
Discussed as a needed supporting infrastructure in a paragraph or two, not a main subject.
Brief section on middleware for multicast, which is explicitly classed as infrastructure rather than middleware.
Mentioned as the access protocol for CIM/DEN, but not discussed as a protocol.
Mentioned as an example of yesterday's middleware only.

gaps.name: middleware
gaps.why: The document's core subject has no taxonomy tag; internet architecture is the closest fit.

RFC2769.title: Routing Policy System Replication
RFC2769.summary: Specifies how routing registries (RPSL-based IRR repositories) replicate and mirror data via signed transaction flooding, heartbeats, snapshots, and commit protocol, plus RPSL additions (repository object, delegated and integrity attributes) preserving the authorization model.

RPSL.why: The document extends RPSL with repository, delegated and integrity attributes, and defines replication of routing registry (IRR) data between repositories and mirrors.
RPSL.quote: This document addresses the need to distribute data over multiple repositories and delegate authority for data subsets to other repositories

rejected.why: The authorization and authentication model is defined in RFC 2725; this document only replicates data under it, and the taxonomy children (RPKI, BGPsec) are unrelated.
Queries via whois are mentioned only as an access method and queries are out of scope.
PGP is used only as the signature mechanism for transactions, not specified here.
Routing policy registry data supports BGP filters but BGP itself is not addressed.

RFC2770.title: GLOP Addressing in 233/8
RFC2770.summary: RFC 2770 defines an experimental static allocation of multicast addresses in 233/8 (GLOP), embedding the 16-bit AS number in the address to give each AS a /24 of globally scoped multicast space.

multicast.why: The document specifies a multicast address allocation scheme (static, AS-based in 233/8). It is about IP multicast addressing in its own right, and no more specific multicast child tag fits.
multicast.quote: This describes an experimental policy for use of the class D address space using 233/8 as the experimental statically assigned subset of the class D address space.

rejected.why: MADCAP and MASC are mentioned only as parallel dynamic allocation work from MALLOC. This document defines a static scheme, not those protocols.
It is IP address allocation, but the multicast tag is the more specific fit, since the scheme only concerns class D space.
The IANA allocation of 233/8 is described only in the IANA Considerations boilerplate. The body is about the addressing scheme itself.
The single-source address space is only cited as an alternative source of addresses, and the document does not address it.
RWhois is only mentioned as the database where AS numbers are registered. It is not specified or discussed.

RFC2771.title: An Abstract API for Multicast Address Allocation
RFC2771.summary: Informational RFC defining an abstract (language-neutral) API for applications to allocate, extend, deallocate and query dynamic multicast addresses and administrative scopes from a multicast address allocation service.

MADCAP.why: The document defines the application-facing interface of the MALLOC multicast address allocation service, which MADCAP implements. Readers of the MADCAP/MALLOC subject would expect it. The tag also covers the allocation architecture.
MADCAP.quote: This document describes the "abstract service interface" for the dynamic multicast address allocation service, as seen by applications.

rejected.why: Multicast is the general domain, but MADCAP, which covers MADCAP and the MALLOC allocation architecture, is a more specific child that fits.
The API is abstract and language-neutral and is not a sockets extension. Concrete APIs are left to other documents.
IPv4 and IPv6 appear only as an AddressFamily parameter, so the document is not about IPv6.
Language tags are used only to name scopes, which is incidental to the document.

RFC2772.title: 6Bone Backbone Routing Guidelines
RFC2772.summary: Informational guidelines for 6Bone IPv6 testbed backbone operators covering which prefixes may be advertised via IGP/EGP (BGP4+), aggregation and peering policy, registry maintenance, and pTLA qualification.

IPv6.why: The document governs deployment and addressing/prefix handling on the 6Bone IPv6 testbed (pTLA/pNLA/TLA allocation, special IPv6 prefixes).
IPv6.quote: The 6Bone is an IPv6 testbed to assist in the evolution and deployment of IPv6.

BGP.why: Much of the document is BGP4+ route advertisement, filtering, and peering policy for backbone operators.
BGP.quote: This document uses BGP-4 with Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4 as defined [RFC 2283], commonly referred to as BGP4+, as the currently accepted EGP.

routing architecture.why: Aggregation model, default-free core, and peering policies are routing architecture/scalability rules for the backbone.
routing architecture.quote: Route aggregation MUST be performed by any border router talking EGP with any other IPv6 sites.

rejected.why: Only a short section on when pTLAs may announce the 6to4 prefix; not a substantial subject.
Multicast prefix handling is a brief rule, not a main subject.
The 6Bone registry uses RIPE-181 objects, but only as an administrative requirement, not a specification of RPSL.
DNS delegation for joining sites is mentioned only as a requirement.
The 6Bone is a transition testbed, but the document is about routing rules rather than transition mechanisms.

RFC2773.title: Encryption using KEA and SKIPJACK
RFC2773.summary: Experimental profile of the FTP Security Extensions (RFC 2228) that uses KEA for mutual authentication and key establishment and SKIPJACK to encrypt the FTP command channel and file data, including a pre-encrypted file token.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP with a new AUTH mechanism (KEA-SKIPJACK), protected commands, and a file-transfer token, and it updates RFC 959.
FTP.quote: This document defines a method to encrypt a file transfer using the FTP specification STD 9, RFC 959, "File Transfer Protocol (FTP)"

key management.why: A substantial part of the document covers KEA key establishment, MEK/TEK/FEK key wrapping and a key-usage table, so key management readers would want it.
key management.quote: The client and server use KEA to generate a shared SKIPJACK symmetric key, called the TEK.

rejected.why: SKIPJACK and KEA are used as given, and no algorithm is specified here. The key-management tag covers the keying aspects.
Mutual authentication is a result of the KEA exchange, not the main subject. The document is a profile for FTP encryption.
Security labels (MSP) are carried in the token but are not the subject of the document.
Base64 is only the encoding used for protected command data.
The FTP security framework is RFC 2228 ADAT/AUTH. GSS-API is not used or discussed.
Certificates carrying KEA keys are mentioned in passing but are not profiled.

gaps.name: FTP Security Extensions (RFC 2228)
gaps.why: The document profiles the FTP security framework (AUTH/ADAT/ENC/PROT), and the taxonomy has no separate tag for it beyond FTP.

gaps.name: SKIPJACK/KEA (Fortezza) algorithms
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for these NSA algorithms or the Fortezza card.

RFC2774.title: An HTTP Extension Framework
RFC2774.summary: Experimental RFC defining a generic HTTP extension framework using URI-identified extension declarations (Man, Opt, C-Man, C-Opt headers), header prefixes, the "M-" method prefix, Ext/C-Ext acknowledgements, and a 510 Not Extended status code.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with new header fields, a method prefix, and a status code, and covers proxy, origin server and caching behaviour. Its whole subject is HTTP extensibility.
HTTP.quote: This document describes a generic extension mechanism for HTTP, which is designed to address the tension between private agreement and public specification

rejected.why: Caching is discussed (Ext with no-cache, Expires, Vary), but only as a side effect of the extension headers. It is not the document's subject.
Extensions are identified by URIs, but the document only uses them as identifiers and defines nothing new about URI syntax or schemes.
Digest and ProxyAuth appear only as example extensions, so the document is not about authentication.
WebDAV is named in the abstract only as one of the extensions that motivated the framework. The document does not specify it.

RFC2775.title: Internet Transparency
RFC2775.summary: Informational IAB-input document analysing the Internet's loss of end-to-end address transparency (NATs, firewalls, private addresses, dynamic addressing, proxies, split DNS) and outlining future network-layer scenarios around IPv6 success, failure or partial deployment.

internet architecture.why: The whole document is an architectural analysis of the end-to-end argument and the loss of transparency in the Internet.
internet architecture.quote: This document describes the current state of the Internet from the architectural viewpoint, concentrating on issues of end-to-end connectivity and transparency.

NAT.why: NATs and their ALGs are a central cause of lost transparency, discussed in its own section and in the future scenarios.
NAT.quote: address translation on the fly destroys end-to-end address transparency and breaks any middleware or applications that depend on it.

firewall.why: Firewalls and SOCKS are discussed as a major cause of non-transparency, with their own sections.
firewall.quote: Firewalls, by their nature, fundamentally limit transparency.

IPv6 transition.why: Section 5 and the conclusion compare IPv6 migration, failure and partial deployment scenarios, which is coexistence/transition analysis.
IPv6 transition.quote: Partial deployment of IPv6, which is a required step on the road to full deployment, is also messy but avoids the dead ends.

rejected.why: Discussed as a casualty of lost transparency, but the document does not specify or analyse IPsec itself.
Private addresses and IPv4 exhaustion are covered, but as causes within the architectural analysis rather than as an address-allocation document.
Split DNS and round-robin DNS are briefly mentioned; the document explicitly excludes namespace issues.
Only a short footnote subsection on SOCKS as a firewall traversal mechanism.
Mentioned only as a source of transient addresses.
Scenarios are about the future of the network layer and transparency, not IPv6 specification; the transition tag better fits.

gaps.name: end-to-end principle / transparency
gaps.why: The document's core subject is end-to-end transparency of the network layer, which has no dedicated tag beyond the broad internet architecture topic.

RFC2776.title: Multicast-Scope Zone Announcement Protocol (MZAP)
RFC2776.summary: RFC 2776 defines MZAP, a protocol by which zone boundary routers announce multicast administrative scope zones and detect misconfigurations such as non-convex or leaky scope zones.

multicast.why: MZAP is an IP multicast administrative scoping protocol that has no dedicated technology tag. The multicast topic tag fits its subject of scope zones, boundary routers and multicast address ranges.
multicast.quote: discovering the multicast administrative scope zones that are relevant at a particular location

rejected.why: MADCAP is only the means by which servers hand MZAP-learned scope information to applications. It is not specified or extended here.
MZAP messages are carried over UDP port 2106. UDP is only the substrate.
IPsec AH is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an authentication option.
Language tags appear only as a field in the zone name encoding. They are not what the document is about.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the zone name field.
IPv6 addresses are supported in the message formats, but the document is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: Administratively scoped multicast / multicast scope zones (MZAP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for multicast administrative scoping or zone announcement, so only the generic multicast topic fits. A dedicated tag would help readers of RFC 2365 and related documents.

RFC2777.title: Publicly Verifiable Nomcom Random Selection
RFC2777.summary: Describes a publicly verifiable method for randomly selecting IETF NomCom voting members from volunteers, using future public randomness sources (e.g. lotteries) mixed with MD5, with a worked example and reference C code.

NomCom.why: The document specifies how NomCom voting members are selected, with an appendix on the history of selection methods. This is NomCom procedure.
NomCom.quote: each year 10 persons are randomly selected from among the eligible persons who volunteer to be the voting members of the nominations committee (NomCom)

randomness.why: A substantial part of the document covers sources of randomness, skew, and entropy needed. This is about randomness requirements and use.
randomness.quote: The crux of the unbiased nature of the selection is that it is based exactly on random information which will be revealed in the future

rejected.why: MD5 is only the mixing function used in the algorithm and reference code. The document does not specify or analyse MD5.
It is implied as the parent of NomCom, so it is not listed separately.
The document uses a hash function to mix inputs but is about verifiable selection procedure, not cryptographic algorithms.

RFC2778.title: A Model for Presence and Instant Messaging
RFC2778.summary: RFC 2778 defines an abstract model and common vocabulary for presence and instant messaging systems, describing the presence service, instant message service, their entities, and presence information structure.

instant messaging.why: The whole document models presence and instant messaging: PRESENCE SERVICE, INSTANT MESSAGE SERVICE, watchers, presentities, inboxes. It is the foundational IMPP model.
instant messaging.quote: This document defines an abstract model for a presence and instant messaging system. It defines the various entities involved, defines terminology

rejected.why: The model describes presence tuples abstractly but does not define the PIDF data format, which came in later work.
SIMPLE is a SIP-based extension set developed later; this model is protocol-neutral and does not specify it.
Email is mentioned only as a possible reuse for instant message delivery; the document is not about it.
SPAM appears as a defined term and in security considerations, but only briefly; it is not a subject of the document.
The document provides vocabulary, but its subject is presence and instant messaging, and the more specific instant messaging tag covers it.

gaps.name: Presence
gaps.why: The model covers presence services (presentities, watchers, subscriptions, notifications) as a whole, but the taxonomy only has presence under 'instant messaging' and PIDF, with no general presence tag.

RFC2779.title: Instant Messaging / Presence Protocol Requirements
RFC2779.summary: RFC 2779 specifies the minimum requirements that the IMPP working group's instant messaging and presence protocol must meet, covering shared, presence-specific, message-specific and security requirements.

instant messaging.why: The whole document sets out requirements for a standard instant messaging and presence protocol, covering both presence information and instant messages.
instant messaging.quote: Instant messaging is a means for sending small, simple messages that are delivered immediately to online users.

rejected.why: MIME is only cited as a basis the common message format SHOULD build on (4.1.10). The document does not specify or extend it.
SIMPLE is a later SIP-based solution. This document is protocol-neutral requirements and does not mention SIP.
The document requires a common presence format but does not define one. PIDF came later.
Privacy-related requirements such as polite blocking and hiding IP addresses are part of the security requirements for IM/presence. They do not amount to a general privacy threat model.
vCard is mentioned only as a possible basis for the presence format (3.1.6).
The security requirements are specific to presence and IM, so the instant messaging tag covers them. A general security tag would be over-broad.

gaps.name: presence service
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no standalone tag for presence. It is only covered by the 'instant messaging' entry (instant messaging and presence), and presence-specific browsing would benefit from its own subject.

RFC2780.title: IANA Allocation Guidelines For Values In the Internet Protocol and Related Headers
RFC2780.summary: BCP giving IANA guidelines on which approval processes govern allocation of values in IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, UDP and TCP header fields.

IANA.why: The document exists to set IANA allocation policy for protocol header field registries, which is what the IANA topic covers.
IANA.quote: This memo provides guidance for the IANA to use in assigning parameters for fields in the IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, UDP and TCP protocol headers.

IPv4.why: A large part of the document sets allocation rules for IPv4 header fields and address ranges.
IPv4.quote: The IPv4 header [V4] contains the following fields that carry values assigned by the IANA: Version, Type of Service, Protocol, Source Address, Destination Address, and Option Type.

IPv6.why: A full section covers IPv6 header fields, address format prefixes, and neighbor discovery values.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 header [V6] contains the following fields that carry values assigned from IANA-managed name spaces: Version (by definition always 6 in IPv6), Traffic Class, Next Header

ICMP.why: Sections 6 and 7 give allocation policy for ICMP and ICMPv6 Type and Code values.
ICMP.quote: The IPv4 ICMP header [ICMP] contains the following fields that carry values assigned from IANA-managed name spaces: Type and Code.

UDP.why: The document gives the port allocation policy for UDP.
UDP.quote: The UDP header [UDP] contains the following fields that carry values assigned from IANA-managed name spaces: Source and Destination Port.

TCP.why: The document gives allocation policy for TCP ports, reserved bits, and option kinds.
TCP.quote: The TCP header [TCP] contains the following fields that carry values assigned from IANA-managed name spaces: Source and Destination Port, Reserved Bits, and Option Kind.

rejected.why: The DS field is mentioned only to point to RFC 2474 for its allocation rules. The document does not address Diffserv itself.
It gets one short subsection of allocation rules. That is not enough to make the document about neighbor discovery.
IPv4 and IPv6 multicast address assignment is mentioned briefly within the address rules. The document is not about multicast.
It covers address-space assignment rules only as part of header fields, and delegates unicast allocation to ICANN and the RIRs.

RFC2781.title: UTF-16, an encoding of ISO 10646
RFC2781.summary: Informational RFC describing the UTF-16 encoding of Unicode/ISO 10646, its serialization and byte order mark handling, and registering the MIME charsets UTF-16, UTF-16BE and UTF-16LE.

Unicode.why: The document specifies the UTF-16 encoding of Unicode, including surrogate pair encoding/decoding, BOM and endianness, so it belongs under Unicode usage in Internet protocols.
Unicode.quote: This document describes the UTF-16 encoding of Unicode/ISO-10646, addresses the issues of serializing UTF-16 as an octet stream for transmission over the Internet

character sets.why: A substantial part (Section 3, 4 and Appendix A) covers charset labelling and registration of three MIME charsets, which is character set registration and use.
character sets.quote: contains the registration for three MIME charset parameter values: UTF-16BE (big-endian), UTF-16LE (little-endian), and UTF-16.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only referenced as the mandatory IETF encoding; the document describes UTF-16, not UTF-8.
MIME charset labels are used, but the document is about the encoding and charset names, not MIME body structure or encodings.
It notes the charsets are unsuitable for text/* types, but does not register media types or define registry rules.
The IANA charset registrations are boilerplate-like registration templates, not guidance about IANA registries.
The parent is implied by the Unicode/character sets tags; no need to tag it directly.

RFC2782.title: A DNS RR for specifying the location of services (DNS SRV)
RFC2782.summary: Specifies the DNS SRV resource record (type 33), which lets clients look up the servers, ports, priorities and weights for a given service and protocol in a domain, and defines the client selection algorithm.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS resource record, its format, query procedure and resolver behaviour.
DNS.quote: Here is the format of the SRV RR, whose DNS type code is 33:
DNS.section: The format of the SRV RR

service discovery.why: The SRV RR's purpose is discovering servers for a service in a domain, with priority and weight based selection, so service discovery readers would want it.
service discovery.quote: This document describes a DNS RR which specifies the location of the server(s) for a specific protocol and domain.

rejected.why: LDAP is only an illustrative example and the document says it is not a definitive statement on LDAP use.
DNS-SD is a separate service discovery mechanism; SRV is merely a building block it uses and not specified here.
Only a one-line type value assignment in the IANA Considerations; boilerplate.
The underscore-prefixed labels are naming convention for service/proto labels, not reserved special-use domain names.

RFC2783.title: Pulse-Per-Second API for UNIX-like Operating Systems, Version 1.0
RFC2783.summary: Specifies a UNIX-style C API (time_pps_* functions, pps_params_t, mode bits) for capturing pulse-per-second timestamps from precise time sources and disciplining the kernel timebase, complementing the RFC 1589 kernel model used with NTP.

time synchronization.why: The document defines an API for PPS timestamping and kernel timebase disciplining, which is clock synchronization. It is not about the NTP protocol itself, so the topic tag fits better than NTP.
time synchronization.quote: One aspect of this model is an accurate interface to the high-accuracy, one pulse-per-second (PPS) output typically available from precise time sources

rejected.why: NTP is the intended consumer, and its 64-bit timestamp format is one optional representation. The document does not specify or extend the NTP protocol; it defines a local OS API.
This is a C API for UNIX, but it concerns PPS sources via file descriptors, not sockets.
PTP is not discussed; the document is about local PPS signals, not network time distribution.

gaps.name: Pulse-per-second (PPS) API / kernel timekeeping
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for operating-system timekeeping interfaces or reference clock hardware. The closest fit is the general time synchronization topic.

RFC2784.title: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE)
RFC2784.summary: RFC 2784 specifies the GRE header format and processing rules for encapsulating an arbitrary network-layer payload in another network-layer protocol, with IPv4 delivery/payload details and interoperation with RFC 1701.

GRE.why: The document defines the GRE header, its fields, and processing rules, so it is the core GRE specification.
GRE.quote: This document specifies a protocol for encapsulation of an arbitrary network layer protocol over another arbitrary network layer protocol.

rejected.why: IPv4 is only the payload and delivery protocol (protocol 47); the document does not specify IPv4 itself.
The child tag GRE already covers this and the parent is implied.
The optional GRE checksum field uses the standard Internet checksum, but the document does not address checksums as a subject.
Path MTU discovery is only listed as a known issue in the appendix and is not addressed by the document.
The introduction mentions IP-over-IP encapsulations only as prior proposals; the document specifies GRE, not IP-in-IP.
PPTP's use of GRE version 1 is mentioned only in IANA considerations, which is not evidence of PPP being the subject.

RFC2785.title: Methods for Avoiding the "Small-Subgroup" Attacks on the Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement Method for S/MIME
RFC2785.summary: Informational RFC describing when S/MIME v3 implementations using Diffie-Hellman key agreement need protection from small-subgroup attacks and five methods (public key validation, CA validation, prime choice, cofactor exponentiation) to prevent them.

key management.why: The document is about securing Diffie-Hellman key agreement, a key establishment mechanism, against small-subgroup attacks, including public key validation and prime selection. No Diffie-Hellman-specific tag exists, so key management is the closest fit.
key management.quote: This document will describe the situations relevant to implementations of S/MIME version 3 in which protection is necessary and the methods that can be used to prevent these attacks.

S/MIME.why: The document is scoped to S/MIME v3 implementations that use Diffie-Hellman, and analyses sender and recipient situations arising in S/MIME, so readers of S/MIME would want it.
S/MIME.quote: in implementations of S/MIME version 3 [RFC2630, RFC2633]. Thus, the ephemeral-static and static-static modes of Diffie-Hellman will be focused on.

rejected.why: CMS is the message syntax in which Diffie-Hellman is used and is only mentioned as a possible non-S/MIME usage. The document is not about CMS itself.
Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman is mentioned in a single sentence saying the methods may also apply. It is not a substantial part of the document.
The CA performing public key validation is only one of the five methods (Section 3.2). The document is not about PKI in general.
The parent is implied only if the document is about the broader subject. Here key management fits more specifically.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key agreement / small-subgroup attacks
gaps.why: The document is about Diffie-Hellman key agreement and its attacks, but the taxonomy has no Diffie-Hellman or discrete-log cryptography tag. Readers browsing for DH would expect to find it.

RFC2786.title: Diffie-Helman USM Key Management Information Base and Textual Convention
RFC2786.summary: Experimental SNMP MIB module defining the DHKeyChange textual convention and objects extending the USM usmUserTable so keys can be changed or bootstrapped ("kickstarted") via Diffie-Hellman exchange, giving forward secrecy.

MIB.why: The document's core content is an SMIv2 MIB module (SNMP-USM-DH-OBJECTS-MIB) with a textual convention, tables, and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module in a manner that is compliant to the SNMP SMIv2[5][6][7].

SNMP.why: It extends SNMPv3 USM security, adding forward-secret key change and kickstart provisioning for SNMPv3 agents, so SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: a set of objects which extend the usmUserTable to permit the use of a DH key exchange in addition to the key change method

key management.why: A substantial part concerns key establishment and provisioning: Diffie-Hellman key change and key ignition with PBKDF2 key derivation for USM keys.
key management.quote: this MIB adds the possibility of forward secrecy to the USM model.

rejected.why: Only used as the derivation function for kickstart keys; the document is not about PBKDF2.
Oakley group parameters from RFC 2409 are borrowed as defaults; IKE is not specified or extended.
Not a taxonomy tag; DOCSIS is only cited as a motivating large-scale deployment, not what the document specifies.
Security Considerations merely refers to RFC 1750 on randomness; the document is not about it.
The generic authentication topic is too broad; the document concerns SNMP USM key management specifically.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key agreement
gaps.why: The core mechanism is DH key agreement; the taxonomy has no Diffie-Hellman tag, so key management is the closest fit.

RFC2787.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol
RFC2787.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module for configuring, monitoring and controlling routers running the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP), with operations, statistics and notification objects.

VRRP.why: The MIB exists to manage VRRP routers: virtual router state, priority, associated addresses, authentication and statistics. VRRP readers would want it.
VRRP.quote: it defines objects for configuring, monitoring, and controlling routers that employ the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP)

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, conformance groups and notifications, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This specification defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with SNMP-based network management.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework used; the MIB tag sits under SNMP and is more specific, so SNMP is not tagged separately.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible protection, and the IP authentication header is just an enumerated auth type value.
The MIB uses IPv4-specific IpAddress syntax because VRRP is IPv4 only, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
The parent topic is implied by the MIB and SNMP tags, so it is not listed.

RFC2788.title: Network Services Monitoring MIB
RFC2788.summary: Defines the NETWORK-SERVICES-MIB, an SNMP MIB module with applTable and assocTable for monitoring network service applications and their associations, obsoleting RFC 2248.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SMIv2) defining objects for monitoring network service applications; it belongs on the MIB page.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB which contains the elements common to the monitoring of any network service application.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is written for, but the document only defines a MIB module; the more specific MIB tag covers it.
Only referenced for the distinguished name string format in applDirectoryName; not about LDAP.
applDirectoryName relates entries to the X.500 Directory, but this is a minor linkage, not the document's subject.
MTAs are given as an example of extension MIBs and in assocRemoteApplication text; the MIB is generic, not about email.
Defines a URLString textual convention only incidentally; not about URIs.
Parent topic of the MIB tag, so it is implied; not chosen separately.

RFC2789.title: Mail Monitoring MIB
RFC2789.summary: Defines the SMIv2 Mail Monitoring MIB (MTA-MIB), extending the Network Services Monitoring MIB with tables of counters and status for monitoring Message Transfer Agents, obsoleting RFC 2249 and RFC 1566.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (MTA-MIB) defining objects, tables, and conformance groups for monitoring MTAs, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

email.why: The subject being monitored is mail transfer: message flow, storage, recipients, loops and errors in MTAs, covering both SMTP and X.400 based MTAs.
email.quote: this memo extends the basic Network Services Monitoring MIB defined in RFC 2788 [16] to allow monitoring of Message Transfer Agents (MTAs).

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried over; the document defines no SNMP protocol changes, only a MIB module.
SMTP is mentioned as an example of an MTA protocol and for error codes, but the document does not specify or extend it.
X.400 is mentioned only as an alternative MTA type in volume and error descriptions, not as a subject of the document.
The more specific MIB tag already covers this and sits under SNMP within network management.

RFC2790.title: Host Resources MIB
RFC2790.summary: Defines the SMIv2 Host Resources MIB (obsoleting RFC 1514), with objects for host system, storage, devices, file systems, running and installed software, plus a HOST-RESOURCES-TYPES module.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to specify a MIB module (HOST-RESOURCES-MIB) in SMIv2 for managing hosts, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a MIB for use with managing host systems.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through; the document defines only managed objects, not protocol changes. The SNMP framework section is boilerplate.
NFS appears only as a file system type identifier (hrFSNFS) in the type registry.
AFS appears only as a file system type identifier (hrFSAFS), not as a subject of the document.
The IANA Considerations section only sets up registration of new type values; this is boilerplate relative to the main subject.
Printer objects here are simple host-device status, not the Internet Printing Protocol.
The more specific MIB tag covers this; the parent is implied.

RFC2791.title: Scalable Routing Design Principles
RFC2791.summary: Informational RFC analysing factors that limit routing scalability in large ISP networks (IGP flooding, I-BGP full mesh, route flapping) and giving design principles such as hierarchy, compartmentalization, aggregation and out-of-band route processing.

routing architecture.why: The whole document is about routing scalability and design principles for large networks, which is the routing architecture subject.
routing architecture.quote: This document identifies major factors affecting routing scalability as well as basic principles of designing scalable routing for large networks.

BGP.why: A substantial part analyses BGP scaling: I-BGP full mesh, route flapping, dampening, E-BGP session load, and policy.
BGP.quote: The major scaling issue associated with BGP lie in the full mesh I-BGP connections.

route reflection.why: Route reflectors and confederations are discussed as the main way to build a BGP hierarchy and cut I-BGP mesh scaling cost.
route reflection.quote: The introduction of a routing hierarchy in BGP, through I-BGP Route Reflectors [7] and BGP Confederations [8], for example, will help alleviate the scaling problem

route server.why: The appendix proposes route servers at exchange points, at customer aggregation and at POPs as an out-of-band way to scale BGP peering.
route server.quote: The use of a Route Server(RS) at NAPs is an example of achieving routing scalability through an out-of-band routing process.

OSPF.why: OSPF flooding, SPF cost, area hierarchy and adjacency scaling are analysed in detail.
OSPF.quote: Link-state IGPs also do not scale well to carry a large number of routes

IS-IS.why: IS-IS scaling and its two-level limits are discussed alongside OSPF as a key factor in hierarchy design.
IS-IS.quote: Although IS-IS supports multi-area routing, it imposes a strict hierarchy between backbone and sub-areas

rejected.why: CIDR aggregation is one principle in section 6.4.2.1, but it is a brief mention of an existing mechanism and not a main subject.
IRR is only mentioned as a proposed mechanism for prefix filtering.
Prefix filtering and the TCP MD5 option are touched on briefly, mostly in the Security Considerations, and the document is not about routing security.
RIP and EGP are only named as previous-generation protocols.

RFC2792.title: DSA and RSA Key and Signature Encoding for the KeyNote Trust Management System
RFC2792.summary: Defines how RSA and DSA public keys, signatures, and binary identifiers are normalized, ASN.1-encoded, ASCII-encoded (hex/base64) and named for KeyNote trust-management assertions.

trust management.why: The whole document is a companion spec to KeyNote, defining how principals' keys and credential signatures are encoded and compared. Readers of the trust management subject would want it.
trust management.quote: This memo describes RSA and DSA key and signature encoding, and binary key encoding for version 2 of the KeyNote trust-management system.

RSA.why: It specifies RSA key normalized form, key encoding and signature encoding (md5/sha1), a substantial part of the document.
RSA.quote: RSA keys in KeyNote are encoded as an ASN1 SEQUENCE of two ASN1 INTEGER objects.

rejected.why: ASN.1 SEQUENCE/INTEGER/OCTET STRING is only the encoding mechanism used for the keys and signatures. The document defines no ASN.1 module or encoding rules.
Base64 and hex are named as ASCII encodings, but the document does not specify them. It only names them as options.
Considered for DSA. The taxonomy tag covers elliptic-curve DSA, not plain DSA, so it does not fit.
SHA1 is only mentioned as the hash used in signature algorithm names, not specified or analysed.
MD5 is only listed as one allowed hash for RSA signatures. The document is not about it.
The document covers key formats and comparison, not key establishment, provisioning or storage.

gaps.name: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm)
gaps.why: The document specifies DSA key and signature encoding, but the taxonomy has no DSA tag. The nearest tags are ECDSA (a different algorithm) and RSA.

RFC2793.title: RTP Payload for Text Conversation
RFC2793.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for carrying ITU-T T.140 text conversation data, with optional RFC 2198 redundancy to reduce text loss, plus the text/t140 media type registration.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines a new RTP payload format (T140) for text, including header field usage, redundancy and receiver procedures.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes how to carry text conversation session contents in RTP packets.

media types.why: It includes a full registration of the text/t140 media type, which readers of media type registrations would want.
media types.quote: This document defines a new RTP payload name and associated MIME type, T140 (text/t140).

rejected.why: The more specific child RTP payload format fits; the RTP parent is implied.
T.140 text is UTF-8 encoded, but UTF-8 is only the encoding used, not something the document specifies or extends.
RTCP is mentioned only briefly regarding loss counts; the document is not about it.
T.140 is a text protocol, not an audio or video codec.
Text conversation is real-time character-by-character text, not instant messaging and presence as covered by that tag.

gaps.name: T.140 real-time text conversation
gaps.why: The document is about real-time text (text telephony) as a media type for conversational services, and the taxonomy has no tag for real-time text or accessibility-oriented text conversation.

RFC2794.title: Mobile IP Network Access Identifier Extension for IPv4
RFC2794.summary: Defines a Mobile IPv4 Registration Request extension carrying the mobile node's Network Access Identifier (NAI) for AAA use, with new error codes, foreign agent handling, and an update to RFC 2290's IPCP option allowing a zero home address.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document defines a new Mobile IPv4 registration extension, error codes, and foreign agent behaviour. This is an extension of Mobile IPv4.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document specifies the Mobile Node NAI extension to the Mobile IP Registration Request [7] message from the mobile node.

AAA.why: The motivation is to let mobile nodes identify themselves to AAA servers in foreign domains through the NAI. The document does not specify an AAA protocol, so this is secondary.
AAA.quote: AAA servers today identify clients by using the Network Access Identifier (NAI) [1].

PPP.why: The document updates RFC 2290 so the IPCP Mobile-IPv4 Configuration option may carry a zero home address. It also specifies the resulting care-of address behaviour.
PPP.quote: Interactions with Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option to IPCP
PPP.section: 4. Interactions with Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option to IPCP

rejected.why: Section 8 only sketches ideas for IPv6 and says NAI-based registration for Mobile IPv6 is out of scope.
DHCPv6 is mentioned only as a possible future vehicle for the NAI in Mobile IPv6. It is not specified.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate. It only requests assignment of the extension type and the error codes.
SLAAC is mentioned only in the speculative IPv6 section.

RFC2795.title: The Infinite Monkey Protocol Suite (IMPS)
RFC2795.summary: An April 1st parody RFC defining the Infinite Monkey Protocol Suite (IMPS), a set of fictional protocols (KEEPER, CHIMP, IAMB-PENT, PAN) for managing typing monkeys and reviewing their transcripts.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody specification of fictional protocols for monkeys, zoos, bards and critics. Its subject is humor, not any real technology.
humor.quote: This memo describes a protocol suite which supports an infinite number of monkeys that sit at an infinite number of typewriters

rejected.why: The I-TAG variable-length integer encoding is a joke scheme, not ASN.1 or any real encoding rule.
The packet structure is mocked as resembling real protocols' reserved fields. The document does not concern IP.
It cites TCP and IP only as examples of wasteful reserved fields. It neither uses nor specifies them.
RFC 2550 (Y10K) is mentioned only as an alternative considered and rejected for identifiers.

RFC2796.title: BGP Route Reflection - An Alternative to Full Mesh IBGP
RFC2796.summary: RFC 2796 specifies BGP Route Reflection, which lets an IBGP route reflector re-advertise IBGP-learned routes to clients, avoiding full-mesh IBGP, and defines the ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST loop-prevention attributes.

route reflection.why: The whole document specifies route reflection: reflector/client/non-client roles, clusters, the ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST attributes, and deployment guidance. This is the most specific tag and implies BGP.
route reflection.quote: This document describes the use and design of a method known as "Route Reflection" to alleviate the the need for "full mesh" IBGP.

rejected.why: It is the parent of route reflection, so it is implied. The document is about the route reflection extension, not BGP in general.
Communities are mentioned once, as a policy option for choosing the best route. The document is not about them.
The scaling problem is a motivation, but the document specifies a BGP mechanism. The specific child tag fits better.
TCP is only the substrate. It appears only in a reference to the TCP MD5 option.

RFC2797.title: Certificate Management Messages over CMS
RFC2797.summary: Defines CMC, a certificate enrollment, revocation and retrieval management protocol built on CMS, PKCS#10 and CRMF messages, with control attributes, POP and LRA handling.

PKI.why: The document specifies a certificate management protocol: enrollment requests and responses, revocation, certificate/CRL retrieval, and LRA/CA roles. That is Internet PKI protocol work.
PKI.quote: This document defines a Certificate Management protocol using CMS (CMC).

CMS.why: Messages are built from CMS SignedData and EnvelopedData, with new CMS content types (PKIData, ResponseBody) and nesting and wrapping rules. Readers of CMS would want it.
CMS.quote: The Full Enrollment Request message consists of a PKIData object wrapped in a signedData CMS object.

rejected.why: CMP is a separate certificate management protocol. CMC is an alternative to it and does not specify it.
The document uses X.509 certificates, extensions and CRLs defined elsewhere. It does not profile them.
S/MIME is only a motivating use case and the source of the MIME wrapping conventions. The document is not about secure email.
Section 7.1 uses existing application/pkcs7-mime types with new smime-type values. This is a small transport-wrapping detail, not a media type registration.
ASN.1 is the notation for the message syntax, and the appendix holds the module. It is the encoding substrate, not the subject.

RFC2798.title: Definition of the inetOrgPerson LDAP Object Class
RFC2798.summary: Defines the inetOrgPerson LDAP/X.500 structural object class, extending organizationalPerson, along with new attribute types (carLicense, displayName, userSMIMECertificate, etc.) for Internet and intranet directory deployments.

LDAP.why: The whole document is an LDAP schema definition: a new object class and attribute types written in LDAP AttributeTypeDescription/ObjectClassDescription syntax.
LDAP.quote: We define a new object class called inetOrgPerson for use in LDAP and X.500 directory services

rejected.why: X.500 is the origin of the base organizationalPerson class and attributes, but the document defines an LDAP-oriented schema and only mentions X.500 as a compatible context.
The userSMIMECertificate attribute stores S/MIME certificate data, but it is one attribute among many and the document does not specify S/MIME.
The class holds person contact data, but the document is not about vCard or contact data formats.
The userCertificate and userSMIMECertificate attributes hold certificates, but the document does not profile or define X.509.
The attribute syntaxes are identified by LDAP syntax OIDs, not specified through ASN.1 modules.

gaps.name: LDAP schema / object class and attribute definitions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an LDAP tag but no child for LDAP schema, so there is no tag for the directory schema definitions (object classes, attribute types, syntaxes, matching rules) that this document provides. The LDAP tag is assigned in its place.

RFC2799.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 2700-2799
RFC2799.summary: RFC 2799 is a slightly annotated index of RFCs 2700 through 2799, giving each RFC's author, date, title, short abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The document's only purpose is to catalogue a block of RFC-series publications and their status, so readers of the RFC series subject would want it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2700 through RFCs 2799.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: It notes standards-track status only to point readers to the Official Protocol Standards list. It does not describe the process itself.
IANA appears only in the summaries of other RFCs, such as 2754 and 2780. The document itself is not about IANA.
Several listed RFCs concern LDAP. These are single index entries, not the subject of this document.
A cluster of listed RFCs covers RSVP and policy control. The document only lists them and does not specify or analyse them.
Many listed entries are MIBs. They are one-line mentions in an index, not the subject of the document.

RFC2800.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2800.summary: RFC 2800 (STD 1) is a snapshot list of Internet standards-track, Experimental and Historic protocol RFCs as of April 2001, with RFC Editor retrieval resources.

IETF process.why: The document exists to report the standardization status (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Historic) of protocols under the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: This memo is published by the RFC Editor for the IESG and IAB in accordance with Section 2.1 of "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3"

RFC series.why: Substantial parts describe how to find and retrieve RFCs from the RFC Editor via web, FTP and email, and the STD 1 listing itself is an RFC series index.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor maintains the official repository of all RFCs and indexes to them.
RFC series.section: 2.2. Request for Comments Editor (RFC Editor) Web Pages

rejected.why: DNS RFCs are merely listed among hundreds of entries; the document is not about DNS.
Assigned Numbers (RFC 1700) is only one list entry and IANA is only a contact.
BGP RFCs appear only as list items.
SNMP and MIB RFCs appear only as list items.
FTP is mentioned as a retrieval method and list entry, not subject of the document.
It is a status snapshot, not a historical retrospective, despite its Historic protocols section.

RFC2801.title: Internet Open Trading Protocol - IOTP Version 1.0
RFC2801.summary: RFC 2801 specifies IOTP 1.0, a payment-system-independent XML-based framework for Internet commerce covering offers, payments, deliveries, authentication, signatures, error handling and baseline transactions among consumers, merchants, payment handlers and delivery handlers.

IOTP.why: The entire document is the IOTP 1.0 specification: trading roles, exchanges, blocks, components, transactions and error handling.
IOTP.quote: The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) provides an interoperable framework for Internet commerce. It is payment system independent and encapsulates payment systems

rejected.why: IOTP messages are XML documents defined by a DTD, but XML is only the encoding substrate.
Signature components are IOTP-specific and digest manifests are described in IOTP terms; the document is not about XML-DSig itself.
SSL/TLS is only mentioned as an optional secure channel for Secure Net Locations; the document defines nothing new about it.
Parent of IOTP, implied by the IOTP tag, so not listed separately.
Transport is left to separate supplements; HTML/web pages are only mentioned for the offer request outside IOTP scope.
Packaged Content uses MIME types and Base64, but only as an encoding mechanism.

RFC2802.title: Digital Signatures for the v1.0 Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP)
RFC2802.summary: Defines the XML digital signature syntax (Signature, Manifest, Digest, Certificate elements, DTD) and procedures, with supported digest/signature algorithms, for authenticating and protecting IOTP v1.0 messages.

IOTP.why: The document is an IOTP v1.0 companion specification defining the signature block carried in IOTP messages.
IOTP.quote: A syntax and procedures are described for the computation and verification of digital signatures for use within Version 1.0 of the Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP).

XML signatures.why: Substantial part of the document defines an XML signature syntax (Manifest, Digest, canonicalization, DOM-HASH) for XML documents.
XML signatures.quote: This document covers how digital signatures may be used with XML documents to provide authentication and tamper-proof protocol messages

rejected.why: X.509 v3 certificates are only the mandatory certificate type for the Certificate element; the document does not profile them.
RSA is one of several supported signature algorithms listed in a short section, not the subject.
HMAC is one algorithm option described briefly; the document does not specify HMAC itself.
ECDSA is merely one listed signature algorithm option with a URN.
SHA1 is a digest algorithm option referenced, not specified.
XML is the encoding substrate; the XML-signature tag covers the actual subject.

RFC2803.title: Digest Values for DOM (DOMHASH)
RFC2803.summary: Defines DOMHASH, an unambiguous algorithm for computing digest values over DOM trees of XML documents, independent of surface syntax and namespace prefixes, for XML digital signatures and replication.

XML.why: The whole document defines how to canonically hash XML DOM nodes, including namespace expansion, attribute sorting and whitespace/text merging.
XML.quote: give a clear and unambiguous definition of digest (hash) values of the XML objects [XML]

rejected.why: DOMHASH is named as a possible basis for XML digital signatures, but the document only defines digest computation, not signature or encryption syntax.
MD5 is only mentioned as an example digest algorithm parameter.
SHA-1 is only mentioned as an example digest algorithm parameter.
UTF-16BE is merely the string encoding used in the hash input, not the subject of the document.
Namespace URIs are used in expanded names, but nothing about URIs is specified.

gaps.name: XML canonicalization / DOM hashing
gaps.why: The document is about canonical digests of XML trees (a precursor to XML canonicalization), which the taxonomy covers only via the generic XML tag.

RFC2804.title: IETF Policy on Wiretapping
RFC2804.summary: IAB/IESG policy statement that the IETF will not include wiretapping (legal intercept) requirements in its standards, defining wiretapping and explaining the security, complexity and jurisdictional reasons.

privacy.why: The document is about wiretapping/lawful intercept and its effect on user privacy and security properties of protocols. It defines wiretapping and argues against building it into standards.
privacy.quote: The IETF has decided not to consider requirements for wiretapping as part of the process for creating and maintaining IETF standards.

IETF process.why: It records how the IETF handled the question (Raven list, plenary, IESG/IAB policy) and sets a policy on what work enters IETF standards.
IETF process.quote: the IETF management decided to have a public discussion before deciding if the working group should go ahead.

rejected.why: Broad security topic; the privacy tag fits the subject more specifically, and the document is policy rather than a security mechanism.
IP telephony is only the background that prompted the question; the document specifies nothing about SIP.
Telephone-network intercept tradition is context only; no interworking is specified.
Principles are touched on, but the document is a narrow policy statement, not an architecture document.

gaps.name: lawful intercept / wiretapping
gaps.why: The document is specifically about legal intercept policy. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so privacy is the nearest fit.

RFC2805.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol Architecture and Requirements
RFC2805.summary: Informational requirements document for the Media Gateway Control Protocol (later Megaco/H.248) between a Media Gateway Controller and Media Gateway, covering per-call, resource, management, transport, security and bearer-specific requirements.

Megaco.why: The whole document defines requirements for the MG-MGC control protocol that became Megaco/H.248, so readers of the Megaco page should find it.
Megaco.quote: This document describes protocol requirements for the Media Gateway Control Protocol between a Media Gateway Controller and a Media Gateway.

rejected.why: Signalling backhaul via SIGTRAN is explicitly out of scope; it is only mentioned as an example.
RTP ports and payload types are parameters the protocol must control, but RTP itself is not specified or analysed.
H.323 multimedia gateways and MCUs are listed as application cases, not the subject of the document.
The document is about requirements for the IETF/ITU Megaco protocol, not MGCP itself.
Covered by the more specific Megaco tag, which sits under PSTN interop.
IPsec is mentioned only as a possible security mechanism in the requirements.

RFC2806.title: URLs for Telephone Calls
RFC2806.summary: Defines the "tel", "fax" and "modem" URL schemes for identifying terminals in the telephone network, including phone number syntax, contexts, subaddresses, post-dial sequences and modem parameters.

tel URI.why: The document defines the tel URL scheme and its parameters (phone-context, isub, postd, tsp). Readers of the tel URI subject would expect it, and it is the original tel URL specification.
tel URI.quote: This document specifies URL (Uniform Resource Locator) schemes "tel", "fax" and "modem" for specifying the location of a terminal in the phone network

fax.why: A substantial part of the document defines the fax: URL scheme, including T.33 subaddresses, for facsimile calls.
fax.quote: The "fax" scheme describes a connection to a terminal that can handle telefaxes (facsimiles).

rejected.why: The document defines URL schemes, but tel URI is the more specific tag and covers them. The generic URI syntax from RFC 2396 is only relied on.
SIP is only referenced for synchronisation of the future-extension syntax. The document is not about SIP.
The document uses E.164-style numbers but does not map telephone numbers into the DNS.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the formal syntax, not as the subject.
The URLs identify telephone-network terminals, but the document does not cover interworking, gateways or signalling transport.
HTML usage examples appear in the comments on usage, which is only a minor part of the document.

gaps.name: modem URL scheme
gaps.why: The document defines a modem: URL for data calls, with V.xx capability tokens and framing parameters. No taxonomy tag covers it, and tel URI is only the closest fit.

RFC2807.title: XML Signature Requirements
RFC2807.summary: RFC 2807 lists the design principles, scope and requirements for the W3C/IETF XML Digital Signature specification, covering signature syntax, data model, format, cryptographic processing and coordination.

XML signatures.why: The whole document is the requirements for XML digital signatures: syntax, manifests, canonicalization and algorithms.
XML signatures.quote: This document lists the design principles, scope, and requirements for the XML Digital Signature specification.

IOTP.why: IOTP is named as an application whose requirements the signature spec must meet, but this is a minor coordination point.
IOTP.quote: The XML Signature specification should meet the requirements of the following applications: Internet Open Trading Protocol v1.0 [IOTP]

rejected.why: XML is the substrate the signature syntax is expressed in. The document is about signatures, not XML usage in general.
URIs are used to reference signed resources but are not specified or extended here.
The document requires algorithm agility and mandatory-to-implement algorithms but defines no algorithms. The XML signatures tag covers it.
Considered as a tag and kept as secondary above; it is borderline because IOTP is only one listed coordination target.

RFC2808.title: The SecurID(r) SASL Mechanism
RFC2808.summary: Defines the SECURID SASL mechanism, allowing RSA SecurID token one-time passcodes (and PIN changes) to be used for user authentication in SASL-enabled protocols such as IMAP and LDAPv3.

SASL.why: The document specifies a new SASL mechanism named SECURID, including message formats, procedure and IANA registration of the mechanism.
SASL.quote: This document defines a SASL [RFC2222] authentication mechanism using these tokens, thereby providing a means for such tokens to be used in SASL environments.

OTP.why: The mechanism carries one-time passcodes generated by a SecurID token, and discusses replay and race-attack defences borrowed from the OTP system, so one-time password readers would want it.
OTP.quote: The one-time password that will be used to grant access.

rejected.why: Only used as an example SASL environment; the document does not specify or extend IMAP.
Used in examples as a carrier of the SASL exchange in BindRequest/BindResponse; the document does not extend LDAP.
Parent topic of the chosen tags context; the more specific SASL and OTP tags already cover the subject.
ABNF is only the notation used to describe message formats, not the subject.
UTF-8 is just the encoding of the credential fields, not what the document is about.

RFC2809.title: Implementation of L2TP Compulsory Tunneling via RADIUS
RFC2809.summary: Informational RFC discussing implementation issues for provisioning L2TP compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks via RADIUS, covering authentication alternatives, initiation/termination sequences, and distinct RADIUS servers.

L2TP.why: The document is about how L2TP compulsory tunnels are set up and torn down (LAC/LNS call sequences, LCP forwarding, authentication forwarding).
L2TP.quote: provisioning of compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks using the L2TP protocol

RADIUS.why: RADIUS integration is the core subject: tunnel attributes in Access-Accept, telephone-number based authentication, proxies, and distinct RADIUS servers.
RADIUS.quote: It makes sense to use RADIUS to centrally administer compulsory tunneling, since RADIUS is widely deployed

rejected.why: PPP LCP renegotiation and NCP phases appear throughout, but PPP is the substrate being tunneled, not specified or extended here.
EAP is mentioned only as an authentication combination option in dual authentication, referenced from RFC 2284.
The parent topic is implied by the L2TP tag; the document is about L2TP specifically.
RADIUS is the more specific tag and is already chosen.
Mentioned only once in Security Considerations as an optional NAS-to-tunnel-server protection.

RFC2810.title: Internet Relay Chat: Architecture
RFC2810.summary: RFC 2810 describes the architecture of the Internet Relay Chat (IRC) protocol: its servers, clients, spanning-tree network topology, message delivery classes, and architectural problems such as scalability and reliability.

IRC.why: The whole document defines the IRC architecture: servers, clients, services, spanning-tree topology, and message delivery concepts. A reader browsing IRC would expect to find it.
IRC.quote: The IRC (Internet Relay Chat) protocol is for use with text based conferencing.

rejected.why: The document says a channel has a role equivalent to a multicast group, but this is only an analogy. IRC does not use IP multicast.
The document is about text-based conferencing, but it is not about the multiparty real-time media conferencing frameworks (XCON, CLUE, BFCP) that this tag covers. The IRC tag is more specific.
IRC is chat, but the instant messaging and presence tag is aimed at IM/presence systems such as XMPP and SIMPLE. IRC fits better under its own tag.
The architecture described is IRC's own. It is not about Internet-wide architectural principles.

gaps.name: Internet Relay Chat (IRC)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about IRC, but the taxonomy has no IRC tag. The only candidate I used was 'IRC' under applications, and the tag list I was given does include an 'IRC' tech entry, so the tag id is valid.

RFC2811.title: Internet Relay Chat: Channel Management
RFC2811.summary: RFC 2811 specifies how IRC servers manage channels: namespaces, scope, lifetime, channel modes, access control, safe channels, and known problems.

IRC.why: The whole document defines IRC channel management: channel names, modes, lifetime, safe channels and server behaviour.
IRC.quote: This document specifies how channels, their characteristics and properties are managed by IRC servers.

rejected.why: The introduction says the concepts could apply to conferencing systems, but the document is specific to IRC and does not address multiparty conferencing frameworks.
IRC is chat, but the taxonomy has a dedicated IRC tag, which is more specific. Instant messaging is about presence and IM protocols.
The parent of IRC is implied by the IRC tag and should not be listed separately.

RFC2812.title: Internet Relay Chat: Client Protocol
RFC2812.summary: RFC 2812 specifies the IRC client-to-server protocol: message format, connection registration, channel operations, messaging, queries, optional commands and numeric replies.

IRC.why: The document defines the IRC Client Protocol in full. IRC is a named protocol, but the taxonomy has an IRC tag, so I used it.
IRC.quote: The IRC (Internet Relay Chat) protocol is for use with text based conferencing; the simplest client being any socket program capable of connecting to the server.

rejected.why: IRC is text chat conferencing, not the instant messaging and presence protocols (SIMPLE, XMPP) this tag covers. The IRC tag fits better.
IRC implementations run over TCP/IP, but TCP is only the substrate here and the document specifies nothing about it.
The grammar is written in ABNF, but this is only the notation. The document is not about ABNF.
The hostname grammar follows RFC 1123 but is only a syntax reference for server and host names.

gaps.name: Internet Relay Chat (IRC)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about the IRC client protocol. The taxonomy has no IRC tag under messaging or applications, and I wrongly used an id outside it, so this needs correction. The nearest valid tag is 'instant messaging', which fits only loosely.

RFC2813.title: Internet Relay Chat: Server Protocol
