RFC2813.summary: RFC 2813 specifies the IRC server-to-server protocol: the global state database, server/user/service registration, SQUIT/NJOIN messages, link options, nickname tracking, flood control, and known scalability problems.

IRC.why: The whole document specifies the IRC server protocol: PASS, SERVER, NICK, SERVICE, SQUIT, NJOIN, and the state exchange between servers.
IRC.quote: This document defines the protocol used by servers to talk to each other.

rejected.why: DNS lookups are mentioned only as a non-blocking implementation detail and for authentication, not as the subject.
The Ident protocol is only used for username lookups in implementation notes.
Compressed links use zlib/DEFLATE/gzip by reference only; the document defines no new compression format.
TLS is only suggested in Security Considerations as a way to protect PASS and OPER.
The grammar is in the IRC client protocol RFC; this document only references it.
IRC is real-time chat, but the taxonomy's instant messaging tag is for IM and presence systems, and this document is specific to IRC. IRC has its own tag, and I judged the IRC tag fits better.

RFC2814.title: SBM (Subnet Bandwidth Manager): A Protocol for RSVP-based Admission Control over IEEE 802-style networks
RFC2814.summary: RFC 2814 specifies the Subnet Bandwidth Manager (SBM) protocol, which gives RSVP-based admission control over IEEE 802-style LANs. It defines the Designated SBM election, new RSVP objects (LAN_NHOP, RSVP_HOP_L2, LAN_LOOPBACK, TCLASS) and PATH/RESV forwarding rules through layer-2 devices.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with new objects, message types (DSBM_WILLING, I_AM_DSBM) and PATH/RESV processing rules at DSBMs and clients. It is an RSVP extension for LAN admission control.
RSVP.quote: This document defines SBM, a signaling protocol for RSVP-based admission control over IEEE 802-style networks.

QoS.why: It covers QoS admission control and bandwidth management for Integrated Services over LANs, including user_priority/TCLASS traffic-class selection. Readers of QoS architectures would want it, in addition to the RSVP tag.
QoS.quote: allows a system using SBM admission control combined with per flow shaping at end systems and IEEE-defined traffic control at link layer to realize some approximation of Controlled Load

Ethernet.why: The protocol targets IEEE 802 LANs, bridges and switches (802.1D forwarding, 802.1p user_priority, MAC address handling). It is link-layer Ethernet and IEEE 802 interworking for RSVP.
Ethernet.quote: The IEEE 802.1p defines a way for switches to differentiate among several "user_priority" values encoded in packets representing different traffic classes

rejected.why: Integrated Services is the service model that SBM maps onto LANs, but the mappings are in separate documents (RFC 2815, 2816). This document specifies the signalling protocol, so Intserv is background.

Reserved multicast addresses (224.0.0.16 and 224.0.0.17) are used for DSBM communication, and multicast sessions are covered in examples. The document is not about multicast routing or group management.
Token Ring is mentioned only as one 802 medium, in the user_priority and canonical-address discussion. The document is not about IP over token ring.
SNMP appears only in Section 6 as an alternative non-RSVP reservation mechanism that SBM does not address.

RFC2815.title: Integrated Service Mappings on IEEE 802 Networks
RFC2815.summary: Defines mappings of IETF Integrated Services (Controlled Load, Guaranteed Service) onto IEEE 802 LANs and 802.1D user_priority traffic classes, including default priority mappings, characterization parameter computation, and RSVP/SBM object merging.

Intserv.why: The document specifies how Controlled Load and Guaranteed Service and their characterization parameters map onto IEEE 802 networks.
Intserv.quote: This document describes mappings of IETF Integrated Services over LANs built from IEEE 802 network segments

Ethernet.why: A substantial part concerns 802.1D/802.1Q bridged LAN user_priority queuing and mapping of IP flows to those classes; Ethernet is the closest link-layer tag.
Ethernet.quote: The IEEE 802.1Q specification [802.1Q] extends the capabilities of Ethernet/802.3 media to carry a traffic class indicator, or "user_priority" field

RSVP.why: Section 5 specifies merging rules for RSVP RESV/SBM TCLASS objects and ResvErr handling in the layer-2 cloud.
RSVP.quote: Where reservations that use the SBM protocol's TCLASS object [SBM] need to be merged, an algorithm needs to be defined

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen Intserv and RSVP tags, so implied.
Parent of Ethernet, implied; document is not about a link layer in general.
Not discussed; the aggregated class approach uses 802.1D priorities, not Diffserv.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.1D bridging / SBM (Subnet Bandwidth Manager)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for 802.1D MAC bridges/user_priority or for SBM admission control, which are central to the document.

RFC2816.title: A Framework for Integrated Services Over Shared and Switched IEEE 802 LAN Technologies
RFC2816.summary: Informational framework for supporting IETF Integrated Services and RSVP-based admission control over shared and switched IEEE 802 LANs, describing a Bandwidth Manager architecture, switch/end-station models, and per-technology access latency.

Intserv.why: The whole document is about mapping Integrated Services (Controlled Load, Guaranteed Service) onto IEEE 802 LANs, including admission control and the Bandwidth Manager.
Intserv.quote: This memo describes a framework for supporting IETF Integrated Services on shared and switched LAN infrastructure.

RSVP.why: The functional model is built around RSVP and its filter styles, receiver heterogeneity and the SBM/DSBM extension, so RSVP readers would want it.
RSVP.quote: It outlines a functional model for supporting the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) in such LAN environments.

Ethernet.why: Substantial coverage of Ethernet/IEEE 802.3 framing overhead, 802.1D/Q priorities, switching, and shared/half/full duplex access latency.
Ethernet.quote: There is no explicit traffic class or user_priority field carried in Ethernet packets.

token ring.why: Detailed treatment of Token Ring user priority, reserved priority, encapsulation overhead and bounded access time, plus FDDI and 802.12 for the same purpose.
token ring.quote: The Token Ring standard [6] provides a priority mechanism that can be used to control both the queuing of packets for transmission

rejected.why: Parent of Intserv, implied by the more specific tag.
FDDI is covered only briefly and is treated as a 100 Mbps token ring. The document does not address IP over FDDI as such.
ARP is mentioned only as a lookup used for address mapping in the Requester Module.
SNMP appears only in a list of higher-layer protocols that might use the Requester Module.

gaps.name: Subnet Bandwidth Manager (SBM) / IEEE 802.1D traffic classes
gaps.why: The document centres on a link-layer bandwidth management architecture (SBM, user_priority mapping, 802.1D/Q bridging), but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC2817.title: Upgrading to TLS Within HTTP/1.1
RFC2817.summary: RFC 2817 specifies using the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism (with the TLS/1.0 token and new 426 status code) to start TLS on an existing HTTP connection, documents the CONNECT method for tunnels through proxies, and creates IANA registries for HTTP status codes and Upgrade tokens.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP/1.1: it defines the TLS/1.0 Upgrade token, the 426 Upgrade Required status code, and the CONNECT method, and it updates RFC 2616.
HTTP.quote: This memo explains how to use the Upgrade mechanism in HTTP/1.1 to initiate Transport Layer Security (TLS) over an existing TCP connection.

TLS.why: The document specifies how TLS is negotiated and started inside HTTP, including TLS-based name-based virtual hosting. It is deployment guidance for TLS on a shared port, not just a mention of TLS.
TLS.quote: Either the client or server can use the HTTP/1.1 [1] Upgrade mechanism (Section 14.10) to indicate that a TLS-secured connection is desired or necessary.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. CONNECT tunnels TCP connections, but the document defines nothing new about TCP.
The memo explicitly says it does not change the https URI scheme. It only discusses the implications for that scheme.
It creates registries for HTTP status codes and Upgrade tokens, but this is a supporting part of an HTTP/TLS document, and the IANA tag covers governance and stewardship.
Proxy-Authorization appears only as a passing example in a CONNECT request.
The CONNECT tunnelling through proxies is a proxy matter. Its security considerations are limited to a short caution about tunnelling to arbitrary ports.

RFC2818.title: HTTP Over TLS
RFC2818.summary: RFC 2818 describes how to run HTTP over TLS (HTTPS): connection setup and closure, default port 443, the https URI scheme, and server and client identity checks against certificates.

HTTP.why: The document specifies how HTTP is carried over TLS (HTTPS). That covers connection handling, truncation handling using Content-Length, and the https scheme. HTTP readers would want it.
HTTP.quote: This memo describes how to use TLS to secure HTTP connections over the Internet.

TLS.why: It gives TLS deployment guidance for HTTP: handshake initiation, closure alerts, incomplete closes, session reuse, and server identity checking.
TLS.quote: TLS implementations MUST initiate an exchange of closure alerts before closing a connection.

URI.why: It defines the https URI scheme and how a client derives the server hostname from the URI. The section is short, but it is a core part of the spec.
URI.quote: HTTP/TLS is differentiated from HTTP URIs by using the 'https' protocol identifier in place of the 'http' protocol identifier.

X.509.why: It sets rules for matching the server's hostname against certificate fields (dNSName, Common Name, wildcards, iPAddress). Certificate-profile readers would want this.
X.509.quote: If a subjectAltName extension of type dNSName is present, that MUST be used as the identity.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document notes that TLS only presumes a reliable stream and defines nothing new about TCP.
The topic fits loosely. HTTP and TLS are the more specific tags, and the document defines no web-platform mechanism such as HSTS.
The document uses certificates for identity checks, but it does not specify PKI mechanisms. X.509 is the closer fit.
The identity checks are done with certificates and are covered by the X.509 tag. The document is not about authentication in general.

RFC2819.title: Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base
RFC2819.summary: RFC 2819 (STD 59) defines the RMON MIB in SMIv2 format, with objects for remote network monitoring probes: Ethernet statistics, history, alarms, hosts, matrix, filters, packet capture and events. It obsoletes RFC 1757.

RMON.why: The document is the RMON MIB itself, defining the groups and tables that remote monitoring probes implement.
RMON.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing remote network monitoring devices.

MIB.why: It is a MIB module in SMIv2 format, with textual conventions OwnerString and EntryStatus and compliance statements. MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through. The document defines managed objects, not protocol changes, so the MIB and RMON tags cover it.
Ethernet statistics and history groups are defined, but they are monitored objects in a management MIB. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The Packet Capture group is one part of the MIB. The tag is about capture and trace file formats, which this document does not define.
The probes collect statistics, but the document specifies a monitoring MIB, not performance metrics or measurement methods.

RFC2820.title: Access Control Requirements for LDAP
RFC2820.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements for an access control list (ACL) model for LDAP directories, covering general, semantics/policy and usability requirements.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies requirements for access control in LDAP directories, e.g. ACLs as LDAP attributes and administration via the protocol.
LDAP.quote: fundamental requirements of an access control list (ACL) model for the Lightweight Directory Application Protocol (LDAP) directory service

authorization.why: The requirements concern ACL semantics, policy combination, default grant/deny, and delegation of administration, which is access control and authorization.
authorization.quote: More specific policies must override less specific ones (e.g. individual user entry in ACL SHOULD take precedence over group entry)

rejected.why: The more specific child tag LDAP fits, so the parent is implied and not listed.
The document is about LDAP. It mentions administrative areas and DNs but does not address X.500 itself.
The more specific tag authorization captures the subject, so the parent is not listed.

RFC2821.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
RFC2821.summary: RFC 2821 is the consolidated, self-contained specification of SMTP (obsoleting RFC 821 and 974), covering the protocol model, extension mechanism, commands, replies, relaying, gatewaying, trace fields, retry strategies and MX-based address resolution.

SMTP.why: The whole document specifies SMTP: commands, replies, sessions, relaying, extensions model, and implementation requirements.
SMTP.quote: This document is a self-contained specification of the basic protocol for the Internet electronic mail transport.

rejected.why: DNS MX/A lookup is used for next-hop resolution (section 5), but the document does not specify DNS itself; it is a mechanism SMTP relies on.
The Internet message format is explicitly left to a companion document (RFC 2822); this RFC only covers Received and Return-Path trace fields.
TCP is only the transport substrate (Appendix A); nothing new is defined about it.
MIME and 8BITMIME are mentioned only as the body structure and extension SMTP can carry, not specified here.
Parent of SMTP, implied by the more specific SMTP tag.
EXPN harvesting and relay abuse are brief security remarks, not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC2822.title: Internet Message Format
RFC2822.summary: RFC 2822 specifies the Internet Message Format: the syntax and semantics of text email message headers and bodies, obsoleting RFC 822.

message format.why: The whole document defines Internet message format: header fields, addressing, dates, message identifiers, and obsolete syntax. This is exactly the 'message format' tag.
message format.quote: This standard specifies a syntax for text messages that are sent between computer users, within the framework of "electronic mail" messages.

rejected.why: The envelope and transport are explicitly out of scope; RFC 2821 is only referenced.
MIME extensions for non-text bodies are explicitly outside the scope of this standard.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammar, not the subject.
US-ASCII is the character repertoire used, not the subject of the document.
The date-time syntax is only one header field's syntax within the message format, not a general timestamp specification.

RFC2823.title: PPP over Simple Data Link (SDL) using SONET/SDH with ATM-like framing
RFC2823.summary: Experimental RFC defining PPP encapsulation using Simple Data Link (SDL) framing over SONET/SDH, including a new LCP option, PSL values, scramblers, CRC and header error correction.

SONET.why: The document specifies a new PPP framing for SONET/SDH links, including path signal labels, payload mapping and scrambling.
SONET.quote: This document extends these standards to include a new encapsulation for PPP called Simple Data Link (SDL) [6]. SDL provides a very low overhead alternative to HDLC-like

PPP.why: It defines a new PPP encapsulation and a new LCP option, and specifies how LCP negotiation and default configuration interact with SDL.
PPP.quote: A new LCP Configuration Option is used to request Simple Data Link (SDL) [6] operation for the PPP link.

rejected.why: CRC-16 and CRC-32 are used for framing and header error correction, but the document does not choose or analyse polynomials as its subject; it just applies the ITU-T polynomials.
The document borrows ATM HEC delineation and the x^43+1 scrambler, but it is not about IP over ATM.
Not related; considered only because this is a link-layer framing document.
CRCs are only a framing integrity mechanism here, not the subject.

gaps.name: Simple Data Link (SDL) framing
gaps.why: The document's central subject is SDL, a length-prefixed link framing with CRC-based delineation and scrambling. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so it is covered only by the PPP and SONET tags.

RFC2824.title: Call Processing Language Framework and Requirements
RFC2824.summary: Informational RFC describing the architectural framework, usage scenarios, feature-interaction issues and language requirements for a Call Processing Language (CPL) that lets users script call handling on Internet telephony signalling servers (SIP proxies/redirect servers, H.323 gatekeepers).

CPL.why: The whole document is the framework and requirements for the Call Processing Language, which is exactly what the CPL tag covers.
CPL.quote: We call this language a call processing language.

SIP.why: The network model uses SIP terminology and SIP proxy/redirect/registrar behaviour, and requirements address SIP headers and caller preferences. SIP is the primary signalling protocol the language controls, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: A CPL script runs in a signalling server, and controls that system's proxy, redirect, or rejection actions for the set-up of a particular call.

rejected.why: H.323 gatekeepers and RAS are mentioned as an alternative signalling environment, but the document uses SIP terminology and is not about H.323.
Sieve is only cited as an analogous non-Turing-complete mail filtering language, not specified or discussed in its own right.
Mentioned in passing as a possible means of locating CPL servers; not a subject of the document.
A more specific tag (CPL, under SIP) already covers the subject, so the parent topic is not needed.
Not a taxonomy tag, and feature interactions are a section of the document rather than a tag-worthy subject here.

RFC2825.title: A Tangled Web: Issues of I18N, Domain Names, and the Other Internet protocols
RFC2825.summary: IAB statement outlining architectural issues in internationalizing domain names, showing how non-ASCII names would affect DNS, email, routing registries, SNMP, and TLS/PKI/IPsec identification.

IDN.why: The whole document is about the interoperability issues of internationalizing domain names and evaluating IDN proposals.
IDN.quote: The Internationalized Domain Names (IDN) Working Group is one component of the IETF's continuing comprehensive effort to internationalize language representation facilities

internationalization.why: It addresses i18n of text in Internet protocols, including character restrictions across protocols, beyond just DNS.
internationalization.quote: In many technical respects, the IDN work is not different from any other effort to enable multiple character set representations
internationalization.section: 2. Technical Challenges within the Domain Name System (DNS)

internet architecture.why: An IAB statement on architectural concerns: global interoperability, avoiding islands, and deployment latency.
internet architecture.quote: It is not a protocol specification, but an attempt to clarify the range of architectural issues that the internationalization of domain names faces.

rejected.why: DNS is the subject being internationalized, but the more specific IDN tag covers it; the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Email is only one example of an affected protocol in section 3.1, not a main subject.
TLS is cited briefly as an example of a protocol that relies on name matching; the document is not about it.
RPSL is mentioned in one short example in section 3.2 only.
SNMP appears only as a brief example of a protocol affected by name restrictions.
PKIX is cited as an example of reliance on hostnames, not discussed in its own right.

RFC2826.title: IAB Technical Comment on the Unique DNS Root
RFC2826.summary: IAB statement arguing that the public DNS must have a single, globally unique root administered by one coordinated naming authority, for technical reasons inherent in DNS design.

DNS.why: The whole document analyses DNS root uniqueness, update coordination and root server relocation. This is about DNS design and operations.
DNS.quote: it is not technically feasible for there to be more than one root in the public DNS

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only briefly, as a partial mitigation that still leaves an out-of-band root key problem. The document is not about it.
The document makes an architectural argument about a globally unique name space. It is specific to the DNS root, so DNS is the better fit.
This is the parent of DNS, and the document is specifically about DNS, so the child tag is used.

RFC2827.title: Network Ingress Filtering: Defeating Denial of Service Attacks which employ IP Source Address Spoofing
RFC2827.summary: BCP 38 recommends that ISPs apply ingress traffic filtering at customer-facing routers so that packets with forged source addresses outside the customer's legitimately advertised prefixes are dropped, mitigating spoofed-source DoS attacks such as SYN floods.

DDoS.why: The whole document is about mitigating denial of service attacks that rely on spoofed source addresses, via a filtering practice.
DDoS.quote: using ingress traffic filtering to prohibit DoS attacks which use forged IP addresses to be propagated from 'behind' an Internet Service Provider's (ISP) aggregation point

SAVI.why: Ingress filtering is source address validation. The SAVI tag is the closest fit for source address validation work.
SAVI.quote: restricting transit traffic which originates from a downstream network to known, and intentionally advertised, prefix(es), the problem of source address spoofing can be virtually eliminated

operational security.why: It is an operator best-practice recommendation for securing network infrastructure at the provider edge.
operational security.quote: All providers of Internet connectivity are urged to implement filtering described in this document

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a case broken by ingress filtering, with reverse tunneling as the remedy. It is a liability note, not the document's subject.
The SYN flood is used as an example attack, and the document does not specify or extend TCP.
The filtering is router-based ingress filtering. The document is not about firewall or middlebox traversal.
ICMP flooding and directed-broadcast smurf attacks are mentioned briefly as related attacks only.
Mentioned only as a caveat that 0.0.0.0 source packets must be permitted for DHCP/BOOTP relays.

gaps.name: Ingress filtering / BCP 38 anti-spoofing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for network ingress filtering or anti-spoofing practice. SAVI is the nearest match, but it is a specific IETF working group effort.

RFC2828.title: Internet Security Glossary
RFC2828.summary: RFC 2828 (FYI 36) is the Internet Security Glossary, defining and giving usage recommendations for information system security terminology for use in Internet Standards documents.

terminology.why: The document is a glossary whose purpose is to standardize security terminology across RFCs, so terminology is its core subject.
terminology.quote: This Glossary provides an internally consistent, complementary set of abbreviations, definitions, explanations, and recommendations for use of terminology related to information system security.

user guides.why: Published as FYI 36, and the glossary is tutorial in places so that security novices can use it. Readers of the FYI series would expect it.
user guides.quote: This memo provides information for the Internet community.

security.why: A broad, general-purpose security reference spanning threats, services, cryptography, PKI and policy, not tied to one mechanism.
security.quote: improve the comprehensibility of writing that deals with Internet security

rejected.why: Many PKI terms are defined, but as part of a broad glossary, not a PKI specification.
Cryptographic terms are defined, but the document is not about cryptography in particular.
IPsec, AH, ESP and IKE appear only as glossary entries.
X.509 terms are defined as entries only; the document does not profile X.509.
SET payment terms are defined, but only as a small part of the glossary.

RFC2829.title: Authentication Methods for LDAP
RFC2829.summary: RFC 2829 specifies the mandatory and recommended authentication mechanisms for LDAPv3 (anonymous, DIGEST-MD5 SASL, simple over TLS, certificate-based with TLS/EXTERNAL), the authorization identity format, and TLS ciphersuite guidance.

LDAP.why: The whole document defines the conformance requirements for authenticating LDAP clients and servers, including bind procedures and authzId format.
LDAP.quote: This document specifies particular combinations of security mechanisms which are required and recommended in LDAP [1] implementations.

SASL.why: A substantial part covers how SASL mechanisms (DIGEST-MD5, EXTERNAL) are used in LDAP binds, authorization identity, and the LDAP SASL service name.
SASL.quote: Implementations providing password-based authenticated access MUST support authentication using the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism [4]

authentication.why: The document defines authentication and authorization concepts and specifies anonymous, password and certificate authentication methods.
authentication.quote: Authentication credentials are the evidence supplied by one party to another, asserting the identity of the supplying party

rejected.why: TLS is the mechanism used (Start TLS, ciphersuite recommendations), but the document does not define TLS itself; the ciphersuite guidance is a minor part.
Certificate-based authentication is used but only briefly; certificate validation is explicitly out of scope.
Authorization identity is discussed, but it is tied to SASL and LDAP binds rather than being a general access control specification.
DIGEST-MD5 is a SASL mechanism specified elsewhere; MD5 the hash is not the subject.

RFC2830.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (v3): Extension for Transport Layer Security
RFC2830.summary: Defines the LDAP Start TLS extended operation, which lets an LDAP client and server establish TLS on an existing LDAP association, and specifies sequencing, server identity checks, closure, and effects on authorization identity (including SASL EXTERNAL).

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAPv3 with a new extended request/response (Start TLS), so it is a specification extending LDAP and belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: This document defines the "Start Transport Layer Security (TLS) Operation" for LDAP [LDAPv3, TLS].

TLS.why: A substantial part covers how TLS is established, used, and closed on an LDAP association, including server identity checking against certificates. It defines new usage of TLS (StartTLS upgrade, identity matching rules) that TLS readers would want.
TLS.quote: The client will send PDUs in the TLS Record Protocol directly over the underlying transport connection to the server to initiate TLS negotiation [TLS].

rejected.why: The SASL EXTERNAL bind is used to assert authorization identity, but SASL is only a mechanism relied on, not the subject of the document.
Server certificate identity matching (subjectAltName dNSName, wildcards) is covered, but only as part of the TLS server identity check, not as a certificate profile.
Effects on authentication and authorization identity are discussed, but the LDAP and TLS tags already cover this and it is not a cross-protocol treatment.
IPsec is mentioned once, as an alternative external source of credentials, so it is not a subject of the document.

RFC2831.title: Using Digest Authentication as a SASL Mechanism
RFC2831.summary: Specifies DIGEST-MD5, a SASL mechanism based on HTTP Digest (md5-sess) authentication, with challenge/response exchange, subsequent authentication, and optional integrity and confidentiality protection.

SASL.why: The document defines the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism, so SASL readers would want it.
SASL.quote: This specification defines how HTTP Digest Authentication [Digest] can be used as a SASL [RFC 2222] mechanism for any protocol that has a SASL profile.

HTTP authentication.why: It adapts HTTP Digest authentication, with directives and computations tied to HTTP Digest, for use outside HTTP.
HTTP authentication.quote: This specification is intended to be upward compatible with the "md5-sess" algorithm of HTTP/1.1 Digest Access Authentication

rejected.why: MD5 and HMAC-MD5 are the primitives used in the computations, but the document does not specify them.
HMAC-MD5 is used for the integrity MAC but is not what the document is about.
IMAP and ACAP appear only as example protocols that use the mechanism.
DES, 3DES and RC4 are only the optional ciphers for confidentiality protection, not the subject.
SASL and HTTP authentication are the more specific tags.

RFC2832.title: NSI Registry Registrar Protocol (RRP) Version 1.1.0
RFC2832.summary: Documents the NSI Registry Registrar Protocol (RRP) 1.1.0, a TCP/SSL text protocol by which registrars register and manage second-level domain names and name servers at a TLD registry.

domain registration.why: The whole document specifies a registry-registrar protocol with commands for add, renew, transfer, delete and status of domains and name servers. No specific child tag (EPP, RDAP, WHOIS) fits this protocol, so the parent topic is used.
domain registration.quote: a protocol for the registration and management of second level domain names and associated name servers in both generic Top Level Domains (gTLDs) and country code Top Level Domains (ccTLDs)

rejected.why: RRP is a predecessor/precursor to a standards-track registry protocol, but the document does not specify or discuss EPP.
The document requires SSL v3.0 for session encryption and mentions TLS only as a successor. It is a substrate, not the subject.
Name servers and zone file inclusion are registry data, but the document specifies registration, not DNS protocol behaviour.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.
TCP port 648 is merely the transport the protocol runs over.
The STATUS command returns registration data to the sponsoring registrar only. It is not a WHOIS directory service.

gaps.name: Registry-registrar provisioning protocol (RRP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has EPP, RDAP and WHOIS under domain registration, but no tag for this earlier proprietary registry-registrar protocol. The parent topic is the closest fit.

RFC2833.title: RTP Payload for DTMF Digits, Telephony Tones and Telephony Signals
RFC2833.summary: Defines two RTP payload formats, "telephone-event" and "tone", for carrying DTMF digits, telephony line/trunk/fax events and multi-frequency tones in RTP packets, with SDP/MIME registration.

RTP payload format.why: The document's core is defining two new RTP payload formats (telephone-event and tone), their fields, timing and redundancy.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes how to carry dual-tone multifrequency (DTMF) signaling, other tone signals and telephony events in RTP packets.

PSTN interop.why: Gateway and RTP-trunk scenarios carrying PSTN line and trunk signalling (MF, ABCD, wink, seizure) over IP are a substantial part of the document.
PSTN interop.quote: the Internet telephony gateway detects DTMF on the incoming circuits and sends the RTP payload described here instead of regular audio packets

media types.why: Section 6 registers audio/telephone-event and audio/tone media types with an events parameter and IANA event registration rules.
media types.quote: The RTP payload format is designated as "telephone-event", the MIME type as "audio/telephone-event".

rejected.why: The child tag RTP payload format fits more specifically.
SDP is used only for a small fmtp capability indication in Section 3.9; it is not what the document is about.
Only mentions jitter calculation for receiver reports; no RTCP specification.
Mentions G.723.1/G.729 as audio that tones must bypass, but defines no codec.
Not mentioned; the document concerns RTP transport of signalling events, not call signalling.

gaps.name: Telephony tones and DTMF signalling events
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag specifically for DTMF or telephony tone/event signalling; PSTN interop and RTP payload format only approximate it.

RFC2834.title: ARP and IP Broadcast over HIPPI-800
RFC2834.summary: Specifies HARP (HIPPI Address Resolution Protocol) and InHARP for resolving IP addresses to HIPPI-800/HIPPI-6400 hardware addresses in a logical IP subnet, plus IP broadcast emulation via PIBES, obsoleting RFC 1374.

ARP.why: The document defines HARP/InHARP, an ARP variant for HIPPI, with registration and operational phases, server behaviour, message formats and table aging.
ARP.quote: HARP is a combination and adaptation of the Internet Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) RFC-826 [13] and Inverse ARP (InARP)

link layer.why: HIPPI has no specific child tag, so the parent link-layer tag covers IP over HIPPI-800/HIPPI-6400 encapsulation, hardware addressing and LIS configuration.
link layer.quote: HIPPI switches can be used to connect a variety of computers and peripheral equipment for many purposes

rejected.why: Multicast is only mentioned: IP multicast is sent using the broadcast emulation algorithm, with no multicast routing specified.
IP is the carried protocol, but the document is about link-level address resolution, not IPv4 itself.
Classical IP and ARP over ATM (RFC 2225) is a model for the HARP server, not the subject.
Not involved; addresses are configured manually or by switch address discovery.

gaps.name: HIPPI (High-Performance Parallel Interface)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for HIPPI or HIPPI-6400/GSN networks; the document is entirely about IP over HIPPI.

RFC2835.title: IP and ARP over HIPPI-6400 (GSN)
RFC2835.summary: Specifies IP over HIPPI-6400 (GSN) switched networks as logical IP subnets, including LLC/SNAP encapsulation, MTU, and HARP, an ARP/InARP-based address resolution protocol with server and broadcast emulation (PIBES).

ARP.why: The core of the document is HARP, an adaptation of ARP and InARP for HIPPI-6400, with message formats, server and client behaviour, and table aging.
ARP.quote: HARP is a combination and adaptation of the Internet Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) RFC-826 [14] and Inverse ARP (InARP)

rejected.why: IPv4 datagrams are carried over HIPPI-6400, but the document does not specify or extend IP itself. It only defines encapsulation and MTU.
Multicast is mentioned only briefly. It is handled by sending packets as broadcast, with no multicast mapping defined.
Classical IP and ARP over ATM (RFC 2225) is only a model that the document borrows from.
The document fits link layer, but the specific tag ARP is a better match for its main content. HIPPI has no dedicated tag.

gaps.name: HIPPI / HIPPI-6400 (GSN)
gaps.why: The document is about IP over HIPPI-6400 links. The taxonomy has no HIPPI technology tag under link layer.

RFC2836.title: Per Hop Behavior Identification Codes
RFC2836.summary: Defines a 16-bit binary encoding to identify individual Diffserv Per Hop Behaviors or sets of PHBs in protocol messages, and creates an IANA registry for PHB identification codes for non-standard PHBs.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies how Diffserv Per Hop Behaviors (and sets such as AF classes) are identified in signalling, built on DSCP values; it is squarely about Differentiated Services.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines a binary encoding to uniquely identify PHBs and/or sets of PHBs in protocol messages.

rejected.why: MPLS support of diffserv is only cited as a usage scenario for the encoding; the document does not specify MPLS behaviour.
ATM Forum signalling is mentioned only as a prospective user of the codes.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level consideration; the main body is about the encoding, not IANA stewardship.
RSVP and LDP are mentioned only as protocols that might carry the encoding, via an external draft.
LDP is mentioned only as a protocol that might carry the encoding, per an external draft.

RFC2837.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Fabric Element in Fibre Channel Standard
RFC2837.summary: Defines the FIBRE-CHANNEL-FE-MIB SMIv2 module with objects for managing a Fibre Channel Fabric Element and its F_Ports/FL_Ports: configuration, status, error counters, class accounting and capabilities.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (FIBRE-CHANNEL-FE-MIB) written in SMIv2, defining managed objects, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

fibre channel.why: The managed subject is the Fibre Channel Fabric Element, its FxPorts, fabric login, and class of service parameters, which readers of Fibre Channel would want.
fibre channel.quote: it defines the objects for managing the operations of the Fabric Element portion of the Fibre Channel Standards.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework used; the document defines a MIB, not SNMP itself, so the more specific MIB tag applies.
Fibre Channel is a storage fabric but this document only manages fabric element hardware, not storage access protocols.
iFCP carries Fibre Channel over TCP/IP; this MIB is about the Fabric Element itself, not IP transport.
Accounting counters are per-port statistics within the MIB, not a measurement methodology.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel fabric element management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a 'fibre channel' tag only as the parent of iFCP (Fibre Channel over IP transports); there is no tag for managing native Fibre Channel fabrics or Fibre Channel MIBs.

RFC2838.title: Uniform Resource Identifiers for Television Broadcasts
RFC2838.summary: Defines the "tv:" URI scheme for referring to television broadcasts using DNS-style identifiers (or the current broadcast), with BNF and notes on obsolete forms.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme (tv:), including syntax and BNF, so it belongs under URIs.
URI.quote: In this context there is a need to reference television broadcasts using the URI format described in [RFC 2396]. This document describes a widely-implemented URI scheme

rejected.why: Identifiers are DNS-style names but explicitly are not resolved via DNS; DNS is only a naming-uniqueness model.
The identifier syntax mirrors hostnames, but the document is not about host naming conventions.
HTML content broadcast alongside video is mentioned only as a usage context.
Concerns naming broadcast signals, not media streaming delivery protocols.

RFC2839.title: Internet Kermit Service
RFC2839.summary: Describes the Internet Kermit Service, a file transfer service that runs the Kermit protocol over a Telnet connection on port 1649 as an alternative to FTP, with Telnet-based authentication and encryption options.

Telnet.why: The service is built on Telnet option negotiation (Kermit option, Authentication, Encryption, START_TLS) and defines how the server behaves as a Telnet server. Telnet readers would want it.
Telnet.quote: based on Telnet Protocol for option negotiation and Kermit Protocol for file transfer and management

FTP.why: The document positions the service as an FTP alternative, with a detailed comparison and anonymous FTP-like behaviour. It is a file transfer service, so FTP readers would find it relevant.
FTP.quote: The Internet Kermit Service resembles an FTP server in that it performs its own authentication and uses a well-defined protocol

rejected.why: The Telnet START_TLS option is used for privacy, but only as a security mechanism. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
Kerberos is only listed as one supported Telnet authentication method.
Secure Remote Password is only mentioned as a supported authentication method.
X.509 certificates are mentioned only in passing as part of TLS authentication.
Authentication is covered only as part of the service's login methods. The document does not address AAA frameworks.

gaps.name: Kermit file transfer protocol
gaps.why: The document is about the Kermit protocol and the Internet Kermit Service, and the taxonomy has no Kermit tag. Telnet and FTP are only the nearest fits.

RFC2840.title: TELNET KERMIT OPTION
RFC2840.summary: RFC 2840 defines a Telnet option (option 47) with subnegotiation codes to negotiate and coordinate starting and stopping a Kermit file-transfer server within a Telnet connection.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new Telnet option (KERMIT, 47) with WILL/DO negotiation and subnegotiations, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: an extension to the Telnet protocol to allow the negotiation, coordination, and use of the Kermit file transfer and management protocol over an existing Telnet protocol connection

rejected.why: Kermit is a different file transfer protocol, not FTP. The document does not specify or discuss FTP.
TCP is only the substrate carrying Telnet and is not discussed.
ASCII control characters are mentioned only as the allowed values for the start-of-packet octet. The document is not about ASCII.

gaps.name: Kermit file transfer protocol
gaps.why: The document is about embedding Kermit sessions in Telnet. The taxonomy has no tag for Kermit or for general file transfer protocols other than FTP and TFTP.

RFC2841.title: IP Authentication using Keyed SHA1 with Interleaved Padding (IP-MAC)
RFC2841.summary: Historic RFC specifying how to compute the IP Authentication Header authentication data using keyed SHA1 with leading/trailing key and interleaved padding (IP-MAC), obsoleting RFC 1852.

SHA.why: The document defines a keyed MAC construction built on SHA1, including digest calculation, padding and output truncation, so SHA readers would look for it.
SHA.quote: This specification describes the AH use of keys with the Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA1) [FIPS-180-1].

IPsec.why: It is a transform specification for the IP Authentication Header, part of the IPsec architecture. AH has no dedicated tag, so IPsec is the closest fit.
IPsec.quote: The Authentication Header (AH) [RFC-1826] provides integrity and authentication for IP datagrams.

rejected.why: The construction is a envelope-method keyed hash (leading and trailing key), not HMAC.
MD5 is mentioned only for performance and chaining comparison; the document is not about it.
DES is mentioned only in a performance comparison.
Key management is only referenced as the place where output size is negotiated; the document does not specify it.
The document concerns AH, not ESP.

gaps.name: IP Authentication Header (AH)
gaps.why: The document specifies an AH authentication transform, but the taxonomy has no AH-specific tag, so it is covered only under IPsec.

RFC2842.title: Capabilities Advertisement with BGP-4
RFC2842.summary: Defines the BGP-4 Capabilities Optional Parameter in the OPEN message, letting speakers advertise optional capabilities without session termination, plus a new Unsupported Capability NOTIFICATION error subcode.

BGP.why: The RFC extends the BGP-4 protocol with a new OPEN Optional Parameter and a new error subcode, so it is about BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: This document defines new Optional Parameter, called Capabilities, that is expected to facilitate introduction of new capabilities in BGP

rejected.why: The IANA Considerations section only creates a Capability Code registry. That is boilerplate, not the main subject.
BGP runs over TCP and the document cites the TCP MD5 option only in Security Considerations. It is not about TCP.
Security Considerations states only that the extension does not change BGP's security issues.

RFC2843.title: Proxy-PAR
RFC2843.summary: Informational overview of Proxy-PAR, a minimal client/server version of ATM Forum's PNNI Augmented Routing that lets ATM-attached IP devices register and discover services (e.g. OSPF, BGP neighbours) via PNNI flooding, with VPN ID scoping.

ATM.why: The document specifies a protocol for service registration and discovery over ATM networks using PNNI flooding, interworking with ILMI, ATMARP and NHRP. ATM is the best fit in the taxonomy.
ATM.quote: Proxy-PAR is a minimal version of PAR (PNNI Augmented Routing) that gives ATM-attached devices the ability to interact with PNNI devices

service discovery.why: A registration/query protocol for automatic discovery of services and peers is central to the document.
service discovery.quote: allow non-ATM devices to use the flooding mechanisms provided by PNNI for registration and automatic discovery of services offered by ATM attached devices

rejected.why: OSPF is only an example of a protocol whose neighbours are discovered. Its use over Proxy-PAR is in the companion RFC 2844.
BGP is only an example of a registered protocol, and the document says nothing about its operation.
The VPN ID is used for scoping and filtering. The document is not about provider-provisioned VPN technology as in the taxonomy's VPN tag.
NHRP appears only in the table of supported protocols and in references to ILMI-based discovery.
PNNI routing is the substrate whose flooding is used. The document does not address general routing architecture.

gaps.name: PNNI / PAR (PNNI Augmented Routing)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is a PNNI-based protocol from the ATM Forum. The taxonomy has no PNNI or ATM routing tag, so ATM is the nearest fit.

RFC2844.title: OSPF over ATM and Proxy-PAR
RFC2844.summary: Experimental RFC describing how OSPF operates over ATM PVC/SVC meshes as logical NBMA, point-to-multipoint or point-to-point interfaces, using Proxy-PAR for neighbor autodiscovery, registration and IP-to-NSAP resolution.

OSPF.why: The document specifies how OSPF interfaces (NBMA, Point-to-MultiPoint, point-to-point) are configured, registered and operated, including DR election and Hello behaviour.
OSPF.quote: mechanisms describing how the protocol operates in ATM networks over PVC and SVC meshes with the presence of Proxy-PAR

ATM.why: It covers IP over ATM: modelling VCs as logical interfaces, PVC and SVC environments, VC setup races, and ATM address resolution via Proxy-PAR/PNNI.
ATM.quote: this document elaborates on how to handle virtual OSPF interfaces over ATM such as NBMA, Point-to-MultiPoint or point-to-point

rejected.why: It is only mentioned in the references (ILMI server discovery for NHRP), not discussed in the body.
RFC 1586 on OSPF over Frame Relay is only cited as a parallel model, and the document is not about frame relay.
Classical IP and ARP over ATM and Inverse ARP appear only as alternatives that Proxy-PAR replaces, so the document is not about ARP.
Proxy-PAR does act as a discovery mechanism, but the document uses it to autoconfigure OSPF neighbors. The specification of Proxy-PAR itself is in RFC 2843.

gaps.name: Proxy-PAR / PNNI Augmented Routing
gaps.why: The document is substantially about Proxy-PAR, the ATM Forum registration and query mechanism for non-ATM services. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC2845.title: Secret Key Transaction Authentication for DNS (TSIG)
RFC2845.summary: RFC 2845 specifies TSIG, a DNS resource record and protocol that uses shared secrets and HMAC-MD5 to authenticate DNS transactions such as dynamic updates, forwarded responses and zone transfers.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS meta-RR type, error codes, and the message processing rules for clients, servers and forwarders. It is about DNS protocol behaviour and operations.
DNS.quote: To provide secret key authentication, we use a new RR type whose mnemonic is TSIG and whose type code is 250.

rejected.why: TSIG is a shared-secret alternative to the public-key RFC 2535 mechanisms. It is not DNSSEC signing or validation, and DNSSEC appears only as background.
Authenticating dynamic updates is one use case, but the document does not specify the update protocol itself.
HMAC-MD5 is the MAC algorithm that TSIG relies on. The document defines no new HMAC behaviour.
MD5 is only the hash underlying HMAC-MD5 and is not the subject of the document.
The generic authentication topic is too broad. The DNS tag is the more specific home for this transaction authentication mechanism.
The document states that key distribution is out of scope: shared secrets are configured out of band.

RFC2846.title: GSTN Address Element Extensions in E-mail Services
RFC2846.summary: Defines the full syntax for representing GSTN (telephone/fax) addresses inside Internet e-mail addresses, extending the minimal RFC 2303 format with local phone numbers, ISDN subaddresses, post-dial sequences, recipient names and qualifiers, and IANA registration templates.

fax.why: The address syntax serves e-mail-to-fax gateways (onramp/offramp), with the FAX service-selector and T.33 subaddress registered. Readers of fax-over-email would want it.
fax.quote: A pstn-mbox address in Italy for the fax service, dialled from U.S.A., using local-phone, without sub-addr-spec and without written-sep

email.why: The document extends the local part of e-mail addresses with GSTN elements and is about e-mail addressing and gateway services.
email.quote: This memo defines a full syntax for one specific case, where there is a need to represent GSTN addresses within Internet e-mail addresses.

rejected.why: It defines address content within the local-part. It does not specify headers or the message format in general.
An SMTP transaction appears only as an example, and the document specifies nothing new about SMTP.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax. The document is not about ABNF.
The IANA registration templates are boilerplate-like apparatus for the new elements. The document is not about IANA stewardship.
X.400 and MIXER are cited only for compatibility and naming. The document does not address X.400 interworking.
The document mentions that URL work is in progress but defines an e-mail address syntax, not a tel URI.

gaps.name: GSTN/PSTN addresses in e-mail (telephone-number addressing)
gaps.why: The main subject is the syntax for embedding telephone numbers, subaddresses and DTMF post-dial sequences in e-mail addresses. No taxonomy tag covers telephone-number addressing outside the tel URI and ENUM.

RFC2847.title: LIPKEY - A Low Infrastructure Public Key Mechanism Using SPKM
RFC2847.summary: RFC 2847 defines LIPKEY, a GSS-API mechanism layered over a new SPKM-3 variant that authenticates a client by password and a server by public key certificate, mimicking low-infrastructure TLS usage.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies a new GSS-API mechanism (LIPKEY), including its mechanism OID, name types, token formats and how it invokes GSS-API calls over SPKM-3.
GSS-API.quote: This memorandum describes a new security mechanism under the GSS-API called the Low Infrastructure Public Key Mechanism (LIPKEY).

rejected.why: TLS is only the analogy for the low-infrastructure model; the document does not specify or extend TLS.
HMAC-MD5 is mandated as an SPKM-3 integrity algorithm, but the document is not about HMAC itself.
Server certificates and trusted CAs are assumed; the document does not define PKI mechanisms.
ONC RPC and RPCSEC_GSS are mentioned only as a motivating use case for GSS-API.
Password authentication is the purpose, but GSS-API is the more specific tag, and the topic tag is implied only as an ancestor.
MD5 weaknesses are discussed only in the justification for algorithm choices.

gaps.name: SPKM (Simple Public-Key GSS-API Mechanism)
gaps.why: The document defines SPKM-3 as a variant of SPKM-1 and its algorithm and QOP changes. The taxonomy has no tag for SPKM.

RFC2848.title: The PINT Service Protocol: Extensions to SIP and SDP for IP Access to Telephone Call Services
RFC2848.summary: Specifies PINT Service Protocol 1.0, SIP and SDP extensions (TN network type, voice/fax/pager transports, fmtp data object references, SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY/UNSUBSCRIBE, require mechanisms) letting IP hosts invoke telephone call, fax and content-reading services in the PSTN.

PINT.why: The document is the PINT protocol specification: milestone services, architecture, gateway behaviour and parameter mapping for requesting PSTN call, fax and content services from IP.
PINT.quote: This document contains the specification of the PINT Service Protocol 1.0, which defines a protocol for invoking certain telephone services from an IP network.

SIP.why: Substantial SIP extensions: SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY/UNSUBSCRIBE methods, Require tags, PINT URLs with tsp parameter, Warning header use, BYE/REGISTER semantics.
SIP.quote: The protocol is specified as a set of enhancements and additions to the SIP 2.0 and SDP protocols.

SDP.why: Extends SDP with TN network type, voice/fax/pager transport keywords, fmtp data object references, phone-context, clir, Q763 and require attributes.
SDP.quote: A new network type "TN" and address types "RFC2543" and "X-..."

rejected.why: Multipart/related is used to carry included data objects, but only as a mechanism, not the subject.
The document explicitly says it does not relate to Fax over IP; fax is only a requested PSTN service.
Parent of PINT, implied by the PINT tag.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection option.
URI references used in fmtp lines, but the document defines nothing new about URIs as a scheme.
SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY here is a PINT-specific monitoring scheme, not the SIMPLE event framework.

RFC2849.title: The LDAP Data Interchange Format (LDIF) - Technical Specification
RFC2849.summary: Specifies LDIF, a text file format for representing LDAP directory entries and change records (add, delete, modify, modrdn) for import/export between directory servers.

LDAP.why: LDIF is the LDAP Data Interchange Format; it maps directly to LDAP operations, controls and attribute syntax, so LDAP readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document describes a file format suitable for describing directory information or modifications made to directory information.

rejected.why: Base64 is only used as an encoding for unsafe values; the document does not define it.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.
UTF-8 is required for DNs and values, but it is not the subject of the document.
The application/directory content-type is mentioned only for context, and base64 is borrowed from MIME.
Language tags appear only in examples as attribute options.

RFC2850.title: Charter of the Internet Architecture Board (IAB)
RFC2850.summary: RFC 2850 (BCP 39) defines the IAB's membership, selection, roles (architectural oversight, standards process oversight and appeals, IESG confirmation, RFC Editor/IANA oversight, liaisons) and internal organization, replacing RFC 1601.

IETF process.why: The charter defines the IAB's composition, IESG confirmation role, appeal function, and relationships with IESG/IRTF/IETF chair, which are IETF process and administration matters.
IETF process.quote: The IAB provides oversight of the process used to create Internet Standards [BCP 9].

RFC series.why: A dedicated responsibility (d) covers IAB oversight of the RFC Editor and the RFC series.
RFC series.quote: The IAB must approve the appointment of an organization to act as RFC Editor and the general policy followed by the RFC Editor.

IANA.why: The charter covers IAB oversight of IANA appointment and adds an IANA liaison seat, though this is a smaller part of the document.
IANA.quote: The IAB must approve the appointment of an organization to act as IANA on behalf of the IETF.

internet architecture.why: Architectural oversight is a core IAB role, expanded in Section 2.1 (long-range planning, charter review for architectural consistency).
internet architecture.quote: The IAB provides oversight of the architecture for the protocols and procedures used by the Internet.

rejected.why: The NomCom and BCP 10 are only referenced for member selection; the document does not define NomCom procedures.
Mentions the IAB convening workshops, but the document is not a workshop report.
Copyright statement is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC2851.title: Textual Conventions for Internet Network Addresses
RFC2851.summary: Defines the INET-ADDRESS-MIB module with SMIv2 textual conventions (InetAddressType, InetAddress, IPv4, IPv6, DNS) so MIB modules can represent IPv4, IPv6 and DNS-name addresses, with usage guidance on indexing and resolution.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining reusable SMIv2 textual conventions, plus guidance for MIB designers on indexing, subtyping and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This MIB module defines textual conventions to represent commonly used Internet network layer addressing information.

addressing.why: A substantial part concerns representing IPv4/IPv6 addresses, scoped IPv6 addresses and their uniqueness in management data.
addressing.quote: The IpAddress SMIv2 base type can only contain 4 byte IPv4 addresses.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB sits in; the document specifies no protocol behaviour, just textual conventions (covered by MIB).
IPv6 addresses are represented but IPv6 itself is not specified or deployed here; addressing covers it.
DNS names are only a value type; resolution timing is a MIB design note, not DNS protocol content.

RFC2852.title: Deliver By SMTP Service Extension
RFC2852.summary: Defines the Deliver By SMTP service extension (DELIVERBY EHLO keyword, BY parameter on MAIL FROM) letting a client request delivery within a time limit, with return or delayed-DSN handling, relaying rules, and a new Deliver-By-Date DSN field.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension: the DELIVERBY EHLO keyword, the BY parameter on MAIL FROM, and server and relay behaviour.
SMTP.quote: A SMTP client wishing to use the Deliver By SMTP service extension may issue the EHLO command to start a SMTP session
SMTP.section: 3. The Deliver By SMTP service extension

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by SMTP. The document is about an SMTP extension, not email architecture in general.
It adds a Deliver-By-Date field to DSNs, but that is a small part of the document. The DSN format itself is defined elsewhere, in RFC 1894.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the syntax. The document is not about it.
MX records are mentioned only for relaying considerations. The document does not specify or extend DNS.

gaps.name: Delivery Status Notifications (DSN)
gaps.why: The document extends the DSN format (Deliver-By-Date) and defines when failed, delayed and relayed DSNs are generated. The taxonomy has no DSN tag.

RFC2853.title: Generic Security Service API Version 2 : Java Bindings
RFC2853.summary: Specifies the Java language bindings (org.ietf.jgss package) for GSS-API Version 2, defining classes and interfaces such as GSSManager, GSSName, GSSCredential, GSSContext, MessageProp and GSSException.

GSS-API.why: The whole document is the Java API binding of GSS-API: credentials, contexts, per-message wrap/unwrap/getMIC, names, channel bindings and error reporting.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies Java language bindings for the Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface Version 2 (GSS- API).

rejected.why: Kerberos V5 is only named as an example mechanism pluggable via providers; the document does not specify it.
The Oid class uses ASN.1 DER encoding for object identifiers, but only as an encoding detail, not as the document's subject.
Parent of GSS-API, which is implied by the more specific tag.
Authentication is a service GSS-API provides, but the specific tech tag covers it.

RFC2854.title: The 'text/html' Media Type
RFC2854.summary: RFC 2854 registers the text/html media type, summarizes HTML's history, points to W3C specifications as the definition of HTML, and obsoletes the earlier IETF HTML RFCs.

HTML.why: The document is about HTML: its history, its definition via W3C recommendations, and obsoleting the IETF HTML RFCs.
HTML.quote: defines the "text/html" MIME type by pointing to the relevant W3C recommendations

media types.why: A large part of the document is the media type registration template for text/html, with charset parameter, encoding, fragment identifier and recognition rules.
media types.quote: Registration of MIME media type text/html
media types.section: 2. Registration of MIME media type text/html

rejected.why: Only referenced as a way to bundle HTML with included resources; the document does not specify it.
Mentioned as the retrieval protocol and for charset defaults, but only a dependency.
Fragment identifier semantics for text/html are described, but the document is not about URIs.
Charset parameter and default rules are discussed, but as part of the media type registration, not as a subject in itself.
XHTML is mentioned as a profile that may be labeled text/html, but XML is not the subject.
Registration is within MIME, covered by the more specific media types tag.

RFC2855.title: DHCP for IEEE 1394
RFC2855.summary: Specifies how DHCP message fields (htype, hlen, chaddr, BROADCAST flag, client identifier with EUI-64) must be used by clients on IEEE 1394 networks.

DHCP.why: The document profiles DHCP message field usage (htype, hlen, chaddr, client identifier) for 1394 clients, so it is about DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This memo describes the 1394 specific usage of some fields of DHCP messages.

FireWire.why: It addresses IP configuration over IEEE 1394, dealing with transient node_IDs, EUI-64 identifiers and 1394 ARP.
FireWire.quote: Since 1394 uses a different link-layer addressing method than conventional IEEE802/Ethernet, the usage of some fields must be clarified

rejected.why: 1394 ARP is mentioned only as the way link addresses get resolved. The document does not specify or extend it.
IPv4 over 1394 is the substrate defined in RFC 2734. This document does not cover it.
The document concerns DHCP for IPv4 only.

RFC2856.title: Textual Conventions for Additional High Capacity Data Types
RFC2856.summary: Defines a SMIv2 MIB module (HCNUM-TC) with two textual conventions, CounterBasedGauge64 and ZeroBasedCounter64, giving 64-bit gauge and zero-based counter types built on Counter64 syntax.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining SMIv2 textual conventions for use by other MIB modules, which is the MIB/SMI subject.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies new textual conventions for additional high capacity data types, intended for SNMP implementations which already support the Counter64 data type.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the textual conventions are used within; the document defines data types, not protocol behaviour. The MIB tag sits under SNMP and is the more specific fit.
The Counter64 ASN.1 tag is mentioned for encoding compatibility, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
ZeroBasedCounter32 from the RMON-2 MIB is only cited as the model for ZeroBasedCounter64; the document does not address RMON.

RFC2857.title: The Use of HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 within ESP and AH
RFC2857.summary: Specifies use of HMAC with RIPEMD-160, truncated to 96 bits, as the authentication algorithm within IPsec ESP and AH, including key length and truncation requirements.

HMAC.why: The document defines the HMAC-RIPEMD-160-96 construction, its truncation to 96 bits and its 160-bit key requirement.
HMAC.quote: This memo describes the use of the HMAC algorithm [RFC 2104] in conjunction with the RIPEMD-160 algorithm [RIPEMD-160] as an authentication mechanism

ESP.why: The algorithm is specified as an authentication transform for ESP and AH, so readers of ESP would want it. No separate AH tag exists, and the ESP tag sits under IPsec.
ESP.quote: within the revised IPSEC Encapsulating Security Payload [ESP] and the revised IPSEC Authentication Header [AH]

rejected.why: IPsec is implied by the more specific ESP tag. The document only defines an algorithm transform and does not specify the architecture.
SHA-1 is mentioned only as an alternative hash that could replace RIPEMD-160 in HMAC.
Key generation randomness is mentioned briefly, with a pointer to RFC 1750, but it is not a main subject.
HMAC-MD5 is mentioned only in the acknowledgements, so MD5 is not a subject of the document.
Automatic key management is mentioned only in passing, with no specification of key exchange.

gaps.name: RIPEMD-160 hash function
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RIPEMD-160. HMAC is the closest fit, but RIPEMD hash readers would not find this RFC under it.

RFC2858.title: Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4
RFC2858.summary: RFC 2858 defines Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4, adding MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes, AFI/SAFI identifiers, and capability advertisement so BGP can carry routing information for multiple network layer protocols.

BGP.why: The document specifies new BGP-4 path attributes (MP_REACH_NLRI, MP_UNREACH_NLRI), NLRI encoding, SAFI values, error handling and capability use. It is a core BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: This document defines extensions to BGP-4 to enable it to carry routing information for multiple Network Layer protocols (e.g., IPv6, IPX, etc...).

rejected.why: IPv6 is only one example of a network layer protocol that BGP can carry. The document does not specify or discuss IPv6 itself.
SAFI value 2 marks NLRI used for multicast forwarding, but this is only a code point. The document does not address multicast routing.
The SAFI registry rules are boilerplate-like IANA considerations. They are not the main subject of the document.
TCP is only the transport BGP runs over, and the document does not use it beyond a reference to the TCP MD5 option in Security Considerations.
IPv4 is mentioned as the existing limitation of BGP-4, not as a subject of the document.

RFC2859.title: A Time Sliding Window Three Colour Marker (TSWTCM)
RFC2859.summary: Defines the Time Sliding Window Three Colour Marker, a rate-estimator-plus-marker that colours packets green/yellow/red against CTR and PTR for Diffserv Assured Forwarding traffic conditioning.

Diffserv.why: The TSWTCM is a Diffserv traffic conditioner component that marks packets to DS codepoints for AF PHB drop precedence. The document specifies the marker, so readers of Diffserv would want it.
Diffserv.quote: which can be used as a component in a Diff-Serv traffic conditioner

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS aspect.
TCP flows are only the traffic being metered and marked. The document does not specify TCP.
The marker's probabilistic marking benefits TCP, but the document is about metering and marking, not congestion control.

RFC2860.title: Memorandum of Understanding Concerning the Technical Work of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority
RFC2860.summary: Records the IETF–ICANN Memorandum of Understanding defining how IANA performs technical protocol parameter assignment work on behalf of the IETF and IRTF, including dispute resolution via IESG and IAB.

IANA.why: The whole MoU defines the technical work, responsibilities and oversight of IANA registries and assignments, so it belongs on the IANA page.
IANA.quote: The IANA will assign and register Internet protocol parameters only as directed by the criteria and procedures specified in RFCs

IETF process.why: It sets out the roles of the IESG and IAB in directing IANA, handling appeals and disputes, and IETF liaison and Last Call review, which are IETF procedural matters.
IETF process.quote: If in doubt or in case of a technical dispute, IANA will seek and follow technical guidance exclusively from the IESG.

rejected.why: It is the parent of the chosen tags. A more specific child fits, so the parent is not listed.
The MoU mentions domain name assignment only to exclude its policy issues from scope. It does not address registry or registrar operations.
IP address block assignment is mentioned only as an out-of-scope policy matter.

RFC2861.title: TCP Congestion Window Validation
RFC2861.summary: Experimental RFC proposing TCP Congestion Window Validation (CWV): decaying cwnd after idle or application-limited periods, using ssthresh as memory, and not growing cwnd when application-limited.

TCP.why: The document specifies a modification to TCP's sender behaviour (cwnd, ssthresh handling), with pseudo-code, simulations and a FreeBSD implementation.
TCP.quote: a simple modification to TCP's congestion control algorithms to decay the congestion window cwnd after the transition from a sufficiently-long application-limited period

congestion control.why: The whole document concerns congestion window management (decay, ssthresh, increase rules). No more specific congestion control child tag (e.g. NewReno, CUBIC) fits.
congestion control.quote: The goal of these algorithms is for TCP's congestion window to reflect recent knowledge of the TCP connection about the state of the network path

rejected.why: Document concerns window validation for idle/application-limited senders, not fast recovery or retransmit modifications.
HTTP 1.1 persistent connections are mentioned only as motivation.
ssh was merely the application used in experiments.
Unrelated; no relevance beyond keyword confusion with other transport topics.

RFC2862.title: RTP Payload Format for Real-Time Pointers
RFC2862.summary: Defines an RTP payload format carrying real-time presentation pointer coordinates, icon number and button flags, and registers the video/pointer media type.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies a new RTP payload format (packet layout, RTP header usage, payload fields) for pointer coordinates.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format to transmit the pointer coordinates captured in one of the ways described above using RTP.

media types.why: A full section registers the video/pointer media type, which readers of media type registrations would want.
media types.quote: This document defines a new RTP payload name, "pointer," and associated MIME subtype, "video/pointer."

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format is defined for; the specific child tag RTP payload format fits better.
Only says RTCP SHOULD be used as in RFC 1889; nothing new is defined about it.
Remote conferencing is the motivating use case, but the document does not address conferencing frameworks or control.
Pointer coordinates are not an audio or video codec, even though the media type is registered under video.

RFC2863.title: The Interfaces Group MIB
RFC2863.summary: RFC 2863 defines the IF-MIB, the SNMP MIB module for the interfaces group (ifTable, ifXTable, ifStackTable, ifRcvAddressTable), clarifying the sub-layer model, interface numbering, 64-bit counters, and linkUp/linkDown traps, and obsoletes RFC 2233.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (IF-MIB) defining generic managed objects for network interface sub-layers, which is the core of the MIB subject.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing Network Interfaces.

SNMP.why: The document defines SNMP managed objects, including linkUp/linkDown traps and their generation rules, and the SNMP counter and agent behaviour semantics. SNMP is the management framework it extends, so SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: This memo discusses the 'interfaces' group of MIB-II [17]

rejected.why: Parent topic of SNMP and MIB, which are already tagged, so it is implied.
Mentioned only as an example of a high-speed interface (OC-48) to justify ifHighSpeed.
Used only as an example of a sub-layer in the layering discussion.
Mentioned only as an example of a fixed-length-cell interface.
IANAifType is referenced as an external textual convention registry, but the document is not about IANA stewardship.
Cited only in counter wrap-time examples; the document is media-independent.

RFC2864.title: The Inverted Stack Table Extension to the Interfaces Group MIB
RFC2864.summary: Defines the IF-INVERTED-STACK-MIB module, which adds ifInvStackTable, a read-only inverted version of the IF-MIB ifStackTable, so managers can efficiently find which interfaces run on top of a given interface.

MIB.why: The document defines a new SMIv2 MIB module (IF-INVERTED-STACK-MIB) extending the Interfaces Group MIB. MIB modules and SMI are the subject of this tag.
MIB.quote: This MIB provides an inverted Interfaces Stack Table, the ifInvStackTable.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is used with. The boilerplate in Section 2 and the Security Considerations describe it, but the document does not specify or extend the protocol. The more specific MIB tag covers the content.
This is the parent of the SNMP and MIB tags, so it is implied by the MIB tag.
The MIB describes interface sub-layer relationships generically in the ifTable. It is not about any particular link technology, though it mentions PPP and HDLC only as examples.
PPP appears only as an example of a sub-layer in the interface stack. The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC2865.title: Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)
RFC2865.summary: RFC 2865 specifies the RADIUS protocol, a UDP-based client/server protocol carrying authentication, authorization and configuration information between a Network Access Server and a shared authentication server, including packet formats, attributes and proxying.

RADIUS.why: The document is the core specification of the RADIUS protocol: packet types, attributes, proxy operation and examples.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes a protocol for carrying authentication, authorization, and configuration information between a Network Access Server which desires to authenticate its links and a shared Authentication Server.

rejected.why: RADIUS only uses UDP as transport (section 2.4 justifies the choice), and the document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
PPP PAP/CHAP is interworked with and PPP is a service the NAS provides, but the document specifies RADIUS, not PPP.
MD5 is used for password hiding and the authenticators, but only as a mechanism, not as the subject.
RADIUS is a child of the AAA tag, so the more specific tag is used and the parent is implied.
It is mentioned only to recommend monitoring with SNMP and for secret distribution, so it is not a subject of the document.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like registration guidance, not the main body's subject.

RFC2866.title: RADIUS Accounting
RFC2866.summary: RFC 2866 specifies the RADIUS Accounting protocol, which carries accounting records (Start/Stop/Interim) from a Network Access Server to an accounting server, with its packet formats, authenticators and accounting attributes.

RADIUS.why: The whole document specifies the RADIUS Accounting protocol: packet codes 4 and 5, authenticators, proxy behaviour and the Acct-* attributes.
RADIUS.quote: This memo extends the use of the RADIUS protocol to cover delivery of accounting information from the Network Access Server (NAS) to a RADIUS accounting server.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport; the document just says packets are carried in UDP port 1813 and defines nothing new about UDP.
MD5 is used only to compute the Request and Response Authenticators. The document is not about the hash algorithm.
RADIUS is the more specific tag under AAA, so the AAA parent is implied and not listed separately.
PPP and multilink sessions appear only as examples of services and in the Acct-Link-Count attribute. The document does not specify PPP.
UTF-8 is mentioned only for the encoding of text attribute values, which is incidental to the accounting protocol.

RFC2867.title: RADIUS Accounting Modifications for Tunnel Protocol Support
RFC2867.summary: RFC 2867 defines new RADIUS accounting attributes and Acct-Status-Type values so RADIUS accounting can record compulsory tunneling (L2TP/PPTP) in dial-up networks.

RADIUS.why: The document extends RADIUS accounting with new Acct-Status-Type values (Tunnel-Start, Tunnel-Stop, and others) and two new attributes. RADIUS is the protocol it specifies extensions for.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines new RADIUS accounting Attributes and new values for the existing Acct-Status-Type Attribute [1]

rejected.why: L2TP is the tunnel protocol being accounted for. The document defines nothing about L2TP itself, and the L2TP specifics are left to RFC 2809.

RFC2868.title: RADIUS Attributes for Tunnel Protocol Support
RFC2868.summary: Defines RADIUS attributes (Tunnel-Type, Tunnel-Medium-Type, endpoints, Tunnel-Password, group/assignment IDs, preference, auth IDs) to support compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks, e.g. for L2TP.

RADIUS.why: The document extends RADIUS with new tunnel-related attributes, their packet usage and encoding. It updates RFC 2865.
RADIUS.quote: this document defines a set of RADIUS attributes designed to support the provision of compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks

tunneling.why: Much of the document concerns configuring and selecting tunnels (type, endpoints, preference, assignment). The tunnel protocols themselves (L2TP, PPTP, GRE, IP-in-IP) are only referenced, not specified.
tunneling.quote: Tunnel-Type Attribute indicates the tunneling protocol(s) to be used (in the case of a tunnel initiator)

rejected.why: L2TP is the main motivating use case, but the document defines RADIUS attributes and refers to RFC 2809 for L2TP specifics.
AH and ESP appear only as Tunnel-Type values, not as subjects of the document.
GRE is only one value in the Tunnel-Type list.
IP-in-IP is only one value in the Tunnel-Type list.
MD5 is used only as the mechanism to hide the Tunnel-Password value.
RADIUS is the more specific tag.

RFC2869.title: RADIUS Extensions
RFC2869.summary: RFC 2869 defines additional RADIUS attributes for interim accounting updates, Apple Remote Access Protocol authentication, and EAP encapsulation (EAP-Message and Message-Authenticator) between a NAS and RADIUS server.

RADIUS.why: The whole document extends RADIUS with new attributes (Acct-Interim-Interval, ARAP attributes, EAP-Message, Message-Authenticator, etc.) and describes their operation.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes additional attributes for carrying authentication, authorization and accounting information between a Network Access Server (NAS) and a shared Accounting Server

EAP.why: A substantial portion (section 2.3, 5.13, 7.2) specifies how EAP packets are encapsulated in RADIUS, including message flows, retransmission, fragmentation and EAP-specific security issues.
EAP.quote: This memo describes how the EAP-Message and Message-Authenticator attributes may be used for providing EAP support within RADIUS.

rejected.why: PPP and LCP are the context in which EAP is negotiated, but the document specifies RADIUS attributes, not PPP itself.
HMAC-MD5 is just the mechanism for Message-Authenticator; the document doesn't define anything new about HMAC.
ARAP is carried over RADIUS here; the tag covers AppleTalk protocols and tunnelling, and the document only maps ARAP authentication to RADIUS attributes.
One-time passwords are used only as an illustrative EAP method in examples.
RADIUS is the more specific tag under AAA and already covers this document.
MD5 is used only inside HMAC-MD5 for the Message-Authenticator and is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: ARAP (Apple Remote Access Protocol) authentication over RADIUS
