gaps.why: Section 2.2 and several attributes (ARAP-Password, ARAP-Features, ARAP-Zone-Access, ARAP-Security) are devoted to ARAP, but the taxonomy has no tag for it. The AppleTalk tag is about AppleTalk protocols and tunnelling, so it doesn't fit.

RFC2870.title: Root Name Server Operational Requirements
RFC2870.summary: BCP defining operational, security and communications requirements for DNS root name servers, including DNSSEC signing and zone transfer authentication.

DNS.why: The document specifies operational requirements for root DNS servers: authoritative-only behaviour, load capacity, zone transfer restrictions, and update timing.
DNS.quote: The primary focus of this document is to provide guidelines for operation of the root name servers.

DNSSEC.why: Section 3.3 requires root zone signing, DNSSEC-capable root servers, and DNSSEC-authenticated zone transfers, a substantial part of the document.
DNSSEC.quote: The root zone MUST be signed by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) in accordance with DNSSEC

rejected.why: NTP is only mentioned as a means of clock synchronisation for the servers, not specified or profiled here.
Physical and network security requirements are substantial, but they are tied to root server operation and covered under the DNS tag; considered as an additional topic tag and decided against.
IANA is mentioned as signer and statistics recipient, but the document is not about IANA registries or stewardship.
Mentioned only in passing as a possible administrative access mechanism.

RFC2871.title: A Framework for Telephony Routing over IP
RFC2871.summary: Informational framework document describing the architecture, elements, and motivation for Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), an inter-domain protocol for exchanging IP telephony gateway routing tables between providers' location servers.

TRIP.why: The whole document defines the TRIP problem, architecture, elements and interactions; it is the TRIP framework.
TRIP.quote: This document serves as a framework for Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), which supports the discovery and exchange of IP telephony gateway routing tables between providers.

rejected.why: BGP is discussed only as a comparison (Section 5); TRIP is a separate application-layer protocol, so the document is not about BGP.
SIP servers and registration are mentioned as signaling servers and possible intra-domain mechanisms, but the document does not specify or extend SIP.
SLP is suggested as a possible intra-domain or front-end protocol, only in passing.
H.323 gatekeepers are cited as signaling servers; the document is not about H.323.
Gateways to the GSTN are the context, but the document concerns routing between providers, which TRIP covers more specifically.
Mentioned only as a possible intra-domain or front-end protocol.

RFC2872.title: Application and Sub Application Identity Policy Element for Use with RSVP
RFC2872.summary: Defines an RSVP policy element (AUTH_APP) carrying application identity (vendor GUID, application name, version, sub-application) as an X.500 DN policy locator so network elements can apply QoS policy per application.

RSVP.why: The document specifies a policy element carried in RSVP signaling messages for application identity, extending RSVP policy data usage.
RSVP.quote: This memo describes a structure for a policy element that can be used to identify application traffic flows.

COPS.why: The document addresses policy-based QoS control with PEP/PDP architecture, the policy framework area COPS covers; the element is consumed by PEPs/PDPs for policy decisions.
COPS.quote: RSVP aware network elements may act as policy enforcement points (PEPs). These work together with policy decision points (PDPs) to enforce QoS policy.

rejected.why: X.500 DN format is only used to encode the policy locator string; the document is not about the directory service.
Parent of RSVP; implied by the RSVP tag.
UNICODE_DN/ID sub-types are mentioned in passing only.
Policy is the context, but the document specifies an RSVP object, not an information model.

RFC2873.title: TCP Processing of the IPv4 Precedence Field
RFC2873.summary: Standards-track memo describing a conflict between TCP's strict precedence checking and DiffServ's rewriting of the IPv4 TOS/DSCP bits, and modifying TCP to ignore the precedence of received segments.

TCP.why: The document modifies TCP's connection setup and reset processing for the precedence field, so it is a TCP protocol change.
TCP.quote: The proposed modification to TCP is that TCP must ignore the precedence of all received segments.

Diffserv.why: The problem arises from DiffServ nodes rewriting the DSCP, which overlaps the old precedence bits. The memo analyses the interaction between TCP and the DS field, and DiffServ readers would want it.
Diffserv.quote: The manipulation of the DSCP to achieve the desired PHB by DiffServ-capable nodes may conflict with TCP's use of the precedence field.

rejected.why: The IPv4 TOS octet is the location of the conflict, but the document does not specify or extend IPv4. The change is made in TCP.
IPv6 is mentioned only to say that it has no such conflict.
Diffserv is the more specific tag. The document does not address QoS architectures in general.

RFC2874.title: DNS Extensions to Support IPv6 Address Aggregation and Renumbering
RFC2874.summary: Defines the DNS A6 resource record for chained, renumberable IPv6 addresses, DNAME/bit-string-label based IP6.ARPA reverse lookup zone structure, and revised additional-section processing, with transition from RFC 1886 AAAA/nibble labels.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS RR type, its processing, reverse-lookup zone structure under IP6.ARPA, and changes to additional section processing for existing query types.
DNS.quote: A new resource record type, "A6", is defined to map a domain name to an IPv6 address, with a provision for indirection for leading "prefix" bits.

renumbering.why: A central goal is making network renumbering feasible by storing prefixes by indirection so zones survive renumbering events.
renumbering.quote: This document defines changes to the Domain Name System to support renumberable and aggregatable IPv6 addressing.

IPv6.why: The document concerns IPv6 address storage and lookup in DNS, including transition from AAAA and coexistence with IPv4 A records.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 addresses are stored in one or more A6 resource records.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is only discussed in passing regarding signing of A6 chains and costs; the document is not about it.
Multihomed provider and site examples illustrate A6 chains, but multihoming architecture is not the subject.
Section 6 covers AAAA to A6 transition, but this is DNS record transition, not IPv4/IPv6 coexistence mechanisms.
Aggregatable address format is assumed in examples, but the document is about DNS representation, not address architecture.

RFC2875.title: Diffie-Hellman Proof-of-Possession Algorithms
RFC2875.summary: Defines two Diffie-Hellman proof-of-possession algorithms (static DH HMAC-SHA1 and a DSA-like discrete logarithm signature) for producing integrity check values on PKCS #10 certification requests, with ASN.1 encodings and worked examples.

PKI.why: The document specifies proof-of-possession for certification requests (PKCS #10) in the PKIX working group, which is certificate enrolment in the Internet PKI. No more specific PKI child fits, since it is not CMP, EST or X.509 profile.
PKI.quote: This document describes two new proof-of-possession algorithms using the Diffie-Hellman key agreement process to provide a shared secret as the basis of an integrity check value.

cryptography.why: A substantial part defines DH-based key derivation, HMAC-SHA1 computation, digest expansion and a DSA-style signature and verification algorithm. No specific child tag covers Diffie-Hellman or DSA, so the parent topic is used.
cryptography.quote: This POP is based on the Digital Signature Algorithm, but we have removed the restrictions imposed by the [FIPS-186] standard.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is used as a building block in the static DH POP; the document is not about HMAC itself.
SHA-1 is only the hash used inside the algorithms, not the subject.
ASN.1 structures and OIDs are given as encodings, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as such.
DH certificates and PKIX profile types are referenced and imported, but the document does not profile certificates.
The shared secret is used only for an integrity check, not for key establishment or provisioning.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman / DSA discrete-log cryptography
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Diffie-Hellman key agreement or DSA, which are the core subject of this document, so only the generic cryptography parent applies.

RFC2876.title: Use of the KEA and SKIPJACK Algorithms in CMS
RFC2876.summary: Informational RFC defining conventions for using the KEA key agreement algorithm and SKIPJACK cipher with CMS enveloped-data and encrypted-data content types, including key wrapping, SMIMECapabilities and OIDs.

CMS.why: The document profiles how CMS EnvelopedData and EncryptedData fields are populated when using KEA and SKIPJACK, so it belongs on the CMS page.
CMS.quote: conventions for using the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) and SKIPJACK encryption algorithm in conjunction with the Cryptographic Message Syntax [CMS] enveloped-data and encrypted-data content types

key management.why: A large part of the document covers KEA key agreement, UKM handling, and CEK wrapping and unwrapping with the FORTEZZA wrap function.
key management.quote: The SKIPJACK CEK is uniquely wrapped for each recipient using a pairwise symmetric key-encryption key (KEK) generated using KEA

rejected.why: Only the SMIMECapabilities attribute encodings are given in one short section. The document is about CMS content types, not S/MIME messaging.
KEA X.509 v3 certificates are referenced as sources of public keys, but the certificate profile is defined in RFC 2528, not here.
The algorithms are used but not specified (the wrap function is unpublished). The specific key-management tag fits better.
ASN.1 is used only as the encoding for the CMS structures and OIDs, not as the subject.

RFC2877.title: 5250 Telnet Enhancements
RFC2877.summary: Informational RFC describing IBM 5250 Telnet server enhancements: NEW-ENVIRON-based device name/printer negotiation, auto-signon with DES-based password substitutes, device name collision handling, and printer pass-through records.

Telnet.why: The whole document specifies extensions to Telnet option negotiation (NEW-ENVIRON USERVARs, new printer terminal types) for the 5250 Telnet server; it updates RFC 1205.
Telnet.quote: The 5250 Telnet server enables clients to negotiate both terminal and printer device names through Telnet Environment Options Negotiations

DES.why: A substantial portion (sections 5.1-5.3) specifies the DES-based password substitute computation used for encrypted auto-signon.
DES.quote: This would use the same 7-step DES-based password substitution scheme as APPC and Client Access.
DES.section: 5. Enhanced Display Auto-Signon and Password Encryption

rejected.why: The document uses SNA/LU6.2 GDS headers and APPC password substitution, but only as inherited formats. It is about Telnet for 5250 devices, not SNA interworking.
The working group is tn3270e and 3270 is mentioned as a device mode. The document itself covers 5250 Telnet, not TN3270 emulation.
Auto-signon is covered, but it is a feature of the Telnet server and is better represented by the Telnet and DES tags.
EBCDIC/ASCII conversion of values is mentioned in passing; it is not a main subject.

gaps.name: 5250 / IBM AS/400 Telnet interface
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IBM 5250 display and printer emulation over Telnet. Telnet is the closest fit.

RFC2878.title: PPP Bridging Control Protocol (BCP)
RFC2878.summary: Defines the PPP Bridging Control Protocol (BCP), a Network Control Protocol for configuring remote MAC bridging (transparent and source-route, with 802.1Q VLAN support) over PPP links, obsoleting RFC 1638.

PPP.why: The document specifies a PPP NCP (protocol 0x8031) with its configuration options and bridged-frame encapsulation over PPP.
PPP.quote: This document defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring Remote Bridging for PPP links.

Ethernet.why: A substantial part concerns MAC bridging of IEEE 802 LANs: spanning tree, VLAN-tagged frames, GARP/GVRP, and carrying Ethernet/802.x frames over PPP.
Ethernet.quote: This document extends that specification by including the IEEE 802.1D-1998 MAC Bridge[8] and IEEE 802.1Q Virtual LAN (VLAN)[9] standards.

rejected.why: Source routing and 802.5 frames are bridged, but the document is not about IP over token ring.
FDDI is only one supported MAC type for bridged frames, not the subject.
LAN FCS preservation is a bridging service, not a CRC polynomial discussion.
Tinygram compression removes zero padding from small frames; it is not protocol header compression.

gaps.name: MAC bridging / spanning tree (IEEE 802.1D/802.1Q VLAN bridging)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for LAN bridging, spanning tree or VLANs, which are central to this document.

RFC2879.title: Content Feature Schema for Internet Fax (V2)
RFC2879.summary: Defines the Internet fax content media feature tag schema (image size, resolution, color, image coding, TIFF file structure, MRC) used for capability identification between extended Internet fax systems, replacing RFC 2531.

fax.why: The whole document defines fax capability feature tags for extended Internet fax systems, with examples mapping to Group 3 fax and TIFF profiles.
fax.quote: This document defines a content media feature schema for Internet fax.

content negotiation.why: It registers media feature tags and shows sender/receiver feature-set matching, which is the media feature and content negotiation framework.
content negotiation.quote: It is a profile of the media feature registration mechanisms [1,2,3] for use in performing capability identification between extended Internet fax systems

rejected.why: Extended Internet fax rides on Internet mail, but this document only defines feature tags, not mail transport.
Feature tags are registered, but these are media feature tags rather than MIME media type registrations.
The IANA section is boilerplate for tag registration and is not the main subject.

gaps.name: TIFF / image file formats and image coding (MRC, JBIG, JPEG)
gaps.why: The document describes TIFF-FX file structures and image coding capabilities, but the taxonomy has no tag for image formats.

RFC2880.title: Internet Fax T.30 Feature Mapping
RFC2880.summary: Informational RFC defining how to map ITU T.30 Group 3 fax DIS/DTC capability bits into the Internet fax media feature schema (feature set expressions), with decision tables and worked examples.

fax.why: The whole document is about Internet fax capability identification and mapping Group 3 fax T.30 capabilities to Internet fax feature expressions.
fax.quote: This document describes how to map Group 3 fax capability identification bits, described in ITU T.30 [6], into the Internet fax feature schema

content negotiation.why: It uses the media feature tag and feature set framework (RFC 2506/2533) for capability description, i.e. media feature and content negotiation.
content negotiation.quote: A feature set contains a number of feature collections. Thus, a feature set can describe a number of different fax document instances.

rejected.why: Extended Internet fax runs over Internet mail, but this document only maps T.30 bits to feature expressions and does not address email.
Media feature tags are not media type registrations; the document does not register or define media types.
MIME is not discussed beyond the eifax context; TIFF is mentioned only in passing.

RFC2881.title: Network Access Server Requirements Next Generation (NASREQNG) NAS Model
RFC2881.summary: Informational RFC defining terminology and a reference model of a Network Access Server (NAS) and its AAA server interactions, to frame evaluation of NAS service protocols such as RADIUS and Diameter.

AAA.why: The document models a NAS and its separation from AAA(A) servers, covering authentication, authorization, accounting and auditing as the framework for evaluating NAS protocols such as RADIUS and Diameter.
AAA.quote: The purpose of this effort is to set the reference space for describing and evaluating NAS service protocols

rejected.why: Cited as an example protocol the model is meant to evaluate; the document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
Mentioned only as a follow-on protocol; not specified or analysed here.
PPP appears as an access method and authentication context, not the subject of the document.
Tunnel servers are described as virtual NAS, but L2TP itself is only referenced.
VPN use of NAS is a brief analysis subsection about customer/compulsory tunnelling, not provider-provisioned VPNs.
Mentioned only as a possible policy management interface.

gaps.name: Network Access Server (NAS) model
gaps.why: The document is about the NAS device and its reference architecture; the taxonomy only has AAA as the nearest fit and no NAS-specific tag.

RFC2882.title: Network Access Servers Requirements: Extended RADIUS Practices
RFC2882.summary: Informational survey of vendor-specific NAS practices that extend RADIUS beyond RFCs 2138/2139 (VSAs, new message codes, pseudo-users, resource management, disconnect/change-filter, policy services, accounting extensions), presented to motivate standardization in future AAA protocols.

RADIUS.why: The whole document catalogs extensions and ad-hoc practices of the RADIUS protocol, including attributes, VSAs, new message types and accounting extensions.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes current practices implemented in NAS products that go beyond the scope of the RADIUS RFCs 2138, 2139

rejected.why: RADIUS is the more specific child tag; AAA frameworks only mentioned as motivation for future protocols.
Only mentioned as one technique for checking session status for concurrent login limits.
Tunnel accounting attributes mentioned only via references; not a subject of the document.
Not mentioned; document only refers to 'future AAA protocols' generically.
Policy services section describes RADIUS-based policy proxies briefly, but the document is not about policy information models.

RFC2883.title: An Extension to the Selective Acknowledgement (SACK) Option for TCP
RFC2883.summary: RFC 2883 extends the TCP SACK option (RFC 2018) with D-SACK, using the first SACK block to report duplicate segments so a sender can detect spurious retransmissions, ACK loss, replication and early timeouts.

TCP.why: The document specifies an extension to the TCP SACK option (D-SACK), including block format rules and examples, so it is a TCP protocol extension.
TCP.quote: This note extends RFC 2018 by specifying the use of the SACK option for acknowledging duplicate packets.

rejected.why: Sender responses such as undoing window reductions are only noted as research issues; the document does not specify any congestion control action.
Fast Retransmit/Recovery is discussed only as context for false retransmits; NewReno is not addressed.

gaps.name: TCP Selective Acknowledgement (SACK) option
gaps.why: The document is about SACK/D-SACK specifically, but the taxonomy has no SACK or loss-recovery tag under TCP, so the generic TCP tag is used.

RFC2884.title: Performance Evaluation of Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) in IP Networks
RFC2884.summary: Informational performance study of ECN, using a Linux implementation on a testbed with RED routers, comparing ECN and non-ECN TCP flows for bulk and transactional transfers.

ECN.why: The whole document evaluates ECN: router marking, TCP ECE/CWR behaviour, and throughput and transaction-rate gains over non-ECN flows.
ECN.quote: This memo presents a performance study of the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) mechanism in the TCP/IP protocol using our implementation on the Linux Operating System.

AQM.why: The document reviews Tail Drop versus RED active queue management. It tunes RED parameters (minth, maxth, maxp) for the experiments, so AQM readers would want it.
AQM.quote: Active queue management mechanisms detect congestion before the queue overflows and provide an indication of this congestion to the end nodes

rejected.why: TCP is the transport whose ECN behaviour is measured, but the document does not specify or extend TCP itself. ECN is the subject.
NewReno, Reno and SACK are only compared as baseline congestion-control variants. The document is not about them.
The study is a performance evaluation, but of a congestion mechanism, not network measurement methods or metrics in general.
The parent of ECN and AQM, so it is implied by the ECN tag.
Diffserv appears only as context for transactional traffic and in the conclusion. It is not a subject of the study.

RFC2885.title: Megaco Protocol version 0.8
RFC2885.summary: RFC 2885 specifies the Megaco/H.248 version 0.8 media gateway control protocol between a Media Gateway Controller and Media Gateway, covering the connection model, commands, transactions, packages, text/binary encodings and transport over UDP/TCP.

Megaco.why: The whole document is the Megaco/H.248 protocol specification: Contexts, Terminations, commands, transactions, packages and encodings.
Megaco.quote: This document defines the protocol used between elements of a physically decomposed multimedia gateway.

rejected.why: SDP is used as the text encoding of Local/Remote descriptors, with small syntax exceptions. It is a substrate here, not the subject.
IPsec (AH/ESP) and an interim AH scheme appear only in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
RTP streams appear only as example terminations. The document does not specify RTP.
UDP and TCP transport is defined in Annex D, but it is a binding for Megaco and does not define UDP or TCP. Transport mapping was also considered but is not needed.
The binary encoding uses ASN.1, but this is only the encoding mechanism.
The text encoding is written in ABNF, which is only the notation used.

RFC2886.title: Megaco Errata
RFC2886.summary: Errata document for the Megaco/H.248 protocol (RFC 2885), listing errors in its text, ASN.1 and ABNF syntax, packages and examples, with the corrections to apply.

Megaco.why: The whole document corrects the Megaco/H.248 gateway control protocol: commands, descriptors, transactions, digit maps, packages and syntax.
Megaco.quote: This document records the errors found in the Megaco/H.248 protocol document [2], along with the changes proposed in the text of that document to resolve them.

rejected.why: Another gateway control protocol. It is not discussed in this document.
The errata fix ASN.1 productions, but only as the binary encoding of Megaco. The document is not about ASN.1.
Annex D.1 changes to UDP application-level framing retransmission are Megaco transport procedures, not UDP itself.
The document does not address IANA registries or IANA considerations.

RFC2887.title: The Reliable Multicast Design Space for Bulk Data Transfer
RFC2887.summary: Informational overview of the design space for reliable multicast protocols for one-to-many bulk data transfer, covering application and network constraints, ACK/NACK/FEC/replication throughput mechanisms and multicast congestion control approaches.

reliable multicast.why: The whole document surveys reliable multicast protocol design (ACK trees, NACK suppression, FEC, layered schemes), which is the subject of this tag.
reliable multicast.quote: In this document we attempt to review the design space for reliable multicast protocols intended for bulk data transfer.

FEC.why: Packet-level proactive/reactive FEC and layered FEC erasure codes are discussed as a substantial loss-recovery mechanism for reliable multicast.
FEC.quote: The simplest form of packet-level FEC is to take a group of packets that is to be sent, and to XOR the packets together

rejected.why: Section 5 covers multicast congestion control classes, but it is one part of a reliable multicast overview, so the multicast tag fits better.
PGM is mentioned only as one example of router-assisted NACK suppression, not specified or analysed in depth.
Parent of the reliable multicast tag, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Security Considerations briefly mention re-keying, but this is boilerplate-level and not the document's main subject.
IGMPv3 is cited only in Security Considerations for pruning unwanted senders.

RFC2888.title: Secure Remote Access with L2TP
RFC2888.summary: Informational RFC proposing a Secure Remote Access Server that combines an L2TP LNS with an IPsec security gateway, and defines three new RADIUS attributes (IPSEC_MANDATE, SECURITY_PROFILE, IKE_NEGOTIATION_PROFILE) to mandate IPsec for dial-in users coming through the Internet.

L2TP.why: The document builds the secure remote access model on L2TP LAC/LNS tunnelling and discusses its limitations and operation.
L2TP.quote: L2TP protocol is a virtual extension of PPP across IP network infrastructure.

IPsec.why: The core proposal is mandating tunnel-mode IPsec (AH/ESP, IKE) for PPP-carried IP packets at a combined LNS/security gateway.
IPsec.quote: The objective of this document is to extend security characteristics of IPsec to remote access users, as they dial-in through the Internet.

RADIUS.why: The document defines three new RADIUS attributes to configure the SRAS's security behaviour per user.
RADIUS.quote: A new RADIUS attribute IPSEC_MANDATE (91) may be defined for each user.

rejected.why: PPP is the carried link protocol and is discussed (LCP, EAP), but the document does not specify or extend PPP itself.
EAP is only suggested as a way to unify LCP and IKE authentication; not a substantial part of the document.
IKE is used for dynamic key negotiation and referenced in a RADIUS profile, but the document does not specify IKE; IPsec covers it.
Firewall and security gateway placement is discussed as background for the SRAS model, not as the subject.

RFC2889.title: Benchmarking Methodology for LAN Switching Devices
RFC2889.summary: RFC 2889 defines benchmarking methodology for LAN switching devices (MAC-layer Ethernet switches), extending RFC 2544 with tests for meshed throughput, congestion control, forwarding rate, address caching and learning, errored frame filtering, and broadcast latency.

benchmarking.why: The whole document specifies benchmarking test procedures, setup parameters and reporting formats for LAN switches, which is exactly the benchmarking methodology subject.
benchmarking.quote: This document is intended to provide methodology for the benchmarking of local area network (LAN) switching devices.

rejected.why: Ethernet frames and IEEE 802.3 are the test medium, but the document is about benchmarking methodology rather than IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Benchmarking is the more specific child-like subject for lab device testing; this is not active or passive network performance measurement.
Section 5.5 tests head-of-line blocking and backpressure of a device, but it does not specify congestion control algorithms.
The tested devices work at the MAC layer, but the document addresses test methodology, not link-layer protocols.

RFC2890.title: Key and Sequence Number Extensions to GRE
RFC2890.summary: Extends GRE with optional Key (traffic-flow identification) and Sequence Number (in-order delivery) header fields, specifying their bits, formats, and receiver sequencing/buffering behaviour.

GRE.why: The whole document defines extensions to the GRE header, adding Key and Sequence Number fields and their processing rules.
GRE.quote: This document describes extensions by which two fields, Key and Sequence Number, can be optionally carried in the GRE Header

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a required protection for the GRE tunnel; the document does not specify or extend IPsec.
Referenced only in Security Considerations as a protection mechanism; not the subject.
Parent of GRE, which is the more specific tag and already implies it.
Not discussed; GRE is the encapsulation being extended.

RFC2891.title: LDAP Control Extension for Server Side Sorting of Search Results
RFC2891.summary: Defines two LDAPv3 controls (sort request and sort response) letting a client ask the server to sort search results by specified attribute types and matching rules, with client-server behaviour, chaining, and paged-results interaction.

LDAP.why: The document specifies new LDAP controls extending search operations, so it belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: This document describes two LDAPv3 control extensions for server side sorting of search results.

rejected.why: ASN.1 and BER are only used to define the control values; the document is not about ASN.1.
Implied as the parent of LDAP; the more specific LDAP tag is used.
Not about X.500; matching rules and attribute types are LDAP concepts here.

RFC2892.title: The Cisco SRP MAC Layer Protocol
RFC2892.summary: Specifies Cisco's Spatial Reuse Protocol (SRP) v2, a ring-based MAC layer protocol with packet formats, a fairness algorithm, topology discovery, and SONET BLSR-style Intelligent Protection Switching, usable over SONET/SDH and other point-to-point media.

link layer.why: The whole document defines a new data-link/MAC protocol for ring media (header, fairness, protection switching). No more specific link-layer tag fits SRP itself.
link layer.quote: This document specifies the MAC layer protocol, "Spatial Reuse Protocol" (SRP) for use with ring based media.

SONET.why: A dedicated section covers running SRP over SONET/SDH (POS framing, STS-Nc mapping, interaction with SONET protection). IPS is modelled on SONET BLSR.
SONET.quote: SRP over SONET/SDH is the first media type perceived for SRP applications.

rejected.why: SRP supports carrying ATM cells, but this is a minor mode and the document is not about IP over ATM.
It reuses the RFC 1662/POS CRC-32 and does not define or choose generator polynomials.
The SRP fairness algorithm governs ring access at the MAC layer, not transport congestion control.
It borrows POS/PPP HDLC-like framing and the CRC, but the document is not about PPP.
The frame format after the SRP header resembles Ethernet v2, but the document is not about Ethernet.

gaps.name: Spatial Reuse Protocol (SRP) / ring MAC protocols with protection switching
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ring-based MAC protocols or Resilient Packet Ring-style technologies. The document is therefore only tagged to the generic link layer topic.

RFC2893.title: Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 Hosts and Routers
RFC2893.summary: Specifies IPv6/IPv4 transition mechanisms for hosts and routers: dual-stack operation, configured and automatic IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling, and IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses (obsoletes RFC 1933).

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document defines transition mechanisms (dual stack, configured and automatic tunneling) for IPv6/IPv4 coexistence. No more specific child tag fits, since 6to4, ISATAP and similar are other documents.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document specifies IPv4 compatibility mechanisms that can be implemented by IPv6 hosts and routers.

tunneling.why: Sections 3-5 specify encapsulation, MTU/fragmentation, hop limit, ICMP error handling and decapsulation for IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels. This is generic tunneling, so it is tagged directly, since no child tag (GRE, IP-in-IP) matches.
tunneling.quote: IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling: The technique of encapsulating IPv6 packets within IPv4 so that they can be carried across IPv4 routing infrastructures.

rejected.why: Section 2.2-2.3 covers resolver handling of A/A6/AAAA records during transition, but this is a minor part of the document and DNS is not specified or extended.
The document is about transition rather than the IPv6 specification itself. The more specific IPv6 transition tag applies.
ICMP error handling in tunnels is discussed, but ICMP is not the subject of the document.
Path MTU Discovery is used for tunnel MTU determination but is a mechanism the document relies on, not one it defines.
The encapsulation is IPv6 in IPv4 (protocol 41), not IP-in-IP as defined for IPv4-in-IPv4.
Section 3.8 says how Neighbor Discovery applies to tunnels, but it is a short subsection and not a subject of the document.

RFC2894.title: Router Renumbering for IPv6
RFC2894.summary: Defines the Router Renumbering (RR) protocol, carried in ICMPv6 type 138, letting a management station command IPv6 routers to add, change or delete interface prefixes site-wide, with IPsec authentication, replay protection and reliability guidance.

renumbering.why: The whole document specifies a router renumbering mechanism, including prefix control operations and examples of renumbering a subnet and global prefixes.
renumbering.quote: This document defines a mechanism called Router Renumbering ("RR") which allows address prefixes on routers to be configured and reconfigured

IPv6.why: It is an IPv6-specific protocol that interacts with Neighbor Discovery prefix advertisement and IPv6 addressing, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: Router Renumbering messages are carried in ICMPv6 packets with Type = 138.

ICMP.why: It defines a new ICMPv6 message type (138) with Command, Result and Sequence Number Reset codes.
ICMP.quote: The three types of messages are distinguished the ICMPv6 "Code" field and differ in the contents of the "Message Body" field.

rejected.why: IPsec AH/ESP is required to authenticate RR messages, but the document only uses it as a security mechanism and gives SPD/SAD entry advice.
RR affects the prefixes and flags advertised in Router Advertisements, but it does not extend or specify Neighbor Discovery itself.
SNMP is mentioned only for the interface index and for peeking at OSPF to list routers.
OSPF is mentioned only as a way to discover the set of routers.
RR is a configuration mechanism, but the renumbering tag is more specific.

RFC2895.title: Remote Network Monitoring MIB Protocol Identifier Reference
RFC2895.summary: Defines the notation and encoding rules for protocol identifier strings used as INDEX values in the RMON-2 protocolDirTable, plus the base layer identifiers (ether2, llc, snap, vsnap, ianaAssigned) and the 802.1Q encapsulation layer.

RMON.why: The document is a normative companion to the RMON-2 MIB, defining protocolDirID and protocolDirParameters encoding.
RMON.quote: This memo defines a notation describing protocol layers in a protocol encapsulation, specifically for use in encoding INDEX values for the protocolDirTable, found in the RMON-2 MIB

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework boilerplate; the document says it specifies no MIB module.
The document explicitly does not specify a MIB module; it defines encoding rules for index strings.
ether2/llc/snap are base-layer identifier values for monitoring, not about IP over Ethernet.
ATM-RMON relationship is a brief note on mapping encapsulations and counting, not the subject.

gaps.name: RMON (Remote Network Monitoring)
gaps.why: The document is about the RMON-2 protocol directory, but the taxonomy has no RMON tag in the selected form; the nearest ids are RMON under network management. I used id RMON, which does exist in taxonomy as a tech under SNMP.

RFC2896.title: Remote Network Monitoring MIB Protocol Identifier Macros
RFC2896.summary: Informational, non-normative collection of RMON-2 protocol identifier macros (PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER definitions for TCP/IP, IPX, XNS, AppleTalk, Vines, DECnet, SNA, NetBIOS) used to build protocolDirTable INDEX values.

RMON.why: The document exists to supply protocol identifier macros for the RMON-2 MIB protocolDirTable, so RMON readers need it.
RMON.quote: protocol identifier examples, which can be used to produce valid protocolDirTable INDEX encodings, as defined by the Remote Network Monitoring MIB (Management Information Base) Version 2

rejected.why: The memo explicitly says it does not specify a MIB module; it only supplies identifier examples for an existing one.
The SNMP framework section is boilerplate and SNMP appears only as one of many listed protocols.
TCP, UDP, IP and the many other protocols are only entries in a catalogue of identifiers, not specified or analysed here.
Novell IPX is one stack among many catalogued; the document is not about it.
Only a single SNA identifier macro is given.

gaps.name: RMON (Remote Network Monitoring) protocol identifiers
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists RMON under network management, but I used the id 'RMON' on the assumption that it exists. The taxonomy shown has an RMON tech tag under SNMP, so it is valid.

RFC2897.title: Proposal for an MGCP Advanced Audio Package
RFC2897.summary: Proposes a new MGCP event/signal package (AU, Advanced Audio) controlling an Audio Resource Function for IVR operations PlayAnnouncement, PlayCollect and PlayRecord, with audio segments, variables, selectors, aliases and a formal syntax.

MGCP.why: The document defines a new MGCP package with events, signals, parameters and return codes, extending MGCP.
MGCP.quote: This document is a proposal to add a new event/signal package to the MGCP (Media Gateway Control Protocol) protocol to control an ARF

rejected.why: Only referenced for digit map syntax and the DTMF detection package; the document extends MGCP, not Megaco.
Parent of MGCP; implied, and the document is about a specific MGCP package rather than broad PSTN interworking.
Speech services control is related in function (IVR, text-to-speech) but the document does not define or extend MRCP.
The formal syntax is ABNF, but only as a notation for the package syntax, not the subject.

gaps.name: IVR (Interactive Voice Response) audio server control
gaps.why: The document is about announcement, digit collection and recording by an audio server, which the taxonomy has no tag for apart from MGCP itself.

RFC2898.title: PKCS #5: Password-Based Cryptography Specification Version 2.0
RFC2898.summary: RFC 2898 republishes PKCS #5 v2.0, specifying password-based key derivation functions (PBKDF1, PBKDF2), encryption schemes (PBES1, PBES2), the PBMAC1 message authentication scheme, and their ASN.1 syntax.

PBKDF2.why: The document specifies PBKDF2, its salt and iteration count, and its ASN.1 parameters. It is the recommended KDF and underlies PBES2 and PBMAC1.
PBKDF2.quote: PBKDF2 applies a pseudorandom function (see Appendix B.1 for an example) to derive keys.

password hashing.why: The document covers password-based key derivation with salt and iteration count to resist dictionary and search attacks. PBKDF1 is also covered, so the parent topic applies beyond PBKDF2 alone.
password hashing.quote: Another approach to password-based cryptography is to construct key derivation techniques that are relatively expensive, thereby increasing the cost of exhaustive search.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to identify algorithms and parameters. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
HMAC-SHA-1 is only the default pseudorandom function and an example MAC. The document does not specify HMAC.
DES and RC2 appear as underlying ciphers in PBES1 and as examples. The document does not define them.
MD2, MD5 and SHA-1 are only the hash options for PBKDF1. The document does not define them.
Key derivation from passwords is covered more specifically by the password hashing and PBKDF2 tags.
Password-based key exchange protocols are explicitly out of scope.

gaps.name: Password-based encryption (PBES1/PBES2) and PBMAC1
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for password-based encryption or MAC schemes, or for the PKCS series. The nearest fits are the password hashing and cryptography topics.

RFC2899.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 2800-2899
RFC2899.summary: RFC 2899 is an annotated summary list of the 100 RFCs numbered 2800 through 2899, giving each one's author, date, title, short abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The document is a catalogue of a block of the RFC series. A reader browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find it there.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2800 through RFCs 2899.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: It notes standards-track status, but only as annotations on the listed RFCs. It does not describe the process itself.
It lists RFC 2860, the IANA MoU, as one entry among 100. The document is not about IANA.
Several listed RFCs cover RADIUS, but each is only a one-line entry. The document is not about the protocol.
RFCs 2810-2813 are listed, but only as summary entries.
The list is a status report, not a history or retrospective.

RFC2900.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC2900.summary: RFC 2900 (STD 1) is a July 2001 snapshot listing the Internet standards-track, BCP, Experimental and Historic RFCs by maturity level, plus pointers to RFC Editor resources.

IETF process.why: The memo's purpose is to report the standardization status (Standard, Draft, Proposed, BCP, Experimental, Historic) of protocols under the IETF standards process (RFC 2026).
IETF process.quote: a snapshot of the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet

RFC series.why: The memo is an index-style publication of the RFC series and explains how to retrieve and search RFCs by web, FTP and email.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor maintains the official repository of all RFCs and indexes to them.
RFC series.section: 2.2. Request for Comments Editor (RFC Editor) Web Pages

rejected.why: IANA appears only as a contact and in BCP titles listed in tables; the document is not about IANA registries.
DNS RFCs are merely entries in the lists; the document does not address DNS itself.
BGP specifications are only listed entries, not the subject.
Many SNMP/MIB RFCs appear in the tables, but only as list items.
FTP is used as a retrieval method and its RFCs are listed, but the document is not about FTP.
Listing RFC 2119 as a BCP does not make the document about requirements language.

RFC2901.title: Guide to Administrative Procedures of the Internet Infrastructure
RFC2901.summary: An informational FYI guide walking new networks through the administrative steps for joining the Internet: obtaining IP address space from ISPs and regional registries, ASNs, routing registry (IRR/RADB) registration, country-code domain registration, and IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation.

addressing.why: The core of the guide is how to request, justify and register IP address space through ISPs, LIRs and the RIRs (ARIN, APNIC, RIPE NCC), including CIDR sizing and renumbering considerations.
addressing.quote: STEP TWO: OBTAIN ADDRESS SPACE ALLOCATION AND REGISTRATION FROM THE ISP YOU ARE CONNECTING TO, OR (AS A LAST RESORT) YOUR REGIONAL REGISTRY.

user guides.why: This is FYI 37, an introductory how-to guide for network operators new to the Internet administrative infrastructure.
user guides.quote: This information is intended to help new or expanding networks understand and follow the Internet administrative procedures

RPSL.why: A full section covers registering maintainer, aut-num and route objects in the IRR/RADB and the transition to the Routing Policy Specification Language.
RPSL.quote: The Internet Routing Registry (IRR) describes registries maintained by several national and international networking organizations.
RPSL.section: IV.C How do I choose a routing database?

domain registration.why: A section covers ccTLD registration, IANA's role, second-level registration and domain disputes. It also covers IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation requests through the registries.
domain registration.quote: To apply to manage a country code top-level domain you should:
domain registration.section: V.B How do I register as a country domain?

CIDR.why: The guide explains CIDR, gives a prefix/mask table, and ties allocation sizes to bit boundaries and aggregation.
CIDR.quote: CIDR stands for Classless Inter-Domain Routing.  Historically, IP addresses were assigned within classes

rejected.why: DNS is touched on only for ccTLDs and reverse delegation as registration procedures. The document does not specify or analyse DNS protocol or operations.
BGP4 is mentioned only in passing for route registration and multi-homing. The document is not about the protocol.
Multi-homing drives the decisions about ASNs and address space, but it is not treated as an architecture topic in its own right.
IANA and ICANN are described as agencies in an appendix and as the ccTLD registrar. The document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
The whois command and whois.ra.net queries are mentioned as practical tools only. The document is not about the WHOIS protocol.
Renumbering is mentioned only as a cost of taking provider-assigned space, not as a procedure.

gaps.name: Regional Internet Registry procedures / Internet number resource management
gaps.why: The document is mainly about RIR, LIR and ISP address and ASN allocation and registration policy and forms. The taxonomy has only the generic addressing tag, and no specific tag for ASN or number-resource administration.

RFC2902.title: Overview of the 1998 IAB Routing Workshop
RFC2902.summary: Overview of the March 1998 IAB routing workshop, summarizing discussions, conclusions and action items on unicast routing scaling, NAT, multicast, routing stability, QoS, routing security, BGP policy, anycast and other topics.

routing architecture.why: The core of the workshop is scaling and architecture of Internet routing: flaps, multihoming, hierarchy levels, and candidate solutions.
routing architecture.quote: Most of the current unicast routing stability problems can be fixed with improved implementation.

multicast.why: A dedicated section evaluates multicast routing model and protocols (DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM, CBT, Express) and scaling.
multicast.quote: The group acknowledged that the current multicast model does not scale well for all scenarios that applications use.

NAT.why: A section discusses NAT deployment, its problems and options for the Internet.
NAT.quote: Identified various problems with the use of NAT devices within the internet

routing security.why: Section on securing routers and routing protocols with conclusions and action items.
routing security.quote: The IETF should encourage work on "wire speed" authentication, pair-wise authentication of routers in routing protocols

anycast.why: Short topic with conclusions on anycast advantages and well-known anycast addresses.
anycast.quote: A BOF should be held to plan work on anycast.

RPSL.why: Routing policy and BGP policy discussion concludes a better policy specification language is needed and raises RPSL concerns.
RPSL.quote: Pass the concerns about the Routing Policy Syntax Language (RPSL) [1] to chairs of the Routing Policy Syntax (RPS) working group

rejected.why: BGP policy limitations are discussed in one section, but the document is not about the protocol itself; RPSL and routing architecture cover it better.
Fits as a document type (IAB workshop report), but a more specific subject set was chosen; it would be a reasonable additional tag.
ToS/CoS/QoS terminology and constraint-based routing are discussed briefly without specifying QoS mechanisms.
Renumbering and geographical addressing were mentioned but explicitly discussed without conclusions.
Only a brief remark that OSPF should support richer metrics.
SNMPv3 is mentioned only as a tool recommendation.

RFC2903.title: Generic AAA Architecture
RFC2903.summary: RFC 2903 proposes a generic AAA server architecture with Application Specific Modules, multi-domain forwarding among AAA servers, and a layered AAA protocol model (application, presentation, transaction/session management, transport).

AAA.why: The whole document defines a generic AAA architecture: rule-based authorization engine, ASMs, multi-domain AAA server forwarding and a layered AAA protocol model. It fits the AAA frameworks tag exactly.
AAA.quote: This memo proposes an Authentication, Authorization, Accounting (AAA) architecture that would incorporate a generic AAA server along with an application interface

rejected.why: RADIUS is only discussed as a legacy protocol to be encapsulated via an AAA gateway and as an AVP example; the document does not specify or extend it.
Diameter is mentioned only in a protocol stack example figure, not as a subject of the document.
Authorization is central, but the AAA tag is the more specific fit for this AAA framework, so the broader topic is not added.
COPS appears only as one example presentation-layer protocol in the stack figure.
KeyNote is cited only as an analogy for the policy server idea.
IPsec is mentioned in Security Considerations as a possible hop-by-hop protection mechanism, which is boilerplate-level substrate use.

RFC2904.title: AAA Authorization Framework
RFC2904.summary: Informational framework from the AAAarch RG describing entities, trust relationships, message sequences (agent/pull/push), policy, attribute certificates, resource management and security requirements for multi-domain authorization of Internet services, as a basis for deriving AAA authorization protocol requirements.

AAA.why: The whole document is an AAA authorization architecture: entities, roaming, distributed services, resource manager, message forwarding, and end-to-end security for AAA servers.
AAA.quote: It presents an architectural framework for understanding the authorization of Internet resources and services and derives requirements for authorization protocols.

authorization.why: Authorization decisions, policy retrieval, evaluation and enforcement points (PDP/PEP), and attribute certificates for authorization data are substantial parts of the document.
authorization.quote: One view of an authorization is that it is the result of evaluating policies of each organization that has an interest in the authorization decision.

rejected.why: RADIUS is mentioned only as an example (NAS with RADIUS server) and as a protocol with roaming weaknesses; it is not specified or analysed here.
Attribute certificates are described conceptually, based on PKIX work, but the document does not profile or specify X.509 certificates.
Policy framework is discussed in relation to authorization, but the document is not about policy information models; authorization covers it.
Diameter is not mentioned or specified; the document is a generic framework, not tied to it.
Certificate authorities and CRLs appear only in passing in the streamlined process section.

RFC2905.title: AAA Authorization Application Examples
RFC2905.summary: Informational memo giving five application examples (PPP dialin roaming, Mobile-IP, Bandwidth Broker, Internet printing, e-commerce, distance learning) modelled on the AAA authorization framework to derive requirements for a generic AAA authorization protocol.

AAA.why: The whole memo explores AAA authorization requirements through application examples, using AAA servers, brokers and roaming models.
AAA.quote: examples of applications requiring authorization. Each application is described in terms of a consistent framework

Mobile IPv4.why: A full section develops the Mobile-IP multi-domain AAA model, key distribution and authorization requirements.
Mobile IPv4.quote: The Mobile-IP protocol is used to manage mobility of an IP host across IP subnets

QoS.why: A large section covers bandwidth broker authorization of QoS resource allocation, SLSs and inter-domain signalling.
QoS.quote: describes authorization aspects derived from the Bandwidth Broker architecture as discussed within the Internet2 Qbone BB Advisory Council

e-commerce.why: A dedicated section analyses SET trust and contractual relationships and derives e-commerce authorization requirements.
e-commerce.quote: This section will examine one e-commerce protocol called SET (Secure Electronic Transaction) that provides for credit and debit card payments.

rejected.why: PPP dialin is only the example scenario; the memo is about authorization, not PPP itself.
RADIUS is mentioned only as a possible AAA protocol for the NAS-to-server hop.
IPP print-by-reference is a brief illustration, explicitly not an IPP WG product.
The more specific AAA tag fits better.
Certificates and CAs appear in the SET and bandwidth broker examples but only as trust mechanisms.
Mentioned only as a possible intra-domain protocol between a bandwidth broker and routers.

RFC2906.title: AAA Authorization Requirements
RFC2906.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements that AAA protocols must meet to support authorization services (attributes, security, time, topology, proxying, trust, administration, negotiation), derived from mobile-IP, roamops and other application studies.

AAA.why: The whole document is a list of requirements for AAA protocols and authorization, so it belongs under the AAA frameworks tag.
AAA.quote: specifies the requirements that Authentication Authorization Accounting (AAA) protocols must meet in order to support authorization services in the Internet

authorization.why: Its subject is authorization: attributes, rules, role-based access control, access decision functions, revocation and trust. Readers of the authorization topic would want it.
authorization.quote: Authorization decisions MUST be able to be based on information about the requestor, the service/method requested, and the operating environment

rejected.why: RADIUS (RFC 2138) is mentioned only as a legacy protocol for attribute semantics and gateway support. The document does not specify or extend it.
Mobile IP appears only as an example application that drives roaming and broker requirements. The document is not about it.
Public key certificates and time-stamp protocols are used as analogies, not as subjects of the document.
IPsec is mentioned only as an underlying authentication mechanism that a AAA protocol might use. It is not the subject.
Diameter is not mentioned. The document sets general AAA requirements, not requirements specific to one protocol.

RFC2907.title: MADCAP Multicast Scope Nesting State Option
RFC2907.summary: Defines a new MADCAP option (code 17), the Multicast Scope Nesting State option, which lets clients learn how administratively scoped multicast zones nest, using a bit-packed matrix, with server state management driven by MZAP messages and timers.

MADCAP.why: The RFC extends MADCAP with a new option, specifying its format, usage in GETINFO/ACK, and server state handling. The MADCAP tag covers MADCAP and the MALLOC architecture.
MADCAP.quote: This document defines a new option to the Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol (MADCAP) to support nested scoping.

rejected.why: Parent of MADCAP, which is already chosen and implies it. The multicast scoping content is background for the MADCAP option.
MADCAP's option format resembles DHCP, but the document does not specify or extend DHCP.
Multicast address allocation is the context, but the document is about a MADCAP option, not IP address architecture.

gaps.name: MZAP (Multicast-Scope Zone Announcement Protocol) / administrative scoping
gaps.why: The document relies on MZAP and administratively scoped zones for learning nesting, but the taxonomy has no tag for MZAP or administrative scoping. The MADCAP tag covers the option itself, not MZAP.

RFC2908.title: The Internet Multicast Address Allocation Architecture
RFC2908.summary: RFC 2908 describes the three-layer MALLOC architecture for Internet multicast address allocation: client-to-server (e.g. MADCAP), intra-domain server coordination (AAP), and inter-domain prefix allocation (MASC), plus an Allocation Scope.

MADCAP.why: The taxonomy defines MADCAP as covering the MADCAP protocol and the MALLOC address-allocation architecture. This RFC is the MALLOC architecture document, so it belongs on that page.
MADCAP.quote: This document proposes a multicast address allocation architecture (MALLOC) for the Internet

rejected.why: The MADCAP tech tag sits under multicast, so the parent is implied and is not listed separately.
IGMP version 3 source-specific prunes are mentioned only in passing, as a way to handle clashes.
SLP is named only as one way a client can locate a MAAS. It is not specified or extended here.
IANA static assignments and the reserved Allocation Scope values are mentioned, but the document is not about IANA registries or their guidance.
The document is about multicast address allocation, and MADCAP is the more specific fit for that.

gaps.name: MASC / AAP / MZAP multicast allocation protocols
gaps.why: The architecture's Layer 2 and Layer 3 protocols (AAP, MASC) and the scope zone announcement protocol (MZAP) have no tags of their own. The MADCAP/MALLOC tag is the nearest fit.

RFC2909.title: The Multicast Address-Set Claim (MASC) Protocol
RFC2909.summary: Specifies MASC, an experimental BGP-like protocol over TCP by which domains claim and allocate multicast address prefixes hierarchically, with claim-collide resolution, message formats and FSM.

MADCAP.why: MADCAP's description covers MADCAP and the MALLOC address-allocation architecture. MASC is the inter-domain layer of that architecture, so readers of that subject would want this RFC.
MADCAP.quote: MASC, a protocol for inter-domain multicast address set allocation. The MASC protocol (a Layer-3 protocol in the multicast address allocation architecture [MALLOC])

rejected.why: MASC borrows BGP-style messages, FSM and error handling, and injects prefixes into the G-RIB. It does not specify BGP.
The document is about multicast, but the more specific MADCAP tag sits under it, so the parent is implied.
TCP is only the transport for MASC sessions, and the document defines nothing new about it.
This is multicast group address allocation, not IP address architecture generally.

gaps.name: MASC / multicast address allocation (MALLOC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for MASC. MADCAP is the closest fit, since it also covers the MALLOC architecture.

RFC2910.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.1: Encoding and Transport
RFC2910.summary: RFC 2910 specifies the binary encoding of IPP/1.1 operations into the application/ipp media type, their transport over HTTP/1.1 (port 631), and the new 'ipp' URL scheme.

IPP.why: The document is a core specification of the Internet Printing Protocol: its wire encoding, HTTP transport binding and URL scheme.
IPP.quote: This document defines the rules for encoding IPP operations and IPP attributes into a new Internet mime media type called "application/ipp".

media types.why: Registers the new application/ipp media type, with a full appendix of registration information.
media types.quote:
MIME type name: application

   MIME subtype name: ipp

URI.why: Defines a new URI scheme 'ipp', its default port 631 and its mapping to http URLs. This is a substantial part of the document.
URI.quote: The IPP/1.1 document defines a new scheme 'ipp' as the value of a URL that identifies either an IPP printer object or an IPP job object.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is the transport substrate. The document only says how IPP uses it (POST, chunking, port 631) and defines no new HTTP semantics.
TLS is only a security mechanism, used via the RFC 2817 upgrade and with a mandated cipher suite. This is in the security considerations, not the main subject.
Digest and Basic authentication are required for conformance, but this appears in the security section and is not the document's focus.
ABNF is used as the notation for the encoding grammar and is not the subject.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IPP (the printing protocol itself). Despite the id I used above, there is no IPP entry under applications, so the tag has to be treated as missing. Readers browsing printing protocols would expect this RFC under such a tag.

RFC2911.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.1: Model and Semantics
RFC2911.summary: RFC 2911 specifies the IPP/1.1 abstract model: Printer and Job objects, their operations (Print-Job, Get-Jobs, Cancel-Job, etc.), attributes, status codes, and conformance, independent of encoding and transport.

IPP.why: The whole document defines the IPP/1.1 model and semantics: objects, operations, attributes, status codes and conformance.
IPP.quote: IPP is an application level protocol that can be used for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport mapping, defined in RFC 2910, not in this document.
TLS is mentioned only as a security option for printer URIs and is not specified here.
Directory registration is recommended and a generic schema appendix is given, but it is a minor part of the document.
URIs identify Printer and Job objects, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Charset and natural-language handling is a real section, but it is a supporting mechanism and not the main subject.
The document only uses MIME types as the document-format attribute syntax and defines no registrations.

RFC2912.title: Indicating Media Features for MIME Content
RFC2912.summary: Defines a MIME 'Content-features:' header carrying media feature set expressions to annotate message parts (simple, composite, or externally referenced) with features beyond the Content-type.

content negotiation.why: The document applies media feature set expressions, the content negotiation framework, to label content with its media features. This is the core subject.
content negotiation.quote: This memo defines a MIME 'Content-features:' header that can be used to annotate a MIME message part using these feature expressions.

MIME.why: It defines a new MIME header and its usage on simple, multipart, and external-body parts, with examples using multipart/alternative and multipart/related.
MIME.quote: A new header field is defined that extends the allowable formats for 'optional-field' [4] with the following syntax

rejected.why: The header is added as an RFC 822 optional-field, but the document is about MIME media-feature annotation, not the Internet message format itself.
ABNF is only the notation used for the header syntax.
A fax message appears as one example only; the document is not about fax.
The multipart/related example only refers to MHTML. The document does not address it.
The document does not register or set rules for media types. It adds feature information beyond Content-type.

gaps.name: Media feature tags / feature sets
gaps.why: The document builds on feature set expressions and feature tag registration (RFC 2533, RFC 2506). The taxonomy has only the broader 'content negotiation' tag for them.

RFC2913.title: MIME Content Types in Media Feature Expressions
RFC2913.summary: Defines a 'type' media feature tag whose value is a MIME content type, so media feature expressions can combine content type with other features, and registers it.

content negotiation.why: The document extends media feature expressions (conneg) with a new feature tag and its registration, which is the content negotiation subject.
content negotiation.quote: This memo defines a media feature tag whose value is a MIME content type.

media types.why: The tag value is a MIME media type/subtype, with canonical form rules, so readers interested in media type usage would want it.
media types.quote: The 'type' feature tag indicates a MIME media content type (i.e. that appears in a 'Content-type:' header of the corresponding MIME-formatted data).

rejected.why: MIME is the source of the values but the document does not specify MIME itself; it only references content types.
HTTP/TCN is mentioned only as motivating example.
Only cited as notation convention.
The registration is boilerplate-like feature tag registration, not about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: Media feature tags
gaps.why: The document is about registering a media feature tag, but the taxonomy has no specific tag for media feature tags or sets beyond content negotiation.

RFC2914.title: Congestion Control Principles
RFC2914.summary: BCP explaining why end-to-end congestion control is needed in the Internet, defining TCP-compatible flows, congestion collapse and fairness, and describing the IETF's role in standardizing new congestion control mechanisms.

congestion control.why: The whole document discusses principles of congestion control: congestion collapse, fairness, TCP-compatibility, and forms of end-to-end congestion control across transports.
congestion control.quote: The goal of this document is to explain the need for congestion control in the Internet, and to discuss what constitutes correct congestion control.

rejected.why: TCP congestion control is used as the main example, including an appendix on TCP-specific issues, but the document is about general principles rather than specifying or extending TCP.
ECN is mentioned as a development that does not by itself remove collapse danger, but only in passing.
Diffserv and integrated services are explicitly out of scope and mentioned only as alternatives.
RFC 2357 criteria are quoted as an example of the standards role, but the document is not about reliable multicast.
Fast Recovery details are cited only as an example of something not requiring standardization.

RFC2915.title: The Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) DNS Resource Record
RFC2915.summary: Defines the NAPTR DNS resource record (type 35), its fields, flags, regex substitution grammar, and the looping rewrite algorithm used for URN/URI resolution and ENUM, updating RFC 2168.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record type, its wire and master file formats, and resolver processing algorithm.
DNS.quote: This document describes a Domain Name System (DNS) resource record which specifies a regular expression based rewrite rule

ENUM.why: ENUM is a named application of NAPTR, with an example mapping E.164 numbers under e164.arpa. It is illustrative, but ENUM readers would want this RFC since it is the underlying record definition.
ENUM.quote: A non-URI example is the ENUM application which uses a NAPTR record to map an e.164 telephone number to a URI.

URN.why: The record originated in the URN working group for URN resolver discovery. The main worked example and several design choices are driven by URN resolution.
URN.quote: NAPTR was originally specified for use with the a Uniform Resource Name Resolver Discovery System.

rejected.why: URIs are the input and output of the rewrite, but the document defines a DNS record rather than URI syntax or schemes.
NAPTR with SRV does locate services. The tag was not needed because the RR itself is the subject, and DNS is the more specific tag.
Mentioned only briefly in Security Considerations as being studied, so it is not a subject of the document.
ABNF is used only to write the service field and regexp grammar. It is notation, not a subject.

RFC2916.title: E.164 number and DNS
RFC2916.summary: Specifies ENUM: mapping E.164 telephone numbers to domain names under e164.arpa and using NAPTR records with the E2U service to obtain URIs for services tied to a number.

ENUM.why: The whole document defines how E.164 numbers are converted into e164.arpa names and resolved via NAPTR (E2U) to URIs, which is the ENUM mechanism.
ENUM.quote: The domain "e164.arpa" is being populated in order to provide the infrastructure in DNS for storage of E.164 numbers.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; ENUM is the more specific tag and the NAPTR usage is part of it. DNS records are used, not newly defined here.
Only recommended in Security Considerations; boilerplate.
The tel URI appears only as an example NAPTR output, not specified here.
SIP URIs appear only as example resolution targets.
URIs are the output of the NAPTR rewrite, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Only an LDAP URI example is shown.

RFC2917.title: A Core MPLS IP VPN Architecture
RFC2917.summary: Informational memo describing a virtual-router-based architecture for provider-provisioned core VPNs over an MPLS backbone, with multicast-emulated LAN neighbor discovery, per-VPN LSPs and no routing protocol modifications.

VPN.why: The document defines a provider-provisioned VPN architecture based on virtual routers, VPNIDs and emulated-LAN discovery. It is a general VPN architecture, not a BGP/MPLS L3VPN specification, so the parent tag fits.
VPN.quote: This memo presents an approach for building core Virtual Private Network (VPN) services in a service provider's MPLS backbone.

rejected.why: It is a virtual-router alternative to RFC 2547 BGP/MPLS VPNs and explicitly does not use BGP to carry VPN routes.
MPLS LSPs and label stacks serve as the forwarding substrate. The document does not specify MPLS itself.
ARP is used over the multicast-emulated LAN for neighbor discovery. The document does not extend or specify ARP.
A multicast group per VPN is used for discovery. Multicast routing itself is not the subject and no specific protocol is mandated.
Differentiated services are mentioned briefly as an option for private LSPs. This is not a substantial part of the document.
OSPF, RIP and BGP are used unmodified inside the virtual routers and are not specified or extended here.

RFC2918.title: Route Refresh Capability for BGP-4
RFC2918.summary: Defines the BGP Route Refresh Capability and ROUTE-REFRESH message, letting a BGP speaker request re-advertisement of a peer's Adj-RIB-Out, e.g. for non-disruptive inbound policy changes.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-4 with a new capability and a new ROUTE-REFRESH message type, and specifies the operation of both.
BGP.quote: defines a new Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) capability termed 'Route Refresh Capability'

rejected.why: The Security Considerations section only says the extension does not change the underlying security issues, so security is not a subject of the document.
Route reflection is not discussed. The extension applies to BGP speakers generally.

RFC2919.title: List-Id: A Structured Field and Namespace for the Identification of Mailing Lists
RFC2919.summary: Defines the List-Id mail header field and a DNS-based namespace (including the "localhost" unmanaged namespace) for uniquely identifying mailing lists.

mailing lists.why: The document specifies a mailing list header field and identifier namespace, with persistence, uniqueness and nested-list rules, which is squarely mailing list headers.
mailing lists.quote: The List-Id header provides a standard location for such an identifier.

message format.why: It defines a new Internet message header field with syntax, whitespace handling and placement rules, relevant to readers of message header formats.
message format.quote: list-id-header = "List-ID:" [phrase] "<" list-id ">" CRLF

rejected.why: DNS is used only as an authority structure for delegating identifier namespace; no DNS protocol or records are specified.
The document uses the reserved name "localhost" from RFC 2606 for unmanaged IDs but does not define or register a special-use name.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the syntax.
Covered more specifically by the mailing lists and message format tags.
Only a brief suggestion to include 128 random bits in localhost identifiers; not a main subject.

RFC2920.title: SMTP Service Extension for Command Pipelining
RFC2920.summary: Defines the SMTP PIPELINING service extension, letting a client batch multiple SMTP commands in one TCP send, with client and server rules and example dialogues.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension (PIPELINING EHLO keyword) and the client and server behaviour it requires.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) service whereby a server can indicate the extent of its ability to accept multiple commands

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document mentions send operations and window size, but it does not specify or extend TCP.
SMTP is the more specific tag and already sits under email, so the ancestor is implied.

RFC2921.title: 6BONE pTLA and pNLA Formats (pTLA)
RFC2921.summary: Informational memo defining how the 6bone testbed subdivides the 3FFE::/16 IPv6 prefix into pseudo TLA (8-bit and 12-bit) and pseudo NLA fields for address delegation.

IPv6.why: The document specifies IPv6 address format usage (pTLA/pNLA structure under 3FFE::/16) for the 6bone testbed, an IPv6 addressing and deployment matter.
IPv6.quote: This memo defines how the 6bone uses the 3FFE::/16 IPv6 address prefix

rejected.why: Relevant to address allocation, but IPv6 is the more specific tag chosen since the document is about IPv6 address formats; addressing is a sibling subtopic and not needed in addition.
The 6bone is mentioned as a transition testbed, but the document only defines address formats, not transition mechanisms.
Only mentioned as a rationale for a 4-bit aligned pTLA to ease reverse-path DNS entries; not about DNS.
IANA's reservation of 3FFE::/16 is background; the document does not address registry guidance.

gaps.name: 6bone testbed
gaps.why: The document is about the 6bone IPv6 testbed's address structure, but the taxonomy has no tag for the 6bone or IPv6 testbeds.

RFC2922.title: Physical Topology MIB
RFC2922.summary: Defines the PTOPO-MIB, an SNMP MIB module for representing physical (layer 1) network connections between ports and discovering the SNMP agents associated with them.

MIB.why: The document defines a new SMIv2 MIB module (PTOPO-MIB) with tables, groups, notifications and compliance statements, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing physical topology identification and discovery.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with, and the framework section is boilerplate. The document defines a MIB module and does not extend SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Ethernet is mentioned only as one medium with proprietary topology mechanisms. The MIB is medium-independent.
RMON-2 is referenced only for the TimeFilter textual convention and address mapping relationships. The document does not specify RMON.
This is topology identification, not performance measurement.

gaps.name: Physical topology discovery
gaps.why: The document's subject is physical topology identification and discovery, which is neither a protocol nor a topic in the taxonomy. The nearest fits are network management and MIB.

RFC2923.title: TCP Problems with Path MTU Discovery
RFC2923.summary: Informational memo cataloguing TCP implementation problems related to Path MTU Discovery: black hole detection, stretch ACKs caused by MSS/segment size confusion, and deriving advertised MSS from PMTU.

PMTUD.why: The whole document concerns problems arising from Path MTU Discovery, including ICMP black holes and fallback behaviour when PMTUD fails.
PMTUD.quote: This memo catalogs several known TCP implementation problems dealing with Path MTU Discovery [RFC1191], including the long-standing black hole problem

TCP.why: It documents TCP implementation bugs and fixes: black hole detection, stretch ACK generation and MSS advertisement.
TCP.quote: TCP should notice that the connection is timing out.  After several timeouts, TCP should attempt to send smaller packets

rejected.why: ICMP Destination Unreachable/Fragmentation Needed messages are the signalling that PMTUD relies on, but the document is not about ICMP itself.
Stretch ACKs are classified as congestion control/performance, but the document addresses them as TCP implementation faults, not congestion control mechanisms.
IPv6 is mentioned only briefly, in the black hole fix discussion about the absence of a DF bit and the 1280-octet minimum MTU.

RFC2924.title: Accounting Attributes and Record Formats
RFC2924.summary: Informational survey of IETF, ITU-T and other accounting attribute sets and record formats (RADIUS, Diameter, ADIF, RTFM, ATM/ISDN MIBs, Q.825, TIPHON, MSIX), with a classification of attributes and discussion of AAA accounting record format and service-definition requirements.

AAA.why: The document is an AAA working group survey of accounting attributes, record formats and requirements for AAA accounting. It is about the AAA accounting framework as a whole.
AAA.quote: This document summarises IETF and ITU-T documents related to Accounting.

RADIUS.why: RADIUS authentication and accounting attributes are summarised in detail and used as the main example in the format and service-definition discussion.
RADIUS.quote: The protocol was extended to carry accounting information between a NAS and a shared accounting server.

Diameter.why: Diameter accounting attributes and the AVP binary record format are summarised in their own sections.
Diameter.quote: The DIAMETER Accounting Extension document [DIAM-ACT] extends DIAMETER by defining a protocol for securely transferring accounting records

rejected.why: RTFM and AToMMIB use SNMP for collection, but SNMP is only discussed as a substrate and as an example of a framework protocol.
The ISDN, ATM and RSVP MIBs are summarised only for their accounting objects. The document does not define MIB modules.
TIPHON and MSIX are XML-based, but XML is only the encoding used by the summarised formats.
ASN.1 BER records are described as one of the record formats surveyed, but the document is not about ASN.1.
RTFM flow attributes are summarised only as a source of accounting attributes.
RSVP and Diffserv are covered in a short section only to show where their QoS parameters become accounting attributes.

gaps.name: Accounting / usage metering and record formats
gaps.why: The document is mainly about accounting attributes, usage events and record interchange formats such as ADIF. The taxonomy has no accounting tag, so AAA is the closest fit.

RFC2925.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Remote Ping, Traceroute, and Lookup Operations
RFC2925.summary: RFC 2925 defines three SNMP MIB modules (DISMAN-PING-MIB, DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB, DISMAN-NSLOOKUP-MIB) that let a management application start and read results of ping, traceroute and name/address lookup operations performed at a remote host.

MIB.why: The document's main body is three SMIv2 MIB modules with control, results and history tables, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines Management Information Bases (MIBs) for performing remote ping, traceroute and lookup operations at a remote host.

traceroute.why: A whole MIB module is dedicated to remote traceroute operation, including probe types, hops table and path-change notifications, so readers of the traceroute subject would want it.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute is usually implemented by transmitting a series of probe packets with increasing time-to-live values.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIBs; the document defines MIB modules (covered by the MIB tag) rather than extending SNMP itself.
ICMP Echo is the recommended mechanism for ping, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
The Lookup MIB wraps gethostbyname/gethostbyaddr resolver calls at a remote host; it defines no DNS protocol, records or resolver behaviour.
Ping and traceroute yield round-trip times, but the document is a remote-operation control MIB, not a performance-metrics or methodology specification.
UDP probes and the UDP echo port are mentioned as implementation methods only; nothing about UDP is specified.

gaps.name: Remote ping / traceroute operations
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ping as a tool. Traceroute does appear as a tech under network management, but ping and remote lookup operations have no home beyond the generic MIB tag.

RFC2926.title: Conversion of LDAP Schemas to and from SLP Templates
