RFC2926.summary: Defines mappings between SLP service type templates and LDAP directory schemas, and a recommended representation of SLP service advertisements in an LDAP DIT so SLP DAs can use LDAP back ends.

SLP.why: The document specifies how SLP templates and service advertisements map to LDAP, and how SLP DAs interoperate with LDAP back ends. SLP is a main subject.
SLP.quote: This document describes a procedure for mapping between Service Location Protocol (SLP) service advertisements and lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP) descriptions of services.

LDAP.why: The document defines LDAP object classes, attribute types and syntaxes for SLP, and a DIT layout for service advertisements. This is LDAP schema work, so readers of LDAP would want it.
LDAP.quote: mapping between SLP service type templates and LDAP directory schema

rejected.why: The document maps ASN.1 types to SLP types, but ASN.1 is only the schema notation being converted. It does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
This is the parent of LDAP. The LDAP tag is more specific, so the parent is not listed.
This is the parent of SLP in the taxonomy. SLP is more specific, so the parent is not listed.
X.520 attribute types are referenced only as a source of attribute definitions. The document is not about the X.500 directory service.

RFC2927.title: MIME Directory Profile for LDAP Schema
RFC2927.summary: Defines a text/directory MIME profile ("schema-ldap-0") and associated types for transferring a single LDAPv3 schema definition, for use with the Internet schema listing service.

LDAP.why: The document specifies how LDAPv3 schema (object classes, attribute types, matching rules, syntaxes) is represented, and defines new LDAP attribute ldapSchemas and its syntax in the appendix.
LDAP.quote: This document defines how a MIME type may be used to transfer a single LDAPv3 schema definition.

media types.why: The document is largely a set of MIME text/directory profile and type registrations, so readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: Registration of text/directory MIME profile "schema-ldap-0"

rejected.why: MIME is the carrier mechanism; the document registers a profile and types for text/directory, and media types is the more specific fit.
Parent of LDAP; the more specific LDAP tag is used instead.
vCard is another text/directory profile but is not discussed here; only the text/directory framework is reused.
OIDs and BNF syntax are used but ASN.1 modules and encodings are not the subject.

gaps.name: MIME text/directory content type (RFC 2425) profiles
gaps.why: The document defines a profile of the text/directory MIME type, but the taxonomy has no tag for the directory content type itself.

RFC2928.title: Initial IPv6 Sub-TLA ID Assignments
RFC2928.summary: Informational RFC recording the initial assignment of IPv6 Sub-TLA IDs (blocks of 64 under 2001::/16) to the regional address registries (APNIC, ARIN, RIPE NCC) and IANA, as input to IANA for IPv6 address allocation.

addressing.why: The document is about allocation of IPv6 address space blocks to registries, which is IP address architecture, allocation and use. No more specific addressing child fits.
addressing.quote: This document defines initial assignments of IPv6 Sub-TLA Aggregation Identifiers (Sub-TLA ID) to the Address Registries.

IPv6.why: It specifies IPv6 prefix ranges (2001::/16 sub-TLA blocks) under the aggregatable global unicast address format, so IPv6 addressing readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: The initial Sub-TLA ID assignments to IP address registries are in blocks of 64 Sub-TLA IDs.

rejected.why: The RFC gives technical input to IANA on address block assignment, but it is not about IANA registries or guidance in general; the subject is IPv6 address allocation.
Prefixes are written in CIDR notation but the document is not about CIDR or aggregation mechanics.
Not relevant; the document concerns only IPv6 address allocation.

RFC2929.title: Domain Name System (DNS) IANA Considerations
RFC2929.summary: RFC 2929 is a BCP setting IANA allocation policies for DNS parameters: header bits, opcodes, RCODEs, RR TYPEs, CLASSes, and label types.

DNS.why: The document defines how DNS protocol parameters (opcodes, RCODEs, RR types, classes, label types) are allocated, so DNS readers would look for it.
DNS.quote: general IANA parameter assignment considerations applying across DNS query and response headers and all RRs

IANA.why: It is an IANA considerations/registry policy document, specifying the registration procedures (Standards Action, IETF Consensus, Specification Required, Private Use) for the DNS registries.
IANA.quote: New OpCode assignments require an IETF Standards Action.

rejected.why: The OPT RR and its extended RCODE are discussed, but only as part of the RCODE and RR TYPE allocation. EDNS is not the subject.
RFC 2535 is cited and the document states it does not address security. It does not cover signing or validation.
The Update opcode and its RCODEs appear in the registry tables only as references.

RFC2930.title: Secret Key Establishment for DNS (TKEY RR)
RFC2930.summary: Defines the TKEY resource record and its modes (Diffie-Hellman, server/resolver assignment, GSS-API, deletion) for establishing shared secret keys between DNS resolvers and servers, for use with TSIG.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record type (249) and the query/response exchanges that use it, so it belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: This document describes a Transaction Key (TKEY) RR that can be used in a number of different modes to establish shared secret keys between a DNS resolver and server.

rejected.why: TKEY keys are tied to servers and resolvers, not zones, and the document states they give no zone-based data origin authentication. DNSSEC KEY RRs are only used to carry public keys.
GSS-API mode is only mentioned and deferred to a separate document, so the document is not about it.
The document does establish keys, but it does so through a DNS-specific RR. The DNS tag fits that better.
RFC 2136 is only cited as background, and the document does not specify dynamic update.
HMAC-MD5 is mentioned only as an example of how the keying material is used by a TSIG algorithm.
RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 is used as the encryption method for keying material, but the document does not specify RSA itself.

gaps.name: TSIG / SIG(0) DNS transaction security
gaps.why: TKEY exists to support TSIG, and the document relies on TSIG and SIG(0) for authenticating messages. The taxonomy has no tag for DNS transaction authentication outside DNSSEC.

RFC2931.title: DNS Request and Transaction Signatures ( SIG(0)s )
RFC2931.summary: RFC 2931 revises the SIG(0) resource record used to sign DNS requests and transaction responses with public-key signatures, updating RFC 2535 and contrasting SIG(0) with TSIG.

DNSSEC.why: The document updates the DNSSEC specification (RFC 2535) for SIG(0) request and transaction signature RRs, defining how they are calculated, processed and expire.
DNSSEC.quote: Extensions to the Domain Name System (DNS) are described in [RFC 2535] that can provide data origin and transaction integrity and authentication

rejected.why: The more specific DNSSEC tag fits; DNS itself is the implied parent.
Dynamic update requests are named only as one use case for request signing; the document does not specify update.
Authentication here is DNS-specific and is covered by DNSSEC; the generic topic is not needed.

gaps.name: TSIG / TKEY (DNS transaction signatures)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TSIG or TKEY secret-key transaction security. The document compares SIG(0) with TSIG at length, but it is not about TSIG.

RFC2932.title: IPv4 Multicast Routing MIB
RFC2932.summary: Defines the IPMROUTE-STD-MIB SMIv2 module for managing IPv4 multicast routing independent of the multicast routing protocol, with tables for routes, next hops, interfaces, scope boundaries and scope names.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module definition for multicast routing management, so the MIB tag fits directly.
MIB.quote: This MIB describes objects used for managing IP Multicast Routing [16], independent of the specific multicast routing protocol [17-21] in use.

multicast.why: The managed subject is IP multicast routing state (routes, next hops, scope boundaries). Readers of multicast would want it. No more specific multicast child tag fits because the MIB is protocol-independent.
multicast.quote: the IP Multicast Route Table containing multicast routing information for IP datagrams sent by particular sources to the IP multicast groups known to a router.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document defines objects, not the protocol, and MIB is the more specific tag.
PIM is mentioned only as one of several multicast routing protocols whose state the MIB can describe. The MIB is explicitly protocol-independent.
The MIB covers only IPv4 multicast addresses, but it is not about the IPv4 protocol itself.

RFC2933.title: Internet Group Management Protocol MIB
RFC2933.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module (IGMP-STD-MIB) for managing IGMP versions 1 and 2 on IPv4 multicast hosts and routers, with interface and cache tables and compliance statements.

IGMP.why: The document's whole purpose is to define managed objects for IGMP (interface table, cache table, querier timers, version handling), so readers of the IGMP subject would want it.
IGMP.quote: In particular, it describes objects used for managing the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP).

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition with object groups and compliance statements, which fits the MIB modules subject.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is accessed through. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag sits under SNMP and covers it.
The IGMP tag is more specific and sits under multicast, so the parent is implied.
The document only notes that IGMP applies to IPv4 multicast. It does not address IPv4 itself.

RFC2934.title: Protocol Independent Multicast MIB for IPv4
RFC2934.summary: Defines an experimental SMIv2 MIB module for managing PIM (v1 and v2, sparse and dense modes) on IPv4 multicast routers, with tables for interfaces, neighbors, routes, RP sets, candidate RPs and components, plus a neighbor-loss notification.

PIM.why: The MIB exists to manage PIM routers: interface, neighbor, RP-set, BSR and assert state, so PIM readers would want it.
PIM.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) protocol [16,17,18,19].

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (PIM-MIB) written in SMIv2, with its compliance and object groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried over; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag is the more specific fit.
The MIB covers both PIM versions and both dense and sparse modes, and it is not a sparse-mode specification, so the broader PIM tag fits better.
IGMP is mentioned only as enabled on PIM interfaces; the document defines no IGMP objects.
The parent of PIM, which is already tagged and implies it.

RFC2935.title: Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) HTTP Supplement
RFC2935.summary: Defines how IOTP (Internet Open Trading Protocol) XML messages are carried over HTTP/1.0 and 1.1, including client/server role mapping, startup, POST usage, transaction termination, and registration of the application/iotp media type.

IOTP.why: The document is a supplement to IOTP specifying its HTTP transport binding, including the roles, starting, ongoing messages and stopping of IOTP transactions.
IOTP.quote: This document describes that mapping for the Hyper Text Transport Protocol (HTTP), Versions 1.0 and 1.1.

media types.why: The document registers the application/iotp media type, and section 4.1 explains its role in launching the IOTP client from the browser, so media type readers would want it.
media types.quote: This specification defines the APPLICATION/IOTP MIME type.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport substrate; the document defines no new HTTP semantics or extensions, only how IOTP uses GET and POST.
SSL/TLS is only mentioned as an optional secure channel; nothing new is defined about its use.
IOTP messages are XML documents, but the document is not about XML usage or formats beyond noting that encodings must be compatible.
The HTML browser is merely the consumer's initial agent; the document does not address HTML.
Implied by the IOTP tag, which already sits under e-commerce.

RFC2936.title: HTTP MIME Type Handler Detection
RFC2936.summary: Informational RFC describing practical techniques (HTTP Accept header, JavaScript navigator.mimeTypes, Windows Registry/ActiveX) for web servers to detect whether a browser has a handler installed for a given MIME type such as IOTP.

HTTP.why: A core technique is interpreting the HTTP Accept request header to infer handler availability; the document is about web content/handler detection over HTTP.
HTTP.quote: The problem should be solved by the Hyper Text Transport Protocol [HTTP] request "Accept" header which lists accepted [MIME] types.

content negotiation.why: The document is about detecting client capabilities to vary served content, a form of ad hoc media feature/content negotiation, and notes future standards work on capabilities negotiation.
content negotiation.quote: In some cases they would want to display different web pages or content depending on a MIME handler's availability.

media types.why: The subject is whether handlers exist for particular MIME media types (application/iotp, etc.) at the browser.
media types.quote: frequently have the problem of not knowing what [MIME] types have handlers installed at a user's browser.

rejected.why: IOTP is only the running example MIME type; the document does not specify or extend IOTP.
ECML gets a brief mention as a way to learn supported payment protocols, but it is not a substantial part of the document.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as boilerplate.
HTML comments are used to hide script, but the document is not about HTML.
MIME is the type system being probed. The document is about handler detection, not MIME body structure or encodings; media types fits better.

gaps.name: Browser/client capability detection (JavaScript, ActiveX)
gaps.why: The document's main content is client-side scripting and registry probing to detect browser capabilities, which has no specific tag in the taxonomy.

RFC2937.title: The Name Service Search Option for DHCP
RFC2937.summary: Defines DHCP option 117, which lets a DHCP server tell clients the order in which to consult name services (DNS, NIS, NIS+, NetBIOS, local files) when resolving names.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a new DHCP option (code 117), its format and client behaviour, so it belongs under DHCP.
DHCP.quote: defines a new Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) option which is passed from the DHCP Server to the DHCP Client

naming.why: The option's purpose is name-service search order across DNS, NIS, NIS+, NetBIOS and local files. That is general name resolution, not one system, so the general naming topic fits.
naming.quote: to specify the order in which name services should be consulted when resolving hostnames and other information

rejected.why: DNS is only one of several name services the option can order. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
NetBIOS name server is only an example entry in the list of name service option codes.
The option is defined for DHCP over IPv4 only.

RFC2938.title: Identifying Composite Media Features
RFC2938.summary: Defines an abbreviated hashed reference format (h.<base32 MD5>) for composite media feature set expressions from RFC 2533, including normalization, base-32 encoding and ways to resolve the references.

content negotiation.why: The document extends the RFC 2533 media feature set expression syntax used in content negotiation, defining hashed feature set references. Readers of content negotiation would want it.
content negotiation.quote: This document describes an abbreviated format for a composite media feature set, based upon a hash of the feature expression describing that composite.

rejected.why: MD5 is only the hash function used to compute the identifier. The document does not specify or analyse MD5 itself.
The document defines its own base-32 encoding and only mentions Base64 in a note explaining why it was not used.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the syntax, not a subject of the document.
Internet fax capability expressions appear only as examples of feature sets.
URN resolution via DNS NAPTR is only mentioned in passing as a possible resolution mechanism.
Media feature tags are related to media types, but this document does not register or define media types.

RFC2939.title: Procedures and IANA Guidelines for Definition of New DHCP Options and Message Types
RFC2939.summary: BCP defining the procedure and IANA guidelines for assigning new DHCP option codes and message type codes, requiring IESG-reviewed RFCs and IETF consensus, and replacing RFC 2489.

DHCP.why: The whole document is about how DHCP is extended with new options and message types, including the split of the option number space and the review process. DHCP readers need it.
DHCP.quote: This document describes the procedure for defining new DHCP options and message types.

IANA.why: The document is a guideline for IANA registry assignment of DHCP option and message type codes (Specification Required, Private Use ranges, IETF consensus). It sits within IANA registries guidance.
IANA.quote: IANA is requested to assign DHCP option codes or message type codes only for options or message types that have been approved for publication as RFCs

rejected.why: It describes an IESG review path for DHCP extensions, but this is registry procedure specific to DHCP, not general IETF process.
The document covers only DHCP for IPv4 options and message types, not DHCPv6.

RFC2940.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Common Open Policy Service (COPS) Protocol Clients
RFC2940.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module (COPS-CLIENT-MIB) for monitoring and configuring a COPS protocol client, including capabilities, per-server status and statistics, and server configuration with retry algorithms.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module in SMIv2 for COPS clients. MIB module definitions are the core content.
MIB.quote: In particular it defines objects for managing a client of the Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol.

COPS.why: The MIB manages COPS client state, protocol error counters, server redirect handling, and server configuration. It is about operating the COPS protocol, so COPS readers would want it.
COPS.quote: The COPS protocol [COPS] is a client-server protocol intended for the communication of policy requests and decisions between a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) and a Policy Decision Point (PDP).

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for. The document defines objects only and nothing new about SNMP itself. MIB, the child tag, covers it.
RSVP is mentioned only to say that RSVP-specific COPS client-types are out of scope.
SLP is mentioned only as an alternative way to locate servers, and the document says it is out of scope.
TLS appears only as a value in the authentication-type enumeration, not as a subject of the document.
IPsec AH and ESP appear only as authentication-type enumeration values, not as a subject of the document.
The document manages a COPS client's status and configuration. It does not define a policy information model.

RFC2941.title: Telnet Authentication Option
RFC2941.summary: Specifies the Telnet Authentication option (obsoleting RFC 1416), a generic framework for negotiating authentication type, encryption mode and credential forwarding within a Telnet session.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet option (AUTHENTICATION, code 37) with its commands, suboptions, negotiation rules and examples, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This document describes the authentication option to the telnet [1] protocol as a generic method for negotiating an authentication type and mode

authentication.why: It is a generic authentication negotiation framework (one-way, mutual, credential forwarding, encryption modes) for user and host authentication, with the actual mechanisms left to separate documents.
authentication.quote: The purpose of the AUTHENTICATION option is to provide a framework for the passing of authentication information through the TELNET session

rejected.why: Kerberos V4/V5 appear only as example authentication types; the mechanisms are defined in separate documents.
SRP is merely listed as an assigned authentication type number, not specified here.
SSL is only listed as an authentication type code, and this document does not define its use.
TCP is only the substrate, mentioned for defining client and server roles.
The IANA assignment policy for type numbers is boilerplate-like and a minor part of the document.

RFC2942.title: Telnet Authentication: Kerberos Version 5
RFC2942.summary: Specifies a Telnet authentication suboption that uses Kerberos V5 (KRB_AP_REQ/REP, credential forwarding via KRB_CRED) and supplies a subkey for the Telnet encryption option.

Telnet.why: The RFC defines a new authentication suboption, with command codes and rules, for the Telnet authentication option. Readers of Telnet options would look for it.
Telnet.quote: This document describes how Kerberos Version 5 [1] is used with the telnet protocol.

Kerberos.why: The document profiles how Kerberos V5 messages (AP_REQ, AP_REP, CRED), principals and subkeys are used for authentication, mutual authentication and credential forwarding.
Kerberos.quote: This is used to pass the Kerberos V5 [1] KRB_AP_REQ message to the remote side of the connection.

rejected.why: The document is about a specific mechanism, and the Kerberos and Telnet tags already cover it. The generic authentication topic adds nothing.
Kerberos is used directly through its native messages. GSS-API is not involved.
The document says how a session subkey is chosen and used for the Telnet encryption option. It does not specify cryptographic algorithms.

RFC2943.title: TELNET Authentication Using DSA
RFC2943.summary: Defines a Telnet Authentication Option mechanism using DSA/DSS (per FIPS 196) for unilateral and mutual authentication with X.509 certificates, including command codes and ASN.1 message syntax.

Telnet.why: The document specifies a new authentication type and sub-option exchanges for the Telnet Authentication Option, so Telnet readers need it.
Telnet.quote: This document defines a telnet authentication mechanism using the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) [FIPS186]. It relies on the Telnet Authentication Option [RFC2941].

authentication.why: The document defines client-to-server and mutual entity authentication exchanges using signed tokens and certificates.
authentication.quote: DSA may provide either unilateral or mutual authentication.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates carry the DSS public keys, but the document only uses them and does not profile them.
ASN.1 is the encoding for the tokens, so it is a substrate here and the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
SHA-1 is only mentioned as the hash that DSA uses.
Certificate validation is mentioned in passing and is not the document's subject.

gaps.name: DSA/DSS (Digital Signature Algorithm)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DSA. The cryptography subtree covers RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA but not DSA, and this document specifies DSA-based authentication.

RFC2944.title: Telnet Authentication: SRP
RFC2944.summary: Defines the SRP authentication type for the Telnet Authentication Option, specifying suboption commands, parameter encoding, implementation rules and an example exchange using the SRP-SHA1 mechanism.

Telnet.why: The document defines a Telnet authentication type with suboption commands (AUTH, PARAMS, EXP, CHALLENGE, RESPONSE) and a Telnet negotiation example, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies an authentication scheme for the Telnet protocol under the framework described in [RFC2941]

SRP.why: The document maps SRP's exchange (n, g, s, A, B, M and the server proof) onto Telnet suboptions and sets modulus-size rules. SRP readers would want this binding.
SRP.quote: using the Secure Remote Password Protocol (SRP) authentication mechanism

rejected.why: Telnet authentication option is a distinct framework, not SASL.
SHA-1 is only the hash in the SRP-SHA1 mechanism, which is defined in RFC 2945, not here.
The Telnet and SRP tags already cover this more specifically.
SRP is the more specific child of PAKE and is already tagged.

RFC2945.title: The SRP Authentication and Key Exchange System
RFC2945.summary: Specifies the SRP-SHA1 (SRP-3) password-authenticated key exchange protocol, which authenticates users by password without exposing it to dictionary attacks and derives a shared session key.

SRP.why: The whole document specifies the SRP protocol: verifier generation, message flow, session key derivation (including interleaved SHA) and proofs.
SRP.quote: a cryptographically strong network authentication mechanism known as the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol

rejected.why: It is the parent of SRP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
SHA-1 is only the hash used inside SRP-SHA1, not the subject of the document.
HMAC is mentioned only as an optional keyed-hash construction in Section 3.2.
MD5 is mentioned only as a hash used by earlier SRP versions.
S/Key is cited only as an example of a challenge-response scheme with weaknesses.
The key exchange is part of SRP itself, which a PAKE tag already covers.

RFC2946.title: Telnet Data Encryption Option
RFC2946.summary: Defines the Telnet ENCRYPT option, a generic negotiation mechanism for providing confidentiality of the Telnet data stream, with command and encryption type codes.

Telnet.why: The RFC specifies a Telnet option (ENCRYPT), its commands, negotiation rules and example, so it belongs on the Telnet page.
Telnet.quote: This document describes a the telnet encryption option as a generic method of providing data confidentiality services for the telnet data stream.

rejected.why: TLS is only mentioned in the future-directions section as a possible approach (START_TLS); the document does not specify it.
DES_CFB64 and other cipher type codes are listed, but the document defines no algorithm and only assigns type numbers.
The Telnet Authentication option is referenced for key derivation and active-attack protection, but is specified in a separate RFC.
Parent topic implied by no specific tag; the document is about a Telnet option, and Telnet is the more specific tag.

RFC2947.title: Telnet Encryption: DES3 64 bit Cipher Feedback
RFC2947.summary: Specifies how to use Triple-DES in 64-bit cipher feedback mode as an encryption type for the Telnet ENCRYPT option, including suboption commands, IV handling, algorithm, and key derivation from the AUTHENTICATION option.

Telnet.why: The document defines a new Telnet encryption type (DES3_CFB64) with suboption commands and implementation rules for the Telnet ENCRYPT option, so Telnet readers need it.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies how to use the Triple-DES (data encryption standard) encryption algorithm in cipher feedback mode with the telnet encryption option.

DES.why: The document specifies Triple-DES in 64-bit CFB mode, including the algorithm and key selection rules for 2 to 6 keys and parity correction.
DES.quote: V0 = DES-e(DES-d(DES-e(iV, key1),key2),key3)

rejected.why: The AUTHENTICATION telnet option is only the source of key material; the document does not specify authentication.
The document is covered by the more specific Telnet and DES tags; it has no general security guidance.
Implied as the parent of DES, so not listed separately.

RFC2948.title: Telnet Encryption: DES3 64 bit Output Feedback
RFC2948.summary: Specifies the DES3_OFB64 encryption type (Triple-DES in 64-bit output feedback mode) for the Telnet ENCRYPT option, including its suboption commands, IV handling, and key derivation from the AUTHENTICATION option.

Telnet.why: The RFC defines a new Telnet encryption type with suboption commands (OFB64_IV, OFB64_IV_OK, OFB64_IV_BAD) and negotiation rules, extending the Telnet protocol's ENCRYPT option.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies how to use the Triple-DES (data encryption standard) encryption algorithm in output feedback mode with the telnet encryption option.

DES.why: A substantial part of the document specifies the Triple-DES EDE output-feedback keystream algorithm and how its three keys are derived and parity-corrected.
DES.quote: V(n+1) = DES-e(DES-d(DES-e(Vn, key1),key2),key3)

rejected.why: The DES tag is more specific and already covers the cipher; the parent is implied.
The AUTHENTICATION telnet option is referenced only to supply key material; the document does not specify authentication.
The document is about a specific Telnet encryption option, not security generally; the Security Considerations section is boilerplate-level evidence.

RFC2949.title: Telnet Encryption: CAST-128 64 bit Output Feedback
RFC2949.summary: Specifies how to use the CAST-128 cipher in 64-bit output feedback mode (40- and 128-bit keys) as an encryption type for the Telnet encryption option, including IV negotiation, state handling and key derivation from Telnet authentication.

Telnet.why: The document defines new Telnet ENCRYPT option encryption types, suboption commands and implementation rules, so it is a Telnet option specification.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in output feedback mode with the telnet encryption option.

rejected.why: CAST-128 and OFB are only the cipher used. The document defines Telnet option negotiation and has no CAST-specific taxonomy tag, so a generic cryptography tag would be too broad.
Not related; the cipher is CAST-128, not AES.
The DES OFB Telnet document is mentioned only as the basis this one was adapted from.
Section 5 only describes how to split key bytes from Telnet authentication. This is a minor detail, not key management in its own right.
The AUTHENTICATION option is referenced only as the source of default key material.

RFC2950.title: Telnet Encryption: CAST-128 64 bit Cipher Feedback
RFC2950.summary: Specifies how to use the CAST-128 cipher in 64-bit cipher feedback mode (40- and 128-bit keys) with the Telnet encryption option, including the IV suboption commands, rekeying rules and AUTHENTICATION key integration.

Telnet.why: The document defines new Telnet encryption types and suboption commands (CFB64_IV, IV_OK, IV_BAD) and the Telnet-side negotiation and keying rules. Readers of Telnet options need it.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in cipher feedback mode with the telnet encryption option.

rejected.why: CAST-128 is only the cipher used. The document is about its integration into the Telnet encryption option, and the taxonomy has no CAST tag. It defines no new algorithm.
This is a different block cipher. The AES tag does not apply.
The document is based on the DES CFB64 Telnet document, but that is only an acknowledged ancestor. It does not cover DES.
The AUTHENTICATION option is referenced only for deriving the default key in a short section. The document is not about authentication.

gaps.name: CAST-128 cipher / Telnet encryption option
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the CAST-128 algorithm or for Telnet encryption and the Telnet authentication option. The best fit is the Telnet tech tag.

RFC2951.title: TELNET Authentication Using KEA and SKIPJACK
RFC2951.summary: Informational RFC defining TELNET Authentication Option mechanisms using KEA key exchange with X.509 certificates and SKIPJACK encryption, in modes with and without stream integrity.

Telnet.why: It specifies new authentication types (KEA_SJ, KEA_SJ_INTEG) and sub-option exchanges for the TELNET Authentication Option, extending Telnet.
Telnet.quote: This document defines a method to authenticate TELNET using the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA), and encryption of the TELNET stream using SKIPJACK.

key management.why: A substantial part of the document is KEA-based key establishment for session encryption keys, including nonces, IVs and certificate exchange.
key management.quote: On completing these exchanges, the parties have a common SKIPJACK key.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates containing KEA keys are only used as inputs to the exchange; the document does not profile them.
SHA-1 is used only as a building block for the integrity check.
Telnet authentication is covered by the Telnet tag; no separate generic authentication tag is needed.
The SKIPJACK and KEA algorithms are used, not specified or analysed. There is no tag for them, and the generic cryptography topic is too broad.
Random generation guidance appears only in Security Considerations, referencing RFC 1750.

gaps.name: SKIPJACK / KEA (Key Exchange Algorithm)
gaps.why: The document's core is the use of these NSA-designed algorithms, and the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC2952.title: Telnet Encryption: DES 64 bit Cipher Feedback
RFC2952.summary: Specifies how to use DES in 64-bit cipher feedback mode as an encryption type for the Telnet ENCRYPT option, including suboption commands, rekeying rules, the algorithm and key derivation from Telnet AUTHENTICATION.

Telnet.why: The RFC defines a Telnet option encryption type with its suboption commands (CFB64_IV, etc.) and implementation rules, so it extends the Telnet protocol.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies how to use the DES encryption algorithm in cipher feedback mode with the telnet encryption option.

DES.why: The document specifies the DES cipher in 64-bit cipher feedback mode, including the algorithm and DES key parity handling.
DES.quote: V[0] = DES(V[i], key)

rejected.why: The Telnet AUTHENTICATION option is only referenced for deriving the default key in one section; the document is not about authentication.
Key derivation from the authentication session key is a small part; the main subject is the cipher mode and option commands.

RFC2953.title: Telnet Encryption: DES 64 bit Output Feedback
RFC2953.summary: Specifies the DES_OFB64 encryption type (64-bit output feedback mode) for the Telnet encryption option, including suboption commands, state handling, algorithm, and keying from the AUTHENTICATION option.

Telnet.why: The RFC defines a new encryption type and suboption commands (OFB64_IV, etc.) for the Telnet encryption option, so it extends the Telnet protocol and its options.
Telnet.quote: This document specifies how to use the data encryption standard (DES) encryption algorithm in output feedback mode with the telnet encryption option.

DES.why: The document specifies the use of DES in 64-bit OFB mode, including the keystream algorithm and DES key parity handling.
DES.quote: Data will be encrypted using the DES 64 bit Output Feedback algorithm.

rejected.why: The keys may come from Telnet AUTHENTICATION mechanisms, but Kerberos is not named or specified here.
Section 5 only describes deriving the encryption key from the AUTHENTICATION option. The document is about encryption, not authentication.
The specific tags Telnet and DES already cover the subject, so the general security topic adds nothing.

RFC2954.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Frame Relay Service
RFC2954.summary: RFC 2954 defines the SMIv2 MIB module (FRNETSERV-MIB) for managing a frame relay network service: logical ports, in-channel signaling, PVC endpoints and connections, accounting and notifications. It obsoletes RFC 1604.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (FRNETSERV-MIB) with tables, object groups, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol-based (TCP/IP) internets.

frame relay.why: The MIB models frame relay UNI/NNI logical ports, DLCIs, PVCs, CIR/Bc/Be, LMI/Q.933 signaling and FRF.12 fragmentation.
frame relay.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing the frame relay service.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is accessed through. The document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag covers it.
The FR/ATM interworking MIB is only referenced. This document adds just an index object, frPVCEndptAtmIwfConnIndex, that points to it.
DS1/E1 interface stacking appears only as an example of how ifStackTable is used. The document is not about DSL access networks.
The more specific MIB tag applies, and its ancestors are implied.

RFC2955.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Monitoring and Controlling the Frame Relay/ATM PVC Service Interworking Function
RFC2955.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module for configuring, monitoring and controlling the Frame Relay/ATM PVC service interworking function (FRF.8), including cross-connect and connection descriptor tables and a status-change notification.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (FR-ATM-PVC-SERVICE-IWF-MIB) specified in SMIv2, with tables, groups, notification and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) to configure, monitor, and control a service interworking function (IWF) for Permanent Virtual Connections (PVC)

frame relay.why: The MIB manages the interworking of frame relay PVCs with ATM PVCs, mapping DE/CLP bits, congestion bits and encapsulations. Frame relay is the subject of the managed function.
frame relay.quote: Frame Relay to ATM PVC Service Interworking is defined in [17].

ATM.why: The MIB augments the ATM MIB atmVclTable and cross-connects ATM VCLs to frame relay PVCs, including AAL5 handling. Readers of IP over ATM would want it.
ATM.quote: ATM PVC endpoints are provisioned as rows in the ATM MIB [21] virtual connection link table.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework that carries the MIB. The document defines objects, not protocol changes, and the SNMP framework section is boilerplate.
Not relevant. This is an SMIv2 MIB, not a YANG model.
ARP translation is only one attribute (frAtmIwfConnArpTranslationEnabled) and is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC2956.title: Overview of 1999 IAB Network Layer Workshop
RFC2956.summary: Report of the 1999 IAB workshop on the Internet network layer, covering loss of transparency, NAT/RSIP, address space, routing scaling, renumbering, IPv6 transition, DNS and IPsec identifiers, with recommendations to the IETF.

workshop reports.why: The RFC is a report of an IAB workshop, with conclusions and recommendations.
workshop reports.quote: This document is an overview of a workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) on the Internet Network Layer architecture

NAT.why: NAT, ALGs and RSIP and their effect on transparency are central, with a recommendation on RSIP.
NAT.quote: NAT especially complicates setting up servers, peer to peer communications and "always-on" hosts

IPv6 transition.why: The workshop assessed IPv6 deployment feasibility, transition paths, and NAT/RSIP's role in them.
IPv6 transition.quote: network address translation techniques could play an important role in the transition process from IPv4 to IPv6

renumbering.why: Renumbering for routing scalability and IPv6 is a recurring theme and drives recommendations.
renumbering.quote: Renumbering remains operationally difficult and expensive

internet architecture.why: Discusses end-to-end transparency and identity/locator separation as architectural principles.
internet architecture.quote: transparency was referred to as the original Internet concept of a single universal logical addressing scheme

routing architecture.why: Routing scaling, convergence time and aggregation are discussed, with recommendations in 3.6.
routing architecture.quote: A number of concerns were raised regarding the scaling of the current routing system.

IPsec.why: The workshop recommended non-address identities for IPsec and IKE, a dedicated recommendation section.
IPsec.quote: It is urgent that we implement and deploy IPsec using some other identifier than 32-bit IP addresses

rejected.why: DNS issues (split DNS, A6 updates) are discussed, but as one aspect of network layer concerns rather than the document's main subject.
DNSSEC is recommended for deployment to support IPsec, but only briefly.
IPv6 is discussed but mainly as transition and renumbering; IPv6 transition is the more specific fit.
Mobility was explicitly not discussed in detail, deferred to a separate workshop.
Address space exhaustion is covered, but renumbering and NAT tags capture it more specifically.

gaps.name: RSIP (Realm-Specific IP)
gaps.why: A substantial part of the document covers RSIP as an alternative to NAT, but the taxonomy has no RSIP tag.

RFC2957.title: The application/whoispp-query Content-Type
RFC2957.summary: Registers the application/whoispp-query MIME media type and defines, in ABNF, the syntax of Whois++ queries so that MIME-aware software can carry Whois++ transactions.

WHOIS++.why: The document specifies how Whois++ queries are expressed, including the full query grammar (commands, terms, constraints). That is squarely about WHOIS++.
WHOIS++.quote: defines the expression of Whois++ protocol (RFC 1835) queries within MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) (RFC 2046) media types

media types.why: A substantial part is the media type registration template for application/whoispp-query, which belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: Registration of MIME media type application/whoispp-query

rejected.why: MIME is the carrier for the new media type. The document registers a type but does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the query grammar. The document is not about ABNF itself.
Mail software is the intended consumer, but the document is about the query content type, not email transport or formats.
WHOIS++ is the more specific child tag and fits better than the legacy WHOIS parent.

RFC2958.title: The application/whoispp-response Content-type
RFC2958.summary: Registers the application/whoispp-response MIME media type and gives an ABNF grammar for Whois++ server responses so MIME-enabled software can carry Whois++ transactions.

WHOIS++.why: The document specifies how Whois++ server responses are structured and carried, so it is about the Whois++ protocol.
WHOIS++.quote: This document defines the expression of Whois++ protocol (RFC1835) responses within MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) (RFC2046) media types.

media types.why: A large part of the document is the IANA media type registration template for a new subtype.
media types.quote: Registration of MIME media type application/whoispp-response

rejected.why: MIME is only the carrier. The document registers a type, which the media types tag covers, and does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the response grammar. The document does not describe ABNF itself.
Mail software is the intended carrier, but the document does not specify email transport or access.
WHOIS++ is the more specific child tag and fits better. The legacy WHOIS protocol is only cited in the references.

RFC2959.title: Real-Time Transport Protocol Management Information Base
RFC2959.summary: Defines the SMIv2 RTP-MIB module (session, sender, receiver and inverse-lookup tables) for managing and monitoring RTP/RTCP systems via SNMP.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module definition (RTP-MIB) using SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

RTP.why: The MIB models RTP sessions, senders (SSRC) and receivers, so RTP readers would want it.
RTP.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) systems (RFC1889).

RTCP.why: Many objects are populated from RTCP sender/receiver reports and BYEs, and RTP monitors operate via RTCP.
RTCP.quote: RTP monitors may collect RTCP information on senders and receivers to and from an RTP host or intermediate-system.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management substrate; the document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the more specific MIB tag.
The MIB exposes counters like jitter and loss, but it is a management data model rather than a measurement methodology.
Multicast sessions are mentioned only as a use case for monitoring, not the subject of the document.

RFC2960.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC2960.summary: RFC 2960 specifies SCTP, a reliable, message-oriented, multi-homed, multi-streamed transport protocol over IP originally designed for carrying PSTN signalling, covering packet formats, association setup with cookies, data transfer, congestion control, fault management, and the ULP API.

SCTP.why: The entire document is the base specification of SCTP: chunk formats, association state machine, data transfer, congestion control, and API.
SCTP.quote: This document describes the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP). SCTP is designed to transport PSTN signaling messages over IP networks, but is capable of broader applications.

rejected.why: Section 7 adapts TCP congestion control to SCTP, but it is one part of the SCTP spec and SCTP is the more specific tag.
TCP is the comparison point and congestion control basis, not the subject of the document.
SCTP was developed in the sigtran WG and motivated by SS7 transport, but this document specifies the generic transport, not the adaptation layers.
ECN is only reserved and sketched in Appendix A as an optional feature, not a substantial focus.
Adler-32 is used as the packet checksum, but it is a mechanism within SCTP rather than a subject of its own.
Section 7.3 only describes how existing PMTUD applies to SCTP.

RFC2961.title: RSVP Refresh Overhead Reduction Extensions
RFC2961.summary: RFC 2961 defines RSVP extensions (Bundle message, MESSAGE_ID objects with ACK/NACK, Srefresh summary refresh, and exponential back-off retransmission) to reduce refresh overhead and give reliable per-hop RSVP message delivery.

RSVP.why: The whole document extends RSVP with new messages and objects (Bundle, Ack, Srefresh, MESSAGE_ID). RSVP readers need it.
RSVP.quote: This document describes a number of mechanisms that can be used to reduce processing overhead requirements of refresh messages

rejected.why: The acknowledgments mention the MPLS-TE design team, but the document specifies base RSVP extensions, not MPLS.
The extensions apply to RSVP generally. They do not define TE LSP signalling.
Multicast session handling is covered (ACK implosion, SRC_LIST), but only as a part of the RSVP extension, not as multicast routing.
IPv6 object formats are defined, but the document is not about IPv6.
The exponential back-off applies to retransmission of signalling messages, not to data congestion control.

RFC2962.title: An SNMP Application Level Gateway for Payload Address Translation
RFC2962.summary: Describes an SNMP Application Level Gateway that statically translates IP addresses in SNMP payloads (basic and advanced variants) so managers can manage NATed, overlapping addressing realms, and discusses limitations, security issues and SNMP proxy alternatives.

SNMP.why: The document specifies how SNMP packets are parsed and rewritten, including BER encoding, instance identifiers, SNMPv3 security impact and SNMP proxies as an alternative.
SNMP.quote: This document describes the ALG (Application Level Gateway) for the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) by which IP (Internet Protocol) addresses in the payload of SNMP packets are statically mapped

NAT.why: The ALG exists as a companion to static basic NAT, translating payload addresses that NAT alone leaves unchanged. The document is a product of the NAT working group.
NAT.quote: An SNMP ALG allows network management stations to manage multiple networks that use conflicting IP addresses.

rejected.why: MIB awareness is needed by the advanced ALG, but the document defines no MIB module.
BER encoding is explained in an appendix to show where to find addresses, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
UDP is only the transport. The checksum adjustment is a side detail of address rewriting.
The incremental checksum update is a small implementation detail, not the subject of the document.
IPv4 addresses are the data being translated, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
The SNMP tag already covers this; no separate topic tag is needed.

RFC2963.title: A Rate Adaptive Shaper for Differentiated Services
RFC2963.summary: Informational memo defining rate adaptive shapers (srRAS, trRAS and green variants) placed upstream of the srTCM/trTCM three color markers at Diffserv ingress to reduce burstiness and improve TCP goodput under AF PHB.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies shapers and traffic conditioners for Diffserv networks, working with the srTCM/trTCM markers and AF PHB. Diffserv is the specific subject its readers would look under.
Diffserv.quote: These RAS improve the performance of TCP when a TCM is used at the ingress of a diffserv network by reducing the burstiness of the traffic.

rejected.why: TCP is the traffic whose performance is improved and is simulated, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Diffserv is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
The shaper does not control congestion. It assumes TCP reacts to congestion and only smooths bursts.
RIO is only used in the simulation's core routers and is not what the document defines.

gaps.name: Traffic conditioning (shaping/metering/marking, Three Color Markers)
gaps.why: The document is about traffic shapers and meters/markers for Diffserv. No taxonomy tag covers traffic conditioning specifically, so Diffserv is the closest fit.

RFC2964.title: Use of HTTP State Management
RFC2964.summary: BCP identifying uses of HTTP State Management (cookies) that are not recommended or harmful, such as third-party information leakage and use for authentication, and giving privacy and user-interface guidance for clients.

cookies.why: The whole document is guidance on appropriate and problematic uses of the HTTP State Management mechanism (cookies), including client capabilities and domain-match limitations.
cookies.quote: This memo identifies specific uses of Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) State Management protocol which are either (a) not recommended by the IETF, or (b) believed to be harmful

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate; the document concerns the state management (cookie) extension, which has its own child tag.
Privacy is a major theme, but it is addressed specifically through cookie usage, so the cookies tag is the more specific fit.
The document advises against using cookies for authentication, but does not specify or analyse HTTP authentication schemes.
Security concerns are discussed, but only within the cookie mechanism, which is already tagged more specifically.

RFC2965.title: HTTP State Management Mechanism
RFC2965.summary: RFC 2965 specifies the HTTP state management mechanism (cookies) using the Cookie, Cookie2 and Set-Cookie2 headers, obsoleting RFC 2109, with rules for origin servers, user agents, caches, and privacy.

cookies.why: The whole document defines the cookie state management mechanism: syntax, attributes, user agent and server behaviour, and privacy controls.
cookies.quote: It describes three new headers, Cookie, Cookie2, and Set-Cookie2, which carry state information between participating origin servers and user agents.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate. The document adds headers for state management, which the more specific cookies tag covers.
Caching of Set-Cookie2 is discussed in a subsection, but it is incidental to the cookie mechanism and not a main subject.
Privacy is a section of the document, but its focus is the cookie mechanism, which the cookies tag already covers.
URI syntax and path matching are used only as inputs to cookie matching rules.

RFC2966.title: Domain-wide Prefix Distribution with Two-Level IS-IS
RFC2966.summary: Informational RFC extending IS-IS (RFC 1195) with an up/down bit and rules so IP prefixes can be leaked between level 1 and level 2 (including L2->L1) without forming loops, for domain-wide prefix distribution.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies extensions to IS-IS: up/down bit, external reachability TLV in L1 LSPs, route preference ordering and interoperability.
IS-IS.quote: This document extends the semantics presented in RFC 1195 so that a routing domain running with both level 1 and level 2 Intermediate Systems (IS) [routers] can distribute IP prefixes

rejected.why: BGP shortest-exit routing and MED are only motivations for finer prefix granularity; the document doesn't specify BGP.
The hierarchy/scalability tradeoff is discussed, but the IS-IS tag covers the subject more specifically.
IPv4 prefixes are the payload carried, but the document is about IS-IS routing, not IPv4 itself.

RFC2967.title: TISDAG - Technical Infrastructure for Swedish Directory Access Gateways
RFC2967.summary: RFC 2967 specifies TISDAG, a Swedish white-pages Directory Access Gateway that uses a CIP-based referral index and protocol-translating access points (SMTP, HTTP, Whois++, LDAPv2/v3) to give uniform query access to directory providers.

LDAP.why: LDAPv2 and LDAPv3 are both client-facing and server-facing protocols, with detailed query/result/error mappings and schema mappings (inetOrgPerson, organizationalRole).
LDAP.quote: Input to the LDAPv3 DAG-CAP follows the LDAPv3 definition

WHOIS++.why: Whois++ is a client protocol and a provider protocol, and DAG/IP is itself derived from it. It uses USER/ORGROLE templates and referrals.
WHOIS++.quote: Input to the Whois++ DAG-CAP follows the Whois++ standard ([6]).

directory services.why: The whole document is about a white-pages directory gateway and index spanning many directory providers.
directory services.quote: develop the necessary technical infrastructure to provide a single-access-point service for searching for whitepages information on Swedish Internet users

WHOIS.why: The Whois++ DAG-CAP and DAG-SAP are specified, and the internal protocol derives from Whois++. WHOIS++ is a child of WHOIS, so the more specific tag WHOIS++ is already given; this is noted only for completeness and not tagged separately.
WHOIS.quote: The Whois++ protocol was selected as the basis of the DAG/IP for several reasons

rejected.why: Parent of WHOIS++, which is already tagged; ancestors are implied.
Mail is only one of the client access channels, and CIP objects travel over MIME-encoded SMTP. It is a substrate, not the subject.
The web DAG-CAP is just a form-based front-end over HTTP POST and is not about HTTP itself.
MIME is used for the mail query/response and CIP transport, but only as a substrate.
UTF-8 is mandated for DAG/IP and index objects, but it is one brief constraint, not the document's subject.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammars.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) / Tagged Index Object
gaps.why: The Referral Index is built on CIP index objects, with an appendix defining their use. The taxonomy has no CIP or query-routing tag, and the closest, directory services, is only a general fit.

RFC2968.title: Mesh of Multiple DAG servers - Results from TISDAG
RFC2968.summary: Informational memo describing how multiple TISDAG Directory Access Gateway (DAG) white-pages services could be meshed by exchanging aggregated Common Indexing Protocol index objects, with top-down and bottom-up traversal scenarios.

directory services.why: The document is about meshing distributed directory (white pages) referral-index services, including referral generation, chaining and query scoping. No LDAP or X.500 technology tag fits more specifically, so the parent topic is used.
directory services.quote: The purpose of such a mesh of servers is to implement some kind of distributed sharing of indexing and/or searching tasks across different servers.

rejected.why: The CIP index-object mesh is conceptually derived from WHOIS++ centroids and meshes. This document never specifies or discusses WHOIS++ itself, so the tag does not fit.
The DAG services front directory access protocols, but LDAP is not named or specified here. The protocols appear only as abstract Prot1, Prot2 and so on.
Referrals point to other directory servers, but the subject is directory index meshing, not discovering network services.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP)
gaps.why: The document centres on exchanging CIP index objects among referral index servers, but the taxonomy has no CIP tag. Only the generic directory services topic is available.

RFC2969.title: Wide Area Directory Deployment - Experiences from TISDAG
RFC2969.summary: Informational report of experiences from the TISDAG project deploying a national whitepages directory gateway (DAG) over LDAP, Whois++, HTTP and SMTP, using CIP index objects and referrals, with lessons, performance observations and related projects.

directory services.why: The whole document is about deploying a wide-area whitepages directory service, including referral indexes, schemas and related directory projects.
directory services.quote: catalogues some of the experiences gained in developing the necessary infrastructure for a national (i.e., multi-organizational) directory service

LDAP.why: Substantial parts, including the Appendix, discuss LDAPv2/v3 client and server behaviour, objectclasses, referrals and response codes encountered in deployment.
LDAP.quote: none of the "standard" LDAP person objectclasses included organization ("o") as an attribute

WHOIS++.why: Whois++ is a supported access protocol and centroid index growth is compared with the Tagged Index Object; the index/referral architecture is central to the document.
WHOIS++.quote: Whois++'s centroid (see [centroid]) was the fact that the index object size did not grow linearly with the size of data indexed

rejected.why: HTTP is only one of several client access protocols; the document is not about it.
Only mentioned as an access method (and for mailing CIP objects), not a subject of the document.
Not discussed; the directories are LDAP/Whois++ based.
Appears only in a brief appendix anecdote about character encoding.
Email addresses are looked up through the directory but email is not what the document addresses.

gaps.name: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) / Tagged Index Object
gaps.why: Index objects and referral indexing are central to the document, but the taxonomy has no tag for CIP; it is closest to WHOIS++ centroids and directory services.

RFC2970.title: Architecture for Integrated Directory Services - Result from TISDAG
RFC2970.summary: Informational RFC describing the Directory Access Gateway (DAG) service architecture generalised from the Swedish TISDAG project, using client access points, service access points and an internal protocol to integrate distributed directory servers behind a single entry point.

directory services.why: The document is an architecture for integrating distributed whitepages directory servers (referrals, proxying, schema translation) into one service, which is the directory services topic.
directory services.quote: outlines an approach to providing the necessary infrastructure for integrating such widely-scattered servers into a single service, rather than attempting to mandate a single protocol and schema set

rejected.why: LDAPv2/v3 appear as example CAP and SAP protocols, but the document does not specify, extend or analyse LDAP.
Whois++ is mentioned as one of the CAP protocols in TISDAG, but the document is not about it.
HTTP is cited as a possible internal protocol and as an example CAP protocol only.
AAA servers are mentioned as possible supporting services and DAG/IP requirements, but only in passing.
Although it is an architecture document, it covers a directory service architecture and not Internet-wide architectural principles.

RFC2971.title: IMAP4 ID extension
RFC2971.summary: Defines the IMAP4 ID extension, an ID command and response letting IMAP clients and servers exchange implementation identification (name, version, OS, vendor) for bug reports and statistics.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4rev1 with a new ID command, response, capability and grammar additions, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: The ID extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4rev1 (IMAP4rev1) protocol allows the server and client to exchange identification information

rejected.why: Privacy risks of sending identifying fields are discussed, but only as a caveat. The document is not about privacy considerations in general.
IMAP is an email access protocol, but the more specific IMAP tag already covers this and implies its ancestors.
Section 5 gives guidance on firewalls and intermediaries handling ID, but it is a small part of the document and not about firewall traversal.

RFC2972.title: Context and Goals for Common Name Resolution
RFC2972.summary: Informational RFC setting out the context, terminology and goals for a Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP), which would map human-friendly names such as company names or book titles to Internet resources, distinct from URIs, DNS and general search.

naming.why: The document defines common names, their namespaces (private and public) and resolution as mapping to resources. That is general naming and name resolution, not tied to DNS or any other single system.
naming.quote: Common name "resolution" is a process of mapping from common names to Internet resources; a Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP) is a network protocol used in such a process.

service discovery.why: The document mentions discovery and selection of resolution providers, but it places them mostly out of scope. It is a minor theme, so this tag is secondary.
service discovery.quote: it is key that there exists a standard resolution protocol (and a service discovery mechanism).
service discovery.section: 6. Distributors/integrators of common name resolution services

rejected.why: The document contrasts common names with URIs and URNs. It says common names are not URIs and that URIs are only the resource identifiers a resolution returns. It does not specify anything about URIs.
DNS appears only in passing, as in "DNS TLD categories" in the list of vertical directories. CNRP is a separate mechanism.
LDAP is only a comparison point ("simpler than LDAP"). The document does not specify or extend it.
Directory services are discussed as users of CNRP and are contrasted with search engines. The document is about name resolution rather than directory access or synchronization.
Browsers and portals are the expected clients, but the document does not address web architecture itself.

gaps.name: Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP)
gaps.why: The document is about this proposed lightweight resolution and search protocol for human-friendly names. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so the general naming tag is the nearest fit.

RFC2973.title: IS-IS Mesh Groups
RFC2973.summary: Informational RFC documenting the IS-IS mesh groups mechanism, which modifies ISO 10589 LSP flooding and CSNP rules to reduce redundant LSP transmissions in full-mesh point-to-point topologies.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies modifications to IS-IS flooding (SRM flags, CSNP behavior, circuit attributes) and covers interoperation with non-mesh-group implementations.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes a mechanism to reduce redundant packet transmissions for the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Routing protocol, as described in ISO 10589.

rejected.why: ATM and frame relay VCs are only mentioned as example environments for full-mesh topologies; the document is not about them.
Mentioned only as an example of a network that yields full-mesh point-to-point circuits.
The document is about a specific IS-IS flooding mechanism, so the IS-IS tag fits better than the broader routing architecture topic.
IS-IS is an OSI protocol, but the document does not address OSI network-layer protocols or their coexistence with IP.

RFC2974.title: Session Announcement Protocol
RFC2974.summary: Specifies SAP v2, a protocol for periodically multicasting session descriptions (usually SDP) to announce multicast sessions, including announcement timing, deletion, modification, packet format, optional encryption and authentication, and proxy caching.

service discovery.why: SAP is a session directory announcement protocol: it lets listeners discover multicast sessions on the network. No specific SAP tag exists, so the service discovery topic fits best.
service discovery.quote: In order to assist the advertisement of multicast multimedia conferences and other multicast sessions, and to communicate the relevant session setup information to prospective participants, a distributed session directory may be used.

multicast.why: The protocol is built on IP multicast. It specifies the IPv4 global and administrative scope addresses and the IPv6 announcement addresses, so multicast readers would want it.
multicast.quote: A SAP announcer periodically multicasts an announcement packet to a well known multicast address and port.

rejected.why: SDP is the payload SAP carries. It is specified in a companion memo, and this document only requires support for application/sdp.
UDP is only the substrate. SAP uses best-effort UDP on port 9875 and does not define anything new about UDP.
PGP is one of two authentication formats the document references. It is a mechanism SAP uses, not the subject of the document.
CMS is the other referenced authentication format. The document only defines how to use it for the SAP authentication subheader.
zlib is the compression applied to the payload, used as a mechanism only.
Sessions are multimedia conferences, but the document is about announcing sessions, not the media or signalling itself.

gaps.name: Session Announcement Protocol (SAP) / session directory
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SAP or multicast session directories. The closest tags are service discovery and multicast.

RFC2975.title: Introduction to Accounting Management
RFC2975.summary: RFC 2975 introduces accounting management (collection of resource consumption data for capacity planning, billing, auditing and cost allocation), analyses reliability and scaling issues in accounting systems, and reviews RADIUS, TACACS+, SNMP and SMTP-based transfer as accounting tools.

AAA.why: The document is about the accounting part of AAA: architecture, objectives, inter/intra-domain accounting, and requirements for accounting protocols.
AAA.quote: The field of Accounting Management is concerned with the collection of resource consumption data for the purposes of capacity and trend analysis, cost allocation, auditing, and billing.

RADIUS.why: A dedicated section analyses RADIUS accounting's reliability, scaling and security shortcomings, and it recurs in the summary table.
RADIUS.quote: RADIUS accounting, described in [4], was developed as an add-on to the RADIUS authentication protocol

TACACS+.why: TACACS+ accounting is reviewed as one of three accounting protocols and compared in the summary.
TACACS+.quote: TACACS+ offers an accounting model with start, stop, and interim update messages.

SNMP.why: The longest section covers SNMP for accounting: security, contexts, views, proxy forwarders, domain separation, and NMRG extensions.
SNMP.quote: SNMP, described in [19],[27]-[41], has been widely deployed in a wide variety of intra-domain accounting applications, typically using the polling data collection model.

rejected.why: Only reviewed briefly as a possible accounting data transfer mechanism in section 4.1, not a subject of the document.
Accounting management is a network-management function, but the AAA and SNMP tags cover the content more specifically.
Transport choice (UDP, TCP, SCTP) is discussed for reliability, but TCP is only substrate.
Mentioned as a transport alternative for reliability, not a subject of the document.
The Kerberos Security Model for SNMPv3 is mentioned only as ongoing research.
MIB modules are discussed in the SNMP context only; the document defines none.

gaps.name: Accounting management
gaps.why: The document's main subject is accounting (usage metering, billing, auditing, record production), which has no dedicated tag; AAA is the closest fit.

RFC2976.title: The SIP INFO Method
RFC2976.summary: RFC 2976 defines the SIP INFO method, an extension to SIP for carrying application-level mid-session signalling information (e.g., DTMF, PSTN signalling) along the session signalling path without changing call state.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP method, including its response behaviour, header support, and proxy/UA rules.
SIP.quote: This extension adds the INFO method to the SIP protocol.

rejected.why: ISUP/ISDN signalling is only an example use; the document does not specify PSTN interworking.
Carrying ISUP is mentioned as a potential use, but SIP-T encapsulation is not defined here.
Not discussed; INFO does not alter session parameters.
Message bodies are mentioned but their definition is explicitly out of scope.

RFC2977.title: Mobile IP Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting Requirements
RFC2977.summary: Informational requirements document stating what a AAA protocol and infrastructure must support (security associations, brokers, key distribution, home agent/address allocation, accounting, fast handover) to enable Mobile IP service across administrative domains.

AAA.why: The document's purpose is to define requirements for AAA frameworks: attendants, local/home/broker AAA servers, security associations, and accounting.
AAA.quote: This document contains the requirements which would have to be supported by a AAA service to aid in providing Mobile IP services.

IP mobility.why: The requirements are derived from Mobile IP operation: foreign agent, home agent, registration, key distribution, local home agents, fast handover, and IPv6 considerations.
IP mobility.quote: Mobile IP is a technology that allows a network node ("mobile node") to migrate from its "home" network to other networks

rejected.why: Used as an example of today's roaming deployment and for the attacks that motivate end-to-end security, but the document specifies requirements for a new AAA protocol, not RADIUS.
The document is about Mobile IP in general, with a short IPv6 section, and specifies AAA requirements rather than the Mobile IPv4 protocol; the parent IP mobility tag fits better.
Only a brief IPv6 considerations section; not a substantial part of the document.
IPsec and IKE are mentioned only in passing as possible uses of AAA-distributed keys.
Key distribution during initial registration is one requirement among many, and AAA is the more specific subject.
Mentioned only as a possible attendant and address allocator, and its scope is explicitly outside this document.

RFC2978.title: IANA Charset Registration Procedures
RFC2978.summary: BCP 19 defines the IANA procedure and requirements for registering charsets (names, aliases, MIBenum values, template) for use in MIME and other Internet protocols, obsoleting RFC 2278.

character sets.why: The whole document defines how charsets are registered, named and reviewed. This is the character set registration subject.
character sets.quote: The charset registration procedure exists solely to associate a specific name or names with a given charset

IANA.why: It specifies an IANA registry procedure with a review mailing list, a designated reviewer, and IANA assigning MIBenum values.
IANA.quote: the IANA will register the charset, assign a MIBenum value, and make its registration available to the community.

media types.why: Registered names must fit the MIME charset parameter syntax, and each registration must state suitability for MIME text. This ties the registry closely to MIME content types.
media types.quote: charsets intended for use in MIME content types under the "text" top-level type MUST conform to the restrictions on that type described in RFC 2045.

rejected.why: MIME is the context in which charset labels are used. The document does not specify MIME body structure or encodings.
The Printer MIB is cited only as the source of MIBenum values. The document does not define or extend any MIB.
The parent topic is implied by character sets, so it is not listed separately.
US-ASCII appears only as an example charset and as the syntax for names. The document is not about it.

RFC2979.title: Behavior of and Requirements for Internet Firewalls
RFC2979.summary: Informational RFC defining behavioral characteristics and a transparency requirement for Internet firewalls, with examples (Path MTU Discovery/ICMP, SMTP extensions) and guidance for application protocol designers.

firewall.why: The whole document specifies firewall behavior and interoperability requirements, so it belongs on the firewall subject page.
firewall.quote: The introduction of a firewall and any associated tunneling or access negotiation facilities MUST NOT cause unintended failures of legitimate and standards-compliant usage

PMTUD.why: A full worked example explains that firewalls must not block ICMP Fragmentation Needed errors, which would break PMTUD.
PMTUD.quote: This often creates "black holes" for Path MTU Discovery [3], causing legitimate application traffic to be delayed or completely blocked

rejected.why: SMTP extension handling by firewalls is a short example, not a subject of the document.
ICMP filtering is discussed only within the PMTUD example; PMTUD is the more specific fit.
SOCKS is cited only as an example of an access negotiation facility, not specified or extended.
The document explicitly states NAT is out of scope and disjoint from firewall functions.
The document is about firewall behavior, which the firewall tag covers more specifically.

RFC2980.title: Common NNTP Extensions
RFC2980.summary: Informational RFC documenting popular, non-standard extensions to NNTP (RFC 977): transport commands (CHECK, TAKETHIS, MODE STREAM, XREPLIC), newsreader commands (LIST variants, XOVER, XHDR, XPAT, etc.), AUTHINFO, DATE, wildmat, and implementation issues.

NNTP.why: The whole document specifies and documents extensions to NNTP commands and responses, so NNTP readers would look here.
NNTP.quote: a number of popular extensions to the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) protocol defined in RFC 977 are documented and discussed

rejected.why: NNTP is a child of Netnews and is the more specific fit. Article headers are discussed only incidentally.
AUTHINFO GENERIC is only said to be similar to the IMAP authenticators of RFC 1731. SASL is not specified or profiled.
NTP is mentioned only as background for the DATE command.
AUTHINFO is one section of a larger NNTP extension catalogue. The NNTP tag covers it, and the topic is not addressed in its own right.
DNS reverse lookup is mentioned only for the NNTP-Posting-Host header.

gaps.name: wildmat pattern matching
gaps.why: Section 3.3 specifies the wildmat glob format used by NNTP commands. The taxonomy has no tag for it, but it is a small part of the document.

RFC2981.title: Event MIB
RFC2981.summary: Defines the Event MIB (DISMAN-EVENT-MIB), an SNMP MIB module for configuring triggers (existence, boolean, threshold) on local or remote MIB objects and events that send notifications or perform SNMP sets.

MIB.why: The document's core is a MIB module (DISMAN-EVENT-MIB) with trigger, objects, event and notification tables defined in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects that can be used to manage and monitor MIB objects and take action through events.

SNMP.why: The MIB drives SNMP Get/GetNext/Set operations and notifications, and depends on SNMPv3 target/notification MIBs and VACM. This is part of the SNMP framework.
SNMP.quote: Remote monitoring uses the tag service of the Management Target MIB [RFC2573] to select and access remote systems as an ordinary SNMP-based management application.

rejected.why: The Event MIB is described as a superset of the RMON alarm and event groups, but it does not specify RMON.
It provides simple trigger/action automation, not a policy information model.
It monitors MIB objects and takes actions on thresholds, but it is not about streaming operational data.

RFC2982.title: Distributed Management Expression MIB
RFC2982.summary: Defines the DISMAN-EXPRESSION-MIB, an SNMP MIB module for configuring expressions over existing MIB objects (with wildcarding, delta sampling and error reporting) whose results appear as ordinary MIB objects, e.g. as Event MIB triggers.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SMIv2) defining expression, object, error and value tables, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing expressions of MIB objects.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB lives in. The document defines a MIB module, not changes to the SNMP protocol, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
This is implied as an ancestor of the MIB tag, so I don't list it separately.
The utilization example is only an illustration. The document is not about performance metrics or methods.

RFC2983.title: Differentiated Services and Tunnels
RFC2983.summary: Informational RFC analysing how Differentiated Services interacts with IP tunnels, defining uniform and pipe conceptual models and guidance on where traffic conditioning and DSCP selection occur at tunnel ingress and egress.

Diffserv.why: The whole document is about diffserv traffic conditioning and DSCP handling in the presence of tunnels, supplementing the diffserv architecture.
Diffserv.quote: This document considers the interaction of Differentiated Services (diffserv) (RFC 2474, RFC 2475) with IP tunnels of various forms.

tunneling.why: The document analyses IP tunnel encapsulation and decapsulation generically (IP-in-IP, L2TP, IPsec), not one specific tunnel protocol, so the generic tunneling topic fits.
tunneling.quote: An IP tunnel encapsulates IP traffic in another IP header as it passes through the tunnel

rejected.why: IPsec tunnels are discussed as a constraint (inner DSCP must be selected at egress), but the document is not about IPsec itself.
L2TP is only cited as an example of a reordering-sensitive tunnel.
RFC 2003 IP-in-IP is mentioned as the simplest tunnel example; the document covers tunnels generally.
Section 6 briefly notes translators like SIIT are not tunnels but should allow diffserv edge processing; this is a minor aside.
Diffserv is the more specific tag and is already chosen; QoS parent is implied.

RFC2984.title: Use of the CAST-128 Encryption Algorithm in CMS
RFC2984.summary: Specifies how to use the CAST-128 cipher for content encryption and key wrapping in CMS, giving OIDs, parameters, key wrap procedures and S/MIME capability advertisement.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with new algorithm OIDs, parameters and key wrap procedures for CAST-128.
