CMS.quote: specifies how to incorporate CAST-128 (RFC2144) into the S/MIME Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) as an additional algorithm for symmetric encryption

S/MIME.why: A section covers S/MIME client capabilities advertisement, including the DER-encoded SMIMECapability for CAST-128.
S/MIME.quote: An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the set of cryptographic functions it supports by using the S/MIME capabilities attribute.

rejected.why: No dedicated CAST-128 tag exists. The document defines no new cipher and only profiles an existing one for CMS. Under the rules, a parent topic is not added when a tech tag already covers the document.
AES is not mentioned. 3DES is named only as the mandatory-to-implement baseline.
Triple-DES appears only in the motivation as the mandatory algorithm that CAST-128 is an alternative to. The document is not about it.
The OIDs and parameter structures are written in ASN.1, but that is only notation. The document is not about ASN.1.

gaps.name: CAST-128
gaps.why: The document is about a specific symmetric cipher, but the taxonomy has no CAST-128 tag under cryptography. It would suit the RFC 2144 and RFC 2984 pair.

RFC2985.title: PKCS #9: Selected Object Classes and Attribute Types Version 2.0
RFC2985.summary: Republication of PKCS #9 v2.0 defining two auxiliary LDAP/X.500 object classes (pkcsEntity, naturalPerson) and attribute types and matching rules for PKCS #7/CMS signed data, PKCS #10 certificate requests, PKCS #12 and PKCS #15, with ASN.1 and LDAP schema definitions.

CMS.why: Defines contentType, messageDigest, signingTime, counterSignature, randomNonce and sequenceNumber attributes used in SignerInfo authenticated/unauthenticated attributes of CMS/PKCS #7 signed data.
CMS.quote: defines some attribute types for use in conjunction with PKCS #7 [14] (and S/MIME CMS [3]) digitally signed messages

LDAP.why: Defines LDAP/X.500 auxiliary object classes, attribute types, matching rules and an LDAP-style schema in Appendix B.
LDAP.quote: selection of object classes and attribute types for use in conjunction with public-key cryptography and Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) accessible directories

PKI.why: Defines challengePassword and extensionRequest attributes for certification requests and PKCS #12/#15 key and token storage attributes, supporting PKI data handling.
PKI.quote: PKCS #10 [16] certificate-signing requests

ASN.1.why: A substantial part of the document is a compilable ASN.1 module with all definitions.
ASN.1.quote: This appendix includes all of the ASN.1 type and value definitions contained in this document in the form of the ASN.1 module PKCS-9.

rejected.why: S/MIME attributes (signingDescription, smimeCapabilities) are only mentioned for completeness in one short section; the document isn't about S/MIME.
Object classes are designed for X.500 and LDAP directories, but the document is about attribute definitions, and LDAP is the principal directory tech.
Certificate extensions are referenced only via extensionRequest; the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
Parent of LDAP, which was chosen as the more specific tag.

gaps.name: PKCS (Public-Key Cryptography Standards)
gaps.why: The document republishes PKCS #9 and references PKCS #7, #8, #10, #12 and #15; the taxonomy has no tag for the PKCS series.

RFC2986.title: PKCS #10: Certification Request Syntax Specification Version 1.7
RFC2986.summary: Republication of PKCS #10 v1.7, defining the ASN.1 syntax of a signed certification request (subject DN, public key, attributes) sent to a CA to obtain an X.509 certificate.

PKI.why: The document specifies the certification request format used to request certificates from a CA, which is core PKI. It is a PKI-level request syntax, not an X.509 certificate profile, so the parent PKI tag fits best.
PKI.quote: A certification request consists of a distinguished name, a public key, and optionally a set of attributes, collectively signed by the entity requesting certification.

rejected.why: The request results in an X.509 certificate, but the document defines the request syntax, not the certificate format or a profile of it.
The syntax is written in ASN.1 with an appendix module, but ASN.1 is only the notation used, not the subject of the document.
RFC 2510 is cited as another application of this syntax, but the document does not specify CMP.
PKCS #1 RSA is mentioned only as an example algorithm; the document is not about RSA.
PKCS #7 is mentioned only as a possible way to return the certificate, which is out of scope.

RFC2987.title: Registration of Charset and Languages Media Features Tags
RFC2987.summary: Registers the "charset" and "language" media feature tags (with ASN.1 identifiers, value rules and usage examples) per the RFC 2506 template, so devices can express supported character sets and human languages.

content negotiation.why: The document registers media feature tags used in media feature and content negotiation expressions, which is exactly the subject of this tag.
content negotiation.quote: These media features allow specification of character sets and human languages that can be understood by devices and the devices' users.

character sets.why: One of the two registrations defines a feature tag whose values are registered charset names, so readers of character set registration and use would want it.
character sets.quote: Ability to display particular charsets as defined in [CHARSET].

language tags.why: The language feature tag takes RFC 1766 language tags as values and specifies how they are compared, which is relevant to language tag usage.
language tags.quote: language tags are always handled as a single token, and "subtags" are not used for comparison.

rejected.why: The IANA Considerations only say the document consists of registrations. The document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
Media feature tags are not MIME media types, and the document registers no media type.
The document touches on charsets and languages, but the more specific tags above fit better, so the parent is not needed.

gaps.name: media feature tags
gaps.why: The document registers media feature tags under the RFC 2506 registration procedure. The taxonomy has no tag for the media feature tag registry, so content negotiation is the closest fit.

RFC2988.title: Computing TCP's Retransmission Timer
RFC2988.summary: Specifies the standard algorithm TCP senders must use to compute and manage the retransmission timeout (RTO), including SRTT/RTTVAR estimation, Karn's algorithm, clock granularity and timer backoff.

TCP.why: The whole document specifies a mandatory TCP sender behaviour: RTO computation, RTT sampling and retransmission timer management.
TCP.quote: This document defines the standard algorithm that Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) senders are required to use to compute and manage their retransmission timer.

rejected.why: RFC 2581 congestion control is referenced and explicitly left unaltered. The document concerns the retransmission timer, not window or rate control.

RFC2989.title: Criteria for Evaluating AAA Protocols for Network Access
RFC2989.summary: Informational summary of AAA protocol requirements for network access (authentication, authorization, accounting), collected from NASREQ, ROAMOPS, MOBILEIP and TIA 45.6, to be used as criteria for evaluating AAA protocol submissions.

AAA.why: The whole document is a set of requirements for AAA protocols, split into general, authentication, authorization and accounting requirements, so the AAA frameworks page is the right home.
AAA.quote: This document represents a summary of AAA protocol requirements for network access.

rejected.why: RADIUS is mentioned only as a compatibility requirement (RADIUS gateway capability) and as a reference. The document does not specify or analyse RADIUS.
EAP transport is one requirement among many in the authentication table. The document is not about EAP itself.
Mobile IP requirements feed the criteria, but the document concerns AAA, not Mobile IP protocol mechanics.
CHAP and PPP appear only as authentication mechanisms the AAA protocol must carry.
The document evaluates candidate protocols generically and never names or specifies Diameter.

RFC2990.title: Next Steps for the IP QoS Architecture
RFC2990.summary: IAB informational memo surveying outstanding architectural issues in IP QoS (IntServ/RSVP vs DiffServ state/stateless approaches) and suggesting next steps for end-to-end QoS deployment.

QoS.why: The whole document is about the IP QoS architecture as a whole, comparing IntServ and DiffServ and the gaps in integrating them end-to-end. The general QoS topic tag fits better than any single child.
QoS.quote: This document highlights the outstanding architectural issues relating to the deployment and use of QoS mechanisms within internet networks

Diffserv.why: DiffServ is analysed throughout: its stateless model, boundary-centric operation, classifiers, service set size and DSCP use.
Diffserv.quote: An alternative approach to load control is to decouple the network load control function from the application. This is the basis of the Differentiated Services architecture.

Intserv.why: IntServ with RSVP is the other half of the comparison, covering per-flow state, scalability concerns and its use for end-to-end signalling.
Intserv.quote: This application-signaled approach can be used within the Integrated Services architecture, where the application frames its service request within the resource reservation protocol (RSVP)

rejected.why: RSVP is discussed as the IntServ signalling mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend it. Its subject is the overall QoS architecture.
Section 3.5 discusses TCP interaction with QoS (ACK treatment, token buckets), but it is one sub-issue, not a main subject.
Section 3.4 touches on traffic engineering and QoS routing, but only briefly as a research topic.
TCP is covered only as it interacts with QoS service classes and conditioners, not as a protocol being specified or extended.

RFC2991.title: Multipath Issues in Unicast and Multicast Next-Hop Selection
RFC2991.summary: Informational memo describing problems with multipath (ECMP) next-hop selection in unicast and multicast forwarding and recommending hash-threshold and HRW methods to keep flows on a single path.

ECMP.why: The whole document is about choosing among equal-cost next-hops: modulo-N, hash-threshold and HRW, and when each applies.
ECMP.quote: The effect of multipath routing on a forwarder is that the forwarder potentially has several next-hops for any given destination and must use some method to choose which next-hop

rejected.why: PIM-SM is only mentioned as an example of explicit-join multicast where HRW picks the next-hop toward the RP. The document does not specify or extend it.
OSPF and IS-IS are cited as protocols that allow ECMP, but the document is not about them.
Multicast forwarding is discussed in section 4.2, but the document concerns next-hop selection generally, and ECMP covers it.
Path MTU variation is listed as one problem of naive multipath, but it is not a subject of the document.
TCP reordering and fast retransmit are cited only as a motivation.
Section 6 on redundant parallel links is a brief aside and not the main subject.

RFC2992.title: Analysis of an Equal-Cost Multi-Path Algorithm
RFC2992.summary: Informational analysis of the hash-threshold ECMP next-hop selection algorithm, covering its performance and flow disruption when next-hops change, compared against modulo-N and highest random weight.

ECMP.why: The whole document analyses an algorithm for choosing among equal-cost next-hops, including its performance and its disruption when the next-hop set changes.
ECMP.quote: Equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) is a routing technique for routing packets along multiple paths of equal cost.

rejected.why: TCP is mentioned only as a protocol that suffers when flow paths change. The document is not about TCP.
RFC 2362 is cited only as an example use of HRW, and the document is not about PIM-SM.
CRC16 is named only as an example hash function for the flow key. The document does not analyse CRCs or polynomial choice.
The ECMP tag is more specific and already covers this subject.

RFC2993.title: Architectural Implications of NAT
RFC2993.summary: IAB-stream informational RFC discussing the architectural implications of NAT (NAT, NAPT, RSIP, ALGs): breakage of the end-to-end model, IPsec, DNS and TCP state, plus deployment guidelines and the IPv6 relationship.

NAT.why: The whole document analyses NAT behaviour, problems, advantages and deployment guidelines.
NAT.quote: In light of the growing interest in, and deployment of network address translation (NAT) RFC-1631, this paper will discuss some of the architectural implications

internet architecture.why: A major part of the document argues from end-to-end and fate-sharing principles about how NAT violates Internet architecture.
internet architecture.quote: Foremost is the End-to-End principle (discussed further below), which notes that certain functions can only be performed in the endpoints

rejected.why: NAT's breakage of IPsec AH/ESP is discussed, but IPsec is not specified or profiled; it is an impacted protocol.
Section 8 relates NAT to IPv6 transition, but only briefly; the document is not about IPv6.
DNS/ALG and name-space issues appear in illustrations, but DNS is not the subject.
TCP TIME_WAIT violations are an illustration of NAT problems, not a TCP specification.
Mentioned only as being broken by DNS/ALG in the security section.
Used only as an example VPN tunnel causing address collisions.

RFC2994.title: A Description of the MISTY1 Encryption Algorithm
RFC2994.summary: Informational description of the MISTY1 64-bit block cipher with a 128-bit key, covering key scheduling, the FO/FI/FL round functions, S-boxes, a CBC-mode object identifier, and test vectors.

cryptography.why: The whole document specifies a block cipher algorithm (key schedule, round functions, S-boxes, test vectors). No more specific cipher tag in the taxonomy fits MISTY1, so the parent topic is used.
cryptography.quote: This document describes a secret-key cryptosystem MISTY1, which is block cipher with a 128-bit key, a 64-bit block and a variable number of rounds.

rejected.why: DES is only mentioned as a comparison in the security considerations and as an example of other CBC algorithms; the document is not about DES.
MISTY1 is a different cipher; AES is not discussed.
The OID for MISTY1-CBC is given in ASN.1 notation, but this is incidental apparatus, not the subject.
The Legal Issues section notes a patent and licensing terms, but this is a minor part and not the subject of the document.
Camellia is a different 128-bit block cipher (also from Mitsubishi) and is not discussed here.

RFC2995.title: Pre-Spirits Implementations of PSTN-initiated Services
RFC2995.summary: Informational survey of four pre-SPIRITS implementations (Korea Telecom, Lucent, NEC, Telia/Nortel) of PSTN-initiated services, chiefly Internet Call Waiting, using IN, SIP/PINT and proprietary protocols to inform the SPIRITS working group.

SPIRITS.why: The whole document surveys existing SPIRITS-like implementations (Internet Call Waiting) and their architectures, as input to the SPIRITS working group.
SPIRITS.quote: SPIRITS-like services are those originating in the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) and necessitating the interactions of the Internet and PSTN.

PINT.why: Korea Telecom's implementation is built on PINT (SIP/SDP extensions) and the section describes how its methods and responses are used. This is a substantial part of the document.
PINT.quote: The ICW service uses the PINT Service Protocol 1.0 [1] for communications between the SCP and the ICW Server System

SIP.why: SIP is the base protocol between the PSTN and the Internet in most of the surveyed implementations (Lucent OCC, Telia/Nortel SIP redirect servers and service control gateways).
SIP.quote: The OCC Server interacts with the PSTN entities over the secure intranet via plain-text Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) messages [2].

rejected.why: This is the parent of SPIRITS and PINT, so it is implied by the more specific tags.
SDP is mentioned only as part of PINT. The document does not discuss it in its own right.
H.323 gateways and gatekeepers appear in the Lucent VoIP call-back path, but only as supporting elements.
NEC's SRHDSP uses SSL only for session setup and key exchange. This is a substrate, not a subject of the document.
Firewalls are mentioned as security measures, but the document is not about them.
NEC's interface runs over UDP/IP, but this is only a transport.

gaps.name: Intelligent Network (IN/INAP) service control
gaps.why: All four implementations use IN-based PSTN solutions (SCP, SSP, INAP). The taxonomy has no tag for IN or INAP.

gaps.name: Internet Call Waiting
gaps.why: This benchmark service has no dedicated tag. SPIRITS covers it only indirectly.

RFC2996.title: Format of the RSVP DCLASS Object
RFC2996.summary: Defines the format of the RSVP DCLASS object, which carries Diffserv Code Points in RSVP messages so a DS network can tell upstream nodes which DSCPs to mark, and briefly covers its use and a simple admission control mechanism.

RSVP.why: The document defines a new RSVP object, its class number and encoding, and how it is used in PATH/RESV processing. It is an extension of RSVP.
RSVP.quote: The DCLASS object is used to represent and carry DSCPs within RSVP messages. This document specifies the format of the DCLASS object

Diffserv.why: The object conveys DSCPs and behavior aggregates between a diff-serv network and upstream markers, and covers admission control and DSCP mapping for DS networks. It sits at the Intserv/Diffserv interworking point.
Diffserv.quote: carry Differentiated Services Code Points (DSCPs) in RSVP message objects

rejected.why: Intserv service types and token buckets appear in the appendix on admission control, but the document is about the RSVP DCLASS object and DSCPs, not Intserv itself.
Policy enforcement points (PEP/PDP) are mentioned as context only. The document does not specify COPS or policy provisioning.
A parent of RSVP and Diffserv, so it is implied. The specific tags cover the document.

RFC2997.title: Specification of the Null Service Type
RFC2997.summary: Defines the RSVP/Intserv 'Null Service' type, letting applications signal identity to QoS policy agents via RSVP ADSPEC/TSPEC/FLOWSPEC without quantifying resources, especially for diffserv networks.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP/Intserv with a new service type and defines its ADSPEC, SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC formats.
RSVP.quote: the RSVP sender offers the new service type, 'Null Service Type' in the ADSPEC that is included with the PATH message

Diffserv.why: A major part of the document is RSVP/diffserv interoperation: DCLASS marking of DSCPs and provisioning/classification challenges.
Diffserv.quote: QoS policy agents may direct the signaled application's traffic to a particular diffserv class of service.

Intserv.why: Defines a new Intserv service type alongside Guaranteed and Controlled Load, following the Intserv service template.
Intserv.quote: Using standard RSVP/Intserv signaling, applications running on hosts issue requests for network resources

rejected.why: PEPs/PDPs are mentioned as consumers of the signaling, but COPS itself is not specified or discussed.
Policy enforcement is the motivation, but no policy information model is defined.

RFC2998.title: A Framework for Integrated Services Operation over Diffserv Networks
RFC2998.summary: Informational framework describing how Integrated Services (Intserv) with RSVP signaling can deliver end-to-end QoS across networks containing Diffserv regions, covering service mapping, admission control, resource management, and multicast issues.

Intserv.why: The document's central subject is operating the Integrated Services architecture end-to-end across Diffserv regions, treated as a network element/virtual link.
Intserv.quote: This document describes a framework by which Integrated Services may be supported over Diffserv networks.

Diffserv.why: Diffserv regions, PHBs, DSCP marking, SLSs and policing at region edges are examined at length, including requirements Diffserv regions must meet.
Diffserv.quote: Diffserv regions of the network are treated as virtual links connecting Intserv capable routers or hosts

RSVP.why: Substantial portions cover RSVP signaling across Diffserv regions: RSVP-aware regions, aggregated/tunneled RSVP, per-flow RSVP, and DSCP signaling through RSVP.
RSVP.quote: RSVP is a signaling protocol that applications may use to request resources from the network.

rejected.why: Section 6 discusses multicast with heterogeneous trees, but only as one complication of the framework, not a multicast routing subject.
Mentioned only as a reason host marking or RSVP SPI-based classification helps; not a subject of the document.
Cited only as one way to provision router classification criteria and as a reference; not discussed in its own right.
Parent of the chosen tags (Intserv, Diffserv, RSVP), so it is implied and not listed.

gaps.name: Bandwidth broker
gaps.why: The document discusses bandwidth brokers/oracles as a means of dynamic resource provisioning in Diffserv regions, but the taxonomy has no tag for them; this is minor and covered under QoS.

RFC2999.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 2900-2999
RFC2999.summary: RFC 2999 is a slightly annotated catalogue of RFCs 2900-2999, giving each RFC's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The whole document is a publication-series status summary of one block of 100 RFCs, which is the sort of document a reader browsing the RFC series page would look for.
RFC series.quote: a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2900

rejected.why: It notes which RFCs are standards-track and points to the Official Protocol Standards list, but it does not describe or discuss the standards process.
Many of the listed RFCs are about DNS, but this document only lists them. Tagging individual technologies would be a mistake for an index of abstracts.
A dozen Telnet encryption and authentication RFCs appear only as list entries.
The MIB RFCs are listed but not specified or analysed here.
The AAA requirements RFCs are listed only as entries.
Diffserv-related RFCs are mentioned only as list entries.

RFC3000.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC3000.summary: RFC 3000 (STD 1) is a snapshot index of Internet standards-track, BCP, experimental and historic RFCs as of October 2001, with contact and retrieval information for the RFC series.

RFC series.why: The document is an RFC Editor index of standards status and explains how to retrieve RFCs by web, FTP and email. Readers of the RFC series subject would want it.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor maintains the official repository of all RFCs and indexes to them.
RFC series.section: 2.2 Request for Comments Editor (RFC Editor) Web Pages

IETF process.why: It records the state of standardization (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Historic, BCP) under the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: This memo is published by the RFC Editor for the IESG and IAB in accordance with Section 2.1 of "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3"

rejected.why: IANA appears only as a contact entry and in BCP titles listed in the tables.
DNS RFCs are listed in the tables but the document is not about DNS.
It is a dated status snapshot, not a history or retrospective.
The tables are not a glossary or a set of definitions.

RFC3001.title: A URN Namespace of Object Identifiers
RFC3001.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "oid", which encodes ASN.1 Object Identifiers as URNs (e.g., urn:oid:1.3.6.1), using the URN namespace registration template.

URN.why: The whole document is a URN namespace registration, defining the structure, equivalence and assignment rules for urn:oid identifiers.
URN.quote: This document specifies the "oid" URN namespace [1]. This namespace is for encoding an Object Identifier as specified in ASN.1 [2] as a URI.

rejected.why: OIDs are defined by ASN.1, but the document only encodes them as URNs and does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
The URI scheme is the generic framework here. URN is the more specific tag and it covers the document.
RFC 1778's string encoding is referenced for the syntax, but the document is not about LDAP or directories.
MIB OIDs appear only as examples of OIDs. The document does not define or discuss MIB modules.

RFC3002.title: Overview of 2000 IAB Wireless Internetworking Workshop
RFC3002.summary: Report of the February-March 2000 IAB workshop on wireless internetworking, summarizing presentations, discussions (walled garden, mobility, security, transport, QoS, header compression, IPv6, signalling) and recommendations to the IETF, IRTF and wireless standards bodies.

cellular.why: The workshop centres on using Internet technology over cellular and other wireless systems (3GPP, 3G.IP, GPRS, WAP, IS-95), and the cellular carriers' walled-garden model.
cellular.quote: The wireless operators have not, however, chosen to use IPv4, TCP, full HTTP/HTML, and other applications for a variety of reasons.

IP mobility.why: Sections 3.2 and 4.4 discuss roaming, macro/micro mobility, Mobile IPv4 limitations and IPv6 mobility recommendations.
IP mobility.quote: It was recommended to encourage adoption of IPv6 mobility extensions [37] to support roaming capabilities in the wireless environment.

IPv6.why: Sections 3.10, 4.3 and 4.14 advocate IPv6 adoption for 3G and wireless, and recommend avoiding NAT.
IPv6.quote: The clear consensus of the workshop was to recommend adoption of an IPv6-based solution to support these services requiring large scaling.

TCP.why: Substantial discussion and recommendations on TCP over wireless: non-congestive loss, NCLI/SE, D-SACK, and WAP transport (WTP) versus TCP.
TCP.quote: TCP makes assumptions on loss as congestion indication.

header compression.why: Dedicated section on header overhead and ROHC for wireless.
header compression.quote: Discussion on header compression techniques to alleviate these concerns focused on work being performed within the IETF Robust Header Compression (rohc) working group.

QoS.why: Sections 3.6 and 4.7 discuss last-leg QoS, path QoS discovery, RSVP and Diffserv for mobile hosts.
QoS.quote: Enabling support for voice and other realtime services along with data capabilities requires Quality of Service (QoS) features

internet architecture.why: The workshop addresses end-to-end model, proxies, NAT and open-versus-walled-garden architecture.
internet architecture.quote: end to end operation is sacrificed, security is compromised, and automated content modification in some form becomes necessary.

workshop reports.why: The document is an IAB workshop report.
workshop reports.quote: This document provides an overview of a workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) on wireless internetworking.

rejected.why: SIP and H.323 are discussed only briefly as signalling for VoIP over wireless; the document is not about SIP.
BGP and IDRP extensions for the ATN are discussed in one section and two recommendations, which is too small a part to tag.
NAT is criticised in the IPv6 scaling recommendations but is not a main subject.
Inter-domain AAA gets a brief recommendation, not enough for a tag.
Satellite TCP work is mentioned only as a precedent for collaboration.
WTLS is based on TLS, but TLS is only mentioned in passing.

gaps.name: WAP (Wireless Application Protocol)
gaps.why: WAP's WTP, WTLS, WSP and WAE are discussed throughout, but the taxonomy has no WAP or mobile-application-protocol tag.

RFC3003.title: The audio/mpeg Media Type
RFC3003.summary: Registers the audio/mpeg MIME media type for MPEG-1/MPEG-2 audio (Layer I, II, III) elementary streams, including the registration template, file extensions and security notes.

media types.why: The document is a media type registration for audio/mpeg, with the full registration template. Readers of the media types subject would expect it.
media types.quote: The intention of this document is to define the media type audio/mpeg to refer to this kind of contents.

MP3.why: The media type covers MPEG audio Layer I/II/III streams (.mp1, .mp2, .mp3), including ID3 metadata handling. The content is MP3-family audio coding.
MP3.quote: The audio compression defined as layer I, layer II and layer III in the MPEG-1 [MPEG-1] and MPEG-2 [MPEG-2] standards

rejected.why: MIME is the framework for the registration. The document is about a specific type, which the more specific media types tag covers.
The MPA RTP payload is mentioned only in a note to distinguish it from audio/mpeg. The document does not define it.
Base64 is mentioned only as a suitable encoding for email transport. It is not the subject of the document.
The MP3 tag is the more specific fit, so the parent is not used.

RFC3004.title: The User Class Option for DHCP
RFC3004.summary: Defines the DHCP User Class option (code 77), which lets a client convey opaque user/application class identifiers so a server can select address pools and configuration parameters.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a new DHCP option, including its format, code, and server handling. It is an extension of DHCP, so it belongs under DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This option is used by a DHCP client to optionally identify the type or category of user or applications it represents.

rejected.why: The option is defined only for DHCP for IPv4 (option code 77, referencing RFC 2131/2132). DHCPv6 is not addressed.

The Security Considerations section only notes that DHCP has no authentication, so a server cannot verify a client's right to use a class. This is boilerplate and does not make the document about authentication.

RFC3005.title: IETF Discussion List Charter
RFC3005.summary: BCP 45 defines the charter of the IETF discussion mailing list: its purposes, appropriate and inappropriate postings, and the authority of the IETF Chair, Executive Director or sergeant-at-arms to restrict abusive posters.

IETF process.why: The document sets procedures and administration for the IETF's main discussion forum, including moderation authority and appeals to the IAB. That is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: It also hosts discussions of IETF direction, policy, meetings, and procedures.
IETF process.section: Charter for the IETF Discussion List

mailing lists.why: It is a charter for a specific mailing list, covering scope, acceptable postings and posting restrictions. The 'mailing lists' tag is about list protocols, headers and management, and this is list management and policy.
mailing lists.quote: The IETF discussion list, ietf@ietf.org, serves two purposes.
mailing lists.section: Charter for the IETF Discussion List

rejected.why: Unsolicited bulk email is only listed as one inappropriate posting type. The document is not about spam filtering or reporting.
Email is only the medium for the list. The document specifies no email technology.

RFC3006.title: Integrated Services in the Presence of Compressible Flows
RFC3006.summary: Extends the Intserv sender TSpec with a Compression_Hint parameter so routers that can do link-level (e.g. IP/UDP/RTP header) compression can scale down admission control and resource allocation for compressible RSVP flows.

Intserv.why: The document extends the Integrated Services sender TSpec and defines how int-serv admission control and resource allocation use a compressed TSpec.
Intserv.quote: This specification describes an extension to the TSpec which enables a sender of potentially compressible data to provide hints to int-serv routers

RSVP.why: The hint is carried in the RSVP SENDER_TSPEC object, with RSVP rules for TSpec combination, policing points and PathErr handling for unknown parameters, so RSVP readers would want it.
RSVP.quote: RSVP [RFC 2205] may be used as a signalling protocol by which end nodes and network elements exchange information about resource requirements

header compression.why: The hint identifies the header compression scheme (RFC 1144, 2507, 2508) and the document works out the bandwidth savings. It does not specify the compression itself.
header compression.quote: notify routers performing real-time transport protocol (RTP) header compression that they may allocate fewer resources to RTP flows

rejected.why: The document only references CRTP (RFC 2508) as an example of compression a router may apply. It does not specify or extend it.
RFC 2507 appears only as one hint value. The document does not define IPHC.
RTP flows are the motivating example, but the document does not specify RTP.
The parent of Intserv and RSVP, so it is implied by the more specific tags.
PPP compression protocol numbers are reused for the hint numbering only.

RFC3007.title: Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Dynamic Update
RFC3007.summary: RFC 3007 specifies how to secure DNS dynamic updates using TSIG or SIG(0) message authentication, policy-based authorization at the primary server, and its interaction with DNSSEC-signed zones.

DNS update.why: The whole document specifies secure dynamic update, updating RFC 2136 and obsoleting RFC 2137.
DNS update.quote: This document defines a means to secure dynamic updates of the Domain Name System (DNS), allowing only authorized sources to make changes to a zone's contents.

DNSSEC.why: A substantial part covers interaction with DNSSEC: SIG/NXT handling, zone key signing, the signatory field, and it updates RFC 2535.
DNSSEC.quote: If the updated zone is secured, the RRset affected by an update operation MUST, at the completion of the update, be signed in accordance with the zone's signing policy.

rejected.why: Policy and authorization are covered, but only as part of the DNS update mechanism; the DNS update tag fits better.
TSIG/SIG(0) message authentication is used as a mechanism, not newly specified here.
A parent of the chosen tags, so it is implied.
TKEY is mentioned only as a way to obtain TSIG secrets; no key establishment is specified.

gaps.name: TSIG / SIG(0) DNS transaction security
gaps.why: The document leans on these DNS transaction signature mechanisms, but the taxonomy has no tag for them. It does not define them, so no tag is needed.

RFC3008.title: Domain Name System Security (DNSSEC) Signing Authority
RFC3008.summary: RFC 3008 revises the DNSSEC signing authority model, updating RFC 2535 to restrict which KEY records may authorize SIG records, requiring zone keys for data signatures and specifying SIG field validation rules for resolvers.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies DNSSEC SIG and KEY validation policy for secure resolvers and updates RFC 2535 section 2.3.6.
DNSSEC.quote: This document defines additional restrictions on DNSSEC signatures (SIG) records relating to their authority to sign associated data.

rejected.why: Dynamic update is mentioned only as the rationale for host/user keys, and the update protocol itself is not specified here.
DNS is the underlying system. The document is specifically about DNSSEC, which is the more specific tag.
Key authority is discussed only within the DNSSEC SIG/KEY model, not as general PKI.

RFC3009.title: Registration of parityfec MIME types
RFC3009.summary: Registers the audio, video, text and application/parityfec MIME media types used by the RTP payload format for generic forward error correction (RFC 2733).

media types.why: The whole document is a set of media type registrations in the IETF tree for the parityfec subtypes, so it belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: This document serves as the MIME type registration for those formats.

RTP payload format.why: The registered types name the RTP payload format for generic FEC. The registrations follow the AVT rules for RTP payload formats, so RTP payload format readers would want it.
RTP payload format.quote: This format is only defined for transport within the Real Time Transport protocol (RTP) [4,5].

rejected.why: The FEC scheme itself is specified in RFC 2733. This document only registers MIME type names for it.
SDP is only mentioned as the place where usage is specified, and that usage is in RFC 2733.
RTP is the transport the payload format runs over. The document does not specify RTP.
MIME is the registration framework here. The document defines no body structure or encoding, and media types is the more specific tag.

RFC3010.title: NFS version 4 Protocol
RFC3010.summary: RFC 3010 specifies NFS version 4, a distributed file system protocol with integrated locking, compound operations, delegation-based client caching, ACLs, migration/replication, security negotiation, and UTF-8 internationalization.

NFS.why: The whole document specifies the NFSv4 protocol: operations, attributes, locking, caching, and migration.
NFS.quote: NFS (Network File System) version 4 is a distributed file system protocol which owes heritage to NFS protocol versions 2 [RFC1094] and 3 [RFC1813].

rejected.why: NFSv4 is an RPC application using ONC RPC and XDR as substrate. The document does not define them.
RPCSEC_GSS and GSS-API mechanisms (Kerberos, LIPKEY, SPKM-3) are used as the security substrate. The document only lists which triples are mandatory.
Kerberos V5 is only one of the security mechanisms listed for RPCSEC_GSS. It is not specified here.
UTF-8 is used for file names, and Section 11 is a rationale for choosing it. The document does not define the encoding.
TCP is the preferred transport. The document does not specify or extend it.
The parent topic is implied by the NFS tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC3011.title: The IPv4 Subnet Selection Option for DHCP
RFC3011.summary: Defines a new DHCP option (code 118, subnet selection) that lets a client tell the DHCP server which IPv4 subnet to allocate an address on, overriding the server's normal giaddr/interface-based subnet selection.

DHCP.why: The whole document specifies a new DHCP option and the server and client behaviour around it, so it belongs on the DHCP page. It is an IPv4 option, and DHCPv6 is not involved.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a new Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) option for selecting the subnet on which to allocate an address.

rejected.why: The option is IPv4-only (a single IPv4 address) and extends DHCP for IPv4, not DHCPv6.
IPv4 subnet addresses are used as option content, but the document is about a DHCP option and not about IPv4 itself.
The document is about the DHCP option that selects which subnet an address comes from. It does not cover address architecture or allocation policy, and the DHCP tag already fits.

RFC3012.title: Mobile IPv4 Challenge/Response Extensions
RFC3012.summary: Defines Mobile IPv4 extensions (agent advertisement Challenge, MN-FA Challenge, generalized MN-AAA authentication) letting a foreign agent authenticate a mobile node by challenge/response, including a CHAP/RADIUS-compatible authenticator.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IPv4 registration and agent advertisements with new extensions, error codes and processing rules for mobile node, foreign agent and home agent.
Mobile IPv4.quote: we define extensions for the Mobile IP Agent Advertisements and the Registration Request that allow a foreign agent to a use challenge/response mechanism to authenticate the mobile node

rejected.why: Only referenced for compatibility of the CHAP_SPI authenticator computation; the RADIUS protocol itself is not specified or extended.
The AAA infrastructure is described only as an unspecified verification infrastructure in the appendix, not as the subject.
MD5 and HMAC-MD5 are used as the authenticator algorithms, but the document is not about them.
Authentication is central, but the more specific Mobile IPv4 tag covers the document; a generic topic tag would be redundant.
Router Discovery agent advertisements carry the extension, but ICMP is only the substrate.
HMAC-MD5 is the default authenticator algorithm but is only used, not specified or analysed.

RFC3013.title: Recommended Internet Service Provider Security Services and Procedures
RFC3013.summary: BCP describing what the IETF community expects of ISPs for security: incident communication, acceptable use policies, network infrastructure hygiene (ingress/egress filtering, route filtering, BGP authentication, registry data) and mail system security.

operational security.why: The whole document is a set of operational security practices for ISP network and systems infrastructure, including filtering, system management and policies.
operational security.quote: The purpose of this document is to express what the engineering community as represented by the IETF expects of Internet Service Providers (ISPs) with respect to security.

incident response.why: A substantial section covers incident notification, information sharing and CSIRT interaction for ISPs.
incident response.quote: ISPs SHOULD have clear policies and procedures on the sharing of information about a security incident with their customers

routing security.why: Recommends strong authentication for routing registries, trust in route announcements, BGP session protection and route filtering.
routing security.quote: BGP authentication [RFC2385] SHOULD be used with routing peers.

spam.why: Covers open mail relay prevention and authenticated message submission to curb UBE.
spam.quote: ISPs should take active steps to prevent their mail infrastructure from being used by 'spammers' to inject Unsolicited Bulk E-mail (UBE)

rejected.why: BGP authentication and route filtering are recommended only as security practices; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
SMTP AUTH and the submission port are recommended in passing as mail security measures, not specified here.
Routing registries are mentioned only regarding authenticated updates and contact data.
Whois is cited only as a place to keep contact information accurate.
Ingress/egress source address filtering is a security practice, which is better captured under operational security; the document does not address address architecture.
Denial of service is mentioned as motivation for filtering, but the document does not cover DDoS mitigation as a subject.

RFC3014.title: Notification Log MIB
RFC3014.summary: Defines the Notification Log MIB module (SMIv2) for logging SNMP Notifications (traps and informs) locally, with configuration, statistics and log tables.

MIB.why: The document's core is a MIB module (NOTIFICATION-LOG-MIB) with config, stats and log tables and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for logging Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Notifications.

rejected.why: The MIB is about SNMP notifications, but the MIB tag sits under SNMP and is the more specific fit; the document does not extend the SNMP protocol itself.
It is a logging function, but for SNMP notifications in a MIB, not the syslog protocol.
Access control for logged notifications uses VACM and isAccessAllowed, a minor aspect and not about authorization frameworks.

RFC3015.title: Megaco Protocol Version 1.0
RFC3015.summary: RFC 3015 specifies Megaco/H.248 version 1.0, the master-slave protocol between a Media Gateway Controller and Media Gateway, covering the connection model, commands, descriptors, transactions, packages, encodings and transport.

Megaco.why: The whole document specifies the Megaco/H.248 gateway control protocol: contexts, terminations, commands, descriptors, packages, binary and text encodings.
Megaco.quote: This document defines the protocol used between elements of a physically decomposed multimedia gateway, i.e. a Media Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller.

rejected.why: Used as the text encoding of Local/Remote descriptors with small modifications, but SDP is a substrate here, not the subject.
Security section relies on AH/ESP and defines an interim AH scheme, but this is boilerplate-level security and not the document's subject.
Alternative gateway control protocol; not discussed in the body, and Megaco has its own tag.
Used for the binary encoding in Annex A, merely as the encoding notation.
Used for the text encoding in Annex B, merely as syntax notation.
RTP streams are terminations controlled by the protocol, and an RTP package is defined, but RTP itself is not the subject.

RFC3016.title: RTP Payload Format for MPEG-4 Audio/Visual Streams
RFC3016.summary: Defines RTP payload formats for carrying MPEG-4 Visual and MPEG-4 Audio (LATM) bitstreams directly over RTP without MPEG-4 Systems, with fragmentation rules, header field usage, MIME type registrations and SDP usage.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies RTP payload formats, including header field use and fragmentation rules, for MPEG-4 audio and video.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload formats for carrying each of MPEG-4 Audio and MPEG-4 Visual bitstreams without using MPEG-4 Systems.

media types.why: A substantial part of the document registers the video/MP4V-ES and audio/MP4A-LATM media types with their parameters.
media types.quote:
MIME media type name: video

   MIME subtype name: MP4V-ES

SDP.why: Specifies how the media types and parameters map into SDP m=, a=rtpmap and a=fmtp lines, with examples.
SDP.quote: The MIME media type video/MP4V-ES string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP), RFC 2327, as follows:

codecs.why: The document is about carrying the MPEG-4 Audio and Visual codecs. The taxonomy has no MPEG-4 specific tag, so the generic codecs tag is the closest fit.
codecs.quote: MPEG-4 Audio is a new kind of audio standard that integrates many different types of audio coding tools.

rejected.why: The more specific child RTP payload format applies, and its ancestor is implied.
H.323 terminals are mentioned only as an example use case, with H.245 signalling for configuration.
SIP and RTSP are named only as environments that use MIME and SDP, and the document does not specify them.
RTSP is named only as an example environment that uses the MIME and SDP parameters, and the document does not specify it.
The document is about MPEG-4 Visual (14496-2), not H.264/AVC.
Generic FEC (RFC 2733) is mentioned only as a protection mechanism that may be applied.

gaps.name: MPEG-4 Audio/Visual
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no MPEG-4 codec tag, so readers browsing MPEG-4 would not find this RFC. The generic codecs tag is used instead.

RFC3017.title: XML DTD for Roaming Access Phone Book
RFC3017.summary: Defines an XML DTD for a roaming access phone book, giving the syntax and semantics of ISP point-of-presence entries and the setup, support and provider information a roaming user needs to select an ISP and configure network access.

XML.why: The document's core deliverable is an XML DTD defining the phone book format, including value-type notations and extensibility rules, so it is an XML-based format specification.
XML.quote: All data is specified in XML [5] (Extensible Markup Language) syntax leading to a concise XML DTD (Document Type Declaration) for the phone book.

rejected.why: The DNS server address is only one setup element value in the phone book; the document does not specify DNS.
ISDN is only an enumerated media type value in the phone book, not the subject of the document.
Multilink PPP appears only as a POP property value; PPP is not specified or extended.
L2TP and other tunnelling protocols are only listed as enumerated tunnelProto values.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like registration policy for the DTD's entities and is not the main body's subject.
SMTP, NNTP, POP3 and IMAP appear only as server-name fields in the setup element.

gaps.name: Roaming access phone book / roaming ISP dial-up configuration
gaps.why: The document is about a roaming consortium phone book for selecting ISPs and configuring dial-up access (ROAMOPS). The taxonomy has no roaming or dial-up access tag, so only the XML format is captured.

RFC3018.title: Unified Memory Space Protocol Specification
RFC3018.summary: Specifies the Unified Memory Space Protocol (UMSP), an experimental session/presentation-layer protocol giving immediate access to a 128-bit distributed memory space on remote nodes, with job/task control, instructions, objects, chains and VM discovery, run over TCP/UDP port 2110.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport UMSP runs over; the document defines no TCP extension.
UDP is merely an optional transport for non-acknowledged instructions.
RPC is mentioned as the protocol UMSP's object instructions extend, but the document does not specify or profile ONC RPC.
ABNF is only cited as the syntax notation convention; the document is not about it.
UMSP is not a binding of another protocol onto a transport; it is a new protocol that merely uses TCP/UDP.
Remote memory access resembles distributed storage, but the taxonomy's storage topic covers block/file protocols over IP (NFS, iSCSI, RDMA), which this is not.
UMSP unites nodes but uses a centralized job control point model, not a peer-to-peer overlay.

gaps.name: Distributed shared memory / remote memory access protocol (UMSP)
gaps.why: The document's subject is a 128-bit unified distributed address space with remote read/write, call, jobs, tasks and objects. No taxonomy tag fits; RDMA, ONC RPC and storage are only loosely related.

RFC3019.title: IP Version 6 Management Information Base for The Multicast Listener Discovery Protocol
RFC3019.summary: Defines the IPV6-MLD-MIB SMIv2 MIB module with interface and cache tables for managing implementations of Multicast Listener Discovery (RFC 2710) on IPv6 hosts and routers.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (IPV6-MLD-MIB) with tables, objects, and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: this document is the MIB module that defines managed objects for implementations of the Multicast Listener Discovery Protocol

MLD.why: The managed objects model MLD operation: queriers, query intervals, robustness, group membership cache, and proxying. Readers of MLD would want this management module.
MLD.quote: The MLD Interface Table, which contains one row for each interface on which MLD is enabled.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management substrate; the document only reuses the framework and does not extend SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific fit.
MLD is an IPv6 protocol, but the document is about MLD management, which is tagged under MLD; IPv6 addressing is incidental.
Implied as the parent of MLD, so not listed separately.

RFC3020.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Monitoring and Controlling the UNI/NNI Multilink Frame Relay Function
RFC3020.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring UNI/NNI Multilink Frame Relay (FRF.16) bundles and bundle links, including their relationship to the ifTable, plus notifications and conformance.

MIB.why: The document's sole content is an SMIv2 MIB module (FR-MFR-MIB) with tables, traps and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring and controlling a UNI/NNI Multilink Frame Relay Function as defined in Frame Relay Forum FRF.16.

frame relay.why: The managed subject is the FRF.16 multilink frame relay function (bundles and bundle links), relating to frame relay DTE and service MIBs.
frame relay.quote: Multilink Frame Relay (MFR) for the User-to-Network Interface (UNI) and the Network-to-Network Interface (NNI) provides physical interface emulation for frame relay devices.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB runs under; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Bundles resemble inverse multiplexing, but the taxonomy tag is for IEEE 802.1AX LAG; this is frame relay specific.
ATM LANE and IMA MIBs are cited only as index design examples.
Q.922 and Q.933 appear only in the reference model, not as the subject.

RFC3021.title: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links
RFC3021.summary: RFC 3021 allows 31-bit subnet masks on IPv4 point-to-point links, treating both addresses as host addresses to halve address consumption, and updates RFC 1122, 1700 and 1812 text on broadcast and network addresses.

IPv4.why: The document changes how IPv4 addresses are assigned on point-to-point links and amends IPv4 host and router requirements about network and broadcast addresses, which is about IPv4 address use.
IPv4.quote: it makes sense to consider where relatively minor changes can be made to fielded practice to improve numbering efficiency

rejected.why: This is a parent of the chosen IPv4 tag. The document is specific to IPv4 address use, so the more specific tag is used.
The document assumes classless routing but does not specify or extend CIDR.
PPP is mentioned only as an alternative for numbering links with host addresses. The document is not about PPP.
NAT is mentioned only as background on address conservation.
IPv6 is mentioned only in the motivation as a long-term alternative.
The Address Mask Reply change is a minor point and does not make the document about ICMP.

RFC3022.title: Traditional IP Network Address Translator (Traditional NAT)
RFC3022.summary: RFC 3022 specifies Traditional NAT (Basic NAT and NAPT), describing address/port translation, checksum adjustment, ICMP/FTP/DNS handling, and limitations, obsoleting RFC 1631.

NAT.why: The document specifies Traditional NAT (Basic NAT and NAPT), its translation phases, packet modifications and limitations.
NAT.quote: Together, these two operations, referred to as traditional NAT, provide a mechanism to connect a realm with private addresses to an external realm

rejected.why: Checksum adjustment algorithm is a section, but it serves NAT packet rewriting rather than being about the Internet checksum itself.
FTP ALG is discussed only as a NAT support requirement; FTP is not specified or extended.
ICMP error and query translation is handled as part of NAT, not the ICMP protocol itself.
TCP/UDP headers are rewritten by NAT, but the transport protocols are not the subject.
DNS ALG is mentioned briefly only to say it is unnecessary for traditional NAT.
Not about carrier-grade NAT; it covers SOHO and stub domain NAT.

RFC3023.title: XML Media Types
RFC3023.summary: RFC 3023 registers the text/xml, application/xml, text/xml-external-parsed-entity, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd media types, defines charset/BOM handling, and standardizes the '+xml' suffix convention for XML-based media types.

media types.why: The document's core purpose is registering MIME media types and defining the '+xml' suffix naming convention, which updates the RFC 2048 registration process.
media types.quote: standardizes five new media types -- text/xml, application/xml, text/xml-external-parsed-entity, application/xml-external-parsed-entity, and application/xml-dtd

XML.why: The media types label XML documents, external parsed entities and DTDs. The document discusses XML entities, encodings, BOM, and generic XML processing of '+xml' types.
XML.quote: for use in exchanging network entities that are related to the Extensible Markup Language (XML)

character sets.why: A substantial part of the document covers charset parameter semantics, defaults (us-ascii), authoritative charset, UTF-16/BOM handling and example charsets.
character sets.quote: the UTF-16 family, UCS-4, and UTF-32 are not allowed (except over HTTP[RFC2616], which uses a MIME-like mechanism)

rejected.why: HTTP is only a transport that carries these entities. The document notes charset differences but does not specify or extend HTTP.
WebDAV is cited as a user of XML entities, but the document does not address it.
SGML is discussed only to explain why text/sgml is unsuitable for XML. The document is not about SGML-based interchange.
MIME is the framework in which the media types are registered. The more specific media types tag fits better than MIME body structure and encodings.
Fragment identifiers and base URI are mentioned briefly (Sections 5 and 6), only to point to XPointer and XML Base. This is not substantial enough to tag.
UTF-8 and UTF-16 are recommended charset values, but the document does not specify those encodings.

RFC3024.title: Reverse Tunneling for Mobile IP, revised
RFC3024.summary: RFC 3024 extends Mobile IPv4 with a 'T' bit, new extension and reply codes, and Direct/Encapsulating delivery styles so foreign agents and home agents can set up topologically correct reverse tunnels, obsoleting RFC 2344.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IPv4 registration requests, agent advertisements and reply codes, and specifies mobile node, foreign agent and home agent behavior for reverse tunneling.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document proposes backwards-compatible extensions to Mobile IP to support topologically correct reverse tunnels.

rejected.why: IP-in-IP encapsulation is the assumed tunnel mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend it.
GRE is mentioned only as an alternative encapsulation, mainly in the appendix demultiplexing discussion. It is not a subject of the document.
The tunnels are specific to Mobile IP, so the Mobile IPv4 tag covers them. The document does not address generic tunneling.
Appendix A covers private and disparate address spaces, but it is not about NAT behavior or deployment.
AH and ESP appear only in an assumption about firewalls sharing security associations.

RFC3025.title: Mobile IP Vendor/Organization-Specific Extensions
RFC3025.summary: Defines two new Mobile IP registration extensions (Critical and Normal Vendor/Organization Specific Extensions), with formats, processing rules and error codes, so vendors can carry private data in Mobile IP messages.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends the Mobile IP (RFC 2002) protocol with new registration extensions and Foreign/Home Agent error codes. It builds on RFC 2002 and RFC 2356, both of which are IPv4 Mobile IP.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document defines two new extensions to Mobile IP.

rejected.why: The IANA Considerations section only records the type and error code assignments. The document is not about IANA registries or their stewardship.
Mobile IPv4 is the more specific child tag and already fits, so the parent is implied.
The Vendor/Org-ID uses the SMI Private Enterprise Code, but only as an identifier. The document does nothing with SNMP or MIBs.

RFC3026.title: Liaison to IETF/ISOC on ENUM
RFC3026.summary: An ITU-T WP1/2 liaison statement to the IETF/ISOC describing who is responsible for supplying E.164 number assignment information to DNS administrators for zones under e164.arpa, in the context of ENUM (RFC 2916).

ENUM.why: The whole document sets out administrative responsibilities for E.164 numbers in the e164.arpa DNS tree used by ENUM. Readers of the ENUM subject would want it.
ENUM.quote: the method for administering and maintaining the E.164-based resources in the Domain Name System (DNS) as related to the ENUM protocol

rejected.why: DNS is the storage substrate for ENUM data. The document is about E.164 number administration, not DNS protocol or operations. ENUM is the more specific tag.
The document does not discuss the tel URI scheme. It mentions number portability only as a topic for further study.
The document covers who supplies number information to DNS administrators, not IANA registries or their stewardship.
Proxy servers for PSTN-to-IP call routing are mentioned only in passing, with no specification of SIP.

RFC3027.title: Protocol Complications with the IP Network Address Translator
RFC3027.summary: Informational RFC cataloguing protocols and applications (IPsec/IKE, Kerberos, X11, FTP, RSVP, DNS, SMTP, SIP, H.323, SNMP, etc.) that break or need ALGs when a NAT/NAPT device is en route, with known workarounds.

NAT.why: The whole document is about NAT's effects on protocols, ALGs and workarounds, so readers of the NAT subject page would want it.
NAT.quote: The purpose of this document is to identify the protocols and applications that break with NAT enroute.

IPsec.why: A dedicated section analyses why AH, ESP and IKE fail through NAT; this is substantial, though the document does not specify IPsec.
IPsec.quote: For all practical purposes, end-to-end IPsec is impossible to accomplish with NAT enroute.

Kerberos.why: Two sections analyse Kerberos 4 and 5 ticket IP-address binding problems under NAT and give workarounds.
Kerberos.quote: Kerberos 4 tickets are encrypted.  Therefore, an ALG cannot be written.

rejected.why: One of many protocols surveyed; the FTP ALG discussion is a section, not the document's focus.
Covered in a single survey section as one example of an application needing an ALG.
Single survey section on H.323 and NAT; not the document's subject.
Brief section on DNS-ALG; DNS is one of many affected protocols.
One survey section; document is not about SNMP management.
One survey section on RSVP-ALG problems; not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Application Level Gateway (ALG)
gaps.why: The document's central workaround concept; the taxonomy has no tag for ALGs apart from NAT.

RFC3028.title: Sieve: A Mail Filtering Language
RFC3028.summary: RFC 3028 specifies Sieve, a simple non-Turing-complete language for filtering email at final delivery, covering its syntax, tests, actions, extension mechanism, and the application/sieve media type.

Sieve.why: The document defines the Sieve mail filtering language: its commands, tests, actions, evaluation rules and extension mechanism.
Sieve.quote: This document describes a language for filtering e-mail messages at time of final delivery.

rejected.why: Section 7 registers application/sieve, but that is a small part of the document, which is about the language itself.
IMAP is mentioned only as a possible server environment. The language is independent of access protocol.
The envelope test refers to SMTP MAIL and RCPT data, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
The scripts inspect RFC 822 headers and addresses, but the document does not specify the message format.
ABNF is used only to write the Sieve grammar. It is a notation the document relies on, not its subject.
Scripts are encoded in UTF-8, but this is only the encoding the language relies on.

RFC3029.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Data Validation and Certification Server Protocols
RFC3029.summary: Experimental RFC defining the Data Validation and Certification Server (DVCS), a trusted third party protocol for certifying data possession, validating signed documents and public key certificates, and issuing Data Validation Certificates, with CMS-based messages and HTTP/email transports.

PKI.why: The document specifies a PKI trusted-third-party service and protocol for validating certificates and signed documents, including path validation and revocation status, which is core PKI subject matter.
PKI.quote: A Data Validation and Certification Server (DVCS) is a Trusted Third Party (TTP) providing data validation services, asserting correctness of digitally signed documents, validity of public key certificates

rejected.why: CMS SignedData is the envelope for requests and responses, but the document does not define CMS itself; it is substrate.
OCSP is only an external source of revocation status that a DVCS may consult, and the document states DVCS does not replace it.
Certificates and path validation are used and referenced via RFC2459, but the document does not profile X.509 itself.
HTTP/HTTPS is only one optional transport for application/dvcs messages, with no new HTTP semantics defined.
Email is an optional transport for DVCS messages, not the subject of the document.
TLS is mentioned only as an optional transport protection mechanism.
The application/dvcs registration is a small appendix and boilerplate-like; the document is not about media type rules.

gaps.name: Time stamping / non-repudiation services
gaps.why: The document defines certification of claim of possession of data (time stamping) and evidence for non-repudiation, but the taxonomy has no tag for time-stamping or non-repudiation services.

RFC3030.title: SMTP Service Extensions for Transmission of Large and Binary MIME Messages
RFC3030.summary: RFC 3030 defines two SMTP service extensions, CHUNKING (the BDAT command as an alternative to DATA for large messages) and BINARYMIME (sending MIME messages with binary transfer encoding), obsoleting RFC 1830.

SMTP.why: The document specifies new SMTP service extensions (CHUNKING, BINARYMIME), a new verb BDAT, and a new BODY value for MAIL. This is squarely an SMTP extension.
SMTP.quote: A new SMTP verb, BDAT, is defined as an alternative to the "DATA" command of [RFC821].
SMTP.section: 2. Framework for the Large Message Extensions

MIME.why: BINARYMIME concerns transport of MIME messages with the binary content-transfer-encoding, including constraints on conversion to 7bit/8bit MIME and canonical text encoding.
MIME.quote: permit the negotiated sending of MIME messages that employ the binary transfer encoding.

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific SMTP tag; the document is about SMTP transport, not email in general.
TCP is only the substrate (port 25 in the examples); nothing new is defined about it.
The document does not define header or message syntax. It only references RFC 822 and canonical MIME form.

RFC3031.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture
RFC3031.summary: RFC 3031 specifies the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) architecture: labels, FECs, LSRs, label stacks, LSPs, tunnels and hierarchy, label distribution procedures, and label encodings including over ATM.

MPLS.why: The whole document defines the MPLS architecture, including labels, label stacks, LSPs, label distribution procedures and tunnels.
MPLS.quote: This document specifies the architecture for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS).

rejected.why: LDP is referenced as a separate specification (RFC 3036). This document describes generic label distribution procedures and does not define the protocol.
BGP is used for label distribution and for LSP tunnels between border routers, but the document is not about BGP itself.
ATM label encodings and merging are discussed in depth, but as one MPLS encoding option, not as IP over ATM.
Explicit routing is mentioned as a motivation. The procedures are left out of scope, so this is not a main subject.
Only mentioned as one label distribution option. The document does not specify it.
The multicast sections are marked as left for further study, so there is no substantive content.

RFC3032.title: MPLS Label Stack Encoding
RFC3032.summary: RFC 3032 specifies the MPLS label stack entry encoding, TTL and reserved-label processing, fragmentation/Path MTU handling for labeled packets, and carriage of labeled packets over PPP (MPLSCP) and LAN media.

MPLS.why: The document defines the MPLS label stack encoding, reserved label values, and TTL processing. This is the core MPLS encapsulation specification.
MPLS.quote: This document specifies the encoding to be used by an LSR in order to transmit labeled packets on PPP data links and on LAN data links.

PMTUD.why: A whole section sets out fragmentation and ICMP rules for labeled datagrams and how they affect Path MTU Discovery, which Path MTU Discovery readers would want.
PMTUD.quote: it provides rules which ensure that hosts implementing Path MTU Discovery [4], and hosts using IPv6 [7,8], will be able to generate IP datagrams that do not need fragmentation

PPP.why: It defines the MPLS Control Protocol (MPLSCP), a new PPP NCP, along with the PPP protocol code points for labeled packets.
PPP.quote: This section defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring label Switching over PPP.

rejected.why: Ethernet is covered only briefly, in a short section assigning ethertypes 8847 and 8848. It is not a main subject.
ICMP messages are generated according to the rules, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
The Router Alert Label is one reserved label value, defined by analogy with the IP option. The document is not about the IP option.
IPv4 and IPv6 are only the payloads that carry the label stack, and the IPv6 handling is a few rules.
LDP is mentioned only in passing, for the Implicit NULL label.

RFC3033.title: The Assignment of the Information Field and Protocol Identifier in the Q.2941 Generic Identifier and Q.2957 User-to-user Signaling for the Internet Protocol
RFC3033.summary: Specifies the assignment of Identifier-related standard/application and Identifier type values in the Q.2941 Generic Identifier IE and protocol discriminator/identifier values in the Q.2957 User-to-user IE for IP sessions (IPv4, IPv6, MPLS VCID, RSVP, ST2+) over ATM B-ISDN signaling.

ATM.why: The document defines how IP sessions are identified and carried in ATM B-ISDN UNI signaling (Generic Identifier and User-user IEs) to set up VCs for long-lived and QoS-sensitive sessions.
ATM.quote: designed for advanced B-ISDN signaling support of the Internet protocol, especially the B-ISDN signaling support for the connection that corresponds to the session

RSVP.why: Defines a User-user IE encoding that carries RSVP Resv, ResvConf, ResvErr and ResvTear messages inside ATM SETUP, CONNECT and RELEASE messages.
RSVP.quote: Internet protocol/application identifier field is the RSVP message (0x02).

ST-II.why: An appendix assigns the ST2+ session identifier and SCMP carriage. The appendix is non-normative, and ST2+ also appears in the identifier registry values.
ST-II.quote: This appendix specifies information field and protocol identifier assignment in the Generic Identifier and User-to-user Signaling for ST2+.

rejected.why: MPLS VCID is only one of several identifier types assigned here. The document is about ATM signaling, not MPLS itself.
IPv6 session identifier is one assigned format, but the document does not specify or extend IPv6.
IPv4 appears only as a standard/application value and in the session identifier format, so the document is not about IPv4.
The IANA section merely reserves number ranges, which is boilerplate.
B-ISDN signaling is the ATM context here, so ATM fits better than narrowband ISDN.
QoS-sensitive sessions motivate the work, but the document defines identifier assignments, not a QoS architecture.

gaps.name: B-ISDN signaling (Q.2931/Q.2941/Q.2957 UNI signaling)
gaps.why: The document is fundamentally about ATM UNI signaling information elements, which the taxonomy only covers broadly under ATM.

RFC3034.title: Use of Label Switching on Frame Relay Networks Specification
RFC3034.summary: Specifies how Frame Relay switches act as MPLS label switching routers, carrying the top label in the DLCI field, with TTL handling and Frame Relay-specific LDP extensions.

frame relay.why: The document defines the encapsulation and processing for MPLS over Frame Relay, which is IP-over-Frame-Relay interworking.
frame relay.quote: When a Frame Relay switch is used for label switching, the top (current) label, on which forwarding decisions are based, is carried in the DLCI field

MPLS.why: It extends and clarifies the MPLS architecture for FR-LSRs, covering label stack handling, TTL processing and label processing at ingress, core and egress.
MPLS.quote: This document defines the model and generic mechanisms for Multiprotocol Label Switching on Frame Relay networks.

LDP.why: A substantial part defines Frame Relay Label Range, Merge and Label fields and the downstream-on-demand label allocation procedures for LDP.
LDP.quote: The Label Distribution Protocol [LDP] messages exchanged between two Frame Relay "LDP-peer" LSRs may contain Frame Relay specific information
LDP.section: 7.3 LDP messages specific to Frame Relay

rejected.why: Only a companion document (RFC 3035) and a heterogeneous-LSP example; the document is not about ATM.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as the routing protocols that FR-LSRs run; the document does not specify them.
RSVP is mentioned only as an optional way to pass circuit parameters.
The document covers plain MPLS over Frame Relay, not generalized MPLS.

RFC3035.title: MPLS using LDP and ATM VC Switching
RFC3035.summary: Specifies how ATM switches act as MPLS label switching routers using LDP downstream-on-demand label distribution, VPI/VCI label encoding, shim-header encapsulation, TTL handling and loop detection via path vectors.

ATM.why: The document defines how ATM switches serve as ATM-LSRs, using VPI/VCI as labels, VC-merge, and RFC 2684 encapsulation. This is IP/MPLS over ATM.
ATM.quote: The ATM switches run network layer routing algorithms (such as OSPF, IS-IS, etc.), and their data forwarding is based on the results of these routing algorithms.

LDP.why: It specifies LDP downstream-on-demand procedures for ATM-LSRs, including hop counts, MAXHOP, path vector loop detection, and label request/binding handling.
LDP.quote: specifying in more detail the procedures which are to be used for distributing labels to or from ATM-LSRs

MPLS.why: It covers the MPLS shim header, label stack and TTL handling over LC-ATM interfaces, as a companion to the label stack encoding RFC.
MPLS.quote: This document also specifies the MPLS encapsulation to be used when sending labeled packets to or from ATM-LSRs

rejected.why: OSPF and IS-IS are only named as the network-layer routing the ATM-LSRs run; the document does not specify them.
ICMP is mentioned only as a possible TTL-expiry message.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as unaffected by the procedures.
RSVP is mentioned only as another label distribution protocol that is explicitly out of scope.

RFC3036.title: LDP Specification
RFC3036.summary: RFC 3036 specifies LDP, the Label Distribution Protocol by which MPLS Label Switching Routers discover peers, establish sessions, and exchange label bindings for FECs, including messages, TLVs, procedures and loop detection.

LDP.why: The entire document is the LDP specification: discovery, sessions, messages, TLVs, label distribution procedures and loop detection.
LDP.quote: This document defines a set of such procedures called LDP (for Label Distribution Protocol) by which LSRs distribute labels to support MPLS forwarding along normally routed paths.

rejected.why: LDP is a child of MPLS and is the more specific tag; the parent is implied.
TCP is only the transport for LDP sessions; the TCP MD5 option is used as defined elsewhere (RFC 2385).
Only mentioned as a separate extension for explicitly routed LSPs; not specified here.
ATM and Frame Relay label TLVs and session parameters are encodings within LDP; the ATM and Frame Relay mappings are specified in other RFCs.
MD5 digest is used via the TCP MD5 option as a security mechanism, not the subject.
UDP is just the substrate for Hello discovery messages.

RFC3037.title: LDP Applicability
RFC3037.summary: Informational applicability statement for LDP, describing where LDP is appropriate for MPLS hop-by-hop label distribution, its features, requirement level, and scalability considerations.

LDP.why: The whole document is an applicability statement for LDP, covering its features, requirement level and scalability.
LDP.quote: This document describes the applicability of the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), a new protocol for label distribution designed to support label distribution for MPLS forwarding

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an extension of LDP for explicitly routed LSPs, in contrast to RSVP-TE; not the subject.
Mentioned only as an alternative for traffic-engineered LSPs; not discussed in detail.
LDP is the more specific tag; MPLS is the surrounding context and the architecture is only referenced.
TCP is only the transport for LDP sessions; the document defines nothing new about its use.
MPLS VPNs are mentioned only as a use case for hop-by-hop tunnels.

RFC3038.title: VCID Notification over ATM link for LDP
RFC3038.summary: Specifies procedures and LDP messages/TLVs (VCID/VPID propose, ACK, NACK) for notifying a common Virtual Connection Identifier between neighbouring ATM-LSRs so LDP label mappings can identify ATM VCs.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with new message types and TLVs (VCID Label TLV, VCID Propose/ACK/NACK) so ATM VCs can be named in label mapping messages.
LDP.quote: This document specifies the procedures for the communication of VCID values between neighboring ATM-LSRs

ATM.why: The procedures are specific to ATM links: VPI/VCI rewriting, VP/PVC/SVC cases, and use of ATM signalling BLLI/GIT fields.
ATM.quote: The ATM has several types of VCs (transparent point-to-point link/VP/PVC/SVC).

rejected.why: The document is about LDP extensions for ATM links, which MPLS covers only as the parent. LDP is the more specific tag.
Point-to-multipoint VC procedures are defined only 'for future use'. They are a minor part of the document.
Non-inband VCID messages are sent over TCP as in LDP, so TCP is only the substrate.

RFC3039.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Qualified Certificates Profile
RFC3039.summary: RFC 3039 profiles X.509 v3 certificates for Qualified Certificates issued to natural persons, defining issuer/subject name content, subject directory attributes, key usage, and new biometric-info and QC-statements extensions, with ASN.1 modules and an example.

X.509.why: The document is an X.509 v3 certificate profile, constraining issuer and subject fields and defining new extensions (biometricInfo, qcStatements).
X.509.quote: This document forms a certificate profile for Qualified Certificates, based on RFC 2459, for use in the Internet.

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers this PKI certificate profile; the parent is implied.
ASN.1 modules are the normative encoding of the extensions but the document is about the certificate profile, not ASN.1 itself.
Distinguished names and X.501/X.520 attributes are used for naming, but the document does not specify a directory service.
RSA and SHA-1 appear only in the example certificate.
Subject directory attributes may be used for authorization, but this is only mentioned in passing.

RFC3040.title: Internet Web Replication and Caching Taxonomy
RFC3040.summary: Informational taxonomy memo defining terminology and cataloguing protocols and relationships for web replication and caching (replica selection, inter-replica and inter-proxy communication, proxy configuration, network element control).

HTTP caching.why: The whole document defines caching proxy terms, meshes and arrays, and surveys inter-cache protocols (ICP, HTCP, Cache Digest, CARP, WCCP, NECP). This is the core of the HTTP caching subject.
HTTP caching.quote: This memo specifies standard terminology and the taxonomy of web replication and caching infrastructure deployed in the Internet today.

CDN.why: A substantial part covers replication, replica selection (HTTP and DNS redirection) and cache pre-filling for content distribution, which CDN readers would want.
CDN.quote: Replica origin servers acquire content as needed due to client demand.

SOCKS.why: SOCKS is described as one of the protocols between proxies and network elements in the taxonomy.
SOCKS.quote: SOCKS is primarily used as a caching proxy to firewall protocol.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is the base spec for terminology and redirects, but the document does not specify or extend it.
DNS redirection is one replica-selection mechanism, mentioned briefly, and DNS is also a WPAD substrate. The document does not define DNS behaviour.
A more specific caching tag already covers the web-architecture content.
DHCP appears only as one WPAD discovery mechanism in a list.
