SLP is only listed as a WPAD discovery mechanism.
Terminology is a major part of the document, but it is specific to web caching and replication, and the caching tags cover it.

gaps.name: Web proxies, proxy auto-configuration (PAC/WPAD) and interception proxies
gaps.why: A large part of the document covers proxy configuration, WPAD, CARP and WCCP/NECP interception. The taxonomy has no web proxy or interception tag; HTTP caching is the nearest fit.

RFC3041.title: Privacy Extensions for Stateless Address Autoconfiguration in IPv6
RFC3041.summary: Defines an extension to IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration that generates temporary, randomized (MD5-derived) interface identifiers and addresses that change over time, to reduce correlation and tracking of nodes.

SLAAC.why: The document specifies temporary address generation as an extension to SLAAC, including Prefix Information processing, lifetimes, DAD and regeneration.
SLAAC.quote: This document describes an extension to IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration for interfaces whose interface identifier is derived from an IEEE identifier.

privacy.why: The motivation and a substantial part of the document concern the privacy threat of constant interface identifiers (tracking and correlation) and its mitigation.
privacy.quote: makes it more difficult for eavesdroppers and other information collectors to identify when different addresses used in different transactions actually correspond to the same node.

rejected.why: SLAAC is the more specific child tag and covers the subject; IPv6 itself is only the context.
MD5 is merely used as the hash for generating pseudo-random identifiers, not the subject of the document.
Router Advertisements and DAD are used as mechanisms but the document does not extend neighbor discovery.
DNS names are discussed as a constant identifier and operational implication, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Cookies are mentioned only as an example of identifier correlation in background.
DHCP is mentioned only as an alternative approach and for comparison.

RFC3042.title: Enhancing TCP's Loss Recovery Using Limited Transmit
RFC3042.summary: Specifies the Limited Transmit algorithm, a TCP sender change that sends new data on the first two duplicate ACKs so fast retransmit can trigger instead of a retransmission timeout when the congestion window is small.

TCP.why: The document defines a new TCP sender loss-recovery mechanism that works with fast retransmit and SACK. It is a TCP protocol extension.
TCP.quote: The "Limited Transmit" algorithm calls for sending a new data segment in response to each of the first two duplicate acknowledgments that arrive at the sender.

rejected.why: The document says Limited Transmit follows the conservation-of-packets principle and leaves cwnd unchanged. Its subject is loss recovery in TCP, and the TCP tag already covers it.
ECN appears only in Related Work as a comparison that also reduces reliance on the retransmission timer. The document is not about ECN.
NewReno is mentioned only as an existing loss recovery technique. The document does not specify or modify it.

RFC3043.title: The Network Solutions Personal Internet Name (PIN): A URN Namespace for People and Organizations
RFC3043.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "pin" for Network Solutions' persistent identifiers naming people and organizations, using the URN namespace registration template.

URN.why: The whole document is a formal URN namespace registration (NID "pin") with structure, uniqueness, persistence, resolution and lexical equivalence rules.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace that is engineered by Network Solutions, Inc. for naming people and organizations.

rejected.why: Network Solutions is a registrar, but the document defines an identifier namespace for people and organizations, not registry or registrar operations.
DNS is mentioned only as something the identifiers may outlast; the document does not specify or use it.
Directory applications motivate the namespace, but the document specifies only the URN namespace.
The namespace registration is the subject, not IANA registry guidance.

RFC3044.title: Using The ISSN (International Serial Standard Number) as URN (Uniform Resource Names) within an ISSN-URN Namespace
RFC3044.summary: Informational RFC registering the ISSN (International Standard Serial Number) as a URN namespace (urn:ISSN:), describing ISSN structure, URN compliance, the ISSN-IC resolver demonstrator, and the namespace registration template.

URN.why: The document defines and registers the ISSN URN namespace, including syntax, lexical equivalence rules and resolution, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: can be supported within the Uniform Resource Name (URN) framework as a specific URN namespace identifier

rejected.why: NAPTR/DNS-based resolution is only mentioned as a future RDS direction. The document does not specify anything about DNS.
URN is the more specific child tag and already covers the URI-related content.
The namespace registration form is the document's main body, but it is URN namespace registration content, not IANA registry guidance.
HTML appears only in passing, in the browser plug-in description.

RFC3045.title: Storing Vendor Information in the LDAP root DSE
RFC3045.summary: Informational RFC defining two LDAP root DSE attributes, vendorName and vendorVersion, for advertising server vendor and version for display and anomaly work-arounds, not feature discovery.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAP by defining two new operational attributes for the root DSE, supplementing RFC 2251 section 3.4. A reader browsing LDAP would expect to find it.
LDAP.quote: This document specifies two Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) attributes, vendorName and vendorVersion that MAY be included in the root DSA-specific Entry (DSE)

rejected.why: LDAP is the more specific child tag and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
DSE and DSA terminology come from X.500, but the document specifies only LDAP attributes.
The IANA Considerations section only asks for two attribute OIDs. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The attribute definitions use schema syntax and OIDs, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC3046.title: DHCP Relay Agent Information Option
RFC3046.summary: Defines the DHCP Relay Agent Information option (option 82) with Circuit ID and Remote ID sub-options, inserted by relay agents in circuit access units so servers can apply address assignment policies and resist spoofing and exhaustion attacks.

DHCP.why: The RFC specifies a new DHCP option and the relay agent and server behaviour around it, extending the DHCP protocol.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a new DHCP Option called the Relay Agent Information Option.

rejected.why: DSL and cable access units are only example deployment environments for the relay agent, not the subject.
IPsec is mentioned only to say relay agents must not modify IPsec-protected DHCP packets.
ATM virtual circuits are only listed as possible Circuit ID values.
The document covers DHCP for IPv4 only, so DHCPv6 does not apply.
The spoofing and exhaustion issues are handled by the option itself and are not a separate security mechanism, so the DHCP tag covers it.

RFC3047.title: RTP Payload Format for ITU-T Recommendation G.722.1
RFC3047.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for the ITU-T G.722.1 wideband audio codec (24/32 kbit/s and non-standard rates), including the audio/G7221 MIME registration and SDP usage.

G.722.why: The taxonomy's G.722 tag covers G.722.1 and its payload formats; this document is exactly an RTP payload format for G.722.1.
G.722.quote: This document describes the payload format for including G.722.1 generated bit streams within an RTP packet.

RTP payload format.why: It is a codec-specific RTP payload format, covering framing, timestamps, and multiple frames per packet, so readers of RTP payload formats would want it.
RTP payload format.quote: No additional header specific to this payload format is required.

rejected.why: SDP is used only to signal bitrate via rtpmap/fmtp; the document defines no new SDP mechanism beyond a codec parameter.
A MIME registration for audio/G7221 is included, but it is a small part of the document and ancillary to the payload format.
RTP is the substrate; the document specifies a payload format rather than extending RTP itself, so the more specific payload format tag applies.
The more specific G.722 tag applies; the document doesn't define the codec itself.

RFC3048.title: Reliable Multicast Transport Building Blocks for One-to-Many Bulk-Data Transfer
RFC3048.summary: Informational RMT WG framework document that decomposes one-to-many bulk-data reliable multicast protocols into reusable building blocks (NACK-based reliability, FEC coding, congestion control, router support, tree configuration) and protocol cores.

reliable multicast.why: The whole document is a framework for decomposing reliable multicast transport protocols into building blocks and protocol cores, so it belongs on the reliable multicast page.
reliable multicast.quote: This document describes a framework for the standardization of bulk-data reliable multicast transport.

FEC.why: FEC coding is one of the recommended building blocks, covering codec selection and FEC packet naming, and the ALC family relies on it.
FEC.quote: This building block is concerned with packet level FEC information when FEC codes are used either proactively or as repairs in reaction to lost packets.

congestion control.why: Congestion control is a recommended building block and the first requirement from RFC 2357. The document discusses single-rate and multiple-rate approaches.
congestion control.quote: There will likely be multiple versions of this building block, corresponding to different design policies in addressing congestion control.

rejected.why: ALC is only named as one protocol family in the taxonomy. The document does not specify the ALC protocol.
PGM is cited as an example of the router-assist family and is not specified or analysed here.
Security and group key management are listed as components, but section 4.6 only defers to the IRTF SMuG research group. The document gives no substantive treatment.
SSM gets a brief mention in the security discussion and is not a subject of the document.
Unrelated to the document. It was considered only because the document is a transport-layer framework.

RFC3049.title: TN3270E Service Location and Session Balancing
RFC3049.summary: Specifies how TN3270E clients use SLP to discover TN3270E servers and pick the least-loaded one (session balancing), and defines the SLP service templates for tn3270e and commserver.

SLP.why: The document profiles SLP for locating TN3270E servers, defining service templates, attributes, queries, and scope and time-out configuration.
SLP.quote: This document discusses the implementation of Service Location Protocol (SLP) and session balancing with a TN3270E emulator in a client server implementation with a TN3270E server.

TN3270.why: The document is about locating TN3270E services and balancing sessions across them, and it defines the TN3270E service template. Discovery happens before TN3270E telnet negotiation.
TN3270.quote: The tn3270 service provides 3270 gateway access to an SNA network via the TN3270 protocol.

rejected.why: SLP is a more specific child tag that already covers service discovery.
TLS is only cited for cipher suite names in the template, so the document is not about it.
The Telnet negotiation is a sample trace that follows discovery, and the document does not extend Telnet.
SNA gateways and LU pools appear as context. TN3270 is the more specific tag and already sits under SNA.
The service: URL scheme is used as defined in RFC 2609 and is not specified here.

RFC3050.title: Common Gateway Interface for SIP
RFC3050.summary: Defines SIP CGI, an interface adapting the HTTP Common Gateway Interface so scripts on SIP proxy, redirect and registrar servers can create services by proxying requests, forwarding responses and keeping state across a transaction.

SIP.why: The document specifies a service-creation interface for SIP servers, with metavariables and action lines for proxying, responses, REGISTER, CANCEL and ACK handling. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document defines a SIP CGI interface for providing SIP services on a SIP server.

rejected.why: HTTP CGI is the model being adapted, and HTTP is only compared against. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
CGI originates in web programming, but this document is about SIP server service creation, not the web.
CPL is another way to control call handling, but this document does not specify or discuss it.
The CGI-SET-COOKIE script cookie is an opaque state token for the script, not HTTP state management.

gaps.name: Common Gateway Interface (CGI) / service creation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CGI or for service creation environments in telephony. SIP is the closest fit.

RFC3051.title: IP Payload Compression Using ITU-T V.44 Packet Method
RFC3051.summary: Informational RFC defining how the ITU-T V.44 Packet Method (LZJH) compression algorithm is applied to IP datagram payloads under the IPComp protocol, including transform ID and negotiation parameters.

IPComp.why: The document specifies a new IPComp compression transform (LZJH), including encoder/decoder procedures and the IPCOMP_LZJH transform ID.
IPComp.quote: This document defines the application of V.44 Packet Method to the Internet Protocol (IP) Payload Compression Protocol (RFC 2393).

rejected.why: IKE is only used to negotiate the IPComp association; the document defines nothing new about IKE beyond a transform ID value.
IPsec transform ID space and SA attributes are used only for negotiation; the document is not about IPsec.
RFC 2395 (IPComp using LZS) is only the model for this document; LZS is a different algorithm.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific IPComp tag, which is chosen instead.

gaps.name: ITU-T V.44 / LZJH data compression algorithm
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the LZJH/V.44 lossless compression algorithm itself, which is the core subject; only the IPComp wrapper has a tag.

RFC3052.title: Service Management Architectures Issues and Review
RFC3052.summary: Informational discussion of the problems in defining a framework for IP network and service management, covering centralized versus decentralized architectures, rules/policy-based management, IP QoS management, and the need for a policy protocol.

policy management.why: Much of the document discusses rules/policy-based management, policy-aware devices, information models, and the need for a policy protocol. This is the closest fit for the subject.
policy management.quote: Efforts to devise a framework for policy management is an example of one of the most popular recent activities.

network management.why: The document is about network and service management architectures. It covers centralized versus decentralized frameworks, operator and vendor needs, and element management.
network management.quote: The purpose of this document is to explore the problems of developing a framework for managing the network and services

QoS.why: A substantial section covers the management implications of IP QoS architectures, including provisioning, billing and service assurance for differentiated service.
QoS.quote: Much of the current management efforts are focused on solving control issues for IP QoS [3].

rejected.why: Diffserv and RSVP are mentioned only as targets of policy models. The document does not address them in its own right.
Intserv appears only as an example in the policy protocol scenario. It is not a subject of the document.
Only the element-management reference (RFC 1156) touches this area. The document does not discuss SNMP or MIBs.
The document discusses a generic 'policy protocol' concept. It does not mention or analyse COPS.

RFC3053.title: IPv6 Tunnel Broker
RFC3053.summary: Informational framework describing the IPv6 Tunnel Broker model, in which a broker and tunnel servers automatically set up IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels, addresses and DNS names for isolated dual-stack users.

IPv6 transition.why: The document defines a transition mechanism for giving isolated IPv4-connected hosts IPv6 connectivity. It is compared with 6to4 and 6over4. No specific child tag fits the tunnel broker.
IPv6 transition.quote: The Tunnel Broker idea is an alternative approach based on the provision of dedicated servers, called Tunnel Brokers, to automatically manage tunnel requests coming from the users.

rejected.why: 6to4 is discussed only as an alternative and a possible beneficiary of the broker idea, not specified here.
The tunnels are IPv6-over-IPv4 transition tunnels, so IPv6 transition fits better than generic tunnelling.
Dynamic DNS Update is only suggested as one way for the broker to update the DNS. It is not the document's subject.
RADIUS and AAA are mentioned only as an example of how to authenticate users.
SNMP is listed as one option for broker-to-server communication and is not specified here.
The broader IPv6 tag is replaced by the more specific IPv6 transition tag.

RFC3054.title: Megaco IP Phone Media Gateway Application Profile
RFC3054.summary: Informational profile specifying how an IP telephone is modelled as a Megaco/H.248 Media Gateway, with User Interface and Audio Transducer Terminations, required Packages, and the "IPPhone" Protocol Profile.

Megaco.why: The document profiles Megaco/H.248 for IP phones, defining Termination types, Package support, TerminationID naming, and a Protocol Profile. It is an application of the Megaco protocol.
Megaco.quote: This document specifies a particular application of the Megaco/H.248 Protocol for control of Internet telephones and similar appliances: the Megaco IP Phone Media Gateway.

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned only as a peer-to-peer alternative that complements Megaco. The document does not specify it.
An RTP Termination is required, but it is only the media transport. The document defines nothing about RTP itself.
H.323 is mentioned only as a peer-to-peer alternative, and the document does not cover it.
The parent of Megaco, which is already tagged. The document is about IP phone device control, not PSTN interworking.
UDP and TCP are only the transports the Profile requires or allows, so they are substrate.
ABNF text encoding is only mandated by reference to the Megaco spec. The document defines no syntax of its own.

RFC3055.title: Management Information Base for the PINT Services Architecture
RFC3055.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module (PINT-MIB) for monitoring performance and security-related call statistics of PINT (PSTN/Internet Interworking) servers, clients, users and gateways.

MIB.why: The document's entire purpose is to define a MIB module (PINT-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables, counters and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB which contains the elements for monitoring the performance of a PINT based service.

PINT.why: The MIB monitors PINT services (request-to-talk, fax, fax-back, hear-content) across PINT clients, servers and gateways, so readers of the PINT subject would want it.
PINT.quote: This memo describes a proposed Management Information Base (MIB) for the PSTN/Internet Interworking (PINT) Services Architecture.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management substrate; the document only defines a MIB module and uses the framework without extending it. MIB is the more specific tag.
The counters are service call statistics in a MIB, not a measurement methodology or metrics framework.
PINT extends SIP/SDP, but this document only references the service protocol and defines no SIP behaviour.
RMON is mentioned only as a way to threshold counters and for control mechanism precedent; the MIB doesn't extend it.

RFC3056.title: Connection of IPv6 Domains via IPv4 Clouds
RFC3056.summary: Specifies 6to4, an interim mechanism that assigns a 2002:V4ADDR::/48 IPv6 prefix to sites with a global IPv4 address and encapsulates IPv6 in IPv4 (protocol 41) so IPv6 sites can interconnect over IPv4 and reach native IPv6 via relay routers.

6to4.why: The document defines the 6to4 prefix allocation, encapsulation, sending and decapsulation rules, and relay router scenarios.
6to4.quote: The abbreviated name of this mechanism is 6to4 (not to be confused with [6OVER4]).

NAT.why: A section covers coexistence of 6to4 with NAT and RSIP, giving NAT-fronted sites IPv6 prefixes. It is secondary to the main 6to4 mechanism.
NAT.quote: Combining a 6to4 router with an IPv4 NAT in this way offers the site concerned a globally unique IPv6 /48 prefix
NAT.section: 5.8 Coexistence with firewall, NAT or RSIP

rejected.why: BGP4+ is used only for relay router route advertisement and the document says its usage is completely standard.
6to4 is an IPv6-over-IPv4 transition mechanism, which the 6to4 tag covers; generic IP-in-IP tunnelling is not the subject.
The parent of the chosen 6to4 tag is implied, so it is not listed separately.
The prefix allocation is part of 6to4 and is covered by that tag.
DNS is mentioned only for publishing the 6to4 addresses and is not specified or extended.

RFC3057.title: ISDN Q.921-User Adaptation Layer
RFC3057.summary: Defines IUA, a SIGTRAN adaptation-layer protocol that backhauls ISDN Q.921-user (Q.931/QSIG) messages between a Signaling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller over SCTP, with ASP/AS state management, fail-over and layer-management primitives.

SIGTRAN.why: IUA is one of the SIGTRAN user adaptation layers carrying ISDN signalling over IP between SG and MGC; the document defines its messages, procedures and fail-over.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document defines a protocol for backhauling of ISDN Q.921 User messages over IP using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

rejected.why: SCTP is only the transport IUA runs over; the document registers a payload protocol identifier but does not extend SCTP itself.
ISDN is the signalling being backhauled, but the document is about IP transport adaptation, not IP access over ISDN; the SIGTRAN tag fits better.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a recommended protection.
The MGC and media gateway context is background; no gateway control protocol is specified.
Implied as the parent of SIGTRAN, so not listed separately.

RFC3058.title: Use of the IDEA Encryption Algorithm in CMS
RFC3058.summary: Informational RFC specifying how to use the IDEA block cipher in CMS/S/MIME for content encryption and key wrapping, defining OIDs, the key wrap/unwrap algorithms and SMIMECapabilities encodings.

CMS.why: The document defines CMS content-encryption and key-wrap algorithm identifiers and procedures for IDEA, an extension of CMS algorithm support.
CMS.quote: The intention of this memo is to provide the OIDs and algorithms required that IDEA can be included in S/MIME for symmetric content and key encryption.

S/MIME.why: A substantial part specifies SMIMECapabilities encodings for IDEA and activation in S/MIME clients, relevant to S/MIME readers.
S/MIME.quote: An S/MIME client can announce the set of cryptographic functions it supports by using the S/MIME capabilities attribute

rejected.why: The IDEA cipher is not in the taxonomy as its own tag. The document specifies its use in CMS rather than the algorithm itself, so the parent topic is not warranted separately.
ASN.1 OIDs and structures are used only as the encoding apparatus, not as the subject.
DES is mentioned only in background comments as the algorithm IDEA was meant to replace.
MIME is only the message context via S/MIME; the document is not about MIME body structure.

gaps.name: IDEA (International Data Encryption Algorithm)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the IDEA block cipher, which is the document's core subject; readers browsing ciphers would expect it.

RFC3059.title: Attribute List Extension for the Service Location Protocol
RFC3059.summary: Defines an optional SLPv2 extension (ID 0x0002) letting a User Agent request that Service Replies include each service's attribute list, avoiding extra Attribute Request round trips.

SLP.why: The document specifies a new extension to the Service Location Protocol, including its message format and processing rules, so SLP readers need it.
SLP.quote: This document specifies a SLPv2 extension which allows a UA to request that a service's attributes be included in Service Reply messages.

rejected.why: SLP is the specific technology tag under it and is already chosen, so the broader topic is implied.
The only IANA content is a routine extension ID assignment in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate.
Language tagging is only mentioned as an existing SLPv2 mechanism that the extension reuses.
Authentication blocks are carried over from SLPv2 unchanged, so the document adds nothing new about authentication.

RFC3060.title: Policy Core Information Model -- Version 1 Specification
RFC3060.summary: RFC 3060 defines the Policy Core Information Model (PCIM), an object-oriented, CIM-based information model of policy groups, rules, conditions, actions and repositories for policy-based network management.

policy management.why: The whole document specifies a policy information model (PolicyGroup, PolicyRule, PolicyCondition, PolicyAction, PolicyRepository) for policy-based management. This matches the taxonomy topic for policy-based network management information models.
policy management.quote: This document presents the object-oriented information model for representing policy information developed jointly in the IETF Policy Framework WG

rejected.why: LDAP is only named as a future mapping target and used for comparison with CIM. This document does not specify an LDAP schema.
QoS (DiffServ/IntServ) is only mentioned as an expected application. The model is generic and defines nothing QoS-specific.
IPsec is mentioned only as an expected application area for the model, and nothing IPsec-specific is defined.
The TimePeriod format is reused from RFC 2445, but only as a formatting convention for one property.
SNMP appears only as a comparison (the OctetString qualifier is likened to an SMIv2 textual convention) and as a reference to the DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB encoding. The document is not about SNMP or MIBs.

gaps.name: Common Information Model (CIM) / information modeling
gaps.why: The document extends the DMTF CIM schema and includes the MOF. The taxonomy has no tag for CIM or general information models.

RFC3061.title: A URN Namespace of Object Identifiers
RFC3061.summary: Registers the formal "oid" URN namespace for encoding ASN.1 Object Identifiers as URNs, defining its syntax, uniqueness, persistence and equivalence rules, and obsoletes RFC 3001.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration (the "oid" namespace) following the RFC 2141 template, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace that contains Object Identifiers (OIDs).

rejected.why: OIDs are defined by ASN.1, but the document only encodes them as URNs and does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
ABNF is used only to express the NSS syntax. It is a notation the document relies on, not its subject.
IANA is mentioned only in the examples of OID arcs. The document does not address IANA registries or procedures.
The URN tag is more specific, and the document is not about URI syntax in general.

RFC3062.title: LDAP Password Modify Extended Operation
RFC3062.summary: Defines an LDAP extended operation (Password Modify) letting clients change or generate user passwords independent of DN identity form or password storage mechanism.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAPv3 extended operation, its request/response syntax, and server/client requirements, so it belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: This document describes an LDAP Extended Operation intended to allow directory clients to update user passwords.

rejected.why: SASL is mentioned only as background for why non-DN identities exist; the document does not specify or extend SASL.
Start TLS is only cited as the required confidentiality protection in Security Considerations; nothing new is defined about TLS.
The operation changes passwords but does not define an authentication mechanism; LDAP is the more specific fit.
ASN.1 is just the notation used to define the request and response values, not the subject.

RFC3063.title: MPLS Loop Prevention Mechanism
RFC3063.summary: Experimental RFC defining a "thread"-based mechanism (colors, hop counts, TTL, rewinding, stalling, merging) that prevents MPLS label switched paths from being set up with loops, including an FSM and comparison to path-vector methods.

MPLS.why: The whole document specifies an MPLS LSP setup procedure that guarantees loop freedom, covering VC merge and ordered downstream allocation. MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: a simple mechanism, based on "threads", which can be used to prevent Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) from setting up label switched path (LSPs) which have loops

rejected.why: The thread messages are carried in label request and mapping messages, and LDP is cited as a reference. The document defines a generic algorithm and does not extend LDP's encoding.
Loop prevention touches routing, but the document is about MPLS LSP setup and not general routing design.
The document does not address constraint-based routing or traffic-engineered LSPs.
ATM-LSRs and VC merge are mentioned only in passing. The document is not about IP over ATM.

RFC3064.title: MGCP CAS Packages
RFC3064.summary: Informational RFC defining six MGCP event packages (MS, DT, BL, DO, MD, MO) for channel associated signalling trunks and FXO/FXS lines, with events, signals, glare handling and call flows between Call Agent and media gateway.

MGCP.why: The document defines MGCP event packages, with events, signals and MGCP command call flows (NTFY, RQNT, CRCX, MDCX, DLCX) for CAS trunks.
MGCP.quote: This document contains a collection of media gateway Channel Associated Signaling (CAS) packages for R1 CAS, North American CAS, CAS PBX interconnect as well as basic FXO support.

rejected.why: SDP appears only in the example CRCX/MDCX connection flows as the substrate for media negotiation, and nothing new is defined about it.
Mentioned only in the IESG note as a potential successor; the document is not about Megaco/H.248.
The document is not about ISUP encapsulation or SIP interworking.

gaps.name: MGCP (Media Gateway Control Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists MGCP only as a technology under PSTN interop, and I've used that. I'm not certain the id is exactly 'MGCP'; it appears in the taxonomy as 'MGCP' under PSTN interop. Channel Associated Signaling (CAS) trunk signalling itself has no dedicated tag.

RFC3065.title: Autonomous System Confederations for BGP
RFC3065.summary: RFC 3065 extends BGP with AS confederations (new AS_CONFED_SET/AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE AS_PATH segment types and modification rules) so a group of member ASes appears as one AS, removing the IBGP full-mesh requirement.

route reflection.why: The taxonomy's route reflection tag covers BGP route reflection and confederations. This RFC specifies BGP confederations as an alternative to the IBGP full mesh.
route reflection.quote: an extension to BGP which may be used to create a confederation of autonomous systems that is represented as a single autonomous system

rejected.why: The more specific child tag, route reflection (route reflection and confederations), fits. Its ancestors are implied.
BGP runs over TCP, but the document does not address TCP itself.
The scaling problem is discussed, but the document specifies one BGP mechanism. The BGP child tag covers it.

RFC3066.title: Tags for the Identification of Languages
RFC3066.summary: RFC 3066 (BCP 47) defines the syntax and semantics of language tags for identifying the language of information objects, the IANA registration procedure for tags, and a prefix-based language-range matching rule, obsoleting RFC 1766.

language tags.why: The whole document specifies the language tag syntax, its sources from ISO 639 and 3166, tag choice, registration, and language-range matching.
language tags.quote: This document describes a language tag for use in cases where it is desired to indicate the language used in an information object

rejected.why: The registration procedure for tags is part of the document, but it is about a specific registry for language tags, not IANA registries or stewardship in general. The language tags tag covers it.
The language-range definition is derived from HTTP/1.1 Accept-Language, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
ABNF is used only to write the tag syntax, so it is only the notation the document relies on.
This is the parent of language tags. The more specific child tag fits, so the parent is not listed.
MIME multipart/alternative and Content-Language are mentioned only as usage examples. The Content-Language definition was moved to another document.

RFC3067.title: TERENA'S Incident Object Description and Exchange Format Requirements
RFC3067.summary: Informational RFC from TERENA's Incident Taxonomy and Description WG setting out high-level requirements for IODEF, a common format for describing, archiving and exchanging computer security incident information between CSIRTs.

IODEF.why: The whole document lists requirements for IODEF, so readers browsing IODEF would expect to find it.
IODEF.quote: The purpose of the Incident Object Description and Exchange Format is to define a common data format for the description, archiving and exchange of information about incidents between CSIRTs

rejected.why: The document mentions IDMEF and IDEF and asks for compatibility with them. It does not specify or analyse them.
The document says an XML DTD will come in later documents. It does not cover XML usage.
Section 4.1 has a requirement for localization and UTF-8. It is a minor part of the document, not a main subject.
The IODEF tag sits under incident response, so the parent is implied.

RFC3068.title: An Anycast Prefix for 6to4 Relay Routers
RFC3068.summary: Defines the 6to4 relay anycast prefix 192.88.99.0/24 (and IPv6 address 2002:c058:6301::), how 6to4 routers use it as a default route, and how relay routers advertise it in the IGP and BGP, with monitoring and fault isolation guidance.

6to4.why: The document extends 6to4 by specifying the relay anycast prefix and the behaviour of 6to4 routers and relay routers.
6to4.quote: This memo introduces a "6to4 anycast address" in order to simplify the configuration of 6to4 routers.

anycast.why: A substantial part of the document covers anycast operation: discovery, failover, monitoring and fault isolation of anycast services.
anycast.quote: 6to4 packets will be automatically routed to the nearest available router.

rejected.why: BGP is only used to advertise the anycast prefix between ASes. The document specifies no BGP protocol behaviour beyond a brief note.
The parent of 6to4 is implied, so it is not listed separately.
The IANA prefix reservation is only documented in boilerplate-like considerations. The document is not about IANA registry stewardship.
The document concerns the IPv4/IPv6 transition mechanism, which 6to4 covers more specifically.
6to4 encapsulation is the underlying mechanism but this document does not define tunnelling itself.

RFC3069.title: VLAN Aggregation for Efficient IP Address Allocation
RFC3069.summary: Informational RFC describing VLAN aggregation (super-VLANs and sub-VLANs), which lets hosts in separate virtual broadcast domains share one IPv4 subnet and default gateway to conserve IPv4 address space.

addressing.why: The document is about IP address allocation: sharing one subnet and gateway across VLANs to cut address consumption. No IPv4-specific child tag fits an allocation-efficiency scheme better than the addressing topic.
addressing.quote: hosts that reside in the same physical switched infrastructure, but separate virtual broadcast domains, are addressed from the same IPv4 subnet and share a common default gateway IP address

rejected.why: IPv4 is the address family being conserved, but the document is about an allocation scheme, not the IPv4 protocol or its address lifecycle.
The switched Ethernet/802.1Q VLAN infrastructure is the setting, but the document does not specify IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM. The change is local to the router.
Proxy-ARP-like behaviour is mentioned in passing for inter-sub-VLAN communication, but ARP is not the subject.
The short multicast section only notes the RPF check needs host routes. It is a side consideration, not a substantial part of the document.
Subnet sizing is discussed, but the document is not about CIDR or aggregation of routes.

gaps.name: VLAN aggregation (super-VLAN/sub-VLAN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for VLANs or Layer 2 virtualisation in LAN/MAN switching. Readers looking for VLAN topics would not find this RFC under the existing link layer tags.

RFC3070.title: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) over Frame Relay
RFC3070.summary: Specifies how L2TP is encapsulated over native Frame Relay PVCs and SVCs using SNAP/NLPID encapsulation (OUI 00-00-5E, PID 0x0007), with MTU and tunnel endpoint addressing guidance.

L2TP.why: The document defines a new media binding for L2TP, including its encapsulation format and tunnel endpoint identification, so L2TP readers would want it.
L2TP.quote: This document describes how L2TP is implemented over Frame Relay Permanent Virtual Circuits (PVCs) and Switched Virtual Circuits (SVCs).

frame relay.why: It specifies the Frame Relay encapsulation (Q.922, SNAP, NLPID), MTU requirements, and PVC/SVC endpoint handling for carrying L2TP over Frame Relay.
frame relay.quote: All protocols over this circuit MUST encapsulate their packets within a Q.922 frame.

rejected.why: PPP is the payload that L2TP tunnels; the document does not specify or extend PPP itself.
This is a transport-mapping-like document, but the taxonomy has more specific tags (L2TP, frame relay) that fit better.
Only cited in passing for obtaining tunnel endpoints; not the subject of the document.
L2TP is the more specific tag for this tunneling protocol.

RFC3071.title: Reflections on the DNS, RFC 1591, and Categories of Domains
RFC3071.summary: Klensin's informational memo reflects on RFC 1591's DNS top-level domain delegation principles and proposes recategorizing TLDs (generic, purpose-specific, country) and limiting ICANN/IANA's role, especially for ccTLDs.

DNS.why: The document is about administrative structure and delegation policy of DNS top-level domains (gTLDs, ccTLDs) and the roles of IANA and ICANN. It is not about protocol mechanics, but DNS is the closest fitting tag; naming is the parent and covers this too.
DNS.quote: RFC 1591, "Domain Name System Structure and Delegation", laid out the basic administrative design and principles for the allocation and administration of domains, from the top level down.

rejected.why: It touches registry and registrar policy, but the focus is TLD categorization and delegation governance, not registry/registrar protocols or operations.
IANA's role in delegating ccTLDs is discussed, but the document is not about IANA registries or considerations guidance.
Considered because it covers ICANN policy and governance. The memo is mainly about DNS TLD delegation policy, so DNS is the more specific fit, and I did not add this as a second tag.

gaps.name: TLD delegation policy / ccTLD and gTLD administration (RFC 1591, ICANN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for administration and policy of top-level domains, such as ccTLD/gTLD categories and delegation rules. DNS is only an approximate fit.

RFC3072.title: Structured Data Exchange Format (SDXF)
RFC3072.summary: RFC 3072 specifies SDXF, a self-describing, platform-independent binary chunk-based hierarchical data interchange format, with an accompanying C/C++ API, compression and encryption flags, and a comparison to ASN.1 and XML.

data formats.why: The document defines a new general-purpose data serialization format (chunk header, flags, data types, arrays, big-endian normalization). No more specific data-format tag fits SDXF itself, so the parent topic applies.
data formats.quote: This specification describes an all-purpose interchange format for use as a file format or for net-working. Data is organized in chunks

compression.why: A full section defines the compression header and two methods (run-length and DEFLATE), plus an IANA registry of compression method numbers. The compression topic fits better than the DEFLATE tag, since DEFLATE is only one referenced method.
compression.quote: there is a flag bit which declares that the following data (elementary or structured) are compressed.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used only for notation of the chunk and as a comparison in section 13; the document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
XML is discussed only in a comparison and conversion sketch in section 13; the document is not about XML usage.
DEFLATE is referenced as one compression method (method 02) by pointing to RFC 1951; the document does not define it.
Section 9 only offers a hook for converting UTF-8 and the datatype flag; the document does not specify the encoding.
The ISO 8859-1 normalization and translation tables are a minor part of platform independence, not the document's subject.
The IANA Considerations section registers compression/encryption method numbers, but that is boilerplate-level apparatus and not the document's main body.

gaps.name: Data serialization / binary interchange format
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for general binary serialization formats; SDXF is covered only by the broad 'data formats' parent.

RFC3073.title: Portable Font Resource (PFR) - application/font-tdpfr MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC3073.summary: Registers the application/font-tdpfr MIME media type for Bitstream's Portable Font Resource (PFR) font format, re-registering it in the IETF tree.

media types.why: The document exists to register a media type with IANA, with the standard registration template (encoding, magic number, file extension, usage).
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) sub-type application/font-tdpfr.

rejected.why: The document uses the MIME registration mechanism but does not define body structure or encodings; the more specific media types tag covers it.
The IANA registration is the document's vehicle, but it is not about IANA registry rules or stewardship.
MIME is only the context for the media type; nothing concerns email transport or formats.

gaps.name: Portable Font Resource (PFR) / font formats
gaps.why: The document describes a compact, platform-independent font format. The taxonomy has no tag for fonts or typography.

RFC3074.title: DHC Load Balancing Algorithm
RFC3074.summary: Specifies a deterministic Pearson-hash-based algorithm by which cooperating DHCP servers, or BOOTP relay agents forwarding to them, decide which server serves each client, enabling load balancing without server-to-server exchange.

DHCP.why: The document defines a load balancing extension for DHCP servers and BOOTP relay agents, using client identifiers and chaddr to hash clients to servers. Readers of DHCP would want it.
DHCP.quote: It enables multiple, cooperating servers to decide which one should service a client, without exchanging any information beyond initial configuration.

rejected.why: DHCP/BOOTP broadcasts run over UDP, but this is only the substrate and the document defines nothing about UDP.
The Pearson hash is a load-distribution hash, not a checksum or integrity check.
Server IPs appear only in configuration examples; the document is not about IPv4.

RFC3075.title: XML-Signature Syntax and Processing
RFC3075.summary: Specifies the XML digital signature syntax and processing rules (Signature, SignedInfo, Reference, KeyInfo, Transforms, algorithms) for signing arbitrary data.

XML signatures.why: The whole document defines the XML Signature element, its processing, and algorithms.
XML signatures.quote: This document specifies XML (Extensible Markup Language) digital signature processing rules and syntax.

XML.why: A substantial part covers XML canonicalization, syntax constraints, DOM/SAX processing, and XPath/XSLT transforms for XML-based formats.
XML.quote: XML is subject to surface representation changes and to processing which discards some surface information.
XML.section: 7.0 XML Canonicalization and Syntax Constraint Considerations

rejected.why: X509Data is just one KeyInfo type for conveying certificates; the document is not about X.509 profiles.
URIs are used to reference signed data, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
SHA-1 is one mandated digest algorithm among others, not the subject.
RSA/PKCS1 appears as a recommended signature algorithm identifier, not the document's focus.
HMAC-SHA1 is just one algorithm identifier.
PGPData is a minor KeyInfo element.

gaps.name: XML canonicalization (C14N)
gaps.why: Canonicalization is central to the processing model, but the normative spec is a separate RFC and no specific tag exists.

RFC3076.title: Canonical XML Version 1.0
RFC3076.summary: Specifies Canonical XML 1.0, an algorithm for producing a canonical physical representation of an XML document or document subset (based on the XPath data model) so logically equivalent documents compare equal, e.g. for digital signatures.

XML.why: The whole document defines an XML canonicalization method: processing model, namespace handling, attribute ordering, and examples. This is XML-based format specification.
XML.quote: This specification describes a method for generating a physical representation, the canonical form, of an XML document that accounts for the permissible changes.

rejected.why: Digital signatures are the motivating application (Section 1.2) and the WG is xmldsig, but the document defines only canonicalization, not signature syntax or processing.
UTF-8 encoding and NFC are mentioned as parts of the algorithm, but the document is not about Unicode usage.
Output is encoded in UTF-8, which is only an incidental detail of the canonical form.
Relative URIs and xml:base are discussed only as limitations.

RFC3077.title: A Link-Layer Tunneling Mechanism for Unidirectional Links
RFC3077.summary: RFC 3077 specifies a link-layer tunneling mechanism (GRE-based) and the Dynamic Tunnel Configuration Protocol (DTCP) that emulate bidirectional connectivity over unidirectional links such as satellite broadcast, using a separate bidirectional IP network as the return path.

satellite.why: The document addresses networking over unidirectional links (e.g., broadcast satellite) and specifies how to emulate bidirectional connectivity. Satellite is the closest taxonomy fit for unidirectional-link networking.
satellite.quote: a mechanism to emulate full bidirectional connectivity between all nodes that are directly connected by a unidirectional link

GRE.why: GRE is the recommended encapsulation, with a dedicated section on its packet format and use on the receiver (Tunnel Type 47). This is a substantial profile of how GRE is used for link-layer tunnels.
GRE.quote: Generic Routing Encapsulation [RFC2784] is suggested as the tunneling mechanism as it provides a means for carrying IP, ARP datagrams

rejected.why: GRE is chosen as the more specific child; the generic tunneling parent is implied.
ARP is discussed as an issue (long delays on satellite links make it work poorly), but the document does not specify or extend it.
The DTCP announcement uses a multicast group, and broadcast/multicast packet handling is covered, but multicast routing is explicitly out of scope.
DTCP runs over UDP, but UDP is only the substrate here.
RIP is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that needs bidirectional links.
This parent is implied by the satellite tag, and the document is not about link layers in general.

gaps.name: UDLR (Unidirectional Link Routing) / DTCP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for unidirectional link routing or its Dynamic Tunnel Configuration Protocol. The satellite tag is only an approximate fit for the general subject of unidirectional links.

RFC3078.title: Microsoft Point-To-Point Encryption (MPPE) Protocol
RFC3078.summary: Describes MPPE, which uses RC4 to encrypt PPP packets, negotiated via CCP option 18, with its packet format, key change and synchronization rules.

PPP.why: MPPE is a PPP extension: a CCP configuration option and encrypted PPP packet format (protocol 0x00FD), with PPP-level resynchronization via CCP Reset-Request.
PPP.quote: MPPE is negotiated within option 18 [4] in the Compression Control Protocol.

RC4.why: The RC4 cipher with 40/56/128-bit session keys, its table initialization and key-change procedure are central to the specification.
RC4.quote: MPPE uses the RSA RC4 [3] algorithm to provide data confidentiality.

rejected.why: SHA-1 is only used as a building block in the key-change algorithm; the document is not about the hash.
Initial key derivation is explicitly left to other documents; only periodic session key changes are described.
MPPC is referenced and CCP is used for negotiation, but MPPE does not compress data.
Only mentioned as an ordering constraint (MPPE applied after header compression).

gaps.name: PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP) / MPPE
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CCP or PPP encryption specifically; PPP is the closest fit.

RFC3079.title: Deriving Keys for use with Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption (MPPE)
RFC3079.summary: Informational RFC specifying how initial MPPE (RC4-based PPP encryption) session keys are derived from MS-CHAP-1, MS-CHAP-2 and EAP-TLS credentials, with sample derivations.

PPP.why: The document is about key derivation for MPPE, a PPP encryption option negotiated via CCP. PPP readers would look for it.
PPP.quote: Microsoft Point to Point Encryption (MPPE) is a means of representing PPP packets in an encrypted form.

key management.why: Its core content is session key derivation and the key hierarchy (master keys, send/receive transient keys) from passwords and TLS master secrets.
key management.quote: This document describes the method used to derive initial MPPE session keys from a variety of credential types.

RC4.why: Keys are derived to initialize RC4 tables at 40, 56 and 128 bits, with key-strength reduction discussed. RC4 readers would find it relevant.
RC4.quote: MPPE uses the RSA RC4 algorithm to provide data confidentiality.

EAP.why: A full section derives MPPE keys from EAP-TLS master secrets.
EAP.quote: EAP-TLS [12] is an EAP authentication type which allows the use of TLS within the PPP authentication framework.

rejected.why: TLS master secret is only an input to key derivation; nothing new is defined about TLS.
SHA-1 is used as a building block in the derivation functions, not the subject.
MD4 is only used for the password hash step; the document is not about the hash.
MS-CHAP is the source of credentials, but the document is about key derivation rather than the authentication protocols.

gaps.name: MS-CHAP / MPPE (Microsoft PPP extensions)
gaps.why: The document concerns Microsoft's MS-CHAP and MPPE, which the taxonomy has no tags for, so they fall under PPP and key management.

RFC3080.title: The Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol Core
RFC3080.summary: RFC 3080 specifies the BEEP core, a generic framing and channel-management kernel for asynchronous, connection-oriented application protocols, and defines the TLS transport security profile and the SASL family of profiles for BEEP.

BEEP.why: The document is the core specification of BEEP: framing, channels, channel management, session establishment and release, and transport mapping requirements.
BEEP.quote: a generic application protocol kernel for connection-oriented, asynchronous interactions called the BEEP (Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol) core

SASL.why: A substantial section defines the SASL family of BEEP profiles, including the service name, initiation and exchange sequences, and the blob element. This is new specification of how SASL is used in BEEP.
SASL.quote: This document defines a family of profiles based on SASL mechanisms

TLS.why: The document defines a BEEP profile (ready/proceed messages) for negotiating TLS. It is a specified part of the document, not just a substrate.
TLS.quote: the TLS transport security profile, based on TLS version one [3]

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for the channel-management messages. The application/beep+xml registration is a small subset definition and not the subject of the document.
Messages are MIME content, but MIME is only the payload format the framing relies on.
The TCP mapping is in a separate document (RFC 3081). This one only states the requirements for transport mappings.
The application/beep+xml registration is a minor section and not the main subject.
The document sets out requirements for transport mappings, but it is the BEEP core itself and not a mapping of one protocol onto a transport.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the frame syntax.

RFC3081.title: Mapping the BEEP Core onto TCP
RFC3081.summary: Specifies how a BEEP session maps onto a single TCP connection, covering session establishment and release plus window-based per-channel flow control using SEQ frames.

BEEP.why: The document is a BEEP specification. It defines the TCP mapping for BEEP, including the SEQ frame and the per-channel flow control rules.
BEEP.quote: This memo describes how a BEEP [1] session is mapped onto a single TCP [2] connection.

transport mapping.why: It is a binding of an application protocol onto a transport, which is what the transport mapping topic covers. It defines session setup, release and abort over TCP.
transport mapping.quote: A BEEP session is established when a TCP connection is established between two BEEP peers

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document does not extend or change TCP. It reintroduces window-based flow control at the BEEP layer.
Congestion is mentioned briefly, as a recommendation to use transport APIs that convey congestion information. The document is about flow control, not congestion control.
ABNF is used only to write the SEQ frame syntax.

RFC3082.title: Notification and Subscription for SLP
RFC3082.summary: Experimental RFC extending the Service Location Protocol with Subscribe and NotifyAt extensions and multicast notification so user agents learn of service appearance/disappearance without polling.

SLP.why: The document extends SLP with notification and subscription: new Subscribe and NotifyAt extensions, SA/DA behaviour, and multicast notification of SrvReg/SrvDereg.
SLP.quote: we describe a protocol for allowing such clients to be notified when a change occurs, removing the need for polling.

MADCAP.why: A section specifies how notification multicast group addresses are allocated via MAAA/MADCAP, so readers of MADCAP would find this use relevant.
MADCAP.quote: a DA allocates, using MADCAP, a new multicast group address for each new service type/scope pair to which a UA subscribes.

rejected.why: Multicast is used as the notification delivery mechanism, but the document is about SLP notification, not multicast routing or group management; MADCAP already covers the address allocation part.
Implied by the SLP tag, which is more specific.
IPv6 multicast addresses are mentioned for notification groups, but IPv6 itself is not the subject.
UDP is only the substrate for multicast messages; MTU overflow handling is incidental.

RFC3083.title: Baseline Privacy Interface Management Information Base for DOCSIS Compliant Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems
RFC3083.summary: Defines the DOCS-BPI-MIB SMIv2 module for SNMP management of the DOCSIS 1.0 Baseline Privacy Interface (authorization and TEK state machines, key lifetimes, multicast SID mapping) on cable modems and CMTSs.

MIB.why: The document's core content is a MIB module (DOCS-BPI-MIB) with tables, objects and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: it defines a basic set of managed objects for SNMP-based (Simple Network Management Protocol) management of the Baseline Privacy Interface (BPI)

DOCSIS.why: The MIB manages the DOCSIS BPI on cable modems and CMTSs, extending the DOCSIS RF Interface MIB, so it belongs on the DOCSIS cable access page.
DOCSIS.quote: Baseline Privacy Interface (BPI), which provides data privacy for DOCSIS 1.0 (Data-Over-Cable Service Interface Specifications) compliant Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol substrate; the document defines MIB objects rather than extending SNMP, so MIB is the more specific fit.
RSA public keys are exposed as MIB objects, but the document is not about the RSA algorithm.
DES is mentioned only in the glossary description of TEKs.
The multicast SID mapping and authorization tables are a small part; the document is not about IP multicast routing.
The MIB exposes key lifetimes and state machines, but the key management protocol is defined in the DOCSIS BPI spec, not here.

RFC3084.title: COPS Usage for Policy Provisioning (COPS-PR)
RFC3084.summary: RFC 3084 specifies how the COPS protocol is used for policy provisioning (COPS-PR), defining PIB-based data naming, new S-Num/S-Type objects, message content for REQ/DEC/RPT, error codes, and fault-tolerance behaviour between PDPs and PEPs.

COPS.why: The whole document defines COPS-PR, a client-type usage and extension of COPS: new objects, decision flag, message formats and operation between PDP and PEP.
COPS.quote: This document describes the use of the Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol for support of policy provisioning (COPS-PR).

rejected.why: QoS examples (DiffServ) are used, but the specification is explicitly independent of policy type; COPS is the tag under QoS that fits.
Policy information bases are referenced, but the PIB data models are defined elsewhere (SPPI); this document defines the transport protocol usage.
BER encoding of PRIDs and EPD is used, but ASN.1 is only the encoding mechanism, not the subject.
TCP is only the transport substrate for COPS connections.
SMI-style definitions are used only as an example for encoding instance data; the document is not a MIB module.
DiffServ is only used for illustrative examples.

RFC3085.title: URN Namespace for NewsML Resources
RFC3085.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "newsml" for identifying NewsML NewsItems, defining the identifier syntax (provider domain, date, item ID, revision, update flag) and the registration template.

URN.why: The document defines and registers a new URN namespace, including syntax, uniqueness, persistence, resolution and equivalence rules.
URN.quote: This document describes a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace for identifying NewsML NewsItems.

rejected.why: NewsML is an XML format, but the document only defines identifiers for NewsItems, not XML usage.
ABNF is only the notation used to state the NSS syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
The ProviderId must be a domain name, but the document does not address DNS protocol or operations.
URN is the more specific child tag and is the right fit.

gaps.name: NewsML / news industry metadata (IPTC)
gaps.why: The document concerns identifiers for NewsML news packaging, but the taxonomy has no tag for news-industry or publishing content formats.

RFC3086.title: Definition of Differentiated Services Per Domain Behaviors and Rules for their Specification
RFC3086.summary: Informational RFC defining the Differentiated Services Per-Domain Behavior (PDB) concept, the required format and attributes for PDB specifications, a reference Best Effort PDB, and guidelines for advancing PDB specs in the diffserv WG.

Diffserv.why: The document extends the differentiated services architecture with the PDB concept, building on PHBs, classifiers and traffic conditioners, and specifies how PDBs are written.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines and discusses Per-Domain Behaviors in detail and lays out the format and required content for contributions to the Diffserv WG on PDBs

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS subject.
PDB attributes are measurable metrics, but the document does not define measurement methods or metrics in their own right.
RFC 2434 Expert Review is only cited for the publication process, so this is not an IANA topic.
Section 8 gives WG guidelines for advancing PDB specs, but this is a small part of a technical document and not its main subject.
Traffic engineering is mentioned in passing, but the document is not about it.

RFC3087.title: Control of Service Context using SIP Request-URI
RFC3087.summary: Informational memo describing a convention of using distinctive SIP Request-URIs to convey service context (e.g., deposit vs. retrieve, busy vs. no-answer) to a voice mail application, with scenarios and SIP call flows.

SIP.why: The whole document is a usage convention of SIP Request-URI with proxy routing and extensive SIP call flows, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: Under this proposal, a client or proxy can communicate context through the use of a distinctive Request-URI.

rejected.why: The SIP Request-URI is used as a convention, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes; it is about SIP service control.
SDP bodies appear in the call flows only as incidental session descriptions.
RTP appears only as the media stream in the examples.
Digest Proxy-Authorization appears in the flows but is not discussed in its own right.
PSTN gateway mapping is mentioned in scenarios, but the focus is SIP Request-URI usage, not interworking mechanisms.

RFC3088.title: OpenLDAP Root Service An experimental LDAP referral service
RFC3088.summary: Describes the experimental OpenLDAP Root Service, an LDAP referral server that maps domain-component DNs to domain names and generates LDAP referrals from DNS SRV records.

LDAP.why: The document specifies an LDAP server's behaviour: referrals, bind, controls like ManageDSAit, and LDAPv2/v3 interoperability.
LDAP.quote: The OpenLDAP Project is operating an experimental LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) referral service known as the "OpenLDAP Root Service".

service discovery.why: The service locates LDAP servers for a domain by querying DNS SRV records and building referrals from them.
service discovery.quote: DNS SRV [RFC2782] resource records can be used to locate services [LOCATE].

rejected.why: DNS SRV records are only consumed as the lookup mechanism; the document defines nothing new about DNS.
Mentioned only as a possible future enhancement in Security Considerations.
Start TLS is mentioned only as a possible later feature.
X.500 naming is background; the document is not about the X.500 directory service.
LDAP URLs are constructed in the referrals but the document does not define or extend the URL scheme.

RFC3089.title: A SOCKS-based IPv6/IPv4 Gateway Mechanism
RFC3089.summary: Informational RFC describing a SOCKS-based gateway mechanism in which a SOCKS server on a dual-stack node relays IPv4 and IPv6 connections at the application layer, with DNS name resolution delegated to the gateway via fake IP addresses.

SOCKS.why: The mechanism is built on SOCKSv5: a socksified client library and an enhanced SOCKS server relay connections, and the document discusses CONNECT, BIND and UDP ASSOCIATE applicability.
SOCKS.quote: It is an enhanced SOCKS server that enables any types of protocol combination relays between Client C (IPvX) and Destination D (IPvY).

IPv6 transition.why: The document is a transition mechanism for IPv6/IPv4 coexistence, using an application-layer gateway on a dual-stack node.
IPv6 transition.quote: enables smooth heterogeneous communications between the IPv6 nodes and IPv4 nodes.

rejected.why: DNS name resolving delegation is a feature of the mechanism, but the document explicitly says it does not modify DNS. It only delegates lookups to the gateway.
IPv6 is one endpoint family in the mechanism. The document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself, and the transition tag already covers the subject.
This is an application-layer relay, not stateless or stateful network-layer address translation.
The document uses no DNS address synthesis. Fake IPs are local to the client library.

RFC3090.title: DNS Security Extension Clarification on Zone Status
RFC3090.summary: RFC 3090 clarifies and updates RFC 2535 DNSSEC by defining a zone as globally secured, locally secured, or unsecured regardless of key algorithm, and deprecates "experimentally secure" status.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document defines the DNSSEC secured-zone status, islands of security, on-tree/off-tree validation and KEY/NXT requirements, updating RFC 2535.
DNSSEC.quote: This document changes this to define a zone to be secured or not secured regardless of the key algorithm used (or not used).

rejected.why: Dynamic update servers are mentioned only as one context that needs to know zone status; the document does not specify update behaviour.
The general DNS protocol is only the substrate; the subject is covered by the more specific DNSSEC tag.
Trust chains and certification authorities are mentioned briefly, but the document is about DNSSEC zone status rather than PKI.

RFC3091.title: Pi Digit Generation Protocol
RFC3091.summary: An April 1st parody RFC defining a Pi digit generation service (PIgen) over TCP, UDP and IP multicast, with DNS SRV-based discovery.

humor.why: Published 1 April 2001, this is a whimsical parody protocol for generating digits of Pi, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: The imminent collapse of the Internet is assured if this guideline is not strictly followed.

small services.why: The protocol is modelled on the chargen-style stream services, sending a stream of digits until the client closes the connection. Readers of the small services page would want to find this parody.
small services.quote: One REQUIRED PIgen service is defined as a stateless TCP service.  A server listens on TCP port 314159.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport for the service; the document does not extend or analyse TCP.
UDP is only the datagram substrate for the digit request and reply service.
DNS SRV is used for service discovery in one short section, which is not enough to make the document about DNS.
The multicast digit service is a joke element, and it does not address multicast routing or deployment.
Discovery via SRV is a minor section and does not make the document about service discovery.
ABNF is used only to define the packet format.

RFC3092.title: Etymology of "Foo"
RFC3092.summary: An April 1 humorous RFC explaining the etymology of the metasyntactic variables "foo", "bar" and "foobar", with acronym interpretations and a table of RFCs that use them.

humor.why: A whimsical April 1st document tracing the origin of 'foo' through cartoons, WWII slang and hacker culture. It is a humorous RFC, and no technical tag fits.
humor.quote: Approximately 212 RFCs so far, starting with RFC 269, contain the terms `foo', `bar', or `foobar' as metasyntactic variables without any proper explanation

rejected.why: It defines and explains terms, but it is a joke etymology, not a glossary or requirements-language document.
It surveys RFCs that use foo/bar, but it is not about RFC format, style or publication.
Example domain names such as foo.bar appear only in the appendix table and are not the document's subject.

RFC3093.title: Firewall Enhancement Protocol (FEP)
RFC3093.summary: April 1st parody RFC proposing the Firewall Enhancement Protocol, which tunnels TCP/IP datagrams inside HTTP messages (with TCP/IP header fields rendered as new HTTP headers) to bypass firewalls.

humor.why: This is an April 1st parody RFC, with whimsical header names (TCP_6Os, IP6_Go_with_the_Flow) and a joke Security Considerations section. The humor page is where readers would expect to find it.
humor.quote: Compressing TCP headers in the face of a protocol such as this one that explodes the size of packets is silly, so we ignore it.

firewall.why: The whole document is about getting traffic past firewalls, which is firewall and middlebox traversal.
firewall.quote: With no cooperation from a firewall operator, the FEP allows ANY application to traverse a Firewall.

tunneling.why: The protocol encapsulates IP datagrams in HTTP messages through a tunnel interface, so it is generic tunnelling.
tunneling.quote: We decided to develop a process by which TCP/IP itself is carried over HTTP.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the carrier used to get through firewalls. The document does define some new HTTP headers, but only as a joke encoding of TCP/IP header fields, so HTTP readers would not need it.
TCP headers are encoded, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
The end-to-end argument is cited as motivation, but the document is a parody protocol and not an architecture discussion.
The IPv6 header encoding is a minor section and the document is not about IPv6.

RFC3094.title: Tekelec's Transport Adapter Layer Interface
RFC3094.summary: Vendor-specified Tekelec protocol (TALI, v1.0 and v2.0) that carries SS7 SCCP/TCAP, ISUP and MTP3 messages over TCP/IP between a Signalling Gateway and IP nodes, with routing-key registration, MTP3 primitives and a state machine; an alternative to IETF SIGTRAN.

SIGTRAN.why: TALI is SS7 signalling transport over IP between a Signaling Gateway and IP nodes, the same problem space as SIGTRAN (the IESG note says it is a vendor alternative to SIGTRAN).
SIGTRAN.quote: The Transport Adapter Layer Interface (TALI) is the proposed interface, which provides TCAP (Transaction Capability Application Part), ISUP (ISDN User Part), and MTP (Mail Transport Protocol) messaging over TCP/IP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable substrate on which TALI runs; TALI defines nothing new about TCP.
SCTP is mentioned only as a possible future replacement transport for TCP in one short section; the document is not about SCTP.
Parent of SIGTRAN, which is the more specific fit and is already tagged.
Media Gateways and Controllers appear only as the kinds of node that use TALI; no gateway control protocol is specified.
SAAL/SSCOP is carried inside TALI as an option, but the document does not address IP over ATM.
Mentioned only as a suggestion in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: SS7 / Signalling System No. 7 (SCCP, TCAP, ISUP, MTP3)
gaps.why: The document is largely a specification of how SS7 message types are encapsulated and routed (routing keys, point codes, MTP3 network management primitives). The taxonomy has no SS7 tag outside SIGTRAN.

RFC3095.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Framework and four profiles: RTP, UDP, ESP, and uncompressed
RFC3095.summary: RFC 3095 specifies the ROHC framework and profiles for robust compression of RTP/UDP/IP, UDP/IP, ESP/IP headers (plus an uncompressed profile) over lossy, long-RTT links such as cellular.

ROHC.why: The whole document defines the ROHC framework, modes, packet formats, feedback and profiles.
ROHC.quote: This document specifies a highly robust and efficient header compression scheme for RTP/UDP/IP (Real-Time Transport Protocol, User Datagram Protocol, Internet Protocol), UDP/IP, and ESP/IP

CRTP.why: Existing CRTP is analysed in depth as the motivation, and ROHC RTP is its robust successor; the RTP profile compresses the same headers. Readers of CRTP would want this.
CRTP.quote: CRTP does not perform well.  Each lost packet over the link causes several subsequent packets to be lost

rejected.why: RTP is the compressed protocol, not specified or extended here.
ESP is only a header chain compressed by a profile; IPsec itself isn't addressed.
Cellular links are the motivating environment, but the document is generic header compression.
CRCs are used internally for error detection; the document doesn't address CRC polynomial choice as a subject.
IPHC is mentioned only as an existing scheme for background.
Parent of ROHC, implied by the child tag.

RFC3096.title: Requirements for robust IP/UDP/RTP header compression
RFC3096.summary: Requirements document for the ROHC WG's robust IP/UDP/RTP header compression scheme, covering infrastructure impact, supported headers, and efficiency/robustness needs for lossy, long-delay cellular links.

ROHC.why: The whole document lists requirements for ROHC, the robust header compression scheme for IP/UDP/RTP.
ROHC.quote: This document contains requirements for robust IP/UDP/RTP (Internet Protocol/User Datagram Protocol/Real-Time Transport Protocol) header compression to be developed by the ROHC (Robust Header Compression) WG.

rejected.why: CRTP (RFC 2508) is only referenced as the baseline ROHC must outperform, not specified or extended.
RTP headers are what gets compressed, but the document is not about RTP itself.
Cellular links (WCDMA, EDGE, CDMA-2000) are the motivating environment, but the document specifies header compression requirements, not IP over 3GPP.
Only one requirement says IPsec subheaders should be compressible; this is a minor point.
Mobile IP headers are one supported header kind, a single requirement, not the subject.

RFC3097.title: RSVP Cryptographic Authentication -- Updated Message Type Value
RFC3097.summary: Updates RFC 2747 (RSVP cryptographic authentication) by reassigning the Challenge and Integrity Response message type values to 25 and 26 to resolve a conflict with the RFC 2961 Bundle message type 12.

RSVP.why: The document modifies the RSVP Integrity extension's message type values and discusses compatibility, so it is about RSVP and belongs on the RSVP page.
RSVP.quote: This memo resolves the conflict over RSVP Message Type 12 by assigning a different value to the Message Type of the Integrity Response Message in RFC 2747.

rejected.why: The document resolves a message type value clash, but it is a protocol-specific amendment to RSVP. It is not about IANA registry stewardship or guidance.
The Integrity extension is authentication, but the document only changes message type numbers and does not address authentication itself.
A parent of RSVP, so implied by the RSVP tag. It is not chosen separately.

RFC3098.title: How to Advertise Responsibly Using E-Mail and Newsgroups or - how NOT to $$$$$  MAKE ENEMIES FAST!  $$$$$
RFC3098.summary: RFC 3098 (FYI 38) is an informational guide advising advertisers how to market responsibly over email, Netnews and the web, avoiding spam through opt-in lists, confirmation, privacy practices and ethical behavior.

spam.why: The whole document is about avoiding spam: why it is irresponsible, what alternatives (opt-in lists, confirmation) exist, and what advertisers should and should not do.
spam.quote: The aforementioned practice, of course, is the sending of Unsolicited Commercial and Bulk E-Mail messages, posts to Netnews groups, or other unsolicited electronic communication.

mailing lists.why: Substantial sections cover building, confirming, and maintaining opt-in mailing lists and posting to lists, including subscription confirmation content.
mailing lists.quote: Opt-In mailing lists provide the prospective Internet advertiser with the control they need over the list of their prospective target audience

rejected.why: Privacy of collected personal data is discussed (Section 7A, Appendix B) but as a business/legal practice for advertisers, not protocol privacy considerations.
Netnews groups are a medium where advertising is posted, but the document does not address the article format or distribution.
Email is the medium of the unsolicited messages; the document does not specify or analyse email protocols.
It is an FYI document, but the taxonomy tag is for introductory guides for Internet users; this is guidance for advertisers and the spam tag fits better.
Cookies are mentioned only as a data-gathering caveat in a sentence or two.

gaps.name: Internet advertising / marketing ethics
gaps.why: The document is largely about responsible online advertising practice, pyramid/Ponzi schemes and data protection law, which no taxonomy tag covers beyond spam.

RFC3099.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 3000-3099
RFC3099.summary: RFC 3099 is a slightly annotated index of RFCs 3000 through 3099 that gives each RFC's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The whole document catalogues a block of the RFC series. Readers browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find this periodic summary.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 3000 through RFCs 3099.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: It marks which RFCs are on the standards track, but only as a label on list entries. The memo does not discuss the process.
Many entries (RFC 3031, 3032, 3036 and others) cover MPLS, but each is only a one-paragraph listing. The memo is not about MPLS.
Several listed RFCs concern DNS, DNSSEC and dynamic update. The summary only lists them and does not address the subject.
Several listed RFCs define DHCP options. This memo only lists them.
IANA appears only inside individual abstracts, such as the RFC 3068 prefix reservation. It is not a subject of the memo.
The list includes April 1 RFCs such as 3091, 3092 and 3093. They are only entries in the index, and the memo itself is not humorous.

RFC3101.title: The OSPF Not-So-Stubby Area (NSSA) Option
RFC3101.summary: Specifies the OSPF Not-So-Stubby Area (NSSA) option, which adds the N-bit and Type-7 LSAs so a stub-like area can import limited external routes, with Type-7 to Type-5 translation, and obsoletes RFC 1587.

OSPF.why: The whole document extends OSPF with a new area type, the N-bit, Type-7 LSAs, translator election and route calculation changes.
OSPF.quote: NSSAs are similar to the existing OSPF stub area configuration option but have the additional capability of importing AS external routes in a limited fashion.

rejected.why: RIP appears only as an example of a protocol whose routes are imported into the NSSA; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Not mentioned; external routes come from other protocols or ASes generically.
A child technology tag (OSPF) fits more specifically.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as OSPF's authentication digest; boilerplate.
Mentioned only in passing as another IGP that may leak routes into the NSSA.

RFC3102.title: Realm Specific IP: Framework
RFC3102.summary: Framework document for Realm Specific IP (RSIP), an alternative to NAT in which hosts lease addresses and ports from a gateway and tunnel packets to preserve end-to-end integrity; covers requirements, deployment scenarios, interaction with other layer-three protocols, and complications.

NAT.why: RSIP is a NAT alternative. The document covers cascaded RSIP and NAT, NAT-related complications and gateway behaviour, so readers of the NAT subject would want it.
NAT.quote: RSIP is intended as a alternative to NAT in which the end-to-end integrity of packets is maintained.

tunneling.why: Host-to-gateway tunnelling is central to the architecture. It also covers tunnel DSCP handling and RSVP over tunnels.
tunneling.quote: Using the public parameters assigned by the RSIP gateway, RSIP hosts tunnel data packets across address space A to the RSIP gateway.

IPsec.why: A section covers how SPI and IKE cookies serve as demultiplexing fields, and the IESG note flags IPsec interoperability. IPsec readers would want this.
