MIB.why: SPPI is a modified SMIv2 and the document specifies macro mappings, textual conventions and an algorithmic PIB-to-MIB mapping (Appendix A), so SMI/MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: The SPPI and PIB modules are based on SNMP's SMI and MIB modules

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation basis for the macros, but the document is about SMI-derived structure of provisioning information, not ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
SNMP is not used as a protocol; only its SMI is adapted, and SNMP notifications are explicitly unused.
The document concerns policy information modelling language mechanics rather than policy-based management information models; COPS tag already covers the area.
DSCP maps appear only in the Appendix B example.

gaps.name: Policy Information Base (PIB) / SPPI
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PIB modules or the policy provisioning data definition language; the closest fits are COPS and MIB.

RFC3160.title: The Tao of IETF - A Novice's Guide to the Internet Engineering Task Force
RFC3160.summary: FYI 17 is a newcomer's guide to the IETF: its organizations (ISOC, IESG, IAB, IANA, RFC Editor, Secretariat), meetings, working groups, BOFs, Internet Drafts, and the RFC standards process.

user guides.why: The document is an FYI-series introductory guide for newcomers to the IETF, which is what the user guides subject covers.
user guides.quote: This document describes the inner workings of IETF meetings and Working Groups, discusses organizations related to the IETF, and introduces the standards process.

IETF process.why: A large part of the document explains IETF working groups, BOFs, rough consensus, the IESG, the standards track and Internet Drafts. This is IETF process.
IETF process.quote: The basic steps for getting something published as an IETF standard are:

RFC series.why: The document explains the kinds of RFCs, the sub-series, the RFC Editor's role and how Internet Drafts become RFCs.
RFC series.quote: There are also three sub-series of RFCs, known as FYIs, BCPs, and STDs.

rejected.why: IANA is described only as one of the IETF's supporting organizations, in short passages. The document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
The Nominating Committee is mentioned only in passing as the body that selects IESG and IAB members. There is no procedural treatment.
Patents in standards get one subsection (6.4.5), which is too small a share of the document to tag.
The MUST/SHOULD/MAY discussion in 6.4.1 is a small part of the document, so it does not warrant a terminology tag.

RFC3161.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP)
RFC3161.summary: RFC 3161 specifies the Time-Stamp Protocol: request and response formats for a Time Stamping Authority, the signed time-stamp token (a CMS SignedData), TSA requirements, and optional transports (email, file, TCP, HTTP).

PKI.why: The document defines a PKIX time-stamping service: TSA requirements, certificate key usage (id-kp-timeStamping), token verification and revocation handling. It is a PKI protocol with no more specific PKI child tag that fits.
PKI.quote: This document describes the format of a request sent to a Time Stamping Authority (TSA) and of the response that is returned.

CMS.why: The TimeStampToken is a CMS SignedData with a new eContentType (id-ct-TSTInfo). Appendix A defines a signature time-stamp attribute for CMS SignerInfo. Both are new uses of CMS that CMS readers would want.
CMS.quote: It is defined as a ContentInfo ([CMS]) and SHALL encapsulate a signed data content type.

rejected.why: The document profiles no certificates beyond requiring a critical extended key usage value for the TSA. The X.509 profile itself is in RFC 2459.
ASN.1 is the notation and encoding for the messages and Appendix C holds the module. It is the substrate, not the subject.
HTTP is one optional transport, described in a short subsection with two MIME types. The document is not about HTTP.
Email transport is an optional mechanism and only a minor part of the document.
The application/timestamp-query and application/timestamp-reply MIME types are defined in passing within the transport sections. The document is not about media type registration.
The time-stamp is an evidentiary token of existence at a time. The document does not synchronize clocks.

gaps.name: Time-stamping / trusted timestamp services
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about a time-stamping authority and token format. The taxonomy has no tag for this beyond the general PKI tag.

RFC3162.title: RADIUS and IPv6
RFC3162.summary: RFC 3162 specifies how RADIUS operates over IPv6 and defines six new RADIUS attributes (NAS-IPv6-Address, Framed-Interface-Id, Framed-IPv6-Prefix, Login-IPv6-Host, Framed-IPv6-Route, Framed-IPv6-Pool) for supporting IPv6 network access.

RADIUS.why: The document extends RADIUS with new attributes and specifies its operation over IPv6, so it belongs on the RADIUS page.
RADIUS.quote: This document specifies the operation of RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) when run over IPv6 as well as the RADIUS attributes used to support IPv6 network access.

IPv6.why: The attributes carry IPv6 addresses, prefixes, interface identifiers and routes for IPv6 network access, so IPv6 deployment readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: This Attribute indicates an IPv6 prefix (and corresponding route) to be configured for the user.

rejected.why: IPv6CP is mentioned only as context for when address assignment happens; the document does not specify PPP.
Discussed only in Security Considerations as a way to protect RADIUS; boilerplate, not the subject.
6to4, 6over4 and tunnels are mentioned in passing; the document says the access method has no effect on RADIUS usage.
RADIUS is the more specific tag and already covers this.

RFC3163.title: ISO/IEC 9798-3 Authentication SASL Mechanism
RFC3163.summary: Defines an experimental SASL authentication mechanism (9798-U/M-algorithm) based on ISO/IEC 9798-3 and FIPS 196 that uses X.509 certificates and digital signatures for unilateral or mutual entity authentication, without integrity or confidentiality.

SASL.why: The document specifies a new SASL mechanism, its mechanism names, token exchange, and registration.
SASL.quote: This document defines a SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) authentication mechanism based on ISO/IEC 9798-3 and FIPS PUB 196 entity authentication.

X.509.why: Authentication relies on X.509 certificates carried in tokens (CertData, certificate chains, TrustedAuth), a substantial part of the protocol design.
X.509.quote: This mechanism only provides authentication using X.509 certificates [X509].

rejected.why: Discussed only as an alternative and compared in the Relationship to TLS section; the document does not specify or extend TLS.
Only used as an example profile of the SASL mechanism; IMAP is not what the document is about.
ASN.1 is the encoding for the PDUs and appendix modules, a substrate rather than the subject.
Uses PKI certificates but does not specify PKI; X.509 is the more specific fit.
A parent of SASL; the more specific SASL tag is used instead.

gaps.name: ISO/IEC 9798-3 entity authentication
gaps.why: The challenge-response signature-based entity authentication scheme itself has no dedicated tag; SASL is the closest fit.

RFC3164.title: The BSD Syslog Protocol
RFC3164.summary: RFC 3164 documents the observed behavior of the BSD syslog protocol, which sends event notification messages over UDP port 514. It covers the architecture of devices, relays and collectors, the PRI/HEADER/MSG packet format, relay handling rules, and security concerns.

syslog.why: The whole document specifies the syslog protocol: its architecture, message format with PRI, HEADER and MSG parts, facilities and severities, and relay behavior.
syslog.quote: the syslog protocol provides a transport to allow a machine to send event notification messages across IP networks to event message collectors

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport. The document assigns port 514 but defines nothing new about UDP itself.
The document requires seven-bit ASCII for the message parts, but it only uses ASCII as an encoding and is not about it.
ABNF is cited for character values only. The document does not specify anything in ABNF.
The TIMESTAMP is the traditional 'Mmm dd hh:mm:ss' form, not an Internet timestamp format. ISO 8601 appears only as an optional suggestion.
The HOSTNAME field is one part of the header, but the document is not about host naming conventions.
The document describes syslog's own protocol over UDP. It does not define a binding of another protocol onto a transport.

RFC3165.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Delegation of Management Scripts
RFC3165.summary: Defines the DISMAN-SCRIPT-MIB (Script MIB), an SNMP MIB module for delegating management scripts to distributed managers: transferring, launching, controlling and monitoring scripts. It obsoletes RFC 2592.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (DISMAN-SCRIPT-MIB) with tables for languages, scripts, code, launch and run. Readers browsing MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: it describes a set of managed objects that allow the delegation of management scripts to distributed managers.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB, but the document defines managed objects and does not extend SNMP. The MIB tag sits under SNMP, so SNMP is implied.
The VACM configuration examples in section 8 show access control for the MIB, but they are illustrative and not the subject of the document.
URLs are used for the script pull model, but only as a mechanism for fetching scripts.
FTP is mentioned only as an example protocol for fetching scripts from a URL.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example protocol for fetching scripts from a URL.
The IANA section only notes a language OID registry for IANA-LANGUAGE-MIB. That is boilerplate and not the main subject.

gaps.name: Script MIB / management delegation (DISMAN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for distributed management or delegation of management functions to scripts. The MIB tag covers the format, but not the delegation subject.

RFC3166.title: Request to Move RFC 1403 to Historic Status
RFC3166.summary: An informational request to reclassify RFC 1403 (BGP OSPF Interaction) as Historic because the mechanism is no longer used and is complex to implement.

BGP.why: The document concerns the status of the BGP/OSPF interaction specification, which arose from a review of BGP-related standards. BGP readers would look for it.
BGP.quote: BGP OSPF interaction, as described in RFC 1403, is not common usage (if at all), and requires significant implementation complexity.

OSPF.why: The obsoleted specification defines how OSPF and BGP interact, so the document belongs on OSPF's page as well.
OSPF.quote: RFC 1403, "BGP OSPF Interaction", describes technology which is no longer used.

rejected.why: The document is about retiring one specific BGP/OSPF interaction mechanism, not about routing architecture generally.
It is a status-change request, but it is a short, specific technical reclassification. The process itself is not the subject.

RFC3167.title: Request to Move RFC 1745 to Historic Status
RFC3167.summary: An informational request to reclassify RFC 1745 (BGP4/IDRP for IP--OSPF Interaction) as Historic because the mechanism was never deployed in the public internet.

BGP.why: The document concerns the status of a BGP-OSPF interaction specification (RFC 1745), arising from a review of BGP standards. A reader browsing BGP would expect to find this retirement of a BGP-related spec.
BGP.quote: BGP/IDRP OSPF interaction, as described in RFC 1745, has never been deployed in the public internet

OSPF.why: The retired RFC specifies how BGP interacts with OSPF, so OSPF readers would want to know that this interaction spec is now Historic.
OSPF.quote: RFC 1745, "BGP4/IDRP for IP---OSPF Interaction", describes technology which was never deployed in the public internet.

rejected.why: The document is a request to change an RFC's status, but it is about the retirement of a specific routing technology; it has no discussion of process beyond the one-line proposal.

RFC3168.title: The Addition of Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to IP
RFC3168.summary: RFC 3168 specifies Explicit Congestion Notification: the two-bit ECN field in the IP header, TCP's ECE and CWR flags and negotiation, and ECN handling in IP and IPsec tunnels.

ECN.why: The document defines ECN itself: the ECT/CE codepoints, router marking behaviour, and the TCP support for it.
ECN.quote: This memo specifies the incorporation of ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) to TCP and IP, including ECN's use of two bits in the IP header.

TCP.why: A large part of the document defines TCP changes: ECE and CWR flags, SYN negotiation, sender and receiver behaviour, and retransmissions. It updates RFC 793.
TCP.quote: This proposal specifies two new flags in the Reserved field of the TCP header.

IPsec.why: It updates RFC 2401 tunnel-mode header processing and adds an SAD field and an SA attribute for ECN, so IPsec readers need it.
IPsec.quote: In particular, in tunnel mode the IPsec tunnel MUST support the limited-functionality option outlined in Section 9.1.1

tunneling.why: It specifies limited- and full-functionality ECN handling at IP-in-IP tunnel ingress and egress.
tunneling.quote: This section considers issues related to interactions between ECN and IP tunnels, and specifies two alternative solutions.

AQM.why: ECN is presented as the marking mechanism for active queue management, with rules on when routers mark rather than drop.
AQM.quote: AQM can set a Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint in the packet header instead of dropping the packet

rejected.why: The ECN field shares the octet with the DS field and the document updates RFC 2474. It is not about Diffserv itself.
The parent is implied by ECN, which is already a child of it.
ICMP appears only as an alternative negotiation mechanism that was rejected.
The ECN Tunnel SA attribute is a small ISAKMP/DOI addition. The document does not specify IKE.
Section 17 only covers incremental IPv4 header checksum recalculation as an implementation note.
The document only redefines two bits of the TOS octet. It is not about IPv4 in general.

RFC3169.title: Criteria for Evaluating Network Access Server Protocols
RFC3169.summary: Informational RFC defining requirements for AAA protocols used by Network Access Servers (authentication, authorization, accounting, security, transport), as criteria for evaluating candidate protocols.

AAA.why: The primary focus is requirements for AAA protocols used by NAS: authentication, authorization, accounting, multi-domain support and security. The generic AAA framework tag fits best.
AAA.quote: This document defines requirements for protocols used by Network Access Servers (NAS).

rejected.why: RADIUS is used as the baseline attribute set and legacy infrastructure, but the document specifies criteria for a next-generation AAA protocol, not RADIUS itself.
PPP is the assumed access protocol and authentication framework, but the document doesn't specify or extend it.
Mentioned only as an example access protocol and a tunnel type the AAA protocol must be able to set up.
EAP is one of the credential types the AAA protocol must carry; the document is not about EAP.
Not mentioned; the document sets criteria that later informed AAA protocol selection, but does not discuss Diameter.
Device management protocols are explicitly out of scope (Section 6).

RFC3170.title: IP Multicast Applications: Challenges and Solutions
RFC3170.summary: Informational introductory guide for developers of IP multicast applications, giving a taxonomy of 1toM/MtoM/Mto1 application types and surveying the service requirements (address management, session management, heterogeneous receivers, reliability, security, synchronized play-out) and their solutions.

multicast.why: The whole document is about IP multicast from the application perspective: application taxonomy, service models (ISM/SSM) and the services applications need. The generic multicast topic fits best.
multicast.quote: This document describes the challenges involved with designing and implementing multicast applications.

reliable multicast.why: A substantial section covers reliable multicast transport challenges (NAKs, implosion, shared learning, local recovery) and the IRTF/RMT work. It does not specify any one protocol, so the topic tag applies.
reliable multicast.quote: Although many reliable multicast protocol implementations exist [Obraczka], and a few are already available in commercial products, none of them are standardized.

multicast security.why: A substantial section discusses multicast-specific security needs (limiting senders and receivers, membership revocation, individual authentication) and the msec/IRTF efforts.
multicast security.quote: Multicast security requirements can include any combination of the following services:

rejected.why: SSM is described only as one of two multicast service models the application must be aware of. The document does not specify or analyse it.
IGMP is mentioned as the join mechanism and for join/leave latency. It is the substrate, and the document is not about it.
RTP/RTCP appear only as examples of shared-learning feedback and API needs. The document does not specify or extend them.
SDP and SAP are mentioned briefly as session advertisement mechanisms and are not the subject of the document.
MADCAP and MASC appear only in the references. The address management section does not discuss them.
Congestion adaptation for heterogeneous receivers is discussed within the multicast context, but it is not a subject in its own right here.
Section 6 on service APIs is generic and brief, and it does not address sockets API extensions.

RFC3171.title: IANA Guidelines for IPv4 Multicast Address Assignments
RFC3171.summary: BCP giving IANA guidelines for assigning IPv4 multicast addresses across the defined blocks (Local Network Control, Internetwork Control, AD-HOC, SDP/SAP, SSM, GLOP, Administratively Scoped), plus annual review and reclamation.

multicast.why: The whole document is about how the IPv4 multicast address space is divided and assigned, so readers of the multicast subject would want it. No specific multicast child technology is the main subject.
multicast.quote: This memo provides guidance for the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) in assigning IPv4 multicast addresses.

IANA.why: It is an IANA allocation-policy document. It sets assignment procedures (Expert Review, IESG Approval, Standards Action), annual review and address reclamation for a registry.
IANA.quote: The guidelines described below are reflected in http://www.iana.org/numbers.html.

addressing.why: It covers allocation of IP address space, including block layout, GLOP mapping and relative offsets. Readers of IP address architecture and allocation would want it.
addressing.quote: IPv4 multicast addresses are assigned directly by the IANA.

rejected.why: SSM is only one of the blocks covered. The document just says no IANA assignment policy is needed for it and does not specify SSM.
The document concerns multicast address assignment, not IPv4 itself or its address lifecycle. Multicast is the better fit.
MADCAP and MALLOC appear only in the references. The body does not discuss them.
NTP's multicast address is cited only as an example of a block use.

RFC3172.title: Management Guidelines & Operational Requirements for the Address and Routing Parameter Area Domain ("arpa")
RFC3172.summary: IAB BCP describing management principles and operational requirements for the "arpa" infrastructure DNS top-level domain, including sub-domain criteria, delegation, and name server requirements.

DNS.why: The document is about management and operation of the arpa DNS zone and its sub-domains (in-addr.arpa, ip6.arpa, e164.arpa), including name server operational requirements.
DNS.quote: The "arpa" domain is used to support a class of infrastructural identifier spaces, providing a distributed database that translates elements of a structured name space

rejected.why: arpa is an infrastructure TLD managed by the IAB, not a reserved special-use name under that registry's meaning; document is about its management, not special-use reservation.
e164.arpa is mentioned only as one existing sub-domain, with details deferred to RFC 2916.
IANA administers the domain, but the document is about the DNS domain's management rather than IANA registries in general.
Delegation of sub-domains is discussed, but not registry/registrar operations or protocols.
ip6.arpa is only mentioned briefly as a sub-domain.

RFC3173.title: IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp)
RFC3173.summary: Defines IPComp, a protocol for stateless lossless compression of IP datagram payloads, including its header format, the non-expansion policy, and IPComp Association negotiation via IKE or manual configuration.

IPComp.why: The document specifies IPComp itself: header structure, compression process, and association negotiation.
IPComp.quote: This document defines the IP payload compression protocol (IPComp), the IPComp packet structure, the IPComp Association (IPCA), and several methods to negotiate the IPCA.

rejected.why: IKE is only the negotiation mechanism for the IPCA. Section 4.1 says how to carry the CPI and transforms in IKE proposals, but the document is not about IKE.
IPComp is often used with IPsec, and compression must be applied before encryption. IPsec is context rather than the subject.
The document gives IPv6 header handling rules for IPComp, but it is not about IPv6 as a protocol.
The document describes IPv4 header modifications for IPComp, but it is not about IPv4 itself.
IPComp compresses payloads, not protocol headers on constrained links, so this topic does not fit.

RFC3174.title: US Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA1)
RFC3174.summary: RFC 3174 makes the US SHA-1 hash algorithm (from FIPS 180-1) available to the Internet community. It gives the algorithm specification, a reference C implementation and a test driver.

SHA.why: The whole document specifies SHA-1, including padding, functions, constants, digest computation and C code. It belongs on the SHA hash family page.
SHA.quote: This document specifies a Secure Hash Algorithm, SHA-1, for computing a condensed representation of a message or a data file.

rejected.why: MD4 and MD5 are cited only as stylistic precedent and as the design lineage of SHA-1. The document is not about them.
RFC 1750 is only listed in the references, and the body does not discuss randomness.
The SHA tag is more specific, and the document does not cover cryptography in general.

RFC3175.title: Aggregation of RSVP for IPv4 and IPv6 Reservations
RFC3175.summary: Specifies aggregation of many end-to-end RSVP reservations into a single aggregate RSVP reservation across a transit region, using Diffserv DSCPs for classification, new protocol number, error code, and session objects.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with aggregation procedures, new objects (SESSION, SENDER_TEMPLATE C-Types), a new PathErr code and a new IP protocol number.
RSVP.quote: the use of a single RSVP (Resource ReSerVation Protocol) reservation to aggregate other RSVP reservations across a transit routing region

Diffserv.why: Aggregate reservations are keyed by DSCP and mapped to PHBs, so classification and scheduling in the region rely on Diffserv, and the session definition includes the DSCP.
Diffserv.quote: One or more Diff-Serv DSCPs are used to identify traffic covered by aggregate reservations and one or more Diff-Serv PHBs are used

rejected.why: Guaranteed Service and Controlled Load are discussed for mapping and ADSPEC handling, but the document is about RSVP aggregation rather than the Intserv service definitions.
The router alert option is used to carry the aggregation level, but this is a minor mechanism of the document and not its subject.
The tag is implied by the more specific RSVP tag.
IPsec AH is mentioned only as a way to mitigate protocol number tampering in Security Considerations.
MPLS LSPs appear only as one option for tunnelling aggregate traffic.
The document is about reservation aggregation and does not address traffic engineering as a subject.

RFC3176.title: InMon Corporation's sFlow: A Method for Monitoring Traffic in Switched and Routed Networks
RFC3176.summary: Defines InMon's sFlow traffic monitoring system: packet and counter sampling mechanisms in an agent, the SFLOW MIB for controlling the agent, and the XDR-encoded sFlow datagram format sent over UDP to a collector.

performance measurement.why: The document specifies a sampling-based traffic measurement system (flow and counter sampling, collector datagrams), which is network performance/traffic measurement.
performance measurement.quote: sFlow is a technology for monitoring traffic in data networks containing switches and routers.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document is an SMIv2 MIB module (SFLOW-MIB) defining objects to configure sampling, so MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: The sFlow MIB defines a control interface for an sFlow Agent.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management substrate for the MIB; the document defines a MIB module rather than extending or specifying SNMP itself.
Related flow export technology, but sFlow is a distinct, non-IPFIX sampling system; the document does not specify or reference IPFIX.
XDR is used only as the encoding for datagrams; the document doesn't concern ONC RPC.
UDP is only the transport for sFlow datagrams; nothing new is defined about UDP.
The MIB imports RMON types, but the document is not about RMON.
Packet sampling is a similar subject, but the document is not a PSAMP specification.

gaps.name: sFlow / traffic flow sampling and export
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for sampled flow monitoring technologies other than IPFIX/PSAMP; sFlow is a distinct technology that readers would look up by name.

RFC3177.title: IAB/IESG Recommendations on IPv6 Address Allocations to Sites
RFC3177.summary: IAB/IESG recommendation to the RIRs that IPv6 sites generally receive a /48 (with /64 and /128 for special cases), justified by renumbering, multihoming, reverse-DNS and address-conservation arguments.

addressing.why: The whole document is policy guidance on how much IPv6 address space to allocate to end sites, which is IP address allocation. No more specific addressing child fits, as it is neither CIDR nor multihoming nor renumbering alone.
addressing.quote: recommends the assignment of /48 in the general case, /64 when it is known that one and only one subnet is needed and /128

IPv6.why: The recommendations concern IPv6 address structure, the 64/64 split and the /48 site prefix. The document discusses IPv6 deployment and addressing at length.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 address, as currently defined, consists of 64 bits of "network number" and 64 bits of "host number".

multihoming.why: A full section analyses multihoming approaches for IPv6 sites and how a fixed /48 boundary interacts with them. The Shim6 tag is not appropriate because that protocol did not yet exist.
multihoming.quote: In the realm of multi-homed networks, the techniques used in IPv4 can all be applied, but they have known scaling problems.

renumbering.why: Avoiding costly site renumbering is one of the main arguments for a fixed /48 boundary, and the document discusses renumbering repeatedly.
renumbering.quote: renumbering of IPv6 networks is neither invisible nor completely painless.  Therefore, renumbering should be considered a tolerable event, but to be avoided if reasonably feasible.

rejected.why: Router-advertised prefixes and the 64-bit host part are cited only to justify the 64/64 split. The document does not address autoconfiguration itself.
Reverse-DNS zone maintenance is mentioned as one advantage of a fixed boundary, but only briefly. The document does not address DNS.
6to4 is mentioned only as a minor argument for a /48 boundary. The document is not about it.
The document concerns site-level allocation size and route aggregation in passing, not CIDR as such.
NATs are mentioned only as a thing that ample address space will discourage.

RFC3178.title: IPv6 Multihoming Support at Site Exit Routers
RFC3178.summary: Informational RFC describing how an IPv6 site with multiple upstream ISP-assigned prefixes achieves multihoming via primary and secondary tunnel links at exit routers, using BGP4+ or RIPng, without growing the global routing table.

multihoming.why: The whole document is about site multihoming using multiple provider-assigned prefixes, without impacting routing table size.
multihoming.quote: The document describes a mechanism for basic IPv6 multihoming support, and its operational requirements.

BGP.why: BGP4+ preference configuration for primary/secondary links is a main operational mechanism, with failover timing from BGP hold/keepalive timers measured in section 7.
BGP.quote: Using RFC 2260 with IPv6 and BGP4+

RIP.why: Gives a dedicated section with RIPng metric invariants for implementing the scheme.
RIP.quote: It is possible to run an RFC 2260-like configuration with RIPng [Malkin, 1997] , with careful control of metric.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the context, but the more specific multihoming tag captures the subject; the IPv6 specification itself is not addressed.
Tunnels are used for secondary links but are a building block, not the subject.
6to4 and RFC 2893 tunnels are only mentioned as possible primary link types.
Routing table scalability is the motivation, but the more specific multihoming tag covers it.
Router advertisement deprecation of prefixes is mentioned briefly only.
Router renumbering is only mentioned in passing, with a recommendation not to automate.

RFC3179.title: Script MIB Extensibility Protocol Version 1.1
RFC3179.summary: Defines SMX 1.1, a line-based text protocol between a Script MIB SNMP agent and language-specific runtime systems, covering commands, replies, procedures and pipe/TCP transports; obsoletes RFC 2593.

MIB.why: SMX exists to extend a Script MIB implementation. It maps protocol messages to smRunState, smLaunchStart and other Script MIB objects. Readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: The IETF Script MIB defines an interface for the delegation of management functions based on the Internet management framework.

SNMP.why: The protocol is defined for SNMP agent processing of set-requests and notifications such as smScriptResult. It is an agent-internal extensibility protocol, similar in spirit to AgentX, but it is not SNMP itself.
SNMP.quote: The language and runtime system independent SNMP agent implementing the Script MIB communicates with one ore more runtime systems via the SMX protocol.

rejected.why: AgentX is a different subagent protocol for extending SNMP MIB instrumentation. SMX only resembles it in purpose, so it is not about AgentX.
ABNF is only the notation used to define message syntax.
TCP is one of two transports, used only locally. This memo defines no new TCP behaviour.
Section 8 maps SMX onto pipes and TCP, but this is a minor part of the document and not its subject.

gaps.name: Script MIB / management by delegation
gaps.why: The document is about delegating management scripts to runtime systems. The taxonomy has no tag for distributed or delegated management, so MIB is the nearest fit.

RFC3180.title: GLOP Addressing in 233/8
RFC3180.summary: Defines GLOP, a policy for statically assigning multicast addresses in 233/8 by embedding a 16-bit AS number in the middle two octets, giving each AS a /24 (obsoletes RFC 2770).

multicast.why: The document is about static allocation of IP multicast group addresses in 233/8. No more specific multicast child tag covers address allocation policy of this kind.
multicast.quote: This document defines the policy for the use of 233/8 for statically assigned multicast addresses.

addressing.why: It specifies an address-allocation scheme that maps AS numbers to /24 blocks, covering the 233/8 address architecture and its private-AS and large-AS limits.
addressing.quote: the high-order octet has the value 233, and the next 16 bits are a previously assigned Autonomous System number (AS)

rejected.why: MADCAP and MALLOC are cited only as the dynamic allocation approach that has not been widely deployed. GLOP is a static alternative and does not specify them.
Source-Specific Multicast is mentioned only to scope out the cases this document does not address.
The IANA assignment of 233/8 is noted, but the document is about the allocation scheme itself, not about registry procedures.
RWhois is mentioned only as the place where AS registrations are listed. The document does not specify or use the protocol.
AS numbers are used as the basis for address derivation. The document does not address BGP itself.

RFC3181.title: Signaled Preemption Priority Policy Element
RFC3181.summary: Defines the PREEMPTION_PRI RSVP policy element (preemption and defending priority, merge strategies, error handling) for signaled policy-based admission control, and corrects the P-Type codepoint error in RFC 2751.

RSVP.why: The document specifies an RSVP POLICY_DATA policy element, including P-Type assignment, merging of reservations and error processing for RSVP flows.
RSVP.quote: preemption priority policy element for use by signaled policy based admission protocols (such as the Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP)

COPS.why: The element is designed for PDP/PEP/LDP policy outsourcing and is carried in COPS as stateless decision objects, a part of the usage model.
COPS.quote: these objects are included as COPS Stateless Policy Data Decision objects

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the RSVP and COPS tags, so it should not be listed separately.
Policy-based admission is the context, but the document specifies a signaled RSVP policy element, not a policy information model.
The IANA section only assigns P-Type value 1. That is boilerplate.
RSVP reservations and QoS merging are discussed, but Intserv service models themselves are not the subject.

RFC3182.title: Identity Representation for RSVP
RFC3182.summary: Defines the AUTH_DATA policy element for RSVP POLICY_DATA objects to carry user and application identity (simple, Kerberos, public-key credentials), with processing rules and error signalling; obsoletes RFC 2752.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with a new identity policy element, its encoding, message generation and processing rules, and error signalling.
RSVP.quote: This document describes the representation of identity information in POLICY_DATA object for supporting policy based admission control in the Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP).

COPS.why: Policy-based admission control with PEP/PDP is a substantial part of the document, but COPS itself is not specified. The RSVP policy framework sits under QoS; this is a weaker fit, kept secondary.
COPS.quote: first hop router installs the RSVP state and forwards the new policy element returned by the Policy Decision Point (PDP)

rejected.why: Kerberos tickets are only one credential type carried in the CREDENTIAL attribute. The document does not specify or extend Kerberos.
X.509 certificates are only carried as an opaque credential subtype; the document does not profile them.
Identity-based authentication is the purpose, but the document mainly extends RSVP policy objects, which the RSVP tag already covers.
Distinguished Names are used only as policy locator strings; the directory service is not discussed.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate registry assignment and is not evidence of the document's subject.

RFC3183.title: Domain Security Services using S/MIME
RFC3183.summary: Experimental RFC defining Domain Security Services: how MTAs, guards and gateways generate and process S/MIME domain, review and additional-attributes signatures and domain encryption/decryption, with naming conventions, a SignatureType attribute and mailing list agent handling.

S/MIME.why: The whole document extends S/MIME with domain-level signature types, naming rules and domain encryption, so S/MIME readers need it.
S/MIME.quote: This document describes how the S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) protocol can be processed and generated by a number of components of a communication system

CMS.why: Defines a new CMS signed attribute (SignatureType) and uses signature encapsulation and triple-wrapping of signedData/envelopedData layers, which readers of CMS would find relevant.
CMS.quote: All of the signatures defined here are generated and processed as described in [5].

rejected.why: Certificate subject naming conventions are specified, but only as usage of X.509 certificates, not a profile of X.509 itself.
Section 5 handles Mail List Agents stripping domain signatures, but it is a signature-application rule rather than mailing list protocol.
S/MIME is the specific tag; the document is about secure messaging services, not general email architecture.
An ASN.1 module is supplied, but only as the syntax for the new attribute; the document is not about ASN.1.
X.400 interworking is mentioned only as a motivating scenario.
PKI limitations motivate the work, but the document does not specify PKI mechanisms.

RFC3184.title: IETF Guidelines for Conduct
RFC3184.summary: BCP 54 sets out guidelines for personal conduct of IETF participants: mutual respect, impartial debate of ideas, global engineering judgment, and preparedness at working group meetings.

IETF process.why: The document is a BCP on how IETF participants should behave in meetings and on mailing lists, which is IETF process and procedure administration. No narrower child tag fits.
IETF process.quote: This document provides a set of guidelines for personal interaction in the Internet Engineering Task Force.

rejected.why: It only cites BCP 9 for intellectual property guidelines in one sentence. The document is not about IPR.
The parent is implied by IETF process, so it is not listed separately.
NomCom procedures are not discussed.

RFC3185.title: Reuse of CMS Content Encryption Keys
RFC3185.summary: Defines CMS attributes (CEKReference, CEKMaxDecrypts, KEKDerivationAlgorithm) letting the content-encryption key of one EnvelopedData message be reused to derive the key-encryption key of later messages.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS EnvelopedData with new unprotected attributes for reusing the CEK as a later KEK. CMS readers need it.
CMS.quote: This document describes a way to include a key identifier in a CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) enveloped data structure

key management.why: It specifies a key derivation and reuse scheme (byte reversal, PBKDF2) for establishing symmetric keys, a key management matter. It states that it is not general group key management.
key management.quote: reuse the content-encryption key (CEK) from a message (say MSG1) to derive the key-encryption key (KEK) for a later message

rejected.why: PBKDF2 is used only as the derivation function with the CEK as input instead of a password. The document does not specify or extend it.
It was produced by the S/MIME working group and uses the S/MIME attribute arc. The content is CMS-level and not about secure email.
The ASN.1 module is just the formal definition of the new attributes, not the subject.
HMAC-SHA1 appears only as the mandated default PRF inside PBKDF2.

RFC3186.title: MAPOS/PPP Tunneling mode
RFC3186.summary: Informational RFC specifying a MAPOS/PPP tunneling mode in which a MAPOS switch network gives PPP-over-SONET/SDH customer equipment a transparent point-to-point link by rewriting the first one or two header octets, with UNI and OAM&P procedures.

MAPOS.why: The whole document defines a operating mode of MAPOS switches, including header rewriting, mode transition, path establishment and failure handling.
MAPOS.quote: This document specifies tunneling configuration over MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) networks.

rejected.why: PPP frames are carried transparently and LCP keep-alive is used for failure detection, but the document does not specify or extend PPP; it is a substrate.
SONET/SDH is the physical layer used, per RFC 2615; the document is about the MAPOS mode, and MAPOS sits under SONET in the taxonomy.
Although called tunneling, it is header rewriting with no encapsulation, not IP-in-IP or generic tunnelling.
A latency measurement per RFC 2544 is included as an evaluation, but it is a small part and not a methodology contribution.

RFC3187.title: Using International Standard Book Numbers as Uniform Resource Names
RFC3187.summary: Informational RFC describing how ISBNs are embedded in the URN framework, including the ISBN URN namespace registration, lexical equivalence rules, and resolution via national bibliographies.

URN.why: The document defines the ISBN URN namespace, registers NID "ISBN", and specifies syntax, lexical equivalence and resolution for ISBN-based URNs.
URN.quote: This document discusses how International Standard Book Numbers (ISBN) can be supported within the URN (Uniform Resource Names) framework

rejected.why: DNS records are mentioned only as a possible way to record resolution services for ISBN groups; the document is not about DNS.
The namespace registration is a URN NID registration, but the document body is about the ISBN namespace, not IANA registry guidance.
URN is the more specific tag and fits; URI is its parent and implied.

gaps.name: Bibliographic identifiers (ISBN)
gaps.why: The ISBN system itself and bibliographic identifier schemes have no tag in the taxonomy; URN covers the Internet-side use only.

RFC3188.title: Using National Bibliography Numbers as Uniform Resource Names
RFC3188.summary: Informational RFC describing how National Bibliography Numbers assigned by national libraries can be used as URNs under the RFC 2141 syntax, including the registration request for the "NBN" URN namespace.

URN.why: The document defines and registers the NBN URN namespace, specifying its syntax, equivalence, assignment and resolution. Readers of the URN subject would want it.
URN.quote: URN Namespace ID Registration for the National Bibliography Number (NBN)

rejected.why: Not about host naming; NBNs name publications, not hosts.
NBNs are persistent identifiers, but they are not UUIDs.
Another persistent identifier system. This document does not discuss it.
MD5 checksums are used to generate NBN strings for archived resources, but only as a mechanism. The document is not about MD5.
The namespace registration is handled under the URN registration process, which is part of the URN subject. The document is not about IANA registries.

gaps.name: Bibliographic identifiers / library identifiers (ISBN, ISSN, NBN)
gaps.why: The document is about library persistent identifiers and digital archiving. The taxonomy has no tag for these beyond the URN namespace.

RFC3189.title: RTP Payload Format for DV (IEC 61834) Video
RFC3189.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for DV (IEC 61834 / SMPTE 306M, 314M) compressed video, including packetization rules, SDP signalling parameters and MIME registrations for video/DV and audio/DV.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for DV video, covering header usage, DIF block packing, and bundled or unbundled audio.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the packetization scheme for encapsulating the compressed digital video data streams commonly known as "DV" into a payload format for the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP).

codecs.why: It describes the DV video and audio coding format (DIF blocks, DCT structure) and defines the DV encoding types. This is the codec definition itself, not just transport.
codecs.quote: The DV format only uses the DCT compression technique within each frame, contrasted with the interframe compression of the MPEG video standards

rejected.why: SDP is used to signal the format with rtpmap and fmtp parameters. It is only the signalling mechanism, and no new SDP mechanism is defined.
The MIME registrations for video/DV and audio/DV are IANA boilerplate that accompanies the payload format. The document is not about media type rules.
RTCP is mentioned only for lip synchronization, which is incidental.
HEVC is not related. MPEG2 is mentioned only as being covered by other RFCs.
IEEE 1394 is mentioned only as the source interface of DV streams. The document does not address IP over 1394.

RFC3190.title: RTP Payload Format for 12-bit DAT Audio and 20- and 24-bit Linear Sampled Audio
RFC3190.summary: Defines RTP payload formats for 12-bit nonlinear (DAT12), 20-bit (L20) and 24-bit (L24) linear audio, plus SDP/MIME "emphasis" and "channel-order" parameters and media type registrations.

RTP payload format.why: The document's main purpose is defining RTP payload formats for specific audio encodings (DAT12, L20, L24).
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies a packetization scheme for encapsulating 12-bit nonlinear, 20-bit linear, and 24-bit linear audio data streams using the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

SDP.why: Defines new SDP fmtp parameters (emphasis, channel-order) and encoding names with SDP examples; a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: This document also specifies the format of a Session Description Protocol (SDP) parameter to indicate when audio data is preemphasized before sampling.

media types.why: Contains full registration forms for audio/DAT12, audio/L20 and audio/L24 media types with new parameters.
media types.quote: This document defines some new RTP payload format names which are also registered as MIME subtypes: DAT12, L20 and L24.

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the document specifies payload formats, which the more specific RTP payload format tag covers.
The encodings are simple linear/companded PCM sample packings, and the specific codec children do not fit; the RTP payload format tag covers it.
MIME body structure/encodings is not the subject; only media type registration applies.

RFC3191.title: Minimal GSTN address format in Internet Mail
RFC3191.summary: Defines a minimal encoding of GSTN (telephone) E.164 numbers into the local-part of Internet email addresses (pstn-email), with an IANA-registered extension mechanism for service selectors and qualifiers, used by email-to-fax/voice/SMS gateways.

email.why: The document specifies how telephone numbers are encoded in email addresses for gateways to GSTN services. This is email addressing, so email is the best fit.
email.quote: a simple method of encoding Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN) addresses (commonly called "telephone numbers") in the local-part of Internet email addresses

fax.why: The service-selector mechanism supports fax, voice and SMS gateway services. The fax example and the companion minimal FAX address RFC make fax a substantial use case.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport the addresses travel over. The document defines an address syntax, not SMTP behaviour.
The document uses E.164 numbers but does not map them into the DNS. It only embeds them in email local-parts.
SMS appears only as an example service-selector. The document does not define SMS gateway behaviour.
The IANA registration templates are boilerplate-like support for the extension mechanism. The document is not about IANA stewardship.
It refines the addr-spec syntax of RFC 822. It does not specify headers or message format in general.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the syntax definitions.

gaps.name: GSTN / telephone number addressing in email
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for E.164 telephone numbers or GSTN gateway addressing in email. The closest tags are email and fax.

RFC3192.title: Minimal FAX address format in Internet Mail
RFC3192.summary: Defines a minimal encoding of GSTN fax numbers (FAX= service-selector with optional T33S subaddress) in the local-part of Internet email addresses for email-to-fax gateways, and updates the IANA registrations.

fax.why: The whole document specifies how fax devices are addressed via Internet mail (fax-over-email gateways), so the fax subject page is the natural home.
fax.quote: This memo describes a simple method of encoding Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN) addresses of facsimile devices in the local-part of Internet email addresses.

message format.why: A substantial part defines the fax-email address syntax (local-part structure, quoting, optional slashes) within Internet message addressing.
message format.quote: This object is a an e-mail address which conforms to [2] and [3] "addr-spec" syntax, with structure refinements which allows the FAX number to be identified.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport; the document only requires domains conform to SMTP/RFC 822 rules and specifies nothing new about SMTP.
DNS appears only in Security Considerations boilerplate about mail routing.
ABNF is merely the notation used to define the syntax, not the subject.
Parent of the fax and message format tags; the more specific tags are used instead.
IANA registration forms for FAX and T33S are boilerplate-like apparatus, not the main subject.
X.400 gateways are mentioned only in passing about optional slashes.

gaps.name: GSTN address format in email (minimal GSTN address, RFC 3191)
gaps.why: The document is part of a family encoding telephone-network addresses in email addresses; no taxonomy tag covers GSTN/PSTN address encoding in email beyond fax.

RFC3193.title: Securing L2TP using IPsec
RFC3193.summary: Specifies how to protect L2TP tunnels over IP with IPsec (ESP, IKE), including interoperability guidelines, IPsec filter handling for floating ports/addresses, and authentication and PPP interaction considerations.

L2TP.why: The document defines how L2TP is secured, including changes to L2TP behaviour (StopCCN Try Another, port/address floating), teardown and fragmentation guidance.
L2TP.quote: This document discusses how L2TP (Layer Two Tunneling Protocol) may utilize IPsec to provide for tunnel authentication, privacy protection, integrity checking and replay protection.

IPsec.why: The document profiles IPsec (ESP transport mode, IKE, filters, SA handling) for protecting L2TP.
IPsec.quote: all L2TP security compliant implementations MUST implement IPsec ESP for securing both L2TP control and data packets.

IKE.why: Substantial sections cover IKE phase 1 and 2 negotiations, pre-shared keys and certificate authentication in the L2TP context.
IKE.quote: IKE SHOULD be supported for authentication, security association negotiation, and key management using the IPsec DOI [5].

rejected.why: PPP ECP/CCP interactions are discussed, but the document is about securing L2TP, not specifying PPP.
ESP is mandated, but it is covered as part of the IPsec profile, not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only as an alternative for end-to-end security inside the tunnel.
Certificate authentication in IKE is discussed briefly, but it is not a subject of the document.
UDP port 1701 is the transport for L2TP, only a substrate here.

RFC3194.title: The H-Density Ratio for Address Assignment Efficiency An Update on the H ratio
RFC3194.summary: Defines the HD-ratio (log of allocated objects over log of maximum allocatable objects) as a replacement for the H-ratio of RFC 1715, and uses it to gauge address-space allocation efficiency and capacity limits for telephone and IPv4 address plans.

addressing.why: The document is about measuring the efficiency of address allocation and the capacity of addressing plans, including 32-bit IPv4. It is general address architecture and allocation, not tied to one protocol, so the addressing topic fits.
addressing.quote: the host density ratio HD is defined as follow

rejected.why: IPv4 is only one worked example, a table row on 32-bit capacity. The document is about a general allocation-efficiency metric, not IPv4 itself.
IPv6 is mentioned only in passing, as the already-decided 128-bit answer to the address size question. The document does not address it.
Renumbering pain is the motivation for the metric, but the document does not describe renumbering procedures.
DECnet Phase IV is a single data point in the HD-ratio examples, not a subject of the document.

RFC3195.title: Reliable Delivery for syslog
RFC3195.summary: RFC 3195 defines two BEEP profiles (RAW and COOKED) that map the BSD syslog protocol onto TCP-based BEEP channels for reliable, authenticated and optionally encrypted delivery of syslog event messages between devices, relays and collectors.

syslog.why: The whole document specifies how syslog is delivered reliably, including the RAW and COOKED profiles and the entry, iam and path elements.
syslog.quote: This memo describes two mappings of the syslog protocol to TCP connections, both useful for reliable delivery of event messages.

BEEP.why: The document defines and registers two new BEEP profiles with channel setup, message exchanges and a registered port. Readers of BEEP need these profiles.
BEEP.quote: this memo defines two BEEP profiles.  BEEP [3] is a generic application protocol framework for connection-oriented, asynchronous interactions.

rejected.why: TCP is only the underlying transport, reached through BEEP's TCP mapping, and nothing new is defined about it.
The abstract calls these mappings of syslog to TCP, but they are really BEEP profiles. The BEEP tag covers that better.
DIGEST-MD5 SASL is only recommended as a mechanism for authentication. The document doesn't specify SASL.
The TLS profile is only recommended for privacy and nothing about TLS is defined.
XML and a DTD are used to encode messages, which makes them the encoding substrate, not the subject.
DNS SRV is mentioned only as an optional way to discover relays and collectors.

gaps.name: syslog
gaps.why: The taxonomy does have a syslog tag, so this is not a real gap. The tag was used above.

RFC3196.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.1: Implementor's Guide
RFC3196.summary: Informational implementor's guide for IPP/1.1 that supplements the Model and Semantics and Encoding and Transport specs with suggested request-processing steps, status-code usage, clarifications from interoperability testing, and HTTP header usage tables.

IPP.why: The whole document is guidance for implementing IPP/1.1 clients and printers, covering operations, attributes, status codes and encoding.
IPP.quote: IPP is an application level protocol that can be used for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies.

rejected.why: IPP is carried over HTTP/1.1 and the document has tables of HTTP header usage and chunking advice, but HTTP is the transport substrate, not the subject.
Charset and natural-language handling is discussed (UTF-8 required, natural language override), but only as a minor part of IPP processing.
LPD is mentioned only in the description of a related document.
URI case-sensitivity is a short IPP-specific note; the document is not about URIs.
NTP is mentioned only as one option for a printer to get the time.

gaps.name: IPP (Internet Printing Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IPP. The only printing entries are LPD and IPP under applications, and the id 'IPP' I supplied is used under the assumption that it exists; if it does not, this RFC has no fitting tag. The closest parent is applications.

RFC3197.title: Applicability Statement for DNS MIB Extensions
RFC3197.summary: Applicability statement explaining why the DNS Server and Resolver MIB extensions (RFCs 1611/1612) were never deployed and recommending they be moved to Historical status.

MIB.why: The document is entirely about the DNS Server and Resolver MIB modules: their history, failures, and retirement. Readers browsing MIB modules would want this.
MIB.quote: we recommend that RFCs 1611 and 1612 be reclassified as Historical documents.

DNS.why: The subject is management extensions for DNS servers and resolvers, including cache indexing and BIND statistics, so DNS operations readers would want it.
DNS.quote: The DNS Server and Resolver MIB extensions were one of the first attempts to write MIB extensions for a protocol usually considered to be at the application layer.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol underlying the MIBs and is discussed only as the tool that was a poor fit. The MIB tag is the more specific fit.
AgentX is mentioned only as a subagent protocol that arrived too late to help; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Dynamic update is mentioned only as the motivation for a separate protocol, not as the subject of the document.

RFC3198.title: Terminology for Policy-Based Management
RFC3198.summary: A glossary of policy-based network management terms (policy, PDP/PEP, PCIM, COPS, PIB/SPPI, SLA, roles, etc.) modelled on RFC 2828, intended to make IETF documents use policy terminology consistently.

policy management.why: The whole document defines policy-based management vocabulary (policy rule, PDP, PEP, PCIM, PIB, role combination), so policy management is its subject.
policy management.quote: This document is a glossary of policy-related terms. It provides abbreviations, explanations, and recommendations for use of these terms.

terminology.why: It is a glossary of definitions with recommended usage, which belongs on the terminology page.
terminology.quote: The intent is to improve the comprehensibility and consistency of writing that deals with network policy, particularly Internet Standards documents (ISDs).

COPS.why: COPS, COPS-RSVP and COPS-PR are defined and used to explain outsourced versus provisioned policy, but only as glossary entries.
COPS.quote: A simple query and response TCP-based protocol that can be used to exchange policy information between a Policy Decision Point (PDP) and its clients

rejected.why: QoS, Diffserv and Intserv are defined as areas of use of policy. They are single glossary entries and not the subject of the document.
MIB, SMIv2 and SPPI are defined only as policy-conveyance techniques, and the document specifies no modules.
AAA and RADIUS appear as one glossary entry that illustrates implicit policy, so the document is not about them.
CIM, DEN and LDAP are mentioned in definitions, but the document is not about directories.

RFC3199.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 3100-3199
RFC3199.summary: RFC 3199 is a slightly annotated status list of the 100 RFCs numbered 3100 through 3199, giving each RFC's author, date, title, a short abstract and whether it is on the standards track.

RFC series.why: The document is a periodic RFC Series summary and catalogue of published RFCs. A reader browsing the RFC series subject would expect to find it.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 3100 through RFCs 3199.

rejected.why: It notes standards-track status and mentions the IETF process documents it lists (3160, 3184). It does not itself describe IETF procedures.
DNS-related RFCs (3123, 3152, 3197) appear only as one-paragraph entries in the list. The document is not about DNS.
Several RSVP RFCs are listed. They are only entries in the catalogue.
MIB and SNMP-related RFCs are listed only as entries. The document does not address SNMP.
Several RTP payload RFCs (3189, 3190, 3119) are listed. They are not the subject of this summary.
IANA guideline RFCs such as 3171 are listed. The summary itself does not address IANA registries.

RFC3201.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Circuit to Interface Translation
RFC3201.summary: Defines the CIRCUIT-IF-MIB, an SNMP MIB module that lets selected circuits (frame relay, ATM, etc.) be inserted into the ifTable with ifIndex values so routing, RMON and other MIBs can use them.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (CIRCUIT-IF-MIB) defining managed objects in SMIv2 and its interaction with the Interfaces Group MIB.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the insertion of interesting Circuit Interfaces into the ifTable.

frame relay.why: Frame relay circuits and the Frame Relay DTE and Service MIBs are a main use case, with ifTypes and stack examples.
frame relay.quote: If, for example, the ifType for the logical port is frameRelay(32), the circuits can be located in the frCircuitTable

ATM.why: ATM VCCs and the ATM MIB are a main use case, with ifType and ifStackTable examples.
ATM.quote: the value for ATM virtual circuits is atmVciEndPt(194)

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB runs under; the document defines no new protocol behaviour, only a MIB module (the more specific MIB tag applies).
RMON is mentioned as a motivation for needing an ifIndex, but the document is not about RMON.
Not relevant; only mentioned in passing as part of ifTable usage, not at all in fact.

RFC3202.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Frame Relay Service Level Definitions
RFC3202.summary: Defines the FRSLD-MIB, an SNMP MIB module for managing Frame Relay Forum FRF.13 service level definitions (delay, frame and data delivery ratio, availability) on frame relay PVCs.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a new SMIv2 MIB module (FRSLD-MIB) with control, data and sample tables plus conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an extension of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

frame relay.why: The MIB manages service level measurements on frame relay PVCs and DLCIs, so it belongs on the frame relay subject page.
frame relay.quote: This MIB module addresses the items required to manage the Frame Relay Forum's Implementation Agreement for Service Level Definitions (FRF.13 [17]).

performance measurement.why: A large part of the document defines performance metrics (delay, delivery ratios, availability), their reference points and how to calculate them.
performance measurement.quote: Delay - The amount of time elapsed, in microseconds, from the time a frame exits the source to the time it reaches the destination.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through. The document defines objects, not new SNMP protocol behaviour. The SNMP Management Framework section is boilerplate.
RFC 2021 user history is only mentioned as an optional collection mechanism.
Service level measurement is related to QoS, but the document defines frame relay metrics and not a QoS architecture or signalling.

RFC3203.title: DHCP reconfigure extension
RFC3203.summary: Defines a DHCP extension introducing a unicast FORCERENEW message (message type 9) that lets a server force a client into the RENEW state to trigger reconfiguration, including INFORM-based clients.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCP with a new message type, client state transition and server procedures, so it is squarely about DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This is achieved by introducing a unicast FORCERENEW message which forces the client to the RENEW state.

rejected.why: The document covers only DHCP for IPv4 (option 53, DHCPNAK, etc.), not DHCPv6.
Renumbering is mentioned only as one example use (2.3.3), not the document's subject.
Message authentication is delegated to RFC 3118 in Security Considerations; the document does not define it.

RFC3204.title: MIME media types for ISUP and QSIG Objects
RFC3204.summary: Registers the application/ISUP and application/QSIG MIME media types (with version/base parameters and a 'signal' Content-Disposition type with 'handling' parameter) for carrying PSTN signalling bodies in SIP messages.

media types.why: The document's core content is the registration of two new MIME media types, with their parameters, encoding and registration rules for version symbols.
media types.quote: This document registers the "application/ISUP" and "application/QSIG" MIME media types.

SIP-T.why: It defines how ISUP is encapsulated in SIP messages for PSTN interworking, which is the core of SIP-T/SIP-I style ISUP encapsulation.
SIP-T.quote: ISUP-encoded signaling information needs to be transported between SIP entities as part of the payload of SIP messages

rejected.why: SIP is the carrier of the bodies; the document defines no SIP behaviour beyond a 415 handling rule for body types.
MIME is the encoding framework used; the specific registration is covered by media types.
A parent of SIP-T, already implied by that tag.
SDP appears only in example messages as a companion body.
IANA considerations are boilerplate-like registration of the document's own types; not about IANA guidance.

RFC3205.title: On the use of HTTP as a Substrate
RFC3205.summary: BCP giving guidance to protocol designers on when and how to layer new application protocols over HTTP, covering ports, URL schemes, MIME types, methods, status codes, security and proxy interaction.

HTTP.why: The whole document is guidance on using HTTP as a substrate: methods, status codes, proxies, caching and port reuse. HTTP readers would want it.
HTTP.quote: This document recommends technical particulars of such use, including use of default ports, URL schemes, and HTTP security mechanisms.

URI.why: A full section covers when to reuse http: or register a new URL scheme, the 's' suffix convention, and URL translation for client libraries.
URI.quote: Issues Regarding Reuse of the http: Scheme in URLs

rejected.why: TLS is discussed as a security mechanism and its limits for client authentication, but nothing new is specified about it. It is a supporting topic.
Digest authentication is mentioned in the security discussion of section 2.3, but only briefly as one HTTP security option. It is not the subject of the document.
Section 5 advises on choosing MIME types for layered protocols, but this is one sub-issue and not about the media type registry.
Firewall and NAT traversal motivations are discussed in section 2.4, but the document is not about firewall security mechanisms.
Caching interactions with status codes are mentioned in section 8 as a constraint, but caching is not the focus.

RFC3206.title: The SYS and AUTH POP Response Codes
RFC3206.summary: Defines the POP3 SYS and AUTH extended response codes and the AUTH-RESP-CODE capability so clients can distinguish credential failures from system errors after authentication failure.

POP3.why: The document extends POP3 by defining new response codes and a new CAPA capability, so POP3 readers would want it.
POP3.quote: This memo proposes two response codes: SYS and AUTH, which enable clients to unambiguously determine an optimal response to an authentication failure.

rejected.why: The AUTH command is mentioned only as one command where the AUTH response code is valid. The document does not specify SASL mechanisms.
Authentication failure reporting is the topic, but the document is specific to POP3. The POP3 tag covers it more precisely.
The IANA section only registers the new capability and response codes. That is boilerplate.
POP3 is the more specific tag, so its parent is implied.

RFC3207.title: SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security
RFC3207.summary: RFC 3207 defines the STARTTLS extension to SMTP, letting an SMTP client and server upgrade a connection to TLS for privacy and authentication, and obsoletes RFC 2487.

SMTP.why: The document defines a new SMTP service extension, with a new EHLO keyword and a new STARTTLS verb. It also covers submission-port use and server policy for relaying.
SMTP.quote: The STARTTLS extension to SMTP is laid out as follows:

TLS.why: A large part of the document covers how TLS is negotiated inside an SMTP session. This includes the handling of the handshake result, certificate checks, and resetting protocol state afterwards. Readers of TLS deployment guidance for application protocols would want it.
TLS.quote: allows an SMTP server and client to use TLS (Transport Layer Security) to provide private, authenticated communication over the Internet.

rejected.why: This is a parent of SMTP, and SMTP is the more specific tag that fits.
SASL is mentioned only in passing, for example in the note about the EXTERNAL mechanism and about not advertising a mechanism until a client certificate has been sent. The document is not about SASL.
Server and client certificates are checked as part of the TLS negotiation, but certificate profiles are not the subject of the document.
The document specifies an in-band upgrade to TLS as an SMTP extension, which is a new SMTP command, rather than a general binding of one protocol to a transport.

RFC3208.title: PGM Reliable Transport Protocol Specification
RFC3208.summary: RFC 3208 specifies PGM (Pragmatic General Multicast), an experimental NAK-based reliable multicast transport protocol with router-assisted NAK suppression, local repair, FEC, and congestion-control support.

PGM.why: The document is the PGM specification itself, covering packet formats, source, receiver and network-element procedures, and options.
PGM.quote: Pragmatic General Multicast (PGM) is a reliable multicast transport protocol for applications that require ordered or unordered, duplicate-free, multicast data delivery

FEC.why: Appendix A specifies pro-active and on-demand parity packets and parity NAKs for loss recovery, a substantial part of the document.
FEC.quote: incorporate packet-level Reed Solomon Erasure correcting techniques as described in [11] and [12] into PGM

congestion control.why: Appendix B defines the OPT_CR congestion report option and the network-element procedures that give PGM sources congestion feedback.
congestion control.quote: A source MUST implement strategies for congestion avoidance, aimed at providing overall network stability, fairness among competing PGM flows
congestion control.section: 12.1 Appendix B - Support for Congestion Control

rejected.why: PGM requires the IP Router Alert Option on SPMs, NCFs and RDATA. It only uses the option and does not define or extend it.
This is the parent of PGM, so it is implied by the PGM tag and is not listed separately.
The document is a multicast transport protocol, not about multicast routing or group membership. IP multicast is only its substrate.
MD5 is mentioned only as a recommended way to derive the Global Source ID, so it is incidental.
The PGM header checksum is ordinary packet-format detail and not a subject of the document.
NORM is a different reliable multicast protocol and is not discussed here.

RFC3209.title: RSVP-TE: Extensions to RSVP for LSP Tunnels
RFC3209.summary: RFC 3209 specifies RSVP-TE: extensions to RSVP (new objects, procedures and a Hello extension) for establishing explicitly routed, optionally resource-reserved MPLS LSP tunnels, chiefly for traffic engineering.

RSVP-TE.why: The document is the base specification of RSVP-TE signalling for traffic-engineered LSP tunnels, defining LABEL_REQUEST, LABEL, EXPLICIT_ROUTE, RECORD_ROUTE, SESSION_ATTRIBUTE objects and procedures.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document describes the use of RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol), including all the necessary extensions, to establish label-switched paths (LSPs) in MPLS

RSVP.why: It extends RSVP itself with new objects, C-Types, reservation-style use (SE/FF), a Hello message and error codes, which RSVP readers would want.
RSVP.quote: The RSVP Hello extension enables RSVP nodes to detect when a neighboring node is not reachable.

MPLS.why: It is a label distribution mechanism for MPLS, covering label request/allocation, label ranges for ATM and Frame Relay, and path MTU handling for labeled packets.
MPLS.quote: This document is a specification of extensions to RSVP for establishing label switched paths (LSPs) in MPLS networks.

rejected.why: Traffic engineering is the key application, but the RSVP-TE tag sits under it and already covers the document.
ATM and Frame Relay label ranges are only encoding details of the Label Request object.
Local protection flags are mentioned, but fast reroute is not specified here.
Section 2.6 handles path MTU for LSPs briefly, but the document is not about Path MTU Discovery.
The Hello extension detects neighbour node failure, but it is an RSVP mechanism, not BFD.

RFC3210.title: Applicability Statement for Extensions to RSVP for LSP-Tunnels
RFC3210.summary: Applicability statement for RSVP-TE (RFC 3209), describing its operation, intended MPLS traffic engineering context, deployment guidance, and limitations, and noting CR-LDP as an alternative.

RSVP-TE.why: The whole document discusses the applicability, principles of operation, deployment guidance and limitations of RSVP-TE for setting up explicit LSP-tunnels.
RSVP-TE.quote: The "Extensions to RSVP for LSP tunnels" (RSVP-TE) specification [1] was developed by the IETF MPLS working group to address this requirement.

rejected.why: RSVP is the base protocol being extended; the document is about the LSP-tunnel extensions (RSVP-TE), the more specific tag.
MPLS is the network context, but the document is about the RSVP-TE signalling protocol, which has its own tag.
Mentioned only as an alternative signalling protocol; the document is not about it.
Traffic engineering is the application, but RSVP-TE already sits under it, so the topic tag is not added directly.
Only a passing remark that RSVP-TE may be a component of VPN provisioning.

RFC3211.title: Password-based Encryption for CMS
RFC3211.summary: Defines PasswordRecipientInfo, a new CMS RecipientInfo type that wraps a content-encryption key under a key-encryption key derived from a user-supplied password (via PBKDF2), with a double-encryption key wrap algorithm and test vectors.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with a fourth RecipientInfo type (pwri), so CMS readers would expect to find it.
CMS.quote: This document describes a password-based content encryption mechanism for CMS.  This is implemented as a new RecipientInfo type

key management.why: A substantial part specifies key derivation from passwords and a key wrap algorithm for protecting CEKs, which is key provisioning and wrapping.
key management.quote: Password-based key wrapping is a two-stage process, a first stage in which a user-supplied password is converted into a KEK

rejected.why: PBKDF2 is the mandatory key derivation algorithm but is only referenced from RFC 2898, not specified or extended here.
The document uses PBKDF2 for key derivation, but is not about password hashing or memory-hard functions.
ASN.1 is only the notation for the structures and modules, not the subject.
AES is mentioned only as one optional KEK algorithm.
Triple-DES is the mandatory KEK cipher, but the document does not specify DES itself; it is used as the algorithm in the wrap and test vectors.
The work was done in the S/MIME working group, but the document is about the CMS structure, not secure email.

RFC3212.title: Constraint-Based LSP Setup using LDP
RFC3212.summary: Specifies CR-LDP: LDP extensions (TLVs, procedures, status codes) for setting up constraint-based routed LSPs with explicit routes, traffic parameters, preemption, route pinning and resource classes.

CR-LDP.why: The whole document defines CR-LDP: its TLVs, messages, procedures, FEC element and status codes for signalling explicitly routed, traffic-engineered LSPs.
CR-LDP.quote: This document specifies mechanisms and TLVs (Type/Length/Value) for support of CR-LSPs (constraint-based routed Label Switched Path) using LDP (Label Distribution Protocol).

rejected.why: CR-LDP is the more specific child; the base LDP spec is RFC 3036 and is only extended here.
Traffic engineering is the motivation, but the CR-LDP tag is the more specific fit.
MPLS is the environment; implied by the CR-LDP ancestry.
Traffic parameters and service examples touch QoS, but only as resource-reservation attributes within CR-LDP signalling.
An alternative signalling protocol, not discussed or specified here.
LDP sessions run over TCP, which is only a substrate.

RFC3213.title: Applicability Statement for CR-LDP
RFC3213.summary: Applicability statement for CR-LDP, describing where constraint-based LSP setup using LDP applies, which LDP modes it needs, deployment guidance, and limitations.

CR-LDP.why: The whole document discusses the applicability, required LDP extensions, deployment guidance and limitations of CR-LDP.
CR-LDP.quote: CR-LDP provides mechanisms for establishing explicitly routed Label Switched Paths (LSPs). These mechanisms are defined as extensions to LDP

rejected.why: LDP is the base protocol that CR-LDP extends; the document is about the extension, and CR-LDP is the more specific child tag.
Mentioned only as an alternative signalling protocol, with its applicability described in a separate RFC.
CR-LDP is a traffic engineering signalling protocol, but the specific CR-LDP tag covers the document, so the parent topic is not needed.
TCP is only the substrate that carries LDP/CR-LDP messages.
Differentiated services appears only as one example of QoS scenarios CR-LDP parameters can describe.
MPLS is the general context, and the more specific CR-LDP tag, which sits under it, covers the document.

RFC3214.title: LSP Modification Using CR-LDP
RFC3214.summary: Specifies how an ingress LSR modifies bandwidth, traffic class, route and priorities of an established CR-LSP without service interruption, using the LSPID TLV and a "modify" action flag in CR-LDP.

CR-LDP.why: The document defines the procedure for modifying an established CR-LSP using CR-LDP Label Request, Mapping and Release messages and the LSPID TLV. CR-LDP is the protocol it extends.
CR-LDP.quote: modify the bandwidth and possibly other parameters of an established CR-LSP (Constraint-based Routed Label Switched Paths) using CR-LDP

rejected.why: LDP is the base protocol and the parent of CR-LDP. The document specifically extends CR-LDP, so the child tag is the right one.
MPLS is the general setting for the document, but the content is about CR-LDP signalling. Tagging MPLS would only restate the ancestor.
The dynamic bandwidth management example in Section 4 is an application of the mechanism. It is not the main subject.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only in passing, in the context of flooding available link bandwidth.
Service class and priority changes are parameters that the modification procedure carries. The document does not address QoS architecture.

RFC3215.title: LDP State Machine
RFC3215.summary: Informational RFC defining state machine tables (control blocks, states, events, transitions) for processing LDP messages in ATM-switch LSRs, covering downstream-on-demand with and without VC-merge and downstream unsolicited modes, to aid LDP and CR-LDP interoperability.

LDP.why: The whole document specifies state machines for LDP message processing (Request, Mapping, Release, Withdraw, Abort, NAK) at LSRs, complementing the LDP specification.
LDP.quote: This document provides state machine tables for ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) switch LSRs.  In the current LDP specification, there is no state machine specified for processing LDP messages.

ATM.why: The state machines are specific to ATM switch LSRs, including VC-merge and non-VC-merge capability and label retention modes, so ATM readers would find it relevant.
ATM.quote: A VC-merge capable LSR can map multiple incoming labels (VPI/VCI) into one outgoing label.

rejected.why: Mentioned for the pinned option and interoperability, but the document does not specify CR-LDP procedures; no CR-LDP-specific state machine is given.
LDP is the MPLS signalling protocol and is tagged more specifically; the document is not about MPLS architecture generally.
Next-hop change and local repair are handled, but only as LSP re-routing state handling, not as traffic engineering.
Local repair on next-hop change is described, but it concerns LSP switchover state, not loop-free alternates or fast reroute mechanisms.

RFC3216.title: SMIng Objectives
