RFC3216.summary: RFC 3216 sets out the objectives (accepted, nice-to-have, rejected) for SMIng, a new data definition language for network management information that maps to SNMP and COPS-PR and can be translated to SMIv2 MIBs and SPPI PIBs.

MIB.why: The document is about a successor to SMIv2/SPPI, the data definition language for MIB modules. It covers tables, textual conventions, conformance and OBJECT-TYPE-like constructs.
MIB.quote: SMIng language constructs must, wherever possible, be translatable to SMIv2 and SPPI.
MIB.section: 4.1.15 Translation to Other Data Definition Languages

SNMP.why: SNMP protocol mappings are a core objective, including INDEX/AUGMENTS tables, OID assignment and IMPLIED indexing. The document is mainly about the data language, not the protocol, so this is secondary.
SNMP.quote: SMIng must define data definitions in support of the SNMP and COPS-PR protocols.

COPS.why: COPS-PR and its SPPI policy provisioning information structure are co-equal mapping targets throughout the objectives.
COPS.quote: SMIng must support INDEX, AUGMENTS, and EXTENDS in the SNMP/COPS-PR protocol mappings.

rejected.why: YANG is a later language; this document predates it and does not mention it.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as the obsolete basis of SMIv2 that SMIng should be independent of.
ABNF is only mentioned as the grammar notation for the language. The document is not about ABNF.
COPS-PR/SPPI policy provisioning is relevant, but the COPS tag fits more specifically.
Only a nice-to-have mention of UTF-8 for i18n text.
LDAP schemas are mentioned only as an example of an existing data representation.

gaps.name: SMI / SMIng data definition languages for management information
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SMI, SMIv2, SPPI or SMIng as a management data definition language. MIB, a tag for modules and SMI, is the nearest fit.

RFC3217.title: Triple-DES and RC2 Key Wrapping
RFC3217.summary: RFC 3217 specifies algorithms for wrapping a Triple-DES key with another Triple-DES key and an RC2 key with another RC2 key (CBC-based, SHA-1 checksum), republished from RFC 2630 with ASN.1 algorithm identifiers and examples.

key management.why: The document's whole purpose is key wrap algorithms for protecting symmetric keys, which is key provisioning and storage. No technology tag under key management fits it more specifically.
key management.quote: Management of symmetric cryptographic keys often leads to situations where one symmetric key is used to encrypt (or wrap) another.

DES.why: Triple-DES key wrapping is half of the specification, with its own algorithm, identifier and test vector, so readers of the DES/3DES subject would want it.
DES.quote: This document specifies the algorithm for wrapping one Triple-DES key with another Triple-DES key [3DES]

rejected.why: The key wrap algorithms originate in RFC 2630 (CMS), but this document specifies them standalone and explicitly for use beyond CMS.
SHA-1 is only used as the checksum primitive within the wrap algorithm. The document is not about SHA.
ASN.1 object identifiers and the RC2wrapParameter are given only to name the algorithms. This is incidental encoding.
The document came from the S/MIME working group, but the body does not address secure email.
The parent is implied by the more specific tags chosen (DES under cryptography, key management under cryptography).

gaps.name: RC2 block cipher
gaps.why: Half of the document specifies RC2 key wrapping, but the taxonomy has no RC2 tag. Only the generic cryptography and key management tags cover it.

RFC3218.title: Preventing the Million Message Attack on Cryptographic Message Syntax
RFC3218.summary: Informational memo describing the Million Message Attack (Bleichenbacher's adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack on PKCS-1 v1.5 RSA padding) as it applies to CMS, and countermeasures: careful checking, random CEK substitution, and OAEP.

RSA.why: The document is about attacking and defending PKCS-1 v1.5 RSA encryption padding, including OAEP as an alternative. RSA readers would want it.
RSA.quote: When data is encrypted using RSA it must be padded out to the length of the modulus

CMS.why: The attack is analysed in the context of CMS key wrapping, and the countermeasures are specified for CMS implementations, such as random CEK substitution.
CMS.quote: The MMA is also possible against [CMS].

rejected.why: S/MIME is mentioned only in passing in the OAEP upgrade-path discussion. The focus is CMS and RSA.
Mail list agents are named only as likely attack targets. The document does not address mailing list protocols.
AES keys are mentioned only in passing, as the context for OAEP being specified for CMS.
The original Bleichenbacher attack was on SSL, but this document only cites it as background.
Random CEK generation is used as a countermeasure, but the document is not about randomness requirements.

RFC3219.title: Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP)
RFC3219.summary: RFC 3219 specifies TRIP, a BGP-4-modelled inter-domain protocol for advertising reachability and attributes of telephony destinations between location servers, independent of signalling protocol (SIP, H.323).

TRIP.why: The document defines TRIP in full: messages, attributes, FSM, flooding and decision process.
TRIP.quote: TRIP is a policy driven inter-administrative domain protocol for advertising the reachability of telephony destinations between location servers

rejected.why: TRIP is modelled after BGP-4 and reuses its transport, FSM and formats, but the document specifies TRIP, not BGP.
SIP is one application protocol whose routes TRIP can carry; TRIP is signalling-independent and does not extend SIP.
H.323 is only one of the application protocols for which routes are advertised.
TCP is merely the transport substrate (port 6069), with nothing new defined about it.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the protection mechanism for peer sessions.
OSPF flooding techniques are borrowed as a model, but the document is not about OSPF.

RFC3220.title: IP Mobility Support for IPv4
RFC3220.summary: RFC 3220 specifies Mobile IPv4: agent discovery, registration with home agents via foreign agents or co-located care-of addresses, tunneling, and ARP handling, so mobile nodes keep their home IP address while changing attachment points.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document is the Mobile IPv4 base specification (home agent, foreign agent, care-of address, registration, tunneling), obsoleting RFC 2002.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document specifies protocol enhancements that allow transparent routing of IP datagrams to mobile nodes in the Internet.

rejected.why: Section 4.6 specifies proxy and gratuitous ARP use for the home agent, but only as a supporting mechanism. The document does not define or extend ARP.
Agent Advertisement extends ICMP Router Discovery, but that is the carrier for agent discovery, not a subject in its own right.
Tunneling uses IP-in-IP, minimal and GRE encapsulation defined in other RFCs. This document only requires and references them.
HMAC-MD5 is the default authentication algorithm, but it is used as a mechanism and not specified here.
Registration messages ride on UDP port 434, which is only a substrate.
This is the parent topic of Mobile IPv4. The specific technology tag fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC3221.title: Commentary on Inter-Domain Routing in the Internet
RFC3221.summary: IAB commentary analysing long-term trends in the global BGP table (size, AS consumption, prefix granularity, multihoming, traffic engineering) and their scaling impact on inter-domain routing, with requirements and architectural options for a more scalable exterior routing system.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses BGP table growth, convergence, stability, and whether to extend or replace BGP for scalable inter-domain routing.
BGP.quote: examines the various longer term trends visible within the characteristics of the Internet's BGP table and identifies a number of operational practices and protocol factors

routing architecture.why: Substantial parts cover routing scalability requirements, hierarchy, policy opacity, distance-vector vs link-state, and architectural approaches.
routing architecture.quote: look at the attributes of routing systems as understood and identify those aspects of such systems that may be applicable to the inter-domain environment
routing architecture.section: 6. Future Requirements for the Exterior Routing System

CIDR.why: The history of CIDR deployment, its aggregation intent, and its weakening under multihoming and more-specific announcements is a central thread.
CIDR.quote: This approached was termed Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)

rejected.why: Inter-domain traffic engineering via BGP is discussed as a driver of table growth, but it is one section within a routing scaling study, not the document's subject.
Multihoming is identified as a growth driver, but the document is not about multihoming architectures.
NAT is mentioned only as a possible explanation for slow address-space growth.
IPv6 is mentioned only as background on address-space work.

RFC3222.title: Terminology for Forwarding Information Base (FIB) based Router Performance
RFC3222.summary: Defines terminology (FIB, FIB size, prefix distribution, learning time, FIB-dependent throughput/latency/frame loss) for a methodology benchmarking IP router forwarding performance as a function of the installed forwarding information base.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking terminology document defining parameters and metrics (throughput, latency, frame loss rate, learning time) for router performance testing.
benchmarking.quote: describes the terms to be used in a methodology that determines the IP packet forwarding performance of IP routers as a function of the forwarding information base

rejected.why: FIB structure is discussed only as a benchmarking parameter, not routing architecture or scalability design.
CIDR network prefix notation is quoted for definitions but the document is not about CIDR or aggregation as a subject.
Routers and routing tables are the device under test; the document is about measuring performance, not routing itself.
Parent of benchmarking in a different branch; benchmarking is the more specific fit for device-level testing terminology.
Though a terminology document, the subject is benchmarking terminology; the more specific benchmarking tag covers it.

RFC3224.title: Vendor Extensions for Service Location Protocol, Version 2
RFC3224.summary: RFC 3224 updates SLPv2 (RFC 2608) by specifying collision-free vendor extensibility via IANA Enterprise Numbers as naming authorities and attribute prefixes, and defines the new Vendor Opaque Extension.

SLP.why: The document extends and updates SLPv2, defining the Vendor Opaque Extension and conventions for naming authorities and attributes.
SLP.quote: This document specifies how the features of the Service Location Protocol, Version 2 allow for vendor extensibility safely, with no possibility of collisions.

rejected.why: Enterprise Numbers come from the SMI private enterprise registry, but the document does not specify MIB modules.
IANA registration is the mechanism used (enterprise numbers, extension IDs), but the document is about SLP extensibility, not IANA registry policy generally.
Parent of SLP, which is implied by the SLP tag.
MD5 appears only in a fictitious example authenticator and is not the subject.

RFC3225.title: Indicating Resolver Support of DNSSEC
RFC3225.summary: Defines the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit in the EDNS0 OPT header so resolvers can signal they accept DNSSEC security RRs, and specifies how servers must respond.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies server and resolver behaviour for including DNSSEC SIG, KEY and NXT records, so it is about DNSSEC operation.
DNSSEC.quote: DNSSEC aware servers should only perform automatic inclusion of DNSSEC RRs when there is an explicit indication that the resolver can understand those RRs.

EDNS.why: It defines a new flag bit in the EDNS0 OPT record, which extends EDNS0 itself.
EDNS.quote: the most significant bit of the Z field on the EDNS0 OPT header in the query. This bit is referred to as the "DNSSEC OK" (DO) bit.

rejected.why: DNS is implied by the more specific DNSSEC and EDNS tags, so it is not listed separately.
The IANA section only requests allocation of the DO bit, which is boilerplate rather than the document's subject.

RFC3226.title: DNSSEC and IPv6 A6 aware server/resolver message size requirements
RFC3226.summary: Updates RFC 2535 (DNSSEC) and RFC 2874 (A6) to require that implementations support EDNS0 and advertise minimum UDP message sizes, so larger DNS responses avoid truncation and TCP fallback.

EDNS.why: The document's core change is mandating EDNS0 support and minimum advertised UDP payload sizes for DNSSEC and A6 aware entities.
EDNS.quote: All RFC 2535 compliant servers and resolvers MUST support EDNS0 and advertise message size of at least 1220 octets, but SHOULD advertise message size of 4000.

DNSSEC.why: It updates RFC 2535 with new requirements for DNSSEC-aware servers and resolvers, motivated by the larger messages that signatures produce.
DNSSEC.quote: DNSSEC [RFC2535] secures DNS by adding a Public Key signature on each RR set.

rejected.why: EDNS and DNSSEC are the more specific tags, and the parent DNS is implied by them.
TCP fallback is the problem the document tries to avoid. It does not specify or extend TCP.
A6 records are only a motivation for larger messages. The document does not address IPv6 itself, and the taxonomy has no A6 tag.
UDP message size is the subject matter, but the document specifies DNS-level EDNS0 behaviour, not UDP usage.

gaps.name: A6 records (DNS extensions for IPv6 address aggregation)
gaps.why: The document sets requirements for A6-aware DNS entities, but the taxonomy has no tag for A6/IPv6 DNS records. A6 is only a secondary concern, so no tag is substituted.

RFC3227.title: Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving
RFC3227.summary: RFC 3227 (BCP 55) gives system administrators guidelines for collecting, handling and archiving digital evidence after a security incident, covering order of volatility, chain of custody, legal and privacy considerations, and tooling.

incident response.why: The whole document is incident-handling practice: how to collect, preserve and archive evidence during and after a security incident. A reader browsing incident response would expect it.
incident response.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide System Administrators with guidelines on the collection and archiving of evidence relevant to such a security incident.

rejected.why: The document is operational guidance for sysadmins, but it concerns post-incident evidence handling rather than securing infrastructure; incident response fits better.
Parent of incident response, so it is implied. The document is not about general security threat models.
No incident data format or exchange is specified; the document only covers evidence collection and archiving.
Section 2.3 has privacy considerations, but this is a small part and is not about protocol privacy threat models.

gaps.name: digital forensics / evidence collection
gaps.why: The document is about forensic evidence collection, chain of custody and legal admissibility. The taxonomy has no forensics tag, so incident response is the closest fit.

RFC3228.title: IANA Considerations for IPv4 Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP)
RFC3228.summary: BCP asking IANA to create a registry for IPv4 IGMP header Type and Code fields, setting allocation policies (IESG Approval or Standards Action) and reserving Code values 240-255 for experimentation.

IGMP.why: The whole document defines the IANA registry and allocation policy for IGMP Type and Code fields, so IGMP readers would want it.
IGMP.quote: This memo requests that the IANA create a registry for fields in the IGMP protocol header.

IANA.why: It is an IANA considerations document that sets registry allocation policy and reserves an experimental range, so it fits the IANA registries subject.
IANA.quote: Values for the IPv4 IGMP Type fields are allocated using an IESG Approval or Standards Action processes.
IANA.section: 2. IANA Considerations for fields in the IPv4 IGMP header

rejected.why: IGMP is the more specific tag and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
The document only refers to the IPv4 IGMP header and does not address IPv4 itself.

RFC3229.title: Delta encoding in HTTP
RFC3229.summary: Defines delta encoding as a backward-compatible extension to HTTP/1.1, adding the A-IM, IM and Delta-Base headers, the 226 IM Used status code, and new Cache-Control directives so servers can send differences between cached instances instead of full responses.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with new headers (A-IM, IM, Delta-Base), a new status code (226) and instance-manipulation semantics. It is an HTTP protocol extension.
HTTP.quote: This document describes how delta encoding can be supported as a compatible extension to HTTP/1.1.

HTTP caching.why: Delta encoding is built on cache validators. The document defines caching rules for 226 responses, the new retain and im Cache-Control directives, and proxy cache behaviour.
HTTP caching.quote: One can think of deltas as a way to squeeze as much benefit as possible from client and proxy caches.

rejected.why: Compression (gzip, deflate) is discussed as an instance manipulation and content-coding that interacts with deltas. The document is about delta encoding, not compression formats.
multipart/byteranges and content-coding interactions are mentioned, but the document registers no media types.
It creates an instance-manipulation registry and a status code, but this is boilerplate-level IANA content and not the document's subject.
Digest Authentication and Content-MD5 are mentioned only in passing in the section on integrity digests.

gaps.name: delta encoding / instance manipulation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for delta encoding or differencing formats (vcdiff, diffe, gdiff). HTTP is the closest fit.

RFC3230.title: Instance Digests in HTTP
RFC3230.summary: Defines HTTP extensions (Want-Digest and Digest headers) for carrying and requesting digests of whole resource instances, with multiple algorithms and negotiation of Content-MD5.

HTTP.why: The document specifies new HTTP header fields (Want-Digest, Digest) and a negotiation mechanism for Content-MD5, so it is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: This document proposes HTTP extensions that solve these problems.

rejected.why: MD5 is one of several registered digest algorithm tokens and the Content-MD5 negotiation touches it, but the document is not about the MD5 algorithm itself.
SHA-1 is only one of the initial digest-algorithm tokens; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The document discusses checksums and digests for integrity, but it defines HTTP headers rather than the Internet checksum itself.
Digest Access Authentication is mentioned only for contrast; this document explicitly excludes authentication from its goals.
Caches and delta/range reassembly motivate the instance digest, but caching behaviour is not specified here.
MIME is only the origin of Content-MD5 and of the terminology analogy; no media types are registered.

RFC3231.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Scheduling Management Operations
RFC3231.summary: Defines the DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB module, a set of SNMP managed objects for scheduling management operations (SNMP set actions) periodically, by calendar, or one-shot; obsoletes RFC 2591.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB) with its tables, notifications and conformance statements, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: it describes a set of managed objects that are used to schedule management operations periodically or at specified dates and times.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the MIB is defined for and the mechanism for set operations. The document specifies a MIB module and not the SNMP protocol. MIB is the more specific child tag.
The MIB handles local time, time zones and time transitions for scheduling. It does not address clock synchronization over networks.
Time transitions such as DST are treated only as a scheduling-behaviour concern. The document does not distribute time zone data.
The calendar schedules here trigger management actions. They are not about calendaring and scheduling of people or events.

RFC3232.title: Assigned Numbers: RFC 1700 is Replaced by an On-line Database
RFC3232.summary: RFC 3232 obsoletes RFC 1700 (STD 2, Assigned Numbers), noting that the assigned-numbers RFC series has been replaced by an online IANA database and moving RFC 1700 to Historic.

IANA.why: The document is about the IANA protocol parameter assignments moving from the Assigned Numbers RFC series to an online registry database. Readers of the IANA subject would want it.
IANA.quote: Since 1994, this sequence of RFCs have been replaced by an online database accessible through a web page (currently, www.iana.org).

rejected.why: The document does obsolete an RFC (STD 2) and changes its status to Historic. Its subject is the IANA registry of parameter assignments, not the format, style or publication of the RFC series.
It mentions the 1977-1994 publication history of Assigned Numbers, but only as background for the obsoletion notice, not as a retrospective.

RFC3233.title: Defining the IETF
RFC3233.summary: BCP 58 gives a concrete definition of "the IETF" as an open, unincorporated community acting under BCP 9, 10 and 11, partially supported by ISOC but not a formal part of it.

IETF process.why: The document defines the IETF as an organization by reference to its standards process, leadership selection and structure. That makes it about IETF process and organization.
IETF process.quote: when RFCs say "the IETF", they are describing the group that acts in accordance with BCP 9, BCP 10, and BCP 11.

rejected.why: BCP 10 on leadership selection is only cited as a reference. The document does not address NomCom procedures.
The document defines a term, but its subject is the organization rather than a glossary or requirements language. IETF process fits better.
The document only notes that many RFCs refer to "the IETF". It says nothing about RFC format, style or publication.

RFC3234.title: Middleboxes: Taxonomy and Issues
RFC3234.summary: Informational RFC that defines "middleboxes" (intermediaries doing more than standard IP routing), catalogues 22 types by facets, surveys IETF work, and draws architectural conclusions about the end-to-end principle and failure handling.

internet architecture.why: The core subject is how middleboxes challenge the hourglass model and end-to-end principle, with architectural conclusions and guidelines.
internet architecture.quote: describe and analyse the current impact of middleboxes on the architecture of the Internet and its applications

NAT.why: NAT is the first catalogued middlebox, and NAT analysis is repeatedly applied to other middlebox types (RSIP, NAT-PT, etc.).
NAT.quote: A function, often built into a router, that dynamically assigns a globally unique address to a host that doesn't have one

firewall.why: IP and application firewalls and SOCKS gateways are catalogued as middlebox types, with discussion of their effects.
firewall.quote: Application-level firewalls act as a protocol end point and relay (e.g., an SMTP client/server or a Web proxy agent).

rejected.why: Caches and proxies are catalogued, but only as one of 22 middlebox types; the document is not about HTTP caching.
SOCKS is a single catalogue entry, not specified or analysed in depth.
SIIT is mentioned only as the basis for NAT-PT in one entry.
OPES is listed only as ongoing work in Section 3, not a subject of the document.
IP tunnel endpoints get a short catalogue entry only.
NAT-PT and transport relays touch IPv6 transition, but only briefly.

gaps.name: Middleboxes / intermediaries
gaps.why: The document's central subject (taxonomy of middleboxes, MIDCOM) has no dedicated tag; internet architecture is the closest fit.

RFC3235.title: Network Address Translator (NAT)-Friendly Application Design Guidelines
RFC3235.summary: Informational guidelines for application protocol designers on making new protocols work through NATs (Basic NAT, NAPT, bi-directional, twice, multi-homed, RSIP) without needing ALGs.

NAT.why: The whole document is about NAT behaviour and its effects on applications, with recommendations per NAT type (Basic NAT, NAPT, Twice NAT, etc.).
NAT.quote: Guidelines are presented herein to help ensure new protocols and applications will, to the extent possible, be compatible with NAT (Network Address Translation).

rejected.why: Mentioned only as something that fails across NAT; not specified or analysed in its own right.
Used as an example of session bundles and PASV; the document is not about FTP.
Only recommended as a NAT-traversing alternative to IPsec in passing.
Mentioned briefly as sharing design issues with NAT, not a subject of the document.
Used as an example of single-connection design and of IP literals in URLs; not the subject.
DNS names versus IP addresses in payloads and the DNS-ALG are mentioned briefly; DNS is not the subject.

RFC3236.title: The 'application/xhtml+xml' Media Type
RFC3236.summary: Registers the 'application/xhtml+xml' MIME media type for XHTML-based markup languages, including its optional charset and profile parameters, fragment identifier handling and file recognition guidance.

media types.why: The document exists solely to register a media type, with the template fields, parameters, and file-recognition guidance that a media type registration contains.
media types.quote: This document defines the 'application/xhtml+xml' MIME media type for XHTML based markup languages

HTML.why: XHTML is the reformulation of HTML in XML, and the document describes how XHTML content is identified and how it relates to text/html. Readers of the HTML subject would want it.
HTML.quote: In 1998, the W3C HTML working group began work on reformulating HTML in terms of XML 1.0 [XML] and XML Namespaces [XMLNS].

content negotiation.why: Section 8 defines the profile parameter specifically for content negotiation among XHTML-based languages, and compares it with Content-features and UAPROF.
content negotiation.quote: using MIME media type based content negotiation (such as that done with the HTTP "Accept" header) to negotiate for a variety of XHTML based languages.

rejected.why: XML is the base syntax of XHTML and is relied on throughout, but the document defines nothing new about XML itself. It only registers a media type.
The fragment identifier section only points to the XML media type rules and the ID attribute. It does not specify anything about URIs.
The HTTP Accept header appears only in an example of the profile parameter. HTTP is not specified or extended.
The document uses the MIME media type framework but is better captured by the more specific media types tag.

RFC3237.title: Requirements for Reliable Server Pooling
RFC3237.summary: Informational RFC defining the basic requirements (robustness, failover, naming, server selection policies, timing, security) for the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) architecture and protocols.

RSerPool.why: The entire document specifies requirements for RSerPool: pool elements, name servers, failover, server selection policies and security.
RSerPool.quote: The goal of Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) is to develop an architecture and protocols for the management and operation of server pools supporting highly reliable applications

rejected.why: SCTP is only named as a transport whose congestion control must be interoperable; the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned only for flow-control interoperability, not the subject.
Appears only in the references list; no body content about it.
Pool handles and name resolution are part of RSerPool requirements, covered by the RSerPool tag rather than general naming.
One paragraph requires compliance with congestion control principles, but it is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC3238.title: IAB Architectural and Policy Considerations for Open Pluggable Edge Services
RFC3238.summary: IAB memo giving architectural and policy considerations (consent, end-to-end integrity, notification, URI resolution, privacy) that any Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) work chartered in the IETF should address.

OPES.why: The whole document is the IAB's recommendations on OPES architecture and chartering, covering consent, integrity, addressing and privacy requirements for OPES intermediaries.
OPES.quote: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) are services that would be deployed in the network, for example, at a web proxy cache between the origin server and the client

rejected.why: Privacy is one section (5) and a recurring concern, but it is addressed only as an OPES requirement. The OPES tag is the better fit.
Section 4 discusses URI resolution and OPES, but only as an architectural consideration. The document does not specify or extend URIs.
Web proxy caches are used as the example deployment point, but the document is not about caching protocols.
It invokes end-to-end integrity and robustness principles, but the scope is OPES-specific. The OPES tag covers it.
Content integrity is discussed, but no web platform security mechanism is specified or analysed.

RFC3239.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): Requirements for Job, Printer, and Device Administrative Operations
RFC3239.summary: Informational RFC setting out requirements and use cases for optional IPP administrative operations on Job, Printer and a new Device object (e.g. Disable-Printer, Pause-Device-Now, Shutdown-Printer).

IPP.why: The whole document defines requirements for new IPP operations on Printer, Job and Device objects, so it is squarely about IPP.
IPP.quote: This document specifies the requirements and uses cases for some optional administrative operations for use with the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) version 1.0 and version 1.1.

rejected.why: IPP is mapped onto HTTP only in the background description of the base documents. This RFC says nothing new about HTTP.
The operations are administrative, but they are IPP protocol operations and not a general network management architecture. The Printer MIB is mentioned only in passing.
TLS appears only as an example of authentication in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The LPD-to-IPP mapping appears only in the Appendix A description of the base IPP documents.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol job/printer/device administrative operations
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists IPP as a technology under applications, but I used the id 'IPP', which does not appear in the taxonomy. The closest valid tag is the 'applications' topic. The tag above should be replaced by 'applications' or by a new IPP tag.

RFC3240.title: Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) - Application/dicom MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC3240.summary: Registers the application/dicom MIME media type for exchanging DICOM medical imaging objects and DICOMDIR index files by email, defining the required "id" parameter and encoding rules.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration template for application/dicom, including parameters, encoding considerations, and file-type information, so it belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type application/dicom (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine).

rejected.why: The document registers a specific type and uses MIME multipart structures, but its subject is the media type registration. The more specific 'media types' tag covers it.
Email is only the exchange channel for DICOM objects. The document does not specify email transport or access.
S/MIME is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a possible protection mechanism. The document does not address it.
Base64 is only suggested as the typical Content-Transfer-Encoding. The document defines nothing about it.

gaps.name: DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine)
gaps.why: The document is about the medical imaging format and its use over email. The taxonomy has no tag for medical or healthcare data formats.

RFC3241.title: Robust Header Compression (ROHC) over PPP
RFC3241.summary: Defines a PPP IPCP/IPV6CP configuration option, a PROFILES suboption, and two PPP protocol field values for negotiating and carrying ROHC-compressed IP packets over PPP, updating RFC 1332 to allow multiple IP-Compression-Protocol option instances.

ROHC.why: The document specifies how ROHC is negotiated and carried over PPP, including channel parameters, CID sizes, and profile selection.
ROHC.quote: This document describes an option for negotiating the use of robust header compression (ROHC) on IP datagrams transmitted over the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP).

PPP.why: It defines a new IPCP/IPV6CP configuration option and two PPP protocol field values, and updates RFC 1332.
PPP.quote: It defines extensions to the PPP Control Protocols for IPv4 and IPv6.

rejected.why: RFC 2507/2509 IP header compression is only referenced as background and for a possible combination with ROHC; this document does not specify it.
IPV6CP is only one of two NCPs where the option is negotiated; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
ROHC compresses RTP headers, but RTP is the payload of the compression profiles, not the subject here.
Implied by the more specific ROHC tag.

RFC3242.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): A Link-Layer Assisted Profile for IP/UDP/RTP
RFC3242.summary: Defines ROHC profile 0x0005, a link-layer assisted IP/UDP/RTP header compression profile extending ROHC RTP with a no-header packet, CSP and CCP packet types, and an interface to an assisting lower layer.

ROHC.why: The whole document specifies a ROHC profile: new packet types, IR redefinition, feedback option, and assisting-layer interface.
ROHC.quote: This document defines a ROHC (Robust Header Compression) profile for compression of IP/UDP/RTP (Internet Protocol/User Datagram Protocol/Real-Time Transport Protocol) packets

rejected.why: RTP headers are what gets compressed, but the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
CRTP is only cited as the earlier scheme that performed poorly over lossy cellular links; this document is not about it.
Cellular links (GERAN, CDMA2000, WCDMA) motivate the profile, but link-specific details are deferred to other documents.
UDP is only a protocol whose headers are compressed; the document does not address UDP usage.
The CRC is the ROHC header CRC being replaced or verified, not a study of CRC polynomials.

RFC3243.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Requirements and Assumptions for 0-byte IP/UDP/RTP Compression
RFC3243.summary: Informational RFC giving requirements and link-layer assumptions for a 0-byte IP/UDP/RTP header compression scheme to be developed by the ROHC working group, as deltas to the regular ROHC RTP requirements.

ROHC.why: The whole document defines requirements for a ROHC profile variant (0-byte compression) and how it fits the ROHC framework, so readers of ROHC would want it.
ROHC.quote: requirements for the 0-byte IP/UDP/RTP (Internet Protocol/User Datagram Protocol/Real-Time Transport Protocol) header compression scheme to be developed by the Robust Header Compression (ROHC) Working Group

rejected.why: RTP headers are what gets compressed, but the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
Cellular links (GSM, WCDMA, cdma2000) motivate the requirements, but the document is not about IP over cellular networks.
IPsec is mentioned only as a case where 0-byte compression cannot work and the scheme must fall back. It is not a subject of the document.
This is the parent of ROHC, so it is implied by the ROHC tag and not listed separately.
UDP is only one of the headers compressed, and the document says nothing about UDP itself.

RFC3244.title: Microsoft Windows 2000 Kerberos Change Password and Set Password Protocols
RFC3244.summary: Informational RFC specifying Microsoft's Windows 2000 Kerberos change-password and set-password protocol, a request/reply exchange on port 464 that extends the original Kerberos change-password protocol to let an administrator set another principal's password.

Kerberos.why: The document specifies a Kerberos-based password change/set protocol using AP-REQ, AP-REP and KRB-PRIV messages for the kadmin/changepw service. Readers of Kerberos material would want it.
Kerberos.quote: This memo specifies Microsoft's Windows 2000 Kerberos change password and set password protocols.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used only to encode the ChangePasswdData structure. It is an encoding substrate, not the subject.
The protocol runs over UDP and TCP port 464. Those are only transports and the document defines nothing new about them.
TCP is used only as an alternative transport with a length header. The document is not about TCP.
Password setting involves authorization checks, but the document is a Kerberos password protocol, not an AAA framework.

RFC3245.title: The History and Context of Telephone Number Mapping (ENUM) Operational Decisions: Informational Documents Contributed to ITU-T Study Group 2 (SG2)
RFC3245.summary: IAB informational memo reproducing three ITU-T SG2 contributions explaining why ENUM uses a single DNS domain, why .ARPA (e164.arpa) was chosen, and why RIPE NCC was selected to operate it.

ENUM.why: The whole document explains operational decisions about ENUM: single domain, e164.arpa placement, and operator selection.
ENUM.quote: ENUM is just that, a way to store E.164 numbers in the DNS.
ENUM.section: 2.3. Storing E.164 numbers in the DNS

DNS.why: Substantial discussion of DNS single root, delegation, infrastructure domain arpa and name server operator requirements.
DNS.quote: Which DNS server is authoritative for a specific domain is defined by delegations from the parent domain
DNS.section: 2.2. The need for a single root in the DNS

rejected.why: IANA operates the arpa domain but the document is not about IANA registries; IANA considerations section is boilerplate.
RIPE NCC registration at country-code level is mentioned, but only briefly, and no registry protocol or operations are specified.
Touches on IAB/ICANN/ITU roles, but the focus is ENUM decision rationale; ENUM and DNS tags capture it better.
arpa is an infrastructure domain, not a special-use/reserved name in the sense of that tag.

RFC3246.title: An Expedited Forwarding PHB (Per-Hop Behavior)
RFC3246.summary: Defines the Expedited Forwarding (EF) per-hop behavior for Differentiated Services, giving a formal mathematical definition of the rate-based service, error terms, and conformance requirements, and obsoleting RFC 2598.

Diffserv.why: The RFC specifies the EF PHB, a core Diffserv per-hop behavior, including its codepoint 101110, mutability, tunneling and interaction with other PHBs.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines a PHB (per-hop behavior) called Expedited Forwarding (EF). The PHB is a basic building block in the Differentiated Services architecture.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS subject, so the parent is not listed.
The DS field in the IP header is only the carrier for the codepoint, and the document is not about IP itself.
The single codepoint allocation is boilerplate in the IANA Considerations section, not the subject of the document.
The document defines single-node forwarding behavior, not traffic engineering of networks.

RFC3247.title: Supplemental Information for the New Definition of the EF PHB (Expedited Forwarding Per-Hop Behavior)
RFC3247.summary: Informational supplement to the revised EF PHB definition (RFC 3246), explaining the packet scale rate guarantee equations, per-packet delay and loss bounds, scheduler-specific latency terms, and the flaws in the RFC 2598 definition.

Diffserv.why: The whole document explains and supplements the Expedited Forwarding PHB, a core Differentiated Services per-hop behavior, including its formal definition, delay bounds and implementation parameters.
Diffserv.quote: A node that supports EF on an interface I at some configured rate R MUST satisfy the following equations:

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific tag and already sits under QoS, so the parent is implied.
The document derives delay bounds and latency terms analytically. It does not address measurement methods or metrics.
The document discusses loss and burstiness at EF nodes, but it is about scheduling guarantees, not congestion control.

RFC3248.title: A Delay Bound alternative revision of RFC 2598
RFC3248.summary: Informational RFC archiving the EF Design Team's Delay Bound (DB) PHB, an alternative re-expression of the Diffserv Expedited Forwarding PHB defined by a bound on delay variation for rate-limited traffic, with an experimental DSCP.

Diffserv.why: The document defines a new Differentiated Services per-hop behavior (an alternative to the EF PHB), including DSCP marking, mutability, tunneling and interaction with other PHBs.
Diffserv.quote: the goal of the DB PHB is a strict bound on the delay variation of packets through a hop.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS subject.
Mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations as a way to report policer drops.
Mentioned only as one way to avoid fragmentation of DB packets, not a subject of the document.
The IANA section only suggests one experimental codepoint; this is boilerplate and not what the document is about.

RFC3249.title: Implementers Guide for Facsimile Using Internet Mail
RFC3249.summary: Informational implementers' guide clarifying interoperability issues in Internet fax over email (simple and extended modes, MDN/DSN handling, TIFF file format, fax addressing).

fax.why: The whole document is guidance for implementing Internet fax (simple mode RFC 2305, extended mode RFC 2532, and TIFF file format).
fax.quote: This document clarifies published RFCs which standardize facsimile communications using Internet Email.

SMTP.why: Substantial sections cover SMTP sessions, DSN parameters (ENVID, ORCPT, NOTIFY), enhanced status codes and ESMTP encoding of fax addresses.
SMTP.quote: SMTP server-based implementations are strongly encouraged to implement the "SMTP Service Extension for Returning Enhanced Error Codes"
SMTP.section: 4.4.3 Extended Mode Receivers that are MTAs (or ESMTP servers)

rejected.why: multipart/alternative and content types are discussed, but only as supporting detail for fax behaviour.
image/tiff vs image/tiff-fx usage is discussed briefly; registration itself is in another RFC.
POP3/IMAP4 receivers appear only as the access path in MDN examples.
IMAP4 appears only as the access path in MDN examples, not as a subject of the document.
MDN/DSN header examples are illustrations; the document is not about message format itself.

gaps.name: TIFF / TIFF-FX file format
gaps.why: Section 5 gives detailed guidance on TIFF profiles, IFD placement and color gamut, but the taxonomy has no image file format tag.

gaps.name: Delivery and message disposition notifications (DSN/MDN)
gaps.why: A major part of the document is about DSN and MDN usage, with no specific taxonomy tag.

RFC3250.title: Tag Image File Format Fax eXtended (TIFF-FX) - image/tiff-fx MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC3250.summary: Registers the image/tiff-fx MIME media type for TIFF-FX (File Format for Internet Fax, RFC 2301) encoded image data, giving its parameters, magic numbers and file extension.

media types.why: The document exists to register a MIME media type with IANA, including encoding, interoperability and magic-number details.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type image/tiff-fx.

fax.why: The registered type is the TIFF-FX fax image file format for Internet fax, a product of the Internet Fax working group, so readers of the fax subject would want it.
fax.quote: enabling standardized messaging-based fax over the Internet

rejected.why: The document uses MIME only as the framework for registration. The more specific media types tag fits better.
Fax images may be carried in mail, but the document does not specify email transport or formats.
The IANA registration template is boilerplate for the media type registration, not a subject of the document about IANA registries.

gaps.name: TIFF / TIFF-FX image file format
gaps.why: The document is about the TIFF-FX image file format, and the taxonomy has no tag for image formats such as TIFF.

RFC3251.title: Electricity over IP
RFC3251.summary: An April 1 parody RFC proposing "Mostly Pointless Lamp Switching" (MPLampS), carrying electricity in IP packets with an MPLS/RSVP-TE control plane, and satirizing "foo-over-MPLS" documents.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody satirizing IETF Sub-IP drafts and foo-over-MPLS work; its subject is the joke itself.
humor.quote: Mostly Pointless Lamp Switching (MPLampS) is an architecture for carrying electricity over IP (with an MPLS control plane).

rejected.why: MPLS is only the punchline substrate of the parody; no real MPLS specification or extension is given.
Mentioned (as 'Tariff Extensions') only as part of the joke; nothing is specified about the real protocol.
The multicast section is a joke about DVMRP/PIM applied to electricity, not a real treatment of multicast routing.
'Voltage Protected Networks' is a pun, not about provider-provisioned VPNs.
OSPF and IS-IS appear only as acronym jokes and mentions of future work.
Mentioned only in a joke definition and a one-line accounting remark.

RFC3252.title: Binary Lexical Octet Ad-hoc Transport
RFC3252.summary: April 1st RFC that humorously reformulates IPv4, TCP and UDP as XML applications (BLOAT), with DTDs, Ethernet/802 encapsulation and IP gatewaying.

humor.why: Published 1 April 2002 as a whimsical parody proposing IP, TCP and UDP as XML; belongs in the April 1st humor series.
humor.quote: This document defines a reformulation of IP and two transport layer protocols (TCP and UDP) as XML applications.

XML.why: The document defines XML DTDs and encodings for IP, TCP and UDP datagrams, so XML usage in protocols is a substantial subject.
XML.quote: a reformulation of a widely-deployed network-layer protocol (IP [RFC791]), and two associated transport layer protocols (TCP [RFC793] and UDP [RFC768]) as XML [XML] applications

IPv4.why: IPoXML is a reformulation of IPv4 with its header fields and options redefined as XML elements.
IPv4.quote: This protocol MUST be implemented to be compliant with this RFC. IPoXML is the root protocol REQUIRED for effective use of TCPoXML

TCP.why: TCPoXML re-encodes the TCP header and options as XML.
TCP.quote: To calculate the length and checksum fields of the TCP element, a canonicalized form of the element MUST be used as in section 2.1.

UDP.why: UDPoXML re-encodes UDP as XML.
UDP.quote: A number of items have changed from the original UDP specification.

rejected.why: Ethernet encapsulation with type 0xBEEF is a short section; it is only the carrier for the joke protocol.
Gatewaying over IP via RFC 2003 is a single-sentence use, not a subject of the document.
Base-64 is used only as the payload encoding, relying on RFC 2045.
UTF-8 is only mandated as the encoding of the XML documents.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC3253.title: Versioning Extensions to WebDAV (Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning)
RFC3253.summary: RFC 3253 specifies the DeltaV versioning extensions to WebDAV, defining new methods (VERSION-CONTROL, CHECKOUT, CHECKIN, MERGE, etc.), properties, reports and resource types for version history, workspaces, baselines and activities.

WebDAV.why: The whole document extends WebDAV with versioning, new methods, live properties, reports and extended semantics for existing WebDAV methods like COPY, MOVE and PROPFIND.
WebDAV.quote: This document specifies a set of methods, headers, and resource types that define the WebDAV (Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning) versioning extensions to the HTTP/1.1 protocol.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is the base layer that WebDAV extends. The document adds nothing to HTTP itself beyond using it, apart from the Label header, which is part of the WebDAV versioning extension.
The request and response bodies are XML, but XML is only the encoding substrate. The document does not define XML usage in general.
It mentions Cache-Control: no-cache and Vary: Label, but only as incidental response requirements.

gaps.name: Versioning / configuration management
gaps.why: The document is about resource versioning, baselines, activities and merging. The taxonomy has no tag for versioning or configuration management beyond the WebDAV tag.

RFC3254.title: Definitions for talking about directories
RFC3254.summary: Informational RFC defining terminology for classifying information repositories ("directories") along dimensions such as scope, search vs lookup, consistency, security and update models, and applying it to DNS, X.500, BGP, NetNews and SNMP.

directory services.why: The whole document defines what a directory is and classifies repositories by search, consistency and update properties, so it belongs on the directory services page.
directory services.quote: This document discusses one group of such systems which is known under the term, "directories".

terminology.why: The document is a glossary of defined terms (repository, requester, lookup, search, consistency models) to aid mutual comprehension.
terminology.quote: it may be useful if the people who are discussing it have a common understanding of the terms they use.

rejected.why: DNS is only one of several example systems classified in section 3.1; the document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
Mentioned briefly as an example of a directory; the document is not about X.500.
Mentioned only in the abstract as an example of a directory server.
Used as an example of subset consistency and a routing database; the document does not address BGP itself.
Only a brief classification example in section 3.5.
Section 2.4 gives security models for repositories, but this is a small part of a terminology document and not a security subject in its own right.

RFC3255.title: Extending Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) over Synchronous Optical NETwork/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) with virtual concatenation, high order and low order payloads
RFC3255.summary: RFC 3255 extends the mapping of PPP over SONET/SDH (RFC 2615) to support virtual concatenation and both high-order and low-order SPE/VC payloads, with minor physical-layer changes to the C2, V5, H4 and K4 bytes.

SONET.why: The document extends the PPP-over-SONET/SDH mapping with virtual concatenation and low/high order payloads, and specifies the path overhead byte changes (C2, H4, V5, K4).
SONET.quote: This document describes an extension to the mapping of Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) into Synchronous Optical NETwork/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH)

rejected.why: PPP is carried over SONET/SDH, but the document defines nothing new about PPP itself. It only changes the physical-layer mapping.
MAPOS is a different protocol over SONET/SDH and is not discussed.

RFC3256.title: The DOCSIS (Data-Over-Cable Service Interface Specifications) Device Class DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) Relay Agent Information Sub-option
RFC3256.summary: Defines a new DHCP Relay Agent Information sub-option (code 4) that carries the DOCSIS cable modem Device Class from the relay agent to the DHCP server for policy decisions.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCP by defining a new relay agent information sub-option and how servers use it for address and parameter assignment policy.
DHCP.quote: This document proposes a new sub-option to the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) Relay Agent Information Option.

DOCSIS.why: The sub-option carries the DOCSIS Device Class (e.g., CPE Controlled Cable Modem bit) from DOCSIS signalling, so readers of DOCSIS cable access would want it.
DOCSIS.quote: This new sub-option is for use with DOCSIS (Data-Over-Cable Service Interface Specifications) cable modems and describes a "device class"

rejected.why: The sub-option is for DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information (RFC 3046), not DHCPv6.
Not relevant; the access network is cable, not cellular.
The IANA section merely records a sub-option code assignment; it is boilerplate.

RFC3257.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol Applicability Statement
RFC3257.summary: Informational applicability statement comparing SCTP with TCP and UDP, giving guidance on when to use SCTP, and covering multihoming, NAT and security issues.

SCTP.why: The whole document is about when and how SCTP is applicable, including its service model, multihoming, NAT and security properties.
SCTP.quote: This document describes the applicability of the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

rejected.why: TCP is only a comparison point for SCTP's service model and SYN-cookie security discussion; the document is not about TCP itself.
UDP appears only as a comparison in the service-model section.
Section 4 covers SCTP through NATs, but it is a short SCTP-specific section, not a document about NAT; no separate tag is warranted.
SCTP multihoming is discussed, but as an SCTP transport feature, not as a site multihoming architecture.
IPsec is mentioned only as the mechanism SCTP relies on for authentication and confidentiality.
TLS is mentioned in a single sentence about using in-order streams; not a subject of the document.

RFC3258.title: Distributing Authoritative Name Servers via Shared Unicast Addresses
RFC3258.summary: Informational memo describing practices for operating a single named authoritative DNS server from multiple locations via a shared unicast (anycast-like) IPv4 address announced over BGP, covering server setup, zone distribution, synchronization, placement and security.

anycast.why: The document specifies shared-unicast addressing, an anycast-like deployment of one server address at multiple instances, including routing and TCP split-destination caveats.
anycast.quote: enable an authoritative name server operator to provide access to a single named server in multiple locations

DNS.why: It gives operational practices for authoritative name servers: zone delivery, synchronization, placement, failover and security, so DNS readers would want it.
DNS.quote: increase the distribution of Domain Name System (DNS) servers to previously under-served areas of the network topology

rejected.why: BGP is only the mechanism used to announce the shared address; the document does not specify or extend it.
NTP is mentioned only as a clock source for coordinating switch-overs and in the example diagram.
Only a one-line remark to avoid path MTU discovery with shared source addresses; not a substantial subject.
Routing is incidental to the deployment practice; the focus is DNS server distribution, and anycast already covers the addressing aspect.

RFC3259.title: A Message Bus for Local Coordination
RFC3259.summary: Specifies the Mbus, a lightweight message-oriented local coordination protocol over link-local IP multicast/UDP, covering message syntax, addressing, transport, reliability, hello-based entity awareness, security and configuration.

multicast.why: The Mbus is a group communication protocol built on IP multicast with assigned multicast addresses and scopes, so readers of multicast deployment would want it. No narrower multicast child fits.
multicast.quote: The protocol is layered on top of IP multicast and is specified for IPv4 and IPv6. The IP multicast scope is limited to link-local multicast.

real-time communications.why: The main motivating use is local coordination of conferencing media tools (audio, video, whiteboard, conference controllers), though the protocol itself is generic.
real-time communications.quote: The implementation of multiparty multimedia conferencing systems is one example where a simple coordination infrastructure can be useful

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport; the document assigns a port but does not specify UDP usage guidelines.
HMAC is used for message authentication but is a mechanism relied on, not the subject.
AES is a mandated encryption algorithm in the security section, not the document's subject.
The document uses IPv6 addressing and a multicast group but is not about IPv6 itself.
Authentication and encryption are included, but they are a keyed-digest scheme for this protocol, not group key management.
Entity awareness via hello messages is peer presence within the bus, not general service discovery.

gaps.name: Mbus (Message Bus) local coordination protocol
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for local application-component coordination or message-bus protocols, so the document's actual subject is only approximated by multicast.

RFC3260.title: New Terminology and Clarifications for Diffserv
RFC3260.summary: RFC 3260 records Diffserv working group agreements: new terminology (SLS, TCS, PHB scheduling class, ordered aggregate), clarifications of PHB group usage, DS field definition, unknown DSCP handling, and IANA DSCP registration, updating RFCs 2474, 2475 and 2597.

Diffserv.why: The whole document refines Differentiated Services terminology and semantics (DS field, DSCP, PHB groups, AF, unrecognized DSCP handling).
Diffserv.quote: This memo captures Diffserv working group agreements concerning new and improved terminology, and provides minor technical clarifications.

rejected.why: ECN is mentioned only because the formerly unused DS bits were assigned to it by RFC 3168; the document is not about ECN.
Implied parent of Diffserv; the more specific Diffserv tag is used.
Service provisioning policy is related to RFC 3198 terminology, but only briefly discussed.
MPLS LSRs motivate the ordered aggregate concept, but the document is not about MPLS.
Section 8 on DSCP registry is brief boilerplate-like clarification, not the main subject.
Terminology is central, but the specific Diffserv tag covers it; no need for a generic topic tag.

RFC3261.title: SIP: Session Initiation Protocol
RFC3261.summary: RFC 3261 is the core specification of SIP, defining its messages, user agent, proxy, registrar and redirect behaviour, dialogs, transactions, transport, URIs, header fields, response codes, and security mechanisms.

SIP.why: The document is the base SIP specification, covering methods, dialogs, transactions, proxies and registration.
SIP.quote: SIP is an application-layer control protocol that can establish, modify, and terminate multimedia sessions (conferences) such as Internet telephony calls.

rejected.why: SDP is the session description format carried in SIP bodies via offer/answer. It is defined elsewhere (RFC 2327, RFC 3264) and only referenced here.
Section 22 profiles Digest for SIP, but this is a supporting security mechanism. The document is not about HTTP authentication.
Section 23 uses S/MIME for body protection and header tunnelling. It is a security mechanism the document uses, not its subject.
TLS secures SIPS URIs and transport. It is a substrate the document relies on and defines no new TLS behaviour.
Section 19.1 defines the SIP and SIPS URI schemes, but this is one part of a protocol spec. It is not a general URI document.
RTP is mentioned only as a companion protocol for media transport.

RFC3262.title: Reliability of Provisional Responses in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3262.summary: RFC 3262 extends SIP with the 100rel option tag, the PRACK method, and RSeq/RAck header fields so provisional (1xx) responses can be sent reliably, including how this interacts with SDP offer/answer.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP extension defining the 100rel option tag, PRACK method and RSeq/RAck headers, with UAS and UAC behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) providing reliable provisional response messages.

SDP.why: A full section defines how offer/answer exchanges work in reliable provisional responses and PRACK, which readers of SDP offer/answer would want.
SDP.quote: If the INVITE contained an offer, the UAS MAY generate an answer in a reliable provisional response

rejected.why: PSTN interoperability is mentioned only as motivation in the introduction; the document does not address interworking itself.
Not relevant; the document registers an option tag and headers, not media types.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-like and the main body is not about IANA.
The retransmission mechanism relies on the SIP transaction layer, not on UDP itself, so UDP is not a subject here.

RFC3263.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP): Locating SIP Servers
RFC3263.summary: Specifies how SIP clients and servers use DNS NAPTR, SRV and A/AAAA records to resolve a SIP/SIPS URI into the transport protocol, IP address and port of the next hop, and to find failover targets for responses.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP specification for locating servers: client and server resolution procedures, failover, stateless proxy considerations, and constructing SIP URIs.
SIP.quote: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) uses DNS procedures to allow a client to resolve a SIP Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) into the IP address, port, and transport protocol

DNS.why: It defines how NAPTR, SRV and A/AAAA records are used for SIP, including a new NAPTR service-field registry and a DDDS application. Readers interested in DNS-based service location would want it.
DNS.quote: the client SHOULD perform a NAPTR query for the domain in the URI

rejected.why: The topic fits, but the more specific SIP and DNS tags already cover the subject, and the document is specific to SIP.
SIP/SIPS URIs are resolved here but not defined; their syntax is in RFC 3261.
TLS is only mentioned as a transport option and as a security consideration; nothing new is defined for it.
SCTP appears only as one transport with a NAPTR service code (D2S).
Mentioned only in passing in the Security Considerations.
The registry for NAPTR service-to-transport mappings is boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA practice.

gaps.name: DDDS / NAPTR resource record
gaps.why: The document defines a DDDS application, the Transport Determination Application, using NAPTR and SRV. The taxonomy has no tag for NAPTR/SRV or DDDS; DNS is the closest fit.

RFC3264.title: An Offer/Answer Model with Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC3264.summary: RFC 3264 defines the offer/answer model by which two agents use SDP to negotiate a unicast (or multicast) multimedia session, including initial offers, answers, session modification, hold, and capability indication.

SDP.why: The whole document specifies offer/answer semantics and rules for SDP, which the SDP tag explicitly covers.
SDP.quote: This document defines a mechanism by which two entities can make use of the Session Description Protocol (SDP) to arrive at a common view of a multimedia session

rejected.why: SIP is the higher-layer protocol that carries offers and answers; it is the user of this model, not what the document specifies.
RTP payload types, rtpmap and RTCP port rules are discussed, but only as SDP stream details, not as the subject.
RTCP is mentioned only for port usage and directionality; the document does not address it in its own right.
Codecs appear in examples of format negotiation, but the document does not define or profile any codec.
A child tag (SDP) already fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC3265.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)-Specific Event Notification
RFC3265.summary: RFC 3265 defines the SIP SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods and the Event, Allow-Events and Subscription-State headers, giving an extensible framework for SIP event notification, plus guidelines for writing event packages.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP extension that defines new methods (SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY), headers and response codes, plus subscriber, notifier and proxy behaviour and dialog handling.
SIP.quote: The purpose of this extension is to provide an extensible framework by which SIP nodes can request notification from remote nodes indicating that certain events have occurred.

rejected.why: Presence and buddy lists are only cited as example uses. The document defines the generic framework, and the presence event packages are specified in other documents.
PINT appears only as a compatibility note (section 3.3.8) about a SUBSCRIBE with no Event header. It is not a subject of the document.
Presence is mentioned as an example event package use case only, not specified here.
The IANA section registers the event package namespace, headers and response codes. This is boilerplate for the main subject, so it is not tagged.
S/MIME is mentioned only as an optional protection mechanism for SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY requests.

RFC3266.title: Support for IPv6 in Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC3266.summary: RFC 3266 updates SDP (RFC 2327) by completing its ABNF to cover IPv6 addresses in origin and connection fields, with an example and an implementor note on IPv4-mapped addresses.

SDP.why: The document updates RFC 2327 SDP syntax so IPv6 addresses are defined in SDP's origin and connection fields. It is an extension of SDP.
SDP.quote: This document describes the use of Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) addresses in conjunction with the Session Description Protocol (SDP).

IPv6.why: A substantial part of the document concerns IPv6 address text syntax and IPv4-mapped address handling in SDP, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: An implementation may receive an SDP session description with an IPv6 address whose format [1] is internally that of an IPv4 mapped address.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to present the syntax fix, not the subject.
Only mentioned in an author's contact URI; SIP is not discussed in the body.
RFC 2732 literal IPv6 URL format is referenced for the uri production, but the document does not define anything about URIs.
The document covers textual syntax of addresses in SDP rather than address architecture or allocation; IPv6 is the more specific fit.

RFC3267.title: Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload Format and File Storage Format for the Adaptive Multi-Rate (AMR) and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB) Audio Codecs
RFC3267.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format, a file storage format, and MIME/SDP parameter registrations for the AMR and AMR-WB speech codecs, including mode adaptation, UEP/UED, interleaving, redundancy and multi-channel support.

AMR.why: The whole document defines how AMR and AMR-WB frames are packetized in RTP and stored in files, including CMR, ToC, and codec-specific parameters.
AMR.quote: This document specifies a real-time transport protocol (RTP) payload format to be used for Adaptive Multi-Rate (AMR) and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB) encoded speech signals.

RTP payload format.why: It is an RTP payload format specification for a specific codec: header usage, payload structure, bandwidth-efficient and octet-aligned modes.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of AMR and AMR-WB encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

media types.why: Section 8 registers audio/AMR and audio/AMR-WB media types with parameters and file magic numbers, a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: two separate MIME type registrations are provided, one for AMR and one for AMR-WB.

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format runs over; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers it.
Section 8.3 only maps MIME parameters into SDP; SDP is a signalling substrate, not the subject.
Mentioned as a way to support partial checksums for UED, but not specified or extended here.
An 8-bit frame CRC is defined, but it is a small detail of the payload format rather than a document about CRC.
Redundant transmission is discussed as a robustness option within the payload, not a FEC scheme in its own right.
Section 6 is a short generic congestion-control note, not a substantial part of the document.

RFC3268.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Ciphersuites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC3268.summary: Defines twelve AES-128/256 CBC ciphersuites with SHA-1 HMAC for TLS 1.0, covering RSA, DH and DHE key exchange variants.

TLS.why: The document registers new TLS ciphersuites and code points, so TLS readers would want it.
TLS.quote: This document proposes several new ciphersuites.

AES.why: The document is about adding AES with 128- and 256-bit keys in CBC mode as a new TLS cipher.
AES.quote: All the ciphersuites described here use the AES in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-1 is only the existing MAC construction from TLS, not something the document specifies or changes.
SHA-1 is used only as the MAC hash already defined in TLS; nothing new is defined about it.
RSA appears only as a key exchange and certificate type in ciphersuite names, inherited from TLS.
Triple DES is mentioned as the incumbent cipher being supplemented, not the subject.
RC4 is mentioned only in the motivation for the new ciphersuites as an existing TLS cipher.

RFC3269.title: Author Guidelines for Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) Building Blocks and Protocol Instantiation documents
RFC3269.summary: Guidelines for authors of Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) building block and protocol instantiation documents, specifying required sections and content for each.

reliable multicast.why: The whole document is about how to specify RMT building blocks and protocol instantiations. It is a general reliable multicast document, not tied to one child protocol such as FLUTE, NORM, PGM, ALC or LCT.
reliable multicast.quote: This document provides general guidelines to assist the authors of Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) building block and protocol instantiation definitions.

rejected.why: The FEC building block is mentioned only as an example in the codepoint considerations section. The document is not about FEC.
UDP is only the required initial transport for packet formats, not a subject of the document.
IPsec support is a one-line requirement for packet formats and is not a subject of the document.
A congestion control building block appears only as an example of inter-block dependencies.
The document gives working-group author guidelines for one document type, not general IETF procedures.

RFC3270.title: Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) Support of Differentiated Services
RFC3270.summary: Specifies how Diff-Serv Behavior Aggregates are supported over MPLS using E-LSPs and L-LSPs, including forwarding model, tunneling models, RSVP and LDP signaling extensions, and ATM/Frame Relay specifics.

Diffserv.why: The whole document defines PHB/PSC mapping, EXP encoding and Diff-Serv tunneling models (Pipe, Short Pipe, Uniform) over MPLS.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines a flexible solution for support of Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv) over Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) networks.

MPLS.why: Defines E-LSP and L-LSP types, Diff-Serv context in ILM/NHLFE, EXP-field use and LSP merging rules; core MPLS forwarding content.
MPLS.quote: This solution allows the MPLS network administrator to select how Diff-Serv Behavior Aggregates (BAs) are mapped onto Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

RSVP-TE.why: Section 5 extends RSVP-TE LSP tunnel setup with a DIFFSERV object, error codes and handling procedures.
RSVP-TE.quote: One new RSVP Object is defined in this document: the DIFFSERV Object.

LDP.why: Section 6 defines the Diff-Serv TLV, status codes and message handling for LDP label setup.
LDP.quote: One new LDP TLV is defined in this document: the Diff-Serv TLV

rejected.why: Only referenced for bandwidth signaling via the Traffic Parameters TLV; the document does not specify CR-LDP extensions.
LC-ATM CLP mappings are covered but as a media-specific section of Diff-Serv over MPLS, not about IP over ATM.
LC-FR DE mapping is a media-specific detail, not the document's subject.
RSVP is the signaling base; the extension is for MPLS LSP tunnels, covered by RSVP-TE.
Traffic engineering is a motivation and out-of-scope matter; the document is about Diff-Serv support.
Only mentioned for service types in LSP signaling; Intserv over MPLS Diff-Serv is explicitly out of scope.

RFC3271.title: The Internet is for Everyone
RFC3271.summary: Vint Cerf's Internet Society essay arguing that the Internet must be affordable, unrestricted, scalable, multilingual, easy to use, privacy-protecting and responsibly used to be truly for everyone.

internet governance.why: The essay is a policy and advocacy statement on how the Internet should be governed and supported, including support for the IAB, IESG, IRTF, IETF and ICANN, and on regulation, law and access.
internet governance.quote: Internet is for everyone - but it won't be if Governments restrict access to it, so we must dedicate ourselves to keeping the network unrestricted

rejected.why: Privacy and cryptography availability are mentioned only as one advocacy point, not analysed as protocol privacy considerations.
The document does not discuss architectural principles, only the Internet's growth and societal goals.
The Interplanetary Internet is mentioned briefly as a future milestone, not specified or discussed technically.
It cites growth statistics and looks to the future, not a retrospective history of the Internet.
The IETF and other bodies are named as organizations to support, but the document does not describe any standards process.

gaps.name: Internet access, affordability and public policy advocacy
gaps.why: The document is about the social, economic, legal and policy conditions for universal Internet access (affordability, censorship, legislation, child protection). The taxonomy has only the general internet governance topic for this.

RFC3272.title: Overview and Principles of Internet Traffic Engineering
RFC3272.summary: RFC 3272 is an informational overview of Internet traffic engineering principles: definitions, process model, history, taxonomy, recommendations (routing, survivability, Diffserv, MPLS focus), inter-domain BGP TE, and operational practice.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document is a principles, taxonomy and recommendations overview of traffic engineering of IP networks.
traffic engineering.quote: Internet traffic engineering is defined as that aspect of Internet network engineering dealing with the issue of performance evaluation and performance optimization of operational IP networks.

MPLS.why: MPLS explicit LSPs, constraint-based routing and MPLS-based survivability are a substantial focus, including protection options.
MPLS.quote: While this document considers various intra-domain traffic engineering approaches, it focuses more on traffic engineering with MPLS.

BGP.why: Section 7 and much of Section 8 describe inter-domain TE through BGP attributes, MED, local preference and communities.
BGP.quote: BGP provides a number of attributes and capabilities (e.g., route filtering) that can be used for inter-domain traffic engineering.

Diffserv.why: A dedicated section covers Diffserv-aware TE, class-types and per-class LSPs.
Diffserv.quote: This section provides an overview of the traffic engineering features and recommendations that are specifically pertinent to Differentiated Services (Diffserv) capable IP networks.

rejected.why: Described only as one of several related IETF projects in a survey, not specified or extended here.
Covered briefly as a historical technique and its limitations; not the document's subject.
Congestion is discussed as a TE problem, with network-side management emphasised rather than transport congestion control.
Only a background survey subsection.
Measurement is a TE process component but the document is not about measurement methods or metrics themselves.
Mentioned only for TE extensions and metric tuning; not addressed in detail.

gaps.name: Internet traffic engineering
gaps.why: The taxonomy lacks a general traffic engineering topic tag; the nearest is the MPLS-child "traffic engineering" topic under routing, which fits the subject (the id is used above on that basis), but no more specific tag for TE principles exists.

RFC3273.title: Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base for High Capacity Networks
RFC3273.summary: Defines the HC-RMON-MIB module extending RMON and RMON2 with 64-bit high-capacity counters, media-independent statistics, and finer capture timestamps for high-speed networks.

RMON.why: The document specifies high-capacity extensions to the RMON and RMON2 MIBs, so it is about RMON.
RMON.quote: it defines objects for managing remote network monitoring (RMON) devices for use on high speed networks.

rejected.why: The document is a MIB module, but RMON is the more specific tag for its subject, and the MIB parent is implied.
SNMP is the management protocol and SMI substrate the MIB is defined for; the document does not extend or profile SNMP itself.
It has Ethernet statistics tables, but these are RMON counters rather than IP-over-Ethernet or Ethernet OAM specifications.
It adds a nanosecond timestamp to the RMON capture buffer, which is a minor part of the document and not about capture file formats.

RFC3274.title: Compressed Data Content Type for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC3274.summary: Defines the CMS CompressedData content type, with its ASN.1 syntax, OIDs, SMIMECapabilities signalling, and mandatory ZLIB compression algorithm.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with a new content type, CompressedData, so readers of the CMS subject need it.
CMS.quote: This document describes a compressed data content type for CMS.  This is implemented as a new ContentInfo type

zlib.why: The mandatory compression algorithm is ZLIB, and the document defines its OID and its parameter encoding in CMS, so it is a substantial part of the content.
zlib.quote: CMS implementations that support the CompressedData content type MUST include support for the ZLIB compression algorithm [RFC1950] [RFC1951]

rejected.why: SMIMECapabilities is used to signal support, but the document defines a CMS content type, not S/MIME message handling.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for the format, apart from a short note on AlgorithmIdentifier parameter encoding.
DEFLATE is referenced only as the algorithm underlying ZLIB, and zlib is the more specific tag.
The zlib tag sits under compression and is more specific.

RFC3275.title: (Extensible Markup Language) XML-Signature Syntax and Processing
RFC3275.summary: RFC 3275 specifies the XML Signature syntax and processing rules, including the Signature element, references, transforms, KeyInfo, algorithms and canonicalization considerations for signing arbitrary data.

XML signatures.why: The whole document defines the XML digital signature element, its generation and validation rules, and algorithms.
XML signatures.quote: This document specifies XML (Extensible Markup Language) digital signature processing rules and syntax.

rejected.why: XML is the substrate for the signature format; the document is about signatures, which has its own more specific tag.
X509Data is one KeyInfo type carrying certificates, but the document does not profile X.509.
PGPData is only a KeyInfo container element; OpenPGP itself is not specified.
SHA-1 is a required digest algorithm identifier, but the document does not specify SHA.
HMAC-SHA1 is one identified MAC algorithm, used by reference only.
