RSA keys and signatures are referenced as identifiers and encodings, not specified.
URIs are used for referencing and algorithm identification, not defined here.

gaps.name: XML Canonicalization (Canonical XML)
gaps.why: Section 7 and 6.5 discuss canonicalization needs for signatures, but the taxonomy has no tag for XML canonicalization.

RFC3276.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for High Bit-Rate DSL - 2nd generation (HDSL2) and Single-Pair High-Speed Digital Subscriber Line (SHDSL) Lines Processing
RFC3276.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module for managing HDSL2 and SHDSL DSL lines: span configuration, status, inventory, endpoint performance counters, maintenance, profiles and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (HDSL2-SHDSL-LINE-MIB) defined with SMIv2, integrating with IF-MIB; MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) module for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

DSL.why: The managed subject is HDSL2/SHDSL digital subscriber line access, covering spans, repeaters, EOC, line rates and SNR margins.
DSL.quote: it describes objects used for managing High Bit-Rate DSL - 2nd generation (HDSL2) [18] and Single-Pair High-Speed Digital Subscriber Line (SHDSL) interfaces [19].

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management framework the MIB is defined for; the document specifies no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and the MIB child tag covers it.
The 15-minute and 1-day interval counters are part of the MIB structure, not a performance measurement methodology.
The document does not concern access node control; it manages DSL line modems.
Loopback maintenance objects exist, but they are a minor part of the MIB and not an OAM mechanism in their own right.

RFC3277.title: Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Transient Blackhole Avoidance
RFC3277.summary: Informational RFC describing an interoperable IS-IS mechanism: a recovering router sets the LSP Overload bit until BGP has converged, to avoid transient blackholing of transit traffic.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies an operational use of the IS-IS Overload bit and LSP flooding behaviour, and discusses IS-IS metric limits.
IS-IS.quote: a simple, interoperable mechanism that can be employed in IS-IS [1, 2] networks in order to avoid transition to a newly available path

rejected.why: BGP convergence is the motivating condition, but the document specifies nothing about BGP itself; it only changes IS-IS behaviour.
OSPF Stub Router Advertisement (RFC 3137) is cited as a similar mechanism and alternative only.
The IS-IS tag already covers this document's subject; no broader architecture topic is addressed.

RFC3278.title: Use of Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Algorithms in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC3278.summary: Profiles the use of ECC algorithms (ECDSA signatures, ECDH and 1-pass ECMQV key agreement) in CMS SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthenticatedData, with ASN.1 syntax and S/MIME capability advertisement.

CMS.why: The document specifies how ECC algorithms are incorporated into CMS content types SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthenticatedData.
CMS.quote: This specification defines a profile for the use of Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) public key algorithms in the CMS.

ECDSA.why: ECDSA signature generation, verification and encoding (ECDSA-Sig-Value) in CMS are specified in detail.
ECDSA.quote: This section describes how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) with SignedData.

elliptic curve.why: ECDH and ECMQV key agreement, EC public keys and curve parameter recommendations are core content. These are not covered by the ECDSA tag.
elliptic curve.quote: This section describes how to use the ephemeral-static Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement algorithm with EnvelopedData.

rejected.why: S/MIME is mentioned only for the SMIMECapabilities attribute and in the summary. The document is a CMS profile.
Section 6 only refers to other documents for ECC in certificates and defines nothing itself.
SHA-1 is used only as the digest and KDF hash, not as the subject.
ASN.1 is just the notation used to define the syntax.

RFC3279.title: Algorithms and Identifiers for the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
RFC3279.summary: Specifies algorithm identifiers (OIDs) and ASN.1 encodings for hash functions, signature algorithms and subject public keys (RSA, DSA, DH, KEA, ECDSA/ECDH) used in Internet X.509 certificates and CRLs, supplementing RFC 3280.

X.509.why: The document profiles the signatureAlgorithm and subjectPublicKeyInfo fields of X.509 certificates and CRLs, supplementing the RFC 3280 profile.
X.509.quote: This document specifies algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encoding formats for digital signatures and subject public keys used in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI).

elliptic curve.why: A substantial section defines the ECDSA signature OIDs, the ECDH/ECDSA key OIDs, and the EC parameter encodings (named curves, field IDs, bases).
elliptic curve.quote: When certificates contain an ECDSA or ECDH public key, the id-ecPublicKey algorithm identifier MUST be used.

RSA.why: The document defines the RSA public key encoding and the md2/md5/sha-1 WithRSAEncryption signature identifiers.
RSA.quote: The OID rsaEncryption identifies RSA public keys.

ECDSA.why: The document defines the ecdsa-with-SHA1 identifier and the Ecdsa-Sig-Value encoding, plus the ECDSA key and curve parameters.
ECDSA.quote: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is defined in [X9.62].

MD5.why: The document profiles MD5 (and MD2) as hash functions for certificate signing and discusses their weaknesses.
MD5.quote: MD5 produces a 128-bit "hash" of the input.  MD5 is fully described in [RFC 1321].

SHA.why: The document profiles SHA-1 as the preferred hash for certificate and CRL signatures, with its OID.
SHA.quote: SHA-1 is the preferred one-way hash function for the Internet X.509 PKI.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the encoding notation the document relies on, not its subject. The ASN.1 module only carries the algorithm definitions.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already implies PKI.
KEA and DH keys are carried in certificates, but the document is about key and signature identifiers, not key establishment.
PEM is mentioned only as the reason MD2 is retained, and the document is not about it.
The more specific technology tags already cover the cryptographic content.

gaps.name: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) and Diffie-Hellman/KEA key encodings
gaps.why: The document defines DSA, DH and KEA public key and signature encodings, but the taxonomy has no tags for them.

RFC3280.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
RFC3280.summary: RFC 3280 profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and v2 CRL for the Internet PKI, defines two Internet-specific extensions, and specifies certification path validation and CRL validation algorithms, with ASN.1 modules and examples.

X.509.why: The whole document is a profile of X.509 certificates and CRLs, including extensions, path validation and CRL processing.
X.509.quote: This memo profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and X.509 v2 Certificate Revocation List (CRL) for use in the Internet.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation and DER the encoding for the structures, and the appendices are ASN.1 modules. The document is about certificates, not ASN.1 itself.
OCSP is only referenced through the authority information access extension (id-ad-ocsp). The document does not specify it.
It is the parent of X.509, so it is implied by the X.509 tag.
IPsec is named only as one application of the certificates.
TLS appears only in the serverAuth and clientAuth key purposes, as a use of certificates.
DNS names appear only as a subjectAltName form and in name constraints.

RFC3281.title: An Internet Attribute Certificate Profile for Authorization
RFC3281.summary: Profiles X.509 Attribute Certificates for Internet use: fields, extensions, attribute types (group, role, clearance), validation, revocation, and optional features such as attribute encryption, proxying and AA controls.

X.509.why: The document is a profile of X.509 attribute certificates, defining their fields, extensions, validation and revocation. X.509 certificates and profiles is the closest fitting tag.
X.509.quote: This specification defines a profile for the use of X.509 Attribute Certificates in Internet Protocols.

authorization.why: ACs exist to convey authorization information such as role, group and clearance for access control decisions. The document also covers delegation, targeting and AA controls over which attributes an issuer may assert.
authorization.quote: An AC may contain attributes that specify group membership, role, security clearance, or other authorization information associated with the AC holder.

rejected.why: OCSP is only named as one way to point to revocation status; the document does not specify or extend it.
CMS EnvelopedData is only used as the mechanism for the optional attribute encryption; it is not the subject.
ASN.1 is the notation for the definitions and the module in Appendix B, not the subject.
The more specific X.509 tag fits. The document is about a certificate profile, not PKI in general.
The clearance attribute is imported from X.501, but it is only one of several attribute types and not a labelling framework.
LDAP URLs are allowed in CRL distribution points and LDAP is referenced for the OID string format. It is not specified here.

gaps.name: Attribute certificates / privilege management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag specific to attribute certificates (ACs). X.509 and authorization only partly cover the subject.

RFC3282.title: Content Language Headers
RFC3282.summary: Defines the Content-Language and Accept-Language headers for labelling and requesting the language of MIME body parts and Web documents using language tags, obsoleting RFC 1766.

language tags.why: The document's whole purpose is carrying and requesting language tags/ranges in headers, so the language tags subject is the best fit.
language tags.quote: This document specifies a protocol element for use with protocols that use RFC 822-like headers for carrying language tags as defined in [TAGS].

content negotiation.why: Accept-Language with q-values expresses language preferences for content negotiation, a substantial part of the document.
content negotiation.quote: The "Accept-Language" header is intended for use in cases where a user or a process desires to identify the preferred language(s)

rejected.why: Accept-Language is borrowed from HTTP/1.1 and mentioned for q-value rules, but the document does not specify HTTP.
MIME body parts are one context of use, but the document does not define MIME structure or encodings.
The headers use RFC 822-style syntax, but the document is about language labelling, not the message format itself.
ABNF is only used to define the header syntax; the document is not about the notation.
Parent of language tags; the more specific child tag was chosen instead.

RFC3283.title: Guide to Internet Calendaring
RFC3283.summary: Informational guide describing the Internet calendaring standards (iCalendar, iTIP, iMIP, CAP), how they relate, deployment scenarios, important aspects, and open issues.

iCalendar.why: The document explains iCalendar, iTIP, iMIP and CAP and how they fit together; iCalendar is the common data format and the best-fitting tag for this calendaring suite.
iCalendar.quote: iCalendar is the language used to describe calendar objects.  iTIP describes a way to use the iCalendar language to do scheduling.

calendaring.why: The guide covers calendar access (CAP), scheduling, and open issues in general, which go beyond iCalendar. The taxonomy has no tags for iTIP, iMIP or CAP, so the topic tag covers them.
calendaring.quote: Calendaring and scheduling protocols are intended to aid individuals in obtaining calendaring information and scheduling meetings across the Internet

rejected.why: iMIP carries iTIP over email, but email is only a transport binding here and the document is not about email itself.
Time zones are one of the 'important aspects' in a brief paragraph. The document is not about time zone data distribution.
MIME is mentioned only as the wrapper for scheduling messages and for signing and encryption.
SASL is mentioned only as the authentication mechanism CAP uses, in the Security Considerations.
SMTP appears only as an analogy for iTIP/iMIP.

gaps.name: iTIP / iMIP / CAP (Calendar Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The scheduling protocol, its email binding and the calendar access protocol are described at length, but the taxonomy has no tags for them. They are covered only by the generic calendaring topic.

RFC3284.title: The VCDIFF Generic Differencing and Compression Data Format
RFC3284.summary: RFC 3284 specifies VCDIFF, a portable byte-aligned binary format for delta (differencing) and compressed files, including its instruction set (ADD/COPY/RUN), address caches, code tables and window organization.

compression.why: The whole document defines a lossless compression and delta-encoding data format; no specific compression child tag (DEFLATE, gzip, etc.) fits, so the parent topic is used.
compression.quote: a general, efficient and portable data format suitable for encoding compressed and/or differencing data so that they can be easily transported among computers

rejected.why: gzip is only mentioned as a comparison point in the performance section; the document does not specify it.
HTTP/1.1 delta encoding (RFC 3229) is only cited as a use case for the source code; the format itself is independent of HTTP.
No media type is registered; the IANA section only mentions a Secondary Compressor ID registry, which is not a media type registry.
The IANA section is boilerplate and defines no values.

gaps.name: Delta encoding / data differencing
gaps.why: The document is about delta compression (differencing between source and target files), which has no specific tag in the taxonomy; compression is the closest fit.

RFC3285.title: Using Microsoft Word to create Internet Drafts and RFCs
RFC3285.summary: Informational guide to configuring Microsoft Word styles, page layout, fields and a CRLF fixup program so authors can produce plain-text Internet-Drafts and RFCs in the required format.

RFC series.why: The document is about authoring tooling and the format and submission requirements for I-Ds and RFCs (72 chars per line, 58 lines per page, CRLF line ends). That falls under RFC series format and publication.
RFC series.quote: This document describes the steps to configure the Microsoft Word application to produce documents in Internet Draft and RFC format.

rejected.why: The text output must be plain ASCII and the document checks for stray non-ASCII characters. But it is about Word configuration, not the ASCII character set.
It is a how-to guide, but for RFC authors rather than a general introductory guide for Internet users in the FYI series.
It mentions submission to the I-D and RFC editors, but it describes tooling, not IETF process or procedures.

gaps.name: Authoring tools for Internet-Drafts and RFCs
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for document-authoring tooling or templates. The nearest, RFC series, covers format and publication, so it is only an approximate fit.

RFC3286.title: An Introduction to the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
RFC3286.summary: An informational overview of SCTP's capabilities (multi-streaming, multi-homing, cookie-protected initiation, data exchange, shutdown, message format, error handling, extensions) as a guide for potential users of SCTP as a general purpose transport protocol.

SCTP.why: The whole document introduces and explains SCTP features, so it belongs on the SCTP page.
SCTP.quote: This document provides a high level introduction to the capabilities supported by the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

rejected.why: TCP is used only as a comparison point and as the source of SACK and congestion-control procedures; the document is not about TCP.
Congestion control is described briefly as following TCP algorithms, which is part of the SCTP overview and not a subject in its own right.
Multi-homing is a core SCTP feature that is described, but the SCTP tag covers it. The document is not about multihoming architectures in general.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an option for strong security, so it is boilerplate-level.
The CRC-32c checksum change is noted in passing and defined elsewhere.

RFC3287.title: Remote Monitoring MIB Extensions for Differentiated Services
RFC3287.summary: Defines the DSMON MIB, an RMON-2 extension that lets probes count packets and octets per DiffServ codepoint (DSCP), with counter aggregation profiles and per-protocol, per-host and per-host-pair statistics and TopN reports.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (DSMON-MIB) with its object groups, compliance statements and configuration examples. It extends the RMON-2 MIB, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

RMON.why: It extends RMON-2 and HC-RMON with DSCP-based classification. It reuses protocolDirTable, TimeFilter, zero-based counters and TopN reporting for RMON probes.
RMON.quote: utilizing the monitoring framework defined in the RMON-2 (Remote Network Monitoring Management Version 2) MIB.

Diffserv.why: The MIB monitors DSCP usage in packets. It helps operators tune DiffServ allocations, so Diffserv readers would want it. DiffServ itself is not specified here.
Diffserv.quote: There is a need for a standardized way of monitoring the network traffic usage of Differentiated Services (DS) [RFC2474] codepoint values.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB runs on. The document does not extend or specify the protocol.
Diffserv is the more specific tag, and the document only monitors DSCP usage rather than defining QoS architecture.
It counts traffic per DSCP but defines no performance metrics. It states that delay and jitter are out of scope.
IPv4 and IPv6 prefix lengths appear only in host table configuration, which is incidental.

RFC3288.title: Using the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) in Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP)
RFC3288.summary: Specifies a SOAP 1.1 binding to BEEP: a BEEP profile with boot/feature negotiation, message packaging, message patterns, soap.beep/soap.beeps URL schemes, and a registered TCP port.

BEEP.why: The document defines a new BEEP profile for SOAP, including profile initialization, channel states, and message exchanges, so BEEP readers need it.
BEEP.quote: This memo specifies a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) binding to the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol core (BEEP).

URI.why: A substantial part defines and registers two new URI schemes, with syntax and address resolution rules.
URI.quote: This memo defines two URL schemes, "soap.beep" and "soap.beeps", which identify the use of SOAP over BEEP over TCP.

rejected.why: SOAP envelopes are XML, but the document only carries them and does not specify an XML format of its own beyond the boot message DTD.
TLS is only mentioned as a mandatory tuning profile in Security Considerations; the document defines nothing new about it.
SRV and A record lookups are used for address resolution, but this is only substrate use and no DNS feature is defined.
multipart/related packaging of envelopes is described briefly, but the document does not specify MIME itself.
HTTP is referenced only by analogy for Host and the request path; it is not used.
DIGEST-MD5 SASL is only named as a required tuning profile in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SOAP or web services. The document is a SOAP binding, so readers browsing SOAP would expect it.

RFC3289.title: Management Information Base for the Differentiated Services Architecture
RFC3289.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module (DIFFSERV-MIB and DIFFSERV-DSCP-TC) for monitoring and configuring Differentiated Services router data paths: classifiers, meters, actions, droppers, queues and schedulers.

Diffserv.why: The document models Differentiated Services router functionality (classifiers, meters, markers, droppers, queues, schedulers) including AF and EF PHB configuration examples.
Diffserv.quote: This MIB models the same functional data path elements, allowing the network manager to assemble them in any fashion that meets the relevant policy.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification, with tables, objects, compliance and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo describes an SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2) MIB for a device implementing the Differentiated Services Architecture.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines a module, so the more specific MIB tag applies.
Random Drop parameters (RED-style) are modeled as objects, but the document is not about active queue management itself.
Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS subject.
IPv6 flow ID and addresses are only match fields in the multi-field classifier.

RFC3290.title: An Informal Management Model for Diffserv Routers
RFC3290.summary: RFC 3290 defines an informal, abstract management model of Differentiated Services routers, decomposing them into classifiers, meters, actions, queues, algorithmic droppers, schedulers and Traffic Conditioning Blocks for configuration and management.

Diffserv.why: The whole document models Diffserv router datapath elements (classifiers, meters, markers, PHB realisation via queues and schedulers), so Diffserv readers need it.
Diffserv.quote: This document proposes an informal management model of Differentiated Services (Diffserv) routers for use in their management and configuration.

policy management.why: The model is an abstract configuration and management information model that underpins the Diffserv MIB and policy-management interfaces.
policy management.quote: it is helpful to define a conceptual model of a Diffserv router that abstracts away implementation details of particular Diffserv routers from the parameters of interest for configuration and management.

AQM.why: A substantial section models algorithmic droppers (RED, RIO, head/tail drop) and their parameters, which is active queue management.
AQM.quote: RED, RED-on-In-and-Out (RIO) and Drop-on-threshold are examples of dropping algorithms.

rejected.why: The model is the rationale for the Diffserv MIB (RFC 3289), but this document does not specify SNMP or MIB content itself.
Diffserv is the more specific child; the QoS parent is implied and not separately addressed.
RSVP appears only in the optional QoS agent module description, which is not a substantial part of the document.
COPS is mentioned only as an example management protocol.
TCP is mentioned only as an example of reactive traffic and in the token bucket discussion, not as a subject.
The document does not define MIB modules; it only says it is the rationale for one.

gaps.name: Traffic metering and token bucket / leaky bucket shaping and policing
gaps.why: Meters, token bucket conformance and shapers are a major part of the document, including Appendix A. The taxonomy has no tag for traffic conditioning, policing or shaping apart from the Diffserv tag.

RFC3291.title: Textual Conventions for Internet Network Addresses
RFC3291.summary: Defines the INET-ADDRESS-MIB module of SMIv2 textual conventions (InetAddressType, InetAddress, prefix length, port number, AS number) for representing IPv4, IPv6 and DNS-name addresses in MIB modules, with usage guidance.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module of textual conventions intended to be imported by other MIB modules, with usage hints on table indexing and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This MIB module defines textual conventions to represent commonly used Internet network layer addressing information.

addressing.why: A substantial part concerns representing IPv4/IPv6 addresses, zone indices, prefix lengths and address ranges, and handling multiple addresses per host and address uniqueness.
addressing.quote: A generic Internet address consists of two objects, one whose syntax is InetAddressType, and another whose syntax is InetAddress.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is written for, but the document only defines textual conventions, not the protocol.
IPv6 addresses and zone indices are represented, but the document does not specify IPv6 itself; it only gives MIB representations.
DNS names are one InetAddressType, but the document defines no DNS behaviour beyond noting when names must be resolved.
IPv4 addresses are only represented in the textual conventions; the document does not specify IPv4.

RFC3292.title: General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP) V3
RFC3292.summary: RFC 3292 specifies GSMPv3, an asymmetric master-slave protocol by which external controllers establish and maintain connection state, reservations, ports, statistics, configuration and QoS on label switches (ATM, Frame Relay, MPLS).

GSMP.quote: The GSMPv3 is an asymmetric protocol that allows one or more external switch controllers to establish and maintain the state of a label switch

rejected.why: MPLS labels are one label type GSMP controls; the document is about switch control, not MPLS itself.
ATM is a supported port type with ATM-specific procedures, but the document is not about IP over ATM.
Frame Relay is a port/label type only.
Only referenced as a service definition for traffic parameters.
Explicitly not supported in this version; only mentioned.
Controlled Load is one service definition referenced for traffic parameters; not the subject.
QoS models are a part of GSMP but the tag GSMP covers it; document is not a QoS architecture.

RFC3293.title: General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP) Packet Encapsulations for Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM), Ethernet and Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
RFC3293.summary: Specifies how GSMP v3 messages are encapsulated in ATM AAL-5 (LLC/SNAP), Ethernet frames (Ethertype 0x880C), and TCP (port 6068 with a TLV header), including IPsec ESP requirements for IP use.

GSMP.why: The whole document defines transport encapsulations for GSMP messages, so it belongs on the GSMP page.
GSMP.quote: This memo specifies the encapsulation of GSMP (General Switch Management Protocol) packets in ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode), Ethernet and TCP

ATM.why: A full section defines the AAL-5 LLC/SNAP encapsulation and the default VPI/VCI control channel, which readers interested in IP over ATM would want.
ATM.quote: GSMP packets are variable length and for an ATM data link layer they are encapsulated directly in an AAL-5 CPCS-PDU [3][4] with an LLC/SNAP header

Ethernet.why: A full section defines the Ethernet frame format, addressing, Ethertype, instance fields and the receiver's discard rules.
Ethernet.quote: GSMP packets MAY be encapsulated on an Ethernet data link as illustrated:

transport mapping.why: The document binds one protocol to several transports (ATM, Ethernet, TCP), which is the kind of mapping this topic covers. It has no more specific child tag for this.
transport mapping.quote: When GSMP messages are transported over an IP network, they MUST be transported using the TCP encapsulation.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate carrying GSMP. The document adds a TLV delimiter and a port number but does not specify or extend TCP.
IPsec ESP is only mandated for securing the TCP/IP case in a short section. The document does not define IPsec itself.
GSMP is a switch control protocol, but this document covers only its encapsulations, not the separation of control and forwarding.

RFC3294.title: General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP) Applicability
RFC3294.summary: Informational overview of GSMP (v3) and its applicability to controlling label switches in an IP/MPLS environment, summarising the protocol, its document set, partitioning, QoS models and message set.

GSMP.why: The whole document is an overview and applicability statement for GSMP, covering its description, partitioning, controller interactions, QoS and message set.
GSMP.quote: The General Switch Management Protocol V3 (GSMPv3) [5], is a general purpose protocol to control a label switch.

rejected.why: MPLS is the deployment environment GSMP is applied in, but the document does not specify or analyse MPLS itself.
ATM is explicitly excluded from the deployment discussion; it appears only as one possible switch and label type.
LDP is mentioned only as an example of a control plane protocol that GSMP separates from the forwarder.
The QoS models are part of GSMP's description, not a QoS architecture in their own right, and GSMP already covers them.
TCP/IP is only the transport for the GSMP control channel, and the document defines nothing new about it.
The GSMP MIB is only listed as one document in the set, and the document does not describe it.

RFC3295.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP)
RFC3295.summary: Defines the SMIv2 GSMP-MIB module for configuring, monitoring and sending notifications about GSMP (General Switch Management Protocol v3) controller and switch entities, sessions and encapsulations.

GSMP.why: The MIB is a protocol MIB for GSMP, configuring and monitoring GSMP entities, sessions, encapsulations and events.
GSMP.quote: it describes managed objects for the General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP)

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition with tables, groups, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for the use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried by; the document defines no new SNMP behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
ATM is only one encapsulation option for GSMP; the MIB just holds VPI/VCI/interface config for it.
TCP is merely an encapsulation transport whose address and port are configured; nothing is defined about TCP itself.
GSMP controls label switches generally, but the document does not address MPLS itself.
Ethernet encapsulation is mentioned only in passing (MAC address as entity ID).

RFC3296.title: Named Subordinate References in Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Directories
RFC3296.summary: Defines the LDAP referral object class, the ref attribute, and the ManageDsaIT control for representing named subordinate references, plus server rules for generating referrals and search continuation references.

LDAP.why: The RFC extends LDAP with a schema (referral class, ref attribute), a control (ManageDsaIT), and referral/search-reference processing rules for servers.
LDAP.quote: This document details schema and protocol elements for representing and manipulating named subordinate references in LDAP directories.

rejected.why: The ref attribute holds URIs (LDAP URLs), but URIs are only the value format, not the subject.
X.500 subordinate knowledge and ManageDsaIT are cited as analogies; the document specifies LDAP, not X.500.
Implied parent of LDAP, so not listed separately.

RFC3297.title: Content Negotiation for Messaging Services based on Email
RFC3297.summary: Defines an email-based content negotiation mechanism for Internet fax and other messaging services, using a Content-alternative header, an Original-Message-ID header, and new MDN options and disposition modifiers.

fax.why: The mechanism is designed to give Internet fax a negotiation facility comparable to Group 3 fax. Section 7 and the examples are all Internet fax.
fax.quote: This memo describes a content negotiation mechanism for facsimile, voice and other messaging services that use Internet email.

email.why: It adds new mail headers (Content-alternative, Original-Message-ID) and MDN extensions. It is an email-level negotiation framework that must interwork with existing mail clients.
email.quote: The mechanism described here aims to meet these needs in a fashion that is fully compatible with the current behaviour and expectations of Internet email.

content negotiation.why: The whole document defines content negotiation, including goals, the sender/receiver flow and the capability exchange. The taxonomy tag covers media feature and content negotiation.
content negotiation.quote: An exchange of information (negotiation metadata) which leads to selection of the appropriate representation (variant) when transferring a data resource.

rejected.why: MIME headers and multipart structures are the substrate. The new Content-alternative header is MIME-level, but the document is not mainly about MIME body structure or encodings.
It defines two new headers, but they serve negotiation and are not a general treatment of message format.
SMTP is only the transport and is not specified or extended here.
Media types appear in the examples (image/tiff, application/pdf), but the document does not register or define any.
HTTP content negotiation is mentioned only as a comparison.

gaps.name: Message Disposition Notifications (MDN)
gaps.why: The document extends MDN with new options and disposition modifiers, and the taxonomy has no MDN or DSN tag.

RFC3298.title: Service in the Public Switched Telephone Network/Intelligent Network (PSTN/IN) Requesting InTernet Service (SPIRITS) Protocol Requirements
RFC3298.summary: RFC 3298 lists requirements for the SPIRITS protocol, which lets PSTN/IN entities request Internet services. It covers general, IN, Wireless IN and PINT-related requirements, and it picks SIP as the signalling base.

SPIRITS.why: The whole document specifies the requirements for the SPIRITS protocol, covering IN detection points, wireless IN events and follow-up actions.
SPIRITS.quote: This document describes the SPIRITS protocol requirements, based on the architecture presented in RFC 3136.

PINT.why: A section is devoted to PINT-related requirements: registration, and reuse of the SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY building blocks. The joint PINT/SPIRITS architecture is also central.
PINT.quote: the SPIRITS protocol must meet the PINT-related requirements listed in section 7 of this document.

rejected.why: SIP is the chosen signalling base. The document defines no new SIP extensions beyond SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, so SIP is the substrate, not the subject.
SDP is only mentioned as one way to carry SPIRITS parameters.
MIME is only mentioned as a possible carrier for parameters.
Wireless IN and CAMEL are covered only as event sources for SPIRITS. The document is not about IP over 3GPP systems.
This is the parent of SPIRITS and PINT, so it is implied by those tags.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as the INAP parameter syntax that must be converted to text.

RFC3299.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 3200-3299
RFC3299.summary: RFC 3299 is a slightly annotated index and status report listing the 100 RFCs numbered 3200 through 3299, with author, date, title and abstract for each.

RFC series.why: The document exists to catalogue a block of RFC series publications. Readers browsing the RFC series subject would expect this periodic summary there.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 3200 through RFC 3299.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: Several summarised RFCs concern SIP, but this document only lists them and does not specify or analyse the protocol.
Many listed RFCs define MIB modules, but the summary is not about MIBs itself.
Several entries are about Diffserv, but they appear only as list items, not as the subject of this document.
The memo mentions standards-track status marking, but it does not define or discuss process. It is a list of publications.
One listed RFC concerns IANA considerations. The summary itself is not about IANA registries.

RFC3300.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC3300.summary: RFC 3300 (STD 1) is a snapshot list of Internet standards-track, BCP, experimental and historic RFCs as of October 2002, published by the RFC Editor for the IESG and IAB.

RFC series.why: The document is an RFC Editor index of RFCs by standards maturity level and BCP, with instructions on retrieving RFCs. It is a publication/catalogue of the RFC series.
RFC series.quote: This memo contains a snapshot of the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as of October 24, 2002.

IETF process.why: The memo's organising principle is the standards track maturity levels defined by RFC 2026, and it is published under the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: Sections 3.1 - 3.6 of this memo contain the lists of protocols in each stage of standardization - Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Historic

rejected.why: IANA is mentioned only as a contact and in cited BCP titles; the document is not about IANA registries.
Many SNMP/MIB RFCs appear in the lists, but the document only catalogues them and is not about SNMP.
It is a dated status snapshot, not a history or retrospective.
FTP and email are mentioned only as retrieval methods for RFCs.

RFC3301.title: Layer Two Tunnelling Protocol (L2TP): ATM access network extensions
RFC3301.summary: RFC 3301 extends L2TP (RFC 2661) with new and changed AVPs and procedures so that PPP sessions can be tunnelled from ATM SVC/PVC access networks, supporting asymmetric bandwidth, service category selection and AESA/NSAP addressing.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TP by defining new AVPs (Rx Minimum/Maximum BPS, Service Category, Service Name, VPI/VCI) and changed AVPs (Bearer Type, Called Number).
L2TP.quote: This document augments the procedures described in [RFC2661] to further support ATM SVC or PVC based access networks.

ATM.why: A substantial part of the document concerns ATM access networks: SVC/PVC establishment, AAL5 framing, ATM service categories and AESA addressing. It is about PPP over ATM access via L2TP.
ATM.quote: the traffic management aspects of ATM connections (e.g. asymmetric bandwidth allocation and service category selection capabilities)

rejected.why: PPP is the payload being tunnelled. The document does not extend PPP itself.
ADSL is only mentioned as an example of an ATM-based access network.
The IANA section is boilerplate for allocating AVP values.
Authentication and authorization are discussed only briefly in the service model section. The document does not specify an AAA framework.

RFC3302.title: Tag Image File Format (TIFF) - image/tiff MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC3302.summary: Registers the image/tiff MIME media type for TIFF 6.0 image data, redefining the earlier RFC 1528 registration and adding an optional "application" parameter; obsoletes RFC 2302.

media types.why: The document exists to register the image/tiff media type, including its optional application parameter, encoding and interoperability considerations.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type image/tiff.

rejected.why: MIME is the framework the registration sits in. The document is about one specific media type registration, which the more specific 'media types' tag covers.
The document came from the Internet Fax WG and lists fax as an application. It does not define fax protocol behaviour, and TIFF Class F is only mentioned as the earlier RFC 1528 definition.
Base64 is mentioned only as the transfer encoding for transports that can't carry binary data. It is a substrate, not the subject.
The IANA registration template is the vehicle for the media type. The document is not about IANA registry procedures or stewardship.

gaps.name: TIFF (Tag Image File Format) / image formats
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for raster image formats such as TIFF. The document describes TIFF's scope and features, but only as background for the MIME registration.

RFC3303.title: Middlebox communication architecture and framework
RFC3303.summary: Informational framework for MIDCOM, in which external agents with application intelligence signal firewall and NAT middleboxes through an application-independent protocol, illustrated with SIP flows.

firewall.why: The framework is about middlebox traversal and control of firewalls: agents open pinholes dynamically. Firewall and middlebox security traversal is the core subject.
firewall.quote: Middleboxes implementing Firewall and Network Address Translator services typically embed application intelligence within the device for their operation.

NAT.why: NAT middleboxes are one of the two services in scope. The document includes NAPT timeline flows and NAT-BIND handling.
NAT.quote: create PORT bindings and appropriately modify the SDP content to permit the RTP/RTCP streams through a middlebox implementing NAT service

SIP.why: A substantial part of the document is SIP call flows through middleboxes with a SIP proxy hosting the MIDCOM agent. SIP is the illustrative application, not the thing specified.
SIP.quote: In figure 3 below, we consider SIP applications (Refer [SIP]) to illustrate the operation of the MIDCOM protocol.

rejected.why: The MIDCOM PDP and policy rules are discussed, but only as authorization for agents. The document does not specify a policy information model.
RTP/RTCP media streams are what the middlebox is asked to let through. The document does not specify RTP.
The agent parses SDP to find dynamic ports. SDP is only the payload being examined.
IPsec AH and ESP are mentioned as options for securing MIDCOM messages, and NAT breaking IPsec is noted. This is boilerplate-level and not the document's subject.
H.323 is mentioned as another application needing agent help, but only briefly.
The PDP authorizes agents, but this is a supporting component. The main subject is middlebox communication.

gaps.name: MIDCOM (middlebox communication)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the middlebox communication architecture and agent-to-middlebox protocol. The taxonomy has no tag for it, only the firewall and NAT tags.

RFC3304.title: Middlebox Communications (midcom) Protocol Requirements
RFC3304.summary: Informational RFC listing the requirements a midcom protocol must meet for agents to control middleboxes (NAT and firewalls), covering session machinery, rule semantics and security.

NAT.why: The midcom protocol exists to let agents control NAT middleboxes, including port mapping requirements. Readers of NAT would want this RFC.
NAT.quote: These requirements were developed with a specific focus on network address translation and firewall middleboxes.

firewall.why: Firewall middlebox control (pinholes, filtering rulesets, allow/disallow of subsets) is a core focus of the requirements.
firewall.quote: The Midcom protocol must be able to carry filtering rules, including but not limited to the 5-tuple, from the midcom agent to the middlebox.

rejected.why: RTP is cited only to justify port oddity and sequence requirements; the document is not about RTP.
Mutual authentication of agent and middlebox is required, but the document is not about an AAA framework.
Section 2.3 lists security requirements, but they are a small part of the document and no specific security mechanism is addressed.
The taxonomy's NAT traversal topic is about interactive traversal of NATs for real-time media (ICE, STUN, TURN). This document is about controlling middleboxes.
Rulesets are installed on middleboxes, but the document does not address policy information models.

gaps.name: Middlebox communications (midcom)
gaps.why: The document is about the midcom protocol between agents and middleboxes. The taxonomy has no tag for middlebox control in general, so NAT and firewall are the nearest fits.

RFC3305.title: Report from the Joint W3C/IETF URI Planning Interest Group: Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs), URLs, and Uniform Resource Names (URNs): Clarifications and Recommendations
RFC3305.summary: Joint W3C/IETF interest group report clarifying the relationship between URIs, URLs and URNs, describing registration of URI schemes and URN namespace IDs, and recommending follow-on work.

URN.why: Substantial sections cover registered, pending and unregistered URN NIDs and the NID registration procedures, so URN readers would want this.
URN.quote: A URN namespace is identified by a "Namespace ID" (NID), which is registered with IANA

URI.why: The document's main purpose is clarifying URI partitioning (classical vs contemporary view) and URI scheme registration, with recommendations for URI work.
URI.quote: addresses and attempts to clarify issues pertaining to URIs. This document addresses how URI space is partitioned and the relationship between URIs, URLs, and URNs

rejected.why: IRIs are mentioned only in one bullet as an unresolved follow-on issue, not addressed in their own right.
The IANA registries for schemes and NIDs are discussed, but only as the registration venue for URI/URN subjects; the document is not about IANA considerations or stewardship.
'hdl' is mentioned once as an example of an unregistered namespace; the Handle System is not the subject.
http: is used as an example of a URI scheme only.

RFC3306.title: Unicast-Prefix-based IPv6 Multicast Addresses
RFC3306.summary: Defines an IPv6 multicast address format embedding the unicast network prefix (P flag, plen, network prefix) so multicast addresses can be allocated along with unicast prefixes, including the SSM range FF3x::/32.

multicast.why: The document defines a new IPv6 multicast address format and allocation approach, with no multicast child tag fitting unicast-prefix-based allocation. The address-allocation subtopic (MADCAP/MALLOC) is only referenced as the thing being made unnecessary.
multicast.quote: This specification defines an extension to the multicast addressing architecture of the IP Version 6 protocol.

SSM.why: A dedicated section defines how to set P, plen and prefix to create the SSM range FF3x::/32, so SSM readers would want this.
SSM.quote: The unicast prefix-based IPv6 multicast address format supports Source-specific multicast addresses, as defined by [SSM ARCH].

IPv6.why: It extends IPv6 addressing architecture with a new multicast address format and ties address lifetime to IPv6 prefix valid lifetimes.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies an extension to the multicast portion of the IPv6 addressing architecture [ADDRARCH].

rejected.why: The document mentions MASC, AAP and the allocation architecture only as protocols that this scheme makes unnecessary; it does not specify or extend them.
The IPv6 tag already covers the addressing subject more specifically.
Router Advertisement Valid Lifetime is only referenced to bound address lifetime; the document is not about neighbor discovery.

RFC3307.title: Allocation Guidelines for IPv6 Multicast Addresses
RFC3307.summary: Specifies guidelines for choosing group IDs when allocating IPv6 multicast addresses (permanent addresses, permanent group IDs, dynamic server/host allocation) to avoid collisions at IPv6 and link layers, and creates an IANA registry for permanent group IDs.

addressing.why: The document is about allocation of IPv6 multicast addresses, specifically group ID ranges and flag bits, which is address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: guidelines that must be implemented by any entity responsible for allocating IPv6 multicast addresses

IPv6.why: The document concerns IPv6 multicast addressing and its mapping to link-layer addresses.
IPv6.quote: The purpose of these guidelines is to reduce the probability of IPv6 multicast address collision

MADCAP.why: Sets group ID range for MADCAP and other allocation servers, and the MALLOC-related allocation of dynamic multicast addresses is a substantial part of the guidance.
MADCAP.quote: The allocation of IPv6 multicast addresses, by a server, is defined in [RFC 2730].

rejected.why: IANA registry creation and allocation policy are present, but the document's main body is about address allocation guidelines, not IANA considerations guidance generally.
The parent is implied by MADCAP; the document is about address allocation rather than multicast routing or group membership.
SSM is only mentioned as an application example of the guidelines.
Ethernet mapping is only used as an example of link-layer address derivation.
RFC 1750 is only referenced for generating random group IDs.

gaps.name: IPv6 multicast address allocation
gaps.why: No tag specifically covers IPv6 multicast address assignment and group ID registries; addressing and MADCAP are the closest fits.

RFC3308.title: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) Differentiated Services Extension
RFC3308.summary: Defines two L2TP AVPs (CCDS and SDS) that let peers negotiate Diffserv per-hop behavior codes for the L2TP control connection and for individual sessions.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TP with new AVPs, new result codes and negotiation procedures for control connections and sessions.
L2TP.quote: mechanisms which enable the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) to negotiate desired Per Hop Behavior (PHB) code for the L2TP control connection

Diffserv.why: The extension signals Diffserv PHB codes and maps them to DSCPs in the outer IP header, and it discusses crossing DS domain boundaries. Diffserv readers would want it.
Diffserv.quote: The L2TP specification currently provides no mechanism for supporting diffserv (DS).

rejected.why: PPP is the payload that L2TP tunnels. The document does not specify or extend it.
Diffserv is the more specific tag for the QoS content, so the parent is implied.
L2TP is the specific tag, and the document is about L2TP rather than generic tunnelling.

RFC3309.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Checksum Change
RFC3309.summary: RFC 3309 replaces SCTP's Adler-32 checksum with CRC-32c, specifying the calculation and verification procedures, bit ordering, and sample code, and updates RFC 2960.

SCTP.why: The document is a normative update to SCTP (RFC 2960), changing the checksum in the SCTP common header and the send/receive procedures.
SCTP.quote: This document changes that checksum and updates SCTP to use a 32 bit CRC checksum.

CRC.why: Most of the document specifies the CRC-32c polynomial, bit ordering, register initialisation and implementation techniques, including the choice of generator polynomial.
CRC.quote: The 32 bit CRC is calculated as described for CRC-32c and uses the polynomial code 0x11EDC6F41

rejected.why: CRC is the more specific child covering this document's CRC-32c checksum, so the parent is implied. The document does not address the Internet checksum in general.
Ethernet CRC is only cited as a similar procedure and for bit-order comparison. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
This parent is implied by the SCTP tag. The document is not about transport in general.

RFC3310.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Digest Authentication Using Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA)
RFC3310.summary: Specifies a mapping of UMTS AKA parameters (RAND, AUTN, RES, AUTS) onto HTTP Digest authentication, so AKA acts as a one-time password generator for Digest, with applicability to SIP.

HTTP authentication.why: The document extends HTTP Digest with new algorithm, nonce and auts directives. Readers of HTTP authentication schemes would want it.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document specifies a mapping of AKA parameters onto HTTP Digest authentication.

cellular.why: The document builds on UMTS AKA, with its AuC, ISIM and sequence numbers. It adapts a 3GPP mechanism for use over HTTP and SIP.
cellular.quote: The Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) [6] mechanism performs authentication and session key distribution in Universal Mobile Telecommunications System (UMTS) networks.

rejected.why: SIP is used only as the example (REGISTER flows) and as an applicable embodiment. The document does not specify SIP.
AKA authentication is discussed, but the document does not address AAA frameworks.
Base64 is only the encoding used for the nonce and auts values.
The more specific HTTP authentication tag fits better.

RFC3311.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) UPDATE Method
RFC3311.summary: Defines the SIP UPDATE method, which lets a UA modify session parameters (via SDP offer/answer) within early or confirmed dialogs without affecting dialog state, including sending/receiving rules and a call flow.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new request method, specifying its handling by UAs and proxies and registering it.
SIP.quote: This specification defines the new UPDATE method for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer is the mechanism carried in UPDATE, but the document does not specify or extend SDP; it only applies RFC 3264 rules.
The IANA section only registers the UPDATE method; it is boilerplate relative to the main body.

RFC3312.title: Integration of Resource Management and Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3312.summary: RFC 3312 defines a generic SDP precondition framework (curr/des/conf attributes, qos type) for SIP offer/answer so that session establishment and alerting are suspended until network resource reservation is complete, adding the 580 status code and the "precondition" option tag.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new option tag, a new 580 status code, and call-flow behaviour for suspending/resuming session establishment using PRACK/UPDATE.
SIP.quote: We define the option tag "precondition" for use in the Require and Supported header fields.

SDP.why: It defines new SDP media attributes (curr, des, conf) and their offer/answer negotiation rules, which is central to the document.
SDP.quote: We define the following media level SDP attributes:

QoS.why: The qos precondition type requires reservation of network resources before alerting. It defines no new reservation mechanism, but QoS integration is a main subject.
QoS.quote: This document also discusses how network quality of service can be made a precondition for establishment of sessions initiated by the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

rejected.why: RSVP only appears as an example reservation mechanism in the call flows; the document does not specify or extend it.
RTP is mentioned only to say no RTP/RTCP packets are sent while establishment is suspended.
The IANA section registers a precondition-type registry, but this is boilerplate, not the main subject.

RFC3313.title: Private Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Extensions for Media Authorization
RFC3313.summary: Informational RFC defining the private SIP header P-Media-Authorization, which carries QoS media authorization tokens from a QoS-enabled proxy to user agents for use in RSVP resource reservations within closed administrative domains.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP header field and the UAC, UAS and proxy procedures for it, so it is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines a private SIP header extension to support a media authorization scheme.
SIP.section: 5. Changes to SIP to Support Media Authorization

QoS.why: The aim is to authorize network QoS for media flows through policy control. Tokens are carried as RSVP policy elements, and the PDP and PEP framework is used. No more specific QoS technology tag fits: RSVP and COPS are only used in the example call flows.
QoS.quote: integrate QoS admission control with call signaling and help guard against denial of service attacks

rejected.why: RSVP is the reservation mechanism that consumes the token, and it appears in the example call flows. The document says the reservation mechanism is not specified here, so it is not about RSVP.
COPS is only mentioned in the example flows, as the exchange between the edge router and the PDP. The document does not specify it.
Proxies may inspect SDP bodies to decide what QoS to authorize, but the document does not define or extend SDP.
The document is about authorizing QoS for media. Because QoS is tagged, the generic authorization topic adds nothing.

RFC3314.title: Recommendations for IPv6 in Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Standards
RFC3314.summary: IPv6 WG design-team recommendations to 3GPP: allow multiple /64 prefixes per primary PDP context, never share a prefix across primary PDP contexts, and allow multiple (including random/privacy) interface identifiers, in GPRS/UMTS.

cellular.why: The whole document concerns IPv6 over 3GPP GPRS/UMTS networks (PDP contexts, GGSN, SGSN), which is the cellular IP interworking subject.
cellular.quote: recommendations from the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) IPv6 Working Group to the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) community regarding the use of IPv6 in the 3GPP standards

IPv6.why: Core content is IPv6 addressing architecture, prefix assignment and interface identifiers as applied to 3GPP, and the deployment of IPv6 in that setting.
IPv6.quote: The recommendations in this document are primarily related to IPv6 address assignment.

SLAAC.why: The recommendations hinge on how stateless address autoconfiguration, Router Advertisements and privacy identifiers should work over PDP contexts.
SLAAC.quote: The stateless IPv6 autoconfiguration works differently in GPRS than in Ethernet networks.

rejected.why: PPP is mentioned for laptop attachment and as the basis of GPRS autoconfiguration, but the document is not about PPP itself.
Router Advertisements and DAD are discussed only as part of autoconfiguration, not specified or analysed in their own right.
A child tag (IPv6) already covers the addressing subject; the HD-ratio discussion is a minor part.
NAT is only mentioned as something the recommendations discourage.
Stateful configuration is only mentioned in passing.

RFC3315.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC3315.summary: RFC 3315 specifies DHCPv6, the stateful client/server/relay protocol for assigning IPv6 addresses and configuration parameters, including messages, options, DUIDs, identity associations and authentication.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document defines DHCPv6: message types, client/server/relay behaviour, options, DUIDs and IAs.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes DHCP for IPv6 (DHCP), a client/server protocol that provides managed configuration of devices.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the stateful counterpart and is compatible with SLAAC, but the document does not specify SLAAC.
IPsec is only used to secure relay-to-server messages in section 21.1; it is a security mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
HMAC-MD5 is the algorithm inside the DHCP authentication option. It is a mechanism the document uses, not its subject.
UDP is only the transport for DHCP messages (ports 546 and 547).
Dynamic DNS updates are mentioned as background only.
DHCPv6 is a child of IPv6 in the taxonomy, via DHCP. IPv6 is the environment, not the subject.

RFC3316.title: Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) for Some Second and Third Generation Cellular Hosts
RFC3316.summary: Informational guidance on which IPv6 specifications (basic IP, IPsec, mobility) a cellular host on GPRS/UMTS 3GPP networks should implement, with notes on their use over cellular links.

cellular.why: The document profiles IPv6 usage for hosts on 3GPP GPRS/UMTS cellular networks, including GGSN, PDP context and addressing in the 3GPP model.
cellular.quote: This document considers IPv6 for cellular hosts that attach to the General Packet Radio Service (GPRS), or Universal Mobile Telecommunications System (UMTS) networks.

IPv6.why: It is an IPv6 node-requirements style profile covering addressing, ND, autoconfiguration, ICMPv6, and related specifications for cellular hosts.
IPv6.quote: This document lists IPv6 specifications with discussion on the use of these specifications when operating over cellular interfaces.

IPsec.why: A whole major section covers which IPsec/IKE specifications cellular hosts must support and issues like IKE with ICMPv6 neighbor discovery.
IPsec.quote: IPsec [RFC-2401] is a fundamental part of IPv6, and support for AH and ESP is described as mandatory in the specifications.

rejected.why: Discussed in a subsection with 3GPP-specific notes, but it is one item in a broad profile, not the document's main subject.
Covered briefly and in the appendix, but only as one component of the overall profile.
Section 4 explicitly says IP mobility is not relevant to this document.
Mentioned in one short paragraph as optional.
The document explicitly leaves transition mechanisms for further study.
IPv6 over PPP is one short subsection, not a main subject.

RFC3317.title: Differentiated Services Quality of Service Policy Information Base
RFC3317.summary: Defines the DiffServ QoS Policy Information Base (PIB): provisioning classes for classifiers, meters, actions, droppers, queues, schedulers and device capabilities, used by a COPS-PR diffServ client to configure DiffServ routers.

Diffserv.why: The whole document specifies provisioning classes for configuring DiffServ functional elements (classifier, meter, action, dropper, queue, scheduler, data path).
Diffserv.quote: This document describes a Policy Information Base (PIB) for a device implementing the Differentiated Services Architecture.

COPS.why: The PIB is a policy provisioning data model for COPS-PR, defines a new COPS client type, and the policy provisioning model (PDP/PEP, PRCs) is central.
COPS.quote: The PRCs defined in this DiffServ QoS PIB are intended for use by the COPS-PR diffServ client type.

rejected.why: A PIB is structured with SPPI rather than SMI, and it is a distinct policy provisioning data model, not a MIB module.
The document references SNMP textual conventions but does not use or specify SNMP.
Random and tail dropper parameters are modelled, but the document is about configuration, not queue management algorithms.
Related, but COPS already covers the policy provisioning protocol aspect and Diffserv the main subject; the PIB is a QoS-specific policy model.

gaps.name: Policy Information Base (PIB) / SPPI policy provisioning
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PIBs or the Structure of Policy Provisioning Information. COPS only partly fits.

RFC3318.title: Framework Policy Information Base
RFC3318.summary: Defines the Framework PIB and TC PIB modules: PRovisioning Classes and textual conventions common to all COPS-PR clients, covering roles, capability sets, PIB contexts and incarnation, error reporting, device limits, and basic classifier and marker classes.

COPS.why: The document specifies PIB modules for COPS-PR policy provisioning, including request-state handling, contexts and errors over COPS. COPS and policy provisioning is the subject area.
COPS.quote: This document defines a set of PRovisioning Classes (PRCs) and textual conventions that are common to all clients that provision policy using Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol for Provisioning.

policy management.why: It defines policy information models: roles, role combinations, capability sets, filters and markers used by PDPs to configure PEPs.
policy management.quote: Rather than specifying policies explicitly for each interface of all devices in the network, policies are specified in terms of interface functionality.

rejected.why: A PIB is SMI-based and resembles a MIB, but it is a policy information base for COPS-PR, not a MIB module for SNMP.
It borrows SMIv2 textual conventions but is not carried over SNMP.
It imports DscpOrAny and defines IP filters that match on the DSCP, but the document is not about Diffserv.
The 802 filter and marker classes touch VLAN and 802.1Q priority, but only as generic classifier elements.
The IP filter supports IPv6 addresses and flow labels, but only as match fields.

gaps.name: PIB (Policy Information Base) / SPPI
gaps.why: The document defines PIB modules in the Structure of Policy Provisioning Information. The taxonomy has no tag for policy provisioning information bases; COPS under QoS is the nearest fit.

RFC3319.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv6) Options for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Servers
RFC3319.summary: Defines two DHCPv6 options (SIP Servers Domain Name List and IPv6 Address List) that let a SIP client discover its local outbound proxy server, with client and server operation rules.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 options (codes 21 and 22) and their client and server behaviour, so it belongs on the DHCPv6 page.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol version 6 (DHCPv6) option that contains a list of domain names or IPv6 addresses

SIP.why: The options exist for SIP outbound proxy discovery, and the document ties into RFC 3263 server-location procedures. SIP readers looking for configuration of outbound proxies would want it.
SIP.quote: allow SIP clients to locate a local SIP server that is to be used for all outbound SIP requests, a so-called outbound proxy server

rejected.why: Domain names use RFC 1035 label encoding and NAPTR/SRV resolution is referenced, but DNS is only the encoding and substrate. Nothing new is defined for DNS.
This is a discovery mechanism for SIP servers, but the DHCPv6 tag already covers it more specifically. The topic is not addressed in its own right.
IPv6 addresses are carried in the option, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The DHCPv6 child tag fits more precisely. The IPv4 DHCP option is only an informative reference.

RFC3320.title: Signaling Compression (SigComp)
RFC3320.summary: Defines SigComp, a lossless signaling-message compression layer built on a Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM), with its architecture, message format, state handling, feedback and instruction set, targeted at SIP and RTSP.

SigComp.why: The whole document specifies SigComp: the architecture, message format, state handler and UDVM.
SigComp.quote: This document defines Signaling Compression (SigComp), a solution for compressing messages generated by application protocols such as the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)

rejected.why: SIP is the main application SigComp compresses but is not specified or extended here.
The document is about SigComp, which has its own tag. It is not a generic compression data format, so the child tag fits better.
DEFLATE is only an example algorithm the UDVM can be programmed to decompress.
SCTP is one of several transports listed that SigComp can run over, nothing more.
SHA-1 is used only to compute state identifiers.
The CRC instruction reuses the PPP FCS polynomial as an integrity check and is a minor detail.

RFC3321.title: Signaling Compression (SigComp) - Extended Operations
RFC3321.summary: Describes extended SigComp mechanisms (explicit acknowledgement, shared compression, cross-session state, checkpoint state, implicit deletion) implementable with the UDVM instructions of RFC 3320.

SigComp.why: The whole document specifies extended operations of SigComp: explicit acknowledgement, shared compression, checkpoint state and related state handling.
SigComp.quote: This document describes how to implement mechanisms with [SIGCOMP] to significantly improve the compression efficiency compared to per-message compression.

rejected.why: SIP is only the example signaling protocol that SigComp compresses; the document does not specify or extend SIP.
The SHA-1 UDVM instruction is used only to compute state identifiers; the document is not about the hash algorithm.
This is a general lossless data compression topic, but the document is specifically about SigComp, which is already tagged.
SigComp compresses signaling messages rather than protocol headers on constrained links, so the topic does not fit.

RFC3322.title: Signaling Compression (SigComp) Requirements & Assumptions
RFC3322.summary: RFC 3322 sets out the motivation, assumptions and requirements for a generic signaling compression scheme (later SigComp) to cut SIP/SDP/RTSP message size and call-setup delay over cellular radio links.

SigComp.why: The document exists to state requirements for the signaling compression scheme that became SigComp, so readers of SigComp would expect it.
SigComp.quote: requirements and motivations for the development of a scheme for compression and decompression of messages from signaling protocols

SIP.why: SIP call setup is the main motivating case, with a SIP call-setup delay estimate in section 2.1. SIP is not itself specified or extended here, but SIP readers would want the motivation.
SIP.quote: With the introduction of SIP/SDP (Session Initiation Protocol/Session Description Protocol) to cellular devices, compression of the signaling messages should be considered

rejected.why: The scheme is developed in the ROHC WG and must coexist with ROHC, but the document is about signaling message compression, not header compression.
RTSP is only named as another text-based protocol the scheme should handle, and is not analysed in its own right.
SDP is only the message body carried in SIP, discussed as a target for compression, not specified or extended.
Cellular radio characteristics are the motivation, but the document does not cover IP over 3GPP systems.
The document is about compressing signaling messages, not protocol headers. ROHC is mentioned only as a coexistence requirement.
The taxonomy's compression topic covers lossless data compression formats. This document gives requirements for signaling compression, which SigComp covers more specifically.

RFC3323.title: A Privacy Mechanism for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3323.summary: RFC 3323 defines a SIP Privacy header, a "privacy service" intermediary role, and guidelines for user agents to build messages that withhold personal identity information.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field, option-tag, and a privacy service role, and specifies user agent and intermediary behavior for SIP messages.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new SIP header, Privacy, that can be used to specify privacy handling for requests and responses.

privacy.why: The document is substantively about privacy mechanisms and requirements for identity withholding, which readers of the privacy subject would want.
privacy.quote: Privacy is defined in this document as the withholding of the identity of a person (and related personal information) from one or more parties

rejected.why: SDP bodies are mentioned only as the place where session addresses appear; the document does not specify SDP changes.
Only recommended as end-to-end protection when using session privacy; not specified here.
TLS and SIPS are recommended as transport security to the privacy service, but it is only a substrate.
CPL is mentioned once as a way to route requests to an anonymization service; not a subject of the document.
The reserved 'anonymous.invalid' hostname is used as a recommendation, but the document does not define or analyze special-use names.
Authentication is explicitly out of scope per the Security Considerations.

RFC3324.title: Short Term Requirements for Network Asserted Identity
RFC3324.summary: Informational requirements document for how SIP network intermediaries generate and exchange Network Asserted Identity (sip:, sips:, tel: URIs) within Trust Domains and to directly connected UAs, including privacy indications.

SIP.why: The whole document states requirements for a SIP extension for conveying authenticated identity between proxies and UAs, which is the subject of SIP readers.
SIP.quote: A Network Asserted Identity is an identity initially derived by a SIP network intermediary as a result of an authentication process.

rejected.why: tel: URIs are only one permitted identity type; the document does not specify or extend the scheme.
Privacy indications are a requirement section, but the document is not a privacy threat model; it is a small part of the identity requirements.
Authentication is the source of the asserted identity but the document concerns the exchange of the resulting identity within trust domains, not authentication mechanisms.
STIR is about caller-ID authentication in a later design; this document predates it and addresses trusted network assertion only.

gaps.name: Network Asserted Identity / Trust Domain (P-Asserted-Identity requirements)
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers SIP identity assertion and trust domains specifically; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC3325.title: Private Extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for Asserted Identity within Trusted Networks
RFC3325.summary: Defines SIP private extensions (P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity headers and the "id" Privacy type) letting trusted SIP servers in a Trust Domain assert authenticated user identity and honour privacy requests.

SIP.why: The document specifies new SIP header fields, proxy and UA behaviour, and a new Privacy priv-value for SIP.
SIP.quote: private extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) that enable a network of trusted SIP servers to assert the identity of authenticated users

rejected.why: Privacy is handled through the SIP Privacy header from RFC 3323. This document applies that mechanism to identity and does not define a general privacy model.
The document explicitly leaves the means of authenticating users out of scope. It only consumes the result, for example from Digest authentication.
TLS appears only in the non-normative example Spec(T) and the Security Considerations, as a hop-by-hop security mechanism.
tel URIs are allowed as values in the identity headers but are not specified or extended here.
SIP Digest authentication is only the example way a proxy learns the user's identity. The document does not define it.
Telephony networks motivate the work, but the document does not specify interworking or gateway behaviour.

RFC3326.title: The Reason Header Field for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3326.summary: Defines the SIP Reason header field, which conveys why a SIP request was issued (e.g., a SIP status code or Q.850 cause) and can encapsulate a final status code in a provisional response to address the HERFP problem.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field, its syntax, semantics, proxy behaviour and IANA registry for protocol values.
SIP.quote: This document defines a header field, Reason, that provides this information.

PSTN interop.why: A substantial use case is carrying ITU-T Q.850 cause values from ISUP in SIP requests at PSTN gateways, so readers of PSTN interworking would want it. It is a topic tag chosen directly because no child tag fits: SIP-T covers ISUP encapsulation, which this document does not define.
PSTN interop.quote: The PSTN gateway of figure 2 generates an INVITE that has to be CANCELed when a REL (release) message is received from the ISUP side.

rejected.why: The document only carries a Q.850 cause value in a Reason header field. It does not define ISUP encapsulation or full SIP-T/SIP-I interworking.
SDP offers and answers appear only in the example scenarios and are not the subject of the document.
SIP header syntax is borrowed from HTTP conventions, but nothing about HTTP is specified or extended.
The IANA section creates a Reason Protocols sub-registry. That is boilerplate, not the main body of the document.

RFC3327.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Extension Header Field for Registering Non-Adjacent Contacts
RFC3327.summary: Defines the SIP "Path" extension header field and "path" option tag, letting proxies between a UA and registrar record themselves during REGISTER so the home proxy can route later requests back through them.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field and option tag, and specifies procedures at UA, proxies, registrar and home proxy for REGISTER handling.
SIP.quote: This document defines an extension header field, "Path" which provides such a mechanism.

rejected.why: Only recommended in Security Considerations to protect the Path in responses; not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only as a security mechanism for integrity protection in Security Considerations.
Mentioned only as an alternative integrity mechanism in Security Considerations.
Session descriptions are omitted from the examples and are not discussed.

RFC3329.title: Security Mechanism Agreement for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3329.summary: RFC 3329 defines SIP header fields (Security-Client, Security-Server, Security-Verify), the 494 response code and the sec-agree option tag. They let a SIP user agent and its first-hop entity securely negotiate a security mechanism (TLS, HTTP Digest, IPsec) and resist bidding-down attacks.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with new header fields, a new response code and an option tag for security mechanism agreement.
SIP.quote: This document defines new functionality for negotiating the security mechanisms used between a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) user agent and its next-hop SIP entity.

rejected.why: TLS is one of the negotiable mechanisms and is only selected and initiated. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
IPsec (IKE, manual keying, ipsec-3gpp) is a negotiated option. The document does not specify or extend IPsec itself, though the appendix gives SIP parameter syntax for it.
Digest is reused unchanged to protect the negotiation. The document states it introduces no change to HTTP Digest.
The IANA section registers header fields, a response code and mechanism names. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.

RFC3330.title: Special-Use IPv4 Addresses
RFC3330.summary: Informational IANA catalogue of special-use IPv4 address blocks (private, loopback, link-local, test-net, benchmark, 6to4 relay anycast, multicast, reserved) and the process for assigning new ones.

IPv4.why: The document is a catalogue of special-use IPv4 address blocks and their status, which is the IPv4 address lifecycle.
IPv4.quote: This document describes the global and other specialized IPv4 address blocks that have been assigned by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

IANA.why: Section 4 describes how IANA makes assignments of IPv4 blocks for new specialized uses, and the whole document records IANA allocation practice.
IANA.quote: the IANA is responsible for ensuring assignments of IPv4 addresses as needed in support of the Internet Standards Process.
IANA.section: 4. Assignments of IPv4 Blocks for New Specialized Uses

rejected.why: IPv4 is the more specific tag under internet layer; addressing is a sibling topic and IPv4 already covers the address-block content.
Private-use blocks are listed, but the document does not address NAT behaviour.
224.0.0.0/4 gets a single entry that defers to RFC 3171, so multicast is not a substantial subject here.
The 6to4 relay anycast prefix is one row in the table, defined elsewhere in RFC 3068.
198.18.0.0/15 is listed for benchmark testing, but the document does not cover benchmarking methodology.

RFC3331.title: Signaling System 7 (SS7) Message Transfer Part 2 (MTP2) - User Adaptation Layer
RFC3331.summary: RFC 3331 defines M2UA, a SIGTRAN adaptation layer that backhauls SS7 MTP2-user (MTP3) signalling between a Signalling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller over SCTP, including ASP/AS state management, messages, and link key registration.

SIGTRAN.why: M2UA is one of the SIGTRAN SS7-over-IP signalling transport adaptation layers; the whole document specifies its messages, procedures and state machines.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document defines a protocol for the backhauling of Signaling System 7 Message Transfer Part 2 (SS7 MTP2) User signalling messages over IP
