rejected.why: SCTP is only the underlying transport M2UA runs over; the document defines nothing new about SCTP itself beyond a payload protocol identifier.
IPsec is only recommended in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The MGC is the peer of the SG, but the document doesn't specify gateway control protocols.
A parent of SIGTRAN, so it is implied by the SIGTRAN tag and not listed separately.

RFC3332.title: Signaling System 7 (SS7) Message Transfer Part 3 (MTP3) - User Adaptation Layer (M3UA)
RFC3332.summary: Defines M3UA, the SIGTRAN adaptation layer that carries SS7 MTP3-User messages (ISUP, SCCP) over SCTP between a Signalling Gateway and Application Server Processes, with its messages, procedures, routing keys and redundancy models.

SIGTRAN.why: M3UA is one of the SIGTRAN adaptation layers for SS7 signalling transport over IP. The whole document specifies it: messages, ASP/AS state machines, routing keys and SS7 network management interworking.
SIGTRAN.quote: This memo defines a protocol for supporting the transport of any SS7 MTP3-User signalling (e.g., ISUP and SCCP messages) over IP

rejected.why: M3UA runs over SCTP and uses its streams and association primitives. The document does not specify or extend SCTP, apart from the IANA payload protocol identifier.
The parent topic is implied by SIGTRAN, so it is not listed separately.
IPsec ESP and ISAKMP are mentioned only in Security Considerations.
No SIP or ISUP encapsulation in SIP appears in the document. ISUP is only an example MTP3-User.
TCP is mentioned once as an alternative transport and is not the subject.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and the document's main body is not about IANA registries.

RFC3334.title: Policy-Based Accounting
RFC3334.summary: RFC 3334 describes policy-based accounting: using standardized accounting policies, exchanged between AAA servers, to configure meters, collectors and accounting in intra- and inter-domain scenarios, integrated with the AAA authorization framework.

AAA.why: The document defines how accounting policies are exchanged between AAA servers and how accounting integrates into the AAA authorization framework.
AAA.quote: This document describes building blocks and message sequences for policy-based accounting in the generic AAA architecture (RFC 2903).

policy management.why: Policy conditions and actions that configure meters and collectors are central, making this policy-based management of accounting infrastructure.
policy management.quote: Accounting policies describe rules for generation, transport and storage of accounting data.

rejected.why: COPS-PR is only mentioned as one possible configuration protocol; the document does not specify it.
SNMP is mentioned only as a way to configure and read meters; it is not what the document is about.
Diffserv is used only as one illustrative example scenario.
Metering is a building block, but the document focuses on accounting configuration, not measurement methods.
NetFlow and NeTraMet appear only as example meters, and no flow export protocol is specified.
The printing service is only an illustrative example.

gaps.name: Accounting / charging / billing
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about accounting management, meaning resource-usage accounting records, charging and billing, and the taxonomy has no accounting topic outside AAA.

RFC3335.title: MIME-based Secure Peer-to-Peer Business Data Interchange over the Internet
RFC3335.summary: RFC 3335 specifies how to exchange EDI, XML and other business data securely over SMTP using MIME packaging, S/MIME or OpenPGP security, and signed MDN receipts (with a new Received-content-MIC field) for non-repudiation of receipt.

EDI.why: The whole document defines secure EDI interchange over Internet mail, including message structure and signed receipts.
EDI.quote: This document describes how to exchange structured business data securely using SMTP transport for Electronic Data Interchange, (EDI - either the American Standards Committee X12 or UN/EDIFACT

S/MIME.why: Section 4.3 and 5 profile how S/MIME signing and encryption are applied to EDI messages and signed receipts.
S/MIME.quote: Authentication and privacy are obtained by using Cryptographic Message Syntax (S/MIME) or OpenPGP security body parts.

OpenPGP.why: PGP/MIME is the alternative security format profiled for EDI messages and receipts (section 4.2).
OpenPGP.quote: Digital envelope security based on the Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) standard (Zimmerman), integrated with MIME Security Multiparts [6].

MIME.why: The document defines MIME structures (multipart/signed, multipart/encrypted, multipart/report) for EDI payloads.
MIME.quote: The data is packaged using standard MIME content-types.

message format.why: It extends MDN (message disposition notification) with a new field, profiles disposition values, and registers signed-receipt options.
message format.quote: The "Received-content-MIC" extension field is set when the integrity of the received message is verified.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport; the document defines nothing new about it.
Covered by the more specific tags; the document is not about email architecture generally.
CMS is relied on via S/MIME; the document does not specify it.
It registers only parameters and an MDN field, not a media type; it reuses RFC 1767 types.
EDI is the more specific tag; no payment protocol is involved.
Hash algorithms are only mentioned as MIC choices, not the subject.

RFC3336.title: PPP Over Asynchronous Transfer Mode Adaptation Layer 2 (AAL2)
RFC3336.summary: Specifies PPP encapsulation over ATM AAL2 using SSSAR segmentation and the AAL2 CPS, with a 16-bit CRC, for bandwidth-efficient transport of small packets such as compressed RTP voice.

ATM.why: The document defines how PPP is carried over ATM AAL2 (CPS, SSSAR, CIDs), which is IP over ATM.
ATM.quote: This document describes the use of ATM Adaptation Layer 2 (AAL2) for framing PPP encapsulated packets.

PPP.why: It specifies a PPP encapsulation and link-layer operation (LCP defaults, MRU, framing) over AAL2.
PPP.quote: Applications implementing PPP over AAL2 MUST meet all the requirements of PPP [1].

rejected.why: The 16-bit CRC (Q.921 FCS polynomial) is specified as part of the encapsulation, but the document is not about CRC polynomial choice itself.
CRTP is used in the example implementation and as motivation, but the document does not specify or extend it.
RTP voice is a motivating use case only.
Header compression is only a motivating example, not what the document specifies.
Unrelated PPP transport; this document is over AAL2, not Ethernet.

gaps.name: ATM AAL2 (I.363.2 / I.366.1 SSSAR)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has ATM but no AAL2-specific tag; the ATM tag covers this document adequately.

RFC3337.title: Class Extensions for PPP over Asynchronous Transfer Mode Adaptation Layer 2
RFC3337.summary: Defines class extensions to PPP over AAL2 that give multi-class fragmentation/preemption for real-time traffic over a single ATM VC by using SSSAR segmentation and separate AAL2 CPS Channel IDs per class, as an alternative to Multi-Class Multi-Link PPP.

ATM.why: The document specifies how AAL2 CPS Channel IDs and SSSAR are used on an ATM virtual circuit to carry PPP traffic classes. It is about IP/PPP over ATM AAL2.
ATM.quote: this document defines a set of class extensions to PPP over AAL2 [1] that implement equivalent functionality to Multi Class Multi Link PPP over a single ATM virtual circuit

PPP.why: It extends PPP over AAL2 with multi-class fragmentation and preemption, an alternative to Multi-Class Multi-Link PPP.
PPP.quote: the AAL2 CPS Channel ID is used to identify the preemption class that a packet fragment belongs to
PPP.section: 3. Class Extensions for PPP over AAL2

rejected.why: RTP voice is only the motivating example of small-packet traffic. The document does not specify anything about RTP.
The document is about preemption and scheduling of fragments, but its subject is PPP over AAL2 link-layer encapsulation. It does not define a QoS architecture or signalling.
RFC 2689, which describes header compression, is referenced only as architecture background. This document does not address header compression.

RFC3338.title: Dual Stack Hosts Using "Bump-in-the-API" (BIA)
RFC3338.summary: Experimental spec for Bump-in-the-API (BIA), a dual-stack host mechanism that translates IPv4 socket API calls to IPv6 ones (with name resolver, address mapper and function mapper) so IPv4-only applications can talk to IPv6 hosts.

IPv6 transition.why: The document defines a dual-stack host transition mechanism for IPv4 applications to reach IPv6 hosts, and no child technology tag fits it, so the parent topic is used.
IPv6 transition.quote: allows for the hosts to communicate with other IPv6 hosts using existing IPv4 applications

sockets API.why: The mechanism works by intercepting and translating socket API calls, with an appendix listing the intercepted functions. Readers of sockets API extensions would want it.
sockets API.quote: it translates the IPv4 socket API function into IPv6 socket API function and vice versa

rejected.why: SIIT is referenced as the IP header translation method that BIA avoids, and only for optional ICMP value translation. BIA is not about SIIT.
NAT-PT is compared against and its security considerations are relied on, but this is not a NAT specification.
The name resolver synthesizes A records from AAAA records at the resolver library level. This is not a DNS protocol or operations document.
The document is about transition and coexistence, not the IPv6 specification, addressing or deployment, so the transition topic is the better fit.
The mechanism is a host-local API translator with no network-based stateful translation.

RFC3339.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
RFC3339.summary: RFC 3339 defines an Internet timestamp format, a profile of ISO 8601 with ABNF grammar, covering UTC offsets, leap seconds, and two-digit year avoidance.

date-time formats.why: The whole document specifies the Internet Date/Time format (RFC 3339 timestamps), including offsets, leap seconds and restrictions.
date-time formats.quote: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to express the grammar; the document is not about ABNF itself.
NTP is mentioned only as one mechanism to obtain UTC for devices with local clocks; the document is not about it.
Clock synchronization is only touched on in one section about unqualified local time; the subject is timestamp representation.
Email date format (RFC 2822) is referenced for comparison only.
Two-digit year ambiguity is discussed briefly in one section, but the document is not a Y2K readiness document.

RFC3340.title: The Application Exchange Core
RFC3340.summary: RFC 3340 specifies APEX Core, an extensible asynchronous message relaying service for application programs, defined as a BEEP profile with endpoints, relays, data/attach/bind/terminate operations, options, and a report service.

APEX.why: The document defines the APEX core protocol itself: its entities, operations, options and services.
APEX.quote: APEX provides an extensible, asynchronous message relaying service for application layer programs.

BEEP.why: APEX is registered as a BEEP profile, with profile identification, channel creation and tuning profile requirements specified. Readers of BEEP would want to find this profile.
BEEP.quote: APEX is specified, in part, as a BEEP [1] "profile".

rejected.why: The APEX tag sits under applications, not messaging. It is a datagram relay for applications, not an interpersonal store-and-forward mail system.
XML is only the encoding for control messages, with DTDs as the syntax. It is the substrate, not the subject.
MIME multipart/related is used to carry content, but only as a substrate.
SRV records are used to locate relays, but nothing new is defined for DNS.
TLS and SASL are mentioned only as required BEEP tuning profiles in Security Considerations.
The presence service is only mentioned and is defined in a separate document.

RFC3341.title: The Application Exchange (APEX) Access Service
RFC3341.summary: Specifies the APEX access service, a well-known endpoint (apex=access) on the APEX relaying mesh that manages access-control entries (owner/actor/actions) via query, get, set, allow, deny and reply operations.

APEX.why: The document defines an APEX service: its operations, access entry format, matching rules and registration. Readers of the APEX subject would expect it.
APEX.quote: This memo describes the Application Exchange (APEX) access service, addressed as the well-known endpoint "apex=access".

rejected.why: BEEP is only the substrate carrying APEX messages; the document merely shows example payload framing.
XML and a DTD are used to encode operations, but the document is not about XML usage itself.
It is an access-control service, but the APEX tag is more specific; no additional authorization technology is specified beyond APEX's own mechanism.
MIME multipart framing appears only in examples of BEEP payloads.
The presence service is merely referenced as an example of an action controlled by access entries.

RFC3342.title: The Application Exchange (APEX) Option Party Pack, Part Deux!
RFC3342.summary: RFC 3342 defines four APEX options (attachOverride, dataTiming, hold4Endpoint, dataHopping) that alter the default best-effort behaviour of the APEX relaying mesh, including delivery timing, queuing for unattached endpoints and hop-count loop detection.

APEX.why: The whole document specifies option extensions to the Application Exchange (APEX) core protocol, so the APEX page is the natural home.
APEX.quote: This memo defines various options to change the default behavior of APEX's "relaying mesh".

rejected.why: APEX messages and the DTD are XML-based, but XML is only the encoding substrate; the document defines no XML usage guidance.
The dataTiming option is acknowledged as similar to the SMTP Deliver By extension, but that is only a comparison in the acknowledgements.
IP TTL is mentioned only as an analogy for the dataHopping option.
APEX is a datagram relaying service rather than a store-and-forward messaging system; the APEX tag is the more specific fit.
The document states that dataTiming provides no priority functionality, so it is not about quality of service.

RFC3343.title: The Application Exchange (APEX) Presence Service
RFC3343.summary: Defines the APEX presence service, a well-known endpoint (apex=presence) on the APEX relaying mesh, with subscribe, watch, publish, terminate and notify operations for managing presence information, plus its XML DTD.

APEX.why: The document specifies an APEX service, including its well-known endpoint, operations, access tokens and DTD, so it belongs under APEX.
APEX.quote: This memo describes the Application Exchange (APEX) presence service, addressed as the well-known endpoint "apex=presence".

instant messaging.why: The document defines presence entries, publication, subscription and watcher notification. This is the presence half of instant messaging and presence, so readers of that subject would want it.
instant messaging.quote: The presence service is used to manage presence information for APEX endpoints.

rejected.why: BEEP is only the transport substrate for APEX messages. The document shows how payloads are carried over it but defines nothing new about BEEP.
XML (with a DTD) is only the encoding for the operations, not the subject of the document.
The presence entry format is APEX-specific (tuple, destination, availableUntil), not PIDF.
The document is not SIP-based and does not use SIMPLE event packages.
MIME appears only as the way payloads are wrapped for BEEP, which is a substrate detail.

RFC3344.title: IP Mobility Support for IPv4
RFC3344.summary: RFC 3344 specifies Mobile IPv4: agent discovery, registration of care-of addresses with a home agent, tunnelling of datagrams to mobile nodes, and ARP/proxy ARP handling, replacing RFC 3220.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document defines the Mobile IPv4 protocol: home agents, foreign agents, registration, agent discovery and routing.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document specifies protocol enhancements that allow transparent routing of IP datagrams to mobile nodes in the Internet.

rejected.why: Proxy and gratuitous ARP rules are specified in Section 4.6, but only as a supporting mechanism for Mobile IP, not as a new ARP spec.
Tunnelling (IP-in-IP, minimal, GRE) is used as a mechanism, with encapsulation defined in other RFCs.
ICMP Router Discovery is extended for agent advertisement, but the document is about Mobile IP, not ICMP itself.
HMAC-MD5 is the default authentication algorithm, used only as a mechanism.
Registration messages run over UDP port 434, which is only the substrate.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA.

RFC3345.title: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Persistent Route Oscillation Condition
RFC3345.summary: Informational RFC describing two types (Type I and II) of persistent BGP route oscillation caused by MED comparison with route reflection or AS confederations, with topologies, step-by-step examples, and design workarounds.

route reflection.why: The document analyses how route reflection and confederations (the tag covers both) cause persistent oscillation with MED, and gives design guidance for them.
route reflection.quote: the BGP scaling mechanisms defined in "BGP Route Reflection - An Alternative to Full Mesh IBGP" and "Autonomous System Confederations for BGP" will introduce persistent BGP route oscillation

BGP.why: The document is about a BGP best-path selection and MED problem, and gives operational design workarounds. It is an analysis of BGP behaviour.
BGP.quote: The persistent route oscillation behavior is deterministic and can be avoided by employing some rudimentary BGP network design principles

rejected.why: Design guidance is specific to BGP iBGP scaling, so the more specific BGP and route reflection tags fit better.
The oscillation is a stability problem, not a security issue; the Security Considerations section says no new concerns.

RFC3346.title: Applicability Statement for Traffic Engineering with MPLS
RFC3346.summary: Informational applicability statement describing where MPLS-based traffic engineering is useful in ISP networks, deployment and operational considerations, and its limitations.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document is about when and how traffic engineering with MPLS applies in ISP networks, including use cases (congestion avoidance, parallel links, affinities, re-optimization), operational considerations and limitations.
traffic engineering.quote: This document describes the applicability of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) to traffic engineering in IP networks.

MPLS.why: MPLS LSP-tunnels are the mechanism whose deployment and limitations are discussed, so MPLS readers would want this applicability statement.
MPLS.quote: MPLS combines the ability to monitor point-to-point traffic statistics between two routers and the capability to control the forwarding paths

rejected.why: Referenced as the protocol whose operational applicability this document augments, but the document does not specify or analyse RSVP-TE itself.
Only mentioned as an IGP with TE extensions; not the subject.
Only mentioned as an IGP with TE extensions; not the subject.
Only cited as a signaling protocol with TE extensions.
Section 4.4 on network measurement is brief and supporting, not a substantial focus.
Network management aspects are a short subsection, not the main subject.

RFC3347.title: Small Computer Systems Interface protocol over the Internet (iSCSI) Requirements and Design Considerations
RFC3347.summary: Informational requirements and design-considerations document for iSCSI, which maps SCSI over TCP/IP for block storage; it lists requirements on performance, framing, reliability, interoperability, security, naming, discovery and Internet accessibility.

iSCSI.why: The whole document sets out the requirements and design considerations for iSCSI, so readers of the iSCSI subject page would want it.
iSCSI.quote: The iSCSI protocol is a mapping of SCSI to TCP, and constitutes a "SCSI transport" as defined by the ANSI T10 document SCSI SAM-2

rejected.why: iSCSI runs over TCP and the document discusses framing and connection use. TCP is the substrate, though, and nothing new is specified about TCP.
SCTP is mentioned only as a possible future substitute transport for TCP, in one requirement.
IPsec and TLS are named as mechanisms that could provide confidentiality and integrity. The document is not about them.
The TCP checksum's weakness motivates the requirement for iSCSI CRC digests. That is a minor point, so the checksum tag does not fit.
This is the parent topic of iSCSI. The iSCSI tech tag is more specific, so the parent is implied.
DNS is mentioned only as an example way to resolve the hostname part of a URL.

RFC3348.title: The Internet Message Action Protocol (IMAP4) Child Mailbox Extension
RFC3348.summary: Informational RFC documenting the IMAP4 CHILDREN extension, which adds \HasChildren and \HasNoChildren attributes to LIST responses so clients can tell whether a mailbox has child mailboxes.

IMAP.why: The document specifies an extension to IMAP4: a new CHILDREN capability and two new LIST response attributes. Readers of IMAP would want it.
IMAP.quote: The Internet Message Action Protocol (IMAP4) CHILDREN extension provides a mechanism for a client to efficiently determine if a particular mailbox has children

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the two-line formal syntax; the document is not about the notation.

RFC3349.title: A Transient Prefix for Identifying Profiles under Development by the Working Groups of the Internet Engineering Task Force
RFC3349.summary: BCP defining a transient URI prefix (http://iana.org/beep/transient/XXX/YYY) that IETF working group chairs assign to BEEP profiles under development, with an IANA registry of these identifiers.

BEEP.why: The document defines how BEEP profiles under development are identified and registered; its whole subject is BEEP profile identifiers.

IANA.why: The practice creates an IANA-maintained registry and registration procedure (chair-authorized) under the iana.org namespace, which readers of IANA registry guidance would want.
IANA.quote: The IANA maintains a registry of transient identifiers used for BEEP profiles under development in the IETF

Registration of profiles is not MIME media type registration.
The identifiers use an http URL but nothing about HTTP is specified.

RFC3351.title: User Requirements for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) in Support of Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Speech-impaired Individuals
RFC3351.summary: Informational RFC presenting user requirements for SIP to support deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired users, including user profiles, transcoding/relay services, gateways to legacy textphones, and usage scenarios.

SIP.why: The document specifies user requirements placed on SIP (profiles, transcoding, gateways, media stream changes), so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document presents a set of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) user requirements that support communications for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired individuals.

accessibility.why: The whole document concerns accessibility of Internet real-time communications for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people.

rejected.why: Parent of SIP, which is already tagged; implied.
Media stream negotiation is implied but SDP is never discussed.
One scenario covers a conference call, but it is not a conferencing framework document.

gaps.why: The document centres on transcoding and relay services (text relay, speech-to-text, sign language), but the taxonomy has no tag for them beyond accessibility.

RFC3352.title: Connection-less Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) to Historic Status
RFC3352.summary: Informational RFC that explains why CLDAP (RFC 1798) was never advanced on the Standards Track and recommends moving it to Historic status.

LDAP.why: CLDAP is a connectionless variant of LDAP for directory lookups. The document assesses its limits (anonymous only, read only, no security) and recommends retiring it, so it belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: The CLDAP was designed to complement version 2 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAPv2)

rejected.why: X.500 appears only as the directory model CLDAP's obsolete references point to (X.501, X.511). The document is not about X.500.
CLDAP runs over UDP, but the document does not address UDP usage. UDP is only the substrate. LDAPUDP is mentioned only as an alternative to experiment with.
The parent topic is implied by the LDAP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The document does reclassify an RFC to Historic, but the subject is CLDAP itself, not the IETF process.

RFC3353.title: Overview of IP Multicast in a Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) Environment
RFC3353.summary: Informational framework overviewing issues in deploying IP multicast over MPLS: multicast routing protocol characteristics, LSP triggers, label distribution modes, piggy-backing, L2 limits, QoS and multi-access networks.

multicast.why: The whole document analyses IP multicast routing protocols (DVMRP, PIM, CBT, MOSPF), tree types, and state when mapped to LSPs. No specific multicast child tag is the main subject.
multicast.quote: This document offers a framework for IP multicast deployment in an MPLS environment.

MPLS.why: Covers LSP triggers, label distribution modes, label allocation, merging, and L2 limitations of MPLS for multicast.
MPLS.quote: Issues arising when MPLS techniques are applied to IP multicast are overviewed.

LDP.why: Substantial discussion of LDP label distribution modes, control and retention, and piggy-backing label advertisement for multicast.
LDP.quote: it will send an LDP bind (Upstream Unsolicited mode) or an LDP bind request (Downstream on Demand mode) to LSRd.

rejected.why: Used as a main example, especially for shared/source tree state co-existence, but it is one of several protocols compared, not the subject.
Discussed as a trigger and QoS mechanism, but only in short sections.
Only a brief section on DSCP-specific trees.
ATM limitations are considered as an L2 constraint, but only through references to other documents.
Referenced only as a label-mapping extension in the piggy-backing discussion.
Explicit routing is a short section and does not make the document about traffic engineering.

RFC3354.title: Internet Open Trading Protocol Version 2 Requirements
RFC3354.summary: Requirements document for IOTP Version 2, setting design principles, scope, and the features that will, may, or will not be included, extending IOTP v1 and replacing its ad hoc XML messaging and signature parts with standards-based mechanisms.

IOTP.why: The whole document defines requirements for IOTP v2, including dynamic trading sequences, offer request blocks, and server-based wallets.
IOTP.quote: This document gives requirements for the Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) Version 2 by describing design principles and scope

rejected.why: IOTP v2 will use the existing XML-Signature standard (RFC 3275), and the document explicitly places designing XML digital signatures out of scope.
XML is the messaging substrate. The document explicitly excludes design of an XML messaging layer.
ECML is only mentioned as a protocol IOTP v2 should work well with. The document does not specify or extend it.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations as a way to provide confidentiality.
The IOTP tag sits under e-commerce and already covers this document, so the parent is not listed separately.

RFC3355.title: Layer Two Tunnelling Protocol (L2TP) Over ATM Adaptation Layer 5 (AAL5)
RFC3355.summary: Specifies how L2TP tunnels between a LAC and LNS are carried over ATM AAL5 virtual circuits, covering LLC and VC-multiplexed encapsulation, MTU, and SVC signalling via B-LLI.

L2TP.quote: This standard supplements [RFC2661] by providing details specific to the use of AAL5 for a point-to-point connection between LAC and LNS.

ATM.why: It specifies AAL5 encapsulation (LLC/SNAP and VC-mux), PVC/SVC use and Q.2931 B-LLI signalling, so it belongs under ATM.
ATM.quote: L2TP PDUs shall be carried in the payload field of Common Part Convergence Sublayer (CPCS) PDUs of AAL5

rejected.why: PPP is the payload that L2TP tunnels. The document specifies nothing new about PPP beyond the MRU the tunnel must support.
L2TP is tagged directly. The generic IP-in-IP and GRE tunnelling topic does not fit.
QoS is mentioned briefly and mostly declared out of scope or for further study.

RFC3356.title: Internet Engineering Task Force and International Telecommunication Union - Telecommunications Standardization Sector Collaboration Guidelines
RFC3356.summary: Informational RFC giving guidelines for collaboration between the IETF/ISOC and the ITU-T, covering how each learns of the other's work, representation, liaison communication, mailing lists, and document sharing.

IETF process.why: The document describes IETF procedures for liaison with another standards body: new-work notification, delegate recognition, formal communication, and Internet-Draft contribution handling. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document provides guidelines for collaboration between the ITU-T and the IETF.

rejected.why: It mentions RFC and Internet-Draft submission and references RFC 2223, but only as part of document sharing. It is not about the RFC series format or publication.
The child tag IETF process fits more specifically, so the parent is not listed.
IPR policy pages are only listed as URLs in Additional Items, and the document is not about intellectual property.

gaps.name: Liaison and collaboration between standards development organizations (IETF-ITU-T)
gaps.why: The document is about inter-SDO relations and liaison statements. The taxonomy has no specific tag for this, and IETF process is the nearest fit.

RFC3357.title: One-way Loss Pattern Sample Metrics
RFC3357.summary: Defines two derived IPPM metrics, one-way loss distance and loss period, plus statistics built on them, to characterise packet loss patterns (burstiness) based on the RFC 2680 base loss metric.

performance measurement.why: The document is an IPPM metric definition: derived sample metrics and statistics for active one-way packet loss measurement. Performance measurement is the best fit and no more specific tag exists.
performance measurement.quote: this document defines two derived metrics "loss distance" and "loss period", and the associated statistics that together capture loss patterns experienced by packet streams

rejected.why: The metrics concern measurement of Internet paths and streams, not benchmarking of network devices.
TCP and TCP-friendly models are mentioned only as sampling-model references, not as the subject.
The document defines metrics only; it does not specify or use the OWAMP protocol.
Real-time voice and video are given as motivating applications; the document does not address RTP.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) loss metrics
gaps.why: No specific tag exists for IPPM metric definitions; the generic performance measurement topic is used instead.

RFC3358.title: Optional Checksums in Intermediate System to Intermediate System (ISIS)
RFC3358.summary: Defines an optional IS-IS TLV (type 12) carrying a Fletcher checksum for CSNP, PSNP and IIH PDUs, so receivers can detect corrupted PDUs, and specifies its processing rules and interaction with MD5/HMAC authentication.

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol with a new optional checksum TLV and specifies its handling in CSNP, PSNP and IIH PDUs.

MD5 appears only in the section on interaction with authentication signatures. The document is not about MD5.
HMAC is mentioned only as an example of signatures that coexist with the checksum, so the document is not about it.

RFC3359.title: Reserved Type, Length and Value (TLV) Codepoints in Intermediate System to Intermediate System
RFC3359.summary: Informational RFC listing the IS-IS TLV codepoints in use by ISO 10589, RFC 1195 and pending IETF extensions, to avoid assignment conflicts in the absence of a central registry.

IS-IS.why: The whole document is a table of IS-IS TLV codepoints and their status, so IS-IS readers would look for it.

Not covered. Only IS-IS codepoints are listed.

RFC3360.title: Inappropriate TCP Resets Considered Harmful
RFC3360.summary: BCP arguing that firewalls and load-balancers sending TCP resets in response to SYNs using Reserved-field flags (notably ECN-setup SYNs) is non-conformant, overloads reset semantics, and obstructs TCP and Internet evolution.

TCP.why: The document analyses correct TCP reset semantics under RFC 793/1122, the Reserved field, and SYN handling, and gives best practice on resets.
TCP.quote: a number of firewalls in the Internet that inappropriately reset a TCP connection upon receiving certain TCP SYN packets, in particular, packets with flags set in the Reserved field

ECN.quote: firewalls that send resets in response to TCP SYN packets from ECN-capable hosts

firewall.quote: it is not conformant with current standards for a firewall, load-balancer, or web-server to respond with a reset to a TCP SYN packet

ICMP Administratively Prohibited is only suggested as an alternative for a separate document, not specified here.
Section 4 discusses obstacles to Internet evolution, but this is a motivating argument secondary to the TCP reset practice.

gaps.name: middleboxes / protocol ossification

RFC3361.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP-for-IPv4) Option for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Servers
RFC3361.summary: Defines DHCPv4 option 120 carrying a list of domain names or IPv4 addresses that locate SIP outbound proxy servers for SIP clients.

RFC3362.title: Real-time Facsimile (T.38) - image/t38 MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC3362.summary: Registers the MIME media type image/t38 for ITU-T T.38 real-time Group 3 fax over IP, intended as an SDP media descriptor in SIP call setup rather than for email.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration for image/t38, including the IANA registration template.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type image/t38.

fax.why: The registered type denotes the T.38 real-time fax bit stream. Readers of the fax subject would want it.
fax.quote: transfer facsimile documents in real-time between two standard Group 3 facsimile terminals over the Internet or other networks using IP protocols

SDP.why: The type's purpose is to serve as an SDP media descriptor for T.38 streams. This is a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: the image/t38 media type is intended to indicate a T.38 media stream in SDP.

rejected.why: SIP is only the call-setup context in which T.38 Annex D uses the type. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
The document registers a media type but defines nothing about MIME body structure or encodings, and it says it is not intended for email use. The media types tag fits better.
The document explicitly says the registration is not intended for email usage.
T.38 may run over TCP or UDP, but this is only a transport mention and not the document's subject.

RFC3363.title: Representing Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) Addresses in the Domain Name System (DNS)
RFC3363.summary: Informational document that, after DNSEXT/NGTRANS consensus, recommends AAAA for IPv6 forward mapping and moves A6 (RFC 2874) and bit labels (RFC 2673) to Experimental, deprecating DNAME in the IPv6 reverse tree.

DNS.why: The document is about DNS resource record choices (AAAA vs A6), bit labels and DNAME in the reverse tree, and the standards status of the DNS specifications defining them.
DNS.quote: This document clarifies and updates the standards status of RFCs that define direct and reverse map of IPv6 addresses in DNS.

IPv6.why: It concerns how IPv6 addresses are represented and deployed in the DNS, with deployment of IPv6 as the stated motivation.
IPv6.quote: AAAA records are preferable at the moment for production deployment of IPv6
IPv6.section: 2. IPv6 Addresses: AAAA RR vs A6 RR

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as an indirect impact of the A6 vs AAAA choice. The document is not about it.
The document is about how addresses are represented in DNS, not about IP address architecture or allocation.
The document changes standards status, but only for specific DNS specifications. Its subject is those DNS mechanisms, not the process.

RFC3364.title: Tradeoffs in Domain Name System (DNS) Support for Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6)
RFC3364.summary: Informational note comparing the AAAA (RFC 1886) and A6/DNAME/bit-label (RFC 2874) approaches to IPv6 address and reverse-mapping support in the DNS, weighing tradeoffs and recommending when each should be used.

DNS.why: The whole document analyses DNS resource record types (AAAA, A6, DNAME), bit labels and reverse mapping tree design, resolver behaviour and zone administration.
DNS.quote: The IETF has two different proposals on the table for how to do DNS support for IPv6

IPv6.why: The document is about how IPv6 addresses are represented in the DNS, including renumbering and GSE-like routing considerations, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: RFC 1886 [RFC1886] specified straightforward mechanisms to support IPv6 addresses in the DNS.

DNSSEC.why: A dedicated section compares signing and validation costs for AAAA versus A6 records, including signing-time measurements.
DNSSEC.quote: One of the areas where AAAA and A6 RRs differ is in the precise details of how they interact with DNSSEC.

rejected.why: Rapid renumbering is a motivating scenario for A6, but the document is about DNS record design, not renumbering procedures.
Dynamic update is discussed in only one short paragraph and is not a substantial part of the document.
AAAA synthesis is mentioned only as a transition idea for A6, unrelated to NAT64 address synthesis.
CIDR is mentioned only as a source of experience for the reverse-mapping design.

RFC3365.title: Strong Security Requirements for Internet Engineering Task Force Standard Protocols
RFC3365.summary: BCP documenting the IETF consensus (the "Danvers Doctrine") that IETF standard protocols must implement appropriate strong security mechanisms, with history and rationale.

security.why: The whole document is a general security requirements doctrine for protocols, not tied to a single mechanism, so the general security topic fits.
security.quote: IETF standard protocols MUST make use of appropriate strong security mechanisms.

IETF process.why: It sets IETF policy for standards-track protocols (the Danvers Doctrine, the Security Considerations requirement). Readers of IETF process would want it.
IETF process.quote: The purpose of this document is to document the IETF consensus on security requirements for protocols as well as to provide the background and motivation for them.

rejected.why: TLS is only named as an example of IETF security technology, and the document does not specify or analyse it.
IPsec is mentioned in passing as an example security protocol, and the document is not about it.
SASL is listed as a toolkit example only.
GSSAPI is listed as a toolkit example only.
The document argues cryptography should be used, but it does not cover specific algorithms or parameters.
Authentication is defined as one of three security services, but it is not the document's focus.

RFC3366.title: Advice to link designers on link Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ)
RFC3366.summary: BCP giving link-layer designers advice on link ARQ: persistence levels, packet ordering, multi-flow treatment and service-class differentiation, and their effects on IP/TCP performance.

link layer.why: The document is about link-layer ARQ design for IP traffic across media generally, not a specific link technology, so the general link layer topic fits.
link layer.quote: This document provides advice to the designers of digital communication equipment and link-layer protocols employing link-layer Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) techniques.

rejected.why: TCP behaviour (RTO, dupacks) is discussed heavily as the interacting end-to-end protocol, but the document specifies or extends nothing about TCP.
FEC and hybrid ARQ are mentioned briefly as complementary techniques, not a substantial part of the document.
Diffserv DSCP is listed as one way to classify flows for link service classes; it is only a mechanism mentioned.
Link service class differentiation is a section, but it concerns ARQ persistence per flow class rather than QoS architectures.
Interaction with TCP congestion control is noted only as context for delay effects.
Path MTU discovery is mentioned only in passing regarding fragmentation.

gaps.name: Link ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)
gaps.why: The document's core subject, link-layer retransmission and its persistence, has no dedicated tag. The nearest fit is the link layer topic, and FEC covers only ARQ for transport loss recovery.

RFC3367.title: Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP)
RFC3367.summary: Specifies CNRP, an XML request/response protocol (over HTTP and SMTP) by which clients resolve human-oriented common names/phrases to URIs, with properties, datasets, referrals, status codes and service discovery.

naming.why: The document defines a general name resolution protocol for common names that is not tied to DNS or any other specific naming system, so the generic naming topic fits.
naming.quote: a protocol for client applications to communicate with common name resolution services

service discovery.why: A substantial part of the document covers ServiceQuery and Schema, by which clients discover a resolution service's capabilities, and its servers and datasets.
service discovery.quote: the Service object is essential to discoverability. It constitutes the main entry point for a CNRP client to dynamically discover the capabilities

rejected.why: XML is the encoding for all CNRP messages and the DTD is definitive, but the document is about the resolution protocol, not about XML usage in general.
HTTP is only one of two transports, with a short binding in section 7.1. It is substrate, not the subject.
SMTP is a secondary transport described in a few lines, so it is not tagged.
The application/cnrp+xml registration is boilerplate-like and covers only a short section.
The document uses absoluteURI for resource identification, but the CNRP URI scheme is defined in RFC 3368, not here.
Common names are explicitly not DNS names and DNS is not involved.

gaps.name: Common name resolution (CNRP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for CNRP or for keyword-to-URI resolution services, so only the generic naming topic fits.

RFC3368.title: The 'go' URI Scheme for the Common Name Resolution Protocol
RFC3368.summary: Defines the 'go:' URI scheme for the Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP), giving its syntax, ABNF, defaults, encoding rules and examples, and registering the scheme.

URI.why: The document's purpose is to define a new URI scheme, including its syntax, default values, encoding rules and registration template.
URI.quote: This document defines a URI scheme, 'go:' to be used with the Common Name Resolution Protocol.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the mandatory transport and default port for CNRP; the document defines nothing new about HTTP.
CNRP is a common-name resolution system, but the document is about the URI scheme for it, not about naming in general.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
UTF-8 is cited only as the percent-encoding basis for URI characters; it is not the subject.
The IANA section only requests the scheme registration, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP)
gaps.why: The document is tied to CNRP (RFC 3367), which resolves common names to URIs. The taxonomy has no tag for CNRP or for common-name or keyword resolution systems.

RFC3369.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC3369.summary: Specifies the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), an ASN.1 encapsulation syntax for signing, digesting, encrypting and authenticating arbitrary content, obsoleting RFC 2630 and RFC 3211.

CMS.why: The whole document defines CMS content types (signed, enveloped, digested, encrypted, authenticated data), recipient info types and attributes.
CMS.quote: This document describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).  This syntax is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt arbitrary message content.

rejected.why: S/MIME is a consumer of CMS and is mentioned only for compatibility; the document does not specify S/MIME.
CMS is defined in ASN.1 and includes ASN.1 modules, but ASN.1 is only the notation, not the subject.
Certificates and CRLs are carried and referenced, but X.509 is profiled elsewhere (RFC 3280).
Certificate-based key management is only supported or referenced, not specified here.
Mentioned only as an example MAC algorithm; algorithms are deliberately left to RFC 3369's companion document.
The RecipientInfo types carry keys, but this is within the CMS syntax rather than general key management.

RFC3370.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Algorithms
RFC3370.summary: RFC 3370 specifies conventions for using digest, signature, key management, content encryption and MAC algorithms (SHA-1, MD5, DSA, RSA, X9.42 DH, 3DES/RC2 key wrap, PBKDF2, 3DES/RC2 CBC, HMAC-SHA1) with the Cryptographic Message Syntax, including algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 parameters.

CMS.why: The whole document defines how algorithms are used in CMS fields (SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData), making it a core CMS companion specification.
CMS.quote: This document describes the conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

RSA.why: Specifies RSA signature and key transport conventions, identifiers and public key encoding for CMS, plus the PKCS#1 v1.5 vulnerability discussion.
RSA.quote: The RSA (PKCS #1 v1.5) signature algorithm is defined in RFC 2437

DES.why: Triple-DES CBC content encryption and Triple-DES key wrap are specified for CMS.
DES.quote: The Triple-DES algorithm is described in ANSI X9.52 [3DES].

HMAC.why: Defines HMAC-SHA1 as the MAC algorithm for CMS AuthenticatedData, including identifier and parameter encoding.
HMAC.quote: The HMAC with SHA-1 algorithm is described in RFC 2104 [HMAC].

PBKDF2.why: Specifies PBKDF2 for password-based key management in CMS with its parameter syntax.
PBKDF2.quote: The PBKDF2 key derivation algorithm is specified in RFC 2898

rejected.why: SHA-1 is only one digest identifier specified for CMS; the document does not define or analyse the SHA family itself.
MD5 is only specified as an optional digest identifier in CMS; the document is not about MD5.
ASN.1 is the notation used to define identifiers and parameter structures, not the subject of the document.
S/MIME is mentioned only in passing in the security considerations and acknowledgments; the document is about CMS algorithms.
Key management techniques are covered but within the CMS algorithms context; the specific CMS tag and algorithm tags cover this adequately.
The parent is implied by the specific algorithm tags chosen.

gaps.name: RC2 cipher and key wrap
gaps.why: The document specifies RC2 CBC content encryption and RC2 key wrap but the taxonomy has no RC2 tag.

gaps.name: X9.42 Diffie-Hellman key agreement
gaps.why: Ephemeral-Static and Static-Static DH key agreement are specified but no Diffie-Hellman tag exists.

gaps.name: DSA
gaps.why: DSA signature conventions are specified but the taxonomy has no DSA tag.

RFC3371.title: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol "L2TP" Management Information Base
RFC3371.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module for managing L2TP tunnels, sessions, domains and UDP/IP transport, extending the IP Tunnel and Interfaces MIBs.

L2TP.why: The whole document defines managed objects for L2TP tunnels, sessions and domains, so L2TP readers would want it.
L2TP.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing networks using Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP).

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (L2TP-MIB) with object definitions, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework used to access the MIB; the MIB tag sits beneath SNMP and covers the document.
PPP interfaces are layered over L2TP tunnels and session objects reference PPP, but the document does not specify PPP.
Only a configuration object indicates whether tunnels are IPsec-secured; IPsec is out of scope.
UDP is merely the transport; only port number objects are defined.
L2TP is the more specific tag; the generic tunneling topic is not needed.

RFC3372.title: Session Initiation Protocol for Telephones (SIP-T): Context and Architectures
RFC3372.summary: BCP describing SIP-T, the framework of mechanisms (ISUP encapsulation in MIME bodies, ISUP-to-SIP header translation, INFO for mid-call signalling) for interworking SIP networks with the PSTN via gateways, with call flows and originator/terminator/intermediary roles.

SIP-T.why: The whole document defines the SIP-T context and architectures: encapsulation and translation of ISUP at SIP-ISUP gateways, flows, and role behaviour.
SIP-T.quote: The SIP-T (SIP for Telephones) effort provides a framework for the integration of legacy telephony signaling into SIP messages.

rejected.why: SIP is the substrate SIP-T builds on and the document specifies no new SIP behaviour beyond SIP-T practice; the more specific SIP-T tag covers it.
Parent of SIP-T, implied by the child tag.
Multipart MIME is only the encapsulation vehicle; the ISUP MIME type is defined in another RFC.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as the way to protect ISUP bodies.
Appears only as a body part in the content negotiation examples.
Mentioned only as a possible influence on routing.

gaps.name: ISUP (ISDN User Part) / SS7 signalling
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ISUP/SS7 itself, which is the legacy signalling the document encapsulates and translates; SIP-T covers only the interworking.

RFC3373.title: Three-Way Handshake for Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Point-to-Point Adjacencies
RFC3373.summary: Defines a backward-compatible IS-IS option providing a three-way handshake for point-to-point adjacencies, with an extended circuit ID allowing more than 256 point-to-point links.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies a new IS-IS TLV option and modifications to the IS-IS point-to-point IIH state machine and adjacency procedures.
IS-IS.quote: This paper defines a backward-compatible extension to the protocol that provides for a three-way handshake.

rejected.why: IS-IS is defined in ISO 10589 and runs with CLNP, but the document is about the IS-IS handshake, not OSI network-layer coexistence.
NLSP is mentioned only as a comparable mechanism; the document does not address IPX interworking.
Parent concern is covered by the specific IS-IS tag; the document is not about general routing architecture.
It detects unidirectional link failure like BFD does, but it is an IS-IS adjacency mechanism, not BFD.

RFC3374.title: Problem Description: Reasons For Performing Context Transfers Between Nodes in an IP Access Network
RFC3374.summary: Problem statement from the Seamoby WG arguing why context transfer (moving AAA, header compression and QoS state between access routers) is needed to speed up handover for mobile hosts in IP access networks.

IP mobility.why: The whole document concerns fast handover for mobile hosts by transferring service state between routers, as an enhancement to IP mobility protocols. No specific Mobile IP technology is the subject, so the parent topic fits.
IP mobility.quote: This document discusses the desirability of context transfer for facilitating seamless IP mobility.

AAA.why: AAA context transfer is the first and most compelling example, with its own subsection on re-authentication and AAA server security associations.
AAA.quote: facilitating the re-authentication of the mobile host and re-establishment of the mobile host's authorization for network access in a new subnet

header compression.why: Header compression context transfer is a worked example, covering the cost of re-establishing compression and the timing of the transfer.
header compression.quote: allowing the network entity performing header compression, usually the last hop router, to transfer the header compression context to the new router

QoS.why: QoS re-establishment after handover is the third worked example, with discussion of the limits for end-to-end QoS.
QoS.quote: A method of transferring the mobile host's QoS context from the old network to the new could facilitate faster re-establishment

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the mobility protocol that handles routing changes. The document says routing changes are outside its scope.
Mentioned only as the mobility protocol that handles routing changes, plus the AAA registration keys extension in passing. The document says routing changes are outside its scope.
Cited as the header compression reference, but the document does not specify or analyse ROHC itself.
Mentioned only as the mechanism that should secure the context transfer, in Security Considerations.
Mentioned only as an existing Layer 2 mechanism for redoing AAA exchanges.
Mentioned only as an existing Layer 2 mechanism for redoing AAA exchanges.

gaps.name: Context transfer / Seamoby (fast handover)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is context transfer between access routers for seamless handover. The taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the generic IP mobility topic.

RFC3375.title: Generic Registry-Registrar Protocol Requirements
RFC3375.summary: Informational RFC from the provreg WG stating high-level functional and interface requirements for a generic registry-registrar protocol for provisioning and managing domain names, name servers and contacts in shared registries.

domain registration.why: The whole document specifies requirements for registry-registrar operations: object registration, transfer, renewal, deletion, query and status. It is the requirements basis for EPP but defines no specific protocol, so the parent topic fits better than the EPP tag.
domain registration.quote: high-level functional and interface requirements for a client-server protocol for the registration and management of Internet domain names in shared registries

rejected.why: This RFC is the requirements document that preceded EPP. It does not specify or mention EPP, so the topic tag is more accurate.
DNS zones, name servers and delegation appear only as the context for registry objects. The document does not specify DNS protocol behaviour.
The query requirements are for registrar access to registry objects, not a public directory service.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and says no action is needed.
TCP and SCTP are mentioned only as example transports. The document does not address them.

RFC3376.title: Internet Group Management Protocol, Version 3
RFC3376.summary: Specifies IGMPv3, the protocol by which IPv4 hosts and multicast routers exchange group membership reports with source filtering (INCLUDE/EXCLUDE), including router/host behaviour, timers, and interoperation with IGMPv1/v2.

IGMP.why: The whole document specifies IGMP version 3: message formats, host and router protocol, compatibility with older versions, and timers.
IGMP.quote: IGMP is the protocol used by IPv4 systems to report their IP multicast group memberships to neighboring multicast routers.

SSM.why: Source filtering is the IGMP feature that enables SSM. The document is about the membership side of SSM, though it does not specify SSM itself, so this is secondary.
SSM.quote: the ability for a system to report interest in receiving packets *only* from specific source addresses, as required to support Source-Specific Multicast [SSM]

rejected.why: MLD is only mentioned as the IPv6 counterpart; this document does not specify it.
IPsec AH is only discussed as an optional protection in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate evidence.
The Router Alert option is only required in IGMP message headers. The document does not define anything new about it.
The Internet checksum is merely reused for the IGMP message.
The more specific IGMP tag applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC3377.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (v3): Technical Specification
RFC3377.summary: RFC 3377 defines the LDAPv3 specification as the set of RFCs 2251-2256, 2829 and 2830, and addresses the IESG Note on mandatory authentication by including RFC 2829.

LDAP.why: The document's whole purpose is to define which RFCs make up LDAPv3 and to be the normative reference for the LDAPv3 suite.
LDAP.quote: This document specifies the set of RFCs comprising the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Version 3 (LDAPv3)

rejected.why: RFC 2830 (LDAP over TLS) is only listed as a member of the suite. The document does not specify anything about TLS.
The IESG Note on mandatory authentication motivates the document. But the body only points to RFC 2829 and does not specify any authentication mechanism.
RFC 2256 (X.500 user schema) is only listed as part of the suite. The document does not address X.500.
The IESG Note handling is a procedural detail within the LDAP suite definition. The document is not about the IETF process in general.
RFC 2829 is mentioned only by title. The document does not discuss SASL.

RFC3378.title: EtherIP: Tunneling Ethernet Frames in IP Datagrams
RFC3378.summary: Informational RFC documenting the historic EtherIP protocol, which tunnels Ethernet/IEEE 802.3 MAC frames in IP datagrams (IP protocol 97) with a 16-bit header and sending/receiving procedures.

tunneling.why: The document specifies a tunneling protocol encapsulating Ethernet frames in IP; no more specific tunneling child (GRE, IP-in-IP) fits, so the parent topic is used.
tunneling.quote: EtherIP tunnels Ethernet and IEEE 802.3 media access control frames in IP datagrams so that non-IP traffic can traverse an IP internet.

Ethernet.why: The payload is Ethernet/802.3 MAC frames, with bridge-like station behaviour and Ethernet interworking over IP, which Ethernet readers would want.
Ethernet.quote: The EtherIP protocol is used to tunnel Ethernet [DIX] and IEEE 802.3 [CSMA/CD] media access control (MAC) frames

rejected.why: Pseudowire emulation is mentioned only as the successor work (PWE3) that supersedes EtherIP; the document does not specify it.
L2TPEXT is mentioned only as a successor effort; not the subject.
Only suggested in Security Considerations as a protection for EtherIP datagrams; boilerplate-level mention.
The protocol runs over IPv4 and uses protocol number 97, but IPv4 itself is just the substrate.
Cited only as an example of a weakly secured protocol in the Security Considerations.
The protocol number assignment is incidental; the document is about the protocol, not registry guidance.

RFC3379.title: Delegated Path Validation and Delegated Path Discovery Protocol Requirements
RFC3379.summary: Informational requirements document for Delegated Path Validation (DPV) and Delegated Path Discovery (DPD) protocols, in which servers validate or discover X.509 certification paths for clients, including validation and path discovery policies.

PKI.why: The whole document concerns certification path validation and discovery, validation policies, trust anchors and revocation checking for PKI. No more specific PKI child tag fits the delegated validation protocols.
PKI.quote: specifies the requirements for Delegated Path Validation (DPV) and Delegated Path Discovery (DPD) for Public Key Certificates

rejected.why: OCSP responses are one source of revocation information the server collects or returns, but the document does not specify or extend OCSP.
The document relies on X.509 certificates and the RFC 3280 path validation algorithm, but it does not profile certificates. Its subject is the delegated protocols.
LDAP is mentioned only as a repository access protocol the DPD server would replace for clients.
S/MIME is mentioned only as an example of a message carrying revocation information that a client could copy into a request.
Request and response authentication is a minor requirement, not a main subject of the document.

gaps.name: Delegated Path Validation / Delegated Path Discovery (DPV/DPD)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for delegated certificate validation or path discovery protocols and policies. PKI is the closest parent.

RFC3380.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): Job and Printer Set Operations
RFC3380.summary: RFC 3380 defines three optional IPP operations (Set-Printer-Attributes, Set-Job-Attributes, Get-Printer-Supported-Values), plus new attributes, status code and out-of-band values, extending IPP/1.0 and IPP/1.1 to modify Job and Printer objects.

IPP.why: The whole document extends IPP with new operations, attributes, status codes and out-of-band values, so it belongs on the IPP page.
IPP.quote: This document specifies 3 additional OPTIONAL operations for use with the Internet Printing Protocol/1.0 (IPP) and IPP/1.1.

rejected.why: IPP is carried over HTTP, but HTTP is only the transport substrate and the document defines nothing new about it.
LDAP and SLP are mentioned only in a note on putting the collection attribute into directory schemas; they are not the subject.
The IANA section only registers IPP operations, attributes and values, which is boilerplate and not the subject.
The 'document-format' MIME type attribute is used, but no media type is registered or defined.
Access rights for operator and administrator are noted per operation, but this is incidental and not the focus of the document.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists IPP only as a tech tag under applications; the id 'IPP' is the tag matching 'IPP (Internet Printing Protocol)'. The listed id is exactly 'IPP', so no gap exists apart from checking that the id is valid.

RFC3381.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): Job Progress Attributes
RFC3381.summary: RFC 3381 defines four optional IPP Job Description attributes for monitoring job progress (drawn from the PWG Job Monitoring MIB) and a new "sheet-collate" Job Template attribute, as extensions to IPP/1.0 and IPP/1.1.

IPP.why: The whole document extends IPP with new job attributes (job-collation-type, sheet-completed-copy-number, etc.) and a sheet-collate Job Template attribute, and it updates RFC 2910.
IPP.quote: This document defines four new Job Description attributes for monitoring job progress to be registered as OPTIONAL extensions to IPP/1.0 [RFC2566] and IPP/1.1 [RFC2911].

rejected.why: The attributes are drawn from the PWG Job Monitoring MIB (RFC 2707), but the document defines IPP attributes, not MIB modules or SMI.
IPP is carried over HTTP, but only in the boilerplate description of the base IPP documents. The document defines nothing about HTTP.
The IANA section only registers the new IPP attributes and values. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Printing / job monitoring
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no general printing or job-monitoring topic besides IPP and LPD, so the print-job progress and collation semantics are covered only through the IPP tag.

RFC3382.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): The 'collection' attribute syntax
RFC3382.summary: Defines the OPTIONAL 'collection' attribute syntax for IPP/1.0 and 1.1, including rules for defining collection attributes, handling unsupported values, and the binary encoding tags (begCollection, endCollection, memberAttrName).

IPP.why: The whole document extends IPP with a new attribute syntax, its definition rules, and its wire encoding, updating RFC 2910 and 2911.
IPP.quote: This document specifies an OPTIONAL attribute syntax called 'collection' for use with the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP/1.0 and IPP/1.1).

rejected.why: IPP is carried over HTTP, but this document only defines attribute syntax and encoding tags; HTTP is merely the substrate.
The IANA section merely registers the new tags; boilerplate, not the document's subject.
The 'application/ipp' media type is mentioned only in the background appendix, not defined here.
Mentioned only in the appendix describing the base IPP documents.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IPP tag in the applications branch, but I used it as shown. Without confirmation it exists as written, I'm flagging it. Wait: it is listed (applications > IPP), so no real gap.

RFC3383.title: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Considerations for the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
RFC3383.summary: BCP 64 defines IANA registration procedures and assignment guidelines for extensible LDAP elements (OIDs, descriptors, controls/extensions, result codes, message types, auth methods, attribute options) and lists currently assigned values.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies how LDAP protocol elements (message types, result codes, controls, descriptors, options) are registered, so LDAP readers need it.
LDAP.quote: This document provides procedures for registering extensible elements of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

IANA.why: It is an IANA considerations document defining registries, registration policies (Expert Review, Standards Action, FCFS) and procedures.
IANA.quote: This document also provides guidelines to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) describing conditions under which new values can be assigned.

rejected.why: SASL is only mentioned in a note as an LDAP authentication choice; the document is not about it.
X.500-derived schema names appear in the assigned-values tables, but the document does not address the X.500 service.
ABNF is used only as notation for keyword syntax, not a subject of the document.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of descriptors; not the subject.
Start TLS appears only as one row in the assigned OID table.

RFC3384.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (version 3) Replication Requirements
RFC3384.summary: Informational document setting out requirements for a standard replication mechanism between LDAPv3 directory servers, covering consistency models, protocol, schema, single/multi-master, management and security requirements, with usage scenarios and rationale.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies requirements for replicating LDAP directory data between servers, so readers of the LDAP subject would expect it.
LDAP.quote: This document sets out the requirements for replication between multiple LDAP servers.

rejected.why: X.500/X.525 replication is referenced as background for models and terminology, but the document is about LDAP replication, not X.500.
Parent of LDAP; LDAP is the more specific tag and is chosen instead.
Security requirements mention confidentiality and integrity mechanisms generically; the document does not define or profile TLS use.
Policy data in a directory is only a usage scenario, not the subject.

gaps.name: LDUP (LDAP replication)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an LDAP technology tag only under directory services if it exists; here LDAP is listed, but no specific tag for directory replication or LDUP exists, so the replication-specific subject is covered only by the general LDAP tag.

RFC3385.title: Internet Protocol Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC)/Checksum Considerations
RFC3385.summary: Informational analysis of undetected-error probabilities for CRC codes (especially CRC32C) versus Fletcher/Adler checksums, supporting the choice of CRC32C as iSCSI's error detection code, with hardware implementation code.

CRC.why: The whole memo analyses CRC generator polynomials, undetected error probability, incremental updates and hardware/software implementations of CRC32C versus IEEE-802 CRC.
CRC.quote: CRC32C is a good choice as a basic error detection mechanism for iSCSI.

checksum.why: A substantial part compares CRCs with Fletcher, Adler and TCP checksums for packet integrity (Section 5.2 and the summary table).
checksum.quote: We will also attempt to compare Cyclic Redundancy Checks (CRCs) with other checksum forms (e.g., Fletcher, Adler, weighted checksums)

rejected.why: iSCSI is the motivating protocol, but the memo only evaluates its error detection code and does not specify or extend iSCSI itself; the CRC tag covers the content.
Parent topic of iSCSI; the document is about error-detection codes, not storage access protocols.
IEEE 802.3 CRC32 is used as a comparison polynomial only, not the subject.
The TCP checksum is mentioned only briefly as a comparison point.
AAL5 CRC and ATM are mentioned only in cited literature.

RFC3386.title: Network Hierarchy and Multilayer Survivability
RFC3386.summary: Informational TEWG design-team document that sets out near-term requirements for network survivability mechanisms (protection and restoration), multilayer coordination, and horizontal/vertical hierarchy in service provider networks.

traffic engineering.why: The document is a TEWG output defining survivability (protection/restoration) requirements and multi-area TE needs for traffic-engineered provider networks. No narrower technology tag covers it.
traffic engineering.quote: The team determined that there appears to be a need to define a small set of interoperable survivability approaches in packet and non-packet networks.

routing architecture.why: A large share of the document covers horizontal and vertical hierarchy, multi-area IGP scalability and hierarchy boundaries. These are routing architecture and scalability design matters.
routing architecture.quote: Network hierarchy is an abstraction of part of a network's topology, routing and signaling mechanisms.

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are the setting for the requirements. The document specifies no MPLS mechanism and is not about MPLS itself.
Multi-area OSPF and ABRs are used as examples of horizontal hierarchy. The document does not specify or extend OSPF.
Optical and TDM layers are discussed only as lower layers in multilayer survivability. The document does not cover GMPLS control.
RSVP-TE fast reroute and shared-mesh restoration drafts appear only as references to proposals.
L2 and L3 VPNs are cited as the driver for edge-to-edge signaling across hierarchy. The document is not about VPN technology.
SDH/SONET protection switching is discussed as a lower layer for coordination. The document is not about IP over SONET.

gaps.name: network survivability / protection and restoration
gaps.why: The core subject is survivability: protection switching, restoration, shared risk groups and multilayer recovery coordination. The taxonomy has no survivability tag, so the closest fit is traffic engineering.

RFC3387.title: Considerations from the Service Management Research Group (SMRG) on Quality of Service (QoS) in the IP Network
RFC3387.summary: An SMRG informational survey of the service and network management issues raised by QoS-capable IP networks, covering inter-domain SLAs, bandwidth brokers, billing, policy, DiffServ/IntServ management and comparison with TMN.

QoS.why: The whole document concerns management of QoS in IP networks, including admission control, inter-domain agreements, bandwidth brokers and billing. QoS architectures are the central subject.
QoS.quote: This document examines some of the areas of impact that QoS is likely to have on management and look at some questions that remain to be addressed.

network management.why: It is a service management and network management architecture survey, comparing with TMN and discussing element, network and service management layers. No specific management protocol is covered, so the parent topic fits.
network management.quote: This document intends to evaluate the network and service management issues that will need to be addressed

rejected.why: Discussed in section 7 only as one QoS architecture whose management issues are examined. The document is not about specifying or extending Diffserv.
Mentioned for comparison with Diffserv and for scalability, not a subject of the document.
Policy work (IETF Policy, DMTF CIM) is discussed as context only, not a main focus.
AAA is cited as a promising starting point for billing and security, but only briefly.
Mentioned in passing as an end-to-end QoS example.

RFC3388.title: Grouping of Media Lines in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC3388.summary: Defines the SDP "group" and "mid" attributes for grouping media lines, with LS (lip synchronization) and FID (flow identification) semantics, and their use in SIP offer/answer.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with new attributes and grouping semantics, so it belongs under SDP.
SDP.quote: This document defines two Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes: "group" and "mid".

SIP.why: A substantial section specifies how group and mid behave in SIP offer/answer exchanges, including backward compatibility and capability negotiation.
SIP.quote: We include a section about SIP because the "group" attribute will most likely be used mainly by SIP systems.
SIP.section: 8. Usage of the "group" Attribute in SIP

rejected.why: RTP sessions and RTCP synchronization are discussed as context, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
GSM, AMR and PCM appear only in examples of FID grouping.
RTCP is mentioned only as the usual way to achieve lip synchronization, not specified here.
Cellular access is a motivating use case for FID, not the subject of the document.
The IANA section creates a registry for group semantics, but this is boilerplate relative to the main body.

RFC3389.title: Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload for Comfort Noise (CN)
RFC3389.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for comfort noise (SID frames) carrying noise level and optional reflection-coefficient spectral data, for use with audio codecs lacking built-in DTX such as G.711, G.726, G.727, G.728 and G.722.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies a new RTP payload format (CN, static payload type 13, audio/CN), exactly what this tag covers.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format for transporting comfort noise (CN).

G.711.why: The CN format derives from G.711 Appendix II and is primarily intended for G.711, with a G.711 example solution described. Readers of G.711 would want it.
G.711.quote: The payload format is based on Appendix II of ITU-T Recommendation G.711 [8] which defines a comfort noise payload format

rejected.why: RTP is the framework the payload plugs into; the more specific RTP payload format tag fits and implies RTP.
SDP is used only for examples of signalling the CN payload type; the document does not define anything new about SDP.
G.722 is only one of several codecs listed as possible companions; the document is not about G.722 itself.
G.729 Annex B VAD/DTX is referenced only in an informative example solution.
The audio/CN registration is IANA boilerplate-like, secondary to the payload format definition.
CN is not a codec; it is a payload for noise description used alongside codecs.

RFC3390.title: Increasing TCP's Initial Window
RFC3390.summary: RFC 3390 specifies an optional increase of TCP's initial congestion window to roughly 4K bytes (up to four segments), obsoleting RFC 2414, and discusses its advantages, disadvantages, implementation issues and supporting experiments.

TCP.why: The document modifies TCP's initial window and updates RFC 2581, so it is a TCP protocol extension/implementation specification.
TCP.quote: specifies an increase in the permitted upper bound for TCP's initial window from one or two segment(s) to between two and four segments

congestion control.why: The change concerns the slow-start initial congestion window, and much of the document analyses congestion collapse risk and drop rates.
congestion control.quote: the initial window used by a sender after a correctly transmitted SYN MUST be one segment consisting of MSS bytes

rejected.why: Section 2 discusses interaction with Path MTU Discovery only briefly as an implementation issue; the document is not about PMTUD.
HTTP/1.1 and web transfers are mentioned as motivating examples, not specified or extended.
ECN is only referenced in the appendix; not a subject of the document.
RED/active queue management is mentioned in passing when discussing router behaviour.
Email transfers are named only as an example of short transfers.
Satellite links appear as one set of experimental results, not the subject of the document.

RFC3391.title: The MIME Application/Vnd.pwg-multiplexed Content-Type
RFC3391.summary: Defines and registers the application/vnd.pwg-multiplexed MIME media type, a chunked, interleavable container for compound objects (an alternative to multipart/related), with examples for printing and scanning.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new MIME media type, including its parameter and registration form, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document defines the Application/Vnd.pwg-multiplexed content-type. It also provides examples of its use.

MIME.why: The type is a MIME compound-object representation that parallels Multipart/Related. Much of the document covers MIME body structure, Content-ID/Location and Content-Disposition handling.
MIME.quote: An Application/Vnd.pwg-multiplexed entity contains a sequence of chunks. Each chunk contains a MIME message or a part of a MIME message.

rejected.why: BEEP is only compared as an alternative mechanism, and the IESG note mentions it. The document does not specify or extend it.
HTTP is mentioned only as the typical transport for the entity.
RFC 2557 patterns are referenced for the Content-ID/Content-Location usage and the .mht file is mentioned. The document does not specify MHTML.
ABNF is only the notation used for the chunk syntax.
The XHTML print examples are only sample payloads.

RFC3392.title: Capabilities Advertisement with BGP-4
RFC3392.summary: Defines the BGP-4 Capabilities Optional Parameter in OPEN messages, letting speakers advertise capabilities without session termination, plus the Unsupported Capability NOTIFICATION subcode; obsoletes RFC 2842.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-4 with a capabilities advertisement mechanism in OPEN messages and a new error subcode, so it belongs on the BGP page.
BGP.quote: defines a new Optional Parameter, called Capabilities, that is expected to facilitate the introduction of new capabilities in the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate for BGP sessions; it appears only in a Security Considerations reference to the TCP MD5 option.
The IANA Considerations section only sets up a Capability Code registry. It is boilerplate and not the main subject of the document.
The Security Considerations section only says the extension adds no new security issues.

RFC3393.title: IP Packet Delay Variation Metric for IP Performance Metrics (IPPM)
