RFC3393.summary: Defines the IPPM IP packet delay variation (ipdv) metric as the difference in one-way delay of selected packet pairs, with singleton, sample and statistics definitions and a discussion of clock synchronization error effects.

performance measurement.why: The document is an IPPM metric specification: singleton, sample and statistics definitions, methodology, and error analysis for measuring packet delay variation.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a metric for the variation in delay of packets that flow from one host to another through an IP path.

rejected.why: Clock synchronization, skew and drift are discussed only as error sources for the metric, not as a time synchronization mechanism.
RFC 1889 jitter estimate is mentioned only as a related computation in one paragraph.
Play-out buffer sizing and EF PHB are cited only as motivation or comparison, not as the subject.
This is a metric for live network path measurement, not device benchmarking methodology.

RFC3394.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Key Wrap Algorithm
RFC3394.summary: RFC 3394 specifies the AES Key Wrap algorithm (wrap/unwrap with an integrity-check initial value), gives object identifiers for it, and supplies extensive test vectors.

AES.why: The document defines a key wrapping algorithm built on the AES block cipher, with KEK sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits, OIDs and test vectors. It is squarely an AES mode/algorithm specification.
AES.quote: The purpose of this document is to make the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Key Wrap algorithm conveniently available to the Internet community.

rejected.why: Key wrap is a primitive used within key management, but the document specifies the algorithm itself rather than a key management protocol or architecture. AES is the more specific fit.
The smime working group context suggests CMS use, but the document never discusses CMS; it only defines the algorithm and OIDs.
Object identifiers are given in a short section, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC3395.title: Remote Network Monitoring MIB Protocol Identifier Reference Extensions
RFC3395.summary: RFC 3395 extends the RMON protocol identifier framework (RFC 2895) with a VERB-IDENTIFIER macro and encoding rules so RMON-2 protocolDirTable entries can identify application protocol operations (verbs) such as FTP, POP3, SNMP, HTTP and SMTP commands.

RMON.why: The document extends the RMON protocol identifier reference and specifies how the RMON-2 protocolDirTable is populated for application verbs, so RMON readers need it.
RMON.quote: it describes the algorithms required to identify protocol operations (verbs) within the protocol encapsulations managed with MIBs such as the Remote Network Monitoring MIB Version 2

rejected.why: The memo explicitly states it does not specify a MIB module or define new MIB objects. It only defines how existing RMON-2 objects are mapped.
SNMP is only the management framework boilerplate and one example verb set in the appendix. The document is not about SNMP itself.
FTP, POP3, HTTP and SMTP appear only as appendix examples of verb lists. The document does not specify or extend those protocols.
Per-verb metrics motivate the work, but the document is about identifier encoding, not measurement methods.

RFC3396.title: Encoding Long Options in the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4)
RFC3396.summary: RFC 3396 updates RFC 2131 by specifying how DHCPv4 options longer than 255 octets, or split across the options, file and sname fields, are split by encoders and concatenated by decoders.

DHCP.why: The document defines encoding and decoding rules for DHCPv4 options and updates RFC 2131, so it is squarely about DHCP.
DHCP.quote: When multiple instances of the same option appear in the options, file and/or sname fields in a DHCP packet, the contents of these options are concatenated together

rejected.why: The document only mentions DHCPv6 in passing, to distinguish it from DHCPv4. It specifies nothing for DHCPv6.
DHCPv4 configures IPv4 hosts, but the document is about option encoding within DHCP and not about IPv4 itself.

RFC3397.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Domain Search Option
RFC3397.summary: Defines DHCPv4 option 119, which delivers a DNS domain search list to clients, encoded with RFC 1035 name compression and split across multiple options per RFC 3396.

DHCP.why: The RFC specifies a new DHCP option (code 119), including its format, encoding and client handling, so it belongs on the DHCP page.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a new Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) option which is passed from the DHCP Server to the DHCP Client

rejected.why: DNS is the resolver context the search list is used in, and the option borrows RFC 1035 name compression. The document defines nothing new about DNS itself.
DNSSEC appears only in the Security Considerations, to explain that it does not prevent the rogue-server attack.
The option is for DHCPv4 only. RFC 3396 is cited for DHCPv4 long-option encoding.
Hostname resolution via search lists is the purpose of the option, but the document is not about host naming conventions.

RFC3398.title: Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) User Part (ISUP) to Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Mapping
RFC3398.summary: Specifies how a media gateway controller maps ISUP (SS7) call signalling messages and parameters to SIP messages and headers, and the reverse, including call flows, state machines, cause-code mapping and tel URI construction.

SIP-T.why: The whole document is the ISUP-SIP interworking specification, including encapsulated ISUP in SIP bodies for SIP bridging, which is the SIP-T/SIP-I topic.
SIP-T.quote: describes a way to perform the mapping between two signaling protocols: the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) User Part (ISUP)

SIP.why: The SIP side of the mapping is specified in detail: INVITE, CANCEL, BYE, INFO, provisional responses, status codes, early media and re-INVITE hold.
SIP.quote: SIP is an application layer protocol for establishing, terminating and modifying multimedia sessions.

tel URI.why: A full section maps ISUP number formats to and from tel URLs, including the npdi, rn and cic parameters for number portability and carrier routing.
tel URI.quote: The most common format used in SIP for the representation of telephone numbers is the tel URL [7].

rejected.why: This is the parent of SIP-T, which is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
ISUP over SCTP is mentioned only as a possible transport. The mapping is independent of the underlying transport.
SDP is used to carry media information for early media and hold, but the document does not specify or extend it.
RTP and DTMF carriage per RFC 2833 are mentioned only in passing.
ENUM is mentioned only as an optional query for resolving the called number, not as a subject of the document.
Multipart bodies and the ISUP media type are used as the encapsulation mechanism, which is defined in other RFCs.

gaps.name: ISUP / SS7 signalling
gaps.why: The document is about ISUP call control and its mapping, but the taxonomy has no ISUP or SS7 tag. SIP-T is the closest fit.

RFC3401.title: Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Part One: The Comprehensive DDDS
RFC3401.summary: RFC 3401 is an informational umbrella document that lists the specifications making up the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS), an algorithm for applying dynamically retrieved string-rewrite rules, and its applications and databases (including NAPTR in DNS).

naming.why: DDDS is a general naming/name-resolution and delegation discovery framework, not specific to one system. The document defines it by listing its parts.
naming.quote: DDDS is an abstract algorithm for applying dynamically retrieved string transformation rules to an application-unique string.

DNS.why: The DNS Database part of DDDS defines the NAPTR resource record. It obsoletes RFC 2915, so DNS readers would want this overview.
DNS.quote: This document is the official specification for the NAPTR DNS Resource Record.

rejected.why: ENUM is only cited as a sample application (RFC 2916). This document does not specify it.
URI resolution is mentioned as a sample application (RFC 3404), but this document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
RFC 2276 is updated, but this document does not discuss URN namespaces or resolution in its body.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and says nothing new.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System) / NAPTR
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DDDS or the NAPTR record specifically. The closest fits are the generic naming topic and DNS.

RFC3402.title: Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Part Two: The Algorithm
RFC3402.summary: Specifies the DDDS algorithm, which iteratively applies dynamically retrieved regex rewrite rules to an application-unique string to find delegated data, and defines what applications and databases must specify.

naming.why: DDDS is a general name-to-data delegation and resolution algorithm, not tied to DNS or one system. It fits the general naming topic.
naming.quote: The DDDS functions by mapping some unique string to data stored within a DDDS Database by iteratively applying string transformation rules until a terminal condition is reached.

service discovery.why: The algorithm discovers the authoritative server or service for a string by following delegation rules, with Services and Flags used to select branches.
service discovery.quote: there was the desire to locate an authoritative server for a URN that (by design) contained no information about network locations.

rejected.why: DNS is only an example Database. This part is database-agnostic, and the DNS database is specified in RFC 3403.
URNs are the historical origin of DDDS, but the document is about the general algorithm, not URN namespaces.
URI Resolution is only an example application, and it is specified in RFC 3404.
ENUM is mentioned only as an example of a shared database use, not as a subject of this document.
LDAP appears only in a fictitious example.

RFC3403.title: Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Part Three: The Domain Name System (DNS) Database
RFC3403.summary: Specifies the DNS as a DDDS Rules database, defining the NAPTR resource record (type 35) format, processing, and master-file encoding, and obsoleting RFC 2915 and RFC 2168.

DNS.why: The document defines the NAPTR RR: packet format, additional section processing, master file format and advice for DNS administrators. This is a new DNS record type, so it belongs under DNS.
DNS.quote: it is the official specification for the NAPTR DNS Resource Record

URN.why: A worked URN resolution example covers URN resolver discovery and the document's origin in the URN working group. It is substantial but not the main subject.
URN.quote: The NAPTR record was originally created for use with the Uniform Resource Name (URN) Resolver Discovery Service

ENUM.why: The E.164 example shows NAPTR records under e164.arpa for ENUM. ENUM readers would want it, though the document is application-neutral.
ENUM.quote: The ENUM Working Group in the IETF has specified a service that allows a telephone number to be mapped to a URI

rejected.why: Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to sign NAPTR records. The document is not about DNSSEC.
UTF-8 is only the character set for NAPTR field values. It is a substrate, not the subject.
SIP appears only as a service value in an ENUM example record.
DDDS is a delegation discovery mechanism, but this document specifies the DNS database for it, which the DNS tag covers. The service-discovery topic is a weaker fit.
URI resolution is a DDDS application covered in a separate RFC. This document only mentions it in examples.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System) / NAPTR
gaps.why: The document is part of the DDDS series and the official NAPTR RR specification. The taxonomy has no DDDS or NAPTR tag, so DNS is the closest fit.

RFC3404.title: Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Part Four: The Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI)
RFC3404.summary: Specifies the URI/URN Resolution application of the DDDS, which rewrites a URI or URN into keys and looks up NAPTR records under uri.arpa. and urn.arpa. to locate an authoritative resolver, with flags, service fields and examples.

URI.why: The document specifies how URIs (and URNs) are resolved, including the first well-known rule from the URI scheme and the uri.arpa. registry.
URI.quote: This document describes a DDDS Application for resolving Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI).

URN.why: A substantial part defines URN resolution via the namespace identifier and the urn.arpa. zone.
URN.quote: this document specifies two DDDS Applications. One is for URI Resolution and the other is for URN Resolution.
URN.section: 3. The Distinction Between URNs and URIs

DNS.why: The application specifies how NAPTR and SRV lookups in the DNS are used, including the uri.arpa. and urn.arpa. zones and additional-information processing.
DNS.quote: uses the NAPTR DNS resource record to contain the rewrite rules. The Keys for this database are encoded as domain-names.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in Security Considerations as being studied; the document is not about it.
A more specific tag (DNS, URI, URN) fits better than the general naming parent.
SRV records are used for the terminal lookup, but the document is about URI resolution, not generic service discovery.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System) / NAPTR
gaps.why: The document is part of the DDDS series and uses the NAPTR record, but the taxonomy has no DDDS or NAPTR tag. Readers of this subject would want a dedicated page.

RFC3405.title: Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Part Five: URI.ARPA Assignment Procedures
RFC3405.summary: RFC 3405 (BCP 65) defines the policies and procedures for registering NAPTR records in the URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA DNS zones, which hold DDDS resolution hints for URI schemes and URN namespaces.

URI.why: The document governs how URI scheme resolution hints are registered in URI.ARPA and ties registration to URI scheme registration under the IETF tree. Readers of URI topics would want it.
URI.quote: This document describes the procedures for inserting a new rule into the 'URI.ARPA' and 'URN.ARPA' zones.

URN.why: A substantial part covers URN.ARPA registration and its relationship to URN namespace ID registration, including the 'urn' rule in URI.ARPA.
URN.quote: The registration of a NAPTR record for a URN NID MUST NOT precede proper registration of that NID

DNS.why: It specifies requirements on NAPTR records in the DNS zones, such as TTLs and delegation to less stable zones, and DNS zone registration procedures. It is about DNS operations for these zones.
DNS.quote: it is anticipated that the resource records in those zones will have extremely long "times to live" (TTLs), perhaps measured in years.

rejected.why: IANA is the registration authority and the Considerations section creates the zones, but the main body is about DNS-hint registration policy for URI/URN, not IANA registry guidance in general.
NAPTR records are used, but the document does not concern telephone numbers or E.164 mapping.
Security Considerations only vaguely mention signing zones when possible; the body is not about DNSSEC.
The IESG review and submission procedure is specific to these zones and is not general IETF process.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System)
gaps.why: The document is part of the DDDS series, and the taxonomy has no tag for DDDS or NAPTR-based delegation discovery.

RFC3406.title: Uniform Resource Names (URN) Namespace Definition Mechanisms
RFC3406.summary: BCP defining the mechanisms, template, and registration process (experimental, informal, formal) for establishing URN namespaces and obtaining NIDs from IANA, obsoleting RFC 2611.

URN.why: The whole document defines URN namespace types, NID assignment, and the namespace definition template, which is squarely about URNs and URN namespaces.
URN.quote: This document lays out general definitions of and mechanisms for establishing Uniform Resource Names (URN) "namespaces".

rejected.why: The document uses an IANA registry for NIDs, but the registration process is for URN namespaces, not general IANA guidance. The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate.
DNS appears only in the hypothetical example namespace based on FQDNs, and in DDDS references; the document is not about DNS.
Formal NID registration uses IETF Consensus and RFC publication, but this is a means to the URN registration, not the subject.
URNs are a URI subset; the more specific URN tag fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC3407.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Simple Capability Declaration
RFC3407.summary: Defines SDP attributes (sqn, cdsc, cpar, cparmin, cparmax) that let an endpoint declare a capability set of supported media formats, as input to later negotiation such as offer/answer.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with new attributes for capability declaration and registers them, so it is squarely about SDP.
SDP.quote: This document defines a set of Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes that enables SDP to provide a minimal and backwards compatible capability declaration mechanism.

rejected.why: SIP is only mentioned as a protocol that uses SDP; the document does not specify or extend SIP.
RTP appears only in example media lines (RTP/AVP); the document is not about RTP.
MGCP is mentioned only as another user of SDP, not addressed by the document.
Codecs such as G.711 and G.729 appear only as example formats; the document defines no codec.

RFC3408.title: Zero-byte Support for Bidirectional Reliable Mode (R-mode) in Extended Link-Layer Assisted RObust Header Compression (ROHC) Profile
RFC3408.summary: Extends the ROHC link-layer assisted (zero-byte) profile of RFC 3242 to support Bidirectional Reliable mode (R-mode) by mapping R-0 packets to No-Header Packets, with assisting-layer interface additions and mode-specific differences.

ROHC.why: The whole document specifies an extension to a ROHC profile (zero-byte/LLA) for R-mode, covering packet mapping, ACK handling, CRC and CCP behaviour.
ROHC.quote: This document adds the zero-byte operation for ROHC Bidirectional Reliable mode (R-mode) to the ones specified for Unidirectional (U-mode) and Bidirectional Optimistic (O-mode) modes

rejected.why: RTP packets are the compressed payload; the document specifies header compression, not RTP itself.
Parent of ROHC; implied by the more specific ROHC tag.
ROHC framework mentions ESP profile in references only; not relevant to this document.
Radio air interfaces are the motivation but the document does not specify cellular interworking.

RFC3409.title: Lower Layer Guidelines for Robust RTP/UDP/IP Header Compression
RFC3409.summary: Informational guidelines describing what functionality lower (link) layers, especially cellular systems, must provide to support ROHC (RFC 3095) RTP/UDP/IP header compression.

ROHC.why: The whole document specifies requirements ROHC places on lower layers: error detection, inferred fields, feedback transport, packet type identification, reordering and duplication.
ROHC.quote: This document describes lower layer guidelines for robust RTP/UDP/IP header compression [RFC3095] as specified by the ROHC working group.

cellular.why: Section 3 gives cellular-specific guidance (handover, unequal error detection and protection), so readers of cellular IP topics would want it.
cellular.quote: These guidelines should simplify incorporation of the robust header compression algorithms into cellular systems like those standardized by 3GPP, 3GPP2, ETSI, etc

rejected.why: CRTP (RFC 2508) is only mentioned as an earlier scheme for comparison; the document is about ROHC.
RFC 2507 is cited as a prior scheme, not the subject.
RTP headers are what gets compressed, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
PPP is mentioned only as an example link layer for incorporation.
The more specific ROHC tag fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC3410.title: Introduction and Applicability Statements for Internet-Standard Management Framework
RFC3410.summary: RFC 3410 is an informational roadmap and applicability statement for the SNMPv3 Internet-Standard Management Framework. It relates SNMPv3 to SNMPv1 and SNMPv2, summarizes the specification documents, and recommends moving SNMPv1/SNMPv2c documents to Historic.

SNMP.why: The whole document is an overview and roadmap of the SNMP framework (v1, v2, v3), including architecture, USM and VACM security, and standardization status. The SNMP tag covers the framework and its security.
SNMP.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide an overview of the third version of the Internet-Standard Management Framework, termed the SNMP version 3 Framework (SNMPv3).

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document summarizes SMIv1/SMIv2, textual conventions, conformance statements, and MIB modules. Readers of the MIB/SMI subject would want it.
MIB.quote: STD 58, RFC 2578 specifies the base data types for the data definition language

rejected.why: USM's use of keyed hashing for digest computation is mentioned only in passing.
DES in CBC mode for USM privacy is mentioned only as a detail of the USM summary.
The UDP transport mapping is mentioned only as the preferred mapping. The document does not specify it.
The SMI is described as derived from ASN.1, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding.
Authentication and access control are part of SNMP security here, not a general AAA framework.
MD5 appears only as a hash algorithm used by USM.

RFC3411.title: An Architecture for Describing Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Management Frameworks
RFC3411.summary: RFC 3411 defines the modular architecture for SNMP Management Frameworks (SNMPv3): the SNMP engine with dispatcher, message processing, security and access control subsystems, applications, abstract service primitives, and the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies the SNMP architecture (engine, subsystems, applications, primitives), which is the core of the SNMP framework.
SNMP.quote: This document describes an architecture for describing Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Management Frameworks.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB module and textual conventions such as SnmpEngineID and SnmpSecurityModel, which MIB readers would want.
MIB.quote: Section 5 defines a collection of managed objects used to instrument SNMP entities within this architecture.

rejected.why: Access control is an architectural subsystem here but is only described abstractly (VACM is in RFC 3415); the document is not about authorization in its own right.
SnmpAdminString only references UTF-8 as an encoding in a textual convention; it is incidental.
Security Models and the User-Based Security Model are only framed here; the mechanisms are defined elsewhere (RFC 3414).
IANA sections only register number spaces for security models and engine ID formats, and that is boilerplate-level.

RFC3412.title: Message Processing and Dispatching for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC3412.summary: RFC 3412 (STD 62) specifies the SNMP Dispatcher and Message Processing Subsystem procedures, the SNMPv3 message format and Message Processing Model (v3MP), and the SNMP-MPD-MIB module of related statistics counters.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the SNMP engine's Dispatcher and the SNMPv3 message processing model and message format, which is core SNMP framework content.
SNMP.quote: It defines the procedures for dispatching potentially multiple versions of SNMP messages to the proper SNMP Message Processing Models, and for dispatching PDUs to SNMP applications.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-MPD-MIB module (snmpUnknownSecurityModels, snmpInvalidMsgs, snmpUnknownPDUHandlers) in Section 5, a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: This document defines these managed objects, the MIB module which contains them, and how these managed objects might be used to provide useful management.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used only to define the SNMPv3 message syntax and the MIB module; the document is not about ASN.1.
The authFlag and privFlag bits are covered, but only as message flags. The authentication mechanisms are in the Security Models defined elsewhere (USM, RFC 3414).
Transport mappings are only referenced (RFC 3417) and are not defined here.

RFC3413.title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Applications
RFC3413.summary: RFC 3413 (STD 62) specifies the five SNMP application types (command generator, command responder, notification originator, notification receiver, proxy forwarder) and defines the SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB and SNMP-PROXY-MIB modules.

SNMP.why: The document specifies the procedures of SNMP applications on top of the SNMPv3 architecture, including notification originators and receivers and proxy forwarding.
SNMP.quote: This document describes five types of Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) applications which make use of an SNMP engine

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document consists of the SNMP-TARGET-MIB, SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB and SNMP-PROXY-MIB module definitions, which readers browsing MIB modules would want.
MIB.quote: This document also defines Management Information Base (MIB) modules for specifying targets of management operations, for notification filtering, and for proxy forwarding.

rejected.why: Security names and levels appear only as parameters of management targets; the document is not about AAA frameworks.
UTF-8 appears only in the tag textual convention descriptions as an encoding, not as a subject of the document.
Access control is invoked via isAccessAllowed, but the access control model itself (VACM) is defined elsewhere.
The document uses SMIv2 MIB modules, not YANG.

RFC3414.title: User-based Security Model (USM) for version 3 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv3)
RFC3414.summary: Specifies the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3, providing message-level authentication (HMAC-MD5-96, HMAC-SHA-96), privacy (CBC-DES), timeliness/replay protection, key localization and key change, discovery, and the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB.

SNMP.why: The document is a core SNMPv3 security specification (STD 62): the Elements of Procedure for generating and processing SNMP messages under USM, so it belongs on the SNMP page.
SNMP.quote: This document describes the User-based Security Model (USM) for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) version 3 for use in the SNMP architecture.

MIB.why: Section 5 defines SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB with usmUserTable, usmStats counters and the KeyChange textual convention, a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: This document also includes a Management Information Base (MIB) for remotely monitoring/managing the configuration parameters for this Security Model.

HMAC.why: Sections 6 and 7 specify the HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 authentication protocols step by step (K1/K2, IPAD/OPAD, 12-octet MAC), so HMAC usage is a substantial subject.
HMAC.quote: It uses MD5 hash-function which is described in [RFC1321], in HMAC mode described in [RFC2104], truncating the output to 96 bits.

DES.why: Section 8 defines the DES-CBC privacy protocol, including key and IV derivation and the salt, in full.
DES.quote: This section describes the CBC-DES Symmetric Encryption Protocol.

rejected.why: MD5 is used inside HMAC-MD5-96 and for password-to-key, but the document does not specify MD5 itself.
SHA-1 is used as the HMAC hash and for key localization; the SHA algorithm is not specified here.
Key localization and KeyChange are covered, but they are mechanisms within USM; the SNMP and HMAC tags cover them better.
The UsmSecurityParameters BER encoding is only a message-format detail.
Authentication is a generic topic, and the document is about the SNMP-specific model, which the more specific tags capture.
Engine boots/time synchronization is a replay-protection mechanism internal to USM, not general clock synchronization.

RFC3415.title: View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC3415.summary: Specifies the View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for SNMP, defining elements of procedure for access checking (groups, contexts, MIB views) and the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB for remotely configuring it.

SNMP.why: VACM is the access control subsystem of the SNMPv3 architecture; the document specifies it and its elements of procedure, so it belongs under SNMP framework and security.
SNMP.quote: This document describes the View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for use in the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) architecture.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document is the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB module (vacmAccessTable, vacmViewTreeFamilyTable, etc.) for remote configuration.
MIB.quote: A MIB module, the View-based Access Control Model Configuration MIB, which defines these managed object types is included in this document.

authorization.why: The model is fundamentally an authorization/access control mechanism, deciding who may read, write or be notified of which managed objects.
authorization.quote: The Access Control Subsystem of an SNMP engine has the responsibility for checking whether a specific type of access (read, write, notify) to a particular object (instance) is allowed.

rejected.why: VACM explicitly assumes the securityName is already authenticated and provides no authentication of its own.
Not relevant; management data is modelled in SMIv2 MIB, not YANG.
OBJECT IDENTIFIERs and SMIv2 syntax are used, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Parent of SNMP; implied by the more specific SNMP tag.

RFC3416.title: Version 2 of the Protocol Operations for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC3416.summary: RFC 3416 (STD 62) specifies SNMP version 2 protocol operations: the PDU syntax in ASN.1 and the elements of procedure for GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, Response, SetRequest, SNMPv2-Trap and InformRequest, obsoleting RFC 1905.

SNMP.why: The whole document specifies SNMP PDU syntax and processing procedures, so it belongs on the SNMP page.
SNMP.quote: This document defines version 2 of the protocol operations for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

rejected.why: MIB objects are accessed by the operations, and sysUpTime and snmpSilentDrops are referenced, but no MIB module is defined here.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the PDUs, not the subject.
UDP is only the preferred transport, and the mapping is specified in RFC 3417.
The SNMP tag is more specific and already covers this.

RFC3417.title: Transport Mappings for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC3417.summary: RFC 3417 (STD 62) defines how SNMP messages are carried over UDP/IPv4, OSI, AppleTalk DDP and IPX, includes the SNMPv2-TM MIB module, and specifies BER serialization rules.

SNMP.why: The document specifies transport mappings for SNMP, part of the SNMP standard framework (STD 62).
SNMP.quote: defines how the management protocol [RFC3416] may be carried over a variety of protocol suites

transport mapping.why: Core content is X-over-UDP/OSI/DDP/IPX bindings with serialization and well-known ports.
transport mapping.quote: It is the purpose of this document to define how the SNMP maps onto an initial set of transport domains.

MIB.why: Defines the SNMPv2-TM MIB module with transport domain identities and textual conventions for addresses.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: AppleTalk DDP is just one of the transports mapped; the document is not about AppleTalk itself.
UDP is the preferred substrate, but the document does not define anything new about UDP.
BER serialization rules are applied to SNMP messages, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules in general.
IPX is one of several substrates mapped, not the subject.
The OSI transport is a substrate for SNMP here, not the subject of the document.

RFC3418.title: Management Information Base (MIB) for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC3418.summary: RFC 3418 defines the SNMPv2-MIB module, with the system group, snmp group, notification objects, set serial number and conformance statements describing the behaviour of an SNMP entity, obsoleting RFC 1907.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SNMPv2-MIB) written in SMIv2, with object definitions, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This document defines managed objects which describe the behavior of a Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) entity.

SNMP.why: The MIB instruments the SNMP protocol entity itself: message counters, authentication-failure traps, silent drops, proxy drops and the set-coordination lock. SNMP readers would want this standard (STD 62).
SNMP.quote: a collection of objects providing basic instrumentation and control of an SNMP entity.

rejected.why: ASN.1/BER is only mentioned in the snmpInASNParseErrs counter description. It is not a subject of the document.
This is an SMIv2 MIB module, not a YANG model.
IPsec appears only as an example in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC3419.title: Textual Conventions for Transport Addresses
RFC3419.summary: Defines the TRANSPORT-ADDRESS-MIB module, a set of SMIv2 textual conventions and OID registrations for representing transport-layer addresses (UDP/TCP/SCTP over IPv4/IPv6, with zone indices, local IPC, and DNS names) for use by other MIB modules.

MIB.why: The RFC's sole content is a MIB module (TRANSPORT-ADDRESS-MIB) with textual conventions in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules and SMI.
MIB.quote: This document introduces a Management Information Base (MIB) module that defines textual conventions to represent commonly used transport-layer addressing information.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework in which MIB objects are accessed and the document relates to SNMPv2-TM, but it defines no SNMP protocol behaviour; the subject is the MIB module.
SCTP is one of the transports that the address formats and domains cover, but the document does not specify or extend SCTP.
TCP is only one of the transport domains named in the address definitions; the document does not specify TCP.
UDP is only one of the transport domains named in the address definitions; the document does not specify UDP.
IPv6 addresses and zone indices are encoded in the textual conventions, but the document does not address IPv6 itself.
It defines how addresses are represented in MIBs, not IP address architecture or allocation.

RFC3420.title: Internet Media Type message/sipfrag
RFC3420.summary: Registers the message/sipfrag MIME media type, which carries well-formed subsets of SIP messages for S/MIME-based assertions and for REFER status reporting.

media types.why: The document's purpose is to define and register a new MIME media type, including its ABNF, parameters and encoding. Readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document registers the message/sipfrag Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) media type.

SIP.why: The type extends SIP by representing partial SIP messages, used with the REFER method and for identity assertions. A substantial part of the document concerns SIP message structure.
SIP.quote: allows certain subsets of well formed Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) messages to be represented instead of requiring a complete SIP message

rejected.why: S/MIME is only mentioned as the mechanism that could protect sipfrag parts. The document does not specify or extend it.
ABNF is only the notation used for the one grammar rule.
The media-type-specific tag fits better. The document does not address MIME body structure in general.
SDP appears only inside example message bodies.

RFC3421.title: Select and Sort Extensions for the Service Location Protocol (SLP)
RFC3421.summary: Defines two SLP extensions, Select and Sort, letting a User Agent limit the number of URL entries in a Service Reply and have them sorted by attribute keys, so it can find the best-matching service.

SLP.why: The whole document specifies new SLP extensions to SrvRqst/SrvRply processing, including extension IDs and DA/SA behaviour.
SLP.quote: This document defines two extensions (Select and Sort) for the Service Location Protocol (SLP).

rejected.why: SLP is the more specific tag that already covers this; the document is about SLP extensions, not service discovery generally.
RFC 2891 LDAP sort rules are only adapted as a model for the sort semantics; the document does not specify or extend LDAP.
ABNF is only used as notation to define the sort-key-list grammar.
The IANA section merely records extension ID assignments; it is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC3422.title: Forwarding Media Access Control (MAC) Frames over Multiple Access Protocol over Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (MAPOS)
RFC3422.summary: Informational RFC describing how to encapsulate Ethernet/IEEE 802 MAC frames in MAPOS frames (protocol 0xFE31) via network adapters, with MAC-to-MAPOS address table setup and security considerations, giving transparent LAN service over a MAPOS network.

MAPOS.why: The document defines an extension of MAPOS: the bridged-LAN encapsulation (0xFE31), destination MAPOS address determination and address table configuration. MAPOS readers would want it.
MAPOS.quote: This memo describes a method for forwarding media access control (MAC) frames over Multiple Access Protocol over Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (MAPOS)

rejected.why: Ethernet frames are the payload being carried, but the document is about the MAPOS encapsulation, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
ARP is only used as an example of how the address table is learned dynamically; the document does not specify or extend it.
The parent SONET tag is implied by the MAPOS child, so it is not listed separately.
The frame format is based on PPP Bridging Control Protocol, but PPP is only a reference model, not the subject.
The text uses VPN/VLAN terminology for transparent LAN service, but it describes a link-layer MAC bridging service, not provider-provisioned L2/L3 VPNs.
FDDI and token ring frame formats are shown as encapsulation cases, but the document is not about IP over those media.

RFC3423.title: XACCT's Common Reliable Accounting for Network Element (CRANE) Protocol Specification Version 1.0
RFC3423.summary: Defines XACCT's CRANE protocol, an application protocol (preferably over SCTP, or TCP) for reliable, efficient export of accounting data from network elements to mediation/billing systems, with template negotiation, redundant servers, flow control and message formats.

AAA.why: CRANE is a new accounting protocol positioned against RADIUS and Diameter. Accounting is the AAA subject area, and no more specific tag fits.
AAA.quote: enables efficient and reliable delivery of any data, mainly accounting data from Network Elements to any systems, such as mediation systems and Business Support Systems

SCTP.why: The document states a preference for SCTP and explains why. It specifies a transport mapping, but only as a substrate, so this is a weaker secondary tag.
SCTP.quote: SCTP [4] is the preferred way to transmit CRANE messages.

rejected.why: Kept above as secondary only; the document does not define anything new about SCTP itself.
TCP is an alternative substrate; the document only lists rules for running over it.
Only discussed as an inadequate existing mechanism, not specified or extended.
Only mentioned as a comparison in the introduction.
Related, since the IPFIX WG is acknowledged, but this document does not specify IPFIX.
Mentioned only as an alternative with high overhead.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a possible lower-layer protection.

gaps.name: usage/accounting data export
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for accounting or usage-record export from network elements, apart from the general AAA tag.

RFC3424.title: IAB Considerations for UNilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF) Across Network Address Translation
RFC3424.summary: IAB architectural statement on UNSAF (unilateral self-address fixing) mechanisms used across NATs, explaining why they are only short-term workarounds and listing the considerations any such proposal must address.

NAT.why: The whole document analyses NAT behaviour, deployed NAT variations, and the architectural problems of workarounds for address discovery across NATs.
NAT.quote: communicating endpoints that are separated by one or more NATs do not know how to refer to themselves using addresses that are valid in the addressing realms

rejected.why: STUN is an example UNSAF mechanism but is never named; the document is general guidance, not about STUN.
It is an IAB architectural statement, but the subject is specifically NAT workarounds, which the NAT tag covers more precisely.
Firewall and midcom security exposure is mentioned as a concern, but only as a side issue.
Fits the theme, but that tag is scoped to interactive traversal of NATs for real-time media, and this document is a general architectural statement not limited to real-time media.

gaps.name: UNSAF (UNilateral Self-Address Fixing)
gaps.why: The document's central concept is not a taxonomy term. The closest fits are NAT and NAT traversal, but neither names the general class of self-address discovery workarounds.

RFC3425.title: Obsoleting IQUERY
RFC3425.summary: RFC 3425 deprecates the DNS IQUERY (inverse query, opcode 1) operation from RFC 1035, superseding section 6.4 and telling name servers to return Not Implemented.

DNS.why: The document changes the DNS protocol by obsoleting the IQUERY opcode and updating RFC 1035, specifying required server behaviour (return Not Implemented).
DNS.quote: this document deprecates the IQUERY operation, declaring it entirely obsolete.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations as a difficulty if IQUERY were kept; the document is not about it.
The IANA section merely retires opcode 1; this is boilerplate-level and not the subject of the document.

RFC3426.title: General Architectural and Policy Considerations
RFC3426.summary: An IAB document listing general architectural and policy questions (layering, long- vs short-term solutions, robustness, tragedy of the commons, competing interests, evolvability, internationalization, deployability) for IETF protocol designers, illustrated with case studies.

internet architecture.why: The whole document is about Internet architectural principles and considerations such as layering, end-to-end, robustness and evolvability, complementing RFC 1958.
internet architecture.quote: This document suggests general architectural and policy questions that the IETF community has to address when working on new standards and protocols.

rejected.why: OPES is only one case study (Section 8.2) summarizing RFC 3238; the document is not about OPES.
ECN is a robustness case study in Section 9.2, not the subject of the document.
SIP is a case study on decomposing a complex protocol (Section 7.1); not the subject.
Mentioned only in case studies (Congestion Manager, end-to-end congestion control); not the document's subject.
A short section poses an internationalization question, but it is a minor part of the document.
UNSAF/NAT traversal is a brief case study of short-term solutions; not the subject.

RFC3427.title: Change Process for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3427.summary: BCP defining the IETF process for proposing, vetting and registering changes and extensions to SIP, including "P-" headers and SIP event package registration rules.

SIP.why: The whole document governs how SIP is extended: working group roles, P- headers, event packages, and IANA registries for SIP methods, headers and option tags.
SIP.quote: This memo documents a process intended to apply architectural discipline to the future development of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

IETF process.why: It is a process BCP about WG charters, IESG/IAB approval, expert review and RFC publication requirements for one protocol's extensions.
IETF process.quote: All changes or extensions to SIP must first exist as SIP Working Group documents.

rejected.why: IANA registration rules for P-headers and event packages are part of the process, but the document is about SIP change control, not IANA registries generally.
SIMPLE and event packages are mentioned only as sources of requirements and as an extension type, not specified or profiled.
It is listed only as one of the working groups that generate SIP requirements.

RFC3428.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Extension for Instant Messaging
RFC3428.summary: Defines the SIP MESSAGE method, a SIP extension for pager-model instant messages carried as MIME bodies, with processing rules, congestion-control limits and security guidance.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new method and specifies UAC, proxy and UAS processing and header field usage for it.
SIP.quote: This document proposes the MESSAGE method, an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) that allows the transfer of Instant Messages.

instant messaging.why: The document's purpose is to carry instant messages over SIP, following the IM requirements in RFC 2779 and the CPIM message format and im: URIs.
instant messaging.quote: Instant Messaging (IM) is defined as the exchange of content between a set of participants in near real time.

rejected.why: The document is a SIMPLE working group product, but it defines only the MESSAGE method. It does not cover presence, event packages or XCAP.
S/MIME is only required for end-to-end protection in the Security Considerations. It is not the subject of the document.
MIME bodies are only the payload carrier for the message. The document defines nothing new about MIME.
SMS is mentioned only as an analogy for the pager model. The document does not specify SMS.
Section 8 gives MESSAGE-specific size and transaction limits, but congestion control is a side concern of the method. It is not a subject of the document in its own right.
Presence is mentioned only as context. The document does not define a presence format.

RFC3429.title: Assignment of the 'OAM Alert Label' for Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture (MPLS) Operation and Maintenance (OAM) Functions
RFC3429.summary: Informational RFC recording the assignment of reserved MPLS label value 14 as the 'OAM Alert Label' used by ITU-T Y.1711 user-plane MPLS OAM to identify OAM packets, with notes on penultimate hop popping behaviour.

MPLS.why: The document assigns a reserved MPLS label value and explains how OAM packets are handled with penultimate hop popping, which is MPLS encoding and operation.
MPLS.quote: One of the reserved label values defined in RFC 3032 (MPLS label stack encoding [2]) is assigned to 'OAM Alert Label'. A value of 14 is used for this purpose.

OAM.why: The label exists to identify MPLS OAM packets. The document covers OAM objectives such as defect detection, localization and performance monitoring.
OAM.quote: MPLS OAM (Operation and Maintenance) functions provide necessary tools for network operators to operate and maintain the networks.

rejected.why: The label value reservation is recorded in IANA Considerations, which is boilerplate here. The document is about the OAM label, not IANA registry guidance.
This RFC predates MPLS-TP and concerns the Y.1711 user-plane OAM label, not the Transport Profile.
Performance monitoring is only listed as one OAM objective. It is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC3430.title: Simple Network Management Protocol Over Transmission Control Protocol Transport Mapping
RFC3430.summary: Defines an experimental, optional transport mapping for carrying SNMP messages over TCP, covering serialization/framing, well-known ports, connection management, and reliable transport versus confirmed operations.

SNMP.why: The document extends the SNMP transport mappings (STD 62, RFC 3417), specifying how SNMP messages are framed, addressed and managed over TCP. Readers of SNMP would want it.
SNMP.quote: This memo defines a transport mapping for using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) [1] over TCP [2].

transport mapping.why: This is a binding of one protocol (SNMP) onto another transport (TCP), which is what the transport mapping topic covers. SNMP is a tech tag outside this topic's subtree, so the topic tag is given directly.
transport mapping.quote: This memo defines a transport mapping for using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) [1] over TCP [2].

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document defines how SNMP uses it, not anything new about TCP itself.
BER encoding is only referenced for message serialization, by pointing to RFC 3417. Nothing about ASN.1 is defined here.
The snmpTargetTable is discussed only in the appendix on alternatives, and no MIB module is defined.

RFC3431.title: Sieve Extension: Relational Tests
RFC3431.summary: Defines the Sieve "relational" extension, adding :value and :count relational match types (gt, ge, lt, le, eq, ne) to the address, envelope and header tests of the Sieve mail filtering language.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies an extension to Sieve: new match types and their semantics for address, envelope and header tests.
Sieve.quote: This document describes the RELATIONAL extension to the Sieve mail filtering language defined in RFC 3028.

rejected.why: Sieve is a child of email and already implies it; the document is about the filtering language, not mail transport or architecture.
Mentioned only as an example of a server where Sieve may run; not specified or extended here.
The i;ascii-numeric comparator is borrowed from the ACAP RFC, but ACAP is not specified or extended; no ACAP tag is warranted.
The RFC 2822 header and address fields are what the tests inspect, but the document does not define or extend message format.
Spam appears only in a script example that files mail with many recipients; the document is not about spam filtering.

RFC3432.title: Network performance measurement with periodic streams
RFC3432.summary: RFC 3432 defines a periodic-stream sampling method and the Type-P-One-way-Delay-Periodic-Stream metric (with delay and IPDV statistics, error analysis, calibration and reporting) for measuring IP network performance, as an alternative to Poisson sampling.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines an active/passive sampling method and delay/delay-variation metrics, with error, calibration and reporting rules, which is IPPM-style performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo describes a periodic sampling method and relevant metrics for assessing the performance of IP networks.

rejected.why: Multimedia/CBR streams are only the motivating traffic model. The document does not specify or analyse RTP.
QoS is mentioned as a use case, for example verifying service classes. The document defines measurement methods, not QoS mechanisms.
NTP is mentioned only as one way to synchronise clocks, in the discussion of clock error.
Clock synchronisation error is analysed only as a source of measurement uncertainty. The document is not about time synchronisation.
OWAMP is a measurement protocol and is not defined or referenced here. This memo defines only a metric and sampling method.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for IPPM metric definitions such as one-way delay, loss and delay variation. The generic 'performance measurement' topic is the closest fit.

RFC3433.title: Entity Sensor Management Information Base
RFC3433.summary: Defines the ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB module, an SMIv2 extension of the Entity MIB that exposes physical sensor readings (temperature, fan RPM, voltage) with type, scale, precision, value and status objects.

MIB.why: The whole document is a MIB module (ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB) with textual conventions, a table and conformance groups, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects for extending the Entity MIB (RFC 2737) to provide generalized access to information related to physical sensors

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document specifies no SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag sits under SNMP and covers it.
RMON Alarm and Events groups are only recommended for thresholding in one paragraph; the document does not define or extend RMON.
The data model is written in SMIv2, not YANG.

RFC3434.title: Remote Monitoring MIB Extensions for High Capacity Alarms
RFC3434.summary: Defines the HC-ALARM MIB module, extending RMON-1 alarm thresholding to Counter64-based objects with a high-capacity alarm table, capabilities scalar, and rising/falling notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module (HC-ALARM-MIB) defining managed objects, tables and notifications.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects for extending the alarm thresholding capabilities found in the Remote Monitoring (RMON) MIB (RFC 2819), to provide similar threshold monitoring of objects based on the Counter64 data type.

RMON.why: It extends the RMON-1 Alarm Group with a superset high capacity alarm group, so RMON readers need it.
RMON.quote: This MIB is intended to be implemented in Remote Monitoring (RMON) probes, which may also support the RMON-1 MIB [RFC2819].

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB and is only referenced for security; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour.
Threshold alarming on counters is covered by the RMON tag; no measurement methodology is defined.

RFC3435.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Version 1.0
RFC3435.summary: RFC 3435 specifies MGCP 1.0, the master/slave protocol by which a Call Agent controls media gateways through endpoints, connections, events, signals, packages, and UDP transactions, obsoleting RFC 2705.

MGCP.why: The document defines the MGCP protocol itself: commands, parameters, return codes, packages, transport over UDP, failover and race conditions.
MGCP.quote: This document describes an application programming interface and a corresponding protocol (MGCP) which is used between elements of a decomposed multimedia gateway.

rejected.why: SDP is used to carry session descriptions, but it is only the encoding substrate. MGCP adds only a LOCAL network type and an a=MGCPlocalcx attribute.
RTP is the bearer media transport the gateways handle and the source of the connection statistics. The document does not specify RTP.
MGCP runs over UDP, which is substrate only. The retransmission and at-most-once logic is MGCP-specific.
SIP is mentioned only as a possible Call-Agent-to-Call-Agent protocol.
Megaco/H.248 is referenced only in the IESG note as the standards-track alternative. This document does not describe it.
The relation to H.323 is a short architectural comparison and is not a main subject.
DNS is used for endpoint and Call Agent name resolution to support failover. The document does not define anything new about the DNS itself.

RFC3436.title: Transport Layer Security over Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC3436.summary: Specifies how to run TLS over SCTP, mapping TLS connections to SCTP bi-directional streams, requiring SCTP message fragmentation, and forbidding unordered delivery for TLS streams.

TLS.why: The document defines how TLS handshakes, sessions and resumption are used per SCTP stream, and mandates a ciphersuite. It is deployment guidance for TLS.
TLS.quote: This document describes the usage of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, as defined in RFC 2246, over the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)

SCTP.why: It places requirements on SCTP: fragmentation, stream usage and no unordered delivery or limited lifetimes for TLS streams. It is a usage profile of SCTP.
SCTP.quote: SCTP MUST provide fragmentation of user messages, which is an optional feature of [RFC2960].

rejected.why: This fits as a topic, but the guidance says to give a topic tag directly only if no technology tag already sits under it. TLS and SCTP are tagged, but they are not children of transport mapping, so the call is close. I chose the specific technology tags instead.
The document runs ordinary TLS over SCTP's reliable streams. It does not use datagram TLS.
TCP is mentioned only as the usual transport for TLS and as a comparison with SCTP.
The mandatory ciphersuite TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA is only referenced, and the document does not address AES.

RFC3437.title: Layer-Two Tunneling Protocol Extensions for PPP Link Control Protocol Negotiation
RFC3437.summary: Defines new L2TP AVPs (LCP Want Options, LCP Allow Options, LNS Last Sent/Received LCP Confreq) letting the LAC and LNS communicate PPP LCP option negotiation across an L2TP tunnel.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TP by defining four new AVPs carried in ICCN, OCCN and Set-Link-Info messages.
L2TP.quote: This document defines extensions to the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) for enhanced support of link-specific Point to Point Protocol (PPP) options.

PPP.why: A substantial part of the document concerns PPP LCP option negotiation (MRU, ACCM, PFC, ACFC, FCS-ALT) and how the LAC and LNS handle it.
PPP.quote: provides a mechanism for communicating desired LCP options between L2TP endpoints in advance of PPP LCP negotiation at the far end of an L2TP tunnel

rejected.why: The IANA section only requests four AVP attribute numbers. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
L2TP is tagged directly, so the generic tunneling topic is not needed. Tunneling is only the context.

RFC3438.title: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Considerations Update
RFC3438.summary: BCP updating IANA registration policies for several L2TP (RFC 2661) number spaces (Control Message AVPs, Message Type values, Result/Error codes) from IETF Consensus/First Come First Served to Expert Review.

L2TP.why: The document updates registry criteria for L2TP protocol values (AVPs, message types, result codes); readers of L2TP would want it.
L2TP.quote: This document provides guidance to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) regarding the registration of values related to the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP)

IANA.why: The whole document is about IANA registration policy (Expert Review vs IETF Consensus) for registries, so IANA readers would want it.
IANA.quote: This section updates the criteria to be used by the IANA to assign additional numbers in each of these lists.

rejected.why: L2TP has its own more specific tag; the generic tunneling parent is implied and not the document's subject.
L2TP carries PPP but the document does not address PPP.
It cites the Designated Expert/Expert Review process only as applied to IANA registries, not IETF procedures in general.

RFC3439.title: Some Internet Architectural Guidelines and Philosophy
RFC3439.summary: Informational RFC extending RFC 1958 with architectural guidelines for Internet backbone design, centred on the Simplicity Principle, and covering layering, convergence, interworking, packet vs circuit switching complexity, over-provisioning and reliability myths.

internet architecture.why: The document extends RFC 1958 on architectural principles, presenting the Simplicity Principle, end-to-end argument, layering and component proportionality as guidance for Internet architecture.
internet architecture.quote: outlining some of the philosophical guidelines to which architects and designers of Internet backbone networks should adhere

rejected.why: Concerns backbone network design and complexity broadly, not routing architecture or scalability of routing specifically; routing is only an example.
QoS is a brief metric comparison in section 5.2.7, not a substantial subject.
IP over ATM is used as a cautionary example of convergence layering, not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only in passing as an example of reduced transparency.
TCP behaviour serves as an example of cross-layer assumptions; the document does not address TCP itself.
Mentioned only as a proposed convergence layer.

RFC3440.title: Definitions of Extension Managed Objects for Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Lines
RFC3440.summary: Defines the ADSL-LINE-EXT-MIB SMIv2 module, extending the ADSL Line MIB (RFC 2662) with G.Lite transmission mode, power state, fast retrain, severely errored/unavailable seconds counters, profile and threshold-notification objects based on ITU G.997.1.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module in SMIv2 defining new managed objects, tables, notifications and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: it describes additional managed objects used for managing Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line (ADSL) interfaces not covered by the ADSL Line MIB (RFC 2662).

DSL.why: The managed objects concern ADSL lines, transmission modes (G.992.1/G.992.2), G.Lite power states, and ATU-C/ATU-R performance counters, so DSL readers would want it.
DSL.quote: The purpose of this memo is to define a supplemental set of managed objects that is not covered by the ADSL Line MIB

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document specifies no SNMP protocol changes, and the MIB tag sits under SNMP and covers the content.
The counters and 15-minute intervals are part of the MIB objects, not a performance measurement methodology.
Not relevant; the data model is SMIv2, not YANG.

RFC3441.title: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) Package for the Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP)
RFC3441.summary: Defines an MGCP package ("atm") with ATM-specific local connection options, events, signals, connection parameters, and AAL2 profile/codec negotiation procedures for media gateways controlling ATM bearer connections.

MGCP.why: The document extends MGCP with a new package (local connection options, events, signals, connection parameters), so it belongs on the MGCP page.
MGCP.quote: This document describes an Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) package for the Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP).

ATM.why: Large parts parameterize ATM bearers, AAL1/AAL2/AAL5, traffic management and QoS, so ATM readers would want it.
ATM.quote: In the ATM networks addressed in this document, services are carried directly over ATM without an intervening IP layer.

rejected.why: SDP is used to carry negotiation results, but the document defines MGCP options, not SDP itself (that is RFC 3108).
Mentioned only as a potential successor protocol.
ATM QoS parameters are conveyed as MGCP options within ATM bearer setup, not a QoS architecture.
Gateway control for voice trunking is covered by the MGCP tag; the document is not about general PSTN interworking.
Frame relay appears only as AAL application values in a list.

RFC3442.title: The Classless Static Route Option for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) version 4
RFC3442.summary: Defines DHCPv4 option 121, which carries a list of classless static routes (destination with subnet mask width plus router) from server to client, obsoleting option 33, and specifies client and server behaviour.

DHCP.why: The RFC defines a new DHCPv4 option (code 121), its encoding, and client/server behaviour. Readers of DHCP would want it. It is DHCPv4, so the DHCPv6 child does not apply.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a new Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) option which is passed from the DHCP Server to the DHCP Client to configure a list of static routes

rejected.why: The option installs static routes in host routing tables. It does not address routing architecture or routing protocols.
The option uses classless subnet masks, but the document is about DHCP option encoding, not CIDR aggregation.
The document is explicitly DHCP version 4 only.
RIP is mentioned only as an alternative way to maintain a routing table.
IPv4 classful and classless addressing is background. The document specifies a DHCP option, not IPv4 itself.

RFC3443.title: Time To Live (TTL) Processing in Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) Networks
RFC3443.summary: RFC 3443 specifies TTL processing for hierarchical MPLS LSPs under the Uniform, Pipe and Short Pipe models, with and without penultimate hop popping, and updates RFC 3032.

MPLS.why: The whole document defines how the TTL field in MPLS label stack entries is handled at push, swap, and pop, including PHP. It updates the MPLS label stack encoding RFC 3032.
MPLS.quote: This document describes Time To Live (TTL) processing in hierarchical Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) networks

rejected.why: The document ties its Pipe/Uniform/Short Pipe terminology to RFC 3270 (MPLS Diffserv support), but it only covers TTL processing, not Diffserv behaviour.
LDP is mentioned only to say that LSP type signalling is out of scope.
RSVP-TE is mentioned only to say that LSP type signalling is out of scope.
IP TTL is handled when packets are pushed or popped, but the document is not about IP itself.

RFC3444.title: On the Difference between Information Models and Data Models
RFC3444.summary: Informational RFC from the IRTF NMRG explaining the difference between Information Models (conceptual, protocol-neutral) and Data Models (implementation- and protocol-specific) for managed objects in network management, using SMI, SPPI, GDMO and CIM/MOF as examples.

network management.why: The document is a conceptual clarification of modelling terminology for network management, with no specific protocol as its subject. The general network management topic fits best.
network management.quote: There has been ongoing confusion about the differences between Information Models and Data Models for defining managed objects in network management.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document analyses IETF MIB modules and SMI, with their OID assignments, INDEX clauses and MAX-ACCESS, as examples of data models. Readers of MIB/SMI material would want it.
MIB.quote: Management Information Base (MIB) modules defined within the IETF. The language (syntax) used to define these DMs is called the "Structure of Management Information" (SMI)

terminology.why: The document exists to harmonize the definitions of the terms Information Model and Data Model, so it also serves as a terminology reference.
terminology.quote: it turned out that people had a different understanding of the main terms, which caused confusion and long arguments.

rejected.why: SNMP is mentioned only as a protocol the models map onto. The document is about modelling terminology, not the protocol.
PIB and SPPI appear only as examples of data models. The document does not address policy-based management information models as a subject.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as the origin of SMI syntax, not as a subject of the document.
YANG does not appear. The document predates it and only discusses SMIng and SMI.
RFC 3290 is cited once as an example of an informal information model. The document is not about Diffserv.

gaps.name: Information modelling / data modelling (IM vs DM, UML, CIM)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is management modelling methodology, including UML class diagrams, CIM schemas and GDMO. The taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the general network management topic.

RFC3445.title: Limiting the Scope of the KEY Resource Record (RR)
RFC3445.summary: Restricts the DNS KEY resource record to DNSSEC keys only, removing application key sub-types (Email, IPSEC, TLS), redefining the flags and protocol octet, and closing the IANA protocol registry; updates RFC 2535.

DNSSEC.why: The document redefines the DNSSEC KEY RR, its flags and protocol octet, and how zone keys are distinguished from application keys, updating RFC 2535.
DNSSEC.quote: This document limits the Domain Name System (DNS) KEY Resource Record (RR) to only keys used by the Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC).

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific child and fits; the KEY RR is a DNSSEC record here, so the parent is implied.
IPSEC keys are only mentioned as application keys being removed from the KEY RR; the document is not about IPsec.
TLS keys are mentioned only as a removed application key sub-type.
The registry closure is a minor consequence in the IANA Considerations section, not the subject of the document.
The document is about the record format and scope, not key establishment or provisioning.

RFC3446.title: Anycast Rendevous Point (RP) mechanism using Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) and Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP)
RFC3446.summary: Informational RFC describing Anycast RP, a mechanism that lets multiple RPs share one anycast address in a PIM-SM domain, using MSDP between the RPs to share source information, for load sharing and fast failover.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM-SM deployment by relaxing the single active RP per group constraint. It covers RP configuration, group-to-RP mappings and register decapsulation load.
PIM-SM.quote: a mechanism to allow for an arbitrary number of Rendevous Points (RPs) per group in a single shared-tree Protocol Independent Multicast-Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) domain

MSDP.why: MSDP peering between the anycast RPs is an essential part of the mechanism. The document specifies how MSDP peerings and SA messages must use unicast RP addresses, and covers the peer-RPF check interaction.
MSDP.quote: MSDP is required so that the various RPs in the domain maintain a consistent view of the sources that are active

rejected.why: The anycast addressing here is a means of building the RP mechanism and is specific to PIM RPs. The document is about multicast RP redundancy and load sharing, not anycast addressing and operation in general.
BGP and MBGP are only mentioned for peer-RPF checks and for addressing guidelines for the MSDP peerings. The document does not specify or extend BGP.
The parent topic is implied by the PIM-SM and MSDP tags, so it is not listed separately.
OSPF appears only in the security discussion as a way to protect unicast routing.

RFC3447.title: Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.1
RFC3447.summary: RFC 3447 republishes PKCS #1 v2.1, specifying RSA key types, primitives, the RSAES-OAEP and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 encryption schemes, the RSASSA-PSS and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature schemes, and their ASN.1 syntax and OIDs.

RSA.why: The whole document specifies RSA keys, primitives, encryption and signature schemes, and their encodings.
RSA.quote: This document provides recommendations for the implementation of public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm [42]

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used to define key and algorithm identifier syntax in an appendix, but the document is about RSA cryptography, not ASN.1.
SHA-1/SHA-2 are only supported hash functions named for the schemes, not specified here.
MD2/MD5 appear only as hash options for compatibility, not the subject.
X.509 is mentioned as an application context only.
CMS and PKCS #7 are mentioned as users of the schemes, not specified here.
TLS is mentioned once as a user of RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5.

gaps.name: RSA-OAEP / RSA-PSS padding schemes (PKCS #1)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RSA tag but no more specific tag for PKCS #1 schemes; RSA covers them well enough.

RFC3448.title: TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC): Protocol Specification
RFC3448.summary: RFC 3448 specifies TFRC, an equation-based, TCP-friendly congestion control mechanism for unicast flows with smooth sending rate, covering sender and receiver behaviour and loss event rate calculation.

TFRC.why: The entire document specifies TFRC: throughput equation, sender and receiver protocols, and loss event rate calculation.
TFRC.quote: This document specifies TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC).  TFRC is a congestion control mechanism for unicast flows operating in a best-effort Internet environment.

rejected.why: TCP's throughput equation is used as a model for fairness, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
RTP is only mentioned as a transport protocol in which TFRC could be used; no packet formats are specified.
ECN marks are treated as loss events, but ECN itself is not the subject.
Parent of TFRC, which is implied by the more specific tag.
DCCP is not mentioned in the text; it is a later user of TFRC.

RFC3449.title: TCP Performance Implications of Network Path Asymmetry
RFC3449.summary: BCP describing how network path asymmetry (bandwidth and MAC-related) degrades TCP performance via ACK feedback problems, and surveying host, transparent link-layer, header compression, ACK filtering/reconstruction and scheduling mitigations with recommendations.

TCP.why: The whole document analyses TCP ACK clocking, delayed ACKs, byte counting, pacing and stretch ACKs under asymmetry, and recommends TCP host modifications.
TCP.quote: This document describes TCP performance problems that arise because of asymmetric effects.

header compression.why: Type 0 mitigations (VJ and robust header compression) get dedicated sections with recommendations by asymmetry level.
header compression.quote: TCP header compression [RFC1144] (sometimes known as V-J compression) is a Proposed Standard describing use over low capacity links running SLIP or PPP

link layer.why: Document covers asymmetric access links (DOCSIS, DVB satellite, ADSL, packet radio), MAC interactions, and link-layer scheduling mitigations.
link layer.quote: asymmetry in the underlying Medium Access Control (MAC) and Physical (PHY) protocols could make it expensive to transmit TCP ACKs

rejected.why: ACK Congestion Control and byte counting are discussed, but the document's focus is asymmetry effects, not congestion control in general; TCP covers it.
RED/ECN are mentioned only as part of ACC mechanism, not the subject.
DOCSIS is an example network of asymmetry in the Appendix, not specified or profiled.
Used as a mechanism within ACC; not about ECN itself.
Mentioned only as a constraint that prevents some mitigations.
Per-flow queuing and scheduling are discussed, but as ACK-handling mitigations, not QoS architectures.

gaps.name: Performance Enhancing Proxies / asymmetric path TCP performance
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TCP performance over specific link characteristics (PILC); closest are TCP and link layer.

RFC3450.title: Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) Protocol Instantiation
RFC3450.summary: Defines ALC, an experimental massively scalable reliable multicast content delivery protocol that combines the LCT, FEC and multiple-rate congestion control building blocks over UDP/IP multicast.

ALC.why: The document is the ALC protocol instantiation specification: packet format, sender and receiver operation, session description.
ALC.quote: This document describes the Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) protocol, a massively scalable reliable content delivery protocol.

LCT.why: ALC is built on the LCT header and specifies how its fields (TSI, TOI, CCI, codepoint, header extensions) are used, so LCT readers would want it.
LCT.quote: ALC uses the LCT building block [11] to provide in-band session management functionality.

rejected.why: Parent of ALC and LCT; implied, so not listed separately.
ALC relies on the FEC building block for reliability but the FEC codes themselves are specified elsewhere (RFC 3452).
Requires a multiple rate congestion control building block but does not define one; it is only referenced.
UDP is merely the transport carrying ALC packets.
SSM and ASM are discussed as environment considerations, not specified by this document.
Mentioned as an example packet authentication scheme in security recommendations, not specified here.
Only listed as one possible format for the Session Description; the document leaves that out of scope.

RFC3451.title: Layered Coding Transport (LCT) Building Block
RFC3451.summary: RFC 3451 specifies the Layered Coding Transport (LCT) building block, a header format and operations for massively scalable reliable content delivery and streaming over IP multicast, designed to work with layered congestion control and FEC.

LCT.why: The document defines the LCT building block itself: its default header, header extensions, and sender/receiver operation.
LCT.quote: Layered Coding Transport (LCT) provides transport level support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols.

reliable multicast.why: LCT is an RMT working group building block for reliable multicast content delivery, and readers of reliable multicast would want it. It is a parent of LCT, so it is only listed as secondary context.
reliable multicast.quote: This memo contains part of the definitions necessary to fully specify a Reliable Multicast Transport protocol in accordance with RFC 2357.

rejected.why: LCT only provides an opaque CCI field and requires some congestion control to be used. It does not specify any scheme.
FEC is a compatible coding building block referenced from other RFCs, not specified here.
SSM is discussed only as one of the multicast models LCT works over, in the environmental considerations.
UDP is only the underlying transport whose source port may serve as the TSI.
SDP is mentioned only as one possible format for the out-of-band session description.
IP multicast is the substrate LCT is designed for, but the document defines a transport building block and not multicast routing or group membership.

RFC3452.title: Forward Error Correction (FEC) Building Block
RFC3452.summary: Experimental RMT building block describing the FEC information (FEC Encoding ID, Instance ID, Payload ID, Object Transmission Information) needed to use FEC codes for reliable IP multicast content delivery, defining IANA registries and two Under-Specified encoding IDs (128, 129).

FEC.why: The whole document defines how FEC codes are identified, parameterised and signalled in packets (FEC Encoding ID, Payload ID, OTI) and the registries for them.
FEC.quote: This document generally describes how to use Forward Error Correction (FEC) codes to efficiently provide and/or augment reliability for data transport.

reliable multicast.why: It is an RMT working group building block for reliable one-to-many multicast delivery, so readers of reliable multicast would want it.
reliable multicast.quote: The primary focus of this document is the application of FEC codes to one-to-many reliable data transport using IP multicast.

rejected.why: Only recommended in Security Considerations as a packet authentication option; not the subject.
Mentioned only as an example integrity hash in Security Considerations.
The document explicitly provides no congestion control and defers it to other building blocks.
The IANA registries are defined, but they are boilerplate-like support for the FEC code identifiers; the document is about FEC, not IANA stewardship.
A protocol that would use this building block, but ALC is not specified or discussed here.
The multicast context is the application setting; the more specific reliable multicast tag fits better.

RFC3453.title: The Use of Forward Error Correction (FEC) in Reliable Multicast
RFC3453.summary: Informational RFC from the RMT working group describing how forward error correction (erasure) codes (simple parity, small block, large block/Tornado, expandable/LT) can provide or augment reliability in one-to-many IP multicast, with terminology and abstract packet formats.

FEC.why: The whole document describes classes of FEC codes, their properties, terminology and symbol/packet identification, so FEC is the core subject.
