FEC.quote: This memo describes the use of Forward Error Correction (FEC) codes to efficiently provide and/or augment reliability for one-to-many reliable data transport using IP multicast.

reliable multicast.why: The context and goal is reliable multicast transport, comparing ARQ and Data Carousel with FEC and showing how FEC is applied in reliable multicast protocols.
reliable multicast.quote: FEC codes provide a reliability method that can be used to augment or replace other reliability methods, especially for one-to-many reliability protocols such as reliable IP multicast.

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a recommended packet authentication scheme; the document is not about it.
Mentioned only as an example of ARQ working well for one-to-one reliability.
Parent topic implied by the more specific reliable multicast tag.
Raptor codes are not discussed; only Tornado and LT codes are described as examples.
LDPC codes are not described; the large block code example is Tornado.
No framework for real-time/streaming media is specified; streaming is mentioned only briefly as an application.

gaps.name: Erasure codes (Reed-Solomon, Tornado, LT codes)
gaps.why: The document's code families have no dedicated tag; FEC is the nearest fit, though specific code families like Tornado and LT are described in detail.

RFC3454.title: Preparation of Internationalized Strings ("stringprep")
RFC3454.summary: RFC 3454 defines stringprep, a framework for preparing Unicode strings (mapping, NFKC normalization, prohibited output, bidi checks, unassigned code point handling) that protocols profile to make internationalized string comparison and input work consistently.

internationalization.why: The whole document defines the stringprep framework for internationalized text strings: mapping, normalization, prohibition tables and bidi rules. No child tag (PRECIS, Unicode, etc.) fits it better. PRECIS is the successor and is not specified here.
internationalization.quote: This document describes a framework for preparing Unicode text strings in order to increase the likelihood that string input and string comparison work in ways that make sense

Unicode.why: The framework is defined over the Unicode 3.2 repertoire. It specifies normalization form KC, unassigned code points, bidi categories and case folding tables, so it is substantially about Unicode usage in protocols.
Unicode.quote: This document is for Unicode version 3.2, and should not be considered to automatically apply to later Unicode versions.

rejected.why: Internationalized domain names are mentioned as one use, and nameprep is acknowledged. The document defines no IDNA or domain-label rules, only the generic framework.
PRECIS later replaced stringprep, but this RFC does not specify it.
UTF-8 is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as an example encoding. The document is not about it.
The document sets up a registry of stringprep profiles, but that is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the main subject.

gaps.name: stringprep
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for stringprep itself or for text-preparation profiles such as nameprep, SASLprep and the like. The closest fits are the internationalization topic and Unicode.

RFC3455.title: Private Header (P-Header) Extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for the 3rd-Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)
RFC3455.summary: Informational RFC defining six private SIP P-headers (P-Associated-URI, P-Called-Party-ID, P-Visited-Network-ID, P-Access-Network-Info, P-Charging-Function-Addresses, P-Charging-Vector) for 3GPP IMS use, with applicability statements and procedures.

SIP.why: The document specifies new SIP header fields, with UA, proxy and registrar procedures and applicability for each, so it is a SIP extension document.
SIP.quote: This document describes a set of private Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) headers (P-headers) used by the 3rd-Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)

rejected.why: 3GPP IMS is the deployment context, but the document defines SIP headers, not IP over 3GPP link technologies.
Only mentions SIP extensions for messaging and events in the header support table; not about presence or instant messaging.
ABNF is only used to write the formal syntax; the document is not about the notation.
The IANA section merely registers the header fields; boilerplate, not the subject.
DNS is mentioned only as one way to pick unique visited-network identifiers; not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: 3GPP IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) charging and roaming
gaps.why: The document covers IMS charging correlation (ICID, IOI, CCF/ECF) and roaming visited-network identification, for which the taxonomy has no tag.

RFC3456.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4) Configuration of IPsec Tunnel Mode
RFC3456.summary: RFC 3456 specifies how DHCPv4 is used to configure a remote host's virtual intranet address over an IPsec tunnel mode SA to a security gateway acting as DHCP relay, and argues this is preferable to IKECFG.

DHCP.why: The document defines how DHCPv4 messages (DISCOVER, relay behaviour, htype value, client-identifier) are used for IPsec tunnel mode hosts.
DHCP.quote: describes how the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4) may be leveraged for configuration

IPsec.why: A substantial part covers IPsec tunnel mode, DHCP SA setup via IKE quick mode, filters and selectors, and the remote access configuration requirements.
IPsec.quote: The DHCP SA is an IPsec tunnel mode SA established to protect initial DHCPv4 traffic between the security gateway and the remote host.

rejected.why: IKE is used to set up the SAs and compared against (IKECFG), but the document explicitly requires no IKE modifications.
Only DHCPv4 is addressed.
The arp-parameters registry is mentioned only for htype allocation in IANA considerations.
Refers to remote access VPN hosts, not provider-provisioned VPNs.
The htype allocation request is boilerplate-level IANA considerations.

RFC3457.title: Requirements for IPsec Remote Access Scenarios
RFC3457.summary: Informational document enumerating requirements (authentication, host configuration, policy, auditing, NAT/firewall traversal) for five IPsec remote access scenarios, from the IPSRA working group.

IPsec.why: The whole document enumerates requirements for using IPsec in remote access scenarios, including SA, SPD policy and IRAC/IRAS roles.
IPsec.quote: IPsec offers much promise as a secure remote access mechanism.

NAT.why: Intermediary traversal (NAPT and firewalls) is one of five requirement categories, repeated in each scenario, so readers on NAT and IPsec would want it.
NAT.quote: NAPT devices typically modify the source IP address and UDP/TCP port of outgoing packets

rejected.why: Mentioned as a legacy mechanism that IPsec remote access should support, but not specified or extended here.
Referenced for authentication mechanisms, but the document does not specify or extend IKE; it is covered under IPsec.
Endpoint authentication is discussed in depth, but only within IPsec remote access, so the more specific IPsec tag covers it.
Mentioned only as legacy dial-up background.
Firewalls appear only as intermediaries to traverse, not as a subject of the document.

gaps.name: IPsec remote access (IPSRA)

RFC3458.title: Message Context for Internet Mail

Parent of message format; the more specific tag already covers it.

SMS is mentioned only in describing the pager-message class and in the appendix.

RFC3459.title: Critical Content Multi-purpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Parameter

MPLS is the context, but the specific subject is LDP, which is the more specific tag.
BGP graceful restart is only cited as inspiration for the ACK scheme.
RSVP refresh mechanisms are mentioned only as approaches this document avoids.

RFC3480.title: Signalling Unnumbered Links in CR-LDP (Constraint-Routing Label Distribution Protocol)
RFC3480.summary: Defines CR-LDP procedures and new TLVs (LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID and Unnumbered Interface ID ER-Hop) so that MPLS TE LSPs can be signalled over unnumbered links and Forwarding Adjacencies.

CR-LDP.why: The document extends CR-LDP with new TLVs and processing rules for the Explicit Route TLV and IF_ID TLV to support unnumbered links.
CR-LDP.quote: This document defines procedures and extensions to Constraint-Routing Label Distribution Protocol (CR-LDP), one of the MPLS TE signalling protocols that are needed in order to support unnumbered links.

rejected.why: The document leans on GMPLS CR-LDP (IF_ID TLV) and the GMPLS IGP extensions, but it extends plain CR-LDP for MPLS TE and is not about GMPLS itself.
CR-LDP runs over LDP and inherits its TLV space, but the document does not specify LDP itself. CR-LDP is the more specific fit.
RSVP-TE is the other MPLS TE signalling protocol. It is not discussed here.
OSPF and IS-IS TE extensions are mentioned only as the separate IGP component. This document covers signalling only.
The document is about MPLS TE signalling, but the CR-LDP tag already sits under traffic engineering's sibling MPLS branch and is the more specific fit.
CR-LDP is a child of MPLS, so the parent is implied.

RFC3481.title: TCP over Second (2.5G) and Third (3G) Generation Wireless Networks
RFC3481.summary: BCP profile recommending TCP configuration choices (window scaling, initial window, Limited Transmit, SACK, ECN, timestamps, PMTUD, disabling VJ header compression) for paths over 2.5G/3G cellular networks, with link characteristics and deployment examples.

TCP.why: The document's core is recommending TCP algorithm and configuration choices (SACK, timestamps, initial window, Limited Transmit, window scale).
TCP.quote: This document describes a profile for optimizing TCP to adapt so that it handles paths including second (2.5G) and third (3G) generation wireless networks.

cellular.why: Substantial sections cover 2.5G/3G link characteristics and GPRS, W-CDMA and cdma2000 deployments, matching the cellular tag.
cellular.quote: It describes the relevant characteristics of 2.5G and 3G networks, and specific features of example deployments of such networks.

rejected.why: cdma2000 is only one of several example technologies, described briefly. The document is not about its packet-data, AAA or Mobile IP aspects.
ECN is one recommended option in a list, not a main subject.
PMTUD is one recommended option in a list, not a main subject.
Header compression is discussed only as something to disable (RFC 1144) and as an open issue. It is not the subject.
Congestion control mechanisms are mentioned in passing. The document concerns TCP configuration overall.
GPRS and HSCSD are described as GSM extensions only as background, not as a subject.

RFC3482.title: Number Portability in the Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN): An Overview
RFC3482.summary: Informational overview of E.164 telephone number portability in the GSTN: types, the four SPNP call-routing schemes (ACQ, QoR, Dropback, OR), NPDB query interfaces, routing in the US and Europe, national implementations, number pooling, and implications for IP telephony (SIP, tel URI, TRIP, ENUM).

PSTN interop.why: The document explains how number portability works in the PSTN (ISUP, SS7 NPDB queries, call routing) and what it means for interworking with IP telephony. This fits PSTN interop and no more specific child tag.
PSTN interop.quote: This document provides an overview of E.164 telephone number portability (NP) in the Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN).

ENUM.why: A substantial part of the implications section covers how NP affects ENUM delegation and records, and recommends separate carrier and end-user ENUM trees.
ENUM.quote: NP certainly must be considered at the first level because the telephony service providers do not "own" or control the telephone numbers

tel URI.why: The document discusses carrying NP information (rn, cic parameters) in tel URIs and how they affect routing decisions.
tel URI.quote: Another better choice may be to add an extension to the "tel" URL [TEL] that is also supported by SIP.

rejected.why: SIP is discussed only as a way to carry NP data to the GSTN, not as the subject of the document.
TRIP gets one paragraph noting that the routing number should be matched against TRIP tables. The document does not specify or extend it.
LDAP is named only as a candidate common NPDB query interface.
DNS appears only as the substrate of ENUM, which is already tagged.
CMIP appears only in the acronym list.

gaps.name: Number Portability (NP) in the GSTN
gaps.why: The core subject is E.164 number portability, including NPDB, LRN, and number pooling. The taxonomy has no number portability or telephone numbering tag, only the tel URI parameters and ENUM tags.

RFC3483.title: Framework for Policy Usage Feedback for Common Open Policy Service with Policy Provisioning (COPS-PR)
RFC3483.summary: Informational framework describing how a COPS-PR PEP monitors and reports policy usage feedback (accounting reports) to the PDP, covering intervals, solicitation, suspension, shared objects, contexts, delete request state and failover.

COPS.why: The document extends COPS-PR usage with a framework for accounting-type reports, usage feedback policies, Accounting Timer handling and PDP/PEP behaviour. A reader of COPS would want it.
COPS.quote: This document focuses on the COPS Report Type of Accounting and the necessary framework for the monitoring and reporting of usage feedback for an installed state.

rejected.why: QoS policy is only an example of what usage feedback may relate to. The document is about the feedback mechanism, not QoS architecture or signalling.
SIP is mentioned only as an example of a session for which a PDP makes policy. The document does not specify anything about SIP.
Related, because it deals with policy provisioning, but the document defines no information model. COPS is the more specific fit.
Accounting is mentioned, but charging, rating and billing models are explicitly out of scope.

RFC3484.title: Default Address Selection for Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6)
RFC3484.summary: RFC 3484 specifies default source address selection and destination address selection algorithms for IPv6 (and dual-stack IPv4/IPv6) nodes, with a policy table for administrative override.

IPv6.why: The whole document specifies default IPv6 address selection behaviour, including the policy table, scope handling and IPv4 coexistence in dual-stack hosts.
IPv6.quote: This document describes two algorithms, for source address selection and for destination address selection.  The algorithms specify default behavior for all Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) implementations.

addressing.why: It is about choosing among multiple addresses by scope, prefix, and deprecated or temporary status. It also covers multihoming configuration (section 10.5), so address architecture and use readers would want it.
addressing.quote: The IPv6 addressing architecture [1] allows multiple unicast addresses to be assigned to interfaces.

rejected.why: Dual-stack choice between IPv6 and IPv4 and the handling of 6to4 and tunnel addresses are covered. But the document does not specify a transition mechanism, so the topic is secondary at most.
Section 10.5 shows policy-table configuration for a multi-homed site. The main body is about default address selection, not multihoming architecture.
DNS name resolution via getaddrinfo() supplies the address list to be sorted. The document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Home and care-of addresses appear only as inputs to the preference rules (Rule 4). The document does not specify mobility.
getaddrinfo() and the sockets API are the context in which the algorithms run. The document specifies no API extensions.
Preferred and deprecated address states from RFC 2462, and temporary addresses, are used as inputs only. The document does not specify SLAAC.

RFC3485.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and Session Description Protocol (SDP) Static Dictionary for Signaling Compression (SigComp)
RFC3485.summary: Defines the normative static dictionary of SIP and SDP strings (with binary SigComp state representation) that SigComp can use to compress SIP/SDP signalling from the first message.

SigComp.why: The whole document specifies a SigComp static dictionary and its state item representation, so it belongs on the SigComp page.
SigComp.quote: This memo defines the SIP/SDP-specific static dictionary that SigComp may use in order to achieve higher efficiency.

SIP.why: The dictionary's contents are SIP header names, methods and response codes (Appendix A), and its purpose is faster SIP session setup. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: SIP [3] and SDP [24] are text-based protocols that use the UTF-8 charset

SDP.why: Appendix B lists SDP field and attribute strings that make up half of the dictionary, so SDP readers would find it relevant.
SDP.quote: Appendix B contains the collection of strings that SDP contributed to the static dictionary.

rejected.why: DEFLATE is mentioned only as an example of an algorithm that benefits from string ordering. The dictionary is compression-algorithm independent.
The general compression topic is already covered by the more specific SigComp tag, and no lossless format is defined here.
This is signalling compression of SIP/SDP text, not header compression on constrained links, so it was not tagged.

RFC3486.title: Compressing the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3486.summary: RFC 3486 defines the "comp=sigcomp" SIP URI and Via parameter to signal willingness and support for SigComp-compressed SIP messages, and the rules for when to send compressed requests and responses.

SigComp.why: The whole document specifies how SIP entities signal and use SigComp compression for SIP messages, which is exactly the SigComp subject.
SigComp.quote: The presence of this parameter (comp=sigcomp) in a URI indicates that the request has to be compressed using SigComp

SIP.why: It extends SIP with new URI and Via parameters, and defines Record-Route, Contact and OPTIONS handling for them.
SIP.quote: We define two parameters, one for SIP URIs and the other for the Via header field.

rejected.why: DNS NAPTR/SRV is mentioned only in the introduction as the motivation. The document's solution is an application-layer mechanism.
TLS is mentioned only as a layer that could multiply DNS entries and in the note that compression happens before TLS. The document defines nothing about TLS.
The comp URI parameter is a SIP URI parameter, which is covered by the SIP tag. It is not a general URI scheme or syntax contribution.
SigComp compresses SIP signalling messages. It is not compression of protocol headers on constrained links.

RFC3487.title: Requirements for Resource Priority Mechanisms for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3487.summary: Informational requirements document for a SIP resource-priority indication that lets emergency preparedness (ETS) communications get prioritized access to gateway, CSN, end system and proxy resources, along with security requirements.

SIP.why: The document sets out requirements for a SIP priority indication (labelled requests, method-neutral, proxy-visible, routing). It is about extending SIP.
SIP.quote: This document summarizes requirements for prioritizing access to circuit-switched network, end system and proxy resources for emergency preparedness communications using the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

emergency services.why: The document concerns emergency telecommunications service (ETS) priority, such as GETS and MLPP, during emergencies. It also separates this from civilian 911/112 emergency calls. The topic fits the emergency preparedness scope.
emergency services.quote: emergency preparedness communications

PSTN interop.why: A large part of the document covers IP/CSN hybrid topologies, gateway trunk resources, and mapping CSN priority schemes (Q.735, GETS) to SIP without loss of information.
PSTN interop.quote: CSN-to-IP gateways are unlikely to know whether the final destination is in the IP network, the CSN or, via SIP forking, in both.

rejected.why: IP network QoS is explicitly out of scope and deferred to another document; the focus is on SIP-level resource prioritization.
SIP-T and ISUP/MIME encapsulation appear only as references, noted as insufficient for the CSN-IP-CSN case.
The security requirements for authentication and authorization are part of the SIP priority requirements and are not the subject in their own right.
Denial-of-service appears only as a short list of security requirements, so it is not a substantial subject of the document.

gaps.name: Resource priority / ETS (Emergency Telecommunications Service) prioritization
gaps.why: The core subject, which is priority access to resources for emergency preparedness communications (MLPP, GETS), has no dedicated tag. The closest ones are emergency services and SIP.

RFC3488.title: Cisco Systems Router-port Group Management Protocol (RGMP)
RFC3488.summary: Describes Cisco's RGMP, a protocol by which multicast routers tell switches which IPv4 multicast groups to forward to router ports, to restrict flooding in switched backbones.

multicast.why: RGMP is an IP multicast group membership/forwarding-restriction protocol between routers and switches. No child tag (IGMP, PIM) is the subject, so the parent topic fits.
multicast.quote: used between multicast routers and switches to restrict multicast packet forwarding in switches to those routers where the packets may be needed

rejected.why: RGMP's message format resembles IGMPv2 and it is compared with IGMP snooping, but the document specifies a distinct protocol, not IGMP.
RGMP is designed to work alongside PIM-SM and PIM hellos are used to identify router ports, but PIM is not specified here.
RGMP operates on Ethernet switches, but the document is about IP multicast forwarding restriction, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
SSM is only discussed as a compatibility note and a possible future extension.

gaps.name: IGMP/MLD snooping and Layer 2 multicast filtering in switches
gaps.why: The document is largely about constraining multicast at Layer 2 switches, and the taxonomy has no tag for switch-level multicast filtering.

RFC3489.title: STUN - Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Through Network Address Translators (NATs)
RFC3489.summary: RFC 3489 specifies STUN, a lightweight UDP client-server protocol that lets applications detect NATs and firewalls, classify the NAT type, discover their public mapped addresses and binding lifetimes, with security and IAB UNSAF considerations.

STUN.why: The document defines the STUN protocol: message formats, attributes, server and client behavior, and use cases. It is the core subject.
STUN.quote: STUN is a lightweight protocol that allows applications to discover the presence and types of NATs and firewalls between them and the public Internet.

rejected.why: NAT behaviour is the problem context. The document specifies STUN, which is already under NAT traversal, not NAT itself.
TLS only carries Shared Secret Requests. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
HMAC-SHA1 is used for MESSAGE-INTEGRITY as a mechanism only.
RTP is a motivating use case, mentioned for address allocation and keepalives, and is not specified here.
DNS SRV lookup is used only for server discovery.
SIP is mentioned only as an application that uses STUN addresses.

gaps.name: UNSAF (Unilateral Self-Address Fixing)
gaps.why: Section 14 covers the IAB UNSAF considerations: exit strategy, brittleness and requirements for a long-term solution. The taxonomy has no tag for this, though NAT traversal readers would want it.

RFC3490.title: Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA)
RFC3490.summary: RFC 3490 defines Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA), in which applications use the ToASCII and ToUnicode operations and the "xn--" ACE prefix to carry non-ASCII domain labels as ASCII in the existing DNS.

IDN.why: The whole document specifies IDNA: label equivalence, the ToASCII and ToUnicode operations, the ACE prefix and applicability rules.
IDN.quote: This document defines internationalized domain names (IDNs) and a mechanism called Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) for handling them in a standard fashion.

rejected.why: IDNA runs on the existing DNS and explicitly requires no changes to servers, resolvers or protocol elements. DNS is the substrate, so the tag would be too broad. The DNS-specific parts are the IDN rules for zones and RR applicability.
Section 6.5 only notes that DNSSEC authenticates the ASCII (ACE) form. It is a short consideration, not a substantial subject of the document.
Unicode is the character repertoire IDNA draws on. Unicode handling is specified in the companion RFCs (Nameprep, Punycode, Stringprep), not here.
The document discusses LDH host name restrictions (STD3) only as a constraint on label characters. It does not define host naming conventions.

RFC3491.title: Nameprep: A Stringprep Profile for Internationalized Domain Names (IDN)
RFC3491.summary: RFC 3491 defines Nameprep, a stringprep profile specifying Unicode 3.2 mapping, NFKC normalization, prohibited characters and bidi checks for preparing internationalized domain name labels used by IDNA.

IDN.why: Nameprep is the string preparation profile for IDNA labels, so it belongs under Internationalized Domain Names.
IDN.quote: This document describes how to prepare internationalized domain name (IDN) labels in order to increase the likelihood that name input and name comparison work

rejected.why: DNS is the context for the names, but the document specifies no DNS protocol or record behaviour, only label string preparation.
The profile uses Unicode 3.2 tables and normalization, but the document is about domain label preparation, not general Unicode usage; stringprep itself is a separate RFC.
PRECIS is the later successor framework for string preparation, but this document is not PRECIS.
The parent topic is implied by IDN and the more specific tag fits.

gaps.name: stringprep
gaps.why: The document is a profile of stringprep (RFC 3454), a general internationalized string preparation framework. The taxonomy has no stringprep tag; PRECIS is the nearest but is a different framework.

RFC3492.title: Punycode: A Bootstring encoding of Unicode for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA)
RFC3492.summary: RFC 3492 specifies Punycode, an instance of the general Bootstring algorithm, which reversibly encodes Unicode strings into ASCII letter-digit-hyphen strings for use in IDNA domain labels, with parameters, pseudocode, examples and a C reference implementation.

IDN.why: Punycode is the encoding used for ACE labels in IDNA. The whole document specifies it, so the IDN page is where readers would look for it.
IDN.quote: Punycode is a simple and efficient transfer encoding syntax designed for use with Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA).

rejected.why: Unicode code points are the input being encoded. The document defines an encoding algorithm and does not address Unicode usage in protocols.
Domain labels are the context and motivation, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour, records or operations.
ASCII is only the output alphabet of the encoding. The document is not about ASCII.
The document notes that the encoding conforms to the RFC 952 hostname label rules, but it only touches on host naming conventions.
Its subject is covered more specifically by IDN, so the parent topic is not added.

gaps.name: Bootstring / Punycode encoding algorithm
gaps.why: The general Bootstring algorithm (variable-length integer, bias adaptation) is a standalone encoding. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so IDN is the closest fit.

RFC3493.title: Basic Socket Interface Extensions for IPv6
RFC3493.summary: Informational RFC (obsoleting RFC 2553) specifying the basic sockets API extensions for IPv6: sockaddr_in6, interface-index functions, IPv6 socket options including multicast, getaddrinfo/getnameinfo, and inet_pton/inet_ntop.

sockets API.why: The whole document defines extensions to the sockets API: new address structures, functions and socket options.
sockets API.quote: changes are required to the sockets API to support IPv6 and this memo describes these changes

IPv6.why: It covers IPv6 addressing in the API (AF_INET6, in6_addr, IPv4-mapped addresses, wildcard/loopback, IPV6_V6ONLY), so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: This memo defines a set of extensions to the socket interface to support the larger address size and new features of IPv6.

rejected.why: Multicast socket options (join/leave, hops, loop) are only one part of the API; the document does not address multicast routing or group membership protocols.
getaddrinfo/getnameinfo resolve names, but DNS is only the underlying resolution mechanism and no DNS behaviour is specified.
IPv4-mapped addresses and IPV6_V6ONLY give IPv4 compatibility, but the document is about the API, not transition mechanisms.
SIIT is cited only in a note about IPv4-mapped addresses and is not specified here.
TCP and UDP are the transports sockets are used with; the document does not specify them.

RFC3494.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol version 2 (LDAPv2) to Historic Status
RFC3494.summary: Informational memo recommending that LDAPv2 (RFCs 1777, 1778, 1779, 1781, 2559 and their predecessors) be moved to Historic status in favour of LDAPv3, explaining interoperability and security shortcomings.

LDAP.why: The whole document concerns LDAPv2's retirement, why LDAPv3 supersedes it, and which dependent specifications go Historic, so LDAP readers would want it.
LDAP.quote: This document recommends the retirement of version 2 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAPv2) and other dependent specifications, and discusses the reasons for doing so.

rejected.why: X.500 is mentioned only as the directory LDAPv2 gave access to; the document is not about X.500 itself.
RFC 2559 (X.509 PKI operational protocols over LDAPv2) is mentioned as a dependent specification to retire, but only briefly; the document isn't about PKI.
Moving RFCs to Historic is a status action, but the document's subject is the technical retirement of LDAPv2, so the process tag does not fit better than LDAP.
X.509 appears only as an authentication mechanism LDAPv2 lacks and in the title of RFC 2559; the document is not about certificates.

RFC3495.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Option for CableLabs Client Configuration
RFC3495.summary: Defines DHCP option code 122, the CableLabs Client Configuration option, with sub-options for configuring PacketCable MTAs and cable modems (DHCP/provisioning server addresses, Kerberos retry timers, realm name, provisioning timer).

DHCP.why: The document's whole purpose is a new DHCP option with sub-option formats and usage, extending DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) option that will be used to configure various devices deployed within CableLabs architectures.

rejected.why: Kerberos timers and realm name are configured via the option, but the document does not specify or extend Kerberos itself.
Cable modems and CMTS are the deployment context, but the document defines no DOCSIS mechanism.
FQDN encoding follows RFC 1035 and the realm is used for DNS lookup, but DNS is only used as a substrate.
PacketCable VoIP is the context, but no call signalling is specified.

RFC3496.title: Protocol Extension for Support of Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) Service Class-aware Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering
RFC3496.summary: Defines a new optional RSVP-TE PATH message object, ATM_SERVICECLASS, to signal that an MPLS traffic-engineered LSP must support a given ATM Forum service class (UBR, VBR-NRT, VBR-RT, CBR).

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE with a new ATM_SERVICECLASS object in PATH messages for LSP tunnels, and specifies how LSRs handle it.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document specifies a Resource ReSerVation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) signaling extension for support of Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) Service Class-aware Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering.

rejected.why: ATM service classes are only signalled as a property of the MPLS TE path. The document does not cover IP over ATM or ATM links.
The DIFFSERV object appears in the PATH message format and is referenced for coexistence. It is not what the document is about.
MPLS is the setting, but the content is the RSVP-TE signalling extension, so the more specific RSVP-TE tag fits better.
The document builds on base RSVP only through the RSVP-TE extension and its unknown-object handling rules. RSVP-TE is the more specific tag.
The RSVP-TE tag is more specific and sits under traffic engineering, so the parent is implied.

RFC3497.title: RTP Payload Format for Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) 292M Video
RFC3497.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for carrying uncompressed SMPTE 292M HDTV serial digital video over IP, with a 4-octet payload header extending the sequence number, a 148.5 MHz timestamp, pgroup alignment, a media type registration and SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document's sole purpose is a new RTP payload format for a specific video medium, so readers of RTP payload formats would look for it.
RTP payload format.quote: this memo defines an RTP payload format for SMPTE 292M format video.

rejected.why: The child tag RTP payload format fits more specifically; the parent is implied.
SDP is used only for a brief parameter mapping example (section 8), which is not a substantial part of the document.
A video/SMPTE292M media type is registered, but that is boilerplate IANA-style registration for the payload format, not a document about media type rules.
Section 6 notes counter rollover at high data rates, but this is a minor consideration and not a specification of RTCP.
The payload carries uncompressed video; it defines no codec.
QoS and congestion are mentioned only as cautions in the introduction and Security Considerations.

gaps.name: SMPTE 292M / HDTV uncompressed video
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for uncompressed or studio video formats; the closest, RTP payload format, covers the packetization but not the video interface itself.

RFC3498.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Synchronous Optical Network (SONET) Linear Automatic Protection Switching (APS) Architectures
RFC3498.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (APS-MIB) for configuring and monitoring SONET linear Automatic Protection Switching groups (1+1 and 1:n), including K1/K2 byte status, switch commands, counters and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defined with SMIv2, specifying tables, textual conventions, notifications and conformance groups for SONET linear APS.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing networks using Synchronous Optical Network (SONET) linear Automatic Protection Switching (APS) architectures.

SONET.why: The subject is SONET linear APS: K1/K2 bytes, protection switching of SONET LTE interfaces, 1+1 and 1:n architectures. Readers of the SONET subject would want this MIB.
SONET.quote: This management information module supports the configuration and management of SONET linear APS groups.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Implied as an ancestor of MIB; no need to list it separately.
APS is protection switching between lines, not bundling parallel links.
The document covers SONET line-level APS, not generalized MPLS control of optical networks.

RFC3499.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 3400-3499
RFC3499.summary: RFC 3499 is a slightly annotated catalogue of RFCs 3400 through 3499, giving each RFC's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The document exists only to summarise a block of the RFC series. A reader browsing the RFC series page would expect it, since it is a publication-level index of the series.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 3400 through RFC 3499.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: The listed RFCs include the SNMPv3 documents, but this memo only lists them. Each subject belongs to the RFC it describes, not to the summary.
Many entries cover MPLS, LDP, RSVP-TE and GMPLS. They are only listed here, so the summary is not about MPLS.
Several SIP RFCs are listed, but the memo does not address SIP itself.
The DDDS, IDNA and DNS entries are only items in the list.
Some listed RFCs concern IANA assignments, but the memo does not discuss IANA itself.

RFC3501.title: INTERNET MESSAGE ACCESS PROTOCOL - VERSION 4rev1
RFC3501.summary: RFC 3501 specifies IMAP4rev1, the protocol by which a client accesses and manipulates email messages and mailboxes on a server, obsoleting RFC 2060.

IMAP.why: The entire document specifies the IMAP4rev1 protocol: commands, responses, states, message attributes and formal syntax.
IMAP.quote: The Internet Message Access Protocol, Version 4rev1 (IMAP4rev1) allows a client to access and manipulate electronic mail messages on a server.

rejected.why: STARTTLS is defined as an IMAP command, but TLS is only the security mechanism used; the document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
AUTHENTICATE uses SASL mechanisms but the document does not specify SASL; it is a substrate.
BODYSTRUCTURE and part fetching parse MIME structure, but the document does not define MIME; it only relies on it.
The ENVELOPE and header fetches parse RFC 2822 messages, but the message format is not the subject.
Mentioned only to say IMAP does not post mail; SMTP is out of scope.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.

RFC3502.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - MULTIAPPEND Extension
RFC3502.summary: RFC 3502 defines the IMAP MULTIAPPEND extension, which lets an IMAP client upload multiple messages in one atomic APPEND command, with the syntax change and its interaction with UIDPLUS.

IMAP.why: The document specifies an extension to IMAP: the MULTIAPPEND capability, the modified APPEND command, its formal syntax and its UIDPLUS interaction.
IMAP.quote: The MULTIAPPEND extension permits uploading of multiple messages with a single command.

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag. The document is about the IMAP access protocol and not about email in general.
The document refers to RFC 2822 messages only as the content of the APPEND literal. It does not define anything about message format.
MIME appears only in a reference to a content transfer encoding for 8-bit data, which is incidental.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax change. The document is not about ABNF.
SMTP is mentioned only in a note saying APPEND is not used for message delivery.

RFC3503.title: Message Disposition Notification (MDN) profile for Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)
RFC3503.summary: Defines the $MDNSent IMAP keyword and client/server behaviour so multiple IMAP MUAs can coordinate generation of Message Disposition Notifications (RFC 2298) without sending duplicates.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP with a new keyword and specifies client and server behaviour (PERMANENTFLAGS, STORE, COPY, APPEND, SEARCH KEYWORD, ACL interaction).
IMAP.quote: This memo defines an additional [IMAP4] mailbox keyword that allows multiple Mail User Agents (MUAs) to know if a requested receipt notification was sent.

rejected.why: Parent of IMAP and implied by it; the document is about IMAP behaviour, not email in general.
MDNs are the subject, but the document does not specify their format; it only profiles when MDNs are sent in IMAP. RFC 2298 defines the format.
MSA/MTA appear only in the timeline borrowed from RFC 2298; nothing about SMTP is specified.
The formal syntax is a tiny ABNF snippet used as apparatus, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Message Disposition Notification (MDN)
gaps.why: The document is substantially about coordinating MDN (read-receipt) generation, but the taxonomy has no MDN tag. The closest are message format and email, which don't fit well.

RFC3504.title: Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) Version 1, Errata
RFC3504.summary: An informational errata document listing and correcting errors in the IOTP Version 1.0 specification (RFC 2801), including DTD attribute fixes, a wording fix, and extended signature type lists.

IOTP.why: The whole document corrects the IOTP v1.0 specification, so readers of IOTP would expect to find it.
IOTP.quote: Several errors have been noted in the IOTP v1.0 specification, particularly RFC 2801, which was the largest RFC ever issued.

rejected.why: The DTD fixes are to IOTP's own element definitions. XML is only the notation, not the subject.
The document extends the list of IOTP signature types. It does not address XML digital signatures in general. RFC 2802 covers those.
This is the parent of IOTP and is implied by the IOTP tag.

RFC3505.title: Electronic Commerce Modeling Language (ECML): Version 2 Requirements
RFC3505.summary: RFC 3505 lists the design principles, scope and requirements for ECML version 2, an XML-based set of payment-processing fields that extends ECML v1.1 to cover more payment types such as ACH, eCheck, mobile phone and PDA payments.

ECML.why: The whole document sets out the requirements for the ECML v2 specification, so it belongs on the ECML page.
ECML.quote: ECML Version 2.0 will describe the syntax of a class of data objects called Payment Processing Objects.

rejected.why: IOTP is mentioned only as a related standard that ECML v2 is not replacing and as an application the spec should meet. The document is not about IOTP.
XML is the syntax ECML v2 uses, so it is the substrate. The document does not specify XML usage in its own right.
TLS is mentioned only as a standard that ECML does not replace.
The parent topic is already implied by the ECML tag, so it is not listed separately.
Improved internationalization support appears as a single bullet in the list of requests. It is not a substantial part of the document.

RFC3506.title: Requirements and Design for Voucher Trading System (VTS)
RFC3506.summary: Informational RFC defining the voucher concept, the Voucher Trading System model and terminology, and design requirements for a VTS and an XML-based Generic Voucher Language for coupons, loyalty points and tickets in electronic commerce.

e-commerce.why: The whole document specifies requirements and a model for trading digital vouchers (coupons, gift certificates, loyalty points) in electronic commerce. No narrower e-commerce tag fits, since it is not IOTP, ECML or CyberCash itself.
e-commerce.quote: Crediting loyalty points and collecting digital coupons or gift certificates are common functions in purchasing and trading transactions.

rejected.why: IOTP is referenced as a model and coordination target, and vouchers may be used within IOTP transactions, but the document does not specify or extend IOTP.
ECML is only listed as a specification the GVL should be consistent with.
GVL syntax must be based on XML and an example is given, but XML is the encoding substrate, not the subject.
XML-Signature is only listed under coordination requirements; it is not what the document is about.
Trust manageability is one minor requirement, and the tag concerns systems like KeyNote, which this document does not address.

gaps.name: Voucher Trading System / Generic Voucher Language
gaps.why: Digital vouchers (tickets, coupons, loyalty points) and a language to describe them have no specific taxonomy tag; only the general e-commerce topic applies.

RFC3507.title: Internet Content Adaptation Protocol (ICAP)
RFC3507.summary: RFC 3507 specifies ICAP, a lightweight HTTP-like request/response protocol by which ICAP clients (e.g. caching surrogates) vectoring HTTP requests and responses to ICAP servers for adaptation such as virus checking, filtering and ad insertion.

OPES.why: ICAP is the intermediary content adaptation protocol that the IESG note ties to the OPES charter; the OPES tag covers intermediary content adaptation, so the document belongs there.
OPES.quote: ICAP is, in essence, a lightweight protocol for executing a "remote procedure call" on HTTP messages.

HTTP.why: ICAP encapsulates HTTP requests and responses, reuses HTTP semantics, headers, status codes and chunking, and defines ICAP-related headers in HTTP messages. HTTP readers would want it, though it is a separate protocol.
HTTP.quote: ICAP is a request/response protocol similar in semantics and usage to HTTP/1.1 [4]. Despite the similarity, ICAP is not HTTP

rejected.why: Caching is discussed (ISTag, Section 5), but only as a minor aspect of ICAP, not the document's subject.
The introduction mentions CDNs and surrogates as motivation. The protocol itself is about content adaptation, not CDN interconnection.
TCP is only the transport, with port 1344. Nothing new is defined about TCP.
Upgrade-based TLS negotiation is mentioned only briefly, as an option.
The icap URI scheme is defined, but only as a small part of the protocol.
A more specific tag (OPES, HTTP) fits, so the broader parent is not needed.

gaps.name: ICAP (Internet Content Adaptation Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ICAP itself. OPES is the nearest fit, but ICAP is a distinct, widely deployed protocol that predates and differs from the OPES specifications.

RFC3508.title: H.323 Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Scheme Registration
RFC3508.summary: RFC 3508 reproduces the ITU-T H.323 version 4 "h323:" URL scheme definition (ABNF syntax, encoding, usage) so the scheme can be registered with IANA.

H.323.why: The document defines the addressing scheme for H.323 entities and is intended for H.323 readers; it is an extension to H.323 for call addressing.
H.323.quote: H.323 version 4 [3] introduced an H.323-specific URL, which may be used to resolve the address of a network entity to which H.323 calls may be directed.

URI.why: The document is a URL scheme registration specifying the syntax, character encoding and usage of the h323 scheme.
URI.quote: The H.323 URL is defined in ABNF as shown below.
URI.section: 2. URL Scheme Formal Syntax Definition and Character Encoding

rejected.why: SIP is only mentioned as a protocol that may carry H.323 URLs; the document does not specify anything about SIP.
TRIP is only mentioned as another protocol that may carry the URL.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the syntax, not the subject.
The IANA section is boilerplate registration of the scheme; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
UTF-8 is merely the encoding applied to the user field, not the subject.

RFC3509.title: Alternative Implementations of OSPF Area Border Routers
RFC3509.summary: Informational RFC describing alternative OSPF Area Border Router behaviors (Cisco and IBM) for routers attached to multiple areas without an active backbone connection, changing ABR definition, router-LSA B-bit, inter-area route calculation, and summary-LSA origination.

OSPF.why: The whole document modifies OSPFv2 ABR behavior: ABR definition, summary-LSA origination and routing table calculation. OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: This document describes alternative ABR behaviors implemented in Cisco and IBM routers.

rejected.why: The document concerns a specific OSPF mechanism, not general routing architecture; the OSPF tag is more specific.
Only OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328) is discussed; OSPFv3 is not covered.

RFC3510.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.1: IPP URL Scheme
RFC3510.summary: Defines the "ipp" URL scheme for locating IPP print services and jobs, updating RFC 2910 section 5 with applicability, port 631, syntax, comparison rules and conformance requirements.

IPP.why: The document specifies and clarifies the IPP URL scheme, an integral part of the Internet Printing Protocol, including Printer and Job URLs and client/printer conformance.
IPP.quote: This memo defines the "ipp" URL (Uniform Resource Locator) scheme.

URI.why: It defines a URI scheme with syntax, character encoding, and comparison rules, which is what URI scheme readers would look for.
URI.quote: ipp-URL = "ipp:" "//" host [ ":" port ] [ abs_path [ "?" query ]]

rejected.why: IPP URLs are mapped to HTTP URLs and IPP runs over HTTP, but HTTP is only the transport substrate here and nothing new is defined for it.
The IANA Considerations section only points to RFC 2910 and 2911; it is boilerplate here.
The application/ipp type is mentioned only as an existing association and is not registered or specified here.
ABNF is only used to write the URL syntax; the document is not about the notation.

gaps.name: IPP (Internet Printing Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IPP tech tag under applications, but I was unable to confirm it is the right id because the document is primarily about the IPP URL scheme; if the taxonomy lacked it, a printing tag would be needed.

RFC3511.title: Benchmarking Methodology for Firewall Performance
RFC3511.summary: RFC 3511 defines benchmarking methodologies and reporting formats for firewall performance (throughput, TCP connection capacity/rate, DoS handling, HTTP transfer, illegal traffic, fragmentation, latency).

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a BMWG benchmarking methodology with test setups, procedures, measurements and reporting formats for a device under test.
benchmarking.quote: This document provides methodologies for the performance benchmarking of firewalls.

firewall.why: The device under test is the firewall (dual-homed/tri-homed, rule sets, NAT, SYN-attack handling), so firewall readers would want it.
firewall.quote: This document focuses on benchmarking firewall performance, wherever possible, independent of implementation.

rejected.why: HTTP 1.1 is only the test traffic generator and validation method, not specified or extended.
TCP connection setup and teardown are measured, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Benchmarking is the more specific tag for device benchmarking methodology.
NAT is only a configuration option to toggle during tests, not the document's subject.
The SYN flood test is one test among many, not the document's focus.

RFC3512.title: Configuring Networks and Devices with Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC3512.summary: Informational BCP-style guidance from the SNMPCONF WG on using SNMP and the Internet Standard Management Framework for configuration management, covering MIB module design, agent implementation, management software design, security, policy-based management, and an example HVAC MIB module.

SNMP.why: The whole document is about applying SNMP and the Internet Standard Management Framework to configuration: transactions, notifications, agent and manager behaviour, and SNMPv3 security.
SNMP.quote: it offers guidance in the effective use of SNMP for configuration management.

MIB.why: Much of the document gives MIB module design practice (RowStatus, indexing, textual conventions, persistence, notifications) and includes an example MIB module, BLDG-HVAC-MIB.
MIB.quote: Carefully considered MIB module designs are crucial to practical configuration with SNMP.

policy management.why: Section 7 and the template-based example MIB cover policy-based management with SNMP, including template objects, conflict detection and the Policy MIB.
policy management.quote: Policy-Based Configuration Management is a methodology wherein configuration information is derived from rules and network-wide objectives
policy management.section: 1.2. Configuration and the Internet Standard Management Framework

rejected.why: NETCONF is not discussed. The document is about configuration over SNMP only.
OSPF and its MIB appear only as examples of configuration stability and activation, not as the subject.
The parent is implied by SNMP, and the document is specific to SNMP rather than network management in general.
DNS is mentioned only as an example of a system where change verification is commonly done.
UDP is the SNMP transport and appears only incidentally, for example in the discussion of message size limits.

RFC3513.title: Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Addressing Architecture
RFC3513.summary: RFC 3513 specifies the IPv6 addressing architecture: address types (unicast, anycast, multicast), text representations, interface identifiers, special addresses, and a node's required addresses.

IPv6.why: The whole document defines IPv6 addressing: formats, text representation, unicast, anycast, multicast addresses and required node addresses.
IPv6.quote: This specification defines the addressing architecture of the IP Version 6 (IPv6) protocol.

addressing.why: The document is an address architecture specification, including address types and scoping. It covers anycast address semantics and restrictions, and the IANA address space allocation table. Addressing is a substantial subject beyond IPv6 as a whole.
addressing.quote: IPv6 addresses are 128-bit identifiers for interfaces and sets of interfaces

rejected.why: Anycast is covered in sections 2.6 and 2.6.1, but only as one address type within the broader addressing architecture. The document is not about anycast operation.
Multicast addresses are defined in section 2.7, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
CIDR notation is referenced only for the prefix text representation and for aggregation, not as a subject of the document.
Neighbor discovery appears only as a use of link-local addresses and solicited-node addresses, not as the topic.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like, even though it carries an address allocation table. The main body is not about IANA registries.

RFC3514.title: The Security Flag in the IPv4 Header
RFC3514.summary: An April 1st parody RFC defining an "evil" bit in the IPv4 header's fragment offset field so firewalls and IDSs can distinguish malicious from benign packets.

humor.why: Dated 1 April, this is a whimsical parody specification of a flag marking malicious packets. It belongs on the humorous RFCs page.
humor.quote: we define a security flag, known as the "evil" bit, in the IPv4 [RFC791] header. Benign packets have this bit set to 0

IPv4.why: The document defines a new flag in the IPv4 header and how fragmentation affects it, so IPv4 readers would find it relevant.
IPv4.quote: The high-order bit of the IP fragment offset field is the only unused bit in the IP header.

firewall.why: The stated purpose is to help firewalls, packet filters and IDSs, and the processing rules cover their behaviour.
firewall.quote: Devices such as firewalls MUST drop all inbound packets that have the evil bit set.

rejected.why: The IDS processing rules are only part of the joke. The tag covers intrusion detection message exchange, which the document does not address.
The IPv6 evil options appear only as a brief related-work aside.
A DDoS diffserv code point is mentioned in one sentence in Related Work and nothing is specified.
The application/evil MIME type is a passing joke and is not registered or specified.
NAT boxes are mentioned only in one rule about setting the bit.
DDoS packets are mentioned only in the Related Work sketches and the document does not address DDoS mitigation.

RFC3515.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Refer Method
RFC3515.summary: Defines the SIP REFER method, the Refer-To header field and the "refer" event package, letting a UA ask another to contact a third party and report the outcome via NOTIFY, as used for call transfer.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP method and header field, with UA, registrar and proxy behaviour and call transfer use. It is a core SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines the REFER method.  This SIP [1] extension requests that the recipient REFER to a resource provided in the request.

SIMPLE.why: A substantial part of the document defines the refer event package, using SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and Subscription-State, which is the SIP event framework in the SIMPLE area.
SIMPLE.quote: This document defines an event package as defined in [2].

rejected.why: message/sipfrag is only used as the NOTIFY body and is defined in RFC 3420, not here.
Refer-To carries URIs of arbitrary schemes, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
HTTP URIs appear only as examples of Refer-To targets.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate that follows from the main body.

RFC3516.title: IMAP4 Binary Content Extension
RFC3516.summary: Defines the IMAP4 BINARY extension, letting servers decode MIME content-transfer-encodings and send or accept binary body data via new FETCH items, literal8 and APPEND changes.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 with new FETCH data items, response items, APPEND changes and a capability. It is an IMAP extension specification.
IMAP.quote: This memo defines the Binary extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP4).

rejected.why: The document works with MIME content-transfer-encodings. It only uses MIME as the thing being decoded and defines nothing new about MIME itself.
ABNF is used only to write the formal syntax, so it is notation and not the subject.
Header handling is mentioned only to say that MIME-encoded headers are not converted. The document is not about message format.

RFC3517.title: A Conservative Selective Acknowledgment (SACK)-based Loss Recovery Algorithm for TCP
RFC3517.summary: RFC 3517 specifies a conservative SACK-based loss recovery algorithm for TCP senders (scoreboard, pipe, NextSeg) that replaces fast recovery while following RFC 2581 congestion control.

TCP.why: The document specifies a TCP sender loss recovery algorithm using the SACK option, including scoreboard handling, retransmission and RTO interaction. It is a TCP extension and implementation specification.
TCP.quote: This document presents a conservative loss recovery algorithm for TCP that is based on the use of the selective acknowledgment (SACK) TCP option.

rejected.why: The algorithm follows RFC 2581 congestion control and uses a pipe estimate to limit sending. But it is a loss recovery algorithm, and the text says the SACK decisions are 'largely decoupled from the congestion control algorithms'.
NewReno is mentioned only as another advanced recovery algorithm in the introduction. This document is not about it.
The Research section cites satellite throughput results only as supporting evidence. The document is not about satellite networking.

RFC3518.title: Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) Bridging Control Protocol (BCP)
RFC3518.summary: Defines the PPP Bridging Control Protocol (BCP), the NCP that negotiates and configures remote MAC bridging over PPP links, including frame formats, VLAN tagging, and a new Bridge Control Packet Indicator option; obsoletes RFC 2878.

PPP.why: The document specifies a PPP Network Control Protocol, its configuration options, PPP protocol field values and negotiation behaviour. Readers of PPP would expect it.
PPP.quote: This document defines the NCP for establishing and configuring Remote Bridging for PPP links.

rejected.why: The document bridges Ethernet and other LAN frames over PPP. It is about PPP encapsulation, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Token Ring and FDDI are only MAC types carried in bridged frames, and source routing is described as background. The document is not about IP over token ring.
The parent is implied by PPP, and no broader link-layer topic is addressed.
LAN FCS preservation is a minor traffic service within the bridging protocol, not the subject.
Tinygram compression only strips zero padding from small frames. It is not header compression.

gaps.name: MAC bridging / Spanning Tree / VLAN bridging
gaps.why: The document covers transparent and source-route bridging, STP BPDUs, GARP/GVRP and 802.1Q VLAN tagging over a remote link. The taxonomy has no tag for LAN bridging.

RFC3519.title: Mobile IP Traversal of Network Address Translation (NAT) Devices
RFC3519.summary: RFC 3519 defines Mobile IPv4 extensions and a UDP-based tunnelling method (using the home agent port 434) so mobile nodes and foreign agents behind NAT devices can register and receive tunnelled traffic, including keepalives and NAT mapping loss handling.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IPv4 with new registration extensions, a tunnel data message, an agent advertisement flag and new reply codes for home agents, foreign agents and mobile nodes.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document presents extensions to the Mobile IP protocol and a tunnelling method which permits mobile nodes using Mobile IP to operate in private address networks

NAT.why: The whole purpose is NAT traversal: NAT detection by the home agent, keepalives to hold NAT mappings, handling of mapping loss, fragmentation concerns with NAPT, and UNSAF considerations.
NAT.quote: Mobile IP's datagram tunnelling is incompatible with Network Address Translation (NAT).

rejected.why: IP-in-UDP, GRE-in-UDP and minimal encapsulation are used, but they are Mobile IP specific tunnelling within the Mobile IP extension, which the Mobile IPv4 tag covers.
GRE is only one of the encapsulations that can be carried inside the UDP tunnel. The document does not specify or change GRE.
UDP is the substrate for the tunnel and for registration messages. The document does not define anything new about UDP itself.
IPsec is mentioned only in the security considerations, as a way to protect user data across the tunnel.
ICMP echo is used as the keepalive payload, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
The parent topic is implied by Mobile IPv4, which is the more specific tag.

RFC3520.title: Session Authorization Policy Element
RFC3520.summary: Defines the AUTH_SESSION RSVP policy element (carried in a POLICY_DATA object) conveying session authorization information, with attribute encodings, integrity protection options (shared key, Kerberos, public key), processing rules and error signalling.

RSVP.why: The document specifies a new RSVP policy element and the RSVP host/router/PDP processing rules for it, so RSVP readers would want it.
RSVP.quote: this element MUST be encapsulated in the Policy Data object [RFC-2750] of an RSVP PATH message

QoS.why: The purpose is policy-based admission control for QoS resource reservations. The QoS parent is implied by RSVP, so this tag is not needed separately.
QoS.quote: per-session authorization and admission control

rejected.why: Kerberos is only one of three mechanisms used to authenticate the policy element; the document does not specify or extend Kerberos.
SIP is only mentioned as one way the host obtains the AUTH_SESSION; the document does not specify SIP behaviour.
The PDP/PEP model is used, but COPS is never specified or profiled here.
HMAC-MD5 is a mandatory-to-implement algorithm for the authentication data, not the subject of the document.
X.509 certificates are used for authentication only. The document does not profile them.
Authentication is a supporting mechanism for the policy element, not the document's subject. Authorization of resource reservation is the subject.

RFC3521.title: Framework for Session Set-up with Media Authorization
RFC3521.summary: Informational framework describing three models (Coupled, Associated, Non-Associated) for linking SIP-style session set-up to RSVP resource reservation via an opaque media authorization token validated by policy servers, to prevent theft of service.

QoS.why: The document is about authorizing network resource reservations for QoS against session-level media authorization, using policy servers and tokens. QoS signalling and policy control is its core subject.
QoS.quote: some linkage is required to verify that the resources being used to provide the requested QoS are in-line with the media streams requested (and authorized) for the session.

authorization.why: The token-based media authorization across policy servers, session servers and edge routers is an authorization framework in its own right, aimed at preventing fraud and theft of service.
authorization.quote: describe these various scenarios and the mechanisms used for exchanging information between network elements in order to authorize the use of resources for a service

rejected.why: SIP is used only to illustrate session signalling. Protocol extensions are explicitly out of scope.
RSVP is the illustrative reservation protocol. The document only notes that the token rides in the existing Policy Data object and defines no RSVP extension.
COPS is used as the example policy protocol. The document specifies no COPS changes, and the new token object is left to RFC 3520.
The AAA authorization framework is cited only as an informative reference, and the document does not profile it.
SDP parameters are cited only as a source of token contents.

RFC3522.title: The Eifel Detection Algorithm for TCP
RFC3522.summary: Defines the Eifel detection algorithm, which uses TCP Timestamps to let a TCP sender detect after the fact that it entered loss recovery unnecessarily (spurious timeout, reordering or duplication).

TCP.why: The document specifies a sender-side TCP algorithm for detecting spurious retransmissions, using the Timestamps option. It is an extension to TCP loss recovery.
TCP.quote: The Eifel detection algorithm allows a TCP sender to detect a posteriori whether it has entered loss recovery unnecessarily.

rejected.why: The algorithm only detects spurious loss recovery. Congestion-state restoration is a response algorithm that is explicitly out of scope, and it is covered by the TCP tag.
NewReno is mentioned only in passing, as a way to avoid a later spurious fast retransmit.
ECN is mentioned only as an analogy for a nonce idea.

RFC3523.title: Internet Emergency Preparedness (IEPREP) Telephony Topology Terminology
RFC3523.summary: Defines four named topologies (IP Bridging, IP at the Start, IP at the End, End-to-End IP) for IEPREP emergency-preparedness phone calls crossing circuit-switched and IP networks, to give the working group common terminology.

emergency services.why: The document is about emergency preparedness telephony, and it names the call topologies used to discuss it. The emergency services topic covers emergency preparedness communications.
emergency services.quote: This document defines the topology naming conventions that are to be used in reference to Internet Emergency Preparedness (IEPREP) phone calls.

PSTN interop.why: Each topology describes how circuit-switched networks and IP networks interwork through gateways. Readers interested in PSTN/Internet interworking would want it.
PSTN interop.quote: a CSN phone of any type initiates (dials) a call to another CSN phone with an IP core between the two CSNs.

rejected.why: The memo says it is agnostic about signalling protocols such as SIP and MEGACO, so it does not address SIP.
QoS mechanisms (Diffserv, RSVP, NSIS) are named only as things the memo stays agnostic about.
It is a terminology document, but the terms cover only IEPREP topologies. The emergency services tag is the more specific subject.
Megaco is mentioned only as an example of a signalling protocol that the memo does not address.

RFC3524.title: Mapping of Media Streams to Resource Reservation Flows
RFC3524.summary: Defines a new "SRF" (Single Reservation Flow) semantics value for the SDP grouping framework, letting an SDP description request that a group of media lines be mapped to a single resource reservation flow.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP by defining a new group semantics token (SRF) and its syntax and meaning for media lines.
SDP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Session Description Protocol (SDP) grouping framework.

QoS.why: The purpose is mapping media streams to resource reservation flows to provide QoS for multimedia sessions, so QoS readers would want it. It does not specify RSVP itself, so the QoS topic is used rather than the RSVP tag.
QoS.quote: Resource reservation protocols assign network resources to particular flows of IP packets.

rejected.why: RSVP is only used as an example reservation mechanism in the Examples section; the document does not specify or extend it.
SIP only carries the SDP in the example and for integrity protection; nothing about SIP is defined.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect SDP integrity.
The registration of the SRF token is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.

RFC3525.title: Gateway Control Protocol Version 1
RFC3525.summary: RFC 3525 specifies the Megaco/H.248 Gateway Control Protocol version 1, used between a Media Gateway Controller and Media Gateway, covering its connection model, commands, transactions, packages, text and binary encodings, and transport.

Megaco.why: The whole document specifies the Megaco/H.248 gateway control protocol: contexts, terminations, commands, transactions, packages and encodings.
Megaco.quote: This document defines the protocol used between elements of a physically decomposed multimedia gateway, i.e., a Media Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller.

rejected.why: A different, competing gateway control protocol; it is not specified or discussed here.
SDP is used as the text encoding of Local and Remote descriptors, which makes it a substrate. The document defines no new SDP semantics beyond small syntax relaxations.
IPsec (AH/ESP) is only the security mechanism, covered in Security Considerations, apart from a small interim AH scheme.
ASN.1 is the notation for the binary encoding, not the subject of the document.
ABNF is the syntax notation for the text encoding, not the subject of the document.
Megaco already sits under this parent, so the child tag is chosen instead of the parent.
H.323 and H.245 are referenced for interworking and mux types, but the document does not specify H.323.

RFC3526.title: More Modular Exponential (MODP) Diffie-Hellman groups for Internet Key Exchange (IKE)
RFC3526.summary: Defines the 1536-bit group 5 and new 2048-, 3072-, 4096-, 6144- and 8192-bit MODP Diffie-Hellman groups (ids 14-18) for IKE, with primes, generators and strength estimates.

IKE.why: The document extends IKE by defining new Diffie-Hellman groups and their IKE group ids. IKE readers need it.
IKE.quote: This document defines new Modular Exponential (MODP) Groups for the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol.

rejected.why: AES is mentioned only to motivate stronger groups; the document does not specify AES or its modes.
IKE is the specific subject; IPsec is the parent and is implied.
IKE is the more specific tag covering the key exchange parameters; no separate key-management topic is needed.
The IANA section only registers group ids, which is boilerplate, not the subject.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman MODP groups
gaps.why: The document is about finite-field Diffie-Hellman group parameters. The taxonomy has no tag for Diffie-Hellman or MODP groups; the nearest is the generic cryptography topic.

RFC3527.title: Link Selection sub-option for the Relay Agent Information Option for DHCPv4
RFC3527.summary: Defines the Link Selection sub-option (code 5) for the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information Option, letting a relay agent specify the subnet/link for address allocation separately from the giaddr used to reach the relay.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 by defining a new relay agent information sub-option and the server behaviour when it is present.
DHCP.quote: This document describes the link selection sub-option of the relay-agent-information option for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4).

rejected.why: The document covers only DHCPv4, not DHCPv6.
IPv4 addressing is only the context; the document is about a DHCP sub-option.
The IANA section only assigns sub-option value 5; it is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC3528.title: Mesh-enhanced Service Location Protocol (mSLP)
RFC3528.summary: Defines mSLP, an experimental enhancement of SLPv2 in which Directory Agents sharing scopes form a fully-meshed peer set and exchange registrations by anti-entropy and direct forwarding, with a new MeshFwd extension and AntiEtrpRqst message.

SLP.why: The document extends SLPv2 with new DA peering behaviour, a new extension (MeshFwd), a new message type and a DAAdvert attribute, so it is squarely about SLP.
SLP.quote: mSLP enhances the Service Location Protocol (SLP) with a scope-based fully-meshed peering Directory Agent (DA) architecture.

rejected.why: SLP is the specific technology tag under it and already covers the subject, so the parent is implied.
Peering connections use TCP only as a reliable substrate; nothing new is defined for TCP.
IBGP is mentioned only as an analogy for the full-mesh peering; the document is not about BGP.
DHCP is listed only as one way to learn about peers, via an existing RFC; the document defines nothing about it.

RFC3529.title: Using Extensible Markup Language-Remote Procedure Calling (XML-RPC) in Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP)
RFC3529.summary: Defines a BEEP profile for carrying XML-RPC requests and responses, including profile initialization, the xmlrpc.beep and xmlrpc.beeps URL schemes, SRV-based address resolution, and IANA registrations including TCP port 602.

BEEP.why: The document defines a new BEEP profile (boot/ready states, bootmsg/bootrpy, one-to-one exchanges), so BEEP readers need it.
BEEP.quote: This memo specifies how messages encoded in the XML-RPC [1] format are transmitted using a BEEP profile [2].

URI.why: A substantial part defines and registers two new URL schemes with syntax and resolution rules.
URI.quote: This memo defines two URL schemes, "xmlrpc.beep" and "xmlrpc.beeps", which identify the use of XML-RPC over BEEP over TCP.

rejected.why: XML-RPC messages are carried as XML, but the document only uses XML as the message encoding and does not specify XML-based formats of its own. No fitting XML-RPC tag exists, so this is noted under gaps.
TLS is used only as a privacy tuning mechanism for xmlrpc.beeps, with no new TLS extension or behaviour defined.
SRV lookup is used for address resolution, but the document defines nothing new about DNS.
HTTP is mentioned only as an analogy for serverName and resource, and as the transport XML-RPC normally uses.
DIGEST-MD5 SASL is listed as a mandatory tuning profile in Security Considerations only, which is boilerplate.
The document uses application/xml but registers no media type.

gaps.name: XML-RPC
gaps.why: The document is about carrying XML-RPC remote procedure calls over BEEP. The taxonomy has no tag for XML-RPC or for RPC over XML in general, other than ONC RPC, which is unrelated.

RFC3530.title: Network File System (NFS) version 4 Protocol
RFC3530.summary: RFC 3530 specifies NFS version 4, a distributed filesystem protocol with integrated locking, compound operations, delegation-based client caching, security negotiation via RPCSEC_GSS, migration/replication and UTF-8 internationalization; it obsoletes RFC 3010.

NFS.why: The document is the definition of the NFSv4 protocol: operations, attributes, locking, caching, and migration.
NFS.quote: The Network File System (NFS) version 4 is a distributed filesystem protocol which owes heritage to NFS protocol version 2, RFC 1094, and version 3, RFC 1813.

rejected.why: NFSv4 is an ONC RPC application and the RPC/XDR definitions are relied upon, but they are specified elsewhere; this document only uses them as substrate.
RPCSEC_GSS with Kerberos V5, LIPKEY and SPKM-3 is used as the security mechanism, but those are specified in other RFCs.
Kerberos V5 is a mandatory security triple but is only referenced, not specified.
TCP is the required transport, but the document defines nothing new about it.
Section 11 defines stringprep profiles for NFS strings, but this is a secondary detail of NFS, not a document about UTF-8.
The ACL attribute is a part of the NFS file attribute model, so it is covered by the NFS tag rather than a separate tag.

RFC3531.title: A Flexible Method for Managing the Assignment of Bits of an IPv6 Address Block
RFC3531.summary: Informational RFC proposing a bit-assignment scheme (leftmost, rightmost, centermost) for allocating parts of an IPv6 (or IPv4) address block so prefix boundaries can be moved later without renumbering, generalizing RFC 1219.

addressing.why: The whole document is about how address authorities allocate address space and sub-prefixes. That is address allocation and use, so the addressing topic fits. No technology tag under addressing is a better match.
addressing.quote: This document proposes a method to manage the assignment of bits of an IPv6 address block or range.

rejected.why: The scheme is aimed first at IPv6 but is stated to apply to any bit-addressing scheme, including IPv4. The document does not specify IPv6 itself, and addressing is the more specific fit.
IPv4 is mentioned only as the setting of RFC 1219 and as another place the scheme can apply. The document is not about IPv4.
The document deals with prefix boundaries and hierarchical allocation, but it does not cover CIDR or aggregation as such.
The scheme reduces the need to renumber when prefix lengths change. The document is about allocation order, not renumbering procedures.

RFC3532.title: Requirements for the Dynamic Partitioning of Switching Elements
RFC3532.summary: Informational requirements document for mechanisms to dynamically reallocate switching element resources among partitions (virtual SEs), primarily for GSMP switches, including leasing partitions to third-party controllers.

GSMP.why: The requirements target GSMP-controlled switches. They require partitioning of all resources discoverable through GSMP, so GSMP readers would want this RFC.
GSMP.quote: This document is primarily intended to facilitate the partitioning of GSMP switches.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example control protocol between controller and partition. The document is not about it.
An ATM switch is given only as an example of a switching element. The document is not about ATM.
An MPLS LSR is mentioned only as an example switching element.
Separated control and switching is related, but the document is about partitioning resources, not a programmable control plane. GSMP is the more specific fit.

gaps.name: Switching element partitioning / virtual switches
gaps.why: The document's own subject is dynamic partitioning of a switch into virtual SEs, with a partition manager and controllers. The taxonomy has no tag for it beyond GSMP.

RFC3533.title: The Ogg Encapsulation Format Version 0
RFC3533.summary: RFC 3533 specifies the Ogg bitstream format version 0, a generic container/encapsulation format that frames, interleaves and multiplexes logical media bitstreams (such as Vorbis audio) into pages with CRC error detection and seeking landmarks.

Ogg.why: The entire document specifies the Ogg encapsulation format: pages, segments, grouping and chaining, and the page header layout.
Ogg.quote: This document describes the Ogg bitstream format version 0, which is a general, freely-available encapsulation format for media streams.

rejected.why: Vorbis is only used as an example media mapping. The document does not specify the codec or its payload format.
Ogg is codec-independent. The Ogg tag already sits under codecs and covers the container, so the parent is implied.
The application/ogg registration is only mentioned in passing and is defined in RFC 3534, not here.
The page header carries a CRC-32 checksum with generator polynomial 0x04c11db7, but this is one field of the format. The document is not about CRC choice.
Matroska is another media container. It is not discussed in this document.
