RFC3534.title: The application/ogg Media Type
RFC3534.summary: Registers the MIME media type application/ogg for the Ogg bitstream container format, giving registration template fields such as magic number, file extension and security notes.

Ogg.why: The document registers the media type for the Ogg bitstream format and describes the format's magic number, extension and usage, so it belongs on the Ogg page.
Ogg.quote: The intention of this document is to define the MIME media type application/ogg to refer to this kind of content when transported across the Internet.

media types.why: The body is mostly a media type registration template sent to ietf-types, so readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: Subject: Registration of MIME media type application/ogg

rejected.why: Vorbis is mentioned only as an example of content carried in Ogg; the document does not specify it.
RTP is mentioned only as a separate wrapping mechanism under development, not specified here.
MIME is the registration framework; the document defines one media type, which the media types tag covers more specifically.
The Ogg tag is more specific, and the document defines a container media type rather than a codec.

RFC3535.title: Overview of the 2002 IAB Network Management Workshop
RFC3535.summary: Report of the 2002 IAB workshop on network management, summarizing operator requirements, assessments of SNMP, COPS-PR, CIM, CLI, HTTP/HTML and XML management technologies, and recommendations to the IETF.

network management.why: The whole document is about network management needs and IETF direction. It covers operator requirements and cross-technology recommendations, so the general topic tag fits.
network management.quote: The goal of the workshop was to continue the important dialog started between network operators and protocol developers, and to guide the IETFs focus on future work regarding network management.

SNMP.why: Sections 2.1 and 4 critique the SNMP framework, SMI and MIBs in detail, and Section 6 gives recommendations about MIB modules.
SNMP.quote: SNMP works reasonably well for device monitoring.  The stateless nature of SNMP is useful for statistical and status polling.

COPS.why: A full section assesses COPS-PR provisioning, and the recommendations address whether to continue COPS-PR and PIB work.
COPS.quote: COPS-PR allows high-level transactions for single devices, including deleting one configuration and replacing it with another.

rejected.why: XML is assessed as a configuration technology and recommended for IETF work, but the document is not about XML usage itself. It is one of several technologies reviewed.
SSH and Telnet appear only as access methods for the CLI in a short pros-and-cons list.
HTTP/HTML embedded web servers are only briefly assessed as a configuration interface.
The workshop's recommendations led to NETCONF, but the document does not mention it or specify anything about it.
This fits as a report from an IAB workshop. Network management is the more specific subject, and the parent would be listed only if the report type were the main reason to tag it.
PCIM and CIM are discussed in a single section only, not as a main subject of the document.

RFC3536.title: Terminology Used in Internationalization in the IETF
RFC3536.summary: RFC 3536 is an informational glossary of internationalization terminology (scripts, characters, charsets, encodings, normalization, rendering, text in IETF protocols) to help IETF participants frame i18n discussions.

internationalization.why: The whole document defines i18n vocabulary: characters, scripts, charsets, normalization, collation, bidi, locale. It is about internationalization of text in protocols.
internationalization.quote: This document provides a glossary of terms used in the IETF when discussing internationalization.

terminology.why: It is a glossary with an index of defined terms, so readers browsing terminology would expect it.
terminology.quote: This document provides a glossary of terms used in the IETF when discussing internationalization.

character sets.why: Substantial parts cover charsets, CCSs, CES, native charsets and IANA charset registration.
character sets.quote: A charset is a method of mapping a sequence of octets to a sequence of abstract characters.

Unicode.why: Covers Unicode and ISO/IEC 10646, UCS-2/4, normalization and case mapping, and the Unicode Consortium.
Unicode.quote: The Unicode Standard is a CCS whose repertoire and code points are identical to ISO/IEC 10646.

UTF-8.why: Section 3.2 defines UTF-8 and the other UTF encodings, with UTF-8 stated as the preferred IETF encoding.
UTF-8.quote: UTF-8, a transformation format specified in [RFC2279], is the preferred encoding for IETF protocols.

rejected.why: MIME is only one glossary entry among many, not a subject of the document.
Base64 and quoted-printable are brief glossary entries under transfer encoding syntax.
Language identification is mentioned briefly and RFC 3066 is only referenced.
XML is a single glossary entry.
The ASN.1 text string types appear as one short glossary entry.
The ACE entry mentions host name internationalization only in passing.

RFC3537.title: Wrapping a Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) key with a Triple-Data Encryption Standard (DES) Key or an Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Key
RFC3537.summary: RFC 3537 specifies two algorithms for wrapping an arbitrary-length HMAC key with a Triple-DES or AES key-encryption key, with algorithm identifiers and test vectors, for use in CMS Authenticated Data.

HMAC.why: The document defines how to wrap HMAC keying material. HMAC is the key type being protected, and the wrap algorithms exist to handle HMAC key properties such as variable length and no parity.
HMAC.quote: This document specifies a mechanism for the encryption of an HMAC key of arbitrary length by a 3DES KEK or an AES KEK.

AES.why: Half of the document specifies an AES-based key wrap, built on the AES key wrap algorithm with padding, and gives an algorithm identifier and test vector.
AES.quote: The second method defined uses an AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) key to encrypt the HMAC key.

DES.why: Half of the document specifies a Triple-DES CBC-based key wrap with its own algorithm identifier and test vector.
DES.quote: The first method defined uses a Triple DES (Data Encryption Standard) key to encrypt the HMAC key.

rejected.why: CMS Authenticated Data is mentioned only as one place the algorithm is used. The document does not specify CMS itself.
Key wrapping is a key-protection primitive. The document is about specific wrap algorithms, which the cryptography technology tags cover more precisely.
ASN.1 object identifiers are only used to name the algorithms, so this is a supporting mechanism and not the subject.
Random IV and padding generation appear only in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate for tagging purposes.

gaps.name: Key wrap algorithms
gaps.why: The document is about symmetric key wrapping, which is a primitive. The taxonomy has no key-wrap tag, so only the HMAC, AES and DES tags apply.

RFC3538.title: Secure Electronic Transaction (SET) Supplement for the v1.0 Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP)
RFC3538.summary: Informational supplement defining how SET (Secure Electronic Transaction) payments are carried within IOTP v1.0, specifying Payment API input/output parameters, the SET Bridge procedures, identifiers, message flows and error handling.

IOTP.why: The whole document profiles IOTP v1.0 for SET payments, specifying the IOTP Payment API parameters and Payment Bridge procedures. Readers of IOTP would want it.
IOTP.quote: This document describes how SET (SET Secure Electronic Transaction) works within the IOTP (Internet Open Trading Protocol).

rejected.why: IOTP is the more specific tag under e-commerce, and it already covers the subject. SET is a payment protocol with no tag of its own in the taxonomy.
IOTP messages and packaged content are XML, but XML is only the encoding substrate here.
Packaged content is BASE64-encoded, but only as a transform. The document does not address Base64 itself.
SHA1 is used to hash the order information into the SET OD. This is a minor detail, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: SET (Secure Electronic Transaction)
gaps.why: The document specifies how the SET card payment protocol is used inside IOTP, but the taxonomy has no tag for SET. The closest is the IOTP tag under e-commerce.

RFC3539.title: Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) Transport Profile
RFC3539.summary: RFC 3539 gives a transport profile for AAA protocols, covering TCP/SCTP use, congestion, failover, an application-layer watchdog, duplicate detection and head-of-line blocking, with recommendations for Diameter-style AAA.

AAA.why: The document is a transport profile for AAA protocols: a watchdog, failover, duplicate detection and agent behaviour. Readers of AAA would want it.
AAA.quote: This document discusses transport issues that arise within protocols for Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA).

transport mapping.why: It defines how AAA protocols map onto TCP and SCTP, including Nagle use, connection count and SCTP stream distribution.
transport mapping.quote: AAA Servers MUST support TCP and SCTP.  AAA clients SHOULD support SCTP, but MUST support TCP if SCTP is not available.

congestion control.why: A large part of the document covers congestion avoidance, congestion window validation, RTO validation and self-clocking for application-driven AAA traffic.
congestion control.quote: AAA implementations MAY implement the Congestion Manager (CM) [RFC3124].

rejected.why: TCP is the substrate whose behaviour is discussed. The document extends no TCP protocol, only recommends existing options such as SACK and Limited Transmit.
SCTP is used as a transport and its streams and heartbeats are applied to AAA. The document does not specify or extend SCTP.
RADIUS is cited as motivating examples (Identifier field, failover) but is not specified or profiled here.
Diameter is mentioned in the SCTP stream text and its watchdog messages (DWR/DWA) are used. The document is a generic AAA transport profile, not the Diameter protocol.

RFC3540.title: Robust Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Signaling with Nonces
RFC3540.summary: Defines the ECN-nonce, an optional extension to ECN that uses the ECT(0)/ECT(1) codepoints and a TCP Nonce Sum header flag so a TCP sender can detect receivers or middleboxes concealing congestion marks or drops.

ECN.why: The document specifies an extension to ECN signaling, the nonce sum mechanism built on ECT codepoints, ECE and CWR. Readers of the ECN subject would want it.
ECN.quote: an optional addition to ECN that protects against accidental or malicious concealment of marked packets from the TCP sender

TCP.why: It defines a new TCP header flag (NS) and sender and receiver TCP behavior, including ACK processing and resynchronization, so TCP implementers need it.
TCP.quote: It is carried in a single "NS" (Nonce Sum) bit in the TCP header.

rejected.why: ECN is the more specific child tag and already sits under congestion control, so the parent is implied.
Only the IP header ECN field is used; IPv4 itself is not the subject.
Mentioned only briefly in the interactions section, as a note about the lack of a header checksum.
Discussed only as an interaction in Section 7.1, not a substantial part of the document.
The nonce's random-number requirements get only a short note in the Security Considerations; the document is not about randomness.

RFC3541.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Web3D Consortium (Web3D)
RFC3541.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "web3d" for the Web3D Consortium, defining its syntax, assignment, persistence and resolution rules for naming VRML/X3D files, schemas and other resources.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration, specifying NID, syntax, uniqueness, assignment and resolution for the web3d namespace. Readers of URN namespaces would look for it.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Web3D Consortium (Web3D) for naming persistent resources

rejected.why: XML DTDs and Schemas are merely among the resources that may be named; the document does not specify anything about XML.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level; the document's body is the namespace specification itself, not registry guidance.
URN is the more specific child tag and fits; URI parent is implied.
VRML/X3D are 3D formats, not hypertext documents; they are only named resources here.

gaps.name: VRML / X3D (Web3D 3D graphics formats)
gaps.why: The named resources are VRML97 and X3D 3D content, but the taxonomy has no tag for 3D graphics formats; the document only names them rather than specifying them.

RFC3542.title: Advanced Sockets Application Program Interface (API) for IPv6
RFC3542.summary: RFC 3542 specifies the advanced sockets API for IPv6: raw sockets, ICMPv6 structures and filtering, packet information and extension header access via ancillary data, routing and options header helper functions, path MTU controls, and IPv6-capable rcmd/rexec library variants.

sockets API.why: The whole document defines sockets API extensions: raw sockets, ancillary data, socket options and helper functions.
sockets API.quote: This document provides sockets Application Program Interface (API) to support "advanced" IPv6 applications, as a supplement to a separate specification, RFC 3493.

IPv6.why: It defines API access to IPv6 header fields, extension headers (routing, hop-by-hop, destination options), traffic class, hop limit and interface selection.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 defines many new values for the Next Header field.

ICMP.why: A substantial part defines the icmp6_hdr structures, type/code constants, ICMPv6 raw sockets, checksum handling and the ICMP6_FILTER.
ICMP.quote: Therefore this API includes a method of filtering ICMPv6 messages by the ICMPv6 type field.

PMTUD.why: Section 11 defines IPV6_USE_MIN_MTU, IPV6_DONTFRAG, IPV6_RECVPATHMTU and IPV6_PATHMTU for path MTU discovery control.
PMTUD.quote: UDP and raw socket applications need to be able to determine the "maximum send transport-message size"

rejected.why: The document only defines header structures and constants for ND messages for use with raw sockets. It does not specify the protocol.
TCP is discussed only for what the options mean on TCP sockets, and received information on TCP is explicitly left undefined.
Only the rcmd_af/rresvport_af/rexec_af library functions are extended. The rlogin protocol itself is not specified.
Only MLD message constants and structures are defined for raw socket use.
Only an option structure and constants are defined, and the option itself is not specified.
The IPV6_TCLASS traffic class access is a minor feature and does not make this document about QoS or Diffserv.

RFC3543.title: Registration Revocation in Mobile IPv4
RFC3543.summary: Defines Mobile IPv4 Registration Revocation: an agent advertisement flag, a revocation support extension, and Revocation and Revocation Acknowledgment messages that let a home or foreign agent (or a co-located mobile node) signal early termination of a binding, with replay protection.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document extends Mobile IPv4 (RFC 3344) with new messages, an extension and an advertisement bit for revoking bindings between home agents, foreign agents and mobile nodes.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document defines a Mobile IPv4 Registration Revocation mechanism whereby a mobility agent involved in providing Mobile IP services to a mobile node can notify the other mobility agent

rejected.why: Mobile IPv4 is the specific child tag that fits, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
IPsec is only mentioned as an alternative way to protect revocation messages. The document uses Mobile IP authenticators.
The messages are carried over UDP port 434, but UDP is only the substrate and nothing new is defined about it.
AAA appears only in an informational reference and a passing mention as an alternative protection mechanism.
Reverse tunnels and tunnel endpoints are mentioned for context, but the document is about signalling binding revocation, not tunnelling.

RFC3544.title: IP Header Compression over PPP
RFC3544.summary: RFC 3544 defines IPCP/IPV6CP configuration option suboptions and PPP protocol field values for negotiating IP header compression (IPHC, CRTP) over PPP, obsoleting RFC 2509.

IPHC.why: The document specifies how IPHC (RFC 2507) is negotiated and demultiplexed over PPP, which is the IPHC-over-PPP tag's subject.
IPHC.quote: This document describes an option for negotiating the use of header compression on IP datagrams transmitted over the Point-to-Point Protocol

PPP.why: It defines new IPCP/IPV6CP configuration option suboptions and nine PPP Data Link Layer Protocol Field values, so PPP readers would want it.
PPP.quote: it defines extensions to the PPP Control Protocols for IPv4 and IPv6 (RFC 1332, RFC 2472)

CRTP.why: It defines the RTP-Compression and Enhanced RTP-Compression suboptions, and the protocol identifiers for compressed RTP/UDP, to negotiate CRTP and enhanced CRTP.
CRTP.quote: One suboption negotiates usage of Enhanced RTP-Compression (specified in [RFC3545])

rejected.why: RFC 3241 (ROHC over PPP) is cited only for allowing multiple IP-Compression-Protocol option instances. This document does not specify ROHC.
RTP headers are only what CRTP compresses. The document does not specify or extend RTP.
IPV6CP is one of the two NCPs the option runs in, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The more specific tags IPHC and CRTP apply, so the parent is implied.

RFC3545.title: Enhanced Compressed RTP (CRTP) for Links with High Delay, Packet Loss and Reordering
RFC3545.summary: Specifies enhanced CRTP, extending RFC 2508 IP/UDP/RTP header compression with repeated updates, absolute-value fields in COMPRESSED_UDP, and a headers checksum so it works over links with delay, loss and reordering.

CRTP.why: The document defines extensions to CRTP (COMPRESSED_UDP flags, HDRCKSUM, N+1 repetition), so it is squarely about CRTP.
CRTP.quote: This document describes a header compression scheme for point to point links with packet loss and long delays. It is based on Compressed Real-time Transport Protocol (CRTP)

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an alternative compression scheme in the introduction; the document does not specify or extend it.
RTP headers are the compressed payload of the scheme, but the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
RFC 2507 is only referenced for compressing authentication headers; the document extends CRTP, not IPHC.
Mentioned as an example tunnel causing loss and reordering, not specified here.
UDP headers and checksums are compressed/validated, but UDP itself is not the subject.
Link negotiation is left to other documents (RFC 3544); PPP is only an example context.

RFC3546.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions
RFC3546.summary: RFC 3546 defines a generic extension mechanism for TLS 1.0 ClientHello/ServerHello and six specific extensions (server_name, max_fragment_length, client_certificate_url, trusted_ca_keys, truncated_hmac, status_request), plus new alerts and the application/pkix-pkipath media type.

TLS.why: The whole document specifies TLS extensions, the extended hello formats, new handshake messages and alerts, so it belongs on the TLS page.
TLS.quote: It provides both generic extension mechanisms for the TLS handshake client and server hellos, and specific extensions using these generic mechanisms.

rejected.why: The status_request extension carries OCSP responses, but OCSP itself is not specified or changed. It is used as the payload.
Section 8 registers application/pkix-pkipath, but this is a minor IANA item supporting the client certificate URL extension, not the document's subject.
Certificates and PkiPath appear as payloads for the extensions. The document does not profile X.509.
IDNA is only referenced for encoding the HostName in server_name, not specified here.
Truncated HMAC is a TLS record-layer negotiation. HMAC itself is not defined or analysed.
The extensions are defined for TLS 1.0 only. DTLS is not discussed.

RFC3547.title: The Group Domain of Interpretation
RFC3547.summary: Specifies GDOI, an ISAKMP Domain of Interpretation for group key management in which a group controller/key server distributes group SAs and keys (KEK/TEK, optional LKH) to members via GROUPKEY-PULL and GROUPKEY-PUSH, initially for IPsec ESP.

GDOI.why: The whole document defines GDOI: its payloads, GROUPKEY-PULL exchange, GROUPKEY-PUSH message and registries.
GDOI.quote: This document presents an ISAMKP Domain of Interpretation (DOI) for group key management called the "Group Domain of Interpretation" (GDOI).

rejected.why: GDOI uses IKE/ISAKMP Phase 1 as its protecting substrate and reuses its header and hash conventions, but does not specify or extend IKE.
Only the first data-security protocol for which GDOI carries SA parameters. ESP itself is not specified or changed.
IPsec ESP SAs are the keyed output, but the document is about group key management, not the IPsec architecture.
This is the parent of GDOI. The child tag is more specific and implies the parent.
Mentioned only in Appendix A as a possible alternate Phase 1 protocol, which the document says is not part of its scope.
Covered by the more specific GDOI tag under multicast security.

RFC3548.title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings
RFC3548.summary: RFC 3548 specifies the Base64, URL/filename-safe Base64, Base32 and Base16 data encodings and gives guidance on line feeds, padding, non-alphabet characters and alphabet choice.

Base64.why: The whole document defines the Base64, Base32 and Base16 encodings, including alphabets, padding and decoder behaviour. This is what the Base64 tag covers.
Base64.quote: This document describes the commonly used base 64, base 32, and base 16 encoding schemes.

rejected.why: MIME is cited only as the source of the base64 Content-Transfer-Encoding and its line-length limit. The document is not about MIME.
US-ASCII is only the character repertoire the encodings are built from. The document does not discuss ASCII itself.
Email appears only as the historical background (PEM, MIME, SMTP line limits). The document is not about mail.
PEM is mentioned only as an origin of the base64 encoding and its 64-character line length.

RFC3549.title: Linux Netlink as an IP Services Protocol
RFC3549.summary: Informational RFC describing Linux Netlink as a protocol between a Forwarding Engine Component and a Control Plane Component for IP services (routing, neighbor, traffic control, firewall, ARPD), written as prior art for the ForCES working group.

ForCES.why: The document describes control/forwarding separation as prior art for the ForCES working group, defining FEC/CPC and the protocol between them.
ForCES.quote: The focus of this document is to describe Netlink's functionality as a protocol between a Forwarding Engine Component (FEC) and a Control Plane Component (CPC)

QoS.why: A substantial section covers the Linux Traffic Control service (qdiscs, classes, filters, policing) with its message template and an example.
QoS.quote: This service provides the ability to provision, query or listen to events under the auspices of traffic control.

firewall.why: NETLINK_FIREWALL is specified with mode and verdict messages for packet redirection to user space.
firewall.quote: This service allows CPCs to receive, manipulate, and re-inject packets via the IPv4 firewall service modules in the FE.

rejected.why: IPv4 forwarding is the service being controlled, but the document is about the Netlink protocol, not IPv4 itself.
NETLINK_ARPD and the neighbor table are covered briefly as a service module, but the document does not specify ARP.
OSPF is only mentioned as an example of a control plane component.
The control/forwarding split is related, but the document is framed around ForCES prior art, which has its own tag.
COPS appears only as an example CPC in the diagrams.
The route service module is a configuration interface for the forwarding table, not a routing architecture discussion.

gaps.name: Linux Netlink / kernel-user control interface
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about Netlink, a Linux kernel/user-space messaging protocol for configuring forwarding. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so ForCES is the closest fit.

RFC3550.title: RTP: A Transport Protocol for Real-Time Applications
RFC3550.summary: RFC 3550 specifies RTP, the real-time transport protocol for audio/video and similar data, together with its control protocol RTCP, translators/mixers, SSRC handling, and the scalable RTCP timer algorithm.

RTP.why: The document is the core RTP specification: header format, sessions, SSRC/CSRC, translators and mixers, and profile framework.
RTP.quote: This memorandum describes RTP, the real-time transport protocol. RTP provides end-to-end network transport functions suitable for applications transmitting real-time data

RTCP.why: A large part of the document defines RTCP packet types (SR, RR, SDES, BYE, APP), the transmission interval algorithm, and report analysis; the main change from RFC 1889 is the RTCP timer.
RTCP.quote: the RTP control protocol (RTCP), to monitor the quality of service and to convey information about the participants in an on-going session

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a profile under development; this document defines its own RTP-specific confidentiality method and defers to SRTP.
UDP is the typical substrate for RTP, with port conventions in Section 11, but the document is not about UDP.
SDP is referenced as a non-RTP means of session description and for a conflicting port rule note, but not specified here.
Section 10 is short and only requires profiles to define congestion control; it is not a substantial subject of the document.
RTP is designed to scale over IP multicast, but the document does not address multicast routing or group management.
DES in CBC mode is the default encryption in Section 9.1 but is a minor, deprecated aspect.

RFC3551.title: RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences with Minimal Control
RFC3551.summary: RFC 3551 defines the RTP/AVP profile for audio/video conferences with minimal control, including static payload type assignments and descriptions of audio and video encodings and payload formats.

RTP.why: The document is an RTP profile giving interpretations of generic RTP fields, default payload type mappings, RTCP behaviour and port assignment.
RTP.quote: This document describes a profile called "RTP/AVP" for the use of the real-time transport protocol (RTP), version 2

RTP payload format.why: Large parts define or reference RTP payload formats for specific codecs (G.723, G.726, G.728, G.729, GSM, DVI4, VDVI, H.261, H.263, JPEG, MPEG) with bit packing and static payload type tables.
RTP payload format.quote: This document also defines a set of encodings and payload formats for audio and video.

rejected.why: RTCP is only touched on for report interval and SDES usage in the profile; no new RTCP mechanism is defined.
SDP is mentioned only as a way to bind dynamic payload types and as the place the profile name is used.
PCMU/PCMA are covered in a short subsection among many; the document is not about G.711 specifically, and the RTP payload format tag covers it.
One of many codecs described; covered under the general payload format tag.
Registration of encoding names as MIME subtypes is done by RFC 3555, only referenced here.
The document lists encodings for RTP carriage but does not define codecs themselves; the RTP payload format tag fits better.

RFC3552.title: Guidelines for Writing RFC Text on Security Considerations
RFC3552.summary: BCP guidance for RFC authors on writing Security Considerations sections, including a security tutorial, the Internet threat model, common security issues (authentication, DoS, channel vs object security), and worked examples for SMTP and VRRP.

security.why: The document is a general security guidance and threat-model handbook not specific to one mechanism, which is exactly what the security topic covers.
security.quote: This document provides guidelines to RFC authors on how to write a good Security Considerations section.

DDoS.why: Section 4.6 substantially covers denial of service attacks and countermeasures, including blind, distributed attacks and SYN flood and Photuris examples.
DDoS.quote: Even more dangerous are DISTRIBUTED denial of service attacks (DDoS) [DDOS].

authentication.why: Section 4.1 and 4.4 survey user and host authentication mechanisms and distinguish authentication from authorization, a substantial part of the document.
authentication.quote: Essentially every system which wants to control access to its resources needs some way to authenticate users.

rejected.why: Discussed in 4.5.1 as a channel security option, but only as one example among several, not the subject.
Section 4.5.2 discusses using TLS, but as one channel security option; the document is not about TLS.
SMTP's security considerations are a retrospective worked example, not the document's subject.
VRRP appears only as a second worked example of a Security Considerations section.
It sets requirements on RFC authors, but the content is security guidance rather than process. The security tag fits better.
Section 4.4 covers authorization vs authentication briefly, but it is a small part of the document.

gaps.name: Internet threat model
gaps.why: The document defines the standard Internet threat model (passive and active attacks, on-path vs off-path). The taxonomy has no dedicated threat-model tag beyond the general security topic.

RFC3553.title: An IETF URN Sub-namespace for Registered Protocol Parameters
RFC3553.summary: Defines the 'params' sub-namespace of the 'ietf' URN namespace for naming IANA-registered protocol parameters, with its structure, assignment process and registration template.

URN.why: The document defines a new URN sub-namespace (urn:ietf:params), including its structure, persistence, lexical equivalence and assignment rules. This is squarely about URN namespaces.
URN.quote: This document creates a new sub-delegation below the "ietf" URN namespace called 'params' which acts as a standardized mechanism for naming the items registered for IETF standards.

rejected.why: The URNs name IANA registry items and IANA operates the sub-namespace. The document's subject is the URN namespace, not IANA registry guidance or stewardship generally.
DNS RR type codes appear only as an example of a URN name (urn:ietf:params:dns:rr-type-codes). The document says nothing about DNS itself.
MIME media types are mentioned only as one example of IANA registries. The document does not address them.

RFC3554.title: On the Use of Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) with IPsec
RFC3554.summary: Specifies requirements for IPsec and IKE to secure SCTP traffic, including SPD/SA handling of multiple addresses and a new IKE ID_LIST identification payload type.

SCTP.why: The document addresses how SCTP's multi-address associations are secured with IPsec; SCTP readers would want it.
SCTP.quote: This document describes functional requirements for IPsec (RFC 2401) and Internet Key Exchange (IKE) (RFC 2409) to facilitate their use in securing SCTP (RFC 2960) traffic.

IKE.why: Defines a new IKE identification payload type and Phase 1/Phase 2 negotiation requirements for multiple addresses.
IKE.quote: Define a new type of ID, ID_LIST, that allows for recursive inclusion of IDs.

IPsec.why: Specifies SPD selector and SA database handling changes needed for SCTP in IPsec implementations.
IPsec.quote: the SPD should be able to accommodate this.

rejected.why: ESP and AH are only mentioned as the protocols providing protection; nothing new is specified about them.
Certificates with multiple SubjAltName entries are used for authentication, but the document does not specify or profile X.509.
SCTP multi-address associations are the motivation, but the document is about IPsec/IKE support, not multihoming architecture.
Not a binding of a protocol over a transport; it is security-policy support for SCTP.

RFC3555.title: MIME Type Registration of RTP Payload Formats
RFC3555.summary: Defines the procedure for registering RTP payload formats as MIME audio/video subtypes, the mapping of MIME parameters to SDP, and registers all payload formats from the RTP Audio/Video Profile (RFC 3551) as MIME types.

media types.why: The document is a media type registration procedure plus a batch of audio/video subtype registrations, which is the core subject of media types.
media types.quote: This document defines the procedure to register RTP Payload Formats as audio, video or other MIME subtype names.

RTP payload format.why: Every registration describes an RTP payload format (rate, channels, ptime, fmtp parameters), so readers of RTP payload formats would want it.
RTP payload format.quote: registers all the RTP payload formats defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences, RFC 3551 [3], as MIME subtypes

SDP.why: A full section defines how MIME type and parameters map onto SDP m=, a=rtpmap, a=fmtp, a=ptime and a=maxptime.
SDP.quote: The information carried in the media type string has a specific mapping to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the formats are carried over; the document is specifically about payload format registrations, covered by the child tag.
MIME registration procedure is used, but the subject is media type registration, which is the more specific tag.
Codecs such as G.723, GSM and H.263 are only registered by name and referenced to other specifications, not defined here.
Registers audio/G729, G729D and G729E with annexb parameter, but only as one of many entries; not substantially about G.729.
Only a single boilerplate registration entry among many.
PCMU/PCMA are registered as minor entries among many, not a focus.

RFC3556.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Bandwidth Modifiers for RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Bandwidth
RFC3556.summary: Defines two new SDP bandwidth modifiers, RS and RR, that specify the RTCP bandwidth allocated to active data senders and to other participants in an RTP session, with defaults and precedence rules.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with new b= bandwidth modifiers (RS and RR), including syntax, precedence at session and media level, and bwtype registration.
SDP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Session Description Protocol (SDP) to specify two additional modifiers for the bandwidth attribute.

RTCP.why: The modifiers control RTCP bandwidth allocation between senders and receivers, including how the RTCP interval algorithm is affected and the default 5% split. Readers of RTCP would want this.
RTCP.quote: These modifiers may be used to specify the bandwidth allowed for RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) packets in a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) session.

rejected.why: RTP is the session context. The document only configures the RTCP bandwidth share, so the more specific RTCP tag covers it.
The IANA section only registers the RS and RR bwtype names. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The RTP A/V profile is mentioned only for its default RTCP bandwidth rules. The document does not define any payload format.

RFC3557.title: RTP Payload Format for European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) European Standard ES 201 108 Distributed Speech Recognition Encoding
RFC3557.summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for carrying ETSI ES 201 108 distributed speech recognition front-end feature frame pairs, including DTX support, RTP header usage, and the audio/dsr-es201108 media type with SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The whole document defines an RTP payload format for a specific media encoding (DSR front-end features), including packing, timestamps and marker usage.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies an RTP payload format for encapsulating European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) European Standard (ES) 201 108 front-end signal processing feature streams

media types.why: The document registers audio/dsr-es201108 with rate and maxptime parameters, a substantial part of the content, and maps them into SDP.
media types.quote: One new MIME subtype registration is required for this payload type, as defined below.

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers it.
Only a short parameter mapping to SDP is given; SDP is not the subject.
The DSR front-end is defined by ETSI, not by this document; this RFC only defines the payload format. It is not a speech codec in the listed sense.
Header compression is only mentioned as a bandwidth-efficiency suggestion.
ROHC is only referenced in passing as a bandwidth-efficiency option.
Speech recognition services are the motivating use, but MRCP is not discussed.

gaps.name: Distributed Speech Recognition (ETSI ES 201 108)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for speech recognition or DSR front-end feature encodings, which is the actual media being carried.

RFC3558.title: RTP Payload Format for Enhanced Variable Rate Codecs (EVRC) and Selectable Mode Vocoders (SMV)
RFC3558.summary: Defines the RTP payload formats (interleaved/bundled and header-free) for the 3GPP2 EVRC and SMV speech codecs, plus a storage format, media type registrations and SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document exists to define RTP payload formats for specific speech codecs (EVRC, SMV), including packet layout, interleaving and bundling.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes the RTP payload format for Enhanced Variable Rate Codec (EVRC) Speech and Selectable Mode Vocoder (SMV) Speech.

media types.why: A substantial part registers audio/EVRC, EVRC0, SMV and SMV0 media types with parameters, and defines a file storage format with magic numbers.
media types.quote: Four new MIME sub-types as described in this section have been registered by the IANA.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by RTP payload format; the document does not extend RTP itself.
Section 13 only maps media type parameters to SDP attributes; SDP is used as a substrate, not specified.
The codecs are defined by 3GPP2 specs, not this document; it only specifies their RTP carriage, so the RTP payload format tag fits better.
CDMA2000 is only background context for where the codecs are used; the document is not about those networks.
Security considerations only refer generally to RTP encryption; boilerplate, not subject matter.

RFC3559.title: Multicast Address Allocation MIB
RFC3559.summary: Defines the MALLOC-MIB SMIv2 module for configuring and monitoring multicast address allocation (scopes, allocation ranges, requests, addresses) plus MADCAP-specific configuration and statistics objects.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (MALLOC-MIB) with tables, objects, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

MADCAP.why: A substantial part of the MIB defines MADCAP configuration parameters and message/error counters, so it manages and monitors MADCAP.
MADCAP.quote: Protocol-specific objects related to the MADCAP client-server protocol.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB. The document does not specify or extend SNMP, so the MIB tag is the more specific fit.
The multicast topic is implied by the MADCAP tag, which already sits under it. A direct topic tag is not needed.
Source-specific multicast appears only as a boolean flag (mallocScopeSSM) on a scope. The document is not about SSM.

gaps.name: Multicast address allocation (MALLOC architecture, MAAS, Prefix Coordinator)
gaps.why: The document manages multicast address allocation servers, clients and prefix coordinators. The closest taxonomy tag is MADCAP, which also covers the MALLOC allocation architecture, but it is a protocol-specific tag.

RFC3560.title: Use of the RSAES-OAEP Key Transport Algorithm in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC3560.summary: Specifies conventions for using the RSAES-OAEP RSA key transport algorithm to encrypt content-encryption keys in CMS EnvelopedData, including algorithm identifiers/parameters, certificate conventions, and SMIMECapabilities.

CMS.why: The document profiles how CMS EnvelopedData and KeyTransRecipientInfo fields are populated when RSAES-OAEP is used.
CMS.quote: This document describes the conventions for using the RSAES-OAEP key transport algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

RSA.why: Defines OIDs, parameters (hash, MGF1, P), and key usage for RSA OAEP encryption, replacing PKCS #1 v1.5 key transport.
RSA.quote: The RSAES-OAEP key transport algorithm is the RSA encryption scheme defined in RFC 3447 [PKCS#1v2.1], where the message to be encrypted is the content-encryption key.

S/MIME.why: A full section defines how RSAES-OAEP is advertised via SMIMECapabilities, with DER encodings for the S/MIME context.
S/MIME.quote: RFC 2633 [MSG], Section 2.5.2 defines the SMIMECapabilities signed attribute

rejected.why: Section 4 adds certificate conventions for RSA keys, but this is a small part and the document is not an X.509 profile.
ASN.1 is used for the module and syntax but is only the notation, not the subject.
SHA-1/SHA-2 are hash parameters used within OAEP, not the subject.
Only mentioned in the introduction as having countermeasures against the attack.
Certificate usage is incidental; the document is about key transport in CMS.

RFC3561.title: Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector (AODV) Routing
RFC3561.summary: Specifies AODV, a reactive unicast distance-vector routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks, including RREQ/RREP/RERR messages, sequence numbers, route maintenance, local repair and parameters.

AODV.why: The document defines the AODV protocol: message formats, operation, route maintenance and configuration parameters.
AODV.quote: The Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector (AODV) routing protocol is intended for use by mobile nodes in an ad hoc network.

rejected.why: Parent of AODV, implied by the AODV tag, so not listed separately.
AODV messages are carried over UDP port 654, but UDP is only the substrate.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a suggested way to authenticate messages.
Used incidentally for connectivity checks and host-unreachable messages, not the subject.
A one-paragraph section defers IPv6 details to another document.
The IANA section only creates message-type registries and is boilerplate.

RFC3562.title: Key Management Considerations for the TCP MD5 Signature Option
RFC3562.summary: Informational RFC giving key-length, key-sharing and key-lifetime guidance for the keying material used with the TCP MD5 Signature Option (RFC 2385), mainly for BGP sessions.

TCP.why: The document is about the TCP MD5 Signature Option, a TCP extension, and the requirements for its keys. A reader browsing TCP extensions would expect to find it.
TCP.quote: The TCP MD5 Signature Option (RFC 2385), used predominantly by BGP, has seen significant deployment in critical areas of Internet infrastructure.

key management.why: It covers key length, entropy, lifetime, sharing limits and secure key handling. These are key management practices.
key management.quote: In current operational use, TCP MD5 Signature keys [RFC2385] may be shared among significant numbers of systems.

MD5.why: The analysis is built on MD5 performance and on key-guessing attacks against the MD5-based MAC. A substantial part of the document concerns MD5 strength.
MD5.quote: the minimum required key entropy is approximately 68 bits

BGP.why: The guidance is aimed at BGP session protection and the BGP routing machinery. BGP operators are the main readers.
BGP.quote: Key sharing SHOULD be limited so that keys aren't shared among multiple BGP peering arrangements.

rejected.why: It only points to RFC 1750 for generating random keys. It does not address randomness requirements itself.
The concern is BGP session authentication keys, but the document is about keying material for a TCP option, not routing security architecture. BGP and TCP already cover the readers.
TLS, S/MIME and SSH are named only as ways to protect key transport.
The EFF DES cracker is cited only as a hardware attack-cost benchmark.
The keyed-MD5 construction is discussed in general terms and HMAC is not mentioned.

RFC3563.title: Cooperative Agreement Between the ISOC/IETF and ISO/IEC Joint Technical Committee 1/Sub Committee 6 (JTC1/SC6) on IS-IS Routing Protocol Development
RFC3563.summary: Informational RFC reproducing the ISOC/IETF and ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6 cooperative agreement that divides IS-IS standardization work between the two bodies, requests an IANA IS-IS TLV codepoint registry, and sets collaboration guidelines.

IS-IS.why: The whole agreement is about who develops and standardizes IS-IS: it defines Core IS-IS Mechanisms versus Internet-specific extensions. IS-IS readers would want it.
IS-IS.quote: regarding cooperative development of the IS-IS routing protocol

IANA.why: A substantial part of the agreement sets up an IANA-maintained IS-IS TLV codepoint registry, with a designated expert and a later transfer of allocation authority to JTC1.
IANA.quote: IANA is requested to temporarily maintain such a registry as described below.

IETF process.why: The agreement sets IETF process rules for IS-IS documents: standards-track requirements, Informational RFCs, fast-track submission to JTC1, liaison and mutual review.
IETF process.quote: IETF SHALL apply to them the procedures for Proposed Standard submission according to [RFC2026]

rejected.why: IS-IS is the more specific tag, and it sits under routing.
IETF process and IANA are more specific children, so the parent is not needed.
IS-IS originated in ISO/OSI, but the document is about its development agreement, not OSI network-layer coexistence with IP.
MPLS and GMPLS are named only as examples of technologies in IETF scope, not as subjects of the document.

RFC3564.title: Requirements for Support of Differentiated Services-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC3564.summary: Informational requirements document stating Service Provider needs, scenarios, and solution evaluation criteria for Diff-Serv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE), including Class-Types, bandwidth constraints, and preemption.

traffic engineering.why: The document defines requirements for per-class MPLS traffic engineering: bandwidth constraints, preemption, constraint-based routing and overbooking. No narrower traffic engineering tech tag fits, because it specifies no protocol.
traffic engineering.quote: it may be desirable to perform traffic engineering at a per-class level instead of at an aggregate level

Diffserv.why: Diff-Serv classes of service, PHBs, PSCs and PDBs are central to the Class-Type and bandwidth constraint requirements.
Diffserv.quote: This document presents Service Provider requirements for support of Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv)-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE).

MPLS.why: The requirements concern LSPs, E-LSPs and L-LSPs and how traffic trunks map onto them, so MPLS readers would want this document.
MPLS.quote: By mapping the traffic from a given Diff-Serv class of service on a separate LSP, it allows this traffic to utilize resources available to the given class

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is only mentioned as an existing mechanism that a solution might extend. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Diffserv is the more specific tag under QoS.
OSPF-TE and ISIS-TE are only cited as existing TE extensions that a solution might change.

RFC3565.title: Use of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Encryption Algorithm in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC3565.summary: Specifies conventions for using AES (CBC content encryption and AES key wrap) with CMS EnvelopedData and EncryptedData, including OIDs, key management options and S/MIME capability encodings.

AES.why: The document defines AES CBC content-encryption identifiers, AES key wrap usage and KEK/CEK sizing rules, which is the core of the AES subject.
AES.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithm for encryption with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

CMS.why: It profiles how EnvelopedData and EncryptedData fields and RecipientInfo types are populated for AES in CMS.
CMS.quote: The CMS enveloped-data content type consists of encrypted content and wrapped content-encryption keys for one or more recipients.

S/MIME.why: A full section defines the SMIMECapabilities encodings for AES key sizes, which S/MIME readers need.
S/MIME.quote: An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the set of cryptographic functions it supports by using the S/MIME capabilities attribute.

rejected.why: RSAES-OAEP is only used as the key transport mechanism, defined elsewhere (RFC 3560).
Key wrap and recipient types are covered but only as part of the CMS profile; the AES and CMS tags capture it.
ASN.1 module is only the encoding apparatus for the OIDs.
Random CEK generation is mentioned only in passing and in Security Considerations.
DES is mentioned only as the algorithm AES replaced.

RFC3566.title: The AES-XCBC-MAC-96 Algorithm and Its Use With IPsec
RFC3566.summary: Specifies AES-XCBC-MAC-96, an AES-based CBC-MAC variant safe for arbitrary-length messages, for use as an authentication algorithm in IPsec ESP and AH, with test vectors.

AES.why: The document defines a MAC construction built on the AES block cipher in CBC mode, requiring AES with a 128-bit key, so AES readers would want it.
AES.quote: This memo specifies the use of AES in CBC mode with a set of extensions to overcome this limitation.

IPsec.why: The algorithm is profiled for IPsec ESP and AH, covering keying, truncation to 96 bits, padding and ESP/AH interaction. IPsec readers need it.
IPsec.quote: AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is used as an authentication mechanism within the context of the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and the Authentication Header (AH) protocols.

rejected.why: ESP is the context in which the MAC is used, not the subject being specified. The IPsec tag covers the use.
HMAC is only cited as the precedent for truncation. The document defines a different MAC.
Key derivation of K1-K3 is internal to the algorithm and the document does not address key management in its own right.

gaps.name: CBC-MAC / AES-XCBC-MAC message authentication code
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for block-cipher-based MAC algorithms (CBC-MAC, XCBC, CMAC). HMAC covers only hash-based MACs.

RFC3567.title: Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Cryptographic Authentication
RFC3567.summary: Informational RFC defining HMAC-MD5 cryptographic authentication for IS-IS PDUs, allocating authentication type 54 and specifying computation, verification, purge handling and password rollover considerations.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new authentication type and modifies PDU handling (LSPs, SNPs, Hellos, purges), so it belongs on the IS-IS page.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes the authentication of Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Protocol Data Units (PDUs) using the Hashed Message Authentication Codes - Message Digest 5 (HMAC-MD5) algorithm

HMAC.why: The mechanism is HMAC-MD5 applied to IS-IS PDUs, with specifics on key, text and zeroed fields; readers of HMAC usage in protocols would find it relevant.
HMAC.quote: The HMAC-MD5 algorithm requires a key K and text T as input [2].

rejected.why: MD5 is only the hash inside HMAC; the document does not address MD5 itself.
Topic is relevant, but the IS-IS technology tag is more specific and no child (RPKI, BGPsec) applies; parent implied by neither, though IS-IS sits under routing.
Generic topic; the specific tags already cover the authentication mechanism.
Document explicitly rejects adding a Key-ID and key management; only mentions it in passing.

RFC3568.title: Known Content Network (CN) Request-Routing Mechanisms
RFC3568.summary: Informational summary of request-routing techniques (DNS-based, transport-layer, application-layer, and combinations, plus measurement metrics) used to direct client requests to surrogates in content delivery networks as of 2000.

CDN.why: The whole document surveys how client requests are directed to surrogates in content delivery networks, which is the core subject of the CDN page.
CDN.quote: Request-Routing techniques are commonly used in Content Networks (also known as Content Delivery Networks)

DNS.why: A substantial section covers DNS-based request routing: single and multiple replies, NS and CNAME redirection, object encoding, TTL issues and limitations.
DNS.quote: a specialized DNS server is inserted in the DNS resolution process.  The server is capable of returning a different set of A, NS or CNAME records

anycast.why: A dedicated subsection discusses anycast as a request-routing mechanism, including its drawbacks.
anycast.quote: the Request-Routing DNS server can advertise an anycast address as its IP address.  The same address is used by multiple physical DNS servers.

rejected.why: HTTP redirects, headers and cookies are the mechanisms that application-layer routing inspects, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Cookie-based routing gets only a short paragraph and the document is not about cookie state management.
TLS is mentioned only for session identifiers and in the security considerations, and TLS-based techniques are declared out of scope.
RFC 3238 is cited as an architectural constraint on content modification, but the document does not address OPES itself.
BGP attributes are mentioned only as one possible proximity metric in the appendix.
The appendix on proximity metrics and probing is brief and supports surrogate selection; it is not a performance measurement framework.

gaps.name: Content Internetworking / request routing
gaps.why: The document is about request routing within content networks (the CDI working group). The taxonomy has a CDN tag but nothing specific to request-routing or content internetworking.

RFC3569.title: An Overview of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM)
RFC3569.summary: Informational overview of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM): the channel (S,G) service model, how it solves ASM deployment problems, required changes to IGMPv3/MLDv2, PIM-SM and applications, and interoperability with ASM.

SSM.why: The whole document is an overview of the SSM service model, its benefits, framework and deployment/interoperability issues.
SSM.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide an overview of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) and issues related to its deployment.

PIM-SM.why: A substantial section describes the PIM-SM changes and subset needed for SSM routing, and the document is framed around deploying SSM with PIM-SM.
PIM-SM.quote: Rendezvous Points (RPs) MUST NOT accept PIM Register messages or (*,G) Join messages in the SSM address range.

IGMP.why: The host reporting section explains IGMPv3 source filtering as the mechanism for channel subscription, a substantial part of the framework.
IGMP.quote: The ability to specify an SSM channel address c is provided by IGMP version 3 [3] and MLD version 2 [20].

MLD.why: MLDv2 is the IPv6 counterpart for SSM channel subscription and is discussed alongside IGMPv3.
MLD.quote: MLD version 2 is derived from, and provides the same support for source-filtering as, IGMPv3.

rejected.why: MSDP is discussed only as being unnecessary for SSM and as an interoperability concern with ASM; the document is not about it.
MBGP is mentioned as part of the ASM suite, with no difference in use for SSM; not a subject here.
The multicast address allocation architecture is mentioned only as a complex ASM solution that SSM avoids.
Parent of the specific tags chosen (SSM, PIM-SM, IGMP, MLD), so it is implied.

RFC3570.title: Content Internetworking (CDI) Scenarios
RFC3570.summary: Informational RFC giving example scenarios (general, brokering, publishing, local request-routing content networks) of how content networks interconnect via content internetworking gateways, to illustrate CDI and evaluate proposals.

CDN.why: The whole document is about content networks interconnecting (content internetworking): request-routing, distribution and accounting interconnection among CDNs, which matches the CDN tag covering CDN interconnection.
CDN.quote: it's useful to provide examples of the sequence of events that may occur when two content networks decide to interconnect.

rejected.why: Content networks serve web content, but the document is not about web architecture in general. The CDN tag is more specific.
Caching proxies and surrogates are mentioned only in passing. The document does not specify or analyse HTTP caching.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate-like threat enumeration for the CDI model, not web platform security mechanisms.
The document gives business and deployment scenarios, not architectural principles of the Internet.

RFC3571.title: Framework Policy Information Base for Usage Feedback
RFC3571.summary: Defines a COPS-PR Policy Information Base module (frwkFeedbackPib) with classes letting a PDP select which policy objects collect usage data, what to collect, and when PEPs report it.

COPS.why: The document specifies a PIB for COPS-PR (policy provisioning), including solicited/unsolicited report behaviour, suspend/resume and failover between PEP and PDP. COPS and policy provisioning is the subject area.
COPS.quote: The provisioning classes specified here allow a Policy Decision Point (PDP) to select which policy objects should collect usage information

rejected.why: The module is a PIB written in SPPI for COPS-PR, not an SNMP MIB module. It only imports IF-MIB's InterfaceIndex.
The PIB is policy-based, but COPS is the more specific tag for this document. Policy management is the parent of neither choice, so I used the specific technology tag.
The document borrows SMIv2 textual conventions but does not use or specify SNMP.
The usage counters are policy usage feedback for provisioning, not network performance metrics or methods.
QoS enforcement policies are mentioned only as an example use of frwkRoleCombo. The document is not about QoS.

gaps.name: Policy Information Base (PIB) / SPPI
gaps.why: The document is a PIB module defined in SPPI for COPS-PR provisioning. The taxonomy has no tag for PIBs or policy provisioning data models apart from COPS.

RFC3572.title: Internet Protocol Version 6 over MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol Over SONET/SDH)
RFC3572.summary: Informational RFC specifying how IPv6 datagrams are encapsulated in MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) frames, including multicast address mapping, interface identifier formation, duplicate address detection, and the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option format.

MAPOS.why: The document defines how IPv6 runs over MAPOS (v1 and MAPOS 16): frame format, MTU, unicast/multicast address mapping, and ND option format. It is a MAPOS extension and the page's readers would want it.
MAPOS.quote: This document specifies the frame format for encapsulating an IPv6 datagram in a MAPOS frame.

IPv6.why: A substantial part specifies IPv6-specific link behaviour: interface identifier construction from EUI-64, DAD timing, and Neighbor Discovery option encoding.
IPv6.quote: the method of forming IPv6 interface identifiers, the method of detecting duplicate addresses, and the format of the Source/Target Link-layer Addresses option field

rejected.why: The document only defines the link-layer address option encoding for MAPOS within ND; it does not specify or extend ND itself, so IPv6 plus MAPOS covers it.
SONET/SDH is the physical substrate; MAPOS is the more specific child tag and covers this.
DAD is referenced from the autoconfiguration RFC, but the document does not address SLAAC itself.
Only the HDLC-like framing of PPP is borrowed as the basis for MAPOS framing; the document is not about PPP.

RFC3573.title: Signalling of Modem-On-Hold status in Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP)
RFC3573.summary: Extends L2TP with a new Modem-Status control message and two AVPs so a LAC can tell the LNS when a V.92 client modem goes on hold or returns online.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TP with a new control message (MDMST) and AVPs (Modem On-Hold Capable, Modem On-Hold Status), so L2TP readers would want it.
L2TP.quote: This document describes a method to let the LNS know when a client modem connected to a LAC has placed the call on hold.

rejected.why: PPP is the payload that L2TP tunnels. The document does not specify or extend PPP. It only mentions LCP echo and similar mechanisms as things an LNS might pause.
The modem connects over the PSTN, but the document only adds L2TP signalling. It does not cover gateway control or telephony interworking.
TCP is mentioned only as a higher-layer protocol that may be affected by on-hold time.
The IANA section only requests assignments of a message type and AVP numbers. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC3574.title: Transition Scenarios for 3GPP Networks
RFC3574.summary: Informational document listing IPv4/IPv6 transition scenarios in 3GPP GPRS networks and the IMS, where a UE connects to nodes outside the GPRS network, for further study in v6ops.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document enumerates IPv6/IPv4 coexistence scenarios (dual stack, IPv6 over IPv4 network, IPv4 over IPv6 network, IPv6-to-IPv4 communication) for 3GPP networks.

cellular.why: The document is about IP over 3GPP GPRS networks, including UE, GGSN and PDP Contexts, and the IMS access over GPRS.
cellular.quote: This document describes different scenarios in Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) defined packet network, i.e., General Packet Radio Service (GPRS)

rejected.why: SIP is the basis of the IMS, but only described as background. The document specifies nothing about SIP itself.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag fits. The document does not specify IPv6 itself.
The translation boxes in the figures are marked only with '?'. No translation mechanism is discussed, and solutions are left to other documents.
PPP PDP Contexts are mentioned in passing only.
No specific mechanism is described. The dual-stack scenario is a generic case and is covered by the IPv6 transition tag.

RFC3575.title: IANA Considerations for RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service)
RFC3575.summary: RFC 3575 gives IANA guidance on registering RADIUS Packet Type Codes, Attribute Types and attribute values, and allocates and reserves packet type codes, updating RFC 2865.

RADIUS.why: The document is about RADIUS registries: packet type codes, attribute types and values, with Appendix A listing RADIUS packet types. It updates RFC 2865.
RADIUS.quote: This document provides guidance to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) regarding registration of values related to the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)

IANA.quote: in accordance with BCP 26, [RFC2434]

rejected.why: RADIUS is an AAA protocol, but the document is about registry allocation for RADIUS, and the RADIUS tag is the more specific fit.
Diameter is not mentioned or addressed.
RFC2869bis on EAP appears only as a reference in the security section.

RFC3576.title: Dynamic Authorization Extensions to Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)
RFC3576.summary: Informational RFC describing the deployed RADIUS extensions for Disconnect and Change-of-Authorization messages sent from server to NAS, with packet format, attributes, error causes, and security guidance.

RADIUS.quote: This document describes a currently deployed extension to the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) protocol, allowing dynamic changes to a user session

rejected.why: IPsec is recommended in the security section as protection, but the document does not specify it; it is a security mechanism relied upon.
Diameter is discussed only to explain translation and semantic differences with RADIUS, not specified or extended here.
UDP port 3799 is used as transport substrate; nothing new about UDP is defined.
Considered since CoA changes session authorizations, but the RADIUS tag is the more specific fit for this protocol extension.
MD5 is used for authenticators and mentioned for weaknesses, but only as a mechanism, not the subject.
Time synchronization is mentioned only in passing for replay protection.

RFC3577.title: Introduction to the Remote Monitoring (RMON) Family of MIB Modules
RFC3577.summary: Informational overview of the RMON family of SNMP MIB modules (RMON-1, Token Ring, RMON-2, SMON, DSMON, HCRMON, APM, TPM, SSPM, RAQMON etc.), describing each document and the shared framework components.

RMON.why: The whole document is an introduction to the RMON framework and its MIB modules, so the RMON tag is the main fit.

MIB.why: The document describes a family of SMIv2 MIB modules, their tables, groups and shared components such as control tables and capabilities objects. Readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: Each document that makes up the RMON framework defines some new useful behavior (i.e., an application) and managed objects that configure, control and monitor that behavior.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIBs. The document does not specify or extend it.
DSMON monitors DSCP values and is one section among many. The document is not about Diffserv itself.
The APM, TPM and SSPM MIBs cover application performance measurement. This is a sub-part of the RMON family, which is already tagged, and the document only summarizes them.
The Token Ring RMON extensions are summarized in one subsection. The document is not about IP over token ring.
RTCP is mentioned only as a transport in the RAQMON paragraph.

RFC3578.title: Mapping of Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) User Part (ISUP) Overlap Signalling to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3578.summary: Specifies how a SIP/PSTN gateway maps ISUP overlap signalling (IAM plus SAMs) to SIP, either by collecting digits into one en-bloc INVITE using timers or by sending multiple INVITEs, and the reverse direction.

rejected.why: SIP is the protocol being mapped to, but the document's subject is the PSTN interworking. It adds no new SIP extension, and SIP-T already sits under SIP.
This is the parent of SIP-T. A specific child tag fits, so the parent is implied.
The document covers ISUP message mapping, not the transport of SS7 signalling over IP.
Gateway control between the media gateway controller and the media gateway is not addressed.

RFC3579.title: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) Support For Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)
RFC3579.summary: RFC 3579 specifies how RADIUS carries EAP packets between a NAS and a RADIUS server using the EAP-Message and Message-Authenticator attributes, with usage guidelines, security analysis and examples, and updates RFC 2869.

Message-Authenticator is computed with HMAC-MD5, but HMAC is only used as a mechanism.
PPP is one link type over which EAP runs, and the document only gives PPP examples.
RADIUS is the more specific tag for this document. AAA is its ancestor and is implied.
MD5 is used inside HMAC-MD5 and in attribute hiding. The document is not about the MD5 algorithm.

RFC3580.title: IEEE 802.1X Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) Usage Guidelines
RFC3580.summary: Informational guidelines on how IEEE 802.1X Authenticators should use RADIUS attributes for authentication, authorization and accounting, including VLAN assignment via tunnel attributes and the RC4 EAPOL-Key frame.

RADIUS.why: The whole document is attribute-by-attribute guidance on using RADIUS authentication and accounting attributes with 802.1X, so RADIUS readers would want it.

WiFi.why: Much of the guidance is specific to 802.11 access points. It covers association IDs, SSID in Called-Station-Id, the RC4 EAPOL-Key frame for WEP keys, and 802.11 integration issues.

rejected.why: RC4 is used in the EAPOL-Key frame and its weaknesses are discussed, but the document is not about the cipher itself.
HMAC-MD5 is only the key signature mechanism in the EAPOL-Key frame.
IPsec is recommended in the Security Considerations to protect RADIUS, but the document is not about it.
RADIUS is the more specific tag, which already sits under AAA.

RFC3581.title: An Extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for Symmetric Response Routing
RFC3581.summary: RFC 3581 defines the "rport" parameter for the SIP Via header field so a server sends responses back to the request's source IP address and port, enabling symmetric response routing and NAT traversal for SIP over UDP.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new Via parameter and specifies client and server behaviour changes to SIP transport processing.

NAT.why: The motivation and much of the content (binding lifetimes, symmetric NATs, UNSAF considerations) concern NAT behaviour and traversal for SIP.

rejected.why: This taxonomy tag covers interactive NAT traversal for real-time media (ICE/STUN/TURN); the document is a SIP signalling extension for response routing, not a media traversal mechanism.

UDP is the transport the behaviour applies to, not the subject of the document.

RFC3582.summary: Informational RFC from the multi6 working group listing goals (redundancy, load sharing, performance, policy, simplicity, transport survivability, scalability, etc.) that any new IPv6 site-multihoming architecture should meet.

multihoming.why: The whole document defines goals and requirements for site-multihoming architectures for IPv6, which is the multihoming topic. No specific solution (e.g. Shim6) is specified, so the parent topic fits.

IPv6 is the context for the goals, but the document is about multihoming, not the IPv6 specification, addressing or deployment; multihoming is the more specific fit.
BGP is mentioned only as an example of failure modes and of current IPv4 multihoming practice; the document does not specify or analyse BGP.
CIDR is cited as the background for the aggregation problem, not the subject of the document.
Routing table scalability is a motivation and a goal, but the document is about multihoming specifically, which already covers it.
Impact on DNS is one brief goal (3.1.7); not a substantial part of the document.

RFC3583.title: Requirements of a Quality of Service (QoS) Solution for Mobile IP
RFC3583.summary: Informational requirements document listing what an IP QoS mechanism must satisfy to work well with Mobile IP, covering handover QoS interruption, localized re-establishment, state release, interoperability, and security.

QoS.why: The core subject is QoS forwarding treatment and (re)establishment of QoS state along new paths after handover, with Intserv/Diffserv heterogeneity considered.
QoS.quote: This document describes requirements for an IP QoS mechanism for its satisfactory operation with Mobile IP.

rejected.why: RSVP is discussed as an example whose shortcomings arise with a changing care-of address, but the document does not specify or extend it.
The document is version-agnostic (IPv4 and IPv6), so the general IP mobility tag fits better than a specific version.
The document is version-agnostic and Mobile IPv6 is only cited in examples.
Mentioned only as an example of a QoS paradigm along the path; not the subject.
Mentioned only as an example of a QoS paradigm along the path; not the subject.

RFC3584.title: Coexistence between Version 1, Version 2, and Version 3 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework
RFC3584.summary: BCP describing coexistence of SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3: SMIv1-to-SMIv2 MIB conversion rules, notification parameter translation, multi-lingual and proxy behaviour, community-based message processing/security models, and the SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB module.

SNMP.why: The document's core subject is how SNMPv1, v2c and v3 entities interoperate: PDU translation, error mapping, proxy forwarding, and community-based message processing and security models.
SNMP.quote: describe coexistence between version 3 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, (SNMPv3), version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework (SNMPv2), and the original

rejected.why: SMI uses an ASN.1 subset as its notation, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
Community strings and VACM mapping touch access control, but the document is not about AAA frameworks.

RFC3585.title: IPsec Configuration Policy Information Model
RFC3585.summary: Defines an object-oriented (UML/CIM-based) information model of IPsec and IKE configuration policy, extending PCIM/PCIMe with classes for rules, conditions, actions, proposals, transforms and IKE service/identity.

policy management.why: It is a policy information model derived from PCIM/PCIMe, which fits policy-based network management information models.

RFC3586.title: IP Security Policy (IPSP) Requirements

ESP and AH are cited only in the statement that IPSP requires no protocol modifications to them.

RFC3587.title: IPv6 Global Unicast Address Format
RFC3587.summary: Obsoletes RFC 2374, making the TLA/NLA IPv6 aggregatable global unicast address structure historic and describing the general global unicast format (global routing prefix, subnet ID, 64-bit interface ID) in line with RIR allocation policy.

RFC3588.summary: RFC 3588 specifies the Diameter base protocol, an AAA framework covering message format, peer capabilities exchange, routing through agents, error handling, session state machines and accounting.

Used as an optional transmission-level security mechanism; the document defines nothing new about TLS.
Mandated as a security mechanism but only as a substrate; not specified here.
One of the transports Diameter runs over; only brief usage guidelines are given.

RFC3589.title: Diameter Command Codes for Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 5
RFC3589.summary: Informational RFC recording IANA's allocation of Diameter Command Codes 300-313 for 3GPP Release 5 IMS applications (Cx/Dx and Sh interfaces), not for reuse in later releases.

Diameter.why: The document's sole purpose is a block of Diameter command codes allocated for 3GPP Release 5 applications, so Diameter readers would look for it.

cellular.why: The codes serve 3GPP Release 5 IMS Cx/Dx and Sh interfaces, and the document mentions needs of the cellular community, so it is relevant to 3GPP cellular interworking.

Parent of MLD, implied by the MLD tag.

RFC3591.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Optical Interface Type
