IPv6.quote: The flow identifier or Flow Label in an IPv6 packet header that may be used to discriminate traffic flows.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework through which MIB objects are accessed. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Flow labels are used for traffic classification, but the document does not address QoS architectures or signalling.

RFC3596.title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6
RFC3596.summary: Standards-track spec adding the AAAA resource record type and IP6.ARPA reverse-lookup domain to DNS for IPv6 addresses, and redefining NS/SRV/MX additional section processing to include AAAA records; obsoletes RFC 1886 and 3152.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS resource record type (AAAA), the IP6.ARPA reverse domain, and changes to additional section processing, all core DNS protocol extensions.
DNS.quote: A resource record type is defined to map a domain name to an IPv6 address.

IPv6.why: The extensions exist to support IPv6 addresses in the DNS, so IPv6 readers would want it, though the protocol specified is DNS.
IPv6.quote: This document defines the changes that need to be made to the Domain Name System (DNS) to support hosts running IP version 6 (IPv6).

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a technique whose usage model is unchanged.
Transition issues are only referenced to RFC 2893, not addressed here.
No EDNS content; unrelated.
IANA section says no assignments; the AAAA type value mention is incidental.

RFC3597.title: Handling of Unknown DNS Resource Record (RR) Types
RFC3597.summary: Specifies how DNS name servers and resolvers must handle RRs of unknown type transparently, including compression rules, generic \# text representation, equality comparison, and DNSSEC canonical form.

DNS.why: The whole document defines DNS server and resolver behaviour for new or unknown resource record types, including name compression, master file text format and equality comparison.
DNS.quote: name servers and resolvers MUST handle RRs of unknown type transparently.

rejected.why: Section 7 defines the canonical form for unknown RR types, but this is one section of a document whose main subject is general RR handling, not signing or validation.
Dynamic Update is mentioned only as a protocol that requires RR equality comparison; the document does not specify or extend it.

RFC3598.title: Sieve Email Filtering -- Subaddress Extension
RFC3598.summary: Defines the Sieve "subaddress" extension, adding :user and :detail address-part arguments so Sieve scripts can compare the sub-parts of a subaddressed email local-part (e.g., ken+sieve@example.org).

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies a new extension to the Sieve language (capability "subaddress", :user and :detail address parts), so it belongs on the Sieve page.
Sieve.quote: This document defines an extension to the Sieve mail filtering language that allows users to compare against the user and detail parts of an address.

rejected.why: The document relies on the Internet message format (RFC 2822) only for the address local-part definition; it does not specify or extend message headers or addressing.
Email is the general context, but the child tag Sieve fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
The IANA section only registers the Sieve capability keyword; it is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The ABNF augmentation of ADDRESS-PART is a one-line syntax detail, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: subaddressing / detailed addressing
gaps.why: The document concerns the practice of plus-addressing (user+detail@domain) in mail systems. The taxonomy has no tag for it, though EAI and message format cover neighbouring areas.

RFC3599.title: Request for Comments Summary RFC Numbers 3500-3599
RFC3599.summary: An annotated index of the 100 RFCs numbered 3500 through 3599, giving each one's author, date, title, abstract and standards-track status.

RFC series.why: The document is a catalogue of a block of the RFC series, its publication status and standards-track markings. It belongs on the RFC series subject page.
RFC series.quote: This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 3500 through RFC 3599.  This is a status report on these RFCs.

rejected.why: RFC 3597 and RFC 3596 appear only as one-paragraph entries in the list. The document does not specify or analyse DNS.
Several SIP RFCs are listed. The summary itself says nothing about SIP, so a SIP reader would not look here.
RTP, RTCP and payload-format RFCs are listed as entries. The document is not about RTP.
RFCs 3501, 3502, 3503 and 3516 are listed. The document is only an index and does not cover IMAP itself.
Many of the listed RFCs concern IPv6, but they are only entries in the list.
Several MIB and SNMP RFCs are listed. The summary does not address SNMP or MIBs.

RFC3600.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC3600.summary: RFC 3600 (STD 1) is a snapshot list of Internet standards-track, BCP and Experimental RFCs as of October 2003, plus pointers on retrieving RFCs from the RFC Editor.

RFC series.why: The document is an RFC Editor publication that indexes the standards-track status of RFCs and explains how to retrieve and search RFCs. A reader browsing the RFC series would look for it there.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor maintains the official repository of all RFCs and indexes to them.
RFC series.section: 2.2. Request for Comments Editor (RFC Editor) Web Pages

IETF process.why: The memo records the standards maturity levels (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, BCP) under RFC 2026, so it documents the state of the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: Sections 3.1 - 3.7 of this memo contain the lists of protocols in each stage of standardization

rejected.why: It is a dated snapshot of standards status, not a history or retrospective.
IANA is only listed as a contact and a few IANA BCPs appear in the lists. The document is not about IANA registries.
Many SNMP and MIB RFCs appear in the lists, but the document does not specify or discuss any of those protocols.
It lists RFC titles and mnemonics but is not a glossary or definitions document.

RFC3601.title: Text String Notation for Dial Sequences and Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN) / E.164 Addresses
RFC3601.summary: Defines a standard text string notation (ABNF) for Dial Sequences, including DTMF elements, pause/wait actions, GSTN phone numbers (global E.164 and local), subaddresses and post-dial sequences.

tel URI.why: The document specifies the text notation for telephone numbers (global-phone with leading +, local-phone, pause/wait, subaddresses, post-dial). This is the closest taxonomy fit, sharing the tel URI's telephone-number syntax subject.
tel URI.quote: A GSTN address in Germany, using global-phone and written-sep ".": +49.81.7856345

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax, not the subject.
Concerns E.164 numbers in the DNS; this document does not involve DNS mapping.
Only a text representation of dial strings; no Internet/PSTN interworking protocol is defined.
Related RFCs (3191, 3192, 2846) are email-based but are only informative references here.

gaps.name: Dial Sequences / GSTN telephone number text notation
gaps.why: No dedicated tag exists for general telephone number and DTMF dial string representation outside the tel URI scheme; tel URI is the nearest approximation.

RFC3602.title: The AES-CBC Cipher Algorithm and Its Use with IPsec
RFC3602.summary: RFC 3602 specifies using the AES cipher in CBC mode with an explicit IV as the confidentiality algorithm for IPsec ESP, including key size, padding, IV rules, IKE identifiers and test vectors.

AES.why: The document defines AES-CBC parameters (key sizes, rounds, block size, IV handling) and provides AES-CBC test vectors.
AES.quote: This document describes the use of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Cipher Algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) Mode, with an explicit Initialization Vector (IV)

ESP.why: It specifies the ESP payload layout, padding and sample ESP packets in transport and tunnel mode for AES-CBC.
ESP.quote: as a confidentiality mechanism within the context of the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

IKE.why: A section covers IKE interactions: Phase 1 and 2 identifiers and the mandatory Key Length attribute.
IKE.quote: For Phase 1 negotiations, IANA has assigned an Encryption Algorithm ID of 7 for AES-CBC.

rejected.why: The more specific children ESP and IKE are tagged, and the ancestor is implied.
Hash algorithms are only discussed briefly in section 5.4 about key generation strength.
HMAC-SHA-1 and HMAC-MD5 are mentioned only as ESP authenticators, not specified here.
The IANA assignments are boilerplate-level and the document is not about IANA registries.
DES is mentioned only as the predecessor of AES.

RFC3603.title: Private Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Proxy-to-Proxy Extensions for Supporting the PacketCable Distributed Call Signaling Architecture
RFC3603.summary: Defines private SIP header extensions (P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID, P-DCS-OSPS, P-DCS-Billing-Info, P-DCS-LAES, P-DCS-Redirect) for trusted proxy-to-proxy exchange of billing, trace, operator services and lawful surveillance information in the PacketCable DCS architecture.

SIP.why: The document specifies new SIP header fields and the UAC, UAS and proxy procedures for them, so it is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document describes private extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) (RFC3261) for supporting the exchange of customer information and billing information between trusted entities

rejected.why: Operator services (BLV/EI) and PSAP calls relate to PSTN interworking, but the document defines SIP headers, not PSTN gateway signalling or interworking.
9-1-1 and PSAP handling are mentioned as motivation and in the OSPS ringback, but emergency calling is not the document's subject.
IPsec or TLS between proxies is required only in the Security Considerations, so they are security substrate.
tel: URLs with E.164 numbers appear only as parameter values in the billing header; the document defines nothing new about the tel scheme.
Authorization for Quality of Service (PacketCable DQoS) is referenced but not specified here.

gaps.name: Lawfully authorized electronic surveillance (lawful intercept)
gaps.why: Section 8 defines P-DCS-LAES and P-DCS-Redirect for lawful intercept, and the taxonomy has no lawful intercept or wiretapping tag.

gaps.name: Billing and accounting for telephony
gaps.why: P-DCS-Billing-Info carries billing correlation and charging data for call accounting, and the taxonomy has no usage accounting or billing tag.

RFC3604.title: Requirements for Adding Optical Support to the General Switch Management Protocol version 3 (GSMPv3)
RFC3604.summary: Informational requirements document listing extensions needed for GSMPv3 to control optical switches and cross-connects (labels, port/switch configuration, protection, burst switching), plus implementer clarifications to GSMPv3.

GSMP.why: The whole document specifies requirements and clarifications for extending GSMPv3 to optical switching.
GSMP.quote: This memo provides requirements for adding optical switching support to the General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP).

rejected.why: GMPLS is referenced for label alignment and as a signaling context, but the document is about GSMP, not GMPLS itself.
SONET/SDH is a switched technology to be controlled, not the subject of the document.
Only a brief note that the encapsulation group of the MIB may need updating.
Mentioned in passing in service model issues; not a subject of the document.

RFC3605.title: Real Time Control Protocol (RTCP) attribute in Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC3605.summary: Defines the SDP "a=rtcp" media-level attribute to state the RTCP port (and optional address) explicitly, so RTP/RTCP sessions can be set up across port-mapping NATs.

SDP.why: The document specifies a new SDP attribute, its ABNF syntax and examples, and registers it with IANA. It is an extension to SDP.
SDP.quote: The RTCP attribute is a "value" attribute, and follows the general syntax specified page 18 of [RFC2327]: "a=<attribute>:<value>".

RTCP.why: The attribute exists to document the RTCP port and address separately from the RTP port. RTCP readers would want it.
RTCP.quote: there is a need to specify RTCP ports explicitly in SDP.

NAT traversal.why: The motivation is port mapping by NATs breaking the RTP/RTCP port pairing. The document discusses STUN-based discovery and UNSAF exit strategies.
NAT traversal.quote: The RTCP attribute in SDP is used to enable establishment of RTP/RTCP flows through NAT.

rejected.why: It is only the suggested way to discover the translated ports. The document does not specify or extend it.
SIP is the context that carries the SDP. The document does not specify or extend it.
RTP is the media protocol whose RTCP port is described. The document does not change RTP itself.
NAT is the problem environment. The document covers a signalling workaround for real-time media and does not address NAT behaviour generally. The NAT traversal tag fits better.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an integrity mechanism.

RFC3606.title: Definitions of Supplemental Managed Objects for ATM Interface
RFC3606.summary: RFC 3606 defines the ATM2-MIB, an SNMP MIB module that supplements the ATM-MIB (RFC 2515) with objects for managing ATM SVCs and PVCs, signalling statistics, ILMI, logical ports, cross-connects and PVC failure traps.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a new SMIv2 MIB module (ATM2-MIB) with tables, objects, traps and conformance groups, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines objects used for managing ATM-based interfaces, devices, and services, in addition to those defined in RFC 2515, the ATM-MIB

ATM.why: The managed objects cover ATM interfaces, VPLs/VCLs, cross-connects, signalling and ILMI. Readers interested in ATM would want this RFC.
ATM.quote: to provide additional support for the management of ATM Switched Virtual Connections (SVCs) and ATM Permanent Virtual Connections (PVCs)

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, so it is only the substrate.
SMDS is mentioned only as an example of an out-of-scope MIB for applications using ATM.
SONET/DS3 MIBs are cited only as other MIBs needed for physical interfaces, and are out of scope.
The NHRP server is only one of the service types registered via ILMI, and is not the document's subject.
OAM cells are mentioned only in the cell-counting description. The document does not address OAM mechanisms.
The parent is implied by the MIB tag, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: ILMI / ATM signalling (UNI/PNNI) management
gaps.why: The document covers ATM Forum ILMI and UNI signalling counters in depth, but the taxonomy has no tag for ATM signalling or ILMI beyond the general ATM tag.

RFC3607.title: Chinese Lottery Cryptanalysis Revisited: The Internet as a Codebreaking Tool
RFC3607.summary: An informational memo revisiting the Chinese Lottery brute-force attack, estimating how a stealthy Internet worm harnessing infected hosts could crack DES and MD5-based keys, and concluding DES should be abandoned.

DES.why: The document's quantitative analysis centres on brute-forcing DES and concludes that DES is weak and must be abandoned. Readers of the DES page would want this feasibility estimate.
DES.quote: It is clear that DES needs to be abandoned; in favor of either 3DES or the newer AES

MD5.why: A substantial part of the analysis computes MD5 key and password brute-force times and gives guidance on MD5 key lengths.
MD5.quote: The picture for MD5 (when used in simple MAC constructions) is much brighter.

rejected.why: The DES and MD5 tags already sit under cryptography and cover the subject, so the parent is implied.
Worms are discussed as the attack vehicle, but the document is not about operational security practice.
IRC is mentioned only as a possible covert channel for worm control, not specified or analysed.
AES is only named as a replacement for DES, not addressed in its own right.
The more specific cryptography tags fit better than the general security parent.

gaps.name: brute-force cryptanalysis / distributed key cracking
gaps.why: The document's main subject is massively parallel brute-force attacks using compromised hosts. The taxonomy has no cryptanalysis or malware/worm tag, so only the DES and MD5 tags apply.

RFC3608.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Extension Header Field for Service Route Discovery During Registration
RFC3608.summary: Defines the SIP Service-Route header field, which a registrar returns in 2xx REGISTER responses so a UA can learn a preloaded route for outbound requests through home service proxies.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP extension defining a new header field, with UA, proxy and registrar procedures and SIP message examples.
SIP.quote: This document defines a header field called "Service-Route" which can contain a route vector that, if used as discussed above, will direct requests through a specific sequence of proxies.

rejected.why: 3GPP is the motivating requirement, but the mechanism is generic SIP and not about cellular networks.
Session descriptions are omitted from the examples and play no role.
S/MIME is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a protection for the response and is not the subject.
DHCP is cited only as an example of how a UA discovers its outbound proxy.
DNS is assumed to be available for proxy lookup but is not discussed.

RFC3609.title: Tracing Requirements for Generic Tunnels
RFC3609.summary: Informational RFC specifying requirements for a generic route-tracing application, a successor to traceroute, and its supporting stateless UDP probe/response protocol, able to reveal details of tunnels (GRE, MPLS, IPsec, GMPLS, IP-in-IP, L2TP) in the IP forwarding path.

traceroute.why: The whole document defines requirements for a traceroute successor that traces paths and reveals tunnel details, so it belongs on the traceroute and path-discovery page.
traceroute.quote: The generic route-tracing application, specified herein, supports a superset of the functionality that "traceroute" currently offers.

tunneling.why: Tunnel detection and display across nested, heterogeneous tunnels (GRE, IP-in-IP, L2TP, MPLS, IPsec) is a core requirement, so readers of tunnelling would want this RFC.
tunneling.quote: Unlike traceroute, this application can reveal details regarding tunnels that support the IP forwarding path.

OAM.why: The document is about operator tools for verifying the forwarding plane and diagnosing faults, which falls under OAM. It has no more specific OAM technology tag.
OAM.quote: Network operators will use the generic route-tracing application to verify proper operation of the IP forwarding plane.

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are one of several tunnel types the tracer must support. The document does not specify MPLS itself.
GMPLS appears only in the list of tunnel technologies to be supported.
GRE appears only in the list of tunnel technologies to be supported.
IPsec appears only in the list of tunnel technologies to be supported.
UDP is only the proposed transport for the probe and response messages. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
ICMP is discussed only to explain why it was rejected as a transport.
The IP Router Alert option is mentioned only to explain why the protocol avoids it.

RFC3610.title: Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM)
RFC3610.summary: Specifies CCM, a generic authenticated-encryption block cipher mode combining CTR encryption with CBC-MAC for 128-bit block ciphers such as AES, with rationale, nonce guidance and test vectors.

AES.why: CCM is a block cipher mode designed with AES in mind. The test vectors all use AES, so readers of the AES modes page would want it.
AES.quote: CCM is defined for use with 128-bit block ciphers, such as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).

rejected.why: The AES tag sits under cryptography and already covers this document. A direct parent tag would be redundant.
ESP is cited only as an example of where sequence numbers are available for use as nonces. It is not the subject of the document.
ESP is mentioned only in the nonce suggestions. The document does not specify or profile it.
CCM uses CBC-MAC, not HMAC. No hash-based MAC is involved.

gaps.name: Authenticated encryption / block cipher modes of operation (CCM, CTR, CBC-MAC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for generic block cipher modes or AEAD constructions. CCM is neither specific to AES nor to any protocol. AES is the closest fit, and it fits only loosely.

RFC3611.title: RTP Control Protocol Extended Reports (RTCP XR)
RFC3611.summary: Defines the RTCP Extended Report (XR) packet type with seven report block types (loss/duplicate RLE, receipt times, reference time, DLRR, statistics summary, VoIP metrics) and SDP "rtcp-xr" attribute signaling.

RTCP.why: The document extends RTCP with a new packet type and report blocks, which is the core subject.
RTCP.quote: This document defines the Extended Report (XR) packet type for the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP)

SDP.why: A substantial section defines a new SDP attribute and its offer/answer usage.
SDP.quote: This section defines one new SDP attribute "rtcp-xr" that can be used to signal participants in a media session

rejected.why: RTP is the parent of RTCP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The blocks carry measurement data, but the document is an RTCP extension and the RTCP tag covers it.
Multicast inference (MINC) is a motivating use case, not the subject of the document.
SIP is mentioned only as a usage scenario for the SDP signaling.
The reference-time blocks were conceived for multicast congestion control, but the document does not specify congestion control.
Secure RTCP is mentioned only in the security considerations.

RFC3612.title: Applicability Statement for Restart Mechanisms for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)
RFC3612.summary: Applicability statement advising when and which LDP restart mechanism (RFC 3478 Graceful Restart vs RFC 3479 Fault Tolerance) to implement, comparing them across failure scenarios, recovery speed, scalability, complexity and CR-LDP applicability.

LDP.why: The whole document analyses LDP restart and fault-tolerance extensions and their applicability to LDP networks.
LDP.quote: This document provides guidance on when it is advisable to implement some form of Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) restart mechanism and which approach might be more suitable.

CR-LDP.why: The abstract says the issues apply equally to CR-LDP, and a section covers how each restart mechanism applies to it.
CR-LDP.quote: [RFC3479] is suitable for use in a network entirely based on CR-LDP or in one that is mixed between LDP and CR-LDP.

rejected.why: MPLS is the context in which LDP runs. The document is about LDP restart, which sits under the LDP tag.
TCP is only the transport for LDP sessions. The document notes that fault-tolerant TCP is hard but does not specify anything about TCP.
BGP is mentioned once, as another TCP application with the same fault-tolerance difficulty.
MPLS Layer 2 VPN FECs are mentioned only as an example of LDP sessions with a low rate of state change.

RFC3613.title: Definition of a Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Middleware Architecture Committee for Education (MACE)
RFC3613.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "mace" for the Internet2 Middleware Architecture Committee for Education, defining its NSS syntax, hierarchical delegation of naming authorities, persistence, and resolution.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration (NID "mace") with syntax, uniqueness, persistence, assignment and resolution rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Internet2 Middleware Architecture Committee for Education (MACE).

rejected.why: The IANA registration of NID 13 is boilerplate-level; the document is about the namespace, not IANA registries or guidance.
ABNF is only used as notation to state the NSS syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
LDAP object classes are mentioned only as examples of resources to be named; the document does not address directory services.
DNS names are only suggested as a way to ensure uniqueness of naming authority names; not a subject of the document.

RFC3614.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Motion Picture Experts Group (MPEG)
RFC3614.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "mpeg" for naming persistent MPEG standards resources (schemas, classification schemes, etc.) using the RFC 3406 template.

URN.why: The document defines and registers a formal URN namespace (NID mpeg), including structure, assignment, resolution and lexical equivalence rules.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Motion Picture Experts Group (MPEG) for naming persistent resources

rejected.why: MPEG is the subject matter of the identified resources, not media type registration.
MPEG codecs are mentioned only as background on the registrant; the document defines no codec.
XML schemas are just example resources to be named, not the document's subject.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level; the namespace registration is covered by the URN tag.

RFC3615.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for SWIFT Financial Messaging
RFC3615.summary: Registers the "swift" URN namespace ID for SWIFT financial messaging, using the RFC 3406 specification template to describe syntax, assignment, persistence and resolution.

URN.why: The whole document defines a new URN namespace (NID "swift") with its syntax, uniqueness, persistence, assignment and resolution rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace that is managed by SWIFT for usage within messages standardized by SWIFT.

rejected.why: XML schemas are only mentioned as an example of items that get URNs; the document is not about XML.
The IANA registration of the NID is boilerplate-level and not the document's subject; the URN tag covers the namespace registration.
The financial messaging context is the motivation for the namespace; the document does not specify payment or trading protocols.
URN is the more specific child tag and fits; the parent is implied.

RFC3616.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents (FIPA)
RFC3616.summary: Registers the "fipa" URN namespace ID for identifying specifications and components published by the Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents, using the RFC 3406 registration template.

URN.why: The document registers a new URN namespace (fipa), defining its structure, uniqueness, persistence, assignment and resolution rules. That is the core subject of the URN tag.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name Namespace Identification (URN NID) for the Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents (FIPA).

rejected.why: The IANA registration of NID 14 is only a boilerplate-style consideration. The body is about the URN namespace itself, not IANA registry practice.
DNS appears only in the discussion of why DNS-based schemes (tag, voc) were rejected. The document specifies nothing about DNS.
URN is the more specific child tag and fits. The document is about a URN namespace, not general URI syntax.

RFC3617.title: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Scheme and Applicability Statement for the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP)
RFC3617.summary: Defines the tftp URI scheme (syntax, semantics, examples, registration template) and gives an applicability statement strongly discouraging continued use of TFTP.

URI.why: The document's main deliverable is the tftp URI scheme: syntax, semantics, examples and scheme registration.
URI.quote: we do define a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme, as well as discuss the protocol's applicability

TFTP.why: The document is also an applicability statement for TFTP, analysing its limitations (no access control, no integrity check, lock-step, NAT problems) and discouraging its use.
TFTP.quote: WE STRONGLY RECOMMEND AGAINST THE CONTINUED USE OF TFTP, FOR REASONS LISTED IN SECTION 5

rejected.why: FTP and HTTP are only mentioned as more robust alternatives; the document is not about them.
ABNF is only the notation used for the URI syntax.
Scheme registration is boilerplate-level and the template is an appendix for the URI scheme itself.
UDP is only mentioned as TFTP's transport in the security discussion.
Section 5 criticises TFTP's weaknesses but is part of the TFTP applicability statement, not a security-mechanism document.

RFC3618.title: Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP)
RFC3618.summary: RFC 3618 specifies the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP), which lets PIM-SM domains with independent RPs exchange Source-Active messages over TCP peerings to discover inter-domain multicast sources, including peer-RPF flooding, mesh groups, timers, state machine and TLV formats.

MSDP.why: The document is the specification of MSDP itself: SA messages, peer-RPF forwarding, caching, timers, connection state machine and TLV formats.
MSDP.quote: The Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) describes a mechanism to connect multiple PIM Sparse-Mode (PIM-SM) [RFC2362] domains together.

rejected.why: MSDP interoperates with PIM-SM RPs and triggers (S,G) joins, but PIM-SM itself is not specified or extended here; it is the context that MSDP connects.
MBGP/BGP is referenced for the MRIB, policy and peer-RPF route selection, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
TCP (port 639) is only the transport for MSDP peerings; nothing new is defined about TCP.
Anycast-RP is mentioned as a deployment scenario in the applicability statement, but it is specified in RFC 3446, not here.
Keyed MD5 and HMAC-SHA1 appear only in Security Considerations as protection mechanisms; this is boilerplate-level evidence.

RFC3619.title: Extreme Networks' Ethernet Automatic Protection Switching (EAPS) Version 1
RFC3619.summary: Describes Extreme Networks' EAPS, a proprietary Ethernet ring protection protocol using a master node, health-check polling and link-down alerts to achieve fast fault recovery, with its frame format.

Ethernet.why: The document specifies a protocol for protecting Ethernet ring topologies, blocking a secondary port to avoid loops and flushing bridging tables on faults, including its frame format. Ethernet interworking and OAM is the closest fit in the taxonomy.
Ethernet.quote: increase the availability and robustness of Ethernet rings

rejected.why: The more specific Ethernet tag already covers this, and the parent is implied.
The health-check polling is a fault-detection mechanism, but the document's focus is ring protection switching, not general OAM.
EAPS is layer-2 loop avoidance and protection, not routing.
TRILL is a different layer-2 technology, not related to EAPS ring protection.
SONET rings are only mentioned as a resilience comparison, not as the subject.

gaps.name: Ethernet ring protection / Ethernet Automatic Protection Switching (EAPS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for layer-2 ring protection or loop-avoidance protocols (such as EAPS, spanning tree or ERPS), so the RFC is placed under the general Ethernet tag.

RFC3620.title: The TUNNEL Profile
RFC3620.summary: Defines the BEEP TUNNEL profile, which lets BEEP peers act as application-layer proxies, using source-routed or provisioned "tunnel" elements to reach a final endpoint through a firewall and then pass octets transparently.

BEEP.why: The document specifies a new BEEP profile, including its message syntax, semantics, reply codes and IANA profile registration.
BEEP.quote: This memo describes a Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) profile that allows a BEEP peer to serve as an application-layer proxy.

firewall.why: The main use is proxying through a firewall for authorized users, and the Security Considerations section discusses firewall traversal. This is a substantial part of the document's purpose.
firewall.quote: a BEEP peer implementing the TUNNEL profile is co-resident with a firewall.

rejected.why: That tag covers IP-in-IP and generic IP tunnelling. This is an application-layer BEEP proxy, not IP-level encapsulation.
TLS can be negotiated end-to-end through the tunnel, but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
SASL is mentioned only as a way to authenticate users before tunnelling. The document does not specify or extend it.
DNS A and SRV lookups are used to find the next hop. This is a substrate use, not a subject of the document.
TCP is only the transport that BEEP is mapped onto.
The tunnel element is described with a DTD, but XML is only the encoding used.

RFC3621.title: Power Ethernet MIB
RFC3621.summary: Defines the POWER-ETHERNET-MIB SMIv2 module for managing IEEE 802.3af Power over Ethernet Power Sourcing Equipment (ports, main power supply, notifications).

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMIv2, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: it defines a set of MIB objects to manage Power Ethernet [IEEE-802.3af] Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE).

Ethernet.why: The MIB manages Power over Ethernet (802.3af) ports and devices, extending the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB.
Ethernet.quote: extends the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB [RFC3635] with the management objects required for the management of the powered Ethernet devices and ports.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Not related; this is an SMIv2 module.
It manages PoE power supply but is specific to the 802.3af PSE; the Ethernet tag fits better, and this is not about general energy monitoring frameworks.

RFC3622.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Liberty Alliance Project
RFC3622.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "liberty" for the Liberty Alliance Project, defining NSS syntax, assignment, persistence and equivalence rules for identifying Liberty Architecture objects such as XML schemas.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration, specifying the NID, NSS syntax, uniqueness, persistence and lexical equivalence rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace that will identify various objects within the Liberty Architecture for federated network identity.

rejected.why: The Liberty Architecture is about federated identity, but this RFC only defines identifier naming for its objects, not the federation mechanisms.
XML Schema and Namespaces are the things being named, but the document does not specify or profile XML usage.
The IANA registration of the NID is boilerplate; the document is not about registry guidance.
ABNF is only used to write the NSS grammar and is not a subject of the document.

RFC3623.title: Graceful OSPF Restart
RFC3623.summary: Specifies an OSPF enhancement (graceful restart) using link-local Grace-LSAs so a restarting router stays on the forwarding path while neighbors act as helpers, with fallback to normal restart on topology change.

OSPF.why: The whole document defines restarting-router and helper-neighbor procedures and the Grace-LSA for OSPF.
OSPF.quote: an OSPF router can stay on the forwarding path even as its OSPF software is restarted. This is called "graceful restart" or "non-stop forwarding".

rejected.why: Only a brief pointer to TE extensions interaction in Section 6; the document is not about traffic engineering.
The document specifies OSPF version 2 behaviour (references RFC 2328, IPv4 addresses), not OSPFv3.
Mentioned only via a reference for TE interaction; not a subject of the document.
Security Considerations is boilerplate-like and only mentions OSPF authentication; not the document's subject.

RFC3624.title: The Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Bulk Audit Package
RFC3624.summary: Defines an MGCP package ("BA") that adds a BulkRequestedInfo parameter to AuditEndpoint so a Call Agent can audit endpoint names, instantiated endpoints, connection counts/modes and endpoint state for groups of gateway endpoints in one request.

MGCP.why: The whole document specifies an extension package to MGCP, adding bulk audit parameters, return codes and examples for the AuditEndpoint command.
MGCP.quote: This document describes a new MGCP package for bulk auditing of a group of gateway endpoints.

rejected.why: Only cited in Security Considerations as the mechanism for message authentication; boilerplate, not the subject.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the parameter syntax; the document is not about it.
Mentioned only in the IESG note as the standards-based alternative; the document does not specify or discuss it.
The parent topic is implied by MGCP, and the document addresses only the MGCP audit package.

RFC3625.title: The QCP File Format and Media Types for Speech Data
RFC3625.summary: Specifies the QCP (RIFF-based) file format for storing QCELP 13K, EVRC and SMV vocoder speech frames, updates the audio/qcelp media type registration, and registers audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp.

media types.why: The document updates audio/qcelp and audio/vnd.qcelp and registers two new audio media types, so it belongs on the media type registrations page.
media types.quote: registers the audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp media types for EVRC and SMV (respectively) data stored in this format

codecs.why: It defines a storage container for speech codec data (QCELP, EVRC, SMV), including codec GUIDs, versions and packet/rate structure, which fits audio codec definitions and containers.
codecs.quote: This document specifies the QCP format for storage of [QCELP] 13K, [EVRC], and [SMV] vocoder frames in files

rejected.why: The document is explicitly a file storage format, not a streaming payload format. RFC 2658 and RFC 3558 are referenced only for context.
ABNF is only the notation used to describe the file layout. The document is not about ABNF itself.
Email is mentioned only as one way the files may be transmitted. The document does not specify anything about email.
cdma2000 handsets are mentioned only as users of the format. The document is not about those networks.
Codec GUIDs are used as identifiers inside the file format. The document does not define or discuss UUIDs.

RFC3626.title: Optimized Link State Routing Protocol (OLSR)
RFC3626.summary: Specifies OLSR, a proactive link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks that uses multipoint relays to reduce flooding overhead and topology advertisement.

OLSR.why: The entire document specifies the OLSR protocol: packet format, HELLO/TC/MID/HNA messages, MPR selection and route calculation.
OLSR.quote: This document describes the Optimized Link State Routing (OLSR) protocol for mobile ad hoc networks.

rejected.why: The parent of OLSR, so it is implied by the OLSR tag and not listed separately.
OLSR's HELLO-based neighbor sensing is built into this protocol. NHDP is a separate later specification.
OLSR is carried over UDP port 698 but only uses it as a substrate.
Mentioned only as an example of classical flooding. The document is not about OSPF.
Security Considerations mention IPsec authentication headers as a possible countermeasure only.
Section 17 notes that IPv6 only needs address substitution. This is a minor remark, not a substantive subject.

gaps.name: OLSR
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists OLSR under MANET (id 'OLSR'), so the tag fits. No gap beyond that.

RFC3627.title: Use of /127 Prefix Length Between Routers Considered Harmful
RFC3627.summary: Informational memo explaining that using /127 prefixes on point-to-point router links can break due to the IPv6 Subnet-router anycast address, and recommending alternatives such as /64, /126 or /112.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 addressing: prefix length choice and the Subnet-router anycast address defined in the IPv6 addressing architecture.
IPv6.quote: In some cases, the operational decision may be to use IPv6 /127 prefix lengths, especially on point-to-point links between routers.

addressing.why: Much of the document discusses prefix length allocation, the subnet-router and reserved anycast addresses, and u/g bits. This is IP address architecture and use, which the addressing topic covers beyond the IPv6 tag.
addressing.quote: One could use /64 for subnets, including point-to-point links.

rejected.why: Duplicate Address Detection and the Router bit are mentioned, but only as the mechanism through which the problem shows up. The document does not specify or extend neighbor discovery.

The Subnet-router anycast address is central to the problem. However, the document is about prefix length choice, not anycast addressing or operation as a subject, so the more specific addressing tag fits better.
The Home Agents anycast address is mentioned only briefly, to bound the minimum prefix length. The document does not address Mobile IPv6.
The ICMPv6 ping-pong issue is a passing mention in the Introduction and not a subject of the document.
Traceroute appears in one example against using only link-local addresses, so it is not a subject of the document.

RFC3628.title: Policy Requirements for Time-Stamping Authorities (TSAs)
RFC3628.summary: Informational RFC (technically equivalent to ETSI TS 102 023) defining baseline policy requirements for Time-Stamping Authorities issuing time-stamp tokens, covering TSU key management, UTC clock synchronization, operational security, disclosure and organizational controls.

PKI.why: The document is a policy and practice framework for a trusted PKI service (the TSA). It covers certificate policy, TSU key lifecycle, certificate issuance and revocation, similar to CA policy requirements.
PKI.quote: This document defines requirements for a baseline time-stamp policy for Time-Stamping Authorities (TSAs) issuing time-stamp tokens, supported by public key certificates

time synchronization.why: A substantial part of the document covers clock calibration, UTC traceability, drift detection and leap-second handling, plus Annex A on UTC. This is the time-synchronization topic, though it does not use NTP.
time synchronization.quote: The TSA shall ensure that its clock is synchronized with UTC within the declared accuracy.

rejected.why: TSU certificates are mentioned, but the document sets no certificate profile. It only requires a certificate issued under an equivalent policy.

Section 7.4 covers operational controls such as physical security, personnel and incident handling. These are TSA-specific policy requirements within the PKI framing rather than general network infrastructure operational security.
NTP is never mentioned. Synchronization is required through UTC(k) laboratory traceability, not a network time protocol.
Time-stamp token format (RFC 3161) is referenced only as out of scope. The document explicitly does not specify protocols.
Section 7.2 covers TSU key lifecycle, but it is one component of the TSA policy. The PKI tag already covers it.

gaps.name: Time-stamping / Time-Stamp Authorities
gaps.why: The document is about trusted time-stamping services and TSA policy, and the taxonomy has no tag for time-stamping (RFC 3161 TSP) or CA/TSA policy frameworks.

RFC3629.title: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646
RFC3629.summary: RFC 3629 (STD 63) specifies UTF-8, the variable-length 1-4 octet encoding of ISO 10646/Unicode characters, including its byte syntax, BOM handling, MIME charset registration and security issues with invalid sequences.

UTF-8.why: The document exists to define the UTF-8 encoding form, its encoding/decoding algorithms, ABNF syntax, BOM guidance and security considerations.
UTF-8.quote: In UTF-8, characters from the U+0000..U+10FFFF range (the UTF-16 accessible range) are encoded using sequences of 1 to 4 octets.

rejected.why: Unicode is the character repertoire UTF-8 encodes, but the document specifies an encoding, so the more specific UTF-8 tag fits.
It does register the MIME charset label UTF-8, but this is a short section and the UTF-8 tag already covers it.
ABNF is only used to express the UTF-8 byte syntax in one section, as a notation rather than a subject of the document.
The MIME charset registration is incidental to defining the encoding, not about media type registration rules.
US-ASCII compatibility is a design property of UTF-8, not the subject of the document.
The MIME charset parameter registration is a minor section; the document is not about MIME body structure or encodings.

RFC3630.title: Traffic Engineering (TE) Extensions to OSPF Version 2
RFC3630.summary: RFC 3630 defines OSPFv2 traffic engineering extensions using a Type 10 Opaque LSA carrying Router Address and Link TLVs with sub-TLVs for bandwidth, metric and administrative group, for intra-area TE topology distribution.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 with a new Traffic Engineering LSA and TLVs, and specifies origination and flooding procedures.
OSPF.quote: This document describes extensions to the OSPF protocol version 2 to support intra-area Traffic Engineering (TE), using Opaque Link State Advertisements.

traffic engineering.why: The extensions build a traffic engineering database for constraint-based routing and are tied to MPLS TE requirements. Readers of traffic engineering would want this RFC.
traffic engineering.quote: The extensions provide a way of describing the traffic engineering topology (including bandwidth and administrative constraints) and distributing this information within a given OSPF area.

rejected.why: MPLS tunnels are only mentioned as one way to instantiate computed paths. The document does not specify MPLS.
The IS-IS TE extensions are referenced as a parallel work and for mapping topologies, but this document does not specify IS-IS.
Only cited in the references for unnumbered links. The document does not specify RSVP-TE.
The document covers OSPF version 2 only.

RFC3631.title: Security Mechanisms for the Internet
RFC3631.summary: IAB informational guidance surveying standard Internet security mechanisms (OTP, HMAC, IPsec, TLS, SASL, GSS-API, DNSSEC, S/MIME, OpenPGP, firewalls, Kerberos, SSH) and the factors for choosing among them, plus weak mechanisms to avoid.

security.why: The document is general guidance on choosing security mechanisms, threat models, mandatory-to-implement mechanisms and layering, not specific to one mechanism, so the general security topic fits.
security.quote: We attempt here to provide guidance, spelling out the factors and the currently-standardized (or about-to-be-standardized) solutions

IPsec.why: A dedicated section reviews IPsec's granularity, deployment, NAT conflict and VPN use.
IPsec.quote: IPsec [RFC2401],[RFC2402],[RFC2406],[RFC2407],[RFC2411] is the generic IP-layer encryption and authentication protocol.

TLS.why: A dedicated section analyses TLS properties and deployment trade-offs versus IPsec.
TLS.quote: TLS [RFC2246] provides an encrypted, authenticated channel that runs on top of TCP.

SASL.why: Section compares SASL with TLS and explains when to combine them.
SASL.quote: SASL [RFC2222] is a framework for negotiating an authentication and encryption mechanism to be used over a TCP stream.

GSS-API.why: Dedicated review section of GSS-API.
GSS-API.quote: GSS-API [RFC2744] provides a framework for applications to use when they require authentication, integrity, and/or confidentiality.

DNSSEC.why: Dedicated section on DNSSEC's role against cache contamination.
DNSSEC.quote: DNSSEC [RFC2535] digitally signs DNS records.

Kerberos.why: Dedicated section on Kerberos.
Kerberos.quote: Kerberos [RFC1510] provides a mechanism for two entities to authenticate each other and exchange keying material.

SSH.why: Dedicated section on SSH.
SSH.quote: SSH provides a secure connection between client and server.

HMAC.why: Section recommends HMAC over keyed hashes and explains per-packet use.
HMAC.quote: HMAC [RFC2104] is the preferred shared-secret authentication technique.

OTP.quote: One-time password schemes, such as that described in [RFC2289], are very much stronger than conventional passwords.

S/MIME.why: Section compares S/MIME's CA model with PGP's web of trust.
S/MIME.quote: two different secure mail protocols, OpenPGP [OpenPGP] and S/MIME [S/MIME], have been proposed to replace PEM [PEM]

OpenPGP.why: Compared alongside S/MIME in the same section.
OpenPGP.quote: PGP uses the so-called "web of trust", where any user can sign anyone else's certificate.

firewall.why: Dedicated section on firewall strengths and limits.
firewall.quote: Firewalls are a topological defense mechanism.

rejected.why: Authentication is discussed, but the specific technologies chosen are tagged more precisely.
Certificates are discussed only as part of the S/MIME vs PGP comparison.
NAT is mentioned only as a conflict with IPsec.
MD5 appears only as a weak keyed-hash example to avoid.
Layering and end-to-end remarks are incidental to the security guidance.
Random numbers are mentioned only briefly for DSA signing.

RFC3632.title: VeriSign Registry Registrar Protocol (RRP) Version 2.0.0
RFC3632.summary: RFC 3632 updates the NSI Registry Registrar Protocol (RFC 2832) to RRP version 2.0.0, adding two response codes, a transfer-cancel option, and IPv6 name server address syntax.

domain registration.why: The document specifies updates to the registry-registrar protocol (RRP), a domain registry/registrar provisioning protocol. RRP is not EPP, so the generic domain registration tag fits best.

rejected.why: RRP is a predecessor/alternative registry provisioning protocol, not EPP; the document does not specify EPP.
IPv6 addresses are only added to the RRP name server grammar; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Response code 510 mentions internationalized name encoding errors, but the document does not define IDN behaviour.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammar, not the subject.
Name servers are registry objects here, but the document does not address DNS protocol or operations.

gaps.name: Registry Registrar Protocol (RRP)

RFC3633.title: IPv6 Prefix Options for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) version 6
RFC3633.summary: RFC 3633 defines DHCPv6 options (IA_PD, IA_PD Prefix) and procedures for delegating IPv6 prefixes from a delegating router to a requesting router, e.g., ISP to CPE.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 options and message-exchange behaviour for prefix delegation, extending DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: The Prefix Delegation options provide a mechanism for automated delegation of IPv6 prefixes using the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP).

rejected.why: IPv6 prefixes are the thing delegated, but the document specifies a DHCPv6 mechanism, not IPv6 itself.
Renumbering is mentioned only in passing in the introduction; it is not the subject.
The more specific child DHCPv6 applies.
RADIUS is only cited as one example of how a delegating router might select prefixes.
Prefix delegation is covered by the DHCPv6 tag; a general addressing tag is not needed.

RFC3634.title: Key Distribution Center (KDC) Server Address Sub-option for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) Option
RFC3634.summary: Defines a new sub-option (code 10) of the DHCP CableLabs Client Configuration option carrying IPv4 addresses of Kerberos KDC servers for CableHome residential gateways.

DHCP.why: The RFC extends DHCP by defining a new sub-option of the CCC option, specifying its encoding and semantics.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a new sub-option for the CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) option code for conveying the network addresses of Key Distribution Center (KDC) servers.

Kerberos.why: The sub-option exists to tell clients where Kerberos KDCs are, so Kerberos bootstrapping readers would want it. The document does not specify Kerberos itself, so this is secondary.
Kerberos.quote: configured to use Kerberos for authentication as the first step in establishing a secure SNMPv3 link

rejected.why: SNMPv3 is only the eventual use case for the Kerberos exchange; the document does not specify or discuss SNMP.
The sub-option uses IPv4 address encoding and extends the DHCP (v4) CCC option, not DHCPv6.
DOCSIS cable networks are mentioned only as the deployment context in Security Considerations, not as the subject.
DNS lookup of the Kerberos realm is mentioned only as the alternative this option avoids.

RFC3635.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types
RFC3635.summary: Defines the EtherLike-MIB SMIv2 module for managing Ethernet-like interfaces (statistics, collision histograms, MAC Control/PAUSE, rate control, 64-bit counters for 10 Gb/s), obsoleting RFC 2665 and mapping IEEE 802.3 managed objects and IF-MIB counters.

MIB.why: The document's core is an SMIv2 MIB module (EtherLike-MIB) with object tables, groups and compliance statements for Ethernet-like interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: Subject is IEEE 802.3 Ethernet interface management, including 10 Gb/s support, MAC Control/PAUSE, duplex, and mapping of 802.3 managed objects and IF-MIB counters to Ethernet.
Ethernet.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself (MIB is the more specific child tag).
Mentioned only as an example of sublayering in the layering model section.
Counters are interface statistics, not performance measurement methodology.
SMIv2 syntax is used as the notation for the module, not the subject.

RFC3636.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs)
RFC3636.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MAU-MIB module for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (repeater and interface MAUs, auto-negotiation, jacks), extending RFC 2668 with 10 Gb/s support.

MIB.why: The document's core is a MIB module (MAU-MIB) with object definitions, conformance groups and compliance statements for 802.3 MAUs.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Ethernet.why: The MIB manages IEEE 802.3 Ethernet MAUs, including auto-negotiation and 10 Gb/s types, which readers of Ethernet pages would want.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet technology, as defined by the 802.3 Working Group of the IEEE, continues to evolve, with scalable increases in speed, new types of cabling and interfaces

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself (MIB is the more specific tag).
Covered by the more specific Ethernet tag.

RFC3637.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet WAN Interface Sublayer
RFC3637.summary: Defines the ETHER-WIS MIB module, a sparse extension of the SONET-MIB, for managing the Ethernet WAN Interface Sublayer (10GBASE-W) of IEEE 802.3ae, including test patterns, trace messages and path status.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (ETHER-WIS) in SMIv2 defining managed objects, tables and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing the Ethernet Wide Area Network (WAN) Interface Sublayer (WIS).

SONET.why: The WIS is SONET-compatible and the module extends SONET-MIB tables for section, line and path layers, with SONET/SDH defects and terminology discussed in depth.
SONET.quote: the MIB module defined in this memo is a sparse augmentation of the SONET-MIB

Ethernet.why: It manages the 10GBASE-W Ethernet PHY sublayer and works with the EtherLike-MIB and MAU-MIB, so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: An interface which includes the Ethernet WIS is, by definition, an Ethernet-like interface

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself.
Not related; this is an SMIv2 MIB module, not a YANG model.
Clause 30 of IEEE 802.3 is mentioned only in passing, and the document is not about link aggregation.
ATM over SONET is mentioned only as other users of the SONET-MIB, so it is not a subject here.
PPP over SONET is mentioned only as other users of the SONET-MIB, so it is not a subject here.

RFC3638.title: Applicability Statement for Reclassification of RFC 1643 to Historic Status
RFC3638.summary: Applicability statement recommending that RFC 1643, the Ethernet-like Interface Types MIB, be reclassified as Historic because later updates (RFC 3635 and others) superseded it.

MIB.why: The document is about the status of the EtherLike-MIB module (RFC 1643/1650) and its successors, which are MIB modules; readers of the MIB subject would want it.
MIB.quote: RFC 1643 is an obsolete specification, overtaken by events.

Ethernet.why: The MIB concerns Ethernet interfaces, and the rationale is the development of faster and full-duplex Ethernet. Ethernet readers would find the Ethernet-like interface MIB history relevant.
Ethernet.quote: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types", and its SMIv2 equivalent, RFC 1650, are applicable to half-duplex 10 Mb/s Ethernet interfaces only.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework behind the MIB, but the document is about the status of one MIB module and not about SNMP itself; MIB is the more specific tag.
The document is a reclassification to Historic, but it is about one specific MIB's obsolescence, not about the IETF process in general.

RFC3639.title: Considerations on the use of a Service Identifier in Packet Headers
RFC3639.summary: IAB statement arguing that intermediate systems should not filter or act on port/protocol numbers as service identifiers, since this has limited effect and pushes applications to obscure identifiers via encapsulation or dynamic ports.

firewall.why: The document is about port-based filtering and blocking by intermediate systems (firewalls, ISP port blocking) and its effectiveness and side effects.

internet architecture.why: An IAB architectural statement on the role of end systems versus intermediate systems and on the visibility of service identifiers in packet headers.
internet architecture.quote: it is preferable that no action or activity be undertaken by any agency, carrier, service provider, or organization which would cause end-users and protocol designers to generally obscure service identification

rejected.why: TCP ports are discussed as service identifiers, but the document does not specify, extend, or analyse TCP itself.
The port and protocol registries are only cited as references for well-known ports; the document is not about registry management.
ESP and IPsec are mentioned only as examples of encapsulation that obscures ports.
QoS marking is mentioned in passing as one use of stable ports; it is not a subject of the document.
SIP is cited only as an example of dynamic port allocation.
UDP port numbers are mentioned only as service identifiers, not as the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Port numbers / service identifiers in packet headers

RFC3640.title: RTP Payload Format for Transport of MPEG-4 Elementary Streams
RFC3640.summary: Defines a generic, configurable RTP payload format (mpeg4-generic) for carrying MPEG-4 elementary streams, with AU headers, fragmentation, interleaving, signalling via MIME/SDP parameters, and modes for CELP and AAC.

SDP.why: Payload configuration is signalled via SDP rtpmap/fmtp, with examples for each mode.
SDP.quote: a=fmtp:<format> <parameter name>=<value>[; <parameter name>=<value>]

gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for GSER or for ASN.1 text encoding rules specifically; ASN.1 is the closest fit.

RFC3643.title: Fibre Channel (FC) Frame Encapsulation
RFC3643.summary: Defines the common Fibre Channel frame encapsulation header and SOF/EOF encoding for carrying FC frames over IP (used by FCIP and iFCP), plus a procedure for measuring frame transit time using timestamps.

fibre channel.why: The whole document specifies how FC frames are encapsulated for IP transport, including header format, SOF/EOF codes and frame lifetime enforcement. This is the Fibre Channel over IP transport subject.
fibre channel.quote: This document describes common mechanisms for the transport of Fibre Channel frames over an IP network, including the encapsulation format

rejected.why: iFCP is only one of two encapsulating protocols that use this format (Protocol# 2). It is specified in a separate document and is mentioned here only in the IANA assignment.
TCP is only the substrate. The document says byte ordering is mapped to TCP but defines nothing new about TCP.
The timestamp format is borrowed from SNTP, but the document does not specify, extend or analyse NTP.
The header CRC reuses the FC-FS polynomial. The document is not about CRC polynomial choice.
The Protocol# registry is created in an appendix, but this is boilerplate-level material and not the main subject.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel frame encapsulation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no id 'fibre channel'. The only Fibre Channel entries are iFCP, a child of storage/fibre channel, and the fibre channel parent, which does exist as a child of storage ('Fibre Channel over IP transports'). The tag used above should be confirmed to match that parent id exactly. If the intended parent id is 'fibre channel', it fits as written.

RFC3644.title: Policy Quality of Service (QoS) Information Model
RFC3644.summary: Defines QPIM, an object-oriented information model extending the IETF Policy Core Information Model for representing QoS policies (RSVP/IntServ admission, DiffServ policing, shaping, marking, per-hop behaviour actions, traffic profiles and RSVP variables).

policy management.why: The document is a policy-based management information model built on PCIM/PCIMe, which is exactly this topic.
policy management.quote: This document presents an object-oriented information model for representing Quality of Service (QoS) network management policies.

QoS.why: Substantial content on QoS actions: policing, shaping, marking, PHB bandwidth and congestion control, and traffic profiles.
QoS.quote: It defines an information model for QoS enforcement for differentiated and integrated services using policy.

RSVP.why: Defines RSVP policy actions, admission control and many RSVP variable classes for conditions.
RSVP.quote: QPIM provides actions that control the reservation of such requests within the network.

Diffserv.why: Models DiffServ edge policing, shaping, DSCP marking and per-hop behaviours (EF, AF).
Diffserv.quote: QPIM provides actions and conditions that control the classification, policing and shaping done within the differentiated service domain boundaries

Intserv.why: Defines IntServ traffic profiles comparing TSPEC/FLOWSPEC for Controlled-Load and Guaranteed Service.
Intserv.quote: The QoSPolicyIntservTrfcProf class models both such traffic profiles.

COPS.why: Actions map directly to COPS for RSVP decision types, but COPS itself is only referenced.
COPS.quote: QPIM follows the COPS for RSVP specification and models each decision using a different action class.

rejected.why: LDAP is mentioned only as an example mapping and for DN string syntax; the model is storage-independent.
Directory schemas are only a possible data model; not the subject.
MIBs only mentioned as a possible data model; DIFF-MIB is a reference.

gaps.name: Policy Core Information Model (PCIM)
gaps.why: The document extends the policy framework information model, which is covered only by the generic 'policy management' topic.

RFC3645.title: Generic Security Service Algorithm for Secret Key Transaction Authentication for DNS (GSS-TSIG)
RFC3645.summary: Specifies the GSS-TSIG algorithm, a TSIG algorithm for DNS that uses GSS-API security contexts negotiated via TKEY records to sign and verify DNS transactions, and updates RFC 2845.

DNS.why: The document defines a new TSIG algorithm for DNS transaction authentication, using TKEY and TSIG resource records and modifying RFC 2845 server-response rules. DNS is the protocol being extended.
DNS.quote: This document specifies an algorithm based on the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) (RFC2743). This document updates RFC 2845.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies in detail how GSS_Init_sec_context, GSS_Accept_sec_context, GSS_GetMIC and GSS_VerifyMIC are called with specific parameters. It is a profile of GSS-API use for DNS.
GSS-API.quote: The GSS-GetMIC and GSS_VerifyMIC APIs are used to generate and verify signatures

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only as something TSIG can off-load; the document is not about DNSSEC.
Kerberos v5 is the required underlying mechanism for interoperability, but the document does not specify Kerberos itself.
SPNEGO is recommended as the mech_type in the Conformance section, but that is a small part of the document.
Dynamic update is only mentioned as a use case for TSIG; the document does not specify it.

review: GSS-API: quote not found in the text

notes: GSS-API: quote not found in the text

RFC3646.title: DNS Configuration options for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC3646.summary: Defines two DHCPv6 options, DNS Recursive Name Server (23) and Domain Search List (24), for giving clients DNS resolver addresses and a search list.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 options, their formats and which messages may carry them. It is a DHCPv6 extension.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes two options for passing configuration information related to Domain Name Service (DNS) (RFC 1034 [6] and RFC 1035 [1]) in DHCPv6 (RFC 3315 [2]).

rejected.why: DNS is the subject of the configuration data, not the protocol being specified. The options only tell a resolver which servers and search domains to use, and nothing new is defined about DNS itself.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations, to say it does not prevent the search-list attack.
DHCPv4 is mentioned only as the source of the search-option analysis. The document is about DHCPv6, so DHCPv6 is the right tag.
IPv6 is only the address family used in the option data. The document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC3647.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Policy and Certification Practices Framework
RFC3647.summary: RFC 3647 is an informational framework listing the topics to cover when writing a certificate policy (CP) or certification practice statement (CPS) for an X.509 PKI. It obsoletes RFC 2527.

PKI.why: The whole document is about CP and CPS drafting for PKIs: CA and RA roles, certificate life-cycle, and operational and legal controls. PKI is the most specific tag that covers this.
PKI.quote: This document presents a framework to assist the writers of certificate policies or certification practice statements for participants within public key infrastructures

X.509.why: Section 3.3 explains the X.509 v3 Certificate Policies, Policy Mappings and Policy Constraints extensions and policy qualifiers. Section 4.7 covers certificate and CRL profiles. This is a substantial part of the document.
X.509.quote: A Version 3 X.509 certificate may contain a field declaring that one or more specific certificate policies apply to that certificate

rejected.why: OCSP appears only as one profile topic in the CP/CPS outline. The document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
Section 4.9.5 on intellectual property is only one item in the legal-matters checklist. It does not concern IETF IPR.
Privacy of personal information (4.9.4) is one checklist item, not a protocol privacy analysis.
Key pair generation, escrow and protection are CA-practice checklist items, not a key management mechanism.
This is a parent tag. PKI is more specific and is already chosen.

gaps.name: Certificate Policy / Certification Practice Statement (CP/CPS) framework
gaps.why: The document is about CP and CPS drafting, covering PKI governance, legal and audit practices. The taxonomy has no tag for PKI policy or practice documents, so PKI is the nearest fit.

RFC3648.title: Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) Ordered Collections Protocol
RFC3648.summary: RFC 3648 extends WebDAV with server-side ordered collections, defining the ORDERPATCH method, Position and Ordering-Type headers, the DAV:ordering-type property, and interaction with versioned collections.

WebDAV.why: The document is a WebDAV extension defining a new method (ORDERPATCH), new headers, a new property and a compliance class for ordered collections.
WebDAV.quote: This specification extends the Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) Protocol to support the server-side ordering of collection members.

rejected.why: WebDAV is built on HTTP, but the document specifies a WebDAV extension rather than HTTP semantics; WebDAV is the more specific tag.
XML is used for request/response bodies and DTD notation only; the document is not about XML.
URIs identify ordering types and segments, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.

RFC3649.title: HighSpeed TCP for Large Congestion Windows
RFC3649.summary: RFC 3649 proposes HighSpeed TCP, an experimental modification of TCP's congestion control response function (additive increase a(w) and multiplicative decrease b(w) parameters) so TCP can sustain very large congestion windows on high bandwidth-delay paths, with fairness and deployment analysis including comparison to Scalable TCP.

TCP.why: The document specifies a TCP sender-side extension (new increase/decrease parameters as a function of window), so it is about TCP protocol extensions.
TCP.quote: HighSpeed TCP, a modification to TCP's congestion control mechanism for use with TCP connections with large congestion windows.

congestion control.why: The core content is a modified TCP response function and AIMD parameters, with fairness analysis against Standard TCP and Scalable TCP; readers of congestion control would want it.
congestion control.quote: for HighSpeed TCP let the congestion window increase by a(w) segments per round-trip time in the absence of congestion
congestion control.section: 7. Translating the HighSpeed Response Function into Congestion Control Parameters

rejected.why: Mentioned as an equation-based mechanism that could use the modified response function directly, but the document is not about TFRC.
Drop-Tail versus RED/AQM behaviour is discussed in tradeoffs and simulations, but only as environment context, not as the subject.
ECN is mentioned as an environment where the design should still work, not specified or analysed.
Only referenced in a mailing list citation about burst limiting; the document does not address NewReno.

RFC3650.title: Handle System Overview
RFC3650.summary: Overview of the Handle System, CNRI's global name service with its namespace, distributed service architecture, security model, and relationship to DNS, LDAP/X.500 and URN.

handle system.why: The whole document describes the Handle System: its namespace, Global Handle Registry and Local Handle Services, resolution and administration.
handle system.quote: The Handle System is a general-purpose global name service that allows secured name resolution and administration over networks such as the Internet.

rejected.why: Compared against the Handle System in section 6.1 but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
Section 6.3 discusses the relationship, but the Handle System is defined outside URI/URN namespaces and the document does not define a URN namespace.
Only compared with the Handle System in section 6.2; not specified or profiled.
UTF-8 is mandated as the handle encoding but only as a substrate.
Mentioned only as a directory that could be used alongside the Handle System.
The more specific handle system tag applies.

RFC3651.title: Handle System Namespace and Service Definition
RFC3651.summary: Describes the Handle System's namespace syntax, data model (handle values and pre-defined types), service components (GHR, LHS, caching, proxy), and operation model including its challenge-response authentication protocol.

handle system.why: The whole document defines the Handle System namespace, data model, service model and operation model, so it belongs on the Handle System page.
handle system.quote: The Handle System is a general-purpose global name service that allows secured name resolution and administration over the public Internet.

rejected.why: DNS is only mentioned as a comparison and as the name of the HTTP proxy host; the document does not specify or extend it.
The hdl: URI scheme and HTTP proxy URLs are mentioned briefly, and the syntax is deferred to a separate document.
HTTP appears only as a transport option and as the proxy interface, not as something the document is about.
The challenge-response protocol is specific to the Handle System and is a part of its operation model, so the handle system tag covers it.
This is the parent of handle system, so the child tag is the right choice.

RFC3652.title: Handle System Protocol (ver 2.1) Specification
RFC3652.summary: Specifies the Handle System protocol (v2.1) by which clients locate handle servers and perform handle resolution, administration, authentication and session management over UDP/TCP.

handle system.why: The whole document defines the Handle System client-server protocol: messages, query, administration, naming authority operations, and sessions.
handle system.quote: The Handle System is a general-purpose global name service that allows secured name resolution and administration over the public Internet.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the mandated string encoding, not the subject.
UDP and TCP are only transports for the protocol; no new usage guidance for UDP itself.
HMAC is only mentioned as an option for challenge-response MACs.
MD5 and SHA-1 are used for digests but are not the subject.
Challenge-response client authentication is a substantial part, but it is specific to the Handle protocol and is covered by the handle system tag.
The handle system tag is the more specific fit under naming.

RFC3653.title: XML-Signature XPath Filter 2.0
RFC3653.summary: Defines a new XML Signature transform (XPath Filter 2.0) that uses a sequence of XPath expressions combined with intersect/subtract/union set operations to select document subsets for signing more efficiently than the original XPath transform.

XML signatures.why: The document specifies a new transform for XML Signature, including its algorithm identifier, syntax and processing model, so it belongs under XML digital signatures.
XML signatures.quote: This specification defines a new XML Signature transform to facilitate the development of efficient document subsetting implementations that interoperate under similar performance profiles.

rejected.why: XML and XPath are the substrate on which the transform operates. The document is about signature transforms, not XML usage in protocols as a subject.
Not related; no certificates are discussed.
The algorithm identifier is a URI, but only as a naming mechanism for the transform.

gaps.name: XPath
gaps.why: The transform is defined in terms of XPath expression evaluation and node-set operations, but the taxonomy has no XPath or XML processing-language tag.

RFC3654.title: Requirements for Separation of IP Control and Forwarding
RFC3654.summary: RFC 3654 introduces the ForCES architecture and terminology and sets architectural, forwarding-element model, and protocol requirements for separating the control and forwarding planes of an IP network element.

ForCES.why: The whole document defines the ForCES architecture, FE model requirements and ForCES protocol requirements, so ForCES is its central subject.
ForCES.quote: defines a set of architectural, modeling, and protocol requirements to logically separate the control and data forwarding planes of an IP (IPv4, IPv6, etc.) networking device

rejected.why: IntServ and DiffServ are mentioned only as functions the FE model must be able to express, not as a subject of the document.
NAT appears as an example of a logical function or high-touch capability in the FE model, but the document is not about NAT.
SNMP is mentioned once as a management tool that must not change FE state without the CE being notified, which is incidental.
IPFLOW and PSAMP are cited as functions the FE model should be able to express, which is a minor requirement and not a main subject.
TCP and SCTP are named as example transports for multihop ForCES, so they are only a substrate.
The document is about the internal architecture of a network element, and ForCES is the more specific tag.

RFC3655.title: Redefinition of DNS Authenticated Data (AD) bit
RFC3655.summary: RFC 3655 redefines the DNSSEC Authenticated Data (AD) bit in DNS response headers so it is set only when all answer/authority data is cryptographically verified, and gives rules for recursive and authoritative servers and for resolvers trusting the bit.

DNSSEC.why: The document updates RFC 2535 DNSSEC semantics for the AD bit, specifying when validating servers set it and when resolvers may trust it.
DNSSEC.quote: This document redefines the AD bit such that it is only set if all data in the response has been cryptographically verified

rejected.why: Parent of DNSSEC; implied, and the document's subject is specifically the DNSSEC AD bit.
The DO bit (RFC 3225) is referenced as a condition, but the document does not specify or extend EDNS.
Trust in the AD bit is discussed, but the subject is DNSSEC validation status, which the DNSSEC tag covers.

RFC3656.title: The Mailbox Update (MUPDATE) Distributed Mailbox Database Protocol
RFC3656.summary: Defines MUPDATE, a protocol by which IMAP/POP3 servers share a unified, consistent mailbox namespace via a master/slave mailbox database, with its commands, responses, syntax and a mupdate URL scheme.

IMAP.why: MUPDATE is a companion protocol for IMAP server clusters, coordinating mailbox creation, location and ACLs. The IMAP tag is the closest fit, since the taxonomy has no distributed mailbox database tag.
IMAP.quote: allows a group of Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) or Post Office Protocol - Version 3 (POP3) servers to function with a unified mailbox namespace

URI.why: The document defines and registers the mupdate URL scheme, with a registration form. That is a substantial section.
URI.quote: This document defines the a URL scheme for the purposes of referencing MUPDATE resources

rejected.why: AUTHENTICATE uses SASL and requires GSSAPI, but the document only relies on it as an authentication mechanism and does not define anything new about it.
STARTTLS is supported, but TLS is only a security substrate here and nothing new is defined about TLS.
There is no ACAP tag in the taxonomy as a separate subject, and the document only borrows ACAP's atom and string syntax.
POP3 is mentioned only as another client of the mailbox database, and the document does not specify or extend it.
The document uses ABNF for its formal syntax but is not about the notation.
The IMAP tag is more specific, and email is implied as its ancestor.

gaps.name: Distributed mailbox database / mailbox namespace synchronization
gaps.why: The document's core subject is a master/slave replicated mailbox database with reserve/activate semantics for IMAP clusters. No tag covers it directly.

RFC3657.title: Use of the Camellia Encryption Algorithm in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
