RFC3657.summary: Specifies conventions, OIDs, key-wrap procedure and SMIMECapabilities encoding for using the Camellia block cipher for content and key encryption in CMS.

Camellia.why: The whole document defines how Camellia is used for content and key encryption: OIDs, CBC parameters, key wrap with Camellia, and S/MIME capability encoding.
Camellia.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the Camellia encryption algorithm [CamelliaSpec] for encryption with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [CMS].

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with new content-encryption and key-wrap algorithm identifiers and an ASN.1 module, so CMS readers need it.
CMS.quote: Camellia is added to the set of symmetric content encryption algorithms defined in [CMSALG].

S/MIME.why: A section defines the SMIMECapabilities encoding for Camellia in S/MIME clients, which is relevant to S/MIME readers.
S/MIME.quote: An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the set of cryptographic functions it supports by using the S/MIME capabilities attribute.

rejected.why: The AES key wrap (RFC 3394) is reused with Camellia substituted, and AES is only the model. The document is not about AES.
The ASN.1 module in the appendix is only the formal definition of the OIDs, and the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Key wrap is specified, but only as part of the Camellia/CMS algorithm conventions. Key generation and distribution are explicitly out of scope.

RFC3658.title: Delegation Signer (DS) Resource Record (RR)
RFC3658.summary: Defines the DNSSEC Delegation Signer (DS) resource record placed at zone cuts to indicate a secure child zone, replacing the NULL KEY mechanism of RFC 2535 and changing DNSSEC chain-of-trust, referral and resolver behaviour.

DNSSEC.why: The document defines the DS RR and modifies the DNSSEC chain of trust, NXT/KEY handling, and validation rules, updating RFC 2535, 3008 and 3090.
DNSSEC.quote: The delegation signer (DS) resource record (RR) is inserted at a zone cut (i.e., a delegation point) to indicate that the delegated zone is digitally signed

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and implies DNS; the document is about the security extension, not general DNS.
SHA-1 is only the digest algorithm used in the DS record; the document is not about the hash family.
It requires the OK bit (RFC 3225) and larger messages but defines nothing new about EDNS.
The DS type code and digest registry are boilerplate-level IANA actions, not the subject of the document.

RFC3659.title: Extensions to FTP
RFC3659.summary: RFC 3659 updates FTP (RFC 959) with the SIZE, MDTM, MLST and MLSD commands, REST restart in STREAM mode, an optional Trivial Virtual File Store naming scheme, and UTF-8 pathname handling.

FTP.why: The whole document extends FTP with new commands, a modified REST, feature-line conventions and a virtual file store naming model.
FTP.quote: This document updates the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) [3].  Four new commands are added: "SIZE", "MDTM", "MLST", and "MLSD".

rejected.why: Pathnames are recommended to be UTF-8, but this is a small part of the document and UTF-8 is just the encoding used, not something it defines.
The FTP control connection uses Telnet NVT conventions, but this is only a substrate and the document does not specify Telnet.
ABNF is used only as the notation for syntax definitions.
Character handling is addressed briefly (sections 8 and 9) but mainly defers to RFC 2640. It is not the focus of the document.
The document creates two small IANA registries, but this is boilerplate-level and the document is not about IANA considerations.

RFC3660.title: Basic Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Packages
RFC3660.summary: Informational RFC defining a basic set of MGCP 1.0 packages (generic, DTMF, trunk, line, handset, RTP, announcement, script, plus new signal list, resource reservation, media format, supplementary tones and digit map extension packages) for media gateway control.

MGCP.why: The whole document specifies MGCP packages, their events, signals and local connection options, updating RFC 2705.
MGCP.quote: This document provides a basic set of Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) packages.

rejected.why: The RES package uses RSVP PATH/RESV messages for reservations, but RSVP is only the mechanism being controlled, not specified or extended.
RFC 3525 is mentioned only in the IESG note as the standards-track alternative; the document is not about it.
The fmtp local connection option is modelled on the SDP attribute, but SDP is not specified or extended here.
The R package defines events on RTP connections, but this is MGCP event reporting rather than RTP itself.
The parent topic is implied by the MGCP tag, and the document is about MGCP specifically.

RFC3661.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Return Code Usage
RFC3661.summary: Informational guidelines that categorize MGCP 1.0 (RFC 3435) return codes by expected Call Agent behavior and advise gateways and Call Agents on consistent usage.

MGCP.why: The whole document specifies how MGCP return codes should be used and categorized, so it belongs on the MGCP page.
MGCP.quote: This document provides implementation guidelines for the use of return codes in the Media Gateway Control Protocol MGCP 1.0 [1].

rejected.why: SDP is mentioned only for the rule that unrecognized attributes are ignored. It is not what the document is about.
Megaco/H.248 is a different gateway control protocol and is not discussed.
The parent topic is implied by the MGCP tag. CAS and ISUP trunks appear only as endpoint types.
RSVP is cited only as an example of a bandwidth check.

RFC3662.title: A Lower Effort Per-Domain Behavior (PDB) for Differentiated Services
RFC3662.summary: RFC 3662 defines the Lower Effort (LE) Differentiated Services per-domain behavior, which forwards traffic at lower priority than best-effort, with PHB configuration guidance, example uses and simulation results.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies a new Diffserv PDB, covering classification, PHB configuration (CS1, AF, scheduler setup) and attributes, so it belongs on the Diffserv page.
Diffserv.quote: This document proposes a differentiated services per-domain behavior (PDB) whose traffic may be "starved" (although starvation is not strictly required) in a properly functioning network.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS subject, so the parent is implied.
The document protects best-effort traffic through scheduling and queueing in the network. It does not define a transport congestion control mechanism.
WRED and RED appear only as PHB implementation variants in the simulation appendix, not as the subject of the document.
TCP flows are used only as simulation traffic.
Netnews is mentioned only as an example of traffic suited to LE.

RFC3663.title: Domain Administrative Data in Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
RFC3663.summary: Experimental RFC describing VeriSign's Referral LDAP Service, which uses LDAP directory trees and referrals between registry, registrar and registrant servers to expose domain registration (administrative) data as an alternative to Nicname/Whois, with lessons learned.

LDAP.why: The document defines DIT structures, allowed searches, access control and referral use over LDAP, and reports LDAP client and referral experience.
LDAP.quote: an experimental service using LDAP and well-known LDAP types to make domain administrative data available

domain registration.why: The service exposes registry/registrar/registrant domain data, name servers and contacts, as a directory alternative to Whois. No EPP/RDAP/WHOIS-specific tag fits as the subject itself, so the parent is used.
domain registration.quote: Domain registration data has typically been exposed to the general public via Nicname/Whois for administrative purposes.

rejected.why: Nicname/Whois is the historical service being replaced or compared against; the document does not specify or extend it, apart from a brief gateway sub-project.
Mentioned only in the historical background as a prior attempt; not specified or extended here.
Mentioned for history and naming guidelines (RFC 1617) but the service is LDAP-based, not X.500.
DNS hierarchy is mirrored in the DIT naming and SRV/NAPTR is mentioned only as an unimplemented idea.
Only noted as out of scope in Internationalization Considerations.

RFC3664.title: The AES-XCBC-PRF-128 Algorithm for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE)
RFC3664.summary: Defines AES-XCBC-PRF-128, a 128-bit pseudo-random function derived from AES-XCBC-MAC by omitting the truncation to 96 bits, for use in IKE versions 1 and 2.

AES.why: The document specifies a new AES-based pseudo-random function built from the AES-XCBC construction, so it is about an AES mode and its use.
AES.quote: The AES-XCBC-PRF-128 algorithm is identical to [AES-XCBC-MAC] except that the truncation step in section 4.3 of [AES-XCBC-MAC] is *not* performed.

IKE.why: The PRF is defined specifically for IKE, which uses it for key derivation. The motivation and title concern IKE, so IKE readers will want this RFC.
IKE.quote: it is too short to be useful as a long-lived pseudo-random (PRF) in either IKE version 1 or version 2.

rejected.why: IPsec is the surrounding context. The document only specifies a PRF for IKE, so the more specific IKE tag covers it.
The construction is an AES-based CBC-MAC, not HMAC, so HMAC is not the subject.
The PRF feeds IKE key derivation, but the document does not address key management as a subject in its own right.

RFC3665.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Basic Call Flow Examples
RFC3665.summary: A BCP of annotated SIP call flow examples (registration, proxy/redirect/ALG session setup, re-INVITE, CANCEL and failure cases) with full message details, based on RFC 3261.

SIP.why: The whole document illustrates SIP registration and session establishment with proxies, redirect servers and ALGs, and failure scenarios.
SIP.quote: This document gives examples of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) call flows.

rejected.why: SDP bodies appear in INVITE/200 messages, but only as payload in the examples. The document does not specify or analyse SDP.
HTTP Digest is used for UA authentication in the flows, but only as a mechanism SIP relies on. Nothing new is defined about it.
RTP media is only indicated as the media path and PCMU payload in the SDP. The RTP protocol is not addressed.
TLS is the transport for the registration examples only. It is a substrate here and nothing new is defined about it.
PSTN interworking call flows are explicitly in the companion RFC 3666, not this document.

RFC3666.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) Call Flows
RFC3666.summary: BCP document giving example SIP call flows with full message details for interworking with the PSTN (SIP to PSTN, PSTN to SIP, PSTN to PSTN via SIP), using ISUP, ISDN and FGB signaling through gateways, including an ENUM lookup example.

PSTN interop.why: The whole document is gateway-mediated SIP/ISUP/ISDN/FGB interworking call flows; SIP-T and RFC 3398 mapping are referenced but no child tag fits as the main subject.
PSTN interop.quote: best current practice examples of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) call flows showing interworking with the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN)

SIP.why: Every scenario shows detailed SIP messages (INVITE, 183, CANCEL, BYE, error responses) with proxy and gateway behaviour, so it is a SIP deployment/usage document.
SIP.quote: These call flows are based on the current version 2.0 of SIP in RFC 3261 [2] with SDP usage described in RFC 3264 [3].

ENUM.why: A dedicated call flow shows an ENUM query and NAPTR response used to route a call over IP bypassing the PSTN.
ENUM.quote: performs an ENUM query [9] on the E.164 number (2.2.2.2.5.5.5.2.7.9.1.e164.arpa), which returns a NAPTR record

rejected.why: The document explicitly says it does not implement the SIP-T framework and has no encapsulated ISUP examples.
SDP bodies appear in messages but only as the substrate for media setup; the document does not specify or extend SDP.
Digest is used in examples as an assumption, not the subject.
Mentioned only as an alternative to SIP URIs; not addressed in its own right.
RTP media paths are shown in diagrams only; the document is not about RTP.
ISDN Q.931 messages appear in PBX flows but no ISDN tag fits as IP access; it is part of the PSTN interworking subject.

RFC3667.title: IETF Rights in Contributions
RFC3667.summary: BCP 78 specifies the IETF's policy on rights (copyright licences, representations, required notices) that Contributors grant in IETF and RFC Editor Contributions, with rationale, updating and partly replacing Section 10 of RFC 2026.

IPR.why: The whole document defines copyright licences, warranties, and mandatory notices for Contributions, which is IETF IPR and copyright policy.
IPR.quote: This memo details the IETF policies on rights in Contributions to the IETF.

rejected.why: It is process-related and updates RFC 2026, but its subject is rights in contributions, which IPR covers more specifically.
It specifies notices in RFCs, but the document is about contributor rights, not RFC format or publication.
MIB modules are mentioned only as examples of extractable code and abbreviated notices.

RFC3668.title: Intellectual Property Rights in IETF Technology
RFC3668.summary: BCP 79 defines IETF policy on intellectual property rights (patents etc.) in IETF technology: disclosure obligations, timing, licensing assurances, notices in RFCs, and how working groups evaluate technologies with IPR claims.

IPR.why: The whole document specifies IPR disclosure, licensing assurance and notice rules for IETF Contributions, which is the IPR subject.
IPR.quote: This memo details the IETF policies concerning IPR related to technology worked on within the IETF.

rejected.why: The document is IETF process-related and updates RFC 2026, but IPR is the more specific child-like subject that fits; IETF process is a sibling, not required beyond IPR.
It mandates a notice in RFCs, but that is incidental to the IPR policy, not about RFC format or publication.

RFC3669.title: Guidelines for Working Groups on Intellectual Property Issues
RFC3669.summary: Informational guidance for IETF working groups on evaluating and handling intellectual property rights claims when choosing technologies, with case studies and general principles.

IPR.why: The whole document is about how working groups should handle IPR claims, licensing terms, and third-party disclosures.
IPR.quote: This memo lays out a conceptual framework and rules of thumb to assist working groups dealing with IPR issues.

rejected.why: The document is about working group process, but IPR is the more specific child-like subject; IPR is the better fit and IETF process is not independently the focus.
One case study discusses SRP being dropped by the IPS WG over IPR, but the document is not about the protocol.
Only a case study mention of IPR claims; the protocol itself is not addressed.
SecSH trademark case study only; not about the protocol.
IDN WG patent claims appear as a case study; not about IDN technology.
PPP CCP/ECP is a case study of IPR handling, not a subject of the document.

RFC3670.title: Information Model for Describing Network Device QoS Datapath Mechanisms
RFC3670.summary: RFC 3670 defines an information model (CIM-derived classes, associations, aggregations) describing QoS datapath mechanisms in network devices: classifiers, meters, markers, droppers, queues and schedulers, for Diffserv and Intserv, to be used with QPIM for policy-based QoS management.

QoS.why: The whole document models QoS datapath mechanisms (classification, metering, marking, dropping, queuing, scheduling) across both QoS architectures. No narrower QoS tag fits.
QoS.quote: define an information model to describe the quality of service (QoS) mechanisms inherent in different network devices, including hosts.

Diffserv.why: Substantial parts of the model are Diffserv-specific: DSCP markers, AF service classes, PHB identification codes, and a mapping of the DiffServ informal management model.
Diffserv.quote: DiffServService ... A concrete class used to represent a DiffServ service associated with a particular Per Hop Behavior.

policy management.why: The model is intended as the device-mechanism half of policy-based QoS management, extending the PCIM/PCIME policy information model family. Large sections discuss the policy continuum and policy translation.
policy management.quote: This document should be used with the QoS Policy Information Model (QPIM) to model how policies can be defined to manage and configure the QoS mechanisms

rejected.why: Considered, but the document only models the datapath aspects of Intserv. It explicitly excludes admission control and RSVP signalling, and the focus is on Diffserv-style conditioning.
RSVP is mentioned only as the Intserv signalling context. It is not specified or extended here.
The RED dropper is modelled as one dropper class, but the document is not about active queue management as a subject.
The document is a protocol-independent information model. MIBs and PIBs are referenced only as possible mappings.
A directory schema mapping is only suggested as a future separate document. This document does not define one.
IPv4 and IPv6 headers appear only as fields that markers and filters act on.

gaps.name: CIM (Common Information Model) based information models
gaps.why: The classes derive from DMTF CIM and PCIM. The taxonomy has no tag for CIM or information modelling, so policy management is the closest fit.

RFC3671.title: Collective Attributes in the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
RFC3671.summary: Defines how X.500 collective attributes (shared by entry collections) are used in LDAP, giving system schema for collective attribute subentries and exclusions plus a set of collective attribute types.

LDAP.why: The document specifies LDAP schema (object class, operational attributes, collective attribute types) for collective attributes. Readers of LDAP would expect it.
LDAP.quote: This document details their use in the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) [RFC3377].

rejected.why: The document is based on the X.500 information model but specifies LDAP usage and schema. X.500 is the source model, not the subject.
Implied as the parent of LDAP, so it is not listed separately.
The IANA section only registers LDAP descriptors. That is boilerplate and not the subject.
Only the OID-based schema description formats are used. The document is not about ASN.1.

RFC3672.title: Subentries in the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
RFC3672.summary: Adapts X.501 subentries to LDAP: defines the SubtreeSpecification syntax, administrativeRole and subtreeSpecification attributes, the subentry object class, and the subentries search control.

LDAP.why: The RFC extends LDAP with subentry schema elements and a new search control, so LDAP readers would want it.
LDAP.quote: This document adapts X.500 subentries mechanisms for use with the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

rejected.why: The document borrows X.501 concepts but specifies their LDAP adaptation; X.500 is the source model, not the subject.
ASN.1 types and BER encoding are used to describe the syntax and control value, but the document is not about ASN.1.
The ABNF appendix is a non-normative convenience for the string encoding, not the subject.
The IANA considerations are boilerplate registrations of descriptors and mechanisms.

RFC3673.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol version 3 (LDAPv3): All Operational Attributes
RFC3673.summary: Defines an LDAPv3 extension in which the attribute description "+" in a Search Request asks the server to return all operational attributes, with a feature OID for discovery in the root DSE.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAP search semantics with a new mechanism for requesting all operational attributes. LDAP readers would want it.
LDAP.quote: The presence of the attribute description "+" (ASCII 43) in the list of attributes in a Search Request [RFC2251] SHALL signify a request for the return of all operational attributes.

rejected.why: X.500 is mentioned only as the origin of the all-operational-attributes mechanism. The document specifies an LDAP extension, not X.500.
The IANA section only registers the feature OID. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The more specific LDAP tag already covers this parent topic.

RFC3674.title: Feature Discovery in Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
RFC3674.summary: Defines a general LDAP feature-discovery mechanism: servers list feature OIDs in the 'supportedFeatures' root DSE attribute, with registration of features as LDAP Protocol Mechanisms.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAP with a new operational attribute (supportedFeatures) for clients to discover elective server features, so it belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: A server advertises its support for a given feature by providing the OID associated with the feature as a value of the 'supportedFeatures' attribute held in the root DSE.

rejected.why: It adds a registration usage ('Feature') to the LDAP Protocol Mechanism registry, but that is boilerplate-like IANA considerations. The main body is about discovery, not registry stewardship.
This is the parent of LDAP. The LDAP tag is more specific, so the parent is implied.
The OID syntax and the attribute definition use ASN.1-derived identifiers only incidentally. The document is not about ASN.1.
SASL is mentioned only as one of the existing discovery mechanisms. The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC3675.title: .sex Considered Dangerous
RFC3675.summary: Informational RFC arguing that mandating a special TLD (.sex, .xxx, .kids) or IP address bit to flag adult content is legally, philosophically and technically unworkable, and that third-party PICS labels are the only reasonable alternative.

DNS.why: The core technical argument concerns DNS hierarchy, TLD delegation, zones and resource records, and why name-based content labeling fails. DNS is the main subject analysed.
DNS.quote: Using special top level domain names (TLDs) multiplies the number of DNS zones the site has to worry about.

addressing.why: A substantial part examines using IPv4/IPv6 address bits or ranges for content labeling, and why address allocation is tied to routing topology.
addressing.quote: the practical constraints of hierarchical routing make the allocation of even a single IPv4 address bit or a significant number of IPv6 address bits impossible.

rejected.why: The document discusses hypothetical content-labeling TLDs, not reserved or special-use names as a technical mechanism.
Email forgery of headers is used only as an example of why name labeling is ineffective, not specified or analysed as a protocol.
HTTP 1.0/1.1 Host handling and redirects are mentioned briefly as illustrations.
Newsgroup namespaces are a brief illustration of a non-DNS name space, not the subject.
IRC channel names appear only as a short example of a non-hierarchical name space.
IPv6 addresses are discussed only as a place where label bits might be allocated; the document is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: Content labeling / filtering and PICS (Platform for Internet Content Selection)
gaps.why: Section 4.3 and the conclusions treat PICS rating labels as the viable alternative to names or addresses for content classification. The taxonomy has no tag for content rating, censorship or filtering.

gaps.name: Internet content regulation and censorship policy
gaps.why: Sections 2 and 3 cover legal, philosophical and political issues of mandating adult domains, free speech and governance. The taxonomy has no tag for content regulation policy.

RFC3676.title: The Text/Plain Format and DelSp Parameters
RFC3676.summary: RFC 3676 defines the Format=Flowed and DelSp parameters for the text/plain media type, using trailing spaces to mark soft line breaks and ">" quote marks, with space-stuffing, so flowed paragraphs interoperate with plain text mail clients.

media types.why: The document defines new parameters (Format, DelSp) for the text/plain media type and updates its registration. Readers of media type topics would want it.
media types.quote: This specification defines two MIME parameters for use with Text/Plain:

message format.why: A substantial part concerns how email body text is line-wrapped, quoted, space-stuffed and signature-separated in replies and forwards.
message format.quote: If the first character of a line is a quote mark (">"), the line is considered to be quoted

rejected.why: MIME is the framework the parameters live in; the document's specific subject is the text/plain parameters, captured by the more specific media types tag.
The more specific message format tag fits better; email is the general substrate.
Mentioned only in the digital signatures section as an interaction caveat, not the subject of the document.
ABNF is used just as notation for the grammar; the document is not about it.
Referenced for line-length limits and dot-stuffing analogy only.
The DelSp parameter addresses languages without spaces, but this is a feature of the flowed format rather than a subject of its own; only one short section addresses it.

RFC3677.title: IETF ISOC Board of Trustee Appointment Procedures
RFC3677.summary: Defines the IAB-run process by which the IETF selects, with IESG confirmation, its annual appointee to the ISOC Board of Trustees, including qualifications, timeline and mid-term vacancies.

IETF process.why: The document specifies an IETF organizational procedure (IAB selection, IESG confirmation, timeline, vacancies) for an appointment, which falls under IETF process administration.
IETF process.quote: This memo outlines the process by which the IETF makes that selection.

rejected.why: The document explains why the NomCom is deliberately not used for this appointment; it does not define NomCom procedures.
Parent of IETF process; the more specific child tag fits, so the parent is not listed.

RFC3678.title: Socket Interface Extensions for Multicast Source Filters
RFC3678.summary: Informational RFC specifying socket API options and functions (delta-based and full-state, IPv4 and protocol-independent) for applications to manage multicast source filters on group memberships.

sockets API.why: The whole document defines extensions to the sockets API: setsockopt options, setsourcefilter/getsourcefilter functions, and structures.
sockets API.quote: This document specifies new socket options and functions to manage source filters for IP Multicast group memberships.

SSM.why: It defines Source-Specific Multicast APIs (IP_ADD_SOURCE_MEMBERSHIP, MCAST_JOIN_SOURCE_GROUP) as one of two main API categories, so SSM readers would want it.
SSM.quote: Source-Specific Multicast: Only sources in a given list are allowed.  The list may change over time.

multicast.why: The API manages IP multicast group membership and source filters (any-source and include/exclude modes), tying it to multicast group membership generally.
multicast.quote: The reception of multicast packets is controlled by the setsockopt() options summarized below.

rejected.why: IGMPv3 is only the protocol the source filters are communicated through; the document defines only host APIs, not IGMP.
MLDv2 is referenced as background; the document does not specify or extend it.
The protocol-independent APIs accommodate IPv6 addresses, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC3679.title: Unused Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Option Codes
RFC3679.summary: RFC 3679 lists DHCP option codes that were assigned but never used, directing IANA to return them for reassignment, and lists several undocumented option codes (PXE, Apple) that must be kept reserved.

DHCP.why: The whole document is about the DHCP option code space: which codes are unused and reclaimable and which must remain reserved. DHCP readers need this.
DHCP.quote: This document lists those unused option codes and directs IANA to make these option codes available for assignment to other DHCP options in the future.

IANA.why: The document is an IANA registry housekeeping action: it reclaims and reserves entries in the BOOTP/DHCP parameters registry, so readers of IANA registry guidance would want it.
IANA.quote: IANA has returned the DHCP option codes listed in Section 2 to the list of available option codes.

rejected.why: The document concerns DHCP for IPv4 option codes only; DHCPv6 is not discussed.
The Service Location Protocol Naming Authority option is just one reclaimed code entry; the document does not address SLP.
UUID/GUID Client Identifier is merely a listed PXE option code, not discussed in its own right.
The LDAP Servers option is only an entry in the list of reserved codes, not about LDAP.
The IPv6 Transition option code is only a reclaimed entry in the list; the document does not address transition mechanisms.

RFC3680.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Event Package for Registrations
RFC3680.summary: Defines the SIP "reg" event package, letting subscribers get NOTIFY messages about changes in SIP registration state, with an application/reginfo+xml document format and registration/contact state machines.

SIMPLE.why: The SIMPLE tag covers SIP event packages and their XML bodies. This RFC defines the 'reg' event package, using SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, a new XML document format and registration state machines. It is also relevant to presence composition.
SIMPLE.quote: This document defines a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) event package for registrations.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP and tracks the state of SIP registrations. This is substantial, but SIMPLE is the more specific tag for the event package itself.
SIP.quote: Through its REGISTER method, SIP allows a user agent to create, modify, and delete registrations.

rejected.why: The reginfo document is XML-based, but XML is only the encoding for the notification body. The document is not about XML usage in general.
It registers application/reginfo+xml, but this is IANA boilerplate rather than the main subject.
Presence is discussed as a use case and MESSAGE appears in an example, but the document is not about instant messaging or presence formats.
It registers an XML namespace URN, which is IANA boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC3681.title: Delegation of E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA
RFC3681.summary: BCP requesting that IANA delegate the E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA reverse DNS zone to the 6bone so reverse lookups for 3ffe::/16 6bone IPv6 test addresses can be served under IP6.ARPA, with further delegation to the pTLAs.

DNS.why: The document is about delegating a reverse DNS zone (E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA) for 6bone addresses and how it is further delegated. This is DNS zone delegation and operations.
DNS.quote: This memo requests that the IANA delegate the E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA domain to the 6bone

IPv6.why: The zone serves the 6bone IPv6 testing address space (3ffe::/16), so IPv6 address allocation and deployment is a substantial part of the context.
IPv6.quote: During this remaining 6bone lifetime IP6.ARPA reverse lookup services for the 3ffe::/16 address space are required.

rejected.why: The IANA request is the mechanism, but the document is about DNS zone delegation, not about IANA registries or stewardship in general.
It concerns reverse lookups for a specific test address block, not address architecture or allocation policy. IPv6 already covers it.
IP6.ARPA subzones are ordinary reverse-mapping delegations, not special-use or reserved names.

RFC3682.title: The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM)
RFC3682.summary: Defines the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM), which sets outbound TTL/Hop Limit to 255 and drops packets from peers lacking the expected TTL to protect router control planes (BGP, MSDP, LDP, BFD) from CPU-exhaustion attacks.

routing security.why: The document specifies a mechanism for securing routing protocol sessions and router infrastructure against forged-packet attacks, a general routing-security topic not tied to one child technology.
routing security.quote: GTSM is designed to protect a router's TCP/IP based control plane from CPU-utilization based attacks.

BGP.why: BGP is the principal motivating protocol and the original use case of the TTL check, with iBGP and multi-hop peering discussed explicitly. The mechanism is generalized to other protocols, so this is secondary.
BGP.quote: The special case of iBGP peers can be protected by filtering at the network edge

rejected.why: Hop Limit is covered only as equivalent to TTL; the document is not about IPv6.
MPLS TTL handling is analysed only as a tunnelling case where the check fails; the document is not about MPLS.
IP-in-IP, GRE and MPLS tunnelling appear only as a spoofing exception in Security Considerations.
TCP/IP is only the substrate. The TCP MD5 option is mentioned in passing.
The document only says an ICMP message must not be generated for dropped packets.
LDP is only listed as one protocol that GTSM could protect.

gaps.name: TTL-based protection / GTSM
gaps.why: No tag exists for the TTL-based generalized security mechanism itself. It sits closest to routing security, but it is an IP-layer technique usable by many protocols.

RFC3683.title: A Practice for Revoking Posting Rights to IETF Mailing Lists
RFC3683.summary: BCP defining the IESG "PR-action" process for revoking an individual's posting rights to IETF mailing lists after abusive disruption of the consensus process.

IETF process.why: The document defines an IESG procedure for revoking and restoring mailing list posting rights, including last call, community discussion and appeals. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This memo recommends that the IESG also undertake a new type of action, termed a PR-action ("posting rights" action).

rejected.why: This tag covers mailing list protocols, headers and management. The document sets IETF policy on who may post, not any mailing list technology.
Unsolicited bulk email appears only as one example of abusive posting. The document is not about spam filtering.
Email is only the medium for the discussion lists. The document specifies no email technology.

RFC3684.title: Topology Dissemination Based on Reverse-Path Forwarding (TBRPF)
RFC3684.summary: RFC 3684 specifies TBRPF, an experimental proactive link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks, including its neighbor discovery (differential HELLO), topology update, association messages, and flooding mechanism.

TBRPF.why: The entire document specifies TBRPF: its packet formats, neighbor discovery, routing module and flooding.
TBRPF.quote: TBRPF is a proactive, link-state routing protocol designed for mobile ad-hoc networks (MANETs), which provides hop-by-hop routing along shortest paths to each destination.

rejected.why: Mentioned only for comparison (MPR selectors); TBRPF is a different protocol.
Used only as a comparison point for HELLO size and link-state behaviour; the document does not specify or extend OSPF.
TBRPF's own neighbor discovery (TND) is specified here, but NHDP is a separate protocol and is not discussed.
Parent of TBRPF, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Only the transport substrate for TBRPF packets (port 712); nothing new is defined about UDP.
The flooding mechanism and the use of 224.0.0.2 are mentioned, but multicast routing is not what the document is about.

RFC3685.title: SIEVE Email Filtering: Spamtest and VirusTest Extensions
RFC3685.summary: RFC 3685 defines two Sieve email filtering extensions, "spamtest" and "virustest", which give scripts portable tests against numeric spam and virus scores.

Sieve.why: The document specifies two new Sieve tests and registers them as Sieve extensions, so it belongs on the Sieve page.
Sieve.quote: The SIEVE mail filtering language "spamtest" and "virustest" extensions permit users to use simple, portable commands for spam and virus tests on email messages.

spam.why: The spamtest test, which gives a 0-10 spam score, is half of the document. Readers interested in spam filtering would want it.
spam.quote: The purpose of this document is to introduce two SIEVE tests that can be used to implement 'generic' tests for spam and viruses in messages

rejected.why: Email is the general setting, but the more specific Sieve tag covers it.

RFC3686.title: Using Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Counter Mode With IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC3686.summary: Specifies the use of AES Counter Mode (AES-CTR) with an explicit 8-octet IV as an IPsec ESP confidentiality transform, including counter block format, IKE keying/nonce conventions, transform ID, and test vectors.

AES.why: The document defines how the AES block cipher is used in counter mode, including counter block layout, key sizes, rounds and test vectors.
AES.quote: This document describes the use of AES Counter Mode (AES-CTR), with an explicit initialization vector (IV), as an IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

ESP.why: It specifies a new ESP confidentiality transform: payload layout, IV, padding, mandatory authentication, and IKE transform identifier.
ESP.quote: The ESP payload is comprised of the IV followed by the ciphertext.

rejected.why: IKE is used only for fresh keys, nonce derivation and the transform ID. The document does not specify or extend IKE itself.
The parent tag is implied by ESP. The document says it gives no IPsec overview.
HMAC-SHA-1-96 is only cited as a likely companion authentication function.
The AES tag is more specific, so the parent is implied.

RFC3687.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and X.500 Component Matching Rules
RFC3687.summary: Defines generic LDAP and X.500 component matching rules (componentFilterMatch, rdnMatch, presentMatch, allComponentsMatch, directoryComponentsMatch) that match arbitrary ASN.1-described components within directory attribute values.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAP (and X.500) with new matching rules, usable in extensible match search filters, with LDAP-style definitions and encodings.
LDAP.quote: This document defines generic matching rules that can match any user selected component parts in an attribute value of any arbitrarily complex attribute syntax.

X.500.why: The rules are defined for X.500 directories as well, with X.500-style MATCHING-RULE definitions, so X.500 readers would want this.
X.500.quote: Attribute type and matching rule definitions in this document are provided in both the X.500 [10] and LDAP [4] description formats.

ASN.1.why: Component references and equality rules are defined over all ASN.1 type constructs (SET, SEQUENCE, CHOICE, open types), and values are encoded with GSER.
ASN.1.quote: This document defines a generic way of matching user selected components in an attribute value of any arbitrarily complex attribute syntax, where that syntax is described using ASN.1 type notation.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used as notation for component reference and GSER encoding syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
Certificate Extension is used only as an example of contained-type referencing.
ComponentReference is a UTF8String, which is merely an encoding substrate.
The IANA section only registers LDAP descriptors; it is boilerplate here.

RFC3688.title: The IETF XML Registry
RFC3688.summary: Defines an IANA-maintained registry for XML namespaces, DTD public identifiers, XML schemas and RDF schemas, with URN assignment under urn:ietf:params:xml and a registration template.

XML.why: The registry exists for XML namespaces, DTD public identifiers, schemas and RDF schemas used in IETF standards. Readers of XML-related subjects would look for it.
XML.quote: an IANA maintained registry for IETF standards which use Extensible Markup Language (XML) related items such as Namespaces, Document Type Declarations (DTDs), Schemas

IANA.why: The document creates a new IANA registry. It specifies the registration procedures, the policy (First Come First Served with Specification Required) and the registration template.
IANA.quote: This document seeks to create a rather large registry for which the IANA (at the direction of the IESG) will be primarily responsible.

URN.why: The document defines a new URN sub-namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml, with its structure and assignment rules. This is new URN-namespace content, not just use of URNs.
URN.quote: a URN of the form urn:ietf:params:xml:<class>:<id> will be assigned where <class> is the type of the document being registered

rejected.why: The registry covers XML namespaces and schemas, not MIME media type registrations.
URIs are used as identifiers, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes. It is about URN assignment and registration.
SGML appears only in the reference for Formal Public Identifiers and in the discussion of PUBLIC identifiers. The document is not about SGML interchange.
The document requires that an item has been through IETF consensus before a URN is assigned. It does not define IETF process.

RFC3689.title: General Requirements for Emergency Telecommunication Service (ETS)
RFC3689.summary: Informational IEPREP document listing general requirements (signaling, labels, policy separation, network functionality, and security) for Emergency Telecommunication Service, without specifying solutions.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about requirements for emergency telecommunications service, covering GETS, IEPS and the IAA system. The taxonomy has no more specific child that fits, since LoST and eCall do not apply.
emergency services.quote: This document presents a list of general requirements in support of Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS).

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned only as an example of optional signaling and in a pointer to RFC 3487. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document touches better-than-best-effort functionality and cites Assured Forwarding as a label example. It sets no QoS mechanism or architecture, so QoS is only peripheral.
RFC 2597 is cited only as an example of a related label set. The document does not address Diffserv itself.
Security requirements (authorization, integrity, confidentiality) are included, but they are a subsection of ETS requirements. They are not a general security subject.
H.460.4 is listed only as an existing emergency standard. The document does not address H.323 itself.

gaps.name: Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) / IEPS / NS/EP priority communications
gaps.why: Priority and preparedness communications for authorized emergency users is a distinct subject, separate from emergency calling by the public. The 'emergency services' tag covers it only loosely.

RFC3690.title: IP Telephony Requirements for Emergency Telecommunication Service (ETS)
RFC3690.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements for Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) in IP telephony signalling, mainly that signalling carry extensible labels mappable to PSTN emergency labels, and that gateways and proxies support best-available service. It extends RFC 3689 and gives no solutions.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about requirements for emergency telecommunications service over IP telephony, including labelling and priority handling of emergency calls. This is the best-fitting topic, because LoST and eCall are narrower technologies that do not apply.
emergency services.quote: This document presents a list of requirements in support of Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) within the context of IP telephony.

PSTN interop.why: A key requirement is mapping IP telephony signalling labels to PSTN/SS7 emergency labels at PSTN/Internet boundaries, so the document is substantially about interworking.
PSTN interop.quote: Certain requirements must be defined in order to achieve peering across hybrid networks (networks that communicate between IP and other types of networks

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned only as the subject of the related RFC 3487. This document explicitly says it is not SIP-specific.
The requirements explicitly exclude IP-layer mechanisms such as Diffserv and Intserv. Best-available service is treated at the application layer only.
Application-layer accounting is mentioned only in passing, as something the requirements must not preclude.
The document makes no reference to ISUP encapsulation. It only discusses label mapping at a general level.

gaps.name: Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) / IEPREP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for priority or preparedness communications for authorised emergency responders. 'emergency services' is the closest fit, but it is oriented toward emergency calling.

RFC3691.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) UNSELECT command
RFC3691.summary: Defines the IMAP UNSELECT command, advertised by the UNSELECT capability, which closes the selected mailbox without expunging deleted messages.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 with a new command and capability, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an UNSELECT command that can be used to close the current mailbox in an Internet Message Access Protocol - version 4 (IMAP4) session without expunging it.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the one-line formal syntax. The document is not about it.
IMAP is the more specific tag, so the parent email tag is implied and not listed separately.
The IANA section only registers the UNSELECT capability. That is boilerplate and the document's main body is not about IANA.

RFC3692.title: Assigning Experimental and Testing Numbers Considered Useful
RFC3692.summary: BCP 82 recommends that IANA Considerations sections reserve small ranges of numbers for experimentation and testing, reserves IP protocol values 253 and 254 for that purpose, and sets rules on how products may use such numbers.

IANA.why: The document is guidance on writing IANA Considerations sections and on reserving experimental values in IANA registries. It also updates RFC 2434 and makes the IP Protocol field assignment of 253 and 254.
IANA.quote: authors should consider assigning a small range of numbers for experimentation purposes that implementers can use when testing protocol extensions or other new features.

rejected.why: The IP Protocol field is only one example registry where values 253 and 254 are reserved. The document is about registry assignment practice, not IP itself.
The document touches on IANA assignment policies such as Standards Action and IESG Approval. It is registry guidance, so IANA is the better fit.
DHCP options appear only as an illustrative example of why a test number is needed.

RFC3693.title: Geopriv Requirements
RFC3693.summary: Informational requirements document for the Geopriv Location Object and its using protocols, covering authorization, security, and privacy (privacy rules, pseudonyms, authentication) for transferring location information.

geolocation.why: The RFC specifies requirements for the Geopriv Location Object that conveys location information with privacy protection. This is the core subject of the geolocation topic.
geolocation.quote: This document focuses on the authorization, security and privacy requirements for such location-dependent services.

privacy.why: A large part of the document covers privacy rules, unlinked pseudonyms, anonymity, and identity protection for location data, which a reader of the privacy subject would want.
privacy.quote: A critical role is played by user-controlled Privacy Rules, which describe the restrictions imposed or permissions given by the "user"

rejected.why: HELD is a later protocol for acquiring location; this RFC only sets requirements for the Location Object and does not define it.
SIP is mentioned only as one example of a protocol that could carry the Location Object.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example using protocol, not as a subject of the document.
Authorization appears as a concept in the privacy rules, but the document is about location privacy, so the privacy tag covers it better.
Emergency calling appears only as an override scenario and an authentication bypass requirement, not as a main subject.

gaps.name: Geopriv Location Object / location privacy rules
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the Location Object format or for the privacy-rule-controlled disclosure of location. Geolocation covers it only broadly.

RFC3694.title: Threat Analysis of the Geopriv Protocol
RFC3694.summary: Informational threat analysis of the Geopriv location-privacy architecture, covering protocol, host-storage and usage attacks and deriving security properties and countermeasures such as rules, pseudonyms and fair information practices.

geolocation.why: The document analyses threats to Location Information and the Location Object in the Geopriv architecture. That is the geolocation privacy and conveyance subject.
geolocation.quote: The proliferation of location-based services that integrate tracking and navigation capabilities gives rise to significant privacy and security concerns.

privacy.why: Much of the document covers privacy threats such as overcollection, traffic analysis, and identity protection through short-lived identifiers and pseudonyms. It also covers fair information practices as countermeasures.
privacy.quote: Principles of fair information practices require entities that handle personal information to meet certain obligations with respect to its collection, use, maintenance and security

rejected.why: Authentication of entities is derived as a required security property, but it is one of many properties and not the main subject.
Denial of service and amplification attacks get one subsection (4.1.4). That is not enough to make the document about DDoS mitigation.
Rules control who may see what, but the document treats them as privacy countermeasures. It does not specify an authorization mechanism.
The document is a threat analysis, but the more specific privacy and geolocation tags fit better, and it is not general security guidance.

gaps.name: Geopriv (location privacy architecture)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the Geopriv location object, privacy rules or Location Server architecture. The geolocation topic covers it only partly.

RFC3695.title: Compact Forward Error Correction (FEC) Schemes
RFC3695.summary: RFC 3695 defines two Compact FEC schemes (FEC Encoding IDs 0 "Compact No-Code" and 130 "Compact FEC") with a compact 32-bit FEC Payload ID, supplementing the FEC Building Block for reliable bulk and block-stream delivery.

FEC.why: The document specifies new FEC schemes, their FEC Payload ID format and Object Transmission Information, and a no-code scheme for interoperability testing.
FEC.quote: This document describes two new Forward Error Correction (FEC) schemes corresponding to FEC Encoding IDs 0 and 130

rejected.why: The schemes are RMT building-block components and are used in reliable multicast, but the document is about FEC payload formats rather than multicast transport itself.
FECFRAME is the FEC framework for real-time and streaming media; this document supplements the RMT FEC Building Block (RFC 3452), not FECFRAME.
The document is meant for use with RMT protocol instantiations, but it does not define or extend LCT, ALC, or FLUTE.
TCP is mentioned only as an analogy for byte-stream delivery.

RFC3696.title: Application Techniques for Checking and Transformation of Names
RFC3696.summary: Informational guidance on correctly validating and transforming domain names, email addresses, and HTTP/MAILTO URLs in applications, including TLD checking, LDH rule, quoting, percent-encoding and IDN implications.

DNS.why: Core of the document is the syntax rules and validity checking of DNS names, including TLD lists, label and name length limits.
DNS.quote: The LDH rule, as updated, provides that the labels (words or strings separated by periods) that make up a domain name must consist of only

URI.why: A substantial section covers URI/URL syntax, reserved characters, percent-encoding, and HTTP and MAILTO URL checks.
URI.quote: applications that intend to check or validate URIs should normally identify the scheme name and then apply scheme-specific tests.

message format.why: A full section summarizes email address syntax, quoting and length limits from RFC 2821/2822.
message format.quote: Contemporary email addresses consist of a "local part" separated from a "domain part" (a fully-qualified domain name) by an at-sign ("@").

IDN.why: Section discusses xn-- encoded labels, punycode length effects, and why IDNA names cannot be validated with simple heuristics.
IDN.quote: The IDNA specification describes the exact process to be used to validate a name or encoded string.

rejected.why: HTTP URLs are only described for syntax checking; the protocol itself is not specified or analysed.
RFC 2821 is a reference for address syntax only; no mail transport content.
The LDH hostname rule is discussed, but only as the basis of DNS name validation, which DNS covers.
IDN is the more specific fit; broad text internationalization is not addressed.

RFC3697.title: IPv6 Flow Label Specification
RFC3697.summary: Specifies the 20-bit IPv6 Flow Label field, minimum requirements for source nodes labeling flows and nodes forwarding labeled packets, and basic requirements for flow state establishment methods.

IPv6.why: The document specifies an IPv6 header field and the host and router behaviour around it, so IPv6 readers would look for it.
IPv6.quote: The 20-bit Flow Label field in the IPv6 header [IPv6] is used by a source to label packets of a flow.

rejected.why: Section 5.2 only notes that IPsec does not cover the Flow Label and how tunnel mode interacts with it. This is a security consideration, not the subject of the document.
Flow-specific treatment and flow state establishment are explicitly out of scope. The document only sets generic requirements that let different methods co-exist.
Load spreading is mentioned only as one benefit of labeling. The document does not specify ECMP or load balancing.
RFC 1750 is cited for choosing initial label values, but the document is not about randomness requirements.

RFC3698.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Additional Matching Rules
RFC3698.summary: Defines LDAP schema descriptions for twelve additional matching rules adapted from X.500 (X.520), such as booleanMatch, caseExactMatch and wordMatch, and updates RFC 2798.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies LDAP matching rules with schema definitions, extending LDAP's schema for attribute comparison.
LDAP.quote: This document provides a collection of matching rules for use with the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

rejected.why: X.500 is only the source of the matching rules, which are adapted for LDAP. The document does not specify or operate the X.500 directory.
The IANA section only registers the LDAP descriptors. It is boilerplate and the document's main body is not about IANA.
This is the parent of LDAP, so it is implied by the LDAP tag.
Syntax OIDs and SEQUENCE types are mentioned, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding.

RFC3700.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC3700.summary: STD 1 is a July 2004 snapshot listing the IETF's Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental and BCP documents, plus pointers to RFC Editor retrieval resources.

IETF process.why: The memo exists to report the standardization status (maturity level) of protocols and BCPs under RFC 2026. Readers browsing IETF process would look for it.
IETF process.quote: snapshot of the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet

RFC series.why: It is a published index of RFCs and explains how to find, search and retrieve RFCs from the RFC Editor by web, FTP and email.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor maintains the official repository of all RFCs and indexes to them.

rejected.why: The memo cites RFC 2119 only as an entry in a list, not as its subject.
IANA appears only as a contact organization and in list entries; the memo is not about registries.
It is a dated snapshot of standards status, not a history or retrospective, even though it is now of historical interest.
It appears in the lists, as do IP, DNS, SMTP, SNMP and hundreds of other protocols. The memo does not specify or analyze any of them, so none gets its own tag.

RFC3701.title: 6bone (IPv6 Testing Address Allocation) Phaseout
RFC3701.summary: RFC 3701 sets a multi-year plan to phase out the 6bone IPv6 testbed and reclaim its 3FFE::/16 test address allocation by June 2006, obsoleting RFC 2471.

IPv6 transition.why: The 6bone was the IPv6 testbed to help transition IPv6 into the Internet; the document is about retiring it and its 3FFE::/16 addresses, so the IPv6 coexistence/transition subject fits.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document establishes a plan for a multi-year phaseout of the 6bone and its address allocation

IANA.why: The plan requires IANA to reclaim the 3FFE::/16 allocation. This is a substantive part of the plan (prefix reclamation and reallocation advice), not mere boilerplate.
IANA.quote: The IANA MUST reclaim the 3FFE::/16 prefix upon the date specified in section 2.0.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the subject of the testbed, but the document is specifically about phasing out the 6bone, which is covered by the more specific IPv6 transition tag.
The document concerns the retirement of a particular test prefix allocation, not address architecture or allocation practice in general; the IPv6 transition tag fits better.
Routing practice rules are mentioned only in references to earlier RFCs; the document does not address BGP.
The document argues the IETF Informational RFC process is appropriate for deciding the phaseout, but this is a brief justification, not the subject.

gaps.name: 6bone
gaps.why: The 6bone IPv6 testbed network has no dedicated tag. The IPv6 transition topic is the nearest fit.

RFC3702.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting Requirements for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3702.summary: Informational requirements document for the interface between SIP entities (proxies) and AAA servers, covering common, authentication, authorization and accounting requirements, with scenarios and a note on RADIUS/Diameter applicability.

SIP.why: The document specifies requirements for how SIP entities (proxies, UAs) interact with AAA servers for authentication, authorization and accounting of SIP sessions. Readers of SIP deployment topics would want it.
SIP.quote: This document provides requirements for the interface between SIP entities and AAA servers.

AAA.why: The core subject is AAA requirements (authentication, authorization, credit control, accounting records) for an application; it is a general AAA framework requirements document.
AAA.quote: The AAA working group is chartered to work on authentication, authorization, and accounting solutions for the Internet.

rejected.why: Discussed in section 1.1 only to say which requirements it could or could not meet; the document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
Mentioned as a possible candidate protocol for implementing the requirements, but the document does not define or extend it.
Digest authentication is mentioned once as a SIP mechanism the interface must accommodate; not a subject of the document.
Parent-level topic; the AAA tag covers the authentication, authorization and accounting requirements more specifically.

RFC3703.title: Policy Core Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Schema
RFC3703.summary: RFC 3703 defines the Policy Core LDAP Schema, mapping the Policy Core Information Model (RFC 3060) into LDAP object classes and attributes, with additional classes that optimize retrieval of policy data from an LDAP directory.

LDAP.why: The document is an LDAP schema specification: it defines object classes, attributes, OIDs and DIT usage for policy data stored in LDAP directories, including retrieval optimization classes.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a mapping of the Policy Core Information Model to a form that can be implemented in a directory that uses Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

rejected.why: The topic is related, but it sits under network management as a general information-model topic. The tag LDAP is more specific to this document, which is a directory schema mapping. The policy information model itself is RFC 3060.
This is the parent of LDAP, so it is implied by the LDAP tag and is not listed separately.
The document refers to X.500 and X.501 concepts such as DIT structure rules and name forms. It does not specify the X.500 directory service.
The policy repository concepts and PDP/PEP roles are mentioned, but COPS is not specified or used here.
The OID and descriptor registrations are boilerplate IANA Considerations. They do not make the document about IANA registries.

gaps.name: Policy Core Information Model / policy-based management schema
gaps.why: The document is about policy information representation (rules, conditions, actions, groups, repositories). The taxonomy has only a generic 'policy management' topic, which fits loosely, and no tag for the PCIM schema mappings.

RFC3704.title: Ingress Filtering for Multihomed Networks
RFC3704.summary: BCP 38 update describing ingress filtering mechanisms (ACLs, strict/feasible/loose RPF) to block spoofed source addresses, and how to apply them in multihomed and asymmetric-routing networks.

multihoming.why: Section 4 analyses how ingress filters break multihomed edge networks and offers solutions. Multihoming is a core subject.
multihoming.quote: examines generic issues related to ingress filtering and delves into the effects on multihoming in particular

DDoS.why: Ingress filtering against spoofed source addresses is a DDoS mitigation and traceability practice. The whole document covers its mechanisms and tradeoffs.
DDoS.quote: is designed to limit the impact of distributed denial of service attacks, by denying traffic with spoofed addresses access to the network

operational security.why: It is an operator best current practice for ISPs and edge networks, including protecting routers from spoofed management access.
operational security.quote: by deploying ingress filtering, one does not just help the Internet as a whole, but protects against several classes of threats to your own infrastructure
operational security.section: 3.2 Ingress Filtering to Protect Your Own Infrastructure

rejected.why: BGP is mentioned as the source of routes for RPF checks and for communities, but the document is not about the protocol itself.
Mentioned in one sentence as a way to automate route preference. It is not a subject of the document.
SAVI covers source address validation inside a local network. This document is about ISP and edge ingress filtering.
The document concerns packet source-address filtering, not securing routing protocols, and no routing-security tag fits better than the tags chosen.
RADIUS, TACACS and Diameter appear only as sources for generating filter lists.

gaps.name: Ingress filtering / Reverse Path Forwarding (BCP 38)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for source-address spoofing prevention or uRPF. This is the document's central subject, so readers would want a dedicated tag.

RFC3705.title: High Capacity Textual Conventions for MIB Modules Using Performance History Based on 15 Minute Intervals
RFC3705.summary: Defines a MIB module of 64-bit High Capacity textual conventions (HCPerfValidIntervals, HCPerfCurrentCount, etc.) for performance history based on 15-minute intervals, extending RFC 3593 using Counter64.

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module defining textual conventions for reuse by other MIB modules, which is exactly the MIB/SMI subject.
MIB.quote: This document presents a set of High Capacity Textual Conventions for use in MIB modules which require performance history based upon 15 minute intervals.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for MIB objects; the document defines textual conventions, not SNMP protocol behaviour.
ADSL and SHDSL MIBs are mentioned as users of the conventions, but the document is not about DSL itself.
SONET/SDH MIBs are merely cited as existing users of the 15-minute conventions.
The conventions are for storing performance history counters in MIBs, but the document does not define measurement methods or metrics; MIB is the better fit.

RFC3706.title: A Traffic-Based Method of Detecting Dead Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Peers
RFC3706.summary: Informational RFC describing Dead Peer Detection (DPD), a traffic-based method that uses IKE Notify messages (R-U-THERE/R-U-THERE-ACK) to detect dead IKE peers while minimizing message exchange.

IKE.why: The document defines an IKE extension: new ISAKMP Notify types, a vendor ID and message exchange for peer liveness detection. IKE readers would want it.
IKE.quote: This scheme, called Dead Peer Detection (DPD), relies on IKE Notify messages to query the liveliness of an IKE peer.

rejected.why: IPsec traffic is used as the liveness signal and SAs are deleted, but the document specifies an IKE mechanism. IKE is the more specific tag.
BFD is a different liveness-detection protocol for routing. It is not discussed here, and DPD is specific to IKE.

RFC3707.title: Cross Registry Internet Service Protocol (CRISP) Requirements
RFC3707.summary: Informational requirements document for CRISP, defining functional and feature requirements for a protocol providing directory-service access to domain registry (and other Internet registry) data, as a replacement for whois-style services.

domain registration.why: The document specifies requirements for domain registry and registrar directory services: lookups, searches, and information sets for domains, nameservers and contacts.
domain registration.quote: This document defines functional requirements for the directory services of domain registries and the common base requirements for extending the use of these services

WHOIS.why: The requirements are motivated by shortcomings of whois and rwhois and aim to replace legacy registration data directory services, so readers of WHOIS would want it.
WHOIS.quote: the uses of their administrative directory services have expanded from the original and traditional use of the whois [6] protocol

rejected.why: DNS is only referenced for the delegation model used to locate authoritative registry servers, not specified or extended.
RWhois is mentioned only as an example of existing protocol usage in the background, not the subject.
RPSL is mentioned only in describing Internet Routing Registries as another registry type; requirements for them are out of scope.
LDAP is mentioned only as a proposed technology in the background.
The document is about registry directory services but the domain registration tag is more specific; no LDAP/X.500 aspects.
Provisioning protocols are explicitly out of scope; only data-set alignment with them is mentioned.

gaps.name: CRISP (Cross Registry Internet Service Protocol) requirements
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the CRISP/IRIS registry directory protocol family or for protocol requirements documents on registry lookup services.

RFC3708.title: Using TCP Duplicate Selective Acknowledgement (DSACKs) and Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Duplicate Transmission Sequence Numbers (TSNs) to Detect Spurious Retransmissions
RFC3708.summary: Experimental RFC specifying conservative algorithms for TCP and SCTP senders to use DSACK and duplicate TSN notifications to detect spurious retransmissions, including a disambiguation algorithm for undoing unnecessary congestion control changes.

TCP.why: The document specifies a TCP sender algorithm using DSACK information and a SACK scoreboard to detect spurious retransmissions. TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: TCP [RFC793] and SCTP [RFC2960] provide notification of duplicate segment receipt through duplicate selective acknowledgment (DSACK) [RFC2883]

SCTP.why: The algorithm applies equally to SCTP duplicate TSN notifications, and SCTP is named in the title and abstract.
SCTP.quote: The following steps MUST be taken upon the receipt of each DSACK or duplicate TSN notification

congestion control.why: The main algorithm decides whether congestion control state can be reverted after spurious retransmissions. It is a congestion control matter at the transport level.
congestion control.quote: a conservative algorithm to disambiguate unnecessary retransmissions from loss events for the purpose of undoing unnecessary congestion control changes

rejected.why: RFC 3540 (ECN nonces) is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible mitigation. The document is not about ECN.
The document does not specify NewReno or any particular fast recovery algorithm. It only references loss recovery in passing.

gaps.name: spurious retransmission detection / loss recovery
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TCP/SCTP loss recovery or spurious retransmission detection (Eifel, F-RTO, DSACK). TCP and SCTP are the closest fit.

RFC3709.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure: Logotypes in X.509 Certificates
RFC3709.summary: RFC 3709 defines a non-critical X.509 certificate and attribute certificate extension that carries community, issuer, subject and other logotypes (image and audio) by URI and hash, for human recognition only.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 certificate extension (id-pe-logotype) and supplements the RFC 3280 profile. Readers of X.509 certificate profiles and extensions need it.
X.509.quote: This document specifies a certificate extension for including logotypes in public key certificates and attribute certificates.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation for the extension syntax and the module in the appendix. The document is not about ASN.1.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already covers the PKI context.
The document only uses MIME types (image/jpeg, image/gif, audio/mpeg) to label logotype files. It registers nothing.
HTTP and FTP are only used to fetch the logotype data. The document specifies nothing new about them.
MP3 is only a mandatory audio format for the optional audio logotypes. The document is not about the codec.

RFC3710.title: An IESG charter
RFC3710.summary: RFC 3710 documents the charter of the IESG: its composition, decision-making, openness, and its roles in working group management, document review, area management, staff supervision, process management and appeals.

IETF process.why: The whole document describes IESG tasks within the IETF standards process: WG creation and termination, document review, appeals and area management. This fits the IETF process topic.
IETF process.quote: The IESG charters and terminates working groups, selects their chairs, monitors their progress and coordinates efforts between them.

rejected.why: NomCom is mentioned only briefly as the selector of IESG members and is cited via BCP 10. The document is not about NomCom procedures.
The IESG's review of documents for RFC publication is described, but the document is about IESG governance, not RFC format or publication.
IANA appears only as a liaison body and in a BCP 26 reference. The document does not address IANA registries.
The IAB is mentioned for its relationship to the IESG. The document does not address architectural principles.

RFC3711.title: The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC3711.summary: RFC 3711 specifies SRTP and SRTCP, a profile of RTP providing confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection for RTP/RTCP, with default AES-based and HMAC-SHA1 transforms, key derivation and key management guidance.

SRTP.why: The document is the SRTP specification itself, covering packet formats, cryptographic contexts, processing, and SRTCP.
SRTP.quote: This document describes the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP), a profile of the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

key management.why: Substantial sections cover master/session key derivation, re-keying via MKI and <From, To>, and the parameters key management must supply.
key management.quote: This section provides guidance for key management systems that service SRTP session.

rejected.why: SRTP is a child of RTP and is the more specific tag; RTP is the base protocol that SRTP profiles, not the subject.
SRTCP is covered, but as part of SRTP; the document does not specify RTCP itself.
AES counter mode and f8 are used as the default transforms, but the document is about SRTP rather than the AES cipher.
HMAC-SHA1 is used as the default authentication transform; it is a building block, not the subject.
MIKEY is mentioned only as an example key management protocol; key management for SRTP is explicitly out of scope.
The cryptographic transforms are part of SRTP; the SRTP tag fits better.

RFC3712.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Schema for Printer Services
RFC3712.summary: Defines an LDAP v3 schema (object classes and attributes) for printers and printer services, based on IPP/1.1 directory attributes, the Printer MIB, and the SLP printer service template.

LDAP.why: The document is an LDAP schema specification, defining object classes and attribute types for LDAP directories.
LDAP.quote: This document defines several object classes to provide Lightweight Directory Access Protocol v3 [LDAP-TS] applications with flexible options in defining printer information using LDAP schema.

IPP.why: The schema is derived from IPP/1.1 Appendix E directory attributes and includes an IPP-specific auxiliary class. Printer readers would want it.
IPP.quote: This auxiliary class defines Internet Printing Protocol (IPP/1.1) [RFC2911] information.

SLP.why: The schema is aligned with the SLP service:printer: template and includes an SLP auxiliary class for interworking with SLP service discovery.
SLP.quote: This auxiliary class defines Service Location Protocol (SLPv2) [RFC2608] specific information.

rejected.why: The printerLPR class only identifies entries that support LPR. LPR is referenced, not specified or extended.
The Printer MIB is only a source for a few attribute definitions. No MIB module is defined.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations and in IPP security keyword values.
URI-valued attributes are stored as DirectoryString. The document does not specify URIs.

gaps.name: LDAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists LDAP under directory services, but I tagged it as 'LDAP' per the taxonomy; no gap. IPP is likewise under applications.

RFC3713.title: A Description of the Camellia Encryption Algorithm
RFC3713.summary: Specifies the Camellia 128-bit block cipher (128/192/256-bit keys): key schedule, Feistel data-randomizing part, F/FL functions, S-boxes, CBC object identifiers, and test vectors.

Camellia.why: The whole document is the algorithm description of Camellia: key schedule, encryption/decryption, components, OIDs and test data.
Camellia.quote: Camellia is a block cipher with 128-bit block size and 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys.

rejected.why: AES is only mentioned as having the same interface as Camellia; the document does not specify or analyse AES.
Object identifiers and a parameter type are given in ASN.1 notation, but this is minor apparatus, not the subject.
RFC 2315 (PKCS #7) is referenced only for plaintext padding with the CBC OIDs; the document is not about CMS.

RFC3714.title: IAB Concerns Regarding Congestion Control for Voice Traffic in the Internet
RFC3714.summary: IAB statement of concern that best-effort VoIP/real-time voice with a minimum sending rate needs end-to-end congestion control, analysing the drop rates at which such flows should terminate or suspend relative to TCP and recommending that IETF protocols specify such a drop rate.

congestion control.why: The whole document is about congestion control for non-adaptive/minimum-rate voice flows: congestion collapse, fairness to TCP, and when a flow must stop sending.
congestion control.quote: This document discusses IAB concerns about effective end-to-end congestion control for best-effort voice traffic in the Internet.

TFRC.why: A section examines TFRC and its packet-size variant TFRC-PS as the relevant mechanism for voice, and the document says the TFRC-PS draft must address minimum rates.
TFRC.quote: TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) is the equation-based congestion control mechanism that has been standardized in the IETF.

DCCP.why: DCCP and its CCIDs are discussed as the transport for congestion-controlled voice, and the document anticipates a new CCID for TFRC-PS.
DCCP.quote: The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport protocol being standardized in the IETF for unreliable flows

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport and its profile's congestion text is quoted, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
TCP behaviour and its response function are used as the fairness yardstick, but TCP is not what the document is about.
ECN is discussed briefly as a variation in how congestion is signalled, not as a main subject.
Explicitly excluded: the document concerns best-effort traffic and sets QoS mechanisms aside.
AMR is mentioned as an example adaptive codec, but only in passing.
RTCP loss reports appear only in a one-paragraph heuristic.

RFC3715.title: IPsec-Network Address Translation (NAT) Compatibility Requirements
RFC3715.summary: Informational RFC that catalogues known incompatibilities between NAT/NAPT and IPsec/IKE and sets requirements for any IPsec-NAT traversal solution, reviewing existing approaches (IPsec tunnel mode, RSIP, 6to4).

IPsec.why: The document analyses how AH, ESP, IKE, SPIs and SPD entries break under NAT and specifies requirements for IPsec NAT compatibility.
IPsec.quote: This document describes known incompatibilities between Network Address Translation (NAT) and IPsec, and describes the requirements for addressing them.

NAT.why: Analyses NAT/NAPT behaviours (checksums, fragments, mapping timeouts, helpers, directionality) and their effect on IPsec; NAT traversal requirements.
NAT.quote: The incompatibilities between NA(P)T and IPsec can be divided into three categories
NAT.section: 2. Known Incompatibilities between NA(P)T and IPsec

rejected.why: IKE issues (identifiers, port floating, cookies) are discussed, but as part of the broader IPsec-NAT analysis; IPsec tag covers it and the document does not specify IKE itself.
Only briefly evaluated as one existing solution in Section 4.3; not a main subject.
VPN here means telecommuter remote-access use of IPsec, not provider-provisioned VPNs.
ESP is discussed as part of IPsec behaviour under NAT, not specified or extended.
Mentioned only as a checksum/multihoming side note.
TCP/UDP checksum dependency on pseudo-header is one incompatibility among many, not the subject.

gaps.name: NAT traversal for IPsec (IPsec-NAT compatibility)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has NAT traversal only for real-time media (ICE/STUN/TURN); no tag for IPsec NAT traversal, and RSIP has no tag either.

RFC3716.title: IETF in the Large:  Administration and Execution
RFC3716.summary: IAB Advisory Committee report reviewing IETF administrative structure and relationships (Secretariat, RFC Editor, IANA, ISOC), listing stress points and requirements, and proposing formalizing the IETF as a single organizational entity.

IETF process.why: The whole document concerns IETF administration, governance and organizational structure, including funding, accountability and support functions. It explicitly excludes the standards process itself, but it remains IETF administration and procedure.
