IETF process.quote: review the existing IETF administrative structure and relationships (RFC Editor, IETF Secretariat, IANA) and to propose changes to the IETF management process or structure

RFC series.why: Appendix C is a substantial consultation with the RFC Editor covering its functions, staffing, publication process, costs and independent submissions.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor is the publisher of RFCs and is responsible for the final editorial review of the documents

IANA.why: Appendix E is a long consultation on IANA protocol parameter assignment, including IANA Considerations clarity and the RFC 2860 MoU relationship.
IANA.quote: the IETF parameter assignment function consists of accepting requests for protocol numbers for extensible protocols

rejected.why: The more specific child tags (IETF process, RFC series, IANA) fit, so the parent is not listed.
The document mentions the history of CNRI, ISI and ISOC support only briefly as background, and it is not a retrospective.
IPR notices appear only in boilerplate and in a passing mention of Secretariat duties.

gaps.name: IETF administrative support and finance (IASA precursor)
gaps.why: The document is about IETF funding, budget, contracts and the Secretariat, and the taxonomy has no specific tag for IETF administration or finance beyond the general IETF process topic.

RFC3717.title: IP over Optical Networks: A Framework
RFC3717.summary: Informational framework for IP over optical networks, covering IP-based (GMPLS-style) control plane for optical networks, service models (domain/unified), interconnection models (peer/overlay/augmented), routing, signaling, protection and restoration.

GMPLS.why: The document frames the IP-based optical control plane around GMPLS signaling and routing for lightpaths across OXCs, which is the core subject of the framework.
GMPLS.quote: The assumption in this framework is that an IP-based control plane [1] is used, such as GMPLS.

traffic engineering.why: Lightpath provisioning, constraint-based route computation, SRLG-disjoint paths and protection/restoration are substantial parts of the framework.
traffic engineering.quote: Use of stable traffic engineering control systems to engineer lightpath connections to enhance network performance

rejected.why: Mentioned as a possible IGP with optical extensions, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Section 5.2.2.1 discusses BGP for domain-specific routing, but only as one option; not the document's subject.
Referenced as a signaling protocol to be adapted, not specified or extended here.
SONET/SDH is mentioned as an optical network type, but the document is not about IP over SONET framing.
Optical VPNs are mentioned briefly in 4.4.1; this is not a substantial part of the document.
Too generic; GMPLS fits the optical control-plane subject better.

gaps.name: IP over optical networks / optical control plane (IPO)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for optical transport networks, OXCs, lightpaths, UNI/NNI interfaces, or WDM; the document's core subject is only partially covered by GMPLS.

RFC3718.title: A Summary of Unicode Consortium Procedures, Policies, Stability, and Public Access
RFC3718.summary: Informational memo describing the Unicode Consortium's structure, the Unicode Technical Committee's decision procedures, stability policies, coordination with ISO/IEC 10646, and public access to the character encoding process.

Unicode.why: The whole memo is about how the Unicode Standard is developed, kept stable, and made publicly accessible, including normalization stability relevant to IETF protocols. Readers of the Unicode subject page would want it.
Unicode.quote: Once published, each version of the Unicode Standard is absolutely stable and will never be changed retroactively.

rejected.why: The memo describes governance of the Unicode Consortium, not governance of the Internet or IETF standards. It is a process description of an external body, so the tag would mislead.
IDN is mentioned only as an example of a consumer of normalization stability. The document does not specify or analyse IDNA.
The memo touches on character encoding standards but deals with the consortium's procedures, not character set registration or use.
UTFs are mentioned only in passing as architectural changes coordinated with ISO.
It describes Unicode's processes, not the IETF's.

gaps.name: Unicode Consortium procedures and policies (standards body liaison)
gaps.why: The taxonomy's closest tag is Unicode, which is defined as usage in Internet protocols. A tag for external standards bodies and their processes (Unicode, ISO, W3C) would fit this memo better.

RFC3719.title: Recommendations for Interoperable Networks using Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS)
RFC3719.summary: Informational RFC documenting differences between the IS-IS protocol as specified in ISO 10589 and as deployed, with interoperability recommendations on timers, constants, LSP buffer sizes, hello padding, checksums, CSNPs and the overload bit.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies recommended deployed behaviour of IS-IS, covering MaxAge, hold multiplier, ID length, LSP buffer sizes, padding, CSNPs and overload.
IS-IS.quote: This document addresses differences between the protocol described in ISO 10589 and the protocol that can be observed on the wire today.

rejected.why: IS-IS is defined over CLNP/ISO 8473, but the document is about IS-IS behaviour, not OSI network-layer coexistence.
The IS-IS MIB is cited only for notification names, not specified here.
Parent of the IS-IS tag, so it is implied and not listed separately.
DECnet Phase V is mentioned only as historical background for hold multiplier values.

RFC3720.title: Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI)
RFC3720.summary: RFC 3720 specifies iSCSI, the mapping of the SCSI protocol over TCP, covering sessions, login and negotiation, PDU formats, error recovery, naming, and authentication.

iSCSI.why: The document is the core iSCSI specification: sessions, login, PDU formats, error recovery and text keys.
iSCSI.quote: This document describes a transport protocol for Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) that works on top of TCP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport iSCSI runs over; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
IPsec is specified as a protection mechanism with iSCSI-specific requirements in Security Considerations only, not the subject of the document.
No CHAP tag exists in the taxonomy. CHAP and SRP are authentication methods used in iSCSI login, not the document's subject.
iSCSI names are designed to meet URN requirements, but the document does not define a URN namespace.
This is the parent of iSCSI, which is implied, so it is not listed separately.

RFC3721.title: Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) Naming and Discovery
RFC3721.summary: Informational companion to the iSCSI protocol RFC giving examples of iSCSI name construction (iqn. and eui. formats), aliases, discovery mechanisms (static, SendTargets, SLP/iSNS), and notes on proxies, firewalls and security identifiers.

iSCSI.why: The whole document is about iSCSI naming, aliases and target discovery, complementing the iSCSI protocol specification.
iSCSI.quote: This document provides examples of the Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI; or SCSI over TCP) name construction and discussion of discovery of iSCSI resources

rejected.why: SLP is only recommended as one zero-configuration discovery option; the document does not specify or extend it.
Discovery is a section, but it is specifically iSCSI target discovery; it is more specific under the iSCSI tag, and the sub-tag SLP is not specified here.
Reversed domain names are used only as naming authority strings; DNS itself is not the subject.
Appendix B describes SOCKS as one proxy type affecting iSCSI, but this is a minor part and SOCKS is not specified.
Firewalls and proxies are discussed only in an appendix regarding their effect on iSCSI naming and discovery.
Port redirector/NAT is mentioned briefly in an appendix only.

RFC3722.title: String Profile for Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) Names
RFC3722.summary: Defines a stringprep profile (based on nameprep) specifying character repertoire, mapping, normalization and prohibited characters for internationalized iSCSI initiator and target names.

iSCSI.why: The document specifies how iSCSI names are prepared and compared, and it says the profile MUST be used with iSCSI. Readers of iSCSI need it.
iSCSI.quote: This document describes how to prepare internationalized iSCSI names to increase the likelihood that name input and comparison work in ways that make sense

internationalization.why: It is a stringprep profile covering Unicode mapping, normalization form KC, prohibited characters and bidi checks. That is internationalized string handling.
internationalization.quote: This document specifies the valid character set for iSCSI names, along with the rules for normalizing and generating iSCSI names based on user input

rejected.why: The profile is modelled on nameprep, but it applies to iSCSI names, not to domain names.
Unicode 3.2 tables are used, but they are the input to the profile. The document is about stringprep profiling, so the internationalization tag fits better.
iSCSI names are UTF-8 strings, but the document does not specify the encoding.
PRECIS replaced stringprep. This RFC predates it and does not define a PRECIS profile.

gaps.name: stringprep profile
gaps.why: The document is a stringprep profile, and the taxonomy has no tag for stringprep. PRECIS and internationalization are the nearest tags.

RFC3723.title: Securing Block Storage Protocols over IP
RFC3723.summary: Specifies how to secure iSCSI, iFCP, FCIP and their discovery protocols (iSNS, SLPv2) using IPsec and IKE, covering threat models, mandatory transforms, IKE usage, iSCSI CHAP/SRP authentication, and performance and resource analysis.

IPsec.why: The document profiles IPsec (ESP, tunnel/transport mode, transforms, rekeying, NAT traversal) and IKE usage requirements for IP storage protocols.
IPsec.quote: This document discusses how to secure block storage and storage discovery protocols running over IP (Internet Protocol) using IPsec and IKE (Internet Key Exchange).

iSCSI.why: iSCSI security requirements, CHAP/SRP authentication, session/IPsec interaction and CRC are a major part of the document.
iSCSI.quote: iSCSI SHOULD use one of its in-band authentication mechanisms or the authentication provided by IKE

iFCP.why: iFCP security requirements and IKE/IPsec interaction are specified (Section 4).
iFCP.quote: iFCP does not have a native, in-band security mechanism. Rather, it relies upon the IPsec protocol suite

SLP.why: A full section analyses SLPv2 threats and how to secure it with IPsec.
SLP.quote: Both iSCSI and FCIP protocols use SLPv2 as a way to discover peer entities and management servers.

service discovery.why: iSNS discovery security (and SLPv2) is covered; iSNS has no tag, so the service discovery topic is used.
service discovery.quote: these discovery protocols would constitute a 'weak link' were they not secured at least as well as the protocols whose security they configure

rejected.why: SRP is only an iSCSI authentication option; the document defines well-known groups for it in an appendix but is not mainly about SRP.
TCP is the substrate for the storage protocols; it is mentioned for checksum and NAT issues only.
NAT traversal is discussed in one subsection and defers to RFC 3715.
AES modes appear as transform choices and performance data, not as the subject.
IPsec is the broader tag for this profile, and the IKE usage is part of that profile.

gaps.name: iSNS (Internet Storage Name Service)
gaps.why: A discovery and management protocol whose security is specified in Section 2.6. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

gaps.name: FCIP (Fibre Channel over TCP/IP)
gaps.why: A protocol whose security is specified here. The taxonomy has no specific tag, only the fibre channel parent under storage.

RFC3724.title: The Rise of the Middle and the Future of End-to-End: Reflections on the Evolution of the Internet Architecture
RFC3724.summary: IAB reflection on how the end-to-end principle has evolved and how pressures such as lack of trust, new service models, and third-party intermediaries affect the Internet architecture going forward.

internet architecture.why: The whole document examines the end-to-end principle, fate-sharing, and trust as architectural principles, and how the architecture should evolve.
internet architecture.quote: The end-to-end principle is the core architectural guideline of the Internet.

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6/IPv4 is discussed only as an example of end-to-end influence in one subsection, not as the subject.
RFC 3238 on OPES is cited as related IAB work; the document is not about OPES itself.
NATs are mentioned as a cause of reduced transparency, but only in passing.
Interdomain QoS appears as one example of conflict in Section 5, not a substantial topic.
Trust and authentication are discussed as architectural pressures, but the document does not address security mechanisms in their own right.
Privacy is mentioned only briefly as a concern raised by in-network services.

RFC3725.title: Best Current Practices for Third Party Call Control (3pcc) in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3725.summary: BCP describing recommended SIP call flows (Flows I-IV) for third party call control by a B2BUA controller, including early media, preconditions, error handling, and click-to-dial and mid-call announcement examples.

SIP.why: The whole document specifies how to use SIP INVITE/re-INVITE/UPDATE/PRACK flows for 3pcc, with recommendations and deployment guidance.
SIP.quote: This document discusses best current practices for the usage of SIP for third party call control.

SDP.why: A substantial part concerns offer/answer handling: black-hole 0.0.0.0 connection addresses, reordering media lines, origin version changes and no-media SDP.
SDP.quote: The controller does need to perform SDP manipulations.

rejected.why: PINT is only compared against in the click-to-dial example; the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an example of call handling policy.
PSTN gateways and phones appear in examples, but the document is about SIP call control, not PSTN interworking.
HTTP POST merely triggers the click-to-dial example.
Mentioned only as a security mechanism for authenticating INVITEs in Security Considerations.

RFC3726.title: Requirements for Signaling Protocols
RFC3726.summary: Informational NSIS working group document listing requirements, assumptions and use-case scenarios for signaling protocols across network domains, mainly for QoS resource reservation and middlebox state setup.

NSIS.why: The whole document defines requirements for the NSIS signaling protocol (Initiator, Forwarder, Responder, path-coupled signaling, state management).
NSIS.quote: This document is the product of the Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) Working Group.  It defines requirements for signaling across different network environments.

QoS.why: QoS signaling and resource reservation are the main driving use cases and examples, with many QoS scenarios in the appendix.
QoS.quote: Signaling is mainly considered for Quality of Service (Qos) such as the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP).

rejected.why: Mentioned as the existing QoS signaling protocol; the document explicitly does not analyse it or list its problems.
Mobility scenarios and handover re-establishment requirements appear, but the document is not about Mobile IP itself.
Section 5.7 lists security requirements, but only as one part of the requirements set; NSIS and QoS tags cover the subject.
Label distribution is only mentioned in the abstract as another signaling application.
Only mentioned in passing as a QoS technology in a mobility scenario.
PSTN gateway scenarios are use cases but not the subject of the document.

RFC3727.title: ASN.1 Module Definition for the LDAP and X.500 Component Matching Rules
RFC3727.summary: Collects the ASN.1 definitions of the LDAP and X.500 component matching rules (from RFC 3687) into a standalone, identified ASN.1 module so other specifications can import them.

LDAP.why: The document defines the matching rules (componentFilterMatch, allComponentsMatch, etc.) for LDAP directory attribute values. Readers of LDAP would look for it.
LDAP.quote: collecting the Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) definitions of the component matching rules into an appropriately identified ASN.1 module

X.500.why: The matching rules apply equally to X.500 directories. The module imports from X.501 InformationFramework and is shared by both.
X.500.quote: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) [LDAP] or X.500 [X500] directory is described by the attribute's syntax.

ASN.1.why: The body of the document is an ASN.1 module definition, published so that other ASN.1 modules can import it.
ASN.1.quote: ComponentMatching {iso(1) 2 36 79672281 xed(3) module(0) component-matching(4)}

rejected.why: LDAP is the more specific child tag and it fits, so the parent is not listed.
ComponentReference is a UTF8String, but this is only an incidental type choice, not a subject of the document.

RFC3728.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Lines (VDSL)
RFC3728.summary: Defines an SNMP MIB module (VDSL-LINE-MIB) for managing VDSL line interfaces, including physical, channel, performance-history, profile and notification objects, integrated with the IF-MIB.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is a new SMIv2 MIB module with tables, textual conventions, notifications and compliance groups for VDSL interfaces.
MIB.quote: This document describes an SNMP MIB module for managing VDSL Lines.

DSL.why: The managed subject is VDSL access lines (Vtuc/Vtur, band plans, PBO, PSD templates), so DSL access networks readers would want it.
DSL.quote: In particular, it describes objects used for managing Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line (VDSL) interfaces.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines a MIB module, which the more specific MIB tag covers.
The 15-minute and 1-day interval counters are part of the MIB's objects, not a performance-measurement methodology.
No YANG content; the data model is in SMIv2.

RFC3729.title: Application Performance Measurement MIB
RFC3729.summary: Defines the APM MIB, an SNMP MIB module (extending RMON) for measuring end-user application availability and responsiveness, with reports, transactions, exceptions and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (APM-MIB) defined in SMIv2, with tables, groups, compliance and notifications.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

performance measurement.why: The subject is measuring application availability and responsiveness (response time, throughput, streaming quality), aggregated into reports.
performance measurement.quote: it defines objects for measuring the application performance as experienced by end-users.

RMON.why: The module extends RMON/RMON2, building on the protocol directory and RMON-style control and data tables, so RMON readers would want it.
RMON.quote: This document continues the architecture created in the RMON MIB [7] by providing analysis of application performance as experienced by end-users.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document specifies no SNMP protocol changes. The MIB tag is the more specific fit.
The HTTP filter table measures HTTP transactions by URL, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
POP3 appears only as an example of an application with verbs, so it is not a subject.
The overview mentions quality of service delivered to users, but this is measurement, not a QoS architecture or signalling.

RFC3730.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC3730.summary: RFC 3730 specifies EPP 1.0, an XML-based stateful client-server protocol for provisioning objects (originally domain names) in a shared registry, with its commands, responses, result codes, extension framework, schemas and the application/epp+xml media type.

EPP.why: The document is the base specification of EPP: commands, responses, result codes, extension framework and schemas.
EPP.quote: an XML text protocol that permits multiple service providers to perform object provisioning operations using a shared central object repository

media types.why: Appendix B registers the application/epp+xml media type, which media-type readers would want to find.
media types.quote: EPP content is identified by MIME media type application/epp+xml.

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are the specification substrate; the document is not about XML usage in general.
Domain names are the motivating object but the base protocol defines no DNS objects or behaviour.
The EPP tag sits under it and is more specific; domain-object mappings are in separate documents.
Only requirements for future transport mappings are listed; no mapping is defined here.
PLAIN SASL is cited only as an analogy for EPP's login authentication.
IANA section only registers XML namespaces and schemas; boilerplate.

RFC3731.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Domain Name Mapping
RFC3731.summary: Specifies the EPP mapping for provisioning and managing domain name objects in a shared registry repository, defining XML commands (check, info, transfer, create, delete, renew, update), status values, and schema.

EPP.why: The document is an EPP object mapping defining command syntax, semantics, status values and the XML schema for domain objects.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Internet domain name mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP).

rejected.why: Domain delegation data (name servers, glue) is provisioned, but the document specifies registry provisioning rather than DNS protocol or resolver behaviour.
XML and XML Schema are only the encoding substrate for the mapping.
Parent of EPP, so it is implied by the EPP tag.
Mentioned only briefly in name syntax and internationalization considerations; not a subject of the document.
The IANA section only registers the XML namespace and schema, which is boilerplate.

RFC3732.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Host Mapping
RFC3732.summary: Defines the EPP mapping for provisioning and managing host name objects in a shared registry repository, including check, info, create, delete and update commands, status values, and the XML schema.

EPP.why: The RFC is an EPP object mapping defining host object commands, attributes, status values and schema for registry provisioning.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for the provisioning and management of Internet host names stored in a shared central repository.

rejected.why: Hosts may be used as name servers and glue records are mentioned, but the document is about registry provisioning, not DNS protocol.
XML and XML Schema are only the specification and encoding substrate for the mapping.
Host name syntax is merely referenced to RFC 952/1123; the document is about provisioning host objects, not naming conventions.
Implied as the parent of EPP; the more specific EPP tag is chosen.
IDNA is only mentioned in passing regarding host name syntax conformance.

RFC3733.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Contact Mapping
RFC3733.summary: Specifies the EPP object mapping for contact objects (personal/organizational identifiers) in a shared registry repository, defining attributes, commands, responses and an XML schema.

EPP.why: The document defines the EPP contact object mapping: attributes, check/info/transfer/create/delete/update commands, and schema. Readers of EPP need it.
EPP.quote: an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for the provisioning and management of individual or organizational social information identifiers (known as "contacts")

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the notation used to specify the mapping, not the subject.
Implied as the parent of EPP; the contact mapping is tagged at the more specific EPP level.
UTF-8 is used for names and addresses but only as an encoding requirement, not the subject.
Telephone numbers use an E.164-derived string format, not the tel URI scheme.
RFC 3339 is merely referenced for date-time representation.

RFC3734.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Transport Over TCP
RFC3734.summary: Specifies how an EPP session maps onto a single TCP connection, including session management, message exchange, a 32-bit length-framed data unit, and a mandatory TLS requirement.

EPP.why: The document is a transport mapping for EPP, defining session handling, message exchange and data unit framing for EPP clients and servers; EPP readers need it.
EPP.quote: This document describes how an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) session is mapped onto a single Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection.

transport mapping.why: The document is a binding of one protocol over TCP, which is what the transport mapping topic covers. EPP is under naming, not transport, so this topic tag is not implied by the EPP tag.
transport mapping.quote: Section 2.1 of the EPP core protocol specification [RFC3730] describes considerations to be addressed by protocol transport mappings.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate EPP is mapped onto. The document defines no new TCP behaviour or extension.
TLS is required for security but only used as a mechanism, with no new extension or TLS specification defined.
EPP messages are XML, but XML is only the encoding and the document does not address XML usage.

RFC3735.title: Guidelines for Extending the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC3735.summary: Informational guidelines for using EPP's extension mechanisms (protocol-level, object-level, command-response, authentication info), covering extension identification by URI/XML namespace, announcement and selection, and choosing an extension form.

EPP.why: The whole document specifies how to extend EPP: documenting, identifying, announcing and selecting extensions, and choosing among extension forms.
EPP.quote: This document presents guidelines for use of EPP's extension mechanisms to define new features and object management capabilities.

rejected.why: XML is the representation and schema language the extension model relies on. The document is about EPP extension, not XML usage in general.
Extensions are identified by URIs and XML namespaces, but this is only a mechanism used by the guidelines. It is not the subject.
EPP's original use is domain registration, but this document is generic and covers extension of any provisioning object. The EPP tag already sits under this topic.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and the document has no registry content of its own.

RFC3736.title: Stateless Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Service for IPv6
RFC3736.summary: Specifies which parts of DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) clients, servers and relay agents must implement to provide stateless DHCP service, where nodes obtain configuration such as DNS and SIP server lists without address assignment.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document profiles DHCPv6 for stateless operation, listing required messages (Information-request, Reply) and options.
DHCPv6.quote: This document explains which messages and options defined in RFC 3315 are required for stateless DHCP service.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the typical way a stateless DHCP node obtained its addresses; not the subject.
DNS server list options are carried by DHCP, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
SIP server option is only listed as an example of configuration information passed.
Parent of DHCPv6; the more specific child tag applies.

RFC3737.title: IANA Guidelines for the Registry of Remote Monitoring (RMON) MIB modules
RFC3737.summary: Defines IANA procedures for administering the OID registry under the RMON root (mib-2.rmon), lists the existing assignments, and describes how new RMON MIB modules request an OID.

RMON.why: The whole document is about the registry of RMON MIB module OID assignments, listing every RMON MIB and the rules for new ones.
RMON.quote: This document defines the procedures for IANA to administer and maintain the Object Identifier (OID) tree under the Remote Monitoring (rmon) root.

IANA.why: The document is an IANA registry guideline, transferring registry administration to IANA and setting assignment policy. It belongs on the IANA registries page.
IANA.quote: IANA is requested to maintain this registry for future assignments. New assignments can only be made via Standards Action

rejected.why: The document assigns OIDs under rmon for MIB modules, but it defines no MIB module itself. It only covers the registry of module roots, so RMON and IANA fit better.
SNMP and SMI are the background for the MIB OID tree. The document does not specify or extend SNMP.

RFC3738.title: Wave and Equation Based Rate Control (WEBRC) Building Block
RFC3738.summary: Specifies WEBRC, an experimental receiver-driven, equation-based multi-rate congestion control building block for IP multicast sessions using a base channel and wave channels, with packet header fields for congestion control information.

congestion control.why: The whole document defines a congestion control scheme (TFRC-like equation, slow start, target rate, join/leave decisions) for multicast sessions. No more specific congestion-control child tag fits, so the parent topic is used.
congestion control.quote: WEBRC is a congestion control building block that is designed to be massively scalable when used with the IP multicast network service.

reliable multicast.why: It is an RMT working group building block, and its congestion control is meant to be combined with other building blocks for reliable multicast content delivery. Readers of reliable multicast would want it.
reliable multicast.quote: This memo contains part of the definitions necessary to fully specify a Reliable Multicast Transport protocol in accordance with RFC 2357.

multicast.why: The scheme works through IP multicast group joins and leaves, and it discusses ASM versus SSM, RP placement and route assumptions.
multicast.quote: Receivers join and leave channels using the appropriate multicast join and leave messages.

rejected.why: WEBRC borrows TFRC's rate equation and loss-estimation approach, but it is a different multicast layered protocol and does not specify or extend TFRC.
LCT is only a companion building block that can carry the WEBRC congestion control information field. It is not specified here.
ALC is mentioned only as an example of a compatible protocol that could be combined with WEBRC.
SSM is discussed as an environmental consideration, but the document is not about SSM itself.
IGMP and MLD are only the mechanism used to join and leave channels.
TESLA is only suggested in Security Considerations for authenticating packets.

RFC3739.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure: Qualified Certificates Profile
RFC3739.summary: RFC 3739 profiles RFC 3280 X.509 certificates for Qualified Certificates issued to natural persons, defining subject/issuer naming conventions, subject directory attributes, biometric information and qcStatements extensions.

X.509.why: The document is an X.509 v3 certificate profile that defines naming conventions and new certificate extensions (biometricInfo, qcStatements) for qualified certificates.
X.509.quote: This document forms a certificate profile, based on RFC 3280, for identity certificates issued to natural persons.

rejected.why: ASN.1 modules are the means of defining the extensions, not the subject of the document.
X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers this profile.
HTTP/HTTPS is only mentioned as a URI scheme for the biometric sourceDataUri.
LDAP is mentioned only for DN string syntax and attribute definitions, not specified here.
The profile is about certificate content, not an authentication mechanism.

RFC3740.title: The Multicast Group Security Architecture
RFC3740.summary: Informational RFC describing the Multicast Security Reference Framework, its functional areas (data handling, group key management, policy), the Group Security Association concept, and the security services for securing large multicast groups.

multicast security.why: The whole document is the architecture for group key management and security of multicast groups, including GSAs, GCKS, and security services. The topic tag fits since it is about the architecture rather than a single protocol.
multicast security.quote: This document provides an overview and rationale of the multicast security architecture used to secure data packets of large multicast groups.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example protocol implementing group key management; the document does not specify it.
Only cited as an example instance of group key management protocols.
Only cited as an example group key management protocol.
Mentioned only as the algorithm used by another document for source authentication; not specified here.
IPsec/ESP is referenced as background and as off-the-shelf transforms, not the subject.
The document is about securing multicast groups, and explicitly is independent of multicast routing and admission control; the security child tag fits better.

RFC3741.title: Exclusive XML Canonicalization, Version 1.0
RFC3741.summary: RFC 3741 specifies Exclusive XML Canonicalization, a variant of Canonical XML that excludes ancestor namespace and xml: attribute context so XML digital signatures over subdocuments survive re-enveloping.

XML.why: The document defines an XML canonicalization (serialization) algorithm, handling namespaces, node-sets and xml: attributes. It is about XML processing and XML-based formats.
XML.quote: The goal of this specification is to establish a method for serializing the XPath node-set representation of an XML document or subset

XML signatures.why: The motivation is signatures that do not break when a signed subdocument is moved to another context. It defines algorithm identifiers and the InclusiveNamespaces parameter for XML-DSig transforms.
XML signatures.quote: Exclusive Canonicalization may be used as a Transform or CanonicalizationMethod algorithm in XML Digital Signature [XML-DSig] and XML Encryption [XML-Enc].

rejected.why: Not relevant; the document concerns XML serialization, not ASN.1 encoding rules.
Digital signatures are the use case, but the document has no key or certificate infrastructure content.
Not about JSON signing; it covers only XML signature canonicalization.

gaps.name: XML canonicalization (Exclusive C14N)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for XML canonicalization. XML and XML signatures are the nearest fits.

RFC3742.title: Limited Slow-Start for TCP with Large Congestion Windows
RFC3742.summary: Experimental RFC defining Limited Slow-Start, an optional modification to TCP's slow-start that caps congestion window growth per RTT once cwnd exceeds max_ssthresh, for connections with large congestion windows.

TCP.why: The document specifies a modification to TCP's slow-start algorithm. TCP is the protocol being extended, and TCP readers would expect to find it.
TCP.quote: This document describes an optional modification for TCP's slow-start for use with TCP connections with large congestion windows.

congestion control.why: Limited Slow-Start is a congestion control mechanism. It changes how cwnd grows during slow-start to reduce drops and queueing. No more specific congestion-control tag fits, since it is not NewReno, CUBIC or similar.
congestion control.quote: limiting the number of segments by which the congestion window is increased for one window of data during slow-start

rejected.why: The document does not modify fast recovery or fast retransmit. It only changes the slow-start window increase.
Active queue management is mentioned only in passing as insufficient to prevent the drops. The document is not about it.
ECN is not discussed. Loss is the only congestion signal considered.

RFC3743.title: Joint Engineering Team (JET) Guidelines for Internationalized Domain Names (IDN) Registration and Administration for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean
RFC3743.summary: Informational guidelines from the CJK Joint Engineering Team for registering and administering internationalized domain labels in zones, using per-language Language Variant Tables and IDL Packages to reserve and activate character variants.

IDN.why: The whole document is about administering internationalized domain names built on IDNA, Nameprep and Punycode, covering label validity and variant handling for CJK.
IDN.quote: This document defines a set of guidelines for applying restrictions of that type for Chinese, Japanese and Korean (CJK) scripts and the zones that use them

domain registration.why: It specifies registry and registrar procedures for registering, activating, deactivating, transferring and deleting labels, using IDL Packages. A reader browsing domain registration would want it.
domain registration.quote: the term "registration" refers to the process by which a potential domain name holder requests that a label be placed in the DNS

rejected.why: The DNS is only the substrate where labels are published. The document defines registration policy mechanisms, not DNS protocol or server behaviour.
Unicode code points are the basis of the variant tables, but the document is not about how Unicode is used in protocols in general. It is specific to IDN registration.
The IDN tag already covers this document's internationalization content, and IDN is the more specific fit.
RFC 3066 language tags are used to associate languages with labels, but this is incidental to the main subject.
ABNF is used only to write down the table syntax. It is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: IDN variant tables / CJK character variants
gaps.why: The document's core mechanism is the Language Variant Table for managing Chinese, Japanese and Korean character variants. The taxonomy has no tag for IDN variant handling or registration policy beyond IDN generally.

RFC3744.title: Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) Access Control Protocol
RFC3744.summary: RFC 3744 specifies WebDAV Access Control extensions: principals, privileges, ACL properties, the ACL method, and REPORTs for searching principals, so clients can read and modify access control lists on WebDAV resources.

WebDAV.why: The whole document defines the WebDAV ACL extension: the ACL method, access control properties, privileges and reports built on PROPFIND/REPORT.
WebDAV.quote: This document specifies a set of methods, headers, message bodies, properties, and reports that define Access Control extensions to the WebDAV Distributed Authoring Protocol.

authorization.why: Core subject is access control: principals, privileges, ACEs and ACL evaluation determining who may do what. WebDAV is the more specific tag, but authorization is a substantial independent theme.
authorization.quote: The goal of the WebDAV access control extensions is to provide an interoperable mechanism for handling discretionary access control for content and metadata managed by WebDAV servers.

rejected.why: Basic and Digest are only referenced; the document explicitly omits authentication discussion.
XML is the encoding for requests and responses, with a DTD appendix, but it is substrate rather than the subject.
Only mentioned as a possible alternate-URI-set value and repository backend; not specified here.
WebDAV builds on HTTP but the document does not extend HTTP semantics in general beyond WebDAV methods and headers.
Unrelated access control language; not discussed.
NFSv4 ACL evaluation is cited only as a comparison.

RFC3745.title: MIME Type Registrations for JPEG 2000 (ISO/IEC 15444)
RFC3745.summary: Registers the MIME media types image/jp2, image/jpx, video/mj2 and image/jpm for the JPEG 2000 (ISO/IEC 15444) family of image and motion file formats.

media types.why: The document exists to register four media type templates with IANA, giving their parameters, magic numbers, extensions and contacts. It belongs on the media type registrations page.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME [MIME1] sub- types image/jp2, video/mj2, image/jpx, and image/jpm.

rejected.why: MIME is the framework in which the types are registered. The document does not specify body structure or encodings beyond the registration templates, so the more specific media types tag is the fit.
JPEG 2000 is described as background, but the codec and file formats are defined in ISO specifications. The document only registers their media types.
This tag covers lossless data compression formats. JPEG 2000 is an image codec described only as background, and the RFC does not define or profile it.
Messaging is listed among the applications that use these types, but the document is not about email.

gaps.name: JPEG 2000 / still image formats
gaps.why: The document is about image and motion file formats (JPEG 2000, Motion JPEG 2000, compound images). The taxonomy has no tag for image formats, so only the media type registration aspect can be captured.

RFC3746.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Framework
RFC3746.summary: Informational RFC defining the ForCES architectural framework: control elements, forwarding elements, managers, reference points, operational phases, applicability to RFC 1812 routers, and security recommendations.

ForCES.why: The whole document is the ForCES architecture framework: CE/FE entities, reference points, and association phases.
ForCES.quote: This document defines the architectural framework for the ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation) network elements, and identifies the associated entities and their interactions.

rejected.why: Section 8.2.1 only outlines how TLS could secure the Fp interface. It is a security substrate and is not specified or extended here.
Section 8.2.2 recommends IPsec/ESP and IKE for securing ForCES. That is a substrate recommendation, not the subject of the document.
AgentX appears only as a suggestion for managing FEs as subagents under a CE master agent, in one short paragraph.
The document is about separating router control and forwarding planes, but the ForCES tag already covers that. It does not address routing architecture or scalability in general.
RFC 1812 applicability is discussed, but only as a requirement to be mapped onto CE/FE functions, not as a subject about IPv4.

RFC3747.title: The Differentiated Services Configuration MIB
RFC3747.summary: Defines the DIFFSERV-CONFIG-MIB module, which provides configuration templates for Differentiated Services datapaths that sit above the DIFFSERV-MIB and are cloned onto interfaces when a policy is activated.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (DIFFSERV-CONFIG-MIB) with its table, objects and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a MIB module that can be used to convey management information about desired network-wide Differentiated Services based policy behavior.

Diffserv.why: The MIB configures Diffserv per-hop-behaviour traffic treatment templates (classifier, meter, mark, drop), so Diffserv readers would want it.
Diffserv.quote: provides a conceptual Application Program Interface (API) for configuration of the Differentiated Services parameters

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol the MIB is used through. The document defines a MIB module, not anything new about SNMP itself.
The Policy-based Management MIB is an optional companion and is explicitly not required. The document does not define policy information models.
Diffserv is a child of QoS, so the more specific Diffserv tag is used instead.

RFC3748.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)
RFC3748.summary: RFC 3748 specifies the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), a link-layer authentication framework supporting multiple methods, defining its packet formats, pass-through behaviour, lower-layer requirements, initial method types, IANA rules and a threat model/security-claims framework (obsoletes RFC 2284).

EAP.why: The document is the core EAP specification: packet format, Request/Response/Success/Failure, method types, and security claims for methods.
EAP.quote: This document defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), an authentication framework which supports multiple authentication methods.

PPP.why: Defines the PPP authentication configuration option and encapsulation for EAP, a substantial section for PPP readers.
PPP.quote: Exactly one EAP packet is encapsulated in the Information field of a PPP Data Link Layer frame where the protocol field indicates type hex C227 (PPP EAP).

OTP.why: Defines the EAP OTP method type (Type 5) and its use with the OTP system, plus the related GTC token card method.
OTP.quote: The EAP OTP method is intended for use with the One-Time Password system only, and MUST NOT be used to provide support for cleartext passwords.

rejected.why: RADIUS and Diameter are discussed as the backend transport for pass-through, but the document does not specify them.
Referenced as the AAA protocol carrying EAP (RFC 3579); defined elsewhere, so only a substrate here.
EAP-TLS is mentioned as an example method with fragmentation, but this document is not about TLS.
No such tag exists; 802.1X and 802.11 encapsulation is delegated to IEEE specs, so WiFi was not tagged.
MD5-Challenge is an EAP method analogous to CHAP, but the document is not about the MD5 hash algorithm.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate for registries and not the document's main subject.

RFC3749.title: Transport Layer Security Protocol Compression Methods
RFC3749.summary: RFC 3749 defines the DEFLATE compression method for TLS, restructures the TLS CompressionMethod identifier value ranges, and specifies compression history and session-resumption rules.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS by defining a new CompressionMethod value, a registry range split, and resumption rules for compression state.
TLS.quote: This document describes an additional compression method associated with a lossless data compression algorithm for use with TLS

DEFLATE.why: The sole new compression method specified is DEFLATE, and the document gives requirements for how it is used in TLS (stateful, flushing). Readers of DEFLATE usage would want it.
DEFLATE.quote: The DEFLATE compression method and encoding format is described in RFC 1951

rejected.why: A DEFLATE tag sits under it and already covers the compression subject, so the parent is implied.
The IANA section only sets up a registry for compression method identifiers. That is boilerplate here, and the main body is not about IANA process.
XML is mentioned only as motivation for compression because it is verbose.
The document cites raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951), not the zlib wrapper format.

RFC3750.title: Unmanaged Networks IPv6 Transition Scenarios
RFC3750.summary: Informational document defining IPv6 transition scenarios (cases A-D) for unmanaged home/small-office networks, analysing application classes and their connectivity, naming and security requirements.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document defines transition scenarios and requirements for IPv4 to IPv6 migration in home/small-office networks.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document defines the scenarios in which IPv6 transition mechanisms are to be used in unmanaged networks.

home networking.why: Scope is the single-subnet home/small office network with an unmanaged gateway, including topology, prefix delegation and naming needs.
home networking.quote: One specific scope is the "unmanaged networks", which typically correspond to home networks or small office networks.

rejected.why: Naming services are discussed as requirements per case, but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
NAT is part of the assumed gateway environment, not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only as one example of an automatic tunnel; it is not analysed here.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag fits better than the general IPv6 tag.
NAT-PT translation is discussed and argued against, but only briefly.
Section 4.2.1 discusses RFC 3041 privacy addresses, but this is a minor part of the document.

RFC3751.title: Omniscience Protocol Requirements
RFC3751.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing requirements for an "Omniscience Protocol" by which copyright enforcers would install invisible clients on users' computers to determine users' intent, satirizing legislative proposals to attack alleged infringers' machines.

humor.why: Dated 1 April, it is a satirical document with absurd requirements (the client must determine user intent, discern server operators' motives, and so on), so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: This memo proposes a number of requirements for a new protocol, the Omniscience Protocol, that could be used to enable such efforts.

rejected.why: The document discusses client authentication, anti-spoofing and hacking resistance only as parody requirements. It does not address security mechanisms in earnest.
FR7 mentions user privacy, but only as a satirical requirement. The document is not a privacy analysis.
OR3 asks for communication through uncooperative firewalls and NATs, but this is a single joke requirement and not a subject of the document.
GMPLS appears only in a joke reference to 'GMPLS for Worm Holes' and the document does not address it.
Peer-to-peer networks are mentioned only as the target of the legislative proposals and in a passing remark about a future P2P version of the protocol.

RFC3752.title: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) Use Cases and Deployment Scenarios
RFC3752.summary: Informational memo presenting use cases (request/response modification, response creation) and deployment scenarios (surrogate and delegate overlays, enterprise, callout servers, chaining, failure notification) for Open Pluggable Edge Services.

OPES.why: The entire document is about OPES use cases and deployment scenarios, including surrogate/delegate overlays, callout servers and chaining.
OPES.quote: The document presents examples of services in which Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) would be useful.

rejected.why: OPES services act on HTTP requests and responses, but HTTP is only the application protocol being processed; the document specifies nothing new about HTTP.
The tag covers data-plane virtualization overlays (VXLAN, Geneve, NVGRE); OPES overlays here are application-level service networks, not that.
A CDN is mentioned only in one failure-case bullet; it is not a focus of the document.
Caching proxy is mentioned only as an example of encoding/decoding at activation points.

RFC3753.title: Mobility Related Terminology
RFC3753.summary: RFC 3753 is an informational glossary defining terminology for IP mobility (access networks, mobile networks, handover types, paging, context transfer, MANET and mobility security terms), originating from the Seamoby WG.

IP mobility.why: The whole document defines mobility terms: mobile nodes, home agents, handover, macro/micro mobility, paging. IP mobility is the subject area, and no specific child (Mobile IPv4/v6, NEMO) is the sole focus.
IP mobility.quote: There is a need for common definitions of terminology in the work to be done around IP mobility.

terminology.why: The document is a glossary with an index of terms, so readers of the terminology subject would expect it.
terminology.quote: This document defines terms for mobility related terminology.

rejected.why: Mobile network terms (MR, MNN) are defined, but only briefly and defer to the NEMO WG documents. The document is not about NEMO.
Terms such as care-of address and home agent are taken from Mobile IPv6/IPv4, but the document does not specify or analyse those protocols.
Section 5 has a short list of ad-hoc terms, which is too small a part of the document to warrant a tag.
UMTS and GPRS appear only as examples in handover definitions.

RFC3754.title: IP Multicast in Differentiated Services (DS) Networks
RFC3754.summary: Informational RFC analysing problems of IP multicast in Differentiated Services domains (the Neglected Reservation Subtree problem, heterogeneous groups, any-source multicast), proposing DSCP re-marking at branching nodes to a Limited Effort PHB, with an implementation model, Linux tests and simulations.

Diffserv.why: The whole document concerns DiffServ behaviour with multicast: EF/AF PHBs, DSCP re-marking, boundary and interior node conditioning, and the Limited Effort PHB.
Diffserv.quote: This document discusses the problems of IP Multicast use in Differentiated Services (DS) networks, expanding on the discussion in RFC 2475

multicast.why: It addresses multicast tree growth, packet replication, heterogeneous groups and any-source multicast, and proposes changes to the multicast routing table (DSCP field per outgoing interface).
multicast.quote: the reduced complexity in DS nodes makes it more complex to use those "better" services together with IP Multicast

rejected.why: RSVP is discussed only as a possible signalling mechanism and its interaction with the NRS problem; it is not the subject.
PIM-SM, DVMRP and PIM-DM are only mentioned as routing protocols that graft new branches.
Diffserv is the more specific tag under QoS, so the parent is implied.
Only mentioned as a planned migration for the management daemon protocol.
Mentioned only in contrast on half-duplex reservation checking.

RFC3755.title: Legacy Resolver Compatibility for Delegation Signer (DS)
RFC3755.summary: RFC 3755 changes the DNSSEC resource record type codes and mnemonics (SIG, KEY, NXT to RRSIG, DNSKEY, NSEC) so legacy RFC 2535 resolvers are not broken by DS-aware servers' unsecure referrals, and updates the related IANA registries.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies a change to the DNSSEC resource records (RRSIG, NSEC, DNSKEY) and how resolvers must treat the old and new types, so it belongs on the DNSSEC page.
DNSSEC.quote: This document changes the type codes and mnemonics of the DNSSEC RRs (SIG, KEY, and NXT) to avoid those interactions.

rejected.why: EDNS0 DO bit and EDNS version are discussed only as rejected alternatives in Section 2, not specified or extended.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag, and the DNS parent is implied by it.

RFC3756.title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) Trust Models and Threats
RFC3756.summary: Informational document from the SEND WG defining three trust models (corporate intranet, operator-run public network, ad hoc) and cataloguing threats to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Router Discovery, to set requirements for securing ND.

SEND.why: The document is the SEND working group's trust-model and threat analysis, defining the requirements for securing IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
SEND.quote: The purpose of this document is to define the types of networks in which the Secure IPv6 Neighbor Discovery mechanisms are expected to work, and the threats that the security protocol(s) must address.

neighbor discovery.why: Analyses attacks on NS/NA, NUD, DAD, Router Advertisement and Redirect messages of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: In this section we discuss threats against the current IPv6 Neighbor Discovery mechanisms, when used in multi-access links.

rejected.why: AH and its key-management problems are discussed as the existing but impractical remedy, not specified or extended here.
Address autoconfiguration and DAD attacks are covered, but only as part of the ND threat analysis, which the neighbor discovery tag already captures.
A bogus DHCPv6 server is mentioned only as one parameter-spoofing attack variant.
Dynamic DNS update appears only as an extended consequence of a bogus prefix attack, and the document says it is not an ND security issue.
The IKE chicken-and-egg problem is mentioned only as motivation for the SEND work.

RFC3757.title: Domain Name System KEY (DNSKEY) Resource Record (RR) Secure Entry Point (SEP) Flag
RFC3757.summary: Defines the Secure Entry Point (SEP) flag bit in the DNSKEY resource record flags field, used administratively to mark keys for DS generation or static trust-anchor configuration, and not used in DNS validation.

DNSSEC.why: The document extends the DNSKEY RR with the SEP flag and gives operational guidance for KSK/ZSK, DS generation, and key rollover, all of which are DNSSEC subjects.
DNSSEC.quote: A flag bit in the DNSKEY RR is defined to indicate that DNSKEY is to be used as a SEP.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific child tag. The document does not change DNS resolution itself, and it says so explicitly.
Key rollover is discussed, but only as an operational use of the flag. The document is about a DNSKEY flag bit, not a key management mechanism.
The IANA assignment of the 15th flag bit is boilerplate. It is not the subject of the document.

RFC3758.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Partial Reliability Extension
RFC3758.summary: Defines the SCTP Partial Reliability extension (PR-SCTP): a Forward-TSN-Supported INIT/INIT-ACK parameter and the FORWARD TSN chunk, letting a sender abandon data chunks, plus a "timed reliability" service.

SCTP.why: The whole document extends SCTP with a new parameter and chunk type, plus sender and receiver procedures and a partially reliable service.
SCTP.quote: an extension to the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) that allows an SCTP endpoint to signal to its peer that it should move the cumulative ack point forward

rejected.why: The document only requires that congestion adjustments follow RFC 2960 when chunks are abandoned. It does not define congestion control itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations, advising against transport layer security (RFC 3436). That is boilerplate and not the subject.
UDP appears only as a comparison for unreliable delivery. The document does not specify or use it.
This is the parent of SCTP, which is already tagged. The parent is implied.

RFC3759.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Terminology and Channel Mapping Examples
RFC3759.summary: Informational RFC that clarifies terminology from RFC 3095 (ROHC): ROHC instances, channels, feedback channels and contexts, with examples mapping them to network elements, IP interfaces and link types, to support ROHC MIB work.

ROHC.why: The whole document defines and explains ROHC terminology (instances, channels, feedback, contexts) and how they map to link environments.
ROHC.quote: This document aims to clarify terms and concepts presented in RFC 3095. RFC 3095 defines a Proposed Standard framework with profiles for RObust Header Compression (ROHC).

rejected.why: MIB development is mentioned as motivation, but the document defines no MIB module or SMI content.
PPP is only cited as an example link over which header compression is applied.
Cellular links appear only as an example of multi-channel links.
Ethernet is mentioned only as an example of a multipoint shared channel.
RTP is only among the headers compressed by RFC 3095 profiles and is not discussed here.

RFC3760.title: Securely Available Credentials (SACRED) - Credential Server Framework
RFC3760.summary: Informational framework for SACRED client/server credential exchange protocols, defining abstract GET/PUT/DELETE operations, mutual authentication, secured credential formats and candidate transports for roaming users' credentials.

authentication.why: The framework centres on authenticating roaming users and credential servers to each other, with a dedicated section on authentication methods. It is cross-protocol, so the generic authentication topic fits.
authentication.quote: mutual authentication/key negotiation - using a strong password protocol (or equivalent) the client authenticates to the server, the server authenticates to the client

key management.why: Secure upload, storage and download of private keys and certificates (credential mobility) is credential and key provisioning and storage, which a key management reader would want.
key management.quote: This document proposes a general framework for secure exchange of such credentials

rejected.why: TLS is one of the authentication options (sTLS/cTLS), but the document defines nothing new about TLS; it is only a mechanism the framework may use.
RFC 2945 is cited as one possible strong password protocol, but the document does not specify or analyse SRP.
Strong password protocols are referenced as a class of authentication method, but the document does not specify or analyse any of them.
BEEP is listed as one candidate transport in a brief subsection; the document does not specify BEEP use.
HTTP is a candidate transport only and is not specified or extended here.
X.509 certificates and PKCS formats are credentials carried opaquely; the document is not about PKI operation.
LDAP is mentioned only as a possible protocol between server and credential store, and is explicitly out of scope.

gaps.name: credential mobility / roaming credentials (SACRED)
gaps.why: The document is about securely storing and exchanging users' private keys and certificates via a credential server. The taxonomy has no tag for credential exchange or roaming credentials, so the closest tags are only partial matches.

RFC3761.title: The E.164 to Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI) Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Application (ENUM)
RFC3761.summary: Specifies the ENUM DDDS application, which maps E.164 telephone numbers to URIs via NAPTR records under e164.arpa in the DNS, and defines the Enumservice registration procedure; obsoletes RFC 2916.

ENUM.why: The document defines ENUM itself: E.164 number to domain name conversion under e164.arpa, NAPTR service field syntax, and the Enumservice registry.
ENUM.quote: Through transformation of International Public Telecommunication Numbers in the international format [5], called within this document E.164 numbers, into DNS names

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR records are the substrate; the document's subject is the ENUM application, which is a child of DNS in the taxonomy and is already tagged.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a mitigation, not specified or profiled here.
URIs are the output of the DDDS loop, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Appears only in examples as a service type, not specified.
The Enumservice registry is a part of ENUM and is covered by the ENUM tag; the document is not about IANA registries in general.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System)
gaps.why: The document is an application of DDDS (RFC 3401-3404), with the rewrite rules, Application Unique String and flags. The taxonomy has no DDDS or NAPTR tag, and ENUM is the closest fit.

RFC3762.title: Telephone Number Mapping (ENUM) Service Registration for H.323
RFC3762.summary: Registers the E2U+H323 ENUM service (h323: URI scheme) under the RFC 3761 ENUM DDDS framework so telephone numbers can be mapped to H.323 URLs via DNS.

ENUM.why: The document's sole purpose is an ENUM enumservice registration (E2U+H323), so readers of the ENUM subject would expect it.
ENUM.quote: This document registers an ENUM service for H.323 according to specifications and guidelines in RFC 3761

H.323.why: It defines how H.323 entities use ENUM-retrieved h323 URLs and refers to H.323 Annex O procedures for locating destinations, which H.323 readers need.
H.323.quote: The H.323 related ENUM record MUST be populated with a standard H.323 URL as defined in [2].

rejected.why: DNS is only the substrate ENUM lookups run over; the document defines no new DNS record type or behaviour beyond the ENUM service registration.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a pointer to RFC 3761's threat analysis.
The h323: scheme is defined by ITU-T H.323, not by this document; it is only referenced in the template.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-like and incidental to the ENUM service definition.

RFC3763.title: One-way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) Requirements
RFC3763.summary: Informational requirements document for OWAMP, a one-way active measurement protocol (OWAMP-Control and OWAMP-Test) for measuring one-way delay and loss across Internet paths.

OWAMP.why: The whole document defines requirements for OWAMP, covering its test and control protocols, result retrieval, and security modes.
OWAMP.quote: This document specifies requirements for a one-way active measurement protocol (OWAMP) standard.

rejected.why: This is the parent of OWAMP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The document covers only the one-way protocol. TWAMP is a later two-way protocol.
DSCP and PHB ID are mentioned only as the packet types the protocol must support. The document is not about Diffserv.
NTP stratum 1 servers are cited only as a source of accurate timestamps.
UDP is named as the transport the test protocol should allow. It is a substrate, not the subject.

RFC3764.title: enumservice registration for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Addresses-of-Record
RFC3764.summary: Registers the 'E2U+SIP' ENUM enumservice for provisioning SIP/SIPS addresses-of-record in NAPTR records under telephone numbers, per RFC 3761.

ENUM.why: The document is an ENUM enumservice registration defining E2U+SIP and how NAPTR records map E.164 numbers to SIP URIs.
ENUM.quote: This document registers an Electronic Number (ENUM) service for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), pursuant to the guidelines in RFC 3761.

SIP.why: A substantial part explains SIP addresses-of-record versus contact addresses, registration and capability negotiation, to justify what belongs in ENUM.
SIP.quote: An address-of-record, however, represents an identity of the user, generally a long-term identity, and it does not have a dependency on any device

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR records are only the substrate for ENUM; the document defines nothing new about DNS itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a pointer to analysis elsewhere.
SIP/SIPS URIs are the values carried, but the document does not define or specify URI syntax or schemes.
Mentioned only as one means of SIP capability negotiation.
The IANA registration is the enumservice template itself, covered by ENUM; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

RFC3765.title: NOPEER Community for Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Route Scope Control
RFC3765.summary: Defines the NOPEER well-known transitive BGP community (0xFFFFFF04), which lets an origin AS advise that a route need not be readvertised across bilateral peer links, to limit propagation of more-specific multihoming/traffic-engineering routes.

BGP communities.why: The document specifies a new well-known BGP community and its semantics, so it belongs on the BGP communities page.
BGP communities.quote: This memo defines the use a new well-known bgp transitive community, NOPEER.

rejected.why: The more specific child, BGP communities, covers the document, so the parent is implied.
Multihoming and traffic engineering motivate the community, but the document is not about multihoming architectures.
Routing table growth is the motivation, but the document specifies a community, not architecture or scalability principles.
The community registration appears only in IANA Considerations boilerplate, which is not evidence.
Traffic engineering is mentioned as a use case; the document is not about TE of packet and transport networks.

RFC3766.title: Determining Strengths For Public Keys Used For Exchanging Symmetric Keys
RFC3766.summary: BCP guidance on choosing RSA/Diffie-Hellman public key sizes so key-exchange strength matches the symmetric key strength, with factoring-effort estimates, compute costs, and key-size equivalence tables.

cryptography.why: The whole document is about cryptographic strength and key-size selection for public-key exchange (RSA, DH, EC), not about a single named protocol. The general cryptography topic fits best.
cryptography.quote: This document explains how to determine the length of an asymmetric key as a function of a symmetric key strength requirement.

key management.why: Key exchange and deriving symmetric keys from DH output (section 4.5) is a substantial part, so key establishment readers would want it.
key management.quote: Implementors of systems that use public key cryptography to exchange symmetric keys need to make the public keys resistant to some predetermined level of attack.

rejected.why: RSA is analysed as one of two key-exchange examples, but the document is about key strength equivalence generally, not the RSA algorithm itself.
EC groups get only brief comparison paragraphs (3.1.1), not a substantial treatment.
AES is mentioned only for key-size equivalence illustration.
Randomness is a short subsection (4.6) that mainly points to RFC 1750.
RFC 2409 is cited only for group type notation and timing examples.
TripleDES is used as an illustrative symmetric cipher for brute-force cost estimates, not the subject.

RFC3767.title: Securely Available Credentials Protocol
RFC3767.summary: Specifies the SACRED protocol, an XML-based protocol (with a BEEP profile) by which a user retrieves, uploads and manages cryptographic credentials such as private keys and PKCS #15 structures on a credential server from an unconfigured workstation.

key management.why: The protocol's purpose is secure storage, download, upload and deletion of users' private keys and credentials on a server. No specific tech tag fits, so the key management topic is the best match.
key management.quote: a user can acquire cryptographic credentials (e.g., private keys, PKCS #15 structures) from a credential server

BEEP.why: Section 3 defines a BEEP profile for SACRED, including the profile URI, message exchanges and error codes. It is a substantial part of the document.
BEEP.quote: This memo also specifies a Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) profile of the protocol.

authentication.why: The document defines password-based account authentication with mutual-authentication requirements per operation, DIGEST-MD5 verifiers and account management, which is a substantial part of the protocol.
authentication.quote: the SACRED protocol is designed to give no information with which an attacker can acquire information for launching a dictionary attack

rejected.why: TLS is mandated as a security mechanism, but the document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
SASL DIGEST-MD5 is used as the client authentication mechanism, but this is only a substrate and nothing new is defined for SASL.
XML is only the payload encoding, and the schema is protocol-specific.
ds:KeyInfo is reused for the credential payload, but the document is not about XML signatures.
PKCS #15 credentials and certificates are carried, but the document does not address PKI operation.

gaps.name: SACRED (Securely Available Credentials)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for credential-server protocols or roaming credentials. The key management topic only approximates the subject.

RFC3768.title: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP)
RFC3768.summary: RFC 3768 specifies VRRP version 2, an IPv4 election protocol that lets a group of routers on a LAN share responsibility for a virtual router and fail over automatically. It obsoletes RFC 2338 and removes the authentication types.

VRRP.why: The document specifies VRRP: its packet format, state machine, Master election and operational issues.
VRRP.quote: This memo defines the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP). VRRP specifies an election protocol that dynamically assigns responsibility for a virtual router

rejected.why: HSRP is only mentioned as a similar proprietary protocol. The document does not specify or analyse it.
VRRP relies on ARP behaviour, including gratuitous ARP and proxy ARP, but the document is not about ARP itself.
Section 9.2 describes VRRP operation over token ring. It is a small part of the document, and the subject is VRRP rather than IP over token ring.
Section 9.1 covers VRRP over FDDI, but only as a brief operational note.
VRRP advertisements use a link-local multicast address, but that is only the transport. The document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
ICMP redirects are discussed only as an operational issue for VRRP, not as the subject of the document.

RFC3769.title: Requirements for IPv6 Prefix Delegation
RFC3769.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements for a mechanism by which an ISP delegates IPv6 address prefixes (e.g. /48 to /64) to a customer site's CPE, covering prefix length, policy, authentication, accounting and link independence.

IPv6.why: The whole document is about requirements for delegating IPv6 prefixes from ISP to customer site, an IPv6 addressing and deployment matter.
IPv6.quote: This document describes requirements for how IPv6 address prefixes should be delegated to an IPv6 subscriber's network (or "site").

rejected.why: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation is the likely solution, but this document never mentions DHCP; it only states mechanism-independent requirements.
Prefix delegation touches address allocation, but IPv6 is the more specific tag, and the document is IPv6-specific.
Dynamic assignment is mentioned, but the document does not address site renumbering procedures.
ADSL is mentioned only as an example of an always-on medium; the document is link-technology independent.
Authentication and accounting requirements are stated briefly, but no AAA framework is specified.

gaps.name: IPv6 prefix delegation
gaps.why: The document is specifically about prefix delegation requirements, which the taxonomy has no dedicated tag for; IPv6 is the closest fit.

RFC3770.title: Certificate Extensions and Attributes Supporting Authentication in Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) and Wireless Local Area Networks (WLAN)
RFC3770.summary: Defines two EAP extended key usage values (EAP over PPP, EAP over LAN) and a WLAN SSID list certificate extension and attribute certificate attribute to help automatically select X.509 certificates for PPP and IEEE 802.1X authentication.

X.509.why: The document defines new X.509 certificate extensions (extended key usage values, SSID extension) and an attribute certificate attribute, extending the certificate profile.
X.509.quote: This document defines two EAP extended key usage values and a public key certificate extension to carry Wireless LAN (WLAN) System Service identifiers (SSIDs).

EAP.why: The new key purposes and SSID lists exist to support certificate selection for EAP methods such as EAP-TLS over PPP and 802.1X, so EAP readers would want it.
EAP.quote: Several Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) [EAP] authentication methods employ X.509 public key certificates.

WiFi.why: A substantial part of the document addresses WLAN SSIDs in certificates for IEEE 802.11 network access.
WiFi.quote: Including a list of SSIDs in a certificate extension facilitates automated selection of an appropriate X.509 public key certificate

rejected.why: PPP is only one environment named by the EKU value; the document specifies nothing about PPP itself.
Mentioned only in passing as the usual authentication service in WLAN deployments.
ASN.1 is just the notation used to define the extensions, not the subject.
EAP-TLS is mentioned as an example consumer; the document does not specify TLS.
The more specific X.509 tag fits; the document is about certificate extensions rather than PKI generally.

RFC3771.title: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Intermediate Response Message
RFC3771.summary: Defines the LDAP IntermediateResponse message, a general mechanism for single-request/multiple-response operations used with extended operations and request controls, updating RFC 2251.

LDAP.why: The document extends the LDAP protocol with a new message type (protocolOp CHOICE addition), specifying its behavior with extended operations and controls.
LDAP.quote: This document defines and describes the LDAP IntermediateResponse message.

rejected.why: LDAP is the more specific child tag and already covers this; the parent is implied.
The ASN.1 definition of the message is just notation for the LDAP extension, not the subject.
The LDAP message type registration is boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not the main body.

RFC3772.title: Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) Vendor Protocol
RFC3772.summary: RFC 3772 defines four vendor-specific PPP protocols (VSNP, VSP, VSNCP, VSAP) with OUI-based identification, enabling proprietary network, control and authentication protocols to be negotiated and carried over PPP.

PPP.why: The document extends PPP by defining new vendor-specific protocol numbers, packet formats, LCP authentication option, and phase rules; it is a PPP extension.
PPP.quote: This document extends these features to cover vendor-specific Network, Authentication, and Control Protocols.

rejected.why: EAP is only mentioned as an example of Success/Failure code use; the document is not about it.
IANA protocol number and OUI assignments are boilerplate-level registrations here, not the subject of the document.
VSAP carries vendor authentication messages but does not specify an AAA framework.

RFC3773.title: High-Level Requirements for Internet Voice Mail
RFC3773.summary: RFC 3773 sets out high-level goals and requirements for Internet Voice Mail (IVM), an extension of VPIM v2 for interoperability among voice mail systems, unified messaging systems, email servers and desktop email clients.

VPIM.why: The whole document defines requirements for IVM, the successor profile to VPIM v2 for voice messaging over Internet mail, including backward compatibility with VPIM v2.
VPIM.quote: IVM is an extension of the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) version 2 designed to support interoperability with desktop clients.

rejected.why: MIME is the substrate for the profile. The document states requirements on body parts and content types but specifies nothing new about MIME.
SMTP is only the transport used by VPIM and IVM. The document does not specify or extend it.
Internet Fax is mentioned only as a compatibility requirement for unified messaging. It is not a subject of the document.
The document lists criteria for choosing a mandatory codec, but only briefly. It defines no codec itself, so VPIM covers it.
The document concerns voice messaging profiles. The more specific VPIM tag covers its mail interoperability aspects.

RFC3774.title: IETF Problem Statement
RFC3774.summary: RFC 3774 summarizes perceived problems in the IETF's structure, mission, engineering practices, standards hierarchy, management and working group dynamics, and distills them into root causes to guide process reform.

IETF process.why: The whole document analyses IETF processes, the standards track maturity levels, IESG workload, WG dynamics and appeals, so it belongs under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: This memo summarizes perceived problems in the structure, function, and processes of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

rejected.why: NomCom is mentioned only briefly in the discussion of concentration of influence; the document is not about NomCom procedures.
The document mentions the lack of architectural views and engineering in the large, but it is about organizational process, not Internet architecture principles.
It notes the IETF's growth since 1989 as context, but it is a problem statement, not a retrospective.

RFC3775.title: Mobility Support in IPv6
