RFC3775.summary: RFC 3775 specifies Mobile IPv6, which lets IPv6 nodes stay reachable at a home address while moving, using home agents, care-of address bindings, a return routability procedure, a Mobility Header, and Neighbor Discovery modifications.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document defines Mobile IPv6: binding updates, home agents, correspondent nodes, route optimization, the Home Address option and the type 2 routing header.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document specifies a protocol which allows nodes to remain reachable while moving around in the IPv6 Internet.

rejected.why: IPsec ESP protects home registration and tunnelled return routability traffic, but it is a security mechanism the protocol relies on, not the subject.
Section 7 modifies Router Advertisements and adds options, and proxy ND is used, but this is a supporting part of Mobile IPv6 rather than the document's focus.
Mobile IPv6 runs over IPv6, but the more specific Mobile IPv6 tag covers it.
Home agent tunnelling uses IPv6 encapsulation defined elsewhere; the document does not define a tunnelling method.
The multicast membership handling via the home agent (MLD) is a minor subsection.
The document defines new ICMP message types for home agent discovery and prefix advertisement, but these are part of Mobile IPv6 and not an ICMP specification.

RFC3776.title: Using IPsec to Protect Mobile IPv6 Signaling Between Mobile Nodes and Home Agents
RFC3776.summary: Specifies how IPsec (ESP, manual keying and IKEv1) must be used to protect Mobile IPv6 signaling and optional payload traffic between mobile nodes and home agents, with packet formats, requirements, SPD/SAD examples and processing steps.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document profiles Mobile IPv6 signaling (Binding Updates, return routability, prefix discovery) between mobile node and home agent and how it is protected.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document illustrates the use of IPsec in securing Mobile IPv6 [7] traffic between mobile nodes and home agents.

IPsec.why: Defines how IPsec ESP in transport and tunnel mode, SPD/SAD policy and processing order are applied for Mobile IPv6; a substantial IPsec profile.
IPsec.quote: Mobile IPv6 uses IPsec to protect signaling between the home agent and the mobile node.

IKE.why: Dynamic keying requirements (aggressive mode, care-of address use, phase 1 identities, endpoint movement) are a substantial part of the document.
IKE.quote: Great care is needed when using IKE [4] to establish security associations to Mobile IPv6 home agents.

rejected.why: ESP is covered under the IPsec tag; the document uses ESP rather than defining anything new about it.
IPv6 is the substrate; the document is about Mobile IPv6 specifically.
IPv6 encapsulation tunnels are used but only as the means of carrying traffic; the focus is IPsec protection.
Mentioned only in passing as a protocol needing payload protection.
Mentioned only as an example of protocols whose payload may be protected.

RFC3777.title: IAB and IESG Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Operation of the Nominating and Recall Committees
RFC3777.summary: RFC 3777 (BCP 10) specifies the process by which IAB and IESG members are selected by the Nominating Committee, confirmed, and recalled, including NomCom composition, volunteer selection, operation, dispute resolution, and recall rules.

NomCom.why: The whole document defines NomCom selection, operation, and the related recall committee procedures; this is the NomCom subject page's core content.
NomCom.quote: The process by which the members of the IAB and IESG are selected, confirmed, and recalled is specified.

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child tag and fits; the parent is implied.
No IANA registry content; only boilerplate.
Random volunteer selection is required, but the method is in RFC 2777/3797; this document does not specify randomness generation.

RFC3778.title: The application/pdf Media Type
RFC3778.summary: Informational RFC that updates the IANA registration of the application/pdf media type, giving an overview of PDF, its fragment identifiers, encryption and digital signature mechanisms, and security considerations.

media types.why: The document exists to update the application/pdf media type registration, with the registration template and security discussion. Readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document provides an overview of the PDF format, explains the mechanisms for digital signatures and encryption within PDF files, and updates the media type registration of 'application/pdf'.

URI.why: A full section defines fragment identifier syntax and parameters (page, zoom, nameddest, etc.) for URLs that point into PDF documents.
URI.quote: A fragment identifier consists of one or more PDF-open parameters in a single URL, separated by the ampersand (&) or pound (#) character.

rejected.why: PKCS#7 is used to hold PDF signatures and encryption recipients, but only as a mechanism; the document does not specify or extend CMS.
RC4 is mentioned as the default encryption algorithm in PDF, but the document is not about RC4 or its deprecation.
X.509 certificates are included in signature dictionaries, but only as a component; the document does not profile X.509.
RSA/PKCS#1 signatures are named as a SubFilter encoding, only incidentally.
PDF is exchanged over the web, but the document is about a document format and not web architecture.

gaps.name: PDF (Portable Document Format)
gaps.why: The document is chiefly an overview of the PDF format, including its encryption and digital signatures. The taxonomy has no document-format tag for PDF or page-description formats, so only the media type registration aspect can be tagged.

RFC3779.title: X.509 Extensions for IP Addresses and AS Identifiers
RFC3779.summary: Defines two X.509 v3 certificate extensions that bind IP address blocks and AS identifiers to a certificate subject, with encoding and path-validation rules, to convey right-to-use of Internet number resources (basis for RPKI).

X.509.why: The document specifies new X.509 certificate extensions, their ASN.1 syntax, criticality and path validation processing.
X.509.quote: This document defines two X.509 v3 certificate extensions.

RPKI.why: These extensions are the foundation of the Resource PKI, with certificates authorizing IP and AS resource holdings through the IANA/RIR/ISP hierarchy, used for validating routing information.
RPKI.quote: These certificates provide a scalable means of verifying the right-to-use for a set of IP address prefixes and AS identifiers.

rejected.why: BGP and S-BGP are only mentioned as a motivating use; the document does not specify BGP.
ASN.1/DER is the encoding vehicle for the extensions, not the subject.
IP address allocation hierarchy is context; the document is about certificate extensions representing it.
Parent of RPKI, which is already tagged and more specific.
IPv6 addresses are encoded but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC3780.title: SMIng - Next Generation Structure of Management Information
RFC3780.summary: RFC 3780 specifies the base SMIng data definition language, a protocol-independent language for modelling management information (types, classes, identities, extensions), with an ABNF grammar and a core NMRG-SMING module.

MIB.why: SMIng is a successor to SMIv2, the language for writing MIB modules. It defines the types, classes and modules for management information, and the NMRG-SMING module of derived types.
MIB.quote: SMIng is a data definition language that provides a protocol-independent representation for management information.

ABNF.why: A large part of the document is the formal ABNF grammar for the language. Extensions can also carry ABNF grammars, but this is the weaker of the two tags.
ABNF.quote: Appendix B contains the grammar of SMIng in ABNF [RFC2234] notation.

rejected.why: SNMP mappings are defined in the companion RFC 3781. This document is protocol-independent and mentions SNMP only as background.
YANG is a different data modelling language that came later. SMIng is not about it.
COPS-PR and SPPI appear only as history and as a possible future mapping.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as the basis of SMIv1/v2. SMIng deliberately moves away from it.
UTF-8 is used only in the display format and the Utf8String type. It is not the subject.

gaps.name: SMI / management data definition languages
gaps.why: The taxonomy has MIB for MIB modules and SMI, but no separate tag for a protocol-independent management data modelling language such as SMIng. MIB is the closest fit.

RFC3781.title: Next Generation Structure of Management Information (SMIng) Mappings to the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC3781.summary: Defines an SMIng language extension (the snmp statement) mapping SMIng classes, attributes and events to SNMP nodes, scalars, tables, columnar objects, notifications, groups and compliance statements, plus SNMP-specific derived types such as RowStatus.

MIB.why: The document is a data-definition mapping for SNMP MIB modules: it specifies how SMIng definitions become SNMP managed objects. It also defines derived types (RowStatus, StorageType, TestAndIncr) and compliance statements, which are SMI/MIB content.
MIB.quote: mapping of SMIng definitions of identities, classes, and their attributes and events to dedicated definitions of nodes, scalar objects, tables and columnar objects, and notifications

SNMP.why: A large part of the document covers SNMP object naming, instance identification, indexing, data type mapping to SNMP types, and row creation semantics. It is the target framework of the mapping.
SNMP.quote: The SNMP network management framework [RFC3410] is based on the concept of "managed objects".

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used for a few type definitions for new SNMP types, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal grammar of the extension. The document is not about ABNF.
YANG is a different data modelling language. SMIng is its conceptual cousin but is not discussed here.

gaps.name: SMIng (Structure of Management Information, Next Generation)
gaps.why: The document extends the SMIng data definition language, and the taxonomy has no tag for SMIng itself or for management data definition languages other than MIB/SMI.

RFC3782.title: The NewReno Modification to TCP's Fast Recovery Algorithm
RFC3782.summary: Specifies the NewReno modification to TCP's Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery algorithms (the Careful variant) for connections without SACK, advancing RFC 2582 to Standards Track.

NewReno.why: The document specifies the NewReno fast recovery algorithm, including partial acknowledgement handling, the recover variable and variants. NewReno is a tag under congestion control.
NewReno.quote: The purpose of this document is to advance NewReno TCP's  Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery algorithms in RFC 2582 from Experimental to Standards Track status.

rejected.why: NewReno is a TCP congestion/loss-recovery algorithm, and the more specific NewReno tag covers it. Tagging TCP too would be redundant.
This is the parent of NewReno, so it is implied by the NewReno tag.
The document concerns loss recovery by retransmission in TCP, not forward error correction, ARQ frameworks or network coding schemes.

RFC3783.title: Small Computer Systems Interface (SCSI) Command Ordering Considerations with iSCSI
RFC3783.summary: Informational RFC explaining the iSCSI session model's ordered command delivery guarantee, relating SCSI command ordering features (CRN, task attributes, ACA, UA interlock) to iSCSI, and giving guidance to storage system designers.

iSCSI.why: The whole document analyses iSCSI's command ordering design intent, session model, connection failure handling and reservation considerations.
iSCSI.quote: This document goes into the design considerations that led to the iSCSI session model as it is defined today, relates the SCSI command ordering features

rejected.why: iSCSI runs over TCP, but TCP is only the substrate; the document doesn't specify or extend it.
Parent of iSCSI, implied by the iSCSI tag, so not listed separately.
The iSCSI CRC digest is mentioned only in passing as an error example.

gaps.name: SCSI architecture and command ordering (SAM-2, ACA, UA interlock)
gaps.why: The document covers SCSI-layer ordering features in depth, but the taxonomy has no SCSI tag. iSCSI is the closest fit.

RFC3784.title: Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Extensions for Traffic Engineering (TE)
RFC3784.summary: Defines IS-IS TLV extensions (extended IS reachability with TE sub-TLVs, extended IP reachability, TE router ID) to carry traffic engineering information and wider metrics in LSPs.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs (types 22, 134, 135), extending the protocol itself.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes extensions to the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol to support Traffic Engineering (TE).

traffic engineering.why: Sub-TLVs advertise bandwidth, administrative groups, TE default metric and router ID for TE computations, so TE readers would want this RFC.
traffic engineering.quote: The characteristics described in this document are needed for Traffic Engineering [4] (TE).

rejected.why: Mentioned only in passing for mapping OSPF and IS-IS topologies via the router ID.
Only referenced for keeping the TE router ID equal to the BGP router ID.
TE is motivated by MPLS (RFC 2702) but the document does not specify MPLS.
IANA registries are boilerplate-level here; the body is about IS-IS encoding.

RFC3785.title: Use of Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) Metric as a second MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) Metric
RFC3785.summary: BCP documenting the common practice of using the IGP metric as a second metric, alongside the TE metric, for constraint-based routing of MPLS TE tunnels, with no protocol extensions.

traffic engineering.why: The document is about choosing between the IGP metric and the TE metric for constraint-based path computation of TE tunnels, which is traffic engineering practice.
traffic engineering.quote: the existing metric of Interior Gateway Protocols (IGP) can be used as an alternative metric to the Traffic Engineering (TE) metric for Constraint Based Routing

MPLS.why: The practice applies to MPLS TE LSPs, covering head-end LSR implementation, deployment and migration for MPLS TE.
MPLS.quote: Constraint Based Routing of MultiProtocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering tunnels

rejected.why: OSPF TE extensions are only the existing mechanism that advertises the metrics; nothing new is specified about OSPF.
IS-IS TE extensions are only a background mechanism; the document does not specify or change them.
RSVP-TE is cited only as a signalling protocol; the document gives no RSVP-TE specification or extension.
CR-LDP is mentioned only as a signalling protocol that is already in place.
Path computation components are mentioned only in the interoperability note, as a case where the chosen metric must be signalled.

RFC3786.title: Extending the Number of Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Link State PDU (LSP) Fragments Beyond the 256 Limit
RFC3786.summary: RFC 3786 defines a mechanism, including a new IS Alias ID TLV and two operation modes, that lets an IS-IS router originate more than 256 LSP fragments by advertising extra LSPs under Additional system-ids (virtual systems).

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol's LSP generation, purging, SPF handling and adjacency formation, and defines a new IS-IS TLV.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes a mechanism that allows a system to originate more than 256 Link State PDU (LSP) fragments, a limit set by the original Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS)

rejected.why: OSI-only routers are mentioned as a supported deployment, but the document is about IS-IS LSP fragmentation, not OSI network-layer protocols.
The IS Alias ID TLV type code appears only as a protocol definition and a pointer to the TLV code registry. The document is not about IANA registries.
The document extends one specific protocol, so the more specific IS-IS tag fits and the general topic does not.

RFC3787.title: Recommendations for Interoperable IP Networks using Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS)
RFC3787.summary: Informational RFC describing differences between IS-IS for IP as specified in RFC 1195 and as deployed (overload bit, wide metric migration, ISH, attached bit, default routes, adjacency formation), to aid interoperability.

IS-IS.why: The whole document is about IS-IS operation for IP routing and interoperability recommendations, covering overload bit, wide metrics migration, adjacency formation and default routes.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes some of the differences between the protocol as described in RFC 1195 [2] and the protocol that can be observed on the wire today.

rejected.why: BGP is mentioned only in the overload bit rationale (setting overload until BGP converges); it is not the subject.
SONET/SDH DCN adjacency requirement is mentioned briefly; the document is not about IP over SONET.
CLNS/OSI is background for ISH and homogeneity discussion, but the document focuses on IS-IS for IP, not OSI network-layer protocols.
Wide metric TLVs come from the TE extensions but the document covers metric migration, not traffic engineering.

RFC3788.title: Security Considerations for Signaling Transport (SIGTRAN) Protocols
RFC3788.summary: Specifies the minimum security mechanisms (mandatory IPsec, optional TLS) for SIGTRAN nodes carrying SS7/ISDN signalling over SCTP, including IKE/ESP requirements and a STARTTLS session upgrade procedure.

SIGTRAN.why: The whole document is about securing the SIGTRAN protocols (IUA, M2UA, M2PA, M3UA, SUA) and defines the STARTTLS message exchange for them.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document discusses how Transport Layer Security (TLS) and IPsec can be used to secure communication for SIGTRAN protocols.

IPsec.why: A substantial section profiles IPsec ESP and IKE use for SIGTRAN, and IPsec support is made mandatory.
IPsec.quote: All SIGTRAN nodes using IPsec MUST implement IPsec ESP [4] in transport mode with non-null encryption and authentication algorithms

TLS.why: Defines how TLS is used for SIGTRAN, including mutual authentication and a session upgrade procedure with new STARTTLS messages.
TLS.quote: A SIGTRAN node that initiates a SCTP association to another SIGTRAN node acts as a TLS client

rejected.why: SCTP is the transport all SIGTRAN protocols run over; the document only notes its security features and interactions, not specifying it.
IKE requirements are part of the IPsec profile; covered by the IPsec tag rather than being a separate focus.
The parent is implied by the SIGTRAN tag.
Parent of the chosen security technologies, implied by them.

RFC3789.title: Introduction to the Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3789.summary: Introduction to a v6ops survey set that catalogues IPv4 address dependencies in IETF Standards Track and Experimental RFCs, describing methodology, per-area summary statistics, and a brief discussion of address stability for protocols.

IPv4.why: The whole survey is about where IPv4 addresses are embedded in specifications, supporting IPv6 readiness; IPv4 is the subject throughout, including its address history.
IPv4.quote: document all usage of IPv4 addresses in IETF standards track and experimental RFCs

IPv6 transition.why: The survey's purpose is to identify IPv4 dependencies to support the transition to IPv6, a coexistence/transition concern.
IPv6 transition.quote: This memo examines the IPv6-readiness of specifications

rejected.why: The document states it does not discuss IPv6's merits; it only surveys IPv4 dependencies.
IPv4 tag is more specific and covers the address lifecycle discussed.
Section 1.2 comments on standards classification, but it is an observation, not the main subject.
NATs are mentioned only in the historical perspective.
The historical perspective is brief background, not the document's purpose.
BGP and CIDR appear only in the historical narrative.

RFC3790.title: Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Internet Area Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3790.summary: Informational survey of all Internet Area Standards Track and Experimental RFCs, identifying which contain IPv4 address dependencies that would need change for IPv6 transition, and noting which later RFCs fixed them.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is an IPv6-readiness audit of IPv4 dependencies in existing protocols, supporting IPv4-to-IPv6 transition.
IPv6 transition.quote: In order to successfully transition from an all IPv4 Internet to an all IPv6 Internet, many interim steps will be taken.

IPv4.why: The survey is about where IPv4 addresses are used and embedded in protocol specifications, so IPv4 address usage is substantial subject matter.
IPv4.quote: This document seeks to document all usage of IPv4 addresses in currently deployed IETF Internet Area documented standards.

rejected.why: IPv6 specs appear only as fixes or are marked 'not discussed'; the document is about IPv4 dependencies.
DNS RFCs are among many surveyed items, not a focus.
DHCP options are only a few of many entries in the survey.
ICMP is one of ~186 surveyed RFCs, not a subject of the document.
The document surveys IPv4 address dependencies rather than addressing architecture; IPv4 is the more specific tag.

RFC3791.title: Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Routing Area Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3791.summary: Informational survey of IPv4 dependencies in IETF Routing Area Standards Track and Experimental RFCs (RIP, OSPF, BGP, IS-IS, VRRP, GRE, CIDR, multicast routing), assessing IPv6 readiness and noting which have been fixed.

IPv6 transition.why: The document exists to identify IPv4 dependencies in routing protocols so they can be evolved for IPv6 and dual-stack support.
IPv6 transition.quote: In order to successfully transition from an all IPv4 Internet to an all IPv6 Internet, many interim steps will be taken.

BGP.why: A substantial part of the survey covers BGP-4 and its extensions, and how multiprotocol extensions fix the IPv4-only limitation.
BGP.quote: This RFC defines a protocol used for exchange of IPv4 routing information and does not support IPv6 as is defined.

OSPF.why: OSPFv2 and its extensions (demand circuits, NSSA, opaque LSA, multicast) are surveyed repeatedly, with OSPFv3 as the fix.
OSPF.quote: This RFC defines a protocol for IPv4 routing.  It is highly assumptive about address formats being IPv4 in nature.

RIP.why: RIPv2 and its demand-circuit extensions are assessed, with RIPng noted as the IPv6 solution.
RIP.quote: RIPv2 is only intended for IPv4 networks.

rejected.why: DVMRP, CBT and PIM-SM are surveyed only briefly for IPv4 dependence; the document is not about multicast routing itself.
Only a short entry noting IPv4-specific 32-bit addresses; a minor part of the survey.
CIDR RFCs get brief entries stating they deal with IPv4 addressing; not a focus.
IPv4 addresses are the object of the survey, but the document is about IPv6 readiness and transition rather than IPv4 itself.
One short entry noting GRE is IPv4-only; minor.

RFC3792.title: Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Security Area Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3792.summary: Informational survey of IPv4 address dependencies across Security Area Standards Track and Experimental RFCs, finding few (RADIUS, RIP-2 MD5, Mobile IPv4 challenge/response, DHCP authentication, SMKD, OSPF with digital signatures) and noting their IPv6 status.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is an IPv4-dependency survey supporting IPv4-to-IPv6 transition, assessing IPv6-readiness of each Security Area specification.
IPv6 transition.quote: In order to successfully transition from an all IPv4 Internet to an all IPv6 Internet, many interim steps will be taken.

RADIUS.why: RADIUS receives the most detailed analysis, with its IPv4-specific attributes enumerated and the IPv6 fix in RFC 3162 noted.
RADIUS.quote: NAS-IP-Address, Framed-IP-Address, Framed-IP-Netmask, Framed-Routing, Login-IP-Host, Framed-Route

IPsec.why: Many surveyed entries cover the IPsec architecture (AH, ESP, ISAKMP, IKE), judged IP-version independent.
IPsec.quote: This specification is both IPv4 and IPv6 aware.

rejected.why: The document surveys IPv4 dependencies but is not about IPv4 itself; it is a transition-readiness survey.
IPv6 is the target of the assessment, not specified or deployed here; the transition tag fits better.
RFC 2617 is one of about 124 surveyed RFCs, with only a brief nonce/IP note.
RFC 2154 (OSPF with digital signatures) is one item among many, not a main subject.
RFC 3118 is one item among many, not a main subject.
The document is about IPv4 dependencies, not about security mechanisms in general; the Security Area is just the survey scope.

RFC3793.title: Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Sub-IP Area Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3793.summary: Survey finding no IPv4 dependencies in the Sub-IP area's Proposed Standard and Experimental RFCs (MPLS architecture, label stack encoding, LDP, MPLS over frame relay/ATM, loop prevention), as part of an IPv6-readiness document set.

IPv4.why: The document's purpose is surveying IPv4 address dependencies in specs for IPv6 transition readiness; IPv4 address usage is its core subject.
IPv4.quote: This document seeks to document all usage of IPv4 addresses in currently deployed IETF Sub-IP Area documented standards.

MPLS.why: All surveyed documents are MPLS specifications (architecture, label stack encoding, LDP, ATM/frame relay, loop prevention), and each is assessed for IPv4 dependency.
MPLS.quote: RFC 3031 Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture (MPLS)

rejected.why: The survey supports transition readiness, but it does not define or analyse transition mechanisms.
LDP RFCs are only items checked in the survey, not analysed in depth; MPLS covers them.
ATM and frame relay appear only in titles of surveyed RFCs.
Only mentioned as the goal; the document examines IPv4 dependencies, not IPv6 specification or deployment.

RFC3794.title: Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Transport Area Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3794.summary: A survey of Standards Track and Experimental RFCs in the IETF Transport Area that records each IPv4 address dependency, to support the move from IPv4 to IPv6.

IPv6 transition.why: The document audits transport-area protocols for IPv4 dependencies and says what each needs in order to work over IPv6. That is IPv6 readiness and coexistence work, so it fits the transition topic.
IPv6 transition.quote: In order to successfully transition from an all IPv4 Internet to an all IPv6 Internet, many interim steps will be taken.

rejected.why: IPv4 addresses are what the survey looks for. The document does not specify or analyse IPv4 itself or its address lifecycle.
The IPv6 transition topic is the more specific fit, since the document is about readiness and migration rather than the IPv6 specification.
TCP, UDP, RSVP, SCTP, RTP and many other protocols are each covered by a short entry. None of them is the subject of the document.
NetBIOS gets the longest entry (RFC 1001/1002), but it is one item among about 100 surveyed RFCs.
Many RTP payload format RFCs are listed, each with one line saying it has no IPv4 dependency. The document is not about RTP.
The RSVP and Diffserv RFCs are surveyed in passing only.

RFC3795.title: Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Application Area Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3795.summary: A v6ops survey of IETF Application Area Full, Draft, Proposed and Experimental standards that identifies which specifications contain IPv4 address dependencies and what must change to support IPv6.

IPv6 transition.why: The document surveys IPv4 dependencies in application protocols to guide making them IPv6-capable or dual-stack, which is IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and transition.
IPv6 transition.quote: it is necessary to survey and document all IPv4 dependencies experienced by current standards (Full, Draft, and Proposed) as well as Experimental RFCs.

IPv4.why: The subject of analysis is IPv4 address usage and its embedding in application specifications, so readers of IPv4 address matters would want it.
IPv4.quote: This document describes IPv4 addressing dependencies in an attempt to clarify the necessary steps in re-designing and re-implementing specifications

rejected.why: The document analyses IPv4 dependencies and only notes needed IPv6 changes; it doesn't specify IPv6. The transition tag fits better.
FTP is one of many protocols surveyed (PORT/PASV in RFC 959); it is not the document's subject.
URL literal-address problems (RFC 1738, 2396) are discussed as one among many findings, not the focus.
RFC 1305 is analysed as one entry in a large survey; the document is not about NTP.
SLP RFCs are surveyed as individual entries, not the subject of the document.

RFC3796.title: Survey of IPv4 Addresses in Currently Deployed IETF Operations & Management Area Standards Track and Experimental Documents
RFC3796.summary: Survey of IPv4 address dependencies in IETF Operations & Management Area Standards Track and Experimental RFCs, mostly SNMP MIB modules, noting which need IPv6 updates.

MIB.why: The survey examines MIB modules and SMI definitions (IpAddress type, textual conventions) one by one for IPv4 dependence.
MIB.quote: Section 3.2.3.2.  IpAddress defines the following:

IPv6.why: The document assesses IPv6-readiness of management standards and says where new IPv6 MIB objects are needed, supporting the IPv6 transition.
IPv6.quote: In order to successfully transition from an all IPv4 Internet to an all IPv6 Internet, many interim steps will be taken.

rejected.why: SNMP is the framework the surveyed MIBs sit in, but the document surveys address types in the MIBs and does not specify SNMP.
IPv4 addresses are the object of the survey, but the document is about IPv6 transition and MIB readiness, not the IPv4 protocol.
It concerns evolving protocols for address independence, not coexistence mechanisms like tunnelling or translation.

gaps.name: IPv4 address dependency survey
gaps.why: The document is one of a series surveying IPv4 usage across IETF standards, and the taxonomy has no tag for that.

RFC3797.title: Publicly Verifiable Nominations Committee (NomCom) Random Selection
RFC3797.summary: Describes a method for making publicly verifiable random selections, using NomCom voting member selection as the example, with an algorithm based on future public randomness sources hashed with MD5, plus reference code.

NomCom.why: The document's worked example and purpose is the selection of voting NomCom members, including the history of NomCom selection methods in Appendix A. It is the IETF NomCom procedure for random selection.
NomCom.quote: each year ten people are randomly selected from among eligible volunteers to be the voting members of the IETF nominations committee (NomCom)

randomness.why: A substantial part covers sources of randomness, skew, and entropy needed, which readers of the randomness subject would want.
randomness.quote: The crux of the unbiased nature of the selection is that it is based in an exact, predetermined fashion on random information

rejected.why: MD5 is only the mixing hash used in the algorithm. The document does not specify or analyse it.
NomCom is the more specific child and already covers the process aspect.
It is mentioned only as a one-off use by IANA to pick the ACE prefix. The document is not about IDN.
SHA-1 is mentioned only as an optional stronger hash.

gaps.name: Publicly verifiable random selection
gaps.why: The core subject is a verifiable lottery-style selection method. The taxonomy has only the general randomness tag and no tag for verifiable selection.

RFC3798.title: Message Disposition Notification
RFC3798.summary: RFC 3798 defines the message/disposition-notification MIME report type and the Disposition-Notification-To, Disposition-Notification-Options and Original-Recipient headers so mail user agents can send and request read receipts (MDNs), with gatewaying guidance for foreign mail systems.

email.why: The document specifies the MDN mechanism, which extends Internet Mail with read-receipt functionality, including request headers and gatewaying to X.400 and other mail systems.
email.quote: report the disposition of a message after it has been successfully delivered to a recipient

media types.why: It defines and registers a new MIME media type, message/disposition-notification, used within multipart/report, and sets IANA registries for its fields and parameters.
media types.quote: The message/disposition-notification content-type is defined as follows:

rejected.why: It adds a few headers (Disposition-Notification-To, Original-Recipient), but the document is about the notification mechanism overall, not the base message format.
SMTP is only the transport; the ORCPT/null envelope sender usage is incidental to MDN.
MIME is the substrate; the document defines one media type under it, which the media types tag covers.
X.400 appears in gatewaying guidance only, not as a subject of the document.
Mailing list exploder behaviour is a brief conformance note, not a substantial part of the document.
The IANA registration sections are boilerplate and do not make the document about IANA.

RFC3801.title: Voice Profile for Internet Mail - version 2 (VPIMv2)
RFC3801.summary: RFC 3801 specifies VPIMv2, a restricted profile of Internet mail (SMTP/MIME) for interchanging voice and fax messages between voice messaging platforms, obsoleting RFC 2421 and defining the multipart/voice-message type and voice Content-Disposition parameter.

VPIM.why: The document defines VPIM itself: message format, addressing, headers, content types, and conformance for voice messaging interchange.
VPIM.quote: This document specifies a restricted profile of the Internet multimedia messaging protocols for use between voice processing server platforms.

MIME.why: Defines the multipart/voice-message subtype and the voice Content-Disposition parameter, and profiles MIME content types (audio, TIFF-F, message/rfc822) for voice messages.
MIME.quote: This MIME multipart structure provides a mechanism for packaging a voice message into one container that is tagged as VPIM v2 conforming.

SMTP.why: Section 5 profiles which ESMTP commands and extensions (DSN, SIZE, PIPELINING, CHUNKING, BINARYMIME) are required or optional for VPIM transport.
SMTP.quote: VPIM utilizes a number of SMTP Service Extensions to provide full-featured voice messaging service.

rejected.why: Header fields are profiled for VPIM use, but the document is not about defining the Internet message format; it is a voice-specific profile.
Fax (TIFF-F attachments) is supported as secondary content, but the document is mainly about voice messaging, not fax-over-mail.
Audio/32KADPCM is mandated as the default encoding, but the codec is defined in RFC 3802 and only referenced here.
SNMP and MIB-II management are mentioned only briefly in a short section on management.
DNS is used only as the basis of address host parts; nothing about DNS is specified.
The multipart/voice-message registration appears in an appendix, but it is not the main subject.

gaps.name: Voice messaging
gaps.why: VPIM is covered by an existing tag under email, so no gap remains.

RFC3802.title: Toll Quality Voice - 32 kbit/s Adaptive Differential Pulse Code Modulation (ADPCM) MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC3802.summary: Registers the MIME audio sub-type audio/32KADPCM for G.726 32 kbit/s ADPCM toll-quality audio, specifying little-endian code word packing, for use primarily in VPIM voice messaging; obsoletes RFC 2422.

media types.why: The document exists to register a MIME media type (audio/32KADPCM), including the IANA registration template and packing rules.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type audio/32KADPCM for toll quality audio.

codecs.why: The registered type carries G.726 ADPCM audio; the document defines how the codec's 4-bit code words are packed into octets, which is codec-format content.
codecs.quote: The conversion is applied to the PCM stream using an Adaptive Differential Pulse Code Modulation (ADPCM) transcoding technique.

VPIM.why: The type is intended primarily for voice messaging in VPIM, and the document was produced by the VPIM working group; readers of VPIM would want it.
VPIM.quote: The audio/32KADPCM sub-type is a primary component of the VPIM specification [VPIM].

rejected.why: The document uses MIME only as the framework for registering a sub-type; the more specific 'media types' tag fits.
G.711 PCM is mentioned only as the input to the G.726 conversion; the document is not about G.711.
X.420 is cited only as the source of the little-endian ordering default; the document is not about X.400.
Content transfer encodings and mail are only the carrier context; the document is not about email itself.

gaps.name: G.726 ADPCM codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for G.726 or ADPCM; the generic 'codecs' tag is the nearest fit.

RFC3803.title: Content Duration MIME Header Definition
RFC3803.summary: Defines the Content-Duration MIME header field, giving the duration in seconds of time-varying media content (audio/video), used notably in VPIM voice messages; obsoletes RFC 2424 with editorial changes only.

MIME.why: The document's sole purpose is to define a new MIME header field, its syntax and semantics, for media body parts.
MIME.quote: This document describes the MIME header Content-Duration that is intended for use with any time varying media content (typically audio/* or video/*).

VPIM.why: A section addresses use of the header in Voice Profile for Internet Mail messages; the work came from the vpim WG and readers of VPIM would want it.
VPIM.quote: All VPIM Messages MUST contain this sub-type to carry the audio of a voice message.

rejected.why: The header is a MIME content header field rather than a general Internet message format header or addressing matter; MIME is the closer fit.
The document defines a header, not a media type registration or registry rules; audio/* and video/* are only mentioned as applicable content.
Email is the context, but the document does not address email architecture or transport; more specific MIME and VPIM tags cover it.

RFC3804.title: Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) Addressing
RFC3804.summary: RFC 3804 defines VPIM email address formats (VPIM, VOICE, AMIS, fax) for submission mode, based on GSTN address syntax, and registers new GSTN service-selectors and qualifiers with IANA.

VPIM.why: The whole document specifies addressing for Voice Profile for Internet Mail, including the vpim-address, voice-address and amis-address formats and their email forms.
VPIM.quote: This document lists the various VPIM email address formats that are currently in common use and defines several new address formats for special case usage.

rejected.why: VPIM is the more specific tag under email; the general email tag is implied as an ancestor.
The document defines address local-part syntax for VPIM, not the Internet message format itself, which it only references for LHS/RHS terms.
Fax addresses are only referenced to RFC 3192 in a couple of one-line subsections; the document is not about fax.
Gateways (onramps/offramps) are mentioned, but their behaviour is declared out of scope; the document is about address syntax.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the address syntax, not the subject.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-like registration forms for the address elements, not a document about IANA registries.

gaps.name: GSTN address (Minimal GSTN address format in Internet Mail)
gaps.why: The document builds on and extends GSTN email addresses (service-selectors, qualif-type1) for telephone numbers, but the taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC3805.title: Printer MIB v2
RFC3805.summary: RFC 3805 defines the Printer MIB v2 (and the IANA Printer MIB), an SNMP MIB module modelling printer sub-units (inputs, outputs, markers, media paths, channels, interpreters, console, alerts) for management; it obsoletes RFC 1759.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define the Printer MIB and IANA Printer MIB modules with their managed objects, textual conventions and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines MIB objects, not SNMP itself, so MIB is the more specific tag.
IPP appears only as one enumerated channel type (chIPP) in a textual convention; the document is not about IPP.
The IANA Printer MIB registry mechanism is part of the document, but the main subject is the printer MIB itself.
Localization uses IANACharset, but this is a minor part of the document.
LPD is only listed as a channel type enumeration value.

gaps.name: Printing / printer management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no printing subject tag (apart from the LPD and IPP technology tags), so the printer-specific subject matter of this MIB has no fitting home.

RFC3806.title: Printer Finishing MIB
RFC3806.summary: Defines the Finisher MIB and companion IANA-FINISHER-MIB, SMIv2 modules for managing printer finishing subunits (stapling, folding, binding, punching, etc.) as an extension of the Printer MIB.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to specify new SMIv2 MIB modules (Finisher-MIB and IANA-FINISHER-MIB) with tables, textual conventions and conformance groups for finisher management.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB module for the management of printer finishing device subunits.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB objects; the document defines MIB content, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
IPP is referenced only for terminology; the document does not specify or extend IPP.
The IANA-FINISHER-MIB registry and Designated Expert process are part of the MIB's design but the document is not about IANA registries in general.
Implied as the parent of MIB; no need to list it separately.

gaps.name: Printer Finishing / Printer MIB
gaps.why: The document is about managing printers and their finishing devices (staplers, punchers, folders); the taxonomy has no printing-management tag other than IPP and LPD, which don't fit.

RFC3807.title: V5.2-User Adaptation Layer (V5UA)
RFC3807.summary: Defines V5UA, an extension of IUA (RFC 3057) for backhauling V5.2 signalling between a Signaling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller over SCTP, adding message header changes, link-status, Sa-bit and error messages.

SIGTRAN.why: V5UA is a SIGTRAN user adaptation layer that carries V5.2 signalling between SG and MGC, extending IUA; it is the document's whole subject.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document defines a mechanism for the backhauling of V5.2 messages over IP using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

rejected.why: SCTP is only the transport carrying V5UA. The document gives stream-usage guidance and a payload protocol identifier but does not specify or extend SCTP.
ISDN access is among the services V5.2 supports, but the document is about V5.2 backhaul rather than ISDN access in its own right.
This is the parent of SIGTRAN, which is already tagged, so it is implied.
The IANA section (PPID and port assignment) is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: V5.2 interface (ETSI V5.2 LE-AN)
gaps.why: The document concerns backhaul of the ETSI V5.2 access network interface, but the taxonomy has no V5.2 or IUA tag beyond SIGTRAN.

RFC3808.title: IANA Charset MIB
RFC3808.summary: Defines the IANA-CHARSET-MIB module with the IANACharset textual convention, an enumeration of IANA-registered charsets for labelling string encodings in MIB objects, and describes machine-generating it from the IANA Charset Registry.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module defining a textual convention for use by other MIB modules, so readers of MIB modules and SMI would look for it.
MIB.quote: This IANA Charset MIB [CHARMIB] module defines the single textual convention 'IANACharset'.

character sets.why: The TC enumerates IANA-registered charsets and is kept in sync with the IANA Charset Registry, so it is substantially about charset labelling.
character sets.quote: Specifies an IANA registered 'charset' - coded character set (CCS) plus optional character encoding scheme (CES)

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework through which MIB objects are accessed; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour.
The document concerns a MIB derived from an IANA registry, but its IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like and it does not address IANA registry policy itself.
UTF-8 is only mentioned as best practice via SnmpAdminString; the document is not about the encoding.
The Internationalization Considerations section is secondary; the more specific character sets tag covers the subject.

RFC3809.title: Generic Requirements for Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPN)
RFC3809.summary: Informational RFC giving generic service, provider and engineering requirements that all provider-provisioned VPN technologies (L2VPN and L3VPN) must meet.

VPN.why: The whole document defines umbrella requirements for provider-provisioned VPNs of both L2 and L3 kinds. The generic VPN tag fits better than the L2VPN or L3VPN children, because the requirements are explicitly not specific to either.
VPN.quote: This document describes generic requirements for Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPN).

rejected.why: Layer 3 specific requirements are in a separate document ([L3REQTS]). This one is generic across L2 and L3.
Layer 2 specific requirements are in [L2REQTS]. This document only covers generic requirements.
QoS and SLA/SLS monitoring are one requirement area among many, and Diffserv is mentioned only in passing.
IPsec is mentioned only as an example tunnelling and security mechanism. The document does not specify or analyse it.
MPLS appears only as a possible tunnelling technique that solutions must not preclude.
PWE3 encapsulations are referenced only as the ones L2VPN solutions should use.

RFC3810.title: Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 (MLDv2) for IPv6
RFC3810.summary: RFC 3810 specifies MLDv2, the IPv6 protocol by which routers discover multicast listeners on attached links, adding source filtering (INCLUDE/EXCLUDE) and MLDv1 interoperability; it updates RFC 2710.

MLD.why: The document is the specification of MLDv2, covering message formats, listener and router behaviour, timers and MLDv1 interoperation.
MLD.quote: MLD is used by an IPv6 router to discover the presence of multicast listeners on directly attached links

SSM.why: Source filtering, the main addition of MLDv2, exists to support SSM. Readers of SSM would want this RFC, though it is not the document's sole focus.
SSM.quote: as required to support Source-Specific Multicast [RFC3569]

rejected.why: MLDv2 is described as a translation of IGMPv3 for IPv6, but IGMP is only a reference point and the document does not specify it.
MLDv2 messages are carried as a subset of ICMPv6 and use its checksum. ICMPv6 is only the substrate here.
The Router Alert option is required on MLD messages, but the document only uses it and defines nothing new about it.
MLD runs on IPv6, but the document is about the multicast listener protocol rather than IPv6 itself. The more specific MLD tag already covers it.
Neighbor Discovery and DAD are mentioned only to explain why Reports may use the unspecified source address.

RFC3811.title: Definitions of Textual Conventions (TCs) for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Management
RFC3811.summary: RFC 3811 defines the MPLS-TC-STD-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module of textual conventions (labels, LSP IDs, tunnel indices, TE hop addresses, etc.) for reuse by MPLS management MIB modules.

MIB.why: The whole document is a MIB module of textual conventions written in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module which contains Textual Conventions to represent commonly used Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) management information.

MPLS.why: The conventions model MPLS concepts: labels, LSP types, label distribution and retention modes, LDP identifiers and tunnels. Readers of MPLS management material would want this RFC.
MPLS.quote: These Textual Conventions should be imported by MIB modules which manage MPLS networks.

rejected.why: LDP identifiers and modes are represented, but the document defines no LDP protocol behaviour.
Tunnel and LSP ID conventions refer to RSVP-TE, but the document does not specify or extend it.
GMPLS labels are mentioned only as one label format within MplsLabel.
SNMP is only the framework the MIB module is accessed through. The document specifies no SNMP protocol behaviour.
CR-LDP LSP IDs are mentioned only as one case within MplsLSPID, so the document does not specify CR-LDP.

RFC3812.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering (TE) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC3812.summary: Defines the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring MPLS traffic-engineered tunnels, including hop, resource, performance and CR-LDP resource tables.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (MPLS-TE-STD-MIB) defining managed objects for MPLS TE tunnels. The MIB tag is the most specific fit.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

traffic engineering.why: The MIB manages MPLS TE tunnels, explicit hops, resources and affinities, so readers of MPLS traffic engineering would want it. No MPLS-TE-specific tech tag exists, and RSVP-TE is only referenced.
traffic engineering.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) [RFC3031] based traffic engineering.

rejected.why: The MIB models tunnels signalled by RSVP-TE but does not specify or extend that protocol.
There is a CR-LDP resource table, but it is one optional part of a management module, not a specification of CR-LDP.
The MIB manages MPLS TE tunnels but does not define MPLS architecture or operations. The traffic engineering topic is the closer fit.
SNMP is the access protocol the MIB is used with. The document defines objects, not SNMP itself, and the MIB tag covers it.

gaps.name: MPLS traffic engineering MIB / MPLS management
gaps.why: No tag covers MPLS-specific management modules. The MPLS tag is for architecture and operations, and MIB is generic.

RFC3813.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switching Router (LSR) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC3813.summary: Defines the MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB SMIv2 module with managed objects to configure and monitor an MPLS Label Switching Router: interfaces, in-segments, out-segments, cross-connects, label stacks and performance counters.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB) in SMIv2, so MIB is the most specific tag for it.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects to configure and/or monitor a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switching Router (LSR).

MPLS.why: The managed objects model MPLS LSR forwarding state (ILM/NHLFE, labels, cross-connects, label stacks), so readers of MPLS would want it.
MPLS.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) [RFC3031] Label Switching Router (LSR).

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
The TE MIB (RFC 3812) is only referenced via RowPointer for traffic parameters; this document is not about RSVP-TE.
TE is only mentioned as an optional use of the traffic parameter pointer; the document is not about TE.
ATM appears only as an example underlying layer and in modeling reference to RFC 2515.

RFC3814.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Forwarding Equivalence Class To Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (FEC-To-NHLFE) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC3814.summary: Defines the MPLS-FTN-STD-MIB SMIv2 module, with managed objects for configuring and monitoring FEC-to-NHLFE mappings (packet matching rules, per-interface application, and performance counters) on MPLS LSRs.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SNMP MIB module (MPLS-FTN-STD-MIB) with tables, objects and compliance statements for MPLS FTN management.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects for defining, configuring, and monitoring Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) to Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE) mappings

MPLS.why: The MIB manages the MPLS FTN mapping at ingress LSRs, redirecting packets into LSPs and TE tunnels, so it belongs on the MPLS subject page.
MPLS.quote: packets entering the MPLS domain are assigned to an FEC. Those packets belonging to an FEC are associated with an NHLFE (i.e., MPLS label) via the FEC-to-NHLFE (FTN) mapping

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and the MIB tag sits under SNMP already.
CIDR prefixes are discussed only to justify using address ranges instead. The document is not about CIDR.
The DSCP is only one of the packet-match fields, and the Dscp textual convention is imported from another MIB.
The MIB points to TE tunnels defined in MPLS-TE-STD-MIB. It does not specify RSVP-TE signalling.
IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are supported as match fields. That is incidental to the MIB and does not make the document about IPv6.

RFC3815.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS), Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)
RFC3815.summary: Defines four SMIv2 MIB modules (LDP base, ATM, Frame Relay, Generic) for configuring and monitoring the MPLS Label Distribution Protocol on LSRs/LERs.

LDP.why: The whole document models LDP entities, peers, sessions, hello adjacencies, FECs and notifications as managed objects, so LDP readers would look for it.
LDP.quote: This document defines 4 MIB Modules which together support the configuration and monitoring of the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

MIB.why: The document's deliverable is a set of SMIv2 MIB modules with compliance statements, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself.
MPLS is the context, but the document is specifically about LDP, a child tag.
ATM label ranges and VPI/VCI are LDP parameters in one module, not a document about IP over ATM.
Frame Relay DLCI label ranges are LDP parameters in one module; the document is not about frame relay itself.
CR-LDP is only mentioned in passing as another protocol whose LIB is represented in the LSR MIB.

RFC3816.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for RObust Header Compression (ROHC)
RFC3816.summary: Defines three SMIv2 MIB modules (ROHC-MIB, ROHC-UNCOMPRESSED-MIB, ROHC-RTP-MIB) for monitoring and configuring RObust Header Compression instances, channels, profiles and contexts via SNMP.

ROHC.why: The MIB models ROHC compressors/decompressors, channels, profiles (uncompressed, RTP, UDP, ESP, LLA) and contexts, so readers of ROHC would want it.
ROHC.quote: it describes a set of managed objects that allow monitoring of running instances of robust header compression.

MIB.why: The document's main body is SMIv2 MIB module definitions with compliance statements, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines MIB modules, and the more specific MIB tag covers it.
The RTP, UDP and ESP profiles are only ROHC profiles being monitored, not RTP itself.
Implied as the parent of ROHC, so not listed separately.
Mentioned only as a ROHC profile name, not as a subject of the document.
Mentioned only as a ROHC profile name, not as a subject of the document.

RFC3817.title: Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) Active Discovery Relay for PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE)
RFC3817.summary: Informational RFC defining how L2TP LACs relay PPPoE Active Discovery (PAD) messages over the L2TP control channel, with two new message types (SRRQ/SRRP) and PPPoE-specific AVPs.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TP with two new control message types and new AVPs, so it is about L2TP.
L2TP.quote: describes a method to relay Active Discovery and Service Selection functionality from PPPoE over the reliable control channel within L2TP.

PPPoE.why: The document is about relaying PPPoE PAD messages (PADI/PADO/PADR/PADS/PADT) and their Host-Uniq and AC-Cookie TAG handling, so PPPoE readers would want it.
PPPoE.quote: PPPoE defines a simple method for discovering services offered by PPPoE Access Concentrators

rejected.why: PPP is the payload being tunnelled; the document does not specify or extend PPP itself.
Ethernet is only the medium PPPoE runs over; the document is not about IP over Ethernet.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to protect L2TP.
The IANA section merely requests AVP and message type numbers; this is boilerplate.

RFC3818.title: IANA Considerations for the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP)
RFC3818.summary: BCP 88 changes IANA allocation policy for fourteen PPP protocol and option number registries from First Come First Served to IETF Consensus, so that PPP extensions get review.

PPP.why: The document sets the registration policy for PPP's name spaces (protocol numbers, LCP/IPCP/CCP options, CHAP algorithms and others). Readers of PPP material would want it.
PPP.quote: IETF Consensus, usually through the Point-to-Point Protocol Extensions working group (pppext), is required for assigning new values in the following address spaces

IANA.why: The document is an IANA allocation-policy BCP. It changes registry policy from First Come First Served to IETF Consensus.
IANA.quote: the allocation of PPP protocol and other assigned numbers will no longer be "first come first served."

rejected.why: The document touches on IETF Consensus and the pppext working group. Its subject is IANA registry policy for PPP, not IETF process in general.
No CHAP tag exists in the taxonomy. CHAP authentication algorithms are only one of the registries listed, so it is not a subject of the document.
The IPV6CP configuration options registry is only listed. IPv6 is not a subject of the document.

RFC3819.title: Advice for Internet Subnetwork Designers
RFC3819.summary: BCP giving link-layer and subnetwork designers advice on supporting IP efficiently: MTU, framing, multicast, error control and ARQ, TCP performance, QoS, compression, reordering, mobility, routing and security.

link layer.why: The whole document is design guidance for link/subnetwork layers beneath IP, not for one specific medium.
link layer.quote: advice to the designers of digital communication equipment, link-layer protocols, and packet-switched local networks (collectively referred to as subnetworks)

TCP.why: Large sections explain how TCP works and its performance formulae and interactions with link-layer ARQ, outages and asymmetry.
TCP.quote: The discussion below focuses on TCP, which is the most widely-used transport protocol in the Internet.

header compression.why: A dedicated section recommends and analyses VJ, CRTP, IPHC and ROHC over lossy links.
header compression.quote: We make a strong recommendation that subnetworks operating at low speed or with small MTUs compress IP and transport-level headers

QoS.why: Section summarises Intserv and Diffserv and lists desirable subnet QoS capabilities.
QoS.quote: There are presently two architectural approaches to providing mechanisms for QoS support in the Internet.

multicast.why: Section gives guidance on native link-layer multicast support, filtering and IGMP/MLD snooping.
multicast.quote: Multicasting is considerably more efficient when a subnetwork explicitly supports it.

AQM.why: Discusses RED, buffering, ECN and discard policies for subnets.
AQM.quote: There is a rough consensus in the research community that active queue management is important to improving fairness, link utilization, and throughput

rejected.why: Mentioned as a framing example and for in-order delivery, but not the subject.
Used repeatedly as an example subnetwork, but the document is not about ATM.
Path MTU discovery is discussed within the MTU section, but only as context.
Mobility section is brief and general, covering several layers.
Error detection is one subsection among many, not a document-level subject.
The end-to-end principle underlies the advice, but the document is design guidance for subnetworks rather than architecture itself.

gaps.name: Link-layer ARQ and error control (PILC)
gaps.why: A major theme (ARQ persistency, FEC vs retransmission, TCP interaction) with no dedicated tag; FEC exists only as a transport-level loss-recovery tag.

RFC3820.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Proxy Certificate Profile
RFC3820.summary: Defines a profile for X.509 Proxy Certificates, including the critical ProxyCertInfo extension, naming rules, proxy policy languages and path validation, to support single sign-on and restricted delegation in PKI-based systems such as Grids.

X.509.why: The document profiles X.509 certificates for proxying: it defines the ProxyCertInfo extension, subject and issuer rules, and a path validation algorithm for proxy certificate chains.
X.509.quote: This document forms a certificate profile for Proxy Certificates, based on X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) certificates as defined in RFC 3280

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers the PKI aspects, so the ancestor is not listed.
Kerberos tickets are discussed only as a comparison in commentary (Section 5.2), not as a subject of the document.
TLS is only mentioned as a protocol that needs no changes to use proxy certificates; it is a substrate.
Delegation and proxy policies relate to authorization, but the document's subject is the certificate profile. The X.509 tag is the better fit.
OCSP is mentioned once in Security Considerations as a possible revocation mechanism; the document does not address it.
The appendix gives an ASN.1 module, but that is only the encoding apparatus for the extension and not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Proxy certificates / credential delegation and single sign-on
gaps.why: The document's core subject is delegation via proxy certificates, which the taxonomy covers only through the generic X.509 tag.

RFC3821.title: Fibre Channel Over TCP/IP (FCIP)
RFC3821.summary: Specifies FCIP, which encapsulates Fibre Channel frames in TCP/IP to join FC SAN islands into a single fabric, covering the FCIP model, encapsulation, special frame, TCP connection management, security via IPsec/IKE, and QoS/performance.

fibre channel.why: The document is the FCIP specification, tunnelling FC frames over TCP/IP to extend FC fabrics. The taxonomy has no plain FCIP tag, so the Fibre Channel over IP transports node fits best.
fibre channel.quote: Fibre Channel Over TCP/IP (FCIP) describes mechanisms that allow the interconnection of islands of Fibre Channel storage area networks over IP-based networks

rejected.why: iFCP is a different gateway protocol; FCIP is a tunnel between fabrics, so it only fits the parent fibre channel node.
TCP is the transport substrate; the document only recommends options (SACK, window scale, NODELAY) and does not extend TCP.
IPsec/IKE/ESP are mandated for security, but the document profiles their use rather than being about IPsec. It is a secondary concern.
SLPv2 is used for dynamic discovery but is defined in a separate document (RFC 3822).
QoS and Diffserv are only mentioned as options in section 10.2; the document does not specify any particular QoS.
The parent of fibre channel is implied, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: FCIP (Fibre Channel over TCP/IP) as a distinct technology
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic fibre channel node and iFCP; there is no dedicated FCIP tag, so FCIP-specific browsing is not possible.

RFC3822.title: Finding Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP) Entities Using Service Location Protocol version 2 (SLPv2)
RFC3822.summary: Defines how FCIP Entities use SLPv2 to discover peer FCIP Entities, including the service:fcip abstract and service:fcip:entity concrete SLP templates and discovery domains.

SLP.why: The document specifies SLPv2 usage and service type templates for FCIP entity discovery, so it belongs on the SLP page.
SLP.quote: This document defines the use of Service Location Protocol version 2 (SLPv2) by Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP) Entities.

fibre channel.why: The subject being discovered is FCIP, Fibre Channel over TCP/IP, so readers of that subject would want the discovery mechanism.
fibre channel.quote: describes the use of the Service Location Protocol version 2 in performing dynamic discovery of participating Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP) Entities

rejected.why: SLP is the more specific tag and already sits under this topic.
IPsec is only recommended in Security Considerations as a countermeasure, which is boilerplate.
This is a different protocol. The document is about FCIP, not iFCP.
TCP is only the substrate that FCIP runs over.

gaps.name: FCIP (Fibre Channel over TCP/IP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no FCIP tag. Only the generic 'fibre channel' tag under storage covers it, and FCIP is a distinct protocol (RFC 3821).

RFC3823.title: MIME Media Type for the Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML)
RFC3823.summary: Registers the MIME media type application/sbml+xml for the XML-based Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) used to exchange biochemical reaction network models.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration under the IANA/MIME registration procedures, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document registers the MIME sub-type application/sbml+xml, a media type for SBML, the Systems Biology Markup Language.

rejected.why: SBML is an XML format and the registration refers to RFC 3023 XML media types, but the document does not specify XML usage in protocols; XML is only the encoding substrate.
The parent of media types is implied; the document is about a registration, not MIME body structure or encodings.
IANA registration is the mechanism, boilerplate-like template; the document is about the specific media type, not IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML)
gaps.why: The document's subject is a domain-specific scientific data format for biochemical models; the taxonomy has no tag for scientific or domain data formats.

RFC3824.title: Using E.164 numbers with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3824.summary: Informational guidance on using ENUM (E.164 numbers mapped to URIs via DNS NAPTR records) with SIP, covering NAPTR authoring for E2U+sip, client processing of ENUM results, and fallback handling when ENUM is not used.

ENUM.why: The document clarifies authoring and processing of ENUM NAPTR records, the E2U+sip enumservice, and compatibility with RFC 3761/2916.
ENUM.quote: there is nevertheless a need to define procedures for integrating ENUM with SIP implementations.

SIP.why: It specifies how SIP user agents, proxies and redirect servers handle E.164 numbers, including forking, 3xx responses and Request-URI processing.
SIP.quote: This document therefore provides an account of how SIP can handle telephone numbers by making use of ENUM.

tel URI.why: A substantial section covers using tel URLs and sip:+number;user=phone as the fallback when ENUM is unavailable, and avoiding recursive ENUM queries on them.
tel URI.quote: If a user agent is unable to translate an E.164 number with ENUM, it can create a type of SIP Request-URI that contains a telephone number.

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR records are the substrate for ENUM; the document does not extend DNS itself and ENUM is the more specific fit.
PSTN gateways are mentioned as context, but the document is about number-to-URI resolution rather than PSTN interworking.
TRIP is only mentioned once as a way to provision proxy routing policy.
SIP URIs and address-of-record usage are discussed, but only as the content of NAPTR records, not as a URI-scheme specification.

RFC3825.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Option for Coordinate-based Location Configuration Information
RFC3825.summary: Defines a DHCP option (code 123, GeoConf) that delivers coordinate-based location configuration information (latitude, longitude, altitude with resolution fields, and datum) to a client, motivated by emergency calling.

geolocation.why: The document defines the format and semantics of coordinate location information (lat/long/altitude, resolution, datum) and its conveyance to hosts. This is geolocation formats and conveyance.
geolocation.quote: This document specifies a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Option for the coordinate-based geographic location of the client.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a new DHCP option, including its binary layout, server behaviour and parameter request list usage.
DHCP.quote: IANA has assigned a DHCP option code of 123 for the GeoConf option defined in this document.

rejected.why: Emergency calling is the motivation, but the document specifies a location option and not emergency-call mechanisms.
The option is defined for DHCP (IPv4) only.
HELD is a different location acquisition protocol and the document does not use it.
Privacy is only touched on in the resolution notes and the security considerations, which is not enough to tag it.
Wired Ethernet hosts are the example use case, but the document is not about Ethernet.

RFC3826.title: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Cipher Algorithm in the SNMP User-based Security Model
RFC3826.summary: Defines the CFB128-AES-128 privacy (encryption) protocol as an alternative to CBC-DES in the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model, including key/IV derivation, procedures, and a small MIB module registering the protocol OID.

AES.why: The document specifies how AES in CFB128 mode with 128-bit keys is used, including key, IV, encryption and decryption steps.
AES.quote: The symmetric encryption protocol described in this document is based on the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher algorithm used in Cipher FeedBack Mode (CFB), with a key size of 128 bits.

SNMP.why: It extends SNMPv3's User-based Security Model with a new privacy protocol, so it belongs under the SNMP framework and security subject.
SNMP.quote: This memo describes the use of CFB128-AES-128 as an alternative privacy protocol for the User-based Security Model.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-USM-AES-MIB module with the usmAesCfb128Protocol object identity, a MIB module readers of that subject would want.
MIB.quote: This MIB is written in SMIv2 [RFC2578].

rejected.why: DES/CBC-DES is only the existing privacy protocol this document supplements; the document is not about it.
HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 are the RFC 3414 authentication protocols the AES privacy protocol is used with, not subjects of this document.
Key localization is referenced from RFC 3414 and only briefly summarised; the document does not specify key management.
OCTET STRING serialization follows RFC 3417 and is merely a substrate; the document defines nothing new about it.

RFC3827.title: Additional Snoop Datalink Types
RFC3827.summary: RFC 3827 adds new datalink type codes (Fibre Channel, ATM, ATM Classical IP, IP over InfiniBand) to the snoop packet capture file format and creates an IANA registry for snoop datalink types.

packet capture.why: The document extends the snoop packet capture file format with new datalink type codes and sets up a registry for them.
packet capture.quote: The snoop file format provides a way to store and exchange datalink layer packet traces.

rejected.why: IP over InfiniBand is only one of the media whose type code is assigned; the document does not specify IPoIB itself.
ATM appears only as a datalink type code value, not as a subject the document addresses.
Fibre Channel is only a type code label; the document is not about Fibre Channel over IP.
The registry creation is a small part of the document and is its IANA Considerations boilerplate; the subject is the snoop format.

RFC3828.title: The Lightweight User Datagram Protocol (UDP-Lite)
RFC3828.summary: Specifies UDP-Lite, a UDP variant that replaces the Length field with a Checksum Coverage field so applications can receive partially damaged payloads, with its own IP protocol number (136).

UDP-Lite.why: The whole document defines the UDP-Lite protocol: header format, checksum coverage, pseudo header, and compatibility with UDP.
UDP-Lite.quote: UDP-Lite provides a checksum with an optional partial coverage.

rejected.why: The partial checksum is the core feature, but it is part of defining UDP-Lite. The document is not about the Internet checksum in general, so the UDP-Lite tag covers it.
UDP-Lite is a child of UDP and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied. UDP itself is only the base protocol.
RTP is mentioned only as an example of an application that would use UDP-Lite.
IPsec appears only in the Security Considerations, as a note on how it interacts with partial checksums.
Voice and video codecs are given only as motivating examples of error-tolerant applications.
The protocol number assignment is a short boilerplate section, not what the document is about.

RFC3829.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Authorization Identity Request and Response Controls
RFC3829.summary: Defines the LDAP Authorization Identity Request and Response controls, which let a client ask for and receive the authorization identity granted by a bind operation.

LDAP.why: The document specifies new LDAP controls on the bind operation, including OIDs, control values and result codes, so it is an extension of LDAP.
LDAP.quote: This document extends the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) bind operation with a mechanism for requesting and returning the authorization identity it establishes.

rejected.why: SASL (including the EXTERNAL mechanism) appears only as an example of where the controls are useful. The document does not specify or extend SASL.
The controls report the authorization identity granted at bind, but the document is about an LDAP protocol extension. LDAP is the more specific tag.
Bind and certificate authentication are the context for the controls. The document defines no authentication mechanism.
Certificate-based authentication is mentioned only as an example of identity mapping. The document does not profile certificates.
The IANA section only reserves OIDs and registers the control. It is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC3830.title: MIKEY: Multimedia Internet KEYing
RFC3830.summary: RFC 3830 specifies MIKEY, a key management protocol for real-time multimedia sessions (pre-shared key, public-key and Diffie-Hellman methods), with detailed support for keying SRTP.

MIKEY.why: The document defines MIKEY itself: its key transport/exchange methods, payloads, key derivation and message handling.
MIKEY.quote: This document describes a key management scheme that can be used for real-time applications (both for peer-to-peer communication and group communication).

SRTP.why: The SRTP policy, SRTP-ID map type, Data SA retrieval and Appendix A describe in detail how MIKEY keys SRTP, which SRTP readers will want.
SRTP.quote: In particular, its use to support the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol is described in detail.

rejected.why: SIP and RTSP are only the session-establishment protocols MIKEY is tunnelled in; the integration is defined in a separate document.
Parent of MIKEY, so implied and not listed separately.
Group key management is touched on (GKMARCH, small groups), but MIKEY targets peer-to-peer and small groups, and GDOI/GSAKMP are only mentioned as alternatives.
HMAC-SHA-1 is used as the MAC and PRF building block, but the document does not specify or extend HMAC.
The application/mikey registration is only a small IANA-section item.
Certificates are used for authentication, but the document does not profile X.509.

RFC3831.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Fibre Channel
RFC3831.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IPv6 packets over Fibre Channel, including LLC/SNAP and Network_Header framing, MTU, interface identifier and link-local address formation from N_Port_Names, and Neighbor Discovery address mapping for unicast and multicast.

IPv6.why: The document defines how IPv6 runs over Fibre Channel, including link-local addresses, interface IDs, MTU, and multicast mapping.
IPv6.quote: The purpose of this document is to specify a way of encapsulating IP version 6 [IPv6] over Fibre Channel

fibre channel.why: Carrying IP over Fibre Channel is the document's core subject, and the Fibre Channel tag fits this IP-over-FC transport.
fibre channel.quote: Fibre Channel (FC) is a high speed serial interface technology that supports several Upper Layer Protocols including Small Computer System Interface (SCSI)

SLAAC.why: A substantial section defines how to derive interface IDs from N_Port_Names for stateless autoconfiguration.
SLAAC.quote: Stateless address autoconfiguration MUST be performed as specified in [ACONF].
SLAAC.section: 6.1. IPv6 Interface Identifier and Address Prefix

neighbor discovery.why: The document defines the Source/Target Link-layer Address option format for Fibre Channel.
neighbor discovery.quote: The procedure for mapping IPv6 unicast addresses into Fibre Channel link-layer addresses uses the Neighbor Discovery Protocol [DISC].

rejected.why: ESP and AH are only mentioned as optional security mechanisms; the document is not about them.
Path MTU Discovery is merely recommended in the MTU section, not specified here.
Address resolution is done via IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, not ARP.
iFCP carries Fibre Channel over TCP/IP, which is a different subject; this document carries IPv6 over FC.

RFC3832.title: Remote Service Discovery in the Service Location Protocol (SLP) via DNS SRV
RFC3832.summary: Defines the DNS SRV resource records (_slpda._tcp/_udp) for SLP Directory Agents and the steps for a User Agent to discover services in remote DNS domains by finding DAs via DNS SRV and then querying them with SLP.

SLP.why: The document extends SLP with a new way to discover Directory Agents in remote domains, covering scopes, DA usage and discovery steps.
SLP.quote: This document describes remote service discovery in the Service Location Protocol (SLP) via DNS SRV.

DNS.why: It defines a new SRV service name (slpda) and the DNS query procedure for locating DAs, which is a DNS RR usage readers of DNS SRV would want. It also registers the service name with IANA.
DNS.quote: It defines the DNS SRV Resource Records for SLP Directory Agent services

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the SLP tag, and SLP is the more specific tag that fits.
The document uses plain DNS SRV records for locating SLP DAs. It does not use DNS-Based Service Discovery (PTR/TXT instance enumeration).
