DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommendation. The document is not about it.
DHCP is mentioned only as an existing local DA discovery mechanism, and the document does not specify or extend it.

RFC3833.title: Threat Analysis of the Domain Name System (DNS)
RFC3833.summary: Informational threat analysis of the DNS that catalogs known attacks (packet interception, ID guessing, name chaining, untrustworthy servers, DoS, authenticated denial, wildcards) and assesses how far DNSSEC defends against them, plus DNSSEC weaknesses and future work.

DNSSEC.why: The document evaluates DNSSEC against each threat, discusses authenticated denial, wildcards, and DNSSEC weaknesses such as root key rollover and time synchronization.
DNSSEC.quote: attempts to document some of the known threats to the DNS, and, in doing so, attempts to measure to what extent (if any) DNSSEC is a useful tool

DNS.why: It analyses DNS-specific attacks (cache poisoning, name chaining, ID guessing, amplification) and dynamic update and zone transfer security, which DNS readers would want.
DNS.quote: There are several distinct classes of threats to the DNS, most of which are DNS-related instances of more general problems

rejected.why: Secure dynamic update is discussed only as a future-work topic in section 4.2, not as the document's main subject.
Mentioned only as an alternative channel security mechanism that is rejected for DNS message protection.
The general security topic is covered by the more specific DNSSEC tag.
Data disclosure was explicitly ruled out of scope, and the document does not address encrypted DNS transport.
Mentioned only in passing as how a trusted server is advertised to clients.

gaps.name: TSIG / TKEY (DNS transaction security)
gaps.why: The document discusses TSIG and TKEY as channel-security mechanisms for DNS, but the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC3834.title: Recommendations for Automatic Responses to Electronic Mail
RFC3834.summary: RFC 3834 recommends how automatic email responders (vacation notices, filters, service responders) should decide when to reply and how to format and address responses, and defines the Auto-Submitted header field.

email.why: The whole document is about email behaviour: when automatic responders reply, how responses are formed, and where they are sent. It does not fit a narrower email tag better.
email.quote: This memo makes recommendations for software that automatically responds to incoming electronic mail messages, including "out of the office" or "vacation" response generators

message format.why: It defines a new Internet message header field with ABNF syntax and semantics. It also gives detailed guidance on setting From, To, Subject, Reply-To and other header fields in responses.
message format.quote: The purpose of the Auto-Submitted header field is to indicate that the message was originated by an automatic process, or an automatic responder, rather than by a human

rejected.why: The envelope guidance (MAIL FROM <>, NOTIFY=NEVER) uses SMTP as the transport. The document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Spam avoidance is one motivation for the recommendations. The document is not about spam filtering or reporting.
MIME encoded-words and content types are mentioned only in passing as formatting details.
ABNF is used only as notation for the Auto-Submitted syntax.

RFC3835.title: An Architecture for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES)
RFC3835.summary: Informational RFC defining the OPES architecture: OPES entities, processors, data dispatchers, flows, rulesets, callout servers, tracing, trust domains and how it addresses the IAB considerations.

OPES.why: The whole document specifies the Open Pluggable Edge Services architecture: entities, flows, rules, callout servers, and tracing.
OPES.quote: This memo defines an architecture that enables the creation of an application service in which a data provider, a data consumer, and zero or more application entities

rejected.why: HTTP is only the example application protocol for OPES flows; the document does not specify or extend it, though it notes tracing may need header extensions.
Trust domains and privacy sections are part of the OPES architecture and not a general security treatment; OPES tag covers it.
Privacy is discussed briefly in section 3.4 within OPES context; not a privacy threat-model document.
Authorization requirements are deferred to a separate document (RFC 3838); only touched on here.
Rulesets are referenced, but the rule schema and configuration are out of scope.

RFC3836.title: Requirements for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) Callout Protocols
RFC3836.summary: Specifies the functional, performance and security requirements that an OPES callout protocol, used between an OPES processor and a remote callout server, must meet.

OPES.why: The whole document is about the OPES callout protocol, which connects OPES processors to callout servers. The OPES page is where readers would look for it.
OPES.quote: This document specifies the requirements that the OPES (Open Pluggable Edge Services) callout protocol must satisfy in order to support the remote execution of OPES services.

rejected.why: HTTP is only an application protocol the callout protocol must be compatible with. The document does not specify or extend it.
TCP is only a suggested transport for reliability and congestion control. The document does not specify or extend it.
SCTP is only mentioned as an alternative transport. The document does not specify or extend it.
RTP is only an example of another application protocol the callout protocol should support.
The congestion avoidance requirement is a single short section that points to existing guidance. It is not a substantial subject of the document.
The document gives one sentence saying the protocol should be NAT-friendly. It is not about NAT.

RFC3837.title: Security Threats and Risks for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES)
RFC3837.summary: RFC 3837 analyses security threats and risks to the Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) architecture, covering data-flow threats at the network and application levels and threats to out-of-band data, without recommending solutions.

OPES.why: The whole document is a threat analysis of the OPES architecture (processors, callout servers, data flow, out-of-band control). Readers of the OPES subject would expect to find it.
OPES.quote: The document investigates the security threats associated with the Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) and discusses the effects of security threats on the underlying architecture.

rejected.why: It concerns threats to an intermediary architecture, not web platform mechanisms such as HSTS or cookies.
HTTP is only used as the example base protocol. The document does not specify or extend it.
CDNs and web caches are mentioned only as similar overlay networks. The document says content services outside OPES are out of scope.
Privacy exposure is one of several threat categories (Sections 3.4-3.7), not the document's main subject.
DoS attacks on OPES processors are listed as one threat among many. The document does not address DDoS mitigation.
It is a threat analysis of one architecture. It specifies no operational practices and recommends no solutions.

RFC3838.title: Policy, Authorization, and Enforcement Requirements of the Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES)
RFC3838.summary: Informational OPES document specifying requirements for policy decision/enforcement points, rule interfaces, and authentication, authorization, integrity and privacy for selecting services applied to an OPES flow.

OPES.why: The whole document specifies requirements for OPES policy, PDP/PEP, rules and authorization of services on OPES processors.
OPES.quote: describes policy, authorization, and enforcement requirements for the selection of the services to be applied to a given Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) flow

rejected.why: Policy-based management is used as a model (PDP/PEP) but the document is about OPES policy requirements, already covered by the OPES tag.
Authorization is a substantial section but specific to OPES services; the OPES tag covers it.
Privacy requirements are a short section within OPES policy, not a general privacy threat model.
HTTP is only mentioned as an example encapsulated protocol and in references.
SLP/UDDI are mentioned in passing as possible resolvers for service names; not a subject of the document.
XML is only suggested as a desirable rule language format in one sentence.

RFC3839.title: MIME Type Registrations for 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Multimedia files
RFC3839.summary: Registers the audio/3gpp and video/3gpp MIME media types for the 3GPP (3GP) multimedia file format, an ISO-media-file-family format used on cellular phones.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration for audio/3gpp and video/3gpp, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document registers the MIME types audio/3gpp and video/3gpp, defined above.

rejected.why: AMR is only mentioned as one of the codecs that 3GP files can contain, and the RTP payload format is cited only to say it is a separate type. The document does not specify AMR.
The document registers a file-format MIME type, not a codec or container definition. The 3GP container is defined by 3GPP, and the codecs are only mentioned.
3GPP is the context for the file format, but the document is not about IP over cellular networks.
MIME is the framework for these registrations, but the document defines no new MIME body structure or encoding. The media types tag is more specific.
HTTP is mentioned only as one way the types are served. The document does not specify anything about HTTP.

RFC3840.title: Indicating User Agent Capabilities in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3840.summary: RFC 3840 defines how a SIP user agent conveys its capabilities and characteristics as feature parameters in the Contact header field (in REGISTER, OPTIONS, and dialog-forming messages), based on the media feature tag content negotiation framework, and registers an initial set of sip.* media feature tags.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's Contact header field with feature parameters and defines REGISTER, OPTIONS and dialog processing rules plus the 'pref' option tag. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This specification defines mechanisms by which a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) user agent can convey its capabilities and characteristics to other user agents and to the registrar

content negotiation.why: It builds on RFC 2533 feature set predicates and RFC 2506 media feature tag registration. It creates a new SIP feature tag registration tree and defines 18 tags, with an appendix overviewing the framework.
content negotiation.quote: This specification makes heavy use of the terminology and concepts in the content negotiation work carried out within the IETF
content negotiation.section: 4. Usage of the Content Negotiation Framework

rejected.why: The 'media feature tags' registered here are not MIME media type registrations. The document only distinguishes its tags from MIME types.
The audio, video, and similar tags align with SDP media types, but SDP is only referenced, not specified or extended.
The IANA section creates a registration tree, but that is boilerplate for this protocol extension and not a main subject.
MESSAGE and event packages appear only as motivating examples and tag values. The document does not specify SIMPLE.

gaps.name: Media feature tags / caller preferences and callee capabilities
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for media feature tags or SIP user agent capability indication, apart from the generic content negotiation tag.

RFC3841.title: Caller Preferences for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3841.summary: RFC 3841 defines SIP extensions letting a caller express request-handling and feature preferences via new Accept-Contact, Reject-Contact and Request-Disposition header fields, with proxy matching and scoring rules.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with three new header fields and specifies UAC, UAS and proxy behaviour for caller preferences.
SIP.quote: a set of extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) which allow a caller to express preferences about request handling in servers

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example of how callee preferences are expressed; the document is not about CPL.
Not used; feature sets come from media feature tags (RFC 3840/2533), not SDP.
The feature-set matching uses RFC 2533 media feature syntax, but the document is about SIP routing preferences, not content negotiation itself.
Event packages and SUBSCRIBE are only referenced as implicit preference inputs.
Not relevant.

RFC3842.title: A Message Summary and Message Waiting Indication Event Package for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3842.summary: Defines the SIP "message-summary" event package and the application/simple-message-summary MIME type, which carry message-waiting status and message counts from a messaging system to a subscribing SIP user agent.

SIMPLE.why: The document specifies a new SIP event package, with subscriber/notifier behaviour and a body format. That is the SIMPLE-style event-package work, so it fits under SIMPLE. It is a more specific fit than SIP.
SIMPLE.quote: This document defines a SIP Event Package as defined in RFC 3265 [2].

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new media type with its own syntax. It devotes a section to the format and a registration section to the type.
media types.quote: The formal syntax for the application/simple-message-summary MIME type is described below.

rejected.why: The document extends SIP through an event package. SIMPLE is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied and not listed.
The format resembles RFC 2822 headers and uses the Message-Context header from Internet mail. It is not about email transport or access.
The document only borrows RFC 2822-style headers inside the body. It does not specify the Internet message format.
ABNF is only the notation used for the body syntax. The document is not about it.
The voice-mail context is incidental. The document does not specify voice profiles for Internet mail.

RFC3843.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): A Compression Profile for IP
RFC3843.summary: Defines ROHC profile 0x0004 for compressing IP-only header chains of arbitrary length, based on the RFC 3095 IP/UDP profile, with static chain termination, constant IP-ID flag, mode transition cancellation and a CONTEXT_MEMORY feedback option.

ROHC.why: The document specifies a new ROHC compression profile and its changes to ROHC mechanisms (mode transitions, feedback option, packet formats).
ROHC.quote: This document defines a ROHC compression profile for IP, similar to the IP/UDP profile defined by RFC 3095, but simplified to exclude UDP

rejected.why: IPv6 headers are compressed, but IPv6 is only the data being compressed, not the subject.
IPv4 IP-ID handling is part of the profile, but IPv4 itself is not specified or extended.
IP-in-IP header chains are compressed, but tunneling is not defined or analysed.
Parent of ROHC; implied by the more specific ROHC tag.

RFC3844.title: IETF Problem Resolution Process
RFC3844.summary: Informational record of the Problem WG's 2003 discussions decomposing the IETF Problem Statement's problems and proposing process improvements for routine IETF processes, with no consensus on structural changes, which it hands to the IESG.

IETF process.why: The whole document analyses IETF process and organizational problems (WG quality, IESG overload, standards maintenance, WG chair selection and training) and proposes how to resolve them.
IETF process.quote: Expeditious and non-disruptive solutions are proposed for the problems affecting routine processes.

rejected.why: The child tag IETF process fits more specifically, so the parent is not listed.
NomCom is mentioned only in passing as a selection method for a proposed panel, not as a subject of the document.
The ASCII format for RFCs appears only in a list of non-core values, and the document is not about RFC publication.
The document lists core values, but it is not about glossaries or definitions.

RFC3845.title: DNS Security (DNSSEC) NextSECure (NSEC) RDATA Format
RFC3845.summary: Redefines the wire format of the Type Bit Map field in the DNSSEC NSEC resource record RDATA to cover the full RR type space, using windowed bitmaps.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies the NSEC RR RDATA format, a core DNSSEC authenticated denial-of-existence mechanism, and updates RFC 2535 and RFC 3755.
DNSSEC.quote: The DNS [6][7] NSEC [5] Resource Record (RR) is used for authenticated proof of the non-existence of DNS owner names and types.

rejected.why: DNS is the underlying system; DNSSEC is the more specific tag and its ancestors are implied.
Not about EDNS; the document concerns the NSEC RR type bitmap encoding only.
IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and states no new considerations.

RFC3846.title: Mobile IPv4 Extension for Carrying Network Access Identifiers
RFC3846.summary: Defines a Mobile IPv4 extension (type 136) carrying NAIs, with subtypes for Home Agent and Home AAA server identities, so re-authentication after moving between foreign networks reaches the same HA/AAAH.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document defines a new extension to Mobile IPv4 registration and advertisement messages, with processing rules for MN, HA and FA.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This section defines the NAI Carrying Extension which may be used in Mobile IP Registration Request and Reply messages, and also in Mobile IP Agent Advertisements

AAA.why: The extension exists to support AAA re-authentication with multiple home AAA servers, and conveys AAAH identities for AAA routing.
AAA.quote: A foreign agent which receives the Home Agent NAI by this extension in a registration request SHOULD include the Home Agent NAI when requesting Mobile Node authentication through the AAA infrastructure

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example of an AAA infrastructure using realm-based routing; the document does not specify or extend Diameter.
FQDNs and a reverse lookup are mentioned only in passing; nothing about DNS is specified.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate for registering the new extension type and subtype space.

gaps.name: Network Access Identifier (NAI)
gaps.why: The NAI is the central identifier carried by the extension, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC3847.title: Restart Signaling for Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS)
RFC3847.summary: Informational RFC defining an IS-IS restart TLV (type 211) in IIH PDUs and procedures (timers T1-T3, RR/RA/SA bits, CSNP-based synchronization) so restarting or starting routers keep adjacencies and minimize routing disruption.

IS-IS.why: The whole document extends IS-IS with restart signaling, a new IIH TLV, adjacency handling, LSP database synchronization and state tables.
IS-IS.quote: A new TLV is defined to be included in IIH PDUs.

rejected.why: IS-IS is the more specific tag and already implies the routing parent.
Not about failure detection; only adjacency hold-time handling during restart.
IS-IS is an OSI protocol, but this document concerns IS-IS restart behaviour, not OSI/CLNP coexistence.

gaps.name: Graceful restart
gaps.why: The document is about router restart without disrupting forwarding. The taxonomy has no graceful-restart tag, so IS-IS is the closest fit.

RFC3848.title: ESMTP and LMTP Transmission Types Registration
RFC3848.summary: Registers seven new "with" clause transmission type keywords (ESMTPA, ESMTPS, ESMTPSA, LMTP, LMTPA, LMTPS, LMTPSA) for the Received header in Internet messages.

SMTP.why: The document extends the registry of SMTP/ESMTP and LMTP protocol types used in trace information, indicating SMTP AUTH and STARTTLS use. It is about SMTP and LMTP mail transfer.
SMTP.quote: This registers seven new mail transmission types (ESMTPA, ESMTPS, ESMTPSA, LMTP, LMTPA, LMTPS, LMTPSA) for use in the "with" clause of a Received header

message format.why: The keywords are values in the Received trace header field of Internet messages, so readers of message header conventions would want this.
message format.quote: for use in the "with" clause of the Received header in an Internet message

rejected.why: The registry update is the document's content, but it concerns a mail-specific registry, not IANA guidance or stewardship in general.
STARTTLS is only referenced as a condition for the ESMTPS keyword. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
SMTP AUTH is only referenced as a condition for the ESMTPA keyword. The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC3849.title: IPv6 Address Prefix Reserved for Documentation
RFC3849.summary: Reserves the IPv6 unicast prefix 2001:DB8::/32 for use in documentation examples and advises operators to treat it as non-routable and filter it.

addressing.why: The document is about reserving and using a specific IP address prefix, an address allocation matter. No specific child tag (CIDR, anycast, etc.) fits, so the addressing topic is used directly.
addressing.quote: an IPv6 unicast address prefix is reserved for use in examples in RFCs, books, documentation, and the like.

rejected.why: The document concerns an IPv6 prefix, so IPv6 is a plausible tag. Its subject is the allocation of a documentation prefix, an addressing matter, and addressing is chosen as the more specific fit. IPv6 is only the context.
The IANA instruction to record the prefix is in the IANA Considerations boilerplate and is not the main subject.
RFC 2606 on reserved TLDs is mentioned only as an analogy, and this document is about addresses, not domain names.
Multicast address derivation from the prefix is mentioned only briefly and is largely out of scope.

RFC3850.title: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Version 3.1 Certificate Handling
RFC3850.summary: RFC 3850 specifies how S/MIME 3.1 agents handle X.509 certificates and CRLs: CMS certificate options, email addresses in certificates, path validation, signing algorithms, and required PKIX extensions.

S/MIME.why: The document is the S/MIME v3.1 certificate handling specification, defining agent requirements for certificates in secure email.
S/MIME.quote: This document specifies conventions for X.509 certificate usage by Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) agents.

X.509.why: A large part of the document profiles X.509 certificate and CRL usage: extensions, key usage, subjectAltName, validation, and signature algorithms.
X.509.quote: Sending and receiving agents MUST correctly handle the basic constraints, key usage, authority key identifier, subject key identifier, and subject alternative names certificate extensions

rejected.why: CMS provides the data types and message format S/MIME uses; this document only specifies certificate options within it, and the CMS spec is separate.
The X.509 tag is more specific; the document profiles certificate handling rather than PKI in general, and relies on RFC 3280 for the PKIX profile.
The Internet message format is only referenced for From/Sender address matching with certificate email addresses.
The document's subject is certificate handling, covered by S/MIME; email is the context only.
X.500 is mentioned only as an example certificate retrieval mechanism.
MD5 and MD2 appear only as signature algorithms to be verified; the document is not about them.

RFC3851.title: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Version 3.1 Message Specification
RFC3851.summary: RFC 3851 specifies S/MIME version 3.1, defining how to create signed, enveloped and compressed MIME body parts using CMS, including the application/pkcs7-mime and application/pkcs7-signature types, algorithm requirements, and multipart/signed usage.

S/MIME.why: The whole document is the S/MIME v3.1 message specification, obsoleting RFC 2633.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data.

CMS.why: Section 2 profiles CMS options (SignedData, EnvelopedData, CompressedData, SignerInfo attributes, algorithm identifiers), a substantial part of the document.
CMS.quote: This specification defines how to create a MIME body part that has been cryptographically enhanced according to CMS [CMS]

MIME.why: Defines MIME types (application/pkcs7-mime, pkcs7-signature), smime-type parameter, canonicalization and transfer encoding for secured MIME entities.
MIME.quote: This document also discusses how to use the multipart/signed MIME type defined in [MIME-SECURE] to transport S/MIME signed messages.

rejected.why: S/MIME is usable with any MIME transport; the more specific S/MIME tag covers it.
Certificate handling is delegated to RFC 3850; this document only touches certificates in passing.
The ASN.1 module is only an appendix defining a few attributes; not the subject.
It defines pkcs7-mime usage but is not about media type registration rules.
AES is only mentioned as a SHOULD-implement content-encryption algorithm.
RSA is only mentioned as a required algorithm and key size guidance, not the subject.

RFC3852.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC3852.summary: RFC 3852 specifies the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), an ASN.1-based encapsulation syntax for digitally signing, digesting, authenticating, and encrypting arbitrary content, obsoleting RFC 3369.

CMS.why: The document is the core CMS specification, defining ContentInfo and the signed-, enveloped-, digested-, encrypted- and authenticated-data content types.
CMS.quote: This document describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).  This syntax is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt arbitrary message content.

rejected.why: CMS is defined using ASN.1 and includes ASN.1 modules, but ASN.1 is the notation and encoding substrate, not the subject.
S/MIME is a major user of CMS and is mentioned for compatibility, but this document does not specify S/MIME.
Certificates and CRLs are carried in CMS structures, but the document does not profile X.509; it defers to RFC 3280.
CMS relies on certificate-based key management but does not define PKI mechanisms; path validation is explicitly out of scope.
Specific algorithms are explicitly excluded and moved to a separate document (CMSALG).
RecipientInfo types are a part of the CMS syntax, but the document does not define key management protocols in their own right.

RFC3853.title: S/MIME Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Requirement for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3853.summary: Updates RFC 3261 to make AES (with RSA/SHA1) the mandatory-to-implement S/MIME algorithm set for SIP instead of 3DES, to align with TLS requirements and the evolving S/MIME specs.

SIP.why: The document amends SIP's normative requirements (RFC 3261 Section 23.3) for S/MIME ciphersuites, so SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: This document updates the normative guidance of RFC 3261 to require the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) for S/MIME.

S/MIME.why: It defines the SIP profile of S/MIME: mandatory algorithms, key sizes, and Content-Transfer-Encoding.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME implementations MUST at a minimum support RSA as a digital signature algorithm and SHA1 as a digest algorithm [5], and AES as an encryption algorithm

AES.why: The central change is mandating AES in place of 3DES, with key-size requirements, so AES readers would want it.
AES.quote: S/MIME implementations of AES MUST support 128-bit AES keys, and SHOULD support 192 and 256-bit keys.

rejected.why: TLS is mentioned only as motivation for unifying algorithm requirements; the document does not specify anything about TLS.
CMS and its AES usage RFCs are referenced as the underlying specification, but the document does not define CMS content.
3DES is the algorithm being demoted to RECOMMENDED; the document is not about DES itself.
RSA is named as a required signature and key transport algorithm, but only in passing within the profile.

RFC3854.title: Securing X.400 Content with Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME)
RFC3854.summary: Specifies how to use S/MIME (CMS SignedData and EnvelopedData) to sign and encrypt X.400 message content, including optional MIME wrapping with new smime-type values and X.400 addresses in certificates.

S/MIME.why: The document profiles S/MIME and CMS for X.400 content: algorithm requirements, signed and enveloped formats, nesting, and the application/pkcs7-mime smime-type values.
S/MIME.quote: This document describes a protocol for adding cryptographic signature and encryption services to X.400 content with Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME).

X.400.why: The subject is X.400 message content and its interworking with SMTP/MIME. It covers the X.400 envelope and content, ORAddress in certificates, and carrying X.400 content in SMTP.
X.400.quote: This document describes how S/MIME CMS is used to secure the content part of X.400 messages.

rejected.why: CMS is the underlying mechanism and is profiled only through S/MIME, which is the more specific tag. S/MIME already sits under CMS in the taxonomy.
MIME is used only as an optional outer wrapper for 7-bit transport. The document defines no new MIME structure beyond the smime-type values.
Certificates are mentioned only for carrying X.400 addresses in subjectAltName. Certificate handling is deferred to other documents.
SMTP is one possible transport. The document explicitly says transport is out of scope.
ASN.1 is used as the encoding but is not the subject of the document.

RFC3855.title: Transporting Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Objects in X.400
RFC3855.summary: Specifies how CMS/S/MIME-protected objects are carried as content or body parts in native X.400 messages, including the S/MIME Encoded Information Type OIDs and guidance on X.400 services (conversion, redirection, DL expansion).

X.400.why: The document defines how S/MIME objects are carried in X.400 content, body parts, EITs, and interacts with X.400 elements of service.
X.400.quote: This specification defines the options and values necessary to enable interoperable transport of S/MIME messages over an X.400 system.

S/MIME.why: It profiles S/MIME v3.1 message transport, defining smime-type equivalents as EITs and RecipientInfo handling for X.400 redirection and DLs.
S/MIME.quote: This document describes a mechanism for using CMS objects as the message content of X.400 messages in a native X.400 environment.

rejected.why: CMS is the protected object being carried; the document does not specify CMS itself, and S/MIME (its child) is the better fit.
MIME wrapping is only discussed as optional and generally not used in homogeneous X.400; the document is not about MIME.
ASN.1 OIDs are used to define values, but ASN.1 is only notation here.
Gateways between X.400 and SMTP are explicitly out of scope.

RFC3856.title: A Presence Event Package for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3856.summary: Defines the SIP "presence" event package, specifying how presence agents handle SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY for presence information, including authorization, state agents, and use of PIDF bodies.

SIMPLE.why: The document is a SIMPLE-WG event package for SIP presence: it defines the presence package, presence agents, and subscription/notification behaviour, which is exactly SIMPLE's subject.
SIMPLE.quote: This document describes the usage of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for subscriptions and notifications of presence.

SIP.why: It extends SIP with an event package and specifies SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY processing, forking, migration and registration usage, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: Specifically, this document defines an event package, as described in RFC 3265 [2].

instant messaging.why: Presence as a service in the RFC 2778 model, with CPP interworking, is a core part of instant messaging and presence, so readers of that subject will look for it.
instant messaging.quote: This document proposes the usage of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [1] as a presence protocol.

rejected.why: The package requires application/pidf+xml bodies but does not define the format; it is specified in a separate RFC.
TLS is only a security mechanism used for hop-by-hop protection.
S/MIME is only mentioned as an option for encryption and integrity, not specified here.
The pres URI usage is discussed, but the URI scheme is defined elsewhere (CPP).
DNS appears only in passing for address resolution procedures defined in another RFC.
Authorization is discussed within the package, but means are explicitly out of scope.

RFC3857.title: A Watcher Information Event Template-Package for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3857.summary: Defines the "winfo" SIP event template-package, which lets users subscribe to watcher information (the set of subscribers to a resource in another event package, e.g. presence), including its subscription state machine, notifier/subscriber behaviour and examples.

SIMPLE.why: The document defines a SIMPLE-working-group event package for presence authorization, using the application/watcherinfo+xml format. It falls under the SIMPLE event package area.
SIMPLE.quote: This document defines the watcher information template-package for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) event framework.

SIP.why: It extends the SIP event framework (RFC 3265) with a new template-package and specifies SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY handling, forking and state agents.
SIP.quote: The framework defines the methods SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY, and introduces the notion of a package.

rejected.why: Presence is the motivating use case, but the document does not define a presence data format. It defines watcher information about subscriptions.
Presence authorization is only a usage scenario. The document specifies a SIP event package, not presence or IM as a system.
The watcherinfo XML format is defined in RFC 3858, not here. XML is only the body encoding.
The document only references the application/watcherinfo+xml type, which is defined elsewhere.

RFC3858.title: An Extensible Markup Language (XML) Based Format for Watcher Information
RFC3858.summary: RFC 3858 defines an XML document format (application/watcherinfo+xml, with its own namespace) describing the state of watchers subscribed to a resource, for use with the SIP watcher information event package in presence systems.

SIMPLE.why: SIMPLE WG document defining the watcher information data format for SIP presence subscriptions, which the SIMPLE tag covers (event packages, presence data formats).
SIMPLE.quote: A watcher information document begins with the root element tag "watcherinfo". It consists of any number of "watcher-list" sub- elements

XML.why: The document specifies a new XML format with namespace and schema, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: Watcher information is an XML document [4] that MUST be well-formed and SHOULD be valid.

media types.why: Registers the application/watcherinfo+xml media type, a deliverable of the document, though the IANA section is boilerplate-like and so only secondary.
media types.quote: This document registers a new MIME type, application/watcherinfo+xml, and registers a new XML namespace.

rejected.why: SIP and the event framework are the substrate; the document only defines the data format, while the event package is in RFC 3857.
Presence is the motivating application, but this document describes subscription state, not presence data itself; SIMPLE covers it.
Watcher information is not the presence information data format; it is a distinct format.
The URN namespace registration is IANA boilerplate; the document is not about URN namespaces.

RFC3859.title: Common Profile for Presence (CPP)
RFC3859.summary: RFC 3859 defines the Common Profile for Presence (CPP), an abstract presence service (subscribe, notify, response operations) with PIDF as the common format and the pres URI scheme, to enable gateways between presence/instant messaging services.

instant messaging.why: The document specifies an abstract presence service (subscribe/notify/response) for interoperability among presence and instant messaging systems, which is the instant messaging and presence subject.
instant messaging.quote: This specification defines semantics and data formats for common services of presence to facilitate the creation of gateways between presence services

PIDF.why: The document mandates PIDF as the common end-to-end presence content format for notify operations through gateways, a substantial part of the profile.
PIDF.quote: applications that send notification operations through a CPP gateway MUST support the format defined in PIDF [4]

rejected.why: The pres URI scheme is defined here, but it serves as the presentity identifier within the presence profile, so the instant messaging tag covers it better.
S/MIME is only the mechanism for end-to-end security of PIDF bodies, mentioned in Security Considerations.
The document does not define SIP event packages or SIMPLE extensions. It is protocol-neutral.
SIP is not mentioned. The profile is abstract and protocol-independent.
RFC 2822 mailbox syntax is only borrowed for the pres URI syntax.
AES is mentioned only as a preferred algorithm in Security Considerations.

RFC3860.title: Common Profile for Instant Messaging (CPIM)
RFC3860.summary: RFC 3860 defines the Common Profile for Instant Messaging (CPIM), an abstract set of message and response operations, plus the im: URI scheme, to let gateways interwork between different instant messaging protocols.

instant messaging.why: The whole document specifies an abstract instant messaging service (message and response operations, looping control, gateways) for interworking IM protocols.
instant messaging.quote: This specification defines common semantics and data formats for instant messaging to facilitate the creation of gateways between instant messaging services.

URI.why: The document defines and registers the im: URI scheme, with syntax in Appendix A, which is a substantial part of its content.
URI.quote: An INSTANT INBOX is specified using an instant messaging URI with the 'im:' URI scheme.

rejected.why: S/MIME is only the mechanism named in Security Considerations for end-to-end protection. The document does not specify it.
The im: URI borrows mailbox syntax from RFC 2822, but the document is not about Internet message format. The IM message format is defined in a separate document (MSGFMT).
SIP is not mentioned in the document. It is a possible IM transport, but the profile is protocol-neutral.
The document covers instant messages only. Presence information formats are out of scope.
Address resolution is delegated by reference to another document, and the text only mentions resolving the domain name portion.

RFC3861.title: Address Resolution for Instant Messaging and Presence
RFC3861.summary: RFC 3861 specifies how to resolve 'im' and 'pres' URIs for instant messaging and presence to servers using DNS SRV records with _im and _pres service labels and IANA-registered protocol labels.

instant messaging.why: The document defines address resolution for the im and pres URI schemes of instant messaging and presence, so readers of that subject need it.
instant messaging.quote: This document provides rules for locating the resources associated with URIs that employ these schemes via the Domain Name Service (DNS)

DNS.why: It defines new use of DNS SRV records (service labels, lookup, SRV/A/CNAME processing) for IM and presence, and creates SRV protocol label registries.
DNS.quote: The symbolic name used in the Service field of the SRV record is "_im" for instant messaging and "_pres" for presence

rejected.why: The im and pres URI schemes are defined in the CPIM and CPP documents; this document only specifies how to resolve them.
The document concerns CPIM/CPP address resolution, not SIP-based SIMPLE extensions.
Presence data format is not addressed; only locating presence services.
SRV-based lookup is a form of service discovery, but the more specific DNS and instant messaging tags cover it.
The registries creation is boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not the main body subject.

RFC3862.title: Common Presence and Instant Messaging (CPIM): Message Format
RFC3862.summary: Defines the Message/CPIM MIME content type, a canonical, securable message format with metadata headers and encapsulated MIME content, for CPIM-compliant instant messaging protocols.

instant messaging.why: The document defines the common message format used for interworking between instant messaging protocols under CPIM.
instant messaging.quote: a message format for protocols that conform to the Common Profile for Instant Messaging (CPIM) specification

media types.why: The document defines and registers the Message/CPIM media type, and its main body specifies that type's structure.
media types.quote: A new MIME content-type value, Message/CPIM, per RFC 2048

MIME.why: The format is a MIME entity that encapsulates MIME content and is secured via MIME multiparts, so MIME readers would want it.
MIME.quote: The CPIM message format encapsulates arbitrary MIME message content, together with message- and content-related metadata.

rejected.why: That tag covers the Internet email message format (RFC 2822). This document defines a different, stricter format that only resembles RFC 2822 headers.
S/MIME appears only as an example of how to sign a Message/CPIM. The format deliberately stays agnostic about security mechanisms.
The document registers a URN sub-namespace for CPIM headers, but this is IANA boilerplate and is not a main subject.
UTF-8 and language tagging are used in the headers, but they are not the document's subject.
The document is related to CPIM and presence, but it defines no SIMPLE event packages or extensions.
The document borrows RFC 2822 syntax, but it is not about email.

gaps.name: CPIM (Common Profile for Instant Messaging)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CPIM-specific tag. The nearest fit is instant messaging, which is broader than CPIM.

RFC3863.title: Presence Information Data Format (PIDF)
RFC3863.summary: RFC 3863 specifies the XML-based Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), its extensibility framework, and the application/pidf+xml media type for CPP-compliant presence protocols.

PIDF.why: The whole document defines PIDF: the presence, tuple, status, contact, note and timestamp elements, plus its extensibility rules.
PIDF.quote: This memo specifies the Common Profile for Presence (CPP) Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) as a common presence data format

media types.why: It defines and registers the application/pidf+xml media type with a full registration template, and a reader of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: This memo defines a new content type "application/pidf+xml" for an XML MIME entity that contains presence information.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding. The document defines a presence format and does not cover XML usage in general, although namespace-based extensibility is a significant part of it.
This is the parent of PIDF, which is the more specific tag. PIDF is the document's subject, so the parent is implied.
The document is from the IMPP working group and defines a base format. It does not specify SIP event packages or XCAP.
S/MIME is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the recommended way to secure PIDF.
The document registers URN namespaces for its XML namespaces. This is IANA boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC3864.title: Registration Procedures for Message Header Fields
RFC3864.summary: BCP defining IANA registration procedures and the permanent and provisional registries for message header field names used by Internet mail, HTTP, Netnews and MIME.

message format.why: The document is about registering and managing message header field names, anchored on the Internet message format (RFC 2822). Readers of the message format subject would want this header registry.
message format.quote: This specification defines registration procedures for the message header field names used by Internet mail, HTTP, newsgroup feeds and other Internet applications.

IANA.why: The main body defines registries, templates, designated-expert review and change control. This is IANA registry procedure, not just boilerplate.
IANA.quote: A new IANA registry for permanent message header fields per Section 4 of this document.

rejected.why: HTTP header fields fall within the registry's scope, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
MIME Content-* headers are discussed only as one class of registered fields, not specified.
This is a header field registry, not a media type registry.
Netnews is only one of the applications whose headers are covered.
The document is about header registration across several protocols, so the narrower message format tag fits better.

RFC3865.title: A No Soliciting Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) Service Extension
RFC3865.summary: Defines a NO-SOLICITING SMTP service extension, a SOLICIT parameter on MAIL FROM, a new Solicitation: message header, and Received: trace-field extensions so receiving MTAs can signal and refuse classes of unsolicited mail.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension, a MAIL FROM parameter, reply codes and Received: trace changes, so it extends SMTP.
SMTP.quote: Per [RFC2821], a "NO-SOLICITING" SMTP service extension is defined. The service extension is declared during the initial "EHLO" SMTP exchange.

spam.why: The extension exists to let receivers refuse classes of unsolicited bulk mail before transfer, so it is an anti-spam mechanism.
spam.quote: Unsolicited Bulk Email (UBE), otherwise known as spam, has become as one of the most pressing issues on the Internet.

message format.why: It defines a new message header field and extends the Received: trace field, and registers the header in the IANA message header registry.
message format.quote: Per [RFC2822], a new "Solicitation:" header field is defined which contains one or more solicitation class keywords.

rejected.why: The extension explicitly does not deal with authentication or consent, so it is not about domain authentication.
Blacklists and whitelists appear only as background in the introduction. The document defines no DNS-based lists.
ABNF is used only as notation for the syntax, not as a subject of the document.
SMTP and message format are more specific children, so the parent is implied.

RFC3866.title: Language Tags and Ranges in the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
RFC3866.summary: Standards-track RFC (obsoleting RFC 2596) specifying how language tag options and language range options on attribute descriptions are used in LDAP search, compare, add and modify operations, plus feature discovery and interoperability.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAP by defining language tag and range options on attribute descriptions and how search, compare, add and modify operations treat them, plus root DSE feature discovery.
LDAP.quote: This document details the use of Language Tags and Ranges in the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

language tags.why: The document is about carrying BCP 47 language tags and defining language range matching semantics in a protocol, which is what readers of the language tags subject would want.
language tags.quote: This document describes how language tags and ranges [RFC3066] are carried in LDAP and are to be interpreted by LDAP implementations.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to write the option syntax; the document is not about it.
The parent topic is implied by the LDAP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The parent topic is implied by the language tags tag, so it is not listed separately.
X.500 contexts are discussed only in Appendix B as an informative comparison, not as a subject of the document.
ASCII is only cited to describe the character set of tag strings.

RFC3867.title: Payment Application Programmers Interface (API) for v1.0 Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP)
RFC3867.summary: Defines an XML-formalised Payment API between the IOTP Application Core and payment modules (IOTP Payment Bridges/existing payment software) for Consumer, Merchant and Payment Handler roles, with message flows, error codes, process states and API calls.

IOTP.why: The entire document specifies the payment-module API for IOTP v1.0, covering its transaction types, brand selection, payment, inquiry and error handling.
IOTP.quote: This document addresses a common interface between the IOTP application core and the payment modules, enabling the interoperability between these kinds of modules.

rejected.why: XML (DTD syntax) is only the notation used to formalise the API parameters, not the subject.
IOTP is a child of e-commerce, so the more specific IOTP tag already covers it.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect pass phrases, so it is not a subject of the document.
Payment schemes such as SET, Mondex and CyberCoin are only examples of what the API must accommodate; CyberCash is not discussed.

gaps.name: SET (Secure Electronic Transaction) payment protocol
gaps.why: The document references SET repeatedly as an example payment scheme, but the taxonomy has no tag for it and it is not the document's subject.

RFC3868.title: Signalling Connection Control Part User Adaptation Layer (SUA)
RFC3868.summary: RFC 3868 specifies SUA, a SIGTRAN adaptation layer that carries SS7 SCCP-user signalling (TCAP, RANAP, etc.) over SCTP between signalling gateways and IP signalling endpoints, or peer-to-peer between IP endpoints.

SIGTRAN.why: SUA is one of the SIGTRAN user adaptation layers (SS7 signalling transport over IP) and is the document's whole subject.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document defines a protocol for the transport of any Signalling Connection Control Part-User signalling over IP using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol.

rejected.why: SCTP is the transport substrate SUA runs over. The document only uses it and assigns a payload protocol ID and port, and does not extend SCTP.
This is the parent of SIGTRAN and is implied by the SIGTRAN tag, so it is not listed separately.
Accepted, see tags.
The IANA section registers a payload protocol ID, a port and an extension registry. That is boilerplate and not the subject.
DNS is mentioned only as one possible implementation of the address mapping function. The document does not specify it.
RFC 3761 is cited only as an example of a lookup mechanism for the address mapping function.

gaps.name: SS7 / SCCP signalling
gaps.why: SS7 SCCP and TCAP user-part transport has no dedicated tag. The SIGTRAN tag covers it adequately.

RFC3869.title: IAB Concerns and Recommendations Regarding Internet Research and Evolution
RFC3869.summary: IAB document arguing that Internet infrastructure research needs sustained non-commercial funding, with a history of research funding and a survey of open research topics (naming, routing, security, management, QoS, congestion control, middleboxes, measurement).

internet architecture.why: The document concerns the evolution of the Internet infrastructure and architectural issues such as layering, middleboxes and end-to-end transparency. Its subject is the Internet's evolution and the research it needs.
internet architecture.quote: research is needed to understand architectural mechanisms that can accommodate increased complexity without decreasing robustness of performance in unknown environments
internet architecture.section: 3.8 Studying the Evolution of the Internet Infrastructure

internet history.why: Section 2 is a historical account of Internet research and its funding from the ARPAnet onward. This is a substantial part of the document.
internet history.quote: Most of the early research into packet-switched networks was sponsored by the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)

rejected.why: Routing is one of several example research areas. The document does not specify or analyse routing architecture in depth.
BGP convergence and scaling are mentioned briefly as research examples. The document is not about BGP.
Section 3.7 is one among many research topic summaries, so it is not a main subject.
QoS is a single research topic section among many.
DNS stress points are discussed briefly as examples. The document is not about DNS.
Security is one example research area. The document does not address security as a whole in depth.
Network management is one of several topic summaries, covered briefly.

gaps.name: Internet research funding
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the funding of Internet research. No taxonomy tag covers research policy or funding.

RFC3870.title: application/rdf+xml Media Type Registration
RFC3870.summary: Registers the application/rdf+xml media type for the RDF/XML serialization of RDF, including parameters, fragment identifier handling and historical notes.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration for application/rdf+xml, so readers browsing media type registrations would expect it.
media types.quote: This is a media type registration as defined in RFC 2048, "Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Four: Registration Procedures"

XML.why: The registered type is for an XML-based format (+xml suffix), sharing charset and encoding rules with application/xml; RDF/XML usage is a substantial subject.
XML.quote: the W3C has defined the RDF/XML syntax [1] to allow RDF to be serialized in an XML format.

rejected.why: Fragment identifiers section discusses URI fragment semantics only briefly as it applies to RDF media type; not about URIs themselves.
MIME registration procedure is the framework used; the document's subject is a specific media type, covered by media types.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible securing mechanism.
Only listed in Security Considerations as a securing option.

gaps.name: RDF (Resource Description Framework) / Semantic Web
gaps.why: The document is about the media type for RDF/XML, but the taxonomy has no tag for RDF or the Semantic Web.

RFC3871.title: Operational Security Requirements for Large Internet Service Provider (ISP) IP Network Infrastructure
RFC3871.summary: Informational RFC listing operational security requirements (management, filtering, logging, AAA, documentation, assurance) that large ISPs can require of router and switch vendors, with profiles for different topology contexts.

operational security.why: The whole document is a catalogue of operational security requirements for network infrastructure devices, which is what this topic covers.
operational security.quote: This document defines a list of operational security requirements for the infrastructure of large Internet Service Provider (ISP) IP networks (routers and switches).

rejected.why: Syslog is cited as one way to meet the logging requirements. The document does not specify or extend it.
A section lists AAA requirements for devices, but RADIUS, TACACS+, Diameter and Kerberos are only named as examples. It is a minor part of a broader requirements list.
SNMP is mentioned as a management mechanism and in a security note. It is not the subject of the document.
The packet filtering requirements are for router and switch ACLs, not firewall systems. They fall under the operational security requirements already tagged.
This id is not in the taxonomy. Anti-spoofing (BCP 38) is only one requirement among many.
The requirements on open-review algorithms and strong cryptography are generic guidance. They are a small part of the document.

RFC3872.title: Management Information Base for Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP)
RFC3872.summary: Defines the TRIP-MIB and TRIP-TC-MIB SMIv2 modules for managing Telephony Routing over IP location servers: configuration, peers, routes, ITAD topology, statistics and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SMIv2) with tables, groups, notifications and compliance statements; readers of MIB pages would look for it.
MIB.quote: it describes a set of managed objects that are used to manage Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) devices.

TRIP.why: The MIB covers TRIP location servers, peers, routes (TRIBs), ITADs and communities, so it is about operating TRIP.
TRIP.quote: This MIB module provides managed objects for TRIP devices defined in Telephony Routing over IP [RFC3219].

rejected.why: TRIP is modeled after BGP-4 and the MIB after the BGP-4 MIB, but the document does not manage BGP.
SNMP is only the access mechanism; the MIB tag is more specific and SNMP is not the subject.
SIP appears only as an application protocol value in a textual convention.
H.323 variants are only enumeration values in a textual convention.

RFC3873.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC3873.summary: Defines the SCTP-MIB SMIv2 module, with statistics, parameters, association tables and reverse-lookup tables, for managing SCTP implementations via SNMP.

MIB.why: The document's sole purpose is to define an SMIv2 MIB module for SCTP, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the Management Information Base (MIB) module which describes managed objects for implementations of the SCTP.

SCTP.why: The MIB models SCTP associations, chunks, multihoming, timers and states for managing SCTP implementations, so SCTP readers would want it.
SCTP.quote: The sctpAssocTable  is the main MIB table, where all the association related information is stored on a per association basis.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB. The document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
The MIB is modelled on the TCP MIB, but TCP is not the subject.
DNS names appear only as the format of the remote host name object, and the document is not about DNS.
IPv4 and IPv6 addresses appear only as InetAddress index types.
The document was produced by the sigtran working group, but it manages SCTP itself and does not cover signalling transport adaptation layers.

RFC3874.title: A 224-bit One-way Hash Function: SHA-224
RFC3874.summary: RFC 3874 specifies the SHA-224 one-way hash function (SHA-256 with a different initial value, truncated to 224 bits), gives test vectors and publishes its ASN.1 object identifier.

SHA.why: The whole document defines SHA-224, a member of the SHA family, with its initial values, truncation, test vectors and OID.
SHA.quote: This document specifies a 224-bit one-way hash function, called SHA-224.  SHA-224 is based on SHA-256, but it uses a different initial value

rejected.why: Only the object identifier is published in ASN.1 notation; the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
CMS is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that uses hash OIDs; it is not specified or extended here.
Triple-DES is cited only as a comparison for the 112-bit security strength.
NIST key management guidance motivates the hash size but the document does not address key management.

RFC3875.title: The Common Gateway Interface (CGI) Version 1.1
RFC3875.summary: Specifies CGI/1.1, the interface by which an HTTP server invokes external scripts, defining request meta-variables, request/response handling, NPH scripts, and system-specific bindings.

web.why: CGI is a web-server-to-program gateway interface, a cross-protocol web architecture matter. No more specific taxonomy tag covers it, so the parent topic fits.
web.quote: The Common Gateway Interface (CGI) allows an HTTP [1], [4] server and a CGI script to share responsibility for responding to client requests.

HTTP.why: A substantial part of the document maps HTTP request methods, headers and status codes to CGI variables and responses, including NPH scripts returning full HTTP responses.
HTTP.quote: Meta-variables with names beginning with "HTTP_" contain values read from the client request header fields, if the protocol used is HTTP.

rejected.why: The Script-URI and URL encoding are used to define meta-variables, but the document is not about URI syntax itself.
Form submission is mentioned only as an example of POST and query strings.
Mentioned only for the scheme and security model; it is only the substrate.
AUTH_TYPE and REMOTE_USER pass through Basic/Digest information, but the document does not specify authentication.
The BNF is just the notation used, not the subject.
REMOTE_IDENT references RFC 1413 in one variable, which is a minor mention.

gaps.name: CGI (Common Gateway Interface)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for server-side gateway or script interfaces such as CGI. The nearest fit is the general web topic.

RFC3876.title: Returning Matched Values with the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol version 3 (LDAPv3)
RFC3876.summary: Defines the LDAPv3 valuesReturnFilter (matched values) control that lets a Search return only those attribute values matching a filter, replacing X.500's matchedValuesOnly boolean.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAPv3 control, its ASN.1 syntax, server behaviour, and interactions with other LDAP controls, so it is squarely about LDAP.
LDAP.quote: This document describes a control for the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol version 3 that is used to return a subset of attribute values from an entry.

rejected.why: X.500 DAP's matchedValuesOnly is discussed only as background in a short section; the document specifies an LDAP control.
ASN.1/BER is only the encoding used for the control value, not the subject.
userCertificate matching appears only in an example; the document is not about certificate profiles.
The IANA section merely registers the control OID; it is boilerplate.
ABNF is used only to write the string filter representation in the examples.

RFC3877.title: Alarm Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC3877.summary: Defines the ALARM-MIB and ITU-ALARM-MIB (plus IANA-ITU-ALARM-TC-MIB) SMIv2 modules for modelling alarms, storing active and cleared alarms, and mapping to ITU M.3100/X.733 alarm attributes.

MIB.why: The document's core content is the ALARM-MIB, ITU-ALARM-MIB and related textual-convention MIB modules in SMIv2, so it belongs on the MIB modules page.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

SNMP.why: The alarm framework builds on SNMP Notifications, the notification and target MIBs, and VACM. It specifies how SNMP fault management is done, beyond just defining objects.
SNMP.quote: This memo describes a method of using alarm management in SNMP to address these problems.

rejected.why: Logging is addressed via the Notification Log MIB, not the syslog protocol.
RMON alarms appear only as one modelling example in section 6.5; the document is not about RMON.
Alarm management is fault management of devices through SNMP, not an OAM mechanism. The generic network management tag fits better, but the specific MIB and SNMP tags are already assigned.
bgpBackwardTransition is only used as an example of resource ID derivation.
The IANA-maintained probable cause textual convention is a small part of the document. It is a registry of enumerations inside a MIB module, not a document about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: Alarm management / fault management
gaps.why: The document is about alarm modelling and fault management, which the taxonomy lacks as a topic. It could sit under network management, alongside telemetry and OAM.

RFC3878.title: Alarm Reporting Control Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC3878.summary: Defines the ARC-MIB SMIv2 module, whose table lets a manager suppress or defer alarm reporting per resource and alarm type, modelled on ITU-T M.3100 Amd3 ARC states.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification (ARC-MIB) with object definitions, textual conventions and conformance groups, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: This document defines an alarm reporting control (ARC) MIB module, which provides a mechanism for a manager to suppress or defer the reporting of alarm conditions

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Alarm reporting control is related to operations and maintenance, but the document is a MIB module and the MIB tag already covers it.
It imports the IANA-maintained probable-cause textual convention, but it only references that registry. It does not address IANA stewardship.

gaps.name: Alarm management / alarm reporting control
gaps.why: The document is about controlling the reporting of alarm conditions (ITU-T M.3100 ARC states: nalm, nalmQI, nalmTI). The taxonomy has no alarm-management tag, so only the generic MIB tag applies.

RFC3879.title: Deprecating Site Local Addresses
RFC3879.summary: Formally deprecates the IPv6 site-local unicast prefix FEC0::/10, explaining the ambiguity and ill-defined-site problems for developers, managers and routers, while allowing existing use to continue.

addressing.why: The document is about IPv6 address architecture: it deprecates a unicast address prefix, discusses address scope and ambiguity, and asks IANA to mark the prefix deprecated. IPv6 is only the context, and the subject is address allocation and use, so the addressing topic fits better than the broader IPv6 tag.
addressing.quote: This document formally deprecates the IPv6 site-local unicast prefix defined in [RFC3513], i.e., 1111111011 binary or FEC0::/10.

rejected.why: The document is about a specific part of IPv6 addressing, the site-local prefix. The addressing topic captures that better than the general IPv6 tag.
The IANA request to mark FEC0::/10 as deprecated is boilerplate-level and does not make the document about IANA registries.
RFC 1918 private addresses are mentioned only as an analogy for leaks, and the document does not address NAT.
The scope identifier problem for developers touches socket address structures, but the document does not extend or specify the sockets API.
Multi-homed hosts are mentioned only as an example of developer pain, and the document is not about multihoming architecture.

RFC3880.title: Call Processing Language (CPL): A Language for User Control of Internet Telephony Services
RFC3880.summary: Defines the Call Processing Language (CPL), an XML-based, non-Turing-complete language for describing user control of Internet telephony services (call routing, screening, forwarding) on servers or user agents, independent of SIP or H.323.

CPL.why: The whole document specifies CPL: its nodes, switches, location modifiers, operations, extensions and XML schema.
CPL.quote: This document defines the Call Processing Language (CPL), a language to describe and control Internet telephony services.

rejected.why: SIP is the main signalling protocol CPL maps onto (per-node SIP usage subsections), but the document specifies CPL, not SIP; it is the substrate.
CPL syntax is XML with a schema, but XML is only the encoding; the document is about the language, not XML usage as such.
Appendix B gives a non-normative H.323 mapping, a minor part; H.323 is not the subject.
Time switches reuse iCalendar recurrence rules from RFC 2445, but the document defines a CPL construct and does not specify iCalendar.
Sieve is only cited as inspiration for the language's design.
Registers application/cpl+xml in IANA Considerations, which is boilerplate-level registration, not the main subject.

RFC3881.title: Security Audit and Access Accountability Message XML Data Definitions for Healthcare Applications
RFC3881.summary: Defines an XML schema and data elements for security audit messages (who accessed healthcare data, when, from where, which records) as a reference for healthcare standards developers.

XML.why: The document's main deliverable is an XML schema (Section 6) defining the audit message format. It is an XML-based format specification, so readers of XML-based formats would look for it.
XML.quote: The format is defined as an XML schema, which is intended as a reference for healthcare standards developers and application designers.

operational security.why: The document is about security auditing and access accountability: what to log, trigger events, and how to review use of data. It fits operational security practice, with no more specific tag available.
operational security.quote: This data collection and review process is called security auditing.

rejected.why: It defines an audit message format and does not specify the syslog protocol or transport. The document says transport and implementation are out of scope.
Healthcare privacy is the motivation, but the document defines audit record data, not privacy threat models or protocol privacy considerations.
IDMEF is for intrusion detection alerts. This audit schema is for retrospective access accountability, not intrusion detection.
NTP is mentioned once as a suggested common time base. The document is not about it.
Event timestamps use ISO 8601 UTC, but that is a minor field detail and not a subject of the document.
Role-based access control appears only as audit trigger events and role identifiers in records. The document does not specify authorization mechanisms.

gaps.name: Healthcare security audit / health informatics
gaps.why: The document is domain-specific to healthcare audit logging (HL7, DICOM, IHE). The taxonomy has no tag for audit logging or healthcare applications. The closest matches are operational security and XML.

RFC3882.title: Configuring BGP to Block Denial-of-Service Attacks
RFC3882.summary: Describes an operational technique using BGP communities to trigger selective remote black-holing of attacked destinations on chosen border routers, plus sinkhole tunnels (e.g. MPLS TE) to pull attack traffic to a sinkhole router for analysis.

BGP communities.why: The core technique assigns community values per border router and matches them in iBGP import policy to selectively alter next hop; this is an operational use of BGP communities.
BGP communities.quote: uses BGP communities to remotely trigger black-holing of a particular destination network to block denial-of-service attacks

DDoS.why: The document is about mitigating DoS attacks via remotely triggered black-holing and sinkholing, which is DDoS mitigation practice.
DDoS.quote: Configuring BGP to Block Denial-of-Service Attacks

rejected.why: The more specific child BGP communities fits; the document is about community-driven policy, not the BGP protocol generally.
MPLS TE tunnels are only mentioned as an example transport for sinkhole tunnels, not specified or analysed.
Considered as a broad fit, but the DDoS tag is more specific for attack mitigation.
ICMP unreachable messages are mentioned only as a side effect used to trace attack sources.
MPLS Traffic Engineering is mentioned only as an example tunnel mechanism.

gaps.name: Remotely triggered black hole (RTBH) filtering
gaps.why: The document describes BGP-triggered black-holing and sinkhole routing as operational techniques; the taxonomy has no specific tag for RTBH or sinkholing, so they are covered only under DDoS and BGP communities.

RFC3883.title: Detecting Inactive Neighbors over OSPF Demand Circuits (DC)
RFC3883.summary: RFC 3883 updates RFC 1793 by adding a "neighbor probing" mechanism, using LSA flooding and acknowledgements, so OSPF routers can detect inactive neighbors over demand circuits where Hello packets are suppressed.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF demand circuit behaviour (RFC 1793) with a new probing mechanism based on OSPF flooding, new interface parameters and adjacency handling.
OSPF.quote: This memo introduces a new mechanism called "neighbor probing" to address the above problem.

rejected.why: The document concerns OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328) and RFC 1793 only, not OSPF for IPv6.
BFD is a different liveness detection mechanism and is not mentioned. This document builds on OSPF's own LSA flooding and acknowledgements.
The document is about one protocol's behaviour, so the specific OSPF tag fits better than the general routing topic.

RFC3884.title: Use of IPsec Transport Mode for Dynamic Routing
RFC3884.summary: Informational RFC proposing IIPtran, which uses RFC 2003 IPIP tunnel interfaces plus IPsec transport mode instead of IPsec tunnel mode so dynamic routing and source address selection work inside IPsec-secured virtual networks/VPNs, and compares it with alternatives.

IPsec.why: The document analyses IPsec tunnel vs transport mode, SAs, SADs and selectors, and proposes a configuration of IPsec to avoid routing conflicts.
IPsec.quote: An alternative to tunnel mode uses non-IPsec IPIP encapsulation together with IPsec transport mode, which we call IIPtran.

IP-in-IP.why: IPIP encapsulation is a core element of the proposal, and the appendix addresses IPIP encapsulation/decapsulation issues (DF flag, protocol 4) with IPsec.
IP-in-IP.quote: IIPtran uses IPIP tunnels (as defined in RFC 2003 [2]), followed by IPsec transport mode on the encapsulated packet.

VPN.why: The document is about securing virtual network and VPN links and supporting dynamic routing within them.
VPN.quote: IPsec can secure the links of a multihop network to protect communication between trusted components, e.g., for a secure virtual network (VN), overlay, or virtual private network (VPN).

rejected.why: IKE impact is discussed in one subsection, but the document is not about IKE itself.
ESP/AH are only referenced as the headers inserted by IPsec; not specified or analysed.
Dynamic routing is the motivation, but no routing protocol is specified or changed; the focus is IPsec/tunnel configuration.
Overlays are mentioned as virtual networks, but the taxonomy tag concerns data-plane encapsulations like VXLAN, which this is not.
Parent of IP-in-IP, which is already chosen.
Mobile IP is mentioned only as the origin of RFC 2003.

RFC3885.title: SMTP Service Extension for Message Tracking
RFC3885.summary: Defines the MTRK SMTP service extension, adding an MTRK parameter to MAIL (with mandatory ENVID/ORCPT) so a sender can mark a message for later tracking and MTAs retain and forward tracking certifiers.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new ESMTP extension (EHLO keyword MTRK, MAIL parameter) and its relay behaviour between MTAs, so it belongs on the SMTP page.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby a client may mark a message for future tracking.

rejected.why: SHA-1 is used only to hash the random secret and long host names; the document is not about the hash family.
SMTP is the more specific tag and covers the extension, so the parent is not needed.
Base64 is only imported as an encoding for the certifier, not a subject of the document.
The document extends the SMTP envelope, not the message headers or format.

gaps.name: Message Tracking (MTRK / MTQP)
gaps.why: The document is about tracking messages through MTAs and the companion Message Tracking Query Protocol. The taxonomy has no tag for message tracking or delivery status.

RFC3886.title: An Extensible Message Format for Message Tracking Responses
RFC3886.summary: Defines the message/tracking-status MIME content type, modeled on RFC 3464 DSNs, used to return message tracking status (per-message and per-recipient fields, actions, a new enhanced status code) for undelivered email.

email.why: The document specifies a status-report message format for tracking email delivery, alongside DSNs and MDNs. It is about email delivery status and tracking, and no narrower child tag fits.
email.quote: This memo defines a MIME [RFC-MIME] content-type for message tracking status in the same spirit as RFC 3464

media types.why: It defines and registers a new MIME media type, message/tracking-status, with its encoding and parameter rules.
media types.quote: MIME type name:           message MIME subtype name:        tracking-status

rejected.why: The SMTP extension for tracking is defined in a separate memo (RFC 3885). This one only defines the status format.
MIME is the substrate here. The document defines one new content type, which the media types tag covers.
This is a MIME status body modeled on RFC 3464, not the Internet message header and addressing format itself.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax.

gaps.name: Message Tracking (MTRK) / Delivery Status Notifications
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for email message tracking or DSN/MDN delivery status reporting. These subjects are central to the document and would help readers browsing related RFCs 3885, 3887 and 3888.

RFC3887.title: Message Tracking Query Protocol
RFC3887.summary: Specifies the Message Tracking Query Protocol (MTQP), a line-oriented TCP protocol (port 1038) for querying the path and status of messages sent via SMTP, with TRACK, STARTTLS, COMMENT and QUIT commands, SRV-based server discovery, and an mtqp URI scheme.

email.why: The whole protocol exists to track email messages sent via SMTP and report their routing status. No narrower email tag fits a tracking query protocol, so the general email tag is used.
email.quote: Message tracking is the ability to find out the path that a particular message has taken through a messaging system and the current routing status of that message.

URI.why: The document defines and registers a new URI scheme, mtqp, with syntax, encoding rules and a registration template.
URI.quote: mtqp://<mserver>/track/<unique-envid>/<mtrk-secret>

rejected.why: The document relies on SMTP extensions defined in a companion RFC. It only queries the status of messages that were sent via SMTP and does not specify SMTP itself.
STARTTLS is used as a security mechanism, following the RFC 3207 model. The document defines no new TLS extension.
Responses carry message/tracking-status bodies defined in a companion RFC. MIME is only the encoding for the response.
SRV lookup is used for server discovery, but the document defines no new DNS record type.
SASL is mentioned only to say it is not used.

gaps.name: Message tracking
gaps.why: The document is about tracking messages through a messaging system. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it, so the general email tag is the closest fit.

RFC3888.title: Message Tracking Model and Requirements
RFC3888.summary: RFC 3888 provides a model and requirements for tracking messages through the Internet email infrastructure, defining tracking entities, enabling/request models, and a hash-based authentication scheme.

email.why: The document models tracking of Internet mail through MUAs, MSAs, MTAs, with DSN/MDN integration and requirements for tracking solutions; this is email architecture.
email.quote: Message tracking is the ability to find out the path that a particular message has taken through a messaging system and the current routing status of that message.

rejected.why: The SMTP tracking extension is specified in RFC 3885, not here; this document only references SMTP DSN extensions.
Message-Id and headers are mentioned only incidentally; the Message/Tracking-Status format is in RFC 3886.
One-time passwords are only cited as an analogy for the hash-based authentication technique.
The authentication scheme is a minor illustrative part of the security section, not a main subject.
Multipart/Report is referenced only in passing as the format for DSN/MDN.

RFC3890.title: A Transport Independent Bandwidth Modifier for the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC3890.summary: Defines the SDP TIAS (Transport Independent Application Specific maximum) bandwidth modifier and the maxprate packet-rate attribute, so transport-dependent bit-rates can be computed independent of IP version or other lower-layer overhead.
