SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new bandwidth modifier (TIAS) and a new maxprate attribute, and registers them for SDP.
SDP.quote: A new session and media level bandwidth modifier is defined: b=TIAS:<bandwidth-value>

RTP.why: A substantial part defines how TIAS maps to RTP session bandwidth and how RTP payload is counted, which RTP readers need.
RTP.quote: For RTP transported media streams, TIAS at the SDP media level can be used to derive the RTP "session bandwidth"

RTCP.why: The document specifies how to derive RTCP bandwidth from TIAS and analyses RTCP fairness across IPv4/IPv6 hosts.
RTCP.quote: This section provides a consistent way of calculating the bit-rate to assign to RTCP, if not explicitly given.

rejected.why: SIP is only one of the protocols that carries SDP; Section 7.2 notes usage is no different from AS, which is a brief interaction note.
RTSP is a protocol that carries SDP and appears in a short interaction section; the document does not specify or extend it.
IPv4/IPv6 header size differences motivate the problem, but the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
Header compression is mentioned only as background on mechanisms that change overhead (Section 1.3.2).
IPsec is mentioned only briefly as another source of extra overhead.

RFC3891.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) "Replaces" Header
RFC3891.summary: Defines the SIP Replaces header and "replaces" option tag, letting an INVITE logically replace an existing dialog (for attended transfer, call pickup), with UAS/UAC behaviour, syntax and authorization security guidance.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP extension header and option tag, specifying UAS, UAC and proxy behaviour for it.
SIP.quote: The Replaces header is used to logically replace an existing SIP dialog with a new SIP dialog.

rejected.why: Not discussed; the document concerns dialog matching in SIP signalling, not session description.
Authorization of replacement is discussed, but it relies on existing Digest/S/MIME mechanisms and is not the document's subject.
Mentioned only as an existing mechanism to authenticate replacement requests.
Digest is referenced only as an existing authentication option, with nothing new defined about it.
The dialog event package is only mentioned as a way to learn dialog information.

RFC3892.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Referred-By Mechanism
RFC3892.summary: Defines the SIP Referred-By header field, an S/MIME-protected Referred-By token (an Authenticated Identity Body), and the 429 "Provide Referrer Identity" response. These let a REFER's referrer convey its identity to the refer target through the referee.

SIP.why: The RFC extends SIP with a new header field (Referred-By), a new 429 response code, and referrer, referee and refer-target behaviour for the REFER method.
SIP.quote: This document extends the REFER method, allowing the referrer to provide information about the REFER request to the refer target using the referee as an intermediary.

rejected.why: S/MIME protects the token, but the RFC only uses it through the Authenticated Identity Body defined in RFC 3893. It does not specify S/MIME itself.
SDP appears only in the example messages and is not part of the mechanism.
The token carries a signed claim of the referrer's identity. The RFC's subject is a SIP header mechanism, and the SIP tag already covers it.
The token is carried in a MIME body part identified by Content-ID. MIME is only the container, not the subject.
The IANA section only registers the header and response code, which is boilerplate.

RFC3893.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Authenticated Identity Body (AIB) Format
RFC3893.summary: Defines the Authenticated Identity Body (AIB), a signed (optionally encrypted) message/sipfrag MIME body with Content-Disposition 'aib' that gives SIP requests and responses a verifiable sender identity, plus rules for populating and processing it.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP security by defining the AIB format and rules for INVITE, non-INVITE and response identity and for recipient processing.
SIP.quote: provides a more specific mechanism to derive integrity and authentication properties from an 'authenticated identity body', a digitally-signed SIP message, or message fragment.

S/MIME.why: AIBs are signed and optionally encrypted using S/MIME, with signing-versus-encryption ordering rules and examples. This is a substantial part of the document, though S/MIME itself is not newly specified.
S/MIME.quote: Many SIP entities that support the use of S/MIME for signatures also support S/MIME encryption, as described in RFC 3261, Section 23.4.3.

rejected.why: The document only defines a new Content-Disposition value and reuses message/sipfrag. It does not register a media type.
MIME is the container for the AIB, and the document only adds a new disposition-type value.
SDP appears only as another body in the example INVITE.
The PKCS#7 signatures are used via S/MIME, and CMS is not discussed in its own right.
The parent topic is covered by the more specific SIP and S/MIME tags. STIR is also not applicable, since it came later.
This is a precursor mechanism for caller identity in SIP, but the document does not specify STIR.

RFC3894.title: Sieve Extension: Copying Without Side Effects
RFC3894.summary: Defines the Sieve ":copy" extension to the "fileinto" and "redirect" actions, letting a script file or forward a copy of a message without cancelling the implicit "keep".

Sieve.why: The RFC is a Sieve language extension. It adds the ":copy" tag and the "copy" capability string to the fileinto and redirect commands.
Sieve.quote: This document defines a new keyword parameter, ":copy", to be used with the Sieve "fileinto" and "redirect" actions.

rejected.why: Email is the domain Sieve filters, but the document specifies only a filtering-language extension. The more specific Sieve tag covers it.
IMAP is mentioned only as an example of a local message store that fileinto can target. The document says nothing about IMAP itself.
The redirect action forwards mail, but the document does not specify or discuss SMTP.
LDAP over TLS appears only in the Security Considerations as advice for protecting write access to scripts. It is not a subject of the document.
The document registers the 'copy' Sieve capability, but that is boilerplate registration and not the subject.

RFC3895.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the DS1, E1, DS2, and E2 Interface Types
RFC3895.summary: RFC 3895 defines the SMIv2 MIB module for managing DS1, E1, DS2 and E2 interfaces (configuration, line status, loopbacks, 15-minute performance statistics, far-end data, channelization), obsoleting RFC 2495.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification for DS1/E1/DS2/E2 interface types, with object definitions, compliance statements and groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

SNMP.why: The MIB is built for SNMP management, including traps, proxy agent behaviour and SNMPv3 security guidance, so SNMP readers would want it. MIB is a child of SNMP, so this tag is arguably implied, but the SNMP-specific content (agents, proxy, traps) is substantial.
SNMP.quote: MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

rejected.why: ISDN Primary Rate appears only in compliance statements for T1/E1 PRI lines; the document is not about ISDN access.
The 15-minute interval error statistics are counters inside the MIB, which is already covered by the MIB tag; the document is not a measurement methodology.
SONET/SDH is mentioned only as a companion MIB document, not as a subject of this one.
The transmit clock source object is a line configuration option, not about clock synchronization over networks.

gaps.name: DS1/E1/DS2/E2 (T1/E1) TDM interfaces
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TDM digital hierarchy carrier circuits such as DS0/DS1/DS3 and E1/E3. The document covers their framing, line coding, alarms, loopbacks and error-event terminology, which readers of that subject would want.

RFC3896.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the DS3/E3 Interface Type
RFC3896.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces (configuration, near/far-end performance statistics, loopbacks, line status traps, channelization), obsoleting RFC 2496.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (DS3-MIB) for DS3/E3 interfaces, with tables, notifications and conformance groups written in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document specifies no SNMP protocol behaviour, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
SONET/SDH is mentioned only as a companion MIB document. This document is about DS3/E3 interfaces.
The document defines error-second counters and 15-minute interval statistics, but only as objects inside the interface MIB, not as a measurement methodology.
DS3/E3 is a physical/transmission interface. The taxonomy has no DS3/E3 tag, and the generic link layer topic is not specific enough to justify a tag.

gaps.name: DS3/E3 (T-carrier/PDH) transmission interfaces
gaps.why: The document is about DS3/E3 digital hierarchy interface management. The taxonomy has no tag for PDH/T-carrier interfaces such as DS0, DS1 or DS3, so it is covered only by the generic MIB tag.

RFC3897.title: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) Entities and End Points Communication
RFC3897.summary: RFC 3897 documents requirements for OPES entities (systems, processors, callout servers) to support in-band tracing of adaptations and a bypass (non-blocking) feature, leaving application-protocol encodings to separate binding documents.

OPES.why: The whole document specifies tracing and bypass requirements for OPES systems, processors and callout servers, so it belongs on the OPES subject page.
OPES.quote: This memo documents tracing and non-blocking (bypass) requirements for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES).

rejected.why: HTTP is mentioned only as an analogy (reload) and as a future binding target; the document defines no HTTP behaviour.
A CDN appears only as an example of an OPES system; the document is not about content delivery networks.
The document covers application-level adaptation in general, and OPES already sits under web. No broader web tag is needed.
Bypass instructions identify services by URI, but the document defines nothing new about URIs.

RFC3898.title: Network Information Service (NIS) Configuration Options for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC3898.summary: Defines four DHCPv6 options (NIS servers, NIS+ servers, NIS domain name, NIS+ domain name) for configuring clients with Network Information Service information over IPv6.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines new DHCPv6 options, with option codes, formats and the messages in which they may appear, extending DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes four options for passing configuration information related to Network Information Service (NIS) [3] in DHCPv6 (RFC 3315 [1]).

rejected.why: IPv6 is the address family the options carry, but the document is about DHCPv6 options, not IPv6 itself; the DHCPv6 tag covers it.
Domain names are encoded using the DHCPv6 domain name representation, but the NIS domain names are not DNS and the document says nothing new about DNS.
The parent tag is implied by DHCPv6, and the document concerns only the IPv6 variant.
The IANA section only records option code assignments, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Network Information Service (NIS / NIS+)
gaps.why: The document is about configuring NIS and NIS+ clients, but the taxonomy has no tag for NIS or Sun's directory and naming services.

RFC3901.title: DNS IPv6 Transport Operational Guidelines
RFC3901.summary: BCP giving operational guidelines to avoid DNS name space fragmentation in mixed IPv4/IPv6 networks: recursive servers must be IPv4-only or dual-stack, and every zone must have at least one IPv4-reachable authoritative server.

DNS.why: The document is operational guidance for DNS resolvers and authoritative servers, covering referral chains, zone delegation and name server reachability.
DNS.quote: guidelines and Best Current Practice for operating DNS in a world where queries and responses are carried in a mixed environment of IPv4 and IPv6 networks

IPv6 transition.why: It addresses IPv4/IPv6 coexistence for DNS, with dual-stack recommendations to keep the name space unfragmented during the transition.
IPv6 transition.quote: the transition will be from IPv4 only to a mixture of IPv4 and IPv6, with three categories of DNS data

rejected.why: IPv6 is the transport context. The document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself, and the more specific IPv6 transition tag already covers the IPv6 subject.
The document does not discuss address synthesis for NAT64. It only recommends dual-stack recursive servers.
IPv4 is only one side of the coexistence discussion and is not itself the subject of the document.

RFC3902.title: The "application/soap+xml" media type
RFC3902.summary: Registers the "application/soap+xml" media type for SOAP 1.2 message envelopes serialized as XML 1.0, defining its charset and action parameters and registration template fields.

media types.why: The document's sole purpose is a media type registration, with parameters, encoding and security considerations in the registration template.
media types.quote: This specification defines the media type "application/soap+xml" which can be used to identify SOAP 1.2 message envelopes that have been serialized with XML 1.0.

XML.why: The media type is an XML-based (+xml) type and inherits charset, encoding, fragment and base URI rules from the XML media types; XML-based formats are a substantial part of the document.
XML.quote: SOAP 1.2 message envelopes that have been serialised with XML 1.0; message envelopes with a different SOAP namespace version or using another XML serialisation MUST NOT use it.

rejected.why: The action parameter replaces the SOAPAction HTTP header, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
The action parameter is a URI-reference, but this is only a parameter value and the document does not address URIs themselves.
The media type registration falls under the more specific 'media types' tag.
SOAP is a web-services messaging framework but the document only registers a media type.

gaps.name: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) 1.2 / web services
gaps.why: The document concerns identifying SOAP 1.2 envelopes, but the taxonomy has no tag for SOAP or web services messaging.

RFC3903.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Extension for Event State Publication
RFC3903.summary: Defines the SIP PUBLISH method, with SIP-ETag and SIP-If-Match headers and the 412 response code, letting event publication agents publish soft event state (first use: presence) to an event state compositor.

SIMPLE.why: The PUBLISH extension is a core SIMPLE specification, extending SIP events and presence with event state publication by a presence user agent to a presence compositor.
SIMPLE.quote: This document describes an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for publishing event state used within the SIP Events framework.

SIP.why: It extends SIP with a new method, two new header fields and a new response code, and specifies UAC/UAS processing rules. SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new SIP method, PUBLISH, for publishing event state.

rejected.why: PIDF is the default body format for presence publication. The document does not define or extend it.
Entity-tags are adapted from HTTP/1.1 for conceptual similarity only. The document does not specify HTTP.
Presence is the first application, but the document defines a SIP event publication mechanism, not presence or instant messaging as such.
Used only as a security mechanism in Security Considerations.
Digest authentication is required only through SIP, in the security section.

RFC3904.title: Evaluation of IPv6 Transition Mechanisms for Unmanaged Networks
RFC3904.summary: Informational analysis of IPv6 transition mechanisms (automatic vs configured tunnels, NAT traversal, prefix delegation, ND proxy, name resolution) for home and small-office unmanaged networks across four deployment cases, with recommendations for v6ops.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document evaluates IPv6/IPv4 transition mechanisms (6to4, Teredo, tunnel brokers, IPv4-over-IPv6) and recommends which to develop.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document analyzes issues involved in the transition of "unmanaged networks" from IPv4 to IPv6.

6to4.why: 6to4 is evaluated at length: relays, anycast relay discovery, scarcity and the parallel-Internet risk.
6to4.quote: The requirements of case C can be solved by an automatic tunneling mechanism such as 6to4 [6TO4].

Teredo.why: Teredo is analysed as the main automatic NAT-traversing tunnel, including relay deployment and parallel-Internet risk.
Teredo.quote: An automatic solution like Teredo appears to be a good fit for providing IPv6 connectivity to hosts behind NAT, in case A of IPv6 deployment.

home networking.why: The scope is home/small-office gateways: prefix delegation, ND proxy, local naming and security for these networks.
home networking.quote: Unmanaged networks typically correspond to home networks or small office networks.

DHCPv6.why: DHCPv6 prefix delegation and DNS configuration are evaluated, including authentication gaps, as the explicit delegation method.
DHCPv6.quote: Several networks have already started using an explicit prefix delegation mechanism using DHCPv6.

rejected.why: NAT traversal is discussed as a transition requirement, but the document is not about NAT behaviour itself; the NAT-traversal tunnelling content falls under transition.
ND proxy for multi-link subnets is discussed and recommended for standardization, but only as one connectivity option, not the document's main subject.
Tunnelling is central, but the specific IPv6 transition tags and parent IPv6 transition fit better.
Mentioned only as a possible reusable NAT traversal piece, not specified or analysed in depth.
Name resolution for IPv6 hosts is discussed (DDNS, resolver provisioning), but only as a requirement at a high level; DNS is not the subject.
Mentioned in passing as an existing VPN tunnel that could carry IPv6.

gaps.name: LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution)
gaps.why: The document recommends LLMNR for local name resolution in unmanaged networks, but the taxonomy has no tag for it; mDNS or naming are only loosely related.

gaps.name: Tunnel broker / Tunnel Setup Protocol
gaps.why: Configured tunnels via tunnel brokers and TSP are evaluated, but the taxonomy has no specific tag.

RFC3905.title: A Template for IETF Patent Disclosures and Licensing Declarations
RFC3905.summary: Informational RFC providing an optional template for IETF patent disclosures and licensing declarations, with commentary on the licensing options, to help disclosers meet RFC 3668 obligations.

IPR.why: The whole document is a template and commentary for patent disclosures and licensing declarations under the IETF IPR policy (RFC 3668), which is the IPR subject.
IPR.quote: this document proposes a patent disclosure and licensing declaration template that may be optionally used as one method for IETF participants and patent holders

rejected.why: The document concerns IETF process, but its subject is specifically IPR disclosure, which the IPR tag covers more precisely.
It is not about RFC format or publication; it only mentions RFC numbers as fields in the template.

RFC3906.title: Calculating Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) Routes Over Traffic Engineering Tunnels
RFC3906.summary: Informational RFC describing how link-state IGPs (IS-IS, OSPF) adapt the SPF computation to install IP routes over MPLS traffic engineering tunnels (IGP shortcuts), including metric adjustment of such routes.

traffic engineering.why: The document is about how IGP route calculation interacts with TE tunnels (IGP shortcuts), including metric adjustment for steering traffic over them. This is a traffic engineering subject.
traffic engineering.quote: this document describes how Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm can be adapted so that link-state IGPs will calculate IP routes to forward traffic over tunnels

OSPF.why: The SPF modification applies to OSPF and the document extends its route calculation, so OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: Link-state protocols like integrated Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) [1] and OSPF [2] use Dijkstra's SPF algorithm to compute a shortest path tree

IS-IS.why: The SPF modification equally applies to IS-IS, and the text uses IS-IS terms such as the TENTative and PATHS lists.
IS-IS.quote: Link-state protocols like integrated Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) [1] and OSPF [2] use Dijkstra's SPF algorithm

rejected.why: The TE tunnels are LSPs, but the document does not specify MPLS behaviour. It assumes the tunnels are already set up.
RSVP-TE is only cited as the way tunnels are created. The document says the shortcut mechanism assumes the tunnels already exist.
The document is a specific SPF enhancement, not general routing architecture or scalability.
Fast reroute is mentioned only as one reason tunnels exist, not as the subject.

RFC3909.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Cancel Operation
RFC3909.summary: Defines an LDAP extended operation (OID 1.3.6.1.1.8) that lets a client cancel an outstanding operation and receive a response indicating the outcome, with new result codes.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAP extended operation, its request/response encoding, semantics and result codes, so it belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: The Cancel operation is defined as an LDAP Extended Operation [RFC2251, Section 4.12] identified by the object identifier 1.3.6.1.1.8.

rejected.why: ASN.1 and BER are only used to describe the protocol elements; the document is not about them.
Start TLS is mentioned only as an operation that cannot be canceled; the document does not address TLS.
The X.511 DAP Abandon operation is cited as the model, but the document specifies an LDAP operation, not X.500.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-like and the body is not about IANA guidance.

RFC3910.title: The SPIRITS (Services in PSTN requesting Internet Services) Protocol
RFC3910.summary: RFC 3910 specifies the SPIRITS protocol, which uses SIP event packages (spirits-INDPs and spirits-user-prof) with an XML payload so PSTN/IN entities can notify Internet hosts of call-related and non-call events.

SPIRITS.why: The document defines the SPIRITS protocol itself: its event packages, detection-point parameters, XML schema and example services such as Internet Call Waiting.
SPIRITS.quote: The purpose of the SPIRITS protocol is to enable the execution of services in the Internet based on certain events occurring in the PSTN.

SIP.why: It defines two new SIP event packages, with SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY rules, Event and Allow-Events header usage, and forking prohibitions, extending SIP for PSTN notification.
SIP.quote: The SPIRITS protocol is a set of two "event packages" [3].

rejected.why: PINT is mentioned only as the reverse-direction protocol (Internet to PSTN) and as the secured interfaces A and E. This document is not about it.
XML is only the encoding for the payload. The XML schema is part of the SPIRITS definition and not a general XML topic.
S/MIME is mandated in Security Considerations only, which is boilerplate evidence.
The packages use RFC 3265 event notification, but they are not SIMPLE presence or event-package work. The presence example is incidental.
A MIME type is registered in the IANA section, but that is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
SIP-T appears only in the acronym list. There is no ISUP encapsulation work.

RFC3911.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) "Join" Header
RFC3911.summary: RFC 3911 defines the SIP Join header and "join" option tag, which let a new INVITE dialog be logically joined to an existing dialog for peer-to-peer multi-party call control (barge-in, screening, monitoring).

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP extension header, with UAS/UAC behaviour, syntax and an option tag.
SIP.quote: The Join header is used to logically join an existing SIP dialog with a new SIP dialog.

conferencing.why: Join creates or transitions to conferences, using a focus and conference URI. It is a multiparty call-control primitive, though it does not define a conferencing framework or data model.
conferencing.quote: One use of the "Join" header is to insert a new participant into a multimedia conversation (which may be a two-party call or a SIP conference [15]).

rejected.why: Digest is mentioned only as one way to authorize a join. The document is not about it.
Mentioned only as an authentication mechanism for join requests.
SDP is not discussed in the body.
ABNF is only the notation used for the header syntax.
Authorization of join requests is part of the UAS behaviour, but it is not the main subject, and the SIP tag covers it.

RFC3912.title: WHOIS Protocol Specification
RFC3912.summary: RFC 3912 re-specifies the WHOIS protocol as a TCP port 43 text query/response service, obsoleting RFC 954 and stripping out non-wire-protocol material.

WHOIS.why: The document is the standard specification of the WHOIS protocol itself, including its request/response framing and connection handling.
WHOIS.quote: A WHOIS server listens on TCP port 43 for requests from WHOIS clients.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport substrate for WHOIS; the document defines nothing new about TCP.
RDAP is not described; the document only mentions that a successor effort (CRISP) exists.
WHOIS was used for registered domain names, but the document only specifies the wire protocol; the WHOIS tag already sits under this parent.
Section 4 only notes that WHOIS has no character set indication; it defines no internationalization mechanism.
ASCII is mentioned for CR/LF terminators and the legacy encoding, but the document is not about ASCII.

RFC3913.title: Border Gateway Multicast Protocol (BGMP): Protocol Specification
RFC3913.summary: Specifies BGMP, an inter-domain multicast routing protocol that builds bidirectional shared trees of domains rooted at a root domain, with optional source-specific branches, its interaction with M-IGPs, message formats, error handling and FSM.

multicast.why: The document specifies an inter-domain multicast routing protocol. No more specific multicast tag exists for BGMP itself (PIM, MSDP, MOSPF and SSM are only referenced or interacted with), so the parent topic applies.
multicast.quote: BGMP, a protocol for inter-domain multicast routing.  BGMP builds shared trees for active multicast groups

rejected.why: BGMP borrows BGP's message structure, error handling and FSM, and uses BGP/MBGP as the EGP for its multicast RIB. The document specifies BGMP, not BGP.
PIM-SM is an M-IGP that BGMP interoperates with (section 4.4.2). It is not the subject of the document.
Only discussed as an M-IGP that BGMP must interact with (section 4.4.4).
The abstract says BGMP natively supports SSM. That is a feature of BGMP, not a specification of SSM.
TCP is only the transport BGMP runs over (port 264). The document defines nothing new about TCP.
Keyed MD5 is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the authentication mechanism.
Route reflectors are mentioned only in the terminology as one way internal BGP peers are connected.

RFC3914.title: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) Treatment of IAB Considerations
RFC3914.summary: Informational RFC explaining how the OPES framework addresses the nine IAB architectural considerations (consent, IP-layer addressability, notification via tracing, bypass, URI resolution, reference validity, privacy, encryption).

OPES.why: The whole document analyses the OPES framework's treatment of IAB considerations, covering tracing, bypass and consent mechanisms.
OPES.quote: IETF Internet Architecture Board (IAB) expressed nine architecture-level considerations for the Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) framework. This document describes how OPES addresses those considerations.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the example application protocol for trace headers; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
TLS is mentioned only as an example of hop-by-hop encryption in the encryption consideration.
CDNs appear as an example environment for notification, not as the subject.
The privacy consideration is only one short section about locating OPES privacy policies, not a privacy threat model.
It answers IAB considerations for OPES specifically; it is not about general Internet architecture principles.
URI resolution is discussed only as an out-of-scope consideration for OPES, not as a subject of the document.

RFC3915.title: Domain Registry Grace Period Mapping for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC3915.summary: Defines an EPP extension mapping to the domain name mapping that supports ICANN registry grace period policies, including redemption grace period restore requests and reports and new grace period status values.

EPP.why: The document specifies an extension of EPP's domain mapping: new status values, an extended <update> command with restore elements, and an <info> response extension.
EPP.quote: This document describes an extension mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) described in RFC 3730

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the notation used to specify the mapping. The document does not address XML usage in its own right.
The document concerns domain registration lifecycle policy, not DNS protocol, records or resolver behaviour.
WHOIS is mentioned only as an example of registration data that can go in a restore report.
This is the parent of EPP and is implied by the EPP tag.
The IANA section only registers the XML namespace and schema, which is boilerplate.

RFC3916.title: Requirements for Pseudo-Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3)
RFC3916.summary: Informational requirements document for the PWE3 working group, setting guidelines for pseudo-wire emulation of Ethernet, ATM and Frame Relay over packet switched networks: encapsulation, maintenance, management (MIBs), faithfulness, QoS and inter-domain issues.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines base requirements for pseudo-wire emulation.
pseudowire.quote: Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) is a mechanism that emulates the essential attributes of a service such as ATM, Frame Relay or Ethernet over a Packet Switched Network

rejected.why: MPLS is only one possible PSN/tunnel type; the document explicitly assumes no particular PSN or PW type.
L2TPv3 is only mentioned as an example PW or tunnel type, not specified or profiled.
Section 6 states MIB requirements for PWs, but it is a small part of the document and no MIB module is defined.
ATM is an example emulated service, but the document is about PWs generically.
Frame Relay is an example emulated service, not the subject.
Ethernet is an example emulated service, not the subject.

RFC3917.title: Requirements for IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC3917.summary: Informational requirements document for the IPFIX protocol, specifying what metering, exporting and collecting processes must do to export IP flow information from routers, probes and middleboxes.

IPFIX.why: The whole document defines requirements for IPFIX flow metering, information model, data model and export, so it belongs on the IPFIX page.
IPFIX.quote: This memo defines requirements for the export of measured IP flow information out of routers, traffic measurement probes, and middleboxes.

rejected.why: Sampling is covered only as a metering requirement (section 5.2), not as the PSAMP framework.
QoS monitoring is only one of several example applications; the document is about flow export, and IPFIX is the more specific tag.
SNMP and the Meter MIB are mentioned only for sysUpTime resolution and as a protocol-converter example.
Attack/intrusion detection is only one application used to derive requirements, not a subject of the document.
Anonymization is a minor optional requirement (6.7), not a substantial part of the document.
Traffic engineering is only an example application that drives requirements.

RFC3918.title: Methodology for IP Multicast Benchmarking
RFC3918.summary: Defines benchmarking methodology for IP multicast forwarding devices: throughput, forwarding, latency, IGMP join/leave delay, group capacity, and tunnel encapsulation tests, extending RFC 2544 and RFC 2432.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a BMWG benchmarking methodology defining test procedures, objectives and reporting formats for multicast forwarding devices.
benchmarking.quote: The purpose of this document is to describe methodology specific to the benchmarking of multicast IP forwarding devices.

multicast.why: The subject under test is IP multicast forwarding and group membership behaviour, so readers of the multicast subject would want this RFC.
multicast.quote: This document defines tests for measuring and reporting the throughput, forwarding, latency and Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) group membership characteristics of devices that support IP multicast

rejected.why: IGMP is used as the stimulus for join/leave delay tests, but the document does not specify or extend IGMP. It only measures device behaviour.
The more specific benchmarking tag applies, and this is device benchmarking rather than network performance metrics.
Encapsulation/decapsulation throughput tests exist, but they are one test among many and no particular tunnel protocol is covered.

RFC3919.title: Remote Network Monitoring (RMON) Protocol Identifiers for IPv6 and Multi Protocol Label Switching (MPLS)
RFC3919.summary: Informational RFC defining RMON-2 protocol identifier macros for MPLS (unicast and multicast), IPv6, IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling and ICMPv6, to extend RFC 2896 for protocolDirTable indexing.

RMON.why: The document extends RMON-2 by defining protocol identifier macros used in protocolDirTable INDEX encodings; this is the RMON subject area.
RMON.quote: This memo defines additional (to those in RFC 2896) protocol identifier examples for IP version 6 and MPLS protocols.

MPLS.why: A substantial part defines mplsu and mplsm identifiers for MPLS label stack encoding over ether2, snap, 802-1Q and PPP.
MPLS.quote: This section defines protocol identifiers for MPLS with unambiguous names to distinguish MPLS Unicast from MPLS Multicast.

IPv6.why: Defines ip6, ipip6 and icmp6 identifiers, with child encoding and address format for IPv6, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: The protocol identifiers for the Internet Protocol, Version 6 [RFC2460].

rejected.why: The document references SMIv2 boilerplate but defines no MIB module; it provides protocol identifier macros for the RMON-2 MIB, so RMON fits better.
SNMP appears only in the management framework boilerplate and is not the subject.
icmp6 is defined only as a protocol identifier entry, not specified or analysed as ICMPv6.
ipip6 is a single identifier for IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling; tunnelling itself is not the subject.

RFC3920.title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Core
RFC3920.summary: RFC 3920 specifies the core of XMPP 1.0: XML streams, JID addressing, TLS and SASL stream negotiation, resource binding, server dialback, message/presence/IQ stanzas, and error handling.

XMPP.why: The document is the core specification of XMPP, defining streams, stanzas, addressing, and negotiation.
XMPP.quote: This memo defines the core features of the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP), a protocol for streaming Extensible Markup Language (XML) elements

rejected.why: TLS is used via STARTTLS to secure streams. The document defines XMPP's use of it, not new TLS features, so it is only a substrate.
The document profiles SASL for XMPP authentication, but the focus is XMPP. SASL is the mechanism relied on.
Instant messaging and presence semantics are deferred to RFC 3921 (XMPP-IM). The parent XMPP tag already covers this document.
XML is the encoding substrate, and the XML usage restrictions in Section 11 are specific to XMPP.
Nodeprep and Resourceprep are stringprep profiles for JIDs. PRECIS is the successor framework and is not defined here.
DNS SRV lookups are used for server resolution, but only as supporting infrastructure.

gaps.name: stringprep profiles (Nodeprep, Resourceprep)
gaps.why: The document defines two new stringprep profiles for internationalized JIDs, and the taxonomy has no stringprep tag. PRECIS and IDN are the nearest tags.

RFC3921.title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Instant Messaging and Presence
RFC3921.summary: RFC 3921 specifies the XMPP extensions for basic instant messaging and presence: session establishment, message and presence stanzas, subscriptions, rosters, privacy-list blocking, and IM-specific server routing rules.

XMPP.why: The whole document specifies XMPP's IM and presence application: sessions, rosters, subscriptions, privacy lists, and routing rules.
XMPP.quote: This memo describes extensions to and applications of the core features of the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) that provide the basic instant messaging (IM) and presence

rejected.why: XMPP is the more specific child tag under instant messaging, so the parent is implied.
The document defines XMPP presence stanzas, not the PIDF format.
SIMPLE is only mentioned as an alternative protocol label in SRV resolution; this document is not about it.
XML is the encoding substrate for XMPP stanzas; the document does not define anything new about XML itself.
SRV lookups for server-to-server routing are a brief substrate use, not the subject of the document.
TLS and SASL are used by the XMPP core, which is defined in RFC 3920; this document does not address them.

RFC3922.title: Mapping the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) to Common Presence and Instant Messaging (CPIM)
RFC3922.summary: Defines a mapping between XMPP message/presence stanzas and the CPIM formats (Message/CPIM, PIDF, im:/pres: URIs) for gateways between XMPP and non-XMPP instant messaging and presence services.

XMPP.why: The document specifies how XMPP stanzas, addresses and presence subscriptions map to CPIM, so XMPP readers would look for it.
XMPP.quote: This memo describes a mapping between the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) and the Common Presence and Instant Messaging (CPIM) specifications.

instant messaging.why: The document covers CPIM instant messaging and presence interworking, including the gateway acting as a presence service with subscribe, notify and unsubscribe semantics.
instant messaging.quote: Syntax Mapping of Instant Messages

PIDF.why: A large part of the document maps XMPP presence stanzas to and from PIDF documents (tuples, basic status, contact, priority).
PIDF.quote: The XMPP <status/> element maps to the PIDF <note/> child of the PIDF <tuple/> element.

rejected.why: Message/CPIM and MIME content types are used as the bearer format but MIME itself is not the subject.
XML is the encoding of stanzas and PIDF only; the document does not address XML as such.
The im: and pres: address mapping is a small section and does not define the schemes.
Not about SIP-based presence; CPIM gateway mapping only.

gaps.name: CPIM (Common Presence and Instant Messaging)
gaps.why: The abstract IM/presence interoperability framework and Message/CPIM format are central to this document, but the taxonomy has no tag for them; instant messaging is the closest fit.

RFC3923.title: End-to-End Signing and Object Encryption for the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)
RFC3923.summary: Defines end-to-end signing and encryption of XMPP messages, directed presence and arbitrary stanzas by wrapping S/MIME (CMS) objects of CPIM/PIDF/application/xmpp+xml content in an <e2e/> element, and registers the application/xmpp+xml media type.

XMPP.why: The document extends XMPP with an <e2e/> wrapper element and namespace, defining how to secure message, presence and iq stanzas and handle errors.
XMPP.quote: This memo defines methods of end-to-end signing and object encryption for the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP).

S/MIME.why: Signing and encryption use S/MIME; Section 6 gives rules for S/MIME generation and handling, certificate names, ordering and mandatory algorithms.
S/MIME.quote: Signing MUST use [SMIME] signatures with [CMS] SignedData.

media types.why: The document defines and registers the new application/xmpp+xml media type to carry arbitrary XMPP stanzas.
media types.quote: The "application/xmpp+xml" media type adheres to the guidelines specified in [XML-MEDIA].

PIDF.why: Presence securing is done by signing/encrypting PIDF objects, and the document ties its interworking requirement to the CPIM presence format.
PIDF.quote: Generate an "application/pidf+xml" object as defined in [PIDF].

rejected.why: CMS SignedData/EnvelopedData is used via S/MIME, and the document specifies mandatory algorithms but not CMS itself.
The document is about XMPP, the more specific tag, and the CPIM interworking is a requirement rather than the main subject.
XML is the encoding substrate (CDATA wrapping, schema); the document does not address XML usage in its own right.
RSA and AES are only listed as mandatory-to-implement algorithms, not discussed in their own right.
Certificate names (subjectAltName with JIDs) are specified, but this is a small part and mainly the S/MIME certificate handling.

RFC3924.title: Cisco Architecture for Lawful Intercept in IP Networks
RFC3924.summary: Informational Cisco-specific architecture for lawful interception of voice and data traffic in IP networks, defining a reference model (IAPs, mediation device, LEA handover interfaces) and using SNMPv3 with a TAP-MIB to control content intercepts.

security.why: The whole document is an architecture for lawful interception, including undetectability, access control and protection of intercept existence. The taxonomy has no lawful-intercept tag, so the general security topic is the closest fit.
security.quote: lawful intercept is the lawfully authorized interception and monitoring of communications

SNMP.why: SNMPv3 with the TAP-MIB is the specified mechanism for the content intercept request interface (d). Section 5.1 covers USM and VACM controls for it, so SNMP readers would want this document.
SNMP.quote: It makes use of a common request protocol (SNMPv3) regardless of the type of application (e.g., voice, data)

rejected.why: SIP, H.323, MGCP and H.248 appear only as example call-signalling protocols. The architecture is independent of them.
RTP retransmission is only a suggested option for reliable delivery of intercepted content, and the document says its use is still under investigation.
The document covers confidentiality of intercepts and the subject's inability to detect them, not protocol privacy threat models.
The TAP-MIB is defined in a separate document. This one only references it.
RADIUS is mentioned once as an example IRI IAP for data services.
The IESG note and the reference to RFC 2804 concern why this is not standardised, but the document is not about IETF process.

gaps.name: Lawful intercept
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the lawful interception of communications (IAPs, mediation device, HI1/HI2/HI3 handover interfaces, IRI). The taxonomy has no tag for it, so readers browsing that subject would have no page.

RFC3925.title: Vendor-Identifying Vendor Options for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol version 4 (DHCPv4)
RFC3925.summary: Defines two new DHCPv4 options (V-I Vendor Class, option 124, and V-I Vendor-Specific Information, option 125) that carry IANA Enterprise Numbers to disambiguate vendor data when a client represents multiple vendors.

DHCP.why: The document specifies new DHCPv4 options, their formats and usage in DHCP messages, so it is squarely about DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This document defines two new options, modeled on the IPv6 options for vendor class and vendor-specific information defined in RFC 3315

rejected.why: The IPv6 DHCP options are only the model for the new options; the document specifies DHCPv4 options.
Enterprise Numbers and option code assignments are referenced, but this is boilerplate-level use of IANA registries, not a document about IANA registries.

RFC3926.title: FLUTE - File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport
RFC3926.summary: RFC 3926 specifies FLUTE, a protocol for unidirectional file delivery over ALC/LCT, mainly via multicast, defining the File Delivery Table (FDT), FDT Instance headers, FEC object transmission information delivery, and session description requirements.

FLUTE.why: The document defines the FLUTE protocol itself: file delivery sessions, FDT, EXT_FDT and EXT_CENC headers, and FEC OTI delivery.
FLUTE.quote: This document defines FLUTE, a protocol for the unidirectional delivery of files over the Internet, which is particularly suited to multicast networks.

ALC.why: FLUTE is a specific application of ALC and defines ALC-specific extensions (EXT_FTI formats, TOI usage). ALC readers would want it.
ALC.quote: The specification builds on Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC), version 1 [2], the base protocol designed for massively scalable multicast distribution.

rejected.why: LCT is the building block ALC inherits from; FLUTE defines new LCT header extensions but is not about LCT itself.
FLUTE carries FEC Object Transmission Information but relies on the FEC building block rather than specifying FEC schemes.
FDT Instance is an XML structure, but XML is just the encoding used.
FLUTE is aimed at multicast delivery, but the more specific reliable multicast tag FLUTE covers it.
Section 4 discusses channels and congestion control only as an inherited ALC matter; no congestion control is defined.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible packet authentication scheme.

RFC3927.title: Dynamic Configuration of IPv4 Link-Local Addresses
RFC3927.summary: Specifies how an IPv4 host autoconfigures a link-local address in 169.254/16 using ARP probing, announcement and conflict defense, plus forwarding rules, multi-interface issues and router behaviour.

IPv4.why: The document defines IPv4 link-local address selection, claiming, defense and forwarding rules for the 169.254/16 prefix, an IPv4 address lifecycle matter.
IPv4.quote: This document describes how a host may automatically configure an interface with an IPv4 address within the 169.254/16 prefix

ARP.why: Defines ARP Probe and ARP Announcement usage for conflict detection and defense, a substantial part of the protocol.
ARP.quote: A host probes to see if an address is already in use by broadcasting an ARP Request for the desired address.

addressing.why: Covers address scope, selection, multi-homing address ambiguity and use of link-local versus routable addresses.
addressing.quote: A host SHOULD NOT have both an operable routable address and an IPv4 Link-Local address configured on the same interface.

rejected.why: DHCP is discussed only for interaction (Section 2.11) and as the alternative configuration source; the document does not specify it.
IPv6 link-local is mentioned only in passing in the introduction.
Multi-interface considerations are discussed, but as hazards for link-local use rather than a multihoming architecture; addressing covers it.
Only prohibits link-local addresses in DNS and queries for 254.169.in-addr.arpa; DNS is not the subject.
IEEE 802 LANs are only the applicability context, not the document's subject.

gaps.name: IPv4 link-local autoconfiguration (zeroconf)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for zero-configuration or link-local address autoconfiguration; IPv4 and addressing are the closest fits.

RFC3928.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Client Update Protocol (LCUP)
RFC3928.summary: Defines LCUP, an LDAP extension using Sync Request/Update/Done controls and cookies so clients can synchronize with and be notified of changes to directory content.

LDAP.why: The document specifies new LDAP controls, result codes and search behaviour for client synchronization, so it is an extension of LDAP.
LDAP.quote: The protocol is intended to allow an LDAP client to synchronize with the content of a directory information tree (DIT) stored by an LDAP server

rejected.why: UUIDs are used to identify entries, but the document only relies on them as an identifier mechanism and defines nothing new about UUIDs.
Controls are described in ASN.1, which is just the notation and encoding used, not the subject.
The parent is implied by the LDAP tag.
The IANA section only registers result codes and OIDs, which is boilerplate.
The document mentions DSAs and DIT but does not address X.500 itself.

gaps.name: LDAP directory synchronization / persistent search
gaps.why: LDAP is in the taxonomy, but a tag for LDAP extensions and controls, or for directory synchronization and replication, would fit this RFC more precisely.

RFC3929.title: Alternative Decision Making Processes for Consensus-Blocked Decisions in the IETF
RFC3929.summary: An experimental RFC defining four alternative decision-making processes (external review team, mixed review team, qualified short-straw selection, random assignment) for IETF working groups deadlocked on a decision they agree must be made.

IETF process.why: The document specifies procedures for working group decision making and consensus-blocked decisions, which is IETF standards process and procedure.
IETF process.quote: This document proposes an experimental set of alternative decision-making processes for use in IETF working groups.

rejected.why: NomCom eligibility rules and random selection (RFC 3777, RFC 3797) are only reused for picking review team members; the document is not about NomCom procedures.
IANA is only asked to make random assignments in Method Four; this is a minor mention, not a registry or stewardship topic.
The IDN working group is mentioned only as an example of a random-selection case, not as subject matter.

RFC3930.title: The Protocol versus Document Points of View in Computer Protocols
RFC3930.summary: An informational essay contrasting the "document" and "protocol" points of view on digital objects, covering meaning, processing, canonicalization, signatures, encryption and unique labels, and advising that protocol design start from the protocol view.

internet architecture.why: The document gives general design principles for Internet protocols (extensibility, canonicalization, labelling, processing models). That is the closest fit for a general protocol-design philosophy in this taxonomy, although the match is imperfect.
internet architecture.quote: adherence to a document point of view can be damaging to protocol design. By understanding both points of view, conflicts between them may be clarified and reduced.

rejected.why: Canonicalization and signing are discussed generically, with XML only one example. The document does not specify or analyse XML-Signature.
XML is cited as something that can be viewed both ways, but it is an example and not the subject.
X.509 is mentioned once as an example of a document-oriented design.
IOTP appears only as an example of hierarchical qualified tags and of a protocol viewpoint.
ASN.1 is mentioned only as a syntax with a standard canonicalization.
Digital authentication is one subsection, discussed from the two viewpoints. The document is not about authentication mechanisms as such.

gaps.name: Protocol design philosophy / canonicalization
gaps.why: The document is about design viewpoints for protocol messages and about canonicalization before signing. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol design principles, and only the broad internet architecture tag comes close.

RFC3931.title: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol - Version 3 (L2TPv3)
RFC3931.summary: RFC 3931 specifies L2TPv3, the base control protocol and data encapsulation for tunneling multiple Layer 2 connections (pseudowires) between two IP nodes, with its AVPs, state machines, reliable control channel, and migration from L2TPv2.

L2TP.why: The document defines L2TPv3 itself.
L2TP.quote: L2TPv3 defines the base control protocol and encapsulation for tunneling multiple Layer 2 connections between two IP nodes.

rejected.why: L2TP sessions are pseudowires, but the document is about the L2TP protocol; the pseudowire tag is implied context, and L2TP is the more specific tag.
Only a section on securing L2TP with IPsec; IPsec is a substrate/security mechanism, not the subject.
UDP is one of two transports used (port 1701), not specified here.
PPP-specific parts are explicitly separated into a companion document.
HMAC-MD5/SHA-1 is used for control message authentication but is a mechanism relied on, not the subject.
Appendix A borrows TCP slow start for the control channel, a minor part.

gaps.name: L2TP (Layer Two Tunneling Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an L2TP tech id in the link layer hierarchy, but it was not in the listed tags I could verify; if absent, the closest option would be tunneling/pseudowire.

RFC3932.title: The IESG and RFC Editor Documents: Procedures
RFC3932.summary: BCP describing how the IESG reviews RFC Editor (independent submission) documents solely for conflicts with IETF work, the possible responses, and the standard IESG notes placed on such RFCs.

RFC series.why: The document defines how independent submissions to the RFC Editor are reviewed and what notes are placed on published RFCs, which is about RFC publication.
RFC series.quote: This document describes the IESG's procedures for handling documents submitted for RFC publication via the RFC Editor

IETF process.why: It specifies an IESG procedure and updates RFC 2026 and RFC 3710, which makes it an IETF process document.
IETF process.quote: The new review model will have the IESG take responsibility ONLY for checking for conflicts between the work of the IETF and the documents submitted

rejected.why: IANA registration procedures are mentioned only as one kind of conflict the IESG checks for, and the document is not about IANA registries.
Photuris and IKE appear only as an example of a rejected alternative published after the WG product.

RFC3933.title: A Model for IETF Process Experiments
RFC3933.summary: BCP 93 defines a lightweight procedure for the IESG to run time-limited IETF process experiments (I-D, four-week Last Call, Experimental RFC, sunset, then BCP or expiry) as a middle ground between informal IESG changes and full BCP processes.

IETF process.why: The whole document specifies how the IETF and IESG change and experiment with IETF procedures, which is the IETF standards process and its administration.
IETF process.quote: This document specifies a middle-ground approach to the system of making changes to IETF process

rejected.why: It mentions publishing Experimental and BCP RFCs, but it is about process change, not RFC format, style or publication.
RFC 3667 and RFC 3668 are mentioned only as examples of past process changes, and the IPR boilerplate is not evidence.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific IETF process tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC3934.title: Updates to RFC 2418 Regarding the Management of IETF Mailing Lists
RFC3934.summary: BCP update to RFC 2418 giving IETF WG chairs authority to suspend a disruptive individual's mailing list posting privileges for up to 30 days without IESG approval.

IETF process.why: The document changes IETF working group procedures, specifically WG chair authority over mailing list management, by updating RFC 2418.
IETF process.quote: It gives WG chairs the authority to temporarily suspend the posting privileges of disruptive individuals without IESG approval.

rejected.why: This tag covers mailing list protocols, headers and management as technology. This document sets IETF WG governance policy on posting privileges, not list software or protocol behaviour.
Email is only the medium for the WG discussions. The document says nothing about email architecture or transport.

RFC3935.title: A Mission Statement for the IETF
RFC3935.summary: RFC 3935 (BCP 95) states the IETF's mission, goal and cardinal principles (open process, technical competence, volunteer core, rough consensus and running code, protocol ownership), defines key terms, and explains why the IETF needs a mission statement and how its scope is bounded.

internet governance.why: The document states the IETF's mission and cardinal principles and discusses its scope and how it makes decisions. That is how the IETF is governed and run, which is the subject of internet governance. No narrower child tag fits, since it is not a specific process procedure, NomCom, IPR or IANA document.
internet governance.quote: The goal of the IETF is to make the Internet work better.

rejected.why: The memo explicitly says procedures such as appeals and who declares a document ready for publication are outside the mission statement (Section 4.3). It covers mission and principles, not process mechanics.
Section 4.1 touches on scope of the Internet and values such as decentralized control, but it does not set out architectural principles of the Internet itself.
Section 2 defines terms such as mission, standard and quality, but only to support the mission statement. It is not a glossary or a requirements-language document.

RFC3936.title: Procedures for Modifying the Resource reSerVation Protocol (RSVP)
RFC3936.summary: BCP defining IANA assignment policies (Standards Action, Expert Review, Vendor Private) for RSVP message types, class numbers, class types, sub-objects and error codes, and the RFC types required to modify RSVP procedures.

RSVP.why: The document governs how RSVP is extended and updates RFC 2205 and RFC 3209, specifying the registry ranges for RSVP entities and the procedures for changing them.
RSVP.quote: This memo specifies procedures for modifying the Resource reSerVation Protocol (RSVP), including (but not limited to) adding, updating, extending or obsoleting: messages

IANA.why: A large part of the document defines IANA assignment policies (Standards Action, Expert Review, Vendor Private) for the RSVP registries.
IANA.quote: This memo specifies ranges for each name space and assignment policies for each range.

rejected.why: The document updates the IANA considerations of RFC 3209 and covers EXPLICIT_ROUTE/RECORD_ROUTE sub-object ranges, but it does not specify RSVP-TE itself. The RSVP tag covers it.
It sets which RFC track is needed for changes, but this is specific to RSVP registries, so IANA is the better fit.
RSVP-TE objects are mentioned only as part of the registries, not as a subject of the document.

RFC3937.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC)
RFC3937.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "iptc" for persistent resources published by the International Press Telecommunications Council (XML DTDs, schemas, namespaces, documents), defining its hierarchical NSS structure and assignment/resolution policies.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration for the NID "iptc", specifying syntax, uniqueness, persistence and resolution for the namespace.
URN.quote: This document describes a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace for identifying persistent resources published by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC).

rejected.why: XML resources (DTDs, schemas, namespaces) are what the URNs identify, but the document does not specify or profile XML usage.
The IANA registration is boilerplate for the namespace template; the document is not about IANA registries or guidance generally.
URN is the more specific fit; the document does not address URI syntax generally.

RFC3938.title: Video-Message Message-Context
RFC3938.summary: Extends the Message-Context email header (RFC 3458) with a new "video-message" value, registered with IANA, as a hint to mail user agents for presenting video email.

email.why: The document defines a new value for an Internet mail header describing message context, so it belongs with email. No finer child fits: it is a message-context header extension, not a message-format overhaul.
email.quote: This specification extends the Message-Context header with one additional context value: video-message.

rejected.why: The header is a message header, but the document only adds one context value to an existing registry. It does not specify header syntax or addressing.
Video bodies may be embedded as body parts, but the document does not define MIME structure or encodings.
It registers a Message-Context class name, not a media type.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level here and is not the subject of the document.
Video is only the content the context describes. No codec or container is defined.

gaps.name: Message-Context header
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the Message-Context header from RFC 3458. The closest tag is email, and that is what this RFC uses.

RFC3939.title: Calling Line Identification for Voice Mail Messages
RFC3939.summary: Defines two new Internet message header fields, Caller-ID and Caller-Name, to record the calling party's number and name in stored voice mail messages (VPIM context), with syntax and a numbering-plan registry.

VPIM.why: The headers are designed for voice mail messages in VPIM format, so readers of VPIM would expect this extension.
VPIM.quote: This information is intended for use when the VPIM message format is used for storing "Call Answer" voice messages in an Internet Mail message store

message format.why: The document defines new Internet message header fields with formal syntax, extending the message header set.
message format.quote: Two new header fields are defined for this purpose: Caller_ID and Called_Name.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to give the syntax, not a subject of the document.
E.164 numbers are carried in the header, but the document does not map numbers into the DNS.
The tel URL is mentioned only as a different mechanism for dialable numbers that this document does not define.
Character set handling for the caller name is a minor detail. The document mainly says to use ASCII, or RFC 2047 encoding if that is not possible.
It creates a small numbering-plan registry, but that is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the document's subject.
The more specific message format and VPIM tags cover this; email is only the general context.

RFC3940.title: Negative-acknowledgment (NACK)-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) Protocol
RFC3940.summary: RFC 3940 specifies the NORM protocol, a NACK-based reliable multicast transport for bulk data objects and streams, with FEC-based repair, feedback suppression, and the TFMCC-based NORM-CC congestion control.

NORM.why: The document is the NORM protocol specification itself: message formats and detailed operation.
NORM.quote: This document describes the messages and procedures of the Negative- acknowledgment (NACK) Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) protocol.

congestion control.why: Section 5.5.2 defines NORM-CC, a TFMCC-based multicast congestion control with CLR selection, rate adjustment and feedback suppression. This is a substantial part of the document.
congestion control.quote: A congestion control scheme is specified to allow the NORM protocol to fairly share available network bandwidth with other transport protocols such as

FEC.why: FEC-based repair is central to NORM: parity-symbol repair strategy, the FEC payload ID, the EXT_FTI extension and the object segmentation algorithm.
FEC.quote: NORM provides for the use of packet-level forward error correction (FEC) techniques for efficient multicast repair and optional proactive transmission robustness

rejected.why: NORM is the more specific child tag under multicast > reliable multicast, so the parent is implied.
NORM sits under this topic, so it is implied by the NORM tag.
NORM messages are encapsulated in UDP, but UDP is only the substrate.
TCP appears only as the fairness benchmark and as an analogy for streams.
The document uses the RMT FEC Building Block, not the FECFRAME framework for real-time media.
IPsec is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a way to counter replay attacks.
Source-Specific Multicast is mentioned only as a deployment topology that affects backoff values.

RFC3941.title: Negative-Acknowledgment (NACK)-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) Building Blocks
RFC3941.summary: RFC 3941 describes the NORM (NACK-oriented reliable multicast) building blocks: sender transmission, NACK repair process with timer-based suppression, and GRTT round-trip timing, along with their relationship to FEC and congestion control.

NORM.why: The whole document defines the building blocks of NORM: sender transmission, NACK repair with suppression, and RTT/GRTT collection.
NORM.quote: This document addresses the creation of negative-acknowledgment (NACK)- oriented reliable multicast (NORM) protocols.

rejected.why: FEC is discussed as a related building block, but it is specified in other RFCs (RFC 3452/3453). This document only states NORM's requirements on it.
Congestion control is only referenced as a required external building block (TFMCC, PGMCC), not defined here.
The parent topic is implied by NORM and reliable multicast, and NORM is the more specific tag.
IPsec appears only in Security Considerations as a compatible protection mechanism.
SSM is mentioned only as one network environment NORM should handle.

RFC3942.title: Reclassifying Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol version 4 (DHCPv4) Options
RFC3942.summary: RFC 3942 updates RFC 2132 by reclassifying DHCPv4 option codes 128-223 from site-specific to publicly defined options managed by IANA, with a transition procedure for vendors already using them.

DHCP.why: The document changes the DHCPv4 option code space, updating RFC 2132. It is squarely about DHCP option allocation.
DHCP.quote: reclassify Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol version 4 (DHCPv4) option codes 128 to 223 (decimal) as publicly defined options to be managed by IANA

rejected.why: IANA registry management is the mechanism for the change, but the subject is the DHCPv4 option space. The IANA instructions are largely a restatement of the procedure.
The document covers only DHCPv4, not DHCPv6.

RFC3943.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Compression Using Lempel-Ziv-Stac (LZS)
RFC3943.summary: Defines a TLS compression method (identifier 64) that applies the LZS lossless compression algorithm to TLS record payloads, including the record header format, history handling and anti-expansion rules.

LZS.why: The document defines how LZS is applied to TLS records, including the TLSComp header, history reset and flushing, and encoding. LZS is the central subject.
LZS.quote: This document specifies the application of Lempel-Ziv-Stac (LZS) compression, a lossless compression algorithm, to TLS record payloads.

TLS.why: It extends TLS with a new compression method negotiated in the handshake and applied in the Record Protocol, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document describes an additional compression method associated with a lossless data compression algorithm for use with TLS.

rejected.why: The LZS child tag already covers the compression topic, so the parent is not listed separately.
RFC 2395 (LZS for IP payload compression) is only an informative reference for the encoding, and the document is not about IPComp.
RFC 1967 and RFC 1974 (PPP LZS) are cited only as sources of the encoding format.
The compression method identifier assignment is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the document's subject.
VPN use of TLS is mentioned only as motivation, and the document does not address provider-provisioned VPNs.

RFC3944.title: H.350 Directory Services
RFC3944.summary: Republishes ITU-T H.350 and H.350.4 as an informational RFC, defining an LDAP schema (commObject, commURI, SIPIdentity) to store multimedia conferencing endpoints and SIP user agent data in enterprise directories.

LDAP.why: The document's core content is an LDAP schema (object classes, attributes, LDIF files, indexing profiles) for representing conferencing endpoints in directories.
LDAP.quote: This Recommendation describes a directory services architecture for multimedia conferencing using LDAP.

SIP.why: H.350.4 defines the SIPIdentity schema for SIP user agents, registrar, proxy and SIP URIs; a substantial half of the document is SIP-specific.
SIP.quote: This Recommendation describes an LDAP directory services architecture for multimedia conferencing using SIP.

H.323.why: The H.350 architecture is designed to cover H.323, H.235 and H.320 endpoints alongside SIP, but only H.350 and H.350.4 text is reproduced.
H.323.quote: H.350.1 - Directory Services Architecture for H.323

rejected.why: Parent of LDAP; the document is specifically about LDAP schema, so the child tag LDAP is used.
HTTP Digest is only referenced as the credential type for the SIPIdentityPassword/UserName attributes; not the subject.
userSMIMECertificate attribute is merely referenced in the SIPIdentity class and security section.
Parent of SIP and H.323 tags, which are chosen as more specific.

RFC3945.title: Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Architecture
RFC3945.summary: Describes the GMPLS architecture, extending MPLS control plane (signaling, routing, link management) to TDM, wavelength and fiber switching, including link bundling, unnumbered links, forwarding adjacencies, LMP, and protection/restoration.

GMPLS.why: The whole document is the architecture of GMPLS: building blocks, signaling, routing, link management, and recovery.
GMPLS.quote: GMPLS extends MPLS to encompass time-division (e.g., SONET/SDH, PDH, G.709), wavelength (lambdas), and spatial switching

traffic engineering.why: Substantial coverage of TE links, TE extensions to IGPs, bandwidth accounting, and LSP protection/restoration.
traffic engineering.quote: GMPLS is indeed based on the Traffic Engineering (TE) extensions to MPLS, a.k.a. MPLS-TE

SONET.why: Substantial treatment of SONET/SDH traffic parameters, labels and concatenation as a GMPLS layer.
SONET.quote: GMPLS extensions for SONET and SDH control [RFC3946].

rejected.why: GMPLS signaling is built on RSVP-TE extensions, but the document is an architecture, with the extensions specified in other RFCs; GMPLS is the better fit.
Referenced as one of two signaling bases, but not specified here.
Routing extensions are specified in other documents; OSPF is only the substrate.
Used as routing substrate for TE link advertisement; extensions defined elsewhere.
Network management section mentions SNMP and MIBs only briefly as recommendations.
GMPLS is the more specific child tag, and MPLS is implied as its parent.

gaps.name: Link Management Protocol (LMP)
gaps.why: Substantial section (6) covers LMP control channel management, link verification and fault localization, but the taxonomy has no LMP tag.

gaps.name: Optical transport networks (G.709/OTN, WDM)
gaps.why: Document covers wavelength and G.709 switching control, with no dedicated optical networking tag.

RFC3946.title: Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Extensions for Synchronous Optical Network (SONET) and Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) Control
RFC3946.summary: RFC 3946 defines SONET/SDH-specific GMPLS signaling traffic parameters (signal type, concatenation, transparency, multiplier) and the SUKLM label format, with RSVP-TE objects and CR-LDP TLV encodings.

GMPLS.why: The document is a GMPLS signaling companion defining SONET/SDH-specific traffic parameters and labels for TDM LSPs.
GMPLS.quote: It defines the Synchronous Optical Network (SONET)/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) technology specific information needed when using GMPLS signaling.

rejected.why: Defines SENDER_TSPEC/FLOWSPEC object formats in section 2.2, but only as one carrier of the GMPLS parameters, not a protocol extension in its own right.
Defines a TLV type in section 2.3, but only as a secondary carrier of the GMPLS traffic parameters.
The taxonomy's SONET tag covers IP and multi-access protocols over SONET/SDH links. This RFC is about control-plane signaling for SONET/SDH LSPs, not IP over SONET.
GMPLS is the more specific tag, so MPLS is implied.
The RFC extends TE signaling, but its subject is the SONET/SDH technology-specific parameters. The GMPLS tag covers it.

RFC3947.title: Negotiation of NAT-Traversal in the IKE
RFC3947.summary: Specifies how IKE Phase 1 and Quick Mode detect NAT between IPsec peers (NAT-D payloads, vendor ID), switch to port 4500, negotiate UDP-encapsulated tunnel/transport modes, and convey original addresses via NAT-OA payloads.

IKE.why: The document extends IKE (Phase 1 and Quick Mode) with new payloads, port changes and encapsulation modes for NAT traversal.
IKE.quote: how to negotiate the use of UDP encapsulation of IPsec packets through NAT boxes in Internet Key Exchange (IKE)

NAT.why: NAT detection and handling of NAT behaviour (port changes, expiring mappings, checksum fixes) is central, so readers of NAT would want it.
NAT.quote: how to detect one or more network address translation devices (NATs) between IPsec hosts

rejected.why: IKE is the more specific child; the document is about IKE negotiation, with ESP/UDP encapsulation specified in RFC 3948.
UDP encapsulation of ESP is defined in RFC 3948; this document only negotiates it.
UDP is only the transport used for IKE and encapsulation, not the subject.
MD5 is only used to compute the vendor ID value.
IANA considerations are boilerplate; registrations are incidental.
The NAT traversal tag in the taxonomy is for real-time media; not applicable to IPsec.

RFC3948.title: UDP Encapsulation of IPsec ESP Packets
RFC3948.summary: Specifies encapsulating IPsec ESP packets in UDP (port 4500, shared with IKE) with NAT-keepalive packets and encapsulation/decapsulation procedures so ESP can traverse NATs.

ESP.why: The document defines how ESP packets are encapsulated in UDP in transport and tunnel modes, an extension of ESP's packet format.
ESP.quote: This protocol specification defines methods to encapsulate and decapsulate ESP packets inside UDP packets for traversing Network Address Translators (NATs)

NAT.why: The document addresses IPsec-NAT traversal: NAT keepalives, checksum fixing after NAT, and multiple clients behind the same NAT.
NAT.quote: Because SGW will now see two possible SAs that lead to 10.1.2.3, it can become confused about where to send packets

rejected.why: IKE only negotiates the SAs and shares port 4500. The document adds a Non-ESP Marker format but does not specify IKE itself; the NAT-T negotiation is in RFC 3947.
UDP is only the encapsulating substrate, and the document does not define new UDP behaviour.
ESP is the more specific tag here. The document is about ESP encapsulation, not the IPsec architecture.
The document only notes that IPv6 headers could be used. It does not specify IPv6 behaviour.
The document defines ESP in UDP, which is specific to IPsec. It is not generic IP tunnelling.

RFC3949.title: File Format for Internet Fax
RFC3949.summary: RFC 3949 revises RFC 2301 and defines TIFF-FX, the TIFF-based file format for Internet fax, with profiles S, F, J, C, L and M covering black-and-white, JBIG, JPEG color and Mixed Raster Content fax data.

fax.why: The whole document specifies the file format for Internet fax (TIFF-FX) and its profiles, so fax is the subject.
fax.quote: This document defines a TIFF-based file format specification for enabling standardized messaging-based fax over the Internet.

media types.why: The document defines a content format carried as the image/tiff and image/tiff-fx media types, with registrations in companion RFCs. It is a small section, so this is secondary.
media types.quote: The MIME content-types image/tiff and image/tiff-fx are used for TIFF-FX encoded image data, as defined in this document.

rejected.why: Fax is carried by Internet mail, but this document defines only the file format, not mail transport.
VPIM is mentioned only as an example use of TIFF-F in Section 4.6, which is not what the document is about.
The T.4, T.6, JBIG and JPEG codings are referenced and mapped to TIFF fields, but the document defines no codec.
MIME is only the carrier for the media types. The document does not specify MIME body structure or encodings.

gaps.name: TIFF (Tag Image File Format) / TIFF-FX
gaps.why: The document is mainly a specification of TIFF profiles, fields and file structure for fax. The taxonomy has no tag for image file formats such as TIFF.

RFC3950.title: Tag Image File Format Fax eXtended (TIFF-FX) - image/tiff-fx MIME Sub-type Registration
RFC3950.summary: Registers the image/tiff-fx MIME media type for TIFF-FX (Internet fax file format, RFC 3949) encoded image data, and obsoletes RFC 3250.

media types.why: The document's whole purpose is registering a MIME media type, including its parameters, encoding, magic numbers and usage guidance versus image/tiff.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type image/tiff-fx.

fax.why: The registered type carries Internet fax image data (TIFF-FX profiles), so readers of the fax subject would want it, though the file format itself is defined in RFC 3949.
fax.quote: TIFF-based file format specification for enabling standardized messaging-based fax over the Internet.

rejected.why: The document registers a type but does not define MIME body structure or encodings; the more specific media types tag fits.
Fax messaging is store-and-forward, but the document specifies no email transport or format.
The IANA registration section is just the registration template for this type, not about IANA registries or guidance in general.
Base64 is only mentioned as an encoding for transports that cannot carry binary data.

gaps.name: TIFF / TIFF-FX image file format
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for image file formats such as TIFF-FX, which this document and RFC 3949 are about.

RFC3951.title: Internet Low Bit Rate Codec (iLBC)
RFC3951.summary: RFC 3951 specifies the iLBC narrowband speech codec for robust VoIP, describing its encoder, decoder, packet loss concealment, bitstream, and C reference implementation.

iLBC.why: The entire document defines the iLBC codec algorithm, bitstream and reference code.
iLBC.quote: This document specifies a speech codec suitable for robust voice communication over IP.

RFC3952.title: Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload Format for internet Low Bit Rate Codec (iLBC) Speech
RFC3952.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for the iLBC speech codec, including bitstream packing, multiple frames per packet, a storage file format, the audio/iLBC MIME registration, and SDP parameter mapping.

iLBC.why: The document specifies the payload format for the iLBC codec, including bitstream class layout and frame packetization, so it belongs on the iLBC page.
iLBC.quote: This document describes how compressed iLBC speech, as produced by the iLBC codec [1], may be formatted for use as an RTP payload type.

RTP payload format.why: The document's core is an RTP payload format for a specific codec: timestamp units, M bit use, multiple frames per packet, and payload type assignment.
