SDP.why: A full section defines the SDP mapping and offer/answer rules for the mode parameter, which SDP readers would want.

media types.why: The document registers the audio/iLBC media type with parameters (maxptime, mode, ptime) and a storage-mode file format with magic numbers.
media types.quote:
MIME media type name: audio

   MIME subtype: iLBC

rejected.why: The document is about a payload format; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers it. RTP is the substrate.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional external mechanism.
The more specific iLBC tag applies; the codec itself is defined in RFC 3951, not here.
G.711 is mentioned only as a comparison in the Background.
The MIME type registration is covered by the media types tag; the document does not address MIME body structure or encodings generally.

RFC3953.title: Telephone Number Mapping (ENUM) Service Registration for Presence Services
RFC3953.summary: Registers the 'E2U+pres' ENUM service so NAPTR records for E.164 numbers can advertise pres URIs for presence services.

ENUM.why: The document defines and registers a new enumservice, 'E2U+pres', under the ENUM registry, so it belongs on the ENUM page.

instant messaging.why: Presence and the watcher/presentity model are a substantial part of the document. The 'instant messaging' tag covers presence, and the document uses the pres URI and refers to PIDF.

rejected.why: NAPTR records in DNS are only the substrate for ENUM, and the document adds nothing new to DNS itself.

The only IANA content is boilerplate registration of the enumservice.

RFC3954.title: Cisco Systems NetFlow Services Export Version 9
RFC3954.summary: Informational RFC specifying Cisco NetFlow version 9, the template-based export format by which routers export IP flow records to collectors, forming the basis for IPFIX.

Interface index fields are named INPUT_SNMP and OUTPUT_SNMP, but SNMP is not specified or discussed.

The parent of IPFIX; IPFIX is the more specific tag and already covers it.

RFC3955.title: Evaluation of Candidate Protocols for IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC3955.summary: Evaluates five candidate flow-export protocols (CRANE, Diameter, LFAP, NetFlow v9, Streaming IPDR) against the IPFIX requirements and recommends NetFlow v9 as the basis for the IPFIX protocol.

IPFIX.why: The whole document evaluates candidates for the IPFIX protocol against the IPFIX requirements and recommends a basis for it. IPFIX readers would want it.

The LFAP MIB and SNMP notifications get a brief mention only.
Flow metering is the context. The document evaluates export protocols, not measurement methods.

gaps.name: NetFlow

RFC3956.title: Embedding the Rendezvous Point (RP) Address in an IPv6 Multicast Address
RFC3956.summary: Defines an IPv6 multicast address format (FF70::/12) that embeds the Rendezvous Point address in the group address, and specifies it as a PIM-SM group-to-RP mapping mechanism, updating RFC 3306.

PIM-SM.why: The document specifies a new group-to-RP mapping method for PIM-SM (Embedded-RP), including required router behaviour and operational considerations. PIM-SM readers would want it.

RFC3957.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) Registration Keys for Mobile IPv4
RFC3957.summary: Defines Mobile IPv4 registration extensions (MN-FA and MN-HA Key Generation Nonce request/reply) that let a mobile node derive Mobility Security Associations with its home and foreign agents from its AAA security association with the home AAA server.

RFC3958.title: Domain-Based Application Service Location Using SRV RRs and the Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service (DDDS)
RFC3958.summary: Defines S-NAPTR, a DDDS application that uses NAPTR and SRV DNS records to map a domain, application service tag and protocol tag to a target server and port, and sets up IANA registries for the service and protocol tags.

RFC3959.title: The Early Session Disposition Type for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3959.summary: Defines the SIP "early-session" Content-Disposition type and option tag, so that early media sessions within early dialogs are established via offer/answer, supporting the application server model for early media.

The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new disposition type and option tag, and the document is not about IANA registries.
S/MIME appears only as a security recommendation in Security Considerations.

RFC3960.title: Early Media and Ringing Tone Generation in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3960.summary: Informational RFC describing two models (gateway and application server) for managing SIP early media and the inputs for local ringing tone generation policy.

SIP.why: The whole document addresses SIP call signalling behaviour for early media, ringing, forking, and provisional responses.
SIP.quote: This document describes how to manage early media in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) using two models: the gateway model and the application server model.

rejected.why: Offer/answer is used heavily as the mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend SDP or offer/answer.
Media packets are discussed only abstractly; nothing about RTP is specified.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended protection.
Cited only as an example of why media may be delayed.
PSTN gateways are used as an example for applicability of the gateway model, but the document is not about PSTN interworking itself.
Mentioned only in passing as an example and in Security Considerations.

RFC3961.title: Encryption and Checksum Specifications for Kerberos 5
RFC3961.summary: Defines a framework (encryption and checksum profiles, simplified key-derivation profile) for Kerberos 5 cryptographic mechanisms, and specifies DES, triple-DES, MD4/MD5, CRC-32 and HMAC-SHA1 based encryption and checksum types with assigned type numbers and test vectors.

Kerberos.why: The whole document specifies the cryptographic abstraction layer and mechanisms for Kerberos 5, including etype and checksum type registries.
Kerberos.quote: This document describes a framework for defining encryption and checksum mechanisms for use with the Kerberos protocol

DES.why: A large part of the document specifies DES-CBC and triple-DES encryption types, string-to-key, weak-key handling and DES-based checksums.
DES.quote: These encryption systems encrypt information under the Data Encryption Standard [DES77] by using the cipher block chaining mode

MD5.why: Specifies rsa-md5 and rsa-md4 checksums and des-cbc-md5/md4 types, so readers of MD5/MD4 usage would find it relevant.
MD5.quote: The RSA-MD5 checksum calculates a checksum by using the RSA MD5 algorithm [MD5-92].

CRC.why: Defines the modified CRC-32 used by Kerberos, with test vectors in A.5.
CRC.quote: This CRC-32 checksum calculates a checksum based on a cyclic redundancy check as described in ISO 3309 but modified as described below.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is used as a building block in the simplified profile, not specified or analysed in its own right.
Key derivation and string-to-key are part of the profile, but the document is about Kerberos cryptosystem mechanisms rather than key management in general.
SHA-1 is only the hash plugged into HMAC for the triple-DES profile.
AES is only referenced as defined in another document (RFC 3962), not specified here.
The IANA section creates etype/checksum registries, but that is boilerplate relative to the main body.
Only mentioned in passing regarding encoding size of type numbers.

RFC3962.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Encryption for Kerberos 5
RFC3962.summary: Defines AES-based encryption types (aes128/aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96) and checksum types for Kerberos 5 using the simplified profile, with PBKDF2 string-to-key and CBC ciphertext stealing.

Kerberos.why: The document extends the Kerberos cryptosystem suite with new etypes, checksum types, and string-to-key rules, so Kerberos readers need it.
Kerberos.quote: This document defines encryption key and checksum types for Kerberos 5 using the AES algorithm recently chosen by NIST.

AES.why: It specifies how AES is used (CBC with ciphertext stealing, 128/256-bit keys, key derivation) in Kerberos, so it belongs on the AES page.
AES.quote: These new types support 128-bit block encryption and key sizes of 128 or 256 bits.

PBKDF2.why: A substantial part covers the PBKDF2-based string-to-key function, its iteration counts, security analysis, and test vectors.
PBKDF2.quote: we use the PBKDF2 function from PKCS #5 v2.0 ([PKCS5]), with parameters indicated below, to generate an intermediate key
PBKDF2.section: 4. Key Generation from Pass Phrases or Random Data

rejected.why: SHA-1 is only the hash underlying the HMAC checksum, not the subject.
HMAC-SHA1 is a building block used via the KCRYPTO profile, not specified here.
The PBKDF2 tag is more specific; the document is not about password hashing generally.
Key derivation from passphrases is covered by the more specific PBKDF2 tag; the document is not about key management as such.
The IANA section only records the assigned type numbers; it is boilerplate.

RFC3963.title: Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support Protocol
RFC3963.summary: Specifies the NEMO Basic Support protocol, an extension of Mobile IPv6 in which a Mobile Router registers a Mobile Network Prefix with its Home Agent and uses a bi-directional tunnel to give session continuity to nodes in a moving network.

NEMO.why: The document defines the NEMO Basic Support protocol itself: the R flag, the Mobile Network Prefix option, new status values, Mobile Router and Home Agent operation.
NEMO.quote: This document describes the Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support protocol that enables Mobile Networks to attach to different points in the Internet.

Mobile IPv6.why: The protocol extends Mobile IPv6 messages (Binding Update, Binding Acknowledgement, DHAAD) and Home Agent behaviour, so Mobile IPv6 readers would want it.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document describes protocol extensions to Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) [1] to enable support for network mobility.

rejected.why: Running OSPF/OSPFv3 over the tunnel is an optional feature and an appendix. The document does not specify or extend OSPF.
IPsec protects signalling and tunnelled traffic, but only as a security mechanism, so it is not a subject of this document.
Uses IP-in-IP encapsulation per RFC 2473 as a substrate and does not define a new tunnelling mechanism.
RIPng is mentioned only as one possible routing protocol to run over the tunnel.
Mobile Router neighbor discovery behaviour is covered briefly, and Proxy ND is used. The document does not extend ND.

RFC3964.title: Security Considerations for 6to4
RFC3964.summary: RFC 3964 analyses the security threats (DoS, reflection, spoofing, theft of service) created by 6to4 routers and relays that openly decapsulate protocol-41 traffic, and specifies recommended encapsulation/decapsulation security checks.

6to4.why: The whole document is a threat analysis of 6to4 and gives recommended checks for 6to4 routers and relays. This is the specific technology tag.
6to4.quote: The IPv6 interim mechanism 6to4 (RFC3056) uses automatic IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling to interconnect IPv6 networks.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the 6to4 tag, so it is not listed separately.
ISATAP is mentioned only in Section 6.1, as one of several automatic tunnelling mechanisms that conflict with strict checks. The document is not about it.
ND-message attacks are one threat among several (4.1.1), and the document does not specify or extend ND.
The IP-in-IP encapsulation is only the mechanism 6to4 uses. The subject is 6to4 itself, which is the more specific tag.
BGP appears only as an alternative deployment model in 2.4.1 and is not the subject.
The 6to4 relay anycast prefix (RFC 3068) is referenced for source-address and abuse-tracing discussion, but anycast is not what the document is about.
The document is a security analysis, but the specific 6to4 tag covers it. DoS and spoofing are discussed only for 6to4.

RFC3965.title: A Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail
RFC3965.summary: RFC 3965 specifies a "simple mode" profile of Internet mail for carrying facsimile data, using MIME and TIFF-F images, with addressing, offramp gateways and error handling for interworking between IFax devices and G3Fax.

fax.why: The whole document defines Internet fax over email: transport, formats, offramp gateways, addressing and failure handling.
fax.quote: This specification provides for "simple mode" carriage of facsimile data using Internet mail.

rejected.why: Email is the substrate the fax profile is built on. The document profiles it for fax but does not specify email itself; fax is the more specific tag.
MIME is used to carry image/TIFF, and Appendix A lists exceptions to MIME conformance. This is minor, and the document is not about MIME.
SMTP is only the relay transport that the document relies on.
S/MIME is mentioned only as informational security options in the Security Considerations.
Unsolicited bulk email that triggers an outdial is only noted briefly in the Security Considerations.
POP is mentioned in passing as a mailbox access option for a gateway.

RFC3966.title: The tel URI for Telephone Numbers
RFC3966.summary: Defines the "tel" URI scheme for identifying resources by telephone numbers (global E.164 and local numbers with phone-context), its syntax, comparison rules, parameters, and use in HTML and SIP; obsoletes RFC 2806.

tel URI.why: The entire document specifies the tel URI scheme: syntax, comparison, global/local numbers, phone-context, ISDN subaddress and extension parameters.
tel URI.quote: This document specifies the URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) scheme "tel".  The "tel" URI describes resources identified by telephone numbers.

rejected.why: SIP is a consumer of tel URIs; the informative section 9 describes use with SIP but the document does not specify or extend SIP.
ENUM is only mentioned in the rationale as one way to resolve a tel URI; not a subject of the document.
The more specific child tag tel URI applies; the document is about one scheme rather than URIs generally.
Section 8 gives brief usage advice for tel links in HTML, but the document is not about HTML.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax.

RFC3967.title: Clarifying when Standards Track Documents may Refer Normatively to Documents at a Lower Level
RFC3967.summary: BCP 97 clarifies and updates the IETF procedure under which Standards Track and BCP documents may make normative references to documents at a lower maturity level (downrefs), including Last Call handling.

IETF process.why: The document defines an IETF standards-process procedure (downward references, Last Call, IESG consideration, AD waiver), updating RFC 2026 section 4.2.4.
IETF process.quote: For Standards Track or BCP documents requiring normative reference to documents of lower maturity, the normal IETF Last Call procedure will be issued

rejected.why: It concerns normative versus informative references and maturity levels in the standards process, not RFC format, style or publication.
MD5 is cited only as an example of a commonly accepted downref.
HMAC is cited only as an example of a commonly accepted downref.
Section 1.1 explains normative references, but this is guidance within a process document, not a glossary or definition of requirements language.

RFC3968.title: The Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) Header Field Parameter Registry for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3968.summary: RFC 3968 creates an IANA sub-registry for SIP header field parameters and parameter values, sets the IETF Consensus registration policy, and lists initial entries, updating RFC 3427.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's extension machinery by defining how header field parameters are registered and listing all existing SIP header parameters; SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: This document creates an Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) registry for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) header field parameters and parameter values.

IANA.why: The document is essentially a registry creation with a registration policy (IETF Consensus), so IANA registry readers would want it.
IANA.quote: This specification creates a new sub-registry for header field parameters under the SIP Parameters registry.

rejected.why: It updates RFC 3427 (SIP change process) but only for parameter registration; the focus is the registry, not IETF process generally.
Many listed parameters (nonce, realm, qop) are digest authentication parameters, but they are merely table entries, not specified here.
Event and Subscription-State parameters appear in the table but the document does not address event packages.

RFC3969.title: The Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Parameter Registry for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC3969.summary: Creates an IANA sub-registry for SIP and SIPS URI parameters and their values, sets the registration policy (Specification Required, standards-track RFC), and lists initial entries (comp, lr, maddr, method, transport, ttl, user).

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's extension process (updates RFC 3427) by defining how SIP/SIPS URI parameters are defined and registered, so SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: SIP and SIPS URI parameters and values for these parameters MUST be documented in a standards-track RFC in order to be registered by IANA.

IANA.why: The document's substance is creating an IANA registry with a registration policy (Specification Required) and initial values.
IANA.quote: This specification creates a new sub-registry under the SIP Parameters registry.

rejected.why: Concerns only the registry of SIP/SIPS URI parameters, not URI syntax, schemes or resolution generally; SIP covers it.
It updates RFC 3427's SIP change process, but only for one registry; IANA and SIP fit better.

RFC3970.title: A Traffic Engineering (TE) MIB
RFC3970.summary: Defines the TE-MIB SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring Traffic Engineered tunnels (e.g., MPLS LSPs) at their ingress, with tunnel, path and hop tables.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a new MIB module (TE-MIB) using SMIv2, which is what the MIB tag covers.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects for Traffic Engineered (TE) Tunnels; for example, Multi-Protocol Label Switched Paths

traffic engineering.why: The managed objects model TE tunnels, paths with constraints, administrative groups, and setup/hold priorities, so readers of traffic engineering would want it.
traffic engineering.quote: The MIB module defined by this memo allows one to configure TE Tunnels, to assign one or more paths to a Tunnel

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is only the signaling protocol the ingress is expected to use; the MIB does not specify or extend it.
MPLS LSPs are given as an example of TE tunnels, but the MIB is generic and does not define MPLS itself.
SNMP is the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB module, which falls under the MIB tag.
Only listed as a possible signaling protocol value and referenced; not specified here.
IS-IS appears only as an enumerated value of teDistProtocol.

RFC3971.title: SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND)
RFC3971.summary: RFC 3971 specifies SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), which secures IPv6 NDP using CGA, RSA signature, timestamp and nonce options plus certification path discovery for router authorization.

SEND.why: The document is the SEND specification itself, defining new NDP options, ADD messages and processing rules.
SEND.quote: This document specifies security mechanisms for NDP. Unlike those in the original NDP specifications, these mechanisms do not use IPsec.

neighbor discovery.why: SEND is an extension of NDP, so readers of the IPv6 neighbor discovery subject would want it. It covers NS/NA, RS/RA, Redirect, DAD and NUD processing changes.
neighbor discovery.quote: IPv6 nodes use the Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) to discover other nodes on the link

PKI.why: A substantial part defines Authorization Delegation Discovery, a router authorization certificate profile, trust anchors and certification path transport. This is PKI-based router authorization.
PKI.quote: Certification paths, anchored on trusted parties, are expected to certify the authority of routers.

rejected.why: Router Authorization Certificates are profiled in Section 6.3.1, but this is a small use of the standard X.509/RFC 3280/3779 profile. PKI covers the authorization delegation theme.
NDP and the new CPS/CPA messages are carried in ICMPv6, which is only the substrate here.
RSA signatures are mandated but only used as the mechanism, not defined or analysed here.
IPsec is mentioned only as the original approach that SEND replaces.
Address autoconfiguration and DAD are discussed only as functions that SEND protects. The document does not specify them.
The more specific neighbor discovery and SEND tags fit better than the parent IPv6 tag.

gaps.name: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA)
gaps.why: SEND relies on CGA, which is specified in RFC 3972. The taxonomy has no CGA tag, and this document only uses it, so it is a minor gap.

RFC3972.title: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA)
RFC3972.summary: Specifies Cryptographically Generated Addresses: IPv6 interface identifiers derived from a hash of a public key and parameters, with generation, verification and signature procedures for use in Secure Neighbor Discovery.

SEND.why: CGA is the address-ownership and signature mechanism defined for SEND, and the working group is send. The document specifies how SEND binds keys to addresses and signs messages.
SEND.quote: This document specifies a method for securely associating a cryptographic public key with an IPv6 address in the Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) protocol

IPv6.why: The document defines a new IPv6 address format, including the interface identifier bits, Sec encoding, and the u/g bits. It is about IPv6 addressing, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA) are IPv6 addresses for which the interface identifier is generated by computing a cryptographic one-way hash function

rejected.why: RSA keys and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures are used as the mechanism, but the document does not specify RSA itself.
SHA-1 is only the hash function used to compute Hash1 and Hash2. The document does not specify it.
Only the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure is borrowed. There are no certificates and no PKI.
Section 7.3 covers privacy, but it is a minor part of the Security Considerations and not the document's subject.
SEND, a child of neighbor discovery, fits more specifically, so the ancestor is implied.

RFC3973.title: Protocol Independent Multicast - Dense Mode (PIM-DM): Protocol Specification (Revised)
RFC3973.summary: Specifies PIM-DM, a flood-and-prune multicast routing protocol using the unicast RIB for RPF checks, with Hello, Prune/Join/Graft, State Refresh and Assert state machines, packet formats and timers.

multicast.why: No PIM-DM-specific tag exists in the taxonomy. PIM-DM is a multicast routing protocol, so the multicast topic is the closest fit.
multicast.quote: PIM-DM is a multicast routing protocol that uses the underlying unicast routing information base to flood multicast datagrams to all multicast routers.

rejected.why: The document is about PIM-DM and shares only the PIM packet format with PIM-SM. PIM is a tech tag whose children include PIM-SM. The document specifies dense mode, so it does not warrant the PIM tag.
The document explicitly says PIM-DM is not intended to interact directly with PIM-SM. It only reuses the common packet formats and references PIM-SM for definitions.
IGMP is used only as a local membership source (section 5.2). The document does not specify or extend it.
The document makes no special considerations for SSM (section 5.3), which is only a brief interaction note.
IPsec AH is recommended for authenticating PIM messages, but only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
GDOI is mentioned once as a possible future negotiation protocol for Security Associations.

gaps.name: PIM-DM (Protocol Independent Multicast - Dense Mode)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has PIM and PIM-SM but no dense-mode tag. PIM-DM readers would expect it under PIM, and the parent multicast topic is the only available fit.

RFC3974.title: SMTP Operational Experience in Mixed IPv4/v6 Environments
RFC3974.summary: Informational RFC describing operational experience and requirements for SMTP in IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack environments, including a dual-stack MX-lookup sender algorithm and MX/A/AAAA record configuration guidance for recipient domains.

SMTP.why: The document's subject is SMTP sender behaviour and MX-based mail routing in dual-stack networks, including a step-by-step sender algorithm.
SMTP.quote: certain configurations of MX records are necessary for stable dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) SMTP operation.

IPv6 transition.why: It addresses IPv4/IPv6 coexistence for mail: dual-stack MX configuration, reachability between MXes, and translator considerations.
IPv6 transition.quote: During the transition period from IPv4 to IPv6, more care should be applied to IPv4/v6 interoperability.

DNS.why: A substantial part covers MX/A/AAAA record configuration, lookup procedure, and broken DNS servers returning SERVFAIL on AAAA queries.
DNS.quote: MX RRs are looked up in DNS to retrieve the names of hosts running MTAs associated with the domain part of the mail address.
DNS.section: 2. Basic DNS Resource Record Definitions for Mail Routing

rejected.why: IPv6 is the environment, but the specific subject is covered more precisely by IPv6 transition; no IPv6 specification is addressed.
Translators are mentioned only briefly in an appendix; no particular translation protocol is specified.
The more specific SMTP tag fits; email as a whole is not addressed.
Mentioned only in passing as a protocol needing special consideration with translators.
Mentioned only as one possible alternative transport between MX hosts.

RFC3975.title: OMA-IETF Standardization Collaboration
RFC3975.summary: An IAB-stream informational RFC setting out the principles and liaison framework for collaboration between the Open Mobile Alliance and the IETF, covering document sharing, liaisons, contributions and IPR.

IETF process.why: The document defines how the IETF interacts with an external standards body: liaison roles, formal liaison statements, participation in the IETF process and contributions. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document contains a set of principles and guidelines that serves as the basis for establishing a cooperation framework between the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

rejected.why: IPR is mentioned only to say each organization follows its own rules and to cite BCP 78 and BCP 79. It is not the subject of the document.
SIMPLE appears only in the Appendix A list of areas of common interest, and the document does not specify or analyse it.
ENUM appears only as one item in the Appendix A list of work areas, and the document does not address it.
Instant messaging is listed as a common work area, but the document says nothing technical about it.
Location services are one bullet in the Appendix A list, and the document does not address them.

gaps.name: Standards liaison relationships with other standards development organizations (SDOs)
gaps.why: The document is one of a series of IETF collaboration agreements with outside bodies (3GPP, 3GPP2, OMA). The taxonomy has no tag for inter-SDO liaison, so IETF process is the nearest fit.

RFC3976.title: Interworking SIP and Intelligent Network (IN) Applications
RFC3976.summary: Informational RFC describing how a SIP entity can access PSTN Intelligent Network services by mapping the SIP protocol state machine onto the IN basic call state models (O_BCSM and T_BCSM) and querying an SCP via INAP.

PSTN interop.why: The document is about interworking SIP endpoints with PSTN Intelligent Network services (SSP/SCP, INAP, BCSM). No specific child tag fits IN/INAP interworking, so the parent topic is used.
PSTN interop.quote: this document describes the mechanism for interworking SIP and Intelligent Network Application Part (INAP)

SIP.why: A large part of the document maps SIP states, responses and proxy/B2BUA roles to IN call model states, so SIP readers would want it. It proposes no SIP extensions.
SIP.quote: One way to gain access to IN services transparently from SIP ... is to map the SIP protocol state machine to the IN call models

rejected.why: Only mentioned as one possible way to carry INAP between the SIN entity and the SCP; the interface is explicitly unspecified.
SIP-T concerns ISUP encapsulation and interworking, whereas this document maps SIP to IN call models and INAP.
TRIP is mentioned once as a way to select an egress gateway in the SELECT_ROUTE PIC, and it is not a subject of the document.
SPIRITS covers IN invoking Internet-hosted services, the opposite direction; this document gives SIP endpoints access to IN services.
PINT covers Internet applications requesting telephone services, not SIP access to IN services.

gaps.name: Intelligent Network (IN) / INAP
gaps.why: The document is about IN call models (BCSM, SSP/SCP) and INAP interworking with SIP, and the taxonomy has no IN-specific tag.

RFC3977.title: Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP)
RFC3977.summary: RFC 3977 specifies NNTP version 2, replacing RFC 977: the commands, response codes, capabilities/extension mechanism, wildmat format, overview/header access commands, and formal syntax for distributing, retrieving and posting Netnews articles.

NNTP.why: The document is the core NNTP specification, obsoleting RFC 977 and defining all commands, responses and extension mechanisms.
NNTP.quote: This document specifies the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP), which is used for the distribution, inquiry, retrieval, and posting of Netnews articles

rejected.why: Netnews is the article format and system NNTP carries; NNTP is the more specific tag and the parent is implied.
The document moves NNTP's default charset to UTF-8 but UTF-8 is only an encoding it adopts, not what it is about.
TCP is only the substrate NNTP commonly runs over.
Section 9 uses ABNF to define NNTP syntax; it is a notation used, not the subject.
STARTTLS and authentication are defined in separate extension RFCs and only referenced here.
The capability registry is a small boilerplate-like part; the document is not about IANA practice.

RFC3978.title: IETF Rights in Contributions
RFC3978.summary: BCP 78 (RFC 3978) specifies the IETF's policy on rights, licenses, representations and required legal notices for Contributions, Internet-Drafts and RFCs, replacing RFC 3667 and updating RFC 2026 Section 10.

IPR.why: The whole document defines copyright licensing, grants, warranties, and required notices for IETF Contributions, which is the IPR/copyright subject.
IPR.quote: This memo details the IETF policies on rights in Contributions to the IETF.

rejected.why: The document updates RFC 2026 and relates to process, but its subject is rights in contributions, which IPR covers more specifically.
It requires notices in RFCs and Internet-Drafts, but it is about legal rights, not RFC format, style or publication.

RFC3979.title: Intellectual Property Rights in IETF Technology
RFC3979.summary: BCP 79 sets IETF policy on intellectual property rights (patents) in IETF technology: disclosure obligations, timing, licensing information, RFC notices, and how working groups treat IPR-encumbered technology.

IPR.why: The whole document defines IETF IPR disclosure rules, licensing assurances, and the required RFC IPR notice, which is the subject of the IPR tag.
IPR.quote: This memo details the IETF policies concerning IPR related to technology worked on within the IETF.

rejected.why: The document is an IETF process BCP and updates RFC 2026, but it is specifically about IPR, which is the more specific child-level subject under internet governance.
It mandates a notice in RFCs, but that is a small part and not about RFC format or publication in general.
Section 1 defines terms, but only as apparatus for the IPR policy.

RFC3980.title: T11 Network Address Authority (NAA) Naming Format for iSCSI Node Names
RFC3980.summary: Defines a new "naa." iSCSI node name type that embeds a T11 Network Address Authority identifier in ASCII hex, so devices with both SAS and iSCSI ports can share one device name; updates RFC 3720.

iSCSI.why: The document extends iSCSI by adding a new node name format and updates RFC 3720, the iSCSI specification. Readers of iSCSI would need it.
iSCSI.quote: This document defines an additional iSCSI node name type format to enable use of the "Network Address Authority" (NAA) worldwide naming format

rejected.why: The document is about naming, but only iSCSI node names. The iSCSI tag fits that more specifically, and this isn't general name resolution.
NAA is defined by Fibre Channel (T11), but the document does not specify or extend FC over IP. It only reuses the NAA identifier format.
iSCSI runs over TCP, which is only the substrate here.
SRP over InfiniBand appears only in the background table and terminology, not as a subject of the document.

RFC3981.title: IRIS: The Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) Core Protocol
RFC3981.summary: Specifies the IRIS core protocol, an XML-based framework for query/result exchanges with Internet registries, including the extension mechanism for registry types, an iris: URI scheme and its resolution via S-NAPTR/SRV.

domain registration.why: IRIS is a registry information lookup service, a successor-style alternative to WHOIS for domain and address registries. No more specific tag (RDAP, WHOIS) fits, since IRIS is its own protocol.
domain registration.quote: an application layer client-server protocol for a framework to represent the query and result operations of the information services of Internet registries

XML.why: The protocol is defined as an XML schema with XML-namespace-identified extension by derivation, and the document gives the full formal schema.
XML.quote: IRIS is specified by using the Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0 as described in [2], XML Schema notation as described in [4] and [5]

URI.why: Section 7 defines the IRIS URI scheme, with its syntax, default values and resolution rules. Readers of URI schemes would want it.
URI.quote: iris:<registry>/<resolution>/<authority>/<class>/<name>

rejected.why: DNS NAPTR/SRV records are used only for locating servers via S-NAPTR. The document defines no new DNS behaviour.
BEEP is the default transport, specified in a separate document (RFC 3983). This document only refers to it.
WHOIS is mentioned only as a protocol that may coexist with IRIS. The document does not specify or extend it.
Registry types are identified by URNs in the IETF XML namespace registry, but the document defines no URN namespace.
The appendix calls IRIS a directory service for registries, but it is not a general directory service like LDAP or X.500.
S-NAPTR service location is used for server resolution, but it is a supporting mechanism and not the document's subject.

gaps.name: IRIS / CRISP (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: No tag covers the IRIS protocol family or the CRISP working group's registry lookup work. domain registration is the closest fit.

RFC3982.title: IRIS:  A Domain Registry (dreg) Type for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS)
RFC3982.summary: Defines the IRIS "dreg1" registry type, an XML schema extending IRIS with queries and results (domain, host, contact, registration authority) for domain registries and registrars.

domain registration.why: The document specifies a lookup service for domain registry and registrar data (domains, hosts, contacts, registrars, status). No IRIS-specific tag exists in the taxonomy, so the domain registration topic is the best fit.
domain registration.quote: This document describes an Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) registry schema for registered DNS information.

rejected.why: IRIS is a successor to WHOIS-style directory services, but the document does not specify or discuss WHOIS.
RDAP is a different protocol serving a similar purpose and is not discussed here.
XML Schema is the notation used to define the registry type. It is the substrate and the document is not about XML usage.
The BEEP transport compliance section is a short conformance statement, and the actual BEEP binding is defined in a separate RFC.
Domain names and name servers appear as registry data, but the document does not specify DNS protocol, records or server behaviour.
The IDN query and the nameprep normalization are used, but they are one feature among many and IDN itself is not specified here.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IRIS or CRISP, the family of registry information protocols this document extends. The parent topic 'domain registration' is only an approximate fit.

RFC3983.title: Using the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) over the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP)
RFC3983.summary: Specifies how the IRIS registry information protocol is bound to BEEP as its application transport, including the BEEP profile identifier, message patterns, server authentication via TLS, and the iris.beep URI scheme, port and S-NAPTR registrations.

BEEP.why: The document defines a new BEEP profile for IRIS, with its channel creation, message exchange patterns and registrations. Readers of BEEP would want it.
BEEP.quote: This document specifies how to use the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) as the application transport substrate for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS).

transport mapping.why: It is a transport binding of IRIS onto BEEP over TCP, which defines the URI scheme, application protocol label and character sets.
transport mapping.quote: This section lists the definitions required by IRIS [6] for transport mappings.

domain registration.why: IRIS is the registry information service for domain and address registries, and this document sets the transport rules for registry types. The core IRIS protocol is not itself in the taxonomy, so the general topic fits.
domain registration.quote: Specifications of registry types MUST include the following explicit definitions:

rejected.why: TLS is only used as the BEEP tuning profile for server authentication. The document defines no new TLS mechanism.
HTTP appears only in the introduction, as an alternative that was rejected.
XML is only the encoding of IRIS messages and is not specified here.
SASL tuning profiles are only listed in the Security Considerations.
The document registers the iris.beep scheme, but this is a minor part of the binding and not the subject.
The S-NAPTR registration is only an application protocol label entry, so the document is not about DNS.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The document binds this registry lookup protocol to BEEP, but the taxonomy has no tag for IRIS or the CRISP family. Only the generic domain registration topic is available.

RFC3984.title: RTP Payload Format for H.264 Video
RFC3984.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for H.264/AVC video: NAL unit packetization modes (single NAL, non-interleaved, interleaved), aggregation and fragmentation units, decoding order numbers, and the video/H264 media type with SDP parameters and offer/answer rules.

H.264.why: The document defines how H.264 NAL units are carried in RTP, including packetization modes, parameter sets and codec-specific signalling; it is the H.264 RTP payload format.
H.264.quote: This memo describes an RTP Payload format for the ITU-T Recommendation H.264 video codec and the technically identical ISO/IEC International Standard 14496-10 video codec.

SDP.why: Section 8.2 defines the mapping of H.264 parameters to SDP fmtp lines, offer/answer rules, and declarative usage, a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: A mapping of the parameters into the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [5] is also provided for applications that use SDP.

rejected.why: The tag is a parent of H.264? No: H.264 sits under codecs, while RTP payload format is under RTP. The document is an RTP payload format, so this is a close candidate. I chose H.264 as the specific tag and considered RTP payload format only as an alternative; the RTP payload format tag is arguably also fitting.
RTP is the transport the payload format is built for; the document does not extend RTP itself, only defines a payload.
The document registers video/H264, but this is incidental to the payload format and not about media type registry rules.
FEC appears only in informative application examples (RFC 2733 with FUs), not as a main subject.
Mentioned only in security considerations as an example protection mechanism.
Mentioned only regarding jitter calculation caveats.

RFC3985.title: Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) Architecture
RFC3985.summary: Informational architecture for Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3): emulating Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet, TDM and SONET/SDH services over IP or MPLS packet switched networks, defining terminology, protocol layering, encapsulation, control and management models.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines the pseudo wire architecture, layering, encapsulation, control plane and management.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes an architecture for Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3).

rejected.why: MPLS is one of the PSNs carrying PWs and the label/control word are discussed, but the document is about pseudo wires, not MPLS itself.
Section 8.2 outlines a PW MIB architecture, but it is a minor part of the document and the MIBs themselves are defined elsewhere.
RTP is only suggested as an option for timing and sequencing, not specified or extended here.
L2TP is one possible demultiplexing/tunnel substrate; the document does not specify it.
ATM is one of several emulated services, only mentioned as a payload type.
PWs underpin L2VPN services, but this document does not describe VPN services.

RFC3986.title: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax
RFC3986.summary: RFC 3986 (STD 66) defines the generic URI syntax, percent-encoding, reference resolution for relative references, and normalization/comparison rules, obsoleting RFC 2396.

URI.why: The whole document specifies URI syntax, components, reference resolution, and normalization/comparison, so it belongs on the URI page.
URI.quote: This specification defines the generic URI syntax and a process for resolving URI references that might be in relative form

rejected.why: DNS is only one registered-name lookup mechanism that the host syntax can reuse. The document does not specify DNS.
The document defines the ABNF for IPv6 literals in URI hosts, but it does not specify or analyse IPv6 itself.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar. The document is not about ABNF.
HTTP appears only in examples and in the security discussion. The document does not specify it.
URNs are mentioned only in the URI/URL/URN classification discussion (Section 1.1.3). The document does not define a URN namespace or URN syntax.
The document explicitly leaves internationalized identifiers undefined. It only says that non-ASCII characters are percent-encoded as UTF-8.

RFC3987.title: Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs)
RFC3987.summary: Defines the Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI), a Unicode-based complement to URIs, with its syntax, IRI-to-URI mapping, bidi rules, comparison and normalization, and deployment guidelines.

IRI.why: The whole document specifies IRIs: ABNF syntax, mapping to and from URIs, bidirectional IRIs, normalization and comparison, and usage guidance.
IRI.quote: This document defines a new protocol element called Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI) by extending the syntax of URIs to a much wider repertoire of characters.

rejected.why: IRI is a child of URI and is the more specific fit. The document builds on RFC 3986 but defines the IRI element rather than URI syntax.
IDNA/ToASCII is used for the ireg-name conversion, but only as a supporting mechanism. The document is not about IDN.
UTF-8 is the encoding used in the IRI-to-URI mapping, so it is a substrate here. The document does not specify it.
Unicode characters, normalization and the bidi algorithm are relied on, but the subject is the identifier type, not Unicode usage in general.
HTTP appears only in examples and applicability notes.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the IRI grammar.

RFC3988.title: Maximum Transmission Unit Signalling Extensions for the Label Distribution Protocol
RFC3988.summary: Experimental extension to LDP defining an MTU TLV in Label Mapping messages and a hop-by-hop procedure so ingress LSRs can learn an LSP's MTU for RFC 1191 path MTU discovery.

LDP.why: The document defines a new LDP TLV (0x0601) carried in Label Mapping messages and the procedure for computing and advertising LSP MTU.
LDP.quote: This document specifies experimental extensions to LDP in support of LSP MTU discovery.

PMTUD.why: The goal is LSP MTU discovery supporting path MTU discovery, and Section 4 specifies how the ingress LSR responds per RFC 1191 using ICMP fragmentation-needed.
PMTUD.quote: This functionality is essential to the proper functioning of RFC 1191 path MTU detection

rejected.why: Mentioned only in the interaction section as being unaffected; the document is not about CR-LDP.
Only mentioned as a tunnel type that LDP LSPs may traverse; not specified here.
ICMP Destination Unreachable is used as the response mechanism but is not itself specified or extended.
LDP is the more specific tag; MPLS is implied as an ancestor.

RFC3989.title: Middlebox Communications (MIDCOM) Protocol Semantics
RFC3989.summary: Specifies the abstract semantics (transactions, state machines, parameters) of the MIDCOM protocol by which agents configure middleboxes such as firewalls and NATs via policy reserve/enable rules, sessions and rule groups.

NAT.why: The protocol semantics configure NAT bindings, address/port reservations and twice-NAT behaviour on middleboxes; the NAT readers would want this RFC.
NAT.quote: The MIDCOM protocol semantics ... for interacting with middleboxes such as firewalls and Network Address Translators (NATs).

firewall.why: MIDCOM dynamically configures firewall pinholes and packet filters on behalf of applications, so firewall/middlebox traversal is a core subject.
firewall.quote: At a firewall, the enable action is interpreted as one or more allow actions configuring pinholes.

rejected.why: SIP is only used as an example scenario in section 4.2; the document does not specify or extend SIP.
TLS and IPsec are only mentioned as underlying security for the session, not specified here.
Policy rules are used in the MIDCOM sense, but the document is not a policy information model; it is a protocol semantics for NAT/firewall control.
That tag covers interactive traversal for real-time media (ICE/STUN/TURN); MIDCOM is explicitly positioned as an alternative, not UNSAF traversal.
Only listed as a possible way to secure sessions.

gaps.name: MIDCOM (middlebox communication)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for middlebox communication/control protocols; firewall (with NAT) is the nearest fit.

RFC3990.title: Configuration and Provisioning for Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Problem Statement
RFC3990.summary: Problem statement describing the management, configuration, provisioning, radio-coordination and security problems of large-scale 802.11 WLAN deployments, motivating a standard interoperable interface between wireless access points and a central access controller (CAPWAP).

CAPWAP.why: The document is the CAPWAP problem statement, motivating the AP-to-controller control and provisioning protocol work.
CAPWAP.quote: a standardized, interoperable interface between access points and a centralized controller addressing the problems seems desirable.

WiFi.why: The problems described concern large 802.11 WLAN deployments, so readers of Wi-Fi would want this RFC.
WiFi.quote: This document will describe the problems introduced by the large-scale deployment of 802.11 WLANs in enterprise networks.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an example of a shared secret stored in the AC in Security Considerations; the document is not about RADIUS.
Management burden is part of the problem, but the CAPWAP tag covers the AP configuration/provisioning subject more specifically.
Security Considerations are brief boilerplate-like remarks, not the main subject.

RFC3991.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Redirect and Reset Package
RFC3991.summary: Defines an MGCP package (RED) that lets a Call Agent redirect or reset groups of endpoints via EndpointConfiguration, including a NotifiedEntityList of ordered backup Call Agents.

MGCP.why: The whole document specifies a new MGCP package (RED) with new parameters, return codes and procedures for redirecting and resetting endpoints.
MGCP.quote: This document provides extensions in the form of a new MGCP package that provides mechanisms for redirecting and resetting a group of endpoints.

rejected.why: Only mentioned in the IESG note as the standards-based alternative; the document does not specify or extend Megaco/H.248.
Only cited in Security Considerations as the required protection mechanism; the document is not about IPsec.
Domain names and Max1/Max2 DNS queries are used in retransmission procedures, but nothing new about DNS is defined.
Parent of MGCP and implied by the MGCP tag; the document is specifically about MGCP, so the child tag is used instead.

RFC3992.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Lockstep State Reporting Mechanism
RFC3992.summary: Defines an MGCP package (LCK) that lets a Call Agent configure endpoints to report, via a new RSIP restart method, being stuck in the lockstep state after failures such as Call Agent failover.

MGCP.why: The document specifies an extension package to MGCP, adding an EndpointConfiguration parameter and a new RSIP restart method. MGCP readers would want it.
MGCP.quote: The Lockstep package defined in this document defines extensions to the EndpointConfiguration and RestartInProgress commands

rejected.why: The IESG note mentions the Megaco-based RFC 3015 only as the standards-based alternative. The document does not cover Megaco/H.248.
IPsec appears only in Security Considerations as the required protection mechanism, so it is boilerplate.
The package registration is a routine IANA Considerations item and not the subject of the document.
ABNF is used only to write the parameter syntax. The document is not about it.

RFC3993.title: Subscriber-ID Suboption for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Relay Agent Option
RFC3993.summary: Defines a new Subscriber-ID suboption (code 6) for the DHCP relay agent information option, carrying a provider-assigned, network-independent ASCII subscriber identifier from relay agent to DHCP server.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCP by defining a new relay agent information option suboption, with relay agent and server behavior.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a new Subscriber-ID suboption for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol's (DHCP) relay agent information option.

rejected.why: The document concerns DHCP for IPv4 (RFC 2131) only.
DOCSIS is mentioned only as an example network environment, not the subject.
xDSL is mentioned only as an example environment where relay agent options are used.
The suboption value is an NVT ASCII string, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
Subscriber-ID may trigger accounting, but the document does not specify AAA mechanisms.

RFC3994.title: Indication of Message Composition for Instant Messaging
RFC3994.summary: Defines the isComposing status message, an XML content type and namespace that tells an instant messaging recipient the other party is composing a message, with sender and receiver state machines.

instant messaging.why: The whole document specifies an IM status indication, its composer and receiver behaviour, and its use in page and session mode.
instant messaging.quote: it is useful to know during an IM conversation whether the other party is composing a message; e.g., typing or recording an audio message.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new media type, application/im-iscomposing+xml, and an XML namespace and schema for it.
media types.quote: labeled as an application/im-iscomposing+xml content type.

rejected.why: Presence information was considered and rejected as an alternative. The document does not extend PIDF.
The document came from the SIMPLE working group, but it defines no event package, PIDF extension or XCAP usage. It is an in-band message mechanism.
XML is only the encoding for the status message. The document does not address XML usage in general.
SIP is mentioned only as one carrier for page-mode delivery (the 415 response). The document does not extend SIP.
Session mode is mentioned generically. The document does not specify MSRP behaviour.

RFC3995.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): Event Notifications and Subscriptions
RFC3995.summary: RFC 3995 defines an optional IPP/1.1 extension for event notifications: Subscription Objects, per-job and per-printer subscriptions, new operations (Create-Job-Subscriptions, Create-Printer-Subscriptions, Get-Subscriptions, Renew-Subscription, Cancel-Subscription), event types, notification content, and a delivery-method registration framework.

IPP.why: The document extends IPP with subscription objects, new operations, status codes, attribute tags and events for printer and job notifications.
IPP.quote: This IPP notification specification is an OPTIONAL extension to Internet Printing Protocol/1.1: Model and Semantics [RFC2911, RFC2910].

rejected.why: IPP runs over HTTP, which is only the transport substrate here and is not specified or extended.
The IANA Considerations section registers attributes, operations and delivery methods. That is boilerplate for this document, not its subject.
Email is mentioned only as a possible delivery method; the document defines none.
Spam is mentioned only in the security considerations as a threat of unwanted notifications.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IPP tech tag under applications that is the correct fit, but its definition above reads 'IPP (Internet Printing Protocol)' and was used here. No gap remains.

RFC3996.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): The 'ippget' Delivery Method for Event Notifications
RFC3996.summary: Defines the 'ippget' pull delivery method for IPP event notifications, including the new Get-Notifications operation, Event Wait Mode, a new status code, and the ippget-event-life Printer attribute.

IPP.why: The document extends IPP/1.1 with a new operation (Get-Notifications), a status code, and Printer attributes. Readers of the IPP subject would expect it.
IPP.quote: This document specifies the 'ippget' Pull Delivery Method for use with the "Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): Event Notifications and Subscriptions" specification

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport for IPP. The document defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
It uses multipart/related with application/ipp parts for Event Wait Mode, but it registers no media type.
The Job Monitoring MIB is mentioned only as a source for the recommended event-life value.
The Security Considerations remark that pull delivery avoids spam notifications. That is boilerplate and not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IPP tech tag under applications, but I should confirm the id. The id used above is 'IPP', and it is in the taxonomy as 'IPP' (Internet Printing Protocol).

RFC3997.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): Requirements for IPP Notifications
RFC3997.summary: Informational requirements document for event notifications and subscriptions as an optional part of an IPP print service, with terminology, usage scenarios and 17 requirements.

IPP.why: The RFC states requirements for notification and subscription extensions to the Internet Printing Protocol, so readers of the IPP subject would want it.
IPP.quote: This document provides a statement of the requirements for notifications as an optional part of an IPP Service.

rejected.why: IPP runs over HTTP and HTTP authentication and TLS are mentioned only in Security Considerations; it is substrate, not the subject.
Email is given only as an example notification delivery method; the document does not specify email.
The application/ipp media type is mentioned in passing in Internationalization Considerations only.
The LPD-to-IPP mapping document is only listed in the appendix description of base IPP documents.
Notification abuse (spam) is a Security Considerations concern, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IPP tech tag only in the abstract sense. The id 'IPP' is not listed. The closest tag is 'IPP', which does not appear in the taxonomy as written. The taxonomy does list 'IPP' under applications. Using the listed id 'IPP' is correct.

RFC3998.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP): Job and Printer Administrative Operations
RFC3998.summary: Defines 16 optional IPP/1.1 administrative operations for Printers and Jobs (enable/disable, pause, hold, deactivate, restart, reprocess, suspend, promote, schedule), plus new attributes, values, a status code, and Printer fan-out/fan-in semantics.

IPP.why: The whole document extends IPP/1.1 with new Printer and Job operations, attributes, values and status codes, and Printer object fan-out/fan-in.
IPP.quote: This document specifies the following 16 additional OPTIONAL system administration operations for use with the Internet Printing Protocol/1.1 (IPP)

rejected.why: IPP is carried over HTTP via RFC 2910, but this document only references it in the summary of base documents.
TLS client authentication is required in Security Considerations only; nothing new is specified about TLS.
Subordinate printer URIs are mentioned, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
The operations are administrative, but they are IPP printer operator functions rather than general network management architecture or protocols.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the IPP tech tag under directory services/applications? Actually IPP exists as 'IPP' under applications, so it fits; no gap beyond that.

RFC4001.title: Textual Conventions for Internet Network Addresses
RFC4001.summary: Defines the INET-ADDRESS-MIB module, a set of SMIv2 textual conventions for representing IPv4, IPv6 (with zone index) and DNS-name Internet addresses, prefix lengths, ports and AS numbers in MIB modules, with usage guidance.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining SMIv2 textual conventions intended to be imported by other MIB modules, with usage hints on table indexing and compliance.
MIB.quote: This MIB module defines textual conventions to represent commonly used Internet network layer addressing information.

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses and scoped zones are represented, but the document only defines MIB encodings for them, not IPv6 itself.
SNMP is the access mechanism for MIB objects; the document is about MIB data definitions (MIB), not the protocol.
DNS names are one address type, with only brief guidance on resolution timing; the DNS protocol is not specified or extended.
It covers MIB representation of addresses, not IP address architecture, allocation or use; MIB is the more specific fit.
IPv4 addresses are encoded as one address type only; the IPv4 protocol is not the subject.

RFC4002.title: IANA Registration for Enumservice 'web' and 'ft'
RFC4002.summary: Registers the ENUM Enumservices 'web' (http, https) and 'ft' (ftp) with IANA under the RFC 3761 E2U DDDS process, mapping E.164 numbers to web and file-transfer URIs via NAPTR records.

ENUM.why: The document's whole purpose is to define two ENUM Enumservices for NAPTR records in E.164 number mapping, which is the ENUM subject.
ENUM.quote: This document registers the Enumservices 'web' and 'ft' by using the URI schemes 'http:', 'https:' and 'ftp:'

rejected.why: http: and https: are only the URI schemes named in the registration. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
ftp: is only the URI scheme named by the 'ft' Enumservice. FTP itself is not specified or extended.
NAPTR records in DNS are the substrate for ENUM. The document adds nothing new to DNS itself, and ENUM is the more specific tag.
The document uses URI schemes as the outcome of Enumservice lookup but does not define or change any URI scheme.
The registration is an IANA action, but it is a registry entry for ENUM, not guidance on IANA procedures or stewardship.
DNSSEC appears only as a reference in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate evidence.

RFC4003.title: GMPLS Signaling Procedure for Egress Control
RFC4003.summary: Clarifies GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling procedures (ERO and RRO handling) by which an LSP's head-end controls the label used on the egress node's output/downstream interface, updating RFC 3473 without changing its mechanisms.

GMPLS.why: The whole document clarifies GMPLS signaling procedures (egress control) specified in RFC 3471/3473, so GMPLS readers would look for it.
GMPLS.quote: This document clarifies the procedures for the control of the label used on an output/downstream interface of the egress node of a Label Switched Path (LSP).

RSVP-TE.why: The procedures are RSVP-TE ERO, RRO and PathErr processing at the egress, as extended by RFC 3473, so the document updates RSVP-TE signalling behaviour.
RSVP-TE.quote: any errors encountered while processing the ERO, including if the listed label(s) are not acceptable or cannot be supported in forwarding, SHOULD result in the generation of a PathErr message

rejected.why: GMPLS is the more specific tag; MPLS is its parent and is implied.
RSVP-TE is the specific tag; plain RSVP for QoS reservation is not what the document addresses.
RSVP-TE is the more specific fit, and the document is about label control, not traffic engineering in general.

RFC4004.title: Diameter Mobile IPv4 Application
RFC4004.summary: Specifies a Diameter application (Application-Id 2) with AMR/AMA and HAR/HAA commands, AVPs, session management, accounting and session-key distribution so AAA servers can authenticate, authorize and account for Mobile IPv4 mobile nodes, including in foreign networks.

Diameter.why: The whole document defines a new Diameter application: command codes, AVPs, result codes and session handling.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies a Diameter application that allows a Diameter server to authenticate, authorize and collect accounting information for Mobile IPv4 services rendered to a mobile node.

Mobile IPv4.why: The application supports HA/FA operation, registration, handoff and mobility security associations for Mobile IPv4, so Mobile IPv4 readers would want it.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Mobile IPv4 [MOBILEIP] allows a Mobile Node (MN) to change its point of attachment to the Internet while maintaining its fixed home address.

key management.why: A substantial part of the document (sections 3.4, 8 and 9) covers generating and distributing MN-HA, MN-FA and FA-HA session keys and nonces.
key management.quote: The Diameter Mobile IPv4 application solves this by including key distribution functionality, which means that after a Mobile Node is authenticated the authorization phase includes the generation of session keys and nonces.

rejected.why: The more specific Mobile IPv4 tag applies, and the document says it is not applicable to Mobile IPv6.
TLS is only used to protect key transport between AAAH and agents; the document defines nothing new about it.
IPsec is only a substrate for securing key transport; the document does not specify or extend it.
HMAC-SHA-1 is merely the algorithm value used for key derivation and authentication extensions.
CDMA2000 appears only as a requirements reference, not as the subject of the document.
The more specific Diameter tag applies, so the AAA parent is implied.

RFC4005.title: Diameter Network Access Server Application
RFC4005.summary: RFC 4005 specifies the Diameter Network Access Server application: NAS commands and AVPs for authentication, authorization, tunneling and accounting, plus rules for translating between RADIUS and Diameter.

Diameter.why: The whole document defines a Diameter application: commands, AVPs, session handling and accounting for NAS.
Diameter.quote: This document describes the Diameter protocol application used for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) services in the Network Access Server (NAS) environment.

RADIUS.why: Section 9 specifies RADIUS/Diameter translation, including dynamic authorization and VSAs, and the AVP space reuses RADIUS attributes.
RADIUS.quote: this application has been carefully designed to ease the burden of protocol conversion between RADIUS and Diameter.

rejected.why: PPP, CHAP and PAP are carried as access types and authentication data; the document does not specify PPP.
EAP is handled by a separate Diameter EAP application and is only referenced.
Tunnel-Type values are listed, but the document defines AVPs and not tunneling protocols.
The more specific Diameter tag covers this document.
IPsec is mentioned only as a base-protocol security mechanism.
DSCP is referenced only inside the QoS-Filter-Rule syntax.

RFC4006.title: Diameter Credit-Control Application
RFC4006.summary: Specifies the Diameter Credit-Control application (application id 4, CCR/CCA commands 272) for real-time credit authorization, rating, direct debiting, refunds and graceful service termination for prepaid services, including RADIUS prepaid interworking.

Diameter.why: The RFC defines a new Diameter application with new commands, AVPs, state machines and result codes, so it belongs on the Diameter page.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies a Diameter application that can be used to implement real-time credit-control for a variety of end user services

AAA.why: It extends AAA infrastructure with credit authorization for prepaid users and describes interaction with AAA servers and accounting flows. This is a secondary aspect.
AAA.quote: a new type of server is needed in the AAA infrastructure: Diameter credit-control server

rejected.why: Only section 11 sketches RADIUS prepaid interworking at a high level; the document does not specify RADIUS.
SIP is only a service example and in the appendix flows; it is not specified or extended here.
Not a taxonomy tag; the NAS application is merely referenced.
TLS and IPsec appear only as underlying security in the Security Considerations.
IANA sections are boilerplate registrations for the application's own AVPs.

gaps.name: Diameter
gaps.why: The taxonomy as shown has no 'Diameter' tag under AAA that I could confirm exists; I used the id 'Diameter' as listed under AAA in the taxonomy.

RFC4007.title: IPv6 Scoped Address Architecture
RFC4007.summary: Specifies the IPv6 scoped address architecture: address scopes, zones, zone indices, packet send/receive/forward rules, multicast scoped routing, and the textual %zone_id representation for non-global addresses.

addressing.why: The document defines address scope, scope zones, zone indices and their textual notation. This is IP address architecture. IPv6 is the technology, but the specific subject is addressing, so addressing is the best fit.
addressing.quote: This document specifies the architectural characteristics, expected behavior, textual representation, and usage of IPv6 addresses of different scopes.

IPv6.why: The document is an IPv6 architecture specification. It also covers IPv6 forwarding behaviour, including Routing Header handling and ICMPv6 Code 2 for packets beyond the scope of the source address.
IPv6.quote: Internet Protocol version 6 includes support for addresses of different "scope"; that is, both global and non-global (e.g., link-local) addresses.

rejected.why: Section 10 covers scoped multicast routing, but only as one part of the scoped address architecture. The document is not about multicast routing in its own right.
It defines ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable Code 2 (beyond scope of source address) as a minor item. ICMP is not the subject.
Neighbor Discovery is mentioned once, as a mechanism used when forwarding link-local packets. It is not the subject.
The sin6_scope_id field and the related API are only referenced. The API itself is specified in other documents.
Section 11.7 discusses the conflict between % zone IDs and URI syntax, but only to decline to specify how they combine.

RFC4008.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Network Address Translators (NAT)
RFC4008.summary: Defines the NAT-MIB SMIv2 module for configuring and monitoring Network Address Translator devices, covering interfaces, address maps, binds, sessions, protocol statistics and notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is a MIB module (NAT-MIB) in SMIv2, with tables, textual conventions, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for devices implementing Network Address Translator (NAT) function.

NAT.why: The MIB models NAT behaviour: address maps, binds, sessions, realms, and the RFC 3489 NAPT variations, so NAT readers would want it.
NAT.quote: The MIB module identifies four types of NAT services: Basic NAT, NAPT, twice NAT and bidirectional NAT.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol changes. MIB is the more specific tag.
RFC 3489 is referenced only for NAPT terminology (cone/symmetric NAT classification), not specified or extended.
ICMP identifiers are mentioned for bind port fields, but ICMP is not the subject.
The MIB supports IPv4 and IPv6 address types via InetAddress, but IPv6 is not a subject of the document.
Implied by the MIB tag's ancestry; no broader management topic is addressed.

RFC4009.title: The SEED Encryption Algorithm
RFC4009.summary: RFC 4009 describes the SEED 128-bit Feistel block cipher developed by KISA, including its round function, key schedule, S-boxes, test vectors, and OIDs for CBC, MAC and PBE use.

cryptography.why: The document specifies a block cipher algorithm. No SEED-specific tag exists in the taxonomy, so the cryptography topic is the best fit.
cryptography.quote: SEED is a 128-bit symmetric key block cipher that has been developed by KISA (Korea Information Security Agency)

rejected.why: The OIDs are defined with ASN.1 notation, but this is incidental to the cipher specification.
SEED is a different cipher and is not related to AES.
The PBE OID refers to RFC 2898, but the document does not define password-based key derivation.
The document is not about CMS. It only defines OIDs that could be used in such contexts.
E-commerce is mentioned only as a use case for SEED in Korea.

gaps.name: SEED block cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the SEED cipher. Similar national ciphers such as ARIA, Camellia and GOST each have their own tag.

RFC4010.title: Use of the SEED Encryption Algorithm in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC4010.summary: Specifies how to use the SEED block cipher for content encryption (CBC) and key wrapping (AES key wrap adapted to SEED) in CMS, with OIDs, S/MIME capabilities and an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document defines OIDs, parameters and processing for SEED content and key encryption in CMS, extending CMS's algorithm set.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the SEED encryption algorithm for encryption with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

S/MIME.why: A section defines the SEED SMIMECapability value and its DER encoding for S/MIME clients.
S/MIME.quote: An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the set of cryptographic functions it supports by using the S/MIME capabilities attribute.

rejected.why: The AES key wrap algorithm (RFC 3394) is reused with AES replaced by SEED. The document is not about AES.
The document is about a specific cipher's use in CMS. The CMS tag fits better, and no SEED tag exists.
The ASN.1 module is only the apparatus for defining the OIDs. The document is not about ASN.1.
Key wrapping is covered, but it is part of the CMS algorithm conventions. Key generation and distribution are explicitly out of scope.

gaps.name: SEED block cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SEED, the Korean 128-bit block cipher. Similar ciphers such as ARIA and Camellia do have tags, and the RFC 4009 companion document would use one too.

RFC4011.title: Policy Based Management MIB
RFC4011.summary: Defines the Policy-Based Management MIB, an SNMP MIB module plus the PolicyScript language and function libraries for distributing and executing policy conditions/actions on managed devices, with scheduling, roles, capabilities, tracking and debugging tables.

MIB.why: The document's core is a MIB module (POLICY-BASED-MANAGEMENT-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables for policies, code, roles, capabilities, schedules, tracking and notifications.
MIB.quote: this MIB defines objects that enable policy-based monitoring and management of Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) infrastructures, a scripting language, and a script execution environment

policy management.why: The document specifies a policy-based management architecture (policyCondition/policyAction, precedence groups, execution environment) and relates to the Policy Core Information Model.
policy management.quote: This practice is called Policy-Based Management.  This document defines managed objects for the Simple Network Management Protocol that are used to distribute policies in a common form

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol the MIB is accessed through and the PolicyScript library functions issue SNMP operations, but the document defines a MIB module rather than extending the protocol itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
PmUTF8String and the international string library use UTF-8, but this is a supporting encoding, not the subject.
The schedule table borrows RFC 2445 date and time formats, but only as a format reference.
The PolicyScript grammar is given in EBNF, but the notation is just the vehicle for defining the language.
The schedule table has local and UTC time handling, but this is scheduling, not time zone data distribution.

gaps.name: PolicyScript scripting language
gaps.why: The document defines a C-like scripting language and a script execution environment with function libraries, but the taxonomy has no tag for embedded management scripting languages.

RFC4012.title: Routing Policy Specification Language next generation (RPSLng)
RFC4012.summary: RFC 4012 extends RPSL (and the RFC 2725 authorization model) with mp- attributes, an afi attribute, route6 and inet6num classes, and class updates so routing policy can be documented for IPv6 and multicast.

RPSL.why: The whole document extends RPSL with mp-import/mp-export, afi, route6 and updated set classes, and the RFC 2725 authorization extensions for route6/inet6num objects used in routing registries.
RPSL.quote: This memo introduces a new set of simple extensions to the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL), enabling the language to document routing policies for the IPv6 and multicast address families

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses are the subject of the policy extensions, but the document is about the policy language, not IPv6 itself.
MPBGP is added as a protocol value in the dictionary, but BGP itself is not specified or extended.
Multicast is only an address family that policy can be written for; no multicast routing is specified.
The RFC 2725 authorization extensions to route6 objects are a minor part, and the document says it adds no new security functionality.

RFC4013.title: SASLprep: Stringprep Profile for User Names and Passwords
RFC4013.summary: Defines SASLprep, a stringprep profile (Unicode 3.2, NFKC, prohibited characters, bidi checks) for preparing user names and passwords for comparison, intended for SASL mechanisms.

SASL.why: The profile exists to prepare user names and passwords for SASL mechanisms, so SASL readers would want it.
SASL.quote: The profile is designed for use in Simple Authentication and Security Layer ([SASL]) mechanisms, such as [PLAIN], [CRAM-MD5], and [DIGEST-MD5].

PRECIS.why: It is a stringprep profile for internationalized strings, which is the predecessor approach to PRECIS and is about preparation and comparison of internationalized strings.
PRECIS.quote: This document defines the "SASLprep" profile of the "stringprep" algorithm [StringPrep].

rejected.why: Unicode is the character set and normalization basis, but the document is about a string-preparation profile, not Unicode usage in general. PRECIS covers it better.
The profile supports authentication, but SASL is the more specific tag and already covers it.
The profile registration is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the main subject.

gaps.name: stringprep
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for stringprep (RFC 3454) and its profiles such as nameprep and SASLprep. PRECIS is the nearest fit.

RFC4014.title: Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Attributes Suboption for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Relay Agent Information Option
RFC4014.summary: Defines a new DHCP Relay Agent Information option suboption (code 7) that lets a relay/NAS pass RADIUS attributes from authentication to the DHCP server for selecting client configuration.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a new DHCP relay agent option suboption and the behaviour of relay agents and servers with it.
DHCP.quote: The RADIUS Attributes suboption is a new suboption for the DHCP Relay Agent option.

RADIUS.why: The suboption carries RADIUS attributes and constrains which attributes may be used, so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: The RADIUS attributes are encoded according to the encoding rules in RFC 2865, in octets o1...oN.

rejected.why: IEEE 802.1X is only the example context; EAP is not discussed.
RADIUS is the more specific tag; the document is not about an AAA framework in general.
Only a single suboption code assignment, which is boilerplate.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a defense.
The document concerns DHCPv4 relay agent option; IPv6 pool attribute is just a table entry.

RFC4015.title: The Eifel Response Algorithm for TCP
RFC4015.summary: Specifies the Eifel response algorithm, which lets a TCP sender react to a detected spurious retransmission timeout by suppressing go-back-N retransmits, restoring congestion control state, and adapting the retransmission timer.

TCP.why: The document defines a TCP sender-side algorithm that changes retransmission, congestion window and RTO handling. It is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: the Eifel response algorithm provides a way for a TCP sender to respond to a detected spurious timeout.

rejected.why: The algorithm does restore cwnd and ssthresh, but it is a TCP loss-recovery response. The TCP tag covers it, and no congestion-control-specific technology tag fits.
NewReno is discussed only as a loss recovery scheme to combine with, with a small modification to its step 1. The document is not about NewReno.
ECN-Echo is only a condition that blocks reversing the congestion state.
SCTP appears only in references to other detection algorithms.
