RFC4016.title: Protocol for Carrying Authentication and Network Access (PANA) Threat Analysis and Security Requirements
RFC4016.summary: Informational threat analysis of PANA (protocol for carrying authentication for network access), enumerating threats in PAA discovery, authentication, disconnect, service theft and PAA-EP communication, and deriving eight security requirements for the PANA protocol design.

PANA.why: The whole document is a threat analysis and requirements set for PANA, the protocol being designed by the PANA working group.
PANA.quote: This document discusses the threats to protocols used to carry authentication for network access.

rejected.why: EAP is mentioned as an example of an authentication protocol with success/failure messages and compound methods, but the document does not specify or extend EAP.
Only cited for the PAA-AS path threats already covered in RFC 3579; not discussed here.
Mentioned once as a possible mitigation for DAD attacks; not a subject of the document.
The AS is described as an AAA server, but the AAA framework is incidental.
The parent is implied by the PANA tag; the document is about a specific protocol's threats.
DAD and ND/ARP activity are touched on in one threat (T6.6.2) only.

RFC4017.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Method Requirements for Wireless LANs
RFC4017.summary: Informational RFC defining mandatory, recommended and optional requirements that EAP authentication methods must meet for use in IEEE 802.11i wireless LAN deployments, and listing non-compliant methods.

EAP.why: The whole document specifies requirements on EAP methods (key derivation, mutual authentication, MSK/EMSK, fragmentation, channel binding) and names non-compliant methods.
EAP.quote: This document defines requirements for EAP methods used in IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN deployments.

WiFi.why: The requirements are scoped to IEEE 802.11 WLAN security (802.11i, 4-Way Handshake), so Wi-Fi readers would want it.
WiFi.quote: EAP authentication methods suitable for use in wireless LAN authentication MUST satisfy the following criteria:

rejected.why: RADIUS is only referenced for AAA transport of the MSK and authorization in Security Considerations; the document does not specify it.
EAP-TLS and TTLS are only mentioned as example deployed methods, not addressed.
AAA servers are mentioned only in passing and the document is not about AAA frameworks.
Key derivation requirements are part of EAP method requirements; the document is not about key management in its own right.

RFC4018.title: Finding Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) Targets and Name Servers by Using Service Location Protocol version 2 (SLPv2)
RFC4018.summary: Defines how iSCSI initiators, targets and storage management servers use SLPv2 for discovery, including the service:iscsi abstract, target and sms service templates.

SLP.why: The document specifies SLP service types and templates and how SLP UAs, SAs and DAs are used for iSCSI discovery, so it is an SLP usage and template specification.
SLP.quote: This document defines the use of the Service Location Protocol (SLP) by iSCSI hosts, devices, and management services, along with the SLP service type templates

iSCSI.why: The document is about discovering iSCSI targets and name servers, including target names, auth attributes and portal groups, so it belongs on the iSCSI page.
iSCSI.quote: This document describes how SLP can be used in iSCSI environments to discover targets, addresses providing targets, and storage management servers.

rejected.why: IPsec is only required for distributing sensitive policy attributes. It is mentioned in Security Considerations and the document is not about it.
The more specific SLP tag already covers this parent topic.
DNS host names appear only in the URL syntax and are not a subject of the document.
TCP is only the transport for SLP and iSCSI. The document does not define anything new about it.
The iSCSI tag is more specific, and it sits under storage.

RFC4019.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Profiles for User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Lite
RFC4019.summary: Defines two ROHC profiles (RTP/UDP-Lite/IP 0x0007 and UDP-Lite/IP 0x0008) as modifications of the RFC 3095 UDP profiles, handling the UDP-Lite Checksum Coverage field with a new CCE packet type, plus IP-only-profile features.

ROHC.why: The document specifies new ROHC profiles, context parameters, packet types and feedback option.
ROHC.quote: This document defines Robust Header Compression (ROHC) profiles for compression of Real-Time Transport Protocol, User Datagram Protocol-Lite, and Internet Protocol (RTP/UDP-Lite/IP) packets

UDP-Lite.why: A substantial part analyses UDP-Lite header fields and behaviour (Checksum Coverage) in order to compress them.
UDP-Lite.quote: UDP-Lite replaces the Length field of the UDP header with a Checksum Coverage field.

rejected.why: UDP is only the baseline the profiles are defined against; the subject is UDP-Lite.
RTP headers are compressed via the RFC 3095 profile; this document does not specify RTP itself.
The checksum coverage field is treated for compression purposes, not as a subject about Internet checksums.
IPv6 is mentioned only in passing regarding checksum use.

RFC4020.title: Early IANA Allocation of Standards Track Code Points
RFC4020.summary: BCP defining a process by which IANA may make temporary early allocations of code points from Standards Action registries for Standards Track drafts, including request, follow-up, and expiry/deprecation.

IANA.why: The whole document defines IANA allocation procedure changes for Standards Action registries, including temporary allocations, expiry and deprecation.
IANA.quote: under strictly controlled circumstances, IANA make an early allocation of code points

IETF process.why: It prescribes roles of WG chairs, Area Directors and IESG in the standards process for early allocation, a procedural BCP.
IETF process.quote: The WG chairs determine whether the conditions for early allocations described in section 2 are met

rejected.why: Routing Area is only mentioned as an example of where pre-RFC implementations are desired; the document is not about routing.
Only boilerplate copyright and IPR sections; not the subject.

RFC4021.title: Registration of Mail and MIME Header Fields
RFC4021.summary: RFC 4021 makes the initial IANA registrations of permanent mail and MIME message header fields (Date, From, Content-Type, List-*, X.400 mapping fields, etc.) in the registry defined by RFC 3864.

message format.why: The body is a catalogue of Internet message header fields (Date, From, Message-ID, Received, etc.) with their specifications, so readers of message format would want it.
message format.quote: This document defines IANA registration for a number of mail message and MIME header fields

MIME.why: Section 2.2 registers MIME header fields such as MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding and Content-Disposition.
MIME.quote: Section 2.2 contains templates for initial registration of MIME header fields.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is populating an IANA registry, but this is the main body rather than boilerplate. Registry readers would want it.
IANA.quote: provides initial registrations of mail and MIME header fields in the "Permanent Message Header Field Registry"

rejected.why: The List-* header fields are only 7 of about 88 registrations. The document does not specify mailing list protocols.
About 20 registered fields are X.400/MIXER mapping fields, but they are only registry entries. The document does not address X.400 interworking.
A more specific child, message format, fits better.
VPIM is only mentioned in passing in the Importance and Sensitivity entries.
The document registers header fields, not media types.

gaps.name: Message header field registry
gaps.why: The document populates the IANA permanent message header field registry defined by RFC 3864. There is no tag for header field registries or registration procedures.

RFC4022.title: Management Information Base for the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
RFC4022.summary: Defines the IP-version-independent SMIv2 MIB module (TCP-MIB) for managing TCP implementations, with scalar parameters/statistics, a connection table and a listener table, obsoleting RFC 2012 and RFC 2452.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module in SMIv2 format, the core subject of the MIB tag.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

TCP.why: The managed objects cover TCP connection state, listeners, retransmission parameters and counters, so readers interested in TCP would want this RFC. It does not change the protocol itself.
TCP.quote: it describes managed objects used for implementations of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) in an IP version independent manner.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines objects, not SNMP behaviour; the MIB tag already sits under SNMP.
The module is IP version neutral and replaces the IPv6-specific MIB. It is not about IPv6 itself.
The retransmission algorithm object only mentions Van Jacobson's algorithm and RFC 2988. It does not address congestion control.

RFC4023.title: Encapsulating MPLS in IP or Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE)
RFC4023.summary: Specifies MPLS-in-IP (protocol 137) and MPLS-in-GRE encapsulations that replace the top MPLS label with an IP or GRE header so MPLS can cross non-MPLS IP networks, with common procedures for fragmentation, TTL, Diffserv and IPsec security.

MPLS.why: The document defines how MPLS packets and label stacks are carried over IP networks, with LSRs and LSP adjacencies tunnelled across non-MPLS cores. MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: This document specifies two IP-based encapsulations: MPLS-in-IP and MPLS-in-GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation).

GRE.why: It specifies the MPLS-in-GRE encapsulation, including the protocol type values and the handling of optional GRE checksum, key and sequence fields.
GRE.quote: The MPLS-in-GRE encapsulation encapsulates an MPLS packet in GRE [RFC2784].

IP-in-IP.why: MPLS-in-IP is a direct IP encapsulation with its own protocol number. It is a generic IP tunnelling mechanism, so readers of IP-in-IP encapsulation would be interested.
IP-in-IP.quote: The IPv4 Protocol Number field or the IPv6 Next Header field is set to 137, indicating an MPLS unicast packet.

rejected.why: IPsec is only an optional way to secure the tunnel, described in Security Considerations. The document does not define it.
Path MTU Discovery is used as a procedure within the tunnel head, but the document is not about PMTUD itself.
It only notes that RFC 2983 and RFC 3270 apply to the DS field in these tunnels, in a short subsection.
IPv6 is supported as the outer header alongside IPv4. The document is not about IPv6.
The parent tag is implied by the more specific GRE and IP-in-IP tags.

RFC4024.title: Voice Messaging Client Behaviour
RFC4024.summary: Informational RFC describing how voice/fax/text messaging clients should behave (icon, sender number column, message size, media viewer, read marking) for VPIM and other voice or fax messages, using Message-Context and related headers.

VPIM.why: The whole document specifies client behaviour for VPIM and voice/fax messages, so voice messaging readers would look for it.
VPIM.quote: This document defines the expected behaviour of a client to various aspects of a Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) message or any voice and/or fax message.

email.why: It addresses mail client (MUA) behaviour for multimedia messages, including message list display and read marking.
email.quote: As Internet messaging evolves into unified messaging, the term "e-mail" no longer refers to text-only messages.

rejected.why: IMAP is mentioned only as an example of where the \SEEN flag is set and how length could be passed; the document does not specify or extend it.
MIME headers (Content-Duration, Content-Type parameters) are proposed for conveying length, but the document does not define MIME structure or encodings.
It suggests using the Subject header and Message-Context header, but these are defined elsewhere; the document is about client behaviour, not message format.
Fax messages are treated as one media type in client behaviour; the document is not about fax transport.

RFC4025.title: A Method for Storing IPsec Keying Material in DNS
RFC4025.summary: Defines the IPSECKEY DNS resource record (type 45) for publishing IPsec public keys and gateway information, with RDATA and presentation formats, IANA registries, and security analysis.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS RR type (IPSECKEY, type 45), including RDATA layout, presentation format and reverse-map lookup conventions.
DNS.quote: This document describes a new resource record for the Domain Name System (DNS). This record may be used to store public keys for use in IP security (IPsec) systems.

IPsec.why: The record's purpose is to supply keying material and gateway location for establishing IPsec tunnels, so IPsec readers would want it.
IPsec.quote: The IPSECKEY resource record (RR) is used to publish a public key that is to be associated with a Domain Name System (DNS) [1] name for use with the IPsec protocol suite.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is recommended for authenticating the record, but the document does not specify or extend DNSSEC; it only reuses KEY RR key encodings.
IKE is the consumer of the keying material and is mentioned in the Security Considerations, but the document does not specify or change IKE.
RSA and DSA key formats are inherited by reference from other RFCs, with only a length-limit change; the document is not about the algorithms.
Base64 is just the presentation encoding of the public key.
The IANA registries created are boilerplate-like and specific to this RR, not a topic of the document.

RFC4026.title: Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Network (VPN) Terminology
RFC4026.summary: RFC 4026 is an informational terminology document defining and unifying terms for provider-provisioned VPN services (L3VPN, L2VPN, VPLS, VPWS, IPLS), their building blocks (CE, PE, P), functions and related concepts.

VPN.why: The whole document defines the terminology of provider-provisioned VPNs, covering both L2 and L3 services and generic building blocks, so the parent VPN tag fits best.
VPN.quote: This document proposes a foundation for a unified terminology for the L2VPN and L3VPN working groups.

VPLS.why: VPLS and its related terms (VSI, MAC learning, flooding, U-PE/N-PE, LPE) are a substantial part of the terminology.
VPLS.quote: A VPLS is a provider service that emulates the full functionality of a traditional Local Area Network (LAN).

L3VPN.why: BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, VRF, Route Distinguisher, Route Target and virtual-router style L3VPNs are defined, which are of interest to L3VPN readers.
L3VPN.quote: An L3VPN interconnects sets of hosts and routers based on Layer 3 addresses; see [L3VPN-FRAME].

L2VPN.why: L2VPN service types VPWS, VPLS and IPLS, along with attachment circuits and related terms, are defined.
L2VPN.quote: Three types of L2VPNs are described in this document: Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS)

rejected.why: Pseudo wire is defined briefly for reference only; the PWE3 specification is not the subject of this document.
This is a glossary, but it is about VPN terminology, so the specific VPN tags are better. The generic terminology topic is for glossaries of general terms, so it was not tagged.
BGP appears only in the definitions of RD and RT and BGP/MPLS VPNs, which does not make the document about BGP.
MPLS labels and tunnels are mentioned as mechanisms in definitions, but the document does not specify MPLS.
Route reflector gets a one-line definition only.
Tunnel is defined as a VPN building block, but the document is not about tunnelling in general.

RFC4027.title: Domain Name System Media Types
RFC4027.summary: Registers the MIME media types application/dns (for detached DNS information per RFC 2540) and text/dns (for DNS master files per RFC 1035).

media types.why: The document's sole purpose is registering two MIME media types, so it belongs on the media type registrations page.
media types.quote: This document registers the media types application/dns and text/dns in accordance with RFC 2048.

DNS.why: The registered types identify DNS master files and detached DNS data, so DNS readers would want it, though it adds no protocol behaviour.
DNS.quote: The text/dns media type is used to identify master files as described in RFC 1035.

rejected.why: MIME is the registration framework, and the more specific media types tag already covers it.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in the security considerations as a possible content type. The document is not about it.
It is cited only as a way to secure the content further, and that is declared out of scope.
It is cited only as a way to secure the content further, and that is declared out of scope.

RFC4028.title: Session Timers in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4028.summary: Defines the SIP session timer extension: Session-Expires and Min-SE header fields, the 422 response code and the 'timer' option tag, so UAs and proxies can periodically refresh sessions via re-INVITE/UPDATE and detect dead sessions.

SIP.why: The document specifies a SIP extension with new header fields, a response code and an option tag, along with UAC, proxy and UAS behavior.
SIP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). This extension allows for a periodic refresh of SIP sessions through a re-INVITE or UPDATE request.

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer is mentioned only for how refresh re-INVITEs carry unchanged offers; the document does not specify SDP.
NAT ALGs are mentioned as one motivating application of the timer, not the subject of the document.
TLS and SIPS are only recommended in Security Considerations for hop-by-hop integrity; they are not the subject.
RTCP is mentioned only as an alternative session liveness indicator.

RFC4029.title: Scenarios and Analysis for Introducing IPv6 into ISP Networks
RFC4029.summary: Informational v6ops document describing scenarios and stages for an ISP introducing IPv6 alongside its existing IPv4 service, analysing backbone, customer-connection and operations actions and evaluating existing transition mechanisms.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document analyses ISP IPv6 deployment stages and evaluates transition mechanisms (tunnels, 6to4, Teredo, dual-stack).
IPv6 transition.quote: This document describes different scenarios for the introduction of IPv6 into an ISP's existing IPv4 network without disrupting the IPv4 service.

6to4.why: 6to4 is evaluated for small and large end sites, including relays and NAT incompatibility.
6to4.quote: Several tunneling techniques have already been defined: configured tunnels with tunnel broker, 6to4 [RFC3056], Teredo [TEREDO], and so on.

Teredo.why: Teredo's applicability to ISP customer connections is analysed alongside 6to4.
Teredo.quote: Teredo is not applicable in this scenario, as it can only provide IPv6 connectivity to a single host, not the whole site.

rejected.why: BGP multiprotocol extensions for IPv6 are discussed briefly as a deployment choice, not the subject of the document.
IGP choice and single-topology convexity (Appendix A) are discussed, but as one part of the transition analysis; not the document's subject.
IPv6 over MPLS backbones is a short subsection; the document is not about MPLS.
Multihoming gets only a brief paragraph and is flagged as follow-on work.
Mentioned for prefix delegation and configuration of customer equipment, but not specified or analysed in depth.
Mentioned as an IGP option only.

RFC4030.title: The Authentication Suboption for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Relay Agent Option
RFC4030.summary: Defines the Authentication suboption (code 8) for the DHCP Relay Agent Information Option, carrying an HMAC-SHA1 keyed hash and replay-detection counter to protect integrity of relayed DHCP messages between relay agents and servers.

DHCP.why: The document extends the DHCP Relay Agent Information Option with a new suboption and specifies relay agent and server behavior for it.
DHCP.quote: This specification defines an authentication suboption for that option, containing a keyed hash in its payload.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is only the mandatory algorithm used for the checksum; the document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
SHA-1 is only the hash underlying the HMAC computation and is not the subject.
IPsec is mentioned only as an alternative approach in the Security Considerations and is not addressed by this document.
The authentication is specific to DHCP relay messages, so the DHCP tag covers it; the generic topic adds nothing.
The document covers DHCP for IPv4 only (RFC 2131 relay agents).
The IANA section merely creates registries for this suboption, which is boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC4031.title: Service Requirements for Layer 3 Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs)
RFC4031.summary: RFC 4031 is an informational document setting out customer and service-provider requirements for Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs (PE-based and CE-based), serving as a checklist for evaluating L3VPN approaches.

L3VPN.why: The whole document is a requirements checklist for L3VPN approaches (PE-based and CE-based), from customer and provider viewpoints.
L3VPN.quote: This document provides requirements for Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks (L3VPNs).

rejected.why: QoS, Diffserv and Intserv requirements are one aspect of the L3VPN requirements, not the subject of the document.
IPsec is named as a CE-based tunnelling and security option, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
BGP is mentioned as a required CE-PE and inter-AS routing protocol, but it is not the subject of the document.
MPLS appears as one tunnelling and backbone technology in the requirements, not as a subject of the document.
Section 7 covers provider management requirements (FCAPS), but this is a sub-part of the L3VPN requirements and not the main subject.
The child tag L3VPN fits more specifically.

RFC4032.title: Update to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Preconditions Framework
RFC4032.summary: Updates RFC 3312's SIP preconditions framework by giving guidelines for defining new precondition types and revising current-status offer/answer rules for session mobility (moved streams, answerer downgrades).

SIP.why: The document updates the SIP preconditions framework, covering SIP extension procedures, re-INVITE/UPDATE handling and UA behaviour.
SIP.quote: RFC 3312 [3] defines the framework for SIP [2] preconditions, which is a generic framework that allows SIP UAs (User Agents) to suspend the establishment of a session

rejected.why: The offer/answer exchange of SDP current-status values is the mechanism the rules operate on, but the document is about SIP preconditions rather than specifying SDP itself.
QoS preconditions are only the example precondition type; the document is a generic framework update and defines no QoS mechanism.
Mentioned only as an example source of local status information.
RTP is mentioned only in a quoted RFC 3312 paragraph about not sending media during suspension.
Appears only in Security Considerations as the recommended integrity protection.

RFC4033.title: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements
RFC4033.summary: RFC 4033 introduces DNSSEC, describing the services it does and does not provide, key terminology, resolver, stub resolver, zone and name server considerations, and the DNSSEC document family.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is the introduction and requirements for DNSSEC: definitions, services, limitations, and the document set.
DNSSEC.quote: The Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) add data origin authentication and data integrity to the Domain Name System.

rejected.why: DNS is the base protocol that DNSSEC extends; the more specific DNSSEC tag covers it and its ancestors are implied.
EDNS0 and the DO bit are only prerequisites mentioned for DNSSEC; the document defines nothing new about EDNS.
Only a passing mention of certificate storage in DNS under 'New Security Uses'; not the subject.
Mentioned only as a channel security option for stub resolver to recursive server and zone transfers.
Dynamic update is discussed only for its interaction with online signing keys; not the subject.

RFC4034.title: Resource Records for the DNS Security Extensions
RFC4034.summary: RFC 4034 defines the DNSSEC resource record types (DNSKEY, RRSIG, NSEC, DS), their wire and presentation formats, canonical form and ordering, and key tag calculation.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies the core DNSSEC resource records, including signing, validation material, and authenticated denial of existence. It is part of the DNSSEC specification family.
DNSSEC.quote: This document defines the public key (DNSKEY), delegation signer (DS), resource record digital signature (RRSIG), and authenticated denial of existence (NSEC) resource records.

rejected.why: DNS is the parent of DNSSEC and is implied. The document is specifically about the security extensions.
RSA/SHA-1 and RSA/MD5 appear only as algorithm-table entries that reference other documents. The document is not about RSA.
SHA-1 is only the digest type used for DS records, listed in a table. The document does not specify it.
Base64 is only the presentation encoding for keys and signatures, referenced from RFC 3548.
Appendix B notes that the key tag algorithm resembles the ones-complement checksum but is explicitly not that checksum.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate that summarizes existing registry state. It is not the subject of the document.

RFC4035.title: Protocol Modifications for the DNS Security Extensions
RFC4035.summary: RFC 4035 specifies the DNSSEC protocol modifications: signed zones, authoritative and recursive server behaviour, resolver behaviour, and validation of DNS responses, including authenticated denial of existence via NSEC.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies DNSSEC protocol operations: zone signing, serving with RRSIG/NSEC/DS, validation, trust anchors, and the CD/AD/DO bits.
DNSSEC.quote: This document defines the concept of a signed zone, along with the requirements for serving and resolving by using DNSSEC.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is a child of DNS and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The document requires EDNS0 support and uses the DO bit, but it does not define EDNS. It is only the substrate, and the DO bit is defined in RFC 3225.
Dynamic update is only mentioned in passing, in the CNAME/KEY allowance and the caching rationale.
Trust anchors and chains of trust are DNSSEC-specific here, not the Internet PKI.

RFC4036.title: Management Information Base for Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS) Cable Modem Termination Systems for Subscriber Management
RFC4036.summary: Defines the DOCS-IETF-SUBMGT-MIB, an SNMP MIB module for DOCSIS CMTS subscriber management that controls CPE IP addresses behind cable modems and binds filter groups to modems, using the Differentiated Services MIB for packet classification and drop.

DOCSIS.why: The MIB manages DOCSIS CMTS subscriber behaviour, covering CM registration, filter groups and CPE address control. Readers of DOCSIS cable access networks would want it.
DOCSIS.quote: it defines a set of managed objects for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)-based management of Data-over-Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS)-compliant Cable Modem Termination Systems

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module definition with tables, objects, compliance and groups.
MIB.quote: This MIB module provides a set of objects required for the management of DOCSIS Cable Modem Termination Systems (CMTS).

Diffserv.why: A substantial part of the document defines how filter groups extend and plug into the Diffserv MIB classifier tables, adding classification items. Diffserv is not just a substrate here.
Diffserv.quote: The filtering capability is implemented using the Classification, Counting, and Drop facilities of the Differentiated Services MIB [RFC3289].

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document does not specify or extend it, and the MIB tag already covers the subject.
TFTP is mentioned only as how modems get provisioning parameters and is not part of what the document specifies.
The filtering is packet classification and drop for subscriber management, not a firewall or middlebox traversal specification. The tiny-fragment guidance is a minor note.
IPv4-only compliance is a scoping remark, not a subject of the document.
The Diffserv MIB is used for filtering, not for quality of service. The more specific Diffserv tag already covers that dependency.

RFC4037.title: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) Callout Protocol (OCP) Core
RFC4037.summary: Specifies the OPES Callout Protocol (OCP) Core, the application-agnostic protocol by which an OPES processor sends application messages to a callout server and receives adapted messages back, including message format, transactions, negotiation, and dataflow optimizations.

OPES.why: The whole document defines the OCP protocol used between an OPES processor and callout server, which is the core of OPES.
OPES.quote: This document specifies the core of the Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) Callout Protocol (OCP).

rejected.why: HTTP is only an example application protocol being adapted; HTTP adaptation is left to a separate profile document.
BEEP is mentioned only as one possible transport; OCP is not defined over it.
TCP is the usual substrate transport only; nothing new is defined for it.
ABNF is used only to define the message syntax, so it is not a subject of the document.
Mapping onto transports is explicitly out of scope.
Transport encryption is only mentioned as a negotiable feature; no TLS specifics are defined.

RFC4038.title: Application Aspects of IPv6 Transition
RFC4038.summary: Informational guide to how IPv6 transition affects applications, describing dual-stack application scenarios and porting guidelines for writing IP version-independent socket applications.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document covers application-level IPv6/IPv4 coexistence: dual-stack scenarios, IPv4-mapped addresses, BIS/BIA, and porting guidance.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document specifies scenarios and aspects of application transition. It also proposes guidelines on how to develop IP version-independent applications during the transition period.

sockets API.why: A large part of the document is guidance and code on getaddrinfo, sockaddr_storage, IPV6_V6ONLY and socket loops for version-independent applications.
sockets API.quote: How to develop IPv6-capable or protocol-independent applications ("application porting guidelines") using standard APIs [RFC3493][RFC3542].

rejected.why: DNS behaviour (AAAA, address lists) is discussed only as it affects applications, not specified or analysed in its own right.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag fits better; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
NAT-PT is mentioned only briefly in Section 7 as a case applications must not distinguish.
Multicast porting is covered in one short subsection, not enough to be a main subject.
TCP is only the transport used in the example code.

RFC4039.title: Rapid Commit Option for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol version 4 (DHCPv4)
RFC4039.summary: Defines the DHCPv4 Rapid Commit option (code 80), enabling a 2-message DHCPDISCOVER/DHCPACK exchange instead of the usual 4-message exchange, modeled on the DHCPv6 option.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv4 option and revises the DHCP client/server message flow from RFC 2131 to support a 2-message exchange.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a new Rapid Commit option for DHCPv4, modeled on the DHCPv6 Rapid Commit option [RFC3315]

rejected.why: The DHCPv6 Rapid Commit option is only the model for this work. The document specifies DHCPv4 only.
ARP is mentioned only as the client's final address-in-use check. The document is not about it.
ICMP Echo Request is mentioned only as a way for servers to probe addresses. The document is not about it.
The IANA section only records the assignment of option code 80. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC4040.title: RTP Payload Format for a 64 kbit/s Transparent Call
RFC4040.summary: Defines the "Clearmode" pseudo-codec RTP payload format for transparently carrying 64 kbit/s clear-channel data, and registers the audio/clearmode media type with its SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification, defining packetization, timestamp, marker bit and sample rate rules for Clearmode.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes how to carry 64 kbit/s channel data transparently in RTP packets, using a pseudo-codec called "Clearmode".

media types.why: A substantial part of the document is the registration of the audio/clearmode media type with its parameters (ptime, maxptime), which is stated as a purpose in the abstract.
media types.quote: This document registers the following MIME subtype: audio/clearmode.

SDP.why: A dedicated section defines how the media type parameters map to SDP m=, a=rtpmap, a=ptime and a=maxptime lines, with an example.
SDP.quote: The MIME subtype (clearmode) goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name.
SDP.section: 5. Mapping to Session Description Protocol (SDP) Parameters

rejected.why: Clearmode is explicitly a pseudo-codec with no encoding or decoding; the RTP payload format tag fits better and a codec definition is not provided.
Packetization is described as similar to PCMU/PCMA, and G.711 is mentioned only for sharing the SDP m= line, but the document is not about G.711.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to get confidentiality.
RTP is the substrate; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers the document.
ISDN data is only an example use case, and the document does not address IP access over ISDN.
Media gateways are the context of use, but no gateway control protocol is specified; RFC 2719 is only an informative reference.

RFC4041.title: Requirements for Morality Sections in Routing Area Drafts
RFC4041.summary: An April 1st parody RFC that requires Routing Area Internet-Drafts to include a "Morality Considerations" section, satirising IETF process conventions and routing jargon.

humor.why: The document is a 1 April whimsical parody. It mocks IETF document-section requirements with jokes about morality and routing terms.
humor.quote: This document specifies a requirement for all new Routing Area Internet-Drafts to include a "Morality Considerations" section

rejected.why: It parodies a requirement for a new section in drafts, but it is a joke and does not change any real IETF process.
It mentions ECMP, MPLS, protection and multicast only as puns. It says nothing real about routing.
ECMP appears only in a joke glossary entry ('Some kind of Communism?').
MPLS appears only in a joke glossary entry.
The glossary in Section 4 is a joke. It is not a real set of definitions.
Differentiated Services appears only as a pun on segregating packets by color.

RFC4042.title: UTF-9 and UTF-18 Efficient Transformation Formats of Unicode
RFC4042.summary: An April 1st RFC defining UTF-9 and UTF-18, humorous nonet-based transformation formats of Unicode for 9-bit platforms like the PDP-10, with sample conversion routines.

humor.why: Published 1 April 2005 as an April Fools' RFC; the premise of 9-bit nonet encodings for PDP-10 platforms is whimsical.
humor.quote: The current representation formats for Unicode (UTF-7, UTF-8, UTF-16) are not storage and computation efficient on platforms that utilize the 9 bit nonet

Unicode.why: The document defines new Unicode transformation formats (UTF-9, UTF-18), including codepoint mappings and conversion routines.
Unicode.quote: This document describes a transformation format of Unicode that takes advantage of the nonet so that the format will be storage and computation efficient.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only compared against and used as a conversion source; the document does not specify or extend it.
It only asks IANA to reserve charset names; the main body is about encoding formats, so Unicode is the more specific fit.
FTP is mentioned only as an example of a protocol supporting nonet transport.
The IANA section is boilerplate-like and a minor charset name reservation.

RFC4043.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Permanent Identifier
RFC4043.summary: Defines the PermanentIdentifier otherName form for the subjectAltName extension of X.509 certificates, letting a CA indicate that multiple certificates relate to the same entity despite changes in subject name.

X.509.why: The RFC specifies a new name form for X.509 certificate subjectAltName, with its ASN.1 syntax, matching rules and OID. It extends the X.509 certificate profile.
X.509.quote: This document defines a new form of name, called permanent identifier, that may be included in the subjectAltName extension of a public key certificate

rejected.why: Parent of X.509, which fits more specifically; the document is about a certificate name form, not PKI in general.
ASN.1 modules are supplied, but only as the formal definition of the new name form; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
identifierValue uses UTF8String, but this is only an encoding it relies on.
IANA Considerations says no actions are needed; the appendix on Private Enterprise Numbers is only about obtaining OIDs.
Access control is mentioned as a use case, but the document does not specify access control mechanisms.

RFC4044.title: Fibre Channel Management MIB
RFC4044.summary: Defines the FC-MGMT-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for managing Fibre Channel instances, switches, ports, statistics, errors, fabric logins and links, and obsoletes RFC 2837.

MIB.why: The whole document is a MIB module (FC-MGMT-MIB) with object definitions, groups and compliance statements, and it is the media-specific MIB for Fibre Channel interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

fibre channel.why: The managed objects describe Fibre Channel switches, ports, classes of service, logins and links, so readers of the Fibre Channel subject need this RFC.
fibre channel.quote: The Fibre Channel provides a general transport vehicle for higher level protocols such as Intelligent Peripheral Interface (IPI) and Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) command sets
fibre channel.section: 3. Short Overview of the Fibre Channel

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, so the MIB tag is the better fit.
AgentX is mentioned only as the reason the tables are indexed by fcmInstanceIndex. It is not specified or extended here.
iSCSI is mentioned only in passing, in the gateway function example and in a comparison with the iSCSI MIB. The document is not about iSCSI.
Fibre Channel is covered by the more specific fibre channel tag, so the parent storage topic is not added.

RFC4045.title: Extensions to Support Efficient Carrying of Multicast Traffic in Layer-2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP)
RFC4045.summary: Experimental extension to L2TP defining new control messages and AVPs so an LNS can send multicast traffic once per tunnel in a dedicated multicast session and the LAC replicates it to the subscribed unicast sessions.

L2TP.why: The document defines new L2TP control messages (MSRQ, MSRP, MSE, MSI, MSEN) and AVPs, so it extends L2TP directly.
L2TP.quote: This document describes an extension to L2TP, to make efficient use of L2TP tunnels within the context of deploying multicast services

multicast.why: A substantial part concerns IP multicast delivery: group state determination from IGMP/MLD, replication contexts and LAC-side replication. No child tag such as IGMP or MLD fits, since those are used but not specified here.
multicast.quote: The solution described herein provides a mechanism for transmitting multicast data only once for all the L2TP sessions that have been established in a tunnel

rejected.why: IGMP/MLD are used by the LNS to track group membership. The document does not specify or extend them.
MLD is referenced as a group management protocol the LNS must support. It is not extended or specified here.
PPP is the framing carried by L2TP sessions. The document only notes that the LAC frames multicast packets for each user's PPP link.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate listing new L2TP values, so it is not evidence of this subject.
xDSL is mentioned only as a deployment context in the Introduction.

RFC4046.title: Multicast Security (MSEC) Group Key Management Architecture
RFC4046.summary: Informational MSEC architecture defining the group key management model: GCKS, registration and rekey protocols, and the group security association (Registration, Rekey and Data SAs), with rekey reliability, implosion and scalability considerations.

multicast security.why: The whole document is the architecture for group key management for secure multicast: GCKS, registration and rekey protocols, GSA contents and scalability. This is the multicast security / group key management topic.
multicast security.quote: This document defines the common architecture for Multicast Security (MSEC) key management protocols to support a variety of application, transport, and network layer security protocols.

key management.why: Key establishment, rekeying and key distribution algorithms (LKH, OFT, Subset Difference) are a substantial part of the document. This is a general key management matter, not MIKEY-specific.
key management.quote: The goal of a group key management protocol is to provide legitimate group members with the up-to-date cryptographic state they need for secrecy and authentication.

reliable multicast.why: Sections 5.3-5.5 discuss reliable delivery of rekey messages, FEC, NACK feedback and implosion. It surveys reliable multicast without specifying a protocol, so only the parent topic fits.
reliable multicast.quote: The rekey message may be sent using reliable multicast.  There are several types of reliable multicast protocols with different properties.

rejected.why: Cited as an example of a registration protocol that reuses IKE phase 1. The document is an architecture and does not specify or analyse GDOI.
Mentioned as an example protocol and for subordinate GCKSs. The document does not specify it.
Cited as an example of a protocol tunnelled in SIP and RTSP. It is not the subject of the document.
IPsec ESP and the SAD/SPD are examples of data security protocols, and the registration SA may run over IPsec. The document is not about IPsec.
Mentioned only as one possible data authentication parameter in 6.3.4.
Named as an example data security protocol in the requirements and Data SA sections, but not specified or analysed.

gaps.name: Group key management architecture / group security association (GSA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no node under multicast security for the group key management architecture or its algorithms (LKH, OFT, Subset Difference). The nearest tags are multicast security and key management.

RFC4047.title: MIME Sub-type Registrations for Flexible Image Transport System (FITS)
RFC4047.summary: Registers the MIME media types application/fits and image/fits for the Flexible Image Transport System astronomical data format, with background on FITS and usage guidance for applications.

media types.why: The RFC exists to register two media types and gives full registration templates, with guidance on when to use each. A media type registration is what the media types subject covers.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME media sub-types "application/fits" and "image/fits".

rejected.why: MIME is the framework the registration fits into. The document does not extend or analyse MIME itself, and the more specific media types tag covers it.
HTTP is mentioned only as a transport where content-coding such as gzip may be used, so it is a substrate and not the subject.
gzip, compress and deflate appear only as optional content-codings in the encoding considerations, not as a subject of the document.

The IANA Considerations section holds the registration templates, but those templates are the document's main body and are covered by media types. The document gives no guidance on IANA registries in general.

gaps.name: FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) astronomical data format
gaps.why: A substantial part of the document describes FITS structure, history and conformance. The taxonomy has no tag for scientific or image data formats, so only the media type registration can be tagged.

RFC4048.title: RFC 1888 Is Obsolete
RFC4048.summary: Recommends that the IESG reclassify RFC 1888 (OSI NSAPs and IPv6) as Historic because its NSAP-in-IPv6 mappings were never used and its section mapping IPv6 inside NSAPs has errors in IDP format.

OSI.why: The document is about OSI NSAP addressing and its mapping with IPv6 as defined in RFC 1888, including errors in the OSI IDP/ICP usage. OSI network-layer addressing coexistence with IP is the subject.
OSI.quote: RFC 1888, on Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Network Service Access Points (NSAPs) and IPv6, be reclassified as Historic

IPv6.why: The document concerns IPv6 address mappings and the IPv6 prefix 0000 001 reserved for NSAP allocation, which IANA now marks Reserved. IPv6 addressing readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: it defines mappings of certain OSI Network Service Access Point (NSAP) addresses inside IPv6 addresses

rejected.why: ATM is mentioned only as a context in which people want to express IP addresses; the document is not about ATM.
The IANA Considerations only note the prefix being marked Reserved and a registry held in abeyance; this is boilerplate-level and not the main body.
CLNP is not discussed; the document concerns NSAP address mappings, not the connectionless network protocol.
The IPv6 tag already covers the address mapping content; the generic addressing topic would be redundant.

RFC4049.title: BinaryTime: An Alternate Format for Representing Date and Time in ASN.1
RFC4049.summary: Defines BinaryTime, an ASN.1 INTEGER type for representing date and time as seconds since 1970, and a CMS binary-signing-time attribute that uses it as an alternative to signing-time.

date-time formats.why: The document's main contribution is a new date/time representation (seconds since 1970 UTC), an alternative to UTCTime and GeneralizedTime.

ASN.1.why: Defines a new ASN.1 type, its encoding considerations and an ASN.1 module in Appendix A.
ASN.1.quote: This document specifies a new ASN.1 [ASN1] type for representing time: BinaryTime.

CMS.why: Specifies a new CMS signed/authenticated attribute for SignedData and AuthenticatedData, alternative to signing-time.
CMS.quote: The binary-signing-time attribute MUST be a signed attribute or an authenticated attribute

rejected.why: Time-stamp protocol (RFC 3161) is only mentioned in Security Considerations; the document is not about PKI.
Concerns time representation in data, not synchronizing clocks.
About time zone data distribution; BinaryTime is UTC-only and not about time zones.

RFC4050.title: Using the Elliptic Curve Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) for XML Digital Signatures
RFC4050.summary: Informational RFC specifying how to use ECDSA as an additional signature method within XML Signatures (XMLDSIG), defining the signature value encoding, the ECDSAKeyValue element, EC domain parameters and point encodings in XML Schema and DTD.

ECDSA.why: The document defines how ECDSA signatures, public keys and curve domain parameters are represented and used; ECDSA readers would want it.
ECDSA.quote: This document specifies how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) with XML signatures

XML signatures.why: It extends XML-Signature with a new signature algorithm identifier and KeyValue element, so it belongs on the XML digital signatures page.
XML signatures.quote: [XMLDSIG] defines only two digital signature methods: RSA and DSA (DSS) signatures.  This document introduces ECDSA signatures as an additional method.

rejected.why: XML Schema and DTD are the means of specifying the syntax; the document is about signatures, not XML usage generally, and XML signatures is the more specific tag.
The parent of ECDSA is implied, so it is not listed separately.
SHA-1 is only mentioned as the hash used with ECDSA; the document says nothing new about it.
RFC 3279 for carrying ECDSA keys in certificates is only referenced in passing.
URN with OID namespace is merely used to name curves; nothing new is defined about URNs.
Base64 is just the encoding of the signature value, a substrate detail.

RFC4051.title: Additional XML Security Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC4051.summary: Defines additional URIs identifying algorithms (digest, MAC, signature, encryption, key wrap, transforms) and KeyInfo types for use with XML Digital Signature, Encryption and Canonicalization.

XML signatures.why: The whole document extends XMLDSIG/XMLENC with new algorithm identifiers and KeyInfo elements/types.
XML signatures.quote: A number of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) intended for use with XML Digital Signatures, Encryption, and Canonicalization are defined.

RC4.why: Defines an XML Encryption identifier for ARCFOUR (RC4-compatible); a short but distinct section.
RC4.quote: ARCFOUR is a fast, simple stream encryption algorithm that is compatible with RSA Security's RC4 algorithm.

Camellia.why: Defines Camellia block encryption and key wrap identifiers for XML Encryption (two subsections).
Camellia.quote: Camellia is an efficient and secure block cipher with the same interface as the AES

rejected.why: The URIs are used merely as algorithm identifiers (namespace-style names), not as a URI scheme or syntax topic.
HMAC is used as a signature method identifier, but the document does not specify HMAC itself.
Only an identifier list with a pointer to RFC 4050; the ECDSA specification is elsewhere.
XML is the substrate; the subject is XML security specifically.
MD5 digest identifier is defined, but only as one of many items; not a main subject.
RSA-SHA* identifiers are defined using PKCS#1 padding, but RSA itself is not the subject.

RFC4052.title: IAB Processes for Management of IETF Liaison Relationships
RFC4052.summary: BCP describing how the IAB establishes and maintains liaison relationships with other SDOs and fora, appoints IETF liaison managers and representatives, and approves and sends liaison statements.

IETF process.why: The document sets out IETF/IAB procedures and administration for liaison relationships, manager appointments, and approval of liaison statements by WG chairs, ADs, IETF Chair and IAB Chair. This is IETF process.
IETF process.quote: the establishment and maintenance of liaison relationships, and the appointment and responsibilities of IETF liaison managers and representatives.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the more specific IETF process tag, so it is not listed separately.
The IAB is the author, but the document covers organizational procedure, not architectural principles.
It defines terms like 'liaison manager' in passing, but it is not a glossary or definitions document.

RFC4053.title: Procedures for Handling Liaison Statements to and from the IETF
RFC4053.summary: BCP describing how the IETF receives, tracks, and responds to liaison statements from other SDOs and how it generates its own, including submission tools and consensus guidance.

IETF process.why: The document defines IETF procedures and responsibilities (chairs, ADs, assignees, consensus levels) for handling liaison statements, which is IETF process administration.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the procedure for generating and handling liaison statements between the IETF and other SDOs

rejected.why: RFCs are mentioned only as documents that may be transmitted in liaison statements; the document is not about RFC format or publication.
The parent is implied by IETF process, and the chosen child fits more specifically.
Email is used for notifications and contacts but is only a substrate for the process.
There is no IANA content; the document is not about registries.

gaps.name: Liaison relationships with other SDOs
gaps.why: The document concerns IETF external relations and liaison statements. No taxonomy tag covers this, so IETF process is the nearest fit.

RFC4054.title: Impairments and Other Constraints on Optical Layer Routing
RFC4054.summary: Informational survey of optical-layer constraints (reconfigurable elements, transmission impairments like PMD and ASE, multi-island networks, and diversity/SRLG) that affect routing and path selection in GMPLS-controlled optical networks.

GMPLS.why: The whole document frames optical layer routing constraints and their implications for GMPLS routing and control plane design, including SRLG and impairment-aware path computation.
GMPLS.quote: This contribution surveys some of the aspects of optical networks that impact routing and identifies possible GMPLS responses for each

rejected.why: Mentioned only as routing logic that would need significant additions for wavelength probing; not specified or extended here.
CSPF and SRLG penalties are touched on, but the document is about optical constraints on routing, not traffic engineering mechanisms.
GMPLS is the more specific fitting tag; MPLS in general is not the subject.
The document covers routing constraints specific to optical networks, which the GMPLS tag covers more specifically.

gaps.name: Optical layer routing / all-optical networks (WDM, impairments)
gaps.why: The core subject is physical-layer optical impairments (PMD, ASE, crosstalk) and lightpath diversity (SRLG), and the taxonomy has no optical networking or shared-risk tag apart from GMPLS.

RFC4055.title: Additional Algorithms and Identifiers for RSA Cryptography for use in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
RFC4055.summary: RFC 4055 specifies algorithm identifiers, parameters and encodings for using RSASSA-PSS, RSAES-OAEP and SHA-2 hashes with PKCS#1 v1.5 RSA signatures in Internet X.509 certificates and CRLs, supplementing RFC 3279.

RSA.why: The document specifies RSA signature and encryption schemes (PSS, OAEP, PKCS#1 v1.5) and their parameters and identifiers.
RSA.quote: describes the conventions for using the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS) signature algorithm, the RSA Encryption Scheme - Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding (RSAES-OAEP) key transport algorithm

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificate and CRL fields, including keyUsage and public key encodings, for the new RSA algorithms.
X.509.quote: This specification defines the contents of the signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue, signature, and subjectPublicKeyInfo fields within Internet X.509 Certificates and CRLs.

rejected.why: SHA-224/256/384/512 are used as hash functions and given OIDs, but the document is not about the hash algorithms themselves.
ASN.1 is the notation for the module and encodings, a substrate rather than the subject.
Covered by the more specific X.509 tag, which is implied by its parent.
CMS is mentioned only incidentally regarding signature value representation.
MD5 is only mentioned as existing in RFC 3279, not addressed.

RFC4056.title: Use of the RSASSA-PSS Signature Algorithm in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC4056.summary: Specifies conventions for using the RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm (algorithm identifiers, parameters, and validation checks) with the CMS signed-data content type.

CMS.why: The document defines how RSASSA-PSS is used in CMS signed-data: signatureAlgorithm, digestAlgorithms, and parameter-consistency checks.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS) [P1v2.1] digital signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax [CMS] signed-data content type.

RSA.why: The RSASSA-PSS RSA signature scheme, its identifiers, public key encoding and parameter handling are the core subject.
RSA.quote: signatureAlgorithm MUST contain id-RSASSA-PSS.  The algorithm parameters field MUST contain RSASSA-PSS-params.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used for the structures, which are defined in RFC 4055; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Certificate public key identifiers are mentioned, but the document is about CMS signatures and the profile lives in RFC 4055.
Random number generation appears only in Security Considerations boilerplate-style guidance.
The document targets CMS signed-data generally and does not specify S/MIME message handling.

RFC4057.title: IPv6 Enterprise Network Scenarios
RFC4057.summary: Informational RFC defining three base IPv6 deployment scenarios for enterprise networks, example networks, and the infrastructure components (DNS, routing, host configuration, security, management, addressing, multicast, multihoming) enterprises must analyze for IPv4 coexistence and transition.

IPv6 transition.why: The document's core purpose is scenarios and requirements for enterprise IPv6 deployment and IPv4 coexistence (dual-stack, sparse dual-stack, IPv6-only with legacy IPv4), which is the IPv6/IPv4 transition topic.
IPv6 transition.quote: Enterprise deployment requirements are discussed in terms of coexistence with IPv4 nodes, networks and applications

rejected.why: The child topic IPv6 transition fits more specifically; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
DNS is only one infrastructure component briefly noted in 4.1 and deferred to another document.
Host configuration is mentioned only in passing as a question for the enterprise to decide.
Multihoming gets a short paragraph in 4.9 and is not a substantial part of the document.
Network management is one listed component with a brief section, not a main subject.
NAT appears only in example network characteristics and application questions.

RFC4058.title: Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) Requirements
RFC4058.summary: Requirements document for PANA, a link-layer-agnostic network-layer protocol that carries EAP between a client and an access network agent for network access authentication.

PANA.why: The whole document defines requirements and terminology for PANA (PaC, PAA, EP), so PANA is the subject.
PANA.quote: identify the requirements for a link-layer agnostic protocol that allows a host and a network to authenticate each other for network access

EAP.why: PANA is defined as a carrier for EAP. The document sets EAP lower-layer requirements and discusses EAP method selection and keying, which EAP readers would want.
EAP.quote: EAP is a candidate protocol that satisfies many requirements for authentication.  PANA would be a carrier protocol for EAP.

rejected.why: A backend AAA infrastructure (RADIUS, Diameter) is mentioned, but the interaction is explicitly out of scope.
IPsec is mentioned only as a possible way to protect traffic after PANA, and a separate secure association protocol is out of scope.
It appears only as an analogy for carrying authentication and as a protocol PANA must not interfere with.
It appears only in the problem statement as an inadequate alternative for access authentication.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific PANA and EAP tags, so it is not listed separately.
COPS is only one possible PAA-to-EP candidate protocol, listed without being specified or analysed.

RFC4059.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Warranty Certificate Extension
RFC4059.summary: Defines a non-critical X.509 certificate extension (id-pe-warranty) by which a CA states the monetary warranty, validity period, type and terms URL for a certificate, with ASN.1 syntax and semantics.

X.509.why: The document specifies a new X.509 certificate extension, its OID, ASN.1 syntax and semantics, so readers of X.509 certificate profiles and extensions would want it.
X.509.quote: The warranty certificate extension identifies the warranty policy associated with a X.509 public key certificate

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the extension; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
X.509 is the more specific fit; the document is about a certificate extension, not PKI in general.
The terms-and-conditions URL must be http and follow RFC 3986, but that is incidental use of URIs.
The IANA section only says no action is needed; it is boilerplate.

RFC4060.title: RTP Payload Formats for European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) European Standard ES 202 050, ES 202 211, and ES 202 212 Distributed Speech Recognition Encoding
RFC4060.summary: Defines RTP payload formats for ETSI ES 202 050, ES 202 211 and ES 202 212 distributed speech recognition front-end feature streams (frame pair layouts, null FPs), and registers the audio/dsr-es202050, dsr-es202211 and dsr-es202212 media types with SDP mappings.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is to define RTP payload formats for specific DSR codec feature streams, including frame pair layouts and RTP header usage.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies RTP payload formats for encapsulating European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) European Standard ES 202 050 DSR Advanced Front-end (AFE)

media types.why: A substantial part registers three audio media subtypes with parameters (rate, maxptime, ptime) and their SDP mapping.
media types.quote: a new MIME subtype registration has been registered by the IANA for the corresponding payload type

rejected.why: SDP is used only to map the media type parameters and for offer/answer. The document defines nothing new about SDP itself.
The DSR front-end codecs are defined by ETSI. This RFC only specifies their RTP packetization, so RTP payload format fits more specifically.
The CRCs are defined in the ETSI specifications and are only referenced here to fill the frame pair layouts.
MRCP covers speech services control. This document concerns transporting DSR features, not controlling media resources.
RFC 3267 is cited only for the maxptime parameter definition.

gaps.name: Distributed Speech Recognition (DSR)
gaps.why: The document is about transporting DSR front-end features to a speech recognition server, and the taxonomy has no tag for DSR or speech recognition transport.

RFC4061.title: Benchmarking Basic OSPF Single Router Control Plane Convergence
RFC4061.summary: Informational BMWG document giving black-box and white-box methodologies for benchmarking OSPF single-router control plane convergence (LSA processing, flooding, SPF time, adjacency formation, DR election, link-down detection).

OSPF.why: All tests measure OSPF behaviour (LSA processing, flooding, SPF, adjacency formation, DR election), so OSPF readers would want this RFC.
OSPF.quote: This document attempts to provide a framework for Open Shortest Path First [OSPF] performance testing, and to provide some tests for measuring some aspects of OSPF performance.

benchmarking.why: It is a benchmarking methodology document defining DUT test setups, reference topologies and measurement procedures from the BMWG.
benchmarking.quote: The motivation of the document is to provide a set of tests that can provide the user comparable data from various vendors

rejected.why: The benchmarking tag is the better fit, since this is lab device benchmarking rather than network performance metrics.
Implied as an ancestor of OSPF; the document is specific to OSPF.
Only OSPF Version 2 (RFC 2328) is referenced; OSPFv3 is not addressed.

RFC4062.title: OSPF Benchmarking Terminology and Concepts
RFC4062.summary: Informational BMWG companion document defining terminology and concepts (white/black box measurement, single-router control plane convergence, network event types) for benchmarking OSPF implementations.

benchmarking.why: The document defines benchmarking terminology and concepts such as white box vs black box measurements, DUT, and convergence measurement for device testing.
benchmarking.quote: This document explains the terminology and concepts used in OSPF benchmarking.

OSPF.why: The subject under test is OSPF; the document discusses OSPF-specific terms (hello interval, router dead interval, SPF execution time, DR election, adjacency) as they relate to convergence benchmarking.
OSPF.quote: an OSPF device must flood any new information it has received, rebuild its shortest path first (SPF) tree

rejected.why: Document concerns OSPF Version 2 (RFC 2328) only.
Benchmarking of devices is the closer fit; this is not about active/passive network performance metrics.
Convergence is considered per-device, not as a routing architecture matter.

RFC4063.title: Considerations When Using Basic OSPF Convergence Benchmarks
RFC4063.summary: Informational BMWG document discussing advantages, limitations, and pitfalls of the OSPF single-router control plane convergence benchmark tests from RFC 4061, including LSA mix, SPF tree shape, measurement noise and topology generation.

benchmarking.why: The document is about the applicability and pitfalls of benchmarking methodology for routing convergence, including measurement noise, test topology generation and LSA mix.
benchmarking.quote: This document describes in detail various benefits and pitfalls of tests described in [BENCHMARK].

OSPF.why: The tests and observations concern OSPF implementation behaviour: LSA types, SPF calculation, flooding and acknowledgements. OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: This document discusses the applicability of various tests for measuring single router control plane convergence, specifically in regard to the Open Shortest First (OSPF) protocol.

rejected.why: Benchmarking of device convergence in a lab is the better fit than active or passive network performance metrics.
The document is about test methodology, not routing design or scalability principles.
Only OSPF version 2 is discussed.

RFC4064.title: Experimental Message, Extensions, and Error Codes for Mobile IPv4
RFC4064.summary: RFC 4064 reserves an experimental Mobile IPv4 message type (255), experimental skippable and non-skippable extension types (also for ICMP router discovery), and experimental FA/HA error codes, for evaluating enhancements before standardization.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IPv4 by defining an experimental message type, extension types and error codes in the Mobile IPv4 number space.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document reserves a message type for use by an individual, company, or organization for experimental purposes, to evaluate enhancements to Mobile IPv4 messages

rejected.why: The document reserves values in the Mobile IPv4 number space, but its subject is the experimental Mobile IPv4 message, extensions and error codes. IANA registry stewardship is not the topic.
ICMP router discovery extensions are reserved for experimental use, but this is a minor part of the document. It adds nothing to ICMP itself.
UDP port 434 is only the transport for the message, so UDP is substrate.

RFC4065.title: Instructions for Seamoby and Experimental Mobility Protocol IANA Allocations
RFC4065.summary: Instructs IANA on the ICMP types, Mobile IPv4/ND option codes, SCTP ports, and new registries (CARD AVP types, L2 access technology IDs, CXTP profile types, experimental mobility ICMP subtypes) needed by the Seamoby CARD and Context Transfer protocols.

IANA.why: The whole document is IANA allocation instructions and registry definitions for the Seamoby protocols.
IANA.quote: This document contains instructions to IANA about which allocations are required for the Seamoby protocols.

IP mobility.why: Seamoby CARD and CXTP are IP handover/mobility protocols, and the document defines an ICMP subtype format for experimental mobility protocols. No narrower mobility tag fits.
IP mobility.quote: experimental protocols designed to accelerate IP handover between wireless access routers

ICMP.why: The document allocates ICMP types 41 and 150 and defines the Experimental Mobility ICMP subtype header and registry.
ICMP.quote: IANA has assigned ICMP type 41 for IPv4 identifying ICMP messages utilized by experimental mobility protocols such as Seamoby.

rejected.why: SCTP is only the transport for CARD and CXTP, and the document just assigns port numbers.
Only Foreign Agent Discovery option codes are allocated, and the document does not specify or extend Mobile IPv4.
Two ND option type codes are assigned, but the document is not about ND itself.
HMAC_SHA1 is mentioned only as an algorithm indicator value for the authorization token.

gaps.name: Seamoby (CARD and Context Transfer Protocol)
gaps.why: The document concerns the Seamoby protocols CARD and CXTP for fast handover between access routers. The taxonomy has no tag for them, so IP mobility is the nearest fit.

RFC4066.title: Candidate Access Router Discovery (CARD)
RFC4066.summary: Experimental protocol letting a mobile node discover candidate access routers' IP addresses (via L2 ID reverse address translation) and capabilities ahead of IP-layer handover, with MN-AR over ICMP and AR-AR over SCTP, and piggybacking on Fast Mobile IPv6.

IP mobility.why: CARD is a handover-support protocol for IP mobility (Mobile IPv6, Fast Mobile IPv6, Mobile IPv4 low latency handoffs). No Mobile IP child tag fits since the document defines a new discovery protocol, not a Mobile IP extension itself.
IP mobility.quote: To enable seamless IP-layer handover of a mobile node (MN) from one access router (AR) to another, the MN is required to discover the identities and capabilities of candidate ARs

service discovery.why: CARD discovers network resources (access routers and their capabilities), which is a service discovery function.
service discovery.quote: The CAR discovery protocol enables the acquisition of information about the access routers that are candidates for the mobile node's next handover.

rejected.why: Used only as the inter-router transport for CARD messages; the document does not extend SCTP.
MN-AR messages are carried in an experimental ICMP type, but this is only the transport substrate.
Fast Mobile IPv6 messages are piggybacked on and used in scenarios, but the document does not specify or extend Mobile IPv6 itself.
IPsec ESP/IKE is required for AR-AR protection but is a security mechanism relied on, not the subject.
SEND signature option is used to authenticate replies in Security Considerations; it is boilerplate-level reliance, not the topic.
Router certificates are carried in sub-options, but that is an incidental part of the document.

gaps.name: Candidate Access Router Discovery / seamless handover support (Seamoby)
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers access-router discovery for fast handover; IP mobility is only the nearest parent.

RFC4067.title: Context Transfer Protocol (CXTP)
RFC4067.summary: Defines the Context Transfer Protocol (CXTP), an experimental protocol for transferring feature contexts between access routers during IP handover, with messages, authorization tokens, SCTP/ICMP transport and security guidance.

IP mobility.why: CXTP supports seamless IP handover between access routers, working with Fast Mobile IP. No specific mobility child tag fits, since it is a separate protocol, so the parent topic applies.
IP mobility.quote: Context transfers allow better support for node based mobility so that the applications running on mobile nodes can operate with minimal disruption.

rejected.why: SCTP is only the inter-router transport CXTP uses. The document defines nothing new about SCTP beyond configuration choices.
ICMP carries CTAR/CTAA on the MN-AR link and is only a substrate. CXTP uses the Experimental Mobility type.
IPsec is mandated to protect inter-router traffic. It is a security mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
Fast Mobile IPv6 handover is related work that CXTP complements. It is not specified here.
MLD context transfer is only the worked example in Appendix B, not the document's subject.
HMAC-SHA1 is used only to compute the authorization token.

gaps.name: Context transfer / Seamoby
gaps.why: CXTP and handover context transfer between access routers has no dedicated tag. It is only partly covered by the IP mobility parent.

RFC4068.title: Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6
RFC4068.summary: Specifies an experimental protocol (FMIPv6) that reduces Mobile IPv6 handover latency using proxy router advertisements, access-router handover initiate/acknowledge messages, fast binding updates and tunnelling between previous and new care-of addresses.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document is an extension of Mobile IPv6 that defines new messages (FBU, FBack, FNA, RtSolPr, PrRtAdv, HI, HAck) to speed up handovers.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document specifies a protocol to improve handover latency due to Mobile IPv6 procedures.

rejected.why: The document adds new ND-style messages and options, but its subject is Mobile IPv6 handover. Neighbor discovery is only the substrate the new messages are built on.
RtSolPr, PrRtAdv, HI and HAck are carried as ICMPv6 messages, which is only the transport format.
Tunnelling between PCoA and NCoA is a mechanism inside the handover protocol. It is not the document's subject.
The more specific child tag Mobile IPv6 applies, so the parent is not used.
AH is only mentioned as the way to protect messages between routers. The document says SA establishment is out of scope.

gaps.name: Fast handover / handover latency reduction (FMIPv6)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for fast handovers or the MIPSHOP work. Mobile IPv6 is the closest fit, but a separate tag would help readers looking for handover optimisation.

RFC4069.title: Definitions of Managed Object Extensions for Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Lines (VDSL) Using Single Carrier Modulation (SCM) Line Coding
RFC4069.summary: Defines a SMIv2 MIB module (VDSL-LINE-EXT-SCM-MIB) extending the VDSL-LINE-MIB with line-code-specific configuration and monitoring objects for VDSL lines using Single Carrier Modulation.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition with SMIv2 tables and objects for SNMP management.
MIB.quote: it describes objects used for managing the Line Code Specific parameters of Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line (VDSL) interfaces using Single Carrier Modulation (SCM) Line Coding

DSL.why: The managed subject is VDSL, a DSL access technology, covering its SCM bands, symbol rates, constellation sizes and PSD levels.
DSL.quote: This document describes an SNMP MIB module for managing the Line Code Dependent, Physical Medium Dependent (PMD) Layer of SCM VDSL Lines.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB. The document defines objects, not SNMP itself, and the MIB tag sits under SNMP anyway.
The document is not about the Access Node Control Protocol. It only manages VDSL line parameters.

RFC4070.title: Definitions of Managed Object Extensions for Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Lines (VDSL) Using Multiple Carrier Modulation (MCM) Line Coding
RFC4070.summary: Defines the VDSL-LINE-EXT-MCM-MIB, an optional SNMP MIB module extending the VDSL-LINE-MIB with line-code-specific configuration profile tables (bands, PSD masks, transmit window) for VDSL lines using Multiple Carrier Modulation.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module in SMIv2 defining managed objects for MCM VDSL lines; MIB is the most specific tag under SNMP.
MIB.quote: it describes objects used for managing the Line Code Specific parameters of Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line (VDSL) interfaces using Multiple Carrier Modulation (MCM) Line Coding

DSL.why: The managed subject is VDSL, a DSL access technology; the MIB configures its PMD-layer band and PSD parameters, so readers of DSL would want it.
DSL.quote: This document describes an SNMP MIB module for managing the Line Code Dependent, Physical Medium Dependent (PMD), Layer of MCM VDSL Lines.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the objects; the specific MIB tag is more precise and implies SNMP.
Not related; the module is written in SMIv2, not YANG.
Implied by MIB under SNMP; no broader network-management content beyond the MIB.
Not about the Access Node Control Protocol; only DSL line configuration objects are defined.

RFC4071.title: Structure of the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA)
RFC4071.summary: RFC 4071 defines the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA) housed within ISOC, specifying the roles of the IAOC, the IAD and ISOC, IAOC membership and selection, funding, and budget process for administrative support of the IETF.

IETF process.why: The document is about IETF administrative structure and procedures: IAOC composition, NomCom appointments, review and appeal of decisions, budgeting. This falls under IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: It defines the roles and responsibilities of the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC), the IETF Administrative Director (IAD), and ISOC in the fiscal and administrative support of the IETF standards process.

rejected.why: IPR management is mentioned as one IASA responsibility and in data/software rights clauses, but it is not the main subject of the document.
The NomCom appoints two IAOC members, but the document does not define NomCom procedures. It defers to RFC 3777.
IANA is only one contracted function the IASA supports. The document is not about IANA registries.
The RFC Editor is mentioned as an ISOC-sponsored function managed under the IASA, but the document does not address RFC format or publication.

gaps.name: IASA / IAOC / IAD administrative and financial structure
gaps.why: The document is about IETF administrative support, funding, and budgeting. The taxonomy only has the broad IETF process tag, with no specific tag for IETF administration or finance.

RFC4072.title: Diameter Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Application
RFC4072.summary: Specifies the Diameter EAP application, defining the DER/DEA commands and new AVPs to carry EAP packets between a NAS acting as EAP authenticator and a back-end Diameter server, with RADIUS translation rules and security analysis.

Diameter.why: The document defines a new Diameter application with new Command-Codes (DER/DEA) and AVPs, extending the Diameter protocol.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies the Diameter EAP application that carries EAP packets between a Network Access Server (NAS) working as an EAP Authenticator and a back-end authentication server.

EAP.why: The document defines how EAP packets are transported in Diameter, including pass-through validation, retransmission, fragmentation and key delivery (MSK), so it is about EAP backend transport.
EAP.quote: The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) provides a standard mechanism for support of various authentication methods.

RADIUS.why: Section 6 gives RADIUS/Diameter translation rules for the EAP application, a substantial part of the document of interest to RADIUS readers.
RADIUS.quote: Diameter EAP-Payload AVP is translated to RADIUS EAP-Message attribute(s).
RADIUS.section: 6.1. RADIUS Request Forwarded as Diameter Request

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a hop-by-hop transport protection mechanism for Diameter; not specified here.
Only a substrate security mechanism for Diameter peers; nothing new defined.
