Mentioned as one link layer over which EAP runs; the document is not about PPP.
Diameter and RADIUS tags are more specific children of AAA, so the parent is implied.
IEEE 802.11i is only an example link layer; the document is not about IP over 802.11.

RFC4073.title: Protecting Multiple Contents with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC4073.summary: Defines two new CMS content types, content-collection and content-with-attributes, for carrying multiple ContentInfo items (optionally with attributes) in ASN.1-only environments, with an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS by defining new content types (ContentCollection, ContentWithAttributes) with OIDs and syntax, so CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: This document describes a convention for using the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [CMS] to protect a content collection.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the structures and the module in the appendix; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The document says the convention is not needed with MIME/S/MIME; S/MIME is mentioned only as a contrasting case.
MIME multipart is mentioned only as the alternative for carrying multiple items; not the subject.
CompressedData is merely one content type implementations should handle; not about compression.

RFC4074.title: Common Misbehavior Against DNS Queries for IPv6 Addresses
RFC4074.summary: Informational memo describing known misbehaviors of DNS authoritative servers when queried for AAAA records (ignoring queries, wrong RCODEs, broken responses, lame delegation) and their effects on IPv6-capable resolvers.

DNS.why: The whole document analyses authoritative server, caching server and stub resolver behaviour for DNS queries and responses (RCODEs, caching, lame delegation).
DNS.quote: There is some known misbehavior of DNS authoritative servers when they are queried for AAAA resource records.

rejected.why: AAAA queries are the context, but the document is about DNS server behaviour, not IPv6 specification, addressing or deployment.
It touches IPv4 fallback for IPv6-capable resolvers but does not define or discuss a transition mechanism.
The denial-of-service remark appears only in Security Considerations and is a minor aside.

RFC4075.title: Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) Configuration Option for DHCPv6
RFC4075.summary: Defines a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_SNTP_SERVERS, code 31) that delivers an ordered list of IPv6 SNTP server addresses to clients.

DHCPv6.why: The document extends DHCPv6 with a new option, specifying its format, the messages it may appear in, and the option-code assignment.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes a new DHCPv6 option for passing a list of Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) server addresses to a client.

NTP.why: The option exists to configure time synchronization via SNTP servers, so readers of NTP/time configuration would want it. It does not change SNTP itself.
NTP.quote: The clients use these SNTP servers to synchronize their system time to that of the standard time servers.
NTP.section: 4. Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) Servers Option

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses are carried in the option, but the document is not about IPv6 itself; DHCPv6 is the more specific subject.
DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag; the IPv4 DHCP option is only mentioned as a pointer to RFC 2132.
NTP, the more specific tag, is already chosen under this topic.
The option-code assignment is boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the subject of the document.

RFC4076.title: Renumbering Requirements for Stateless Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC4076.summary: Problem statement describing how IPv6 hosts using SLAAC plus stateless DHCPv6 cannot learn of renumbering or changes to DHCPv6-assigned options, with requirements and candidate solutions.

DHCPv6.why: The document is a problem statement about stateless DHCPv6 lacking a reconfiguration/update mechanism, and it proposes candidate solutions such as Reconfigure, lifetimes and the RA 'O' flag.
DHCPv6.quote: hosts using this combination currently have no means by which to be informed of changes in stateless DHCPv6 option settings

renumbering.why: Renumbering is in the title and is the core scenario, covering requirements for handling planned and unplanned renumbering of hosts.
renumbering.quote: Any such site renumbering will require hosts to reconfigure both their own address and default router settings and their stateless DHCPv6-assigned settings.

rejected.why: SLAAC is the context the hosts operate in, but the document concerns the DHCPv6 side. It does not specify or extend SLAAC.
Router Advertisements are mentioned only as a possible hint mechanism in the solution space. The document is not about neighbor discovery.
IPv6 is the setting for the document. A more specific tag covers the subject.
NTP server address changes are only an example of a DHCPv6 option, so the document is not about NTP.

RFC4077.title: A Negative Acknowledgement Mechanism for Signaling Compression
RFC4077.summary: RFC 4077 defines a Negative Acknowledgement (NACK) mechanism for SigComp, letting a receiver report precise decompression failure reasons to the sender so it can adjust compression and recover quickly.

SigComp.why: The whole document extends SigComp with a NACK message format, reason codes and node behaviour.
SigComp.quote: This document describes a mechanism that allows Signaling Compression (SigComp) implementations to report precise error information upon receipt of a message which cannot be decompressed.

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned only as an example application that uses SigComp and DNS SRV; the document does not specify or extend SIP.
UDP and TCP are only the transports over which NACK delivery behaviour is described; nothing new is defined about them.
TCP is only the transport whose behaviour (reset, stream delimiters) is referenced; the document is not about TCP.
SHA-1 is used merely as a message identifier hash in the NACK; the document does not address the hash algorithm.
DNS SRV is mentioned only as background for the server failover problem.

gaps.name: SigComp (Signaling Compression)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists SigComp only as a child of SIP, and SigComp is not tied to SIP exclusively. I used SigComp as the tag id, but it sits in the taxonomy under SIP in real-time communications, and header compression has no SigComp-specific tag outside that. This RFC would be best served by a SigComp tag or a compression-of-signalling tag.

RFC4078.title: The TV-Anytime Content Reference Identifier (CRID)
RFC4078.summary: Defines and registers the "crid:" URI scheme, the TV-Anytime Content Reference Identifier used to reference scheduled broadcast programme content, reproducing the TV-Anytime specification for IANA registration.

URI.why: The document defines a new URI scheme, its syntax, character encoding and examples, and registers it under the URL scheme registration procedure.
URI.quote: The CRID URL takes the form crid://<DNS name>/<data>

rejected.why: The DNS name is only used as an authority identifier; the document says DNS resolution need not be used for CRID resolution.
Mentions streaming/file delivery as possible locator forms, but the document is about an identifier scheme, not streaming delivery.
The IANA section is just scheme registration boilerplate; the body is not about IANA registries.
CRID is a URL-form scheme with an authority, not a URN namespace.
Concerns broadcast programme referencing, not IPTV service delivery or operations.

gaps.name: TV-Anytime CRID / broadcast content referencing
gaps.why: The document is about identifying and resolving broadcast programme content, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy; URI covers only the scheme aspect.

RFC4079.title: A Presence Architecture for the Distribution of GEOPRIV Location Objects
RFC4079.summary: Informational RFC arguing that presence architectures (CPP, PIDF, SIMPLE, XMPP, XCAP) map onto GEOPRIV and that presence protocols can serve as GEOPRIV using protocols for distributing location objects via subscription/notification.

geolocation.why: The document is about distributing GEOPRIV location objects and mapping GEOPRIV entities (Location Server, Recipient, Target) onto presence architecture.
geolocation.quote: GEOPRIV is a standard for the transmission of location information and privacy policies over the Internet.

instant messaging.why: The core argument is that the presence model (watchers, presentities, subscriptions, notifications) is reused for location distribution.
instant messaging.quote: Presence is a service defined in RFC2778 [2] that allows users of a communications service to monitor one another's availability and disposition

PIDF.why: A whole section analyses PIDF's extensibility and security as a container for location information.
PIDF.quote: PIDF is an XML format that provides presence information about a presentity.

rejected.why: SIMPLE and XCAP are cited only as existing presence protocols that could be using protocols; the document does not specify or extend them.
Mentioned only as an example presence protocol instantiating CPP, not analysed in its own right.
SIP appears only via the presence event package reference; the document does not address SIP itself.
XML is merely the encoding of PIDF and is not itself a subject of the document.
Privacy and security are discussed only briefly in terms of requirement mapping, and the main subject is location distribution architecture.

gaps.name: GEOPRIV
gaps.why: The GEOPRIV location object and privacy framework has no specific tag; geolocation is the closest fit.

gaps.name: Presence (RFC 2778 model, CPP)
gaps.why: There is no general presence-model tag. Presence abstractions (watcher, presentity, CPP) are only covered by the instant messaging tag.

RFC4080.title: Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS): Framework
RFC4080.summary: Informational framework for the IETF NSIS working group describing a two-layer architecture (generic NTLP transport layer plus application-specific NSLPs) for path-coupled signaling of per-flow network control state, with QoS signaling as the main example.

NSIS.why: The document defines the NSIS framework itself. The taxonomy has no NSIS tag, so the closest fit is NSIS under QoS.
NSIS.quote: this document proposes an architectural framework for these signaling protocols.

QoS.why: QoS signaling is the principal signaling application, covered in detail in Section 6.1 with QNI/QNR/QNF roles and resource management interactions.
QoS.quote: The example of signaling for QoS (comparable to core RSVP QoS signaling functionality) is given in detail in Section 6.1

rejected.why: RSVP is the comparison baseline and a source of concepts, but the document specifies NSIS, not RSVP.
NAT interaction is one section (5.3), not a main subject.
Mobility and multihoming interactions are discussed in Section 5.2 only as a consideration for the signaling design.
The router alert option is mentioned as an addressing and interception mechanism but is not the subject.
TLS, IPsec and SSH appear only as possible channel security mechanisms, and no specific one is mandated.
Diffserv appears only in passing as an aggregation or marking example.

gaps.name: NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an NSIS tag, so the primary subject fits it. The tag is nested under QoS, though, and the framework also covers middlebox and other non-QoS signaling.

RFC4081.title: Security Threats for Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS)
RFC4081.summary: Informational threat analysis of the NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling) protocol suite, covering communication models, generic threats (MITM, replay, injection, negotiation downgrade) and NSIS-specific threats (flooding, spoofing, DoS, session ownership, etc.) for QoS and NAT/Firewall signaling.

NSIS.why: The whole document is a threat analysis of the NSIS protocol suite (NTLP/GIMPS and NSLPs), so readers of NSIS would expect it.
NSIS.quote: This threats document provides a detailed analysis of the security threats relevant to the Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) protocol suite.

rejected.why: Security is the document's subject area, but the NSIS technology tag is more specific; the generic topic is not needed on top of it. It is not a general security handbook.
RSVP is referenced as a comparison point (PATH messages, tokens, diagnostic messages) but the document is not about RSVP.
The Router Alert Option is mentioned only as a flooding-threat vector in one paragraph, not as a subject of the document.
NAT/Firewall NSLP is discussed only as an example application of NSIS threats; the document does not specify firewall traversal.
DiffServ is mentioned only as an example of marking-based spoofing attacks.
Authentication weaknesses (missing, unilateral, weak) are discussed as threats, but only in the NSIS context; no authentication mechanism is specified.

gaps.name: NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an NSIS tag only under QoS; I used it, but the NSIS tag id was not confirmed. Checking: NSIS is listed under QoS in the taxonomy, so the tag is valid.

RFC4082.title: Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication (TESLA): Multicast Source Authentication Transform Introduction
RFC4082.summary: Informational introduction to TESLA, a multicast/broadcast source authentication scheme using symmetric MACs with time-delayed key disclosure and loosely synchronized clocks, including DoS protections and layer placement.

TESLA.why: The entire document introduces and describes the TESLA protocol, which is the TESLA tag's subject (delayed-key-disclosure source authentication for multicast streams).
TESLA.quote: TESLA allows all receivers to check the integrity and authenticate the source of each packet in multicast or broadcast data streams.

rejected.why: NTP is only mentioned as one possible way to obtain the clock-offset bound; the document is not about it.
Loose time synchronization is a TESLA assumption and a short sketch is given, but the document is not about clock synchronization in its own right.
Parent of TESLA, implied by the TESLA tag, so not listed separately.
MACs and PRFs are used generically; no specific HMAC construction is specified.
IPsec and TLS appear only as examples of unicast authentication and as possible layer placement contexts.
S/KEY is mentioned only as an analogy for the one-way key chain in the key-non-reuse variant.

RFC4083.title: Input 3rd-Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 5 Requirements on the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4083.summary: Informational document listing the requirements 3GPP Release 5 IMS places on SIP for operation in cellular networks, covering registration, compression, QoS coordination, identity, privacy, charging, and security.

SIP.why: The whole document is a set of requirements on SIP (registration, routing, outbound proxy, session release, identity) from 3GPP IMS, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: we express the requirements identified by 3GPP to support SIP for Release 5 of the 3GPP IMS in cellular networks.

cellular.why: The document is about IMS and SIP over 3GPP GPRS cellular networks, including radio-interface efficiency and access/visited/home network models.
cellular.quote: 3GPP cellular IP Multimedia terminals use the existing General Packet Radio Service (GPRS) [27] as a transport network for IP datagrams.

SigComp.why: A dedicated section states requirements for SIP signaling compression between UA and outbound proxy, which is the need SigComp addresses.
SigComp.quote: there must be a mechanism to efficiently transport SIP signaling packets over the radio interface, by compressing the SIP messages

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer is discussed only briefly in requirements on codec negotiation; not a main subject.
Mentioned only as a proposed solution for network domain security in one sentence.
Section 4.5 covers SIP/QoS coordination but is a small part; the focus is SIP, not a QoS architecture.
Identity presentation and anonymity requirements are SIP-specific (RFC 3323/3325) and are a minor portion of the document.
Authentication and charging are discussed as requirements, but no AAA framework or protocol is the subject.
Only cited as a possible mechanism for outbound proxy discovery.

gaps.name: 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS)
gaps.why: The document is fundamentally about IMS requirements, and the taxonomy has no IMS tag; cellular and SIP only partly cover it.

RFC4084.title: Terminology for Describing Internet Connectivity
RFC4084.summary: BCP defining terminology for describing types of Internet connectivity service (Web-only, client-only, firewalled, full) and related filtering/disclosure items that ISPs should state to consumers.

terminology.why: The document exists to define standard terms for describing Internet connectivity offerings; it is a glossary-style BCP.
terminology.quote: This document provides a list of terms and definitions that may be helpful to providers, consumers, and, potentially, regulators in clarifying the type and character of services being offered.

operational security.why: A substantial part covers provider-imposed filtering, port blocking, proxies, and firewalling, and disclosure of these practices.
operational security.quote: it is important that providers disclose the services they are making available and the filters and conditions they are imposing.
operational security.section: 3. Filtering or Security Issues and Terminology

rejected.why: NAT is mentioned as a characteristic of some service types, but the document does not specify or analyse NAT behaviour.
Email filtering against spam motivates Section 3, but the document is about disclosure of connectivity restrictions, not spam handling.
Firewalled connectivity is one defined service term, but the document does not address firewall technology itself.
Mail submission blocking is discussed only as a filtering example, not as protocol content.
HTTP/HTTPS only appear in the definition of Web connectivity.

gaps.name: Internet access service types / ISP service descriptions
gaps.why: The document is about classifying consumer Internet access offerings and provider disclosure, for which the taxonomy has no specific tag beyond general terminology.

RFC4085.title: Embedding Globally-Routable Internet Addresses Considered Harmful
RFC4085.summary: BCP discouraging hard-coding of globally-routable IP addresses in host firmware (e.g., the NetGear/University of Wisconsin NTP server flood), explaining the problems and recommending DNS names, reserved documentation addresses, and local service discovery.

addressing.why: The document is about the proper use of IP addresses: not using them as fixed identifiers, address block reuse, reserved documentation blocks (192.0.2.0/24, 2001:DB8::/32). That is address architecture and use.
addressing.quote: This document discourages the practice of embedding references to unique, globally-routable IP addresses in Internet hosts, describes some of the resulting problems

service discovery.why: Substantial recommendations on discovering services via DNS names, SRV records and DHCP advertisement of local services instead of hard-coded addresses.
service discovery.quote: Internet hosts should use the Domain Name System to determine the IP addresses associated with the Internet services they require.

rejected.why: DNS is recommended as the indirection mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend DNS; it is the substrate for the recommendation.
The NetGear NTP server flood is the motivating example, but the document is not about NTP protocol or operations.
DHCP is mentioned only as a way to configure servers; not specified or extended here.
RFC 2606 example domains are mentioned only as documentation examples, not the document's subject.
IANA address reallocation is mentioned as affected context, not the focus.
Security considerations are brief boilerplate-like; the document's focus is addressing practice, not security operations.

RFC4086.title: Randomness Requirements for Security
RFC4086.summary: BCP describing how to generate unguessable random quantities for security use: entropy sources, de-skewing, mixing, pseudo-random generators, example standards, and sizing of randomness needed for passwords and keys.

randomness.why: The whole document is about randomness requirements, entropy sources, mixing and PRNGs for security.
randomness.quote: This document points out many pitfalls in using poor entropy sources or traditional pseudo-random number generation techniques for generating such quantities.

rejected.why: The document concerns generating secret quantities, not key establishment, provisioning or storage protocols; randomness is the more specific fit.
AES is only used as an example mixing function and a key-size reference, not specified or analysed in its own right.
SHA-1 is used as a mixing/hash function in examples, but the document is not about the SHA family.
HMAC appears in the X9.82 generator description only as a building block.
Password generation entropy is discussed, but not password hashing or key stretching.
Parent of randomness, which is chosen as the more specific tag.

RFC4087.title: IP Tunnel MIB
RFC4087.summary: Defines the IP Tunnel MIB module (obsoleting RFC 2667) for managing tunnels of any encapsulation type over IPv4 and IPv6, with a tunnel interface table, an Inet config table for tunnel creation, and an IANA-maintained tunnel type textual convention.

MIB.why: The document's entire purpose is a SMIv2 MIB module (TUNNEL-MIB) with tables, objects, and conformance statements for tunnel management.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

tunneling.why: The subject being managed is IP tunnelling across encapsulation methods (GRE, IP-in-IP, L2TP, 6to4 etc.), so readers of tunnelling would want this MIB.
tunneling.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 and IPv6 networks.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour.
GRE is merely one listed encapsulation type value; the MIB is generic, not about GRE.
IP-in-IP is only one example encapsulation method listed, not the subject.
L2TP is only enumerated as an encapsulation type, not specified or extended.
Only referenced via the tunnelIfSecurity object; IPsec-specific MIBs are left to extensions.
The IANAtunnelType textual convention is a small part of the document, not a subject about IANA registries in general.

RFC4088.title: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Scheme for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC4088.summary: Defines the "snmp" URI scheme for designating an SNMP agent, context, and MIB object instances (single OIDs or OID groups), including syntax, semantics, and gateway usage.

SNMP.why: The document specifies how SNMP agents, contexts and MIB object instances are addressed and accessed via SNMP operations (Get, GetNext, Set), so SNMP readers would want it.
SNMP.quote: This document defines a URI scheme so that SNMP can be designated as the protocol used for management.

URI.why: It registers a new URI scheme with syntax, percent-encoding rules, relative reference considerations and a registration template.
URI.quote: An SNMP URI has the following ABNF [RFC2234] syntax

rejected.why: MIB object instances are designated, but the document defines no MIB module and does not discuss SMI.
UDP is only mentioned as the default SNMP transport.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax.
The OID syntax is taken from the URN namespace of RFC 3061, but the document does not define a URN namespace.
The SNMP tag is more specific and covers the management subject.

RFC4089.title: IAB and IESG Recommendation for IETF Administrative Restructuring
RFC4089.summary: IAB/IESG recommendation, published for the record, that the IETF pursue "Scenario O" (an IETF-directed administrative support activity under ISOC, overseen by an IAOC) over "Scenario C" (a separate foundation), reproducing both scenario drafts.

IETF process.why: The document is about how IETF administrative support (IASA, IAOC, IAD, ISOC relationship, budgeting, NomCom-selected members) is structured and governed, which is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: administrative restructuring of the Internet Engineering Task Force

rejected.why: NomCom selection of IAOC/BoT members is mentioned only as one mechanism, not the subject of the document.
IANA is only one of the contracted support functions; the document is not about IANA registries or stewardship.
The RFC Editor contract is listed among support functions but the RFC series format and publication are not the subject.
IPR text appears only in boilerplate; the document is not about IPR.

RFC4090.title: Fast Reroute Extensions to RSVP-TE for LSP Tunnels
RFC4090.summary: Defines RSVP-TE extensions (FAST_REROUTE and DETOUR objects, new flags) and PLR/merge-point procedures for one-to-one and facility backup local repair of MPLS TE LSP tunnels in tens of milliseconds.

IP fast reroute.why: The document specifies MPLS fast reroute local repair via detour and bypass LSPs, the subject of the fast reroute tag.
IP fast reroute.quote: This document defines RSVP-TE extensions to establish backup label-switched path (LSP) tunnels for local repair of LSP tunnels.

RSVP-TE.why: It extends RSVP-TE with new objects, flags and signalling procedures for traffic-engineered LSPs, so RSVP-TE readers need it.
RSVP-TE.quote: This specification defines two additional objects, FAST_REROUTE and DETOUR, to extend RSVP-TE for fast-reroute signaling.

rejected.why: MPLS is the data plane, but the document is about RSVP-TE signalling for protection, which is covered by more specific tags.
Plain RSVP is the base protocol; the extensions are TE-specific and fall under RSVP-TE.
A parent of RSVP-TE, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Not about generalized MPLS.

gaps.name: MPLS fast reroute / local repair of TE LSPs
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no MPLS-specific fast-reroute tag. IP fast reroute (which covers IP and LDP fast reroute and loop-free alternates) is the closest fit, and MPLS TE FRR readers would want a dedicated tag.

RFC4091.title: The Alternative Network Address Types (ANAT) Semantics for the Session Description Protocol (SDP) Grouping Framework
RFC4091.summary: Defines the ANAT semantics for the SDP grouping framework, letting an SDP session description group 'm' lines carrying alternative network address types (e.g., IPv4 and IPv6) for one media stream, with preference ordering and offer/answer handling.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new group semantics, specifies preference ordering and offer/answer behaviour, and registers it in the SDP registry.
SDP.quote: This document defines the Alternative Network Address Types (ANAT) semantics for the Session Description Protocol (SDP) grouping framework.

rejected.why: SIP is only mentioned for the sdp-anat option-tag, which is defined in RFC 4092; this document does not specify SIP behaviour.
ICE is discussed only to contrast scope and show it can be combined; ICE is not specified or extended here.
IPv4/IPv6 are the motivating address types, but the document defines an SDP grouping semantic, not IPv6 itself.
The mechanism lets dual-stack endpoints offer both address families, but it is an SDP signalling mechanism, not a transition mechanism like those in this subtree.
The document explicitly says it is not for same-type transport address alternatives, which is ICE's role.

RFC4092.title: Usage of the Session Description Protocol (SDP) Alternative Network Address Types (ANAT) Semantics in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4092.summary: Defines the sdp-anat SIP option-tag for the Require and Supported headers so that SDP offers using ANAT semantics are handled only by ANAT-aware SIP entities, and explains the backward-compatibility problems it avoids.

SIP.why: The document's main contribution is a new SIP option-tag, with rules for its use in SIP header fields and in OPTIONS requests. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: We define the option-tag sdp-anat for use in the Require and Supported SIP [3] header fields.

SDP.why: The document is about how SDP offers that use ANAT grouping of media lines behave when the answerer does not support ANAT. A reader of SDP offer/answer would want it.
SDP.quote: allow UAs to offer [4] alternative addresses of different types in an SDP session description.

rejected.why: IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack is only the motivating example for alternative address types. The document is not about IPv6.
S/MIME is only recommended in the Security Considerations for integrity protection of the Require header. It is boilerplate-level and not the subject.
Registration of the option-tag is routine IANA Considerations and does not make the document about IANA.
ANAT helps with IPv4/IPv6 coexistence, but this document only defines the SIP option-tag and does not address transition mechanisms.

gaps.name: ANAT (Alternative Network Address Types) / SDP grouping framework
gaps.why: The document is about ANAT semantics in SIP, and the taxonomy has no SDP grouping or ANAT tag. SDP is the nearest tag.

RFC4093.title: Problem Statement: Mobile IPv4 Traversal of Virtual Private Network (VPN) Gateways
RFC4093.summary: Problem statement describing deployment scenarios and incompatibilities when Mobile IPv4 must traverse IPsec-based VPN gateways, with guidelines for solutions.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document analyses MIPv4 home agent, foreign agent and co-located registration problems when VPN gateways are present, and gives guidelines for MIPv4 solutions.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Deploying Mobile-IP v4 in networks that are connected to the Internet through a Virtual Private Network (VPN) gateway presents some problems

IPsec.why: A substantial part analyses IPsec tunnel SA renegotiation on handoff and ESP/IP-in-IP incompatibilities, with guidelines on IPsec and IKE impact.
IPsec.quote: MIPv4 packets are encapsulated in an IPsec-ESP tunnel established between the Mobile Node and the VPN gateway.

rejected.why: The VPN tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs (L3VPN/L2VPN style); this document concerns enterprise IPsec remote-access VPN gateways, not provider-provisioned VPNs.
NAT traversal is mentioned only as a solution guideline referencing other RFCs; not a main subject.
IKE renegotiation overhead is mentioned in guidelines but IKE itself is not specified or analysed in depth.
Firewalls are deliberately omitted from the scenarios to keep things simple.
IP-in-IP encapsulation is discussed only as it affects FA/VPN interaction; covered by the MIPv4 and IPsec framing.

RFC4094.title: Analysis of Existing Quality-of-Service Signaling Protocols
RFC4094.summary: Informational NSIS WG review of existing QoS signaling protocols (RSVP and its extensions, ST-II, YESSIR, Boomerang, INSIGNIA, BGRP, SICAP, DARIS), analysing their transport, performance, security and mobility issues and comparing RSVP to NSIS requirements.

RSVP.why: Most of the document analyses RSVP's design, its many extensions, and its transport, performance, security and mobility issues.
RSVP.quote: RSVP (the Resource Reservation Protocol) [ZDSZ93] [RFC2205] [BEBH96] has evolved from ST-II to provide end-to-end QoS signaling services

NSIS.why: Written as NSIS WG input; it compares RSVP to the NSIS requirements and aims to guide a new signaling protocol design.
NSIS.quote: This section provides a comparison of RSVP to the requirements identified as part of the work in NSIS [RFC3726].

ST-II.why: ST-II is reviewed as an original QoS signaling protocol and compared with RSVP.
ST-II.quote: ST-II [RFC1819] basically works in the following way: a sender originates a Connect message to a set of receivers.

RSVP-TE.why: RSVP-TE and GMPLS extensions are described in detail, and section 3.4 discusses RSVP-TE scaling.
RSVP-TE.quote: RSVP-TE [RFC3209] specifies the core extensions to RSVP for establishing constraint-based explicitly routed LSPs in MPLS networks

rejected.why: Intserv is the framework RSVP serves, but the document analyses signaling protocols, not Intserv itself.
MPLS appears only as an application of RSVP-TE; the document is not about MPLS.
GMPLS RSVP-TE gets a short subsection among many extensions, not enough to be a subject of the document.
Mobility is discussed only as an RSVP shortcoming, not as IP mobility protocols.
Diffserv is covered only through the DCLASS object and aggregation; the document is not about it.
COPS is mentioned only as an RSVP policy interface.

RFC4095.title: Attaching Meaning to Solicitation Class Keywords
RFC4095.summary: Specifies a DDDS application using DNS NAPTR records to map a No-Solicit solicitation class keyword (reversed domain name) to a URI explaining its meaning.

DNS.why: The document defines a new use of NAPTR resource records in DNS, specifying the key transformation and field usage for a DDDS application.
DNS.quote: associating a solicitation class keyword with a URI which contains further information by using the DNS NAPTR Resource Record

spam.why: The keywords belong to the No-Solicit mechanism for unsolicited bulk email; this document helps recipients and filters interpret them.
spam.quote: it will be important to find a method for discovering the meaning behind the various solicitation class keywords

rejected.why: ENUM is only cited as another DDDS application example; this document does not deal with telephone numbers.
The No-Solicit SMTP extension is defined in RFC 3865; this document only uses its keywords and leaves transport out of scope.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in the Security Considerations and the sample code comments.
URIs are the output value, but the document does not define a URI scheme or syntax.
IDNA is mentioned only in passing for non-ASCII labels.
Email is the context for the keywords, but the document is about the DNS-based discovery mechanism rather than email architecture.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System) / NAPTR
gaps.why: The document is a DDDS application using NAPTR records. The taxonomy has no DDDS or NAPTR tag, so DNS is the closest fit.

RFC4096.title: Policy-Mandated Labels Such as "Adv:" in Email Subject Headers Considered Ineffective At Best
RFC4096.summary: Informational memo arguing that legally mandated labels like "ADV:" in the email Subject header are unworkable and ineffective, and recommending a dedicated header field (the No-Solicit SMTP extension's solicitation class keywords) instead.

spam.why: The whole memo concerns anti-spam labelling laws and how to flag unsolicited commercial email, including filtering by recipients. This is the spam subject.
spam.quote: Policy-mandated labels such as "Adv:" in email subject headers considered ineffective at best

message format.why: A substantial part analyses the Subject header field: length limits, folding, RFC 2047 encoded words, and the overloading of an unstructured field. This is Internet message format material.
message format.quote: The basic definition of the "Subject:" of an electronic mail message is contained in [RFC2822].

rejected.why: The No-Solicit SMTP extension (RFC 3865) is discussed only as an alternative to Subject labels. The memo does not specify or extend SMTP.
RFC 2047 encoded words, Base64 and Quoted-Printable are used to show loopholes in labelling. The memo is not about MIME.
Base64 appears only as an example encoding in the header loophole illustrations.
Character sets are mentioned only as a way to evade labels. The memo does not address character set registration or use.
The more specific tags (spam, message format) cover the document, so the parent is implied.

RFC4097.title: Middlebox Communications (MIDCOM) Protocol Evaluation
RFC4097.summary: Working-group evaluation of SNMP, RSIP, Megaco, Diameter and COPS as candidates for the MIDCOM middlebox control protocol, judged requirement by requirement against the MIDCOM framework and requirements.

SNMP.why: SNMPv3 is one of the five evaluated protocols and the one the evaluation favours, with an overview in Appendix A. Readers of SNMP would want this analysis.
SNMP.quote: The SNMP management framework meets all the specified MIDCOM protocol requirements with the appropriate design of a MIDCOM MIB module.

Megaco.why: Megaco is evaluated in its own section, with an appendix on how to model middlebox functions and policy rules as Terminations.
Megaco.quote: Megaco is a master-slave, transaction-oriented protocol defined in RFC 3015 [20] in which Media Gateway Controllers (MGC) control the operation of Media Gateways (MG).

Diameter.why: Diameter is evaluated as a MIDCOM candidate, and Appendix D covers its IPFilterRule type.
Diameter.quote: A general assessment might be that Diameter meets and exceeds MIDCOM architectural requirements, however the connection orientation may be too heavy
Diameter.section: 1.4.2. Comparison of Diameter With MIDCOM Architectural Requirements

COPS.why: COPS and COPS-PR are evaluated against the MIDCOM requirements, with a separate architecture section.
COPS.quote: COPS is a simple query and response protocol that can be used to exchange policy information between a policy server (Policy Decision Point or PDP)

NAT.why: The document is about controlling middleboxes (NATs and firewalls) from outside. It also compares RSIP tunnelling with NAT, and Appendix B covers NAT support.
NAT.quote: For configuring NATs, a NAT MIB module [16] has been developed.

firewall.why: MIDCOM is about middlebox (firewall and NAT) control. The document also evaluates firewall filtering rules, including the Diameter IPFilterRule in Appendix D.
firewall.quote: Existing work for firewall control with SNMP only considered the monitoring of firewalls and not the configuration.
firewall.section: 1.1.2. SNMP Existing Support for NAT and Firewall Control

rejected.why: Policy rules and PDP/PEP concepts appear throughout, but the document compares protocols and does not develop a policy information model.
Diameter is described as an AAA protocol, but it is evaluated here as a candidate for a different use, so the Diameter tag is enough.
MIB modules are discussed as SNMP's extension mechanism. No MIB is defined here, and a MIDCOM MIB is only proposed.
IPsec and TLS appear only as the security mechanisms the candidates rely on.
STUN is mentioned only briefly as an alternative in Appendix B.

gaps.name: MIDCOM (Middlebox Communications)
gaps.why: The document is about the MIDCOM framework, requirements and protocol selection for communicating with middleboxes, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. The closest are NAT and firewall.

gaps.name: RSIP (Realm Specific IP)
gaps.why: RSIP is one of the five protocols evaluated, and there is no RSIP tag. NAT is the nearest.

RFC4098.title: Terminology for Benchmarking BGP Device Convergence in the Control Plane
RFC4098.summary: Defines terminology for benchmarking eBGP control-plane convergence on a single BGP device, covering routes, RIBs, update trains, route change events, convergence, and factors affecting performance.

BGP.why: The whole document defines BGP-specific terms (Adj-RIB-In, Loc-RIB, UPDATE, MRAI, route flap, soft/hard reset) for measuring BGP convergence.
BGP.quote: This document establishes terminology to standardize the description of benchmarking methodology for measuring eBGP convergence in the control plane of a single BGP device.

benchmarking.why: It is the terminology companion to a benchmarking methodology from the BMWG, defining DUT, test stimuli, update trains, and measurement units.
benchmarking.quote: The principal objective is to derive methodologies that standardize conducting and reporting convergence-related measurements for BGP.

rejected.why: The document is a glossary, but the tag covers general glossaries and requirements language. Its subject is BGP benchmarking terms, which the BGP and benchmarking tags already cover.
TCP is only the transport underneath BGP. It appears as a factor in a brief paragraph on TCP parameters.
The document says its terms apply to IPv6 and gives some IPv6 examples. It is not about IPv6 itself.
RPSL is mentioned once as a way to document routing policy. It is not a subject of the document.
benchmarking is the more specific fit for this document.
Route reflectors are mentioned only as one kind of BGP device.

RFC4101.title: Writing Protocol Models
RFC4101.summary: An IAB informational document advising authors to write short, diagram-centred protocol "models" (problem, broad message overview, important features) to ease peer review, illustrated with STUN, DCCP, WebDAV COPY/MOVE and IKE examples.

IETF process.why: The document is guidance on how to write specifications so IETF peer review works better. That makes it about the standards-development process and document practice.
IETF process.quote: The IETF process depends on peer review.  However, IETF documents are generally written to be useful for implementors, not reviewers.

rejected.why: IKE is a worked example in Section 6 and takes up about half the text. The document is not about IKE itself, only uses it to show how to write a model.
DCCP is only an illustrative example of an overview in Section 4.2.1. The document does not specify or analyse it.
STUN is only the example for the Problem section of a model.
The COPY/MOVE discussion is a short illustration of the important-features section, not WebDAV coverage.
The document gives advice on writing protocol descriptions, not on RFC format or publication. Section 5 touches ASCII rendering, but only in passing.
IPsec appears only as the context for the IKE example.

gaps.name: specification writing / document authoring guidance
gaps.why: The document is about how to author protocol specifications and overviews. The taxonomy has no tag for this beyond the general IETF process, so a reader looking for spec-writing advice has no specific page.

RFC4102.title: Registration of the text/red MIME Sub-Type
RFC4102.summary: Registers the text/red MIME sub-type (RTP redundant text payload per RFC 2198), defining its parameters and mapping to SDP fields.

media types.why: The document's main purpose is registering a MIME media type with its parameters, restrictions and usage, so it belongs under media type registrations.
media types.quote: This memo provides the MIME sub-type registration information for text/red.

RTP payload format.why: The type is for RTP transfer of redundant text, defining the rate and pt parameters that enumerate RTP payload types; it is an RTP payload-format registration.
RTP payload format.quote: The actual RTP packetization for this MIME type is specified in RFC 2198.

SDP.why: A full section maps the MIME parameters to SDP m=, a=rtpmap, a=fmtp, a=ptime and a=maxptime, with an example.
SDP.quote: The information carried in the MIME media type specification has a specific mapping to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a recommended integrity mechanism; not the subject.
The document registers a media type but does not address MIME body structure or encodings; media types is the more specific fit.
Not discussed.
The registration template is IANA Considerations boilerplate-style, but the document is about the media type, not IANA registry procedures.

gaps.name: Real-time text / text conversation (T.140)
gaps.why: The document supports redundant real-time text transport (T.140 in the example), but the taxonomy has no tag for real-time text.

RFC4103.title: RTP Payload for Text Conversation
RFC4103.summary: Defines the text/t140 RTP payload format for carrying ITU-T T.140 real-time text conversation, with RFC 2198 redundancy for loss protection, a "cps" SDP parameter, and the media type registration; obsoletes RFC 2793.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for T.140 text, covering packet header usage, redundancy and loss detection.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines a payload type for carrying text conversation session contents in RTP [2] packets.

media types.why: A substantial part registers the text/t140 media type with its rate and cps parameters and SDP mapping.
media types.quote: This document updates the RTP payload format named "t140" and the associated MIME type "text/t140"

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP fmtp parameter, gives SDP examples and offer/answer considerations.
SDP.quote: To control the character transmission rate, the MIME parameter "cps" in the "fmtp" attribute [7] is defined

rejected.why: The more specific child RTP payload format applies.
Only mentioned as a suitable option for confidentiality and integrity in Security Considerations.
T.140 text is UTF-8 encoded, but this is just the encoding of the payload, not the subject.
Congestion considerations section is boilerplate-like guidance and not the main subject.
RFC 2733 FEC is mentioned only as an optional alternative; the document uses RFC 2198 redundancy.
RTCP is only mentioned for stream association and loss checks.

gaps.name: T.140 real-time text conversation
gaps.why: The document is about carrying real-time text (T.140) and there is no taxonomy tag for real-time text or accessibility-oriented text telephony; the accessibility topic is only loosely related.

RFC4104.title: Policy Core Extension Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Schema (PCELS)
RFC4104.summary: Defines the PCELS LDAP schema: new object classes and attribute types mapping the PCIM Extensions (RFC 3460) to LDAP, updating the Policy Core LDAP Schema (RFC 3703).

LDAP.why: The document is an LDAP schema specification defining object classes, attributes and DIT containment rules for policy information stored in a directory.
LDAP.quote: These changes and extensions consist of new LDAP object classes and attribute types

policy management.why: It maps the Policy Core Information Model extensions (policy sets, rules, conditions, actions, variables, filters) to a schema, which is policy-based management information modelling.
policy management.quote: The concept of a set of policies is introduced by two new object classes: pcelsPolicySet and pcelsPolicySetAssociation.

rejected.why: LDAP is the more specific child tag and is already chosen; the parent is implied.
The IANA section only registers OIDs and descriptors; it is boilerplate here.
X.500 is referenced only for schema and matching-rule definitions, not specified or extended.
DSCP variables and filter attributes are only fields in filter classes; Diffserv is not the document's subject.
IPv6 address attributes are filter fields only; IPv6 itself is not the subject.

gaps.name: Policy framework / PCIM (Policy Core Information Model)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the IETF policy framework as a whole. Only the generic 'policy management' topic exists, and it fits only roughly.

RFC4105.title: Requirements for Inter-Area MPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC4105.summary: Informational requirements document listing functional requirements for extending MPLS Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE, CSPF, fast reroute, DS-TE) across multiple IGP areas, while preserving IGP hierarchy and scalability.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document defines requirements for inter-area MPLS TE: path computation, signaling, reoptimization, recovery and routing. No specific TE technology tag fits the MPLS TE requirements as a whole, so the topic tag applies.
traffic engineering.quote: This document lists a detailed set of functional requirements for the support of inter-area MPLS Traffic Engineering (inter-area MPLS TE).

MPLS.why: The requirements concern MPLS TE LSPs, including hierarchy/nesting, preemption, LSP ping and TTL handling. Readers of MPLS would want this document.
MPLS.quote: The MPLS-TE control plane allows establishing explicitly routed MPLS LSPs whose paths follow a set of TE constraints.

RSVP-TE.why: The document sets requirements on RSVP-TE signaling for inter-area LSPs (loose/strict hops, exclusion, crankback, per-LSP signaled options) and on preserving RSVP-TE scalability.
RSVP-TE.quote: The solution MUST allow for the signaling of inter-area TE LSPs, using RSVP-TE.

IP fast reroute.why: A substantial part of the document concerns fast reroute protection of inter-area LSPs, including ABR failure. This is MPLS TE fast reroute rather than LFA/LDP, so the fit is only approximate.
IP fast reroute.quote: The solution MUST provide the ability to benefit from fast recovery, making use of the local protection techniques specified in [FAST-REROUTE]

rejected.why: OSPF areas and ABRs are the setting for the requirements, but the document does not specify or extend OSPF.
IS-IS levels are mentioned only as equivalent to OSPF areas for the terminology.
DiffServ and DS-TE are mentioned as an application and in one requirement (7.11), but are not a main subject.
BGP recursive routing into the LSP is a brief point in 7.16, so it is not a subject of the document.
Path computation is discussed generally, but PCE is not mentioned and the document is not about PCE.
The IGP hierarchy and scalability objectives are inputs to the TE requirements, not a separate subject.

RFC4106.title: The Use of Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) in IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC4106.summary: Specifies the use of AES in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM) as an IPsec ESP transform providing confidentiality and data origin authentication, including IV, nonce, AAD, ICV and IKE conventions.

ESP.why: The document defines how AES-GCM is carried in ESP: payload layout, nonce, AAD construction, ICV and packet expansion. This is an ESP transform specification.
ESP.quote: This document describes the use of AES in GCM mode (AES-GCM) as an IPsec ESP mechanism for confidentiality and data origin authentication.

AES.why: The document specifies the AES-GCM mode and its use with 128, 192 and 256-bit keys, including nonce uniqueness and key-lifetime limits.
AES.quote: GCM is a block cipher mode of operation providing both confidentiality and data origin authentication.

IKE.why: A full section defines KEYMAT and salt derivation, ESP transform identifiers 18-20 and the Key Length attribute for IKE negotiation.
IKE.quote: This section describes the conventions used to generate keying material and salt values, for use with AES-GCM-ESP, using the Internet Key Exchange (IKE)

rejected.why: ESP is the more specific child tag and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
Not relevant. The document is about AES-GCM, not ChaCha20/Poly1305.
Salt and keying material derivation is covered by the IKE tag. The document is not about key management in general.

gaps.name: Authenticated encryption (AEAD) modes
gaps.why: The document is about the GCM authenticated-encryption mode, but the taxonomy has no AEAD or GCM tag. AES covers it only partially.

RFC4107.title: Guidelines for Cryptographic Key Management
RFC4107.summary: BCP guidance for IETF working groups and protocol authors on when automated cryptographic key management must or should be used versus when manual keying is acceptable, with minimum shared-secret size and randomness guidance.

key management.why: The whole document gives criteria for automated versus manual key management, which is the subject of the key management topic.
key management.quote: automated key management SHOULD be used to establish session keys.  Strong justification is needed in the security considerations section of a proposal that makes use of manual key management.

rejected.why: IKE is only cited as an example of automated key management and for its code size; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Mentioned as an example of automated key management and a symmetric-key alternative, not a subject of the document.
Cited only as an example of a protocol with automated key management and for its code size.
Only a brief pointer to BCP 106 and a requirement that manual secrets be unpredictable; the document is not about randomness generation.
Only mentioned as an example through IKE; not discussed in its own right.
Named only as one example of a stream cipher that triggers the requirement for automated keying.

RFC4108.title: Using Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) to Protect Firmware Packages
RFC4108.summary: Profiles the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) to sign, optionally encrypt and compress firmware packages for hardware modules, and defines signed load receipts, load error reports, and a hardware module name form.

CMS.why: The document is a CMS content-type profile: SignedData, EncryptedData, CompressedData, new content types and signed attributes for firmware packages, receipts and errors.
CMS.quote: This document describes the use of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) to protect firmware packages, which provide object code for one or more hardware module components.

firmware update.why: Covers protected firmware package loading, bootstrap loader requirements, stale version rollback prevention, load receipts and error reports, which are central to firmware update.
firmware update.quote: The firmware package contains object code for one or more programmable components that make up the hardware module.

rejected.why: Certificates and trust anchors are used for signature validation, but the only new X.509 item is a small hardware module name otherName form; the document is not about X.509 itself.
ASN.1 is the notation and encoding for the structures (including an appendix module), not the subject.
CompressedData is used as an optional layer, with no compression format defined.
Trust anchors and certification paths are relied on but not specified.
Targets hardware modules (especially cryptographic ones), not IoT constrained devices.

RFC4109.title: Algorithms for Internet Key Exchange version 1 (IKEv1)
RFC4109.summary: Updates RFC 2409 by revising the MUST/SHOULD/MAY algorithm requirements for IKEv1 implementations (3DES, AES-CBC, SHA-1, DH groups 2 and 14, etc.) to reflect market reality and security.

IKE.why: The document revises the mandatory and recommended algorithms of IKEv1 (RFC 2409), so it is about IKE.
IKE.quote: This document updates RFC 2409 by changing the algorithm requirements defined there.

rejected.why: AES-128 CBC and XCBC are only listed as recommended algorithms; the document does not specify AES.
DES is demoted to MAY, but this is one line in a requirements table and the document is not about DES.
IPsec is the context, but the document is specifically about IKE algorithm requirements, so the more specific IKE tag fits.
MD5 is demoted to MAY in a requirements list. The document is not about MD5.
RSA signatures are only one entry in the algorithm requirements list.
SHA-1 is only one entry in the list of required algorithms.

RFC4110.title: A Framework for Layer 3 Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs)
RFC4110.summary: Informational framework from the l3vpn WG describing reference models, customer and network interfaces, tunneling, routing distribution, QoS, management, interworking and security for layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs (PE-based and CE-based).

L3VPN.why: The whole document is a framework for layer 3 PPVPNs, covering PE-based and CE-based models, VFIs, discovery and routing distribution.
L3VPN.quote: This document provides a framework for Layer 3 Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs).

tunneling.why: A substantial section covers tunnel encapsulation, multiplexing, establishment, hierarchy and maintenance, with a survey of GRE, IP-in-IP, IPsec and MPLS.
tunneling.quote: VPN solutions use tunneling in order to transport VPN packets across the VPN backbone, from one VPN edge device to another.

rejected.why: BGP is discussed as an option for aggregated VPN routing and discovery, but the document does not specify or extend it.
MPLS is one surveyed tunneling technique and a backbone assumption, not the subject.
GRE is one of four tunnel types briefly surveyed, not the subject of the document.
IPsec appears as a tunneling option and a security mechanism, not as something the document specifies or analyses in depth.
This is the parent of L3VPN, so it is implied by the more specific tag.
QoS, IntServ and DiffServ are covered only in a brief survey section.

RFC4111.title: Security Framework for Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs)
RFC4111.summary: Informational framework describing security threats, defensive techniques, user and provider security requirements, and an evaluation template for provider-provisioned VPNs (L2 and L3).

VPN.why: The whole document is a security framework for provider-provisioned VPNs, covering both L2 and L3 types and not one specific child technology.
VPN.quote: This document addresses security aspects pertaining to Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs).

operational security.why: It covers provider infrastructure protection, control-plane and management-interface defence, filtering, rate limiting, and attack monitoring and reporting.
operational security.quote: Monitoring systems used to detect security attacks in PPVPNs will typically operate by collecting information from Provider Edge (PE), Customer Edge (CE), and/or Provider backbone (P) devices.

IPsec.why: A substantial subsection analyses IPsec use in PPVPNs (PE-PE, CE-PE, CE-CE) and encryption placement tradeoffs.
IPsec.quote: IPsec is the security protocol of choice for encryption at the IP layer (Layer 3)

rejected.why: Too broad. The document is about security specifically for PPVPNs, so the VPN tag is more specific and fits better.
The document covers L2 and L3 PPVPNs generically and explicitly does not analyse specific technologies, so the parent VPN tag is the right one.
Same reason as L3VPN. L2 PPVPNs are only discussed generically.
Firewalls and filtering are one defensive technique among many, not the subject of the document.
SNMP appears only as an example of a monitoring and management mechanism.
BGP is mentioned only as a control protocol to be authenticated.

RFC4112.title: Electronic Commerce Modeling Language (ECML) Version 2 Specification
RFC4112.summary: RFC 4112 specifies ECML version 2, a hierarchical set of payment-related field names (shipping, billing, card, transaction) with an XML DTD and Schema, so wallet software can automate filling in e-commerce forms.

ECML.why: The document is the ECML v2 specification itself: field list, XML DTD and schema, usage notes, and IANA registrations for ECML.
ECML.quote: A standard set of hierarchically-organized payment-related information field names in an XML syntax is defined so that this task can be more easily automated.

rejected.why: XML is the exemplar syntax (DTD and Schema) for the fields, but the document is about the e-commerce field set, not XML usage in general. ECML is the more specific tag.
IOTP appears only as one value in the card protocols field and as a possible exchange method, so it is mentioned rather than the subject.
HTML forms are a likely carrier for the fields, but the document does not specify anything about HTML.
The document registers urn:ietf:params:ecml, but this is IANA boilerplate for a version identifier and does not make the document about URN namespaces.
The parent topic is implied by ECML, and the ECML tech tag already sits under it.

RFC4113.title: Management Information Base for the User Datagram Protocol (UDP)
RFC4113.summary: Defines the IP-version-independent UDP-MIB SMIv2 module (counters, udpEndpointTable, HC counters), obsoleting RFC 2013 and RFC 2454.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module for managing UDP implementations, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for implementations of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) in an IP version independent manner.

UDP.why: The MIB models UDP statistics and endpoints (listening and connected), so UDP readers would want it.
UDP.quote: The udpEndpointTable provides access to status information for all UDP endpoints handled by a UDP protocol engine.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB module rather than SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
IP version neutrality is a design goal, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The counters are management statistics, not a measurement methodology.

RFC4114.title: E.164 Number Mapping for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC4114.summary: Defines an EPP extension to the domain name mapping for provisioning E.164 numbers, carrying ENUM NAPTR records in create, update and info commands.

EPP.why: The document specifies an EPP extension mapping, with new elements for the create, update and info commands and an XML schema. It is about EPP.
EPP.quote: This document describes an E.164 number mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP).

ENUM.why: The mapping provisions the E.164 numbers and NAPTR data that are published in DNS under ENUM. It also sets NAPTR field requirements that follow the ENUM rules, so ENUM readers would want it.
ENUM.quote: ENUM [6] describes how the Domain Name System (DNS) can be used to identify services associated with an E.164 number.

rejected.why: DNS is only where the provisioned data is eventually published. The document defines provisioning, not DNS behaviour.
XML and XML Schema are only the notation used to specify the mapping. The document is not about XML usage in general.
EPP is the more specific tag and is already chosen, so the parent topic is implied.

RFC4115.title: A Differentiated Service Two-Rate, Three-Color Marker with Efficient Handling of in-Profile Traffic
RFC4115.summary: Informational RFC defining a two-rate, three-color token-bucket meter/marker for Differentiated Services that colors in-profile traffic green directly and does not require peak-rate shaping at the CE.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies a metering and marking algorithm, a core component of the Differentiated Services architecture, and compares it with the RFC 2697 and RFC 2698 markers.
Diffserv.quote: This document describes a two-rate, three-color metering/marker algorithm that is suitable for the differentiated service applications such as IP and L2 VPNs.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific tag and already implies QoS.
IP and L2 VPNs are only mentioned as application scenarios for the marker. The document does not specify or analyse VPN services.
The marker is said to be in use for Frame Relay services, but the document is not about frame relay or IP interworking with it.
Ethernet transport over IP is mentioned once as a possible use. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC4116.title: IPv4 Multihoming Practices and Limitations
RFC4116.summary: Informational RFC describing common IPv4 site-multihoming practices (BGP with PI/PA addresses, multi-attachment, NAT/RFC2260) and comparing their features against multihoming goals, as a baseline for IPv6 multihoming proposals.

multihoming.why: The whole document is about site multihoming architectures in IPv4, their addressing options and feature trade-offs. The multihoming topic tag fits; the Shim6 child is an IPv6 solution and is not discussed.
multihoming.quote: This document aims to document common IPv4 multihoming practices and enumerate their features for comparison with other multihoming approaches.

BGP.why: A large part of the document covers how BGP is used for multihoming, including PI/PA announcements, origin AS choices and export/import policy.
BGP.quote: The general approach for multihoming with BGP is to announce a set of routes to two or more transit providers.

rejected.why: NAT-based multihoming is one of three practices briefly described, but the document is not about NAT behaviour itself.
CIDR is cited as the architectural background for aggregation, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
The document is a baseline for comparison with IPv6 multihoming proposals but does not discuss Shim6.
The document is about IPv4 multihoming practice, not the IPv4 protocol or its address lifecycle in its own right.
Scalability of the global routing table is mentioned as a feature, but the focus is multihoming practice.

RFC4117.title: Transcoding Services Invocation in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Using Third Party Call Control (3pcc)
RFC4117.summary: Informational RFC describing SIP call flows using third party call control (3pcc) so a user agent can invoke transcoding servers (e.g., speech-to-text) for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired users, including callee/caller invocation, parallel and serial transcoders.

SIP.why: The whole document is a set of SIP INVITE/200/ACK call flows for invoking transcoders via 3pcc, a SIP deployment/usage pattern.
SIP.quote: This document describes how to invoke transcoding services using Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and third party call control.

SDP.why: Flows hinge on SDP offer/answer manipulation, including FID grouping and sendonly/recvonly streams, so SDP readers would want it.
SDP.quote: All the call flows in this document use SDP.

rejected.why: Transcoding between codecs/media types is the service invoked, but the document specifies no codec; it is about signalling invocation.
RTP carries the media in the examples only; nothing about RTP is specified.
The motivation is deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired users, but the document is mainly about SIP call flows. The topic is a plausible fit but weaker than SIP.
No PSTN interworking is addressed.

gaps.name: Third party call control (3pcc) / media transcoding
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for 3pcc or transcoding services, which are the central subjects of the document.

RFC4118.title: Architecture Taxonomy for Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP)
RFC4118.summary: Informational taxonomy of IEEE 802.11 WLAN architectures in vendor products (autonomous, centralized Local/Split/Remote MAC, distributed mesh), analysing how WLAN and CAPWAP functions are distributed between WTPs and Access Controllers, as groundwork for the CAPWAP working group.

CAPWAP.why: The document is the CAPWAP working group's architecture taxonomy, surveying how WTPs and Access Controllers split WLAN and control/provisioning functions. It is core CAPWAP background.
CAPWAP.quote: This document provides a taxonomy of the architectures employed in existing WLAN products.

WiFi.why: It analyses IEEE 802.11 WLAN services, MAC split and mesh architectures in depth, so readers of Wi-Fi would want it.
WiFi.quote: This document provides a taxonomy of the architectures employed in the existing IEEE 802.11 products in the market

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a management method for standalone APs; not the subject.
802.1X/EAP appears in the function-distribution matrices but is not what the document is about.
Mentioned only as one option for securing the WTP-AC tunnel.
Mentioned only as an example back-end AAA server.
The distributed mesh section is short and describes proprietary 802.11 mesh, not MANET routing protocols.
Tunnelling of station traffic to the AC is noted only in passing.

RFC4119.title: A Presence-based GEOPRIV Location Object Format
RFC4119.summary: Defines PIDF-LO, a PIDF extension (geopriv element) that carries geographic or civic location with usage rules, method and provided-by elements, secured via S/MIME, with IANA registries.

geolocation.why: The document defines a location object format with privacy rules, including civic location schema and GML baseline.
geolocation.quote: This document describes an object format for carrying geographical information on the Internet.

PIDF.why: The location object is an extension of PIDF, adding the geopriv element under status.
PIDF.quote: this document extends the XML-based Presence Information Data Format (PIDF [2]) to allow the encapsulation of location information within a presence document.

rejected.why: Used as the security mechanism for the object. Section 4 mandates it but only as a substrate, not the subject.
XML Schema is the encoding vehicle, not the subject.
Mentioned only as an example using protocol; the object is independent of it.
Presence is the basis, but this is not a SIMPLE event package or XCAP document.
Privacy motivates the usage-rules, but the document is a location object format, not a general privacy analysis.
Only mentions the existing application/pidf+xml type; it registers no media type.

gaps.name: PIDF-LO / GEOPRIV location object
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for presence-based location objects. The geolocation topic is the closest fit, and a PIDF-LO tech tag would help. PIDF exists only as a child of instant messaging, and I tagged it with an id that I could not confirm in the taxonomy.

RFC4120.title: The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)
RFC4120.summary: RFC 4120 specifies Version 5 of the Kerberos network authentication protocol, including the AS, TGS and client/server exchanges, ticket formats, ASN.1 message definitions, naming conventions, KDC transport and DNS SRV-based KDC discovery, and interoperability requirements, obsoleting RFC 1510.

Kerberos.why: The entire document specifies the Kerberos V5 protocol: exchanges, tickets, messages, constants and interoperability.
Kerberos.quote: This document provides an overview and specification of Version 5 of the Kerberos protocol, and it obsoletes RFC 1510

rejected.why: GSS-API is mentioned only as an application interface and for the separate Kerberos mechanism in RFC 4121; this document does not specify it.
ASN.1/DER is the notation and encoding used to define the messages; the document is not about ASN.1 itself, though it gives compatibility notes.
DNS SRV records are used for KDC discovery in a short subsection (7.2.3); DNS is a substrate here and the document defines no new DNS record type.
UDP and TCP are only transports for KDC messaging (7.2); the document does not specify or analyse them.
The generic authentication topic is implied by the Kerberos tag, which is already the more specific tag.
AES-based encryption types are required only by reference to RFC 3961 and RFC 3962; the document does not specify them.

gaps.name: Kerberos
gaps.why: The taxonomy contains Kerberos as a technology under security, but the tag list shown uses the id 'Kerberos'. If this id is not accepted by the validator, no alternative fits as precisely.

RFC4121.title: The Kerberos Version 5 Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Mechanism: Version 2
RFC4121.summary: RFC 4121 defines version 2 of the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism, specifying context establishment tokens, new per-message MIC/Wrap token formats based on the Kerberos crypto framework, and related parameters, updating RFC 1964.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies a GSS-API mechanism: token formats, channel bindings, minor status codes and buffer sizes for GSS-API calls.
GSS-API.quote: This document defines protocols, procedures, and conventions to be employed by peers implementing the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) when using the Kerberos Version 5 mechanism.

Kerberos.why: It defines the Kerberos V5 mechanism, using Kerberos AP-REQ/AP-REP/KRB-ERROR messages, session keys, subkeys and key usages derived under the Kerberos cryptosystem framework.
Kerberos.quote: The approach taken in this document obviates the need for algorithm identifiers. This is accomplished by using the same encryption algorithm, specified by the crypto profile [RFC3961]

rejected.why: Only a pseudo-ASN.1 framing structure is used for tokens; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
MD5 is merely used to hash channel bindings, not the subject of the document.
RFC 2478 is mentioned only as a possible negotiation mechanism for backwards compatibility.
AES is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an example enctype.
Key derivation for per-message tokens is a part of the Kerberos mechanism, already covered by the Kerberos tag.

RFC4122.title: A Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) URN Namespace
RFC4122.summary: Defines the UUID (GUID) URN namespace, the 128-bit UUID format, its versions (time-based, name-based with MD5/SHA-1, random), generation algorithms, and a sample implementation.

UUID.why: The whole document specifies the UUID format, versions, string representation, and generation algorithms, plus its URN namespace registration.
UUID.quote: This specification defines a Uniform Resource Name namespace for UUIDs (Universally Unique IDentifier), also known as GUIDs (Globally Unique IDentifier).

URN.why: The document registers the urn:uuid namespace, giving syntax, equivalence rules, persistence and resolution considerations, so URN namespace readers would want it.
URN.quote: Namespace ID:  UUID

rejected.why: MD5 is only one hash option for version 3 name-based UUIDs; it is not the subject.
SHA-1 is used as the hash for version 5 UUIDs; it is a building block, not the subject.
Random number generation is used for version 4 UUIDs and node IDs but only referenced via RFC 4086; not the subject.
ABNF is only used to write the UUID string grammar.
DNS names appear only as an example name space for name-based UUIDs.
The namespace registration template is a URN registration, not IANA registry guidance.

RFC4123.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)-H.323 Interworking Requirements
RFC4123.summary: Informational document specifying requirements for a SIP-H.323 Interworking Function (IWF) that translates call signalling, addressing, capability negotiation and registration between SIP and H.323 networks.

H.323.why: The document exists to define requirements for interworking H.323 with SIP, covering gatekeepers, RAS, H.225.0, H.245 and Fast Connect mapping.
H.323.quote: The SIP-H.323 Interworking function (IWF) converts between SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) [RFC3261] and the ITU Recommendation H.323 protocol [H.323].

SIP.why: SIP is one of the two protocols being interworked, with requirements on registration, address resolution, call flows, and sips/TLS handling.
SIP.quote: The IWF also acts as a SIP user agent client and server.

rejected.why: SDP is mentioned only for capability mapping with H.245; it is not specified or extended here.
RTP is assumed as the common media transport and the IWF does not process media.
This is IP-to-IP interworking between SIP and H.323, not PSTN interworking; TGREP and DTMF are mentioned only in passing.
TRIP/TGREP is only one example of an address translation method.
DNS SRV is only referenced for server location, not specified here.
SIP-over-TLS is mentioned only in security considerations as a matching requirement.

RFC4124.title: Protocol Extensions for Support of Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC4124.summary: Specifies IGP (OSPF/IS-IS) and RSVP-TE protocol extensions, including the Bandwidth Constraints sub-TLV and the CLASSTYPE object, to support Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering.

RSVP-TE.why: Defines the new CLASSTYPE RSVP object, its handling in Path messages and the new Diffserv-aware TE error code and values.
RSVP-TE.quote: This also includes extensions to RSVP-TE signaling beyond those already specified in RFC 3209 for existing MPLS Traffic Engineering.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document is about DS-TE: Class-Types, TE-Classes, bandwidth constraints, preemption and admission control.
traffic engineering.quote: This document specifies the protocol extensions for support of Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE).

OSPF.why: Defines a new OSPFv2 TE sub-TLV and generalizes the semantics of existing OSPF-TE sub-TLVs.
OSPF.quote: With OSPF, the sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the "Link TLV" and its sub-TLV type is 17.

IS-IS.why: Defines a new IS-IS TE sub-TLV and generalizes existing IS-IS TE sub-TLV semantics.
IS-IS.quote: With ISIS, the sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the "extended IS reachability TLV" and its sub-TLV type is 22.

Diffserv.why: DS-TE ties Class-Types to Diffserv PSCs/PHBs, with consistency checks against the DIFFSERV object and scheduler adjustment.
Diffserv.quote: DS-TE has capabilities for traffic that Diffserv does not:  Diffserv does not indicate preemption, by intent

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific RSVP-TE and traffic engineering tags.
Diffserv is the more specific tag; the document does not address QoS architecture generally.
RSVP-TE is the more specific tag; plain RSVP is only extended via an optional object for LSP tunnels.
Mentioned only as an extension that must interoperate with DS-TE, not a subject of the document.
IANA Considerations is boilerplate, so it is not evidence of subject.

RFC4125.title: Maximum Allocation Bandwidth Constraints Model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC4125.summary: RFC 4125 specifies the Maximum Allocation Model (MAM), a bandwidth constraints model for Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering that sets per-Class-Type bandwidth limits and an aggregate cap on a link.

traffic engineering.why: The document defines a bandwidth constraints model for DS-TE: per-Class-Type constraints, Max Reservable Bandwidth, TE-Class unreserved bandwidth, and preemption. This is traffic engineering admission control and bandwidth allocation.
traffic engineering.quote: This document provides specifications for one Bandwidth Constraints Model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering, which is referred to as the Maximum Allocation Model.

rejected.why: LSPs and MPLS TE are the setting, but the document is about the bandwidth constraints model, not MPLS architecture or encapsulation.
The signalling extensions that carry MAM are specified in RFC 4124 (DSTE-PROTO). This document only defines the model.
Diffserv classes motivate Class-Types, but the document does not specify or extend Diffserv itself.
The model supports QoS objectives, but the document is limited to a TE bandwidth allocation model.
Shared Mesh Restoration from GMPLS recovery is mentioned only for compatibility.

gaps.name: Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) Bandwidth Constraints Models
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DS-TE tag. The closest fit is the traffic engineering topic, which covers the subject only generally. A DS-TE tag would also collect RFC 3564, 4124, 4127 and 4128.

RFC4126.title: Max Allocation with Reservation Bandwidth Constraints Model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering & Performance Comparisons
RFC4126.summary: Specifies the Maximum Allocation with Reservation (MAR) Bandwidth Constraints Model for Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering, with examples and simulation-based performance comparison against MAM and no-DSTE.

traffic engineering.why: The document defines a DS-TE bandwidth constraints model for allocating link bandwidth to class types in MPLS traffic engineering, and analyses its performance. No more specific tag exists for DS-TE bandwidth constraints models.
traffic engineering.quote: giving a functional specification for the Maximum Allocation with Reservation (MAR) Bandwidth Constraints Model

Diffserv.why: The model is about Diffserv-aware TE: class types, per-class bandwidth allocation, priorities and QoS protection. Readers of Diffserv would want it.
Diffserv.quote: Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering (DS-TE) requirements and protocol extensions are specified in [DSTE-REQ, DSTE-PROTO].

rejected.why: MPLS is the setting for the model, but the document is about the bandwidth allocation model and not about MPLS architecture or encapsulation.
It is mentioned only as the mechanism the LER uses to check link bandwidth. The document does not specify or extend it.
