Protection against QoS degradation is an objective, but the subject is bandwidth constraints for TE. The Diffserv tag already covers the QoS aspect.
The simulation comparisons serve to evaluate the model. They are not network performance measurement methods.
OSPF-TE and the IGP are referenced only in passing for advertised unreserved bandwidth. The document adds no IGP extensions.

gaps.name: Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) Bandwidth Constraints Models
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DS-TE or its bandwidth constraints models (MAM, RDM, MAR). RFCs 4125, 4127 and 4128 would fit the same tag, so a dedicated DS-TE tag under traffic engineering would help.

RFC4127.title: Russian Dolls Bandwidth Constraints Model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC4127.summary: Specifies the Russian Dolls Model (RDM), a nested bandwidth constraints model for Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering, including its constraint definitions, example unreserved-bandwidth formulas, and usage scenarios.

traffic engineering.why: The document defines a bandwidth constraints model for DS-TE, governing per-class-type bandwidth allocation, admission control and preemption on TE LSPs. This is traffic engineering of MPLS networks. No more specific technology tag (RSVP-TE, PCE) is specified here, so the topic tag applies directly.
traffic engineering.quote: This document provides specifications for one Bandwidth Constraints Model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering, which is referred to as the Russian Dolls Model.

Diffserv.why: The model is for Diffserv-aware TE, with Class-Types mapped to Diffserv classes and PHBs. A substantial part of the document covers how bandwidth constraints per class relate to Diffserv, so Diffserv readers would want it.
Diffserv.quote: the Russian Dolls Bandwidth Constraints Model can be used to support each of the scenarios described in [DSTE-REQ].

rejected.why: MPLS is the environment, but the document defines a bandwidth model, not MPLS architecture or encapsulation. Traffic engineering covers the subject.
The signalling extensions are defined in RFC 4124 (DSTE-PROTO). This document only references them and defines the model.
Diffserv is the more specific tag, and the document is about TE bandwidth constraints rather than QoS architectures in general.
The IGP sub-TLV is mentioned only briefly in Section 6, and the extensions themselves are defined elsewhere.
The IGP sub-TLV is mentioned only briefly in Section 6, and the extensions themselves are defined elsewhere.
Shared Mesh Restoration from GMPLS recovery is mentioned only for compatibility in the definitions.

gaps.name: Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) bandwidth constraints models
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DS-TE tag. A reader looking for the RDM and MAM bandwidth constraints models would have to find them under traffic engineering and Diffserv.

RFC4128.title: Bandwidth Constraints Models for Differentiated Services (Diffserv)-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering: Performance Evaluation
RFC4128.summary: Informational RFC presenting a Markov-chain performance evaluation of the Maximum Allocation and Russian Dolls bandwidth constraints models for Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering, comparing LSP blocking and preemption under normal load, overload, partial preemption, pure blocking and complete sharing.

traffic engineering.why: The document evaluates bandwidth constraints models for DS-TE, covering per-class LSP admission, bandwidth allocation and preemption. This is traffic engineering of MPLS networks, and no more specific child tag fits, since it is not RSVP-TE or PCE.
traffic engineering.quote: presenting the results of a performance evaluation of these two models under various operational conditions: normal load, overload, preemption fully or partially enabled

MPLS.why: The analysis concerns LSP establishment, blocking and preemption on MPLS links, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: Differentiated Services (Diffserv)-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) mechanisms operate on the basis of different Diffserv classes of traffic

Diffserv.why: The bandwidth constraints are enforced per Diffserv class (Class-Type), and the document discusses how LSP admission interacts with the Diffserv scheduler's QoS objectives.
Diffserv.quote: To achieve per-class traffic engineering, rather than on an aggregate basis across all classes, DS-TE enforces different Bandwidth Constraints (BCs) on different classes.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is only cited in the references and the security section, and the document does not specify or analyse its signalling.
Diffserv is the more specific tag, and the document is about LSP-level bandwidth admission rather than QoS architectures generally.
The document is an analytical model of blocking and preemption probabilities, not network measurement metrics or methods.

gaps.name: Diffserv-aware MPLS TE (DS-TE) bandwidth constraints models
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DS-TE or for the MAM and RDM bandwidth constraints models. The closest fit is a combination of the traffic engineering, MPLS and Diffserv tags.

RFC4129.title: Digital Private Network Signaling System (DPNSS)/Digital Access Signaling System 2 (DASS 2) Extensions to the IUA Protocol
RFC4129.summary: Defines DUA, an extension of the IUA protocol (RFC 3057) for backhauling DPNSS 1 and DASS 2 signalling between a Signaling Gateway and Media Gateway Controller over SCTP/IP, with a new message class, DLCI format, DLC status messages, error codes and message sequences.

SIGTRAN.why: The document is a SIGTRAN user adaptation layer (DUA) extending IUA to carry DPNSS/DASS 2 signalling between an SG and an MGC over IP.
SIGTRAN.quote: defines a mechanism for backhauling Digital Private Network Signaling System 1 (DPNSS 1) and Digital Access Signaling System 2 (DASS 2) messages over IP

rejected.why: SCTP is only the transport; the document just assigns a payload protocol ID and does not define anything new about SCTP itself.
IUA is ISDN-based, but DUA targets DPNSS/DASS 2, not ISDN access. ISDN-specific features are explicitly marked invalid.
This is the parent of SIGTRAN, which is the more specific tag and already covers the document.
The IANA section only records a payload protocol ID assignment, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: DPNSS/DASS 2 (private PBX signalling)
gaps.why: The document is about backhauling these PBX signalling protocols, but the taxonomy has no tag for them. SIGTRAN is the closest fit.

RFC4130.title: MIME-Based Secure Peer-to-Peer Business Data Interchange Using HTTP, Applicability Statement 2 (AS2)
RFC4130.summary: RFC 4130 (AS2) is an applicability statement defining how to exchange EDI/XML business data securely over HTTP using MIME, S/MIME signing/encryption, and signed (a)synchronous MDN receipts for non-repudiation of receipt.

EDI.why: The document is the AS2 applicability statement for EDI/business data interchange over HTTP, the HTTP counterpart of AS1 (RFC 3335).
EDI.quote: describes how to exchange structured business data securely using the HTTP transfer protocol

S/MIME.why: Defines how S/MIME signing and encryption structures are applied to AS2 messages and signed MDNs, a substantial part of the specification.
S/MIME.quote: Authentication and data confidentiality are obtained by using Cryptographic Message Syntax with S/MIME security body parts.

HTTP.why: Defines new AS2-Version, AS2-From, AS2-To headers and HTTP POST usage, status codes and error recovery for AS2.
HTTP.quote: The following headers are to be included in all AS2 messages and all AS2 MDNs

MIME.why: Specifies the MIME structure of AS2 messages and MDNs (multipart/signed, multipart/report, EDI content types).
MIME.quote: The data is packaged using standard MIME structures.

rejected.why: MDN and MIME formats derive from email, but this document is about HTTP transport; SMTP is only mentioned as an alternative.
SMTP variant is AS1 (RFC 3335); only referenced for async MDNs.
HTTPS/TLS only mentioned as an optional transport; not specified.
Certificates are required but handled as a trading-partner setup matter, not profiled.
B2B data exchange is covered more specifically by EDI.
Lists required content types but does not register new media types.

RFC4131.title: Management Information Base for Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS) Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems for Baseline Privacy Plus
RFC4131.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module (DOCS-IETF-BPI2-MIB) for SNMP management of DOCSIS Baseline Privacy Plus (key exchange, certificate authentication, multicast encryption, secure software download) on cable modems and CMTSs.

DOCSIS.why: The MIB manages DOCSIS cable modems and CMTSs' Baseline Privacy Plus, so readers of DOCSIS cable access networks need it.
DOCSIS.quote: defines a set of managed objects for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) based management of the Baseline Privacy Plus features of DOCSIS 1.1 and DOCSIS 2.0

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module definition with tables, textual conventions and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This MIB module (BPI+ MIB) provides a set of objects required for the management of the Baseline Privacy Interface Plus features

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Certificates are carried in tables as DER blobs, but the document does not profile X.509.
IP multicast address to SAID mapping tables are only a part of the security MIB; the document is not about multicast routing.
Key exchange state and counters are managed, but the document is not a key management protocol specification.
DES and AES appear only as enumerated algorithm values and in security considerations.
IPv6 is mentioned only for netmask and address type handling.

RFC4132.title: Addition of Camellia Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC4132.summary: Defines twelve TLS cipher suites using the Camellia block cipher in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA-1 and various RSA/DH key exchanges, with 128- and 256-bit keys.

Camellia.why: The document exists to add Camellia-based cipher suites to TLS; Camellia and its use in TLS is the tag's exact subject.
Camellia.quote: to support the Camellia encryption algorithm as a bulk cipher algorithm

TLS.why: It extends TLS by registering new cipher suite code points and defining their cipher, hash and key exchange, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: proposes the addition of new cipher suites to the TLS protocol [TLS]

rejected.why: AES is only mentioned as a comparison point and for the AES-TLS precedent; the document does not specify AES.
HMAC-SHA-1 is just the MAC used per the TLS spec, not something the document defines or profiles.
SHA-1 is used only as the MAC hash by reference; the document says nothing new about it.
RSA is only a key exchange option in the suite names, defined by TLS itself.
CMS is mentioned only in a reference to another Camellia RFC.

RFC4133.title: Entity MIB (Version 3)
RFC4133.summary: Defines version 3 of the Entity MIB module, SNMP managed objects for representing multiple physical and logical entities, their containment and mappings, managed by a single agent, obsoleting RFC 2737.

MIB.why: The document specifies the ENTITY-MIB module in SMIv2, with tables, textual conventions and compliance statements, so it belongs on the MIB modules page.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing multiple logical and physical entities managed by a single SNMP agent.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through. The document defines a MIB module and does not extend the protocol, so the more specific MIB tag fits.
entPhysicalUris holds URIs (CLEI URNs), but this is a small use of existing URI syntax and does not define anything new about URIs.
The CLEI URN namespace is defined in RFC 4152 and only used here as an example value.
Ethernet and repeater devices appear only in the usage examples.

RFC4134.title: Examples of S/MIME Messages
RFC4134.summary: Informational RFC giving worked examples of CMS objects (signed, enveloped, digested, encrypted data) and S/MIME messages, with test keys, certificates and CRLs, to aid interoperability.

S/MIME.why: The document exists to provide S/MIME message examples, including MIME formatting for multipart/signed and application/pkcs7-mime messages.
S/MIME.quote: This document gives examples of message bodies formatted using S/MIME.

CMS.why: Most examples are CMS ContentInfo, SignedData, EnvelopedData, DigestedData and EncryptedData structures, so CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: Specifically, it has examples of Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) objects and S/MIME messages (including the MIME formatting).

rejected.why: Certificates and CRLs are included only as test constants used by the CMS examples. The document says it explicitly does not cover PKIX examples.
MIME headers appear only in the few S/MIME message examples, as the transport wrapper. The document is not about MIME itself.
ASN.1 dumps are the presentation format for the examples. The document is not about ASN.1.
Triple-DES and RC2 are used only as algorithms in the example EnvelopedData and EncryptedData objects.
RSA and DSS are used for the example signatures and key transport. They are not the subject of the document.
Base64 is used only as the encoding for the binaries in the appendix and the MIME bodies.

RFC4135.title: Goals of Detecting Network Attachment in IPv6
RFC4135.summary: Informational RFC from the DNA working group stating the problems in detecting network attachment (link change) in IPv6 and listing ten goals (G1-G10) that DNA solutions should meet.

IPv6.why: The document defines goals for detecting link change and validity of IP configuration for IPv6 hosts, which is IPv6 host attachment and configuration behaviour.
IPv6.quote: This document considers the DNA procedure only from the IPv6 point of view, unless explicitly mentioned otherwise.

neighbor discovery.why: Much of the problem analysis concerns Router Advertisement/Solicitation behaviour, link-local router addresses, and ND random delays, and goals reference NS/NA, RS/RA and SEND compatibility.
neighbor discovery.quote: The DNA process is intimately related to the Neighbor Discovery protocol [1]

rejected.why: Only referenced in goal G7 as something DNA schemes should be compatible with; the document is not about SEND.
Mentioned only as defining RA interval timer expiry as a hint; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only to say actual configuration retrieval is out of DNA scope.
Mobility motivates rapid detection but the document is about link change detection, not mobility protocols.
Address configuration is explicitly out of scope; DNA only decides whether configuration is still valid.

gaps.name: Detecting Network Attachment (DNA)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is detecting link change/network attachment, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy; it is closest to IPv6 and neighbor discovery.

RFC4136.title: OSPF Refresh and Flooding Reduction in Stable Topologies
RFC4136.summary: Informational RFC extending OSPF to reduce periodic LSA refresh flooding in stable topologies by generalizing use of DoNotAge LSAs, with configuration parameters for flooding reduction.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF flooding and refresh behaviour, defining new router behaviour, backward compatibility and configuration parameters.
OSPF.quote: This document describes an extension to the OSPF protocol to reduce periodic flooding of Link State Advertisements (LSAs) in stable topologies.

rejected.why: The document concerns OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328) and the demand circuit extensions, not OSPF for IPv6.
The document addresses scalability of one protocol, OSPF, and is covered by the OSPF tag rather than general routing architecture.

RFC4137.title: State Machines for Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Peer and Authenticator
RFC4137.summary: Informational RFC giving illustrative state machines for the EAP peer, stand-alone authenticator, AAA backend authenticator and full/pass-through authenticator, based on the EAP Switch model and RFCs 3748 and 3579.

EAP.why: The whole document specifies how EAP peers and authenticators can be implemented as state machines, including the Switch model and method interface.
EAP.quote: This document describes a set of state machines for Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) peer, EAP stand-alone authenticator (non-pass-through), EAP backend authenticator

AAA.why: Substantial parts (Sections 6 and 7) cover the backend authenticator on AAA servers and pass-through operation over an AAA interface.
AAA.quote: The backend and full/pass-through authenticators illustrate how EAP/AAA protocol support defined in RFC 3579 may be implemented.

rejected.why: RADIUS appears only as the example AAA protocol and in RFC 3579 references; the document does not specify RADIUS itself.
PPP is mentioned only as an example lower layer for peer-to-peer operation.
Not a taxonomy tag; state machine notation is just the presentation form.

RFC4138.title: Forward RTO-Recovery (F-RTO): An Algorithm for Detecting Spurious Retransmission Timeouts with TCP and the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
RFC4138.summary: Specifies F-RTO, a TCP sender-only algorithm (with a SACK-enhanced variant, also applicable to SCTP) for detecting spurious retransmission timeouts and avoiding unnecessary retransmissions.

TCP.why: The document defines a TCP sender-side algorithm modifying RTO recovery behaviour, with a SACK-enhanced variant.
TCP.quote: This document describes the F-RTO detection algorithm for detecting spurious TCP retransmission timeouts.

SCTP.why: Section 5 is dedicated to applying F-RTO to SCTP, covering multi-homing and chunk bundling considerations.
SCTP.quote: The F-RTO algorithm can also be applied to the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)

rejected.why: The document explicitly leaves the response to spurious timeouts (congestion window reversion) unspecified; it is about detection, and congestion control is only discussed as consequences.
NewReno is referenced for its recover variable and fast recovery interaction but is not specified or extended here.

RFC4139.title: Requirements for Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Signaling Usage and Extensions for Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON)
RFC4139.summary: Informational requirements document describing what GMPLS signaling (RSVP-TE based) must support for ITU-T ASON: soft permanent connections, call/connection separation, call segments, restart, extended label association, crankback, extra errors, and backward compatibility.

GMPLS.why: The whole document sets requirements for GMPLS signaling extensions to support ASON, so it belongs on the GMPLS page.
GMPLS.quote: It identifies the features to be covered by the GMPLS signaling protocol to support the capabilities of an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON).

rejected.why: RFC 3473 RSVP-TE is the signaling protocol relied on, but the document states requirements at the functional level and does not specify RSVP-TE extensions.
SONET/SDH appears only as an example data plane for the label association scenario; the document is not about IP over SONET.
The RSVP-TE/TE aspects are implicit; the document is about optical control plane signaling, which GMPLS covers.
Control plane restart and failure recovery requirements are part of the signaling requirements, not an OAM mechanism.

gaps.name: Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is the ITU-T ASON control plane architecture (UNI, E-NNI, I-NNI, call/connection separation), and the taxonomy has no optical or transport network control tag besides GMPLS.

gaps.name: Crankback
gaps.why: Crankback signaling is a substantial section (4.6) but has no dedicated tag.

RFC4140.title: Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 Mobility Management (HMIPv6)
RFC4140.summary: Defines Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 (HMIPv6), adding a Mobility Anchor Point acting as a local home agent, a local Binding Update M flag, and a Neighbour Discovery MAP option to reduce handover signalling.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document extends Mobile IPv6 with a MAP (local home agent), local binding updates with the M flag, and RCoA/LCoA handling. It is the core subject.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document introduces extensions to Mobile IPv6 and IPv6 Neighbour Discovery to allow for local mobility handling.

neighbor discovery.why: It defines a new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement option (type 23) used for MAP discovery. This is a substantial part of the specification.
neighbor discovery.quote: Neighbour Discovery Extension: The MAP Option Message Format
neighbor discovery.section: 5. Neighbour Discovery Extension: The MAP Option Message Format

rejected.why: AH/ESP and IKE only secure MN-MAP binding updates, in Security Considerations. They are a security mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
This is the parent of Mobile IPv6. The child tag fits, so the parent is not listed.
IPv6 is the substrate. The document is about mobility extensions, not IPv6 itself.
It is mentioned only as a possible future way to recover from MAP failures.
It is used only to establish the MN-MAP security association and is not specified here.

gaps.name: Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6)
gaps.why: Appendix A discusses integrating Fast Handovers with HMIPv6, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. It is only an appendix, so it is not a main subject here.

RFC4141.title: SMTP and MIME Extensions for Content Conversion
RFC4141.summary: Defines two ESMTP extensions (CONPERM, CONNEG) and MIME header fields (Content-Convert, Content-Previous, with Content-Features) enabling authorized, accountable content-form conversion by mail intermediaries.

SMTP.why: The document defines the CONPERM and CONNEG SMTP service extensions with MAIL-FROM and RCPT-TO parameters and relay behaviour.
SMTP.quote: This specification integrates two ESMTP extensions and three MIME content header fields, which defines a cooperative service that permits authorized, accountable content form conversion

MIME.why: It defines new MIME body-part header fields (Content-Convert, Content-Previous) and uses Content-Features to record conversion guidance and history.
MIME.quote: Content-Convert is a header field that specifies preferred conversions for the associated content.

rejected.why: Related to media feature negotiation, but the document's own subject is intermediary conversion; the feature syntax is borrowed from RFC 2533/2912.
Examples use IFAX/TIFF-FX, but fax is only the illustrative case; the mechanism is general.
RFC 3238 is cited informatively only; this is not an OPES specification.
Header fields are defined, but they are MIME body-part headers rather than Internet message format headers.
Appendix C registers header fields, not media types.

RFC4142.title: Full-mode Fax Profile for Internet Mail (FFPIM)
RFC4142.summary: RFC 4142 defines the "full mode" fax profile for Internet mail, extending simple and extended mode fax with mandatory content negotiation (UA-based and optional ESMTP CONNEG) and enhanced TIFF content format.

fax.why: The document is the full-mode fax profile for Internet mail, exactly what the fax subject covers.
fax.quote: This specification defines "full mode" carriage of facsimile data over the Internet, building upon previous work in A Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail

content negotiation.why: A substantial part of the document specifies UA-based and ESMTP-based content/capability negotiation for fax.
content negotiation.quote: Implementations that are conformant to FFPIM MUST support content negotiation as described there.

rejected.why: ESMTP CONNEG is referenced from RFC 4141 as a negotiation mechanism; the document does not specify SMTP itself.
Mail is the substrate for the fax profile; the more specific fax tag covers the subject.
TIFF content is mentioned but MIME structure is defined in other RFCs, not here.
RFC 3238 is cited only in a note about intermediaries' risk.

RFC4143.title: Facsimile Using Internet Mail (IFAX) Service of ENUM
RFC4143.summary: Registers the ENUM NAPTR service "E2U+ifax" with a mailto URI so a telephone number can be resolved via DNS to the email address of an Internet fax (IFax) system.

ENUM.why: The document defines a new ENUM NAPTR service registration (E2U+ifax) mapping E.164 numbers to mailto URIs.
ENUM.quote: An IFax client makes a [ENUMbis] DNS query, using the target system's telephone number. The returned NAPTR record specifies an email address

fax.why: The service lets email-based Internet fax use telephone numbers to locate the recipient, so fax readers would want this RFC.
fax.quote: IFax is "facsimile using Internet mail".

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate for the ENUM lookup. The document defines only a NAPTR service registration, not DNS behaviour.
The mailto address is just the result of the lookup. Fax over mail is specified in other RFCs, and this one only references them.
The mailto scheme is used as the target of the NAPTR record, but nothing new is defined about URIs.
The Security Considerations mention junk faxes and harvesting, but this is boilerplate-level discussion, not the subject of the document.
The registration is the core content, but it is covered by the ENUM tag. The IANA section itself is boilerplate.

RFC4144.title: How to Gain Prominence and Influence in Standards Organizations
RFC4144.summary: An Independent-stream informational memo giving practical, non-technical advice (attend, sit up front, socialize, volunteer, learn the traditions) for newcomers who want to gain prominence and influence in standards organizations.

IETF process.why: The document is newcomer guidance on participating in standards bodies: meetings, working group chairs and editors, procedures and traditions. That is the closest taxonomy subject, even though the advice is not specific to the IETF.
IETF process.quote: following some simple guidelines can greatly accelerate the rate at which you will become favorably known in an organization.

rejected.why: It is a guide of sorts, but it is not an FYI-series introduction for Internet users. It is advice on organizational behaviour.
It mentions being selected for positions such as chair or editor, but it says nothing about NomCom procedures.
It is published as an RFC but says nothing about the RFC series itself.

gaps.name: Standards organization participation / social dynamics
gaps.why: The document is about how individuals gain influence in standards bodies generally. The taxonomy has no tag for participant guidance or community culture, so IETF process is only an approximate fit.

RFC4145.title: TCP-Based Media Transport in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC4145.summary: RFC 4145 defines how SDP describes TCP-based media: a new 'TCP' proto identifier, the 'setup' attribute for connection initiation roles, and the 'connection' attribute for reusing or re-establishing connections, negotiated via offer/answer.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new proto value and two new attributes, and specifies their offer/answer negotiation.
SDP.quote: This document describes how to express media transport over TCP using the Session Description Protocol (SDP).

TCP.why: A substantial part covers TCP connection setup, reestablishment and termination as signalled in SDP. This is how TCP is described and managed, not a change to TCP itself, so it is secondary.
TCP.quote: Media described using an 'm' line containing the 'TCP' protocol identifier are carried using TCP [1].

rejected.why: SIP is only one of several carriers of SDP, mentioned for examples and security. The document is not about SIP.
Considered because it carries media over TCP. The document defines SDP signalling for TCP, not a binding of a protocol over a transport.
The IANA section mentions MIME registration for formats, but only as boilerplate guidance.
T.38 fax appears only in the examples.

RFC4146.title: Simple New Mail Notification
RFC4146.summary: Documents the long-standing "notify mail" technique where a mail server sends the string "nm_notifyuser" CRLF to port 79 on a user's client to signal new mail.

email.why: The document specifies a new-mail notification mechanism from mail servers to mail clients, which is an email-system function not tied to SMTP, IMAP or POP3 specifically.
email.quote: allows users to be notified of new mail

rejected.why: Only the finger port (79) is borrowed; the document states the finger protocol itself is not used, and requires that no finger daemon be active.
TCP (or sometimes UDP) is just the substrate for sending the one-line message.
The notification prompts a client to fetch mail, but IMAP is not specified or extended here.
Mail fetching is only mentioned in passing; POP3 is not specified or extended here.
The IANA note about port 79 is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC4147.title: Proposed Changes to the Format of the IANA IPv6 Registry
RFC4147.summary: Proposes a revised format for the IANA IPv6 address space and global unicast assignment registries, aligning them with the current IPv6 addressing architecture (RFC 3513) and dropping TLA/sub-TLA terminology.

IANA.why: The document's whole purpose is to redefine the layout and content conventions of IANA registries, and it advises IANA to adopt them.
IANA.quote: This document proposes a revised format for the IANA IPv6 address registries.

addressing.why: The registry contents are the IPv6 address space allocation: prefix dispositions, RIR allocations, and reserved blocks. Readers of IP address architecture and allocation would want it.
addressing.quote: The IPv6 Unicast space encompasses the entire IPv6 address range with the exception of FF00::/8.

rejected.why: It concerns the registry format for IPv6 address space, not the specification of IPv6. Addressing is the more specific fit.
6to4 only appears as one registry entry (2002::/16) and is not specified or discussed.
The Security Considerations briefly mention using the registry as a trust point, but the body is not about routing security.
Only a passing remark about file signatures and certificates in Security Considerations; the document is not about RPKI.

RFC4148.title: IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) Metrics Registry
RFC4148.summary: Defines an IANA-administered registry (a MIB module of OBJECT-IDENTITYs) for IP Performance Metrics, registering the 33 IPPM WG metrics and setting rules for adding future metrics.

performance measurement.why: The document registers and identifies IPPM metrics (delay, loss, connectivity, delay variation) and defines how new ones are added, which is the performance measurement subject.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a registry for IP Performance Metrics (IPPM). It assigns and registers an initial set of OBJECT IDENTITIES to currently defined metrics in the IETF.

MIB.why: The registry is implemented as an SMIv2 MIB module of OBJECT-IDENTITYs for other MIB modules to reference, so MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: IANA-IPPM-METRICS-REGISTRY-MIB DEFINITIONS ::= BEGIN

rejected.why: The IANA registry is the mechanism, but the document is about the IPPM metrics registry content, not general IANA guidance or stewardship.
The MIB is accessed via SNMP, but the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour and no management objects.
The metrics concern network performance measurement, not benchmarking methodology for devices.

RFC4149.title: Definition of Managed Objects for Synthetic Sources for Performance Monitoring Algorithms
RFC4149.summary: Defines the SSPM-MIB, an SNMP MIB module for configuring synthetic sources (active probes) and sinks that inject packets for performance monitoring within the RMON/APM-MIB framework.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a MIB module (SSPM-MIB) in SMIv2 with source, sink and general groups, so the MIB subject page is where readers would look.
MIB.quote: In particular, it describes objects for configuring Synthetic Sources for Performance Monitoring (SSPM) algorithms.

performance measurement.why: The MIB configures active probes for one-way and round-trip performance measurement and relates to IPPM metrics, APM-MIB and TPM-MIB.
performance measurement.quote: remotely controlling synthetic sources (or 'active' probes) and sinks in order to enhance remote performance monitoring capabilities within IP networks and services

RMON.why: It is an RMON WG work item, placed under the rmon OID and designed to complement the RMON performance monitoring architecture.
RMON.quote: This is useful within the Remote Monitoring (RMON) framework [RFC3577] for performance monitoring

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
The OWDP one-way protocol is mentioned only as related work that the SSPM-MIB could replace for control purposes.
NTP stratum is only referenced in a textual convention for clock source.
The ping and traceroute MIBs are discussed only as related DISMAN work.
IPv4/IPv6 header fields such as flow label and loose source route are set in objects, but the document is not about IPv6.

RFC4150.title: Transport Performance Metrics MIB
RFC4150.summary: Defines the TPM-MIB, an RMON2 extension MIB module for monitoring sub-application transaction performance metrics (delay, loss, connect) with aggregated statistics, current reports and exception reports, as a drill-down to the APM-MIB.

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module (TPM-MIB) extending RMON2, defining tables, objects, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part concerns performance metrics (delay, loss, round-trip) referencing IPPM and ITU metrics, and statistical aggregation of them.
performance measurement.quote: it describes managed objects used for monitoring selectable performance metrics and statistics derived from the monitoring of network packets and sub-application level transactions.

rejected.why: The MIB extends RMON2 and is in the rmonmib WG, but it defines new performance-metric objects for transactions rather than specifying RMON itself; MIB tag covers it.
SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document does not specify SNMP.
Implied as an ancestor of the chosen tags.
Active measurement protocols are not specified; IPPM metrics are only referenced.
DNS transactions are merely examples of monitored sub-application transactions.

gaps.name: Application Performance Measurement / RMON2 monitoring
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RMON-family probes; RMON appears only as an entry under network management and is not available as a tag here.

RFC4151.title: The 'tag' URI Scheme
RFC4151.summary: Defines the 'tag' URI scheme, a non-resolvable URI scheme for globally unique, human-tractable identifiers minted from a domain name or email address plus a date, with syntax, minting rules and equality rules.

URI.why: The whole document specifies a new URI scheme: its syntax, minting rules, resolution (none) and equality comparison.
URI.quote: This document describes the "tag" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an existing identifier scheme that is hard for humans to read; the document is not about UUIDs.
Domain names are used as authority names in tags, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
The date component uses ISO 8601 formats (YYYY, YYYY-MM, YYYY-MM-DD), but this is a small part of the scheme definition, not a subject of the document.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the syntax.
Atom is listed in IANA considerations as an application that may use tag URIs; the document is not about it.
Tags are not URNs; URN namespaces are only mentioned in the reference to OIDs.

RFC4152.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Common Language Equipment Identifier (CLEI) Code
RFC4152.summary: Registers the "CLEI" URN namespace for Common Language Equipment Identifier codes, managed by Telcordia, using the RFC 3406 template.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration for CLEI. It gives the NID, syntax, uniqueness, persistence and resolution rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace (RFC 3406) for the assignment of the Common Language Equipment Identifier (CLEI) code

rejected.why: The IANA registration of the NID is boilerplate. The document is not about IANA registries or their guidance.
URN is the more specific child tag and already covers this document.

RFC4153.title: XML Voucher: Generic Voucher Language
RFC4153.summary: RFC 4153 defines an XML schema (the Voucher Component, namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:vts-lang) for describing voucher properties such as issuer, holder, value, merchandise and validity period, for use with a Voucher Trading System.

e-commerce.why: The document defines a language for vouchers (coupons, tickets, gift certificates) processed in payment and delivery transactions, which is an e-commerce subject. No more specific e-commerce tag fits, since it is not IOTP, ECML or CyberCash.
e-commerce.quote: A voucher can be used to transfer a wide range of electronic values, including coupons, tickets, loyalty points, and gift certificates

XML.why: The main body is an XML vocabulary with an XML Schema definition, namespace and element semantics, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: This document specifies rules for defining voucher properties in XML syntax.

rejected.why: The IANA section only registers an XML namespace and schema URN. That is boilerplate and not the subject.
The URN namespace is used only to name the XML namespace and schema, and the document defines nothing new about URNs.
TLS and IPsec are mentioned only as channels for protecting delivery of the Voucher Component, so they are substrate.
XML-Signature is only suggested as a way to secure the Voucher Component. The document does not specify or extend it.
IOTP appears only in the example coupon title and is not specified or profiled.

gaps.name: Voucher Trading System (VTS) / voucher language
gaps.why: The document is about generic electronic vouchers and the VTS. The taxonomy has no tag for voucher or trading systems, so e-commerce is the closest fit.

RFC4154.title: Voucher Trading System Application Programming Interface (VTS-API)
RFC4154.summary: RFC 4154 specifies the Java-syntax Voucher Trading System API (VTS-API), letting wallets and other applications issue, transfer, consume and present vouchers independent of VTS implementation.

e-commerce.why: The document defines an API for trading vouchers in payment and delivery transactions, which is an e-commerce/payment subject with no more specific tag in the taxonomy.
e-commerce.quote: The VTS is a system for securely transferring vouchers; e.g., coupons, tickets, loyalty points, and gift certificates.

rejected.why: Voucher components are XML documents (GVL), but this API only handles them as DOM objects; the XML format is defined in a separate RFC.
TLS is only recommended for securing login channels; not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only as a possible upper-layer branding negotiation mechanism.
Mentioned only as an optional negotiation standard; not the subject.
Only cited as an example of a directory service that could back a ParticipantRepository.
Login and authentication are implementation-specific and the document explicitly does not specify an authentication scheme.

gaps.name: Voucher Trading System (VTS)
gaps.why: The document's subject is voucher issuing, transfer and redemption; the taxonomy has only the generic e-commerce topic, not a VTS/voucher-specific tag.

RFC4155.title: The application/mbox Media Type
RFC4155.summary: Registers the application/mbox media type, with a "format" parameter and IANA registry, and defines a default mbox database format for storing and interchanging email messages as a file.

media types.why: The document's core purpose is a media type registration, including a format parameter and a new IANA registry of format values.
media types.quote: This memo requests that the application/mbox media type be authorized for allocation by the IESG, according to the terms specified in RFC 2048.

email.why: The mbox format is a mail storage format. The document defines its default format with separator lines and message terminators. Readers interested in email would want it.
email.quote: mbox databases typically contain a linear sequence of electronic mail messages.

rejected.why: MIME is the framework for the registration. The document does not extend MIME itself, so the more specific media types tag covers it.
The default format requires messages to follow RFC 2822. The document does not define or change the Internet message format itself.
The new format-parameter registry is a minor part of a media type registration. The document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC4156.title: The wais URI Scheme
RFC4156.summary: Historic RFC that copies the wais URI scheme definition from RFC 1738 so that RFC 1738 could be obsoleted, specifying wais:// URLs for WAIS databases, searches and documents.

URI.why: The document's purpose is to define a URI scheme, including its syntax forms and default port, so it belongs under URI.
URI.quote: This document specifies the wais Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme that was originally specified in RFC 1738.

WAIS.why: The scheme exists solely to address WAIS resources, and the document discusses WAIS types, document-ids and the protocol, so readers of WAIS would want it.
WAIS.quote: The WAIS URL scheme is used to designate WAIS databases, searches, or individual documents available from a WAIS database.

rejected.why: This is a URL scheme, not a URN namespace.
Nothing about internationalized identifiers is addressed.
WAIS is covered by its own tag. The document does not address directory access in general.

RFC4157.title: The prospero URI Scheme
RFC4157.summary: Re-specifies the historic prospero URI scheme (copied from RFC 1738) for resources accessed via the Prospero Directory Service, so RFC 1738 could be obsoleted.

URI.why: The document's sole purpose is defining a URI scheme, its syntax (host, port, hsoname, fields) and default port. No more specific URI child tag (URN, IRI) applies.
URI.quote: The prospero URL scheme is used to designate resources that are accessed through the Prospero Directory Service.

rejected.why: Prospero is a directory service, but the document only defines the URI scheme for it, not the directory protocol or its access. Prospero is also not in the taxonomy.
Prospero host-specific object names are opaque to the URL; the document does not address naming or name resolution generally.

gaps.name: Prospero Directory Service / Prospero protocol
gaps.why: The scheme exists to access resources through Prospero, a historic distributed directory and file naming system. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so readers looking for Prospero have no page.

RFC4158.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure: Certification Path Building
RFC4158.summary: Informational guidance for developers on building X.509 certification paths (forward/reverse, sorting and elimination optimizations, policy chaining, loop/dead-end avoidance, certificate and CRL retrieval, revocation signer paths).

PKI.why: The whole document is about building certification paths in PKIs, including trust anchors, cross-certification, bridge CAs and revocation signer paths. It is general PKI guidance, not a profile of the X.509 certificate format.
PKI.quote: This document provides guidance and recommendations to developers building X.509 public-key certification paths within their applications.

rejected.why: The document builds paths over X.509 certificates and discusses extensions such as AIA and basicConstraints. It does not define or profile the certificate format. The path validation it relies on lives in RFC 3280.
OCSP responder certificates and responses come up as revocation signers and in sorting criteria. OCSP itself is not specified or extended here.
Section 6.1 covers retrieving certificate attributes from LDAP directories. That is only one retrieval mechanism among several, and the document does not specify LDAP.
TLS and S/MIME appear only as application protocols that may carry certificates. The document does not address them.
HTTP is only one of several certificate and CRL retrieval transports, so it is just a substrate here.

RFC4159.title: Deprecation of "ip6.int"
RFC4159.summary: BCP advising that the DNS reverse-mapping domain "ip6.int" is deprecated for IPv6 implementations as of 1 September 2005 and that "ip6.arpa" should be used instead.

DNS.why: The document is about which DNS domain is used for IPv6 reverse mapping (address-to-name), deprecating ip6.int in favour of ip6.arpa. This is DNS operations and naming-tree usage.
DNS.quote: the DNS domain "ip6.int" should no longer be used to perform reverse mapping of IPv6 addresses to domain names, and that the domain "ip6.arpa" should be used henceforth

IPv6.why: The deprecation applies to standards-conformant IPv6 implementations, so IPv6 readers need to find it.
IPv6.quote: its use in IPv6 implementations that conform to the IPv6 Internet Standards is discontinued

rejected.why: The IANA Considerations section is only a short advisory note; the document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
ip6.int is a deprecated infrastructure reverse-mapping domain, not a special-use or reserved name in the sense of that tag.
The request to RIRs to stop maintaining delegations in ip6.int is incidental to the deprecation, not about registry or registrar protocols.

RFC4160.title: Internet Fax Gateway Requirements
RFC4160.summary: Informational RFC giving recommendations for Internet Fax gateways (onramp and offramp) between GSTN fax and store-and-forward email-based i-fax, covering addressing, image format conversion, authorization and error notification.

fax.why: The whole document specifies recommended behaviour of gateways between GSTN fax and email-based Internet Fax, which is exactly the fax subject.
fax.quote: To allow connectivity between the General Switched Telephone Network facsimile service (GSTN fax) and the e-mail-based Internet Fax service (i-fax) an "Internet Fax Gateway" is required.

rejected.why: Internet Fax is carried over email, but the document is about fax gateway functions, not email architecture or transport.
S/MIME is mentioned as one optional way to authorize users, and is not specified or profiled here.
Only mentioned as an alternative signature method for user authorization; not the subject.
The document only references the Internet message format for addr-spec definitions.
This is about GSTN fax gateways, but the more specific fax tag covers it; the document does not address telephony signalling or gateway control protocols.
Faxes are MIME messages, but MIME is only the substrate and is not discussed in its own right.

RFC4161.title: Guidelines for Optional Services for Internet Fax Gateways
RFC4161.summary: Informational guidelines for optional services of Internet Fax gateways (offramp and onramp) between GSTN fax and email-based i-fax, covering duplicate dropping, retransmission, return notices, logging, and DTMF/caller-ID authorization.

fax.why: The whole document specifies optional offramp/onramp gateway behaviour for Internet fax between GSTN fax and email-based i-fax.
fax.quote: This document provides guidelines for the optional functionality of Internet Fax Gateways.

rejected.why: SMTP envelope RCPT TO and Message-ID are used as mechanisms for duplicate detection, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Gateway to the GSTN is involved, but the document is about fax gateways, not SS7/media gateway control or telephony interworking; fax covers it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as not protecting across gateways.
Caller-ID, station ID and DTMF authorization are a small part of the document, fitting within the gateway services scope; not a substantial standalone treatment.
POP/IMAP only mentioned as a way the gateway retrieves messages.

RFC4162.title: Addition of SEED Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC4162.summary: Defines six TLS cipher suites using the SEED 128-bit block cipher in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA-1 and various RSA/DH key exchange methods.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS by registering new cipher suite code points, which is the core of the RFC.
TLS.quote: This document proposes the addition of new cipher suites to the TLS protocol [TLS] to support the SEED encryption algorithm as a bulk cipher algorithm.

cryptography.why: The document introduces the SEED block cipher and its use as a bulk cipher in an Internet protocol. No specific algorithm tag exists for SEED, so the parent cryptography topic fits.
cryptography.quote: SEED is a symmetric encryption algorithm that was developed by Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and a group of experts, beginning in 1998.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-1 is only the MAC specified by TLS for these suites; the document does not specify or analyse it.
SHA-1 is used only as the hash inside the TLS MAC and is not the subject of the document.
RSA is only one of the key exchange options named in the suites, not something the document specifies or extends.
AES cipher suites RFC is referenced only for security considerations and is not the subject.
The SEED CMS RFC is mentioned only as another submission of SEED, not as part of this document.

gaps.name: SEED block cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SEED tag, unlike AES, ARIA or Camellia, so the cipher falls back on the generic cryptography topic.

RFC4163.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Requirements on TCP/IP Header Compression
RFC4163.summary: Requirements document from the ROHC working group for a TCP/IP header compression profile, covering scope, performance, link-layer assumptions and IPR concerns.

ROHC.why: The whole document sets requirements for a ROHC TCP/IP compression profile, so readers of ROHC would expect it.
ROHC.quote: This document contains requirements on the TCP/IP header compression scheme (profile) to be developed by the RObust Header Compression (ROHC) Working Group.

TCP.why: A substantial part covers how TCP headers, options (SACK, Timestamp), flags and ECN bits must be compressed, and TCP behaviour under misordering and loss.
TCP.quote: The scheme must support compression of packets with any TCP option present, even if the option itself is not compressed.

rejected.why: CRTP covers IP/UDP/RTP compression over serial links; this document concerns TCP/IP and ROHC.
RFC 2507 is only a baseline for efficiency comparison, not the subject.
ECN bits are only a header field the scheme must compress efficiently.
IPsec headers are mentioned only as one case the scheme should handle.
Mobile IP headers are only one kind of header to support; the document is not about mobility.
The IPR section is a short requirement on the working group, not a subject of the document.

RFC4164.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Context Replication for ROHC Profiles
RFC4164.summary: Defines context replication for ROHC profiles, a mechanism letting a compressor and decompressor create a new header compression context from an existing base context, with the compressor and decompressor logic and the IR-CR packet format.

ROHC.why: The document extends ROHC (RFC 3095) with a new compressor state, decompressor logic, feedback handling and the IR-CR packet. ROHC is the technology it specifies.
ROHC.quote: Context replication is introduced to reduce the overhead of the context establishment procedure.

rejected.why: Short-lived TCP flows are the motivating use case and ROHC-TCP is referenced. The document does not specify TCP or TCP header compression itself.
It defines CRC-7 and CRC-8 polynomials for the IR-CR packet. These are small details of the ROHC mechanism, not the subject of the document.
This is the parent of ROHC, so it is implied by the ROHC tag and not listed separately.

RFC4165.title: Signaling System 7 (SS7) Message Transfer Part 2 (MTP2) - User Peer-to-Peer Adaptation Layer (M2PA)
RFC4165.summary: Defines M2PA, an adaptation layer that carries SS7 MTP3 signalling messages between IP Signaling Points over SCTP associations, replacing MTP2 with peer-to-peer link state, alignment, processor outage, flow control and changeover procedures.

SIGTRAN.why: M2PA is a SIGTRAN adaptation layer (M2PA) carrying SS7 MTP3 over SCTP/IP, which is exactly the SS7 signalling transport over IP that this tag covers.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document defines a protocol supporting the transport of Signaling System Number 7 (SS7) Message Transfer Part (MTP) Level 3 signaling messages over Internet Protocol (IP)

rejected.why: SCTP is the transport substrate M2PA runs over; the document uses its streams and notifications but does not specify or extend SCTP.
Parent of SIGTRAN, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Gateway control is not the subject. The document only mentions MGCs and signaling gateways as context.
The IANA section registers a port, a payload protocol identifier and the extension rules. This is boilerplate, not the main subject.

gaps.name: SS7 MTP3/MTP2 signalling (M2PA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SS7 itself, which is the subject the M2PA adaptation serves. SIGTRAN is the closest fit.

RFC4166.title: Telephony Signalling Transport over Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Applicability Statement
RFC4166.summary: Applicability statement describing how SCTP and the SIGTRAN user adaptation layers (IUA, V5UA, DUA, M2UA, M2PA, M3UA, SUA) transport telephony signalling over IP, with SCTP tuning guidance for signalling.

SIGTRAN.why: The whole document explains the SIGTRAN architecture and the applicability of each user adaptation layer (IUA, V5UA, DUA, M2UA, M2PA, M3UA, SUA).
SIGTRAN.quote: the whole architecture is called SIGTRAN (Signalling Transport) and is composed of a transport protocol (SCTP) and several User Adaptation Layers (UALs)

SCTP.why: Section 3 gives SCTP usage guidance for signalling: congestion control, RTO, heartbeat, retransmissions, bundling and stream usage.
SCTP.quote: Transport of telephony signalling requires special considerations. In order to use SCTP, an implementation must take special care to meet the performance, timing, and failure management requirements.
SCTP.section: 3. Issues for Transporting Telephony Signalling over SCTP

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the SIGTRAN tag, which is more specific.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as the recommended way to secure SIGTRAN; the document is not about it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations, as an option via RFC 3436.
Section 3.1 discusses SCTP congestion control for signalling, but it is a sub-point of SCTP usage and not a main subject.
MGC appears only as the role of the IP endpoint; gateway control protocols are not discussed.
ISDN Q.921/Q.931 are the signalling being carried via IUA, but the document is about transporting it over IP via SIGTRAN, not about ISDN access.

RFC4167.title: Graceful OSPF Restart Implementation Report
RFC4167.summary: An implementation report for Graceful OSPF Restart (RFC 3623), surveying eleven vendors' implementations, their differences, MIB objects, and a minimal set of test scenarios.

OSPF.why: The document reports on implementation experience of Graceful OSPF Restart, an extension to OSPF, covering interoperability, differences and test scenarios.
OSPF.quote: This document provides an implementation report for this extension to the base OSPF protocol.

rejected.why: Section 3 only references MIB objects added to the OSPF MIB; the document is not about MIB definitions.
BGP/MPLS VPNs are mentioned only as an example of extensions some vendors implemented.
Mentioned only in passing regarding MPLS VPN interaction.
It satisfies the RFC 1264 implementation report requirement, but the document is about OSPF graceful restart, not process.
Control/forwarding separation is the motivation, but the document is not about ForCES.

RFC4168.title: The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) as a Transport for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4168.summary: Specifies how SIP is carried over SCTP (and TLS over SCTP): benefits, the TLS-SCTP Via transport value, stream mapping rules, and the SIPS+D2S NAPTR service value.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new transport binding, defining the TLS-SCTP Via transport value, SIP transaction mapping and server location via NAPTR.
SIP.quote: This document specifies a mechanism for usage of SCTP (the Stream Control Transmission Protocol) as the transport mechanism between SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) entities.

SCTP.why: It specifies SCTP usage for SIP: stream selection, unordered delivery, payload protocol identifier and its advantages over TCP and UDP.
SCTP.quote: a SIP entity SHOULD send every SIP message (request or response) over stream zero with the unordered flag set.

rejected.why: TLS over SCTP (RFC 3436) is relied on for secure transport, but this document defines nothing new about TLS itself.

Fits somewhat, but the SIP and SCTP technology tags already cover the binding, and a topic tag is only given directly when no technology tag under it was chosen. SCTP is under transport, not under this topic.
The NAPTR service value is registered via DNS-based server location, but it is a minor part; the document does not define DNS behaviour.
TCP is compared against SCTP but is not the subject.

RFC4169.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Digest Authentication Using Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) Version-2
RFC4169.summary: Informational RFC defining the "AKAv2" algorithm version for HTTP Digest AKA (RFC 3310), which derives the Digest password from RES, IK and CK via HMAC-based PRF to resist man-in-the-middle and interleaving attacks in tunnelled authentication.

HTTP authentication.why: The document extends HTTP Digest authentication with a new AKA algorithm version, specifying password generation and session key derivation for Digest.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document specifies version 2 of the HTTP Digest AKA algorithm (RFC 3310).

rejected.why: TLS appears only as the tunnel in the man-in-the-middle attack discussion; nothing new is specified about TLS.
HMAC is used as the PRF but is only a building block, not the subject.
AKA comes from UMTS/3GPP, but the document specifies an HTTP Digest algorithm, not IP over cellular networks.
SIP is mentioned as an example HTTP-authentication-compatible protocol and for ABNF notation only.
EAP is mentioned only as an example context for the tunnelled authentication attack.
MD5 appears only as an example digest algorithm (AKAv2-MD5), not as the subject.

RFC4170.title: Tunneling Multiplexed Compressed RTP (TCRTP)
RFC4170.summary: Describes TCRTP, a BCP combining Enhanced CRTP header compression, PPP Multiplexing and L2TP tunneling to save bandwidth for many parallel RTP streams (e.g., voice trunking), with bandwidth analysis and negotiation examples.

CRTP.why: The document centres on using (Enhanced) CRTP compression of IP/UDP/RTP headers end-to-end, including ECRTP state synchronization and out-of-order handling.
CRTP.quote: Header compression is accomplished using Enhanced CRTP (ECRTP, [ECRTP]). ECRTP is an enhancement to classical CRTP [CRTP] that works better over long delay links

L2TP.why: L2TP is a core component of TCRTP; the document profiles its use, tunnel/session negotiation and overhead.
L2TP.quote: L2TP tunnels should be used to tunnel the ECRTP payloads end to end.

PPP.why: PPP Multiplexing, with LCP/IPCP negotiation, is one of the three combined protocols and the document specifies transmitter modifications for tunneling.
PPP.quote: [PPP-MUX] describes an encapsulation that combines multiple PPP payloads into one multiplexed payload.

RTP.why: The document is about carrying many RTP streams efficiently, with bandwidth analysis for voice and video RTP flows.
RTP.quote: improve the bandwidth utilization of RTP streams over network paths that carry multiple Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) streams in parallel

rejected.why: Only mentioned for contrast; ROHC is not what the document specifies.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible encryption profile.
ATM/AAL2/AAL5 appear in bandwidth comparisons only; the document is not about IP over ATM.
EF marking of tunnel headers is a brief subsection, not a substantial focus.
IPHC is cited only for IPCP negotiation; the document is about ECRTP, not RFC 2507.

RFC4171.title: Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS)
RFC4171.summary: RFC 4171 specifies the iSNS protocol (iSNSP), by which iSCSI and iFCP storage devices register with and query an iSNS server for discovery, discovery-domain login control, and state change notification.

iSCSI.why: iSNS is the name/discovery service for iSCSI devices, with iSCSI attributes, node types, and boot list features specified.
iSCSI.quote: facilitates automated discovery, management, and configuration of iSCSI and Fibre Channel devices (using iFCP gateways) on a TCP/IP network

rejected.why: The taxonomy has an iFCP tag only as a child of fibre channel, which is a child of storage, and I cannot tag it here without a clear fit; iFCP support is a major part of the document though. See gaps.
SLP is only one of several server discovery mechanisms and is referenced, not extended.
The iSNS MIB is only referenced and indexing requirements are brief.
IKE/IPsec is used as a security mechanism; only attribute carriage of policy is defined.
The DHCP option is defined in a separate RFC.
Considered, but the document specifies a registry/name service for storage, which the storage tags cover better.

gaps.name: iSNS (Internet Storage Name Service)
gaps.why: No tag exists for iSNS itself; the document is the iSNS protocol specification.

RFC4172.title: iFCP - A Protocol for Internet Fibre Channel Storage Networking
RFC4172.summary: RFC 4172 specifies iFCP, a gateway-to-gateway protocol that carries Fibre Channel frames over TCP/IP. It covers session management, frame encapsulation, address translation, link services, and security via IPsec/IKE, and it uses iSNS for discovery.

iFCP.why: The whole document defines the iFCP protocol: its network model, sessions, encapsulation, link service handling and fabric services.
iFCP.quote: iFCP is a gateway-to-gateway protocol that provides fibre channel fabric services to fibre channel devices over a TCP/IP network.

rejected.why: IPsec and IKE are the security mechanism iFCP relies on (Section 10), with profile requirements, but the document is not about IPsec itself.
TCP is the transport substrate for iFCP sessions. The TCP feature guidance (Nagle, window scale, PAWS) is a small part of the document.
Section 11 only notes that Diffserv, Intserv and MPLS can be used underneath iFCP. It is not a substantive QoS specification.
SNTP is used to synchronize gateway clocks for R_A_TOV enforcement. This is a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
This id is not in the taxonomy. The Fibre Channel concepts are covered by the iFCP tag, which sits under 'fibre channel'.

gaps.name: iSNS (Internet Storage Name Service)
gaps.why: iFCP depends on iSNS for discovery and configuration, but the taxonomy has no tag for it. It is specified in a separate RFC.

RFC4173.title: Bootstrapping Clients using the Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) Protocol
RFC4173.summary: Standards-track memo defining how diskless clients bootstrap from an iSCSI boot server, using DHCP Root Path option encoding ("iscsi:" string) and SLP/iSNS discovery to obtain the information needed to open an iSCSI session.

iSCSI.why: The whole document specifies how iSCSI boot clients obtain target name, address, port and LUN to open an iSCSI session with a boot server.
iSCSI.quote: This memo describes a standard mechanism for enabling clients to bootstrap themselves using the iSCSI protocol.

DHCP.why: A substantial section defines how the DHCP/BOOTP Root Path option is used and formatted to carry iSCSI boot parameters.
DHCP.quote: This is done using the variable-length option named Root Path [Alexander93, Reynolds93].  The use of the option field is reserved for iSCSI boot use by prefacing the string with "iscsi:".

SLP.why: The discovery stage specifies querying SLP using the iSCSI Target service type template query strings to find boot servers.
SLP.quote: The Discovery Service may be based on the SLP protocol [Guttman99, Bakke02] and is an instantiation of the SLP Service or Directory Agent.

rejected.why: iSCSI runs over TCP, but this is only the substrate; the document doesn't extend TCP.
Security Considerations only recommend IPsec support for the stages; the subject is not about IPsec.
Mentioned only in related work as a boot image transport.
The option string is UTF-8, which is merely an encoding detail.
The servername only references URI syntax rules for host format; not about URIs.
The parent topic is implied by the iSCSI tag; iSCSI is the more specific fit.

gaps.name: iSNS (Internet Storage Name Service)
gaps.why: The document describes iSNS as an alternative discovery service, but the taxonomy has no iSNS tag; it is only a secondary part, so it is left untagged.

RFC4174.title: The IPv4 Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Option for the Internet Storage Name Service
RFC4174.summary: Defines DHCPv4 option 83 that lets iSNS clients (iSCSI and iFCP devices) discover iSNS servers and learn their functions, discovery domain access, administrative flags and security settings.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv4 option, including its format and fields, so it belongs on the DHCP page.
DHCP.quote: This document describes the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) option to allow Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS) clients to discover the location of the iSNS server

storage.why: The option carries iSNS configuration for IP storage networks. No iSNS-specific tag exists, so the storage topic fits. iSCSI and iFCP are only the context, not the subject.
storage.quote: iSNS provides discovery and management capabilities for Internet SCSI (iSCSI) and Internet Fibre Channel Protocol (iFCP) storage devices

rejected.why: iSCSI devices are the clients that use the option, but the document does not specify or extend iSCSI.
iFCP is mentioned as a client of iSNS and is not specified or changed here.
The security bitmap advertises IKE/IPsec settings, but this is a small part of the option and the document does not define IPsec.
The bitmap only signals IKE modes (Main, Aggressive, PFS). IKE itself is not specified or extended.
The option does help clients find iSNS servers. The DHCP tag already covers the document, and the taxonomy has no discovery tag for this narrower case.

gaps.name: iSNS (Internet Storage Name Service)
gaps.why: The document's subject is configuring iSNS discovery, and the taxonomy has no iSNS tag.

RFC4175.title: RTP Payload Format for Uncompressed Video
RFC4175.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for packetizing uncompressed studio-quality video (BT.601, SMPTE 274M/296M), including scan-line headers, pixel groups, extended sequence numbers, the video/raw media type registration, and SDP parameter mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document's whole purpose is a new RTP payload format for uncompressed video, specifying payload header, packing and packetization rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo defines a scheme to packetize uncompressed, studio-quality video streams for transport using RTP

media types.why: Registers the video/raw media type with required and optional parameters and creates sub-parameter registries, a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: MIME media type name: video  MIME subtype name: raw

SDP.why: A dedicated section defines how the media type parameters map into SDP m=, rtpmap and fmtp lines, with an example.
SDP.quote: Remaining parameters go in the SDP "a=fmtp" attribute by copying them directly from the MIME media type string

rejected.why: The specific child tag RTP payload format fits; RTP itself is the substrate, used per RFC 3550.
Section 5 only notes counter wrap-around for high-rate streams; it is a brief remark, not a substantial subject.
The video is uncompressed, so this defines no codec; it only packetizes raw samples.
The Security Considerations text on monitoring loss is boilerplate-level and not the document's subject.

RFC4176.title: Framework for Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks (L3VPN) Operations and Management
RFC4176.summary: Informational framework describing the operations and management of Layer 3 VPNs, covering customer service management, provider network management (FCAPS), and device information models and management communication.

L3VPN.why: The whole document is a management framework for L3VPNs (PE-based and CE-based), so the L3VPN page is where readers would look for it.
L3VPN.quote: This document provides a framework for the operation and management of Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks (L3VPNs).

network management.why: A large part of the document is general FCAPS network and service management architecture, reference models and requirements for management interfaces and information models. No specific management protocol is specified, so the parent topic fits.
network management.quote: This section presents detailed customer management functions in the traditional fault, configuration, accounting, performance, and security (FCAPS) management categories.

rejected.why: SNMP is only mentioned as an example of a standards-track management protocol; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Section 4.1 only says each L3VPN solution must specify management information such as MIBs; no MIB is defined.
IPsec appears only as an example of a service template and provisioned security service.
QoS and SLS parameters are mentioned as service-level objectives but QoS mechanisms are not the subject.
AAA is cited only in passing for supervising operations, not discussed in its own right.
Policy information models are not discussed; the SLA/SLS information model is service-level, not policy-based management.

RFC4177.title: Architectural Approaches to Multi-homing for IPv6
RFC4177.summary: Informational multi6 analysis giving an architectural taxonomy of IPv6 site multi-homing approaches (routing, mobility, new/modified identity-locator protocol elements, site-exit rewriting) and a framework for comparing them.

multihoming.why: The whole document classifies multi-homing approaches for IPv6, including identity/locator split, locator selection and re-homing triggers.
multihoming.quote: This memo provides an analysis of the architectural aspects of multi-homing support for the IPv6 protocol suite.

Shim6.why: It describes the host-based identity/locator shim approaches that Shim6 grew out of. It does not specify Shim6 itself, but readers of the Shim6 subject would want this architectural background.
Shim6.quote: the transport session to use an invariant endpoint identity value to initiate and maintain a session, while allowing the forwarding layer to dynamically change paths

rejected.why: Section 5.2 analyses MIPv6 and its Return Routability procedure as a candidate multi-homing approach, but only as one of five approaches. The RFC does not specify or extend it.
IPv6 is the scope of the document, but the subject is multi-homing, so the more specific addressing/multihoming tag fits better.
Section 5.1 covers the IPv4-style routing approach (announcing prefixes in the inter-domain table) only briefly, and BGP is not named or analysed.
The identity/locator split touches end-to-end architecture, but the document's subject is multi-homing, which is more specific.
DNS is mentioned as one way to map endpoints to locators, but it is only a supporting mechanism and is not specified or extended.
It is concerned with routing-table scalability, but the main subject is host/site multi-homing rather than routing system design.

gaps.name: identity/locator split
gaps.why: The core theme is separating endpoint identity from locator, which is not a distinct tag. Shim6 and HIP only partly cover it, and ILNP and LISP are specific solutions.

RFC4178.title: The Simple and Protected Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Negotiation Mechanism
RFC4178.summary: RFC 4178 specifies SPNEGO, a GSS-API pseudo-mechanism that lets peers negotiate a common security mechanism in-band, with MIC-protected mechanism list, replacing RFC 2478.

SPNEGO.why: The document defines the SPNEGO negotiation mechanism itself: tokens, negotiation procedure, and mechListMIC processing.
SPNEGO.quote: The Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation (SPNEGO) mechanism defined here is a pseudo security mechanism that enables GSS-API peers to determine in-band

rejected.why: SPNEGO is the more specific child tag; the parent GSS-API is implied.
DER-encoded ASN.1 is only the encoding for tokens and the module in the appendix; the document is not about ASN.1.
Kerberos V5 appears only as an example mechanism OID and legacy Windows quirk.
Negotiation concerns mechanism selection, covered by the SPNEGO and GSS-API tags.

RFC4179.title: Using Universal Content Identifier (UCI) as Uniform Resource Names (URN)
RFC4179.summary: Registers the "UCI" formal URN namespace for the National Computerization Agency (Korea), defining its syntax, assignment, resolution and registration-agency delegation for persistent digital content identifiers.

URN.why: The RFC is a URN namespace registration (NID "UCI") with syntax, uniqueness, persistence, resolution and lexical equivalence rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the National Computerization Agency (NCA) for naming persistent digital resources

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to write the namespace syntax. The document is not about ABNF.
The IANA section only records the NID registration. The main body is about the namespace itself, not IANA registries or guidance.
UCI is a persistent identifier scheme, but it is not the Handle System and does not use it.
Resolution is done through an NCA HTTP resolution server and registration agencies, not through DNS.

RFC4180.title: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files
RFC4180.summary: RFC 4180 documents the de facto Comma-Separated Values (CSV) file format, gives an ABNF grammar for it, and registers the "text/csv" MIME media type.

CSV.why: The whole document defines the CSV record, field and quoting rules and the text/csv type with its header parameter. This is the core subject of the CSV tag.
CSV.quote: This RFC documents the format used for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) files and registers the associated MIME type "text/csv".

rejected.why: The text/csv registration is a real part of the document. The taxonomy has a dedicated CSV tag that covers the text/csv media type, so the more specific tag fits better.
The document uses ABNF to write the CSV grammar but is not about ABNF itself. It is only the notation.
MIME is the registration framework the document uses. The document does not define anything new about MIME structure or encodings.
The IANA Considerations section only records the registration. It is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

RFC4181.title: Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of MIB Documents
RFC4181.summary: BCP giving guidelines for authors and reviewers of IETF standards-track MIB documents, covering documentation structure and SMIv2 usage rules for data types, tables, notifications, compliance statements and module revisions.

MIB.why: The whole document is about writing and reviewing MIB modules in SMIv2: data types, textual conventions, tables, notifications, compliance statements and revisions.
MIB.quote: This memo provides guidelines for authors and reviewers of IETF standards-track specifications containing MIB modules.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol context, but the document is about MIB module authoring and SMIv2, not the protocol itself.
It describes what a MIB document's IANA Considerations section must contain, but that is a small part of the document, and IANA is not its subject.
It sets IETF review practice for MIB documents, but the subject is MIB module design, and the process material is only the review framing.
YANG is not mentioned. The document is about SMIv2 modules.

RFC4182.title: Removing a Restriction on the use of MPLS Explicit NULL
RFC4182.summary: RFC 4182 updates RFC 3032 to remove the restriction that the MPLS IPv4/IPv6 Explicit NULL labels may appear only at the bottom of the label stack, so they are legal anywhere, motivated by the Diffserv Pipe Model.

MPLS.why: The document amends the MPLS label stack encoding (RFC 3032) reserved label semantics for Explicit NULL, which is core MPLS architecture and encapsulation.
MPLS.quote: these label values may legally occur anywhere in the stack.

Diffserv.why: A substantial part of the document justifies the change by the Diffserv Pipe Model over MPLS LSPs, and the change is needed for proper Pipe Model operation.
Diffserv.quote: if one is supporting the Pipe Model of RFC 3270 [RFC3270], there are good reasons to create label stacks in which Explicit NULL is at the top

rejected.why: LDP label bindings of Explicit NULL are mentioned in motivation and deployment, but the document does not specify or extend LDP.
IPv6 Explicit NULL is just one of the two reserved labels changed; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Diffserv is the more specific tag and is already chosen; no general QoS architecture is addressed.

RFC4183.title: A Suggested Scheme for DNS Resolution of Networks and Gateways
RFC4183.summary: Informational RFC suggesting a DNS PTR-record scheme under in-addr.arpa, with masked-octet labels, that lets a client find the network, netmask and first-hop gateways for an IPv4 address, including non-octet-boundary delegation.

DNS.why: The whole document defines a DNS naming and lookup convention using PTR and A records and in-addr.arpa delegation. It is about DNS usage and zone contents.
DNS.quote: This document suggests a method of using DNS to determine the network that contains a specified IP address, the netmask of that network, and the address(es) of first-hop routers(s)

rejected.why: The scheme handles variable-length subnet masks and builds on RFC 2317 classless delegation, but the document is not about CIDR itself.
It operates on IPv4 addresses and subnets, but only as the data being resolved. The subject is the DNS lookup scheme.
Subnet and netmask discovery touches addressing, but the DNS tag fits more specifically.
Section 4.2 explicitly declines to provide an IPv6 mechanism.
It is mentioned only in passing as an alternative for IPv6 anycast queries.
ABNF is used only to describe the domain name syntax and is not the subject.

RFC4184.title: RTP Payload Format for AC-3 Audio
RFC4184.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio, including header fields, frame fragmentation, media type registration and SDP usage.
