RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for a specific codec (AC-3), with payload header, fragmentation rules and media type registration.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for transporting audio data using the AC-3 audio compression standard.

rejected.why: AC-3 is only summarised for context; the document defines transport, not the codec. RTP payload format is the more specific fit, and no AC-3 tag exists.
SDP mapping and offer/answer notes are a small part of the document, which only uses SDP to describe the payload.
RTP is the transport the payload format is for. The more specific RTP payload format tag already covers this.
The media type registration for audio/ac3 is part of a standard payload format document, not the main subject.
SRTP is only mentioned in Security Considerations as an external protection mechanism.

gaps.name: AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for AC-3. Readers interested in this codec would look for it by name.

RFC4185.title: National and Local Characters for DNS Top Level Domain (TLD) Names
RFC4185.summary: Informational RFC reviewing motivations and constraints for internationalized/national-character TLD names and proposing client-side local translation tables mapping local-language strings to existing TLDs, as an alternative to new IDNA-based TLDs or DNS changes.

IDN.why: The document is about internationalized TLD names, how IDNA applies to them, and a client-side alternative that works alongside IDNA and punycode.
IDN.quote: That much could be accomplished, given updated applications, by using a new TLD name with IDNA encoding.

DNS.why: A substantial part of the document analyses DNS constraints (administrative hierarchy, CNAME/DNAME aliasing, TLD structure) that shape the proposal.
DNS.quote: the DNS does not have facilities for either. Instead, it supports a "CNAME" record, whose label can refer only to a particular label and not to a subtree.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only briefly as a constraint on defining a new alias record type; the document is not about it.
Unicode is only the character repertoire underlying IDNA; the document does not address Unicode usage itself.
IRIs are mentioned only in passing for copy/paste behaviour.
The parent topic is implied by IDN; the document's concern is domain names specifically, not general text internationalization.
Registry policy and ccTLD administration are discussed as background, but the document is not about registration protocols or operations.

RFC4186.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol Method for Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) Subscriber Identity Modules (EAP-SIM)
RFC4186.summary: Specifies EAP-SIM, an EAP method (type 18) for authentication and session key derivation using GSM SIM triplets, with mutual authentication, identity privacy, result indications and fast re-authentication.

EAP.why: The document defines a new EAP method, its messages, attributes, key hierarchy and security claims.
EAP.quote: This document specifies an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) [RFC3748] mechanism for authentication and session key distribution using the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) Subscriber Identity Module (SIM).

GSM.why: The method is built on GSM SIM authentication (A3/A8 triplets, IMSI, AuC) and the GSM-specific security properties, so GSM readers would want it.
GSM.quote: GSM is a second generation mobile network standard.  Second generation mobile networks and third generation mobile networks use different authentication and key agreement mechanisms.

rejected.why: AAA protocols only carry EAP messages between authenticator and server; the document does not specify them.
GSM is a child of cellular and is the more specific fit; the document does not address IP over 3GPP systems more broadly.
HMAC-SHA1-128 is used only as the MAC primitive for AT_MAC; the document is not about HMAC.
AES-CBC is only the encryption mechanism for AT_ENCR_DATA.
SHA-1 is used in key derivation as a substrate, not the subject.
Identity privacy via pseudonyms is a feature of the EAP method, not a general privacy treatment; the method is covered by the EAP tag.

RFC4187.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol Method for 3rd Generation Authentication and Key Agreement (EAP-AKA)
RFC4187.summary: Specifies EAP-AKA, an EAP method using 3G UMTS/CDMA2000 AKA for mutual authentication and session key derivation, with identity privacy, fast re-authentication, notifications and key generation.

EAP.why: The whole document defines the EAP-AKA method: messages, attributes, identity handling, fast re-authentication and key derivation.
EAP.quote: This document specifies an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) mechanism for authentication and session key distribution that uses the Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) mechanism.

cellular.why: The method reuses 3GPP/3GPP2 SIM-based AKA authentication infrastructure (USIM, (R)UIM, IMSI, AuC) and interworks with mobile networks.
cellular.quote: AKA is used in the 3rd generation mobile networks Universal Mobile Telecommunications System (UMTS) and CDMA2000.

rejected.why: CDMA2000 AKA is supported alongside UMTS, but the document is not about cdma2000 packet-data networks; cellular covers it.
GSM and EAP-SIM are mentioned only for contrast; the document is about 3G AKA.
AAA protocols only carry EAP messages and keys between authenticator and server; not specified here.
Only referenced for transporting MSK keying material via MS-MPPE attributes.
SHA-1 and FIPS 186-2 PRF are used as building blocks, not the subject.
HMAC-SHA1-128 is used for AT_MAC as a mechanism only.
AES-CBC encrypts AT_ENCR_DATA; it is a substrate, not the subject.

RFC4188.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges
RFC4188.summary: Defines the SMIv2 BRIDGE-MIB module for managing IEEE 802.1D MAC bridges (base, spanning tree, transparent bridging forwarding database, static filtering), obsoleting RFC 1493.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define the BRIDGE-MIB module in SMIv2, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

Ethernet.why: The managed objects cover MAC bridging, spanning tree, forwarding databases and filtering for LAN bridges. Ethernet is the closest fit for interworking and OAM of bridged LANs.
Ethernet.quote: it defines objects for managing MAC bridges based on the IEEE 802.1D-1998 standard between Local Area Network (LAN) segments.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
Implied as an ancestor of MIB, so it is not listed separately.
The document does not address bundling parallel links.
The document covers classic 802.1D bridging, not TRILL.

gaps.name: Spanning Tree Protocol / MAC bridging
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IEEE 802.1D bridging or the Spanning Tree Protocol, which are the subject of the managed objects.

RFC4189.title: Requirements for End-to-Middle Security for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4189.summary: Informational requirements document for an "end-to-middle security" mechanism for SIP, letting a UA selectively disclose message bodies/headers to trusted proxies while keeping confidentiality and integrity end-to-end.

SIP.why: The whole document defines requirements for a new SIP security mechanism between UAs and proxy servers, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) User Agent (UA) does not always trust all intermediaries in its request path to inspect its message bodies and/or headers

rejected.why: Used as the existing end-to-end mechanism and referenced, but the document does not specify or extend S/MIME.
Mentioned as hop-by-hop security that is unsuitable; only a substrate, not the subject.
Appears only as an example of a body that proxies need to read for firewall traversal.
Digest authentication is cited as an existing mechanism for user authentication, not addressed in its own right.
SIP MESSAGE logging is one use-case example, not the focus.
The security subject is covered by the more specific SIP tag; no broader security tag is needed beyond that.

gaps.name: End-to-middle security
gaps.why: The core subject of SIP intermediary-selective confidentiality and integrity has no dedicated tag; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC4190.title: Framework for Supporting Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) in IP Telephony
RFC4190.summary: Informational framework describing how authorized emergency telecommunications service (ETS) can be supported in IP telephony, surveying SIP, Diff-Serv, RTP, H.248, policy, traffic engineering, security, alternate routing and fault tolerance, with PSTN-interworking scenarios.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about emergency telecommunications service (ETS/GETS/IEPS) in IP telephony; the general emergency services topic fits since no child tag (LoST, eCall) applies.
emergency services.quote: This document presents a framework for supporting authorized, emergency-related communication within the context of IP telephony.

Diffserv.why: Substantial sections discuss DSCP marking, new PHBs, AF/EF use and queuing/AQM variations for emergency traffic.
Diffserv.quote: One approach discussed on the IEPREP mailing list is the specification of a new Per-Hop Behaviour (PHB) for emergency-related flows.

SIP.why: SIP priority and the resource-priority requirements are the main application-layer signalling discussed for ETS.
SIP.quote: SIP has an existing "priority" field in the Request-Header-Field that distinguishes different types of sessions.

PSTN interop.why: The key scenarios center on signalling gateways and SS7/SIP interworking between PSTN and IP carriers, plus GETS/GTPS PSTN schemes.
PSTN interop.quote: we assume there is a signaling and data interaction between the PSTN and the IP network with respect to supporting emergency-related telephony traffic.

rejected.why: RTP is discussed only to conclude that adding an emergency classifier extension was not pursued; not the document's subject.
GCP/H.248 priority and emergency fields get a short subsection only; minor coverage.
Brief section recommending no specific mechanism; MPLS and OSPF only mentioned.
Intserv/RSVP appear in the introduction as background; Diffserv is the more specific tag chosen.
TRIP is mentioned briefly as a possible alternate-path mechanism.
FEC and redundant transmission are described as tangential value-added objectives in a short subsection.

gaps.name: Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) / IEPS / GETS preparedness communications
gaps.why: The taxonomy's emergency services topic covers this only generally; there is no specific tag for authorized priority emergency preparedness service.

RFC4191.title: Default Router Preferences and More-Specific Routes
RFC4191.summary: Defines an optional IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement extension: default router preference bits and a new Route Information Option so hosts, especially multi-homed ones, can choose appropriate routers and more-specific routes.

neighbor discovery.why: The RFC extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisements with a Prf field and a new Route Information Option (type 24), and specifies host behaviour for router selection and reachability probing.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document describes an optional extension to Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement messages for communicating default router preferences and more-specific routes from routers to hosts.

rejected.why: Multi-homed hosts are the motivating scenario, but the document specifies a Neighbor Discovery extension, not a multihoming architecture.
The parent of neighbor discovery is implied, and the document is not about IPv6 in general.
RIP is mentioned only as an alternative that was rejected.
6to4 appears only as an example scenario, not as a subject of the document.
The preferences are explicitly not routing metrics, and the document affects host next-hop selection only, not router forwarding.

RFC4192.title: Procedures for Renumbering an IPv6 Network without a Flag Day
RFC4192.summary: Informational procedure for renumbering an IPv6 network from an old prefix to a new one via make-before-break, covering DNS TTL/update management, DHCP/SLAAC timing, router/filter configuration, and pitfalls.

renumbering.why: The whole document is a renumbering procedure, which is the renumbering topic.
renumbering.quote: This document describes a procedure that can be used to renumber a network from one prefix to another.

IPv6.why: The procedure relies on IPv6 multiple addresses per interface, preferred lifetimes and prefix handling, and is aimed at IPv6 deployment and operation.
IPv6.quote: This document addresses the key procedural issues in renumbering an IPv6 [RFC2460] network without a "flag day".

DNS.why: A substantial part covers DNS record updates, TTL management, reverse zones, and Appendix A on DNS latency.
DNS.quote: During the renumbering process, the DNS database must be updated to add information about addresses assigned to interfaces from the new prefix

rejected.why: DHCP timers and Reconfigure are discussed as part of the procedure, but the document does not specify or extend DHCP.
SLAAC is used as an address-assignment mechanism during renumbering and the RA flag handling is mentioned, but it is not the subject.
Dynamic DNS is suggested as a strategy and the call to action mentions it, but only briefly.
The document states it is not about multihoming per se; it only mentions ingress filtering issues during provider overlap.
Only a short section on BGP link flaps when renumbering router addresses.
Security considerations are mostly misconfiguration and attack notes tied to the renumbering procedure; not a main subject.

RFC4193.title: Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses
RFC4193.summary: Defines the Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Address format (FC00::/7) with pseudo-randomly generated 40-bit Global IDs, and gives operational guidance for routing, filtering, DNS, renumbering and VPN use.

IPv6.why: The RFC specifies a new IPv6 unicast address type, its format, allocation and usage. No narrower IPv6 child tag fits, so IPv6 is the most specific one.
IPv6.quote: This document defines an IPv6 unicast address format that is globally unique and is intended for local communications

addressing.why: Much of the document concerns address allocation, uniqueness analysis, scope and site renumbering/merging. These are address-architecture matters, but the IPv6 tag already sits under addressing, so this tag is only a weak supplement.
addressing.quote: Local IPv6 addresses can be used for inter-site Virtual Private Networks (VPN) if appropriate routes are set up.
addressing.section: 4.7. Use of Local IPv6 Addresses with VPNs

rejected.why: Section 4.4 gives DNS guidance (no AAAA/PTR in global DNS, empty d.f.ip6.arpa), but it is a small operational part and DNS is not the subject.
BGP filtering of FC00::/7 is mentioned in routing guidance, but BGP is not specified or extended here.
Renumbering is touched on in 4.2 as a benefit, but the document does not describe renumbering procedures.
Section 4.7 mentions inter-site VPN use briefly, but this is about customer VPNs, not provider-provisioned VPN technology.
SHA-1 is only used inside the sample algorithm for generating Global IDs.
Pseudo-random generation is required and cited from RFC 4086, but the document does not address randomness requirements itself.

RFC4194.title: The S Hexdump Format
RFC4194.summary: Specifies the S Hexdump Format (SHF), an XML-based format for describing binary data dumps in hexadecimal, with SHA-1 block checksums, a DTD, examples, and the application/shf+xml media type registration.

XML.why: The document defines a new XML-based data format with dump and block elements, attributes and a DTD. Readers of XML-based formats would look for it.
XML.quote: a new, XML-based open format for describing binary data in hexadecimal notation

media types.why: The document registers the application/shf+xml media type with a full registration template, which is a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: Registration: application/shf+xml

rejected.why: SHA-1 is only the checksum mechanism used for block integrity. The document defines nothing new about it.
The checksum here is a SHA-1 digest attribute in a data format. It is not the Internet checksum or a packet integrity scheme.
RFC 3275 is mentioned only as an external way to protect a whole file, in the Security Considerations.
The data is hexadecimal text. This is not one of the Base16/32/64 encodings.
Firmware is named only as a typical use of the dumps. The document does not address firmware update architecture.

gaps.name: Hexadecimal binary dump formats (S-records, SHF)
gaps.why: The document is about a format for hex dumps of memory and firmware images. The taxonomy has no data-format tag for binary or memory image representations beyond XML.

RFC4195.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the TV-Anytime Forum
RFC4195.summary: Registers the "tva" URN namespace for the TV-Anytime Forum, to give persistent names to its specifications, schemas, namespaces and other documents.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration (NID "tva") with structure, lexical equivalence, persistence and assignment rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace that is engineered by the TV-Anytime Forum for naming persistent resources

rejected.why: XML DTDs and schemas are only examples of the resources being named. The document does not specify anything about XML.
This is a namespace registration, but it is not guidance on IANA registries or their stewardship. The URN tag covers it.
TV-Anytime is a broadcast and television domain, but the document only names the Forum's documents and does not address media delivery.

RFC4196.title: The SEED Cipher Algorithm and Its Use with IPsec
RFC4196.summary: Specifies use of the SEED 128-bit block cipher in CBC mode with explicit IV as an IPsec ESP confidentiality transform, including IKE identifiers and test vectors.

ESP.why: The document defines how SEED-CBC is used as an ESP encryption transform: payload layout, IV, padding, IKE transform ID, and ESP test packets.
ESP.quote: as a confidentiality mechanism within the context of the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

IKE.why: A dedicated section covers Phase 1 and Phase 2 identifiers, key length attribute and hash considerations for negotiating SEED-CBC SAs.
IKE.quote: This section describes the use of IKE [IKE] to establish IPsec ESP security associations (SAs) that employ SEED in CBC mode.

rejected.why: SEED is a cipher, but the document is about its use in ESP. No more specific cryptography tag fits SEED, and a topic tag is only used when no technology tag already sits under it. ESP sits under security, not cryptography.
ESP is the more specific child tag and already implies IPsec.
AES is mentioned only when describing the NIST modes of operation. The document is not about it.
HMAC-SHA-1 and HMAC-MD5 are only mentioned as the authenticators and key generators to use. The document defines nothing new about them.
The requirement for an unpredictable IV is a brief aside within the ESP payload specification.

gaps.name: SEED block cipher
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about the Korean SEED cipher's use in ESP. The taxonomy has tags for AES, Camellia, ARIA and others but none for SEED, so readers browsing national block ciphers would not find it.

RFC4197.title: Requirements for Edge-to-Edge Emulation of Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) Circuits over Packet Switching Networks
RFC4197.summary: Informational requirements document for PWE3 emulation of TDM circuits (PDH T1/E1/T3/E3 and SONET/SDH) over packet-switched networks, complementing the generic PWE3 requirements with TDM-specific needs such as clock recovery, jitter, signalling and loss handling.

pseudowire.why: The whole document specifies requirements for TDM pseudowires, aligned to the PWE3 architecture and complementing the generic PWE3 requirements.
pseudowire.quote: defines the specific requirements for edge-to-edge emulation of circuits carrying Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) digital signals

SONET.why: A substantial part covers emulating SONET STS-1/STS-Nc and VT circuits and SDH analogs. The SONET tag fits, since the document is about carrying these circuits rather than IP over them.
SONET.quote: This document discusses the requirements for emulation of SONET/SDH services.

rejected.why: RTP is mentioned only as one possible way to carry timing information in the adaptive scenario.
Section 7.8 briefly covers shutting down a TDM PW under congestion, but that is a minor requirement, not a main subject.
CAS/CCS signalling is discussed, but the document is about circuit emulation, not PSTN gateway interworking.
Clock recovery and network synchronization are treated only as requirements for the emulated circuits. The document is not about time protocols like NTP or PTP.
Header compression compatibility is a single sentence in Section 7.7.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation (PDH T1/E1/T3/E3, CESoPSN/SAToP requirements)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a pseudowire tag, but it has no tag for TDM circuit emulation or for PDH circuits specifically. Readers looking for TDM PW work would want one.

RFC4198.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for Federated Content
RFC4198.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "fdc" for identifying content resources in federated content collections, with provider-domain/date/resource-id syntax and a recommended HTTP-based resolution convention.

URN.why: The document defines and registers a new URN namespace (fdc), including syntax, uniqueness, persistence, lexical equivalence and resolution rules.
URN.quote: This document describes a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace for identifying content resources within federated content collections.

rejected.why: RFC 2169 HTTP-based URN resolution is only recommended as the resolution mechanism; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Domain names are used as provider identifiers for uniqueness, but the document is not about DNS itself.
ABNF is only the notation used to express the namespace syntax.
The NID registration is boilerplate-level; the document is about the namespace itself, not IANA registry procedure.
The DateId uses ISO 8601 basic format, but only as a component of the identifier, not as a document subject.

RFC4201.title: Link Bundling in MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE)
RFC4201.summary: Defines link bundling for GMPLS/MPLS-TE: grouping component links into a bundled TE link, how routing parameters are advertised for the bundle, how component links are identified in RSVP-TE and CR-LDP signaling (updating RFC 3471/3472/3473 interface identification TLVs), and bandwidth accounting.

GMPLS.why: The document defines a GMPLS TE link construct (bundled links) and updates GMPLS signaling interface identification TLVs and routing parameters.
GMPLS.quote: For the purpose of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) signaling, in certain cases a combination of <link identifier, label> is not sufficient

RSVP-TE.why: A substantial part specifies how component links are identified in RSVP-TE Path messages, IF_ID RSVP_HOP and ERROR_SPEC objects.
RSVP-TE.quote: Component link identifiers are carried in RSVP messages, as described in section 8 of [RFC3473].

traffic engineering.why: Defines how TE parameters (bandwidth, metric, resource classes) are aggregated for bundled links and how bandwidth accounting is done.
traffic engineering.quote: we define the Traffic Engineering parameters to be advertised for a bundled link, based on the configuration of the component links

rejected.why: Signaling for CR-LDP is covered only briefly by reference to RFC 3472/3473; the document is not about CR-LDP.
OSPF/IS-IS TE parameters are referenced as substrate for the bundle's advertised attributes; no OSPF extension is defined here.
The more specific GMPLS and traffic engineering tags fit better.
Despite the similar name, this is TE link bundling for LSP resource identification, not IEEE 802.1AX LAG.

RFC4202.title: Routing Extensions in Support of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)
RFC4202.summary: RFC 4202 defines the GMPLS routing extensions: new TE link attributes (unnumbered links, link protection type, SRLG, interface switching capability descriptors, bandwidth encoding) that IGPs advertise, extending MPLS TE routing to non-packet links such as OXCs and TDM.

GMPLS.why: The whole document defines GMPLS TE link properties, including interface switching capabilities, protection types and SRLGs, for optical and transport network control.
GMPLS.quote: This document specifies routing extensions in support of carrying link state information for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

rejected.why: The OSPF encoding is in RFC 4203. This document is protocol-independent and only mentions OSPF as a place where the extensions are encoded.
The IS-IS encoding is in RFC 4205. This document is protocol-independent.
It extends TE link attributes, but the GMPLS tag is the more specific fit.
MPLS is the base technology that GMPLS generalizes. GMPLS is the more specific tag.

RFC4203.title: OSPF Extensions in Support of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)
RFC4203.summary: Defines OSPFv2 TE LSA sub-TLVs (Link Local/Remote Identifiers, Link Protection Type, Interface Switching Capability Descriptor, SRLG) and a link-local TE opaque LSA to support GMPLS, plus graceful restart implications.

GMPLS.why: The extensions carry GMPLS-specific TE link information such as switching capability, protection type and SRLGs; readers of GMPLS would want this RFC.
GMPLS.quote: This document specifies encoding of extensions to the OSPF routing protocol in support of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

OSPF.why: It extends OSPFv2 TE opaque LSAs with new sub-TLVs and a new link-local TE LSA, and updates RFC 3630.
OSPF.quote: This document specifies extensions to the OSPF routing protocol [OSPF] in support of carrying link state information for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

rejected.why: Only referenced for restart procedures; the document does not specify RSVP-TE signalling.
TE link attributes are advertised, but the OSPF and GMPLS tags cover this more specifically.
GMPLS is the more specific tag; MPLS is its parent and is implied.
The document specifies only OSPFv2 Opaque LSAs.
SONET/SDH appears only as a switching-capability indication field, not as a subject of the document.

RFC4204.title: Link Management Protocol (LMP)
RFC4204.summary: RFC 4204 specifies the Link Management Protocol (LMP), run between neighbouring nodes to manage TE links in GMPLS networks: control channel management, link property correlation, data link connectivity verification, and fault localization.

GMPLS.why: LMP is a GMPLS control-plane protocol that manages TE links, data links and control channels. The taxonomy has no LMP-specific tag, so GMPLS is the closest fit.
GMPLS.quote: LMP will be used to maintain control channel connectivity, verify the physical connectivity of the data links, correlate the link property information, suppress downstream alarms

traffic engineering.why: The document is about managing TE links: aggregating data links, correlating their properties, and feeding them to Constrained SPF and signaling.
traffic engineering.quote: multiple data links can be combined to form a single traffic engineering (TE) link

rejected.why: Security Considerations only recommends IPsec/IKE to protect LMP. That is a substrate mechanism, not the subject.
LMP runs over UDP port 701, but UDP is only the transport.
Mentioned only as a companion signaling protocol that uses the control channels.
Fault localization and link verification are OAM-like, but the document is a GMPLS link management protocol, not a general OAM mechanism. The GMPLS tag is the better fit.
The parent of GMPLS, so it is implied. LMP is specific to GMPLS, so no separate MPLS tag is needed.
Named only as a source of the Node_Id and as a consumer of link properties.

gaps.name: Link Management Protocol (LMP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for LMP itself. It is a GMPLS-specific protocol for control channel management, link verification and fault localization, so a dedicated tag would suit it better than GMPLS.

RFC4205.title: Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Extensions in Support of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)
RFC4205.summary: Defines IS-IS sub-TLVs (Link Local/Remote Identifiers, Link Protection Type, Interface Switching Capability Descriptor) and a new SRLG TLV to carry GMPLS traffic-engineering link state, plus graceful restart implications.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with new TLVs and sub-TLVs and gives restart behaviour for IS-IS LSPs; it updates RFC 3784.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies extensions to the IS-IS routing protocol in support of carrying link state information for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

GMPLS.why: The encodings carry GMPLS TE link properties (switching capability, protection type, SRLG, unnumbered link identifiers) for optical/TDM/packet networks, so GMPLS readers need it.
GMPLS.quote: we enhance the sub-TLVs for the extended IS reachability TLV (see [ISIS-TE]) in support of GMPLS.

rejected.why: Only referenced for restart procedures; the document does not specify RSVP-TE signalling.
TE link attributes are advertised, but the GMPLS and IS-IS tags cover this subject more specifically.
GMPLS is the more specific child tag and fits; plain MPLS is not the subject.
SONET/SDH appears only as a TDM capability indication field, not as a subject of the document.

RFC4206.title: Label Switched Paths (LSP) Hierarchy with Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Traffic Engineering (TE)
RFC4206.summary: Defines LSP hierarchy in GMPLS TE via forwarding adjacencies: an LSP advertised as a TE link into IS-IS/OSPF, with routing parameters, region boundaries, and RSVP-TE/CR-LDP signalling for nesting LSPs.

GMPLS.why: The whole document specifies LSP hierarchy and forwarding adjacencies within GMPLS TE, including regions based on interface switching capability.
GMPLS.quote: it may be useful to aggregate Label Switched Paths (LSPs) by creating a hierarchy of such LSPs

RSVP-TE.why: Defines specific RSVP-TE procedures for tunnelling LSPs over an FA-LSP: IF_ID RSVP_HOP, no Router Alert, TTL check changes.
RSVP-TE.quote: If one uses RSVP-TE to signal an LSP to be tunneled over an FA-LSP, then the Path message MUST contain an IF_ID RSVP_HOP object

CR-LDP.why: Specifies the CR-LDP signalling procedures for FA-LSPs, including targeted LDP sessions.
CR-LDP.quote: If one uses CR-LDP to signal an LSP to be tunneled over an FA-LSP, then the Request message MUST contain an IF_ID TLV

rejected.why: OSPF is the carrier of the FA's TE link advertisement, but the document defines no OSPF extension. It only says how to populate existing TE parameters.
Like OSPF, IS-IS only floods the FA as a TE link. The document does not specify or extend IS-IS.
The parent topic is implied by the GMPLS, RSVP-TE and CR-LDP tags and not chosen separately.
The document only says the Router Alert option must not be set on Path messages. It does not specify the option.

RFC4207.title: Synchronous Optical Network (SONET)/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) Encoding for Link Management Protocol (LMP) Test Messages
RFC4207.summary: Defines SONET/SDH-specific encoding for LMP link verification Test messages (J0/J1/J2 trace correlation) and new trace monitoring messages and objects for LMP.

SONET.why: The document specifies how SONET/SDH overhead bytes (J0, J1, J2 trace, DCC) are used for LMP test and trace monitoring, so readers of the SONET/SDH subject need it.
SONET.quote: the SONET/SDH technology-specific information for LMP is defined. Specifically, the SONET/SDH test procedures used for link verification and link property correlation are detailed.

GMPLS.why: It extends LMP, a GMPLS component, with new messages and objects (TraceMonitor, TRACE, etc.) for optical/transport TE link management.
GMPLS.quote: The Link Management Protocol (LMP) [RFC4204] has been developed as part of the Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) protocol suite to manage TE links.

rejected.why: HDLC framing is cited from RFC 1662 only as the framing for DCC test messages; the document is not about PPP.
TE links are the context for LMP, but the document does not address traffic engineering itself; GMPLS covers the area.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as LMP's message security mechanism.
The IANA section only lists new LMP message type and class assignments; it is boilerplate.

gaps.name: LMP (Link Management Protocol)
gaps.why: The document extends LMP with new messages and objects, but the taxonomy has no LMP tag, so GMPLS is the closest fit.

RFC4208.title: Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) User-Network Interface (UNI): Resource ReserVation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) Support for the Overlay Model
RFC4208.summary: Specifies how GMPLS RSVP-TE signalling is applied at the overlay-model User-Network Interface between edge nodes and core nodes, covering addressing, ERO/RRO handling, notification, graceful deletion and VPN connections.

GMPLS.why: The document profiles GMPLS signalling for the overlay model and UNI, defining restrictions and procedures between edge and core nodes.
GMPLS.quote: Specifically, it addresses RSVP-TE procedures between an edge-node and a core-node in the overlay model.

RSVP-TE.why: Substantial parts specify RSVP-TE message and object handling (ERO, RRO, NOTIFY_REQUEST, PathErr, PathTear) at the UNI.
RSVP-TE.quote: A core-node MAY reject a Path message that contains an ERO.

rejected.why: Section 7 covers VPN connections only briefly as a compatibility case; the document is not about provider-provisioned VPNs.
GMPLS is a more specific child tag and fits better than the MPLS parent.
RSVP-TE already sits under this topic, so it is implied and not added separately.
Alarm-free deletion is a signalling procedure, not an OAM mechanism.

gaps.name: GMPLS UNI / overlay model (ASON)
gaps.why: The core subject is the overlay UNI reference point for optical networks, which the taxonomy has no specific tag for, so it is covered only by the GMPLS tag.

RFC4209.title: Link Management Protocol (LMP) for Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) Optical Line Systems
RFC4209.summary: Extends the Link Management Protocol (LMP) for use between a GMPLS peer node and an adjacent DWDM optical line system, adding a WDM CONFIG object, new Data Link sub-objects (link group, SRLG, BER, protection, span length, admin group) and a link-group channel status object.

GMPLS.why: LMP is part of the GMPLS suite and manages TE links for optical networks. This document extends it for DWDM line systems, so readers of GMPLS/optical control would look for it.
GMPLS.quote: extensions to LMP are proposed to allow it to be used between a peer node and an adjacent optical line system (OLS)

rejected.why: TE links are the subject matter, but the document extends link management rather than TE routing or signalling. GMPLS is the more specific tag.
Only cited for the 32-bit administrative group definition in RFC 3630. The document does not specify OSPF behaviour.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as the mechanism securing LMP messages.
GMPLS signalling is referenced only for the Admin Status object and for path selection. The document does not specify RSVP-TE.
SONET/SDH appears only as the user-port types of the OLS and in the use of the RFC 4207 trace function for verification. The document is not about IP over SONET.

gaps.name: Link Management Protocol (LMP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no LMP tag. The document is about LMP itself (control channel management, link verification, link summarization, fault management), so GMPLS is only the nearest fit.

RFC4210.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Management Protocol (CMP)
RFC4210.summary: RFC 4210 specifies the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP), the PKIX message formats and procedures for X.509v3 certificate enrollment, update, revocation, cross-certification, CA key update and proof-of-possession between end entities, RAs and CAs.

CMP.why: The document is the CMP specification itself, defining its messages, data structures, mandatory functions and profiles.
CMP.quote: This document describes the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Certificate Management Protocol (CMP).

rejected.why: CMP manages X.509v3 certificates but does not define the certificate format or profile; X.509 is the object being managed.
The protocol is expressed in ASN.1 with a compilable module in Appendix F, but ASN.1 is only the notation and encoding used.
The more specific child CMP fits and implies PKI as its parent.
HMAC and PasswordBasedMac are used for message protection, but the document is not about HMAC.
CMP covers key update and recovery in a PKI context, but CMP is the more specific tag.

RFC4211.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF)
RFC4211.summary: Specifies the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF), an ASN.1 syntax for requesting X.509 certificates from a CA/RA, including proof-of-possession methods, controls, and registration info; it is not itself a protocol.

X.509.why: The document defines the message format for requesting X.509 certificates, including the CertTemplate. This is X.509 PKI certificate enrolment syntax, and X.509 is the most specific fitting tag.
X.509.quote: This syntax is used to convey a request for a certificate to a Certification Authority (CA), possibly via a Registration Authority (RA), for the purposes of X.509 certificate production.

PKI.why: A substantial part covers PKI enrolment concerns: proof-of-possession, RA/CA roles, key archival and escrow controls, and password-based MAC. These belong to general PKI management, beyond the certificate format itself.
PKI.quote: Any CRP referencing this document MUST enforce POP by some means.

rejected.why: CMS EnvelopedData is used to carry encrypted private keys, but CRMF only uses it as a building block and defines a new content type only for that purpose.
The syntax is expressed in ASN.1, but ASN.1 is just the notation. The document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
HMAC-SHA1 is used inside the password-based MAC, which is only a mechanism the document relies on.
CRMF is explicitly not a protocol and is designed to be referenced by CMP and other protocols. CMP itself is not specified here.
Private key archival and escrow controls are discussed, but they are a part of certificate enrolment, which the PKI tag already covers.

RFC4212.title: Alternative Certificate Formats for the Public-Key Infrastructure Using X.509 (PKIX) Certificate Management Protocols
RFC4212.summary: Informational RFC defining how CRMF certificate templates, PKIX-CMP and CMC can request and carry alternative certificate formats (X.509 attribute certificates and OpenPGP certificates).

CMP.why: The document extends PKIX-CMP (CMPCertificate CHOICE) and CMC and the CRMF request syntax to handle alternative certificate types. CMP is the closest taxonomy tag for PKIX certificate management protocols.
CMP.quote: This document proposes extensions to the PKIX-CMP and CMC protocols that are required to manage certificates in alternative formats.

OpenPGP.why: A large part of the document defines OpenPGP CertTemplates, Key and Signature Templates, and examples built from OpenPGP packets, so OpenPGP readers would want it.
OpenPGP.quote: A CertTemplate for an OpenPGP certificate can be used by defining an object identifier (OID) and corresponding value for use in the id-regCtrl-altCertTemplate control.

X.509.why: It defines the AttCertTemplate for X.509 attribute certificates and extends the CMP and CMC certificate choices to carry them.
X.509.quote: A CertTemplate for an X.509 attribute certificate can be used by simply defining an object identifier (OID) and corresponding value

rejected.why: CMS is only the syntax CMC uses. The document merely extends its CertificateChoices CHOICE for OpenPGP certificates, which is minor.
ASN.1 is the notation used for the definitions, not the subject of the document.
The more specific tags (CMP, X.509) already cover the PKI subject area.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to get confidentiality for CMP.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a lower-layer option.

gaps.name: CRMF / CMC (Certificate Request Message Format, Certificate Management Messages over CMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a CMP tag but no tag for CRMF or CMC, which the document extends substantially.

RFC4213.title: Basic Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 Hosts and Routers
RFC4213.summary: RFC 4213 specifies the basic IPv6 transition mechanisms, dual-stack operation and configured IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnelling, including encapsulation, tunnel MTU, ICMP error handling, decapsulation checks and link-local addresses.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document defines the core IPv4/IPv6 coexistence mechanisms (dual stack and configured tunnels), which is the IPv6 transition topic.
IPv6 transition.quote: Two mechanisms are specified, dual stack and configured tunneling.

tunneling.why: Much of the body specifies encapsulation, hop limit, header construction, decapsulation and source-address checks for IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels. No child tag fits: GRE and IP-in-IP are not what is specified.
tunneling.quote: Configured tunneling of IPv6 over IPv4: A technique for establishing point-to-point tunnels by encapsulating IPv6 packets within IPv4 headers

rejected.why: The IPv6 transition tag is the more specific fit, and the document is about coexistence rather than IPv6 itself.
Path MTU discovery is used for dynamic tunnel MTU, but the document only relies on it as a mechanism.
ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 error handling is covered, but only as part of tunnel behaviour, not as a subject in its own right.
Section 2.2 mentions A and AAAA handling in resolvers. This is brief, and the document defines nothing new for DNS.
The document is specific to IPv6-in-IPv4 configured tunnels, so the general tunneling tag fits better.
IPsec is only mentioned in Security Considerations as an alternative for authenticated tunnels.

RFC4214.title: Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP)
RFC4214.summary: Specifies ISATAP, an experimental mechanism for automatically tunnelling IPv6 packets over an IPv4 site network, including ISATAP interface identifiers, a Potential Router List, and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery behaviour over the tunnel.

ISATAP.why: The document defines ISATAP itself, including addressing, automatic tunnelling and neighbor discovery over ISATAP interfaces.
ISATAP.quote: connects IPv6 hosts/routers over IPv4 networks. ISATAP views the IPv4 network as a link layer for IPv6

rejected.why: The document adapts IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for ISATAP interfaces (PRL, router discovery). This is part of ISATAP rather than a separate subject, so the ISATAP tag covers it.
This is the parent of ISATAP and is implied by the ISATAP tag, so it is not listed separately.
DNS is only one way to learn the PRL (the isatap.domainname FQDN convention). It is used as a mechanism and is not the subject.
A DHCPv4 option is mentioned only as one way to initialise the PRL, with no DHCP specification.
Generic tunnelling is relied on through RFC 4213 mechanisms, and the more specific ISATAP tag fits better.
IPv6 is the payload protocol. The document is about tunnelling it, which the transition tag covers.

RFC4215.title: Analysis on IPv6 Transition in Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Networks
RFC4215.summary: Informational analysis of IPv6 transition scenarios in 3GPP GPRS/UMTS packet networks and IMS, evaluating dual stack, tunneling and translation mechanisms and recommending which to use.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document analyzes IPv6/IPv4 transition scenarios and applicable mechanisms (dual stack, tunneling, translators) for 3GPP networks.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document analyzes the transition to IPv6 in Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) packet networks.

cellular.why: The document is specific to 3GPP GPRS/UMTS networks: GGSN, PDP contexts, UE configuration and IMS, so it belongs under cellular networks.
cellular.quote: IPv6 in Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) General Packet Radio Service (GPRS) packet networks [3GPP-23.060]

SIP.why: Section 4 analyzes SIP/SDP IPv4/IPv6 interworking in the IMS, including B2BUA drawbacks, and recommends SIP working group solutions.
SIP.quote: the transition of IMS traffic from IPv6 to IPv4, must be handled at two levels
SIP.section: 4.1. UE Connecting to a Node in an IPv4 Network through IMS

rejected.why: NAT-PT and NAPT-PT are discussed (with an appendix on their problems), but NAT64 is a different, later mechanism not covered here.
Only mentioned as a candidate tunneling mechanism; the document does not specify or analyze it in detail.
Section 2.4 has brief DNS transport guidelines, but the document is not about DNS.
Tunneling is one of the transition mechanisms discussed, but the more specific IPv6 transition tag covers it.
DHCPv6 is mentioned only as one way to configure DNS and P-CSCF addresses in the UE.
SIIT is only cited as the header-translation algorithm used by NAT-PT; the document does not analyze it.

RFC4216.title: MPLS Inter-Autonomous System (AS) Traffic Engineering (TE) Requirements
RFC4216.summary: Informational requirements document describing objectives, application scenarios and detailed requirements for extending MPLS Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE LSPs) across autonomous system boundaries, within one or several service providers.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document sets out requirements, scenarios and policies for inter-AS TE LSPs (bandwidth guarantees, optimization, fast recovery, re-optimization, DS-TE).
traffic engineering.quote: This document discusses requirements for the support of inter-AS MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS TE).

MPLS.why: It concerns MPLS TE LSPs, hierarchy, fast reroute and OAM extended across ASes, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: requirements for an inter-AS MPLS Traffic Engineering mechanism that may be used to achieve the same set of objectives across AS boundaries

RSVP-TE.why: Requirements for RSVP-TE signalling: ERO/RRO with AS subobjects, Path Error on policy violations, and rewriting of session attributes at AS boundaries.
RSVP-TE.quote: end-to-end Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) signaling (eventually with loose paths) traversing across the interconnected ASBRs

rejected.why: BGP-based inter-AS TE appears only as background and in Appendix A for comparison. The document is not about BGP itself.
PCE/PCC is mentioned briefly for confidentiality of path computation, but it is not a substantial part of the document.
Diffserv and DS-TE are drivers for the requirements, but the document does not specify or analyse Diffserv.
MPLS TE fast reroute is required, but this is RSVP-TE FRR and not the IP/LDP fast-reroute subject.
A MIB requirement is stated, but no MIB module is defined, so this is only a small part of the document.

RFC4217.title: Securing FTP with TLS
RFC4217.summary: Specifies how to use TLS to secure FTP control and data connections, using the RFC 2228 AUTH, PBSZ, PROT and CCC commands, with negotiation policy, reply codes and timing diagrams.

FTP.why: The document profiles and extends FTP security. It defines the AUTH TLS negotiation, data connection protection, and the behaviour of REIN, ABOR and STAT under TLS.
FTP.quote: This document describes how the AUTH, PBSZ, PROT, and CCC commands, defined therein, should be implemented with the TLS protocol.

TLS.why: A large part of the document defines how TLS is applied to FTP: client/server roles, TLS negotiation on data connections, cached sessions, and certificate cross-checking. Readers of TLS deployment guidance would want it.
TLS.quote: The FTP client MUST be the TLS client and the FTP server MUST be the TLS server.

rejected.why: Certificates appear only in the security considerations, as the assumed identity token. The document does not profile them.
CCC and firewall-friendly PASV are discussed as motivations. The document does not address firewall traversal as a subject.
RFC 2228 is the underlying security extension framework. This document does not use ADAT or GSS mechanisms.
SMTP over TLS (RFC 3207) is mentioned only as an analogy.

RFC4218.title: Threats Relating to IPv6 Multihoming Solutions
RFC4218.summary: Informational threat analysis cataloguing redirection, third-party DoS, packet injection and privacy threats inherent to IPv6 site multihoming solutions that separate locators from identifiers.

multihoming.why: The whole document analyses threats common to all IPv6 multihoming solutions. It is not about any one solution, so the multihoming topic fits better than the Shim6 child.
multihoming.quote: This document lists security threats related to IPv6 multihoming. Multihoming can introduce new opportunities to redirect packets to different, unintended IP addresses.

privacy.why: Sections 3.5 and 4.5 analyse address privacy and host tracking risks of stable identifiers and multiple locators. This is a substantial part of the document.
privacy.quote: Designers of solutions to multihoming need to be aware of this concern.

rejected.why: The document deliberately analyses no specific solution, and Shim6 is never named. It covers multihoming threats in general.
Mobile IPv6 threats are cited as background and as an analogy, but the document is not about mobility.
IPv6 is the setting for the multihoming work, but the document does not specify or analyse IPv6 itself.
HIP appears only as an example of a proposal in the analysis and the appendix.
Third-party DoS is a main threat discussed, but the document is about multihoming threats and not DDoS mitigation as such.
TCP is used as an example for injection and flooding attacks, but the document is not about TCP.

RFC4219.title: Things Multihoming in IPv6 (MULTI6) Developers Should Think About
RFC4219.summary: RFC 4219 is a questionnaire that authors of IPv6 site-multihoming (multi6) solutions should answer, covering on-the-wire behaviour, identifier/locator split, routing, DNS, and application compatibility.

multihoming.why: The whole document is a questionnaire for evaluating IPv6 multihoming solutions, so the multihoming architectures page is where readers would look for it.
multihoming.quote: This document specifies a set of questions that authors should be prepared to answer as part of a solution to multihoming with IPv6.

rejected.why: The questionnaire mentions shim approaches only generically and does not specify or analyse the Shim6 protocol.
Section 5 asks how a solution interacts with DNS, but DNS is not the subject of the document.
IPv6 is the context, but the document is about multihoming. The multihoming tag is more specific.
NAT and middleboxes come up in a few questions, but the document does not address them in its own right.
Section 4 asks about aggregation and traffic engineering, but only as questions for solution authors. It is not a routing architecture document.

RFC4220.title: Traffic Engineering Link Management Information Base
RFC4220.summary: Defines the TE-LINK-STD-MIB SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring MPLS/GMPLS traffic engineering links, bundled links and component links, including their ifTable/ifStackTable usage.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module (TE-LINK-STD-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables, conformance groups and interface-group applicability.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

GMPLS.why: The managed objects model GMPLS/MPLS TE links: SRLGs, switching capabilities, encoding types, protection types and priority-based bandwidth for link bundling.
GMPLS.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling TE links as described in the Link Bundling in MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) document.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag is more specific.
OSPF TE extensions are referenced for semantics of attributes, but the document doesn't specify or extend OSPF.
The GMPLS tag already covers the TE link subject; this is a management module, not a TE architecture document.
MPLS is the context; the document manages TE links rather than specifying MPLS itself.
The data model is SMIv2, not YANG.

RFC4221.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Management Overview
RFC4221.summary: Informational overview of the MPLS management architecture, describing the MPLS MIB modules (TC, LSR, LDP, TE, FTN, TE-LINK), their tables, notifications, and interdependencies, plus related PWE3/PPVPN/CCAMP/TEWG MIBs.

MIB.why: The whole document surveys the MPLS MIB modules, their tables, scalars, notifications, OID tree and dependencies, which is MIB/SMI subject matter.
MIB.quote: This document describes the management architecture for MPLS and indicates the interrelationships between the different MIB modules used for MPLS network management.

MPLS.why: The document is about managing MPLS networks: LSRs, LSPs, TE tunnels, FTN mappings, and TE links.
MPLS.quote: MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB describes managed objects for modeling an MPLS Label Switching Router (LSR).

LDP.why: A substantial part (section 6 and subsections 4.4-4.7) covers the LDP MIB modules and their tables and notifications.
LDP.quote: MPLS-LDP-STD-MIB describes managed objects used to model and manage the MPLS Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) [RFC3036].

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol and framework context; the document defines nothing new about SNMP itself.
TE tunnels and TE links are covered, but only as managed objects. The MPLS MIB tags already capture that, and the TE MIB is not a TE protocol.
Mentioned only as a future CCAMP MIB direction, not a subject of the document.
The PPVPN MPLS VPN MIB is covered only in a brief background note.
PWE3 MIBs are mentioned only in a brief background note.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific MIB tag.

RFC4222.title: Prioritized Treatment of Specific OSPF Version 2 Packets and Congestion Avoidance
RFC4222.summary: BCP recommending OSPFv2 implementation practices (prioritizing Hello and LSA Ack packets, exponential retransmission backoff, implicit congestion detection, adjacency throttling) to keep large networks stable during LSA storms.

OSPF.why: The whole document specifies recommended OSPFv2 packet-handling, retransmission and adjacency-formation behaviour to avoid LSA storm instability.
OSPF.quote: recommends methods that are intended to improve the scalability and stability of large networks using Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) Version 2 protocol

rejected.why: The congestion avoidance here is control-plane flooding behaviour within OSPF, not transport-layer congestion control.
Only mentioned as possibly applicable with further study; the document targets OSPFv2.
Only mentioned in Appendix C to note TOS/Precedence bits were redefined; not a subject of the document.
Packet prioritisation is internal to router OSPF processing, not a QoS architecture or signalling.
Mentioned only as another link-state protocol that suffered outages.

RFC4223.title: Reclassification of RFC 1863 to Historic
RFC4223.summary: This memo reclassifies RFC 1863 (BGP/IDRP route server as an alternative to full mesh routing) to Historic status because no implementations exist, and obsoletes it.

BGP.why: The document concerns the status of a BGP-related route server specification, an alternative to BGP full mesh, so BGP readers would look for it.
BGP.quote: RFC 1863 [1] describes the use of route servers as an alternative to BGP/IDRP full mesh routing.

route reflection.why: Names route reflection and confederations as the current replacements for the obsolete approach, so it is relevant to that subject.
route reflection.quote: Current techniques that serve as an alternative to full mesh routing include BGP Route Reflectors [2], BGP Confederedations [3]

rejected.why: The tag covers Internet exchange route servers. The memo explicitly excludes those and covers only the RFC 1863 route server.
IDRP (the OSI inter-domain routing protocol) is mentioned only in passing as obsolete. It is not the same as Inter-Domain Policy Routing.
IDRP is an OSI protocol, but the document says nothing about OSI network-layer coexistence.

RFC4224.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): ROHC over Channels That Can Reorder Packets
RFC4224.summary: Informational guidance on implementing ROHC (RFC 3095 and derived profiles) over channels that can reorder packets, covering LSB interpretation interval offset p, R-mode and U/O-mode behaviour, and suggestions for compressor, decompressor and new profile design.

ROHC.why: The whole document analyses ROHC behaviour under packet reordering and gives implementation and profile-design guidance, so it belongs on the ROHC page.
ROHC.quote: This document discusses aspects of using ROHC over channels that can reorder packets. It provides guidelines on how to implement existing profiles over such channels

rejected.why: Parent of ROHC; implied, so not listed separately.
ESP tunnels are mentioned only as an example where external sequence numbers could detect reordering, and that is explicitly out of scope.
RTP headers are what ROHC compresses (profile 0x0001), but the document is not about RTP itself.
UDP-Lite profiles 0x0007/0x0008 are listed as in scope but only as ROHC profiles; the document is not about UDP-Lite.
CRTP is a different header compression scheme and is not discussed.

RFC4225.title: Mobile IP Version 6 Route Optimization Security Design Background
RFC4225.summary: Informational RFC explaining the rationale behind Mobile IPv6 route optimization security design: threats (address stealing, flooding, reflection), the return routability mechanism, and residual risks.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document analyses Mobile IPv6 route optimization security, binding updates, and return routability.
Mobile IPv6.quote: an account of the rationale behind the Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) Route Optimization security design

rejected.why: IPsec is discussed (Section 3.5, 5.2) as an alternative that was rejected and as protection of HA-MN tunnel, but the document is not about IPsec.
Only a brief hypothetical of using secure reverse DNS for a global key infrastructure in Section 3.5.
The document is about mobility binding security, not securing routing protocols; routing infrastructure is only an assumption.
Security is the theme, but the specific technology tag Mobile IPv6 covers it; no general security guidance beyond that.
Neighbor Discovery is mentioned only in passing as a comparison and for the Destination Cache.

gaps.name: Return routability / binding update security
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag specific to Mobile IPv6 route optimization security; it is covered by the Mobile IPv6 tag.

RFC4226.title: HOTP: An HMAC-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
RFC4226.summary: Informational RFC specifying HOTP, an HMAC-SHA-1 counter-based one-time password algorithm for two-factor authentication, with security analysis, deployment requirements, reference code and test values.

OTP.why: The whole document specifies the HOTP one-time password algorithm, its truncation, counter resynchronization, throttling and shared secret management.
OTP.quote: This document describes an algorithm to generate one-time password values, based on Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC).

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-1 is the building block used by HOTP; the document does not specify or extend HMAC itself, only uses it as a pseudorandom function.
SHA-1 is used internally; Appendix B discusses SHA-1 attacks only to assess HOTP impact, so the document is not about the SHA family.
The more specific OTP tag already covers two-factor authentication; the parent is implied.
Section 7.5 only recommends following RFC 4086 for generating shared secrets; this is a minor mention.
Shared secret management in 7.5 is a part of deploying OTP, not a main subject of the document.

RFC4227.title: Using the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) in Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP)
RFC4227.summary: Specifies a BEEP profile binding for SOAP envelopes, including profile identification, message patterns, MTOM/XOP packaging, soap.beep/soap.beeps URL schemes and port registration; obsoletes RFC 3288.

BEEP.why: The document defines a new BEEP profile (boot/ready states, channel creation, message exchanges) for carrying SOAP, so BEEP readers need it.
BEEP.quote: This memo specifies a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) binding to the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) core.

URI.why: Defines and registers two new URI schemes with syntax and resolution rules, a substantial part of the document.
URI.quote: This memo defines two URL schemes, "soap.beep" and "soap.beeps", which identify the use of SOAP over BEEP over TCP.

rejected.why: SOAP envelopes are XML, but the document defines a transport binding, not an XML format or usage guidance.
MTOM/XOP multipart packaging is used, but the document only applies existing MIME packaging; it does not define MIME structure.
TLS is only mentioned as a mandatory tuning profile in Security Considerations and for soap.beeps; it is boilerplate-level substrate.
SRV lookup is used for address resolution of the URL scheme, but nothing new is defined about DNS.
HTTP is referenced only by analogy (Host header, abs_path); not about HTTP.
DIGEST-MD5 SASL is merely named as a required authentication tuning profile.

gaps.name: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about binding SOAP messaging to a transport, but the taxonomy has no SOAP or web services tag.

RFC4228.title: Requirements for an IETF Draft Submission Toolset
RFC4228.summary: Specifies requirements for an IETF toolset that automates Internet-Draft submission, validation, meta-data extraction, authentication and posting, replacing the Secretariat's manual process.

IETF process.why: The document is about IETF administrative procedure for Internet-Draft submission and posting, including WG approval, Secretariat handling, submission blackout and draft naming rules. No narrower tag fits, so the IETF process topic applies.
IETF process.quote: This document specifies requirements for an IETF toolset to facilitate Internet-Draft submission, validation, and posting.

rejected.why: XML drafts (RFC 2629 format) are one accepted input format and are validated, but the document is not about XML itself.
It concerns Internet-Drafts, not RFC publication. The RFC Editor is only mentioned as a downstream consumer of the drafts.
The xml2rfc vocabulary is only a draft input format that the toolset preprocesses and validates. The document does not define or change that vocabulary.
The web upload interface runs over HTTP, but HTTP is only the substrate. Nothing new is specified about it.
An email submission interface is one section, but the document does not specify email protocols. It uses email only for confirmation and notification.
The IPR boilerplate check is one validation rule among many. The document is not about IPR.

gaps.name: IETF tools / Internet-Draft submission tooling
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IETF tooling or the Internet-Draft submission and posting infrastructure. The closest is IETF process.

RFC4229.title: HTTP Header Field Registrations
RFC4229.summary: Defines the initial contents of the IANA permanent registry and provisional repository of HTTP header field names, listing each header with its status, controller and specification.

HTTP.why: The whole document catalogs HTTP header fields (Accept, Cache-Control, Host, etc.), so HTTP readers would look for it.
HTTP.quote: This document defines the initial contents of a permanent IANA registry for HTTP header fields and a provisional repository for HTTP header fields

IANA.why: It populates IANA registries per RFC 3864, so it is relevant to registry readers.
IANA.quote: This document defines the initial contents of an IANA registry that catalogs permanent HTTP header field-names

rejected.why: Cookie and Set-Cookie are only two of many registered entries; the document is not about state management.
DAV, Depth, Overwrite etc. are listed only as registry entries, not specified here.
Cache-Control, Age and Surrogate-* appear only as entries in a list.
Authorization and WWW-Authenticate are just registry entries.
Registry procedure for message headers is referenced, but this document is HTTP-specific entries.

RFC4230.title: RSVP Security Properties
RFC4230.summary: Informational analysis of the security properties of RSVP (INTEGRITY object, identity representation, integrity handshake, Kerberos/public-key user authentication, IPsec interactions) written for the NSIS working group.

RSVP.why: The whole document analyses RSVP's security mechanisms: INTEGRITY object, POLICY_DATA identity, integrity handshake, and shortcomings.
RSVP.quote: This document summarizes the security properties of RSVP.

Kerberos.why: Substantial parts cover Kerberos tickets in AUTH_DATA, session keys, last-hop issues, and an appendix on dictionary attacks against Kerberos.
Kerberos.quote: Kerberos may be used to create the key for the RSVP INTEGRITY object.

NSIS.why: Written for the NSIS working group as input to the design of a new signaling protocol, drawing lessons from RSVP.
NSIS.quote: This document summarizes the security properties of RSVP and is part of the overall process of analyzing other signaling protocols

rejected.why: Section 5.4 and 5.6 discuss IPsec interactions with RSVP, but only as a side issue, not the subject of the document.
Explicitly out of scope per the Introduction.
COPS is only the PEP-to-PDP transport mentioned in passing.
HMAC-MD5 is the keyed hash used in the INTEGRITY object; it is a mechanism relied upon, not the subject.
Authorization is discussed in several subsections but is not the main subject; the RSVP and security tags cover it.
Certificates appear only as one credential type among several, not as a subject of the document.

RFC4231.title: Identifiers and Test Vectors for HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512
RFC4231.summary: RFC 4231 provides ASN.1 object identifiers, XML algorithm URIs, and conformance test vectors for HMAC-SHA-224, -256, -384 and -512.

HMAC.why: The whole document is test vectors and identifiers for HMAC instantiated with SHA-2 hashes, so readers of the HMAC subject need it.
HMAC.quote: This document provides test vectors for the HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512 message authentication schemes.

SHA.why: The schemes are HMAC built on the SHA-2 family (SHA-224/256/384/512), and the test vectors exercise those block sizes. Readers of SHA would find it relevant.
SHA.quote: HMAC-SHA-224 is the realization of the HMAC message authentication code [1] using the SHA-224 hash function

rejected.why: ASN.1 OIDs are assigned, but ASN.1 is only the identification mechanism, not the subject; no ASN.1 modules or encoding rules are specified.
The algorithm URIs are meant for XML Signature use, but the document does not specify or extend XML-Signature; it is only a context reference.
CMS/S/MIME is only cited as an example of a protocol using the OIDs, via an informative reference.
Mentioned only as an example consumer of the identifiers.
The algorithm URIs are identifier values, not a subject about URI syntax or schemes.

RFC4233.title: Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) Q.921-User Adaptation Layer
RFC4233.summary: RFC 4233 specifies the ISDN Q.921-User Adaptation Layer (IUA), a SIGTRAN protocol that backhauls Q.921/Q.931 signalling between a Signaling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller over SCTP, and it obsoletes RFC 3057.

SIGTRAN.why: IUA is a SIGTRAN adaptation layer that carries ISDN signalling over IP between an SG and an MGC. The whole document specifies its messages, ASP/AS state machines and procedures.
SIGTRAN.quote: This document defines a protocol for backhauling of Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) Q.921 User messages over IP using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

rejected.why: SCTP is only the transport IUA runs over. The document does not define anything new about SCTP beyond a payload protocol identifier and a port number.

ISDN is the signalling system being backhauled. The document does not cover ISDN access or IP over ISDN. The ISDN-specific content is the Q.921/Q.931 primitive mapping, which belongs to the SIGTRAN adaptation layer.
The MGC and SG are the endpoints, but gateway control protocols such as Megaco and MGCP are not specified here.
This is the parent of SIGTRAN, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The IANA section only registers a payload protocol identifier and sets extension rules. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.

RFC4234.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF
RFC4234.summary: RFC 4234 specifies Augmented BNF (ABNF), the formal syntax notation used in Internet specifications, including its operators, its own ABNF definition, and a set of core rules.

ABNF.why: The document exists to define the ABNF notation: rule naming, operators, terminal values, the ABNF grammar of ABNF, and core rules.
ABNF.quote: a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications.

rejected.why: US-ASCII is only the character encoding assumed for the core rules and terminal strings, not the subject of the document.
RFC 733/822 are mentioned only as historical origin of ABNF; the document does not specify email message format.
External encodings are mentioned briefly but declared beyond the scope of ABNF.

RFC4235.title: An INVITE-Initiated Dialog Event Package for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4235.summary: Defines the SIP "dialog" event package and its application/dialog-info+xml format for subscribing to and notifying about INVITE-initiated dialog state, plus two new SIP media feature tags (sip.byeless, sip.rendering).

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new event package (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY), a dialog state machine, and new caller-capability feature parameters. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines a dialog event package for the SIP Events architecture, along with a data format used in notifications for this package.

media types.why: A substantial part defines and registers the application/dialog-info+xml media type with its schema and URN namespace, which readers of media type registrations would want.
media types.quote: This document registers a new MIME type, application/dialog-info+xml;

rejected.why: Related to presence/events but the document is an INVITE dialog event package, not a presence or XCAP extension; SIP covers it.
XML is only the encoding for the dialog-info format; the document is not about XML usage in general.
Presence and IM are mentioned only as motivating applications, not specified.
The sip.byeless and sip.rendering feature tags are defined under RFC 3840 caller capabilities, but this is a minor part and not about media feature negotiation as such.
Only mentioned as a SHOULD in Security Considerations; boilerplate substrate.

gaps.name: SIP Events framework / event packages
gaps.why: The document specifies a SIP event package (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, RFC 3265), but the taxonomy has no tag for SIP event notification; SIP is the nearest fit.

RFC4236.title: HTTP Adaptation with Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES)
RFC4236.summary: Specifies the HTTP profile for OPES: HTTP-specific OCP callout protocol extensions (message parts, profile features, AMS/DUM parameters), HTTP header correctness rules, and OPES-System/OPES-Via/OPES-Bypass HTTP headers for tracing and bypass.

OPES.why: The document is the HTTP application profile of the OPES callout protocol, tracing and bypass; it belongs on the OPES subject page.
OPES.quote: This document extends those generic mechanisms for adaptation of a specific application protocol, HTTP [RFC2616].

HTTP.why: It defines new HTTP extension headers (OPES-System, OPES-Via, OPES-Bypass) and rules for Content-Length, Content-MD5, transfer encodings and hop-by-hop headers when HTTP messages are adapted.
HTTP.quote: OPES processors MUST ensure correctness of all computable HTTP headers documented in specifications that the processors intend to be compliant with.

rejected.why: Only an IANA registration of profile feature URIs; not about media types.
The IANA section registers two profile URIs; that is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
The example trace uses a cdn.example.com host, but the document is not about content delivery.
Content-Encodings: (gzip) appears only as an example value; the document is not about gzip.
The document does not address caching; it covers message adaptation.

RFC4237.title: Voice Messaging Directory Service
RFC4237.summary: Defines the VPIM directory LDAP schema (vPIMUser object class and attributes) that maps a telephone number to a voice mailbox email address, spoken name, and media capabilities for voice messaging.

VPIM.why: The document is the directory service companion to VPIM, defining the schema for voice messaging addressing and capabilities.
VPIM.quote: This document provides details of the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) directory service.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAP schema (object class and attributes) with syntaxes and matching rules, so readers of LDAP would want it.
LDAP.quote: This query is expected to use LDAP [LDAP], a connection-oriented protocol.

rejected.why: It maps telephone numbers to email addresses but via LDAP, not E.164 numbers in the DNS.
DNS is only mentioned for redundancy and load balancing of the directory server.
Only the inter-domain SMTP address is stored; SMTP is not specified or extended.
The attribute carries MIME audio subtypes but the document does not register or define media types.

RFC4238.title: Voice Message Routing Service
RFC4238.summary: Defines two ways to route voice messages by telephone number: a complete service using ENUM to find a VPIM LDAP directory, and a basic send-and-pray service using ENUM NAPTR rewrite to build a mailto address routed via DNS MX records.

ENUM.why: Registers and specifies the E2U+VPIM:LDAP and E2U+VPIM:Mailto ENUM services and the NAPTR rewrite rules; ENUM is the core mechanism.
ENUM.quote: The VPIM directory server is found by using the ENUM protocol and querying for the VPIMDIR service associated with the telephone number of the recipient.

VPIM.why: The document is about routing VPIM voice messages by telephone number, including constructing VPIM addresses and intradomain routing of VPIM messages.
VPIM.quote: The complete service uses the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) Directory service to lookup a VPIM email address with a telephone number

rejected.why: LDAP is only used to query the VPIM directory; the directory schema is in RFC 4237, not here.
DNS NAPTR and MX are substrate for ENUM; nothing new is defined about DNS itself.
Message delivery uses ordinary SMTP/MX routing with no changes; SMTP is only substrate.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a mitigation.
Covered by the more specific VPIM tag; the document does not address email in general.
The document uses E.164 telephone numbers but does not specify the tel URI scheme.

RFC4239.title: Internet Voice Messaging (IVM)
RFC4239.summary: Defines how voicemail messages are carried over Internet mail (SMTP/MIME) for unified messaging, mandating G.711 mu-law audio/basic encoding, message context, critical content, notifications, and optional VPIM v2 interoperability.

VPIM.why: The taxonomy lists VPIM as the id for voice messaging over Internet mail.
VPIM.quote: This document describes the carriage of voicemail messages over Internet mail as part of a unified messaging infrastructure.

RFC4240.title: Basic Network Media Services with SIP
RFC4240.summary: Informational RFC defining a SIP Request-URI user-part convention (annc, dialog, conf) by which application servers invoke announcement, prompt-and-collect (VoiceXML), and basic conference services on multifunction media servers.

SIP.why: The document defines a SIP URI convention and parameters (play, repeat, delay, etc.) and INVITE handling with response codes for media servers. It is a SIP deployment/usage convention.
SIP.quote: This document describes how to identify to a multifunction media server what sort of session the client is requesting, without modifying the SIP protocol.

conferencing.why: A substantial section defines the basic conference (media mixing) service, with the media server acting as a Focus under the SIP conferencing framework.
conferencing.quote: sip:conf=uniqueIdentifier@mediaserver.example.net

MRCP.why: The prompt-and-collect/IVR service is a speech and media-resource service on media servers. MRCP is the closest taxonomy fit for that media-server control area, though this RFC does not specify MRCP itself.
MRCP.quote: The dialog service takes a parameter, voicexml=, indicating the URI of the VoiceXML script to execute.

rejected.why: The document defines SIP URI user-part conventions and parameters, but this is SIP-specific and not about generic URI syntax or schemes.
SDP negotiation is explicitly unmodified and only mentioned in passing.
RTP is only the media transport for announcements and mixing. The document does not specify it.
MIME types appear only as a content-type parameter value. The document has no media type registration.
The registration of SIP URI parameters is boilerplate-level and does not make the document about IANA.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.

gaps.name: Media server control / SIP media services (netann)
gaps.why: There is no tag for application-server-to-media-server interfaces or IVR/announcement services. MRCP is only an approximate fit.

RFC4241.title: A Model of IPv6/IPv4 Dual Stack Internet Access Service
RFC4241.summary: Informational digest of NTT Communications' IPv6/IPv4 dual stack ADSL access service, describing PPP/PPPoE-based dual stack connectivity with DHCPv6 prefix delegation and DNS server address delivery to CPE.

DHCPv6.why: The core of the automatic configuration is DHCPv6 prefix delegation plus DNS server options, so DHCPv6 readers would want this deployment model.
DHCPv6.quote: The PE delegates prefixes to CPE using Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) [RFC3633] with the prefix delegation options

PPPoE.why: The access architecture runs IPv4 and IPv6 (IPCP and IPV6CP) over a single PPPoE session with CHAP, and this is a substantial part of the specification.
PPPoE.quote: Only PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) and its upper layers are mentioned

IPv6 transition.why: The document models a dual stack service in which IPv6 and IPv4 run independently over one link, which is an IPv6/IPv4 coexistence mechanism.
IPv6 transition.quote: IPv6/IPv4 dual stack service is specified as follows.
