DSL.why: The service is an ADSL access network offering, so DSL access readers would find it relevant.
DSL.quote: The architecture is mainly targeted at a leased-line ADSL service for home users.

rejected.why: DNS server addresses are only delivered via DHCPv6 options; the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
ICMPv6 Echo is used for connectivity monitoring only as a minor point.
Hosts use conventional stateless autoconfiguration, but it is only mentioned in passing.
Targets home users, but it specifies the ISP access interface rather than home network architecture.
An AAA server supplies prefixes to the PE, but this is a supporting detail and AAA is not specified.
Parent of the chosen IPv6 transition tag; the document is about the dual stack model, not IPv6 in general.

RFC4242.title: Information Refresh Time Option for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC4242.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 Information Refresh Time option, an upper bound on how long a stateless DHCPv6 client waits before refreshing its configuration data, with client and server behaviour and option format.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option, including its format and client and server behaviour in Information-Request/Reply exchanges.
DHCPv6.quote: a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) option for specifying an upper bound for how long a client should wait before refreshing information

rejected.why: Stateless autoconfiguration is mentioned only as background for why stateless DHCPv6 needs a refresh time. The document does not specify it.
Renumbering is cited as one use case for the option. The document does not address renumbering procedures.
This is the parent of DHCPv6, so it is implied and not listed separately.
IPv6 is only the environment the option runs in. The document is about DHCPv6 and not the IPv6 protocol.

RFC4243.title: Vendor-Specific Information Suboption for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Relay Agent Option
RFC4243.summary: Defines a new Vendor-Specific Information suboption (code 9) for the DHCP relay agent information option, letting relay agents carry opaque vendor-defined data keyed by enterprise number in forwarded DHCP messages.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCP's relay agent information option with a new suboption and specifies relay agent and server behaviour for it.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a new DHCP relay agent option suboption that carries vendor-defined data.

rejected.why: The document covers DHCP for IPv4 only (DHCPv4 relay agent option).
DOCSIS cable networks are mentioned only as an example environment where relay agent information is used.
xDSL is mentioned only as an example environment, and the document is not about DSL access networks.
The IANA section only assigns suboption number 9, which is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC4244.title: An Extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for Request History Information
RFC4244.summary: Defines the SIP History-Info header, the "histinfo" option tag and the "history" Privacy priv-value, which capture the retargeting history of a SIP request, along with requirements, processing rules, and example call flows.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field, option tag and privacy value, and specifies UAC, UAS, proxy and redirect server behaviour for them.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new optional SIP header, History-Info, for capturing the history information in requests.

rejected.why: TLS is only the recommended hop-by-hop security mechanism for protecting History-Info. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
SDP bodies appear only in the example messages and are not part of the subject.
The Privacy header handling (RFC 3323) is a substantial part of the document. However, it is SIP-specific privacy for one header, and the general privacy-considerations topic doesn't fit.
RTP appears only as media lines in the example SDP.
The IANA section registers the header, option tag and priv-value. It is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC4245.title: High-Level Requirements for Tightly Coupled SIP Conferencing
RFC4245.summary: Informational RFC listing high-level requirements for tightly coupled SIP conferencing: discovery, creation, termination, participant manipulation, conference state, focus migration, side-bars, cascading, and SIMPLE coordination.

conferencing.why: The whole document defines requirements for a multiparty conferencing framework (focus, participants, conference state, policies), which is the conferencing topic. XCON is a specific framework that this RFC does not itself define, so the parent topic fits.
conferencing.quote: This document examines a wide range of conferencing requirements for tightly coupled SIP conferences.

SIP.why: The requirements are for SIP-based conferencing: dialogs, dial-in/dial-out, invitations, and focus behaviour built on SIP call control. Readers of SIP would want it.
SIP.quote: A SIP conference is an association of SIP user agents (i.e., conference participants) with a central point (i.e., a conference focus)

rejected.why: Section 3.9 only requires coordination between SIMPLE presence/IM and SIP conferencing. SIMPLE is not specified or extended here.
This RFC predates the XCON framework and data model. It supplies requirements but does not define the framework.
Floor control is mentioned only as a topic for separate documents.
Instant messaging appears only in one coordination requirement (3.9), not as a main subject.

RFC4246.title: International Standard Audiovisual Number (ISAN) URN Definition
RFC4246.summary: Registers the ISAN (International Standard Audiovisual Number) URN namespace identifier using the RFC 3406 template, giving its structure, formal syntax, uniqueness, persistence, assignment and resolution rules.

URN.why: The whole document is a URN namespace registration for ISAN, so it belongs on the URN page. It follows the RFC 3406 template and defines the URN syntax.
URN.quote: This document is the definition of the formal Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace Identifier (NID) for ISAN.

rejected.why: The document gives a short BNF for the ISAN-NSS, but it only uses the notation. It is not about the notation.
The IANA section only requests the NID registration. That is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
Streaming media is mentioned only as a possible future use in Community Considerations. It is not what the document is about.

RFC4247.title: Requirements for Header Compression over MPLS
RFC4247.summary: Informational requirements document for carrying compressed RTP/UDP/IP headers (via ECRTP or ROHC) across an MPLS LSP without per-hop compression/decompression, with problem statement, goals, candidate methods and signalling needs.

header compression.why: The whole document states requirements for header compression of RTP/UDP/IP over MPLS, which is the general header compression subject.
header compression.quote: We consider using MPLS to route compressed packets over an MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) without compression/decompression cycles at each router.

ROHC.why: ROHC is one of the two candidate compression methods analysed, including its reordering and packet type identification needs.
ROHC.quote: [ROHC] is also very tolerant of packet loss, and therefore is a candidate method to guard against frequent resynchronizations.

CRTP.why: Enhanced compressed RTP and cRTP are analysed as candidates, with needed extensions for packet type identification over MPLS.
CRTP.quote: [ECRTP] uses mechanisms that make cRTP more tolerant to packet loss

MPLS.why: The document is about using MPLS LSPs to carry compressed headers, including reordering and signalling (LDP, RSVP-TE) extensions needed.
MPLS.quote: the compressed packet routed on an MPLS LSP using MPLS labels, and the compressed header would be decompressed at the egress router/gateway

rejected.why: RTP headers are what gets compressed, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
Signalling extensions are suggested as needed, but are to be developed in a separate document.
Mentioned as a possible signalling protocol needing extension; not the subject of this document.
Not relevant; the document concerns VoIP only as an application context.

RFC4248.title: The telnet URI Scheme
RFC4248.summary: RFC 4248 re-specifies the telnet URI scheme (copied from RFC 1738) so that RFC 1738 can be obsoleted, defining the telnet://user:password@host:port/ form for designating interactive Telnet services.

URI.why: The document defines a URI scheme: its syntax, default port, and handling of user and password. It belongs on the URI page.
URI.quote: The Telnet URL scheme is used to designate interactive services that may be accessed by the Telnet protocol

Telnet.why: The scheme exists to designate Telnet services. The document also discusses how Telnet security extensions relate to the scheme, so Telnet readers would want it.
Telnet.quote: Many RFCs have added various services to the Telnet protocol for better authentication, encryption of traffic, or both.

rejected.why: The document does not mention TLS. It only mentions secure Telnet extensions generally.
The Telnet authentication option appears only in the Security Considerations and in passing. The document is not about authentication.
The scheme is a URI matter. The document is not about web architecture.

RFC4249.title: Implementer-Friendly Specification of Message and MIME-Part Header Fields and Field Components
RFC4249.summary: Informational guide for authors of extension header fields in Internet messages and MIME parts, listing what a specification should state (naming, ABNF, cardinality, semantics, compatibility).

message format.why: The whole memo is guidance on specifying message header fields and field components under the Internet Message Format, including naming prefixes, categories and Resent- rules.
message format.quote: Message headers and MIME-part headers consist of fields.

MIME.why: MIME-part header fields are co-equal subject of the guidance, including the Content- prefix rule and context of MIME-part headers.
MIME.quote: This prefix must be used for all MIME extension fields and must not be used for fields that are not MIME extension fields

rejected.why: ABNF is discussed as a thing extension specs should use correctly, but the memo does not specify or profile ABNF itself.
Only brief advice about registries for keywords; the main body is about header field specification.
Parent of message format; the more specific tag is chosen.
Guides spec authors, but about header fields rather than RFC format or publication.
MIME media types are only mentioned as a context where fields might appear.
Only a short note on language tagging of human-readable field text.

RFC4250.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Assigned Numbers
RFC4250.summary: RFC 4250 initializes the IANA registries for the SSH protocol, listing initial message numbers, reason codes, terminal mode opcodes, and algorithm/method names, and gives allocation policies for future assignments.

SSH.why: The entire document enumerates SSH protocol message numbers, reason codes, channel types, and algorithm names. SSH readers would look here for the assigned numbers.
SSH.quote: This document does not define any new protocols.  It is intended only to create the initial state of the IANA databases for the SSH protocol

IANA.why: The document's purpose is to set up IANA registries and the allocation policies (STANDARDS ACTION, IETF CONSENSUS, PRIVATE USE) for future assignments.
IANA.quote: This entire document is the IANA considerations for the SSH protocol, as defined in [SSH-ARCH], [SSH-TRANS], [SSH-USERAUTH], [SSH-CONNECT].

rejected.why: AES appears only as algorithm names in a registry table; the document does not specify or analyse it.
hmac-sha1 and hmac-md5 are listed only as registered MAC names, not specified.
IKE/Oakley groups are mentioned only to explain naming of SSH key exchange methods.
des-cbc is listed as a HISTORIC name only in one registry row.
Pseudo-terminal opcodes are SSH connection protocol items, not Telnet.

RFC4251.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Architecture
RFC4251.summary: RFC 4251 describes the overall architecture of the SSH protocol (transport, user authentication, connection layers), its host key trust models, extensibility, data type notation, algorithm naming, message numbers, and consolidated security considerations.

SSH.why: The document is the architectural specification of the SSH protocol, defining its components, host key model, notation, naming, and security properties.
SSH.quote: Secure Shell (SSH) is a protocol for secure remote login and other secure network services over an insecure network.

rejected.why: TCP is only the typical substrate the SSH transport runs over; nothing new is specified about TCP.
X11 forwarding is discussed only in the security considerations as a connection protocol use; the document is not about X.
Algorithms are negotiated and discussed in passing; the document explicitly says it does not analyze or recommend specific ciphers.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate summarizing RFC 4250; the main body is not about IANA registries.
Host key trust models mention CAs briefly, but the document is not about PKI itself.
Pseudo-random number generation is a short security-considerations subsection, not a main subject.

gaps.name: SSH (Secure Shell) protocol architecture
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists SSH under security, but the id I used is the taxonomy's 'SSH'; the taxonomy entry is 'SSH' [tech], so no real gap.

RFC4252.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Authentication Protocol
RFC4252.summary: RFC 4252 specifies the SSH user authentication protocol framework and the publickey, password, and hostbased client authentication methods, which run over the SSH transport layer.

SSH.why: The document is one of the core SSH protocol specifications, defining the ssh-userauth service, its message formats and authentication methods.
SSH.quote: This document describes the SSH authentication protocol framework and public key, password, and host-based client authentication methods.

rejected.why: Generic authentication topic; the SSH tech tag is more specific and the document is about SSH user authentication, not cross-protocol authentication.
Password normalization refers to SASLprep (RFC 4013), but SASL is not specified or used by this protocol.
Usernames and passwords are encoded in UTF-8, but this is just an encoding used, not the document's subject.
Public key blobs may contain certificates, but this is only a passing mention.
Not discussed; the protocol runs over the SSH transport layer, which is the substrate.

RFC4253.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol
RFC4253.summary: Specifies the SSH transport layer protocol: connection setup, version exchange, binary packet protocol, algorithm negotiation, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, key re-exchange and service requests, providing encryption, host authentication and integrity.

SSH.why: The document defines the SSH transport layer protocol in full, including packet format, negotiation, key exchange and messages.
SSH.quote: This document describes the SSH transport layer protocol, which typically runs on top of TCP/IP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the usual substrate; Section 4.1 just notes port 22 use over TCP/IP.
AES is one of many negotiated ciphers listed in Section 6.3; the document is not about it.
HMAC-SHA1/MD5 are listed as MAC algorithms; used, not specified or analysed.
ssh-rsa key format is defined in Section 6.6, but only as one public key type; the document is not about RSA.
Key exchange here is part of the SSH protocol itself, already covered by the SSH tag.
3des-cbc is a required cipher but only one of many negotiated algorithms; the document is not about DES.

RFC4254.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Connection Protocol
RFC4254.summary: RFC 4254 specifies the SSH Connection Protocol, which multiplexes interactive sessions, remote command execution, TCP/IP port forwarding and X11 forwarding as channels over an SSH transport.

SSH.why: The document defines one layer of the SSH protocol: channel mechanism, session requests, port forwarding and terminal mode encoding.
SSH.quote: This document describes the SSH Connection Protocol. It provides interactive login sessions, remote execution of commands, forwarded TCP/IP connections, and forwarded X11 connections.

rejected.why: X11 forwarding is one channel type, but the document does not specify the X protocol itself; it only forwards it.
TCP/IP port forwarding relays connections over SSH channels. It does not specify or extend TCP.
The IANA considerations only point to RFC 4250 and are boilerplate. The reason code and data type registry notes are minor.
Interactive login sessions with pty requests are functionally similar to Telnet, but Telnet is not discussed or used.
The DNS extensibility naming convention is only borrowed for naming request and channel types.

RFC4255.title: Using DNS to Securely Publish Secure Shell (SSH) Key Fingerprints
RFC4255.summary: Defines the SSHFP DNS resource record for publishing SSH host key fingerprints and describes how SSH clients verify host keys using DNSSEC-authenticated lookups.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS RR type (code 44), its RDATA and presentation format, so it belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: this document defines a new DNS resource record, "SSHFP", to carry the fingerprint.

SSH.why: It specifies a host key verification method for SSH clients, with fingerprint matching and client policy guidance.
SSH.quote: the SSH client MAY look up the SSHFP resource record(s) for the host it is connecting to.

DNSSEC.why: The method relies on DNSSEC validation, and the document sets requirements for how clients validate or obtain validated responses. It defines no new DNSSEC mechanism, so this is secondary.
DNSSEC.quote: A public key verified using this method MUST NOT be trusted if the SSHFP resource record (RR) used for verification was not authenticated by a trusted SIG RR.

rejected.why: DANE covers TLSA records and certificate association. SSHFP is a precursor of that idea, but the document does not mention or specify DANE.
Secure dynamic update is mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations as a way to transfer fingerprints.
SHA-1 is only the one fingerprint digest type that is assigned. The document is not about the hash family.
RSA and DSS are only algorithm number values in the RR format.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-level here and support the new RR type, so this is not a subject of the document.

RFC4256.title: Generic Message Exchange Authentication for the Secure Shell Protocol (SSH)
RFC4256.summary: Defines the SSH "keyboard-interactive" user authentication method, a generic server-driven prompt/response exchange that lets clients support arbitrary interactive authentication mechanisms without knowing their specifics.

SSH.why: The RFC specifies a new SSH userauth method, including its message formats (INFO_REQUEST/INFO_RESPONSE), client UI behaviour and message numbers. Readers of the SSH subject would expect it.
SSH.quote: This document describes a general purpose authentication method for the SSH authentication protocol.

rejected.why: The SSH tag already sits under security, and the document is specific to SSH user authentication. The generic authentication topic is not needed.
One-time passwords and challenge-response are mentioned as supported use cases and shown in an example, but the document does not specify them.
SASLprep is cited only for password normalization. SASL itself is not specified or used.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the string fields. The document does not define anything new about it.
The deprecated language tag field is a minor detail and not a substantial part of the document.
Not relevant. The method relies on the SSH transport layer for confidentiality, which is boilerplate-level substrate reliance.

RFC4257.title: Framework for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)-based Control of Synchronous Digital Hierarchy/Synchronous Optical Networking (SDH/SONET) Networks
RFC4257.summary: Informational framework describing how GMPLS routing and signaling extensions can control SDH/SONET TDM networks, covering switching capabilities, protection, capacity advertisement, path computation, and label structure and signaling elements.

GMPLS.why: The whole document is a framework for applying GMPLS routing and signaling to circuit-switched SDH/SONET networks.
GMPLS.quote: This document illustrates this process by describing those extensions to GMPLS protocols that are aimed at controlling Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) or Synchronous Optical Networking (SONET) networks.

SONET.why: A large part of the document describes the SDH/SONET multiplex, concatenation, transparency and protection, and how each is controlled. Readers of the SONET/SDH subject would want it.
SONET.quote: SDH and SONET are two TDM standards widely used by operators to transport and multiplex different tributary signals over optical links

rejected.why: The signaling elements section relies on RSVP-TE objects but only summarizes RFC 3473 and RFC 3946. It does not specify or extend them.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned as the link-state routing protocols that carry the information. The document does not define the extensions.
The document mentions traffic engineering and path computation, but they are not its main subject. GMPLS is the more specific tag.
The MPLS overview is background. The document is about GMPLS, which is a child of MPLS and is already tagged.
The document compares centralized NMS control with distributed control. This is a side discussion and not the subject.

gaps.name: SDH/SONET optical transport networks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SDH/SONET TDM transport as a circuit-switched technology. SONET exists only as IP-over-SONET under link layer, which does not fit a document about controlling the TDM multiplex.

RFC4258.title: Requirements for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Routing for the Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON)
RFC4258.summary: Informational CCAMP document stating the routing requirements that the ITU-T ASON control plane architecture (G.8080, G.7715, G.7715.1) places on GMPLS routing protocols: hierarchical routing areas, information dissemination between levels, configuration, evolution and routing attributes.

GMPLS.why: The whole document is a set of requirements on GMPLS routing for ASON, so readers of the GMPLS subject would look for it.
GMPLS.quote: This document concentrates on the routing requirements placed on the GMPLS suite of protocols in order to support the capabilities and functionalities of an Automatically Switched Optical Network

routing architecture.why: A large part of the document covers hierarchical routing areas, routing controllers, information abstraction and scalability, which is routing architecture.
routing architecture.quote: The ASON routing architecture defines a multi-level routing hierarchy of RAs based on a containment model to support routing information abstraction.

rejected.why: OSPF multi-areas are mentioned only as an example of a protocol realization. The document explicitly leaves protocol design and applicability out of scope.
SONET/SDH appear only as switching technologies GMPLS can control. The document is not about IP over SONET.
TE link information is mentioned in passing in terminology. The document is not about traffic engineering.
No IS-IS content. The document is protocol-neutral and does not specify any particular routing protocol.

gaps.name: ASON (Automatically Switched Optical Network) control plane / optical transport network control
gaps.why: The document is about ITU-T ASON routing requirements. The taxonomy has no optical or transport-network control tag beyond GMPLS.

RFC4259.title: A Framework for Transmission of IP Datagrams over MPEG-2 Networks
RFC4259.summary: Informational framework describing the architecture and requirements for carrying IPv4/IPv6 datagrams over MPEG-2 Transport Streams (DVB/ATSC), covering encapsulation requirements, address resolution and multicast support.

DVB.why: The whole document is about IP over MPEG-2/DVB broadcast links: encapsulation requirements, address resolution to PIDs and multicast mapping.
DVB.quote: This document describes an architecture for the transport of IP Datagrams over ISO MPEG-2 Transport Streams (TS).

rejected.why: Multicast support and address resolution for multicast is a section, but it is applied to MPEG-2 link mapping, not IP multicast routing; the DVB tag is the better fit.
Address resolution is discussed in analogy to ARP/ND, but the document defines requirements for an MPEG-2-specific AR, not ARP itself.
Satellite scenarios are examples of MPEG-2 networks, but the document is about MPEG-2 TS generally rather than satellite networking.
ROHC is mentioned only as a type-field requirement; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned in security considerations only as an end-to-end mechanism.
IPv6 is supported as a payload but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

gaps.name: ULE / MPEG-2 Transport Stream encapsulation
gaps.why: The document motivates Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation and MPEG-2 TS address resolution; taxonomy only has the broad DVB tag rather than a specific ULE/ipdvb tag.

RFC4260.title: Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers for 802.11 Networks
RFC4260.summary: Informational RFC describing how Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers (FMIPv6) can be applied over IEEE 802.11 links, tracing 802.11 handover steps against FMIPv6 message exchanges in predictive and reactive scenarios.

IP mobility.why: The document is about Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover (FMIPv6) deployment, which is IP-layer mobility. The taxonomy has no FMIPv6-specific tag, and Mobile IPv6 is a technology tag that would fit only the base protocol, so the parent IP mobility topic is used.
IP mobility.quote: This document describes how a Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover could be implemented on link layers conforming to the 802.11 suite of specifications.

WiFi.why: A large part of the document details 802.11 handover steps (scan, join, authenticate, re-associate), AP/AR deployment architectures and beacon scanning, so it belongs under IP over 802.11.
WiFi.quote: This document gives a set of deployment examples for Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers on 802.11 networks.

rejected.why: The document builds on Mobile IPv6 but specifies fast handover (RFC 4068) over 802.11. Basic Mobile IPv6 is only mentioned as the fallback.
802.1X/EAPOL authentication is discussed only in the security considerations as it affects handover delay. It is not the document's subject.
RtSolPr/PrRtAdv are FMIPv6 messages derived from router discovery, but the document does not specify neighbor discovery.
RADIUS and Diameter are mentioned in passing as back-end servers in the 802.1X exchange.

gaps.name: Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is FMIPv6 (RFC 4068), and the taxonomy has no tag for it under Mobile IPv6 or IP mobility.

RFC4261.title: Common Open Policy Service (COPS) Over Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC4261.summary: Specifies how to secure COPS connections with TLS using upward negotiation via a new Integrity-TLS object in Client-Open/Client-Accept, defines error codes, closure behaviour, certificate-based endpoint identification and cipher suite requirements, and updates RFC 2748's Client-Accept message.

COPS.why: The document extends COPS with a new Integrity-TLS object, error codes and a modified Client-Accept message, so it belongs on the COPS page.
COPS.quote: This document describes how to use COPS over TLS. "COPS over TLS" is abbreviated COPS/TLS.

TLS.why: It profiles TLS use for COPS: handshake initiation, closure alerts, certificate identity checks and a mandatory cipher suite. Readers of TLS deployment guidance would want it.
TLS.quote: Once the TLS connection is established, all COPS data MUST be sent as TLS "application data".

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are required for endpoint identity, but only by reference to RFC 3280. The document defines nothing new about the certificate profile.
The document does bind COPS to TLS. The more specific COPS and TLS tags cover it better, and the taxonomy says to give a topic tag directly only when no technology tag under it is chosen.
Trust anchors and CAs are mentioned only as deployment requirements, not as a subject of the document.
COPS is policy provisioning, not AAA. The access control discussion is limited to PDP/PEP authorization.

RFC4262.title: X.509 Certificate Extension for Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Capabilities
RFC4262.summary: Defines an X.509 certificate extension that carries S/MIME Capabilities (e.g., content encryption algorithms) so senders can pick suitable encryption for recipients with unknown capabilities.

S/MIME.why: The extension complements the S/MIME SMIMECapabilities attribute and helps S/MIME senders choose content encryption algorithms. S/MIME readers would want it.
S/MIME.quote: This document defines a certificate extension for inclusion of S/MIME Capabilities in X.509 public key certificates

X.509.why: It defines a new X.509 v3 certificate extension, including its content and criticality rules, as profiled by RFC 3280.
X.509.quote: This extension MUST NOT be marked critical.

rejected.why: The SMIMECapabilities attribute is reused, but CMS is not specified or extended here.
ASN.1 is only the notation for illustrating the structure, which is identical to the existing attribute.
The X.509 tag is the more specific fit. The document does not address PKI operations in general.
S/MIME is the specific subject. The document does not deal with MIME body structure.

RFC4263.title: Media Subtype Registration for Media Type text/troff
RFC4263.summary: Registers the text/troff media subtype for troff-family source (text plus formatting directives), defining its optional parameters (charset, process, resources, versions), encoding, interoperability and security considerations.

media types.why: The document is a media type registration (text/troff) using the registration form of RFC 4288, so it belongs under media type registrations.
media types.quote: A text media subtype for tagging content consisting of juxtaposed text and formatting directives as used by the troff series of programs

rejected.why: MIME is the framework the registration lives in; the document defines no new MIME mechanism beyond the subtype, which the media types tag covers.
The charset parameter is described, but only as an ordinary parameter of the registration, not as a charset topic.
SMTP appears only as the subject of an example diagram.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as a possible 8bit encoding of Unicode input in the encoding considerations.
The Internationalization Considerations section is short boilerplate-like content, not the document's main subject.

gaps.name: troff document formatting language
gaps.why: The document is about the troff/nroff formatting format and its preprocessors and macro packages, and the taxonomy has no tag for typesetting or document markup formats of this kind.

RFC4264.title: BGP Wedgies
RFC4264.summary: Informational problem-statement memo describing "BGP Wedgies": BGP policy configurations (primary/backup via communities and local preference) with multiple stable states, including unintended ones that BGP may select non-deterministically.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses BGP policy interaction and convergence to unintended stable states, i.e. BGP behaviour and operations.
BGP.quote: a class of BGP configurations for which there is more than one potential outcome, and where forwarding states other than the intended state are equally stable

BGP communities.why: The wedgie examples hinge on communities marking routes as 'backup only' or 'primary', which set local preference; a substantial part of the analysis.
BGP communities.quote: An alternative approach to routing policy specification uses BGP communities [RFC1997].

rejected.why: Concerns BGP policy behaviour specifically, so the BGP tag fits better than the general architecture topic.
Primary/backup inbound traffic engineering is the motivating context, but the document does not address traffic engineering mechanisms such as MPLS-TE.
The Security Considerations mention possible exploitation by session resets, but this is boilerplate-level and not the main subject.

RFC4265.title: Definition of Textual Conventions for Virtual Private Network (VPN) Management
RFC4265.summary: Defines the VPN-TC-STD-MIB module with SMIv2 textual conventions (VPNId, VPNIdOrZero) for the Global VPN Identifier of RFC 2685, for use in VPN-related MIBs.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining SMIv2 textual conventions, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

VPN.why: The conventions model the VPN identifier used by provider-provisioned VPN MIBs, so VPN readers would want it. No specific VPN flavour (L3VPN etc.) is addressed beyond the working group.
VPN.quote: it defines Textual Conventions used in Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) and IETF VPN-related MIBs.

rejected.why: Produced by the l3vpn WG, but the VPN-ID textual convention is generic and not specific to BGP/MPLS L3VPN.
SNMP is only the framework in which MIBs are accessed; the document defines no SNMP protocol behavior.
Implied as an ancestor of MIB; not chosen directly.

RFC4266.title: The gopher URI Scheme
RFC4266.summary: Copies the gopher URI scheme definition from RFC 1738 so it stays on standards track, specifying syntax for Gopher and Gopher+ resources, searches, attributes, views and forms.

URI.why: The document defines a URI scheme: its syntax, defaults and encoding of components. It belongs on the URI page.
URI.quote: The gopher URL scheme is used to designate Internet resources accessible using the Gopher protocol.

Gopher.why: Much of the body explains how URLs map to Gopher and Gopher+ selectors, searches, attributes, views and forms. Readers of the Gopher subject would want it.
Gopher.quote: Gopher clients specify which item to retrieve by sending the Gopher selector string to a Gopher server.

rejected.why: The document covers only URIs and does not address internationalized identifiers.
There is no IANA section, and the scheme registration is not the subject of the body.

RFC4267.title: The W3C Speech Interface Framework Media Types: application/voicexml+xml, application/ssml+xml, application/srgs, application/srgs+xml, application/ccxml+xml, and application/pls+xml
RFC4267.summary: Registers six W3C Speech Interface Framework media types (VoiceXML, SSML, SRGS in ABNF and XML forms, CCXML, PLS) with IANA.

media types.why: The RFC exists to register six MIME media types, giving their encoding, file extensions, magic numbers and change controller.
media types.quote: This document defines the media types for the languages of the W3C Speech Interface Framework

rejected.why: The registered types are XML-based and refer to RFC 3023, but the RFC registers media types and does not specify XML usage.
MRCP is a speech services control protocol. This RFC only registers markup language media types and does not define or discuss MRCP.
SRGS has an ABNF form, but the RFC only gives its magic number and media type. It does not define ABNF.
The Security Considerations cite RFC 3986, but that is boilerplate. The document is not about URIs.

gaps.name: W3C Speech Interface Framework (VoiceXML, SSML, SRGS, CCXML, PLS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for speech markup languages or voice browser technology. The closest existing tags are MRCP and media types, which only partly cover it.

RFC4268.title: Entity State MIB
RFC4268.summary: Defines the ENTITY-STATE-MIB, extending the Entity MIB with administrative, operational, usage, alarm and standby state objects for physical entities, plus a companion module of state textual conventions.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification (ENTITY-STATE-MIB and ENTITY-STATE-TC-MIB) in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it describes extensions to the Entity MIB to provide information about the state of physical entities.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not protocol behaviour.
Parent of MIB and implied by the MIB tag; no need to list it separately.
Alarm and state reporting touch on OAM, but the document is a MIB definition, not an OAM mechanism.
SMIv2 syntax is used for the definitions, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encodings.

RFC4269.title: The SEED Encryption Algorithm
RFC4269.summary: RFC 4269 specifies the SEED 128-bit Feistel block cipher (round function, S-boxes, key schedule, OIDs, test vectors), obsoleting RFC 4009 with clarified definitions.

cryptography.why: The document specifies a block cipher algorithm. No child tag fits SEED (Korean ARIA and GOST are different ciphers), so the parent topic cryptography is used.
cryptography.quote: This document describes the SEED encryption algorithm, which has been adopted by most of the security systems in the Republic of Korea.

rejected.why: ARIA is a different Korean block cipher; SEED is not covered by it.
The OIDs are given in ASN.1 notation, but only as a small incidental piece of the document.
A SEED-based MAC OID is defined, but it is not HMAC.
SEED is a separate cipher and AES is not specified or discussed in the document.
DES is a different, older cipher and is not covered here.
The PBE OID refers to RFC 2898, but the document does not address password hashing.

gaps.name: SEED block cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SEED. Other national ciphers (ARIA, Camellia, GOST) each have a tag, so SEED readers can only find the document under the generic cryptography topic.

RFC4270.title: Attacks on Cryptographic Hashes in Internet Protocols
RFC4270.summary: Informational RFC summarizing collision attacks on MD5 and SHA-1, how Internet protocols use hashes, which uses are affected (signatures, certificates), mitigations for PKIX certificates, and advice on migrating to stronger hashes.

MD5.why: The document analyses attacks on MD5 and urges migration away from it, especially MD5, so MD5 readers would want it.
MD5.quote: the MD5 hash algorithm was susceptible to collision attacks

SHA.why: It covers attacks on SHA-1 and discusses migration to SHA-256, so it belongs under the SHA family.
SHA.quote: The Internet protocol community needs to migrate in an orderly manner away from SHA-1 and MD5

X.509.why: A substantial section covers collision attacks on PKIX certificates and ways to make certificate fields unpredictable.
X.509.quote: shows how to thwart known attacks on digital certificates

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example of a protocol that uses signatures. The document is not about it.
Mentioned only as an example of a protocol that uses signatures. The document is not about it.
X.509 is the more specific fit for the certificate discussion.
Message authentication with shared secrets is only briefly said to be unaffected, and HMAC is not named.
The parent tag is implied by the MD5 and SHA tags.

RFC4271.title: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)
RFC4271.summary: RFC 4271 specifies BGP-4, the inter-AS routing protocol: message formats, path attributes, error handling, the finite state machine, the decision process, and aggregation, obsoleting RFC 1771.

BGP.why: The document is the base specification of BGP-4, covering messages, path attributes, FSM, decision process and timers.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol.

rejected.why: BGP only uses TCP as transport (port 179) and the TCP MD5 option for authentication; the document does not define anything new about TCP.
BGP-4 supports CIDR via prefix advertisement and aggregation, but the document specifies BGP, not CIDR itself.
Route reflection and confederations are only referenced as separate extensions (RFC 2796, RFC 3065).
Security Considerations only mention TCP MD5 protection; the body is not about routing security.
IANA registries for BGP message types and attributes are boilerplate-level considerations, not the document's subject.

RFC4272.title: BGP Security Vulnerabilities Analysis
RFC4272.summary: Informational analysis of security vulnerabilities in BGP-4 message processing and its TCP substrate, covering attacks by outsiders and legitimate peers, residual risks, and operational protections.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses BGP message types, FSM events and path attributes for vulnerabilities, so it belongs on the BGP page.
BGP.quote: This document discusses the vulnerabilities of BGP, based on the BGP specification [RFC4271].

routing security.why: It is a threat and vulnerability analysis of routing protocol security, including origination and AS_PATH protection options and operational filtering. No RPKI or BGPsec technology is specified, so the parent topic fits.
routing security.quote: no mechanism has been specified within BGP to validate the authority of an AS to announce NLRI information.

rejected.why: TCP attacks (SYN, RST) are discussed only as the substrate BGP runs over, not as a TCP specification or extension.
Mentioned only as an alternative to TCP MD5 for confidentiality in Security Considerations; the document is not about IPsec.
TCP MD5 signature option is referenced as an existing protection, but the document does not address MD5 itself.
DoS against port 179 is mentioned briefly and operational filtering is discussed, but this is a minor part of the document.
Section 4.2 on ISP filtering is a small portion; the document's focus is vulnerability analysis.
Origination signing is only mentioned as a possible future solution, with no RPKI specification.

RFC4273.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for BGP-4
RFC4273.summary: Defines the BGP4-MIB SMIv2 module (obsoleting RFC 1269 and 1657) for managing BGP-4 implementations, with peer table, received path attribute table, notifications and conformance groups.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (BGP4-MIB) defining managed objects, tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

BGP.why: The managed objects model BGP peers, FSM state, timers and received path attributes, so BGP readers will want this MIB.
BGP.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the Border Gateway Protocol Version 4 or lower

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag covers it.
Only referenced as the connection transport for BGP peer ports; not a subject.
Parent of MIB, implied by the MIB tag.
Security Considerations is boilerplate about SNMP access to objects, not routing security.

RFC4274.title: BGP-4 Protocol Analysis
RFC4274.summary: RFC 4274 is an informational report analysing BGP-4 for Draft Standard advancement, summarizing its features, FSM, capabilities, scaling and performance, and policy-expressiveness implications.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses BGP-4: features, path vector algorithm, FSM, scalability, policy-induced instability and applicability.
BGP.quote: this report augments RFC 1774 and summarizes the key features of BGP-4, as well as analyzes the protocol with respect to scaling and performance

rejected.why: Communities are only mentioned as an example of policy expressiveness, not the subject.
TCP is only the transport BGP runs over.
Security Considerations only summarise TCP MD5, IPsec and GTSM; not the main body.
RPSL is only cited as an example of a policy language.
CIDR is mentioned as the reason for BGP-4 aggregation, not analysed.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations.

RFC4275.title: BGP-4 MIB Implementation Survey
RFC4275.summary: A survey of three vendor implementations (Cisco, NextHop, Redback) of the BGP-4 MIB (RFC 1657 / RFC 4274) agents, reporting which MIB objects, read-write objects, and traps are implemented, with SNMP manager interoperability and raw MIB walks.

MIB.why: The whole document reports implementation coverage of the BGP-4 MIB objects, notifications and counters, including MIB walks. Readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: This document provides a survey of BGP-4 v1 MIB [RFC4274] implementations.

BGP.why: It surveys BGP-4 implementations (peer state, path attributes, FSM transitions) and their management, so BGP operators and implementers would look here.
BGP.quote: This survey asked for information about the implementations of the BGP-4 [RFC4271] that support MIB agents [RFC1657]

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB; the survey notes SNMPv1/v2c/v3 testing only as interoperability detail. The MIB tag covers the subject.
Implied as an ancestor of MIB and SNMP; no need to tag the parent.

RFC4276.title: BGP-4 Implementation Report
RFC4276.summary: RFC 4276 reports results of a 259-question survey of four vendors' BGP-4 implementations (Alcatel, Cisco, Laurel, NextHop) against the RFC 4271 specification, with brief information from three other implementers.

BGP.why: The whole document is an implementation report on BGP-4 conformance to RFC 4271, covering messages, path attributes, FSM, decision process, and aggregation.
BGP.quote: This document reports the results of the BGP-4 implementation survey. The survey had 259 questions about implementations' support of BGP-4 as specified in RFC 4271.

rejected.why: Route reflectors are only mentioned as part of deployed BGP; no survey questions address them in their own right.
TCP port 179, PUSH and DSCP are touched on in a few questions, but TCP is only the substrate for BGP.
Communities appear only in a vendor comment on attribute ordering, not as a subject of the report.
The only security-related question is the RFC 2385 TCP MD5 requirement, and the Security Considerations section says no security issues are addressed.

RFC4277.title: Experience with the BGP-4 Protocol
RFC4277.summary: Informational report documenting operational experience with BGP-4 (MED, LOCAL_PREF, update packing, route flap damping, IBGP scaling, security) to satisfy the requirement for the second report for advancing the protocol to Standard.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses BGP-4 deployment experience, covering metrics, update handling, damping and implementation pitfalls.
BGP.quote: The purpose of this memo is to document how the requirements for publication of a routing protocol as an Internet Draft Standard have been satisfied by Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4).

route reflection.why: A substantial section discusses IBGP scaling and how route reflection and confederations address it.
route reflection.quote: To alleviate the need for "full mesh" IBGP, several alternatives have been defined, including BGP Route Reflection [RFC2796] and AS Confederations for BGP [RFC3065].
route reflection.section: 9. Internal BGP In Large Autonomous Systems

RPSL.why: Two sections cover Internet Routing Registries, RPSL and the history of the IRR and PRDB.
RPSL.quote: These databases provide access to information using the RPSL language, as defined in [RFC2622].

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport BGP runs over. The TCP-awareness notes are implementation caveats, not a specification of TCP.
The security section briefly mentions TCP MD5, IPsec and S-BGP/soBGP efforts. This is boilerplate-level coverage, not a main subject.
IPsec appears only as an optional way to protect BGP sessions.
The MIB gets a short descriptive section only. The document does not define it.

RFC4278.title: Standards Maturity Variance Regarding the TCP MD5 Signature Option (RFC 2385) and the BGP-4 Specification
RFC4278.summary: Informational IESG-supporting memo explaining why a standards-maturity variance is warranted so the revised BGP-4 spec can advance to Draft Standard despite normatively referencing the Proposed Standard TCP MD5 Signature Option (RFC 2385), which is weak and not to be advanced.

BGP.why: The document concerns advancing the BGP-4 specification and analyses how BGP sessions are protected and BGP's threat environment and deployment patterns.
BGP.quote: RFC 2385 is the only transmission security mechanism defined for BGP-4.

TCP.why: A substantial part evaluates the TCP MD5 Signature Option (RFC 2385), a TCP extension, its weaknesses, and why it should not be advanced.
TCP.quote: Protection of BGP Sessions via the TCP MD5 Signature Option

IETF process.why: The document's purpose is to justify a variance from the standards-track normative reference rule, discussing Proposed vs Draft Standard requirements.
IETF process.quote: RFC 2026 section 9.1 allows the IESG to grant a variance to the standard practices of the IETF.

MD5.why: The analysis of RFC 2385's weakness rests on the keyed-MD5 MAC construction and MD5 cryptanalysis.
MD5.quote: the underlying hash function, MD5, has shown signs of weakness

LDP.why: A dedicated section explains that RFC 2385 will not be deprecated for LDP because its threat environment resembles BGP's.
LDP.quote: The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) [RFC3036] also uses [RFC2385].

rejected.why: HMAC is mentioned only as the IETF's standard MAC that supersedes the keyed-hash construction; the document is not about it.
IPsec is mentioned only as a rarely-used alternative mechanism that would do the job better.
TLS is mentioned only in passing as an alternative that is rarely used for BGP.
The document is mainly about standards maturity; S-BGP is mentioned only to note it would address a different threat.
Lack of key management in RFC 2385 is noted briefly, not a main subject.

review: BGP: quote not found in the text

notes: BGP: quote not found in the text

RFC4279.title: Pre-Shared Key Ciphersuites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC4279.summary: Defines three sets of TLS ciphersuites (PSK, DHE_PSK, RSA_PSK) that authenticate TLS connections using pre-shared symmetric keys, with identity encoding and conformance requirements.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS with new key exchange algorithms, ciphersuites, handshake message formats and a new alert. Readers of TLS extensions and deployment guidance need it.
TLS.quote: This document specifies three sets of new ciphersuites for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to support authentication based on pre-shared keys (PSKs).

rejected.why: RC4 ciphersuites are defined, but RC4 is just one of the ciphers reused. The document is not about RC4 itself.
AES ciphersuites are reused from RFC 3268. The document does not specify or analyse AES.
Triple-DES is only one of the reused cipher options.
RSA_PSK uses RSA key transport as in standard TLS. The document does not define anything new about RSA.
SRP is mentioned only as an alternative in the applicability statement.
PSK use is motivated by key management convenience. The document defines TLS key exchange methods, not a key management scheme.
UTF-8 is only the encoding used for the PSK identity. It is a substrate here.

RFC4280.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Options for Broadcast and Multicast Control Servers
RFC4280.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options (domain name list and IP address options) that let mobile nodes discover the 3GPP2 Broadcast and Multicast Service (BCMCS) controller.

DHCP.why: The document's main content is new DHCPv4 option codes 88 and 89 and their client and server behaviour.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines extensions for both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 so that DHCP can be used to provide necessary configuration information to a mobile device

DHCPv6.why: It defines two new DHCPv6 options, OPTION_BCMCS_SERVER_D and OPTION_BCMCS_SERVER_A, with their formats.
DHCPv6.quote: option-code: OPTION_BCMCS_SERVER_D (33).

cdma2000.why: The options serve 3GPP2 (cdma2000) BCMCS controller discovery, and the overview section describes the 3GPP2 BCMCS network. The quote comes from a reference title, so this tag is weaker evidence than the DHCP tags.
cdma2000.quote: Broadcast and Multicast Service in cdma2000 Wireless IP Network

rejected.why: Domain names are only encoded in the option and used for SRV lookups. The document defines nothing new for DNS.
BCMCS is a cellular broadcast/multicast service. The document does not address IP multicast routing or group membership.
cdma2000 is the more specific tag for the 3GPP2 context. The document does not cover general IP-over-cellular matters.
The options do serve controller discovery, but the DHCP tags already cover that.

RFC4281.title: The Codecs Parameter for "Bucket" Media Types
RFC4281.summary: Defines a new optional "codecs" parameter for container ("bucket") media types such as audio/3gpp and video/3gpp2, letting a Content-Type header list the codecs inside, with a syntax and an ISO Base Media File Format name space.

media types.why: The RFC defines a new parameter for MIME media types (audio/3gpp, video/3gpp2, etc.) and updates their registrations. That is media type parameter registration.
media types.quote: This document adds a parameter to allow unambiguous specification of all codecs indicated to render the content in the MIME part.

codecs.why: The parameter's purpose is to identify the codecs (AMR, AAC, H.263, MPEG-4 and others) needed to render container content. It defines codec naming, such as mp4a.40.2, for the ISO file format family.
codecs.quote: it would be helpful to know from the Content-Type alone if the content can be rendered

rejected.why: The document relies on MIME parameter syntax (RFC 2045, RFC 2231). It adds a media type parameter and does not change MIME body structure or encodings, so the more specific media types tag fits.
AMR appears only as an example codec that a container may hold. The document is not about AMR.
H.264 is listed only as one possible content codec in the examples and background. The document is not about it.
MMS and email messages are mentioned only as motivation. The document does not specify mail behaviour.

gaps.name: 3GPP/ISO base media file format
gaps.why: The document defines the codec name space for the ISO Base Media File Format (3GP/3GP2 files). The taxonomy has no tag for container file formats outside Matroska and Ogg.

RFC4282.title: The Network Access Identifier
RFC4282.summary: Defines the syntax and semantics of the Network Access Identifier (user@realm), the user identity submitted during network access authentication in roaming, with internationalization, username privacy, length limits and realm construction.

AAA.why: The NAI is the user identity for network access authentication and AAA routing in roaming; the document defines it for AAA systems (RADIUS/Diameter) and is best placed under the AAA framework.
AAA.quote: NAIs are used, among other purposes, for routing AAA transactions to the user's home realm.

authentication.why: The NAI is an identity format for network access authentication, including username privacy and anonymous forms; the general authentication topic fits as it is not a specific AAA protocol.
authentication.quote: the user identity submitted by the client during network authentication

IDN.why: A substantive section specifies how realms use IDNA/ToASCII as IDN-unaware domain name slots, and the DNS-compatible realm grammar is revised.
IDN.quote: Internationalization of the realm portion of the NAI is based on "Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA)"

PRECIS.why: Usernames are internationalized via UTF-8 and SASLprep stringprep (mapping, normalization, prohibited output), which is the precursor of PRECIS string handling.
PRECIS.quote: characters of the username portion in an NAI MUST fulfill the ABNF in this specification as well as the requirements specified in [RFC4013]

rejected.why: RADIUS is only a transport carrying the NAI in User-Name; the document discusses length limits but does not specify or extend RADIUS.
Diameter is mentioned only as another transport for NAIs, as with RADIUS.
The realm is based on the DNS namespace and syntax, but the document does not specify DNS itself; the IDN tag covers the relevant part.
EAP is mentioned only for method-specific pseudonyms in the Security Considerations; the document is not about EAP.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the grammar.
UTF-8 is the encoding used for international usernames, but the document does not define or discuss the encoding itself.

gaps.name: Network Access Identifier (NAI) / roaming identity
gaps.why: There is no tag for network access identity or roaming user identifiers; AAA and authentication are the nearest fits.

RFC4283.title: Mobile Node Identifier Option for Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6)
RFC4283.summary: Defines a new Mobile IPv6 mobility option (Mobile Node Identifier) with subtypes, including the MN-NAI subtype, so mobility entities can identify themselves by NAI or other identifiers instead of the home address.

Mobile IPv6.why: The RFC extends Mobile IPv6 with a new mobility option carried in the Mobility header, so it belongs on the Mobile IPv6 page.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document defines a new mobility option that can be used by Mobile IPv6 entities to identify themselves in messages containing a mobility header.

rejected.why: AAA infrastructure is mentioned only as one use case for the identifier. The document does not specify or profile AAA.
IPsec is mentioned only as an alternative way to protect binding updates and as a privacy mitigation.
The IANA section only registers the option type and a subtype namespace, which is boilerplate.
Privacy appears only in the Security Considerations, and the document's main body is not about privacy.

RFC4284.title: Identity Selection Hints for the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)
RFC4284.summary: Informational RFC (from 3GPP work) defining a mechanism for an access network to send NAI realm identity-selection hints to an EAP peer inside the EAP-Request/Identity message, with RADIUS proxy behaviour and delivery options.

EAP.why: The document extends EAP's Request/Identity message with a NAIRealms hint attribute to help the peer pick an NAI. It is about EAP behaviour.
EAP.quote: This document defines a mechanism that allows an access network to provide identity selection hints to an EAP peer

RADIUS.why: It specifies how RADIUS proxies respond to unknown realms, replying with an Access-Challenge carrying a hint instead of an Access-Reject. The appendix delivery options are also RADIUS-based.
RADIUS.quote: This document specifies behavior of Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) proxies that handle EAP messages.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an alternative to RADIUS in the appendix, with no specification of it.
AAA routing is the context, but the specified behaviour is concretely EAP and RADIUS. RADIUS is the more specific tag.
The 802.11 access network is the example setting for the delivery options. The document does not specify IP over 802.11.
ABNF is only used to write the packet format, so it is not a subject of the document.
The 3GPP WLAN interworking application is mentioned as the immediate use, but the document is not about cellular networks.

gaps.name: Network Access Identifier (NAI)
gaps.why: The document centres on NAI selection and realm formatting, including decorated NAIs. The taxonomy has no tag for NAI.

RFC4285.title: Authentication Protocol for Mobile IPv6
RFC4285.summary: Defines an alternate, shared-key authentication mechanism for Mobile IPv6 Binding Updates/Acknowledgements (MN-HA and MN-AAA authentication options plus a timestamp replay protection option) for use in 3GPP2 networks instead of IPsec.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document defines new Mobile IPv6 mobility options, status codes and processing rules for Binding Update/Acknowledgement authentication, extending the Mobile IPv6 protocol.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document proposes an alternate method for securing MIPv6 signaling messages between Mobile Nodes and Home Agents.

cdma2000.why: The mechanism is designed for and applicability-limited to 3GPP2 cdma2000 networks, with AAA and PPP/DHCPv6 bootstrapping assumptions.
cdma2000.quote: One such example of networks that have such characteristics are CDMA networks as defined in [3GPP2].

rejected.why: IPsec is the mechanism being replaced; the document does not specify or extend it.
A home AAA server is used as an authenticator, but the AAA interaction is explicitly out of scope.
Only the NTP timestamp format is borrowed for the replay option.
HMAC-SHA1 is merely the algorithm used to compute authentication data; nothing new is defined about HMAC.
IKEv2 is mentioned only as a reason for the alternative, not addressed itself.
A broad topic, but the more specific Mobile IPv6 tag captures the document's subject.

RFC4286.title: Multicast Router Discovery
RFC4286.summary: Specifies Multicast Router Discovery (MRD), a set of IGMP/MLD-carried Advertisement, Solicitation and Termination messages that let snooping switches locate multicast routers independent of routing protocol.

multicast.why: MRD is a multicast-specific protocol for identifying multicast routers for IGMP/MLD snooping switches. No child tag specifically covers MRD, so the multicast topic is the best fit.
multicast.quote: This document introduces a general mechanism that allows for the discovery of multicast routers.

IGMP.why: MRD is defined as new IGMP message types for IPv4, with IANA IGMP Type assignments, and it conveys IGMP variables such as Query Interval and Robustness Variable.
IGMP.quote: All Advertisements are sent as Internet Group Management Protocol (for IPv4) or Multicast Listener Discovery (for IPv6) messages

MLD.why: The IPv6 form of MRD is defined as new MLD messages carried in ICMPv6, so it is a substantial extension of the MLD message set.
MLD.quote: This document also introduces three new MLD messages.

rejected.why: ICMPv6 is only the carrier for the IPv6 messages and its checksum is reused. The document does not define anything new about ICMP itself.
The messages carry the Router Alert option, but the document only uses it and does not specify it.
SEND is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible mitigation.
ESP is mentioned only as an optional protection in Security Considerations.
The ICMP Router Discovery model is acknowledged, but this is not IPv6 neighbor discovery.

RFC4287.title: The Atom Syndication Format
RFC4287.summary: Specifies Atom 1.0, an XML-based syndication format for feeds and entries of web content and metadata, including its constructs, elements, security and extension rules, and the application/atom+xml media type and link relation registry.

Atom.why: The whole document defines the Atom syndication format: feed and entry documents, constructs, elements and extensibility.
Atom.quote: This document specifies Atom, an XML-based Web content and metadata syndication format.

XML.why: Atom is an XML-based format; the document covers XML namespaces, xml:base, xml:lang, a RELAX NG schema, and XML signature/encryption use, so XML-format readers would want it.
XML.quote: Both kinds of Atom Documents are specified in terms of the XML Information Set, serialized as XML 1.0

media types.why: Registers the application/atom+xml media type, and atom:content type handling relies on media types.
media types.quote: MIME media type name:  application MIME subtype name:  atom+xml

web linking.why: Defines atom:link with rel values and creates the IANA Registry of Link Relations (alternate, related, self, enclosure, via).
web linking.quote: The "atom:link" element defines a reference from an entry or feed to a Web resource.

rejected.why: Section 5 only says to use XML-Signature and XML Encryption as-is with a few algorithm requirements; it is a small part, not the subject.
HTML/XHTML is only a permitted payload type in text constructs and content, not specified by the document.
IRIs are used as identifiers and references per RFC 3987, but the document does not define them.
Date constructs simply require RFC 3339 date-time; this is reuse, not new definition.
URIs/IRIs are relied on for atom:id and links, but not specified or profiled here.
hreflang and xml:lang use language tags only as an attribute value.

gaps.name: Syndication feeds (RSS/Atom feed formats)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has Atom under web, but no general syndication/feeds topic; fine for this RFC since Atom has its own tag.

RFC4288.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures
RFC4288.summary: BCP 13 defining the procedures, trees, naming and content requirements for specifying and registering media (MIME) types with IANA, obsoleting RFC 2048.

media types.why: The whole document defines media type registration trees, naming and parameter rules, and the registration procedure and template.
media types.quote: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in MIME and other Internet protocols.

IANA.why: A substantial part is the IANA registration procedure, the reviewer role, and the registry's change procedures, so readers of IANA registry guidance would want it.
IANA.quote: This document defines media type specification and registration procedures that use the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as a central registry.

rejected.why: MIME is the original context, but this document deliberately separates the registration procedure from MIME; media types is the more specific fit.
Only a pointer to RFC 3023 for XML media type rules; not a subject of the document.
ABNF is used only as notation for the name syntax.
The registration procedure is explicitly not a formal standards process, and it involves the IESG only as an approver.
RTP is mentioned only as a framed-encoding transport example.

RFC4289.title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Four: Registration Procedures
RFC4289.summary: RFC 4289 (BCP 13) defines IANA registration procedures and requirements for MIME external-body access types and content-transfer-encodings, obsoleting RFC 2048.

MIME.why: The document specifies how MIME extension values (access types and transfer encodings) are registered and what requirements they must meet. This is about MIME's extensibility framework, not about media types, which are handled in a separate RFC.
MIME.quote: This document specifies IANA registration procedures for MIME external body access types and content-transfer-encodings.

rejected.why: Media type registration is explicitly out of scope; it is covered in RFC 4288.
The document creates IANA registries, but the main subject is MIME-specific registration rules. It is not general IANA guidance or stewardship, so the MIME tag fits better.
MIME is used in email, but the document is about MIME registries rather than email architecture or transport.
Base64 and quoted-printable are mentioned only as examples of existing transfer encodings.

RFC4290.title: Suggested Practices for Registration of Internationalized Domain Names (IDN)
RFC4290.summary: Informational RFC suggesting practices and a model table format and CreateBundle algorithm by which domain registries can restrict and bundle IDN registrations (variants, language tables) to reduce user confusion, adapting the JET CJK guidelines.

IDN.why: The whole document is about IDN registration policy: variants, language tables, registration bundles and the CreateBundle procedure built around IDNA/nameprep/ToASCII.
IDN.quote: This document explores the issues in the registration of internationalized domain names (IDNs).

domain registration.why: It addresses registry operations: registration restrictions, reserved versus activated labels, zone policy for variants, and the IANA language table registry.
domain registration.quote: the IDN registration process must impose rules that disallow some otherwise-valid name combinations.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; the document concerns registry policy for labels, not DNS protocol or operations.
Unicode code points are used to describe characters and tables, but the document is about registration practice, not Unicode usage in protocols.
Terminology on scripts and charsets is background, not the document's subject.
RFC 3066 language codes are only used to label tables and are not the subject.
Whois is mentioned only in passing about display of the base registration and in security considerations.
The IANA considerations only review an existing ICANN-managed language table registry and give no new IANA instructions.

RFC4291.title: IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture
RFC4291.summary: RFC 4291 specifies the IPv6 addressing architecture: address types (unicast, anycast, multicast), text representations, interface identifiers, special addresses, and the addresses a node must recognize.

IPv6.why: The whole document defines IPv6 addressing: formats, unicast/anycast/multicast types, interface identifiers and required node addresses.
IPv6.quote: This specification defines the addressing architecture of the IP Version 6 protocol.

anycast.why: Defines anycast addresses, routing implications and the required Subnet-Router anycast address.
anycast.quote: An IPv6 anycast address is an address that is assigned to more than one interface

rejected.why: IPv6 is the more specific tag for IPv6 address architecture, and the anycast child is tagged separately; the parent is implied.
Multicast address format and scopes are defined, but only as address format. The document does not cover multicast routing or group membership protocols.
Only referenced for prefix notation, not about CIDR.
The solicited-node multicast address is used by neighbor discovery, but ND itself is not specified here.
Embedded IPv4 addresses are defined, but only briefly and one is deprecated; transition mechanisms are not the subject.

RFC4292.title: IP Forwarding Table MIB
RFC4292.summary: Defines the IP version-independent IP-FORWARD-MIB module (inetCidrRouteTable and related objects) for managing IP forwarding/routing tables via SNMP, obsoleting RFC 2096.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition (IP-FORWARD-MIB) with the inetCidrRouteTable, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects related to the forwarding of Internet Protocol (IP) packets in an IP version-independent manner.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the more specific MIB tag.
CIDR routes are the content of the table, but the document is not about CIDR itself.
Version independence is a feature of the MIB, but the document does not specify IPv6.
The document defines managed objects for the forwarding table, not routing architecture.

RFC4293.title: Management Information Base for the Internet Protocol (IP)
RFC4293.summary: Defines the IP-version-independent SNMP MIB module (IP-MIB) for managing IPv4/IPv6 and ICMP implementations, merging and obsoleting RFCs 2011, 2465 and 2466.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (IP-MIB) with tables, objects, and conformance groups for managing IP and ICMP.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

IPv6.why: Substantial part merges the IPv6 MIBs and adds IPv6 objects (scope zones, router advertisements, default routers, interface tables).
IPv6.quote: Another purpose of this document is to increase the manageability of a node running IPv6 by adding new objects.

IPv4.why: The MIB covers IPv4 objects (forwarding, TTL, reassembly, address table) and migration of the old IPv4-only IP-MIB.
IPv4.quote: The somewhat more specific changes that are required for IPv4 follow.
IPv4.section: 4.1. Updating an Implementation of the IPv4-only IP-MIB

ICMP.why: Defines ICMP statistics tables (icmpStatsTable, icmpMsgStatsTable) for both ICMPv4 and ICMPv6.
ICMP.quote: There are two sets of statistics for ICMP.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself.
Neighbor discovery is referenced by tables (ipNetToPhysical, router advertisement) but not specified or extended.
ARP is merely a mechanism that may populate the translation table.
Address status states derive from SLAAC but the document does not specify it.
Not related; this is an SMIv2 MIB.

RFC4294.title: IPv6 Node Requirements
RFC4294.summary: Informational RFC consolidating in one place the requirements for IPv6 nodes (hosts and routers) across link layers, IP layer, addressing, DNS, DHCPv6, transition, Mobile IPv6, IPsec, and MIBs, by pointing to other specifications.

IPv6.why: The whole document defines what an IPv6 node must implement, covering the IPv6 specification, ICMPv6, extension headers and addressing.
IPv6.quote: The goal of this document is to define the common functionality required from both IPv6 hosts and routers.

neighbor discovery.why: Gives a detailed breakdown of which ND functions (router/prefix discovery, NUD, DAD, redirect) are required for hosts and routers.
neighbor discovery.quote: Router Discovery MUST be supported for implementations.

SLAAC.why: Has dedicated requirement subsections for SLAAC and privacy extensions to it.
SLAAC.quote: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration is defined in [RFC-2462]. This specification MUST be supported for nodes that are hosts.

DHCPv6.why: A whole section covers DHCPv6 managed address configuration and other configuration information, including the stateless subset.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv6 [RFC-3315] is the standard stateful address configuration protocol

IPsec.why: Section 8 specifies IPsec requirements for IPv6 nodes: architecture, ESP/AH, algorithms and key management.
IPsec.quote: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol [RFC-4301] MUST be supported.

MLD.why: Specifies when MLDv1 or MLDv2 must be supported.
MLD.quote: Nodes that need to join multicast groups SHOULD implement MLDv2 [RFC-3810].
MLD.section: 4.6. Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) for IPv6 - RFC 2710

Mobile IPv6.why: A dedicated section sets requirements for mobile nodes, correspondent nodes, home agents and routers.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Hosts SHOULD support route optimization requirements for correspondent nodes described in Section 8.2 of [RFC-3775].

IPv6 transition.why: Covers IPv4 support and transition requirements for dual-stack nodes.
IPv6 transition.quote: If an IPv6 node implements dual stack and tunneling, then [RFC-4213] MUST be supported.
IPv6 transition.section: 6.1.1. Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 Hosts and Routers - RFC 2893

DNS.why: Specifies stub-resolver requirements, AAAA, ip6.arpa and EDNS0 support for IPv6 nodes.
DNS.quote: All nodes that need to resolve names SHOULD implement stub-resolver [RFC-1034] functionality

PMTUD.why: Has its own subsection stating PMTUD requirements.
PMTUD.quote: Path MTU Discovery [RFC-1981] SHOULD be supported, though minimal implementations MAY choose to not support it and avoid large packets.

rejected.why: ICMPv6 gets a single requirement sentence; the document is not about ICMP itself.
Only two MIBs are recommended for SNMP agents; a minor part of the document.
DNSSEC is only recommended in one sentence.
A one-line pointer to RFC 2464; link-layer coverage is brief and not the document's subject.
Mentioned only as an example of key management.
Only a short subsection noting the option is needed when other protocols mandate it.

RFC4295.title: Mobile IPv6 Management Information Base
RFC4295.summary: Defines the MOBILEIPV6-MIB SMIv2 module for monitoring and controlling Mobile IPv6 mobile node, home agent and correspondent node entities, including binding cache, traffic counters, statistics and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMIv2, which is the core of the MIB subject.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB), the Mobile-IPv6 MIB, for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

Mobile IPv6.why: All managed objects model Mobile IPv6 entities (binding cache, binding update list, home agent list), so Mobile IPv6 readers would want it.
Mobile IPv6.quote: the Mobile-IPv6 MIB will be used to monitor and control the mobile node, home agent, and correspondent node functions of a Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) entity.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; MIB is the more specific child tag.
MIPv6 is the subject; IPv6 itself is only the underlying protocol.
ICMP messages are merely counted by some objects; not the subject.
Mentioned only in passing as an existing MIB to reuse and in security considerations.
Router Advertisement parameters are configured but ND itself is not specified.

RFC4296.title: The Architecture of Direct Data Placement (DDP) and Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) on Internet Protocols
RFC4296.summary: Informational RFC defining an abstract architecture for Direct Data Placement (DDP) and RDMA protocols layered over IP-suite transports, with abstract operations, transport characteristics and security requirements.

RDMA.why: The whole document defines the architecture of DDP and RDMA, including RDMA Read/Write/Send operations, buffer registration, and Steering Tags. DDP is covered under the same RDMA tag since no separate DDP tag exists.
RDMA.quote: The goal of the RDMA protocol is to provide the semantics to enable Remote Direct Memory Access between peers in a way consistent with application requirements.

rejected.why: Only cited as an example transport DDP can run over; the document does not specify or extend SCTP.
Discussed in Security Considerations as the preferred security layer for RDMA, but only as a mechanism, not the subject.
Mentioned only as a less natural fit for securing RDMA; not about TLS.
Framed TCP is listed as an example transport; the document is transport independent.
The RDMA tag sits under storage and implies it; storage protocols are only mentioned as potential upper layers.

gaps.name: Direct Data Placement (DDP)
gaps.why: DDP is a core subject of the document, but the taxonomy has no dedicated tag; it is only covered by the RDMA tag.

RFC4297.title: Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over IP Problem Statement
RFC4297.summary: Problem statement showing that data-copying overhead in end-host network I/O limits high-speed IP use, and motivating an IP-based copy-avoidance solution via direct data placement and RDMA.

RDMA.why: The whole document is a problem statement for RDMA over IP and its DDP/RDMA conceptual framework, so readers browsing RDMA would expect it.
RDMA.quote: RDMA is a set of mechanisms that allow the network adapter, under control of the application, to steer data directly into and out of application buffers.

rejected.why: TCP processing overhead is analysed as background, but the document says TCP offload is not addressed and does not specify or extend TCP.
IPsec and TLS appear only in the Security Considerations, as boilerplate-level discussion of how they fit with RDMA.
TLS is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as a less natural fit for protecting RDMA. The document is not about TLS.
InfiniBand is cited as an example RDMA fabric, and the document is not about it.
Fibre Channel is cited as an example RDMA fabric, not as a subject of the document.

RFC4298.title: RTP Payload Format for BroadVoice Speech Codecs
