RFC4298.summary: Defines the RTP payload formats, bit packing, MIME registrations (audio/BV16, audio/BV32) and SDP mappings for the BroadVoice16 narrowband and BroadVoice32 wideband speech codecs.

RTP payload format.why: The document's core purpose is an RTP payload format for the BV16 and BV32 codecs, including frame packing, timestamps and marker bit rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for sending BroadVoice encoded speech or audio signals using the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

codecs.why: It describes the BroadVoice codec family and defines the bit allocation of the encoded parameters for each frame, which is of interest to codec readers.
codecs.quote: BroadVoice is a speech codec family developed for VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) applications

rejected.why: SDP is used only to carry the codec's rtpmap/ptime parameters; no new SDP mechanism is defined, and offer/answer needs no special handling.
The document registers audio/BV16 and audio/BV32, but this is boilerplate-like IANA registration that accompanies the payload format and is not the main subject.
RTP is the transport that the payload format is built on. The more specific RTP payload format tag already covers it.
The congestion control section only refers to general RTP considerations and is too brief to count as a subject.
RFC 3267 is cited only for the maxptime parameter definition, and AMR is not the subject of this document.

gaps.name: BroadVoice (BV16/BV32) codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for BroadVoice. The generic codecs tag is the closest fit, but readers browsing for BroadVoice would benefit from a dedicated tag.

RFC4301.title: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
RFC4301.summary: RFC 4301 specifies the base IPsec security architecture: security associations, the SPD/SAD/PAD databases, inbound and outbound IP traffic processing, ICMP, fragment and PMTU handling, and auditing, obsoleting RFC 2401.

IPsec.why: The whole document defines the IPsec architecture: SAs, SPD, SAD, PAD, tunnel/transport modes, and traffic processing.
IPsec.quote: This document specifies the base architecture for IPsec-compliant systems.

rejected.why: ESP is specified in RFC 4303; this document only references it as one of the two protocols the architecture uses.
IKEv2 is defined in RFC 4306. The PAD links to IKE, but IKE is not specified here.
ICMP error handling is covered in Section 6, but only as it relates to IPsec processing. ICMP itself is not the subject.
Section 8 covers PMTU handling for SAs, but this is a small part of the document and not about PMTUD as a protocol.
IPsec includes minimal firewall functionality, but the document is about the IPsec architecture, not firewalls.
Appendix C gives an illustrative ASN.1 module for SPD entries. It is incidental and not a document about ASN.1.

RFC4302.title: IP Authentication Header
RFC4302.summary: Specifies version 2 of the IPsec Authentication Header (AH), providing connectionless integrity, data origin authentication and optional anti-replay for IPv4/IPv6 packets, including header format, mutable field handling, processing rules and 64-bit extended sequence numbers.

IPsec.why: The whole document specifies AH, one of the core IPsec protocols, with its SA lookup, transport and tunnel modes, and anti-replay. IPsec is the most specific fitting tag, since AH has no child tag.
IPsec.quote: The IP Authentication Header (AH) is used to provide connectionless integrity and data origin authentication for IP datagrams

rejected.why: ESP is only compared with AH and referenced. It is specified in a separate RFC (4303).
IKE is mentioned only as an SA management and negotiation mechanism, for example for ESN negotiation. The document does not specify it.
AH is defined for both IPv4 and IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 itself. IPv6 headers appear only as the carrier.
IPv4 header and option mutability is covered only as it affects the ICV calculation. The document is not about IPv4.
Multicast SAs and SPI demultiplexing are handled, but this is a minor part of the document. Group key management is not addressed.
Integrity algorithms are only mentioned as examples and are specified in a separate document.

RFC4303.title: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC4303.summary: RFC 4303 specifies the updated IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol, covering packet format, transport and tunnel mode processing, anti-replay with extended sequence numbers, and traffic flow confidentiality padding.

ESP.why: The entire document specifies the ESP protocol: packet format, inbound and outbound processing, anti-replay, and the ESN appendix.
ESP.quote: This document describes an updated version of the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol, which is designed to provide a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6.

rejected.why: ESP is a child of IPsec in the taxonomy and is the more specific tag. The parent is implied, so it is not listed separately.
IKE is mentioned only as an SA management protocol for negotiating ESN and other features. The document does not specify it.
ESP runs over IPv4 and IPv6 and the document gives IPv6 header placement, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Encryption and integrity algorithms are left to separate RFCs. This document defines only how ESP uses them.
GDOI appears only as an example of a group SA management protocol.

RFC4304.title: Extended Sequence Number (ESN) Addendum to IPsec Domain of Interpretation (DOI) for Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol (ISAKMP)
RFC4304.summary: Defines a new IPsec DOI attribute for ISAKMP/IKE Phase II that negotiates use of 64-bit extended sequence numbers for AH and ESP security associations.

IKE.why: The document adds an SA attribute to the IPsec DOI used in IKE Phase II negotiation, i.e. it extends IKEv1/ISAKMP negotiation. IKE is the most specific fitting tag.
IKE.quote: These extensions support negotiation of the use of traditional 32-bit sequence numbers or extended (64-bit) sequence numbers (ESNs) for a particular AH or ESP security association.

ESP.why: The ESN option for ESP and AH is the feature being negotiated, and the document discusses its implications for ESP. ESP is the closest tag for the sequence-number-bearing protocol.
ESP.quote: In using ESNs with ESP, it is important to employ an encryption mode that is secure when very large volumes of data are encrypted under a single key.

rejected.why: It is the parent of IKE and ESP, so it is implied by those tags.
DES is mentioned only as an example of a cipher unsuitable for use with ESN in the Security Considerations.
The document is about the IKE negotiation attribute, and the more specific IKE tag covers it.

RFC4305.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Implementation Requirements for Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH)
RFC4305.summary: RFC 4305 specifies the mandatory-to-implement and recommended cryptographic algorithms (encryption, authentication, combined mode) for IPsec ESP and AH, obsoleting the requirements in RFC 2402/2406.

ESP.why: The document's core content is the algorithm conformance tables for ESP (encryption, authentication, combined mode). ESP is the most specific IPsec tag that fits.
ESP.quote: This document defines the current set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms for ESP and AH

IPsec.why: AH is covered by the IPsec architecture tag, which has no separate AH child. Half of the document sets requirements for AH and the IPsec SA protections in general.
IPsec.quote: The implementation conformance requirements for security algorithms for AH are given below.

cryptography.why: The document is about selecting cryptographic algorithms (3DES, AES-CBC, AES-CTR, HMAC-SHA1, DES deprecation) and their requirement levels. No single algorithm tag covers the whole selection, so the topic tag applies.
cryptography.quote: MUST-          TripleDES-CBC [RFC2451]

rejected.why: IKE is only mentioned as one way algorithms are negotiated. The document sets no IKE requirements.
AES-CBC, AES-CTR and AES-CCM are listed as entries in the tables. The document is not about AES itself.
Single DES is deprecated in a note, and 3DES is a table entry. This is a minor part of the document.
HMAC-SHA1-96 and HMAC-MD5-96 are table entries only. The document does not specify HMAC.
HMAC-SHA1-96 is cited as a required algorithm, but the document is not about the SHA family.

RFC4306.title: Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2) Protocol
RFC4306.summary: RFC 4306 specifies IKEv2, the IPsec key exchange and mutual authentication protocol for establishing and maintaining IKE and CHILD security associations, replacing RFCs 2407, 2408 and 2409.

IKE.why: The whole document specifies IKEv2: exchanges, payload formats, key derivation, rekeying, and error handling.
IKE.quote: This document describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol.  IKE is a component of IPsec used for performing mutual authentication and establishing and maintaining security associations

NAT.why: Section 2.23 defines NAT detection notifications and UDP port 4500 encapsulation, a substantial NAT traversal part of the spec.
NAT.quote: IKEv2 can negotiate UDP encapsulation of IKE and ESP packets.  This encoding is slightly less efficient but is easier for NATs to process.

rejected.why: IKE is a child of IPsec in the taxonomy, so the ancestor is implied and not listed.
ESP SAs are negotiated by IKE, but ESP itself is specified in RFC 4303, not here.
EAP is supported as an authentication option (sections 2.16 and 3.16), but it is a mechanism used rather than the subject of the document.
IPComp negotiation is covered in a short section only. The IPComp tag sits under compression, and the document's main subject is not compression.
Certificates are carried in CERT payloads, but the document does not profile X.509.
UDP is only the transport substrate (ports 500 and 4500).

RFC4307.title: Cryptographic Algorithms for Use in the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC4307.summary: RFC 4307 specifies which cryptographic algorithms (encryption, PRF, integrity, and Diffie-Hellman groups) are mandatory or recommended to implement for IKEv2, using MUST-/SHOULD+ style requirement levels.

IKE.why: The document is entirely about the algorithm suite for IKEv2, including transform types and DH groups negotiated in IKEv2.
IKE.quote: This document defines the current set of algorithms that are mandatory to implement as part of IKEv2

cryptography.why: The document is about selecting cryptographic algorithms, parameters and groups for use in an Internet protocol. It covers several algorithms and no single algorithm tag fits.
cryptography.quote: For confidentiality, implementations MUST- implement 3DES-CBC and SHOULD+ implement AES-128-CBC.  For integrity, HMAC-SHA1 MUST be implemented.

rejected.why: IPsec is the parent of IKE, so it is implied. The document is specifically about IKEv2 algorithms.
AES-CBC, AES-CTR and AES-XCBC are listed in the tables, but AES is only one of many algorithms and is not the subject.
HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC-MD5 are listed as algorithm choices only. The document does not specify or analyse HMAC.
3DES is listed only as a MUST- algorithm. The document does not cover DES itself.
The ESP-related algorithm RFCs are referenced, but the document concerns IKEv2 negotiation rather than ESP.

RFC4308.title: Cryptographic Suites for IPsec
RFC4308.summary: Defines two optional named cryptographic suites (VPN-A and VPN-B) of algorithms and parameters for IPsec ESP, IKE and IKEv2, plus IKEv1 SA lifetimes, and creates an IANA registry for suite names.

IPsec.why: The document defines UI suites for IPsec, specifying ESP algorithms and parameters for VPN use; IPsec administrators are the audience.
IPsec.quote: This document specifies optional suites of algorithms and attributes that can be used to simplify the administration of IPsec when used in manual keying mode, with IKEv1 or with IKEv2.

IKE.why: Each suite specifies IKE and IKEv2 encryption, PRF, integrity and DH group values, plus IKEv1 Phase 1/2 lifetimes and rekeying requirements.
IKE.quote: IKE and IKEv2: Encryption TripleDES in CBC mode [RFC2451] Pseudo-random function HMAC-SHA1 [RFC2104]

rejected.why: VPN-B uses AES-CBC and AES-XCBC, but the document only selects them in a suite and does not specify AES.
VPN-A uses TripleDES, but only as a referenced choice, not as the subject.
HMAC-SHA1 appears as a suite component only.
ESP is named as the protocol in the suites, but the document does not specify ESP itself; IPsec covers it.
This tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs (L3VPN, L2VPN); the suites target corporate IPsec VPNs and do not address that subject.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA Considerations, not the main subject.

RFC4309.title: Using Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) CCM Mode with IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC4309.summary: Specifies the use of AES in CCM mode with an explicit IV as an IPsec ESP transform providing confidentiality, data origin authentication and integrity, including nonce/AAD construction, IKE keying conventions and ESP transform identifiers.

ESP.why: The document defines a new ESP encryption/authentication transform: payload layout, IV, ICV, AAD and packet expansion within ESP.
ESP.quote: as an IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) [ESP] mechanism to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, and connectionless integrity.

AES.why: The document is about using the AES block cipher in CCM mode: parameters M and L, key sizes, nonce format.
AES.quote: This document describes the use of AES in CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC) mode (AES CCM), with an explicit initialization vector (IV)

IKE.why: A full section defines IKE keying material and salt derivation, Phase 2 transform identifiers and the Key Length attribute for negotiating AES CCM.
IKE.quote: This section describes the conventions used to generate keying material and salt values for use with AES CCM using the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) [IKE] protocol.

rejected.why: The more specific ESP tag fits; the parent is implied.
Jumbograms are only referenced to justify the length field size.
IANA transform assignments are boilerplate-level here.
CCM uses CBC-MAC, not HMAC, and HMAC is not discussed.
Key derivation is specific to IKE conventions, covered by the IKE tag.

RFC4310.title: Domain Name System (DNS) Security Extensions Mapping for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC4310.summary: Defines an EPP extension mapping (secDNS-1.0) that lets registrars provision DNSSEC delegation signer (DS) and key data for domains in a shared registry via create, update and info commands.

EPP.why: The document is an EPP extension defining new elements for domain create, update and info commands.
EPP.quote: This document describes an extension mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)

DNSSEC.why: The extension conveys DNSSEC DS records and DNSKEY data to the parent zone, so DNSSEC operators and readers would want it.
DNSSEC.quote: provisioning and management of DNS security extensions in a shared central repository

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the specification notation for the mapping, not the subject.
DNS is background; the document is about DNSSEC provisioning, which is the more specific tag.
Implied as the parent of EPP; EPP is the more specific tag.
The IANA section only registers the XML namespace and schema, which is boilerplate.

RFC4311.title: IPv6 Host-to-Router Load Sharing
RFC4311.summary: RFC 4311 updates the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery conceptual sending algorithm so hosts can load-share outgoing traffic among equivalent default routers using a destination-address hash.

neighbor discovery.why: The document updates the RFC 2461 Neighbor Discovery conceptual sending algorithm, specifically next-hop (router) selection among equivalent routers.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document updates the conceptual sending algorithm in RFC 2461 so that traffic to different destinations can be distributed among routers in an efficient fashion.

rejected.why: ECMP is router-side equal-cost multipath forwarding. This document covers host-side selection among default routers. RFC 2991 is only referenced.
The parent tag is implied by the more specific neighbor discovery tag.
RFC 3484 source address selection is mentioned only as background. The document is not about address selection.
The document concerns host next-hop choice, not routing system architecture.

RFC4312.title: The Camellia Cipher Algorithm and Its Use With IPsec
RFC4312.summary: RFC 4312 specifies how to use the Camellia block cipher in CBC mode with an explicit IV as the confidentiality algorithm for IPsec ESP, including key sizes, padding, and IKE identifiers.

Camellia.why: The document specifies the Camellia cipher's use (mode, key sizes, rounds, IV) and its IKE/ESP identifiers. The Camellia tag covers its cipher suites in IPsec.
Camellia.quote: This document describes the use of the Camellia block cipher algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining Mode, with an explicit Initialization Vector

ESP.why: The document defines the ESP payload layout, padding and keying material for Camellia-CBC, and assigns an ESP transform identifier. Readers of ESP would want it.
ESP.quote: as a confidentiality mechanism within the context of the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

rejected.why: Section 4 only defines the Phase 1 and Phase 2 identifiers and defers all other IKE interaction to the AES-CBC RFC. IKE is not what the document is about.
AES is mentioned only for comparison and as the interface model. The document is not about AES.
ESP is the more specific child tag, so the IPsec parent is implied.

RFC4313.title: Requirements for Distributed Control of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speaker Identification/Speaker Verification (SI/SV), and Text-to-Speech (TTS) Resources
RFC4313.summary: Requirements document for a protocol (SPEECHSC) to control distributed ASR, speaker identification/verification, and TTS servers, covering framework, general, per-service, and duplexing requirements plus security considerations.

MRCP.why: The document sets requirements for a speech services control protocol, the successor to MRCP, for controlling ASR, SI/SV and TTS servers. That is the MRCP subject area.
MRCP.quote: The SPEECHSC framework MUST accommodate at a minimum all of the protocol parameters currently defined in Media Resource Control Protocol (MRCP)

real-time communications.why: The framework is built on RTP media streams and SDP descriptions, with barge-in, full-duplex operation and playback controls. It addresses real-time media control but is not about one specific child technology.
real-time communications.quote: The SPEECHSC framework MUST allow a 1:N mapping between session and RTP channels.

rejected.why: SIP appears in examples and as an existing protocol to reuse, but the document does not specify or extend it.
RTSP is discussed as a candidate to extend for VCR controls, but the document is not about it.
RTP is only the media transport the framework assumes.
SDP is assumed for media session description. The document defines nothing new about it.
Section 3.9 is a short requirement on users with disabilities, not a substantial part of the document.
OPES compliance is a single general requirement in section 3.5, which is too minor for a tag.

gaps.name: Speech services control (ASR, SI/SV, TTS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for distributed speech processing control apart from MRCP, which is only its predecessor protocol.

RFC4314.title: IMAP4 Access Control List (ACL) Extension
RFC4314.summary: RFC 4314 revises the IMAP4 ACL extension, defining access rights, the SETACL/DELETEACL/GETACL/LISTRIGHTS/MYRIGHTS commands and responses, and which rights each IMAP command requires.

IMAP.why: The document is an extension to IMAP defining new commands, responses, a RIGHTS= capability and the rights needed for existing IMAP commands.
IMAP.quote: The ACL (Access Control List) extension of the Internet Message Access Protocol [IMAP4] permits mailbox access control lists to be retrieved and manipulated through the IMAP protocol.

rejected.why: It concerns access control, but the IMAP tag is the more specific home. The document is an IMAP extension rather than a general authorization treatment.
SASLprep is used only to prepare identifier strings; the document does not specify SASL.
Identifiers are UTF-8 strings, but this is only a clarification of encoding and not the subject.
ABNF is only used to write the formal syntax.
STARTTLS is mentioned only in the Security Considerations and in a capability example.

gaps.name: IMAP4 ACL extension
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IMAP-specific tag below email except through the IMAP tag; the chosen tag, 'IMAP', is listed in the taxonomy but I should verify it.

RFC4315.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - UIDPLUS extension
RFC4315.summary: Specifies the IMAP UIDPLUS extension, adding the UID EXPUNGE command and the APPENDUID, COPYUID and UIDNOTSTICKY response codes to help disconnected-use clients, obsoleting RFC 2359.

IMAP.why: The document is an extension to IMAP, defining a new command (UID EXPUNGE), new response codes and the UIDPLUS capability. It is squarely about IMAP.
IMAP.quote: The UIDPLUS extension defines an additional command.  In addition, this document recommends new status response codes in IMAP

rejected.why: ABNF is only used as the notation for the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
The example message has MIME headers, but MIME is not a subject of the document.
IMAP is the more specific tag and its ancestor email is implied.
The example message shows headers, but the document does not address message format.

RFC4316.title: Datatypes for Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) Properties
RFC4316.summary: RFC 4316 extends WebDAV so PROPPATCH and PROPFIND can carry XML Schema datatype information (xsi:type) on property elements, letting clients and servers declare and return property datatypes.

WebDAV.why: The document defines extensions to WebDAV's PROPPATCH and PROPFIND methods for typed properties, so it belongs on the WebDAV subject page.
WebDAV.quote: This specification extends the Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning Protocol (WebDAV) to support datatyping.

rejected.why: XML Schema datatypes and xsi:type are used as the encoding mechanism for the property types, but the document is about WebDAV property typing, not XML usage in general.
WebDAV runs over HTTP and the examples show HTTP messages, but the document does not extend HTTP itself.
Content-Type headers appear only in examples; no media type is registered.

RFC4317.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer Examples
RFC4317.summary: Informational RFC giving worked examples of SDP offer/answer exchanges (codec negotiation, hold/resume, adding/deleting streams, 3pcc scenarios) based on RFC 3264.

SDP.why: The whole document consists of SDP offer/answer examples illustrating RFC 3264 usage, so SDP readers would want it.
SDP.quote: This document gives examples of Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer/answer exchanges.

rejected.why: SIP is only the assumed transport for offers and answers; the document specifies nothing about SIP itself.
RTP/AVP appears in m= lines as the media transport, but the document is not about RTP.
Codecs like iLBC and telephone-event are only referenced in rtpmap lines; no payload format is defined.
iLBC is merely a codec used in the examples.
Codec negotiation is shown through SDP, but no codec is defined or discussed in its own right.

RFC4318.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges with Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol
RFC4318.summary: Defines the SMIv2 RSTP-MIB module supplementing the BRIDGE-MIB with managed objects for Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1t/802.1w) bridge and per-port parameters.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is to define a MIB module (RSTP-MIB) in SMIv2, with objects, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines an SMIv2 MIB module for managing the Rapid Spanning Tree (RSTP) capability defined by the IEEE P802.1t [802.1t] and P802.1w [802.1w]

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Bridging and spanning tree concern LAN bridges, but the document is about managed objects, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
RSTP is a link-layer bridging protocol, but the taxonomy has no specific spanning tree/bridging tag and the document is about the MIB, so the parent is not warranted.
Implied by the MIB tag as its ancestor, so listing it separately is unnecessary.
Aggregators are mentioned only in the point-to-point object description; not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Spanning Tree Protocol / transparent bridging (IEEE 802.1D RSTP)
gaps.why: The MIB manages bridge Rapid Spanning Tree, but the taxonomy has no tag for bridging or spanning tree, so readers browsing that subject would not find this RFC.

RFC4319.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for High Bit-Rate DSL - 2nd generation (HDSL2) and Single-Pair High-Speed Digital Subscriber Line (SHDSL) Lines
RFC4319.summary: Defines the HDSL2-SHDSL-LINE-MIB SMIv2 module for managing HDSL2 and SHDSL (including G.shdsl.bis) lines, obsoleting RFC 3276 with extra wire pairs, payload rates and wire-pair status objects.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (SMIv2 tables, notifications, conformance groups) for HDSL2/SHDSL lines.
MIB.quote: it describes objects used for managing High Bit-Rate Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) - 2nd generation (HDSL2) and Single-Pair High-Speed Digital Subscriber Line (SHDSL) interfaces

DSL.why: The managed subject is the HDSL2/SHDSL DSL access line: spans, units, wire pairs, EOC, loopbacks, and line performance. A reader browsing DSL would expect this MIB.
DSL.quote: This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for use with network management protocols in the Internet community for the purpose of managing HDSL2/SHDSL lines.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB, not the subject; the MIB tag covers the module itself.
No access node control protocol is involved; this is line management only.
The 15-minute and 1-day counters are part of the MIB's line statistics, not a performance measurement methodology.

RFC4320.title: Actions Addressing Identified Issues with the Session Initiation Protocol's (SIP) Non-INVITE Transaction
RFC4320.summary: Updates RFC 3261 to change SIP non-INVITE transaction behavior: restricts provisional responses (only 100 Trying, timed), forbids 408 responses to non-INVITE requests, and prevents proxies from forwarding late/stray non-INVITE responses.

SIP.why: The document normatively updates SIP (RFC 3261) transaction behavior for provisional responses, 408 responses and stray response forwarding.
SIP.quote: This document describes modifications to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) to address problems that have been identified with the SIP non-INVITE transaction.

rejected.why: UDP is mentioned only as an unreliable transport affecting Timer E behavior; the document does not specify UDP.
DNS poisoning appears only in the Security Considerations as an attack example.
Some changes mitigate flooding and DoS, but this is a protocol robustness fix to SIP transactions, not operational security guidance.
The DoS and flooding mitigation is a side benefit discussed in Security Considerations; the document is not about DDoS mitigation.

RFC4321.title: Problems Identified Associated with the Session Initiation Protocol's (SIP) Non-INVITE Transaction
RFC4321.summary: Informational RFC describing problems with the SIP non-INVITE transaction model, including fixed-duration races, provisional response delays, blacklisting, useless 408s, forking proxy failure, and mismatched timers.

SIP.why: The whole document analyses flaws in SIP's non-INVITE transaction state machines, timers, and proxy behaviour under RFC 3261 and RFC 3263.
SIP.quote: This document describes several problems that have been identified with the Session Initiation Protocol's (SIP) non-INVITE transaction.

rejected.why: DNS SRV is mentioned only in the blacklisting discussion as the mechanism for locating servers; the document is not about DNS.
UDP is only the unreliable transport whose retransmission behaviour is relevant to Timer E; not a subject of the document.

RFC4322.title: Opportunistic Encryption using the Internet Key Exchange (IKE)
RFC4322.summary: Describes opportunistic encryption as implemented by Linux FreeS/WAN, in which IPsec gateways use IKE and DNS-published KEY and TXT records (secured by DNSSEC) to set up tunnels with strangers without pre-arrangement.

IKE.why: The document specifies how IKE phase 1 and phase 2 are used for opportunistic tunnels, including required proposal types, IDs and impacts on IKE. IKE is the child of IPsec, so IPsec is implied.
IKE.quote: OE uses the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) and IPsec protocols. The objective is to allow encryption for secure communication without any pre-arrangement

DNSSEC.why: Peer authentication depends on DNSSEC-validated KEY and TXT records, and Section 4.5 covers interactions with DNSSEC. The document is not about DNSSEC itself, though.
DNSSEC.quote: The use of DNS Security (DNSSEC) secures this system against active attackers as well.

DNS.why: The document defines a TXT delegation record format in the reverse map, the use of KEY records, key roll-over and DNS failure modes. This is a substantial DNS usage and record definition.
DNS.quote: DNS is used to distribute the public keys of each system involved.

rejected.why: Section 6 on NAT interaction is brief and only notes the usual IPsec NAT traversal issues.
Section 8 discusses multi-homing with multiple gateway delegation records. It is a short section, not a main subject.
The document uses DNS to publish keys for IPsec, not TLSA records for certificate association.
The document explicitly avoids an X.509-based infrastructure, using DNS keys instead.
ESP is only the data-plane encryption mechanism. The document is about policy and key discovery, not ESP.

gaps.name: Opportunistic encryption
gaps.why: The main subject is opportunistic, pre-arrangement-free encryption between strangers. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so IKE is the closest fit.

RFC4323.title: Data Over Cable System Interface Specification Quality of Service Management Information Base (DOCSIS-QoS MIB)
RFC4323.summary: Defines the DOCS-IETF-QOS-MIB SMIv2 module for SNMP management of DOCSIS 1.1/2.0 cable modem and CMTS quality-of-service features: packet classifiers, QoS parameter sets, service flows, service classes, PHS and dynamic service statistics.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification with tables and conformance groups, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: This document defines a basic set of managed objects for SNMP-based management of extended QoS features of Cable Modems (CMs) and Cable Modem Termination Systems (CMTSs)

DOCSIS.why: The MIB models DOCSIS service flows, classifiers, PHS and dynamic service messages on cable access networks.
DOCSIS.quote: conforming to the Data over Cable System (DOCSIS) specifications versions 1.1 and 2.0

QoS.why: A large part covers QoS parameter sets, scheduling types, policing and service classes. It is a management model for DOCSIS QoS, not a general QoS architecture, so this is secondary.
QoS.quote: The Active QPS is the set of services actually being used by the Service Flow.

rejected.why: Diffserv is only discussed for how ToS/DSCP overwrite objects relate to it. The document does not specify or profile Diffserv.
ECN appears only as a caution that the ToS mask objects must not modify the ECN bits. The document is not about ECN.
SNMP is the management substrate. The MIB is the subject, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Payload Header Suppression is one table among eleven and is a DOCSIS-specific feature. It is not general header compression.
The ToS octet and IPv4 address objects are used for classification only. The document does not address IPv4 itself.

RFC4324.title: Calendar Access Protocol (CAP)
RFC4324.summary: Specifies the Calendar Access Protocol (CAP), an experimental BEEP-profile protocol letting a calendar user agent query, create, modify, delete and search iCalendar data in a calendar store, with a SQL-like query language, access-rights components and new iCalendar properties.

CalDAV.why: CAP is a calendar access protocol, the IETF alternative to CalDAV. The taxonomy has no CAP-specific tag, so CalDAV is the closest tech; the calendaring topic itself would also fit, but a tech tag under it is preferred.
CalDAV.quote: The Calendar Access Protocol (CAP) described in this memo permits a Calendar User (CU) to utilize a Calendar User Agent (CUA) to access an iCAL-based Calendar Store (CS).

iCalendar.why: The document adds many new iCalendar components, properties, parameters and value types (VAGENDA, VCAR, CAL-QUERY, etc.) and extends iTIP handling. Readers of the iCalendar page would want it.
iCalendar.quote: The protocol data units of CAP leverage the standard iCalendar format iCAL [iCAL] to convey calendar-related information.

BEEP.why: The document defines a BEEP profile with registration, exchange styles and connection details (Section 12), so it is substantially about a BEEP profile.
BEEP.quote: CAP is specified as a BEEP (Block Extensible Exchange Protocol) "profile" [BEEP] [BEEPGUIDE].

rejected.why: TLS is used only as a BEEP tuning profile for confidentiality; nothing new is defined for it.
Authentication is delegated to BEEP's SASL profiles; the document only maps authenticated identities to UPNs.
CAP messages are carried as text/calendar MIME objects, which is substrate rather than the subject.
VCAR/VRIGHT access rights are a substantial part, but they are specific to the calendar store and are best covered under the calendaring subject.
iTIP is explicitly unchanged; CAP only stores and fetches iTIP objects.
The text/calendar type is used, not registered or defined here.

gaps.name: Calendar Access Protocol (CAP) / iCalendar
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CAP itself or for iCalendar and iTIP; only the calendaring topic and the CalDAV, JSCalendar and time zones techs exist. A dedicated iCalendar/CAP tag would let readers of the calendaring subject find this RFC.

RFC4325.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Authority Information Access Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Extension
RFC4325.summary: Defines the use of the Authority Information Access extension in X.509 CRLs, so applications can discover and retrieve CRL issuer certificates via id-ad-caIssuers, updating RFC 3280.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 CRL extension and updates the PKIX certificate and CRL profile (RFC 3280). It is about X.509 certificate and CRL profile content.
X.509.quote: This document updates RFC 3280 by defining the Authority Information Access Certificate Revocation List (CRL) extension.

rejected.why: LDAP URIs are one way to locate certificates, but LDAP is only a retrieval mechanism and is not specified or extended here.
HTTP is only a retrieval mechanism for certificate files, with content-type guidance. The document is not about HTTP.
The extension syntax is given in ASN.1, but ASN.1 is only the notation used.
The .p7c certs-only CMS message is only referenced as a file format for certificate collections.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already covers this document.
The document concerns CRL revocation checking, not OCSP.

RFC4326.title: Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) for Transmission of IP Datagrams over an MPEG-2 Transport Stream (TS)
RFC4326.summary: Specifies Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE), which encapsulates IPv4/IPv6 datagrams and bridged Ethernet frames into SNDUs carried over MPEG-2 Transport Streams, with extension headers, a CRC-32 trailer, and encapsulator/receiver processing rules.

DVB.why: The whole document defines an encapsulation of IP over MPEG-2 TS, the DVB/ATSC broadcast link; this is exactly the IP over MPEG-2/DVB link-layer tag.
DVB.quote: transport of IPv4 and IPv6 Datagrams and other network protocol packets directly over the ISO MPEG-2 Transport Stream as TS Private Data

rejected.why: The document specifies a CRC-32 trailer but it reuses the standard Ethernet/DSM-CC polynomial; error detection is a minor component, not the subject.
IPv6 is merely one of the payload types carried; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
IPv4 is only one payload carried by the encapsulation.
Bridged Ethernet frames are one optional payload type (Bridged SNDU); the document is about MPEG-2 encapsulation, not Ethernet.
ULE is a link-layer encapsulation over MPEG-2, not IP-in-IP or generic IP tunnelling.
The ULE Next-Header registry is created in IANA Considerations boilerplate; the main body is not about IANA registries.

RFC4327.title: Link Management Protocol (LMP) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC4327.summary: Defines the LMP-MIB SMIv2 module for configuring and monitoring Link Management Protocol (LMP) implementations, including neighbors, control channels, TE links, link verification, data-bearing links, performance counters and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (SMIv2) with tables, counters, notifications and compliance statements for LMP.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

GMPLS.why: LMP is a GMPLS control-plane protocol for managing TE links; the MIB models its control channels, link verification and data-bearing links, so readers of GMPLS would want it.
GMPLS.quote: Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) [RFC3471] and the Link Management Protocol [RFC4204] are key components of this standardization activity.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines a MIB module, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag fits better.
The module goes with the TE Link MIB and was modelled on the MPLS LSR MIB, but the subject is LMP/GMPLS link management and the GMPLS tag is more specific.
TE links are managed objects here, but the document is about LMP management rather than traffic engineering in its own right.
Ethernet appears only as an example of an underlying layer in the interface stacking discussion.

gaps.name: Link Management Protocol (LMP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no LMP tag. GMPLS is the nearest parent, but LMP and its MIB deserve a dedicated tag.

RFC4328.title: Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Signaling Extensions for G.709 Optical Transport Networks Control
RFC4328.summary: Specifies GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling extensions for ITU-T G.709 Optical Transport Networks: new LSP Encoding Types, G-PIDs, traffic parameters (signal type, NMC, NVC, multiplier), and ODUk/OCh label spaces.

GMPLS.why: The document is a GMPLS technology-specific signaling extension for G.709 OTN, defining new LSP Encoding Types, G-PIDs, traffic parameters and labels.
GMPLS.quote: It describes the technology-specific information needed to extend GMPLS signaling to control Optical Transport Networks (OTN)

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signaling carrier for the new objects (SENDER_TSPEC/FLOWSPEC C-Types) and Section 6 is short; the subject is GMPLS G.709 extensions, so RSVP-TE is a substrate here. The RSVP-TE tag is also a child of traffic engineering.
SONET/SDH is covered by RFC 3946; this document only references it for pre-OTN items and G-PID mappings.
GMPLS is the more specific tag, and the document is not about MPLS generally.
RSVP is only the underlying protocol; the document defines G.709 traffic parameter objects for it but is not about RSVP itself.

gaps.name: G.709 Optical Transport Network (OTN)
gaps.why: The document is about controlling OTN (ODUk/OCh layers, optical transport hierarchy), but the taxonomy has no optical transport or OTN tag; the nearest is GMPLS, which covers optical/transport network control.

RFC4329.title: Scripting Media Types
RFC4329.summary: Registers four media types (text/javascript, text/ecmascript, application/javascript, application/ecmascript) for JavaScript and ECMAScript programs, and defines charset parameter handling, encoding detection and error-handling requirements.

media types.why: The document exists to register four media types in the IANA registry and define their processing requirements, so it belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of media types for the ECMAScript and JavaScript programming languages and conformance requirements for implementations of these types.

character sets.why: A substantial part of the document defines charset parameter use, signature-based encoding detection, UTF-8 default and error handling for script source text.
character sets.quote: The media types defined in this document allow an optional charset parameter to explicitly specify the character encoding scheme used to encode the source text.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is required as a baseline encoding, but the document does not specify or extend UTF-8; it only relies on it.
Unicode signatures (BOMs) and normalization are mentioned, but they are supporting details of encoding detection, covered by character sets.
RFC 3023 is referenced only for encoding considerations of the registrations; the document is not about XML.
Scripts are used in web contexts, but the document is about media type registration rather than web architecture.

gaps.name: JavaScript/ECMAScript programming language
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for scripting or programming languages. Readers interested in JavaScript or ECMAScript would want this RFC, but it can only be found through media types.

RFC4330.title: Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) Version 4 for IPv4, IPv6 and OSI
RFC4330.summary: RFC 4330 specifies SNTPv4, a simplified subset of NTP for clock synchronization using a stateless RPC-style exchange over UDP, with IPv6/OSI header changes, the kiss-o'-death packet, and client best practices.

NTP.why: The whole document specifies SNTPv4, its packet format, client and server operations, kiss-o'-death and best practices for NTP/SNTP clients.
NTP.quote: This memorandum describes the Simple Network Time Protocol Version 4 (SNTPv4), which is a subset of the Network Time Protocol (NTP) used to synchronize computer clocks

rejected.why: SNTP merely runs over UDP port 123; it defines nothing new about UDP.
The header reference identifier is adapted for IPv6 addressing, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Broadcast/multicast/manycast addressing modes are used, but multicast routing and group membership are out of scope.
DNS is recommended for resolving server names in best practices, but only as a supporting mechanism.
MD5 is used only to hash IPv6/NSAP addresses for the reference identifier and to fill timestamp bits; incidental.
OSI addressing is accommodated in the header, but the document is not about OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC4331.title: Quota and Size Properties for Distributed Authoring and Versioning (DAV) Collections
RFC4331.summary: RFC 4331 defines two live WebDAV properties, DAV:quota-available-bytes and DAV:quota-used-bytes, plus 507 error preconditions, so clients can discover and interoperate with storage quotas on DAV collections.

WebDAV.why: The document extends WebDAV with new live properties (quota-available-bytes, quota-used-bytes), PROPFIND behaviour and 507 error preconditions. A reader browsing WebDAV would expect it.
WebDAV.quote: The approach to meeting the requirements and scenarios outlined above is to define two live properties.

rejected.why: WebDAV runs over HTTP, but the document specifies WebDAV properties and does not extend HTTP semantics. WebDAV is the more specific tag.
NFS quota definitions are cited as the model for the properties, and its error codes are mentioned. The document is not about NFS.
XML is only the encoding for property values and error bodies. The document adds nothing new about XML itself.
The topic is storage access protocols over IP. Here quota is a WebDAV property concern, and WebDAV is already tagged.

RFC4332.title: Cisco's Mobile IPv4 Host Configuration Extensions
RFC4332.summary: Informational RFC defining Cisco vendor-specific extensions to Mobile IPv4 Registration Request/Reply messages so a Mobile Node can obtain home-network host configuration (prefix length, DNS, DHCP, gateway, suffix, URL) from the Home Agent.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document defines new extensions to Mobile IPv4 registration messages, so it extends the Mobile IPv4 protocol and belongs on that subject's page.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document describes the Cisco vendor-specific extensions to Mobile IPv4 to provide the base host configuration in Registration Request and Reply messages.

rejected.why: DHCP is only the comparison point and a source of the configuration values (DHCP Client ID and Server fields echo DHCP data). The document does not specify or extend DHCP itself.
The DNS Server and DNS Suffix extensions only carry configuration values for the host. They say nothing about DNS protocol behaviour.
PPP/IPCP is mentioned only as another way to obtain host configuration, which the document says is inadequate.
The Configuration URL extension merely carries a URL string and defines nothing about URIs.

RFC4333.title: The IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) Member Selection Guidelines and Process
RFC4333.summary: BCP defining the guidelines and process by which the IAB and IESG select their member of the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC), including qualifications, nominations, terms and vacancies.

IETF process.why: The document specifies an IETF administrative selection procedure (nominations, selection, terms, vacancies) for the IAOC, which is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This memo outlines the process by which the IAB and IESG make their selections.

rejected.why: The IETF Nominations Committee is only mentioned as also using the qualification guidance; the document defines the IAB/IESG process, not NomCom procedures.
Nothing about RFC format or publication; the IAOC oversees administrative support generally.

gaps.name: IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA) / IAOC
gaps.why: The document is about the IAOC and IASA governance structure, for which the taxonomy has no specific tag; IETF process is the nearest fit.

RFC4334.title: Certificate Extensions and Attributes Supporting Authentication in Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) and Wireless Local Area Networks (WLAN)
RFC4334.summary: Defines two EAP extended key usage values (EAP over PPP, EAP over LAN) and a WLAN SSID certificate extension and attribute certificate attribute to help select X.509 client certificates for PPP and 802.1X authentication.

X.509.why: The document defines new X.509 certificate extensions (extended key usage values, SSID extension) and an attribute certificate attribute, so it belongs to X.509 certificates and profiles.
X.509.quote: This document defines two Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) extended key usage values and a public key certificate extension to carry Wireless LAN (WLAN) System Service identifiers (SSIDs).

EAP.why: The new key purposes identify certificates suitable for EAP authentication in PPP and LAN environments, and the extensions exist to support EAP-TLS certificate selection.
EAP.quote: This specification defines two KeyPurposeId values: one for EAP over PPP, and one for EAP over LAN (EAPOL).

WiFi.why: A substantial part of the document defines the WLAN SSID extension and attribute for IEEE 802.11 networks, so readers interested in Wi-Fi authentication would want it.
WiFi.quote: The list of SSIDs MAY be used to select the correct certificate for authentication in a particular WLAN.
WiFi.section: 3. WLAN SSID Public Key Certificate Extension

rejected.why: PPP is only one of the environments in which the EAP key usage applies. The document defines certificate extensions, not anything about PPP itself.
RADIUS is mentioned only as the usual authentication service in WLAN deployments, and the document specifies nothing about it.
EAP-TLS is cited only as an example of a method that uses certificates. The document defines nothing about TLS.
ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the extensions, and the document is not about ASN.1.
The more specific X.509 tag fits better than the PKI parent.

RFC4335.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Session Channel Break Extension
RFC4335.summary: Defines a new SSH connection-protocol session channel request, "break", that lets an SSH client send a BREAK signal to a remote host, with guidance on break duration and cascading.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH connection protocol with a new channel request type ('break'), so it is about SSH.
SSH.quote: The following channel-specific request can be sent over a session channel (as described in [4]) to request that the remote host perform a BREAK operation.

rejected.why: Telnet's BREAK is the motivating precedent and console servers are discussed, but the document specifies nothing about Telnet itself.
The IANA section only registers the 'break' channel request name. That is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC4336.title: Problem Statement for the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)
RFC4336.summary: Informational problem statement explaining the motivation for DCCP, a congestion-controlled unreliable datagram transport protocol, and why a new transport is preferable to congestion control above/below UDP or modifying TCP, SCTP or RTP.

DCCP.why: The whole document is the problem statement and design rationale for DCCP.
DCCP.quote: the motivation behind the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), an unreliable transport protocol incorporating end-to-end congestion control

congestion control.why: A substantial part of the document analyses where congestion control for unreliable flows should live, plus TFRC-like and TCP-like choices.
congestion control.quote: We aim to bring easy-to-use congestion control mechanisms to applications that generate large or long-lived flows of unreliable datagrams

rejected.why: UDP is the baseline the document compares against and seeks to replace for these applications; the document does not specify or extend it.
ECN is discussed as a requirement and its difficulties above UDP, but the document is not about ECN itself; it falls under the congestion control topic.
SCTP is considered and rejected as a basis in one subsection only.
TCP is discussed only as an alternative that is not modified.
TFRC is mentioned as a desired congestion control choice but is not specified or analysed here.
RTP is discussed only as a layer that would run over the new protocol or be modified.

RFC4337.title: MIME Type Registration for MPEG-4
RFC4337.summary: Registers five MIME media types (video/mp4, audio/mp4, application/mp4, application/mpeg4-iod, application/mpeg4-iod-xmt) for MPEG-4 MP4 files and gives guidance on choosing among them.

media types.why: The document's whole purpose is registering MIME media types for MP4 content and recommending which type to use for which content.
media types.quote: Sections from 4.1 to 4.5 register five new MIME types with the IANA.

rejected.why: MPEG-4 is the content format, but the document only registers media types and does not define codecs or containers.
AVC is mentioned only in passing in the introduction; the document is not about it.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example of how the files might be served; it is not specified or extended.
RFC 3550 is cited only as a reference for MPEG-4 delivery; the document does not address RTP.
The IANA Considerations section holds the registrations themselves, but the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

RFC4338.title: Transmission of IPv6, IPv4, and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) Packets over Fibre Channel
RFC4338.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IPv6, IPv4 and ARP packets over Fibre Channel, including IPv6 interface ID and link-local formation, a Fibre Channel ARP format, multicast mapping, and sequence and exchange management. It obsoletes RFC 2625 and RFC 3831.

ARP.why: The document defines a new FC ARP packet format and the IPv4 address resolution procedure over Fibre Channel. It also covers ARP encapsulation and compatibility with RFC 2625's Ethernet-format ARP.
ARP.quote: defining a Fibre Channel specific version of the ARP protocol (FC ARP), carrying both N_Port_Name and N_Port_ID as Hardware (HW) Address.

SLAAC.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how to derive IPv6 interface identifiers from N_Port_Names, for stateless autoconfiguration and link-local addresses.
SLAAC.quote: IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration MUST be performed as specified in [ACONF]. An IPv6 Address Prefix used for stateless address autoconfiguration of an Nx_Port MUST have a length of 64 bits.
SLAAC.section: 5.1. IPv6 Interface Identifier and Address Prefix

rejected.why: This tag covers Fibre Channel over IP transports such as iFCP and FCIP, the opposite direction. This document carries IP over Fibre Channel.
The document only defines the Source/Target Link-layer Address option format for Fibre Channel. Neighbor Discovery is used as the resolution mechanism and is not itself specified or extended.
IPv6 is the payload being encapsulated. The document is about the link-layer mapping, not the IPv6 protocol itself.
IPv4 is the payload being encapsulated, not the subject being specified.
Fibre Channel is described as a storage network technology, but the document is about IP over FC, not storage access.
Multicast address mapping is covered in one section, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.

gaps.name: IP over Fibre Channel
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no link-layer tag for IP over Fibre Channel. The existing 'fibre channel' tag covers Fibre Channel over IP, which is the opposite direction. Readers looking for link-layer mappings would want this RFC listed with the other IP-over-X documents.

RFC4339.title: IPv6 Host Configuration of DNS Server Information Approaches
RFC4339.summary: An informational analysis comparing three approaches (RA option, DHCPv6 option, well-known anycast addresses) for configuring recursive DNS server addresses on IPv6 hosts, with deployment scenarios for ISP, enterprise, 3GPP and unmanaged networks.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 host autoconfiguration of DNS resolver information, including ND/RA-based configuration and deployment scenarios in IPv6 networks.
IPv6.quote: This document describes three approaches for IPv6 recursive DNS server address configuration.

DHCPv6.why: One of the three approaches is analysed in depth: the DHCPv6 DNS option and stateless DHCPv6, with advantages and disadvantages.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv6 [3] includes the "DNS Recursive Name Server" option, through which a host can obtain a list of IP addresses of recursive DNS servers [5].

neighbor discovery.why: The RA option approach extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and is analysed in detail.
neighbor discovery.quote: The RA approach defines a new ND option, called the RDNSS option, that contains a recursive DNS server address [6].

anycast.why: A third approach is well-known anycast addresses for recursive DNS servers, discussed with its own operational semantics.
anycast.quote: The approach with well-known anycast addresses is to set multiple well-known anycast addresses in clients' resolver configuration files

rejected.why: DNS is the service being configured, not the subject. The document covers how hosts learn resolver addresses, not DNS protocol or operation.
It appears only in Security Considerations, as a remark about autoconfiguration and key rollover.
Stateless address autoconfiguration is mentioned as the context for the RA option but is not what the document analyses.
3GPP is one deployment scenario section, but the document is not about IP over 3GPP systems in general.
Secure ND is only referenced in the security discussion.

gaps.name: IPv6 DNS configuration / RDNSS discovery
gaps.why: The document's central subject, host configuration of recursive DNS server addresses, has no dedicated tag. The closest are IPv6, DHCPv6 and neighbor discovery.

RFC4340.title: Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)
RFC4340.summary: RFC 4340 specifies DCCP, a transport protocol providing congestion-controlled unreliable datagram connections, with handshakes, feature negotiation, acknowledgement options, ECN support, partial checksums, PMTU handling, and pluggable CCIDs.

DCCP.why: The document is the core DCCP specification, defining its packet formats, states, feature negotiation, and registries.
DCCP.quote: The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport protocol that provides bidirectional unicast connections of congestion-controlled unreliable datagrams.

ECN.why: A full section covers ECN Incapable, ECN Nonces and aggression penalties, so ECN readers would want this.
ECN.quote: The DCCP protocol is fully ECN-aware [RFC3168]. Each CCID specifies how its endpoints respond to ECN marks.

rejected.why: DCCP is the more specific tag for this RFC. The CCID profiles are in RFC 4341 and RFC 4342, not here.
CCID 3 (TFRC) is only referenced and defined in a separate profile document.
Partial checksum coverage was inspired by UDP-Lite, but the document is not about it.
Section 17.1 discusses RTP over DCCP only briefly, as a relation to other specifications.
PMTU measurement is one section of a larger protocol specification, and the document does not define PMTUD itself.
The checksum and Data Checksum material is a sub-part of DCCP, not the subject of the document.

RFC4341.title: Profile for Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) Congestion Control ID 2: TCP-like Congestion Control
RFC4341.summary: Defines DCCP Congestion Control ID 2 (CCID 2), a TCP-like AIMD congestion control profile for DCCP using Ack Vectors, SACK-like loss inference, Ack Ratio control of acknowledgements, and ECN support.

DCCP.why: The document is a DCCP CCID profile, specifying congestion control behaviour, options and features, and registries within DCCP.
DCCP.quote: This document contains the profile for Congestion Control Identifier 2 (CCID 2), TCP-like Congestion Control, in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)

congestion control.why: It specifies an AIMD congestion control algorithm (cwnd, ssthresh, pipe) plus congestion control of acknowledgements. The DCCP tag has no congestion control tag as a child, so this topic tag is added directly.
congestion control.quote: CCID 2's congestion control mechanisms are based on those for SACK- based TCP [RFC3517], since the Ack Vector provides all the information

rejected.why: TCP congestion control is the model that CCID 2 follows, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
ECN is supported (Section 7), but only by reference to RFC 3168, RFC 3540 and RFC 4340. The document defines nothing new about ECN.
CCID 3 (TFRC) is mentioned only as the alternative, and it is specified in another RFC.
The document does not specify or discuss NewReno. It follows SACK-based TCP loss recovery.

RFC4342.title: Profile for Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) Congestion Control ID 3: TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC)
RFC4342.summary: Profile of DCCP Congestion Control ID 3 (CCID 3), which applies TFRC rate-based, TCP-friendly congestion control to DCCP half-connections, defining its loss-interval feedback, options, features and ECN nonce verification.

TFRC.why: The document profiles TFRC for use in DCCP, specifying loss event rate, nofeedback timer, initial rate and receive rate handling.
TFRC.quote: TFRC is a receiver-based congestion control mechanism that provides a TCP-friendly sending rate while minimizing the abrupt rate changes characteristic of TCP

DCCP.why: It defines CCID 3 for DCCP, including new options (Loss Intervals, Receive Rate, Loss Event Rate), a feature number and IANA registries.
DCCP.quote: This document contains the profile for Congestion Control Identifier 3, TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC), in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)

ECN.why: A substantial part covers ECN use, ECN Nonce reporting in Loss Intervals and verifying receiver compliance (Sections 7 and 9).
ECN.quote: CCID 3 supports Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) [RFC3168].

rejected.why: TCP is only the reference for fairness and the throughput equation, not specified or extended here.
The parent topic is implied by the TFRC tag; the document is about a specific mechanism.
Not discussed; DCCP is the substrate-level protocol here.
IANA registries are boilerplate-like and secondary to the main body.

gaps.name: DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists DCCP as a transport tag, but I used the id 'DCCP'; if it is not exactly present, the closest fits are TFRC and congestion control.

RFC4343.title: Domain Name System (DNS) Case Insensitivity Clarification
RFC4343.summary: RFC 4343 clarifies what "case insensitive" means for DNS names, specifying label comparison, escaping, case preservation on input and output, and the relationship to label types, CLASS and IDNs.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies DNS name-matching and case-preservation behaviour for resolvers and servers, updating RFCs 1034, 1035 and 2181.
DNS.quote: Domain Name System (DNS) names are "case insensitive". This document explains exactly what that means and provides a clear specification of the rules.

rejected.why: Section 5 only notes that IDN case handling happens in a separate application-level transformation and is not part of DNS. The document is not about IDNA.
The document relies on ASCII letter ranges for its matching rule, but it is about DNS name comparison, not the ASCII character set.
RFC 4034 is cited only for a canonical name form in Security Considerations. That is boilerplate-level evidence.
Dynamic update is mentioned only as one input source for case preservation. The document does not specify it.

RFC4344.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Encryption Modes
RFC4344.summary: RFC 4344 defines new counter-mode (SDCTR) symmetric encryption methods for the SSH Transport Protocol and gives rekeying recommendations to fix attacks on the original CBC-based authenticated encryption.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH Transport Protocol with new encryption methods and rekeying guidance, so SSH readers need it.
SSH.quote: This document describes new symmetric encryption methods for the Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Protocol and gives specific recommendations on how frequently SSH implementations should rekey.

AES.why: The RECOMMENDED methods are AES in counter mode with 128, 192 and 256-bit keys. The document specifies how AES is used in SSH, and the counter mode applies to all the ciphers.
AES.quote: The "aes128-ctr" method uses AES (the Advanced Encryption Standard, formerly Rijndael) with 128-bit keys [AES].

rejected.why: 3des-ctr is just one of thirteen cipher options. The document is not about DES.
The MAC is discussed only as a source of information leakage that motivates rekeying. The document does not specify it.
Rekeying is the SSH transport's own key exchange cadence. The document gives no key-management mechanism.
The parent topic is implied by the AES tag, and the document is better described by the more specific tag.

RFC4345.title: Improved Arcfour Modes for the Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol
RFC4345.summary: Defines two new SSH transport-layer encryption algorithms, arcfour128 and arcfour256, which use RC4 but discard the first 1536 bytes of keystream to mitigate key-scheduling weakness.

RC4.why: The document specifies how to use RC4 (Arcfour) safely, with keystream discard to mitigate its weak key schedule. It also discusses attacks on RC4 and says it should be used with caution.
RC4.quote: The first 1536 bytes of keystream generated by the cipher MUST be discarded, and the first byte of the first encrypted packet MUST be encrypted using the 1537th byte of keystream.

SSH.why: It defines new SSH transport-layer encryption algorithm names (arcfour128, arcfour256), so it extends SSH and belongs on the SSH page.
SSH.quote: This document specifies new cipher algorithms for SSH that follow this recommendation.

rejected.why: The RC4 tag is more specific and already sits under cryptography, so the parent is implied.
This is general security. The SSH and RC4 tags cover the document more specifically.
The document only registers two algorithm names. That is boilerplate, not its subject.

RFC4346.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1
RFC4346.summary: RFC 4346 specifies TLS version 1.1, defining the record protocol, handshake protocols, alerts, cipher suites and security analysis, as a revision of TLS 1.0 with explicit CBC IVs and related fixes.

TLS.why: The whole document is the TLS 1.1 protocol specification: record layer, handshake, alerts, cipher suites, backward compatibility and security analysis.
TLS.quote: This document specifies Version 1.1 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

rejected.why: Certificates are used for authentication, but the document defers certificate profiles to PKIX and does not specify X.509 itself.
RSA is used for key exchange and signatures, but only as a mechanism the protocol relies on, not as the subject.
HMAC is used for record MACs and the PRF, but it is a building block defined elsewhere.
TCP is only the reliable transport substrate under TLS.
DES and 3DES appear as cipher suite components, but the document is not about them.
MD5 and SHA-1 are used in the PRF and handshake hashes but are not the subject.

RFC4347.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security
RFC4347.summary: RFC 4347 specifies DTLS 1.0, a datagram variant of TLS 1.1 that adds explicit record sequence numbers, a cookie exchange against DoS, and handshake fragmentation and retransmission over unreliable transport.

DTLS.why: The document defines the DTLS protocol itself, including record layer changes, handshake modifications, retransmission and replay detection.
DTLS.quote: This document specifies Version 1.0 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

rejected.why: DTLS is a child of TLS and is the more specific tag. TLS 1.1 is the base that the document describes deltas from, not the subject.
UDP is the datagram transport DTLS runs over and is not specified or profiled here.
IPsec is mentioned only as an alternative and as the source of the replay-window technique.
DCCP is mentioned only as another possible transport, with a future mapping noted.
The PMTU handling section is a supporting detail of the record layer. The document does not define PMTUD.
SIP is cited only as an example of an application that uses UDP.

RFC4348.title: Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload Format for the Variable-Rate Multimode Wideband (VMR-WB) Audio Codec
RFC4348.summary: Specifies the RTP payload formats (header-free and octet-aligned), SDP/MIME parameters, and a media type registration for the VMR-WB wideband speech codec, designed to interoperate with AMR-WB.

RTP payload format.why: The document's core purpose is an RTP payload format for a specific speech codec, including header usage, ToC, interleaving and parameters.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of VMR-WB-encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

AMR.why: A substantial part of the document addresses AMR-WB interoperability (mode 3, FT mapping, gateway scenarios, offer/answer declaring AMR-WB capability).
AMR.quote: VMR-WB is a variable-rate multimode wideband speech codec that has a number of operating modes, one of which is interoperable with AMR-WB

media types.why: The document includes a full audio/VMR-WB media type registration with parameters.
media types.quote: The MIME subtype for the Variable-Rate Multimode Wideband (VMR-WB) audio codec is allocated from the IETF tree

SDP.why: Defines the SDP mapping of parameters and offer/answer considerations for the payload format.
SDP.quote: When SDP is used to specify sessions employing the VMR-WB codec, the mapping is as follows:

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the specific payload-format tag covers this document.
The codec itself is specified by 3GPP2; this RFC only defines packetization, so the payload format tag fits better.
Redundant transmission is discussed briefly as a robustness feature, but it is not a main subject.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible external mechanism.
CDMA2000 gateway scenarios provide context, but the document is not about cellular network IP interworking.
Short section referring to general RTP congestion rules; not a substantial topic.

RFC4349.title: High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC) Frames over Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol, Version 3 (L2TPv3)
RFC4349.summary: Specifies how to carry HDLC frames as pseudowires over L2TPv3: pseudowire type, session setup and teardown, Circuit Status signalling, encapsulation, sequencing and MTU.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TPv3 with a new HDLC pseudowire type, new result codes, session handling and encapsulation rules. L2TP is the protocol it specifies.
L2TP.quote: This document describes the specifics of how to tunnel High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC) frames over L2TPv3.

pseudowire.why: The document defines an HDLC pseudowire emulation: port-to-port transport, link status notification, and an applicability statement on emulation fidelity. Readers of pseudowire emulation would want it.
pseudowire.quote: Such emulated circuits are referred to as HDLC Pseudowires (HDLCPWs).

rejected.why: PPP is only one example of a protocol that can ride over the HDLC pseudowire. The LCCEs do not take part in its negotiation.
Frame Relay is mentioned only as a transparent payload example, not specified or profiled here.
LAPB/X.25 is only an example of a transported payload.
IPsec is mentioned once as an option for payload integrity and is not the subject of the document.
The tunnelling is done by L2TP, which is the more specific tag.
The FCS/CRC is only noted as stripped and regenerated, and the document is not about CRC error detection.

gaps.name: HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control)
gaps.why: The document is about carrying HDLC frames, but the taxonomy has no HDLC tag. The nearest tags are link layer and PPP.

RFC4350.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Formal Namespace for the New Zealand Government
RFC4350.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace identifier "NZL" for the New Zealand Government, defining its urn:nzl:<specifier>:... structure, assignment, persistence, resolution and lexical equivalence rules.

URN.why: The document is a URN formal namespace registration (NID NZL) with its structure, uniqueness, persistence and lexical equivalence rules, so it belongs under URN namespaces.
URN.quote: urn:nzl:<nz-specifier>[:<nz-specifier defined string>]+

rejected.why: XML artefacts are the motivating use case, but the document specifies a URN namespace, not XML usage or formats.
UTF-8 and percent-encoding of Maori macrons are discussed for lexical equivalence, but only as part of URI syntax rules, not as the subject.
The IANA section only registers the NID and is boilerplate; the document is not about IANA registry policy.
The more specific URN tag fits; URI syntax (RFC 3986) is only the basis for the namespace.

RFC4351.title: Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload for Text Conversation Interleaved in an Audio Stream
RFC4351.summary: Defines the audio/t140c RTP payload format for PSTN gateways to interleave T.140 real-time text with audio in one RTP session, with T140block counters, RFC 2198 redundancy, and a "cps" SDP parameter; now Historic.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines a new RTP payload format (audio/t140c) for T.140 text, including packet layout, redundancy and media type registration.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes how to carry real-time text conversation session contents in RTP packets.

PSTN interop.why: The format is restricted to PSTN gateway applications that interleave textphone signals with voice over IP, so PSTN interworking readers would want it.
PSTN interop.quote: The payload format for real-time text transmission with RTP [2] described in this memo is intended for use between Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) gateways

rejected.why: SDP is used for the fmtp 'cps' parameter and examples, but the document is not about SDP itself.
SRTP is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a suitable protection mechanism.
The audio/t140c registration is IANA boilerplate for the payload format, not a document about media type rules.
G.711 audio only appears as the audio interleaved in the SDP examples.
RFC 2198 redundancy is used, but this is part of the payload format and not a general loss-recovery scheme. FEC is only mentioned as an alternative.
RTCP is only mentioned for CNAME-based stream association.

gaps.name: T.140 real-time text
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for real-time text conversation (T.140, RFC 4103). This is the main subject of the document.

RFC4352.title: RTP Payload Format for the Extended Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB+) Audio Codec
RFC4352.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format (basic and interleaved modes, ToC, timestamps, ISF handling) for the AMR-WB+ audio codec, with a media type registration and SDP parameter mapping.

AMR.why: The document defines how AMR-WB+ (an AMR-WB extension) frames are packetized in RTP. The AMR tag covers AMR and AMR-WB speech codecs and fits this closely.
AMR.quote: This document specifies a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format for Extended Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB+) encoded audio signals.

RTP payload format.why: It is an RTP payload format specification for a specific codec: payload header, ToC, timestamp derivation, and interleaving.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of Extended Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB+) [1] encoded audio signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

media types.why: A full audio/AMR-WB+ media type registration with parameters (channels, interleaving, int-delay) is a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: The media type for the Extended Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB+) codec is allocated from the IETF tree

SDP.why: It defines the SDP mapping and offer/answer rules for the payload parameters, which SDP readers would want.
SDP.quote: The information carried in the media type specification has a specific mapping to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
SDP.section: 7.2. Mapping Media Type Parameters into SDP

rejected.why: AMR is a more specific tag under codecs and already covers the codec subject.
SRTP is only mentioned as an external security mechanism that may be used.
The redundancy scheme is a small, AMR-WB+-specific feature of the payload. The document is not about FEC as a subject.
RTCP is mentioned only as a source of feedback for choosing redundancy.
Section 5 is a short boilerplate-style note referring to general RTP congestion considerations.
RTSP appears only as a declarative SDP usage example in a reference.

RFC4353.title: A Framework for Conferencing with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4353.summary: Informational framework describing the architecture, terminology and SIP protocol components (focus, mixers, notification service, conference policy) for tightly coupled multiparty conferencing with SIP.

conferencing.why: The document is a conferencing framework defining focus, mixer, policy server and physical realizations. XCON is a specific framework/data model, so the general conferencing topic is the best fit.
conferencing.quote: This document defines a framework for how such conferencing can occur. This framework describes the overall architecture, terminology, and protocol components needed for multi-party conferencing.

SIP.why: The framework is built on SIP dialogs, INVITE/BYE/REFER/Join, SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and the isfocus feature tag, describing how SIP is used for tightly coupled conferences.
SIP.quote: Users usually join the conference by sending an INVITE to the conference URI.

rejected.why: XCON is the later centralized conferencing framework and data model; this RFC is the SIP-specific framework, and the conference policy interfaces are explicitly non-SIP-specific.
RTP is only the media transport that mixers handle; the document does not specify or extend it.
Offer/answer is only used for adding and removing media via re-INVITE; the document does not extend it.
Single-source multicast is mentioned once as a media distribution option in distributed mixing, not a subject of the document.
The conference notification service uses SIP event notification, but only briefly and without defining an event package.

RFC4354.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Event Package and Data Format for Various Settings in Support for the Push-to-Talk over Cellular (PoC) Service
RFC4354.summary: Defines the SIP "poc-settings" event package and the application/poc-settings+xml document format, letting Push-to-talk over Cellular terminals publish and subscribers receive Incoming Session Barring, Answer Mode, Instant Personal Alert Barring and Simultaneous Sessions settings.

SIMPLE.why: The document is a SIP event package using SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and PUBLISH with an EPA/ESC model, which is the SIMPLE event-package family. It defines the package's details for RFC 3265 and RFC 3903.
SIMPLE.quote: We define a new "poc-settings" event package.  Event Publication Agents (EPA) use PUBLISH requests to inform an Event State Compositor (ESC)

SIP.why: It extends SIP for the PoC service, with a new Event header value and rules for notifiers and subscribers. Readers of SIP extensions would want it.
SIP.quote: This document defines a SIP event package to support publication, subscription, and notification of additional capabilities required by the PoC service.

media types.why: It defines the PoC-settings document format and registers the application/poc-settings+xml media type.
media types.quote: PoC-settings documents are identified with the MIME type "application/poc-settings+xml" and are instances of the XML schema defined in Section 6.1.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for the settings document. The document defines a schema but is not about XML usage in general.
PoC runs over cellular networks, but the document is about SIP signalling of user settings, not IP over 3GPP systems.
S/MIME is only mentioned as an option for protecting NOTIFY bodies. The document is not about it.
It covers PoC settings, and instant messaging is mentioned only in passing. The event-package mechanism is the focus.
Conference focus and URI-list servers are mentioned as PoC network roles. The document does not address conferencing frameworks.

gaps.name: Push-to-talk over Cellular (PoC)
gaps.why: The OMA PoC service is the document's whole context, but the taxonomy has no tag for push-to-talk or PoC services.

RFC4355.title: IANA Registration for Enumservices email, fax, mms, ems, and sms
RFC4355.summary: RFC 4355 registers the ENUM Enumservices "email", "fax", "sms", "ems" and "mms" (with tel: and mailto: URI schemes) for use in NAPTR records under the E2U DDDS application of RFC 3761.
