ENUM.why: The whole document is a set of Enumservice registrations under the ENUM specification (RFC 3761), indicating service classes in NAPTR records for E.164 numbers.
ENUM.quote: This document registers the Enumservices "email", "fax", "sms", "ems", and "mms" using the URI schemes 'tel:' and 'mailto:'

SMS.why: Three of the five registrations (sms, ems, mms) concern mobile short and multimedia messaging, including carrying them over SMTP to gateways; SMS readers would want this.
SMS.quote: This Enumservice indicates that the resource identified by the associated URI scheme is capable of receiving a message using the Short Message Service (SMS)

tel URI.why: The tel: URI scheme is the subtype for fax, sms, ems and mms registrations, so readers interested in tel URI usage with ENUM would find it relevant.

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR records are only the substrate for ENUM; the document defines no new DNS behaviour.
The email Enumservice only registers the mailto: scheme as a hint; it does not specify email protocols or architecture.
The fax Enumservice is a registration pointing to PSTN fax standards (T.4/T.30), not a specification of fax over Internet mail or IP.
MIME sub-parts are mentioned only in passing and no media type is registered.
SMTP is only the bearer for MMS and SMS content in the mailto: registrations; the document does not specify or extend it.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as boilerplate-level reference.

RFC4356.title: Mapping Between the Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS) and Internet Mail
RFC4356.summary: Specifies how to map messages, X-Mms-* headers, and delivery/disposition reports between the cellular Multimedia Messaging Service (MM3 interface) and Internet mail (SMTP and Internet message format).

email.why: The document is a gateway specification between MMS and Internet mail, covering SMTP envelope and header mapping, delivery and disposition reports. Email is the general tag that fits it.
email.quote: This document specifies how to exchange messages between these two services, including mapping information elements as used in MMS X-Mms-* headers

SMS.why: MMS is the mobile messaging service that sits alongside SMS. It is the closest taxonomy tag for mobile message interworking with Internet mail, though MMS is not SMS itself.
SMS.quote: The cellular telephone industry has defined a service known as the Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS).

VPIM.why: The mapping explicitly supports VPIM voice messages, including Sensitivity header handling and status code 5.6.0.
VPIM.quote: This document includes support for voice messages specified by the Voice Profile for Internet Mail [VPIM].

rejected.why: SMTP is the transport the mapping uses, including DSN and DELIVER-BY extensions. The document defines no new SMTP behaviour and only specifies how to populate it.
The document uses RFC 2822 headers, but its subject is the MMS-to-Internet mapping, not the message format.
multipart/report and charset handling are used but not specified. They are not the subject.
MMS is a cellular-industry service, but the document covers only mail interworking, not IP over 3GPP networks.

gaps.name: Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MMS. It is the document's main subject and would be a natural child of messaging.

RFC4357.title: Additional Cryptographic Algorithms for Use with GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001, and GOST R 34.11-94 Algorithms
RFC4357.summary: Informational RFC from CRYPTO-PRO that supplements the Russian GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94/2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms with CBC mode, key meshing, HMAC/PRF, VKO key derivation, key wrap, key diversification, and ASN.1 OIDs and parameter sets.

GOST.why: The whole document defines supplementary modes, key wrap, key derivation, and parameter sets for the Russian GOST algorithms for use in Internet protocols.
GOST.quote: This document describes the cryptographic algorithms and parameters supplementary to the original GOST specifications, GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001, and GOST R 34.11-94

rejected.why: ASN.1 modules are the notation used to define OIDs and parameters, but the document is about the GOST algorithms, not ASN.1 itself.
HMAC_GOSTR3411 is a short section applying HMAC to the GOST hash; it is a minor part, not what the document is about.
GOST R 34.10-2001 elliptic curve parameters are defined, but they are covered by the GOST tag as a GOST-specific algorithm.
VKO key derivation and key wrap are included, but they are GOST-specific pieces and the GOST tag covers them.
PRF_GOSTR3411 follows the TLS PRF construction, but TLS is only referenced and not specified or extended here.

RFC4358.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA)
RFC4358.summary: Registers the "oma" URN namespace identifier for the Open Mobile Alliance, defining its syntax urn:oma:{OMAresource}:{ResourceSpecificString} and the OMNA naming authority that manages assignments.

URN.why: The whole document is a URN namespace registration under RFC 3406, specifying the NID, syntax, assignment and uniqueness rules for "oma".
URN.quote: This document describes the Namespace Identifier (NID) for Uniform Resource Namespace (URN) resources published by the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA).

rejected.why: XML namespaces are the motivation for the URNs, but the document does not specify any XML usage or format.
The IANA section only notes the NID was entered in the URN namespaces registry; that is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
URN is the more specific tag; the document is not about general URI syntax or schemes.

RFC4359.title: The Use of RSA/SHA-1 Signatures within Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH)
RFC4359.summary: Specifies the use of RSA digital signatures with SHA-1 as an authentication algorithm (ICV) in IPsec ESP and AH, to give data origin authentication for group/multicast traffic.

ESP.why: The document defines a new authentication transform for ESP (and AH), specifying ICV sizing, interaction with ESP combined-mode ciphers, and SA attributes.
ESP.quote: This memo describes how RSA digital signatures can be applied as an ESP and AH authentication mechanism to provide data origin authentication.

RSA.why: Specifies RSA signature encodings, modulus sizes, key lifetimes, and performance of RSA/SHA-1 signatures.
RSA.quote: RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 MUST be supported by a conforming implementation.

multicast security.why: The motivating use is source authentication for group traffic, with public key distribution through group key management such as GDOI.
multicast security.quote: One example is the use of ESP and AH to authenticate the sender of an IP multicast packet.

rejected.why: SHA-1 is mandated as the hash but the document is not about the hash family.
Mentioned only as an example group key management system for distributing the public key.
IKEv2 is mentioned only as an example for pairwise SAs where this transform is not recommended.
HMAC is the contrasting mechanism that this document explains is insufficient for group origin authentication.
ESP is the more specific tag; AH has no separate child tag and the parent is implied.

RFC4360.title: BGP Extended Communities Attribute
RFC4360.summary: Defines the BGP Extended Communities attribute (type code 16), its 8-octet encoding, the two-octet-AS, IPv4-address and opaque types, Route Target and Route Origin communities, operational rules, and IANA registries.

BGP communities.why: The whole document specifies the Extended Communities attribute, its encoding, types, and handling, which is exactly the BGP communities subject (extended communities).
BGP communities.quote: This document describes the "extended community" BGP-4 attribute. This attribute provides a mechanism for labeling information carried in BGP-4.

rejected.why: The document extends BGP with an attribute, but the more specific BGP communities tag covers it; BGP itself is the substrate.
Route Target and Route Origin are used by BGP/MPLS VPNs, but that use is only referenced as one possible use (RFC 4364), not specified here.
IANA registries are created, but this is boilerplate-level apparatus for the main subject.

RFC4361.title: Node-specific Client Identifiers for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Version Four (DHCPv4)
RFC4361.summary: Specifies that DHCPv4 clients identify themselves using an RFC 3315-style DUID and IAID in the client identifier option (type 255), updating RFC 2131/2132 so identifiers are node-specific and consistent with DHCPv6.

DHCP.why: The document redefines the DHCPv4 client identifier option format and client/server behaviour, updating RFC 2131 and RFC 2132.
DHCP.quote: DHCPv4 clients MUST send a 'client identifier' option containing an Identity Association Unique Identifier, as defined in section 10 of RFC 3315

DHCPv6.why: It reuses DHCPv6 DUID/IAID identifiers, updates RFC 3315, and sets DHCPv6 client behaviour (section 6.2) so dual-stack hosts use the same DUID.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv4 client implementations that conform to this specification use a DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID) as specified in Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

rejected.why: DNS updates made by the DHCP server are only a motivating example, not the subject of the document.
The IPv4-to-IPv6 transition is only the motivation. The document is about DHCP identifiers, not IPv6 itself.
Dynamic DNS updates are mentioned only as a use of client identity. The document does not specify them.

RFC4362.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): A Link-Layer Assisted Profile for IP/UDP/RTP
RFC4362.summary: Defines ROHC profile 0x0005, a link-layer assisted IP/UDP/RTP header compression profile extending ROHC RTP with a header-free packet (NHP), new CSP/CCP packet types, and an interface to an assisting lower layer; obsoletes RFC 3242.

ROHC.why: The document specifies a new ROHC profile as an extension to the ROHC RTP profile, with additional packet types, feedback option and parameters.
ROHC.quote: This document defines a ROHC (Robust Header Compression) profile for compression of IP/UDP/RTP (Internet Protocol/User Datagram Protocol/Real-Time Transport Protocol) packets

rejected.why: RTP headers are what is compressed, but the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
Parent of ROHC; the more specific ROHC tag is used instead.
Mentioned only as prior art for comparison.
Mentioned only as prior art in the introduction and not specified here.
Cellular links such as GERAN and CDMA2000 motivate the profile, but the document gives no link-specific specification.
UDP headers are compressed, but the document does not specify or extend UDP.

RFC4363.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges with Traffic Classes, Multicast Filtering, and Virtual LAN Extensions
RFC4363.summary: RFC 4363 defines the P-BRIDGE-MIB and Q-BRIDGE-MIB SNMP MIB modules for managing IEEE 802.1D traffic classes and multicast filtering and IEEE 802.1Q VLANs on MAC bridges, obsoleting RFC 2674.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is to define SMIv2 MIB modules (P-BRIDGE-MIB and Q-BRIDGE-MIB) for bridge management, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it defines two MIB modules for managing the capabilities of MAC bridges defined by the IEEE 802.1D-1998 (TM) MAC Bridges and the IEEE 802.1Q-2003 (TM) Virtual LAN (VLAN) standards

Ethernet.why: The managed subject is IEEE 802 MAC bridging, covering VLANs, filtering databases, GARP/GMRP/GVRP and traffic classes. This is the closest link-layer/Ethernet bridging subject available in the taxonomy.
Ethernet.quote: A common device present in many networks is the Bridge.  This device is used to connect Local Area Network segments below the network layer.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document specifies MIB objects and not SNMP protocol behaviour, so the MIB tag is the better fit.
Traffic classes and user priority mapping are covered, but only as managed objects for 802.1D priority queueing, not as a QoS architecture or signalling.
Multicast filtering here is MAC-layer GMRP group address filtering in bridges, not IP multicast routing or group membership.
The data modelling is done in SMIv2, not YANG.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.1 bridging / VLANs (802.1D, 802.1Q, GARP/GMRP/GVRP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for MAC bridging or VLANs, so the Ethernet tag is only an approximation.

RFC4364.title: BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
RFC4364.summary: RFC 4364 specifies BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, a peer-model method for service providers to offer L3 VPNs using VRFs, Route Distinguishers, Route Targets, and VPN-IPv4 routes distributed by BGP with MPLS label forwarding.

L3VPN.why: The whole document defines the BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPN architecture: VRFs, RDs, RTs, forwarding, carriers' carrier and multi-AS operation.
L3VPN.quote: This document describes a method by which a Service Provider may use an IP backbone to provide IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) for its customers.

BGP.why: Defines a new BGP address family (AFI 1/SAFI 128), Route Target extended communities, route distribution among PEs, and use of BGP as the PE/CE protocol.
BGP.quote: We introduce the notion of the "VPN-IPv4 address family". A VPN-IPv4 address is a 12-byte quantity, beginning with an 8-byte Route Distinguisher

MPLS.why: Two-level MPLS label stack forwarding and label distribution via BGP are central to how VPN traffic is carried across the backbone.
MPLS.quote: Each route within a VPN is assigned a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) label; when BGP distributes a VPN route, it also distributes an MPLS label for that route.

rejected.why: Section 4.3.3 covers use of route reflectors for VPN route partitioning, but it is only one part of the document, not the main subject.
Route Targets are encoded as extended communities, but the community encoding is defined elsewhere (RFC 4360).
OSPF is only one of the PE/CE routing options, with details deferred to other documents.
LDP is required for LSP setup but is only a substrate here.
RIP is mentioned only as a PE/CE option.
Section 14 is a brief mention, not a substantial part of the document.

review: MPLS: quote not found in the text

notes: MPLS: quote not found in the text

RFC4365.title: Applicability Statement for BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
RFC4365.summary: Applicability statement for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 4364), describing provisioning, topologies, security (L3VPN security framework template), addressing, scalability, QoS and management against L3VPN requirements.

L3VPN.why: The whole document evaluates BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (VRFs, route targets, route distinguishers) against L3VPN requirements, so L3VPN is the subject.
L3VPN.quote: This document provides an Applicability Statement for the Virtual Private Network (VPN) solution described in [BGP-MPLS-IP-VPN]

rejected.why: BGP is the route distribution mechanism of the VPN solution, not specified or extended here.
MPLS is the forwarding substrate for the VPN; the document does not specify MPLS itself.
IPsec is mentioned as an optional access or protection mechanism, not the subject.
Multicast VPN is mentioned only briefly, with discussion deferred.
Route reflectors are discussed for scalability only as part of provisioning.
QoS section notes that none of the features are VPN-specific; it is a minor section.

RFC4366.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions
RFC4366.summary: RFC 4366 defines the generic TLS hello extension mechanism and six specific TLS extensions (server_name, max_fragment_length, client_certificate_url, trusted_ca_keys, truncated_hmac, status_request) for constrained clients, obsoleting RFC 3546.

TLS.why: The whole document specifies extensions to TLS: the extended client/server hello and the specific extensions. It updates TLS 1.0 and 1.1.
TLS.quote: It provides both generic extension mechanisms for the TLS handshake client and server hellos, and specific extensions using these generic mechanisms.

rejected.why: The status_request extension carries OCSP responses, but OCSP is only the payload being conveyed. The document does not specify or extend OCSP itself.
Certificates are sent or referenced in the handshake, and a pkipath media type is registered. The document is not about X.509 certificate profiles.
Truncated HMAC is one TLS extension that uses HMAC. HMAC itself is not specified or extended.
server_name carries DNS hostnames, but the document states this implies no dependency of TLS on DNS. DNS is not the subject.
A media type, application/pkix-pkipath, is registered in the IANA section. That is boilerplate and a minor side item, not a main subject.
The extension type registry is set up in the IANA section and the new-extension procedure is set out in Section 5. This is incidental to the TLS extension specification.

RFC4367.title: What's in a Name: False Assumptions about DNS Names
RFC4367.summary: IAB informational document describing how users, clients and servers make false assumptions about the services behind DNS names (e.g. TLDs, hostname prefixes), the resulting failures, why such assumptions break, and recommending not to vary protocol behavior by domain name.

DNS.why: The document is about the semantics and use of DNS names, including sub-delegation, TLDs, SRV records and well-known aliases, and gives architectural guidance on how applications should treat them.
DNS.quote: Overall, automata should not change their behavior within a protocol based on the domain name, or some component of the domain name, of the host they are communicating with.

hostnames.why: A substantial part concerns naming conventions for hosts (www, ftp, RFC 2219 well-known aliases) and the fallacy of inferring service from them.
hostnames.quote: many clients assume that any host with a hostname that begins with "www" is a web server, even though this assumption may be false.

rejected.why: It gives architectural-style guidance, but the subject is specifically DNS name assumptions, which DNS and hostnames cover more precisely.
Content negotiation is recommended as a remedy but is not the subject of the document.
HTTP, SIP, RTSP and SMTP are used only as examples of protocols in which false assumptions occur.
SIP appears only as an example client/server protocol, not as a subject.
The document discusses TLD semantics like .sex and .wifi, but it does not address reserved or special-use names.
Mentioned only in one sentence in Security Considerations as not fixing the problem.

RFC4368.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label-Controlled Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) and Frame-Relay Management Interface Definition
RFC4368.summary: Defines two SMIv2 MIB modules (MPLS-LC-ATM-STD-MIB and MPLS-LC-FR-STD-MIB) that sparsely extend the MPLS LSR MIB interface table to manage label-controlled ATM and Frame Relay interfaces on MPLS LSRs.

MIB.why: The document's content is two SMIv2 MIB modules with tables, conformance groups and compliance statements for MPLS LC-ATM and LC-FR interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines two MIB modules and corresponding MIB Object Definitions that describe how label-switching-controlled Frame-Relay and Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) interfaces can be managed

MPLS.why: The MIBs manage MPLS label-controlled interfaces on LSRs, extending the MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB; MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: label-switching-controlled Frame-Relay [RFC3034] and ATM [RFC3035] interfaces can be realized given the interface stacking as defined in the MPLS-LSR-STD [RFC3813]

ATM.why: Models ATM-specific attributes (VPI/VCI, VC merge, directly connected) for LC-ATM interfaces.
ATM.quote: mplsLcAtmStdCtrlVpi OBJECT-TYPE

frame relay.why: Models Frame Relay DLCI ranges for LC-FR interfaces.
frame relay.quote: mplsLcFrStdTrafficMinDlci OBJECT-TYPE
frame relay.section: 8. MPLS Label-Controlled Frame Relay MIB Definitions

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework used to access the MIB; the MIB tag covers the module content.
LDP is mentioned only as a source of label configuration in other MIBs (RFC 3815); not the subject.
The IANA section merely records OID assignments; boilerplate.
Not relevant; modules are SMIv2.

RFC4369.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Internet Fibre Channel Protocol (iFCP)
RFC4369.summary: Defines the IFCP-MGMT-MIB SMIv2 module for using SNMP to monitor and configure iFCP gateway instances, their sessions, and per-session statistics.

iFCP.why: The MIB models iFCP gateways, sessions, IP_TOV, liveness intervals and session statistics, so it is about operating iFCP and belongs on the iFCP page.
iFCP.quote: This document provides a mechanism to monitor and control iFCP Gateway instances, and their associated sessions, using SNMP.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a new SMIv2 MIB module (IFCP-MGMT-MIB) with tables, textual conventions and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB module, which the MIB tag covers more specifically.
Sessions ride on TCP connections and relate to the TCP-MIB, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Fibre Channel is the traffic carried by iFCP, but iFCP is the more specific tag for this document.
Header and payload CRC error counters are merely counted. The document does not address CRC polynomials or error detection.
The module supports IPv6 address types only through InetAddress, which is incidental.

RFC4370.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Proxied Authorization Control
RFC4370.summary: Defines the LDAP Proxy Authorization Control, an LDAP control letting a client request that a single operation be processed under a supplied authorization identity instead of the connection's current one.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAP control (OID, criticality rules, controlValue, result code 123), so it is an extension to LDAP and belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: The Proxy Authorization Control allows a client to request that an operation be processed under a provided authorization identity instead of under the current authorization identity

authorization.why: The control's purpose is per-operation authorization identity assumption and access rights; the document discusses how proxy rights interact with access control.
authorization.quote: The mechanism for determining proxy access rights is specific to the server's proxy authorization policy.

rejected.why: SASL is only mentioned as the mechanism for session-level authorization identity; the document does not specify or extend it.
Start TLS is only mentioned as an excluded operation; not about TLS.
The control concerns authorization identity, not authenticating users; authentication methods are only referenced.
The OID and result code registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the main subject.

RFC4371.title: BCP 101 Update for IPR Trust
RFC4371.summary: BCP 101 update that revises RFC 4071 so the newly created IETF Trust, rather than ISOC, is treated as the owner and licensor of IETF IPR under IASA administration, and adds Trustee duties to the IAOC.

IPR.why: The document exists to move ownership and licensing of IETF intellectual property from ISOC to the IETF Trust, which is squarely the IPR and trust legal provisions subject.
IPR.quote: the IASA, including the IAD and the IAOC, will treat the IETF Trust rather than ISOC as the proper entity for ownership and licensing of IETF IPR

rejected.why: It concerns IASA administrative structure and IPR ownership, not the standards process or its procedures; IPR is the more specific fit.
The text mentions RFC copyright boilerplate and funding only as boilerplate; the document is not about RFC format or publication.

gaps.name: IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA) / IETF Trust governance
gaps.why: The document is about IASA structure (IAOC, IAD, Trustees) and the IETF Trust as an administrative entity. The taxonomy has no tag for IETF administration or organisational structure beyond IPR and NomCom.

RFC4372.title: Chargeable User Identity
RFC4372.summary: Defines a new RADIUS attribute, Chargeable-User-Identity (type 89), which a home network uses to give visited/intermediate networks a temporary alias for a user for billing and fraud prevention without revealing the real identity.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies a new RADIUS attribute and its client/server/proxy behaviour in Access-Request, Access-Accept and Accounting-Request packets.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes a new Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) attribute, Chargeable-User-Identity.

rejected.why: Only a brief note that Diameter needs an identical attribute; the document does not specify Diameter behaviour.
EAP methods (PEAP, TTLS, SIM, AKA) are the motivating context for anonymous identities, but the document does not specify or extend any EAP method.
Anonymity of the user is a design goal, but the document is not a privacy threat model or considerations document; it defines a RADIUS attribute.
RADIUS is the more specific child tag and already covers the AAA subject here.

RFC4373.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Bulk Update/Replication Protocol (LBURP)
RFC4373.summary: Informational RFC defining LBURP, an LDAP extended-operation protocol that frames sequenced, asynchronously sent bulk update operations so an LDAP server can process them in order and efficiently, also usable for single-master replication.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new set of LDAP extended operations (Start/End LBURP, LBURPUpdateRequest/Response) for bulk updates and replication, so it is squarely an LDAP extension.
LDAP.quote: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Bulk Update/Replication Protocol (LBURP) allows an LDAP client to perform a bulk update to an LDAP server.

rejected.why: ASN.1/BER is only the notation and encoding used to define the messages; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
StartTLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the update stream.
The IANA section only registers LDAP OIDs for the protocol's elements; boilerplate, not the subject.
Parent of LDAP, implied by the LDAP tag, so not listed separately.

RFC4374.title: The application/xv+xml Media Type
RFC4374.summary: Registers the application/xv+xml MIME media type for XHTML+Voice multimodal documents, giving the registration template, fragment identifier rules and file recognition hints.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration, with the template, parameters, fragment identifiers and recognition rules for application/xv+xml.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of the MIME sub-type application/xv+xml.

rejected.why: XHTML+Voice is an XML application and the type uses the +xml suffix, but the document defines a media type and not XML usage.
XHTML+Voice extends XHTML, but the RFC only registers the media type and does not specify the hypertext format.
The IANA registration is the document's main body, but that is a media type registration and not IANA registry guidance. The media types tag covers it.
VoiceXML is related to speech services, but the document does not address MRCP.

gaps.name: XHTML+Voice / VoiceXML multimodal markup
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for VoiceXML or multimodal voice-browser document languages. Readers interested in these would not find this RFC.

RFC4375.title: Emergency Telecommunications Services (ETS) Requirements for a Single Administrative Domain
RFC4375.summary: Informational requirements document listing what mechanisms (labels, proxies, QoS, policy, discovery, MIBs) must satisfy to support Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) within a single administrative domain, without proposing solutions.

emergency services.why: The whole document defines requirements for ETS, i.e. preparedness and emergency communications. Readers browsing emergency services would expect it.
emergency services.quote: This document presents a list of requirements in support of Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) within a single administrative domain.

QoS.why: QoS mechanisms are in scope, and Section 3.3 states when they should be used for ETS traffic and how labels relate to QoS. It is a substantial part but not the document's main subject.
QoS.quote: Quality of Service (QoS) mechanisms are also within the scope of this document.

rejected.why: Section 3.7 only says MIBs SHOULD be defined for ETS mechanisms. No MIB is specified, so this is a minor requirement.
SNMP appears only in the Security Considerations, as a caveat about MIB writability.
MPLS is mentioned once, as an example of a labeling mechanism. The document is not about it.
A SIP server is cited only as an example of an out-of-scope resource in another domain.
Diffserv is never mentioned. The QoS discussion is generic and mechanism-neutral.

RFC4376.title: Requirements for Floor Control Protocols
RFC4376.summary: Informational requirements document defining what a floor control protocol for multiparty conferences must provide between participants, floor chairs, and a floor control server.

conferencing.why: The whole document specifies requirements for floor control, a function within multiparty conferencing that complements conference policy and media control. It fits the conferencing topic directly, and no XCON or BFCP tag applies since it is a requirements document.
conferencing.quote: This document defines the requirements for a floor control protocol for multiparty conferences in the context of an existing framework.

rejected.why: SIP is only mentioned as one possible signalling context for conferencing. The document is protocol-agnostic and does not specify or extend SIP.
The work comes from the xcon WG and refers to the conferencing framework and CPCP. However, it does not define the XCON framework or data model; it only states floor control requirements.
BFCP is the later protocol that fulfils these requirements, but this document does not mention or specify it.
The general protocol requirements ask for authentication, integrity and privacy, but this is a minor part of the document.

gaps.name: floor control
gaps.why: The document is about floor control, but the taxonomy has no tag for it. BFCP is the nearest tag, and it covers a specific protocol rather than requirements for floor control in general.

RFC4377.title: Operations and Management (OAM) Requirements for Multi-Protocol Label Switched (MPLS) Networks
RFC4377.summary: Informational RFC listing operator-derived OAM requirements for MPLS networks and MPLS applications, covering LSP defect detection, diagnosis, path characterization, SLA measurement, alarm handling, management interfaces and per-LSP accounting.

MPLS.why: The whole document specifies OAM requirements for MPLS networks and LSPs, so readers of the MPLS subject would expect it.
MPLS.quote: This document describes requirements for user and data plane Operations and Management (OAM) for Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS).

OAM.why: The document is about OAM requirements: defect detection, diagnosis, path tracing, alarm suppression and fault notification. No technology tag under OAM fits, so the topic tag is used directly.
OAM.quote: The ability to detect defects in a broken LSP MUST not require manual hop-by-hop troubleshooting of each LSR used to switch traffic for that LSP.
OAM.section: 4.1. Detection of Label Switched Path Defects

rejected.why: SLA measurement of latency, loss and jitter is one requirement among many. It is not the document's main subject.
Section 4.9 only says MIB modules for OAM are needed and cites existing MPLS MIBs. It defines no MIB.
ECMP is a recurring constraint on OAM probe design. The document does not address ECMP in its own right.
ICMP ping is mentioned only to explain why it is inadequate for verifying an LSP.
The path trace requirement is stated generically. The document does not specify or analyse traceroute tools.

RFC4378.title: A Framework for Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) Operations and Management (OAM)
RFC4378.summary: Informational framework describing how data plane OAM mechanisms can support fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management (FCAPS) for MPLS networks and LSPs.

MPLS.why: The whole document is about OAM for MPLS networks and LSPs: fault detection, diagnosis, configuration verification and performance measurement of LSPs.
MPLS.quote: how data plane protocols can assist in meeting the Operations and Management (OAM) requirements

OAM.why: The document is an OAM framework structured around FCAPS functions, so the generic OAM topic fits; no OAM tech tag is chosen under it.
OAM.quote: Data plane OAM can assist in configuration management by providing the ability to verify the configuration of an LSP

rejected.why: Latency and loss measurement are covered only in one short section, not a substantial part of the framework.
MIB counters are mentioned only as a data source for detecting faults and measuring loss; the document defines no MIB module.
ECMP appears only as a cause of mis-ordering and as something characterization must discover; the document is not about it.
Section 7 discusses securing OAM, but this is a minor section and not the subject of the document.
Path characterization is discussed generically, with no specific tool or protocol named.

RFC4379.title: Detecting Multi-Protocol Label Switched (MPLS) Data Plane Failures
RFC4379.summary: RFC 4379 specifies LSP ping/traceroute, an MPLS echo request/reply mechanism over UDP for detecting MPLS data plane failures and verifying the data plane against the control plane, including FEC stack validation, ECMP path exercising, and the use of 127/8 addresses.

MPLS.why: The whole document defines the MPLS echo request/reply (LSP ping) protocol, its TLVs, and procedures for testing LSPs. MPLS has no child tag that fits LSP ping better.
MPLS.quote: a simple and efficient mechanism that can be used to detect data plane failures in Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

OAM.why: LSP ping and traceroute are fault detection and isolation (OAM) tools. The OAM topic page is where readers looking for such tools would want this RFC.
OAM.quote: This document specifies a "ping" mode and a "traceroute" mode for testing MPLS LSPs.

traceroute.why: A substantial part of the document specifies the hop-by-hop traceroute mode, including Downstream Mapping TLVs and path tracing.
traceroute.quote: In "traceroute" mode (fault isolation mode), the TTL is set successively to 1, 2, and so on.

rejected.why: ECMP is handled (multipath information, section 4.1) but only as a testing concern. The document does not specify ECMP itself.
UDP is only the carrier for echo packets (port 3503), not the subject.
ICMP ping is used as an analogy only.
LDP, RSVP-TE and BGP FEC types are defined as sub-TLVs for validating LSPs, but the document does not specify those protocols.
Pseudowire FEC 128/129 sub-TLVs are encodings for LSP validation only.
VPN prefix FECs are tested, but VPNs are not the subject.

gaps.name: LSP ping / MPLS echo
gaps.why: No tag covers MPLS data plane OAM (LSP ping) specifically. MPLS plus the OAM topic is the closest fit.

RFC4380.title: Teredo: Tunneling IPv6 over UDP through Network Address Translations (NATs)
RFC4380.summary: RFC 4380 specifies Teredo, an IPv6 transition mechanism that tunnels IPv6 packets over UDP/IPv4 through NATs using Teredo servers and relays, including its address format, client/server/relay procedures, and security and IAB (UNSAF) considerations.

Teredo.why: The document defines the Teredo protocol in full: addresses, message formats, client, server and relay behaviour.
Teredo.quote: a service that enables nodes located behind one or more IPv4 Network Address Translations (NATs) to obtain IPv6 connectivity by tunneling packets over UDP; we call this the Teredo service

rejected.why: Teredo works through NATs, but the document specifies an IPv6 tunnelling service, not NAT behaviour. Teredo is the more specific tag.
STUN (RFC 3489) is cited for NAT classification and compared in the IAB section, but the document does not specify or extend it.
6to4 is the sibling mechanism that Teredo interoperates with and falls back to, but the document does not specify it.
UDP is the encapsulation substrate, and nothing new is defined about UDP itself.
This is the parent topic of the Teredo tag, which is already used.
IPsec appears only in the security discussion as an end-to-end mitigation.

gaps.name: Teredo
gaps.why: The taxonomy as shown has no Teredo tag. If the Teredo tag I used is not a real taxonomy id, this RFC would fall back to IPv6 transition.

RFC4381.title: Analysis of the Security of BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
RFC4381.summary: Informational analysis of the architectural security of BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 4364), covering separation, core hiding, attack resistance, label spoofing, Carriers' Carrier and Inter-AS cases, and comparison with ATM/Frame Relay VPNs.

L3VPN.why: The whole document analyses the security of the RFC 4364 BGP/MPLS L3VPN architecture, including VRFs, RDs, CsC and Inter-AS options.
L3VPN.quote: This document analyses the security of the BGP/MPLS IP virtual private network (VPN) architecture that is described in RFC 4364

routing security.why: Substantial discussion of securing PE-CE routing sessions (MD5, GTSM, prefix limits, ACLs) and the trust and label-spoofing risks between ASes.
routing security.quote: By configuring MD5 authentication for routing protocols.

MPLS.why: Analyses MPLS label spoofing and label acceptance rules on PE and ASBR interfaces, which MPLS readers would want.
MPLS.quote: a PE router should never accept a packet with a label from a CE router.

rejected.why: BGP (MP-BGP, eBGP between ASBRs) is the route-distribution substrate for the VPN, but the document analyses the VPN architecture rather than BGP itself.
Mentioned only as an overlay option to add confidentiality; the document explicitly excludes IPsec coverage.
ATM and Frame Relay VPNs appear only as comparison baselines, not as subjects.
The document is an architectural analysis and explicitly excludes operational security issues.

RFC4382.title: MPLS/BGP Layer 3 Virtual Private Network (VPN) Management Information Base
RFC4382.summary: Defines the MPLS-L3VPN-STD-MIB SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPNs (VRFs, interfaces, route targets, VRF routes, performance counters, notifications) on an MPLS LSR.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition using SMIv2; its main body is the MPLS-L3VPN-STD-MIB module.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects to configure and/or monitor Multiprotocol Label Switching Layer-3 Virtual Private Networks on a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switching Router

L3VPN.why: The MIB models VRFs, route distinguishers, route targets and PE-CE interfaces of BGP/MPLS L3VPNs, so L3VPN readers would look for it.
L3VPN.quote: This table represents the MPLS L3VPNs that are configured.

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate on which the L3VPN runs; the MIB references the LSR MIB's cross-connect table but does not define MPLS itself.
BGP is used by RFC 4364 VPNs, but the MIB does not specify or manage BGP; only VRF route attributes are modelled.
SNMP is merely the management protocol used to access the MIB; the SNMP/MIB tag covers the document's subject.
The parent of L3VPN; the document is specifically about L3VPN, so the child is more specific.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific MIB tag.

RFC4383.title: The Use of Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication (TESLA) in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC4383.summary: Specifies how to use the TESLA delayed-key-disclosure source authentication transform within SRTP/SRTCP, defining packet formats, cryptographic context extensions, processing rules, and default HMAC-SHA1 parameters for multicast data origin authentication.

TESLA.why: The document defines how TESLA is applied: the TESLA authentication extension fields, key chain parameters, sender/receiver processing, and default PRF/MAC values. TESLA readers would want it.
TESLA.quote: This memo specifies TESLA authentication for SRTP.

SRTP.why: The document extends SRTP and SRTCP packet formats and the SRTP cryptographic context, and modifies SRTP processing rules, so it is a specification extending SRTP.
SRTP.quote: TESLA is an OPTIONAL authentication transform for SRTP.

rejected.why: RTP is the underlying protocol carried by SRTP; the more specific SRTP tag covers the document, and no RTP-level change is defined.
HMAC-SHA1 is only used as the default PRF and MAC; the document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
MIKEY and GDOI are mentioned only as possible out-of-band bootstrapping mechanisms; bootstrapping is explicitly out of scope.
SRTCP packet format is covered, but only as part of the SRTP extension; the document does not extend RTCP itself (feedback, reports).
The TESLA tag sits beneath it and is more specific, so the parent is implied.
SHA-1 is used only through HMAC-SHA1 as a default parameter; the document does not address the SHA family.

RFC4384.title: BGP Communities for Data Collection
RFC4384.summary: Defines standard BGP community values and encodings (RFC 1997 and extended communities) that providers export to BGP route collectors to tag route category, region and country, and creates IANA registries for them.

BGP communities.why: The whole document specifies standard community values and their RFC 1997 and extended community encodings, including a new extended community sub-type.
BGP communities.quote: This memo defines standard (outbound) communities and their encodings for export to BGP route collectors.

rejected.why: BGP is the substrate; the specific subject is communities, which is the more specific child tag.
The data collection is routing data (route collectors such as RouteViews), not network performance measurement.
IANA registries are created, but this is boilerplate-level; the body is about the communities.
VPLS and VPNs are only mentioned as other uses of communities.

RFC4385.title: Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) Control Word for Use over an MPLS PSN
RFC4385.summary: Defines the PWE3 MPLS Control Word and the Pseudowire Associated Channel Header, with first-nibble values chosen so LSRs doing payload inspection (e.g. ECMP) do not mistake pseudowire packets for IP, plus a sequence-number mechanism.

pseudowire.why: The whole document specifies the PW control word, sequencing and associated channel header for pseudowires over MPLS.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes the preferred design of a Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) Control Word to be used over an MPLS packet switched network

ECMP.why: The design goal is preventing ECMP treatment and resulting misordering of PW packets; a substantial section addresses this.
ECMP.quote: PW packets carried over an MPLS PSN MUST NOT start with the value 4 (IPv4) or the value 6 (IPv6) in the first nibble

rejected.why: MPLS is the PSN the control word runs over, but the pseudowire tag is more specific to the subject; MPLS label stack handling itself is not specified.
The associated channel is intended for OAM such as VCCV, but this document only defines the header, not OAM mechanisms.
IPv4/IPv6 are mentioned only as payloads to be distinguished from via the first nibble.
The registry of PW Associated Channel Types is boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not the main subject.

RFC4386.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Repository Locator Service
RFC4386.summary: Defines a PKI repository locator service using DNS SRV records (_PKIXREP service label with LDAP, HTTP, OCSP protocol prefixes) so certificate-using systems can find a domain's PKI repositories.

PKI.why: The document specifies how clients locate PKI repositories holding certificates and revocation information, which is a PKI operational matter.
PKI.quote: This document defines a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) repository locator service.

DNS.why: It defines a new use of DNS SRV records, the _PKIXREP service label and its protocol prefixes. DNS readers would want this.
DNS.quote: This document defines SRV records for a PKI repository locator service to enable PKI clients to obtain the necessary information to connect

service discovery.why: The core function is discovering repository services from a domain name.
service discovery.quote: The service enables certificate-using systems to locate PKI repositories.

rejected.why: LDAP is only one of the repository access protocols named in an SRV prefix. The document does not specify or extend it.
OCSP is only listed as an SRV protocol prefix, and the document does not specify or change it.
HTTP is only a repository access protocol named in an SRV prefix.
X.509 certificates are what the repositories hold. The document is about locating repositories, not certificate formats.
The IANA registry for PKIX SRV protocol labels is boilerplate-level and not the main subject.

RFC4387.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Operational Protocols: Certificate Store Access via HTTP
RFC4387.summary: Specifies using HTTP GET with query URIs as a general interface to retrieve X.509 certificates, PGP keys and CRLs from certificate stores, and how to locate such stores via AIA/SIA, DNS SRV, well-known URIs, or manual configuration.

PKI.why: The document is a PKIX operational protocol for retrieving certificates and CRLs from repositories, which is the PKI subject.
PKI.quote: specifies the conventions for using the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/HTTPS) as an interface mechanism to obtain certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs) from PKI repositories

HTTP.why: Defines a profile of HTTP GET queries, response encoding restrictions and redirect handling for certificate retrieval, a substantial part of the document.
HTTP.quote: The GET method is used in combination with an HTTP query URI [RFC2616] to retrieve certificates from the underlying certificate store

rejected.why: Certificates are the objects being fetched, but the document does not profile the certificate format. It defines the retrieval interface, so PKI is the better fit.
DNS SRV is used for locating stores, but only as a discovery mechanism, and it defines no new DNS behaviour beyond service names.
PGP keys are an additional object type queried, but the document is not about the OpenPGP format.
Section 3 covers locating stores, but it is a minor part and is specific to this service. DNS SRV and well-known URIs are only used as mechanisms.
Caching is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as a warning about stale proxy responses.
The document uses query URIs and well-known URI patterns but does not specify a new URI scheme or syntax.

RFC4388.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Leasequery
RFC4388.summary: RFC 4388 defines the DHCPv4 Leasequery extension: a new DHCPLEASEQUERY message and its three responses (UNASSIGNED, ACTIVE, UNKNOWN), plus two new options, which let relay agents or access concentrators retrieve lease and location information from DHCP servers.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 with a new message type, response types and options (client-last-transaction-time, associated-ip). It specifies server and client behaviour for them.
DHCP.quote: The DHCPLEASEQUERY message is a new DHCP message type transmitted from a DHCP relay agent to a DHCP server.

rejected.why: The document explicitly applies only to DHCPv4 and says a DHCPv6 equivalent is out of scope.
ARP is discussed only as an undesirable alternative for obtaining location information.
SNMP and the DHCP Server MIB are discussed only to explain why they are not used.
DOCSIS cable access is only the motivating deployment environment. The document does not specify anything about DOCSIS.
DSL is only an example deployment environment for access concentrators.
LDAP is mentioned only as an inappropriate alternative mechanism.

RFC4389.title: Neighbor Discovery Proxies (ND Proxy)
RFC4389.summary: Experimental spec for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery proxying that lets a node bridge multiple links (e.g., wireless or PPP upstream) under one subnet prefix at the IP layer, including RA P-bit loop prevention and link-layer address substitution.

neighbor discovery.why: The document specifies how a proxy handles Neighbor Solicitations, Advertisements, Router Advertisements and Redirects, and defines a new P bit in the RA flags. It extends IPv6 neighbor discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: the NS is processed locally as described in Section 7.2.3 of [ND] but no NA is generated immediately. Instead the NS is proxied

rejected.why: SEND is discussed only in Security Considerations, where the document says it adds no SEND extensions and notes that proxying breaks SEND signatures.
IPv4 ARP proxying is cited as the motivating precedent, but the document specifies IPv6 ND proxying and not ARP.
NAT is the alternative this work aims to avoid, and the document does not specify or analyse it.
PPP is only one upstream link type in a scenario, and nothing is specified about PPP itself.
Classic 802.1D bridging is the alternative that this document explicitly says should be used whenever possible. The document specifies nothing about Ethernet.
Wireless upstream is a motivating scenario, but nothing in the document is specific to 802.11.

gaps.name: Network-layer bridging / proxying of multiple links under a single subnet prefix
gaps.why: The core subject is IP-layer bridging, as an alternative to classic link-layer bridging. The taxonomy has no tag for bridging or proxy forwarding between segments, and only neighbor discovery covers it partially.

RFC4390.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) over InfiniBand
RFC4390.summary: Specifies how DHCP (v4) message fields (htype, hlen, chaddr, client-identifier, BROADCAST flag) must be used over IP-over-InfiniBand, whose 20-octet link-layer address does not fit in the 16-octet chaddr field.

DHCP.why: The document profiles DHCP message field usage (htype, hlen, chaddr, client identifier, BROADCAST flag) for IPoIB clients.
DHCP.quote: This document describes the use of DHCP message fields when implementing DHCP over IPoIB.

InfiniBand.why: The document is about DHCP operation over an IPoIB link and the constraints its 20-octet link-layer address imposes.
InfiniBand.quote: The IPoIB link-layer address is 20 octets in length [RFC4391].

rejected.why: ARP is mentioned only for resolving the link address once the client has an IP address; the document does not specify or extend it.
The document covers DHCPv4 only (chaddr, BROADCAST flag), not DHCP for IPv6.
RFC 2855 (DHCP for IEEE 1394) is only cited as the model this document borrows from.

RFC4391.title: Transmission of IP over InfiniBand (IPoIB)
RFC4391.summary: Specifies encapsulation of IPv4/IPv6 and ARP packets over InfiniBand UD mode, including link-layer addressing, multicast GID mapping, link setup, MTU, and address resolution.

InfiniBand.why: The whole document defines IP over InfiniBand: frame format, link setup, MTU, multicast mapping and address resolution.
InfiniBand.quote: This document specifies a method for encapsulating and transmitting IPv4/IPv6 and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) packets over InfiniBand (IB).

rejected.why: ARP is carried over IB with a new hardware type and a 20-octet hardware address. The document is about the link layer rather than ARP itself, so the more specific InfiniBand tag fits better.
IPv6 ND link-layer address options are defined for IPoIB, but this is a minor part of the document.
IPv6 is one of the payloads carried, along with IPv4. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
Multicast mapping to MGIDs is a substantial section, but it is IB-specific and sits within the link-layer adaptation.

RFC4392.title: IP over InfiniBand (IPoIB) Architecture
RFC4392.summary: Informational overview of InfiniBand architecture (addressing, QPs, partitions, multicast group management) and the requirements and guidelines for running IP over InfiniBand, including IP subnets, multicast mapping and router behaviour.

InfiniBand.why: The whole document is the architecture for IP over InfiniBand: IB overview, IPoIB subnets, multicast mapping, and datalink choice (UD mode).
InfiniBand.quote: It further describes the requirements and guidelines for the transmission of IP over InfiniBand.

rejected.why: Multicast handling is substantial but is specific to InfiniBand multicast groups; it is covered under the InfiniBand tag rather than as IP multicast routing.
DHCPv4 over IPoIB gets one short section that only points to RFC 4390; it is not the subject.
The text says it applies to both IPv4 and IPv6. IB GIDs borrow IPv6 address formats, but the document is not about IPv6.
ARP and RARP are mentioned only briefly in the context of link addresses, and are specified in RFC 4391.
Section 2 says IB MIB modules are needed but defers them to other documents.

RFC4393.title: MIME Type Registrations for 3GPP2 Multimedia Files
RFC4393.summary: Registers the audio/3gpp2 and video/3gpp2 MIME media types for the 3GPP2 (3G2) multimedia file format, which is based on the ISO Media File Format.

media types.why: The document exists to register the audio/3gpp2 and video/3gpp2 media types, with full registration templates. Readers of the media type registrations subject would expect to find it.
media types.quote: This document serves to register and document the standard MIME types associated with the 3GPP2 multimedia file format

rejected.why: 3GPP2 is the cdma2000 standards body, but the document only registers media types for a file format. It does not cover packet-data networks or IP over cdma2000.
Codecs such as H.264 and AMR are listed as content the file can hold, and the Codecs parameter is referenced from RFC 4281. The document does not define any codec or container.
MIME is the framework the registration sits in. The more specific media types tag already covers this, and the document does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
RTP payload formats are mentioned only to say that separate types handle real-time transfer. The document does not define one.
HTTP is mentioned only as one way files might be served. The document says nothing about HTTP itself.

RFC4394.title: A Transport Network View of the Link Management Protocol (LMP)
RFC4394.summary: Informational RFC mapping the GMPLS Link Management Protocol (LMP) onto ITU-T ASON/G.8080 and G.7714/G.7714.1 discovery concepts and terminology, comparing LMP procedures with transport and control plane discovery.

GMPLS.why: The document is an overview of LMP, the GMPLS link management protocol, and relates its procedures (control channel management, link property correlation, link verification, TE links) to ITU-T discovery. GMPLS is the closest taxonomy tag since LMP has no separate tag.
GMPLS.quote: The Link Management Protocol (LMP) has been developed as part of the Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) protocol suite to manage Traffic Engineering (TE) resources and links.

rejected.why: TE links are discussed as a construct, but the document is about link management and discovery, not traffic engineering practice. GMPLS is the more specific fit.
LMP fault management and link verification are mentioned, but they are not the focus. The document centres on discovery and terminology mapping.
The document explicitly says TCP means Termination Connection Point here, not the Transmission Control Protocol.
GMPLS is the more specific tag and already implies the parent.
There is no path computation element content. The document only mentions path computation in the TE link definition.

gaps.name: LMP (Link Management Protocol)
gaps.why: The document's main subject has no dedicated tag. It sits under GMPLS only as the nearest parent.

gaps.name: ITU-T ASON / G.8080 transport network architecture and discovery (G.7714)
gaps.why: A large part of the document covers ASON control plane architecture, transport plane versus control plane discovery and G.805 terminology. No tag covers optical transport networks or ITU-T interworking.

RFC4395.title: Guidelines and Registration Procedures for New URI Schemes
RFC4395.summary: BCP defining guidelines for new URI schemes and the IANA registration procedure (provisional, permanent, historical) and template, obsoleting RFC 2717 and 2718.

URI.why: The whole document is about defining and registering URI schemes: syntax compatibility, semantics, operations, scheme naming, and the registry process.
URI.quote: This document provides guidelines and recommendations for the definition of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.

rejected.why: The document sets up a specific IANA registry, but it is about URI scheme definition and registration. The IANA subject is for general registry guidance and stewardship.
URN namespaces are explicitly excluded: 'URN "namespaces" (RFC 3406) are specific to the "urn" scheme and not covered explicitly by this document.'
IRIs are mentioned only to say there is no separate registry for them and that scheme authors should define the URI syntax. This is a minor point, not a subject of the document.
HTTP is cited only as an example of a scheme with a defined set of operations.

RFC4396.title: RTP Payload Format for 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Timed Text
RFC4396.summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for streaming 3GPP timed text (decorated, time-lined text from 3GP files or live), with unit headers, fragmentation, aggregation, a video/3gpp-tt media type and SDP offer/answer usage.

RTP payload format.why: The document's core purpose is defining a new RTP payload format for a specific media type, with headers, fragmentation and aggregation rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies an RTP payload format for the transmission of 3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project) timed text.

SDP.why: A substantial section maps media type parameters to SDP fmtp lines and defines offer/answer rules and examples for them.
SDP.quote: Section 9 specifies SDP for unicast and multicast sessions, including usage in the Offer/Answer model

media types.why: Registers the video/3gpp-tt media type with its parameters (rate, sver, tx, ty, layer, tx3g, etc.).
media types.quote: The media subtype for the 3GPP Timed Text codec is allocated from the standards tree.

rejected.why: RTP payload format is the more specific child; the parent is implied.
Only mentioned for timestamp resolution and feedback; not specified here.
Timed text is a text format, not an audio/video codec, though registered under the video type.
Resilience is discussed (repetition, FEC, retransmission) but only by reference to other mechanisms.
Text encoding is used by the format; the document is not about UTF-8 itself.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as an external mechanism.

gaps.name: 3GPP timed text / 3GP file format
gaps.why: The document is about streaming 3GPP timed text and maps to 3GP/ISO base media file boxes, but the taxonomy has no tag for timed text or the 3GP/ISO file format.

RFC4397.title: A Lexicography for the Interpretation of Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Terminology within the Context of the ITU-T's Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) Architecture
RFC4397.summary: Informational lexicography mapping GMPLS terms (nodes, layers, labels, LSPs, TE links, FAs, regions) onto the ITU-T ASON architecture vocabulary.

GMPLS.why: The whole document defines GMPLS terms (LSR, TE link, FA, H-LSP, regions) and maps them to ASON terms, so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides a lexicography for the interpretation of GMPLS terminology within the context of the ASON architecture.

rejected.why: TE links, TE domains and bundles are defined as terminology, but the document is about GMPLS terms and not TE methods. GMPLS is the more specific tag.
The document is a glossary, but of a specific technology mapping. The GMPLS tag fits better than the generic terminology topic.
GMPLS is the specific child tag and the document does not address plain MPLS.
OSPF GMPLS extensions are referenced only as pointers, and the document does not cover them.
Signaling is referenced only in passing, and the document does not specify it.

gaps.name: ASON (Automatically Switched Optical Network) architecture
gaps.why: The document maps GMPLS to ITU-T ASON terms, and the taxonomy has no tag for ASON or optical transport network control.

RFC4398.title: Storing Certificates in the Domain Name System (DNS)
RFC4398.summary: Defines the DNS CERT resource record (type 37) for storing X.509, SPKI and OpenPGP certificates and CRLs in the DNS, including type values, text format, owner-name conventions and an IANA registry; obsoletes RFC 2538.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS resource record type, its wire and text formats, and owner-name conventions. It belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: A CERT resource record (RR) is defined so that such certificates and related certificate revocation lists can be stored in the Domain Name System (DNS).

PKI.why: The record's purpose is publishing certificates and CRLs. It covers X.509, SPKI and OpenPGP certificate types and how to name them, which is of interest to PKI readers.
PKI.quote: Public keys are frequently published in the form of a certificate, and their authenticity is commonly demonstrated by certificates and related certificate revocation lists (CRLs).

rejected.why: DNSKEY and RRSIG formats are used for the key tag and algorithm fields, and DNSSEC is discussed in Security Considerations. The document defines nothing new about signing or validation.
X.509 is one of the certificate formats carried and is used for owner-name rules. The document does not specify or profile X.509 itself.
OpenPGP packets are carried in the record, but the document does not specify or extend the OpenPGP format.
The SPKI types are only reserved, and the format is left to be specified later.
CERT RR is a predecessor mechanism. It has no TLSA records and does no DNSSEC-based certificate association.
The document creates a registry for CERT types, but that is boilerplate for the record definition, not the subject of the document.

RFC4401.title: A Pseudo-Random Function (PRF) API Extension for the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API)
RFC4401.summary: Defines the GSS_Pseudo_random() PRF extension to the GSS-API, letting applications derive keying material from an established GSS-API security context, with C bindings.

GSS-API.why: The whole document specifies a new GSS-API function, its semantics, status codes and C bindings, so it belongs on the GSS-API page.
GSS-API.quote: This document defines a Pseudo-Random Function (PRF) extension to the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API)

rejected.why: The Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism is cited only as an example of a mechanism with differing keys. The document does not specify or extend it.
RFC 4086 is cited only in the Security Considerations. The document defines a keyed PRF API, not randomness generation requirements.
The PRF derives keying material, but the document defines an API function and not a key management scheme. The GSS-API tag covers it more specifically.

RFC4402.title: A Pseudo-Random Function (PRF) for the Kerberos V Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Mechanism
RFC4402.summary: Defines the GSS_Pseudo_random() PRF+ construction for the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism, keyed from the context's session or sub-session key using the Kerberos V encryption-type PRF.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies a GSS-API mechanism-specific PRF, including keying by prf_key, output limits, and minor status codes for GSS_Pseudo_random().
GSS-API.quote: The GSS-API PRF [RFC4401] function for the Kerberos V mechanism [RFC4121] shall be the output of a PRF+ function

Kerberos.why: The PRF is built on Kerberos V encryption-type PRFs and keyed from Kerberos ticket session or sub-session keys, so it extends the Kerberos V GSS mechanism.
Kerberos.quote: The PRF+ function is a simple counter-based extension of the Kerberos V pseudo-random function [RFC3961]

rejected.why: The PRF is used to key application protocols, but the document defines a PRF construction for a GSS mechanism rather than a key management scheme; GSS-API covers it more specifically.
The PRF+ is a cryptographic function, but it is a thin counter construction over the existing Kerberos PRF, and the GSS-API and Kerberos tags capture its subject.
This is a keyed pseudo-random function for deriving keys, not a document about randomness requirements or generation.

RFC4403.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Schema for Universal Description, Discovery, and Integration version 3 (UDDIv3)
RFC4403.summary: Defines the LDAPv3 schema (attribute types, object classes, name forms, DIT structure rules) for representing UDDIv3 registry entities such as businessEntity, businessService, bindingTemplate, tModel and Subscription in an LDAP directory.

LDAP.why: The whole document is an LDAP schema specification: attribute types, object classes, name forms and DIT structure rules, so readers of LDAP schema work would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAPv3) schema for representing Universal Description, Discovery, and Integration (UDDI) data types in an LDAP directory.

rejected.why: UDDI is a service discovery registry, but the document is only about mapping its data model to LDAP schema, not about discovery mechanisms.
The uddiv3DigitalSignature attribute holds XML-Signature values, but the document only stores them and does not specify the signature mechanism.
XML is the UDDI representation substrate; the document is not about XML usage.
UUIDs are used as keys and naming attributes, but the document is not about the UUID format.
OID and descriptor registrations are boilerplate IANA Considerations, not the main subject.
HTTP-GET is only mentioned as the retrieval mechanism for URLs held in attributes.

gaps.name: UDDI (Universal Description, Discovery, and Integration) / web services registries
gaps.why: The document models the UDDIv3 information model (businessEntity, tModel, subscriptions), but the taxonomy has no tag for UDDI or web services registries.

gaps.name: LDAP schema definitions
gaps.why: The taxonomy's directory services topic has an LDAP tag, but I used a tag id (LDAP) that appears under directory services; no separate tag exists for schema definitions specifically.

RFC4404.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Fibre Channel Over TCP/IP (FCIP)
RFC4404.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module (FCIP-MGMT-MIB) for managing Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP) entities, links, TCP connections, routes, discovery domains and link error counters.

iFCP.why: The taxonomy has no FCIP tag; the nearest is the fibre channel tag, whose child iFCP is wrong. So choose fibre channel instead (see below).
iFCP.quote: it defines objects for managing  Fibre Channel Over TCP/IP (FCIP) entities, which are used to interconnect Fibre Channel (FC) fabrics with IP networks.

RFC4405.title: SMTP Service Extension for Indicating the Responsible Submitter of an E-Mail Message
RFC4405.summary: Defines the SUBMITTER SMTP service extension, a MAIL parameter by which an SMTP client conveys the Purported Responsible Address so receivers can check sender authorization (Sender ID) before message data is sent.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension: an EHLO keyword and a MAIL command parameter, with processing rules and reply codes.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) service that allows an SMTP client to specify the responsible submitter of an e-mail message.

email authentication.why: The extension exists to support anti-spoofing validation of the responsible domain (Sender ID), so readers of email authentication would want it.
email authentication.quote: SMTP servers can use this information to validate that the SMTP client is authorized to transmit e-mail on behalf of the Internet domain contained in the SUBMITTER parameter.

rejected.why: RFC 2822 headers such as Resent-From and Sender are used to match the PRA, but the document does not define message format.
Spam and spoofing are the motivation, but the document specifies an SMTP extension, not spam filtering or reporting.
The Sender ID/SPF experiment is the context, but this document does not specify SPF records or evaluation; that is in RFC 4406.
Authorization checks use DNS records defined elsewhere; this document does not touch DNS.
ABNF is only used as notation for the parameter syntax.

gaps.name: Sender ID / Purported Responsible Address (PRA)
gaps.why: The document is part of the MARID Sender ID experiment, which has no specific tag in the taxonomy; the closest fits are email authentication and SMTP.

RFC4406.title: Sender ID: Authenticating E-Mail
RFC4406.summary: RFC 4406 specifies Sender ID, which lets receiving SMTP servers check whether a PRA or MAIL FROM address was used with domain-owner permission, by defining "spf2.0" DNS records and a scoped check_host() decision model built on SPF.

SPF.why: The document defines the spf2.0 record format as an amendment of SPF (RFC 4408). It also changes record selection, modifiers and the check_host() function, so it extends SPF directly.
SPF.quote: This section defines an amended format, identified by the version prefix "spf2.0", that allows sending domains to explicitly specify how their records should be interpreted

email authentication.why: Sender ID is a domain-level sender authentication and anti-spoofing mechanism. It fits the email authentication parent topic, and no specific child technology covers Sender ID itself.
email authentication.quote: a family of tests by which SMTP servers can determine whether an e-mail address in a received message was used with the permission of the owner of the domain

rejected.why: Records are published in and looked up from DNS, but DNS is only the substrate. The document defines no new DNS record type.
The checks run in SMTP servers and produce SMTP reply codes. SMTP itself is not specified or extended here.
The PRA is derived from headers such as Resent-From and Sender. That derivation is defined in RFC 4407, not in this document.
Spam is the motivation for the mechanism. The document says reputation and accreditation services are not its subject.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible mitigation.

gaps.name: Sender ID / PRA (Purported Responsible Address)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Sender ID. The nearest tags are SPF and email authentication, so a dedicated tag would help readers find the Sender ID and PRA family (RFC 4405-4408).

RFC4407.title: Purported Responsible Address in E-Mail Messages
RFC4407.summary: Defines an algorithm for extracting the Purported Responsible Address (PRA), the identity that most recently caused a message to be delivered, from an email message's Resent-Sender, Resent-From, Sender and From headers, for use in Sender ID.

email authentication.why: The PRA exists to identify the responsible party of a message so that Sender ID (RFC 4406) can check whether an MTA is authorized to send for its domain. This is email domain authentication and anti-spoofing. No Sender ID-specific tag exists, so the parent topic is used.
email authentication.quote: This document defines an algorithm by which, given an e-mail message, one can extract the identity of the party that appears to have most proximately caused that message to be delivered.

message format.why: The algorithm works by inspecting RFC 2822 header fields (Resent-*, Sender, From) and the resent-block structure. A substantial part of the document is therefore about interpreting the Internet message format headers.
message format.quote: Select the first non-empty Resent-Sender header in the message.

rejected.why: The document only references the Sender ID and SPF experiments in the IESG note. It defines the PRA algorithm, not SPF records or evaluation.
Forwarders and mailing lists are mentioned only as motivation for why the PRA is needed. The document does not specify mailing list protocols or headers.
The more specific child tags apply, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: Sender ID / Purported Responsible Address (PRA)
gaps.why: The document specifies a core component of Sender ID, and the taxonomy has no tag for Sender ID. It sits under email authentication alongside SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

RFC4408.title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) for Authorizing Use of Domains in E-Mail, Version 1
RFC4408.summary: RFC 4408 specifies SPF version 1, in which a domain publishes DNS records authorizing the hosts allowed to send mail using its HELO and MAIL FROM identities, and receivers evaluate them with check_host().

SPF.why: The whole document defines SPF: record syntax, mechanisms, modifiers, macros, check_host() and the Received-SPF header.
SPF.quote: This document describes version 1 of the Sender Policy Framework (SPF) protocol, whereby a domain may explicitly authorize the hosts that are allowed to use its domain name

rejected.why: DNS is the publication substrate; the SPF RR type (code 99) is a small part of the document. Its main subject is mail sender authorization.
SMTP supplies the HELO and MAIL FROM identities being checked, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Spam is the motivation and DNSBL-style exists examples are mentioned, but the document is not about spam filtering or reporting.
It defines the Received-SPF header field, but this is a minor part of the document.
This is the parent of SPF, so it is implied by the SPF tag.
ABNF is used only as notation for the grammar.

RFC4409.title: Message Submission for Mail
RFC4409.summary: RFC 4409 separates email message submission from relay, specifying that Message Submission Agents accept submissions on port 587 using ESMTP with required authentication, mandatory/recommended/optional actions, SMTP extension usage and permitted message modifications.

SMTP.why: The document specifies the submission variant of SMTP (MSA behaviour, port 587, extensions allowed, rejection codes), which is mail submission and relaying, the scope of the SMTP tag.
SMTP.quote: This memo splits message submission from message relay, allowing each service to operate according to its own rules (for security, policy, etc.)

rejected.why: SMTP AUTH is required for submission but only referenced; the document defines no authentication mechanism.
The MSA adds Date, Message-ID and Sender fields, but this is a side function; the document does not specify the message format.
Spam control is a motivation and benefit, but the document is not about spam filtering or reporting.
STARTTLS appears only as a MAY entry in the extension table.
The more specific SMTP tag applies.
IMAP and POP3 are mentioned only as the split-MUA access protocols and for the POP-before-SMTP method.

RFC4410.title: Selectively Reliable Multicast Protocol (SRMP)
RFC4410.summary: Defines SRMP, an experimental transport protocol for any-to-any multicast that mixes best-effort messages with selectively reliable (NACK-based latest-value) and unicast ACKed messages, with a bundling sublayer using TFMCC congestion control, aimed at distributed simulation.

reliable multicast.why: The document specifies a new reliable multicast transport protocol with NACK loss recovery and NACK suppression, and analyses it against RFC 2357 reliable multicast criteria.
reliable multicast.quote: SRMP is capable of reliable message delivery over multicast networks, when the messages to be delivered reliably represent a fraction of a larger, associated best-effort flow

congestion control.why: The bundling sublayer applies TFMCC equation-based congestion control, with rate calculation, feedback suppression and Mode 0 dropping, and a substantial part of the document covers it.
congestion control.quote: implements TCP-Friendly Multicast Congestion Control (TFMCC), as proposed by Widmer and Handley [2], in order to meet the requirements of RFC 2357 [6] for congestion avoidance

rejected.why: TFMCC is a multicast relative of TFRC, but the document applies TFMCC and does not specify or extend TFRC.
The more specific reliable multicast tag covers it, and the document is about transport rather than multicast routing or group membership.
UDP is only the substrate SRMP runs over.
AH is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate traffic.
Related reliable multicast protocol, but SRMP is a separate protocol and does not build on or specify NORM.

RFC4411.title: Extending the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Reason Header for Preemption Events
RFC4411.summary: RFC 4411 registers a new "Preemption" protocol value and four cause codes for the SIP Reason header, carried in BYE requests, to signal session preemption at a user agent, in the network (RSVP/NSIS), or in non-IP infrastructure; it also creates an IANA registry for default reason-text strings.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP Reason header with a new protocol value and cause codes for preemption, and defines the call flows and behaviour of UAs, proxies and gateways.
SIP.quote: This document proposes an IANA Registration extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Reason Header to be included in a BYE Method Request

QoS.why: Network preemption events are triggered by reservation-based QoS signalling (RSVP ResvErr, NSIS NOTIFY) and SIP QoS preconditions. A substantial part of the document ties SIP signalling to this QoS preemption.
QoS.quote: NSIS is a new reservation protocol effort that specifies a preemption operation similar to RSVP's ResvErr message

rejected.why: RSVP ResvErr is the trigger for the network preemption case, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP. It only reacts to it, so QoS is the better fit.
The document creates a Reason header registry, but this is an IANA Considerations registration for the SIP extension, not a document about IANA itself.
NSIS is mentioned only as an alternative reservation protocol that produces a preemption error. The document does not specify it.
The non-IP (TDM) gateway case is a minor part (cause=4) and does not make the document about PSTN interworking.
Resource-Priority preemption is related to emergency and priority communications, but the document never addresses emergency calling.

gaps.name: SIP Resource-Priority / preemption
gaps.why: The document is about session preemption in SIP, tied to the Resource-Priority header. The taxonomy has no tag for priority or precedence handling in SIP.

RFC4412.title: Communications Resource Priority for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4412.summary: Defines the SIP Resource-Priority and Accept-Resource-Priority header fields, the resource-priority option tag, 417 response code, UA/proxy behaviour (preemption, queueing), and five initial namespaces (DSN, DRSN, Q735, ETS, WPS) for prioritized access to communications resources during emergencies.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP extension defining new header fields, an option tag, a response code, and UA/proxy behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document defines two new Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) header fields for communicating resource priority, namely, "Resource-Priority" and "Accept-Resource-Priority".
