emergency services.why: The motivation and namespaces (ETS, WPS, DSN) target emergency preparedness communications, so readers of emergency services would want it.
emergency services.quote: During emergencies, communications resources (including telephone circuits, IP bandwidth, and gateways between the circuit-switched and IP networks) may become congested.

rejected.why: The header does not influence IP router forwarding or packet priority. It concerns SIP-level resource prioritization, not QoS signalling.
Gateways and Q.735.3 mapping are mentioned, but the document does not define PSTN interworking. Its subject is the SIP header mechanism.
TLS is only a security mechanism the document requires in Security Considerations. It is not what the document is about.
The IANA registries for namespaces and priority values are boilerplate-like registrations of the document's own protocol elements, not guidance on IANA itself.
RTP is mentioned only for transparency requirements. The document does not specify or extend it.

gaps.name: Resource priority / precedence and preemption (MLPP)
gaps.why: The document is about prioritized access and preemption of communications resources. No taxonomy tag covers this beyond SIP and emergency services.

RFC4413.title: TCP/IP Field Behavior
RFC4413.summary: Informational memo analysing the behaviour of IP (v4/v6) and TCP header fields and options, classifying them by static/changing patterns and replicability, to inform ROHC-based TCP/IP header compression design.

ROHC.why: The document exists to supply the field-behaviour analysis needed to design a ROHC TCP/IP compression profile, following RFC 3095's method.
ROHC.quote: This memo describes TCP/IP field behavior in the context of header compression.

TCP.why: A large part of the document analyses TCP header fields, sequence/ack behaviour, and TCP options (MSS, SACK, timestamps, etc.).
TCP.quote: TCP header fields are classified and analyzed in two steps.

rejected.why: IPv6 header fields are classified, but only as input to compression analysis; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
IPv4 header fields (ID, DF, TTL) are analysed for compression, not as a subject in their own right; ROHC and TCP tags cover it.
ECN flags are discussed as header fields for compression, but the document does not specify or analyse ECN itself.
The parent is implied by ROHC, which is the more specific tag.
Mentioned only as a reference; the memo does not cover RFC 2507 or its use over PPP.

RFC4414.title: An ENUM Registry Type for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS)
RFC4414.summary: Defines the IRIS "ereg1" registry type, an XML schema of queries and results for looking up ENUM domain registrations, hosts, contacts, registration authorities, validation entities and communication service providers.

ENUM.why: The whole document defines how ENUM (E.164 numbers in the DNS) registration data is queried and returned, including E.164 prefix searches and ENUM domain results.
ENUM.quote: This document describes an IRIS registry schema for registries of ENUM data

domain registration.why: It specifies a registry information service for registry and registrar data (status, grace periods, contacts, validation events), which is domain registration directory access. No tag for IRIS exists, so this parent topic fits best.
domain registration.quote: The <registrationAuthority> result represents an entity capable of registering domains.

rejected.why: XML Schema is only the notation used to define the schema, so XML is the substrate and the document is not about it.
ENUM domains and name servers appear as data, but the document does not specify DNS protocol or operations.
The BEEP section is only a short transport compliance statement that defers to IRIS-BEEP.
IRIS is a successor to WHOIS-style lookup, but the document does not discuss WHOIS or legacy directory services.
EPP is cited only through RFC 3915 for grace-period status names, and the document does not extend EPP.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The document is an IRIS registry type, and the taxonomy has no IRIS tag. Related IRIS registry-type RFCs would need one.

RFC4415.title: IANA Registration for Enumservice Voice
RFC4415.summary: Registers the ENUM Enumservice "voice" with subtype "tel" under RFC 3761, indicating a NAPTR's URI can be used to place an interactive voice call via the PSTN/PLMN using a tel: URI.

ENUM.why: The document defines a new Enumservice for ENUM NAPTR records, including its functional specification and an example record. Readers of ENUM would expect to find it.
ENUM.quote: This document registers the Enumservice "voice" (which has a defined subtype "tel"), as per the IANA registration process defined in the ENUM specification RFC 3761.

tel URI.why: The Enumservice's URI scheme is tel:, and the registration gives guidance on using global versus local phone number forms in it. It does not define the scheme itself.
tel URI.quote: The "tel:" URI value SHOULD be fully qualified (using the "global phone number" form of RFC 3966 [10]).

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR records are only the substrate for ENUM. The document adds no new DNS behaviour or record type.
The document is a registration under an existing IANA registry. It is not about IANA registry procedures or guidance.
SIP and H.323 appear only as possible ways a provider may reach the PSTN. The document does not specify or extend them.
The PSTN is the target network of the voice call. The document does not address interworking mechanisms such as gateways or signalling transport.
Spam appears only in the Security Considerations, as a risk of data harvesting. The document is not about it.

RFC4416.title: Goals for Internet Messaging to Support Diverse Service Environments
RFC4416.summary: Informational history of the LEMONADE working group's goals: requirements and principles for enhancing Internet email (mainly IMAP retrieval and message submission) to support mobile, telephone-based and multi-modal clients, plus interoperation with MMS.

email.why: The whole document is about enhancing Internet mail architecture, retrieval, submission and notification for mobile and diverse clients.
email.quote: The LEMONADE Working Group -- Internet email to support diverse service environments -- is chartered to provide enhancements to Internet mail

IMAP.why: A substantial part of the document lists IMAP extension requirements (streaming, binary, mailbox summary, sort, multiple access).
IMAP.quote: IMAP [10] is the Internet protocol for rich message retrieval and manipulation.  The project MUST limit itself to extending IMAP where necessary

VPIM.why: Voice messaging profiles and TUI voice mail clients drive many of the requirements, so VPIM readers would want it.
VPIM.quote: These profiles, RFC3801 [13] to RFC3803 [15], enable the transport of voice messages using the Internet mail system.

rejected.why: Message submission and LMTP extensions are discussed only as requirements, not as the document's subject.
SMS is background for the mobile messaging infrastructure, not specified or analysed here.
iFax is briefly surveyed as an existing profile, and fax guaranteed delivery is explicitly out of scope.
MMS and 3GPP are discussed as interoperation context, not as IP over cellular.
MIME is a substrate; the document only touches on base64 inflation.
Mentioned only in the IAB note's example of notification.

gaps.name: Mobile messaging / MMS interoperation
gaps.why: The document covers MMS (3GPP/OMA) interworking and mobile email, and the taxonomy has no tag for MMS or mobile messaging beyond SMS.

gaps.name: LEMONADE (mobile email enhancements)
gaps.why: No tag for the LEMONADE effort itself or for event notification protocols between message stores and clients.

RFC4417.title: Report of the 2004 IAB Messaging Workshop
RFC4417.summary: Report of the October 2004 IAB workshop on Internet messaging, summarizing discussions on authorization, multiple channels, negotiation, user control, transport, and key distribution across email, IM, and voice messaging, with recommended engineering and research work.

messaging.why: The whole report is about messaging in general across email, IM and voice, with cross-protocol themes, so the general messaging topic fits better than any single technology.
messaging.quote: examine the current state of different messaging technologies on the Internet (including, but not limited to, electronic mail, instant messaging, and voice messaging)

workshop reports.why: It is an IAB workshop report, which matches the workshop reports tag directly.
workshop reports.quote: This document reports the outcome of a workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) on the future of Internet messaging.

rejected.why: Email is one of several media discussed and a main example, but the report treats messaging generally across media and does not specify or extend email.
IM is used as a comparison example alongside email and voice. The report is not about IM specifically.
The Introduction says spam was deliberately kept off the agenda. Reputation and allow/block lists are discussed only as general authorization topics.
Sieve is mentioned once as existing work to extend for recipient rules. It is not a subject of the document.
Authorization of senders and recipients is a discussion theme, but it is one of six topics in a general messaging report, and the messaging tag already covers it.
The report mentions in passing building key distribution into Secure DNS. This is a brief suggestion and not a substantial subject.

RFC4418.title: UMAC: Message Authentication Code using Universal Hashing
RFC4418.summary: RFC 4418 specifies UMAC, a fast Wegman-Carter message authentication code built on the UHASH universal hash function and an AES-based key and pad derivation, with 32/64/96/128-bit tags, security analysis and test vectors.

cryptography.why: The document specifies a MAC algorithm, which is a cryptographic primitive. No more specific tag exists for universal-hash MACs (HMAC is a different construction), so the parent topic is used.
cryptography.quote: This specification describes how to generate an authentication tag using the UMAC message authentication algorithm.

rejected.why: AES is only the default block cipher used inside the KDF and PDF. The document is not about AES itself.
HMAC is mentioned only as an alternative way to realise the KDF or PDF. UMAC is a different MAC construction.
SHA-1 is mentioned only as a comparison, and the document says UHASH is not a replacement for it.
ESP is cited only as an example of a protocol that could supply the nonce. The document is not about IPsec.
The KDF derives internal keys, but the document does not address key establishment or provisioning.

gaps.name: Message authentication code (MAC) / universal hashing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MAC algorithms in general. Only HMAC has its own tag, so UMAC falls back to the cryptography parent.

RFC4419.title: Diffie-Hellman Group Exchange for the Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol
RFC4419.summary: Defines two new SSH key exchange methods (diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1 and -sha256) in which the server proposes safe-prime DH groups to the client, with message formats, hash computation, and implementation notes.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport layer with new key exchange methods and message types, so it belongs on the SSH page.
SSH.quote: This memo describes a new key exchange method for the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol.

key management.why: The core content is a Diffie-Hellman key establishment with dynamic group selection, safe prime generation, generator choice and private exponent sizing, which is key establishment.
key management.quote: It allows the SSH server to propose new groups on which to perform the Diffie-Hellman key exchange to the client.

rejected.why: SHA-1 and SHA-256 are only the hash functions named in the method names, not the subject of the document.
The parent is implied by key management, which fits more specifically. No cryptographic algorithm is newly specified apart from the DH group exchange.
Host key signing is mentioned generically, and no RSA-specific content appears.
The message number section says the numbers are private to this document and not IANA-assigned, so it is only boilerplate-level.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key exchange
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for finite-field Diffie-Hellman groups or safe prime generation, which is the main technical subject. Key management is the closest fit.

RFC4420.title: Encoding of Attributes for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Path (LSP) Establishment Using Resource ReserVation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE)
RFC4420.summary: Defines the LSP_ATTRIBUTES and LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES RSVP-TE objects, a TLV-based Attributes Flags encoding, and an RRO Attributes subobject to signal and record LSP attributes beyond the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE flags.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE with new objects, TLVs, an RRO subobject and error codes for LSP attributes.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines a new object for RSVP-TE messages that allows the signaling of further attributes bits

MPLS.why: The attributes are for MPLS LSP establishment, and the document is a product of the MPLS working group. The mechanisms are explicitly applicable to MPLS LSPs.
MPLS.quote: Traffic-Engineered Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) [RFC3031] may be set up using the Path message

GMPLS.why: The document updates RFC 3473 and states the mechanisms apply to GMPLS PSC and non-PSC LSPs.
GMPLS.quote: The extensions described in this document are equally applicable to MPLS and GMPLS.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the subject, not base RSVP. The RSVP object class rules are only the underlying mechanism the new objects rely on.
The IANA section creates registries, but it is boilerplate here and not the main subject.
The RSVP-TE tag is the more specific fit. This document does not address traffic engineering in its own right.

RFC4421.title: RTP Payload Format for Uncompressed Video: Additional Colour Sampling Modes
RFC4421.summary: RFC 4421 extends the RTP payload format for uncompressed video (RFC 4175) with six new colour sampling modes (RGB+, RG+B, R+GB, BGR+, BG+R, B+GR) signalled via SDP fmtp parameters, and registers them for the video/raw media type.

RTP payload format.why: The document extends the RTP payload format for uncompressed video (RFC 4175) with new sampling modes and parameters, so readers of RTP payload formats need it.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo defines six new colour sampling modes that MAY be signalled for use with [1].

rejected.why: SDP is only used to show how the new modes are signalled in an example; the document does not specify or extend SDP.
RTP is the transport substrate; the document is about a payload format, which is covered by the more specific child tag.
The IANA section just adds new values for the sampling parameter of video/raw; this is boilerplate registration, not the main subject.
Uncompressed video is not a codec definition; the document only adds sampling-mode signalling to a payload format.

RFC4422.title: Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL)
RFC4422.summary: RFC 4422 specifies the SASL framework, which provides replaceable authentication mechanisms and an optional data security layer for connection-oriented protocols. It sets out protocol and mechanism requirements and the IANA mechanism registry, and defines the EXTERNAL mechanism.

SASL.why: The whole document specifies SASL: the authentication exchange, protocol and mechanism requirements, security layers, the mechanism registry, and the EXTERNAL mechanism.
SASL.quote: The Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) is a framework for providing authentication and data security services in connection-oriented protocols via replaceable mechanisms.

rejected.why: GSSAPI is only mentioned for the service name registry and as an example mechanism, which is now specified separately. The document is not about it.
TLS appears only as an example of an external security layer and in the EXTERNAL examples. It is not specified or extended here.
The SASL mechanism registry procedures are part of the SASL specification and are not a general IANA topic. They are boilerplate-like registration rules for this one registry.
Unicode and UTF-8 are used to define the authorization identity string, but the document does not address Unicode usage in its own right.
This broad topic is covered by the SASL tag, which is more specific.
ACAP is used only for the EXTERNAL examples.

gaps.name: SASL
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a SASL tech tag under security, and the tag list I was given is exactly as shown. However, I wrote 'SASL' as the id, and it is in the taxonomy as 'SASL'.

RFC4423.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Architecture
RFC4423.summary: Informational architecture document describing the Host Identity namespace (public-key host identifiers) and the Host Identity Protocol layer between internetworking and transport, covering mobility, multihoming, IPsec use, NATs and security.

HIP.why: The entire document is the architecture of HIP: its namespace, identifiers (HIT, LSI), base exchange, mobility and policies.
HIP.quote: a new protocol layer, the Host Identity Protocol (HIP), between the internetworking and transport layers

IPsec.why: A dedicated section explains how HIP base exchange sets up ESP SAs, transport mode only, and why a new protocol rather than IKE; readers of IPsec would want it.
IPsec.quote: The preferred way of implementing HIP is to use IPsec to carry the actual data traffic.

IP mobility.why: Mobility, multihoming, rendezvous and readdress flooding protection are a substantial part of the architecture.
IP mobility.quote: HIP can provide for a degree of internetworking mobility and multi-homing at a low infrastructure cost.

rejected.why: DNS is used only to store Host Identifiers (a to-be-defined RR); the document is not about DNS itself.
HIP-aware NAT behaviour is discussed in one section, but it is a secondary aspect, not the document's subject.
Mentioned as the expected authenticator for HIs, but only as a supporting mechanism.
Compared against and explicitly not used; HIP defines its own exchange.
The HI namespace is central, but the HIP tag already covers it and no more specific naming tag fits.
Considered since it is an architecture memo, but it is specific to HIP, which is covered by the HIP tag.

RFC4424.title: Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload Format for the Variable-Rate Multimode Wideband (VMR-WB) Extension Audio Codec
RFC4424.summary: Addendum to RFC 4348 updating the RTP payload format tables (frame types, CMR values, mode-set parameter) to support the new VMR-WB mode 4 of the 3GPP2 wideband speech codec.

RTP payload format.why: The document updates the RTP payload format for the VMR-WB codec, changing the frame type and CMR tables and the mode-set parameter.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies some updates in RFC 4348 to enable support for the new operating mode of VMR-WB standard (i.e., VMR-WB mode 4).

rejected.why: VMR-WB is a codec, but the document only updates its RTP payload format tables. The codec itself is specified by 3GPP2. RTP payload format is the more specific tag.
AMR-WB interoperable modes appear in the tables, but the document is not about AMR.
The mode-set parameter value in the existing registration is modified. That is a small IANA change, and the document states that no new media type registration is required.
The offer/answer model is mentioned only briefly for negotiating modes. It is not a subject of the document.
CDMA2000 is the target network and the source of the rate sets, but the document does not address IP over cdma2000 networks.

RFC4425.title: RTP Payload Format for Video Codec 1 (VC-1)
RFC4425.summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for SMPTE 421M VC-1 compressed video, including AU header syntax, fragmentation, timestamps, and the video/vc1 media type with SDP parameters and offer/answer rules.

RTP payload format.why: The document's whole purpose is defining how VC-1 video is packetized in RTP: access units, fragmentation, timestamps, and random access signalling.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo specifies an RTP payload format for the video coding standard Video Codec 1, also known as VC-1.

codecs.why: VC-1 is a video codec with no dedicated child tag. The document overviews its profiles, levels, bit stream layering and HRD, so readers of codecs would want it.
codecs.quote: SMPTE 421M defines the VC-1 bit stream syntax and specifies constraints that must be met by VC-1 conformant bit streams.

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document maps media type parameters to SDP fmtp lines and defines offer/answer and declarative usage rules.
SDP.quote: Section 6.3 defines rules specific to the SDP Offer/Answer model, and section 6.4 defines rules for when SDP is used in a declarative style.

media types.why: It registers the video/vc1 media type with detailed parameters, which is a significant section.
media types.quote: Type name:  video  Subtype name:  vc1

rejected.why: SRTP is only mentioned as an example for confidentiality and integrity in Security Considerations.
RTP is the substrate. The more specific RTP payload format tag covers the document.
Section 8 only applies RTP congestion control rules to this payload. It defines no new mechanism.
RTSP is mentioned only as an example of declarative SDP use.
SIP appears only in passing, as a re-invite example for changing parameters.

gaps.name: VC-1 (SMPTE 421M) video codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no VC-1 codec tag. Sibling codecs such as H.264 and VP8 each have one, so VC-1 readers would be served only by the generic codecs tag.

RFC4426.title: Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Recovery Functional Specification
RFC4426.summary: Functional specification of GMPLS-based recovery (span protection, end-to-end path protection, shared mesh restoration, reversion) describing the signaling messages and procedures needed, with protocol formats left to companion documents.

GMPLS.why: The whole document specifies GMPLS recovery functions (span, end-to-end and shared mesh protection, reversion, messages), so it belongs under GMPLS.
GMPLS.quote: This document presents a functional description of the protocol extensions needed to support Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)-based recovery (i.e., protection and restoration).

rejected.why: TE links and bandwidth announcements are mentioned, but the subject is GMPLS recovery, which GMPLS covers more specifically.
GMPLS is a child of MPLS and is the more specific tag.
Signaling is described abstractly; protocol-specific encodings are deferred to companion documents.
OSPF and IS-IS are only cited for encoding Link Protection Type in other RFCs; not the document's subject.
Failure detection is mentioned but the document is about recovery procedures, not OAM mechanisms.

gaps.name: Protection and restoration (network recovery/survivability)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is recovery (1+1, 1:1, M:N, shared mesh, reversion); the taxonomy has no recovery/survivability tag, so only GMPLS captures it.

RFC4427.title: Recovery (Protection and Restoration) Terminology for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)
RFC4427.summary: Defines common terminology for GMPLS-based recovery (protection and restoration) of LSPs and spans, independent of transport technology, borrowing from ITU-T G.808.1 and G.841.

GMPLS.why: The whole document defines recovery terms (protection types, restoration schemes, bridges, selectors, switch-over) for LSPs controlled by a GMPLS control plane, so readers of GMPLS would look for it.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines a common terminology for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)-based recovery mechanisms (i.e., protection and restoration).

rejected.why: Protection and restoration relate to survivability, but the document is terminology specific to GMPLS recovery, and GMPLS is the more specific fit.
GMPLS is the more specific tag under MPLS; the document does not address plain MPLS.
It is a terminology document, but the subject-specific tag GMPLS fits better and the terminology topic is for general glossaries and requirements language.
Failure detection and reporting are discussed only as recovery phases and definitions, not as OAM mechanisms.
SDH protection (G.841) is only a source of borrowed terminology; the document is technology-independent.

gaps.name: Network survivability / protection and restoration
gaps.why: The document's subject is recovery (protection switching and restoration) of LSPs. The taxonomy has no tag for survivability or recovery, so GMPLS is the nearest fit.

RFC4428.title: Analysis of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)-based Recovery Mechanisms (including Protection and Restoration)
RFC4428.summary: Informational CCAMP analysis grid evaluating GMPLS-based protection and restoration mechanisms across the recovery phases (detection, localization, notification, recovery, reversion), hierarchies, SRLG disjointness and recovery resource sharing for SONET/SDH, OTN and pre-OTN transport planes.

GMPLS.why: The whole document analyses GMPLS signalling and routing capabilities for LSP/span protection and restoration, including reversion, hierarchies and shared-mesh recovery.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides an analysis grid to evaluate, compare, and contrast the Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) protocol suite capabilities with the recovery mechanisms

rejected.why: GMPLS RSVP-TE signalling is the mechanism relied on for recovery, but the document explicitly does not cover protocol specifications.
SRLG-aware path computation and bandwidth sharing are discussed, but the focus is recovery, which GMPLS covers more specifically.
SONET/SDH is the transport technology whose failure detection and APS are described, but the document is not about IP over SONET.
Failure detection and notification are fault management, but they are examined as recovery phases rather than as an OAM mechanism.
Path computation is explicitly out of scope.
The document mentions OSPF-TE only in the security considerations and says no routing extensions are needed.

gaps.name: Protection and restoration / network survivability (transport-plane recovery)
gaps.why: The document is about LSP/span recovery, covering protection switching, restoration, reversion and SRLG disjointness. The taxonomy has no survivability or resilience tag, so only GMPLS fits.

RFC4429.title: Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) for IPv6
RFC4429.summary: Specifies Optimistic DAD, a modification to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration that lets a host use an address before Duplicate Address Detection completes, with restrictions to avoid disrupting neighbors.

SLAAC.why: The document modifies the SLAAC DAD process (RFC 2462 sections 5.4, 5.5) by introducing an Optimistic address state, so SLAAC readers need it.
SLAAC.quote: Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection is an interoperable modification of the existing IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 2461) and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 2462) processes.

neighbor discovery.why: It specifies normative changes to RFC 2461 Neighbor Discovery behaviour (NS, NA Override flag, RS SLLAO, redirects) for Optimistic addresses.
neighbor discovery.quote: A node MUST NOT use an Optimistic Address as the source address of a Neighbor Solicitation.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in Security Considerations as providing protection; the document does not specify or extend SEND.
Only cited as one source of likely-unique addresses; not the subject.
Mentioned as motivation and an example of packets sent during the optimistic period; the document does not specify Mobile IPv6 behaviour.
ICMP Redirect is used as a mechanism for neighbor contact, but the document is not about ICMP itself.
A more specific child tag (SLAAC, neighbor discovery) fits, so the parent is implied.

RFC4430.title: Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys (KINK)
RFC4430.summary: Specifies KINK, a Kerberos-based protocol that creates, deletes and maintains IPsec security associations by reusing IKE Quick Mode payloads, with message flows, formats, dead peer detection and key derivation.

KINK.why: The document defines the KINK protocol itself: message flows, payloads, key derivation and dead peer detection.
KINK.quote: KINK defines a low-latency, computationally inexpensive, easily managed, and cryptographically sound protocol to establish and maintain security associations using the Kerberos authentication system.

rejected.why: Kerberos is the authentication substrate KINK relies on; the document does not extend or profile Kerberos itself.
KINK reuses IKE Quick Mode payloads but replaces IKE's authentication and phase 1. The document is not about IKE, and KINK is its own tag under IKE.
KINK establishes IPsec SAs, but IPsec ESP/AH and architecture are the target of keying, not what is specified here.
GDOI is only mentioned as an example of a possible future DOI carried over KINK.
The KINK tag is more specific, so this parent is implied.

RFC4431.title: The DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) DNS Resource Record
RFC4431.summary: Defines the DLV DNS resource record, which has the same format as DS, for publishing DNSSEC trust anchors outside the DNS delegation chain.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies a new DNSSEC record type used for trust anchors and validation, so it belongs under DNSSEC, which also covers DNS resource records of this kind.
DNSSEC.quote: defines a new DNS resource record, called the DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) RR, for publishing DNSSEC trust anchors outside of the DNS delegation chain

rejected.why: The parent of DNSSEC is implied. The record is a security-specific RR, so DNSSEC is the more specific tag.

RFC4432.title: RSA Key Exchange for the Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol
RFC4432.summary: Defines two SSH transport-layer key-exchange methods (rsa1024-sha1 and rsa2048-sha256) that use RSAES-OAEP encryption of a client-generated secret under a transient server RSA key, as a faster alternative to Diffie-Hellman for slow clients.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport layer with new key-exchange methods, new messages and message numbers, and IANA-registered method names.
SSH.quote: This memo describes a key-exchange method for the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol based on Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) public-key encryption.

RSA.why: The key exchange is built on RSA encryption with OAEP padding, a transient RSA key and RSA modulus size requirements, and the document discusses RSA key reuse and strength.
RSA.quote: The encryption is performed according to the RSAES-OAEP scheme of [RFC3447], with a mask generation function of MGF1-with-HASH

rejected.why: The document does describe key establishment, but the SSH tag already covers it as the specific protocol and the RSA tag covers the algorithm, so the broader topic is not needed.
SHA-1 and SHA-256 are only parameters of the two methods and are not themselves specified or analysed.
Randomness is mentioned only in Security Considerations, with a reference to RFC 4086. It is not the document's subject.
The IANA registration of the method names is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC4433.title: Mobile IPv4 Dynamic Home Agent (HA) Assignment
RFC4433.summary: Defines a Mobile IPv4 messaging mechanism (ALL-ZERO-ONE-ADDR in the HA field, Requested/Redirected HA extensions, REDIRECT-HA-REQ error code) for dynamic home agent assignment and redirection during registration.

Mobile IPv4.why: The RFC extends Mobile IPv4 registration with new extensions, an error code and HA assignment/redirection procedures for the MN, FA and HA.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document adds to the Mobile IP protocol [1], by proposing a messaging mechanism for dynamic home agent assignment and home agent redirection during initial registration.

rejected.why: DHCP Mobile IP Home Agent Option 68 is only mentioned as one example method for selecting the Requested HA; the document does not specify DHCP.
AAA servers are mentioned as a possible HA selection source and for key derivation via RFC 3957, but the document is not about AAA.
DNS lookup is listed as one example selection method only; nothing new is defined for DNS.
The document is about a specific child, Mobile IPv4, so the parent tag is implied and not listed separately.

RFC4434.title: The AES-XCBC-PRF-128 Algorithm for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE)
RFC4434.summary: Defines AES-XCBC-PRF-128, a 128-bit-output pseudo-random function derived from AES-XCBC-MAC by omitting truncation and relaxing key length rules, for use in IKEv1 and IKEv2; obsoletes RFC 3664.

AES.why: The document specifies a new AES-based PRF algorithm (AES-XCBC-PRF-128), including key handling and test vectors, so it belongs under AES.
AES.quote: Some implementations of IP Security (IPsec) may want to use a pseudo-random function derived from the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).

IKE.why: The algorithm is defined for use as an IKE PRF, and the document explains its fixed vs variable key-length semantics in IKEv2 key generation and authentication.
IKE.quote: Both versions of IKE use the PRF to create keys in a fashion that is dependent on the length of the output of the PRF.

rejected.why: IPsec is the context, but the document only specifies a PRF for IKE rather than IPsec architecture, ESP or AH.
HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC-MD5 are mentioned only as comparison PRFs for key-length alignment; the document is not about HMAC.
The PRF is used to derive keys, but the document defines a cryptographic algorithm and not a key management mechanism; IKE already covers that context.

RFC4435.title: A Framework for the Usage of Internet Media Guides (IMGs)
RFC4435.summary: Informational framework defining a generalized model (data types, entities, operations) for delivering Internet Media Guides, collections of multimedia session descriptions, and assessing how existing protocols (SDP, SAP, HTTP, SIP events, RTSP, ALC/FLUTE) fit and what is missing.

streaming.why: IMGs describe media services such as TV program schedules and content delivery schedules and how guide metadata is delivered. This is media delivery and guide infrastructure with no more specific tag, so the streaming topic fits best.
streaming.quote: An IMG is a structured collection of multimedia session descriptions expressed using the Session Description Protocol (SDP), SDPng, or some similar session description format.

SDP.why: The document analyses SDP as a session description format for IMG metadata, including its limitations. It is one of several candidate formats, so the role is secondary.
SDP.quote: The SDP format [2] could be used to describe session-level parameters (e.g., scheduling, addressing, and the use of media codecs) to be included in Complete IMG Descriptions.

ALC.why: The document recommends ALC and FLUTE as the basis for a new IMG multicast announcement protocol. That is a substantial part of the gap analysis.
ALC.quote: we recommend that ALC and FLUTE be the starting points for this protocol's design.

FLUTE.why: FLUTE is the recommended starting point for the IMG multicast announcement protocol. Readers interested in FLUTE applications would want this document.
FLUTE.quote: FLUTE seems to be the only fully specified transport and open specification on which a new IMG announcement protocol could be designed.

rejected.why: HTTP is evaluated as one possible unicast transport for QUERY/RESOLVE, but the document does not specify or extend it.
SIP events (RFC 3265) are mentioned only as a possible way to implement SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, not as a subject of the document.
RTSP DESCRIBE and ANNOUNCE are discussed briefly as a possible fit, not as a subject.
Multicast distribution is a deployment case, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
SDPng, MPEG-7 and TV-Anytime are XML-based, but XML is only incidental.
IMGs resemble session discovery, but the document is about guide metadata delivery. It is not a discovery protocol.

gaps.name: Internet Media Guides (IMG) / media guide metadata delivery
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for program-guide and session-metadata delivery frameworks. The nearest fit, streaming, is only approximate.

gaps.name: Session Announcement Protocol (SAP)
gaps.why: SAP is analysed as a candidate transport but has no tag of its own.

RFC4436.title: Detecting Network Attachment in IPv4 (DNAv4)
RFC4436.summary: Specifies DNAv4, a procedure using a unicast ARP reachability test to a known router, run in parallel with DHCP INIT-REBOOT, so a host re-attaching to a previously visited network can quickly confirm its still-valid IPv4 configuration and reduce handover latency.

ARP.why: The core mechanism of DNAv4 is a unicast ARP request/reply exchange with specific field rules, extending how ARP is used.
ARP.quote: The reachability test is performed by sending a unicast ARP Request.

DHCP.why: The document specifies how DNAv4 interacts with DHCP INIT-REBOOT/INIT states, lease validity, client identifiers and retransmission, and is a DHCP working group document.
DHCP.quote: it is RECOMMENDED that the host attempt to obtain IPv4 configuration via DHCPv4 in parallel with the reachability tests

rejected.why: IPv4 configuration is the subject matter, but the document is about ARP/DHCP-based attachment detection rather than the IP protocol or addressing itself.
ICMP Echo is discussed only as an unacceptable alternative to the ARP reachability test.
Link-local and private addresses are discussed only as they bear on the reachability test; the document does not address addressing architecture.
The document concerns handover latency when moving between networks, but it is not about Mobile IP or its successors.

gaps.name: Detecting Network Attachment (DNA)
gaps.why: The document defines a link-change and network-attachment detection procedure for hosts, and the taxonomy has no tag for movement detection or fast re-attachment.

RFC4437.title: Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) Redirect Reference Resources
RFC4437.summary: Experimental WebDAV extension defining redirect reference resources, with new MKREDIRECTREF and UPDATEREDIRECTREF methods, Redirect-Ref and Apply-To-Redirect-Ref headers, properties, and capability discovery.

WebDAV.why: The document extends WebDAV with new methods (MKREDIRECTREF, UPDATEREDIRECTREF), properties, XML elements, and a compliance class.
WebDAV.quote: This specification defines an extension to Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) to allow clients to author HTTP redirect reference resources

rejected.why: HTTP 3xx redirection and new headers are used, but the document's subject is the WebDAV extension; HTTP is the substrate.
URIs and relative-reference resolution are used as targets, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
XML is the request/response encoding for the new methods, not the subject.
Redirect references resemble links, but the document does not define typed link relations or the Link header.

RFC4438.title: Fibre-Channel Name Server MIB
RFC4438.summary: Defines the T11-FC-NAME-SERVER-MIB SMIv2 module, giving SNMP managed objects for monitoring the Fibre Channel Name Server: registered ports, statistics, reject information and notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module in SMIv2 for the Fibre Channel Name Server, with tables, counters, notifications and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects for information related to the Name Server function of a Fibre Channel network.

fibre channel.why: The MIB manages the Fibre Channel Name Server function (FC-GS-4, RSCN, WWNs, FC-4 types), so readers of Fibre Channel topics would want it.
fibre channel.quote: The Fibre Channel Name Server provides a way for N_Ports and NL_Ports to register and discover Fibre Channel attributes.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines objects and does not extend SNMP itself, so the MIB tag is the more specific fit.
It is mentioned only as an example of how management instances may be grouped, and the document is not about AgentX.
The Name Server registers and discovers FC names, but it is a Fibre Channel function rather than a directory service in the IETF sense.
The Name Server is a Fibre Channel mechanism and is not about general naming or name resolution.
IP addresses appear only as OCTET STRING objects, so the document is not about IPv6.

RFC4439.title: Fibre Channel Fabric Address Manager MIB
RFC4439.summary: Defines the T11-FC-FABRIC-ADDR-MGR-MIB and T11-TC-MIB SMIv2 modules for managing Fibre Channel Fabric Address Manager functionality (Domain_ID assignment, Principal Switch selection, FC address identifiers, RCF/BF) in FC switches via SNMP.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification with SMIv2 tables, objects, notifications and conformance groups for Fibre Channel fabric address management.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

fibre channel.why: The managed subject is Fibre Channel fabric behaviour (Domain_IDs, Principal Switch, FC IDs, RCF/BF). The taxonomy has only a Fibre Channel over IP tag, which is the closest match for readers of Fibre Channel management.
fibre channel.quote: it describes managed objects for information related to a Fibre Channel network's Fabric Address Manager.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
Fibre Channel is a storage networking technology, but this document covers fabric address management and not storage access protocols.
AgentX is mentioned only as an example of how management instances may be grouped; the document is not about it.
iFCP carries Fibre Channel over TCP/IP; this MIB manages native FC fabric switches and is not about iFCP.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel (native fabric, FC-SW, FC-FS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has Fibre Channel only as 'fibre channel' (over IP transports) under storage. Native FC switch fabric management, such as the other T11 MIBs in the series, has no tag of its own.

RFC4440.title: IAB Thoughts on the Role of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF)
RFC4440.summary: An IAB report discussing the role of the IRTF on its own and in relation to the IETF and IAB, covering research group structures, architecture work, IETF/IRTF interchange, and the RFC publication track for IRTF documents.

IETF process.why: The document is about how the IRTF is organised and relates to the IETF, IAB and IESG, including research group chartering, differences from working groups and the RG-to-WG interchange. That is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: The IRTF has generally focused on investigation into areas that are not considered sufficiently mature for IETF standardization
IETF process.section: 2. The Relationship between the IRTF, the IAB, and the IETF

RFC series.why: A section discusses whether a distinct RFC publication track is needed for IRTF research group output, and how to shorten its publication delay.
RFC series.quote: RFCs produced by RGs are published as individual submissions, under the review of the RFC Editor
RFC series.section: 4.4. The RFC Track for IRTF Documents

rejected.why: The document discusses how IRTF groups can contribute to architecture work, but it is about the IRTF's role, not architectural principles themselves.
It gives brief history of the IAB, IRTF and its chairs, but only as background to the discussion of the IRTF's role.
The HIP research group is mentioned only as an example of an RG.
The Reliable Multicast RG is cited only as an example of work tossed over the fence to the IETF.

gaps.name: IRTF (Internet Research Task Force)
gaps.why: The document is about the IRTF and its research groups. The taxonomy has no IRTF tag, so the closest fit is the broader IETF process topic.

RFC4441.title: The IEEE 802/IETF Relationship
RFC4441.summary: IAB informational RFC describing the policies, procedures and history of coordination between IEEE 802 and the IETF, covering liaisons, document access, MIB review, EAP/AAA review and EtherType allocation.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document (Section 1.4 and Appendix A.1) covers MIB Doctor review and the history of Bridge, Hub, MAU and 802.1 MIB development between the two organizations.
MIB.quote: it is recommended that Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) MIBs developed in IEEE 802 follow the MIB guidelines [RFC4181] and be reviewed as part of the IETF SNMP quality control process

EAP.why: The EAP review process for IEEE 802.1X, 802.11i and 802.16e, plus the EAP WG history in Appendix A.2, forms a major part of the relationship described.
EAP.quote: IEEE 802 working groups should send a liaison letter to the IETF, outlining the required functionality or requesting a review of draft text.

RADIUS.why: The document gives guidance on RADIUS attributes and VSAs for IEEE 802 and on IETF review of 802 RADIUS extensions, including the 802.11F history.
RADIUS.quote: allocation from the IETF standard attribute space is preferred to creation of IEEE 802 Vendor-Specific Attributes (VSAs).

IETF process.why: The document's main purpose is to describe liaison, new-work review, document access and review procedures between the IETF and another standards body.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the policies and procedures that have been put in place to encourage cooperation between the IETF and IEEE 802.

rejected.why: EtherType allocation is only a short section and the document is not about IP over Ethernet itself.
IEEE 802.11 is discussed only as a liaison partner, not as the subject of the document.
EtherType and RADIUS allocation policies are mentioned briefly, but the main subject is not IANA registries.
SNMP is the management framework for the MIBs discussed, but the document's focus is MIB review and not the SNMP protocol.
The more specific RADIUS and EAP tags fit better than the general AAA framework tag.
CAPWAP appears only as one example of a document reviewed by IEEE 802.11.

gaps.name: Liaison relationships between the IETF and other standards bodies (IEEE 802)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for inter-SDO liaison and coordination. IETF process is the nearest fit, but it is only approximate.

RFC4442.title: Bootstrapping Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication (TESLA)
RFC4442.summary: Specifies new MIKEY payloads (TESLA policy in the Security Policy payload, and an initial-key General Extension payload) to bootstrap TESLA parameters for SRTP source authentication in group communication.

TESLA.why: The document defines how TESLA parameters and the initial key are bootstrapped, including time synchronization and policy encoding. TESLA readers would want it.
TESLA.quote: TESLA, the Timed Efficient Stream Loss-tolerant Authentication protocol, provides source authentication in multicast scenarios.

MIKEY.why: It extends MIKEY with a new Prot type value, TESLA policy TLVs and a new General Extension payload type, plus new IANA registries.
MIKEY.quote: This document specifies payloads for the Multimedia Internet Keying (MIKEY) protocol for bootstrapping TESLA

SRTP.why: The bootstrapped parameters serve the SRTP-TESLA profile (RFC 4383), and the document supplies the missing parameter distribution for it.
SRTP.quote: bootstrapping TESLA for source authentication of secure group communications using SRTP

rejected.why: NTP is only one of two options mentioned for time synchronization; the document does not specify or extend it.
SDP is only mentioned as the transport MIKEY uses for parameter carriage in Security Considerations; not the subject.
SIP is mentioned only as a possible session setup context in Security Considerations.
HMAC-SHA1 appears only as a default PRF and MAC identifier value, not as a subject.
The parent topic is implied by the TESLA and MIKEY tags, and the document is about specific mechanisms rather than the general topic.

RFC4443.title: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMPv6) for the Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
RFC4443.summary: RFC 4443 specifies ICMPv6, the Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6: its message format, error messages (Destination Unreachable, Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem), Echo Request/Reply, processing rules, rate limiting, and IANA assignment procedures.

ICMP.why: The document is the core ICMPv6 specification, defining message formats, codes, and processing rules.
ICMP.quote: This document describes the format of a set of control messages used in ICMPv6 (Internet Control Message Protocol).

rejected.why: ICMPv6 runs over IPv6, but the document specifies ICMP, not IPv6 itself. ICMP is the more specific fit.
The Packet Too Big message supports Path MTU Discovery, but the document explicitly says the PMTUD procedures are described elsewhere.
Neighbor Discovery messages are only mentioned as other ICMPv6 types defined in other documents.
IPsec AH and ESP appear only in the Security Considerations as ways to protect ICMP messages.
The checksum calculation is a short subsection of the message format and is not a subject of the document in its own right.
The IANA Considerations section sets type and code assignment procedures, but this is boilerplate relative to the main body.

RFC4444.title: Management Information Base for Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS)
RFC4444.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module for managing IS-IS routers (used for IP routing per RFC 1195), covering system, circuit, adjacency, reachable address, LSP database objects, counters and notifications.

IS-IS.why: The managed protocol is IS-IS; the MIB models its adjacencies, LSPs, circuits, levels, metrics and notifications, so readers of IS-IS would want it.
IS-IS.quote: this document describes a MIB for the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Routing protocol when it is used to construct routing tables for IP networks

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (ISIS-MIB) with tables, conformance groups and notifications.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines a MIB module rather than SNMP itself, and the MIB tag sits under SNMP already.
OSI NSAP addresses and ISO 10589 are the basis of IS-IS, but the document is about managing IS-IS, not OSI network-layer protocols generally.
Only wide metrics and a TE-enabled flag are included; TE is not the subject.
Listed only as a route source type enumeration value.

RFC4445.title: A Proposed Media Delivery Index (MDI)
RFC4445.summary: Defines the Media Delivery Index (MDI), a Delay Factor and Media Loss Rate measurement for monitoring jitter and loss of streaming media flows such as MPEG-TS over UDP in IPTV networks.

performance measurement.why: The document defines a network performance metric (delay factor and media loss rate) for monitoring jitter and loss, which is a performance measurement topic.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a Media Delivery Index (MDI) measurement that can be used as a diagnostic tool or a quality indicator for monitoring a network

IPTV.why: The metric is aimed at monitoring delivery quality of streaming video in IPTV deployments, so readers of IPTV operations would find it useful.
IPTV.quote: An example application is the burgeoning deployments of Internet Protocol Television (IPTV) by cable and telecommunication service providers.

rejected.why: RTP and RTCP are only mentioned as related work; the MDI is independent of stream encapsulation.
UDP is the transport of the monitored streams, not the subject of the document.
IPTV is the more specific child tag, so the parent streaming is not chosen.
QoS mechanisms such as RSVP and Diffserv are cited as background, but the document is about measuring delivery, not about QoS architecture.
RTCP XR is only mentioned as an alternative reporting approach.

RFC4446.title: IANA Allocations for Pseudowire Edge to Edge Emulation (PWE3)
RFC4446.summary: BCP defining the IANA registries and initial code point allocations (PW types, interface parameter sub-TLVs, AII/AGI types, status codes) for pseudowire emulation (PWE3) protocols, with expert-review rules.

pseudowire.why: The whole document allocates pseudowire type, interface parameter, attachment identifier and status code registries for PWE3, so pseudowire readers would want it.
pseudowire.quote: IANA has set up the registry of "MPLS Pseudowire Type".

IANA.why: It sets IANA registry policies and expert review directives, ranges and vendor FCFS rules, for the PWE3 registries.
IANA.quote: allocation procedures for several registries call for an expert review process according to [RFC2434]

rejected.why: MPLS is the PSN carrying the pseudowires and its types are referenced, but the document is about pseudowire registries, not MPLS itself.
Signalling via LDP (RFC 4447) is referenced for status codes and sub-TLVs, but this document does not specify LDP.
AII/AGI types come from the L2VPN signalling draft, but the document does not address L2VPN services.
ATM, Frame Relay, Ethernet and SONET appear only as PW type names in a table, not as subjects.

RFC4447.title: Pseudowire Setup and Maintenance Using the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)
RFC4447.summary: Specifies LDP extensions (new FEC elements, TLVs, status codes and procedures) for setting up, maintaining and signaling status of point-to-point pseudowires over an MPLS network.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines pseudowire signaling: PWid and Generalized PWid FEC elements, PW status, control word negotiation.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies a protocol for establishing and maintaining the pseudowires, using extensions to Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with new FEC element types, TLVs and status codes, so LDP readers need it.
LDP.quote: we define new TLVs, FEC elements, parameters, and codes for LDP, which enable LDP to identify pseudowires and to signal attributes of pseudowires.

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate carrying pseudowires; tunnel setup is explicitly out of scope, and LDP/pseudowire are the more specific tags.
Mentions VPWS/VPLS provisioning models only in passing; the document does not specify L2VPN services.
ATM, Frame Relay and Ethernet are emulated services whose encapsulations are in companion documents.
TDM/SONET circuit emulation is referenced only as a service handled by companion documents.
The LDP MD5 option is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a mechanism, not the subject.

RFC4448.title: Encapsulation Methods for Transport of Ethernet over MPLS Networks
RFC4448.summary: Specifies the encapsulation of Ethernet/802.3 PDUs in a pseudowire over MPLS (raw and tagged modes, control word, QoS, MTU) to provide an emulated point-to-point Ethernet service.

pseudowire.why: The document defines the Ethernet pseudowire type: its encapsulation, control word, raw/tagged modes and point-to-point service procedures.
pseudowire.quote: An Ethernet pseudowire (PW) is used to carry Ethernet/802.3 Protocol Data Units (PDUs) over an MPLS network.

rejected.why: MPLS is the underlying PSN used for transport; the document is about the pseudowire encapsulation, not MPLS itself.
The Ethernet tag covers IP over Ethernet and Ethernet OAM; here Ethernet is the emulated service carried over a PW, and the pseudowire tag is the better fit.
LDP is used only for PW signalling, and the one sub-TLV defined here is a PW interface parameter. The signalling is specified in RFC 4447.
ECMP is mentioned only as the reason for the control word, not as a subject of the document.
QoS mapping of 802.1Q priority to the PSN is a short section and appendix, not a main subject.

RFC4449.title: Securing Mobile IPv6 Route Optimization Using a Static Shared Key
RFC4449.summary: Defines an alternative to return routability for Mobile IPv6 route optimization, in which a mobile node and correspondent node preconfigure a shared key and nonces to precompute the Binding Management Key used to authenticate Binding Updates.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 with a preconfigured-key way of computing Kbm for authorizing Binding Updates. Readers of Mobile IPv6 route optimization security would want it.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This specification introduces an alternative, low-latency security mechanism for protecting signaling related to the route optimization in Mobile IPv6.

rejected.why: It does involve manually configured shared keys. But the document is about a Mobile IPv6 binding authorization mechanism, not key management in general.
It cites RFC 4086 for generating Kcn. That is a passing requirement, not a subject of the document.
It authenticates Binding Updates, but only inside Mobile IPv6. The Mobile IPv6 tag covers that, so the broader topic isn't needed.
Mobile IPv6 is the specific subject. The general IPv6 tag is a parent of it and is implied.

RFC4450.title: Getting Rid of the Cruft: Report from an Experiment in Identifying and Reclassifying Obsolete Standards Documents
RFC4450.summary: Reports on an experiment to identify obsolete Proposed Standards (RFCs below 2000) and reclassify about 61 of them as Historic, describing the bulk-decommissioning procedure and its results and next steps.

IETF process.why: The document is about the IETF standards-track process: review of immature standards under RFC 2026, and a bulk procedure for moving them to Historic.
IETF process.quote: This memo documents an experiment to review and classify Proposed Standards as not reflecting documented practice within the world today.

rejected.why: It concerns the standards status of documents, not RFC format, style or publication; the RFC Editor is only asked to mark statuses.
Many Telnet options appear in the input list, but they are not the subject; they are only discussed as a category removed from the list.
X.400 documents appear in the list of reclassified RFCs, but the document is not about X.400.
Whois++ RFCs are listed among the reclassified documents only; the document does not address the protocol.
The PEM RFCs appear in the results list; the document is not about PEM itself.
IDPR RFCs are items in the list, not the subject of the document.

RFC4451.title: BGP MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) Considerations
RFC4451.summary: Informational RFC discussing implementation and deployment considerations for the BGP MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute, including hot/cold potato routing, route oscillation with route reflection/confederations, flap damping, and update packing.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses the BGP MED attribute, its decision-process behaviour, implementation quirks and operational deployment issues.
BGP.quote: The BGP MED attribute provides a mechanism for BGP speakers to convey to an adjacent AS the optimal entry point into the local AS.

route reflection.why: A dedicated section covers how MED interacts with route reflectors and confederations to cause persistent route oscillation, with mitigation advice.
route reflection.quote: the BGP scaling mechanisms defined in "BGP Route Reflection - An Alternative to Full Mesh IBGP" [RFC2796] and "Autonomous System Confederations for BGP" [RFC3065]
route reflection.section: 3.4. MEDs, Route Reflection, and AS Confederations for BGP

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example of an IGP metric space differing from IS-IS; not a subject of the document.
Only a passing example of a contrasting IGP metric space.
The document is about a specific BGP attribute, so the BGP tag fits better than a general routing architecture tag.
Hot/cold potato and MED-based path preference touch on traffic engineering, but the document does not address TE as a subject.
The Security Considerations section is brief boilerplate-like content and not the main body subject.

RFC4452.title: The "info" URI Scheme for Information Assets with Identifiers in Public Namespaces
RFC4452.summary: Defines the "info" URI scheme and its registry, which lets identifiers from public namespaces (Dewey, LCCN, SICI, PubMed, etc.) be referenced as URIs, with syntax, normalization rules and rationale versus URN.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme, including its ABNF syntax, allowed characters and normalization and comparison rules.
URI.quote: This document defines the "info" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme for information assets that have identifiers in public namespaces

rejected.why: Section 6.3 only explains why a URN namespace was not used. The document defines a URI scheme, not a URN namespace.
The IANA section only requests a URI scheme registration. That is boilerplate. The "info" Registry is run by NISO, not IANA.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax. The document is not about it.
UTF-8 is only mentioned as the encoding for percent-escaping. The document is not about it.

RFC4453.title: Requirements for Consent-Based Communications in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4453.summary: Informational requirements document listing 17 requirements for a consent-based framework in SIP, to stop relays (forking proxies, URI-list services) from delivering requests without recipient permission, mitigating spam and amplification DoS.

SIP.why: The whole document defines requirements for extending SIP with consent for relays, proxies and URI-list services; SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document identifies a set of requirements for extensions to SIP that add consent-based communications.

spam.why: A key motivation is preventing SIP spam (telemarketer calls, unwanted MESSAGE content) via a consent framework, so readers on spam would find it relevant.
spam.quote: Without such consent, it is possible for SIP to be used for malicious purposes, including spam and denial-of-service attacks.

DDoS.why: Describes amplification DoS attacks via URI-list servers and requires consent to prevent them.
DDoS.quote: A SIP URI-list service could be used as an amplifier, allowing a single SIP request to flood a single target host or network.

rejected.why: SUBSCRIBE and watcher info are mentioned only as an example of existing consent; the document is not about presence or event packages.
MESSAGE requests are one example method affected; the document is not about instant messaging itself.
Consent is a form of authorization, but the document is framed as SIP requirements, and the SIP/spam/DDoS tags cover it better.
Email spam is only an analogy for the SIP problem.

RFC4454.title: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) over Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3)
RFC4454.summary: Specifies how to use the L2TPv3 control plane and encapsulation to emulate ATM pseudowires (AAL5 SDU and cell relay modes), defining new AVPs, an ATM-specific sublayer, OAM handling and alarm status signalling.

pseudowire.why: The document defines ATM pseudowire emulation over IP using L2TPv3: encapsulation, session setup, cell relay and AAL5 modes.
pseudowire.quote: describes the specifics of how to use the L2TP control plane for Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) Pseudowires

L2TP.why: It extends L2TPv3 with a new ATM-specific sublayer, three new AVPs and a new result code.
L2TP.quote: Any ATM-specific AVPs or other L2TP constructs for ATM Pseudowire (ATMPW) support are defined here as well.

ATM.why: The document covers how ATM services (AAL5, VCC/VPC/port cell relay, OAM cells and alarms) are carried across an IP network.
ATM.quote: carrying various ATM services, such as AAL5 SDU, ATM VCC/VPC/Port cell relay over L2TP

rejected.why: IPsec is only mentioned as an optional way to preserve payload integrity, not specified or profiled here.
Diffserv is mentioned only as an example of QoS mapping for the PSN, not what the document is about.
The congestion control section is short and applies PWE3 guidance. It is a minor part of the document.
The ATM over MPLS draft is only an informative reference for encoding alignment.

RFC4455.title: Definition of Managed Objects for Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) Entities
RFC4455.summary: Defines the SCSI-MIB SNMP module for configuring and monitoring SCSI initiator/target devices, ports, logical units, LUN maps and statistics, independent of the interconnect/transport.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to specify an SMIv2 MIB module (SCSI-MIB) with tables, conformance groups and notifications for SCSI entities.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB), for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

storage.why: The subject is SCSI storage entities (initiators, targets, logical units, LUN mapping, virtualization), which belongs under storage; no SCSI-specific tag exists.
storage.quote: it describes a set of managed objects to configure and monitor Small Computer System Interface entities (SCSI entities)

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag is the better fit.
iSCSI is only one possible transport, referenced via a transport pointer; its MIB is a separate document.
Fibre Channel is mentioned as another transport type identity only; not the subject.
Implied by the SNMP/MIB children; a more specific tag was chosen.
Discovered targets are mentioned (SLP, iSNS) but the document only models results, not discovery mechanisms.

gaps.name: SCSI (Small Computer System Interface) architecture and management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SCSI tag; the document is about SCSI protocol-layer entities, and only the generic storage topic is available.

RFC4456.title: BGP Route Reflection: An Alternative to Full Mesh Internal BGP (IBGP)
RFC4456.summary: RFC 4456 specifies BGP route reflection, which lets IBGP route reflectors re-advertise IBGP-learned routes to clients and so removes the need for a full IBGP mesh. It defines the ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST attributes for loop avoidance and obsoletes RFC 2796 and RFC 1966.

route reflection.why: The whole document specifies BGP route reflection: RR and client roles, clusters, the ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST attributes, and the effect on route selection. The taxonomy has a dedicated tag for this.
route reflection.quote: This document describes the use and design of a method known as "route reflection" to alleviate the need for "full mesh" Internal BGP (IBGP).

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by the more specific route reflection tag, so it is not listed separately.
The document touches on scaling, but the scaling problem is addressed through the specific BGP route reflection mechanism, which has its own tag.
BGP runs over TCP, but TCP is only the substrate and the document says nothing new about it.
Communities are mentioned only in passing as a way to influence route selection, and the document is not about them.

RFC4457.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) P-User-Database Private-Header (P-Header)
RFC4457.summary: Defines the SIP P-User-Database P-header, which an I-CSCF uses to give an S-CSCF the Diameter URI of the HSS holding a user's profile in 3GPP IMS, avoiding a second SLF lookup.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP header field for use between proxies in 3GPP IMS. It extends SIP, so readers of the SIP subject would expect to find it.
SIP.quote: This document specifies the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) P-User-Database Private-Header (P-header).

rejected.why: The Cx and Dx interfaces use Diameter, and the header value is a DiameterURI. Diameter is only the substrate. The document does not specify or extend it.
The header is registered in the SIP Parameters registry, but this is boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the subject of the document.
ABNF is only used to write the header syntax. The document is not about it.
The document concerns IMS signalling between CSCF proxies in 3GPP networks, not IP over cellular links. It sits in the SIP header domain, so cellular is not a good fit.

gaps.name: 3GPP IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about IMS call-control entities (P-CSCF, I-CSCF, S-CSCF, HSS, SLF). The taxonomy has no IMS tag, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC4458.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) URIs for Applications such as Voicemail and Interactive Voice Response (IVR)
RFC4458.summary: Defines SIP URI parameters 'target' and 'cause' so proxies and endpoints can request voicemail/IVR/unified messaging services when retargeting calls, including PSTN gateway mapping and History-Info interaction.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with new Request-URI parameters (target, cause) for retargeted calls to voicemail/IVR, with SIP call-flow examples and a registration in the SIP URI parameters registry.
SIP.quote: This specification describes a convention for forming SIP service URIs that request particular services based on redirecting targets from such applications.

rejected.why: Cause values map to ISUP redirecting reasons and gateways are discussed, but the document is about the SIP URI convention, not about interworking mechanisms.
The document defines SIP URI parameters, but is SIP-specific and not about URI syntax in general.
No ISUP encapsulation is specified; ISUP is only referenced for mapping names of redirect reasons.
The IANA section merely registers two SIP URI parameters; it is boilerplate here.
ABNF is just used to write the grammar for the parameters.
TLS is only mentioned in Security Considerations as protection for the signalling.

RFC4459.title: MTU and Fragmentation Issues with In-the-Network Tunneling
RFC4459.summary: Informational memo analysing MTU, fragmentation and Path MTU Discovery problems for router-to-router IP-in-IP-style tunnels, and comparing four solutions (outer fragmentation/reassembly, PMTUD signalling, operational MTU provisioning, inner-packet fragmentation).

tunneling.why: The whole document is about packet size handling in generic IP tunnelling (IP-in-IP, GRE, L2TP, IPsec) rather than one specific tunnel protocol, so the generic tunneling topic fits.
tunneling.quote: Tunneling techniques such as IP-in-IP when deployed in the middle of the network, typically between routers, have certain issues regarding how large packets can be handled

PMTUD.why: Path MTU Discovery, its reliability problems, ICMP Packet Too Big handling and MSS clamping are a central part of the analysis, as is the DF bit handling in section 3.4.
PMTUD.quote: Another approach is to use techniques like Path MTU Discovery (or potentially a future derivative [13]) to signal to the sources whose packets will be encapsulated

rejected.why: GRE is only listed as one example tunnelling mechanism; the document does not specify or analyse it specifically.
L2TP is mentioned as an example and as the origin of the discussion, but the memo is not about it.
IPsec tunnel mode is only listed as one example encapsulation; the cryptographic-cost remark is in Security Considerations.
ICMP Packet Too Big is the signalling vehicle for PMTUD but the document is not about ICMP itself.
IPv6 is compared against IPv4 throughout, but the document is not about IPv6 in particular.
IP-in-IP is the leading example but the memo covers tunnelling generally, so the parent tunneling tag is the better fit.
Mentioned as an example of a lower-MTU link, but explicitly declared out of scope.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation and reassembly
gaps.why: A major theme is the cost, buffering and IPv4 ID wrapping problems of fragmenting and reassembling at tunnel endpoints; the taxonomy has no tag for IP fragmentation.

RFC4460.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Specification Errata and Issues
RFC4460.summary: RFC 4460 compiles errata, clarifications and fixes (as text deltas) to the SCTP specification in RFC 2960, covering chunk/parameter handling, restart security, congestion control, fast retransmit, heartbeats, shutdown/abort, ICMP handling and the CRC32c checksum change.

SCTP.why: The whole document is a set of corrections and clarifications to the SCTP specification (RFC 2960), so it is squarely about SCTP.
SCTP.quote: This document is a compilation of issues found during six interoperability events and 5 years of experience with implementing, testing, and using Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)

rejected.why: Several errata cover SCTP cwnd, fast retransmit and initial window, but they are SCTP-specific and part of the SCTP errata, not a cross-transport congestion control subject.
Section 2.38 incorporates the CRC32c checksum change from RFC 3309, but that is one erratum inside the SCTP spec, not the document's subject.
Appendix C describes how SCTP endpoints process ICMP messages, which is SCTP behaviour; the document does not specify ICMP.
TCP is only referenced for comparison of congestion and fast retransmit behaviour.
IPv4/IPv6 address parameters in INIT are handled, but only as SCTP parameter processing.

RFC4461.title: Signaling Requirements for Point-to-Multipoint Traffic-Engineered MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC4461.summary: Informational requirements document listing the signaling requirements for establishing and maintaining point-to-multipoint traffic-engineered MPLS (and GMPLS) LSPs, without specifying a solution.

traffic engineering.why: The document's core subject is P2MP TE LSP signaling requirements: explicit routing, re-optimization, make-before-break, fast protection and CAC for traffic-engineered LSPs. No specific child technology is the subject, so the parent topic is used.
traffic engineering.quote: This document presents a set of requirements for Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) traffic engineering (TE) extensions to Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS).

MPLS.why: The document defines requirements for extending MPLS LSPs to point-to-multipoint, covering the tree terminology, labels, branch/bud LSRs and coexistence with P2P LSPs.
MPLS.quote: A P2MP TE LSP is a TE LSP (per [RFC2702] and [RFC3031]) that has a single ingress LSR and one or more egress LSRs, and is unidirectional.

GMPLS.why: The requirements are stated to apply equally to GMPLS (L2SC, TDM, lambda, port switching). A dedicated section lists GMPLS compatibility requirements.
GMPLS.quote: Solutions for MPLS P2MP TE-LSPs, when applied to GMPLS P2MP PSC or non-PSC TE-LSPs, MUST be compatible with the other features of GMPLS

rejected.why: It is the expected signaling protocol (RFC 3209 is cited), but the document explicitly does not restrict the choice of protocol and specifies no RSVP-TE extensions.
The document is about P2MP LSPs for TE, not IP multicast routing or group membership. It only mentions coexistence with IP multicast.
CAC, DiffServ and DS-TE are mentioned as requirements within one subsection, but they are not a substantial subject of the document.
OAM is explicitly out of scope and deferred to another document. Section 4.17 only requires MIB enhancements.
Fast reroute for P2MP LSPs is required (RFC 4090), but this is one requirement among many and the tag concerns IP and LDP fast reroute.

gaps.name: Point-to-multipoint LSPs (P2MP TE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for P2MP MPLS LSP signaling or tree-based LSPs. The nearest tags are the MPLS, traffic engineering and GMPLS entries used here.

RFC4462.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Authentication and Key Exchange for the Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol
RFC4462.summary: Defines GSS-API-based user authentication methods (gssapi-with-mic, gssapi-keyex), GSS-API-authenticated Diffie-Hellman key exchange methods, and a "null" host key algorithm for the Secure Shell protocol.

SSH.why: The document extends SSH with new key exchange methods, user authentication methods and a host key algorithm.
SSH.quote: This memo describes methods for using the GSS-API for authentication and key exchange in SSH.

GSS-API.why: It specifies how GSS-API calls and tokens are used for SSH authentication and key exchange, including naming, channel bindings and SPNEGO considerations.
GSS-API.quote: These definitions allow any GSS-API mechanism to be used with the Secure Shell protocol.

rejected.why: Section 7.3 only says SPNEGO must not be used as the underlying mechanism; the document is not about SPNEGO.
Kerberos is only mentioned as an example GSS-API mechanism.
The Diffie-Hellman key exchange is SSH-specific and covered by the SSH tag.
SHA-1 is only the hash used in the method names, not the subject.
MD5 is used only to form method names.
The GSS-API tag already covers the authentication content more specifically, and the document does not address authentication across protocols.

RFC4463.title: A Media Resource Control Protocol (MRCP) Developed by Cisco, Nuance, and Speechworks
RFC4463.summary: Informational RFC describing the original Cisco/Nuance/Speechworks MRCP, a text-based protocol for controlling speech synthesizer and recognizer resources on a media server, tunnelled over RTSP (or SIP) with RTP carrying media.

MRCP.why: The whole document specifies MRCP: its requests, responses, events, state machines, and synthesizer and recognizer resources.
MRCP.quote: MRCP controls media service resources like speech synthesizers, recognizers, signal generators, signal detectors, fax servers, etc., over a network.

rejected.why: RTSP is the substrate that carries MRCP in ANNOUNCE messages. The document does not specify or extend RTSP. Section 3.2 only says how MRCP messages ride on it, so it is not tagged.
SIP is only mentioned as another possible tunnel for MRCP messages. It is not specified or profiled here.
SDP is used in SETUP and DESCRIBE exchanges for media negotiation. The document defines nothing new about SDP.
RTP is the media delivery mechanism the resources feed from or into. The document does not specify RTP.
The document uses application/mrcp and application/x-nlsml. The IESG note says application/mrcp is unregistered, and this is not a registration document.
SSML, grammar and NLSML are XML-based payloads. They are carried as content and are not what the document is about.

RFC4464.title: Signaling Compression (SigComp) Users' Guide
RFC4464.summary: Informational users' guide for SigComp implementers, giving UDVM assembly language, example bytecode for LZ77, LZSS, LZW, DEFLATE, LZJH and a modified DEFLATE, and robustness mechanisms such as acknowledgements, static dictionary, CRC, and shared compression.

SigComp.why: The whole document is a guide to implementing SigComp compressors, UDVM assembly and SigComp mechanisms.
SigComp.quote: This document provides an informational guide for users of the Signaling Compression (SigComp) protocol.

rejected.why: DEFLATE is only one of several example algorithms for which UDVM bytecode is given; the document is about SigComp, not DEFLATE itself.
The general compression topic is implied by SigComp's use of algorithms like LZ77, LZSS, LZW and LZJH; the document is about SigComp usage, so a more specific tag fits better.
SIP and SDP appear only as the protocols for which a static dictionary exists; the document does not address SIP.
The CRC section is a short example of a SigComp robustness mechanism, not a treatment of CRC polynomials.
ABNF is used only to describe the assembly syntax.
