RFC4465.title: Signaling Compression (SigComp) Torture Tests
RFC4465.summary: Provides a set of torture tests (UDVM bytecode and assembly, with expected outputs and cycle counts) for implementers of SigComp, covering UDVM instructions, the dispatcher and the state handler.

SigComp.why: The whole document is test material for SigComp implementations: UDVM instructions, dispatcher and state handler boundary and error cases.
SigComp.quote: This document provides a set of "torture tests" for implementers of the Signaling Compression (SigComp) protocol.

rejected.why: SIP appears only via the RFC 3485 SIP/SDP static dictionary state test in one subsection; SigComp is the subject, not SIP.
The SHA-1 instruction is tested only as a UDVM instruction; the document is not about the hash family.
The CRC instruction is exercised as one UDVM test; the document is not about CRC polynomial choice.
SigComp is already the specific tag; generic lossless compression formats are not the subject.

RFC4466.title: Collected Extensions to IMAP4 ABNF
RFC4466.summary: RFC 4466 collects and generalizes the ABNF syntax extensions to IMAP4 commands (SELECT, EXAMINE, CREATE, RENAME, FETCH, STORE, SEARCH, APPEND) and defines the ESEARCH response, providing standard patterns for future IMAP extensions.

IMAP.why: The document updates and extends the IMAP4 command syntax and defines the new ESEARCH response and extension patterns. IMAP readers would look for it.
IMAP.quote: this document collects most of such ABNF changes in one place.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to specify IMAP syntax. The document is not about the ABNF notation itself.
IMAP is the more specific tag, and the document is about IMAP command syntax rather than email in general.
MIME is not addressed. The BINARY and literal8 content only concerns IMAP syntax.

RFC4467.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - URLAUTH Extension
RFC4467.summary: Defines the IMAP URLAUTH extension, which adds URLAUTH-authorized IMAP URLs and the RESETKEY, GENURLAUTH and URLFETCH commands so clients can grant limited access to message data, e.g. for BURL submission.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP with new commands (RESETKEY, GENURLAUTH, URLFETCH), a response code, and a capability, updating RFC 3501.
IMAP.quote: This document describes the URLAUTH extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) (RFC 3501) and the IMAP URL Scheme (IMAPURL) (RFC 2192).

URI.why: A substantial part of the document extends the IMAP URL scheme syntax with authorization components, and specifies how they are generated and validated.
URI.quote: [IMAPURL] is extended by allowing the addition of ";EXPIRE=<datetime>" and ";URLAUTH=<access>:<mech>:<token>" to IMAP URLs

rejected.why: BURL message submission is only the motivating use case and is specified in a separate RFC, 4468.
HMAC-SHA1 is merely recommended as an example token algorithm for the INTERNAL mechanism, and the document is not about HMAC.
The document does deal with authorization, but it is specific to IMAP URLs, and the IMAP and URI tags cover that.
IMAP is the more specific tag and already implies the parent email.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.
SASL is mentioned only in passing, in a note about authorization identifiers.

RFC4468.title: Message Submission BURL Extension
RFC4468.summary: RFC 4468 defines the BURL extension to SMTP message submission, letting a client have the submit server fetch message content from an IMAP server via IMAP URLs (including URLAUTH) rather than downloading and re-uploading it, and adds new enhanced status codes.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP submission extension (BURL EHLO keyword and command), plus new enhanced status codes and response codes. This is the core subject.
SMTP.quote: This specification extends the submission profile by adding a new BURL command that can be used to fetch submission data from an Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) server.

IMAP.why: A substantial part of the document defines how the submit server acts as an IMAP client, resolving IMAP URLs and URLAUTH URLs, authenticating to the IMAP server and trusting it. IMAP readers would want this.
IMAP.quote: the BURL command supports the URLAUTH [RFC4467] extended form of IMAP URLs [RFC2192] and that the submit server is configured with the necessary credentials

rejected.why: SASL PLAIN and SMTP AUTH are only used for authentication. The document defines nothing new about SASL.
IMAP URLs are consumed as BURL arguments. The document defines no new URI scheme or syntax, and only the BURL command grammar.
STARTTLS appears only in the configuration and security guidance. The document is not about TLS.
8-bit and binary conversion and MIME header encoding are mentioned in passing, but they are not the subject.
SMTP is the more specific tag, and it already sits under email.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the formal syntax.

RFC4469.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) CATENATE Extension
RFC4469.summary: Defines the IMAP CATENATE extension, which extends APPEND so a client can build a new message on the server from literals and URLs of existing messages or message parts, and adds the BADURL and TOOBIG response codes.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies an IMAP extension: a new capability, an extended APPEND command, new response codes and syntax.
IMAP.quote: The CATENATE extension extends the APPEND command so that, instead of a single message literal, the command can take as arguments any combination of message literals

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag and already sits under email, so the parent is implied.
The client must build valid MIME messages, but the document does not specify MIME. It only notes that the server copies octets unchanged.
RFC 2822 message format is referenced only as a requirement on the client. The document defines nothing about it.
ABNF is used only to write the formal syntax. It is a notation the document relies on, not its subject.
IMAP URLs are used as an input to the extension but are defined elsewhere (RFC 2192).

RFC4470.title: Minimally Covering NSEC Records and DNSSEC On-line Signing
RFC4470.summary: RFC 4470 describes how to build DNSSEC NSEC records that cover minimal name ranges, generated and signed on demand, to prevent zone walking, and it updates RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies a modification to NSEC record construction and on-line signing in DNSSEC, and it updates RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. DNSSEC is its core subject.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes how to construct DNSSEC NSEC resource records that cover a smaller range of names than called for by RFC 4034.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already implies DNS. The document does not address general DNS behaviour.
Preventing zone walking limits disclosure of zone contents. The document treats this as a DNSSEC NSEC design problem and does not discuss protocol privacy in general.

RFC4471.title: Derivation of DNS Name Predecessor and Successor
RFC4471.summary: Experimental RFC describing two methods (absolute and modified) for deriving the canonically ordered predecessor and successor of a DNS name, used for dynamic NSEC record synthesis in DNSSEC online signing to provide authenticated denial of existence without revealing other owner names.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies algorithms for dynamic NSEC synthesis in DNSSEC-signed zones, relying on canonical name order from RFC 4034. Readers of DNSSEC (NSEC, online signing) would want it.
DNSSEC.quote: enabling security-aware name servers to provide authenticated denial of existence without disclosing other owner names in a DNSSEC secured zone

rejected.why: General DNS name rules (label length, case) are used only as background. The subject is DNSSEC NSEC synthesis, so the child tag DNSSEC covers it.
The document is about DNS name ordering specifically, not naming in general. DNSSEC covers it more precisely.
Uppercase US-ASCII letters are skipped when incrementing and decrementing octets, but this is a case-handling detail, not the subject.

RFC4472.title: Operational Considerations and Issues with IPv6 DNS
RFC4472.summary: Informational memo summarising operational considerations for IPv6 in the DNS: special addresses, implementation misbehaviour, service naming, resolver support, and forward/reverse dynamic updates.

DNS.why: The whole document concerns DNS operations with IPv6: AAAA/PTR records, server and resolver behaviour, TTLs, and additional data handling.
DNS.quote: This memo presents operational considerations and issues with IPv6 Domain Name System (DNS)

DNS update.why: Sections 6 and 7 analyse forward and reverse dynamic DNS updates with SLAAC, DHCP and prefix delegation, including authentication concerns.
DNS update.quote: Dynamic DNS updates (DDNS) [RFC2136] [RFC3007] is a standardized mechanism for dynamically updating the DNS.

IPv6.why: It covers how special IPv6 address types (link-local, temporary, 6to4, ULA) relate to DNS publication, and IPv6 service provisioning and deployment.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 addressing architecture [RFC4291] includes two kinds of local-use addresses: link-local (fe80::/10) and site-local (fec0::/10).

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is mentioned only for resolver discovery and as an address configuration source for DDNS; the memo doesn't specify or extend it.
EDNS0 is mentioned only as a protocol fix for large additional data in Appendix B; it is not a subject of the document.
6to4 reverse DNS is discussed briefly, but only as one special-address case. The memo is not about 6to4 itself.
SLAAC is discussed only as an address configuration case for DDNS.
Transition mechanisms (6to4, Teredo, NAT-PT) get short mentions only. The focus is DNS operations.
Renumbering gets a short section (8.2) on applications ignoring DNS TTL, but it is not a main subject.

RFC4473.title: Requirements for Internet Media Guides (IMGs)
RFC4473.summary: Informational requirements document from MMUSIC for Internet Media Guides (IMGs): delivery, update, customization, reliability, description envelope and security requirements for distributing multimedia session/program metadata via multicast and unicast.

service discovery.why: IMGs are guides for discovering and selecting multimedia sessions and content on a network, with metadata delivery and update. The closest fit is the service discovery topic.
service discovery.quote: Internet Media Guide (IMG) information for media-on-demand and multicast applications

multicast.why: Much of the document concerns scalable multicast and unicast delivery of guide metadata, including carousels and sender-driven delivery.
multicast.quote: For traditional broadcast-style scenarios, multicast-based (push) distribution of IMG metadata needs to be supported.

rejected.why: SDP is the session description format that IMGs build on and is discussed as background. The document specifies requirements for IMGs, not SDP.
SIP and its event notification are mentioned only as an existing mechanism. The document notes that an event package would be needed but does not define one.
TV and radio programs are the content that IMGs describe. The document is about the guide metadata, not about media streaming delivery.
Reliability, FEC and carousel delivery are mentioned in use cases, but the document does not address reliable multicast transport itself.
HTTP is cited only as an existing retrieval mechanism and its polling limitations are noted. The document does not extend or profile it.
EPP-style guides and TV program delivery are use cases. The document does not cover IPTV service delivery or operational requirements.

gaps.name: Internet Media Guides (IMG) / electronic program guide metadata delivery
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IMG metadata distribution, so service discovery is used as the nearest fit. The subject is a whole family of related IMG RFCs from MMUSIC.

RFC4474.title: Enhancements for Authenticated Identity Management in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4474.summary: Defines the SIP Identity and Identity-Info header fields, letting an authentication service in a domain sign key request headers and body so verifiers can validate the sender's identity using the domain's certificate.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with new headers, response codes (428, 436, 437, 438) and authentication service and verifier roles.
SIP.quote: This document defines a mechanism for securely identifying originators of SIP messages. It does so by defining two new SIP header fields, Identity

STIR.why: Caller-ID authentication in SIP is the subject; this is the precursor to STIR, with signed From identity including TEL URIs and telephone-number identity (Section 11).
STIR.quote: It is desirable for SIP user agents to be able to send requests to destinations with which they have no previous association

authentication.why: The document is about authenticating the originator identity of requests across domains via signed assertions.
authentication.quote: The existing security mechanisms in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) are inadequate for cryptographically assuring the identity of the end users

rejected.why: TLS is only recommended as the hop-by-hop channel between the UAC and the authentication service; nothing new is defined for it.
Domain certificates are used for signing and validated per RFC 3280, but the document does not profile certificates.
rsa-sha1 is the single signing algorithm, used as a mechanism rather than the subject of the document.
Section 11 discusses TEL URIs as identities, but the document does not define the scheme or its parameters.
Digest authentication is how the authentication service authenticates the user, but it is not the subject of the document.
SDP bodies are covered by the signature, but SDP itself is not specified or extended.

RFC4475.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Torture Test Messages
RFC4475.summary: Informational collection of SIP torture-test messages (valid, invalid, semantic, backward-compat) for exercising SIP parsers and implementations, developed at SIPit events.

SIP.why: The whole document is a set of SIP messages and expected element behaviour for interoperability testing of SIP parsers, transaction and application layers.
SIP.quote: examples of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) test messages designed to exercise and "torture" a SIP implementation.

rejected.why: SDP bodies appear in many messages only as payload; the document is not about SDP.
One multipart MIME test message exists, but it is a minor part of a SIP parser test suite.
Several tests touch URI escaping and schemes, but only as SIP syntax edge cases, not URI specification.
Refers to SIP message syntax, not Internet email message format.
Only appears in SDP m= lines as example content.

RFC4476.title: Attribute Certificate (AC) Policies Extension
RFC4476.summary: Defines a PKIX certificate extension (id-pe-acPolicies) for Attribute Certificates that lists the Attribute Certificate Policies applying to an AC, with policy qualifiers (ACPS pointer, user notice), so relying parties can check policy acceptability.

X.509.why: The document specifies a new X.509 attribute certificate extension and its syntax and processing rules, so it belongs with X.509 certificate profiles and extensions.
X.509.quote: This document describes one certificate extension that explicitly states the Attribute Certificate Policies (ACPs) that apply to a given Attribute Certificate (AC).

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the extension; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Considered as the parent; X.509 is the more specific fit, so the parent is implied.
ACs carry authorization attributes, but the document only defines a policy extension, not authorization mechanisms.

gaps.name: Attribute Certificates / Attribute Certificate Policies
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for attribute certificates (RFC 3281) or certificate policy extensions; X.509 is the nearest fit.

RFC4477.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP): IPv4 and IPv6 Dual-Stack Issues
RFC4477.summary: Informational problem statement describing issues in operating DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 together on dual-stack nodes (merging responses, option variations, separate vs. single server) and recording the dhc WG's consensus for separate servers.

DHCPv6.why: The document analyses DHCPv4/DHCPv6 interaction and whether DHCPv6 should be extended to carry IPv4 configuration. DHCPv6 is the more specific child of DHCP and the main subject of the dual-stack discussion.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes issues identified with dual IP version DHCP interactions, the most important aspect of which is how to handle potential problems in clients processing configuration information

DHCP.why: DHCPv4 behaviour, its options and the DHCPv4 server/client role are analysed equally with DHCPv6, so the parent DHCP tag is also warranted.
DHCP.quote: The principal choice is whether separate DHCP and DHCPv6 services should be maintained by a site, or whether DHCPv6 should be extended to carry IPv4 configuration settings

rejected.why: The document is about dual-stack configuration via DHCP, not a transition mechanism; dual-stack is only context.
Stateless address autoconfiguration is mentioned only in passing as an alternative for address configuration.
The document notes overlap with multihoming but explicitly defers it to other WGs.
DNS server and search path options are examples of configuration data, not the subject of the document.
IPv6 is the environment, but the document is specifically about DHCP; the DHCP tags capture it.

RFC4478.title: Repeated Authentication in Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2) Protocol
RFC4478.summary: Experimental extension to IKEv2 defining an AUTH_LIFETIME notification that lets the original Responder tell the Initiator how many seconds remain before it must repeat the Initial exchange (re-authenticate).

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new AUTH_LIFETIME notify payload and the procedures for repeated authentication. IKE is the most specific tag that fits.
IKE.quote: This document describes a new notification that the original Responder can send to the original Initiator with the number of seconds before the authentication needs to be repeated.

rejected.why: EAP is mentioned only as a reason the gateway cannot initiate re-authentication. The document does not specify or extend it.
IPsec SAs are the thing whose lifetime is limited, but the document specifies an IKEv2 notification. IKE is the more specific tag.
Repeated authentication is the subject, but the IKE tag already covers it and the mechanism is IKEv2-specific.

RFC4479.title: A Data Model for Presence
RFC4479.summary: RFC 4479 defines the presence data model (presentity, person, service, device) used by SIMPLE presence agents and its encoding as an extension of PIDF, with XML schemas for the new person and device elements.

PIDF.why: The document extends PIDF with the person and device elements and defines how services map to tuples. It is a PIDF data model specification.
PIDF.quote: This document defines the underlying presence data model used by Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for Instant Messaging and Presence Leveraging Extensions (SIMPLE) presence agents.

SIMPLE.why: It is a SIMPLE working group specification of the presence model used by SIMPLE presence agents, so readers of SIMPLE would want it.
SIMPLE.quote: This data model is defined in terms of an extension to RFC 3863.

rejected.why: SIP is only the context in which presence is used. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
XML is only the encoding for the schemas. The document is about the presence model, not XML usage.
The UUID URN is recommended only as an interim device ID, which is a minor mention.
Location is mentioned only for where to place geopriv objects in a document. This is not a main subject.
PIDF is the more specific tag, and the broader instant messaging and presence tag is implied by it.

RFC4480.title: RPID: Rich Presence Extensions to the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF)
RFC4480.summary: RFC 4480 defines RPID, an XML extension to PIDF adding rich presence elements (activities, mood, place-is, privacy, sphere, status-icon, time-offset, user-input, etc.) for persons, services and devices.

PIDF.why: The whole document specifies extension elements to PIDF, the presence document format; this is the core subject.
PIDF.quote: The Rich Presence Information Data format (RPID) described here is an extension that adds optional elements to the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF).

SIMPLE.why: Produced by the SIMPLE working group as a presence format extension, within the SIMPLE family of presence specifications; readers of that subject would want it.
SIMPLE.quote: Registrant Contact:  IETF, SIMPLE working group, simple@ietf.org

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding substrate for the presence extension elements; the document is not about XML usage in general.
Parent of PIDF and implied by the PIDF tag; no need to list it separately.
Only referenced for alignment of some activity values with calendar categories; not about iCalendar.
SIP URIs appear in examples and the presence event package is referenced in security considerations only; not about SIP.
Place-is and place-type describe environment and type of place, not location formats; location types come from a separate registry RFC.
The document reuses application/pidf+xml and needs no new media type.

RFC4481.title: Timed Presence Extensions to the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) to Indicate Status Information for Past and Future Time Intervals
RFC4481.summary: RFC 4481 extends PIDF with a <timed-status> element so a presentity can declare its status for a past or future time interval, defining the XML schema and IANA namespace registration.

PIDF.why: The document is a PIDF extension defining a new tuple child element with from/until attributes; readers of PIDF want it.
PIDF.quote: This document extends PIDF, adding a timed status extension (<timed-status> element) that allows a presentity to declare its status for a time interval fully in the future or the past.

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding substrate for the extension; the document is not about XML usage in general.
Produced in the SIMPLE WG, but the document defines a PIDF data format extension, not SIP event packages or XCAP; PIDF is the more specific fit.
Parent of PIDF, so implied by the PIDF tag and not listed separately.
Uses xs:dateTime for from/until but does not define or extend timestamp representation.
The namespace and schema registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject of the document.
PIDF-LO is mentioned only as an example of an element that could appear within timed-status.

RFC4482.title: CIPID: Contact Information for the Presence Information Data Format
RFC4482.summary: RFC 4482 defines CIPID, an XML extension to PIDF adding contact-information elements (card, display-name, homepage, icon, map, sound) to presence documents for a presentity or its contacts.

PIDF.why: The document specifies an extension to PIDF, defining new elements and an XML namespace and schema for presence documents.
PIDF.quote: The Contact Information for the Presence Information Data format (CIPID) is an extension that adds elements to PIDF that provide additional contact information about a presentity

rejected.why: XML is the encoding substrate for the schema; the document is about presence contact elements, not XML usage generally.
vCard is only one of the formats the <card> element may point to; the document does not specify it.
Produced by the SIMPLE WG, but it defines no SIP event package or SIP mechanism; PIDF is the more specific fit.
Implied by PIDF as its ancestor, so not listed separately.
No new media type is registered; only an XML namespace and schema are registered.
The URN namespace is registered only for the XML namespace, which is IANA boilerplate rather than the subject.

RFC4483.title: A Mechanism for Content Indirection in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Messages
RFC4483.summary: Defines a SIP content indirection mechanism by profiling the RFC 2017 message/external-body MIME URL access-type, with parameters for expiration, size, hash, and versioning, so any SIP body part can be referenced by URI.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP extension that lets any SIP message body part be carried indirectly via a URI, including Accept-header negotiation, 415 rejection and SIP examples.
SIP.quote: This document defines an extension to the URL MIME External-Body Access-Type to satisfy the content indirection requirements for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

MIME.why: A substantial part of the document specifies new parameters (expiration, size, hash) and header usage for the message/external-body MIME type.
MIME.quote: allowing any MIME part in a SIP message to be referred to indirectly via a URI.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the retrieval channel for the indirect content and is mandated as a URI scheme, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
It profiles an existing media type's parameters rather than registering a media type or defining registry rules.
URIs are used to locate content, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
Presence notification is only a use-case example; the document is not about presence event packages.
S/MIME is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the protection mechanism borrowed from RFC 3261.
SHA-1 is used only as the hash for the integrity parameter and is not the subject of the document.

RFC4484.title: Trait-Based Authorization Requirements for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4484.summary: Informational requirements document for trait-based authorization in SIP, in which signed assertions of principal attributes are carried in or referenced from SIP requests, with use cases and 18 requirements.

SIP.why: The document specifies requirements for extending SIP to carry and verify authorization assertions in requests, involving UACs, UASs and proxies.
SIP.quote: This document explores requirements of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [1] for enabling trait-based authorization.

authorization.why: The core subject is authorization based on asserted attributes (traits) rather than identity, including federation and an assertion model. No technology tag fits it better than the general authorization topic.
authorization.quote: trait-based authorization provides information used to make policy decisions based on the attributes of a participant in a session.

rejected.why: The document contrasts authorization with authentication and only requires that clients authenticate to the authorization service. Authentication is not its subject.
Privacy is a stated benefit, notably requirements for identity-free assertions and selective sharing. It is not the document's main focus.
Federation is a necessary concept, but the document addresses authorization assertions, not cross-domain authentication frameworks.
QoS reservation is only one example in the 'Linking Different Protocols' use case.
SAML and X.509 attribute certificates are mentioned only as example assertion schemes, and neither is specified or profiled here. XACML is not mentioned.
RFC 3281 attribute certificates are cited in one requirement as an example assertion scheme. That is a passing reference.

RFC4485.title: Guidelines for Authors of Extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4485.summary: Informational guidelines for authors of SIP extensions: when an extension is appropriate, SIP's architectural model, backward compatibility, syntax, semantics, IANA registration, and interactions with SIP features like forking.

SIP.why: The whole document is about designing, evaluating and specifying SIP extensions (methods, headers, body types), covering SIP's solution space, architecture, and feature interactions.
SIP.quote: In order to facilitate effective and interoperable extensions to SIP, some guidelines need to be followed when developing SIP extensions.

rejected.why: Section 4.8 only lists which SIP registries extension authors must use; it is a part of the SIP guidance, not about IANA registries in general.
Offer/answer is mentioned only briefly in the new-method considerations; not a subject of the document.
Syntax rules require ABNF per RFC 4234, but this is a use of the notation, not the document's subject.
It supplements the SIP change process (RFC 3427) with technical guidance, but is mainly about SIP technical design rather than IETF procedures.
Mentioned only as an alternative for message compression; not addressed in its own right.
A single requirement that freeform text be UTF-8; incidental.

RFC4486.title: Subcodes for BGP Cease Notification Message
RFC4486.summary: Defines eight subcodes for the BGP Cease NOTIFICATION message, says when a speaker should send each, and recommends a retry backoff after certain subcodes.

BGP.why: The document extends the BGP protocol with new Cease NOTIFICATION subcodes and recommends connection retry behaviour for BGP speakers.
BGP.quote: This document defines several subcodes for the BGP Cease NOTIFICATION message that would provide more information to aid network operators in correlating network events

rejected.why: The IANA section only sets up the subcode registry. The main body is about BGP, and boilerplate is not evidence.
The subcodes help operators diagnose peering, but the document specifies a BGP protocol extension, not a management mechanism.
BGP runs over TCP and the document mentions the transport connection only in passing.

RFC4487.title: Mobile IPv6 and Firewalls: Problem Statement
RFC4487.summary: Informational problem statement describing how firewalls (stateful packet filters, ESP dropping) interfere with Mobile IPv6 signalling, return routability and route optimization in MN, CN and HA scenarios, including 3G networks.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document analyses how Mobile IPv6 signalling (Binding Updates, Return Routability, route optimization) breaks in the presence of firewalls.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document captures the issues that may arise in the deployment of IPv6 networks when they support Mobile IPv6 and firewalls.

firewall.why: Firewall behaviour (stateful filtering, state tables, ESP drops, state sharing across firewalls) is half of the problem statement, with a dedicated overview section.
firewall.quote: Unless firewalls are aware of Mobile IPv6 protocol details, these security devices will interfere with the smooth operation of the protocol

rejected.why: ESP is mentioned as the protection for MIPv6 signalling that firewalls drop, but the document does not specify or extend it.
IPsec protects Binding Updates and Home Test messages; it is a dependency, not the subject.
3G/GPRS/UMTS applicability is only a short appendix referencing another document.
The document concerns firewalls, not address translation.

RFC4488.title: Suppression of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) REFER Method Implicit Subscription
RFC4488.summary: Defines a new SIP header field, Refer-Sub, and option tag, norefersub, letting a REFER issuer suppress the implicit subscription and NOTIFYs that RFC 3515 otherwise creates.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's REFER method with a new header field and option tag, and covers REFER forking and dialog behaviour. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new SIP header field: "Refer-Sub" meaningful within a REFER transaction only.

rejected.why: The implicit subscription uses SIP event notification (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY), but the document does not define an event package or presence/IM extension. It only suppresses the subscription.
No session description content is involved. The example REFER carries no body.
The IANA section only registers the header field and option tag. That is boilerplate and not the subject.
S/MIME appears only in Security Considerations as a suggested integrity protection.

RFC4489.title: A Method for Generating Link-Scoped IPv6 Multicast Addresses
RFC4489.summary: Defines a method for forming link-scoped IPv6 multicast addresses by embedding the interface identifier of a node's link-local unicast address in the multicast address, updating RFC 3306's unicast-prefix-based format.

addressing.why: The document is about allocating and generating IPv6 multicast addresses from IIDs. It is an address architecture and allocation matter. It extends RFC 3306's format rather than specifying a multicast routing protocol, so addressing fits better than a multicast child.
addressing.quote: The extension allows the use of Interface Identifiers (IIDs) to allocate multicast addresses.

rejected.why: The document is an IPv6 addressing extension, but addressing is the more specific fitting tag. IPv6 is the parent of the broader technology and is implied only for its children.
The document concerns multicast address format, not multicast routing, group membership or deployment, so the addressing topic fits better.
It depends on link-local address configuration and DAD, but only as the source of the IID and does not specify autoconfiguration.
ND address resolution and DAD are mentioned only as the substrate the method relies on.

RFC4490.title: Using the GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.11-94, GOST R 34.10-94, and GOST R 34.10-2001 Algorithms with Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC4490.summary: Specifies conventions for using the Russian GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms in CMS, covering digests, signatures, key agreement/transport, content encryption, MACs, and S/MIME usage.

GOST.why: The whole document defines OIDs, parameters and encodings for the Russian GOST ciphers, hashes and signature algorithms, so GOST is the core subject.
GOST.quote: This document describes the conventions for using the cryptographic algorithms GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001, and GOST R 34.11-94 with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

CMS.why: The document is a companion specification profiling which CMS fields (SignerInfo, KeyAgreeRecipientInfo, EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData) carry the GOST algorithms.
CMS.quote: The Cryptographic Message Syntax [CMS] is used for digital signature, digest, authentication, and encryption of arbitrary message contents.

S/MIME.why: A dedicated section defines S/MIME micalg and SMIMECapabilities values for the GOST algorithms.
S/MIME.quote: micalg parameter SHOULD be set to "gostr3411-94"; otherwise, it MUST be set to "unknown".

rejected.why: ASN.1 modules are provided, but ASN.1 is the notation used to define the identifiers, not the subject.
Section 6.1 defines HMAC with GOST R 34.11-94, but it is a small part and a GOST-specific construction covered by the GOST tag.
The certificate profile is in a separate companion RFC (RFC 4491); this document only references it.
Key agreement and transport are described, but only as CMS recipient-info conventions for GOST, so the GOST and CMS tags already cover them.

RFC4491.title: Using the GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001, and GOST R 34.11-94 Algorithms with the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile
RFC4491.summary: Specifies algorithm identifiers, parameter encodings, key and signature formats, and keyUsage rules for using the Russian GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms in X.509 certificates and CRLs, supplementing RFC 3279.

GOST.why: The document defines how the Russian GOST signature and hash algorithms are identified and encoded for use in IETF PKI, which is the core subject of the GOST tag.
GOST.quote: describes encoding formats, identifiers, and parameter formats for the algorithms GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001, and GOST R 34.11-94

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificate and CRL fields for these algorithms, including keyUsage rules and example certificates, and it updates RFC 3279.
X.509.quote: This specification defines the contents of the signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue, signature, and subjectPublicKeyInfo fields within X.509 Certificates and CRLs.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation for the OIDs and structures, but the document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules itself. Those are in RFC 4357.
The parent of X.509 is implied, so I did not list it separately.
CMS is mentioned only once, to note that signature values are directly usable there. It is not a subject of the document.
GOST R 34.10-2001 is elliptic-curve based, but the document only specifies key encoding and does not address elliptic curve cryptography in general.

RFC4492.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC4492.summary: Specifies ECC-based TLS key exchange algorithms (ECDH, ECDHE with ECDSA/RSA authentication, anonymous ECDH), two new TLS extensions for curve and point-format negotiation, and the associated cipher suites.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS with new key exchange methods, client authentication mechanisms, handshake message changes, extensions and cipher suites.
TLS.quote: This document describes new key exchange algorithms based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

elliptic curve.why: ECDH, named curves, point formats and curve selection guidance are central, so ECC readers would want this RFC.
elliptic curve.quote: it specifies the use of Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement in a TLS handshake

ECDSA.why: ECDSA is specified as the signature mechanism for ServerKeyExchange, CertificateVerify and certificates, including signature encoding.
ECDSA.quote: the use of Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) as a new authentication mechanism

rejected.why: RSA certificates and signatures are used in the ECDH_RSA and ECDHE_RSA variants, but RSA itself is not the subject.
Certificates carry ECC keys, but the document only refers to an existing profile (RFC 3279) and defines nothing new about X.509.
AES cipher suites are listed in the cipher suite table, but AES is defined elsewhere and is not what the document is about.
RC4 suites appear only as entries in the cipher suite table.
ASN.1 is used only to encode the ECDSA signature value.
Certificate usage is incidental to the key exchange and authentication mechanisms specified here.

RFC4493.title: The AES-CMAC Algorithm
RFC4493.summary: Informational RFC specifying AES-CMAC, a message authentication code built on the CMAC mode with AES-128, including subkey generation, MAC generation and verification algorithms, test vectors and reference C code.

AES.why: The document specifies a MAC algorithm built on AES-128 as a block cipher mode (CMAC/OMAC1), which is exactly the AES block cipher and its modes subject.
AES.quote: This memo specifies an authentication algorithm based on CMAC with the 128-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). This new authentication algorithm is named AES-CMAC.

rejected.why: HMAC is only mentioned as a comparison point (similar security goal); the document does not specify or extend it.
RFC 4086 is cited only in Security Considerations for key generation; boilerplate-level reference, not the subject.
Checksums are mentioned only to contrast integrity assurance of a MAC with error-detecting codes.
Parent topic is implied by the more specific AES tag.

gaps.name: Message authentication codes (CMAC/OMAC1/CBC-MAC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has HMAC but no general MAC tag; CMAC itself, the block-cipher-based MAC, is not separately represented, so AES is the closest fit.

RFC4494.title: The AES-CMAC-96 Algorithm and Its Use with IPsec
RFC4494.summary: RFC 4494 specifies AES-CMAC-96, a truncated AES-CMAC MAC, as an integrity/authentication algorithm for IPsec ESP and AH, with test vectors and an IKEv2 transform ID.

IPsec.why: The document defines a new authentication algorithm for IPsec ESP and AH and its use there, so IPsec readers need it. ESP is a child of IPsec, but the document covers both AH and ESP, so the parent tag fits.
IPsec.quote: This memo specifies the use of CMAC mode on the authentication mechanism of the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and the Authentication Header (AH) protocols.

AES.why: AES-CMAC is an AES-based MAC mode. The document defines AES-CMAC-96 with AES-128 and gives test vectors. Readers of the AES page would want it.
AES.quote: CMAC [NIST-CMAC] is a message authentication code that is based on a symmetric key block cipher such as the Advanced Encryption Standard [NIST-AES].

rejected.why: HMAC is mentioned only as a comparison to AES-CMAC. The document is not about it.
The document covers both AH and ESP, so the broader IPsec tag fits better.
The IKEv2 transform ID allocation appears only in the IANA considerations, which is boilerplate.
The AES child tag already covers the cryptographic subject, so the parent topic is not given directly.

gaps.name: CMAC / message authentication code modes
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for block-cipher-based MAC modes such as AES-CMAC, OMAC1 or XCBC. AES is the closest fit.

RFC4495.title: A Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Extension for the Reduction of Bandwidth of a Reservation Flow
RFC4495.summary: Extends RSVP (updating RFC 2205) so a router can signal partial preemption via a new ResvErr subcode (ERR_PARTIAL_PREEMPT, 102) and suppress ResvTear, letting an individual or aggregate reservation be reduced in bandwidth rather than torn down.

RSVP.why: The document specifies an RSVP extension: a new ResvErr error subcode and changed ResvTear behaviour, updating RFC 2205, including for aggregated reservations.
RSVP.quote: This document proposes an extension to the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) [1] to allow an existing reservation to be reduced in allocated bandwidth

rejected.why: IPsec tunnels are treated only as a case of an individual reservation; the document does not specify or extend IPsec.
ECN is mentioned only to explain why it is insufficient for bandwidth indication.
SIP is only an example of a session protocol the endpoints might use to renegotiate a codec.
Intserv flowspecs are referenced, but the document is about the RSVP reduction mechanism rather than the Intserv model.
Covered by the more specific RSVP tag, which sits under QoS.

RFC4496.title: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) SMTP Use Cases
RFC4496.summary: Informational RFC describing use cases and deployment scenarios for applying OPES (Open Pluggable Edge Services) callout filtering to SMTP mail flows, such as security, spam, access control, rewriting and blocking filters.

OPES.why: The whole document is about applying the OPES framework (processors, callout servers, OCP) to SMTP; it exists to define OPES use cases.
OPES.quote: This document describes OPES SMTP use cases and deployment scenarios in preparation for SMTP adaptation with OPES.

SMTP.why: The use cases operate on SMTP dialog commands and responses at MTAs, with an SMTP overview and example dialog, so SMTP readers would want it.
SMTP.quote: This work focuses on SMTP-based services that want to modify command values or want to block SMTP commands.

spam.why: A dedicated use case section covers spam filtering via callout servers, including actions on classified spam.
spam.quote: Next to security filters, spam filters are probably the most wanted filtering application today.

rejected.why: HTTP is only referenced as the analogous earlier OPES adaptation (OCP/HTTP); this document is not about HTTP.
Parent of SMTP, which is the more specific tag chosen; the document does not address email architecture generally.
Secure email handling is a brief use case with no S/MIME specifics.
MIME types and sections are only mentioned in passing in filter examples.
POP3 and IMAP are mentioned only as client access protocols in the flow description.

RFC4497.title: Interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and QSIG
RFC4497.summary: Specifies how a gateway interworks SIP and QSIG (enterprise PISN signalling) for basic calls, covering message mapping, call clearing, cause/response code mapping, number and identity mapping, and bearer/SDP media derivation.

SIP.why: The document specifies how SIP INVITE/provisional/final responses, PRACK, CANCEL and BYE map to QSIG messages, plus SIP identity headers (P-Asserted-Identity, Privacy), at a SIP gateway.
SIP.quote: This document specifies interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and QSIG within corporate telecommunication networks

PSTN interop.why: Gateway interworking between an IP/SIP network and a circuit-switched PISN signalling protocol (QSIG, ISDN-like) is PSTN-style interop; no narrower child tag fits QSIG.
PSTN interop.quote: Such calls are supported by gateways that perform interworking between SIP and QSIG.

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer is used and its media type derivation is touched on, but it is a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
SIP-T concerns ISUP encapsulation/interworking; this is QSIG mapping, and QSIG encapsulation is explicitly out of scope.
RTP is mentioned only as media carrier and media interworking is out of scope.
QSIG is ISDN-like, but the document is about SIP-QSIG interworking, not IP over ISDN access.
Privacy header and presentation restriction mapping is a part of number mapping, not a privacy-focused document.
TLS and SCTP are only optional SIP transports mentioned in the architecture.

gaps.name: QSIG / Private Integrated Services Network signalling
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for QSIG or enterprise PBX (PISN) signalling, which is the other half of this interworking specification.

RFC4498.title: The Managed Object Aggregation MIB
RFC4498.summary: Defines two experimental SNMP MIB modules (AGGREGATE-MIB and TIME-AGGREGATE-MIB) that let an agent aggregate multiple managed object instances, or repeated samples of one, into a single object to reduce polling overhead.

MIB.why: The document's main body is two SMIv2 MIB modules, AggrMIB and TAggrMIB, with their tables, textual conventions and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: the Aggregation MIB modules will be used to configure a network management agent to aggregate the values of a user-specified set of Managed Object instances

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol the MIB is used through. The document adds no new protocol operations, only MIB modules, so the more specific MIB tag fits.
DEFLATE appears only as one selectable compression option in an object, referenced to RFC 1951. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Time-based aggregation samples values, but the document is about polling efficiency and not about performance metrics or methods.
RMON-MIB is imported only for the OwnerString textual convention.

RFC4501.title: Domain Name System Uniform Resource Identifiers
RFC4501.summary: Defines the "dns" URI scheme for referencing DNS resource record sets by name, class, type and optional authority, and registers it.

URI.why: The document's main content is a URI scheme registration template, with syntax, escaping rules and examples for the dns: scheme.
URI.quote: This document defines Uniform Resource Identifiers for Domain Name System resources.

DNS.why: The scheme identifies DNS resource record sets by owner name, class and type, and describes how to resolve them via DNS queries, so DNS readers would want it.
DNS.quote: The DNS URI scheme defined here can be used to reference any data stored in the DNS.

rejected.why: Mentioned only to say the dnsname is an IDN-unaware domain name slot; not the document's subject.
Used only as the notation for the syntax.
The text/dns and application/dns types are only mentioned, and they are defined in RFC 4027.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect data.
Mentioned only as a way to render DNS responses in data browsers.

RFC4502.title: Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base Version 2
RFC4502.summary: RFC 4502 defines the RMON2-MIB module, an SNMP MIB for remote network monitoring probes covering protocol directory, protocol distribution, address mapping, network/application-layer host and matrix groups, user history and probe configuration; it obsoletes RFC 2021 and updates RFC 3273.

RMON.why: The whole document specifies the RMON2 MIB, extending RMON (RFC 2819) with protocol directory, host/matrix and user history groups.
RMON.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing remote network monitoring devices.

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module definition including textual conventions such as TimeFilter and LastCreateTime and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself. MIB and RMON sit under SNMP and are more specific.
Probes collect traffic statistics, but the RMON tag is the more specific fit for this MIB.
RMON filter/capture is only augmented slightly here; the document is not about capture formats.
Token Ring RMON tables are only augmented and deprecated here, not the subject.

RFC4503.title: A Description of the Rabbit Stream Cipher Algorithm
RFC4503.summary: RFC 4503 describes the Rabbit stream cipher (128-bit key, 64-bit IV): its key and IV setup, counter system, next-state function, extraction and encryption scheme, with usage rules and test vectors.

cryptography.why: The whole document specifies a symmetric stream cipher algorithm and its proper use. No child tag fits Rabbit, so the parent topic is used.
cryptography.quote: This document describes the encryption algorithm Rabbit. It is a stream cipher algorithm with a 128-bit key and 64-bit initialization vector (IV).

rejected.why: RC4 is mentioned only as an example of IV/keystream misuse (Word and Excel); the document is not about RC4.
Rabbit is a different cipher and does not use AES or its modes.
The cipher is a pseudorandom bitstream generator, but the document specifies an encryption algorithm, not randomness requirements.
RFC 3447 is cited only for the OS2IP/I2OSP conversion primitives in the test vectors appendix.

gaps.name: Stream cipher (Rabbit)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for stream ciphers or for the Rabbit cipher specifically, so it falls under the generic cryptography topic.

RFC4504.title: SIP Telephony Device Requirements and Configuration
RFC4504.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements and a configuration-settings glossary for SIP telephony devices (phones, soft clients, adaptors), based on deployment experience, to promote multi-vendor interoperability.

SIP.why: The whole document specifies what SIP user agents (telephony devices) must support: call hold, transfer, early media, forking, digest authentication, and so on.
SIP.quote: This document describes the requirements for SIP telephony devices, based on the deployment experience of large numbers of SIP phones and PC clients

emergency services.why: A dedicated section covers emergency calling and Resource-Priority support for emergency preparedness, and a related section covers real-time text for emergency services.
emergency services.quote: Emergency calling: For emergency numbers (e.g., 911, SOS URL), SIP telephony devices SHOULD support the work of the ECRIT WG

NAT traversal.why: The document has a requirements section and a security subsection on firewall and NAT traversal (STUN, ICE, TURN, symmetric RTP) for SIP devices.
NAT traversal.quote: SIP telephony devices SHOULD support the Simple Traversal of UDP through NATs (STUN) protocol [48] for determining the NAPT public external address.

accessibility.why: The interactive text section covers real-time text conversation (RFC 4103) and V.18 text-telephone handling for deaf and hard-of-hearing users.
accessibility.quote: SHOULD support the accessibility requirements for deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-impaired individuals as per RFC 3351

rejected.why: The document only requires RTP/RTCP support as one of many device requirements and does not specify or extend it.
The codec section lists which codecs devices should support, but it is a small part of a broader device requirements document.
DHCP is used for acquiring settings and the time server, but it is only a mechanism the devices rely on.
TLS is required for secure transport but is only a security mechanism the document relies on, not defines anything new about it.
ENUM gets one MAY requirement (Req-11), which is too small a part of the document to tag.
Req-18 requires tel URI support, but the document does not define or extend the scheme.

gaps.name: SIP user agent configuration settings / device provisioning
gaps.why: Section 3 is a glossary of configuration settings for SIP devices and refers to auto-configuration and profile delivery. The taxonomy has no tag for endpoint provisioning or configuration.

RFC4505.title: Anonymous Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) Mechanism
RFC4505.summary: Defines the ANONYMOUS SASL mechanism, which lets clients log in anonymously with optional trace information, plus a "trace" stringprep profile, and replaces RFC 2245.

SASL.why: The document specifies a new SASL mechanism (ANONYMOUS), so readers of the SASL subject would expect to find it.
SASL.quote: This document defines an anonymous mechanism for the Simple Authentication and Security Layer ([SASL]) framework. The name associated with this mechanism is "ANONYMOUS".

rejected.why: The document defines a stringprep profile, which is the predecessor of PRECIS. It is not PRECIS itself, and the profile is a small supporting part of the document.
UTF-8 is only the encoding for the trace string. The document does not define anything new about it.
IMAP appears only in the example of an ANONYMOUS login. The document does not specify or extend IMAP.
The SASL tag is more specific and already covers this.
ABNF is only the notation used for the message grammar.
Unicode is only the character repertoire for the trace string. The document does not address Unicode usage in its own right.

RFC4506.title: XDR: External Data Representation Standard
RFC4506.summary: RFC 4506 specifies XDR, the External Data Representation Standard: a data description language and canonical binary encoding for types such as integers, floats, opaque data, strings, arrays, structs and unions, obsoleting RFC 1832.

ONC RPC.why: The ONC RPC tech tag is defined as covering ONC RPC and XDR, so this XDR specification belongs there. It is the standard data representation used by ONC RPC and NFS.
ONC RPC.quote: Protocols such as ONC RPC (Remote Procedure Call) and the NFS* (Network File System) use XDR to describe the format of their data.

rejected.why: NFS is only cited as a protocol that uses XDR. The document does not specify or profile it.
The document compares XDR with ASN.1 (X.409) in one sentence in the introduction. The document is not about ASN.1, and ASN.1 is a different encoding.
Section 6 gives an extended BNF grammar for the XDR language. That grammar only defines XDR's own syntax and is not about BNF notations.
Strings are defined as ASCII bytes, but only as an incidental detail of the string type.

gaps.name: XDR (External Data Representation)
gaps.why: The document is about XDR as a data description language and encoding. The only fitting tag is ONC RPC, which is defined to include XDR. No tag in the data formats area covers XDR as a general serialization standard.

RFC4507.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Session Resumption without Server-Side State
RFC4507.summary: Defines a TLS extension (SessionTicket) and NewSessionTicket handshake message letting a server resume sessions by giving the client an encrypted ticket, so the server keeps no per-client session state.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS with a new extension (SessionTicket, number 35) and a new handshake message (NewSessionTicket), so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document defines a way to resume a Transport Layer Security (TLS) session without requiring session-specific state at the TLS server.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is only used in the recommended ticket protection format, not what the document is about.
AES-CBC is only the recommended ticket encryption, a supporting mechanism.
SHA-1 is used only inside HMAC for ticket integrity; not a subject of the document.
Ticket key management is explicitly out of scope beyond a short list of recommended practices.
Kerberos is mentioned only as inspiration and as an alternative identity type.

RFC4508.title: Conveying Feature Tags with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) REFER Method
RFC4508.summary: Extends the SIP REFER Refer-To header field to carry RFC 3840 feature tags, letting a REFER issuer tell the recipient about the capabilities of the referred target.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP REFER method and the Refer-To header ABNF with feature-param, so it is a SIP extension and belongs on the SIP page.
SIP.quote: This document extends the SIP [2] REFER method defined in RFC 3515 [3] to be used with feature parameters defined in RFC 3840 [4].

rejected.why: SDP is only mentioned in an example about offering video; the document does not specify or extend it.
The conference subscription is mentioned only as a motivating example, and the document is not about event packages or presence.
The isfocus tag is used only as an example of a feature tag. The document does not address conferencing frameworks.
The conference focus appears only in an example, and the document is not about conferencing.

RFC4509.title: Use of SHA-256 in DNSSEC Delegation Signer (DS) Resource Records (RRs)
RFC4509.summary: Specifies digest type 2 (SHA-256) for DNSSEC DS resource records, including field values, wire format, an example, implementation requirements, deployment advice and downgrade-attack considerations.

DNSSEC.why: The document extends DNSSEC DS records with a new digest type, defining the digest calculation, wire format, validator behaviour and downgrade considerations.
DNSSEC.quote: This document specifies how to use the SHA-256 digest type in DNS Delegation Signer (DS) Resource Records (RRs).

rejected.why: SHA-256 is used as the digest algorithm, but the document is about its use in DS records, not the hash function itself.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag and covers the DS record subject; DNS is its ancestor.
The IANA section only records the digest type assignment, which is boilerplate.

RFC4510.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Technical Specification Road Map
RFC4510.summary: RFC 4510 is the road map for the LDAP version 3 technical specification, listing the component RFCs, LDAP's relationship to X.500, and which earlier specifications it obsoletes.

LDAP.why: The document defines the composition of the LDAPv3 technical specification and is the formal reference for the LDAP suite.
LDAP.quote: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an Internet protocol for accessing distributed directory services that act in accordance with X.500 data and service models.

X.500.why: A full section covers how LDAP relates to X.500 data and service models and how servers must conform to them.
X.500.quote: This technical specification defines LDAP in terms of [X.500] as an X.500 access mechanism.

rejected.why: The IANA considerations for LDAP are only referenced (BCP 64); the document is not about IANA registries.
Parent of LDAP and X.500, which are chosen instead, so it is implied.
Describes which RFCs it obsoletes, but this is a technical specification road map, not a process document.
Authentication and security mechanisms are covered in RFC 4513, not in this document.

RFC4511.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): The Protocol
RFC4511.summary: RFC 4511 specifies the LDAPv3 protocol elements, operations (bind, search, modify, add, delete, compare, abandon, extended, StartTLS), ASN.1/BER encoding and TCP mapping, obsoleting RFCs 2251, 2830 and 3771.

LDAP.why: The document is the core LDAP protocol specification, defining all operations, result codes, controls, referrals and encoding.
LDAP.quote: This document describes the protocol elements, along with their semantics and encodings, of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

rejected.why: StartTLS is defined as an LDAP extended operation, but TLS itself is a security substrate; details are in RFC 4513.
ASN.1/BER is the notation and encoding used for the protocol, not the subject of the document.
SASL is used for Bind authentication; semantics are delegated to RFC 4513 and RFC 4422.
TCP is only the transport mapping (Section 5.2), not specified or extended.
X.500 is the model LDAP is based on and gateways to, but the document specifies LDAP, not X.500.
LDAP URLs and URIs appear in referrals but are defined elsewhere (RFC 4516).

RFC4512.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Directory Information Models
RFC4512.summary: RFC 4512 specifies the X.500 directory information models as used by LDAP: the DIT, entries, attributes, object classes, operational attributes, schema definitions, subschema discovery, and the root DSE server information model.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies the LDAP directory data model, schema description formats, and root DSE attributes.
LDAP.quote: This document describes the X.500 Directory Information Models, as used in LDAP.

rejected.why: X.500 is the source model that LDAP adapts. The document is about its use in LDAP, so LDAP is the better tag.
ASN.1 is only referenced for describing LDAP syntaxes. The document does not specify ASN.1.
ABNF is only the notation used for the schema description formats. The document does not specify it.
SASL appears only in the 'supportedSASLMechanisms' root DSE attribute. It is a minor mention.
The IANA section only updates the LDAP descriptor registry. It is boilerplate.

RFC4513.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Authentication Methods and Security Mechanisms
RFC4513.summary: RFC 4513 specifies LDAP authentication methods and security mechanisms: StartTLS establishment, simple Bind (anonymous, unauthenticated, name/password), the SASL Bind profile including EXTERNAL, and authorization state transitions.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies the security and authentication behaviour of LDAP: Bind, StartTLS, authorization state and mandatory-to-implement mechanisms.
LDAP.quote: This document describes authentication methods and security mechanisms of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

SASL.why: A substantial section defines the LDAP SASL protocol profile (service name, exchange, layers, authzId, EXTERNAL mechanism), which SASL readers would want.
SASL.quote: LDAP allows authentication via any SASL mechanism [RFC4422].

TLS.why: Defines TLS establishment via StartTLS in LDAP, server identity checks, ciphersuite requirements and effects on authorization state.
TLS.quote: The goals of using the TLS protocol with LDAP are to ensure data confidentiality and integrity, and to optionally provide for authentication.

rejected.why: Generic topic; the more specific LDAP and SASL tags cover the authentication content.
Certificates are used for the server identity check, but the document does not profile X.509.
IDNA ACE conversion is referenced only for DNS name comparison in the identity check.
Parent of LDAP, so it is implied by the LDAP tag.
Authorization state is discussed, but only within LDAP sessions; the LDAP tag covers it.
ABNF is used only as notation for the authzId grammar.

RFC4514.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): String Representation of Distinguished Names
RFC4514.summary: RFC 4514 defines the LDAP string representation of X.500 distinguished names, giving the ASN.1-to-string conversion algorithm, the ABNF grammar for parsing, escaping rules and examples.

LDAP.why: The document is a core part of the LDAP technical specification and defines how DNs are represented in LDAP.
LDAP.quote: This document defines the string representation used in the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) to transfer distinguished names.

rejected.why: X.500 DNs are the source structure, but the document specifies the LDAP string form, not the X.500 directory service.
ASN.1 structures and BER are the input to the conversion, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
ABNF is only the notation used to express the grammar.
UTF-8 is the character encoding of the strings and is used as a dependency, not defined or profiled here.
X.509 certificates appear only as an example in the Security Considerations.

RFC4515.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): String Representation of Search Filters
RFC4515.summary: Defines the human-readable UTF-8 string representation (ABNF grammar, escaping rules, examples) of LDAP version 3 search filters, obsoleting RFC 2254, for use in LDAP URLs and other applications.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies the string form of LDAP search filters, a part of the LDAP technical specification, so readers of the LDAP subject page would expect it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a human-readable string format for representing the full range of possible LDAP version 3 search filters, including extended match filters.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to define the grammar. The document is not about ABNF.
UTF-8 is the encoding of the filter string. The document does not define or profile it.
The ASN.1 filter definition is quoted from RFC 4511 as background, and BER is only the network encoding. The document does not specify ASN.1.
LDAP URLs (RFC 4516) are named only as an example consumer of the string format. This document does not define the URL scheme.
Parent of LDAP, which is implied. The document is about LDAP specifically, so the broader topic is not chosen.

gaps.name: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists LDAP only as a child of directory services, and the id is written as 'LDAP' there. It appears in the taxonomy, so no real gap exists, but the LDAP tag id is the correct choice.

RFC4516.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Uniform Resource Locator
RFC4516.summary: Defines the LDAP URL format (ldap:// scheme) describing an LDAP search operation or referral target, including grammar, percent-encoding, defaults, extension mechanism and examples; obsoletes RFC 2255.

LDAP.why: The document is part of the LDAP technical specification and defines how LDAP searches and referrals are expressed as URLs, so LDAP readers need it.
LDAP.quote: This document describes a format for a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Uniform Resource Locator (URL).

URI.why: It defines a URI scheme with its grammar, percent-encoding rules and defaults, which URI readers would look for.
URI.quote: An LDAP URL begins with the protocol prefix "ldap" and is defined by the following grammar

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar; the document is not about it.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as acceptable input encoding for percent-encoding; not the subject.
Literal IPv6 hosts are noted only in passing through RFC 3986 and are not the subject.
The parent is implied by the LDAP tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC4517.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Syntaxes and Matching Rules
RFC4517.summary: RFC 4517 defines the base set of LDAP attribute syntaxes (with their LDAP-specific encodings) and matching rules used to compare attribute and assertion values, obsoleting parts of RFC 2252 and 2256.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies LDAP schema building blocks: syntaxes, their encodings and matching rules, part of the core LDAP technical specification.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a base set of syntaxes and matching rules for use in defining attributes for LDAP directories.

rejected.why: Parent of LDAP, which is the more specific tag and already implied.
X.500 types are referenced for correspondence of syntaxes, but the document specifies LDAP, not X.500.
ASN.1 types are mapped to LDAP syntaxes, but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
ABNF is only the notation used to define encodings.
UTF-8 is only the encoding used for Directory String; not the subject.
Generalized Time and UTC Time syntaxes are LDAP-specific syntax definitions, a minor part of the document.

RFC4518.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Internationalized String Preparation
RFC4518.summary: Defines the six-step string preparation algorithm (transcode, map, normalize, prohibit, check bidi, insignificant character handling) for character-based LDAP matching rules, based on stringprep.

LDAP.why: The document is an integral part of the LDAP technical specification, defining how string matching in LDAP matching rules is performed.
LDAP.quote: This document defines string preparation algorithms for character-based matching rules defined for use in LDAP.

PRECIS.why: It is a stringprep-style internationalized string preparation profile (Unicode mapping, normalization KC, prohibited code points), which readers of internationalized string handling would want.
PRECIS.quote: The character string preparation algorithms described in this document are based upon the "stringprep" approach [RFC3454].

rejected.why: Unicode is the character repertoire used, but the document is about LDAP matching preparation; PRECIS covers the string-handling subject better.
The algorithms align with X.500 matching rules, but X.500 is only the background model; the document is about LDAP.
ASN.1 string types are only inputs to transcoding, not the subject.

RFC4519.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Schema for User Applications
RFC4519.summary: RFC 4519 specifies the LDAP schema for user applications: standard attribute types and object classes (person, organization, group, country, etc.) derived from X.520/X.521, obsoleting RFC 2256.

LDAP.why: The document is a core part of the LDAP technical specification, defining the user schema (attribute types and object classes) for LDAP directories.
LDAP.quote: It provides a technical specification of attribute types and object classes intended for use by LDAP directory clients for many directory services, such as White Pages.

rejected.why: The schema originates in X.500 (X.520/X.521) but the document specifies it for LDAP use, not the X.500 directory service itself.
The 'dc' attribute holds DNS labels but DNS is only referenced for syntax; the document is not about DNS.
Only a brief note on using ToASCII for domain component labels; not a substantial subject of the document.
Schema definitions use LDAP's description syntax (ABNF-based), not ASN.1 modules.
IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like registry update of LDAP descriptors; not the main subject.
Parent of LDAP, implied by the LDAP tag.

RFC4520.title: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Considerations for the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
RFC4520.summary: BCP 64 defines IANA registration procedures and assignment guidelines for extensible LDAP elements (OIDs, descriptors, attribute options, message types, result codes, auth methods, search scopes, etc.), obsoleting RFC 3383.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies registries and registration rules for LDAP protocol elements, so LDAP readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document provides procedures for registering extensible elements of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

IANA.why: It is an IANA considerations document defining registry policies (Expert Review, Standards Action, First Come First Served) and registration templates.
IANA.quote: The document also provides guidelines to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) describing conditions under which new values can be assigned.

rejected.why: ASN.1 identifiers and BER tags are mentioned for message types, but the document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
SASL is only noted as an authentication choice in LDAP Bind; nothing about SASL is specified.
ABNF is used as notation for descriptor syntax only, not the subject.
UTF-8 is only the encoding restriction for descriptors and options; the document is not about it.
The parent is implied by LDAP, so it is not listed separately.
RFC 2578 is referenced only for how private enterprise and experimental OID numbers are assigned.

gaps.name: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no LDAP tag; I intended it as a tag but the listed taxonomy only has a 'directory services' topic with an LDAP child. If LDAP is not present as a valid id, 'directory services > LDAP' is the intended fit.

RFC4521.title: Considerations for Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Extensions
RFC4521.summary: BCP giving LDAP extension designers guidance on controls, extended operations, ASN.1 extension, schema elements, and other extension mechanisms.

LDAP.why: The whole document is guidance on extending LDAP operations, result codes, schema, and URLs, so LDAP readers would want it.
LDAP.quote: This document discusses considerations for designers of LDAP extensions.

rejected.why: The document covers extending LDAP's ASN.1 definition and BER restrictions, but only as part of LDAP extensibility. It does not specify ASN.1 itself.
It recommends defining new authentication as SASL mechanisms, but only in passing.
Start TLS controls are discussed only as an LDAP operation being extended.
It requires registering protocol values under BCP 64, but that is a brief pointer to RFC 4520, not the main subject.
The LDAP tech tag sits under this topic and is more specific.

RFC4522.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): The Binary Encoding Option
RFC4522.summary: Defines the LDAP "binary" attribute description option, which specifies that attribute or assertion values are BER-encoded rather than using the LDAP-specific encoding, and sets rules for its use in search requests.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies an LDAP protocol extension (the binary option) and how servers and clients handle it in search requests and results.
LDAP.quote: This document defines an attribute option, the binary option, which can be used in an attribute description [RFC4512] in an LDAP operation

rejected.why: BER is only the encoding the option selects. The document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
X.500 is only referenced as the origin of BER and the directory model. The document does not specify the X.500 directory service.
Certificate syntaxes are mentioned only as examples of syntaxes that need binary transfer. Their schema is defined in RFC 4523.
The only IANA content is a routine registration of the option name, which is boilerplate.

RFC4523.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Schema Definitions for X.509 Certificates
RFC4523.summary: Defines LDAP schema elements (syntaxes, matching rules, attribute types, object classes) for representing X.509 certificates, CRLs, cross-certificate pairs and related X.521 security information in LDAP directories, obsoleting RFCs 2252, 2256 and 2587.

LDAP.why: The document is an LDAP schema specification: it defines LDAP syntaxes, matching rules, attribute types and object classes for directories accessed via LDAP.
LDAP.quote: This document provides LDAP [RFC4510] schema definitions [RFC4512] for a subset of elements specified in X.509 [X.509] and X.521 [X.521]

X.509.why: The schema exists to represent X.509 certificates, certificate lists, certificate pairs and their matching rules, so X.509 readers would want it.
X.509.quote: The userCertificate attribute holds the X.509 certificates issued to the user by one or more certificate authorities

rejected.why: GSER and DER encodings of ASN.1 types are used for values, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
ABNF grammars appear in the appendix, but only as a notation for describing the encodings.
The document covers directory storage of PKI objects, but X.509 is the more specific fit and it does not specify PKI operations.
The schema derives from X.500 specifications, but the document is about the LDAP representation, not the X.500 directory service.

RFC4524.title: COSINE LDAP/X.500 Schema
RFC4524.summary: Standards-track document defining COSINE LDAP schema elements (attribute types and object classes) for LDAP directories, replacing RFC 1274 and updating RFCs 2247 and 2798.

LDAP.why: The document specifies LDAP attribute types and object classes using LDAP schema description formats, so LDAP readers need it.
LDAP.quote: This document provides a collection of schema elements for use with the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) from the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilot projects.

X.500.why: The schema originates from X.500 pilot projects and is meant for use in modern X.500 and LDAP directory services, with X.500 names reserved for legacy recognition.
X.500.quote: RFC 1274 was published to standardize the directory schema and naming architecture for use in the COSINE and other Internet X.500 pilots

rejected.why: DNS names appear only as values in the associatedDomain attribute and the domain object class; the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Only a brief note that applications use ToASCII for internationalized labels; not a subject of the document.
The mail attribute holds mailbox addresses, but the document does not address email protocols or formats.
The IANA section merely updates the LDAP descriptors registry; boilerplate-like and not the main body.

gaps.name: LDAP schema
gaps.why: The document defines LDAP/X.500 schema elements (attribute types, object classes), and the taxonomy lists no LDAP tag. LDAP and X.500 are listed under 'directory services' but I used the ids as given; if the ids LDAP and X.500 are not valid, tag choice should fall to directory services.

RFC4525.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Modify-Increment Extension
RFC4525.summary: Defines an extension to the LDAP Modify operation adding an increment operation value (OID 1.3.6.1.1.14), with LDIF representation, for atomic attribute value increments.

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the LDAP Modify operation, including a new operation enumeration value, feature OID in the root DSE, and LDIF syntax. LDAP readers would want it.
LDAP.quote: This document extends the LDAP Modify Operation [RFC4511] to support an increment values capability.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used as notation to extend the LDIF mod-spec production; the document is not about it.
The IANA section registers an OID and operation type, but this is boilerplate and the document's main body is not about IANA registries.
This is the parent of LDAP, so it is implied by the LDAP tag and not listed separately.

RFC4526.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Absolute True and False Filters
RFC4526.summary: RFC 4526 extends LDAPv3 to allow empty 'and' and 'or' search filters as absolute True "(&)" and False "(|)" filters, and extends the LDAP filter string representation accordingly.

LDAP.why: The document defines an extension to LDAPv3 search filters and their string representation, so it is about LDAP.
LDAP.quote: An 'and' filter consisting of an empty set of filters SHALL evaluate to True.  This filter is represented by the string "(&)".

rejected.why: X.500 DAP is cited as the source of the feature and for DAP-to-LDAP gateway mapping, but the document specifies only an LDAP extension.
The parent topic is implied by the LDAP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The IANA section only records the registration of the feature OID. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
