RFC4527.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Read Entry Controls
RFC4527.summary: RFC 4527 defines the LDAP Pre-Read and Post-Read request/response controls, which let a client retrieve the target entry before and/or after an update operation (Modify, Delete, ModifyDN, Add) as an atomic part of that update.

LDAP.why: The document specifies new LDAP controls (Pre-Read and Post-Read) extending LDAP update operations, so it belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) to allow the client to read the target entry of an update operation

rejected.why: BER-encoded ASN.1 is only the encoding used for control values; the document defines no ASN.1 module or encoding rules.
Parent of LDAP and implied by the LDAP tag, so it is not listed separately.
DAP functionality is mentioned only as the model for these controls; the document does not specify X.500.
entryUUID is only cited as an example operational attribute that could be read; the document is not about UUIDs.
The IANA section only registers OIDs and protocol mechanisms. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC4528.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Assertion Control
RFC4528.summary: Defines the LDAP Assertion Control, an LDAP control carrying a filter that must evaluate true against the target entry for an operation to be processed, enabling atomic test-and-set style conditional operations.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new extension control for LDAP, defining its OID, value, semantics per operation, and the assertionFailed result code.
LDAP.quote: The assertion control is an LDAP Control [RFC4511] whose controlType is 1.3.6.1.1.12 and whose controlValue is a BER-encoded Filter

rejected.why: ASN.1 and BER are only the notation and encoding used for the control value; the document is not about them.
The parent is implied by the LDAP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The IANA section registers the OID, protocol mechanism and result code, but that is boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC4529.title: Requesting Attributes by Object Class in the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol
RFC4529.summary: RFC 4529 extends the LDAP search operation so clients can request all attributes of an object class by prefixing the class identifier with "@" in attribute lists, and defines a feature OID for servers to advertise support.

LDAP.why: The document specifies an extension to the LDAP search operation (attribute selection syntax and feature advertisement), so it belongs on the LDAP page.
LDAP.quote: This document extends LDAP to allow an object class identifier to be specified in attributes lists, such as in Search requests

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the grammar extension; the document is not about the notation.
LDAP URLs are mentioned as one place the attribute selector may appear, but the document does not define or profile URIs.
Implied as the parent of LDAP; the more specific LDAP tag is chosen instead.
The IANA section only records the feature OID registration, which is boilerplate and not the main subject.
DSE/DSA terminology is inherited from X.500, but the document is about LDAP only.

RFC4530.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) entryUUID Operational Attribute
RFC4530.summary: Defines the LDAP entryUUID operational attribute, plus the UUID syntax and uuidMatch/uuidOrderingMatch matching rules, giving each directory entry a server-assigned immutable UUID.

LDAP.why: The document extends LDAP's schema with a new operational attribute, syntax and matching rules, so LDAP readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document describes the LDAP/X.500 'entryUUID' operational attribute and associated matching rules and syntax.

UUID.why: The document defines how UUIDs are represented (UUID syntax) and assigned in LDAP, a substantial part of its content.
UUID.quote: The attribute holds a server-assigned Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) for the object.

rejected.why: X.500 is the data model LDAP derives from, but the document specifies an LDAP schema element, not X.500 itself.
ASN.1 is used only to state the UUID type; the document is not about ASN.1.
RFC 4122's UUID URN namespace is referenced only for the UUID definition and generation; no URN is defined.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and do not make the document about IANA.
ASCII is only the character encoding of the UUID string representation.

RFC4531.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Turn Operation
RFC4531.summary: Defines an experimental LDAP extended operation, Turn, that reverses client/server roles of an LDAP session (or lets both peers act as both), with authentication scenarios and TLS/SASL layering rules.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAP extended operation (OID 1.3.6.1.1.19) with request/response encodings, extending LDAP itself.
LDAP.quote: This specification describes a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) extended operation to reverse (or "turn") the roles of client and server

rejected.why: TLS is used as a security substrate in the examples; the document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
SASL EXTERNAL and GSSAPI appear in authentication scenarios, but the document does not specify or extend SASL; it only notes layer constraints.
ASN.1/BER is only the notation and encoding for turnValue, a substrate.
Parent of LDAP, implied by the LDAP tag.
IANA registrations are boilerplate for the OID and mechanism, not the document's subject.

RFC4532.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) "Who am I?" Operation
RFC4532.summary: Defines the LDAP "Who am I?" extended operation, which lets a client obtain the primary authorization identity (authzId) the server associates with it, intended to replace the Bind-control-based Authorization Identity Controls.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAP extended operation, including request and response encoding, semantics, and control extension. It is squarely about LDAP.
LDAP.quote: The "Who am I?" operation is defined as an LDAP Extended Operation [RFC4511] identified by the whoamiOID Object Identifier (OID).

rejected.why: The operation reports the authorization identity after authentication. It does not define an authentication mechanism.
It returns the authzId the server already associates with the client. It defines no access control or authorization model.
The authzId format comes from RFC 4513, but the document does not specify SASL or its mechanisms.
StartTLS and security layers are mentioned only as context for why an extended operation is protected. They are not the subject.
The hex-encoded examples are BER, which is the encoding LDAP already uses. The document defines no ASN.1 module.

RFC4533.title: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Content Synchronization Operation
RFC4533.summary: Defines the experimental LDAP Content Synchronization (Sync) Operation, a set of controls extending LDAP Search that lets a client maintain a synchronized copy of a DIT fragment via polling (refreshOnly) or listening (refreshAndPersist).

LDAP.why: The whole document specifies a new LDAP extension (controls, intermediate response, result code) built on the Search operation, so LDAP readers would expect it.
LDAP.quote: This specification describes the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Content Synchronization Operation. The operation allows a client to maintain a copy of a fragment of the Directory Information Tree (DIT).

rejected.why: Entry UUIDs are used as stable keys, but the document only relies on the UUID format and the entryUUID attribute; it defines nothing new about UUIDs.
Protocol elements are written in ASN.1 with BER, but this is just the notation/encoding substrate, not the subject.
X.500/DISP shadowing is mentioned only as related work and for background on the information model; the document is not about X.500.
The parent topic is implied by the LDAP tag and no more specific fit is needed.

gaps.name: LDAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy as shown has directory services as a topic with LDAP and X.500 listed as child technologies. I used LDAP as the tag id, but the taxonomy text lists it under 'directory services' with the id 'LDAP', so this is fine; no gap remains.

RFC4534.title: Group Security Policy Token v1
RFC4534.summary: Defines the Group Security Policy Token, an ASN.1/DER structure signed with CMS by the Group Owner that specifies registration, rekey and data security policy for a secure multicast group, with GSAKMP base policy payloads.

multicast security.why: The token expresses group security policy for secure multicast groups under the MSEC architecture, which is the group key management and multicast security topic.
multicast security.quote: The Group Security Policy Token is a structure used to specify the security policy and configurable parameters for a cryptographic group, such as a secure multicast group.

GSAKMP.why: A large part of the document (Appendix B) defines GSAKMPv1 registration, de-registration and rekey policy payloads, so GSAKMP readers would want it.
GSAKMP.quote: This appendix provides the data structures needed for when GSAKMP exchanges are used as the GroupMngmtProtocol for the registration, de-registration, and/or Rekey SAs.

rejected.why: CMS SignedData is only the signing mechanism for the token; the document defines no new CMS usage beyond a content type OID.
ASN.1 is the notation used to define the token, not the subject of the document.
IPsec and SRTP are mentioned only as examples of data SA protocols the token may reference.
Only mentioned as an example of a Data SA protocol.
X.509 KeyIdentifier is imported for naming certification authorities; the document does not profile certificates.

RFC4535.title: GSAKMP: Group Secure Association Key Management Protocol
RFC4535.summary: Specifies GSAKMP, a protocol for creating and managing cryptographic groups: policy token distribution, group key download, rekey (optionally LKH), member registration/de-registration, and DoS cookies, with message and payload formats.

GSAKMP.why: The entire document specifies GSAKMP: its architecture, group life cycle, messages, payloads and state machine.
GSAKMP.quote: This document specifies the Group Secure Association Key Management Protocol (GSAKMP).

rejected.why: GSAKMP borrows from ISAKMP/IKEv2 (cookies, DH group, ID types) but is a distinct group key management protocol, not IKE.
Parent of GSAKMP, implied by the child tag.
X.509 certificates and CRLs are relied on for authentication but not the subject.
Groups are typically multicast, but the document does not specify multicast routing or membership.
Related group key management protocol, only background; not discussed.
Policy token is a CMS signed object, but only as encoding; defined in RFC 4534.

RFC4536.title: The application/smil and application/smil+xml Media Types
RFC4536.summary: Registers the application/smil and application/smil+xml media types for SMIL 1.0, 2.0 and 2.1, with registration templates, file-recognition guidance, and a "profile" parameter for content negotiation.

media types.why: The RFC exists to register the application/smil and application/smil+xml media types, with full registration templates.
media types.quote: This document specifies the media type for versions 1.0, 2.0, and 2.1 of the Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language

content negotiation.why: A whole section defines a new profile parameter for negotiating SMIL language variants, which is of interest to content negotiation readers.
content negotiation.quote: This parameter is meant to be used in MIME media-type-based content negotiation (such as that done with the HTTP "Accept" header)

rejected.why: The +xml suffix and RFC 3023 are relied on, but the document does not specify XML usage beyond a media type registration.
HTTP Accept is only an example of where the profile parameter is used; the document does not extend HTTP.
The document is a registration of subtypes. The more specific media types tag covers it, so the MIME parent is not needed.
Fragment identifier semantics are only mentioned in the registration template and deferred to the SMIL spec.

gaps.name: SMIL (Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language)
gaps.why: The document is about the media type for this W3C multimedia presentation format, but the taxonomy has no SMIL or multimedia presentation format tag.

RFC4537.title: Kerberos Cryptosystem Negotiation Extension
RFC4537.summary: Extends Kerberos V5 so a client can send an ordered list of supported encryption types in AP-REQ authorization data and the server selects one, returning a negotiated subkey in the AP-REP.

Kerberos.why: The document extends Kerberos V5 (updating RFC 4120) with a new authorization data element, AD-ETYPE-NEGOTIATION, for enctype negotiation between client and server.
Kerberos.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Kerberos protocol to allow clients and servers to negotiate use of a different and possibly stronger cryptosystem

rejected.why: The EtypeList type is defined in ASN.1 and DER-encoded, but ASN.1 is only the encoding substrate, not the subject.
The document concerns negotiating among encryption types and generating a subkey, but it defines no algorithms. The negotiation mechanism is Kerberos-specific.
A negotiated subkey is produced, but the document is about enctype negotiation within the Kerberos AP exchange, not key management in general.
GSS-API is not mentioned; the extension operates in the Kerberos AP-REQ and AP-REP messages.

RFC4538.title: Request Authorization through Dialog Identification in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4538.summary: Defines the SIP Target-Dialog header field and the tdialog option tag, which let a dialog-creating request (e.g., REFER or SUBSCRIBE) prove awareness of an existing dialog's identifiers so the recipient can authorize it.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP extension that adds a new header field, option tag, and UAC/UAS behavior for dialog-creating requests.
SIP.quote: This specification defines the Target-Dialog header field for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), and the corresponding option tag, tdialog.

rejected.why: Authorization is the purpose of the header field, but the document specifies a SIP mechanism. The SIP tag is the more specific fit.
The sips URI gives hop-by-hop TLS, which the document relies on to keep dialog identifiers secret. It defines nothing new about TLS.
SDP appears only as the body in the example call flow and is not discussed.
Cryptographically random dialog identifiers are required, but this is a security consideration and not the subject of the document.
SUBSCRIBE and the dialog and conference event packages are mentioned only as use cases for the header field.
The mechanism proves awareness of dialog identifiers for authorization. It does not authenticate the identity of users, hosts, or messages.

RFC4539.title: Media Type Registration for the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) Material Exchange Format (MXF)
RFC4539.summary: Registers the application/mxf media type for the SMPTE Material Exchange Format (MXF), an audiovisual wrapper format, including an optional ULs parameter carrying URNs of SMPTE Universal Labels.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration for application/mxf, with parameter definition, encoding and interoperability considerations. A reader browsing media type registrations would expect it.
media types.quote: The IANA has registered the media type application/mxf as specified in Section 3.1.  The registration uses the template present in [RFC4288].

rejected.why: MXF is a wrapper/container for essence types, but the document only registers its media type. It does not define a codec or container format itself; SMPTE 377M does.
The ULs parameter holds URNs (OID namespace, RFC 3061), but the document defines no URN namespace. It only uses existing ones.
HTTP is mentioned only as one way MXF files may be served. The document says nothing about HTTP itself.

The document uses the MIME media type framework and cites RFC 2045 for quoting. It specifies nothing new about MIME body structure beyond the media type registration, which the media types tag covers.
SMPTE Universal Labels are OIDs per ASN.1, but this is a passing reference and the document is not about ASN.1.

RFC4540.title: NEC's Simple Middlebox Configuration (SIMCO) Protocol Version 3.0
RFC4540.summary: Specifies SIMCO 3.0, a binary TLV-encoded protocol implementing MIDCOM semantics by which agents configure firewalls and NATs (pinholes, NAT bindings, policy rules) on middleboxes.

NAT.why: The protocol configures NAT bindings (traditional and twice NAT) on middleboxes; the document largely specifies NAT reservation and enabling processing.
NAT.quote: The Simple Middlebox Configuration (SIMCO) protocol is used to control firewalls and Network Address Translators (NATs).

firewall.why: SIMCO is a firewall/middlebox control protocol, including pinhole configuration and the PDR block rule for attack mitigation.
firewall.quote: Applications can request pinholes at firewalls and address bindings at NATs.

rejected.why: Only used as a security mechanism for sessions in Security Considerations; not the subject.
Mentioned only as an optional session securing mechanism.
Merely the transport substrate (port 7626); nothing new defined about TCP.
Only referenced in UNSAF considerations as an alternative NAT-traversal approach.
PDR is intended for blocking attack traffic, but only as one use case; not a focus of the document.
Address tuples support IPv6 but the document is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: MIDCOM (Middlebox Communications)
gaps.why: The document is a concrete protocol implementing MIDCOM semantics (RFC 3989); the taxonomy has no tag for middlebox communication/control, so NAT and firewall are the closest fits.

RFC4541.title: Considerations for Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) Snooping Switches
RFC4541.summary: Informational RFC giving recommendations for IGMP and MLD snooping switches: forwarding rules for IGMP/MLD control and data traffic, IGMPv3/MLDv2 considerations, spanning-tree topology changes, IPv6 differences, and a vendor questionnaire.

multicast.why: The document is about IP multicast forwarding in snooping switches, covering group membership and multicast router tracking. No single child tag fits the snooping-switch subject, so the parent multicast topic is used.
multicast.quote: This memo describes the recommendations for Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) snooping switches.

IGMP.why: Most of the body specifies how switches process IGMPv2/IGMPv3 reports, queries and leaves, and what Querier-election and spoofing behaviour to follow.
IGMP.quote: A snooping switch should forward IGMP Membership Reports only to those ports where multicast routers are attached.

MLD.why: A full section covers MLD/MLDv2 snooping differences: ICMPv6 identification, unspecified source address, and IPv6 address mapping.
MLD.quote: The control and data forwarding rules in the IGMP section can, with a few considerations, also be applied to MLD.

Ethernet.why: The document addresses Ethernet bridging behaviour for multicast, including MAC-address mapping ambiguity and spanning-tree topology changes, which are link-layer switch concerns.
Ethernet.quote: When processing a packet whose destination MAC address is a multicast address, the switch will forward a copy of the packet into each of the remaining network interfaces

rejected.why: MLDv2 runs over ICMPv6 and the document discusses filtering it, but ICMP itself is not the subject.
IPv6 is covered only as it relates to MLD snooping; the document is not about IPv6 specification or deployment.
Neighbor Discovery is mentioned only as a false-positive risk when identifying ICMPv6 traffic for MLD snooping.
Ethernet is the more specific tag and already covers the link-layer aspects.
PIM is not discussed; the router side is limited to IGMP queriers and multicast router discovery.

gaps.name: IGMP/MLD snooping
gaps.why: The document's central subject, snooping in layer-2 switches, has no dedicated tag. It is covered here through the multicast, IGMP, MLD and Ethernet tags.

RFC4542.title: Implementing an Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) for Real-Time Services in the Internet Protocol Suite
RFC4542.summary: Informational architecture document describing how to implement emergency telecommunications service (MLPP/GETS/IEPS) precedence and preemption for real-time SIP/H.323 calls using SIP Resource-Priority, RSVP admission with policy, and Diffserv EF PHB.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about implementing ETS/IEPS (MLPP, GETS) emergency preference calling in IP networks.
emergency services.quote: The key requirement is to guarantee an elevated probability of call completion to an authorized user in time of crisis.

RSVP.why: Bandwidth admission and preemption via RSVP, its policy extensions, aggregation and tunnels, and a long RSVP appendix example are a substantial part.
RSVP.quote: The use of Capacity Admission using RSVP with SIP is described in [RFC3312].

SIP.why: Call admission/preemption uses SIP Resource-Priority and Reason headers, with SIP preconditions flows shown in detail.
SIP.quote: The SIP Communications Resource Priority Header (or RP Header) serves the call setup process with the precedence level chosen by the initiator of the call.

Diffserv.why: Data-plane treatment uses Diffserv DSCPs and EF PHB, with DCLASS interaction with RSVP.
Diffserv.quote: In the data path, the Expedited Forwarding PHB [RFC3246] [RFC3247] describes the fundamental needs of voice and video traffic.

rejected.why: Mentioned as an alternative signalling system the CAC applies to, but not specified or analysed.
Used in the appendix example for QoS preconditions, but only as a substrate.
Parent of RSVP and Diffserv, which are tagged more specifically.
Policy model mentions COPS only as one possible PDP protocol.
RFC1633 is referenced for admission, but the document is not about the Intserv architecture itself.

gaps.name: Multi-Level Precedence and Preemption (MLPP) / call preemption
gaps.why: Core subject of the document; the taxonomy's emergency services topic covers it only broadly, with no precedence/preemption tag.

RFC4543.title: The Use of Galois Message Authentication Code (GMAC) in IPsec ESP and AH
RFC4543.summary: Specifies the use of AES-GMAC (GCM with zero-length plaintext) as a data-origin authentication-only algorithm in IPsec ESP and AH, including nonce, AAD, ICV formats and IKE conventions.

ESP.why: The document defines a new ESP combined-mode algorithm, with IV, nonce, AAD and ICV formats for ESP packets.
ESP.quote: ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC is a companion to the AES Galois/Counter Mode ESP [RFC4106]

IPsec.why: It also defines AUTH_AES_GMAC for the Authentication Header, which sits under IPsec rather than ESP, and gives IKE keying conventions.
IPsec.quote: The use of AES-GMAC in AH
IPsec.section: 4. The Use of AES-GMAC in AH

AES.why: AES-GMAC, a GCM-based AES mode, is the algorithm specified. Readers of AES modes would want this RFC.
AES.quote: GMAC is a block cipher mode of operation providing data origin authentication.

rejected.why: IKE is used only for key negotiation, identifiers and keying material derivation. This is a small section, not the document's subject.
Section 5.4 covers KEYMAT and salt derivation, but it is a minor part of an algorithm-specification document.

gaps.name: GCM/GMAC authenticated encryption mode
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the Galois/Counter Mode or GMAC. The nearest tag is AES, which is only approximate.

RFC4544.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI)
RFC4544.summary: Defines the ISCSI-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing iSCSI instances, portals, nodes, targets, initiators, sessions and connections, with statistics and notifications.

iSCSI.why: The MIB exists to manage iSCSI devices: targets, initiators, sessions, connections and login negotiation parameters.
iSCSI.quote: it defines objects for managing a client using the Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) protocol (SCSI over TCP).

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, conformance groups and notifications.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB module for iSCSI [RFC3720], used to manage devices that implement the iSCSI protocol.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport iSCSI runs over. The MIB links connections to the TCP MIB but does not specify TCP.
SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB. The MIB is tagged instead, and SNMP is not extended here.
The MIB points to the IPS authorization MIB (RFC 4545) for identities, but defines only pointer tables. It is not about authentication frameworks.
The parent topic is implied by the iSCSI tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC4545.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IP Storage User Identity Authorization
RFC4545.summary: Defines the IPS-AUTH-MIB module for configuring user identities (names, address ranges, CHAP/SRP/Kerberos credentials) used in access lists for iSCSI and other IP storage protocols.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module, IPS-AUTH-MIB, defining tables for managing user identities.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

authorization.why: The module models identities, names, addresses and credentials that other modules tie to access lists, so authorization of users to resources is a substantial subject.
authorization.quote: this MIB module provides only the set of identities to be used within access lists

iSCSI.why: The MIB was designed primarily for configuring iSCSI initiator identities, so iSCSI readers would want it.
iSCSI.quote: This document was motivated by the need for the configuration of authorized user identities for the iSCSI protocol

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol through which the MIB is accessed. The document only discusses its relationship to USM and contexts.
Kerberos is only one credential type for which a principal name is stored. The document does not specify or extend it.
SRP is only one credential type for which a user name is stored; the document does not extend it.
The MIB stores identity and credential data for authorization lists. It does not define an authentication mechanism.
Fibre Channel addresses are accepted as an address type, but the document is not about Fibre Channel transports.

RFC4546.title: Radio Frequency (RF) Interface Management Information Base for Data over Cable Service Interface Specifications (DOCSIS) 2.0 Compliant RF Interfaces
RFC4546.summary: RFC 4546 defines the DOCS-IF-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing DOCSIS 2.0 RF interfaces on cable modems and CMTSs, obsoleting RFC 2670.

DOCSIS.why: The document is entirely about DOCSIS RF interface management objects (downstream/upstream channels, modulation profiles, CM/CMTS status).
DOCSIS.quote: it defines a set of managed objects for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) based management of the Radio Frequency (RF) interfaces for systems compliant with the Data Over Cable Service Interface Specifications (DOCSIS)

rejected.why: The document is a MIB module and would fit, but the DOCSIS cable-access subject is its specific topic; both could apply. Considered as secondary.
SNMP is only the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines objects rather than extending SNMP.
QoS profile table is part of the MIB, but the document does not address QoS architecture or signalling.
Downstream follows J.83/MPEG framing, but the document is not about IP over DVB.

RFC4547.title: Event Notification Management Information Base for Data over Cable Service Interface Specifications (DOCSIS)-Compliant Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems
RFC4547.summary: Defines the DOCS-IETF-CABLE-DEVICE-NOTIFICATION-MIB, an SNMP MIB module of event notifications and control objects for DOCSIS cable modems and CMTSs, extending the DOCSIS Cable Device MIB.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module defining notification objects, control objects and conformance groups for DOCSIS devices.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

DOCSIS.why: The MIB is specifically about DOCSIS CM and CMTS events (registration, dynamic service, BPI, DCC, software upgrade), so readers of DOCSIS cable access would want it.
DOCSIS.quote: event notification management of Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS) compliant Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems.

rejected.why: SNMP is the protocol used to carry notifications; the document defines a MIB module, which is tagged under MIB instead.
Only a DHCP failure notification references the DHCP server address. The document is not about DHCP.
A time-of-day failure notification is defined, but the document is not about time synchronization.
Software upgrade notifications are included, but they report events and do not specify firmware update architecture.

RFC4548.title: Internet Code Point (ICP) Assignments for NSAP Addresses
RFC4548.summary: Defines the initial Internet Code Point assignments (ICP 0 for IPv6, ICP 1 for IPv4) under IANA's NSAP AFI 35, specifies how IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are embedded in 20-octet NSAP addresses, and sets IETF consensus as the policy for further ICP assignments.

OSI.why: The document specifies how IP addresses are encoded in OSI NSAP addresses (AFI 35, IDI/ICP, DSP). This is the OSI network-layer addressing coexistence subject.
OSI.quote: to establish an "initial" Internet Code Point (ICP) assignment for each of IPv4 and IPv6 address encoding in Network Service Access Point (NSAP) Addresses

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document sets up the ICP registry under IANA's AFI '35', with initial assignments and a future assignment policy.
IANA.quote: Remaining decimal values '2' through '9999' MUST be assigned on an IETF consensus basis [2434].

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses are only embedded as payload in NSAP addresses. The document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself.
IPv4 addresses are only embedded in the NSAP format. The document does not specify or extend IPv4 itself.
CLNP is mentioned only as a possible use of the embedding, not specified or profiled here.
The ATM Forum address format is mentioned only as an example use of the embedding.
OSI is more specific for NSAP address encodings, and the document is not about IP address architecture or allocation.
RFC 4301 appears only in boilerplate Security Considerations.

gaps.name: NSAP addressing (Internet Code Points under AFI 35)
gaps.why: The OSI tag covers NSAP coexistence in general, but there is no tag for NSAP address formats or ICP registrations, which are the specific subject of this RFC.

RFC4549.title: Synchronization Operations for Disconnected IMAP4 Clients
RFC4549.summary: Informational guide for building disconnected IMAP4 clients, describing synchronization strategies, IMAP command usage (UIDPLUS, MULTIAPPEND, CONDSTORE, etc.), error recovery and optimizations.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies how disconnected clients should use IMAP commands and extensions (UIDPLUS, CONDSTORE, MULTIAPPEND, UNSELECT) to synchronize mailboxes.
IMAP.quote: it deals with the issues of what might be called the "driver" portion of the synchronization tool: the portion of the code responsible for issuing the correct set of IMAP4 commands

rejected.why: Only mentioned in passing for sending messages composed offline; not part of IMAP synchronization.
MIME part fetching appears in examples but the document is not about MIME.
IMAP is the more specific tag and covers the subject.
Only the underlying transport; flow control is mentioned in passing.

RFC4550.title: Internet Email to Support Diverse Service Environments (Lemonade) Profile
RFC4550.summary: Defines the Lemonade profile: a set of required IMAP and SMTP submission extensions (CATENATE, URLAUTH, BURL, CONDSTORE, etc.) letting constrained mobile clients forward mail without download, submit efficiently, and resynchronize quickly.

IMAP.why: The profile mandates IMAP extensions (CATENATE, URLAUTH, UIDPLUS, CONDSTORE, NAMESPACE, LITERAL+, IDLE) and defines the $Forwarded keyword, so it is about IMAP usage and extensions.
IMAP.quote: This document describes a profile (a set of required extensions, restrictions, and usage modes) of the IMAP and mail submission protocols.

SMTP.why: The document profiles mail submission, requiring BURL, CHUNKING, PIPELINING, DSN, SIZE, ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES and STARTTLS on submission servers.
SMTP.quote: Lemonade-compliant mail submission servers are expected to implement the following set of SMTP extensions to make message submission efficient.

rejected.why: TLS and STARTTLS are only required as the security mechanism for IMAP and submission. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
MIME message assembly appears only in examples. The document is not about MIME structure or encodings.
Message headers appear only in the example messages. The document does not address message format.
The parent tag is implied by the more specific IMAP and SMTP tags.
URLAUTH URLs are used as the mechanism for authorizing access to message parts. The document does not specify URI syntax.

RFC4551.title: IMAP Extension for Conditional STORE Operation or Quick Flag Changes Resynchronization
RFC4551.summary: RFC 4551 defines the IMAP CONDSTORE extension, which adds per-message modification sequences, a conditional STORE (UNCHANGEDSINCE), CHANGEDSINCE FETCH, MODSEQ search and HIGHESTMODSEQ so that multiple clients can coordinate flag changes and quickly resynchronize.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP extension (CONDSTORE) that changes STORE, FETCH, SEARCH, SELECT/EXAMINE and STATUS, so it belongs under IMAP.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an extension to IMAP (RFC 3501).

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section; the document is not about ABNF.
IMAP is the specific tag that applies; email is its ancestor and is implied.
ACAP is only mentioned as a source of borrowed text in the acknowledgements and references.
NTP is mentioned only as a reason mod-sequences cannot be derived from the system clock.

RFC4552.title: Authentication/Confidentiality for OSPFv3
RFC4552.summary: Specifies how IPsec AH/ESP with mandatory manual keying is used to provide authentication and confidentiality for OSPFv3 packets, including SA granularity, virtual links, rekeying, and SPD rules.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends/profiles OSPFv3 security, including virtual link address selection and per-link SA handling specific to OSPFv3.
OSPFv3.quote: This document describes how IPv6 AH/ESP extension headers can be used to provide authentication/confidentiality to OSPFv3.

IPsec.why: A substantial part specifies IPsec requirements, SPD rules, SA granularity, manual keying and rekeying for using AH/ESP with OSPFv3.
IPsec.quote: The IPsec protection barrier MUST be around the OSPF protocol.

rejected.why: ESP is used as the mechanism but the document does not define anything new about ESP itself; covered under IPsec.
Discussed only to explain why it cannot be used for one-to-many keying; manual keying is mandated.
The OSPFv3 tag is more specific; the document is about securing one routing protocol, though a reader browsing routing security could find it relevant.
Manual keying and rekeying are covered, but only as part of the IPsec profile for OSPFv3.
HMAC-MD5/SHA-1 are only mentioned in the rekeying analysis.
IPv6 is the substrate on which OSPFv3 runs; the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC4553.title: Structure-Agnostic Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) over Packet (SAToP)
RFC4553.summary: RFC 4553 specifies SAToP, a pseudowire encapsulation for structure-agnostic transport of T1/E1/T3/E3 TDM bit-streams over packet-switched networks (MPLS, UDP/IP, L2TPv3), including control word, optional RTP header, payload sizes, IWF operation, defects and congestion considerations.

pseudowire.why: The document defines a new pseudowire encapsulation (SAToP) for TDM circuits within the PWE3 architecture, so it belongs under pseudowire emulation.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a method for encapsulating Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) bit-streams (T1, E1, T3, E3) as pseudowires over packet-switching networks (PSN).

rejected.why: RTP header is optionally used for timestamps, but only as a substrate; the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
L2TPv3 is only one of the PW demultiplexing layers; the document does not define L2TP behavior beyond referencing it.
MPLS is one of the underlying PSNs; the document is about the PW encapsulation, not MPLS.
QoS section only recommends using Diffserv/Intserv of the underlying PSN; not the subject.
Congestion section is brief and mostly defers specifics; not a substantial subject of the document.
Mentioned only to say it is NOT RECOMMENDED as a substitute for PW security.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation (T1/E1/T3/E3)
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is emulation of TDM circuits; the taxonomy has no TDM/circuit emulation tag, and pseudowire only partially covers it.

RFC4554.title: Use of VLANs for IPv4-IPv6 Coexistence in Enterprise Networks
RFC4554.summary: Informational document describing how Ethernet VLANs can overlay a parallel IPv6 routing infrastructure onto existing IPv4 enterprise networks for early dual-stack IPv6 deployment, with a FreeBSD configuration example.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is a deployment/coexistence method for introducing IPv6 into IPv4 enterprise networks, and positions itself as an alternative to ISATAP-style tunnelling.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document describes how such VLANs can be readily used to deploy IPv6 networking in an enterprise

Ethernet.why: A substantial part covers 802.1Q VLAN tagging, trunking and per-interface VLAN configuration for carrying IPv6 links over Ethernet.
Ethernet.quote: The IEEE 802.1Q VLAN standard allows separate LANs to be deployed over a single bridged LAN, by inserting "Virtual LAN" tagging

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an alternative tunnelling method the VLAN approach is contrasted with; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The parent is implied by or less specific than IPv6 transition; the document is about coexistence, not the IPv6 protocol itself.
Router Advertisements are mentioned only in passing as part of autoconfiguration on the VLAN links.
Stateless autoconfiguration is only briefly referenced; not a substantive subject.
RIPng appears only in the FreeBSD configuration example, not as a subject.
Multicast routing via pim6sd appears only as a configuration line in the appendix.

gaps.name: VLANs (IEEE 802.1Q virtual LANs)
gaps.why: VLAN tagging and trunking is a core subject of the document but the taxonomy has no VLAN tag; Ethernet is the closest fit.

RFC4555.title: IKEv2 Mobility and Multihoming Protocol (MOBIKE)
RFC4555.summary: Specifies MOBIKE, an IKEv2 extension that lets the IP addresses of IKE and tunnel-mode IPsec SAs change for mobility and multihoming, with return routability checks, NAT handling and new Notify payloads.

MOBIKE.why: The document defines the MOBIKE protocol itself, including its exchanges, notifications and security considerations.
MOBIKE.quote: This document describes the MOBIKE protocol, a mobility and multihoming extension to Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2).

rejected.why: MOBIKE is the more specific child tag. IKE is the base protocol being extended, and the parent is implied.
IPsec SAs are what MOBIKE updates, but the document is about the IKEv2 extension and does not specify IPsec itself.
Section 2.3 and Sections 3.8-3.9 cover NAT interaction, but only as a limitation and a use of IKEv2 NAT Traversal. The document does not specify NAT behaviour.
The document relates itself to Mobile IP but is an IKEv2-level mechanism, not an IP-layer mobility protocol.
Multihoming is a motivating scenario, but MOBIKE only moves traffic between address pairs. It is not a multihoming architecture.

RFC4556.title: Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos (PKINIT)
RFC4556.summary: RFC 4556 specifies PKINIT, Kerberos V5 pre-authentication extensions that let clients and KDCs use public-key signatures and encryption or Diffie-Hellman, with X.509 certificates and CMS, to authenticate in the initial AS exchange and establish the AS reply key.

Kerberos.why: The whole document extends the Kerberos V5 AS exchange with new pre-authentication types, error codes and authorization data.
Kerberos.quote: These extensions provide a method for integrating public key cryptography into the initial authentication exchange, by using asymmetric-key signature and/or encryption algorithms in pre-authentication data fields.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are used and profiled for KDC and client identity (SAN, EKU), but the document is not about X.509 itself. Certificate use is a mechanism it relies on.
CMS SignedData and EnvelopedData carry the PKINIT messages, so CMS is the substrate and is not being specified.
PKI supplies the trust infrastructure the protocol depends on, but the document defines a Kerberos extension and not PKI mechanisms.
The document derives the AS reply key through DH or public-key delivery, but this is part of the Kerberos protocol and not a general key management topic.
An ASN.1 module is defined in Appendix A, but it is only the notation for the protocol structures.

RFC4557.title: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Support for Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos (PKINIT)
RFC4557.summary: Defines a Kerberos pre-authentication type (PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE) letting PKINIT clients and KDCs piggyback OCSP responses to validate each other's certificates in the AS exchange.

OCSP.why: The document extends OCSP usage by carrying OCSP responses in-band to verify certificate validity, defining the PKOcspData structure and processing rules.
OCSP.quote: This document defines a mechanism to enable in-band transmission of Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) responses in the Kerberos network authentication protocol.

Kerberos.why: It defines a new Kerberos pre-authentication type (PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE) extending PKINIT, so Kerberos readers need it.
Kerberos.quote: This document defines a pre-authentication type [RFC4120], where the client and the KDC MAY piggyback OCSP responses for certificates used in authentication exchanges

rejected.why: Certificates are validated, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
Covered by the more specific OCSP tag; the document is not about PKI in general.
Defines a small ASN.1 type but only uses ASN.1/DER as encoding; not about ASN.1 itself.
Document explicitly says the pre-auth data does not authenticate principals; Kerberos tag covers it.

RFC4558.title: Node-ID Based Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Hello: A Clarification Statement
RFC4558.summary: Clarifies and formalizes the use of Node-ID based RSVP Hello sessions (Node-ID as source/destination of Hello packets) for detecting signaling adjacency failure in RSVP-TE for MPLS and GMPLS, e.g. with unnumbered links or separated control and data planes.

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies how RSVP-TE Hello sessions use Node-IDs for signaling adjacency failure detection, extending/clarifying RFC 3209 and RFC 3473 behavior.
RSVP-TE.quote: this document formalizes use of the Node-ID based RSVP Hello session in some scenarios.

GMPLS.why: Control/data plane separation in GMPLS motivates the Node-ID Hello procedure, and the procedure explicitly applies to GMPLS-capable nodes and GR.
GMPLS.quote: in GMPLS networks, the control plane information is carried over a control network whose end-points are IP capable

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific tag under traffic engineering for this document; the RSVP Hello is used in the TE context.
Mentioned only as an example of alternative link failure detection; not specified here.
Only referenced for the definition of Node-ID via TE Router Address TLV; not the subject.
Only referenced for the TE Router ID TLV definition; not the subject.
Document is about RSVP-TE signaling, covered by the more specific RSVP-TE and GMPLS tags.

RFC4559.title: SPNEGO-based Kerberos and NTLM HTTP Authentication in Microsoft Windows
RFC4559.summary: Informational RFC describing the HTTP "Negotiate" auth-scheme used by Microsoft IE and IIS, which carries SPNEGO GSS-API tokens (Kerberos or NTLM) in WWW-Authenticate and Authorization headers.

SPNEGO.why: The SPNEGO tag covers negotiation of a common security mechanism and its use in HTTP authentication. This document defines exactly that use: the Negotiate scheme carrying SPNEGO tokens, with Kerberos or NTLM selected.
SPNEGO.quote: The "Negotiate" auth-scheme calls for the use of SPNEGO GSSAPI tokens that the specific mechanism type specifies.

HTTP authentication.why: The document defines a new HTTP authentication scheme, with its challenge and credentials syntax, the 401 flow and an example exchange.
HTTP authentication.quote: Use of Kerberos is wrapped in an HTTP auth-scheme of "Negotiate".

Kerberos.why: Kerberos v5 is the main mechanism the Negotiate scheme is used with, including the HTTP/hostname principal naming. The document describes its use for web authentication but does not define Kerberos itself.
Kerberos.quote: Microsoft has provided support for Kerberos authentication in Microsoft Internet Explorer (MSIE) and Internet Information Services (IIS)

rejected.why: GSS-API is the token format and API the scheme is built on, but SPNEGO is the more specific tag, and the GSS-API tag is its parent.
HTTP is the substrate. The document only adds an auth-scheme, which the HTTP authentication tag covers.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations, as an alternative for confidentiality and channel binding.
Base64 is only used to encode the gssapi-data tokens.

gaps.name: NTLM (NT LAN Manager) authentication
gaps.why: The Negotiate scheme can select NTLM as well as Kerberos. The taxonomy has no tag for NTLM.

RFC4560.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Remote Ping, Traceroute, and Lookup Operations
RFC4560.summary: Defines three SNMP MIB modules (DISMAN-PING-MIB, DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB, DISMAN-NSLOOKUP-MIB) letting a management station initiate and retrieve ping, traceroute and name/address lookup operations at a remote host; obsoletes RFC 2925.

MIB.why: The document's core content is three SMIv2 MIB modules with control, results, and history tables plus compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines Management Information Bases (MIBs) for performing ping, traceroute, and lookup operations at a host.

traceroute.why: One of the three modules (DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB) controls remote traceroute, with hop tables and path-change notifications.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute is usually implemented by transmitting a series of probe packets with increasing time-to-live values.

performance measurement.why: Ping tests with RTT statistics, probe counts and periodic repetition are active network measurements, and the document's measurement results are the subject of its MIB objects.
performance measurement.quote: Both ping and traceroute yield round-trip times measured in milliseconds.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIBs; the document does not extend the protocol itself. MIB is the more specific fit.
ICMP echo is the recommended ping method and traceroute relies on ICMP errors, but the document defines no ICMP behaviour.
The lookup MIB uses getaddrinfo/gethostbyname, and the text says results may differ from a pure DNS lookup; it defines nothing about DNS itself.
Ping and traceroute are diagnostic tools, but the document is about SNMP MIB modules for network management, and the OAM topic targets link- and layer-specific OAM mechanisms.
The lookup operation resolves host names, but the document is a MIB for remote invocation, not about naming conventions.

gaps.name: ping
gaps.why: Remote ping is a main subject of the document (DISMAN-PING-MIB), but the taxonomy has no ping tag. The traceroute tag covers only half of the ping/traceroute pair.

RFC4561.title: Definition of a Record Route Object (RRO) Node-Id Sub-Object
RFC4561.summary: Defines a node-id flag (0x20) for RSVP-TE Record Route Object IPv4/IPv6 sub-objects so a Point of Local Repair can identify the Merge Point for facility-backup MPLS Fast Reroute of inter-area and inter-AS TE LSPs.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE's RRO sub-objects with a new node-id flag, so it is an RSVP-TE extension.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document specifies the use of existing Record Route Object (RRO) IPv4 and IPv6 sub-objects (with a new flag defined) thus defining the node-id sub-object

IP fast reroute.why: The node-id sub-object exists to support merge point discovery and backup tunnel selection for MPLS facility-backup Fast Reroute. The taxonomy's closest fast-reroute tag covers IP and LDP fast reroute, so this is a weaker fit.
IP fast reroute.quote: MPLS Fast Reroute (FRR) [FAST-REROUTE] is a fast recovery local protection technique used to protect Traffic Engineering LSPs from link/node/SRLG failure.

rejected.why: The RSVP-TE tag is more specific. MPLS is the context, not the subject.
The RSVP-TE tag, which sits under it, already covers this.
OSPF-TE Router Address is only referenced to define what a node-id is. The document does not specify OSPF.
The IS-IS TE Router ID is cited only to define node-id. The document does not specify IS-IS.
PCE is mentioned only as one way to compute backup paths. The document does not address it.
Base RSVP is only the substrate. The extension is specific to RSVP-TE.

gaps.name: MPLS TE Fast Reroute (facility backup)
gaps.why: The document is about MPLS RSVP-TE Fast Reroute merge point discovery. The taxonomy has only IP fast reroute, which covers IP and LDP fast reroute, so it fits imperfectly.

RFC4562.title: MAC-Forced Forwarding: A Method for Subscriber Separation on an Ethernet Access Network
RFC4562.summary: Informational RFC describing MAC-Forced Forwarding, where an Ethernet access node acts as an ARP proxy and filter so subscribers in the same IPv4 subnet are separated at layer 2 and all upstream traffic goes via an access router.

ARP.why: The core mechanism is an ARP proxy in the access node that replies with the access router's MAC address. The document specifies how ARP requests are intercepted, answered and discarded.
ARP.quote: implements an Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) proxy function that prohibits Ethernet Media Access Control (MAC) address resolution between hosts located within the same IPv4 subnet

Ethernet.why: The document addresses Ethernet-based access and aggregation networks. It specifies bridge filtering behaviour of the Ethernet Access Node for broadcast, multicast and unicast frames.
Ethernet.quote: ensure layer-2 separation of Local Area Network (LAN) stations accessing an IPv4 gateway over a bridged Ethernet segment

DSL.why: The scenario is a broadband DSL access network with access nodes, aggregation and BRAS, and it references DSL Forum TR-101. The mechanism is aimed at Ethernet-based DSL aggregation.
DSL.quote: for xDSL access, the EAN is an Ethernet-centric DSLAM

rejected.why: The EAN snoops DHCP messages and uses Option 82 to learn router addresses, but DHCP is only an input to the mechanism. The document specifies nothing new about DHCP.
Mentioned only as an existing alternative that the document finds suboptimal because it handles multicast poorly.
IGMP snooping is a brief multicast consideration in Section 6. It is not a substantial part of the document.
Section 7 says the mechanism is not directly applicable to IPv6 and gives only brief notes.
Only a note that ICMP redirects must be disabled on the access router.

RFC4563.title: The Key ID Information Type for the General Extension Payload in Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY)
RFC4563.summary: Defines a new Key ID Information type (Type 3) for the MIKEY General Extension Payload, plus an "empty map" CS ID map type, to identify key types and identities in 3GPP MBMS three-level group key management.

MIKEY.why: The document extends MIKEY with a new General Extension Payload type and a new CS ID map type, and registers new values for them.
MIKEY.quote: This memo specifies a new Type (the Key ID Information Type) for the General Extension Payload in the Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) Protocol.

rejected.why: SRTP is only mentioned as an example of what the MTK might be used for. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document relates to MSEC group key management (GKMARCH) and MBMS multicast re-keying. MIKEY is the specific technology and sits under key management, so it is the better fit.
SRTP-TESLA is mentioned only to say that this extension is not compatible with it.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate. It registers values but the document is not about IANA practice.
3GPP MBMS is the application context. The document does not address IP over cellular networks.

RFC4564.title: Objectives for Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP)
RFC4564.summary: Informational RFC setting out prioritized objectives (mandatory, desirable, non-objectives, operator requirements) for a CAPWAP protocol that controls and provisions wireless access points (WTPs) from a WLAN controller in large-scale WLAN deployments.

CAPWAP.why: The whole document defines requirements and objectives for the CAPWAP protocol between WLAN controllers and WTPs, so the CAPWAP subject page is the natural home.
CAPWAP.quote: This document presents objectives for an interoperable protocol for the Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP).

rejected.why: The document concerns IEEE 802.11 WLAN management, but the Wi-Fi tag is for IP over 802.11. CAPWAP is the more specific fit, and the ancestor is implied by it.
Mutual authentication and access control are discussed as requirements, but no AAA framework is specified or analysed.
The Resource Control objective maps 802.11e priorities across segments, but it is one objective among many and is not about QoS architectures or signalling.
NAT Traversal is a single short objective (CAPWAP must not prevent established traversal methods), not a substantial treatment of NAT.
The firmware trigger objective is a single protocol requirement; the document says actual firmware delivery is outside the protocol and the tag targets IoT firmware update architecture.

RFC4565.title: Evaluation of Candidate Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocols
RFC4565.summary: Records the CAPWAP working group evaluation team's process and findings in rating four candidate protocols (LWAPP, SLAPP, CTP, WiCoP) against the CAPWAP objectives and recommending LWAPP as the basis for the CAPWAP protocol.

CAPWAP.why: The whole document evaluates candidate CAPWAP protocols (LWAPP, SLAPP, CTP, WiCoP) for controlling and provisioning wireless access points, and recommends a basis for the CAPWAP protocol.
CAPWAP.quote: This document is a record of the process and findings of the Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points Working Group (CAPWAP WG) evaluation team.

rejected.why: The candidates control 802.11 access points, but the document is about evaluating AP control protocols, not IP over 802.11. CAPWAP is the more specific tag.
DTLS is discussed as SLAPP's control channel and as a recommended security option, but only as a substrate, not the document's subject.
GRE is mentioned as SLAPP's data tunnelling and a recommended encapsulation, but only in passing.
CTP's use of SNMP for configuration is evaluated, but SNMP is not the subject of the document.
WiCoP's proposed use of EAP is mentioned briefly; the document is not about EAP.

RFC4566.title: SDP: Session Description Protocol
RFC4566.summary: RFC 4566 specifies the Session Description Protocol (SDP), a text format for describing multimedia sessions (fields, attributes, media descriptions, grammar, IANA registries), obsoleting RFC 2327 and 3266.

SDP.why: The document is the core SDP specification, defining all session- and media-level fields, attributes, registration rules and grammar.
SDP.quote: This memo defines the Session Description Protocol (SDP). SDP is intended for describing multimedia sessions for the purposes of session announcement, session invitation

rejected.why: SIP is only a transport/use-case for SDP; the document defines nothing about SIP itself.
RTP is referenced for rtpmap and RTP/AVP proto values, but the document is not about RTP.
Registers application/sdp, but that is boilerplate-like IANA content and not the main subject.
RTSP is mentioned as a user of SDP only.
The grammar is written in ABNF but the document is not about ABNF.
The registries for SDP parameters are SDP-specific and secondary to the specification.

RFC4567.title: Key Management Extensions for Session Description Protocol (SDP) and Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP)
RFC4567.summary: Defines a framework of SDP attribute (a=key-mgmt) and RTSP header (KeyMgmt, status 463) for carrying key management protocol messages to secure media, with bidding-down protection, an IANA registry of protocol identifiers, and the integration of MIKEY.

MIKEY.why: Section 7 specifies how MIKEY is integrated into SDP and RTSP, including the 'mikey' identifier, authenticated protocol list and the MIKEY interface; examples all use MIKEY.
MIKEY.quote: The usage with the Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) key management protocol is also defined.

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP attribute, with offer/answer processing rules and SAP usage, extending SDP.
SDP.quote: key-mgmt-att-field = "key-mgmt"

RTSP.why: Defines a new RTSP header and status code 463 with usage rules for DESCRIBE and SETUP.

key management.why: The document is a generic framework for carrying key management protocols, with requirements for adding new ones; MIKEY is a child tag but the framework is broader.
key management.quote: defines general extensions for Session Description Protocol (SDP) and Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) to carry messages, as specified by a key management protocol

rejected.why: SRTP is the security protocol whose keys are established, but the document only relies on it as the target of keying.
SIP is used as the offer/answer carrier with some usage guidance, but nothing new is specified for SIP itself.
Only used as the encoding of key management data.
Only used as notation for grammar.
Not about MIME type registrations; the IANA registry is for SDP/RTSP key management identifiers.
IANA registrations are boilerplate-like and secondary to the main body.

RFC4568.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Security Descriptions for Media Streams
RFC4568.summary: Defines the SDP "crypto" attribute for conveying inline keying material and session parameters for unicast media streams, with SRTP-specific crypto-suites, session parameters, offer/answer rules and IANA registries.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new media-level attribute and defines its offer/answer use and grammar.
SDP.quote: This document specifies a new SDP attribute called "crypto", which is used to signal and negotiate cryptographic parameters for media streams in general

SRTP.why: It defines SRTP crypto-suites, master key format, session parameters (KDR, FEC, WSH) and crypto context handling for SRTP.
SRTP.quote: In Section 6, we define the crypto attribute details needed for SRTP, and in Section 7, we define SRTP-specific use of the attribute

key management.why: It is an in-band key distribution mechanism for media security, with key-method registry and directionality rationale; positioned relative to MIKEY and other AKE protocols.
key management.quote: The inline parameter conveys the SRTP master key used by an endpoint to encrypt the SRTP and SRTCP streams transmitted by that endpoint.

rejected.why: SIP is the main encapsulating protocol and forking is discussed, but the document is not about SIP itself.
Mentioned only as an alternative key management approach, not specified here.
AES modes are used in the crypto-suites but only as referenced SRTP transforms, not defined.
IANA registries are created but that is boilerplate for this document's subject; the document is not about IANA stewardship.
HMAC-SHA1 appears only as part of the crypto-suite names borrowed from SRTP.
Mentioned only as a possible protection for the SDP message in Security Considerations.

RFC4569.title: Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) Registration of the Message Media Feature Tag
RFC4569.summary: Registers the SIP media feature tag 'sip.message' with IANA, indicating a device supports 'message' (session-based instant messaging) as a streaming media type, filling a gap left by RFC 3840.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's caller-preferences/user agent capability mechanism with a new feature tag (sip.message) used to route calls to capable devices.
SIP.quote: This specification registers a new media feature tag in the SIP [3] tree per the procedures defined in RFC 2506 [2] and RFC 3840 [4].

SDP.why: The tag corresponds to the SDP 'message' media type introduced in RFC 4566; the registration completes the mapping of SDP media types to feature tags.
SDP.quote: This media type was defined by the revised SDP specification [5], which was published after RFC 3840.

rejected.why: Session-based instant messaging is only the example use; the document registers a SIP capability tag and does not specify messaging.
MSRP is implied by 'session-based instant messaging' but never named or specified here.
The 'message' here is an SDP streaming media type, and the registry involved is the media feature tag registry, not MIME type registration.
This is a single registration under existing procedures. It gives no IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: media feature tags
gaps.why: The document is about registering a SIP/media feature tag under RFC 2506 and RFC 3840 procedures. The taxonomy has no tag for feature tag registries, apart from the broader 'content negotiation'.

RFC4570.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Source Filters
RFC4570.summary: Defines the SDP "source-filter" attribute, which lists inclusive or exclusive source addresses for destination connection addresses, notably to describe Source-Specific Multicast sessions.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new attribute, including syntax, processing rules, offer/answer considerations and an IANA attribute registration.
SDP.quote: It defines the syntax and semantics for an SDP "source-filter" attribute that may reference either IPv4 or IPv6 address(es)

SSM.why: A key use case is expressing SSM sessions, with a dedicated example (3.2.1) and discussion of the ASM/SSM relationship in Section 4. Readers of SSM would want this.
SSM.quote: In particular, an inclusive source-filter can be used to specify a Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) session.

rejected.why: RTP/RTCP are mentioned only in an example's side-effect note; the document is not about RTP.
IGMPv3 is mentioned as a possible mechanism to convey filters to routers, which is explicitly out of scope.
The SSM tag is more specific and already covers the multicast aspect.
ABNF is only used to write the grammar in the appendix.
NAT is only mentioned as a caveat about address translation.
FQDNs are permitted in filters, but DNS is not specified or extended.

RFC4571.title: Framing Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) and RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Packets over Connection-Oriented Transport
RFC4571.summary: Defines a 16-bit length-prefix framing method for carrying RTP and RTCP packets over TCP and other connection-oriented transports, and defines the SDP "TCP/RTP/AVP" protocol token and the procedures for signalling it.

RTP.why: The document specifies how RTP and RTCP packets are framed and carried over TCP, and extends RTP/AVP usage with a new transport binding. RTP readers need it.
RTP.quote: This memo defines a method for framing Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) and RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) packets onto connection-oriented transport (such as TCP).

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document defines a new SDP media-line proto token and its offer/answer procedures, including RTCP bandwidth lines and the setup/connection attributes.
SDP.quote: Below, we define a token value ("TCP/RTP/AVP") that signals the use of RTP/AVP in a TCP session.
SDP.section: 4. Session Descriptions for RTP/AVP over TCP

transport mapping.why: The document is a transport mapping that carries RTP/RTCP over TCP. It defines the framing and the related connection semantics.
transport mapping.quote: This memo defines a method for framing Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) and RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) packets onto connection-oriented transport

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate the framing runs over. The document defines nothing new about TCP itself.
RTCP packets are framed in the same way as RTP packets, but the document adds nothing about RTCP feedback or reports. The RTP tag covers it.
The congestion control section only notes that TCP competes fairly. It is a short remark and not a subject of the document.
The document covers only the plain AVP profile. SRTP is not discussed.

RFC4572.title: Connection-Oriented Media Transport over the Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC4572.summary: RFC 4572 defines the SDP 'TCP/TLS' protocol identifier and the 'fingerprint' attribute so that connection-oriented media sessions can run over TLS, using certificate fingerprints to authenticate even self-signed certificates, and updates RFC 4145.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new proto value and a new attribute, and updates RFC 4145 (SDP TCP-based media transport).
SDP.quote: It defines a new SDP protocol identifier, 'TCP/TLS'.  It also defines the syntax and semantics for an SDP 'fingerprint' attribute

TLS.why: It specifies how TLS is used for media connections: certificate choice and presentation, fingerprint matching, and bad_certificate handling. Readers of TLS usage guidance would want it.
TLS.quote: extends the Connection-Oriented Media specification to allow session descriptions to describe media sessions that use the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are used and their identity fields (subjectAltName) are constrained, but the document is not about X.509 profiling itself.
SIP is only an example carrier of SDP and an integrity mechanism (sips); the document doesn't specify or extend SIP.
TCP is the underlying transport (defined by RFC 4145); nothing new is specified about TCP.
Explicitly out of scope; the document notes that it defines no mechanism for secure RTP over connection-oriented transport.
Hash functions are used for fingerprints and listed in an IANA registry, but the document is not about the SHA algorithms.
Only TLS over TCP is covered; TLS over other transports is explicitly excluded.

RFC4573.title: MIME Type Registration for RTP Payload Format for H.224
RFC4573.summary: Registers the application/h224 media type and defines its SDP mapping and offer/answer usage for carrying H.224 far-end camera control (H.281) over RTP.

media types.why: The document's core purpose is registering the application/h224 MIME media type using the RFC 4288 template.
media types.quote: The document registers the H224 media type, which may be used by systems that use SDP [RFC4566].

SDP.why: It defines the SDP parameters (m= line, rtpmap, clock rate, bandwidth) and offer/answer semantics with sendonly/sendrecv for this media type.
SDP.quote: The media name in the "m=" line of SDP MUST be application.

RTP payload format.why: The registration is for an RTP payload format (H.224 frames per H.323 Annex Q) and follows RFC 3555 for RTP payload media types.
RTP payload format.quote: This media type depends on RTP framing and thus is only defined for transfer via RTP [RFC3550].
RTP payload format.section: 4.1.1. Registration of MIME Media Type application/h224

rejected.why: H.323 Annex Q defines the RTP packetization and is referenced for gateway interworking, but this document does not specify or extend H.323 itself.
SRTP is only suggested in Security Considerations as an example protection mechanism.
RTP is the transport substrate; the document does not extend RTP itself, and the more specific RTP payload format tag fits.
The document does not mention SIP; only SDP and offer/answer are used.

gaps.name: Far-end camera control protocol (FECC, ITU-T H.281/H.224)
gaps.why: The document is about signalling far-end camera control, but the taxonomy has no tag for camera control or H.224/H.281.

RFC4574.title: The Session Description Protocol (SDP) Label Attribute
RFC4574.summary: Defines the SDP 'label' media-level attribute, which gives an application-defined token pointing to a media stream so external documents can refer to streams across multiple SDP sessions.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new media-level attribute, specifies its ABNF syntax, its use in offer/answer, and registers it. It is squarely about SDP.
SDP.quote: This document defines a new Session Description Protocol (SDP) media-level attribute: "label".

rejected.why: XCON is only the motivating example in the Introduction. The document defines nothing specific to the XCON framework.
SIP appears only as one carrier of SDP, and in the Security Considerations (S/MIME integrity protection). The document does not specify or extend SIP.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the attribute syntax. The document is not about it.
Conferencing is background motivation. The attribute is generic and applies to any application that uses SDP.

RFC4575.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Event Package for Conference State
RFC4575.summary: Defines the SIP "conference" event package and the application/conference-info+xml data format (with partial-notification state handling) for notifying subscribers about conference membership, media, and sidebars.

SIMPLE.why: The SIP event package for conference state is a SIP event-notification package with an XML body, the kind of work the SIMPLE tag covers. It is more specific than SIP alone.
SIMPLE.quote: This document defines a conference event package for tightly coupled conferences using the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) events framework

conferencing.why: The document gives conference state notification for the SIP conferencing framework: focus, participants, sidebars, and cascaded foci. It fits the conferencing topic, and no more specific child tag applies.
conferencing.quote: The conference event package allows a user to subscribe to the information relating to a conference.

rejected.why: The package fits the SIP conferencing framework (RFC 4353), but it is not the XCON centralized conferencing framework or data model.
SDP media types, labels and direction attributes are referenced for element values, but the document does not specify or extend SDP.
The conference-info XML schema is the notification body format, but the document is about the event package. XML is only the encoding.
It registers application/conference-info+xml, but that is IANA boilerplate, not the main subject.
SIP is the substrate. The more specific SIMPLE tag covers the event-package work, so the ancestor is not listed.
The <src-id> element carries an RTP SSRC identifier, but this is only a passing reference to RTP.

RFC4576.title: Using a Link State Advertisement (LSA) Options Bit to Prevent Looping in BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
RFC4576.summary: Specifies use of the high-order LSA Options bit (the DN bit) in OSPFv2 so that PEs in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs ignore LSAs already forwarded by a PE, preventing routing loops.

OSPF.why: The document defines a new use of an OSPFv2 LSA Options bit (DN bit) and how OSPF route calculation and LSA handling treat it.
OSPF.quote: The high-order bit of the LSA Options field (a previously unused bit) is used to solve the problem described in the previous section.
OSPF.section: 4. Using the LSA Options to Prevent Loops

L3VPN.why: The document addresses loop prevention in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs when OSPF is the PE-CE protocol, so L3VPN readers need it.
L3VPN.quote: A procedure is needed to ensure that once a route is sent from a PE to a CE, the route will be ignored by any PE that receives it back from a CE.

rejected.why: BGP carries the VPN-IPv4 routes between PEs, but the document specifies nothing new about BGP. The change is in OSPF LSA handling.
MPLS is the backbone substrate of the VPN service. The document is not about MPLS itself.
The document covers only OSPFv2, not OSPFv3.

RFC4577.title: OSPF as the Provider/Customer Edge Protocol for BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
RFC4577.summary: Specifies how PE routers in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs use OSPF as the PE/CE routing protocol, including BGP/OSPF interaction, domain identifiers, loop prevention via DN bit and route tags, and optional sham links; updates RFC 4364.

L3VPN.why: The document extends and updates the BGP/MPLS IP VPN specification (RFC 4364) with OSPF as PE/CE protocol, so L3VPN readers need it.
L3VPN.quote: This document extends that specification by allowing the routing protocol on the PE/CE interface to be the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) protocol.

OSPF.why: Specifies OSPF procedures on PEs: LSA types, area handling, domain identifiers, DN bit/route tags, and sham links as OSPF links.
OSPF.quote: A PE router that attaches to more than one OSPF domain MUST run an independent instance of OSPF for each domain.

rejected.why: BGP carries VPN-IPv4 routes and extended communities here, but it is the substrate; the BGP extended community values are defined only to carry OSPF information.
MPLS is the tunnelling substrate of BGP/MPLS VPNs and is not specified or extended here.
New extended community types are registered, but only as a mechanism for conveying OSPF domain, route type and router ID, not a general BGP communities topic.
Mentioned only as an alternative PE/CE protocol and in a loop example.

RFC4578.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Options for the Intel Preboot eXecution Environment (PXE)
RFC4578.summary: Informational RFC documenting the DHCP options (93, 94, 97, and the requested 128-135 range) used by Intel PXE/EFI clients to identify architecture, network interface, and machine GUID so a boot server can return the right bootstrap image.

DHCP.why: The document defines new DHCPv4 options (Client System Architecture Type, Network Interface Identifier, Machine Identifier) and PXE's use of options 128-135, so it belongs on the DHCP page.
DHCP.quote: We define Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) options being used by Preboot eXecution Environment (PXE) and Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI) clients

rejected.why: The options are DHCPv4 options (codes 93, 94, 97 per RFC 2132); DHCPv6 is not addressed.
PXE boot typically downloads images via TFTP, but the document does not discuss TFTP.
The machine identifier is a 16-octet GUID, but it is only a field value, not a subject of the document.
The IANA section only updates option registry references, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: PXE (Preboot eXecution Environment) network booting
gaps.why: The document is about network boot/pre-OS client identification; the taxonomy has no tag for PXE or network booting, so DHCP is the closest fit.

RFC4579.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Call Control - Conferencing for User Agents
RFC4579.summary: BCP defining SIP call control for tightly coupled conferences from the user agent perspective: focus, conference-aware and unaware UAs, the isfocus feature parameter, and dial-in, dial-out, REFER, Join, Replaces and OPTIONS call flows.

SIP.why: The document specifies SIP UA behaviour and call flows for conferencing, including use of the isfocus feature tag, REFER, Join and Replaces.
SIP.quote: This specification defines conferencing call control features for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

conferencing.why: The document is about tightly coupled conferencing with a focus. It covers creating, joining, adding and removing participants and deleting a conference. No more specific child tag (XCON, BFCP, telepresence) fits.
conferencing.quote: This document builds on the Conferencing Requirements and Framework documents to define how a tightly coupled SIP conference works.

rejected.why: XCON is the centralized conferencing framework and data model. This document only uses SIP primitives and does not define the XCON framework or data model.
SDP appears in the examples and in a few informational fields the focus may populate. It is not the subject of the document.
The conference event package is used in the flows, but it is defined in RFC 4575. This document only says UAs subscribe to it.
Conference URIs and the factory URI are discussed, but only as SIP call-control concepts, not URI syntax or schemes.
The conference-info XML bodies appear only as example NOTIFY payloads, not as the subject of the document.

RFC4580.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) Relay Agent Subscriber-ID Option
RFC4580.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 Relay Agent Subscriber-ID option (code 38), which lets a relay agent pass a stable, provider-assigned subscriber identifier to DHCPv6 servers independent of the physical network.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option, its format, and relay agent and server behaviour, so it belongs under DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: This memo defines a new Relay Agent Subscriber-ID option for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6).

rejected.why: This is the parent of DHCPv6, so it is implied. The DHCPv4 Subscriber-ID suboption is only mentioned for encoding guidance.
NVT ASCII is mentioned only as a suggested encoding for interoperability with DHCPv4. The option format itself is not standardized.
IPv6 is only the context for DHCPv6. The document is about the DHCPv6 option, not IPv6 addressing.
The IANA section only records the option code assignment, which is boilerplate.

RFC4581.title: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA) Extension Field Format
RFC4581.summary: Defines a Type-Length-Value format for Extension Fields in the CGA Parameter Data Structure, updating RFC 3972, and creates an IANA registry of CGA Extension Types.

IPv6.why: CGAs are IPv6 addresses whose interface identifiers are derived cryptographically. This document specifies the extension field format for them, so it belongs under IPv6 addressing. The taxonomy has no CGA-specific tag.
IPv6.quote: Data items to be included in Extension Fields of the CGA Parameter Data Structure MUST be encoded using the following Type-Length-Value (TLV) format

rejected.why: The IANA registry for CGA Extension Types is boilerplate-level here. The document's main body is the TLV format, not IANA guidance.
This is a general addressing topic, and the IPv6 technology tag I chose is more specific for a document about IPv6 CGAs.
CGAs are used by SEND, but this document does not mention or specify SEND.
The document does not address public key infrastructure. It only defines a generic TLV field format.

gaps.name: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA)
