gaps.why: The document is about CGA, a cryptographic binding of IPv6 addresses to public keys. The taxonomy has no CGA tag, so the closest fit is IPv6.

RFC4582.title: The Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP)
RFC4582.summary: RFC 4582 specifies the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP), a TCP/TLS-carried binary TLV protocol by which floor participants and chairs request, grant, release and query floors at a floor control server in multiparty conferences.

BFCP.why: The document is the core specification of BFCP: message formats, attributes, transactions, and client and server operations.
BFCP.quote: This document specifies the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP). BFCP is used between floor participants and floor control servers, and between floor chairs

rejected.why: BFCP complements the XCON framework, which the document references for context, but it does not specify the XCON framework or data model.
TLS is only the lower-layer security mechanism, with a mandatory ciphersuite named. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
TCP is only the transport substrate. The document does not extend TCP.
SDP offer/answer is the way BFCP connection information is exchanged, but that is defined in RFC 4583, not here.
SIP is only mentioned as an example of a session establishment protocol; it is not specified here.
BFCP sits under this parent, so the child tag BFCP already implies it.

RFC4583.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Format for Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) Streams
RFC4583.summary: Defines SDP encoding for BFCP streams: new TCP/BFCP and TCP/TLS/BFCP proto values, and the floorctrl, confid, userid and floorid attributes, plus TCP connection management and authentication rules for offer/answer.

BFCP.why: The document specifies how BFCP connections are described and negotiated, including floor control server determination and floor-to-stream association.
BFCP.quote: This document specifies how to describe Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) streams in Session Description Protocol (SDP) descriptions.

SDP.why: It defines new SDP proto values and media-level attributes (floorctrl, confid, userid, floorid) and their offer/answer use.
SDP.quote: We define the 'floorctrl' SDP media-level attribute to perform floor control determination.

rejected.why: TLS is only the secure transport for BFCP; nothing new is defined about TLS itself.
SIP is only the typical carrier of the offer/answer exchange; the document specifies nothing about SIP.
TCP connection setup uses the existing setup/connection attributes from RFC 4145; no new TCP behaviour is defined.
BFCP is the more specific tag for floor control, so this parent is implied.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the SDP attributes defined in the body.

RFC4584.title: Extension to Sockets API for Mobile IPv6
RFC4584.summary: Informational RFC defining C data structures, constants and socket-option/ancillary-data usage extending the Advanced Sockets API for IPv6 so applications can access Mobile IPv6 Mobility Header messages, Home Address destination options and Type 2 Routing Headers.

sockets API.why: The document is a sockets API extension: structures, header files, setsockopt options, ancillary data and raw sockets for Mobile IPv6.
sockets API.quote: This document describes data structures and API support for Mobile IPv6 as an extension to the Advanced Socket API for IPv6.

Mobile IPv6.why: The API exposes Mobile IPv6 protocol elements (Mobility Header messages, Home Address option, Type 2 Routing Header, MIPv6 ICMP messages) and is aimed at implementing and monitoring Mobile IPv6.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Mobility Support in IPv6 [2] defines a new Mobility Protocol header, a Home Address destination option and a new Routing Header type.

rejected.why: IPv6 extension headers and the Advanced Sockets API are the substrate; the document is about Mobile IPv6 specifics, not IPv6 itself.
Defines ICMPv6 message structures for Mobile IPv6 only as part of the API headers; not about ICMP itself.
Neighbor Discovery changes for Mobile IPv6 appear as a small constants/struct section only.
AH/ESP are mentioned only in header ordering and explicitly excluded as a non-goal.
Network mobility API is explicitly out of scope.

RFC4585.title: Extended RTP Profile for Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)-Based Feedback (RTP/AVPF)
RFC4585.summary: RFC 4585 defines the RTP/AVPF profile, extending RTP/AVP with early RTCP feedback timing rules, generic NACK, PLI, SLI, RPSI and application-layer feedback messages, and SDP signalling (rtcp-fb, trr-int).

RTCP.why: The document specifies RTCP-based feedback: early RTCP scheduling algorithm, new RTCP packet types RTPFB/PSFB, and feedback message formats.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Audio-visual Profile (AVP) that enables receivers to provide, statistically, more immediate feedback to the senders

SDP.why: A substantial section defines the RTP/AVPF profile identifier, the rtcp-fb attribute, trr-int, and offer/answer usage in SDP.
SDP.quote: A new payload format-specific SDP attribute is defined to indicate the capability of using RTCP feedback as specified in this document: "a=rtcp-fb".

rejected.why: Implied as the parent of RTCP; the document's specific subject is RTCP feedback, so the child tag is the right one.
The document only notes that RTCP feedback is insufficient for congestion control and refers to TFRC; it does not specify congestion control.
Mentioned only as an underlying transport and for suppressing duplicate feedback.
Referenced only in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate RTCP (SAVPF); not specified here.
PLI, SLI and RPSI are video-codec-oriented feedback, but the document defines generic feedback messages rather than a codec.
FEC and repair mechanisms are cited as background motivation; not specified.

RFC4586.title: Extended RTP Profile for Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)-Based Feedback: Results of the Timing Rule Simulations
RFC4586.summary: Informational RFC reporting ns2 simulation results of the AVPF (RTP/AVPF) RTCP feedback timing rules, covering RTCP bandwidth use, feedback delay and suppression, the dither parameter "l", and NEWPRED video error-resilience feedback.

RTCP.why: The whole document evaluates RTCP feedback timing rules (early packets, T_dither_max, 5% bandwidth, feedback suppression) of the AVPF profile, so RTCP readers would want it.
RTCP.quote: This document describes the results achieved when simulating the timing rules of the Extended RTP Profile for Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)-Based Feedback, denoted AVPF.

rejected.why: RTP is the parent of RTCP and is implied; the document's subject is RTCP feedback timing, not RTP generally.
SDP bandwidth modifiers (RFC 3556) are only mentioned in passing.
NEWPRED (MPEG-4/H.263 error resilience) is an application used to test the feedback timing, not something the document defines.
Multicast topologies are simulated, but the document is about RTCP timing, not multicast routing or group membership.
Congestion losses are a simulated scenario, but the document does not address congestion control algorithms.

RFC4587.title: RTP Payload Format for H.261 Video Streams
RFC4587.summary: RFC 4587 specifies the RTP payload format for packetizing ITU-T H.261 video streams, including SDP parameters and the video/H261 media type registration, and obsoletes RFC 2032.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines the H.261 RTP payload header, macroblock-level packetization and packet loss handling, which is a codec-specific RTP payload format.
RTP payload format.quote: The purpose of this memo is to specify the RTP payload format for encapsulating H.261 video streams in RTP [RFC3550].

media types.why: A substantial part of the document is the registration and update of the video/H261 media type, with optional parameters CIF, QCIF and D.
media types.quote: MIME media type name: video  MIME subtype name: H261
media types.section: 6.1.1. Registration of MIME Media Type video/H261

SDP.why: The document defines the SDP mapping and offer/answer usage of the H.261 parameters, which is a substantial section.
SDP.quote: The encoding name in the "a=rtpmap" line of SDP MUST be H261 (the MIME subtype).

rejected.why: H.261 has no dedicated codec child tag. The document covers only its RTP packetization, not the codec definition, so RTP payload format is the better fit.
RTP is the protocol the payload format sits on. The document does not extend RTP itself, so the more specific child tag is used.
RTCP appears only in the discussion of deprecating the H.261-specific FIR and NACK control packets and in the pointer to RFC 4585. It is not a main subject.
SRTP is mentioned only as an example in the Security Considerations section, which is boilerplate.
H.245 FastUpdateRequest is mentioned in passing as one way to request image refreshment. The document is not about H.323.

gaps.name: H.261 video codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the H.261 codec, though it has tags for H.264, VP8 and others. Readers browsing codecs would expect this RFC there.

RFC4588.title: RTP Retransmission Payload Format
RFC4588.summary: Defines an RTP payload format (rtx) that carries retransmitted RTP packets in a separate stream (session- or SSRC-multiplexed) with an OSN header, plus RTCP NACK usage under AVPF, congestion control, SDP/MIME registration and RTSP considerations.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies a new RTP payload format (rtx) with an OSN payload header, and its rules for sender and receiver.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for performing retransmissions.

RTCP.why: A substantial part covers RTCP feedback usage (NACK, SR/RR handling, timing rules under AVPF) for retransmission requests.
RTCP.quote: The NACK feedback message format defined in the AVPF profile SHOULD be used by receivers to send retransmission requests.

media types.why: Registers audio/rtx, video/rtx, text/rtx and application/rtx with apt and rtx-time parameters.
media types.quote: A new MIME subtype name, "rtx", has been registered for four different media types

SDP.why: Defines SDP mapping, fmtp parameters and example descriptions for session- and SSRC-multiplexing.
SDP.quote: The SDP MUST provide the grouping of the original and associated retransmission sessions' "m" lines, using the Flow Identification (FID) semantics

RTSP.why: A dedicated section covers RTSP control, aggregate control and cache control for retransmission streams.
RTSP.quote: This section looks at the issues involved in controlling RTP sessions that use retransmissions.

rejected.why: FEC is only mentioned as an alternative repair technique; the document is about retransmission.
Section 7 gives brief congestion guidance, but it is not a main subject.
Only mentioned in the Security Considerations about two-time pads.
Streaming is the target use case, but the document is about the RTP payload format rather than streaming delivery generally. RTSP is already tagged.

gaps.name: RTP retransmission / packet loss repair
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RTP retransmission or loss repair other than FEC, so the central subject is covered only by the RTP payload format tag.

RFC4589.title: Location Types Registry
RFC4589.summary: Creates an IANA registry of location type tokens (e.g., aircraft, office, train-station) with an XML schema and namespace, for use by other protocols such as DHCP civic addresses, RADIUS and RPID.

geolocation.why: The document defines a common vocabulary of location types (place types) for conveying location context. Readers of the geolocation subject would want it.
geolocation.quote: This document creates a registry for describing the types of places a human or end system might be found.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is to create a registry with an Expert Review policy and registration template, so it is relevant to IANA registries.
IANA.quote: This document creates new IANA registries for location types as listed in Section 3, starting with 'aircraft' and finishing with 'watercraft'.

rejected.why: XML schema and namespace are only the encoding for the tokens. The document does not specify an XML-based protocol.
RPID uses these values, but this document does not define or extend PIDF.
DHCP civic address options are only a referenced consumer of the registry.
RADIUS location carrying is only a referenced consumer of the registry.

RFC4590.title: RADIUS Extension for Digest Authentication
RFC4590.summary: Defines new RADIUS attributes and client/server behaviour so a RADIUS server can perform HTTP Digest (including SIP and AKA digest) authentication on behalf of HTTP-style servers.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS attributes (103-122) and RADIUS client/server processing for Digest authentication.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines an extension to the RADIUS protocol to enable support of Digest Authentication for use with SIP, HTTP, and other HTTP-style protocols

HTTP authentication.why: The attributes carry HTTP Digest directives (realm, nonce, qop, rspauth, etc.) and the document specifies how Digest is mapped to and from RADIUS, so Digest readers would want it.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document defines new attributes that enable the RADIUS server to perform the digest calculation defined in [RFC2617]

rejected.why: SIP is one of the HTTP-style protocols being authenticated and supplies the SIP-AOR attribute, but the document does not specify or extend SIP itself.
HTTP is the client-side protocol whose Digest headers are translated; the document does not specify HTTP semantics.
Only mentioned as a companion document (SIP-APP) and compatibility note; the document does not define Diameter behaviour.
Mentioned as an optional protection for RADIUS traffic in conditions for Digest-HA1 and in security considerations only; not the subject.
RADIUS is the more specific tag and already covers the AAA aspect.
MD5 is the default digest algorithm used inside Digest, not a subject the document addresses.

RFC4591.title: Frame Relay over Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3)
RFC4591.summary: Specifies how to carry Frame Relay PVCs as pseudowires over L2TPv3, covering control connection setup, PVC status signalling, session lifecycle, Frame Relay header encapsulation, sequencing and MTU.

frame relay.why: The document defines Frame Relay PVC emulation: DLCI encapsulation, FECN/BECN/DE handling, and Q.933 status interworking. Readers of the Frame Relay subject would want it.
frame relay.quote: This document describes the specifics of how to tunnel Frame Relay over L2TPv3, including frame encapsulation, virtual-circuit creation and deletion, and status change notification.

L2TP.why: It extends L2TPv3 with a new pseudowire type, a new AVP (Frame Relay Header Length), new result codes, and procedures for sessions, SLI and Circuit Status.
L2TP.quote: This document defines the specifics necessary for tunneling Frame Relay over L2TPv3.

rejected.why: It is a pseudowire type, but the document is specific to L2TPv3 and the L2TP tag is the better fit. Pseudowire emulation here is the mechanism rather than the subject area.
The generic tunnelling parent is implied by the L2TP tag and is not the subject here.
The document does not address L2VPN services or architecture, only a point-to-point pseudowire encapsulation.
QoS (CIR, bc, be) is mentioned only briefly in the applicability statement.

RFC4592.title: The Role of Wildcards in the Domain Name System
RFC4592.summary: RFC 4592 refines the RFC 1034 definition of DNS wildcards, defining new terms (wildcard domain name, closest encloser, source of synthesis), changing CNAME handling at wildcards, and discussing wildcard behaviour for special RR types including DNSSEC-related ones.

DNS.why: The whole document clarifies and updates core DNS wildcard synthesis, existence rules, and name server response algorithm from RFC 1034.
DNS.quote: This is an update to the wildcard definition of RFC 1034. The interaction with wildcards and CNAME is changed, an error condition is removed

rejected.why: DNSSEC motivated the clarification and RRSIG/NSEC/DS at wildcards are discussed briefly, but the document is about base DNS wildcard semantics, not DNSSEC signing or validation.
Not related to the document.
Dynamic update is only mentioned in passing when discussing banning NS wildcards.

RFC4593.title: Generic Threats to Routing Protocols
RFC4593.summary: Informational RFC describing a protocol-independent threat model for routing protocols: threat sources, capabilities, consequences, and generic threat actions such as spoofing, falsification, interference and overload.

routing security.why: The whole document is a threat analysis of routing protocols, a precursor to routing security requirements. This is the routing security subject area, and no specific child (RPKI, BGPsec) is its focus.
routing security.quote: This document provides a description and a summary of generic threats that affect routing protocols in general.

rejected.why: BGP is used as one example among several (OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, PIM). The document is protocol independent and does not specify or analyse BGP in particular.
OSPF appears only as an example for illustrating threats, not as the subject.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific routing security tag.
RIP is mentioned only as an example of a forwarder modifying hop counts.
IS-IS is cited only as an example of a routing protocol in scope.
The document is a protocol threat model, not operational practice guidance.

RFC4594.title: Configuration Guidelines for DiffServ Service Classes
RFC4594.summary: Informational guideline defining twelve Diffserv service classes and recommending DSCP markings, traffic conditioners, PHBs, queuing and AQM settings for each, with deployment examples.

Diffserv.why: The whole document is about configuring Diffserv service classes, DSCP marking, PHBs (EF, AF, CS, DF) and conditioning.
Diffserv.quote: describes service classes configured with Diffserv and recommends how they can be used and how to construct them using Differentiated Services Code Points (DSCPs), traffic conditioners, Per-Hop Behaviors (PHBs)

AQM.why: Each service class includes AQM guidance (RED thresholds per DSCP, when to apply or not), a substantial recurring part of the configuration recommendations.
AQM.quote: Active Queue Management, or AQM, is a generic name for any of a variety of procedures that use packet dropping or marking to manage the depth of a queue.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the more specific child and is already chosen.
Mentioned only as an admission control option and signaling mapping, not the subject.
SIP is only an example of signaling traffic mapped to the CS5 class.
ECN is mentioned as an optional companion to AQM, not addressed in its own right.
Section 5.3 on VPN service mapping is brief and concerns Diffserv in tunnels, not provider-provisioned VPNs.
TCP is referenced as the transport of elastic traffic classes only.

RFC4595.title: Use of IKEv2 in the Fibre Channel Security Association Management Protocol
RFC4595.summary: Informational RFC specifying IKEv2 extensions (new ID type, protocol IDs, integrity transforms, traffic selector type) so the Fibre Channel Security Association Management Protocol (FC-SP) can negotiate SAs for FC ESP_Header and CT_Authentication.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with Fibre Channel-specific ID types, protocol IDs, transforms and traffic selectors, so it is about IKEv2 usage and extension.
IKE.quote: This document describes the use of IKEv2 to negotiate security protocols and transforms for Fibre Channel

fibre channel.why: The document defines security protocols and SA management for Fibre Channel (FC-SP), so readers of the Fibre Channel subject would want it.
fibre channel.quote: Fibre Channel (FC) is a gigabit-speed network technology primarily used for Storage Networking.

ESP.why: The FC ESP_Header protocol is an ESP-equivalent encapsulation described in Section 3.1 and negotiated via new IKEv2 protocol IDs.
ESP.quote: The ESP_Header protocol is a transform applied to FC-2 Fibre Channel frames.  It is based on the IP Encapsulation Security Payload

rejected.why: IPsec for IP is explicitly not what is negotiated. The document says the new values MUST NOT be used for IPsec, and it only borrows IPsec/IKE machinery.
HMAC-MD5-128 and HMAC-SHA1-160 are transforms used, but the document does not specify HMAC itself.
MD5 is only mentioned as a hash underlying one integrity transform.
FCIP and FC encapsulation over IP are mentioned only as a source of potential confusion, and iFCP is not the subject.

RFC4596.title: Guidelines for Usage of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Caller Preferences Extension
RFC4596.summary: Informational guidelines document giving use cases, feature-tag usage examples, and a sample implementation of the matching algorithm for the SIP Caller Preferences (RFC 3841) and callee capabilities (RFC 3840) extensions.

SIP.why: The whole document explains how to use the SIP caller preferences and callee capabilities extensions (Accept-Contact, Reject-Contact, feature tags) through use cases and an implementation approach.
SIP.quote: This document contains guidelines for usage of the Caller Preferences Extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

rejected.why: CPL is mentioned as an alternative for called-party routing features, but the document is not about it.
SDP is referenced only incidentally in the audio/video example.
MESSAGE and presence appear only as example contact capabilities.
Presence and dialog event packages are used only as routing examples.
RFC 2533 feature matching is the basis of the matching algorithm, but the document is about SIP routing preferences, not media feature negotiation in general.

RFC4597.title: Conferencing Scenarios
RFC4597.summary: Informational RFC describing basic and advanced multimedia conferencing scenarios (ad hoc, reserved, lecture, sidebars, media policy control, text chat) to guide requirements and evaluation of protocols in the XCON working group.

conferencing.why: The whole document is a set of multiparty conferencing scenarios (ad hoc, reserved, sidebars, media policy, floor control). It supports XCON work but defines no protocol itself, so the parent topic fits better than the XCON tech tag.
conferencing.quote: These scenarios will help with the definition and evaluation of the protocols being developed in the centralized conferencing XCON working group.

rejected.why: The document is a scenarios input to XCON, but it does not specify or profile the XCON framework or data model, which is only referenced. The general conferencing topic fits better.
The document states its scenarios are not specific to SIP. SIP is mentioned only through the referenced SIP Conferencing Framework.
RTP is mentioned once as the carrier for interactive text (RFC 4103), which is not what the document is about.
Group chat and text sidebars are described as conference scenarios, with no IM protocol discussed.
Floor control is mentioned as a possible mechanism, but BFCP is not discussed.
Recorders appear only as passive participants in a feature list, so the document is not about SIP session recording.

RFC4598.title: Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload Format for Enhanced AC-3 (E-AC-3) Audio
RFC4598.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for Enhanced AC-3 (E-AC-3) audio, including header fields, fragmentation and concatenation of frames, the audio/eac3 media type registration, and SDP usage with offer/answer.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is an RTP payload format for a specific audio codec, with payload header, fragmentation, and concatenation rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format for transporting Enhanced AC-3 (E-AC-3) encoded audio data.

media types.why: A substantial section registers the audio/eac3 media type with its rate and bitStreamConfig parameters.
media types.quote: To: ietf-types@iana.org Subject: Registration of media type audio/eac3

SDP.why: Specifies the SDP mapping and offer/answer considerations for the new payload format.
SDP.quote: The optional parameter "bitStreamConfig" goes in the SDP "a=fmtp" attribute.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by RTP payload format, and no specific E-AC-3 or AC-3 codec tag exists. The codec is described only as background.
The document builds on RTP but only defines a payload format, which the more specific child tag covers.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an external protection mechanism.
IPTV appears only as one example application in the Introduction.
The congestion control section is a brief pointer to the general RTP considerations.

gaps.name: Enhanced AC-3 (E-AC-3) / AC-3 / Dolby Digital Plus audio codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the AC-3 family of audio codecs, so the codec itself cannot be tagged apart from its RTP payload format.

RFC4601.title: Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM): Protocol Specification (Revised)
RFC4601.summary: RFC 4601 is the Standards Track specification of PIM-SM, a multicast routing protocol that builds RP-rooted shared trees and optional shortest-path trees, obsoleting experimental RFC 2362.

PIM-SM.why: The document is the full protocol specification of PIM-SM: state, forwarding, Hello/DR election, Register, Join/Prune, Assert, RP discovery and packet formats.
PIM-SM.quote: PIM-SM is a multicast routing protocol that can use the underlying unicast routing information base or a separate multicast-capable routing information base.

SSM.why: A dedicated section specifies protocol modifications for SSM addresses and PIM-SSM-only router behaviour.
SSM.quote: The Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) service model [6] can be implemented with a strict subset of the PIM-SM protocol mechanisms.

rejected.why: Used only as the source of local membership information; not specified or extended here.
Mentioned alongside IGMP as a membership mechanism only.
MBGP is mentioned only as a possible source of MRIB routes.
Only referenced in Security Considerations for authenticating PIM messages; boilerplate.
Parent of PIM-SM; implied and not listed separately.
The PIM checksum is just a standard field description, not a subject of the document.

RFC4602.title: Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) IETF Proposed Standard Requirements Analysis
RFC4602.summary: Informational document supplying the RFC 1264 requirements analysis (specification, MIB, security, implementations, testing, suitability, authentication) to justify advancing PIM-SM from Experimental to Proposed Standard.

PIM-SM.why: The whole document analyses PIM-SM's readiness: implementations, interoperability testing of Hello, Register, Join/Prune, Assert and Bootstrap mechanisms, and suitability. PIM-SM readers would want it.
PIM-SM.quote: supporting documentation to advance the Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) routing protocol from IETF Experimental status to Proposed Standard.

rejected.why: AH is mentioned only briefly as PIM-SM's message authentication mechanism, not a subject of the document.
The PIM MIB (RFC 2934) is only cited as one requirement being satisfied; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The more specific child PIM-SM applies, so the parent is implied.
IGMP packets appear only as test-traffic generators in XORP testing.

RFC4603.title: Additional Values for the NAS-Port-Type Attribute
RFC4603.summary: Defines five new NAS-Port-Type RADIUS attribute values (PPPoA, PPPoEoA, PPPoEoE, PPPoEoVLAN, PPPoEoQinQ) and requests their IANA registration.

RADIUS.why: The whole document extends the RADIUS NAS-Port-Type attribute with new values, so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines a set of values for the NAS-Port-Type RADIUS Attribute.

PPPoE.why: Four of the five new values name PPPoE encapsulation variants (over ATM, Ethernet, VLAN, QinQ). The document defines labels for these access types and does not specify PPPoE itself.

rejected.why: PPP appears only inside the names of the port types. The document does not specify or extend PPP.
PPPoA and PPPoEoA are named in the values, but the document says nothing about ATM itself.
The IANA section is boilerplate registration of the values. The document is not about IANA registries in general.
Ethernet and VLAN appear only as part of the attribute value names. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.

RFC4604.title: Using Internet Group Management Protocol Version 3 (IGMPv3) and Multicast Listener Discovery Protocol Version 2 (MLDv2) for Source-Specific Multicast
RFC4604.summary: RFC 4604 defines "SSM-aware" hosts and routers and specifies modifications and clarifications to IGMPv3 and MLDv2 behavior for source-specific multicast addresses.

SSM.why: The document defines how SSM-aware hosts and routers behave, including handling of SSM address ranges and ignoring EXCLUDE-mode records for SSM addresses.
SSM.quote: This document defines the notion of an "SSM-aware" router and host, and clarifies and (in some cases) modifies the behavior of IGMPv3 and MLDv2

IGMP.why: It updates RFC 3376 (IGMPv3), modifying host and router behavior for report and query handling.
IGMP.quote: IGMP version 3 (IGMPv3) [IGMPv3] provides the ability for a host to selectively request or filter traffic from individual sources within a multicast group.

MLD.why: It updates RFC 3810 (MLDv2) with the same SSM-specific modifications for IPv6.
MLD.quote: MLD version 2 (MLDv2) provides the analogous "source filtering" functionality of IGMPv3 for IPv6.

rejected.why: Parent topic is implied by the more specific SSM, IGMP and MLD tags.
MLDv2 is IPv6-related, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The API requirement is only a brief reference to RFC 3678 and not a substantial part of the document.
PIM is not discussed; the document covers only host-router group management.

RFC4605.title: Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) / Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD)-Based Multicast Forwarding ("IGMP/MLD Proxying")
RFC4605.summary: Specifies IGMP/MLD proxying: a device in a simple tree topology acts as an IGMP/MLD host upstream and router downstream, merging membership into a database and forwarding multicast without a multicast routing protocol.

IGMP.why: The document defines forwarding based solely on IGMP membership, with the proxy acting as IGMP router downstream and host upstream, and merging IGMPv1/v2/v3 subscriptions.
IGMP.quote: It performs the router portion of the IGMP [RFC1112, RFC2236, RFC3376] or MLD [RFC2710, MLDv2] protocol on its downstream interfaces

MLD.quote: A group is in MLD version 1 (MLDv1) [RFC2710] mode if an MLDv1 report is heard.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a router behaviour upstream of the proxy tree (Register-encapsulation); the document replaces PIM, not specifies it.
Section 4.3 only says the proxy should comply with the IGMPv3/MLDv2 SSM spec; a minor consideration, not a substantial subject.
PIM is named as the kind of routing protocol this mechanism avoids; the document does not specify or extend it.
A DSLAM is given as a motivating deployment example only.

RFC4606.title: Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Extensions for Synchronous Optical Network (SONET) and Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) Control
RFC4606.summary: Defines SONET/SDH-specific GMPLS signaling traffic parameters (signal type, concatenation, transparency, multiplier) and SUKLM label encoding for RSVP-TE and CR-LDP, obsoleting RFC 3946.

GMPLS.why: The document is a GMPLS companion specifying SONET/SDH traffic parameters and labels for GMPLS signaling.
GMPLS.quote: It defines the Synchronous Optical Network (SONET)/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) technology-specific information needed when GMPLS signaling is used.

SONET.why: It defines SONET/SDH signal types, concatenation, transparency and the SUKLM label encoding over SONET/SDH.
SONET.quote: The format of the label for SONET and/or SDH TDM-LSR link is

RSVP-TE.why: Defines new RSVP-TE object class/C-types and error handling for SONET/SDH.
RSVP-TE.quote: the SONET/SDH traffic parameters are carried in the SONET/SDH SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects.

CR-LDP.why: Defines a new CR-LDP TLV (0x0838) and NOTIFICATION behaviour for SONET/SDH.
CR-LDP.quote: the SONET/SDH traffic parameters are carried in the SONET/SDH Traffic Parameters TLV.

rejected.why: The parent of GMPLS; GMPLS is the more specific fit.
RSVP is only the carrier for the objects; the document is about RSVP-TE extensions, not RSVP itself.
CR-LDP is the more specific child and is already chosen.

RFC4607.title: Source-Specific Multicast for IP
RFC4607.summary: Defines the Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) service model for IP: the 232/8 and FF3x::/32 address ranges, (S,G) channel semantics, and the host and router requirements (IGMPv3/MLDv2, PIM-SSM) to support it.

SSM.why: The whole document specifies the SSM service model, channel semantics, address allocation, and host/router requirements.
SSM.quote: This document defines an extension to the Internet network service that applies to datagrams sent to SSM addresses and defines the host and router requirements to support this extension.

rejected.why: Router requirement is to implement the PIM-SSM subset of PIM-SM, but the document does not specify or extend PIM-SM itself.
IGMPv3 is the host-to-router signalling mechanism relied on; specified in other RFCs (RFC 3376, RFC 4604).
MLDv2 is used as the IPv6 membership mechanism but not specified here.
Only discussed in Security Considerations as caveats; not the main subject.
IPv6 SSM address prefix is covered, but the document is about multicast service, not IPv6 itself.

RFC4608.title: Source-Specific Protocol Independent Multicast in 232/8
RFC4608.summary: BCP giving operational recommendations for routers, RPs and MSDP so that the 232/8 range behaves as source-specific multicast only, with no shared trees, RP registration, (*,G) joins or MSDP SAs.

SSM.why: The whole document defines operational practices to ensure source-specific behaviour in 232/8, the SSM address range.
SSM.quote: IP Multicast group addresses in the 232/8 (232.0.0.0 to 232.255.255.255) range are designated as source-specific multicast destination addresses

PIM-SM.why: Recommendations modify PIM-SM RP/DR behaviour (registers, (*,G) joins, RP candidates, BSR) for 232/8 while keeping ASM coexistence.
PIM-SM.quote: preventing the RP from accepting registers for 232/8 groups from the DR

MSDP.why: A section is devoted to MSDP SA handling, and the document discusses MSDP's Experimental status and BCP variance.
MSDP.quote: To prevent propagation of SAs in the 232/8 range, an RP SHOULD never originate an SA for any 232/8 groups

rejected.why: The more specific SSM, PIM-SM and MSDP tags already cover it, so the parent is implied.
The 232/8 allocation is mentioned only as background; the document is not about IANA registry matters.
The variance procedure and normative-reference discussion is apparatus, not the main subject.

RFC4609.title: Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) Multicast Routing Security Issues and Enhancements
RFC4609.summary: Informational memo analysing denial-of-service and integrity threats to PIM-SM multicast routing (ASM with MSDP, SSM, Embedded-RP) and proposing mitigations such as rate-limiters, remote routability signalling and a passive PIM mode.

PIM-SM.why: The whole document analyses PIM-SM threats (join flooding, register attacks) and proposes enhancements to PIM-SM operation, so it belongs on the PIM-SM page.
PIM-SM.quote: This memo describes security threats for the larger (intra-domain or inter-domain) multicast routing infrastructures. Only Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) is analyzed

MSDP.why: MSDP flooding is described as the most serious threat in ASM, and a dedicated MSDP SA rate-limiter is proposed, so a substantial part addresses MSDP.
MSDP.quote: A MSDP source-active rate-limiter is a token-bucket-based, source-based rate-limiter, that would limit new groups per source

SSM.why: SSM is one of the three analysed operational models, with its threat resistance compared in the threat matrix.
SSM.quote: The SSM service model prevents injection of packets to (S,G) channels, avoiding this problem.

routing security.why: The document is a threat analysis and mitigation proposal for multicast routing infrastructure, which is routing security.
routing security.quote: This memo analyzes the security of PIM routing infrastructures in some detail and proposes enhancements to mitigate the observed threats.

rejected.why: Group management protocols are only the attack vector for receiver-based attacks. Host-to-router attacks are explicitly out of scope.
MLD appears only as a trigger for PIM joins. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible authentication mechanism. The document does not discuss it in its main body.
Parent of the specific multicast technology tags chosen (PIM-SM, MSDP, SSM), so it is implied.
The threats are DoS attacks, but the document is about multicast routing security specifically. The DDoS mitigation and signalling subject is a different topic.

RFC4610.title: Anycast-RP Using Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM)
RFC4610.summary: Specifies Anycast-RP within a PIM-only domain by having an RP replicate PIM Register messages to the other RPs in the Anycast-RP set, removing the need for MSDP between RPs.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM-SM Register handling at the RP (Register copying, Register-Stop, (S,G) state) and is defined as blending with the PIM-SM specification.
PIM-SM.quote: This memo extends the Register mechanism in PIM so Anycast-RP functionality can be retained without using MSDP.

anycast.why: The document is about operating a Rendezvous Point using anycast addressing, with the same RP address on several routers and unicast routing delivering to the nearest one.
anycast.quote: Assume RP1, RP2, and RP3 are all assigned the same IP address, which is used as the Anycast-RP address

MSDP.why: A whole section covers how Anycast-RP via PIM interacts with MSDP peering in stub and transit domains. It is the alternative this document replaces.

Mentioned only in the interoperability considerations.

RFC4635.summary: Registers HMAC-SHA TSIG algorithm identifiers (SHA-1, 224, 256, 384, 512) for DNS TSIG, sets implementation requirements, and specifies MAC truncation handling and the BADTRUNC error code.

RFC4638.title: Accommodating a Maximum Transit Unit/Maximum Receive Unit (MTU/MRU) Greater Than 1492 in the Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet (PPPoE)
RFC4638.summary: Defines an optional PPPoE discovery tag, PPP-Max-Payload, that lets a client and server negotiate a PPP MRU/MTU greater than 1492 over jumbo-capable Ethernet, with LCP MRU negotiation rules and an Echo-Request test.

PPP.quote: the Maximum-Receive-Unit (MRU) option MUST NOT be negotiated to a size larger than 1492, unless both the PPPoE client and server have indicated

rejected.why: Jumbo frames are the motivation, but the document specifies PPPoE behaviour, not IP over Ethernet.

ATM and PPPoA appear in the network diagrams as context. The document does not cover IP over ATM.
The document concerns MRU negotiation and an Echo-Request test, not Path MTU Discovery.

RFC4639.title: Cable Device Management Information Base for Data-Over-Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS) Compliant Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems

MIB.quote: it defines a basic set of managed objects for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)-based management of Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS)-compliant Cable Modems

DOCSIS.why: The MIB manages DOCSIS cable access devices, so readers of DOCSIS would expect it.
DOCSIS.quote: This MIB module provides a set of objects required for the management of DOCSIS-compliant Cable Modems (CM) and Cable Modem Termination Systems (CMTS).

TFTP and HTTP are only used for software download selection via an object; they are not the subject.
Syslog is one event reporting mechanism that objects control; not the document's subject.
Only a single object, docsDevIgmpModeControl, touches IGMP mode; not a substantial subject.
The more specific MIB tag already covers this, so the parent is implied.

RFC4640.title: Problem Statement for bootstrapping Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6)
RFC4640.summary: Informational problem statement defining Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping (obtaining home address, home agent address, and security association), its motivations, AAA-based service models, deployment scenarios, and seed parameters.

Mobile IPv6.quote: This document discusses issues involved with how the mobile node can be bootstrapped for Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6)

AAA.quote: One typical way of verifying the trust relationship is using authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) infrastructure.

rejected.why: IPsec SAs are the outcome to be bootstrapped, but the document does not specify or analyse IPsec itself.
IKEv1/IKEv2 limitations are mentioned as motivation, but IKE is not the subject.
Mentioned only as one possible address assignment or discovery means.
DNS lookup is mentioned only as a possible home agent discovery method.
Only referenced for threat information; not discussed in the body.
Key establishment is part of bootstrapping, but the document is mainly about Mobile IPv6 provisioning and the Mobile IPv6 tag covers it.

RFC4641.title: DNSSEC Operational Practices
RFC4641.summary: Informational guide for zone administrators on operating DNSSEC: key generation, storage, sizes, signature validity and timing, ZSK/KSK rollovers, emergency rollover, and parental DS policies; obsoletes RFC 2541.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is operational guidance for signed zones: KSK/ZSK, rollovers, signature timing, chain of trust and DS handling.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes a set of practices for operating the DNS with security extensions (DNSSEC).

RFC4642.title: Using Transport Layer Security (TLS) with Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP)
RFC4642.summary: Defines the STARTTLS extension to NNTP, letting NNTP clients and servers negotiate TLS within a session for confidentiality, integrity and optional certificate authentication.

NNTP.why: The document extends NNTP with a new STARTTLS command, capability label and response codes 382/580.
NNTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) that allows an NNTP client and server to use Transport Layer Security (TLS).

RFC4643.title: Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) Extension for Authentication
RFC4643.summary: Defines the NNTP AUTHINFO extension (AUTHINFO USER/PASS and AUTHINFO SASL) for client authentication and optional security-layer negotiation, formalizing the legacy USER/PASS method, deprecating AUTHINFO GENERIC/SIMPLE, and profiling SASL for NNTP.

NNTP.why: The document specifies a new NNTP extension (AUTHINFO capability, commands and response codes), so NNTP readers need it.
NNTP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) that allows a client to indicate an authentication mechanism to the server

SASL.why: Defines the NNTP profile of SASL (AUTHINFO SASL, service name nntp, base64 challenge/response encoding, mechanism requirements), a substantial part of the document.
SASL.quote: This section defines a formal profile of the Simple Authentication and Security Layer [SASL].

rejected.why: TLS is referenced as the security layer under which USER/PASS should be used and its interaction with SASL layers, but the document defines nothing new about TLS; STARTTLS is specified elsewhere (RFC 4642).

Base64 is only the encoding used for SASL challenges and responses.
ABNF is only used as notation for the formal syntax.

RFC4644.title: Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) Extension for Streaming Feeds
RFC4644.summary: Defines the NNTP STREAMING extension, formalizing the CHECK and TAKETHIS commands (and deprecating MODE STREAM) for pipelined, asynchronous server-to-server article transfer.

NNTP.why: The document specifies an extension to NNTP, adding the STREAMING capability and the CHECK, TAKETHIS and MODE STREAM commands with new response codes.
NNTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) to provide asynchronous (otherwise known as "streaming") transfer of articles.

RFC4645.title: Initial Language Subtag Registry
RFC4645.summary: RFC 4645 describes the criteria used to build the initial contents of the IANA Language Subtag Registry for BCP 47 language tags (from ISO 639, ISO 15924, ISO 3166-1, UN M.49 and the RFC 3066 registry). The registry contents themselves were removed before publication.

RFC4646.title: Tags for Identifying Languages
RFC4646.summary: BCP 47 specification of the structure, subtag registry, registration procedures, extension mechanism and processing rules for language tags used to identify the language of information objects, replacing RFC 3066.

RFC4647.summary: BCP 47 companion to RFC 4646 that defines language ranges (basic and extended), language priority lists, and the filtering and lookup schemes for matching language ranges against language tags.

RFC4648.summary: RFC 4648 specifies the base64, base64url, base32, base32hex and base16 data encodings, along with guidance on line feeds, padding, non-alphabet characters, alphabet choice and canonical encoding.

RFC4649.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) Relay Agent Remote-ID Option
RFC4649.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 Relay Agent Remote-ID option (option code 37), the DHCPv6 equivalent of the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Remote-ID suboption, along with relay agent and server behaviour for it.

DHCPv6.quote: This memo defines a new Relay Agent Remote-ID option for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6).

RFC4650.title: HMAC-Authenticated Diffie-Hellman for Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY)
RFC4650.summary: RFC 4650 specifies MIKEY-DHHMAC, a MIKEY key management variant that uses Diffie-Hellman key agreement authenticated with HMAC over pre-shared secrets, completing in one roundtrip with perfect forward secrecy and no PKI.

MIKEY.why: The document defines a new MIKEY key management mode (DHHMAC), including its message exchange, payload usage, re-keying and data type values.
MIKEY.quote: This document describes a lightweight point-to-point key management protocol variant for the multimedia Internet keying (MIKEY) protocol MIKEY, as defined in RFC 3830.

SIP/SDP is only a transport container for MIKEY messages; the document does not extend SIP.
H.323/H.235 usage appears only in an informative appendix.
SRTP is the consumer of the keys; the document does not define SRTP behaviour.

RFC4651.title: A Taxonomy and Analysis of Enhancements to Mobile IPv6 Route Optimization
RFC4651.summary: An IRTF MobOpts research group document that surveys and evaluates strategies (a "toolbox") for enhancing Mobile IPv6 Route Optimization in terms of handoff latency, security, signaling overhead and robustness.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document analyses enhancements to Mobile IPv6 Route Optimization and the return-routability procedure, so Mobile IPv6 is the subject.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document describes and evaluates strategies to enhance Mobile IPv6 Route Optimization, on the basis of existing proposals

Location privacy is a short subsection (3.14) and is not a substantial focus.

RFC4652.title: Evaluation of Existing Routing Protocols against Automatic Switched Optical Network (ASON) Routing Requirements
RFC4652.summary: Informational RFC evaluating OSPF and IS-IS (with GMPLS/TE extensions) against the ITU-T ASON routing requirements from RFC 4258, and listing the additions needed to each protocol.

GMPLS.quote: The Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) suite of protocols has been defined to control different switching technologies as well as different applications.

OSPF.quote: OSPFv2 [RFC2328] prevents inter-area routes (which are learned from area 0) from being passed back to area 0.

rejected.why: BGP is explicitly excluded as a candidate protocol, with only a short note explaining why.

It is mentioned only as a protocol the algorithm could be adapted to. The document does not specify anything for SCTP.

RFC4654.summary: Specifies TFMCC, a single-rate, TCP-friendly congestion control mechanism for multicast sessions in which receivers compute a TCP-friendly rate and the sender adapts to the limiting receiver, using feedback suppression and loss-event-rate measurement.

IPv6.quote: This document allows support for an IPv6 VPN service over an IPv4 backbone, as well as over an IPv6 backbone.

BGP.why: Defines AFI/SAFI usage, NLRI and next-hop encoding, capability negotiation and multi-AS BGP redistribution approaches.
BGP.quote: The BGP Multiprotocol Extensions [BGP-MP] are used to advertise the IPv6 VPN routes in the MP_REACH Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI).

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are the forwarding substrate; the document does not specify MPLS itself.
Tunnelling options (GRE, IP-in-IP, IPsec, L2TPv3) are used as transport per other RFCs, not defined here.
IPsec-protected tunnels are only mentioned as an option for PE-PE transport.
IPv4/IPv6 interworking is explicitly out of scope; only IPv6 VPN over IPv4 core is covered, which is not a transition mechanism.

RFC4660.title: Functional Description of Event Notification Filtering
RFC4660.summary: RFC 4660 specifies the SIP subscriber, Resource List Server and notifier procedures for placing XML filtering rules in SUBSCRIBE requests and for generating filtered, trigger-driven NOTIFY requests for SIP event notification, with presence and watcher-info examples.

SIMPLE.why: The document is a SIMPLE working group specification extending SIP event notification with filtering, applied to presence and watcher information event packages. SIMPLE is the most specific tag for SIP event notification filtering.
SIMPLE.quote: This document describes the operations a subscriber performs in order to put filtering rules associated with a subscription to event notification information in place.

SIP.why: It extends SIP SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY behaviour with new handling for filter bodies, response codes (200, 202, 415, 488) and the 'badfilter' event reason. Readers of SIP extensions would want it.
SIP.quote: The SIP event notification framework describes the usage of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for subscriptions and notifications of changes to the state of a resource.

rejected.why: PIDF documents appear only as the example content being filtered. The document does not define or extend PIDF.
XML is the encoding of the filter and the filtered content. The filter format itself is defined in RFC 4661, not here.
Presence is used for the examples, but the document is about notification filtering rather than presence or instant messaging.
The document uses the application/simple-filter+xml type but does not register it. Registration is in RFC 4661.

gaps.name: SIP event notification filtering
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for SIP event notification framework or filtering. SIMPLE is the closest fit.

RFC4661.title: An Extensible Markup Language (XML)-Based Format for Event Notification Filtering
RFC4661.summary: Defines an XML format (simple-filter, application/simple-filter+xml) that lets a SIP event subscriber specify what content and which state-change triggers should produce notifications, with XPath-like selection syntax and an extensible schema.

SIMPLE.why: This is a SIMPLE working group document defining a filter format for SIP event notifications (presence/watcher info). It is the event-notification filtering extension SIMPLE covers.
SIMPLE.quote: The SIP event notification framework describes the usage of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for subscriptions and notifications of changes to a state of a resource.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document defines an XML document format, its schema, namespace and extensibility rules, plus an XPath-compatible expression syntax.
XML.quote: The structure of the filter criteria is described using the XML schema.  The filter criteria is presented as an XML document.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new media type, application/simple-filter+xml, and gives its identification rules.
media types.quote: The MIME type for the simple-filter document is "application/ simple-filter+xml".

rejected.why: SIP is the carrier of the subscriptions. The document defines a filter format, not SIP behaviour; SIMPLE is the more specific fit.
PIDF documents are used only as filtering examples; the document does not specify or extend PIDF.
ABNF is only used to write the selection syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
The document registers an XML namespace URN but is not about URN namespaces in general.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to encrypt requests.
The IANA section is boilerplate registration, not the document's subject.

RFC4662.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Event Notification Extension for Resource Lists
RFC4662.summary: Defines a SIP event notification extension (eventlist) letting a subscriber subscribe to a list of resources via a resource list server, with NOTIFY bodies as multipart/related carrying an application/rlmi+xml meta-information document.

SIMPLE.why: The document is a SIMPLE working group specification extending SIP event notification (RFC 3265) with resource list subscriptions, RLS, RLMI and the eventlist option tag, so it belongs under SIMPLE.
SIMPLE.quote: This document presents an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)-Specific Event Notification mechanism for subscribing to a homogeneous list of resources.

rejected.why: SIP is the base protocol being extended, but SIMPLE is the more specific child tag that fits event-notification extensions.
It registers application/rlmi+xml, but that is IANA boilerplate; the main body is about list subscriptions.
RLMI is XML-based, but XML is only the encoding for the new format.
PIDF documents appear only as example payloads in the call flow, not as the subject of the document.
multipart/related is used as the container for notification bodies, but the document does not define MIME itself.
Signing of bodies is discussed only in security considerations and the example.

RFC4663.title: Transferring MIB Work from IETF Bridge MIB WG to IEEE 802.1 WG
RFC4663.summary: Informational plan describing the transfer of bridging-related MIB module development and maintenance from the IETF Bridge MIB WG to the IEEE 802.1 WG, covering OID arcs, IPR/copyright permissions, MIB Doctor review arrangements and freezing of existing IETF Bridge MIB modules.

MIB.why: The whole document concerns who develops and maintains the Bridge MIB modules, how they are registered, reviewed (MIB Doctors, RFC 4181 guidelines), and SMI rules constraining updates.
MIB.quote: transition responsibility for bridging-related MIB modules from the IETF Bridge MIB WG to the IEEE 802.1 WG

IPR.why: A substantial part (Section 3.1, Section 9, Appendix B) addresses copyright and rights permissions needed to hand derivative-work rights to IEEE.
IPR.quote: the IETF does not have sufficient legal authority to make the transfer without the consent of the document authors
IPR.section: 3.1. Transferring Current Bridge MIB WG Documents

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol context for the MIB modules, but the document is about transferring MIB work, not specifying or extending SNMP.
Bridging technology (802.1D/Q) is what the MIBs manage, but the document does not address bridging protocols themselves.
Touches liaison and review processes between SDOs, but is specific to MIB work transfer rather than general IETF process.
OID registration arcs are discussed but no IANA registry guidance is provided; the IANA section states no actions.

RFC4664.title: Framework for Layer 2 Virtual Private Networks (L2VPNs)
RFC4664.summary: Informational framework document defining reference models and functional components (attachment circuits, pseudowires, forwarders, tunnels, signaling, provisioning, auto-discovery) for provider-provisioned Layer 2 VPNs, covering VPWS, VPLS and IPLS.

L2VPN.why: The whole document is the L2VPN framework.
L2VPN.quote: This document provides a framework for Layer 2 Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (L2VPNs).
L2VPN.section: 1.2 Objectives and Scope of the Document

RFC4665.title: Service Requirements for Layer 2 Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks
RFC4665.summary: Informational requirements document for provider-provisioned Layer 2 VPNs (VPWS and VPLS), stating customer, service provider and engineering requirements as a checklist for evaluating L2VPN approaches.

L2VPN.why: The whole document defines service requirements for L2VPNs, covering both point-to-point VPWS and multipoint VPLS, from customer and provider perspectives.
L2VPN.quote: This document provides requirements for Layer 2 Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (L2VPNs).

VPLS.why: VPLS is one of the two L2VPN types. Many requirements cover VSIs, MAC learning, broadcast domains and loop prevention that are specific to VPLS.
VPLS.quote: the PE devices provide a logical interconnect such that CE devices belonging to a specific VPLS appear to be connected by a single LAN.

rejected.why: Pseudowires are the building block that PWE3 encapsulation and congestion techniques are drawn from. The document only says to reuse them and does not specify them.
IPsec appears only as an optional method for securing L2VPN traffic carried over IP. It is not the subject.
QoS requirements are one section among many. The document points to RFC 3809 and RFC 4031 for details.
Ethernet is used as the access and service frame type. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
L2VPN is the more specific child of VPN, so the parent is not listed.

RFC4666.title: Signaling System 7 (SS7) Message Transfer Part 3 (MTP3) - User Adaptation Layer (M3UA)
RFC4666.summary: RFC 4666 specifies M3UA, the SIGTRAN adaptation layer that carries SS7 MTP3-User signalling (ISUP, SCCP) over SCTP between Signalling Gateways and IP-based application servers or between IP server processes, obsoleting RFC 3332.

SIGTRAN.why: M3UA is one of the SIGTRAN adaptation layers for SS7 signalling transport over IP. The whole document defines its messages, procedures and state machines.
SIGTRAN.quote: This memo defines a protocol for supporting the transport of any SS7 MTP3-User signalling (e.g., ISUP and SCCP messages) over IP

rejected.why: SCTP is the transport M3UA runs over. The document uses its associations and streams but defines nothing new about SCTP.
The document concerns SS7 MTP3-User transport, not SIP/ISUP encapsulation.
Media Gateway Controllers are mentioned only as example ASPs. Gateway control protocols are not specified here.
A parent of SIGTRAN, so it is implied and not listed separately.
TCP is mentioned only as an optional alternative transport in back-to-back scenarios.
The IANA section is boilerplate, retained only for historical purposes.

RFC4667.title: Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) Extensions for Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP)
RFC4667.summary: Defines L2TPv3 protocol extensions (new AGI, Local End ID and Interface MTU AVPs, new CDN result codes, forwarder identifiers, tie detection and a generic signaling algorithm) for setting up L2VPN pseudowires between PEs.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TPv3 with new AVPs, result codes and signaling procedures, so it is squarely about L2TP.
L2TP.quote: This document defines the protocol extensions for L2TP to set up different types of L2VPNs in a unified fashion.

L2VPN.why: The document's purpose is signaling L2VPNs (cross-connect, VPLS, VPWS) using L2TP, including forwarder identifiers and pseudowire setup.
L2VPN.quote: Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) applications are typically in the scope of the LAC-LAC reference model.

pseudowire.why: Pseudowire setup, capability negotiation and tie detection are a substantial part of the signaling procedures.
pseudowire.quote: Each L2TP session acts as an emulated circuit, also known as pseudowire.

rejected.why: VPLS is mentioned only as one forwarder type (VSI); the document is not about VPLS specifically.

RFC4668.title: RADIUS Authentication Client MIB for IPv6
RFC4668.summary: Defines the RADIUS Authentication Client MIB module (obsoleting RFC 2618), deprecating the IPv4-only server table and adding a version-neutral IPv4/IPv6 table plus UNITS/REFERENCE clauses.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (RADIUS-AUTH-CLIENT-MIB) with tables, objects, and conformance groups for managing RADIUS authentication clients.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a set of extensions that instrument RADIUS authentication client functions. These extensions represent a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB)

RADIUS.why: The MIB instruments RADIUS client behaviour (Access-Requests, accepts, rejects, timeouts), so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: The objects defined within this memo relate to the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Authentication Client as defined in RFC 2865

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag sits under SNMP and is the more specific fit.
IPv6 appears in the title, but the change is only adding version-neutral InetAddress objects. The document does not specify IPv6 itself.
RADIUS is the more specific tag under AAA, so the parent is not needed.
The port number object refers to the UDP port, but UDP is only the transport.

RFC4669.title: RADIUS Authentication Server MIB for IPv6
RFC4669.summary: Defines the RADIUS Authentication Server MIB module (obsoleting RFC 2619) by deprecating the IPv4-only client table and adding a version-neutral IP address table, for SNMP management of RADIUS servers.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (RADIUS-AUTH-SERVER-MIB) with scalars, tables, and conformance groups for managing RADIUS authentication servers.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a set of extensions that instrument RADIUS authentication server functions. These extensions represent a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB)

RADIUS.why: The MIB instruments RADIUS authentication server behaviour (Access-Request/Accept/Reject/Challenge counters, per-client statistics), so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: The objects defined within this memo relate to the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Authentication Server as defined in RFC 2865

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines a MIB module (tagged MIB, the more specific child) rather than anything about SNMP itself.
The IPv6 aspect is only using version-neutral InetAddress textual conventions in a table; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
RADIUS is the more specific tag covering the AAA protocol here; no general AAA framework is addressed.
Version-neutral address handling is a MIB-level change, not about IP address architecture.

RFC4670.title: RADIUS Accounting Client MIB for IPv6
RFC4670.summary: Defines the RADIUS-ACC-CLIENT-MIB SMIv2 module for managing RADIUS accounting clients, obsoleting RFC 2620 by deprecating the IPv4-only server table and adding a version-neutral (IPv4/IPv6) table.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, objects, and conformance groups for RADIUS accounting clients.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a set of extensions that instrument RADIUS accounting client functions. These extensions represent a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB)

RADIUS.why: The MIB instruments RADIUS accounting client behaviour (requests, responses, timeouts, malformed packets), so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: The objects defined within this memo relate to the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Accounting Client as defined in RFC 2866

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag sits under SNMP and covers this.
IPv6 appears in the title, but the document only adds version-neutral InetAddress objects to a MIB table, not anything about IPv6 itself.
RADIUS is the specific tag under AAA; the document is not about AAA frameworks generally.
UDP port numbers are mentioned only as an object value; the document is not about UDP.

RFC4671.title: RADIUS Accounting Server MIB for IPv6
RFC4671.summary: Defines a MIB module (obsoleting RFC 2621) for managing RADIUS accounting servers, deprecating the IPv4-only client table and adding a version-neutral IP address table.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (RADIUS-ACC-SERVER-MIB) with objects, tables, and conformance statements for managing RADIUS accounting servers.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a set of extensions that instrument RADIUS accounting server functions.  These extensions represent a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB)

RADIUS.why: The MIB instruments RADIUS accounting server behaviour (requests, responses, malformed packets, bad authenticators), so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: The objects defined within this memo relate to the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Accounting Server as defined in RFC 2866

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
IPv6 appears in the title, but the document only switches the address columns to version-neutral InetAddress types; it is not about IPv6 itself.
RADIUS is the more specific tag, and the document does not address AAA frameworks generally.

RFC4672.title: RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client MIB
RFC4672.summary: Defines the RADIUS-DYNAUTH-CLIENT-MIB SMIv2 module for managing the Dynamic Authorization Client (Disconnect and CoA messages per RFC 3576), with per-server counters and conformance groups.

MIB.why: The document's entire content is a MIB module definition (RADIUS-DYNAUTH-CLIENT-MIB) with objects, tables, and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

RADIUS.why: The MIB manages RADIUS dynamic authorization client entities, counting Disconnect and CoA packets exchanged with servers; readers of RADIUS would want this.
RADIUS.quote: it describes the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) (RFC2865) Dynamic Authorization Client (DAC) functions

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines a module, not SNMP itself (MIB covers it).
RADIUS is the more specific tag under AAA; ancestors are implied.
UDP port is only mentioned as a managed object attribute; not about UDP.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate.
Parent of MIB, implied by the more specific tag.

RFC4673.title: RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server MIB
RFC4673.summary: Defines the RADIUS-DYNAUTH-SERVER-MIB SMIv2 module, giving SNMP-managed counters and a client table for a RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server handling Disconnect and CoA messages per RFC 3576.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define an SMIv2 MIB module (RADIUS-DYNAUTH-SERVER-MIB) with scalar objects and a per-client table.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

RADIUS.why: The MIB manages the RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server function, counting Disconnect and CoA packets, so RADIUS readers would expect it.
RADIUS.quote: It is becoming increasingly important to support Dynamic Authorization extensions on the network access server (NAS) devices to handle the Disconnect and Change-of-Authorization (CoA) messages

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific fit.
RADIUS is the more specific child tag; the document does not address AAA frameworks in general.
UDP is mentioned only as the port the DAS listens on; the document is not about UDP.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as boilerplate.

RFC4674.title: Requirements for Path Computation Element (PCE) Discovery
RFC4674.summary: Informational requirements document for an automatic PCE discovery mechanism letting PCCs discover PCEs, their domains, inter-domain functions and capabilities, with scope, policy, security, scalability and manageability requirements.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies requirements for discovering PCEs in the PCE architecture, including location, domains, inter-domain functions and capabilities.
PCE.quote: a set of requirements for a Path Computation Element (PCE) discovery mechanism that would allow a Path Computation Client (PCC) to discover dynamically and automatically a set of PCEs

rejected.why: PCE discovery is a form of service discovery, but the document is specific to PCEs, which the PCE tag covers more specifically.
Section 4.10.2 requires PCE discovery MIB modules but does not define any; it is only a manageability requirement.
IGP areas and ABRs are used as examples of domains; the document is not about OSPF.
Requirements apply equally to MPLS-TE and GMPLS PCEs, but GMPLS is only mentioned as applicability.
TE-LSPs are the context for path computation, not the subject of the document.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering and covers it.

RFC4675.title: RADIUS Attributes for Virtual LAN and Priority Support
RFC4675.summary: Defines four new RADIUS attributes (Egress-VLANID, Ingress-Filters, Egress-VLAN-Name, User-Priority-Table) for dynamic VLAN assignment and user-priority remapping on IEEE 802 ports, usable in RADIUS and Diameter.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS attributes (types 56-59), their packet applicability and encoding, so it belongs on the RADIUS page.
RADIUS.quote: This document proposes additional Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) attributes for dynamic Virtual LAN assignment and prioritization

Diameter.why: A dedicated section gives Diameter AVP flag rules and message mapping, and the abstract says the attributes are usable in Diameter.
Diameter.quote: the attributes defined in this specification can be used as Diameter attribute-value pair (AVPs) from the Code space 1-255

rejected.why: IEEE 802.1Q VLANs and bridges are the subject of the provisioning, but the document is about RADIUS attributes, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
RADIUS and Diameter, the more specific tags, already sit under AAA, so the parent is implied.
The User-Priority-Table attribute remaps 802.1D user priority, but this is a small part of a RADIUS attribute specification and not a QoS architecture or signalling document.
802.1X and EAP are the deployment context only; the document defines no EAP method or EAP behaviour.
RFC 4363 is cited as an analogue for the management variables, but the document defines no MIB module.

RFC4676.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) Option for Civic Addresses Configuration Information
RFC4676.summary: Defines DHCPv4 (code 99) and DHCPv6 (option 37) options carrying civic/postal location of a client or server, with civic address element types (CAtypes), multi-language/script renditions, and a new IANA CAtype registry.

DHCP.why: The document defines a new DHCP option for both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, so it belongs under DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) option containing the civic location of the client or the DHCP server.

DHCPv6.why: It specifies the DHCPv6 option format (OPTION_GEOCONF_CIVIC) in its own section, which readers of DHCPv6 would want.
DHCPv6.quote: The DHCPv6 [6] civic address option refers generally to the client as a whole.

geolocation.why: The document is about conveying civic location information within the GEOPRIV architecture. It defines the address elements and their mapping to PIDF-LO.
geolocation.quote: The Location Configuration Information (LCI) includes information about the country, administrative units such as states, provinces, and cities, as well as street addresses

rejected.why: Emergency calling is the motivation, but the document explicitly leaves emergency-service handling to ECRIT and other applications.
UTF-8 is only the encoding used for the component values. The document defines nothing new about it.
Language and script tags are used in the language and script elements, but the document is not about them.
The document creates a CAtype registry. That is boilerplate-level IANA content and is not a document about IANA registries in general.
The elements align with PIDF-LO, but the document does not specify PIDF.

RFC4677.title: The Tao of IETF - A Novice's Guide to the Internet Engineering Task Force
RFC4677.summary: RFC 4677 (FYI 17) is an informational newcomer's guide to the IETF, explaining its structure, meetings, working groups, BOFs, and the RFC/Internet-Draft standards process.

IETF process.why: The whole document explains how the IETF works: meetings, working groups, BOFs, rough consensus, the IESG, and the standards track.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the inner workings of IETF meetings and Working Groups, discusses organizations related to the IETF, and introduces the standards process.

user guides.why: It is FYI 17, an introductory guide for newcomers, which fits the user guides subject.
user guides.quote: FYIs provide topical and technical overviews that are introductory or appeal to a broad audience

RFC series.why: Section 8 covers RFC kinds, the FYI/BCP/STD sub-series, the RFC Editor's role and Internet Draft formatting.
RFC series.quote: Every IETF standard is published as an RFC (a "Request for Comments," but everyone just calls them RFCs), and every RFC starts out as an Internet Draft

rejected.why: IANA is described briefly as one of the organizations around the IETF. The document is not about IANA registries or their guidance.
Patents and BCP 78/79 get a short subsection (8.4.5). That is not a substantial part of the document.
The NomCom appears only in passing, as the body that selects IESG and IAB members.
The MUST/SHOULD/MAY discussion in 8.4.1 is a small subsection, so the document is not about requirements language.
Jabber is mentioned only as a tool used for meeting chat rooms.

RFC4678.title: Server/Application State Protocol v1
RFC4678.summary: Informational RFC specifying SASP, a binary TLV protocol over long-running TCP connections by which load balancers register server groups with and receive load-distribution weights from a Group Workload Manager.

rejected.why: SSL/TLS is only the security substrate; the document explicitly leaves connection and security to implementations and defines nothing new for TLS.
SASP runs over a long-running TCP connection on port 3860, but TCP is just the transport and nothing new is defined about it.
The document defines an application protocol's own messages, not a binding of another protocol onto a transport.
Strings use UTF-8, but this is an encoding detail, not what the document is about.
A UUID is only mentioned as an example of an LB UID; identifiers are local and unstructured.
The generic applications topic is too broad. SASP is a load-balancing and workload-management protocol, and the taxonomy has no more specific fit.

gaps.name: Load balancing / workload management (SASP, Server/Application State Protocol)
gaps.why: The whole document is about communication between load balancers and workload managers to distribute work across server group members. The taxonomy has no load balancing, server clustering or workload management tag, so no tag fits.

RFC4679.title: DSL Forum Vendor-Specific RADIUS Attributes
RFC4679.summary: Informational RFC defining the DSL Forum's RADIUS vendor-specific attributes (Vendor-Id 3561) that carry DSL line identification, data rate, interleaving delay and encapsulation information from the DSLAM via the BRAS into RADIUS Access and Accounting requests.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS vendor-specific attributes, their encoding, and which RADIUS packet types may carry them, so it extends RADIUS.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes the set of Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service Vendor-Specific Attributes (RADIUS VSAs) defined by the DSL Forum.

DSL.why: The attributes describe DSL access loop characteristics (actual/attainable/min/max rates, interleaving delay, loop encapsulation) for DSL access networks with DSLAM and BRAS.
DSL.quote: These attributes are designed to transport Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) information that is not supported by the standard RADIUS attribute set.

rejected.why: PPPoE tags are only the means by which the DSLAM forwards line information to the BRAS; the document does not specify or extend PPPoE.
DHCP Relay Agent option and Vendor-Specific suboption are only mentioned as sources of the information; not specified here.
RADIUS is the more specific tag; the document does not address AAA frameworks generally.
AAL5 and IPoA appear only as encapsulation values in one attribute, not as a subject of the document.

RFC4680.title: TLS Handshake Message for Supplemental Data
RFC4680.summary: Defines a new TLS handshake message, supplemental_data, negotiated via hello extensions, for carrying application-level supplemental data during the TLS handshake, and creates an IANA registry for supplemental data types.

TLS.why: The document extends the TLS handshake protocol with a new message type, its message flow, and error handling, updating RFC 4346.
TLS.quote: This specification defines a TLS handshake message for exchange of supplemental application data.

rejected.why: Only TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are discussed; datagram TLS is not addressed.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA Considerations and not the main subject of the body.
Authorization data such as SAML assertions is mentioned only as motivating examples; the document defines no authorization mechanism.

RFC4681.title: TLS User Mapping Extension
RFC4681.summary: Defines a TLS extension (user_mapping) and a SupplementalData payload letting clients send unauthenticated user mapping hints (e.g., UPN domain hint) so a server can map a client certificate to a directory account.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS extension (user_mapping) and handshake payload, and updates RFC 4346. TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a TLS extension that enables clients to send generic user mapping hints in a supplemental data handshake message

rejected.why: Client certificates are mapped to accounts, but the document does not profile or specify certificates.
Only TLS 1.0/1.1 are discussed; DTLS is not addressed.
The domain_name field refers to IDNA processing, but only as a minor encoding detail.
A directory is where the account is located, but no directory protocol is specified.
The hint is explicitly unauthenticated. The document extends TLS client authentication handling and does not define an authentication mechanism.

RFC4682.title: Multimedia Terminal Adapter (MTA) Management Information Base for PacketCable- and IPCablecom-Compliant Devices
RFC4682.summary: Defines the PKTC-IETF-MTA-MIB, an SNMP MIB module for managing PacketCable/IPCablecom Multimedia Terminal Adapters, covering device base, provisioning server, and Kerberos/security objects.
