MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a new MIB module (PKTC-IETF-MTA-MIB) in SMIv2 for MTA devices.
MIB.quote: it defines a basic set of managed objects for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)-based management of PacketCable- and IPCablecom-compliant Multimedia Terminal Adapter devices.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through; the document defines MIB objects, so MIB is the more specific tag.
Kerberos realms, tickets and key management timers appear as managed objects, but the document does not specify or extend Kerberos.
DHCP options 43, 60 and 122 are referenced as the sources of object values; DHCP is not specified or extended here.
X.509 certificates are held in objects and referenced for the organization name, but the document does not profile them.
DOCSIS is only context. Cable modems are described, and the S-MTA compliance requires existing DOCSIS MIB groups, but the document is not about DOCSIS.
Real-time signalling in PacketCable uses NCS, not SIP. The MIB covers only provisioning and security, and the NCS signalling MIB is a separate document.

gaps.name: PacketCable / IPCablecom MTA provisioning
gaps.why: The MIB centres on cable-telephony MTA provisioning (DOCSIS cable access, CMS, KDC). The taxonomy has a DOCSIS tag under link layer, but it covers cable access networks rather than PacketCable voice provisioning.

RFC4683.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Subject Identification Method (SIM)
RFC4683.summary: Defines the Subject Identification Method (SIM) and PEPSI hashed-identifier format, carried as an otherName in the X.509 subjectAltName extension, letting a certificate subject prove a privacy-sensitive identifier to relying parties without exposing it, plus an Encrypted PEPSI for certificate requests.

X.509.why: The document defines a new otherName form for the X.509 subjectAltName extension, so it is about X.509 certificate content and profiles.
X.509.quote: This document defines the Subject Identification Method (SIM) for including a privacy-sensitive identifier in the subjectAltName extension of a certificate.

privacy.why: A major goal is letting the subject control disclosure of a sensitive identifier (e.g., SSN) while still proving it, using a salted, password-protected double hash.
privacy.quote: privacy-sensitive identifiers of this sort should not be included in certificates in plaintext form.

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific tag; the document is about certificate content, not PKI operations broadly.
SHA-1/SHA-256 are only the hash functions used inside the construction; the document does not specify them.
ASN.1 is just the notation for the syntax definitions; the document is not about ASN.1.
Certificate request formats (PKCS#10, CRMF) are only carriers for the EPEPSI in regInfo, not specified or extended here.
Stringprep is referenced for password preparation, but PRECIS is a different, later framework and is not the subject.

RFC4684.title: Constrained Route Distribution for Border Gateway Protocol/MultiProtocol Label Switching (BGP/MPLS) Internet Protocol (IP) Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
RFC4684.summary: RFC 4684 defines an MP-BGP Route Target membership NLRI (AFI 1, SAFI 132) that lets BGP speakers exchange RT membership information so VPN route distribution can be constrained inter-AS and for route reflectors, updating RFC 4364.

L3VPN.why: The document extends BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 4364) with constrained route distribution based on Route Targets, and updates RFC 4364. L3VPN readers need it.
L3VPN.quote: PE routers use Route Target (RT) extended communities to control the distribution of routes into VRFs.

BGP.why: It defines a new MP-BGP NLRI type, with its encoding, capability advertisement, path-selection and advertisement rules, and End-of-RIB behaviour.
BGP.quote: Route Target membership NLRI is advertised in BGP UPDATE messages using the MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes

route reflection.why: A main motivation is limiting the VPN routes held by route reflectors. It specifies route reflector and client advertisement rules and the scaling benefits.
route reflection.quote: When advertising RT membership NLRI to a route-reflector client, the Originator attribute shall be set to the router-id of the advertiser

rejected.why: It is only mentioned as another application that uses Route Targets, so it is not the subject.
MPLS is the substrate for BGP/MPLS VPNs, and the document is about BGP route distribution, not MPLS.
L3VPN is the more specific child tag and fits better.
Route Target extended communities are used as keys, but the document does not define or extend the community mechanism.

RFC4685.title: Atom Threading Extensions
RFC4685.summary: Defines Atom syndication format extensions (thr:in-reply-to, the 'replies' link relation with thr:count/thr:updated, and thr:total) for expressing threaded discussions in feeds.

Atom.why: The whole document extends the Atom Syndication Format with new elements and a link relation, so readers of Atom would want it.
Atom.quote: This document defines an extension for expressing threaded discussions within the Atom Syndication Format [RFC4287].

rejected.why: It registers the 'replies' link relation, but this is one part of an Atom extension. The document is not about web linking in general.
The extension elements are XML, but XML is only the encoding substrate. The document defines nothing new about XML itself.
in-reply-to is compared to the RFC 2822 headers, but only as an analogy.
IRIs and URIs are used for identifiers and references, but the document says nothing new about them.
The only IANA content is boilerplate registration of the 'replies' link relation.

RFC4686.title: Analysis of Threats Motivating DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
RFC4686.summary: Informational threat analysis of attackers, bad acts, and attacks against DKIM message signatures and Sender Signing Practices, deriving requirements for the DKIM design.

DKIM.why: The whole document analyses threats to DKIM signatures and signing practices, and derives requirements for DKIM.
DKIM.quote: This document provides an analysis of some threats against Internet mail that are intended to be addressed by signature-based mail authentication, in particular DomainKeys Identified Mail.

rejected.why: Spam and reputation attacks are discussed as motivations, but the document is about DKIM threats, not spam filtering.
DNS is the key-publication substrate; attacks like cache poisoning and amplification are discussed, but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
Mentioned only as the preferred mitigation for falsified key replies, not a subject of the document.
SMTP is explicitly noted as irrelevant to DKIM verification.
DKIM is the more specific tag and already implies this parent.
IDN abuse is one attack (look-alike domains), a brief mention rather than a subject of the document.

RFC4687.title: Operations and Management (OAM) Requirements  for Point-to-Multipoint MPLS Networks
RFC4687.summary: Informational requirements document for data plane OAM (detection, diagnosis, path characterization, SLA measurement, alarms, MIBs, accounting) for point-to-multipoint MPLS LSPs, building on RFC 4377.

MPLS.why: The document specifies OAM requirements for P2MP MPLS LSPs, including P2MP TE LSPs and multicast LDP LSPs. MPLS is the subject technology, and no more specific child tag fits.
MPLS.quote: This document describes requirements for data plane operations and management (OAM) for point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS).

OAM.why: The whole document is about OAM requirements: defect detection, diagnosis, path characterization, alarm suppression and fault notification.
OAM.quote: The ability to diagnose a broken P2MP LSP and to isolate the failed component (i.e., link or node) in the path is REQUIRED.
OAM.section: 4.2. Diagnosis of a Broken Label Switch Path

rejected.why: P2MP LSPs are multicast-like, but the document addresses MPLS OAM, not IP multicast routing or group membership.
P2MP RSVP-TE is referenced as one kind of LSP and as a recovery technique, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Multicast LDP LSPs are mentioned only as one form of P2MP LSP covered by the requirements.
Section 4.9 says existing MPLS MIBs should be extended, but this is a single requirement rather than a main subject.
SLA measurement is one requirement among many, not a substantial focus.
P2MP TE LSPs are among the LSPs covered, but TE is not what the document is about.

RFC4688.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for Aerospace and Defence Industries Association of Europe (ASD) Specification 1000D
RFC4688.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "S1000D" for naming persistent resources (data modules, publication modules, illustrations, etc.) defined by ASD Specification 1000D for technical publications.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration, defining the S1000D NID, its structure, uniqueness, persistence and resolution.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for naming persistent resources defined by Aerospace and Defence Industries Association of Europe (ASD) Specification 1000D.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used as the notation to define the identifier syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
The parent of URN is implied; the document is specifically about a URN namespace.
The IANA registration of the NID is boilerplate-level; the document's body is the namespace definition, not registry guidance.
S1000D uses XML-based standards but the document does not address XML.

RFC4689.title: Terminology for Benchmarking Network-layer Traffic Control Mechanisms
RFC4689.summary: Defines benchmarking terminology (forwarding capacity, forwarding delay, jitter, sequence tracking, and rate/loss/delay/jitter vectors) for measuring IP traffic control and classification mechanisms in a DUT/SUT, especially during congestion.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a benchmarking terminology for network devices under test, defining measurement terms such as Forwarding Capacity, Forwarding Delay and vectors.
benchmarking.quote: This document describes terminology for the benchmarking of devices that implement traffic control using packet classification based on defined criteria.

Diffserv.why: Traffic control is evaluated via DSCP classification and per-hop behaviors, with an undifferentiated-response baseline, so Diffserv readers would want it.
Diffserv.quote: Rules for packet classification can be based on any field in the IP header, such as the Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP)

congestion control.why: Defines Forwarding Congestion and Congestion Management, with measurements of how traffic-control mechanisms deal with congestion.
congestion control.quote: This document introduces several new terms that will allow measurements to be taken during periods of congestion.

rejected.why: The more specific benchmarking tag fits, since this is device benchmarking terminology rather than general performance metrics.
Diffserv is the more specific tag for the QoS mechanism involved.
ECN is only mentioned as a method not used in this methodology.
The benchmarking tag is more specific; the document is domain terminology, not general glossary or requirements language.
RED is only mentioned in passing in the discussion of incipient congestion.

RFC4690.title: Review and Recommendations for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs)
RFC4690.summary: IAB review of problems with Internationalized Domain Names and IDNA (Stringprep, Nameprep, Punycode), recommending IETF/ICANN next steps such as restricting permitted characters, handling Unicode version migration, and registry policy.

IDN.why: The whole document reviews IDNA, its tables, confusables, normalization and Unicode migration, and recommends changes to IDNA.
IDN.quote: This note describes issues raised by the deployment and use of Internationalized Domain Names.

domain registration.why: Substantial parts address registry policy, dispute resolution, IDN TLDs and whois databases for IDNs.
domain registration.quote: The IAB recommends that registries use an inclusion-based model when choosing what characters to allow at the time of registration.

Unicode.why: Section 3 and much of Section 2 address Unicode version migration, normalization and combining characters as they affect IDNA.
Unicode.quote: Unicode is used as the base, and defining, character set for IDNs.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; the document is about IDN labels, not DNS protocol itself. IDN is the more specific tag.
Mentioned only briefly in Section 5.4 as needing non-ASCII support, not a main subject.
Parent topic; the Unicode tag already covers the text-handling aspects and IDN is the specific subject.
Confusable-character spoofing is discussed but is not the primary focus; Security Considerations is boilerplate.
IDN TLDs in the root are discussed, but this is not about reserved or special-use names.

RFC4691.title: Guidelines for Acting as an IETF Liaison to Another Organization
RFC4691.summary: An IAB-stream informational RFC giving guidelines on the mandate, expectations, responsibilities and tasks of IETF liaison managers and representatives to other standards organizations, supplementing RFC 4052.

IETF process.why: The document describes IETF procedures and administration for liaison relationships, including how IETF consensus is conveyed and how liaison statements are handled. This falls under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: This document expands on the role of liaison managers and liaison representatives, giving guidelines on their mandate and the expectations, tasks, and responsibilities placed on them.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the more specific IETF process tag, so it is not listed separately.
IANA appears only in the boilerplate IANA Considerations section, which says there are no requests. The document is not about IANA.
The document mentions RFC number assignment for referencing by other organizations only in passing. It is not about the RFC series.
The terms defined in Section 2.4 are local to this document and cover only a small part of it.

RFC4692.title: Considerations on the IPv6 Host Density Metric
RFC4692.summary: Analyses the HD-Ratio address-efficiency metric used by RIRs for IPv6 allocation, contrasts it with IPv4's fixed 80% efficiency, and suggests a higher HD-Ratio (about 0.94) might be more appropriate.

addressing.why: The document is about address allocation efficiency metrics (HD-Ratio) used by registries to size IPv6 allocations. No child tag fits (CIDR, multihoming, anycast, renumbering are not the focus), so the addressing topic is used directly.
addressing.quote: This memo provides an analysis of the Host Density metric as it is currently used to guide registry allocations of IPv6 unicast address blocks.

IPv6.why: The analysis is specifically about IPv6 unicast address structure (/48 end-site, /32 allocations) and how allocation policy maps customer counts to prefix sizes. Readers of IPv6 deployment and addressing would want it.
IPv6.quote: The general format for IPv6 global unicast addresses is defined in [RFC4291] as follows

rejected.why: IPv4's 80% fixed-efficiency metric is used only as a comparison baseline, not the subject.
Renumbering is mentioned as a consequence of high utilisation thresholds, but the document does not address renumbering procedures.
Prefix-length notation is used, but aggregation and classless routing are not the subject.
Routing hierarchy and aggregation are discussed only as input to the efficiency model, not as the topic.
Concerns RIR allocation policy rather than IANA registries or their stewardship.

gaps.name: Address allocation policy / Regional Internet Registry (RIR) policy
gaps.why: The document is about RIR allocation efficiency metrics (HD-Ratio) and thresholds. The taxonomy has no tag for address registry allocation policy, so it falls under the broader addressing topic.

RFC4693.title: IETF Operational Notes
RFC4693.summary: Defines the IETF Operational Notes (IONs), a new approved-but-ephemeral document series for IETF operational procedures, established as an RFC 3933 process experiment with approval rules, a public store and sunset criteria.

IETF process.why: The document sets up a process experiment under RFC 3933. It covers who approves IONs, how appeals work, and the experiment's success criteria. All of this is IETF procedure and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document series is intended to capture the set of procedures that the IETF follows, but for which the RFC process is an inappropriate documentation vehicle.

rejected.why: IONs are explicitly a separate series from RFCs. The document is about the new series rather than the RFC series's format, style or publication, so it fits IETF process better.
RFC 3978 and RFC 3979 appear only as examples of BCPs that might later be split. The document is not about IPR.
Mailing list management BCPs are mentioned only as possible future split candidates, not as a subject of the document.
HTTP and FTP are mentioned only as ways to reach the ION store. They are substrate and are not specified or extended here.

RFC4694.title: Number Portability Parameters for the "tel" URI
RFC4694.summary: Defines five number-portability parameters (rn, npdi, cic, rn-context, cic-context) for the "tel" URI and the rules for handling, adding and mapping them in call signaling nodes after an NP database dip.

tel URI.why: The RFC extends the tel URI with new NP parameters and specifies their syntax and processing rules; the taxonomy entry explicitly covers tel URI parameters such as number portability.
tel URI.quote: This document defines five parameters in the "tel" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) to carry the number portability (NP)-related information.

rejected.why: SIP is only one of the signaling protocols carrying the tel URI; the document does not specify or extend SIP itself.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax, not a subject of the document.
H.323 is mentioned as another signaling protocol that may carry the URI, but the document is not about it.
Section 5.2.4 maps ISUP parameters to tel URI parameters at gateways, but this is a minor part of a document focused on the URI parameters.
The more specific tel URI tag fits; the document is not about URIs generally.

gaps.name: Number portability
gaps.why: The document is about telephone number portability (NP) information in call routing, and the taxonomy has no tag for it; the tel URI tag captures it only partly.

RFC4695.title: RTP Payload Format for MIDI
RFC4695.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for MIDI commands, including a recovery journal for packet-loss resilience, SDP media type parameters for session configuration, and an mpeg4-generic mode.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is to define an RTP payload format and its media types for MIDI, so it belongs under RTP payload formats.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format for the MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) command language.

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document defines fmtp parameters and SDP session descriptions for configuring streams, with offer/answer and declarative usage.
SDP.quote: Section 6 and Appendices C-D define the media types identifying the payload format, the parameters needed for configuration, and how the parameters are utilized in SDP.

rejected.why: The document is a payload format, which is the more specific child tag. RTP itself is only specified in RFC 3550.
It registers rtp-midi, mpeg4-generic mode and asc media types, but these are IANA boilerplate for the payload format. The document is not about media type registration rules.
SIP is used only for the interoperability examples in Appendix C.7.2. It is not specified or extended here.
RTSP is used only for content-streaming interoperability guidance. The document does not define it.
MIDI is a command language, not an audio codec. The mpeg4-generic mode is a rendering context, so no codec tag fits.
RTCP receiver reports serve as feedback for the closed-loop journal policy. The document does not specify RTCP.

gaps.name: MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface)
gaps.why: The document is about transporting MIDI. The taxonomy has no tag for MIDI or musical-instrument networking.

RFC4696.title: An Implementation Guide for RTP MIDI
RFC4696.summary: Non-normative implementation guide for the RTP MIDI payload format (RFC 4695), using a two-party network musical performance example to describe session setup, sender and receiver algorithms, and recovery journal handling.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an implementation guide for the RTP MIDI payload format, covering sending and receiving algorithms and recovery journal structures specific to that format.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo offers non-normative implementation guidance for the Real-time Protocol (RTP) MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) payload format.

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate. The document's focus is the MIDI payload format, which has its own more specific tag.
RTCP receiver reports are used to trim the recovery journal, but RTCP itself is not specified or extended here.
SDP session descriptions are used as setup examples, but the document is not about SDP.
Unicast UDP is only the transport, and the socket code is incidental.
NAT is mentioned only as a caveat in the session setup and keep-alive discussion.
Section 4.3 lists rate-control methods briefly, but this is not a substantial focus of the document.

gaps.name: MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) / network musical performance
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MIDI or musical performance applications. The RTP payload format tag is the closest fit but does not cover the MIDI-specific content.

RFC4697.title: Observed DNS Resolution Misbehavior
RFC4697.summary: BCP describing observed misbehaviors of DNS iterative resolvers (requeries, lame server retries, aggressive retransmission, bad NS records, etc.) that burden root and TLD servers, with implementation recommendations.

DNS.why: The whole document analyses and gives operational and implementation advice on DNS resolver and server behaviour.
DNS.quote: This memo describes DNS iterative resolver behavior that results in a significant query volume sent to the root and top-level domain (TLD) name servers.

DNS update.why: A full section recommends how dynamic update agents should locate the zone, instead of probing with UPDATE messages.
DNS update.quote: Dynamic update agents SHOULD send SOA or NS queries to progressively higher-level names to find the closest enclosing zone

rejected.why: AS112 black-hole servers are mentioned only in passing as a possible target for numeric TLD delegations.
Not discussed anywhere in the document.
Not discussed; security considerations concern DoS load only.

RFC4698.title: IRIS: An Address Registry (areg) Type for the Internet Registry Information Service
RFC4698.summary: Defines the "areg" registry type for IRIS, an XML schema of queries and results for looking up IP network, autonomous system, contact and organization records held by Internet address registries.

WHOIS.why: IRIS is a registration-data lookup service that replaces WHOIS. This document defines its address-registry queries and results (networks, ASNs, contacts, organizations). It is the closest fit in the taxonomy, which has no IRIS tag.
WHOIS.quote: This document describes an IRIS registry schema for IP address and Autonomous System Number information.

rejected.why: The schema is written in XML Schema, but XML is only the encoding. The document is not about XML usage in general.
The BEEP transport is referenced only in a short compliance section, and only to say the default patterns apply.
The document deals with IP address registry records and nesting of ranges for lookup. It does not address IP address architecture or allocation itself.
DNS is used only for NAPTR-based top-down resolution of areg.iris.arpa and for name server fields. The document is not about DNS.
RDAP is a later, different protocol. It is not specified or discussed here.
The registry type covers address and ASN registries, not domain registration. The more specific WHOIS tag already covers the lookup-service aspect.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The document extends IRIS with a new registry type. The taxonomy has no IRIS tag, so readers browsing IRIS and CRISP registry types cannot find it directly.

RFC4701.title: A DNS Resource Record (RR) for Encoding Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Information (DHCID RR)
RFC4701.summary: Defines the DHCID DNS resource record (type 49), which stores a SHA-256 hash of a DHCP client identifier plus FQDN so DHCP clients and servers can resolve conflicts in dynamic DNS updates.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS resource record type, including its RDATA format, presentation format and IANA registries, so it belongs under DNS.
DNS.quote: The DHCID RR is defined with mnemonic DHCID and type code 49.  The DHCID RR is only defined in the IN class.

DHCP.why: A large part of the document specifies how DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 client identifiers (DUID, Client Identifier option, htype/chaddr) are used to compute the RDATA, and how DHCP updaters behave. Readers of DHCP would want it.
DHCP.quote: DHCP clients or servers use the DHCID RR to associate a DHCP client's identity with a DNS name

rejected.why: The RR is used in dynamic updates, but the document does not specify the update protocol. It only defines the record that updaters use for conflict detection.
SHA-256 is used only as the digest algorithm for the record. The document is not about the hash family.
DHCPv6 identifiers are one input among several. The document is not specifically about DHCPv6, so the DHCP tag is the better fit.
Base64 is only the presentation encoding for the RDATA.

RFC4702.title: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Client Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) Option
RFC4702.summary: Defines the DHCPv4 Client FQDN option (code 81) by which clients and servers exchange the client's FQDN and negotiate who performs the A and PTR DNS updates.

DHCP.why: The document defines a new DHCPv4 option and specifies client and server behaviour for it, so it belongs under DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies a DHCP option, the Client FQDN option, which can be used by DHCP clients and servers to exchange information about the client's fully qualified domain name

DNS update.why: A large part of the document covers which party performs dynamic DNS updates of A and PTR records, plus TTLs and conflicts. Readers of DNS update would want it.
DNS update.quote: who has the responsibility for updating the DNS with the associated A and PTR RRs.

rejected.why: DNS is the thing being updated, but the document defines no DNS protocol or record changes. The more specific DNS update tag covers it.
This is DHCPv4 only. The DHCPv6 FQDN option is defined elsewhere.
EDNS0 is mentioned only as a reason to deprecate the RCODE fields.
It deals with FQDNs and mentions the Host Name option, but it is not about host naming conventions or host tables.

RFC4703.title: Resolution of Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) Conflicts among Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Clients
RFC4703.summary: Specifies how DHCP clients and servers use the DHCID RR with DNS UPDATE to detect and resolve FQDN conflicts when adding or removing A, AAAA and PTR records.

DNS update.why: The document defines procedures for performing dynamic DNS updates (prerequisites, RCODE handling, add/delete sequences) to resolve name conflicts, so it belongs under Dynamic DNS updates.
DNS update.quote: The updater prepares a DNS UPDATE request that includes as a prerequisite the assertion that the FQDN does not exist.

DHCP.why: The document is about the behaviour of DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 clients and servers when they update DNS on behalf of clients, including client identifiers and lease expiry or release handling.
DHCP.quote: This document identifies situations in which conflicts in the use of FQDNs may arise among DHCP clients and servers

rejected.why: The document covers DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 equally, so the parent DHCP tag fits better than the DHCPv6 child.
DNS UPDATE and the DHCID RR are the specific subject, and the DNS update tag already sits under DNS.
The document explicitly says the DHCID mechanism is advisory and not a substitute for DNS security. It only briefly mentions TSIG in the security considerations.
FQDNs are the objects being managed, but the document does not address host naming conventions or host tables.

gaps.name: DHCID resource record
gaps.why: The document's strategy rests on the DHCID RR, which is specified in RFC 4701. The taxonomy has no tag for DNS resource record types or the DHCID RR, so DNS update is the nearest fit.

RFC4704.title: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) Client Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) Option
RFC4704.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 Client FQDN option (code 39), by which clients and servers exchange the client's FQDN and negotiate who performs the AAAA and PTR DNS updates.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option and specifies client and server behaviour for it.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies a new DHCPv6 option, the Client FQDN option, which can be used by DHCPv6 clients and servers to exchange information

DNS update.why: A substantial part of the document negotiates who performs dynamic DNS updates, covering RR TTLs, deletion of records and update conflicts. It does not define the update protocol itself.
DNS update.quote: about who has the responsibility for updating the DNS with the associated AAAA and PTR RRs

rejected.why: DNS RRs are the subject of the updates, but the document adds nothing to DNS itself. The more specific DNS update tag already covers the DNS side.
The option is carried in DHCPv6 and concerns IPv6 addresses, but the document does not address IPv6 specification or addressing.
The document deals with FQDNs only as option content for DNS updates, not with host naming conventions.

RFC4705.title: GigaBeam High-Speed Radio Link Encryption
RFC4705.summary: Describes GigaBeam's WiFiber radio link security: a custom AES-GCM link-frame protocol for subscriber traffic, IPsec ESP for management traffic, and IKEv1 key management with certificates.

IKE.why: A large part of the document specifies how IKEv1 is profiled for the radio link: Phase 1 and 2 modes, Oakley group 14, a new protocol identifier and transform, ID types, and keying material.
IKE.quote: In the GigaBeam environment, the Phase 1 exchange is IKE Aggressive Mode with signatures and certificates.

AES.why: The core of the document is the use of AES-GCM to encrypt and authenticate radio link frames. It defines the counter block construction, the 96-bit tag, and the key and salt usage.
AES.quote: AES-GCM [GCM] with a custom security protocol specified in this document to provide confidentiality and integrity protection of subscriber traffic on the radio link

IPsec.why: IPsec ESP with AES-CBC and HMAC-SHA-1 protects management traffic. The document also registers a new IPsec security protocol identifier, PROTO_GIGABEAM_RADIO, for the IPsec DOI.
IPsec.quote: IPsec ESP [ESP] is used in the usual fashion to protect all non-IKE traffic on the data control channel.

rejected.why: PPP only runs over the serial data channel to create a two-node IP network. It is substrate, not the subject.
HMAC-SHA-1 is used only as a mechanism within ESP and IKE. The document does not specify or extend it.
Certificates are used for authentication, and the document gives a name format. This is minor, and the document is not about X.509 profiles.
RSA signatures are only the authentication mechanism used within IKE.
ESP is used in the standard way for management traffic. The document adds nothing new to ESP itself.
The product is a proprietary point-to-point radio link, not IEEE 802.11. IP over 802.11 is not covered.

gaps.name: Point-to-point radio link encryption / link-layer encryption
gaps.why: The document is about securing a proprietary high-speed wireless link frame format (FEC, scrambling, AES-GCM framing). The taxonomy has no tag for link-layer encryption or non-IP radio links.

RFC4706.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line 2 (ADSL2)
RFC4706.summary: RFC 4706 defines the ADSL2-LINE MIB, an SNMP MIB module for managing ADSL, ADSL2 and ADSL2+ lines, including line/channel configuration profiles, status, performance monitoring counters, and threshold notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (ADSL2-LINE-MIB and its TC MIB) using SMIv2 for managing ADSL2 interfaces.
MIB.quote: This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for use with network management protocols in the Internet community

DSL.why: The managed subject is the DSL access line itself (ATU-C/ATU-R, G.992.x modes, DELT, rate adaptation, power states), so DSL readers would expect it.
DSL.quote: it describes objects used for managing parameters of the "Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line" family of interface types: ADSL, ADSL2, ADSL2+, and their variants.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself. MIB tag, a child of SNMP, covers it.
ATM status bits appear for the data path, but the document is not about IP over ATM.
Only SMIv2 is used; no YANG.
Not about access node control protocol; only manages DSL lines.
PM counters and thresholds are part of the MIB objects, but not a general performance measurement methodology.

RFC4707.title: Netnews Administration System (NAS)
RFC4707.summary: Defines the Netnews Administration System (NAS), an experimental TCP client-server protocol and hierarchical database for distributing signed administrative data about Usenet newsgroups and hierarchies to news servers, administrators and readers, outside of control messages.

Netnews.why: The whole document specifies a protocol and database for administering newsgroups and hierarchies in Netnews. Readers browsing Netnews would expect it there.
Netnews.quote: NAS is a framework to simplify the administration and usage of network news (also known as Netnews) on the Internet.

rejected.why: NAS is explicitly out-of-band and does not use NNTP commands. It is only loosely inspired by NNTP.
PGP signing and key blocks are used for data authenticity, but this is a supporting mechanism. The document does not specify or extend OpenPGP.
The document compares NAS to DNS, LDAP and NIS, but it defines a separate news-specific protocol, not a directory service.
Registers application/nasdata only in IANA Considerations boilerplate. The main body is not about media type rules.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify commands, not the subject.
DNS is mentioned only as an analogy for the hierarchical root-server design.

RFC4708.title: CellML Media Type
RFC4708.summary: Registers the application/cellml+xml media type for CellML Umbrella 1.0 mathematical model documents, following the +xml suffix convention of RFC 3023.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration template for application/cellml+xml, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document standardises a new media type -- application/cellml+xml -- for use in exchanging mathematical models represented in a CellML Umbrella 1.0 compliant markup language.

XML.why: CellML is an XML-based format and the registration covers XML-specific charset handling, interoperability and security rules. It is a substantial part of the document but secondary to the media type registration.
XML.quote: As all well-formed CellML Umbrella documents are also well-formed XML documents, the convention described in Section 7 of [RFC3023] has been observed by use of the +xml suffix.

rejected.why: The document only registers a subtype and does not define MIME body structure or encodings. The more specific media types tag covers it.
UTF-8 is only mentioned as a required charset for CellML documents. It is not a subject of the document.
Email appears only as an example in the Security Considerations about retrieval of external URLs.
URLs are referenced only in security considerations about external resource retrieval.

gaps.name: CellML (mathematical model interchange format)
gaps.why: The document is about a specific scientific modelling markup language. No taxonomy tag covers domain-specific XML formats of this kind.

RFC4709.title: Mounting Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) Servers
RFC4709.summary: Defines the application/davmount+xml media type and a small XML format (dm:mount) that lets a WebDAV server tell a browser to hand off a collection URL to the user's native WebDAV client for mounting.

WebDAV.why: The whole document extends WebDAV deployment with a mount-description format for WebDAV clients and servers.
WebDAV.quote: This document specifies a mechanism and a document format that enables WebDAV servers to send "mounting" information to a WebDAV client.

media types.why: The mechanism depends on dispatch by a newly registered media type, and Section 6.1 gives the full registration, so readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: The browser in turn passes the content to the application that was registered to handle the "application/davmount+xml" MIME type

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for the mount document. The document defines no general XML usage.
The document relies on HTTP for retrieval and caching headers but specifies nothing new about HTTP.
The document uses URI syntax for the dm:url and dm:open values. Its brief discussion of custom URI schemes is in an appendix and is not the subject of the document.
The document uses MIME-type dispatch but does not address MIME body structure or encodings. The media types tag covers the registration.

RFC4710.title: Real-time Application Quality-of-Service Monitoring (RAQMON) Framework
RFC4710.summary: Defines the RAQMON framework, an RMON extension in which end-devices (RDS) report application-level QoS metrics to report collectors (RRC), with PDU information model, transport requirements, congestion-safe operation, and predefined metrics.

performance measurement.why: The document defines application QoS metrics (delay, jitter, loss, discards) and a monitoring architecture, which is performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines the framework, architecture, relevant metrics, and transport requirements for real-time QoS monitoring of applications.

RMON.why: RAQMON is explicitly an extension of the RMON family, with an RRC implementing a RAQMON MIB extending the RMON MIB.
RMON.quote: This memo extends the remote network monitoring (RMON) family of specifications to allow real-time quality-of-service (QoS) monitoring

rejected.why: The MIB itself is defined in RFC 4711; this framework document only references it.
RTP is referenced for metric methodologies (RFC 3550) but the document is not about RTP.
SNMP is an optional transport mapping, specified in RFC 4712, not the subject here.
TCP is the mandatory transport for RAQMON PDUs but only as substrate.
Section 3 covers congestion-safe operation, but it is a small part of the document and not its main subject.
The document monitors QoS rather than defining QoS architectures or signalling.

RFC4711.title: Real-time Application Quality-of-Service Monitoring (RAQMON) MIB
RFC4711.summary: Defines the RAQMON MIB module, an SMIv2 extension of the RMON MIB, giving a RAQMON Report Collector tables of per-session participant and QoS data, exception thresholds with notifications, and collector configuration objects.

MIB.why: The whole document is an SMIv2 MIB module (RAQMON-MIB) extending the RMON MIB, so readers of MIB modules would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

performance measurement.why: The MIB holds collected QoS metrics (delay, jitter, packet loss, discards) for real-time sessions, with exception thresholds. This is performance measurement of applications.
performance measurement.quote: it describes managed objects used for real-time application Quality of Service (QoS) monitoring.

rejected.why: The MIB extends RFC 2819 and sits under the rmon subtree, but it does not define or change RMON itself. It only imports the rmon OID and registers under it.
SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The SNMP transport mapping of RAQMON PDUs is in RFC 4712, not here.
The document monitors QoS metrics but does not define a QoS architecture or signalling. It reports DSCP and L2 priority values only as measured data.
RTP appears only through the payload-type references. The document is not about RTP.
DSCP values are reported as monitored fields only; Diffserv itself is not specified or analysed.

gaps.name: RAQMON (Real-time Application QoS Monitoring)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the RAQMON framework, its data sources and collectors, or its PDU transport. RFC 4710 and RFC 4712 are its sibling documents. The MIB tag and the performance measurement tag only partly cover it.

RFC4712.title: Transport Mappings for Real-time Application Quality-of-Service Monitoring (RAQMON) Protocol Data Unit (PDU)
RFC4712.summary: Specifies two transport mappings for the RAQMON PDU (RFC 4710 information model): native TCP with a binary PDU format and optional TLS protection, and SNMP notifications via a new RAQMON-RDS-MIB module.

transport mapping.why: The document's purpose is to map the RAQMON PDU onto TCP and SNMP transports, which is the transport mapping topic.
transport mapping.quote: This memo specifies two transport mappings of the Real-Time Application Quality-of-Service Monitoring (RAQMON) information model defined in RFC 4710 using TCP as a native transport

MIB.why: Defines the new RAQMON-RDS-MIB module (SMIv2) with notification objects, a substantial normative part of the document.
MIB.quote: The RAQMON RDS MIB module is used to map RAQMON PDUs onto SNMP Notifications for transport purposes.

performance measurement.why: The PDU carries application QoS metrics (delay, jitter, loss) reported from data sources to collectors, so performance measurement readers would want it.
performance measurement.quote: RAQMON monitoring carried by the common protocol data unit (PDU) used between a RDS and RRC to report QoS statistics.

TLS.why: Defines a StartTLS request/response PDU exchange, sequencing, and identity checks for using TLS with RAQMON over TCP.
TLS.quote: The protection of a RAQMON session starts with the RDS client's StartTLS request upon successful establishment of the TCP session.

rejected.why: SNMP notifications are the carrier; the document defines a MIB module (tagged MIB) but does not extend the SNMP protocol itself.
TCP is merely the substrate used to carry PDUs; nothing new is specified about TCP.
RTP is referenced only for the DSRC generation algorithm and payload types, not a subject of the document.
RAQMON extends the RMON family conceptually but this document does not specify RMON MIB objects beyond placing its module under the rmon OID.
UDP is the underlying transport of SNMP and mentioned only for congestion considerations.
Congestion safety is a short section relying on TCP and RFC 4710 rather than new congestion control content.

gaps.name: RAQMON (Real-time Application QoS Monitoring)
gaps.why: The document is about the RAQMON framework's PDU and transports, but the taxonomy has no tag for RAQMON or application-level QoS monitoring.

RFC4713.title: Registration and Administration Recommendations for Chinese Domain Names
RFC4713.summary: Informational RFC specifying how CNNIC and TWNIC register Chinese domain name labels, applying the RFC 3743 JET variant-table procedure to Simplified and Traditional Chinese so each name gets SC and TC forms.

IDN.why: The document defines how internationalized domain labels containing Chinese characters are registered, using variant tables on top of IDNA. This is IDN registration practice.
IDN.quote: This memo builds on the basic concepts, general guidelines, and framework of RFC 3743 to specify proposed registration and administration procedures for Chinese domain names.

rejected.why: The document does concern registry procedures, but the IDN tag is more specific to its subject. The registry operations it describes are about IDN variant handling, not registry or registrar protocols.
Zone file entries are mentioned only as where the variant labels end up. The document does not change DNS protocol or operations.
The Chinese character tables are central, but the document is about domain label registration rather than Unicode usage in protocols generally.
The IANA language tables are referenced as the source of the character tables. The document is not about IANA registry administration.

RFC4714.title: Requirements for IETF Technical Publication Service
RFC4714.summary: Sets out the IETF's requirements for its technical publisher (the RFC Editor): the publication tasks, derived requirements and performance goals for producing, indexing and distributing IETF technical specifications.

RFC series.why: The whole document is about RFC publication: editing, identifiers (RFC numbers), errata, the index and archive, and publisher performance goals. This is the RFC Series subject.
RFC series.quote: This document sets forth requirements on the duties of the IETF technical publisher and how it interacts with the IETF in the production of those publications.

IETF process.why: It describes how publication fits into the IETF standards process (WGLC, IESG review, shepherd and AD roles) and the IETF-side process implications in Section 5.
IETF process.quote: Under the IETF standards process stream, the post-approval processing is initiated by the IESG after technical approval.
IETF process.section: 2.1. Stages in the Technical Specification Publication Lifetime

rejected.why: IANA parameter value insertion is one small task (Section 3.6). It is not a substantial part of the document.
The document only says the publisher should validate formal languages such as ABNF, XML and ASN.1. It does not specify those languages.
MIBs are mentioned only as an example of formal language to validate and of boilerplate to preserve.
Section 3.18 on a vocabulary document says the RFC Editor does not maintain one and derives no requirements.

RFC4715.title: The Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) Subaddress Encoding Type for tel URI
RFC4715.summary: Defines a new optional tel URI parameter, "isub-encoding", that carries the encoding type of an ISDN subaddress so ISUP/SIP gateways can interwork correctly with the "isub" parameter.

tel URI.why: The document's whole purpose is to define a new parameter for the tel URI, extending the "isub" parameter of RFC 3966.
tel URI.quote: this document specifies a new optional tel URI parameter to carry the encoding type of ISDN subaddress.

ISDN.why: The ISDN subaddress and its NSAP encoding (AFI, IA5, BCD) are the substance. The appendices describe the Q.931 subaddress information element and NSAP structure, and gateway behaviour is specified for ISDN-SIP interconnection.
ISDN.quote: Without a tel URI parameter to carry an encoding type of ISDN subaddress, the problems described in Sections 3.1. and 3.2. might be observed.

rejected.why: SIP is only the network the tel URI travels in. The document defines nothing new about SIP itself.
The document concerns ISUP/SIP interworking, but it only defines a tel URI parameter. It does not specify ISUP encapsulation as in SIP-T.
Gateway interworking is the motivation, but the work is the tel URI parameter and ISDN subaddress encoding. The tags tel URI and ISDN fit more specifically.
ABNF is only used to write the syntax of the new parameter.

RFC4716.title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Public Key File Format
RFC4716.summary: RFC 4716 documents the existing SSH public key file format (BEGIN/END markers, RFC822-style headers, base64 body) for exchanging public keys between SSH implementations, and defines a textual MD5-based public key fingerprint representation.

SSH.why: The whole document specifies an SSH-related file format and SSH public key fingerprints, so SSH readers would want it.
SSH.quote: This document formally documents an existing public key file format in use for exchanging public keys between different Secure Shell (SSH) implementations.

rejected.why: MD5 is only the hash used to compute fingerprints; the document is not about MD5 itself.
PEM is mentioned only to contrast formats in Section 3.5; the document does not specify or extend it.
Base64 is just the encoding used for the key body, with no new specification.
PKI is mentioned only in passing; the document covers raw public key files, not PKI.
The header-tag registry appears only in IANA Considerations boilerplate.
OpenPGP is mentioned only in a comparison of formats.

RFC4717.title: Encapsulation Methods for Transport of Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) over MPLS Networks
RFC4717.summary: Specifies encapsulation of ATM cells and AAL5 frames in pseudowires over MPLS PSNs, including control words, cell and AAL5 modes, OAM handling, and ATM-specific interface parameters.

pseudowire.why: The document defines the ATM pseudowire encapsulations (N-to-one, one-to-one, AAL5 SDU/PDU) and procedures for providing an ATM service over a PW.
pseudowire.quote: An Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) Pseudowire (PW) is used to carry ATM cells over an MPLS network.

ATM.why: Substantial content concerns ATM cells, VCC/VPC, AAL5, OAM and ILMI behaviour, so readers of ATM and IP over ATM would want it.
ATM.quote: ATM cell ordering can be preserved using the OPTIONAL sequence field in the control word

rejected.why: MPLS is the PSN carrying the pseudowire; the pseudowire tag is more specific and the document only uses MPLS labels and TTL/S-bit as substrate.
PW signalling via LDP is defined in RFC 4447; this document only references it for status and interface parameters.
ECMP is mentioned only as a reason for the control word, not a subject of the document.
Diffserv appears only in the informational class-of-service mapping and congestion sections.
ATM OAM cell handling is a section, but the main subject is the encapsulation; the pseudowire and ATM tags cover it better.

RFC4718.title: IKEv2 Clarifications and Implementation Guidelines
RFC4718.summary: Informational document that clarifies ambiguous areas of the IKEv2 specification (IKE_SA creation, authentication, CHILD_SA creation and rekeying, exchange collisions, configuration payloads) to improve interoperability, without changing the protocol.

IKE.why: The whole document is about IKEv2 behaviour: IKE_SA_INIT, cookies, AUTH, CREATE_CHILD_SA, rekeying, collisions, configuration payloads, and implementation mistakes.
IKE.quote: This document clarifies many areas of the IKEv2 specification that may be difficult to understand to developers not intimately familiar with the specification

rejected.why: IPsec architecture (ESP/AH, SAs, PAD) is the context IKEv2 negotiates for, but the document's subject is IKEv2 itself, which is a child tag.
EAP is discussed only for the identity type and PRF key size when used within IKEv2 authentication. It is not specified or extended here.
RSA signature hash and encoding are clarified as part of AUTH payload handling, in a small section only. The document is not about RSA.
ESP appears only as the SA type that IKEv2 negotiates, not as a subject of the document.
NAT traversal port 4500 details are minor clarifications within IKEv2 (sections 7.5 and 7.6).
RADIUS is mentioned only as the way an AAA server communicates the authenticated identity, and in comparisons of address attributes.

RFC4719.title: Transport of Ethernet Frames over Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3)
RFC4719.summary: Specifies how Ethernet port and Ethernet VLAN frames are carried as pseudowires over L2TPv3, covering PW signalling, status monitoring via SLI/Circuit Status AVP, encapsulation, MTU handling and applicability.

L2TP.why: The document defines the Ethernet pseudowire types, session establishment, status signalling and encapsulation for L2TPv3, so it extends L2TP.
L2TP.quote: This document describes the transport of Ethernet frames over the Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol, Version 3 (L2TPv3).

pseudowire.why: It specifies Ethernet port and Ethernet VLAN pseudowire emulation, including an applicability statement and congestion considerations for PWs.
pseudowire.quote: The mechanism described in this document can be used in the creation of Pseudowires to transport Ethernet frames over an IP network.

Ethernet.why: A substantial part covers Ethernet frame and VLAN handling: preamble/FCS stripping, VLAN tag rewriting, link status and QoS mapping for Ethernet emulation.
Ethernet.quote: The PW termination point receives untagged (also referred to as 'raw') or tagged Ethernet frames and delivers them unaltered to the PW termination point

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an option for payload integrity transparency; not a subject of the document.
The 802.1p to DS field mapping is mentioned but explicitly left out of scope.
Section 5 gives brief congestion guidance but offers no mechanism, so it is not a primary subject.
Pseudowire emulation here runs over L2TPv3 and IP, not MPLS.
UDP appears only as an optional encapsulation of L2TPv3 and as a factor in the MTU calculation.

RFC4720.title: Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) Frame Check Sequence Retention
RFC4720.summary: Defines an optional mechanism, with LDP and L2TPv3 signaling, for retaining the original Frame Check Sequence across Ethernet, Frame Relay, HDLC and PPP pseudowires instead of stripping it at ingress and regenerating it at egress.

pseudowire.why: The whole document extends PWE3 pseudowire encapsulations with FCS retention and defines the signaling for it, including an MPLS/LDP interface parameter.
pseudowire.quote: This document defines a mechanism for preserving Frame Check Sequence (FCS) through Ethernet, Frame Relay, High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC), and PPP pseudowires.

L2TP.why: A full section defines a new L2TPv3 AVP, with its format and negotiation rules, for signaling FCS retention. L2TP readers need this.
L2TP.quote: When using the signaling procedures in [7], the FCS Retention AVP, Attribute Type 92, is used.
L2TP.section: 4. Signaling FCS Retention with L2TPv3-Based Pseudowires

rejected.why: The FCS is the thing being carried, but the document doesn't define polynomials or error-detection algorithms. It only decides whether to retain the FCS.
The document uses LDP signaling (a new interface parameter sub-TLV) but doesn't specify or extend LDP itself. The pseudowire tag already covers it.
Ethernet is one of the carried payload types. The document is about pseudowire encapsulation, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Frame Relay is only a payload type that pseudowires carry. The document does not address Frame Relay networking or IP interworking.
PPP is only a payload type that pseudowires carry. The document does not specify or extend PPP.
MPLS is the underlying transport for the pseudowires. The document does not define anything new about MPLS itself.

RFC4721.title: Mobile IPv4 Challenge/Response Extensions (Revised)
RFC4721.summary: Defines Mobile IPv4 Challenge extensions for agent advertisements and registration requests, plus a generalized Mobile-AAA authentication extension, so foreign agents can authenticate mobile nodes and protect against replay; obsoletes RFC 3012 and updates RFC 3344.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document specifies new Mobile IPv4 extensions, error codes and processing rules for mobile node, foreign agent and home agent, and updates RFC 3344.
Mobile IPv4.quote: we define extensions for the Mobile IP Agent Advertisements and the Registration Request that allow a foreign agent to use a challenge/ response mechanism to authenticate the mobile node.

rejected.why: Only the CHAP_SPI authenticator computation is made compatible with RADIUS servers. RADIUS itself is not specified or extended.
AAA infrastructure is referenced as an external verification infrastructure and is explicitly out of scope. The document defines only a Mobile IP extension.
MD5 and HMAC-MD5 are used as authenticator algorithms, but the document is not about the hash functions.
The authentication here is specific to Mobile IPv4, which is the more specific tag already chosen.
The Router Discovery (RFC 1256) advertisement is extended with a Challenge extension, but ICMP itself is not the subject.

RFC4722.title: Media Server Control Markup Language (MSCML) and Protocol
RFC4722.summary: RFC 4722 specifies MSCML, an XML markup carried in SIP INVITE and INFO requests for controlling a media server's advanced conferencing, IVR (play, collect, record), call-leg events and fax functions.

SIP.why: MSCML is defined as payloads for SIP INVITE and INFO, with SIP dialogs as the control context and a justified use of INFO. It extends SIP-based media server control.
SIP.quote: Media Server Control Markup Language (MSCML) is a markup language used in conjunction with SIP to provide advanced conferencing and interactive voice response (IVR) functions.

conferencing.why: A major part of the document covers advanced conferencing: control leg, leg configuration, active talker events, personalized mixes and video switching. It fits the generic conferencing topic and is not XCON itself.
conferencing.quote: MSCML serves as the interface between the conference server or focus and a centralized conference mixer.

MRCP.why: The IVR half of MSCML (play, playcollect, playrecord) provides media resource control similar to MRCP and VoiceXML speech services. It is the nearest taxonomy fit for media server IVR control.
MRCP.quote: The second class comprises primitives for interactive voice response (IVR).  These include collecting DTMF digits and playing and recording multimedia content.

media types.why: The document registers the application/mediaservercontrol+xml media type, a minor but real contribution.
media types.quote: MIME subtype name: mediaservercontrol+xml

rejected.why: XML and an XML Schema are the encoding for MSCML, so they are the substrate and not the subject.
The document is cited as input to the XCON work and satisfies RFC 4353, but it does not define the XCON framework or data model.
It includes faxrecord/faxplay for T.30/T.38 fax, but these are a small part of the document. The taxonomy tag is about fax over Internet mail and IP, not media-server fax control.
SDP appears only as a co-carried body part, for example hold SDP, and is not specified or extended.
Media flows over RTP, but the document does not address RTP itself.
HTTP is used for content fetch and the managecontent put and post operations, but only as a mechanism.

gaps.name: Media server control / IVR (MSCML)
gaps.why: The document is about application-level media server control. The taxonomy has no media server control tag apart from MRCP, which is a speech-services protocol, so MRCP is only an approximate fit.

RFC4723.title: Registration of Media Type audio/mobile-xmf
RFC4723.summary: Registers the audio/mobile-xmf media type for Mobile XMF files (SP-MIDI and Mobile DLS content), defining its optional parameters (revision, prl, minimum-pr, total-pr) and other registration template fields.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration template for audio/mobile-xmf, with parameters, encoding and interoperability considerations.
media types.quote: This document registers the media type audio/mobile-xmf.

rejected.why: Only cited as a suitable encoding for email transport of the binary data; the document does not define anything about it.
The MIME registration is covered by the more specific media types tag; the document does not address MIME body structure or encodings generally.
Mobile XMF is a file container for MIDI data, but the document only registers the media type and does not define a codec or container format.
The IANA section merely states that one subtype is registered; it is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: MIDI / Mobile XMF (musical instrument data formats)
gaps.why: The document is about a MIDI-related audio file format (Mobile XMF, SP-MIDI, Mobile DLS), but the taxonomy has no tag for MIDI or synthetic audio formats.

RFC4724.title: Graceful Restart Mechanism for BGP
RFC4724.summary: Defines the BGP Graceful Restart Capability (code 64), the End-of-RIB marker, and procedures and FSM changes for retaining stale routes across BGP session restarts to avoid routing flaps.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new capability, End-of-RIB marker, restarting/receiving speaker procedures, and modifications to the BGP finite state machine.
BGP.quote: A new BGP capability, termed "Graceful Restart Capability", is defined that would allow a BGP speaker to express its ability to preserve forwarding state during BGP restart.

rejected.why: TCP session termination is the trigger for the procedures, but the document does not specify or extend TCP; it is only the transport.
BFD is mentioned only as an example way to check peer forwarding viability and is out of scope; it is not in the taxonomy as a subject for this document.
The IANA section only registers capability code 64; this is boilerplate, not the document's subject.
The document is protocol-specific to BGP, so the BGP tag fits better than the general routing architecture topic.

RFC4725.title: ENUM Validation Architecture
RFC4725.summary: RFC 4725 describes the roles, requirements and a high-level architecture for validating that an ENUM domain registrant is the assignee of the corresponding E.164 number, including workflows and trust relations among registry, registrar and validation entity.

ENUM.why: The whole document is about ENUM provisioning and the validation of ENUM domain delegations against E.164 numbers, so readers of the ENUM subject would expect it.
ENUM.quote: This document describes validation requirements and a high-level architecture for an ENUM validation infrastructure.

domain registration.why: A substantial part of the document defines registry, registrar and registrant roles, the registration workflow and the trust relations between them. This is domain registration operations applied to ENUM.
domain registration.quote: The ENUM Registry operates the master database of ENUM domain delegations and runs the authoritative nameservers for the relevant zone under e164.arpa.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate for ENUM. The document does not specify DNS protocol or server behaviour.
EPP is mentioned only as a typical Registry-Registrar protocol, and the document does not specify or extend it.
The document concerns E.164 numbers, but it does not cover the tel URI scheme.

RFC4726.title: A Framework for Inter-Domain Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering
RFC4726.summary: Informational framework describing signaling options (nesting, contiguous, stitching), path computation techniques (head-end, domain boundary, PCE) and advanced functions for establishing MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs across multiple domains (IGP areas and ASes).

traffic engineering.why: The whole document is a framework for inter-domain MPLS/GMPLS traffic engineering: signaling, path computation, TE information distribution and advanced functions.
traffic engineering.quote: a framework for establishing and controlling Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Traffic Engineered (TE) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in multi-domain networks

MPLS.why: The framework concerns establishing MPLS TE LSPs across domains, including LSP nesting, stitching and fast reroute, all MPLS mechanisms.
MPLS.quote: Hierarchical LSPs form a fundamental part of MPLS [RFC3031] and are discussed in further detail in [RFC4206].

PCE.why: A full section covers use of PCEs for multi-domain path computation, including confidentiality-preserving and per-domain PCE models.
PCE.quote: An alternative technique places the responsibility for path computation with a Path Computation Element (PCE) [RFC4655].

GMPLS.why: The framework explicitly covers GMPLS LSPs, including non-packet technologies and segment protection.
GMPLS.quote: the term "MPLS Traffic Engineering" is used equally to apply to MPLS and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) traffic.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signaling protocol the framework relies on (ERO, RRO, Path messages), but the document does not specify or extend it.
Section 5.4 discusses MPLS TE Fast Reroute (RFC 4090) in the inter-domain context, but only as one advanced function; the tag is for IP and LDP fast reroute.
BGP is mentioned only as a possible vehicle for future cross-domain TE advertisement, not addressed in its own right.
OSPF and IS-IS TE extensions are cited only as the existing means of distributing TE information within domains.
Section 5.8 comments briefly on inter-domain OAM, but it is a minor part of the document.

RFC4727.title: Experimental Values In IPv4, IPv6, ICMPv4, ICMPv6, UDP, and TCP Headers
RFC4727.summary: Reserves RFC 3692-style experimental code points and ports in IPv4, IPv6, ICMPv4/ICMPv6, Neighbor Discovery, UDP and TCP headers, and lists the corresponding IANA registry assignments.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is making assignments in IANA-managed number registries for experimental use, following RFC 2780 and RFC 3692.
IANA.quote: This document reserves some ranges of numbers for experimentation purposes in specific protocols where the need to support experimentation has been identified

IPv4.why: A substantial part covers IPv4 header fields: protocol 253/254, multicast groups, and option type codes.
IPv4.quote: This document assigns a single option number, with all defined values of the "copy" and "class" fields, resulting in four distinct option type codes.

IPv6.why: Substantial coverage of IPv6 header fields: Next Header, multicast group FF0X::114, hop-by-hop/destination options, routing types, and Neighbor Discovery options.
IPv6.quote: This document assigns two values for the Routing Type field in the IPv6 Routing Header, 253 and 254.

rejected.why: TCP option kinds 253/254 and ports 1021/1022 are reserved, but only briefly; the document is not about TCP itself.
Only a one-line port reservation shared with TCP.
Experimental ICMP type numbers are assigned in short sections only; the document is not about ICMP as a protocol.
Only one experimental option type pair is assigned, in a short subsection.

RFC4728.title: The Dynamic Source Routing Protocol (DSR) for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks for IPv4
RFC4728.summary: RFC 4728 specifies the Dynamic Source Routing (DSR) protocol, an on-demand source-routing protocol for multi-hop wireless mobile ad hoc networks carrying unicast IPv4 packets, including Route Discovery, Route Maintenance, option formats and an optional flow state extension.

DSR.why: The whole document specifies DSR: Route Discovery, Route Maintenance, the DSR Options header, options, and the flow state extension.
DSR.quote: The Dynamic Source Routing protocol (DSR) is a simple and efficient routing protocol designed specifically for use in multi-hop wireless ad hoc networks of mobile nodes.

rejected.why: Parent of DSR, so it is implied. The document is about the DSR protocol specifically, not MANET routing in general.
DSR uses ARP to map next-hop IP addresses to MAC addresses, but only as a substrate. The document defines nothing new about ARP.
The specification is for IPv4 packets, but it defines a routing protocol, not IPv4 itself.
Mentioned only as one possible way a node's IP address could be assigned, which the document puts out of scope.
IEEE 802.11 appears as an example MAC layer and for default parameter values. The document is not about IP over 802.11.
IP-in-IP encapsulation is used only for fragmentation handling in a single subsection (8.5).

RFC4729.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for  the Near Field Communication (NFC) Forum
RFC4729.summary: Registers the "nfc" URN namespace identifier for the NFC Forum, specifying the urn:nfc:{NFCresource}:{ResourceSpecificString} structure and its assignment, uniqueness and persistence policies per RFC 3406.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration for the 'nfc' NID, defining its syntax, uniqueness, persistence and assignment process. This is the URN namespace subject.
URN.quote: This document describes the Namespace Identifier (NID) for Uniform Resource Name (URN) resources published by the Near Field Communication (NFC) Forum.

rejected.why: The IANA section only notes the NID was entered in the registry. That is boilerplate, and the document is about the namespace itself.
Domain names are mentioned only as a way to make self-assigned names unique. The document does not specify anything about DNS.
XML schema namespaces appear only as examples of named resources, not as a subject of the document.
URN is the more specific tag and already implies URI.

gaps.name: Near Field Communication (NFC)
gaps.why: The namespace serves NFC Forum specifications, but the taxonomy has no NFC tag. The RFC itself is only about the URN registration, so this gap is minor.

RFC4730.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Event Package for Key Press Stimulus (KPML)
RFC4730.summary: Defines the SIP event package "kpml" and the Key Press Markup Language (XML request/response bodies, DRegex digit patterns) letting an application server subscribe to and receive DTMF key-press reports from a user agent or gateway.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP event package using SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, with notifier/subscriber procedures, dialog parameters, forking and proxy behaviour. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document describes a SIP Event Package "kpml" that enables monitoring of key presses and utilizes XML documents referred to as Key Press Markup Language (KPML).

media types.why: It registers application/kpml-request+xml and application/kpml-response+xml, a significant part of the specification.
media types.quote: The "kpml" event package requires the definition of two new MIME types, two new URN sub-namespaces, and two schemas

rejected.why: XML is the encoding for KPML bodies and schemas, i.e. substrate; the document is not about XML usage generally.
RFC 2833 DTMF packets are only referenced as the in-band alternative; the document does not specify RTP behaviour.
Uses SIP event notification but is not presence/IM or SIMPLE-specific.
Gateways are a common notifier, but the document is not about PSTN interworking as such.
ABNF is only used to define DRegex syntax.
TLS/sips is required only as a security mechanism, nothing new defined.

gaps.name: DTMF / key press signalling (KPML)
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers DTMF digit reporting or application interaction/stimulus signalling in SIP.

RFC4731.title: IMAP4 Extension to SEARCH Command for Controlling What Kind of Information Is Returned
RFC4731.summary: Extends IMAP SEARCH and UID SEARCH with result options (MIN, MAX, ALL, COUNT) and the ESEARCH capability/response, including interaction with CONDSTORE.

IMAP.why: The document is an extension to the IMAP protocol, defining new SEARCH result options and the ESEARCH capability.
IMAP.quote: This document extends IMAP (RFC 3501) SEARCH and UID SEARCH commands with several result options, which can control what kind of information is returned.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
IMAP is the more specific child tag; email is implied as its ancestor.
Mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations as a comparison to IMAP.
IANA section only registers the ESEARCH capability; boilerplate.

RFC4732.title: Internet Denial-of-Service Considerations
RFC4732.summary: IAB informational overview of denial-of-service attack avenues against Internet hosts, routers, links, DNS, firewalls and more, with attack amplification and mitigation strategies for protocol designers and operators.

DDoS.why: The whole document surveys DoS/DDoS attacks, amplification and mitigation, which is the DDoS topic.
DDoS.quote: This document provides an overview of possible avenues for denial- of-service (DoS) attack on Internet systems.

operational security.why: Substantial operator guidance: out-of-band access, ingress filtering, router configuration hardening, monitoring.
operational security.quote: Network operators are strongly encouraged to establish a monitoring framework to detect and log abnormal network activity.

routing security.why: Large portions cover attacks on routers via routing protocols, authenticating adjacencies, and BGP route validity checks.
routing security.quote: The routing protocols themselves can be used to stage a DoS attack on a router or a network of routers.

rejected.why: BGP is used as an example throughout, but the document is not about specifying or operating BGP itself.
DNS attacks and reflection are one section among many; DNS is not the subject.
SYN-flood and reset attacks are examples; the document is not about TCP.
Hopes for architectural solutions are expressed, but the content is a threat survey rather than architectural principles.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific DDoS tag.
Spam and black-hole lists get one short subsection only.

RFC4733.title: RTP Payload for DTMF Digits, Telephony Tones, and Telephony Signals
RFC4733.summary: RFC 4733 defines RTP payload formats for named telephone events (DTMF digits and similar signals) and for general telephony tones, with sending/receiving procedures, an IANA event-code registry, and media type registrations, obsoleting RFC 2833.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies the telephone-event and tone RTP payload formats, with header field use, procedures and media type registrations. This is exactly what the RTP payload format tag covers.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo defines two RTP [5] payload formats, one for carrying dual-tone multifrequency (DTMF) digits and other line and trunk signals as events

PSTN interop.why: A large part of the document covers carrying PSTN in-band tones and out-of-band signals across IP, including gateway scenarios, so readers of PSTN interworking would want it.
PSTN interop.quote: the receiver must propagate tone signalling accurately into the PSTN for machine consumption. One example of this is a gateway passing DTMF tones to an IVR.

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the formats ride on. The RTP payload format tag is the more specific fit, and the document does not change RTP itself.
SDP is used for negotiation (fmtp mapping of the events parameter). That is a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
The document registers audio/telephone-event and audio/tone, but this is boilerplate for the payload formats and not about media type registry rules in general.
It creates an event-code registry, but that is a supporting part of the payload spec and not about IANA guidance itself.
SRTP is only recommended in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
Congestion and performance are discussed, but only as considerations for these payloads and not as a congestion control mechanism.

gaps.name: DTMF / telephony events and tones signalling
gaps.why: The document is about carrying DTMF digits and telephony tone signals in-band over IP. The taxonomy has no tag for telephony signalling events, so the RTP payload format tag is the closest fit.

RFC4734.title: Definition of Events for Modem, Fax, and Text Telephony Signals
RFC4734.summary: RFC 4734 defines new telephone-event codes in the RTP telephony event payload for modem, fax (T.30) and text telephony signals (V.8, V.8 bis, V.21, V.25, V.32, Baudot, V.23, V.18), updating RFC 4733 and obsoleting the corresponding part of RFC 2833.

RTP payload format.why: The document extends the telephone-event RTP payload format with new event codes and usage rules, and registers them in the telephony event registry.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo updates RFC 4733 to add event codes for modem, fax, and text telephony signals when carried in the telephony event RTP payload.

PSTN interop.why: The events let gateways carry fax, modem and text telephony call setup signalling between PSTN terminals across IP, which is PSTN/Internet interworking.
PSTN interop.quote: The typical application of these events is to allow the Internet to serve as a bridge between terminals operating on the PSTN.

fax.why: A substantial section defines T.30 fax events (CED, CNG, V.21 preamble) for fax over IP gateways.
fax.quote: ITU-T Recommendation T.30 [8] defines the procedures used by Group III fax terminals.

rejected.why: SRTP is only recommended in Security Considerations for protecting the event streams; the document does not specify it.
SDP fmtp is used only in the examples to signal supported events; it is not the subject.
The more specific RTP payload format tag fits; the document does not extend RTP itself.
G.711 voice-band data is only the companion payload carried alongside the events, not defined here.
The IANA section merely registers the event codes; this is boilerplate relative to the main subject.

gaps.name: Telephony events / DTMF and tone signalling over RTP
gaps.why: The document is about named telephony events for modem/fax/text signals; the taxonomy has no tag for telephone-event signalling beyond the generic RTP payload format tag.

RFC4735.title: Example Media Types for Use in Documentation
RFC4735.summary: Registers the 'example' media type and 'example' subtypes under application, audio, image, message, model, multipart, text and video in the standards tree, for use only in documentation examples.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration under RFC 4288 rules, defining new example type and subtypes. Readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document is registration for the 'example' media type and 'example' subtypes within the standards tree.

rejected.why: Media types are a MIME concept, but the document registers specific types and does not specify MIME body structure or encodings. The more specific 'media types' tag fits.
The IANA Considerations section only restates the registrations, and the document is not about IANA registries or guidance in general.
The example types serve as illustrative placeholders in documentation. The document is not a glossary or a definition of requirements language.

RFC4736.title: Reoptimization of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering (TE) Loosely Routed Label Switched Path (LSP)
RFC4736.summary: Defines RSVP-TE extensions (a SESSION_ATTRIBUTE path re-evaluation flag and PathErr Notify sub-codes) letting a head-end or mid-point LSR detect and signal a better path or needed maintenance reroute for loosely routed inter-area/inter-AS MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling with a new SESSION_ATTRIBUTE flag and new PathErr Notify sub-codes to trigger and report path re-evaluation of TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: A new flag in the SESSION ATTRIBUTE object and new Error Value sub-codes in the ERROR SPEC object are proposed in this document.
