traffic engineering.why: Reoptimization of TE LSPs across inter-area and inter-AS domains is a traffic engineering matter; RSVP-TE only covers the signalling, so the broader topic is warranted as a secondary tag.
traffic engineering.quote: Both requirements documents specify the need for some mechanism providing an option for the head-end LSR to control the reoptimization process

rejected.why: The mechanism applies to GMPLS LSPs per RFC 3473, but the document does not specify GMPLS-specific behaviour; it is mentioned only as an applicable context.
MPLS is the general setting, but the specific subject is covered by the RSVP-TE and traffic engineering tags.
OSPF is used only in examples of area topology and ABRs; the document does not specify OSPF behaviour.
Path computation is done by ERO expansion on LSRs, not by a PCE; the document makes no assumption about the computation method.
Mentioned only as an alternative IGP to which the mechanism applies equally; the document does not specify IS-IS behaviour.
Sub-ASes and BGP confederations appear only in a terminology definition; the document does not cover BGP.

RFC4737.title: Packet Reordering Metrics
RFC4737.summary: Defines IPPM metrics for packet reordering (a reordered-packet singleton plus sample metrics for ratio, extent, late time, byte offset, gaps, reordering-free runs, and a TCP-relevant n-reordering metric) with measurement guidance and examples.

performance measurement.why: The document is an IPPM performance metric specification, defining reordering metrics and measurement methodology (active/passive, stream parameters), so it belongs under performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines metrics to evaluate whether a network has maintained packet order on a packet-by-packet basis.

rejected.why: Section 5 defines an n-reordering metric relevant to TCP's DUP-ACK threshold, but the document does not specify or extend TCP; it only measures reordering relevant to it.
Fast Retransmit and congestion window behavior are mentioned only to motivate the n-reordering metric, not as the subject.
OWAMP is referenced only in Security Considerations as a data collection protocol, not specified here.
RTP is mentioned only in passing as a place sequence numbers might be carried for passive measurement.
IP is the substrate being measured; Appendix B uses IP fragmentation fields but the document is not about IP itself.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) packet reordering metrics
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for IPPM metrics or packet reordering; the generic performance measurement topic is the closest fit.

RFC4738.title: MIKEY-RSA-R: An Additional Mode of Key Distribution in Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY)
RFC4738.summary: RFC 4738 defines MIKEY-RSA-R, a new reverse-mode public-key exchange for MIKEY in which the Responder selects and sends the TGK, supporting unknown responders and member-initiated group key download; it updates RFC 3830.

MIKEY.why: The document specifies a new MIKEY mode (RSA-R), including message formats, processing rules and new registry values, and updates RFC 3830.
MIKEY.quote: We propose a new MIKEY mode that works well in such scenarios.

multicast security.why: A substantial part covers group key distribution (Section 3.2 and applicability compared to GDOI/GSAKMP) in line with the MSEC group key management architecture.
multicast security.quote: it supports member-initiated group key download (in contrast to group manager pushing the group keys to all members).

rejected.why: SRTP is only the consumer of the keys derived; the document does not specify or extend SRTP.
Certificates are handled by reference to RFC 3830 and RFC 2585; no new certificate profile is defined.
RSA is the underlying public-key mechanism for the envelope key; the document is about the key transport mode, not the algorithm.
OCSP is only recommended for certificate validation in one paragraph.
SIP is mentioned only as a use case or source of identities, not specified here.
GDOI and GSAKMP are cited only for comparison in the applicability discussion.

RFC4739.title: Multiple Authentication Exchanges in the Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2) Protocol
RFC4739.summary: Experimental extension to IKEv2 defining two notify payloads (MULTIPLE_AUTH_SUPPORTED, ANOTHER_AUTH_FOLLOWS) that allow multiple authentication exchanges (certificate, shared secret, EAP) within one IKE_AUTH phase.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new notifications and message flows for multiple authentications in IKE_AUTH, so it belongs under IKE.
IKE.quote: This document specifies an extension to IKEv2 that allows the use of multiple authentication exchanges, using either different mechanisms or the same mechanism.

EAP.why: A substantial part addresses running multiple independent EAP conversations within IKEv2, with examples, and how this relates to EAP's rules on sequences of methods.
EAP.quote: In case of several EAP authentications, it is important to notice that they are not a "sequence" (as described in Section 2.1 of [EAP])

rejected.why: IPsec SAs are the context, but the document extends the IKE key exchange, not IPsec architecture; the IKE tag is more specific.
Backend AAA servers are mentioned as a scenario, but the document explicitly places AAA protocol details out of scope.
Certificates are used for authentication in the examples, but the document is not about PKI.
PANA is only mentioned as a similar multi-stage authentication concept in the introduction.
The general authentication topic is covered by the more specific IKE and EAP tags.

RFC4740.title: Diameter Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Application
RFC4740.summary: Defines the Diameter SIP application, a Diameter application with new commands (UAR/UAA, SAR/SAA, LIR/LIA, MAR/MAA, RTR/RTA, PPR/PPA) and AVPs that let a SIP server's co-located Diameter client obtain HTTP Digest authentication, authorization, user profiles and routing information from a Diameter server.

Diameter.why: The document specifies a new Diameter application with its commands, AVPs, Result-Codes and IANA registrations.
Diameter.quote: This is a Diameter application that allows a Diameter client to request authentication and authorization information.

SIP.why: The application is designed for SIP servers (registrars, proxies) and maps SIP REGISTER/INVITE processing, digest challenges and soft state onto Diameter exchanges, so SIP deployment readers would want it.
SIP.quote: provides a Diameter client co-located with a SIP server, with the ability to request the authentication of users and authorization of SIP resources usage

rejected.why: RADIUS Digest attributes are imported and a RADIUS migration section exists, but the document specifies a Diameter application, not RADIUS.
HTTP Digest is the authentication mechanism carried in the AVPs, but the document does not define or extend the scheme; it only transports its parameters.
The more specific Diameter tag covers the AAA framework used here.
TLS is mentioned only as a transport protection option in the security considerations.
CPL is only an example of a server capability, mentioned in passing.

RFC4741.title: NETCONF Configuration Protocol
RFC4741.summary: Specifies the NETCONF protocol, an XML/RPC-based mechanism for installing, manipulating and deleting network device configuration, with its operations, datastores, subtree filtering and capabilities.

NETCONF.why: The document is the base NETCONF protocol specification: RPC layer, operations, datastores, capabilities and error handling.
NETCONF.quote: The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) defined in this document provides mechanisms to install, manipulate, and delete the configuration of network devices.

rejected.why: XML is the encoding substrate for messages and schema; the document is not about XML usage in general.
SSH is only the mandatory transport mapping, defined in a separate document (RFC 4742).
Data modeling is explicitly out of scope; no data modeling language is defined here.
SNMP is mentioned only as another interface that locks must guard against, not a subject.
BEEP is listed only as an example transport.
TLS is mentioned only as an example of a transport security mechanism.

RFC4742.title: Using the NETCONF Configuration Protocol over Secure SHell (SSH)
RFC4742.summary: Defines the mapping of NETCONF onto SSH as the "netconf" SSH subsystem on TCP port 830, covering session startup, hello capability exchange, ]]>]]> message framing, and session close.

NETCONF.why: The document specifies a transport mapping for NETCONF: subsystem invocation, capability exchange, framing and session close. NETCONF readers need it.
NETCONF.quote: This document describes a method for invoking and running the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) within a Secure Shell (SSH) session as an SSH subsystem.

SSH.why: It defines a new SSH subsystem name, "netconf", and how it is invoked over SSH connection and session channels. SSH readers would want this.
SSH.quote: IANA is also requested to assign "netconf" as an SSH Service Name as defined in [RFC4250]

rejected.why: NETCONF messages are XML, but XML is only the encoding. The document defines nothing new about XML.
This topic fits the document's nature, but the NETCONF tag already covers it. A technology tag was chosen under network management, not under this topic.
No data modelling is involved. The document is only about the transport.
Port 830 is assigned, but TCP is only the substrate.

RFC4743.title: Using NETCONF over the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP)
RFC4743.summary: Defines a SOAP binding for NETCONF over HTTP and BEEP, including session handling, SOAP fault mapping, and a WSDL definition.

NETCONF.why: The document specifies how NETCONF operations, sessions, hello exchange and errors are carried in SOAP. It is a NETCONF transport binding.
NETCONF.quote: Herein, we describe SOAP over HTTP and SOAP over Blocks Exchange Extensible Protocol (BEEP) bindings for NETCONF.

BEEP.why: BEEP is one of the two bindings specified, with its own session establishment and teardown behaviour, and a port assignment. Readers of BEEP would want it.
BEEP.quote: The BEEP profile for SOAP simply makes use of a single BEEP channel for exchanging SOAP messages

HTTP.why: Substantial normative guidance on using HTTP as the substrate: caching prohibition, persistent connections, chunking, BCP56 concerns, and the port.
HTTP.quote: HTTP caches SHOULD NOT be inserted between NETCONF managers and agents as NETCONF session state is tied to the state of the underlying transport connection.

XML.why: The document is built around SOAP envelopes, WSDL and XSD usage, which are XML-based formats.
XML.quote: With the right tools, the WSDL combined with the base NETCONF XML Schemas provides machine-readable descriptions

rejected.why: TLS is mandated as the secure transport in Security Considerations, but the document defines nothing new about it.
Mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations as an integration option.
Digest authentication is only listed as an option in Security Considerations.
This does fit, as the document carries NETCONF over HTTP and BEEP. I chose the NETCONF technology tag as the more specific home for the binding.

gaps.name: SOAP / Web Services (WSDL)
gaps.why: The document is largely about the SOAP messaging framework and WSDL service definitions, but the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC4744.title: Using the NETCONF Protocol over the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP)
RFC4744.summary: Specifies the mapping of the NETCONF configuration protocol onto BEEP, covering session establishment with TLS/SASL, channel setup with the NETCONF profile, usage, teardown, and the BEEP profile registration.

NETCONF.why: The document defines how NETCONF sessions, hello exchange, RPCs and teardown are carried over BEEP, so NETCONF readers need it.
NETCONF.quote: This document specifies an application protocol mapping for the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) over the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP).

BEEP.why: It defines a new BEEP profile for NETCONF (greetings, channel start, profile definition, TCP port 831), which is something new about how BEEP is used.
BEEP.quote: The manager now establishes a new channel and specifies the single NETCONF profile.

rejected.why: TLS is only the security mechanism BEEP uses for confidentiality; no new TLS extension is defined.
SASL is used for authentication via BEEP's profile; the document does not define a new SASL mechanism.
XML is only the encoding of NETCONF messages, not the subject.

Considered since this is a transport mapping, but the NETCONF and BEEP tech tags are more specific; the topic is only given directly when no tech tag sits under it, and BEEP and NETCONF sit elsewhere in the hierarchy, so I did not add it.
TCP is only the underlying transport (port 831) via BEEP's TCP mapping.

RFC4745.title: Common Policy: A Document Format for Expressing Privacy Preferences
RFC4745.summary: RFC 4745 defines Common Policy, an XML-based framework and schema for authorization rules (conditions, actions, transformations, permission combining) controlling access to presence and location data, extensible to other domains.

authorization.why: The document specifies a generic authorization policy framework: rules with conditions, actions, transformations and a permission-combining procedure.
authorization.quote: This document defines a framework for authorization policies controlling access to application-specific data.

privacy.why: The policy language expresses privacy preferences for presence and location data, with transformations that reduce disclosed information.
privacy.quote: This functionality is particularly helpful in reducing the granularity of information provided to the WR, as, for example, required for location privacy.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document is the XML schema and XML namespace and media type definitions for the policy format.
XML.quote: Rules are encoded in XML. To this end, Section 13 contains an XML schema defining the Common Policy Markup Language.

rejected.why: Location policy is only a downstream extension specified elsewhere. This document is the common framework.
Presence policy is specified in a separate document. RPID is mentioned only in passing for sphere.
The application/auth-policy+xml registration is IANA boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
IDNA ToASCII is used only for domain comparison, as a minor detail.
Presence is only an example application domain. The document is not about presence protocols.

RFC4746.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Password Authenticated Exchange
RFC4746.summary: Defines EAP-PAX, an EAP method for lightweight shared-key mutual authentication with optional key provisioning via Diffie-Hellman, identity protection via a server public key, and authenticated data exchange.

EAP.why: The whole document specifies a new EAP method: packet format, exchanges, key derivation, and EAP security claims.
EAP.quote: This document defines an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method called EAP-PAX (Password Authenticated eXchange).

rejected.why: Despite the 'Password Authenticated Exchange' name, EAP-PAX is a shared-key protocol with a PAX_SEC option; it is not presented as a PAKE family protocol. The main subject is the EAP method.
Certificates are used for server authentication, but only as a mechanism; the document does not profile X.509.
HMAC-SHA1/SHA256 are used as the MAC and KDF primitive, but the document doesn't specify or extend HMAC.
Wireless LANs motivate the design and appear in the appendix, but the document does not define IP over 802.11.
Key derivation is internal to the EAP method, so the EAP tag covers it.

RFC4747.title: The Virtual Fabrics MIB
RFC4747.summary: Defines the T11-FC-VIRTUAL-FABRIC-MIB SMIv2 module, giving SNMP managed objects for monitoring and configuring Fibre Channel Virtual Fabrics (core/virtual switches, port VF_ID tagging, locally enabled VF_IDs).

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification extending the FC-MGMT-MIB, defined with SMIv2 for SNMP-based management.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: The Fibre Channel tag covers Fibre Channel over IP transports (e.g., FCIP/iFCP), not a management MIB for native FC Virtual Fabrics.
SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, so the more specific MIB tag fits.
Fibre Channel is a storage networking technology, but the document is about managing FC switch virtualization, not storage access protocols over IP.
AgentX is only mentioned as an example of how management instances may be grouped.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel Virtual Fabrics
gaps.why: The document is about native Fibre Channel fabric management (T11 FC-SW-4 Virtual Fabrics); the taxonomy has no tag for Fibre Channel management or non-IP FC networking beyond FC over IP transports.

RFC4748.title: RFC 3978 Update to Recognize the IETF Trust
RFC4748.summary: BCP 78 update that amends RFC 3978 (IETF Rights in Contributions) to replace ISOC with the IETF Trust as the licensee/custodian of rights in IETF Contributions and in the copyright statement.

IPR.why: The document is entirely about IETF copyright and licensing provisions, changing the license-grant path from ISOC to the IETF Trust in BCP 78.
IPR.quote: updates RFC 3978 "IETF Rights in Contributions" to recognize that the IETF Trust is now the proper custodian of all IETF-related intellectual property rights

rejected.why: Although it is a BCP affecting the standards process, its subject is the IPR/copyright provisions, which IPR covers more specifically.
It changes the copyright statement text in RFCs, but the document is about rights and licensing, not RFC format or publication.

RFC4749.title: RTP Payload Format for the G.729.1 Audio Codec
RFC4749.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for the ITU-T G.729.1 scalable wideband audio codec, including the MBS in-band bit-rate request, and registers the audio/G7291 media type with SDP parameter mappings and offer/answer rules.

G.729.why: The document is the RTP payload format for G.729.1, a scalable extension of G.729. The G.729 tag explicitly covers wideband extensions and their payload formats.
G.729.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of G.729.1 encoded audio signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

SDP.why: A substantial section maps the media type parameters to SDP and defines offer/answer and declarative rules for maxbitrate and mbs.
SDP.quote: The media subtype ("G7291") goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name. The RTP clock rate in "a=rtpmap" MUST be 16000 for G.729.1.

media types.why: The document includes a full media type registration for audio/G7291 with defined parameters.
media types.quote: Type name: audio  Subtype name: G7291

rejected.why: This is the closest-fitting concept, but G.729 is the more specific tag, and the taxonomy places RTP payload format under RTP rather than under codecs. I chose G.729 because it names G.729.1 and its payload formats explicitly.
RTP is the substrate. The document uses RTP header fields in a standard way and defines nothing new about RTP itself.
Section 7 is short and refers to RFC 3550. The MBS mechanism can help with congestion, but the document is not about congestion control.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional external mechanism.
SIP appears only in a passing example of a re-INVITE for an out-of-band bit-rate request.

RFC4750.title: OSPF Version 2 Management Information Base
RFC4750.summary: RFC 4750 defines the SMIv2 MIB module and companion trap MIB for managing OSPF version 2, obsoleting RFC 1850 with additions for graceful restart, NSSA, opaque LSAs, and stub routers.

MIB.why: The document is an SNMP MIB module (OSPF-MIB and OSPF-TRAP-MIB) written in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing version 2 of the Open Shortest Path First Routing Protocol.

OSPF.why: The MIB models OSPFv2 areas, interfaces, neighbors, LSDBs, NSSA, opaque LSAs and graceful restart, and it covers OSPF-specific traps. Readers of OSPF would want it.
OSPF.quote: The MIB module to describe the OSPF Version 2 Protocol.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol through which the MIB is accessed. The document defines objects, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
The document is specific to OSPFv2/IPv4 and only mentions OSPFv3 in the abstract.
OSPF is already tagged, and it sits under routing.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate, recording only the ospf OID assignment.

RFC4752.title: The Kerberos V5 ("GSSAPI") Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) Mechanism
RFC4752.summary: Specifies the SASL "GSSAPI" mechanism, which uses the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism for authentication and optional security layers, replacing Section 7.2 of RFC 2222.

SASL.why: The document defines a SASL mechanism (GSSAPI), including its exchange, security layer negotiation, and IANA registration of the mechanism name.
SASL.quote: This document describes the method for using the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Kerberos V5 in the SASL.

GSS-API.why: The mechanism is specified in terms of detailed GSS-API calls (Init/Accept_sec_context, Wrap/Unwrap), so GSS-API readers would want it.
GSS-API.quote: The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context, passing in input_context_handle of 0 (initially), mech_type of the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism

Kerberos.why: The mechanism is bound specifically to Kerberos V5 and checks that the negotiated mech is Kerberos V5, so Kerberos readers would find it relevant.
Kerberos.quote: the mechanism is specifically tied to Kerberos V5 and GSS-API's Kerberos V5 mechanism.

rejected.why: Only used to encode the authorization identity; it is an encoding substrate, not the subject.
Parent topic implied by the more specific SASL and GSS-API tags.
Not discussed; the document is tied directly to the Kerberos V5 mechanism with no negotiation.

RFC4753.title: ECP Groups For IKE and IKEv2
RFC4753.summary: Defines three new elliptic curve (modular prime, ECP) Diffie-Hellman groups (NIST P-256, P-384, P-521) for IKE and IKEv2, with parameters, key exchange data formats, IANA assignments and test vectors.

IKE.why: The document extends IKE and IKEv2 with new Diffie-Hellman groups, specifies KE payload formats and gives IKEv2 test vectors.
IKE.quote: This document describes new Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) groups for use in the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) and Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) protocols

elliptic curve.why: It defines specific prime-field elliptic curves (P-256, P-384, P-521) with their parameters, generators and alignment with NIST/SECG/ANSI curve standards.
elliptic curve.quote: IKE and IKEv2 implementations SHOULD support an ECP group with the following characteristics.

rejected.why: IKE is the key exchange component under IPsec, but the document only adds DH groups to IKE; the more specific IKE tag suffices.
AES is mentioned only to compare security strength of the groups.
SHA-1 is used only to verifiably generate the curve seeds, not the subject.
The curves are used for Diffie-Hellman key exchange, not signatures; ECDSA appears only in references.

RFC4754.title: IKE and IKEv2 Authentication Using the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)
RFC4754.summary: Defines ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521 as digital signature authentication methods for IKE and IKEv2, with signature encoding and test vectors.

ECDSA.why: The document specifies ECDSA instantiations (curve and hash pairs), signature encoding and test vectors.
ECDSA.quote: This document describes how the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) may be used as the authentication method within the Internet Key Exchange (IKE)

IKE.why: It extends IKE/IKEv2 authentication with a new signature method and registers new authentication method IDs.
IKE.quote: This document adds ECDSA capability to IKE and IKEv2 without introducing any changes to existing IKE operation.

rejected.why: IPsec is only the context in which IKE is used; the document is about IKE authentication.
The more specific ECDSA child tag fits; the curve groups themselves are defined in RFC 4753.
SHA-256/384/512 are only the hash functions paired with the signatures, not the subject.
Mentioned only to compare security strength in Security Considerations.
Certificates are mentioned only in passing regarding key size.

RFC4755.title: IP over InfiniBand: Connected Mode
RFC4755.summary: Specifies how IPv4/IPv6 packets are transmitted and addresses resolved over InfiniBand's connected modes (RC/UC), as an optional extension to IPoIB over UD, covering link-layer address flags, connection setup, Service-IDs, and per-connection MTU.

InfiniBand.why: The whole document defines IP over InfiniBand connected mode (IPoIB-CM): link-layer address extension, CM connection setup, Service-ID, MTU and private-data format.
InfiniBand.quote: This document specifies transmission of IPv4/IPv6 packets and address resolution over the connected modes of InfiniBand.

rejected.why: Address resolution is mentioned but is defined in RFC 4391; this document only extends the link-layer address with flags and does not specify ARP itself.
TCP appears only in a cautionary note on RC-mode timeouts interacting with TCP congestion control; the document is not about TCP.
IPv4/IPv6 are the carried payload; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
Per-destination MTU is discussed, but it is a link MTU negotiation, not Path MTU Discovery.
Neighbor Discovery is only mentioned as responses that must use UD mode; it is not specified here.

RFC4756.title: Forward Error Correction Grouping Semantics in Session Description Protocol
RFC4756.summary: Defines a new "FEC" semantics token for the SDP "a=group" attribute (RFC 3388) so that FEC streams can be grouped with the payload streams they protect.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP media-line grouping with a new FEC semantics token and gives SDP examples and offer/answer handling. SDP is the subject.
SDP.quote: This document defines the semantics that allow for grouping of Forward Error Correction (FEC) streams with the protected payload streams in Session Description Protocol (SDP).

FEC.why: The document covers how FEC streams are associated with protected payload streams, and the readers of the FEC subject would want it. It does not define a FEC scheme, only the signalling of the association.
FEC.quote: In general, the FEC data can be sent in two different ways: (1) multiplexed together with the original payload stream or (2) as a separate stream.

rejected.why: The examples use RTP payload types such as ulpfec, but the document defines nothing about RTP itself.
SIP appears only in the offer/answer failure response codes (488, 606), as a substrate.
FECFRAME is for real-time and streaming media FEC frameworks. This document only groups streams in SDP and does not define a framework.
The generic FEC payload format is only referenced as an informative work in progress. This document does not define it.

RFC4757.title: The RC4-HMAC Kerberos Encryption Types Used by Microsoft Windows
RFC4757.summary: Informational (historic) RFC documenting Microsoft Windows 2000's RC4-HMAC Kerberos encryption and checksum types (etypes 23 and 24), including key generation, encryption, and GSS-API token changes.

Kerberos.why: The document defines new Kerberos encryption and checksum types, their key derivation per message type, and key strength negotiation, so Kerberos readers need it.
Kerberos.quote: The Microsoft Windows 2000 implementation of Kerberos introduces a new encryption type based on the RC4 encryption algorithm and using an MD5 HMAC for checksum.

RC4.why: The RC4-based cipher suites are the subject. The document also discusses RC4 keystream weaknesses and recommends against high-volume use.
RC4.quote: RC4 is a stream cipher licensed by RSA Data Security.  In this document, the function is referred to as RC4(Key, Data)

GSS-API.why: Section 7 specifies changes to the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism: MIC and WRAP token formats, new flags, and sequence number handling.
GSS-API.quote: The Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) per-message tokens also require new checksum and encryption types.

rejected.why: HMAC-MD5 is used as a building block for checksums and key derivation, but the document does not specify or extend HMAC itself.
MD5 and MD4 are used as primitives, with MD4 hashing the password to produce the key. The document is not about them; MD4 weaknesses appear only in the security discussion.
AES is mentioned only as a stronger alternative (aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96) recommended in Security Considerations.
DES-based Kerberos types are mentioned only as the existing types that RC4-HMAC is an alternative to.
NetBIOS addresses are mentioned only in passing as a GSS-API address type value.

RFC4758.title: Cryptographic Token Key Initialization Protocol (CT-KIP) Version 1.0 Revision 1
RFC4758.summary: Informational RFC specifying CT-KIP, an XML-based client-server protocol for securely initializing cryptographic (OTP) tokens with secret keys via nonce exchange and a pseudorandom function, with an HTTP binding.

key management.why: The protocol's purpose is secure key generation and provisioning into tokens, with keys known only to server and token. This is key establishment and provisioning.
key management.quote: CT-KIP is a client-server protocol for initialization (and configuration) of cryptographic tokens.

OTP.why: It is part of the OTPS series and provisions OTP token keys, with OTP format, length and mode configuration. Readers of one-time password systems would want it.
OTP.quote: carries additional configuration data that the cryptographic token should use (subject to local policy) when generating OTP values from the newly generated OTP key.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is only the transport binding (Section 4.2); it defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
XML Schema is the message encoding for the protocol, not the subject.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations as a protective transport.
HMAC and OMAC appear only in the example PRF realizations in Appendix D, a minor part of the document.
AES is only used in an example PRF realization in the appendix; the document is not about AES.
Token key initialization is the subject, not user or message authentication in general; the MACs are auxiliary.

gaps.name: Cryptographic token provisioning (CT-KIP, PSKC-style symmetric key provisioning)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for token or symmetric key provisioning protocols. 'key management' and 'OTP' are the closest, but neither is specific.

RFC4759.title: The ENUM Dip Indicator Parameter for the "tel" URI
RFC4759.summary: Defines the "enumdi" parameter for the "tel" URI, signalling that an ENUM query has already been performed on an E.164 number, and specifies how VoIP network elements add, pass on, and handle it.

tel URI.why: The document extends the tel URI with a new parameter, including ABNF syntax extending the 'par' production, and defines handling rules for it.
tel URI.quote: This document defines a new parameter "enumdi" for the "tel" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI)

ENUM.why: The parameter exists to handle ENUM queries and avoid redundant lookups. The rules cover NXDOMAIN results, NAPTR records and e164.arpa. queries.
ENUM.quote: The presence of the "enumdi" parameter indicates that an ENUM query has already been performed on the E.164 number by a previous VoIP network element.

rejected.why: SIP is only the signalling context. The parameter can appear in a SIP URI, but the document does not specify or extend SIP.
DNS NAPTR queries and NXDOMAIN are the mechanism underlying ENUM. The document adds nothing new about DNS itself.
ABNF is only the notation used for the one-line syntax extension.
The more specific tel URI tag fits, and the document defines nothing about URIs in general.
The IANA section only points to the existing tel URI parameter registry, which is boilerplate.

RFC4760.title: Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4
RFC4760.summary: Defines Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4 (MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes, AFI/SAFI, capability advertisement) so BGP can carry routing information for multiple network layer protocols; obsoletes RFC 2858.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies new BGP-4 path attributes, NLRI encoding, SAFI values, error handling and capability use, so it is a BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: This document defines extensions to BGP-4 to enable it to carry routing information for multiple Network Layer protocols (e.g., IPv6, IPX, L3VPN, etc.).

rejected.why: IPv6 is only named as one example of a network layer protocol that the extensions can carry. The document does not specify anything about IPv6.
SAFI 2 marks NLRI used for multicast forwarding, but this is a single value in the registry. The document does not cover multicast routing.
L3VPN appears only as an example in the abstract. The document does not define VPN behaviour.
The SAFI registry rules are boilerplate-like IANA Considerations text. The main body is not about IANA.

RFC4761.title: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Using BGP for Auto-Discovery and Signaling
RFC4761.summary: RFC 4761 specifies VPLS using BGP (Multiprotocol BGP with a new L2VPN AFI/SAFI NLRI and label blocks) for PE auto-discovery and pseudowire signaling, plus the forwarding/data-plane rules, multi-AS methods, and deployment options.

VPLS.why: The whole document defines the BGP-based VPLS functional model, control plane, and data plane.
VPLS.quote: This document describes the functions required to offer VPLS, a mechanism for signaling a VPLS, and rules for forwarding VPLS frames across a packet switched network.

BGP.why: A substantial part defines a new BGP NLRI (AFI 25/SAFI 65), the Layer2 Info Extended Community, multi-AS EBGP methods and BGP path selection for multi-homing.
BGP.quote: The control plane described in this document uses Multiprotocol BGP [4] to establish VPLS service, i.e., for the auto-discovery of VPLS members

rejected.why: Pseudowires are the mechanism VPLS uses, set up via BGP, but the document is about VPLS, not pseudowire emulation itself.
MPLS labels serve as demultiplexors and for inter-AS label swapping, but MPLS is a substrate here.
Route reflectors are discussed only briefly as a scaling technique in Section 3.6.
VPLS is a child of L2VPN, so the more specific tag is chosen and L2VPN is implied.
The service emulates an Ethernet LAN with MAC learning and flooding, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
BGP/MPLS IP VPNs are referenced as the model for Route Targets and inter-AS methods but are not the subject.

RFC4762.title: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Using Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) Signaling
RFC4762.summary: Specifies VPLS using LDP-signaled pseudowires (extending RFC 4447): topology, MAC learning and withdrawal (new MAC List TLV), data forwarding on Ethernet PWs, and hierarchical H-VPLS models.

VPLS.why: The whole document specifies VPLS: emulated LAN, MAC learning, flooding, split horizon, and hierarchical VPLS.
VPLS.quote: This document describes a Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) solution using pseudowires

LDP.why: Defines LDP signaling of PW labels for VPLS using the Generalized PWid FEC and a new LDP MAC List TLV in Address Withdraw messages.
LDP.quote: We introduce an optional MAC List TLV in LDP to specify a list of MAC addresses that can be removed or unlearned

pseudowire.why: VPLS is built from a mesh of pseudowires, with Ethernet and Ethernet tagged PW types and spoke PWs. The document extends RFC 4447 PW signaling.
pseudowire.quote: A full mesh of LDP sessions is used to establish the mesh of PWs.

rejected.why: Ethernet is the service carried, with MAC learning and VLAN handling. The document is about VPLS over MPLS, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
MPLS is the transport substrate for the PWs. The document does not define anything about MPLS itself.
VPLS is a child of L2VPN, so the L2VPN tag is implied by the more specific tag.
BGP is mentioned only as an auto-discovery option and in comparison to BGP VPNs. It is not specified here.

RFC4763.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol Method for Shared-secret Authentication and Key Establishment (EAP-SAKE)
RFC4763.summary: Specifies EAP-SAKE, an EAP method for mutual authentication and session key derivation from a pre-shared Root Secret, with message formats, key hierarchy, identity management and security claims, published as documentation for an IANA EAP Type assignment.

EAP.why: The document defines a new EAP method (EAP-SAKE) with its exchanges, attributes, key derivation and security claims per RFC 3748.
EAP.quote: This document specifies an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) mechanism for Shared-secret Authentication and Key Establishment (SAKE).

rejected.why: AES-CBC is only the default attribute-encryption cipher; the document is not about AES.
HMAC-SHA1 is used inside the KDF, taken from IEEE 802.11i, as a building block only.
Backend AAA communication is explicitly out of scope.
Key hierarchy and derivation are part of the EAP method, which the EAP tag already covers.
IEEE 802.11i is referenced for its KDF and as a usage context, but the document is not about IP over 802.11.
SHA-1 is used only within the HMAC-based KDF as a primitive.

RFC4764.title: The EAP-PSK Protocol: A Pre-Shared Key Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Method
RFC4764.summary: Specifies EAP-PSK, an experimental EAP method for mutual authentication and session key derivation from a 16-byte pre-shared key using AES-128, CMAC and EAX, with a protected channel for result indications and extensions.

EAP.why: The document defines a new EAP method, including its message flows, formats, key hierarchy and protected result indications.
EAP.quote: This document specifies EAP-PSK, an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method for mutual authentication and session key derivation using a Pre-Shared Key (PSK).

rejected.why: AES-128 is the sole cryptographic primitive used (CMAC, EAX, modified counter mode), but the document is not about AES itself.
Key hierarchy (AK, KDK, TEK, MSK, EMSK) is part of the EAP method design, not a general key management topic; EAP covers it.
Mentioned only in a discouraged appendix for deriving a PSK from a password.
MSK is transported to AAA/authenticators, but AAA is only context.
IEEE 802.11 is the motivating deployment environment, but the document doesn't specify anything about it.
The generic topic is implied by the more specific EAP tag.

RFC4765.title: The Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF)
RFC4765.summary: Defines IDMEF, an XML/DTD data model and format for intrusion detection analyzers to send alerts and heartbeats to managers, including extension rules and IANA registries.

IDMEF.why: The document is the specification of IDMEF itself: data model, DTD, extension and registration rules.
IDMEF.quote: The purpose of the Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF) is to define data formats and exchange procedures for sharing information of interest to intrusion detection

XML.why: A substantial part of the document is the XML implementation: DTD, schema, namespaces, validity and well-formedness rules, and XML-based extension mechanisms.
XML.quote: An implementation of the data model in the Extensible Markup Language (XML) is presented, an XML Document Type Definition is developed

rejected.why: The SNMPService class only carries fields of SNMP traffic seen in alerts; the document does not specify or extend SNMP.
NTP timestamps are used as a data type and synchronization is discussed as out of scope; NTP is not specified or profiled here.
The parent topic is implied by the IDMEF tag, so it is not listed separately.
The IANA section only creates an attribute value registry for IDMEF; this is boilerplate relative to the main subject.
Digital signatures are only recommended and explicitly left out of scope.
The document uses an ISO 8601 subset for its DATETIME type, which is a supporting detail rather than the subject.

RFC4766.title: Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Requirements
RFC4766.summary: Informational requirements document from the IDWG for the Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF) and its communication protocol (IDP), covering general, message format, protocol security and message content requirements.

IDMEF.why: The whole document specifies requirements for IDMEF message format and content, so IDMEF is the main subject.
IDMEF.quote: This document defines requirements for the Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF) [5], a product of the Intrusion Detection Exchange Format Working Group (IDWG).

IDXP.why: Section 5 sets requirements for the IDMEF Communication Protocol (IDP): reliability, mutual authentication, confidentiality, integrity, firewall traversal, DoS resistance. Readers of IDXP, the protocol later developed to meet these, would want it.
IDXP.quote: This document also specifies requirements for a communication protocol for communicating IDMEF.

rejected.why: Parent topic of IDMEF and IDXP, so it is implied by the specific tags chosen.
Mentioned only as one possible illustrative design for carrying IDMEF; not the subject.
Section 3.2 only requires IDMEF to work in IPv4 and IPv6 environments; this is incidental.
Sections 6.14 to 6.16 cover timestamps in alerts, not clock synchronization protocols.
Mentioned only in a scenario about internationalization of message strings.
Section 5.2 requires traversal of firewalls, but the document is not about firewalls or middlebox traversal mechanisms.

RFC4767.title: The Intrusion Detection Exchange Protocol (IDXP)
RFC4767.summary: RFC 4767 specifies IDXP, a BEEP profile for exchanging IDMEF intrusion detection messages, text and binary data between analyzers and managers, with options, DTDs and a mapping to IDWG requirements.

IDXP.why: The document defines IDXP itself: its BEEP profile, greeting element, options, DTDs and reply codes.
IDXP.quote: IDXP, an application-level protocol for exchanging data between intrusion detection entities.

BEEP.why: IDXP is defined as a BEEP profile, with profile registration, channel management, TUNNEL use, and BEEP-specific message exchanges. Readers of BEEP would want to see this profile.
BEEP.quote: IDXP is specified, in part, as a Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) [4] "profile".

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy as a tag under intrusion detection other than IDMEF; IDMEF is defined in RFC 4765, and this document only carries it.
TLS is the recommended security profile but only used as a mechanism, not specified or extended here.
XML/DTDs are only the encoding of the profile messages.
SASL is only required to be offered for TUNNEL authentication, not specified here.
Ancestor of IDXP, implied by the more specific tag.
Firewall traversal via TUNNEL is a requirement addressed briefly, not the subject of the document.

RFC4768.title: Desired Enhancements to Generic Security Services Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Version 3 Naming
RFC4768.summary: Informational document motivating and describing proposed extensions to GSS-API naming (composite names with attributes, credential extensions, export-name mechanisms, source identity selection) for GSS-API Version 3, driven by Kerberos and X.509 naming problems.

GSS-API.why: The whole document is about GSS-API naming, name attributes, credentials and compatibility with GSS-API V2 in preparation for V3.
GSS-API.quote: This document motivates extensions to GSS-API naming and describes the extensions under discussion.

rejected.why: Kerberos enterprise names and authorization data are used as a motivating case, but the document is about GSS-API naming, not Kerberos itself.
X.509 subject names and subjectAltName are discussed as a problem for GSS-API mechanisms; the document does not specify or profile X.509.
Name-based authorization and ACLs are the motivation, but the subject of the document is GSS-API naming; the GSS-API tag covers it.
This is GSS-API name architecture, not naming and name resolution in the DNS-style sense the tag covers.

RFC4769.title: IANA Registration for an Enumservice Containing Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) Signaling Information
RFC4769.summary: Registers the ENUM Enumservice type "pstn" with subtypes "tel" and "sip" so NAPTR records can carry PSTN routing and number portability data for telephone numbers.

ENUM.why: The document is an ENUM Enumservice registration under RFC 3761, with NAPTR examples and E2U+pstn call processing.
ENUM.quote: This document registers the Enumservice type "pstn" and subtype "tel" using the URI scheme 'tel', as well as the subtype "sip"

tel URI.why: The tel URI scheme with number portability parameters (npdi, rn) is a main part of the registration and examples.
tel URI.quote: The URIs returned in this service may use the TEL URI parameters defined in RFC 4694 [10], and implementations must be prepared to accept them.

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR records are the substrate for ENUM; the document defines no new DNS behaviour beyond the Enumservice registration.
The sip URI is a subtype scheme but SIP itself is not specified or extended.
Considered because of PSTN routing, but the document is an ENUM registration, not about PSTN/Internet interworking mechanisms.
The IANA registration is the document's purpose but it is a registration in the ENUM registry, so the ENUM tag fits better than the IANA governance topic.

gaps.name: Number portability
gaps.why: The document is about routing calls for ported telephone numbers, but the taxonomy has no tag for number portability.

RFC4770.title: vCard Extensions for Instant Messaging (IM)
RFC4770.summary: Defines the IMPP vCard type (with TYPE parameters) so a vCard can hold an instant messaging or presence URI, registered under the text/directory MIME types.

vCard.why: The whole document extends vCard with a new IMPP type, its TYPE parameter values and ABNF, so readers of vCard material need it.
vCard.quote: This document defines a new type in a vCard for representing instant IM and PP URIs.

instant messaging.why: The extension exists to carry IM and presence addresses (sip, xmpp, im, pres URIs) in contact data. It is a substantial subject of the document, though no IM protocol is specified.
instant messaging.quote: it becomes important for them to be able to share this contact address information

rejected.why: URIs are only the value type carried in the IMPP entry. The document defines no new URI scheme and does not specify URI syntax.
SIP appears only as an example of a URI scheme that can appear in an IMPP value.
XMPP is only an example of a URI type that can appear in IMPP. It is not specified or extended here.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammar and is not a subject of the document.
The text/directory registration entry is IANA boilerplate for the vCard type. It is not a media type registration document.
The document mentions presence only as a URI purpose. It does not use or define a presence data format.

RFC4771.title: Integrity Transform Carrying Roll-Over Counter for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC4771.summary: Defines the Roll-over Counter Carrying (RCC) integrity transform for SRTP, which carries the ROC in the authentication tag of selected packets, with three modes and MIKEY parameter negotiation.

SRTP.why: The document specifies a new SRTP integrity transform and how it changes SRTP packet processing, so it is an extension of SRTP.
SRTP.quote: This document defines an integrity transform for Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP; see RFC 3711), which allows the roll-over counter (ROC) to be transmitted in SRTP packets

MIKEY.why: A substantial section defines new MIKEY parameters and transform values for the RCC transform and for separate SRTP and SRTCP integrity settings.
MIKEY.quote: To perform the parameter negotiation using MIKEY, three integrity transforms have been registered -- RCCm1, RCCm2, and RCCm3 in Table 6.10.1.c of [RFC3830]

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is used as the MAC computation, but the document does not specify or extend HMAC.
SRTCP is mentioned only to say the transform does not apply to it.
The broadcast and multicast setting motivates the work, but the document is about SRTP synchronization and integrity, not group key management.
RTP sequence numbers are the background to the ROC problem, but the document is about the secure profile, not RTP itself.

RFC4772.title: Security Implications of Using the Data Encryption Standard (DES)
RFC4772.summary: Informational RFC analysing the security weaknesses of DES (brute-force and cryptanalytic attacks, EFF DES Cracker, FPGAs, botnets) and recommending against its use, with an appendix on 3DES.

DES.why: The whole document analyses DES and 3DES security, attacks on them, and recommends deprecating DES; the Appendix covers 3DES in detail.
DES.quote: The Data Encryption Standard (DES) is susceptible to brute-force attacks, which are well within the reach of a modestly financed adversary.

rejected.why: AES is mentioned only as the recommended replacement, not analysed or specified.
Covered by the more specific DES tag, which is a child of this topic.
Botnets and DDoS are mentioned only as a vehicle for distributed key search, not addressed in their own right.
Site-to-site VPNs appear only as an example application threatened by weak encryption.

RFC4773.title: Administration of the IANA Special Purpose IPv6 Address Block
RFC4773.summary: Directs IANA to open and maintain a Special Purpose IPv6 Address Registry for blocks designated from 2001:0000::/23, defining what each registry entry records and how designations are made.

IANA.why: The document's whole purpose is an instruction to IANA on running an address registry, including the fields recorded and the criteria for designations.
IANA.quote: This document directs IANA to open a Special Purpose IPv6 address registry for the management of these IANA-designated address blocks.
IANA.section: 2. IANA IPv6 Special Purpose Address Block

IPv6.why: The registry concerns IPv6 address space (2001:0000::/23) and special-purpose IPv6 prefix designations such as experimental and anycast uses.
IPv6.quote: IANA maintains an "IANA IPv6 Address Special Purpose Registry".  The registry records current IANA address designations

rejected.why: It is a parent of the chosen tags' subject area, but the document is about the IANA registry, and IPv6 is the more specific tag. Allocation policy itself is not defined here.
Anycast is mentioned only as an example purpose for designated blocks, not as a subject of the document.
Only the Security Considerations touch on authenticating address blocks, and those are boilerplate-like. The document does not address routing security.

RFC4774.title: Specifying Alternate Semantics for the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Field
RFC4774.summary: BCP describing issues and requirements for defining alternate semantics for the IP ECN field (signalling via diffserv, incremental deployment with old routers, coexistence with competing traffic) so they can safely coexist with RFC 3168 ECN.

ECN.why: The whole document concerns the ECN field semantics, codepoints and how alternate semantics must coexist with default RFC 3168 ECN.
ECN.quote: This document discusses some of the issues in defining alternate semantics for the ECN field, and specifies requirements for a safe coexistence

Diffserv.why: A substantial section covers using diffserv codepoints (new or redefined) to signal alternate ECN semantics and the effects of DSCP re-marking.
Diffserv.quote: a codepoint in the diffserv field is used to signal the use of these alternate ECN semantics to the router
Diffserv.section: 3. Signalling the Use of Alternate ECN Semantics

rejected.why: Congestion-control response requirements are discussed, but ECN is the more specific tag and the document is about the ECN field itself.
Pre-congestion notification is only cited as an example proposal for alternate semantics, not the subject.
TCP is mentioned only as an example of conformant congestion control.
TFRC is only listed as a conformant congestion control mechanism.
The IP header is the location of the ECN field, but the document is not about IP itself.
Tunnel interaction is mentioned in one short subsection (5.4) as a consideration only.

RFC4775.title: Procedures for Protocol Extensions and Variations
RFC4775.summary: BCP 125 gives procedures and guidance for how other SDOs and vendors should handle extensions to or variations of IETF protocols, urging early IETF review, proper IANA registration and liaison use, without changing formal IETF processes.

IETF process.why: The document defines procedures for how protocol extensions interact with IETF review, liaison, IESG, IRTF and Independent Submission routes.
IETF process.quote: including when it is reasonable to extend IETF protocols with little or no review, and when extensions or variations need to be reviewed by the IETF community

IANA.why: A substantial section covers registered values, IANA assignments and the need for IANA Considerations in extension documents.
IANA.quote: It is essential that such new values are properly registered by the applicable procedures, including expert review where applicable

rejected.why: The document explicitly says it does not describe architectural principles of extensibility design; it is procedural.
Mentioned only as an example of an extensible protocol needing expert review of new attributes.
Section 5 only points to BCP 111 for MIB modules; not the subject of the document.
Section 6 is a brief boilerplate-like note on IETF IPR rules, not a main subject.
SIP change process is only cited as an example of a protocol-specific change process.

RFC4776.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) Option for Civic Addresses Configuration Information
RFC4776.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that carry the civic (street/postal) address of a client or server, with multilingual and multi-script renderings and an IANA registry of civic address element types (CAtypes).

DHCP.why: The document defines a new DHCPv4 option (code 99) for civic location, extending DHCP.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) option containing the civic location of the client or the DHCP server.

DHCPv6.why: It also defines the DHCPv6 option OPTION_GEOCONF_CIVIC with its own format.
DHCPv6.quote: OPTION_GEOCONF_CIVIC (36)

geolocation.why: The subject is the format and conveyance of civic location information within the GEOPRIV architecture.
geolocation.quote: There are two common ways to identify the location of an object, either through geospatial coordinates or by so-called civic addresses.

rejected.why: Emergency calling is the motivation, but the document defines only DHCP location delivery and leaves emergency use to ECRIT.
UTF-8 is only the encoding used for the values.
Language and script tags are used as element values but are not the subject.
The document creates a CAtype registry, but this is boilerplate-level and not the main subject.
Privacy appears only in the Security Considerations section.

gaps.name: Civic address format / GEOPRIV civic location
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for civic address formats. The geolocation topic is used instead.

RFC4777.title: IBM's iSeries Telnet Enhancements
RFC4777.summary: Informational RFC describing IBM iSeries Telnet server enhancements: NEW-ENVIRON USERVARs for device names, printer pass-through, auto-sign-on with DES/SHA-1 password substitutes and Kerberos tokens, and startup response records.

Telnet.why: The document extends Telnet with new environment-option USERVARs, terminal types and printer pass-through on the iSeries Telnet server.
Telnet.quote: This document describes the interface to the Telnet server on IBM's iSeries line of midrange business computers.

Kerberos.why: A full section defines Kerberos services-ticket automatic sign-on via the IBMTICKET USERVAR, with an SSPI example and error codes.
Kerberos.quote: Enhanced Telnet clients will need to obtain the Kerberos services ticket from a Key Distribution Center (KDC).

rejected.why: DES is only used as the algorithm in IBM's password-substitute scheme; the document is not about DES itself.
SHA-1 is used to build password substitutes; the document does not specify or analyse SHA.
GSS tokens carry the Kerberos ticket, but GSS-API itself is not specified or extended.
Auto-sign-on is covered, but it is specific to this Telnet interface and is better captured by the Telnet and Kerberos tags.
EBCDIC conversion is mentioned incidentally for object names and passwords, not as a subject of the document.

gaps.name: 5250 terminal emulation / IBM iSeries (AS/400) printer pass-through
gaps.why: A large part of the document covers 5250 pass-through, virtual device creation and printer data-stream records. The taxonomy has no 5250 tag; TN3270 covers only 3270.

RFC4778.title: Operational Security Current Practices in Internet Service Provider Environments
RFC4778.summary: RFC 4778 surveys operational security practices ISPs use to protect layer 2/3 infrastructure devices: physical access, in-band/OOB management, data path filtering, routing control plane, software/config integrity, logging, filtering and DoS tracing.

operational security.why: The whole document catalogues operational security practices for ISP network infrastructure, which is exactly this topic.
operational security.quote: This document is a survey of the current practices used in today's large ISP operational networks to secure layer 2 and layer 3 infrastructure devices.

DDoS.why: A dedicated section covers DoS tracking and mitigation techniques, and the DoS Mitigation service is listed in every section.
DDoS.quote: ISPs are using a variety of mitigation techniques including: sinkhole routing, black hole triggered routing, uRPF, rate limiting, and specific control plane traffic enhancements.

rejected.why: BGP appears as the context for prefix filters, max-prefix limits and black-hole triggered routing, but the document does not specify or extend BGP; it surveys security practices.
AAA, RADIUS and TACACS+ are used for device management authentication, but only as practices within the survey, not the subject of the document.
SSH is the preferred management channel mentioned throughout, but is only a mechanism used, not specified or analysed.
Logging is discussed in one section, including syslog weaknesses, but the document is not about the syslog protocol itself.
Routing control plane protection (MD5, GTSM, prefix filters) is one section of a broader survey; the document as a whole is operational security, so the broader tag fits better.
SNMP is mentioned as a management mechanism with community string practices, but is not the subject.

RFC4779.title: ISP IPv6 Deployment Scenarios in Broadband Access Networks
RFC4779.summary: Informational document describing how ISPs can deploy IPv6 alongside IPv4 in broadband access networks (cable/DOCSIS, DSL, Ethernet, WLAN, PLC), covering tunneling, native dual-stack, addressing, routing, multicast, QoS, security and management, with a gap analysis.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document is about deploying IPv6 in coexistence with IPv4 using tunneling and dual-stack in ISP broadband access networks.
IPv6 transition.quote: detailed description of IPv6 deployment and integration methods and scenarios in today's Service Provider (SP) Broadband (BB) networks in coexistence with deployed IPv4 services

DOCSIS.why: A large section analyses IPv6 deployment over DOCSIS cable networks, including bridged and routed CMTS models and needed spec changes.
DOCSIS.quote: DOCSIS 2.0 and prior specifications have limitations that do not allow for a smooth implementation of native IPv6 transport.

DSL.why: A major section covers IPv6 deployment models (point-to-point, PTA, LAA, hybrid) over DSL access networks.
DSL.quote: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) broadband services provide users with IP connectivity over the existing twisted-pair telephone lines

WiFi.why: A dedicated section covers IPv6 deployment over WLAN hotspots and routers, including security and multicast concerns.
WiFi.quote: WLAN enables subscribers to connect to the Internet from various locations without the restriction of staying indoors.

Ethernet.why: Covers IPv6 over broadband Ethernet/VLAN access with point-to-point, PTA and LAA models.
Ethernet.quote: This section describes the IPv6 deployment options in currently deployed Broadband Ethernet Access Networks.

DHCPv6.why: DHCPv6 and prefix delegation are the primary addressing mechanisms discussed across every access technology.
DHCPv6.quote: followed by a request via DHCP-PD for a prefix shorter than /64, typically /48 [RFC3177]

multicast.why: Each access technology has an IPv6 multicast section covering MLD, ASM/SSM, PIM and embedded RP.
multicast.quote: The deployment of IPv6 multicast services relies on MLD, identical to IGMP in IPv4 and on PIM for routing.

L2TP.why: The LAA model using L2TPv2 for IPv6 PPP sessions is a repeated deployment model in DSL, Ethernet and WLAN sections.
L2TP.quote: The BRAS tunnels the subscriber PPP sessions to the ISP by encapsulating them into L2TPv2 [RFC2661] tunnels.
L2TP.section: 6.2. Deploying IPv6 in IPv4 DSL Networks

rejected.why: PPP/PPPoE/PPPoA are the access encapsulations in the PTA model but are used as given, not specified or extended.
Tunneling overview is a part, but the specific IPv6 transition tag fits better; tunnels (6to4, Teredo, ISATAP) are only surveyed.
OSPFv3 and IS-IS are mentioned as the IGP choices in each scenario but are not the subject.
Network management sections only briefly say SNMP/MIBs should support IPv6.
IPv6 QoS subsections are brief and say to reuse IPv4 methodologies.
RADIUS/AAA servers appear in diagrams and authentication but are not discussed in their own right.

gaps.name: Power Line Communications (PLC/BPL)
gaps.why: A full section covers IPv6 over broadband power line access, but the taxonomy has no tag for PLC/BPL.

RFC4780.title: Management Information Base for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4780.summary: Defines the SIP-TC-MIB, SIP-COMMON-MIB, SIP-UA-MIB and SIP-SERVER-MIB SMIv2 modules for managing SIP user agents, proxies, redirect servers and registrars, including configuration, timers, statistics and notifications.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a set of SMIv2 MIB modules with objects, tables, notifications and compliance statements, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: Four MIB modules are specified: SIP-COMMON-MIB, SIP-SERVER-MIB, SIP-UA-MIB, and SIP-TC-MIB.

SIP.why: The MIB models SIP entities, methods, timers, status codes and option tags, so SIP readers would want this management specification.
SIP.quote: a set of managed objects that are used to manage Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) entities, which include User Agents, and Proxy, Redirect and Registrar servers.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
SCTP appears only as a transport bit in a textual convention referencing RFC 4168.
TLS is only listed as an authentication method bit and a transport option, not specified or profiled.
HTTP Digest is mentioned only as a value of the proxy authentication method object.
This is a parent of MIB, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.

RFC4781.title: Graceful Restart Mechanism for BGP with MPLS
RFC4781.summary: Extends BGP Graceful Restart (RFC 4724) so that an LSR restarting its BGP component can preserve MPLS forwarding state and label bindings for labels carried in BGP, with procedures for the restarting LSR and its neighbors.

BGP.why: Specifies an extension to BGP Graceful Restart: capability advertisement, restarting-speaker and receiving-neighbor procedures for labeled BGP routes.
BGP.quote: This document extends this mechanism to minimize the negative effects on MPLS forwarding caused by the Label Switching Router's (LSR's) control plane restart

MPLS.why: A substantial part concerns preserving MPLS forwarding state, label bindings and label reuse rules across control-plane restart.
MPLS.quote: it may be desirable not to perturb the LSPs going through that LSR (and specifically, the LSPs established by BGP) after failure or restart

rejected.why: Mentioned only as another protocol that may assign labels; not specified or extended.
Mentioned only in passing as another label-assigning component.
TCP MD5 and session failure appear only in Security Considerations.
Security Considerations discuss DoS only as boilerplate; document is not about routing security.

RFC4782.title: Quick-Start for TCP and IP
RFC4782.summary: Specifies the experimental Quick-Start mechanism, an IPv4/IPv6 option plus a TCP Quick-Start Response option, by which routers approve a higher initial or post-idle TCP sending rate, along with tunnel/MPLS interactions, security and deployment analysis.

congestion control.why: The document defines a router-assisted mechanism for determining the initial and post-idle sending rate, which is congestion-control subject matter. No more specific child tag fits.
congestion control.quote: Quick-Start is designed to allow connections to use higher sending rates when there is significant unused bandwidth along the path

TCP.why: It specifies a TCP Quick-Start Response option, how the sender computes QS-cwnd, paces packets, and reacts to loss, and it registers a TCP option.
TCP.quote: The Quick-Start Mechanisms in TCP

IPv4.why: It defines a new IPv4 option (option number 25) and its processing at routers, including header checksum updates.
IPv4.quote: The Quick-Start Request for IPv4 is defined as follows:

IPv6.why: It defines an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option and discusses its compatibility with flow labels and with checksums.
IPv6.quote: The Quick-Start Option for IPv6 is placed in the Hop-by-Hop Options extension header

tunneling.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how tunnels must handle Quick-Start options, and when tunnels cause false positives.
tunneling.quote: This section considers interactions between Quick-Start and IP tunnels, including IPsec ([RFC4301]), IP in IP [RFC2003], GRE

rejected.why: It is compared and may be used alongside Quick-Start, but the document is not about ECN.
Section 5 only shows AH ICV compatibility and mentions tunnels. This is peripheral to the document.
Section 6.4 gives a brief discussion of interaction. The document is not about MPLS.
It is discussed only as an issue with large initial windows in Section 4.7.1.
Appendix C discusses possible issues only, and the document explicitly does not specify Quick-Start for DCCP.
Section 9.3 only briefly notes that Quick-Start is orthogonal to differentiated services.

RFC4783.title: GMPLS - Communication of Alarm Information
RFC4783.summary: Extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling (updating RFC 3473) with a new ALARM_SPEC object, new IF_ID TLVs, an Admin_Status inhibit bit and an "Alarms" error code so alarm information can be communicated along an LSP in Path and Resv messages.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS signaling (RFC 3473 GMPLS-RSVP) with alarm communication objects, TLVs and procedures, so it belongs on the GMPLS page.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes an extension to Generalized MPLS (Multi-Protocol Label Switching) signaling to support communication of alarm information.

RSVP-TE.why: The extension is specified as new RSVP objects (ALARM_SPEC), Path/Resv message formats, error code and Admin_Status changes, so RSVP-TE readers would want it.
RSVP-TE.quote: This section provides the GMPLS-RSVP [RFC3473] specification for communication of alarm information.

rejected.why: RSVP is the base protocol, but the document is specifically about the RSVP-TE/GMPLS extensions rather than QoS reservation.
The more specific GMPLS tag fits; MPLS in general is not the subject.
Alarm reporting is related to fault management, but the document is a signaling extension rather than an OAM mechanism.
The Alarm MIB (RFC 3877) is only referenced for probable-cause values and severity; the document defines no MIB.
The IANA section only registers values for the new protocol elements; it is boilerplate here.

RFC4784.title: Verizon Wireless Dynamic Mobile IP Key Update for cdma2000(R) Networks
RFC4784.summary: Describes Verizon Wireless's deployed Dynamic Mobile IP Key Update (DMU) procedure, which uses RSA-encrypted key payloads carried in Mobile IP extensions and RADIUS VSAs to bootstrap MIP keys between a mobile node and home AAA server in cdma2000 networks.

cdma2000.why: The whole procedure is defined for cdma2000 1X and HRPD/1xEV-DO packet data networks (PDSN, HLR/AC, IS-835), so readers of cdma2000 would look for it.
cdma2000.quote: mechanism for distributing and updating Mobile IP (MIP) cryptographic keys in cdma2000(R) networks (including High Rate Packet Data, which is often referred to as 1xEV-DO)

Mobile IPv4.why: It defines new Mobile IP vendor-specific extensions and a key bootstrapping procedure for MN-AAA and MN-HA keys within Mobile IPv4 registration.
Mobile IPv4.quote: The MIP_Key_Data Payload is appended to the MN's MIP Registration Request (RRQ) as a MIP Vendor/Organization-Specific Extension

RADIUS.why: Defines new vendor-specific RADIUS attributes and an Access-Reject based flow, which the IESG note flags as incompatible with RADIUS.
RADIUS.quote: Three new RADIUS Attributes are required to support the DMU Procedure and are specified as follows

key management.why: Core subject is key distribution and provisioning, including RSA key management, pre-generation of keys and key lifetimes.
key management.quote: The DMU procedure utilizes RSA public key cryptography to securely distribute unique MIP keys to potentially millions of cdma2000(R) 1X and HRPD/1xEV-DO Mobile Nodes

rejected.why: RSA (PKCS#1 v1.5) is the encryption mechanism used for the payload, not the subject; the document does not specify or analyse RSA itself.
Section 4.3 explicitly explains why PKI is not used, so the document is not about PKI.
Mentioned only in passing as an alternative to RADIUS; nothing is specified for it.
RFC 4086 is only cited for key generation requirements; not a substantial subject of the document.
The child RADIUS tag fits better; the document does not address AAA frameworks generally.

RFC4785.title: Pre-Shared Key (PSK) Ciphersuites with NULL Encryption for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC4785.summary: Defines three TLS pre-shared key ciphersuites (PSK, DHE_PSK, RSA_PSK with NULL encryption and SHA) that provide authentication and integrity without confidentiality.

TLS.why: The document specifies new TLS ciphersuites and registers them in the TLS Cipher Suite registry. Readers of TLS extensions and ciphersuites need it.
TLS.quote: This document augments [TLS-PSK] by adding three more ciphersuites (PSK, DHE_PSK, RSA_PSK) with authentication and integrity only - no encryption.

rejected.why: SRP is mentioned only as an alternative in the applicability statement. The document does not specify or analyse it.
SHA is only the hash named in the ciphersuites. The document says nothing new about the hash family.
RSA_PSK is only a key exchange name inherited from TLS-PSK. The document does not specify RSA itself.
Pre-shared keys are the premise, but the document does not address key provisioning or management.
PKI is mentioned only as something that PSK avoids.

RFC4786.title: Operation of Anycast Services
RFC4786.summary: BCP describing how network operators should design, deploy, route, and monitor anycast-distributed services (e.g., DNS root servers) using IGPs and BGP, including node placement, covering prefixes, ECMP, dampening, RPF, and security.

anycast.why: The whole document is operational best practice for anycast service distribution, which is exactly the anycast topic.
anycast.quote: This document presents commentary and recommendations for distribution of services using anycast.

rejected.why: BGP is the routing system over which global anycast is advertised, and some BGP-specific issues are discussed (dampening, communities), but the document is not about specifying or operating BGP itself.
DNS is the main example service, but the document is service-agnostic and does not specify DNS behaviour.
Equal-cost paths are discussed in one subsection as a hazard to anycast; not a substantial subject of the document.
RPF checks and multi-homed sites are mentioned only in relation to anycast nodes.
IGP anycast is discussed generically without reference to OSPF specifically.
NO_EXPORT and NOPEER are mentioned briefly for local-scope propagation, not a main subject.

RFC4787.title: Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP
RFC4787.summary: BCP defining terminology for NAT mapping, filtering, hairpinning and related behaviors for unicast UDP, and a set of 14 requirements so that real-time and gaming applications work through NATs.

NAT.why: The whole document specifies required NAT behaviors (mapping, filtering, hairpinning, ALGs, timers, ICMP, fragmentation) for UDP.
NAT.quote: defines a set of requirements that would allow many applications, such as multimedia communications or online gaming, to work consistently

rejected.why: UDP is the traffic type NATs handle, not specified or extended here; the document is about NAT behavior.
STUN is discussed as a motivating UNSAF traversal technique but is not specified or extended.
ICE is referenced as the way applications cope with NATs; out of scope here.
Traversal techniques are explicitly out of scope; the document sets NAT requirements, so the NAT tag fits better.
ICMP handling by NATs is one requirement (REQ-12/13), a minor part of the document.
RTP port parity and contiguity are mentioned as motivation only.

RFC4788.title: Enhancements to RTP Payload Formats for EVRC Family Codecs
RFC4788.summary: RFC 4788 updates RFC 3558 by defining EVRC-B RTP payload support, a compact bundled packet format for EVRC/EVRC-B, DTX (silence suppression) SDP parameters, and new audio media type registrations.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines RTP payload formats (header-free, interleaved/bundled, compact bundled) for the EVRC and EVRC-B codecs.
RTP payload format.quote: This document updates the Enhanced Variable Rate Codec (EVRC) RTP payload formats defined in RFC 3558 with several enhancements and extensions.

media types.why: A large part of the document is media type registrations (EVRC1, EVRCB, EVRCB0, EVRCB1) and updates to EVRC and EVRC0, with parameter definitions.
media types.quote: Four (4) new MIME subtype registrations - "EVRC1", "EVRCB", "EVRCB0", and "EVRCB1" - are defined in this document

SDP.why: The document maps the new parameters (fixedrate, silencesupp, dtxmax, dtxmin, hangover) into SDP and gives offer/answer rules for negotiating DTX.
SDP.quote: When SDP is used to specify sessions employing the compact bundled format for EVRC/EVRC-B-encoded speech, the mapping is as follows:

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload formats ride on. The more specific RTP payload format tag already covers the document.
The EVRC-B codec is defined in 3GPP2 specifications. This RFC only specifies how to carry its frames in RTP, and RTP payload format already covers that.
EVRC comes from the cdma2000 world and DTX is cited from a cdma2000 spec. The document does not address cdma2000 networks themselves.
AMR is a different speech codec. It plays no part in this document.

RFC4789.title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) over IEEE 802 Networks
RFC4789.summary: Defines an optional SNMP transport mapping that carries serialized SNMP messages directly in IEEE 802 frames (Ethernet type 0x814C, SNAP over LLC), adds the snmpIeee802Domain transport domain OID, and obsoletes RFC 1089.

SNMP.why: The document is a new SNMP transport mapping that updates RFC 3417 and defines a transport domain for SNMP, so it belongs on the SNMP page.
SNMP.quote: This document specifies how Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) messages can be transmitted directly over IEEE 802 networks.

Ethernet.why: A substantial part of the document specifies the frame format, Ethernet type value and SNAP/LLC encapsulation for carrying SNMP directly over IEEE 802 LANs.
Ethernet.quote: Serialized SNMP messages are sent in IEEE 802.3 frames with an Ethernet type field of 33100 (hexadecimal 814C).

rejected.why: The MIB module only defines a module identity and an OID for the transport domain. It defines no managed objects, so it is not really about MIB modules.
This is a close fit as a topic. However, SNMP is already tagged, and the taxonomy places this topic outside the SNMP subtree, so I did not add it.
IEEE 802.11 is mentioned only as an example of a LAN that uses LLC/SNAP encapsulation.
The OID registry assignment is boilerplate IANA Considerations text and not the main subject.

RFC4790.title: Internet Application Protocol Collation Registry
RFC4790.summary: Defines the collation abstraction for string comparison (equality, substring, ordering) in Internet application protocols, creates an IANA collation registry with registration procedure, and registers the initial collations i;octet, i;ascii-numeric and i;ascii-casemap.

internationalization.why: The document is about comparing and sorting international strings in protocols, and about the requirements application protocols must meet when allowing non-ASCII characters. No specific child tag fits.
internationalization.quote: Many Internet application protocols include string-based lookup, searching, or sorting operations. However, the problem space for searching and sorting international strings is large

IANA.why: A major part of the document defines the collation registry, the registration procedure and format, the designated expert guidelines, and the initial registrations.
IANA.quote: it is now time to create that registry and populate it with some initial values appropriate for an international community.

rejected.why: ACAP is the origin of the comparator concept, but this document generalizes it into a registry and does not specify or extend ACAP.
IMAP is an example protocol that uses collations and is discussed informatively only.
Sieve is only an example of a protocol that uses collations.
The document relies on the Unicode Collation Algorithm and stringprep by reference but does not define Unicode usage itself.
UTF-8 is mentioned as the usual encoding and in the security considerations, but the document is not about it.
Charsets appear only as an analogy for the abstraction, and the document does not register or define character sets.

gaps.name: Collation / string comparison
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for collation, string comparison or sorting, which is the main subject of this document. internationalization is only the closest parent.

RFC4791.title: Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV (CalDAV)
RFC4791.summary: Defines CalDAV, a set of WebDAV extensions (calendar collections, MKCALENDAR, properties, privileges and calendaring REPORTs) for accessing, managing and sharing iCalendar data on a server.
