CalDAV.why: The whole document specifies the CalDAV calendar-access feature: calendar collections, MKCALENDAR, calendar-query, calendar-multiget and free-busy-query reports.
CalDAV.quote: This document defines extensions to the Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) protocol to specify a standard way of accessing, managing, and sharing calendaring and scheduling information

WebDAV.why: CalDAV is defined as extensions to WebDAV, building on its ACL, REPORT, properties, ETags and locking. Readers of WebDAV extensions would want it.
WebDAV.quote: This document proposes a way to model calendar data in WebDAV, with additional features to make an interoperable calendar access protocol.

iCalendar.why: The document profiles how iCalendar objects (components, UIDs, recurrence, VTIMEZONE, VFREEBUSY) are stored and queried in calendar object resources.
iCalendar.quote: MUST support iCalendar [RFC2445] as a media type for the calendar object resource format;

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate; CalDAV adds WebDAV-level methods and does not define new HTTP semantics.
XML is only the encoding for requests, responses and properties.
TLS is only required as transport security and is not specified here.
The calendar-timezone property is used for resolving floating times, but the document does not distribute time zone data.
Basic authentication is mentioned only in a Security Considerations remark.

RFC4792.title: Encoding Instructions for the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER)
RFC4792.summary: Defines the notation for GSER encoding instructions and the CHOICE-OF-STRINGS encoding instruction, which lets GSER encode a CHOICE of restricted string types without its identifier, and applies it to X.520 DirectoryString.

ASN.1.why: The document specifies ASN.1 encoding instruction notation and the CHOICE-OF-STRINGS instruction for GSER. It is about ASN.1 modules and encoding rules.
ASN.1.quote: defines the supporting notation for encoding instructions that apply to the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER)

rejected.why: DirectoryString from X.520 is used as the example, but the document is about ASN.1 encoding instructions and not directory access or synchronization.
X.520 is referenced only to amend the DirectoryString definition. The X.500 directory service itself is not specified or analysed.
ABNF is only the notation used to reproduce the GSER ChoiceValue rule. The document is not about ABNF.
The restricted string types are the subject of the CHOICE alternatives, but the document does not register or discuss character sets.

gaps.name: GSER (Generic String Encoding Rules)
gaps.why: The document extends GSER, an ASN.1 encoding rule set, and the taxonomy has no tag for GSER specifically. The ASN.1 tag covers it only approximately.

RFC4793.title: The EAP Protected One-Time Password Protocol (EAP-POTP)
RFC4793.summary: RFC 4793 specifies EAP-POTP, an EAP method for authenticating users with one-time-password tokens, providing optional mutual authentication, key derivation, session resumption, and PIN change via a TLV-based protocol.

EAP.why: The document defines a new EAP method (type 32 for SecurID profile) with its TLVs, negotiation, key derivation and security claims.
EAP.quote: This document describes a general Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method suitable for use with One-Time Password (OTP) tokens

OTP.why: The method is built around carrying one-time passwords from tokens, including challenge, next-OTP, PIN change and an RSA SecurID profile, so readers of OTP systems would want it.
OTP.quote: This document describes an EAP method intended to meet the needs of organizations wishing to use OTP tokens in an interoperable manner to authenticate users over EAP.

rejected.why: PBKDF2 is used as the key derivation function but the document is not about password hashing; it is a building block.
RADIUS is only mentioned as a typical backend protocol and in Appendix C for MPPE key attribute population; it is not the subject.
HMAC is used as the default MAC algorithm, not specified or analysed here.
AES-CBC is a default negotiated encryption algorithm, merely a substrate.
PPP is named only as an example protocol that carries EAP.
Key derivation is part of the EAP method, and the EAP tag already covers it; the document is not a general key management treatment.
SHA-256 is the default hash used by the method, not the subject of the document.

RFC4794.title: RFC 1264 Is Obsolete
RFC4794.summary: RFC 4794 reclassifies RFC 1264 (IETF routing protocol standardization criteria) as historic, removing the blanket extra requirements for routing documents on the Standards Track and leaving implementation-experience demands to normal RFC 2026 IESG discretion.

IETF process.why: The document changes IETF standards-track procedure by retiring special rules for routing protocols and deferring to the RFC 2026 standards process.
IETF process.quote: this document reclassifies RFC 1264 as historic. While that does not prohibit the Routing Area Directors from requiring implementation and/or operational experience under the RFC 2026 rules

rejected.why: The document concerns the standardization process for routing protocols, not routing technology itself.
MIB modules are mentioned only as a past RFC 1264 requirement now merely encouraged; the document does not define or discuss MIBs substantively.
Manageability is mentioned briefly as a consideration but is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC4795.title: Link-local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR)
RFC4795.summary: Informational RFC specifying LLMNR, a DNS-packet-format-based multicast protocol for link-local name resolution when conventional DNS is unavailable, including sender/responder behavior, conflict resolution and security.

DNS.why: LLMNR is a DNS-derived name resolution protocol using DNS formats, RR types, and a distinct resolver cache; DNS readers would want it. No narrower tag fits (mDNS is a different protocol).
DNS.quote: LLMNR is based on the DNS packet format defined in [RFC1035] Section 4 for both queries and responses.

naming.why: Document addresses general name resolution mechanism, usage model as secondary resolver and name uniqueness/conflict resolution on a link, beyond DNS itself.
naming.quote: The goal of Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) is to enable name resolution in scenarios in which conventional DNS name resolution is not possible.

rejected.why: LLMNR is a distinct protocol (port 5355, different addresses); mDNS is only mentioned as acknowledged prior work.
Only mentioned as an optional authentication mechanism in Security Considerations.
EDNS0 support is required but only as a used mechanism, not defined or extended.
DHCP is only referenced for configuring names and enabling LLMNR; not the subject.
UDP/TCP are just transport substrate for LLMNR.
Explicitly stated as out of scope in the Introduction.

RFC4796.title: The Session Description Protocol (SDP) Content Attribute
RFC4796.summary: Defines a new SDP media-level attribute, 'content', whose values (slides, speaker, sl, main, alt) describe the content of a media stream, with offer/answer usage, examples, and an IANA subregistry.

SDP.why: The RFC extends SDP with a new media-level attribute, including its ABNF, offer/answer semantics and examples.
SDP.quote: This document defines a new Session Description Protocol (SDP) media-level attribute, 'content'.

rejected.why: SIP is only the typical context in which SDP is used and a means for integrity protection; the document does not specify or extend it.
RTP/AVP appears only in example m= lines; nothing is specified about RTP.
Conferencing scenarios such as lectures are motivating use cases, but the document defines an SDP attribute, not a conferencing framework.
TLS and S/MIME are mentioned only in Security Considerations as integrity protection.
The new subregistry is boilerplate registration for the attribute, not the subject of the document.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the attribute syntax.

RFC4797.title: Use of Provider Edge to Provider Edge (PE-PE) Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) or IP in BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks
RFC4797.summary: Informational RFC describing how BGP/MPLS IP VPNs can replace the MPLS tunnel label with an MPLS-in-IP or MPLS-in-GRE encapsulation between PE routers, so VPNs work across non-MPLS cores, and discussing spoofing implications.

L3VPN.why: The document modifies how BGP/MPLS IP VPN PE routers carry VPN traffic, replacing the tunnel LSP with an IP/GRE tunnel; L3VPN readers would want it.
L3VPN.quote: an implementation strategy for BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) in which the outermost MPLS label (i.e., the tunnel label) is replaced with either an IP header

GRE.why: GRE (and plain IP) encapsulation of MPLS packets is the core mechanism specified, including encapsulation and decapsulation procedures at PEs.
GRE.quote: An MPLS-in-GRE or MPLS-in-IP [6] encapsulation will be used to turn the MPLS packet, described above, back into an IP packet.

rejected.why: MPLS labels are used for the VPN route label, but the document's point is to remove the MPLS tunnel LSP; MPLS is the substrate, not the subject.
BGP next-hop is used to infer tunnel endpoints, but BGP is not extended or specified here.
Plain IP encapsulation is mentioned as an alternative, but the encapsulation itself is defined in RFC 4023; GRE and L3VPN cover the subject.
Parent of GRE and IP-in-IP; GRE is chosen as the more specific tag.
Packet spoofing implications are discussed, but this concerns tunnel filtering rather than routing protocol security.

RFC4798.title: Connecting IPv6 Islands over IPv4 MPLS Using IPv6 Provider Edge Routers (6PE)
RFC4798.summary: Specifies 6PE, in which dual-stack provider edge routers interconnect IPv6 islands across an IPv4 MPLS core by exchanging labeled IPv6 routes over MP-BGP with IPv4-mapped next hops and carrying traffic over IPv4-signaled LSPs, including multi-AS cases.

IPv6 transition.why: 6PE is a mechanism for IPv6/IPv4 coexistence, providing IPv6 connectivity across an IPv4-only MPLS core without upgrading the core.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document explains how to interconnect IPv6 islands over a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS)-enabled IPv4 cloud.

MPLS.why: The document specifies IPv6 transport over MPLS LSPs, including two-level label stacks, PHP, explicit null and MTU handling.
MPLS.quote: The IPv4-signaled LSPs can be established using any existing technique for label setup [RFC3031] (LDP, RSVP-TE, etc.).
MPLS.section: 3. Transport over IPv4-signaled LSPs and IPv6 Label Binding

BGP.why: Core of the mechanism is MP-BGP with the IPv6 AFI, label SAFI and IPv4-mapped next hop, plus multi-AS eBGP and route reflector procedures.
BGP.quote: The 6PE routers MUST exchange the IPv6 prefixes over MP-BGP sessions as per [RFC2545] running over IPv4.

rejected.why: Only referenced for analogy; the document explicitly says IPv6 VPNs are out of scope and 6PE provides global IPv6 reachability.
LDP is mandated as the baseline LSP signalling but is a substrate, not what the document is about.
IPv6 is the payload being carried, but the document's subject is the transition mechanism, which sits under the more specific IPv6 transition tag.
Route reflectors are mentioned in passing as an option for distributing routes, not specified.
MTU and Packet Too Big handling is a short operational note, not a substantial part of the document.

RFC4801.title: Definitions of Textual Conventions for Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Management
RFC4801.summary: Defines the GMPLS-TC-STD-MIB module of SMIv2 textual conventions (label, label type, segment direction) for reuse by GMPLS-related MIB modules.

GMPLS.why: The TCs represent GMPLS labels, label types and LSP segment direction, so the document belongs on the GMPLS page.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines a MIB module that contains textual conventions (TCs) for Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) networks.

MIB.why: The document's content is an SMIv2 MIB module of textual conventions, which is what the MIB tag covers.
MIB.quote: This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module that contains textual conventions (TCs) to represent commonly used

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for MIB objects, and the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour.
It supplements the MPLS TC MIB (RFC 3811), but the subject is GMPLS, which is a more specific tag.
SONET and SDH labels appear only as enumerated label types referencing RFC 4606.
The document defines TCs only and does not address traffic engineering.

RFC4802.title: Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Traffic Engineering Management Information Base
RFC4802.summary: RFC 4802 defines the GMPLS-TE-STD-MIB SNMP MIB module (plus the IANA-GMPLS-TC-MIB textual conventions) for managing GMPLS traffic-engineered tunnels, extending the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module, with tables, objects, notification and compliance statements for GMPLS TE tunnels.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

GMPLS.why: The managed objects model GMPLS tunnels, their hops, labels, encoding, switching type and G-PID, so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) [RFC3945] based traffic engineering (TE).

rejected.why: The MIB objects reflect RSVP-TE signalling parameters (Notify recipients, Admin Status), but the document does not specify or extend that protocol; it only manages state.
SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document's subject is the MIB module, which the MIB tag covers.
The MIB extends the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB, but the document is about GMPLS TE management, and the GMPLS tag is more specific.
TE tunnels are the managed subject, but the GMPLS tag already covers them and the document does not address TE in its own right.
The IANA-GMPLS-TC-MIB is defined in the IANA Considerations section, but that is boilerplate-style apparatus and not the main subject.

RFC4803.title: Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Label Switching Router (LSR) Management Information Base
RFC4803.summary: Defines the GMPLS-LSR-STD-MIB and GMPLS-LABEL-STD-MIB SNMP MIB modules, which sparse-augment the MPLS LSR MIB to configure and monitor GMPLS label switching routers, including generalized labels and bidirectional LSPs.

GMPLS.why: The document models GMPLS LSR interfaces, segments, and generalized labels (SONET/SDH, wavelength, waveband), so GMPLS readers need it.
GMPLS.quote: it describes managed objects to configure and/or monitor a Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Label Switching Router (LSR).

MIB.why: The document's main content is two SMIv2 MIB modules with tables, objects and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: The GMPLS tag is more specific; the MPLS LSR MIB (RFC 3813) is extended but not the subject here.
SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the MIB tag covers the subject.
Only referenced by a signaling capability bit and hello period object; the document does not specify RSVP-TE.
SONET/SDH label fields are represented in the label table, but the document is not about IP over SONET.
The TE MIB is a companion document (RFC 4802); this one covers LSR and labels.

RFC4804.title: Aggregation of Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) Reservations over MPLS TE/DS-TE Tunnels
RFC4804.summary: Specifies aggregation of end-to-end RSVP reservations over pre-established MPLS TE/DS-TE tunnels, adapting RFC 3175 procedures so the tunnel head-end acts as Aggregator and tail-end as Deaggregator.

RSVP.why: The document specifies RSVP Path/Resv processing by Aggregator and Deaggregator, modifying RFC 3175 procedures. RSVP aggregation is its core subject.
RSVP.quote: This document specifies aggregation of RSVP end-to-end reservations over MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) tunnels or MPLS Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) tunnels.

RSVP-TE.why: TE tunnels signalled with RSVP-TE act as the aggregate reservations, and the document reuses LSP-hierarchy procedures such as IF_ID RSVP_HOP and tunnel resizing.
RSVP-TE.quote: Aggregator SHOULD use "make-before-break" procedures as described in [RSVP-TE] to alter the TE tunnel bandwidth.

MPLS.why: The aggregate reservations are MPLS TE and DS-TE tunnels, and the document handles MPLS-specific issues such as penultimate hop popping and label-based encapsulation of traffic.
MPLS.quote: aggregation of end-to-end RSVP reservations over MPLS TE tunnels (which act as aggregate reservations in the core)

rejected.why: Diffserv PHBs and classes are the data-plane mechanism in the core, and DS-TE class types guide tunnel mapping. The document does not specify Diffserv itself.
Intserv service types are used in mapping policy and ADSPEC updates. The document is not about the Intserv architecture.
MPLS TE tunnels are used as aggregate reservations, but the document does not address traffic engineering in its own right. RSVP-TE already covers the subject.
IPsec gateways are mentioned only as an optional deployment case in which E2E messages and data are sent into IPsec tunnels.
SIP appears only in the informative VoIP call admission control example in Appendix B.
The document reuses LSP-hierarchy procedures from a GMPLS RFC but states that the GMPLS-specific aspects are not relevant here.

RFC4805.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the DS1, J1, E1, DS2, and E2 Interface Types
RFC4805.summary: Standards-track SMIv2 MIB module for managing DS1, J1, E1, DS2 and E2 interfaces (configuration, line status, loopbacks, 15-minute performance statistics, channelization), obsoleting RFC 3895.

MIB.why: The document's entire purpose is to define a MIB module (DS1-MIB) with objects, tables, groups and compliance statements for DS1/J1/E1/DS2/E2 interfaces.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines managed objects, not SNMP itself (security text is boilerplate).
ISDN Primary Rate appears only in compliance statements for T1/E1 PRI; the document is not about ISDN access.
SONET/SDH is mentioned only as a companion MIB document.
The subject is a management MIB for telco interfaces; the specific tag MIB fits better and no specific link-layer tag covers DS1/E1.
PPP/HDLC is mentioned only as an analogy for ifStackTable usage.

gaps.name: DS1/E1/T1 digital transmission interfaces (PDH)
gaps.why: The document is about T1/E1/J1/DS2/E2 plesiochronous digital hierarchy line interfaces, performance monitoring and alarms, but the taxonomy has no tag for PDH/T-carrier physical-layer links.

RFC4806.title: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Extensions to IKEv2
RFC4806.summary: Defines an "OCSP Content" Cert Encoding for IKEv2 CERTREQ and CERT payloads so peers can exchange bounded-size OCSP responses in-band to convey certificate revocation status.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new Cert Encoding value and specifies its use in CERTREQ/CERT payloads and the IKEv2 exchanges.
IKE.quote: This document defines the "OCSP Content" extension to IKEv2.

OCSP.why: It specifies how OCSP responses are requested and carried in IKEv2 and how responders are identified, so readers of OCSP would want it.
OCSP.quote: This document defines an extension to IKEv2 that enables the use of OCSP for in-band signaling of certificate revocation status.

rejected.why: Certificate revocation status and path validation are discussed, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
EAP appears only as an example exchange in which the OCSP extension is used; the document does not specify or extend EAP.
IKEv2 is the IPsec key management protocol, but the document is about the IKE extension, not IPsec architecture, ESP or AH; IKE is the more specific tag.
The parent of OCSP is implied, and the document is specifically about OCSP rather than PKI in general.

RFC4807.title: IPsec Security Policy Database Configuration MIB
RFC4807.summary: Defines the IPSEC-SPD-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for configuring an IPsec security policy database (endpoints, rule groups, filters, compound filters, static actions and notifications), designed to be extensible with IPsec and IKE action MIBs.

MIB.why: The document's core content is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, textual conventions, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB module for configuration of an IPsec security policy database (SPD).

IPsec.why: The MIB configures the IPsec security policy database based on the IPsec architecture and the IPCP model, so IPsec readers would want it.
IPsec.quote: This MIB module defines configuration objects for managing IPsec Security Policies.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag sits under SNMP and covers it.
Considered since it configures policy-based filtering and relates to the DMTF/IPCP policy model, but the MIB tag and IPsec tag fit more specifically.
The filtering and accept/drop actions are noted as usable for firewall configuration, but the document is about the IPsec SPD, not firewalls.
IKE actions are defined in a companion document, explicitly not in this one.
The DIFFSERV-MIB multi-field classifier is imported and reused for filtering, but the document does not address Diffserv itself.
UTF-8 is only used for encoding the time period textual convention.

RFC4808.title: Key Change Strategies for TCP-MD5
RFC4808.summary: Informational RFC describing single-ended heuristic strategies for changing the long-term TCP-MD5 (RFC 2385) key, mostly used for BGP sessions, with reception/transmission algorithms, operations, and suggestions for a future TCP authentication option.

TCP.why: The document specifies key-change behaviour for the TCP-MD5 option, including receive/transmit algorithms, retransmission-based key fallback and Timestamp disambiguation, i.e. an extension/implementation strategy for TCP authentication.
TCP.quote: Fortunately, a heuristic permits key change despite this protocol deficiency. The change can be installed unilaterally at one end of a connection

key management.why: The whole document concerns rekeying practice for a long-term shared key, and Section 4 states requirements for a Key ID and automated key management in a future TCP authentication option.
key management.quote: The proper solution involves some sort of key management protocol.

rejected.why: BGP is the motivating use case for TCP-MD5, but the document does not specify or change BGP; it only mentions BGP keepalives.
The MD5-based option is the subject, but the document is about key change strategy, not the MD5 algorithm; it only suggests replacing it with a stronger MAC.
HMAC-SHA1 is only mentioned as a preferred future MAC in the Moving Forward section.
It secures BGP sessions, but the document is about TCP option key rollover rather than securing routing protocols as a subject.
Operational monitoring of key usage is discussed, but this is a small part and not a general operational security practices document.

gaps.name: TCP-MD5 signature option / TCP authentication
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the TCP MD5 signature option or TCP-AO; TCP is the closest fit but readers of TCP authentication would want it.

RFC4809.title: Requirements for an IPsec Certificate Management Profile
RFC4809.summary: Informational requirements document for certificate lifecycle management transactions (authorization, generation, enrollment, rekey/renewal/update, revocation, repository lookup, trust) between IPsec/IKE VPN systems and PKI systems, intended to drive a later certificate management profile.

PKI.why: The document is about certificate enrollment, renewal, revocation, repositories, CRLs and trust anchors for a PKI used with IPsec; this is PKI certificate management.
PKI.quote: requirements for transactions to handle Public Key Certificate (PKC) lifecycle transactions between Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) Virtual Private Network (VPN) Systems

IPsec.why: The requirements are driven by large-scale IPsec/IKE VPN deployments, covering gateway and remote-access peers and certificate use in IKE; readers of IPsec would want it.
IPsec.quote: The Peers authenticate themselves in the IKE negotiation using digital signatures generated with PKCs from a PKI System.

rejected.why: Only touches on certificate fields and CRL/AIA/CDP as requirements; it does not define a certificate profile itself (defers to RFC 3280 and the IKE cert profile).
IKE is the consumer of the certificates; IKE transactions are explicitly out of scope ([I] interactions).
CMP is not named; the Security Considerations mention CMC/CRMF only as candidate protocols for a later profile, and this document specifies no protocol.
Revocation checking is by CRLs; OCSP is not discussed.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a candidate protocol for the future profile.

RFC4810.title: Long-Term Archive Service Requirements
RFC4810.summary: Informational RFC from the LTANS working group describing long-term archive services that preserve data and evidence records (time stamps, verification data) over long periods, and listing the technical requirements for interacting with such services.

LTANS.why: The whole document defines requirements for long-term archive services, which is the subject of the LTANS tag (long-term archive and notary services for signed data).
LTANS.quote: This document describes a class of long-term archive services to support such scenarios and the technical requirements for interacting with such services.

rejected.why: Certificates, revocation and trust anchors are mentioned as evidence content, but the document does not specify or profile PKI.
RFC 3280 is cited only for trust anchors; nothing about certificate formats is defined here.
The archive stores data, but this tag covers storage access protocols like NFS and iSCSI, not a preservation and evidence service.
The parent is implied by LTANS, and the document is not general security guidance.
Algorithm weakening and cryptographic maintenance policy are discussed, but only as motivation for archive requirements.

RFC4811.title: OSPF Out-of-Band Link State Database (LSDB) Resynchronization
RFC4811.summary: Informational RFC documenting a vendor-specific OSPF mechanism for out-of-band LSDB resynchronization using an LR capability bit in LLS Extended Options and an R-bit in Database Description packets, so adjacencies need not be dropped from router-LSAs.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 with a new DBD R-bit, a neighbor data structure flag, and modified DBD processing and neighbor state treatment for LSDB resynchronization.
OSPF.quote: the format of the OSPF Database Description (DBD) packet is changed to include a new R-bit indicating OOB LSDB resynchronization.

rejected.why: The document modifies OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328) packet formats; OSPFv3 is not addressed.
The subject is a specific OSPF protocol mechanism, so the OSPF tag is the more specific fit.
The document concerns LSDB resynchronization without topology change, not fast reroute. It also notes it predates Graceful OSPF Restart (RFC 3623) but does not specify restart.

gaps.name: OSPF Link-Local Signaling (LLS) / Graceful OSPF Restart
gaps.why: The mechanism relies on the LLS Extended Options TLV (RFC 4813) and is related to Graceful Restart (RFC 3623), but the taxonomy has no tag for either. The document only uses the LLS capability bit and does not define LLS.

RFC4812.title: OSPF Restart Signaling
RFC4812.summary: Describes a vendor-specific OSPF mechanism, using an RS-bit in the Link-Local Signaling Extended Options TLV, by which a restarting router tells neighbors not to reset adjacencies when its Hellos omit them.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF Hello processing and neighbor state machine behavior with a restart signaling bit, so it is about OSPF.
OSPF.quote: a new bit, called RS (restart signal), is introduced into the Extended Options (EO) TLV in the Link-Local Signaling (LLS) block

rejected.why: The document applies to OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328) and does not address OSPF for IPv6.
The document is about a specific OSPF mechanism, not general routing architecture or scalability.

RFC4813.title: OSPF Link-Local Signaling
RFC4813.summary: Experimental RFC defining OSPF Link-Local Signaling: an LLS data block with TLVs (Extended Options, Cryptographic Authentication) appended to OSPF Hello and DBD packets, signalled by a new L-bit in the Options field.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF packet formats with an LLS block, a new Options bit and TLVs, so it is squarely about OSPF.
OSPF.quote: To perform link-local signaling (LLS), OSPF routers add a special data block at the end of OSPF packets

rejected.why: The document extends OSPF Version 2 (RFC 2328) only; it does not address OSPF for IPv6.
MD5 is only the digest used in the cryptographic authentication TLV, as a mechanism for authenticating the LLS block, not the subject.
The LLS block uses the standard IP checksum, but this is incidental to the format.
The CA-TLV authenticates the LLS block, but this is a small part of the document, which is about signalling, not routing security.

RFC4814.title: Hash and Stuffing: Overlooked Factors in Network Device Benchmarking
RFC4814.summary: Informational BMWG document explaining how test-traffic contents (MAC, IP, MPLS, port addresses) and PPP/HDLC bit- and byte-stuffing affect network device benchmark results, with recommendations and formulas for stuffing probability.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is about benchmarking methodology for network devices: declaring and choosing test traffic contents and compensating for stuffing overhead to make results repeatable.
benchmarking.quote: existing methodologies do not require the reporting of addresses or other test traffic contents, even though these fields can affect test results.

PPP.why: Section 5 analyses PPP with HDLC-like framing (RFC 1662) bit- and byte-stuffing, ACCM negotiation, and overhead probabilities, which PPP readers would want.
PPP.quote: PPP and HDLC-like framing introduce two kinds of escape sequences: bit- and byte-stuffing.

SONET.why: Byte-stuffing probabilities and load-reduction recommendations are given specifically for POS circuits.
SONET.quote: A common implementation of PPP in HDLC-like framing is in PPP over SONET/SDH (POS), as defined in [RFC2615].

ECMP.why: The document discusses how hashing of IP addresses in ECMP link assignment is affected by nonrandom test addresses, and recommends address patterns for testing ECMP devices.
ECMP.quote: the equal cost multipath (ECMP) feature performs load-sharing across multiple links.

rejected.why: MPLS labels are only briefly addressed as a field for pseudorandom test values; the document is not about MPLS.
L2TP is mentioned only as an example of nonzero ACCM use; not a subject of the document.
CRC/checksum fields are mentioned as sources of stuffing in test packets, but the document isn't about them.
Pseudorandom patterns are recommended for test traffic, but this is not about randomness generation requirements for security; it is a benchmarking concern.
TCP and UDP headers appear in example frames and port number guidance only as test traffic contents.
MAC addresses are used in hash examples but the document does not specify Ethernet protocol behaviour.

RFC4815.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): Corrections and Clarifications to RFC 3095
RFC4815.summary: RFC 4815 provides corrections, additions and clarifications to the ROHC framework and profiles of RFC 3095 (CRC coverage, mode transitions, timestamp encoding, list compression, context updating and reuse), plus clarifications to the ROHC-over-PPP, IP-only and UDP-Lite profile RFCs.

ROHC.why: The whole document corrects and clarifies the ROHC framework and its profiles (RTP/UDP/ESP/IP), including mode transitions, TS encoding and list compression.
ROHC.quote: This document provides corrections, additions, and clarifications to RFC 3095; this document thus updates RFC 3095.

rejected.why: CRC calculation and coverage are discussed (Section 2, Appendix A) but only as ROHC-specific details, not as a general CRC polynomial subject.
RTP header fields are compressed, but RTP itself is not specified or extended; it is the thing being compressed.
Section 10 clarifies the ROHC PROFILES sub-option for ROHC over PPP, but this is a small part and the subject is ROHC.
ESP/AH header compression is covered only as ROHC list-compression details; IPsec itself is not the subject.
IPHC (RFC 2507) is not discussed; only the ROHC IP-only profile is mentioned.

RFC4816.title: Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) Transparent Cell Transport Service
RFC4816.summary: Defines an ATM transparent cell transport service over PWE3 pseudowires (type 0x0003), using the N-to-one cell relay encapsulation to emulate a port-to-port ATM connection across a PSN.

pseudowire.why: The document specifies a PWE3 pseudowire service (type 0x0003) carrying ATM cells across a PSN, including cell concatenation and failure handling.
pseudowire.quote: The transparent port service is a natural application of the "N-to-one" Virtual Circuit Connection (VCC) cell transport mode for PWE3 ATM encapsulation

ATM.why: The service emulates ATM port connectivity, handling OAM and ILMI cells and idle cell discard, so ATM readers would want it.
ATM.quote: The ATM transparent port service emulates connectivity between two remote ATM ports.

rejected.why: The encapsulation in RFC 4717 and LDP signalling in RFC 4447 are relied on, but this document only defines a service application of them.
LDP is used for pseudowire setup, but is only referenced for the interface parameter and status signalling, not specified here.
The document describes a point-to-point pseudowire port service, not an L2VPN service framework.

RFC4817.title: Encapsulation of MPLS over Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol Version 3
RFC4817.summary: Defines how to carry an MPLS label stack and its payload over the L2TPv3 data encapsulation across an IP network, with applicability, congestion and security guidance.

L2TP.why: The document specifies a new payload encapsulation over L2TPv3, including Session ID and Cookie usage, so L2TP readers would want it.
L2TP.quote: This document defines how to carry an MPLS label stack and its payload over the L2TPv3 data encapsulation.

MPLS.why: It defines carrying MPLS label stacks over an IP network as an alternative to an MPLS-enabled core, and compares it with MPLS-in-IP/GRE and MPLS over IPsec.
MPLS.quote: MPLS over L2TPv3 allows tunneling of an MPLS stack [RFC3032] and its payload over an IP network

rejected.why: IPsec is discussed only as an optional way to secure the tunnel in Security Considerations; the document does not specify or extend it.
GRE is mentioned only as an alternative encapsulation in the applicability comparison (RFC 4023).
A more specific tag fits: L2TP is a child of link layer, and MPLS is covered by its own tag. The generic tunnelling topic is not the document's subject.
The Congestion Considerations section is standard boilerplate-style guidance and not a substantial subject of the document.
VPNs are mentioned only as context for the applicability discussion; the document does not address provider-provisioned VPNs.
IPv4 and IPv6 are both mentioned only as possible outer IP headers, not as a subject of the document.

RFC4818.title: RADIUS Delegated-IPv6-Prefix Attribute
RFC4818.summary: Defines the RADIUS Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute (type 123) carrying an IPv6 prefix to be delegated to a user, usable in RADIUS and Diameter, e.g. for DHCP Prefix Delegation.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies a new RADIUS attribute, its format, and which packet types may carry it.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) attribute that carries an IPv6 prefix that is to be delegated to the user.

Diameter.why: A full section covers use as a Diameter AVP, including flag rules and translation between RADIUS and Diameter.
Diameter.quote: When used in Diameter, the attribute defined in this specification can be used as a Diameter AVP from the Code space 1-255

DHCPv6.why: The attribute's purpose is to supply prefixes for DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation between the delegating router and a RADIUS server.
DHCPv6.quote: the prefix in a Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute can be delegated to another node through DHCP Prefix Delegation

rejected.why: IPv6 prefixes are the payload, but the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
Prefix delegation is the use case, but the document defines an AAA attribute rather than addressing architecture.
Only a routine type value assignment in the IANA Considerations; boilerplate.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations.

RFC4819.title: Secure Shell Public Key Subsystem
RFC4819.summary: Defines the SSH "publickey" subsystem, a protocol letting authenticated clients add, remove and list their public keys on an SSH server, with attributes that restrict key use.

SSH.why: The RFC specifies a new SSH subsystem ("publickey") running over the SSH connection protocol, with requests, responses, status codes and key attributes tied to SSH public-key user authentication.
SSH.quote: This document describes a subsystem that can be used to configure public keys in an implementation-independent fashion.

rejected.why: The document explicitly says it is not a PKIX replacement; it is simple key configuration on a server, not a public key infrastructure.
It supports public-key user authentication by provisioning keys, but the protocol itself is key management for SSH rather than an authentication mechanism.
Considered since it distributes public keys, but SSH is the more specific fit and the document concerns configuring authorized keys in SSH only.
IANA section only registers names and codes, which is boilerplate evidence and not the subject.
Key attributes restrict what a key may do, but this is a side feature of the SSH subsystem rather than the focus.

RFC4820.title: Padding Chunk and Parameter for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
RFC4820.summary: Defines the SCTP padding chunk (PAD, type 0x84) and padding parameter (0x8005 for INIT chunks), with receiver-side procedures and IANA registrations.

SCTP.why: The document extends SCTP with a new chunk type and a new INIT parameter and specifies how receivers process them.
SCTP.quote: This document defines a padding chunk and a padding parameter and describes the required receiver side procedures.

rejected.why: Packetization Layer PMTUD (RFC 4821) is the intended use of the PAD chunk. This document only mentions that use in one sentence and defines no PMTUD procedure.
The IANA section only registers the new chunk and parameter types. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC4821.title: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery
RFC4821.summary: Specifies Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD), a method in which TCP, SCTP or applications probe a path with progressively larger packets to find the path MTU without relying on ICMP messages, extending RFC 1191 and RFC 1981.

PMTUD.why: The whole document defines a probing-based Path MTU Discovery method, covering its state variables, search strategy, probe handling and verification.
PMTUD.quote: This document describes a robust method for Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) that relies on TCP or some other Packetization Layer to probe an Internet path with progressively larger packets.

rejected.why: TCP is one of the packetization layers PLPMTUD is applied to (Section 10.1). The document does not specify or extend TCP itself.
Section 10.2 gives SCTP probing details, but SCTP is only one example packetization layer. The PAD chunk is defined in RFC 4820, not here.
The classical ICMP-based PMTUD is the mechanism that PLPMTUD supplements or replaces. The document does not define or extend ICMP.
The document says probe loss must not be treated as a congestion signal, and it constrains how often that can happen. This is a constraint on the method, not a congestion control specification.
The document applies to both IPv4 and IPv6, with IPv6 terminology preferred. It does not specify IPv6.

RFC4822.title: RIPv2 Cryptographic Authentication
RFC4822.summary: RFC 4822 revises RIPv2 cryptographic authentication (obsoleting RFC 2082), adding HMAC-SHA family support alongside Keyed-MD5, defining the packet trailer, security associations, key rollover, and security considerations.

RIP.why: The document specifies the RIPv2 authentication packet format, processing and key management, and updates RFC 2453.
RIP.quote: This note describes a revision to the RIPv2 Cryptographic Authentication mechanism originally specified in RFC 2082.

HMAC.why: A substantial part defines HMAC-SHA1/SHA-256/384/512 computation (ipad/opad, key prep) for the authentication data.
HMAC.quote: This section describes the processing steps for HMAC Authentication.

routing security.why: Securing a routing protocol against passive and active attacks, with key management and rollover, is the central purpose.
routing security.quote: Growth in the Internet has made us aware of the need for improved authentication of routing information.

rejected.why: SHA-1/SHA-2 are used as hash functions within HMAC, but the document does not define or analyse them.
Keyed-MD5 is retained for backward compatibility and defined briefly, but the document is not about MD5 itself.
Only discussed in security considerations as a not-recommended way to configure keys, and the RIPv2 MIB is only mentioned for future revision.
Key management is deliberately omitted; only requirements and future work are discussed, and manual keys plus rollover are covered under the routing authentication scheme.
UDP is only the transport; the document just notes the checksum may be zero.
Routing authentication is better covered by RIP and routing security tags than the generic authentication topic.

RFC4823.title: FTP Transport for Secure Peer-to-Peer Business Data Interchange over the Internet
RFC4823.summary: Applicability Statement (AS3) specifying how to exchange EDI, XML and other business data securely over FTP, using S/MIME-signed/encrypted MIME packaging and signed MDN receipts for non-repudiation.

EDI.why: The document is the EDIINT AS3 specification for carrying EDI/B2B data over an Internet transport (FTP), so it belongs on the EDI page.
EDI.quote: This Applicability Statement (AS) describes how to exchange structured business data securely using the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) for XML, Binary, Electronic Data Interchange (EDI

FTP.why: The document profiles FTP as the transport, with FTP security requirements, FTP URL for MDN return, server interface rules and deployment configurations.
FTP.quote: conforming implementations of AS3 SHALL employ FTP client/servers that support the AUTH command described within [4]

S/MIME.why: Substantial parts specify how S/MIME signing, encryption and multipart/signed receipts are applied to the messages, and certificate handling.
S/MIME.quote: Authentication and data confidentiality are obtained by using Cryptographic Message Syntax (S/MIME) security body parts.

MIME.why: Defines the MIME message structure, required content types, AS3-specific headers, and the multipart/report MDN format.
MIME.quote: The basic structure of AS3 messages comprises MIME encapsulated data with both customary MIME headers and a few additional AS3-specific outer headers.

rejected.why: AUTH TLS is required for FTP security but TLS is only a relied-upon mechanism, with nothing new defined about it.
Earlier EDIINT work (RFC 3335) used SMTP; this document only adapts it to FTP and does not specify SMTP.
Certificates are required, but the section only states trading partners exchange and self-certify them, not a profile.
CMS is the underlying format for S/MIME and compression, referenced rather than specified here.
Lists required content types but does not register any new media types.

RFC4824.title: The Transmission of IP Datagrams over the Semaphore Flag Signaling System (SFSS)
RFC4824.summary: April 1 humor RFC specifying IP-SFS, a method for encapsulating and transmitting IPv4/IPv6 datagrams over the Semaphore Flag Signaling System, with framing, coding, and a half-duplex link control protocol.

humor.why: An April 1st RFC with whimsical content (hollering, cigarette-length timeouts, human interfaces waving flags). It belongs on the humor page.
humor.quote: This document specifies IP-SFS, a method for the encapsulation and transmission of IPv4/IPv6 packets over the Semaphore Flag Signaling System (SFSS).

rejected.why: The document nominally defines a link layer for IP, but it is a parody. The humor tag fits better, and no real link technology is specified.
IPv4/IPv6 are only the payload being encapsulated, not the subject.
It uses a CCITT CRC-16 checksum as a framing detail only, and does not discuss polynomial choice.
gzip is mentioned only as a protocol code value for compressed frames.

RFC4825.title: The Extensible Markup Language (XML) Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP)
RFC4825.summary: RFC 4825 specifies XCAP, a protocol that maps XML document sub-trees and attributes to HTTP URIs so clients can read, write and modify per-user application configuration data (e.g. SIP presence and resource lists) on a server via HTTP GET/PUT/DELETE.

SIMPLE.why: XCAP is a SIMPLE working group protocol (XCAP under the SIMPLE umbrella) for manipulating per-user presence authorization and resource list data used by SIP presence and messaging. The taxonomy lists XCAP under SIMPLE.
SIMPLE.quote: XCAP allows a client to read, write, and modify application configuration data stored in XML format on a server.

rejected.why: XCAP is a usage of HTTP and relies on it as substrate (GET/PUT/DELETE, etags, conditional requests); it defines no new HTTP semantics or extensions.
XML is the data format of the managed documents, but the document is about a protocol for accessing them, not XML usage per se. Marginal; XML schemas and namespaces are the substrate.
Defines URI construction conventions for XCAP resources, but this is part of the protocol rather than a contribution to URI syntax or schemes.
Registers several application/xcap-*+xml types, but this is IANA boilerplate supporting the protocol, not the main subject.
Only cited as inspiration; XCAP explicitly has no dependency on or extension of ACAP.
SIP applications are the motivating use case, but XCAP itself is not SIP signalling.

gaps.name: XCAP (XML Configuration Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated XCAP tag; the nearest fit is SIMPLE, which only partly describes a generic XML-over-HTTP configuration access protocol.

RFC4826.title: Extensible Markup Language (XML) Formats for Representing Resource Lists
RFC4826.summary: Defines two XML document formats (resource-lists and rls-services) for representing lists of resources and SIP resource list server service definitions, with XCAP application usages, media types and URN registrations.

SIMPLE.why: Placeholder
SIMPLE.quote: this document defines two Extensible Markup Language (XML) document formats.

RFC4827.title: An Extensible Markup Language (XML) Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP) Usage for Manipulating Presence Document Contents
RFC4827.summary: Defines an XCAP application usage ('pidf-manipulation') that lets clients manipulate persistent PIDF presence documents on an XCAP server, as an input to the SIP presence Event State Compositor alongside SIP PUBLISH.

SIMPLE.why: The document is a SIMPLE working group specification defining an XCAP application usage for presence documents; SIMPLE covers XCAP and PIDF extensions for SIP presence.
SIMPLE.quote: This document describes a usage of the Extensible Markup Language (XML) Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP) for manipulating the contents of Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) based presence documents.

PIDF.why: The manipulated documents are PIDF presence documents, including RPID and CIPID extensions in the example, and the document specifies how they are stored and edited.
PIDF.quote: Presence Information Document Format (PIDF) [3] is used as the presence document format

rejected.why: SIP PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE are context for the presence system; the document specifies no SIP behaviour.
Digest authentication is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a mechanism inherited from XCAP.
HTTP over TLS is mentioned only as a security mechanism in Security Considerations.
XML is the data encoding for the presence documents, not the subject of the document.
The document merely names application/pidf+xml as the MIME type and registers no new media type.
Presence is the subject, but the SIMPLE and PIDF tags are more specific fits.

gaps.name: XCAP (XML Configuration Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for XCAP itself. The document defines an XCAP application usage (AUID 'pidf-manipulation'), and readers browsing XCAP usages would expect to find it. SIMPLE is the closest fit.

RFC4828.title: TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC): The Small-Packet (SP) Variant
RFC4828.summary: Specifies TFRC-SP, an experimental small-packet variant of TCP-Friendly Rate Control that targets fairness in bytes per second with 1460-byte TCP flows, enforces a 10 ms minimum packet interval, counts losses differently in short loss intervals, and evaluates the design by simulation.

TFRC.why: The document defines and analyses TFRC-SP, a modification of TFRC's rate calculation, header accounting and loss event rate measurement.
TFRC.quote: This document proposes TFRC-SP, a Small-Packet (SP) variant of TFRC, that is designed for applications that send small packets.

rejected.why: DCCP is mentioned as a transport that could use TFRC-SP (CCID), but the CCID is to be specified in a separate document. DCCP is not the subject here.
TCP is the fairness reference and its response function is compared against, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
ECN appears only in the simulations and the security discussion, so it is not a subject of the document.
RED and Drop-Tail queue behaviour is only the simulation environment used to evaluate TFRC-SP fairness.
The more specific TFRC tag covers this topic, so the parent is not listed separately.
PMTUD is mentioned only as a question left to the transport protocol that uses TFRC-SP.

RFC4829.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Preemption Policies for MPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC4829.summary: Informational RFC presenting a flexible, weighted-cost heuristic for selecting which lower-priority TE LSPs to preempt in MPLS (DiffServ-aware) traffic engineering, with examples and simulation comparisons against other preemption policies.

traffic engineering.why: The document is about LSP preemption policy in MPLS traffic engineering: choosing which TE LSPs to preempt, cascading, bandwidth wastage and blocking probability.
traffic engineering.quote: a node has to make a local decision to select which TE LSPs will be preempted

MPLS.why: The preemption policy applies to MPLS TE LSPs and is aimed at MPLS TE networks, so MPLS readers would want it. The traffic engineering tag is the more specific fit, so this is secondary.
MPLS.quote: preemption also plays an important role in regular MPLS Traffic Engineering environments (with a single pool of bandwidth)

rejected.why: DS-TE bandwidth constraint models and TE-Classes are background context. The document defines a preemption heuristic, not Diffserv itself.
RFC 3209 is cited only for the preemption attributes. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as IGPs that already carry the needed parameters, so they are not subjects of the document.
The centralized manager approach is discussed only briefly as an alternative to the chosen distributed approach, so the document is not about PCE.
Preemption priority serves differentiated traffic, but the document is about LSP selection for preemption, not QoS architecture or signalling.

RFC4830.title: Problem Statement for Network-Based Localized Mobility Management (NETLMM)
RFC4830.summary: Informational problem statement arguing that localized IP mobility management should be network-based (no host stack involvement) because host-based solutions like FMIPv6/HMIPv6 and proprietary WLAN-switch protocols have shortcomings.

IP mobility.why: The whole document is a problem statement for localized (network-based) IP mobility management, which fits the IP-mobility topic. No specific child (Mobile IPv6, PMIPv6) is specified here, so the parent topic is used.
IP mobility.quote: Localized Mobility Management is a generic term for any protocol that maintains the IP connectivity and reachability of a mobile node

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6, FMIPv6 and HMIPv6 are discussed as existing host-based solutions and global mobility protocols, but the document does not specify or extend them.
This problem statement motivates network-based mobility, which led to PMIPv6, but PMIPv6 is not defined or mentioned here.
HIP is mentioned only as an alternative global mobility protocol that localized mobility should be independent of.
MOBIKE is mentioned only as an example of a global mobility protocol.
WLAN switches are used as a motivating example of proprietary localized mobility, but the document is not about IP over 802.11.
Mobile IPv4 appears only in passing as an existing deployment, not as a subject of the document.

RFC4831.title: Goals for Network-Based Localized Mobility Management (NETLMM)
RFC4831.summary: Informational RFC setting out eleven design goals for a network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM) protocol, with LMA/MAG functional architecture, so mobile nodes need no localized-mobility software.

PMIPv6.why: NETLMM is the network-based localized mobility work that led to Proxy Mobile IPv6; the document defines the LMA/MAG architecture and goals for it.
PMIPv6.quote: design goals for a network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM) protocol are discussed

IP mobility.why: Goals address handover, global vs local mobility independence, and support for Mobile IPv4/IPv6, HIP and MOBIKE as global protocols; general IP-layer mobility subject.
IP mobility.quote: mobility between localized mobility management domains is not covered here. It is assumed that this is covered by the global mobility management protocols.

rejected.why: Used as the example global mobility protocol for signaling counts, but the document is not about specifying or extending it.
Mentioned as a way to secure movement detection; not the subject.
ESP tunnels mentioned only as one forwarding option in Goal 11.
IP-in-IP forwarding is one configurable option mentioned briefly, not a main topic.
Goal 8 says both IPv4 and IPv6 should be supported; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Goal 3 on location privacy is one goal among eleven, not enough to make the document about privacy.

gaps.name: Network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for NETLMM itself; PMIPv6 is the closest tech, and IP mobility the parent topic.

RFC4832.title: Security Threats to Network-Based Localized Mobility Management (NETLMM)
RFC4832.summary: Informational threat analysis of network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM), covering threats on the LMA-MAG interface, the MAG-mobile node interface, and from the Internet.

IP mobility.why: The document analyses threats to NETLMM, an IP-layer localized mobility architecture with LMA and MAG. No NETLMM-specific tag exists, and the PMIPv6 tag covers a specific protocol rather than this threat analysis, so the IP mobility parent topic fits best.
IP mobility.quote: This document discusses security threats to network-based localized mobility management.

security.why: A substantial part of the document is a general threat model covering compromise, impersonation, man-in-the-middle and denial-of-service attacks. No narrower security tag fits.
security.quote: This document identifies and discusses security threats on both interfaces of the localized mobility management architecture.

rejected.why: The NetLMM protocol is the precursor to PMIPv6, but this document does not specify or analyse PMIPv6 itself.
The architecture serves IPv6 mobile nodes, but the document is about mobility management threats, not IPv6 itself.
SEND is mentioned only in passing as a countermeasure for on-link attacks.
Denial-of-service is one threat among several in the document, not its main subject.
Neighbor discovery is only referenced in the context of on-link impersonation.

gaps.name: Network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM)
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no dedicated tag. The taxonomy has IP mobility children for Mobile IPv4, Mobile IPv6, PMIPv6 and NEMO only.

RFC4833.title: Timezone Options for DHCP
RFC4833.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options carrying client timezone information as POSIX TZ strings or TZ database names, and deprecates the DHCPv4 time offset option.

DHCP.why: The document defines new DHCPv4 options and deprecates an existing one (updating RFC 2132), so it is about DHCP option specification.
DHCP.quote: This memo specifies DHCP options for each of those methods.  The DHCPv4 time offset option is deprecated.

DHCPv6.why: A substantial section defines OPTION_NEW_POSIX_TIMEZONE(41) and OPTION_NEW_TZDB_TIMEZONE(42) for DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: The semantics and content of the DHCPv6 encoding of these options are exactly the same as the encoding described for DHCPv4

time zones.why: The options convey time zone data via POSIX TZ strings and TZ database names, and the document discusses choosing between them and DST accuracy.
time zones.quote: Reference to the name of the time zone entry in the TZ Database

rejected.why: VTIMEZONE is discussed only as an alternative that was not chosen; the document does not specify or extend iCalendar.
This is about timezone configuration, not clock synchronization; the time offset option is merely deprecated.
IANA option allocations are boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

RFC4834.title: Requirements for Multicast in Layer 3 Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs)
RFC4834.summary: Informational requirements document specifying end-user and service-provider functional requirements for supporting IP multicast within Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs.

MVPN.why: The whole document lists requirements for multicast VPNs in L3 PPVPNs (BGP/MPLS-style), the exact subject of the MVPN tag.
MVPN.quote: functional requirements for network solutions that allow the deployment of IP multicast within Layer 3 (L3) Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs)

rejected.why: Child MVPN is more specific and fits; the L3VPN parent is implied.
PIM-SM, bidir-PIM and PIM-DM are required at the PE-CE interface but only as existing protocols the solution must support, not specified here.
IGMPv3/MLDv2 are listed as PE-CE protocols to support; the document does not specify or extend them.
MPLS P2MP LSPs are listed as possible tunneling technologies only; not the subject.
Mentioned as QoS mechanisms to be supported; only a minor part of the document.
SNMP/MIB and IPFIX are named only as monitoring means for SLA/OAM data.

RFC4835.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Implementation Requirements for Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH)
RFC4835.summary: RFC 4835 specifies which cryptographic algorithms (encryption, authentication, combined mode) are mandatory or recommended to implement for IPsec ESP and AH, obsoleting RFC 4305.

ESP.why: The document sets algorithm implementation requirements for ESP, with encryption, authentication and combined-mode tables.
ESP.quote: This document defines the current set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms for ESP and AH

IPsec.why: It covers IPsec conformance requirements for both ESP and AH. AH has no child tag, so IPsec is the right tag for it.
IPsec.quote: The IPsec series of protocols makes use of various cryptographic algorithms in order to provide security services.

rejected.why: IKE is mentioned only as a way to negotiate algorithms. The document does not specify it.
AES-CBC, AES-CTR, AES-CCM and AES-GCM appear as entries in the requirement tables. The document is not about AES itself.
HMAC-SHA1-96 and HMAC-MD5-96 are listed as algorithms, but the document does not specify them.
DES-CBC appears only as a SHOULD NOT entry. The document does not address DES.
A more specific IPsec tag fits. The document is about IPsec algorithm requirements, not cryptography in general.

RFC4836.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs)
RFC4836.summary: Defines the MAU-MIB SMIv2 module for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (repeater and interface MAUs, auto-negotiation, jacks), and splits MAU type identities and textual conventions into a new IANA-maintained IANA-MAU-MIB, adding EFM and 10GBASE-CX4 support; obsoletes RFC 3636.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (MAU-MIB) plus an IANA-maintained MIB module, written in SMIv2. This is the MIB/SMI subject.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs)

Ethernet.why: The managed objects cover IEEE 802.3 MAU types, auto-negotiation, jack types and link state across 10 Mb/s to 10 Gb/s, plus EFM and 10GBASE-CX4. Readers of Ethernet interworking and OAM would want it.
Ethernet.quote: This specification is intended to provide for management of all types of Ethernet/802.3 MAUs.

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document sets up an IANA-maintained registry-like MIB module with Expert Review rules for adding new MAU types.
IANA.quote: all relevant object identities and textual conventions have been moved to a separate, IANA-maintained MIB module IANA-MAU-MIB

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour, so MIB is the more specific fit.
The 2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS PME aggregation (PAF) is mentioned only in passing, in media-available state descriptions.
2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS are EFM copper types that appear only as enumerated values. The document is not about DSL access networks.
The WIS and 10GBASE-W layering requirements are interface-stack notes, and the document is not about SONET.

RFC4837.title: Managed Objects of Ethernet Passive Optical Networks (EPON)
RFC4837.summary: Defines the DOT3-EPON-MIB module, an SMIv2 MIB for managing IEEE 802.3ah Ethernet Passive Optical Network interfaces (MPCP, point-to-point emulation, FEC, extended package with queues and optical interface status).

MIB.why: The document's purpose is a MIB module with tables, objects and conformance groups for EPON interfaces, extending the Interfaces and Ethernet-like MIBs.
MIB.quote: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP based Internets.

Ethernet.why: It manages IEEE 802.3ah EPON Ethernet interfaces (MPCP, P2P emulation, FEC, virtual links) and ties them to Ethernet-like MIBs, MAU MIB and EFM OAM.
Ethernet.quote: EPON interface is a kind of Ether-like interface.  This MIB module extends the objects of the Interface MIB and the Ether-like Interfaces MIB
Ethernet.section: 4.1. Relation to the Interfaces MIB and Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP behaviour.
The FEC here is the EPON PHY-layer Reed-Solomon code managed via counters; it is not about packet-loss recovery schemes.
EPON is optical access, not DSL, though it is a similar access-network context.
The EFM OAM MIB is only mentioned as a complementary module in a short section, not defined here.
Not relevant; the model is SMIv2 only.

gaps.name: EPON (Ethernet Passive Optical Network) / IEEE 802.3ah EFM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for optical access or Ethernet PON as a link technology; the closest fits are Ethernet and MIB.

RFC4838.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking Architecture
RFC4838.summary: RFC 4838 describes the architecture for delay- and disruption-tolerant networking: a message-oriented store-and-forward "bundle layer" overlay with EIDs, custody transfer, contacts-based routing, fragmentation, and optional security.

DTN.why: The whole document defines the DTN architecture: bundle layer, nodes, endpoints, custody transfer, contacts, convergence layers.
DTN.quote: This document describes an architecture for delay-tolerant and disruption-tolerant networks, and is an evolution of the architecture originally designed for the Interplanetary Internet

rejected.why: EIDs are expressed as URIs, but RFC 3986 is only the naming syntax relied on; the document defines no URI scheme.
Section 3.13 discusses bundle-layer congestion/flow control but explicitly leaves it unresolved; a minor part.
TCP is only an underlying protocol used via convergence layers, not the subject.
The document contrasts with Internet assumptions but is about the DTN architecture, covered by the DTN tag.
Routing and forwarding is one section within DTN; the DTN tag covers it.
Section 3.12 only states DTN depends on time sync supplied by external protocols.

RFC4839.title: Media Type Registrations for the Open eBook Publication Structure (OEBPS) Package File (OPF)
RFC4839.summary: Registers the application/oebps-package+xml media type for Open eBook Publication Structure (OEBPS) Package Files (.opf), XML files describing an eBook publication.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration (application/oebps-package+xml) using the RFC 4288 template, so it belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: This document serves to register a media type for the Open eBook Publication Structure (OEBPS) Package Files.

rejected.why: OPF is an XML file and the subtype uses the +xml suffix, but the document only registers the media type; XML is the underlying format, not the subject.
Media type registration is covered by the more specific media types tag; the document does not address MIME body structure or encodings generally.
The IANA Considerations section is just the registration boilerplate; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
Only mentioned in the encoding considerations field of the template; not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Open eBook Publication Structure (OEBPS) / eBook packaging
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for electronic publishing or eBook formats, though the document registers a type for them.

RFC4840.title: Multiple Encapsulation Methods Considered Harmful
RFC4840.summary: IAB informational RFC describing architectural and operational problems when a link-layer protocol supports multiple IP encapsulation methods (Ethernet, IEEE 802, trailers, PPP, IEEE 802.16), and recommending a single mandatory encapsulation per link.

link layer.why: The whole document is about link-layer encapsulation of IP and its negotiation, generality, and interoperability across media, not one specific medium.
link layer.quote: architectural and operational issues that arise from link-layer protocols supporting multiple Internet Protocol encapsulation methods

Ethernet.why: Ethernet experience (RFC 894, RFC 1042 IEEE 802 SNAP, RFC 948, trailers) is the main case study in section 1.2.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet [DIX] encapsulation as defined in "A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks"

WiMAX.why: IEEE 802.16 convergence sublayers and classification drive much of the Section 3 analysis of multiple encapsulations.
WiMAX.quote: IEEE 802.16 [IEEE-802.16.2004] splits the Media Access Control (MAC) layer into a number of sublayers.

rejected.why: PPP is discussed as an example where multiple encapsulations rarely coexist, but the document is not about PPP itself.
ARP appears in trailer negotiation and CS discussion but is not the subject.
Recommended as a solution to the efficiency argument, but only as a supporting point.
Cites RFC 1958 principles, but the focus is link-layer encapsulation rather than general Internet architecture.
IPv6 is mentioned as an example of affected protocols, not the topic.

RFC4841.title: RFC 4181 Update to Recognize the IETF Trust
RFC4841.summary: A short BCP that updates RFC 4181 (MIB authoring guidelines) so the Section 3.7 copyright notice templates name "The IETF Trust" instead of "The Internet Society", following RFC 4748.

IPR.why: The whole document changes the copyright notice required in MIB documents to reflect the IETF Trust. That is a copyright and trust legal provisions matter.
IPR.quote: In the copyright notice templates in Section 3.7, replace all occurrences of "The Internet Society" with "The IETF Trust".

MIB.why: It amends the MIB authoring guidelines (RFC 4181), so readers looking for MIB document guidance would want to find it.
MIB.quote: This document updates RFC 4181, "Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of MIB Documents", to recognize the creation of the IETF Trust.

rejected.why: SNMP is not discussed. Only the MIB guidelines document's copyright templates are changed.
The change is to copyright notice text, not to IETF standards procedures. IPR is the better fit.

RFC4842.title: Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) Circuit Emulation over Packet (CEP)
RFC4842.summary: Specifies encapsulation formats and semantics (CEP) for emulating SONET/SDH circuits as pseudowires over MPLS PSNs, including maintenance signals, pointer management, performance monitors, payload compression and LDP signalling parameters.

pseudowire.why: CEP is a PWE3 pseudowire encapsulation for SONET/SDH circuits over MPLS, including the CEP header following the PW control word and PW signalling parameters.
pseudowire.quote: This document provides encapsulation formats and semantics for emulating SONET/SDH circuits and services over MPLS.

SONET.why: The document is about carrying SONET/SDH SPEs, VTs, VCs, with pointer handling, alarms (AIS, RDI), and fractional STS-1/VC-4 formats.
SONET.quote: SONET/SDH fragments MUST be byte aligned with the SONET/SDH SPE or VT.

rejected.why: RTP header is optionally reused purely as a format for timing; the document says RTP mechanisms are not applicable, so it is not about RTP.
MPLS is the PSN substrate; CEP is defined over it but the document is about the pseudowire emulation, not MPLS itself.
LDP is used for optional PW signalling; the document only defines CEP-specific interface parameters, which is minor relative to LDP itself.
Congestion section only suggests Intserv/Diffserv-enabled PSNs; not a subject of the document.
Short section stating CEP is inelastic CBR and recommending TE networks; not a substantial subject.
Transport timing is declared mostly out of scope and relies on external mechanisms.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation
gaps.why: CEP is a circuit emulation of TDM services; the taxonomy has no tag for TDM circuit emulation beyond pseudowire.

RFC4843.title: An IPv6 Prefix for Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers (ORCHID)
RFC4843.summary: Defines ORCHIDs, experimental IPv6-address-like cryptographic hash identifiers under a temporary 2001:10::/28 prefix, for use at APIs and routable only in overlays, and requests the IANA prefix allocation.

addressing.why: The document allocates an IPv6 prefix and defines the construction of address-like identifiers within it, which is IP address architecture and allocation. No more specific technology tag fits, since it is not IPv6 specification itself.
addressing.quote: This document requests IANA to allocate a temporary prefix out of the IPv6 addressing space for Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers.

HIP.why: HIP HITs are the main intended use of ORCHIDs, and the document is motivated by HIP experimentation. HIP readers would want it, though HIP is not specified here.
HIP.quote: Examples of these include Host Identity Tags (HIT) in the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) [HIP-BASE]

IPv6.why: The document is about an IPv6 prefix and how its identifiers coexist with IPv6 addresses at APIs, which readers of IPv6 would want.
IPv6.quote: The ORCHID prefix is allocated under the IPv6 global unicast address block.  Hence, ORCHIDs are indistinguishable from IPv6 global unicast addresses.

rejected.why: The IANA allocation is part of the request but the document is not about IANA registry guidance itself; it is boilerplate-like here.
SHA1 is only cited as the hash used by HIP contexts; the document is not about the hash algorithm.
Mobile IPv6 TMIs are mentioned only as an example context of use.
That tag covers data-plane virtualization overlays such as VXLAN; the overlay routing here is a research discussion of DHT-based identifier routing.
Overlay routing is discussed only as background to why ORCHIDs are non-routable at IP layer.

RFC4844.title: The RFC Series and RFC Editor
RFC4844.summary: IAB framework document defining the RFC Series mission, the roles of the RFC Editor, IAB and IASA, and the four RFC streams (IETF, IAB, IRTF, Independent) with their approval and publication processes.

RFC series.why: The whole document defines the framework, roles, streams and publication requirements of the RFC Series and RFC Editor function.
RFC series.quote: this document provides a brief charter for the RFC Series, describes the role of the RFC Editor, the IAB, and the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA)

IETF process.why: A substantial part covers stream approval processes and IASA/IAOC administrative oversight of the RFC Editor, which is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: Any document being published as part of the IETF standards process must follow this stream -- no other stream can approve Standards-Track or Best Current Practice (BCP) RFCs.

rejected.why: Copyright and IPR rules are only listed as existing series-wide documents; the document is not about them.
IANA is mentioned only in passing regarding stream interdependence.

RFC4845.title: Process for Publication of IAB RFCs
RFC4845.summary: Defines the IAB's process for reviewing, approving, and publishing its documents as Informational RFCs in the RFC Series, including the call for comment and handoff to the RFC Editor.

RFC series.why: The document specifies how IAB-stream RFCs are produced and published, which is a matter of RFC Series publication streams and procedure.
RFC series.quote: This document defines the process by which those documents are produced, reviewed, and published in the RFC Series.

IETF process.why: Describes a community review and approval procedure, including BCP handoff to the IESG, which is part of IETF standards process and administration.
IETF process.quote: The chair of the IAB issues an IETF-wide Call for Comment on the IETF Announce mailing list.

rejected.why: Parent topic; the more specific children RFC series and IETF process fit, so the parent is implied.
Copyright and IPR sections are boilerplate only and not the subject of the document.

RFC4846.title: Independent Submissions to the RFC Editor
RFC4846.summary: RFC 4846 describes the Independent Submission stream for the RFC Series, explaining its role and defining the review, IESG conflict-review, Editorial Board and IPR processing norms for documents published via the RFC Editor outside the IETF process.

RFC series.why: The document defines how the RFC Editor handles Independent Submissions: submission, review, Editorial Review Board, and publication. This is the RFC Series publication process.
RFC series.quote: use of the RFC Series to publish materials that are not rooted in the IETF standards process and its review and approval mechanisms

IPR.why: Section 8 consolidates the copyright and licensing terms for Independent Submissions extracted from BCP 78. It is substantive body content, not boilerplate.
IPR.quote: By submission of an RFC Editor Contribution, each person actually submitting the RFC Editor Contribution, and each named co- Contributor, is deemed to agree to the following terms

rejected.why: The document is about the stream that sits outside the IETF standards process. Its IESG review is limited to conflict checks, so it is not about IETF process itself.
IANA allocation policy is mentioned only briefly in Section 4.2, and the historical IANA policy statements only in the list of roles. Neither is a substantive subject of the document.
The document gives some history of the RFC Series, but it is a process description, not a retrospective.

gaps.name: Independent Submission stream / RFC Editor publication streams
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for the Independent Submission stream or for the IAB/RFC Editor stream structure. RFC series is the closest fit.

RFC4847.title: Framework and Requirements for Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks
RFC4847.summary: Informational framework and service-level requirements for Layer 1 VPNs (L1VPNs) provided over GMPLS-controlled TDM/optical networks, covering motivations, reference model, service models, recovery, control plane connectivity, manageability and security.

L1VPN.why: The whole document defines the L1VPN framework, reference model, service models and requirements.
L1VPN.quote: This document provides a framework and service level requirements for Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks (L1VPNs).

GMPLS.why: The service models are built on GMPLS signaling, routing, UNI overlay and recovery, and the document discusses needed GMPLS extensions.
GMPLS.quote: the realization of the framework by those networks being controlled by Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) protocols.

rejected.why: L1VPN is the more specific child and fits; the parent is implied.
Only referenced as the GMPLS signaling mechanism underlying the UNI; not specified or extended here.
Only mentioned as an example security mechanism in Security Considerations.
Mentioned for comparison and manageability references, not the subject.
TE links and routing information are used in the models, but the document is about VPN services, not TE itself.
SDH/SONET appears only as examples of layer 1 technologies.

RFC4848.title: Domain-Based Application Service Location Using URIs and the Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service (DDDS)
RFC4848.summary: Defines U-NAPTR, a DDDS application extending S-NAPTR with a "U" flag and a restricted regexp so DNS NAPTR records can map a domain name to a URI for an application service and protocol.

service discovery.why: The document specifies a DDDS application for locating application services for a domain, using NAPTR records and URIs. No specific discovery technology tag fits U-NAPTR, so the general service discovery topic applies.
service discovery.quote: define a new, straightforward Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service (DDDS) application to allow mapping of domain names to URIs for particular application services

DNS.why: U-NAPTR defines how NAPTR resource records are used, including the new "U" flag, the regexp form and the service parameter syntax. It also covers resolver handling of SRV and A records and the additional section, so DNS readers would want it.
