DNS.quote: [4] specifies a DDDS Database that uses the NAPTR DNS resource record to contain the rewrite rules.

rejected.why: URIs are only the output of the rule. The document does not specify URI syntax or schemes and refers to STD 66 for them.
DNSSEC appears only in the Security Considerations, as a way to trust the retrieved URI.
The IANA Considerations section reuses the existing registries and places no new requirements on IANA. It is boilerplate-level evidence.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the service parameter syntax.

gaps.name: DDDS / NAPTR (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System, U-NAPTR, S-NAPTR)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about a DDDS application using NAPTR records. The taxonomy has no DDDS or NAPTR tag, so it falls back on the generic service discovery and DNS tags.

RFC4849.title: RADIUS Filter Rule Attribute
RFC4849.summary: Defines the RADIUS NAS-Filter-Rule attribute (type 92), carrying explicit IPFilterRule-syntax filter rules from RADIUS server to NAS, and describes Diameter interworking.

RADIUS.why: The document extends RADIUS with a new attribute, including its format, packet usage table and proxy behaviour.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines the NAS-Filter-Rule attribute within the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS).

Diameter.why: A dedicated section specifies translation between the RADIUS attribute and the Diameter AVP, including a new Diameter Result-Code error.
Diameter.quote: Diameter/RADIUS gateways will need to be configured to translate RADIUS attribute 92 to Diameter NAS-Filter-Rule AVP (400) and vice versa.

rejected.why: The attribute carries packet filter rules, but the document specifies a AAA attribute, not firewall or middlebox security.
RFC 3579 is only cited in Security Considerations.
The more specific RADIUS and Diameter tags apply instead of the AAA parent.
The IANA section only records the attribute and result-code allocations, which is boilerplate.

RFC4850.title: Declarative Public Extension Key for Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) Node Architecture
RFC4850.summary: Defines a declarative iSCSI public extension key, X#NodeArchitecture, that lets initiators and targets exchange node architecture details during login for logging and support, and updates RFC 3720 to allow standards-track and experimental RFCs to define iSCSI extension items.

iSCSI.why: The document specifies a new iSCSI login key and updates RFC 3720's rules for extension items. It extends the iSCSI protocol, so it belongs on the iSCSI page.
iSCSI.quote: This document describes a declarative Public Extension Key, as defined by Section 12.22 of RFC 3720 [2], that may be used to communicate additional iSCSI node information

rejected.why: The key is only modeled on the HTTP Server and User-Agent header fields. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
IPsec is mentioned only as a countermeasure in Security Considerations. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The IANA section registers the key and changes the rules for extension registries. This is registry bookkeeping for iSCSI and not guidance on IANA in general.
TCP is only part of the substrate that iSCSI runs over.
iSCSI is a child of storage, so the ancestor is implied by the iSCSI tag.

RFC4851.title: The Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling Extensible Authentication Protocol Method (EAP-FAST)
RFC4851.summary: Defines EAP-FAST, an EAP method that builds a TLS tunnel (optionally resumed via a PAC/ticket) and carries inner authentication in TLVs, with crypto-binding, key derivation and security analysis.

EAP.why: The document specifies a new EAP method, including message formats, TLVs, phases, MSK/EMSK derivation and EAP security claims.
EAP.quote: EAP-FAST is an EAP method that enables secure communication between a peer and a server by using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) to establish a mutually authenticated tunnel.

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate for the tunnel; the document uses RFC 4507 session tickets rather than defining a new TLS extension, and its focus is the EAP method.
RADIUS is only a carrier protocol for EAP, mentioned in the layering model.
HMAC-SHA1 is used in the T-PRF and Compound MAC but is a building block, not the subject.
RC4 appears only as a mandatory TLS ciphersuite listing, not as a subject.
Network access authentication is the context, but the document specifies an EAP method rather than an AAA framework.
Certificates are used for Peer-Id and Server-Id determination only incidentally.

RFC4852.title: IPv6 Enterprise Network Analysis - IP Layer 3 Focus
RFC4852.summary: Informational analysis of IPv6 transition in enterprise networks at IP Layer 3, defining a matrix of ten notional dual-IP scenarios and recommending transition mechanisms (tunnelling, ISATAP, Teredo, 6to4, tunnel brokers) plus staged deployment guidance.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document analyses IPv6/IPv4 coexistence and recommends transition mechanisms per scenario.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document analyzes the transition to IPv6 in enterprise networks focusing on IP Layer 3.

IPv6.why: Substantial parts cover IPv6 deployment: addressing plan, /48 allocation, routing, SLAAC/DHCPv6 host configuration, security.
IPv6.quote: This document covers deployment of IPv6 "on the wire", including address management and DNS services.

rejected.why: Mentioned as one available mechanism in Section 8.1, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
Only recommended in passing as a mechanism when behind a NAT; not the subject.
Cited briefly as an option for enterprises without an assigned prefix; not the document's subject.
Tunnelling is discussed as a means, but the specific subject is IPv6 transition, covered by the more specific tag.
Referenced in host configuration section only briefly; the document doesn't specify or analyse it.
Only a pointer to RFC 4192 for provider changes; not a substantial topic here.

RFC4853.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Multiple Signer Clarification
RFC4853.summary: RFC 4853 updates RFC 3852 (CMS) with replacement text clarifying that a SignedData with multiple signatures is validly signed by a signer if any one of that signer's signatures validates.

CMS.why: The whole document amends the CMS specification (RFC 3852) SignedData processing rules for multiple signers, so it belongs on the CMS page.
CMS.quote: The CMS SignedData protected content type allows multiple digital signatures, but the specification is unclear about the appropriate processing by a recipient of such a signed content.

rejected.why: RSA is only used as an example algorithm for multiple signatures; the document is not about it.
ECDSA is only mentioned as an example of a second signature algorithm.
SHA-1 to SHA-256 transition appears only as an illustrative example.
Certificates are only referenced in the quoted CMS text for identifying signer keys; nothing new is specified about them.

RFC4854.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for Extensions to the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)
RFC4854.summary: Registers the "xmpp" URN namespace ID, administered by the XSF's XMPP Registrar, for naming XML namespaces of XMPP extensions (urn:xmpp:{ShortName}:{SubName}).

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration: it defines the syntax, uniqueness, persistence and assignment rules for the "xmpp" NID. A reader browsing URN namespaces would expect it.
URN.quote: this document registers a formal namespace identifier (NID) for Uniform Resource Names [URN] associated with XMPP extensions

XMPP.why: The namespace exists to name XMPP extensions (XEPs). It does not change XMPP itself, but XMPP readers will want to know about the new naming of extension namespaces.
XMPP.quote: uniquely identifying Extensible Markup Language (XML) formats and protocols that provide extensions to the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)

rejected.why: XML namespaces are what the URNs name, but the document does not define or use XML as a format. XML is only the substrate.
The IANA section just records the NID registration. The document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
The parent of XMPP, which is implied by the XMPP tag. The document is not about instant messaging in general.

RFC4855.title: Media Type Registration of RTP Payload Formats
RFC4855.summary: Specifies the procedure and template requirements for registering RTP payload formats as IANA media types, including sharing rules between RTP and non-RTP transfer and the mapping of media type parameters to SDP fields; obsoletes RFC 3555.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration procedure for RTP payload formats, with required/optional parameters and rules for sharing subtype names.
media types.quote: This document specifies the procedure to register RTP payload formats as audio, video, or other media subtype names.

RTP payload format.why: It sets requirements on how payload formats are described and registered (rate, channels, ptime, clock rate in specification), which readers of RTP payload formats need.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines the specific requirements for registration of media types for use with the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), RFC 3550, to identify RTP payload formats.

SDP.why: A full section defines how media type parameters map to SDP m=, a=rtpmap, a=fmtp, a=ptime and a=maxptime.
SDP.quote: The information carried in the media type string has a specific mapping to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the registered formats are carried over; the document does not specify or extend RTP itself, and the more specific payload format tag covers it.
MIME header syntax is referenced only for parameter format; the subject is media type registration, covered by media types.
IANA registry is the venue, but the IANA Considerations section says no registrations are defined; the registration procedure is media-type specific.

RFC4856.title: Media Type Registration of Payload Formats in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences
RFC4856.summary: RFC 4856 updates the media type registrations (audio/DVI4, G722, G723, G726, G728, G729, GSM, L8, L16, LPC, PCMA, PCMU, VDVI, video/nv) for the RTP payload formats of the RFC 3551 Audio/Video Profile to the revised RFC 4288/4855 template, obsoleting RFC 3555.

media types.why: The document consists of media type registrations under audio and video, conforming to the RFC 4288/4855 registration template, so media type readers expect it.
media types.quote: This document specifies media type registrations for the RTP payload formats defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences.

RTP payload format.why: Each registration covers an RTP payload format from the RFC 3551 profile, with RTP clock rate, ptime and channel parameters.
RTP payload format.quote: This media type depends on RTP framing, and hence is only defined for transfer via RTP (RFC 3550 [6]).

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the formats are carried in; the document registers media types for payload formats rather than specifying RTP, so the more specific payload format tag fits.
PCMA and PCMU are registered here, but only as one of many registrations, and the document defines no G.711 coding itself.
G729, G729D and G729E are registered, but only as part of a broad list of registrations, not as a G.729 specification.
audio/G722 is one registration among many; the document does not define G.722.
ptime and maxptime are referenced from SDP, which is only the source of those parameter definitions.
The IANA section only renames registry headings and changes references, so the document's main body is not about IANA stewardship.

RFC4857.title: Mobile IPv4 Regional Registration
RFC4857.summary: Defines an experimental optional extension to Mobile IPv4 that adds a Gateway Foreign Agent and regional registration messages so a mobile node can register locally within a visited domain, reducing signalling to the home agent.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document specifies new entities (GFA), messages, extensions and code values extending Mobile IPv4 registration.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document is an optional extension to the Mobile IPv4 protocol, and proposes a means for mobile nodes to register locally within a visited domain.

rejected.why: AAA is only touched in an appendix and as a key distribution option; the document is not about AAA.
The more specific Mobile IPv4 tag fits, so the parent is implied.
Router discovery is extended with one flag, but the document is not about ICMP itself.
New authentication extensions are defined, but only as part of the Mobile IPv4 registration mechanism.

RFC4858.title: Document Shepherding from Working Group Last Call to Publication
RFC4858.summary: RFC 4858 describes the IETF's PROTO document shepherding process, in which a working group chair or secretary acts as Document Shepherd for a document from WG Last Call through AD evaluation, IESG evaluation, IANA actions and RFC Editor publication.

IETF process.why: The whole document defines an IETF standards-process procedure for document flow after WG Last Call, covering AD evaluation, IESG evaluation and post-approval steps.
IETF process.quote: It specifies a set of procedures under which a working group chair or secretary serves as the primary Document Shepherd for a document that has been submitted to the IESG for publication.

rejected.why: Section 4 covers the shepherd's handling of IANA actions, but this is one part of the process and the document is not about IANA registries or guidance themselves.
The RFC Editor's post-approval requests (AUTH48, copy-edits) are discussed briefly, but the document is not about RFC format, style or publication policy.
The RTP MIDI example write-up in Appendix A.1 is only an illustrative announcement, not subject matter.
The IP-over-Fibre-Channel write-up in Appendix A.2 is only an example announcement.

RFC4859.title: Codepoint Registry for the Flags Field in the Resource Reservation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) Session Attribute Object
RFC4859.summary: Informational RFC that instructs IANA to create the "Session Attribute Object Flags" registry for the RSVP-TE Session Attribute object's flags field and lists the existing bit assignments from RFCs 3209, 4090 and 4736.

RSVP-TE.why: The whole document concerns the flags field of the RSVP-TE Session Attribute object, cataloguing the bit assignments made by RSVP-TE extensions and creating a registry for them. RSVP-TE readers would want it.
RSVP-TE.quote: There is a need for a codepoint registry to track the use of the bit flags in this field, to ensure that bits are not assigned more than once

rejected.why: The document creates an IANA registry, but only for one protocol's field. The subject is RSVP-TE codepoints, not IANA guidance or stewardship generally.
MPLS and GMPLS are the context in which RSVP-TE is used. The document is about the RSVP-TE object, not MPLS architecture.
GMPLS is mentioned as a use of RSVP-TE, but nothing in the document is specific to GMPLS.
Base RSVP is only background. The Session Attribute object is an RSVP-TE extension, so RSVP-TE is the more specific tag.

RFC4860.title: Generic Aggregate Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) Reservations
RFC4860.summary: Defines generic aggregate RSVP reservations (new SESSION C-Types with virtual destination port and PHB-ID, plus a SESSION-OF-INTEREST object) so multiple aggregate reservations can exist per PHB between an Aggregator and Deaggregator, and specifies the E2E aggregation procedures over them in a Diffserv network.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with new SESSION objects, a SESSION-OF-INTEREST class, processing rules and aggregation procedures. This is a direct RSVP specification.
RSVP.quote: defines a more flexible type of aggregate RSVP reservations, referred to as generic aggregate reservation.

Diffserv.why: Reservations are made per PHB, identified by PHB-ID, in a Diffserv aggregation region. The document covers the RSVP-Diffserv interworking, including classification by DSCP and PHB-ID.
Diffserv.quote: allowing resources to be reserved in a Diffserv network for a given Per Hop Behavior (PHB), or given set of PHBs

rejected.why: GRE appears only as an example encapsulation in Section 5 and is not a subject of the document.
The Extended Tunnel ID concept is borrowed from RSVP-TE, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE or MPLS.
IPsec ESP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional confidentiality mechanism.
IPv6 object variants are defined alongside the IPv4 ones, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The C-Type and class number assignments are boilerplate IANA Considerations, not the main subject.

RFC4861.title: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)
RFC4861.summary: RFC 4861 specifies the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol: router and prefix discovery, address resolution, neighbor unreachability detection, redirects, and the ICMPv6 message and option formats.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document defines IPv6 Neighbor Discovery: its messages, options, host/router behaviour, NUD and redirects.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document specifies the Neighbor Discovery protocol for IP Version 6.

rejected.why: Stateless address autoconfiguration and DAD are specified in RFC 4862; this document only supplies the RA prefix options it uses.
ND messages are carried as ICMPv6 types, but ICMPv6 itself is the substrate and is not specified here.
SEND is only referenced as the cryptographic security solution defined elsewhere. Also, SEND is not a taxonomy tag beyond being a child of neighbor discovery.
IPsec AH/ESP are discussed briefly in Security Considerations as a possible, limited protection, not the subject.
ARP is compared with ND in the IPv4 comparison, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Only the M and O flags pointing to DHCPv6 are defined; DHCPv6 itself is not specified.

RFC4862.title: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
RFC4862.summary: Specifies how IPv6 hosts autoconfigure interfaces: link-local address creation, stateless global address generation from Router Advertisement prefixes, address lifetimes, and the Duplicate Address Detection procedure.

SLAAC.why: The whole document specifies IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, including link-local and global address formation and lifetime handling.
SLAAC.quote: The IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration mechanism requires no manual configuration of hosts, minimal (if any) configuration of routers, and no additional servers.

neighbor discovery.why: The document defines Duplicate Address Detection, which is built on Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement messages. Its sections on sending and receiving them are a substantial part of the document, and readers of neighbor discovery would want it.
neighbor discovery.quote: The procedure for detecting duplicate addresses uses Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement messages as described below.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is mentioned as a complementary mechanism. DAD applies to its addresses, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Site renumbering is a design goal, and Section 4.1 covers it briefly. The document is about autoconfiguration, not renumbering procedures.
Secure Neighbor Discovery is only referenced, for authenticating Router Advertisements and in Security Considerations.
This is implied as the parent of SLAAC. The document is about the more specific SLAAC subject.
The document uses solicited-node multicast and MLD reports as machinery for DAD. It does not address multicast itself.

RFC4863.title: Wildcard Pseudowire Type
RFC4863.summary: Defines a Wildcard Pseudowire Type (codepoint 0x7FFF) so a PE lacking knowledge of the PW Type can initiate LDP-signaled pseudowire LSP setup, with sending and receiving procedures.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines a new pseudowire type and the signaling procedures for it, extending PW setup via LDP.
pseudowire.quote: In order to allow a PE to initiate the signaling exchange for a pseudowire without knowing the pseudowire type, a new PW Type is defined.

rejected.why: LDP is the signaling substrate. The document extends pseudowire signaling (RFC 4447) and defines nothing new in LDP itself beyond using existing status codes.
LSPs are mentioned only as the underlying mechanism. The document is not about MPLS architecture or operations.
The IANA section only records a single registry allocation. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC4864.title: Local Network Protection for IPv6
RFC4864.summary: Informational document showing how IPv6 techniques (privacy addresses, ULAs, DHCPv6-PD, stateful firewalling, untraceable addresses) can deliver the perceived benefits of IPv4 NAT without address translation, with case studies and gap analysis.

NAT.why: The document analyses the perceived benefits and disadvantages of NAT and how to achieve them without it; NAT readers would want it.
NAT.quote: this document shows how Local Network Protection (LNP) using IPv6 can provide the same or more benefits without the need for address translation

IPv6.why: Core subject is IPv6 deployment: ULAs, privacy addresses, multihoming, renumbering and addressing in IPv6 networks.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 was designed with the intention of making NAT unnecessary

firewall.why: Simple security via stateful filtering and pinholes replacing NAT's perceived firewall role is a substantial part.
firewall.quote: the broadband gateway/router should be equipped with stateful firewall capabilities

DHCPv6.why: DHCPv6 prefix delegation is used as the simple-gateway mechanism and for renumbering throughout.
DHCPv6.quote: The Prefix Delegation (DHCP-PD) options [12] provide a mechanism for automated delegation of IPv6 prefixes

privacy.why: Device profiling, privacy addresses and topology hiding are a main theme.
privacy.quote: IPv6 privacy addresses were defined to provide that capability

rejected.why: Discussed only as one protection available without NAT; not the subject.

RFC4887.title: Network Mobility Home Network Models
RFC4887.summary: Informational RFC describing four-plus models for organizing the Home Network (extended, aggregated, virtual, mobile) for NEMO Basic Support Mobile Routers, with configuration, returning-home behaviour and deployment caveats.

NEMO.why: The whole document is about Home Network organization for NEMO Basic Support Mobile Routers, Home Agents and Mobile Network Prefixes.
NEMO.quote: documents some of the usage patterns and the associated issues when deploying a Home Network for Network Mobility (NEMO)-enabled Mobile Routers, conforming to the NEMO Basic Support

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 is the base the models extend and a short reminder section covers it, but the document's subject is NEMO home network organization, not MIPv6 itself.
ND proxying, DAD and ND extensions are mentioned as mechanisms in the models but are not the subject.
IPv6 prefixes and autoconfiguration are the substrate for the examples; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Multihoming is mentioned only briefly as a caveat and deferred to another document.
Only mentioned in passing as an example of an interchange point.
Only mentioned in passing as an example of an interchange point.

RFC4888.title: Network Mobility Route Optimization Problem Statement
RFC4888.summary: Informational problem statement describing why NEMO Basic Support's mandatory mobile router/home agent tunnel causes sub-optimal routing, bottlenecks, nesting amplification and stalemates, motivating Route Optimization for network mobility.

NEMO.why: The whole document analyses limitations of NEMO Basic Support and motivates route optimization for it.
NEMO.quote: With current Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support, all communications to and from Mobile Network Nodes must go through the bi-directional tunnel

rejected.why: Discussed as it interacts with NEMO (MIPv6 route optimization over a mobile network), but the document's subject is NEMO, not MIPv6 itself.
The MRHA tunnel and nested encapsulation are the problem's mechanism, but the document is about mobility routing, not tunnelling generally.
IPv6 is the substrate; nothing specific about IPv6 is specified or analysed.
Route optimization is considered, but the NEMO tag is the more specific home for it.

RFC4889.title: Network Mobility Route Optimization Solution Space Analysis
RFC4889.summary: Informational NEMO WG analysis of the solution space for Route Optimization in IPv6 Network Mobility: benefits, scenarios, issues and design questions (entities, binding, signalling, data transmission, security).

NEMO.why: The whole document analyses route optimization approaches for NEMO Basic Support, nested mobile networks and mobile routers.
NEMO.quote: With current Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support, all communications to and from Mobile Network Nodes must go through the Mobile Router and Home Agent (MRHA) tunnel

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 Return Routability and binding updates are discussed as the basis for RO, but the document is about network mobility, not specifying or analysing MIPv6 itself.
Section 5.8 covers security of address binding and location privacy, but it is a sub-part of the NEMO analysis, not the document's main subject.
Location privacy is discussed as a tradeoff in sections 4.8 and 5.8.3, but it is a secondary concern, not a subject in its own right.
The work is IPv6-based but IPv6 itself is the substrate, not the subject.
Tunnels are central to the analysis, but they are the mechanism being optimized rather than the subject of the document.
DHCP prefix delegation is only mentioned as one candidate approach.

gaps.name: Network Mobility (NEMO) route optimization
gaps.why: The taxonomy's IP mobility topic has a NEMO technology tag, but no tag covers NEMO route optimization specifically. I used NEMO, which fits the document's scope.

RFC4890.title: Recommendations for Filtering ICMPv6 Messages in Firewalls
RFC4890.summary: RFC 4890 gives recommendations for which ICMPv6 message types and codes firewalls should pass or drop, for transit and local traffic, with an example Netfilter script.

ICMP.why: The whole document analyses ICMPv6 message types, codes, scopes and roles and recommends which to allow or drop.
ICMP.quote: This document provides some recommendations for ICMPv6 firewall filter configuration that will allow propagation of ICMPv6 messages that are needed to maintain the functioning of the network

firewall.why: It is a firewall filtering guide covering firewall/routers, firewall/bridges and end-host firewalls, with an example ip6tables script.
firewall.quote: This document recommends a set of rules that seek to balance effective IPv6 communication against the needs of site security.

IPv6.why: The document addresses operating IPv6 networks securely, including scanning risk and Teredo and Mobile IPv6 considerations, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: ICMPv6 is essential to the functioning of IPv6, but there are a number of security risks associated with uncontrolled forwarding of ICMPv6 messages.

rejected.why: Neighbor Discovery messages are classified and filtered, but the document does not specify or extend ND.
Mobile IPv6 ICMPv6 messages get filtering advice, but only as one message group among many.
Packet Too Big is stressed as essential to path MTU discovery, but the document is not about PMTUD itself.
MLD messages are only listed as local-link messages with filter rules.
Considered as a topic tag. The firewall tag is more specific and fits better.
SEND certificate path messages are only mentioned as messages to filter.

RFC4891.title: Using IPsec to Secure IPv6-in-IPv4 Tunnels
RFC4891.summary: Informational guidance on securing manually configured IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels with IPsec, recommending transport mode with ESP and IKE, with SPD examples and tunnel-mode alternatives in appendices.

IPsec.why: The document profiles IPsec usage (transport vs tunnel mode, SPD entries, PAD, ESP/AH choice) for protecting tunnels.
IPsec.quote: This document gives guidance on securing manually configured IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels using IPsec in transport mode.

IPv6 transition.why: It addresses the security of the manually configured IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnel transition mechanism, including threats like address spoofing.
IPv6 transition.quote: The IPv6 Operations (v6ops) working group has selected (manually configured) IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling [RFC4213] as one of the IPv6 transition mechanisms

IKE.why: A substantial section compares IKEv1 and IKEv2 for this use, covering identities, traffic selectors, PAD, and recommending IKEv2 over manual keying.
IKE.quote: IKEv2 supports legacy authentication methods by carrying them in Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) payloads.

rejected.why: The generic tunnelling topic is covered by the IPv6 transition tag; the document is specific to IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels.
Mentioned only as a reason tunnel mode might be acceptable; not specified or profiled.
ESP is used as the protection mechanism but is not itself specified or extended; covered under IPsec.
NAT traversal is discussed only briefly in an appendix on optional features.
Mentioned only as another tunnel type where transport mode is used.
Explicitly out of scope.

RFC4892.title: Requirements for a Mechanism Identifying a Name Server Instance
RFC4892.summary: Informational requirements document describing the existing BIND CHAOS-class TXT (HOSTNAME.BIND / ID.SERVER) convention for identifying which DNS name server instance answered a query, its pros and cons, and requirements for an improved in-band mechanism (later NSID).

DNS.why: The whole document concerns DNS server behaviour: the CHAOS-class TXT query convention and requirements for an in-band DNS mechanism to identify a name server instance, in anycast and load-balanced deployments.
DNS.quote: A standardized mechanism to determine the identity of a name server responding to a particular query would be useful, particularly as a diagnostic aid for administrators.

anycast.why: The motivating problem is telling which instance of an anycast or shared-address server pool answered, so readers of anycast operations would want this.
anycast.quote: With the increased use of DNS anycast, load balancing, and other mechanisms allowing more than one DNS name server to share a single IP address

rejected.why: The document says the mechanism should use the OPT pseudo-RR, but it only states requirements. The actual EDNS option (NSID) is specified in a separate document.
DNSSEC is mentioned only as a hypothetical way to authenticate the response, and the document says this is impossible in practice for the CHAOS class. It is not about DNSSEC.
The security considerations discuss information leakage, but the document is not a general operational security practice document.

RFC4893.title: BGP Support for Four-octet AS Number Space
RFC4893.summary: RFC 4893 extends BGP to carry four-octet AS numbers, defining a new capability, the AS4_PATH and AS4_AGGREGATOR attributes, the AS_TRANS reserved AS number, and rules for interworking and transition between NEW and OLD BGP speakers.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies extensions to BGP: a new capability, two new path attributes, and update generation and processing rules for four-octet AS numbers.
BGP.quote: this document defines a new BGP capability, Four-octet AS Number Capability, that can be used by a BGP speaker to indicate its support for the four-octet AS numbers.

rejected.why: Section 5 only notes that RFC 1997 communities cannot carry four-octet AS numbers and points to a separate extended-community document. That is a minor aside, not a substantial part of the RFC.

Confederations are mentioned only in connection with excluding confederation path segments from AS4_PATH and with transition constraints. The RFC does not address route reflection or confederations in their own right.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate for this purpose. It records code assignments and the expansion of the AS number pool but is not what the document is about.
The Security Considerations only note a possible loss of path information and routing loops. The document does not address routing security.

RFC4894.title: Use of Hash Algorithms in Internet Key Exchange (IKE) and IPsec
RFC4894.summary: Informational review of how IKEv1, IKEv2 and IPsec (AH/ESP) use hash functions, concluding they are not vulnerable to known MD5/SHA-1 collision-reduction attacks and suggesting algorithm-agility and PKIX-related changes for implementors.

IKE.why: Section 2 and much of the document analyse hash use in IKEv1 and IKEv2 (PRFs, integrity, signatures, key identifiers, NAT-T) and whether they need changes.
IKE.quote: This document reviews the many ways that three protocols (IKEv1 [IKEv1], IKEv2 [IKEv2], and IPsec [ESP] and [AH]) use hash functions.

IPsec.why: The document analyses IPsec (AH/ESP) hash use in HMACs and the effect of reduced collision resistance, and gives implementor guidance.
IPsec.quote: AH uses hash functions for authenticating packets; the same is true for ESP when ESP is using its own authentication.

HMAC.why: The vulnerability of HMAC with MD5/SHA-1 in IKEv2 integrity and IPsec packet authentication is a central finding.
HMAC.quote: MD5 used in HMACs is susceptible to forgery, and it is suspected that full SHA-1 used in HMAC is susceptible to forgery.

MD5.why: The MD5 collision weaknesses are the motivating subject, and the document assesses their impact on IKE/IPsec.
MD5.quote: explains the level of vulnerability of these protocols to the reduced collision resistance of the MD5 and SHA-1 hash algorithms.

SHA.why: SHA-1 weakness and a move to the SHA-2 family are discussed in the recommendations.
SHA.quote: implementors of IKE that allow certificate authentication should strongly consider allowing the use of certificates that are signed with the SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 hash algorithms.

rejected.why: PKIX certificates are discussed only as a dependency whose weaknesses IKE inherits (Section 4); the document is not about PKI itself.
Colliding X.509 certificates are cited as a known attack, but the document does not specify or profile certificates.
The subject is covered more specifically by the HMAC, MD5 and SHA tags.
NAT traversal appears only as one place where IKE uses hashes to obscure addresses.
ESP is only one of two IPsec protocols examined, and the document does not address ESP specifically, so the IPsec tag covers it.

RFC4895.title: Authenticated Chunks for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
RFC4895.summary: Defines the SCTP AUTH chunk, the RANDOM, CHUNKS and HMAC-ALGO parameters, and the procedures that let SCTP endpoints authenticate chunks with HMAC and association shared keys.

SCTP.why: The document extends SCTP with a new chunk type, new parameters, an error cause and procedures. It is an SCTP extension specification.
SCTP.quote: This new chunk type can be used to authenticate SCTP chunks by using shared keys between the sender and receiver.

rejected.why: HMAC is the primitive used to compute the AUTH chunk's MAC. The document does not specify or extend HMAC itself.
SHA-1 and SHA-256 are only listed as HMAC identifiers. The document does not specify them.
TLS appears only to explain why it is insufficient (it secures only user data) and as one way to establish endpoint pair shared keys. The document is not about TLS.
Association shared keys are derived within the protocol, but establishing endpoint pair shared keys is explicitly out of scope.
The general authentication topic is covered by the SCTP tag, since the mechanism is SCTP-specific. The document is an SCTP extension, not a cross-protocol authentication topic.

RFC4896.title: Signaling Compression (SigComp) Corrections and Clarifications
RFC4896.summary: RFC 4896 corrects and clarifies ambiguities in SigComp (RFC 3320), SigComp Extended Operations (RFC 3321) and the SIP/SDP static dictionary (RFC 3485), covering decompression memory, UDVM instructions, state handling, feedback and advertisement of resources.

SigComp.why: The whole document is a corrigendum for SigComp and its extensions, so it belongs on the SigComp page.
SigComp.quote: This document describes common misinterpretations and some ambiguities in the Signaling Compression Protocol (SigComp), and offers guidance to developers to resolve any resultant problems.

rejected.why: SIP is the application protocol SigComp compresses. It is only mentioned in examples and in the SIP/SDP static dictionary section. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
ABNF is only used to describe the dummy application protocol message format in the appendix.
SigComp already sits under the real-time communications hierarchy. The generic lossless compression topic is for data compression formats, which this document is not about.
SDP appears only as part of the SIP/SDP static dictionary content. The document does not define SDP behaviour.

RFC4897.title: Handling Normative References to Standards-Track Documents
RFC4897.summary: BCP 97 update to RFC 3967 that replaces the rule of holding documents for normative downward references to Standards-Track RFCs with a "note and move on" annotation procedure.

IETF process.why: The document defines an IETF standards-process procedure for handling normative downward references, updating RFC 3967 and relating to RFC 2026.
IETF process.quote: a document at a given maturity level cannot be published until all of the documents to which it makes a normative reference are at that maturity level or higher

rejected.why: The document concerns the IETF standards-track process and reference annotations, not RFC format, style or editor publication practice in itself.
It defines 'source document' and 'target document' briefly, but is not about terminology or requirements language.

RFC4898.title: TCP Extended Statistics MIB
RFC4898.summary: Defines the TCP-ESTATS-MIB, an SNMP MIB module exposing extended per-connection and listener TCP statistics (performance, path, stack, application, tuning) for diagnosing performance problems and SYN-flood attacks.

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module with tables, scalars, notifications and conformance groups, so it belongs under MIB modules.
MIB.quote: The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) objects defined in this document extend TCP MIB, as specified in RFC 4022

TCP.why: The objects instrument TCP internals: congestion control, retransmission, SACK, window scaling, listener backlog. TCP readers would want this instrumentation.
TCP.quote: This document describes extended performance statistics for TCP. They are designed to use TCP's ideal vantage point to diagnose performance problems

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB module, which the MIB tag covers more specifically.
Congestion window and ssthresh objects are instrumented, but the document does not specify congestion control; it is TCP instrumentation.
ECN counters are included, but only as a few statistics objects.
It is about TCP-stack self-instrumentation via a MIB rather than network measurement metrics or methods.
The listener table supports diagnosing SYN floods, but this is a small part and no mitigation is specified.
Not applicable; the data model is SMIv2.

RFC4901.title: Protocol Extensions for Header Compression over MPLS
RFC4901.summary: Specifies how header-compressed packets (ROHC, CRTP, ECRTP, IPHC) are carried over MPLS pseudowires set up with LDP, including PW types, reused PPP configuration options as interface parameter sub-TLVs, and an HC control parameter encapsulation.

header compression.why: Placeholder
header compression.quote: This specification defines how to use Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) to route Header-Compressed (HC) packets over an MPLS label switched path.

RFC4902.title: Integrity, Privacy, and Security in Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) for SMTP
RFC4902.summary: Informational RFC analysing integrity, privacy and security issues (tracing, bypass, cryptographic compatibility) of adapting the OPES framework to SMTP, and listing requirements and IAB-consideration mappings for a future OPES/SMTP specification.

OPES.why: The whole document concerns OPES adaptation to SMTP: tracing, bypass, IAB considerations and requirements for OPES/SMTP.
OPES.quote: This document analyzes aspects about the integrity of SMTP and mail message adaptation by OPES systems and about privacy and security issues

SMTP.why: The document analyses SMTP gateway adaptation, NDR behaviour, Received trace headers and proposes SMTP-dialog bypass extensions, so SMTP readers would want it.
SMTP.quote: Adding SMTP adaptations with OPES allows us to define a standardized way for SMTP gateway filtering

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific SMTP tag; the document's email focus is on SMTP gateways.
Trace headers are discussed but no header format is defined; the document leaves open whether Received or new headers are used.
Cryptographic protections (OpenPGP, CMS, XML-Signature) are only discussed for compatibility with OPES, not specified or profiled.
Spam filters are mentioned only as examples of existing out-of-band bypass mechanisms.
Privacy is discussed only within the OPES/IAB context; the document is not a general privacy considerations document.
HTTP is referenced only as the contrasting protocol used in earlier OPES work.

RFC4903.title: Multi-Link Subnet Issues
RFC4903.summary: IAB memo documenting the problems with multi-link subnets (a subnet spanning multiple routed links) for IP, TTL/Hop Limit assumptions, link-scoped multicast/broadcast and duplicate address detection, and recommending link models and IPv6 prefix assignment practice.

addressing.why: The document is about the relationship between subnet prefixes and links, and how prefixes should be assigned (RA on-link vs DHCP-PD). This is IP address architecture, with no more specific child tag fitting.
addressing.quote: A multi-link subnet model should be avoided.

neighbor discovery.why: Substantial parts cover ND's Hop Limit 255 check, DAD and DIID, ND proxying/caching and the Prefix Information Option L flag, all in the context of multi-link subnets.
neighbor discovery.quote: Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) uses link-scoped multicast in IPv6 and link-scoped broadcast in IPv4 and so has the issues mentioned in Section 2.3 above.

rejected.why: The document is IPv4/IPv6 generic and concerns the link model; the IPv6-specific parts are covered by the neighbor discovery tag.
SEND is mentioned only as breaking under multi-link subnets in a short security discussion; it is not specified or extended.
Mobile IPv6 is cited as one example of a multi-link subnet approach, but the document is not about mobility.
DHCPv6 prefix delegation is contrasted with RAs briefly; the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
Link-scoped multicast is a source of issues, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership in its own right.
MANETs are mentioned as one context where multi-link subnets arise, not the subject.

gaps.name: IP link model / subnet-link relationship
gaps.why: The central subject, the architecture of links versus subnets and the multi-link subnet problem, has no dedicated tag under internet layer; addressing is the closest.

RFC4904.title: Representing Trunk Groups in tel/sip Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC4904.summary: Defines the tgrp and trunk-context parameters as an extension to the tel URI (and its sip URI equivalent) for conveying originating and terminating trunk groups in SIP requests, with UA/proxy behaviour and call flows.

tel URI.why: The document's core content is new tel URI parameters (tgrp, trunk-context), their ABNF, scoping and equivalence rules.
tel URI.quote: An extension to the tel URI is defined for this purpose.

SIP.why: A substantial part specifies UAC, UAS and proxy behaviour and SIP call flows for using trunk groups in R-URI and Contact headers.
SIP.quote: The terminating (or egress) trunk group parameters MUST be specified in the R-URI.
SIP.section: 6. Normative Behavior of SIP Entities Using Trunk Groups

rejected.why: Trunk groups come from the PSTN and gateways are discussed, but the document specifies a URI parameter and SIP behaviour, not interworking or gateway control.
TGREP is only cited as one way a proxy might choose trunk groups, which is out of scope.
The tel URI tag is more specific; the sip URI is only the equivalent form of the same parameters.
TLS and SIPS appear only in Security Considerations as protection.
MGCP, Megaco and H.323 are mentioned only as possible non-SIP users of the tel URI.

RFC4905.title: Encapsulation Methods for Transport of Layer 2 Frames over MPLS Networks
RFC4905.summary: Historic document describing the "draft-martini" encapsulation of layer 2 PDUs (Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet, HDLC, PPP) with a control word for transport over MPLS emulated virtual circuits, superseded by PWE3 RFCs.

pseudowire.why: The document specifies emulated VC (pseudowire) encapsulations over MPLS, the draft-martini precursor of the PWE3 specifications, including the control word and per-protocol details.
pseudowire.quote: methods for encapsulating the Protocol Data Units (PDUs) of layer 2 protocols such as Frame Relay, Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM), or Ethernet for transport across an MPLS network

rejected.why: MPLS is the tunnel and demultiplexer substrate; the pseudowire tag is more specific and covers the subject.
ATM cells and AAL5 are carried as payload and encapsulated; the document is not about IP over ATM.
Frame Relay is one of several layer 2 payloads carried; it is not the subject of the document.
Ethernet is one of the carried payloads, not the focus of the document.
PPP is only one carried payload type (section 5.6), not what the document is about.
Signaling is deferred to RFC 4906 and RFC 4447; this document specifies only the encapsulation.

RFC4906.title: Transport of Layer 2 Frames Over MPLS
RFC4906.summary: Historic RFC documenting the deployed "draft-martini" LDP-based signalling for transporting layer 2 frames (Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet, HDLC, PPP) over MPLS using VC labels, now superseded by PWE3 specs (RFC 4447).

pseudowire.why: The document defines the draft-martini pseudowire setup: VC labels, VC FEC element, control word negotiation, and LDP withdrawal procedures for emulating layer 2 circuits over MPLS. It is the predecessor of the PWE3 specifications.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies the necessary label distribution procedures for accomplishing this using the encapsulation methods in [RFC4905].

LDP.why: A substantial part defines a new LDP FEC element (type 128), interface parameters, new status codes, and label withdraw/release procedures. These are LDP extensions that LDP readers would need.
LDP.quote: The VC label bindings are distributed using the LDP downstream unsolicited mode described in [RFC3036].

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate; the more specific pseudowire tag covers the subject.
ATM is one of several transported payloads, and the document only references its encapsulation without being about IP over ATM.
Frame Relay is one of several payloads carried; the document is not about frame relay itself.
Ethernet is only one of the carried layer 2 types, and the encapsulation details are in RFC 4905.
PPP frames are just one transported payload type.
The SONET circuit emulation service is only mentioned and is defined in the separate CEM document.

RFC4907.title: Architectural Implications of Link Indications
RFC4907.summary: IAB informational document describing the role of link-layer indications (Link Up/Down, rate, frame loss) within the Internet architecture, giving architectural principles and advice on appropriate and inappropriate use across Internet, transport and application layers, with a literature review focused on WLANs.

internet architecture.why: The document gives architectural principles (layering, robustness, race conditions, layer compression) for how link-layer information should be used by higher layers.
internet architecture.quote: This document describes the role of link indications within the Internet architecture.

link layer.why: Subject is link-layer state indications (Link Up/Down, rate, frame loss), with substantial discussion of 802.11 link behaviour, rate adaptation and handoff in the appendix.
link layer.quote: A link indication represents information provided by the link layer to higher layers regarding the state of the link.

rejected.why: 802.11 is the main example and literature focus, but the document is about link indications generally, not IP over 802.11.
DHCP and DNA are cited as consumers of link indications, not the subject.
Mobile IP binding updates appear as examples of path-change signals, not the document's subject.
Transport parameter estimation is discussed in the layered model, but TCP itself is not specified or extended.
Congestion control is one architectural consideration (Section 2.4), not a main subject.

gaps.name: Link indications / link-layer triggers
gaps.why: The document's core subject (Link Up/Down events, IEEE 802.21 triggers) has no dedicated taxonomy tag; link layer is the nearest fit.

RFC4908.title: Multi-homing for small scale fixed network Using Mobile IP and NEMO
RFC4908.summary: Experimental RFC proposing a multihoming architecture for small fixed networks using Mobile IPv6 and NEMO Basic Support, with multiple Care-of Addresses and geographically distributed redundant Home Agents advertising aggregated prefixes.

NEMO.why: The document's architecture is built on NEMO Basic Support: a mobile router with multiple tunnels to home agents, and it requires extensions to NEMO for multiple CoAs and multiple HAs.
NEMO.quote: we propose a multihoming architecture using mobile IP [1] and NEMO [2] for small-scale fixed networks.

Mobile IPv6.why: It specifies requirements for extending Mobile IPv6 (multiple CoA registration, multiple synchronized home agents) and applies it to fixed hosts and networks.
Mobile IPv6.quote: The current Mobile IPv6 and the NEMO Basic Support protocol does not allow registration of more than one Care-of Address

multihoming.why: Multihoming architecture, its goals and its contrast with BGP-based multihoming are a central theme. The multihoming topic is a child of addressing. Mobile IP/NEMO tags are chosen as technology, but this document addresses multihoming in its own right, with no multihoming technology tag chosen.
multihoming.quote: Multihoming technology improves the availability of host and network connectivity.

rejected.why: BGP is discussed only as the conventional multihoming approach whose problems motivate the proposal, and as an analogy for HA synchronization. The document does not specify or extend it.
The IBGP route reflector is only used as an analogy for HA binding synchronization.
Not mentioned. The document deals with Mobile IP-based multihoming, not the Shim6 host shim.
CDN is mentioned only as an example of proven same-prefix advertisement from several sites.
Advertising the same prefix from multiple HAs is an anycast-like technique, but the document does not use or discuss anycast addressing as such.
Parent of the chosen Mobile IPv6 and NEMO tags, so it is implied and not listed separately.

gaps.name: Multihoming
gaps.why: The document is largely about multihoming architecture. The taxonomy has only the multihoming topic under addressing, and it is the only tag that fits that subject.

RFC4909.title: Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) General Extension Payload for Open Mobile Alliance BCAST LTKM/STKM Transport
RFC4909.summary: Defines a new MIKEY General Extension payload type (Type 5, with LTKM and STKM subtypes) to carry OMA BCAST long-term and short-term key messages, and records the IANA allocation.

MIKEY.why: The document extends MIKEY by defining a new General Extension payload type and subtypes for OMA BCAST key messages. Readers of MIKEY extensions would want it.
MIKEY.quote: This document specifies the use of the General Extension payload of MIKEY to carry the LTKMs or STKMs.

rejected.why: OMA BCAST and 3GPP MBMS are mobile broadcast contexts, but the document defines no IP-over-cellular behaviour, only a key-management payload.
The payload is used for broadcast key delivery, but the document specifies only a MIKEY payload format, not group key management. MIKEY is the more specific fit.
The IANA section registers a new General Extension type and subtypes, but this is boilerplate here and the document is not about IANA registries.
MIKEY is a child of key management and the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.

RFC4910.title: Robust XML Encoding Rules (RXER) for Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1)
RFC4910.summary: Defines the Robust XML Encoding Rules (RXER) and Canonical RXER (CRXER) for ASN.1, which encode ASN.1 abstract values as XML, along with supporting basic types (Markup, QName, etc.).

ASN.1.why: The document specifies new ASN.1 encoding rules, including translation of every ASN.1 built-in type and canonical form, plus an ASN.1 module.
ASN.1.quote: defines a set of Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) encoding rules, called the Robust XML Encoding Rules or RXER

XML.why: The encoding produces XML documents via Infoset translation, namespaces, serialization and canonicalization, so it is an XML-based format specification.
XML.quote: produce an Extensible Markup Language (XML) [XML10][XML11] representation of ASN.1 values of any given ASN.1 type

rejected.why: Not related; only a different binary encoding family is discussed (BER/DER/PER).
No media type registration; IANA section only registers an XML namespace.
Unicode normalization and character handling are discussed but only incidentally to XML encoding.
AnyURI type merely references URI syntax; not about URIs.

gaps.name: ASN.1 encoding rules (RXER/CRXER)
gaps.why: ASN.1 tag covers modules and encoding rules, but a dedicated tag for ASN.1 encoding rules / XER family would be more specific.

RFC4911.title: Encoding Instructions for the Robust XML Encoding Rules (RXER)
RFC4911.summary: Defines the RXER encoding instructions (ATTRIBUTE, GROUP, LIST, UNION, VALUES, insertion and reference instructions, etc.) that modify how ASN.1 values are encoded by RXER/CRXER and translated to ASN.X, and rules for keeping the resulting encodings unambiguous.

ASN.1.why: The whole document specifies ASN.1 encoding instructions for RXER and their effect on ASN.1 type definitions and ASN.X translation. It is about ASN.1 notation and encoding.
ASN.1.quote: defines encoding instructions that may be used in an Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) specification to alter how ASN.1 values are encoded

XML.why: The instructions control XML encodings, and the reference instructions incorporate XML Schema, RELAX NG and DTD definitions. XML-based encoding of ASN.1 is a substantial subject of the document.
XML.quote: encode a component of an ASN.1 value as an Extensible Markup Language (XML) attribute rather than as a child element

rejected.why: Not about media type registration.
URIs appear only as namespace names and context identifiers, not as the subject.
Not relevant.

gaps.name: Robust XML Encoding Rules (RXER) / ASN.X
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RXER or ASN.X; the ASN.1 tag is the closest.

RFC4912.title: Abstract Syntax Notation X (ASN.X)
RFC4912.summary: Defines ASN.X, an XML representation of ASN.1 specifications, via translation rules from ASN.1 modules to XML, designed to be an RXER-encodable ASN.1 type (ModuleDefinition) and to serve as an XML schema language.

ASN.1.why: The whole document specifies how ASN.1 modules, types, values, classes and objects are translated into ASN.X, and gives an ASN.1 module for ASN.X.
ASN.1.quote: Abstract Syntax Notation X (ASN.X) is a semantically equivalent Extensible Markup Language (XML) representation for Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) specifications.

rejected.why: XML is the serialization format for ASN.X modules, but the document is about the ASN.1 notation translation, not XML usage in protocols generally.
Parent of ASN.1 and XML; the specific child ASN.1 is the better fit.

gaps.name: ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists ASN.1 only in prose under data formats; I used the id 'ASN.1' as written in the taxonomy, so this is not a gap.

gaps.name: RXER (Robust XML Encoding Rules)
gaps.why: ASN.X is tightly tied to RXER and its encoding instructions, but the taxonomy has no tag for ASN.1 encoding rules such as RXER, XER or GSER.

RFC4913.title: Abstract Syntax Notation X (ASN.X) Representation of Encoding Instructions for the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER)
RFC4913.summary: Specifies the ASN.X (XML) representation of GSER encoding instructions, i.e. the choiceOfStrings instruction and the empty GSER encoding-instruction assignment list, with ASN.1 and ASN.X modules.

ASN.1.why: The document defines how ASN.1 encoding instructions for GSER are translated to ASN.X, and provides normative ASN.1 and ASN.X modules. It is about ASN.1 notation and encoding rules.
ASN.1.quote: This document specifies the ASN.X representation for EncodingInstructionAssignmentList and EncodingInstruction as they are defined for the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER)

XML.why: ASN.X is an XML-based format, and the translation rules are given in terms of XML Infoset element and attribute items.
XML.quote: Abstract Syntax Notation X (ASN.X) [ASN.X] is an Extensible Markup Language (XML) [XML10][XML11] representation for Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1)

rejected.why: Only XML is used as a representation; nothing concerns XML digital signatures or encryption.
No JSON content; GSER is a string encoding of ASN.1 types, which no tag covers.
The example mentions UTF8String and VisibleString only as ASN.1 types in an encoding instruction, not as a Unicode topic.

gaps.name: GSER / RXER / ASN.X (ASN.1 encoding rules)
gaps.why: The document is about ASN.X and GSER encoding instructions, but the taxonomy has no tags for them. ASN.1 is the closest, and readers of the ASN.1 encoding-rules family would want this RFC.

RFC4914.title: Abstract Syntax Notation X (ASN.X) Representation of Encoding Instructions for the XML Encoding Rules (XER)
RFC4914.summary: Specifies how XER (XML Encoding Rules) encoding instructions and target lists in ASN.1 are translated into ASN.X, the XML representation of ASN.1, with the supporting ASN.1 and ASN.X modules.

ASN.1.why: The document defines ASN.X translation rules for ASN.1 encoding instructions and gives normative ASN.1 modules and their ASN.X forms. This is ASN.1 notation and encoding work.
ASN.1.quote: This document specifies the ASN.X representation of encoding instructions for the XML Encoding Rules (XER).

XML.why: The translations are specified as XML Infoset element and attribute items, and ASN.X is an XML-based format. A substantial part of the document addresses this XML representation.
XML.quote: ASN.X is defined in terms of rules for translating from an ASN.1 specification.

rejected.why: The document does not register or define media types.
URIs appear only as namespace values in the instructions and are not the subject of the document.
Unicode is cited only for code point notation, which is incidental.

gaps.name: ASN.X / XER encoding instructions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ASN.X, XER or RXER. ASN.1 is the closest fit but does not cover the XML encoding rules specifically.

RFC4915.title: Multi-Topology (MT) Routing in OSPF
RFC4915.summary: Extends OSPFv2 to support multiple independent IP topologies (MT-IDs) by redefining TOS metric fields in LSAs, with optional exclusion of links from the default topology, interoperability, and migration guidance.

OSPF.why: The document specifies an extension to OSPFv2: MT-ID metrics in Router, Summary and AS-external LSAs, per-MT SPF computation, and the MT option bit.
OSPF.quote: This document describes an extension to Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) in order to define independent IP topologies called Multi-Topologies (MTs).

rejected.why: The document is a specific OSPF protocol extension, so the OSPF tag fits better than the general architecture topic.
M-ISIS is mentioned only as a similar mechanism in the Introduction; the document does not cover IS-IS.
A default multicast topology MT-ID is reserved, but multicast routing is not a subject of the document.
The MT-ID registry is created, but that is boilerplate IANA considerations and not the document's main subject.
Diffserv/TOS appears only in comparing MT with historic TOS-based routing; classification of traffic to topologies is out of scope.
The document extends OSPF Version 2 (RFC 2328) only.

RFC4916.title: Connected Identity in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC4916.summary: RFC 4916 extends SIP so a UA can convey its connected identity in the From header of a mid-dialog UPDATE or re-INVITE, signed via the RFC 4474 Identity header, and adds the "from-change" option tag, updating RFC 3261.

SIP.why: The document specifies a SIP extension and updates RFC 3261: new UA, proxy and Authentication Service behaviour, a new option tag, and relaxed To/From URI reflection in mid-dialog requests.
SIP.quote: This document extends the use of the From header field to allow it to convey what is commonly called "connected identity" information

rejected.why: The document relies on RFC 4474 Identity header signing for caller-ID authentication, but it does not define STIR. It only applies the existing mechanism to mid-dialog requests.
The document uses SIP Identity signing as a means to authenticate connected identity. Its subject is SIP signalling behaviour, not authentication mechanisms.
SDP appears only in the example messages and as a note on early media. The document does not specify or extend it.
PSTN call transfers behind gateways are mentioned as a motivation for identity changes. The document does not address interworking.

RFC4917.title: Mobile IPv4 Message String Extension
RFC4917.summary: Defines a new skippable Mobile IPv4 extension (type 145) that Home Agents and Foreign Agents add to Registration Reply/Revocation messages to carry a human-readable UTF-8 text string for the Mobile Node's user.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document specifies a new extension to Mobile IPv4 registration messages, its format, and its operation between HA, FA and MN.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document specifies a new extension for use in Mobile IPv4. This extension can be added by the Home Agent and the Foreign Agent to Registration Reply messages.

rejected.why: The text field must be UTF-8, but this is only an encoding used by the extension, not something the document is about.
Mentioned only as one possible source of the message string; the document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
The more specific Mobile IPv4 tag applies, so the parent is not listed.
The IANA section reserves type 145 and a subtype space, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC4918.title: HTTP Extensions for Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV)
RFC4918.summary: RFC 4918 specifies WebDAV, a set of HTTP/1.1 extensions (PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE, LOCK, UNLOCK, new headers, status codes and XML formats) for managing resource properties, collections, namespace operations and locking, and it obsoletes RFC 2518.

WebDAV.why: The whole document specifies WebDAV: its methods, headers, properties, locking model, multi-status responses, XML elements and compliance classes.
WebDAV.quote: Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) consists of a set of methods, headers, and content-types ancillary to HTTP/1.1

rejected.why: WebDAV extends HTTP, but the WebDAV tag sits under HTTP and is the more specific fit. The ancestor is implied.
XML is the encoding for WebDAV properties and request and response bodies. The document does not define XML itself, and its XML extensibility rules are part of WebDAV.
UUID URNs are only suggested as a form for lock tokens, which is incidental to the document.
Basic and Digest authentication appear only in the security considerations and in guidance on triggering an authentication challenge. They are not the subject of the document.
The document defines the 'opaquelocktoken' and 'DAV:' URI schemes only in passing. Its subject is the WebDAV protocol, not URI mechanics.

RFC4919.title: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs): Overview, Assumptions, Problem Statement, and Goals
RFC4919.summary: Informational overview of the assumptions, problems and goals for carrying IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 low-power wireless personal area networks (6LoWPANs), setting out the initial work list for the 6lowpan WG.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document frames the problem and goals for IPv6 over 802.15.4 LoWPANs, including the adaptation layer, header compression and address autoconfiguration.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document describes the assumptions, problem statement, and goals for transmitting IP over IEEE 802.15.4 networks.

IoT.why: It addresses constrained, low-power, large-scale sensor devices and guidance for using IP on them, which matches the IoT topic.
IoT.quote: A LoWPAN typically includes devices that work together to connect the physical environment to real-world applications, e.g., wireless sensors.

rejected.why: Mesh routing is one goal and AODV, OLSR and TBRPF are cited as examples, but the document does not specify or analyse them.
SNMP is mentioned only as a candidate management protocol needing further study, in one goal.
IPsec and TLS appear only as alternatives to evaluate in the security considerations, not as the document's subject.
AES appears only as the 802.15.4 link-layer cipher, mentioned in passing.
Address autoconfiguration is a goal, but the document only motivates it and defers the specification to other work, so the 6LoWPAN tag covers it.
Header compression is one goal among eight. The 6LoWPAN tag covers it and the document does not specify any scheme.

RFC4920.title: Crankback Signaling Extensions for MPLS and GMPLS RSVP-TE
RFC4920.summary: Specifies crankback signaling extensions to MPLS and GMPLS RSVP-TE: new IF_ID ERROR_SPEC TLVs, re-routing flags in LSP_ATTRIBUTES, and an error value, so failed LSP setups or recoveries can be retried around blocked links or nodes.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling with new TLVs, flags and an error code for crankback re-routing of TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document specifies crankback signaling extensions for use in MPLS signaling using RSVP-TE as defined in "RSVP-TE: Extensions to RSVP for LSP Tunnels", RFC 3209

GMPLS.why: The extensions apply equally to GMPLS signalling, using the GMPLS IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object and Notify message, and GMPLS recovery is a key motivation.
GMPLS.quote: GMPLS signaling as defined in "Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Signaling Functional Description", RFC 3473

rejected.why: The more specific RSVP-TE and GMPLS tags cover the subject; MPLS in general is implied as an ancestor.
Base RSVP is the substrate; the document's extensions are to RSVP-TE specifically.
OSPF and IS-IS are only sources of TE information and area identifiers carried in TLVs, not specified here.
PCE is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to detect bogus reports.
Fast reroute (RFC 4090) is referenced only as related background, not the subject.
Parent of the RSVP-TE tag chosen, so it is implied; the document does not address traffic engineering more broadly than RSVP-TE signalling.

gaps.name: Crankback routing / LSP re-routing and recovery
gaps.why: The core subject is crankback re-routing of failed LSP setups and LSP recovery, which has no dedicated tag; RSVP-TE is the closest fit.

RFC4923.title: Quality of Service (QoS) Signaling in a Nested Virtual Private Network
RFC4923.summary: Informational memo describing how RSVP reservations, aggregation (RFC 3175) and precedence-based preemption work across nested IPsec-style VPNs, including data and signaling flows within a VPN router and via a Network Guard.

RSVP.why: The whole document explains RSVP reservation setup, aggregation/deaggregation, and preemption (RFC 3181/4495) across nested VPN tunnels, including RSVP message handling in VPN routers.
RSVP.quote: Let us discuss how a resource reservation protocol, and specifically RSVP, might be used in a nested virtual private network.
RSVP.section: 2. Reservation and Preemption in a Nested VPN

VPN.why: Nested VPN architecture and VPN router structure are central. They are customer-provisioned IPsec VPNs, but the VPN tag covers the nesting and tunnel structure readers would look for.
VPN.quote: Some networks require communication between an interior and exterior portion of a VPN or through a concatenation of such networks resulting in a nested VPN

IPsec.why: The VPN tunnels are IPsec security associations; the document addresses how reservations map onto SAs and how signalling crosses the plaintext/ciphertext boundary.
IPsec.quote: The thrust of the memo surrounds VPNs that use encryption in some form, such as IPsec and their subsequent nesting across multiple network domains.

rejected.why: DSCP marking and DCLASS are used for the aggregate reservations, but Diffserv is a supporting mechanism rather than the subject.
Parent of RSVP, which is chosen; ancestors are implied.
SIP and H.323 are mentioned only as call management systems that interoperate with the reservations.
GRE, IP/IP and MPLS tunnels are mentioned only as alternative aggregation tunnels; the focus is IPsec VPN.
The Network Guard is discussed as a signaling path across the crypto boundary, but it is not a firewall specification.
Integrated Services is background framing for RSVP; the document is about RSVP operation in nested VPNs, not Intserv itself.

RFC4924.title: Reflections on Internet Transparency
RFC4924.summary: IAB document reviewing prior statements on Internet transparency and the end-to-end principle, and discussing new transparency barriers: application filtering, QoS, ALGs, IPv6 address restrictions, DNS namespace mangling, and load balancing/redirection.

internet architecture.why: The document is an architectural reflection on transparency, oblivious transport and the end-to-end principle, reaffirming core Internet architectural tenets.
internet architecture.quote: the IAB has published a number of documents relating to Internet transparency and the end-to-end principle

NAT.why: A substantial section addresses NATs and ALGs as barriers to transparency, and the risk of NAT for IPv6.
NAT.quote: it has become apparent that there are problems inherent in the deployment of Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) (frequently embedded within firewalls and devices implementing NAT)

QoS.why: A dedicated section analyses how QoS mechanisms (Diffserv classes, RSVP) affect transparency.
QoS.quote: Deployment of QoS technology has potential implications for Internet transparency, since the QoS experienced by a flow can make the Internet more or less oblivious to that flow.

DNS.why: DNS section covers the unique root and namespace mangling by resolvers, and DNS-based redirection, as transparency issues.
DNS.quote: providers implementing recursive nameservers and/or DNS forwarders that replace answers that indicate that a name does not exist in the DNS hierarchy

IPv6.why: A section on IPv6 address restrictions and allocation as they affect transparency, including IKEv2 IPv6 assignment.
IPv6.quote: it is important that IPv6 networks of all sizes be supplied with a prefix sufficient to enable allocation of addresses and sub-networks
IPv6.section: 2.4.1. Allocation of IPv6 Addresses by Providers

rejected.why: Firewalls and filtering are discussed as transparency barriers, but the document is not about firewall mechanisms themselves.
Mentioned only as being broken by DNS ALGs and mangling; the document does not specify or analyse DNSSEC.
IKEv2 IPv6 address assignment is a brief subsection, not the focus of the document.
Diffserv classes are cited as examples of QoS impact; QoS is the broader and fitting subject.
Anycast gets one sentence in the load balancing section, not enough to be about it.
RFC 4084 terminology is discussed, but this document does not itself define terminology.

gaps.name: Internet transparency / end-to-end principle / oblivious transport
gaps.why: The central subject has no dedicated tag. The closest is internet architecture, which fits only broadly.

RFC4925.title: Softwire Problem Statement
RFC4925.summary: Problem statement for the Softwires WG describing the Hubs-and-Spokes and Mesh scenarios for carrying IPv4 across IPv6-only networks and IPv6 across IPv4-only networks via tunnels, with requirements and non-requirements.

softwire.why: The whole document defines the softwire problem space (Hubs and Spokes, Mesh), requirements for discovery, control and encapsulation.
softwire.quote: connecting IPv4 networks across IPv6-only networks as well as IPv6 networks across IPv4-only networks

rejected.why: Parent of softwire; implied, so not listed separately.
NAT traversal is a requirement for softwires but the document is not about NAT itself.
Mentioned only as an analogy; the document explicitly says multiple address space support is out of scope.
BGP is used between AFBRs in the mesh scenario but is not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only as a contrasting mechanism.
Softwires are the more specific tag; generic tunnelling is implied.

RFC4926.title: A URN Namespace for GEANT
RFC4926.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "geant" managed by DANTE for naming persistent resources of the GEANT European research and education network consortium, specifying its syntax, assignment, resolution and delegation rules.

URN.why: The document defines and registers a new URN namespace (NID geant), including syntax, uniqueness, persistence, assignment and resolution, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a proposed URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace that would be managed by DANTE

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to state the NSS syntax; the document is not about the notation.
The IANA registration of the NID is a boilerplate-level step; the document's body is the namespace definition itself.
DNS names are only mentioned as one way to guarantee uniqueness of subordinate authority names; the document is not about DNS.
URN is the more specific tag that fits; URI syntax is only background.

RFC4927.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCECP) Specific Requirements for Inter-Area MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC4927.summary: Informational RFC listing inter-area-specific requirements on the PCE Communication Protocol (PCECP) for computing inter-area MPLS/GMPLS TE-LSP paths, complementing the generic PCECP requirements.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies requirements on PCECP request/response messages, PCE selection, recording, and loop avoidance for inter-area path computation. This is PCE architecture and protocol work.
PCE.quote: This document lists a detailed set of PCECP-specific requirements for support of inter-area TE-LSP path computation.

traffic engineering.why: The document concerns inter-area MPLS/GMPLS TE-LSP path computation, including diversity and constrained shortest paths. The PCE tag sits under traffic engineering, so this tag is a topic tag only if it adds something beyond PCE; it does add the inter-area TE motivation.
traffic engineering.quote: An inter-area Traffic Engineered Label Switched Path (TE-LSP) is an LSP that transits through at least two IGP areas.

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are the setting for the computed paths, but the document does not specify MPLS itself.
GMPLS is named in the title and scope, but nothing GMPLS-specific is specified.
OSPF areas appear only as the definition of IGP areas; the document does not address OSPF.
IS-IS levels are mentioned only as a definition of IGP area; the document is not about IS-IS.
The RSVP-TE ERO is mentioned in the terminology only; the document is not about RSVP-TE signalling.
The Manageability section calls for PCECP MIB modules to record statistics, but this is a minor requirement.

RFC4928.title: Avoiding Equal Cost Multipath Treatment in MPLS Networks
RFC4928.summary: BCP describing how deployed MPLS LSRs apply equal-cost multipath by guessing IP payloads from the first nibble, and recommending that applications over MPLS restrict the first payload nibble to 0x0 or 0x1 to avoid ECMP-induced reordering.

ECMP.why: The whole document is about ECMP behaviour in MPLS networks (IP ECMP vs label ECMP) and how to avoid it for flows that need in-order delivery.
ECMP.quote: This document describes the Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP) behavior of currently deployed MPLS networks.

MPLS.why: The document analyses MPLS label stack and payload identification and gives recommendations for application FEC and payload design over MPLS.
MPLS.quote: The MPLS label stack does not carry a Protocol Identifier. Instead the payload of an MPLS packet is identified by the Forwarding Equivalence Class

rejected.why: Only cited as an example (RFC 4385 control word); the document is not about pseudowires.
IPv4/IPv6 version nibbles are inspected, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
MPLS IPv4 VPN mentioned only as a trivial case where being mistaken for IPv4 is harmless.
IANA section only marks IP version 0x1 as reserved; boilerplate-level.
Appears only in references listing other MPLS specs.

RFC4929.title: Change Process for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Protocols and Procedures
RFC4929.summary: BCP defining the IETF process by which other SDOs and fora must propose, review and develop extensions or changes to MPLS and GMPLS protocols, clarifying the MPLS and CCAMP working groups' ownership of those protocols.

IETF process.why: The document is a procedural BCP describing stages (requirements evaluation, WG charter, IESG review, solutions work, rejection, appeals) within the IETF standards process as applied to MPLS/GMPLS.
IETF process.quote: This section defines the (G)MPLS change process and the rules that must be followed in order to make extensions or changes to the (G)MPLS protocols.

MPLS.why: The document concerns governance and ownership of MPLS/GMPLS protocols and which WGs are responsible, so readers of MPLS would want it, though it specifies no protocol.
MPLS.quote: The (G)MPLS working groups are REQUIRED to protect the architectural integrity of the (G)MPLS protocols

GMPLS.why: GMPLS change control and CCAMP's authority over GMPLS are a central subject of the document.
GMPLS.quote: The technology that the CCAMP working group focuses on is called Generalized MPLS (GMPLS)
GMPLS.section: 2.1.2. Common Control & Measurement Plane Working Group

rejected.why: IANA codepoint allocation is mentioned only as a consequence of following the process; the main body is not about IANA registries.
Only boilerplate IPR text; not a subject of the document.
P2MP TE LSPs are mentioned only as an example of work division between WGs.
Mentioned in a survey of related working groups only.

RFC4930.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC4930.summary: RFC 4930 specifies EPP 1.0, an XML-based stateful client-server protocol for provisioning objects (e.g., domain names) in a shared registry repository, with generic commands, an extension framework, result codes, schemas, an object mapping template and the application/epp+xml media type.
