EPP.why: The document is the core specification of EPP: commands, responses, extension framework, result codes and schemas.
EPP.quote: an application layer client-server protocol for the provisioning and management of objects stored in a shared central repository

XML.why: A substantial part is the XML schema definition, namespaces and XML-based extension framework, and the application/epp+xml media type registration; readers of XML-based protocol formats would want it.
XML.quote: EPP is specified using the Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0

rejected.why: The EPP tag sits under it and already covers the registry-registrar provisioning subject; the parent is implied.
Appendix B registers application/epp+xml, but it is a small appendix of a protocol spec, not the document's subject.
Domain names are the motivating use case, but the document defines no DNS protocol behaviour and no object mappings.
Section 2.1 only lists requirements for future transport mappings; this document defines none.
The login mechanism is merely compared to SASL PLAIN; it does not specify or extend SASL.
Security is delegated to lower layers; the document does not specify TLS use.

RFC4931.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Domain Name Mapping
RFC4931.summary: Specifies the XML-based EPP mapping for provisioning and managing domain name objects in a shared registry (commands, attributes, status values, schema), obsoleting RFC 3731.

EPP.why: The document is the EPP domain object mapping: it defines check, info, transfer, create, delete, renew and update command semantics, status values and the XML schema for domain objects.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for the provisioning and management of Internet domain names stored in a shared central repository.

rejected.why: Domain delegation data (name servers, glue) is provisioned, but the document is about registry provisioning, not DNS protocol or resolver behaviour.
XML and XML Schema are only the specification notation and encoding for the mapping, not the subject.
Implied parent of EPP; the more specific EPP tag is used.
Internationalized names are only mentioned as a conformance note referencing IDNA; not a subject of the document.
IANA section only registers XML namespace and schema; boilerplate.

RFC4932.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Host Mapping
RFC4932.summary: Specifies the EPP mapping for provisioning and managing host name objects (check, info, create, delete, update, pending-action notification) in a shared registry repository, obsoleting RFC 3732.

EPP.why: The document is the EPP host object mapping, defining command syntax, semantics, status values and XML schema for host objects.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for the provisioning and management of Internet host names stored in a shared central repository.

rejected.why: Host objects are used as name servers and glue records, but the document defines a registry provisioning mapping, not DNS protocol or resource records.
XML and XML Schema are only the specification notation for the mapping, not the subject.
Host name syntax is merely referenced (RFC 952/1123) as an attribute constraint; the document is about provisioning host objects.
Implied as the parent of EPP; the specific EPP tag is the better fit.
Only mentioned briefly in the context of host name syntax conformance.

RFC4933.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Contact Mapping
RFC4933.summary: RFC 4933 specifies the EPP object mapping for contacts (social information identifiers) in a shared registry repository, defining XML command and response syntax for check, info, transfer, create, delete and update, and obsoletes RFC 3733.

EPP.why: The whole document is an EPP object mapping for contacts, defining command syntax, semantics, status values and the XML schema for registry contact objects.
EPP.quote: an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for the provisioning and management of individual or organizational social information identifiers (known as "contacts")

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the notation used to specify the mapping. The document is not about XML usage in general.
This is the parent of EPP and is implied by the EPP tag. The document covers contact objects, not domain objects.
UTF-8 is mentioned for name and address strings and in the internationalization section, but only as an encoding the mapping relies on.
The document only requires XML Schema dateTime in UTC. It defines no date-time format of its own.
The contact data is similar in kind to vCard, but the document does not use or discuss vCard.

RFC4934.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Transport Over TCP
RFC4934.summary: Specifies how an EPP session maps onto a single TCP connection, including session management, message exchange, a 32-bit length-framed data unit, and mandatory TLS protection; obsoletes RFC 3734.

EPP.why: The document is a transport mapping for EPP, defining session, message exchange and framing for EPP over TCP. Readers of EPP would expect to find it.
EPP.quote: This document describes how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) is mapped onto a single client-server TCP connection.

transport mapping.why: It is a classic X-over-TCP binding, covering connection mapping, framing and the transport considerations required of EPP mappings. It also adds a topic-level tag that is not an ancestor of EPP.
transport mapping.quote: This mapping addresses each of the considerations using a combination of features described in this document and features provided by TCP

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document defines no new TCP behaviour or extension.
TLS is mandated for security but is only a security mechanism. No new TLS extension is defined.
EPP XML instances are only the payload that is framed. The document does not specify XML usage.
EPP is already tagged, and it sits under domain registration, so the parent is implied.

RFC4935.title: Fibre Channel Fabric Configuration Server MIB
RFC4935.summary: Defines the T11-FC-FABRIC-CONFIG-SERVER-MIB SMIv2 module for managing the Fibre Channel Fabric Configuration Server: discovery control and status, discovered interconnect elements, ports and platforms, statistics, and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, groups, notifications and compliance statements for the Fibre Channel Fabric Configuration Server.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

fibre channel.why: The managed subject is Fibre Channel fabric topology, switches, ports and platforms. Fibre Channel is the subject matter rather than a transport for something else, though the taxonomy entry covers FC over IP transports.
fibre channel.quote: it describes managed objects for information related to the Fabric Configuration Server function of a Fibre Channel network.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag covers the content.
The FC fabric topology relates to storage networking. The document does not address storage access protocols, and LUN map information is explicitly left to the SCSI-MIB.
AgentX is mentioned only as an example of how management instances can be grouped.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel fabric management (FC-GS Fabric Configuration Server)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has Fibre Channel only as IP-over-FC transports (fibre channel under storage, iFCP). It has no tag for native Fibre Channel fabric management MIBs such as this one, the Name Server MIB or the Fabric Address Manager MIB.

RFC4936.title: Fibre Channel Zone Server MIB
RFC4936.summary: Defines two SMIv2 MIB modules (T11-FC-FABRIC-LOCK-MIB and T11-FC-ZONE-SERVER-MIB) for managing Fibre Channel Zone Servers, zoning databases, active zone sets, fabric locks, statistics and notifications via SNMP.

MIB.why: The whole document is two MIB modules written in SMIv2 for Fibre Channel zoning management; readers browsing MIB modules would expect it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

fibre channel.why: The subject is Fibre Channel zoning (zone sets, zones, members, fabric locks, Basic and Enhanced modes). The fibre channel tag is the closest fit in the taxonomy for Fibre Channel transport over IP/storage networking.
fibre channel.quote: it describes managed objects for information related to a Fibre Channel network's Zone Server.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol used by the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag covers it.
iFCP carries Fibre Channel over TCP/IP; this MIB manages FC zone servers and is not about iFCP.
Parent of fibre channel, so it is implied; no need to list it separately.
Zoning controls access between devices but the document is a management MIB, not about firewalls.
Parent of SNMP/MIB, implied by the MIB tag.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel zoning / FC native fabric management
gaps.why: The taxonomy only has a fibre channel tag scoped to Fibre Channel over IP transports, so native FC zone server management is not precisely covered.

RFC4937.title: IANA Considerations for PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE)
RFC4937.summary: Defines IANA registries and registration policies (First Come First Served) for PPPoE TAG values and PPPoE Active Discovery Code fields, and reserves the values already in use.

PPPoE.why: The whole document is about PPPoE's TAG and Code field name spaces, listing reserved values from RFC 2516, 4638 and 4938. Readers of the PPPoE subject would want it.
PPPoE.quote: This document provides guidance to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) regarding the registration of values related to the PPP over Ethernet Protocol (PPPoE)

rejected.why: The document is an IANA considerations document, but only for the PPPoE registries. It is not general IANA guidance, so the specific PPPoE tag fits better.
PPPoE is carried over Ethernet and is the subject here. PPP itself is only the payload and is not specified or extended.
Ethernet is only the substrate PPPoE runs over. The document does not address Ethernet itself.

RFC4938.title: PPP Over Ethernet (PPPoE) Extensions for Credit Flow and Link Metrics
RFC4938.summary: Extends PPPoE with a credit-based flow control mechanism (PADG/PADC packets, Credit tag) and a link quality metrics report (PADQ, Metrics tag) for variable-bandwidth media such as radio links.

PPPoE.why: The document defines new PPPoE discovery packets (PADG, PADC, PADQ) and tags, extending the PPPoE protocol itself.
PPPoE.quote: This document extends the Point-to-Point over Ethernet (PPPoE) Protocol with a credit-based flow control mechanism and Link Quality Metric report.

rejected.why: PPP is the payload that PPPoE carries; the document does not change PPP, only the PPPoE encapsulation.
Ethernet is only the medium under PPPoE; no Ethernet behaviour is specified.
The credit scheme is hop-by-hop flow control between a host radio and an access concentrator, not transport congestion control.
The IANA section only records PPPoE tag and code assignments, which is boilerplate.
Radio links are the motivating example, but the document does not cover cellular networks.

RFC4939.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for iSNS (Internet Storage Name Service)
RFC4939.summary: Defines the ISNS-MIB SMIv2 module for monitoring iSNS servers and their registered entities, portals, iSCSI/FC nodes, discovery domains and notifications via SNMP.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (ISNS-MIB) defined in SMIv2 with tables, textual conventions, notifications and compliance statements; MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: The iSNS MIB is designed to allow Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) to be used to monitor iSNS servers supporting iSCSI [RFC3720] and iFCP [RFC4172].

iSCSI.why: A substantial part of the MIB models iSCSI nodes, portal groups, control nodes and authentication methods registered in iSNS for iSCSI storage.
iSCSI.quote: The isnsRegIscsiNodeInfo section provides information on the registered iSCSI Nodes for a specific iSNS Server instance.

iFCP.why: The MIB includes FC node and port tables supporting iFCP clients, with a dedicated iFCP compliance statement.
iFCP.quote: The isnsRegFcPortInfo section provides information on the registered FC Ports for a specific iSNS Server instance.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
iSNS is a discovery/registration service, but this document only defines management objects for monitoring it, not the discovery protocol.
Mentioned only as a server discovery method bit in a textual convention.
Mentioned only as a server discovery method bit in a textual convention.
Portal security bits mention IKE/IPsec settings, but only as registered attributes; the document is not about IPsec.

gaps.name: iSNS (Internet Storage Name Service)
gaps.why: The protocol whose servers this MIB monitors has no tag of its own in the taxonomy (nearest are storage and service discovery); a storage name service tag would fit RFC 4171 and this MIB.

RFC4940.title: IANA Considerations for OSPF
RFC4940.summary: RFC 4940 (BCP 130) creates IANA registries for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 code points (options, packet types, LSA types, link types, opaque LSA types, Grace LSA TLVs) and defines assignment policies for their value ranges.

OSPF.why: The whole document defines registries and assignment policies for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 code points, so OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: This memo creates a number of OSPF registries and provides guidance to IANA for assignment of code points within these registries.

IANA.why: It is an IANA considerations BCP that defines assignment policies (Standards Action, Experimentation, Vendor Private Use, Reserved) for registries.
IANA.quote: This memo defines various OSPF registries for IANA to set up and maintain for OSPF code points.

rejected.why: The document covers OSPFv3 registries only alongside OSPFv2 registries; it is about OSPF as a whole, so the parent OSPF tag fits better.
RFC 3630 (OSPF TE extensions) is only cited in a note about the Opaque LSA registry, not addressed by the document.
Assignment policies are IANA registry rules for one protocol, not IETF process in its own right.

RFC4941.title: Privacy Extensions for Stateless Address Autoconfiguration in IPv6
RFC4941.summary: RFC 4941 specifies an extension to IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration that generates temporary, randomized interface identifiers and addresses that change over time, to prevent correlation and tracking of nodes by their IEEE-derived identifiers.

SLAAC.why: The document extends SLAAC with temporary addresses, defining how they are generated, lifetimes handled and regenerated on receipt of Router Advertisements.
SLAAC.quote: This document describes an extension to IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration for interfaces whose interface identifier is derived from an IEEE identifier.

privacy.why: The motivating problem is privacy: correlation and tracking via constant interface identifiers; the document analyses this threat and its limits (prefix, DNS names, cookies) in substantial depth.
privacy.quote: makes it more difficult for eavesdroppers and other information collectors to identify when different addresses used in different transactions actually correspond to the same node.

rejected.why: SLAAC is the more specific child tag and already covers the IPv6 addressing aspect.
MD5 is only used as the hash for generating identifiers and the document allows other algorithms; not about MD5.
Mentioned only as an alternative approach for temporary addresses; not specified or extended here.
Router Advertisements and DAD are used as mechanisms, but the document does not extend neighbor discovery.
DNS names as constant identifiers and reverse-lookup issues are discussed as implications only, not DNS specification.
Random generation is used in the algorithm but the document refers to RFC 4086 rather than addressing randomness requirements.

RFC4942.title: IPv6 Transition/Co-existence Security Considerations
RFC4942.summary: Informational overview of security considerations for IPv6 and IPv4/IPv6 coexistence, grouped into issues from the IPv6 protocol, transition mechanisms (6to4, Teredo, tunnelling) and deployment practice.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is about security of IPv6/IPv4 coexistence and transition mechanisms (6to4, Teredo, automatic tunnels, relays, IPv4-mapped addresses). The IPv6 transition topic fits directly.
IPv6 transition.quote: The transition from a pure IPv4 network to a network where IPv4 and IPv6 coexist brings a number of extra security considerations

IPv6.why: A large part of the document analyses security issues in the IPv6 protocol itself: extension headers, fragmentation, routing headers, privacy addresses, and deployment.
IPv6.quote: All IPv6 nodes must be able to process routing headers [RFC2460].

operational security.why: Section 4 gives operational security guidance on piloting, firewalls, router securing, and address planning for dual-stack networks.
operational security.quote: Sometimes the default IPv6 configuration is insecure.
operational security.section: 4.8. Operational Factors when Enabling IPv6 in the Network

firewall.why: Firewall handling of extension headers, fragments, ICMPv6 and tunnels is a recurring theme, with explicit firewall placement recommendations.
firewall.quote: The network architecture must provide separate IPv4 and IPv6 firewalls with tunneled IPv6 traffic
firewall.section: 3.3. Tunneling IPv6 through IPv4 Networks May Break IPv4 Network Security Assumptions

rejected.why: 6to4 is discussed as an example of automatic tunnelling, but the document is not specifically about it; RFC 3964 covers that.
It is mentioned alongside 6to4 as an automatic tunnelling mechanism, not as a main subject.
Neighbor discovery and SEND are covered in a few subsections, but they are only one of many issues.
ICMPv6 issues are covered in several subsections, but the document is not mainly about ICMP.
It gets only a short subsection, with security discussion deferred to other RFCs.
Appendix B covers IPv6 privacy, but it is a minor part of the document.

RFC4943.title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery On-Link Assumption Considered Harmful
RFC4943.summary: Informational memo explaining why the "on-link assumption" (treating all destinations as on-link when the default router list is empty) was removed from IPv6 Neighbor Discovery in RFC 4861, covering address selection, delay, multi-interface and security problems.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document analyses and documents a change to the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery conceptual sending algorithm (RFC 2461 to RFC 4861).
neighbor discovery.quote: This document describes the historical and background information behind the removal of the "on-link assumption" from the conceptual host sending algorithm defined in Neighbor Discovery for IP Version 6

rejected.why: Implied as the parent of neighbor discovery; the document is about a specific ND behaviour, not IPv6 in general.
Security discussion refers to ND threats (RFC 3756) but does not discuss Secure Neighbor Discovery.
DNS lookups returning AAAA/A records are only background for the problem scenario.
VPN software leaking IPv6 is a brief example of a security side effect; it is not about provider-provisioned VPNs.
ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable is mentioned only as the resulting behaviour.
The document discusses connection delays with multiple addresses but does not specify or discuss Happy Eyeballs racing.

RFC4944.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over IEEE 802.15.4 Networks
RFC4944.summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over IEEE 802.15.4 networks: a LoWPAN adaptation layer with fragmentation, mesh addressing and broadcast headers, interface identifier/link-local formation, address mapping, and the HC1/HC_UDP header compression.

6LoWPAN.why: The RFC is the base 6LoWPAN specification: adaptation layer, fragmentation, mesh headers and header compression for IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document defines the frame format for transmission of IPv6 [RFC2460] packets as well as the formation of IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses

rejected.why: IPv6 is the payload carried; the document is a link-layer adaptation, and the 6LoWPAN tag is more specific.
HC1/HC_UDP compression is substantial, but it is part of the 6LoWPAN tech tag chosen; no ROHC/IPHC compression is defined.
Interface identifier formation is defined for 802.15.4, but it is a small section within the 6LoWPAN adaptation.
Only the link-layer address option format is specified; ND itself is used, not extended.
UDP header compression is defined, but UDP itself is not the subject.
Mesh routing protocol is explicitly out of scope; only mesh addressing headers are defined.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.15.4 link layer
gaps.why: The document is about IP over IEEE 802.15.4 low-power PANs, but the taxonomy has no 802.15.4-specific tag other than the 6LoWPAN umbrella.

RFC4945.title: The Internet IP Security PKI Profile of IKEv1/ISAKMP, IKEv2, and PKIX
RFC4945.summary: Profiles IKEv1/ISAKMP, IKEv2 and the PKIX certificate profile for IPsec, specifying ID, CERTREQ and CERT payload handling, X.509 certificate and CRL requirements, and configuration data exchange formats.

IKE.why: The document specifies how IKEv1/ISAKMP and IKEv2 ID, CERTREQ and CERT payloads must be populated and processed, so it is about IKE.
IKE.quote: This document provides a profile of IKE and PKIX that defines the requirements for using PKI technology in the context of IKE/IPsec.

X.509.why: A large part of the document profiles X.509 certificate fields, extensions and CRL extensions for IKE use.
X.509.quote: Certificate Profile for IKEv1/ISAKMP and IKEv2
X.509.section: 5. Certificate Profile for IKEv1/ISAKMP and IKEv2

PKI.why: Covers trust anchors, CA behaviour, revocation checking via CRL/OCSP pointers and certificate exchange conventions for IPsec.
PKI.quote: defines the requirements for using PKI technology in the context of IKE/IPsec

rejected.why: IPsec is the context; the specified content is IKE/PKI, so the more specific IKE tag is used.
OCSP is mentioned only as an alternative revocation method in the AIA discussion.
Used only as an encoding for configuration data, not the subject.
Mentioned only in passing for securely mapping FQDNs.
Section 5.3 briefly discusses hash strength, but it is a small part of the document.
Only mentioned as the signature algorithm in certificates, not the subject.

RFC4946.title: Atom License Extension
RFC4946.summary: Defines an experimental Atom Syndication Format extension: a "license" link relation for associating machine-readable licenses with feeds and entries, including inheritance rules and relation to atom:rights.

Atom.why: The whole document extends the Atom Syndication Format with a license link relation, inheritance rules for entries/feeds/sources, and interaction with atom:rights.
Atom.quote: This document defines an extension to the Atom Syndication Format that can be used to add links to Atom feed or entry documents

web linking.why: The extension is essentially a new typed link relation ("license") with defined semantics, comparison and multiplicity rules, which readers of link relations would want.
web linking.quote: This specification defines one new Atom link relation type to be registered in the IANA Registry of Link Relations

rejected.why: URIs/IRIs are only referenced for href values and comparison; the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
IRI comparison and mapping are cited from RFC 3987 as supporting mechanisms, not the subject.
Atom is XML-based, but the document is not about XML usage itself; xml:base and xml:lang are mentioned only as Atom conventions.
Licenses here are content licenses on feeds, not IETF IPR or copyright provisions.
The IANA section merely registers one link relation; the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC4947.title: Address Resolution Mechanisms for IP Datagrams over MPEG-2 Networks
RFC4947.summary: Informational review of address resolution mechanisms (static, MPEG-2 SI/PSI tables such as INT/MMT/AIT, ARP/ND, DHCP, UDLR) for binding IPv4/IPv6 addresses to MPEG-2 Transport Streams over DVB, ATSC and DOCSIS, with link-layer encapsulation (ULE/MPE) implications.

DVB.why: The whole document is about address resolution for IP over MPEG-2/DVB broadcast links, including DVB INT, MMT, AIT tables and ULE/MPE encapsulation.
DVB.quote: This document describes the process of binding/associating IPv4/IPv6 addresses with MPEG-2 Transport Streams (TS).

ARP.why: A substantial part analyses ARP behaviour, scalability, delay and security over MPEG-2 links and encapsulations.
ARP.quote: Two IETF-defined protocols for mapping IP addresses to MAC/NPA addresses are the Address Resolution Protocol, ARP [RFC826], and the Neighbor Discovery protocol
ARP.section: 5. Mapping IP Addresses to MAC/NPA Addresses

neighbor discovery.why: IPv6 ND is analysed for large-delay links, DAD, SEND interaction and tuning over MPEG-2 networks.
neighbor discovery.quote: The default parameters specified in the ND protocol [RFC2461] can introduce interoperability problems
neighbor discovery.section: 5. Mapping IP Addresses to MAC/NPA Addresses

DHCP.why: A dedicated section gives DHCP tuning guidance for MPEG-2 links, and DOCSIS DHCP usage is discussed.
DHCP.quote: DHCP [RFC2131] and DHCPv6 [RFC3315] may be used over MPEG-2 Networks with bidirectional connectivity.

rejected.why: DOCSIS is only discussed as one example of static well-known PID configuration, not a main subject.
SEND is mentioned as a security option for ND, not examined in its own right.
Multicast address mapping is covered, but it is part of address resolution rather than multicast routing; no specific multicast protocol is the subject.
IPv6 is addressed alongside IPv4 but is not the document's subject.
Satellite links (DVB-S, DVB-RCS) appear as examples; the document is about MPEG-2 generally and DVB covers it.

gaps.name: MPEG-2 Transport Stream / ULE encapsulation
gaps.why: The document is largely about IP over MPEG-2 TS, including ULE and MPE encapsulations. The taxonomy has only DVB for this, which covers it only loosely.

RFC4948.title: Report from the IAB workshop on Unwanted Traffic March 9-10, 2006
RFC4948.summary: Report of the IAB workshop on unwanted Internet traffic (DDoS, spam, phishing, botnets), covering the underground economy, operator impact, existing and future countermeasures, research, and recommended IETF/IRTF/IAB actions.

DDoS.why: DDoS traffic and its mitigation (ACLs, BGP null routes, BCP 38, uRPF, research on filtering) are a central thread of the workshop report.
DDoS.quote: DDoS attacks often saturate access networks and make a significant impact on customers.

spam.why: Spam is one of the two main kinds of unwanted traffic discussed, along with its filtering and impact on enterprises.
spam.quote: Methods to discourage the dissemination of spam by punishing the spammers, such as Spam Harassment Reduction via Economic Disincentive (SHRED), were discussed.

operational security.why: Large parts of the report cover operator practice, incentives, tools, education and wishes for securing network infrastructure.
operational security.quote: Currently, backbone networks do not have effective diagnosis or mitigation tools against DDoS attacks.

rejected.why: The document is an IAB workshop report, so this tag fits well. However, it is the more specific subject tags above that readers would look for, and I chose those. Reconsider if workshop reports should be tagged alongside them.
BGP null routing and route hijacking are mentioned only as mitigation tools and vulnerabilities, not specified or analysed.
Core routing security is raised only briefly as a recommended step, not as a main subject.
Section 3.4 discusses DDoS against DNS servers, but only as one operator perspective.
IRC is mentioned as the underground market's command channel, not specified or analysed.
IDS is described briefly under research, not as a main subject.

gaps.name: Unwanted traffic / underground economy / botnets
gaps.why: The report's core subject is unwanted traffic and the underground economy behind it, which the taxonomy covers only partly through DDoS, spam and operational security.

RFC4949.title: Internet Security Glossary, Version 2
RFC4949.summary: RFC 4949 is a comprehensive glossary of information system security terminology, giving definitions and usage recommendations (endorsed/deprecated) for terms used in IETF documents.

terminology.why: The whole document is a glossary that standardizes security terms for use in IETF documents, which is exactly what a terminology page covers.
terminology.quote: This Glossary provides definitions, abbreviations, and explanations of terminology for information system security.

security.why: The subject matter of every entry is general security concepts, threats, models and mechanisms, not one specific mechanism.
security.quote: terminology that concerns information system security

rejected.why: There are many PKI entries (CA, certificate, CRL), but they are definitions within a general glossary, not the subject of the document.
Cryptographic terms are defined throughout, but the document is not about cryptographic algorithms or their use in protocols.
X.509 terms are defined in many entries, but X.509 is not profiled or specified here.
AH, ESP and IPsec are defined only as glossary entries.
The glossary guides terminology in IDOCs, but it is not about RFC format, style or publication.

RFC4950.title: ICMP Extensions for Multiprotocol Label Switching
RFC4950.summary: Defines an ICMP extension object (MPLS Label Stack Object) that lets LSRs append the incoming MPLS label stack to ICMP Time Exceeded and Destination Unreachable messages, enabling enhanced traceroute.

ICMP.why: The document specifies a new ICMP extension object, a new class number and C-type registry for ICMPv4/ICMPv6 multi-part messages.
ICMP.quote: This memo defines an extension object that can be appended to selected multi-part ICMP messages.

MPLS.why: The object carries the MPLS label stack entries as received by the LSR, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: This extension permits Label Switching Routers to append MPLS information to ICMP messages

traceroute.why: A dedicated section describes enhanced traceroute output showing MPLS labels at each hop.
traceroute.quote: The ICMP extension defined in this memo supports enhancements to TRACEROUTE.

rejected.why: The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA guidance.
ICMPv6 is mentioned only as one of two ICMP versions the extension applies to equally.
Not a taxonomy id; MPLS covers it.

RFC4951.title: Fail Over Extensions for Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) "failover"
RFC4951.summary: Defines L2TP extensions (failover capability negotiation, recovery tunnels, control/data channel reset, and new FSQ/FSR messages and AVPs) so L2TPv2/v3 endpoints can recover tunnel and session state after a failure.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TPv2 and L2TPv3 with new messages, AVPs and recovery procedures for failover, which is squarely about L2TP.
L2TP.quote: this document introduces a mechanism to bring the dynamic stateful information of a tunnel to a correct and consistent state after a failure.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a possible external failure-detection protocol for separate devices; the document is not about it.
L2TP MIBs are mentioned only to say they are rarely used for configuration; not a subject of the document.
L2TP is the specific tech tag that applies; the generic tunneling topic is not addressed in its own right.
Configuration parameters section is brief and defers to CLI or proprietary mechanisms; not a substantial subject.

RFC4952.title: Overview and Framework for Internationalized Email
RFC4952.summary: Informational overview and framework for the EAI (email address internationalization) document set, describing the UTF8SMTP SMTP extension, UTF-8 headers, downgrading, and related issues.

EAI.why: The document is the overview and framework for email address internationalization (EAI), introducing the series of specifications.
EAI.quote: Full use of electronic mail throughout the world requires that people be able to use their own names, written correctly in their own languages and scripts, as mailbox names

SMTP.why: A substantial part describes the UTF8SMTP SMTP extension, relay behaviour, and downgrading during SMTP transactions.
SMTP.quote: An SMTP extension, "UTF8SMTP" is specified as follows:

rejected.why: The IMAP UTF-8 extension is only mentioned as a companion document; this RFC does not specify it.
POP3 UTF-8 support is only listed in the document plan.
UTF-8 headers are defined in a companion document; here they are only summarized, and EAI is the more specific tag.
IDNA is referenced as background for the domain part; the document is about the local part and headers.
UTF-8 is the encoding relied upon, not the subject of the document.
DKIM is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a future coordination issue.

RFC4953.title: Defending TCP Against Spoofing Attacks
RFC4953.summary: Informational RFC analysing off-path spoofed RST (and related ICMP) attacks on TCP connections, notably BGP sessions, showing vulnerability grows with the square of bandwidth, and comparing transport-layer (TCP MD5, RST window attenuation, timestamps) and network-layer (address filtering, GTSM, IPsec) defences.

TCP.why: The document analyses TCP's RST handling and receive-window vulnerability and compares proposed TCP modifications (RST window attenuation, timestamp authentication, TCP/MD5).
TCP.quote: increases in the path bandwidth-delay product of a connection have sufficiently increased the receive window space that off-path third parties can brute-force generate a viable RST sequence number

IPsec.why: IPsec is discussed at length as the network-layer defence, with its keying challenges and the BTNS/anonymous-security alternatives, in Sections 3.2.2 and 5.2.
IPsec.quote: IPsec was designed specifically to establish and enforce authentication of a packet's source and contents in order to most directly and explicitly address this security vulnerability.

operational security.why: The document gives operational guidance on defending core infrastructure (BGP routers) against spoofing, including ingress filtering and TTL-based filtering (GTSM).
operational security.quote: address filtering is not a local solution that can be deployed to protect communicating pairs, but rather relies on a distributed infrastructure of trusted gateways

rejected.why: BGP sessions are the motivating example, but the document is about TCP's spoofing vulnerability, not BGP protocol or policy.
Section 4 discusses spoofed ICMP attacks on TCP, but the document says it is not the focus and treats it briefly.
The attacks affect BGP sessions, but the proposed defences are transport and network layer, not routing-protocol security mechanisms such as RPKI or BGPsec.
TCP MD5 is discussed as a defence, but the document is not about the MD5 algorithm itself.
The parent topic is too broad. IPsec is tagged directly, and the TCP-specific content fits better under the transport tags.

gaps.name: TCP spoofing / blind in-window attacks
gaps.why: The document is about transport-layer spoofing attack analysis and mitigation, and no taxonomy tag covers that threat subject. The nearest tag is TCP.

RFC4954.title: SMTP Service Extension for Authentication
RFC4954.summary: RFC 4954 defines the SMTP AUTH extension: an AUTH command that runs a SASL exchange (with optional security layer), an AUTH parameter on MAIL FROM, related status codes and Received header requirements. It obsoletes RFC 2554.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension: the AUTH verb, the AUTH parameter on MAIL FROM, and new reply codes.
SMTP.quote: This document defines a Simple Mail Transport Protocol (SMTP) extension whereby an SMTP client may indicate an authentication mechanism to the server

SASL.why: It defines the SASL profile for SMTP: service name, challenge/response encoding, initial response handling, and mandatory PLAIN over TLS. SASL readers would want this.
SASL.quote: This extension includes a profile of the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) for SMTP.

rejected.why: TLS is a security substrate (STARTTLS, PLAIN over TLS). The document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
This is a parent of SMTP, which is the more specific tag.
Base64 is only the encoding of challenges and responses, not the subject.
Certificate verification rules for PLAIN over TLS are a small part, not the subject.
SASL is the more specific tag for authentication here.

RFC4955.title: DNS Security (DNSSEC) Experiments
RFC4955.summary: RFC 4955 defines a methodology for deploying experimental, non-backwards-compatible DNSSEC changes by using unknown or private algorithm identifiers so standard validators treat experimental zones as insecure.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies how to run DNSSEC experiments using unknown algorithm identifiers in DS records and signatures, relying on validator behaviour from RFC 4035. It is about DNSSEC deployment and algorithm identifiers.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes a standard methodology for setting up DNSSEC experiments.

rejected.why: DNS is the underlying system. The document is specifically about DNSSEC, which is the more specific tag, and it explicitly excludes experiments with the core DNS protocol.
Algorithm number allocation is mentioned only briefly as an option (private vs IANA-allocated numbers). It is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC4956.title: DNS Security (DNSSEC) Opt-In
RFC4956.summary: Defines an experimental DNSSEC "Opt-In" extension that lets zones omit NSEC records for insecure delegations by tagging covering NSEC records via the NSEC type-bit, specifying server and resolver validation changes.

DNSSEC.why: The document extends DNSSEC NSEC semantics, validation rules, AD bit use and server behaviour for insecure delegations. It is squarely about DNSSEC.
DNSSEC.quote: Using "Opt-In", a zone administrator can choose to remove insecure delegations from the NSEC chain.

rejected.why: DNS is implied as the parent of DNSSEC; the document is about the security extension specifically, not general DNS.
Dynamic Update is mentioned only to say servers must refuse updates to Opt-In zones until rules are defined; it is not a substantial subject.
The DO bit is cited only in the appendix algorithm; the document does not specify EDNS.

RFC4957.title: Link-Layer Event Notifications for Detecting Network Attachments
RFC4957.summary: Informational catalogue of link-layer event notifications (link up and auxiliary info) available from GPRS, cdma2000, IEEE 802.11 and IEEE 802.3 that IP can use to detect network attachment (DNA) changes.

cellular.why: A substantial section covers GPRS/3GPP and cdma2000/3GPP2 link-up events, PDP context and PPP/IPCP, and the IP configuration they provide.
cellular.quote: GSM Packet Radio System (GPRS) provides packet-switched data transmission over a cellular network

WiFi.why: A dedicated section covers when 802.11 generates link up and what BSSID/SSID information means for subnet change.
WiFi.quote: In a WiFi network that uses Robust Secure Network (RSN [IEEE-802.11i]), successful completion of the 4-way handshake between the STA and AP commences the availability of IP service.

Ethernet.why: The largest section covers Ethernet link integrity tests, bridging/STP delays and LLDP, and their effect on link-up notifications.
Ethernet.quote: IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD (commonly referred to as Ethernet) is the most commonly deployed Local Area Network technology in use today.

link layer.why: The document is a cross-technology catalogue of link-layer events delivered to IP, not tied to one medium, so the general link layer topic fits.
link layer.quote: Link-layer event notifications can help IP expeditiously detect configuration changes.

rejected.why: DNAv6 is the motivating use case, but the document does not specify IPv6 behaviour.
PPP/IPCP is only how cdma2000 signals link up, not the subject.
Router solicitation is mentioned only as an example action after link up.
Fast handover work is explicitly out of scope; the document only mentions it in passing.
It fits the cdma2000 subsection, but the child tag is too narrow for a document covering four technologies. The parent cellular tag is used instead.
GPRS is covered in one subsection only, and the GSM tag is about SIM authentication and SMS transport.

gaps.name: Detecting Network Attachment (DNA)
gaps.why: The document supports DNA solutions, and the taxonomy has no tag for detecting network attachment or link-layer indications.

RFC4958.title: A Framework for Supporting Emergency Telecommunications Services (ETS) within a Single Administrative Domain
RFC4958.summary: Informational framework surveying protocols and mechanisms (MPLS, RSVP, COPS policy, subnetwork QoS, multicast, discovery, Diffserv) that could support Emergency Telecommunications Services within a single administrative domain, without specifying solutions.

emergency services.why: The whole document is a framework for ETS, emergency preparedness communications; no more specific child (LoST, eCall) applies.
emergency services.quote: This document presents a framework for supporting Emergency Telecommunications Services (ETS) within the scope of a single administrative domain.

QoS.why: Central theme is QoS and preferential treatment via reservations, labels and queuing; the document surveys several QoS mechanisms collectively.
QoS.quote: The primary objective is to provide a target measure of service within a domain for flows that have been labeled for ETS.

RSVP.why: Has a dedicated section on RSVP, its intra-domain deployment and relation to ETS.
RSVP.quote: The original design of RSVP, together with the Integrated Services model, was one of an end-to-end signaling capability to set up a path of reserved resources

Diffserv.why: Dedicated section on Diffserv codepoints (AF, EF) for ETS within a domain.
Diffserv.quote: There are a number of examples where Diffserv [rfc2474] has been deployed strictly within a domain, with no extension of service to neighboring domains.

COPS.why: Policy section discusses COPS, COPS-RSVP and COPS-PR deployment status for ETS.
COPS.quote: The Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol [rfc2748] was defined to provide policy control over QoS signaling protocols, such as RSVP.

MPLS.why: Dedicated section on MPLS and its Diffserv support for traffic engineering of ETS traffic.
MPLS.quote: MPLS signaling produces Labeled Switched Paths (LSPs) through a network of Label Switch Routers [rfc3031].

rejected.why: Section 4.5 covers multicast for ETS, but it is one of seven topic areas surveyed; less central than the QoS mechanisms.
Mentioned only as one discovery candidate in Section 4.6.
Only a subsection on cable subnetwork QoS; not the focus.
802.11e is briefly described in one subsection only.
Mobile IP is only borrowed for terminology and a brief scenario.
Anycast is mentioned briefly as a discovery option.

gaps.name: Emergency Telecommunications Services (ETS) / IEPREP
gaps.why: The taxonomy's emergency services tag covers it generally, but there is no tag specific to ETS or priority/preferential service for emergency preparedness.

RFC4959.title: IMAP Extension for Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) Initial Client Response
RFC4959.summary: Defines the IMAP SASL-IR capability, which adds an optional initial client response argument to the IMAP AUTHENTICATE command to save a round trip during SASL authentication.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP by adding an optional argument to AUTHENTICATE and a new SASL-IR capability.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an extension to IMAP which allows clients and servers to avoid this round trip by allowing an initial client response argument to the IMAP AUTHENTICATE command.

SASL.why: The extension is about how SASL's initial client response is carried in IMAP, including handling for mechanisms that do or do not support it. SASL readers would want it.
SASL.quote: If this second argument is present, it represents the contents of the "initial client response" defined in Section 5.1 of [RFC4422].
SASL.section: 3. IMAP Changes to the IMAP AUTHENTICATE Command

rejected.why: TLS only appears in the examples as the protection layer. The document defines nothing about TLS.
The initial response is Base64-encoded per RFC 4648, but the document only uses the encoding. It does not define or extend it.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the formal syntax section.
IMAP is covered by its own tag, which sits under email. The email parent is implied.

RFC4960.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC4960.summary: RFC 4960 is the standards-track specification of SCTP, a reliable, message-oriented, multi-homed transport protocol with multiple streams. It defines the packet and chunk formats, association setup and teardown, data transfer, congestion control, fault management and the upper-layer interface, and it obsoletes RFC 2960 and RFC 3309.

SCTP.why: The document is the core specification of SCTP, covering its protocol, procedures and parameters.
SCTP.quote: SCTP is a reliable transport protocol operating on top of a connectionless packet network such as IP.

rejected.why: Section 7 specifies SCTP's congestion control, but it adapts the TCP algorithms for SCTP and does not define a general scheme. The SCTP tag covers it.
TCP is only a comparison point and the source of the algorithms SCTP adapts. The document does not specify or extend it.
CRC32c is defined in Appendix B as SCTP's packet checksum. That is a component of SCTP and not a general checksum topic.
Section 7.3 only says endpoints should apply the existing PMTU discovery methods per destination address. It adds no new mechanism.
PSTN signaling transport is the motivation for SCTP. The document specifies a general transport and not the SIGTRAN adaptation layers.

RFC4961.title: Symmetric RTP / RTP Control Protocol (RTCP)
RFC4961.summary: BCP recommending that bidirectional RTP and RTCP sessions use one UDP port pair for sending and receiving ("symmetric RTP/RTCP"), defining the terms and explaining why NATs and relays need it.

RTP.why: The document defines and recommends a port-usage practice for RTP and RTCP sessions. RTCP has no separate tag because it is covered by the same recommendation, and the parent RTP tag fits.
RTP.quote: it is RECOMMENDED that symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP always be used for bidirectional RTP media streams.

NAT traversal.why: A substantial part of the document explains that symmetric ports are required for media to traverse NATs and media relays. This is the main motivation for the practice.
NAT traversal.quote: Such NATs require that endpoints use symmetric UDP ports to establish bidirectional traffic.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport whose ports are used. The document gives guidance specific to RTP/RTCP, not about UDP itself.
NAT behaviour is cited as a motivation and is specified elsewhere (RFC 4787). The document does not specify NAT behaviour.
RTCP is covered by the same recommendation as RTP. The document is not about RTCP feedback or reports, so the parent RTP tag is the better fit.
SDP is mentioned only as a way to communicate the receive port.
TURN is cited only as an example of a media relay.

RFC4962.title: Guidance for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) Key Management
RFC4962.summary: BCP giving architectural guidance and requirements for designers of AAA key management protocols (EAP, RADIUS, Diameter, secure association protocols), such as algorithm independence, fresh keys, key scope, key naming and context binding.

AAA.why: The whole document sets requirements for AAA key management and the AAA protocols involved. RADIUS and Diameter are discussed as examples, not specified, so the AAA framework tag fits best.
AAA.quote: This document provides guidance to designers of Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) key management protocols.

key management.why: The core requirements cover session key freshness, key scope, key naming, key hierarchy and binding keys to context. These are key-management design guidance.
key management.quote: The overall goal of AAA key management is to provide cryptographic keying material in situations where key derivation cannot be used by the peer and authenticator.

EAP.why: EAP pass-through keying and EAP method requirements are a substantial part of the guidance, including the mandatory algorithm and key-strength rules for EAP methods.
EAP.quote: This section provides guidance to AAA protocol designers, EAP method designers, and security association protocol designers.

rejected.why: RADIUS is cited as an example and criticised (MD5 integrity, no algorithm negotiation), but the document does not specify or extend it.
Diameter is mentioned only as an example AAA protocol and for key confidentiality; the document is not about it.
IKEv2 and IPsec appear only in the history appendix and as an example of EAP use.
The EAP and AAA tags already cover the authentication aspects, so a generic authentication tag would be redundant.
The document advises on algorithm independence generally but does not address any particular algorithm or cryptographic primitive.

RFC4963.title: IPv4 Reassembly Errors at High Data Rates
RFC4963.summary: Informational note showing that the 16-bit IPv4 ID field wraps quickly at high data rates, causing mis-associated fragments that slip past 16-bit transport checksums and corrupt data, with experiments and operational mitigations.

IPv4.why: The document analyses a failure of IPv4 fragmentation and reassembly caused by the ID field size, so it is about IPv4 itself.
IPv4.quote: At high data rates, the 16-bit IP identification field is not large enough to prevent frequent incorrectly assembled IP fragments

checksum.why: A substantial part analyses how weak 16-bit transport checksums let corrupted reassembled datagrams through, and suggests stronger integrity checks.
checksum.quote: The TCP/UDP checksum is only 16 bits in length.

PMTUD.why: Path MTU Discovery is the main prevention discussed, including how disabling DF handling exposes protocols to the problem.
PMTUD.quote: The most straightforward way to avoid mis-association is to avoid fragmentation altogether by implementing Path MTU Discovery

rejected.why: UDP bulk transfer was only the test vehicle for the experiments; the document is not about UDP itself.
TCP is mentioned only for its checksum and congestion control effects, not specified or analysed.
Tunnels are discussed as one case of fragmentation exposure, but only briefly, not as a subject of the document.
IPv6 is mentioned only as less vulnerable because of its 32-bit identification field.
IPsec AH is mentioned only as one mitigation by integrity checking.
Effects on loss-based congestion control are mentioned in passing only.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation and reassembly
gaps.why: The core subject is IPv4 fragmentation and reassembly errors; the taxonomy has no specific tag for fragmentation, so IPv4 is the closest fit.

RFC4964.title: The P-Answer-State Header Extension to the Session Initiation Protocol for the Open Mobile Alliance Push to Talk over Cellular
RFC4964.summary: Informational RFC defining the private SIP P-Answer-State header, used by OMA Push to talk over Cellular so PTT Servers can signal Unconfirmed/Confirmed answer state and enable media buffering, with applicability limits and example flows.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP header field, its syntax, procedures for UAs, B2BUAs and proxies, and IANA registration in the SIP registry. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document describes a private Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) header (P-header) used by the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) for Push to talk over Cellular (PoC)

rejected.why: SDP offers and answers appear in the flows, but the document only notes that a new SDP attribute was rejected as an alternative. It does not specify or extend SDP.
The conference focus appears in the example flows, but the document is about answer-state signalling, not conferencing frameworks.
PoC is a cellular service, but the document defines a SIP header and has no IP-over-3GPP content.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as hop-by-hop protection, so it is boilerplate rather than subject matter.
The document uses SIP REFER, NOTIFY and sipfrag, but these are not SIMPLE event packages or presence.

gaps.name: Push to talk over Cellular (PoC)
gaps.why: The document is specific to OMA PoC half-duplex push-to-talk, and the taxonomy has no PoC or push-to-talk tag.

RFC4965.title: CableLabs - IETF Standardization Collaboration
RFC4965.summary: Informational RFC describing the liaison and collaboration framework between the IETF and CableLabs, covering document sharing, participation, liaison managers, formal liaison statements and contributions.

IETF process.why: The document defines how the IETF interacts with an external SDO: liaison managers, liaison statements, participation and contribution procedures. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document contains a set of principles and guidelines that serves as the basis for establishing a liaison relationship between the Cable Television Laboratories, Inc. and the Internet Engineering Task Force

rejected.why: DOCSIS is mentioned only as one CableLabs project. The document does not specify or discuss the technology.
IPR policy is referenced only as the rules governing contributions and liaison statements. It is not the subject of the document.
The IANA section only asks IANA to use a stable URL format when citing CableLabs specifications. It is boilerplate-like and not the main body.
DHCP options are mentioned as an example of a submission, and DHCWG appears in a list of working groups. The document is not about DHCP.

RFC4966.title: Reasons to Move the Network Address Translator - Protocol Translator (NAT-PT) to Historic Status
RFC4966.summary: Informational analysis of the problems with NAT-PT (RFC 2766), IPv6-IPv4 protocol translation with a DNS ALG, concluding that RFC 2766 should be reclassified as Historic.

IPv6 transition.why: The document analyses NAT-PT as an IPv6/IPv4 transition and translation mechanism and recommends moving it to Historic. NAT-PT has no child tag of its own, so the IPv6 transition topic is the best fit.
IPv6 transition.quote: defines a set of network-layer translation mechanisms designed to allow nodes that only support IPv4 to communicate with nodes that only support IPv6

NAT.why: NAT-PT and NAPT-PT are NAT variants. Much of the analysis carries over from traditional NAT issues (RFC 2663, RFC 3027): embedded addresses, binding state decay, fragmentation and port redirection.
NAT.quote: NAT-PT has a different status as a transition mechanism for IPv6

SIIT.why: NAT-PT is built on SIIT, and the generic translator issues in Section 2 apply to any SIIT-based translator. Section 2.4 analyses the semantic loss in SIIT header translation.
SIIT.quote: Protocol translation is performed using the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT) defined in [RFC2765].

DNS.why: Sections 3 and 4 cover the DNS-ALG: its address selection, translated RR validity, A and AAAA query handling and multi-addressed nodes.
DNS.quote: issues with the DNS-ALG must be considered as issues for the whole specification.

rejected.why: Only Section 4.5 discusses it, as one of many issues, namely that the DNS-ALG breaks signatures. The document is not about DNSSEC.
Only Section 2.6 covers SCTP multihoming through NAT-PT. It is one issue among many.
Section 2.7 covers it briefly as an issue for NAT-PT. The document is not about Mobile IPv6.
Mentioned only as being broken by translation in Section 2.1, so it is not a subject of the document.
Section 2.8 is a short discussion of multicast being untranslatable by NAT-PT, not a main subject.

gaps.name: NAT-PT (Network Address Translator - Protocol Translator)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for NAT-PT or for IPv6/IPv4 protocol translators in general. IPv6 transition is used as the closest fit.

RFC4967.title: Dial String Parameter for the Session Initiation Protocol Uniform Resource Identifier
RFC4967.summary: RFC 4967 defines a new "dialstring" value for the SIP/SIPS URI "user" parameter, so a dial string with a required phone-context can be carried in a SIP URI and distinguished from a plain user part.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP/SIPS URI with a new user-parameter value and defines its syntax and proxy/B2BUA handling. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This memo creates a new value for the user parameter "dialstring", so that one may specify "user=dialstring" to encode a dial string as a 'sip:' or 'sips:' URI.

tel URI.why: The document builds on the tel URI's phone-context parameter and visual-separator syntax. It also addresses the tel URI's exclusion of dial strings and the translation of dial strings to tel URIs.
tel URI.quote: When the "user=dialstring" is used, a context parameter, as defined in [RFC3966], MUST be specified.

rejected.why: The change is to the SIP URI parameter, which is covered by the SIP tag. It is not about URI syntax or schemes in general.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as protection for dial strings sent across the Internet.
The IANA section only registers the new parameter value, which is boilerplate.
Dial strings and DTMF come from the PSTN, but the document only defines a URI parameter and does not cover interworking or gateway control.

RFC4968.title: Analysis of IPv6 Link Models for 802.16 Based Networks
RFC4968.summary: Informational analysis of three IPv6 link models (shared prefix, point-to-point, Ethernet-like) for IEEE 802.16/WiMAX networks, covering prefix assignment, autoconfiguration, DAD, renumbering, dormant mode and routing, with applicability recommendations.

WiMAX.why: The whole document analyses how to run IPv6 over IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) networks and which link model fits each deployment.
WiMAX.quote: This document provides different IPv6 link models that are suitable for IEEE 802.16 based networks

IPv6.why: Substantial discussion of IPv6 prefix assignment, address autoconfiguration, DAD and link definitions under each model.
IPv6.quote: In this model, all MSs attached to an AR share one or more prefixes for constructing their global IPv6 addresses

renumbering.why: A dedicated section analyses renumbering effects on each link model, including RA withdrawal and DHCP lease handling.
renumbering.quote: If the downstream prefixes managed by the AR are involved in renumbering, it may be necessary to renumber each link under the AR.

rejected.why: Neighbor Discovery and DAD are used and discussed, including a Relay DAD optimisation, but the document does not specify or extend ND itself.
PPP and PPPoE are mentioned only as one way to realise the point-to-point link model.
MLD snooping is used as a supporting mechanism for Relay DAD and multicast, but it is not the subject of the document.
The Ethernet-like link model is one option analysed, but the document is about IPv6 over 802.16 rather than IP over Ethernet.
Stateless autoconfiguration is applied as specified in RFC 2462 and is not analysed as a subject in its own right.
DHCP is only mentioned in passing for address assignment and renumbering.

RFC4969.title: IANA Registration for vCard Enumservice
RFC4969.summary: Registers the "vCard" ENUM Enumservice (E2U+vcard) with http/https URIs, allowing an ENUM domain name for an E.164 number to point to a vCard describing its user, with privacy and access-control considerations.

ENUM.why: The document is an ENUM Enumservice registration, defining how NAPTR records for E.164 numbers refer to vCards.
ENUM.quote: This memo registers the Enumservice "vCard" using the URI schemes "http" and "https".

vCard.why: The Enumservice's purpose is to locate vCard contact data for a number; vCard readers would want this RFC.
vCard.quote: refer from an ENUM domain name to a vCard instance describing the user of the respective E.164 number.

rejected.why: DNS (NAPTR records) is the substrate for ENUM; nothing new is defined about DNS itself.
HTTP/HTTPS is only the URI scheme used to fetch the vCard, not specified or extended.
Mentioned only briefly in security considerations (NSEC zone-walking advice).
Digest authentication is mentioned as a way to restrict access, but is not the subject.
Privacy considerations are a section of the document, but the document is not about privacy threat models in its own right.
URI schemes http/https are just listed in the registration template.

RFC4970.title: Extensions to OSPF for Advertising Optional Router Capabilities
RFC4970.summary: Defines the OSPF Router Information (RI) LSA for OSPFv2 (opaque type 4) and OSPFv3 (function code 12) to advertise optional router capabilities, with an informational capabilities TLV and flooding-scope rules.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with a new RI LSA and capability TLV.
OSPF.quote: This document proposes extensions to OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 for advertising optional router capabilities.

OSPFv3.why: A substantial part specifies the OSPFv3 RI LSA format, function code and registry.
OSPFv3.quote: The OSPFv3 Router Information LSA has a function code of 12 while the S1/S2 bits are dependent on the desired flooding scope for the LSA.

rejected.why: TE is only one capability bit advertised; the document is not about traffic engineering.
IANA section is boilerplate-like registry creation; not the main subject.
Parent of OSPF, implied.

RFC4971.title: Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) Extensions for Advertising Router Information
RFC4971.summary: Defines the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV (type 242), carrying sub-TLVs, with flooding scope flags (S and D bits), leaking rules between levels, and procedures for advertising router capabilities.

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol with a new TLV, flooding scope flags, level leaking rules and procedures for LSP updates.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines a new optional IS-IS TLV named CAPABILITY, formed of multiple sub-TLVs, which allows a router to announce its capabilities

rejected.why: MPLS Traffic Engineering is only used as illustrative motivation; the document states the mechanism is generic and not limited to it.
TE examples (mesh-group, P2MP, inter-area TE) are illustrations only; sub-TLV definitions are out of scope.
PCE discovery is mentioned only as a possible future use to be discussed in the PCE WG.
Authentication (RFC 3567, IS-IS HMAC) is mentioned only in Security Considerations as boilerplate.
The TLV code point assignment is a routine IANA Considerations item, not the document's subject.

RFC4972.title: Routing Extensions for Discovery of Multiprotocol (MPLS) Label Switch Router (LSR) Traffic Engineering (TE) Mesh Membership
RFC4972.summary: Defines OSPF and IS-IS TLVs (carried in Router Information LSA / Router Capability TLV) so LSRs can advertise membership in MPLS TE mesh-groups, enabling automatic discovery for building full meshes of TE LSPs.

traffic engineering.why: The document's purpose is automating discovery of TE mesh-group members to set up meshes of MPLS TE LSPs; it addresses MPLS traffic engineering deployment in its own right.
traffic engineering.quote: The setup of a full mesh of TE LSPs among a set of LSRs is a common deployment scenario of MPLS Traffic Engineering

OSPF.why: Specifies a new OSPF TLV and procedures for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 flooding scopes.
OSPF.quote: The OSPF TE-MESH-GROUP TLV (advertised in an OSPF router information LSA defined in [RFC4970]) has the following format:

IS-IS.why: Specifies a new IS-IS sub-TLV in the Router Capability TLV and its procedures.
IS-IS.quote: The IS-IS TE-MESH-GROUP sub-TLV (advertised in the IS-IS CAPABILITY TLV defined in [RFC4971]) is composed of 1 octet for the type

MPLS.why: The mesh members are MPLS LSRs connected by TE LSPs; MPLS readers would want this, though the work is IGP extensions.
MPLS.quote: Routing extensions are specified in this document, allowing for dynamic discovery of the TE mesh-group members.

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is covered by the OSPF extension; its handling is brief and the TLV is the same, so the OSPF tag suffices.
TE LSP signalling is explicitly out of scope; the mechanism for creating LSPs is implementation specific.
The document concerns plain MPLS TE, not generalized MPLS.
IPv6 addresses are merely one address format in the TLV, not a subject of the document.

RFC4973.title: OSPF-xTE: Experimental Extension to OSPF for Traffic Engineering
RFC4973.summary: Defines OSPF-xTE, an experimental OSPF extension with new TE LSAs, a separate TE-LSDB and TE adjacency handling for packet and non-packet (SONET/TDM, optical) networks, as an alternative to the Opaque-LSA approach of RFC 3630.

OSPF.why: The document specifies new LSA types, TLVs, adjacency and flooding changes and interface data structure changes to OSPF.
OSPF.quote: This document defines OSPF-xTE, an experimental traffic engineering (TE) extension to the link-state routing protocol OSPF.

traffic engineering.why: The document is about advertising TE metrics (bandwidth, SRLG, color, cost) into a TE-LSDB for computing TE circuit paths.
traffic engineering.quote: The objective of OSPF-xTE is to discover TE network topology and disseminate TE metrics within an autonomous system (AS).

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are the TE circuits being served, but the document only advertises TE metrics and does not specify MPLS.
Non-packet TDM/lambda/fiber switching is covered, but only through OSPF advertisement, not GMPLS itself.
Only referenced for signalling and listed as a supported protocol code; signalling is explicitly out of scope.
Only referenced for signalling and listed as a supported protocol code; signalling is explicitly out of scope.
SONET/SDH rings are modelled by a positional-ring LSA, but the document is not about IP over SONET.
The IANA section only registers LSA types, TLV values and a multicast address, so it is boilerplate here.

RFC4974.title: Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) RSVP-TE Signaling Extensions in Support of Calls
RFC4974.summary: Specifies GMPLS RSVP-TE extensions (Notify-based Call setup/teardown, Call IDs, LINK_CAPABILITY object, ADMIN_STATUS C bit) to support Calls separate from LSP Connections, e.g., for ASON.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling (updating RFC 3473) with Call procedures, new objects, and error codes; this is the GMPLS signalling subject.
GMPLS.quote: This document specifies how GMPLS Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) signaling may be used and extended to support Calls.

rejected.why: Closely related, but RSVP-TE is the substrate here, and GMPLS is the more specific home for this GMPLS-specific extension.
RSVP messages (Notify, SESSION) are used as the carrier, but the document is about GMPLS Call signalling rather than RSVP itself.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as an optional protection mechanism.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a suggested key exchange.
LSPs are the Connections, but the document is specifically about GMPLS Calls, so the more specific GMPLS tag applies.
IANA Considerations only register a new RSVP object, error codes and a bit; boilerplate.

RFC4975.title: The Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)
RFC4975.summary: Specifies MSRP, a text-based, connection-oriented protocol for exchanging instant messages in sessions, with SEND/REPORT methods, chunking, msrp/msrps URIs, and SIP/SDP offer/answer negotiation.

MSRP.why: The document defines MSRP itself: framing, chunking, SEND/REPORT requests, response codes, connection model, and URIs.
MSRP.quote: This document describes the Message Session Relay Protocol, a protocol for transmitting a series of related instant messages in the context of a session.

SDP.why: A substantial section defines new SDP attributes (path, accept-types, accept-wrapped-types, max-size) and the TCP/MSRP proto values, which SDP readers need.
SDP.quote: This document defines a handful of new SDP parameters to set up MSRP sessions.
SDP.section: 8. Using MSRP with SIP and SDP

rejected.why: SIP is the rendezvous mechanism for MSRP sessions, not specified or extended here.
TLS is used for msrps security; the document defines no new TLS extension or mechanism.
TCP is only the transport substrate for MSRP.
S/MIME protection of payloads is discussed only in security considerations.
MSRP is already a child of instant messaging, so MSRP is the more specific tag.
The msrp/msrps URI schemes are defined, but as part of the MSRP protocol, so a separate URI tag is not needed.

RFC4976.title: Relay Extensions for the Message Sessions Relay Protocol (MSRP)
RFC4976.summary: RFC 4976 extends MSRP with relay intermediaries, defining the AUTH method, Use-Path header, HTTP Digest client authentication, TLS requirements for relays, forwarding rules, and DNS SRV-based relay discovery.

MSRP.why: The document is an extension of MSRP that specifies relay behavior, the AUTH method, and new headers.
MSRP.quote: This document introduces the notion of message relay intermediaries to MSRP and describes the extensions necessary to use them.

HTTP authentication.why: A substantial part of the document profiles HTTP Digest authentication for AUTH requests, with restrictions and modifications (no Basic, no auth-int, required qop/cnonce) and new header usage within MSRP.
HTTP authentication.quote: The client uses HTTP Digest authentication [1] to authenticate to the relay.

rejected.why: TLS is used as the security substrate for relay connections; the document sets requirements for its use but defines no new TLS extension or mechanism.
SIP is only the rendezvous/signaling protocol that MSRP sessions are set up with; the document leaves that relationship unchanged.
SDP is used only to carry the path attribute and appears in an example; the document does not define SDP extensions.
A DNS SRV lookup for _msrps is used for relay discovery, but this is a small part of the document and uses existing DNS mechanisms.
S/MIME is mentioned in the security section as an optional end-to-end protection mechanism but the document is not about it.
NAT traversal is mentioned only as an example of why a relay might be used.

gaps.name: MSRP (Message Session Relay Protocol)
gaps.why: The MSRP tag id in my tags list is not in the taxonomy. The closest fit is instant messaging, which covers session-mode instant messaging and the MSRP sibling, so MSRP itself has no taxonomy entry.

RFC4977.title: Problem Statement: Dual Stack Mobility
RFC4977.summary: Problem statement explaining why dual stack mobile nodes should not need to run both Mobile IPv4 and Mobile IPv6, and recommending work so that either protocol can manage mobility for both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document recommends extending MIPv6 to handle IPv4 home addresses and care-of addresses, and analyses its signalling coupling to address family.
Mobile IPv6.quote: It should be possible to create IPv4 extensions to Mobile IPv6 so that an IPv4 and IPv6 capable mobile node can register its IPv4 and IPv6 home addresses

Mobile IPv4.why: The document equally recommends extending MIPv4 to support IPv6 addresses, and discusses its burdens in dual stack deployments.
Mobile IPv4.quote: It should be possible to create IPv6 extensions to Mobile IPv4 so that an IPv4 and IPv6 capable mobile node can register its IPv4 and IPv6 home addresses

rejected.why: Section 3.5 only briefly says existing transition mechanisms do not help. The document is about mobility, not transition mechanisms.
IPv6 is the context for dual stack, but the document is about mobility protocols and not IPv6 itself.
Security associations are mentioned only as duplicated credentials, not as a subject of the document.
SIP is cited once as an example of a protocol independent of address family.
The two specific child technology tags fit better, and the parent is implied.

RFC4978.title: The IMAP COMPRESS Extension
RFC4978.summary: Defines the IMAP COMPRESS extension, which adds a COMPRESS command and COMPRESS=DEFLATE capability so an IMAP connection can be compressed with DEFLATE, including ordering with SASL/TLS layers and efficiency guidance.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP command, capability and response code, so it is an extension of IMAP.
IMAP.quote: The COMPRESS extension allows an IMAP connection to be effectively and efficiently compressed.

DEFLATE.why: DEFLATE is the sole compression mechanism specified, and section 4 gives zlib/DEFLATE usage guidance (flushes, levels, windowBits) for implementers.
DEFLATE.quote: The DEFLATE algorithm (defined in [RFC1951]) is standard, widely available and fairly efficient, so it is the only algorithm defined by this document.

rejected.why: TLS and its compression (RFC 3749) are compared and the layering order is specified, but the document defines nothing new in TLS; it is only a related mechanism.
Only the ordering of compression relative to SASL security layers is mentioned; SASL itself is not the subject.
The more specific DEFLATE tag fits the compression subject, so the parent is not listed.
ABNF is used only to write the formal syntax, so it is notation rather than the subject.
The document is about IMAP, which is the more specific tag; email in general is not the subject.
The zlib API is mentioned in informative efficiency guidance, but the document does not specify the zlib format.

RFC4979.title: IANA Registration for Enumservice 'XMPP'
RFC4979.summary: Registers the 'XMPP' Enumservice with IANA so that xmpp URIs can be provisioned in ENUM NAPTR records for E.164 numbers, with guidance on authority components and IRI-to-URI mapping.

ENUM.why: The document defines a new ENUM Enumservice registration, with a template, usage rules and a NAPTR example. Readers of ENUM would want it.
ENUM.quote: This Enumservice specifically allows the use of 'xmpp' Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) in the context of E.164 Number Mapping (ENUM).

XMPP.why: The Enumservice is specifically for XMPP entities. The document covers how xmpp URIs/IRIs are used in this context, including authority component handling.
XMPP.quote: This Enumservice indicates that the resource identified is an XMPP entity.

rejected.why: DNS is only the substrate that ENUM NAPTR records are stored in. The document defines nothing new about DNS.
The document uses the xmpp URI scheme registered in RFC 4622 and mentions IRI-to-URI mapping. It does not define or extend a URI scheme.
The IRI-to-URI mapping section only points to RFC 3987 for the procedure. It is a minor point and not the subject of the document.
The IANA registration is the mechanism for this ENUM-specific document. It is not a subject of IANA guidance.

RFC4980.title: Analysis of Multihoming in Network Mobility Support
RFC4980.summary: Informational analysis of multihoming in IPv6 network mobility (NEMO Basic Support): proposes an (MRs,HAs,MNPs) taxonomy of eight configurations, describes deployment scenarios, analyses issues such as fault tolerance, ingress filtering and synchronization, and recommends which WGs should address them.

NEMO.why: The whole document analyses multihomed mobile networks under NEMO Basic Support (RFC 3963), including MR/HA/MNP configurations and tunnels.
NEMO.quote: This document is an analysis of multihoming in the context of network mobility (NEMO) in IPv6.

multihoming.why: Multihoming is the central subject: configurations, fault tolerance, path selection, source address selection and ingress filtering are analysed, with reference to Shim6.
multihoming.quote: a taxonomy is proposed to classify the possible configurations.

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 is the basis for NEMO Basic Support and is referenced for comparison, but the document analyses NEMO, not MIPv6 itself.
The document is IPv6-only, but IPv6 is the environment rather than the subject.
Shim6 is cited as a source of related solutions for path exploration and re-homing, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
DHCP and DHCPv6 prefix delegation are mentioned only in passing as ways to make prefixes available.

RFC4981.title: Survey of Research towards Robust Peer-to-Peer Networks: Search Methods
RFC4981.summary: An independent-stream survey of academic research on peer-to-peer search networks (index types, DHT routing geometries, keyword/IR indexes, and range/multi-attribute/join/aggregation queries) with emphasis on robustness.

P2P.why: The whole document surveys P2P overlay search: Gnutella, Freenet, DHTs (Chord, Pastry, CAN), and P2P queries. The P2P tag is the best fit in the taxonomy.
P2P.quote: P2P search methods are first couched within an overall P2P taxonomy.

rejected.why: Section 3.4 covers DHT-based application-level multicast, but only as one part of the survey. It is overlay multicast, not IP multicast routing.
DNS appears only as an example of semantic naming and in a reference. The document does not address DNS.
Distributed indexes and queries are discussed, but not directory access protocols like LDAP or X.500.
Service discovery is mentioned only in passing (SDS in Section 5.2). The document is not about it.
The web is mentioned only for caching and CDN context. The document does not address HTTP.

gaps.name: Distributed hash tables (DHTs) / structured overlay search
gaps.why: The core subject is DHT routing geometries and P2P indexes and queries. The taxonomy has only the broad P2P tag, not a DHT-specific one.

gaps.name: Robustness/dependability of distributed systems
gaps.why: The document's stated theme is robustness under churn, which has no fitting taxonomy tag.

RFC4982.title: Support for Multiple Hash Algorithms in Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs)
RFC4982.summary: RFC 4982 analyses the impact of hash-function collision attacks on Cryptographically Generated Addresses and updates RFC 3972 to support multiple hash algorithms by encoding the hash choice in the Sec bits, creating an IANA "CGA SEC" registry.

IPv6.why: CGAs are IPv6 addresses whose interface identifier is derived from a hash of a public key. The document updates the CGA address generation procedure (RFC 3972).
IPv6.quote: The proposal is to encode in the Sec bits, not only information about brute force attack protection but also to encode the hash function used to generate the hash.

SHA.why: A large part of the document analyses collision attacks on SHA-1 and how to migrate CGAs to alternative hash functions.
SHA.quote: including SHA-1 that is the hash function used by CGAs [2].

rejected.why: Secure Neighbor Discovery is only one of the listed CGA applications, discussed in the impact analysis. The document does not specify or extend it.
Shim6 is mentioned as a CGA user in the impact analysis, but the document is not about it.
It is mentioned only as an application of CGAs in the analysis.
The new CGA SEC registry is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the main subject.
