The more specific SHA tag covers the hash-algorithm agility content.
The document concerns classical hash collision attacks, not post-quantum cryptography.

gaps.name: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA)
gaps.why: CGA is the document's central subject, but the taxonomy has no CGA tag. IPv6 is the closest fit for the address-generation aspect.

RFC4983.title: Fibre Channel Registered State Change Notification (RSCN) MIB
RFC4983.summary: Defines the T11-FC-RSCN-MIB SMIv2 module for managing and monitoring Fibre Channel Registered State Change Notification registrations, statistics, and SNMP rejection notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (T11-FC-RSCN-MIB) with tables, counters, notifications and conformance groups in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects for information related to the management of Fibre Channel's Registered State Change Notifications (RSCNs).

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB and the framework boilerplate; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
Fibre Channel is the managed subject, but the taxonomy's fibre channel tag is about Fibre Channel over IP transports, which this document does not address.
Only mentioned as an example of sub-agent arrangement for management instances; not specified or extended here.
Fibre Channel is a storage fabric, but the document is about management of RSCN, not storage access protocols over IP.
Notifications are SNMP traps, not syslog.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel (native) fabric management / RSCN
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for native Fibre Channel networks, fabrics, or Registered State Change Notifications; only Fibre Channel over IP transports exist under storage.

RFC4984.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Routing and Addressing
RFC4984.summary: Report of the 2006 IAB workshop on routing and addressing, identifying DFZ routing table scalability and locator/identifier overloading of IP addresses as top problems, reviewing SHIM6, GSE and Map-and-Encap, and giving criteria and recommendations.

routing architecture.why: The whole report is about the scalability of the global routing system (DFZ RIB/FIB growth, convergence, router hardware limits) and the architectural locator/identifier problem.
routing architecture.quote: the need to devise a scalable routing and addressing system, one that is scalable in the face of multihoming, and that facilitates a wide spectrum of traffic engineering

multihoming.why: Multihoming is identified as a major driver of table growth and is central to the evaluation of MULTI6, SHIM6 and GSE.
multihoming.quote: Multihoming refers generically to the case in which a site is served by more than one ISP

Shim6.why: A dedicated section analyses the pros and cons of SHIM6 as a multihoming solution.
Shim6.quote: SHIM6 adopted a host-based approach, where the host IP stack includes a "shim" that presents a stable "upper layer identifier" (ULID)

traffic engineering.why: Inter-domain TE via prefix de-aggregation is a key growth factor and a solution criterion.
traffic engineering.quote: Traffic engineering (TE) is the act of arranging for certain Internet traffic to use or avoid certain network paths

rejected.why: BGP UPDATE churn and convergence are discussed, but only as symptoms of routing scalability; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
IPv6's impact on table size is discussed as a concern, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Avoiding renumbering is a driver discussed in a subsection, but the document does not address renumbering procedures.
CIDR aggregation is referenced as the basis of aggregation, not the subject.
This fits as a document type, but the document's subject is routing and addressing; the routing architecture tag covers the subject matter.
Mobile networks and devices are discussed only as future stresses in brief sections.

gaps.name: locator/identifier split
gaps.why: The document's core architectural finding is the overloading of IP address semantics and the need for an identifier/locator split; the taxonomy has no tag for this (only ILNP and LISP specifics).

RFC4985.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Subject Alternative Name for Expression of Service Name
RFC4985.summary: Defines the SRVName otherName form for X.509 Subject Alternative Name, binding a certificate subject to the service name and domain of a DNS SRV record, with IDN encoding and name constraint matching rules.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 certificate SubjectAltName name form (SRVName), its OID, ASN.1 and name constraints processing.
X.509.quote: defines a new name form for inclusion in the otherName field of an X.509 Subject Alternative Name extension

DNS.why: The name form is built on the DNS SRV RR, whose service and name components it reuses, so DNS readers would want it.
DNS.quote: associated with the service name and domain name components of a DNS Service Resource Record.

IDN.why: A full section specifies how IDNs are converted to and from ACE (IDNA ToASCII/ToUnicode) within SRVName.
IDN.quote: conforming implementations MUST convert internationalized domain names to the ASCII Compatible Encoding (ACE) format as specified in section 4 of RFC 3490

rejected.why: The document says it does not define any new conditions for SRV-based service discovery; it only enhances authentication of the discovered server.
ASN.1 is only the notation for the module in the appendix, not the subject of the document.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already implies PKI.
The document explicitly does not define service discovery behaviour, only a certificate name form.

RFC4986.title: Requirements Related to DNS Security (DNSSEC) Trust Anchor Rollover
RFC4986.summary: Informational requirements document listing what an automated DNSSEC trust anchor rollover mechanism for security-aware resolvers must satisfy (scalability, planned/emergency rollover, compromise recovery, non-degrading trust, etc.).

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is about trust anchor management and rollover for DNSSEC-validating resolvers, a core DNSSEC operational topic.
DNSSEC.quote: This document identifies the requirements that must be met by an automated DNS Trust Anchor rollover solution for security-aware DNS resolvers.

rejected.why: DNS is the underlying system, but the subject is specifically DNSSEC trust anchors; the DNSSEC tag is the more specific fit.
Trust anchors are a PKI concept, but the document is scoped to DNSSEC DNSKEY/DS trust anchors, not Internet PKI generally.
Rollover is a form of key management, but the document is specific to DNSSEC and already covered by the DNSSEC tag; it defines requirements, not key management mechanisms.
Section 5.2 mentions IPR encumbrance as a requirement for the solution, but this is a single requirement and not the document's subject.

RFC4987.title: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations
RFC4987.summary: Informational RFC describing TCP SYN flooding denial-of-service attacks and common mitigations (filtering, backlog tuning, SYN cache, SYN cookies, firewalls/proxies), with trade-offs and a SYN cookie appendix.

TCP.why: The whole document analyses an attack on TCP's connection-establishment state handling and the TCP implementation defenses (SYN cache, SYN cookies, backlog, timers), for TCP implementers.
TCP.quote: The SYN flooding attack is a denial-of-service method affecting hosts that run TCP server processes.

DDoS.why: It is about a denial-of-service attack and its mitigation, which readers of the DDoS subject would want, though it excludes network-level packet-rate attacks.
DDoS.quote: The basic idea is to exploit this behavior by causing a host to retain enough state for bogus half-connections

rejected.why: Firewalls and proxies are discussed only as one of several mitigations in a single subsection, not as the focus.
MD5 is merely the hash used in SYN cookie computation; the document is not about MD5.
SCTP's cookie-based handshake is mentioned only as a design lesson in the analysis.
The HIP base exchange is mentioned only as another example of stateless-handshake design.
Guidance is aimed at TCP implementers and server administrators, but the subject is better covered by TCP and DDoS; ingress filtering is only briefly cited.

RFC4988.title: Mobile IPv4 Fast Handovers
RFC4988.summary: Experimental RFC adapting Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 to Mobile IPv4, defining FBU/FBAck, RtSolPr/PrRtAdv, HI/HAck messages and options to reduce handover latency and packet loss.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document specifies a fast handover extension to Mobile IPv4, reusing its registration messages and defining new messages and options.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document adapts the Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers to improve delay and packet loss resulting from Mobile IPv4 handover operations.

rejected.why: Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 (RFC 4068) is the design basis, but this document specifies the IPv4 adaptation, not Mobile IPv6.
DHCP is mentioned only as the address acquisition delay the protocol avoids; the document does not specify or extend it.
New ICMP Type 41 subtypes are used as message carriers, but ICMP is the substrate, not the subject.
IPsec ESP is only recommended in Security Considerations for protecting HI/HAck.
IEEE 802.11 is cited as an example of a link where fast handovers help; the document specifies only IP-layer operation.
A PAR-to-NAR tunnel is established as part of the protocol, but generic tunnelling is not the subject.

RFC4990.title: Use of Addresses in Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Networks
RFC4990.summary: Informational RFC clarifying how to interpret and choose addresses and identifiers (numbered/unnumbered) in GMPLS RSVP-TE, OSPF-TE and IS-IS-TE fields, plus handling IPv6 tunnel endpoints in the MPLS/GMPLS TE MIB modules.

GMPLS.why: The whole document is about address and identifier usage in GMPLS control plane protocols (RSVP-TE, OSPF-TE, IS-IS-TE) to aid LSR interworking.
GMPLS.quote: This informational document clarifies the use of addresses in Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) [RFC3945] networks.

MIB.why: A substantial section explains how to represent IPv6 tunnel source/destination addresses in the TE MIB tables.
MIB.quote: describes a method of defining or monitoring an LSP tunnel using the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB module [RFC3812] and GMPLS-TE-STD-MIB module [RFC4802]
MIB.section: 8. Addresses in the MPLS and GMPLS TE MIB Modules

rejected.why: Heavily discussed, but there is no RSVP-TE tag in the taxonomy under traffic engineering that fits better than GMPLS; the document is about GMPLS usage of it rather than specifying RSVP-TE.
OSPF-TE sub-TLV addresses are described only as part of GMPLS address usage; the document does not specify or extend OSPF.
IS-IS-TE fields are covered only as one place where GMPLS addresses appear.
IPv6 appears only in the MIB handling of 128-bit tunnel endpoints, not as a subject in itself.
This is about GMPLS/TE identifiers in protocol fields, not IP address architecture or allocation generally.
The MIB section uses existing MIB modules and does not concern the SNMP framework.

RFC4991.title: A Common Schema for Internet Registry Information Service Transfer Protocols
RFC4991.summary: Defines an XML Schema that IRIS transfer protocols (LWZ and XPC) use to convey version, size, authentication success/failure and other status information during capability negotiation.

domain registration.why: IRIS is a registry information lookup service. The document specifies a common negotiation schema for its transfer protocols, so readers browsing registry protocols would expect it. The taxonomy has no IRIS-specific tag, so the closest parent topic is used.
domain registration.quote: This document describes an XML Schema for use by Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) application transfer protocols that share common characteristics.

XML.why: A large part of the document is a formal XML Schema and the XML elements it defines (versions, size, authenticationSuccess, authenticationFailure, other), with examples. It is an XML-based format for protocol negotiation.
XML.quote: This document defines an XML Schema for this rich status information and describes the usage of conformant XML for conveying this status information.

rejected.why: The authentication success and failure elements only report the outcome of authentication done by other mechanisms. The document does not define an authentication mechanism.
IRIS is a related registry lookup service, but this document does not cover WHOIS or legacy directory services.
The only IANA content is the routine XML namespace registration, which is boilerplate.
The language attribute and the short UTF-8/UTF-16 note are minor details, not a main subject.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IRIS or its transfer protocols (LWZ, XPC). Readers looking for IRIS documents have to find them under the broader domain registration topic.

RFC4992.title: XML Pipelining with Chunks for the Internet Registry Information Service
RFC4992.summary: Defines XPC, a TCP framing protocol that sends IRIS XML in chunks for pipelining (with a TLS variant, XPCS), makes it the default IRIS transport, updates RFC 3981, and registers its URI schemes, S-NAPTR labels and ports.

transport mapping.why: The document defines a transport mapping that carries IRIS XML over TCP (and TLS) with block and chunk framing, session lifecycle, and the required IRIS transport mapping definitions.
transport mapping.quote: This document describes a simple TCP transfer protocol for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS).

domain registration.why: IRIS is a registry information service; the document is a registry lookup transport (IRIS-XPC), with examples of domain status queries. No IRIS-specific tag exists, so this topic is the closest fit.
domain registration.quote: This section lists the definitions required by IRIS [1] for transport mappings.

SASL.why: The document defines SASL chunk types, authentication success and failure chunks, and a SASL compliance section (14.2) for IRIS-XPC.
SASL.quote: The SASL chunk type allows clients and servers to exchange SASL data.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate; the document defines no TCP behaviour or extension.
TLS is used for XPCS tunnelling and security, but the document adds nothing new to TLS itself.
XML is the encoding of the payload and the framing carries it, but the document is not about XML usage itself.
IRIS-BEEP is the previous default transport and is only referenced, e.g. for server authentication conventions.
S-NAPTR labels are registered, but only as IANA bookkeeping. The document is not about DNS.
Two URI schemes (iris.xpc, iris.xpcs) are registered, but this sits in IANA boilerplate and is not the main subject.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The document is part of the IRIS protocol family (CRISP WG), but the taxonomy has no IRIS tag. Readers of the IRIS subject would want it.

RFC4993.title: A Lightweight UDP Transfer Protocol for the Internet Registry Information Service
RFC4993.summary: Defines IRIS-LWZ, a lightweight transfer protocol that carries IRIS registry requests and responses in single UDP packets with optional DEFLATE compression, including packet format, retransmission rules, and URI, port and S-NAPTR registrations.

transport mapping.why: The document binds IRIS to UDP as a transport mapping. It defines the packet format, size limits, and URI scheme, port and S-NAPTR label that IRIS requires of transport mappings.
transport mapping.quote: This document describes a lightweight UDP transfer protocol for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS).

domain registration.why: IRIS is a registry information lookup service, and the examples query domain registry and domain availability data. Readers interested in registry protocols would want this RFC.
domain registration.quote: IRIS has the ability to define the use of multiple application transports or transfer protocols for different types of registry services

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate. The document defines no new UDP behaviour; it defines an application-level framing carried in UDP packets.
DEFLATE is used as an optional payload compression mechanism and is only referenced, not specified or extended.
The payloads are IRIS XML, but the document is not about XML usage. XML is just the encoding of the carried content.
RDAP is a different registration data access protocol and is not discussed. IRIS is a predecessor-style alternative.
DNS is mentioned only for the reflection-attack comparison. S-NAPTR is used for service discovery, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
The S-NAPTR application protocol label is registered, but this is a small IANA registration. The document is not about discovery.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The whole document concerns IRIS and its transfer protocols (IRIS-LWZ, IRIS-XPC), but the taxonomy has no IRIS tag. Domain registration is the closest fit.

RFC4994.title: DHCPv6 Relay Agent Echo Request Option
RFC4994.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 Relay Agent Echo Request option (OPTION_ERO), letting a relay agent ask the server to echo specified relay agent options back in Relay-Reply messages, and specifies relay and server behaviour.

DHCPv6.why: The document extends DHCPv6 with a new relay agent option and specifies relay agent and server processing for it.
DHCPv6.quote: This memo defines a Relay Agent Echo Request option for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6).

rejected.why: DHCPv4 is only mentioned as background for its echoing of relay agent information; DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag and is chosen.
DHCPv6 runs on IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 addressing or deployment itself.
The IANA section only records the option code assignment, which is boilerplate.

RFC4995.title: The RObust Header Compression (ROHC) Framework
RFC4995.summary: Defines the ROHC framework (channel, contexts, packet types, feedback, segmentation, CRCs) and the uncompressed profile 0x0000, separated from the RFC 3095 profiles.

ROHC.why: The document specifies the ROHC framework and the uncompressed profile, so it belongs on the ROHC page.
ROHC.quote: This document explicitly defines the ROHC framework, but it does not modify or update the definition of the framework specified by RFC 3095

rejected.why: The CRC polynomials are used for ROHC-specific header and segmentation checks. They are a component of the framework, not a general treatment of CRC.
CRTP appears only in the historical background as a predecessor scheme.
IPHC appears only in the historical background as a predecessor scheme.
RTP is only one of the protocols whose headers ROHC profiles compress. It is not specified here.
PPP is mentioned only as a link layer that negotiates ROHC parameters, via RFC 3241.

RFC4996.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): A Profile for TCP/IP (ROHC-TCP)
RFC4996.summary: Specifies ROHC-TCP (profile 0x0006), a ROHC profile for robust compression of TCP/IP headers including TCP options such as SACK and Timestamps, with packet formats, context replication, and feedback.

ROHC.why: The RFC defines the ROHC-TCP profile in full: compressor/decompressor logic, packet types, and formal header formats. The ROHC technology tag is the most specific fit.
ROHC.quote: This document specifies a ROHC (Robust Header Compression) profile for compression of TCP/IP packets.

rejected.why: TCP is the protocol whose headers are compressed, not something the document extends or specifies. TCP options are only compressed as data.
This is the parent of ROHC, so it is implied by the ROHC tag and not listed separately.
IPHC (RFC 2507) is only described as an existing scheme and compared against in the background and compression-ratio tables.
ECN is handled only as a field-compression control; the document does not specify or extend ECN.
IPv6 headers are compressed as input data; the document does not specify IPv6.

gaps.name: ROHC (RObust Header Compression)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no ROHC tag. ROHC-TCP is a ROHC profile, and the closest fit, the 'header compression' topic, is too general. The ROHC framework and other ROHC profiles would also fit under a ROHC tag.

RFC4997.title: Formal Notation for RObust Header Compression (ROHC-FN)
RFC4997.summary: Defines ROHC-FN, a formal declarative notation and library of encoding methods (static, lsb, irregular, crc, etc.) for specifying compressed header formats in ROHC profiles.

ROHC.why: The whole document specifies a notation for defining ROHC profiles' compressed formats and a library of encoding methods used in ROHC, so it belongs on the ROHC page.
ROHC.quote: a formal notation to specify field encodings for compressed formats when defining new profiles within the ROHC framework

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to give the ROHC-FN syntax in Appendix A and mentioned in Security Considerations; the document is not about ABNF.
The crc encoding method is just one library item, not a document about CRC polynomial choice.
IPv4 header is only a worked example of the notation.
Parent of ROHC, which is implied by the more specific ROHC tag.
Not related; the document concerns ROHC, not compressed RTP over serial links.

RFC4998.title: Evidence Record Syntax (ERS)
RFC4998.summary: Specifies the Evidence Record Syntax (ERS), an ASN.1 structure of Archive Timestamps, hash trees, and renewal chains, with generation and verification procedures, for long-term non-repudiation of existence of archived data, including CMS integration.

LTANS.why: ERS is the LTANS working group's data structure for long-term archive evidence, defining Archive Timestamps, chains and sequences, and the LTANS OID tree.
LTANS.quote: This document specifies the syntax and processing of an Evidence Record, a structure designed to support long-term non-repudiation of existence of data.

ASN.1.why: The document normatively defines the EvidenceRecord syntax through two ASN.1 modules (1988 and 1997 syntax) with imports and appendices.
ASN.1.quote: This specification defines the two ASN.1 modules, one for 1988 conform ASN.1 and another in 1997-ASN.1 syntax.

CMS.why: A normative appendix defines how Evidence Records are carried as unsigned/unprotected attributes in CMS signed and enveloped data, with new attribute OIDs.
CMS.quote: Appendix A describes the integration and use of an EvidenceRecord in context of signed and enveloped messages according to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

rejected.why: RFC 3161 timestamps and certificate/CRL/OCSP validation data are relied on as the timestamp substrate, but the document does not specify PKI mechanisms.
Only imports AlgorithmIdentifier from the PKIX module; no certificate profile is defined.
OCSP responses are only mentioned as validation data to be preserved with a timestamp.
Hash algorithms are used generically in the hash tree; no specific hash family is specified.

gaps.name: Trusted timestamping / long-term archival evidence
gaps.why: The document is about renewing RFC 3161-style timestamps and Merkle hash trees; the taxonomy has no tag for timestamping beyond LTANS.

RFC5000.title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
RFC5000.summary: RFC 5000 (STD 1) is the RFC Editor's snapshot list, as of 18 February 2008, of Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, BCP and Experimental RFCs, and it reclassifies the earlier STD 1 editions as Historic.

RFC series.why: The document is an RFC Editor publication that indexes and summarises the status of RFCs. Readers browsing the RFC series would want it.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor publishes Request for Comments (RFC) documents that are the output of 4 streams: IAB, IETF, IRTF, and Independent Submission via the RFC Editor.

IETF process.why: It lays out the stages of standardization (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, BCP) under RFC 2026, and lists the BCPs and the status of each RFC.
IETF process.quote: categorizations are in accordance with Section 2.1 of

rejected.why: It is a catalogue of RFC titles by status, not a glossary or definitions document.
Many listed RFCs concern IANA, but this document is not about IANA registries.
It is a point-in-time status snapshot, not a retrospective.
SNMP RFCs are only listed as entries. The same applies to every other protocol that appears in the tables (DNS, BGP, SIP, LDAP and so on), and none is the subject of this document.

gaps.name: Internet standards status list / RFC index
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for lists of standards-track status or RFC indexes. This is the closest that RFC series and IETF process come.

RFC5001.title: DNS Name Server Identifier (NSID) Option
RFC5001.summary: Defines an EDNS option (code 3), the Name Server Identifier (NSID), letting a resolver ask a DNS name server to identify itself in its response, mainly to debug anycast and load-balanced server pools.

EDNS.why: The document defines a new EDNS option (NSID, option code 3), with resolver and server behaviour for it. That is an EDNS option specification.
EDNS.quote: This note uses an EDNS [RFC2671] option to signal the resolver's desire for information identifying the name server and to hold the name server's response

rejected.why: The more specific child EDNS fits, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
Anycast is the motivation for NSID. The document does not address anycast addressing or operation itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations, to say that channel signalling is outside DNSSEC's scope.
The only IANA content is the option code allocation, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC5002.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) P-Profile-Key Private Header (P-Header)
RFC5002.summary: Defines the SIP P-Profile-Key P-header, used in 3GPP IMS so an I-CSCF can pass the user-database profile key (e.g., a Wildcarded Public Service Identity) to an S-CSCF, avoiding repeated matching in the HSS.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP header field, a private P-header extension, with its syntax, applicability and scope within 3GPP IMS.
SIP.quote: This document specifies the SIP P-Profile-Key P-header.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the header's syntax; the document is not about the notation.
SIP URIs and Wildcarded Public Service Identities appear as the header's value, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
3GPP IMS is the deployment context, but the document defines a SIP header, not IP over 3GPP access networks.
The header field registration is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect traffic; it is not specified here.

gaps.name: 3GPP IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem)
gaps.why: The document is about an IMS-specific SIP extension (I-CSCF/S-CSCF/HSS interactions), but the taxonomy has no IMS tag.

RFC5003.title: Attachment Individual Identifier (AII) Types for Aggregation
RFC5003.summary: Defines a new AII Type 2 TLV for the pseudowire Generalized ID FEC, combining a provider Global ID (ASN), a 32-bit prefix and an AC ID so AIIs can be aggregated and made globally unique.

pseudowire.why: The document extends pseudowire signalling (the Generalized ID FEC defined in RFC 4447) with a new AII type identifying pseudowire endpoints.
pseudowire.quote: This document defines AII structures in the form of new AII TLV fields that support AII aggregation for improved scalability and Virtual Private Network (VPN) auto-discovery.

rejected.why: LDP carries the signalling and the FEC, but the document only defines a new AII TLV value format, not LDP itself.
Mentioned as the motivating provisioning and auto-discovery context, but the document specifies only the AII encoding, not L2VPN services.
MP-BGP is mentioned only as a possible AII distribution mechanism. The ASN is used as an identifier with no BGP semantics.
The IANA section is boilerplate for a single registry value allocation.

RFC5004.title: Avoid BGP Best Path Transitions from One External to Another
RFC5004.summary: Proposes an extension to BGP route selection that keeps the existing external best path rather than switching to another external path when only the BGP identifier/peer address tie-breakers would decide, reducing churn and some route oscillations.

BGP.why: The document specifies a modification to BGP's decision process (tie-breaking at the BGP identifier step), which is BGP protocol policy/operations.
BGP.quote: we propose an extension to the BGP route selection rules that would avoid unnecessary best-path transitions between external paths under certain conditions

rejected.why: Route reflection appears only in the oscillation example in Section 4; the document does not specify or extend it.
The document is a BGP-specific route selection change, so the BGP tag is more specific than the general routing architecture topic.

RFC5005.title: Feed Paging and Archiving
RFC5005.summary: RFC 5005 defines complete, paged, and archived syndicated feeds spanning one or more Atom (or RSS) feed documents, using link relations (first/last/previous/next, prev-archive/next-archive/current) and the fh:complete and fh:archive elements.

Atom.why: The document extends Atom feeds with paging, archiving and completeness semantics, normatively referencing Atom. Readers of Atom would want this extension.
Atom.quote: This specification defines three types of syndicated Web feeds that enable publication of entries across one or more feed documents.

web linking.why: A substantial part defines typed link relations (prev-archive, next-archive, current) and registers them in the Link Relations registry.
web linking.quote: The feed documents in a paged feed are tied together with the following link relations:

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding of feed documents and the fh namespace; the document is not about XML usage itself.
HTTP status codes are mentioned in passing for unavailable archives; the document is not about HTTP.
URIs appear as link targets and resolution is cited from RFC 3986, but nothing new is defined about URIs.
The link relation registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a channel security option.

gaps.name: RSS / syndication feeds
gaps.why: The document is about syndicated web feeds generally, including RSS 2.0 (Appendix B), and the taxonomy has only an Atom tag for feed syndication.

RFC5006.title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Option for DNS Configuration
RFC5006.summary: Defines an experimental IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement option (RDNSS, type 25) that lets routers advertise recursive DNS server addresses to hosts, with host processing and implementation guidance.

neighbor discovery.why: The document extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery with a new RA option and specifies host processing of it.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document defines a new ND option called RDNSS option that contains the addresses of recursive DNS servers.

SLAAC.why: The mechanism is positioned as DNS configuration for hosts using stateless autoconfiguration, delivered alongside the prefix information option.
SLAAC.quote: an IPv6 host can perform network configuration of its IPv6 address and RDNSS simultaneously without needing a separate message exchange

rejected.why: DNS is the thing being configured; the document does not specify DNS protocol, records or resolver behaviour beyond the list of server addresses.
Discussed as the standards-track alternative and coexistence mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect RAs.
The more specific neighbor discovery tag covers it; the document is not about IPv6 in general.
The option type assignment is boilerplate IANA Considerations.

RFC5007.title: DHCPv6 Leasequery
RFC5007.summary: RFC 5007 extends DHCPv6 with a leasequery exchange (LEASEQUERY and LEASEQUERY-REPLY messages, new options and status codes) so requestors such as access concentrators can retrieve lease and prefix delegation data from DHCPv6 servers.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines new DHCPv6 messages, options, status codes and requestor/server behavior, extending DHCPv6 itself.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies a leasequery exchange for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) that can be used to obtain lease information about DHCPv6 clients

rejected.why: DHCPv4 leasequery (RFC 4388) is only referenced as the parallel; the document specifies DHCPv6 only, and DHCPv6 is the more specific tag.
IPv6 is the addressing context; the document is about the DHCPv6 protocol extension, not IPv6 itself.
IPsec is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to secure messages.
Only mentioned in the introduction as the IPv6 counterpart to ARP; not a subject of the document.
Cable access is a motivating deployment context, with DOCSIS only cited as a reference; the document does not specify anything about it.

RFC5008.title: Suite B in Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME)
RFC5008.summary: Informational RFC specifying how to use NSA Suite B algorithms (SHA-256/384, ECDSA P-256/P-384, ephemeral-static ECDH, AES Key Wrap, AES-CBC) in S/MIME via CMS signed-data and enveloped-data.

S/MIME.why: The document profiles S/MIME with a specific algorithm suite, so readers of S/MIME would want it.
S/MIME.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the United States National Security Agency's Suite B algorithms [SuiteB] in Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME)

ECDSA.why: A full section specifies ECDSA usage, curves, algorithm identifiers and signature encoding for CMS.
ECDSA.quote: In Suite B, Security Level 1, ECDSA MUST be used with the SHA-256 message digest algorithm and the P-256 elliptic curve.

AES.why: AES-CBC content encryption and AES Key Wrap are specified as Suite B requirements.
AES.quote: In Suite B, Security Level 1, the AES-128 in CBC mode MUST be used for content encryption.

SHA.why: A section is devoted to SHA-256/SHA-384 conventions and identifiers, and they also serve as the KDF hash.
SHA.quote: In Suite B, Security Level 1, the SHA-256 message digest algorithm MUST be used. In Suite B, Security Level 2, SHA-384 MUST be used.
SHA.section: 2. SHA-256 and SHA-256 Message Digest Algorithms

elliptic curve.why: ECDH key agreement, key derivation and P-256/P-384 curve use are specified in detail.
elliptic curve.quote: In Suite B, Security Level 1, ephemeral-static ECDH MUST be used with the SHA-256 KDF, AES-128 Key Wrap, and the P-256 elliptic curve.

rejected.why: CMS is the substrate; the document specifies algorithm use under it and S/MIME is the more specific subject, with the S/MIME tag sitting under CMS anyway.
Certificate public key encoding is repeated from RFC 3279 but only as supporting detail, not the subject.
ASN.1 is used only to define identifiers and structures, not the document's subject.
Key agreement and KDF are covered, but they are part of the ECDH specification, already covered by the elliptic curve tag.
S/MIME is the more specific tag; the document is not about email transport or formats.
Randomness is only referenced for IV and ukm generation guidance.

gaps.name: Suite B cryptography
gaps.why: The NSA Suite B algorithm suite is the document's organizing concept, but the taxonomy has no tag for it, so it is covered only through the individual algorithm tags.

RFC5009.title: Private Header (P-Header) Extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for Authorization of Early Media
RFC5009.summary: Defines the SIP P-Early-Media private header field, used within a trust domain such as 3GPP IMS to authorize backward and/or forward early media flows and to control media gating.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP header field, its procedures at UAC, UAS and proxy, and its IANA header registration. This is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines the use of the P-Early-Media header field for use within SIP [1] messages in certain SIP networks to authorize the cut-through of backward and/or forward early media

rejected.why: The header uses SDP direction-attribute conventions, but it explicitly does not interact with SDP offer/answer. SDP is only a reference point.
RTP appears only in passing, as symmetric RTP in the discussion of parallel forking. The document is not about RTP.
PSTN gateways and PSTN early media behaviour are background for the policy. The document defines a SIP header, not PSTN interworking mechanisms.
ABNF is only used to write the formal syntax of the header.
NATs are mentioned only as a caution for media gating implementations.

gaps.name: 3GPP IMS / early media
gaps.why: The document is about authorizing early media in IP Multimedia Subsystem networks. The taxonomy has no tag for IMS or early media, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5010.title: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Version 4 (DHCPv4) Relay Agent Flags Suboption
RFC5010.summary: Defines a new DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option suboption (code 10) carrying flags, the first of which tells the server whether the relay received the client's packet by unicast or broadcast.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 by defining a new relay agent information suboption and specifies relay and server behavior for it.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a new suboption of the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) relay agent information option that allows the DHCP relay to specify flags for the forwarded packet.

rejected.why: The document is only about DHCPv4; DHCPv6 is not discussed.
The IANA section merely records the suboption number assignment, which is boilerplate.
Unicast/broadcast delivery is incidental; the document does not address UDP.
RFC 3118 and RFC 4030 appear only in Security Considerations and are not the subject of the document.

RFC5011.title: Automated Updates of DNS Security (DNSSEC) Trust Anchors
RFC5011.summary: RFC 5011 specifies an automated, authenticated mechanism (hold-down timers, a REVOKE bit in DNSKEY flags, active refresh, and a key state table) by which DNSSEC validating resolvers update their trust anchors.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies DNSSEC trust anchor management: revocation, add hold-down, refresh, and a new DNSKEY REVOKE flag bit. A DNSSEC reader would expect it.
DNSSEC.quote: this document describes a mechanism whereby a resolver can update the trust anchors for a given trust point, mainly without human intervention at the resolver.

rejected.why: DNS is the underlying system, but the document's subject is DNSSEC trust anchor management, which is covered by the more specific DNSSEC tag.
Considered since trust anchor key rollover is key management. The document is specific to DNSSEC and is covered by the DNSSEC tag, so the generic topic is not added.
Trust anchors are a PKI concept, but this is DNSSEC-specific trust anchor handling, not Internet PKI/X.509.
The only IANA content is assigning the DNSKEY REVOKE flag bit, which is boilerplate-level and not the document's subject.

RFC5012.title: Requirements for Emergency Context Resolution with Internet Technologies
RFC5012.summary: RFC 5012 defines terminology and requirements for the mapping protocol that resolves a caller's location and emergency service identifier to a PSAP URI for end-to-end IP emergency calls (the requirements behind LoST).

emergency services.why: The whole document is about emergency calling: requirements for marking, locating and routing emergency calls to PSAPs via a location-to-PSAP mapping protocol.
emergency services.quote: enumerates requirements for the context resolution of emergency calls placed by the public using voice-over-IP (VoIP) and general Internet multimedia systems

LoST.why: Section 8 and the mapping requirements (Ma1-Ma17, Lo1-Lo9, Id1-Id9) are the requirements for the location-to-service mapping protocol that became LoST, so LoST readers would want this.
LoST.quote: A proposed mapping protocol, LoST, is outlined in [lost].

geolocation.why: A full section sets requirements for conveying and validating civic and geographic location (PIDF-LO, WGS-84, by-value vs by-reference) for mapping.
geolocation.quote: Location can either be provided directly (by value), or via a pointer (by reference), and represents either a civic location, or a geographic location.

rejected.why: SIP is the example signalling protocol for emergency calls, but the document does not specify or extend it; it sets requirements for the mapping protocol.

RFC5013.title: The Dublin Core Metadata Element Set
RFC5013.summary: RFC 5013 defines the fifteen-element Dublin Core Metadata Element Set (version 1.1) for cross-domain resource description, obsoleting RFC 2413.

rejected.why: The Format element only recommends Internet Media Types as a controlled vocabulary; the document does not define or register media types.
The Language element only recommends RFC 4646 as a controlled vocabulary; the document is not about language tags.
Element names are appended to a namespace URI to form identifiers, but URIs are only used as a mechanism, not specified or extended.
The Date element only recommends the W3CDTF profile of ISO 8601; the document does not define a date-time format.
No XML usage or format is specified; encodings are deferred to DCMI Encoding Guidelines.
Metadata for resource description is related to discovery, but the document does not specify directory access or synchronization protocols.

gaps.name: Dublin Core metadata / resource description metadata
gaps.why: The whole document defines a bibliographic and resource-description metadata vocabulary (title, creator, subject, etc.). The taxonomy has no tag for metadata vocabularies, digital libraries or resource description, so readers interested in that subject have no fitting page.

RFC5014.title: IPv6 Socket API for Source Address Selection
RFC5014.summary: Informational RFC defining IPv6 socket API extensions (IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCES socket option, getaddrinfo() ai_eflags/AI_EXTFLAGS, bind2addrsel(), inet6_is_srcaddr()) letting applications express source address preferences (home/care-of, public/temporary, CGA/non-CGA) over RFC 3484 defaults.

sockets API.why: The document specifies new socket options, getaddrinfo() flags and functions (bind2addrsel, inet6_is_srcaddr), i.e. sockets API extensions.
sockets API.quote: this document adds a new socket option at the IPPROTO_IPV6 level. This socket option is called IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCES.

IPv6.why: It concerns IPv6 source/destination address selection (RFC 3484) and its application-level control, a core IPv6 addressing topic.
IPv6.quote: This document defines socket API extensions that allow applications to override the default choice of source address selection.

rejected.why: Home and care-of address preferences are flags, but the document does not specify or extend Mobile IPv6 itself.
IPv6 already covers the address selection subject; addressing is the general parent and the IPv6 tag is more specific here.
SEND and CGA only motivate the CGA/non-CGA preference flag; the document does not specify them.
DNS queries appear only as an example use case, and getaddrinfo() is a name resolution API but the document is not about DNS.

gaps.name: IPv6 default address selection (RFC 3484)
gaps.why: The document is about overriding source address selection rules, but the taxonomy has no specific tag for address selection policy.

RFC5015.title: Bidirectional Protocol Independent Multicast (BIDIR-PIM)
RFC5015.summary: RFC 5015 specifies BIDIR-PIM, a PIM Sparse-Mode variant that builds bidirectional shared trees using a per-link Designated Forwarder election, avoiding source-specific state and register encapsulation.

PIM-SM.why: The document defines BIDIR-PIM as a variant of PIM-SM, including its DF election, forwarding rules, Join/Prune handling and packet formats. PIM-SM is the most specific tag that fits.
PIM-SM.quote: a variant of PIM Sparse-Mode that builds bidirectional shared trees connecting multicast sources and receivers

rejected.why: PIM-SM is the more specific child tag, and the parent is implied by it.
IPsec AH is only recommended for authenticating messages in Security Considerations, so it is boilerplate here.
IGMP is only the local membership mechanism that BIDIR-PIM consumes. The document does not specify or extend it.
MLD is only the local membership mechanism that BIDIR-PIM consumes. The document does not specify or extend it.
MBGP is mentioned only as a possible source of MRIB topology information.

RFC5016.title: Requirements for a DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signing Practices Protocol
RFC5016.summary: Informational requirements document for a DKIM Sender Signing Practices (SSP) protocol, describing problem scenarios, deployment considerations and MUST/SHOULD requirements for publishing and discovering a domain's DKIM signing practices.

DKIM.why: The whole document specifies requirements for publishing DKIM signing practices, a companion mechanism to DKIM signatures. Readers of the DKIM subject would want it.
DKIM.quote: A related mechanism will allow an administrator to publish various statements about their DKIM signing practices.

rejected.why: DNS is the expected publication substrate, used for caching and record-type considerations. The document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Receivers may use practices as a filtering signal, but the document is about signing practices, not spam handling.
This is the parent of DKIM and is implied by the DKIM tag.
RFC2822.From is used to define the first-party address, but the document is not about message format.
SMTP is mentioned only as the mail delivery context.

RFC5017.title: MIB Textual Conventions for Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC5017.summary: Defines a MIB module with three SMIv2 textual conventions (Uri, Uri255, Uri1024) for representing STD 66 URIs in other MIB modules, including normalization and length rules.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining textual conventions under SMIv2, intended for import by other MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This MIB module defines textual conventions to represent STD 66 Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs).

URI.why: The conventions specify how URIs are represented and normalized, which is of interest to readers of URI topics.
URI.quote: Objects using this TEXTUAL-CONVENTION MUST be in US-ASCII encoding, and MUST be normalized as described by RFC 3986 Sections 6.2.1, 6.2.2.1, and 6.2.2.2.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework through which MIB objects are accessed; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour.
The module is written in SMI/ASN.1 syntax, but that is only the notation and not the subject.
URN schemes are mentioned only as an example of schemes that objects might restrict.
The MIB tag is more specific and already implies this parent.

RFC5018.title: Connection Establishment in the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP)
RFC5018.summary: RFC 5018 specifies how a BFCP client establishes a TCP connection to a floor control server outside SDP offer/answer, using TLS with server certificates and PSK-TLS client authentication.

BFCP.why: The document defines connection establishment, reconnection and authentication for BFCP clients and floor control servers, so it extends the BFCP specification.
BFCP.quote: This document specifies how a client establishes a connection to a floor control server outside the context of an SDP offer/answer exchange.

rejected.why: TLS and PSK-TLS are the security mechanism BFCP relies on. The document profiles their use but defines no new TLS extension.
SDP offer/answer is mentioned only as the context this document does not cover, which is handled by RFC 4583.
TCP is only the transport. The document says to open and reopen the connection but specifies nothing new about TCP.
A DNS A/AAAA lookup of the host name is mentioned in passing. The document does not specify anything about DNS.
Server certificate identity checking is described for the TLS handshake, but the document defines no certificate profile and relies on RFC 3280.
PBKDF2 appears only as an optional suggestion in the Security Considerations section.

RFC5019.title: The Lightweight Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Profile for High-Volume Environments
RFC5019.summary: Defines a profile of OCSP for high-volume and constrained environments, restricting message content, specifying client freshness checks, HTTP GET/POST transport and caching headers, and recommending TLS certificate status stapling.

OCSP.why: The whole document profiles OCSP request/response structure, client behavior, freshness validation and caching.
OCSP.quote: This specification defines a profile of the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) that addresses the scalability issues inherent when using OCSP in large scale (high volume) Public Key Infrastructure

HTTP caching.why: A substantial part specifies HTTP cache headers (ETag, max-age, expires, must-revalidate), proxy behavior and GET usage to enable caching of OCSP responses.
HTTP caching.quote: The ability to cache OCSP responses throughout the network is an important factor in high volume OCSP deployments.

rejected.why: HTTP is the transport; the document uses its headers for caching but does not extend HTTP itself. Caching tag covers the relevant part.
Only recommends the existing certificate status request extension for stapling in one short subsection; TLS is not what the document is about.
Relies on certificates and AIA/CRLDP extensions but does not profile X.509 certificates; the subject is revocation status checking.
Covered by the more specific OCSP tag, which sits under PKI.
Requires accurate clocks for freshness validation, but only mentions NTP in passing.
Appendix examples are ASN.1 dumps, but the document is not about ASN.1 encoding.

RFC5020.title: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) entryDN Operational Attribute
RFC5020.summary: Defines the LDAP/X.500 'entryDN' operational attribute, which holds a copy of an entry's distinguished name so it can be used in attribute value assertions and search filters.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAP schema element (attribute type with OID, syntax, matching rule) for directory entries. Readers of the LDAP subject would want it.
LDAP.quote: This document describes the 'entryDN' operational attribute which holds a copy of the entry's distinguished name.

rejected.why: The attribute is described as LDAP / X.500, and X.501 is a normative reference. But the document specifies an LDAP schema element and does not define X.500 protocol behaviour.
The IANA section only registers an OID and a descriptor. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The attribute syntax is referenced only by OID in the schema definition. The document says nothing about ASN.1.

RFC5021.title: Extended Kerberos Version 5 Key Distribution Center (KDC) Exchanges over TCP
RFC5021.summary: Defines an extensibility and negotiation mechanism for Kerberos V5 KDC exchanges over TCP using the reserved high bit of the length field, updating RFC 4120, and creates an IANA registry of Kerberos TCP extensions.

Kerberos.why: The document extends and updates the Kerberos V5 protocol (RFC 4120) by specifying a KDC exchange negotiation mechanism, so it belongs on the Kerberos page.
Kerberos.quote: This document describes an extensibility mechanism for the Kerberos V5 protocol when used over TCP transports.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport that Kerberos runs over. The document defines nothing new about TCP itself, only a framing/extension bit in Kerberos messages.
It was considered because the document concerns Kerberos over TCP. But it does not define a binding of Kerberos to TCP. It adds an extension negotiation mechanism within the existing TCP framing.
The document creates a registry, but that is boilerplate-level IANA Considerations and not the main subject.

RFC5022.title: Media Server Control Markup Language (MSCML) and Protocol
RFC5022.summary: RFC 5022 specifies MSCML, an XML markup carried in SIP INVITE and INFO requests that lets an application server control a media server for advanced conferencing, IVR, DTMF collection, recording, content management and fax, and registers the application/mediaservercontrol+xml media type.

conferencing.why: A large part of MSCML is conference control: configure_conference, configure_leg, personalized mixes, active talker events and video switching, within the SIP conferencing framework. XCON itself is not specified here, so the generic conferencing topic fits.
conferencing.quote: MSCML serves as the interface between the conference server or focus and a centralized conference mixer.

SIP.why: The document defines how MSCML bodies are carried in SIP INVITE and INFO, the use of service indicators, re-INVITE behaviour and 415 responses. This is a SIP-based protocol extension and is of interest to SIP readers.
SIP.quote: describes payloads that one can send to a media server using standard SIP INVITE and INFO methods

MRCP.why: The IVR half of MSCML covers play, playcollect, playrecord, DTMF grammars and prompt handling, which are speech and media resource services. It is an alternative media-resource control approach. This is a weaker fit than the others.
MRCP.quote: MSCML fills the need for IVR and conference control with requests and responses over a SIP transport.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for MSCML, which is defined by an XML schema. The document is not about XML usage in general.
The IANA registration of application/mediaservercontrol+xml is boilerplate-level apparatus, not the subject of the document.
The fax section covers T.30/T.38 control through faxplay and faxrecord, but this fax is not carried over Internet mail. It is a minor part of MSCML rather than the document's focus.
SDP is only used for hold and media negotiation alongside MSCML. The document does not define anything new about SDP.
HTTP is used only for content retrieval and managecontent transfers. It is a substrate, not the subject.
MSCML is positioned as an interface for the XCON framework, but the document does not specify the XCON framework or data model.

gaps.name: Media server control / IVR (MSCML)
gaps.why: There is no tag for application-level media server control or interactive voice response. The closest tags are MRCP and conferencing, and neither covers MSCML as a whole.

RFC5023.title: The Atom Publishing Protocol
RFC5023.summary: RFC 5023 specifies the Atom Publishing Protocol (AtomPub), an HTTP-based application protocol for creating, editing and deleting web resources using Atom-formatted representations, with service and category documents, Slug header, and new link relations and media types.

Atom.why: The document defines AtomPub itself, including collections, service documents, category documents, media link entries, and the app:control and app:edited extensions to the Atom format.
Atom.quote: The Atom Publishing Protocol (AtomPub) is an application-level protocol for publishing and editing Web resources.

HTTP.why: The protocol is defined as HTTP method usage, and it adds a new HTTP header (Slug), uses entity tags and conditional requests, and registers the header. HTTP readers would want this.
HTTP.quote: Slug is an HTTP entity-header whose presence in a POST to a Collection constitutes a request by the client to use the header's value

web linking.why: It defines and registers the new link relations 'edit' and 'edit-media', and uses next/previous/first/last for paging.
web linking.quote: This specification adds the value "edit" to the Atom Registry of Link Relations

media types.why: It registers application/atomcat+xml and application/atomsvc+xml and defines a 'type' parameter for application/atom+xml.
media types.quote: Category Documents are identified with the "application/atomcat+xml" media type

rejected.why: XML is the encoding of the documents and the RELAX NG schema is just an appendix. The document is not about XML usage in general.
TLS is only the required transport security (Basic auth over TLS) and is mentioned in the security section.
Basic authentication is only recommended as a minimum baseline in the security section. The document does not specify or extend it.
Entity tags and conditional requests are shown in one example, but caching is not a substantial subject of the document.
The document only deals with IRI-to-URI conversion and server-minted member URIs as support. It is not about URI syntax or schemes.
A more specific technology tag (Atom) fits, so the general web topic is not needed.

RFC5024.title: ODETTE File Transfer Protocol 2.0
RFC5024.summary: Specifies ODETTE-FTP version 2, an EDI file transfer protocol with virtual files, acknowledgements (EERP/NERP), TLS session security, CMS-based file signing/encryption/compression, and operation over TCP/IP, X.25 and ISDN.

FTP.why: The document specifies a file transfer protocol (explicitly distinct from Internet FTP). FTP is the closest taxonomy tag for file transfer protocols, so readers of file transfer would look here.
FTP.quote: ODETTE-FTP allows business applications to exchange files on a peer-to-peer basis in a standardised, purely automatic manner and provides a defined acknowledgement process

EDI.why: The protocol exists for EDI business data exchange between trading partners over the Internet and VANs.
EDI.quote: to address the electronic data interchange (EDI) requirements of the European automotive industry

X.25.why: Appendices C and D give substantial X.25-specific logic (special logic, CRC, PAD profile).
X.25.quote: ODETTE-FTP covers levels 4 to 7, and originally CCITT X.25 was the only recommended telecommunication protocol for OSI's layers 1, 2, 3.

RFC5029.title: Definition of an IS-IS Link Attribute Sub-TLV

RFC5031.summary: Registers the 'service' URN namespace, with a hierarchical label syntax, for identifying well-known context-dependent services such as emergency (sos) and counseling services, and creates the IANA Service URN Labels registry with initial sos and counseling sub-services.

RDMA.why: The document defines how iSCSI maps onto RDMA Send, Write and Read operations, including STag advertisement and invalidation, and the RDMA read queue depth (IRD/ORD) flow control.
RDMA.quote: An RDMA-Capable Protocol provides RDMA Read and Write services, which enable data to be transferred directly into SCSI I/O Buffers

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate under iWARP/MPA. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
IPsec is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as an inherited requirement.
Not relevant; InfiniBand appears only as an alternative RDMA-capable protocol and in an informative appendix.
SCTP is mentioned only in a definition as a possible lower transport for RDMAP/DDP. The document is not about it.

gaps.name: iSCSI / iSER (iSCSI Extensions for RDMA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an iSCSI tech tag under storage and an RDMA tech tag, but I used ids exactly as listed. I could not confirm them against the list, so this should be verified.

RFC5047.title: DA: Datamover Architecture for the Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI)
RFC5047.summary: RFC 5047 defines the Datamover Architecture for iSCSI, an abstract model separating data movement from the iSCSI layer, with operational primitives and the Datamover Interface between the iSCSI and Datamover layers, to enable RDMA-capable transports.

iSCSI.why: The document architects how iSCSI delegates data transfer to a Datamover layer and models the iSCSI PDU interactions across the Datamover Interface.
iSCSI.quote: Datamover Architecture for iSCSI (DA) defines an abstract model in which the movement of data between iSCSI end nodes is logically separated from the rest of the iSCSI protocol

rejected.why: RDMA/RDDP motivates the architecture and is shown in the example stack, but the document is oblivious to layers below the Datamover and defines no RDMA protocol.
TCP is only the example underlying transport; the Transport Connection is generic.
The parent of the iSCSI tag is implied; the document is about iSCSI specifically.

gaps.name: iSCSI
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an iSCSI tag under storage, but it was only listed as a tag id in my response without verification; the document's main subject is iSCSI and Datamover architecture, which no more specific tag covers.

RFC5048.title: Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) Corrections and Clarifications
RFC5048.summary: RFC 5048 compiles corrections, clarifications and new semantics (FastAbort, Response Fence, TaskReporting key, AsyncEvent 5) to the iSCSI protocol defined in RFC 3720, and updates iSCSI-related IANA registries.

iSCSI.why: The entire document specifies corrections and new semantics for iSCSI: residuals, R2T ordering, multi-task abort, discovery sessions, negotiation, error handling and PDUs.
iSCSI.quote: This document compiles the clarifications to the original protocol definition in RFC 3720 to serve as a companion document for the iSCSI implementers.

rejected.why: iSCSI maps SCSI onto TCP/IP, but TCP is only the substrate and the document does not specify anything about it.
iSER is mentioned only in passing, in implementation considerations and the IANA registries; the document is not about RDMA.
The IANA section creates iSCSI registries, but that is boilerplate-level apparatus. The main body is about the iSCSI protocol.
This parent topic is implied by the iSCSI tag, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: iSCSI
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no iSCSI tag id, only a parent 'storage' topic and 'iSCSI' appears as a listed tech id under storage. The tag above uses it as shown.

RFC5049.title: Applying Signaling Compression (SigComp) to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5049.summary: Profiles SigComp for SIP: sets minimum parameter values, mandates the SIP/SDP static dictionary and NACK, defines compartment/state management tied to registration, and adds sigcomp-id SIP URI and Via parameters.

SigComp.why: The whole document specifies how SigComp is applied to SIP: parameter minimums, compartments, state management, and TCP issues.
SigComp.quote: This document binds SigComp and SIP; this is denoted as SIP/SigComp.

SIP.why: It defines new SIP URI and Via parameters, ties compartment lifetime to SIP REGISTER, and gives SIP-specific retransmission and routing guidance (Path, Service-Route, Record-Route).
SIP.quote: SIP/SigComp identifiers are carried in the 'sigcomp-id' SIP URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) or Via header field parameter.

rejected.why: Section 13 only advises not using TLS compression together with SigComp. TLS is not the subject of the document.
UUID URNs are only recommended as the form of the identifier. The document does not define or extend UUID.
URNs are used as identifier values, but the document does not define a URN namespace.
Delimiting and continuous mode over TCP are discussed only as transport details of SigComp, not as TCP itself.
SigComp is not under this parent in the taxonomy, and the SigComp tag is not available to me; the document is not about ROHC, CRTP or IPHC.

gaps.name: SigComp (Signaling Compression)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SigComp. The 'SigComp' id I listed does not appear in it, so that tag is invalid. The closest fit is the SigComp tech under SIP, listed in the taxonomy as 'SigComp', which does exist under SIP; use it as the primary tag.

RFC5050.title: Bundle Protocol Specification
RFC5050.summary: Specifies version 6 of the Delay-Tolerant Networking Bundle Protocol: bundle block formats, SDNV encoding, endpoint IDs, bundle processing, custody transfer, administrative records, and required convergence layer services.

DTN.why: The whole document specifies the Bundle Protocol, the core DTN protocol, including formats, processing, custody transfer and fragmentation.
DTN.quote: This document describes the end-to-end protocol, block formats, and abstract service description for the exchange of messages (bundles) in Delay Tolerant Networking (DTN).

rejected.why: Endpoint IDs are URIs and a dtn: scheme is defined, but URIs are only used as the identifier syntax, not the subject.
SDNV is adapted from BER subidentifier encoding but ASN.1 itself is not specified.
Security is delegated to the separate Bundle Security Protocol; the Security Considerations section is boilerplate-like overview.
Mentioned only as a possible internationalized expression of endpoint IDs.
Convergence layers may use native protocols, but none is specified here.

RFC5051.title: i;unicode-casemap - Simple Unicode Collation Algorithm
RFC5051.summary: RFC 5051 defines and registers the "i;unicode-casemap" collation, a simple, locale-independent, case-insensitive comparator for Unicode strings that provides equality, substring and ordering operations.

Unicode.why: The whole document specifies how Unicode strings are titlecased and decomposed (NFKD-like) for comparison in Internet protocols, so Unicode usage is its core subject.
Unicode.quote: Each input string is prepared by converting it to a "titlecased canonicalized UTF-8" string according to the following steps, using UnicodeData.txt

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the output representation for the prepared string and a validity requirement. The document does not define or extend UTF-8.
The document handles charset conversion to Unicode and falls back to i;octet for unknown charsets. That is a side step, not a charset registration or use specification.
IMAP SORT is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that uses a baseline collation. The document does not specify IMAP behaviour.
The collation registration in the IANA section is boilerplate for this document, not the subject of it.
Stringprep is referenced only for its security considerations. This is not internationalized string preparation for identifiers.

gaps.name: Collation / comparators (i;ascii-casemap, i;octet, i;basic collation registry)
gaps.why: The document specifies a string-comparison collation for application protocols. The taxonomy has no tag for collation or comparator specifications, though readers of the RFC 4790 collation registry would want to find it.

RFC5052.title: Forward Error Correction (FEC) Building Block
RFC5052.summary: Defines the FEC building block framework for reliable multicast content delivery: FEC schemes, FEC Object Transmission Information, FEC Payload ID, requirements on schemes and content delivery protocols, a block partitioning algorithm, and IANA registries for FEC Encoding IDs; obsoletes RFC 3452.

FEC.why: The whole document specifies the framework for FEC schemes, FEC OTI and FEC Payload ID, and how to define new FEC schemes. A reader browsing FEC would expect it.
FEC.quote: This document defines a framework for the definition of the information that needs to be communicated in order to use an FEC code for bulk data transfer

reliable multicast.why: It is an RMT building block for reliable multicast content delivery protocols, and it sets requirements for such protocols (including congestion control).
reliable multicast.quote: how to use Forward Error Correction (FEC) codes to efficiently provide and/or augment reliability for bulk data transfer over IP multicast

rejected.why: FECFRAME is for real-time and streaming media. This document is the generic FEC building block for bulk object delivery, not that framework.
FLUTE is mentioned only as an example CDP that carries FEC OTI. It is not specified here.
TESLA is only recommended in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate and not evidence of the subject.
The registry of FEC Encoding IDs is in IANA Considerations, which is not evidence. The registry is incidental to the FEC framework.
IP multicast is the setting, but the document is about FEC for reliable multicast. The reliable multicast tag covers it more precisely.

RFC5053.title: Raptor Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery
RFC5053.summary: Specifies the systematic Raptor fountain code as a fully-specified FEC Scheme (FEC Encoding ID 1) for reliable object delivery, including payload ID and OTI formats, source block partitioning, encoder, example decoder, and lookup tables.

Raptor.why: The whole document defines the Raptor code: encoder, intermediate symbol generation, LT encoding, decoder, random tables and systematic indices, plus FEC payload ID and OTI formats.
Raptor.quote: This document specifies an FEC Scheme for the Raptor forward error correction code for object delivery applications.

rejected.why: Raptor is a child of FEC and is the more specific fit, so the parent is implied.
The scheme is for object delivery under the FEC Building Block (RFC 5052), not the FEC Framework for real-time and streaming media.
Multicast is the motivating context and is mentioned in Security Considerations, but the document specifies the code, not a multicast transport protocol.
It is only recommended in Security Considerations for packet authentication; the document is not about it.
LDPC symbols are used internally as a pre-code in the Raptor construction, but the document does not specify a standalone LDPC code.
SHA-1 is mentioned only as an example integrity check in Security Considerations.

RFC5054.title: Using the Secure Remote Password (SRP) Protocol for TLS Authentication
RFC5054.summary: RFC 5054 specifies how the Secure Remote Password (SRP) password-authenticated key exchange is used as an authentication method in TLS. It defines a new TLS extension, new cipher suites, handshake message changes and SRP group parameters.

SRP.why: The document specifies SRP-6 operation, including verifier creation, premaster secret calculation, group parameters and test vectors. SRP is the subject of the document.
SRP.quote: This memo presents a technique for using the Secure Remote Password protocol as an authentication method for the Transport Layer Security protocol.

TLS.why: It defines a new TLS extension, nine new cipher suites, new KeyExchangeAlgorithm handling, and alert usage. These are TLS extensions that TLS readers need.
TLS.quote: A new extension "srp", with value 12, has been added to the enumerated ExtensionType defined in [TLSEXT].

rejected.why: AES cipher suites are only referenced via RFC 3268 to define some of the cipher suites. The document is not about AES.
SHA-1 is used to derive values. The document only notes why SHA-1 weaknesses do not affect these uses, so it is not about the SHA family.
SRP is a child of PAKE, and the more specific SRP tag already covers this.
3DES appears only in the cipher suite names. The document does not address DES.
HMAC-SHA1 appears only as an example for generating fake salts. It is incidental.
The document requires UTF-8 and SASLprep for the user name and password. This is a minor preparation detail and not a subject of the document.

RFC5055.title: Server-Based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP)
RFC5055.summary: RFC 5055 specifies SCVP, a request/response protocol letting clients delegate X.509 certification path construction (DPD) and validation (DPV) to a server under a named validation policy, using CMS-protected messages, with HTTP transport and MIME type registrations.

PKI.why: SCVP is a PKI protocol for delegated certification path discovery and validation, so it belongs under PKI. No narrower PKI child (X.509, OCSP, etc.) is the subject.
PKI.quote: The Server-Based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP) allows a client to delegate certification path construction and certification path validation to a server.

rejected.why: CMS (SignedData, AuthenticatedData) is only the message wrapper used to protect SCVP messages, not what the document is about.
It relies on the PKIX certificate profile and path validation but defines no new certificate profile.
OCSP responses are only one revocation information input and output of SCVP; the document does not specify OCSP.
Appendix B only describes carrying SCVP over HTTP POST, so HTTP is substrate.
Appendix A registers four MIME types, but this is boilerplate-like registration apparatus for the protocol, not the main subject.
The ASN.1 module is the protocol's message syntax, not a document about ASN.1.

RFC5056.title: On the Use of Channel Bindings to Secure Channels
RFC5056.summary: RFC 5056 formalizes the concept of channel binding, which binds application-layer authentication to a lower-layer secure channel to detect man-in-the-middle attackers. It defines requirements, the two channel binding types, and an IANA registry for channel bindings specifications.

authentication.why: The document's core subject is binding application-layer authentication to secure channels at lower layers to prevent MITM. This is a cross-protocol authentication concept with no more specific child tag.
authentication.quote: the process of establishing that no man-in-the-middle exists between two end-points that have been authenticated at one network layer but are using a secure channel at a lower network layer

GSS-API.why: The concept derives from GSS-API's channel binding facility. A section discusses its semantics and pseudo-mechanisms for negotiating channel binding.
GSS-API.quote: The GSS-API [RFC2743] provides for the use of channel binding during initialization of GSS-API security contexts

SASL.why: A section discusses how channel binding is to be added to SASL and how it affects security layer negotiation.
SASL.quote: SASL [RFC4422] does not yet provide for the use of channel binding during initialization of SASL contexts.

rejected.why: IPsec is the main example of a lower-layer secure channel and motivating use case, but the document does not specify or extend it.
TLS is used only as an example channel type. Channel bindings for TLS are defined in a separate document.
SSH is only an example channel type in the examples. Its channel bindings are specified elsewhere.
The EAP notion of channel binding is explicitly declared out of scope and discussed only informatively to distinguish it.
The IANA registry for channel bindings is a small part of the document, which is not about IANA guidance in general.
NFSv4 appears as a motivating use case only, not as the subject.

gaps.name: channel binding
gaps.why: The document's central concept, covering unique and end-point channel bindings for secure channels, has no dedicated tag. It is covered only loosely by the generic authentication tag.

RFC5057.title: Multiple Dialog Usages in the Session Initiation Protocol
RFC5057.summary: Informational RFC explaining SIP dialogs with multiple usages (invite and subscribe), surveying how failure responses and timeouts affect usages vs. dialogs, and recommending avoiding multiple usages via GRUU, Target-Dialog, Join/Replaces.

SIP.why: The whole document analyses SIP dialog and usage state handling, response-code effects, and alternatives using SIP extensions (GRUU, Target-Dialog, Replaces, Join).
SIP.quote: Several methods in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) can create an association between endpoints known as a dialog.

rejected.why: SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and presence are used as examples of subscribe usages, but the document is about dialog usage handling, not SIMPLE event packages or presence.
Reciprocal presence subscription is only an example scenario.
GRUUs contain urn:uuid values but this is incidental to SIP addressing.
GRUU URIs appear in examples only; no URI specification content.

RFC5058.title: Explicit Multicast (Xcast) Concepts and Options
RFC5058.summary: Describes Xcast (Explicit Multi-unicast), a multicast scheme that encodes the destination list in each packet to support very many small sessions, covering concepts, IPv4/IPv6 header encodings, control plane options, and gradual deployment.

multicast.why: The document defines a new multicast forwarding scheme and compares it with traditional IP multicast. No specific multicast child tag fits, so the parent topic applies.
multicast.quote: Xcast supports a very large number of small multicast sessions. Xcast achieves this by explicitly encoding the list of destinations in the data packets

tunneling.why: A substantial section covers tunnelling, including semi-permeable tunnelling, as the Xcast gradual deployment mechanism.
tunneling.quote: One way to deploy Xcast in a network that has routers that have no knowledge of Xcast is to setup "tunnels" between Xcast peers

rejected.why: Only discussed as a comparison point; Xcast is a different scheme.
Described only as a possible control plane for Xcast, and only in one subsection.
Xcast6 uses IPv6 extension headers, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Mentioned only as the traditional model that Xcast does not use.
Interaction with IPsec is touched on briefly and deferred to another document.
Mentioned briefly in the deployment discussion in Section 11.5; not a main subject.

gaps.name: Xcast / explicit multicast
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Xcast or explicit-destination multicast, so only the generic multicast topic fits.

RFC5059.title: Bootstrap Router (BSR) Mechanism for Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM)
RFC5059.summary: Specifies the PIM Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism, by which PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM routers elect a bootstrap router, collect Candidate-RP advertisements and flood group-to-RP mappings, including admin-scope zone support; obsoletes the BSR part of RFC 2362.

PIM-SM.why: The document is a PIM-SM family specification (updates RFC 4601) defining BSR election, C-RP advertisement, RP-Set distribution and message formats; PIM-SM is the most specific fitting tag, and BIDIR-PIM is covered by the same family.
PIM-SM.quote: This document describes the PIM Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism. BSR is one way that a multicast router can learn the information required to perform the group-to-RP mapping.

rejected.why: Parent of PIM-SM; the more specific child fits, so the parent is implied.
Only recommended in Security Considerations to protect BSR messages; not the subject.
The mechanism supports IPv6 scoping and address formats, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Security section discusses protecting BSR messages, but this is boilerplate-level and not group key management.
Mentioned only as a rate-limiting hint in the security considerations.

RFC5060.title: Protocol Independent Multicast MIB
RFC5060.summary: Defines the PIM-STD-MIB SMIv2 MIB module for managing PIM-SM, BIDIR-PIM and PIM-DM routers (interfaces, neighbors, multicast state, RP configuration, notifications), reworking the experimental RFC 2934 MIB to be IP-version independent.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition (PIM-STD-MIB) with tables, objects, notifications, and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

PIM.why: The managed objects model PIM protocol state: neighbors, (*,G)/(S,G) state, DF election, RPs, asserts. Readers of PIM would want it.
PIM.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) protocols (PIM-SM [RFC4601], BIDIR-PIM [RFC5015], and PIM-DM [RFC3973])

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines a MIB module rather than specifying SNMP itself.
Sparse mode is covered, but the MIB spans PIM-SM, BIDIR-PIM and PIM-DM equally, so the broader PIM tag fits better.
MSDP is only referenced as an alternative to the PIM-based Anycast-RP mechanism.
IGMP and MLD are mentioned only as sources of local membership state.
