SSM appears as a PIM mode value and in a compliance statement, but the document is not about SSM.
Anycast-RP configuration is one table within the PIM MIB; it is not the main subject.

RFC5061.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Dynamic Address Reconfiguration
RFC5061.summary: RFC 5061 extends SCTP with ASCONF and ASCONF-ACK chunks and new parameters so an association can dynamically add or delete IP addresses and request a peer's primary address, using SCTP-AUTH for protection.

SCTP.why: The whole document defines new SCTP chunks, parameters, error causes and procedures. It is an extension of SCTP.
SCTP.quote: This document describes an extension to SCTP that will allow an SCTP stack to dynamically add an IP address to an SCTP association

rejected.why: SCTP multihoming is the motivation, but the document specifies SCTP protocol extensions rather than general multihoming architecture. The SCTP tag covers it.
IPv6 renumbering is mentioned as motivation only. The document does not define site renumbering procedures.
Authentication is via SCTP-AUTH (RFC 4895), which this document relies on. It is not specified here and is not IPsec.
The IANA section only registers SCTP chunk, parameter and error cause values, which is boilerplate.
Section 5.1.1 limits ASCONF transmissions to avoid congestion, but this is a small part of the document and is not congestion control in its own right.
IPv6 is mentioned only as an address type that the extension can carry. The document is not about IPv6.

RFC5062.title: Security Attacks Found Against the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) and Current Countermeasures
RFC5062.summary: Informational RFC describing known security attacks against SCTP (address camping, association hijacking, redirection, bombing/amplification) and the countermeasures included in RFC 4960 and related SCTP specifications.

SCTP.why: The whole document analyses attacks on SCTP (multihoming, INIT/cookie handling, HEARTBEAT, ADD-IP) and the mitigations in the SCTP specification, so SCTP readers would want it.
SCTP.quote: This document describes certain security threats to SCTP. It also describes ways to mitigate these threats

rejected.why: DHCP appears only as an example mechanism for reassigning an IP address in the hijacking scenario; the document is not about DHCP.
ICMP handling is one mitigation detail for SCTP, not a subject of the document.
Path MTU discovery is mentioned only in the amplification attack 5 description; the document is not about it.
The security topic is implied as a general area, but the document concerns one specific protocol, so the SCTP tag fits better.
The bombing/amplification attacks are DoS-related, but the document does not address DDoS mitigation or signalling as a subject.

RFC5063.title: Extensions to GMPLS Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Graceful Restart
RFC5063.summary: Extends GMPLS RSVP-TE graceful restart with a new RecoveryPath message and Capability object in Hello messages, letting a restarting node recover its previously sent Path state (including ERO) from downstream neighbors, with optional Summary Refresh support.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE/GMPLS signalling graceful restart for traffic-engineered LSPs, defining a new message, a new object and recovery procedures.
RSVP-TE.quote: The extensions enable the recovery of RSVP signaling state based on the Path message last sent by the node being restarted.

GMPLS.why: It updates RFC 3473 (GMPLS RSVP-TE) and applies to LSPs of all GMPLS switching types, so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes extensions to the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Graceful Restart mechanisms defined in RFC 3473.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific tag, and the document is about the TE extension. It uses base RSVP Summary Refresh (RFC 2961) only as a mechanism.
LSPs are the subject matter, but the document's content is RSVP-TE signalling recovery, which is covered by the more specific tags.
A parent of RSVP-TE, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC5064.title: The Archived-At Message Header Field
RFC5064.summary: Defines the Archived-At email/netnews header field, carrying a URI to the archived copy of a message, plus the obsolete X-Archived-At variant, with usage and implementation guidance.

message format.why: The document specifies a new Internet message header field with ABNF syntax, multiple-field rules and fragmentation handling, which is message format subject matter.
message format.quote: This memo defines a new email header field, Archived-At:, to provide a direct link to the archived form of an individual email message.

mailing lists.why: The header complements the List-* headers of RFC 2369 and is mainly added by list expanders; the document discusses list-to-sublist handling and list archive implementation.
mailing lists.quote: This provides quick access to the location of a mailing list message in the list archive.

rejected.why: URIs are only the value carried in the header; the document defines no new URI scheme or syntax.
Section 2.4 only says an IRI replaces the URI in internationalized headers; this is a minor note, not the document's subject.
The internationalized-header extension is a brief note, and the document does not specify email address internationalization.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the syntax.
The header registrations are boilerplate IANA Considerations, not the subject of the document.
Media types such as message/rfc822 and text/html are mentioned only as formats an archive may serve; the document registers none.

RFC5065.title: Autonomous System Confederations for BGP
RFC5065.summary: RFC 5065 specifies BGP AS confederations, new AS_CONFED_SET/AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE AS_PATH segment types and associated rules, which remove the IBGP full-mesh requirement by presenting a group of member ASes as a single AS externally.

BGP.why: The document defines a BGP extension: new AS_PATH segment types, AS_PATH modification rules, MED/LOCAL_PREF handling and path selection changes for confederations.
BGP.quote: This document describes an extension to BGP that may be used to create a confederation of autonomous systems that is represented as a single autonomous system

rejected.why: Route reflection (RFC 4456) is only mentioned as an alternative way to avoid the full mesh. The document specifies confederations, not route reflection.
The scaling motivation is architectural, but the document is a specific BGP extension and the BGP tag fits it better.
TCP is only the transport that BGP sessions run over. The document defines nothing about TCP.

RFC5066.title: Ethernet in the First Mile Copper (EFMCu) Interfaces MIB
RFC5066.summary: Defines the EFM-CU-MIB and IF-CAP-STACK-MIB SNMP MIB modules for managing Ethernet in the First Mile Copper (2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS) interfaces, including PME aggregation, profiles, and cross-connect capability of stacked interfaces.

MIB.why: The document's whole content is two SMIv2 MIB modules (EFM-CU-MIB and IF-CAP-STACK-MIB) extending IF-MIB, EtherLike-MIB and MAU-MIB.
MIB.quote: This document defines Management Information Base (MIB) modules for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets.

DSL.why: The managed interfaces are SHDSL/VDSL-based copper PHYs with PME bonding, profiles, SNR margin and line attenuation objects, so DSL readers would want it.
DSL.quote: 2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS physical interfaces (PHYs), defined over voice-grade copper pairs, have been specified for the long and short reach

Ethernet.why: Manages IEEE 802.3ah Ethernet-like PHYs and extends EtherLike-MIB and MAU-MIB, including PCS/MAC layering and PAF.
Ethernet.quote: This document describes extensions to the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB and Medium Attachment Unit (MAU) MIB modules

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines modules, not SNMP itself (MIB is the more specific tag).
PME aggregation (PAF) is bonding of copper pairs within one PHY under 802.3ah, not IEEE 802.1AX link aggregation.
Implied by the MIB tag as an ancestor.
IANA section only notes OID allocation; boilerplate.

RFC5067.title: Infrastructure ENUM Requirements
RFC5067.summary: Informational requirements document for "infrastructure" (carrier) ENUM, which uses RFC 3761 E.164-to-URI mapping in DNS to let carriers publish points of interconnection for VoIP and other E.164-addressed services.

ENUM.why: The whole document defines requirements for infrastructure ENUM, a variant of ENUM where carriers publish E.164-to-URI mappings in the DNS.
ENUM.quote: Infrastructure ENUM is defined as the use of the technology in RFC 3761 [1] by the carrier-of-record

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate for ENUM here; the requirements concern ENUM namespace and records, not DNS protocol itself (ENUM is a child of naming, not DNS).
VoIP interconnection is the motivating use case, but SIP is not specified or discussed.
Peering between providers is mentioned in background, but the document does not address SPEERMINT architecture.
IRIS is mentioned as a SHOULD-support capability, but no matching tag for IRIS exists and RDAP is not the subject.
Registrar and registrant roles are touched on, but only as part of ENUM requirements.

RFC5068.title: Email Submission Operations: Access and Accountability Requirements
RFC5068.summary: BCP recommending operational policies for email message submission (MUA to MSA), including use of port 587, mandatory authentication/authorization, accountability, and not blocking port 587, to improve accountability against spam and abuse.

SMTP.why: The document sets operational requirements for SMTP message submission and relaying: port 587 use, MSA authentication, open relay prevention. Readers of SMTP submission operations would want it.
SMTP.quote: MSAs MUST perform authentication on the identity asserted during all mail transactions on the SUBMISSION port

spam.why: The motivation and goal is combating spam and worms via accountability at submission, though it explicitly does not cover rejection standards.
spam.quote: Its goal is to improve lines of accountability for controlling abusive uses of the Internet mail service.

rejected.why: The document concerns authenticating the submitting user to the MSA, not domain-level anti-spoofing technologies such as SPF/DKIM. It only says it builds on them.
SMTP AUTH is only mentioned as an available mechanism; the document gives no recommendations on specific security implementations.
STARTTLS is only mentioned in passing as one possible mechanism; nothing about TLS is specified.
Port 25 and 587 are referenced only as the substrate for SMTP; nothing new is defined about TCP.
Considered since it gives operational practices to reduce abuse, but the content is specific to email submission and is covered better by SMTP and spam.

RFC5069.title: Security Threats and Requirements for Emergency Call Marking and Mapping
RFC5069.summary: Informational ECRIT document analysing security threats to emergency call marking and to the location-to-PSAP-URI mapping process, and deriving security requirements for the mapping protocol and emergency-marked call handling.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about emergency call routing: marking calls as emergency and mapping locations to PSAP URIs, with threats and security requirements. No child (LoST, eCall) is named, so the parent topic is used.
emergency services.quote: This document reviews the security threats associated with the marking of signalling messages to indicate that they are related to an emergency

security.why: A threat analysis and requirements set (flooding, impersonation, integrity, confidentiality) is a substantial part of the document. It is a general threat model rather than a specific mechanism, so the generic security topic fits.
security.quote: Based on the identified threats, this document establishes a set of security requirements for the mapping protocol and for the handling of emergency-marked calls.

rejected.why: The document never names LoST. It states requirements for an unspecified mapping protocol, so the specific protocol tag would overreach.
SIP is only mentioned as an example signalling protocol (e.g. Request-URI). The document does not specify or extend it.
Location information is an input to mapping, but the document does not address location formats, privacy or conveyance, and explicitly scopes out faked-location attacks.
Confidentiality of mapping requests is one requirement (R9), but the document is not a privacy threat model in its own right.
Flooding attacks are discussed only as one of the threats against the mapping system, not as DDoS mitigation or signalling.

RFC5070.title: The Incident Object Description Exchange Format
RFC5070.summary: RFC 5070 defines IODEF, an XML-based data model and schema for CSIRTs to exchange computer security incident information across administrative domains.

IODEF.why: The document specifies the IODEF information model and XML schema. IODEF is a [tech] under incident response.
IODEF.quote: The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) is a format for representing computer security information commonly exchanged between Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs).

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are the implementation substrate for the data model, not the subject of the document.
IDMEF only influenced the design of IODEF and is referenced for some derived classes. It is not specified here.
RID is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a transport that can carry IODEF documents.
The document is about incident exchange between CSIRTs, not intrusion detection message exchange.
RFC 3339 timestamps are used for the DATETIME data type but are not the subject of the document.
The XML namespace and schema registrations in the IANA section are boilerplate and not what the document is about.

RFC5071.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Options Used by PXELINUX
RFC5071.summary: Informational RFC documenting PXELINUX's use of DHCPv4 option codes 208-211 (MAGIC, ConfigFile, PathPrefix, RebootTime), assigning them in IANA and specifying client/server behaviour.

DHCP.why: The document defines four DHCPv4 options, their packet formats, and the client and server behaviour for them, and records their IANA assignment. A reader browsing DHCP options would expect to find it.
DHCP.quote: PXELINUX uses DHCP options 208-211 to govern parts of this bootstrap process

rejected.why: TFTP is only the transport PXELINUX uses to load the config file and images. The document defines nothing new about TFTP.
The options are DHCPv4 only. DHCPv6 is not covered.
The IANA section only moves option codes 208-211 to Assigned. That is boilerplate for the DHCP option definitions, not a document about IANA registries.

gaps.name: PXE / network boot (Preboot eXecution Environment)
gaps.why: The document is about network bootstrapping with PXE and PXELINUX. The taxonomy has no tag for network boot or bootloaders, so DHCP is the closest fit.

RFC5072.title: IP Version 6 over PPP
RFC5072.summary: RFC 5072 specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over PPP links, defines the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP) with its Interface-Identifier option, and gives rules for link-local address formation and when Duplicate Address Detection can be skipped; it obsoletes RFC 2472.

PPP.why: The document defines IPV6CP, a PPP Network Control Protocol, its encapsulation (protocol 0x0057/0x8057) and the Interface-Identifier option. It is a PPP control protocol specification.
PPP.quote: This document defines the method for sending IPv6 packets over PPP links, the NCP for establishing and configuring the IPv6 over PPP

IPv6.why: A substantial part covers IPv6 interface identifiers, link-local address format, and the conditions for DAD on addresses configured by stateless autoconfiguration.
IPv6.quote: the method for forming IPv6 link-local addresses on PPP links

rejected.why: SLAAC is relied on and its DAD behaviour is tuned for PPP, but the document does not specify SLAAC itself. IPv6 covers the addressing content.
Mentioned only in Appendix A as an example of stateful address configuration.
3GPP2 and 3GPP networks are cited only as examples of PPP use satisfying the DAD conditions.
Referenced only in Security Considerations as a threat model reference.
Duplicate Address Detection is discussed as part of autoconfiguration, but the document does not specify neighbor discovery.

RFC5073.title: IGP Routing Protocol Extensions for Discovery of Traffic Engineering Node Capabilities
RFC5073.summary: Defines OSPF and IS-IS extensions (a TE Node Capability Descriptor TLV/sub-TLV) to advertise data-plane and control-plane TE node capabilities such as P2MP branch/bud LSR and GMPLS support, for use in MPLS/GMPLS TE path selection.

OSPF.why: The document specifies a new OSPF TLV, its format, and OSPF elements of procedure (flooding scope, LSA origination).
OSPF.quote: A new TLV is defined for OSPF, the TE Node Capability Descriptor TLV, to be carried within the Router Information LSA

IS-IS.why: The document specifies a new IS-IS sub-TLV, its format, and IS-IS procedures, in parallel with the OSPF extension.
IS-IS.quote: A new sub-TLV is defined for IS-IS, the TE Node Capability Descriptor sub-TLV, to be carried within the IS-IS Capability TLV

traffic engineering.why: The purpose is to advertise TE node capabilities for constraint-based TE-LSP path computation. This is the general TE topic, and no more specific tag fits this use.
traffic engineering.quote: These TE node capabilities will be taken into account as constraints during path selection.

rejected.why: MPLS TE LSPs are the context, but the document only extends IGPs to advertise capabilities. It does not specify MPLS itself.
RSVP-TE signaling support is one of the advertised capability bits. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
GMPLS signaling support is only one advertised capability bit. The document is not about GMPLS itself.
Path computation uses the advertised capabilities, but PCE is not specified or discussed.

RFC5074.title: DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV)
RFC5074.summary: Informational RFC (now historic) defining DNSSEC Lookaside Validation, a mechanism for publishing DNSSEC trust anchors in DLV domains outside the delegation chain, with validator behaviour and aggressive negative caching.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies a DNSSEC validation mechanism: DLV domains, validator procedures, trust anchors, and NSEC-based aggressive negative caching.
DNSSEC.quote: DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) is a mechanism for publishing DNS Security (DNSSEC) trust anchors outside of the DNS delegation chain.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and implies DNS. Authoritative server behaviour in Section 8 is a small part of the document.
The IANA section only points to the DLV RR type assigned in RFC 4431. It is boilerplate.
Trust anchors here are DNSSEC trust anchors, not Internet PKI. DNSSEC covers the subject.

RFC5075.title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Flags Option
RFC5075.summary: Defines a new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement option (Expanded Flags Option, type 26) that adds 48 extra flag bits, and sets up an IANA registry for RA flags.

neighbor discovery.why: The document extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery with a new RA option, specifying its format and sender/receiver processing rules.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document defines an option for the Router Advertisement message that expands the available number of flag bits by adding an additional 48 flag bits to NDP messages.

rejected.why: Neighbor discovery is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
The IANA section only creates a registry and assigns an option type. That is boilerplate here, and the body is about the ND option.
The Mobile IPv6 Home Agent flag is only listed as an existing RA flag. The document doesn't address mobility.
ND messages are carried in ICMPv6, but the document only relies on that as a substrate, and the registry sits in icmpv6-parameters.

RFC5076.title: ENUM Validation Information Mapping for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol
RFC5076.summary: Defines an EPP domain-name mapping extension framework for conveying ENUM E.164 number validation information (add/rem/chg/inf) in EPP commands and responses, with an example XML schema.

EPP.why: The document is an EPP extension to the domain name mapping, defining new elements for create, update, renew, transfer and info commands.
EPP.quote: an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension framework for mapping information about the validation process

ENUM.why: The extension exists to provision validation information for ENUM domain names, supporting registration of E.164 numbers in the DNS.
ENUM.quote: ENUM validation process has to be applied before the ENUM domain name can be inserted into the DNS.

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the notation used to specify the mapping, not the subject.
DNS is the background for ENUM, but the document is about registry provisioning, not DNS protocol or operations.
Implied as the parent of EPP; EPP is the more specific tag.
The IANA section only registers XML namespaces and schemas, which is boilerplate.
No media types are registered; only XML namespaces and schemas.

RFC5077.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Session Resumption without Server-Side State
RFC5077.summary: Defines a TLS extension (SessionTicket) and NewSessionTicket handshake message letting a server resume sessions by giving the client an encrypted ticket, avoiding per-client server-side state; obsoletes RFC 4507.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension (SessionTicket, type 35) and a new handshake message (NewSessionTicket), which is a TLS protocol extension for session resumption.
TLS.quote: This document defines a way to resume a Transport Layer Security (TLS) session without requiring session-specific state at the TLS server.

rejected.why: AES-128-CBC is only used in the recommended ticket format as a protection mechanism; the document is not about AES.
HMAC-SHA-256 is used for ticket integrity in the recommended format only; it is a building block, not the subject.
The document applies to TLS 1.0 and 1.1 only; DTLS is not addressed.
Ticket protection key management is explicitly out of scope beyond a short list of recommended practices.
Section 5.8 briefly discusses unlinkability, but this is a small part of the Security Considerations, not a main subject.

RFC5078.title: IAB and IESG Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Revision of the Nominating and Recall Committees Timeline
RFC5078.summary: Informational RFC that restructures the sample timeline for the IETF Nominating and Recall Committee (NomCom) process from RFC 3777 Appendix B so NomCom starts earlier, without normative changes.

NomCom.why: The whole document is about NomCom scheduling: a revised sample timeline for volunteer solicitation, self-organization, candidate selection and confirmation.
NomCom.quote: This document describes a timeline that meets this need, replacing RFC 3777, Appendix B, and makes no other changes to [RFC3777].

rejected.why: It is the parent of NomCom, which fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
The document updates an RFC about process but is not about RFC format, style or publication.

RFC5079.title: Rejecting Anonymous Requests in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5079.summary: Defines the SIP 433 (Anonymity Disallowed) response code so a server can reject anonymous requests and the caller can retry non-anonymously with user consent.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new response code and specifies server and UAC behavior for it.
SIP.quote: This specification defines the 433 (Anonymity Disallowed) response code.

rejected.why: Concerns anonymity in SIP calls, but the document specifies a response code, not privacy threat models or considerations in general.
Spam/telemarketing is mentioned only in Security Considerations, noting the code is likely ineffective against SIP spam.
RFC 4474 Identity header is mentioned only as a case that does not affect anonymity determination; the document is not about caller-ID authentication.
The response code registration is boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC5080.title: Common Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) Implementation Issues and Suggested Fixes
RFC5080.summary: RFC 5080 clarifies ambiguities and errors in the RADIUS specifications (RFC 2865, 2866, 2869, 3579) and recommends fixes for common implementation issues: State attribute use, retransmission/backoff, duplicate detection, accounting, Access-Reject semantics, addressing and Framed-IPv6-Prefix.

RADIUS.why: The whole document clarifies and updates RADIUS protocol behaviour (State, retransmission, duplicate detection, accounting, Access-Reject), so it belongs on the RADIUS page.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes common issues seen in Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) implementations and suggests some fixes.

rejected.why: EAP session tracking via State is discussed, but only as a RADIUS client/server concern; the document does not specify or extend EAP.
Section 2.3.5 clarifies RADIUS client MIB counters, but this is one small subsection and the MIB modules are not defined here.
RADIUS is the more specific tag; the generic AAA framework is not the subject.
Retransmission backoff and jitter is discussed, but only as RADIUS client behaviour, not as general congestion control.
The retransmission model is borrowed from DHCPv6, which is not itself addressed.
Framed-IPv6-Prefix and link-local addressing are handled as RADIUS attributes, not as IPv6 itself.

RFC5081.title: Using OpenPGP Keys for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authentication
RFC5081.summary: Experimental RFC defining a TLS extension ("cert_type") to negotiate certificate type and modifying TLS handshake messages so OpenPGP keys/fingerprints can be used for TLS authentication.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS extension (cert_type) and changes to Client Hello, Server Hello, Certificate and Certificate Request messages in the TLS handshake.
TLS.quote: This memo proposes extensions to the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to support the OpenPGP key format.

OpenPGP.why: The document is about using OpenPGP keys and certificates, including sending OpenPGP fingerprints, as TLS authentication credentials, so readers of the OpenPGP subject would want it.
OpenPGP.quote: This document specifies a way to negotiate use of OpenPGP certificates for a TLS session, and specifies how to transport OpenPGP certificates via TLS.

rejected.why: X.509 is only the default certificate type that the new negotiation sits alongside. The document does not specify or profile it.
Web of trust and certificate verification procedures are explicitly out of scope. The document only transports OpenPGP certificates.
The new extension type and the TLS Certificate Types registry appear only in the IANA Considerations boilerplate section, not in the main body.
The generic topic is covered by the more specific TLS tag, and the document gives no cross-protocol authentication treatment.

RFC5082.title: The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM)
RFC5082.summary: Specifies GTSM, which protects a router's control plane by sending protocol packets with TTL/Hop Limit 255 and checking that received packets have TTL 255, so that packets from non-adjacent attackers are rejected. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 3682.

operational security.why: The document defines a mechanism to protect router infrastructure from spoofed-packet resource-exhaustion attacks. That is operational security for network infrastructure, and there is no more specific tag for it.
operational security.quote: GTSM) is designed to protect a router's IP-based control plane from CPU-utilization based attacks.

routing security.why: GTSM secures routing protocol sessions (BGP, LDP, MSDP) between adjacent peers, so readers interested in routing security would want it. It was originally BGP-specific.
routing security.quote: cryptographic techniques can protect the router-based infrastructure (e.g., BGP [RFC4271], [RFC4272]) from a wide variety of attacks

rejected.why: BGP is the motivating example, but GTSM is generic and the document does not specify or extend BGP.
The tunnel analysis (IP-in-IP, GRE, MPLS) is a security consideration for GTSM. The document is not about tunneling itself.
The MPLS TTL models are discussed only as a case where the GTSM check can fail. The document does not cover MPLS.
TTL and Hop Limit are the mechanism's substrate. The document does not specify IP.
Hop Limit is covered only as equivalent to TTL. The document does not specify IPv6.
PMTUD is mentioned only as a way to avoid fragmentation, in the security considerations.

RFC5083.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Authenticated-Enveloped-Data Content Type
RFC5083.summary: Defines the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type (AuthEnvelopedData), an ASN.1 structure for authenticated encryption with all CMS key management techniques, updating RFC 3852.

CMS.why: The document specifies a new CMS content type, AuthEnvelopedData, with its processing rules and ASN.1 module, and updates the CMS specification.
CMS.quote: This document describes an additional content type for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

rejected.why: AES-CCM and AES-GCM conventions are in a separate document (RFC 5084). This document only references them.
ASN.1 is only the notation and encoding used to define the structure. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Randomness appears only in the Security Considerations, as a pointer to RFC 4086.
Key management techniques are reused from CMS enveloped-data. The document defines nothing new about key management.
S/MIME is only the working group context. The document does not specify S/MIME.

RFC5084.title: Using AES-CCM and AES-GCM Authenticated Encryption in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC5084.summary: Specifies conventions for using AES-CCM and AES-GCM authenticated encryption as content-authenticated-encryption algorithms in the CMS AuthEnvelopedData content type, including algorithm identifiers, parameters, and an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document defines how AES-CCM and AES-GCM are used in CMS AuthEnvelopedData, including OIDs and parameter structures. CMS readers need it.
CMS.quote: specifies the conventions for using the AES-CCM and the AES-GCM authenticated encryption algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) authenticated-enveloped-data content type

AES.why: The document specifies AES-CCM and AES-GCM modes, with their algorithm identifiers per key size and nonce and ICV parameters. This falls under AES and its modes.
AES.quote: CCM is defined for use with any 128-bit block cipher, but in this document, CCM is used with the AES block cipher.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the parameter structures and module. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The automated key management section is a requirement for safe use of the nonce and key. It is not the document's subject.
Random key generation is mentioned only in Security Considerations, with a pointer to RFC 4086.
The document targets CMS AuthEnvelopedData generally. It does not specify S/MIME secure email.

RFC5085.title: Pseudowire Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV): A Control Channel for Pseudowires
RFC5085.summary: Defines VCCV, a control channel associated with a pseudowire for OAM/connectivity verification, with CC and CV types for MPLS and L2TPv3 PWs and capability advertisement via LDP sub-TLV and an L2TPv3 AVP.

pseudowire.why: The document specifies a control channel and connectivity verification for pseudowires, including MPLS PW encapsulation and capability signalling.
pseudowire.quote: VCCV, which provides a control channel that is associated with a pseudowire (PW), as well as the corresponding operations and management functions

OAM.why: VCCV is an OAM mechanism for verifying PW forwarding path, so OAM readers would want it.
OAM.quote: There is a need for fault detection and diagnostic mechanisms that can be used for end-to-end fault detection and diagnostics for a Pseudowire

L2TP.why: A substantial part defines the VCCV control channel, V-bit and the VCCV Capability AVP for L2TPv3 pseudowires.
L2TP.quote: A new optional AVP is defined in Section 6.3.1 to indicate the VCCV capabilities during session establishment.

rejected.why: MPLS is the PSN substrate for PWs; the document is about the pseudowire layer, though it uses the router alert label and TTL tricks.
LDP is only the signalling carrier for the VCCV capability sub-TLV, defined by RFC 4447.
ICMP Echo is used as a CV type payload but not specified or extended here.
Congestion considerations section only gives rate-limiting guidance for VCCV traffic; minor boilerplate-like content.
Connectivity verification is fault detection, not performance measurement.

RFC5086.title: Structure-Aware Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) Circuit Emulation Service over Packet Switched Network (CESoPSN)
RFC5086.summary: Specifies CESoPSN, an encapsulation for carrying structured NxDS0 TDM circuits (with or without CAS) as pseudowires over MPLS or IP (UDP/L2TPv3) packet networks, including control word, payload formats, IWF operation, and performance monitoring.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines a TDM pseudowire encapsulation within the PWE3 architecture, including control word, payload layer and IWF operation.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a method for encapsulating structured (NxDS0) Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) signals as pseudowires over packet-switching networks (PSN).

rejected.why: RTP header is only optionally reused as a formal timestamp/sequence header; the document says RTP mechanisms are not applicable.
MPLS is one of the PSN/demultiplexing substrates; setup is defined in other documents.
L2TPv3 is merely a demultiplexing layer option; setup is defined elsewhere.
UDP port is used as PW label but nothing new about UDP is defined.
QoS section only recommends using Diffserv PDBs; not the subject.
Congestion section is short guidance for CBR pseudowires; not a main subject.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation (CESoPSN, NxDS0)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TDM circuit emulation; the closest tag, pseudowire, is the only fit and was used as the primary tag.

RFC5087.title: Time Division Multiplexing over IP (TDMoIP)
RFC5087.summary: Informational RFC specifying TDMoIP, a structure-aware pseudowire method for transporting TDM circuits (T1/E1/T3/E3) over UDP/IP, MPLS, L2TPv3 and Ethernet using AAL1, AAL2 and HDLC payload formats, with defect handling and OAM.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines a TDM pseudowire encapsulation, control word, payload adaptation, defect handling and OAM; pseudowire emulation is the subject.
pseudowire.quote: TDMoIP is a structure-aware method for transporting Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) signals using pseudowires (PWs).

DTN.why: placeholder
DTN.quote: placeholder

review: DTN: quote not found in the text

notes: DTN: quote not found in the text

RFC5088.title: OSPF Protocol Extensions for Path Computation Element (PCE) Discovery
RFC5088.summary: Defines OSPFv2/OSPFv3 extensions, a PCED TLV with sub-TLVs carried in the Router Information LSA, for advertising Path Computation Element discovery information within an OSPF area or domain.

PCE.why: The document specifies how PCEs advertise their location, scope, domains and capabilities so PCCs can discover and select them. This is PCE discovery, which falls under the PCE architecture tag.
PCE.quote: this document defines extensions to the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing protocol for the advertisement of PCE Discovery information

OSPF.why: It extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with a new TLV and flooding-scope procedures in Router Information LSAs.
OSPF.quote: This document defines a new TLV (named the PCE Discovery TLV (PCED TLV)) to be carried within the OSPF Router Information LSA

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is covered alongside OSPFv2 with only brief LSA flooding-scope notes. The document is about OSPF generally, so the parent tag fits better.
The IS-IS counterpart is only mentioned as RFC 5089 and is not specified here.
GMPLS and MPLS TE LSPs are the context for path computation, not the subject of this document.
TE LSPs are the use case for PCE, but the document addresses discovery, not traffic engineering mechanisms.

gaps.name: PCE (Path Computation Element) discovery
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a PCE tag only under traffic engineering as 'PCE architecture and PCEP'. I used it for PCE discovery, but there is no separate tag for discovery.

RFC5089.title: IS-IS Protocol Extensions for Path Computation Element (PCE) Discovery
RFC5089.summary: Defines IS-IS Router Capability sub-TLVs (PCED) for advertising Path Computation Element discovery information (address, path scope, domains, capabilities) within an IS-IS area or routing domain.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new PCED sub-TLV in the Router Capability TLV, with flooding scope and procedures.
IS-IS.quote: this document defines extensions to the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) routing protocol for the advertisement of PCE Discovery information

PCE.why: The purpose is PCE discovery: advertising PCE location, scope, domains and capabilities so PCCs can select PCEs.
PCE.quote: it is highly desirable to have a mechanism for automatic and dynamic PCE discovery that allows PCCs to automatically discover a set of PCEs

rejected.why: Only the companion RFC 5088 covers OSPF; here it is mentioned as the sibling IGP and for the shared capability registry.
MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs are the context for PCE, but the document is not about them.
TE LSPs are the use case for PCE, not the subject of this document.
A PCED MIB is only referenced informatively.
PCE is a path computation component for TE, but this document is about discovery advertisement, and the PCE tag already covers it.

gaps.name: PCE (Path Computation Element) discovery
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no PCE tag; PCE sits only under traffic engineering as a tech. IS-IS and PCE tags used above are not in the taxonomy as listed, so the best fits may be IS-IS and PCE under traffic engineering.

RFC5090.title: RADIUS Extension for Digest Authentication
RFC5090.summary: Defines RADIUS attributes that let a RADIUS server perform HTTP Digest authentication (including AKA) for HTTP-style clients such as SIP and HTTP servers acting as RADIUS clients; obsoletes RFC 4590.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS attributes and client/server behaviour for Digest authentication, so it is an extension of RADIUS.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines an extension to the RADIUS protocol to enable support of Digest Authentication for use with SIP, HTTP, and other HTTP-style protocols

HTTP authentication.why: The whole mechanism carries HTTP Digest Access Authentication parameters (nonce, qop, rspauth, etc.) over RADIUS. Readers of HTTP authentication would want this.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document defines new attributes that enable the RADIUS server to perform the digest calculation defined in [RFC2617]

rejected.why: SIP is a client protocol that uses Digest and is authenticated via RADIUS. The document does not specify or extend SIP, apart from the SIP-AOR attribute.
Only mentioned as a companion document (RFC 4740) defining the Diameter equivalent. The document itself is not about Diameter.
IPsec is mentioned only as an optional protection for RADIUS traffic in the security considerations and in conditions for Digest-HA1.
HTTP is the protocol being authenticated, not the one being extended. The HTTP authentication tag covers the relevant subject.
RFC 3579 is cited only for Message-Authenticator. EAP is not part of the document.
Mentioned only as a way to secure HTTP-style client connections, in the security discussion.

RFC5091.title: Identity-Based Cryptography Standard (IBCS) #1: Supersingular Curve Implementations of the BF and BB1 Cryptosystems
RFC5091.summary: Specifies the Boneh-Franklin (BF) and Boneh-Boyen (BB1) identity-based encryption algorithms on supersingular type-1 elliptic curves, including Tate pairing computation, hashing, key derivation, encryption/decryption, test vectors and an ASN.1 module.

elliptic curve.why: The document specifies pairing-based IBE algorithms on supersingular elliptic curves, including point arithmetic, Miller algorithm and Tate pairing. No identity-based encryption tag exists, so elliptic curve cryptography is the closest fit.
elliptic curve.quote: Fully secure and practical implementations are described for each system

key management.why: Setup, public parameters, master secret, and private key extraction from a PKG are a substantial part of the document.
key management.quote: a Private-key Generator (PKG). The PKG contains the cryptographic material, known as a master secret, for generating an individual's IBE private key.

rejected.why: TLS 1.1 is only required as the transport for PPS/PKG communication, not specified here.
CMS is only referenced as the message format; the usage is defined in another document.
The ASN.1 module is just an encoding apparatus for the keys and ciphertexts, not the subject.
SHA hash functions are used as building blocks, not specified or analysed.
RSA is mentioned only as a security-level comparison.
The schemes are classical pairing-based and not post-quantum.

gaps.name: Identity-based encryption (IBE) / pairing-based cryptography
gaps.why: The document is about IBE (Boneh-Franklin, Boneh-Boyen) and bilinear pairings, but the taxonomy has no tag for identity-based or pairing-based cryptography.

RFC5092.title: IMAP URL Scheme
RFC5092.summary: Defines the imap: URI scheme for referencing IMAP servers, mailboxes, messages, message parts and searches, including URLAUTH authorized URLs and relative URL rules; obsoletes RFC 2192 and updates RFC 4467.

IMAP.why: The document specifies how IMAP servers, mailboxes, messages and searches are addressed, mapping URLs to IMAP commands (SELECT, UID FETCH, SEARCH) and incorporating URLAUTH.
IMAP.quote: This document defines a URL scheme for referencing objects on an IMAP server.

URI.why: It defines a URI scheme with ABNF, relative reference resolution and a scheme registration, so it belongs on the URI page.
URI.quote: The IMAP URL follows the common Internet scheme syntax as defined in [URI-GEN].

rejected.why: SASL mechanisms (AUTH=, ANONYMOUS, GSSAPI) are used for authentication in URLs but SASL itself is not specified or extended.
STARTTLS and TLS are mentioned only as security advice; they are a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
Modified UTF-7 to UTF-8 percent-encoding conversion is a supporting detail of mailbox naming, not the subject of the document.
The document gives ABNF for its own syntax, but ABNF is just the notation used and the document is not about it.
The relative-URL use in MHTML is mentioned only in the change list, where that text was removed.
The Internationalization Considerations section is short and covers only encoding of mailbox names, user names and search strings as UTF-8.

RFC5093.title: BT's eXtended Network Quality RTP Control Protocol Extended Reports (RTCP XR XNQ)
RFC5093.summary: Defines BT's vendor-specific RTCP XR report block (block type 8, XNQ) carrying packet delay variation, jitter buffer, and errored/severely errored second metrics, documented to register the block type with IANA.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP Extended Report block type and its fields, extending RTCP XR (RFC 3611) with network quality metrics.
RTCP.quote: This document describes an RTCP XR report block, which reports packet transport parameters.

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport being monitored; the document extends RTCP, not RTP itself, and RTCP is the more specific tag.
The metrics are performance measures, but the document is about the RTCP XR report block carrying them. RTCP is the more specific fit and covers it.
The block type registration is only boilerplate-like motivation, not the subject of the document.

RFC5094.title: Mobile IPv6 Vendor Specific Option
RFC5094.summary: Defines a new Vendor-Specific mobility option for Mobile IPv6 Mobility Header messages, identified by an SMI enterprise number, so vendors can carry vendor data in MIPv6 exchanges.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 by defining a new mobility option for Mobility Header messages, allocated from the MIPv6 Mobility Options registry.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document defines a new mobility option, the Vendor-Specific Mobility Option, which can be carried in any Mobility Header message.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as another protocol that could use the option; the document is not about NEMO.
Only mentioned as able to use the option; not specified or extended here.
The IANA section merely assigns the option type value; the body is not about IANA registries.
The more specific Mobile IPv6 tag fits, so the parent is not listed.

RFC5095.title: Deprecation of Type 0 Routing Headers in IPv6
RFC5095.summary: Standards-track RFC that deprecates the IPv6 Type 0 Routing Header (RH0) because it enables traffic amplification DoS, updating RFC 2460 and RFC 4294, and gives ingress filtering and firewall guidance.

IPv6.why: The document modifies the IPv6 specification (RFC 2460) by deprecating a routing header type and changing node processing behaviour for it.
IPv6.quote: This document updates the IPv6 specification to deprecate the use of IPv6 Type 0 Routing Headers, in light of this security concern.

operational security.why: A substantial part of the document gives operational guidance on ingress filtering and firewall policy to mitigate RH0 attacks.
operational security.quote: A site security policy intended to protect against attacks using RH0 SHOULD include the implementation of ingress filtering at the site border.

rejected.why: Section 4.2 gives firewall policy guidance, but it is a short part of a document about deprecating RH0; operational security covers it.
The amplification DoS attack motivates the deprecation, but the document does not address DDoS mitigation or signalling as a subject.
Mentioned only as a user of the Type 2 Routing Header that firewalls must not block; the document is not about Mobile IPv6.
The ICMP Parameter Problem message is only the error behaviour inherited from RFC 2460 for unrecognised routing types.
The Routing Header is an IPv6 source-routing extension header, not a routing protocol or routing system.

RFC5096.title: Mobile IPv6 Experimental Messages
RFC5096.summary: Defines an Experimental Mobility Header message type and an Experimental Mobility option for experimental extensions to Mobile IPv6.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 by defining a new Mobility Header message type and a new Mobility option for experiments.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document defines a new experimental Mobility Header message and a Mobility option that can be used for experimental extensions to the Mobile IPv6 protocol.

rejected.why: NEMO is only mentioned as another protocol that can use these messages; the document does not specify it.
Proxy Mobile IPv6 is only mentioned as another user of Mobility Header messages.
The IANA section only records the code point assignments; the document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
ICMP Parameter Problem is mentioned only as an error response for unrecognized message types.

RFC5097.title: MIB for the UDP-Lite protocol
RFC5097.summary: Defines the UDPLITE-MIB SMIv2 module with counters and an endpoint table for managing and monitoring UDP-Lite implementations, including partial checksum coverage statistics.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module in SMIv2 (UDPLITE-MIB), so it belongs on the MIB page; this is a more specific tag than SNMP.
MIB.quote: This document specifies a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the Lightweight User Datagram Protocol (UDP-Lite).

UDP-Lite.why: The MIB models UDP-Lite behaviour: partial checksum coverage counters, bad checksum counts and minimum coverage per endpoint. Readers of UDP-Lite would want it.
UDP-Lite.quote: It defines a set of new MIB objects to characterise the behaviour and performance of transport layer endpoints deploying UDP-Lite.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB. The more specific MIB tag already covers this document.
The MIB is modelled on the UDP-MIB, but UDP itself is not specified or extended here. UDP-Lite is the subject.
Checksum coverage is monitored through counters. The document defines no new checksum mechanism.
DCCP is mentioned once as an example of a protocol that negotiates checksum coverage. It is not the subject.
The counters support monitoring, but the document is a MIB definition rather than a measurement methodology.
IPv6 appears only in the endpoint address types.

RFC5098.title: Signaling MIB for PacketCable and IPCablecom Multimedia Terminal Adapters (MTAs)
RFC5098.summary: Defines the PKTC-IETF-SIG-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing signaling (NCS/MGCP-derived call signaling, tones, ring cadence, caller ID, endpoint config) on PacketCable/IPCablecom Multimedia Terminal Adapters.

MIB.why: The document's core content is a SMIv2 MIB module with tables, objects and conformance groups for MTA signaling.
MIB.quote: it defines a basic set of managed objects for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)-based management of PacketCable- and IPCablecom-compliant Multimedia Terminal Adapter devices.

rejected.why: NCS is an MGCP derivative, but the document only defines managed objects (timers, ports, tones) for it, not the protocol itself.
MTAs may embed a DOCSIS cable modem, but DOCSIS is only context; no DOCSIS behavior is specified.
DSCP objects use the DIFFSERV-DSCP-TC textual convention only as a syntax import.
SNMP is the management substrate; the MIB tag sits under it and is the more specific fit.
The signaling here is NCS, not SIP.

gaps.name: PacketCable/IPCablecom cable telephony
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for cable-industry VoIP (PacketCable MTA provisioning and signaling), which would group this with RFC 4682 and related MIBs.

RFC5101.title: Specification of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol for the Exchange of IP Traffic Flow Information
RFC5101.summary: RFC 5101 specifies the IPFIX protocol: message, set, template and data record formats, template management, collector behaviour, and transport over SCTP, UDP and TCP with TLS/DTLS security, for exporting IP traffic flow information.

IPFIX.why: The document is the core IPFIX protocol specification: message format, templates, options templates, template management and collecting process behaviour.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol that serves for transmitting IP Traffic Flow information over the network.

rejected.why: SCTP/PR-SCTP is the mandatory transport that IPFIX runs over, with no new SCTP mechanism defined. It is substrate only.
TCP is an optional transport for IPFIX. The document only describes how to use it, not TCP itself.
UDP is an optional transport. The document describes template refresh and loss handling over it but does not specify UDP.
TLS and DTLS are the security mechanisms IPFIX relies on, described only in Security Considerations, and the document defines no new TLS extension.
Section 10 does map IPFIX onto SCTP, TCP and UDP, but this is a part of the IPFIX protocol specification, which the IPFIX tag already covers.
RFC 5102 defines the information model separately. This document only references it and does not define MIB modules.

RFC5102.title: Information Model for IP Flow Information Export
RFC5102.summary: RFC 5102 defines the IPFIX information model: the registry of Information Elements (flow keys, counters, timestamps, process statistics), abstract data types, naming and extension rules, with an XML specification in the appendices.

IPFIX.why: The whole document specifies the IPFIX Information Elements, data types and IANA registry used by the IPFIX protocol.
IPFIX.quote: This memo defines an information model for the IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) protocol.

rejected.why: XML is only used to generate the specification and appendices; not the subject.
SNMP counter semantics and ifIndex are referenced for comparison only.
BGP AS-number elements merely reference BGP; the document isn't about BGP.
MPLS label stack elements only describe observed header fields.
TCP header fields are reported as elements; TCP itself is not specified.
IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level here, secondary to the information model.

RFC5103.title: Bidirectional Flow Export Using IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC5103.summary: RFC 5103 defines a method for exporting bidirectional flows (Biflows) in IPFIX using a single Flow Record per Biflow, via a Reverse Information Element PEN and a new biflowDirection Information Element.

IPFIX.why: The document extends the IPFIX information model with Reverse Information Elements and biflowDirection, and specifies how Biflow records and templates are exported.
IPFIX.quote: describes an efficient method for exporting bidirectional flow (Biflow) information using the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol, representing each Biflow using a single Flow Record

rejected.why: Flow metering is the context, but the document is about IPFIX export encoding, which IPFIX already covers.
The PEN and Information Element assignments appear only in the IANA Considerations boilerplate, not as the main subject.
UDP is mentioned only for reliability of Options export; it is not a subject of the document.
The MIB tag is not relevant; IPFIX is the only management-related technology the document covers.

RFC5104.title: Codec Control Messages in the RTP Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback (AVPF)
RFC5104.summary: RFC 5104 defines Codec Control Messages (FIR, TSTR/TSTN, VBCM for H.271, TMMBR/TMMBN) as RTCP feedback extensions to AVPF, plus SDP "ccm" signalling, for conversational multimedia and centralized multipoint conferencing.

RTCP.why: The document's core content is new RTCP transport-layer and payload-specific feedback messages (FIR, TSTR, TSTN, VBCM, TMMBR, TMMBN) extending AVPF, with message formats, semantics and timing rules.
RTCP.quote: This memo specifies six new feedback messages.

SDP.why: A substantial section extends the SDP rtcp-fb attribute with the "ccm" value and its parameters, and specifies offer/answer rules and examples.
SDP.quote: In this document, we define a new feedback value "ccm", which indicates the support of codec control using RTCP feedback messages.

rejected.why: The messages are motivated by MCU/mixer-based multipoint conferencing, but the document specifies RTCP feedback messages, not a conferencing framework or control protocol.
TMMBR is explicitly not a substitute for congestion control; the document only requires that senders obey congestion control, in a short section.
H.264 is mentioned only as an example of codec decoder refresh points; the messages are codec-generic.
SIP is mentioned only as the heavier alternative and signalling path the messages avoid; the document does not specify SIP.
SRTP/SAVPF is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the feedback messages.

gaps.name: RTP Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback (AVPF) / RTCP feedback
gaps.why: The taxonomy has RTP and RTCP tags, but the first tag id I used above, "RTCP", is a child of RTP in the taxonomy and the tag id should be confirmed; AVPF itself has no dedicated tag.

RFC5105.title: ENUM Validation Token Format Definition
RFC5105.summary: Defines the ENUM Validation Token, a signed XML document (XML-DSIG) that a Validation Entity sends to a registry to certify that an ENUM domain registrant is the assignee of the E.164 number, with its fields and schemas.

ENUM.why: The document defines a token format for validating ENUM domain delegations against E.164 number assignment, so it belongs on the ENUM page.
ENUM.quote: An ENUM domain name is tightly coupled with the underlying E.164 number.

XML signatures.why: A substantial part of the document profiles XML-DSIG for the token: enveloped signature, exclusive canonicalization, mandatory algorithms and key sizes, and the signature checks a registry must make.
XML signatures.quote: The cryptographic signature on the token follows RFC 3275 (XML-DSIG [4]).

XML.why: The token is a new XML format defined by XML schemas, with registered namespaces and examples, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: Two schemas are defined: The "token core schema" contains mandatory attribute definitions, and the "token data schema" defines the format of the optional "tokendata" section.

rejected.why: EPP is only the protocol that may carry the token and is cited as informative. The document does not specify or extend it.
X.509 certificates may be embedded in the signature, but the document only relies on them. It does not profile them.
The token supports registry delegation decisions, but the document defines a data format rather than registry or registrar protocols.
RSA-SHA1 and RSA-SHA256 are required signature algorithms only through XML-DSIG. The document is not about RSA itself.
RFC 3339 full-date is merely used for the date fields.

RFC5106.title: The Extensible Authentication Protocol-Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (EAP-IKEv2) Method
RFC5106.summary: Specifies EAP-IKEv2, an experimental EAP method based on IKEv2 message formats providing mutual authentication, session key (MSK/EMSK) derivation, ciphersuite negotiation, fragmentation and fast reconnect.

EAP.why: The document defines a new EAP method with its message flows, key export (MSK/EMSK), Session-ID/Peer-ID/Server-ID, fast reconnect, and EAP security claims.
EAP.quote: This document specifies EAP-IKEv2, an EAP method that is based on the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2)

IKE.why: The method reuses IKEv2 payloads, SA negotiation, key derivation and CREATE_CHILD_SA rekeying, adapting them with deviations (new NFID payload, own payload registry), so IKEv2 readers would want it.
IKE.quote: The semantics and formats of EAP-IKEv2 messages are similar, albeit not identical, to those specified in IKEv2 [1]

rejected.why: Certificates are only an optional credential type carried in payloads; the document is not about PKI.
AAA infrastructure is mentioned only for realm routing of identities; not a subject of the document.
Key derivation is specific to the EAP method, already covered by the EAP tag.
IKEv2 is used as the basis, but no IPsec SAs are established or specified.
Exports MSK/EMSK per the EAP key management framework, but does not define handover keying or ERP.

RFC5107.title: DHCP Server Identifier Override Suboption
RFC5107.summary: Defines a new DHCP Relay Agent Information suboption (code 11, Server Identifier Override) letting a relay agent make the DHCP server set the Server Identifier to the relay's address so clients' RENEW DHCPREQUESTs pass through the relay.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 relay agent behaviour with a new suboption and specifies how servers and relays must handle it.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a new suboption of the DHCP relay information option that allows the DHCP relay to specify a new value for the Server Identifier option

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is mentioned only as a comparison, since its relay already behaves this way; the document is about DHCPv4.
DHCPv4 runs on IPv4, but the document does not address IPv4 itself.
The suboption number assignment is boilerplate IANA Considerations only.
Authentication of DHCP messages and relay agent information is mentioned only in Security Considerations.

RFC5109.title: RTP Payload Format for Generic Forward Error Correction
RFC5109.summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for generic XOR-parity forward error correction with Uneven Level Protection, including recovery procedures, media type registrations and SDP signalling, obsoleting RFC 2733 and RFC 3009.

FEC.why: The whole document defines an XOR-parity FEC scheme with unequal level protection, packet formats and recovery. It is a loss-recovery scheme for packet transport.
FEC.quote: This document specifies a payload format for generic Forward Error Correction (FEC) for media data encapsulated in RTP.

RTP payload format.why: It is an RTP payload format, with FEC packet structure, RTP header usage and ulpfec media types registered for RTP.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines a payload format for RTP [1] that allows for generic forward error correction of real-time media.

rejected.why: RTP is the carrier; the specific child tag RTP payload format covers the document's relation to it.
SDP is used for signalling the FEC stream (grouping, rtpmap, offer/answer), but this is a small section, not the document's subject.
Media type registrations for ulpfec exist but are IANA boilerplate-like registrations, not the main subject.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations.
The document predates and does not use the FEC Framework; it defines its own packet format.
The Congestion Considerations section is brief boilerplate-style guidance.

RFC5110.title: Overview of the Internet Multicast Routing Architecture
RFC5110.summary: Informational overview of deployed Internet multicast routing architectures (PIM variants, topology distribution, source discovery, RP configuration, redundancy, host interaction, link-layer flooding reduction), which also reclassifies BGMP, CBT and MOSPF to Historic.

multicast.why: The whole document is an architectural overview of multicast routing. It covers many protocols across the multicast subtree and has no single child tag that fits.
multicast.quote: This document describes multicast routing architectures that are currently deployed on the Internet.

PIM-SM.why: PIM-SM is the central protocol in the overview. RP configuration, anycast RP and source discovery are all discussed in its context.
PIM-SM.quote: By far, the most common multicast routing protocol is PIM-SM [RFC4601].

MSDP.why: MSDP is described as the de-facto IPv4 inter-domain source discovery mechanism and as a means of anycast RP redundancy.
MSDP.quote: Multicast Source Discovery Protocol [RFC3618] was invented as a stop-gap mechanism, when it became apparent that multiple PIM-SM domains

MOSPF.why: MOSPF is one of the protocols reclassified to Historic by this memo, and Section 2.1.5 discusses it.
MOSPF.quote: This memo reclassifies to Historic [RFC2026] the following RFCs:

SSM.why: SSM is covered as a source discovery model and in the host interaction summary.
SSM.quote: Source-specific Multicast [RFC4607] (sometimes also referred to as "single-source Multicast") does not count on learning active sources

IGMP.why: Host-to-router group membership signalling is a section of the overview. IGMP snooping and proxying are also discussed.
IGMP.quote: Hosts signal their interest in receiving a multicast group or channel by the use of IGMP [RFC3376] and MLD [RFC3810].

PIM.why: The document covers several PIM variants (PIM-DM, BIDIR-PIM, anycast-RP using PIM, BSR). These go beyond PIM-SM, so the PIM parent tag also applies.
PIM.quote: Bidirectional PIM [RFC5015] is a multicast forwarding protocol that establishes a common shared-path for all sources with a single root.

rejected.why: Multiprotocol BGP (SAFI=2) is described only briefly as a way to carry multicast topology information. The document is not about BGP.
MLD is mentioned alongside IGMP as the host signalling protocol, but only in passing.
PGM and reliable multicast appear only in a short appendix on router-assisted payload transport.
Multicast group security appears only as a brief appendix pointer to RFC 3740.
IS-IS multi-topology is mentioned only in one sentence on topology distribution.
Link-layer flooding reduction (IGMP snooping, CGMP, GMRP) is one section on Ethernet switch behaviour, not the document's subject.

RFC5111.title: Experiment in Exploratory Group Formation within the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
RFC5111.summary: Defines an RFC 3933 process experiment in which the IESG may charter short-lived Exploratory Groups as a step toward or between a BOF and Working Group formation.

IETF process.why: The whole document specifies an experimental change to the IETF working group formation procedure, including chartering, durations, milestones and success metrics.
IETF process.quote: This document describes an RFC 3933 [RFC3933] experiment in the Working Group (WG) formation process, known as the Exploratory Group (EG).

rejected.why: Unrelated to nominating committee procedures.
The document is about WG formation, not RFC format or publication.
No IANA registry content; the document has no IANA section.

RFC5112.title: The Presence-Specific Static Dictionary for Signaling Compression (Sigcomp)
RFC5112.summary: Defines a static, presence-specific dictionary (strings from PIDF and its extensions) loaded as a SigComp state so SigComp can compress SIP presence documents better from the first message.

SigComp.why: The document specifies a SigComp static dictionary, including its binary state item and STATE-ACCESS usage. It extends SigComp in the same way RFC 3485 does for SIP/SDP.
SigComp.quote: This memo defines the presence-specific static dictionary that SigComp can use in order to compress presence documents to achieve higher efficiency.

PIDF.why: The dictionary strings come from PIDF and its extensions (RPID, CIPID, timed status, partial PIDF). Readers of presence formats would want to find the dictionary.
PIDF.quote: The Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) [8] defines the format for the basic presence document that supplies presence information.

rejected.why: SIP is the protocol whose presence documents are being compressed. The document does not specify or extend SIP itself.
The dictionary covers SIMPLE-related XML formats (watcher info, filters, resource lists), but it is a compression dictionary and does not define those formats.
The strings come from XML-based documents, but the document does not specify XML usage.
DEFLATE is mentioned only as an example of an algorithm that benefits from string ordering. The dictionary is algorithm independent.
This is a general lossless data compression tag. SigComp is the more specific fit.

RFC5113.title: Network Discovery and Selection Problem
RFC5113.summary: Informational RFC defining the network discovery and selection problem for access networks (point-of-attachment discovery, identity/realm selection, AAA routing, capability discovery), outlining design constraints and the limitations of existing solutions such as RFC 4284 realm hints and 802.11 beacons.

AAA.why: A major part of the problem is AAA routing: realm routing tables, proxies, default-free zone, route selection policy and NAI source routing in RADIUS/Diameter roaming.
AAA.quote: AAA routing. This involves routing of the AAA conversation back to the home AAA server, based on the realm of the selected NAI.

EAP.why: Substantial analysis of EAP-based identity selection hints (realm hints), their scalability, latency and security limits, and EAP method downgrade risks.
EAP.quote: This is the problem that RFC 4284 [RFC4284] attempts to solve, using the EAP-Request/Identity to communicate a list of supported realms.

WiFi.why: Analyses 802.11 beacon/probe discovery, virtual APs and their scaling (channel utilisation calculation) as central to access network discovery.
WiFi.quote: In IEEE 802.11 Wireless Local Area Networks (WLAN), the Beacon and Probe Request/Response mechanism provides a way for Stations to discover Access Points

rejected.why: Mentioned as an AAA protocol in the roaming discussion but not specified or extended; covered by the AAA tag.
Discussed for its discovery and redirect features, but only as part of the AAA routing background, not the subject.
3GPP PLMN selection and I-WLAN appear only in an appendix survey of existing work.
The problem is network/realm discovery for access, which is not the generic service discovery subject; SLP is mentioned only in passing.
Mentioned only in passing as one of the WGs and in NAS terminology.

gaps.name: Network discovery and selection / access network selection
gaps.why: The document's central subject is choosing among access networks and realms, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC5114.title: Additional Diffie-Hellman Groups for Use with IETF Standards
RFC5114.summary: Defines eight additional Diffie-Hellman groups (three MODP, five ECP) with parameters and test data, and explains how to use them with X.509, IKE, TLS, SSH and S/MIME.

cryptography.why: The document's core content is cryptographic group parameters (MODP and elliptic-curve prime groups) and test data for Diffie-Hellman key agreement. No more specific child tag fits generic DH groups.
cryptography.quote: This document describes eight Diffie-Hellman groups that can be used in conjunction with IETF protocols to provide security for Internet communications.

IKE.why: A substantial section gives IKE transform IDs for each group and specifies the ECP key exchange format to use with IKEv1 and IKEv2. The IANA section also updates the IKE registries.
IKE.quote: In order to use a Diffie-Hellman group with IKE, it is required that a transform ID for the group be registered with IANA.

rejected.why: TLS is one of several protocols the groups can be used with. The section mapping curves to named-curve IDs is short and the document defines nothing new for TLS.
The SSH section only says that RFC 4419 already allows these groups. No new SSH specification is given.
The section only points to RFC 3279 for encoding DH keys in certificates.
The section only points to CMS and RFC 2631 for DH use and defines nothing new.
Five of the groups are NIST elliptic curves, but the document is about DH groups in general rather than elliptic-curve cryptography as a subject. The parent cryptography tag covers it.
The groups serve key agreement, but the document specifies group parameters rather than key management procedures.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman groups (MODP and ECP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Diffie-Hellman key agreement or group parameters. This is the main subject of the document, so the generic cryptography tag stands in for it.

RFC5115.title: Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) Attribute for Resource Priority
RFC5115.summary: Defines a new TRIP attribute, ResourcePriority, that advertises which SIP Resource-Priority NameSpaces (e.g., for GETS/GTPS emergency preferential service) are supported by PSTN gateways reachable via a TRIP gateway.

TRIP.why: The document extends TRIP with a new ResourcePriority attribute, specifying its flags, syntax, and route origination, aggregation and dissemination rules.
TRIP.quote: This document defines a new attribute for the Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) protocol.

SIP.why: The attribute is based on the SIP Resource-Priority header's NameSpace token, and a substantial part of the document explains that header's background and benefits.
SIP.quote: defines a new header for SIP called Resource-Priority. This new header, which is optional, is divided into two parts: a NameSpace and a Value.

rejected.why: The document concerns emergency/preferential-service priority, but it is a TRIP routing attribute, not emergency calling such as LoST or eCall.
TRIP is modeled after BGP-4, but BGP itself is not specified or extended here.
The gateways connect to the PSTN, but the document defines a routing attribute rather than gateway control or ISUP interworking.
The attribute is registered in an IANA registry, but that appears only in boilerplate IANA Considerations.
ABNF is used only to write the namespace syntax and is not the subject of the document.

RFC5116.title: An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption
RFC5116.summary: RFC 5116 defines a uniform interface for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD), guidance on nonce use, an IANA AEAD registry, and four AES-GCM and AES-CCM AEAD algorithms.

AES.why: The document defines AEAD_AES_128/256_GCM and AEAD_AES_128/256_CCM, specifying AES modes of operation, parameters and nonce-reuse consequences.
AES.quote: We populate this registry with four AEAD algorithms based on the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode [GCM] with 128- and 256-bit keys

cryptography.why: The AEAD interface, nonce requirements and algorithm specification requirements are general cryptography, not tied to one narrower tag; AES covers only the concrete algorithms.
cryptography.quote: This document defines algorithms for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD), and defines a uniform interface and a registry for such algorithms.

rejected.why: ESP with GCM/CCM is used only as an example of AEAD use and nonce format; the document is not about IPsec.
Mentioned as an example (Section 3.4) only; RFC 4106/4309 define the ESP usage.
The AEAD registry is created, but it is boilerplate-like and the subject is cryptographic, not IANA stewardship.
Only mentioned as a possible future generic composition in Other Considerations.
Nonce generation and uniqueness are discussed, but randomness requirements are not the subject; RFC 4086 is only referenced.

gaps.name: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for AEAD interfaces or AEAD algorithm registries, which is the document's central subject; cryptography and AES are the nearest fits.

RFC5117.title: RTP Topologies
RFC5117.summary: Informational RFC describing multi-endpoint RTP topologies (point-to-point, multicast, translators, mixers, video-switching and RTCP-terminating MCUs), mapping deployed conferencing MCUs to RTP terminology and comparing their properties.

RTP.why: The whole document clarifies RTP Translator and Mixer concepts, SSRC/CSRC handling and topology behaviours from RFC 3550.
RTP.quote: This document discusses multi-endpoint topologies used in Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)-based environments.

RTCP.why: Much of each topology discussion concerns how RTCP reports and feedback messages are forwarded, rewritten or terminated.
RTCP.quote: The RTCP translation process can be trivial, for example, when Transport Translators just need to adjust IP addresses

conferencing.why: Maps MCU-based multipoint conferencing topologies to RTP roles and compares their properties.
conferencing.quote: centralized topologies commonly employed in the video conferencing industry are mapped to the RTP terminology.

rejected.why: Only discussed in Security Considerations as an interaction with Mixers/Translators; not the subject of the document.
Multicast is one topology among several, used as a transmission model rather than the subject of routing/group management.
Mentioned only as the origin of deployed MCU models; the document is not about H.323.
Cited only for conference state signalling of contributing sources.

RFC5118.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Torture Test Messages for Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6)
RFC5118.summary: Informational companion to the SIP torture tests (RFC 4475) giving example SIP messages with IPv6 addresses (URIs, Via, SDP, IPv4-mapped, ABNF bug) to exercise IPv6-enabled SIP parsers.

SIP.why: The document consists of SIP test messages and parsing guidance for SIP implementations handling IPv6 references in headers and URIs.
SIP.quote: examples of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) test messages designed to exercise and "torture" the code of an IPv6-enabled SIP implementation

IPv6.why: All test cases concern IPv6 address representation (delimiters, ports, IPv4-mapped addresses, ABNF bug) in SIP, relevant to IPv6 deployment readers.
IPv6.quote: it tries to focus on areas that may cause interoperability problems in IPv6 deployments

rejected.why: SDP bodies appear in a few test messages with IPv6 addresses, but SDP itself is not specified or analysed.
SIP URI IPv6 references are tested, but this is within SIP parsing rather than URI syntax work.
The RFC 3261 ABNF is quoted and a bug discussed, but the document is not about the notation.
IPv6 address textual forms are used in tests, but the document does not address address architecture or allocation.

RFC5119.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE)
RFC5119.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "smpte" for persistent resources produced or managed by SMPTE, with a "ul" subnamespace for SMPTE Universal Labels.

URN.why: The document defines and registers a new URN namespace (NID smpte) with its structure, assignment, resolution and lexical equivalence rules, which is what the URN subject page covers.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) for naming persistent resources

rejected.why: Universal Labels are noted as ISO/IEC 8824-1 object identifiers, but only as an informative aside. The document is not about ASN.1.
ABNF is only the notation used to describe the identifier structure. The document is not about it.
The IANA section only records the NID registration, which is boilerplate. The namespace definition is the subject, not IANA registry guidance.
Despite the media industry context, the document concerns naming Universal Labels, not MIME types.

RFC5120.title: M-ISIS: Multi Topology (MT) Routing in Intermediate System to Intermediate Systems (IS-ISs)
RFC5120.summary: Specifies Multi-Topology (MT) extensions to IS-IS, adding TLVs for MT adjacency, reachability and prefixes, per-MT SPF computation, and forwarding/management considerations for running multiple independent IP topologies in one IS-IS domain.

IS-IS.why: The whole document extends IS-IS with new TLVs, adjacency rules and per-topology SPF computation.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes how to run, within a single IS-IS domain, a set of independent IP topologies that we call Multi-Topologies (MTs).

rejected.why: IPv6 prefixes are carried in one of the MT TLVs and an MT is reserved for IPv6 routing, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Multicast RPF topologies are mentioned only as one use case and reserved MT IDs, not as the subject.
The TE TLV encodings (RFC 3784) are reused as the basis for the MT TLVs, but TE is not the subject.
Not mentioned; the document is IS-IS only.
Section 9 briefly discusses in-band management topologies, but this is a minor part of the document.
The IANA section creates a registry for MT IDs, but that is boilerplate for this document, not its subject.

gaps.name: Multi-Topology Routing
gaps.why: The document's core subject is MT routing in IS-IS. The taxonomy has the IS-IS tech tag but no tag for multi-topology routing generally, and the document is also the basis for MT in other IGPs.

RFC5121.title: Transmission of IPv6 via the IPv6 Convergence Sublayer over IEEE 802.16 Networks
RFC5121.summary: Specifies how IPv6 is transmitted over the IP-specific part of the Packet Convergence Sublayer on IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) air interfaces, covering link model, prefix assignment, router discovery, MTU, addressing and MLD.

WiMAX.why: The whole document defines IPv6 operation over IEEE 802.16 via the IP CS, including WiMAX appendices on architecture, link and MTU.
WiMAX.quote: This document specifies the operation of IPv6 over the IEEE 802.16 air interface.
