rejected.why: The document is about IPv6 on a specific link layer, so the more specific WiMAX tag fits better. IPv6 is the carried protocol, not the subject.
Router discovery parameters are tuned for 802.16 (lifetime, MaxRtrAdvInterval), but this is a link-specific profile of RFC 4861 rather than a document about ND.
Addressing is specified only by reference to RFC 4862, with a small DAD note.
A single short section says MLDv2 SHOULD be supported; this is not a main subject.
GRE is used between BS and AR only in the WiMAX appendix as the tunnelling substrate.
DHCP is mentioned only as an optional prefix delegation and stateful configuration method.

RFC5122.title: Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs) and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) for the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)
RFC5122.summary: Defines the xmpp URI scheme and XMPP IRIs: their syntax, how to generate and process them, IRI/URI conversion, and IANA registration of the scheme, obsoleting RFC 4622.

URI.why: The document registers and specifies the xmpp URI scheme, with its syntax, semantics, generation and processing rules.
URI.quote: Formally defines the syntax for XMPP IRIs and URIs.

IRI.why: It defines an IRI form for XMPP addresses and the IRI-to-URI mapping and internationalization handling, so IRI readers need it.
IRI.quote: Specifies how to transform XMPP IRIs into URIs and vice versa.

XMPP.why: The identifiers address XMPP entities and define how applications generate stanzas from them, including query types for XMPP actions. It extends how XMPP entities are identified externally.
XMPP.quote: applications external to an XMPP network may need to identify XMPP entities either as URIs or, in a more modern fashion, as Internationalized Resource Identifiers

rejected.why: IDNA is relied on for the domain part of addresses, but the document defines nothing new about IDNs.
Unicode and stringprep are inherited from XMPP core and the IRI spec. The document only references them.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the syntax.
HTTP authentication is mentioned only as an analogy in the processing notes.
SASL appears only in the Security Considerations, as the mechanism XMPP uses for authentication.
DNS SRV is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as the way port numbers are discovered.

RFC5123.title: Considerations in Validating the Path in BGP
RFC5123.summary: Informational analysis of why validating the BGP AS Path is hard, examining route, destination and transit authorization and forwarding consistency under aggregation, filtering and interior/exterior path mismatches.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses BGP AS Path semantics, aggregation, policy and forwarding behaviour through worked BGP examples.
BGP.quote: This document examines the implications of hop-by-hop forwarding, route aggregation, and route filtering on the concept of validation within a BGP Autonomous System (AS) Path.

routing security.why: The motivation and analysis concern securing and validating routing information (path validation, authorization), a routing security topic. No specific mechanism such as RPKI or BGPsec is specified.
routing security.quote: the security of the information carried within routing systems running BGP, as described in [RFC4271], is being looked at with great interest.

rejected.why: The document evaluates concepts relevant to path validation schemes but does not specify or analyse BGPsec itself.
Origin authorization is explicitly declared out of scope, and RPKI is not discussed.
Route reflectors are only mentioned as a source of forwarding inconsistency; no real discussion.
Only cited as a reference on AS-level traceroute; not a subject of the document.
Aggregation and suballocation are discussed, but only as they affect authorization, not CIDR itself.

RFC5124.title: Extended Secure RTP Profile for Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)-Based Feedback (RTP/SAVPF)
RFC5124.summary: Defines the RTP/SAVPF profile, combining the Secure RTP profile (SAVP) with the RTCP-based feedback profile (AVPF), with rules for combining them, SDP negotiation, and interworking.

SRTP.why: The document defines a secure RTP profile that combines SRTP (SAVP) with feedback. It specifies SRTCP packet encapsulation, overhead, and key-usage rules.
SRTP.quote: this document specifies a new RTP profile ("SAVPF") that combines the features of SAVP and AVPF.

RTCP.why: The AVPF feedback profile is combined with SRTP. The document covers its effect on RTCP packet size and timing (avg_rtcp_size).
RTCP.quote: AVPF modifies timing rules for transmitting RTCP packets and adds extra RTCP packet formats specific to feedback.

SDP.why: A substantial part defines the SDP RTP/SAVPF proto, its profile negotiation via offer/answer, RTSP and SAP, and examples. It also registers the SDP proto name.
SDP.quote: The combined profile specified in this document is referred to as "SAVPF".

rejected.why: RTSP is only one of the ways the profile is negotiated (Section 3.3.2). The document does not specify or extend RTSP.
MIKEY is used only as the key management protocol in the examples. The document does not specify anything about it.
SIP is mentioned only as a carrier for SDP offer/answer in the examples.
The document only refers to RFC 4567 and RFC 4568 for keying and adds nothing on key management itself.

RFC5125.title: Reclassification of RFC 3525 to Historic
RFC5125.summary: Reclassifies RFC 3525 (Gateway Control Protocol Version 1, Megaco/H.248) to Historic because ITU-T H.248.1 has since been revised and superseded it.

Megaco.why: RFC 3525 specifies the Megaco/H.248 gateway control protocol. This document concerns its status and its relationship to later H.248.1 versions, so readers of the Megaco subject would want it.
Megaco.quote: The purpose of this document is to reclassify RFC 3525, Gateway Control Protocol Version 1, to Historic Status.

rejected.why: The document applies RFC 2026 to move an RFC to Historic. That is a one-off status change, not a document about the IETF process.
The IANA section only says the existing registries stay in force. The body is not about IANA.
MGCP is a related gateway control protocol but is not mentioned in the document.

RFC5126.title: CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures (CAdES)
RFC5126.summary: RFC 5126 defines CAdES, CMS-based advanced electronic signature formats (BES, EPES, -T, -C, -X, -A) using signed and unsigned attributes, time-stamps and validation data to keep signatures valid long-term and support non-repudiation.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS SignedData with new signed and unsigned attributes, defining the CAdES formats and their ASN.1 syntax.
CMS.quote: The format can be considered as an extension to RFC 3852 and RFC 2634, where, when appropriate, additional signed and unsigned attributes have been defined.

PKI.why: Substantial parts cover certification paths, revocation data, time-stamping authorities and attribute certificates for long-term validation.
PKI.quote: Validation data includes CA certificates as well as revocation status information in the form of Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) or certificate status information (OCSP)

rejected.why: S/MIME is only illustrated in an informative annex on MIME packaging; the document defines signature formats, not S/MIME.
OCSP responses are referenced and stored as validation data, but OCSP itself is not specified or extended.
X.509 certificates and CRLs are imported structures; the document does not profile them.
ASN.1 is just the notation for the definitions, not the subject.
MIME is only used for content typing in an informative annex.
Considered as a general topic, but the specific tags above cover the subject better.

gaps.name: Electronic signatures / long-term signature validation and time-stamping (RFC 3161 TSP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for digital signature formats, time-stamping or non-repudiation, which are central to this document.

RFC5127.title: Aggregation of Diffserv Service Classes
RFC5127.summary: Informational guidelines for aggregating RFC 4594 Diffserv service classes into four forwarding treatment aggregates (Network Control, Real-Time, Assured Elastic, Elastic), with an appendix mapping them onto MPLS E-LSP EXP values.

Diffserv.why: The whole document defines treatment aggregates of Diffserv service classes, their DSCP mappings and PHBs (CS, EF, AF, Default).
Diffserv.quote: This document provides guidelines for the aggregation of Diffserv service classes into forwarding treatments.

MPLS.why: Appendix A gives a recommended MPLS EXP field mapping for each treatment aggregate and discusses E-LSP and L-LSP, which is useful to MPLS Diffserv readers.
MPLS.quote: an example (in the appendix) of performing this aggregation over MPLS using E-LSP, EXP Inferred PHB Scheduling Class (PSC) Label Switched Path (LSP).

rejected.why: AQM/RED thresholds are used to configure the Assured Elastic aggregate, but AQM is not the subject of the document.
ECN is mentioned only as an alternative to dropping for marking excess traffic.
Diffserv is the more specific child tag under QoS and is already chosen.
VPLS is mentioned only as an example of a multipoint service with an unpredictable traffic pattern.
MPLS-based traffic engineering is mentioned only briefly as another control on offered traffic levels.

RFC5128.title: State of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Communication across Network Address Translators (NATs)
RFC5128.summary: Informational memo describing the techniques P2P applications use to establish direct TCP/UDP communication across NATs (relaying, connection reversal, UDP/TCP hole punching, port prediction), with observations and security advice.

NAT.why: The whole document is about NAT behaviour (endpoint mapping, filtering, hairpinning) and how applications traverse it.
NAT.quote: This memo documents the various methods known to be in use by applications to establish direct communication in the presence of Network Address Translators (NATs) at the current time.

NAT traversal.why: The techniques surveyed (hole punching, relaying, port prediction) are NAT traversal for peers, which the NAT traversal topic covers. The taxonomy's NAT traversal topic is framed around real-time media, but it is the closest fit for the traversal techniques.
NAT traversal.quote: UDP hole punching relies on the properties of EIM-NATs to allow appropriately designed peer-to-peer applications to "punch holes" through the NAT device(s)

P2P.why: The document is framed around peer-to-peer applications such as gaming and file sharing, with rendezvous servers and direct peer connections.
P2P.quote: The asymmetric addressing and connectivity regimes established by these NAT devices have created unique problems for peer-to-peer (P2P) applications and protocols

rejected.why: ICE is described only as related work and explicitly scoped out as a solution for a specific class of applications.
STUN is mentioned for terminology and as an ICE dependency, but it is not specified or analysed here.
TURN is mentioned once as a relay protocol; relaying is described generically.
TCP simultaneous open is used by TCP hole punching, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Teredo is mentioned briefly in the survey of recent work, and the document is not about it.
UDP is the substrate for the traversal techniques; the document does not cover UDP usage guidelines.

RFC5129.title: Explicit Congestion Marking in MPLS
RFC5129.summary: Defines how MPLS EXP field codepoints can encode explicit congestion notification (CM/Not-CM), with per-domain ECT checking and label push/pop procedures, plus an appendix extending to PCN marking.

ECN.why: The document specifies how ECN marking is encoded and processed in MPLS, including egress checking and copying CE into the IP header.
ECN.quote: This document defines how an operator might define some of the EXP codepoints for explicit congestion notification, without precluding other uses.

MPLS.why: It specifies use of the MPLS EXP field and LSR push/pop behaviour, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: Our intent is to specify how the MPLS shim header [RFC3032] should denote ECN marking

PCN.why: The appendix and Section 9.4 define AM/TM/NM codepoint handling for pre-congestion notification in MPLS.
PCN.quote: This appendix describes how the mechanisms described in the body of the document can be extended to support PCN [PCN].

Diffserv.why: The design is constrained by Diffserv E-LSP/L-LSP encodings of PHBs in EXP, and it covers tunnelling models and domain boundaries.
Diffserv.quote: [RFC3270] defines two possible approaches for requesting differentiated service treatment from an LSR:

rejected.why: TCP ECN-Echo/CWR is only mentioned as an example use; the document does not specify TCP.
Shayman's congestion-feedback TE is only a brief example application; the document does not specify it.
RSVP and NSIS appear only in descriptions of other proposals for PCN admission control.
RFC 4301 is cited only as consistent precedent for copying ECN into tunnel headers.
Section 7 compares MPLS behaviour with RFC 3168 IP tunnel modes, but the document is about MPLS rather than generic tunnelling.

RFC5130.title: A Policy Control Mechanism in IS-IS Using Administrative Tags
RFC5130.summary: Defines two new IS-IS sub-TLVs (32-bit and 64-bit Administrative Tags) attached to IP reachability TLVs so operators can control prefix distribution and redistribution policy across levels.

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol with new administrative tag sub-TLVs for IP prefix policy control, so it belongs on the IS-IS page.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines 2 new sub-TLVs for TLV 135, TLV 235, TLV 236 and TLV 237 that may be used to carry administrative information about an IP prefix.

rejected.why: BGP communities are mentioned only as an example use of the tags; the document does not specify or discuss them.
The sub-TLVs apply to IPv6 reachability TLVs 236 and 237, but only incidentally; the document is not about IPv6.
The document is about a specific IS-IS extension, not general routing architecture. The IS-IS tag already covers it.

RFC5131.title: A MIB Textual Convention for Language Tags
RFC5131.summary: Defines the LANGTAG-TC-MIB module with the LangTag SMIv2 textual convention for representing BCP 47 language tags in MIB modules, replacing the older LanguageTag convention from RFC 2932.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module defining a textual convention in SMIv2, to be imported by other MIB modules. Readers of MIB/SMI material would look for it.
MIB.quote: This MIB module defines a textual convention to represent BCP 47 language tags.

language tags.why: The convention constrains how BCP 47 language tags are represented (lowercase, well-formed, length limits), so language tag readers would find the representation rules useful.
language tags.quote: A language tag, constructed in accordance with BCP 47.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework through which MIB objects are accessed. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour.
The parent is implied by language tags, and the document is about a data-type representation, not internationalization of text in general.
The only IANA content is the mib-2 OID assignment in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate.

RFC5132.title: IP Multicast MIB
RFC5132.summary: Defines the IPMCAST-MIB SNMP MIB module (obsoleting RFC 2932) for managing IP multicast function and routing independent of the specific multicast protocol, covering IPv4/IPv6, SSM ranges, scope zones, and local listeners.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (IPMCAST-MIB) in SMIv2, with tables, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

multicast.why: The managed subject is IP multicast: routes, next hops, scope boundaries, listeners, TTL thresholds. Readers of multicast would want this.
multicast.quote: it describes objects used for managing multicast function, independent of the specific multicast protocol(s) in use.

SSM.why: A substantial table manages SSM address ranges, with IPv6 FF3x handling.
SSM.quote: The IP Multicast SSM Range Table, which contains one row per range of multicast group addresses to which Source-Specific Multicast semantics [RFC3569] should be applied.

rejected.why: PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM are only referenced in DESCRIPTION clauses as examples; the MIB is protocol-independent.
SNMP is merely the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB, which is tagged separately.
IPv6 addressing support is a feature of the objects, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Parent of MIB, implied by the MIB tag.

RFC5133.title: Terminal Endpoint Identifier (TEI) Query Request Number Change
RFC5133.summary: Updates RFC 4233 (ISDN Q.921-User Adaptation Layer, IUA) so that TEI Query Request messages use message type 8 instead of 5, avoiding a clash with the DUA DLC Status message type.

SIGTRAN.why: The document changes a message type value in IUA, a SIGTRAN ISDN signalling transport adaptation protocol. SIGTRAN covers IUA, so readers of that subject need this update.
SIGTRAN.quote: Terminal Endpoint Identifier (TEI) Query messages MUST be encoded with a message type of 8 instead of 5 as described in [RFC4233].
SIGTRAN.section: 3. New Message Type of the TEI Query Message

rejected.why: ISDN is the signalling environment IUA serves. The document is about the IUA message encoding over IP, not ISDN access, so SIGTRAN fits better.
This is the parent of SIGTRAN, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The IANA registry reservation is boilerplate for a one-value change. The document is not about IANA registries or guidance.

RFC5134.title: A Uniform Resource Name Namespace for the EPCglobal Electronic Product Code (EPC) and Related Standards
RFC5134.summary: Registers two formal URN namespaces, 'epc' (identifying physical objects such as GTIN/SGTIN, GLN, SSCC in the EPCglobal supply-chain system) and 'epcglobal' (naming XML schemas and system components), with registration templates.

URN.why: The document exists to register the 'epc' and 'epcglobal' URN namespaces, with structure, assignment, persistence and resolution templates.
URN.quote: a single Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace ID (NID) is being requested: 'epc'.

rejected.why: ONS resolution via DDDS is only mentioned for some sub-namespaces; the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
XML schema namespaces are named by 'epcglobal', but XML is just the context and the document does not specify XML usage.
Supply chain and e-commerce are the application context, but the document is about URN naming, not payment or trading protocols.
The IANA section merely notes the NID registrations; that is boilerplate, not the main subject.
ABNF is only used to define the syntax; the document is not about the notation.

gaps.name: EPCglobal Electronic Product Code / RFID supply chain identifiers
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for product identification systems (GTIN, SGTIN, EPC), which is the real-world subject of the identifiers being named.

RFC5135.title: IP Multicast Requirements for a Network Address Translator (NAT) and a Network Address Port Translator (NAPT)
RFC5135.summary: BCP defining requirements for NAT/NAPT devices doing IGMP proxying to correctly forward IP multicast (ASM and SSM) data and IGMP messages between inside and outside interfaces, including UDP mapping behaviour.

NAT.why: The document specifies NAT/NAPT behaviour requirements for multicast, as a companion to RFC 4787 unicast UDP requirements.
NAT.quote: This document specifies requirements for a for a Network Address Translator (NAT) and a Network Address Port Translator (NAPT) that support Any Source IP Multicast or Source-Specific IP Multicast.

multicast.why: Core subject is IP multicast forwarding and group membership handling through a NAT, covering ASM and SSM deployment.
multicast.quote: A NAT MUST forward IP multicast UDP datagrams from its 'outside' interface to multicast receivers on its 'inside' interface(s).

IGMP.why: A substantial section covers IGMPv1/v2/v3 support and proxying requirements for the NAT.
IGMP.quote: If a NAT supports IGMPv3, the NAT MUST implement IGMP/MLD Proxying [RFC4605].

SSM.why: SSM requirements (REQ-13) and the SSM application considerations appendix are a meaningful part of the document.
SSM.quote: If a NAT supports IGMPv3, the NAT MUST implement Source- Specific Multicast (SSM) for IP [RFC4607] and IGMPv3/MLDv2 for SSM [RFC4604].

rejected.why: RTP's SSRC collision and RTCP behaviour motivate REQ-14, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
Explicitly out of scope; the IGMP proxy devices do not forward PIM-SM.
UDP mapping timers are discussed within NAT behaviour, but the document is not about UDP itself.
Only mentioned as an example of address discovery and in the appendix; not a subject of the document.
Explicitly out of scope because NAT is not considered necessary with IPv6.
Mentioned only as an example of a non-UDP multicast protocol to be forwarded.

RFC5136.title: Defining Network Capacity
RFC5136.summary: RFC 5136 defines terminology and formulas for IP-layer link and path Capacity, Usage, Utilization and Available Capacity, as a common framework for capacity measurement techniques, building on the IPPM framework.

performance measurement.why: The document defines IP-layer capacity and available capacity metrics from the IPPM working group, which are network performance measurement quantities and the methods for reporting them.
performance measurement.quote: This document provides definitions for the terms 'Capacity' and 'Available Capacity' related to IP traffic traveling between a source and destination in an IP network.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an example of compression whose bits must be counted as uninflated; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only in the comparison with Bulk Transfer Capacity as the congestion-aware transport used there.
BTC comparison touches congestion-aware transport, but the document defines IP-layer capacity metrics, not congestion control.
The document defines metrics for paths in operation, not benchmarking methodology for devices.
Though definitional, the subject is network capacity metrics, which fits performance measurement more specifically.

RFC5137.title: ASCII Escaping of Unicode Characters
RFC5137.summary: BCP giving guidance on which ASCII escape syntax for Unicode code points new or internationalized IETF protocols should use, recommending code-point escapes with explicit delimiters (\u'NNNN' and &#xNNNN;) over UTF-8/UTF-16 octet or C/Perl/Java forms.

Unicode.why: The whole document is about how to escape Unicode code points in protocols, comparing code point versus UTF-8/UTF-16 escapes and recommending specific syntaxes.
Unicode.quote: Unicode represents characters as code points: numeric values from 0 to hex 10FFFF.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is discussed only as an alternative serialization whose octet escapes are discouraged. The document does not specify or profile UTF-8.
The parent topic is implied by the Unicode tag, so I did not list it separately.
The XML &#xNNNN; character reference is recommended as one presentation form, but the document is not about XML usage.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the syntax definitions.
Punycode is mentioned briefly as a comparable ACE encoding and nothing more.

RFC5138.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Commission for the Management and Application of Geoscience Information (CGI)
RFC5138.summary: Registers the "cgi" URN namespace identifier for the Commission for the Management and Application of Geoscience Information, defining its syntax, assignment authority (CGINA), and example URNs.

URN.why: The RFC is a URN namespace registration per RFC 3406, defining the NID "cgi", its syntax, persistence and assignment rules.
URN.quote: This document describes a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace that is engineered by the Commission for the Management and Application of Geoscience Information (CGI)

rejected.why: The IANA registry entry is boilerplate for this namespace registration; the document is not about IANA registry policy.
GeoSciML XML namespaces appear only as example URNs, not as a subject of the document.
URN is the more specific tag and covers this document; the parent is implied.

RFC5139.title: Revised Civic Location Format for Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO)
RFC5139.summary: Defines a revised XML civic address format for PIDF-LO, replacing RFC 4119's civic format with new CAtypes from the DHCP civic option, hierarchical road elements, xml:lang support and tighter value restrictions.

geolocation.why: The whole document specifies how civic location is represented in PIDF-LO. No more specific geolocation child tag fits, since HELD is about acquiring location and is not relevant here.
geolocation.quote: This document defines an XML format for the representation of civic location.

PIDF.why: The format is the civic address element of PIDF-LO and updates RFC 4119. Readers of PIDF would want it.
PIDF.quote: This format is designed for use with Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) documents and replaces the civic location format in RFC 4119.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document is an XML schema with design choices on token whitespace handling, xml:lang and namespace registration.
XML.quote: The XML schema defined for civic addresses allows for the addition of the "xml:lang" attribute to all elements except "country" and "PLC"

rejected.why: The DHCP civic address option (RFC 4776) is the source of the new types, but this document does not specify or extend DHCP. It only defines how to convert DHCP civic data into XML.
xml:lang is used with script subtags, but this is a minor feature and the document does not specify language tags or matching.
SIP and HTTP Accept-Language are mentioned only as an example of how language preferences might be conveyed.
The IANA section registers a namespace, a schema and CAtype updates, which is boilerplate and not the subject.

gaps.name: PIDF-LO / civic location format
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the GEOPRIV location object or civic address format. The geolocation topic is the closest match, and the PIDF tag only partly covers it.

RFC5140.title: A Telephony Gateway REgistration Protocol (TGREP)
RFC5140.summary: Specifies TGREP, a TRIP-derived protocol by which telephony gateways register prefixes, trunk groups, carriers and circuit-capacity/call-success information with a location server or signaling proxy, which can feed it into TRIP.

TRIP.why: The taxonomy's TRIP tag explicitly covers TRIP and the TGREP gateway registration protocol. This document defines TGREP, so this is the primary subject.
TRIP.quote: TGREP allows PSTN gateways or soft switches to inform a signaling server, such as a SIP proxy server or H.323 gatekeeper, of routes it has to the PSTN.

rejected.why: SIP proxies are only the signaling servers fronting the gateways. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
The TrunkGroup and Carrier syntax reuses parameters defined in tel/sip URI RFCs, but the document does not define anything new about the tel URI.
IPsec is used only for peering-session security, as described in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
H.323 gatekeepers are mentioned only as an alternative signaling proxy.
The document concerns gateway routing registration. TRIP is the more specific fit, and it already covers this.

RFC5141.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
RFC5141.summary: Registers and specifies the "iso" URN namespace, defining the syntax (originator, type, number, part, edition, version, language, supplements, document elements) for persistent identifiers of ISO standards documents and related resources, with resolution to http URIs.

URN.why: The document registers and defines a new URN namespace (NID "iso") with its NSS structure, equivalence rules, and resolution process.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name Namespace Identification (URN NID) for the International Organization for Standardization (ISO).

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the NSS grammar; the document is not about the notation.
The IANA section merely notes the NID assignment; boilerplate, not the subject.
ISO 639-1 language codes are used as an element in the identifier; the document does not address language tags themselves.
Resolution maps URNs to http URIs, but HTTP is only the substrate, not specified or extended.
Appendix A discusses the OID scheme only as a rejected alternative.

RFC5142.title: Mobility Header Home Agent Switch Message
RFC5142.summary: Defines a new Mobility Header message (Home Agent Switch, MH type 12) in Mobile IPv6 that lets a home agent tell a mobile node to stop using it and acquire a new home agent, with sender and receiver procedures.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) with a new Mobility Header message and specifies home agent and mobile node behaviour for it.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document specifies a new Mobility Header message type that can be used between a home agent and mobile node to signal to a mobile node that it should acquire a new home agent.

rejected.why: ESP security associations protect the message, but they are only the security mechanism relied on, not the subject.
The document only requires existing ESP SAs for integrity and confidentiality and defines nothing new about ESP.
Home agent renumbering is one scenario, but the document does not address site renumbering procedures.
The message carries IPv6 addresses, but the subject is Mobile IPv6 mobility signalling, not IPv6 itself.
The IANA section only assigns the new MH type value and is boilerplate.

RFC5143.title: Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) Circuit Emulation Service over MPLS (CEM) Encapsulation
RFC5143.summary: Historic RFC specifying a CEM encapsulation (header, DBA, maintenance signal mapping, clocking, LDP signaling) for carrying SONET/SDH SPE circuits over MPLS or IP packet networks, superseded by RFC 4842.

pseudowire.why: The document defines a circuit emulation pseudowire encapsulation for SONET/SDH over MPLS/IP, signalled with the PWE3 PW Type and the LDP PWid FEC.
pseudowire.quote: MPLS labels and a new circuit emulation header are used to encapsulate TDM signals and provide the Circuit Emulation Service over MPLS (CEM) function.

SONET.why: A large part of the document covers SONET/SDH SPE fragmentation, pointer adjustments, AIS-P and unequipped maintenance signals, and rates and formats (Appendix A).
SONET.quote: This document describes a historical method for encapsulating SONET/SDH Path signals for transport across packet-switched networks (PSNs).

rejected.why: MPLS is the transport substrate for the encapsulation; the document's subject is pseudowire circuit emulation, which is a child of MPLS in the taxonomy and is already tagged.
LDP with the PWid FEC from RFC 4447 is used only for signalling in a short section, and the document defines nothing new about LDP itself.
The IP transport option just refers to RFC 4023 for carrying MPLS over IP and does not specify any new tunnelling mechanism.
ECMP is mentioned only in a note about the header's conflict with RFC 4928, which is incidental.
The ECC-6 header error correction code is a Hamming-style code, not a CRC polynomial.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation
gaps.why: The document is about circuit emulation of TDM (SONET/SDH) services over packet networks. The pseudowire tag covers it only approximately.

RFC5144.title: A Domain Availability Check (DCHK) Registry Type for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS)
RFC5144.summary: Defines the DCHK registry type for IRIS, a lightweight domain availability check service whose data model is a strict subset of the DREG schema, with an XML schema, entity lookups, URI resolution and registrations.

domain registration.why: The document specifies a domain availability service reporting registration status (active, reserved, grace periods, etc.) for domain registries. No tech tag for IRIS exists, so the parent domain registration topic fits.
domain registration.quote: This document describes a lightweight service for checking the availability of domain names.

rejected.why: Domain names and DNS availability are only the subject matter of the lookup; the document does not specify DNS protocol behaviour.
XML Schema is the notation used to define the registry schema, i.e. a substrate, not the subject.
BEEP is an optional transport, only referenced by default message pattern and authentication; nothing new is defined about it.
IRIS/DREG is a successor to WHOIS-type services but this document does not specify WHOIS or legacy directory services.
The idn element and nameprep form are mentioned only as data fields, not as the document's subject.
Only references EPP grace period statuses from RFC 3915; the document does not specify EPP.

gaps.name: IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service)
gaps.why: The document is a registry type for IRIS, a CRISP-WG protocol framework, but the taxonomy has no IRIS tag; domain registration is the closest fit.

RFC5145.title: Framework for MPLS-TE to GMPLS Migration
RFC5145.summary: Informational framework describing migration models (island, integrated, phased) and an interworking toolkit (layering, routing, signaling, PCE) for evolving an MPLS-TE control plane to GMPLS.

GMPLS.why: The whole document concerns migrating to GMPLS and the MPLS-TE/GMPLS interworking this requires, so GMPLS is the primary subject.
GMPLS.quote: Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) to Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) migration is the process of evolving an MPLS-TE-based control plane to a GMPLS-based control plane.

PCE.why: PCE is presented as one tool in the migration toolkit for computing paths across layers. The section is short, so the role is secondary.
PCE.quote: The Path Computation Element (PCE) [RFC4655] may provide an additional tool to aid MPLS to GMPLS migration.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE signaling is what is being interworked, but the document specifies no extensions to it. It is discussed only as part of the GMPLS migration.
The routing interworking discussion refers to IGP TE extensions generally (OSPF-TE and IS-IS TE) without being about either protocol.
MPLS-TE is the starting point of the migration. The GMPLS tag sits under MPLS and fits more specifically, and the document is about moving off MPLS-TE.
TE is the context for MPLS-TE and GMPLS. The document does not address traffic engineering as a subject in its own right.
GRE is mentioned once as a possible tunnel between island border nodes and is not a subject of the document.
The manageability section briefly notes that GMPLS MIBs build on MPLS MIBs. This is incidental.

RFC5146.title: Interworking Requirements to Support Operation of MPLS-TE over GMPLS Networks
RFC5146.summary: Informational framework and Service Provider requirements for operating an MPLS-TE client network over a GMPLS server network, recommending the Border Peer Model with hierarchical LSPs.

GMPLS.why: The whole document concerns interworking of MPLS-TE with a GMPLS server network, including triggered GMPLS LSP setup, border routers and the Border Peer Model.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes a framework and Service Provider requirements for operating MPLS-TE networks over GMPLS networks.

MPLS.why: MPLS-TE LSPs, Fast Reroute, hierarchical LSPs and stitching in the client network are substantial parts of the requirements and architecture.
MPLS.quote: MPLS-TE network connectivity is provided through a GMPLS LSP which is created between Border Routers.

rejected.why: PCE is only mentioned briefly as a possible aid for inter-layer path computation, not a subject of the document.
RSVP-TE signalling is referenced indirectly via LSP setup and FRR but the document does not specify or extend it.
FRR is discussed only as a protection requirement for MPLS-TE LSPs over GMPLS; this tag is about IP/LDP fast reroute and loop-free alternates.
The more specific GMPLS and MPLS tags cover it; the document is not a general traffic engineering treatment.
GRE is just a suggested tunnelling mechanism for control plane connectivity in one sentence.

RFC5147.title: URI Fragment Identifiers for the text/plain Media Type
RFC5147.summary: RFC 5147 defines URI fragment identifiers for the text/plain media type, allowing references to character or line positions and ranges, with optional length or MD5 integrity checks, and updates RFC 2046.

URI.why: The document specifies a fragment identifier syntax and processing rules for URIs that point into text/plain resources. Readers of the URI subject would look for it.
URI.quote: This memo defines URI fragment identifiers for text/plain MIME entities.

media types.why: It updates the text/plain media type registration with a fragment identification method, and IANA adds a reference to the registration. Media type registration readers would want it.
media types.quote: This memo updates the text/plain media type defined in RFC 2046 [3] by defining URI fragment identifiers for text/plain MIME entities.

rejected.why: MD5 is only used as an optional integrity-check value. The document does not specify or analyse MD5 itself.
ABNF is only the notation for the syntax definition, so the document is not about it.
The document leans on MIME entities, but it does not define body structure or encodings. The media types tag fits better.
IRIs appear only as a reference in the Security Considerations section.
HTTP is mentioned only in examples and in the discussion of line endings. The document does not extend it.
Character encoding affects how characters are counted, but the document does not register or define character sets.

RFC5148.title: Jitter Considerations in Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs)
RFC5148.summary: Informational RFC giving recommendations for randomly jittering timing of periodic, triggered, and forwarded control message transmissions in MANET routing protocols to reduce wireless collisions.

MANET.why: The whole document is guidance for MANET routing protocols on applying jitter to control message generation and forwarding. It is generalized from OLSR's jitter mechanism, and readers of MANET routing would want it.
MANET.quote: provides recommendations for jittering (randomly modifying timing) of control traffic transmissions in Mobile Ad hoc NETwork (MANET) routing protocols to reduce the probability of transmission collisions

rejected.why: OLSR is the source the jitter mechanism was generalized from and is cited as an example. The document does not specify or extend OLSR.
AODV is mentioned only as an example of a reactive protocol that uses event-triggered messages.
Jitter here means deliberate random timing variation to avoid collisions, not a measured network performance metric.
The word jitter might suggest RTP jitter or buffering, but the document is not about real-time media.

RFC5149.title: Service Selection for Mobile IPv6
RFC5149.summary: Defines a Service Selection Mobility Option for Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6 Binding Updates, letting a home agent choose and authorize a specific service for a mobility subscription, plus a new status code.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document specifies a new Mobile IPv6 mobility option and status code used in binding registration, with mobile node, home agent and correspondent node processing rules.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document describes a Service Selection Mobility Option for Mobile IPv6 that is intended to assist home agents to make specific service selections

PMIPv6.why: The option is explicitly designed to also be used by the Proxy Mobile IPv6 client in Binding Updates, a substantial part of the scope.
PMIPv6.quote: a Service Selection Mobility Option for both conventional Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6

rejected.why: ESP and IKEv2 are only mentioned for confidentiality and identification; the document is not about IPsec.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the identifier string, a substrate detail.
The IANA section merely records the option type and status code assignments, which is boilerplate.
Authorization of the service by the home agent is described only briefly and is not about an AAA framework.
QoS treatment is only mentioned as a possible effect of the selected service.

RFC5150.title: Label Switched Path Stitching with Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering (GMPLS TE)
RFC5150.summary: RFC 5150 defines LSP stitching for GMPLS TE: it extends RSVP-TE signaling (new LSP_ATTRIBUTES/RRO flags and an error code) and routing advertisement so that an end-to-end LSP is built from LSP segments joined in the data plane, and compares this with LSP hierarchy.

GMPLS.why: The document specifies GMPLS TE extensions for stitching LSP segments into end-to-end LSPs, covering both signaling and routing aspects, so it is squarely about GMPLS.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes extensions to the existing GMPLS signaling protocol (Resource Reservation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP- TE)) to establish e2e LSPs created from S-LSPs

RSVP-TE.why: A substantial part of the document extends RSVP-TE with a new attribute flag, an RRO flag, an error sub-code, and Path, Resv and teardown procedures for stitched LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: In order to request LSP stitching on the S-LSP, we define a new bit in the Attributes Flags TLV of the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object

rejected.why: The document is about GMPLS, a child of MPLS. Tagging GMPLS covers it, and the ancestor is implied.
RSVP-TE is the more specific tag that applies, and the document gives no general treatment of traffic engineering beyond it.
OSPF-TE and ISIS-TE are mentioned only as the way to flood S-LSP TE link information. The document defines nothing new for them.
PCE is cited only in passing as a way to compute inter-domain paths. The document does not specify or extend it.
IPsec appears only in the Security Considerations, which are boilerplate-like and do not make the document about IPsec.
The document extends RSVP-TE specifically, which sits under traffic engineering. It does not extend the general RSVP QoS protocol.

RFC5151.title: Inter-Domain MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering -- Resource Reservation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) Extensions
RFC5151.summary: Defines RSVP-TE procedures and extensions (a Contiguous LSP attribute flag and new error codes) for border nodes to signal, protect, and reoptimize inter-domain MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs using contiguous, nested, or stitched methods.

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies RSVP-TE extensions (new Attributes Flags bit, error codes) and border-node procedures for inter-domain LSP signaling.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document describes procedures and protocol extensions for the use of Resource Reservation Protocol-Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) signaling

GMPLS.why: The procedures apply to GMPLS LSPs, including segment recovery, nesting via hierarchy and Notify handling, and the document updates RFC 3473.
GMPLS.quote: Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) packet and non-packet networks to support the establishment and maintenance of Label Switched Paths that cross domain boundaries

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen tags; implied.
Path computation is explicitly out of scope; PCE is only mentioned as an option.
Fast Reroute (RFC 4090) is discussed in the protection section but only as applied without extensions; not the focus.
Parent of RSVP-TE; implied.
ASBRs and ASes are mentioned only as examples of domains.

RFC5152.title: A Per-Domain Path Computation Method for Establishing Inter-Domain Traffic Engineering (TE) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC5152.summary: Specifies a per-domain path computation method, using loose-hop ERO expansion at boundary LSRs, for establishing inter-area and inter-AS MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs, including optimality, diversity and reoptimization considerations.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document defines how inter-domain TE LSP paths are computed per domain, covering ERO expansion, crankback, diversity and reoptimization. It is a traffic engineering path computation method.
traffic engineering.quote: a per-domain path computation technique for establishing inter-domain Traffic Engineering (TE) Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

MPLS.why: The document covers MPLS and GMPLS LSP establishment procedures: contiguous, stitched and nested LSPs, H-LSP/S-LSP, and boundary LSR behaviour. Readers of MPLS would want it.
MPLS.quote: The inter-domain TE LSPs are signaled using RSVP-TE ([RFC3209] and [RFC3473]).

rejected.why: PCE-based computation is mentioned only as an alternative technique. The document specifies a per-domain method that does not use PCE.
RSVP-TE is the signaling substrate. The procedures are defined in RFC 3209 and RFC 5151, not here. The document only specifies path computation.
GMPLS is mentioned as applicable, but the document is not about GMPLS-specific mechanisms.
OSPF-TE and IS-IS TE are assumed as the IGP substrate. The document does not extend them.
BGP is only a source of reachability for auto-discovery of boundary nodes. It is not the subject.

RFC5153.title: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Implementation Guidelines
RFC5153.summary: Informational implementation guidelines for the IPFIX protocol covering template management, exporter/collector behaviour, SCTP/UDP/TCP transport issues, middlebox deployment, TLS/DTLS security use, information model extension, and common mistakes (including NetFlow v9 differences).

IPFIX.why: The whole document is implementation guidance for IPFIX: templates, exporting and collecting processes, transport, middleboxes, and information elements.
IPFIX.quote: This document provides guidelines for the implementation and use of the IPFIX protocol.

rejected.why: SCTP and PR-SCTP are discussed as IPFIX transport options, but the document is about IPFIX use of them, not SCTP itself.
UDP template refresh and sizing guidance is IPFIX-specific transport usage, not about UDP.
TCP is only a transport option for IPFIX.
TLS/DTLS is the security substrate for IPFIX; there is no new TLS extension.
DTLS is used as the security mechanism for IPFIX over UDP and SCTP, not specified or extended here.
NAT and other middleboxes are discussed only as places where IPFIX measurement is deployed.
Firewalls appear as middlebox examples for IPFIX reporting; the document is not about firewall security.

RFC5154.title: IP over IEEE 802.16 Problem Statement and Goals
RFC5154.summary: Problem statement and goals document describing the gaps in running IPv4/IPv6 over IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) MACs, covering the convergence sublayers, IP subnet link models, and goals for IETF work.

WiMAX.why: The whole document is about IP over IEEE 802.16: MAC overview, convergence sublayers, link models, and per-CS problems and goals.
WiMAX.quote: This document specifies problems in running IP over IEEE 802.16 networks by identifying specific gaps in the IEEE 802.16 Media Access Control (MAC) for IPv4 and IPv6 support.

rejected.why: Address resolution, router discovery, NUD and DAD are discussed as problems over 802.16, but the document does not specify or extend neighbor discovery itself.
ARP is mentioned only as not applicable to the IP CS and as a multicast source in the Ethernet CS. The document is not about ARP.
The Ethernet CS is part of 802.16 and is covered under WiMAX. The document is not about IP over Ethernet in its own right.
PPP is mentioned only as an unavailable option for the point-to-point link model.
IPv6 matters here only as one of the IP versions carried over 802.16. IPv6 is not specified, extended or analysed in its own right.
SEND appears only as goal #4, applicability of security schemes. The document does not address SEND itself.

RFC5155.title: DNS Security (DNSSEC) Hashed Authenticated Denial of Existence
RFC5155.summary: RFC 5155 specifies the NSEC3 and NSEC3PARAM DNS resource records, which give DNSSEC authenticated denial of existence using hashed owner names to prevent zone enumeration, and which add an Opt-Out flag for delegation-centric zones.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document defines a DNSSEC extension: the NSEC3 and NSEC3PARAM RRs, how signers, servers and validators use them, and how a zone moves between NSEC and NSEC3.
DNSSEC.quote: This document introduces an alternative resource record, NSEC3, which similarly provides authenticated denial of existence.

rejected.why: DNS is the parent of DNSSEC, so it is implied by the DNSSEC tag. The document does not address DNS in general.
Section 7.5 covers dynamic update only as it affects NSEC3 zones. It is a minor consideration, not a substantial part of the document.
SHA-1 is only the hash algorithm used for NSEC3 hashing. The document does not specify or analyse SHA.
The IANA section creates registries for NSEC3 flags and hash algorithms. This is boilerplate for the tags, not the subject of the document.

RFC5156.title: Special-Use IPv6 Addresses
RFC5156.summary: Informational compilation of special-use IPv6 address blocks defined in other RFCs, serving as a checklist of prefixes that should be filtered from routes and packets on the public Internet.

addressing.why: The document catalogs special-purpose IPv6 address blocks (loopback, link-local, ULA, documentation, multicast, etc.) and their routing treatment, which is IP address architecture and use. No more specific technology tag fits the address compilation itself.
addressing.quote: This document is a compilation of special IPv6 addresses defined in other RFCs.

IPv6.why: The whole document is about IPv6 address space and its special blocks, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: ::FFFF:0:0/96 are the IPv4-mapped addresses [RFC4291].  Addresses within this block should not appear on the public Internet.

routing security.why: The stated purpose is route and packet filtering of invalid prefixes, which is a routing hygiene and security concern.
routing security.quote: It can be used as a checklist of invalid routing prefixes for developing filtering policies for routes and IP packets.

rejected.why: 6to4 and Teredo prefixes are only listed as entries in the checklist, with filtering notes; the document does not specify or extend those mechanisms.
Only one entry (2001::/32) in the list; the document is not about the Teredo protocol.
It refers to the IANA special-purpose registry and adds a header note, but the body is about the addresses, not registry administration.
The transition mechanisms are mentioned only as sources of special prefixes.
Route filtering is relevant to BGP but the document does not discuss BGP itself.

RFC5157.title: IPv6 Implications for Network Scanning
RFC5157.summary: Informational document analysing how IPv6's large 64-bit subnets limit traditional network scanning, how attackers may still discover IPv6 addresses, and how administrators can mitigate via address allocation choices.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 addressing and deployment implications: subnet size, address numbering, and how these affect scanning. No more specific IPv6 child tag covers the whole subject.
IPv6.quote: The 128 bits of IPv6 [1] address space is considerably bigger than the 32 bits of address space in IPv4.

operational security.why: It gives administrators defence-in-depth guidance on site address allocation and management to mitigate scanning and worm propagation.
operational security.quote: administrators should be aware that attackers may use other techniques to discover IPv6 addresses on a target network

SLAAC.why: EUI-64 SLAAC addresses shrink the scan search space, and privacy addresses, CGAs and random interface identifiers are discussed as mitigations. A substantial part of the document concerns this.
SLAAC.quote: in the case of statelessly autoconfiguring [1] hosts, the host part of the address will usually take a well-known format that includes the Ethernet vendor prefix

rejected.why: Section 5.4 only suggests configuring DHCPv6 pools with non-sequential addresses. It is a mitigation option, not the subject.
DNS-published hosts and zone transfers are discussed as address-discovery channels, but the document does not specify or analyse DNS itself.
Section 3.7 notes that 6to4, ISATAP and Teredo reveal address patterns, but this is a brief mention.
Privacy addresses are discussed as a scan mitigation, not as a privacy threat-model topic.
SEND and CGAs get a two-sentence mention as a way to enlarge the search space.
Multicast group addresses are mentioned only as an address-leak vector.

gaps.name: Network scanning / port scanning and worm propagation
gaps.why: The document's central subject is scanning and worm address discovery. The taxonomy has no tag for scanning or attack techniques, so it is covered only loosely by operational security.

RFC5158.title: 6to4 Reverse DNS Delegation Specification
RFC5158.summary: Informational RFC describing a web-based service that lets 6to4 sites enter DNS delegations for their reverse zone under 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa, authenticated by 6to4 source address and updated via dynamic DNS.

6to4.why: The document is about operating reverse DNS for 6to4 addresses, with authorization tied to the 6to4 address prefix. It belongs on the 6to4 page.
6to4.quote: This memo describes the service mechanism for entering a delegation of DNS servers that provide reverse lookup of 6to4 IPv6 addresses into the 6to4 reverse zone file.

DNS.why: It specifies reverse-zone delegation structure, NS/SOA consistency checks, low TTLs and zone operation, which are DNS operations.
DNS.quote: This specification uses a single delegation level in the 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa zone, delegating zones only at the 48th bit position.

rejected.why: Dynamic updates (RFC 2136) are only the mechanism used to edit the zone; the document defines nothing new about them.
TLS only secures the web delegation interface; it is a substrate and nothing new is defined about it.
The web interface is just the access channel for the service, not the subject.
6to4 is the more specific child tag and already covers this; the parent should not be listed.
The document only says it does not compromise DNS security functions; it does not discuss signing or validation.
The IANA section only notes the delegation of 2.0.0.2.ip6.arpa; it is boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC5159.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Attributes for Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) Broadcast (BCAST) Service and Content Protection
RFC5159.summary: Informational RFC describing four new SDP attributes (bcastversion, stkmstream, SRTPAuthentication, SRTPROCTxRate) used by OMA BCAST service and content protection, and registering them with IANA.

SDP.why: The document defines and registers new SDP attributes, so it extends SDP; readers of SDP attributes would want it.
SDP.quote: several new SDP attributes are necessary to allow the broadcast server to signal the service and content protection parameters to clients

SRTP.why: Two of the four attributes (SRTPAuthentication, SRTPROCTxRate) configure SRTP authentication transforms and ROC transmission rate for protected broadcast media.
SRTP.quote: When SRTP is used, the attribute SRTPAuthentication states which authentication algorithm to use.

rejected.why: The IANA registrations are the mechanism for publishing the attributes, not a document about IANA registries or guidance.
Content protection key streams (STKM) are mentioned, but the document only defines SDP signalling attributes, not group key management.
MBMS/BCMCS are named only as systems expected to use OMA BCAST; the document does not address cellular networking.
The stkmstream attribute only maps key message streams to media streams; key management itself is specified by OMA.

gaps.name: OMA BCAST mobile broadcast service and content protection
gaps.why: The document's subject is the Open Mobile Alliance broadcast protection system (STKM streams, MBMS/BCMCS/DVB-H); the taxonomy has no tag for mobile broadcast services.

RFC5160.title: Considerations of Provider-to-Provider Agreements for Internet-Scale Quality of Service (QoS)
RFC5160.summary: Informational memo analysing provider-to-provider inter-domain QoS agreements, arguing for single-domain guarantees and introducing the Meta-QoS-Class (MQC) concept and MQC planes for an Internet-scale QoS framework.

QoS.why: The whole document is a framework for inter-domain QoS agreements, defining l-QCs and Meta-QoS-Classes. No specific QoS protocol tag fits, so the QoS topic is the right level.
QoS.quote: This memo analyzes provider-to-provider Quality of Service (QoS) agreements suitable for a global QoS-enabled Internet.

rejected.why: BGP is assumed as the peering and inter-domain routing substrate, and Section 7 only suggests it could carry QoS values. The document specifies nothing about BGP.
Diffserv and PDBs are mentioned only to relate an l-QC to a PDB. MQC is explicitly indifferent to how networks are engineered.
RSVP-TE/MPLS-TE is mentioned in one sentence as a possible mechanism for route pinning.
The (D, J, L) metrics reference the IPPM RFCs only as parameters for defining classes. The document does not address measurement.
Section 7 touches on QoS routing using BGP, but this is a secondary discussion within a QoS agreement framework.

gaps.name: inter-domain QoS / provider interconnection agreements (Meta-QoS-Class)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is inter-provider QoS business and technical agreements. The taxonomy has only the general QoS topic and no inter-domain QoS or peering-agreement tag.

RFC5161.title: The IMAP ENABLE Extension
RFC5161.summary: RFC 5161 defines the IMAP ENABLE command and ENABLED response, letting an IMAP client explicitly tell the server which extensions (currently only CONDSTORE) it supports.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP extension (ENABLE command, ENABLED response, capability) and is entirely about IMAP protocol behaviour.
IMAP.quote: The ENABLE extension allows an IMAP client to say which extensions it supports.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax; the document isn't about it.
IMAP is already the specific tag; the parent is implied.
The IANA section only adds ENABLE to the IMAP capabilities registry, which is boilerplate.
No media type registration is involved; it was considered only because of the registry reference.

RFC5162.title: IMAP4 Extensions for Quick Mailbox Resynchronization
RFC5162.summary: Defines the IMAP QRESYNC extension, which lets a reconnecting client resynchronize a mailbox in a single SELECT/EXAMINE round-trip, and adds the VANISHED response, the VANISHED UID FETCH modifier and the CLOSED response code.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to IMAP: a new SELECT/EXAMINE parameter, a UID FETCH modifier, the VANISHED response, and updates to EXPUNGE, CLOSE and UID EXPUNGE.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an IMAP4 extension, which gives an IMAP client the ability to quickly resynchronize any previously opened mailbox as part of the SELECT command

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag. The document is not about email architecture generally.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax in Section 6. The document is not about ABNF.
Not a taxonomy tag. Mobile clients are only mentioned as a motivating use case.

RFC5163.title: Extension Formats for Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) and the Generic Stream Encapsulation (GSE)
RFC5163.summary: Defines three Extension Headers (TS-Concat, PDU-Concat, TimeStamp) for ULE and GSE, the encapsulations for carrying IP over MPEG-2 TS and DVB-S2 Generic Streams.

DVB.why: The document specifies extension formats for ULE and GSE, the IP encapsulations over MPEG-2/DVB links, including DVB-S2 Generic Stream. DVB is the closest taxonomy tag.
DVB.quote: This document describes a set of Extension Headers for the Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE), RFC 4326.

rejected.why: DVB-S2 is a satellite physical layer, but the document is about encapsulation framing for DVB broadcast links, not satellite networking issues.
IPv4/IPv6 packets are only mentioned as PDUs that may be concatenated; nothing IPv6-specific is defined.
The TimeStamp extension may support monitoring and benchmarking, but it is a minor part of the document and not a measurement method.
CRC-32 appears only as part of the ULE/GSE SNDU format and is not what the document specifies.
The IANA section registers Next-Header values, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
ULE is an encapsulation, but it is a link-layer encapsulation for DVB, not IP-in-IP or generic tunnelling.

gaps.name: ULE / GSE (Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation / Generic Stream Encapsulation)
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is the ULE/GSE encapsulation and its extension header mechanism. The taxonomy has only the broader DVB tag (IP over MPEG-2/DVB), so a dedicated ULE/GSE tag would fit better.

RFC5164.title: Mobility Services Transport: Problem Statement
RFC5164.summary: Informational problem statement for a generic Mobility Services Transport protocol that carries IEEE 802.21 MIH handover signalling over IP, covering discovery, security, latency, reliability, congestion control, fragmentation, multihoming and IPv4/IPv6 requirements.

IP mobility.why: The document is about transporting handover-support signalling (MIH) for heterogeneous IP handover, complementing Mobile IP and related mobility mechanisms. It fits IP mobility better than any specific child.
IP mobility.quote: The mobility support services are complementary to IP mobility mechanisms [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9] to enhance the overall performance and usability perception.

transport.why: A large part of the document sets out requirements for a generic transport layer: reliability, congestion control, fragmentation, low latency and multihoming.
transport.quote: The Mobility Service Transport Layer provides certain functionality (outlined in Section 5.2) to the higher-layer mobility support services

rejected.why: IEEE 802.21 handover spans heterogeneous links, and 3GPP is only cited as a reference. The document is not about cellular networks.
No transport protocol is chosen or analysed. The document explicitly takes no position on which protocol to use.
UDP usage guidelines are cited only as input for the reliability and congestion control discussion, so the document is not about UDP.
Discovery of mobility service nodes is one requirement among many, and the document defers to existing directory and configuration mechanisms.
Mobile IPv6 appears only as a complementary mobility mechanism in the references, not as a subject of the document.
The security requirements are generic and support the transport problem. They do not make security a subject in its own right.

gaps.name: Media Independent Handover (IEEE 802.21 MIH) services
gaps.why: The document exists to provide transport for MIH handover signalling. The taxonomy has no tag for MIH or inter-technology handover support, so IP mobility is the nearest fit.

RFC5165.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC)
RFC5165.summary: Registers the "ogc" URN namespace ID for the Open Geospatial Consortium, defining its syntax (urn:ogc:{OGCresource}:{ResourceSpecificString}), the OGC Naming Authority's assignment and persistence procedures, and examples for naming OGC specifications, service types and coordinate reference systems.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration (NID "ogc") per RFC 3406, so it belongs on the URN and URN namespaces page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace that is engineered by the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) for naming persistent resources published by the OGC.

rejected.why: URN is the more specific child tag and already implies URI; the document is not about URI syntax in general.
XML namespaces and schemas are only among the resources the URNs identify; the document does not specify any XML format.
The IANA registration of the NID is boilerplate for a URN namespace RFC; the document is not about IANA registry policy.
The identified resources are geospatial standards, but the document does not address location information formats, privacy or conveyance.

RFC5166.title: Metrics for the Evaluation of Congestion Control Mechanisms
RFC5166.summary: An informational TMRG/IRTF document discussing the metrics (throughput, delay, loss, fairness, convergence, robustness, deployability) to consider when evaluating new or modified congestion control mechanisms, transport protocols and AQM.

congestion control.why: The whole document is about how to evaluate congestion control mechanisms: throughput, delay, loss, fairness, convergence, oscillations and deployability trade-offs.
congestion control.quote: This document discusses the metrics to be considered in an evaluation of new or modified congestion control mechanisms for the Internet.

performance measurement.why: The document is about performance metrics and relates them to IPPM metrics, though its purpose is evaluating congestion control in simulation and experiments rather than defining measurement methods.
performance measurement.quote: The IPPM Working Group [IPPM] was established to define performance metrics to be used by network operators, end users, or independent testing groups.

rejected.why: TCP is discussed as a baseline and example (TCP-friendliness, modifications) but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
AQM is mentioned as one class of mechanism to be evaluated, but the document does not address AQM specifically.
The document explicitly says it is not a benchmark test suite; it lists metrics for research evaluation, not benchmarking methodology for devices.
ECN is only mentioned in passing when discussing loss/mark rates.
Equation-based congestion control and TFRC are cited as examples in metric discussions, not as the subject.
Only a brief mention of QoS-enabled environments in Section 2.7.

RFC5167.title: Media Server Control Protocol Requirements
RFC5167.summary: Informational requirements document for a Media Server Control Protocol (MCP) letting an application server control a media server for announcements, IVR and conferencing, produced by the MEDIACTRL working group.

conferencing.why: The requirements cover conference mixing, video layouts, active speaker notification and splitting call legs into sub-conferences, built on the XCON/SIP conferencing framework. This makes conferencing the main fit.
conferencing.quote: This document presents the requirements for a Media Server Control Protocol (MCP) that enables an application server to control a media server.

MRCP.why: The protocol covers IVR, announcements, DTMF and recording, which are media resource control and speech-service functions. MRCP is the closest existing tag, though the document does not discuss MRCP itself.
MRCP.quote: The AS shall be able to instruct the MS to perform one or more IVR scripts and receive the results.

rejected.why: SIP/SDP is only the mechanism for establishing media connections (REQ-MCP-07) and for authentication. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
SDP is named only as the means of setting up media connections. Nothing new is defined about it.
The XCON framework is referenced for terminology and architecture, but this document specifies a different interface (AS to MS), not XCON itself.
RFC 4733 tones are mentioned in passing as a media type. The document is not about RTP.

gaps.name: Media Server Control (MEDIACTRL)
gaps.why: The document is about control of media servers by application servers (the MEDIACTRL framework and protocol). The taxonomy has no tag for this, so conferencing and MRCP are only approximate fits.

RFC5168.title: XML Schema for Media Control
RFC5168.summary: Informational RFC documenting a legacy XML schema (application/media_control+xml) carried in SIP INFO for requesting a video fast update (intra frame) from a remote encoder, superseded by the RTCP Full Intra Request.

SIP.why: The document defines a SIP-based media control mechanism for video fast update, deployed in SIP systems and carried via SIP INFO. Readers of SIP extensions would want it.
SIP.quote: The defined XML document is conveyed using the SIP INFO method [3] with the "Content-Type" set to "application/media_control+xml".

XML.why: The core deliverable is an XML schema for media control commands and error reports, so XML-based formats readers would look here.
XML.quote: This document defines an Extensible Markup Language (XML) Schema for video fast update request in a tightly controlled environment

media types.why: The document registers a new media type, application/media_control+xml, as a substantive part of its content.
media types.quote: Type name:   application   Subtype name:   media_control+xml

rejected.why: The RTCP Full Intra Request (RFC 5104) is the recommended replacement and is only discussed for comparison. This document does not specify or extend RTCP.
RTP is background for the media being controlled; the document does not define anything about RTP.
Intra and inter frames are explained only as context for the fast update command; no codec is defined.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to secure signalling.

RFC5169.title: Handover Key Management and Re-Authentication Problem Statement
RFC5169.summary: Problem statement for the HOKEY working group describing why EAP lacks efficient re-authentication and handover keying, and setting design and security goals for a method-independent, lower-layer-independent re-authentication and key management protocol.

HOKEY.why: The document is the HOKEY problem statement: it defines goals for reusing EAP keying material for fast re-authentication and handover.
HOKEY.quote: This document describes the Handover Keying (HOKEY) re-authentication problem statement.

EAP.why: Substantial parts analyse EAP keying (MSK/EMSK), method-specific fast re-authentication (EAP-SIM/AKA, TTLS, PEAP, FAST) and EAP method independence.
EAP.quote: The current Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) keying framework is not designed to support re-authentication and handovers without re-executing an EAP method.

rejected.why: AAA protocols (RADIUS/Diameter) carry the MSK and must remain compatible, but they are the transport for keys, not the subject.
CAPWAP is discussed only as a use case in Section 6.3 for inter-AC roaming, not specified or extended.
Key management is a topic parent; the HOKEY tag is more specific and already covers the keying subject.
TLS session resumption is mentioned only as a mechanism in some EAP methods; the document is not about TLS.
IEEE 802.11r is discussed as related work in Section 6.2 but the document is not about IP over 802.11.

RFC5170.title: Low Density Parity Check (LDPC) Staircase and Triangle Forward Error Correction (FEC) Schemes
RFC5170.summary: Specifies two fully-specified FEC schemes, LDPC-Staircase (Encoding ID 3) and LDPC-Triangle (ID 4), including FEC payload IDs, object transmission information, parity check matrix construction, encoding and decoding for packet erasure channels.

LDPC.why: The whole document specifies LDPC Staircase and Triangle codes: matrix creation, encoding and decoding, and FEC OTI formats.
LDPC.quote: This document describes two Fully-Specified Forward Error Correction (FEC) Schemes, Low Density Parity Check (LDPC) Staircase and LDPC Triangle

rejected.why: LDPC is a child of FEC, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The document is a scheme for object delivery built on the RFC 5052 FEC building block, not the real-time FECFRAME framework.
ALC is mentioned only as a protocol that may carry the FEC OTI in EXT_FTI; the document does not specify it.
FLUTE is only mentioned for carrying FEC OTI in the FDT instance, an optional use of the scheme.
NORM is cited only as another protocol that can use the EXT_FTI mechanism.
TESLA appears only in the Security Considerations as one source authentication option.
The Park-Miller PRNG is specified only as a building block for matrix construction, not as a randomness topic.

gaps.name: LDPC
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists LDPC only under FEC with the description 'low-density parity-check staircase and triangle codes for packet erasure correction'. I used the id 'LDPC' as it appears there, but the exact id is listed as 'LDPC' under FEC, which is valid.

RFC5171.title: Cisco Systems UniDirectional Link Detection (UDLD) Protocol
RFC5171.summary: Informational RFC describing Cisco's UDLD, a Layer 2 protocol over LLC/SNAP that detects and disables unidirectional Ethernet links using neighbor advertisements, echo messages and TLVs.

Ethernet.why: UDLD is a Layer 2 link-fault detection protocol for Ethernet links, working alongside IEEE 802.3 Layer 1 mechanisms and protecting spanning tree. This is the closest fit for Ethernet interworking and OAM.
Ethernet.quote: detect and disable unidirectional Ethernet fiber or copper links caused, for instance, by mis-wiring of fiber strands, interface malfunctions

rejected.why: Section 8 only compares UDLD with BFD. BFD is not specified or extended here.
Ethernet is the more specific tag that fits, so the parent is implied.
UDLD is fault detection, but the Ethernet tag already covers Ethernet OAM and fits better.
The PDU uses an IP-like checksum, but this is a minor packet-format detail and not a subject of the document.
The Device Name TLV is said to be used by the CLI or SNMP, but that is a passing mention.

gaps.name: Spanning Tree Protocol / UDLD
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Layer 2 bridging or spanning tree, nor for vendor-specific Layer 2 link-fault detection. UDLD exists mainly to prevent STP loops.

RFC5172.title: Negotiation for IPv6 Datagram Compression Using IPv6 Control Protocol
RFC5172.summary: Defines the IPv6-Compression-Protocol configuration option for IPV6CP, letting PPP peers negotiate IPv6 datagram compression (e.g., IPHC or ROHC); obsoletes the corresponding part of RFC 2472 with no protocol changes.

PPP.why: The document specifies a new IPV6CP configuration option, a PPP Network Control Protocol option, negotiated over PPP links.
PPP.quote: This document defines the IPv6 datagram compression option that can be negotiated by a node on the link through the IPV6CP.

IPHC.why: The option negotiates IP header compression over PPP, with IPHC as one of the assigned protocol values; readers of IPHC would want this.
IPHC.quote: IPv6-Compression-Protocol field values have been assigned in [4, 5] for IP Header Compression (0061)

ROHC.why: ROHC is the other compression protocol whose value is negotiated through this option.
ROHC.quote: and in [6] for Robust Header Compression (ROHC) (0003)

rejected.why: IPv6 is the network protocol being carried over PPP. The document is about a PPP NCP option, not IPv6 itself.
The specific child tags IPHC and ROHC apply, so the parent topic is implied.
This is lossless data compression formats, such as CCP-style whole-datagram compression. The document explicitly distinguishes its option from CCP.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate. It only updates registry references.

RFC5173.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Body Extension
RFC5173.summary: RFC 5173 defines the Sieve "body" extension, a new test for matching strings in an email message body, with :raw, :content and :text transforms.

Sieve.why: The document specifies a new test extension to the Sieve email filtering language, including its syntax, semantics and capability string.
Sieve.quote: The "body" test checks for the occurrence of one or more strings in the body of an email message.

rejected.why: MIME structure is traversed by the :content transform, but the document does not specify MIME; it only relies on it.
Text is converted to UTF-8 as comparator input, which is a substrate detail, not the subject.
Sieve is the more specific tag and already sits under email.
The document only references the header/body split of messages and does not define message format.

RFC5174.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the European Broadcasting Union (EBU)
RFC5174.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "ebu" for the European Broadcasting Union, specifying its structure, assignment, resolution and persistence for EBU resources such as XML schemas and classification schemes.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration (NID 'ebu') with the full registration template, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: URNs assigned by the EBU will have the following hierarchical structure based on the organizational structure of the EBU resources

rejected.why: XML schemas are among the resources to be named, but the document does not specify or profile XML.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-like; the document is about the namespace, not IANA registry guidance.
URN is the more specific tag and already covers this.

RFC5175.title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Flags Option
RFC5175.summary: Defines a new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement option (type 26, Expanded Flags Option) that adds 48 more flag bits beyond the 8-bit RA flags field, and creates the IANA registry for RA flags.

neighbor discovery.why: The document specifies a new NDP option for Router Advertisement messages, extending IPv6 Neighbor Discovery with processing rules for sender and receiver.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document defines an option for the Router Advertisement message that expands the available number of flag bits by adding an additional 48 flag bits to NDP messages.

rejected.why: It creates an IANA registry for RA flags, but that is a small part of the document; the main subject is the NDP option itself.
The Mobile IPv6 Home Agent flag is only listed as an existing flag, and the document is not about mobility.
The more specific child tag neighbor discovery applies, so the parent is implied.
NDP runs over ICMPv6 and the registry sits in icmpv6-parameters, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP itself.

RFC5176.title: Dynamic Authorization Extensions to Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)
RFC5176.summary: Informational RFC documenting the deployed RADIUS Dynamic Authorization extensions (Disconnect-Request and Change-of-Authorization messages on UDP port 3799), including attributes, Error-Cause codes, Diameter translation, and security guidance; obsoletes RFC 3576.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS packet codes (Disconnect and CoA), attributes and Error-Cause values, extending the RADIUS protocol.
RADIUS.quote: allowing dynamic changes to a user session, as implemented by network access server products. This includes support for disconnecting users and changing authorizations

Diameter.why: A dedicated section covers translation between RADIUS CoA/Disconnect and Diameter RAR/ASR, including Error-Cause to Result-Code mapping, which Diameter readers would want.
Diameter.quote: it may be difficult or impossible for a Diameter/RADIUS gateway to successfully translate a Diameter Re-Auth-Request (RAR) to a CoA-Request and vice versa.

rejected.why: IPsec is only recommended as a security mechanism with a short policy profile in Security Considerations; the document is not about IPsec.
The parent framework tag is implied by the RADIUS and Diameter tags, so it is not listed separately.
UDP port 3799 is merely the transport substrate.
