MD5 and HMAC-MD5 are used for authenticators but are not the subject of the document.
Time synchronization (SNTP) is mentioned only in passing for replay protection.

RFC5177.title: Network Mobility (NEMO) Extensions for Mobile IPv4
RFC5177.summary: Specifies NEMOv4, Mobile IPv4 registration extensions that let a Mobile Router register Mobile Network Prefixes with its Home Agent, with tunnelling, forwarding, and security rules.

NEMO.why: The document defines network mobility support, with the Mobile Router and its Mobile Network Prefixes, for IPv4. This is the NEMO tag, whose parent IP mobility is implied.
NEMO.quote: This document describes a protocol for supporting Mobile Networks between a Mobile Router and a Home Agent by extending the Mobile IPv4 protocol.

Mobile IPv4.why: It defines new Mobile IPv4 registration extensions (type 148) and new reply codes, and specifies Home Agent and Mobile Router operation built on RFC 3344.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Extensions to Mobile IPv4 are introduced to support Mobile Networks.

rejected.why: IPsec ESP is only recommended for protecting routing updates in one security subsection. The document is not about IPsec.
OSPF, BGP and RIP are mentioned only as examples of dynamic routing protocols that could run over the tunnel.
The document uses IP-in-IP tunnelling between the Mobile Router and Home Agent, but this is a mechanism of the mobility protocol, not the subject.
The IANA section only registers the new extension type, sub-types and codes. It is boilerplate, not the subject.
MIB definitions for Mobile Routers are explicitly stated to be out of scope.

RFC5178.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Internationalization and Domain-Based Service Names and Name Type
RFC5178.summary: Defines a new GSS-API name type for domain-based service names (service@domain@hostname), which lets clients authorize servers found via insecure discovery, and adds UTF-8/ACE internationalized import and display functions to the GSS-API.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies a new GSS-API name type (GSS_C_NT_DOMAINBASED_SERVICE) and new GSS-API functions, so it is squarely about GSS-API.
GSS-API.quote: This document describes domain-name-based service principal names and the corresponding name type for the Generic Security Service Application Programming Interface (GSS-API).

internationalization.why: A full section defines how internationalized domain names are imported and displayed in GSS-API names using UTF-8 and ACE encoding.
internationalization.quote: We introduce new versions of GSS_Import_name() and GSS_Display_name() to better support Unicode.

rejected.why: DNS names and SRV lookups are the setting for the names. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
IDNA/ACE encoding is used to handle internationalized names, but the document defines GSS-API behaviour, not IDN itself.
NFSv4 is only a non-normative application example.
LDAP server discovery is only a non-normative application example.
SASL is mentioned in passing in the LDAP example and is not what the document is about.
DNSSEC is mentioned only as the secure discovery alternative that domain-based names avoid needing.

RFC5179.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Domain-Based Service Names Mapping for the Kerberos V GSS Mechanism
RFC5179.summary: Specifies how GSS-API domain-based service names (GSS_C_NT_DOMAINBASED_SERVICE) map onto Kerberos V principal names in the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism, including name type and IDN handling.

GSS-API.why: The document defines a GSS-API name mapping for the Kerberos V mechanism, so GSS-API readers need it.
GSS-API.quote: this document provides the mechanism-specific details needed to implement GSS-API [RFC2743] domain-based service names with the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism [RFC4121]
GSS-API.section: 1. Domain-Based Names for the Kerberos V GSS-API Mechanism

Kerberos.why: It specifies the mapping to Kerberos V principal names, the realm derivation and the NTT-SRVT-HST-DOMAIN name type.
Kerberos.quote: the <service> name becomes the first (0th) component of the Kerberos V principal name;
Kerberos.section: 1. Domain-Based Names for the Kerberos V GSS-API Mechanism

rejected.why: IDNA/ACE-encoded names are only referenced for interoperability in one short internationalization section. The document does not specify IDNs.
The internationalization discussion is brief and defers to ACE encoding, so it is not a substantial subject of the document.
Domain names are used as hostnames in the principal name, but no DNS protocol behaviour is specified.

RFC5180.title: IPv6 Benchmarking Methodology for Network Interconnect Devices
RFC5180.summary: RFC 5180 supplements the RFC 2544 benchmarking methodology with IPv6-specific guidance (extension headers, addressing, filters, IPv4/IPv6 coexistence) for evaluating forwarding performance of network interconnect devices.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking methodology for network devices (throughput, latency, frame loss, reset, recovery), which is exactly the benchmarking topic.
benchmarking.quote: This document provides additional benchmarking guidelines, which in conjunction with RFC 2544, lead to a more complete and realistic evaluation of the IPv6 performance of network interconnect devices.

IPv6.why: A substantial part of the document covers IPv6-specific aspects: extension headers, prefix lengths, address selection, and IPv4/IPv6 coexistence testing. Readers of IPv6 would want it.
IPv6.quote: This document provides benchmarking methodology recommendations that address IPv6-specific aspects, such as evaluating the forwarding performance of traffic containing extension headers

rejected.why: Neighbor discovery is only mentioned as a test setup note (static vs dynamic neighbor entries). The document does not specify or analyse it.
The abstract says transition mechanisms are out of scope. The IPv4/IPv6 traffic mix is coexistence testing, not a transition mechanism.
Ethernet and SONET frame sizes are test parameters. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
Packet over SONET frame sizes and rates appear only as test parameters and in an appendix.
The document is device benchmarking in a lab, which the benchmarking tag covers more specifically. It is not about active or passive network performance measurement.
AH and ESP appear only as extension header types used in test traffic.

RFC5181.title: IPv6 Deployment Scenarios in 802.16 Networks
RFC5181.summary: Informational document describing IPv6 deployment scenarios (mobile shared-prefix and point-to-point link models, fixed/nomadic) in IEEE 802.16 broadband wireless access networks coexisting with IPv4.

WiMAX.why: The whole document is about deploying IPv6 over IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) access networks: link models, convergence sublayers, addressing, transport, routing and mobility.
WiMAX.quote: This document provides a detailed description of IPv6 deployment and integration methods and scenarios in wireless broadband access networks

IPv6 transition.why: Covers dual-stack upgrades, IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling and coexistence with deployed IPv4 services in the access network.
IPv6 transition.quote: IPv6 will be deployed in this scenario by upgrading the following devices to dual stack: MS, AR, and ER.

Mobile IPv6.why: A substantial part of the mobility discussion covers MIPv6 and FMIPv6 over 802.16e, including L2 triggers and cross-layer design.
Mobile IPv6.quote: IP layer handover for MSs is handled by Mobile IPv6 [RFC3775].

rejected.why: Not chosen because IPv6 transition and WiMAX are the more specific tags, and the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
DHCPv6 is only mentioned as one address-assignment option. The document does not specify or extend it.
SLAAC is only mentioned as an addressing option. The document does not specify or extend it.
OSPFv3 and IS-IS are only suggested as routing protocols, in passing.
The multicast section is a brief pointer to another document (IP-ETHERNET).
The QoS section only describes 802.16 scheduling services, in a short paragraph.

RFC5182.title: IMAP Extension for Referencing the Last SEARCH Result
RFC5182.summary: RFC 5182 defines the IMAP SEARCHRES extension, adding a SAVE search result option and a "$" marker so a client can reuse the last SEARCH result in later commands without a round trip, and it updates RFC 3501.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP capability (SEARCHRES), with the SAVE result option, the "$" marker and the NOTSAVED response code. It also updates RFC 3501.
IMAP.quote: This document proposes an IMAP extension that allows a client to tell a server to use the result of a SEARCH (or UID SEARCH) command as an input to any subsequent command.

rejected.why: IMAP is the email access protocol, but the document is about one IMAP extension. The IMAP tag is more specific and implies email.
The document uses ABNF for its formal syntax, but only as a notation. It is not about ABNF.
The only MIME-related content is a UTF-8 charset in the SEARCH examples. The document is not about MIME.

RFC5183.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Environment Extension
RFC5183.summary: Defines the Sieve "environment" extension, adding an environment test and an IANA registry of environment items (domain, host, location, remote-host, remote-ip, etc.) giving scripts access to interpreter and execution context information.

Sieve.why: The document specifies an extension to the Sieve email filtering language, including a new test and an item registry.
Sieve.quote: The "environment" extension gives a Sieve script access to information about the Sieve interpreter itself, where it is running, and about any transport connection

rejected.why: Only referenced for the remote-host/remote-ip items and address-literal syntax; the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
PTR lookup is mentioned only in security considerations as one way to derive remote-host; not about DNS.
The document creates an IANA registry, but this is boilerplate-like registration for the extension itself, not about IANA guidance in its own right.
Mentioned only in the introduction as an example server environment.

RFC5184.title: Unified Layer 2 (L2) Abstractions for Layer 3 (L3)-Driven Fast Handover
RFC5184.summary: Defines nine L2 abstraction primitives (e.g., L2-LinkUp, L2-PoAList, L2-LinkConnect) that let the IP layer obtain link information and drive L2/L3 fast handovers for mobile nodes, with an FMIPv6 example and IEEE 802.11/802.16e mappings.

IP mobility.why: The document is about IP-layer handover optimisation for mobile nodes, using link-layer indications to trigger fast handover (including FMIPv6 operation). It fits the IP mobility topic, and no specific Mobile IP technology tag fits better because it is a cross-protocol abstraction.
IP mobility.quote: This document proposes unified Layer 2 (L2) abstractions for Layer 3 (L3)-driven fast handovers.

WiFi.why: Substantial parts (Appendix C, Appendix D, Appendix E implementation) map the primitives onto IEEE 802.11 events, and the implementation and testbed are 802.11a. Readers of Wi-Fi would want this.
WiFi.quote: in case of the infrastructure mode in IEEE 802.11 [7] (WiFi), this primitive is provided when an association to an access point is established.

rejected.why: FMIPv6 and Mobile IPv6 are the context and an example use, but the document does not specify or extend them. It defines link-layer primitives.
IEEE 802.16e appears only in a mapping table, with no substantive treatment.
The document is about L3 using L2 information, but it is covered better by the IP mobility topic and the WiFi tag. Link layer in general is not its subject.
Neighbor Discovery and DAD are mentioned only as handover preparation steps.
Section 7 addresses RFC 4907 architectural considerations, but this is a checklist about the proposal and not an architecture document.

gaps.name: Media-independent link-layer triggers / link indications for handover
gaps.why: The document's core subject is a link-layer-to-IP-layer event and control primitive interface (like IEEE 802.21 MIH and RFC 4957). The taxonomy has no tag for it, so IP mobility is the closest fit.

RFC5185.title: OSPF Multi-Area Adjacency
RFC5185.summary: Extends OSPF (v2, with OSPFv3 applicability) so a single physical link can carry multiple per-area adjacencies, each advertised as a point-to-point link, letting the link be intra-area in several areas.

OSPF.why: The whole document specifies an extension to OSPF: packet reception changes, interface/neighbor handling, and Router LSA advertisement for multi-area adjacencies.
OSPF.quote: an extension to the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) protocol to allow a single physical link to be shared by multiple areas

OSPFv3.why: A dedicated section describes how the extension applies to OSPFv3, including router-LSA, link-LSA and intra-area-prefix-LSA handling.
OSPFv3.quote: The mechanisms defined in this document also apply to OSPFv3

rejected.why: The document is a specific OSPF protocol extension, not a general discussion of routing architecture.
IPv6 is only the address family OSPFv3 runs over; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Neighbor address discovery is mentioned only as external to OSPF; not a subject of the document.

RFC5186.title: Internet Group Management Protocol Version 3 (IGMPv3) / Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 (MLDv2) and Multicast Routing Protocol Interaction
RFC5186.summary: Informational RFC describing how multicast routing protocols (DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM-DM, PIM-SM, PIM-SSM) should use source-filter information from IGMPv3 and MLDv2 group membership reports to build forwarding state and generate joins, prunes and grafts.

IGMP.why: The document defines how routing protocols interpret IGMPv3 source-filter records (INCLUDE/EXCLUDE) and act on them.
IGMP.quote: The definitions of the Internet Group Management Protocol Version 3 (IGMPv3) and Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 (MLDv2) require new behavior within the multicast routing protocols.

MLD.why: MLDv2 is treated in parallel with IGMPv3 throughout; the group management database interaction applies equally to it.
MLD.quote: The definitions of IGMPv3 [IGMP3] and MLDv2 [MLDv2] require new behavior within the multicast routing protocols.

PIM-SM.why: A substantial section specifies PIM-SM join and prune behaviour triggered by IGMPv3/MLDv2 state.
PIM-SM.quote: If this is due to an IGMPv3 or MLDv2 report with a zero-length EXCLUDE list, then the join is sent as a (*,G) join towards the RP.

PIM.why: PIM-DM prune and graft behaviour is specified; PIM-DM has no dedicated child tag, so the PIM parent covers it.
PIM.quote: The PIM-DM protocol [PIMDM] interaction with a source-filtering group management protocol is important in two areas: multicast distribution tree pruning and multicast distribution tree grafting.

MOSPF.why: The document has a section on how MOSPF uses source filter information.
MOSPF.quote: In Multicast Extensions to OSPF (MOSPF) [MOSPF], the consideration of source filter information in the group management database is limited

SSM.why: The document distinguishes ASM from SSM ranges and addresses SSM interaction, though it defers the behaviour to RFC 4601.
SSM.quote: A PIM-SSM interaction takes place when a PIM-SM router receives an IGMPv3 or MLDv2 message regarding a group address that is in the Source Specific Multicast range.

rejected.why: Parent topic; implied by the specific multicast technology tags chosen.
Not mentioned; irrelevant.
MOSPF is only mentioned as a multicast routing protocol; the MOSPF tag fits better.

gaps.name: DVMRP
gaps.why: The document has a short section on DVMRP, but the taxonomy has no DVMRP tag; it is only covered by the multicast parent.

RFC5187.title: OSPFv3 Graceful Restart
RFC5187.summary: RFC 5187 specifies the OSPFv3 graceful restart, defining the OSPFv3 grace-LSA format (LS type 0x000b) and OSPFv3-specific requirements such as preserving LSA ID-to-prefix mappings and Interface IDs across restarts.

OSPFv3.why: The document specifies graceful restart for OSPFv3, defining a new grace-LSA type and OSPFv3-specific considerations; it belongs on the OSPFv3 page.
OSPFv3.quote: OSPFv3 will use a grace-LSA with a different format to signal that a router is initiating (or is about to initiate) a graceful restart.

rejected.why: OSPFv2 graceful restart (RFC 3623) is the base mechanism referenced; this document is specific to OSPFv3, the more specific child tag.
Mentions MIB-II IfIndex only as a common source for Interface IDs; the document is not about MIBs.
OSPFv3 authentication is mentioned only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The IANA section only records a function code assignment; the document is not about IANA practice.

RFC5188.title: RTP Payload Format for the Enhanced Variable Rate Wideband Codec (EVRC-WB) and the Media Subtype Updates for EVRC-B Codec
RFC5188.summary: Specifies RTP payload formats, an email/file storage format, SDP/offer-answer rules and media type registrations for the EVRC-WB wideband speech codec, and updates the EVRC-B media types of RFC 4788 with new recvmode/sendmode parameters.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines header-free, interleaved/bundled and compact bundle RTP payload formats for EVRC-WB and updates EVRC-B ones.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload formats for packetization of EVRC-WB encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

media types.why: A large part of the document is registration of audio/EVRCWB, EVRCWB0, EVRCWB1 and updated EVRCB/EVRCB0 media types.
media types.quote: this section registers new 'audio' media subtypes for EVRC-WB and updates the audio/EVRCB and audio/EVRCB0 media type registrations

SDP.why: Defines SDP parameter mappings, offer/answer considerations and declarative SDP rules for the new fmtp parameters.
SDP.quote: 'mode-set-recv' is defined for use with EVRC-WB. A decoder can use this attribute to inform an encoder of its preference
SDP.section: 10. SDP Mode Attributes for EVRC-WB and EVRC-B

rejected.why: The specific EVRC-WB codec is not in the taxonomy; the RTP payload format tag is the better fit and the codec itself is specified externally by 3GPP2.
RTP is the transport the payload format is carried in; the more specific RTP payload format tag already covers it.
The storage format mentions email attachments only as a use case for a file format.
A different speech codec family; not related beyond being a speech codec.

gaps.name: EVRC family codecs (EVRC, EVRC-B, EVRC-WB)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the 3GPP2 EVRC speech codec family, which is the central subject of this and related RFCs (3558, 4788).

RFC5189.title: Middlebox Communication (MIDCOM) Protocol Semantics
RFC5189.summary: Specifies the transaction semantics (session control, policy reserve/enable rules, lifetime changes, groups, notifications) of the MIDCOM protocol by which agents configure firewalls and NATs, obsoleting RFC 3989.

NAT.why: The document defines the protocol semantics for dynamically configuring NAT bindings and address/port reservations on NATs, so NAT readers would look for it.
NAT.quote: semantics description is targeted at packet filters and Network Address Translators (NATs), and it supports applications that require dynamic configuration of these middleboxes

firewall.why: MIDCOM is a protocol for agents to configure firewall pinholes and other middlebox policy rules; firewall traversal and control is the core subject.
firewall.quote: At a firewall, the enable action is interpreted as one or more allow actions configuring pinholes.

rejected.why: SIP only appears in the usage example (B2BUA scenario); the document does not specify or extend SIP.
TLS is only mentioned as a possible underlying security mechanism; nothing new is defined about it.
IPsec is named only as an alternative substrate for authentication and protection of MIDCOM sessions.
Policy rules are used, but the document defines middlebox-specific transactions rather than a policy information model.
STUN is mentioned only in the UNSAF section as a contrasting workaround.
The topic concerns interactive traversal of NATs for real-time media; MIDCOM is a control protocol for middleboxes, which NAT and firewall capture better.

gaps.name: MIDCOM (middlebox communication)
gaps.why: The document's primary subject, the MIDCOM agent-to-middlebox control protocol, has no dedicated tag; NAT and firewall cover it only partially.

RFC5190.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Middlebox Communication
RFC5190.summary: Defines the MIDCOM-MIB SMIv2 module that lets a MIDCOM client use SNMP to configure and monitor firewalls and NATs (pinholes, NAT bindings), mapping the RFC 5189 MIDCOM semantics onto SNMP operations.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a MIB module (MIDCOM-MIB) with tables, notifications and conformance groups, plus guidance on VACM configuration and SNMP usage.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

NAT.why: The MIB controls NAT bindings and sessions, covers twice-NAT and port translation, and relates to the NAT-MIB. Readers interested in NAT would want it.
NAT.quote: it describes a set of managed objects that allow configuring middleboxes, such as firewalls and network address translators, in order to enable communication across these devices.

firewall.why: Policy rules open firewall pinholes and the MIB configures firewall rule priority and groups. Middlebox/firewall traversal control is a central purpose.
firewall.quote: applications can, for example, request pinholes at firewalls and address bindings at NATs.

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to carry the MIB; the document defines objects and mappings, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
The 'policy rules' are firewall/NAT pinhole rules, not a policy-based management information model.
VACM-based access control is recommended in a configuration section, but it is supporting guidance, not the document's subject.
RTP is mentioned only as a reason for requesting consecutive port pairs.
Security sections address securing the MIB's access; this is boilerplate-level guidance, not the subject.

gaps.name: MIDCOM (Middlebox Communication)
gaps.why: The document implements the MIDCOM protocol semantics (RFC 5189) via SNMP; the taxonomy has no tag for middlebox communication or middlebox control frameworks.

RFC5191.title: Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA)
RFC5191.summary: Specifies PANA, a UDP-based network-layer EAP lower-layer protocol between a PANA Client and Authentication Agent for network access authentication, including session phases, messages, AVPs, PANA SA and retransmission.

PANA.why: The document defines the PANA protocol itself: its messages, phases, AVPs, security association and processing rules.
PANA.quote: PANA is a UDP-based EAP lower layer that runs between the EAP peer and the EAP authenticator.

EAP.why: PANA is specified as an EAP lower layer, and the document covers EAP encapsulation, MSK-derived keys and EAP-Payload AVP, so EAP readers would want it.
EAP.quote: PANA carries EAP, which can carry various authentication methods.

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate PANA runs over (port 716); the document does not define UDP usage guidance.
Back-end AAA is mentioned as an optional offload in the EAP model, but the document is not about AAA frameworks.
DHCP is only the default way to discover the PAA, and is specified in a separate RFC (5192).
Only the prf+ function and transform IDs are borrowed from IKEv2; the document is not about IKE.
The AVP format and data types are borrowed from Diameter, but the document does not specify or extend Diameter.
The generic authentication topic is implied by the more specific PANA and EAP tags.

RFC5192.title: DHCP Options for Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) Authentication Agents
RFC5192.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options carrying lists of IP addresses so PANA Clients can discover PANA Authentication Agents.

PANA.why: The options exist solely for PANA Clients to discover PANA Authentication Agents, so the document extends PANA's agent-discovery mechanism.
PANA.quote: This document defines new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that contain a list of IP addresses to locate one or more PANA

DHCPv6.why: Defines a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_PANA_AGENT, 40) and its client and server behaviour.
DHCPv6.quote: This DHCPv6 option carries a list of 128-bit (binary) IPv6 addresses indicating PANA Authentication Agents (PAAs)

DHCP.why: Defines a new DHCPv4 option (OPTION_PANA_AGENT, 136) and its client and server behaviour.
DHCP.quote: This DHCPv4 option carries a list of 32-bit (binary) IPv4 addresses indicating PANA Authentication Agents (PAAs)

rejected.why: PANA is an EAP lower layer, but this document only covers PAA discovery and does not specify or extend EAP.
Network access authentication is the context, but the document defines only DHCP discovery options, not an AAA framework.
The DHCPv6 option carries IPv6 addresses, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The options are a discovery mechanism, but the more specific DHCP and PANA tags cover that.

RFC5193.title: Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) Framework
RFC5193.summary: Informational framework describing the functional entities (PaC, PAA, AS, EP), high-level call flow, and deployment environments for PANA, an EAP lower layer for network access authentication.

PANA.why: The whole document is the PANA framework: functional model, call flow and deployment environments.
PANA.quote: This document defines the general framework for describing how these various PANA and other network access authentication elements interact with each other

rejected.why: PANA carries EAP as a lower layer, but the document does not specify or extend EAP or its methods.
The document mentions an AAA and access control framework, but only as context; RADIUS/Diameter are named as options between PAA and AS.
Only mentioned as a possible PAA-to-AS protocol.
Only mentioned as a possible PAA-to-AS protocol.
IPsec/IKE is only one option for per-packet protection after PANA, and its use is out of scope.
Only cited as an example protocol between the PAA and EP.

RFC5194.title: Framework for Real-Time Text over IP Using the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5194.summary: Informational framework listing requirements for real-time text over IP (ToIP) and describing its implementation with SIP and RTP (RFC 4103/T.140), including transcoding relay services and interworking with PSTN text telephony, cellular and instant messaging.

SIP.why: The framework specifies how SIP session setup, registration, caller preferences and transcoding invocation are used for real-time text conversations.
SIP.quote: ToIP services MUST use the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [2] for setting up, controlling, and terminating sessions for real-time text conversation

RTP payload format.why: Transport of T.140 real-time text via the RFC 4103 RTP payload, with redundancy and cps parameters, is a core part of the framework.
RTP payload format.quote: ToIP services MUST support the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) [3] according to the specification of RFC 4103 [4] for the transport of real-time text

PSTN interop.why: A substantial part covers text gateways interworking with PSTN textphones (V.18, Baudot, V.21) and cellular text telephony.
PSTN interop.quote: Text gateways MUST use the ITU-T V.18 [16] standard at the PSTN side. A text gateway MUST act as a SIP User Agent on the IP side

accessibility.why: Requirements are driven by accessibility needs of deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-impaired users, including relay services and alerting.
accessibility.quote: deaf, hard-of-hearing, and speech-impaired people are amongst the most prolific users of real-time, conversational, text

rejected.why: SDP is used to negotiate text media but the document defines nothing new about it beyond an example.
IM is discussed only as an interworking target and contrasted with real-time text.
Emergency access is a brief recommendation in section 7.1, not a substantial part.
UTF-8 is merely the mandated character encoding for T.140 text.
Multipoint text conferencing is mentioned in requirements but not specified.

gaps.name: Real-time text (T.140 / ToIP)
gaps.why: The document's main subject, real-time text conversation, has no dedicated tag; closest are the RTP payload format and SIP tags.

RFC5195.title: BGP-Based Auto-Discovery for Layer-1 VPNs
RFC5195.summary: Defines a BGP-based auto-discovery mechanism for Layer-1 VPNs, using a new SAFI (69) and NLRI to distribute <CPI, PPI> port information among PEs filtered by Route Targets.

L1VPN.why: The whole document specifies auto-discovery for Layer-1 VPNs, including PITs, route target filtering, and the new NLRI for port information.
L1VPN.quote: The purpose of this document is to define a BGP-based auto-discovery mechanism for Layer-1 VPNs (L1VPNs)

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new SAFI and NLRI format, and defines route-target filtering, refresh and scalability procedures for it.
BGP.quote: We introduce a new subsequent address family identifier, called Layer-1 VPN auto-discovery information (value 69), and also a new Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) format

rejected.why: GMPLS is only the backbone in the reference figure and the signalling that the discovered information supports; the document does not specify it.
Route Target extended communities are used for filtering but are defined elsewhere (RFC 4360); this document only uses them.
Route reflectors are mentioned only in the scalability discussion, not specified or profiled.
The more specific L1VPN tag fits; this is not about L3/L2 provider-provisioned VPNs in general.

RFC5196.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) User Agent Capability Extension to Presence Information Data Format (PIDF)
RFC5196.summary: Defines an XML extension to PIDF (urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:caps) that expresses SIP user agent service and device capabilities (RFC 3840 feature tags) within presence documents.

PIDF.why: The document specifies a new extension to the Presence Information Data Format, with elements, schema and namespace for carrying capabilities in presence documents.
PIDF.quote: This memo defines a PIDF extension to represent SIP User Agent capabilities.

SIMPLE.why: Produced by the SIMPLE WG; it extends SIP-based presence with capability information for watchers and PUAs, mapping RFC 3840 SIP feature tags into presence.
SIMPLE.quote: presence applications based on SIP can have richer and more usable presence information compared to the baseline PIDF.

rejected.why: SIP feature tags are represented, but the document defines a presence data format extension rather than SIP protocol behaviour; SIMPLE covers the SIP presence context.
XML schema is the encoding mechanism for the extension, not the subject.
Parent of PIDF; implied, and the document is about the presence format specifically.
The <type> element carries MIME types, but the document does not address media type registration.
IANA namespace and schema registrations are boilerplate and not the main subject.

RFC5197.title: On the Applicability of Various Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) Modes and Extensions
RFC5197.summary: Informational overview of MIKEY (RFC 3830) key distribution modes and extensions, comparing their advantages and disadvantages and their applicability to SIP scenarios such as early media, forking, retargeting and shared-key conferencing.

MIKEY.why: The whole document compares MIKEY modes (PSK, RSA, DH-SIGN, DH-HMAC, RSA-R, SAML-DH) and extensions (ECC, TESLA payload, Key ID type, OMA BCAST) and advises on mode selection.
MIKEY.quote: This document provides an overview about the MIKEY base document in general as well as the existing extensions for MIKEY

rejected.why: MIKEY is mainly used to bootstrap SRTP, but the document does not specify or extend SRTP. It only touches the rollover-counter transform in passing.
SIP call scenarios (forking, redirect, retarget) are used to evaluate MIKEY modes, but SIP itself is not the subject.
The TESLA bootstrapping payload gets one short subsection, but this is a MIKEY extension and not a treatment of TESLA.
SDP is the transport for MIKEY messages and is mentioned only as a substrate.
ECC algorithms for MIKEY are summarised in one subsection. That is a MIKEY extension, not a document about elliptic curve cryptography.
The parent topic of MIKEY, so it is implied by the MIKEY tag and not listed separately.

RFC5198.title: Unicode Format for Network Interchange
RFC5198.summary: RFC 5198 defines "Net-Unicode", a standard network text interchange format using UTF-8, NFC normalization, CRLF line endings and no BOM, as an internationalized successor to NVT ASCII, updating Telnet (RFC 854).

Unicode.why: The whole document defines a Unicode-based text format, with NFC normalization, handling of unassigned code points, and Unicode version stability. Readers of Unicode usage in Internet protocols would want it.
Unicode.quote: This document proposes to establish "Net-Unicode" as a new standardized text transmission form for the Internet

UTF-8.why: UTF-8 is the mandated encoding, and the document adds profile rules such as no BOM and treating untagged UTF-8-looking strings as UTF-8. It does not define UTF-8 itself, so this is secondary.
UTF-8.quote: Characters MUST be encoded in UTF-8 as defined in [RFC3629].

Telnet.why: It updates RFC 854 (Telnet) and revises the NVT definition, including control characters, CR/LF handling and IAC interaction with UTF-8.
Telnet.quote: The main body of this specification is intended as an update to, and internationalized version of, the Net-ASCII definition.

rejected.why: ASCII and NVT ASCII are the historical baseline being replaced. The document is about the Unicode successor, not about ASCII.
It is about a specific text format. It does not cover character set registration or labeling.
Whois is only cited as an example of a protocol that could adopt Net-Unicode. The document does not specify it.
FTP is mentioned only as historical context and in a future-work note.
Stringprep and Nameprep are mentioned only for comparison of normalization and Unicode versions. The document does not define string preparation.
The parent is implied by the Unicode and UTF-8 tags.

RFC5201.title: Host Identity Protocol
RFC5201.summary: Specifies the base Host Identity Protocol (HIP): a Sigma-style four-packet Diffie-Hellman base exchange with puzzles, using public-key Host Identities to separate identifier and locator roles, plus packet formats, UPDATE/CLOSE procedures and state machine.

HIP.why: The whole document defines HIP: Host Identity namespace, HITs, base exchange, packet formats, state machine and processing rules.
HIP.quote: This memo specifies the details of the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

rejected.why: ESP is the mandatory data transport (specified in RFC 5202) and HIP is compared to IKE, but this document does not specify IPsec.
The ESP transport format is defined in a separate document; here it is only referenced as the required transport.
IKE is mentioned only as a comparison; HIP is explicitly not a replacement for it.
DNS is used only to look up HITs and HIs; the DNS extensions are in RFC 5205.
Mobility and multihoming are explicitly left to separate specifications (RFC 5206).
No DDoS tag is chosen; the puzzle mechanism is part of the HIP protocol design.

RFC5202.title: Using the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) Transport Format with the Host Identity Protocol (HIP)
RFC5202.summary: Specifies how ESP is used with the Host Identity Protocol: HIP parameters (ESP_INFO, ESP_TRANSFORM) for setting up and rekeying ESP SAs during the base exchange and UPDATE, with keying material, SPI semantics and packet processing.

HIP.why: Defines new HIP parameters, base exchange modifications and UPDATE-based rekeying for HIP's ESP data transport.
HIP.quote: This memo specifies an Encapsulated Security Payload (ESP) based mechanism for transmission of user data packets, to be used with the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

ESP.why: Specifies ESP SA setup, SPI semantics, BEET mode, transforms and sequence numbers when ESP is used with HIP.
ESP.quote: This document specifies how ESP is used with HIP to carry actual user data.

rejected.why: ESP is the more specific tag; IPsec architecture is only discussed for coexistence, and ESP is the child tag chosen.
Mentioned only as an alternative key-establishment method; the document uses HIP instead.
AES-CBC is only a mandatory transform named, not specified or analysed.
Only a brief note on Parameter Problem for unknown SPI.

RFC5203.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Registration Extension
RFC5203.summary: Defines an experimental HIP extension with REG_INFO, REG_REQUEST, REG_RESPONSE and REG_FAILED parameters letting hosts register with services such as rendezvous servers or middleboxes via the HIP base exchange or UPDATE.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with new parameters, packet processing rules and registries for registering with HIP services.
HIP.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) [RFC5201].  The extension provides a generic means for a host to register with a service.

rejected.why: Middleboxes such as NATs and firewalls are mentioned only as examples of services and for lifetime baselines; the document is not about NAT.
Firewalls are only an example service; the document does not specify firewall traversal.
The IANA section merely creates registries for this extension; it is boilerplate and not the main subject.
The document explicitly states it does not specify discovery of services or registrars.

RFC5204.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Rendezvous Extension
RFC5204.summary: Defines the HIP rendezvous extension: rendezvous servers that relay HIP base exchange I1 packets to registered, mobile or multihomed clients, with new RVS_HMAC, FROM and VIA_RVS parameters and a RENDEZVOUS registration type.

HIP.why: The whole document extends HIP with rendezvous servers, new parameters and modified I1/R1 processing.
HIP.quote: This document defines a rendezvous extension for the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

rejected.why: Rendezvous helps mobile nodes be reachable, but the document specifies a HIP mechanism, not an IP mobility protocol; HIP already sits under internet layer.
Multihoming is a motivation mentioned in the abstract; the document does not address multihoming architecture.
The RVS address is recorded in the HIP DNS record, which is defined elsewhere (RFC 5205); it is only referenced here.
RVS_HMAC reuses the HIP HMAC construction with a different type code; the document is not about HMAC.
NAT traversal is explicitly out of scope; egress filtering only motivates source address rewriting.

RFC5205.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Domain Name System (DNS) Extensions
RFC5205.summary: Defines the HIP DNS resource record (type 55) for storing a node's Host Identity, HIT and rendezvous server names, and describes how HIP initiators use DNS lookups to find them.

HIP.why: The document specifies how the Host Identity Protocol uses DNS to publish HIs, HITs and rendezvous servers, and how initiators use it to start HIP exchanges.
HIP.quote: This RR allows a HIP node to store in the DNS its Host Identity (HI, the public component of the node public-private key pair)

DNS.why: It defines a new DNS RR type, with its wire and presentation formats, and the query behaviour (RCODE handling, A/AAAA/HIP lookups) for it.
DNS.quote: This document specifies a new resource record (RR) for the Domain Name System (DNS)

rejected.why: DNSSEC is only recommended as a way to secure the HIP RR in Security Considerations. The document does not specify anything new about it.
The IPSECKEY RR is reused for algorithm types and key formats, but the document is not about IPsec.
Base16 and Base64 are used only for the presentation format and are not the subject.
The RR type allocation is boilerplate IANA considerations.
Mobility and RVS are the motivating scenario, but the document specifies only the DNS record, not mobility mechanisms.

gaps.name: Host Identity Protocol (HIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a HIP tag in the internet layer group, which I used. No tag exists for the HIP rendezvous extension specifically, but HIP is a close enough fit.

RFC5206.title: End-Host Mobility and Multihoming with the Host Identity Protocol
RFC5206.summary: Defines the HIP LOCATOR parameter and procedures for end-host mobility (readdressing via UPDATE, address verification, credit-based authorization) and basic multihoming with the Host Identity Protocol.

HIP.why: The whole document extends HIP with a LOCATOR parameter and mobility/multihoming procedures.
HIP.quote: This document defines mobility and multihoming extensions to the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

IP mobility.why: The document specifies end-to-end network-layer mobility procedures, an alternative to Mobile IP, so readers of IP mobility would want it.
IP mobility.quote: end-host mobility of a HIP host -- the sequential change in the preferred IP address used to reach a host.

multihoming.why: Defines basic host multihoming using LOCATOR with multiple SAs and preferred locators, though detailed procedures are left open.
multihoming.quote: a host has multiple locators simultaneously rather than sequentially, as in the case of mobility.

rejected.why: ESP SAs are the substrate for the HIP data plane and are only referenced, not specified or extended here.
IPsec is used via ESP SAs, but the document is about HIP signalling, not IPsec architecture.
Mentioned only for comparison and for the credit-based authorization background; the document is not about Mobile IPv6.
Mentioned once as possible future alignment; not covered.
Flooding attacks are discussed in Security Considerations, as boilerplate-like analysis; not the main subject.

gaps.name: Host Identity Protocol (HIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a HIP tag, but this document's most specific subject is HIP mobility and multihoming extensions; no child tag exists for it.

RFC5207.title: NAT and Firewall Traversal Issues of Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Communication
RFC5207.summary: IRTF informational RFC describing problems that NATs and firewalls cause for HIP base exchange and ESP data traffic, and discussing possible solutions such as UDP encapsulation, rendezvous, SPINAT and NSIS signalling.

HIP.why: The whole document analyses HIP and its base exchange and ESP phases across middleboxes, and identifies issues in HIP specifications.
HIP.quote: This document discusses the problems associated with HIP communication across network paths that include specific types of middleboxes, namely, network address translators and firewalls.

NAT.why: NAT traversal problems (NAPT, SPI demultiplexing, receiver behind NAT, legacy NATs) are a central subject, so readers of NAT would want it.
NAT.quote: This section focuses on the traversal of HIP across network address translator (NAT) middleboxes.

firewall.why: Firewall traversal for HIP is a full section and part of the title, covering blocking of base exchange and ESP and SPI-based flow identification.
firewall.quote: This section focuses on the traversal of HIP across IP firewalls and packet filters.

rejected.why: ESP is the data-plane substrate of HIP. The document discusses how NATs treat it but does not specify or extend it.
NSIS NATFW NSLP is mentioned as one possible SPI signalling solution, not a main subject.
IPsec NAT compatibility is referenced via RFC 3715, but the document is about HIP, not IPsec itself.
UDP encapsulation is proposed as a remedy, but the document is not about UDP.
The HIP mobility and multihoming extension is mentioned only briefly as a way to announce rendezvous points.

RFC5208.title: Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) #8: Private-Key Information Syntax Specification Version 1.2
RFC5208.summary: Republication of PKCS #8 v1.2 defining ASN.1 syntax for private-key information (PrivateKeyInfo) and encrypted private-key information (EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo), with change control moved to the IETF.

key management.why: The document defines how private keys are represented and protected (encrypted) for storage and transfer, which is key storage and provisioning. No more specific tag fits.
key management.quote: This document describes a syntax for private-key information.

ASN.1.why: The specification consists of ASN.1 type definitions and an ASN.1 module in Appendix A, with BER encoding of the structures.
ASN.1.quote: Private-key information shall have ASN.1 type PrivateKeyInfo:

rejected.why: The document concerns private-key container syntax, not certificates or public key infrastructure operation.
RSA is only given as an example private-key algorithm, via PKCS #1 rsaEncryption.
Password-based encryption (PKCS #5) is referenced as an example of an encryption algorithm. This document does not specify it.
AlgorithmIdentifier is imported from X.509 but the document does not profile certificates.

gaps.name: PKCS (Public-Key Cryptography Standards) private-key syntax
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PKCS #8 or private-key container formats. Key management is the closest fit.

RFC5209.title: Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA): Overview and Requirements
RFC5209.summary: RFC 5209 defines the problem statement, scope, reference model (PA, PB, PT protocols), use cases and protocol requirements for Network Endpoint Assessment, which checks endpoint security posture against network compliance policy.

NEA.why: The whole document specifies the NEA reference model, use cases and requirements for the PA, PB and PT protocols, which is exactly what the NEA tag covers.
NEA.quote: This document defines the problem statement, scope, and protocol requirements between the components of the NEA (Network Endpoint Assessment) reference model.

rejected.why: EAP and 802.1X are only candidate transports for PT, and the document does not specify or extend them.
TLS is named only as an example PT carrier, so it is substrate and not the subject.
IPsec and IKEv2 are mentioned only as environments over which PT could run.
Detecting lying endpoints and TCG-style attestation are explicitly out of scope.
There is a Privacy Considerations section, but it is secondary to the NEA requirements. NEA is the more specific tag and the primary subject.
RADIUS is only listed as a possible lower-layer carrier for PT.

RFC5210.title: A Source Address Validation Architecture (SAVA) Testbed and Deployment Experience
RFC5210.summary: Experimental report on a prototype multiple-fence Source Address Validation Architecture (access network, intra-AS, inter-AS) deployed on the IPv6 CNGI-CERNET2 testbed, with test results and lessons learned.

SAVI.why: The whole document describes and evaluates source address validation mechanisms at access, intra-AS and inter-AS levels, which is the subject of the SAVI tag.
SAVI.quote: In an effort to enhance the Internet with IP source address validation, a prototype implementation of the IP Source Address Validation Architecture (SAVA) was created

rejected.why: The testbed is IPv6-only and uses hop-by-hop extension headers, but IPv6 is the substrate, not the subject.
Spoofed-source attacks are the motivation, but the document does not address DDoS mitigation or signalling itself.
Considered because of deployment experience, but the focus is a specific validation architecture, which SAVI covers better.
Inter-AS rules reflect AS relationships (customer/provider/peer), but BGP is not specified or analysed.
Variant B uses network access authentication keys, but this is a minor mechanism rather than a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Ingress filtering / IP source address spoofing prevention (SAVA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy only has SAVI, which is the nearest fit. A dedicated tag for source address validation architecture and ingress filtering (BCP 38 family) would group this RFC with RFC 2827 and RFC 3704.

RFC5211.title: An Internet Transition Plan
RFC5211.summary: An Independent-stream informational memo proposing a three-phase plan (preparation, transition, post-transition, 2008–2012) for moving the Internet from predominantly IPv4 to predominantly IPv6 connectivity.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document is a transition plan for IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and migration, with phased requirements for service providers and organizations. This fits the IPv6 transition topic directly.
IPv6 transition.quote: This memo provides one possible plan for transitioning the Internet from a predominantly IPv4-based connectivity model to a predominantly IPv6-based connectivity model.

rejected.why: The document is about the transition plan, which is the more specific child tag. It does not specify IPv6 itself.
IPv4 address exhaustion is mentioned only as the motivation for the timeline. The IANA note about IPv4 availability is boilerplate.
DNS servers appear only as examples of Internet-facing servers, and RFC 4472 is cited for separate service names. DNS is not the subject.
The plan cites RFC 1958 but does not discuss architectural principles in its own right.
IPv4 address pool exhaustion is context only. The document does not cover address allocation or architecture.

RFC5212.title: Requirements for GMPLS-Based Multi-Region and Multi-Layer Networks (MRN/MLN)
RFC5212.summary: Informational requirements document defining a framework and functional requirements for GMPLS control of multi-region and multi-layer networks (MRN/MLN), covering ISCs, hybrid nodes, FA-LSPs, virtual network topology, scalability, and management.

GMPLS.why: The whole document specifies requirements for GMPLS control of multi-layer and multi-region networks, covering ISCD, FA-LSPs, and triggered signaling.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines a framework for GMPLS based multi-region / multi-layer networks and lists a set of functional requirements.

traffic engineering.why: Substantial parts address integrated TE, the unified TED, virtual network topology, virtual TE links and path computation across layers.
traffic engineering.quote: a path across multiple regions or layers can be computed using this TED. Thus, optimization of network resources can be achieved across the whole MLN/MRN.

rejected.why: MPLS is the base technology that GMPLS extends. The document's subject is GMPLS, so the more specific tag fits.
Signaling is discussed only at requirements level, and the document says it does not specify protocol elements.
Path computation is discussed generically and PCE or PCEP is not specified.
OAM requirements appear in one subsection of the management section. That is not a substantial part of the document.
MIB modules are only mentioned briefly as a way to manage GMPLS layers.

RFC5213.title: Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC5213.summary: RFC 5213 specifies Proxy Mobile IPv6, a network-based mobility management protocol in which a Mobile Access Gateway signals a Local Mobility Anchor with Proxy Binding Updates on behalf of a mobile node, extending Mobile IPv6 messages and options.

PMIPv6.why: The document defines the PMIPv6 protocol.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification describes a network-based mobility management protocol and is referred to as Proxy Mobile IPv6.

RFC5214.title: Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP)
RFC5214.summary: RFC 5214 specifies ISATAP, an automatic intra-site tunnelling mechanism that carries IPv6 packets over an IPv4 network treated as an NBMA link layer, including interface identifier construction, encapsulation and Neighbor Discovery adaptations with a Potential Router List.

ISATAP.why: The document specifies ISATAP itself: addressing, automatic tunnelling, and neighbor discovery over ISATAP interfaces.
ISATAP.quote: ISATAP connects dual-stack (IPv6/IPv4) nodes over IPv4 networks.

rejected.why: The document adapts IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) for ISATAP interfaces, but this is part of ISATAP's specification rather than a subject in its own right. The ISATAP tag covers it.
This is the parent of ISATAP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Generic tunnelling is covered by the more specific ISATAP tag; the basic mechanisms come from RFC 4213.
DNS is only used to resolve the isatap FQDN into the Potential Router List. It is substrate, not the subject.
A DHCPv4 option is mentioned only as one way to obtain PRL addresses. This is incidental.
The IPv6 tag is the parent of ISATAP and is implied. The addressing details are specific to ISATAP.

RFC5215.title: RTP Payload Format for Vorbis Encoded Audio
RFC5215.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for Vorbis audio, including packetization, fragmentation, in-band and out-of-band delivery of codebook configuration headers, media type registrations, and SDP mapping.

Vorbis.why: The document defines how Vorbis audio is carried in RTP, including raw data, configuration (codebook) and comment packets, and fragmentation. Vorbis and its RTP payload format are the subject.
Vorbis.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for transporting Vorbis encoded audio.

rejected.why: Vorbis is the more specific tag; its description includes its RTP payload format, and the RTP payload format parent is implied only via codecs/RTP, so the Vorbis tag covers it.
SDP mapping of media type parameters is a section, but SDP is the signalling mechanism used, not something newly specified.
Registers audio/vorbis and audio/vorbis-config, but this is boilerplate-like IANA registration for the payload format, not about media type rules.
The payload format builds on RTP, but RTP itself is the substrate.
Ogg is mentioned only as the usual encapsulation that is dropped for RTP transport.
Base64 is used only to encode the configuration parameter.

RFC5216.title: The EAP-TLS Authentication Protocol
RFC5216.summary: Defines EAP-TLS, an EAP method that carries TLS handshake messages inside EAP packets to give certificate-based mutual authentication and key derivation (MSK/EMSK), including fragmentation, privacy, session resumption and certificate validation rules; obsoletes RFC 2716.

EAP.why: The document specifies a new EAP method: packet formats, conversation flows, fragmentation, key hierarchy (MSK/EMSK), and EAP security claims.
EAP.quote: This document defines EAP-TLS, which includes support for certificate-based mutual authentication and key derivation.

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate EAP-TLS encapsulates. The document defines how TLS records are carried in EAP and does not specify or extend TLS itself.
Certificate validation, identity and revocation rules appear in the security considerations, but they apply TLS and RFC 3280 and do not define certificate profiles.
OCSP and CRLs are only referenced as revocation-checking requirements for implementations. The document is not about them.
RADIUS is mentioned only for its packet size limit and the MS-MPPE key attributes. The document does not specify it.
PPP is one of several EAP lower layers named in the introduction. The document is not PPP-specific.

RFC5217.title: Memorandum for Multi-Domain Public Key Infrastructure Interoperability
RFC5217.summary: Informational memo defining terminology, PKI domain requirements, and models (unifying, bridge, direct cross-certification, trust lists) for interoperability among multiple X.509 PKI domains operating under distinct policies.

PKI.why: The whole document concerns PKI architectures, CA relationships, cross-certification, bridge CAs, PKI domains and trust lists.
PKI.quote: establish a terminology framework and to suggest the operational requirements of Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) domain for interoperability of multi-domain Public Key Infrastructure

rejected.why: Certificates and policy extensions are used, but the document is about PKI trust relationships and domain models, not the X.509 certificate profile itself.
The parent is implied by PKI; no broader security topic is addressed separately.
Revocation status is mentioned only briefly in passing (CRLs); not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only as an example repository in Security Considerations.

RFC5218.title: What Makes for a Successful Protocol?
RFC5218.summary: IAB informational document that uses case studies (HTTP/HTML, IPv4 vs IPX, SSH, inter-domain multicast, WAP, WEP, RADIUS vs TACACS+, NAT) to identify factors that make protocols succeed or fail, as guidance for future protocol work.

internet architecture.why: The document gives architectural/design guidance on what makes protocols succeed: deployability, extensibility, scalability, and threat mitigation. It also cites the Architectural Principles of the Internet. No narrower tag fits.
internet architecture.quote: this document identifies some of the factors influencing success and failure of protocol designs.

IETF process.why: It is aimed at IETF decision-making, such as chartering, choosing among proposals and evaluating BOFs. It also discusses open maintenance processes and open specification availability.
IETF process.quote: IESG members deciding whether to charter a Working Group to do work on a specific protocol;

rejected.why: NAT is one case study among eight. The document does not specify or analyse NAT in its own right.
HTTP/HTML is a case study of success factors and not the subject of the document.
SSH is only a case study, with brief commentary on its success.
RADIUS is compared with TACACS+ only as a success-factor case.
Inter-domain multicast is discussed as an example of an unsuccessful protocol and is not the subject of the document.
Freedom from usage restrictions is one success factor, but the document is not about IPR provisions.

RFC5219.title: A More Loss-Tolerant RTP Payload Format for MP3 Audio
RFC5219.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for MP3 audio that repackages frames as Application Data Units with optional interleaving for better packet-loss tolerance, obsoleting RFC 3119.

MP3.why: The document specifies a loss-tolerant RTP payload format for MP3 audio, which is exactly what the MP3 tag covers.
MP3.quote: This document describes an RTP (Real-Time Protocol) payload format for transporting MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) 1 or 2, layer III audio (commonly known as "MP3").

RTP payload format.why: It defines the packing rules, RTP header field usage, media type (audio/mpa-robust) and SDP usage of an RTP payload format for a specific codec.
RTP payload format.quote: In this new payload format for MP3 audio, however, each RTP packet payload contains "ADU frames", each preceded by an "ADU descriptor".

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format is carried over. The specific tag RTP payload format covers the subject, so the parent is implied.
SDP appears only in a short usage section giving the rtpmap line, which is boilerplate-level use of SDP rather than anything new about it.
The IANA section registers audio/mpa-robust. This is registration boilerplate, not a document about media type rules.
The document does not define a codec. It covers packetization of an existing one, and MP3 is the more specific tag.
Interleaving is used to reduce the effect of packet loss, but the document does not specify any forward error correction or loss recovery coding scheme.

RFC5220.title: Problem Statement for Default Address Selection in Multi-Prefix Environments: Operational Issues of RFC 3484 Default Rules
RFC5220.summary: Informational problem statement describing operational problems of RFC 3484 default source and destination address selection for hosts with multiple prefixes (multi-homing, ULA, IPv4/IPv6, renumbering, temporary addresses), with brief solution analysis.

addressing.why: The whole document is about source and destination IP address selection for hosts with multiple addresses/prefixes, which is IP address architecture and use; no more specific child tag fits.
addressing.quote: RFC 3484 defines default source and destination address selection rules and is implemented in a variety of OSs. But, it has been too difficult to use operationally

IPv6.why: The problems are IPv6-specific: ULA vs global addresses, IPv4/IPv6 prioritization, deprecated addresses, and temporary addresses. Readers of IPv6 deployment would want it.
IPv6.quote: In IPv6, a single physical link can have multiple prefixes assigned to it.

renumbering.why: A dedicated subsection discusses how old-prefix addresses persist during site renumbering and affect address selection.
renumbering.quote: RFC 4192 [RFC4192] describes a recommended procedure for renumbering a network from one prefix to another.

rejected.why: Scope section explicitly excludes multi-homing techniques for redundancy; multi-homed sites are only example scenarios.
Autoconfiguration is mentioned (lifetimes, RFC 4862) but not the subject.
IPv4/IPv6 prioritization is one case, but the document is not about transition mechanisms.
RFC 5014 is only mentioned as a possible solution for temporary address selection.
Only mentioned in passing as an analogous HA/CoA selection situation.

gaps.name: Default address selection (RFC 3484 source/destination address selection)
gaps.why: The central subject has no specific tag; it is covered only by the broader addressing tag.

RFC5221.title: Requirements for Address Selection Mechanisms
RFC5221.summary: Informational RFC listing eleven requirements for an address-selection mechanism (autoconfiguration/central control) that works alongside RFC 3484 default address selection for IPv6 hosts in multi-prefix environments.

addressing.why: The whole document is about source/destination address selection policy for hosts, including multiple prefixes and interfaces. This fits the addressing topic; no more specific technology tag covers address selection.
addressing.quote: This document contains requirements for address-selection mechanisms that enable hosts to perform appropriate address selection automatically.

IPv6.why: RFC 3484 is Default Address Selection for IPv6. The requirements target IPv6 host behavior, and they cover compatibility with the IPv6 socket API (RFC 3493) and next-hop selection (RFC 4191).
IPv6.quote: Though RFC 3484 made the address-selection behavior of a host configurable, typical users cannot make use of that

rejected.why: The multi-prefix problem is the context, but the document gives requirements for address selection and not a multihoming architecture.
A DHCP-based solution is not specified here. Only generic autoconfiguration requirements are given.
It appears only as an example of a security mechanism in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-like and not the subject of the document.
RFC 3493 compatibility is one requirement, but the document does not extend the sockets API.

gaps.name: Default address selection (RFC 3484 policy table)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for source/destination address selection, so addressing is the closest fit.

RFC5222.title: LoST: A Location-to-Service Translation Protocol
RFC5222.summary: RFC 5222 specifies LoST, an XML-over-HTTP protocol that maps service URNs and civic or geodetic locations to service contact URIs, mainly to find the right PSAP for emergency calls.

LoST.why: The document defines the LoST protocol itself: its queries, responses, location profiles, errors and transport.
LoST.quote: This document describes an XML-based protocol for mapping service identifiers and geodetic or civic location information to service contact URIs.

emergency services.why: The protocol's main use is emergency call routing to PSAPs. LoST is already under this topic, so the parent adds only a little.
emergency services.quote: In particular, it can be used to determine the location-appropriate Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) for emergency services.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport for LoST messages (POST, 2xx responses). The document does not extend HTTP.
U-NAPTR/DNS is used only to discover LoST servers. It is a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
XML and the Relax NG schema are the encoding for LoST messages. The document is about the protocol, not XML usage.
Civic and geodetic location formats are reused from PIDF-LO, not defined here. The location profiles only select which formats LoST carries.
TLS is recommended for protecting LoST exchanges, but it is only the security substrate.
The application/lost+xml registration is IANA boilerplate, not a main subject.

RFC5223.title: Discovering Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Servers Using the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)
RFC5223.summary: Defines DHCPv4 (code 137) and DHCPv6 (code 51) options that carry a domain name so a LoST client can discover a local LoST server for emergency service location-to-URL mapping.

DHCP.why: The document's main content is defining new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options, so DHCP readers need it. DHCPv6 is a child tag, but the document covers both versions, so the parent DHCP is the better fit.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies a DHCPv4 and a DHCPv6 option that allows LoST clients to discover local LoST servers.

LoST.why: The document is about discovering LoST servers, which is a companion to the LoST protocol. It sits under emergency services and readers of LoST would want it.
LoST.quote: This document describes how a LoST client can discover a LoST server using the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP).

rejected.why: The document defines options for both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 equally, so the parent DHCP covers it better than the DHCPv6 child.
The domain name is encoded per RFC 1035 and fed into U-NAPTR resolution, but the document defines nothing new about DNS. DNS is only the substrate.
The document is a discovery mechanism, but it is specific to LoST via DHCP. The generic service discovery topic is not a better fit than the technology tags.
LoST is XML-based, but the document does not use or specify XML formats.

RFC5224.title: Diameter Policy Processing Application
RFC5224.summary: Informational RFC documenting the new Diameter vendor-specific Policy Processing Application (Command Code 314, Policy-Data AVP, application id 16777243) used for the OMA PEEM PEM-1 interface.

Diameter.why: The document defines a new Diameter application with a new command code, AVP and application id, extending the Diameter base protocol. Readers of Diameter would want it.
Diameter.quote: This document describes the need for a new IANA Diameter Command Code to be used in a vendor-specific new application for invocation of Policy Processing

rejected.why: The document concerns policy evaluation and enforcement invocation, but it is a Diameter application registration and is not about policy-based network management information models.
Diameter is already tagged and sits under AAA, so the parent is implied.
The IANA section only registers Command Code 314, the AVP and the application id. It is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: OMA PEEM (Policy Evaluation, Enforcement and Management)
gaps.why: The document exists to support the Open Mobile Alliance PEEM enabler's PEM-1 interface. The taxonomy has no tag for OMA policy enablers.

RFC5225.title: RObust Header Compression Version 2 (ROHCv2): Profiles for RTP, UDP, IP, ESP and UDP-Lite
RFC5225.summary: Specifies the ROHCv2 header compression profiles (0x0101-0x0108) for RTP/UDP/IP, UDP/IP, ESP/IP, IP, RTP/UDP-Lite/IP and UDP-Lite/IP, with header formats, reordering robustness, and feedback.

ROHC.why: The document defines the second version of the ROHC profiles, their formats, and feedback.
ROHC.quote: This document specifies ROHC (Robust Header Compression) profiles that efficiently compress RTP/UDP/IP

rejected.why: RTP headers are compressed by the profile, but the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
UDP-Lite is a compressed header type, not the subject of the document.
ESP headers are compressed by one profile; the document does not specify ESP.
IPsec is only touched via the ESP and AH header compression.
GRE is one of the extension headers that can be compressed, not a subject of the document.
IPv6 headers are compressed, but the document does not address IPv6 itself.

gaps.name: ROHC (RObust Header Compression) ROHCv2 profiles
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the parent 'header compression' topic with ROHC, CRTP and IPHC children. I tagged ROHC, which exists in the taxonomy under header compression.

RFC5226.title: Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs
RFC5226.summary: BCP 26 gives guidelines for authors on writing IANA Considerations sections, defining registry assignment policies (Expert Review, IETF Review, Standards Action, etc.), designated expert roles, and procedures for registering, updating and reclaiming values.

IANA.why: The whole document is about IANA registries, registration policies, and what to put in IANA Considerations sections.
IANA.quote: This document discusses issues that should be considered in formulating a policy for assigning values to a namespace and provides guidelines for authors on the specific text

rejected.why: Designated experts, IESG approval and appeals touch IETF process, but they are in service of registry management, so the more specific IANA tag fits.
DHCP options appear only as examples of registries and sample text.
IPsec transforms are mentioned only as an example of values needing assignment.
Media types are cited only as an example namespace, not specified here.
DNS is mentioned only as an example of a delegated namespace.

RFC5227.title: IPv4 Address Conflict Detection
RFC5227.summary: RFC 5227 specifies IPv4 Address Conflict Detection: ARP Probes before using an address, ARP Announcements after, and ongoing passive conflict detection and defense, updating RFC 826.

ARP.why: The whole document specifies how ARP Requests are used as probes and announcements, and how received ARP packets are checked for conflicts. It updates RFC 826.
ARP.quote: a host implementing this specification MUST test to see if the address is already in use, by broadcasting ARP Probe packets.

IPv4.why: The document is about avoiding and detecting duplicate IPv4 address use on a link, and about address acquisition and rate-limiting. This is IPv4 address lifecycle management.
IPv4.quote: IPv4 Address Conflict Detection (ACD)

rejected.why: DHCP is mentioned as a motivating use case, and DHCPDECLINE is the notification path. The document does not specify or extend DHCP.
Ethernet and other IEEE 802 links are only the applicability scope. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
The IPv4 tag already covers address lifecycle, so the parent topic is not needed.

RFC5228.title: Sieve: An Email Filtering Language
RFC5228.summary: RFC 5228 specifies the Sieve language, a simple, extensible, non-Turing-complete scripting language for filtering email messages at final delivery, covering its syntax, tests, actions, control commands, extension mechanism and application/sieve media type.

Sieve.why: The whole document defines the Sieve language: grammar, tests, actions, control commands, extensibility and the capability registry.
Sieve.quote: This document describes a language for filtering email messages at time of final delivery.

rejected.why: Sieve inspects headers and addresses defined by the Internet Message Format but does not specify or extend it.
The envelope test reads SMTP MAIL/RCPT data and redirect resubmits mail, but SMTP is only the substrate, not specified here.
Mentioned only as a server environment and for mailbox-name encoding in fileinto; the language is access-protocol independent.
Section 7 registers application/sieve, but this is a small part of the document and the registry rules are not the subject.
MIME encoded-word header decoding is used for comparisons, but MIME itself is not being specified.
Scripts and comparisons use UTF-8, but it is just the encoding relied upon.

RFC5229.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Variables Extension
RFC5229.summary: Specifies the Sieve "variables" extension, which adds variable substitution in strings, match variables, a "set" action with modifiers, and a "string" test for the Sieve email filtering language.

Sieve.why: The whole document defines an extension to the Sieve email filtering language: the set action, string test, modifiers and match variables.
Sieve.quote: This document updates the Sieve filtering language (RFC 5228) with an extension to support variables.

rejected.why: Sieve is already the specific tag under email; the document is about the filtering language, not email generally.
Spam and virus checking are mentioned only in Security Considerations, as something Sieve is not suited for.
Characters are defined by reference to ISO 10646/UTF-8, but this is only the substrate for string handling.
ABNF is used only as notation for the grammar; the document is not about it.

RFC5230.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Vacation Extension
RFC5230.summary: Defines the Sieve "vacation" extension, an autoresponder action with response tracking, loop-prevention safeguards, and rules for generating the reply message.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies a Sieve extension (the vacation action, its arguments, capability identifier and interaction with other Sieve actions).
Sieve.quote: This document defines an extension to the Sieve language defined in [RFC5228] for notification that messages to a particular recipient will not be answered immediately.

rejected.why: Only used as the transport for responses (MAIL FROM <>, NOTIFY=NEVER); the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Header generation rules (Auto-Submitted, In-Reply-To, References) are applied to the reply but the document doesn't define message format.
The :mime parameter carries a MIME entity, but MIME is a substrate here, not the subject.
List headers are only checked to suppress replies; the document does not address mailing list protocols.
A short section covers UTF-8 and language selection, but it is a minor consideration, not the subject.

RFC5231.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Relational Extension
RFC5231.summary: Defines the Sieve "relational" extension, adding :value and :count match types with relational operators (gt, ge, lt, le, eq, ne) to Sieve address, envelope and header tests; obsoletes RFC 3431.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the Sieve email filtering language, defining new match types and their semantics.
Sieve.quote: The RELATIONAL extension to the Sieve mail filtering language [Sieve] provides relational operators on the address, envelope, and header tests.

rejected.why: Internet message format (RFC 2822) is only referenced for counting mailbox elements and header fields; the document does not specify it.
Covered by the more specific Sieve tag; the document is about filtering language tests, not mail architecture.
ABNF is used only as notation for the new syntax; it is not the subject.
The IANA section merely registers the capability name; it is boilerplate and not the subject.
Envelope MAIL FROM is mentioned only to define the envelope test count, not as SMTP specification.

RFC5232.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Imap4flags Extension
RFC5232.summary: RFC 5232 defines the Sieve "imap4flags" extension, adding setflag, addflag and removeflag actions, a hasflag test and a :flags argument so Sieve scripts can set IMAP system flags and keywords on delivered messages.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies a Sieve language extension: new actions, a test and a tagged argument for keep and fileinto.
Sieve.quote: This document describes an extension to the Sieve mail filtering language for setting IMAP flags.

rejected.why: IMAP flags are the thing being set, but the document doesn't specify or extend IMAP. It only refers to IMAP's flag definitions and may act as an IMAP client or have direct mailstore access.
The parent of Sieve, so it is implied by the Sieve tag and not listed separately.
The document doesn't deal with message headers or format. It only uses header tests in examples.

RFC5233.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Subaddress Extension
RFC5233.summary: Defines the Sieve "subaddress" extension, adding :user and :detail address parts so scripts can compare against the user and detail sub-parts of an email local-part (e.g. ken+sieve@example.org); obsoletes RFC 3598.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies a Sieve extension (capability "subaddress") adding :user and :detail address parts to address and envelope tests.
Sieve.quote: This document defines an extension to the Sieve Email Filtering Language that allows users to compare against the user and detail sub-parts of an address.

rejected.why: Subaddressing refers to the local-part of RFC 2822 addresses, but the document does not specify or extend the message format; it only relies on it.
Email is the context, but the document is specific to the Sieve filtering language, which is the more specific tag.
The IANA registration of the Sieve capability is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.

RFC5234.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF
RFC5234.summary: RFC 5234 specifies Augmented BNF (ABNF), the metalanguage for defining formal syntax in Internet specifications, including its operators, its own ABNF definition, and a set of core rules.

ABNF.why: The document is the standard definition of ABNF: rule naming, operators, terminal values, the ABNF grammar of ABNF, and the core rules.
ABNF.quote: a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications.

rejected.why: US-ASCII is used as the character set for terminals and the core-rule encoding, but the document is not about ASCII itself.
The email specs RFC 733 and RFC 822 are mentioned only as historical origins of ABNF, not as subjects.
The external-encodings section only notes that encoding is beyond the scope of ABNF. It does not address character set registration or use.

RFC5235.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Spamtest and Virustest Extensions
RFC5235.summary: RFC 5235 defines the Sieve email filtering extensions "spamtest", "spamtestplus" and "virustest", which add tests that match normalized numeric spam and virus scores, and it obsoletes RFC 3685.

Sieve.why: The document specifies new Sieve tests and their capability identifiers, so it is a Sieve extension.
Sieve.quote: The Sieve email filtering language "spamtest", "spamtestplus", and "virustest" extensions permit users to use simple, portable commands for spam and virus tests on email messages.

spam.why: A substantial part of the document is a portable spam-scoring test, with a 0-10 scale and a 0-100 :percent scale. Readers of spam filtering would want it.
spam.quote: The purpose of this document is to introduce two Sieve tests that can be used to implement "generic" tests for spam and viruses in messages

rejected.why: Sieve and spam are more specific tags under email, and the document is about filtering rather than email architecture.
The tests depend on headers added by third-party checkers, but the document does not define or discuss message format.
The document mentions black-listed senders only as an example and does not cover DNS-based blocklists.
The IANA registrations of Sieve capability names are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC5236.title: Improved Packet Reordering Metrics
RFC5236.summary: Defines two packet reordering metrics, Reorder Density (RD) and Reorder Buffer-occupancy Density (RBD), with thresholds for loss/duplicate detection, O(N) algorithms and worked examples, as an alternative to RFC 4737.
