performance measurement.why: The document defines IP performance metrics for packet reordering and algorithms to measure them, which is the performance measurement subject.
performance measurement.quote: This document presents two improved metrics for packet reordering, namely, Reorder Density (RD) and Reorder Buffer-occupancy Density (RBD).

rejected.why: TCP is mentioned only as an example application sensitive to reordering and for window-size limits on DT; the document is not about TCP.
OWAMP appears only in the Security Considerations pointer to RFC 4656/3763; not the subject.
Mentioned only as a cause of reordering.
The metrics are for measuring network traffic reordering, not benchmarking methodology for devices.

gaps.name: packet reordering metrics
gaps.why: The document is specifically about packet reordering measurement, which has no dedicated tag; performance measurement is the closest parent.

RFC5237.title: IANA Allocation Guidelines for the Protocol Field
RFC5237.summary: BCP update to RFC 2780 that removes the Expert Review option from IANA allocation rules for the IPv4 Protocol field (and thus IPv6 Next Header), leaving only IESG Approval or Standards Action.

IANA.why: The document's whole purpose is to revise IANA registry allocation policy for the Protocol field and Next Header values, so it belongs under IANA registries and considerations guidance.
IANA.quote: IANA allocates values from the IPv4 Protocol name space following an IESG Approval or Standards Action process.

rejected.why: The Protocol field is in the IPv4 header, but the document only changes the registry allocation policy. It doesn't specify or analyse IPv4.
The change also covers IPv6 Next Header values, but only through the IANA rule. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
The IESG Approval and Standards Action processes are mentioned only as allocation policies. The document is about the registry, not IETF procedures in general.

RFC5238.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) over the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)
RFC5238.summary: Specifies how to carry DTLS records in DCCP-Data packets, covering handshake interaction, congestion control effects, PMTU handling, session/connection relationships and DCCP Service Codes.

DTLS.why: The document defines how DTLS is used over a new transport, DCCP, including handshake, PMTU and session behaviour. Readers of DTLS would want it.
DTLS.quote: DTLS records are transmitted in the Application Data fields of DCCP-Data and DCCP-DataAck packets

DCCP.why: The document specifies how applications using DCCP get transport security. It covers DCCP handshake, CCIDs, MPS and Service Codes.
DCCP.quote: DCCP is a transport protocol that provides a congestion-controlled unreliable datagram service.

rejected.why: DTLS is the TLS variant being used. The document is about DTLS, a child of TLS, so TLS is implied and not tagged separately.
Section 3.3 discusses how DCCP congestion control affects the DTLS handshake. It defines no congestion control mechanism, and the DCCP tag already covers it.
Section 3.5 reconciles DTLS and DCCP PMTU handling. This is a small part of the document, not its subject.
UDP appears only as the comparison transport for DTLS and DCCP.
TFRC and CCID 3 are mentioned only as a suggestion for applications. The document is not about them.

RFC5239.title: A Framework for Centralized Conferencing
RFC5239.summary: RFC 5239 defines the XCON framework for centralized conferencing: logical entities (focus, conference control server, floor control server, notification service), conference object/identifier constructs, a cloning tree model, and scenario realizations such as sidebars and whispers.

XCON.why: The document is the XCON centralized conferencing framework itself, defining the conference object, identifiers, cloning tree, and conferencing system entities.
XCON.quote: This document defines the framework for Centralized Conferencing.

BFCP.why: Floor control via BFCP is a framework component. Sections 8.4, 9.5 and 11.3 cover floor control, its SDP attributes and server authentication.
BFCP.quote: A floor control protocol (e.g., Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP)) provides the interface between a floor control client and the floor control server.

rejected.why: SIP is one supported call signaling protocol and the default, but the framework treats signaling as out of scope and generic.
SDP offer/answer is used only to carry floor control connection info, with attributes defined in RFC 4583.
iCal objects are referenced for scheduling in Section 7.4 only. The document is not about the iCalendar format.
This is the parent of XCON and BFCP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The SIP conference event package is referenced for notifications, but the document does not specify it.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations as boilerplate-level guidance.

RFC5240.title: Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) Bootstrap Router MIB
RFC5240.summary: Defines the PIM-BSR-MIB SMIv2 module with tables and notifications for managing the PIM Bootstrap Router mechanism: Candidate-RP, Elected BSR RP-Set, Candidate-BSR and Elected-BSR.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is a new MIB module (PIM-BSR-MIB) written in SMIv2, with tables, notifications and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

PIM.why: The MIB manages the PIM BSR mechanism (C-RP, C-BSR, elected BSR, RP-sets, BIDIR-PIM vs PIM-SM ranges), so PIM readers would look for it. PIM-SM is the closest fit for the BSR mechanism.
PIM.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism for PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast).

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol; the document defines a MIB module and does not extend SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
The BSR mechanism is part of the PIM-SM family, but this document manages BSR through a MIB rather than specifying PIM-SM, so the more general PIM tag fits.
The parent topic is implied by the PIM tag, so it is not listed separately.
The parent topic is implied by the MIB tag.

RFC5241.title: Naming Rights in IETF Protocols
RFC5241.summary: An April 1 humorous RFC proposing that the IETF sell and lease commercial naming rights to protocol fields, with IANA, RFC Editor and xml2rfc changes to produce branded "Real_RFCs".

humor.why: A dated 1 April satirical proposal (Real_RFCs, Viagra Total Length, Microsoft Evil bit) that belongs in the humorous RFCs series.
humor.quote: This document proposes a new revenue source for the IETF to support standardization activities: protocol field naming rights, i.e., the association of commercial brands with protocol fields.

rejected.why: The IANA considerations section sets up a brand-name catalog, but that is a satirical proposal rather than a document about IANA registries or stewardship.
The RFC Editor Considerations describe producing branded Real_RFCs, but this is a small joke part of the proposal, not a real change to the RFC series.
Mentions a pfield XML element and xml2rfc changes, but only as part of the parody, not a real vocabulary specification.
Naming rights and indemnification are trademark-flavored satire, not a document about IETF IPR or copyright provisions.

RFC5242.title: A Generalized Unified Character Code: Western European and CJK Sections
RFC5242.summary: An April 1st parody RFC describing a fully unified coded character set (composing Latin, Greek, Cyrillic and CJK glyphs from base shapes, modifiers and joiners) as a spoof alternative to Unicode for internationalized domain names.

humor.why: Published 1 April with absurd design choices (23-bit code space because 3 and 23 are prime, an expert on angels on pinheads). It is a parody of character-set and IDN design.
humor.quote: The generation of other numbers is left as an exercise for the reader.

internationalization.why: The document is, in jest, about a coded character set for internationalized text. It compares itself to Unicode and unifies look-alike characters across scripts.
internationalization.quote: This memo describes a fully unified coded character set for scripts based on Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and Chinese (CJK) characters.

rejected.why: IDNs are the stated motivation and IDNA is cited, but the document defines a parody character set. It does not specify IDNA, punycode or label validity.
Unicode is the foil and the source of the character names. The document proposes a rival encoding, not a way of using Unicode in Internet protocols.
It defines a character set, but it is a joke that no one would register or use. The broader internationalization tag fits better.
The IANA section only asks for a registry as part of the joke. It is boilerplate.

RFC5243.title: OSPF Database Exchange Summary List Optimization
RFC5243.summary: Describes a backward-compatible optimization to the OSPFv2/OSPFv3 Database Exchange process that omits LSAs from Database Description packets when the neighbor already listed the same or newer instance, reducing DD overhead by about 50%.

OSPFv3.why: The document modifies the OSPFv2 database exchange procedure and applies equally to OSPFv3. It is about OSPF, and OSPFv3 is the most specific child tag covering the IPv6 variant.
OSPFv3.quote: This document describes a backward-compatible optimization for the Database Exchange process in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

OSPF.why: The document's core content is a change to the OSPFv2 specification in RFC 2328 (Database Description packet handling). OSPF is tagged directly because the OSPFv2 portion is not covered by the OSPFv3 child tag.
OSPF.quote: The Database Exchange summary list optimization is defined by modifying Section 10.6 "Receiving Database Description Packets" of RFC 2328 as follows.

rejected.why: The introduction mentions large mobile ad hoc networks only as a place where the optimization is especially beneficial. The document does not specify MANET routing.
The optimization is a protocol-level change to OSPF. It is not about routing architecture or scalability principles in general.

RFC5244.title: Definition of Events for Channel-Oriented Telephony Signalling
RFC5244.summary: RFC 5244 updates RFC 4733 by defining RTP telephone-event codes for carrying PSTN channel-associated signalling (SS No. 5, R1/MF, R2, ABCD bit states, continuity tones, trunk unavailable, metering pulse) between gateways in an "RTP trunk" application.

RTP.why: The document defines new event codes for the telephone-event RTP payload format, extending RFC 4733; RTP users would look for it.
RTP.quote: This memo updates RFC 4733 to add event codes for telephony signals used for channel-associated signalling when carried in the telephony event RTP payload.

PSTN interop.why: It concerns carrying PSTN trunk signalling systems (SS No. 5, R1, R2, ABCD) over IP between gateways, which is PSTN interworking. No more specific child tag fits.
PSTN interop.quote: The events defined in this document support an application where such PSTN signalling is carried between two gateways without being signalled in the IP network

rejected.why: This tag is for payload formats of specific codecs and media. The document only adds event codes to the existing telephone-event payload defined in RFC 4733, so the generic RTP tag fits better.
SRTP is only mentioned in Security Considerations as the protection mechanism to use. The document is not about it.
G.723.1 and G.729 appear only as examples of encodings that destroy in-band signalling. The document does not define or profile them.
The document concerns channel-associated trunk signalling, not SS7 or ISDN signalling transport over IP.
The IANA section registers event codes, but this is boilerplate relative to the main body, which is about the events themselves.

gaps.name: Telephony events / DTMF and telephony signals over RTP (telephone-event payload)
gaps.why: The document extends the telephone-event payload for signalling events. The taxonomy has no tag for DTMF or telephony tone events, so RTP and PSTN interop only partly cover it.

RFC5245.title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal for Offer/Answer Protocols
RFC5245.summary: RFC 5245 specifies Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE), an offer/answer-based NAT traversal protocol for UDP media that gathers candidate addresses, runs STUN connectivity checks, nominates pairs, and defines SDP attributes and STUN extensions, with SIP usage guidance.

ICE.why: The entire document specifies ICE: candidate gathering, prioritization, connectivity checks, nomination, lite/full implementations and restarts.
ICE.quote: This document describes a protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal for UDP-based multimedia sessions established with the offer/answer model.

SDP.why: ICE is an extension to offer/answer and defines new SDP attributes with grammar and IANA registrations, which SDP readers need.
SDP.quote: This specification defines seven new SDP attributes -- the "candidate", "remote-candidates", "ice-lite", "ice-mismatch", "ice-ufrag", "ice-pwd", and "ice-options" attributes.

STUN.why: Defines new STUN attributes and error code 487, and details STUN client/server procedures for connectivity checks and keepalives.
STUN.quote: ICE extends STUN by defining several new attributes, including PRIORITY, USE-CANDIDATE, ICE-CONTROLLED, and ICE-CONTROLLING.

SIP.why: Section 12 gives SIP-specific usage: latency guidelines, provisional response reliability, forking, preconditions, and third-party call control.
SIP.quote: ICE requires a series of STUN-based connectivity checks to take place between endpoints.

rejected.why: TURN supplies relayed candidates, but the document only uses it as a substrate and defines nothing new for TURN.
NAT traversal is the motivation, but the ICE tag already covers it under NAT traversal; the document does not specify NAT behaviour.
RTP is the media being established; ICE only demultiplexes and handles RTP/RTCP components, without extending RTP.
ICE supports dual-stack address selection, but this is a side benefit, not the subject.
Deprecation of ANAT (RFC 4091/4092) is touched on in Section 13 only briefly.

RFC5246.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2
RFC5246.summary: RFC 5246 specifies TLS version 1.2, defining the record protocol, handshake, alerts, cipher suites, key derivation, backward compatibility and security analysis.

TLS.why: The whole document is the TLS 1.2 protocol specification: record layer, handshake, alerts, extensions framework and cipher suites.
TLS.quote: This document specifies Version 1.2 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

rejected.why: Algorithms (AES, RSA, HMAC, DH) are used within cipher suites but the document specifies the protocol, not the algorithms.
Certificates are carried in the handshake but profiling X.509 is not the document's subject.
HMAC is used to build the PRF but is only a building block here.
TCP is only the reliable transport substrate for TLS.
IANA Considerations is boilerplate; the registries are TLS-specific and not the document's subject.
DTLS is not discussed; only TLS over reliable transport.

RFC5247.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Key Management Framework
RFC5247.summary: Specifies the EAP key hierarchy and a framework for transport and use of EAP-derived keying material, with identifiers, secure association, handoff and a system-level security analysis against RFC 4962 requirements.

EAP.why: The whole document defines EAP keying material (MSK, EMSK), Session-Id/Peer-Id/Server-Id and their handling, updating RFC 3748.
EAP.quote: This document specifies the EAP key hierarchy and provides a framework for the transport and usage of keying material and parameters generated by EAP methods.

key management.why: Large parts cover key naming, scope, lifetimes, freshness, caching and secure association management, and the analysis against RFC 4962 key management requirements.
key management.quote: provides a detailed security analysis, describing the conditions under which the requirements described in "Guidance for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) Key Management" [RFC4962] can be satisfied.

rejected.why: RADIUS and Diameter are the AAA key transport substrate discussed throughout, but the document does not specify or extend them.
AAA key transport (phase 1b) is one phase of the framework and is discussed heavily, but the document is about EAP keying, not AAA frameworks themselves.
IEEE 802.11 and its 4-way handshake are used as examples of lower layers, not the subject.
IKEv2 appears as an example EAP lower layer only.
EAP-TLS and TLS are mentioned as example method and substrate only.

RFC5248.title: A Registry for SMTP Enhanced Mail System Status Codes
RFC5248.summary: RFC 5248 (BCP 138) creates the IANA registry for SMTP Enhanced Mail System Status Codes, sets its review and update rules, populates it with initial codes from RFC 3463, 3886, 4468 and 4954, and registers new codes X.7.10, X.7.13 and X.7.14.

SMTP.why: The document defines and populates the registry of SMTP enhanced status codes, extending SMTP's reply code space. It also updates RFC 4468 and RFC 4954, both SMTP extensions. SMTP readers need it.
SMTP.quote: This document specifies an IANA registry for mail system enhanced status codes

IANA.why: A large part of the document sets up the registry, with its review process, update rules and initial values. It is a registry-creation document, so readers of the IANA subject would expect it.
IANA.quote: Entries in this registry are expected to follow the "Specification Required" model ([RFC5226])

rejected.why: The more specific SMTP tag covers this. The document concerns SMTP status codes, not email architecture generally.
TLS appears only in the X.7.10 description as an example of a security layer a client may activate. The document is not about TLS.
The codes come from SMTP AUTH (RFC 4954), but the document does not specify or extend SASL. It only registers status codes.
The document is about SMTP reply codes, not message headers or addressing.

RFC5249.title: Templates for Internet-Drafts Containing MIB Modules
RFC5249.summary: BCP 5249 points editors to three MIB Doctor-produced templates (XML2RFC, annotated text, plain text) for Internet-Drafts that define MIB modules, to make such documents uniform and easier to review.

MIB.why: The whole document is about templates and authoring practice for documents defining MIB modules, so readers of the MIB subject would want it.
MIB.quote: three annotated templates for IETF documents that contain the definition of MIB modules

rejected.why: MIB modules are used with SNMP, but the document only covers document templates, not the SNMP protocol; MIB is the more specific fit.
The templates concern Internet-Draft authoring, but they are specific to MIB documents and the document does not address RFC format or style in general.
An XML2RFC template is one of the three, but the document does not define or discuss the RFC XML vocabulary itself.
It mentions IESG requirements and MIB Doctor review, but only as context for the templates; it does not specify process.

RFC5250.title: The OSPF Opaque LSA Option
RFC5250.summary: Defines OSPF Opaque LSAs (types 9, 10, 11) as a generalized extensibility mechanism, with flooding scope rules, neighbor state machine changes, and a mechanism to validate AS-scope Opaque LSAs from other areas; obsoletes RFC 2370.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with Opaque LSAs, modifying flooding procedures and the neighbor state machine. It is squarely an OSPF specification.
OSPF.quote: This document defines enhancements to the OSPF protocol to support a new class of link state advertisements (LSAs) called Opaque LSAs.

rejected.why: The IANA section only updates the Opaque LSA type registry. This is boilerplate relative to the main body, which is about OSPF.
The Management Considerations section only points to the OSPF MIB (RFC 4750) for Opaque LSA support. The document does not define or analyse a MIB.
The TE LSA appears only as a registry entry for Opaque type 1. The document is not about traffic engineering.
OSPFv3 is cited only for a remark about reachability validation. The document specifies OSPFv2.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate-like and restates existing OSPF authentication. It adds no routing security mechanism.

RFC5251.title: Layer 1 VPN Basic Mode
RFC5251.summary: Specifies the Layer 1 VPN Basic Mode: a port-based VPN service over GMPLS networks, defining port identifiers, Port Information Tables, auto-discovery information encoding, and the CE-PE RSVP-TE signaling (shuffling, stitching/nesting) and recovery procedures.

L1VPN.why: The whole document defines the L1VPN Basic Mode operational model, port information tables, and signaling extensions.
L1VPN.quote: L1VPN Basic Mode (L1VPN BM) is a port-based VPN.  In L1VPN Basic Mode, the basic unit of service is a Label Switched Path (LSP)

GMPLS.why: The service is realized with GMPLS signaling in the overlay model, including RSVP-TE address shuffling, stitching/nesting and segment recovery. A substantial part of the document is GMPLS signaling procedure.
GMPLS.quote: GMPLS RSVP-TE is used for signaling both within the service provider (between PEs), as well as between the customer and the service provider

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signaling mechanism used, but the document defines its use specifically within GMPLS L1VPN rather than the protocol itself.
The document relies on MPLS/GMPLS background but is not about MPLS architecture or encapsulation; GMPLS is the more specific fit.
L1VPN is the more specific child tag; parent is implied.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional protection for the control channel.
BGP-based auto-discovery is only referenced; its mechanisms are defined in other RFCs.

RFC5252.title: OSPF-Based Layer 1 VPN Auto-Discovery
RFC5252.summary: Defines an OSPFv2 Opaque LSA (type 5, L1VPN LSA) and L1VPN Info TLV that lets PE routers auto-discover L1VPN membership and CE-link port mappings for L1VPN basic mode.

L1VPN.why: The document specifies auto-discovery of L1VPN membership and port mappings for basic mode, so readers of the L1VPN subject need it.
L1VPN.quote: This document defines an Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) based Layer 1 Virtual Private Network (L1VPN) auto-discovery mechanism.

OSPF.why: It extends OSPFv2 with a new Opaque LSA type and TLV, including flooding and processing rules and backward compatibility.
OSPF.quote: The approach used in this document to provide OSPF-based L1VPN auto-discovery uses a new type of Opaque Link State Advertisement (LSA) that is referred to as an L1VPN LSA.

rejected.why: The backbone is GMPLS and TE Link TLVs from the GMPLS OSPF extensions are reused, but the document does not specify GMPLS itself.
Explicitly out of scope; the document covers only OSPF version 2.
Only mentioned as the parallel BGP-based auto-discovery in RFC 5195; this document does not address BGP.
TE TLVs and the TED are reused, but the document is not about traffic engineering in its own right.
Considered because it is auto-discovery, but the L1VPN tag is more specific and the discovery here is VPN membership among PEs.

RFC5253.title: Applicability Statement for Layer 1 Virtual Private Network (L1VPN) Basic Mode
RFC5253.summary: Applicability statement describing how GMPLS protocols and mechanisms (RSVP-TE signalling, BGP/OSPF auto-discovery) satisfy the requirements of Basic Mode Layer 1 VPNs, covering provider/customer control, addressing, scalability, resiliency and security.

L1VPN.why: The whole document is about Basic Mode L1VPNs: PIT provisioning, PE-to-PE segment control, topology control and security.
L1VPN.quote: This document provides an applicability statement on the use of Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) protocols and mechanisms to support Basic Mode Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks (L1VPNs).

GMPLS.why: The document examines how GMPLS signalling, recovery and control-plane mechanisms are applied to meet L1VPN requirements, which is a substantial part of its content.
GMPLS.quote: The provider network is controlled by GMPLS.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signalling mechanism relied on, but the document does not specify or extend it. It is covered under GMPLS.
BGP-based auto-discovery is only referenced from RFC 5195 and is not specified here.
OSPF-based auto-discovery is only referenced from RFC 5252 and is not specified here.
PCE is mentioned only as one option for computing PE-to-PE paths.
L1VPN is the more specific child tag and already covers the VPN subject.
IPsec appears only in the security discussion as an option customers or providers may use.

RFC5254.title: Requirements for Multi-Segment Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3)
RFC5254.summary: Requirements document for multi-segment pseudowires (MS-PWs) in PWE3, covering switching PEs, setup mechanisms, resiliency, QoS, congestion control, OAM, management and security across multiple PSN domains.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines requirements for multi-segment pseudowires, so pseudowire emulation is the central subject.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies requirements for extending pseudowires across more than one packet switched network (PSN) domain and/or more than one PSN tunnel.

rejected.why: MPLS is the usual PSN substrate for the PWs; the document is about pseudowires, not MPLS itself.
LDP signalling for PW setup is mentioned (FEC 128/129) but only as an existing mechanism, not specified or extended.
Inter-AS L2VPN appears as a use case only; the document is not about L2VPN services.
There is an OAM section, but it is one part of the requirements and does not warrant a separate tag; the document is not primarily about OAM.
QoS and congestion requirements are one section of the MS-PW requirements, not the subject of the document.

RFC5255.title: Internet Message Access Protocol Internationalization
RFC5255.summary: RFC 5255 defines IMAP4rev1 extensions (LANGUAGE, I18NLEVEL=1 and I18NLEVEL=2 with COMPARATOR) for negotiating the language of server text, translating namespace prefixes, and choosing collations for SEARCH, SORT and THREAD.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies new IMAP commands, responses, capabilities and response codes (LANGUAGE, COMPARATOR, BADCOMPARATOR, I18NLEVEL), so it is an IMAP extension.
IMAP.quote: This specification defines two IMAP4rev1 [RFC3501] extensions to enhance international support.

language tags.why: Language negotiation relies on language tags and language-range matching (RFC 4646/4647), with i-default as the default. This is a substantial part of the document.
language tags.quote: requests that human-readable text emitted by the server be localized to a language matching one of the language range argument as described by Section 2 of [RFC4647].

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the child tags, so it is not listed separately.
UTF-8 is the encoding for localized text, but the document does not define or profile it.
IDNA is mentioned only in Section 5.3 as an unresolved issue for future work.
MIME decoding is a step in the collation procedure, but MIME itself is not the subject.
EAI is cited only as the venue for work on issues this document leaves unresolved.
SASL is mentioned only for security-layer interaction and for Unicode userids.
TLS appears only in a security note about re-issuing LANGUAGE after STARTTLS.

gaps.name: collation / comparator framework
gaps.why: I18NLEVEL=2 and the COMPARATOR command are built on the Internet Application Protocol Collation Registry (RFC 4790) and i;unicode-casemap. The taxonomy has no tag for collation.

RFC5256.title: Internet Message Access Protocol - SORT and THREAD Extensions
RFC5256.summary: RFC 5256 defines the IMAP SORT and THREAD extensions, which let a server sort and thread messages (ORDEREDSUBJECT and REFERENCES algorithms), including base-subject extraction, the new commands and responses, and their formal syntax.

IMAP.why: The document specifies new IMAP commands (SORT, UID SORT, THREAD, UID THREAD), untagged responses, capabilities and IANA registries as extensions to IMAP.
IMAP.quote: The SORT and THREAD extensions to the [IMAP] protocol provide a means of server-based sorting and threading of messages

rejected.why: The threading algorithm uses Message-ID, References, In-Reply-To and Subject headers, but it does not define or change the Internet message format.
IMAP is the more specific tag. The document does not address email architecture more broadly.
UTF-8 is only the charset used for collation and for decoding subjects. The document defines nothing new about it.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax. The document is not about the notation.
The Internationalization Considerations section requires I18NLEVEL=1 collation, but this is a supporting requirement. The main body is about sorting and threading.
The IANA section registers the capabilities and creates a threading algorithms registry. This is boilerplate and the main body is not about IANA.

gaps.name: IMAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IMAP tag. Only the entry named IMAP exists, so this is a fit with the tag I used, not a gap.

RFC5257.title: Internet Message Access Protocol - ANNOTATE Extension
RFC5257.summary: Defines the experimental IMAP ANNOTATE extension, which lets clients and servers store private and shared metadata annotations on messages and message parts, adding FETCH, STORE, APPEND, SEARCH, SORT, COPY and ACL changes.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to IMAP: new FETCH, STORE, APPEND, SEARCH and SORT items, response codes, a SELECT parameter and an ACL right.
IMAP.quote: The ANNOTATE extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol permits clients and servers to maintain "meta data" for messages, or individual message parts, stored in a mailbox on the server.

rejected.why: The data model is based on ACAP (RFC 2244), but the document does not specify or extend ACAP.
IMAP is a child of email, and the more specific IMAP tag fits, so the parent is implied.
Entry registrations carry content-types, but this is IANA boilerplate and not media type registration rules.
The registries for entries and attributes are a minor part of the document and are specific to the extension.
The formal syntax is written in ABNF, which serves only as notation.

RFC5258.title: Internet Message Access Protocol version 4 - LIST Command Extensions
RFC5258.summary: RFC 5258 extends the IMAP4 LIST command (LIST-EXTENDED capability) with selection options, return options, multiple patterns, new mailbox attributes, and the CHILDINFO extended data item, and obsoletes the Child Mailbox Extension (RFC 3348).

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to IMAP4's LIST command, including syntax, options, attributes and IANA registries for IMAP LIST-EXTENDED.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an IMAP4 extension that is identified by the capability string "LIST-EXTENDED".

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section; the document is not about it.
The IANA registries for LIST-EXTENDED options and data items are boilerplate-like registrations in service of the IMAP extension, not the main subject.
IMAP is the more specific tag; the parent is implied.
Mailbox listing is not directory service access; the LIST command concerns IMAP mailbox hierarchy.

gaps.name: IMAP4 mailbox access and extensions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IMAP tech tag (messaging > email > IMAP) but I used it above; however the tag id list shows 'IMAP' exactly, so no real gap. Listed only to note that IMAP extension mechanisms (capability registries) have no finer-grained tag.

RFC5259.title: Internet Message Access Protocol - CONVERT Extension
RFC5259.summary: Defines the IMAP CONVERT extension, adding CONVERSIONS and CONVERT/UID CONVERT commands so clients (especially mobile) can ask the server to transcode or adapt message body parts, with parameters, responses and error codes.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies a new IMAP extension with new commands, responses and response codes, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document defines the CONVERT extension to IMAP4 [RFC3501]. CONVERT provides adaptation and transcoding of body parts as needed by the client.

content negotiation.why: Conversion parameters are media feature tags. The document registers the unknown-character-replacement feature tag and uses feature tags to negotiate target formats.
content negotiation.quote: This document relies on the registry of conversion parameters established by [MEDIAFEAT-REG].

rejected.why: MIME types and body parts are the objects being converted, but the document does not define MIME itself.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommendation.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.
IMAP is the more specific tag, and the email parent is implied by it.
Charset conversion is one mandatory conversion, but the document does not register or define character sets.

RFC5260.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Date and Index Extensions
RFC5260.summary: Defines the Sieve "date" and "index" extensions: date and currentdate tests for matching date/time values, and :index/:last arguments to select specific occurrences of repeated header fields in header, address and date tests.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies two extensions to the Sieve filtering language, including new tests and tagged arguments.
Sieve.quote: This document describes the "date" and "index" extensions to the Sieve email filtering language.

rejected.why: RFC 3339 timestamps are only used for the iso8601 date-part; the document is about Sieve tests, not the timestamp format.
Tests operate on RFC 2822 headers, but the document does not specify or extend the message format.
Mentioned only as an example of a server where Sieve may run.
Sieve is the more specific tag; the parent is implied.

RFC5261.title: An Extensible Markup Language (XML) Patch Operations Framework Utilizing XML Path Language (XPath) Selectors
RFC5261.summary: Defines an XML patch framework using restricted XPath selectors and <add>, <replace>, <remove> operations, with namespace handling, error elements, a new patch-ops-error media type and schemas.

XML.why: The whole document specifies how to patch XML documents: selectors, namespace mangling, operations and XML-based error documents. It is an XML-based format and framework.
XML.quote: This document describes an XML patch framework that utilizes XML Path language (XPath) selectors.

rejected.why: Partial PIDF and XCAP-diff use this framework, but the document is generic and applies to any application exchanging XML. SIP and presence are only examples.
It registers application/patch-ops-error+xml, but that is IANA boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
Partial PIDF is defined in RFC 5262. Here it is only cited as an example user.
SIP is mentioned only as one example context. The document does not specify anything about SIP.

gaps.name: XPath / XML patching
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for XPath or XML diff/patch. The XML tag is the closest fit.

RFC5262.title: Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) Extension for Partial Presence
RFC5262.summary: Defines the 'application/pidf-diff+xml' media type, an extension of PIDF that carries either full presence documents or XML-patch-based partial updates, to save bandwidth on constrained links.

PIDF.why: The document extends PIDF with a partial-update format (pidf-diff/pidf-full roots), so it is squarely about PIDF.
PIDF.quote: This document introduces a new MIME-Type 'application/pidf-diff+xml', which enables transporting of either only the changed parts or the full PIDF based presence information.

media types.why: A new media type is defined and registered, and its negotiation via Accept is part of the design rationale, so media type readers would want it.
media types.quote: registered a new MIME type 'application/pidf-diff+xml' according to the procedures of RFC 4288

rejected.why: XML and the RFC 5261 patch operations are the encoding and mechanism it uses, not the subject of the document.
SIP only carries the content and negotiates its use via RFC 5263; this document does not specify SIP behaviour.
It is a SIMPLE WG work item, but the document defines only a PIDF data format, not event packages or XCAP. PIDF is the more specific fit.
Redundant, since PIDF is the more specific child tag for presence formats.

gaps.name: XML patch operations / partial presence
gaps.why: The document builds on the RFC 5261 XML patch framework (add/replace/remove with XPath selectors), but the taxonomy has no tag for XML patching.

RFC5263.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Extension for Partial Notification of Presence Information
RFC5263.summary: Defines a SIP presence event package extension letting watchers negotiate via Accept header and receive only changed presence data (application/pidf-diff+xml partial PIDF) in NOTIFY requests, with version-counter handling.

SIMPLE.why: The document extends the SIP presence event package with partial notifications, specifying watcher and presence agent behaviour. This is squarely SIMPLE work (event packages and PIDF extensions).
SIMPLE.quote: This memo defines an extension allowing delivery of only the presence data that has actually changed.

PIDF.why: A substantial part of the document concerns constructing and applying partial PIDF documents (pidf-full/pidf-diff, add/replace/remove). The PIDF format is used and profiled for delta delivery.
PIDF.quote: the presence agent MUST build a presence document according to the PIDF extension for Partial Presence [2]

rejected.why: SIP is the substrate (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, Accept header); the more specific SIMPLE tag covers the presence event package extension.
XML patch operations are defined in other RFCs (5261/5262). This document only uses them.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended hop-by-hop protection.
Parent of PIDF and implied; the document does not address messaging beyond presence.
The application/pidf-diff+xml type is defined in RFC 5262, not in this document.

RFC5264.title: Publication of Partial Presence Information
RFC5264.summary: RFC 5264 defines a SIP PUBLISH extension letting a presence user agent publish only changed parts of its presence document (using partial PIDF diff/full formats) after an initial full-state publication, to reduce overhead.

SIMPLE.why: Defines a SIMPLE-working-group extension to SIP event state publication for presence, specifying PUA and compositor behaviour for partial presence publication.
SIMPLE.quote: This memo specifies a mechanism with which the PUA is after an initial full state publication able to publish only those parts of the presence document that have changed

PIDF.why: The mechanism is built on the PIDF and partial PIDF formats (pidf-full / pidf-diff), whose handling in publications is specified here.
PIDF.quote: This is accomplished using the partial PIDF [RFC5262] document format to communicate a set of presence document changes to the PA

rejected.why: SIP PUBLISH is the substrate; the document is a SIMPLE presence extension, and SIMPLE is the more specific tag.
XML patch operations are defined in RFC 5261/5262; this document only uses them.
PIDF is the more specific child under it; the document concerns presence publication, covered by SIMPLE/PIDF.
The application/pidf-diff+xml type is defined in RFC 5262, only used here.

RFC5265.title: Mobile IPv4 Traversal across IPsec-Based VPN Gateways
RFC5265.summary: Specifies a Mobile IPv4 plus IPsec VPN coexistence solution for enterprise remote access, with access modes, a secure internal-network detection algorithm, and a new Trusted Networks Configured registration-reply extension.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document profiles Mobile IPv4 for use with VPN gateways and defines a new Mobile IPv4 extension (Trusted Networks Configured) for home agents and mobile nodes.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document outlines a solution for the Mobile IPv4 (MIPv4) and IPsec coexistence problem for enterprise users.

IPsec.why: The solution layers MIPv4 under IPsec-based VPN tunnels, and the document analyses why IPsec lacks mobility, IPsec NAT traversal, and ESP overhead.
IPsec.quote: another layer of Mobile IPv4 is used underneath IPsec, in effect making IPsec unaware of movement.

VPN.why: The document addresses enterprise remote access VPN gateways, DMZ and firewall deployment, but these are IPsec remote-access VPNs, not provider-provisioned VPNs, so this is a weaker fit.
VPN.quote: VPN, in this document, refers to an IPsec-based remote access VPN.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an alternative that would remove the external MIPv4 layer; out of scope and not specified.
NAT traversal is supported by reference to existing mechanisms (RFC 3519, RFC 3947/3948); the document defines nothing new about it.
IKE is used to establish the VPN tunnel, but the document does not specify or change it.
Firewall configuration assumptions are discussed as deployment context, not as the document's subject.
Only mentioned as one possible VPN tunnel type.

RFC5266.title: Secure Connectivity and Mobility Using Mobile IPv4 and IKEv2 Mobility and Multihoming (MOBIKE)
RFC5266.summary: BCP describing how a mobile node combines Mobile IPv4 (on trusted networks) with MOBIKE-capable IKEv2 IPsec VPNs (on untrusted networks) for enterprise secure connectivity and mobility, including trust-boundary detection and NAT traversal.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document specifies how Mobile IPv4 registration, care-of addresses and home agent are used across trusted and untrusted networks.
Mobile IPv4.quote: The solution described in this document uses Mobile IPv4 when the mobile node is on the trusted network and MOBIKE-capable IPsec VPNs when the mobile node is on the untrusted network.

MOBIKE.why: MOBIKE is used to keep the IPsec VPN tunnel alive across address changes, and the document defines how it interworks with MIPv4 (VPN-TIA as co-located CoA).
MOBIKE.quote: If the mobile node moves and its IP address changes, it initiates the MOBIKE protocol [RFC4555] to update the address on the VPN gateway.

rejected.why: IKEv2 is the substrate for MOBIKE; the document does not extend IKE beyond MOBIKE, which is the more specific tag.
IPsec VPN tunnels are relied upon, but the document does not specify or extend IPsec itself.
NAT traversal is a brief section that only points to existing MIPv4 and IPsec NAT traversal specs.
This tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs (L2/L3 over BGP/MPLS); the enterprise IPsec remote-access VPN here does not fit it.
DHCP is only used to obtain the co-located care-of address.

RFC5267.title: Contexts for IMAP4
RFC5267.summary: RFC 5267 defines the IMAP ESORT and CONTEXT=SEARCH/SORT extensions, adding UPDATE, PARTIAL and CONTEXT return options so clients get live, windowed search and sort results (virtual-mailbox-like views).

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4rev1 with new capabilities (ESORT, CONTEXT=SEARCH, CONTEXT=SORT), new return options, the CANCELUPDATE command and new response data items.
IMAP.quote: The IMAP4rev1 protocol has powerful search facilities as part of the core protocol, but lacks the ability to create live, updated results that can be easily handled.

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific child tag; email is implied as its ancestor.
ACAP is only cited as the source of the windowed-view and update concepts; the document does not specify or extend it.
ABNF is only used to write the formal syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
The IANA section only registers the new capabilities, which is boilerplate.

RFC5268.title: Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers
RFC5268.summary: Specifies the Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers protocol (FMIPv6), which reduces handover latency via RtSolPr/PrRtAdv, FBU/FBack, HI/HAck messages and tunnelling between previous and new access routers, obsoleting RFC 4068.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document defines fast handover extensions to Mobile IPv6: FBU, FBack, HI, HAck, and related options and processing.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document specifies a protocol to improve handover latency due to Mobile IPv6 procedures.

rejected.why: UNA and NAACK use Neighbor Discovery messages and options, but the document extends Mobile IPv6 handover rather than ND itself. ND is a substrate.
SEND is only mentioned as an option for securing RtSolPr and PrRtAdv. The handover key distribution is in the companion RFC 5269.
IPsec ESP and IKEv2 are used to protect HI and HAck, but that is a security mechanism relied upon, not the subject.
DHCP is only an alternative way to configure the new care-of address, not specified here.
DAD and stateless address autoconfiguration are referenced in handling the new care-of address, but the document is not about them.
The messages are carried as ICMPv6 type 154, but this is only the carrier.

gaps.name: Fast handover / handover latency reduction
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for fast handovers specifically, so the IP mobility parent is the best fit. A child for Mobile IPv6 fast handovers (FMIPv6) would also suit the related RFCs.

RFC5269.title: Distributing a Symmetric Fast Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6) Handover Key Using SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND)
RFC5269.summary: Defines a mechanism by which an Access Router provisions a shared handover key to a Mobile Node, encrypted under a MN-generated public key, using SEND-secured RtSolPr/PrRtAdv messages, to authenticate Fast Mobile IPv6 Fast Binding Updates.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Fast Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6) with key provisioning to secure the FBU and defines new options carried in its RtSolPr/PrRtAdv messages.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Fast Mobile IPv6 requires that a Fast Binding Update is secured using a security association shared between an Access Router and a Mobile Node

SEND.why: The key exchange depends on SEND-protected messages (CGA, signature, nonce, certificates), and the document defines new Neighbor Discovery options used with SEND.
SEND.quote: The key exchange messages are required to have SEND security; that is, the source address is a Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA)

rejected.why: SEND, a child of neighbor discovery, is the more specific tag chosen; the new options are ND options but the document is about SEND-secured key provisioning.
RSA is only the public key algorithm inherited from SEND, used via RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5; nothing new is defined about it.
Key provisioning is the topic, but the technology tags chosen already cover the document; this is a narrow, protocol-specific provisioning exchange.
Not about proxy mobility; FMIPv6 is a host-based Mobile IPv6 handover optimization.
RtSolPr/PrRtAdv are ICMP messages, but only as substrate.
FBU authorization via MAC is a part of the work, but the specific Mobile IPv6 and SEND tags cover it.

gaps.name: Fast Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6) handovers
gaps.why: The taxonomy has Mobile IPv6 but no specific tag for Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5268); the document is specifically about securing FMIPv6.

gaps.name: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA)
gaps.why: CGAs are central to the authorization model, but there is no CGA tag in the taxonomy.

RFC5270.title: Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers over IEEE 802.16e Networks
RFC5270.summary: Informational guide describing how Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers (FMIPv6) are interleaved with IEEE 802.16e link-layer handover procedures using link-layer trigger primitives, in predictive and reactive modes.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document is about applying FMIPv6 (RFC 5268) handover procedures, including FBU/FBack, predictive and reactive modes, tunnel setup between PAR and NAR.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document describes how a Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover can be implemented on link layers conforming to the IEEE 802.16e suite of specifications.

WiMAX.why: It specifies how IP-layer handover works over IEEE 802.16e, covering 802.16e handover messages and network entry, and defines link-layer primitives between 802.16e and IP.

rejected.why: UNA and RA/NAACK are used as part of FMIPv6 completion but only as borrowed mechanisms; the document is not about neighbor discovery.
DAD per RFC 4862 is only referenced for the new care-of address; not a subject of the document.
Parent of Mobile IPv6; the more specific child tag applies.
802.16e is a broadband wireless access technology, covered by the WiMAX tag, not a 3GPP cellular system.

RFC5271.title: Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers for 3G CDMA Networks
RFC5271.summary: Informational RFC specifying how Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers (RFC 5268) are applied in 3G CDMA networks, defining predictive and reactive procedures, new Neighbor Discovery options (Handover Assist Information, Mobile Node Identifier), and new FBU/PrRtAdv flags.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document specifies Mobile IPv6 fast handover procedures (predictive and reactive modes, FBU/HI/HAck, new flags) and thus extends Mobile IPv6 fast handover.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document therefore specifies how Mobile IPv6 fast handovers can be applied in the 3G CDMA networks.

cdma2000.why: The handover is specific to 3G CDMA (cdma2000 / 3GPP2) networks, using pilot sets, ANID, SectorID, PDSN and the cdma2000 attachment procedure.
cdma2000.quote: It is adopted in 3G CDMA networks for handling host-based mobility management [12].

rejected.why: The document defines two new ND options (types 29, 30), but this is incidental to the handover specification; ND is the carrier of the options, not the subject.
PPP/LCP/IPv6CP are described only as the 3G CDMA link-layer attachment steps, not specified or extended.
DHCPv6 is only mentioned as a bootstrap step for obtaining the HA address.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional mechanism.
Parent topic; implied by the more specific Mobile IPv6 tag.

RFC5272.title: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC)
RFC5272.summary: RFC 5272 defines CMC, a PKI certificate enrollment and management protocol built on CMS and PKCS #10/CRMF, with Full/Simple PKI requests and responses, controls, and RA processing, obsoleting RFC 2797.

PKI.why: The document is a certificate management/enrollment protocol covering certification requests, revocation, RAs and CAs, trust anchor publication; this is PKI protocol work.
PKI.quote: The need for an interface to public key certification products and services based on CMS and PKCS #10

CMS.why: CMC messages are defined as new CMS content types (PKIData, PKIResponse) wrapped in SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthenticatedData, with nesting and encryption rules specified.
CMS.quote: Full PKI Request: one or more PKCS #10, CRMF or Other Request Messages structures wrapped in a CMS encapsulation as part of a PKIData.

rejected.why: Certificates and extensions are the objects being requested, but the document does not profile X.509 itself; it depends on the PKIX profile.
The ASN.1 module is the notation for the protocol, not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only as a source of algorithm requirements; the document is not about secure email.
Used for identity proof and POP witness computations only as a mechanism.
Revocation handling here is via the Revocation Request and Get CRL controls, not OCSP.

RFC5273.title: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC): Transport Protocols
RFC5273.summary: Defines transport mechanisms (file, MIME mail, HTTP/HTTPS, and TCP) for carrying CMC (Certificate Management over CMS) PKI request and response messages.

PKI.why: CMC is a certificate enrollment/management protocol for PKI. This document specifies how its PKI Request and Response messages are transported. There is no CMC-specific tag, so PKI is the best fit.
PKI.quote: This document defines a number of transport methods that are used to move CMC messages

media types.why: A substantial part of the document specifies MIME content types, smime-type parameters and file extensions for the CMC message types (Table 1).
media types.quote: Full enrollment request messages MUST be encoded as content type "application/pkcs7-mime".  The smime-type parameter MUST be included with a value of "CMC-Request".

rejected.why: HTTP is used only as a transport (POST, 200 response, Content-Type). The document does not extend or profile HTTP in a way that HTTP readers need.
TLS is only mentioned as optional content protection and in Security Considerations. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
CMS is the message format that CMC carries, and it is defined in RFC 5272. This document only transports those messages.
The mail wrapping is borrowed from S/MIME, but the document does not specify S/MIME itself. It notes that its use differs from standard S/MIME messages.
TCP is only a substrate. The document defines framing-free use of TCP and has no TCP protocol content.
MIME wrapping is used for the mail-based transport, but the document does not specify MIME itself. Its content-type registrations are covered by the media types tag.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CMC tag. It has CMP and EST for certificate management protocols, but CMC itself is the subject of this document and its companion RFC 5272.

RFC5274.title: Certificate Management Messages over CMS (CMC): Compliance Requirements
RFC5274.summary: RFC 5274 specifies compliance requirements (MUST/SHOULD levels for algorithms, controls, and CRMF features) for CMC certificate enrollment entities: EEs, RAs, and CAs.

PKI.why: CMC is a PKI certificate enrollment protocol. There is no CMC-specific tag, so PKI is the best fit. The document sets requirements for EEs, RAs and CAs.
PKI.quote: This document provides a set of compliance statements about the CMC (Certificate Management over CMS) enrollment protocol.

CMS.why: Much of the document sets mandatory CMS algorithms and profiles for SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthenticatedData. The CMS content is a substantial part of the document, not just a substrate.
CMS.quote: All entities MUST support Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) as the content encryption algorithm for EnvelopedData

rejected.why: AES is only named as a required algorithm for CMS EnvelopedData. The document is not about AES.
Certificates and CRMF are discussed, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
HTTP is only the mandatory transport, and it is specified in CMC-TRANS rather than here.
PBKDF2 is mentioned only as a required key derivation algorithm.
HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC-SHA256 appear only as required algorithms for particular controls.
RSA appears only as a required key transport and signature algorithm.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the CMC enrollment protocol. It is covered here under PKI and CMS, which loses the protocol-specific grouping with RFC 5272 and RFC 5273.

RFC5275.title: CMS Symmetric Key Management and Distribution
RFC5275.summary: Defines a CMC/CMS-based protocol, with control attributes and administrative and distribution messages, for a Group List Agent to create groups, manage membership and distribute and rekey shared symmetric key-encryption keys, developed for S/MIME Mail List Agents.

CMS.why: The document defines CMC control attributes carried in CMS SignedData/EnvelopedData, and glKey uses CMS RecipientInfos (kekri/ktri/kari) to distribute shared KEKs. This is a CMS-based specification.
CMS.quote: The mechanism uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) protocol and Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol to manage the symmetric keys.

key management.why: The core subject is group symmetric KEK setup, distribution, rekey, compromise handling and refresh. No more specific key-management tag fits.
key management.quote: This document describes a mechanism to manage (i.e., set up, distribute, and rekey) keys used with symmetric cryptographic algorithms.

mailing lists.why: The motivating use case is encrypted distribution through mail list agents, covered in Sections 1.2 and 1.4. It is a substantial application of the mechanism.
mailing lists.quote: This mechanism has been developed to support Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Mail List Agents (MLAs).

rejected.why: S/MIME is the motivating application and is referenced for SMIMECapabilities, but the document specifies key distribution, not S/MIME message handling.
CMC and the PKIX profile are used as the substrate and for certificate validation. The document does not specify certificate management.
Group key distribution is conceptually related, but this is not IP multicast and the document does not address multicast group key management.
SMTP is only the required message transport in Section 7, a one-line mention.
AES-128 key wrap is only the default algorithm, referenced from other RFCs.
An ASN.1 module is the notation for the protocol messages, not the subject.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The protocol is built on CMC control attributes and PKIData/PKIResponse structures, but the taxonomy has no CMC tag; the closest, CMP, is a different protocol.

RFC5276.title: Using the Server-Based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP) to Convey Long-Term Evidence Records
RFC5276.summary: Defines new SCVP WantBack OIDs and ASN.1 structures so an SCVP server can return ERS evidence records covering certification paths, certificates and revocation information, supporting long-term validation of archived data with LTAP.

LTANS.why: The document is an LTANS work item: it conveys ERS evidence records for long-term archive verification and ties into LTAP. Readers of long-term archive and notary services would want it.
LTANS.quote: This document describes usage of the SCVP WantBack feature to convey evidence records, enabling SCVP responders to provide preservation evidence for certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs).

PKI.why: It extends SCVP, the PKI certification path validation protocol, with new WantBacks for certification paths, certificates and revocation information. The taxonomy has no SCVP-specific tag, so the PKI parent is the closest fit.
PKI.quote: SCVP defines an extensible means of delegating the development and validation of certification paths to a server.

rejected.why: The ASN.1 module only defines the OIDs and structures for the extension. ASN.1 is the notation, not the subject.
OCSP responses are mentioned only as one possible form of revocation information. The document does not specify or extend OCSP.
Certificates and CRLs are the objects being preserved, but the document does not profile X.509.
Evidence records are ASN.1 structures from ERS, and the document does not use CMS in any way that matters to its subject.

gaps.name: SCVP (Server-Based Certificate Validation Protocol)
gaps.why: The document extends SCVP, but the taxonomy has no SCVP tag, so it is tagged under the PKI parent.

gaps.name: Evidence Record Syntax (ERS)
gaps.why: ERS is the evidence record format conveyed here, and the taxonomy has no ERS tag. LTANS is the nearest tag.

RFC5277.title: NETCONF Event Notifications
RFC5277.summary: Defines an optional NETCONF capability for asynchronous event notifications: the create-subscription operation, notification messages, event streams, replay, filtering, and the interleave capability.

NETCONF.why: The whole document extends NETCONF with a notification capability, new operations (<create-subscription>, <notification>), and the :interleave capability.
NETCONF.quote: This document defines mechanisms that provide an asynchronous message notification delivery service for the [NETCONF] protocol.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding and schema language for the messages; the document is not about XML usage in general.
SNMP is mentioned only as a possible event stream source, which is out of scope.
syslog is mentioned only as a possible event stream source, which is out of scope.
The data model is given in XML Schema, not YANG.
RFC 3339 timestamps are only used for the time parameters; the document does not define date-time formats.
The notifications are event messages for NETCONF, not a general network telemetry framework, so the more specific NETCONF tag is the better fit.

RFC5278.title: IANA Registration of Enumservices for Voice and Video Messaging
RFC5278.summary: Registers the ENUM service types voicemsg, videomsg and unifmsg (with sip, sips, tel, http, https subtypes) so NAPTR records can route real-time sessions to voice, video or unified messaging systems.

ENUM.why: The document's whole purpose is registering new Enumservices under the ENUM (RFC 3761) registry, with NAPTR examples and implementation advice for ENUM resolvers.
ENUM.quote: This document registers the Enumservice named "vmsg", which is used to facilitate the real-time routing of voice, video, and unified communications to a messaging system.

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR records are only the substrate for ENUM here; the document defines no new DNS behaviour or record type.
VPIM is discussed only to explain why it was not suitable for real-time routing; the document does not specify or extend it.
SIP URIs are used as subtypes, but the document does not specify or extend SIP itself.
The tel URI is a subtype scheme used by voicemsg and is not defined or extended by the document.
http and https are only URI schemes for subtypes; nothing about HTTP is specified.
The registrations go in an existing registry, but the document is about the ENUM service content and not IANA guidance.

RFC5279.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)
RFC5279.summary: Registers the "3gpp" URN Namespace Identifier for 3GPP, specifying its syntax, registration/assignment process, and management by 3GPP per RFC 3406.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration (NID 3gpp) defining syntax, uniqueness, persistence and assignment rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes the Namespace Identifier (NID) for Uniform Resource Namespace (URN) resources published by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP).

rejected.why: 3GPP develops cellular technologies, but the document only registers a URN namespace and says nothing about cellular networking.
The IANA section merely registers the NID; the document body is about the namespace itself, and boilerplate is not evidence.
URN is the more specific child tag and fits better than the parent.

RFC5280.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
RFC5280.summary: RFC 5280 profiles X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for the Internet PKI, defining extensions, the certification path validation algorithm, CRL validation, and rules for internationalized names.

X.509.why: The whole document is the Internet profile of X.509 certificates and CRLs: fields, extensions, path validation, CRL processing.
X.509.quote: This memo profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and X.509 v2 certificate revocation list (CRL) for use in the Internet.

PKI.why: It describes the PKIX architecture model (CA, RA, CRL issuer, repository), trust anchors and certification path validation.
PKI.quote: This specification is one part of a family of standards for the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) for the Internet.

IDN.why: Section 7 sets processing and comparison rules for IDNs in certificates, which IDN readers would want.
IDN.quote: conforming implementations MUST convert internationalized domain names to the ASCII Compatible Encoding (ACE) format as specified in Section 4 of RFC 3490

rejected.why: Only referenced as an alternative revocation mechanism and via the AIA id-ad-ocsp access method; the protocol is not specified here.
ASN.1 is the notation and DER the encoding for the structures; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Section 7.4 gives IRI-to-URI mapping rules for certificate fields, but this is a minor part and the document is not about IRIs.
LDAP is only used as an optional retrieval mechanism for certificates and CRLs via URIs.
HTTP is only a retrieval substrate for CRLs and certificates, with media types noted.
Covered more specifically by IDN; Section 7 is a small part of the document.

RFC5281.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol Tunneled Transport Layer Security Authenticated Protocol Version 0 (EAP-TTLSv0)
RFC5281.summary: Informational specification of EAP-TTLSv0, an EAP method that sets up a TLS tunnel and then carries legacy or EAP client authentication as RADIUS/Diameter-style AVPs inside it, with key derivation (MSK/EMSK).

EAP.why: The document specifies a new EAP method: packet format, version negotiation, fragmentation, tunneled inner authentication, MSK/EMSK generation and the EAP keying framework identifiers.
EAP.quote: EAP-TTLS is an EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) method that encapsulates a TLS (Transport Layer Security) session, consisting of a handshake phase and a data phase.

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate for the tunnel. The document uses the TLS handshake, record layer and PRF but defines no new TLS extension or behaviour.
RADIUS is the AAA carrier and the source of the AVP namespace, but it is not specified or extended here.
Diameter supplies only the AVP encoding format. The document states Diameter support is not required, so it is not a subject.
AAA servers and carrier protocols are architectural context for the EAP method. The document does not define a AAA framework.
PPP is only a possible EAP carrier, and CHAP and MS-CHAP are tunneled inner methods. PPP itself is not the subject.
The parent topic is implied by the EAP tag and the document is not about authentication in general.

RFC5282.title: Using Authenticated Encryption Algorithms with the Encrypted Payload of the Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) Protocol
RFC5282.summary: Specifies how authenticated encryption (AEAD) algorithms, specifically AES GCM and AES CCM, are used with the IKEv2 Encrypted Payload, updating RFC 4306 and defining new AEAD_* algorithm identifiers.

IKE.why: The document updates IKEv2 (RFC 4306): it redefines the Encrypted Payload structure, associated data, key derivation and algorithm selection rules for combined-mode algorithms.
IKE.quote: This document describes the use of AEAD algorithms with the Encrypted Payload of the Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) protocol.

AES.why: It specifies the AES GCM and AES CCM modes for IKEv2: nonce format, ICV sizes, key and salt layout, and new AEAD_AES_* algorithm definitions.
AES.quote: the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode (AES GCM) [GCM] and AES in Counter with CBC-MAC Mode (AES CCM) [CCM].

rejected.why: ESP is referenced as the model for the design and for compatibility, but the document is about IKEv2's Encrypted Payload, not IPsec/ESP itself. IKE is the more specific tag.
ESP usage of AES GCM and CCM is only the basis the document reuses. It does not specify or change ESP.
The new AEAD registry entries are boilerplate-like registrations and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Authenticated encryption (AEAD)
gaps.why: The core subject is AEAD/combined-mode algorithms under RFC 5116, which the taxonomy has no specific tag for; the AES tag covers it only partly.

RFC5283.title: LDP Extension for Inter-Area Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC5283.summary: RFC 5283 defines an optional Longest-Match Label Mapping Procedure for LDP so that LSPs can be established across IGP areas without leaking specific /32 loopback prefixes, allowing ABRs to keep IP aggregation.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP's Label Mapping message procedure (RFC 5036) to use IP longest-match RIB lookup instead of exact match, and specifies how LDP reacts to RIB events.
LDP.quote: this document describes a new optional Longest-Match Label Mapping Procedure for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)

rejected.why: OSPF areas and ABRs form the problem context, but the document does not specify or extend OSPF.
IS-IS levels are the context for inter-area LSPs; the document does not specify or extend IS-IS.
Inter-area RSVP-TE is only discussed as an alternative solution in the problem statement.
BGP with MPLS hierarchy is described only as an inadequate alternative; it is not the subject.
L3VPNs and VPLS are only motivation for needing inter-area LSPs.
The document concerns MPLS LSPs, but its specific subject is the LDP procedure, so the more specific LDP tag fits.

RFC5284.title: User-Defined Errors for RSVP
RFC5284.summary: Defines a new RSVP USER_ERROR_SPEC object (class 194) and Error Code 33 so implementations can carry enterprise-specific, user-defined error codes and descriptions in PathErr, ResvErr and Notify messages.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP with a new error object, a new error code, and procedures for sending and receiving it in PathErr, ResvErr and Notify messages.
RSVP.quote: This document defines a USER_ERROR_SPEC to be used in addition to the ERROR_SPEC to carry additional user information related to errors.

rejected.why: The document references RFC 3473 Notify messages, but it extends base RSVP error signalling rather than traffic-engineering signalling.
RFC 3473 is cited only because the Notify message also requires an ERROR_SPEC. The document does not address GMPLS.
The Error Description field uses UTF-8 per RFC 2277 and RFC 5198. This is only an encoding requirement for one field.
The IANA Considerations section only registers the new error code and object class. It is boilerplate for this purpose.
The Enterprise Numbers registry is referenced only as a source of identifiers. The document defines no MIB.

RFC5285.title: A General Mechanism for RTP Header Extensions
RFC5285.summary: Defines a general mechanism for carrying multiple small header extension elements in RTP packets (one-byte and two-byte forms), with SDP extmap signalling, offer/answer rules, and an IANA registry of URN-named extensions.

RTP.why: The document extends RTP by defining a multi-element header extension format (0xBEDE one-byte and 0x100 two-byte forms) and registry for RTP packets.
RTP.quote: This document provides a general mechanism to use the header extension feature of RTP (the Real-Time Transport Protocol).

SDP.why: Defines the new SDP extmap attribute and its offer/answer semantics, a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: a=extmap:<value>["/"<direction>] <URI> <extensionattributes>

rejected.why: SIP offer/answer is only mentioned as an example signalling context; the document specifies SDP attributes, not SIP.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations about header protection coverage.
URIs are used to name extensions, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes; only a URN-based naming convention within the registry.
Header compression is mentioned only as an efficiency caveat.
The IANA registry is boilerplate-like registration for this specification's own registry, not a document about IANA guidance.

RFC5286.title: Basic Specification for IP Fast Reroute: Loop-Free Alternates
RFC5286.summary: Specifies loop-free alternates (LFAs): precomputed backup next-hops for local protection against single link, node or SRLG failure in OSPF/IS-IS IP and MPLS/LDP networks, reducing packet loss during convergence.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document defines the LFA basic specification for IP Fast Reroute: the loop-free conditions, selection procedure, and how and when alternates are used and removed.
IP fast reroute.quote: This document describes the use of loop-free alternates to provide local protection for unicast traffic in pure IP and MPLS/LDP networks

OSPF.why: Substantial OSPF-specific content: multi-area constraints, virtual links, ASBR and external routes, and a dedicated appendix. LFA computation is run over OSPF topology.
OSPF.quote: Loop-free alternates should not be used for inter-area routes in an area that contains more than one alternate ABR [RFC3509].

IS-IS.why: Defines LFA interactions with the IS-IS overload bit, maximum metric and link attribute flags (RFC 5029). IS-IS is a co-equal IGP for the mechanism.
IS-IS.quote: For computing an alternate, a router MUST NOT use an alternate next-hop that is along a link whose cost or reverse cost is LSInfinity

LDP.why: Section 5 sets requirements on LDP mode (liberal retention, unsolicited distribution) so MPLS/LDP traffic can use LFAs.
LDP.quote: it is necessary for LDP to have the appropriate labels available for the alternate so that the appropriate out-segments can be installed

rejected.why: BGP next-hop synchronization is only briefly discussed. BGP inherits the IGP alternates, and BGP fast reroute is explicitly out of scope.
Multicast traffic is explicitly out of scope for this specification.
ECMP interaction is one subsection about choosing alternates among primary next-hops. The document is not about ECMP itself.
MPLS appears only through the LDP requirements. The LDP tag covers it more specifically.
The document specifies a particular mechanism, not general routing architecture principles.

gaps.name: IP Fast Reroute (IPFRR) / loop-free alternates
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the 'IP fast reroute' tag only as 'IP and LDP fast reroute, loop-free alternates', so it fits here. A more specific LFA tag would only help if later fast-reroute RFCs (remote LFA, not-via, TI-LFA) were to be separated.

RFC5287.title: Control Protocol Extensions for the Setup of Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) Pseudowires in MPLS Networks
RFC5287.summary: Defines LDP extensions (PW types usage, interface parameter sub-TLVs, status codes) for setting up TDM pseudowires (SAToP, CESoPSN, TDMoIP) in MPLS networks, extending RFC 4447.

pseudowire.why: The whole document specifies PW FEC usage, interface parameters, and status codes for setting up TDM pseudowires over MPLS via the PWE3 control protocol.
pseudowire.quote: defines extension to the PWE3 control protocol [RFC4447] and PWE3 IANA allocations [RFC4446] required for the setup of TDM pseudowires in MPLS networks

LDP.why: The document extends LDP-based PW signalling with new interface parameter sub-TLVs and LDP status code usage, which LDP readers would want.
LDP.quote: [RFC4447] defines extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) [RFC5036] that are required to exchange PW labels

rejected.why: RTP header usage is only an option flagged in the TDM Options parameter; the document is not about RTP.
MPLS is the substrate network; the document is about PW setup, which is covered by the pseudowire tag.
TDMoIP AAL1/AAL2 modes are mentioned as parameters, but the document does not address IP over ATM.
L2TPv3 setup is explicitly out of scope, deferred to a separate document.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation (SAToP, CESoPSN, TDMoIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TDM circuit emulation over packet networks; the document's subject is setting up such PWs, only partly covered by pseudowire.

RFC5288.title: AES Galois Counter Mode (GCM) Cipher Suites for TLS
RFC5288.summary: Defines twelve TLS 1.2 cipher suites using AES-GCM authenticated encryption with RSA, DSA and Diffie-Hellman key exchanges, including nonce construction and version restrictions.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS cipher suites, their nonce handling, PRF choice and TLS version restrictions, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This memo defines TLS cipher suites that use AES-GCM with RSA, DSA, and Diffie-Hellman-based key exchange mechanisms.

AES.why: It specifies how AES-GCM (AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM) is used, including nonce uniqueness and counter reuse guidance, which is the AES and its modes subject.
AES.quote: This memo describes the use of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) as a Transport Layer Security (TLS) authenticated encryption operation.

rejected.why: RSA appears only as a key exchange and certificate type in the suite names; the document does not specify RSA itself.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 are only the PRF hash selections inherited from TLS 1.2, not the subject.
ECC cipher suites are explicitly left to a separate document, RFC 5289.
IPsec ESP is mentioned only as another place AES-GCM is used.
Only TLS is addressed; DTLS is not discussed.
The IANA section merely lists code points for the new suites and is boilerplate.

RFC5289.title: TLS Elliptic Curve Cipher Suites with SHA-256/384 and AES Galois Counter Mode (GCM)
RFC5289.summary: Defines sixteen TLS cipher suites combining elliptic curve key exchange/signatures with AES-CBC and HMAC-SHA-256/384, or AES-GCM AEAD with SHA-256/384 PRFs, for TLS 1.2.

TLS.why: The document specifies new TLS cipher suites and their PRF/MAC definitions for TLS 1.2, which is TLS protocol extension material.
TLS.quote: This document defines 16 new cipher suites to be added to TLS.

elliptic curve.why: All suites use ECDH/ECDHE with ECDSA or RSA authentication; ECC cipher suites are the focus, extending RFC 4492.
elliptic curve.quote: All use Elliptic Curve Cryptography for key exchange and digital signature, as defined in RFC 4492.

AES.why: Half the suites use AES-GCM and the other half AES-CBC, so AES modes are a substantial part of the content.
AES.quote: use the new authenticated encryption modes defined in TLS 1.2 with AES in Galois Counter Mode (GCM)

SHA.why: The motivation is moving from SHA-1 to SHA-256/384 for the MAC and PRF in the suites.
SHA.quote: This document specifies TLS ECC cipher suites that use SHA-256 and SHA-384 [SHS] rather than SHA-1.

rejected.why: HMAC is used as the MAC but is only referenced; the document defines nothing new about HMAC itself.
ECDSA is just one authentication option in the suites, defined in RFC 4492; covered by the elliptic curve tag.
RSA appears only as the certificate/signature type in some suite names, not as a subject of the document.
The IANA section merely lists code point assignments; boilerplate-like and not the document's subject.

RFC5290.title: Comments on the Usefulness of Simple Best-Effort Traffic
RFC5290.summary: An Independent-stream informational RFC in which Floyd and Allman argue that simple best-effort traffic is still worth keeping alongside QoS mechanisms, and that rough flow-rate fairness is a reasonable resource-allocation goal for it.

congestion control.why: A large part of the document discusses flow-rate fairness, congestion collapse avoidance, TCP congestion control and the limits of enforcing fairness. These are congestion control subjects, discussed at the level of principles and not one mechanism.
congestion control.quote: some form of rough flow-rate fairness is a useful goal for resource allocation, where "flow-rate fairness" is defined by the goal of equal flow rates for different flows

QoS.why: The document is about the role of simple best-effort service compared with QoS, intserv/diffserv, admission control and cost-based pricing. It argues QoS should supplement best-effort traffic and does not replace it.
QoS.quote: While differential treatment of traffic can clearly be useful, we believe such mechanisms are useful as *adjuncts* to simple best-effort traffic, not as *replacements*

internet architecture.why: It discusses the architectural role of best-effort service and why changes to the Internet infrastructure are hard to deploy, citing RFC 1958.
internet architecture.quote: The problems of deploying interlocking changes to the infrastructure do not necessarily have an easy fix as they stem in part from the underlying architecture of the Internet.

rejected.why: TCP congestion control is cited as the mechanism that gives rough fairness today. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
