Diffserv and Intserv appear only as contrast cases for differential treatment, and the document does not analyse them.
ECN is mentioned only in passing as a marking mechanism that cost-based fairness would need.
The limit on persistent HTTP connections is used only as an example of fairness granularity.

gaps.name: network neutrality / Internet economics and pricing
gaps.why: The document discusses congestion-based pricing, cost-based fairness and network neutrality. The taxonomy has no tag for Internet economics or policy.

RFC5291.title: Outbound Route Filtering Capability for BGP-4
RFC5291.summary: Defines the BGP Outbound Route Filtering capability, letting a BGP speaker send ORFs to a peer in ROUTE-REFRESH messages so the peer filters its outbound updates.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-4 with a new capability (code 3), ROUTE-REFRESH message encoding and operational procedures for ORFs.
BGP.quote: This document defines a BGP-based mechanism that allows a BGP speaker to send to its BGP peer a set of Outbound Route Filters (ORFs)

rejected.why: ORFs are about reducing unwanted routing updates by policy filtering, not securing routing; Security Considerations just says no change.
Flowspec filters traffic; ORF filters route advertisements and is a different mechanism.
Manageability section only suggests management objects be defined elsewhere; it is not the document's subject.

RFC5292.title: Address-Prefix-Based Outbound Route Filter for BGP-4
RFC5292.summary: Defines a new BGP Outbound Route Filter type (Address Prefix ORF, type 64) enabling prefix-length/range, wildcard and exact address-prefix filtering of a peer's outbound routing updates, with its encoding and matching rules.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new ORF type, specifying its fields, encoding and matching rules. No narrower BGP child tag covers ORF.
BGP.quote: defines a new Outbound Router Filter (ORF) type for BGP, termed "Address Prefix Outbound Route Filter", that can be used to perform address-prefix-based route filtering

rejected.why: The IANA section only assigns ORF-type value 64. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
It also filters traffic or routes by prefix, but it is a different mechanism. This document is about ORF for route advertisement filtering.
Filtering here is a route-advertisement optimisation, not a security mechanism. The Security Considerations section says nothing new.

gaps.name: Outbound Route Filtering (ORF)
gaps.why: The ORF capability and its ORF types, such as the Address Prefix ORF in this RFC and the base capability in RFC 5291, have no dedicated tag. BGP is the closest fit but is broader.

RFC5293.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Editheader Extension
RFC5293.summary: Defines the Sieve "editheader" extension, adding the addheader and deleteheader actions that let Sieve scripts add and remove header fields of the message being processed, with interaction rules and security considerations.

Sieve.why: The document is a Sieve language extension specifying the addheader and deleteheader actions and their interaction with other Sieve features.
Sieve.quote: This document defines two new actions for the "Sieve" email filtering language that add and delete email header fields.

rejected.why: Header fields are the object manipulated, but the document does not specify the message format; it relies on RFC 2822 syntax.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as being potentially invalidated by header edits.
Parent of Sieve; the more specific Sieve tag fits.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations regarding signatures.
Referenced only for loop prevention in Security Considerations.

RFC5294.title: Host Threats to Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM)
RFC5294.summary: Informational threat analysis of PIM (PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM) attacks by hosts or rogue routers on host-facing router interfaces, with mitigations (passive mode, IPsec, IP filtering).

PIM-SM.why: The document analyses vulnerabilities in PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM (Register, Hello, DR election, Assert, DF election) on host-facing links. PIM-SM is the most specific tag that fits, and PIM-DM is explicitly out of scope.
PIM-SM.quote: describing Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) threats specific to router interfaces connecting hosts

multicast security.why: It is a security threat analysis of multicast routing infrastructure, and it discusses mitigations and group security (RFC 3740, GDOI). It is not about group key management itself, so the parent topic fits better than GDOI.
multicast security.quote: This memo complements the list of multicast infrastructure security threat analysis documents

rejected.why: IPsec is only one of several mitigations discussed. The document does not specify or extend it.
It is mentioned once, as a possible way to ease SA negotiation. That is not substantial coverage.
IGMP/MLD appear only as context or as out-of-scope related work.
The document is about multicast routing security, which multicast security covers more closely. It is not about unicast routing protocols.
PIM-SM is the more specific child and already captures the subject.

RFC5295.title: Specification for the Derivation of Root Keys from an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK)
RFC5295.summary: Standards-track spec reserving the EAP EMSK solely for deriving cryptographically separate root keys (USRK, DSRK/DSUSRK) via a PRF+/HMAC-SHA-256 KDF, with key naming rules, usage-definition requirements and IANA registries for key labels and PRF numbers.

HOKEY.why: Produced by the HOKEY WG, it specifies the EMSK root key hierarchy (USRK, DSRK) used for handover keying; the HOKEY tag covers EAP key derivation and handover keying.
HOKEY.quote: This memo reserves the EMSK for the sole purpose of deriving root keys.

EAP.why: The document defines how EAP's EMSK keying material is used and what the EAP system must do, updating the EAP key management framework (RFC 5247). It is a substantial EAP keying specification.
EAP.quote: EAP defines two types of keying material: a Master Session Key (MSK) and an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK).

key management.why: Root key derivation, naming, lifetime, distribution and key management domains are core content, which is the kind of material a key management reader wants.
key management.quote: This document also provides guidelines for creating usage definitions for the various uses of EAP key material and for the management of the root keys.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-256 is only the PRF inside the default KDF; the document is not about HMAC itself.
SHA-256 is only referenced as the underlying hash for the PRF; not a subject of the document.
PRF+ is borrowed from IKEv2 (RFC 4306) as a construction; IKE is not specified or profiled here.
The IANA section creates registries for key labels and PRF numbers, but that is boilerplate-level apparatus; the main body is not about IANA stewardship.
AAA frameworks are not discussed beyond mentioning the EAP server; keys transport is explicitly out of scope.

RFC5296.title: EAP Extensions for EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP)
RFC5296.summary: RFC 5296 specifies the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP): new EAP codes (Initiate/Finish), a re-authentication key hierarchy (rRK, rIK, rMSK) derived from the EMSK/DSRK, and procedures for fast method-independent re-authentication with a home or local ER server.

HOKEY.why: The document defines ERP, the EAP Re-authentication Protocol, which is the core HOKEY deliverable, along with its key hierarchy and bootstrapping.
HOKEY.quote: This document specifies extensions to EAP and the EAP keying hierarchy to support an EAP method-independent protocol for efficient re-authentication

EAP.why: It extends EAP with new packet codes, types and TLV attributes, so readers of EAP will want it. HOKEY is a child of EAP, but ERP is the parent-level EAP extension, and the EAP-level packet and registry changes are a substantial part of the document.
EAP.quote: Two new EAP codes, EAP-Initiate and EAP-Finish, are specified in this document for the purpose of EAP re-authentication.

rejected.why: AAA transport of ERP is specified in other documents (RADIUS/Diameter support drafts). This document only references it.
RADIUS carries ERP messages and supplies the channel-binding attributes, but the document does not specify RADIUS behaviour. That is left to a separate document.
The document mentions that RFC 4306 (IKEv2) must be updated to carry ERP, but that is a lower-layer note, not the subject.
The key hierarchy is a major part of the document, but it is EAP-specific and falls under the more specific HOKEY tag.
HMAC-SHA256 is only used as the integrity cryptosuite. The document defines nothing new about HMAC itself.

RFC5297.title: Synthetic Initialization Vector (SIV) Authenticated Encryption Using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
RFC5297.summary: Specifies SIV, an AES-based (CMAC S2V plus CTR) block cipher mode providing deterministic and nonce-misuse-resistant authenticated encryption and key wrapping, with AEAD registrations for RFC 5116 and test vectors.

AES.why: The document defines a new AES-based mode of operation (SIV-AES) with AES-CMAC and AES-CTR, so readers of AES modes would expect it.
AES.quote: SIV-AES uses AES in CMAC mode (S2V) and in counter mode (CTR).

rejected.why: Key wrapping is a motivation and use case, but the document specifies a cipher mode, not key establishment or provisioning.
RADIUS key delivery is mentioned only as a motivating example.
HMAC is mentioned only in the motivation; the PRF used is AES-CMAC.
The IANA section registers AEAD algorithm entries, but that is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Authenticated encryption (AEAD) modes
gaps.why: The document is about a block cipher mode for authenticated encryption and key wrapping, and the RFC 5116 AEAD interface. The taxonomy has no AEAD or block-cipher-mode tag other than the AES-specific one.

RFC5298.title: Analysis of Inter-Domain Label Switched Path (LSP) Recovery
RFC5298.summary: Informational analysis of how existing path computation and signaling techniques (per-domain, PCE/BRPC, path keys, LSP segments) can establish end-to-end diverse working and recovery TE LSPs in multi-domain MPLS/GMPLS networks, with and without domain confidentiality.

GMPLS.why: The document analyzes protection and recovery of inter-domain MPLS/GMPLS LSPs, building on GMPLS recovery work (RFC 4427/4428/4872/4873); GMPLS is the closest tag for LSP recovery.
GMPLS.quote: Protection and recovery are important features of service offerings in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) networks.

PCE.why: A substantial part of the analysis covers PCE-based path computation: BRPC, PCEP XRO, SVEC and path keys for computing diverse inter-domain paths.
PCE.quote: Collaborative simultaneous path computation is achieved using the Synchronization Vector (SVEC) object in the PCE Protocol [PCEP].

traffic engineering.why: Inter-domain TE LSP setup with diverse working and recovery paths is the central subject. Taken alone, this topic tag covers the general TE angle.
traffic engineering.quote: The main focus for this document is on establishing end-to-end diverse Traffic Engineering (TE) LSPs in multi-domain networks.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signaling mechanism used (ERO, RRO, XRO), but the document defines no new RSVP-TE behavior and only notes missing mechanisms; it is a substrate here.
The document applies to MPLS but is mainly about recovery and diversity analysis. GMPLS and traffic engineering capture it better.
Fast Reroute is explicitly out of scope, and the document only points to other RFCs for it.
BGP is mentioned only in passing for domain-level routing (AS_PATH), which is out of scope.
L1VPNs are mentioned only as an example of a multi-domain case with confidentiality, not as a subject of the document.
This is an analysis of LSP recovery rather than a routing architecture or scalability document.

gaps.name: Inter-domain MPLS/GMPLS TE and LSP protection/recovery
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is multi-domain LSP recovery and diversity. The taxonomy has no tag for LSP protection and restoration or inter-domain TE, so GMPLS and traffic engineering are only approximations.

RFC5301.title: Dynamic Hostname Exchange Mechanism for IS-IS
RFC5301.summary: Standards-track document that obsoletes RFC 2763 and defines IS-IS TLV 137 (Dynamic Hostname) so routers flood symbolic name-to-system-ID mappings in their LSPs.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies an IS-IS extension, the Dynamic hostname TLV (type 137), and its handling by IS-IS routers in LSPs.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines a new TLV that allows the IS-IS routers to include the name-to-systemID mapping data in their LSPs.

rejected.why: DNS is discussed only as an alternative that the document rejects, and the TLV carries a domain-name-formatted string. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
The document is about distributing router names within IS-IS, not about host naming conventions or host tables, so the IS-IS tag fits better.
IDNA (RFC 3490) is referenced only for UI conversion of Unicode to ASCII, which is incidental.
The mapping helps operators with diagnostics, but the mechanism is an IS-IS protocol extension and is covered by the IS-IS tag.

RFC5302.title: Domain-Wide Prefix Distribution with Two-Level IS-IS
RFC5302.summary: Standards-track update to RFC 1195 and replacement of RFC 2966 that extends IS-IS so IP prefixes can be leaked between level 1 and level 2 (using the up/down bit in TLVs 128/130), defining route types and preference order to avoid loops.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies IS-IS extensions: L2->L1 prefix leaking, the up/down bit, TLV usage and route preference.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes extensions to the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol to support optimal routing within a two-level domain.

rejected.why: BGP shortest-exit routing and MED are cited only as motivation; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
RFC 5305 (IS-IS TE extensions) is referenced only in a comparison section; this document is not about traffic engineering.
The document addresses scalability tradeoffs of hierarchy, but the specific IS-IS tag already covers it.
IS-IS originates from OSI, but the document concerns IP routing in IS-IS, not OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC5303.title: Three-Way Handshake for IS-IS Point-to-Point Adjacencies
RFC5303.summary: Defines a backward-compatible IS-IS option (TLV 240) giving point-to-point adjacencies a three-way handshake and an extended 4-octet circuit ID, allowing more than 256 point-to-point links.

IS-IS.why: The whole document extends the IS-IS protocol with a new Point-to-Point Three-Way Adjacency option and modifies its IIH state machine procedures.
IS-IS.quote: This paper defines a backward-compatible extension to the protocol that provides for a three-way handshake.

rejected.why: NLSP, an IPX routing variant of IS-IS, is mentioned only as prior art for a similar mechanism; the document is not about IPX.
IS-IS is an OSI protocol (ISO 10589), but the document is specifically about IS-IS, which has its own tag.
The IANA section only notes that option 240 was already allocated; it is boilerplate.
RFC 5304 authentication is only referenced in Security Considerations; the document does not address it.

RFC5304.title: IS-IS Cryptographic Authentication
RFC5304.summary: Defines an HMAC-MD5 authentication type (54) for IS-IS PDUs via the Authentication TLV (TLV 10), replacing RFC 3567, with procedures, security discussion and a new IANA registry for authentication type codes.

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol with a new authentication type and specifies how IS-IS PDUs are authenticated and how purges are handled.
IS-IS.quote: This document extends the above situation by allocating a new authentication type for HMAC-MD5 and specifying the algorithms for the computation of the Authentication Value.

HMAC.why: HMAC-MD5 is the algorithm specified for the IS-IS authentication value, and the security discussion analyses its strength. Readers of HMAC would want this as a usage profile.
HMAC.quote: The HMAC-MD5 algorithm requires a key K and text T as input [RFC2104].

rejected.why: MD5 appears only as the hash inside HMAC-MD5. The document is not about MD5 itself, though its security section discusses attacks on it.
The document is about authentication of IS-IS, and the tech tag IS-IS already covers it. Tagging the parent topic directly would add little.
This is a routing protocol PDU authentication mechanism, not a general cross-protocol authentication document.
The IANA section creates a registry, but this is boilerplate-like and not the main subject of the body.

RFC5305.title: IS-IS Extensions for Traffic Engineering
RFC5305.summary: Standards-track specification of IS-IS extensions for traffic engineering: the extended IS reachability TLV with TE sub-TLVs, the extended IP reachability TLV with a 32-bit metric and up/down bit, and the TE router ID TLV; obsoletes RFC 3784.

IS-IS.why: The document defines new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs (22, 134, 135) and their semantics, so it is a specification and extension of IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: This document extends the IS-IS protocol by specifying new information that an Intermediate System (router) can place in Link State Protocol Data Units (LSP).

traffic engineering.why: The sub-TLVs (administrative group, bandwidth, unreserved bandwidth per priority, TE default metric) and the TE router ID exist to carry link attributes for TE path computation, so TE readers would want this RFC.
traffic engineering.quote: The characteristics described in this document are needed for traffic engineering [RFC2702].

rejected.why: TE is motivated by MPLS (RFC 2702 reference), but the document does not specify anything about MPLS itself.
BGP is mentioned only in a recommendation that the TE router ID match the BGP router ID; the document is not about BGP.
Setup priorities and reservable bandwidth are advertised, but RSVP-TE signalling is not discussed.
OSPF is mentioned in one sentence about mapping OSPF and IS-IS topologies; not a subject of the document.
Security Considerations only refer to RFC 5304 and add nothing new.

RFC5306.title: Restart Signaling for IS-IS
RFC5306.summary: RFC 5306 defines an IS-IS restart TLV (RR, RA, SA bits) and timers T1-T3 so a (re)starting router can keep adjacencies up, synchronize its LSP database and limit routing disruption; it obsoletes RFC 3847.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a Restart TLV and procedures for adjacency reacquisition, LSP database synchronization and overload-bit handling.
IS-IS.quote: A new TLV is defined to be included in IIH PDUs.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the IS-IS tag, and the document is specific to IS-IS.
Only IS-IS is specified. OSPF is not discussed.
Not mentioned. The document is about restart signalling, not failure detection.

RFC5307.title: IS-IS Extensions in Support of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)
RFC5307.summary: RFC 5307 defines IS-IS TLV and sub-TLV encodings (link local/remote identifiers, link protection type, interface switching capability descriptor, SRLG) to carry GMPLS traffic engineering link state, and covers graceful restart implications.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with new sub-TLVs and a new TLV, and specifies restart behaviour of IS-IS LSPs.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies extensions to the IS-IS routing protocol in support of carrying link state information for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

GMPLS.why: The encodings carry GMPLS TE link properties (switching capability, protection type, SRLG, unnumbered link identifiers), so GMPLS readers need this document.
GMPLS.quote: The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor is a sub-TLV (of type 21) of the extended IS reachability TLV.

rejected.why: Only referenced for restart procedures; the document defines IS-IS routing encodings, not RSVP-TE signalling.
TE link attributes are advertised, but the document is about IS-IS/GMPLS encodings; the IS-IS and GMPLS tags cover it.
SONET/SDH appears only as a TDM switching capability indication field, not as a subject of the document.
The IS-IS tag already sits under routing and is more specific.

RFC5308.title: Routing IPv6 with IS-IS
RFC5308.summary: Specifies two new IS-IS TLVs (IPv6 Reachability, IPv6 Interface Address) and an IPv6 NLPID so IS-IS can carry IPv6 routing information alongside IPv4 and OSI.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with new TLVs, an NLPID and modified SPF path preference for IPv6, so it belongs on the IS-IS page.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies a method for exchanging IPv6 routing information using the IS-IS routing protocol.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the address family being routed. The document specifies no IPv6 protocol behaviour, only how IS-IS carries IPv6 prefixes.
Equal-cost multipath is mentioned in one sentence in Operation, but it is not a subject of the document.
The document reuses the extended metrics and up/down semantics from RFC 5305, but it does not address traffic engineering itself.
OSI is mentioned only as one of the protocols IS-IS routes alongside IPv6. The document does not address OSI network-layer protocols.

RFC5309.title: Point-to-Point Operation over LAN in Link State Routing Protocols
RFC5309.summary: Informational RFC describing a configuration mechanism letting IS-IS and OSPF/OSPFv3 treat a two-router LAN as a point-to-point circuit (p2p-over-lan), including unnumbered operation, ARP/ND resolution and misconfiguration detection.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies how IS-IS operates with a point-to-point circuit type over LAN media, including hello contents and link-layer addressing.
IS-IS.quote: the p2p IS-IS Hello (IIH) over this circuit MUST include the IP interface address(es) as defined in [RFC1195]

OSPF.why: Specifies OSPF and OSPFv3 interface behaviour when a LAN interface is configured as point-to-point, so OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: Both routers on the LAN will simply join the AllSPFRouters multicast group and send all OSPF packets with a destination address of AllSPFRouters.

ARP.why: A substantial section covers relaxing ARP source-subnet checks and MAC resolution for unnumbered p2p-over-lan links.
ARP.quote: The ARP process has to be able to resolve the internal IPv4 address used for the unnumbered p2p-over-lan circuits.

rejected.why: ND is mentioned only briefly for resolving link-local next-hop MACs in IPv6; the document does not extend or specify it.
Ethernet/LAN is the medium the mechanism runs over, but the document concerns IGP circuit type, not Ethernet itself.
OSPFv3 is covered jointly with OSPF in one short section; the parent OSPF tag suffices.
The document is protocol-specific to IS-IS/OSPF rather than general routing architecture.
Mentioned only as an example of point-to-point link encapsulation.

RFC5310.title: IS-IS Generic Cryptographic Authentication
RFC5310.summary: Defines a new IS-IS authentication type (CRYPTO_AUTH, code 3) in TLV 10 using Key IDs mapped to security associations and HMAC-SHA algorithms to authenticate IS-IS PDUs.

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol with a new authentication type in TLV 10 and specifies sending and receiving procedures for IS-IS PDUs.
IS-IS.quote: This document proposes an extension to Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) to allow the use of any cryptographic authentication algorithm

HMAC.why: Section 3.3 specifies the HMAC construction (ipad/opad, inner and outer hash) with the SHA family for IS-IS PDUs, a substantial part of the document.
HMAC.quote: This document also explains how HMAC-SHA authentication can be used in IS-IS.

rejected.why: SHA hash functions are used as the underlying primitive inside HMAC; the document does not specify or analyse SHA itself.
Topic parent of the narrower RPKI/BGPsec children, which don't apply. IS-IS is the more specific tag, and the document is primarily about the IS-IS protocol extension.
HMAC-MD5 is mentioned only as the existing RFC 5304 scheme and as background concern; this document does not specify it.
Key IDs and security associations are described, but key management mechanisms are explicitly out of scope (keys are manually configured).
Generic topic; the document concerns PDU authentication within IS-IS, which is covered by the IS-IS and HMAC tags.

RFC5311.title: Simplified Extension of Link State PDU (LSP) Space for IS-IS
RFC5311.summary: Defines a simplified IS-IS mechanism for exceeding the 256 LSP limit using additional system IDs (Extended LSPs), with restricted content, a new IS Alias ID TLV and neighbor attribute TLVs, replacing RFC 3786.

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol with Extended LSPs, new TLVs and processing rules, so it is squarely about IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes a simplified method for extending the Link State PDU (LSP) space beyond the 256 LSP limit.

rejected.why: TE sub-TLVs (RFC 5305) are mentioned only as an example of information carried in the new neighbor attribute TLVs; the document is not about TE.
RFC 5307 is only cited as a source of sub-TLV information.
The document specifies a protocol extension for IS-IS, which the more specific IS-IS tag covers.

RFC5316.title: ISIS Extensions in Support of Inter-Autonomous System (AS) MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC5316.summary: Defines IS-IS extensions (a new inter-AS reachability TLV and sub-TLVs, plus router-capability TE Router ID sub-TLVs) to flood inter-AS TE link information for MPLS/GMPLS inter-AS path computation.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new TLV and sub-TLVs and specifies flooding procedures for them.
IS-IS.quote: It defines ISIS-TE extensions for the flooding of TE information about inter-AS links, which can be used to perform inter- AS TE path computation.

traffic engineering.why: The extensions carry TE link information for inter-AS TE path computation, covering both per-domain and BRPC methods.
traffic engineering.quote: a path computation entity that may be the head-end Label Switching Router (LSR), an AS Border Router (ASBR), or a Path Computation Element

GMPLS.why: The document supports GMPLS TE as well as MPLS TE across multiple ASes.
GMPLS.quote: extensions to the ISIS (ISIS) protocol to support Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Traffic Engineering (TE)

rejected.why: PCE and BRPC are motivating use cases. The document explicitly makes no change to the PCE architecture or usage.
BGP is mentioned only as a possible source of configuration data and for consistency checks. The document is not about BGP.
The document is about the IS-IS advertisement of TE links. MPLS LSPs are the context, not the subject, and GMPLS and traffic engineering already cover that.
The ERO and Path message are cited only as background for the problem statement.
The document gives IPv6 sub-TLVs for completeness, but it is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC5317.title: Joint Working Team (JWT) Report on MPLS Architectural Considerations for a Transport Profile
RFC5317.summary: Archives the IETF–ITU-T Joint Working Team report recommending that MPLS be extended through the IETF to provide a Transport Profile (MPLS-TP), covering forwarding, OAM, control plane, survivability and management.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole report is about defining the MPLS Transport Profile and the decision to develop it in the IETF.
MPLS-TP.quote: extend IETF MPLS forwarding, OAM (Operations, Administration, and Management), survivability, network management and control plane protocols to meet those requirements

rejected.why: The control plane section only notes that existing GMPLS protocols can be reused. The document does not specify or analyse GMPLS.
Pseudowires come up only in passing, in the OAM monitoring discussion. The document is not about them.
OAM is one of the areas the report covers, but it is a sub-topic of MPLS-TP and is not treated on its own.
The document covers IETF–ITU-T cooperation, but the subject is the technical direction for MPLS-TP, not IETF procedures.

RFC5318.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) P-Refused-URI-List Private-Header (P-Header)
RFC5318.summary: Defines the SIP P-Refused-URI-List P-Header, used in OMA Push-to-talk over Cellular, which lets a URI-list server refuse an INVITE containing embedded URI lists with a 403 response and tell the client the members of those lists.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP header field and its parameter, including syntax, 403 response generation rules and an example. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document specifies the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) P-Refused-URI-List Private-Header (P-Header).

rejected.why: The resource-lists XML format only appears in the example bodies and is not specified or extended here.
The multipart bodies and Content-ID references are used as a mechanism, but the document does not define anything new about MIME.
The header is used in OMA PoC networks, but the document is about a SIP header and not IP over 3GPP systems.
The IANA section only registers the header and parameter, which is boilerplate.
The ad-hoc PoC group sessions are only the usage scenario. The document does not address conferencing frameworks or control.
SDP is only a body part in the example INVITE, and its content is not shown.

RFC5320.title: The Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer (SEAL)
RFC5320.summary: Experimental RFC specifying SEAL, a mid-layer encapsulation sublayer for IP tunnels that provides segmentation/reassembly, extended 32-bit packet identification, and fragmentation-reporting probes to handle diverse MTUs and avoid in-network IPv4 fragmentation and classical PMTUD failures.

tunneling.why: SEAL is a new encapsulation sublayer for IP-in-IP/tunnel-mode operation between ingress and egress tunnel endpoints. No more specific tunnel tag (GRE, IP-in-IP) fits, since SEAL is its own encapsulation.
tunneling.quote: This document specifies a Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer (SEAL) that accommodates such virtual topologies over diverse underlying link technologies.

PMTUD.why: The document's core problem is MTU handling. It replaces classical path MTU discovery with fragmentation-reporting probes, and it has a section on SEAL advantages over classical PMTUD plus a historical appendix on PMTUD.
PMTUD.quote: SEAL accommodates links with diverse MTUs and supports efficient duplicate packet detection by introducing a minimal mid-layer encapsulation.

rejected.why: ICMPv4 Fragmentation Needed and PTB messages are used and encapsulated, but ICMP itself is not specified or extended; it is the feedback mechanism.
IPv4 fragmentation and the Identification field are central motivation and mechanism, but the document does not specify IPv4; it adapts around its limits.
IPsec tunnels are discussed as a case SEAL must handle and a placement for the header, but the document is not about IPsec.
Transport mode uses a TCP option for negotiation, but this is a minor part of the document and TCP is only a substrate.
FEC is only mentioned as possible future reliability work in Appendix B.
Teredo is cited only as an example UDP encapsulation context for SEAL.

RFC5321.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
RFC5321.summary: RFC 5321 is the consolidated Draft Standard specification of SMTP, covering its model, extension mechanism, commands, replies, relaying, MX-based address resolution, trace fields, gatewaying and operational/security issues.

SMTP.why: The document is the core SMTP specification: commands, replies, sessions, relaying, extension model, retry and timeout rules.
SMTP.quote: This document is a specification of the basic protocol for Internet electronic mail transport.

rejected.why: MX lookup in Section 5 is used to locate hosts, but the document does not define DNS behaviour; it is a substrate.
Header formats are specified in companion RFC 5322; this document only touches trace fields (Received, Return-Path).
Mentioned only as the body structure carried in DATA; not specified here.
Transport substrate only; Appendix A is a short note.
SPF and DKIM are mentioned only in passing and explicitly not addressed.
The more specific SMTP tag applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC5322.title: Internet Message Format
RFC5322.summary: RFC 5322 specifies the Internet Message Format, the syntax of text email messages including header fields, addressing, dates, and obsolete syntax, obsoleting RFC 2822.

message format.why: The whole document defines the Internet message format: header fields, address syntax, date-time, message identifiers, and obsolete forms. This is the core spec for the message format tag.
message format.quote: This document specifies the Internet Message Format (IMF), a syntax for text messages that are sent between computer users, within the framework of "electronic mail" messages.

rejected.why: SMTP (RFC 5321) handles transport and the envelope. This document only references it and explicitly excludes the envelope.
MIME extensions are named as out of scope. They are only referenced as the way to carry non-ASCII and non-text content.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar. The document is not about ABNF itself.
The date-time syntax is specific to message header fields, as one part of the message format. It is not the RFC 3339 Internet timestamp format.
The more specific child tag, message format, fits better.
The document restricts messages to US-ASCII characters but is not about ASCII as a character set.

RFC5323.title: Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) SEARCH
RFC5323.summary: Specifies WebDAV SEARCH (DASL), an HTTP/1.1 extension adding the SEARCH method, DASL header, query grammar and schema discovery, and the mandatory DAV:basicsearch XML query grammar for server-side search of DAV resources.

WebDAV.why: The document defines a WebDAV extension: the SEARCH method, DASL header, DAV:supported-query-grammar-set property and the DAV:basicsearch grammar, all built on the WebDAV resource and property model.
WebDAV.quote: an application of the HTTP/1.1 protocol to efficiently search for DAV resources based upon a set of client-supplied criteria

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate. The document adds a method and header, but its subject is WebDAV search, which the more specific WebDAV tag covers.
XML is only the encoding of queries and responses, with DTD fragments used as notation.
Not relevant; the document says nothing about authentication schemes.
Media types such as text/xml and application/xml are mentioned only as request body formats, and none are registered.
The only IANA content is boilerplate registration of the DASL header.
xml:lang matching operators are defined, but this is a minor part of the document, not its subject.

RFC5324.title: MIB for Fibre-Channel Security Protocols (FC-SP)
RFC5324.summary: Defines five SMIv2 MIB modules (TC, Authentication, Zoning, Policy, Security Association) for managing Fibre Channel Security Protocols (FC-SP).

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is to define MIB modules using SMIv2 for FC-SP management.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

fibre channel.why: The managed subject is Fibre Channel security (authentication, SAs, policies, zoning). The closest taxonomy tag is fibre channel.
fibre channel.quote: it describes managed objects for information related to FC-SP, the Security Protocols defined for Fibre Channel.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB modules; the SNMP tag covers the framework itself, and MIB is the more specific fit.
The document explicitly says the FC Security Association Management protocol is a subset of IKEv2 and 'not IPsec'. It only mentions ESP_Header as a conceptual parallel.
RADIUS appears only as an OID identity for external authentication servers, not as a subject of the document.
AAA protocols are mentioned only as external servers for verifying DH-CHAP responses.
FC-SP authentication is covered, but only as managed objects within the MIB, not as a general authentication topic.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel Security Protocols (FC-SP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for FC-SP itself. The 'fibre channel' and 'iFCP' tags cover Fibre Channel over IP, not native Fibre Channel security management. The 'fibre channel' tag I used above is an approximation and may not be valid.

RFC5325.title: Licklider Transmission Protocol - Motivation
RFC5325.summary: Informational DTN Research Group document explaining the motivation, environment, and overall design of the Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP), a retransmission-based ARQ convergence layer for long-delay, intermittently connected deep-space links under the Bundle Protocol.

DTN.why: LTP is the DTN convergence layer for the Bundle Protocol over deep-space links; the whole document motivates and overviews it, so DTN readers would want it.
DTN.quote: LTP is intended to serve as a reliable "convergence layer" protocol, underlying the Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) [DTN] Bundle protocol [BP]

rejected.why: TCP is only compared against to explain why it is unsuitable; the document does not specify or extend it.
SCTP is discussed only briefly as a protocol that does not fit the environment.
The TFRC throughput equation is used only to show TCP is infeasible; the document is not about congestion control.
UDP is mentioned only as an optional lower layer for LTP in development or private LANs.
The IP Authentication Header is cited only as a design analogy in the security discussion; the details are in the separate extensions document.
LTP uses ARQ retransmission, not FEC or network coding, and the document does not address loss-recovery coding.

RFC5326.title: Licklider Transmission Protocol - Specification
RFC5326.summary: Specifies the Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP), a retransmission-based (ARQ) reliable transfer protocol with red/green parts, checkpoints and report segments, for links with very long delays or intermittent connectivity, serving as a convergence layer for the DTN Bundle Protocol.

DTN.why: LTP is a core Delay-Tolerant Networking protocol, serving as the reliable convergence layer for the Bundle Protocol in interplanetary and other challenged environments. The whole document specifies it.
DTN.quote: designed to provide retransmission-based reliability over links characterized by extremely long message round-trip times (RTTs) and/or frequent interruptions in connectivity

rejected.why: UDP is only an optional substrate for LTP, for development and private LANs. The document does not specify or extend UDP; it only reserves a port number.
LTP is a transport-like protocol, but the DTN tag is more specific and fits better. I do not add the parent.

ARQ is the loss-recovery mechanism here, but the document is about the protocol itself, not a loss-recovery scheme in the sense of this subject. Forward error correction is only mentioned as something the data-link layer provides.
The document states that LTP has no flow or congestion control, so the subject is not addressed.
LTP runs directly over a data-link protocol, but it only states requirements for that layer and does not specify one.

RFC5327.title: Licklider Transmission Protocol - Security Extensions
RFC5327.summary: Defines security extensions for the Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP): an authentication extension (HMAC-SHA1-80, RSA-SHA256, NULL ciphersuites) and a cookie extension to hinder DoS attacks, for delay-tolerant networking.

DTN.why: LTP is the DTN convergence layer for deep-space links; this document extends it with security features, so DTN readers would look for it.
DTN.quote: LTP is designed to provide retransmission-based reliability over links characterized by extremely long message round-trip times (RTTs) and/or frequent interruptions in connectivity.

authentication.why: A major part of the document defines a segment authentication extension with ciphersuites carrying a MAC or digital signature.
authentication.quote: The LTP authentication mechanism provides cryptographic authentication of the segment.

DDoS.why: The cookie extension is defined to resist denial-of-service attacks on LTP sessions, so it falls under DoS mitigation.
DDoS.quote: The use of cookies is a well-known way to make Denial of Service (DoS) attacks harder to mount.

rejected.why: That tag is for HTTP state management cookies; the LTP cookie here is an anti-DoS random value, unrelated.
HMAC-SHA1-80 is used as a ciphersuite component but the document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
RSA-SHA256 is just a signature algorithm referenced from RFC 3447, not specified here.
IPsec/IKE is only mentioned as unsuitable for general DTN due to long delays; the document is not about it.
TLS is cited only as precedent for the hardcoded ciphersuite numbering scheme.
The document explicitly states it does not address key management.

gaps.name: Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no LTP-specific tag; DTN is the closest fit but LTP, the deep-space ARQ convergence layer, is the actual subject.

RFC5328.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Digital Video Broadcasting Project (DVB)
RFC5328.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "dvb" for persistent resources (XML schemas, classification schemes, metadata) defined by the Digital Video Broadcasting Project, and describes how such URNs are assigned and resolved.

URN.why: The document is a formal URN namespace registration (NID "dvb") following RFC 3406, with structure, assignment, resolution and equivalence rules.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Digital Video Broadcasting Project (DVB) for naming persistent resources defined within DVB standards.

rejected.why: DNS SRV records are used to find SD&S entry points, but DNS is only a supporting mechanism and is not specified or extended here.
DVB Service Discovery and Selection is used to bootstrap URN resolution, but it is defined in ETSI specs; this RFC only references it.
XML schemas are among the resources being named, but the document does not address XML usage itself.
IPTV is mentioned as context for the DVB services that use these URNs, but the document is not about IPTV delivery.
The IANA considerations section only records the NID registration; it is boilerplate here.

RFC5329.title: Traffic Engineering Extensions to OSPF Version 3
RFC5329.summary: Defines the OSPFv3 Intra-Area-TE-LSA and new TLV/sub-TLVs (Router IPv6 Address, Neighbor ID, Local/Remote Interface IPv6 Address) to extend OSPFv2 traffic engineering to IPv6 networks.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends OSPFv3 with a new LSA type and TLVs, so it belongs on the OSPFv3 page.
OSPFv3.quote: This document describes extensions to OSPFv3 to support intra-area Traffic Engineering (TE).

traffic engineering.why: The extensions advertise TE link information for IPv6 networks, which is of interest to readers of traffic engineering.
traffic engineering.quote: This document extends OSPFv2 TE to handle IPv6 networks.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an informative reference that could reuse these TLVs. The document does not specify GMPLS.
IPv6 addresses are carried in the TLVs, but the document is about OSPFv3 TE extensions and not IPv6 itself.
The Management Considerations section lists two MIB variables defined elsewhere. That is not a substantial part of the document.
OSPFv3 is the more specific child tag and it already covers this.
The document is about OSPF TE advertisement, not MPLS itself. MPLS appears only via references to Diff-Serv MPLS.

RFC5330.title: A Link-Type sub-TLV to Convey the Number of Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths Signalled with Zero Reserved Bandwidth across a Link
RFC5330.summary: Defines a new Unconstrained TE LSP Count link sub-TLV for OSPF (v2/v3 TE LSA) and IS-IS (TLV 22/222) to advertise the number of zero-bandwidth MPLS TE LSPs across a link.

traffic engineering.why: The document extends MPLS TE link advertisement with a new sub-TLV counting zero-bandwidth TE LSPs, which supports load balancing and TE path decisions.
traffic engineering.quote: This document specifies a new Link-type Traffic Engineering sub-TLV used to advertise the number of unconstrained TE LSPs signalled across a link.

OSPF.why: Specifies a new sub-TLV for the OSPF TE LSA (and OSPFv3 Intra-Area-TE LSA), so it extends OSPF.
OSPF.quote: The OSPF Unconstrained TE LSP Count sub-TLV is OPTIONAL and MUST NOT appear more than once within the Link TLV (Type 2)

IS-IS.why: Specifies a new sub-TLV for IS-IS extended IS reachability TLVs, so it extends IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: The IS-IS Unconstrained TE LSP Count sub-TLV is OPTIONAL and MUST NOT appear more than once within the extended IS reachability TLV (type 22)

rejected.why: MPLS TE is the context, but the document specifies IGP advertisements rather than MPLS itself. The traffic engineering tag covers the subject.
The LSPs are signalled with RSVP-TE, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
OSPFv3 is mentioned only as a carrier LSA in passing. The document is mainly about the OSPF sub-TLV in general.
Load balancing across equal-cost paths is the motivation only. The document explicitly puts the algorithms out of scope.
MPLS TE Fast Reroute is cited as deployment context only, and it is not LDP or IP fast reroute.

RFC5331.title: MPLS Upstream Label Assignment and Context-Specific Label Space
RFC5331.summary: Extends the MPLS architecture with upstream-assigned labels and generalizes per-interface label spaces into context-specific label spaces, including upstream neighbor label spaces and context labels on LANs.

MPLS.why: The document extends the MPLS architecture (RFC 3031) with upstream label assignment and context-specific label spaces, so it belongs on the MPLS page.
MPLS.quote: This document introduces the notion of upstream-assigned MPLS labels to the MPLS architecture.

rejected.why: Multicast is only the illustrative use case in Section 9. The document itself is about label assignment and label spaces.
Label distribution protocols are mentioned only as a mechanism whose extensions are explicitly out of scope.
GRE is only an example of a tunnel type used to determine the context. The document does not specify or extend it.
Tunnels supply the context for label lookup, but the document does not specify tunneling itself.
The document does not address multicast VPNs. The multicast use case is general MPLS multicast.

RFC5332.title: MPLS Multicast Encapsulations
RFC5332.summary: Redefines the two MPLS data-link codepoints (ethertypes 0x8847/0x8848) so both can carry multicast, with 0x8848 meaning an upstream-assigned top label, specifies the GRE/IP/PPP encapsulation consequences, and defines the Ethernet multicast MAC DA for MPLS.

MPLS.why: The document updates the MPLS label stack encoding (RFC 3032) and the data-link codepoints for MPLS, including upstream-assigned labels and Ethernet MAC DA for MPLS multicast.
MPLS.quote: This specification updates RFC 3032 by redefining the meaning of these two codepoints.

GRE.why: It modifies RFC 4023 MPLS-in-GRE ethertype selection depending on whether the top label is upstream-assigned.
GRE.quote: If the IP destination address of the GRE encapsulation is a multicast IP address, then: the ethertype value 0x8847 MUST be used

rejected.why: The document concerns MPLS encapsulation of multicast packets, not IP multicast routing or group membership. The MPLS tag fits better.
Ethernet is only the link medium for the ethertype and MAC DA rules. The document is not about IP over Ethernet in general.
PPP gets one sentence stating the protocol field is 0x0281. That is not a substantial part of the document.
The IP protocol number 137 section is brief and part of the RFC 4023 MPLS-in-IP update. It is not about generic IP-in-IP.

RFC5333.title: IANA Registration of Enumservices for Internet Calendaring
RFC5333.summary: Registers the ENUM Enumservices "ical-sched" (iMIP via mailto:) and "ical-access" (CalDAV via http/https) so telephone numbers can map to Internet calendaring URIs in the DNS.

ENUM.why: The document's whole purpose is to register new ENUM Enumservices with NAPTR templates and examples for E.164 numbers.
ENUM.quote: This document registers Enumservices for scheduling and accessing Internet calendaring information associated with an E.164 number.

CalDAV.why: The ical-access Enumservice points to CalDAV services. Readers of CalDAV would want to know about this discovery mechanism.
CalDAV.quote: in order to access a user's calendar (for example free/busy status) using the CalDAV [7] protocol for Internet calendaring.

iCalendar.why: The ical-sched Enumservice covers iCalendar scheduling with iMIP. iCalendar is the closest taxonomy tag for this.
iCalendar.quote: This Enumservice indicates that the resource identified can be addressed by the associated URI used for scheduling using Internet calendaring via Internet mail with the iMIP [6] protocol.

rejected.why: DNS is only the substrate that ENUM uses. The document defines nothing new about DNS itself.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a mitigation.
The more specific tags iCalendar and CalDAV cover the calendaring content.
The mailto, http and https URI schemes are used as existing schemes. None is defined or changed.
WebDAV is only the base of CalDAV and is not the subject here.
It appears only in Security Considerations as the protection for https.

RFC5334.title: Ogg Media Types
RFC5334.summary: Registers the application/ogg, video/ogg and audio/ogg media types for the Ogg container format, with usage rules, file extensions, the codecs parameter and Skeleton requirements, obsoleting RFC 3534.

Ogg.why: The document defines the Ogg media types, file extensions and conformance rules, which is exactly the Ogg tag's scope (encapsulation format, its media types).
Ogg.quote: This document describes the registration of media types for the Ogg container format and conformance requirements for implementations of these types.

media types.why: The core purpose is media type registration (video/ogg, audio/ogg, application/ogg) with registration templates and usage restrictions.
media types.quote: this document registers two new media types and redefines the existing application/ogg as defined in the following section.

rejected.why: Codecs (Theora, Vorbis, Speex, etc.) are only listed as content Ogg can carry and mapped to the codecs parameter. The document does not define them.
Vorbis is only mentioned as example content in Ogg, not specified here.
Speex is only mentioned as example content and for the .spx extension, not specified here.
MIME is the general framework for media types, but the document is about specific type registrations, covered by the media types tag.
HTTP is only mentioned as one place where the types are served, not specified or extended.
RTP payload formats are only referenced as separate types for real-time use, not defined here.

RFC5335.title: Internationalized Email Headers
RFC5335.summary: RFC 5335 specifies an experimental variant of Internet message format allowing UTF-8 in email header fields (extended ABNF, addr-spec, trace fields), updates RFC 2045/2822, and registers the message/global media type.

EAI.why: The document defines the header-side of email address internationalization within the EAI work, so it belongs on the EAI page.
EAI.quote: This document specifies an experimental variant of Internet mail that permits the use of Unicode encoded in UTF-8, rather than ASCII, as the base form for Internet email header fields.

message format.why: A substantial part extends RFC 2822 header syntax, including addr-spec, mailbox, Received and Return-Path trace fields.
message format.quote: To permit UTF-8 characters in field values, the header definition in [RFC2822] must be extended to support the new format.

media types.why: It defines and registers the message/global media type and relaxes the content-transfer-encoding rule for message/ subtypes.
media types.quote: The type message/global is similar to message/rfc822, except that it contains a message that can contain UTF-8 characters in the headers

rejected.why: The UTF8SMTP extension is specified in RFC 5336. This document only relies on it as the authorizing transport.
UTF-8 is the encoding the document uses, not something it specifies. The ABNF is copied from RFC 3629.
It updates one rule in RFC 2045 section 6.4, but the main subject is headers. The message/global registration is covered by the media types tag.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax.
The EAI tag fits more specifically.

RFC5336.title: SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email Addresses
RFC5336.summary: Defines the UTF8SMTP SMTP extension permitting internationalized (UTF-8) email addresses in envelopes and UTF-8 headers, with the ALT-ADDRESS parameter for downgrading, UTF8REPLY for VRFY/EXPN, and new enhanced status codes.

EAI.why: The document is a core EAI specification defining the SMTP transport piece of email address internationalization.
EAI.quote: This document specifies an SMTP extension for transport and delivery of email messages with internationalized email addresses or header information.

SMTP.why: It defines a new SMTP service extension, with new MAIL/RCPT/VRFY/EXPN parameters, trace-line changes and reply codes, updating RFC 2821.
SMTP.quote: The extension is identified with the token "UTF8SMTP".

rejected.why: Header internationalization is specified in RFC 5335; this document only references it and updates trace header syntax.
UTF-8 is the encoding used for addresses, not the subject of the document.
IDNA is relied on for domain label handling (ToASCII, validity) but nothing new is defined about it.
Only BODY=8BITMIME/BINARYMIME interaction is discussed, which is an SMTP matter.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the new syntax.

RFC5337.title: Internationalized Delivery Status and Disposition Notifications
RFC5337.summary: RFC 5337 defines a UTF-8 address type for DSN original/final recipient fields and new message/global-delivery-status, message/global-headers and message/global-disposition-notification media types, so delivery status and disposition notifications work with internationalized email.

EAI.why: The document is an EAI working group specification extending DSNs and MDNs to carry internationalized email addresses and UTF-8 headers.
EAI.quote: This specification adds a new address type for international email addresses so an original recipient address with non-US-ASCII characters can be correctly preserved even after downgrading.

media types.why: It defines and registers three new message/* media types (global-headers, global-delivery-status, global-disposition-notification) and their IANA templates.
media types.quote: The first type, message/global-delivery-status, has the syntax of message/delivery-status with three modifications.

SMTP.why: It specifies ORCPT parameter handling for the DSN SMTP extension and requirements on SMTP servers returning undeliverable UTF8SMTP messages.
SMTP.quote: An SMTP [RFC2821] server that advertises both the UTF8SMTP extension [RFC5336] and the DSN extension [RFC3461] MUST accept a UTF-8 address type in the ORCPT parameter

rejected.why: MIME is used as the container (multipart/report, content-transfer-encoding), but the document's subject is the new media types, which fall under media types.
UTF-8 is the charset used by the new formats, but the document is not about the encoding itself.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the syntax.
Internationalized headers are defined in RFC 5335; this document only references them for returned content.

gaps.name: Delivery Status Notifications (DSN) and Message Disposition Notifications (MDN)
gaps.why: The core subject is DSN/MDN report formats, and the taxonomy has no tag for them. Readers would look for them under email, which is only approximated here by EAI, SMTP and media types.

RFC5338.title: Using the Host Identity Protocol with Legacy Applications
RFC5338.summary: Informational overview of techniques for making HIP-aware systems work with legacy, non-HIP-aware applications, covering transparent IP-to-HIT mapping, DNS resolver interposition, user-invoked HITs/LSIs, and local address management for servers.

HIP.why: The whole document is about deploying HIP incrementally with legacy applications: HITs, LSIs, opportunistic mode, and mapping IP addresses to host identifiers.
HIP.quote: This informational document discusses implementation and Application Programming Interface (API) issues relating to using HIP in situations in which the system is HIP-aware but the applications are not

rejected.why: DNS is used for resolver interposition and HIP record lookups, but the document does not specify or extend DNS. It is a mechanism HIP leans on.
The sockets API is the interface legacy applications use, and the document discusses its behaviour. It does not define or extend a sockets API; it explicitly declines to define a native HIP API.
DNSSEC is mentioned only for its security implications in the Security Considerations. The document is not about it.
IPsec is mentioned only as a possible implementation basis for the security policy database. It is not a subject of the document.
NATs are mentioned only as a comparison for referral breakage, not as a topic.
HITs are the same size as IPv6 addresses and LSIs can be 128-bit, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC5339.title: Evaluation of Existing GMPLS Protocols against Multi-Layer and Multi-Region Networks (MLN/MRN)
RFC5339.summary: Informational evaluation of existing GMPLS signaling, routing and management protocols against the multi-layer/multi-region network requirements of RFC 5212, identifying where extensions are needed (virtual TE links, graceful TE link deletion, multi-region signaling, adjustment capacity advertisement, MIB and OAM coordination).

GMPLS.why: The whole document evaluates GMPLS signaling and routing for MLN/MRN and proposes extension areas. GMPLS is the subject.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides an evaluation of Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) protocols and mechanisms against the requirements for Multi-Layer Networks (MLNs) and Multi-Region Networks (MRNs).

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signaling substrate for GMPLS here. The document does not specify or extend it on its own, only evaluates GMPLS signaling as a whole.
OSPF GMPLS extensions are mentioned for ISCD advertisement, but only as the routing substrate.
MIB modules get a short subsection (3.1.5.1), but it is not a substantial part of the document.
PCE is mentioned only as a possible location for VNT path computation, which is out of scope.
OAM coordination is one subsection (3.1.5.2) among many and not the focus.
The document is about traffic engineering of GMPLS networks, but the GMPLS tag is the more specific fit.

gaps.name: GMPLS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a GMPLS tag under MPLS, so no gap exists. It is listed only as a note that the multi-layer/multi-region network (MLN/MRN) concept has no dedicated tag.

RFC5340.title: OSPF for IPv6
RFC5340.summary: RFC 5340 specifies OSPF version 3 (OSPFv3), the modifications to OSPF needed to route IPv6, covering packet and LSA formats, flooding scope, per-link operation, NSSA support, and multiple interfaces per link; it obsoletes RFC 2740.

OSPFv3.why: The whole document defines OSPF for IPv6 (OSPFv3), including its packet formats, LSA types, flooding and SPF changes.
OSPFv3.quote: This document describes the modifications to OSPF to support version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6).

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is a more specific child tag, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
OSPFv3 runs directly over IPv6, but the document is about the routing protocol, not IPv6 specification, addressing or deployment.
Authentication relies on AH and ESP as specified in RFC 4552. This document only references them and defines nothing new about IPsec.
MOSPF support for IPv6 is deprecated here. This is a minor note and the document is not about MOSPF.
The OSPFv3 MIB is mentioned only in Manageability Considerations as a pointer to another document.
The IANA section registers some OSPFv3 option bits and a router properties registry, but this is boilerplate relative to the main body.

RFC5341.title: The Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) tel Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Parameter Registry
RFC5341.summary: Creates an IANA registry for tel URI parameters and values, sets its Specification Required/Designated Expert policy, and populates it with parameters from RFC 3966 and the number portability, ENUM, isub and trunk group extensions.

tel URI.why: The whole document concerns the tel URI parameter registry, its initial contents (isub, ext, phone-context, npdi, rn, cic, tgrp, etc.) and its registration rules. It updates RFC 3966, so readers of the tel URI subject need it.
tel URI.quote: This document creates an Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) registry for tel Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) parameters and their values.

rejected.why: The document is an IANA registry creation, but it is specific to tel URI parameters. The tel URI tag is more specific and fits better. The IANA topic is for registries and stewardship guidance in general.
SIP is mentioned only as the source of the registry structure (RFC 3969) and as a protocol to which tel URIs may be converted. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
The enumdi parameter is listed in the initial table, but the document does not discuss ENUM itself.
The tel URI tag already covers the specific URI scheme, and the document is not about URIs in general.

RFC5342.title: IANA Considerations and IETF Protocol Usage for IEEE 802 Parameters
RFC5342.summary: BCP defining IANA allocation procedures (Expert Review and IESG Ratification) for EUI-48/EUI-64 MAC identifiers, SNAP protocol numbers and other OUI-based parameters under the IANA OUI (00-00-5E), and describing IETF use of IEEE 802 parameters; updates RFC 2153 to stop allocating 'CF Series' OUIs.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is the IANA registry policy for Ethernet parameters under the IANA OUI, including Expert Review and IESG Ratification procedures and templates.
IANA.quote: This document specifies IANA considerations for the allocation of code points under the IANA OUI.

Ethernet.why: Substantial parts cover Ethernet MAC identifiers, Ethertypes, LSAPs, SNAP and OUI Extended Ethertype usage by IETF protocols.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet protocol parameters provide a means of indicating the contents of a frame -- for example, that its contents are IPv4 or IPv6.

rejected.why: Modified EUI-64 use in IPv6 interface identifiers is discussed, but only as one use of MAC-64 identifiers; the document is not about IPv6.
VRRP's unicast MAC block is listed as an allocation example only.
RFC 2153 CF Series OUIs relate to PPP, but the document only deprecates further allocation.
This concerns MAC identifiers, not IP address architecture.
IPv4/MPLS/IPv6 multicast MAC ranges are listed as allocations, not the subject of the document.

RFC5343.title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Context EngineID Discovery
RFC5343.summary: RFC 5343 defines a well-known localEngineID value and a procedure for discovering the snmpEngineID of a remote SNMPv3 engine independent of security models, and updates RFC 3411's IANA rules for the SnmpEngineID format registry.

SNMP.why: The document specifies a new SNMPv3 mechanism (localEngineID and a discovery procedure) and updates RFC 3411, so it belongs under the SNMP framework.
SNMP.quote: This document introduces a well-known localEngineID and a discovery mechanism that can be used to learn the snmpEngineID of a remote SNMP protocol engine.

rejected.why: It reads the snmpEngineID scalar from the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB but defines no MIB module or SMI content.
The SnmpEngineID format registry rules are only a small IANA Considerations clarification. The main body is about discovery.
SNMP is the more specific tag and already covers this.
The mechanism is explicitly independent of security models. USM and TSM are only mentioned for context.

RFC5344.title: Presence and Instant Messaging Peering Use Cases
RFC5344.summary: Informational SPEERMINT WG document describing use cases for peering presence and instant messaging (non-VoIP) services between service providers, to drive later requirements.

SPEERMINT.why: The document is a SPEERMINT WG use-case document on peering between service providers, specifically for presence and IM. The SPEERMINT tag covers peering between SIP providers, and this is the closest fit.
SPEERMINT.quote: This document describes several use cases of peering of non-VoIP (Voice over IP) services between two or more Service Providers.

instant messaging.why: The use cases cover interdomain presence subscription, pager-mode IM and session-based IM, so the document is about presence and IM peering.
instant messaging.quote: drive requirements for peering between domains that provide the non-VoIP based collaboration services with presence and, in particular, Instant Messaging (IM)

MSRP.why: Session-based IM peering is one of the use cases and is based on MSRP. This is a use-case mention rather than a specification, so the tag is secondary.
MSRP.quote: a user from one Peer Network creates a Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) [10] session with a user from another Peer Network.

rejected.why: SIP is referenced only indirectly, through the pager mode and resource list references. The document does not specify or extend it.
Presence subscription and resource lists are the underlying mechanisms, but the document does not define or extend SIMPLE specifications.
Presence documents are mentioned only generically, and PIDF is never named.
Privacy of presence data is discussed in the authorization migration use case and in Security Considerations. The document does not analyse privacy threats in its own right.
Email appears only as an analogy for how prevalent RTC services are.

RFC5345.title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Traffic Measurements and Trace Exchange Formats
RFC5345.summary: An IRTF NMRG informational document describing an approach to large-scale SNMP traffic measurement, including capture, conversion, filtering, storage and analysis, and defining XML (RELAX NG) and CSV trace exchange formats for SNMP messages.

SNMP.why: The whole document studies SNMP usage patterns (versions, operations, table retrieval, traps, row creation) and defines trace formats for SNMP messages.
SNMP.quote: This document describes an approach to carrying out large-scale SNMP traffic measurements in order to develop a better understanding of how SNMP is used in real-world production networks.

performance measurement.why: It specifies a passive measurement methodology (capture, anonymize, analyze traces) and analyses such as message size, latency and concurrency distributions.
performance measurement.quote: This document recommends an approach to collecting, codifying, and handling SNMP traffic traces in order to find answers to some of these questions.

packet capture.why: Capturing pcap traces and defining XML/CSV trace file formats for exchanging them is a substantial part of the document.
packet capture.quote: Capture raw SNMP traffic traces in pcap packet capture files [1].

rejected.why: XML and RELAX NG are the encoding used for the trace format, a substrate rather than the subject.
The CSV format is defined here, but it is a bespoke trace format, not about the CSV/text/csv media type itself.
MIB objects (ifTable, sysUpTime, RowStatus) are discussed only as things to look for in traces; no MIB module is defined.
Anonymization of traces is covered, but mainly as a tool step and in Security Considerations, not as a privacy analysis.
The XML namespace URN registration is boilerplate IANA considerations.

RFC5346.title: Operational Requirements for ENUM-Based Softswitch Use
RFC5346.summary: Informational report on Korean NIDA 2006 Infrastructure ENUM trial, describing operational requirements and lookup/routing rules for ENUM-enabled softswitches between two VoIP carriers during the interim period when DNS has sparse data.

ENUM.why: The document describes ENUM lookup rules, NAPTR handling, Rcode handling and Infrastructure ENUM operation in the e164.arpa tree for call routing.
ENUM.quote: ENUM-based softswitches have to follow a consistent set of rules.

SIP.why: Softswitch call routing to SIP URIs is a substantial part of the operational discussion, including measured SIP answer delay, though the document does not specify SIP itself.
SIP.quote: There is at least one usable URI (such as SIP and/or H.323 URIs)

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate for ENUM; rcode handling is described only in the ENUM routing context, so ENUM is the more specific fit.
EPP is used only for provisioning in the trial and is mentioned briefly; the document does not specify or extend it.
Dynamic Update is only mentioned as the mechanism used to refresh ENUM data in the trial.
Mentioned only as one URI type and signalling protocol a softswitch supports.
Listed only as a protocol a softswitch may support; not discussed.
PSTN fallback is part of routing rules, but the document is not about PSTN interworking mechanisms such as gateway control or signalling transport.

gaps.name: Softswitch / VoIP carrier call routing
gaps.why: The document is about softswitch call routing and migration from prefix-based routing to ENUM; the taxonomy has no softswitch tag, so ENUM is the closest fit.

RFC5347.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol Fax Package
RFC5347.summary: Defines the MGCP FXR (fax) package, giving the Call Agent LocalConnectionOptions, events (t38, gwfax, nopfax) and connection parameters to control T.38 fax relay or let the gateway handle fax itself.

MGCP.why: The document is an MGCP package specification, defining new LCO values, events and connection parameters for MGCP gateways.
MGCP.quote: This document defines a Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) [RFC3435] package that enables MGCP controlled gateways to support fax calls.

fax.why: The subject is fax calls over IP, specifically T.38 fax relay and gateway-controlled fax handling, with fax detection procedures and fax page counters.
fax.quote: The first one utilizes ITU-T Recommendation T.38 using either UDP Transport Layer (UDPTL) or TCP (see [T38]) for fax relay under the control of the Call Agent.

rejected.why: SDP and RFC 3407 capability descriptors are used to signal T.38 support and a negotiation mapping is discussed, but SDP is not the subject.
SIP appears in the call flow examples for Call Agent interworking, but the document does not specify or extend SIP.
RTP is only the alternative audio media transport that T.38 replaces; not specified here.
Parent of MGCP; the document is about MGCP specifically, so the child tag fits better.
Audio codecs like PCMU and G.729 appear in examples only.

gaps.name: T.38 fax relay over IP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no T.38 tag; fax is the closest fit but T.38 is a major subject of the document.

RFC5348.title: TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC): Protocol Specification
RFC5348.summary: RFC 5348 specifies TFRC, an equation-based, TCP-friendly congestion control mechanism for unicast flows, covering sender and receiver behaviour, loss event rate calculation, and responses to idle/data-limited periods; it obsoletes RFC 3448.

TFRC.why: The whole document is the TFRC protocol specification: throughput equation, sender and receiver algorithms, loss interval calculation.
TFRC.quote: This document specifies TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC).  TFRC is a congestion control mechanism for unicast flows operating in a best-effort Internet environment.

rejected.why: DCCP and its CCID 3/4 profiles are the intended host for TFRC, but the document defines the congestion control mechanism and no DCCP packet formats.
TCP behaviour is used only as the fairness reference through its throughput equation. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
ECN marks are counted as loss events, but ECN is only an input signal and the document does not specify it.
This is the parent of TFRC, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a DCCP tag under transport, and it is related because CCID 3 and CCID 4 use TFRC. I chose not to tag it because the RFC is not about DCCP itself.

RFC5349.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Support for Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos (PKINIT)
RFC5349.summary: Informational RFC specifying how to use elliptic curve certificates, ECDSA signatures and ECDH key agreement (with curve and key size choices) within Kerberos PKINIT (RFC 4556), with no change to PKINIT message syntax.

Kerberos.why: The document extends PKINIT, the Kerberos v5 public-key initial authentication extension, defining how ECDH is used for AS reply key delivery and KDC domain parameter negotiation.
Kerberos.quote: the use of Elliptic Curve certificates, Elliptic Curve signature schemes and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement within the framework of PKINIT

elliptic curve.why: Core content is ECC: ECDH key agreement, named curves (P-256, P-384, etc.), key size comparison, curve choice tradeoffs and mandatory-to-implement curves.
elliptic curve.quote: A set of ECDH domain parameters is also known as a "curve".
elliptic curve.section: 5. Choosing the Domain Parameters and the Key Size

ECDSA.why: Section 3 specifies which ECDSA signature algorithm identifiers and paired digests are used in CMS SignedData, with ecdsa-with-Sha256 mandatory.
ECDSA.quote: ecdsa-with-Sha256 [X9.62]
ECDSA.section: 3. Using Elliptic Curve Certificates and Elliptic Curve Signature Schemes

rejected.why: Certificates must comply with RFC 3279, but the document defines nothing new about X.509 profiles; it is a dependency.
SignedData is the substrate carrying the ECDSA signatures; the document only specifies algorithm identifiers used within it.
Certificates are used but PKI itself is not the subject.
SHA digests are only paired with ECDSA algorithm identifiers; nothing new about hash functions.
ECDH key delivery is covered, but it is better captured by the Kerberos and elliptic curve tags.

gaps.name: PKINIT
gaps.why: The document is about PKINIT specifically, but the taxonomy has no PKINIT tag; Kerberos is the closest fit.

RFC5350.title: IANA Considerations for the IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Options
RFC5350.summary: Updates IANA allocation rules and registries for IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Option Values, creating an IPv4 registry, removing a duplicate IPv6 value, and defining experimental ranges.

router alert.why: The whole document concerns the Router Alert Option Value field and its registries for IPv4 and IPv6, so the router alert subject page is the right home.
router alert.quote: This document updates the IANA allocation rules and registry of IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Option Values.

rejected.why: The document is IANA considerations, but only for one specific registry; the router alert tag is more specific and covers the subject for readers.
RSVP aggregation levels appear as values in the registry, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP.
IPv6 is one of two IP versions the option is registered for; the document is about the router alert option, not IPv6 itself.
IPv4 is one of two IP versions the option is registered for; the document is about the router alert option, not IPv4 itself.
IGMP is only mentioned as a user of the option.

RFC5351.title: An Overview of Reliable Server Pooling Protocols
RFC5351.summary: Informational overview of the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) protocol suite, describing ASAP and ENRP, pool handles, failover mechanisms (cookies, business cards), and example usage scenarios.

RSerPool.why: The whole document is an overview of the RSerPool suite, including ASAP, ENRP, pool handles, failover and example usage.
RSerPool.quote: The Reliable Server Pooling effort (abbreviated "RSerPool") provides an application-independent set of services and protocols for building fault-tolerant and highly available client/server applications.

rejected.why: SCTP is only mentioned as an example underlying transport that RSerPool can use; the document is not about it.
DNS appears only as a comparison for how applications resolve hostnames versus pool handles; not about DNS.
TCP is mentioned only as one possible underlying transport.
Pool handle resolution is a form of server selection, but the specific RSerPool tag is more precise and the parent is implied.
Well-known multicast channels are used for server announcement and discovery, but only incidentally.

RFC5352.title: Aggregate Server Access Protocol (ASAP)
RFC5352.summary: Specifies ASAP, the Reliable Server Pooling protocol that registers pool elements, resolves pool handles via ENRP servers, and provides load sharing and failover among server pool members, mainly over SCTP.

RSerPool.why: The document defines ASAP, a core RSerPool protocol: registration, handle resolution, pool element selection, failover and the ASAP user interface.
RSerPool.quote: ASAP defines each logical communication destination as a pool, providing full transparent support for server pooling and load sharing.

rejected.why: SCTP is the transport ASAP runs over and exploits; the document does not extend or specify SCTP itself.
TLS is only the security mechanism mandated in Security Considerations; nothing new is defined about TLS.
DNS is mentioned only in passing for locating ENRP servers, and the handlespace is explicitly contrasted with DNS.
ASAP states other transports need a separate mapping document, but this document does not define such a mapping.
The IANA Considerations only register ASAP message types, ports and a PPID, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool), ASAP and ENRP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RSerPool tag only under SCTP-related transport (listed as 'RSerPool' [tech] under transport), but I used it by id; if the taxonomy intended a different placement, the subject of server pooling and handlespace management has no more specific tag.

RFC5353.title: Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol (ENRP)
RFC5353.summary: Specifies ENRP, the server-to-server protocol of Reliable Server Pooling that keeps a distributed, fault-tolerant handlespace registry synchronized through message formats, initialization, updates, peer monitoring, takeover, and auditing.

RSerPool.why: The document defines ENRP, a core RSerPool protocol.
RSerPool.quote: ENRP defines the procedures and message formats of a distributed, fault-tolerant registry service for storing, bookkeeping, retrieving, and distributing pool operation and membership information.

rejected.why: SCTP is only the transport used between ENRP servers; nothing new is defined about SCTP.
TLS is the mandated security mechanism in the Security Considerations; no new TLS features are defined.
The Internet checksum (RFC 1071) is used for PE checksums but is only a tool, not the subject.
DNS is mentioned only as one administrative means of finding a mentor server and in certificate identity checks.

gaps.name: ENRP / ASAP (Reliable Server Pooling)
