gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RSerPool tech tag but my tag id 'RSerPool' is not in the listed taxonomy; the closest listed tag is RSerPool under transport, which I used. This is a flag to verify.

RFC5354.title: Aggregate Server Access Protocol (ASAP) and Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol (ENRP) Parameters
RFC5354.summary: Defines the common TLV parameter formats, error causes and message framing shared by ASAP and ENRP in the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) architecture, and creates the IANA registries for RSerPool parameter types and error causes.

RSerPool.why: The whole document specifies parameter formats for ASAP and ENRP, the two RSerPool protocols, so a reader of the RSerPool page would expect it.
RSerPool.quote: This document details the common message parameters shared between the two protocols.

rejected.why: SCTP is used as the ASAP/ENRP transport and an SCTP Transport parameter is defined, but the document is not about SCTP itself.
A DCCP Transport parameter is defined only to describe a pool element's user transport. The document does not specify or extend DCCP.
UDP-Lite appears only as one of the user transports a parameter can describe.
The IANA section creates registries, but this is boilerplate and not the main subject.
TCP appears only as a user transport that a parameter can describe, not as the subject.

gaps.name: RSerPool / ASAP / ENRP (Reliable Server Pooling)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RSerPool tech entry listed in the family of transport protocols, and the tag I used is not in the taxonomy as shown. The taxonomy lists RSerPool under transport. The document is entirely about it, so the correct tag id is RSerPool.

RFC5355.title: Threats Introduced by Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) and Requirements for Security in Response to Threats
RFC5355.summary: Informational RFC describing security threats to the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) architecture (ASAP/ENRP) and the security requirements, mostly met with TLS, to counter them.

RSerPool.why: The whole document analyses threats to RSerPool, ASAP and ENRP and sets security requirements for them, so readers of RSerPool would want it.
RSerPool.quote: This document describes security threats to the RSerPool architecture and presents requirements for security to thwart these threats.

security.why: It is a threat analysis with authentication, integrity, confidentiality, replay protection and DoS requirements. It is not tied to a single security mechanism, so the general security topic fits.
security.quote: This informational document characterizes potential security threats targeting the RSerPool architecture.

rejected.why: TLS, including TLS-PSK, is the mechanism selected to meet the requirements. The document does not define new TLS extensions or usage, and the ASAP and ENRP documents describe the actual TLS use.
Flooding and DoS threats are discussed, but only as threats to ENRP servers and PEs. The document does not address DDoS mitigation as a subject.
Authentication requirements recur throughout, but the document is a broader threat analysis. The general security tag covers it better.

RFC5356.title: Reliable Server Pooling Policies
RFC5356.summary: Defines the server pool member selection policies (round robin, weighted random, least used, etc.) for Reliable Server Pooling, with ENRP server and pool user procedures, policy parameter formats, and an IANA registry of policy types.

RSerPool.why: The whole document specifies RSerPool pool member selection policies, their ENRP server and pool user behaviour, and their parameter encodings.
RSerPool.quote: This document describes server pool policies for Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) including considerations for implementing them at Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol (ENRP) servers and pool users.

rejected.why: RSerPool is commonly deployed alongside SCTP, but this document does not discuss SCTP at all.
The document creates a new IANA registry for policy types, but that is boilerplate-level registration and not the document's subject.
Load-based selection is load distribution among servers, not transport congestion control.
Handle resolution resembles name resolution, but the document specifies selection policies, not DNS.

gaps.name: Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RSerPool tag only as a transport child (id 'RSerPool' under transport), and I tagged it by id. Per the instructions the id must appear in the taxonomy, and 'RSerPool' does appear. No gap in tag availability, but a server load-distribution policy topic has no dedicated tag.

RFC5357.title: A Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC5357.summary: RFC 5357 specifies TWAMP, an OWAMP-based protocol (TWAMP-Control and TWAMP-Test) for measuring two-way/round-trip network performance, with a Session-Reflector and an informative TWAMP Light appendix.

TWAMP.why: The document defines TWAMP itself: the control and test protocols, packet formats, reflector behaviour and the Command Number registry.
TWAMP.quote: This memo specifies a Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP), based on the OWAMP, that adds two-way or round-trip measurement capabilities.

rejected.why: TWAMP is derived from OWAMP and reuses much of it, but OWAMP is specified in RFC 4656. This document does not extend or profile OWAMP itself, so it is not tagged.
This is the parent topic of TWAMP, so it is implied by the TWAMP tag and not listed separately.
TCP is only the substrate for TWAMP-Control.
UDP is only the substrate for TWAMP-Test packets.
HMAC and AES are used for integrity protection and encryption in the OWAMP-derived modes. The document does not define them.
AES is used as a mechanism for the test and control modes, and the document is not about AES.

RFC5358.title: Preventing Use of Recursive Nameservers in Reflector Attacks
RFC5358.summary: BCP recommending that operators restrict recursive DNS nameserver service to intended clients (ACLs, interface selection, TSIG/SIG(0)) so open resolvers cannot be used as amplifiers in UDP reflector DoS attacks, and pointing to BCP38 ingress filtering.

DNS.why: The document gives operational configuration guidance for recursive DNS servers, which is DNS server behaviour and operations.
DNS.quote: describes ways to prevent the use of default configured recursive nameservers as reflectors in Denial of Service (DoS) attacks

DDoS.why: It describes reflector/amplification DoS attacks and mitigation, so the DDoS mitigation subject page fits.
DDoS.quote: DNS has been named as a major factor in the generation of massive amounts of network traffic used in Denial of Service (DoS) attacks

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only as a source of larger responses and for key distribution of SIG(0) keys; the document is not about it.
EDNS0 is cited only as raising the amplification factor, not specified or extended.
Considered since the document is operational guidance, but DNS and DDoS tags are more specific.
UDP is the substrate that enables the attack; the document is not about UDP itself.
BCP38 ingress filtering is only referenced as the real solution, not specified here.

RFC5359.title: Session Initiation Protocol Service Examples
RFC5359.summary: BCP document giving detailed SIP call flow examples for IP Centrex/PBX services (hold, transfer, forwarding, conferencing, find-me, screening, park, pickup, redial, click-to-dial) using REFER, Replaces, Join, SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and the dialog event package.

SIP.why: The whole document is SIP message flows showing how telephony services are implemented with SIP and its extensions (REFER, Replaces, Join, dialog events).
SIP.quote: This document gives examples of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) services.

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer is used only in simple form (sendonly/recvonly for hold) as a substrate; the document says it shows only very simple exchanges.
SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and dialog event package are used for call pickup/redial, but the document is not about presence/IM extensions.
The 3-way conference flows are two of eighteen examples; they use the isfocus tag from RFC 4579 rather than addressing conferencing frameworks.
sips URIs imply TLS transport on each hop but TLS is only the substrate.
RTP media paths are merely shown in diagrams.
Digest authentication appears in screening examples only incidentally.

RFC5360.title: A Framework for Consent-Based Communications in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5360.summary: RFC 5360 defines a SIP framework in which relays (proxies, B2BUAs, URI-list services, registrars) must obtain a recipient's permission before translating requests toward it. It adds the 470 response code and the Trigger-Consent and Permission-Missing headers to guard against amplification and DoS.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a consent framework, defining the 470 response code, the Trigger-Consent and Permission-Missing header fields, and relay behaviour for REGISTER and MESSAGE.
SIP.quote: This document identifies a framework for consent-based communications in SIP.

rejected.why: The framework uses MESSAGE, PUBLISH and the Pending Additions event package, but those are defined in companion RFCs. This document is not mainly about presence or IM extensions.
MESSAGE requests carry the permission documents, so IM is only the vehicle for asking permission.
Spam is part of the motivation, but the document addresses consent and amplification in SIP, not spam filtering.
The permission document is XML, but its format is defined in RFC 5361. XML is only the encoding.
The document uses SIP Identity, P-Asserted-Identity, return routability and digest to authenticate grants. This is a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
DoS and amplification are the threats the framework addresses, but it is a SIP consent mechanism, not a DDoS mitigation or signalling scheme.

RFC5361.title: A Document Format for Requesting Consent
RFC5361.summary: Defines an XML permission document format, built on Common Policy, that a SIP relay uses to request a recipient's consent to perform a Request-URI translation, with recipient/target conditions and grant/deny actions.

SIP.why: The document is a SIP-related specification supporting consent-based communications: it defines a permission document for SIP relays, including SIP-specific authentication and identity matching.
SIP.quote: Such permission documents are used by SIP [RFC3261] relays to request permission to perform translations.

XML.why: The main content is a new XML document format with schema, namespace and extensibility rules, extending Common Policy. Readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: This document defines an Extensible Markup Language (XML) format for a permission document used to request consent.

rejected.why: The permission grants are consent for translations, but the document is about a document format in SIP rather than general authorization or access control.
Common Policy is a privacy-preference format, but this document defines consent requests for routing translations and does not address privacy threats or considerations.
HTTP URIs and GET requests are only used as a means of granting or denying permission. The document does not specify HTTP.
The document reuses the existing application/auth-policy+xml type and registers no new media type.
Authentication methods (SIP Identity, P-Asserted-Identity, digest) are referenced from RFC 5360 and used for identity matching, not specified here.
SIP Identity (RFC 4474) is only one of the accepted authentication mechanisms and is not the subject of the document.

RFC5362.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Pending Additions Event Package
RFC5362.summary: Defines the SIP "consent-pending-additions" event package, which lets user agents subscribe to a relay for the consent status of resources being added to a resource list, including an XML consent-status element and partial (diff) notifications.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP event notification package (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY handling, durations, forking, rates) for consent-based SIP relays.
SIP.quote: This document defines the SIP Pending Additions event package.

media types.why: It defines and registers a new media type for partial resource-list notifications, which is a substantive part of the document.
media types.quote: This section registers the 'application/resource-lists-diff+xml' MIME type.

rejected.why: XML is the encoding for the consent-status and diff documents, but the document is not about XML itself.
Uses SIP event packages and resource lists, but is a consent-framework extension, not presence/IM or XCAP work.
A MESSAGE request is mentioned for permission requests, but the document is not about messaging or presence.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as a hop-by-hop protection recommendation.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an end-to-end protection option.
The IANA section is boilerplate registration and does not make the document about IANA.

gaps.name: SIP consent framework / SIP event notification
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SIP event packages or consent-based communications in SIP, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5363.title: Framework and Security Considerations for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) URI-List Services
RFC5363.summary: Defines requirements, a framework (recipient-list Content-Disposition type), and security considerations (authentication, opt-in consent, amplification-attack prevention) for SIP URI-list services that fan out one request to many recipients.

SIP.why: The document specifies a framework and requirements for SIP URI-list services, including a new Content-Disposition type for carrying lists in SIP requests and their security rules.
SIP.quote: The task of a SIP URI-list service is to receive a request that contains or references a URI list

rejected.why: The recipient-list Content-Disposition value is a small registration; the document is not about MIME itself.
MESSAGE is only an example use case; per-method specs are in other RFCs.
Conference servers are only an example of a URI-list service; conferencing is handled by RFC 5366.
TLS and S/MIME are only recommended for list integrity protection; the document is not about them.
Amplification attacks are discussed within security considerations of a SIP service, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation generally.
SUBSCRIBE and resource lists are referenced as examples but not specified here.

RFC5364.title: Extensible Markup Language (XML) Format Extension for Representing Copy Control Attributes in Resource Lists
RFC5364.summary: Defines an XML extension to the SIP resource list format adding 'copyControl' (to/cc/bcc), 'anonymize' and 'count' attributes so URI-list servers can handle recipients like email to/cc/bcc, and defines the 'recipient-list-history' disposition type.

SIMPLE.why: The document extends the XCAP/SIMPLE resource-lists XML format (RFC 4826) used for SIP URI-list services, defining new attributes and a namespace. SIMPLE covers XCAP-related formats like this.
SIMPLE.quote: This specification defines an XML extension to the XML resource list format that allows the sender of the request to qualify a recipient with a copy control level

SIP.why: The extension is used in SIP requests handled by URI-list servers, with a new Content-Disposition type 'recipient-list-history' and handling-parameter guidance for SIP.
SIP.quote: a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) request is distributed to a group of SIP User Agents (UAs)

rejected.why: XML is the encoding of the format extension, but the document is about the SIP resource-list semantics, not XML usage in general. Schema use is substrate-like.
Copy control is analogous to email to/cc/bcc but the document does not define email message headers.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection option.
S/MIME is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection option.
The IANA registration is of a Content-Disposition value, not a media type.

gaps.name: SIP URI-list services / resource lists (RFC 4826)
gaps.why: The document is about resource lists carried in SIP for multi-recipient requests, and the taxonomy has no specific tag for XCAP resource lists or URI-list services beyond SIMPLE.

RFC5365.title: Multiple-Recipient MESSAGE Requests in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5365.summary: Defines how a SIP UAC sends a single MESSAGE request with a recipient-list body to a MESSAGE URI-list service, which fans it out to each recipient, includes a recipient-list-history body for Reply-To-All, and registers the 'recipient-list-message' option-tag.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP MESSAGE with URI-list service procedures for UAC and service, defines a new SIP option-tag, and specifies header handling for the fan-out.
SIP.quote: This document specifies a mechanism that allows a SIP User Agent Client (UAC) to send a SIP MESSAGE request to a set of destinations

instant messaging.why: The purpose is group pager-mode instant messaging with Reply-To-All, so instant messaging readers would want it.
instant messaging.quote: the sending user just wants to send a small pager-mode instant message to an ad hoc group without the burden of setting up a session

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an alternative session-based approach, not specified or used.
The resource-lists XML format is reused from other RFCs as a payload; nothing new about XML itself is defined here.
Only referenced as optional protection for bodies; the document does not address S/MIME itself.
The document extends SIP MESSAGE (RFC 3428), not the SIMPLE event packages, PIDF or XCAP work; XCAP is only referenced for features that are not used.
It uses existing media types and Content-Disposition values defined in RFC 5363/5364; it registers no new media type.
The URI-list fan-out resembles list expansion, but it is SIP instant messaging, not mailing-list protocols.

gaps.name: SIP URI-list services
gaps.why: The document is one of a set (RFC 5363/5364/5365) on SIP URI-list services and copy control, and the taxonomy has no tag for that subject.

RFC5366.title: Conference Establishment Using Request-Contained Lists in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5366.summary: Specifies how a SIP UAC creates an ad hoc conference by sending an INVITE to a conference factory URI carrying a recipient-list URI-list body, defines the 'recipient-list-invite' option-tag, and describes conference server handling.

conferencing.why: The document is about ad hoc conference creation with an initial participant list, using the conference factory and focus procedures of RFC 4579. No XCON/CLUE-specific tag fits, so the general conferencing topic applies.
conferencing.quote: This document describes how to create a conference using SIP URI-list services.

SIP.why: It extends SIP with a new option-tag and INVITE body handling, including re-INVITE and 420 behaviour, and a conference-server flow using INVITE.
SIP.quote: the UAC MUST include the 'recipient-list-invite' option-tag (which is registered with the IANA in Section 8) in a Require header field.

rejected.why: SDP bodies appear only in the INVITE offer/answer examples; the document defines nothing about SDP.
The resource-lists XML format is reused from RFC 4826 and RFC 5364, not defined here.
Multipart bodies and Content-Disposition values are used as a substrate; the document does not define MIME mechanisms.
Resource lists come from XCAP-related specs, but the document does not address event packages, PIDF or XCAP.
The document builds on RFC 4579 SIP conferencing, not the XCON framework or data model.

gaps.name: SIP URI-list services
gaps.why: The document defines a URI-list service (request-contained recipient lists, RFC 5363 framework), but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC5367.title: Subscriptions to Request-Contained Resource Lists in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5367.summary: Specifies how a SIP UAC creates a resource list and subscribes to it in one SUBSCRIBE request by carrying the URI list in the body, with server behaviour, a list-management Call-Info purpose value, and a new option-tag.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP event notification with request-contained resource list subscriptions, defining a new option-tag, Call-Info purpose value, and UAC/server procedures.
SIP.quote: This document specifies a way to create subscription to a list of resources in SIP. This is achieved by including the list of resources in the body of a SUBSCRIBE request.

rejected.why: The tag covers SIMPLE event packages, PIDF extensions and XCAP. This RFC extends SUBSCRIBE and uses the RFC 4662 RLS and the XCAP resource-list format only as building blocks. It is not itself a SIMPLE presence specification, so SIP alone is the fit.
The resource-lists XML format is reused from RFC 4826 and is not defined here.
The RFC registers no media types. It only registers an option-tag and a Call-Info purpose value.
The IANA section is boilerplate and the registrations are minor.

RFC5368.title: Referring to Multiple Resources in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5368.summary: RFC 5368 extends the SIP REFER method so a single request can refer a recipient (a URI-list service) to multiple targets via a URI list body pointed to by Refer-To, defining the "multiple-refer" option-tag and recommending suppression of the implicit subscription.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP REFER method, defines a new SIP option-tag, and specifies REFER-Issuer and REFER-Recipient behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document defines extensions to the SIP REFER method so that it can be used to refer to multiple resources in a single request.

SIMPLE.why: It profiles XCAP resource-list documents with copy-control extensions as the URI-list format for SIP URI-list services, which is SIMPLE-family work. This is a smaller part of the document than the REFER extension.
SIMPLE.quote: The default format for 'recipient-list' bodies for REFER-Issuers and REFER-Recipients is RFC 4826 [RFC4826] extended with RFC 5364 [RFC5364].

rejected.why: XML resource-lists are only the encoding of the URI list, not the subject of the document.
The conference server use case is only a motivating example. The document is not about conferencing.
The document only reuses existing media types and registers no new one.
The only IANA content is the boilerplate registration of the option-tag.

RFC5369.title: Framework for Transcoding with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5369.summary: Informational framework for transcoding in SIP sessions, covering how an endpoint discovers the need for transcoding and two invocation models (3pcc and conference bridge), meeting the RFC 3351 requirements for deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-impaired users.

SIP.why: The document defines how SIP user agents discover the need for and invoke transcoder intermediaries, using 3pcc and B2BUA conference bridge models. This is SIP call signalling deployment guidance.
SIP.quote: This document defines a framework for transcoding with SIP. This framework includes how to discover the need for transcoding services in a session and how to invoke those transcoding services.

conferencing.why: One of the two invocation models is the conference bridge model, which treats the transcoder as a dial-in/dial-out conference server. A substantial part of the document addresses this.
conferencing.quote: we can model a transcoding service as a two-party conference server that may change not only the codec in use, but also the format of the media

accessibility.why: The framework is motivated by and explicitly meets the accessibility requirements for deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-impaired users. Examples include speech-to-text and text-to-speech transcoding.
accessibility.quote: Both models meet the requirements regarding transcoding services invocation in RFC 3351 [RFC3351], which support deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired individuals.

rejected.why: SDP and offer/answer are used to learn media capabilities, but the document does not specify or extend them.
Codec incompatibility is the motivation, but the document defines no codec and is about invoking transcoders, not codec definitions.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate the transcoder.
S/MIME is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate the transcoder.
Presence documents are mentioned briefly as a source of capability information, but the document is not about SIMPLE or presence.
RFC 3238 is cited only for the one-party consent principle. The document does not address OPES.

RFC5370.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Conference Bridge Transcoding Model
RFC5370.summary: Specifies the conference bridge model for invoking SIP transcoding services, where a transcoder acts as a B2BUA invoked by caller (via URI-list INVITE) or callee (via 302 redirect), supporting accessibility needs.

SIP.why: The document specifies SIP procedures (INVITE with URI-list body, B2BUA behaviour, 302 redirect, History-Info) for invoking transcoders.
SIP.quote: a transcoding server that provides a particular transcoding service (e.g., speech-to-text) behaves as a B2BUA (Back-to-Back User Agent) between both UAs

rejected.why: Uses a conference-server-style model but only for two-party transcoding, not a conferencing framework or control.
SDP is only the session description carried in the INVITEs; nothing new is defined about it.
Transcoding is the motivation, but the document defines no codec; it only covers invocation signalling.
Accessibility is mentioned as motivation in the abstract, but the body is about SIP invocation procedures, not accessibility itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an integrity mechanism.
The resource-lists XML body is only carried in an example; XML is not the subject.

RFC5371.title: RTP Payload Format for JPEG 2000 Video Streams
RFC5371.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for carrying JPEG 2000 video (a series of JPEG 2000 images) over RTP, including the payload header, packetization rules, the video/jpeg2000 media type, and SDP parameters and offer/answer usage.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines a new RTP payload format for JPEG 2000 video, with payload header, packetization and RTP header usage.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies a payload format for JPEG 2000 video streams over the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

codecs.why: The JPEG 2000 video codec, its codestream structure and features are explained and packetized. The taxonomy has no JPEG 2000 specific tag, so the generic codecs tag is the closest fit.
codecs.quote: JPEG 2000 is an ISO/IEC International Standard and ITU-T Recommendation (ISO/IEC International Standard 15444-1 | ITU-T Rec. T.800)

SDP.why: Substantial sections cover SDP mapping of the media type parameters and offer/answer rules with examples.
SDP.quote: The media type video/jpeg2000 string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] as follows:

media types.why: The document registers the video/jpeg2000 media type with its parameters (rate, sampling, interlace, width, height).
media types.quote: Type name: video

rejected.why: The payload format tag is more specific; RTP itself is only used, not extended (RTP payload format sits under RTP).
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a recommended mechanism.
The congestion control section is standard boilerplate for RTP payload formats, not a substantial part of the document.
Mentioned only as an example out-of-band signaling protocol.
Mentioned only as an example out-of-band signaling protocol.
Mentioned only in passing regarding timestamp resolution for jitter measurement.

gaps.name: JPEG 2000 (ISO/IEC 15444-1 / ITU-T T.800)
gaps.why: The image/video coding standard being packetized has no dedicated tag in the codecs subtree, so it is covered only by the generic codecs tag.

RFC5372.title: Payload Format for JPEG 2000 Video: Extensions for Scalability and Main Header Recovery
RFC5372.summary: Extends the RTP payload format for JPEG 2000 video (RFC 5371) with a priority-field mapping for scalability, a main header recovery scheme using mh_id, and new SDP/media type parameters (mhc, pt).

RTP payload format.why: The document extends an RTP payload format for JPEG 2000 video, defining priority and mh_id header processing. This is the core subject.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes extended uses for the payload header in "RTP Payload Format for JPEG 2000 Video Streams" as specified in RFC 5371

SDP.why: It defines new SDP fmtp parameters and offer/answer rules with examples. This is a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: The new optional parameters mhc and pt, if presented, MUST be included in the "a=fmtp" line of SDP.

rejected.why: It adds optional parameters to the existing video/jpeg2000 media type, but this is small and tied to the payload format. It is not about media type registry rules.
JPEG 2000 is the coded media, but the document only specifies RTP packetization and signalling. It does not define a codec.
RTP is the transport. The specific child tag RTP payload format fits better.
Multicast is mentioned only as a scenario for the priority field, and the document does not cover multicast routing.

gaps.name: JPEG 2000 image coding
gaps.why: The document is about carrying JPEG 2000 codestreams, but the taxonomy has no still-image or JPEG 2000 tag.

RFC5373.title: Requesting Answering Modes for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5373.summary: Defines the SIP Answer-Mode and Priv-Answer-Mode header fields and the "answermode" option tag, letting an INVITE requester ask whether the target UA answers automatically or after user interaction, with authorization policy and security analysis.

SIP.why: The document specifies a SIP extension: new header fields, option tag, and UAC/proxy/UAS procedures for INVITE and 200 responses.
SIP.quote: This document extends SIP with two header fields and associated option tags that can be used in INVITE requests to convey the requester's preference

rejected.why: SDP is mentioned only in passing (loopback usage in another draft); the document does not specify SDP usage.
Caller identity is relied on via SIP Identity (RFC 4474) and P-Asserted-Identity, but the document does not define caller-ID authentication.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the header syntax.
Parent of SIP, already implied; push-to-talk and loopback are use cases, not a separate subject.
Authorization policy at the UAS is part of the extension's design, but the document is about SIP answering modes, and SIP already captures it.

RFC5374.title: Multicast Extensions to the Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
RFC5374.summary: Extends the IPsec security architecture (RFC 4301) to IP multicast: group security policy database, group peer authorization database, tunnel mode with address preservation, group key management interaction, and rekey rollover.

IPsec.why: The document amends RFC 4301 IPsec architecture (SPD, SAD, PAD, traffic processing) for multicast SAs.
IPsec.quote: This document describes how the IPsec security services are applied to IP multicast packets.

multicast security.why: A substantial part covers group key management interaction (GCKS, GSA, rekey rollover, GPAD) and group data origin authentication, which fits multicast security.
multicast security.quote: It also describes additional semantics for IPsec Group Key Management (GKM) subsystems.

rejected.why: Multicast routing is explicitly out of scope; the document only places requirements on IPsec endpoints, and the multicast security child covers the group aspect.
GDOI is only cited as an example GKM protocol; the document is GKM-agnostic.
Only mentioned as an example GKM protocol, not specified or extended here.
Mentioned as one option for data origin authentication, not the subject.
IKEv2 is only discussed regarding coexistence with GKM and SPI allocation.
ESP/AH are used as is; the document extends the architecture, not ESP itself.

RFC5375.title: IPv6 Unicast Address Assignment Considerations
RFC5375.summary: Informational guidance on planning IPv6 unicast address assignment (global, ULA, subnet prefix length, interface IDs), with enterprise and ISP case studies.

addressing.why: The document is about IP address architecture, allocation and planning: prefix sizing, subnetting, aggregation and IID assignment. IPv6 is the context, but the subject is address planning.
addressing.quote: This document aims to provide the information and recommendations relevant to planning the addressing aspects of IPv6 deployments.

IPv6.why: The whole document concerns IPv6 addressing and deployment, including /64 subnet requirements, ULAs, and IIDs. Readers of the IPv6 page would want it.
IPv6.quote: The Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Addressing Architecture [RFC4291] defines three main types of addresses: unicast, anycast, and multicast.

rejected.why: Renumbering is mentioned in passing and referred to RFC 4192 and another draft. It is not a main subject.
Multihoming is discussed only briefly, as a factor in prefix choice and SP POP multihoming.
Stateless autoconfiguration and EUI-64 IIDs are discussed as assignment options, but the document does not specify or analyse SLAAC itself.
DHCPv6 is only cited as one assignment method and the document says assignment methods are out of scope.
The ISP case study assumes an MPLS backbone with 6PE, but MPLS is only the backdrop for the address plan.

RFC5376.title: Inter-AS Requirements for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCECP)
RFC5376.summary: Informational RFC extending the generic PCECP requirements (RFC 4657) with requirements specific to inter-AS (G)MPLS TE path computation between PCCs and PCEs, covering requests, responses, scalability, management, confidentiality, policy and security.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies requirements for the PCE Communication Protocol in inter-AS use, including request/response content, policy and confidentiality between PCEs.
PCE.quote: This document provides a set of PCECP requirements that are specific to inter-AS (G)MPLS TE path computation.

rejected.why: MPLS TE LSPs are the thing whose paths are computed, but the document's subject is the PCE communication protocol, not MPLS itself.
Signalling is explicitly out of scope; RSVP-TE is only mentioned in references to RFC 4216 and RFC 5151.
GMPLS appears only as the type of LSP whose paths are computed; the document does not specify GMPLS.
Not discussed. The inter-AS setting concerns TE path computation, not BGP.
Management requirements mention a PCECP MIB module, but only briefly, as requirements, not a MIB definition.
Implied as the parent of PCE, so it is not listed separately.

RFC5377.title: Advice to the Trustees of the IETF Trust on Rights to Be Granted in IETF Documents
RFC5377.summary: RFC 5377 gives the IETF's advice to the IETF Trust Trustees on which outbound rights to copy, quote, implement from and reuse text and code in RFCs and other IETF Contributions should be granted to users.

IPR.why: The whole document is about copyright and licensing rights the IETF Trust grants to users of IETF documents, which is the IPR subject.
IPR.quote: This document describes the desires of the IETF regarding outbound rights to be granted in IETF Contributions.

rejected.why: It is a process-flavoured document, but its subject is rights and licensing, which IPR covers more specifically.
It concerns rights in RFCs but not their format, style or publication.
ABNF is only listed as an example of code components that may be reused.
ASN.1 is only listed as an example of code components that may be reused.

RFC5378.title: Rights Contributors Provide to the IETF Trust
RFC5378.summary: BCP 78 specifies the rights contributors grant to the IETF Trust in their IETF Contributions (copyright licenses, representations, warranties, trademarks, copyright in RFCs), obsoleting RFC 3978 and 4748.

IPR.why: The whole document defines copyright and licensing rights contributors grant to the IETF Trust, which is the IPR, copyright and trust legal provisions subject.
IPR.quote: certain limited rights must be granted to the IETF Trust, which then grants the necessary rights to the IETF

rejected.why: Document relates to the IETF process, but its subject is more specifically IPR/copyright; IPR is the more specific fit.
Addresses copyright ownership in RFCs only as part of the rights policy; not about RFC format or publication.
Definitions section is supporting apparatus for the rights policy, not a glossary document.

RFC5379.title: Guidelines for Using the Privacy Mechanism for SIP
RFC5379.summary: Informational guidelines clarifying which SIP headers and SDP parameters a privacy service should delete, anonymize or leave alone for each Privacy header priv-value defined in RFCs 3323, 3325 and 4244.

SIP.why: The whole document clarifies handling of SIP headers (Call-ID, Contact, From, Via, Record-Route, P-Asserted-Identity, etc.) per Privacy priv-value, so it is about SIP privacy deployment.
SIP.quote: provides guidelines for using the privacy mechanism for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) that is specified in RFC 3323 and subsequently extended in RFCs 3325 and 4244

rejected.why: SDP c/m/o/i/u/e/p lines are covered as privacy targets under Privacy:session, but only as a small part. The document does not specify or extend SDP.
The document is about a specific SIP privacy mechanism, not general privacy threat models. The SIP tag is the more specific fit.
Identity/Identity-Info (RFC 4474) is discussed only as a non-target header interacting with privacy services. The document does not address caller-ID authentication.
TURN is mentioned only as a way to obtain anonymous relay addresses. It is not the subject.
No presence or messaging extensions are covered.

RFC5380.title: Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 (HMIPv6) Mobility Management
RFC5380.summary: RFC 5380 specifies Hierarchical Mobile IPv6, introducing the Mobility Anchor Point (MAP), a local binding update and a Neighbour Discovery MAP option to reduce signalling and speed up handover for Mobile IPv6 nodes.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document extends Mobile IPv6 with a local home agent (MAP), a local binding update with the M flag, and MAP selection and operation.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document introduces extensions to Mobile IPv6 and IPv6 Neighbour Discovery to allow for local mobility handling.

rejected.why: The MAP option is carried in Router Advertisements, but ND is only the carrier for the new option. The document is about Mobile IPv6 mobility management.
IKEv2 is required to secure binding updates with the MAP, but it is the security mechanism the document relies on. Nothing new is defined for it.
AH and ESP protect local binding updates, but IPsec is used as a mechanism and is not the subject.
MN-MAP bi-directional tunnelling and its MTU impact are discussed, but the document is not about tunnelling in general.
The more specific Mobile IPv6 tag fits, so the parent is not listed.

RFC5381.title: Experience of Implementing NETCONF over SOAP
RFC5381.summary: Informational report on the authors' experience implementing NETCONF clients and servers over SOAP/HTTP using Apache Axis, WSDL-generated stubs and skeletons, including a cookie-based session binding that is not interoperable with RFC 4743.

NETCONF.why: The whole document is about implementing NETCONF over SOAP: client/server architecture, session maintenance, and development procedures for NETCONF clients and servers.
NETCONF.quote: This document aims to provide NETCONF development guidelines gained from the experience of implementing a SOAP-based NETCONF client and server.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport beneath SOAP; the cookie-based session mapping is a small implementation detail, not an extension of HTTP.
Cookies are used only to map requests to NETCONF sessions in the alternative binding; the document is not about HTTP state management.
XML/XSD/WSDL are the encoding and tooling substrate for the generated APIs; the document is not about XML usage in its own right.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the required transport security.
The document does not address SNMP; it is about NETCONF-based network management.

gaps.name: SOAP / Web Services (WSDL)
gaps.why: The document centres on SOAP and WSDL tooling (Apache Axis) for NETCONF, but the taxonomy has no SOAP or Web Services tag.

RFC5382.title: NAT Behavioral Requirements for TCP
RFC5382.summary: BCP defining behavioral requirements for NATs handling TCP (mapping, filtering, simultaneous-open, timeouts, ALGs, hairpinning, ICMP) so peer-to-peer applications can traverse them.

NAT.why: The whole document specifies NAT behaviour requirements (mapping, filtering, hairpinning, ALGs, session timeouts) for TCP.
NAT.quote: This document defines a set of requirements for NATs that handle TCP that would allow many applications, such as peer-to-peer applications and online games to work consistently.

TCP.why: Substantial content on TCP handshake, simultaneous-open, state machine, idle timeouts and TIME_WAIT handling as they interact with NATs, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: A NAT MUST support all valid sequences of TCP packets (defined in [RFC0793]) for connections initiated both internally as well as externally

rejected.why: ICMP handling is covered in two requirements (REQ-9, REQ-10), but the document is not about ICMP; the NAT ICMP behaviour is in a separate document.
FTP is mentioned only as an ALG exception in REQ-6; the document does not address FTP itself.
Closely related, but that taxonomy tag is for interactive real-time media (ICE/STUN/TURN). This document sets NAT behaviour requirements and does not specify traversal for real-time media.
Mentioned only as a reason to translate ICMP Destination Unreachable messages.

RFC5383.title: Deployment Considerations for Lemonade-Compliant Mobile Email
RFC5383.summary: BCP describing deployment requirements for Lemonade mobile email (IMAP and Message Submission): ports, long-lived TCP connections, idle timeouts, dormancy, firewalls and NAT behaviour.

IMAP.why: The document sets deployment requirements for lemonade IMAP clients and servers: port 143, long-lived connections, idle timers, and unsolicited notifications.
IMAP.quote: The IETF lemonade group has developed a set of extensions to IMAP and Message Submission, along with a profile document

SMTP.why: A substantial part covers Message Submission deployment: port 587 versus 25, application-level SMTP firewalls, and the submission server reaching the IMAP server.
SMTP.quote: Message Submission uses port 587.  It is REQUIRED that the client be able to contact the server on these ports.

firewall.why: Two sections cover firewall traversal, why tunnelling over HTTP is a bad idea, and firewall requirements for mobile email.
firewall.quote: Firewalls deployed in the network path MUST NOT damage protocol traffic.  In particular, both Message Submission and IMAP connections from the client MUST be permitted.

NAT.why: A dedicated section sets NAT idle-timeout requirements so that long-lived mail connections survive.
NAT.quote: Any NAT boxes that are deployed between client and server systems MUST comply with REQ-5 in [BEHAVE-TCP]

TCP.why: Substantial guidance on TCP connection lifetime, idle timeouts, keep-alives and survival during transient loss.
TCP.quote: The client system, the server, as well as all intermediate systems MUST NOT terminate these TCP connections simply because of their duration

rejected.why: The more specific IMAP and SMTP tags cover the subject, and the parent is implied.
Dormancy of cellular data channels is discussed in one short section, but the document is not about IP over 3GPP systems.
TLS and STARTTLS are only recommended in Security Considerations and mentioned as a cost of reconnecting.
ACAP is mentioned once as an example of a configuration protocol needing port 674.
HTTP and webmail appear only as a contrast and as a tunnelling kludge to avoid.
The document concerns mobile devices and TCP survival when the IP address stays the same, not Mobile IP.

gaps.name: Lemonade (mobile email profile)
gaps.why: The document is about deploying the lemonade profile of IMAP and Submission extensions for mobile email, and the taxonomy has no tag for lemonade.

RFC5384.title: The Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) Join Attribute Format
RFC5384.summary: Defines a new PIM Join message encoding (Encoded-Source Address type 1) carrying TLV Join Attributes, a PIM Hello option to signal support, and generic procedures for processing, forwarding and conflict resolution of such attributes.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends the PIM-SM Join message with a new source encoding type and Hello option, and specifies the procedures for handling the attributes. A reader of PIM-SM extensions would want it.
PIM-SM.quote: This document describes a modification of the Join message that allows a node to associate attributes with a particular tree.

rejected.why: PIM-SM is the more specific child tag and is the protocol actually extended. The parent is implied.
The IANA registries for Join Attribute types and Encoding Types are boilerplate here, and the document is not about IANA.
It is implied by the PIM-SM tag, and no broader multicast topic is addressed in its own right.
The new registries are only a small part of the document, so a topic tag is not warranted.

RFC5385.title: Version 2.0 Microsoft Word Template for Creating Internet Drafts and RFCs
RFC5385.summary: Describes a revised Microsoft Word template (.dot) and Perl post-processor for authoring Internet-Drafts and RFCs with output matching RFC Editor ASCII format, obsoleting RFC 3285.

RFC series.why: The document is a tool for authoring RFCs/Internet-Drafts in the RFC-compliant text format, including boilerplate, page layout and line/page limits. It concerns RFC format and publication tooling.
RFC series.quote: This document describes the properties and use of a revised Microsoft Word template (.dot) for writing Internet Drafts and RFCs.

rejected.why: XML is mentioned only as an alternative authoring system the template does not support; the document is about Word, not the RFC XML vocabulary.
XML is only mentioned in passing as an alternative; there is no XML usage or format specified.
Boilerplate updated per BCP 78 is only a minor part of the template; the document is not about IPR provisions.
MD5 is mentioned only in Security Considerations about signing the template files.
The template produces ASCII output, but the document is about authoring tooling, not the ASCII character set.

gaps.name: RFC authoring tools / document preparation
gaps.why: Word templates and post-processing scripts for producing RFCs are covered only by the general RFC series tag; no specific authoring-tools tag exists.

RFC5386.title: Better-Than-Nothing Security: An Unauthenticated Mode of IPsec
RFC5386.summary: Specifies how to use IKEv2 with unauthenticated public keys to set up unauthenticated IPsec SAs (BTNS), by extending the IPsec PAD and SPD with a PUBLICKEY ID type, BTNS PAD entries, and a BTNS_OK SPD flag.

IPsec.why: The document modifies the RFC 4301 IPsec processing model with new PAD entry types and an SPD flag to allow unauthenticated ESP/AH SAs. This is the core subject.
IPsec.quote: The IPsec processing model is hereby modified as follows:

IKE.why: BTNS SAs are established via IKEv2 using bare public key CERT payloads and signature AUTH methods. The document specifies how IKE peers are matched and treated without new wire elements.
IKE.quote: Here we describe how to establish unauthenticated IPsec SAs using IKEv2 [RFC4306] and unauthenticated public keys.

rejected.why: ESP is only the protection protocol used by the resulting SAs. The document specifies nothing about ESP itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to detect MITM via channel binding. It is not the subject.
Referenced only as an example of leap-of-faith behaviour.
The document concerns omitting peer authentication in IPsec, but the IPsec tag covers it more specifically.
NFSv4 appears only as an example application in the usage scenarios.

gaps.name: BTNS (Better-Than-Nothing Security) / unauthenticated IPsec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for BTNS. Other BTNS RFCs, such as the applicability statement RFC 5387 and connection latching, would benefit from a shared tag.

RFC5387.title: Problem and Applicability Statement for Better-Than-Nothing Security (BTNS)
RFC5387.summary: Informational problem and applicability statement for BTNS, which extends IPsec to allow unauthenticated SAs (Stand-Alone and Channel-Bound modes), explaining the motivation, applicable uses, and risks.

IPsec.why: The whole document motivates and scopes an unauthenticated mode of IPsec, covering changes to the PAD/SPD and security services.
IPsec.quote: explains the rationale for extending the Internet network security protocol suite to enable use of IPsec security services without authentication

IKE.why: A large part of the problem statement concerns IKE's authentication requirements and anonymous keying. IKE peer authentication is the thing BTNS relaxes.
IKE.quote: IKE further requires message exchanges that incur round-trip latency to setup security associations.

rejected.why: TCP spoofing and RST injection motivate BTNS, but the document is not about TCP itself.
BGP sessions are cited only as a motivating example, and the document says the routing community chose other solutions.
Authentication is central, but the IPsec and IKE tags cover it more specifically.
SSH's leap-of-faith model is compared in one subsection of the security considerations, but the document is not about SSH.
GSS-API is mentioned only as an existing channel binding mechanism.
KINK is mentioned only as a related effort in Section 6.

gaps.name: Channel binding / connection latching
gaps.why: Channel binding for IPsec channels is a significant theme, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

gaps.name: BTNS (Better-Than-Nothing Security)
gaps.why: There is no tag for BTNS itself, the unauthenticated IPsec mode that this document is about.

RFC5388.title: Information Model and XML Data Model for Traceroute Measurements
RFC5388.summary: Defines an information model and an XML schema for storing and exchanging the configuration and results of traceroute measurements, aligned with DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB and including a comparison of tool implementations.

traceroute.why: The whole document standardizes how traceroute measurement configuration and results are represented, so readers of the traceroute subject would expect it.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute is a network diagnostic tool used to determine the hop-by-hop path from a source to a destination and the Round Trip Time (RTT)
traceroute.section: 3. The Traceroute Tool and Its Operations

performance measurement.why: It is an IPPM work item about storing active measurement results (RTT, hop paths) and comparing them, and it discusses compatibility with IPPM metrics.
performance measurement.quote: The standard metrics defined by the IPPM group in matters of delay, connectivity, and losses do not apply to the metrics returned by the traceroute tool.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document is an XML schema and XML data model, with examples, for the measurement data.
XML.quote: On the basis of the information model, a data model based on XML is defined to store the results of traceroute measurements.

rejected.why: The document contrasts itself with DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB (RFC 4560) in an appendix but defines an XML format, not a MIB module.
IPFIX is discussed only as a rejected alternative data-model option.
ICMP TIME_EXCEEDED is the mechanism traceroute relies on, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
The MPLS label stack entry is just one reported field per probe, so MPLS is not a subject of the document.
The data model is XML Schema, not YANG.
RFC 3339 timestamps are used as a dependency only.

gaps.name: traceroute
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists 'traceroute' under network management, but the id I intended may not match exactly. The tag id is 'traceroute' as in the taxonomy, so no gap exists for it.

RFC5389.title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC5389.summary: RFC 5389 specifies STUN, a protocol and tool for NAT traversal that lets endpoints discover their reflexive transport addresses and keep NAT bindings alive. It defines the message format, Binding method, authentication mechanisms, DNS discovery and attributes, and obsoletes RFC 3489.

STUN.why: The document is the core STUN specification: message structure, Binding method, mechanisms, attributes and registries.
STUN.quote: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) is a protocol that serves as a tool for other protocols in dealing with Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal.

rejected.why: ICE is described only as one STUN usage defined elsewhere; this document does not specify it.
TURN is only referenced as an extension of STUN defined in another document.
STUN is the tool; NAT behaviour itself is not the subject, and the STUN tag is more specific. Not tagged separately.
Section 9 uses SRV records for server discovery, but this is a use of DNS, not new DNS work.
TLS is only a transport option for STUN; nothing new is defined about TLS.
HMAC-SHA1 is used as a mechanism for MESSAGE-INTEGRITY but is not the subject of the document.
SIP Outbound is mentioned as a usage and SIP is referenced for error codes and realm grammar, but the document does not address SIP itself.

RFC5390.title: Requirements for Management of Overload in the Session Initiation Protocol
RFC5390.summary: Informational RFC describing problems with SIP's 503-based overload handling (load amplification, underutilization, off/on Retry-After, ambiguous usage) and listing 23 requirements for a SIP overload control mechanism.

SIP.why: The whole document analyses SIP's 503 overload mechanism and sets requirements for a SIP overload control solution, so it belongs on the SIP page.
SIP.quote: Overload occurs in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [RFC3261] networks when proxies and user agents have insufficient resources to complete the processing of a request

rejected.why: The document is about application-layer overload control in SIP servers. It is not about transport congestion control.
DoS attacks are only one listed cause of overload and one requirement. The document is not about DDoS mitigation.
DNS SRV records and DNS servers are mentioned only as examples of dependencies and scope. The document says nothing about DNS itself.
RFC 3398 ISUP-to-SIP mapping is cited only as an example of ambiguous 503 usage.
The security-related requirements concern an overload mechanism not being an attack avenue. This is not operational security practice.

gaps.name: SIP overload control
gaps.why: The document is about SIP overload control and its requirements. The taxonomy has no overload-control tag, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5391.title: RTP Payload Format for ITU-T Recommendation G.711.1
RFC5391.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for the ITU-T G.711.1 embedded wideband audio codec, including payload header, frame packing, the audio/PCMA-WB and audio/PCMU-WB media type registrations, and SDP offer/answer mapping.

G.711.why: The document exists to define the RTP payload format for G.711.1, an extension of G.711, which the G.711 tag covers (extensions and payload formats).
G.711.quote: This document specifies a payload format for packetization of G.711.1 encoded audio signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

RTP payload format.why: This is an RTP payload format for a specific codec, covering header usage, payload header and frame packing.
RTP payload format.quote: The complete payload consists of a payload header of 1 octet, followed by one or more consecutive G.711.1 audio frames of the same mode.

media types.why: A substantial part of the document registers two media types with their parameters.
media types.quote: two media types with the same parameters will be defined: audio/PCMA-WB for A-law core, and audio/PCMU-WB for mu-law core.

SDP.why: Defines the SDP mapping and offer/answer rules for the new payload format, with examples.
SDP.quote: The parameter "mode-set" goes in the SDP "a=fmtp" attribute by copying it as a "mode-set=<value>" string.

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the more specific RTP payload format tag fits and implies RTP.
The more specific G.711 tag applies; the codec itself is defined by ITU-T, not this document.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as an optional external mechanism.
Section 7 is brief and defers to RFC 3550/3551; not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC5392.title: OSPF Extensions in Support of Inter-Autonomous System (AS) MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC5392.summary: Defines OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 TE extensions (new Inter-AS-TE LSAs and three Link TLV sub-TLVs) to flood inter-AS TE link information for MPLS/GMPLS inter-AS path computation.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 with new Opaque LSA and sub-TLVs for inter-AS TE links.
OSPF.quote: This document describes extensions to the OSPF version 2 and 3 protocols to support Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Traffic Engineering (TE)

OSPFv3.why: Defines the Inter-AS-TE-v3 LSA for OSPFv3, a substantial part of the specification.
OSPFv3.quote: a new LS type is defined for OSPFv3 inter-AS TE link advertisement. The new LS type function code is 13

traffic engineering.why: The purpose is inter-AS MPLS/GMPLS TE path computation, so TE readers would want it.
traffic engineering.quote: OSPF-TE v2 and v3 extensions are defined for the flooding of TE information about inter-AS links that can be used to perform inter-AS TE path computation.

rejected.why: PCE and BRPC motivate the problem, but the document explicitly makes no change to PCE architecture or usage.
BGP is mentioned only as a possible source of configuration and for consistency checking.
GMPLS is named in the scope, but the document only references RFC 4203 and adds no GMPLS-specific mechanism.
MPLS TE LSPs are the context for the extensions, but the document does not specify MPLS behavior.
The RSVP-TE Path message and ERO appear only in the problem statement.

RFC5393.title: Addressing an Amplification Vulnerability in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Forking Proxies
RFC5393.summary: Updates RFC 3261 to require loop detection in forking SIP proxies, corrects the loop-detection algorithm, and defines the Max-Breadth header field and 440 response to limit concurrent forked branches and counter an amplification attack.

SIP.why: The document amends SIP proxy forking and loop-detection behavior and defines a new SIP header field (Max-Breadth) and response code (440).
SIP.quote: This document normatively updates RFC 3261, the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), to address a security vulnerability identified in SIP proxy behavior.

rejected.why: It describes an amplification attack on SIP proxies and mitigations built into the protocol. It is not about general DDoS mitigation or signalling.
The Security Considerations give operator advice, but the main body is a protocol fix specific to SIP.
ABNF is only used to write the Max-Breadth grammar.
It is mentioned only as one acceptable hash for the branch parameter's second part, not as a subject of the document.
It is cited only for the CRC-32c function.

RFC5394.title: Policy-Enabled Path Computation Framework
RFC5394.summary: Informational framework describing how policy (via the Policy Core Information Model, PDP/PEP components) can be applied at PCCs and PCEs in the PCE architecture, with scenarios, requirements, configurations and event sequences.

PCE.why: The whole document extends the PCE architecture with policy: PCC/PCE policy components, requests and responses, cooperating PCEs, and PCEP carrying policy information.
PCE.quote: The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture introduces the concept of policy in the context of path computation.

policy management.why: The framework is built on policy-based management, using PCIM, policy repositories, PDPs and PEPs, and policy information models for path computation. Readers of the policy-based management subject would want it.
policy management.quote: Policy-based Management (PBM), see [RFC3198], is a network management approach that enables a network to automatically perform actions in response to network events

rejected.why: COPS is only cited for the PEP/PDP terminology, and the document explicitly says it does not assume or require the COPS protocol.
RSVP-TE is the signalling context for the LSPs being computed, but the document is not about the protocol itself.
GMPLS LSRs appear as example PCCs, but the document does not specify or extend GMPLS.
The document is about path computation policy in a TE setting. The PCE tag under traffic engineering already covers that, so the parent is implied.
LDAPv3 is mentioned only as one possible access protocol to policy repositories.
BEEP is named only as one possible protocol between PDP and PEP.

gaps.name: Policy-based management / Policy Core Information Model (PCIM)
gaps.why: The document is largely about applying PCIM and the PDP/PEP policy framework. The taxonomy's policy management topic is missing from the supplied taxonomy, so no tag fits.

RFC5395.title: Domain Name System (DNS) IANA Considerations
RFC5395.summary: BCP 42 specifying IANA allocation policies for DNS parameters: RR types, CLASSes, OpCodes, RCODEs, header bits and AFSDB subtypes, obsoleting RFC 2929.

DNS.why: The whole document defines registry policies for DNS protocol parameters (RRTYPEs, CLASSes, OpCodes, RCODEs, header bits), so DNS readers need it.
DNS.quote: IANA parameter assignment considerations are specified for the allocation of Domain Name System (DNS) resource record types, CLASSes, operation codes, error codes

IANA.why: It defines allocation policies, such as Expert Review and IETF Review, and the RRTYPE template process for the DNS Parameters registry, which is IANA registry guidance.
IANA.quote: New OpCode assignments require an IETF Standards Action as modified by [RFC4020].

rejected.why: The OPT RR is mentioned only for its RCODE extension and defers to RFC 2671; the document does not specify EDNS.
Security Considerations only points to the DNSSEC RFCs; the document is not about DNSSEC.
The AFSDB subtype registry is covered, but the document is about the registry policy, not AFS.

RFC5396.title: Textual Representation of Autonomous System (AS) Numbers
RFC5396.summary: Defines "asplain" (decimal) as the single standard textual representation for Autonomous System numbers, and describes the asplain, asdot+ and asdot formats.

routing.why: AS numbers are the identifiers of inter-domain routing, and the document sets a cross-protocol convention for writing them in documents, configuration and tools. It is not tied to one routing protocol, so the general routing topic fits best.
routing.quote: A textual representation for Autonomous System (AS) numbers is defined as the decimal value of the AS number.

rejected.why: AS numbers are used in BGP, but the document does not specify, extend or analyse BGP. It only defines a notation for the numbers.
Only a one-line IANA Considerations section says registries should use asplain. That is boilerplate and not the main subject.
The notation is a textual syntax for an integer. That is too minor to count as a data format subject.

gaps.name: Autonomous System numbers (AS number notation)
gaps.why: The document is about AS number representation specifically. The taxonomy has no tag for AS numbers or inter-domain identifiers, so the general routing topic is the closest fit.

RFC5397.title: WebDAV Current Principal Extension
RFC5397.summary: Defines the DAV:current-user-principal WebDAV property, an extension to WebDAV ACL that lets a client discover the principal resource URL for the currently authenticated user.

WebDAV.why: The document defines a new WebDAV property as an extension to WebDAV ACL (RFC 3744), so it belongs on the WebDAV page.
WebDAV.quote: This specification defines a new WebDAV property that allows clients to quickly determine the principal corresponding to the current authenticated user.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate that WebDAV extends. The document adds nothing new to HTTP itself.
The property value is expressed in XML, but XML is only the encoding. The document does not address XML usage.
WebDAV ACL principals are involved, but the document only defines a property for locating the principal. It does not address access control itself.
CalDAV is mentioned only in the acknowledgments. The document is not about calendar access.

RFC5398.title: Autonomous System (AS) Number Reservation for Documentation Use
RFC5398.summary: Informational RFC reserving two blocks of 16 AS numbers (64496-64511 and 65536-65551) for use in documentation examples, with IANA registry reservations.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is a reservation in the IANA AS Number Registry; readers of IANA registry guidance would look for it.
IANA.quote: IANA has reserved a contiguous block of 16 Autonomous System numbers from the unallocated number range within the "16-bit" number set for documentation purposes

routing.why: AS numbers are routing identifiers, and the reservation has operational routing implications. No more specific routing tag fits, since the document does not specify BGP itself.
routing.quote: BGP operational configurations should not peer with neighboring ASes that are numbered from this reserved AS number set.

rejected.why: BGP is only mentioned in passing for peering guidance; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
It concerns AS numbers, not IP address architecture. IP address documentation reservations are only cited as analogies.
RFC 2606 is only referenced as a similar precedent.

gaps.name: Autonomous System numbers / documentation reservations
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers AS number assignment or special-purpose number reservations for documentation use.

RFC5401.title: Multicast Negative-Acknowledgment (NACK) Building Blocks
RFC5401.summary: Standards-track framework describing building blocks for NACK-based reliable multicast protocols (sender transmission, NACK repair with timer-based suppression, GRTT round-trip timing), obsoleting the experimental RFC 3941.

NORM.why: Better quote: the document is the NACK-oriented reliable multicast building blocks (NORM-derived), defining sender transmission, NACK repair process and RTT collection used by NORM-style protocols.
NORM.quote: NACK-based reliable multicast protocols are expected to be subject to the same security vulnerabilities

reliable multicast.why: The whole document is a framework for reliable multicast transport design.
reliable multicast.quote: This document addresses the creation of reliable multicast protocols that utilize negative-acknowledgment (NACK) feedback.

rejected.why: FEC is used by the repair process but the details are in the separate FEC Building Block (RFC 5052); here it is a dependency, not the subject.
PGM is only mentioned in the applicability comparison, not specified.
Congestion control is a required external input; the document only points to TFMCC/PGMCC.
Security considerations mention IPsec/GSAKMP, which is boilerplate-level here.
SSM is mentioned as a deployment model, not addressed in its own right.

gaps.name: NACK-oriented reliable multicast building blocks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the NORM tech tag only as a leaf under reliable multicast, but the tags I chose must exist in the taxonomy; the document's subject fits reliable multicast with NORM as its main instantiation.

RFC5402.title: Compressed Data within an Internet Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) Message
RFC5402.summary: Specifies how to apply CMS compressed-data (RFC 3274, zlib) as a layer within EDIINT AS1/AS2/AS3 MIME messages, including layering with signing/encryption, MIC calculation, error disposition and version header.

EDI.why: The document extends EDIINT AS1/AS2/AS3 messages with a compression layer, defining MIC calculation, error disposition and version header changes.
EDI.quote: explains the rules and procedures for utilizing compression (RFC 3274) within an Internet EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) 'AS' message

compression.why: Applying lossless compression to business payloads is a core part of the document. Compression is its main purpose, though it uses existing formats rather than defining new ones.
compression.quote: The MIME entity will be compressed using [ZLIB] and placed inside a CMS compressed-data object

S/MIME.why: Much of the document defines how the CMS compressed-data type is layered with S/MIME signed and encrypted parts (Section 3).
S/MIME.quote: The compressed-data object will be MIME encapsulated according to details outlined in [S/MIME3.1], RFC 3851, Section 3.5.

rejected.why: The document uses the CMS compressed-data content type from RFC 3274 but does not define or extend CMS. S/MIME packaging fits better.
MIME is the message substrate. The document defines layering for EDI messages, not new MIME structure.
DEFLATE and zlib are only mandated as the compression format and are not specified here.
AS2 runs over HTTP, but the document does not address HTTP.
AS3 runs over FTP, but the document does not address FTP.

RFC5403.title: RPCSEC_GSS Version 2
RFC5403.summary: RFC 5403 defines RPCSEC_GSS version 2, which extends the RPCSEC_GSS protocol for ONC RPC with channel bindings support (a new BIND_CHANNEL procedure and channel-protection service) on top of GSS-API.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies RPCSEC_GSS v2, a protocol that carries GSS-API tokens and adds channel binding using GSS MICs. Readers of GSS-API would want it.
GSS-API.quote: RPCSEC_GSS allows remote procedure call (RPC) protocols to access the Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface (GSS-API).

ONC RPC.why: It extends the security flavor for ONC RPC, with new RPC credential, procedure, verifier and XDR definitions.
ONC RPC.quote: RPCSEC_GSSv2 and RPCSEC_GSSv1 are protocols that exchange tokens emitted by the Generic Security Services (GSS) framework

rejected.why: IPsec is mentioned only as an example of a lower-layer channel; the document does not specify or extend it.
The document does involve mutual authentication, but the GSS-API and ONC RPC tags cover it more specifically.
The working group is nfsv4, but the text does not mention NFS and defines nothing NFS-specific.

gaps.name: channel bindings
gaps.why: The document is about using channel bindings (RFC 5056) to tie upper-layer authentication to a secure channel. The taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC5404.title: RTP Payload Format for G.719
RFC5404.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for the ITU-T G.719 full-band audio codec, including multi-channel, multi-frame, redundancy and interleaving support, plus the audio/G719 media type and SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines an RTP payload format for a specific codec: ToC structure, basic and interleaved modes, and header usage.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of the G.719 full-band (FB) codec encoded audio signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document defines the SDP mapping and the offer/answer rules for the G.719 parameters (interleaving, int-delay, max-red, CBR).
SDP.quote: The media subtype (payload format name) goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name.

media types.why: The document registers the audio/G719 media type with its parameters in the IETF tree.
media types.quote: This RTP payload format is identified using the media type audio/ G719, which is registered in accordance with [RFC4855]

rejected.why: G.719 is the codec being packetized, but the document specifies the payload format, not the codec. The codec's own entry is the more specific RTP payload format tag.
RTP is the transport the payload format plugs into. The more specific RTP payload format tag covers the document.
Redundant transmission of G.719 frames is a feature of the payload format, but the document does not specify a general FEC scheme.
SRTP is only recommended in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
Section 9 discusses the congestion implications of the payload format, but only briefly.
G.719 is a different ITU-T codec from G.722, so that tag does not apply.

gaps.name: G.719 full-band audio codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the G.719 codec itself. Readers browsing for it would be directed to the generic codecs or RTP payload format pages.

RFC5405.title: Unicast UDP Usage Guidelines for Application Designers
RFC5405.summary: BCP giving application designers guidelines for using unicast UDP, focused on congestion control and also covering message size, reliability, checksums/UDP-Lite, middlebox traversal, sockets programming and ICMP.

UDP.why: The whole document is usage guidance for UDP, which is exactly the subject of the UDP tag.
UDP.quote: This document provides guidelines on the use of UDP for the designers of unicast applications and upper-layer protocols.

UDP-Lite.why: A dedicated subsection gives guidance on when and how to use UDP-Lite and its checksum coverage.
UDP-Lite.quote: Applications that choose to use UDP-Lite instead of UDP should still follow the congestion control and other guidelines described for use with UDP in Section 3.

congestion control.why: Congestion control is stated to be the primary focus, with guidelines for bulk, low-volume and tunnel traffic.
congestion control.quote: applications and upper-layer protocols that choose to use UDP as an Internet transport must employ mechanisms to prevent congestion collapse

rejected.why: Mentioned as the recommended alternative and as a comparison point, not specified or profiled here.
Recommended for bulk UDP transfers, but it is only referenced and not defined or extended here.
Middlebox traversal is covered in one section, but the document is not about NAT behaviour itself.
Applications are advised to use path MTU discovery, but the mechanism is only referenced.
Listed as one security option in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-like and not the subject.
The UDP checksum is covered in a subsection, but it is part of UDP usage and not the Internet checksum as a subject.

RFC5406.title: Guidelines for Specifying the Use of IPsec Version 2
RFC5406.summary: BCP giving protocol designers guidance on when and how to specify the use of IPsec version 2 (AH/ESP/IKEv1) in their specifications, covering availability, selectors/SPD, key management, and a BGP worked example.

IPsec.why: The whole document analyses IPsec architecture (AH, ESP, modes, SPD selectors, key management) and how to specify its use in protocol documents.
IPsec.quote: This memo offers some guidance on when IPsec Version 2 should and should not be specified.

rejected.why: IKEv1 key management is discussed as one piece of IPsec, but only as part of the specification checklist, not as a subject in its own right.
ESP is covered as one of the pieces of IPsec, not specified or extended; the IPsec tag covers it.
BGP is used only as a worked example of evaluating IPsec; the document is not about BGP.
Only mentioned briefly as an alternative key management mechanism.
NAT problems with IPsec are mentioned in passing, not a substantial subject.

RFC5407.title: Example Call Flows of Race Conditions in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5407.summary: A BCP giving example SIP call flows and a dialog state machine showing how user agents should handle race conditions (crossing CANCEL, BYE, re-INVITE, UPDATE, REFER, ACK) around INVITE dialog establishment and termination.

SIP.why: The whole document specifies best-practice SIP UA and dialog behavior in race conditions, with detailed SIP call flows.
SIP.quote: This document clarifies SIP User Agent (UA) behaviors when messages cross each other as race conditions.

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer appears in message details and in the offer/answer collision cases, but it is used as payload and is not the document's subject.
RTP media paths appear only in the flow diagrams as context.
REFER and the subscription usage are mentioned only in one race example, not as SIP event/presence work.

RFC5408.title: Identity-Based Encryption Architecture and Supporting Data Structures
RFC5408.summary: RFC 5408 describes the identity-based encryption (IBE) architecture, with its Public Parameter Server and Private-key Generator, and defines ASN.1/XML data structures, a public-parameter lookup method, a private key request protocol, and three media types.

key management.why: The document defines the architecture and protocols for distributing IBE public parameters and for provisioning private keys from a PKG, which is key provisioning. No more specific child tag fits.
key management.quote: A Private-key Generator (PKG).  The PKG stores and uses cryptographic material, known as a master secret, which is used for generating a user's IBE private key.

cryptography.why: The document is about IBE, a public-key encryption technology. It specifies how IBE algorithms (Boneh-Franklin, Boneh-Boyen) are parameterised and used, though the algorithms themselves are in RFC 5091. No narrower cryptography tag covers IBE.
cryptography.quote: identity-based encryption, a public-key encryption technology that uses a user's identity as a public key.

media types.why: The document defines and registers three new media types, each with a full template in Sections 4.3, 5.4 and 5.7. These are a substantial part of the content.
media types.quote: IANA has registered three media types in the standard registration tree.  These are application/ibe-pp-data, application/ibe-key-request+xml, and application/ibe-pkg-reply+xml.

rejected.why: TLS 1.2 is only the secure transport the protocols rely on. The document defines no new TLS extension.
HTTP GET and POST carry the requests, but HTTP itself is not extended or specified here.
ASN.1 is the notation used to define the structures, not the subject.
XML is used only for the request and response encoding.
CMS use with IBE is defined in the companion RFC 5409. Here it is only referenced.
Basic and Digest authentication are mandated for PKG clients, but that is a minor requirement and not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Identity-based encryption (IBE)
gaps.why: The document is about IBE and its PPS/PKG architecture. The taxonomy has no IBE tag, so only the generic cryptography and key management tags apply.

RFC5409.title: Using the Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen Identity-Based Encryption Algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC5409.summary: Defines how to use the Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen identity-based encryption algorithms in CMS EnvelopedData to encrypt content-encryption keys, including OIDs, the recipient identity encoding (email address plus not-before time), and sender/receiver processing.

CMS.why: The document specifies a new key-encryption convention for CMS EnvelopedData using OtherRecipientInfo, with OIDs and sender/receiver processing. Readers of CMS would want it.
CMS.quote: This document defines the way to use the Boneh-Franklin [IBCS] and Boneh-Boyen [IBCS] identity-based encryption (IBE) public-key algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

rejected.why: TLS only protects communications with the PPS and PKG. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
