ASN.1 is only the notation for the module and the OIDs, not the subject.
The work came from the smime WG, but the text only addresses CMS and does not mention S/MIME message handling.
PKIX is cited only for the rfc822Name encoding. The document is not about certificates.
The document concerns CEK encryption in CMS. Private-key retrieval is defined in RFC 5408, not here.

gaps.name: Identity-based encryption (IBE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for identity-based cryptography. Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen IBE is the core subject, and readers browsing it would want this RFC alongside RFC 5091 and RFC 5408.

RFC5410.title: Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) General Extension Payload for Open Mobile Alliance BCAST 1.0
RFC5410.summary: Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 4909 and defines MIKEY General Extension payload Type 5 with subtypes (LTKM, STKM, LTKM Reporting, Parental Control) to carry OMA BCAST Service and Content Protection messages.

MIKEY.why: The document extends MIKEY by defining a new General Extension payload type and subtype registry values for OMA BCAST key messages, so readers of MIKEY would want it.
MIKEY.quote: This document specifies the use of the General Extension payload of MIKEY to carry the messages mentioned above

rejected.why: MIKEY is the more specific child tag under key management, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The IANA actions (type 5 and subtypes 3 and 4) are boilerplate-like registrations that support the MIKEY extension. The document is not about IANA guidance.
The document mentions broadcast/MBMS transport, but it defines only a payload container and does not address group key management.
3GPP MBMS is only cited as context. The document does not address IP over cellular networks.

RFC5411.title: A Hitchhiker's Guide to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5411.summary: An informational guide to the SIP RFC series that lists, summarizes and groups the specifications under the SIP umbrella (core, PSTN interworking, NAT traversal, events, QoS, security, conferencing, IM/presence, emergency services).

SIP.why: The whole document catalogs and summarizes SIP specifications and extensions, so SIP is its central subject.
SIP.quote: This specification serves as a guide to the SIP RFC series. It lists a current snapshot of the specifications under the SIP umbrella

PSTN interop.why: A dedicated section covers PSTN interworking specs (PINT, SPIRITS, SIP-T, ISUP mapping, QSIG). The section is a substantial part of the guide.
PSTN interop.quote: Numerous extensions and usages of SIP are related to interoperability and communications with or through the PSTN.

SIMPLE.why: The guide has sections on event framework, event packages, and IM/presence, which fall under SIMPLE-related SIP extensions.
SIMPLE.quote: SIP extensions related to IM, presence, and multimedia.

NAT traversal.why: A dedicated section covers ICE, outbound, rport, and GRUU for NAT traversal.
NAT traversal.quote: These SIP extensions are primarily aimed at addressing NAT traversal for SIP.

rejected.why: SDP and its extensions are listed as part of the SIP specification set, but the document is a guide to SIP, not about SDP itself.
Only a short section lists two SigComp-related RFCs; not substantial enough.
A short section lists three extensions (Resource-Priority, location conveyance); minor part of the guide.
A section lists conferencing extensions, but it is a small catalog part, not the document's focus.
ICE is only one entry among many in the listing; the document does not specify or analyse it.
SRTP keying is mentioned in a few entries only; not a substantial subject of the guide.

RFC5412.title: Lightweight Access Point Protocol
RFC5412.summary: Historic RFC specifying LWAPP, the protocol by which a wireless Access Controller manages lightweight Wireless Termination Points, with L2/UDP transports, discovery/join/config, AES-CCM control security, and an IEEE 802.11 binding; precursor to CAPWAP.

CAPWAP.why: The whole document specifies LWAPP, the AC-WTP control and provisioning protocol that is the basis for CAPWAP; readers of the CAPWAP subject would want it.
CAPWAP.quote: This specification defines the Lightweight Access Point Protocol (LWAPP), which addresses the CAPWAP's (Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points) protocol requirements.

WiFi.why: Section 11 gives a substantial IEEE 802.11 binding (split/local MAC, WLAN config, radio message elements), so Wi-Fi readers would want it.
WiFi.quote: this specific document describes the base protocol and an extension that allows it to be used with the IEEE's 802.11 wireless LAN protocol.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an optional means of end-to-end protection of user data; not specified here.
Certificates are used for join authentication, but the document only profiles usage lightly (NetscapeComment) and is not about X.509.
AES-CCM and AES-CMAC are used as mechanisms for control-channel security, not the subject.
UDP is just a transport substrate for LWAPP.
The key exchange is internal to LWAPP security rather than a standalone key-management subject.
A short NAT considerations section only; the document is not about NAT.

RFC5413.title: SLAPP: Secure Light Access Point Protocol
RFC5413.summary: SLAPP is a historic independent-stream protocol for discovery, DTLS-secured association, and control negotiation between wireless Access Controllers and Wireless Termination Points, including an 802.11 control protocol and an image download protocol; it was a basis for CAPWAP.

CAPWAP.why: SLAPP is a proposed solution to the CAPWAP problem, defining AC/WTP discovery, security association and 802.11 control and provisioning.
CAPWAP.quote: The Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) problem statement describes a problem that needs to be addressed

rejected.why: DTLS is only the security substrate for the SLAPP channel; nothing new is defined about DTLS itself.
The 802.11 control protocol is about configuring WTPs, which CAPWAP covers more specifically; the document is not about IP over 802.11 itself.
GRE is only used to tunnel frames between WTP and AC; no new GRE behaviour is specified.
DHCP option 43 is mentioned only as one way for a WTP to discover an AC.
DNS lookups are mentioned only as a discovery method, not specified or extended.
The document leans on TLS cipher suites for authentication but defines nothing new about TLS.

RFC5414.title: Wireless LAN Control Protocol (WiCoP)
RFC5414.summary: RFC 5414 specifies WiCoP, a historic WLAN control and provisioning protocol between access controllers and wireless termination points, submitted as input to the CAPWAP working group and since obsoleted by RFC 5415.

CAPWAP.why: WiCoP is a competing/precursor protocol for Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points, designed to realize the CAPWAP objectives. It defines the AC-WTP control and data packets, messages and state machine.
CAPWAP.quote: The Wireless LAN Control Protocol (WiCoP) described in this document allows for the control and provisioning of large-scale WLANs.

rejected.why: The document uses IEEE 802.11 as its main use case, but it is about a control protocol (CAPWAP family) rather than IP over 802.11 itself; CAPWAP is the more specific fit.
Connection state mentions initiating an IPsec security association, but the security mechanism is explicitly out of scope; it is only a substrate.
EAP frames are carried in message elements for key configuration, but the document does not specify EAP.
TFTP is only used to carry firmware data in a message element; the document does not specify TFTP.
OID message element and MIB-style syntax types are borrowed, but the document is not about SNMP.

gaps.name: WiCoP / CAPWAP (Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points)
gaps.why: I used the CAPWAP tag id above, but it does not appear in the taxonomy. The closest available id is CAPWAP under link layer, which the taxonomy does list, so no gap remains on that point; no other subject lacks a tag.

RFC5415.title: Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocol Specification
RFC5415.summary: RFC 5415 specifies the base CAPWAP protocol by which an Access Controller discovers, configures, secures with DTLS, and manages Wireless Termination Points, including state machine, packet formats, message elements and firmware management.

CAPWAP.why: The document is the base CAPWAP protocol specification.
CAPWAP.quote: This specification defines the Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocol, meeting the objectives defined by the CAPWAP Working Group in RFC 4564.

DTLS.why: Substantial sections define the CAPWAP/DTLS interface, handshake processing, cipher suites, and certificate/PSK authorization, which DTLS readers would want.
DTLS.quote: CAPWAP Control messages, and optionally CAPWAP Data messages, are secured using Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)

UDP-Lite.why: Specifies UDP-Lite as the default data channel transport over IPv6 with checksum coverage rules and a transport-selection message element.
UDP-Lite.quote: The CAPWAP protocol supports both UDP and UDP-Lite [RFC3828] transport protocols.

rejected.why: The IEEE 802.11 binding is defined in a separate RFC (5416); this base protocol is technology-independent.
NAT Considerations section covers middlebox detection but the document is not about NAT behaviour itself.
MTU discovery is used via existing RFCs; no new PMTUD mechanism defined.
EKU values for AC/WTP are defined, but only as a small part of DTLS authorization.
ECN support is a minor message element, not a main subject.
Firmware download is a CAPWAP operation, not the IoT firmware update architecture.

RFC5416.title: Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocol Binding for IEEE 802.11
RFC5416.summary: Defines the CAPWAP binding for IEEE 802.11, specifying Split/Local MAC operation, 802.11-specific control messages, message elements, QoS tagging, and key handling between WTPs and Access Controllers.

CAPWAP.why: The document is the 802.11 binding of CAPWAP, defining message types, message elements and WTP/AC behaviour.
CAPWAP.quote: This specification defines the Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocol Binding Specification for use with the IEEE 802.11 Wireless Local Area Network protocol.

WiFi.why: The whole document concerns managing IEEE 802.11 WLANs: BSSIDs, radios, beacons, RSNA keys, roaming and 802.11 QoS.
WiFi.quote: This section describes use of the CAPWAP protocol with the IEEE 802.11 Wireless Local Area Network protocol, including Local and Split MAC operation

rejected.why: 802.1X/EAP is only located on the AC and forwarded by the WTP. The document does not specify it.
DSCP marking rules for tunnelled and inner packets are a small part of the QoS section. They are not the document's subject.
802.11 QoS tagging is one subsection, and the tag would be secondary at best.
The IANA registries are boilerplate here and are not the main body.
AES-CCMP is mentioned only as a cipher the WTP can advertise or use.

RFC5417.title: Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Access Controller DHCP Option
RFC5417.summary: Defines DHCPv4 (option 138) and DHCPv6 (option 52) options that carry an ordered list of CAPWAP Access Controller addresses so a Wireless Termination Point can discover its AC.

CAPWAP.why: The document is a CAPWAP companion specification defining how a WTP discovers ACs, so CAPWAP readers need it.
CAPWAP.quote: allows a Wireless Termination Point to use DHCP to discover the Access Controllers to which it is to connect

DHCP.why: It specifies a new DHCPv4 option, including its format, client request behaviour and server behaviour.
DHCP.quote: This section defines a DHCPv4 option that carries a list of 32-bit (binary) IPv4 addresses indicating one or more CAPWAP ACs

DHCPv6.why: It specifies a new DHCPv6 option with its format and usage. It is a child of DHCP, but the document is specifically about the DHCPv6 option too.
DHCPv6.quote: This section defines a DHCPv6 option that carries a list of 128-bit (binary) IPv6 addresses indicating one or more CAPWAP ACs

rejected.why: DTLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the mechanism CAPWAP uses to authenticate peers. The document is not about it.
IPv6 addresses are only the payload of the DHCPv6 option. The document does not address IPv6 itself.
AC discovery is the purpose, but the document is specific to a DHCP option and CAPWAP. The CAPWAP and DHCP tags cover it.

RFC5418.title: Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Threat Analysis for IEEE 802.11 Deployments
RFC5418.summary: Informational threat analysis of the security exposure created by splitting a WLAN access point into WTP and AC with CAPWAP in IEEE 802.11 deployments, covering adversary capabilities, goals, countermeasures, and what DTLS does and does not address.

CAPWAP.why: The whole document is a threat analysis of the CAPWAP protocol and its IEEE 802.11 binding, so readers of the CAPWAP subject would want it.
CAPWAP.quote: This document analyzes the security exposure resulting from the introduction of CAPWAP and summarizes the associated security considerations for IEEE 802.11-based CAPWAP implementations and deployments.

rejected.why: DTLS is the proposed security mechanism, and Section 11 lists what it provides and what it does not. The document defines nothing new about DTLS itself, so it is only the substrate.
RADIUS, Diameter and EAP appear only as background (Section 4), and the document says it does not analyse AAA security. Tagging them would overstate their role.
EAP appears only in the trust-relationship background (Section 4). The document does not analyse or extend it.
This is a general threat-analysis topic, but the document is specific to CAPWAP, so the technology tag is the better fit.
X.509 certificate fields (CN, EKU) are discussed briefly as authorization checks, but only as a small part of the countermeasures discussion.

RFC5419.title: Why the Authentication Data Suboption is Needed for Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6)
RFC5419.summary: Informational RFC justifying why the Mobile IPv6 authentication option (RFC 4285) is needed as an alternative to IPsec for MN-HA signaling, mainly for CDMA2000 and WiMAX deployments with AAA backends.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document justifies an authentication mechanism for MIPv6 binding signaling between MN and HA, and discusses its limitations, deployment and route optimization.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Mobile IPv6 relies on the IPsec Security Association between the Mobile Node (MN) and the Home Agent (HA) for authentication of the MN to its HA

cdma2000.why: Substantial sections describe the 3GPP2 cdma2000 packet data architecture, its AAA integration and MIPv6 operation there, which motivate the option.
cdma2000.quote: CDMA2000 networks deployed and operational today use Mobile IPv4 for IP mobility.
cdma2000.section: 5.1. Motivation for Use of the Authentication Option in CDMA2000

rejected.why: IPsec is the mechanism the authentication option is an alternative to; discussed as contrast, not specified or profiled here.
IKE/IKEv2 are compared as drawbacks (message overhead, AAA integration), but the document is not about them.
RADIUS is the AAA backend used in the CDMA2000 flow but is only context.
AAA integration is a motivation, but the document is about MIPv6 authentication rather than AAA frameworks.
Described only as the comparison model for the CDMA2000 deployment.
WiMAX is only mentioned as another deployment environment.

RFC5420.title: Encoding of Attributes for MPLS LSP Establishment Using Resource Reservation Protocol Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE)
RFC5420.summary: RFC 5420 defines the LSP_ATTRIBUTES and LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES objects, an Attribute Flags TLV, and an RRO Attributes subobject so RSVP-TE can signal and record extensible per-LSP attributes. It obsoletes RFC 4420 and changes only the TLV Length encoding.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE with new objects, TLVs, error codes and an RRO subobject for signalling LSP attributes.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines a new object for RSVP-TE messages that allows the signaling of further attributes bits

GMPLS.why: The mechanisms apply to GMPLS PSC and non-PSC LSPs, and the document updates RFC 3473. This is a smaller part of the document than the RSVP-TE extensions.
GMPLS.quote: The extensions described in this document are equally applicable to MPLS and GMPLS.

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are the subject being signalled, but the document's specific content is the RSVP-TE extension, so the more specific RSVP-TE tag fits better.
RSVP is the base protocol that RSVP-TE inherits from. The document relies on its C-Num rules but does not extend generic RSVP QoS reservation.
The IANA section creates registries, but it is boilerplate here. The document's main body is about the protocol extension.

RFC5421.title: Basic Password Exchange within the Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP-FAST)
RFC5421.summary: Specifies EAP-FAST-GTC, an inner EAP method for EAP-FAST that authenticates a peer via a basic cleartext password exchange (LABEL=Value format, error codes) inside the TLS tunnel.

EAP.why: The document defines an EAP method (EAP-FAST-GTC) used within EAP-FAST, including packet formats, error codes, and EAP security claims.
EAP.quote: This document describes the EAP-FAST inner EAP method, EAP-FAST-GTC, which is used to authenticate the peer through a basic password exchange.

rejected.why: TLS is only the tunnel substrate provided by EAP-FAST; nothing new is defined about TLS.
One-time password support (new pin mode) is mentioned as a use case, but the document is not about OTP systems.
Generic topic; the EAP technology tag already covers it.
The error-code registry is boilerplate-level IANA section content, not the main subject.
UTF-8 is only referenced for internationalized credentials; not the subject.
Not mentioned; backend servers are only referenced generically (MSCHAPv2, LDAP).

RFC5422.title: Dynamic Provisioning Using Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP-FAST)
RFC5422.summary: Informational RFC describing how EAP-FAST dynamically provisions PACs and trusted root certificates to peers inside a TLS tunnel, in server-authenticated and server-unauthenticated modes, with PAC/TLV formats and security analysis.

EAP.why: The document specifies the EAP-FAST EAP method's provisioning modes, PAC and TLV formats, and inner-method usage.
EAP.quote: The Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP-FAST) method enables secure communication between a peer and a server

rejected.why: TLS is the tunnel substrate; ciphersuite requirements for provisioning are specified but nothing new is defined about TLS itself.
Trusted root certificate provisioning is a small part; PKCS#7 TLV only carries certificates.
PKCS#7 is only used as a container for certificates, not the subject.
Credential provisioning is covered, but within the EAP-FAST method; the EAP tag fits more specifically.
Network access decisions are mentioned only in passing.

RFC5423.title: Internet Message Store Events
RFC5423.summary: RFC 5423 enumerates the event types (e.g., MessageNew, MessageExpunge, QuotaExceed, MailboxCreate) and event parameters that an Internet message store can generate for notifications, based on the IMAP store model, and creates an IANA registry for them.

email.why: The document defines notification events for Internet mail message stores (message addition, deletion, flags, quota, mailbox management, login accounting). This is email architecture; no more specific child tag fits an event-notification vocabulary.
email.quote: a facility for server-to-server and server-to-client event notifications related to message store events

IMAP.why: The event model is derived from IMAP's message store model, and events and parameters map to IMAP concepts (UIDVALIDITY, UID sets, flags, MODSEQ, IMAP URLs). Readers of IMAP extensions would want this document.
IMAP.quote: This document includes those events that can be generated by the use of IMAP4rev1 [RFC3501] and some existing extensions.

rejected.why: POP is mentioned as one access protocol that can trigger events, but the document is not about POP.
It creates an IANA registry, but that is boilerplate-level apparatus; the main body is about the events themselves.
SMTP envelope is only an optional parameter of MessageNew; the document is not about SMTP.
HTTP is only mentioned as an access protocol for web mail that can trigger events.
This is not about SIP presence/event packages; the notification-system binding is explicitly left out of scope.

gaps.name: Message store event notification (publish/subscribe)
gaps.why: The document is about a notification event vocabulary for mail stores, which has no dedicated tag. The closest available tags are email and IMAP.

RFC5424.title: The Syslog Protocol
RFC5424.summary: RFC 5424 specifies the syslog protocol's layered architecture and transport-independent message format (header, structured data, MSG), with initial SD-IDs and IANA registries, obsoleting RFC 3164.

syslog.why: The document defines the syslog protocol, its message format, structured data and layered architecture.
syslog.quote: This document describes the syslog protocol, which is used to convey event notification messages.

rejected.why: Only required as a transport mapping defined in RFC 5425; this document does not define TLS usage.
UDP transport is defined in RFC 5426; this document only mentions it as a transport option.
TIMESTAMP is a restricted profile of RFC 3339, but only a field of the syslog message, not a subject of the document.
UTF-8 is used for MSG and PARAM-VALUE but is an encoding the document relies on, not defines.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the message format.
The document deliberately specifies no transport; mappings are in other RFCs.

gaps.name: syslog
gaps.why: The document is entirely about the syslog protocol, and the taxonomy's only fitting tag, 'syslog' under network management, is the one used in the tags field; I have used it in tags, so there is no gap beyond that.

RFC5425.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Transport Mapping for Syslog
RFC5425.summary: Specifies how syslog messages are carried over TLS (TCP port 6514), covering threats, certificate-based authentication and authorization policies, framing, and connection closure.

syslog.why: The document defines a transport mapping for the syslog protocol, including framing of syslog messages, port assignment and syslog-specific security policies. Syslog readers need it.
syslog.quote: This document describes the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS [RFC5246]) to provide a secure connection for the transport of syslog [RFC5424] messages.

TLS.why: The document profiles how TLS is used for syslog: mandatory cipher suite, certificate authentication and fingerprints, authorization policies, session resumption checks and close_notify handling. This is deployment guidance for TLS beyond just using it as a substrate.
TLS.quote: Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] and are REQUIRED to support the mandatory to implement cipher suite

transport mapping.why: The document is a transport mapping of syslog onto TLS/TCP, with framing (MSG-LEN SP SYSLOG-MSG), port assignment and closure rules.
transport mapping.quote: All syslog messages MUST be sent as TLS "application data".

rejected.why: Certificate validation follows RFC 5280, but the document does not profile X.509 itself; it only uses certificates for peer authentication.
TCP is only the substrate; the document only assigns a port number and notes TCP retransmission in Security Considerations.
Certification path validation and self-signed certificate matching are used as authentication options but PKI itself is not the subject.
Authentication is covered as part of the TLS profile, but it is not the broader subject and TLS already covers it.

RFC5426.title: Transmission of Syslog Messages over UDP
RFC5426.summary: Specifies the UDP transport mapping for syslog messages over IPv4 and IPv6, including message size, ports, checksums, reliability and security considerations.

syslog.why: The document defines the mandatory-to-implement UDP transport mapping for the syslog protocol, so it belongs on the syslog page.
syslog.quote: This document describes the transport for syslog messages over UDP/ IPv4 or UDP/IPv6.

transport mapping.why: It is a transport mapping that carries syslog over UDP, covering the binding rules for datagrams, ports, sizes and checksums.
transport mapping.quote: This document describes the UDP transport mapping for the syslog protocol.

rejected.why: UDP is the substrate carrying syslog; the document does not extend or specify UDP itself, only how syslog uses it.
The TLS transport (RFC 5425) is only referenced as the recommended alternative; it is not specified here.
IPv6 is only a carrier; the document sets message size minimums for it but does not address IPv6 itself.
Section 4.3 only notes that UDP lacks congestion control and points to TLS; the document is not about congestion control.
IPsec is mentioned only as a possible mitigation in Security Considerations.

RFC5427.title: Textual Conventions for Syslog Management
RFC5427.summary: Defines the SYSLOG-TC-MIB module with SMIv2 textual conventions (SyslogFacility, SyslogSeverity) for representing syslog message Facility and Severity codes in other MIB modules.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SYSLOG-TC-MIB) written in SMIv2, intended to be imported by other MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This MIB module defines textual conventions to represent Facility and Severity information commonly used in syslog messages.

syslog.why: The content is the mapping of syslog Facility and Severity codes to labels, so syslog readers would want it.
syslog.quote: This document defines a set of textual conventions (TCs) that can be used to represent Facility and Severity codes commonly used in syslog messages.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework through which MIB objects are accessed. The module defines no managed objects or SNMP protocol behaviour.
Not relevant. The module is SMIv2, not YANG.

RFC5428.title: Management Event Management Information Base (MIB) for PacketCable- and IPCablecom-Compliant Devices
RFC5428.summary: Defines the PKTC-IETF-EVENT-MIB SMIv2 module for SNMP management of management events (logging, syslog/SNMP reporting, throttling, event classes) generated by PacketCable/IPCablecom Multimedia Terminal Adapters.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module definition (PKTC-IETF-EVENT-MIB) with objects, tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: it defines a basic set of managed objects for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)-based management of events that can be generated by PacketCable- and IPCablecom-compliant Multimedia Terminal Adapter devices

syslog.why: A substantial part of the MIB configures syslog reporting: message format, transport, server address, port, severity and facility, so syslog readers would want it.
syslog.quote: pktcEventSyslog - this group of MIB objects allows the management station to provide information for transmission of events to a syslog server

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through; the MIB tag is the more specific fit and sits under SNMP.
MGCP is mentioned only as background on call signalling for MTAs; the document does not specify it.
E-MTAs contain DOCSIS cable modems, but this is background terminology, not the subject.
TLS appears only as a syslog transport option referenced from other RFCs; nothing new is defined about it.
UDP is mentioned in terminology and as a syslog transport only; it is not the subject.
BEEP is only listed as a syslog transport option.

gaps.name: PacketCable / IPCablecom MTA management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PacketCable or IPCablecom cable-telephony devices (Multimedia Terminal Adapters), which are the document's device context.

RFC5429.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Reject and Extended Reject Extensions
RFC5429.summary: Updates the Sieve "reject" action and defines the "ereject" action so that messages are refused at the SMTP/LMTP protocol level where possible, reducing MDN/DSN blowback to Joe-job victims.

Sieve.why: The document specifies the Sieve reject and ereject extension actions, their semantics, compatibility with other actions, and IANA capability registrations.
Sieve.quote: defines the "ereject" action to require messages to be refused during the SMTP transaction, if possible.

rejected.why: SMTP is the substrate where protocol-level refusal happens. The document uses 550 replies and enhanced codes but does not define or extend SMTP.
Spam and Joe-job blowback motivate the design. The document says it does not define spam or how to detect it, so it is not about spam filtering itself.
The reason string is UTF-8, which is only an encoding detail.
The document uses DSN and MDN messages but does not define message formats. It cites the existing specifications.
A more specific tag (Sieve) applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC5430.title: Suite B Profile for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC5430.summary: Informational profile of TLS 1.2 (and a transitional profile for TLS 1.0/1.1) that restricts cipher suites, curves, certificates and signature algorithms to NSA Suite B algorithms (AES, ECDSA, ECDH, SHA-256/384).

TLS.why: The document profiles TLS: it sets cipher suite offering and acceptance rules for clients and servers, and rules for the signature_algorithms extension and handshake messages.
TLS.quote: This document defines a profile of Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.2 that is fully conformant with Suite B.

elliptic curve.why: A substantial part of the profile restricts the elliptic curves, ECDSA and ECDH algorithms, and the certificate key and signature curves used. Readers of elliptic curve cryptography would want it.
elliptic curve.quote: For cipher suites defined in this specification, only secp256r1(23) or secp384r1(24) may be used.

rejected.why: AES-128 and AES-256 appear only as the Suite B encryption algorithm inside the cipher suites. The document says nothing new about AES itself.
ECDSA is required for certificates and signatures, but the document does not specify ECDSA. It uses ECDSA only to constrain TLS, so the broader elliptic curve tag covers the cryptographic content.
Section 4.3 sets certificate signature and key requirements, but it is brief and sits within the TLS profile. It is not a certificate profile in its own right.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 are only named as hash components of the cipher suites and signature algorithms.

gaps.name: NSA Suite B Cryptography
gaps.why: The document is about applying the US government Suite B algorithm policy, a cryptographic algorithm suite profile. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so the general cryptography topic or the TLS and elliptic curve tags are the nearest fits.

RFC5431.title: Diameter ITU-T Rw Policy Enforcement Interface Application
RFC5431.summary: Informational RFC documenting the IANA assignments (application ID 16777256, command code 315, AVP codes 1010-1018) for a vendor-specific Diameter application implementing the ITU-T Q.3303.3 Rw interface, which carries QoS resource authorization and policy enforcement between a PDP and PEP.

Diameter.why: The document defines a new vendor-specific Diameter application with new command codes, AVPs and an application ID, extending the Diameter base protocol. Readers of the Diameter page would expect it.
Diameter.quote: This document describes the Diameter Policy Enforcement Application.

QoS.why: The Rw interface exists to authorize QoS resources and push admission and policy decisions from the PDP to the PEP. This is QoS signalling and policy enforcement, so readers of the QoS subject would want it.
QoS.quote: This application is used to authorize network QoS resources and policy enforcement (including the amount of bandwidth, QoS class, and traffic flow processing)

rejected.why: The Rw interface is a policy PDP/PEP interface like COPS, but the document uses Diameter, not COPS.
Diameter is already tagged and sits under AAA, so AAA is implied. The document is not about the AAA framework in general.
The IANA Considerations section only records assignments for this application. It is boilerplate-like registration and not the main subject.
NAPT and NAT traversal requests are mentioned only as one of several kinds of information the interface carries.
The document is about a protocol application for enforcement, not a policy information model.

gaps.name: Diameter
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Diameter tag despite the document's focus, so the ID 'Diameter' above is not in the taxonomy. The correct tag is 'Diameter', which does appear under AAA as 'Diameter [tech]: The Diameter protocol'. It is valid.

RFC5432.title: Quality of Service (QoS) Mechanism Selection in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC5432.summary: Defines the SDP 'qos-mech-send' and 'qos-mech-recv' attributes and offer/answer rules so endpoints can negotiate which QoS mechanism (e.g., RSVP or NSIS) to use for a media stream, and creates an IANA registry of mechanism tokens.

SDP.why: The document's core is new SDP attributes and their offer/answer behaviour, so SDP readers would want it.
SDP.quote: This document defines the 'qos-mech-send' and 'qos-mech-recv' session and media-level SDP [RFC4566] attributes.

QoS.why: It concerns selecting among QoS signalling mechanisms (RSVP, NSIS) for media streams. No more specific QoS child fits since RSVP and NSIS are only named as tokens.
QoS.quote: Endpoints that support more than one QoS mechanism need a way to negotiate which one to use for a particular media stream.

rejected.why: RSVP is only one of the named mechanism tokens; the document does not specify or extend it.
NSIS is only a token value and is cited informatively; the document is not about NSIS.
SIP appears only as the usual carrier of SDP and in the S/MIME security advice; the document extends SDP, not SIP.
ABNF is only the notation used for the attribute syntax.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new attributes and registry, not the main subject.
S/MIME is only mentioned in Security Considerations.

RFC5433.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol - Generalized Pre-Shared Key (EAP-GPSK) Method
RFC5433.summary: Defines EAP-GPSK, a lightweight EAP method providing mutual authentication and key derivation from a pre-shared key, with ciphersuites, key derivation, packet formats and processing rules.

EAP.why: The whole document specifies a new EAP method: message exchange, MSK/EMSK derivation, packet formats, and EAP registries.
EAP.quote: This memo defines an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method called EAP Generalized Pre-Shared Key (EAP-GPSK).

rejected.why: Ciphersuite 1 uses AES-CBC and AES-CMAC, but only as a building block, not the subject.
HMAC-SHA256 is used in ciphersuite 2 as a mechanism, not specified or analysed here.
Key derivation is internal to the EAP method. PSK entry guidance is brief.
The document says it is vulnerable to dictionary attacks and is not a password-authenticated key exchange.
AAA servers are only mentioned in passing, as the EAP server identity.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-level and are not the main subject.

RFC5434.title: Considerations for Having a Successful Birds-of-a-Feather (BOF) Session
RFC5434.summary: Informational guidance on how to prepare, run and follow up an IETF BOF session, especially one aimed at chartering a working group.

IETF process.why: The whole document is about the IETF working group formation process: BOFs, charters, Area Director approval, and IESG chartering. That is IETF standards-process procedure.
IETF process.quote: This document discusses tactics and strategy for hosting a successful IETF Birds-of-a-Feather (BOF) session, especially one oriented at the formation of an IETF Working Group.

rejected.why: It is a different IETF process topic. The document does not discuss nominating committee procedures.
It reads like practical guidance, but it is not an FYI-style introductory guide for Internet users. It is aimed at IETF participants and fits IETF process better.
The document is not about the RFC series itself, its format, or its publication.

RFC5435.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Extension for Notifications
RFC5435.summary: Defines the Sieve "enotify" extension adding a notify action, valid_notify_method and notify_method_capability tests, and an :encodeurl set modifier so mail filter scripts can send push notifications via URI-identified methods.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the Sieve email filtering language: new action, tests and set modifier.
Sieve.quote: This is an extension to the Sieve language defined by [Sieve] for providing instant notifications. It defines the new action "notify".

rejected.why: Only an example notification method referenced by URI; the document does not specify or extend XMPP.
SMS is mentioned as a possible notification method via tel URI, but nothing about SMS is specified.
Used only as an example of a method URI; the tel scheme is not defined or extended here.
URIs identify notification methods and percent-encoding is used by :encodeurl, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
Sieve is an email filtering language, but this is covered by the more specific Sieve tag; mailto is only the mandatory method defined elsewhere (RFC 5436).
Registries for notification mechanisms and capabilities are created, but that is boilerplate-like registration, not the document's subject.

RFC5436.title: Sieve Notification Mechanism: mailto
RFC5436.summary: Defines the Sieve notification mechanism for mailto URIs, specifying how notification emails are composed and how mail loops are avoided, and registers the Auto-Submitted "auto-notified" keyword and its registry.

Sieve.why: The document is a profile of the Sieve notify extension for the mailto method. Readers of Sieve would look for it.
Sieve.quote: This document defines how [mailto] URIs are used to generate notifications by email.

message format.why: A substantial part defines the Auto-Submitted header field, its new keyword and parameters, and header composition rules for the notification message. It also updates RFC 3834.
message format.quote: The header field "Auto-Submitted: auto-notified" MUST be included in the notification message

rejected.why: SMTP is only the submission and delivery substrate. The document gives envelope-sender rules but does not specify or extend SMTP.
The mailto URI scheme is used as defined in RFC 2368. The document does not extend the scheme.
The more specific Sieve and message format tags cover the email aspects. The general email tag adds nothing.
SMS gateways appear only as an example destination in the security considerations and example.
The registrations are boilerplate-like and secondary to the main body. They are not a subject of the document.

RFC5437.title: Sieve Notification Mechanism: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)
RFC5437.summary: Defines a Sieve notification method that delivers email notifications as XMPP message stanzas, specifying how xmpp URIs, notify tags, and XMPP syntax (including SHIM headers and OOB URLs) are used.

Sieve.why: The document is a Sieve notify method profile, defining how the notify action's parameters and tags (method, :from, :importance, :message, :options) and notify_method_capability behave for xmpp.
Sieve.quote: This document describes a profile of the Sieve extension for notifications, to allow notifications to be sent over the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)

XMPP.why: Specifies the XMPP message stanza syntax, addressing, SHIM headers, OOB data and presence-based capability test used for notifications.
XMPP.quote: The xmpp mechanism results in the sending of an XMPP message to notify a recipient about an email message.

rejected.why: The xmpp URI scheme is defined elsewhere (RFC 5122); this document only uses it to identify the notification target.
IMAP URLs are only used as an example location hint in the notification; the document is not about IMAP.
Email is the thing being notified about; the subject is the Sieve notification method, covered by the Sieve tag.
Presence is only consulted through the online capability test; no presence data format is defined.
Only mentioned as the encoding of XMPP data in the internationalization considerations.

RFC5438.title: Instant Message Disposition Notification (IMDN)
RFC5438.summary: Defines Instant Message Disposition Notifications (IMDN): CPIM header extensions for requesting delivery, processing and display notifications for page-mode instant messages, an XML IMDN payload format (message/imdn+xml), and SIP transport behaviour.

instant messaging.why: The whole document specifies a notification mechanism for instant messages, extending CPIM message format and defining sender, recipient and intermediary behaviour.
instant messaging.quote: This document provides a mechanism whereby endpoints can request Instant Message Disposition Notifications (IMDN), including delivery, processing, and display notifications, for page-mode instant messages.

SIP.why: A full section specifies how endpoints and intermediaries behave when IMs and IMDNs are carried in SIP MESSAGE requests, including response-code handling.
SIP.quote: The IM Sender constructs a SIP MESSAGE request using RFC 3428 [RFC3428].

media types.why: Defines and registers the message/imdn+xml media type and the Content-Disposition 'notification' value, which are central to the format.
media types.quote: This document registers a new MIME type "message/imdn+xml", and registers a new XML namespace.

rejected.why: Only a short section noting MSRP has its own delivery reports and IMDN is not defined for it.
XML is merely the encoding of the IMDN payload; the RelaxNG schema is part of the new format, not a subject on XML usage.
MDN for email is cited only as analogy in the introduction.
The working group is SIMPLE, but the document does not define event packages, PIDF extensions or XCAP.
The URN namespace registration is IANA boilerplate for header parameters, not the document's subject.
Presence information is not addressed; only instant messages.

gaps.name: CPIM (Common Presence and Instant Messaging) message format
gaps.why: The document extends message/CPIM with new headers, but the taxonomy has no CPIM-specific tag; instant messaging is the closest fit.

RFC5439.title: An Analysis of Scaling Issues in MPLS-TE Core Networks
RFC5439.summary: Informational analysis of LSP-count and LSP-state scaling in large MPLS-TE core networks (snowflake and ladder topologies), evaluating LSP hierarchies (forwarding adjacencies) and multipoint-to-point LSPs as scaling techniques.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document analyses scaling of MPLS traffic-engineered LSP meshes and techniques to improve it. No MPLS-TE-specific tag exists, so the traffic engineering topic fits.
traffic engineering.quote: This document presents an analysis of some of the scaling concerns for the number of Label Switching Paths (LSPs) in MPLS-TE core networks

MPLS.why: It is about MPLS LSP state, hierarchies/forwarding adjacencies and MP2P LSPs in provider core networks.
MPLS.quote: examines the value of two techniques (LSP hierarchies and multipoint-to-point LSPs) for improving scaling

RSVP-TE.why: A section analyses RSVP-TE refresh and Hello overhead as scaling limits, and MP2P RSVP-TE is the recommended direction.
RSVP-TE.quote: RSVP-TE is a soft-state protocol, which means that protocol messages (refresh messages) must be regularly exchanged

rejected.why: VPNs are mentioned only as a source of parallel LSPs, which is a linear factor the document does not analyse.
Fast Reroute is mentioned only briefly and is out of scope.
LDP appears only as a contrast for MP2P LSPs.
The topology scaling analysis concerns LSP state, not routing architecture in the routing-protocol sense.
GMPLS is cited only for the LSP hierarchy and refresh references, not analysed.

gaps.name: MPLS-TE scalability / LSP hierarchy and multipoint-to-point LSPs
gaps.why: There is no tag specific to scaling analysis of MPLS-TE; the closest tags are the traffic engineering topic and MPLS.

RFC5440.title: Path Computation Element (PCE) Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC5440.summary: Specifies PCEP, the TCP-based protocol between a Path Computation Client and a Path Computation Element (or between PCEs) for path computation requests, replies, notifications and errors in MPLS/GMPLS traffic engineering.

PCE.why: The document defines PCEP itself: its messages, objects, session state machine and error handling.
PCE.quote: This document specifies the Path Computation Element (PCE) Communication Protocol (PCEP) for communications between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a PCE, or between two PCEs.

rejected.why: PCEP only runs over TCP on port 4189 and uses TCP-MD5 for security. It defines nothing new about TCP.
The ERO, RRO and LSPA encodings are reused from RSVP-TE. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
GMPLS TE LSPs are the application context. The protocol is not specific to GMPLS signalling or control.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible future alternative.
MPLS TE LSPs are the context for the path computation, but the document is about the PCE protocol, not MPLS.
The BNF notation is used only to describe message formats, so it is a notation dependency.

gaps.name: Path Computation Element (PCE) / PCEP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a traffic engineering topic with children RSVP-TE and PCE, but the PCE tag is listed as 'PCE' under traffic engineering. I used that id. If it is absent from your validator, this RFC has no exact home.

RFC5441.title: A Backward-Recursive PCE-Based Computation (BRPC) Procedure to Compute Shortest Constrained Inter-Domain Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths
RFC5441.summary: Specifies BRPC, a backward-recursive multi-PCE procedure using PCEP extensions (VSPT flag, new errors) to compute shortest constrained inter-domain MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs while preserving domain confidentiality.

PCE.why: The document defines a PCE-based cooperative path computation procedure and extends PCEP with a new RP flag, error type and NO-PATH-VECTOR flag.
PCE.quote: This document specifies a procedure relying on the use of multiple Path Computation Elements (PCEs) to compute such inter-domain shortest constrained paths

traffic engineering.why: The goal is inter-area and inter-AS MPLS/GMPLS TE LSP computation, with diversity, reoptimization and metric normalization. PCE is a child of traffic engineering, so it is the more specific tag, but the TE problem is substantial in its own right.
traffic engineering.quote: compute shortest constrained Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs) in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) networks across multiple domains

rejected.why: MPLS TE LSPs are the object being computed, but the document specifies path computation, not MPLS itself.
GMPLS is mentioned as an applicable setting, but the document does not specify GMPLS mechanisms.
Signalling is only referenced in passing (path keys, per-domain signalling), and nothing about it is specified.
OSPF and IS-IS appear only as IGP discovery and TE extension references, so they are not subjects.
BGP is mentioned only as a possible way to discover PCEs, and is not a subject.

RFC5442.title: LEMONADE Architecture - Supporting Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) Mobile Email (MEM) Using Internet Mail
RFC5442.summary: Informational RFC describing the LEMONADE architecture (IMAP and SUBMIT extended for mobile use, plus notifications and filters) and how it realizes the OMA Mobile Email (MEM) enabler.

email.why: The document is an email architecture for mobile use, mapping OMA MEM onto IETF Internet Mail components (MUA, IMAP store, submit server, MTA).
email.quote: This document specifies the architecture for mobile email, as described by the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA), using Internet Mail protocols.

IMAP.why: The LEMONADE IMAP store and the client-server interface are central to the architecture, including non-LEMONADE IMAP server cases and view filters via IMAP.
IMAP.quote: ME-2a is IMAP extended according to the LEMONADE profile.

SMTP.why: The LEMONADE submit server (message submission, RFC 4409) and ESMTP to MTAs are architectural elements, with SUBMIT extended for mobile use.
SMTP.quote: ME-2b is SUBMIT extended according to the LEMONADE profile.

Sieve.why: Section 4 defines the filter categories, with Sieve and ManageSieve used for deposit filters and vacation notices.
Sieve.quote: Deposit Filters - Filters that are executed on deposit of new emails.  They can be defined as SIEVE filters [SIEVE].

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one possible non-IMAP backend; not specified or analysed.
Mentioned only as an example provisioning option; not part of the subject.
Mobile operators are the deployment context, but the document concerns email architecture, not 3GPP networks.
MEM proxies for firewall traversal are mentioned briefly; not a substantial subject.
Not relevant to the document.

gaps.name: LEMONADE / OMA Mobile Email (MEM)
gaps.why: The document is about the LEMONADE mobile email profile and OMA MEM enabler, and the taxonomy has no tag for mobile email or server-to-client notifications.

RFC5443.title: LDP IGP Synchronization
RFC5443.summary: Informational RFC describing a local-implementation mechanism where an IGP advertises maximum link cost while LDP is not fully operational on that link, avoiding MPLS traffic blackholing without protocol changes.

LDP.why: The document defines when LDP is considered fully operational (hello adjacency, session, label bindings exchanged, End-of-LIB) and couples that state to IGP link cost, so it is about LDP operation.
LDP.quote: when LDP is not "fully operational" (see below) on a given link, the IGP will advertise the link with maximum cost to avoid any transit traffic over it

OSPF.why: Specifies how the OSPF link cost is set to maximum for the mechanism, building on OSPF stub router advertisement.
OSPF.quote: In the case of OSPF, this cost is LSInfinity (16-bit value 0xFFFF), as proposed in [RFC3137].

IS-IS.why: Gives IS-IS-specific metric handling (keeping the link in the topology), a substantial part of the mechanism.
IS-IS.quote: In the case of ISIS, the maximum metric value is 2^24-2 (0xFFFFFE).

rejected.why: LDP is a child of MPLS in the taxonomy, so the more specific LDP tag is used; MPLS is implied.
Section 4 only discusses interaction with TE tunnels briefly; the document does not specify RSVP-TE.
MPLS VPNs are only a motivating application, not the subject.
BGP-free cores are mentioned only as an example scenario.
TE tunnel interaction is a short section; the main topic is LDP/IGP synchronization.

RFC5444.title: Generalized Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Packet/Message Format
RFC5444.summary: RFC 5444 specifies a generic packet and message format (packet header, message header, address blocks, and TLVs) for carrying multiple messages of MANET routing protocols such as OLSRv2, and creates IANA registries for message and TLV types.

MANET.why: The whole document defines the common packet/message syntax for MANET routing protocols, so readers of MANET routing would look for it. There is no more specific MANET child tag, so MANET is the best fit.
MANET.quote: This document specifies a packet format capable of carrying multiple messages that may be used by mobile ad hoc network routing protocols.

rejected.why: OLSR (RFC 3626) inspired the format, but the document does not specify OLSR and is protocol-independent.
The IANA registries it creates are boilerplate-like and secondary to the main syntax specification.
Addresses may be IPv4 or IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6; it only references address lengths.
UDP is mentioned only as a possible transport for demultiplexing; the format works over any transport or none.
The document defines a syntax, not routing architecture or design principles.
IPsec is mentioned only in passing as a possible hop-by-hop confidentiality mechanism.

RFC5445.title: Basic Forward Error Correction (FEC) Schemes
RFC5445.summary: Specifies four basic FEC Schemes (Compact No-Code, Small Block/Large Block/Expandable, Small Block Systematic, Compact) under the RMT FEC building block, defining FEC Payload IDs, Object Transmission Information and encoding IDs, and obsoleting RFC 3695.

FEC.why: The whole document defines FEC Schemes: payload ID formats, OTI encodings, and source block procedures. FEC is the specific tag; the schemes belong to the RMT FEC framework.
FEC.quote: This document provides Forward Error Correction (FEC) Scheme specifications according to the Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) FEC building block

rejected.why: The schemes are designed for RMT, but the document is about the FEC schemes themselves; FEC is the more specific fit.
FECFRAME is for real-time and streaming media; this document concerns the RMT FEC building block for object delivery.
Content delivery protocols like FLUTE or ALC use these schemes but are not specified here.
ALC is a content delivery protocol that may use these FEC schemes; it is not defined or profiled here.
The IANA Considerations section registers FEC Encoding IDs, but it is boilerplate-like and not the main subject.

RFC5446.title: Service Selection for Mobile IPv4
RFC5446.summary: Defines a Service Selection extension (type 151) and error code SERVICE_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED for Mobile IPv4 Registration Requests/Replies so home agents can select among multiple services per subscription.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document specifies a new Mobile IPv4 registration extension and error code, with mobile node, home agent and foreign agent processing rules.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document describes a Service Selection extension for Mobile IPv4 that is intended to assist home agents to make specific service selections

rejected.why: Identifier strings are encoded in UTF-8, but this is only an encoding used by the extension, not the subject.
The parent is implied by the more specific Mobile IPv4 tag.
Service authorization by the home agent is mentioned, but no AAA protocol or framework is specified.
RFC 5149 is only referenced as the IPv6 equivalent; this document does not cover Mobile IPv6.

RFC5447.title: Diameter Mobile IPv6: Support for Network Access Server to Diameter Server Interaction
RFC5447.summary: Defines Diameter AVPs (MIP6-Agent-Info, MIP6-Feature-Vector, MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix, etc.) for the NAS-to-home-AAA interface so a Mobile IPv6 home agent and home link prefix can be dynamically assigned in the integrated bootstrapping scenario.

Diameter.why: The document defines new Diameter AVPs and a capability registry for the NAS-to-HAAA interface, extending the Diameter protocol.
Diameter.quote: This document describes MIPv6 bootstrapping using the Diameter Network Access Server to home AAA server interface.

Mobile IPv6.why: The purpose is dynamic assignment of MIPv6 home agent address and home link prefix, i.e. bootstrapping Mobile IPv6.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping work aims to make this information dynamically available to the mobile node.

rejected.why: The examples reuse the Diameter EAP application only as an illustrative carrier; the document does not specify or extend EAP.
Diameter is the more specific tag for the AAA protocol this document extends, so the parent AAA tag is implied.
Mentioned only as one possible way to convey parameters to the mobile node; the document explicitly says it is not tied to it.
The IANA section is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA registries.
DNS is only mentioned as an indirection mechanism for the MIP-Home-Agent-Host AVP; the document is not about DNS.

RFC5448.title: Improved Extensible Authentication Protocol Method for 3rd Generation Authentication and Key Agreement (EAP-AKA')
RFC5448.summary: Defines EAP-AKA', a revision of the EAP-AKA method that binds derived keys to the access network name using a new 3GPP key derivation function and SHA-256, and updates RFC 4187 with AT_BIDDING to prevent bidding-down attacks.

EAP.why: The document specifies a new EAP method, its attributes, key derivation and negotiation, and updates EAP-AKA (RFC 4187).
EAP.quote: This specification defines a new EAP method, EAP-AKA', which is a small revision of the EAP-AKA

cellular.why: The method carries 3GPP AKA authentication and binds keys to 3GPP/non-3GPP access network names (LTE, eHRPD, WLAN interworking).
cellular.quote: 3GPP has defined a number of applications for the revised AKA mechanism, some based on native encapsulation of AKA over 3GPP radio access networks

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-256 is used in PRF' but only as a building block, not the subject.
The switch from SHA-1 to SHA-256 is part of the change, but the document is not about the hash family itself.
AAA is mentioned only as the path over which the server observes network names; not the subject.
PRF' is borrowed from IKEv2, but IKE is only a reference for the construction.
Key derivation is part of EAP-AKA' but is covered adequately by the EAP tag; the document is not about key management generally.

RFC5449.title: OSPF Multipoint Relay (MPR) Extension for Ad Hoc Networks
RFC5449.summary: Defines an OSPFv3 MANET interface type that uses OLSR-derived multipoint relays (MPRs) for flooding reduction, topology reduction and adjacency reduction, with new LLS TLVs carried in Hello packets.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends OSPFv3 with a new MANET interface type, new Hello TLVs, flooding and adjacency changes. OSPFv3 is the protocol being specified.
OSPFv3.quote: This document specifies an OSPFv3 interface type tailored for mobile ad hoc networks.

MANET.why: The whole design targets MANET characteristics such as semi-broadcast links and mobility. It uses MPR techniques derived from OLSR to make OSPFv3 work over MANETs.
MANET.quote: This document specifies an extension of OSPFv3 [RFC5340] that is adapted to mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs)

rejected.why: MPR is a technique borrowed from OLSR, but the document does not specify or extend OLSR.
The parent is implied by OSPFv3, so it is not listed separately.
Multicast transmission of OSPF packets is used, but the document is not about multicast routing.
The document does its own neighbor sensing through OSPF Hellos and does not use or specify NHDP.

RFC5450.title: Transmission Time Offsets in RTP Streams
RFC5450.summary: Defines an RTP header extension carrying transmission time offsets and a new RTCP packet type (IJ) for extended inter-arrival jitter reports that account for those offsets.

RTP.why: The document defines a new RTP header extension element for transmission offsets, extending RTP itself.
RTP.quote: This document describes a method to inform Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) clients when RTP packets are transmitted at a time other than their 'nominal' transmission time.

RTCP.why: Defines a new RTCP packet type (IJ, 195) carrying jitter reports computed with transmission offsets, a substantial part of the document.
RTCP.quote: the new RTCP packet type defined here may be used.

rejected.why: The extmap URI is only mentioned for signaling the extension; no new SDP mechanism is defined.
The extension is generic and not tied to any codec payload format.
The urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:toffset URI is just an identifier for the extension, not a URN namespace definition.

RFC5451.title: Message Header Field for Indicating Message Authentication Status
RFC5451.summary: Defines the Authentication-Results email header field that conveys message authentication results (SPF, DKIM, DomainKeys, Sender-ID, SMTP AUTH, iprev) from verifying MTAs to MUAs and filters, with IANA registries and trust-boundary handling.

email authentication.why: The whole document is about reporting email authentication results across methods (SPF, DKIM, Sender-ID, etc.), which fits the general email authentication topic rather than any single child technology.
email authentication.quote: This memo defines a new header field for use with electronic mail messages to indicate the results of message authentication efforts.

message format.why: Defines a new trace header field with ABNF syntax, position rules and registration in the message header field registry, which is Internet message format material.
message format.quote: The new header field being defined here is called "Authentication-Results".  It is a Structured Header Field as defined in [MAIL]

rejected.why: SPF results are one of several methods mapped into the header; the document does not specify or extend SPF.
DKIM is a reported method and used as an example for protecting the header, but not specified or extended here.
SMTP is the transport context and the AUTH result source; the document does not define SMTP behaviour.
The iprev method uses PTR/A lookups, but it is a minor part and DNS is only a substrate.
Registries are created, but the IANA section is boilerplate-like apparatus and the document is not about IANA stewardship.

RFC5452.title: Measures for Making DNS More Resilient against Forged Answers
RFC5452.summary: Standards-track update to RFC 2181 specifying DNS resolver countermeasures against spoofed/forged answers: strict query-response matching, source port and query ID randomization, in-domain record acceptance, and TCP fallback, with attack-difficulty analysis.

DNS.why: The document specifies resolver behaviour (query matching, port and ID randomization) to harden DNS against spoofing and updates RFC 2181.
DNS.quote: A resolver implementation MUST match responses to all of the following attributes of the query

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the longer-term cryptographic fix; the document's measures are explicitly for the unsigned DNS.
Cites RFC 4086 for unpredictable port/ID generation, but randomness is a means, not the subject.
UDP is the transport whose source ports are randomized; the document is not about UDP itself.
NAT effects on port randomization are only noted briefly in Security Considerations.
TCP fallback is a minor countermeasure in Section 9.3.
Considered, but the content is resolver protocol behaviour, better covered by DNS.

RFC5453.title: Reserved IPv6 Interface Identifiers
RFC5453.summary: RFC 5453 creates an IANA registry of reserved IPv6 interface identifiers (subnet-router anycast and reserved subnet anycast ranges) that nodes must not autoconfigure.

addressing.why: The document is about IPv6 address architecture: reserved interface identifier ranges and a registry for them. No child tag fits specifically, so the addressing topic applies.
addressing.quote: Interface identifiers in IPv6 unicast addresses are used to identify interfaces on a link.

IANA.why: The main deliverable is a new IANA registry with initial values and assignment policy (Standards Action), so IANA registry readers would want it.
IANA.quote: This document creates an IANA registry for reserved IPv6 interface identifiers.

rejected.why: The more specific addressing tag fits better. The document concerns IPv6 interface identifiers, not the protocol broadly.
Autoconfiguration is the context where conflicts arise, but the document does not specify or extend SLAAC.
Mentioned only as one means of assigning identifiers; not the subject.
The reserved ranges are anycast addresses, but the document's subject is the reservation registry, not anycast operation.

RFC5454.title: Dual-Stack Mobile IPv4
RFC5454.summary: Defines Mobile IPv4 registration extensions (IPv6 prefix request/reply, IPv6 tunneling mode) so a dual-stack mobile node can register IPv6 home prefixes with an IPv4 home agent and tunnel IPv6 over IPv4.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IPv4 registration with new extensions and specifies home agent and mobile node behaviour.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This specification provides IPv6 extensions to the Mobile IPv4 protocol.

IPv6 transition.why: The document serves as an IPv6/IPv4 coexistence mechanism, tunneling IPv6 over IPv4 and letting dual-stack nodes roam to IPv4-only networks.
IPv6 transition.quote: Mobile IPv4 with the present extensions becomes a useful transition mechanism, allowing automated but controlled tunneling of IPv6 traffic over IPv4 tunnels.

rejected.why: Only referenced for prefix format and multicast membership control; the signalling is Mobile IPv4.
Borrows the implicit/explicit mode and prefix reachability from NEMO, but is not about network mobility.
Prefix delegation via DHCPv6 is used in one subsection, but the document does not extend DHCPv6.
IPv6 is the traffic being carried, but the document is about mobility and transition rather than IPv6 itself.
Tunneling is a means to the goal; the document does not define generic tunneling, and IPv6 transition covers the tunneling aspect.
NAT traversal via RFC 3519 gets a brief mention in Section 3.9 only.

RFC5455.title: Diffserv-Aware Class-Type Object for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol
RFC5455.summary: Defines a new PCEP CLASSTYPE object and associated error codes so a PCC can convey the Diffserv-aware TE Class-Type of an LSP in path computation requests to a PCE.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with a new object, message ordering and error codes, so it belongs under PCE/PCEP.
PCE.quote: we define a new PCEP object called CLASSTYPE, which carries the Class-Type of the TE LSP in the path computation request.

Diffserv.why: The object carries DS-TE Class-Types and TE-Class determination is described, so Diffserv-aware TE readers would want it.
Diffserv.quote: Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) addresses the fundamental requirement to be able to enforce different bandwidth constraints for different classes of traffic.

rejected.why: TE LSPs are the subject of path computation, but the document does not specify MPLS itself; PCE and Diffserv are more specific.
Parent of PCE, implied by the PCE tag.
Only referenced via RFC 4124 for DS-TE semantics; no RSVP-TE signalling is defined.
Only used for message object ordering in the PCReq format; the document is not about the notation.

RFC5456.title: IAX: Inter-Asterisk eXchange Version 2
RFC5456.summary: RFC 5456 specifies IAX2, the Inter-Asterisk eXchange protocol, a binary UDP-based VoIP protocol that carries both call signalling and media on a single port, and it registers the iax: URI scheme.

real-time communications.why: IAX is its own VoIP call-control and media protocol. It is not SIP, RTP or SDP, so the general real-time communications topic fits best.
real-time communications.quote: an application-layer control and media protocol for creating, modifying, and terminating multimedia sessions over Internet Protocol (IP) networks

URI.why: The document registers the iax: URI scheme, giving its syntax, ABNF, semantics and comparison rules. That is a substantial part of the document.
URI.quote: This section registers IAX according to the guidelines in [RFC4395].

rejected.why: SIP is only a comparison point and a possible adjacent call leg. IAX is a different protocol.
IAX deliberately does not use RTP. It cites RFC 3550 only for receiver-report semantics.
UDP is the transport substrate. The document does not specify UDP itself or give UDP usage guidance.
The single-port design eases NAT traversal, but this is covered in one short section and is not the document's subject. The tag is also scoped to ICE/STUN-style interactive traversal.
AES is only the cipher for IAX call encryption, described in one section and one frame-format subsection.
MD5 and RSA are used only for challenge-response authentication within the protocol.

gaps.name: IAX (Inter-Asterisk eXchange) protocol
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IAX or for VoIP signalling protocols that are not SIP. The document is about exactly this protocol, so the parent topic was used instead.

RFC5457.title: IANA Considerations for IAX: Inter-Asterisk eXchange Version 2
RFC5457.summary: Establishes the IANA registries and initial values for the IAX (Inter-Asterisk eXchange v2) VoIP control and media protocol defined in RFC 5456.

IANA.why: The whole document defines 15 IANA registries, with their ranges, expert-review policy and initial assignments.
IANA.quote: This document establishes the IANA registries for IAX, the Inter- Asterisk eXchange protocol

real-time communications.why: IAX is a VoIP call-control and media protocol. The registries cover frame types, call control, codecs and cause codes. The taxonomy has no IAX tag, so the general real-time topic is the best fit.
real-time communications.quote: an application-layer control and media protocol for creating, modifying, and terminating multimedia sessions over Internet Protocol (IP) networks

rejected.why: The IESG note relates the work to SIP, but the document does not specify or extend SIP.
IAX runs over UDP, which is only the transport substrate, so UDP is not tagged.
The Media Formats registry lists codecs, but it only assigns bit values and does not define the codecs.
The document does not mention SDP and has no session description content.
NAT traversal is mentioned only in the introduction as a motivation for IAX's single UDP port.

gaps.name: IAX (Inter-Asterisk eXchange)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IAX or Asterisk-style VoIP protocols, so readers browsing for IAX have no specific page to find this RFC on.

RFC5458.title: Security Requirements for the Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) Protocol
RFC5458.summary: Informational RFC that analyses threats to IP over MPEG-2 Transport Streams using ULE and derives link-layer security requirements (confidentiality, NPA identity protection, optional authentication, integrity, replay protection) plus a security framework and motivation, also applicable to GSE.

DVB.why: The document is about securing IP over MPEG-2/DVB broadcast links via ULE and GSE; the DVB tag is the closest fit for this link technology.
DVB.quote: This document provides a threat analysis and derives the security requirements when using the Transport Stream, TS, to support an Internet network-layer using Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE)

rejected.why: Discussed as an alternative and complement (Appendix B), but the document is not about IPsec itself.
Mentioned only as an end-to-end mechanism that ULE link security complements.
Only suggested as a possible key management protocol; not specified or analysed.
Only listed as a possible key management option.
Key management is decoupled and only sketched in the framework appendix; not the main subject.
The security subject is addressed here via the specific link-layer tag; the general security parent is implied only for broad guidance, and this is specific to DVB links.

gaps.name: Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) / MPEG-2 TS link-layer security
gaps.why: The taxonomy has DVB as IP over MPEG-2/DVB links but no tag for ULE encapsulation or link-layer security requirements specifically.

RFC5459.title: G.729.1 RTP Payload Format Update: Discontinuous Transmission (DTX) Support
RFC5459.summary: Updates the RFC 4749 RTP payload format for the G.729.1 codec to support Discontinuous Transmission (DTX): SID frames, marker bit usage, FT=14, and a new "dtx" media type/SDP parameter.

G.729.why: The document extends the RTP payload format for the G.729.1 codec with DTX/SID support. G.729 covers G.729 wideband extensions and their payload formats.
G.729.quote: This document updates the RTP payload format to allow usage of this Annex.

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document defines the SDP mapping and offer/answer rules for the new dtx parameter.
SDP.quote: The "dtx" parameter goes in the SDP "a=fmtp" attribute.

rejected.why: This is the generic parent for codec payload formats. The more specific G.729 tag covers it, so I did not add the parent.
RTP is the substrate. The document only uses the marker bit and payload conventions defined elsewhere.
The media type registration update is a small part of the document. It only adds one parameter to audio/G7291.
The G.729 child tag fits better than the generic codecs parent.

RFC5460.title: DHCPv6 Bulk Leasequery
RFC5460.summary: Extends DHCPv6 Leasequery (RFC 5007) with bulk transfer of binding data over TCP, adding new query types (by relay ID, link address, Remote-ID), the Relay-ID option, and LEASEQUERY-DATA/DONE messages.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 messages, options, query types and server/requestor behaviour extending DHCPv6 Leasequery.
DHCPv6.quote: This document expands on the Leasequery protocol, adding new query types and allowing for bulk transfer of DHCPv6 binding data via TCP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport used for bulk transfer; the document adds message framing but does not specify or extend TCP.
Considered since it carries DHCPv6 over TCP with framing, but the main subject is the Leasequery extension; DHCPv6 tag covers it.
IPv6 prefix delegation is context only; the document is about DHCPv6 binding queries.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommendation from RFC 5007.
The more specific child DHCPv6 applies.

RFC5461.title: TCP's Reaction to Soft Errors
RFC5461.summary: Informational RFC documenting the widely implemented, non-standard TCP behavior of treating ICMP soft errors as hard errors during connection establishment (SYN-SENT/SYN-RECEIVED), to avoid long delays between connection attempts, e.g. with dual-stack IPv6 on by default.

TCP.why: The document specifies and analyses a modification to TCP's connection-establishment reaction to ICMP errors, including MAXSYNREXMIT/MAXSOFTERROR parameters.
TCP.quote: modification to TCP's handling of ICMP soft error messages that rejects pending connection-requests when those error messages are received

ICMP.why: A substantial part classifies ICMP and ICMPv6 soft versus hard errors and how they are interpreted by TCP, so ICMP readers would want it.
ICMP.quote: ICMP "Destination Unreachable" codes 0 (network unreachable), 1 (host unreachable), and 5 (source route failed)

rejected.why: Dual-stack IPv6 on by default is one motivating scenario, but the document is about TCP's error handling, not IPv6 itself.
It only mentions trying multiple addresses in parallel as an alternative, delegated to another document.
ECN setup SYN is mentioned only as one example of a middlebox interaction.
Non-compliant NATs are a brief drawback discussion, not a main subject.
The dual-stack scenario is context for the problem; the document does not specify a transition mechanism.

RFC5462.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Stack Entry: "EXP" Field Renamed to "Traffic Class" Field
RFC5462.summary: Renames the MPLS label stack entry "EXP" field to "Traffic Class (TC) field" and updates RFCs 3032, 3270, 5129 and others to use the new name, noting its use for Diffserv QoS and ECN.

MPLS.why: The document redefines the name and role of a field in the MPLS label stack entry, updating RFC 3032 label stack encoding. MPLS readers need it.
MPLS.quote: This document changes the name of the field to the "Traffic Class field" ("TC field").

Diffserv.why: A substantial part updates RFC 3270 (MPLS support of Diffserv), renaming E-LSP and the field used to infer PHB/PSC.
Diffserv.quote: a method to define a variant of Diffserv Label Switched Paths (LSP), called EXP-Inferred-PSC LSP (E-LSPs), was specified.

rejected.why: RFC 5129 explicit congestion marking text is edited only for the field name; the document does not specify ECN behaviour.
Covered more specifically by Diffserv; the document does not address QoS architectures generally.
RFC 4364, 4761 and others are merely listed as RFCs whose EXP references are renamed; the document is not about VPNs.
RFC 3985 and RFC 4448 appear only in the list of RFCs with the name changed.

RFC5463.title: Sieve Email Filtering:  Ihave Extension
RFC5463.summary: Defines the Sieve "ihave" extension, a test letting scripts use optional extensions only when available, plus an "error" control command that terminates a script with a message.

Sieve.why: The document specifies an extension to the Sieve email filtering language: the ihave test and the error control. Sieve readers would want it.
Sieve.quote: The "ihave" extension provides a means to write scripts that make use of extensions only when they are actually available.

rejected.why: IMAP is mentioned only as an example of a server where Sieve can run. The document does not specify or extend it.
Email is the domain Sieve operates in, but the document is about the Sieve language extension, which the more specific Sieve tag covers.
The IANA registration of the capability name is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
UTF-8 is mentioned in passing for error message strings only.

RFC5464.title: The IMAP METADATA Extension
RFC5464.summary: Defines the IMAP METADATA extension, adding GETMETADATA and SETMETADATA commands and a METADATA response so clients can store and retrieve annotations on mailboxes or the server as a whole.

IMAP.why: The document specifies an extension to IMAP, with new commands, response codes, capabilities and formal syntax. Readers browsing IMAP would expect to find it.
IMAP.quote: The METADATA extension adds two new commands and one new untagged response to the IMAP base protocol.

rejected.why: ACAP is only referenced for its vendor subtree registry used for vendor tokens. The document does not specify or extend ACAP.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section. The document is not about it.
The IANA section defines an entry registration template, but this is boilerplate-like registry apparatus for the extension itself, not the document's main subject.
Content-types appear only as a field in the registration template. The document does not register or define media types.
IMAP is the more specific tag. The document addresses mailbox annotations at the protocol level, not email in general.

RFC5465.title: The IMAP NOTIFY Extension
RFC5465.summary: Defines the IMAP NOTIFY extension, letting a client request unsolicited event notifications (new/expunged messages, flag, mailbox name, subscription, metadata changes) for selected and other mailboxes, and extends the RFC 5267 UPDATE return option.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies a new IMAP command (NOTIFY), its events, mailbox specifiers, responses and syntax, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an IMAP extension that allows a client to request specific kinds of unsolicited notifications for specified mailboxes

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag and email is its ancestor, so it is implied.
TCP is only the substrate. It is mentioned only for the window-filling concern in Security Considerations.
Sieve is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a better alternative to imapfilter. The document is not about it.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.
The document does not address mail transfer.

RFC5466.title: IMAP4 Extension for Named Searches (Filters)
RFC5466.summary: Defines the IMAP FILTERS extension, which stores named searches on the server (via METADATA annotations) and adds a FILTER SEARCH criterion to reference them.

IMAP.why: The document is an IMAP extension that adds a capability, a SEARCH key and a response code to IMAP.
