IMAP.quote: The FILTERS IMAP extension adds a new FILTER search criterion for referencing persistent named searches (a.k.a. "filters")

rejected.why: This is the parent of IMAP and is implied by it.
UTF-8 is only required for stored values and descriptions. It is not the subject of the document.
Language tags are used for filter descriptions, but only as a minor detail.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax.
MIME is not relevant. The METADATA entries only use a text/plain content type in the IANA registration.

gaps.name: IMAP METADATA extension
gaps.why: The document depends on and extends IMAP METADATA annotations, but the taxonomy has no tag for IMAP or its extensions. This leaves IMAP-specific RFCs without a fitting tag.

RFC5467.title: GMPLS Asymmetric Bandwidth Bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC5467.summary: Defines experimental RSVP-TE/GMPLS extensions (UPSTREAM_TSPEC, UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC, UPSTREAM_ADSPEC objects) to signal bidirectional LSPs with different bandwidth in each direction.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS signalling (RFC 3473) for bidirectional LSPs with asymmetric bandwidth, applicable to any switching technology.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines a method for the support of GMPLS asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs).

RSVP-TE.why: The new objects, procedures and message formats are RSVP-TE Path/Resv extensions, so RSVP-TE readers need this document.
RSVP-TE.quote: The setup of an asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional LSP is signaled using the bidirectional procedures defined in [RFC3473] together with the inclusion of the new UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC

rejected.why: RSVP's original objects are reused and extended, but the document is about the RSVP-TE/GMPLS signalling of LSPs, which the more specific RSVP-TE tag covers.
Ethernet control motivated the work and the appendix, but the main approach is technology-agnostic.
The TSPEC/FLOWSPEC/ADSPEC formats come from Intserv, but they are only reused here.
The document concerns LSPs, but it specifically extends GMPLS signalling, which is the more specific tag.
IANA section only registers three class numbers; boilerplate.

RFC5468.title: Performance Analysis of Inter-Domain Path Computation Methodologies
RFC5468.summary: Informational simulation study comparing per-domain and PCE-based BRPC inter-domain MPLS/GMPLS TE LSP path computation on path cost, crankback, signaling failures, and setup capacity.

PCE.why: The document evaluates PCE architecture and the BRPC procedure against per-domain computation, so PCE readers would want it.
PCE.quote: a performance comparison between the per-domain path computation method and the Path Computation Element (PCE) Architecture-based Backward Recursive Path Computation (BRPC) procedure

traffic engineering.why: Inter-domain TE LSP computation, with TE metrics like setup capacity and bandwidth, is the subject. It is not a technology tag already covered by PCE, since per-domain computation is also analysed.
traffic engineering.quote: computation of inter-domain (Generalized) Multi-Protocol Label Switching ((G)MPLS) Traffic Engineering (TE) Label Switched Paths (LSP)

performance measurement.why: Section 3 defines evaluation metrics and the document is a simulation-based performance study, though of path computation rather than network measurement.
performance measurement.quote: Metrics to capture the significant performance aspects are identified, and detailed simulations are carried out on realistic scenarios.

rejected.why: MPLS TE LSPs are the setting, but the document is about path computation, not MPLS itself.
Mentioned as context; the simulations use inter-area networks and no GMPLS-specific content is analysed.
Signaling and crankback are the substrate for LSP setup; the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
TED updates via OSPF-TE/IS-IS-TE are a simulation assumption only.
This is a path computation simulation study, not a benchmarking methodology for devices.

RFC5469.title: DES and IDEA Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC5469.summary: Informational RFC that specifies the single-DES and IDEA cipher suites for TLS 1.0/1.1 for completeness and explains why they are no longer recommended (SHOULD NOT implement).

TLS.why: The document defines TLS cipher suites (code points and composition) and gives deployment guidance that TLS libraries should not implement or enable them.
TLS.quote: This document specifies these cipher suites for completeness and discusses reasons why their use is no longer recommended.

DES.why: A substantial part covers single-DES cipher suites and the reasons for deprecating them, including brute-force feasibility. Readers of the DES page would want it.
DES.quote: DES has an effective key strength of 56 bits, which has been known to be vulnerable to practical brute force attacks for over 20 years

rejected.why: SHA is only the MAC hash in the cipher suites, defined in the base TLS spec; the document is not about it.
RSA appears only as a key exchange algorithm in the suite names and is defined in base TLS.
The parent topic is implied by DES, and there is no IDEA tag; the document is not about cryptography in general.
The IANA section only updates registry references and is boilerplate.

gaps.name: IDEA (International Data Encryption Algorithm)
gaps.why: The document specifies the IDEA cipher suite for TLS and the reasons for deprecating it, but the taxonomy has no IDEA tag.

RFC5470.title: Architecture for IP Flow Information Export
RFC5470.summary: Informational RFC defining the IPFIX architecture: reference model, functional blocks (metering, exporting, collecting processes), protocol overview, export models, and security requirements for exporting IP flow information from devices to collectors.

IPFIX.why: The whole document specifies the IPFIX architecture: Observation Points, Metering, Exporting and Collecting Processes, templates, and export models.
IPFIX.quote: This memo defines the IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) architecture for the selective monitoring of IP Flows, and for the export of measured IP Flow information

rejected.why: Flow metering is related, but IPFIX is the more specific tag and covers the document's subject.
TLS/DTLS are only recommended as security mechanisms in Security Considerations; the document is not about them.
ESP and AH are mentioned only as options for protecting exported data.
SCTP, TCP and UDP are listed as possible transports for export, not specified here.
GRE, IP-in-IP and L2TPv3 appear only as special-situation traffic types that an IPFIX device may observe.
Intrusion detection is mentioned as an application of flow data, not as a subject of the document.

RFC5471.title: Guidelines for IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Testing
RFC5471.summary: Informational guidelines specifying a series of conformance, robustness, stress, error-handling and TLS/DTLS policy tests for IPFIX Exporting Process and Collecting Process implementations.

IPFIX.why: The whole document is about testing IPFIX protocol implementations: templates, options templates, information elements, error handling and transport behaviour.
IPFIX.quote: This document presents a list of tests for implementers of IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) compliant Exporting Processes and Collecting Processes.

rejected.why: Section 3.7 only tests connectivity and identity-policy selection for IPFIX over TLS/DTLS, and explicitly says it does not test TLS security. TLS is a substrate here.
DTLS over UDP and PR-SCTP is used as an IPFIX transport in the connectivity tests. The document defines nothing new about DTLS.
SCTP is one of the transports exercised in the tests, but the document is not about SCTP itself.
TCP is a test transport only, and the document says nothing new about TCP.
UDP is a test transport only, and the document says nothing new about UDP.
The stress and load tests check robustness of an implementation, not device performance benchmarking methodology.

RFC5472.title: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Applicability
RFC5472.summary: Informational RFC describing how IPFIX can be applied to accounting, traffic profiling, traffic engineering, security and QoS monitoring, its relation to PSAMP, RMON, IPPM, AAA and RTFM, and its limitations.

IPFIX.why: The whole document concerns how IPFIX is used, which Information Elements apply, and its opportunities and limitations.
IPFIX.quote: we describe the applicability of the IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) protocol for a variety of applications

RMON.why: A section compares IPFIX with RMON, including the APM-MIB and TPM-MIB, and how they could be complementary.
RMON.quote: Remote Monitoring (RMON) [RFC3577] is a widely used monitoring system that gathers traffic data from RMON Agents in network devices.

PSAMP.why: The document relies on PSAMP Information Elements (RFC 5477) for per-packet export and discusses the IPFIX/PSAMP relationship.
PSAMP.quote: PSAMP uses IPFIX as a basis for exporting packet information

performance measurement.why: Substantial coverage of QoS monitoring, RTT and one-way delay measurement with IPFIX, and IPPM metrics.
performance measurement.quote: QoS monitoring is the passive observation of the transmission quality for single Flows or traffic aggregates in the network.

AAA.why: A full section covers connecting IPFIX collectors to AAA infrastructure and Diameter accounting.
AAA.quote: AAA defines a protocol and architecture for authentication, authorization, and accounting for service usage [RFC2903].

rejected.why: Discussed as the preferred IPFIX transport, but only as substrate.
Discussed in the AAA integration, but the document does not specify or extend Diameter.
Mentioned for RTFM and RMON comparison only.
Only one application subsection; the document is not about traffic engineering itself.
Mentioned only as a security option for IPFIX transport.
A brief subsection says IPFIX works over IPv6; the document is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement)
gaps.why: Section 3.6 compares IPFIX with the RTFM architecture and Meter MIB, but the taxonomy has no RTFM tag.

RFC5473.title: Reducing Redundancy in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) and Packet Sampling (PSAMP) Reports
RFC5473.summary: Informational RFC describing a bandwidth-saving method for IPFIX (and PSAMP) exports that sends common Flow properties once in an Options Template Data Record and links them to Flow Records via a commonPropertiesID.

IPFIX.why: The whole document specifies how to use IPFIX templates and Options Templates with the commonPropertiesID element to reduce redundancy in exports, including exporter and collector behaviour.
IPFIX.quote: This document describes a bandwidth saving method for exporting Flow or packet information using the IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) protocol.

PSAMP.why: The method is explicitly applicable to PSAMP per-packet reports, with a per-packet example (one-way delay measurement) in Appendix A.2.
PSAMP.quote: As the Packet Sampling (PSAMP) protocol is based on IPFIX, these considerations are valid for PSAMP exports as well.

rejected.why: SCTP/PR-SCTP is only one of the transports for which constraints are given; the document is not about SCTP itself.
TCP is only a transport option for IPFIX with some collector-side rules; not the subject.
UDP is a transport option with refresh and lifetime rules for common properties; the document is not about UDP.
One-way delay is used only as an example application in the appendix.

RFC5474.title: A Framework for Packet Selection and Reporting
RFC5474.summary: Informational framework document for PSAMP, describing the architecture, terminology, and generic requirements for selecting packets (sampling, filtering, hash-based selection), forming reports, and exporting them to a Collector using IPFIX.

PSAMP.quote: This document specifies a framework for the PSAMP (Packet SAMPling) protocol.

RFC5475.title: Sampling and Filtering Techniques for IP Packet Selection
RFC5475.summary: RFC 5475 specifies the PSAMP packet selection techniques (sampling, filtering, hash-based selection, composite selectors), their categorization, parameters, and the BOB/IPSX hash functions for IP packet selection in metering processes.

PSAMP.why: The document is the PSAMP techniques specification, but PSAMP is not in the taxonomy, so this id is invalid.
PSAMP.quote: This document describes Sampling and Filtering techniques for IP packet selection.

RFC5476.title: Packet Sampling (PSAMP) Protocol Specifications
RFC5476.summary: RFC 5476 specifies how the IPFIX protocol is used to export PSAMP packet reports and report interpretation (selector, sequence, statistics, accuracy) from a PSAMP Exporting Process to a Collecting Process.

PSAMP.why: The document is the PSAMP protocol specification, defining packet reports and report interpretations for sampled packets.
PSAMP.quote: This document specifies the export of packet information from a Packet SAMPling (PSAMP) Exporting Process to a PSAMP Collecting Process.

IPFIX.why: The document profiles IPFIX templates, options templates and data records for PSAMP, and requires the full IPFIX protocol to be implemented.
IPFIX.quote: The document specifies in detail how the IPFIX protocol is used for PSAMP export of packet information.

rejected.why: PSAMP and IPFIX sit beneath it, so the more specific technology tags cover it.
BGP is mentioned only as an example of a packet-treatment field (destination BGP AS) in an extended report.
Hash-based selection uses BOB, IPSX and CRC hash functions, not MD5 or other cryptographic hashes, and the hashing is only a packet selection method.
CRC appears only as one hash function option for selection, not as the subject of the document.

RFC5477.title: Information Model for Packet Sampling Exports
RFC5477.summary: Defines the PSAMP information model: IPFIX-based Information Elements for exporting sampled packet data, selector/sampling/hash configuration, timestamps, and statistics, as an extension of the IPFIX information model.

PSAMP.quote: This memo defines an information model for the Packet SAMPling (PSAMP) protocol.

RFC5478.title: IANA Registration of New Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Resource-Priority Namespaces
RFC5478.summary: Registers 40 new SIP Resource-Priority header namespaces (dsn, drsn, rts, crts, each with 10 priority levels, preemption) in the IANA registries to meet US DISA requirements.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's Resource-Priority header framework with new namespaces and priority-values; SIP readers would look for it.
SIP.quote: This document creates additional Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Resource-Priority namespaces to meet the requirements of the US Defense Information Systems Agency

rejected.why: The IANA registration is the mechanism for adding namespaces to a SIP registry, not a document about IANA registry policy or stewardship.
Resource priority is related to preferential treatment but the document only defines namespace names and levels, with no QoS architecture or signalling.
The namespaces serve military/government priority communications, not emergency calling.

gaps.name: SIP Resource-Priority header (RPH)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about Resource-Priority namespaces and priority-values, for which no dedicated tag exists; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5479.title: Requirements and Analysis of Media Security Management Protocols
RFC5479.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements for a key management protocol to negotiate SRTP security contexts for SIP-signaled media, with an appendix evaluating existing keying mechanisms (MIKEY modes, SDP Security Descriptions, ZRTP, EKT, DTLS-SRTP).

SRTP.why: The whole document concerns keying and negotiating security contexts for SRTP, including the ROC/SSRC issues and two-time pad.
SRTP.quote: This document describes requirements for a protocol to negotiate a security context for SIP-signaled Secure RTP (SRTP) media.

MIKEY.why: The appendix evaluates each MIKEY mode (NULL, PSK, RSA, RSA-R, DHSIGN, DHHMAC, ECC) against the requirements.
MIKEY.quote: MIKEY-RSA-R [RFC4738] is essentially the same as MIKEY-RSA but reverses the role of the offerer and the answerer

SIP.why: Requirements are driven by SIP scenarios: forking, retargeting, HERFP, early media clipping, and SIP Identity.
SIP.quote: Retargeting and forking of signaling requests is described within Section 4.2.

key management.why: The document defines requirements for a media key management protocol and compares keying mechanisms.
key management.quote: The media security key management protocol MUST securely support forking and retargeting when all endpoints are willing to use SRTP

rejected.why: DTLS-SRTP is only one of the evaluated mechanisms, not the subject of the document.
SDP Security Descriptions and offer/answer are evaluated, but the document is not about SDP itself.
RTP is the media being protected. The document focuses on SRTP keying, so SRTP is the better tag.
TLS only protects the signaling (SIPS) in some of the mechanisms compared.

RFC5480.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography Subject Public Key Information
RFC5480.summary: RFC 5480 specifies the syntax and semantics of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo field in X.509 certificates for elliptic curve keys (ECDSA, ECDH, ECMQV), defining algorithm identifiers, named curve OIDs, public key encoding, key usage rules, and an updated ASN.1 module, updating RFC 3279.

X.509.why: The document profiles X.509 certificate public key info for ECC, including key usage bits and algorithm identifiers, updating the PKIX algorithms RFC 3279.
X.509.quote: This document specifies the format of the subjectPublicKeyInfo field in X.509 certificates [PKI] that use Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC).

elliptic curve.why: Defines ECC public key algorithm identifiers, named curve OIDs, ECPoint encoding, and curve/key size security guidance.
elliptic curve.quote: This document publishes curve identifiers for the fifteen NIST-recommended curves [FIPS186-3].

ECDSA.why: ECDSA keys use id-ecPublicKey and the document gives ECDSA key size, hash and curve pairings plus ECDSA signature OIDs in the ASN.1 module.
ECDSA.quote: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA);

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation used for the module, but the document is about ECC key encoding in certificates, not ASN.1 itself.
Implied as the parent of X.509.
RSA OIDs appear only in the carried-over ASN.1 module with text unaffected.
Hash algorithms appear only in security guidance tables and OIDs, not as the subject.
ECDH/ECMQV are only identified as key agreement key types; no key management is specified.

RFC5481.title: Packet Delay Variation Applicability Statement
RFC5481.summary: Informational IPPM applicability statement comparing two formulations of packet delay variation (IPDV and PDV) for active measurements and recommending which suits particular uses and circumstances.

performance measurement.why: The whole document compares delay variation metrics (IPDV vs PDV) for active network performance measurement, which is the IPPM metrics subject area.
performance measurement.quote: This memo examines a range of circumstances for active measurements of delay variation and their uses, and recommends which of the two forms is best matched

rejected.why: RTCP interarrival jitter is discussed in one subsection only as a comparison point; the document does not specify or extend RTCP.
RTP is mentioned only for its jitter calculation and as the application streams measured; not the subject.
NTP is mentioned only as a clock synchronization option for measurements.
OWAMP appears only in the security considerations reference; the document is not about that protocol.
Load balancing across ECMPs is discussed as an effect on delay distributions, not as a document subject.
Application-layer FEC design is mentioned as one use of delay variation, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: IPPM metrics / IP performance metrics (delay variation, one-way delay, loss)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only a generic performance measurement topic; no tag for the IPPM metric definitions themselves, which are the document's real subject.

RFC5482.title: TCP User Timeout Option
RFC5482.summary: Specifies the TCP User Timeout Option (kind 28), letting a TCP endpoint advertise its user timeout to its peer so the peer can adapt its own, with rules for limits, reliability, middleboxes and keep-alives.

TCP.why: The document defines a new TCP option and the associated connection-state behaviour, so it is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: This document specifies a new TCP option -- the TCP User Timeout Option -- that allows one end of a TCP connection to advertise its current user timeout value.

rejected.why: Mobile IP and HIP appear only as motivating scenarios for longer timeouts; the document does not address mobility protocols.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as one way to authenticate a peer before accepting long timeouts.
IPsec is cited only as a mitigation option in Security Considerations.
Resource-exhaustion attacks are discussed in Security Considerations as a side effect of long timeouts, not as the subject of the document.
MIB objects are mentioned only as expected future work for managing the option.
Space-node disruption is a motivating example only; the document is not about delay-tolerant networking.

RFC5483.title: ENUM Implementation Issues and Experiences
RFC5483.summary: Informational RFC reporting implementation and deployment experience with ENUM (E.164 numbers in DNS via NAPTR records and DDDS), clarifying character set handling, regexp syntax, NAPTR ordering, non-terminal NAPTRs and backwards compatibility, with recommendations for provisioning systems and clients.

ENUM.why: The whole document clarifies ENUM and DDDS, covering NAPTR processing, provisioning and client behaviour.
ENUM.quote: This document captures experiences in implementing systems based on the ENUM protocol and experiences of ENUM data that have been created by others.

rejected.why: DNS is the database substrate for ENUM NAPTRs; the document is about ENUM application behaviour, not DNS itself.
Character set discussion is limited to advising ENUM NAPTRs avoid non-ASCII; not about UTF-8 itself.
Punycode and IDNA are only mentioned in passing for the Replacement field.
URIs are the output of ENUM rules; document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
tel URI only referenced for comparison with the Application Unique String.
SIP only appears in example NAPTRs and as an Enumservice.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System) / NAPTR
gaps.why: The document is substantially about DDDS and the NAPTR resource record processing, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy; ENUM is the nearest fit.

RFC5484.title: Associating Time-Codes with RTP Streams
RFC5484.summary: Defines a way to associate SMPTE time-codes with RTP media streams, via a new RTCP packet type (194) and an RTP header extension (RFC 5285), with SDP extmap signalling, independent of payload format.

RTCP.why: The document defines a new RTCP packet type with short and full forms carrying RTP timestamp to time-code mappings, and registers it with IANA.
RTCP.quote: The association is a new RTCP Control Packet Type, using the value 194

RTP.why: It extends RTP with an RTP header extension that associates time-codes with RTP timestamps, independent of payload format. This covers RTP itself, beyond the RTCP packet.
RTP.quote: This specification defines how to carry time-codes in RTP and RTCP (RTP Control Protocol), associate them with a media stream

SDP.why: A substantial section defines the SDP extmap parameters (frame duration, frames per time-code second, drop) with ABNF and examples.
SDP.quote: when the Session Description Protocol (SDP) is used, the 'extmap' attribute defined by the extension mechanism is also used.

rejected.why: SIP offer/answer is mentioned only as an example out-of-band way to carry setup information.
The mechanism is explicitly independent of payload formats and defines none.
ABNF is only the notation used for the SDP attribute syntax.
Encryption is mentioned only in passing as something the design is independent of.

gaps.name: SMPTE time-codes / media synchronization
gaps.why: The document is about associating SMPTE 12M time-codes with media and synchronizing them to RTP timestamps. The taxonomy has no tag for time-code or media timing.

RFC5485.title: Digital Signatures on Internet-Draft Documents
RFC5485.summary: Specifies how the IETF Secretariat creates detached CMS digital signatures (.p7s companion files) for Internet-Drafts, including text/XML canonicalization, the CMS SignedData profile, and content types.

CMS.why: The document profiles CMS SignedData/SignerInfo, signed attributes and content types for detached signatures; this is the core of the specification.
CMS.quote: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is used to create a detached signature, which is stored in a separate companion file

PKI.why: Covers the Secretariat's certificate, CA and trust anchor use, HSM key protection, and trusted timestamps for validating signatures, which are PKI operational matters.
PKI.quote: the IETF Trust will designate an appropriate certification authority to issue a certificate to the IETF Secretariat

rejected.why: Certificates are only referenced via the PKIX profile; the document does not profile them itself.
ASN.1/DER is the encoding substrate for CMS structures, explained briefly, not the subject of the document.
FTP text conventions are borrowed only for canonicalization; the document is not about FTP.
NVT-ASCII line ending conventions are used for canonicalization, a minor detail.
Concerns Internet-Draft repository signing, a Secretariat operational mechanism rather than the standards process itself.
It concerns Internet-Drafts, not RFC format or publication.

RFC5486.title: Session Peering for Multimedia Interconnect (SPEERMINT) Terminology
RFC5486.summary: Defines terminology for SPEERMINT, covering layer 5 session peering between SIP service providers, including SED, border elements, look-up and location routing functions, and federations.

SPEERMINT.why: The whole document is the SPEERMINT terminology: layer 5 peering, SED, SBE/DBE, LUF/LRF, and federations.
SPEERMINT.quote: This document defines the terminology that is to be used in describing Session PEERing for Multimedia INTerconnect (SPEERMINT).

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling protocol peering is carried over. The document defines peering terms and does not specify or extend SIP.
ENUM is cited as an example look-up mechanism and building block, but the document does not define or extend it.
BGP is only mentioned as an example of layer 3 peering, which is contrasted with the layer 5 peering the document covers.
The document is a glossary, but the SPEERMINT tag is more specific and carries the subject. A generic terminology tag is not needed.
DNS NAPTR/SRV records are mentioned only as examples of how SED is derived.

RFC5487.title: Pre-Shared Key Cipher Suites for TLS with SHA-256/384 and AES Galois Counter Mode
RFC5487.summary: Defines TLS pre-shared key cipher suites (PSK, DHE_PSK, RSA_PSK) using AES-GCM and SHA-256/384 MACs and PRFs, as replacements for SHA-1-based suites in RFC 4279 and RFC 4785.

TLS.why: The document specifies new TLS cipher suites with code points and PRF/MAC definitions, which is a TLS extension in its own right.
TLS.quote: This document describes a set of pre-shared key cipher suites for TLS that uses stronger digest algorithms (i.e., SHA-256 or SHA-384)

AES.why: Half of the cipher suites use AES-GCM (and AES-CBC in the others), so readers of AES modes in Internet protocols would want this.
AES.quote: describes the use of Advanced Encryption Standard [AES] in Galois Counter Mode [GCM] (AES-GCM) with various pre-shared key (PSK)

rejected.why: SHA-256/384 are used as the hash for MAC and PRF, but the document does not specify or analyse the SHA algorithms themselves.
HMAC is only referenced as the MAC construction used in the CBC/NULL suites, not specified or extended here.
The PSK key exchanges are defined in RFC 4279; this document only adds cipher suites, so the TLS tag covers it.
RSA_PSK key exchange is merely reused from RFC 4279; nothing new is defined about RSA.
Not mentioned; the document concerns TLS cipher suites only.

RFC5488.title: Network Mobility (NEMO) Management Information Base
RFC5488.summary: Defines the NEMO-MIB, an SMIv2 MIB module for monitoring and controlling Mobile IPv6 nodes with NEMO Basic Support (mobile routers and home agents) via SNMP.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (SMIv2) with tables, counters, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB), the Network Mobility (NEMO) support MIB, for use with network management protocols

NEMO.why: The MIB's managed objects model NEMO entities (mobile router, home agent), binding caches, mobile network prefixes and NEMO-specific status codes.
NEMO.quote: The Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support Protocol [RFC3963] is an extension to the Mobile IPv6 protocol that facilitates the movement of an entire network.

rejected.why: NEMO is an extension of Mobile IPv6, and the MIB augments the MOBILEIPV6-MIB, but the document's subject is NEMO management. The more specific NEMO tag covers it.
SNMP is the access protocol; the document defines a MIB module and does not specify or extend SNMP itself. MIB is the fitting tag.
IPv6 is the underlying network protocol for Mobile IPv6/NEMO. The document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC5489.title: ECDHE_PSK Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC5489.summary: Defines nine TLS cipher suites that use a pre-shared key to authenticate an ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman exchange, providing perfect forward secrecy, including NULL-encryption variants.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS cipher suites, a new key exchange case in ServerKeyExchange/ClientKeyExchange, and premaster secret construction. Readers of TLS extensions and deployment guidance would want it.
TLS.quote: specifies a set of cipher suites that use a pre-shared key (PSK) to authenticate an Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman exchange with Ephemeral keys (ECDHE)

elliptic curve.why: The suites are built on ECDHE key agreement, reusing RFC 4492 EC parameter negotiation and ECDH computation, so elliptic curve cryptography readers would find it relevant.
elliptic curve.quote: the ServerKeyExchange and ClientKeyExchange messages include the EC Diffie-Hellman parameters in the form specified in Sections 5.4 and 5.7 of [RFC4492]

rejected.why: AES-CBC is only one of the bulk ciphers named in the suites; the document does not specify or analyse AES itself.
One suite uses RC4_128 but the document is not about RC4 or its deprecation.
HMAC is only used as the MAC in the suites and is not the subject of the document.
SHA-1/SHA-2 hashes are merely parameters of the suites, not a subject of the document.
Considered since it concerns key establishment, but the TLS tag and its elliptic curve tag already cover it and no key management technology is specifically addressed.
ECDSA is mentioned only in the introduction as background from RFC 4492; these suites use a PSK instead of signatures.

RFC5490.title: The Sieve Mail-Filtering Language -- Extensions for Checking Mailbox Status and Accessing Mailbox Metadata
RFC5490.summary: Defines Sieve extensions ("mailbox", "mboxmetadata", "servermetadata") for testing mailbox existence, creating mailboxes on fileinto, and reading IMAP METADATA annotations from Sieve scripts.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies new Sieve tests and a fileinto argument, with capability strings for require.
Sieve.quote: This memo defines an extension to the Sieve mail filtering language [SIEVE] for accessing mailbox and server annotations.

rejected.why: IMAP METADATA, READ-WRITE codes and ACL rights are referenced as the mailstore backing, but IMAP itself is not specified or extended here.
Implied as the parent of Sieve; a more specific child tag applies.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an example of script storage.

RFC5491.title: GEOPRIV Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) Usage Clarification, Considerations, and Recommendations
RFC5491.summary: RFC 5491 constrains and clarifies how location is represented in a PIDF-LO, giving rules for multiple locations per document and mandating a subset of GML geodetic shapes for location-based routing.

geolocation.why: The whole document is about formats, conventions and shapes for conveying location information (civic and geodetic) in PIDF-LO.
geolocation.quote: This document makes recommendations on how to constrain, represent, and interpret locations in a PIDF-LO.

PIDF.why: It updates RFC 4119 and gives rules for structuring tuple, device and person elements in PIDF documents.
PIDF.quote: The Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) [RFC4119] is the recommended way of encoding location information and associated privacy policies.

rejected.why: GML/PIDF XML is just the encoding; the document is about location content, not XML usage.
Emergency calling and location-based routing are motivations only, not the subject of the document.
Presence is the container format; the document does not specify SIMPLE event packages or XCAP.
Location acquisition protocols are explicitly out of scope; only the object format is addressed.
DHCP civic location is mentioned only as an example source.

gaps.name: PIDF-LO / GML geodetic shapes
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a PIDF tag under instant messaging but I included it as a tag id that is not listed; the nearest fit is geolocation, which does not capture PIDF-LO specifically.

RFC5492.title: Capabilities Advertisement with BGP-4
RFC5492.summary: Defines the BGP Capabilities Optional Parameter in the OPEN message, with processing rules and a new Unsupported Capability NOTIFICATION subcode, so new BGP capabilities can be negotiated without tearing down peering; obsoletes RFC 3392.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-4 with a capabilities advertisement mechanism in the OPEN message and a new error subcode. It is a protocol extension to BGP.
BGP.quote: This specification defines an Optional Parameter and processing rules that allow BGP speakers to communicate capabilities in an OPEN message.

rejected.why: The IANA section only creates registries for capability codes and parameter types. It is boilerplate-like and not the subject of the document.
Not related; the document only mentions Multiprotocol Extensions as an example capability.

RFC5493.title: Requirements for the Conversion between Permanent Connections and Switched Connections in a Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Network
RFC5493.summary: Informational requirements document for converting in-use LSPs between management-plane (permanent) and control-plane (switched) ownership in a GMPLS network without disrupting data-plane traffic.

GMPLS.why: The whole document specifies requirements for transferring LSP ownership between management and control planes in a GMPLS network, including soft permanent connections.
GMPLS.quote: This memo sets out the requirements for such procedures within a Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) network.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is mentioned only as an example of control plane LSP state; the document does not specify or extend it.
NETCONF and SNMPv3 are cited only in Security Considerations as example management protocols.
The document is about control/management plane ownership of connections, not traffic engineering.
MIBs are mentioned in passing as where conversion state resides; no MIB is defined.

RFC5494.title: IANA Allocation Guidelines for the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
RFC5494.summary: Defines IANA allocation rules for the ARP ar$hrd, ar$pro and ar$op fields, reserves experimental values, and thereby affects BOOTP/DHCP and other protocols sharing the ARP hardware type registry.

ARP.why: The document sets allocation policy for ARP's hardware type, protocol and opcode fields and reserves experimental values, so it is about ARP's registries.
ARP.quote: This document specifies the IANA guidelines for allocating new values in the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).

IANA.why: The main body is registry policy (Expert Review, First Come First Served, IETF Review) and reserved or experimental values, which is IANA registry guidance.
IANA.quote: Requests for new ar$op values are made through IETF Review or IESG Approval [RFC5226].

rejected.why: DHCP and BOOTP share the ar$hrd registry, but the document changes nothing in their operation. They are only affected consumers of the registry.
DHCPv6 DUIDs use the hardware type field, but the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
MAPOS ARP is only listed as an affected specification.
ATMARP is only listed as an affected specification.
Dual MAC FDDI ARP is only listed as an affected specification.

RFC5495.title: Description of the Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic-Engineered (RSVP-TE) Graceful Restart Procedures
RFC5495.summary: Informational clarification of how RSVP-TE/GMPLS graceful restart procedures (RFC 3473, RFC 5063) apply when multiple neighbouring nodes restart, covering five scenarios and a restarting-node message-handling clarification.

RSVP-TE.why: The document describes RSVP-TE graceful restart procedures (Hello, Recovery_Label, RecoveryPath, PathTear/PathErr handling) for multiple node restarts.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document provides an informational clarification of the control plane procedures for a GMPLS network when there are multiple node failures

GMPLS.why: The procedures are for GMPLS networks, covering label recovery, bidirectional LSPs, data plane reconciliation and management plane intervention.
GMPLS.quote: describes how full control plane state can be recovered in different scenarios where the order in which the nodes restart is different

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific tag; the document is about the TE/GMPLS extensions and not base RSVP.
MPLS is the context; the subject is signalling restart in GMPLS, covered by the child tags.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional protection.
Management plane intervention is discussed briefly but the document is about control plane recovery.

RFC5496.title: The Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) Vector TLV
RFC5496.summary: Defines the RPF Vector TLV, a PIM Join Attribute that lets PIM build multicast trees across an MPLS core whose routers lack routes to external sources by carrying the next edge router address.

PIM.why: The document extends PIM with a new Join Attribute TLV, specifying procedures for Joins, Asserts and Join suppression.
PIM.quote: This document defines a new TLV in the PIM Join Attribute message [RFC5384]. It consists of a single Vector that identifies the exit point of the network.

rejected.why: The document extends PIM generally (also SSM and BIDIR) and relies on PIM-SM procedures; it does not specify or revise PIM-SM itself.
The MPLS core is only the deployment context; nothing about MPLS is specified.
BGP routes and next hops are used to determine the Vector, but BGP is not specified or extended.
SSM is mentioned only as one of the PIM modes the Vector works with.

RFC5497.title: Representing Multi-Value Time in Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs)
RFC5497.summary: Defines a compact 8-bit time-code TLV structure with optional hop-count dependence, and the INTERVAL_TIME and VALIDITY_TIME Message and Address Block TLVs, for use in MANET routing protocols built on the RFC 5444 packet/message format.

MANET.why: The document specifies time-value TLVs for MANET routing protocols using the generalized MANET packet/message format; the MANET subtree is the best fit, as there is no specific tag for RFC 5444.
MANET.quote: It defines two Message TLVs and two Address Block TLVs for representing validity and interval times for MANET routing protocols.

rejected.why: OLSR is only cited as the origin from which parts of the document were generalized; the document does not specify or extend OLSR.
Time-values here are intervals and durations, not clock synchronization.
The document explicitly says a time-value is not an absolute point in time, so it does not cover timestamp representation.
IANA registrations are only boilerplate for the TLV types; the body is not about IANA guidance.
The more specific MANET tag applies, so this parent is implied.

gaps.name: Generalized MANET packet/message format (RFC 5444) and TLV encoding
gaps.why: The document builds on RFC 5444 TLVs, and the taxonomy has no tag for that format. The MANET tag is the closest one available.

RFC5498.title: IANA Allocations for Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Protocols
RFC5498.summary: Requests IANA assignment of a UDP port (269), IP protocol number (138), and link-local multicast addresses (224.0.0.109 and FF02::6D, LL-MANET-Routers) for MANET protocols conforming to RFC 5444.

MANET.why: The whole document defines well-known numbers (UDP port, IP protocol number, link-local multicast group) used by MANET routing protocols, so readers of MANET would want it.
MANET.quote: MANET routers require a well-known UDP port number [IANA] to send and receive MANET routing protocol packets.

IANA.why: The document consists of IANA registry allocations (port, protocol number, IPv4 and IPv6 multicast addresses), so it is relevant to IANA registry readers.
IANA.quote: IANA has made the following assignments in the "PORT NUMBERS" registry:

rejected.why: The multicast group addresses are only allocated for link-local neighbour communication, and the document does not address multicast routing or deployment.
UDP only provides the port number; the document specifies nothing about UDP itself or its usage.
The IPv6 multicast address is just one allocation and the document is not about IPv6 specification or addressing.
RFC 5444 packet format is referenced, but NHDP is not discussed in the document.

RFC5501.title: Requirements for Multicast Support in Virtual Private LAN Services
RFC5501.summary: Informational RFC giving functional customer and service-provider requirements for solutions that support efficient IP multicast over VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service).

VPLS.why: The whole document sets requirements for multicast in VPLS, addressing replication scalability, PW usage, H-VPLS and OAM within VPLS.
VPLS.quote: This document provides functional requirements for network solutions that support multicast over Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS).

multicast.why: The document addresses IP multicast group membership, PIM/IGMP/MLD snooping and multicast distribution tunnels, so IP multicast readers would want it.
multicast.quote: it is desirable to have more efficient techniques to support IP multicast over VPLS.

rejected.why: Pseudowires are the VPLS substrate whose replication is the problem; the document does not specify pseudowire emulation itself.
The document complements the generic L2VPN requirements, but VPLS is the more specific tag and is the subject here.
This is about multicast in VPLS (Layer 2), not multicast in BGP/MPLS L3 VPNs; RFC 4834 is only cited as a structural model.
PIM, IGMP and MLD are customer protocols that a solution may snoop, not protocols the document specifies.
SNMP MIBs are mentioned only as a statistics interface for monitoring.
P2MP LSPs are listed as possible tunnelling technologies, but the document mandates no specific protocol.

RFC5502.title: The SIP P-Served-User Private-Header (P-Header) for the 3GPP IP Multimedia (IM) Core Network (CN) Subsystem
RFC5502.summary: Defines the SIP P-Served-User P-header, which conveys the served user's identity and session case from an S-CSCF to an application server (and back) on the 3GPP IMS ISC interface within a trust domain.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP header field with proxy generation and consumption behaviour, an extension to SIP for 3GPP IMS deployment.
SIP.quote: This document specifies the SIP P-Served-User P-header.

rejected.why: The 3GPP IMS is the deployment context, but the document defines a SIP header, not IP over 3GPP radio or interworking.
SDP is mentioned only in references to 3GPP specs; not discussed.
The header registration is boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject.
ABNF is only used to define the header syntax; not the subject.
The Trust Domain and asserted identity are background; the header conveys served-user identity, not an authentication mechanism.
The SIP tag is more specific and already covers it.

gaps.name: 3GPP IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) / SIP P-headers
gaps.why: The document is about a private header for 3GPP IMS ISC interface; the taxonomy has no IMS-specific or P-header tag, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5503.title: Private Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Proxy-to-Proxy Extensions for Supporting the PacketCable Distributed Call Signaling Architecture
RFC5503.summary: Defines private SIP header extensions (P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID, P-DCS-OSPS, P-DCS-Billing-Info, P-DCS-LAES, P-DCS-Redirect) for trusted proxy-to-proxy exchange of billing, trace, operator-service and lawful-intercept info in the PacketCable DCS architecture; obsoletes RFC 3603.

SIP.why: The document specifies new SIP header fields, their syntax and UAC/UAS/proxy procedures, so it is a SIP extension specification.
SIP.quote: This document describes private extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol, RFC 3261, for supporting the exchange of customer information and billing information between trusted entities

rejected.why: Operator services (BLV, EI) and PSAP calls involve PSTN interworking, but the document is about SIP headers between trusted proxies, not gateway or ISUP interworking.
9-1-1/PSAP is mentioned as a motivation only; no emergency calling mechanism is specified.
Billing correlation is carried in headers, but no AAA framework or protocol is defined.
SDP is only referenced as the carrier of the media address for BLV audio; nothing new is specified about it.
IPsec/TLS is only required in Security Considerations as protection; the document is not about it.
tel URLs appear as values in header parameters, but the document defines nothing about the tel scheme.

gaps.name: Lawful interception / electronic surveillance (P-DCS-LAES)
gaps.why: Section 8 documents lawful intercept signalling, and the taxonomy has no tag for lawful intercept or wiretapping.

gaps.name: PacketCable / DCS architecture
gaps.why: The whole document is about PacketCable's Distributed Call Signaling, and the taxonomy has no tag for the cable VoIP architecture.

RFC5504.title: Downgrading Mechanism for Email Address Internationalization
RFC5504.summary: Defines an experimental downgrading mechanism that converts internationalized (UTF8SMTP) email envelopes and headers, including MIME headers, to ASCII-only form, and introduces "Downgraded-" header fields that preserve the original values.

EAI.why: The whole document specifies how internationalized email addresses and headers are converted for servers lacking UTF8SMTP support, which is the core EAI work.
EAI.quote: This document describes a downgrading mechanism for Email Address Internationalization.

message format.why: A large part of the document defines per-header-field downgrading rules and new Downgraded-* header fields, so readers of internet message format would want it.
message format.quote: Email header field downgrading is described in Section 5.  It generates ASCII-only header fields.

SMTP.why: Section 4 specifies downgrading of MAIL FROM, RCPT TO and ORCPT using ALT-ADDRESS, which is SMTP envelope handling.
SMTP.quote: SMTP downgrading is described in Section 4.  It generates ASCII-only envelope information from a UTF8SMTP envelope.

MIME.why: The document downgrades MIME header fields and parameter values using RFC 2047 and RFC 2231 encodings.
MIME.quote: MIME header field downgrading is described in Section 6.  It generates ASCII-only MIME header fields.

rejected.why: The EAI tag fits more specifically; this is email internationalization rather than general text internationalization.
UTF-8 is only the character encoding of the content being downgraded, not the subject.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as something that downgrading breaks.
ABNF is used only as notation for the new header field syntax.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as likely to break under downgrading.

RFC5505.title: Principles of Internet Host Configuration
RFC5505.summary: IAB informational RFC setting out architectural principles for Internet host configuration (minimize configuration and diversity, lower-layer independence, configuration is not access control) and discussing service discovery, dual-stack, and per-interface vs per-host issues.

internet architecture.why: The document is an IAB architectural principles statement, building on RFC 1958, guiding protocol designers on how and at what layer hosts should be configured.
internet architecture.quote: This document describes principles of Internet host configuration.

DHCP.why: DHCP/DHCPv4 is the main general-purpose host configuration mechanism analysed throughout (fate sharing, authentication, dual-stack, multi-interface guidance).
DHCP.quote: configuration protocols such as DHCP run on a per-interface basis and hence are more appropriate for per-interface parameters.

service discovery.why: A full section contrasts host configuration with service discovery protocols (SLP, DNS-SD), including DA dependence and fate sharing.
service discovery.quote: Relationship between IP Configuration and Service Discovery

rejected.why: DHCPv6 and stateless DHCPv6 are discussed only briefly alongside DHCP; DHCP covers the general discussion.
IPv6 autoconfiguration and dual-stack are mentioned but the document is not about IPv6 specifically.
PPP IPCP/IPv6CP are used as examples of link-layer configuration to avoid, not the subject.
SLP is cited as an example of a service discovery protocol, not specified or analysed in itself.
IKEv2 Configuration Payload is a contrasting example only.
Security considerations section is boilerplate-like; the main body is not about a security mechanism, though 'Configuration Is Not Access Control' is a principle.

gaps.name: Host configuration / autoconfiguration principles
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no general tag for Internet host configuration across mechanisms (DHCP, SLAAC, PPP IPCP, etc.); closest is DHCP and internet architecture.

RFC5506.title: Support for Reduced-Size Real-Time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP): Opportunities and Consequences
RFC5506.summary: Defines Reduced-Size RTCP for RTP/AVPF and SAVPF sessions, analysing benefits and issues of relaxing RFC 3550 compound packet rules, and defines the SDP attribute a=rtcp-rsize for signalling support.

RTCP.why: The document changes the RTCP compound packet rules from RFC 3550 and RFC 4585 to allow Reduced-Size RTCP feedback packets.
RTCP.quote: allow feedback messages to be sent as Reduced-Size RTCP packets under certain conditions when using the RTP/AVPF

SDP.why: It defines a new SDP attribute with offer/answer rules, which is a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: This document defines the "a=rtcp-rsize" Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] attribute to indicate if the session participant is capable of supporting Reduced-Size RTCP

rejected.why: The document updates RFC 3711 only to relax the first-packet-must-be-SR/RR rule. It is mostly about RTCP, and SRTP is discussed as an issue and not as the subject.
RTP is the context, but the document is specifically about RTCP, which is the more specific child tag.
ROHC is mentioned only briefly as an issue left for future work.
TFRC for RTP is mentioned only as an example use case.

RFC5507.title: Design Choices When Expanding the DNS
RFC5507.summary: IAB informational RFC comparing mechanisms for extending the DNS with new application data (RDATA subtyping, prefix, suffix, new class, new RR type) and recommending a new Resource Record Type over reusing TXT.

DNS.why: The whole document is about DNS extension design: RR types, RRSets, owner-name prefixes and suffixes, classes, wildcards, and zone boundaries. It is DNS architecture and protocol guidance.
DNS.quote: This document lists different mechanisms to extend the DNS, and concludes that the use of a new DNS Resource Record Type is the best solution.

rejected.why: DNSSEC comes up only as a consideration, such as signing with the same keys and larger responses. The document is not about DNSSEC.
EDNS0 is mentioned only as background on UDP message size limits.
The document explicitly says it does not discuss whether DNS should be used for service discovery. The DNS-SD draft is cited only as an example of structured TXT.
ENUM and NAPTR are given only as examples of subtyping.
The RR type registration process is delegated to RFC 5395 in a one-line section. The document is not about IANA registries.
It is architectural guidance, but it is specific to DNS, so the DNS tag fits better.

RFC5508.title: NAT Behavioral Requirements for ICMP
RFC5508.summary: RFC 5508 (BCP 148) specifies behavioral requirements for NAT devices when handling ICMP Query and ICMP Error messages, including mapping, timeouts, error translation, hairpinning, and RFC 1812 conformance.

NAT.why: The whole document is a set of NAT behavioral requirements (mapping, timeouts, hairpinning, error translation), companion to the TCP and UDP BEHAVE documents.
NAT.quote: This document specifies the behavioral properties required of the Network Address Translator (NAT) devices in conjunction with the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP).

ICMP.why: It classifies ICMP messages into Query, Error and other types. It specifies how each is handled, including payload validation, Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded and code 13 rejection.
ICMP.quote: ICMP Query messages are characterized by an Identifier field in the ICMP header.

rejected.why: Path MTU discovery is discussed only as an application that depends on ICMP errors being forwarded and generated. The document is not about PMTUD itself.
Traceroute and ping are mentioned only as legacy ICMP-based applications that NAT behavior must not break.
The document covers traditional NAT (Basic NAT and NAPT) and does not address carrier-grade NAT.
Checksum validation of ICMP error payloads is a minor detail within the NAT/ICMP requirements.
DS field handling is a single short recommendation (copying the diffserv class) in Section 7.7.
TCP is referenced only for the MSL timeout guideline and for companion documents.

RFC5509.title: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Registration of Instant Messaging and Presence DNS SRV RRs for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5509.summary: Registers the "_sip" protocol label in the IANA Instant Messaging and Presence SRV Protocol Label registries and explains how im: and pres: URIs resolve to SIP URIs via DNS SRV lookups (_im._sip, _pres._sip).

SIMPLE.why: The document concerns SIP-based instant messaging and presence address resolution (SIMPLE), specifying how im:/pres: URIs resolve to SIP via SRV.
SIMPLE.quote: this document defines and registers the "_sip" protocol label in both registries so that computer programs can resolve 'im:' and 'pres:' URIs down to SIP addresses.

DNS.why: Defines DNS SRV service/protocol label usage for locating SIP IM and presence services; SRV lookup is a substantial part of the content.
DNS.quote: the UA performs a SRV lookup for: _im._sip.example.com
DNS.section: 3. DNS SRV Usage of SIP with 'im' and 'pres' URIs

rejected.why: SIP is the target protocol being resolved to, but the document does not specify or extend SIP; SIMPLE is the more specific fit.
Considered as the IM/presence parent, but SIMPLE is the more specific child and already covers the SIP-based IM/presence subject.
The document is a registration action, but the IANA section is boilerplate-like here and the subject is the SRV label usage, not IANA policy.
im: and pres: URIs are resolved, but the document does not define or specify URI schemes.
MSRP is mentioned only as the session IM mode and is not specified or extended.

RFC5510.title: Reed-Solomon Forward Error Correction (FEC) Schemes
RFC5510.summary: Specifies Reed-Solomon FEC schemes (FEC Encoding IDs 2 and 5, and FEC Instance ID 0 under Encoding ID 129) over GF(2^m) for reliable delivery of objects on packet erasure channels, including payload ID, OTI formats, and encoding/decoding algorithms.

FEC.why: The whole document defines Reed-Solomon FEC schemes for packet erasure recovery, including FEC Payload ID, OTI and codec specification.
FEC.quote: This document describes a Fully-Specified Forward Error Correction (FEC) Scheme for the Reed-Solomon FEC codes over GF(2^^m), where m is in {2..16}

rejected.why: The schemes plug into the RFC 5052 FEC building block for content delivery protocols, not the FECFRAME framework for real-time streaming.
LDPC is only cited as a contrasting sparse-graph scheme (RFC 5170); this document is not about it.
Raptor codes (RFC 5053) are only mentioned for comparison.
ALC is a protocol the FEC OTI can be carried in (EXT_FTI); the document does not specify ALC.
FLUTE is only a carrier for FEC OTI via the FDT Instance; not specified here.
NORM is mentioned as a candidate CDP using EXT_FTI; the document does not specify it.

RFC5511.title: Routing Backus-Naur Form (RBNF): A Syntax Used to Form Encoding Rules in Various Routing Protocol Specifications
RFC5511.summary: RFC 5511 formally defines Routing BNF (RBNF), the BNF variant used in RSVP, RSVP-TE, GMPLS, LMP and PCEP specifications to describe message syntax, with its rules, operators, and precedence.

RBNF.why: The document exists to formally define RBNF: rule naming, operators, editorial conventions and precedence.
RBNF.quote: This document provides such a specification and names the BNF variant Routing BNF (RBNF).

rejected.why: ABNF (RFC 5234) is only discussed as an alternative; the document defines a different variant, not ABNF.
RSVP-TE messages supply examples and motivation, but the document does not specify or extend the protocol.
PCEP is named as a protocol that uses RBNF, but it is not specified or changed here.
GMPLS signaling is cited only as an existing use of the notation.
RSVP is the origin of the notation and a source of examples, not a subject of the document.

RFC5512.title: The BGP Encapsulation Subsequent Address Family Identifier (SAFI) and the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute
RFC5512.summary: Defines the BGP Encapsulation SAFI (7) and the Tunnel Encapsulation path attribute (23), plus Color and Encapsulation extended communities, so BGP speakers can signal tunnel (L2TPv3, GRE, IP-in-IP) encapsulation information to each other.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new SAFI, a new optional transitive path attribute and new extended communities, so it is a BGP extension.
BGP.quote: this document specifies a method by which BGP speakers can signal encapsulation information to each other

softwire.why: The work was done in the softwire WG to support softwire mesh tunnelling across IPv4/IPv6 cores. The softwire tag covers tunnelling across a network of the other address family. The body only mentions the mesh case briefly, so this is a lower-confidence secondary tag.
softwire.quote: Security considerations applicable to softwires can be found in the mesh framework [MESH].

rejected.why: GRE is one of the tunnel types signalled, but the document does not specify or extend GRE itself. It only carries the GRE key in a BGP sub-TLV.
L2TPv3 session ID and cookie are signalled via BGP, but L2TP is not specified or changed here.
IP-in-IP is just one of the tunnel types that can be signalled.
The document defines two opaque extended communities (Color, Encapsulation), but its focus is the SAFI and the tunnel attribute, not communities as a subject.
The tunnels are the subject being signalled, but the document is about BGP signalling, which BGP already covers. It does not define a tunnelling mechanism.
The IPv6 AFI is used, but only as an address family option, not as a subject of the document.

RFC5513.title: IANA Considerations for Three Letter Acronyms
RFC5513.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing an IANA registry for Three Letter Acronyms (TLAs), with a mock formal definition, reserved values and allocation policies.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st satirical RFC with whimsical expansions of acronyms and mock reasoning such as World Acronym Depletion.
humor.quote: this document specifies a Badly Construed Proposal (BCP) for the management of a registry of TLAs within the IETF

IANA.why: The document is framed as IANA considerations: it defines a new registry, reserved values and allocation policies (Experimental Use, First Come First Served, IETF Review), though as parody.
IANA.quote: The Internet TLA Registry (ITR) should track the following information:

rejected.why: It jokingly defines acronyms, but it is a parody and not a real glossary or requirements-language document.
TCP and ST2 appear only as jokes about acronym counts and as reserved-value examples.
It is mentioned only in the acknowledgements as the origin of the joke.
It mocks RFC acronym usage and the RFC Editor terminology list, but it is not about RFC format or publication.

RFC5514.title: IPv6 over Social Networks
RFC5514.summary: An April 1st RFC proposing to turn social networking platforms into IPv6 networks, with users as routers, friend links as point-to-point links, SNA-ID-based addressing, RIPng as the IGP, and a Facebook prototype.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical proposal with hours-to-days latency and users manually 'running the CPU'; it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: This document proposes to vastly increase the number of IPv6 hosts by transforming all Social Networking platforms into IPv6 networks.

IPv6.why: The document defines IPv6 addressing (global and link-local) and IPv6 packet carriage over a social network, so IPv6 readers would look for it.
IPv6.quote: the IPv6 global address of the router loopback will be a /64 prefix (such as 2001: db8:face:b00c::/64) followed by the SNA identification.

RIP.why: A section is devoted to choosing the IGP and recommends RIPng over OSPFv3 for the high-latency environment.
RIP.quote: IPoSN SHOULD implement RIPng [RFC2080], which is relatively immune to jitter and does not rely on flooding messages to all neighboring routers.

rejected.why: NAT66 gateway is mentioned only briefly and declared out of scope.
Mentioned only to say it SHOULD NOT be used; the document is not about it.
Only a one-line pointer that DTN routing protocols MAY be used; not a substantial subject.
Prototype ping and traceroute output are shown as illustrations, but the document does not specify or extend traceroute.
An ICMP echo example appears only as a latency illustration.
UDP is recommended over TCP in one sentence; the document does not address UDP itself.

RFC5515.title: Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) Access Line Information Attribute Value Pair (AVP) Extensions
RFC5515.summary: Defines new L2TP AVPs and two control messages (CSUN, CSURQ) that let a DSL BRAS/LAC pass subscriber Access Line identification and speed information to the LNS, and report connection speed changes.

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TP (v2 and v3) with new AVPs and two new control messages, CSUN and CSURQ.
L2TP.quote: describes a set of Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) Attribute Value Pair (AVP) extensions designed to carry the subscriber Access Line identification and characterization information

DSL.why: The AVPs carry DSL line characteristics (data rates, interleaving delay, ADSL/VDSL type) from TR-101 for DSL equipment vendors' interoperability.
DSL.quote: Access Nodes (ANs), referred to as Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexers (DSLAMs) in DSL, are adding enhancement features

rejected.why: ANCP is one of the sources of access line information the LAC may receive. The document does not specify it.
PPPoE vendor-specific tags are only an input source for the information. The document does not define anything about PPPoE.
DHCP relay options are only an input source for the information.
RADIUS is mentioned only as the existing way the BRAS forwards this information (RFC 4679). The document does not specify it.
The IANA section only requests L2TP registry values, which is boilerplate.

RFC5516.title: Diameter Command Code Registration for the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Evolved Packet System (EPS)
RFC5516.summary: Registers IANA Diameter command codes (316-324) for the new 3GPP EPS vendor-specific Diameter applications S6a/S6d and S13/S13' between MME/SGSN and HSS/EIR.

Diameter.why: The document extends the Diameter protocol's command code namespace for new Diameter applications, so Diameter readers would look for it.
Diameter.quote: This document registers a set of IANA Diameter Command Codes to be used in new vendor-specific Diameter applications defined for the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)

cellular.why: The command codes serve 3GPP Evolved Packet System interfaces (MME/SGSN to HSS/EIR), which concern cellular network interworking.
cellular.quote: the 3GPP S6a/S6d application (vendor-specific application id: 16777251) enables the transfer of subscriber-related data between the Mobile Management Entity (MME)

rejected.why: The IANA registration is the document's mechanism, but the subject is Diameter command codes for 3GPP, not IANA registry policy or stewardship.
Diameter is already tagged as the more specific technology under AAA; the document does not address AAA frameworks generally.
The document concerns EPS/LTE and SGSN interfaces, not SIM-based authentication or second-generation interworking specifically.

RFC5517.title: Cisco Systems' Private VLANs: Scalable Security in a Multi-Client Environment
RFC5517.summary: Informational description of Cisco's Private VLANs, a Layer 2 forwarding-constraint mechanism (primary/isolated/community VLAN pairs and promiscuous/isolated/community ports) that isolates devices sharing one IP subnet.

Ethernet.why: The document specifies an Ethernet switch mechanism (802.1Q VLAN pairing and port types) for Layer 2 isolation, and the Ethernet tag is the closest fit for this.
Ethernet.quote: This document describes a mechanism to achieve device isolation through the application of special Layer 2 forwarding constraints.

rejected.why: The shared-subnet address efficiency is a benefit of the design, but the document is about Layer 2 isolation, not IP address architecture.
The parent tag is implied by Ethernet, and the document is specifically about Ethernet VLAN switching.
A DHCP server on a promiscuous port is only mentioned as an example deployment.
Proxy-ARP and ARP poisoning are mentioned only in passing, in routing and security remarks.
The document notes in passing that routing considerations apply to IPv4 and IPv6, but it is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: VLANs / Private VLANs (Layer 2 bridging and port isolation)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for VLANs or Layer 2 switching and bridging. Ethernet is only an approximate fit.

RFC5518.title: Vouch By Reference
RFC5518.summary: Defines Vouch By Reference (VBR), a protocol where email senders add a VBR-Info header field naming third-party certifiers and receivers verify the vouching via DNS TXT queries under _vouch labels, tied to a domain validated by DKIM, DomainKeys, SPF or Sender ID.

email authentication.why: VBR certifies the owner of a domain associated with received mail, building on DKIM/SPF/Sender ID validation; this is email domain assurance and no specific child tag (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC, ARF) fits as the subject.
email authentication.quote: VBR is a protocol for adding third-party certification to email.

spam.why: Vouching reputation is used to adjust spam scoring, and the DNS-based lookup of certifier lists resembles reputation services.
spam.quote: If a recipient uses the results of vouching to adjust spam scores on incoming email, that recipient is placing a great deal of operational trust

message format.why: The document defines a new trace header field with ABNF syntax and registers it, a substantial part of the specification.
message format.quote: A sender provides certification attestations through the use of a new RFC 5322 ([RFC5322]) mail header field, "VBR-Info:".

rejected.why: Used as one mechanism to validate the domain; VBR is not about DKIM itself.
Only one of several validation mechanisms referenced, not specified or extended here.
DNS TXT lookup is the substrate for distributing certification data; no new RR type or DNS behavior is defined.
Similar in being a DNS-based list lookup, but the document defines a certification query, not a blocklist/whitelist of sending hosts.

RFC5519.title: Multicast Group Membership Discovery MIB
RFC5519.summary: Defines the MGMD-STD-MIB SMIv2 module for managing IGMP (v1-v3) and MLD (v1-v2) on hosts and routers, including source-filter tables and proxy support, obsoleting RFC 2933 and RFC 3019.

MIB.why: The document's sole content is an SMIv2 MIB module (MGMD-STD-MIB) with tables, objects, and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

IGMP.why: The MIB manages IGMP hosts and routers, including querier state, timers, and source filtering, so IGMP readers would want it.
IGMP.quote: it describes objects used for managing the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) version 1 [RFC1112], version 2 [RFC2236], or version 3 [RFC3376]

MLD.why: MLD is managed alongside IGMP through a generic MGMD interface, covering MLDv1 and MLDv2.
MLD.quote: the Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) protocol version 1 [RFC2710] or version 2 [RFC3810]

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP behavior. The MIB tag covers it.
Source filtering in IGMPv3/MLDv2 is represented in the source-list tables, but the document does not specify SSM itself.
The parent topic is implied by the IGMP and MLD tags.
MLD is IPv6-specific, but the document is about group membership management, not IPv6 in general.

RFC5520.title: Preserving Topology Confidentiality in Inter-Domain Path Computation Using a Path-Key-Based Mechanism
RFC5520.summary: Defines the Path-Key mechanism, in which a PCE replaces a Confidential Path Segment of an inter-domain TE LSP path with a token (Path-Key Subobject) carried in PCEP and RSVP-TE EROs, and extends PCEP so the token can later be expanded, preserving topology confidentiality.

PCE.why: The RFC extends PCEP with a PATH-KEY object, new RP bit, PKS subobjects and a NO-PATH-VECTOR flag, and specifies PCE behaviour for creating and expanding path-keys.
PCE.quote: This document defines a mechanism to hide the contents of a segment of a path, called the Confidential Path Segment (CPS).

RSVP-TE.why: Path-keys are signalled in RSVP-TE explicit route objects, and the LSR must expand them during LSP setup. The signalling extension itself is in a companion document, so this is secondary.
RSVP-TE.quote: the PKS will be carried in an RSVP-TE Path message

rejected.why: MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs are the context for path computation. The document's subject is PCE path-key handling, not MPLS itself.
GMPLS is mentioned as the setting, but nothing in the document is specific to GMPLS.
RBNF is only the notation used for the message formats, so it is a substrate and not the subject.
The Manageability section calls for a new MIB module for inspecting path-keys, but it does not define one.
ASes and ASBRs appear only as examples of domains and boundary routers, and BGP is not discussed.

RFC5521.title: Extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for Route Exclusions
RFC5521.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (the Exclude Route Object, the Explicit Exclusion Route subobject in the IRO, and Path-Key use in the XRO) that let a PCC tell a PCE which nodes, resources and SRLGs to exclude from a computed path.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with the new XRO object and EXRS subobject, and specifies PCE processing rules for them. PCE (with PCEP) is the subject of this RFC.
PCE.quote: This document presents PCEP extensions for route exclusions.

rejected.why: Only referenced for the RFC 4874 exclude-route extension that this work parallels. The document defines no RSVP-TE changes, only mentions that a PCC may signal an XRO.
The abstract mentions MPLS/GMPLS networks as the context, but the document does not specify anything GMPLS-specific.
Traffic engineering is the general context. The PCE tag is more specific for this document and covers the subject.
MPLS LSPs are the setting for path computation, but the document does not address MPLS itself.
The Manageability section only says the PCEP MIB should be extended. No MIB is defined here.

gaps.name: PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has PCE as a child of traffic engineering and describes it as 'PCE architecture and PCEP'. PCE and PCEP are covered by that single tag, which is the one used here. Reviewers should confirm that this tag is intended to cover PCEP extension documents.

RFC5522.title: Network Mobility Route Optimization Requirements for Operational Use in Aeronautics and Space Exploration Mobile Networks
RFC5522.summary: Informational requirements document specifying the required and desirable properties of a Network Mobility (NEMO) Route Optimization solution for aeronautical and space exploration networks.

NEMO.why: The whole document defines requirements for route optimization in NEMO (mobile routers, MRHA tunnels, MNPs) for aircraft and spacecraft networks.
NEMO.quote: requirements and desired properties of Network Mobility (NEMO) Route Optimization techniques for use in global-networked communications systems for aeronautics and space exploration

rejected.why: NEMO builds on Mobile IPv6 and RO is compared to it, but the document is about NEMO route optimization, not Mobile IPv6 itself.
Req2 covers multihoming of the mobile router, but it is one requirement among nine, and the document is not about multihoming architectures.
BGP is mentioned only as a technique to avoid for RO (Req6 scalability); the document does not specify or analyse it.
Mentioned as a policy database analogy and for adaptability; not a subject of the document.
IPv6 is the assumed substrate for addressing; the document does not address IPv6 itself.
A possible ATN-specific PKI is discussed briefly in the security rationale, but only as an assumption, not a main subject.

gaps.name: Aeronautical and space communications (ATN, ICAO, CCSDS)
gaps.why: The document's scenarios and requirements are driven by aviation and space data networks, and the taxonomy has no tag for these domains.

RFC5523.title: OSPFv3-Based Layer 1 VPN Auto-Discovery
RFC5523.summary: Defines an OSPFv3 L1VPN LSA (function code 14) and an L1VPN IPv6 Info TLV so PEs can auto-discover Layer 1 VPN membership and port mappings, paralleling the OSPFv2 mechanism and adding IPv6 support.

L1VPN.why: The document specifies the auto-discovery mechanism for L1VPN basic mode, carrying VPN membership and port mapping (PIT) information between PEs.
L1VPN.quote: This document defines an OSPFv3-based (Open Shortest Path First version 3) Layer 1 Virtual Private Network (L1VPN) auto-discovery mechanism.

OSPFv3.why: It extends OSPFv3 with a new LSA function code and TLV, and covers flooding, processing and migration from OSPFv2.
OSPFv3.quote: The approach used in this document to provide OSPFv3-based L1VPN auto-discovery uses a new type of Link State Advertisement (LSA), which is referred to as an OSPFv3 L1VPN LSA.

rejected.why: The GMPLS backbone is the setting and TE Link TLVs are reused, but the document does not specify GMPLS itself.
OSPFv3 is the more specific child tag and applies; the OSPFv2 mechanism is only referenced as the parallel.
IPv6 support is only addressing in the TLV; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
MIB modules are mentioned only as informative inspection options in manageability considerations.
TE Link TLVs are optionally carried but defined elsewhere (RFC 3630, 4203, 5329).

RFC5524.title: Extended URLFETCH for Binary and Converted Parts
RFC5524.summary: Defines an IMAP extension (URLAUTH=BINARY) to URLFETCH that lets clients request BODYPARTSTRUCTURE, decoded BINARY content, or raw BODY for a URLAUTH URL, so non-mail applications can get usable data.

IMAP.why: The document extends the IMAP URLFETCH command with new parameters, response metadata, and a capability. It is an IMAP extension.
IMAP.quote: Such servers accept additional, per-URL parameters to the URLFETCH command and will provide, upon request, specific data for each URL dereferenced.

rejected.why: Content transfer encodings and media types are handled, but MIME is only the content being decoded. The document does not specify anything new about MIME.
URLAUTH URLs are dereferenced, but the document defines no URI syntax or scheme. It only adds parameters to the fetch command.
Base64 is only one of the transfer encodings a server must decode. The document is not about it.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section.
The IANA section registers an IMAP capability, not a media type.

RFC5525.title: Reliable Server Pooling MIB Module Definition
RFC5525.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module (RSERPOOL-MIB) for managing RSerPool implementations, with tables for ENRP servers, pool elements and pool users.

MIB.why: The document's sole purpose is to define a MIB module in SMIv2, with tables, textual conventions and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This document defines an SMIv2-compliant (Structure of Management Information Version 2) Management Information Base (MIB) module providing access to managed objects in an RSerPool implementation.

RSerPool.why: The managed objects model ASAP/ENRP components: ENRP servers, pool elements, pool users, pool handles and policies. Readers of RSerPool material would want this MIB.
RSerPool.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module that describes managed objects for RSerPool implementations.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, and the MIB tag sits under SNMP and covers it.
SCTP ports appear only as object values, since ASAP and ENRP run over SCTP. The document says nothing new about SCTP itself.
The more specific MIB tag already covers this topic.
IPv4 and IPv6 appear only as InetAddressType values in the tables. The document is not about IPv6.

RFC5526.title: The E.164 to Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI) Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Application for Infrastructure ENUM
RFC5526.summary: Informational RFC defining the Infrastructure ENUM use case and proposing a parallel DNS namespace to e164.arpa so carriers can provision ENUM records for telephone numbers independently of end users.

ENUM.why: The whole document defines and proposes Infrastructure ENUM, a variant of E.164 number mapping in the DNS using a parallel apex to e164.arpa.
ENUM.quote: Infrastructure ENUM be implemented by means of a parallel namespace to e164.arpa dedicated to Infrastructure ENUM

rejected.why: DNS is only the substrate for ENUM NAPTR lookups. The document adds no DNS protocol behaviour, only a new zone apex for ENUM.
VoIP interconnection is the motivation, but SIP is never specified or discussed.
