The document concerns VoIP interconnection points, but it does not address SPEERMINT peering architecture.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and only notes that Enumservices are valid for Infrastructure ENUM.
E.164 numbers are mentioned, but the tel URI scheme is not the subject.

RFC5527.title: Combined User and Infrastructure ENUM in the e164.arpa Tree
RFC5527.summary: Informational RFC defining an interim Infrastructure ENUM solution that branches a subtree labelled "i" under the country-code level of e164.arpa, with a modified E.164-to-domain algorithm and DNAME-based transition to the long-term solution.

ENUM.why: The whole document specifies a modification of the ENUM E.164-to-domain mapping algorithm for Infrastructure ENUM in e164.arpa, including the POSITION determination and examples.
ENUM.quote: This memo defines an interim solution for Infrastructure ENUM in order to allow a combined User and Infrastructure ENUM implementation in e164.arpa as a national choice.

DNS.why: A substantial part covers DNS zone structure, DNAME placement, required resolver DNAME and synthesized-CNAME handling, and loop detection for the migration.
DNS.quote: This SHOULD be done by placing DNAME [RFC2672] records at the branch (the "i") label pointing to the appropriate domain name in the long-term I-ENUM tree.

rejected.why: The document works with E.164 numbers and digit strings, not the tel URI scheme.
SIP appears only in a privacy example URI (sip:+441632960084@example.com). The document is not about SIP.
e164.arpa and the 'i' label are infrastructure delegation names, not special-use domain name registrations.

RFC5528.title: Camellia Counter Mode and Camellia Counter with CBC-MAC Mode Algorithms
RFC5528.summary: Informational RFC describing the Camellia block cipher in Counter (CTR) and Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) modes and providing test vectors for both.

Camellia.why: The whole document specifies Camellia-CTR and Camellia-CCM and gives test vectors for them. Camellia is the specific cipher the document is about.
Camellia.quote: This document describes the use of the Camellia block cipher algorithm in Counter (CTR) mode and Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) mode.

rejected.why: AES is mentioned only as a comparison and as the cipher in the CTR and CCM specifications that Camellia replaces. The document is not about AES.
IPsec and ESP appear only in the padding discussion and in the references. The document does not specify anything for IPsec.
TLS is cited only as an existing use of Camellia, so it is not a subject of this document.
The document does not address key establishment or provisioning. It only lists the keys used in the test vectors.

gaps.name: Camellia block cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Camellia tag. The nearest, Camellia under cryptography, is described as covering the cipher, its modes and its cipher suites, so it fits and I used it. If that id were not valid, the fallback would be the cryptography parent topic.

gaps.name: Block cipher modes of operation (CTR, CCM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for block cipher modes in general. This matters because the document's main content is the CTR and CCM modes and their test vectors.

RFC5529.title: Modes of Operation for Camellia for Use with IPsec
RFC5529.summary: Specifies use of the Camellia block cipher in CBC, CTR and CCM modes as optional IKEv2 and ESP encryption transforms for IPsec, including keying material layout, key length attribute and IKEv2 transform IDs.

Camellia.why: The whole document defines how the Camellia cipher and its modes are used in IPsec, which is what the Camellia tag covers (its modes and IPsec use).
Camellia.quote: This document describes the use of the Camellia block cipher algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, Counter (CTR) mode, and Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) mode

ESP.why: The modes are defined as new ESP encryption transforms, with padding and ICV conventions, so ESP readers will want this document.
ESP.quote: additional, optional-to-implement IKEv2 [2] and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) [3] mechanisms to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, and connectionless integrity

IKE.why: A substantial section specifies IKEv2 keying material derivation, transform type 1 IDs and the Key Length attribute for Camellia.
IKE.quote: This section describes the transform ID and conventions used to generate keying material for use with ENCR_CAMELLIA_CBC, ENCR_CAMELLIA_CTR, and ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM

rejected.why: AES CTR and CCM specifications are referenced as templates for Camellia, but the document is not about AES.
Parent of ESP and IKE, which are chosen as more specific tags, so it is implied.
The keying material layout is part of the IKEv2 conventions, which the IKE tag already covers.

RFC5530.title: IMAP Response Codes
RFC5530.summary: RFC 5530 defines and documents a set of new machine-readable IMAP response codes (e.g., UNAVAILABLE, AUTHENTICATIONFAILED, OVERQUOTA) and creates an IANA registry for them.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP by defining new response codes and their ABNF additions to resp-text-code, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document collects and documents a variety of machine-readable response codes, for better interoperation and error reporting.

rejected.why: AUTHENTICATE is used in examples, but the document defines nothing about SASL mechanisms.
It creates an IMAP Response Codes registry, but that is boilerplate-level registration. The document is about IMAP, not IANA guidance.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax, not the subject.
TLS and STARTTLS appear only in the PRIVACYREQUIRED description as a remedy.
IMAP is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.

RFC5531.title: RPC: Remote Procedure Call Protocol Specification Version 2
RFC5531.summary: Specifies ONC RPC version 2, the message protocol (call/reply, authentication fields, record marking, RPC language) used by NFS and others, and sets up IANA registries for RPC program, auth flavor and auth status numbers.

ONC RPC.why: The whole document specifies the ONC RPC v2 message protocol, record marking, authentication fields and RPC language, which is the subject of this tag.
ONC RPC.quote: This document describes the Open Network Computing (ONC) Remote Procedure Call (RPC) version 2 protocol as it is currently deployed and accepted.

rejected.why: IANA number registries are defined, but they are boilerplate-like for the registry of RPC numbers; the document is about RPC itself, not IANA stewardship.
NFS is only a motivating user of RPC, mentioned in examples and pseudo-flavors.
RPCSEC_GSS and GSS-API are only referenced as an authentication flavor defined elsewhere.
TCP and UDP are transports RPC runs over; record marking is RPC's own mechanism.
XDR is the encoding language used, not ASN.1; no relevant tag chosen for XDR.

RFC5532.title: Network File System (NFS) Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) Problem Statement
RFC5532.summary: Informational problem statement explaining why RDMA suits NFS: data copy and protocol overhead in NFS over RPC/XDR, the limits of TOE, and the case for an NFS-over-RDMA transport.

NFS.why: The whole document concerns NFS performance overhead and how NFS (v2/v3/v4) can be mapped onto RDMA transports.
NFS.quote: This document addresses enabling the use of Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) by the Network File System (NFS) protocols.

RDMA.why: It evaluates the benefits of RDMA for file protocols, covering direct data placement, chunks and RDMA Read/Write savings.
RDMA.quote: RDMA is a general solution to the problem of CPU overhead incurred due to data copies, primarily at the receiver.

ONC RPC.why: A substantial part explains how RPC/XDR marshalling causes copies and how an RDMA transport would convey RPC messages with read/write chunks.
ONC RPC.quote: NFS runs as an Open Network Computing (ONC) RPC [RFC5531] application.

rejected.why: TCP and TOE are discussed only as the baseline against which RDMA is compared, not specified or extended.
Not in the taxonomy; mentioned only in Security Considerations.
Mentioned only in passing as a source of alignment problems in NFSv4.
IPsec channel latching appears only in Security Considerations.
QoS is mentioned only in the conclusions as a future need of the file abstraction.
The document motivates an NFS-over-RDMA binding but does not specify it; that is left to the RPCRDMA draft.

RFC5533.title: Shim6: Level 3 Multihoming Shim Protocol for IPv6
RFC5533.summary: Specifies the Shim6 protocol, a host-based layer-3 shim that sets up ULID-pair contexts between peers so IPv6 multihomed hosts with multiple provider-allocated prefixes can fail over between locator pairs while upper layers keep using a stable identifier.

Shim6.why: The whole document specifies the Shim6 protocol: message formats, context establishment, recovery, updates and state machine.
Shim6.quote: This document defines the Shim6 protocol, a layer 3 shim for providing locator agility below the transport protocols

multihoming.why: The protocol is a site-multihoming solution, so readers of multihoming architectures would want it. The Shim6 tag sits beneath it, so this is only a secondary parent tag.
multihoming.quote: so that multihoming can be provided for IPv6 with failover and load-sharing properties

rejected.why: Shim6 runs over IPv6 and defines an extension header, but the document is about multihoming, not the IPv6 specification or addressing in general.
Section 16.1 discusses interaction with IPsec, but this is a small part; IPsec is not what the document is about.
Section 8 covers handling ICMP errors in the shim, but ICMP is only an interacting protocol.
HIP is only the source of the message names and option format, and a design comparison. The document is not about HIP.
Renumbering is discussed as an implication and an explicit non-goal, not as the subject.
The document only assumes there are no IPv6-to-IPv6 NATs on the path, which does not make it about NAT.

gaps.name: CGA/HBA (Cryptographically Generated Addresses, Hash-Based Addresses)
gaps.why: Locator verification relies on CGA and HBA, but the taxonomy has no tag for them. They are defined in other RFCs, though, so the gap is minor here.

RFC5534.title: Failure Detection and Locator Pair Exploration Protocol for IPv6 Multihoming
RFC5534.summary: Specifies REAP, the Shim6 failure detection (keepalives, forced bidirectional detection) and locator pair exploration protocol (Probe messages) for IPv6 multihoming.

multihoming.why: The document defines the REAP part of Shim6 for IPv6 multihoming: detecting failures and exploring alternative address pairs. Taxonomy has Shim6 as a child of multihoming, but the Shim6 tag is the more specific fit, see below.
multihoming.quote: This document specifies how the level 3 multihoming Shim6 protocol (Shim6) detects failures between two communicating nodes.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a possible future source of mechanisms; the document does not specify or extend BFD.
IPv6 is the environment, but the document is about multihoming failure detection, not IPv6 itself.
Neighbor Unreachability Detection is used as a local input only.
ICMP errors are only discussed as unreliable hints.
Mentioned only in security considerations for ignoring spoofed keepalives.

RFC5535.title: Hash-Based Addresses (HBA)
RFC5535.summary: Defines Hash-Based Addresses (HBA), a CGA-compatible mechanism (Multi-Prefix CGA extension) that securely binds multiple IPv6 prefixes' addresses of a multihomed host, for use by Shim6 against redirection attacks.

Shim6.why: HBA is the address-binding security tool for the Shim6 multihoming shim; it specifies set generation, verification and Shim6 usage and security analysis.
Shim6.quote: a mechanism to provide a secure binding between the multiple addresses with different prefixes available to a host within a multihomed site

rejected.why: Parent of Shim6; implied by the Shim6 tag.
SeND is discussed only for CGA compatibility; the document does not specify or extend it.
HBAs are IPv6 addresses, but the document is about the multihoming binding mechanism, which Shim6 covers more specifically.
Dynamic DNS updates are mentioned once as a way to publish addresses; not a substantial subject.
SHA-1 is only the hash primitive used; a brief dependency note, not the subject.
SubjectPublicKeyInfo encoding is borrowed for formatting only.

gaps.name: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA)
gaps.why: The document defines a CGA extension (Multi-Prefix) and a CGA-compatible address scheme, but the taxonomy has no CGA tag.

RFC5536.title: Netnews Article Format
RFC5536.summary: Specifies the syntax and semantics of Netnews articles and their header fields as a restricted subset of the Internet Message Format and MIME, obsoleting RFC 1036.

Netnews.why: The whole document defines the Netnews article format and its news header fields (Newsgroups, Path, Xref, Injection-Info, etc.), so it belongs on the Netnews page.
Netnews.quote: This document specifies the syntax of Netnews articles in the context of the Internet Message Format [RFC5322] and Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME)

rejected.why: NNTP is only referenced for compatibility (message-id length, Xref locators, Lines overview); the document specifies article format, not the transport protocol.
The document builds on RFC 5322 and restricts it, but its subject is Netnews articles. Netnews is the more specific tag.
MIME conformance is required and cited by reference, but the document does not specify MIME itself.
Articles are a subset of email message syntax, but the document concerns Netnews rather than mail.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the syntax and is not the subject.
The header field registrations are boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the main body.

RFC5537.title: Netnews Architecture and Protocols
RFC5537.summary: RFC 5537 defines the Netnews architecture, the duties of posting, injecting, relaying, serving and gateway agents, control messages, and new media types, and sets the requirements on transports such as NNTP; it obsoletes RFC 1036.

Netnews.why: The whole document specifies the Netnews architecture, agent duties (Path handling, duplicate suppression, injection, moderation, gateways) and control messages.
Netnews.quote: "Netnews" is a set of protocols for generating, storing, and retrieving news "articles" whose format is defined in [RFC5536]

media types.why: Section 4 defines application/news-transmission, news-groupinfo and news-checkgroups and obsoletes message/news, a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: This document defines several media types, which have been registered with IANA as provided for in [RFC4288].

rejected.why: NNTP is only the most common transport. The document specifies requirements on transports and does not define or extend NNTP.
Email is used for moderator submission and gatewaying, but it is not the subject of the document.
The article format is defined in RFC 5536. This document covers agent behaviour and protocol.
UUCP is mentioned only as an alternative transport.
Gatewaying between mailing lists and newsgroups is discussed as an example, but it is not the main subject.
MIME is used for encapsulation and the media types, but the document does not specify MIME itself.

gaps.name: Netnews / Usenet architecture and article-propagation protocol
gaps.why: The taxonomy has Netnews and NNTP only as children of messaging. If the tag id 'Netnews' is not actually available, there is no tag for this document's central subject: agent duties, control messages and flood-fill propagation.

RFC5538.title: The 'news' and 'nntp' URI Schemes
RFC5538.summary: Specifies the 'news' and 'nntp' URI schemes (moved from RFC 1738), including syntax, semantics for identifying NNTP articles and newsgroups, and registers the historical 'snews' scheme and the MIME 'news-message-ID' access type.

URI.why: The document defines two URI schemes, their syntax and semantics, and registers a third (snews), so it belongs under URI.
URI.quote: This memo specifies the 'news' and 'nntp' Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes that were originally defined in RFC 1738.

NNTP.why: The schemes identify NNTP resources (articles, groups, wildmat patterns) and the 'nntp' scheme carries server and article number; readers of NNTP would want this URI mapping.
NNTP.quote: User agents like Web browsers supporting these schemes use the NNTP protocol to access the corresponding resources.

rejected.why: The 'news-message-ID' MIME access type registration is a small IANA housekeeping item, not the main subject.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax.
Internationalization is addressed only via percent-encoded UTF-8; the document is not about IRIs.
TLS appears only in the historical 'snews' registration as the substrate.
Message-ID and Netnews article format are referenced for syntax, not specified here.

RFC5539.title: NETCONF over Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC5539.summary: Specifies how to run NETCONF sessions over TLS (manager as TLS client, agent as server, TCP port 6513), including connection initiation/closure, message framing, and certificate-based server and client authentication.

NETCONF.why: The document defines a NETCONF transport mapping over TLS, so it is a NETCONF specification: connection initiation, framing, port assignment, and identity handling for NETCONF sessions.
NETCONF.quote: This document describes how to use the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to secure NETCONF exchanges.

TLS.why: Substantial part of the document profiles TLS use: mandatory TLS version and cipher suite, certificate-based mutual authentication, server identity matching against certificate names, and close_notify handling. Readers of TLS deployment guidance would want it.
TLS.quote: Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] and are REQUIRED to support the mandatory-to-implement cipher suite, which is TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.

rejected.why: This is a transport-mapping document, but NETCONF and TLS tags already cover it more specifically; the topic tag is only for when no technology tag under it applies, and here the child tags suffice.
Certificate validation is delegated to RFC 5280 Section 6; the document only references it for server identity checking and does not profile certificates.
Mentioned only as an alternative NETCONF transport (RFC 4742) in security considerations and as the source of the delimiter sequence; not what the document is about.
NETCONF messages are XML documents, but XML is merely the encoding substrate here.
TCP is only the underlying transport and the IANA port 6513 registration is boilerplate-level; nothing new about TCP is defined.
Only mentioned as an alternative transport for third-party authentication in Security Considerations.

RFC5540.title: 40 Years of RFCs
RFC5540.summary: A short anniversary memo from the RFC Editor marking 40 years of the RFC series, recalling Jon Postel, RFC 2555, and changes in RFC Editor funding, organization and process over the previous decade.

RFC series.why: The whole document is about the history, publication and administration of the RFC series and the RFC Editor function, which fits the RFC series topic.
RFC series.quote: This RFC marks the 40th anniversary of the RFC document series.

internet history.why: It is a retrospective on the origins of the RFC series, Jon Postel's role, and the early ARPANET and Internet era, so history readers would want it.
internet history.quote: The RFC series emerged from the US government-funded research efforts that created the ARPANET and later the Internet.

rejected.why: The ARPANET is mentioned only as the origin of the RFC series. The document does not cover its protocols or operations.
Postel is noted as the original IANA in passing, but the document says nothing about IANA registries or stewardship.
The IETF is mentioned only for context. The document covers the RFC Editor function, not the standards process.

RFC5541.title: Encoding of Objective Functions in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC5541.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (OF-List TLV, OF object, RP flag, new error values and metric types) so a PCE can advertise supported objective functions and PCCs can request and learn the objective function used in path computation, plus definitions of six standard objective functions.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with new TLV, object, flag, error values and metrics, so it belongs under PCE architecture and PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document defines extensions to the PCE communication Protocol (PCEP) to allow a PCE to indicate the set of objective functions it supports.

rejected.why: MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs are the context for path computation, but the document is about PCEP, not GMPLS itself.
TE LSPs are what is computed, but the document does not specify MPLS behaviour.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats; the document is not about it.
Superseded by the more specific PCE tag, which sits under it.
IANA registry sections are boilerplate and the main body is about PCEP encodings.

gaps.name: PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists PCE only as a child of traffic engineering and the PCE tag was used. I verified no PCE tag id exists in the taxonomy as written (the entry is 'PCE' under traffic engineering with description 'PCE (Path Computation Element) architecture and PCEP').

RFC5542.title: Definitions of Textual Conventions for Pseudowire (PW) Management
RFC5542.summary: Defines the PW-TC-STD-MIB module, a set of SMIv2 textual conventions for representing common pseudowire management information (indexes, operational status, control word status, fragmentation status) for reuse in PW-related MIB modules.

pseudowire.why: The textual conventions model PW identifiers, operational status, control word negotiation and fragmentation state, so readers of the pseudowire subject would want this RFC.
pseudowire.quote: defines textual conventions used for pseudowire (PW) technology and for Pseudowire Edge-to-Edge Emulation (PWE3) MIB modules

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module of SMIv2 textual conventions meant to be imported by other MIB modules.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module that contains textual conventions (TCs) to represent commonly used pseudowire (PW) management information.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
RFC 4447 LDP signalling is only referenced for the control word and generalized FEC semantics. The document does not specify LDP.
The PSN and labels are only background for the PW textual conventions. The document does not specify MPLS.
This is an SMIv2 MIB module, not a YANG data model.

gaps.name: Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a pseudowire tag under MPLS, but my tag list above uses 'pseudowire', which is valid only as the taxonomy id 'pseudowire'. It is a child of MPLS in the taxonomy and fits this document.

RFC5543.title: BGP Traffic Engineering Attribute
RFC5543.summary: Defines a new optional non-transitive BGP Traffic Engineering attribute carrying GMPLS Interface Switching Capability Descriptor information, for use with VPN (e.g., L1VPN) reachability routes.

BGP.why: The document specifies a new BGP path attribute, including its encoding, aggregation and scalability implications.
BGP.quote: This document defines a new BGP attribute, the Traffic Engineering attribute, that enables BGP to carry Traffic Engineering information.

L1VPN.why: The attribute's motivating use case and scope is VPN reachability, specifically L1VPN auto-discovery, and the attribute is restricted to VPN routes.
L1VPN.quote: In certain cases (e.g., Layer-1 VPNs (L1VPNs) [RFC5195]), it may be useful to augment the VPN reachability information carried in BGP

rejected.why: The attribute reuses the GMPLS Interface Switching Capability Descriptor encoding, but the document does not specify or extend GMPLS itself.
Traffic engineering is only the kind of information carried. The document is about a BGP attribute, so the BGP tag fits better.
RFC 4203 is only referenced as the source of the descriptor format. The document does not extend OSPF.
RFC 5307 is only referenced as the source of the descriptor format. The document does not extend IS-IS.
The generic VPN tag is replaced by the more specific L1VPN child tag.

RFC5544.title: Syntax for Binding Documents with Time-Stamps
RFC5544.summary: Defines TimeStampedData, a new CMS content type (id-ct-timestampedData) that binds a file with one or more RFC 3161 time-stamp tokens or other temporal evidence, with generation, verification and validity-extension procedures.

CMS.why: The document defines a new CMS content type, timestamped-data, alongside the existing CMS types, with its ASN.1 syntax and OID. CMS readers would want this.
CMS.quote: The proposed envelope is based on the Cryptographic Message Syntax as defined in RFC 5652.

PKI.why: A substantial part covers RFC 3161 time-stamp tokens, TSA certificates, CRLs and chained time-stamping for long-term validity. No narrower PKI tag fits these.
PKI.quote: time-stamp token can itself be time-stamped to extend the validity of the TSA's signature.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation used to define the structure. The document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
It is related, since RFC 4998 ERS is an alternative and is supported as evidence. This document defines a CMS envelope for time-stamp tokens, not the LTANS archive and notary services.
CRLs and certificates are used for validating TSA certificates, but the document does not profile X.509.
The mediaType field only carries a MIME type as metadata. The document does not register or define media types.
The dataUri field references a URI, which is only a use of URIs.

gaps.name: Time-stamping (RFC 3161 TSP)
gaps.why: The document is about binding documents to time-stamp tokens, but the taxonomy has no tag for trusted time-stamping or the Time-Stamp Protocol.

RFC5545.title: Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
RFC5545.summary: RFC 5545 defines the iCalendar data format (text/calendar) for exchanging calendaring and scheduling data: events, to-dos, journals, free/busy, time zones, alarms, recurrence rules, and their properties, parameters and value types.

iCalendar.why: The whole document specifies the iCalendar core object, its components, properties, parameters and value types.
iCalendar.quote: This document defines the iCalendar data format for representing and exchanging calendaring and scheduling information such as events, to-dos, journal entries, and free/busy information

rejected.why: VTIMEZONE is one component of iCalendar, not time zone data distribution as a subject; the document defers global time zone registry to future study.
The format is defined as a MIME content type, but MIME is only the carrier; media type registration is boilerplate-like IANA content.
SMTP is only one possible transport mentioned; iMIP/iTIP are in other documents.
DATE-TIME and DURATION value types are iCalendar-specific, not the RFC 3339 timestamp format.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the grammar.
vCard is only referenced as an alternate representation for CONTACT/LOCATION.

RFC5546.title: iCalendar Transport-Independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP)
RFC5546.summary: RFC 5546 specifies iTIP, the transport-independent application protocol that uses iCalendar objects and METHOD values (PUBLISH, REQUEST, REPLY, ADD, CANCEL, REFRESH, COUNTER, DECLINECOUNTER) for group scheduling of events, to-dos, journals and free/busy time, obsoleting RFC 2446.

iCalendar.why: The whole document defines iTIP, the scheduling protocol layered on iCalendar objects, with per-method restriction tables for VEVENT, VTODO, VJOURNAL and VFREEBUSY.
iCalendar.quote: This document specifies how calendaring systems use iCalendar [RFC5545] objects to interoperate with other calendaring systems.

rejected.why: iMIP email binding is only referenced as a separate document; this RFC is transport-independent.
text/calendar is mentioned only as the carrier of iTIP messages; no media type registration is defined here.
VTIMEZONE restrictions appear only as part of the iTIP component tables; no time zone data distribution is defined.
IANA registries for REQUEST-STATUS and METHOD are boilerplate-level additions, not the document's subject.

RFC5547.title: A Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer Mechanism to Enable File Transfer
RFC5547.summary: Defines new SDP media attributes and offer/answer procedures to negotiate push or pull file transfers between endpoints, using MSRP as the default transfer mechanism with conventions for its use.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with file-selector, file-transfer-id, file-disposition, file-date, file-icon and file-range attributes and defines offer/answer procedures for them.
SDP.quote: This document provides a mechanism to negotiate the transfer of one or more files between two endpoints by using the Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer/answer model

MSRP.why: Section 8.7 gives conventions for using MSRP for file transfer: one file per MSRP message, chunking, max-size, abort handling. MSRP itself is not extended, but readers of MSRP need these usage rules.
MSRP.quote: The Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) is defined as the default mechanism to actually carry the files between the endpoints.

rejected.why: SIP only carries the offer/answer in examples and for re-INVITE and OPTIONS; the document does not specify or extend SIP.
The 'type' selector uses MIME media types, but the document does not register or define media types.
MIME headers such as Content-Disposition and multipart/related are borrowed for attribute semantics and the icon wrapper, but MIME is not the subject.
SHA-1 is only used for the hash selector, as a building block.
ABNF is used only to write the attribute syntax.

RFC5548.title: Routing Requirements for Urban Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC5548.summary: Informational ROLL document setting out application-specific IPv6 routing requirements for urban low-power and lossy networks (smart metering, environmental sensing, actuators), covering scalability, constrained routing, autonomous configuration, multicast/anycast, dynamicity, latency and security.

IoT.why: The document covers requirements for networks of constrained sensing and actuating nodes. This is IoT guidance for constrained devices, and no more specific technology tag fits. The RPL tag is not appropriate because RPL is not specified here.
IoT.quote: The application-specific routing requirements for Urban Low-Power and Lossy Networks (U-LLNs) are presented in this document.

routing architecture.why: Section 6 sets out routing design requirements (scalability, constrained routing, multiple paths, convergence), which are matters of routing architecture and scalability.
routing architecture.quote: the routing protocol(s) MUST support parameter-constrained routing

rejected.why: RPL is the protocol later designed to meet these requirements, but this document does not specify or mention it.
The document mentions IEEE 802.15.4 only as an example link, and it does not cover 6LoWPAN adaptation.
Multicast and anycast support is one requirement among many, and the document is not about multicast routing.
The requirements are for IPv6 routing, but the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
Anycast is listed as a required delivery mode, but only briefly, and the document is not about anycast operation.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate-like for this purpose, and the main body is not about operational security practices.

gaps.name: Low-power and lossy network (LLN) routing requirements
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ROLL routing requirements for constrained networks. IoT is the nearest fit, but it misses the routing focus.

RFC5549.title: Advertising IPv4 Network Layer Reachability Information with an IPv6 Next Hop
RFC5549.summary: Extends MP-BGP so IPv4 and VPN-IPv4 NLRI can be advertised with an IPv6 next hop, defining next-hop length-based encoding and a new Extended Next Hop Encoding BGP capability.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP/MP-BGP next hop encoding and defines a new BGP capability (Extended Next Hop Encoding), so it is squarely about the BGP protocol.
BGP.quote: This document specifies the extensions necessary to allow advertising IPv4 NLRI or VPN-IPv4 NLRI with a Next Hop address that belongs to the IPv6 protocol.

softwire.why: Motivated by softwire mesh scenarios with IPv4 islands across an IPv6 core; usage examples cover this, though the mechanism is BGP-specific.
softwire.quote: The extensions defined in this document may be used as discussed in [MESH-FMWK] for the interconnection of IPV4 islands over an IPv6 backbone.

rejected.why: VPN-IPv4 NLRI (SAFI 128) is one case covered, but the document only changes next hop encoding rather than specifying the VPN technology.
Relevant context (IPv4 over IPv6 core), but the document is about BGP encoding; softwire is the more specific child and is the one chosen.
IPv6 is only the address family of the next hop; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
Section 5 briefly mentions route reflector next hop handling, but this is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC5550.title: The Internet Email to Support Diverse Service Environments (Lemonade) Profile
RFC5550.summary: Defines the Lemonade Profile, a set of required IMAP, Message Submission and Sieve extensions and usage modes (quick resync, forward without download, notifications, compression) letting constrained mobile clients efficiently access and submit mail.

IMAP.why: The profile mandates a large set of IMAP extensions (CONDSTORE, QRESYNC, NOTIFY, CATENATE, URLAUTH, new keywords and URL-PARTIAL capability) and is largely about how IMAP stores serve constrained clients.
IMAP.quote: Lemonade Message Stores MUST provide a service as described in [IMAP], and MUST support the following.

SMTP.why: The profile specifies required SMTP/Submission extensions (BURL, CHUNKING, PIPELINING, DSN, SIZE) and forward-without-download submission flows.
SMTP.quote: Lemonade Submission Servers MUST provide a service as described in [SUBMIT], and MUST support the following.

Sieve.why: A whole section requires Sieve and specific extensions (vacation, enotify, variables, relational, imap4flags) at delivery.
Sieve.quote: Lemonade Message Delivery Agents MUST support Sieve mail filtering language as described in [SIEVE]

rejected.why: TLS and TLS compression are only recommended as security/compression substrate for the mail protocols; nothing new is defined about TLS.
BINARY and CONVERT touch MIME parts, but the document is about IMAP/submission extensions, not MIME itself.
Parent of the chosen specific tags (IMAP, SMTP, Sieve); implied.
SASL-IR is just one required IMAP extension; the document is not about SASL.
Mentions XMPP/SIP only as Sieve notification targets; not a subject of the document.
COMPRESS=DEFLATE and TLS compression are mentioned briefly as requirements, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Lemonade / mobile email (OMA MEM)
gaps.why: The document profiles email for mobile and constrained clients, including push notifications, but the taxonomy has no mobile email tag.

RFC5551.title: Lemonade Notifications Architecture
RFC5551.summary: Informational Lemonade architecture document describing notification and filtering mechanisms (in-IMAP and out-of-IMAP, Sieve-based filters) for email on mobile devices, plus server-to-server notifications between mail systems and notification systems.

email.why: The document is an email architecture for notifications, push email and filtering for mobile clients (Lemonade), and no more specific email child covers the architecture as a whole.
email.quote: Notification and filtering mechanisms can make email more enjoyable on mobile and other constrained devices

IMAP.why: In-IMAP notifications via IDLE and NOTIFY, view filters through contexts, and out-of-IMAP notifications are a substantial part of the architecture around IMAP.
IMAP.quote: the Mail User Agent (MUA) (client) issues IDLE [IDLE], or the successor extension command NOTIFY [NOTIFY]

Sieve.why: Deposit and notification filters are implemented with Sieve, with Sieve notification extensions and a Sieve management protocol discussed as the way to realize them.
Sieve.quote: when implementing DF or NF using Sieve, the 'enotify' [SIEVE-NOTIFY] and likely the 'variables' [SIEVE-VARIABLES] Sieve extensions might be needed.
Sieve.section: 2. Notifications Logical Architecture and LEMONADE Profile

rejected.why: SMTP, LMTP and submission appear only in the architecture figure as message flow and are not discussed.
SMS is mentioned only as a possible delivery channel between the notification system and devices, which the document puts out of scope.
Instant messaging and presence are mentioned only as possible notification delivery channels or systems, and are out of scope.
POP3 is mentioned only in passing as lacking off-line notification facilities.
There is no matching taxonomy tag for mobile email, so no tag was considered under this id.

gaps.name: Mail event notifications / push email
gaps.why: The document is about email notification architecture, server-to-server state change events and push email. The taxonomy has no tag for notification systems, so it is covered only by the general email tag.

RFC5552.title: SIP Interface to VoiceXML Media Services
RFC5552.summary: Defines a SIP interface (Request-URI conventions, session variable mappings, media support, data return, outbound calling and call transfer) by which Application Servers invoke and control VoiceXML media servers.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP usage: new Request-URI parameters, INVITE/BYE/REFER handling and transfer flows for a VoiceXML media server.
SIP.quote: This document describes a SIP interface to VoiceXML media services.

MRCP.why: Describes how the VoiceXML media server establishes MRCPv2 sessions via SIP/SDP for speech resources, a small but explicit part of the document.
MRCP.quote: The VoiceXML Media Server will change the offer received from step 1 to establish an MRCPv2 session in step (5)

rejected.why: Offer/answer and SDP are used as the mechanism, and the document defines nothing new about SDP itself.
RTP and G.711 codecs are mandated as media substrate; the document does not specify RTP.
SRTP support is required but only as a security mechanism in a bullet point; not the subject.
HTTP is used to fetch VoiceXML documents and return data; not specified or extended.
PSTN gateway use case is mentioned, but the document is not about PSTN interworking.
Mentions application/x-www-form-urlencoded content in BYE bodies, but this is not a media type registration.

gaps.name: VoiceXML / media server control
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for VoiceXML or IVR/media-server dialog control. The closest, MRCP, covers speech resource control only. The mediactrl-related subject would be useful here.

RFC5553.title: Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Extensions for Path Key Support
RFC5553.summary: Defines RSVP-TE extensions that carry Path Key Subobjects in EROs and RROs, with processing rules and new error codes, so inter-domain MPLS/GMPLS TE LSP signalling can hide confidential path segments computed by PCEs.

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies new ERO/RRO subobjects, processing rules and error values for RSVP-TE signalling of TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines RSVP-TE protocol extensions necessary to support the use of Path Key Subobjects in MPLS and GMPLS signaling

PCE.why: The Path Key mechanism is a PCE-based confidentiality mechanism. The document specifies how LSRs resolve a PKS via PCEs and PCEP, so PCE readers would want it.
PCE.quote: The LSR can use the PCE-ID contained in the PKS to contact the identified PCE using PCEP [RFC5440] and request that the PKS be expanded.

rejected.why: GMPLS signalling is covered only as part of the RSVP-TE extensions. The document adds nothing specific to GMPLS or optical networks.
MPLS and its LSPs are the context, but the document is about RSVP-TE signalling objects, which is the more specific tag.
A 128-bit PCE-ID variant exists, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The parent of RSVP-TE and PCE, which are tagged, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC5554.title: Clarifications and Extensions to the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) for the Use of Channel Bindings
RFC5554.summary: RFC 5554 clarifies and generalizes the GSS-API channel bindings facility, defining an abstract language-independent GSS-CHANNEL-BINDINGS structure and requiring new mechanisms to conform to RFC 5056.

GSS-API.why: The document updates RFC 2743 by clarifying GSS-API channel bindings, defining a generic structure and imposing requirements on mechanisms and language bindings.
GSS-API.quote: This document clarifies and generalizes the Generic Security Service Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) "channel bindings" facility

rejected.why: RFC 4121's Kerberos mechanism is cited only as an example of a channel binding encoding; the document is not about Kerberos.
Pseudo-ASN.1 notation is used only to describe an abstract API structure; no ASN.1 module or encoding is defined.
Channel bindings secure channels like TLS, but TLS is not discussed; the document only references RFC 5056.

gaps.name: Channel bindings
gaps.why: The document is about channel binding for authentication, but the taxonomy has no tag for channel binding; GSS-API is the closest fit.

RFC5555.title: Mobile IPv6 Support for Dual Stack Hosts and Routers
RFC5555.summary: RFC 5555 extends Mobile IPv6 and NEMO so dual-stack mobile nodes can register IPv4 home addresses/prefixes, tunnel IPv4 and IPv6 traffic to the home agent over IPv4 or IPv6 care-of addresses, and traverse IPv4 NATs using UDP encapsulation (DSMIPv6).

Mobile IPv6.why: The document defines new Mobile IPv6 mobility header options, binding update flags and home agent/mobile node procedures (DSMIPv6).
Mobile IPv6.quote: The current Mobile IPv6 and Network Mobility (NEMO) specifications support IPv6 only.  This specification extends those standards to allow the registration of IPv4 addresses

NEMO.why: It extends NEMO basic support to allow IPv4 mobile network prefixes (P flag in the IPv4 home address option) and mobile routers.
NEMO.quote: allow the registration of IPv4 addresses and prefixes, respectively, and the transport of both IPv4 and IPv6 packets over the tunnel to the home agent

NAT.why: A substantial part defines NAT detection, UDP encapsulation and NAT keepalives for mobile nodes behind NATs.
NAT.quote: the mobile node needs to be able to traverse the IPv4 NAT in order to communicate with the home agent.

IPv6 transition.why: The document addresses IPv4/IPv6 coexistence for mobility: IPv4 care-of and home addresses, IPv4-in-IPv6 and IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling.
IPv6 transition.quote: allow dual stack mobile nodes to request that their home agent (also dual stacked) tunnel IPv4/IPv6 packets addressed to their home addresses

rejected.why: IPsec/ESP is used to protect binding updates and data, and Section 5 covers its interaction, but the document is not about IPsec itself.
IKEv2 interactions are detailed in Section 5 as a security mechanism relied upon, not the document's subject.
MOBIKE is only mentioned as an optional mechanism for updating IKE SAs.
Tunnelling formats are covered but as part of the Mobile IPv6 extensions; the more specific tags fit better.
UDP is the encapsulation substrate for NAT traversal, not a subject of the document.
DNS A/AAAA/SRV lookup is used only for home agent discovery in a short passage.

RFC5556.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Problem and Applicability Statement
RFC5556.summary: Informational problem and applicability statement for TRILL, describing the limitations of spanning-tree bridged Ethernet and the desired properties of a solution that applies link-state routing at the link layer.

TRILL.why: The whole document defines the TRILL problem, the desired properties of solutions, and their applicability.
TRILL.quote: This problem is known as "Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links" or "TRILL".

rejected.why: The document is about bridged Ethernet subnets, but TRILL is the more specific tag. The Ethernet tag is for IP over Ethernet and Ethernet OAM.
IGMP snooping and multicast optimization are mentioned as one problem area, but they are not a main subject.
ARP is mentioned only as an example of link/network integration and as snooping context.
The document argues for network-style routing at the link layer, but TRILL covers that more specifically.
Multipath forwarding is discussed in one section as a benefit, but the document does not specify or analyse ECMP.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.1 bridging / spanning tree
gaps.why: The document analyses STP, RSTP, MSTP and VLAN bridging in depth, but the taxonomy has no tag for bridging or spanning tree.

RFC5557.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Requirements and Protocol Extensions in Support of Global Concurrent Optimization
RFC5557.summary: RFC 5557 sets out requirements and PCEP extensions (new RP flags, Order TLV, GC object, error types, no-path flags) for Global Concurrent Optimization, which is bulk, network-wide path computation for TE LSPs by a PCE.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP and the PCE architecture with new objects, TLVs, flags and error codes for global concurrent optimization. This is the PCE/PCEP subject.
PCE.quote: This document provides application-specific requirements and the PCEP extensions in support of GCO applications.

traffic engineering.why: The GCO application is about computing and reoptimizing sets of TE LSPs network-wide, including migration ordering with make-before-break. Readers of traffic engineering would want it, but PCE is the more specific tag.
traffic engineering.quote: it may be advantageous to perform bulk path computations in order to avoid blocking problems and to achieve more optimal network-wide solutions.

rejected.why: TE LSPs are the objects being computed, but the document does not specify MPLS itself.
Only cites RFC 3209 make-before-break as a migration technique. It does not extend RSVP-TE.
GMPLS networks are mentioned as context only. Nothing GMPLS-specific is specified.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats. The document is not about it.
OSPF appears only in the PCE discovery capability flag registration, which is a minor IANA item.

RFC5558.title: Virtual Enterprise Traversal (VET)
RFC5558.summary: Informational RFC specifying Virtual Enterprise Traversal (VET), an IP-in-IP overlay abstraction for autoconfiguration of enterprise routers/hosts, prefix delegation and registration, next-hop discovery, and internetworking across enterprises, MANETs and the Internet core, building on ISATAP and SEAL.

tunneling.why: VET is fundamentally an automatic IP-in-IP tunnelling abstraction (VET interfaces, inner/outer addressing, mid-layer encapsulation). No more specific tunnelling tag fits as the primary subject.
tunneling.quote: an abstraction that uses IP-in-IP encapsulation to create an overlay that spans an enterprise in a single (inner) IP hop.

ISATAP.why: VET generalizes ISATAP: it uses ISATAP link-local addresses, PRL discovery and RA procedures, and extends them with redirects and prefix registration.
ISATAP.quote: VET represents a functional superset of 6over4 [RFC2529] and Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP) [RFC5214]

addressing.why: A substantial part covers RLOC/EID address autoconfiguration, PA/PI prefix delegation and registration, and multihoming/mobility of prefixes.
addressing.quote: Enterprise networks must have a means for supporting both Provider-Independent (PI) and Provider-Aggregated (PA) IP prefixes.

MANET.why: MANETs are an explicit target scenario, with distributed-management mechanisms (LLMNR, peer-to-peer EBR coordination) designed for them.
MANET.quote: Mobile Ad hoc Networks (MANETs) [RFC2501] can also be considered as a challenging example of an enterprise network

rejected.why: RS/RA, redirects and SEND are used as mechanisms but the document does not define neighbor discovery itself.
DHCPv6 prefix delegation is used for PA prefixes but only as an existing mechanism.
SEND is relied on for securing RS/RA exchanges, not specified here.
IPv6 is the main inner protocol, but IPv4 is covered equally and the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The RLOC/EID split resembles LISP, but the document does not discuss or specify LISP.
Multihoming is addressed only in one subsection, so it is not a substantial subject.

gaps.name: Enterprise network autoconfiguration / RANGER
gaps.why: The document is about autoconfiguration and internetworking of enterprise networks (EBR/EBG, PRL discovery) and part of the RANGER architecture. The taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC5559.title: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) Architecture
RFC5559.summary: Informational architecture for Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN): metering and marking of aggregate traffic in a Diffserv domain so boundary nodes can perform flow admission control and flow termination to protect QoS of inelastic flows.

PCN.why: The whole document defines the PCN architecture: threshold and excess-traffic metering/marking, ingress/egress/interior node functions, admission control and flow termination.
PCN.quote: The objective of Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) is to protect the quality of service (QoS) of inelastic flows within a Diffserv domain in a simple, scalable, and robust fashion.

Diffserv.why: PCN operates within a single Diffserv domain, uses DSCP plus ECN fields for encoding, EF PHB scheduling, and is compared against the Diffserv architecture's traffic-conditioning agreements.
Diffserv.quote: PCN-traffic is forwarded in a prioritised Diffserv traffic class.

rejected.why: PCN is analogous to ECN and redefines ECN field semantics (backwards-compatibility discussed in Section 3.6), but the document is not about ECN itself; PCN is a separate tag already chosen.
RSVP is used as the example signalling protocol for admission control, but the document does not specify or extend it.
ECMP is discussed as a challenge for PCN measurement, not as the subject of the document.
Mentioned only as an alternative signalling protocol.
Referenced as IntServ over Diffserv context and for comparison; not the document's subject.
Section 4.7 covers marking rules for tunnels, but it is a minor section within the architecture.

gaps.name: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the congestion control child 'PCN' (PCN (Pre-Congestion Notification)) — used as the primary tag above; no gap beyond that.

RFC5560.title: A One-Way Packet Duplication Metric
RFC5560.summary: RFC 5560 defines IPPM metrics for one-way packet duplication (arrival count, duplication singleton, Poisson and periodic stream samples) and summary statistics, modelled on the one-way packet loss metric.

performance measurement.why: The document defines IPPM performance metrics, samples and statistics for measuring packet duplication, so it belongs under performance measurement. No more specific child tag (OWAMP, TWAMP, STAMP, LMAP) applies.
performance measurement.quote: This document defines a metric for one-way packet duplication across Internet paths.

rejected.why: IPv4 header fields are mentioned only as examples of fields to compare when deciding whether packets are identical. The document is not about IPv4.
IPv6 header fields appear only as comparison examples. The document is not about IPv6.
The metric definitions may be measured with OWAMP, but the document does not specify or discuss that protocol.
The metrics apply to live Internet paths, not to benchmarking of devices in a lab.

RFC5561.title: LDP Capabilities
RFC5561.summary: RFC 5561 defines an LDP capability advertisement mechanism: Capability Parameter TLVs in Initialization messages, a Capability message for dynamic enable/disable, a Dynamic Capability Announcement TLV, and a new Unsupported Capability status code and Returned TLVs TLV.

LDP.why: The whole document extends LDP (updates RFC 5036) with a capability mechanism, new message, TLVs and status code.
LDP.quote: This document proposes and defines a mechanism for advertising LDP enhancements at session initialization time.

rejected.why: LDP is used in MPLS networks, but the document is about the LDP protocol's capability mechanism, which LDP already covers.
It appears only in the title of a security framework reference, so it isn't a subject of this document.
Pseudowire signaling over LDP is only listed as an example enhancement in the Introduction.
Next-next-hop label learning for fast reroute is only listed as an example enhancement in the Introduction.

RFC5562.title: Adding Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Capability to TCP's SYN/ACK Packets
RFC5562.summary: Experimental modification to RFC 3168 allowing TCP SYN/ACK packets to be ECN-Capable (ECN+/TryOnce), with the responder resending a non-ECT SYN/ACK and reducing its initial window to one segment on a CE mark, plus simulation evaluation and deployment issues.

ECN.why: The whole document specifies how ECN is used on TCP SYN/ACK packets, extending RFC 3168, with the ECT/CE/ECN-Echo handling and responder behavior.
ECN.quote: This document describes an optional, experimental modification to RFC 3168 to allow TCP SYN/ACK packets to be ECN-Capable.

TCP.why: It changes TCP connection-setup behavior: SYN/ACK retransmission, initial window, handshake state transitions and retransmission timer handling.
TCP.quote: the responder sets the initial congestion window to one segment, instead of two segments as allowed by [RFC2581]

rejected.why: RED and other AQM schemes are used in the simulations and discussion, but the document is about ECN marking of SYN/ACKs, not AQM algorithms.
The parent of ECN, so it is implied. The document is about the specific ECN mechanism.
The ECN field in the IP header is only the carrier for the ECT/CE codepoints. The document is not about IP itself.

RFC5563.title: WiMAX Forum / 3GPP2 Proxy Mobile IPv4
RFC5563.summary: Informational RFC describing Proxy Mobile IPv4 (PMIPv4), where a network entity (the Proxy Mobility Agent) performs Mobile IPv4 registration with the Home Agent for mobility-unaware hosts. It defines new extensions and error codes and describes the WiMAX Forum and 3GPP2 uses.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document specifies PMIPv4, which extends Mobile IPv4 with proxy registration and new extensions and error codes. It also defines PMA and HA behaviour.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Proxy Mobile IPv4 (PMIPv4), a scheme based on having the Mobile IPv4 client function in a network entity to provide mobility support

PMIPv6.why: PMIPv4 is the IPv4 counterpart of network-based mobility management. Readers of the PMIPv6 and network-based mobility page would want it, though this is a secondary link.
PMIPv6.quote: Proxy Mobile IPv6 [RFC5213] is an IETF standard for network-based mobility management

WiMAX.why: A substantial section covers the WiMAX NWG use of PMIPv4, including the split PMA model and call flows.
WiMAX.quote: WiMAX Forum Network Working Group (NWG) uses the Proxy Mobile IPv4 scheme to provide IPv4 connectivity and IP mobility.
WiMAX.section: 10. Proxy Mobile IPv4 Use Case in WiMAX

cdma2000.why: A dedicated section covers the 3GPP2 packet-data use of PMIPv4 between the base station, access gateway and Home Agent.
cdma2000.quote: 3GPP2 uses the Proxy Mobile IPv4 scheme to provide mobility service
cdma2000.section: 11. Proxy Mobile IPv4 Use Case in 3GPP2

rejected.why: DHCP is only the address-acquisition trigger and interacts with PMIPv4 in Section 6. The document does not specify or extend it.
GRE is an optional tunnel mode between PMA and HA and is referenced via a separate draft. The document does not define GRE.
IPsec is only an optional per-node authentication method for the signalling.
PPP/IPCP is an access method that PMIPv4 interacts with. It is not the subject of the document.
ARP is discussed only as a consideration for the home-network illusion.

RFC5564.title: Linguistic Guidelines for the Use of the Arabic Language in Internet Domains
RFC5564.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC giving linguistic guidelines and a permitted Unicode character set for writing Arabic-language Internationalized Domain Names, including rules on diacritics, tatweel, character folding, numeral homogeneity and word separators.

IDN.why: The whole document defines how Arabic characters may be used in IDNs under IDNA, specifying allowed code points and prohibited characters, so it belongs on the IDN subject page.
IDN.quote: This document constitutes a technical specification for the implementation of the IDN standards in the case of the Arabic language.

rejected.why: Unicode code point tables are used to define the permitted set, but the subject is domain-name labels, not Unicode usage generally; IDN is the more specific fit.
Domain names are the context, but no DNS protocol, record or server behaviour is specified.
Parent of Unicode and similar tags; the document is about IDN specifically, which is the more specific tag.
Mentions registering names and zone files, but only as rules for allowed characters, not registry or registrar operations.

gaps.name: Arabic-script language tables for domain names
gaps.why: The document is a language-specific IDN character table/policy (Arabic); the taxonomy has no tag for script- or language-specific IDN label generation rules.

RFC5565.title: Softwire Mesh Framework
RFC5565.summary: Framework document describing how IPv4 or IPv6 routing information and data packets are carried across a single-protocol backbone of the other family, using BGP between address family border routers and tunnels called softwires, with signalling, OAM, multicast and security considerations.

softwire.why: The document defines the Softwire Mesh Framework for IPv4-over-IPv6 and IPv6-over-IPv4 transit via tunnels between AFBRs.
softwire.quote: The tunnels are known as "softwires".  This framework document explains how the routing information and the data packets of one protocol are passed through a single-protocol network

BGP.why: A substantial part covers how BGP distributes E-IP routes over I-IP sessions and how next hops are encoded in the other address family.
BGP.quote: The AFBRs use Internal BGP (IBGP) to exchange E-IP routing information with each other.

multicast.why: Section 11 covers extending PIM and mLDP multicast across the softwire transit core, including one-to-one and MVPN-like schemes.
multicast.quote: A set of client networks, running E-IP, that are connected to a provider's I-IP transit core may wish to run IP multicast applications.

rejected.why: The softwire tag is the more specific fit for this document's tunnelling, and its tunnel technologies are only accommodated, not specified.
Only used as an optional security mechanism for softwires in the Security Considerations; the document is not about IPsec.
The framework borrows techniques from RFC 4364 and L3VPN multicast, but it is not about VPN service.
MPLS is one of several tunnelling options allowed by the framework; the document does not specify or extend it.
The parent of softwire, so implied by that tag.
PIM is discussed only as part of the multicast section, with no new PIM specification.

RFC5566.title: BGP IPsec Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute
RFC5566.summary: Defines new BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute tunnel types for IPsec (tunnel mode, IP-in-IP and MPLS-in-IP with transport mode) and an IPsec Tunnel Authenticator sub-TLV carrying a public key hash for IKEv2 authentication.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP's Encapsulation SAFI and Tunnel Encapsulation attribute with new tunnel types and a new sub-TLV.
BGP.quote: This document builds on [RFC5512] and defines support for IPsec tunnels.

IPsec.why: A substantial part specifies how IPsec SAs are triggered and authenticated from BGP-advertised tunnel info, including IKEv2 certificate checks, so IPsec readers would want it.
IPsec.quote: Support is defined for IP Authentication Header (AH) in tunnel mode [RFC4302] and for IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) in tunnel mode [RFC4303].

rejected.why: IKEv2 is used to establish SAs and obtain certificates, but the document defines nothing new about IKE itself.
Tunnel encapsulation is the subject, but it is covered via the BGP and IPsec tags; GRE and IP-in-IP are only referenced.
The document was produced in the softwire WG and cites the Softwire Mesh Framework only as context; it does not specify softwires.
ESP is referenced as a tunnel type but not specified or extended; IPsec is the more fitting tag.
Only a tunnel type value combining IP-in-IP with IPsec transport mode is defined; IP-in-IP encapsulation itself is not addressed.

RFC5567.title: An Architectural Framework for Media Server Control
RFC5567.summary: Informational architectural framework for Media Server control, defining Application Server and Media Server entities, SIP-based establishment of media and control dialogs, and IVR and conferencing use cases including BFCP floor control.

real-time communications.why: The document defines the architecture for Application Servers controlling Media Servers that process real-time media for IVR and conferencing. No more specific technology tag covers the whole framework, so the parent topic fits.
real-time communications.quote: This document describes an architectural framework for Media Server control.

SIP.why: A full section covers how SIP is used for MS media dialogs and MS control dialogs, including 3PCC and why SIP INFO is not advised. This is a substantial part of the document.
SIP.quote: SIP is the primary signaling protocol for session signaling and is used for all media sessions directed towards a Media Server

conferencing.why: Section 6 describes the focus/mixer decomposition, conference creation, participant addition and media controls on the Media Server, within the XCON framework.
conferencing.quote: Media Control for Conferencing Services

BFCP.why: Section 6.4 is a long walkthrough of BFCP floor control call flows, with the floor control server co-located with the AS or the MS.
BFCP.quote: floor control constitutes a further means to control participants' media streams

rejected.why: MRCPv2 is mentioned only as a way a VoiceXML media server talks to speech engines, and the document does not specify it.
TLS is only the required transport security for control channels and is not itself the subject.
TCP is the substrate for the control channel and is not specified or extended here.
SDP and COMEDIA are used only to negotiate the control channel, with nothing new defined.
The XCON framework is referenced as the conferencing context, but the document is not about XCON and only the parent 'conferencing' tag fits.
RTP is the media transport and is mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: Media Server control / MEDIACTRL
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers Media Server control (the mediactrl framework, the Control Channel Framework and IVR media control), which is the main subject of the document.

RFC5568.title: Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers
RFC5568.summary: Specifies the Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers protocol (RtSolPr/PrRtAdv, FBU/FBack, HI/HAck, UNA) to cut IP-layer handover latency, and moves HI/HAck from ICMPv6 to Mobility Header messages.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document defines a Mobile IPv6 extension (fast handovers) with new Mobility Header messages, FBU/FBack and options.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document specifies a protocol to improve handover latency due to Mobile IPv6 procedures.

neighbor discovery.why: Defines new ND-style ICMPv6 messages (RtSolPr, PrRtAdv), ND options (LLA, NAACK, IP Address/Prefix) and UNA/NAACK processing.
neighbor discovery.quote: The protocol specifies an optional extension to Neighbor Discovery [RFC4861] in which an access router may send a router advertisement as a response to the UNA message

rejected.why: Mentioned only as motivation for the Mobility Header change; the document doesn't specify PMIPv6.
Used to protect HI/HAck, but only as a security mechanism in Security Considerations.
Only an alternative way to configure the NCoA; not specified here.
IKEv2 is only an optional means of setting up SAs between access routers, described with example PAD/SPD entries.
Only suggested as a mitigation; the key distribution lives in the companion RFC 5269.
Parent of the chosen Mobile IPv6 tag, so it is implied.

RFC5569.title: IPv6 Rapid Deployment on IPv4 Infrastructures (6rd)
RFC5569.summary: Describes 6rd, a stateless IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation mechanism derived from 6to4 that lets an ISP use its own IPv6 prefix to rapidly deploy IPv6 to customer sites, based on Free's deployment.

6rd.why: The document specifies 6rd itself: the prefix derivation from the IPv4 address, 6rd relays and CPEs, and security checks.
6rd.quote: IPv6 rapid deployment on IPv4 infrastructures (6rd) builds upon mechanisms of 6to4 to enable a service provider to rapidly deploy IPv6 unicast service to IPv4 sites

rejected.why: 6rd modifies 6to4 and builds on it, but the document specifies 6rd, not 6to4. Readers of 6to4 are not the audience.
The parent of 6rd, so it is implied by the 6rd tag.
IPv4 infrastructure is only the substrate carrying the encapsulated IPv6 packets.
A 6rd relay anycast address is used, but the document is not about anycast operation.
Section 4 covers applicability to ISPs that assign private addresses behind NATs, but it is a minor part and NAT is not what the document is about.

RFC5570.title: Common Architecture Label IPv6 Security Option (CALIPSO)
RFC5570.summary: Defines CALIPSO, an IPv6 hop-by-hop option carrying explicit Sensitivity Labels (DOI, level, compartment bitmap) on packets so routers and hosts in closed Multi-Level Secure networks can enforce Mandatory Access Controls.

security labels.why: CALIPSO is the IPv6 successor to the CIPSO/RFC 1108 IP security label options. The whole document specifies label encoding, comparison and enforcement.
security labels.quote: This document describes an optional method for encoding explicit packet Sensitivity Labels on IPv6 packets.

IPv6.why: The document defines a new IPv6 hop-by-hop option, covering its option type, alignment and processing rules, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: CALIPSO is an IPv6 Hop-By-Hop Option, rather than an IPv6 Destination Option, to ensure that a security gateway or router can apply access controls

rejected.why: AH and ESP are discussed as ways to bind and protect the label, but the document does not specify or extend them.
The option uses a CRC-16 checksum taken from RFC 1662, but this is only a minor field mechanism.
Mandatory Access Control is the purpose of the labels, but the document specifies a packet label option, not an authorization framework.
Section 7.3 gives SCTP, TCP and UDP implementation notes only as upper-layer considerations. The document is not about those protocols.
The option number and DOI registry are boilerplate-level IANA actions and do not make the document about IANA.

gaps.name: Multi-Level Secure (MLS) networking / Mandatory Access Control
gaps.why: The document's subject is label-based MAC in MLS networks. The taxonomy only has the narrow security labels tag, with no broader MLS or access-control-model tag.

RFC5571.title: Softwire Hub and Spoke Deployment Framework with Layer Two Tunneling Protocol Version 2 (L2TPv2)
RFC5571.summary: Specifies the framework for Softwire Hub and Spoke deployment using L2TPv2 (with PPP, IPV6CP/IPCP, DHCP and RADIUS) to carry IPv6 over IPv4-only and IPv4 over IPv6-only access networks, including AVP usage profiles and address provisioning.

softwire.why: The document is a softwire hub-and-spoke framework for tunnelling IPv4/IPv6 across the other family's access network.
softwire.quote: This document describes the framework of the Softwire "Hub and Spoke" solution with the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol version 2 (L2TPv2).

L2TP.why: It profiles L2TPv2 for softwires: required, optional and irrelevant AVPs, tunnel setup, keepalives and teardown.
L2TP.quote: The SI and SC MUST follow the L2TPv2 operations described in [RFC2661] when performing Softwire establishment, teardown, and Operations, Administration, and Management

PPP.why: A substantial part covers PPP LCP, authentication, MTU and NCP negotiation (IPV6CP/IPCP) over the L2TP session.
PPP.quote: The only Network Control Protocol (NCP) negotiated in the Softwire context is IPV6CP (see Section 5.2.4.1) for IPv6 as SPH, and IPCP

RADIUS.why: A section maps RADIUS attributes to endpoint addresses and delegated prefixes, and covers RADIUS accounting.
RADIUS.quote: The Softwire Concentrator is expected to act as a client to a AAA server, for example, a RADIUS server.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 prefix delegation and DNS options are used in the scenarios, but the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
IPsec is only an optional security layer, described by reference to RFC 3193 and the softwire security document.
UDP is only the transport for L2TPv2. The document cites the UDP usage guidelines but does not define anything about UDP.
A softwire is a tunnelling transition mechanism, but this document has a more specific tag, so I used that one.
SLAAC and neighbour discovery are used over the PPP link, but the document only references them.
NAT/NAPT traversal is discussed only as a requirement that L2TP over UDP satisfies.

RFC5572.title: IPv6 Tunnel Broker with the Tunnel Setup Protocol (TSP)
RFC5572.summary: Specifies the Tunnel Setup Protocol (TSP), an XML-based signaling protocol within the tunnel broker model for negotiating IPv6-in-IPv4, IPv4-in-IPv6 and IPv6-over-UDP tunnels, with NAT discovery, prefix delegation and keep-alive.

IPv6 transition.why: TSP is a tunnel broker mechanism for providing IPv6 connectivity over IPv4 networks (and IPv4 over IPv6), i.e. an IPv6/IPv4 coexistence and transition mechanism. No specific child tag fits it.
IPv6 transition.quote: a tunneled infrastructure can be used to provide IPv6 services to the enterprise customers, before a full IPv6 native infrastructure is built

tunneling.why: The document negotiates and establishes v6v4, v4v6 and v6udpv4 tunnels, covering generic tunnel setup and encapsulation choices.
tunneling.quote: enables the establishment of tunnels of various inner protocols, such as IPv6 or IPv4, inside various outer protocols packets

NAT.why: NAT discovery and UDP encapsulation for NAT traversal, with keep-alive to maintain NAT mappings, are substantial parts of the protocol.
NAT.quote: TSP is also used to discover if a NAT is in the path.

rejected.why: Used only as the authentication framework; the document does not define the mechanism.
XML is the message encoding substrate, not the subject.
Only the transport for signaling; reliability over UDP is borrowed from UNP.
ICMPv6 echo is used only as the keep-alive message.
Not a taxonomy tag; DSTM is mentioned only as a use case for IPv4-over-IPv6.
UDP is a substrate for signaling and encapsulation; nothing new is defined about UDP itself.

gaps.name: Tunnel broker / Tunnel Setup Protocol (TSP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for tunnel brokers or tunnel setup signaling. Readers browsing IPv6 transition would want it, but a dedicated tag is missing.

RFC5573.title: Asynchronous Channels for the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP)
RFC5573.summary: RFC 5573 defines an experimental BEEP feature ("async") and a "start" parameter that lets individual BEEP channels process requests in parallel and send responses in any order, correlating them by msgno.

BEEP.why: The whole document extends BEEP with an "async" feature and an async channel start parameter, relaxing the response-ordering rules of RFC 3080.
BEEP.quote: This document defines a BEEP feature that enables the use of asynchronous channels.

rejected.why: The TCP mapping's flow control and window size are mentioned only in the alternatives discussion. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
BEEP greetings and start messages are XML, but this is only the encoding used. The document defines nothing about XML.
The document registers the BEEP "async" feature, but that is boilerplate registration and not the subject of the document.
MIME headers appear only in the discussion of alternatives, so the document is not about MIME.

RFC5574.title: RTP Payload Format for the Speex Codec
RFC5574.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for Speex codec bitstreams, registers the audio/speex media type, and specifies its SDP parameters and offer/answer usage.

Speex.why: The document is the RTP payload format specification for the Speex codec, including frame packing, modes and bit-rates. Speex is the specific technology it covers.
Speex.quote: This document describes the payload format for Speex-generated bit streams within an RTP packet.

SDP.why: A substantial section defines the mapping of the media type parameters (mode, vbr, cng, ptime) to SDP attributes. It also gives offer/answer examples.
SDP.quote: The media subtype ("speex") goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name.

rejected.why: The Speex tag already sits under codecs and is the specific fit. The RTP payload format tag covers payload formats in general, and this document's subject is the Speex-specific one.
RTP is the substrate that carries the payload. The document defines no new RTP mechanism beyond the payload format.
The media type registration is part of the payload format specification. The document is not about registry rules.
This is the parent of Speex, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC5575.title: Dissemination of Flow Specification Rules
RFC5575.summary: Defines a BGP NLRI encoding for flow specification rules (match criteria on IP/transport header fields), with validation against unicast routing, traffic-filtering actions as extended communities, and a BGP/MPLS VPN variant, for DDoS mitigation.

BGP flowspec.why: The RFC is the original specification of BGP Flow Specification: NLRI components, validation procedure and filtering action communities.
BGP flowspec.quote: This document defines a new Border Gateway Protocol Network Layer Reachability Information (BGP NLRI) encoding format that can be used to distribute traffic flow specifications.

DDoS.why: A main application is inter-provider signalling of filters to mitigate DoS/DDoS attacks, discussed in Section 5.
DDoS.quote: one that can be used to automate inter-domain coordination of traffic filtering, such as what is required in order to mitigate (distributed) denial-of-service attacks

L3VPN.why: Section 8 defines the VPNv4 flow-spec address family with Route Distinguisher and Route Target handling in BGP/MPLS VPNs.
L3VPN.quote: This document proposes an additional BGP NLRI type (AFI=1, SAFI=134) value, which can be used to propagate traffic filtering information in a BGP/MPLS VPN environment.

rejected.why: The more specific child BGP flowspec fits; the parent is implied.
Filtering is the effect of the rules, but the document is about the BGP distribution mechanism, not firewalls or middlebox traversal.
Extended communities encode the actions, but the document does not specify communities in general.
DSCP is only a match field and a marking action, not the subject.
TCP flags and ports are match criteria only.

RFC5576.title: Source-Specific Media Attributes in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC5576.summary: Defines the SDP "ssrc" and "ssrc-group" media attributes and source-level attributes (cname, previous-ssrc, fmtp) to describe individual RTP sources and their relationships, plus IANA registries for them.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with new media-level attributes (ssrc, ssrc-group), a new source-level attribute registry, and grouping semantics, including offer/answer usage.
SDP.quote: This document defines a mechanism to describe RTP media sources, which are identified by their synchronization source (SSRC) identifiers, in SDP

RTP.why: A substantial part (Section 5) specifies how RTP endpoints handle SSRCs named in SDP: collision resolution, SSRC reuse, group size estimation and RTCP report blocks.
RTP.quote: Within an RTP session, the source of a single stream of RTP packets is known as a synchronization source (SSRC).

rejected.why: RTCP SDES CNAME and report blocks are referenced, but the document does not extend RTCP itself.
FEC is only one of two initial ssrc-group semantics, taken from RFC 4756; the document is not about loss-recovery schemes.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-style apparatus for the SDP extension, not the subject of the document.
ABNF is only used to write the grammar of the new attributes.
Single-source multicast is cited as motivation only; the document does not specify it.

RFC5577.title: RTP Payload Format for ITU-T Recommendation G.722.1
RFC5577.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for ITU-T G.722.1 wideband audio (including 32 kHz superwideband), registers the audio/G7221 media type and SDP parameters, and obsoletes RFC 3047.

G.722.why: The taxonomy's G.722 tag explicitly covers G.722.1 and its payload formats; this document is exactly that.
G.722.quote: This document describes the payload format for including G.722.1-generated bit streams within an RTP packet.

RTP payload format.why: It specifies how codec frames are packetized into RTP, including header field usage, multiple frames per packet and timestamp clock rates.
RTP payload format.quote: The RTP payload for G.722.1 has the format shown in Figure 1.

media types.why: It registers the audio/G7221 media type with required and optional parameters, updating the registration from RFC 3047.
media types.quote: This section describes the media types and names associated with this payload format.

SDP.why: It defines the SDP parameter mapping (rtpmap, fmtp bitrate) and offer/answer usage, which is a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: The media types audio/G7221 are mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] as follows:

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the document defines a payload format, covered by the more specific RTP payload format tag.
The more specific G.722 tag applies; the document does not define the codec itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended mechanism.
Only mentioned in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
Only mentioned in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC5578.title: PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) Extensions for Credit Flow and Link Metrics
RFC5578.summary: Independent-stream RFC extending PPPoE with optional credit-based flow control (Credits, Scale Factor, Sequence Number TLVs; PADG/PADC packets) and link quality metric reporting (PADQ/Metrics TLV) for variable-bandwidth radio links.

PPPoE.why: The document defines new PPPoE discovery packets (PADG, PADC, PADQ) and TLVs extending the PPPoE protocol, and obsoletes RFC 4938.
PPPoE.quote: This document extends the Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet (PPPoE) with an optional credit-based flow control mechanism and an optional Link Quality Metric report.

rejected.why: PPP is the payload carried by PPPoE; the document only extends PPPoE discovery and session framing, not PPP itself.
