Ethernet is merely the substrate PPPoE runs over; nothing new about Ethernet is specified.
Credit flow control is a hop-level mechanism within PPPoE, not a transport congestion control scheme.
The metrics TLV reports radio link quality to the router for route cost, within PPPoE; it is not a measurement methodology.
The use case is point-to-point radio links, and routing influence is explicitly out of scope.

RFC5579.title: Transmission of IPv4 Packets over Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP) Interfaces
RFC5579.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC that extends ISATAP interfaces to carry IPv4 packets via IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation, including address configuration, next-hop mapping and IPv4 multicast mapping.

ISATAP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to ISATAP interface behaviour (IPv4 operation over ISATAP interfaces).
ISATAP.quote: This document specifies a method for transmitting IPv4 packets over ISATAP interfaces.

rejected.why: RFC 2003 IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation is the mechanism used, but the document is about ISATAP interface operation, not defining the encapsulation.
ISATAP is its child and already chosen; this document actually extends ISATAP to IPv4, not transition itself.
IPv4 is the payload carried, not the subject of the document.
The multicast mapping is a short subsection mirroring 6over4, not a substantial multicast topic.
DHCP is only mentioned as one way to ensure L3ADDR uniqueness.
The ISATAP tag is more specific; the tunnelling is part of it.

RFC5580.title: Carrying Location Objects in RADIUS and Diameter
RFC5580.summary: Defines new RADIUS (and Diameter-compatible) attributes for conveying operator-name and civic/geospatial location objects with privacy policy rules, plus delivery methods in Access-Request, CoA and accounting messages.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS attributes (Operator-Name, Location-Information, Location-Data, etc.) and their message usage, including CoA and accounting.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines attributes within RADIUS and Diameter that can be used to convey location-related information within authentication and accounting exchanges.

Diameter.why: A dedicated section defines Diameter AVP flag rules and RADIUS-Diameter translation of the attributes.
Diameter.quote: the attributes defined in this specification can be used as Diameter attribute-value pairs (AVPs) from the code space 1-255

geolocation.why: The document is about carrying civic and geospatial location objects with privacy rules, following GEOPRIV requirements.
geolocation.quote: conveying access-network ownership and location information based on civic and geospatial location formats

rejected.why: Privacy is a significant concern, but it is addressed through location policy rules within the geolocation scope rather than as a general privacy-threat-model document.
Only the DHCP civic and LCI location encodings are reused for the Location-Data format. DHCP itself is not specified or extended.
IPsec is mentioned only as a security mechanism protecting RADIUS in the Security Considerations.
EAP is mentioned only as the context for authentication and identity leakage.
The new registries are boilerplate for the new attributes, not the main subject of the document.

RFC5581.title: The Camellia Cipher in OpenPGP
RFC5581.summary: Informational RFC defining how the Camellia block cipher (128/192/256-bit keys) is used in OpenPGP, assigning symmetric-key algorithm numbers 11, 12 and 13 and updating RFC 4880.

Camellia.why: The whole document defines the use of Camellia in OpenPGP, mapping key lengths to OpenPGP algorithm numbers. Camellia is the specific cipher the document is about.
Camellia.quote: This document presents the necessary information to use the Camellia [RFC3713] symmetric cipher in the OpenPGP protocol.

OpenPGP.why: The document extends OpenPGP (updates RFC 4880) with new symmetric algorithm identifiers and discusses interoperability with algorithm preferences and private key encryption.
OpenPGP.quote: OpenPGP applications MAY implement Camellia.  If implemented, Camellia may be used in any place in OpenPGP where a symmetric cipher is usable

rejected.why: AES is only mentioned in passing as another 128-bit block cipher already in OpenPGP; the document is not about it.
The IANA section merely records the three algorithm number assignments; this is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
The document touches on private key encryption interoperability only briefly; it is about a cipher, not key management.

RFC5582.title: Location-to-URL Mapping Architecture and Framework
RFC5582.summary: Informational architecture document describing a global, hierarchical system of seekers, resolvers, authoritative mapping servers (trees) and forest guides that uses LoST to map geographic location to service URLs (e.g., emergency PSAPs) and service numbers.

LoST.why: The whole document defines the architecture (seekers, resolvers, trees, forest guides) built on LoST for location-to-service mapping.
LoST.quote: an architecture for a global, scalable, resilient, and administratively distributed system for mapping geographic location information to URLs, using the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol

emergency services.why: Emergency calling is the motivating use case, with PSAP mapping examples and emergency service numbers discussed, in the ECRIT working group context.
emergency services.quote: Among the best-known public services of this kind is emergency calling, where emergency calls are routed to the most appropriate public safety answering point (PSAP)

rejected.why: DNS is only used as an analogy for the hierarchical tree and forest guides; the document does not specify or extend DNS.
Location objects are inputs to mapping, but the document is about the mapping architecture, not location formats or conveyance.
SIP user agents and proxies are merely possible seekers; no SIP specification is involved.
DHCP is only mentioned as a way to configure resolver addresses, defined elsewhere (RFC 5223).
Mapping location to service URLs is related, but LoST and emergency services tags are more specific and fitting.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a means to sign coverage regions.

RFC5583.title: Signaling Media Decoding Dependency in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC5583.summary: Defines the SDP "DDP" grouping semantics and the "depend" media-level attribute to signal layered and multiple-description decoding dependencies among same-type media descriptions carried over RTP.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new group semantic (DDP) and a new media-level attribute (depend), including offer/answer usage rules.
SDP.quote: This memo defines semantics that allow for signaling the decoding dependency of different media descriptions with the same media type in the Session Description Protocol (SDP).

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the mechanism applies to, but the document specifies only SDP signalling, not RTP itself.
It references the SVC and H.264 payload formats in examples but does not define any payload format.
H264 and H264-SVC appear only as example media subtypes.
RTSP is mentioned briefly for declarative usage; it is not the subject.
Layered and MDC coding is the motivation, but the document defines no codec.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new SDP group semantic and attribute.

gaps.name: SDP (Session Description Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SDP tag under real-time communications. The 'SDP' id I used in the tags is listed in the taxonomy as 'SDP [tech]' under real-time communications, so this is not a true gap.

RFC5584.title: RTP Payload Format for the Adaptive TRansform Acoustic Coding (ATRAC) Family
RFC5584.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for the Sony ATRAC family of audio codecs (ATRAC3, ATRAC-X, ATRAC Advanced Lossless), covering framing, fragmentation, redundancy, scalable base/enhancement layer streaming, and media type/SDP parameter registrations.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is an RTP payload format for specific audio codecs, with header, fragmentation, and redundancy definitions.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for efficient and flexible transporting of audio data encoded with the Adaptive TRansform Audio Coding (ATRAC) family of codecs.

codecs.why: Defines and describes ATRAC3, ATRAC-X and ATRAC Advanced Lossless codec variants and their parameters; no specific ATRAC tag exists, so the generic codecs tag fits.
codecs.quote: The ATRAC family of perceptual audio codecs is designed to address numerous needs for high-quality, low-bit-rate audio transfer.

SDP.why: Substantial sections give SDP fmtp/rtpmap mapping, offer/answer rules, declarative usage and grouping/dependency attributes for layered streams.
SDP.quote: A mapping of these parameters into the Session Description Protocol (SDP) (RFC 4566) [2] is also provided for applications that utilize SDP.

media types.why: Registers three audio media subtypes with full templates in the main body (Section 7).
media types.quote: Three new Media subtypes, audio/ATRAC3, audio/ATRAC-X, and audio/ATRAC-ADVANCED-LOSSLESS, have been registered

rejected.why: RTCP is used only for CNAME binding and SR-based synchronisation of layers; not specified here.
Mentioned only as an external security mechanism in Security Considerations.
RTP is the substrate; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers this document.
The redundancy scheme is simple time-shifted frame duplication, in the spirit of RFC 2198, not a FEC scheme.
Referenced only as an example of declarative SDP usage.

gaps.name: ATRAC (Adaptive TRansform Acoustic Coding)
gaps.why: No specific ATRAC codec tag exists in the taxonomy, so only the generic codecs tag can be used.

RFC5585.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Service Overview
RFC5585.summary: Informational overview of the DKIM service: its goals, signing and verification function, selector construct, service architecture, and how it differs from PEM, PGP, S/MIME and other message-signing technologies.

DKIM.why: The whole document is an overview of DKIM: its value proposition, goals, signing and verification function, and service architecture.
DKIM.quote: DKIM defines a domain-level digital signature authentication framework for email, using public-key cryptography, with the domain name service as its key server technology

rejected.why: DKIM publishes keys in the DNS, but the DNS is only the key-lookup substrate. The document defines nothing new about DNS.
SMTP is only the relay mechanism for the signed message. The document does not specify or extend it.
S/MIME is mentioned only as prior work and a contrast. The document is not about it.
OpenPGP is mentioned only as prior work and a contrast. The document is not about it.
The abstract says DKIM can assist in controlling spam, but the document states explicitly that it does not try to solve spam. It describes an authentication enabler, not a spam-filtering technology.
The DKIM-Signature header field is only described briefly. The document does not cover message format.

RFC5586.title: MPLS Generic Associated Channel
RFC5586.summary: Generalizes the pseudowire Associated Channel Header to MPLS LSPs and Sections (the G-ACh) and assigns reserved label 13 as the Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) to flag such packets in the label stack.

MPLS.why: The document defines a new MPLS encapsulation and reserved-label exception mechanism (GAL) for control channels on LSPs and Sections, updating RFC 3032 label usage.
MPLS.quote: enabling the realization of a control channel associated to MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) and MPLS Sections in addition to MPLS pseudowires

OAM.why: The G-ACh exists to carry OAM and other maintenance messages. The document defines the channel rather than the OAM functions themselves.
OAM.quote: There is a need for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanisms that can be used for fault detection, diagnostics, maintenance

pseudowire.why: It builds on and generalizes the PW Associated Channel Header from VCCV and RFC 4385, and modifies the PW Associated Channel Type registry.
pseudowire.quote: This document generalizes the applicability of the ACH to enable the same associated control channel mechanism to be used for Sections, LSPs, and PWs.

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is used only as the example application. The mechanism is explicitly general to MPLS.
BFD-MPLS and BFD-VCCV are mentioned only as existing tools. They are not specified here.
The IANA section registers label 13 and registry changes, which is boilerplate-level here. The document's main body is not about IANA guidance.
LSP-Ping (RFC 4379) is referenced only as an existing alert mechanism.

RFC5587.title: Extended Generic Security Service Mechanism Inquiry APIs
RFC5587.summary: RFC 5587 adds GSS-API functions and an OID namespace of mechanism attributes so applications can inquire which mechanisms have which properties instead of hardcoding mechanism OIDs.

GSS-API.why: The document extends the GSS-API with new functions (GSS_Indicate_mechs_by_attrs, GSS_Inquire_attrs_for_mech, GSS_Display_mech_attr), C bindings, a new status code, and mechanism attribute sets.
GSS-API.quote: This document introduces new application programming interfaces (APIs) to the Generic Security Services API (GSS-API) for extended mechanism attribute inquiry.

rejected.why: SSHv2 is only mentioned as an example of an application that must exclude SPNEGO. The document does not specify or extend SSH.
SPNEGO is only one mechanism whose attribute set is listed. The document is about the general inquiry APIs, not about SPNEGO.
The Kerberos V mechanism's attribute list is an example. The document does not specify or extend Kerberos.
The IANA section only registers an OID arc and the GSS_C_MA_* namespace. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
OIDs are reused as a data type for attributes, but ASN.1 itself is not the subject of the document.

RFC5588.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Extension for Storing Delegated Credentials
RFC5588.summary: Defines the GSS_Store_cred() GSS-API function (with C bindings) for storing delegated or other credentials into the implicit credential store so acceptors can use them like acquired credentials.

GSS-API.why: The entire document specifies an extension to the GSS-API: the GSS_Store_cred() function, its semantics, status codes, and C bindings.
GSS-API.quote: This document defines a new function for the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API), which allows applications to store delegated (and other) credentials

rejected.why: Only mentioned in passing (KRB5CCNAME environment variable in an example); the document is mechanism-independent.
Credential storage is a GSS-API API matter; the more specific GSS-API tag covers it.
Not discussed; only generic mechanism OIDs are used.

RFC5589.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Call Control - Transfer
RFC5589.summary: BCP describing SIP call transfer (blind, consultative, attended, semi-attended) call flows using REFER, Replaces, Target-Dialog and Referred-By, including ad hoc conference modelling and gateway issues.

SIP.why: The whole document is SIP call control best practice for transfer, with detailed call flows and extension usage.
SIP.quote: This document describes providing Call Transfer capabilities in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). SIP extensions such as REFER and Replaces are used

rejected.why: SDP bodies appear in example messages only as offer/answer payloads; not a subject of the document.
Section 9 models transfer as an ad hoc conference using the focus and conference package, but it is one example section, not the document's subject.
Referred-By signed token example uses S/MIME but only as an illustration.
Examples use sips/TLS transport only as substrate.
Section 11 gateway issues are brief and the document is about SIP transfer, not PSTN interworking.

RFC5590.title: Transport Subsystem for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC5590.summary: Defines a Transport Subsystem for the SNMPv3 architecture (RFC 3411), enabling pluggable Transport Models (e.g., SSH, TLS), with the tmStateReference cache, new sendMessage/receiveMessage ASIs, and changes to existing ASIs.

SNMP.why: The document extends the SNMPv3 architecture with a new subsystem, updating RFCs 3411, 3412, 3414 and 3417, so it is squarely about SNMP framework.
SNMP.quote: This document defines a Transport Subsystem, extending the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) architecture defined in [RFC3411].

rejected.why: TLS is mentioned only as an example of a secure transport a future Transport Model might use; the document defines nothing about TLS.
SSH is only an example secure transport; the SSH Transport Model is in RFC 5592, not this document.
No MIB module is defined here; MIB objects are mentioned only in passing.
The document is about an SNMP architecture subsystem for transport models, but the SNMP tag is the more specific fit; it does not define a specific X-over-Y binding.
RADIUS and AAA are mentioned only as external mechanisms in the motivation.
UDP appears only in the architecture diagram and as an example transport.

RFC5591.title: Transport Security Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC5591.summary: RFC 5591 specifies the Transport Security Model (TSM) for SNMP, a security model that uses secure Transport Models in the Transport Subsystem, and defines the SNMP-TSM-MIB module with its counters and prefix configuration object.

SNMP.why: The document extends the SNMP (RFC 3411) architecture with a new Security Model, including elements of procedure for outgoing and incoming messages and SNMPv3 coexistence.
SNMP.quote: This memo describes a Transport Security Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-TSM-MIB module (counters and snmpTsmConfigurationUsePrefix) in SMIv2, a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: This memo also defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring and managing the Transport Security Model for SNMP.

rejected.why: The Secure Shell Transport Model is only cited as an example of a compatible Transport Model; it is specified in RFC 5592.
Secure transports are not specified here; the model relies on whatever Transport Model supplies security.
The document is a Security Model, not a binding of SNMP to a transport; the transport bindings are in separate Transport Model documents.
The model does not authenticate anything itself; it trusts the Transport Model's assertions, so it is not about authentication as a subject.
ASN.1 appears only in the Appendix B comparison of processing order and as the encoding of the SNMP message.

RFC5592.title: Secure Shell Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC5592.summary: Specifies the Secure Shell Transport Model (SSHTM) for SNMP, which runs SNMP as an SSH subsystem within the SNMP Transport Subsystem, with elements of procedure and the SNMP-SSH-TM-MIB module.

SNMP.why: The document defines a new SNMP Transport Model, its elements of procedure and its cache and session handling, so it is about SNMP.
SNMP.quote: This memo describes a Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), using the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-SSH-TM-MIB module with counters, a transport domain and the SnmpSSHAddress textual convention.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for monitoring and managing the Secure Shell Transport Model for SNMP.

SSH.why: It defines a new SSH subsystem named "snmp" and how SSH authentication maps onto SNMP identities, which SSH readers would want.
SSH.quote: This memo describes how SNMP can be used within a Secure Shell (SSH) session, using the SSH connection protocol [RFC4254] over the SSH transport protocol

rejected.why: RADIUS is mentioned only as a possible password-validation backend for SSH.
TCP is only the substrate. The document merely registers two TCP ports.
AAA appears only in passing, as an optional password-validation infrastructure.
GSS-API authentication for SSH is mentioned only as a supported method, not specified here.
NETCONF is mentioned only as a comparison, since it also uses SSH.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC5593.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - URL Access Identifier Extension
RFC5593.summary: Defines new IMAP URLAUTH <access> identifiers (e.g., "stream"), generic application-entity access identifiers and prefixes, an IANA registry for them, and updates RFC 5092.

IMAP.why: The document extends the IMAP URL/URLAUTH mechanism with new access identifiers and updates RFC 5092, so it is about IMAP.
IMAP.quote: This document proposes a set of new <access> identifiers as well as an IANA mechanism to register new <access> identifiers for future applications.

rejected.why: The IMAP URL scheme is the subject, but the document only extends its authorization access identifiers; the IMAP tag fits better.
It creates a registry, but this is boilerplate-level registration in service of the IMAP extension, not an IANA guidance document.
Streaming is only the motivating application, defined in a separate document.
ABNF is just the notation used for the small syntax update.

RFC5594.title: Report from the IETF Workshop on Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Infrastructure, May 28, 2008
RFC5594.summary: Report of the 2008 IETF P2P Infrastructure workshop on P2P-induced congestion, covering ISP and application-provider views, peer selection/localization, congestion control, QoS, and resulting IETF work items.

P2P.why: The whole workshop is about P2P traffic impact and infrastructure, including peer selection, trackers, caches and iTrackers.
P2P.quote: to understand the technical problems that ISPs and end users are experiencing as a result of high volumes of P2P traffic

congestion control.why: Congestion control is a main outcome: delay-based end-to-end scavenger control, weighted congestion control, and the multiple-TCP-connection fairness discussion.
congestion control.quote: designing a protocol for very deferential end-to-end congestion control for delay-tolerant applications

ALTO.why: Peer selection with ISP-provided network information (iTracker, oracle) is the problem space that led to ALTO.
ALTO.quote: standardizing a format for requests and responses may be useful.

Diffserv.why: A substantial section discusses DSCP/Diffserv deployment and its comparison with weighted congestion control as QoS approaches.
Diffserv.quote: A standardized mechanism that may be useful for implementing QoS is Differentiated Services Code Points (DSCP) [RFC2474].

workshop reports.why: The document is a report on an IETF workshop.
workshop reports.quote: This document reports the outcome of a workshop organized by the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure Area Directors

DOCSIS.why: A full subsection covers DOCSIS upstream contention and the Comcast congestion-management approach.
DOCSIS.quote: In the Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS) architecture [DOCSIS] that is used for many cable systems

rejected.why: TCP flow fairness and multiple connections are discussed, but the document is not about TCP itself.
Diffserv is the more specific tag for the QoS section.
Mentioned only in passing as uncommon at modems.
DNS SRV is only a suggested discovery mechanism.
BGP metrics are mentioned only as ISP knowledge.
Discovery of trackers and oracles is one brief potential work item.

RFC5595.title: The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) Service Codes
RFC5595.summary: Describes and clarifies the use of 32-bit DCCP Service Codes (updating RFC 4340): their motivation, registry, relationship to server ports, middlebox handling, and server-side demultiplexing behaviour.

DCCP.why: The whole document specifies and updates DCCP behaviour regarding Service Codes, port demultiplexing and request handling.
DCCP.quote: This document describes the usage of Service Codes by the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol, RFC 4340.

NAT.why: A substantial section sets requirements for NATs and other middleboxes handling Service Codes.
NAT.quote: A middlebox that does not modify the intended application (e.g., NATs [RFC5597] and Firewalls) MUST NOT change the Service Code.

rejected.why: Firewalls are discussed as consumers of Service Codes, but the document is not about firewall traversal mechanisms; middlebox handling is covered by the NAT tag.
SDP is mentioned only as an out-of-band way to signal ports; the extension is defined elsewhere.
The IANA registry is described, but the document does not change allocation procedures; it is about protocol usage.
Only discussed briefly in security considerations.
DTLS over DCCP is mentioned only as an example of a transport-service using Service Codes.
UDP is mentioned only for comparison in the history of port numbers.

gaps.name: DCCP Service Codes
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DCCP, even though DCCP is the protocol this RFC updates. The congestion control tag is not a fit, so the document is tagged under the parent transport topic.

RFC5596.title: Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) Simultaneous-Open Technique to Facilitate NAT/Middlebox Traversal
RFC5596.summary: RFC 5596 updates DCCP (RFC 4340) by adding the DCCP-Listen packet type and INVITED/LISTEN1 server states so a DCCP server behind a NAT or firewall can punch a hole via near-simultaneous open.

DCCP.why: The document extends DCCP by adding a new packet type, two server states, and updated connection-establishment procedures, so it belongs on the DCCP page.
DCCP.quote: This document specifies an update to the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), a connection-oriented and datagram-based transport protocol.

NAT.why: The whole purpose is NAT/middlebox traversal for DCCP via hole punching. It covers the NAPT scenarios and how middleboxes handle DCCP-Listen, and it complements the DCCP NAT behavioural requirements in RFC 5597.
NAT.quote: This assists DCCP applications to communicate through middleboxes (e.g., a Network Address Port Translator or a DCCP server behind a firewall)

rejected.why: This tag is scoped to interactive traversal of NATs for real-time media (ICE/STUN/TURN). The document is a transport-protocol update, and STUN and ICE appear only in background discussion.
SDP is mentioned only as an example of out-of-band signalling to convey the address, port and Service Code. The document does not specify or extend it.
SIP appears only as a possible rendezvous or signalling mechanism and is not the subject of the document.
TCP simultaneous open is discussed in the appendix as background and a design analogy. The document does not change TCP.
Firewalls are mentioned as middleboxes that block inbound connection requests. The document does not address firewall security traversal in its own right, and NAT is the better fit.

RFC5597.title: Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol
RFC5597.summary: RFC 5597 (BCP 150) defines behavioral requirements for NAT devices handling DCCP traffic, modelled on the TCP NAT requirements, covering mapping, filtering, timeouts, ALGs, ICMP, checksum coverage and Service Codes.

NAT.why: The document specifies NAT behavior requirements (mapping, filtering, hairpinning, timeouts, ALGs) for DCCP, which is squarely NAT behavior and requirements.
NAT.quote: This document defines a set of requirements for NATs handling the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP).

DCCP.why: Includes DCCP-specific requirements: handling of simultaneous-open, DCCP-Listen/Sync packets, checksum coverage and Service Codes, so DCCP readers would want it.
DCCP.quote: NAT devices need to mangle: the DCCP source port for outgoing packets, depending on the NAT mapping

rejected.why: RFC 4787 UDP NAT requirements are inherited and UDP encapsulation is mentioned only as out of scope.
ICMP handling by NATs is addressed in a couple of requirements, but the document is not about ICMP itself.
RFC 5382 TCP NAT requirements serve as the structural model, but the document does not address TCP.
Checksum handling is a requirement for DCCP NAT translation, but this is a minor part and not about checksums in general.

RFC5598.title: Internet Mail Architecture
RFC5598.summary: RFC 5598 describes the architecture of Internet Mail, defining actor roles (User, MHS, ADMD), identities, functional components (MUA, MSA, MTA, MDA, MS), and Mediators such as mailing lists and gateways, to give the community a common vocabulary.

email.why: The whole document is an architectural description of Internet email: actors, components, identities, services and standards. This is the general email tag, not a specific protocol.
email.quote: this document describes the enhanced Internet Mail architecture, reflecting the current service.

mailing lists.why: Mailing lists are treated as Mediators, with detail on which identity fields (List-Id, List-*, Reply-To, Sender, MailFrom) they set. This is a substantial part of the document.
mailing lists.quote: A Mailing List receives messages as an explicit addressee and then re-posts them to a list of subscribed members.

rejected.why: SMTP is described as a component protocol within the architecture, but the document does not specify or extend it. The general email tag covers it.
Header fields and the envelope are discussed as identity carriers, but the document does not define the message format. RFC 5322 does that.
MIME is cited as a core standard and in the internationalization section, but only as background.
IMAP and POP appear as access protocols between the message store and the MUA, with only brief mention.
Section 6.2 mentions EAI briefly in an internationalization overview. It is not a main subject.
Spam appears only in the Boundary Filter and Security Considerations sections, in passing.

RFC5601.title: Pseudowire (PW) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC5601.summary: RFC 5601 defines the PW-STD-MIB and IANA-PWE3-MIB SMIv2 modules for generic management of pseudowires (PWE3) over a packet switched network, including configuration, status, performance tables and notifications.

pseudowire.why: The MIB manages pseudowires: PW type, PSN type, labels, signaling parameters, FCS retention, fragmentation and status.
pseudowire.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling of Pseudowire Edge-to-Edge services carried over a general Packet Switched Network.

MIB.why: The document's main content is the PW-STD-MIB and IANA-PWE3-MIB modules, with tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document is about the MIB module (the MIB tag covers it).
MPLS is one PSN type the MIB can map to, and is used in the example. The MPLS-specific MIB is a separate RFC (5602).
LDP signaling (RFC 4447) is referenced for object semantics and the example, but the document does not specify or extend LDP.
L2TPv3 is only one signaling or PSN option referenced by objects.
The IANA-PWE3-MIB is a small part of the document. Its registry content is a MIB textual convention and not IANA guidance as such.

RFC5602.title: Pseudowire (PW) over MPLS PSN Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC5602.summary: Defines the PW-MPLS-STD-MIB SMIv2 module for managing pseudowire association to MPLS PSN tunnels (MPLS-TE, non-TE/LDP, or PW-label-only), complementing the general PW MIB.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (PW-MPLS-STD-MIB) in SMIv2, with tables, objects and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: it describes a MIB module for PW operation over Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switching Routers (LSRs).

pseudowire.why: The MIB manages pseudowire association to MPLS PSN tunnels, so readers of pseudowire emulation would want it.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a model for managing pseudowire services for transmission over different flavors of MPLS tunnels.

rejected.why: The pseudowire tag is more specific to the subject; MPLS tunnels are modelled via existing MPLS MIBs and referenced, not specified here.
LDP is referenced for signaled outer tunnels and PW signaling identifiers, but the document does not specify or extend LDP.
MPLS-TE tunnels are referenced via the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB indexes only; RSVP-TE is not addressed.
SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; Security Considerations boilerplate about SNMPv3 is not evidence.

RFC5603.title: Ethernet Pseudowire (PW) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC5603.summary: Defines the PW-ENET-STD-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing Ethernet pseudowires over any PSN, covering port/VLAN mapping to a PW, VLAN handling modes, and statistics.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a MIB module (PW-ENET-STD-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables, objects, and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: describes managed objects for modeling of Ethernet pseudowire (PW) services

pseudowire.why: The MIB manages Ethernet PWs per the PWE3 architecture, complementing PW-STD-MIB, so pseudowire readers would expect it.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a model for managing Ethernet pseudowire services for transmission over a Packet Switched Network (PSN).

rejected.why: The MIB maps Ethernet ports and VLANs to PWs and links to Etherlike-MIB, but it is about pseudowire management, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
VPLS is mentioned as a supported service type, but the document only provides the interface to a VPLS virtual interface; bridging is explicitly out of scope.
SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB, not the subject; the MIB tag already covers it.
MPLS appears only as one example PSN; the module is stated to be PSN-agnostic.
L2VPN is referenced only as a framework for service types; the document does not address it.

RFC5604.title: Managed Objects for Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) over Packet Switched Networks (PSNs)
RFC5604.summary: Defines the PW-TDM-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing TDM (T1/E1/T3/E3, NxDS0) pseudowires over packet switched networks, with configuration and performance-monitoring tables.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (PW-TDM-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables, objects, and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

pseudowire.why: The MIB manages TDM pseudowires (SAToP, CESoPSN, TDMoIP) in the PWE3 architecture, so readers of pseudowire emulation would want it.
pseudowire.quote: it describes managed objects for pseudowire encapsulation for structured or unstructured Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) (T1, E1, T3, E3) circuits over a Packet Switched Network (PSN)

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines objects and does not specify or extend SNMP, and the MIB tag sits under it.
The MPLS MIBs appear only as the PSN layer in the layering figure. The document does not address MPLS itself.
The performance tables are interval counters for the PW MIB. They are not a measurement methodology.
RTP header use is a configuration flag, not something the document specifies.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation (SAToP/CESoPSN/TDMoIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TDM circuit emulation over packet networks. Pseudowire is the nearest fit.

RFC5605.title: Managed Objects for ATM over Packet Switched Networks (PSNs)
RFC5605.summary: Defines the PW-ATM-MIB SMIv2 module for managing ATM pseudowires that carry ATM cells over packet switched networks, with configuration tables for 1:1 and N:1 modes and performance counters.

pseudowire.why: The MIB manages ATM pseudowires, i.e. ATM emulated edge-to-edge over a PSN, which is the pseudowire subject.
pseudowire.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling ATM Pseudowire (PW) carrying ATM cells over Packet Switched Networks (PSNs)

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (PW-ATM-MIB) with its tables, objects and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part of the MIB is current, 15-minute and 1-day performance counter tables for ATM PWs.
performance measurement.quote: Report ATM performance metrics for the ATM PW. This includes cells transmit, Cells dropped, Cells received, and unknownCells.

rejected.why: ATM is the emulated service whose parameters (VPI/VCI, traffic descriptors) are managed, but the document is about pseudowire management of ATM, not IP over ATM; the pseudowire and MIB tags cover it better.
MPLS is only the example PSN; the MIB is PSN-agnostic and links to MPLS via other MIB modules.
SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB; the document only references it in framework text and SNMPv3 security considerations.
OAM cell support is mentioned as a requirement but no OAM mechanism is specified.

RFC5606.title: Implications of 'retransmission-allowed' for SIP Location Conveyance
RFC5606.summary: Informational GEOPRIV consensus statement on how the PIDF-LO <retransmission-allowed> element should be interpreted when location is conveyed in SIP, recommending location-by-reference, encryption, or omission to limit access, and a "Location-Routing-Allowed" SIP header.

geolocation.why: The document is about the privacy semantics of PIDF-LO location information, retransmission rules, and location-by-reference vs by-value conveyance. No more specific child tag fits (HELD is not discussed).
geolocation.quote: explores an ambiguity in the interpretation of the <retransmission-allowed> element of the Presence Information Data Format for Location Objects (PIDF-LO)

SIP.why: It recommends how SIP location conveyance should behave, proposes a new SIP header, and gives rules for proxies, UAs and B2BUAs handling location.
SIP.quote: it is the responsibility of the SIP WG ... recommend a "Location-Routing-Allowed" header

rejected.why: PIDF-LO is the object whose element is discussed, but the document is about location privacy semantics in SIP, not the presence data format itself. The geolocation tag covers it.
Privacy is central, but the document is about location-specific policy, which geolocation covers. It is not a general protocol privacy considerations document.
The document mentions SIP presence only in passing and does not specify SIMPLE event packages.
Emergency calling appears only as an example use case for location-based routing.
SIP Digest and RFC 4474 Identity are mentioned briefly as authentication costs for dereferencing, but the document does not address them.

RFC5607.title: Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Authorization for Network Access Server (NAS) Management
RFC5607.summary: Defines new RADIUS attributes and a Service-Type value (Framed-Management) for authorizing local and remote management access to a NAS, including management protocol, transport protection, policy name, and privilege level.

RADIUS.why: The document extends RADIUS with four new attributes and a new Service-Type value for management authorization.
RADIUS.quote: This document specifies Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) attributes for authorizing management access to a Network Access Server (NAS).

rejected.why: Only a short translation-considerations section; the document is about RADIUS attributes.
SNMP is one of the management protocols that can be named in an attribute value, not a subject of the document.
Only listed as an enumerated value and an example of a Framed Management protocol.
RADIUS is the more specific tag and already implies the AAA parent.
The RADIUS tag covers this; no separate topic tag is needed.
SSH is mentioned only as a remote terminal and secure transport, not specified or extended.

RFC5608.title: Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Usage for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Transport Models
RFC5608.summary: Specifies how SNMP secure Transport Models (e.g., SSH Transport Model) use RADIUS to authenticate principals and authorize SNMP sessions, recommending hint and service-provisioning attributes in Access-Request/Accept messages.

RADIUS.why: The document profiles RADIUS attribute usage (Service-Type, Framed-Management-Protocol, Management-Transport-Protection, timeouts) for SNMP service authorization.
RADIUS.quote: This memo describes the use of a Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) authentication and authorization service with Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) secure Transport Models

SNMP.why: The document is about authorizing SNMP access over secure Transport Models, mapping to SNMP security levels (authPriv, authNoPriv).
SNMP.quote: The Transport Subsystem for SNMP [RFC5590] defines a mechanism for providing transport layer security (TLS) for SNMP

rejected.why: SSH is the example secure transport used by the SNMP Transport Model; the document does not define or extend SSH.
TLS is only mentioned as an alternative secure transport; nothing specified for it.
RADIUS is the specific AAA protocol tagged; generic AAA is implied by the child.
EAP is mentioned only as an authentication method and its use is NOT RECOMMENDED here.
Mentioned only as another PAM-integrated authentication service.
No MIB module is defined; the document concerns RADIUS attributes.

RFC5609.title: State Machines for the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA)
RFC5609.summary: RFC 5609 defines informative conceptual state machines for the PANA Client (PaC) and PANA Authentication Agent (PAA), including their interfaces to EAP peer and authenticator state machines.

PANA.why: The whole document specifies PaC and PAA state machines, with variables, procedures and transition tables for PANA.
PANA.quote: This document defines the conceptual state machines for the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA).

EAP.why: A substantial part (Section 3, 7.1, 8.1) defines the interface between PANA and EAP peer/authenticator state machines, including restart, message delivery and result notification.
EAP.quote: The two state machines show how PANA can interface with the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) state machines.

rejected.why: Mentioned only briefly in implementation considerations as the backend protocol; the document is not about it.
Mentioned only as an example of secured transport bootstrapped with keying material; not a subject of the document.
Generic parent topic; the specific technology tags PANA and EAP already cover it.

RFC5610.title: Exporting Type Information for IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Elements
RFC5610.summary: Extends IPFIX with new Information Elements and an Options Template that export Information Element type information (data type, semantics, units, range, name, description) inline in an IPFIX message stream, mainly for enterprise-specific IEs.

IPFIX.why: The document extends IPFIX with new Information Elements and an Options Template for type records.
IPFIX.quote: to allow the encoding of IPFIX Information Model properties within an IPFIX Message stream

rejected.why: It only reuses informationElementId from the PSAMP Information Model. The document is not about packet sampling.
The IANA subregistries are created in the IANA Considerations boilerplate. The main body is not about IANA registry guidance.
It is only the string encoding used for name and description fields.
Language tags are mentioned only for annotating descriptions, which is incidental.

RFC5611.title: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol version 3 - Setup of Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) Pseudowires
RFC5611.summary: Defines L2TPv3 control-plane extensions (new TDM PW and RTP AVPs, PW types, result/error codes) for setting up structure-agnostic and CESoPSN-style TDM pseudowires.

pseudowire.why: The document specifies setup of TDM pseudowires: PW types, TDM PW AVP, session creation and validation.
pseudowire.quote: This document defines extensions to the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3) for support of structure-agnostic [RFC4553] and structure-aware (CESoPSN style, see [RFC5086]) Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) pseudowires.

L2TP.why: It extends L2TPv3 with new AVPs, PW type values, result codes and session negotiation rules.
L2TP.quote: There are two new AVPs for the Session Management messages. One AVP describes the TDM pseudowire attributes.

rejected.why: The RTP AVP only signals whether an RTP header is used in the TDM PW encapsulation; RTP itself is not specified or extended.
MPLS TDM PW setup is mentioned only as a related document (RFC 5287); this document covers L2TPv3.
IANA section only registers values for this document's extensions; it is boilerplate here.

gaps.name: TDM pseudowires / circuit emulation (SAToP, CESoPSN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TDM circuit emulation. The document is about it, and 'pseudowire' only partly covers it.

RFC5612.title: Enterprise Number for Documentation Use
RFC5612.summary: RFC 5612 allocates Enterprise Number 32473 (an SMI Private Enterprise Number) for use in examples in RFCs, books and documentation.

IANA.why: The document reserves a single value in the IANA-administered Private Enterprise Numbers registry for documentation use, so it is about that registry allocation.
IANA.quote: The Enterprise Number 32473 has been allocated for use in examples in RFCs, books, documentation, and the like.

MIB.why: Enterprise Numbers form the 1.3.6.1.4.1 OID subtree under the SMI, used to identify management objects. Readers of SMI and MIB material would want this documentation value.
MIB.quote: created a subtree (arc) of object identifiers (OIDs) for identifying management objects that are defined unilaterally by a single party

rejected.why: Syslog is only one example protocol that uses Enterprise Numbers, and the document does not specify or extend it.
RADIUS Vendor-Specific attributes appear only in a list of protocols that use Enterprise Numbers.
DHCPv4 vendor options are one listed use of Enterprise Numbers, not a subject of the document.
IPFIX enterprise-specific information elements are a listed example only.
The document concerns the Enterprise Number registry and OID arc, not the SNMP protocol or framework.

gaps.name: Reserved values for documentation use
gaps.why: RFC 5612 belongs with other documentation-reserved identifiers, such as AS numbers and example media types. The taxonomy has no tag for this group.

RFC5613.title: OSPF Link-Local Signaling
RFC5613.summary: Defines a backward-compatible OSPFv2/OSPFv3 extension that appends a TLV-based link-local signaling (LLS) data block to Hello and DD packets, with an L-bit, Extended Options and Flags TLV, and a cryptographic authentication TLV; replaces experimental RFC 4813.

OSPF.why: The whole document specifies an extension to OSPF packets (LLS block, L-bit, TLVs) for both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
OSPF.quote: This document describes an extension to OSPFv2 [OSPFV2] and OSPFv3 [OSPFV3] allowing additional information to be exchanged between routers on the same link.

rejected.why: The document covers both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equally; OSPFv3 is not its sole subject, so the parent OSPF tag fits better.
IPsec AH/ESP only mentioned in Security Considerations as the OSPFv3 authentication mechanism.
The LLS block uses the standard IP checksum, but this is incidental to the extension.
IANA registry creation/updates are boilerplate-like and not the main subject.

RFC5614.title: Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Extension of OSPF Using Connected Dominating Set (CDS) Flooding
RFC5614.summary: Specifies OSPF-MDR, an experimental OSPFv3 extension adding a MANET interface type that uses a connected dominating set of MANET Designated Routers for reduced flooding, adjacency reduction, differential Hellos, and partial-topology router-LSAs.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends OSPFv3 with a new interface type, modifying Hello, adjacency, flooding, router-LSA and SPF procedures.
OSPFv3.quote: This document specifies an extension of OSPFv3 [RFC5340] to support a new interface type for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs)

MANET.why: The document's purpose is routing in mobile ad hoc networks, using a distributed CDS-based MDR selection algorithm.
MANET.quote: MANET Interface is a new OSPF interface type that supports broadcast-capable, multihop wireless networks.

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific OSPFv3 child tag; the parent is implied.
The document uses its own OSPF Hello extension for neighbor discovery, not NHDP.
AH/ESP are mentioned only in Security Considerations as boilerplate for authentication.
Security Considerations discuss threats briefly but the document is not about routing security.
OSPFv3 runs over IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC5615.title: H.248/MEGACO Registration Procedures
RFC5615.summary: BCP updating the IANA registration procedures for H.248/MEGACO Packages, Error Codes, ServiceChange Reasons and Profile Names, adding formal IESG expert review.

Megaco.why: The document defines registration and review procedures for packages, error codes, reasons and profiles of the H.248/Megaco gateway control protocol, so Megaco readers need it.
Megaco.quote: This document updates the H.248/MEGACO IANA Package registration procedures in order to better describe the Package registration process

IANA.why: A substantial part is an IANA registry policy: expert review, registration fields and status handling for the H.248/MEGACO Packages registry.
IANA.quote: The process for registering a public Package is deemed to be "specification required" as per [RFC5226].

rejected.why: ABNF is used only to give the PackageName syntax; the document is not about the notation.
It describes appointing an IESG expert, but only for a registry; the IANA tag fits better.

RFC5616.title: Streaming Internet Messaging Attachments
RFC5616.summary: Informational profile for streaming audio/video message attachments from an IMAP server to constrained clients by passing URLAUTH-authorized IMAP URLs to a SIP media server (RFC 4240 announcement or RFC 5022 MSCML IVR), which fetches via URLFETCH and streams over RTP; also defines an IMAP METADATA entry for media server discovery.

IMAP.why: The document profiles IMAP extensions (URLAUTH, URLFETCH BINARY, METADATA, GENURLAUTH) and defines a new IMAP METADATA entry /shared/mediaServers; IMAP readers would want it.
IMAP.quote: a method for streaming multimedia attachments received by a resource- and/or network-constrained device from an IMAP server

SIP.why: Substantial portions specify SIP INVITE/INFO usage with the announcement and MSCML IVR media server services, including SDP negotiation examples and SIPS security.
SIP.quote: The client connects to a SIP Media Server using the announcement service as specified in RFC 4240 [NETANN], or the IVR service as specified in RFC 5022

streaming.why: The goal is streaming audio/video with VCR-style controls to clients, so streaming readers would want this document.
streaming.quote: the media can be streamed to the device, using protocols such as RTP [RTP]

rejected.why: RTP is only the delivery substrate for the stream; nothing new is defined about it.
SDP is used only in illustrative codec negotiation examples, not specified or extended.
MIME headers/content types are used to decide what to stream, but the document is not about MIME.
TLS is only recommended as a security mechanism for the media server to IMAP server connection.
IMAP is the more specific tag; the document is about IMAP-based access rather than email in general.
MSCML is a different media server control protocol and not MRCP.

gaps.name: MSCML / media server control (RFC 4240 announcement and RFC 5022 IVR)
gaps.why: The document profiles SIP media server services and the Media Server Control Markup Language, but the taxonomy has no tag for media server control or IVR services.

RFC5617.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Author Domain Signing Practices (ADSP)
RFC5617.summary: Specifies DKIM Author Domain Signing Practices (ADSP), a DNS TXT record at _adsp._domainkey that lets a domain advertise whether it signs all its mail, plus the lookup procedure and IANA registries.

DKIM.why: ADSP is a DKIM adjunct that defines a record and lookup procedure for author domain signing practices; it extends DKIM and is the core subject.
DKIM.quote: This document specifies an adjunct mechanism to aid in assessing messages that do not contain a DKIM signature for the domain used in the author's address.

rejected.why: DNS is only the publication substrate (TXT record under _adsp._domainkey); no new RR type or DNS behaviour is defined.
A later, different policy mechanism; not discussed here.
Not part of the document.
The From: header is referenced as the author address source, but the document does not specify message format.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as the answer to DNS spoofing.
The parent is implied by the more specific DKIM tag, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: DKIM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DKIM tag, although it has sibling tags SPF, DMARC and ARC under email authentication. The closest fit is the parent tag email authentication, but DKIM is the actual subject.

RFC5618.title: Mixed Security Mode for the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC5618.summary: RFC 5618 extends TWAMP with a mixed security mode (new Modes bit 3) allowing an encrypted TWAMP-Control session with an unauthenticated TWAMP-Test session, and creates the IANA TWAMP Modes registry.

TWAMP.why: The document extends TWAMP by defining a new Modes value for mixed security, updating RFC 5357. It is squarely about TWAMP.
TWAMP.quote: The extension adds the option to use different security modes in the TWAMP-Control and TWAMP-Test protocols simultaneously.

rejected.why: TWAMP derives from OWAMP and the document references its control and test procedures. It does not extend or specify OWAMP itself.
The document creates a TWAMP Modes registry, but that is a small part of a TWAMP-specific extension. It is not about IANA guidance or stewardship in general.
TWAMP already sits under this topic, so the technology tag covers it and the topic tag is not needed.
The security-mode choice is a TWAMP protocol mode negotiation, not a general authentication mechanism.

RFC5619.title: Softwire Security Analysis and Requirements
RFC5619.summary: Security analysis and requirements for softwire Hubs-and-Spokes (L2TPv2) and Mesh (BGP) deployments, specifying threats and the use of IPsec/IKEv2, authentication and BGP protection.

softwire.why: The document is the security analysis for softwire solutions. Softwire is the nearest taxonomy tag, but it is not in the taxonomy. See gaps.
softwire.quote: This document describes security guidelines for the softwire "Hubs and Spokes" and "Mesh" solutions.

RFC5620.title: RFC Editor Model (Version 1)
RFC5620.summary: IAB document defining the RFC Editor model, splitting RFC Series responsibilities among the RFC Series Editor, Independent Submission Editor, RFC Production Center and RFC Publisher, with the RSAG advisory group and selection process.

RFC series.why: The document defines the organizational structure, roles, and oversight of the RFC Editor and RFC Series, which is exactly the RFC series subject.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor model presented in this document divides the responsibilities for the RFC Series into four functions

internet governance.why: Covers IAB/IAOC oversight, contracting, selection processes and dispute resolution for the RFC Editor functions. This is governance of Internet standards publication beyond the series format itself.
internet governance.quote: The exact implementation is a responsibility of the IAOC.

rejected.why: The focus is the RFC Editor's organization and selection of editors, not the IETF standards process itself.
IANA is only mentioned as a coordination partner of the Production Center; the document is not about IANA registries.
The selection process resembles the IAOC selection approach but is not the NomCom procedure.

RFC5621.title: Message Body Handling in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5621.summary: RFC 5621 specifies how SIP user agents encode, generate, process and signal handling for message bodies, including mandatory multipart MIME support, Content-Disposition handling parameters, body-part references, and the new 'by-reference' disposition type.

SIP.why: The whole document defines SIP UA behaviour for message bodies and updates RFC 3261, 3204 and 3459, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document specifies how message bodies are handled in SIP.

MIME.why: A substantial part specifies SIP UA support for multipart MIME types (mixed, alternative, related), nesting, and Content-Disposition use.
MIME.quote: SIP UAs MUST support parsing 'multipart' MIME bodies, including nested body parts.

rejected.why: SDP appears only as an example body type and in the default 'session' disposition; the document doesn't specify or extend it.
Mentioned only for protecting bodies and in Security Considerations; not the subject.
The document registers a disposition type, not a media type, and the multipart handling is better covered by MIME.
Content-Disposition header usage is in SIP messages, not Internet mail message format.

RFC5622.title: Profile for Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) Congestion ID 4: TCP-Friendly Rate Control for Small Packets (TFRC-SP)
RFC5622.summary: Specifies DCCP Congestion Control ID 4 (CCID 4), an experimental profile based on CCID 3 that uses the small-packet variant of TFRC (TFRC-SP), including a new Dropped Packets option.

TFRC.why: The document profiles TFRC-SP congestion control for DCCP, defining header-size adjustment, minimum packet interval and short-loss-interval loss rate handling.
TFRC.quote: CCID 4 uses TFRC-SP [RFC4828], an experimental, small-packet variant of TFRC.

DCCP.why: It defines a new DCCP CCID, with new option type (Dropped Packets), feature numbers and registries.
DCCP.quote: This document specifies an experimental profile for Congestion Control Identifier 4, TCP-Friendly Rate Control for Small Packets (TFRC-SP), in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)

rejected.why: ECN is used by reference to RFC 4342 and is not specified or extended here.
Parent of TFRC; implied by the more specific tag.
Mentioned only as the model for loss intervals.
DCCP is a separate transport; UDP isn't relevant.

RFC5623.title: Framework for PCE-Based Inter-Layer MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC5623.summary: Informational framework describing how the PCE architecture applies to inter-layer MPLS/GMPLS traffic engineering, covering single and multiple PCE computation models, Virtual Network Topology Manager (VNTM) cooperation and signaling-trigger control models, stability and manageability.

PCE.why: The whole document defines how PCEs (single or multiple, with or without inter-PCE communication) compute inter-layer paths and cooperate with a VNTM.
PCE.quote: This document describes a framework for applying the PCE-based architecture to inter-layer Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) traffic engineering.

GMPLS.why: Multi-layer and multi-region GMPLS networks, LSP hierarchy and virtual TE links are the setting and substance of the inter-layer TE models.
GMPLS.quote: the lower-layer network (LSRs, H2, L1, L2, and H3) is a GMPLS optical network

rejected.why: Used for signaling the computed paths (EROs, triggered lower-layer LSP setup), but the document defines no RSVP-TE extensions.
Parent of GMPLS, so implied by the GMPLS tag. The document is about inter-layer TE for both MPLS and GMPLS, so GMPLS is the more specific tag.
MIB modules are mentioned only for notifications and manageability, and the document defines none.
Parent of PCE, so it is implied by the PCE tag.
Inter-layer policy is discussed in the manageability section, but it is not the subject of the document.

RFC5624.title: Quality of Service Parameters for Usage with Diameter
RFC5624.summary: Defines Diameter AVPs for QoS parameters (two token-bucket traffic model AVPs, a Bandwidth AVP, and a PHB-Class AVP), plus a QoS profile registry for extensibility.

Diameter.why: The document defines new Diameter AVPs (codes 495-503) and an extensibility profile for QoS in Diameter, so it extends the Diameter protocol.
Diameter.quote: This document defines a number of Quality of Service (QoS) parameters that can be reused for conveying QoS information within the Diameter protocol

QoS.why: The core subject is QoS parameters (token bucket, bandwidth, PHB class) for resource reservation and signalling.
QoS.quote: The above-mentioned parameters are intended to support basic integrated and differentiated services functionality in the network.

Diffserv.why: The PHB-Class AVP encodes DSCP and PHB identification codes per RFC 3140, and the TMOD-2 AVP supports AF traffic.
Diffserv.quote: Resource reservations might refer to a packet processor with a particular DiffServ per-hop behavior (PHB) (using the <PHB-Class> AVP).

rejected.why: The TMOD semantics are taken from the Intserv/RSVP specifications (RFC 2210, 2215), but those are only the source of the parameter definitions.
RSVP is referenced only for the semantics of the token bucket parameters. The document does not specify or extend RSVP.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the AVP grammar. The document is not about it.
The IANA considerations (AVP codes, QoS profile registry) are boilerplate-like registrations. The main body is not about IANA registry guidance.
NSIS is mentioned only in the acknowledgements, and the QSPEC work is not specified here.

RFC5625.title: DNS Proxy Implementation Guidelines
RFC5625.summary: BCP giving implementation guidelines for DNS proxies in broadband gateways: transparency, protocol conformance (flags, compression, unknown RRs, size limits, TCP, EDNS0, TSIG), DHCP-DNS interaction, and security recommendations.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies how DNS proxies/forwarders should handle DNS messages, so it is about DNS resolver/forwarder behaviour and operations.
DNS.quote: This document provides guidelines for the implementation of DNS proxies, as found in broadband gateways and other similar network devices.

EDNS.why: A dedicated section covers proxy handling of EDNS0 OPT records, buffer sizes and fragmentation, which EDNS readers would want.
EDNS.quote: However, some proxies have been observed to either reject (with a FORMERR response code) or black-hole any packet containing an OPT RR.

DHCP.why: Section 5 is devoted to how DHCP options 6 and 15 and lease behaviour affect client DNS configuration, with recommendations for gateways.
DHCP.quote: Most gateways default to supplying their own IP address in the DHCP "Domain Name Server" option [RFC2132].

rejected.why: Only mentioned for AD/CD/DO bits that proxies must not drop; the document does not specify DNSSEC itself.
UDP packet size and truncation are discussed only as part of DNS transport, not UDP usage in general.
TCP is just a DNS fail-over transport the proxy must support; nothing new about TCP.
NAT source-port randomisation is mentioned briefly in security considerations only.

RFC5626.title: Managing Client-Initiated Connections in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5626.summary: RFC 5626 defines SIP "outbound" behaviors for UAs, edge proxies, registrars and authoritative proxies so requests are delivered over UA-initiated flows (through NATs/firewalls), with multiple registration flows, flow tokens, CRLF and STUN keep-alives, and flow recovery backoff.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP (updating RFC 3261 and 3327) with the outbound option tag, reg-id, ob parameter, Flow-Timer header and new response codes 430 and 439.
SIP.quote: This specification defines behaviors for User Agents, registrars, and proxy servers that allow requests to be delivered on existing connections established by the User Agent.

NAT traversal.why: A central goal is NAT/firewall traversal for SIP signalling via client-initiated flows and keep-alives that hold NAT bindings open.
NAT traversal.quote: This specification allows a SIP User Agent behind such a firewall or NAT to receive inbound traffic associated with registrations or dialogs that it initiates.

STUN.why: Defines a new SIP-specific STUN usage for keep-alives over UDP flows, which STUN readers would want.
STUN.quote: This section describes changes to the SIP transport layer that allow SIP and STUN [RFC5389] Binding Requests to be mixed over the same flow.  This constitutes a new STUN usage.

rejected.why: TCP connections are the substrate for flows and CRLF keep-alives; the document doesn't extend TCP.
TLS is mentioned as motivation (client-initiated connections to servers with certificates) but nothing new is defined for TLS.
Instance-id is recommended to be a UUID URN, but only as a usage of RFC 4122, not about UUIDs.
Only a short subsection on multiplexing STUN with SigComp; not a substantial focus.
DNS SRV is used for load balancing and server location, but only as a mechanism the document relies on.
HMAC is used only in an example flow-token algorithm.

RFC5627.title: Obtaining and Using Globally Routable User Agent URIs (GRUUs) in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5627.summary: Defines a SIP extension by which a registrar issues Globally Routable User Agent URIs (public and temporary GRUUs) to a UA at registration, and how UAs, registrars and proxies use and route them.

SIP.why: The document specifies a SIP extension: new Contact parameters, the gr URI parameter, the gruu option tag, and UA, registrar and proxy behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document describes an extension to SIP for obtaining a GRUU from a registrar and for communicating a GRUU to a peer within a dialog.

rejected.why: Instance IDs are urn:uuid values taken from RFC 5626, but the document does not define or specify UUIDs.
It defines a SIP URI parameter, but only as part of the SIP extension. It is not about URI syntax in general.
NAT and firewall traversal is given as motivation, but the document does not specify NAT behaviour.
AES-ECB and HMAC-SHA256 appear only in the Appendix A example GRUU construction algorithm, so the document is not about them.
Section 10.3 discusses privacy of temporary GRUUs, but it is a security considerations discussion, not the main subject of the document.
SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY (event packages) appear in the call flow only as usage examples.

RFC5628.title: Registration Event Package Extension for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Globally Routable User Agent URIs (GRUUs)
RFC5628.summary: Defines an XML extension (<pub-gruu> and <temp-gruu> elements) to the SIP registration event package's reginfo document so notifiers can deliver GRUUs and subscribers can track temporary GRUU validity.

SIP.why: The document extends a SIP event package (reg event) and specifies notifier and subscriber behaviour for SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, building on SIP GRUUs. It is SIP extension work.
SIP.quote: This specification defines an extension to the registration event package to include GRUUs assigned by the registrar.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document defines new XML elements, an XML schema and a namespace extending the reginfo document format.
XML.quote: The <pub-gruu> and <temp-gruu> elements are defined within a new XML namespace URI.

rejected.why: The registration event package is SIP event-package work, but this RFC does not address presence, PIDF or XCAP. SIP is the better fit.
GRUUs are URIs, but the document only carries them in notifications. It does not define URI syntax or schemes.
The +sip.instance value appears only in examples as an instance ID and is not the subject of the document.
3GPP IMS implicit registration is used as a motivating example, not as the subject.

RFC5629.title: A Framework for Application Interaction in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5629.summary: Framework describing stimulus-based application interaction in SIP, where applications push client-local UI components (HTML, KPML) via REFER/SUBSCRIBE or use client-remote UIs over media, plus UA behaviour, authorization and feature interaction.

SIP.why: The document specifies how SIP applications and user agents interact using REFER, SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, GRUU and Target-Dialog, including UA and application requirements.
SIP.quote: This document describes a framework for the interaction between users and Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) based applications.

rejected.why: RTP and RFC 4733 DTMF carriage are only the media substrate for client-remote UIs, not specified here.
Uses SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and the KPML event package, but is not about presence or instant messaging.
HTML and other markups are used for UI components but not specified or extended.
PSTN gateway appears as a User Device Proxy, but interworking is not the subject.
VoiceXML/IVR are mentioned as UI examples; MRCP is not discussed.

gaps.name: Application interaction / stimulus signaling (KPML)
gaps.why: The framework for user interaction with SIP applications via markup and key-press stimulus has no dedicated tag; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5630.title: The Use of the SIPS URI Scheme in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5630.summary: Clarifies the meaning and use of the SIPS URI scheme in SIP, deprecates the last-hop exception, and specifies normative UA, registrar, proxy and redirect server behaviour, updating RFC 3261 and RFC 3608.

SIP.why: The document updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3608 with normative changes to SIP behaviour for UAC, UAS, registrar, proxy and redirect server regarding SIPS URIs, including GRUU and registration handling.
SIP.quote: This document provides clarifications and guidelines concerning the use of the SIPS URI scheme in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate that SIPS requires on each hop. The document defines no new TLS protocol feature, only how SIP uses it.
SIPS is a URI scheme, but the document is about its SIP routing and security semantics, not about general URI syntax or scheme registration.
Not relevant; the document concerns secure signalling, not ISUP interworking.
RFC 4474 SIP Identity is only mentioned as a preferable alternative for end-to-end assurance, and the document is not about caller-ID authentication.

RFC5631.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Session Mobility
RFC5631.summary: Informational framework describing how SIP (via 3pcc and REFER) can transfer ongoing media sessions between a mobile node and local devices, using SLP as an example for device discovery.

SIP.why: The whole document defines SIP call flows (3pcc re-INVITE, REFER/Replaces, GRUU addressing) for session mobility, so it belongs on the SIP page.
SIP.quote: This document describes the basic approaches and shows the signaling and media flow examples for providing this service using the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

SLP.why: Section 4 describes in detail how SLP (SA/UA/DA, SrvReg, SrvRqst, attributes) is used to discover local devices, and SLP is used throughout the examples.
SLP.quote: Service discovery is essential to locate targets for session transfer and is discussed using the Service Location Protocol (SLP) as an example.

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer is the mechanism for the media parameters, but the document does not define or extend it.
MSRP transfer is covered only as one media type in a subsection (5.3.1.2), and the document does not specify the protocol.
ICE has a short section (5.6) on possible use, but the document is not about it.
Despite the 'mobility' framing, this is application-layer session transfer, not IP-layer mobility.
SLP is tagged directly, which sits under this topic, so the parent is implied.
SRTP and DTLS appear only in the Security Considerations about maintaining media security.

RFC5632.title: Comcast's ISP Experiences in a Proactive Network Provider Participation for P2P (P4P) Technical Trial
RFC5632.summary: Informational report of Comcast's July 2008 P4P iTracker trial with Pando and Yale, describing the iTracker designs (fine, coarse, generic) and measured effects on P2P swarm download speed and ISP traffic, as input to the IETF ALTO work.

ALTO.why: The trial evaluates P4P iTracker, the ISP-to-P2P topology guidance mechanism feeding ALTO. The document shares results to inform ALTO's technical discussion.
ALTO.quote: This trial used P4P iTracker technology, which is being considered by the IETF as part of the Application Layer Transport Optimization (ALTO) working group.

P2P.why: The trial measures P2P swarm localization, download speeds and cancellation rates with a Pando P2P client, so P2P readers would want it.
P2P.quote: P4P iTrackers theoretically allow P2P networks to optimize traffic within each ISP, reducing the volume of data traversing the ISP's infrastructure

rejected.why: Comcast's cable network and CMTS are mentioned only as the trial's setting, and RFC 3083 is cited only for a CMTS definition.
The document reports measured trial results, but these are P2P/ISP traffic outcomes, not a measurement metric or method.
Privacy is touched on briefly (opt-in, topology-only information) in Next Steps, but it is not a substantial subject of the document.
Transit cost and localization effects are discussed, but not traffic engineering of packet networks in the routing sense.

RFC5633.title: Nominating Committee Process: Earlier Announcement of Open Positions and Solicitation of Volunteers
RFC5633.summary: BCP update to RFC 3777 allowing the IETF Executive Director to announce open NomCom positions and solicit volunteers when no NomCom Chair has been named four weeks after the first IETF meeting, and letting the Secretariat do clerical tasks.

NomCom.why: The whole document modifies the Nominating Committee selection process, specifically the announcement of positions and solicitation of volunteers in RFC 3777.
NomCom.quote: The Chair (or the IETF Executive Director, if no Chair has been named four weeks after the first IETF meeting of the year) obtains the list of positions to be reviewed

rejected.why: It is the parent of NomCom. NomCom is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.

RFC5634.title: Quick-Start for the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)
RFC5634.summary: Specifies how DCCP uses the experimental Quick-Start mechanism (IP-option rate requests approved by routers), defining a DCCP Quick-Start Response option, a Quick-Start Interval, a validation phase, and CCID 2, 3 and 4 procedures.

DCCP.why: The document extends DCCP with a new header option and CCID-specific procedures for Quick-Start. DCCP readers need it.
DCCP.quote: This document specifies the use of the Quick-Start mechanism by the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP).

congestion control.why: Quick-Start is a congestion control mechanism for setting the initial or restart sending rate. The document specifies how it interacts with CCID 2, 3 and 4 congestion control (cwnd, TFRC rate).
congestion control.quote: Quick-Start enables a DCCP sender to cooperate with Quick-Start routers along the end-to-end path to determine an allowed sending rate

rejected.why: TCP appears only as a comparison and as the subject of RFC 4782. This document does not specify TCP behaviour.
TFRC and TFRC-SP are the congestion control used by CCID 3 and CCID 4. The document only adapts Quick-Start to them and does not define them.
ECN marks are treated as a congestion signal that ends Quick-Start mode. ECN itself is not the subject.
Section 2.7 only says Quick-Start Requests should not be sent in PMTUD probe packets. This is a minor interaction.
Quick-Start Requests are carried in IP options, but the document is not about IP itself. RFC 4782 covers that.

gaps.name: Quick-Start
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Quick-Start (RFC 4782), the router-assisted initial sending rate mechanism. Both this RFC and RFC 4782 would be grouped under it.

RFC5635.title: Remote Triggered Black Hole Filtering with Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF)
RFC5635.summary: Informational RFC describing how to use BGP-triggered discard routes (RTBH) with unicast RPF to black-hole DoS traffic by destination and by source address, with deployment steps and Cisco/Juniper examples.

DDoS.why: The whole document is a DoS/DDoS mitigation technique (RTBH filtering by destination and source). No DOTS involvement, so the parent topic fits.
DDoS.quote: Remote Triggered Black Hole (RTBH) filtering is a popular and effective technique for the mitigation of denial-of-service attacks.

BGP.why: A substantial part covers BGP policy, communities, NO_EXPORT, trigger routers and egress filters to implement RTBH, so BGP operations readers would want it.
BGP.quote: BGP can be used to distribute discard routes that are based not on destination or target addresses, but on source addresses of unwanted traffic.

operational security.why: The document is an operator practice guide with safety filters and deployment cautions for network infrastructure, produced by the opsec WG.
operational security.quote: There is always a chance that the triggering BGP update could leak from the network and so egress prefix filters are strongly recommended.

rejected.why: Communities are used as triggers, but the document does not define or specify community types; it is a usage detail of the BGP policy.
The technique uses discard routes, not flow specification; flowspec is only an alternative not discussed.
uRPF/ingress filtering is referenced via RFC 3704 but the document is not about address architecture or allocation.
Concerns traffic dropping rather than securing routing protocol or origin validation; the DDoS and operational security tags fit better.
uRPF is used for source-based dropping, not source address validation improvement.

gaps.name: Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) / ingress filtering
gaps.why: The document relies on uRPF strict and loose modes for source-based filtering, but the taxonomy has no tag for uRPF or ingress filtering (BCP 38/84).

RFC5636.title: Traceable Anonymous Certificate
RFC5636.summary: Defines an experimental architecture and protocol for issuing Traceable Anonymous Certificates, in which a Blind Issuer and an Anonymity Issuer jointly sign pseudonymous X.509 certificates with threshold and blind signatures, so a certificate can be traced to the real user only if both cooperate.

PKI.why: The document defines a split-authority CA/RA certificate issuance architecture, with PKCS10/CMC request profiles and CRL revocation handling, for pseudonymous certificates in an Internet PKI.
PKI.quote: offering privacy for a user who requests and uses an X.509 certificate containing a pseudonym, while still retaining the ability to map such a certificate to the real user

X.509.why: It defines a profile of pseudonymous end-entity X.509 certificates, with a second CRL-signing CA certificate and constraints on the Subject field.
X.509.quote: The Traceable Anonymous Certificate MUST be a syntactically valid X.509 certificate in which the Subject field contains a pseudonym.

CMS.why: The Token and related messages are defined as profiled CMS SignedData objects, with a CMS profile in Appendix C, so CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: the value is embedded in a digitally signed CMS object called a Token
