privacy.why: The document's core aim is balancing user privacy and accountability through conditional anonymity, and it analyses linkability in its security considerations.
privacy.quote: there are increasing demands for privacy-enhancing techniques on the Internet

rejected.why: TLS is only the assumed secure channel between parties (Appendix B), with no new TLS extension defined.
No CMC tag exists, and CMC is used only as one of two request formats being profiled.
OCSP is mentioned only in passing as an alternative way to convey revocation status.
S/MIME is mentioned only to note that TACs cannot support it.
RSA is used for threshold and blind signing, but the document is not about RSA itself.
The ASN.1 module is only apparatus for the Token and message definitions.

gaps.name: Threshold and blind signatures / anonymous certificates
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no cryptography tag for threshold signature schemes, blind signatures or pseudonymous certificates, which are central to this document.

RFC5637.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) Goals for Mobile IPv6
RFC5637.summary: Informational document describing scenarios (split and integrated bootstrapping) and listing goals and requirements for AAA interfaces between the Mobile IPv6 Home Agent / NAS and the AAA server.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document sets goals for AAA support of Mobile IPv6 service: authorization, accounting, bootstrapping and Home Agent interaction. Mobile IPv6 readers would want it.
Mobile IPv6.quote: an interface between Mobile IPv6 and AAA protocols needs to be defined

AAA.why: The document lists requirements for AAA interfaces (AAA-HA and AAA-NAS) covering service authorization, accounting and MN authentication.
AAA.quote: The AAA-HA interface MUST support the transfer of accounting records needed for service control and charging.

rejected.why: IKEv2 is used for MN-HA security association setup, but the document only mentions it as the context for authentication goals.
The HA acting as pass-through EAP authenticator is one goal, but EAP is not the subject of the document.
DHCPv6 is mentioned as the Home Agent discovery mechanism in the integrated scenario, but nothing new is defined about it.
DNS is used for Home Agent discovery and update in the split scenario, but only as background.
IPsec protects Mobile IPv6 signaling, but the document is not about IPsec.
The document is protocol-agnostic and states it does not provide solutions, so no specific AAA protocol is addressed.

RFC5638.title: Simple SIP Usage Scenario for Applications in the Endpoints
RFC5638.summary: Informational memo defining "Simple SIP", a minimal set of about 11 SIP-related RFCs for Internet-centric presence, IM and audio/video communications with applications in powerful endpoints combined with rich Internet applications, plus pointers on NAT traversal and security.

SIP.why: The document defines a simplified usage profile of SIP and lists the core SIP specifications (RFC 3261, 3263, 3265, 3840, 3581, 4474) needed for it.
SIP.quote: 'Simple SIP' in this document refers the SIP functions necessary to support only the rendezvous and session-setup functions of SIP

SIMPLE.why: Presence and IM over SIP (presence event package, PIDF, MESSAGE method) are a substantial part of the baseline.
SIMPLE.quote: RFC 3856 [7] defines the usage of SIP as a presence protocol and makes use of the SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods for presence events.

SDP.why: SDP and offer/answer are two of the mandatory references in the simple SIP set.
SDP.quote: This negotiation procedure is specified in RFC 3264 [3].

NAT traversal.why: A dedicated section covers NAT traversal for SIP via STUN/TURN/ICE or HIP, so readers of that subject would want it.
NAT traversal.quote: NAT traversal is also a basic requirement for simple SIP.

rejected.why: Mentioned as an alternative NAT traversal approach in one section, but the document is not about HIP.
Emergency calls are used as an illustrative example of applicability only, not a subject of the document.
Only briefly described as one of the referenced specifications; covered under SIMPLE instead.
DTLS-SRTP and ZRTP are only cited in Security Considerations as pointers.
The SIP MESSAGE method is one item in the list; SIMPLE is the better-fitting tag for presence and IM over SIP.
RIAs are discussed as motivation, but the document does not address web architecture itself.

RFC5639.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool Standard Curves and Curve Generation
RFC5639.summary: Specifies seven pairs of Brainpool elliptic curve domain parameters over prime fields (160–512 bits), their security and technical requirements, ASN.1 object identifiers for use in X.509, and the pseudo-random generation method.

elliptic curve.why: The whole document defines elliptic curve domain parameters, their requirements, and generation, so elliptic curve cryptography is the core subject.
elliptic curve.quote: This RFC specifies elliptic curve domain parameters over prime fields GF(p) with p having a length of 160, 192, 224, 256, 320, 384, and 512 bits.

X.509.why: Section 4 defines object identifiers and the ASN.1 encoding of subjectPublicKeyInfo for using the curves in X.509 certificates, which readers of X.509 would want.
X.509.quote: The domain parameters specified in this RFC SHALL be used with X.509 certificates in accordance with [RFC5480].

rejected.why: TLS is named only as one protocol the curves are consistent with. The document defines no TLS-specific content.
SHA-1 is used only inside the seed-generation algorithm, and the SHA family appears in a key-size table. The document is not about hash functions.
The OIDs and ASN.1 syntax serve the X.509 usage. The document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject in its own right.
The document explicitly does not address the algorithms used with the parameters, and ECDSA appears only in references.
IKE appears only in the list of RFCs the curves are consistent with, so the document says nothing specific about IKE.
CMS is mentioned only as an application area for the curves. The document specifies nothing about it.

RFC5640.title: Load-Balancing for Mesh Softwires
RFC5640.summary: Defines a new BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute sub-TLV, the Load-Balancing Block, letting ingress routers vary the L2TPv3 Session ID or GRE Key per flow so core routers can spread mesh softwire traffic across ECMP paths.

softwire.why: The document extends the mesh softwire signalling with a new sub-TLV so that softwire tunnels can be load-balanced. Softwire readers would want it.
softwire.quote: Payloads transported over a Softwire mesh service (as defined by BGP Encapsulation Subsequent Address Family Identifier (SAFI) information exchange)

ECMP.why: The goal is to give core routers enough entropy to load-balance encapsulated flows across equal-cost paths, which is the subject of ECMP and load-balanced forwarding.
ECMP.quote: It can, in some circumstances, be desirable to distribute these flows over the equal cost multiple paths (ECMPs) that exist in the packet switched network.

rejected.why: The sub-TLV is carried in BGP Encapsulation SAFI updates, but BGP is only the signalling substrate. The new sub-TLV is about tunnel load-balancing, not BGP protocol or policy.
L2TPv3 over IP is one of the two tunnel types whose Session ID is used as the load-balancing field. The document does not specify or extend L2TP.
The GRE Key serves as the load-balancing field, but GRE itself is only used as an encapsulation and is not extended.
The generic tunnelling topic is covered by the softwire tag. The document defines no new encapsulation.

RFC5641.title: Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3) Extended Circuit Status Values
RFC5641.summary: Defines additional bit values in the L2TPv3 Circuit Status AVP for finer-grained attachment circuit and pseudowire fault and standby status, deprecates the New bit, and updates RFCs 3931, 4349, 4454, 4591 and 4719.

L2TP.why: The document extends the L2TPv3 Circuit Status AVP and updates several L2TPv3 specifications, so it is squarely about L2TP.
L2TP.quote: defines additional Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3) bit values to be used within the "Circuit Status" Attribute Value Pair (AVP)

pseudowire.why: The new bits report pseudowire and AC fault and standby states, including redundancy scenarios, which is relevant to readers of pseudowire emulation.
pseudowire.quote: communicate finer-grained error states for Attachment Circuits (ACs) and pseudowires (PWs)

rejected.why: BFD is only mentioned as an example way to detect faults. The document does not specify or extend it.
MPLS and LDP pseudowire status is cited only as precedent for the new bits. The document is not about MPLS.
RFC 4454 (ATM over L2TPv3) is updated only for the Circuit Status bit definitions, so this is not about ATM.
RFC 4591 (Frame Relay over L2TPv3) is updated only for the Circuit Status bit definitions, so this is not about frame relay.
RFC 4719 (Ethernet over L2TPv3) is updated only for the Circuit Status bit definitions, so this is not about Ethernet.
The IANA section only records the bit assignments. The document is not about IANA registries.

RFC5642.title: Dynamic Hostname Exchange Mechanism for OSPF
RFC5642.summary: Defines a new OSPF Router Information TLV (Dynamic Hostname TLV) that lets OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 routers flood hostname-to-Router-ID mappings, mirroring the IS-IS mechanism.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with a new RI LSA TLV, including flooding scope rules for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
OSPF.quote: defines a new OSPF Router Information (RI) TLV that allows OSPF routers to flood their hostname-to-Router-ID mapping information across an OSPF network

OSPFv3.why: The document specifies OSPFv3-specific handling, including S1/S2 flooding scope bits and IPv6 considerations for Router IDs.
OSPFv3.quote: The Dynamic Hostname TLV is applicable to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

rejected.why: DNS is discussed only as an alternative solution and as a naming format reference. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
The tag covers host naming conventions and host tables. Here the hostname is just the payload of an OSPF TLV, so the document is about OSPF, not host naming.
Hostname-to-Router-ID mapping is a naming matter, but it is carried entirely within OSPF. The OSPF tag fits better.
IS-IS is only mentioned as the precedent for this mechanism. The document does not specify or extend it.
The IANA section only registers a TLV type, which is boilerplate.
The IPv6 considerations section is brief and concerns OSPFv3 Router IDs. The document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC5643.title: Management Information Base for OSPFv3
RFC5643.summary: Defines the OSPFv3-MIB SMIv2 module for managing OSPF for IPv6 (OSPFv3) routers via SNMP, including tables for areas, interfaces, neighbors, LSDBs, and notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (OSPFV3-MIB) in SMIv2, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in IPv6-based internets.

OSPFv3.why: The managed protocol is OSPFv3; the MIB covers its areas, interfaces, neighbors, LSDBs, graceful restart and notifications, so OSPFv3 readers would want it.
OSPFv3.quote: it defines objects for managing the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) Routing Protocol for IPv6, otherwise known as OSPF version 3 (OSPFv3).

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag covers it.
The more specific child OSPFv3 applies; OSPFv2 is only referenced for semantics.
IPv6 is the environment OSPFv3 runs in; the document does not specify IPv6.
No YANG model; the module is SMIv2.

RFC5644.title: IP Performance Metrics (IPPM): Spatial and Multicast
RFC5644.summary: Defines IPPM spatial metrics (per-segment delay, loss, ipdv vectors and streams along a path) and one-to-group metrics and statistics for multicast/multiparty delivery, with reporting model and IANA metric registry entries.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines active network performance metrics (delay, loss, ipdv) over path segments and multicast groups, extending the IPPM framework.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines two new categories of metrics that extend the coverage to multiple measurement points.

rejected.why: Multicast trees are the measured topology for one-to-group metrics, but the document defines no multicast routing or group membership mechanism.
Metrics are registered via IANA-IPPM-METRICS-REGISTRY-MIB OBJECT-IDENTITY entries, but this is only registry boilerplate, not a MIB module defined by the document.
Mentioned only as a motivation for spatial metrics; the document does not address traffic engineering itself.
MPLS point-to-multipoint LSPs appear only as example use cases for the metrics.
The metrics are active performance measurements rather than OAM mechanisms; performance measurement is the better fit.

RFC5645.title: Update to the Language Subtag Registry
RFC5645.summary: Describes how the IANA Language Subtag Registry was updated for RFC 5646, adding about 7,500 ISO 639-3/639-5 language subtags and new region subtags, and deprecating or reclassifying grandfathered and redundant tags.

language tags.why: The whole document is about the contents and update of the Language Subtag Registry used to build language tags (BCP 47). It covers new subtags, Preferred-Value changes and grandfathered tags.
language tags.quote: adding support for approximately 7,500 new primary and extended language subtags based on [ISO639-3] and [ISO639-5] alpha-3 code elements

rejected.why: The registry is maintained by IANA, but the document is about the content of one specific registry. It is not about IANA registry policy or stewardship, and the IANA Considerations section is boilerplate.
The more specific child tag 'language tags' fits, so the parent is implied.
ISO language, country and script codes are involved, but the document does not deal with character set registration.

RFC5646.title: Tags for Identifying Languages
RFC5646.summary: BCP 47 core specification defining the syntax, subtag sources, IANA Language Subtag Registry format and registration procedures, extension mechanism, and rules for choosing and canonicalizing language tags.

language tags.why: The whole document specifies language tags, their registry and their use. This is the most specific fit in the taxonomy.
language tags.quote: This document describes the structure, content, construction, and semantics of language tags for use in cases where it is desirable to indicate the language used in an information object.

rejected.why: The document defines the IANA Language Subtag Registry and its registration process. That is registry content specific to language tags, not general IANA guidance, and the IANA Considerations section is boilerplate.
The tag syntax is written in ABNF, but ABNF is only the notation used and the document is not about it.
Content-Language and Accept-Language are mentioned only as places where tags are used, not specified here.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as the encoding of the registry file.

gaps.name: Language tags (BCP 47)
gaps.why: Language tags and their matching (the RFC 4647 companion) are the main subject of this document. The taxonomy has no tag for them: the 'language tags' id I used is listed under internationalization in the taxonomy, so I could not confirm it is valid as written.

RFC5647.title: AES Galois Counter Mode for the Secure Shell Transport Layer Protocol
RFC5647.summary: Informational RFC specifying how AES-GCM (AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM) is used as combined encryption and MAC algorithm in the SSH Transport Layer Protocol, including IV handling, packet formation and the unencrypted packet length field.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport layer with new encryption/MAC algorithms, changes binary packet processing, and registers SSH algorithm names.
SSH.quote: The purpose of this document is to show how GCM with either AES-128 or AES-256 can be integrated into the Secure Shell Transport Layer Protocol

AES.why: The document is about the AES-GCM mode of operation, its parameters (key, IV, tag sizes), and its use for authenticated encryption.
AES.quote: we shall focus on AES GCM, the use of the Advanced Encryption Algorithm (AES) in Galois Counter Mode

rejected.why: Key derivation is only reviewed from RFC 4253; the document defines no new key management.
IANA section only registers algorithm names; boilerplate.
Parent of AES, which is the more specific fitting tag.

RFC5648.title: Multiple Care-of Addresses Registration
RFC5648.summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 with a Binding Identifier mobility option and new flags and status codes so a mobile node can register and use multiple care-of addresses with its home agent and correspondents, also applicable to NEMO and DSMIPv6.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document specifies Mobile IPv6 extensions: the BID mobility option, the O and H flags, new Binding Acknowledgement status values, and home agent and correspondent node processing.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document proposes extensions to the Mobile IPv6 protocol to register and use multiple care-of addresses.

rejected.why: The extensions are said to work for NEMO mobile routers, but that is only a short applicability section (Section 7). The document is not about NEMO.
Section 9 covers how IPsec and IKEv2 interact with multiple care-of addresses. It is a supporting interaction, not the subject of the document.
IKEv2 is discussed only for the care-of address used in the IKE security association. The document defines nothing new for IKE.
Neighbor Discovery behaviour is covered for returning home. The document only relies on it and does not specify or extend it.
Multiple care-of addresses is a multihoming use case. The document is a Mobile IPv6 extension, and the more specific Mobile IPv6 tag fits better.

RFC5649.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Key Wrap with Padding Algorithm
RFC5649.summary: Specifies the AES Key Wrap with Padding algorithm, extending RFC 3394 AES Key Wrap with an alternative initial value and padding so keys of any octet length can be wrapped, and assigns ASN.1 algorithm identifiers.

AES.why: The document defines an AES-based key wrapping algorithm (wrapping and unwrapping processes, AIV, padding) built on the AES codebook; this is an AES mode/algorithm specification.
AES.quote: The AES Key Wrap with Padding algorithm can be used to wrap a key of any practical size with an AES key.

rejected.why: Key wrapping is a key-management primitive, but the document specifies a cryptographic algorithm rather than key establishment or provisioning; AES is the more specific fit.
ASN.1 is only used to define algorithm identifier OIDs and modules in an appendix; it is encoding apparatus, not the subject.
The algorithm identifiers are intended for CMS/S/MIME use, but the document does not specify CMS content or usage; it only references it.
The ASN.1 module mentions S/MIME capabilities, but only as a substrate for identifier definitions.

RFC5650.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line 2 (VDSL2)
RFC5650.summary: Defines the VDSL2-LINE-MIB and VDSL2-LINE-TC-MIB SNMP modules for managing VDSL2, ADSL, ADSL2 and ADSL2+ lines, covering line/channel configuration profiles, status, performance counters, thresholds and notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is a MIB module for DSL line management, specified in SMIv2. MIB covers MIB modules and SMI, and sits under SNMP.
MIB.quote: This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

DSL.why: The MIB manages VDSL2, ADSL, ADSL2 and ADSL2+ access lines, which is DSL access networking.
DSL.quote: objects used for managing parameters of the "Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line 2 (VDSL2)" interface type

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the child tag MIB is the more specific fit.
ATM appears only as a possible data path over the DSL channel (ifStackTable example and ATM status bits), not as the subject.
No Ethernet content; PTM is only a channel status type.
The document does not define or use Access Node Control Protocol.
Data modelling is in SMIv2, not YANG.

RFC5651.title: Layered Coding Transport (LCT) Building Block
RFC5651.summary: RFC 5651 specifies the Layered Coding Transport (LCT) building block, the packet header format, header extensions, and sender/receiver operations for massively scalable reliable content and stream delivery, mainly over IP multicast. It obsoletes RFC 3451.

LCT.why: The document defines LCT itself: the header fields (TSI, TOI, CCI, codepoint), header extensions (EXT_NOP, EXT_AUTH, EXT_TIME), and sender and receiver operation.
LCT.quote: Layered Coding Transport (LCT) provides transport level support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols.

rejected.why: LCT is designed for IP multicast, but the LCT tag sits under reliable multicast, which is itself under multicast. The more specific tag covers it.
The document discusses how LCT channels map onto ASM and SSM channels. That is only an environmental consideration, not the subject.
FEC is a compatible coding building block, referenced via RFC 5052 and carried in the Codepoint field. The document does not specify it.
Congestion control is required and the CCI field carries its information. The document specifies no algorithm and defers to WEBRC (RFC 3738).
NTP is mentioned only as an optional way to synchronize the sender clock for EXT_TIME values.
SDP is named only as one possible session description format, and the document says its format and distribution are out of scope.
UDP is only an underlying transport whose source port may serve as the TSI. The document does not specify it.

RFC5652.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC5652.summary: RFC 5652 specifies the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), an ASN.1-based encapsulation syntax for digitally signing, digesting, encrypting and authenticating arbitrary content, obsoleting RFC 3852.

CMS.why: The whole document defines CMS: ContentInfo, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data content types, RecipientInfo types, and attributes.
CMS.quote: This syntax is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt arbitrary message content.

rejected.why: S/MIME is a major user of CMS and is mentioned for compatibility, but this document does not specify S/MIME.
The syntax is expressed in ASN.1 with BER/DER, but ASN.1 is the notation used rather than the subject.
X.509 certificates and CRLs are referenced and carried, but their profile is defined elsewhere (RFC 5280).
CMS can support certificate-based key management, but the document does not address PKI itself.
OCSP responses are mentioned only as an example for OtherRevocationInfoFormat.
The document deliberately omits specific algorithms, which are covered in a separate document.

RFC5653.title: Generic Security Service API Version 2: Java Bindings Update
RFC5653.summary: RFC 5653 updates and obsoletes RFC 2853, specifying the Java language bindings (org.ietf.jgss classes and interfaces) for GSS-API version 2 with corrections to status code, credential usage and name type OID values.

GSS-API.why: The whole document defines the Java API (GSSManager, GSSContext, GSSName, GSSCredential, etc.) for GSS-API, so it belongs on the GSS-API subject page.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies Java language bindings for the Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface version 2 (GSS- API).

rejected.why: Kerberos v5 is only mentioned as an example mechanism (OID, provider example); the document is not about it.
The Oid class uses ASN.1 DER encoding of object identifiers only incidentally; the document does not specify ASN.1 itself.
Only a passing remark about negotiated mechanisms in getMech; not a topic of the document.
GSS-API is the more specific fitting tag, which already sits under security; the generic authentication topic adds nothing beyond it.

RFC5654.title: Requirements of an MPLS Transport Profile
RFC5654.summary: Specifies the requirements for an MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP), a subset of MPLS/PWE3 for packet transport networks, covering general, layering, data plane, control plane, recovery/protection, ring, and QoS requirements.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is the requirements specification for MPLS-TP, including data plane, control plane, recovery and ring protection requirements.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document specifies the requirements of an MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP).

rejected.why: Referenced for ASON control plane and recovery terminology, but the document is about MPLS-TP requirements, not GMPLS itself.
PWs are mentioned as transport paths, but pseudowire emulation is not the subject.
OAM requirements are explicitly deferred to another document (Section 3.2).
Section 2.6 has a short QoS requirements list, but it is minor and not a substantial part of the document.
The document requires traffic-engineered paths, but MPLS-TP is the more specific tag for the subject.
MPLS-TP is a child of MPLS and is the more specific fit, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: Packet transport network protection/recovery (1+1, 1:n, ring protection)
gaps.why: Much of the document specifies transport-network survivability requirements, and the taxonomy has no dedicated tag for protection switching or recovery.

RFC5655.title: Specification of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) File Format
RFC5655.summary: Specifies the IPFIX File format, a serialized stream of IPFIX Messages for storing flow data, with File Reader/Writer rules, metadata Options Templates and new Information Elements, CMS detached signing, bzip2/gzip compression, and NetFlow V9 storage.

IPFIX.why: The document defines the IPFIX File format, File Readers/Writers as Exporting/Collecting Processes, Options Templates, and registers new IPFIX Information Elements.
IPFIX.quote: This document describes a file format for the storage of flow data based upon the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol.

CMS.why: Section 9.1 specifies a profile of CMS detached signatures (SignedData, SignerInfo, .p7s naming) for IPFIX Files, a substantial normative part.
CMS.quote: Section 9 specifies a CMS-based method for signing IPFIX Files.

rejected.why: Only one of the IPFIX transports the file format emulates; it is not specified or extended here.
TLS/DTLS protect the export sessions whose data is stored; the document only records certificates and discusses interaction, adding nothing about TLS.
gzip and bzip2 are used as external compression encapsulations, not specified here; Section 10 is a short usage profile.
Compression is a section on applying existing tools; the document is not about compression formats themselves.
MD5 is merely used as a simple checksum in an Information Element, not the subject.
Registers application/ipfix, but this is IANA boilerplate-like registration, not the document's subject.

gaps.name: NetFlow
gaps.why: Appendix B describes storing NetFlow V9 data and transforming it to IPFIX, but the taxonomy has no NetFlow tag; IPFIX is the closest.

RFC5656.title: Elliptic Curve Algorithm Integration in the Secure Shell Transport Layer
RFC5656.summary: Specifies ECDH and ECMQV key exchange methods and ECDSA public key algorithms (ecdsa-sha2-*) with named curves for the SSH transport layer, and registers their names with IANA.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport layer with new key exchange methods, host key formats, signature encodings, message numbers and method names.
SSH.quote: This document describes algorithms based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) for use within the Secure Shell (SSH) transport protocol.

ECDSA.why: Defines the ecdsa-sha2-* key format, signature encoding, and hash selection by curve size for SSH. A substantial part of the document concerns ECDSA and its curves.
ECDSA.quote: Signing and verifying is done using the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA).

elliptic curve.why: ECDH and ECMQV key agreement over named curves (required and recommended curves in Section 10) is a core part of the document. No more specific taxonomy tag covers ECDH or ECMQV.
elliptic curve.quote: The Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange method generates a shared secret from an ephemeral local elliptic curve private key

rejected.why: SHA-2 is only used as the hash selected by curve size. The document does not specify or analyse it.
HMAC is used only for ECMQV verification and defined in RFC 2104. The document does not specify anything new about it.
OIDs are only used to name curves, and the document defines no ASN.1 modules.
RSA appears only as a key-size comparison in the introduction table.
Key exchange is covered by the SSH and elliptic curve tags. The document is not about key management in general.

RFC5657.title: Guidance on Interoperation and Implementation Reports for Advancement to Draft Standard
RFC5657.summary: BCP 9 update to RFC 2026 giving guidance on the content, format, and granularity of interoperation and implementation reports required to advance a specification to Draft Standard, and relaxing some RFC 2026 requirements.

IETF process.why: The document updates RFC 2026 standards-track procedures by defining what implementation reports for Draft Standard advancement must contain and how they are submitted to the IESG.
IETF process.quote: Advancing a protocol to Draft Standard requires documentation of the interoperation and implementation of the protocol.

rejected.why: SMTP pipelining and the RFC2821bis survey are used only as examples of reports; the document does not specify or analyse SMTP.
ABNF is cited as an example of a non-protocol standard whose report was filed, not a subject of the document.
The RTP/RTCP report excerpt is an illustration of feature granularity only.
The document uses BCP 14 key words as boilerplate and defines no glossary.
The report format rules (ASCII text, optional Internet-Draft style) apply to implementation reports in the IESG archive, not to the RFC series itself.
The Litmus WebDAV test client is mentioned as a counter-example of a test suite, not a subject.

RFC5658.title: Addressing Record-Route Issues in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5658.summary: RFC 5658 clarifies how SIP proxies should populate Record-Route headers when incoming and outgoing interfaces differ (multi-homed, IPv4/IPv6, transport switching), recommending double Record-Routing over rewriting and giving guidance on the transport URI parameter.

SIP.why: The whole document clarifies SIP proxy Record-Route behaviour and updates RFC 3261 handling, with recommendations for proxies and UAs.
SIP.quote: A typical function of a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Proxy is to insert a Record-Route header into initial, dialog-creating requests

rejected.why: IPv4-to-IPv6 proxy scenarios are one example of interface change, but the document is about SIP Record-Route handling, not transition mechanisms.
comp=sigcomp is only mentioned as one parameter that may differ between interfaces; the document does not address SigComp.
RFC 3263 resolution is cited to explain transport selection, but nothing new is specified about DNS.
TLS and SIPS are mentioned only as a case for Record-Route URI construction; the document is not about TLS.
SIP URIs and their parameters are the content of the header, but the document does not define URI syntax.

RFC5659.title: An Architecture for Multi-Segment Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge
RFC5659.summary: Informational architecture RFC extending the pseudowire emulation architecture (RFC 3985) to multi-segment pseudowires, defining T-PE/S-PE terminology, reference models, protocol stack, maintenance, control plane, congestion and security considerations.

pseudowire.why: The whole document is the architecture for multi-segment pseudowires, with S-PE switching, segment concatenation, and PW demultiplexer handling. Pseudowire emulation is the subject throughout.
pseudowire.quote: This document extends the architecture in RFC 3985 to enable point-to-point pseudowires to be extended through multiple PSN tunnels.

rejected.why: MPLS is only one possible PSN tunnel type here, and label swap is mentioned in passing. The document is about pseudowires, not MPLS.
The document says an MS-PW should not be confused with an L2VPN system. It only notes that an MS-PW is indistinguishable from an SS-PW from the L2VPN perspective.
MPLS-TP is mentioned once as an applicability scenario, with citations to its requirements and framework. The document does not address it substantively.
LDP appears only as an example signaling adjacency in the motivation section. The detailed signaling mechanisms are explicitly out of scope.
L2TPv3 is mentioned only as an alternative PSN type for the S-PE label-mapping discussion.
The congestion section is short and only lists considerations for MS-PWs. The document is not about congestion control as a subject.

gaps.name: pseudowire / PWE3
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a 'pseudowire' tag listed under MPLS in the hierarchy (id: pseudowire), and I used it. I am noting this because the document's core subject is pseudowire emulation, which is described in the taxonomy as 'Pseudowire emulation edge-to-edge'. The document also covers multi-segment switching and S-PE/T-PE roles, which no more specific tag covers.

RFC5660.title: IPsec Channels: Connection Latching
RFC5660.summary: Specifies abstractly how ULPs and applications interface with IPsec to latch connections (packet flows) to fixed SA parameters, creating IPsec channels that protect against configuration changes and weak peer ID/address binding (BTNS).

IPsec.why: The whole document defines a layer atop IPsec (latch database, state machine, key manager interfaces, SPD/SAD monitoring). IPsec architecture is the subject.
IPsec.quote: how to interface applications and transport protocols with IPsec so as to create "channels" by latching "connections" (packet flows) to certain IPsec Security Association (SA) parameters

rejected.why: IKEv2 is relied on for SA negotiation and DPD, but the document does not specify or extend IKE.
TCP is one ULP to which latching is applied in a short section; the document is not about TCP itself.
Section 5.4 covers SCTP multihoming handling, but it is a minor part of an IPsec-focused document.
UDP latching is covered briefly as a ULP binding only.
Peer identity latching is part of the mechanism, but the document is not about authentication in its own right.
The parent topic is implied by the IPsec tag.

gaps.name: BTNS (Better-Than-Nothing Security) / channel binding
gaps.why: The document is motivated by BTNS unauthenticated IPsec and prepares for IPsec channel binding, but the taxonomy has no tag for either.

RFC5661.title: Network File System (NFS) Version 4 Minor Version 1 Protocol
RFC5661.summary: RFC 5661 specifies NFS version 4 minor version 1, adding Sessions, directory delegations and parallel NFS (pNFS) to the NFSv4 file access protocol, including its operations, attributes, locking, caching, ACLs and multi-server namespace.

NFS.why: The whole document defines the NFSv4.1 protocol: operations, state management, locking, delegations, attributes, pNFS and sessions.
NFS.quote: The NFS version 4 minor version 1 (NFSv4.1) protocol is the second minor version of the NFS version 4 (NFSv4) protocol.

rejected.why: NFSv4.1 is an RPC application and relies on ONC RPC/XDR and RPCSEC_GSS as substrate; the document does not specify them.
RDMA is a transport it runs over, with only upper-layer considerations; RPC/RDMA is specified elsewhere.
Used as a security substrate via RPCSEC_GSS; the internal SSV mechanism is a detail of NFS session security.
Mandated security mechanism only, not specified here.
Required transport, not specified or extended.
Used for names and strings, but not the subject of the document.

RFC5662.title: Network File System (NFS) Version 4 Minor Version 1 External Data Representation Standard (XDR) Description
RFC5662.summary: Provides the machine-extractable XDR (RFC 4506) description of the NFSv4.1 protocol, including COMPOUND operations, callback operations, attributes, sessions, and pNFS layout types.

NFS.why: The whole document is the formal wire-format definition of NFSv4.1 operations, attributes, sessions, delegations and callbacks.
NFS.quote: This document provides the External Data Representation Standard (XDR) description for Network File System version 4 (NFSv4) minor version 1.

ONC RPC.why: The document is an XDR specification and defines the RPC program and version definitions for NFS4 and its callback program, so ONC RPC and XDR readers would find it relevant.
ONC RPC.quote: program NFS4_PROGRAM {

rejected.why: RDMA flags appear only as a few fields in the XDR; the document isn't about RDMA.
RPCSEC_GSS and SSV structures appear as data definitions only; the document doesn't specify GSS mechanisms.
The description language is XDR, not ASN.1.

gaps.name: pNFS (parallel NFS) layouts
gaps.why: A substantial part of the XDR defines pNFS layout, device and layout-recall structures, but the taxonomy has no pNFS tag. It falls under NFS.

RFC5663.title: Parallel NFS (pNFS) Block/Volume Layout
RFC5663.summary: Specifies the pNFS block/volume layout type for NFSv4.1: XDR data structures for volume identification and topology, extents, layout commit/return, copy-on-write, fencing, and security responsibilities when clients access SAN storage directly.

NFS.why: The document extends NFSv4.1/pNFS with a block/volume layout type, defining layout, device address, commit, hint and fencing behaviour. It is squarely about NFS.
NFS.quote: this document specifies the additional extensions (primarily data structures) for use of pNFS with block- and volume-based storage.

rejected.why: iSCSI is only one of several block storage protocols (SCSI, FCP, SAS, FCoE) clients may use for data access. The document does not specify or profile it.
Fibre Channel is mentioned as a possible storage access network, not specified or extended here.
XDR is used to describe the data structures, but only as the encoding mechanism. The document does not cover RPC or XDR itself.
The parent topic is implied by the NFS tag, which is the more specific fit.

gaps.name: pNFS (Parallel NFS) layout types
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an NFS tag, but the 'NFS' id given in the tag is not present in the taxonomy as listed; the closest entries are the 'storage' topic and its children. The tag used is therefore not verifiable against the taxonomy, and there is no pNFS-specific tag.

RFC5664.title: Object-Based Parallel NFS (pNFS) Operations
RFC5664.summary: Specifies the NFSv4.1 object-based pNFS layout type (LAYOUT4_OSD2_OBJECTS): XDR data types for OSD addressing, striping/RAID data maps, layout update/return, error reporting, recall, fencing, and OSD capability security.

NFS.why: The document defines a pNFS layout type for NFSv4.1, including layout, layoutreturn, layoutcommit, hint and recall structures. NFS readers would expect it.
NFS.quote: This document specifies the NFSv4.1 Object-Based pNFS Layout Type as a companion to the main NFSv4 Minor version 1 specification.

storage.why: A substantial part covers object storage device addressing, striping, mirroring and RAID algorithms, and SCSI/iSCSI target discovery. This is storage access beyond NFS itself.
storage.quote: This document describes the layouts used with object-based storage devices (OSDs) that are accessed according to the OSD storage protocol standard

rejected.why: iSCSI names and discovery are referenced for addressing OSD devices, but the document does not specify or extend iSCSI.
XDR is used to describe the structures and RPCSEC_GSS is mentioned, but the document is not about ONC RPC.
GSS-API/RPCSEC_GSS is only used as a mechanism to protect capability keys, so it is not tagged.
IPsec is mentioned only as an alternative channel for privacy of the capability key.
Fibre Channel naming (NAA) is mentioned only as a device identifier format, not as a transport the document specifies.

gaps.name: pNFS / OSD object-based storage
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for parallel NFS layout types or SCSI object storage devices (T10 OSD). The NFS and storage tags cover them only partly.

RFC5665.title: IANA Considerations for Remote Procedure Call (RPC) Network Identifiers and Universal Address Formats
RFC5665.summary: Establishes IANA registries for ONC RPC netids and universal address (uaddr) formats, gives their initial contents, and updates RFC 1833.

ONC RPC.why: The document defines the registration rules and initial contents of the RPC netid and uaddr format registries, and updates RFC 1833 (RPC binding). Readers of ONC RPC need it.
ONC RPC.quote: IANA has created a registry called "ONC RPC Netids".

IANA.why: The document's main body is IANA registry creation and policy (FCFS and Standards Action, designated expert, cross-referencing), so IANA registry guidance readers would want it.
IANA.quote: IANA has created a registry called "ONC RPC Uaddr Format Registry"

rejected.why: SCTP is only one registered netid, with a short note on record marking in Section 3. The document is not about the protocol.
TCP and UDP appear only as netid entries in the initial registry and are not specified or extended.
IPv6 address text format is referenced for the uaddr format, but IPv6 itself is not the subject.
RPC/RDMA is only a netid entry, not the subject of the document.
NFSv4 is mentioned as motivation, and Section 5.4 assigns port 2049 for NFS over SCTP, but the document is not about NFS.

gaps.name: ONC RPC / RPC binding (netids, uaddrs, rpcbind)
gaps.why: The ONC RPC tag used above is not in the taxonomy. The closest is 'ONC RPC' under storage, which I listed as an id but which is not exactly the id shown ('ONC RPC' does appear in the taxonomy as 'ONC RPC [tech]' under storage). Nothing else fits the netid/uaddr binding subject.

RFC5666.title: Remote Direct Memory Access Transport for Remote Procedure Call
RFC5666.summary: Specifies RPC-over-RDMA version 1, a transport binding for ONC RPC over RDMA transports (iWARP, InfiniBand), covering header layout, chunk lists, flow control credits, long messages, and an optional connection configuration protocol.

RDMA.why: The document defines how RPC messages are conveyed using RDMA Send, Read and Write, with chunk lists and flow control; RDMA protocols are the subject.
RDMA.quote: This document describes a protocol providing Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) as a new transport for Remote Procedure Call (RPC).

ONC RPC.why: It defines a new ONC RPC transport binding, including XDR encoding with chunks, a new netid, and an RPC program for connection configuration.
ONC RPC.quote: Open Network Computing Remote Procedure Call (ONC RPC, or simply, RPC) [RFC5531] is a remote procedure call protocol that has been run over a variety of transports.

rejected.why: NFS is the motivating upper-layer user, but the document is a generic RPC transport; NFS specifics are in RFC 5667.
Mentioned only as a possible link-level protection in the Security Considerations.
This is a real new transport with its own framing, not merely a binding of one protocol onto an existing transport; the more specific RDMA and ONC RPC tags cover it.
Mentioned only as a comparison and as an underlying layer for iWARP.
RPCSEC_GSS is referenced for security only; the document does not specify it.

RFC5667.title: Network File System (NFS) Direct Data Placement
RFC5667.summary: Defines how NFS versions 2, 3, 4 and 4.1 map their bulk data (READ, WRITE, READLINK, SYMLINK) onto RPC/RDMA Read and Write chunk lists for direct data placement, plus callback and port usage considerations.

NFS.why: The document specifies the bindings of NFSv2, v3, v4 and v4.1 operations to RDMA chunk lists, so it is about NFS.
NFS.quote: This document details the mapping for each version of the NFS protocol

RDMA.why: It specifies use of RDMA Read and Write operations for direct data placement via the RPC/RDMA transport, which readers of the RDMA subject would want.
RDMA.quote: allows an RPC client application to post buffers in a Chunk list for specific arguments and results from an RPC call

rejected.why: RPC and XDR are the layer the mapping sits on. The RPC/RDMA transport itself is defined in RFC 5666, not here.
The document binds NFS to an RDMA transport, but the NFS and RDMA tags cover the subject more specifically.
This is a different storage protocol and is not discussed in the document.
The Security Considerations section only defers to RFC 5666 and says nothing specific.

RFC5668.title: 4-Octet AS Specific BGP Extended Community
RFC5668.summary: Defines a new BGP extended community type (4-octet AS specific, types 0x02/0x42) carrying a 4-octet AS number, with Route Target and Route Origin sub-type assignments.

BGP communities.why: The document's sole purpose is to define a new BGP extended community format and its registry, which is squarely a BGP communities subject.
BGP communities.quote: This document defines a new type of BGP extended community [RFC4360]: a 4-octet AS specific extended community.

rejected.why: The more specific BGP communities tag fits; the document does not otherwise specify BGP protocol behaviour.
Route Target and Route Origin are used in L3VPNs and the WG is l3vpn, but the document only defines the community encoding, not VPN mechanisms.
The registry creation is boilerplate-like IANA considerations, not the main body subject.

RFC5669.title: The SEED Cipher Algorithm and Its Use with the Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC5669.summary: Defines how the SEED block cipher is used in SRTP/SRTCP: counter mode, CCM and GCM transforms, nonce formats, key derivation PRF, mandatory-to-implement transforms, and SDP crypto suite registrations.

SRTP.why: The document specifies new SRTP/SRTCP cipher transforms, nonce formats, key derivation and mandatory-to-implement transforms for SEED.
SRTP.quote: This document describes the use of the SEED block cipher algorithm in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) for providing confidentiality

rejected.why: AES counter mode is only the model that SEED-CTR copies. The document is not about AES.
HMAC-SHA1 is only the default authentication function used with SEED-CTR. The document does not specify or extend it.
SRTCP is covered together with SRTP, and the SRTP tag fits better.
The key derivation PRF is part of the SRTP transform definition, not a key management topic in its own right.
SDP only appears in the IANA registration of crypto suite names. That is boilerplate and not what the document is about.
SEED is not covered by a more specific tag. The document is about using it in SRTP, though, so I used the SRTP tag. See gaps.

gaps.name: SEED block cipher
gaps.why: The document specifies a Korean national block cipher in use. The taxonomy has tags for AES, ARIA, Camellia and GOST but none for SEED.

RFC5670.title: Metering and Marking Behaviour of PCN-Nodes
RFC5670.summary: Defines the threshold-metering/marking and excess-traffic-metering/marking behaviours (token-bucket based) of PCN-nodes in a Diffserv domain, so boundary nodes can make admission control and flow termination decisions.

PCN.why: The document specifies PCN node behaviour, but PCN is not in the taxonomy as its own tag; the closest fit is the congestion control PCN tag, which is the technology for pre-congestion notification.
PCN.quote: This document defines the two metering and marking behaviours of PCN-nodes.

rejected.why: PCN operates within a Diffserv domain and uses DSCP for classification, but the document does not specify or extend Diffserv itself.
The encoding uses ECN field codepoints, defined elsewhere (RFC 5696); this document defines metering and marking, not ECN.
Parent of PCN-related items; PCN tag is more specific under congestion control.
The marking is RED-like in spirit but is a different early-warning metering scheme, not an AQM algorithm.

RFC5671.title: Applicability of the Path Computation Element (PCE) to Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering (TE)
RFC5671.summary: Informational RFC examining how the Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture applies to computing P2MP MPLS and GMPLS TE LSPs, covering motivation, architectural models, tree fragmentation, replication points, reoptimization, repair, and disjoint paths.

PCE.why: The whole document analyses how PCE architecture models (offline, online, cooperating PCEs, capabilities, overload) suit P2MP path computation.
PCE.quote: This document examines the applicability of PCE to path computation for P2MP TE LSPs in MPLS and GMPLS networks.

GMPLS.why: The document is explicitly scoped to both MPLS and GMPLS TE networks, though it is not GMPLS-specific in content.
GMPLS.quote: The Path Computation Element (PCE) provides path computation functions in support of traffic engineering in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) networks.

rejected.why: P2MP RSVP-TE signaling (RFC 4875) is only referenced as the signaling mechanism; the document does not specify or extend it.
MPLS is the network context, but the subject is path computation; the more specific PCE tag fits.
P2MP LSPs are mentioned for multicast VPNs and video distribution, but the document is not about IP multicast routing.
Multicast VPNs are mentioned once as a motivating use case only.
MIB modules and NETCONF are mentioned briefly in manageability considerations only.

RFC5672.title: RFC 4871 DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures -- Update
RFC5672.summary: RFC 5672 updates RFC 4871 in errata style, clarifying the roles of the DKIM d= (SDID) and i= (AUID) identifier tags and specifying that the d= value is the payload delivered to an identity assessor.

DKIM.why: The whole document amends the DKIM signature specification (RFC 4871), redefining SDID/AUID semantics and the d= and i= tags of the DKIM-Signature header field.
DKIM.quote: the document clarifies the nature, roles, and relationship of the two DKIM identifier tag values that are candidates for payload delivery to a receiving processing module

rejected.why: It is the parent of DKIM, so it is implied by the DKIM tag and not listed separately.
DNS is only where the key record is published and the d= name is queried. The document does not specify DNS behaviour.
IDNA is mentioned only in passing, as the encoding rule for internationalized domain names in the quoted tag text. The document does not change it.
Whitelists and reputation assessors are mentioned only as consumers of the identifier. The document is not about spam filtering.
The document touches the From: header and email-address syntax only as a comparison with the identifiers. It does not define message format.

RFC5673.title: Industrial Routing Requirements in Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC5673.summary: Informational requirements document analysing what a routing protocol for industrial low-power and lossy wireless networks (LLNs) of field devices must support, covering traffic, reliability, device constraints, multicast, mobility and manageability.

routing.why: The whole document sets out functional requirements for a routing protocol (multipath, constrained routes, convergence, multicast, mobility), and it specifies no particular routing protocol, so the general routing topic fits.
routing.quote: The aim of this document is to analyze the requirements from the industrial environment for a routing protocol in Low power and Lossy Networks (LLNs)

IoT.why: It covers industrial wireless sensor and actuator networks of constrained, battery-powered field devices. That puts it in the IoT and constrained-device area.
IoT.quote: Wireless, low-power field devices enable industrial users to significantly increase the amount of information collected and the number of control points that can be remotely managed.

rejected.why: Cited only as one of the layer 1-4 technologies that ISA100.11a adapts. The document does not specify or analyse 6LoWPAN.
RPL came out of this ROLL work, but the document predates it and sets requirements without describing the protocol.
IPv6 is the assumed network layer, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
There is one short section on multicast requirements, but the document does not deal with multicast routing in any depth.
The document lists requirements and does not discuss routing architecture or scalability design principles as a subject.

gaps.name: Low-power and Lossy Networks (ROLL) routing requirements
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for LLN or constrained-network routing apart from RPL. A tag for ROLL application-specific requirements would group this RFC with its sibling requirements documents.

RFC5674.title: Alarms in Syslog
RFC5674.summary: Defines an "alarm" syslog structured-data element (SD-ID with SD-PARAMs such as resource, probableCause, perceivedSeverity) and a mapping of ITU perceived severities to syslog severities, reusing X.733 and Alarm MIB terminology.

syslog.why: The document extends syslog with a new alarm SD-ID, its SD-PARAMs, and a severity mapping to syslog SEVERITY, so it belongs on the syslog page.
syslog.quote: This memo defines a set of SD-PARAMs to support logging and defines a mapping of syslog severity to the severity of the alarm.

rejected.why: The Alarm MIB (RFC 3877) is only the source of terminology and value mnemonics; the document defines no MIB module.
SNMP is mentioned as another alarm channel and for the resourceURI syntax, but the document is not about SNMP.
resourceURI must conform to RFC 3986, but URIs are only used as a value format and not specified here.
Alarm management is the subject area, but the syslog tag is the more specific fit and covers it.
Netconf is mentioned only as another way of sending alarms asynchronously.

RFC5675.title: Mapping Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Notifications to SYSLOG Messages
RFC5675.summary: Defines a mapping of SNMP notifications (traps and informs) into RFC 5424 SYSLOG messages, introducing a new "snmp" structured data element that carries the notification PDU's varbinds and context.

syslog.why: The document defines how SYSLOG header, structured data (new SD-ID "snmp") and MSG are populated for SNMP notifications, extending syslog's structured data usage.
syslog.quote: we specify a concrete mapping from SNMP event notifications [RFC3416] into SYSLOG messages [RFC5424]

SNMP.why: The mapping is driven by the SNMP notification format (SNMPv2-Trap, InformRequest, scopedPDU, varbinds, type mapping), and it interworks with SNMP notification receivers and the SYSLOG-MSG-MIB.
SNMP.quote: There are two types of SNMP protocol operations that are associated with SNMP notification messages

rejected.why: The document does not define a MIB module; the companion RFC 5676 does. It only discusses how the two relate.
ASN.1 and BER appear only as background describing the PDU structure and in the example, not as a subject of the document.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the new structured data element.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as the encoding for parameter values and MSG, which is incidental.
The IANA section is boilerplate registering the SD-ID; it is not what the document is about.

RFC5676.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Mapping SYSLOG Messages to Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Notifications
RFC5676.summary: Defines the SYSLOG-MSG-MIB SNMP MIB module that represents received SYSLOG messages in tables and sends them as SNMP notifications, mapping SYSLOG to SNMP.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a SMIv2 MIB module (SYSLOG-MSG-MIB) with tables, notification and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

syslog.why: The MIB represents SYSLOG message fields and structured data and translates SYSLOG messages to SNMP, so syslog readers would want it.
syslog.quote: it defines a mapping of SYSLOG messages to Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) notifications.

rejected.why: SNMP is the vehicle for the MIB, but the more specific MIB tag covers the document. The SNMP framework itself is not specified here.
UTF-8 is only used in a textual convention for parameter values; the document is not about it.
Not a taxonomy id; RFC 3014 is mentioned only for comparison.

RFC5677.title: IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services Framework Design (MSFD)
RFC5677.summary: Defines a framework for carrying IEEE 802.21 MIH messages over IP: discovery of Mobility Services via DHCP and DNS across four deployment scenarios, and guidance on using TCP/UDP transport (message size, rate, retransmission, NAT traversal), with no security mechanisms.

IP mobility.why: The document is about IEEE 802.21 Media Independent Handover services: discovery of mobility servers and transport of MIH messages to support handover. No narrower mobility tag fits, so the parent topic applies.
IP mobility.quote: addresses identified issues associated with the transport of MIH messages

service discovery.why: A substantial part (Section 5) covers how a mobile node discovers Mobility Servers in home, visited and third-party networks using DHCP and DNS.
service discovery.quote: The document also describes mechanisms for Mobility Services (MoS) discovery

transport mapping.why: Section 6 specifies how MIH is carried over TCP and UDP, covering message size, rate, retransmission, NAT behaviour, default port and transport choice. This is a transport binding for MIH.
transport mapping.quote: MIH peers MAY exchange information over TCP, UDP, or any other transport supported by both the server and the client.

rejected.why: The DHCP options are defined in RFC 5678. This document only uses DHCP as a discovery substrate.
The DNS-based discovery is specified in RFC 5679. Here DNS is only a mechanism the framework relies on.
TCP and UDP are only the transports used and discussed. The document does not specify or extend them.
UDP is used as a transport and its trade-offs are discussed, but the document does not extend it or give general UDP guidance.
NAT traversal gets a brief subsection that cites existing NAT requirements. It is not the main subject.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommendation.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.21 Media Independent Handover (MIH)
gaps.why: The document is about carrying this link-layer handover protocol over IP. The taxonomy has no MIH or handover-services tag, so IP mobility is only an approximate fit.

RFC5678.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) Options for IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services (MoS) Discovery
RFC5678.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options (MoS IP address and domain name list, with IS/CS/ES sub-options) that let a mobile node discover IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services servers, and creates IANA registries for the sub-option service types.

DHCP.why: The document's main content is new DHCPv4 options and their client/server usage rules.
DHCP.quote: This document defines new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options and sub-options called the MoS IP Address and Domain Name List Options

DHCPv6.why: Defines two DHCPv6 options (54 and 55) and DHCPv6 client/server behaviour, so DHCPv6 readers would want it.
DHCPv6.quote: OPTION-IPv6_Address-MoS (54) - 2 bytes
DHCPv6.section: 4. MoS IPv6 Address Option for DHCPv6

IP mobility.why: The options support discovery of IEEE 802.21 mobility services for handover, which is a mobility subject. There is no more specific tag for 802.21 MIH.
IP mobility.quote: These Mobility Services are used to assist a mobile node (MN) in handover preparation (network discovery) and handover decision (network selection).

rejected.why: Domain names are carried in the options and resolved using RFC 5679, but this document defines no DNS behaviour.
DNSSEC is mentioned only as a recommendation in Security Considerations.
The document does perform discovery of servers, but the DHCP tags cover it more specifically.
The registries it creates are boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the main subject.
The document is about 802.21 media independent handover services, not Mobile IP protocols.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.21 Media Independent Handover (MIH) services
gaps.why: The document is about discovering MIH Information, Event and Command Services servers. The taxonomy has no tag for 802.21 or MIH, so IP mobility is only a loose fit.

RFC5679.title: Locating IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services Using DNS
RFC5679.summary: Defines DNS-based (NAPTR/SRV) procedures and service tags (MIHIS, MIHES, MIHCS) for a mobile node to discover IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services servers.

DNS.why: The document specifies NAPTR and SRV record usage, service field values and lookup procedures in DNS to locate mobility servers.
DNS.quote: DNS procedures for discovering servers that provide IEEE 802.21-defined Mobility Services

service discovery.why: Its purpose is discovering Mobility Service servers, which is service discovery, though DNS-SD is not used.
service discovery.quote: application service tags that allow service location without relying on rigid domain naming conventions

rejected.why: The mobility services support handover, but the document only covers server discovery via DNS, not IP mobility protocols.
DHCP is mentioned as an input source for the search path, but the DHCP options are defined in RFC 5678, not here.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
SCTP is only one of the transports given a NAPTR service code, so the document is not about it.
The IANA registry for NAPTR service fields is a minor part of the document, not its subject.
The document concerns IEEE 802.21 media-independent handover, not a cellular system.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.21 Media Independent Handover services
gaps.why: The document is about locating MIH Information, Event and Command services. The taxonomy has no tag for MIH or handover services.

RFC5680.title: The Nominating Committee Process: Open Disclosure of Willing Nominees
RFC5680.summary: RFC 5680 updates RFC 3777 to let the IETF NomCom publicly disclose the list of nominees willing to be considered, so it can ask the whole community for feedback.

NomCom.why: The document changes NomCom confidentiality rules by allowing disclosure of willing-nominee lists. This is squarely about NomCom procedures.
NomCom.quote: The list of nominees willing to be considered for positions under review in the current NomCom cycle is not confidential.

rejected.why: NomCom is a more specific child of IETF process, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The document has only boilerplate copyright text and nothing on intellectual property rights in the body.

RFC5681.title: TCP Congestion Control
RFC5681.summary: RFC 5681 specifies TCP's four congestion control algorithms (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery), plus restart after idle periods and ACK generation rules, obsoleting RFC 2581.

TCP.why: The document is a Standards Track specification of TCP sender and receiver behaviour, including idle restart, delayed ACK generation and loss recovery. Readers of TCP would expect to find it.
TCP.quote: This document specifies four TCP [RFC793] congestion control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery.

congestion control.why: The core subject is congestion control: cwnd and ssthresh management, slow start, congestion avoidance and the response to loss. It is a general congestion-control reference, so the topic tag is appropriate and no more specific child tag fits.
congestion control.quote: a TCP MUST NOT be more aggressive than the following algorithms allow (that is, MUST NOT send data when the value of cwnd computed by the following algorithms would not allow the data to be sent)

rejected.why: RFC 3782 NewReno is only cited as an allowed advanced loss recovery algorithm. This document does not specify it.
ECN is mentioned once as an alternative congestion signal, and the algorithms here use loss only.
Path MTU discovery is referenced only for its effect on SMSS and on the initial window, not specified here.
Persistent HTTP connections appear once as an example of why idle detection fails, so HTTP is not a subject of the document.

RFC5682.title: Forward RTO-Recovery (F-RTO): An Algorithm for Detecting Spurious Retransmission Timeouts with TCP
RFC5682.summary: Standards Track specification of F-RTO, a TCP sender-only algorithm (with a SACK-enhanced variant) for detecting spurious retransmission timeouts, moving the TCP part of experimental RFC 4138 to Standards Track.

TCP.why: The whole document specifies a TCP sender algorithm for detecting spurious RTOs and altering retransmission behaviour, including a SACK-enhanced version.
TCP.quote: This document describes the F-RTO detection algorithm for detecting spurious TCP retransmission timeouts.

rejected.why: The document touches on congestion window handling after a spurious RTO, but response algorithms are explicitly out of scope; the subject is spurious timeout detection.
SCTP is mentioned only as a possible application, and the SCTP considerations were removed and remain experimental in RFC 4138.
Used only as a referenced loss recovery algorithm and for the recover variable; the document does not specify or extend it.

RFC5683.title: Password-Authenticated Key (PAK) Diffie-Hellman Exchange
RFC5683.summary: Informational RFC specifying the Password-Authenticated Key (PAK) exchange, which adds mutual password-based authentication to Diffie-Hellman and resists offline dictionary attacks, with parameter guidance for OTASP/WLAN.
review: model chose 'PAK', which is not a tag

notes: model chose 'PAK', which is not a tag

RFC5684.title: Unintended Consequences of NAT Deployments with Overlapping Address Space
RFC5684.summary: Informational RFC describing problems and recommendations for multi-level NAT topologies with overlapping private address space and for remote access VPNs whose clients sit behind NATs with overlapping addresses.

NAT.why: The whole document analyses unconventional NAT deployments (multi-level NAT, overlapping private address space), their anomalies and recommendations for operating them.
NAT.quote: NATs are increasingly, and often unintentionally, used to create hierarchically interconnected clusters of private networks

VPN.why: Half the document covers remote access VPN address conflicts, split/non-split VPN and VIP conflicts, with recommendations. These are client-based remote access VPNs rather than provider-provisioned VPNs, but the VPN tag is the closest fit.
VPN.quote: Enterprises use remote access VPN to allow secure access to employees working outside the enterprise premises.

rejected.why: DHCP is discussed as the way plug-and-play NATs hand out addresses and as a bootstrap service. The document does not specify or extend it.
IPsec is only named as one example of a VPN technology and is not analysed.
Overlapping RFC 1918 address space is central, but the NAT tag already covers it. The document is about NAT deployments rather than address allocation.
ARP is mentioned only in passing, as an example of ambiguity on interfaces that share a subnet.
IPv4 address depletion is given as motivation only. The document does not address IPv4 itself.
L2TP is only listed as an example VPN technology.

RFC5685.title: Redirect Mechanism for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC5685.summary: Defines an IKEv2 extension (REDIRECT_SUPPORTED, REDIRECT, REDIRECTED_FROM notifications) letting a VPN gateway redirect a client to another gateway during IKE_SA_INIT, IKE_AUTH or an active session, including anycast use and Mobile IPv6 home agent redirect.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new notify payloads and exchange behaviour for redirecting clients.
IKE.quote: This document defines an IKEv2 extension that allows an overloaded VPN gateway or a VPN gateway that is being shut down for maintenance to redirect the VPN client

Mobile IPv6.why: A dedicated section specifies how the redirect interacts with Mobile IPv6 home agent discovery and Home Agent Switch.
Mobile IPv6.quote: the mechanism described in this document can also be used by a Mobile IPv6 home agent to redirect a mobile node to another home agent.
Mobile IPv6.section: 8. Using the Redirect Mechanism with Mobile IPv6

rejected.why: IPsec is the context, but the document only extends IKEv2 key exchange; the more specific IKE tag covers it.
Anycast addresses are used as an initial gateway address in one section, but the document does not address anycast operation in its own right.
This tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs (L3VPN/L2VPN style) in routing, not remote-access IPsec VPN clients.
DNS is mentioned only as a gateway discovery method and a possible identity format; nothing new is defined for DNS.

RFC5686.title: RTP Payload Format for mU-law EMbedded Codec for Low-delay IP Communication (UEMCLIP) Speech Codec
RFC5686.summary: Defines the RTP payload format, bitstream layout, transcoding rules with G.711, and media type/SDP parameters for the UEMCLIP embedded wideband speech codec built on u-law G.711.

RTP payload format.why: The RFC's purpose is an RTP payload format for a specific speech codec: frame layout, RTP header usage, multiple frames per packet, and media type registration.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for sending UEMCLIP-encoded (mU-law EMbedded Coder for Low-delay IP communication) speech using the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

G.711.why: The codec embeds a G.711 u-law core layer, and a full section covers transcoding between UEMCLIP and G.711. Readers of G.711 would want this RFC.
G.711.quote: UEMCLIP is an enhanced version of u-law ITU-T G.711, otherwise known as PCMU

SDP.why: It specifies SDP mappings (rtpmap, fmtp mode, ptime) and offer/answer rules with examples for the codec.
SDP.quote: The procedures related to exchanging SDP messages MUST follow [RFC3264].

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate. The document defines a payload format, which is covered by the more specific RTP payload format tag.
The codec is proprietary and its internals are not described. Only the bitstream framing is specified, and G.711 is already tagged.
It registers audio/UEMCLIP, but this is routine payload-format boilerplate and not the subject.
RTCP is mentioned only in connection with MCU topologies and rewriting RTCP during transcoding. The document does not specify RTCP.

RFC5687.title: GEOPRIV Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol: Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC5687.summary: Informational GEOPRIV design-team document giving the problem statement, scenarios, LIS discovery options, identifier analysis and requirements for a Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol by which hosts obtain location by value or reference from an access-network Location Information Server.

geolocation.why: The whole document is about how end hosts obtain location information (by value or by reference) from a LIS, plus PIDF-LO creation requirements. No more specific geolocation child tag (HELD) is named here; the document is a requirements document that precedes it.
geolocation.quote: This document provides a problem statement, lists requirements, and captures design aspects for a GEOPRIV Layer 7 (L7) Location Configuration Protocol (LCP).

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one candidate LIS discovery mechanism and as part of customer-premises scenarios; the document does not specify DHCP.
HELD is the eventual protocol meeting these requirements, but this document does not mention or define it.

LIS discovery is a section, but it is a brief, non-consensus list of options rather than a main subject. The tag could be secondary, but the discovery content is thin and is covered by the geolocation tag.
Only mentioned as a consumer of the obtained location; not discussed.
PIDF-LO is cited in one requirement (L7-10) for LIS output; not a substantial part of the document.
NAT appears as a scenario constraint affecting identifier choice and legacy devices, but the document is not about NAT.

gaps.name: Location Information Server (LIS) / Location Configuration Protocol
gaps.why: The document covers host-to-LIS location acquisition requirements; the taxonomy only has geolocation and HELD (a specific protocol), so geolocation is the closest fit.

RFC5688.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Media Feature Tag for MIME Application Subtypes
RFC5688.summary: Defines the SIP media feature tag 'sip.app-subtype', letting a user agent register and callers request support for specific MIME application subtypes used as streaming formats in SDP.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP caller preferences and UA capability registration (RFC 3840/3841) with a new feature tag used in Contact, Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact headers.
SIP.quote: this specification defines a new media feature tag that indicates which application subtypes are supported by the agent for streaming.

SDP.why: Support for a subtype is defined in terms of the ability to handle an SDP offer with that application format in an m-line, and the example uses SDP m=application lines.
SDP.quote: capable of processing a Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] offer [RFC3264] that contained that subtype as a format in the m-line of the SDP.

rejected.why: It refers to MIME application subtypes but does not define or register media types or alter registry rules; it only registers a SIP feature tag.
MIME subtypes are merely the values of the tag; the document is not about MIME body structure or encodings.
Media feature tags are related, but the document is specifically a SIP capability tag and does not define general media feature negotiation.
Appears only in an example SDP line; the document is not about RTP.

RFC5689.title: Extended MKCOL for Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV)
RFC5689.summary: RFC 5689 extends the WebDAV MKCOL method with an XML request body so collections of arbitrary resourcetype can be created with properties set atomically, and shows it as an alternative to CalDAV's MKCALENDAR.

WebDAV.why: The document defines an extension to WebDAV's MKCOL method, including the DAV:mkcol and DAV:mkcol-response elements, the extended-mkcol DAV header token and the valid-resourcetype precondition. It updates RFC 4918.
WebDAV.quote: This specification extends the Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) MKCOL (Make Collection) method to allow collections of arbitrary resourcetype to be created

CalDAV.why: A substantial section shows extended MKCOL as an alternative to CalDAV's MKCALENDAR, and the document formally updates RFC 4791. Readers of CalDAV material would want it.
CalDAV.quote: The extended MKCOL method can be used instead by specifying both DAV: collection and CALDAV:calendar-collection XML elements

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate WebDAV runs on. The document only extends a WebDAV method and does not specify anything new about HTTP itself.
XML is only the encoding for the request and response bodies, and DTD fragments are used as notation. The document is not about XML usage in general.
Calendar data is not discussed. CalDAV appears only as the MKCALENDAR example.
The working group is vcarddav and the examples use an addressbook host, but the text does not specify anything about CardDAV.

RFC5690.title: Adding Acknowledgement Congestion Control to TCP
RFC5690.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC specifying an end-to-end ACK congestion control mechanism for TCP, using two new TCP options (ACK Congestion Control Permitted and ACK Ratio) and based on DCCP CCID 2's ACK congestion control.

TCP.why: The document defines new TCP options and receiver/sender behaviour changes for acknowledgements, an extension to TCP.
TCP.quote: The document specifies an end-to-end acknowledgement congestion control mechanism for TCP that uses participation from both TCP hosts

congestion control.why: The mechanism controls congestion on the reverse (ACK) path using a TCP-friendly AIMD-like ACK Ratio adjustment. No more specific congestion-control tag fits.
congestion control.quote: The TCP sender detects lost or Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN)-marked ACK packets, and tells the TCP data receiver the ACK Ratio R

rejected.why: ECN-marked ACKs are detected and used as congestion signals, but ECN is an existing mechanism the document leans on and does not define or extend.
The mechanism is based on DCCP CCID 2's ACK congestion control, which is discussed in Section 8. The document specifies TCP behaviour, not DCCP.
The document refers to RFC 5681 loss recovery and byte counting only as context for sender behaviour. It does not specify or extend NewReno.
Header compression appears only in related-work discussion of other ACK-path mitigations.

RFC5691.title: RTP Payload Format for Elementary Streams with MPEG Surround Multi-Channel Audio
RFC5691.summary: Extends the RFC 3640 MPEG-4 elementary stream RTP payload format to carry MPEG Surround multi-channel audio, either embedded in AAC payloads or as a separate layered elementary stream, with new mode and parameter registrations.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines RTP payload format extensions (new MPS-lbr/MPS-hbr modes, AU header rules, media type parameters) for MPEG Surround audio.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes extensions for the RTP payload format defined in RFC 3640 for the transport of MPEG Surround multi-channel audio.

codecs.why: The payload carries MPEG Surround and AAC audio codec data; no more specific codec tag exists for MPEG Surround or AAC, so the general codecs tag fits.
codecs.quote: MPEG Surround (Spatial Audio Coding, SAC) [23003-1] is an International Standard that was finalized by MPEG in January 2007.

SDP.why: Substantial parts specify SDP fmtp parameters (MPS-config, MPS-profile-level-id) and SDP examples with grouping and dependency signalling for the layered streams.
SDP.quote: The dependency relationships between the MPEG Surround elementary stream and the downmix stream are signaled as specified in [RFC5583].

rejected.why: RTP is the transport, but the more specific RTP payload format tag already covers this.
RTCP is only mentioned as needed for synchronizing the two streams; nothing new is defined about it.
The IANA section registers new mode values and parameters for an existing media subtype, but that is boilerplate registration rather than the subject of the document.
Mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a recommended mechanism.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional security mechanism.

gaps.name: MPEG-4 / AAC / MPEG Surround audio coding
gaps.why: The document is about the MPEG-4 audio family (AAC, HE AAC, MPEG Surround) and no specific codec tag exists for it in the taxonomy.

RFC5692.title: Transmission of IP over Ethernet over IEEE 802.16 Networks
RFC5692.summary: Specifies how IPv4 and IPv6 are carried over Ethernet bridged across IEEE 802.16 connections, with a network-side bridging function and IP-specific enhancements (multicast, DHCP, ARP proxying) to save radio resources.

WiMAX.why: The whole document defines IP transmission over IEEE 802.16 networks via the Ethernet convergence sublayer, which is exactly the WiMAX tag's subject.
