WiMAX.quote: This document describes the transmission of IPv4 over Ethernet, as well as IPv6 over Ethernet, in an access network deploying the IEEE 802.16 cellular radio transmission technology.

Ethernet.why: It defines an Ethernet link model on 802.16 using bridging per 802.1D/802.1Q, VLANs, and IP over Ethernet rules, so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet on top of IEEE 802.16 is realized by bridging between IEEE 802.16 radio connections that connect a BS (Base Station) and its associated SSs

rejected.why: ARP is used and Proxy ARP handling is described, but only as one operational enhancement; the document is not about ARP itself.
DHCP broadcast filtering and Option 82 are discussed in one subsection, as a supporting enhancement rather than the main subject.
IPv6 over Ethernet is covered, but the document specifies the link model rather than IPv6 itself.
NDP and SEND are only referenced for address resolution and public access, not specified here.
Multicast and IGMP snooping are handled in the bridge as an enhancement, which is not substantial enough for the multicast tag.
IPv4 over Ethernet is relied on from RFC 894; the document does not address IPv4 as a subject.

RFC5693.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Problem Statement
RFC5693.summary: Informational problem statement for the IETF ALTO working group, describing why P2P and distributed applications need network-topology guidance for better-than-random peer selection, with use cases, definitions and issues such as privacy and topology hiding.

ALTO.why: The whole document defines the ALTO problem, terminology, use cases and design aspects of the ALTO service, so it belongs on the ALTO page.
ALTO.quote: This document discusses issues related to an information-sharing service that enables applications to perform better-than-random peer selection.

P2P.why: The problem is framed around P2P overlay applications and their peer selection (file sharing, DHTs, streaming), a substantial part of the document's subject.
P2P.quote: Distributed applications, both peer-to-peer (P2P) and client/server used for file sharing, real-time communication, and live and on-demand media streaming

rejected.why: MPLS and Diffserv are mentioned only to contrast network-layer traffic optimization with the application-layer problem.
Section 5.6 discusses caching coexisting with ALTO, but only briefly and as orthogonal to it.
Only a brief remark that a discovery mechanism is expected; the document is not about service discovery.
User privacy and topology hiding are short subsections, not the main subject of the document.
CDNs are mentioned only as an example of third-party ALTO providers.
Live media streaming is one use case among several, not the document's subject.

RFC5694.title: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Architecture: Definition, Taxonomies, Examples, and Applicability
RFC5694.summary: IAB informational survey of P2P systems that defines P2P, gives taxonomies (mainly by data indexing), classifies P2P application domains, and offers architectural trade-off guidance and security considerations for choosing P2P versus client-server.

P2P.why: The whole document defines, classifies, exemplifies and gives applicability guidance for P2P systems, so it belongs on the P2P page.
P2P.quote: We consider a system to be P2P if the elements that form the system share their resources in order to provide the service the system has been designed to provide.

rejected.why: P2PSIP is used only as one example when applying the P2P definition (Section 2.3). The document does not specify or analyse it.
Traditional SIP is analysed only to decide whether it counts as P2P. It is not the subject of the document.
DNS is applied to the P2P definition in a short example and judged not P2P. The document is not about DNS.
The document gives architectural guidance but only for P2P versus client-server. The P2P tag covers this more specifically.
NAT traversal and ICE appear only in the historical appendix, as background.
ZebraNet and delay-tolerant networking are mentioned only in one example.

RFC5695.title: MPLS Forwarding Benchmarking Methodology for IP Flows
RFC5695.summary: Defines a laboratory benchmarking methodology (throughput, latency, frame-loss rate, system recovery, reset) for MPLS forwarding devices performing label push, swap and pop on IP flows, building on RFC 2544 and RFC 1242.

MPLS.why: The document is about MPLS forwarding operations (push, swap, pop, PHP) and how to measure them on a device under test.
MPLS.quote: This document describes a methodology specific to the benchmarking of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) forwarding devices

benchmarking.why: It is a BMWG benchmarking methodology extending RFC 2544 and RFC 1242 with test setups, procedures and reporting formats.
benchmarking.quote: This document proposes a methodology using common criteria (such as throughput, latency, frame-loss rate, system recovery, reset, etc.) to evaluate MPLS forwarding

rejected.why: LDP is only one of the label distribution protocols the test setup uses to establish label bindings. The document does not specify or extend it.
BGP, used for label distribution (RFC 3107) and aggregation, is only a supporting mechanism in the test setup.
RSVP-TE is listed as an option for label distribution and is not the subject of the document.
Ethernet frame sizes are chosen for the tests, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet.
IPv6 is allowed as the payload, but the document is not about IPv6.
The benchmarking tag is more specific for lab device benchmarking, so this broader tag is not needed.

RFC5696.title: Baseline Encoding and Transport of Pre-Congestion Information
RFC5696.summary: Specifies the baseline PCN encoding, which redefines the ECN field codepoints together with a PCN-compatible DSCP to carry two PCN states (Not-marked, PCN-marked) plus not-PCN within a Diffserv domain, and sets rules for experimental extensions.

PCN.why: The whole document defines how PCN marks are encoded in the IP header and the valid codepoint transitions at PCN nodes.
PCN.quote: This document specifies how these PCN-marks are encoded into the IP header by reusing the bits of the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) field

ECN.why: The encoding redefines the ECN codepoints within PCN domains. It also discusses coexistence with end-to-end ECN (BCP 124 compliance, Appendix B).
ECN.quote: The baseline PCN encoding closely follows the semantics of ECN [RFC3168].
ECN.section: 4. Encoding Two PCN States in IP

Diffserv.why: The encoding uses a DSCP plus ECN, and the document defines PCN-compatible DSCPs and guidance on which Diffserv service classes to use.
Diffserv.quote: PCN-traffic MUST be marked with a PCN-compatible Diffserv codepoint.
Diffserv.section: 4. Encoding Two PCN States in IP

rejected.why: The encoding uses IP header bits but is not about the IP protocol itself.
Tunnelling through IPsec is only a constraint on the encoding design.
IP-in-IP tunnels are mentioned as an encoding constraint and a coexistence option, not the subject.
PCN is under the QoS area, but the specific child tags fit better.

RFC5697.title: Other Certificates Extension
RFC5697.summary: Defines an experimental X.509 certificate extension (otherCerts) listing SCVPCertID references so a CA can attest that several certificates belong to the same end entity for linking application state.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 certificate extension (id-pe-otherCerts), its syntax, and its issuance and validation rules, building on the RFC 5280 profile.
X.509.quote: This memo defines a new public key certificate extension that supports such linkage

rejected.why: TLS handshakes and the web server use case are only a motivating example. The document specifies nothing about TLS.
The parent of X.509. The document is specifically about an X.509 certificate extension, so the more specific tag is used.
The ASN.1 module is only the normative syntax for the extension, which is a notation substrate.
Web browsers and web servers appear only in the use case.

RFC5698.title: Data Structure for the Security Suitability of Cryptographic Algorithms (DSSC)
RFC5698.summary: Defines the DSSC XML and ASN.1 data structure for publishing signed security suitability policies that evaluate cryptographic algorithms over time, plus processing rules, for use in long-term archiving and signature verification.

LTANS.why: Produced by the LTANS working group, the document supports long-term archive services and Evidence Record Syntax verification, with an appendix on storing policies in Evidence Records.
LTANS.quote: Long-term archiving: The most important use case is long-term archiving of signed data.

cryptography.why: The subject is evaluating the suitability and validity periods of cryptographic algorithms (RSA, DSA, SHA family) and their parameters, which is cryptographic algorithm management. No specific algorithm tag fits.
cryptography.quote: This document specifies a data structure that enables an automated analysis of the security suitability of a given cryptographic algorithm at a given point of time

rejected.why: The policy may carry an enveloped XML signature, but that is only the integrity mechanism, not the subject.
The policy schema is XML, which is only the encoding.
An ASN.1 module is provided as an alternative encoding, which is only the encoding.
The ASN.1 form is wrapped in CMS SignedData, which is only the substrate.
RSA is used as an example algorithm and parameter, but the document is not about RSA.
The media type registrations are IANA boilerplate, not the main body.
Certificate path validation is mentioned only for verifying the policy signature.

gaps.name: Cryptographic algorithm agility / suitability policy
gaps.why: The document is about expressing time-bound evaluations of algorithm security. The taxonomy has no tag for algorithm agility, deprecation or suitability, so only the generic cryptography topic fits.

RFC5701.title: IPv6 Address Specific BGP Extended Community Attribute
RFC5701.summary: Defines a new BGP attribute, the IPv6 Address Specific Extended Community, a 20-octet analogue of the IPv4 Address Specific Extended Community, with IANA registry and Route Target/Route Origin sub-types.

BGP communities.why: The whole document specifies a new BGP extended community attribute carrying an IPv6 address, extending RFC 4360. This is exactly the BGP communities subject.
BGP communities.quote: This document defines a new BGP attribute, the IPv6 Address Specific Extended Community, that has a structure similar to the IPv4 Address Specific Extended Community

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses are only the content of the new community field; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
BGP is the host protocol, but the document is specifically about extended communities, so the more specific child tag fits.
Route Target and Route Origin sub-types are used in L3VPNs, but the document does not specify VPN procedures, though it was produced in the l3vpn WG.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level apparatus for the new attribute, not the main subject.

RFC5702.title: Use of SHA-2 Algorithms with RSA in DNSKEY and RRSIG Resource Records for DNSSEC
RFC5702.summary: Defines DNSSEC algorithm numbers 8 (RSA/SHA-256) and 10 (RSA/SHA-512) for DNSKEY and RRSIG records, specifying key sizes, signature construction with PKCS#1 v1.5 prefixes, and examples.

DNSSEC.why: The document extends DNSSEC's list of signing algorithms and specifies DNSKEY/RRSIG formats, algorithm numbers, key size limits, and validator requirements.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes how to produce RSA/SHA-256 and RSA/SHA-512 DNSKEY and RRSIG resource records for use in the Domain Name System Security Extensions

RSA.why: A substantial part specifies how RSA signatures are computed with SHA-2 hashes (PKCS#1 v1.5 padding, prefixes, key size limits), relevant to RSA readers.
RSA.quote: The value of the signature field in the RRSIG RR follows the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature scheme

SHA.why: The document introduces SHA-256 and SHA-512 into DNSSEC and discusses SHA-1 versus SHA-2 strength, so SHA family readers would want it.
SHA.quote: hash = SHA-XXX(data)

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; the subject is covered more specifically by the DNSSEC tag.
Not related; RSA keys here are in DNSKEY records, not certificates.
IANA registry additions are boilerplate-level; the body is about the algorithms.
ASN.1 DER prefixes are only quoted from PKCS#1, not the subject.

RFC5703.title: Sieve Email Filtering: MIME Part Tests, Iteration, Extraction, Replacement, and Enclosure
RFC5703.summary: Defines Sieve extensions for MIME part handling: foreverypart/break loops, :mime/:anychild tests on header/address/exists, and replace, enclose and extracttext actions.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies Sieve extensions (foreverypart, mime, replace, enclose, extracttext).
Sieve.quote: This document defines extensions to the Sieve email filtering language to permit analysis and manipulation of the MIME body parts of an email message.

rejected.why: MIME structure is the object the Sieve extension operates on; the document does not define MIME itself.
RFC 5322 headers are only referenced as what the tests examine.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as affected by replace.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations.
The document does not register media types or define registry rules.

RFC5704.title: Uncoordinated Protocol Development Considered Harmful
RFC5704.summary: IAB document describing harms from uncoordinated protocol development between SDOs (ITU-T and IETF), using T-MPLS and PPP over SONET as case studies and recommending a universal IETF change process.

IETF process.why: The document recommends inter-SDO coordination procedures and a universal IETF change process, which is about how IETF develops and changes protocols.
IETF process.quote: the IETF has not yet defined a change process that is applicable to all of its work areas.

MPLS-TP.why: MPLS-TP and the T-MPLS conflict are the main case study, and the appendix analyses it in detail. The JWT and MPLS-TP are presented as the model for coordination.
MPLS-TP.quote: the IETF and the ITU-T established a joint working team (JWT) to assess whether it was possible to enhance existing MPLS standards

internet architecture.why: The document covers architectural principles such as invariants, code-point semantics, design authority, and 'ships in the night'.
internet architecture.quote: Some of these problems may cause significant harm to the Internet.

rejected.why: MPLS is the subject of the case study, but the document does not specify or extend MPLS. It is about SDO coordination.
PPP over SONET is a brief second example of miscoordination, not a subject of the document.
Code-point allocation is discussed as a principle, but the document is not about IANA registries or procedures.
ENUM is mentioned only in passing as an example of the design authority split.

gaps.name: Inter-SDO coordination / liaison relationships (IETF-ITU-T)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about coordination between standards bodies, and the taxonomy has no tag specific to it. The closest fit is IETF process.

RFC5705.title: Keying Material Exporters for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC5705.summary: RFC 5705 defines a general exporter mechanism for deriving application-specific keying material from a TLS/DTLS master secret using a label, optional context value and length, and creates the IANA TLS Exporter Label registry.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new mechanism in TLS (keying material exporters) that applies to all TLS versions. It is a TLS extension of the kind readers of TLS would need.
TLS.quote: PRF(SecurityParameters.master_secret, label, SecurityParameters.client_random + SecurityParameters.server_random)[length]

rejected.why: The exporter works with DTLS, but the document only mentions DTLS in passing and defines the mechanism in terms of TLS. DTLS is not the subject.
DTLS-SRTP is only the motivating example of an application that uses exported keys. The document does not specify SRTP.
The document is about deriving keys from a TLS session. TLS is the more specific tag, and the document does not address key management generally.
The document creates a TLS Exporter Label registry, but that is boilerplate-level IANA content. The main body is not about IANA guidance.
EAP-TLS and EAP-TTLS only appear as existing exporter users in the IANA registry table. The document is not about EAP.

RFC5706.title: Guidelines for Considering Operations and Management of New Protocols and Protocol Extensions
RFC5706.summary: Informational guidelines telling protocol designers and reviewers which operations and management aspects (deployment, configuration, fault, performance, security management, information models) to consider and document for new protocols or extensions, with a review checklist.

network management.why: The whole document is about considering operations and manageability of new protocols: fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management, plus operational considerations and documentation guidance.
network management.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide guidance to authors and reviewers of documents that define new protocols or protocol extensions regarding aspects of operations and management

rejected.why: SNMP, SMI and MIBs are discussed as available management technologies and background, but the document does not specify or extend them.
NETCONF is mentioned as one of several management protocols and for multi-device locking, not as a subject of the document.
Syslog is cited as an option for logging and security events, not specified or profiled here.
Section 3.6 touches performance management and points to BMWG/IPPM, but it is a small part of the document and the broader network management tag already covers it.
Security management (Section 3.7) is only one subsection, and it concerns managing the protocol rather than operational security practice for infrastructure.
Section 4 gives documentation guidance for Manageability Considerations sections, but the document is not about IETF procedures.

RFC5707.title: Media Server Markup Language (MSML)
RFC5707.summary: Informational RFC specifying MSML, an XML language for controlling media server conferencing, IVR dialogs, media transforms, fax and auditing, carried over SIP INFO or the SIP Control Framework.

conferencing.why: A large part of MSML defines conference creation, audio mixing, video layout, join/unjoin and sidebars; a media server conference control language belongs under conferencing.
conferencing.quote: MSML can be used, for example, to control media server conferencing features such as video layout and audio mixing, create sidebar conferences or personal mixes

XML.why: MSML is an XML-based language defined with a full set of XML schemas, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: The Media Server Markup Language (MSML) is an XML [n2] language used to control the flow of media streams and services applied to media streams within a media server.

SIP.why: The document specifies MSML usage over SIP INFO and the SIP Control Framework, including Control Package definitions and the msml-param Request-URI parameter.
SIP.quote: SIP INVITE and INFO [i5] requests and responses MAY be used to carry MSML.

MRCP.why: MSML dialogs provide IVR, ASR and TTS speech services control on a media server, which is closely related to MRCP-style media resource control.
MRCP.quote: MSML has been designed to address the control and manipulation of media processing operations (e.g., announcement, IVR, play and record, automatic speech recognition (ASR), text to speech (TTS)

rejected.why: SDP appears only in examples and as a source of stream directionality; the document is not about SDP.
RTP sessions are the media substrate terminated by connections; not specified here.
The IANA registrations of application/moml+xml are boilerplate-like registrations, not the main subject.
Fax send/receive/detect primitives are only one MSML package, and the fax tag concerns fax over Internet mail and IP.
IVR and DTMF primitives do not make this about Internet-PSTN interworking or gateway control.

gaps.name: Media server control / IVR (VoiceXML)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for media server control or IVR dialog languages, which is the core subject of MSML.

RFC5708.title: X.509 Key and Signature Encoding for the KeyNote Trust Management System
RFC5708.summary: Defines X.509 certificate key identifiers and signature encodings for KeyNote assertions, plus new SHA-256/SHA-512/RIPEMD-160 signature types for RSA and X.509 keys.

trust management.why: The document extends KeyNote, the trust management system, with new key identifier and signature encodings and registers new algorithm identifiers for it.
trust management.quote: This memo describes X.509 key identifiers and signature encoding for version 2 of the KeyNote trust-management system (RFC 2704).

X.509.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how X.509 certificates are used directly as principals' keys in KeyNote, including normalization of the subject key.
X.509.quote: X.509 key identifiers in KeyNote are encoded as an ASN1 Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) encoding of the whole X.509 certificate

rejected.why: SHA-256/512 are only hash choices for new signature types; the document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
RSA signatures get new hash identifiers, but RSA itself is defined in RFC 2792 and is not the subject here.
DER and OCTET STRING are used only as the encoding mechanism.
Certificate validity is left to the application; no PKI mechanism is specified.
The IANA section only reserves identifiers and is boilerplate here.
Base64 is just one of the ASCII encodings used, not a subject of the document.

RFC5709.title: OSPFv2 HMAC-SHA Cryptographic Authentication
RFC5709.summary: Updates OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication (RFC 2328 Appendix D) to support HMAC with the SHA-1/224/256/384/512 family, defining the Apad, key preparation, digest computation, and security association parameters.

OSPF.why: The document updates OSPFv2's built-in cryptographic authentication mechanism, specifying packet trailer computation and verification for OSPFv2.
OSPF.quote: This document adds support for Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA) defined in the US NIST Secure Hash Standard (SHS)

HMAC.why: Section 3.3 specifies the HMAC computation (Ipad/Opad, First-Hash, Second-Hash) with SHA algorithms for OSPF authentication.
HMAC.quote: The Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) authentication mode defined in NIST FIPS 198 is used

SHA.why: The document defines use of the SHA family of hash functions, with required and optional algorithm support, in OSPFv2 authentication.
SHA.quote: HMAC-SHA-1 (defined here) HMAC-SHA-256 (defined here) HMAC-SHA-384 (defined here) HMAC-SHA-512 (defined here)
SHA.section: 3. Cryptographic Authentication with NIST SHS in HMAC Mode

routing security.why: The document is about securing a routing protocol's packets against forgery, so routing security readers would want it; no child tag (RPKI, BGPsec) fits.
routing security.quote: This document enhances the security of the OSPFv2 routing protocol by adding, to the existing OSPFv2 Cryptographic Authentication method

rejected.why: Keyed-MD5 is only the existing algorithm retained for backwards compatibility; the document is about the SHA alternatives.
Mentioned only as an alternative that operators chose not to use; the document does not specify it.
The more specific routing-security and OSPF tags cover this; generic authentication is not the document's subject.
The document explicitly notes OSPF has no automated key management; key lifetime parameters are only briefly specified.
The document applies only to OSPFv2.

RFC5710.title: PathErr Message Triggered MPLS and GMPLS LSP Reroutes
RFC5710.summary: RFC 5710 describes how RSVP-TE PathErr messages can trigger non-disruptive rerouting of MPLS and GMPLS point-to-point TE LSPs (e.g., for soft preemption and graceful shutdown), with optional timeout-based forced removal, and defines a new "Reroute" RSVP error code.

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies RSVP-TE PathErr processing at requesting, transit and ingress nodes for reroute requests, and defines a new RSVP error code. It is an RSVP-TE signalling extension.
RSVP-TE.quote: describes how Resource ReserVation Protocol (RSVP) PathErr messages may be used to trigger rerouting of Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) point-to-point Traffic Engineering (TE) Label Switched Paths

GMPLS.why: It applies explicitly to GMPLS LSPs. It uses the GMPLS IF_ID ERROR_SPEC formats, Path_State_Removed and link-bundling TLVs, so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes how Resource ReserVation Protocol (RSVP) PathErr messages may be used to trigger rerouting of Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS)

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific tag. The base RSVP protocol is only the substrate.
The RSVP-TE child tag already sits under this topic, so listing it separately is redundant.
The RFC is about RSVP-TE signalling for LSP rerouting. Plain MPLS architecture and encapsulation are not its subject.
The new error code registration is boilerplate-level IANA content and not the document's main subject.

RFC5711.title: Node Behavior upon Originating and Receiving Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Path Error Messages
RFC5711.summary: Clarifies, without new protocol extensions, how nodes send and receive RSVP-TE PathErr messages for preempted MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs, including state clearing for fatal and non-fatal errors.

RSVP-TE.why: The whole document specifies node behaviour for RSVP-TE PathErr messages when a TE LSP is preempted, clarifying RFC 3209 procedures.
RSVP-TE.quote: the behavior of a node sending a Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Traffic Engineering (TE) Path Error message and to the behavior of a node receiving an RSVP Path Error message

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific tag. The document is about PathErr handling for TE LSPs, not base RSVP.
GMPLS is mentioned and the Path_State_Removed flag from RFC 3473 is noted. The document is not about GMPLS signalling itself.
MPLS TE LSPs are the context, but the subject is the RSVP-TE signalling behaviour, which is covered by the RSVP-TE tag.
The more specific RSVP-TE tag under traffic engineering already covers this.

RFC5712.title: MPLS Traffic Engineering Soft Preemption
RFC5712.summary: Specifies MPLS-TE soft preemption: a SESSION-ATTRIBUTE flag and a "Reroute Request Soft Preemption" PathErr value so preempted TE LSPs can be rerouted make-before-break instead of being torn down.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling with a new SESSION-ATTRIBUTE flag and a PathErr error value, and defines the node procedures for soft preemption of TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: the preempting node MUST issue a PathErr message with the Error Code=34 ("Reroute") and a value=1 ("Reroute Request Soft Preemption")

rejected.why: MPLS is the setting, but the document's subject is the RSVP-TE signalling extension. The more specific RSVP-TE tag fits better.
RSVP-TE is a child of this topic and is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
Diffserv is mentioned only as the context where soft preemption is most useful. The document does not specify or extend it.
The Interoperability section only says soft preemption may not translate to some GMPLS technologies, which is a passing remark.
RSVP is the underlying protocol. The extensions are TE-specific and fall under RSVP-TE.
IGP updates are mentioned only as a side effect of preemption. The document does not specify anything about IGPs.

RFC5713.title: Security Threats and Security Requirements for the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP)
RFC5713.summary: Informational RFC that develops a threat model for the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) between a NAS and an Access Node (DSLAM), enumerates attacks per use case, and derives security requirements for ANCP.

ANCP.why: The whole document analyses threats against ANCP and defines its security requirements, so readers of the ANCP subject would expect it.
ANCP.quote: This document focuses on describing security threats and deriving security requirements for the Access Node Control Protocol

rejected.why: Implied as an ancestor of nothing chosen here, but the document is specific to ANCP; the ANCP tag (under link layer/DSL) captures it. A generic security tag would be less specific.
The AAA server is part of the system overview, but AAA policy negotiation is explicitly out of scope.
Multicast is one ANCP use case discussed in Section 7.4, but the document is not about multicast routing or group membership.
The AN MIB module is mentioned only for management attack context; the document does not specify MIB objects.
IGMP is only mentioned as a source of DoS load on ANCP, not specified or analysed.
DSL is the access technology context; ANCP is the more specific tag.

RFC5714.title: IP Fast Reroute Framework
RFC5714.summary: Informational framework for IP fast-reroute: locally computed, pre-installed repair paths (ECMP, loop-free alternates, multi-hop) protecting against link or node failure in conventionally routed IP networks, with link-state IGPs as initial scope.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document frames IPFRR: problem analysis, repair path categories (ECMP, loop-free alternates, multi-hop), coverage analysis, and management considerations.
IP fast reroute.quote: a framework for the development of IP fast-reroute mechanisms that provide protection against link or router failure by invoking locally determined repair paths

rejected.why: BFD is mentioned only as one possible fast failure detection mechanism; the document does not specify or extend it.
ECMP paths are one of three repair path categories, but the document is about IPFRR overall, not ECMP forwarding.
MPLS fast-reroute is cited only as an analogy; this framework is explicitly for conventional IP routing.
Link-state IGPs are named as the initial scope, but no specific protocol such as OSPF or IS-IS is addressed.
The more specific IP fast reroute tag covers the subject, so the parent is not used.

gaps.name: Micro-loop prevention / loop-free convergence
gaps.why: The document discusses micro-loop avoidance as a companion mechanism to IPFRR, but it is covered mainly by RFC 5715 and has no dedicated taxonomy tag.

RFC5715.title: A Framework for Loop-Free Convergence
RFC5715.summary: Informational framework surveying the causes of micro-loops during IGP routing transitions in IP/LDP networks and the proposed mechanisms (mitigation, prevention, suppression) for loop-free convergence.

IP fast reroute.why: Micro-loops disrupt fast-reroute repairs, and the framework is a companion to the IP Fast Reroute Framework. It surveys loop-free convergence mechanisms (tunnels, not-via, ordered FIB) that work alongside IPFRR.
IP fast reroute.quote: Micro-loops can also form as a result of a network-maintenance action such as adding a new network component

routing architecture.why: The document addresses routing convergence behaviour, FIB consistency and design strategies in general, across IGPs, rather than a specific protocol.
routing architecture.quote: A micro-loop is a packet forwarding loop that may occur transiently among two or more routers in a hop-by-hop, packet forwarding paradigm.

rejected.why: Only the IGP context. No OSPF-specific mechanism is specified; the incremental-cost work is cited from an OSPF paper but is generic.
LDP is mentioned as the label-distribution substrate for the MPLS new-labels method, but the document is not about LDP.
MPLS networks are one applicability context, and one section covers new labels, but this is not a substantial MPLS subject.
NTP is only suggested as a way to synchronise FIB updates and is not the subject.
Tunnels are used as a prevention technique but generic tunnelling is not the subject.

gaps.name: Loop-free convergence / micro-loop avoidance in IGP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IGP convergence or micro-loop prevention (PLSN, oFIB, incremental cost), which is the core subject of the document.

RFC5716.title: Requirements for Federated File Systems
RFC5716.summary: This informational document lists the functional requirements for a federated file system, in which fileservers and namespace database (NSDB) nodes run by different administrators present one namespace built from filesets, FSNs, FSLs and junctions, and it defines the related terms.

storage.why: The whole document is about file-system namespace federation: filesets, junctions, replicas and migration across fileservers. No specific storage technology tag fits as the subject, so the parent topic is used.
storage.quote: Today, there are collections of fileservers that inter-operate to provide a single namespace comprised of filesystem resources provided by different members of the collection

rejected.why: NFSv2, NFSv3, NFSv4 and CIFS appear only as client-facing access protocols that the federation must not change. NFSv4 referrals are the redirection mechanism used. The document does not specify or extend NFS.
LDAP is mentioned only in Security Considerations, as one possible way to implement the NSDB query mechanism.
DNS is mentioned only as one way to locate an NSDB node by its FQDN. The document does not specify anything new about DNS.
UUIDs are suggested as one possible FSN identifier format in an example. The document is not about UUIDs.
TLS is mentioned only as an example mechanism in Security Considerations.
Trust anchor management is touched on only in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: Federated file systems / NFSv4 namespace federation (FedFS)
gaps.why: The document specifies requirements for a federated namespace (filesets, FSN, FSL, junction, NSDB) over NFS and CIFS. The taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the generic storage topic.

RFC5717.title: Partial Lock Remote Procedure Call (RPC) for NETCONF
RFC5717.summary: Defines a NETCONF capability (:partial-lock) with partial-lock and partial-unlock RPCs for locking portions of the running datastore using XPath-selected nodes, plus interactions with existing operations and capabilities.

NETCONF.why: The document extends NETCONF with new lock/unlock operations and a new capability, and specifies their interaction with base operations.
NETCONF.quote: This document defines a capability-based extension to the NETCONF protocol for locking portions of a configuration datastore.

rejected.why: A non-normative YANG module is given in an appendix, but YANG is only an alternative notation for the operations, not the subject.
XML and XML Schema are the encoding for the operations and the normative schema, which makes them substrate, not the subject.
SNMP is mentioned only as another management interface the lock must exclude, not specified or extended here.
The IANA section registers a capability URN and an XML namespace. This is boilerplate and not what the document is about.

RFC5718.title: An In-Band Data Communication Network For the MPLS Transport Profile
RFC5718.summary: Defines how the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) carries Management and Signaling Communication Network (MCN/SCN, together DCN) messages in MPLS-TP, with MCC/SCC channel types, a PID field for payload protocol, and demultiplexing procedures.

MPLS-TP.why: The document specifies an in-band data communication network for MPLS-TP nodes using the G-ACh, with encapsulation, channel types and receiver procedures, so it belongs on the MPLS-TP page.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document describes how the G-ACh may be used to provide the infrastructure that forms part of the Management Communication Network (MCN) and a Signaling Communication Network (SCN).

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate; the more specific MPLS-TP tag fits the document.
The ACH originates in pseudowire work and PW setup is mentioned briefly, but the document is not about pseudowire emulation.
G-ACh is used for OAM generally, but this document carries management and control messages rather than defining OAM mechanisms.
LDP is mentioned only as an example of a signaling protocol that could run over the DCN.
The DCN carries management traffic, but the document defines a transport channel rather than management practice or protocols.
The IANA section allocates two channel types, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC5719.title: Updated IANA Considerations for Diameter Command Code Allocations
RFC5719.summary: RFC 5719 updates RFC 3588 by splitting the Diameter command code space into ranges (RADIUS-compatible, IETF Review, vendor-specific FCFS, experimental) so other SDOs can obtain command codes without overloading existing commands.

Diameter.why: The document updates the Diameter base protocol's extensibility rules and command code allocation policy, so Diameter readers need it.
Diameter.quote: This document aligns the extensibility rules for Diameter command codes with those defined for Diameter application identifiers

IANA.why: The substance of the document is a registry allocation policy (IETF Review, First Come First Served, experimental ranges) for the Diameter command code namespace.
IANA.quote: This section describes changes to the IANA Considerations sections outlined in RFC 3588 regarding the allocation of command codes by IANA.

rejected.why: Only the range 0-255 is reserved for RADIUS backward compatibility; the document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
Diameter is a more specific child of AAA, and the document is not about AAA frameworks generally.
It touches on delegating work to other SDOs, but the actual content is a registry allocation policy, better covered by IANA.

RFC5720.title: Routing and Addressing in Networks with Global Enterprise Recursion (RANGER)
RFC5720.summary: RANGER is an informational architectural framework for scalable routing and addressing using recursively nested enterprise networks, map-and-encaps overlays (VET, SEAL, ISATAP), with mobility, multihoming and IPv6/IPv4 coexistence.

routing architecture.why: The document's core is a routing and addressing scalability architecture with EID/RLOC separation, mapping systems and recursive enterprises.
routing architecture.quote: RANGER is an architectural framework for scalable routing and addressing in networks with global enterprise recursion.

IPv6 transition.why: Uses IPv6 as a virtual overlay over IPv4 and discusses translation, CGN and ISATAP-descended tunnelling for coexistence.
IPv6 transition.quote: The RANGER architecture addresses these requirements and also provides a comprehensive framework for IPv6/ IPv4 coexistence

tunneling.why: Automatic tunnelling overlays (VET, SEAL, ISATAP) are the mechanism that manifests the architecture.
tunneling.quote: The VET approach uses automatic IP-in-IP tunneling in which ITEs encapsulate EID-based inner IP packets within RLOC-based, outer IP headers

IP mobility.why: A dedicated section covers site and host mobility, including aircraft mobile routers and the use of Mobile IPv6 and HIP.
IP mobility.quote: Enterprise mobility use cases must be considered along several different vectors

multihoming.why: Multihoming of enterprises with PI prefixes is a stated goal and has its own section.
multihoming.quote: Within an enterprise, EBRs can discover multiple EBGs and use them in a fault-tolerant and load-balancing fashion

rejected.why: Only cited as a related initiative; RANGER is a separate architecture.
Described as an ancestor technology and component, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned as an optional securing mechanism only.
Used in the descriptive enterprise-within-enterprise framework but not specified or analysed.
CGN and NAT appear only as legacy-service access options.
Listed among related RRG proposals only.

gaps.name: Locator/identifier split (map-and-encaps, EID/RLOC)
gaps.why: The core design separates edge identifiers from routing locators; the taxonomy has only LISP and ILNP as specific tags and no general tag for this topic.

RFC5721.title: POP3 Support for UTF-8
RFC5721.summary: RFC 5721 extends POP3 with LANG and UTF8 capabilities to support un-encoded UTF-8 in headers, user names, passwords, and localized protocol error text, as part of the EAI experiment.

POP3.why: The document defines new POP3 capabilities (LANG, UTF8) and commands extending POP3 via the CAPA mechanism.
POP3.quote: This specification extends the Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) to support un-encoded international characters in user names, passwords, mail addresses, message headers

EAI.why: It is the POP3 piece of the EAI work, handling UTF-8 headers and downgrading of native UTF-8 maildrops.
EAI.quote: This document forms part of the Email Address Internationalization (EAI) experiment described in the EAI Framework document [RFC4952]

language tags.why: A substantial part of the document is the LANG command negotiating response language using language tags and range matching.
language tags.quote: The LANG command requests that human-readable text included in all subsequent +OK and -ERR responses be localized to a language matching the language range argument

UTF-8.why: The UTF8 command switches the session to UTF-8 mode, and UTF-8 text is used for error strings, headers and credentials.
UTF-8.quote: This and subsequent protocol-level human- readable text is encoded in the UTF-8 charset.

rejected.why: It uses SASLprep (the predecessor) for user names and passwords, but PRECIS itself is not specified or discussed.
SASLprep is only applied as a string-preparation profile; AUTH/SASL is merely referenced.
Internationalized headers are handled by other EAI RFCs; this document only passes them through or down-converts them.
STLS is mentioned only as a restriction after UTF8 and as a security mitigation.
SMTP is mentioned only for contrast on downgrading requirements.

RFC5722.title: Handling of Overlapping IPv6 Fragments
RFC5722.summary: RFC 5722 updates the IPv6 base specification to forbid overlapping fragments, explaining a firewall-bypass attack using overlapping fragments and requiring that datagrams with overlapping fragments be silently discarded.

IPv6.why: The document amends RFC 2460's fragmentation and reassembly behaviour and defines new IPv6 node behaviour (MUST NOT create overlapping fragments, discard on reassembly).
IPv6.quote: updates the IPv6 specification to explicitly forbid overlapping fragments

rejected.why: The attack is about bypassing firewalls, but the document specifies host fragment/reassembly behaviour, not firewall mechanisms.
TCP header flags are used only in the attack example; TCP is not specified or extended.
The security issue is specific to IPv6 fragmentation; the IPv6 tag is the more specific fit and the document is not general security guidance.
Path MTU is mentioned only as the reason fragmentation occurs; the document is not about PMTUD.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation and reassembly
gaps.why: The document is specifically about IPv6 fragment reassembly and overlapping fragments, and the taxonomy has no tag for IP fragmentation; it is covered only broadly under IPv6.

RFC5723.title: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Session Resumption
RFC5723.summary: RFC 5723 extends IKEv2 with a session resumption mechanism: the responder issues an opaque ticket (by value or by reference), and the client later presents it in a new IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange to re-establish an IKE SA cheaply without a full key exchange or EAP re-authentication.

IKE.why: The document defines a new IKEv2 exchange type (IKE_SESSION_RESUME), new notify payloads, and key derivation for resumed IKE SAs. This is an extension of IKEv2, so IKE is the most specific fitting tag.
IKE.quote: This document proposes an extension to IKEv2 that allows a client to re-establish an IKE SA with a gateway in a highly efficient manner

rejected.why: IPsec SAs are the context, but the document specifies an IKE extension. IPsec is the parent of IKE and is implied.
TLS session resumption (RFC 5077) is cited as the inspiration for the approach, but the document is not about TLS.
EAP is mentioned as the motivation for avoiding the latency of re-authentication. The document does not specify or extend EAP.
MOBIKE appears only as a state item in the table of what is or is not resumed. It is not a subject of the document.
The document derives new keys from the old SK_d, but this is part of IKE and does not make the document about key management in general.

RFC5724.title: URI Scheme for Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) Short Message Service (SMS)
RFC5724.summary: Defines the "sms" URI scheme for specifying one or more SMS recipients (and an optional body) so user agents can compose GSM SMS messages, including processing, comparison, HTML form use, and registration.

SMS.why: The document defines the URI scheme for SMS and discusses SMS content, infrastructure, SMSCs and security. The SMS tag explicitly covers its URI schemes.
SMS.quote: This memo specifies the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme "sms" for specifying one or more recipients for an SMS message.

URI.why: It specifies a new URI scheme with formal syntax, processing, comparison rules and registration under RFC 4395, so readers of URI schemes would want it.
URI.quote: This memo requests the registration of the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme "sms" for specifying one or more recipients for an SMS message.

rejected.why: The sms scheme reuses the telephone-subscriber syntax from RFC 3966 and reproduces it in an appendix. The document defines nothing new about the tel scheme.
Section 2.6 covers using sms URIs as HTML form actions, but HTML is only the context and is not specified or extended.
GSM is described as background. The document is not about IP over 3GPP networks.
The document is about a URI scheme for SMS, not GSM SIM authentication or interworking. GSM is only the underlying network.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the syntax.

RFC5725.title: Post-Repair Loss RLE Report Block Type for RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Reports (XRs)
RFC5725.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR report block type (Post-repair Loss RLE, BT=10) reporting RTP packets still lost after loss repair, plus its SDP "rtcp-xr" parameter signaling.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block, its format and semantics, and its registration. RTCP is the subject and the document is not just using it.
RTCP.quote: This document defines a new report block type within the framework of RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Reports (XRs).

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP parameter for the rtcp-xr attribute. This is new SDP signaling that readers of SDP would want.
SDP.quote: pkt-loss-rle-post = "post-repair-loss-rle" ["=" max-size]

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport being reported on. The document extends RTCP, so the more specific RTCP tag fits.
FEC and retransmission are mentioned only as examples of loss-repair methods. The document does not specify them.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional protection mechanism.
The report supports evaluating loss-repair effectiveness, but the document defines an RTCP report block rather than measurement methodology.
ABNF is only the notation used for the SDP syntax.

RFC5726.title: Mobile IPv6 Location Privacy Solutions
RFC5726.summary: Experimental IRTF RFC proposing Mobile IPv6 extensions (encrypted home address and pseudo home address, with new options and a routing header) that hide the home address/care-of address binding from eavesdroppers and correspondent nodes.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document specifies extensions to Mobile IPv6 (new destination option, routing header, mobility options, modified return routability and binding update procedures) for location privacy.
Mobile IPv6.quote: we consider the Mobile IPv6 location privacy problem described in RFC 4882, and propose efficient and secure techniques to protect location privacy of the mobile node

privacy.why: The whole document addresses location privacy and profiling attacks, including a profiling discussion appendix.
privacy.quote: The IP address location privacy problem is concerned with unwittingly revealing the current location of a mobile node to eavesdroppers and to communicating parties.

rejected.why: IPsec ESP tunnel mode with non-null encryption is relied on to protect MN-HA signaling, but the document does not specify or extend IPsec.
Mobile IPv6 is the subject; IPv6 itself is only the base protocol, and the extension header formats are Mobile IPv6 specific.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate, not the main subject.
AES is only named as the default encryption algorithm for the encrypted home address.
HMAC_SHA1 is used inside the return routability procedure but is not the subject.

RFC5727.title: Change Process for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure Area
RFC5727.summary: BCP defining the SIPCORE and DISPATCH working groups' roles in managing changes to SIP and RAI Area work, deprecating the "P-" header field process, and setting IANA registration rules for SIP header fields and event packages.

SIP.why: The document governs how SIP is changed and extended, including header field and event package registration rules. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: Documents that update or obsolete RFCs 3261 through 3265 must advance through the SIPCORE WG.

IETF process.why: A large part of the document defines working group roles, chartering and new-work intake for the RAI Area, which is IETF process.
IETF process.quote: DISPATCH identifies the proper venue for work. If no such venue yet exists in the RAI Area, DISPATCH will develop charters and consensus for a BoF

IANA.why: The document changes IANA registration policies for SIP header fields and event packages, and clarifies RFC 3969.
IANA.quote: Previously in RFC 3427, all new SIP header field registrations required a Standards Action (per RFC 5226) with the exception of "P-" header fields

rejected.why: SIMPLE is mentioned only as an example of a working group that generates SIP requirements. Event packages are covered only as a registration policy.
Mentioned only as an example working group in a list.

RFC5728.title: The SatLabs Group DVB-RCS MIB
RFC5728.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module, written by the SatLabs Group, for managing DVB-RCS satellite terminals (RCSTs). It covers system/ODU, network, installation, QoS, control, state, and forward/return link objects.

MIB.why: The whole document is a MIB module definition (DVB-RCS-MIB) with objects, groups and compliance statements, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: SatLabs has specified a common Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Management Information Base (MIB) for DVB-RCS terminals, which is defined in this document.

satellite.why: The managed subject is DVB-RCS satellite terminals and their forward and return links, with new ifTypes for DVB-RCS MAC, TDM and TDMA interfaces.
satellite.quote: MIB module for the Digital Video Broadcasting Return Channel via Satellite system (DVB-RCS)

rejected.why: The MIB uses DSCP and PHB for packet classification, but it only maps them to Request Classes and does not specify or extend Diffserv.
SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB, not something the document specifies. The MIB tag already covers it.
ATM cells and VPI/VCI appear as object parameters for the ATM burst profile, but the document is not about ATM.
A QoS group of objects exists (packet classes, request classes, PID pools), but it is a part of the MIB and not the document's main subject.
Only the DNS server addresses are configured as objects, so DNS is a mere dependency.
FTP and TFTP appear only as the transports for config file URLs.

gaps.name: DVB-RCS / DVB-S2 satellite terminal management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only generic satellite networking and DVB IP-over-MPEG tags, with nothing specific to the DVB-RCS return channel system.

RFC5729.title: Clarifications on the Routing of Diameter Requests Based on the Username and the Realm
RFC5729.summary: RFC 5729 specifies how Diameter agents must route requests when the User-Name AVP holds a multi-realm "Decorated" NAI, updating User-Name and Destination-Realm at each hop, as a clarification of RFC 3588.

Diameter.why: The document clarifies and updates Diameter base protocol request routing (updates RFC 3588) for proxies and agents, so it belongs on the Diameter page.
Diameter.quote: This specification defines the behavior required of Diameter agents to route requests when the User-Name Attribute Value Pair (AVP) contains a Network Access Identifier

rejected.why: Diameter is the specific AAA tag chosen; AAA is its ancestor and is implied, and the document does not address AAA frameworks in general.
RADIUS NAI decoration is mentioned only as prior background; the document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
EAP is only mentioned as an application that assumes decoration support; the document does not specify EAP behaviour.
Internationalization of realms is discussed briefly with assumptions, but the document explicitly does not attempt to address it.
DNS is the namespace for realm names, but the document defines no DNS behaviour.

gaps.name: Network Access Identifier (NAI)
gaps.why: The document is substantially about the NAI and its decorated multi-realm form, but the taxonomy has no NAI tag.

RFC5730.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC5730.summary: RFC 5730 specifies the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) version 1.0, an XML client-server protocol for provisioning objects (originally domain names) in a shared registry, with commands, result codes, an extension framework, schemas, an object mapping template and the application/epp+xml media type.

EPP.why: The document is the core EPP specification: greeting, commands, responses, result codes, extension framework and XML schemas.
EPP.quote: an application-layer client-server protocol for the provisioning and management of objects stored in a shared central repository

rejected.why: EPP is specified in XML and XML Schema, but XML is the encoding substrate, not the subject.
Appendix B registers application/epp+xml, but it is a minor part of the document.
Domain registration is the motivating use case, but EPP is the more specific tag and the document defines no domain object mapping.
Section 2.1 lists requirements for transport mappings, but the document defines none.
The EPP login is only said to be similar to SASL PLAIN, so it is not about SASL.
DNS appears only as an example of repository objects and in the label type, not as a subject.

RFC5731.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Domain Name Mapping
RFC5731.summary: Specifies the EPP mapping for provisioning and managing domain name objects in a shared registry repository, defining XML commands (check, info, transfer, create, delete, renew, update), attributes, statuses and schema; obsoletes RFC 4931.

EPP.why: The document is the EPP domain object mapping, defining command syntax and semantics, status values and the XML schema for domain objects.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for the provisioning and management of Internet domain names stored in a shared central repository.

rejected.why: Domain names and delegation data (name servers, glue) are the objects being provisioned, but the document specifies registry provisioning, not DNS protocol or resolver behaviour.
The mapping is written in XML Schema, but XML is only the encoding substrate and the document is not about XML usage itself.
Parent of EPP; EPP is the more specific tag and already covers it.
Internationalized domain names are mentioned only briefly regarding name syntax conformance, not addressed in their own right.

RFC5732.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Host Mapping
RFC5732.summary: Defines the EPP mapping for host objects (name servers) in a shared registry repository, specifying commands, attributes, status values and the XML schema; obsoletes RFC 4932.

EPP.why: The whole document specifies the EPP host object mapping: check, info, create, delete, update commands, status values and the XML schema.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Internet host name mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP).

rejected.why: Hosts are provisioned as name servers and glue records are mentioned, but the document specifies registry provisioning, not DNS protocol behaviour.
Host name syntax is only referenced to RFC 952/1123; the document is about provisioning host objects, not naming conventions.
XML and XML Schema are only the specification notation and encoding for the mapping.
Implied as the parent of EPP; no need to list ancestors.
Only a brief reference to RFC 3490 in syntax conformance, not a subject of the document.
IPv6 address syntax is merely referenced for host address attributes.

RFC5733.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Contact Mapping
RFC5733.summary: Defines the XML mapping of EPP commands (check, info, transfer, create, delete, update) and attributes for provisioning contact objects in a shared registry repository, obsoleting RFC 4933.

EPP.why: The document is the EPP contact object mapping (STD 69 companion), specifying command syntax and semantics for contacts.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for the provisioning and management of individual or organizational social information identifiers

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the notation used to specify the mapping; the document is not about XML usage itself.
Contacts are associated with domain objects, but the parent is implied by EPP and the document only defines contact objects.
Disclosure elements relate to data exposure policy but the document does not specify WHOIS or directory services.
UTF-8 is mentioned for name and address encoding but is not the subject.
IANA section only registers XML namespace and schema URNs; boilerplate.

RFC5734.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Transport over TCP
RFC5734.summary: Specifies the mapping of an EPP session onto a single TCP connection, including session management, message framing with a 32-bit length header, and a mandatory TLS usage profile.

EPP.why: The document is a transport mapping for EPP, defining session management, message exchange and data unit framing for EPP over TCP. Readers of the EPP subject need it.
EPP.quote: This document describes how an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) session is mapped onto a single Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection.

transport mapping.why: It is a classic X-over-TCP/TLS binding, addressing the transport considerations of the core protocol. The EPP tag is a technology under domain registration, not under transport mapping, so the topic tag is also appropriate.
transport mapping.quote: This document describes how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) is mapped onto a single client-server TCP connection.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate; the document defines nothing new about TCP itself.

TLS is the required security mechanism, but the usage profile is for EPP and defines no new TLS extension or behaviour beyond identity checking and cipher suite requirements. Considered as secondary but it only profiles use as a substrate.
Certificate identity checking rules appear in the TLS profile but are a supporting detail, not the subject.
EPP messages are XML instances but the document only frames them with a length header.

RFC5735.title: Special Use IPv4 Addresses
RFC5735.summary: RFC 5735 (BCP 153) catalogs the global and special-use IPv4 address blocks assigned by IANA (private, loopback, link-local, documentation, benchmarking, 6to4 relay anycast, multicast, reserved), obsoleting RFC 3330.

IPv4.why: The document is a catalog of special-use IPv4 address blocks and their present use, which is the IPv4 address lifecycle.
IPv4.quote: It describes the global and other specialized IPv4 address blocks that have been assigned by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

addressing.why: It covers IP address architecture and allocation, including private-use, link-local, documentation and multicast blocks. IPv4 is the more specific tag for the primary subject, so addressing is kept secondary.
addressing.quote: This block is set aside for use in private networks.
addressing.section: 3. Global and Other Specialized Address Blocks

rejected.why: IANA's role in assigning these blocks is background. The document is about the address blocks, not IANA registry guidance; the IANA Considerations section is boilerplate.
The 192.88.99.0/24 6to4 relay anycast block is only one entry in the table, so the document is not about 6to4.
224.0.0.0/4 is listed as one line in the table. The document does not address multicast routing or deployment.
Private address blocks are listed, but the document does not address NAT behaviour.

RFC5736.title: IANA IPv4 Special Purpose Address Registry
RFC5736.summary: Directs IANA to create and maintain the IANA IPv4 Special Purpose Address Registry, which records IETF protocol designations from 192.0.0.0/24 and the fields kept for each entry.

IANA.why: The document is a direction to IANA on creating and managing a registry, including its policy (IETF Review) and recorded fields. That is IANA registry guidance in its own right.
IANA.quote: This document directs IANA to open an IPv4 Special Purpose Address Registry for the management of these IANA-designated address blocks.
IANA.section: 2. IANA IPv4 Special Purpose Address Block

IPv4.why: The registry covers IPv4 special-purpose address blocks and how they are designated. Readers of IPv4 address lifecycle material would want it.
IPv4.quote: The registry will be used for recording IETF protocol assignments from 192.0.0.0/24 and any other address prefixes allocated to the registry in the future

rejected.why: The IPv4 tag is more specific for IPv4 address designation, and the document is a registry direction rather than a treatment of address architecture.
The Security Considerations mention address validation and trust points, but that is boilerplate and not what the document is about.
The IETF Review requirement is a registry policy and not a description of IETF process.

RFC5737.title: IPv4 Address Blocks Reserved for Documentation
RFC5737.summary: RFC 5737 reserves three IPv4 blocks (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24) for use in documentation and examples, and gives operational guidance on filtering them.

IPv4.why: The document specifies special-use IPv4 address blocks and their allocation. This falls under IPv4 and its address lifecycle.
IPv4.quote: Three IPv4 unicast address blocks are reserved for use in examples in specifications and other documents.

addressing.why: It covers address allocation and reservation and says how the blocks should be treated in filters and routing. It also discusses the status of 128.66.0.0/16. IPv4 is the more specific tag, but readers of the addressing subject would want this RFC for its reserved-block guidance.
addressing.quote: Addresses within the TEST-NET-1, TEST-NET-2, and TEST-NET-3 blocks SHOULD NOT appear on the public Internet

rejected.why: RFC 3849's IPv6 documentation prefix is only mentioned as related work. This document does not define or discuss it.
RFC 2606 example domain names are only cited as a parallel documentation resource. This document deals with address blocks, not domain names.
IANA recording the allocation is a boilerplate IANA Considerations matter. The document is not about IANA registry guidance.
The blocks are written in CIDR prefix notation, but the document is not about CIDR or aggregation.

RFC5738.title: IMAP Support for UTF-8
RFC5738.summary: Experimental IMAP4rev1 extension defining UTF8=ACCEPT/USER/APPEND/ALL/ONLY capabilities, UTF-8 quoted strings, a UTF8 SELECT/EXAMINE parameter, LIST extensions, and server up-conversion rules to support internationalized email headers, mailbox names and credentials.

IMAP.why: The document extends and updates IMAP4rev1 with new capabilities, SELECT parameter, LIST options and APPEND data extensions.
IMAP.quote: This specification extends IMAP4rev1 [RFC3501] to permit UTF-8 [RFC3629] in headers

EAI.why: It is the IMAP part of the Email Address Internationalization work, produced by the EAI working group, covering UTF-8 headers, addresses and up-conversion.
EAI.quote: permit UTF-8 [RFC3629] in headers as described in "Internationalized Email Headers" [RFC5335]

rejected.why: UTF-8 is the encoding the extension carries, but the document is about IMAP/EAI support, not the UTF-8 encoding itself.
SASLprep is only referenced for preparing user names and passwords in UTF8=USER; the document does not specify SASL.
IDNA is mentioned only as an encoding to up-convert in address domains; it is not the subject.
MIME header encodings are handled in up-conversion requirements, but MIME itself is not specified or extended.
The Internet message format is relied on for header fields but not extended here.

RFC5739.title: IPv6 Configuration in Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC5739.summary: Experimental RFC defining new IKEv2 configuration attributes (INTERNAL_IP6_LINK, INTERNAL_IP6_PREFIX) and a LINK_ID notification so a VPN gateway can assign IPv6 prefixes and link-local addresses to remote-access clients over a virtual link.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new configuration payload attributes and a notify payload, including reauthentication and CREATE_CHILD_SA handling.
IKE.quote: This document specifies new configuration attributes for IKEv2 that allows the VPN gateway to assign IPv6 prefixes to clients

IPv6.why: A substantial part concerns IPv6 prefix assignment, link-local addresses, interface IDs, CGAs, DAD and the relationship to Neighbor Discovery on the virtual link.
IPv6.quote: enabling all features of IPv6 to be used with the client-gateway "virtual link"

rejected.why: IKEv2 is the specific subject; IPsec SPD/SAs are only the context, so the more specific IKE tag fits.
Only recommended for fetching extra configuration such as DNS servers; it is not specified or extended here.
Section 4.4 only explains which ND mechanisms are unnecessary on the virtual link; it does not specify ND.
Discussed as a design alternative and goal for sharing access, but the document does not define SLAAC behaviour.
This is remote-access VPN via IKEv2, not provider-provisioned VPNs.
IANA section only registers the new attributes; boilerplate.

RFC5740.title: NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) Transport Protocol
RFC5740.summary: RFC 5740 specifies the NORM protocol, a NACK-based reliable multicast transport with FEC repair, TFMCC-based congestion control, and an IPsec baseline for security. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 3940.

NORM.why: The document is the NORM protocol specification itself, covering message formats and procedures.
NORM.quote: This document describes the messages and procedures of the Negative-ACKnowledgment (NACK) Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) protocol.

FEC.why: FEC parity repair and FTI/FEC payload ID handling are central to NORM's repair strategy, and readers of FEC would want this document.
FEC.quote: NORM provides for the use of packet-level forward error correction (FEC) techniques for efficient multicast repair and OPTIONAL proactive transmission robustness

congestion control.why: The document fully specifies the NORM-CC congestion control scheme, adapted from TFMCC, in Section 5.5.2.
congestion control.quote: A congestion control scheme is specified to allow the NORM protocol to fairly share available network bandwidth with other transport protocols

rejected.why: NORM is already tagged under the reliable multicast branch, and the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
Section 7.1 gives a baseline IPsec profile, but it is a security-considerations mechanism and not the subject of the document.
UDP is only the encapsulation substrate for NORM messages.
NORM-CC is based on TFMCC, which is a multicast congestion control scheme, and TFRC is not specified here.
GDOI is only cited as a recommended key management option.
SSM is only one of the topologies NORM supports, and the document does not specify it.

RFC5741.title: RFC Streams, Headers, and Boilerplates
RFC5741.summary: IAB-stream RFC defining the fixed structural elements of RFCs (title page header, Status of This Memo boilerplate per stream, copyright/ISSN elements) so the source stream and review status of each RFC are clearly communicated.

RFC series.why: The document specifies the format and structure of RFCs and the RFC streams, which is exactly the RFC Series format/style subject.
RFC series.quote: RFC documents contain a number of fixed elements such as the title page header, standard boilerplates, and copyright/IPR statements.

rejected.why: Copyright and IPR statements are mentioned only as one structural element whose content is defined by BCP 78/79; the document is not about IPR.
Section 2 explains streams versus Internet Standards, but only as context for labelling; the document is about RFC format, not IETF process.
xml2rfc is only mentioned in the acknowledgements as the production tool.

RFC5742.title: IESG Procedures for Handling of Independent and IRTF Stream Submissions
RFC5742.summary: BCP 92 describes how the IESG reviews Independent Submission and IRTF stream documents for conflicts with IETF work, including IESG notes and a dispute resolution process, obsoleting RFC 3932.

RFC series.why: The document is about publication procedures for non-IETF RFC streams (Independent and IRTF), the roles of RFC Editor, IESG, IRSG and IAB, and IESG notes on RFCs.
RFC series.quote: This document describes the procedures used by the IESG for handling documents submitted for RFC publication from the Independent Submission and IRTF streams.

IETF process.why: It is a BCP updating RFC 2026 and RFC 3710 on IESG review procedure, conflict checking against IETF standards process, and dispute resolution via the IAB.
IETF process.quote: the IESG taking responsibility only for checking for conflicts between the work of the IETF and the documents submitted.

rejected.why: IANA registration procedures are mentioned only in passing as a type of conflict, not a subject of the document.
Copyright and legal boilerplate appears only in standard boilerplate, not in the main body.
IKE and Photuris appear only as an example of a rejected alternative bypass.

RFC5743.title: Definition of an Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) Document Stream
RFC5743.summary: Defines the IRTF document stream: how IRTF research group documents are reviewed by the RG, IRSG and IESG and published as RFCs, plus the rights and IPR rules for that stream.

RFC series.why: The document defines a publication stream of the RFC series, including approval steps and RFC Editor handling.
RFC series.quote: This memo defines the steps required to publish a document in the IRTF RFC stream.

IETF process.why: Describes the IRSG and IESG review process and administration for non-IETF stream documents, a procedural subject within the IETF process area.
IETF process.quote: The IRTF Chair will then extend the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) an opportunity to review the document

IPR.why: Substantial sections cover copyright, derivative-works rights, IETF Trust procedures, and patent disclosure rules for the IRTF stream.
IPR.quote: Rules for Submission and Use of Material
IPR.section: 3. Rules for Submission and Use of Material

rejected.why: Not related; the document has no IANA content.
No NomCom procedures are described.

gaps.name: IRTF (Internet Research Task Force) and document streams
gaps.why: The document is about the IRTF stream and the IRSG review process. The taxonomy has no tag for the IRTF or for RFC streams other than the broad RFC series and IETF process tags.

RFC5744.title: Procedures for Rights Handling in the RFC Independent Submission Stream
RFC5744.summary: RFC 5744 specifies how authors of Independent Submission stream RFCs grant incoming rights, what outgoing rights (unlimited or no derivative works) readers receive, requests the IETF Trust manage them, and sets patent/trademark disclosure rules.

IPR.why: The whole document defines copyright incoming/outgoing rights and patent/trademark disclosure for Independent Submission RFCs, which is the IPR topic.
IPR.quote: This document defines the copyright procedures for RFC Independent Submission documents.

RFC series.why: It concerns publication policy for the Independent Submission stream of the RFC Series and the role of the Independent Submission Editor.
RFC series.quote: The concept of RFC streams in general, and the Independent Submission stream in particular, are described in Section 5 of [RFC4844]

rejected.why: It touches Internet-Draft submission, but the Independent stream is outside the IETF process, and the document's focus is rights, not IETF procedures.

RFC5745.title: Procedures for Rights Handling in the RFC IAB Stream
RFC5745.summary: RFC 5745 specifies how IAB-stream RFC authors grant incoming copyright rights and how the IETF Trust should manage outgoing rights (unlimited or no derivative works) for readers, plus patent/trademark disclosure rules for the IAB stream.

IPR.why: The whole document is about incoming and outgoing copyright rights, the IETF Trust's management of them, and patent/trademark disclosure for IAB stream documents.
IPR.quote: This document defines the copyright procedures for RFC IAB stream documents.

RFC series.why: It sets publication rules for a specific RFC stream (IAB stream), parallel to the Independent Submission stream rules, so readers of RFC series and stream topics would want it.
RFC series.quote: The goal of the IAB stream of RFCs is to publish information from the IAB to the Internet community.

rejected.why: The document touches Internet-Draft submission and BCP 9/BCP 79 compliance, but its subject is rights handling, which IPR covers more specifically.

RFC5746.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Renegotiation Indication Extension
RFC5746.summary: Defines the TLS renegotiation_info extension and an SCSV that cryptographically bind renegotiation handshakes to the enclosing connection, preventing the renegotiation splicing attack, with backward-compatibility rules (also applying to DTLS).

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension (renegotiation_info) and a signalling cipher suite value, updating TLS 1.0-1.2, and defines client and server handshake behaviour.
TLS.quote: This specification defines a TLS extension to cryptographically tie renegotiations to the TLS connections they are being performed over, thus preventing this attack.

rejected.why: The extension applies equally to DTLS, but this is only a brief note in Section 3.2. The document is about TLS renegotiation.
HTTPS and cookies appear only as examples of vulnerable applications.
Cookies are mentioned once as an attack illustration, not as a subject.
SMTP and IMAP are mentioned only as examples of protocols affected by the attack.
The document is about the TLS protocol, not web platform security mechanisms.
The parent is implied by the TLS tag, and the document is not about general security guidance.

RFC5747.title: 4over6 Transit Solution Using IP Encapsulation and MP-BGP Extensions
RFC5747.summary: Experimental RFC describing 4over6, which uses a new MP-BGP SAFI (67) to automatically discover endpoints and build IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels between dual-stack PE routers across an IPv6-only backbone, with deployment experience on CNGI-CERNET2.

BGP.why: The document defines a new BGP SAFI (4over6, 67) and the procedures by which PE routers advertise and process the routes, so it extends BGP.
BGP.quote: experimental extensions to Multiprotocol Extension for BGP (MP-BGP) [RFC4271] [RFC4760] employed to communicate tunnel endpoint information

IPv6 transition.why: It is a transition mechanism for IPv4 islands to communicate across an IPv6-only backbone, and it is compared with the softwire mesh effort.
IPv6 transition.quote: Some IPv6 backbones will need to offer transit services to attached IPv4 access networks.

softwire.why: The mechanism does mesh IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnelling with BGP-signalled endpoints, and a section compares it with the Softwire Mesh solutions.
softwire.quote: The 4over6 solution can be viewed as a precursor to the Softwire Mesh Framework proposed in the softwire problem statement [RFC4925].

rejected.why: The data plane uses the RFC 2473 encapsulation as is. The document's novelty is the control plane.
Tunnelling is the data plane, but softwire is the more specific tag covering automatic mesh IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnels.
GRE is mentioned only as a possible alternative encapsulation.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an option to protect the iBGP session.
Route reflectors are mentioned only in passing for iBGP peering.

RFC5748.title: IANA Registry Update for Support of the SEED Cipher Algorithm in Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY)
RFC5748.summary: Informational RFC that adds SEED cipher code points (SEED-CTR, SEED-CCM, SEED-GCM) to the IANA MIKEY payload sub-registries for SRTP/SRTCP encryption algorithms and PRF.

MIKEY.why: The document's sole purpose is to add new code points to MIKEY payload tables (Tables 6.10.1.b and 6.10.1.d of RFC 3830) so MIKEY can negotiate SEED for SRTP.
MIKEY.quote: This document updates IANA registries to support the SEED block cipher algorithm for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) and the secure Real-time Transport Control Protocol (SRTCP) in Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY).

rejected.why: SRTP is the protocol whose keys MIKEY sets up. The document defines nothing about SRTP itself. The SEED-in-SRTP specification is RFC 5669.
The registry updates are the mechanism, but the document is about MIKEY algorithm identifiers, not IANA registry guidance or stewardship.
SEED is mentioned, but the cipher is defined in RFC 4269 and its SRTP use in RFC 5669. This document only assigns code points, and no SEED technology tag exists.

gaps.name: SEED cipher
gaps.why: The document's subject is the Korean SEED block cipher, but the taxonomy has no SEED tag. It has tags for AES, ARIA, Camellia and others.

RFC5749.title: Distribution of EAP-Based Keys for Handover and Re-Authentication
RFC5749.summary: Defines an abstract key distribution exchange (KDE) template, run over AAA protocols, for delivering EMSK-derived root keys (USRK, DSRK, DSUSRK) from an EAP/AAA server to servers needing them for handover and ERP re-authentication, with security requirements.

HOKEY.why: The RFC is a HOKEY working group product specifying root key distribution for handover keying and ERP re-authentication, including a section on KDE use in ERP.
HOKEY.quote: This document defines a template for a key distribution exchange (KDE) protocol that can distribute these different types of root keys using a AAA

AAA.why: The KDE is carried in AAA messages and the document sets security requirements for AAA key transport (integrity, replay protection, key wrap, proxy hop-by-hop concerns), so AAA readers would want it.
AAA.quote: The Key Distribution Exchange (KDE) mechanism defined in this document runs over a AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) protocol
