rejected.why: The HOKEY tag sits under EAP and is more specific; EAP is the keying source here, not itself extended.
Only named as a possible instantiation; no RADIUS attributes or messages are defined.
Only named as a possible instantiation; the template defines no Diameter AVPs.
The document is about key distribution, but the HOKEY tag covers this more specifically, so the broader topic is not added.

RFC5750.title: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Version 3.2 Certificate Handling
RFC5750.summary: RFC 5750 specifies how S/MIME v3.2 agents must handle X.509 certificates and CRLs: certificate choices, email address matching, path validation, signing algorithm and key size requirements, and PKIX extension handling.

S/MIME.why: The whole document defines certificate handling requirements for S/MIME agents, so S/MIME readers would expect it.
S/MIME.quote: This document specifies conventions for X.509 certificate usage by Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) v3.2 agents.

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificate and CRL processing: key usage, basic constraints, subjectAltName, extended key usage, signing algorithms and key sizes.
X.509.quote: S/MIME agents MUST use PKIX certificates to validate public keys as described in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKIX) Certificate and CRL Profile [KEYM].

rejected.why: CMS supplies the data types and message format. This document only sets certificate-related options and does not specify CMS.
The document concerns certificates used with mail. It matches certificate addresses to From/Sender headers, but the subject is not mail transport or formats.
X.509 is the more specific child tag and fits better. It covers certificate and path validation, so PKI is implied.
RSA and DSA signature algorithms are listed as requirements for certificate signing, but the document is not about those algorithms.
MIME is the substrate for S/MIME. The document says nothing new about MIME body structure.
X.500 is only mentioned as one example of a certificate retrieval mechanism.

RFC5751.title: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Version 3.2 Message Specification
RFC5751.summary: RFC 5751 specifies S/MIME version 3.2 message handling: how to create signed, enveloped and compressed MIME entities using CMS, the application/pkcs7-mime and application/pkcs7-signature media types, and mandatory algorithms.

S/MIME.why: The whole document is the S/MIME v3.2 message specification: message creation, signing, enveloping, compression and algorithm requirements.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data.

CMS.why: Section 2 profiles CMS options (SignedData, EnvelopedData, CompressedData, signed attributes, algorithms) for S/MIME, and an appendix defines S/MIME CMS attributes in ASN.1.
CMS.quote: This specification defines how to create a MIME body part that has been cryptographically enhanced according to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

media types.why: Defines the application/pkcs7-mime media type with smime-type parameter and file extensions, and updates the registrations of application/pkcs7-mime and application/pkcs7-signature.
media types.quote: The application/pkcs7-mime media type is used to carry CMS content types including EnvelopedData, SignedData, and CompressedData.

rejected.why: MIME is the structure being secured; the document defines S/MIME wrapping rather than MIME itself, so S/MIME and media types are more specific.
S/MIME is usable with any MIME transport (HTTP, SIP), and the document is about message-level security, not mail architecture.
SMTP is mentioned only as a 7-bit transport constraint motivating transfer encoding.
AES is only a mandatory content-encryption algorithm choice, with details left to the CMS AES RFC.
RSA appears as a required algorithm and key-size policy, not as the subject of the document.
The ASN.1 module is an appendix defining attribute syntax, not the subject of the document.

RFC5752.title: Multiple Signatures in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC5752.summary: Defines the CMS multiple-signatures signed attribute, with generation and verification rules, that lets a signer's parallel SignerInfo objects point to each other so removal of a strong-algorithm signature (a downgrade attack) is detectable.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS SignedData/SignerInfo with a new signed attribute and defines generation, verification and evaluation procedures for it.
CMS.quote: This document defines the multiple-signatures attribute, its generation rules, and its processing rules to allow signers to convey multiple SignerInfo objects while protecting against downgrade attacks.

rejected.why: Only referenced for its use of CMS signatures and as an application example (S/MIME message and certificate specs); the document defines a CMS attribute, not S/MIME behaviour.
ASN.1 module is just the formal definition of the attribute, not the subject of the document.
Certificate evaluation is deferred to RFC 5280 and only mentioned in signature evaluation; not the subject.
SHA appears only in the example; the document is algorithm-agnostic regarding hashes.
Concerns the downgrade-attack protection in CMS signature structure and algorithm migration, which is covered by the CMS tag; it does not specify any algorithm.

RFC5753.title: Use of Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Algorithms in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC5753.summary: Profiles the use of ECC algorithms (ECDSA signatures, ECDH and ECMQV key agreement) in CMS SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData, with S/MIME capabilities, ASN.1 modules and algorithm recommendations; obsoletes RFC 3278.

CMS.why: The document specifies how ECC algorithms are used within CMS content types (SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData, AuthEnvelopedData), so CMS readers would look for it.
CMS.quote: This specification defines a profile for the use of Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) public key algorithms in the CMS.

ECDSA.why: ECDSA signature use, identifiers, encoding (ECDSA-Sig-Value) and curve/hash recommendations are a core part of the document.
ECDSA.quote: This section describes how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) with SignedData.

S/MIME.why: A substantial section defines S/MIME capabilities encodings for the ECC algorithms; the work came from the S/MIME WG.
S/MIME.quote: A sending agent MAY announce to receiving agents that it supports one or more of the ECC algorithms specified in this document by using the SMIMECapabilities

rejected.why: The more specific child ECDSA is tagged; ECDH/ECMQV key agreement has no dedicated child tag, and the parent is implied by ECDSA.
Certificates are only referenced to RFC 5480/5280 in a one-paragraph section; nothing new is defined.
ASN.1 modules are the notation for the profile, not the subject of the document.
AES is used for key wrap and content encryption, but is a relied-on algorithm defined elsewhere.
SHA family is used as the digest and KDF hash, defined elsewhere.
HMAC is used for AuthenticatedData MACs but is only referenced, not specified here.

gaps.name: ECDH / ECMQV key agreement
gaps.why: The document specifies ephemeral-static ECDH and 1-Pass ECMQV key agreement with SEC1 KDF, but the taxonomy has no key agreement tag beneath cryptography or elliptic curve.

RFC5754.title: Using SHA2 Algorithms with Cryptographic Message Syntax
RFC5754.summary: RFC 5754 specifies conventions for using SHA-224/256/384/512 message digests, and their combination with DSA, RSA and ECDSA signatures, in CMS, with algorithm identifiers and SMIMECapabilities values.

CMS.why: The document defines how SHA2 digests and signature algorithms are identified and used in CMS structures (SignedData, DigestedData, etc.), updating RFC 3370 CMS algorithms.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the algorithm identifiers and specifies parameters for the message digest algorithms SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 for use with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

SHA.why: The core subject is the SHA-2 family (SHA-224/256/384/512), their identifiers and parameter encoding conventions.
SHA.quote: The SHA-256 message digest algorithm is defined in [SHS].  The algorithm identifier for SHA-256 is:

ECDSA.why: A section specifies ECDSA with each SHA2 digest, including OIDs and absent-parameter rules.
ECDSA.quote: The algorithm identifier for ECDSA with SHA-224 signature values is:

RSA.why: A section specifies RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signature OIDs with SHA2 and the NULL-parameter requirement.
RSA.quote: RSA (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5) [RFC3447] MAY be used with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512.

S/MIME.why: The document supplies SMIMECapabilities attribute DER encodings for each algorithm, which S/MIME implementers need.
S/MIME.quote: This document also specifies the SMIMECapabilities attribute values [RFC5751] for each algorithm.

rejected.why: HMAC with SHA2 is only noted as covered by RFC 4231, not specified here.
OIDs are borrowed from X.509-related RFCs, but the document does not profile certificates.
ASN.1 syntax appears only for AlgorithmIdentifier and OIDs; no module is defined.

RFC5755.title: An Internet Attribute Certificate Profile for Authorization
RFC5755.summary: Profiles X.509 Attribute Certificates for Internet authorization, defining fields, extensions (targeting, audit identity, proxying, AA controls), attribute types, validation and revocation rules; obsoletes RFC 3281.

X.509.why: The document is a profile of X.509 attribute certificates, defining their fields, extensions and validation, so it belongs on the X.509 certificates page.
X.509.quote: This specification defines a profile for the use of X.509 Attribute Certificates in Internet Protocols.

authorization.why: ACs exist to convey authorization information (roles, groups, clearance) for access control decisions, which makes this a substantial part of the document.
authorization.quote: An AC may contain attributes that specify group membership, role, security clearance, or other authorization information associated with the AC holder.

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific tag and already covers this; the PKC profile is only referenced.
OCSP is only referenced as one revocation pointer mechanism; the document does not specify or extend it.
CMS EnvelopedData is used only as a substrate for the optional attribute encryption feature.
ASN.1 is the notation used to define the structures and the module in the appendix; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The clearance attribute is defined, but it is one attribute type and the document is not about security labelling frameworks.

RFC5756.title: Updates for RSAES-OAEP and RSASSA-PSS Algorithm Parameters
RFC5756.summary: RFC 5756 updates RFC 4055 to change how RSAES-OAEP and RSASSA-PSS algorithm parameters are used in X.509 certificate subjectPublicKeyInfo and signature fields, prohibiting RSAES-OAEP parameters in subjectPublicKeyInfo.

RSA.why: The document specifies conventions for RSAES-OAEP and RSASSA-PSS algorithm identifiers and parameters, which are RSA encryption and signature schemes.
RSA.quote: The parameters MUST be absent when used in the subjectPublicKeyInfo field.

X.509.why: It profiles how algorithm parameters appear in X.509 certificates and CRLs (subjectPublicKeyInfo, signatureAlgorithm fields) for the Internet PKI.
X.509.quote: When the id-RSASSA-PSS object identifier appears in the TBSCertificate or TBSCertList signature algorithm field, then the RSASSA-PSS-params structure MUST be included
X.509.section: 2. Changes to Section 3 (Second and Third Paragraphs)

rejected.why: Mentioned only in the Security Considerations as an example of negotiating parameters; the document is not about S/MIME.
Parent of X.509, which is already chosen and implies it.
The parameters are ASN.1 structures, but the document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC5757.title: Multicast Mobility in Mobile IP Version 6 (MIPv6): Problem Statement and Brief Survey
RFC5757.summary: IRTF MobOpts problem statement and survey of multicast mobility in Mobile IPv6, covering listener and source mobility (ASM/SSM), multicast routing and link-layer aspects, and existing solution approaches.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document is a problem statement and survey of multicast support for mobile nodes under MIPv6, including FMIPv6, HMIPv6 and PMIPv6 interplay.
Mobile IPv6.quote: MIPv6 [5] only roughly defines multicast mobility for Mobile Nodes (MNs) using a remote subscription approach or through bidirectional tunneling via the Home Agent (HA).

multicast.why: The document addresses multicast routing trees, ASM/SSM, listener and source mobility, and deployment issues of IP multicast.
multicast.quote: Multicast mobility is a generic term, which subsumes a collection of distinct functions.

SSM.why: A dedicated section and solution subsection address mobile SSM sources, a central problem of the document.
SSM.quote: Source-Specific Multicast has been designed for multicast senders with static source addresses.

MLD.why: MLD behaviour and proposed extensions (Listener Hold, early Done) for mobile listeners are discussed substantially.
MLD.quote: The default timer values and Robustness Variable specified in MLD [17] were not designed for the mobility context.

rejected.why: Discussed as the routing context for source mobility, but the document is not about specifying or extending PIM-SM.
Link-layer multicast on 802.16 is surveyed in one subsection only; the document is not about IP over WiMAX.
3GPP MBMS/BCMCS is covered briefly as a link technology, not a main subject.
DVB-H multicast is surveyed briefly in a subsection; not a primary subject.
Mentioned only as a unicast mobility scheme and its multicast transparency in one paragraph.
Mentioned only in an appendix on implicit source notification.

RFC5758.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure: Additional Algorithms and Identifiers for DSA and ECDSA
RFC5758.summary: Updates RFC 3279 to define algorithm identifiers (OIDs) and encoding rules for DSA and ECDSA signatures using SHA-224/256/384/512 in X.509 certificates and CRLs, and identifies the SHA2 hash OIDs for the X.509 PKI.

X.509.why: The document profiles algorithm identifiers and encodings for signing X.509 certificates and CRLs, updating RFC 3279 in the PKIX profile family.
X.509.quote: This specification defines the contents of the signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue, and signature fields within Internet X.509 certificates and CRLs

ECDSA.why: Defines the ecdsa-with-SHA2 OIDs, parameter encoding, and CA requirements for ECDSA signatures.
ECDSA.quote: The ASN.1 OIDs used to specify that an ECDSA signature was generated using SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 are, respectively:

SHA.why: A full section identifies the four SHA-2 hash algorithm OIDs for use in the X.509 PKI and recommends their use over SHA-1.
SHA.quote: SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 produce a 224-bit, 256-bit, 384-bit, and 512-bit "hash" of the input, respectively

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to express OIDs and AlgorithmIdentifier encodings. The document does not specify ASN.1 itself or define a new module.
RSA is mentioned only in a reference to RFC 4055. The document does not address it.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already covers the PKI profile.

gaps.name: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm)
gaps.why: The document defines DSA with SHA-224/SHA-256 OIDs and requirements, but the taxonomy has no DSA tag. The closest option is the general cryptography topic.

RFC5759.title: Suite B Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
RFC5759.summary: Defines a base profile of RFC 5280 X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for NSA Suite B, requiring ECDSA with P-256/P-384 and SHA-256/384 and specifying extension requirements for CA and end entity certificates.

X.509.why: The document is a profile of RFC 5280 certificates and CRLs, specifying required fields, key usage and extension criticality for each certificate type.
X.509.quote: This document specifies a base profile for X.509 v3 Certificates and X.509 v2 Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs)

ECDSA.why: A substantial part covers ECDSA signature algorithm identifiers, curves P-256/P-384, signature value encoding and public key encoding.
ECDSA.quote: Every Suite B certificate and CRL MUST be signed using ECDSA.

rejected.why: ECDSA is the more specific tag and covers the curve and signature content.
SHA-256/384 are only named as hash choices for the signatures; they are not the subject.
Implied as the parent of X.509, so not listed separately.
DER/ASN.1 is merely the encoding used for signatures and keys, not the subject.
Covered by the more specific ECDSA tag.

gaps.name: Suite B Cryptography
gaps.why: The NSA Suite B algorithm suite is the document's context, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC5760.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extensions for Single-Source Multicast Sessions with Unicast Feedback
RFC5760.summary: RFC 5760 extends RTCP with unicast feedback to a Distribution Source for single-source multicast (SSM) sessions, defining a simple reflection model and a summary model using the new RSI packet and sub-report blocks, plus SDP attributes.

RTCP.why: The document defines a new RTCP packet type (RSI, 209), sub-report blocks, and feedback/reflection behaviour for RTCP.
RTCP.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) to use unicast feedback to a multicast sender.

SSM.why: SSM is the main deployment scenario motivating the extension; readers of SSM would want it.
SSM.quote: useful for single-source multicast sessions such as Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) communication where the traditional model of many-to-many group communication is either not available

SDP.why: Section 10 defines a new SDP attribute (rtcp-unicast) and source-filter/ssrc usage for these sessions.
SDP.quote: A new session-level attribute MUST be used to indicate the use of unicast instead of multicast feedback: "rtcp-unicast".

rejected.why: RTP data stream is explicitly unaltered; the document is about the control protocol, so RTCP (child) is the fit.
SSM is the more specific tag chosen; the document does not address multicast routing in general.
Only recommended as a security solution in Security Considerations.
Only mentioned as a recommended authentication option in security boilerplate.
Mentioned only among recommended security solutions.
Mentioned only as a preferred key distribution mechanism in security discussion.

RFC5761.title: Multiplexing RTP Data and Control Packets on a Single Port
RFC5761.summary: Specifies when and how RTP and RTCP can be multiplexed on a single UDP port, including payload type constraints and SDP "a=rtcp-mux" signalling, and updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551.

RTCP.why: The document defines how RTCP packets are multiplexed with RTP data and constrains RTCP packet type assignments. RTCP is the control half of what is multiplexed.
RTCP.quote: This memo discusses how the RTP and RTCP flows for a single media type can be run on a single port

RTP.why: It restricts RTP payload type choices (64-95 not allowed) and updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551. It is core RTP specification work.
RTP.quote: RTP payload type values used are distinct from the RTCP packet types used

SDP.why: It defines a new SDP attribute, rtcp-mux, and its offer/answer and declarative usage. This is a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: the "a=rtcp-mux" attribute (see Section 8) indicates the desire to multiplex RTP and RTCP onto a single port

rejected.why: Only one subsection explains how rtcp-mux affects ICE candidates. ICE is not the subject.
The document only says multiplexing must happen below the SRTP layer, in Security Considerations.
Header compression effects are discussed in one subsection as a caveat. The document does not specify header compression.
UDP is the substrate carrying the multiplexed port. The document defines nothing about UDP.
SSM sessions are covered in a short section on whether to multiplex. The document does not specify SSM.
NAT traversal is the motivation for the document. The ICE interaction is a minor part, and the document does not specify NAT traversal mechanisms.

RFC5762.title: RTP and the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)
RFC5762.summary: Specifies how RTP and RTCP packets are framed over DCCP connections, and defines SDP signalling (proto identifiers, dccp-service-code attribute, DCCP service codes) for such sessions.

DCCP.why: The document defines how RTP runs over DCCP, including service codes, checksum coverage, congestion control interaction and connection use, so DCCP readers would want it.
DCCP.quote: This memo specifies a mapping of RTP onto DCCP, along with associated signalling, such that real-time applications can make use of the services provided by DCCP.

RTP.why: The document specifies RTP and RTCP framing, session/connection relationships, profile compatibility and translator issues over DCCP.
RTP.quote: The following section defines how RTP and RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) packets can be framed for transport using DCCP.

SDP.why: A substantial part defines new SDP proto identifiers and an attribute for signalling RTP over DCCP, including offer/answer usage and an example.
SDP.quote: A single new SDP attribute ("dccp-service-code") is defined to signal the DCCP service code

rejected.why: RTCP is handled as part of RTP framing; the document does not extend RTCP itself, only discusses timing under congestion control and overlap with DCCP acks.
SRTP profiles are only discussed for compatibility with DCCP partial checksums, not specified or extended.
The document relies on DCCP congestion control as motivation but defines no congestion control mechanism; the DCCP tag covers it.
SIP is mentioned only as a signalling example for renegotiating session parameters.
Considered since this is a mapping of RTP onto DCCP, but the more specific DCCP and RTP tags cover the subject.

RFC5763.title: Framework for Establishing a Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) Security Context Using Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC5763.summary: Framework for using SIP/SDP certificate fingerprints, optionally protected by SIP Identity, to bind a DTLS handshake on the media path that establishes an SRTP security context (DTLS-SRTP).

SRTP.why: The document's purpose is establishing an SRTP security context via DTLS key exchange, with SRTP being the protected media transport.
SRTP.quote: This document provides guidelines on how to establish SRTP [RFC3711] security over UDP using an extension to DTLS

DTLS.why: Specifies how mutual DTLS handshakes with self-signed certificates are used on the media path, including setup roles, multiple associations, and rekeying.
DTLS.quote: The media is transported over a mutually authenticated DTLS session where both sides have certificates.

SIP.why: SIP signalling carries the fingerprints; the document covers SIP forking, early media, delayed offer, UPDATE and SIP Identity interactions with extensive message flows.
SIP.quote: This document specifies how to use the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) to establish a Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) security context

SDP.why: Defines the offer/answer requirements for the fingerprint and setup attributes in SDP.
SDP.quote: a mechanism of transporting a fingerprint attribute in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) that identifies the key that will be presented during the DTLS handshake

rejected.why: ICE interaction is discussed briefly in one subsection but is not a main subject.
A single unauthenticated STUN check is required for latching without ICE, but STUN is only a supporting mechanism.
The document's key management is DTLS-SRTP, already captured by the DTLS and SRTP tags; MIKEY is mentioned only as an alternative.
RTP is the media being protected; the SRTP tag is more specific.
Certificates are used merely as carriers for public keys, not profiled.
Only cited as a contrasting prior approach.

RFC5764.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Extension to Establish Keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC5764.summary: Defines the DTLS use_srtp extension, which negotiates SRTP protection profiles and derives SRTP/SRTCP keys from a DTLS handshake on the media path, with packet demultiplexing, rekeying and SDP proto tokens.

SRTP.why: The document is a key management method for SRTP: it defines SRTP protection profiles, key derivation into the SRTP KDF, MKI use, and how SRTP/SRTCP packets are sent over the DTLS-SRTP channel.
SRTP.quote: This document describes a Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) extension to establish keys for Secure RTP (SRTP) and Secure RTP Control Protocol (SRTCP) flows.

DTLS.why: It specifies a new DTLS extension (use_srtp), the handshake behaviour, exporter-based key derivation and rehandshake/rekey interactions. This is the kind of new TLS/DTLS extension that DTLS readers need.
DTLS.quote: In order to negotiate the use of SRTP data protection, clients include an extension of type "use_srtp" in the DTLS extended client hello.

rejected.why: The document only defines new SDP proto tokens (UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVP) in a short section. The offer/answer use is in RFC 5763, so SDP is not a main subject.
RTP and RTCP are the protected payload. The document does not extend RTP itself, so the more specific SRTP tag covers it.
The TLS exporter and PRF are used as substrate. The document's extension is specific to DTLS, which is already tagged.
The document is a key management method, but the SRTP tag is the more specific subject. The MIKEY tag does not apply.
SIP appears only as an example of the external signalling that may indicate DTLS-SRTP sessions.
STUN is mentioned only in the packet demultiplexing rule.

RFC5765.title: Security Issues and Solutions in Peer-to-Peer Systems for Realtime Communications
RFC5765.summary: IRTF P2PRG informational survey of security attacks and countermeasures in DHT-based peer-to-peer overlays, and how they apply to P2P realtime communication such as P2PSIP.

P2P.why: The whole document analyses security problems of P2P overlays (Sybil attacks, admission control, reputation, routing integrity, peer promotion), so the P2P page is where readers would look for it.
P2P.quote: This document describes some of the known issues found in common P2P networks, analyzing the relevance of such issues and the applicability of existing solutions

P2PSIP.why: Section 7 applies the analysis to P2P SIP overlays: man-in-the-middle on P2PSIP routing, SIP proxies as untrusted peers, and location binding integrity. This makes it relevant to P2PSIP readers.
P2PSIP.quote: Initiatives such as the P2PSIP working group in IETF [P2PSIP] are currently concentrating on achieving this by using a DHT

rejected.why: SIP is discussed as the signalling protocol that P2P overlays would replace or reuse, and the CONNECT method is mentioned. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
SRTP is mentioned only as an example of media encryption in one paragraph. It is not a subject of the document.
Confidentiality of communications is mentioned, but the document is not a privacy threat-model analysis.
The parent is implied by the P2P tag. The document is not a general security handbook, since its scope is P2P overlays specifically.

gaps.name: Sybil attack / DHT overlay security
gaps.why: The core subject is attacks on DHT-based overlays (Sybil, poisoning, eclipse) and their defences. The taxonomy has only the general P2P tag for this.

RFC5766.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC5766.summary: RFC 5766 specifies TURN, a STUN extension that lets a client behind a NAT allocate a relayed transport address on a server and exchange packets with multiple peers through it, designed for use with ICE.

TURN.why: The document defines the TURN protocol: allocations, permissions, channels, Send/Data, new STUN methods and attributes.
TURN.quote: This specification defines a protocol, called TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT), that allows the host to control the operation of the relay

STUN.why: TURN is defined as a STUN extension, and the document registers new STUN methods, attributes and error codes (Sections 13-15).
STUN.quote: TURN is an extension to the STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) protocol [RFC5389].  Most, though not all, TURN messages are STUN-formatted messages.

rejected.why: TURN is designed to be used within ICE, but ICE is specified in RFC 5245, not here. This document only mentions it as the main use case.
NAT behaviour is the problem context. The document does not specify or analyse NAT behaviour, so the NAT traversal tags fit better.
SIP is mentioned only as an example rendezvous protocol.
TLS is an optional client-to-server transport and is not specified here.
The RTP support (even-port allocation) is a small feature. The document is not about RTP.
The document discusses fragmentation avoidance and the DONT-FRAGMENT attribute, but this is only a minor part of it.

RFC5767.title: User-Agent-Driven Privacy Mechanism for SIP
RFC5767.summary: Informational guideline describing how a SIP User Agent can anonymize its own messages using GRUU and TURN, without relying on the RFC 3323 privacy service.

SIP.why: The document specifies UA behaviour for anonymizing SIP header fields (Contact, From, Via) and SDP addresses; it is a SIP privacy extension/guideline.
SIP.quote: This document defines a guideline for a User Agent (UA) to generate an anonymous Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) message

TURN.why: A substantial section covers using TURN relayed addresses for anonymous Via and SDP addresses, which TURN readers would want.
TURN.quote: a UA that is not provided with a functional anonymous IP address through some administrative means MUST obtain a relayed address

privacy.why: The document's central subject is concealing user-identifying information in protocol messages, a privacy mechanism.
privacy.quote: The concept of privacy in this document is the act of concealing privacy-sensitive information.

rejected.why: SDP IP addresses are anonymized, but SDP is only the carrier of the address; the document does not specify or extend SDP.
STUN is mentioned only as the server on which TURN relays run; not the subject.
SIP-Identity (RFC 4474) is discussed only in relation to the From header; STIR is a different mechanism.
TURN is used for anonymity, not for NAT traversal of media; the topic is not addressed.
Not relevant; listed only to note no unrelated addressing tag applies.

RFC5768.title: Indicating Support for Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5768.summary: Defines the "sip.ice" media feature tag and the "ice" SIP option tag so SIP user agents can advertise ICE support to registrars and require ICE for a call.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new option tag (Require header) and a media feature tag in Contact on REGISTER, for gateway routing and mandating ICE.
SIP.quote: This specification defines a media feature tag, "sip.ice", and a SIP option tag, "ice", that can be used by SIP User Agents that make use of ICE.

ICE.why: The tags signal ICE capability and define what counts as ICE support (lite or full), so readers of ICE would want it. ICE itself is not modified.
ICE.quote: The "sip.ice" media feature tag indicates support for ICE. An agent supports ICE if it is either a lite or full implementation

rejected.why: Offer/answer SDP is only the context in which ICE candidates are carried; nothing about SDP is defined.
Only mentioned as the mechanism ICE uses for connectivity checks; not addressed.
Parent of ICE, implied by the ICE tag; the document does not itself address NAT traversal.
The media feature tag registration is a SIP caller-preferences feature tag (RFC 3840), not a MIME media type.

RFC5769.title: Test Vectors for Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC5769.summary: Provides test vectors (sample STUN requests and responses with FINGERPRINT, MESSAGE-INTEGRITY and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attributes, including long-term credential authentication) for testing STUN implementations.

STUN.why: The whole document is a set of STUN message test vectors for implementers, so it belongs on the STUN page.
STUN.quote: This document provides samples of properly formatted STUN messages including these hashes, for the sake of testing implementations of the STUN protocol.

rejected.why: Sample messages follow the ICE connectivity check use case, but ICE is only the context; the document tests STUN attributes.
MESSAGE-INTEGRITY uses HMAC-SHA1, but HMAC is a mechanism within STUN, not the subject.
FINGERPRINT is a CRC32 but only appears as a STUN attribute; the document does not address CRC polynomials.
STUN is tagged directly, and this topic is its parent, so it is implied.

RFC5770.title: Basic Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Extensions for Traversal of Network Address Translators
RFC5770.summary: Experimental RFC extending the Host Identity Protocol with ICE-based NAT traversal, UDP encapsulation of HIP and ESP, and a HIP relay server with registration and new parameters.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with new parameters (NAT_TRAVERSAL_MODE, TRANSACTION_PACING, RELAY_FROM/TO), relay server registration, and notify types.
HIP.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) to facilitate Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal.

NAT.why: NAT traversal is the central goal; it covers NAT keepalives, connectivity checks, hairpin and relaying issues, so NAT readers would want it.
NAT.quote: The purpose of these extensions is to allow two HIP-enabled hosts to communicate with each other even if one or both of the communicating hosts are in a network that is behind one or more NATs.

ICE.why: The document profiles ICE for a non-SIP protocol: candidate gathering, offer/answer in the base exchange, checklists, pacing, and nomination.
ICE.quote: HIP end-hosts use techniques drawn from the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) methodology [RFC5245] to find operational paths for the HIP control protocol and for ESP encapsulated data traffic.

rejected.why: STUN Binding requests and indications are used for connectivity checks and keepalives, but only as a mechanism borrowed from ICE; STUN itself is not extended.
TURN servers are used as relays for data traffic, but the document does not specify or extend TURN.
UDP encapsulation of ESP follows RFC 3948 and the HIP ESP transport in RFC 5202; ESP is a substrate here, not the subject.
IPsec ESP SAs are established by HIP and merely carried over UDP; the document does not specify IPsec itself.
The ICE offer/answer is carried in HIP LOCATOR parameters, not SDP; SDP only appears in quoted ICE background.
UDP is the encapsulation substrate for HIP and ESP; the document does not define UDP usage guidance.

RFC5771.title: IANA Guidelines for IPv4 Multicast Address Assignments
RFC5771.summary: BCP giving IANA guidelines for assigning IPv4 multicast addresses across the multicast address blocks (Local Network Control, Internetwork Control, AD-HOC, SDP/SAP, SSM, GLOP, administratively scoped), obsoleting RFC 3171 and RFC 3138 and updating RFC 2780.

multicast.why: The document defines how the IPv4 multicast address space is divided and assigned, so readers of IP multicast addressing and deployment would want it.
multicast.quote: This document provides guidance for the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) in assigning IPv4 multicast addresses.

IANA.why: It is an IANA allocation-guidelines document: assignment policies (Expert Review, IESG Approval), application form, annual review, reclamation and renewal.
IANA.quote: IPv4 multicast addresses are assigned directly by the IANA.

SSM.why: A dedicated section covers the 232/8 Source-Specific Multicast block and its assignment rules.
SSM.quote: Because the SSM model essentially makes the entire multicast address space local to the host, no IANA assignment policy is required.

rejected.why: The document concerns multicast address assignment, not IPv4 itself or its address lifecycle in general; multicast is the more specific fit.
Addressing is the parent of subjects here, but the document is specifically about multicast address blocks, which the multicast tag covers.
SDP/SAP appears only as the user of the 224.2/16 block; the document does not specify SDP.
NTP's multicast address is cited only as an example of an Internetwork Control assignment.
MADCAP is mentioned only as an example (mdhcpdiscover) and is not the subject.
OSPF All Routers is only an example of a link-local multicast assignment.

RFC5772.title: A Set of Possible Requirements for a Future Routing Architecture
RFC5772.summary: Historic IRTF RRG document presenting two independent sets of requirements (Group A and Group B) for a future inter-domain routing and addressing architecture, covering scaling, multihoming, policy, convergence, security and more.

routing architecture.why: The whole document sets requirements for a new routing architecture, covering scalability, abstraction, separable components and the IGP/EGP split. It does not specify any one protocol.
routing architecture.quote: The new routing and addressing protocols, data structures, and algorithms need to be developed from a clear, well thought-out, and documented architecture.

multihoming.why: Multihoming is a substantial, repeated requirement in both groups' sections. It is tied to routing table growth and path selection.
multihoming.quote: The architecture must provide multi-homing for all elements of the Internet.

routing security.why: Group A has a full routing-system security section and Group B has a security requirements section (R(58)-R(64)). Both cover authentication, integrity, DoS resistance and origin authorization.
routing security.quote: The security of the Internet's routing system is paramount.

rejected.why: BGP is the incumbent system whose shortcomings motivate the requirements. The document does not specify, extend or operate it.
Group A lists it as a non-requirement. Group B gives it only a short subsection, not enough to make it a subject of the document.
Group A explicitly marks it a non-goal. Group B mentions it only in R(16) and R(29).
Group A makes no QoS requirements. Group B treats QoS only as path information to advertise, so it is not a subject of the document.
Renumbering appears as short requirements (2.1.22, R(28)). It is not a main subject.
Mobility appears as short requirements, and Mobile IP and NEMO are mentioned only in passing.

RFC5773.title: Analysis of Inter-Domain Routing Requirements and History
RFC5773.summary: Historic IRTF RRG document analysing the state of inter-domain routing (BGP, IDRP, Nimrod, PNNI) against RFC 1126 requirements and cataloguing BGP/inter-/intra-domain architecture problems, as a counterpart to RFC 5772.

routing architecture.why: The document is an architectural analysis of the domain-based routing system, its requirements, scalability and inter-/intra-domain relationship, rather than one protocol.
routing architecture.quote: This document analyzes the state of the Internet domain-based routing system, concentrating on Inter-Domain Routing (IDR)

BGP.why: Section 5 and much of section 3 analyse BGP's shortcomings (convergence, aggregation, hold-down, policy, AS number exhaustion) and its history.
BGP.quote: the main Internet inter-domain routing protocol, BGP version 4 (BGP-4), appears to have a number of problems

multihoming.why: A dedicated section examines multi-homing's impact on aggregation and routing table growth.
multihoming.quote: the increasing use of multi-homing as a robustness technique by peripheral networks requires that multiple routes have to be advertised

Nimrod.why: A section reviews the Nimrod requirements and their relevance to a future routing architecture.
Nimrod.quote: Nimrod as expressed by Noel Chiappa in his early document, "A New IP Routing and Addressing Architecture"

RPSL.why: Section 5.14.1 describes RPSL, the routing registry database and IRR toolset as tools for inter-domain routing deployment.
RPSL.quote: Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) [RFC2622] enables a network operator to describe routes, routers, and Autonomous Systems (ASs)

rejected.why: Inter-Domain Policy Routing is not discussed; IDRP (the OSI protocol) is covered but has no tag, and that is a different protocol.
MPLS and BGP-based VPNs are mentioned only briefly in a short section on BGP overloading.
IPv6 is discussed only as it affects routing (ships in the night); the document is not about IPv6.
CIDR is mentioned as a background for aggregation and table growth but is not the subject.
OSI routing history is covered in section 3.2, but the document is not about OSI network-layer protocols as such.

gaps.name: Inter-Domain Routing Protocol (IDRP, ISO 10747)
gaps.why: The OSI inter-domain routing protocol is a significant historical subject of section 3.2 but has no tag in the taxonomy.

RFC5774.title: Considerations for Civic Addresses in the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO): Guidelines and IANA Registry Definition
RFC5774.summary: BCP giving guidelines for writing per-country civic address considerations documents for PIDF-LO civic address elements, creating an IANA registry of such documents, and registering the Austrian mapping (and marking RFC 4776 examples obsolete).

geolocation.why: The document is about mapping national civic address data into PIDF-LO civic address elements, which is conveyance and formats of location information. No PIDF-LO or civic-address specific tag exists in the taxonomy, so the geolocation topic is the best fit.
geolocation.quote: This document provides a guideline for creating civic address considerations documents for individual countries

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document defines a new IANA registry with structure, template and Expert Review procedure, and registers Austrian and obsolete RFC 4776 entries.
IANA.quote: IANA has created the registry "PIDF-LO Civic Address Considerations Registry"

rejected.why: RFC 4776 is the DHCP civic address option, but this document only updates its guidance on considerations documents and does not touch DHCP.
PIDF-LO is XML-based, but XML is only the encoding and the document does not address XML usage itself.
PIDF-LO is built on PIDF, but this document only concerns the civic address elements, not the presence data format.
HELD is a location delivery protocol and is not discussed.
Emergency calling is mentioned only as a motivating use case.

gaps.name: PIDF-LO / civic address (GEOPRIV location object)
gaps.why: The document is about civic address format and mapping within PIDF-LO, but the taxonomy has no tag for PIDF-LO or civic location formats beyond the generic geolocation topic.

RFC5775.title: Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) Protocol Instantiation
RFC5775.summary: Specifies ALC, a massively scalable reliable multicast content delivery protocol built from LCT, FEC and multiple-rate congestion control building blocks over UDP/IP multicast; obsoletes the experimental RFC 3450 and defines the EXT_FTI header extension.

ALC.why: The document is the ALC protocol specification itself.
ALC.quote: This document describes the Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) protocol, a massively scalable reliable content delivery protocol.

LCT.why: A substantial part of the document defines how ALC uses LCT: TSI, TOI, CCI, Codepoint, PSI bits and the EXT_FTI header extension.
LCT.quote: ALC uses the LCT building block [RFC5651] to provide in-band session management functionality.

rejected.why: Section 5.1 gives a baseline secure mode using IPsec ESP, but IPsec is only used as a security mechanism and is not specified or extended here.
ALC relies on the FEC building block (RFC 5052) for reliability, but it only references it; the FEC scheme is not specified here.
The document requires a multiple rate congestion control building block (WEBRC, RFC 3738) but does not define one.
UDP is only the substrate over which ALC packets are carried.
SSM and ASM are discussed as deployment considerations in Section 1.3, but only briefly.
TESLA is only referenced as a packet authentication option, via RFC 5776.
ALC runs over IP multicast, but a more specific reliable multicast tag fits better. ALC is already implied under reliable multicast.

RFC5776.title: Use of Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication (TESLA) in the Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) and NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) Protocols
RFC5776.summary: Specifies how the TESLA source-authentication protocol is integrated into ALC and NORM via the EXT_AUTH header extension, covering bootstrapping, time synchronization, key chains, authentication tags, and receiver/sender operations.

TESLA.why: The whole document specifies TESLA's sender and receiver operations, key chains, message formats and bootstrapping for ALC and NORM.
TESLA.quote: This document details the Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication (TESLA) packet source authentication and packet integrity verification protocol

ALC.why: ALC is one of the two protocols the document extends, via the EXT_AUTH header extension and ALC-specific behaviours.
ALC.quote: This document explains how to integrate the TESLA source authentication and packet integrity protocol to the ALC and NORM CDP.

NORM.why: NORM is the other protocol extended, with NORM-specific direct time sync and replay analysis.
NORM.quote: With NORM, the "bootstrap information" TESLA EXT_AUTH MUST be sent in a NORM_CMD(APPLICATION) message.

rejected.why: NTP/SNTP is only one of several options for indirect time synchronization; the document does not specify or extend it.
HMAC is used as the PRF/MAC primitive, not the subject of the document.
RSA signatures (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5/PSS) are used for bootstrap signing, with details deferred to RFC 4359.
MIKEY is only mentioned as an out-of-band bootstrapping example.
FLUTE is mentioned only as an application that benefits; not specified here.
LCT's EXT_AUTH header extension is used, but the document is about TESLA in ALC/NORM, not LCT itself.

RFC5777.title: Traffic Classification and Quality of Service (QoS) Attributes for Diameter
RFC5777.summary: Defines Diameter AVPs for traffic classification (IP, TCP, ICMP, Ethernet/VLAN headers, time-of-day conditions) and actions (drop, shape, mark, permit) with QoS treatment, replacing IPFilterRule/QoSFilterRule.

Diameter.why: The document specifies new Diameter AVPs (codes 508-578) and their use in Diameter applications such as NASREQ, EAP and Credit Control.
Diameter.quote: This document defines a number of Diameter attribute-value pairs (AVPs) for traffic classification with actions for filtering and Quality of Service (QoS) treatment.

QoS.why: The AVPs express QoS authorization, profiles, semantics, shaping/marking and excess treatment, which makes QoS signalling the document's subject.
QoS.quote: The QoS-Resources AVP represents a complete rule set with each rule represented by a Filter-Rule AVP.

rejected.why: Diffserv code points and PHB marking are matched or referenced, but the document does not specify Diffserv. The PHB parameters are defined in RFC 5624.
Ethernet, VLAN and MAC attributes are only match criteria in classifiers, not a specification of IP over Ethernet.
The EAP flow appears only as an example of carrying QoS AVPs.
ICMP types and codes are only header fields to be matched.

gaps.name: Diameter
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Diameter tag outside the 'security > AAA' branch, so the `Diameter` id used above needs checking. The AAA branch does contain a Diameter tag.

RFC5778.title: Diameter Mobile IPv6: Support for Home Agent to Diameter Server Interaction
RFC5778.summary: Defines two Diameter applications (MIP6I and MIP6A), commands and AVPs for a Mobile IPv6 home agent to interact with a Diameter server for authentication, authorization, session management and accounting of mobile nodes.

Diameter.why: The document defines new Diameter applications, command codes, AVPs and result codes for the HA-to-AAA interface.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies the interaction between a Mobile IP home agent and a Diameter server.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document is about bootstrapping and AAA support for Mobile IPv6, including the Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol and home agent behaviour.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Mobile IPv6 deployments may want to bootstrap their operations dynamically based on an interaction between the home agent and the Diameter server

rejected.why: IKEv2 with EAP is the front-end protocol between the mobile node and the HA. The document only maps it onto Diameter and defines nothing new for IKE.
The Diameter EAP application (RFC 4072) is reused as is. The document adds Mobile IPv6 AVPs but does not specify EAP or its methods.
IPsec SAs are only the mechanism that protects Mobile IPv6 signalling, and the document does not specify IPsec.
This is a parent of Diameter, so the more specific Diameter tag is used instead.

RFC5779.title: Diameter Proxy Mobile IPv6: Mobile Access Gateway and Local Mobility Anchor Interaction with Diameter Server
RFC5779.summary: Defines Diameter-based AAA interactions (AVPs, session management, capability bits) between Proxy Mobile IPv6 MAG/LMA entities and a home AAA server for downloading and updating mobile node policy profiles and authorizing PBUs.

Diameter.why: The document defines new Diameter AVPs, extends MIP6-Agent-Info and MIP6-Feature-Vector, and specifies session management usage for the MAG-to-HAAA and LMA-to-HAAA interfaces.
Diameter.quote: This specification defines Diameter-based AAA interactions between the MAG and the HAAA, and between the LMA and the HAAA.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document supports Proxy Mobile IPv6 deployments by providing policy profile download, PBU authorization and address assignment delegation via AAA.
PMIPv6.quote: AAA interactions between a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) and a AAA server, and between a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) and a AAA server within a Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Domain

rejected.why: EAP is used only as an example network access authentication method carried in the Diameter EAP application; the document does not specify EAP itself.
Relies on MIPv6 Diameter AVPs from RFC 5447, but the subject is Proxy Mobile IPv6, which has its own tag.
A DHCP server address AVP is defined, but DHCP is peripheral to the document.
Parent of Diameter; the more specific Diameter tag applies.

review: Diameter: quote not found in the text

notes: Diameter: quote not found in the text

RFC5780.title: NAT Behavior Discovery Using Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC5780.summary: Experimental STUN usage defining new attributes (CHANGE-REQUEST, RESPONSE-PORT, PADDING, RESPONSE-ORIGIN, OTHER-ADDRESS) and test procedures for discovering NAT mapping, filtering, binding lifetime, hairpinning, fragment handling and generic ALGs.

STUN.why: The document defines a new STUN usage with new attributes and client/server behavior for Binding Requests and Responses.
STUN.quote: This specification defines the NAT Behavior Discovery STUN usage, which allows a STUN client to probe the current behavior of the NAT/firewall (NAT/FW) devices

NAT.why: A large part of the document is about discovering and diagnosing NAT behavior (mapping, filtering, binding lifetime, hairpinning, ALGs), which NAT readers would want.
NAT.quote: A client behind a NAT wishes to determine if that NAT is currently using Endpoint-Independent, Address-Dependent, or Address and Port-Dependent Mapping

rejected.why: ICE is only referenced as a complementary technique and a comparison; the document does not specify or extend it.
SRV records are used only for server discovery (stun-behavior service names), which is a substrate use.
The P2P overlay is an example use case in the Introduction, not the subject of the document.
UDP is the transport for most tests, not the subject of the document.
TURN is mentioned only in a comparison with ICE and RFC 3489 relay fallbacks.
The document discovers NAT behavior rather than specifying a traversal mechanism, and the STUN/NAT tags cover the subject.

gaps.name: STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no STUN tag. The document specifies a STUN usage, and the NAT traversal topic has ICE, STUN and TURN children, so I intended STUN as the primary tag. A STUN tag with that id appears in the taxonomy only under NAT traversal, so I cannot tell whether the id above is valid as written. If it is not, the nearest available fit is NAT traversal, and STUN readers will not find this RFC there.

RFC5781.title: The rsync URI Scheme
RFC5781.summary: Registers the provisional "rsync" URI scheme (rsync://[user@]host[:port]/Source, default port 873) for the rsync protocol over TCP.

URI.why: The whole document is a URI scheme registration template defining syntax, semantics and default port for rsync URIs.
URI.quote: This document specifies the rsync Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme.

rejected.why: rsync is a file transfer utility but not FTP; the document does not concern FTP.
ABNF is only used to write the short syntax rule; the document is not about ABNF.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level; the document is about the URI scheme itself, not registry guidance.
TCP is merely the transport the rsync protocol uses; nothing new is defined about it.

gaps.name: rsync protocol / file synchronization
gaps.why: The document is about a URI for rsync, but the taxonomy has no tag for rsync or file synchronization tools.

RFC5782.title: DNS Blacklists and Whitelists
RFC5782.summary: RFC 5782 documents the structure, query protocol, test entries, caching and typical usage of DNS-based blacklists and whitelists (DNSxLs) for IP addresses and domain names, primarily for anti-spam use.

DNSBL.why: The whole document defines DNSBL/DNSWL query and response conventions: name construction, A/TXT records, sublists, test entries and usage.
DNSBL.quote: This memo documents the structure and usage of DNS-based blacklists and whitelists, and the protocol used to query them.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; DNSBL is the more specific tag and its ancestors are implied. No new DNS record types are defined.
Mail servers are the main clients, but the document does not specify SMTP; it only describes how lists are consulted on connection.
Parent of DNSBL and implied by the DNSBL tag; the document does not address spam policy or filtering beyond list queries.
IPv6 DNSxL naming is a small subsection based on ip6.arpa; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Mentioned only as another consumer of DNSBLs.

RFC5783.title: Congestion Control in the RFC Series
RFC5783.summary: An IRTF ICCRG informational survey, in annotated-bibliography form, of congestion control RFCs covering architecture, TCP, link characteristics, ECN and Quick-Start, non-TCP unicast, multicast, guidance, and historic documents.

congestion control.why: The whole document surveys congestion control RFCs across TCP, non-TCP, multicast, router-based and guidance documents; the general topic fits best.
congestion control.quote: we define congestion control as the feedback-based adjustment of the rate at which data is sent into the network.

ECN.why: A dedicated section covers the ECN RFCs (2481, 2884, 3168, 3540), their deployment and blackhole problems.
ECN.quote: There are two Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) bits in the IP header that enable an AQM mechanism

AQM.why: AQM is discussed substantively (RFC 2309, RFC 1812, RFC 1254), though it is not a separate section.
AQM.quote: This RFC recommends to test, standardize, and deploy Active Queue Management (AQM) in routers

TFRC.why: TFRC (RFC 5348), its DCCP profile (RFC 4342) and its multicast derivative TFMCC are surveyed.
TFRC.quote: specifies TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC), a rate-based congestion control mechanism for unicast flows

rejected.why: TCP congestion control is a section of the survey, but it is covered by the congestion control topic; the document does not specify or extend TCP itself.
DCCP and its CCIDs are described only as entries in the survey; the document does not specify or extend DCCP.
Multicast congestion control building blocks (ALC, WEBRC, PGM, TFMCC) are one section among many, not the document's main subject.
The introduction explicitly excludes QoS from scope.
SCTP appears only as one entry among the non-TCP protocols.

RFC5784.title: Sieve Email Filtering:  Sieves and Display Directives in XML
RFC5784.summary: Defines an XML representation of Sieve email filtering scripts, with display directives (displayblock, displaydata) and structured-comment mappings back to regular Sieve syntax, plus XML Schema, Relax NG and XSLT appendices.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies how Sieve scripts map to and from XML and how display metadata is preserved as Sieve comments.
Sieve.quote: This document describes a way to represent Sieve email filtering language scripts in XML.

XML.why: The document defines an XML vocabulary, namespace, XML Schema and Relax NG schemas, and an XSLT stylesheet, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: Sieve controls and actions are represented in XML as "control" or "action" elements, respectively.

rejected.why: Sieve is a child of email and is the more specific tag; the parent is implied.
No media type is registered; the IANA section only registers an XML namespace.
The namespace registration is boilerplate-level and not the subject of the document.
The document does not deal with the Internet message format; it only mentions headers in example filter tests.

RFC5785.title: Defining Well-Known Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC5785.summary: Defines the "/.well-known/" path prefix for site-wide metadata locations in HTTP(S) URIs and establishes an IANA registry of well-known URI suffixes.

URI.why: The document defines a URI path-prefix convention and a registry of names under it, which is a matter of URI structure and scheme usage.
URI.quote: this memo defines a path prefix in HTTP(S) URIs for these "well-known locations", "/.well-known/"

rejected.why: HTTP is only the scheme and substrate; the document defines no new HTTP semantics, though it formally updates RFC 2616.
The Robots Exclusion Protocol appears only as a motivating example of a well-known location. It is not specified here.
The topic is covered by the more specific URI tag, so it isn't also listed.
The registry is created in the IANA Considerations section, but it is boilerplate for this document's subject, which is the URI prefix itself.
PROPFIND is mentioned only as an alternative for per-resource metadata.

RFC5786.title: Advertising a Router's Local Addresses in OSPF Traffic Engineering (TE) Extensions
RFC5786.summary: Defines a new Node Attribute TLV with IPv4 and IPv6 local address sub-TLVs in OSPF TE LSAs so a router can advertise loopback and non-TE interface addresses, enabling CSPF computation of MPLS TE LSPs to them; updates RFC 3630.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF TE LSAs (updating RFC 3630) with a new Node Attribute TLV and sub-TLVs, so it belongs on the OSPF page.
OSPF.quote: this document defines an enhancement to OSPF TE extensions to advertise the local addresses of a node.

traffic engineering.why: The purpose is to let routers populate the TED and compute TE LSPs to a router's loopback and non-TE addresses, so traffic-engineering readers would want it.
traffic engineering.quote: it is desirable to set up constrained shortest path first (CSPF) computed Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineered Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs)

rejected.why: MPLS TE LSPs are the motivating use case, but the document specifies only OSPF advertisement, not MPLS.
OSPFv3 is referenced for IPv6 prefix encoding and as a related TE extension, but the document's main subject is OSPF TE LSAs (OSPFv2 TE).
BGP next-hop for VPN traffic appears only as an example motivating separate loopback addresses.
The IPv6 sub-TLV only reuses RFC 5340 prefix encoding; the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC5787.title: OSPFv2 Routing Protocols Extensions for Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) Routing
RFC5787.summary: Defines experimental OSPFv2 TE LSA extensions (new sub-TLVs, Router Information TLVs, import/export rules between protocol instances) to meet ASON routing requirements for GMPLS-controlled optical networks.

OSPF.why: The document specifies new OSPFv2 Opaque TE LSA sub-TLVs, Router Information LSA TLVs, and inter-instance dissemination and loop prevention rules.
OSPF.quote: This document defines extensions to the OSPFv2 Link State Routing Protocol to meet the requirements for routing in an ASON.

GMPLS.why: The extensions support GMPLS routing for ASON, building on GMPLS ISCD and link attributes (RFC 4202/4203), so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: The Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) protocol suite is designed to provide a control plane for a range of network technologies including optical networks

rejected.why: The OSPF TE LSA is the carrier, but the document is about ASON hierarchical routing information exchange, and GMPLS already covers the TE angle.
It discusses routing area hierarchy, but only as it relates to OSPF extensions; the OSPF and GMPLS tags are more specific.
The Node IPv6 Local Prefix sub-TLV only carries IPv6 prefixes and does not specify IPv6 itself.
The document is OSPFv2 only; RFC 5340 is cited just for IPv6 prefix encoding.
SONET/SDH is mentioned only as an example technology, and technology-specific attributes are out of scope.

gaps.name: ASON (Automatically Switched Optical Network) routing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ITU-T ASON or optical network control. GMPLS is the closest fit, so ASON readers would not find this RFC under a dedicated subject.

RFC5788.title: IMAP4 Keyword Registry
RFC5788.summary: Establishes an IANA registry for IMAP keywords, defines the Expert Review registration procedure and review guidelines, and makes the initial registrations ($MDNSent, $Forwarded, $SubmitPending, $Submitted).

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP by creating a registry of message keywords (flags) and registering initial keywords, so IMAP readers would want it.
IMAP.quote: The aim of this document is to establish a new IANA registry for IMAP keywords and to define a procedure for keyword registration

rejected.why: The IANA registry is the document's main body rather than boilerplate, but the IMAP tag fits it more specifically. The registry is for IMAP keywords and not about IANA stewardship in general.
IMAP is a child of email and is implied by it.
Not a media type registry; unrelated.

RFC5789.title: PATCH Method for HTTP
RFC5789.summary: RFC 5789 defines the HTTP PATCH method for applying partial modifications to a resource, including its semantics, error handling, and the Accept-Patch response header for advertising supported patch formats.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with a new method and a new response header (Accept-Patch), specifying semantics, caching, atomicity and error handling.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines the new HTTP/1.1 [RFC2616] method, PATCH, which is used to apply partial modifications to a resource.

rejected.why: Only cited informatively for the 422 status code; the document is not about WebDAV.
Caching of PATCH responses is addressed briefly, but is a small part of the method definition.
Patch documents are identified by media type, and Accept-Patch lists them, but no media types are registered or governed here.
Security considerations refer to authorization only generally, and that is boilerplate.

RFC5790.title: Lightweight Internet Group Management Protocol Version 3 (IGMPv3) and Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 (MLDv2) Protocols
RFC5790.summary: Specifies lightweight subsets of IGMPv3 and MLDv2 (LW-IGMPv3/LW-MLDv2) that drop EXCLUDE-mode source blocking to simplify host and router behavior while remaining interoperable with full IGMPv3/MLDv2 and IGMPv1/v2/MLDv1.

IGMP.why: The document defines a simplified variant of IGMPv3, including host and router behavior, record types and interoperability with IGMPv1/v2/v3.
IGMP.quote: This document describes lightweight IGMPv3 and MLDv2 protocols (LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2), which simplify the standard (full) versions of IGMPv3 and MLDv2.

MLD.why: MLDv2 is specified in parallel as LW-MLDv2, with its own MLDv1 interoperation rules.
MLD.quote: LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2 are subsets of the standard IGMPv3 and MLDv2.

SSM.why: The document explains SSM support and implementation rules for (*,G) joins in the SSM address range, a substantial part of its motivation and implementation guidance.
SSM.quote: They support both Any-Source Multicast (ASM) and SSM communications without a filtering function that blocks sources.

rejected.why: Security Considerations only says they are the same as the full versions; it is not a subject of the document.
The MSF APIs are only referenced briefly in implementation considerations; the document does not specify them.
Multicast routing protocols are mentioned only as unaffected by the lightweight protocols.

RFC5791.title: RFC 2731 ("Encoding Dublin Core Metadata in HTML") Is Obsolete
RFC5791.summary: Administrative RFC that obsoletes RFC 2731 (Encoding Dublin Core Metadata in HTML) because development moved to the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative.

HTML.why: The document concerns the obsolescence of a specification for embedding Dublin Core metadata in HTML meta and link elements, so readers of HTML-related documents would want it.
HTML.quote: Encoding Dublin Core Metadata in HTML

rejected.why: The document is an obsoleting notice, but its subject is the Dublin Core HTML encoding, not RFC series format or publication policy.
DC-HTML mentions XHTML, but the document does not address XML usage.

gaps.name: Dublin Core metadata
gaps.why: The document is about Dublin Core metadata encoding, and the taxonomy has no tag for metadata schemas or Dublin Core.

RFC5792.title: PA-TNC: A Posture Attribute (PA) Protocol Compatible with Trusted Network Connect (TNC)
RFC5792.summary: RFC 5792 specifies PA-TNC, the NEA posture attribute protocol (identical to TCG IF-M 1.0) carried over PB-TNC, defining message headers, standard attribute types, error codes, and IANA registries, and evaluates it against NEA requirements.

NEA.why: The document specifies the PA protocol of the Network Endpoint Assessment architecture, including posture collector/validator messaging and attributes, and evaluates it against NEA requirements.
NEA.quote: This document specifies PA-TNC, a Posture Attribute protocol identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-M 1.0 protocol.

rejected.why: SMI Private Enterprise Numbers are only used as vendor namespace identifiers; the document does not concern SNMP management.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like apparatus for this protocol; the document is not about IANA guidance in general.
EAP/802.1X and other PT protocols are mentioned only as possible transports below PB-TNC; PA-TNC is transport-agnostic.
UTF-8 is merely the string encoding used in fields.
RFC 3339 is used for one field's timestamp format, not a subject of the document.
The protocol explicitly has no security mechanisms of its own; it relies on the PT layer.

gaps.name: NEA (Network Endpoint Assessment) / TNC posture assessment
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists NEA only as a technology under security in my chosen id, but I used 'NEA', which does not appear exactly: the closest taxonomy entry is 'NEA' under security (NEA (Network Endpoint Assessment) and posture), so this is covered.

RFC5793.title: PB-TNC: A Posture Broker (PB) Protocol Compatible with Trusted Network Connect (TNC)
RFC5793.summary: RFC 5793 specifies PB-TNC, the NEA Posture Broker protocol (identical to TCG IF-TNCCS 2.0), which carries batches of posture attribute messages between Posture Broker Client and Server, and evaluates it against NEA requirements.

NEA.why: The document defines the NEA Posture Broker protocol, its batches, state machine and message types, and evaluates it against the NEA Requirements.
NEA.quote: This document specifies PB-TNC, a Posture Broker (PB) protocol identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-TNCCS 2.0 protocol

rejected.why: EAP is only mentioned as an example of a half-duplex transport that PT protocols may be based on. PB-TNC is not about EAP.
TLS is not discussed. Security is delegated to the unspecified PT protocol.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like sections supporting the protocol. The document is not about IANA guidance.
Language tags and Accept-Language are used in a few message fields only, which is peripheral.
UTF-8 is just the string encoding used in two message fields, so it is not a subject of the document.
The NEA protocol is not SACM. SACM is a separate effort.

RFC5794.title: A Description of the ARIA Encryption Algorithm
RFC5794.summary: Describes the ARIA 128-bit block cipher (128/192/256-bit keys): key schedule, encryption/decryption, S-boxes, diffusion layer, test vectors, and an ASN.1 module of OIDs for its modes of operation.

ARIA.why: The whole document specifies the ARIA cipher: key scheduling, round functions, substitution and diffusion layers, and test data.
ARIA.quote: ARIA is a 128-bit block cipher with 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys.

rejected.why: The appendix ASN.1 module only defines OIDs and parameters for ARIA modes. ASN.1 is the notation used, not the subject.
AES is mentioned only in passing, in a comment about key wrap with padding (RFC 5649). The document is not about AES.
The parent is implied by the ARIA tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC5795.title: The RObust Header Compression (ROHC) Framework
RFC5795.summary: RFC 5795 specifies the ROHC (RObust Header Compression) framework, common to all profiles, including channel parameters, packet types, feedback, segmentation, CRCs, and the uncompressed profile 0x0000; it obsoletes RFC 4995.

ROHC.why: The document is the normative ROHC framework specification: channel, contexts, CIDs, IR/IR-DYN packets, feedback, segmentation, and the uncompressed profile.
ROHC.quote: This document explicitly defines the ROHC framework, but it does not modify or update the definition of the framework specified by RFC 3095

rejected.why: The document defines the CRC polynomials used by ROHC, but only as an internal mechanism for header verification, not as a subject on CRC polynomial choice in general.
The parent topic is implied by ROHC, so it is not listed separately.
Mentioned only in the historical background section, not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only in the historical background section; the document does not specify it.
RTP headers are one of the things ROHC profiles compress, but the document does not address RTP itself.
RFC 3241 (ROHC over PPP) is referenced only as an example of channel negotiation, and the CRC algorithm is borrowed from RFC 1662.

RFC5796.title: Authentication and Confidentiality in Protocol Independent Multicast Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) Link-Local Messages
RFC5796.summary: Specifies how to authenticate (and optionally encrypt) PIM-SM link-local messages using IPsec ESP (or optionally AH), with manual keying mandatory and optional automated group key management, updating RFC 4601.

PIM-SM.why: The document secures PIM-SM link-local messages (Hello, Join/Prune, Assert) and updates RFC 4601, the PIM-SM specification.
PIM-SM.quote: This document specifies mechanisms to authenticate the PIM-SM link-local messages using the IP security (IPsec) Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) or (optionally) the Authentication Header (AH).

IPsec.why: Much of the document profiles IPsec for this use: transport mode, SPD/SAD/PAD handling, SA lookup, anti-replay, ESN, and rekeying.
IPsec.quote: In order to provide authentication of PIM-SM link-local messages, implementations MUST support ESP [RFC4303] and MAY support AH [RFC4302].

multicast security.why: It covers group key management for multicast link-local traffic, including GSPD use and the speaker/listener group pattern. The procedures for automated keying are left to other documents.
multicast security.quote: One option is to use Group Domain Of Interpretation (GDOI) [RFC3547], which enables a group of users or devices to exchange encrypted data using IPsec data encryption.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one option for automated key management. The document does not specify or profile it.
Mentioned only as an alternative option for automated key management, with no specification.
ESP is the mandated mechanism, but the document profiles overall IPsec use rather than defining ESP itself, so the IPsec tag covers it.
Key management is discussed, but multicast security is the more specific fit for the group key management content.
AES-CBC is only named as the required confidentiality algorithm; the document is not about AES.
It is relevant in a general sense, but PIM-SM and IPsec are the more specific tags.

RFC5797.title: FTP Command and Extension Registry
RFC5797.summary: RFC 5797 establishes the IANA "FTP Commands and Extensions" registry, defining its format, registration criteria, and initial contents covering base, historic, security, feature-negotiation and NAT/IPv6 FTP commands.

FTP.why: The whole document defines a registry of FTP commands and extensions, lists the base RFC 959 commands, historic commands, and FEAT features. FTP readers would want it.
FTP.quote: An IANA registry of FTP Command and Feature names is established to reduce the likelihood of conflict of names and the consequent ambiguity.

rejected.why: The document does create an IANA registry, but it is specific to FTP commands. It is not about IANA registries or guidance in general, so the FTP tag fits better.
RFC 4217 (AUTH TLS) appears only as a reference in table entries. The document does not address TLS.
EPRT/EPSV (NAT/IPv6 extensions) are only listed as registry rows. The document is not about IPv6.
The FOOBAR IPng commands LPRT/LPSV are only listed as obsolete entries. The document is not about IPng.

RFC5798.title: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) Version 3 for IPv4 and IPv6
RFC5798.summary: RFC 5798 specifies VRRP version 3 for IPv4 and IPv6, an election protocol that dynamically assigns a virtual router to one of several routers on a LAN, with packet format, state machine and operational issues; it obsoletes RFC 3768.

VRRP.why: The document defines VRRPv3, including packet format, state machine, and operational considerations, so it is the core specification for VRRP.
VRRP.quote: VRRP specifies an election protocol that dynamically assigns responsibility for a virtual router to one of the VRRP routers on a LAN.

rejected.why: HSRP is only mentioned as a similar proprietary protocol in the Introduction; the document does not specify or analyse it.
VRRP interacts with ND (Neighbor Solicitation, Router Advertisements) and is compared to ND failover detection, but the document does not define or extend ND.
The document describes how the Master answers ARP requests with the virtual MAC, but ARP is a mechanism VRRP relies on and is not specified here.
VRRP runs over IPv6 and IPv4, but the document is about the redundancy protocol, not IPv6 itself.
Appendix A covers operation over Token Ring and FDDI, but it is a minor appendix on link-layer specifics and not the main subject.

RFC5801.title: Using Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Mechanisms in Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL): The GS2 Mechanism Family
RFC5801.summary: Defines the GS2 SASL mechanism family, a bridge allowing any GSS-API mechanism supporting channel binding and mutual authentication to be used as a SASL mechanism, including naming, message format, channel binding negotiation and new GSS-API utility calls.

SASL.why: The document defines a new SASL mechanism family (GS2-*), its names, message exchange and IANA registration.
SASL.quote: This document describes how to use a GSS-API mechanism as though it were a SASL mechanism.

GSS-API.why: Specifies how GSS-API context tokens are carried, GSS-API parameter use, and two new GSS-API utility functions (gss_inquire_saslname_for_mech and gss_inquire_mech_for_saslname).
GSS-API.quote: All the SASL authentication messages exchanged are exactly the same as the security context tokens of the GSS-API mechanism

rejected.why: TLS is only the external channel to which GS2 binds via tls-unique; the document defines nothing new about TLS.
Mentioned only to forbid its use as a GS2 mechanism; the document is not about SPNEGO.
Kerberos V5 is just an example mechanism with grandfathered names GS2-KRB5; the document is not about Kerberos itself.
SHA-1 is only used to derive mechanism names, with no cryptographic properties required.
Base32 is used for name encoding; it is incidental to the document.
The generic topic is covered by the more specific SASL and GSS-API tags.

gaps.name: channel binding
gaps.why: Channel binding negotiation (gs2-cb-flag, -PLUS names, tls-unique default) is a substantial part of the document, but the taxonomy has no channel binding tag.

RFC5802.title: Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM) SASL and GSS-API Mechanisms
RFC5802.summary: Defines SCRAM, a family of SASL authentication mechanisms (SCRAM-SHA-1 and -PLUS) with channel binding, which also works as a GSS-API mechanism via GS2.

SASL.why: The document specifies a new family of SASL mechanisms, including naming, message exchange, formal syntax and IANA SASL registry entries.
SASL.quote: This specification describes a family of Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL; RFC 4422) authentication mechanisms called the Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM)

GSS-API.why: A full section defines SCRAM as a GSS-API mechanism: OID, name types, per-message tokens and GSS_Pseudo_random, normative for GSS-API implementors.
GSS-API.quote: SCRAM is actually also a GSS-API mechanism.  The messages are the same

rejected.why: TLS is the external channel SCRAM is used with and binds to. The document defines no new TLS feature, only the use of tls-unique channel bindings.
HMAC is a building block of the SCRAM computation and not the subject of the document.
Hi() is described as essentially PBKDF2, but only as a construction detail. The document does not specify or profile PBKDF2.
LDAP is mentioned only as a possible authentication database. The LDAP schema is in a separate document (RFC 5803).
SHA-1 is the mandatory hash function but is only used, not specified or analysed.
The SASL tag is more specific and already covers the authentication-mechanism subject.

RFC5803.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Schema for Storing Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM) Secrets
RFC5803.summary: Defines how the LDAP authPassword attribute stores SCRAM SASL mechanism secrets (scheme, authInfo with iteration count and salt, authValue with StoredKey and ServerKey), with ABNF syntax.

SASL.why: The document specifies how SCRAM SASL mechanism secrets are stored, so it is about SASL mechanisms and their credential storage. SCRAM has no tag of its own, so SASL is the closest fit.
SASL.quote: how the authPassword LDAP attribute [AUTHPASS] can be used for storing secrets used by [SCRAM] Simple Authentication and Security Layer [RFC4422] Mechanisms
