LDAP.why: It is an LDAP schema document that defines the syntax and use of the authPassword attribute values for SCRAM. LDAP readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document describes how the authPassword LDAP attribute [AUTHPASS] can be used for storing secrets

rejected.why: ABNF is used only to express the attribute syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
Base64 encoding is used for salt and keys, but only as an encoding the document relies on.
StoredKey and ServerKey derive from HMAC-based SCRAM, but the document does not address HMAC itself.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a privacy layer.
The document stores SCRAM verifiers, but it does not specify password hashing or key-derivation functions.

gaps.name: SCRAM (Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SCRAM. Readers browsing SCRAM would want this RFC and RFC 5802, but only the generic SASL tag is available.

RFC5804.title: A Protocol for Remotely Managing Sieve Scripts
RFC5804.summary: Specifies ManageSieve, a line-oriented protocol over TCP for remotely uploading, listing, activating, validating and deleting Sieve email filtering scripts on a server, with SASL/TLS security and a sieve: URL scheme.

Sieve.why: The document defines the protocol for managing Sieve email filtering scripts, including script validation, active script handling and the sieve URL scheme; Sieve readers would want it.
Sieve.quote: This document describes a protocol "ManageSieve" for securely managing Sieve scripts on a remote server.

rejected.why: Authentication is done via SASL, but the document only profiles its use (service name, capabilities); it does not define SASL itself.
STARTTLS is used as a security substrate, with a server identity check, but no new TLS extension is defined.
A sieve: URI scheme is registered, but it is a small part serving the protocol; Sieve is the better subject.
Only cited as a syntactic similarity; the protocol is not about IMAP.
Sieve is the more specific tag; the document is not about general email architecture.
Only referenced for data type syntax and as a possible user-preference store.

RFC5805.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Transactions
RFC5805.summary: Experimental RFC extending LDAP with transactions: Start Transaction and End Transaction extended operations, a Transaction Specification control, and an Aborted Transaction Notice, so multiple update operations can be applied atomically.

LDAP.why: The document defines new LDAP extended operations, a control and an unsolicited notice, and specifies their interaction with other LDAP controls. It is an extension of LDAP itself.
LDAP.quote: This document extends the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) [RFC4510] to allow clients to relate a number of update operations [RFC4511] and have them performed as one unit

rejected.why: ASN.1 and BER are only used to describe and encode the new protocol elements; the document is not about ASN.1.
LDAP is the more specific child tag and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
The X.500 model is mentioned only briefly in the distributed directory considerations; the document is not about X.500.
The OID and protocol mechanism registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject of the main body.

RFC5806.title: Diversion Indication in SIP
RFC5806.summary: Historic, independently published early proposal defining a SIP Diversion header that tells the called party from whom and why a call was diverted, with call-forwarding flow examples and mappings to ISUP/ISDN redirection information.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP header (Diversion), its syntax, and UAC, UAS, proxy and redirect server behaviour, with many call flows.
SIP.quote: This document proposes an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). This extension provides the ability for the called SIP user agent to identify from whom the call was diverted

PSTN interop.why: A substantial section specifies translation of ISUP/ISDN redirection information and reason codes at SIP/ISUP and SIP/ISDN gateways, including information loss.
PSTN interop.quote: Mapping ISUP/ISDN Redirection Information to SIP Diversion Header
PSTN interop.section: 9. Mapping ISUP/ISDN Redirection Information to SIP Diversion Header

rejected.why: The document maps ISUP redirection data to a header but does not define ISUP encapsulation in SIP, so it is not SIP-T/SIP-I.
SDP appears in the example messages only as a body, and the document says its contents are omitted.
RTP is mentioned only in passing in the examples, as the media that starts after call setup.
ISDN is mentioned as a legacy signalling source for the mapping, but the document is not about IP access over ISDN.

gaps.name: Call diversion / redirection information (Diversion header, call forwarding)
gaps.why: The core subject, the SIP Diversion header and call forwarding indications, has no dedicated tag. It is covered here only through the general SIP tag.

RFC5807.title: Definition of Master Key between PANA Client and Enforcement Point
RFC5807.summary: Defines the PaC-EP Master Key (PEMK), derived from the EAP MSK after successful PANA authentication, for bootstrapping lower-layer ciphering between a PANA client and an enforcement point, with key name, scope, context, lifetime and distribution guidance.

PANA.why: The document extends PANA by defining a master key derived from PANA authentication between the PaC and the enforcement point.
PANA.quote: This document defines the PaC-EP Master Key (PEMK) that is used by a secure association protocol as the pre-shared secret between the PaC and EP

rejected.why: The MSK comes from EAP, but EAP is only the underlying method carried by PANA. The document does not specify or change EAP.
IPsec ESP is mentioned only as an example of lower-layer per-packet security that the key could bootstrap.
The prf+ function is borrowed from IKEv2 and IKE is listed as a possible secure association protocol. The document is not about IKE.
The document does define a key, but the PANA tag covers it more specifically. The tag hierarchy does not place this as a separate cryptographic topic.
SHA-1 is used only to compute the key name, so it is a building block and not the subject.
The Security Considerations cite AAA key management guidance, which is boilerplate-level context. The document is not a AAA framework.

RFC5808.title: Requirements for a Location-by-Reference Mechanism
RFC5808.summary: Informational GEOPRIV document defining terminology and high-level requirements for a Location-by-Reference mechanism, in which location URIs are created, configured to a Target and dereferenced by Location Recipients.

geolocation.why: The whole document is about conveying location information by reference: location URIs, configuration and dereference protocol requirements, privacy and authorization of location. No more specific child (HELD) is specified here.
geolocation.quote: This document defines terminology and provides requirements relating to the Location-by-Reference approach using a location Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) to handle location information

rejected.why: HELD is only cited as an example location configuration protocol; the document specifies requirements, not HELD.
SIP is used only as an example for conveyance and subscription; location conveyance in SIP is explicitly out of scope.
Location URIs are the central object, but the document defines requirements on location reference, not URI syntax or scheme registration.
PIDF-LO is the required return format for dereference but is referenced, not specified or extended.
DHCP is listed only as an example location configuration protocol.
Privacy motivates many requirements, but the document is about location-by-reference mechanism in general; geolocation covers it.

RFC5810.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Protocol Specification
RFC5810.summary: Specifies the ForCES protocol (message formats, TLV encoding, transactions, heartbeat, high availability) for communication between Control Elements and Forwarding Elements, and defines requirements for the Transport Mapping Layer.

ForCES.why: The whole document is the ForCES protocol specification: common header, message types, LFB addressing, two-phase commit transactions, heartbeats and HA.
ForCES.quote: This document specifies the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) protocol.  The ForCES protocol is used for communications between Control Elements(CEs) and Forwarding Elements (FEs)

rejected.why: The document only lists requirements a TML must meet. The actual TML is defined in a separate RFC (RFC 5811), so this is a minor part of the document.
TLS and IPsec are only suggested as ways a TML may provide security. They are not specified here.
The SCTP-based TML is defined in RFC 5811, not in this document, which only mentions that implementations must implement it.
The LFB schema is XML and defined in RFC 5812. YANG is not involved.
The document describes control/forwarding separation, but ForCES is the specific tag and SDN is a general topic, so it is not tagged separately.
XML is used only for the Appendix B LFB schema and is not the subject of the document.

RFC5811.title: SCTP-Based Transport Mapping Layer (TML) for the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Protocol
RFC5811.summary: Defines the SCTP-based Transport Mapping Layer for the ForCES protocol, specifying three SCTP channels (ports 6704-6706, PPIDs 21-23) with differing reliability and priority, strict-priority scheduling, and IPsec security usage.

ForCES.why: The document specifies a TML for the ForCES protocol, meeting the ForCES PL's TML requirements, so ForCES readers need it.
ForCES.quote: This document defines the SCTP-based TML (Transport Mapping Layer) for the ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation) protocol.

SCTP.why: Substantial part of the document is how SCTP is used: three sockets, partial reliability, multi-homing, ports and PPIDs registered. It defines new SCTP port and PPID usage.
SCTP.quote: There are three SCTP socket connections opened between any two PL endpoints (whether FE or CE).

rejected.why: IPsec with IKE and ESP is only the security mechanism applied to the TML; the document profiles it briefly in Security Considerations but is not about IPsec.
Considered since this is a transport mapping, but the specific ForCES and SCTP tags capture it; the topic tag is not needed given the technology tags chosen.
Congestion control is relied on from SCTP and tied to node overload, but the document does not define congestion control mechanisms.
Only mentioned as an analogy for ADDIP address migration.
The IANA section merely registers ports and PPIDs; boilerplate, not the subject.

gaps.name: ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation)
gaps.why: If the taxonomy had no ForCES tag the document's central subject would be missing; the routing hierarchy does provide ForCES, so no real gap.

RFC5812.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Forwarding Element Model
RFC5812.summary: Defines the ForCES forwarding element (FE) model: LFB classes, topology, capabilities, events, an XML schema for LFB library documents, and the FE Object LFB used by CEs to control FEs.

ForCES.why: The whole document specifies the ForCES FE model, LFB model and FE Object.
ForCES.quote: This document defines the forwarding element (FE) model used in the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) protocol.

rejected.why: XML Schema is only the modelling language for LFB library documents, not the subject.
A data modelling language of a different kind; this RFC defines its own XML-based model, not YANG.
IANA registries for LFB classes are boilerplate-level; main body is the model.
Frame relay appears only in a fictional example LFB.

gaps.name: ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation)
gaps.why: The document is about ForCES, but the taxonomy's only close tag is ForCES under routing, which I used; I verified the id exists in the taxonomy. No gap.

RFC5813.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) MIB
RFC5813.summary: Defines a read-only SNMP MIB module (FORCES-MIB) exposing ForCES protocol version, and per-association identifiers, timestamps, message counters and up/down notifications for CE-FE associations in a ForCES Network Element.

ForCES.why: The MIB exists to manage ForCES associations between Control Elements and Forwarding Elements, so readers of ForCES would expect it.
ForCES.quote: it defines managed objects for the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Network Element (NE).

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition (FORCES-MIB) with objects, notifications and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific fit.
Implied as an ancestor of MIB; the document is not about management architecture in general.
The message counters are simple association statistics for debugging, not performance metrics or methods.

RFC5814.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Dynamic Provisioning Performance Metrics in Generalized MPLS Networks
RFC5814.summary: Defines IPPM-style performance metrics (setup delay for single/multiple unidirectional and bidirectional LSPs, graceful release delay, samples, and statistics) for evaluating dynamic LSP provisioning via RSVP-TE signalling in GMPLS networks.

GMPLS.why: The whole document defines metrics for LSP setup and release in GMPLS networks, so GMPLS readers will want it.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides a series of performance metrics to evaluate the dynamic Label Switched Path (LSP) provisioning performance in GMPLS networks

performance measurement.why: It defines singleton and sample metrics, methodologies, and statistics in the IPPM framework style. This is a performance measurement topic.
performance measurement.quote: This document defines performance metrics and methodologies that can be used to characterize the dynamic LSP provisioning performance of GMPLS networks

RSVP-TE.why: The metrics are defined over RSVP-TE Path, Resv, PathErr and PathTear exchanges. They characterize the performance of RSVP-TE signalling and serve as a scalability metric for implementations.
RSVP-TE.quote: this reflects the inherent delay of a Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) implementation

rejected.why: GMPLS is the more specific fit, and the document is not about plain MPLS.
RSVP-TE is the more specific tag. The document measures signalling delay, not traffic engineering itself.
SNMP and MIBs appear only in Security Considerations as a way to collect or expose the metrics.
RSVP is the underlying signalling protocol being measured. RSVP-TE is the more specific tag.
The metrics follow the IPPM framework rather than BMWG device benchmarking methodology.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics)
gaps.why: The document builds on the IPPM framework (RFC 2330, 2679, 2681). The taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic, with no IPPM-specific tag.

RFC5815.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IP Flow Information Export
RFC5815.summary: Defines the IPFIX-MIB and IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB SMIv2 modules for monitoring IPFIX Exporters and Collectors, covering transport sessions, templates, export groups, metering, observation points, selection processes and statistics.

IPFIX.why: The document models IPFIX Exporter and Collector state (transport sessions, templates, metering and selection processes) as MIB objects, so it is about IPFIX.
IPFIX.quote: This document defines managed objects for IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX). These objects provide information for monitoring IPFIX Exporters and IPFIX Collectors

MIB.why: Its main content is two SMIv2 MIB modules (IPFIX-MIB and IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB), so it belongs under MIB modules and SMI.
MIB.quote: This document defines two MIB modules for monitoring IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) Devices including Exporters and Collectors.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB. The document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Packet sampling and selection methods are explicitly out of scope. Only a placeholder Select All function is defined, so it is not a substantial part of the document.
SCTP is only referenced as a transport via its association ID in the SCTP MIB. The document does not specify or extend SCTP.
UDP is only a transport option recorded in the transport session objects. The document does not specify UDP.
TCP is only a transport option recorded in the transport session objects. The document does not specify TCP.
The IANA section only records OID assignments and expert review for the selector MIB. This is boilerplate, not the document's subject.

RFC5816.title: ESSCertIDv2 Update for RFC 3161
RFC5816.summary: Updates RFC 3161 (Time-Stamp Protocol) so a TSA's signing certificate may be identified with ESSCertIDv2/SigningCertificateV2, permitting hash algorithms other than SHA-1.

PKI.why: The document amends the PKIX Time-Stamp Protocol (RFC 3161), a PKI protocol, changing how the TSA certificate is identified and verified. No narrower PKI child tag exists for time-stamping.
PKI.quote: The time-stamping protocol defined in RFC 3161 [RFC3161] requires that the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) SignedData [RFC5652]

CMS.why: The changes concern signed attributes (SigningCertificate/SigningCertificateV2) in the CMS SignedData of the time-stamp token, which CMS readers would want to find.
CMS.quote: the SigningCertificateV2 attribute MUST be used if any algorithm other than SHA-1 is used and SHOULD NOT be used for SHA-1.

rejected.why: SHA-1 is mentioned only as the limitation being removed. The document is about algorithm agility in certificate identifiers, not the SHA family.
ESS comes from the S/MIME world, but this document only reuses ESSCertIDv2 for time-stamping and does not address S/MIME.
Certificates are referenced by hash, but the document does not profile or specify X.509 certificates.

gaps.name: Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP)
gaps.why: The document is about RFC 3161 trusted time-stamping, which has no dedicated tag. PKI is the closest parent.

RFC5817.title: Graceful Shutdown in MPLS and Generalized MPLS Traffic Engineering Networks
RFC5817.summary: Informational RFC describing requirements and mechanisms (IGP advertisements plus RSVP-TE PathErr signalling) for gracefully shutting down TE links, component links, labels or nodes in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks to avoid traffic disruption during planned outages.

RSVP-TE.why: The core mechanism is RSVP-TE PathErr signalling that triggers LSP reroute around the resource being shut down, so the document specifies how RSVP-TE is used for graceful shutdown.
RSVP-TE.quote: triggers a PathErr message with the error code "Notify" and error value "Local link maintenance required", for all affected TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.section: 4.2 RSVP-TE Signaling Mechanisms for Graceful Shutdown

GMPLS.why: The document covers graceful shutdown in GMPLS TE networks, including label resources such as lambdas and non-packet switching.
GMPLS.quote: These operations are equally applicable to both MPLS-TE [RFC3209] and its Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extensions [RFC3471] [RFC3473].

traffic engineering.why: The document gives requirements for TE network operations and planned maintenance, which is a TE operational topic beyond RSVP-TE signalling alone.
traffic engineering.quote: MPLS-TE Graceful Shutdown is a method for explicitly notifying the nodes in a Traffic Engineering (TE) enabled network that the TE capability on a link

rejected.why: The document only reuses existing OSPF TE LSA advertisements as a notification mechanism, and defines no new OSPF protocol behaviour.
IS-IS TE advertisements are used in the same way as OSPF ones, as an existing substrate, so the document is not about IS-IS.
GMPLS and RSVP-TE are the more specific tags, so the MPLS parent is implied and not listed.
PCE is mentioned only to say the head-end acting as PCC asks the PCE to avoid the resource, which is a passing reference.
The linkDown trap from RFC 2863 appears only in the manageability considerations and is not a subject of the document.

RFC5818.title: Data Channel Status Confirmation Extensions for the Link Management Protocol
RFC5818.summary: RFC 5818 extends the Link Management Protocol with ConfirmDataChannelStatus, Ack and Nack messages and a Data Channel Status subobject so adjacent GMPLS LSRs can detect mismatched data channel states and report stranded resources to the management plane.

GMPLS.why: LMP is the GMPLS link management protocol, and the document extends it with new messages, a subobject and error codes for data channel status confirmation in GMPLS TE links. No separate LMP tag exists, so GMPLS is the closest fit.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines simple additions to the Link Management Protocol (LMP) to provide a control plane tool that can assist in the location of stranded resources

rejected.why: RSVP-TE restart and soft state are discussed only as background and as mechanisms that may resolve mismatches. The document does not specify or extend them.
GMPLS is the more specific fit, since the document concerns non-packet data channels such as timeslots and lambdas.
OSPF is mentioned only to explain that routing-advertised TE information cannot reveal data channel mismatches.
RBNF is used only as the notation for the message formats. The document is not about it.
The IANA section only records code point allocations, which is boilerplate.
UDP is the transport for LMP messages and is not what the document is about.

gaps.name: Link Management Protocol (LMP)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about extending LMP, but the taxonomy has no LMP tag. GMPLS is the nearest tag, and LMP readers would want a dedicated page.

RFC5819.title: IMAP4 Extension for Returning STATUS Information in Extended LIST
RFC5819.summary: Defines an IMAP LIST extension (LIST-STATUS) adding a STATUS return option so a client can get mailbox STATUS data together with LIST results in one command.

IMAP.why: The document specifies an extension to IMAP4's LIST command, including the LIST-STATUS capability and its syntax, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: this document is extending the LIST command with a new return option, STATUS.
IMAP.section: 2. STATUS Return Option to LIST Command

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag and already implies email as its parent.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax and is not what the document is about.
The IANA section only registers the capability and the LIST-EXTENDED option, which is routine boilerplate.

RFC5820.title: Extensions to OSPF to Support Mobile Ad Hoc Networking
RFC5820.summary: Experimental RFC defining OSPF-OR, extensions to OSPFv3 for mobile ad hoc networks: a MANET interface type, incremental Hellos, overlapping-relay optimized flooding, and smart peering to reduce adjacencies.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends OSPFv3 with a new interface type, LLS TLVs, flooding and peering changes. OSPFv3 is the specific protocol being extended.
OSPFv3.quote: This document proposes modifications to [OSPFv3] to support mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs).

MANET.why: The whole purpose is routing in mobile ad hoc networks, including MANET interfaces and relay-based flooding modelled on OLSR MPR selection.
MANET.quote: This document describes extensions to OSPF to support mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs).

rejected.why: This is the parent of OSPFv3. The document builds on OSPFv3 specifically, so the child tag is the better fit.
The relay selection heuristic is borrowed from OLSR MPR selection, but the document does not specify or extend OLSR.
AH and ESP appear only in the Security Considerations, as the mechanism for authenticating OSPF packets.
Not related. The document concerns flooding and adjacency reduction, not repair paths.
802.11 is only mentioned as an example of a link with Layer 2 broadcast. The document does not specify IP over 802.11.

RFC5824.title: Requirements for Supporting Customer Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) and RSVP Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) over a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN
RFC5824.summary: Informational requirements document describing service-provider needs for supporting customer RSVP paths and RSVP-TE LSPs across a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN, with reference model, scenarios, and detailed requirements.

L3VPN.why: The document is an L3VPN WG requirements document on BGP/MPLS IP-VPNs, covering VRF-context RSVP handling at PEs and CEs.
L3VPN.quote: This document describes service-provider requirements for supporting a customer Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) and RSVP-TE over a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN.

RSVP-TE.why: Customer TE LSPs signalled with RSVP-TE, FRR, reoptimization, and graceful restart requirements are a central part of the document.
RSVP-TE.quote: RSVP-TE signaling for Customer TE LSPs (C-TE LSPs) over BGP/MPLS IP-VPNs

RSVP.why: The C-RSVP path model (native RSVP, aggregation over P-TE LSPs, transparency) is one of the two models whose requirements are specified.
RSVP.quote: The RSVP path may be used to provide QoS guarantees and reserve an adequate bandwidth for the data.

rejected.why: PCE is mentioned as one requirement (6.8) but is not a main subject.
DS-TE and MPLS Diffserv are referenced as supporting features, not the document's subject.
LDP appears only as a non-TE core transport option in some scenarios.
MPLS is the substrate. The document is about RSVP-TE and VPN support, so the more specific tags cover it.
BGP appears only as part of BGP/MPLS VPN and as a scalability concern, not as a subject in its own right.
QoS is the motivation, but RSVP is a more specific tag that already sits under it.

RFC5825.title: Displaying Downgraded Messages for Email Address Internationalization
RFC5825.summary: Experimental EAI-WG document specifying how a mail user agent can reverse the RFC 5504 downgrade of internationalized email messages by reconstructing original header fields from "Downgraded-" fields for display.

EAI.why: The whole document is part of the Email Address Internationalization set. It defines how MUAs restore downgraded EAI messages for display.
EAI.quote: This document describes a method for displaying downgraded messages that originally contained internationalized email addresses or internationalized header fields.

rejected.why: It manipulates header fields, but the subject is EAI downgrade reversal, not the base Internet message format, which RFC 5322 defines.
MIME encoded-word decoding (RFC 2047/2231) is used as a step in the procedure, but the document does not specify or extend MIME.
The UTF8SMTP extension and the delivery path are background only. The document concerns MUA display, not SMTP transport.
EAI is the more specific tag and already implies the email parent.
IMAP servers are mentioned once as a possible place for restoration, but IMAP is not the document's subject.

RFC5826.title: Home Automation Routing Requirements in Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC5826.summary: Informational ROLL WG document specifying routing requirements for home automation low-power and lossy networks, covering use cases and requirements such as constraint-based routing, mobility, scalability, convergence time, manageability and security.

IoT.why: The document is about routing requirements for constrained, battery-powered home automation devices in LLNs. IoT is the closest fitting tag for constrained-device network guidance; no specific protocol tag applies.
IoT.quote: This document presents requirements specific to home control and automation applications for Routing Over Low power and Lossy (ROLL) networks.

rejected.why: RPL is the ROLL routing protocol, but this document only states requirements and does not specify or mention RPL.
Mentions IPv6 packets and 802.15.4 links only as background; the document is not about adaptation layers.
Requirements are for a specific class of constrained networks, not general routing architecture; the IoT tag covers it better.
Mobility is a requirement here, but the document is about low-power lossy networks, not ad hoc routing protocols.
All traffic is IPv6, but this is only the substrate; the document says nothing about IPv6 itself.
Demand-response and demand-side management appear only as use cases, not as the subject of the document.

gaps.name: ROLL / Low-power and Lossy Networks routing requirements
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for routing in low-power and lossy networks (the ROLL WG requirements series). IoT is only a rough fit.

RFC5827.title: Early Retransmit for TCP and Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
RFC5827.summary: Experimental RFC specifying the Early Retransmit mechanism, which lowers the duplicate-ACK threshold for fast retransmit in TCP and SCTP when the congestion window is small and no new data can be sent.

TCP.why: The document specifies a TCP loss-recovery extension (byte-based and segment-based Early Retransmit, SACK and non-SACK variants), so it belongs on the TCP page.
TCP.quote: a new mechanism for TCP and Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) that can be used to recover lost segments when a connection's congestion window is small

SCTP.why: SCTP is a co-equal target of the mechanism. The document gives SCTP-specific rules (SACK-based, chunks, message-to-byte conversion) and the title names it.
SCTP.quote: A TCP or SCTP sender MAY use segment-based Early Retransmit.

rejected.why: The mechanism concerns loss recovery triggered by small congestion windows. It does not change congestion control algorithms. It is mainly TCP and SCTP loss recovery.
NewReno is only mentioned as one of the existing loss recovery variants. The document does not specify or extend it.
ECN appears only in Related Work as an orthogonal technique that helps small windows.

RFC5828.title: Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Ethernet Label Switching Architecture and Framework
RFC5828.summary: Informational architecture and framework document describing how the GMPLS control plane (routing, signaling, link management, path computation) can be applied to transport Ethernet, introducing the Eth-LSP concept.

GMPLS.why: The document's purpose is to frame GMPLS control of Ethernet Label Switched Paths (Eth-LSPs), covering signaling, routing, link management and path selection.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines an architecture and framework for a Generalized-MPLS-based control plane for Ethernet in this "transport network" capacity.

Ethernet.why: A substantial part of the document describes Ethernet switching types (PBB, VLAN, I-TAG), Ethernet OAM (CFM, Y.1731) and PBB-TE, which readers of Ethernet topics would want.
Ethernet.quote: The characteristics of the "transport" Ethernet data plane are not modified in order to apply GMPLS control.

rejected.why: GMPLS signaling is RSVP-TE based, but the document only refers to it generally and defines no extensions.
Path computation is mentioned only briefly with a reference to the PCE architecture; it is not a focus.
Eth-LSPs are traffic-engineered, but the document is about GMPLS control for Ethernet, and GMPLS is the more specific tag.
Ethernet OAM is summarized as background, not the subject of the document.
GMPLS is the specific fit; the document does not address MPLS in general.

RFC5829.title: Link Relation Types for Simple Version Navigation between Web Resources
RFC5829.summary: Defines and registers six Atom/Web link relation types (version-history, latest-version, working-copy, working-copy-of, predecessor-version, successor-version) for navigating among versioned resources, with mapping to WebDAV versioning and JCR.

web linking.why: The whole document defines and registers typed link relations and shows their use in the HTTP Link header, so it belongs on the web linking page.
web linking.quote: This specification defines a set of link relation types that may be used on Web resources

WebDAV.why: The appendix maps each relation to WebDAV versioning properties and uses a VERSION-CONTROL example. WebDAV versioning readers would want this, though it is not the document's main focus.
WebDAV.quote: The link relations defined in Section 3 correspond to various properties used in WebDAV Versioning [RFC3253] and JCR [JSR-283]

rejected.why: Relations are registered per the Atom registry and used in AtomPub bindings of CMIS, but the document does not specify or extend Atom itself.
The Link header appears only in an example appendix; HTTP is the substrate and nothing new is defined for it.
The registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations for the relations, not a document about IANA registries.

RFC5830.title: GOST 28147-89: Encryption, Decryption, and Message Authentication Code (MAC) Algorithms
RFC5830.summary: Informational description of the Russian GOST 28147-89 block cipher, specifying its ECB, counter, and cipher feedback encryption/decryption modes and its MAC generation mode.

GOST.why: The whole document describes the GOST 28147-89 cipher, its modes, and its MAC. This is a Russian national cryptographic algorithm, which is what the GOST tag covers.
GOST.quote: the Russian Federal standard for electronic encryption, decryption, and message authentication algorithms (GOST 28147-89), which is one of the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms

rejected.why: The cipher has a similar Feistel structure and 64-bit blocks, but the document is not about DES.
The document is about a different block cipher, not AES or its modes.
The GOST tag is more specific, and its parent cryptography is implied.
The MAC here is a block-cipher-based MAC, not HMAC.

RFC5831.title: GOST R 34.11-94: Hash Function Algorithm
RFC5831.summary: Informational RFC describing the Russian GOST R 34.11-94 hash function algorithm, including the step function, iterative hashing procedure, and test vectors.

GOST.why: The whole document specifies the GOST R 34.11-94 hash function, one of the Russian national cryptographic algorithms, with its calculation procedure and test examples.
GOST.quote: This document is intended to be a source of information about the Russian Federal standard hash function (GOST R 34.11-94)

rejected.why: Different hash family; not discussed or used in the document.
Not related; the document specifies a different hash function.
No keyed MAC construction is defined or used.

RFC5832.title: GOST R 34.10-2001: Digital Signature Algorithm
RFC5832.summary: Informational description of the Russian GOST R 34.10-2001 elliptic-curve digital signature algorithm, covering its parameters, signature generation and verification processes, and test vectors.

GOST.why: The whole document specifies a GOST national signature algorithm, its parameters, processes and test examples, so the GOST page is where readers would look.
GOST.quote: Russian Federal standard for digital signatures (GOST R 34.10-2001), which is one of the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms (called GOST algorithms)

elliptic curve.why: The signature scheme is built on elliptic curve group arithmetic over GF(p), and a substantial part of the document (Section 5) defines the curve math, so elliptic-curve readers would want it.
elliptic curve.quote: describes the generation and verification processes for digital signatures, based on operations with an elliptic curve points group, defined over a prime finite field

rejected.why: GOST R 34.10-2001 is a distinct elliptic-curve signature algorithm with its own equations; the document is not about ECDSA.
Implied as the ancestor of the chosen tags, so not listed separately.
The hash function used is GOST R 34.11-94, referenced but not specified here, and SHA is not mentioned.

RFC5833.title: Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocol Base MIB
RFC5833.summary: Defines the CAPWAP-BASE-MIB SMIv2 module for SNMP management of CAPWAP Access Controllers and WTPs, covering WTP profiles, state, radio bindings via ifIndex, statistics and notifications.

CAPWAP.why: The document defines the managed objects for CAPWAP, covering configuration and WTP status monitoring.
CAPWAP.quote: it describes the managed objects for modeling the Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocol.

MIB.why: The main body is a MIB module (CAPWAP-BASE-MIB) with tables, notifications and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
DTLS only secures CAPWAP channels; objects merely report DTLS state and failures.
IEEE 802.11 is reused through separate binding MIBs and is only used as an example; the base MIB is technology-independent.
ECN support appears only as a CAPWAP field modeled by one object.
Mentioned only in terminology as a possible CAPWAP transport.

gaps.name: CAPWAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a CAPWAP tag listed under link layer, but the RFC is also about the MIB, so I used both tags; no gap remains.

RFC5834.title: Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Protocol Binding MIB for IEEE 802.11
RFC5834.summary: Defines the CAPWAP-DOT11-MIB SNMP MIB module for managing WLAN profiles, MAC type, tunnel mode and WLAN-to-radio bindings in the CAPWAP protocol's IEEE 802.11 binding, reusing the IEEE 802.11 MIB via ifIndex.

CAPWAP.why: The MIB models CAPWAP's 802.11 binding (WLAN profiles, MAC type, tunnel mode, WLAN binding to radios), so CAPWAP readers would want it.
CAPWAP.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling the Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) protocol for IEEE 802.11 wireless binding

MIB.why: The document's main content is an SMIv2 MIB module (CAPWAP-DOT11-MIB) with tables, conformance groups and ifType assignments.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB module that can be used to manage CAPWAP implementations for IEEE 802.11 wireless binding.

rejected.why: The IEEE 802.11 MIB is reused rather than specified; the document is about CAPWAP management, not IP over 802.11. CAPWAP is the more specific tag.
SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the MIB tag covers the SMI-based module.
DTLS is mentioned only in terminology as the CAPWAP security mechanism.
Mentioned only in the definition of the CAPWAP channels.

RFC5835.title: Framework for Metric Composition
RFC5835.summary: Informational IPPM framework defining how performance metrics (loss, delay, delay variation) are composed and aggregated over time and space, with terminology, requirements and guidelines for composed-metric definitions.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines a framework for composing and aggregating IPPM network performance metrics (delay, loss, delay variation) via temporal aggregation, spatial aggregation and spatial composition.
performance measurement.quote: a detailed framework for composing and aggregating metrics (both in time and in space) originally defined by the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM)

rejected.why: OWAMP is cited only in Security Considerations as relevant to active measurement; the document does not specify or extend it.
TWAMP is cited only in Security Considerations; not a subject of the document.
The document concerns metrics of live network paths, not benchmarking methodology for devices.
The framework concerns performance metric composition, not OAM mechanisms.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metric composition
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic 'performance measurement' topic and no tag for the IPPM metrics framework itself; the generic topic covers it adequately but IPPM-specific readers may want a dedicated tag.

RFC5836.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Early Authentication Problem Statement
RFC5836.summary: Problem statement for EAP early authentication, where a mobile device establishes authenticated keying material on a candidate attachment point before handover, covering usage models, architectural considerations and open AAA issues.

EAP.why: The whole document is a problem statement on using EAP for early authentication, including usage models and EAP keying (MSK) issues.
EAP.quote: EAP early authentication may be defined as the use of EAP by a mobile device to establish authenticated keying material on a target attachment point prior to its arrival.

HOKEY.why: Produced by the HOKEY WG and positions early authentication against ERP and handover key management, which are HOKEY subjects.
HOKEY.quote: security context transfer (e.g., using the EAP Extensions for EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP)) [RFC5296], or as EAP early authentication.

AAA.why: Section 8 is devoted to AAA issues for early authentication: authorization, lifetime, retries, inter-realm and billing.
AAA.quote: Most of the AAA documents today do not distinguish between a normal authentication and an early authentication, and this creates a set of open issues:

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an example AAA transport protocol; the document does not specify or extend it.
Only cited as an example AAA protocol, not the subject.
IEEE 802.11 is used as an example of handover; the document is not about IP over Wi-Fi.
The handover discussed is link and access-network handover with authentication, not Mobile IP or its successors.
3GPP TS33.402 is mentioned only as one example of handover authentication.

RFC5837.title: Extending ICMP for Interface and Next-Hop Identification
RFC5837.summary: Defines an ICMP extension object (Interface Information Object) appended to ICMP Time Exceeded, Destination Unreachable and Parameter Problem messages to identify incoming/outgoing interfaces and next hop by ifIndex, IP address, name and MTU.

ICMP.why: The document specifies a new ICMP extension object, its C-Type encoding and usage rules for ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 messages.
ICMP.quote: This memo defines a data structure that can be appended to selected ICMP messages.

traceroute.why: A main application is enhanced traceroute that identifies interfaces and next hops at each node; readers of traceroute would want it.
traceroute.quote: ICMP extensions defined in this memo provide additional capability to traceroute.

rejected.why: The document uses ifIndex and ifName from the Interfaces Group MIB only as values to carry; it does not define MIB modules.
PMTUD is mentioned only as an example application (identifying the interface that cannot support an MTU); the document is not about it.
Section 5 gives brief NAT considerations for the extension, but this is a small part and not the document's subject.
UTF-8 is only the encoding used for the interface name string.

RFC5838.title: Support of Address Families in OSPFv3
RFC5838.summary: RFC 5838 extends OSPFv3 to carry multiple address families (IPv6 multicast, IPv4 unicast and multicast) by mapping each AF to its own Instance ID and OSPFv3 instance, adding an AF-bit, M6-bit, and an IPv6 MTU LLS TLV.

OSPFv3.why: The whole document specifies extensions to OSPFv3: Instance ID ranges per AF, new Options and DD bits, Hello processing changes, next-hop and forwarding address encoding.
OSPFv3.quote: This document supports these other AFs in OSPFv3 by mapping each AF to a separate Instance ID and OSPFv3 instance.

rejected.why: OSPFv3 runs over IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
IPv4 prefixes are advertised as an AF, but the document does not specify IPv4.
The IPv4/IPv6 multicast AFs are just routing instances. PIM is mentioned only as an example for RPF.
OSPFv3 is the more specific child tag and already covers this document.
The IANA registry for Instance ID values is boilerplate-level here, not the main subject.
IPsec appears only in Security Considerations.

RFC5839.title: An Extension to Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Events for Conditional Event Notification
RFC5839.summary: Defines a SIP events extension (SIP-ETag, Suppress-If-Match header, 204 No Notification response) letting subscribers condition SUBSCRIBE requests so unchanged event state or whole NOTIFYs are suppressed.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's event notification framework with a new header field, a new response code, and subscriber/notifier behavior. Readers of SIP extensions would want it.
SIP.quote: This memo defines an extension to SIP events that allows the subscriber to condition the subscription request to whether the state has changed

rejected.why: Presence and resource-list event packages are cited only as examples. The extension is generic to SIP events and defines no SIMPLE-specific package, PIDF or XCAP.
HTTP conditional requests and entity-tags are only an analogy for the design. The document does not specify HTTP behavior.
Presence is only an example use case for the subscription mechanism. The document is not about presence or instant messaging.
ABNF is used only to write the grammar for the new header field. The document is not about the notation.
The IANA section only registers a response code and a header field, which is boilerplate for this document.

RFC5840.title: Wrapped Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) for Traffic Visibility
RFC5840.summary: Defines Wrapped ESP (WESP), a header wrapper around IPsec ESP that lets intermediate devices deterministically distinguish integrity-only from encrypted ESP traffic for monitoring and access control, including UDP encapsulation and IKEv2 negotiation.

ESP.why: The document specifies a new wrapper header for ESP, with transport and tunnel mode processing, to expose whether ESP payloads are encrypted.
ESP.quote: Wrapped Encapsulating Security Payload (WESP) protocol, which builds on the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) RFC 4303

IKE.why: Defines a new IKEv2 notification to negotiate WESP, a substantive part of the specification.
IKE.quote: The notification, USE_WESP_MODE (value 16415) MUST be included in a request message that also includes an SA payload requesting a CHILD_SA using ESP.

rejected.why: Firewalls and middleboxes are the motivating consumers of the visibility, but the document defines a packet format, not firewall mechanisms.
NAT traversal compatibility is noted via UDP encapsulation, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.
UDP encapsulation per RFC 3948 is used as a substrate with a new protocol identifier, not a UDP topic.
ESP is the more specific child tag and is chosen; IPsec is implied as its ancestor.
IDS/IPS are mentioned only as motivating devices needing visibility, not subject matter.

RFC5841.title: TCP Option to Denote Packet Mood
RFC5841.summary: An April 1st joke RFC proposing TCP option kind 25 carrying ASCII emoticons (e.g. :) , :@ ) to denote the "mood" of a packet, with rules for when to mark packets happy, sad, angry, etc.

humor.why: The document is a 1 April parody RFC with whimsical content (packets that are amused, bored, evil; network psychologists). Readers browsing humorous RFCs would expect it.
humor.quote: In an attempt to anthropomorphize the bit streams on countless physical layer networks throughout the world, we propose a TCP option to express packet mood

TCP.why: The document defines a new (jocky) TCP option, its kind, length and format, and ties mood to TCP events such as retransmission, out-of-order delivery and RST.
TCP.quote: It is proposed that option 25 (released 2000-12-18) be used to define packet mood.

rejected.why: ASCII is merely the encoding used for the emoticon characters; the document is not about the character set.
ICMP destination unreachable is mentioned only as a trigger for the 'surprised' mood.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like and the document is not about IANA registry matters.
The TCP checksum is mentioned only in a Security Considerations joke about swapping emoticon characters.

RFC5842.title: Binding Extensions to Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV)
RFC5842.summary: Defines WebDAV binding extensions: the BIND, UNBIND and REBIND methods, the DAV:resource-id and DAV:parent-set properties, and the 208 and 508 status codes, so a resource can be reached through multiple URIs.

WebDAV.why: The document extends WebDAV with new methods, properties, preconditions and a DAV compliance class, and describes how bindings interact with COPY, MOVE, DELETE, locking, ACL and versioning.
WebDAV.quote: This specification defines bindings, and the BIND method for creating multiple bindings to the same resource.

rejected.why: HTTP is the base protocol. The document adds WebDAV methods and status codes 208 and 508, but it is about WebDAV, and the WebDAV tag already sits under HTTP.
XML request and response bodies and DTD fragments are only the encoding used.
URI mappings are central to the concept, but the document specifies WebDAV methods, not URI syntax or schemes.
The urn:uuid scheme is only mentioned as an example value for DAV:resource-id.

RFC5843.title: Additional Hash Algorithms for HTTP Instance Digests
RFC5843.summary: RFC 5843 updates the IANA registry of HTTP Digest Algorithm Values for Instance Digests (RFC 3230), updating MD5 and SHA references and adding SHA-256 and SHA-512.

HTTP.why: The document extends the HTTP Instance Digest mechanism (RFC 3230) by registering new digest algorithm values for the Digest header.
HTTP.quote: defines values for digest algorithms used by Instance Digests in HTTP

SHA.why: The main change is registering SHA-256 and SHA-512 and updating the SHA-1 reference, so readers of the SHA family would find this relevant.
SHA.quote: The SHA-256 algorithm [FIPS-180-3].  The output of this algorithm is encoded using the base64 encoding [RFC4648].

rejected.why: MD5 registration only has its references updated; the document is not about MD5 itself.
Base64 is only the output encoding referenced for digest values; nothing new is defined about it.
IANA registry is the vehicle for the change, but the document is about the HTTP digest algorithm values, not IANA guidance generally.
The document explicitly notes it is unrelated to HTTP Digest Authentication.
Instance digests are content integrity hashes of representations, not the Internet checksum for packet integrity.

RFC5844.title: IPv4 Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC5844.summary: Extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with IPv4 home address mobility support (new mobility options, status codes, DHCP interaction) and IPv4 transport for PMIPv6 signaling and tunnels, with UDP encapsulation and IPsec.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document extends PMIPv6 with IPv4 home address support and IPv4 transport, defining new options and processing rules for the LMA and MAG.
PMIPv6.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Proxy Mobile IPv6 protocol for adding IPv4 protocol support.

DHCP.why: A substantial section specifies how DHCP server and relay functions co-located with the MAG interact with PMIPv6 signaling, including MTU, Router and relay agent options.
DHCP.quote: This section explains how DHCP-based address configuration support can be enabled for a mobile node in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain.

rejected.why: Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6 is a reference model, but the document specifies network-based PMIPv6, which is the more specific tag.
IPsec protects signaling and payload only as a mechanism, with SPD examples. The document defines nothing new about IPsec itself.
GRE is only one encapsulation mode, and its details are deferred to the GREKEY draft.
The document touches IPv4/IPv6 coexistence, but the subject is mobility signalling, not a transition mechanism.
NAT between MAG and LMA is explicitly unsupported; NAT is mentioned only as an assumption.
Proxy ARP is used by the MAG as a supporting detail, not a subject of the document.

RFC5845.title: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) Key Option for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC5845.summary: Defines a new Mobile IPv6 mobility option (GRE Key option) for Proxy Binding Update/Acknowledgement that lets a MAG and LMA negotiate GRE encapsulation and exchange uplink/downlink GRE keys per mobility session, plus a TLV-header UDP tunneling format.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with a new mobility option, new status codes and BU/BA flag, and MAG/LMA procedures.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification defines a new mobility option for allowing the mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor to negotiate Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) encapsulation mode

GRE.why: The document specifies how GRE and its Key extension are negotiated and used for PMIPv6 tunnels, including header ordering and key-based session identification.
GRE.quote: exchange the downlink and uplink GRE keys that are used for marking the downlink and uplink traffic that belong to a specific mobility session

rejected.why: Mobility header option framework is reused, but the document is about Proxy Mobile IPv6, the more specific tag.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as optional protection for GRE traffic.
NAT traversal via UDP TLV encapsulation is mentioned but only as a scenario; not the subject.
Overlapping private IPv4 addressing is a use case, not the subject of the document.
UDP is only a substrate for the TLV-header encapsulation.

RFC5846.title: Binding Revocation for IPv6 Mobility
RFC5846.summary: Defines a Binding Revocation mechanism (new Mobility Header type 16, BRI/BRA messages) letting a home agent, LMA or MAG terminate one, several or all bindings with a peer, for Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 with revocation signalling between home agent and mobile node, including DSMIPv6 and multiple care-of addresses.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document defines a binding revocation mechanism to terminate a mobile node's mobility session and the associated resources.

PMIPv6.why: Large parts of the document specify LMA and MAG behaviour for revoking Proxy Mobile IPv6 bindings, including bulk and inter-MAG handover cases.
PMIPv6.quote: a mobile access gateway can use this mechanism to notify its local mobility anchor peer with a bulk termination of all or a subset of proxy mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) bindings

rejected.why: IPsec is only the security association reused to protect the revocation messages; the document defines nothing new about it.
RFC 3543 Mobile IPv4 registration revocation is mentioned only as a precedent.
The messages run over IPv6, but the document is about mobility signalling, not IPv6 itself.
The IANA section registers a new MH type and registries, which is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.

RFC5847.title: Heartbeat Mechanism for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC5847.summary: Defines a heartbeat mechanism and Restart Counter mobility option for Proxy Mobile IPv6 so a MAG and LMA can detect peer unreachability and restarts.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with a new Heartbeat Mobility Header message and Restart Counter option between MAG and LMA.
PMIPv6.quote: This document describes a heartbeat mechanism between the MAG and the LMA to detect failures, quickly inform peers in the event of a recovery from node failures

rejected.why: The Mobility Header is reused from Mobile IPv6 as a substrate, but the document is about PMIPv6 nodes, not Mobile IPv6 itself.
Only used to protect Heartbeat messages in Security Considerations; boilerplate-level reliance.
IKEv2 is mentioned only as the option for dynamic key negotiation in Security Considerations.
Serves a similar liveness-detection purpose but the document does not specify or use BFD.
Heartbeat is a liveness mechanism, but the document is specific to PMIPv6 and the more specific tag fits better.
Section 4 only references RFC 5844 for carrying the message over IPv4-UDP; it does not address IPv4 itself.

RFC5848.title: Signed Syslog Messages
RFC5848.summary: Defines syslog-sign, a mechanism that adds origin authentication, integrity, replay resistance, sequencing and missing-message detection to syslog by sending signed Signature Blocks and Certificate Blocks as structured data in special syslog messages.

syslog.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the syslog protocol (Signature Block and Certificate Block messages carried as SD elements), so readers of syslog would want it.
syslog.quote: adds origin authentication, message integrity, replay resistance, message sequencing, and detection of missing messages to syslog

rejected.why: OpenPGP DSA and certificates are one supported signature scheme and key blob type, but the document does not specify OpenPGP itself.
PKIX certificates are a mandatory key blob type and are validated per RFC 5280, but the document only uses them and does not profile them.
RFC 5425 TLS transport is the recommended substrate, and the document defines nothing new about TLS.
UDP transport is discussed only as a not-recommended option, and the document does not specify UDP.
The origin authentication is specific to syslog and covered by the syslog tag, so the generic authentication topic adds nothing.
SHA1 and SHA256 are only the hash algorithms selected via the Version field.

RFC5849.title: The OAuth 1.0 Protocol
RFC5849.summary: Informational specification of OAuth 1.0 (Core 1.0 Rev A), defining a redirection-based flow for resource owners to authorize third-party client access via temporary and token credentials, and a method for signing HTTP requests (HMAC-SHA1, RSA-SHA1, PLAINTEXT).

OAuth.why: The document specifies the OAuth 1.0 protocol: temporary credentials, resource owner authorization, token credentials and signed authenticated requests.
OAuth.quote: OAuth provides a method for clients to access server resources on behalf of a resource owner (such as a different client or an end-user).

HTTP authentication.why: Section 3 defines an HTTP authentication scheme ("OAuth" auth-scheme) with Authorization and WWW-Authenticate usage, which readers of HTTP authentication schemes would want.
HTTP authentication.quote: Protocol parameters can be transmitted using the HTTP "Authorization" header field as defined by [RFC2617] with the auth-scheme name set to "OAuth"

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is used as one signature method, but the document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 is used as a signature method by reference to RFC 3447; the document is not about RSA.
HTTP is the substrate the protocol runs over; the document defines no new HTTP semantics beyond the auth scheme already tagged.
TLS is only required for protecting plaintext credentials; nothing new is defined about TLS.
SHA-1 is used in signatures and discussed in security considerations only (boilerplate); the document is not about the SHA family.
URIs are used for endpoints and the base string URI, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.

RFC5850.title: A Call Control and Multi-Party Usage Framework for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5850.summary: Informational framework defining requirements and an abstract "conversation space" model for SIP call control and multi-party usage, covering signaling/mixing models, event conveyance, and a catalog of call control actions and example features.

SIP.why: The whole document is a SIP call control framework: dialog manipulation primitives (REFER, Replaces, Join, 3pcc), call control actions and example features.
SIP.quote: This document defines a framework and the requirements for call control and multi-party usage of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

conferencing.why: A substantial part covers mixing models (focus, centralized, distributed), conference state events and actions such as add, join, split, which are multi-party conferencing matters.
conferencing.quote: SIP supports both tightly coupled and loosely coupled conferencing, although more sophisticated behavior is available in tightly coupled conferences.

rejected.why: Mentioned for offer/answer and media forking but is only a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
Presence and event packages are referenced as information sources, but the document does not specify or extend them.
Only cited as one way to implement Find-Me in an appendix example.
Section 2.7 discusses SIP URIs for naming users and services, but this is SIP-specific usage rather than a document about URIs in general.
XCON's CCMP is cited only as a reference for mixer media policy; the document does not define or profile XCON.
PSTN is mentioned in comparisons and examples (billing, pre-paid), but interworking is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: SIP call control / multi-party features
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for call control (transfer, hold, park, pickup); SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5851.title: Framework and Requirements for an Access Node Control Mechanism in Broadband Multi-Service Networks
RFC5851.summary: Informational framework and requirements document defining use cases (topology discovery, access-loop configuration, remote connectivity test, multicast control) and protocol/nodal requirements for the Access Node Control Protocol between a NAS and a DSLAM in broadband DSL access networks.

ANCP.why: The document is the ANCP framework and requirements, defining use cases, protocol requirements and nodal requirements for NAS and Access Node.
ANCP.quote: define a framework for an Access Node Control Mechanism between a Network Access Server (NAS) and an Access Node (e.g., a Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer (DSLAM))

rejected.why: DSL access is the deployment context, but the tag taxonomy places ANCP under DSL; the more specific ANCP tag covers it.
IGMP snooping/proxy is the context for the multicast use cases, but the document does not specify or extend IGMP.
Multicast admission control and conditional access are a significant use case, but they are specified as ANCP functions, not as multicast routing or group membership.
RADIUS VSAs are used to report loop attributes to AAA servers, but only as a peripheral mechanism.
PPPoE and DHCP are referenced for circuit identification (ACI) only, not specified.
The remote connectivity test triggers OAM on access loops, but it is one use case within ANCP rather than a document about OAM.

RFC5852.title: RSVP-TE Signaling Extension for LSP Handover from the Management Plane to the Control Plane in a GMPLS-Enabled Transport Network
RFC5852.summary: Defines an RSVP-TE extension (an H bit in ADMIN_STATUS and a new Handover Procedure Failure error code) for transferring LSP ownership between the management plane and the GMPLS control plane without disturbing the data plane, including failure handling.

GMPLS.why: The document specifies GMPLS signalling procedures for handing LSPs between the management plane and the control plane in transport networks.
GMPLS.quote: This memo describes an extension to GMPLS Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) signaling that enables the transfer of connection ownership

RSVP-TE.why: It extends RSVP-TE with a new H bit in ADMIN_STATUS and a new ERROR_SPEC error code. It also defines Path, Resv, PathErr and PathTear handling for Handover.
RSVP-TE.quote: This memo introduces a new flag into the ADMIN_STATUS Object.

rejected.why: Base RSVP is only the substrate; the extension is specific to RSVP-TE/GMPLS, which are the more specific tags.
The procedures apply to transport networks generally, and the document never specifies MPLS-TP.
This is implied as the parent of RSVP-TE, so listing it separately would be redundant.
The document concerns ownership transfer between management and control planes. It does not define OAM mechanisms.

RFC5853.title: Requirements from Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Session Border Control (SBC) Deployments
RFC5853.summary: Informational RFC describing the functions of SIP Session Border Controllers (topology hiding, media traffic management, capability mismatch fixing, NAT binding maintenance, access control, protocol repair, media encryption), their conflicts with SIP architecture, and derived requirements for future SIP work.

SIP.why: The whole document analyses SIP intermediaries (SBCs acting as B2BUAs), their effects on SIP end-to-end principles, and derives requirements for future SIP standardization.
SIP.quote: The purpose of this document is to describe functions implemented in SBCs. A special focus is given to those practices that conflict with SIP architectural principles

rejected.why: SBCs rewrite SDP bodies in examples, but SDP is not specified or extended here; it is the object SBCs manipulate.
Section 3.4 covers SBC NAT-binding maintenance, but it is one of seven functions, and NAT behaviour itself is not the subject.
Media encryption is mentioned as an SBC function (Section 3.7), but SRTP is not specified or analysed.
Access control uses firewalls, but the document is about SBC functions in SIP rather than firewall traversal or security.
Media relaying is discussed, but RTP is only the carried media, not the document's subject.
Topology and identity hiding touch on privacy, but the document is not a privacy threat model or privacy considerations guide.

gaps.name: Session Border Controller (SBC)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is SBC deployments and requirements, and the taxonomy has no SBC or B2BUA tag. SIP is the closest fit.

RFC5854.title: The Metalink Download Description Format
RFC5854.summary: Specifies Metalink, an XML-based download description format listing mirrors, cryptographic hashes, piece hashes, signatures and metadata so clients can reliably download files, and registers its namespace and media type.

XML.why: The document defines a new XML vocabulary with elements, a RELAX NG schema, extension rules and a namespace, so it is an XML-based format.
XML.quote: Metalink is a document format based on Extensible Markup Language (XML) that describes a file or list of files to be downloaded from a server.

media types.why: It registers the application/metalink4+xml media type. It also defines mediatype attribute rules for metaurl and signature elements.
media types.quote: A Metalink Document, when serialized as XML 1.0, can be identified with the following media type:

rejected.why: HTTP is only one of the protocols (with FTP and P2P) that Metalink URLs point to. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Signing of Metalink documents is covered only in Security Considerations, and the main body does not specify it.
URIs and IRIs are used as values. The document defines nothing new about them.
SHA-256 is required as a hash type, but the document is not about the hash family.
The design is modelled on Atom, but Metalink is a separate format and not Atom syndication.
BitTorrent is referenced only through metaurl. The document is not about P2P networks.

gaps.name: Metalink / download description and mirror lists
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for file download metadata or mirror selection, and Metalink is a distinct format that readers would look up by that name.

RFC5855.title: Nameservers for IPv4 and IPv6 Reverse Zones
RFC5855.summary: BCP specifying a stable nameserver naming scheme (X.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA and X.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA) for the DNS reverse zones IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA, with delegation and label-compression analysis.

DNS.why: The document defines nameserver names, delegations and glue for the DNS reverse zones, and analyses label compression and query patterns. This is DNS operations.
DNS.quote: This document specifies a stable naming scheme for the nameservers that serve the zones IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA in the DNS.

rejected.why: IP6.ARPA is only the reverse-mapping zone for IPv6 addresses. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
IANA carried out the delegations, but that appears in the IANA Considerations boilerplate. The main body is about DNS naming, not registry guidance.
DNSSEC is mentioned once in passing as a contributor to response size. The document does not address it.
IN-ADDR.ARPA serves IPv4 reverse mapping, but the document does not address IPv4 itself.

RFC5856.title: Integration of Robust Header Compression over IPsec Security Associations
RFC5856.summary: Informational framework document describing how to integrate ROHC header compression of inner headers over IPsec tunnel-mode SAs, with IKEv2 negotiation and Next Header identification of compressed packets.

ROHC.why: The document's whole subject is extending ROHC to operate at IPsec SA endpoints, covering channel setup, feedback, and integrity checking of decompression.
ROHC.quote: This document outlines a framework for integrating ROHC [ROHC] over IPsec [IPSEC] (ROHCoIPsec).

IPsec.why: It modifies IPsec inbound and outbound processing, adds a ROHC data item to SA state, and uses the Next Header field. It is co-primary because the framework changes IPsec behaviour.
IPsec.quote: The process illustrated in Figure 2 augments the IPsec processing model for outbound IP traffic (protected-to-unprotected).

rejected.why: IKEv2 is only the mechanism for negotiating ROHC channel parameters. The extensions are specified in a separate RFC (5857), not here.
ESP is the security protocol whose Next Header carries the ROHC identifier, but the document does not specify or extend ESP itself.
IPComp is mentioned only briefly as something that can be nested with ROHCoIPsec; the document is not about it.
Path MTU is discussed in one short subsection and the approaches are deferred to another RFC.

RFC5857.title: IKEv2 Extensions to Support Robust Header Compression over IPsec
RFC5857.summary: Defines IKEv2 extensions (a ROHC_SUPPORTED Notify payload and ROHC attribute types) to signal ROHC channel parameters for ROHC-enabled IPsec SAs (ROHCoIPsec).

ROHC.why: The document specifies how ROHC channel parameters (MAX_CID, profiles, integrity, ICV length, MRRU) are negotiated so ROHC can be used over IPsec; ROHC readers need it.
ROHC.quote: this document defines extensions to IKEv2 to signal ROHC parameters for ROHCoIPsec.

IKE.why: It extends IKEv2 with a new Notify message type and attribute registry, so it belongs under IKE.
IKE.quote: a new Notify message type MUST be included in the IKE_AUTH and CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges whenever a new ROHC-enabled IPsec SA is created

rejected.why: IPsec SAs are the context, but the extension itself is to IKEv2; IKE is the more specific tag. The companion IPsec-side work is RFC 5858/5856.
Parent of ROHC, implied by the ROHC tag.
IANA registry creation is boilerplate here, not the main subject.
ESP is not specified or changed here; it only appears in the ROHC profile mentions.

RFC5858.title: IPsec Extensions to Support Robust Header Compression over IPsec
RFC5858.summary: Specifies the IPsec SPD and SAD extensions and processing changes (ROHC protocol identifier, ROHC ICV integrity check, segmentation/MTU handling, nesting with IPComp) needed to run Robust Header Compression over IPsec.

ROHC.why: The document defines how ROHC is integrated with IPsec: ROHC channel parameters, the ROHC protocol identifier, the ROHC ICV and segmentation handling.
ROHC.quote: Integrating Robust Header Compression (ROHC) with IPsec (ROHCoIPsec) offers the combined benefits of IP security services and efficient bandwidth utilization.

IPsec.why: The document extends the IPsec architecture (SPD, SAD, ESP/AH processing order) to support ROHC.
IPsec.quote: extensions to the Security Policy Database (SPD) and Security Association Database (SAD) are required.

IPComp.why: A section specifies the processing order when IPComp is nested with ROHCoIPsec.
IPComp.quote: If IPComp and ROHCoIPsec are implemented in a nested fashion, the following steps MUST be followed for outbound and inbound packets.

rejected.why: IKEv2 signalling of ROHC parameters is only referenced and left to RFC 5857; this document covers the databases and processing.
ESP and AH are the protection mechanisms to which ROHC is applied, not the document's subject. The IPsec tag covers it.
The ASN.1 appendix is only an illustrative representation of the SPD parameters.
HMAC and other integrity algorithms are only listed as options for the ROHC ICV.
Path MTU is discussed only for how it interacts with ROHC segmentation, not as a subject in its own right.

gaps.name: ROHC (RObust Header Compression)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a ROHC tag under header compression, but the RFC is also about ROHC; the id I used is not verified against the taxonomy list below.

RFC5859.title: TFTP Server Address Option for DHCPv4
RFC5859.summary: Documents the existing DHCPv4 option 150 (TFTP Server Address), which carries one or more IPv4 addresses of a configuration server so VoIP devices need not resolve a hostname.

DHCP.why: The document defines a DHCPv4 option, its format, length rules, and client/server behaviour. DHCPv4 is the DHCP tag; the option is not DHCPv6-specific.
DHCP.quote: The TFTP Server Address option is a DHCP option [RFC2132]. The option contains one or more IPv4 addresses that the client MAY use.

rejected.why: TFTP is only the protocol the option is currently used to fetch configuration with. The document defines nothing about TFTP itself.
DNS is mentioned only as the hostname resolution the option avoids.
The option is DHCPv4-only, and the document says there is no IPv6 equivalent.
VoIP devices are the motivating use case, but the document does not address SIP or call signalling.
The IANA section only records the option number assignment, which is boilerplate.

RFC5860.title: Requirements for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in MPLS Transport Networks
RFC5860.summary: Lists architectural and functional requirements for OAM (continuity checks, connectivity verification, route tracing, lock, alarm, RDI, loss and delay measurement) in MPLS Transport Profile, applying to pseudowires, LSPs and Sections.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document specifies OAM requirements for the MPLS Transport Profile, so MPLS-TP readers would want it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document lists architectural and functional requirements for the OAM functionality of MPLS-TP.

OAM.why: The document is about OAM mechanisms and their requirements: continuity checks, connectivity verification, diagnostics, lock, alarm and remote defect indication.
OAM.quote: The MPLS-TP OAM toolset MUST provide a function to enable an End Point to monitor the liveness of a PW, LSP, or Section.

performance measurement.why: Packet loss and delay measurement requirements are a substantial part of the functional requirements.
performance measurement.quote: The MPLS-TP OAM toolset MUST provide a function to enable the quantification of packet loss ratio over a PW, LSP, or Section.

rejected.why: Pseudowires are one of the transport entities that OAM applies to. The document does not specify pseudowire emulation.
BFD for MPLS LSPs and VCCV is only cited as existing OAM protocols that must remain usable. The document does not specify or extend BFD.
Route tracing is one functional requirement among many. The document does not define a traceroute tool.
MPLS-TP is the more specific tag and already implies MPLS as its parent.

RFC5861.title: HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content
RFC5861.summary: Defines two HTTP Cache-Control extensions, stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error, letting caches serve stale responses during background revalidation or on origin errors.

HTTP caching.why: The whole document specifies Cache-Control extensions governing how HTTP caches use stale responses, which is exactly HTTP caching.
HTTP caching.quote: This document defines two independent HTTP Cache-Control extensions that allow control over the use of stale responses by caches.

rejected.why: HTTP caching is the more specific child tag; the parent is implied.
ABNF is used only to write the two directive grammars, not the subject of the document.
DNS failure is mentioned only as one example of an error that triggers stale-if-error.

RFC5862.title: Path Computation Clients (PCC) - Path Computation Element (PCE) Requirements for Point-to-Multipoint MPLS-TE
RFC5862.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements for the PCC-PCE communication protocol (PCEP) to support path computation for point-to-multipoint MPLS/GMPLS traffic-engineered LSPs.

PCE.why: The whole document defines requirements on the PCC-PCE communication protocol for P2MP path computation, which is the PCE architecture and PCEP subject.
PCE.quote: presents a detailed set of PCC-PCE communication protocol requirements for point-to-multipoint MPLS/GMPLS traffic engineering

rejected.why: RSVP-TE P2MP signaling (RFC 4875) is referenced as background and for path encoding, but the document does not specify or extend it.
MPLS TE LSPs are the setting for the computation, but the document is about the PCC-PCE protocol, not MPLS itself.
GMPLS is mentioned as an applicable network type only; nothing GMPLS-specific is addressed.
Multicast VPNs are cited once as a motivation for P2MP TE, not a subject of the document.
Implied as the parent of PCE, and the PCE tag fits more specifically.

RFC5863.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Development, Deployment, and Operations
RFC5863.summary: Informational guide for developers, deployers and operators of DKIM covering trust assessment, key management, signing, verifying, signature taxonomy, ADSP usage, and migration from DomainKeys and between algorithms.

DKIM.why: The whole document is practical guidance on developing, deploying and operating DKIM signing and verification.
DKIM.quote: This document provides implementation, deployment, operational, and migration considerations for DKIM.

rejected.why: DKIM key records are published in DNS and server considerations are discussed, but DNS is the key-publication substrate, not the subject.
Mentioned only briefly as ideal protection for key records in Section 3.2; not a substantial part.
Filtering using DKIM identifiers is discussed, but the document is about DKIM, not spam control itself.
Header fields such as DKIM-Signature and Authentication-Results are used, but message format is not the subject.
Section 3 covers DKIM key management, but it is specific to DKIM and does not warrant a general tag beyond DKIM.

gaps.name: Author Domain Signing Practices (ADSP)
gaps.why: Section 7.3 covers ADSP usage, but the taxonomy has no ADSP tag; it only has DKIM, DMARC and other email authentication tags.

RFC5864.title: DNS SRV Resource Records for AFS
RFC5864.summary: Specifies use of DNS SRV records (afs3-vlserver, afs3-prserver) to locate AFS cell VLDB and PTS servers, maps SRV priority/weight to AFS server ranks, and deprecates the AFSDB RR from RFC 1183 with backward-compatibility guidance.

AFS.why: The document defines how AFS clients locate VLDB and PTS servers for a cell via DNS and how SRV priority/weight map to AFS server ranks. The AFS tag explicitly covers DNS-based service discovery.
AFS.quote: specifies how to use DNS (Domain Name Service) SRV RRs (Resource Records) to locate services for the AFS distributed file system

DNS.why: The document uses SRV RRs, deprecates the AFSDB RR and gives client fallback and TTL handling rules. That is substantial DNS resource record usage, and readers of DNS would want it.
DNS.quote: It updates RFC 1183 to deprecate the use of the AFSDB RR to locate AFS cell database servers

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a mitigation, so the document is not about it.
The document does service discovery, but the more specific AFS tag already covers it.
DNS-SD is a different mechanism. This document uses plain SRV records and does not use DNS-SD.

RFC5865.title: A Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) for Capacity-Admitted Traffic
