RFC5865.summary: RFC 5865 requests a new DSCP (VOICE-ADMIT, 101100) for EF-conforming real-time traffic that undergoes capacity admission control, and recommends admission control for certain video classes, updating RFC 4594 and RFC 4542.

Diffserv.why: The document defines a new DSCP and its EF-based PHB treatment, and updates the Diffserv service class configuration guidelines in RFC 4594.
Diffserv.quote: This document requests one Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) from the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) for a class of real-time traffic.

RSVP.why: RSVP is recommended as the capacity admission signalling mechanism at the UNI, and the admission discussion compares it with NSIS and other approaches. It is a recommendation rather than a new specification, so it is secondary.
RSVP.quote: We therefore RECOMMEND the use of a protocol, such as RSVP, at the UNI.
RSVP.section: 2.3. Recommendations on Implementation of an Admitted Telephony Service Class

rejected.why: The parent QoS topic is implied by the Diffserv and RSVP tags, so it is not listed separately.
NSIS is only named as one possible admission mechanism and is noted as not finalized, so the document is not about it.
The DSCP registration is the core subject and falls under Diffserv. The IANA considerations section is boilerplate for the registry request.
The document mentions VoIP and SIP telephony only as context for the traffic being admitted. It specifies nothing about SIP.
RTP is mentioned only through the RFC 5127 Real-Time Traffic class name, not as a protocol the document addresses.
AAA is mentioned as a supporting function for admission, not specified or analysed here.

RFC5866.title: Diameter Quality-of-Service Application
RFC5866.summary: Defines the Diameter QoS application, with QAR/QAA and QIR/QIA commands, letting network elements obtain QoS authorization from Diameter servers in Pull mode or have it installed in Push mode.

Diameter.why: The document specifies a new Diameter application: command codes, AVPs, state machine and session handling.
Diameter.quote: This document describes the framework, messages, and procedures for the Diameter [RFC3588] Quality-of-Service (QoS) application.

QoS.why: A substantial part of the document is the QoS authorization framework: Pull/Push modes, authorization tokens and IntServ/Diffserv interaction.
QoS.quote: The Diameter QoS application allows Network Elements (NEs) to interact with Diameter servers when allocating QoS resources in the network.

rejected.why: SIP is only the application-layer trigger in the examples; it is not specified or extended here.
RSVP and NSIS are only QoS signalling triggers that the Network Element receives; the document does not define them.
Intserv and Diffserv are discussed only as background for choosing between Pull and Push modes.
The generic AAA framework is background; the document is about the specific Diameter application, and Diameter is the more specific tag.
TLS and IPsec appear only in the Security Considerations as Diameter's protection mechanisms.
SDP appears only in the example flows, where it carries session parameters.

RFC5867.title: Building Automation Routing Requirements in Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC5867.summary: Informational ROLL WG document defining IPv6 routing requirements for low-power and lossy networks in commercial building automation, covering commissioning, scalability, mobility, constrained devices, route selection, manageability and security.

IoT.why: The document sets requirements for routing among resource-constrained sensors, actuators and controllers in LLNs. No more specific IoT technology tag fits, so the IoT topic is used directly.
IoT.quote: this document defines the IPv6 routing requirements for building automation.

routing architecture.why: A substantial part covers routing requirements: scalability to 2,000 nodes, route cost, adaptation, redundancy, discovery time and prioritization. These apply to any protocol that is developed.
routing architecture.quote: The routing protocol MUST support a metric of route quality and optimize selection according to such metrics within constraints established for links along the routes.

rejected.why: The document states requirements for ROLL routing protocols but does not specify or analyse RPL.
IPv6 is the addressing context for the requirements. The document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself.
Mobility is one requirements subsection, and it says Mobile IP is only one possible approach. The document does not address IP mobility protocols.
Multicast, anycast and unicast support appear as a brief addressing requirement, which is not enough to make the document about multicast.
Prioritized routing is a single short requirement and does not amount to a QoS architecture.
The security requirements concern routing protocol features such as authentication and encryption in LLNs. They do not describe operational security practices.

gaps.name: Building automation / LLN routing requirements (ROLL)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for low-power and lossy network routing or building automation. Readers browsing the ROLL requirements series would want to find this RFC under such a subject.

RFC5868.title: Problem Statement on the Cross-Realm Operation of Kerberos
RFC5868.summary: Informational problem statement describing issues with Kerberos V5 cross-realm authentication (RFC 4120) in large-scale industrial automation deployments, listing requirements and issues without proposing solutions.

Kerberos.why: The whole document analyses Kerberos cross-realm operation, its trust models (direct and indirect), and the issues (MITM, scalability, DoS, performance, roaming pre-authentication) it raises.
Kerberos.quote: identifying issues in the current Kerberos cross-realm authentication model as defined in RFC 4120

rejected.why: Authentication is the subject but the document is specifically about Kerberos, not a general AAA framework.
Parent topic of Kerberos is already implied via the Kerberos tag; no need to list separately.
The document concerns protocol deployment issues in industrial settings, not operational security practice for infrastructure.
DNS domain hierarchy is mentioned only in passing for trust path determination.

RFC5869.title: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)
RFC5869.summary: RFC 5869 specifies HKDF, an HMAC-based extract-then-expand key derivation function, with usage guidance and test vectors.

key management.why: The document defines a general-purpose KDF that derives cryptographic keys from input keying material. No tag exists for KDFs specifically, and key management (key establishment and provisioning) is the closest fit.
key management.quote: A key derivation function (KDF) is a basic and essential component of cryptographic systems.

HMAC.why: HKDF is built entirely from HMAC. The document specifies a construction on top of HMAC and does not define HMAC itself, so this is secondary.
HMAC.quote: HMAC-Hash denotes the HMAC function [HMAC] instantiated with hash function 'Hash'.

rejected.why: SHA-1 and SHA-256 are only the hash functions used to instantiate HMAC and to produce test vectors.
IKEv2 is cited as an existing user of HKDF. The document does not specify or change it.
The document says password-based KDFs are out of scope and points to PKCS #5 instead.
Entropy extraction is part of HKDF's rationale, but the document does not specify randomness generation.
A more specific child tag (HMAC) was chosen, and key management covers the KDF subject.

gaps.name: Key derivation function (KDF) / HKDF
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for key derivation functions. HKDF is widely used in TLS 1.3, MLS, and other protocols, so readers would look for a dedicated KDF page.

RFC5870.title: A Uniform Resource Identifier for Geographic Locations ('geo' URI)
RFC5870.summary: Defines the 'geo' URI scheme for identifying geographic locations by WGS-84 coordinates (with optional altitude and uncertainty), registers it with IANA along with a parameter registry, and gives non-normative GML mappings.

URI.why: The document defines a new URI scheme: its syntax, semantics, comparison rules, and registration. Readers of URI scheme pages would expect it.
URI.quote: This document specifies a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) for geographic locations using the 'geo' scheme name.

geolocation.why: The subject is conveying geographic location (coordinates, CRS, uncertainty, location privacy under GEOPRIV). The topic tag applies because no technology tag under geolocation fits (HELD is not involved).
geolocation.quote: A 'geo' URI identifies a physical location in a two- or three-dimensional coordinate reference system

rejected.why: GML mappings in Section 7 are non-normative examples. XML is not the subject.
HTML hyperlinks appear only as a usage example in Section 6.2.
ABNF is just the notation used to give the syntax.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-like apparatus for the scheme and its parameter registry. The document is not about IANA guidance.
Location privacy gets only a short Security Considerations note referring to GEOPRIV.
HELD is not discussed. The document is about a URI, not acquiring location over HTTP.

RFC5871.title: IANA Allocation Guidelines for the IPv6 Routing Header
RFC5871.summary: Specifies IANA allocation policy (IETF Review or IESG Approval) for new Routing Type values in the IPv6 Routing Header, updating RFC 2460.

IPv6.why: The document concerns the IPv6 Routing Header's Routing Type registry and updates the IPv6 specification (RFC 2460), so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: specifies the IANA guidelines [RFC5226] for allocating new values for the Routing Type field in the IPv6 Routing Header

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry allocation policy, so it belongs with IANA registry guidance.
IANA.quote: New Routing Type values are allocated through IETF Review or IESG Approval [RFC5226].

rejected.why: The Routing Header is an IPv6 extension header, not about routing protocols or systems; the IPv6 tag is more fitting.
Security Considerations only mention that Type 0 header problems existed; the document does not address routing security.

RFC5872.title: IANA Rules for the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA)
RFC5872.summary: RFC 5872 updates RFC 5191 by relaxing the IANA allocation rules for several PANA registries (Message Types, Message Flags, AVP Flags, Result-Code and Termination-Cause AVP values) to also permit IESG Approval.

PANA.why: The whole document modifies the registry allocation policies of PANA message types, flags and AVP values, so it belongs on the PANA page.
PANA.quote: This document relaxes the IANA rules for the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) [RFC5191].

rejected.why: The document is a PANA-specific registry policy change. It is not general guidance on IANA registries or stewardship. The IANA Considerations section is where the content sits, but the subject is PANA.
PANA carries EAP, but this document says nothing about EAP or its methods.
The AVP format resembles Diameter, but the document does not address AAA frameworks.

RFC5873.title: Pre-Authentication Support for the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA)
RFC5873.summary: Defines an experimental PANA extension (new 'E' pre-authentication header bit) letting a PaC proactively run EAP authentication and establish a PANA SA with a candidate PAA in a network it may move to.

PANA.why: The whole document extends PANA with a new header flag and negotiation procedure for pre-authentication.
PANA.quote: This document defines an extension to the PANA protocol [RFC5191] used for proactively executing EAP authentication and establishing a PANA SA

rejected.why: EAP is carried by PANA and pre-authentication uses it, but the document specifies nothing new about EAP or its methods; it is the substrate.
Handover motivates the work, but the document does not address IP-layer mobility protocols.
Authorization and accounting are explicitly out of scope.

RFC5874.title: An Extensible Markup Language (XML) Document Format for Indicating a Change in XML Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP) Resources
RFC5874.summary: Defines the XCAP diff XML document format, which reports changes (ETags, XML patches, existing element/attribute content) in XCAP-managed documents, deliverable e.g. via a SIP event package.

SIMPLE.why: The SIMPLE taxonomy entry covers event packages, PIDF extensions and XCAP. This SIMPLE WG document defines the XCAP diff format used by the XCAP diff event package, so it belongs here.
SIMPLE.quote: This specification defines a document format that can be used to indicate that a change has occurred in a document managed by the Extensible Markup Language (XML) Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP).

XML.why: The document specifies an XML-based format with a schema, namespaces and XML patch operations. A reader browsing XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: This data format is an XML document format, called an XCAP diff document.

rejected.why: SIP event notification is only one transport for the format, which the document says is not defined by this specification.
HTTP ETags and PUT/DELETE are the substrate XCAP uses. The document does not extend HTTP.
It registers application/xcap-diff+xml, but that is IANA boilerplate rather than the main subject.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the recommended transport protection.
It registers an XML namespace URN under the IETF URN namespace, which is IANA boilerplate and not the document's subject.

gaps.name: XCAP (XML Configuration Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about changes to XCAP-managed documents, but the taxonomy has no XCAP tag. SIMPLE is the closest fit.

RFC5875.title: An Extensible Markup Language (XML) Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP) Diff Event Package
RFC5875.summary: Defines the "xcap-diff" SIP event package that lets clients subscribe to changes in XCAP documents, collections and components, with notifications carried in the XCAP diff format and a 'diff-processing' parameter controlling patching modes.

SIMPLE.why: The document specifies a new SIP event package for XCAP resource change notification, which belongs with SIMPLE event packages and XCAP. It is the closest taxonomy fit, covering SIP event notification and XCAP.
SIMPLE.quote: This memo defines an "xcap-diff" event package that, together with the SIP event notification framework [RFC3265] and the XCAP diff format [RFC5874]

SIP.why: It extends SIP with a new event package, an Event header parameter and SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY procedures including forking and rate handling.
SIP.quote: The name of this event package is "xcap-diff". As specified in [RFC3265], this value appears in the Event header field present in SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY requests.

rejected.why: XML is the data format of XCAP and the diff documents, but the document is about the event package, not XML usage itself.
HTTP is used by XCAP clients to fetch and modify documents, but it is only a substrate here.
WebDAV is mentioned only for collection URL conventions and a PROPFIND comparison.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations as a hop-by-hop protection mechanism.
The IANA registration of the event package is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.

gaps.name: XCAP (XML Configuration Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The document revolves around XCAP resources, components and the XCAP diff format, but the taxonomy has no XCAP tag. SIMPLE only mentions XCAP in its description.

RFC5876.title: Updates to Asserted Identity in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5876.summary: RFC 5876 updates RFC 3325 to let a trusted SIP UAC insert P-Asserted-Identity, allow P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity in any request except ACK and CANCEL, and define handling of unexpected URI counts and schemes.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP asserted identity mechanism (RFC 3325). It specifies UAC, proxy, registrar and UAS behaviour for the P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity header fields.
SIP.quote: This document extends RFC 3325 by allowing inclusion of the P-Asserted-Identity header field by a UAC in the same Trust Domain as the first proxy

rejected.why: The document concerns asserted identity within a trust domain. Digest authentication is only the precondition for asserting an identity, not the subject.
MESSAGE and PUBLISH are mentioned as methods that may carry the header fields, but the document does not specify presence or IM extensions.
The TEL URI is only one of the URI schemes permitted in the header fields. The document defines nothing new about it.
PSTN gateways are given as examples of trusted UACs. The document does not address PSTN interworking itself.
The Privacy header field with value 'id' appears only in one compatibility provision. The document is not about privacy.

RFC5877.title: The application/pkix-attr-cert Media Type for Attribute Certificates
RFC5877.summary: Registers the application/pkix-attr-cert MIME media type (file extension .ac) for carrying a single RFC 5755 attribute certificate.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration (application/pkix-attr-cert) following BCP 13. Readers browsing media type registrations would expect to find it.
media types.quote: This document specifies a MIME media type used to carry a single attribute certificate as defined in RFC 5755.

X.509.why: Attribute certificates are part of the X.509 PKI family and are used alongside public key certificates. The document ties the media type to that profile and gives an encoding consistency rule for the holder name.
X.509.quote: This document specifies a MIME media type for use with attribute certificates as defined in RFC 5755

rejected.why: Attribute certificates are ASN.1/DER/BER encoded, but the document only mentions this in passing and defines nothing about ASN.1.
The media type is said to be used with HTTP to fetch certificates, but HTTP is only the transport and the document specifies nothing about it.
The document is a registration of a single media type. The more specific media types tag covers it, and nothing in it concerns MIME body structure or encodings.
This is a subject-area parent of X.509. The more specific X.509 tag is already chosen, so the parent is implied.

RFC5878.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authorization Extensions
RFC5878.summary: Experimental RFC defining TLS client_authz and server_authz hello extensions and a supplemental data message type for exchanging authorization data (X.509 attribute certificates, SAML assertions, or URLs to them) during the TLS handshake.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS extensions (client_authz, server_authz), a supplemental data type, alert usage and an IANA registry, so it is squarely a TLS extension document.
TLS.quote: This document specifies authorization extensions to the Transport Layer Security (TLS) Handshake Protocol.

authorization.why: The subject is carrying authorization information (ACs, SAML assertions) in the handshake, with guidance on least privilege and binding to authentication.
authorization.quote: authorization information needs to be exchanged between the client and the server before any protected data is exchanged

X.509.why: Substantial portions specify how X.509 attribute certificates are carried and linked to the TLS certificate holder.
X.509.quote: the authorization data is an X.509 attribute certificate (AC) that conforms to the profile in RFC 5755

rejected.why: SAML assertions are XML, but the document only uses XML as the assertion encoding and defines nothing about XML itself.
HTTP is only used to dereference URLs for ACs and assertions; the document does not specify anything about HTTP.
SAML is a payload format here, not a federated authentication framework being specified or profiled.
Hash algorithms are only used to integrity-protect fetched authorization URLs; the document is not about SHA.
It only references existing media types such as application/pkix-attr-cert; it registers none.

RFC5879.title: Heuristics for Detecting ESP-NULL Packets
RFC5879.summary: Informational RFC describing heuristics that intermediate devices such as deep-inspection engines can use to distinguish IPsec ESP-NULL packets from encrypted ESP packets without changing end hosts.

ESP.why: The whole document analyses ESP packet format (padding, ICV, IV, next header) to detect NULL-encrypted ESP flows, including UDP encapsulation of ESP.
ESP.quote: distinguishing IPsec ESP-NULL (Encapsulating Security Payload without encryption) packets from encrypted ESP packets

rejected.why: ESP is the more specific child tag and covers the subject; the parent is implied.
Deep-inspection engines are the use case, but the document specifies ESP detection heuristics, not firewall or middlebox traversal mechanisms.
TCP header checks are used only as inner-protocol validation heuristics, not as a subject of the document.
SCTP is mentioned only as one inner protocol whose checksum can be checked.
NAT effects on checksums and UDP port 4500 are considered, but NAT is not what the document is about.
Mentioned only because the flow cache must be shared between UDP-encapsulated and plain flows; the document does not cover MOBIKE itself.

RFC5880.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)
RFC5880.summary: RFC 5880 specifies the base Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol: a low-overhead Hello-style mechanism for detecting forwarding-path failures between adjacent systems, covering packet formats, the state machine, modes, timers and authentication.

BFD.why: The document is the base specification of BFD, defining its control packets, state machine, Asynchronous and Demand modes, Echo function and authentication.
BFD.quote: The goal of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is to provide low-overhead, short-duration detection of failures in the path between adjacent forwarding engines

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an example application that may request a BFD session; the document does not specify or extend OSPF.
MD5 is used as one optional authentication digest and discouraged; the document is not about MD5 itself.
SHA1 is used as an authentication hash within BFD; the document does not specify or analyse SHA.
Mentioned only to explain that BFD uses a secret-suffix construction rather than HMAC.
BFD operates independently of routing protocols; the more specific BFD tag applies.
Authentication sections are a part of BFD's packet format, not a standalone treatment of authentication across protocols.

RFC5881.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for IPv4 and IPv6 (Single Hop)
RFC5881.summary: RFC 5881 specifies how BFD is used over IPv4 and IPv6 for single IP hops, covering UDP encapsulation (ports 3784/3785), TTL=255 checks, addressing, Echo function constraints and tunnel use.

BFD.why: The whole document defines the single-hop BFD application: session demultiplexing, encapsulation, TTL/Hop Limit handling, addressing and Echo rules.
BFD.quote: This document describes the use of the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol over IPv4 and IPv6 for single IP hops.

rejected.why: UDP is only the encapsulation for BFD packets. The document assigns ports but does not specify or extend UDP.
IPv4 and IPv6 are the network layers BFD runs over. The document does not define anything about them.
The text calls BFD an OAM mechanism in passing. The BFD tag already covers that.
There is a short section on using BFD to detect liveness of tunnels. It is not about tunnelling mechanisms.
IPv4 is only a substrate over which BFD runs. The document says nothing new about IPv4 itself.

RFC5882.title: Generic Application of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)
RFC5882.summary: Describes the generic application of BFD to client applications such as routing protocols and non-protocol functions, covering session state handling, graceful restart interactions, and non-normative examples for OSPF, IS-IS, BGP and RIP.

BFD.why: The whole document specifies how BFD sessions interact with client applications: hysteresis, AdminDown, adjacency establishment, graceful restart and multiple link subnetworks.
BFD.quote: This document describes the generic application of the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol.

rejected.why: Used only as a non-normative example of a BFD client in Section 10.1. The document is not about OSPF itself.
Section 10.2 gives an illustrative example of BFD with EBGP. BGP is a client and is not the subject.
Appears only as an example BFD client in Section 10.1.
Section 10.3 is a short illustrative example. The document does not specify RIP.
BFD is already covered by its own tag. The routing protocols are only examples of clients.
OAM is mentioned only briefly in Section 8 on tunnels and pseudowires. The BFD tag covers the document.

RFC5883.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for Multihop Paths
RFC5883.summary: Specifies how to use BFD over multihop paths and unidirectional links, covering session demultiplexing options, UDP port 4784 encapsulation, and authentication.

BFD.why: The document extends and profiles BFD for multihop paths, defining demultiplexing approaches, the multihop UDP port 4784 encapsulation and authentication guidance.
BFD.quote: This document describes the use of the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol over multihop paths, including unidirectional links.

rejected.why: OSPF Virtual Links are mentioned only as one use case for BFD; the document is not about OSPF.
BFD for MPLS LSPs is only cited as an example of out-of-band discriminator signaling; it is specified in another RFC.
UDP is merely the encapsulation substrate, and the document only assigns a port number for BFD multihop.
BFD is described as an OAM mechanism in the applicability section, but the BFD tag already covers this and the document is not about OAM in general.
IPv4/IPv6 are only the network layer over which BFD runs, so the document is not about IPv6.
TFRC is mentioned only as a reference for the TCP-friendly behavior required when BFD is used across the Internet.

RFC5884.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC5884.summary: Describes how BFD is applied to detect MPLS LSP data plane failures, using LSP Ping to bootstrap BFD sessions (via a new BFD Discriminator TLV) and defining encapsulation and demultiplexing procedures.

BFD.why: The document specifies procedures for running BFD sessions over MPLS LSPs: session establishment, discriminators, and encapsulation.
BFD.quote: One desirable application of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is to track the liveness of a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Path (LSP).

MPLS.why: It addresses MPLS LSP data plane fault detection, covering LSPs from LDP, RSVP-TE, VPN and pseudowire FECs, and its encapsulation in MPLS label stacks. It also complements LSP Ping, the MPLS OAM mechanism.
MPLS.quote: BFD can be used to detect a data plane failure in the forwarding path of an MPLS LSP.

rejected.why: Pseudowires are only one of several LSP types BFD can monitor. The document does not specify pseudowire emulation.
LDP FECs are one LSP type that can be monitored. The document does not specify LDP.
RSVP-TE tunnels are mentioned only as a FEC type that can be monitored.
UDP is only the encapsulation substrate for BFD Control packets, using ports 3784 and 4784.
The document is about OAM, but BFD and MPLS already cover the subject more specifically.
LSP Ping traceroute is used to discover alternate paths, but the document does not specify it.

gaps.name: LSP Ping (MPLS data plane failure detection, RFC 4379)
gaps.why: The document defines the BFD Discriminator TLV for LSP Ping and bootstraps BFD sessions with it. The taxonomy has no LSP Ping or MPLS OAM tag, only the broad MPLS tag.

RFC5885.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for the Pseudowire Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV)
RFC5885.summary: Defines four new BFD Connectivity Verification types (IP/UDP and PW-ACH encapsulated, with or without status signaling) for use over the pseudowire VCCV control channel, including selection rules and IANA registrations.

BFD.why: The document specifies how BFD is applied over VCCV, with new CV Types, encapsulations and session-bootstrap procedures for pseudowires.
BFD.quote: BFD [RFC5880] is used over the VCCV control channel primarily as a pseudowire fault detection mechanism, for detecting data-plane failures.

pseudowire.why: VCCV is the pseudowire OAM control channel; the document extends it with BFD CV Types, capability selection and PW-ACH channel type, so pseudowire readers need it.
pseudowire.quote: VCCV provides a control channel that is associated with a pseudowire (PW), as well as the corresponding operations and management functions

rejected.why: MPLS PW demultiplexers and the PW-ACH are used, but the document is about pseudowire OAM, not MPLS itself.
L2TPv3 is one of two supported PW demultiplexers and has an IANA registry addition, but is not the subject.
UDP/IP encapsulation of BFD is borrowed from RFC 5881; it is substrate only.
The document is OAM-related, but the specific BFD and pseudowire tags cover it more precisely.
IANA registrations are boilerplate-like and not the main subject.

RFC5886.title: A Set of Monitoring Tools for Path Computation Element (PCE)-Based Architecture
RFC5886.summary: RFC 5886 extends PCEP with new messages (PCMonReq/PCMonRep) and objects (MONITORING, PCE-ID, PROC-TIME, OVERLOAD) to monitor liveness, processing time and overload along a PCE path computation chain.

PCE.why: The document defines new PCEP messages and objects for monitoring PCEs in the PCE architecture, so it is squarely about PCE/PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document specifies procedures and extensions to the Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) in order to gather such information.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part defines gathering state and performance metrics (processing time statistics, overload, liveness) for PCEs, which is a monitoring/performance-measurement topic.
performance measurement.quote: liveness of each element (PCE) involved in the PCE chain and detection of potential resource contention states and statistics in terms of path computation times

rejected.why: TE LSPs in MPLS/GMPLS are the computation target, but the document is about monitoring PCEs, not MPLS itself.
Mentioned only as the network context for the LSPs being computed.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering; the document does not address TE in its own right.
Monitoring of the control-plane path computation chain is not OAM of a data-plane path; performance measurement fits better.
Only a passing remark that a MIB module may be defined in the future.
Not relevant; BRPC is referenced only as an example of a path computation chain.

RFC5887.title: Renumbering Still Needs Work
RFC5887.summary: Informational review of existing IPv4 and IPv6 site renumbering mechanisms, their operational issues, proposed new mechanisms, and a gap analysis for future work.

renumbering.why: The whole document is about site renumbering procedures, issues and gaps, which is exactly the renumbering topic.
renumbering.quote: This document reviews the existing mechanisms for site renumbering for both IPv4 and IPv6, and it identifies operational issues with those mechanisms.

DHCP.why: DHCP/DHCPv6 lease lifetimes, FORCERENEW/RECONFIGURE and prefix delegation are substantial renumbering mechanisms discussed and analysed.
DHCP.quote: DHCP [RFC2131] [RFC3315] offers similar support for renumbering for both versions of IP.

SLAAC.why: SLAAC and RA prefix lifetimes, plus the M/O flag ambiguity, are analysed as core renumbering mechanisms.
SLAAC.quote: setting a preferred lifetime that is zero or finite is SLAAC's warning that renumbering will occur.

rejected.why: Secure Dynamic DNS Update is discussed as a renumbering tool, but only as one subsection and a gap item; the document is not about it.
Shim6 is summarised as a proposed mechanism in a short subsection; not a substantial subject of the document.
IPv6 is the main context, but more specific tags apply and the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Mentioned as needed for secure renumbering and deployment momentum, but only briefly.
NAT state issues are a short subsection; NAT is not the document's subject.
Mentioned as a way to reduce address dependence, only briefly.

gaps.name: Renumbering
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists renumbering only as a topic under addressing; I used that id. I could not confirm the id is exactly 'renumbering', so verify it before applying.

RFC5888.title: The Session Description Protocol (SDP) Grouping Framework
RFC5888.summary: Defines the SDP grouping framework with the "group" and "mid" attributes, plus the LS (lip synchronization) and FID (flow identification) semantics and their use in SIP offer/answer.

SDP.why: The document defines new SDP attributes (group, mid), grouping semantics and a registry, and extends SDP itself.
SDP.quote: we define a framework to group "m" lines in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) for different purposes

SIP.why: A substantial section specifies how group/mid behave in SIP offer/answer, including answers, capability negotiation and backward compatibility.
SIP.quote: SIP systems MUST perform media alignment matching nth lines regardless of the presence of the "group" or "mid" attributes.

rejected.why: RTP sessions and RTCP are discussed as the media context for synchronization and flows, but RTP itself is not specified or extended.
Only mentioned as the usual mechanism for lip synchronization; not the subject of the document.
AMR and GSM appear only as codecs in FID examples.
The registry for group semantics is boilerplate IANA considerations and not the document's main subject.
ABNF is used only to write the attribute syntax.

RFC5889.title: IP Addressing Model in Ad Hoc Networks
RFC5889.summary: Informational model for configuring IP addresses and subnet prefixes on router interfaces attached to links with undetermined connectivity (ad hoc networks): unique addresses within the routing domain and no on-link prefix (IPv6) or /32 prefix (IPv4).

addressing.why: The whole document gives principles and IPv6/IPv4 rules for assigning addresses and subnet prefixes on interfaces, which is IP address architecture and use.
addressing.quote: a model for configuration of IP addresses and subnet prefixes on router interfaces to links with undetermined connectivity properties

MANET.why: The model targets routers in ad hoc networks so that ad hoc routing protocols can function. The document does not specify a particular MANET routing protocol, so the parent tag fits.
MANET.quote: Ad hoc networks are typical examples of networks with undetermined link-level connectivity.

rejected.why: IPv6 is covered only as one of two cases of the addressing model, and the document is not about IPv6 itself.
IPv4 is covered only as one of two cases of the addressing model, and the document is not about IPv4 itself.
The document discusses autoconfiguration only in general and does not specify or analyse SLAAC.
CIDR is cited only for terminology.
The document says addressing is a prerequisite for routing protocols but does not address routing architecture.

RFC5890.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework
RFC5890.summary: RFC 5890 is the definitions and document-framework RFC for IDNA2008, giving the road map of the IDNA2008 document set and defining terms such as LDH label, A-label, U-label, NR-LDH label, ACE prefix and domain name slot.

IDN.why: The whole document defines IDNA2008 terminology and the document set. IDN is the specific tag for IDNA, punycode and label validity.
IDN.quote: An "internationalized domain name" (IDN) is a domain name that contains at least one A-label or U-label

rejected.why: The document assumes DNS and its terminology but does not specify or extend DNS. IDN is the more specific tag and sits under DNS.
Unicode is the character set that U-labels use. The document defines IDNA label terms and does not address how Unicode is used in protocols in general.
LDH label syntax is described in relation to hostname rules, but only as background for the IDNA definitions.
TLS appears only in a Security Considerations aside about local character sets.

RFC5891.title: Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA): Protocol
RFC5891.summary: RFC 5891 specifies the IDNA2008 protocol, defining registration and lookup procedures for internationalized domain labels (U-labels/A-labels via Punycode) without changes to the DNS, obsoleting RFC 3490 and 3491.

IDN.why: The document is the core IDNA2008 protocol definition, covering registration and lookup validation, A-label/U-label handling and Punycode conversion.
IDN.quote: This document specifies the protocol mechanism, called Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA), for registering and looking up IDNs in a way that does not require changes to the DNS itself.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; IDNA explicitly requires no changes to DNS servers, resolvers or protocol elements.
Unicode normalization and code point categories are used, but the code point tables and rules are in separate RFCs (5892, 5893); this document is about the domain name protocol.
Registry label validation is covered, but only as part of the IDNA protocol; registrar/registry operations are out of scope.
IDN is the more specific tag; the document is about domain labels, not general internationalized text.
URIs and IRIs are mentioned only as sources of domain names for lookup input.

RFC5892.title: The Unicode Code Points and Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA)
RFC5892.summary: RFC 5892 specifies the IDNA2008 algorithm and categories for deriving each Unicode code point's property value (PVALID, CONTEXTJ, CONTEXTO, DISALLOWED, UNASSIGNED) for use in internationalized domain name labels, plus a contextual rules registry.

IDN.why: The document is part of the IDNA2008 specification and defines which code points may appear in IDN labels, including the contextual rules registry.
IDN.quote: This document specifies rules for deciding whether a code point, considered in isolation or in context, is a candidate for inclusion in an Internationalized Domain Name (IDN).

rejected.why: The document leans heavily on Unicode properties, but its purpose is IDN code point eligibility, not Unicode usage in general. IDN is the more specific home for it.
IDNs are DNS labels, but the document does not specify DNS protocol, records or resolver behaviour.
It creates the derived property and context registries, but this is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the subject of the document.
The document is about code point properties and normalization, not the UTF-8 encoding.

RFC5893.title: Right-to-Left Scripts for Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA)
RFC5893.summary: RFC 5893 defines the Bidi rule for IDNA2008 U-labels containing right-to-left scripts, replacing the IDNA2003 stringprep Bidi criterion, with requirements, examples (Dhivehi, Yiddish), and compatibility discussion.

IDN.why: The document specifies an additional validity rule for IDNA2008 labels in right-to-left scripts, part of the revised IDNA protocol.
IDN.quote: The purpose of this document is to establish a rule that can be applied to Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) labels in Unicode form (U-labels)

Unicode.why: The rule is defined entirely in terms of Unicode Bidi properties and the Unicode bidirectional algorithm, and addresses display of Unicode text in labels.
Unicode.quote: The terminology used for the Bidi properties of Unicode characters is taken from the Unicode Standard

rejected.why: DNS is only the context where the labels are used; the document defines no DNS protocol behavior (DNAME and wildcards are mentioned only in passing).
The parent topic is implied by the more specific Unicode tag, and the main subject is IDN, so it is not listed separately.
Stringprep (RFC 3454) is discussed only as the IDNA2003 predecessor being replaced, not PRECIS.
The document concerns Bidi properties of Unicode characters, not character set registration.

gaps.name: Bidirectional text (Bidi) display of right-to-left scripts
gaps.why: The document is about the Bidi rule and the Unicode bidirectional algorithm's effect on label display; the taxonomy has no tag specifically for bidi or RTL text handling.

RFC5894.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Background, Explanation, and Rationale
RFC5894.summary: Informational rationale document for IDNA2008, explaining the revised Internationalized Domain Names framework: the inclusion-based character categories, registration vs lookup, mapping removal, Unicode version independence, and migration from IDNA2003.

IDN.why: The whole document explains the background and rationale of IDNA2008 (A-labels, U-labels, Punycode, character tables, migration from IDNA2003), which is exactly the IDN subject.
IDN.quote: Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) is a collection of standards that allow client applications to convert some mnemonic strings expressed in Unicode to an ASCII-compatible encoding form

rejected.why: IDNA explicitly does not extend or change DNS; DNS is the substrate for A-label lookup. Name server considerations are a brief section only.
Unicode properties drive the character rules, but the document is about IDNA's use of them as an IDN mechanism; IDN is the more specific home. Considered but not tagged.
Registry policy and registration-versus-lookup are discussed, but as part of IDNA rules, not registry operations or protocols.
Mentioned only in passing in the root server considerations section.
IRIs appear only as an example of display order issues for IDNs.

RFC5895.title: Mapping Characters for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) 2008
RFC5895.summary: RFC 5895 describes a user-interface mapping (case folding, fullwidth/halfwidth mapping, NFC, ideographic full stop) applied to user input before it is passed to the IDNA2008 protocol, and cautions that it is not a universal algorithm.

IDN.why: The whole document is about preparing user input for IDNA2008 and how it differs from IDNA2003, so a reader browsing IDN would expect it.
IDN.quote: This document describes the operations that can be applied to user input in order to get it into a form that is acceptable by the Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) protocol

Unicode.why: The mapping steps are Unicode operations (lowercase mapping, width decomposition, NFC normalization) from the Unicode Character Database, applied to text in an Internet protocol context.
Unicode.quote: All characters are mapped using Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC).

rejected.why: DNS is only the downstream system that receives the encoded labels. The document defines no DNS behaviour.
This is the parent of Unicode. Unicode is the more specific tag and already covers it.
No encoding of text as UTF-8 is discussed.
The document is about IDNA mapping, not the PRECIS framework for internationalized strings.

RFC5896.title: Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API): Delegate if Approved by Policy
RFC5896.summary: Extends GSS-API with a deleg_policy_req_flag/deleg_policy_state and GSS_C_DELEG_POLICY_FLAG so initiators delegate credentials only when central policy approves, and specifies Kerberos OK-AS-DELEGATE behavior including cross-realm handling.

GSS-API.why: The document extends the GSS-API (RFC 2743) with a new flag, output state, and C binding constant, and specifies the resulting API behavior.
GSS-API.quote: This specification adds a new input flag to gss_init_sec_context() to request delegation when approved by central policy.

Kerberos.why: A substantial section defines Kerberos mechanism behavior for OK-AS-DELEGATE and clarifies cross-realm handling, updating RFC 4120 semantics.
Kerberos.quote: the Kerberos GSS-API mechanism MUST only delegate if OK-AS-DELEGATE is set [RFC4120] in the service ticket.

rejected.why: Delegation policy is a part of this, but the document is about the GSS-API flag and the Kerberos mechanism, which the more specific tags already cover.
Authentication mechanisms are only the context; the document specifies credential delegation behavior in GSS-API and Kerberos.

RFC5897.title: Identification of Communications Services in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5897.summary: Informational RFC that analyses service identification in SIP, argues declarative service identifiers cause fraud, interoperability failure and stifled innovation, and recommends deriving service identity from signaling (Request-URI, content types, feature tags).

SIP.why: The whole document is architectural guidance on how SIP signaling should identify services, covering Request-URI use, feature tags, and device dispatch.
SIP.quote: This document considers the problem of service identification in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

rejected.why: SDP content is used as signaling evidence for deriving services, but the document does not specify or extend SDP.
MSRP and the SIP MESSAGE method appear only as examples in service scenarios.
IPTV is only one example service, and the document explicitly says whether SIP suits IPTV is out of scope.
QoS authorization is just one use of a service identifier, discussed briefly in Section 4.3.
The emergency URN is cited once as a fraud-avoidance example, so the document is not about emergency calling.
Presence is recommended as a source of service URIs, but only in a short section (7.3). The document does not cover presence specifications.

RFC5898.title: Connectivity Preconditions for Session Description Protocol (SDP) Media Streams
RFC5898.summary: Defines a new "conn" connectivity precondition type for the SIP/SDP preconditions framework, delaying session setup until media stream connectivity is verified (via ICE, TCP connection establishment, etc.).

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP precondition type with its syntax, status type, direction tags and strength semantics, extending SDP offer/answer.
SDP.quote: This document defines a new connectivity precondition for the Session Description Protocol (SDP) precondition framework.

SIP.why: The precondition extends the SIP preconditions framework (RFC 3312/4032). It affects INVITE, UPDATE and 183 and 180 handling, and it registers a SIP precondition type.
SIP.quote: The concept of a Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] precondition in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [RFC3261] is defined in RFC 3312

ICE.why: A substantial section defines how ICE full and lite implementations ascertain send and recv connectivity for the precondition. One of the two examples uses ICE, and ICE support is RECOMMENDED.
ICE.quote: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) [RFC5245] provides one or more candidate addresses in signaling between the offerer and the answerer

rejected.why: TCP connection establishment is used as an implicit verification mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
STUN Binding Requests are used only as part of ICE checks and are not themselves specified here.
NAT traversal is mentioned as a motivation, but the document is about preconditions. The ICE tag already covers the traversal aspect.
SCTP is mentioned only in one sentence, which says it should be treated like TCP.
RTP and RTCP connectivity is mentioned only as a detail of verification. The document does not specify RTP.

gaps.name: SDP preconditions framework
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SIP/SDP preconditions. The SDP and SIP tags are the closest fit.

RFC5901.title: Extensions to the IODEF-Document Class for Reporting Phishing
RFC5901.summary: RFC 5901 defines a PhraudReport XML extension to the IODEF-Document format (RFC 5070) for reporting phishing and fraud events, covering lure sources, collection sites, sensors, takedown and archived data.

IODEF.why: The document is an extension of the IODEF data model, defining the PhraudReport element within IODEF AdditionalData.
IODEF.quote: This document extends the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) defined in RFC 5070 to support the reporting of phishing events

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are the encoding substrate for the extension, not the subject.
Phishing lures arrive by email, but the document is about incident reporting, not spam filtering or reputation.
Email is only the lure transport and the EmailRecord element carries a message. The document does not specify email.
DNS data such as nameservers and domain data is recorded in reports, but DNS itself is not specified or extended.
Implied as the parent of IODEF, so not listed separately.

gaps.name: Phishing / fraud reporting
gaps.why: The document's subject is phishing and e-crime event reporting. The taxonomy has no tag for phishing or fraud, so only the IODEF extension angle is covered.

RFC5902.title: IAB Thoughts on IPv6 Network Address Translation
RFC5902.summary: IAB document discussing the architectural issues, pros and cons of IPv6 NAT, and the solution space for renumbering, multihoming and homogeneous edge configuration, recommending end-to-end transparency as a requirement.

NAT.why: The whole document analyses whether and how IPv6 NAT should exist, its benefits, harms to transparency, and obfuscation/security claims.
NAT.quote: This document articulates the architectural issues raised by IPv6 NATs, the pros and cons of having IPv6 NATs

multihoming.why: Site multihoming and routing scalability is one of the key problems NAT is used for and a substantial part of the solution-space discussion.
multihoming.quote: A multihomed site essentially requires that its IP prefixes be present in the global routing table to achieve the desired reliability

renumbering.why: Avoiding renumbering is a major motivation analysed, and the solution space is framed around renumbering and multihoming.
renumbering.quote: the ability to change service providers with minimal operational difficulty is an important requirement in many networks

internet architecture.why: The document argues from end-to-end transparency principles and whether NAT should be a permanent architectural building block.
internet architecture.quote: We believe that the discussions on IPv6 NAT should be put in the context of the overall Internet architecture.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the context, but the document is about NAT rather than specifying or deploying IPv6 itself; NAT sits under the more specific tag.
Firewalls are contrasted with NAT briefly in 2.5 and 3, but not a substantial subject.
Only mentioned as a mechanism that fails with complex NATs.
Only mentioned in passing as failing with complex NATs.
The document concerns IPv6 NAT (IPv6-to-IPv6), not IPv4/IPv6 coexistence mechanisms.
Host counting and topology hiding are discussed, but as network obfuscation, not a privacy threat model.

gaps.name: Internet transparency / end-to-end principle
gaps.why: The document's central argument is about end-to-end transparency, which fits only loosely under internet architecture.

RFC5903.title: Elliptic Curve Groups modulo a Prime (ECP Groups) for IKE and IKEv2
RFC5903.summary: Defines three NIST-curve ECP Diffie-Hellman groups (256, 384, 521-bit; P-256/P-384/P-521) for IKE and IKEv2, with key exchange data formats and test vectors, obsoleting RFC 4753 with a shared-secret format correction.

elliptic curve.why: The document specifies elliptic curve groups modulo a prime (curve parameters, generators, point encodings, test vectors) and aligns them with NIST/SECG curves.
elliptic curve.quote: This document describes three Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) groups for use in the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) and Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) protocols

IKE.why: It defines new Diffie-Hellman groups for IKE/IKEv2, their KE payload formats, shared secret computation and IANA code points.
IKE.quote: IKE and IKEv2 implementations SHOULD support an ECP group with the following characteristics.

rejected.why: The curves are used for Diffie-Hellman key exchange, not signatures; ECDSA is only mentioned in reference titles.
IKE is the specific subject; IPsec is only the broader context and parent.
SHA-1 is only used to verifiably generate curve seeds.
AES is cited only for security-strength comparison.
IANA registry update is boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA stewardship.

RFC5904.title: RADIUS Attributes for IEEE 802.16 Privacy Key Management Version 1 (PKMv1) Protocol Support
RFC5904.summary: Defines seven RADIUS attributes (PKM-SS-Cert, PKM-CA-Cert, PKM-Config-Settings, PKM-Cryptosuite-List, PKM-SAID, PKM-SA-Descriptor, PKM-Auth-Key) to carry IEEE 802.16 PKMv1 authentication and key material between a RADIUS client and server.

RADIUS.why: The document's purpose is defining new RADIUS attributes, with type codes, formats, and packet-presence rules, which is an extension of RADIUS.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines a set of Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Attributes that are designed to provide RADIUS support for IEEE 802.16 Privacy Key Management Version 1.

WiMAX.why: The attributes exist to support IEEE 802.16 PKMv1 between Subscriber Station and Base Station, so readers on IP over 802.16 would want it.
WiMAX.quote: public-key-based authentication and key establishment protocol typically used in fixed wireless broadband network deployments.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are only carried as opaque data fragmented across attributes. The document does not profile them.
RSA is only the mechanism used to encrypt the AUTH-Key as IEEE 802.16 requires. The document defines nothing new about it.
RFC 3579 (RADIUS EAP support) is referenced only for Message-Authenticator. The document does not use EAP.
The Diameter section only notes that no special handling is needed because the attributes are in the standard RADIUS type space.
PKMv1 key handling is the subject, but the document only defines RADIUS attributes to carry it. The AUTH-Key protection is a minor subsection.

RFC5905.title: Network Time Protocol Version 4: Protocol and Algorithms Specification
RFC5905.summary: RFC 5905 specifies NTPv4, the Network Time Protocol: packet format, on-wire protocol, peer/system/poll processes, clock filter, selection, cluster, combine and clock discipline algorithms, SNTP subset, and a code skeleton.

NTP.why: The whole document specifies NTPv4: modes, packet header, on-wire protocol, mitigation and clock discipline algorithms, and the SNTP subset.
NTP.quote: This document defines the Network Time Protocol version 4 (NTPv4), which is widely used to synchronize system clocks among a set of distributed time servers and clients.

rejected.why: NTP packets are carried in UDP datagrams on port 123, but UDP is only the substrate.
MD5 is used only for the symmetric-key MAC; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The parent of NTP is implied by the NTP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The refid field is adapted for IPv6 addresses, but this is a minor header detail and the document is not about IPv6.
Broadcast and manycast modes use multicast addresses, but this is only an operating mode of NTP, not multicast routing or deployment.
The IANA registries for extension field types, reference IDs and kiss codes are boilerplate-level sections, not the main subject.

RFC5906.title: Network Time Protocol Version 4: Autokey Specification
RFC5906.summary: Informational specification of the NTPv4 Autokey security protocol, which authenticates NTP servers to clients using public-key certificates, identity schemes (IFF, GQ, MV), and hash-chained autokey sequences, including message formats and state machines.

NTP.why: The document specifies a security extension to NTPv4: extension fields, client/server/broadcast/symmetric dances, and state machine. It belongs on the NTP page.
NTP.quote: This memo describes the Autokey security model for authenticating servers to clients using the Network Time Protocol (NTP) and public key cryptography.

key management.why: A substantial part covers cookie exchange, autokey key lists, key IDs, and group key distribution by a trusted authority, which is key establishment and provisioning.
key management.quote: Autokey uses specially contrived session keys, called autokeys, and a precomputed pseudo-random sequence of autokeys that are saved in the autokey list.

authentication.why: The document's core purpose is server-to-client authentication, with challenge-response identity schemes and certificate trails.
authentication.quote: Reliability requires that clients can determine that received packets are authentic; that is, were actually sent by the intended server

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an approach deemed unsuitable; not specified or profiled.
Certificates are used and extension fields described, but the document is not about the X.509 profile itself.
PKI is a mechanism relied on; the document defines an NTP-specific trust model, not general PKI.
DER encoding is used for value fields but only as an encoding apparatus in appendices.
RSA/DSA keys are used as building blocks; the document takes no position on algorithms.
MD5 is used to hash autokeys but only as a substrate component.

RFC5907.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Network Time Protocol Version 4 (NTPv4)
RFC5907.summary: Defines the NTPv4-MIB SNMP MIB module for monitoring and managing NTP entities, including status, associations, control objects and notifications.

NTP.why: The MIB models the NTP entity: its stratum, associations, offsets, leap seconds and packet counters. Readers of the NTP subject would want it.
NTP.quote: The NTPv4 MIB module is designed to allow Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) to be used to monitor and manage local NTP [RFC5905] entities.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module (NTPv4-MIB) written in SMIv2, with objects, tables, notifications and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB. The document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the more specific MIB tag, and does not extend SNMP itself.
This is the parent of NTP and is implied by the NTP tag.
The MIB only supports IPv6 addresses in association objects through InetAddress. That is incidental.

RFC5908.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP) Server Option for DHCPv6
RFC5908.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 OPTION_NTP_SERVER option and its suboptions (unicast address, multicast address, FQDN) to deliver NTPv4/SNTP server location to DHCPv6 clients, and deprecates RFC 4075.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option with suboptions, its format, message appearance rules and IANA registry, so DHCPv6 readers need it.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines a DHCPv6 option and associated suboptions to provide Network Time Protocol version 4 [RFC5905] or greater server location information to DHCPv6 hosts.

NTP.why: The option configures NTP/SNTP clients with servers or multicast groups, and the document discusses NTP usage and server load. Readers of NTP would want to find the configuration mechanism.
NTP.quote: This option serves as a container for server location information related to one NTP server or Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) [RFC4330] server.

rejected.why: The FQDN suboption relies on DNS encoding and DNS indirection for misconfiguration mitigation, but the document defines nothing new about DNS.
Uses IPv6 addresses in suboptions, but only as the carried data; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The multicast address suboption carries an NTP multicast group address, but the document does not address multicast routing or deployment.
SEND is mentioned only as an example of a security protocol that depends on time in the Security Considerations.

RFC5909.title: Securing Neighbor Discovery Proxy: Problem Statement
RFC5909.summary: Problem statement describing why IPv6 Neighbor Discovery proxying (Mobile IPv6 Home Agent proxy, bridge-like ND Proxy) cannot be secured with SEND/CGA, and outlining potential approaches such as delegation certificates.

SEND.why: The whole document analyses how proxy ND conflicts with SEND (CGA signatures, authorization delegation, timestamps) and sketches approaches to securing it.
SEND.quote: Neighbor Discovery Proxy currently cannot be secured using Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND).

neighbor discovery.why: ND Proxy behaviour (RFC 4389 bridge-like proxies, proxy NA/DAD/RA) is analysed in detail. Mostly it is covered through SEND, but it is a substantial subject in its own right.
neighbor discovery.quote: Neighbor Discovery Proxy relies upon another device, the proxy, to monitor for Neighbor Solicitations (NSs), and answer with Neighbor Advertisements (NAs).

Mobile IPv6.why: The Home Agent proxy scenario is one of the two main use cases, with its own section on approaches (4.1) for Mobile IPv6.
Mobile IPv6.quote: In Mobile IPv6, the role of the proxy is undertaken by the Home Agent.
Mobile IPv6.section: 2.1. IPv6 Mobile Nodes and Neighbor Discovery Proxy

rejected.why: Certificates are mentioned as a delegation mechanism only; the document is not about X.509 profiles.
IKEv2 is only a scenario where a security gateway assigns an address to be proxied.
Only briefly mentioned in Section 5 as a case of several nodes defending one address.
A passing mention in Section 5; the document is not about anycast.
Delegation certificates are discussed but only as a means for SEND authorization, not as PKI in itself.

gaps.name: CGA (Cryptographically Generated Addresses)
gaps.why: The document centres on CGA-based signatures and ownership proofs, but the taxonomy has no CGA tag. SEND is the closest fit.

RFC5910.title: Domain Name System (DNS) Security Extensions Mapping for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC5910.summary: Defines the secDNS-1.1 EPP extension to the domain name mapping for provisioning DNSSEC delegation signer (DS) and key data in a registry, obsoleting RFC 4310.

EPP.why: The document specifies an EPP extension (secDNS-1.1) extending the domain mapping with create, update and info elements.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension mapping for the provisioning and management of Domain Name System security (DNSSEC) extensions

DNSSEC.why: The extension carries DS and DNSKEY data and maxSigLife for DNSSEC secure delegations, so DNSSEC readers would want it.
DNSSEC.quote: Information exchanged via this mapping can be extracted from the repository and used to publish DNSSEC Delegation Signer (DS) resource records

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the specification notation for the mapping.
DNS records are referenced but the document is about registry provisioning, not DNS protocol behaviour.
Implied as the parent of EPP; the child tag EPP is more specific.
IANA section only registers the namespace and schema; boilerplate.

RFC5911.title: New ASN.1 Modules for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and S/MIME
RFC5911.summary: Republishes the ASN.1 modules for CMS, S/MIME, ESS, CMS AES/AuthEnveloped/firmware/ERS/symmetric key distribution in 2002-version ASN.1, with a common AlgorithmInformation module and no bits-on-the-wire changes.

CMS.why: The core of the document is the CMS ASN.1 module (SignedData, EnvelopedData, etc.) plus CMS algorithm, AES, authenticated-enveloped, firmware and key distribution modules.
CMS.quote: This document updates those ASN.1 modules to conform to the 2002 version of ASN.1.

ASN.1.why: The document's purpose is converting 1988 ASN.1 modules to 2002 ASN.1 with information object classes.
ASN.1.quote: The modules in this document use the object model available in the 2002 ASN.1 documents to a great extent.

S/MIME.why: Includes the S/MIME message module (capabilities, encryption key preference) and ESS module for S/MIME.
S/MIME.quote: RFC 3851, S/MIME Version 3.1 Message Specification [RFC3851]

rejected.why: AES CBC/CCM/GCM/wrap identifiers are only transcribed into modules; the document is not about the cipher.
PKIX modules are imported from RFC 5912, not specified here.
The ERS module is included but is a small part, only an ASN.1 conversion.
The firmware wrapper module is one conversion among many and not the document's subject.

RFC5912.title: New ASN.1 Modules for the Public Key Infrastructure Using X.509 (PKIX)
RFC5912.summary: Informational RFC that rewrites the ASN.1 modules for PKIX (certificates, CRLs, OCSP, CMP, CRMF, CMC, SCVP, attribute certificates, PKCS#10, algorithm definitions) from 1988 to 2002 ASN.1 syntax with no change to the encodings on the wire.

ASN.1.why: The whole document is a set of ASN.1 modules using the 2002 information object class syntax, so a reader of ASN.1 modules would want it.
ASN.1.quote: This document updates those ASN.1 modules to conform to the 2002 version of ASN.1.

X.509.why: It supplies the ASN.1 for the RFC 5280 certificate and CRL profile (explicit and implicit modules), attribute certificates, and the algorithm identifier modules.
X.509.quote: The Public Key Infrastructure using X.509 (PKIX) certificate format, and many associated formats, are expressed using ASN.1.

PKI.why: Also covers modules for CMP, CRMF, CMC, SCVP and PKCS#10 requests, the PKIX management and validation protocols.
PKI.quote: RFC 4210, PKIX CMP (Certificate Management Protocol) [RFC4210]

OCSP.why: Section 4 gives a full updated ASN.1 module for OCSP requests and responses.
OCSP.quote: RFC 2560, PKIX Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) [RFC2560]

rejected.why: CMS and S/MIME modules are in the companion RFC 5911; here CMS is only imported.
RSA OAEP/PSS algorithm objects appear only as part of the RFC 4055 module, not as the document's subject.
The EC and ECDSA algorithm objects are incidental entries in the RFC 3279/5480 algorithm module.
The algorithm class definitions are ASN.1 syntax machinery, not cryptographic specification.
S/MIME capabilities appear only as a class definition; the S/MIME modules are in RFC 5911.

RFC5913.title: Clearance Attribute and Authority Clearance Constraints Certificate Extension
RFC5913.summary: Defines the X.509 Clearance attribute and the Authority Clearance Constraints certificate extension, and the certification path processing rules for computing a subject's effective clearance in public key and attribute certificates.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 certificate attribute and extension and augments RFC 5280 and RFC 5755 certification path validation, so it belongs under X.509 certificates and profiles.
X.509.quote: This document defines the syntax and semantics for the Clearance attribute and the Authority Clearance Constraints extension in X.509 certificates.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the structures in the body and Appendix A. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The parent of X.509. The document is about X.509 certificate extensions specifically, so the child tag is the more specific fit.
Clearance is authorization information held by the subject, but the document specifies certificate syntax and path processing, not an access control framework. The X.509 tag already covers it.
RFC 3114 is cited only as an example of a security policy. The document does not define security labels for networked data.
RFC 3114 on S/MIME security labels is mentioned only as an informative example.

RFC5914.title: Trust Anchor Format
RFC5914.summary: Defines the TrustAnchorInfo ASN.1 structure and TrustAnchorList for representing PKIX trust anchors (public key, name, and certification path controls), optionally carried in CMS SignedData.

PKI.why: The document specifies a trust anchor format used to initialize X.509 certification path validation, which is core PKI subject matter. No narrower PKI child tag fits, since the document is neither a certificate profile nor a status or enrollment protocol.
PKI.quote: This document describes a structure for representing trust anchor information. A trust anchor is an authoritative entity represented by a public key and associated data.

X.509.why: A substantial part of the document defines how name constraints, policy flags and path length constraints replace or supplement X.509 certificate extensions, and TrustAnchorChoice can carry a Certificate or TBSCertificate.
X.509.quote: it provides the controls needed to initialize an X.509 certification path validation algorithm implementation

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the structure. The document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules as a subject.
CMS SignedData is mentioned only as a way to protect a TrustAnchorList. It is a substrate here, and the document defines only a content type OID.
UTF8String is used for the title field and is not the subject of the document.
The language tag field is a minor detail of the title and does not make the document about language tags.

gaps.name: Trust anchor management / trust anchor format
gaps.why: The document is specifically about trust anchor representation. The taxonomy has no trust anchor tag, so PKI is the closest fit.

RFC5915.title: Elliptic Curve Private Key Structure
RFC5915.summary: Defines the ASN.1 ECPrivateKey structure (version, privateKey, parameters, publicKey) for conveying elliptic curve private keys, e.g. inside PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo, with encoding and PEM storage notes.

elliptic curve.why: The whole document defines how EC private keys, their named-curve parameters and optional public keys are represented, so it is about elliptic curve cryptography.
elliptic curve.quote: This document specifies a syntax and semantics for Elliptic Curve (EC) private key information.

ASN.1.why: The specification is an ASN.1 type with an ASN.1 module in Appendix A, and it sets DER/BER encoding requirements. This is a substantial part of the document.
ASN.1.quote: EC private key information SHALL have ASN.1 type ECPrivateKey:

rejected.why: PKCS #8 and PKIX appear only as context and as the carrier for the structure. The document does not specify PKI operations.
It reuses RFC 5480 types and PKIX ASN.1 modules, but it defines no certificates or certificate profiles.
The PEM encoding of the key is mentioned only as a common local storage format, and it is out of scope. The document is not about the historic PEM secure email system.
Base64 is only the encoding used inside the PEM armor, so it is a substrate here.
The document defines a key container for any EC key and does not specify the ECDSA algorithm.

RFC5916.title: Device Owner Attribute
RFC5916.summary: Defines the Device Owner attribute, an OID-valued attribute identifying the entity that owns a device, for inclusion in X.509 public key certificates and attribute certificates, with its ASN.1 definition.

X.509.why: The document defines a new attribute for X.509 public key and attribute certificates, extending the certificate profile content that PKIX readers need.
X.509.quote: This attribute is intended to be used in public key certificates [RFC5280] and attribute certificates [RFC5755].

ASN.1.why: The attribute is specified via an ASN.1 object identifier and information object definition, with a normative ASN.1 module in the appendix.
ASN.1.quote: The ASN.1 syntax for the Device Owner attribute is as follows:

rejected.why: The attribute may feed authorization decisions, but the document only defines the attribute; the approved-list mechanism is out of scope.
The document explicitly does not define an LDAP schema; it is deferred to future work.
X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers the certificate attribute.

RFC5917.title: Clearance Sponsor Attribute
RFC5917.summary: Defines the clearance sponsor attribute (an ASN.1-defined UTF8 DirectoryString with OID) for X.509 public key certificates and attribute certificates, naming the entity that granted the subject's clearance.

X.509.why: The document defines a new attribute for X.509 public key and attribute certificates, extending the certificate profile, so readers of X.509 would want it.
X.509.quote: It is included in public key certificates [RFC5280] and attribute certificates [RFC5755].

ASN.1.why: A substantial part of the document is the normative ASN.1 module and attribute definition with OID, in Appendix A.
ASN.1.quote: The attribute is defined using ASN.1 [X.680], [X.681], [X.682], and [X.683].

rejected.why: The attribute may feed authorization decisions, but the document only defines a certificate attribute; authorization is a use, not the subject.
It uses DirectoryString and caseIgnoreMatch from X.500, but explicitly leaves LDAP schema to future work; directory is only a dependency.
Implied by X.509 parent; the more specific X.509 tag is used.
X.520 types are imported as building blocks only; no X.500 directory service is specified.
UTF8String is merely required for the value; the document is not about the encoding.
The document explicitly does not provide an LDAP schema.

RFC5918.title: Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) 'Typed Wildcard' Forward Equivalence Class (FEC)
RFC5918.summary: RFC 5918 defines the LDP Typed Wildcard FEC Element, its procedures in Label Request/Withdraw/Release messages, and a new LDP capability to advertise support for it.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with a new FEC element type, procedures, and a new capability TLV. LDP is the protocol it specifies extensions to.
LDP.quote: This document addresses those limitations by defining a Typed Wildcard FEC Element and associated procedures.

rejected.why: LDP sits under MPLS, and the more specific LDP tag already covers this. The document is not about MPLS architecture generally.
RFC 4447 is cited only as an example of another FEC type. The document does not address pseudowires.
CR-LDP is a different LDP-related signalling protocol, and this document does not deal with it.

RFC5919.title: Signaling LDP Label Advertisement Completion
RFC5919.summary: Specifies an LDP End-of-LIB Notification status code and an Unrecognized Notification capability so an LDP speaker can signal completion of its initial label advertisements after session establishment.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with a new status code, a new capability TLV, and procedures for signalling label advertisement completion.
LDP.quote: This document specifies use of a Notification message with the End-of-LIB Status Code for an LDP speaker to signal completion of its label advertisements

rejected.why: Not about fast reroute; LDP-IGP sync and graceful restart are only usage scenarios.
LDP is the more specific tag and is the subject; MPLS is implied as its ancestor.
IANA code point assignments are boilerplate here, not the main subject.
The IGP is only mentioned in the LDP-IGP sync usage guideline; the document is not about OSPF.

RFC5920.title: Security Framework for MPLS and GMPLS Networks
RFC5920.summary: Informational security framework for MPLS and GMPLS networks, describing threats, defensive techniques, monitoring, provider requirements, and inter-AS/inter-provider security, with emphasis on RSVP-TE and LDP.

MPLS.why: The whole document analyses security of MPLS/GMPLS networks, including data-plane label spoofing and inter-provider ICI. MPLS is the most specific tag covering the subject.
MPLS.quote: This document provides a security framework for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Networks.

GMPLS.why: GMPLS-specific issues are covered throughout, such as separate control and data planes, misconnection in optical networks, and management interfaces.
GMPLS.quote: the GMPLS control plane may be provided by separate resources from those used in the data plane.

RSVP-TE.why: The abstract emphasizes RSVP-TE security. The document covers attacks and defenses such as neighbor filtering, message pacing, and authentication.
RSVP-TE.quote: RSVP-TE, described in [RFC3209], is the control protocol used to set up GMPLS and traffic engineered MPLS tunnels.

LDP.why: The abstract emphasizes LDP security. The document covers attacks on LDP and its control-plane protection.
LDP.quote: LDP, described in [RFC5036], is the control protocol used to set up MPLS tunnels without TE.

security.why: This is a general security framework covering threats, defenses, and operational requirements, not tied to one security mechanism.
security.quote: It describes the security threats, the related defensive techniques, and the mechanisms for detection and reporting.

rejected.why: IPsec is discussed as a defensive technique, but the document does not specify or profile it.
PPVPNs appear as context and as the source of cross-connection threats, but the document is not about VPN technology.
One subsection covers pseudowire threats, but it is not a main subject.
BGP route filtering and authentication at the ICI are mentioned, but BGP is not the document's subject.
The document points to other RFCs for general operational security. It focuses on MPLS/GMPLS-specific threats, so the more specific MPLS and security tags are enough.

RFC5921.title: A Framework for MPLS in Transport Networks
RFC5921.summary: Informational framework document defining the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) architecture for point-to-point packet transport networks, covering native service adaptation via LSPs and pseudowires, G-ACh, OAM, control plane, static operation, survivability, SPMEs and management.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is the architectural framework for MPLS-TP: its scope, forwarding, adaptation, OAM, control plane, survivability and static operation.
MPLS-TP.quote: the application of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) to the construction of packet-switched transport networks. It describes a common set of protocol functions -- the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP)

pseudowire.why: A substantial part of the document (Section 3.4.4, Figures 7-9) describes PW and MS-PW adaptation, label stacks and PW OAM in MPLS-TP.
pseudowire.quote: MPLS-TP uses IETF-defined pseudowires to emulate certain services, for example, Ethernet, Frame Relay, or PPP / High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC).

rejected.why: GMPLS signaling is named as the LSP control plane, but only referenced briefly; the control-plane details are left to the separate control plane framework.
OAM is a significant part of the framework, but the details are delegated to the OAM framework document; it is an MPLS-TP component and is covered by the MPLS-TP tag.
The parent of MPLS-TP is implied by the more specific tag.
Targeted LDP is mentioned only as the PW signalling protocol; the document does not specify or extend it.
Section 3.14 summarises the management architecture but defers to the NM framework document, so it is too brief to tag.
BFD is mentioned only as an example of an OAM tool that can run over the G-ACh.

RFC5922.title: Domain Certificates in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5922.summary: Specifies how SIP domain identities are encoded in and extracted from X.509 certificates used with TLS, how to compare them, and how clients, servers, proxies and registrars use them for SIP domain authentication; updates RFC 3261.

SIP.why: The document updates RFC 3261 and specifies normative behaviour of SIP clients, servers, proxies, registrars and redirect servers for domain authentication, so SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: Existing SIP specifications do not sufficiently specify how to use certificates for domain (as opposed to host) authentication.
