X.509.why: The core content is profiling X.509 certificate subjectAltName and CN usage for SIP domain identities, and the matching rules for them.
X.509.quote: this document describes how to encode and extract the identity of a SIP domain in a certificate and how to use that identity for SIP domain authentication

TLS.why: The document defines how certificates are validated and matched in SIP-over-TLS connections, including use of the server_name extension for virtual hosting. TLS is the setting, but the guidance on its use for SIP is substantial.
TLS.quote: X.509 certificates used for TLS serve to bind the identities of the per-hop domain sending or receiving the SIP messages.

rejected.why: DNS is used for server location and name comparison rules, but the document does not specify DNS itself.
Digest is discussed only briefly in Security Considerations, as a reason not to infer connection authentication from it.
S/MIME is explicitly out of scope; it is mentioned only for contrast.
The X.509 tag is the more specific fit; the document does not address PKI in general.
Only a one-line pointer to RFC 5280 handling of IDNs in comparisons.

RFC5923.title: Connection Reuse in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5923.summary: Defines the SIP Via "alias" parameter letting two adjacent SIP entities reuse a mutually authenticated TLS connection (over TCP or SCTP) for requests in both directions, with an alias table, virtual-server rules and DNS SRV interaction.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new Via header parameter and specifies client and server behaviour for connection reuse between SIP entities.
SIP.quote: The act of reusing a connection is initiated by P1 when it adds an "alias" header field parameter (defined later) to the Via header field.

rejected.why: TLS is the authentication and transport substrate. The document defines no new TLS extension; it only relies on X.509 certificates exchanged in TLS.
TCP is only an underlying transport used for illustration. The document does not specify or extend it.
SCTP is mentioned only as an alternative stream transport under TLS. The document does not specify or extend it.
Certificates are used for identity checking, with the details deferred to RFC 5922. The document does not profile them.
RFC 3263 SRV resolution is used to match resolved addresses. Section 10 on SRV load balancing is brief, and the document defines nothing new about DNS.
The Via alias parameter registration is boilerplate-level IANA content, not a subject of the document.

RFC5924.title: Extended Key Usage (EKU) for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) X.509 Certificates
RFC5924.summary: Defines the id-kp-sipDomain extended key usage value for X.509 certificates, restricting a certificate's subject names to SIP service use, with validation rules for SIP implementations and guidance for certification authorities.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 certificate extension value (id-kp-sipDomain EKU), a certificate profile item, and gives CA issuance and validation rules.
X.509.quote: This memo documents an extended key usage (EKU) X.509 certificate extension for restricting the applicability of a certificate to use with a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) service.

SIP.why: The EKU is specific to SIP, with rules for SIP implementations validating peer certificates in SIP proxy-to-proxy TLS. SIP readers need it, though the SIP protocol itself is not extended.
SIP.quote: Inclusion of this KeyPurposeId in a certificate indicates that the use of any Subject names in the certificate is restricted to use by a SIP service
SIP.section: 4.1. Extended Key Usage Values for SIP Domains

rejected.why: TLS is only the substrate in which the certificates are presented; the document defines nothing new about TLS.
The parent of X.509, so it is implied by the more specific tag.
ASN.1 is used only to write the OID definition and module in the appendix; the document is not about ASN.1.
DNS names are mentioned only as the identity form in the certificate; nothing about DNS is specified.

RFC5925.title: The TCP Authentication Option
RFC5925.summary: RFC 5925 specifies the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO), which replaces TCP MD5 with a TCP option providing stronger MACs, master key tuples, per-connection traffic key derivation, key-change coordination and replay protection for long-lived connections.

TCP.why: The document defines a new TCP option and specifies how it interacts with TCP states, segments, user interface, ICMP handling and sequence numbers; it is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: This document specifies the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO), which obsoletes the TCP MD5 Signature option of RFC 2385 (TCP MD5).

rejected.why: BGP and LDP are only motivating use cases for protecting long-lived connections; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
IPsec is discussed as an alternative and compared in the applicability statement, but the document is not about IPsec.
HMAC and the MAC/KDF algorithms are specified in RFC 5926, not here; this document only defines the interface.
The document explicitly leaves key management out of band and defines only a simple key coordination mechanism via KeyID/RNextKeyID.
General authentication topic; the more specific TCP tag covers this TCP-level authentication option.
TCP MD5 is reviewed and obsoleted, but the MD5 digest algorithm itself is not the subject.

RFC5926.title: Cryptographic Algorithms for the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO)
RFC5926.summary: Specifies the mandatory MAC algorithms (HMAC-SHA-1-96, AES-128-CMAC-96) and key derivation functions (KDF_HMAC_SHA1, KDF_AES_128_CMAC) for TCP-AO, plus requirements for future algorithms and an IANA registry.

TCP.why: The document is a companion to the TCP Authentication Option and defines the cryptographic algorithms every TCP-AO implementation must support, so TCP readers need it.
TCP.quote: This document specifies the algorithms and attributes that can be used in TCP-AO's current manual keying mechanism and provides the interface for future message authentication codes (MACs).

HMAC.why: HMAC-SHA-1 is one of the two mandatory MACs. The document defines its use, its truncation to 96 bits and its KDF.
HMAC.quote: HMAC-SHA-1-96 [RFC2104][FIPS-180-3]

AES.why: AES-128-CMAC is the second mandatory MAC and also the basis of KDF_AES_128_CMAC. The document specifies how it is used, including handling of variable-length master keys.
AES.quote: AES-128-CMAC-96 [NIST-SP800-38B][FIPS197]

rejected.why: SHA-1 is only the hash inside HMAC. The document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
The KDFs derive traffic keys from a manually configured master key. The document is about algorithm selection, not key management.
This is a generic topic. The more specific TCP tag already covers the subject.
The specific technology tags HMAC and AES already sit under this topic.
The registry it creates is boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: TCP-AO (TCP Authentication Option)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TCP-AO. The TCP tag is the closest fit, but readers of TCP-AO and TCP-MD5 would want a dedicated tag.

RFC5927.title: ICMP Attacks against TCP
RFC5927.summary: Informational document describing ICMP-based blind attacks on TCP (connection reset, throughput reduction via Source Quench, PMTUD performance degradation) and widely implemented non-standard TCP counter-measures.

TCP.why: The document specifies modifications to TCP's handling of ICMP errors (sequence checks, hard errors as soft errors, delayed PMTU update with new variables) and analyses attacks on TCP connections.
TCP.quote: discusses the use of the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) to perform a variety of attacks against the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

ICMP.why: The attacks use forged ICMP error messages and the document covers ICMPv4/ICMPv6 error handling and payload validation.
ICMP.quote: the current specifications do not recommend any kind of validation checks on the received ICMP error messages

PMTUD.why: A large section (7.1-7.4) describes the attack on Path MTU Discovery and a counter-measure with worked examples and pseudo-code.
PMTUD.quote: a modification to the PMTUD mechanism specified in [RFC1191] and [RFC1981] that has been incorporated in OpenBSD and NetBSD

rejected.why: IPsec is discussed only as background on ICMP handling and as an authentication option that cannot be applied to truncated ICMP payloads.
Source Quench is discussed as a throughput-reduction attack vector, but the document is not about congestion control mechanisms.
BGP sessions are mentioned only as an example scenario where the four-tuple is guessable.
The document is about attacks on a specific protocol and its mitigations, which the TCP and ICMP tags already cover.

RFC5928.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) Resolution Mechanism
RFC5928.summary: Defines an S-NAPTR/SRV/A-AAAA based resolution mechanism a TURN client uses to build an ordered list of server transport addresses, registering the RELAY service tag and turn.udp/tcp/tls protocol tags.

TURN.why: The whole document specifies how TURN clients locate TURN servers and select transport, extending TURN.
TURN.quote: defines a resolution mechanism to generate a list of server transport addresses that can be tried to create a Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) allocation

DNS.why: Specifies use of DNS NAPTR, SRV, A and AAAA lookups with DNS configuration examples, defining a new S-NAPTR application.
DNS.quote: the SRV algorithm defined in [RFC2782] is used to generate a list of IP address and port tuples

rejected.why: Applicable in spirit, but DNS is the more specific tag for the S-NAPTR/SRV mechanism; parent not needed.
STUN is only the base protocol of TURN; the document only references its long-term credentials and identity verification.
TLS is only one of the transports selected; nothing new is defined about TLS.
Tag registrations are boilerplate-style IANA considerations, not the main subject.
UDP/TCP are just transport options to be selected, not subjects of the document.

gaps.name: S-NAPTR (Straightforward NAPTR) / DDDS application
gaps.why: The document defines an S-NAPTR application (RELAY service tag), but the taxonomy has no tag for S-NAPTR/DDDS or SRV records; DNS is the closest fit.

RFC5929.title: Channel Bindings for TLS
RFC5929.summary: RFC 5929 defines and re-registers three TLS channel binding types (tls-unique, tls-server-end-point, tls-unique-for-telnet) per RFC 5056, gives applicability advice and required API guidance, and changes the original tls-unique definition.

TLS.why: The document specifies new TLS-related channel binding types derived from TLS Finished messages and server certificates, with API requirements for TLS implementations and renegotiation guidance.
TLS.quote: This document defines three channel binding types for Transport Layer Security (TLS), tls-unique, tls-server-end-point, and tls-unique-for-telnet

rejected.why: tls-unique-for-telnet is one binding type, but the document does not specify Telnet itself or its options; it only references a proposed StartTLS extension.
The server certificate is hashed for tls-server-end-point, but the document only uses certificates and does not profile them.
GSS-API and SASL GS2 are mentioned only as frameworks that do not negotiate channel binding types.
SASL is mentioned only as a framework that consumes channel bindings and does not negotiate binding types. The document does not specify it.
The document re-registers three entries in the channel binding type registry, but the IANA content is registration of its own types, not guidance about IANA registries.
SHA-256 is selected as the hash for certificate bindings, but the document does not address the SHA family itself.
Channel bindings are consumed by authentication mechanisms, but the document defines binding types and not authentication itself.

gaps.name: Channel bindings (RFC 5056)
gaps.why: The document is about channel binding to secure channels, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy. TLS is the closest fit.

RFC5930.title: Using Advanced Encryption Standard Counter Mode (AES-CTR) with the Internet Key Exchange version 02 (IKEv2) Protocol
RFC5930.summary: Specifies how IKEv2 uses AES Counter Mode (ENCR_AES_CTR, transform ID 13) with an 8-octet explicit IV to encrypt the Encrypted Payload of exchanges after IKE_SA_INIT, mirroring RFC 3686 for ESP.

IKE.why: The document defines how IKEv2 encrypts its Encrypted Payload with AES-CTR, including IV size, padding, and negotiation of the transform for the IKE SA.
IKE.quote: This document provides the specification and usage of AES-CTR Counter Mode by IKEv2.

AES.why: The document specifies the AES counter mode construction (nonce, IV, block counter) as used in IKEv2, so readers of AES modes would want it.
AES.quote: The key stream is generated by inputting counter blocks into the AES algorithm.

rejected.why: ESP is referenced only because RFC 3686 defines AES-CTR for ESP and its IV and counter rules are reused. The document is not about ESP.
IPsec is the context, but the document is specifically about IKEv2, which is already tagged. IPsec architecture is not addressed.
The IANA section only records the ENCR_AES_CTR transform ID 13. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC5931.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Authentication Using Only a Password
RFC5931.summary: Specifies EAP-pwd, an EAP method providing mutual authentication and key derivation from a possibly low-entropy shared password using a dictionary-attack-resistant discrete-log key exchange over ECC/FFC groups.

EAP.why: The document defines a new EAP method, including its message exchanges, packet formats, fragmentation, MSK/EMSK derivation and security claims.
EAP.quote: This memo describes an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method, EAP-pwd, which uses a shared password for authentication.

PAKE.why: The core is a password-authenticated key exchange resistant to active, passive and dictionary attack with forward secrecy, which PAKE readers would want to find.
PAKE.quote: EAP-pwd is an EAP method that addresses the problem of password-based authenticated key exchange

rejected.why: ECC groups are used as an underlying primitive, but the document is about the authentication method, not elliptic curve cryptography itself.
HMAC-SHA256 only instantiates the random function H and the PRF; it is a building block, not the subject.
Key derivation and naming of MSK/EMSK is part of the EAP method definition, already covered by EAP.
SASLprep is used only for password preprocessing, not SASL itself.
The method is used with AAA servers and key management, but the document does not specify an AAA framework.
Only mentioned in relation to RFC 4017 requirements for wireless LAN EAP methods; not a Wi-Fi document.

RFC5932.title: Camellia Cipher Suites for TLS
RFC5932.summary: RFC 5932 defines 24 TLS cipher suites using the Camellia block cipher in CBC mode, adding SHA-256 variants to those in RFC 4132, which it obsoletes.

Camellia.why: The document's whole purpose is defining Camellia-based cipher suites and how Camellia is used in them. The Camellia tag covers its cipher suites in TLS.
Camellia.quote: specifies a set of cipher suites for the Transport Security Layer (TLS) protocol to support the Camellia encryption algorithm as a block cipher

TLS.why: It extends TLS with new cipher suites and sets version-negotiation rules for them (TLS 1.2 only for the SHA256 suites). TLS readers need this registry-level addition.
TLS.quote: The PRF is the TLS PRF [RFC5246] with SHA-256 as the hash function.  These cipher suites MUST NOT be negotiated by TLS 1.1 or earlier versions.

rejected.why: SHA-1 and SHA-256 are used only as the MAC and PRF hash inside the suites. The document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
HMAC is used only as the MAC for the suites and is not specified or extended here.
RSA appears only in key exchange names, and key exchange is defined by RFC 5246.
The IANA section only records the cipher suite code points, which is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.

RFC5933.title: Use of GOST Signature Algorithms in DNSKEY and RRSIG Resource Records for DNSSEC
RFC5933.summary: Defines how GOST R 34.10-2001 signatures and GOST R 34.11-94 digests are used in DNSSEC DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS resource records, with algorithm number 12 and digest type 3.

GOST.why: The document specifies use of the Russian GOST signature and hash algorithms, including key, signature and digest wire formats.
GOST.quote: This document describes how to produce digital signatures and hash functions using the GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms

DNSSEC.why: It extends the DNSSEC algorithm list and defines DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS record formats and examples with the new algorithm, and requires NSEC/NSEC3 support.
DNSSEC.quote: for DNSKEY, RRSIG, and DS resource records, for use in the Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC)

rejected.why: DNS is the base system; the document is specifically about DNSSEC, the more specific child tag.
RFC 4491 key encoding is referenced only to help use keys with existing libraries, not the subject.
RFC 4490 is referenced only for signature and digest wire formats.
GOST R 34.10-2001 is elliptic-curve based, but the document is about the GOST algorithm in DNSSEC, which the GOST tag covers.
Registry updates are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the main body.

RFC5934.title: Trust Anchor Management Protocol (TAMP)
RFC5934.summary: RFC 5934 specifies the Trust Anchor Management Protocol (TAMP), a transport-independent CMS-based protocol with signed messages for adding, removing, changing trust anchors, apex trust anchors, community identifiers and sequence numbers in a trust anchor store.

PKI.why: The document defines a protocol for managing trust anchors, a core PKI function, including apex/management/identity trust anchors, subordination checks using X.509 path controls, and TrustAnchorInfo handling.
PKI.quote: a transport independent protocol for the management of trust anchors (TAs) and community identifiers stored in a trust anchor store

CMS.why: Section 2 profiles CMS ContentInfo, SignedData, SignerInfo and attributes for TAMP, and defines new CMS content types and an unsigned attribute.
CMS.quote: TAMP makes use of signed and unsigned messages.  The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is used in both cases.

rejected.why: Certificates are used as trust anchor formats and for path validation, but the document specifies trust anchor management, not the X.509 profile; it only adds one certificate extension.
ASN.1 modules are the normative syntax, but only as the means of defining the protocol messages.
Appendix C binds TAMP to HTTP POST, but HTTP is merely a transport here.
Appendix B registers eleven media types, but this is boilerplate-like registration apparatus, not the subject.
Not relevant; only mentioned for completeness of trust anchor stores, not middleboxes.

gaps.name: Trust anchor management
gaps.why: The taxonomy has PKI but no specific tag for trust anchor formats and management (TAMP, RFC 5914 Trust Anchor Format).

RFC5935.title: Expressing SNMP SMI Datatypes in XML Schema Definition Language
RFC5935.summary: Defines the standard XML Schema (XSD) mapping of the SMIv2 base datatypes (INTEGER, Counter32, OCTET STRING, IpAddress, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, etc.) so MIB data can be faithfully expressed and validated in XML.

MIB.why: The document is about SMI datatypes used by MIB modules and how to map them to XSD, which falls under MIB/SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the IETF standard expression of Structure of Management Information (SMI) base datatypes in XML Schema Definition (XSD) language.

XML.why: The document specifies an XSD schema and XML representation for management data, a substantial part of its content.
XML.quote: The use of a standard mapping from SMIv2 to XML via XSD validation enables and promotes the efficient reuse of existing and future MIB modules

rejected.why: SNMP PDUs and varbinds are the source of the values, but the document only maps SMI datatypes to XSD; it does not specify SNMP itself. MIB is the better fit.
The OBJECT IDENTIFIER rules are referenced from ASN.1/BER only informally; the document does not define ASN.1 modules or encodings.
Only mentioned in acknowledgements as a prior datatypes effort; the document is not about NETCONF.
Not mentioned in the body; the mapping is to XSD, not YANG.

RFC5936.title: DNS Zone Transfer Protocol (AXFR)
RFC5936.summary: RFC 5936 re-specifies the DNS AXFR full zone transfer protocol, covering message formats, zone contents, TCP transport, authorization, zone integrity and backward compatibility, updating RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

DNS.why: The document defines the AXFR zone transfer mechanism of DNS, including message formats, record inclusion rules and server/client behaviour, and updates RFC 1034/1035.
DNS.quote: This document re-specifies the AXFR mechanism as it is deployed in the Internet at large

rejected.why: DNSSEC record placement at zone cuts is discussed briefly, but only as content carried by AXFR; the document is not about DNSSEC.
OPT RR usage in AXFR queries and responses is mentioned, but EDNS is only a supporting element, not defined or extended here.
AXFR runs over TCP and connection management is described, but TCP is the substrate, not the subject.
Dynamic update is mentioned only for its effect on occluded names, not specified or extended.

RFC5937.title: Using Trust Anchor Constraints during Certification Path Processing
RFC5937.summary: Informational RFC specifying how to enforce trust anchor constraints (name constraints, policies, basic constraints) as supplementary initialization steps in RFC 5280 certification path validation.

PKI.why: The document is about trust anchors and certification path validation, core PKI subject matter.
PKI.quote: This document describes how to use information associated with a trust anchor public key when validating certification paths.

X.509.why: It extends the RFC 5280 X.509 path validation algorithm, handling name constraints, policy constraints, inhibitAnyPolicy and basic constraints extensions.
X.509.quote: The supplementary rules specify an additional input and extend the initialization procedures in the [RFC5280] path validation algorithm.

rejected.why: CMS Content Constraints are mentioned only as an example of constraints that may define additional steps; the document is not about CMS.
The parent topic is implied by PKI; the document is about a specific mechanism.

gaps.name: Trust anchor format and management (TAF, TAMP)
gaps.why: The document builds on the Trust Anchor Format and relates to TAMP, but the taxonomy has no tag for trust anchors specifically; PKI is the closest fit.

RFC5938.title: Individual Session Control Feature for the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC5938.summary: RFC 5938 defines an optional TWAMP extension (new Modes bit and Start-N-Sessions, Start-N-Ack, Stop-N-Sessions, Stop-N-Ack commands) letting the Control-Client start and stop individual test sessions by SID, updating RFC 5357.

TWAMP.why: The document extends and updates TWAMP with new control commands, a new mode bit, and sender/reflector behaviour changes.
TWAMP.quote: This memo describes an OPTIONAL feature for TWAMP, that gives the controlling host the ability to start and stop one or more individual test sessions using Session Identifiers.

rejected.why: OWAMP is the base that TWAMP derives from and is referenced for formats; the document does not extend OWAMP itself.
Implied as parent of TWAMP; the document is specifically about TWAMP, so the child tag suffices.
IANA registry assignments are boilerplate-like consequences of the extension, not the subject of the document.
HMAC is only used to terminate messages as already defined in RFC 4656; nothing new is specified about it.

RFC5939.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Capability Negotiation
RFC5939.summary: RFC 5939 defines the SDP Capability Negotiation framework: new SDP attributes (csup, creq, acap, tcap, pcfg, acfg) and offer/answer extensions letting an offerer present alternative transport protocols and attributes as potential configurations, in a backwards-compatible way.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with new attributes and updates the RFC 3264 offer/answer procedures, so it belongs on the SDP/offer-answer page.
SDP.quote: extending SDP with capability negotiation parameters and associated offer/answer procedures to use those parameters in a backwards compatible manner

rejected.why: SRTP and its keying (SDES, MIKEY, DTLS-SRTP) appear as motivating cases and in examples. The document does not specify or extend them.
RTP profiles (RTP/AVP, RTP/AVPF and others) are the transport values being negotiated, not the subject.
SIP is the main protocol that carries SDP offer/answer. Section 3.8 discusses option-tag interactions only briefly, so the document is not about SIP.
Section 3.7 gives guidelines for interaction with ICE. It is a short section and ICE is not the subject.
MIKEY appears only as an example key-management attribute capability.

gaps.name: SDP offer/answer capability negotiation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an SDP tag, but the document is specifically about capability negotiation and potential configurations, a distinct subject within SDP.

RFC5940.title: Additional Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Revocation Information Choices
RFC5940.summary: Defines two additional CMS RevocationInfoChoice formats, carrying OCSP responses and SCVP requests/responses, with object identifiers under id-ri and ASN.1 modules.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS RevocationInfoChoices with new OtherRevocationInfoFormat values for SignedData, EnvelopedData and related content types.
CMS.quote: The other CHOICE MUST be used to convey OCSP responses, SCVP requests, and SCVP responses.

OCSP.why: Defines how OCSP responses are embedded in CMS, which is a substantial part of the document and of interest to OCSP readers.
OCSP.quote: otherRevInfo MUST carry the OCSP response using the OCSPResponse type defined in [OCSP].

rejected.why: ASN.1 modules are given, but they only encode the new CMS structures. ASN.1 is the notation, not the subject.
CRLs and certificates are background. The document does not profile X.509.
The parent PKI tag is implied by the CMS and OCSP tags. The document is about the CMS carriage formats, not PKI in general.
S/MIME is only mentioned in the title of a reference, and the document does not address it.

gaps.name: SCVP (Server-Based Certificate Validation Protocol)
gaps.why: Section 4 specifies how SCVP requests and responses are carried, but the taxonomy has no SCVP tag.

RFC5941.title: Sharing Transaction Fraud Data
RFC5941.summary: Defines Thraud, an IODEF extension and profile for sharing transaction fraud reports (payment, transfer, identity, other) between financial organizations, with a media type and XML namespace registration.

IODEF.why: IODEF is not a tag id in the taxonomy, so this placeholder must be rejected; see the gaps and the replacement tag below.
IODEF.quote: This document describes a document format for exchanging transaction fraud (Thraud) information.  It extends the Incident Handling Working Group (INCH WG) Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF)

RFC5942.title: IPv6 Subnet Model: The Relationship between Links and Subnet Prefixes
RFC5942.summary: RFC 5942 clarifies the IPv6 subnet model, stating that assigning an IPv6 address does not imply an on-link prefix, and updates RFC 4861 by deprecating two bullets of the "on-link" definition for security reasons.

neighbor discovery.why: The document clarifies on-link determination, Prefix List, Destination Cache and Neighbor Cache behaviour in IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. It also updates RFC 4861's on-link definition.
neighbor discovery.quote: The on-link determination is separate from the address assignment.

rejected.why: This is the parent of neighbor discovery. The document is about the ND-specific on-link definition, so the more specific child tag is used.
SLAAC is only mentioned as one way an address gets assigned. The document does not specify or change it.
DHCPv6 IA_NA is cited only as an example of address acquisition with no prefix length. The document is not about DHCPv6.
The document covers the link/prefix relationship in ND, not address architecture or allocation.
The security concern is about spoofed NS/NA/RS messages. The document does not discuss SEND.

RFC5943.title: A Dedicated Routing Policy Specification Language Interface Identifier for Operational Testing
RFC5943.summary: Defines new optional RPSL attributes (pingable and ping-hdl) for route/route6 objects so operators can advertise a diagnostic IP address that outside parties can probe, with a rate-limit guideline.

RPSL.why: The document extends RPSL with new pingable and ping-hdl attributes on route and route6 objects, which are used in routing registries.
RPSL.quote: The pingable attribute is a member of the route and route6 objects in the RPSL.

rejected.why: Pings use ICMP Echo, but the document only mentions it as the service being advertised and does not specify or extend ICMP.
Path MTU discovery is named only as an example of a problem the diagnostic address helps test. The document is not about it.
The document mentions rate limiting and DoS risk, but only in Security Considerations and a brief usage note. That is not its subject.
The document touches on RPSL authentication only in Security Considerations. It does not address securing routing.

RFC5944.title: IP Mobility Support for IPv4, Revised
RFC5944.summary: RFC 5944 is the revised Mobile IPv4 specification, defining agent discovery, registration with home and foreign agents, tunneling-based routing, ARP handling and authentication for mobile nodes, obsoleting RFC 3344.

Mobile IPv4.why: The whole document specifies Mobile IPv4: agent discovery, registration, home/foreign agents, care-of addresses and tunneling.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document specifies protocol enhancements that allow transparent routing of IP datagrams to mobile nodes in the Internet.

rejected.why: Section 4.6 uses proxy and gratuitous ARP as a mechanism for home agent interception, but ARP itself is not specified or extended.
IP-in-IP, minimal and GRE encapsulation are used as the data path but are defined in other RFCs; they are substrates here.
ICMP Router Discovery is extended for Agent Advertisement, but this is part of Mobile IPv4, not a document about ICMP.
Section 4.4 covers multicast for mobile nodes briefly, but it is a minor part of the document.
HMAC-MD5 is the default authentication algorithm but is only used as a mechanism.
Registration messages run over UDP port 434; UDP is only transport.

RFC5945.title: Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Proxy Approaches
RFC5945.summary: Informational RFC describing conceptual RSVP proxy approaches (sender and receiver proxies, triggered by Path messages, inspection, STUN, application entities, policy servers) that let RSVP routers reserve resources when endpoints are not RSVP-capable, with use cases.

RSVP.why: The whole document specifies and analyses RSVP proxy behaviours, Path-triggered receiver proxy, sender proxy and aggregation, so RSVP is the core subject.
RSVP.quote: This document presents RSVP proxy behaviors allowing RSVP routers to initiate or terminate RSVP signaling on behalf of a receiver or a sender that is not RSVP-capable.

rejected.why: SIP is only the application-level signaling that synchronizes reservations; not specified or extended here.
STUN messages are discussed as a possible trigger, but extensions are explicitly out of scope; it is a mechanism relied on, not the subject.
ICE connectivity checks are used as a trigger cue only; the document does not define anything about ICE.
NSIS QoS NSLP is mentioned only as a related protocol with a similar proxy concept.
GRE tunneling is used as a control-interface mechanism in one subsection, not the subject.
Router alert appears only in Security Considerations as a limitation.

RFC5946.title: Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Extensions for Path-Triggered RSVP Receiver Proxy
RFC5946.summary: Specifies RSVP extensions for a Path-Triggered RSVP Receiver Proxy: sender notification of reservation failure via PathErr or Notify, dynamic discovery of downstream RSVP capability, and a Receiver Proxy Control policy element.

RSVP.why: The whole document extends RSVP: new PathErr and Notify procedures, a new error code, and a new policy element for receiver proxies.
RSVP.quote: RSVP extensions are needed to facilitate operations with an RSVP Receiver Proxy whose signaling is triggered by receipt of RSVP Path messages from the sender.

rejected.why: RFC 3209 and RFC 3473 (Notify, Path_State_Removed) are borrowed for procedures, but the document is not about traffic-engineered LSP signalling.
RSVP uses the router alert option, but it is mentioned only in Security Considerations.
IPsec is only cited in Security Considerations as a way to protect RSVP messages.
The policy element is carried in POLICY_DATA objects per RFC 2750, but COPS itself is not involved.
IANA actions (an error code and a policy element registry) are boilerplate-level and do not make the document about IANA.

RFC5947.title: Requirements for Multiple Address of Record (AOR) Reachability Information in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC5947.summary: Informational requirements document for a standardized SIP REGISTER-based mechanism allowing a SIP-PBX to register multiple AORs (E.164 numbers) with a SIP service provider, with a problem statement, requirements, and desirables.

SIP.why: The whole document specifies requirements for a SIP registration mechanism between SIP-PBXs and service providers, including REGISTER, Request-URI, Route and P-header handling.
SIP.quote: This document states requirements for a standardized SIP registration mechanism for multiple addresses of record (AORs)

rejected.why: TEL URIs and E.164 numbers appear as AOR types, and the illegal wildcard syntax is noted, but the document is not about the tel URI scheme.
It covers SIP trunking between a PBX and a provider, but it is about registration of multiple AORs rather than SPEERMINT peering.
TLS is only cited as an example transport for integrity and confidentiality in REQ14.
RFC 3263 DNS-based server location is mentioned only as the procedure that is inadequate for small PBXs and must remain unaffected for other domains.

RFC5948.title: Transmission of IPv4 Packets over the IP Convergence Sublayer of IEEE 802.16
RFC5948.summary: Specifies how IPv4 packets are encapsulated and transmitted over the IPv4-specific Packet Convergence Sublayer of IEEE 802.16, including frame format, MTU and DHCP-based address assignment on a point-to-point link model.

WiMAX.why: The whole document defines IPv4 over the IEEE 802.16 IPv4 CS: frame format, MTU, subnet model, and WiMAX MTU differences.
WiMAX.quote: This document specifies the frame format, the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU), and the address assignment procedures for transmitting IPv4 packets over the IP-specific part of the Packet Convergence Sublayer of IEEE 802.16.

IPv4.why: The document is specifically about carrying IPv4, including its address assignment and MTU on this link, which readers of IPv4 would want.
IPv4.quote: This document specifies a method for encapsulating and transmitting IPv4 [RFC0791] packets over the IPv4 CS of IEEE 802.16.

rejected.why: DHCP is used for address assignment and MTU configuration but is only relied upon, not specified or extended.
The document only notes ARP is not used on this point-to-point link.
Path MTU discovery is mentioned as an encouraged client practice, not the document's subject.
GRE is only an example of an L2 tunnel between BS and AR.
The document is IPv4-specific; IPv6 is mentioned only as a contrast (RFC 5121).
A more specific tech tag exists for this link type, so the parent is implied.

RFC5949.title: Fast Handovers for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC5949.summary: Specifies how Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6) operate with Proxy Mobile IPv6, extending HI/HAck messages and defining new mobility options for context transfer and inter-MAG tunnelling.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document defines fast handover for PMIPv6 between previous and new MAGs, with new HI/HAck flags, codes and mobility options.
PMIPv6.quote: This document specifies the usage of fast handovers for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6; RFC 5568) when Proxy Mobile IPv6 is used as the mobility management protocol.

rejected.why: FMIPv6 and MIPv6 are the base being adapted, but the mobile node is not involved in MIPv6 signalling; the subject is PMIPv6 network-based mobility.
Used only to protect HI/HAck messages in Security Considerations; boilerplate-level dependency.
GRE keys and tunnelling are reused from RFC 5845 for the inter-MAG tunnel; not defined here.
Mobility runs over IPv6 but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
IANA section registers flags and options but is boilerplate.
Inter-MAG tunnelling reuses existing encapsulation modes; it is a supporting mechanism.

RFC5950.title: Network Management Framework for MPLS-based Transport Networks
RFC5950.summary: Informational framework describing the network and element management architecture (ITU-T terminology) and fault, configuration and performance management heuristics for MPLS-TP networks.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is the management framework for MPLS-TP networks and elements, so MPLS-TP readers would look for it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document provides the network management framework for the Transport Profile for Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS-TP).

network management.why: It describes network and element management architectures and FCAPS-style fault, configuration and performance management, which is general network management architecture and practice.
network management.quote: The management of the MPLS-TP network could be based on a multi-tiered distributed management systems

rejected.why: The LSP ownership handover section only references GMPLS/RSVP-TE handover work from other RFCs; it is not the document's subject.
It is mentioned only as the signaling protocol for handover defined in RFC 5852.
SNMP and NETCONF appear only as example management interfaces, with no restriction placed on them.
RMON is cited once as an example of limiting performance data volume.
OAM is defined in the terminology and mentioned, but the document is about management rather than OAM mechanisms.
The performance management section is short and only discusses on-demand versus proactive data volume, not measurement methods.

RFC5951.title: Network Management Requirements for MPLS-based Transport Networks
RFC5951.summary: Specifies network management requirements (fault, configuration, performance, security, management channels) for equipment in MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) networks.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines management requirements for MPLS-TP NEs, so readers of the MPLS-TP subject would expect it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document specifies the requirements for the management of equipment used in networks supporting an MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP).

network management.why: The document is a network management requirements specification covering fault, configuration, performance and security management, with no specific management protocol or data model chosen.
network management.quote: These requirements indicate what management capabilities need to be available in MPLS for use in managing the MPLS-TP.

OAM.why: A substantial part covers management of OAM: supervision, on-demand vs proactive configuration, and connectivity checks.
OAM.quote: The MPLS-TP NE MUST support configuration of the OAM entities and functions specified in RFC 5860

performance measurement.why: Section 7 sets requirements for loss and delay measurement, availability and measurement scope.
performance measurement.quote: The MPLS-TP NE MUST support collection of loss measurement (LM) statistics.

rejected.why: SNMP and NETCONF are mentioned only as examples of management protocols. The document explicitly specifies no preferred management interface.
It is only an example of an allowed management protocol.
The DoS/DDoS section is one short security-management requirement, not a main subject.
MIBs are mentioned only in passing for timer defaults. No MIB module is defined.
It is mentioned only for control-plane hand-off and signaling channel context.

RFC5952.title: A Recommendation for IPv6 Address Text Representation
RFC5952.summary: Defines a canonical text representation for IPv6 addresses (suppress leading zeros, maximal "::" compression, lowercase hex), updating RFC 4291's flexible text format, with notes on special addresses, ports, and prefixes.

IPv6.why: The whole document specifies how IPv6 addresses are to be written as text, updating the IPv6 addressing architecture text rules.
IPv6.quote: This document defines a canonical textual representation format.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the more specific tag covering IPv6 address text representation; the document is not about address allocation or architecture generally.
Only briefly says to follow RFC 3986 bracket literals for addresses with ports; URI syntax is not the subject.
Whois is mentioned only as one example of a search problem caused by inconsistent representation.
ISATAP and IPv4-mapped addresses are mentioned only as special addresses whose mixed notation is addressed in one section.

RFC5953.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC5953.summary: Specifies the TLS Transport Model (TLSTM) for SNMP, carrying SNMP over TLS/TCP and DTLS/UDP with X.509 certificate authentication, and defines the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB module for managing it.

SNMP.why: The document extends the SNMPv3 architecture with a new Transport Model and its elements of procedure, so it is about SNMP.
SNMP.quote: This document describes a Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), that uses either the Transport Layer Security protocol or the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

MIB.why: It defines the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB module with counters, configuration tables, and notifications for managing TLSTM, a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: This document also defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols.

transport mapping.why: The document binds SNMP to TLS and DTLS transports and defines new transport domains, which fits the transport-mapping subject.
transport mapping.quote: It supports the sending of SNMP messages over TLS/TCP and DTLS/UDP.

DTLS.why: The document specifies DTLS-specific handling: demultiplexing, cookies, replay protection, and datagram sizing.
DTLS.quote: For DTLS over UDP, each SNMP message MUST be placed in a single UDP datagram; it MAY be split to multiple DTLS records.

rejected.why: TLS is the security substrate that the model uses. The document defines how SNMP uses it, not anything new about TLS itself.
X.509 certificates are used for authentication and mapped to security names. The document does not profile or extend X.509.
TCP is only the underlying transport beneath TLS. Section 8.4 explicitly leaves its characteristics out of scope.
UDP is only the underlying transport beneath DTLS and is not itself the subject of the document.
Certificate provisioning is discussed only as it applies to the model's use of certificates, which does not make the document about PKI.
Authentication is covered only through the TLS and X.509 mechanisms the model relies on.

RFC5954.title: Essential Correction for IPv6 ABNF and URI Comparison in RFC 3261
RFC5954.summary: RFC 5954 updates RFC 3261 (SIP) by replacing its faulty IPv6address/IPv4address ABNF with the RFC 3986 rules and clarifying that SIP URI comparison uses binary equivalence of IP addresses regardless of textual form.

SIP.why: The document corrects the SIP specification's grammar and its URI comparison rule (Section 19.1.4 of RFC 3261). SIP readers need this essential correction.
SIP.quote: the <IPv6address> and <IPv4address> production rules from RFC 3261 MUST NOT be used and instead, the production rules of the same name in RFC 3986

URI.why: A substantial part of the document clarifies URI comparison rules for URIs containing IP address literals, and it adopts the RFC 3986 URI ABNF.
URI.quote: it is the binary equivalence of the IP address that must be taken into consideration when comparing two URIs

IPv6.why: The document addresses IPv6 address textual representation: the IPv4-mapped literal syntax, equivalence of different text forms, and canonical output.
IPv6.quote: Implementers SHOULD generate IPv6 text representation as defined in RFC 5952

rejected.why: ABNF is the notation in which the corrected rules are written. The document is about fixing specific SIP grammar rules, not about the ABNF notation itself.
The document concerns textual representation of addresses within SIP URIs, not IP address architecture or allocation. The more specific IPv6 tag covers it.

RFC5955.title: The application/timestamped-data Media Type
RFC5955.summary: Registers the application/timestamped-data media type (file extension .tsd) for TimeStampedData envelopes defined in RFC 5544, which bind a file to one or more time-stamp tokens.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration (application/timestamped-data) with the registration template filled in; readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: This document defines a new media type for TimeStampedData envelopes.

rejected.why: TimeStampedData in RFC 5544 is CMS-related, but this document only registers the media type and does not specify or extend CMS syntax.
MIME is only the transport context for the media type; the document does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
Time-stamp tokens relate to PKI, but this document does not address PKI; it only registers a media type.
The IANA section merely records the registration; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: Time-stamping / TimeStampedData envelopes (RFC 5544)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for trusted time-stamping or binding documents to time-stamp tokens, which is the underlying subject of the registered type.

RFC5956.title: Forward Error Correction Grouping Semantics in the Session Description Protocol
RFC5956.summary: Defines the "FEC-FR" SDP grouping semantics (for the group and ssrc-group attributes) to associate source and FEC repair flows, including additive repair flows, and deprecates the RFC 4756 "FEC" semantics.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP by defining new group and ssrc-group semantics, with SDP examples and offer/answer fallback rules.
SDP.quote: This document defines the semantics for grouping the associated source and FEC-based (Forward Error Correction) repair flows in the Session Description Protocol (SDP).

FECFRAME.why: The semantics signal source/repair flow associations and additivity for FEC Framework instances, so readers of FECFRAME would want this RFC.
FECFRAME.quote: The FEC Framework [FEC-FRAMEWK] outlines a general framework for using FEC codes in multimedia applications that stream audio, video, or other types of multimedia content.

rejected.why: RTP is only the carrier of the flows. The SSRC-multiplexing section uses ssrc-group but does not change RTP itself.
The parent tag is implied by FECFRAME, and the document is about the framework's SDP signalling, not FEC codes.
SIP appears only in passing as a source of the 488 and 606 refusal responses in the offer/answer fallback.
The registrations in the IANA section are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC5957.title: Display-Based Address Sorting for the IMAP4 SORT Extension
RFC5957.summary: Defines the IMAP SORT=DISPLAY capability, adding DISPLAYFROM and DISPLAYTO sort criteria that sort messages by the display-name of the first From/To address, updating RFC 5256.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP's SORT extension with new sort criteria and a new capability, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document describes an IMAP protocol extension enabling server-side message sorting on the commonly displayed portion of the From and To header fields.

rejected.why: The document refers to the RFC 5322 display-name, but only as the source of the values it sorts on. It does not specify message format.
RFC 2047 encoded-word decoding is applied as a step in the procedure. The document is not about MIME.
The Internationalization Considerations section is short boilerplate-like text that relies on RFC 5255 collations. It does not define internationalization behaviour of its own.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the formal syntax.

RFC5958.title: Asymmetric Key Packages
RFC5958.summary: RFC 5958 defines the Asymmetric Key Package (OneAsymmetricKey) ASN.1 syntax and CMS content type for conveying private keys, plus EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo, obsoleting PKCS #8 (RFC 5208).

CMS.why: The document defines a new CMS content type and describes how the CMS protecting content types (SignedData, EnvelopedData, etc.) protect it.
CMS.quote: This document defines the syntax for private-key information and a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [RFC5652] content type for it.

ASN.1.why: The core of the document is an ASN.1 module with encoding requirements (DER/BER) for the key structures.
ASN.1.quote: The key package is defined using ASN.1 [X.680], [X.681], [X.682], and [X.683].

key management.why: It covers the format for transporting and encrypting private keys, which falls under key provisioning and storage.
key management.quote: The asymmetric key package CMS content type is used to transfer one or more plaintext asymmetric keys from one party to another.
key management.section: 2. Asymmetric Key Package CMS Content Type

rejected.why: It registers application/pkcs8, but that is IANA boilerplate and not the document's main subject.
It deals with private-key packaging and mentions certificates only as attributes. It doesn't address PKI itself.
RSA keys are given as an example of private-key content, but the document is not about RSA.
Base64 is used only for the PEM encoding of .p8 files, so it is only a substrate.
The PEM-encoded .p8 files mentioned are a file-encoding convention, not the historic Privacy Enhanced Mail system.

gaps.name: PKCS #8 private-key information syntax
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PKCS #8 or private-key container formats, though this is the document's central subject.

RFC5959.title: Algorithms for Asymmetric Key Package Content Type
RFC5959.summary: Specifies which cryptographic algorithms must or should be supported when encrypting EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo (PBES2 with PBKDF2/AES Key Wrap) and when protecting the AsymmetricKeyPackage with CMS content types (SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthenticatedData, AuthEnvelopedData).

CMS.why: The document profiles algorithm use for the CMS protecting content types, which is the core of Section 3.
CMS.quote: conventions necessary to protect the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type with SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthenticatedData, and AuthEnvelopedData

key management.why: It covers key transport, key agreement and key wrap choices for protecting private keys. The 'cryptography' parent holds this subject, and the PBES2 password-based encryption of private keys also fits here.
key management.quote: EncryptedData requires that keys be managed by other means; therefore, the only algorithm specified is the content encryption algorithm.

AES.why: AES Key Wrap with Padding and AES-GCM/CCM are the central algorithm choices mandated throughout.
AES.quote: MUST support AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding [RFC5649] as the content encryption algorithm.

PBKDF2.why: Section 2 mandates PBES2 with PBKDF2 for EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo.
PBKDF2.quote: PBES2 with a key derivation algorithm of PBKDF2 using HMAC with SHA-256 [RFC5754]

rejected.why: S/MIME is only referenced for the SMIMECapabilities attribute values. The document is not about S/MIME messages.
RSA is one of many algorithms mandated, and it is not the subject of the document.
SHA-256 and SHA-1 are only named as hash choices within the algorithm profile.
HMAC-SHA-256 is mentioned only as a required MAC for AuthenticatedData.
Certificates are mentioned only in passing in the key sizes section.
Public key certificates are only the easiest way to implement the algorithms. The document is not about PKI.

gaps.name: Asymmetric Key Packages / PKCS #8 private key format
gaps.why: The document concerns the AsymmetricKeyPackage and EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structures for carrying private keys. The taxonomy has no tag for private key packaging.

RFC5960.title: MPLS Transport Profile Data Plane Architecture
RFC5960.summary: Specifies the MPLS-TP data plane: packet encapsulation and forwarding for LSPs, sections and pseudowires, plus the Generic Associated Channel, as a profile of existing MPLS and PWE3 data plane architectures.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines the MPLS Transport Profile data plane: LSP types, sections, G-ACh/GAL handling, TTL and PHP rules, and ECMP prohibition.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document defines the set of functions that comprise the MPLS-TP data plane: the architectural layer concerned with the encapsulation and forwarding of packets within an MPLS-TP network.

pseudowire.why: Pseudowires are one of three MPLS-TP transport entities, and the document covers PW label TTL handling, the control word and ACH discrimination. It adds no PW changes, so this is secondary.
pseudowire.quote: The data plane architectures for single-segment pseudowires [RFC3985] and multi-segment pseudowires [RFC5659] are included in the MPLS-TP.

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by MPLS-TP, and the document is about the transport profile specifically.
Diffserv LSP modes (E-LSP, L-LSP) and tunnelling models are only referenced from existing RFCs as part of the data plane QoS inclusion.
ECMP is only mentioned in a single prohibition on MPLS-TP LSPs, not a subject of the document.
RSVP-TE TE LSPs are only cited as providing QoS capability; nothing about the protocol is specified.
The G-ACh is described as the channel that carries OAM, but OAM mechanisms themselves are out of scope.
Not discussed in the document body.

RFC5961.title: Improving TCP's Robustness to Blind In-Window Attacks
RFC5961.summary: Specifies small changes to TCP's handling of inbound RST, SYN and data segments (challenge ACKs, stricter ACK checks, ACK throttling) to mitigate blind in-window spoofing attacks.

TCP.why: The document modifies TCP's segment processing rules for RST, SYN and data segments, adding challenge ACKs and a MAX.SND.WND check. It is a TCP protocol change.
TCP.quote: This document specifies small modifications to the way TCP handles inbound segments that can reduce the chances of a successful attack.

rejected.why: BGP is only the motivating example of a long-lived TCP application. The document does not specify or change BGP.
IPsec AH and ESP are mentioned only in Security Considerations as the full protection against on-path attacks.
Forged ICMP attacks are only noted as out of scope in Security Considerations.
The receive window is explicitly distinguished from the congestion window. The document does not address congestion control.

RFC5962.title: Dynamic Extensions to the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO)
RFC5962.summary: RFC 5962 defines a <Dynamic> XML extension to PIDF-LO that conveys orientation, speed and heading of a moving presentity, with schema and IANA namespace registrations.

geolocation.why: The document extends the PIDF-LO location object format with dynamic location information (orientation, speed, heading), which is about location formats and their conveyance.
geolocation.quote: This document defines PIDF-LO extensions to convey information about moving objects. Elements are defined that enable expression of spatial orientation, speed, and heading of the presentity.

PIDF.why: PIDF-LO is an extension of PIDF, and this document extends it further with a new <Dynamic> element, so readers of PIDF would want it.
PIDF.quote: This document extends PIDF-LO to convey spatial orientation, speed, and heading of a presentity.

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding used for the new elements. The document does not define XML usage in general.
Security Considerations discusses privacy risk from predicting future location. This is boilerplate-level discussion and not the main body.
Presence concepts are reused only through PIDF. The document is not about instant messaging or presence protocols.
No SIP event packages or XCAP are involved. The document only extends a data format.

gaps.name: GEOPRIV / PIDF-LO location object
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for the GEOPRIV location object. The geolocation topic is the closest fit.

RFC5963.title: IPv6 Deployment in Internet Exchange Points (IXPs)
RFC5963.summary: Informational guidance for deploying IPv6 at Internet Exchange Points, covering switch fabric configuration, addressing plan, multicast and neighbor discovery, reverse DNS, route servers, and policies.

IPv6.why: The document is about deploying IPv6 at IXPs, including its addressing plan (prefix sizes, IID selection) and operational impact.
IPv6.quote: This document provides guidance on IPv6 deployment in Internet Exchange Points (IXPs).

route server.why: A dedicated section covers IPv6 support for IXP route servers, including MP-BGP for IPv6 and IPv6 transport for sessions.
route server.quote: IXPs may offer a route-server service, either for Multi-Lateral Peering Agreements (MLPA) service, looking-glass service, or route-collection service.

neighbor discovery.why: Substantial discussion of controlling and monitoring ND multicast traffic and RA filtering on the IXP LAN.
neighbor discovery.quote: ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery [RFC4861] implements the following necessary functions in an IXP switching fabric: Address Resolution, Neighbor Unreachability Detection, and Duplicate Address Detection.
neighbor discovery.section: 4.1. Multicast Support and Monitoring for Neighbor Discovery at an IXP

multicast.why: Covers IPv6 multicast exchange at IXPs, including PIM, PIM snooping and multicast BGP for RPF.
multicast.quote: For IPv6 Multicast traffic exchange, an IXP may decide to use either the same LAN being used for unicast IPv6 traffic exchange
multicast.section: 4.2. IPv6 Multicast Traffic Exchange at an IXP

rejected.why: The IXP fabric is Ethernet, but it is assumed substrate; the document does not define new Ethernet behaviour.
BGP is used for sessions and MP-BGP is mentioned, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
Reverse DNS (ip6.arpa PTR records) is a brief recommendation, not a substantial subject.
IPFIX is mentioned only as a way to separate IPv4 and IPv6 statistics.
PIM is mentioned only for multicast exchange, which is covered by the multicast tag.
The IXP addressing plan is a major section, but IPv6 already covers it as the more specific tag.

gaps.name: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs)
gaps.why: The whole document is about IXP operations. The taxonomy has no IXP tag, apart from the route server tag, which covers only one part.

RFC5964.title: Specifying Holes in Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Service Boundaries
RFC5964.summary: Defines a profile of GML polygons with interior boundaries (holes) for specifying LoST service boundaries, with rules for valid holes and a point-in-polygon selection approach for service mapping.

LoST.why: The document extends how LoST service boundaries are expressed, giving rules for holes and showing LoST mapping examples and the server selection algorithm.
LoST.quote: This document describes how holes can be specified in geodetic service boundaries.

rejected.why: Geodetic polygons and GML are central, but the subject is LoST service boundaries; LoST sits under emergency services and is the more specific fit.
GML is XML-encoded, but XML is only the encoding substrate here.
SIP URIs appear only in example mapping responses.
The parent of LoST is implied by the LoST tag, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: GML (Geography Markup Language) polygon profile
gaps.why: The document profiles GML polygons with interior boundaries; the taxonomy has no tag for geospatial shape formats beyond the generic geolocation topic.

RFC5965.title: An Extensible Format for Email Feedback Reports
RFC5965.summary: RFC 5965 defines the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF): a multipart/report-based format and the message/feedback-report MIME type, with IANA registries, for mail operators to send machine-readable email abuse and feedback reports.

ARF.why: The document is the specification of ARF, the format for email feedback and abuse reports.
ARF.quote: This format is intended primarily as an Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) for reporting email abuse but also includes support for direct feedback via end user mail clients

media types.why: It defines and registers the new message/feedback-report media type, and its extensibility registries. This is a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: A new [MIME] content type called "message/feedback-report" is defined.

rejected.why: Abuse reports are related to spam, but the document defines a report format and not spam filtering or reputation. ARF is the more specific tag.
The Authentication-Results field and the mention of SPF and DKIM are only used for vetting reports. The document does not specify them.
SMTP envelope fields are copied into reports, but SMTP is only the substrate. The document does not extend it.
The document builds on MIME multipart/report. Its own contribution is the media type, which is covered by the media types tag.
The report fields reuse the header field syntax from RFC 5322, but the document does not define Internet message format.

RFC5966.title: DNS Transport over TCP - Implementation Requirements
RFC5966.summary: RFC 5966 updates RFC 1035 and RFC 1123 to make TCP support a required part of full DNS implementations, relaxes the UDP-first rule, gives connection-handling guidance, and clarifies response reordering.

DNS.why: The document specifies requirements for DNS implementations (authoritative, recursive, stub) regarding transport selection, connection handling and response reordering, updating core DNS specs.
DNS.quote: support for TCP is henceforth a REQUIRED part of a full DNS protocol implementation.

rejected.why: TCP is the transport DNS runs over; the document sets DNS implementation requirements, not anything new about TCP itself.
EDNS0 is discussed only as background for why UDP truncation and fallback to TCP occur; it is not specified or extended.
DNSSEC and NSEC3 are mentioned only as the cause of larger responses motivating TCP.
UDP is the contrasting default transport; the document does not address UDP usage itself.
Considered since it concerns DNS carried over TCP, but the document is about requiring TCP support in DNS, not defining a binding or transport model for a new mapping.

RFC5967.title: The application/pkcs10 Media Type
RFC5967.summary: Registers the application/pkcs10 media type for carrying PKCS #10 certification requests (DER/BER, base64 for 7-bit transports), carrying over text from the historic RFC 2311 and updating RFC 2986.

media types.why: The document's purpose is to define and register the application/pkcs10 media type, so readers of media type registrations would look for it.
media types.quote: IANA has updated the registration for the application/pkcs10 media subtype in the Application Media Types registry

PKI.why: The media type carries PKCS #10 certification requests sent to a CA, and the document updates RFC 2986. This is a substantial PKI subject, but no more specific PKI tag fits, since it is not X.509 certificate profiling or an enrollment protocol.
PKI.quote: A typical application that allows a user to generate cryptographic information has to submit that information to a Certification Authority (CA), who transforms it into a certificate.

rejected.why: The document only references S/MIME RFCs as the origin of the text and for the certs-only message. It does not specify S/MIME.
Media types are the focus, so the more specific media types tag applies. Content-Transfer-Encoding is only mentioned in passing.
BER/DER encoding of the CertificationRequest is mentioned, but the document defines no ASN.1 module or encoding rules.
Base64 is only the suggested transfer encoding for 7-bit transports, not something the document is about.
Certificates are the end product of the request, but the document does not profile X.509.
PKCS #7 and CMS appear only in a passing note about certs-only messages.

RFC5968.title: Guidelines for Extending the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP)
RFC5968.summary: Informational guidelines for designing extensions to RTCP, covering RTCP capabilities and limitations, common pitfalls, a design checklist, and the appropriate extension points.

RTCP.why: The whole document is about how to design RTCP extensions, reviewing RTCP capabilities, limitations and extension points (SDES, XR, AVPF feedback, APP, new packet types).
RTCP.quote: This document provides guidelines on extending RTCP if those basic mechanisms prove insufficient.

rejected.why: RTP is the parent of RTCP and is implied. The document concerns RTCP specifically, not RTP data transport.
Mentioned only as not affecting RTCP behaviour beyond securing it; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only in passing (RTCP timers, TCP-friendliness note); the document does not address congestion control.
Referenced only for signalling RTCP bandwidth and in security considerations.
Group scalability and SSM are discussed as design considerations, but the document is not about multicast routing or deployment.

RFC5969.title: IPv6 Rapid Deployment on IPv4 Infrastructures (6rd) -- Protocol Specification
RFC5969.summary: RFC 5969 specifies 6rd, a stateless automatic IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling mechanism that lets a service provider delegate IPv6 prefixes to customer sites over its IPv4 network, including prefix derivation, a DHCPv4 option for configuration, and border relay behaviour.

6rd.why: The document is the protocol specification of 6rd itself: prefix delegation, CE/BR behaviour, encapsulation and receiving rules.
6rd.quote: This document specifies an automatic tunneling mechanism tailored to advance deployment of IPv6 to end users via a service provider's IPv4 network infrastructure.

rejected.why: 6rd builds on 6to4 and is described as a superset, but 6to4 is only the basis. The document does not specify or extend 6to4.
The document defines a DHCPv4 option (OPTION_6RD) for configuring 6rd, but this is a provisioning mechanism for 6rd. It is not a substantial treatment of DHCP itself.
This is the parent of 6rd, so it is implied by the 6rd tag.
The document uses IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation from RFC 4213 but defines no new generic tunnelling. The 6rd tag covers it.
The document came from the softwire working group, but it specifies a 6rd-specific mechanism. It is not about the softwire framework.
The document mentions anycast BR addresses for resiliency, but only as a deployment option.

RFC5970.title: DHCPv6 Options for Network Boot
RFC5970.summary: Defines four new DHCPv6 options (boot file URL, boot file parameters, client architecture type, client network interface identifier) for network booting, plus a new IANA registry of processor architecture types.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 options with formats, option codes and message-appearance rules, so it is about DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes new options for DHCPv6 that SHOULD be used for booting a node from the network.

rejected.why: The boot file URL must comply with RFC 3986, but the document defines nothing new about URIs.
TFTP is only mentioned as a possible download protocol and is not specified or extended here.
HTTP is recommended as a download protocol, but the document does not specify or extend it.
iSCSI boot is mentioned briefly in the download considerations, and the document does not define iSCSI behaviour.
The new Processor Architecture Types registry is boilerplate-level IANA content and does not make the document about IANA guidance.
DHCPv6 is the more specific tag, and the DHCPv4 options are only referenced for parity.

gaps.name: Network boot / PXE
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for network booting or the Preboot Execution Environment (PXE). This is the document's real subject, and it ties to RFC 4578 and UEFI.

RFC5971.title: GIST: General Internet Signalling Transport
RFC5971.summary: RFC 5971 specifies GIST, the General Internet Signalling Transport, the NSIS base protocol that discovers peers and transports per-flow signalling messages along a data path using UDP/TCP/TLS messaging associations.

NSIS.why: GIST is the NSIS transport layer protocol (NTLP); the document defines its handshake, routing state, and messaging associations.
NSIS.quote: The combination of GIST and the lower layer transport and security protocols provides a solution for the base protocol component of the "Next Steps in Signalling" (NSIS) framework.

rejected.why: TLS is only the channel security protocol used in messaging associations; the document defines no new TLS extension.
TCP is the C-mode transport substrate; only its use as Forwards-TCP is specified, not TCP itself.
UDP is the D-mode encapsulation substrate, not a subject of the document.
The Router Alert Option is used for Q-mode interception, and Appendix C covers deployment issues, but the RFC is not about the option itself.
NAT traversal is a section of GIST (7.2), but the document is not about NAT behaviour in general.
RSVP is cited as inspiration and example, not specified here.

gaps.name: NSIS (Next Steps in Signalling) / GIST
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag exists for the NSIS protocol suite and its GIST transport layer. The nearest tags (QoS, NSIS under QoS) were considered, but the taxonomy as shown lists NSIS under QoS; I used that tag.

RFC5972.title: General Internet Signaling Transport (GIST) State Machine
RFC5972.summary: Informational document giving illustrative state machines (querying node and responding node, with transition tables) for implementing the GIST signalling transport protocol of the NSIS framework.

NSIS.why: GIST is the NSIS transport-layer protocol (RFC 5971). The document specifies its Message Routing State handling for NSLPs, so it belongs on the NSIS page.
NSIS.quote: This document describes state machines for the General Internet Signaling Transport (GIST).

rejected.why: NSIS is a child of QoS, so QoS is implied. The document does not itself address QoS.
UDP is only mentioned as the D-mode transport carrying peer state info. The document is not about it.
Messaging associations may run over TCP or TLS, but the document only models them abstractly and does not specify TCP.
TLS is only a possible MA security mechanism and is not discussed. The Security Considerations section is boilerplate.
RFC 4137, an EAP state-machine RFC, is cited only for notation conventions, so the document is not about EAP.
RFC 5609 is cited only for state machine details and style. PANA is not the subject.

RFC5973.title: NAT/Firewall NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (NSLP)
RFC5973.summary: Defines the NATFW NSLP, an NSIS signaling layer protocol carried over GIST that lets hosts dynamically configure NATs and firewalls along the data path via CREATE, EXTERNAL, RESPONSE and NOTIFY messages, including proxy mode and security framework.

NSIS.why: The document specifies the NATFW NSLP within the NSIS framework.
NSIS.quote: This memo defines the NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (NSLP) for Network Address Translators (NATs) and firewalls.

RFC5974.title: NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (NSLP) for Quality-of-Service Signaling
RFC5974.summary: Specifies the QoS NSLP, an NSIS signaling layer protocol that runs over GIST to establish and maintain QoS reservations along a data path, RSVP-like but with sender/receiver initiation, bidirectional and aggregate reservations, and no multicast.

NSIS.why: NSIS is not in the taxonomy, so this entry is invalid; see rejected and gaps.
NSIS.quote: This specification describes the NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (NSLP) for signaling Quality of Service (QoS) reservations in the Internet.

RFC5975.title: QSPEC Template for the Quality-of-Service NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (NSLP)
RFC5975.summary: Defines the QSPEC template, the QoS-model-independent object and set of parameters (TMOD, path latency/jitter/loss, priorities, excess treatment, PHB class, etc.) carried in QoS NSLP messages, with processing procedures, flags, encodings and IANA registries.

NSIS.quote: The Quality-of-Service (QoS) NSIS signaling layer protocol (NSLP) is used to signal QoS reservations and is independent of a specific QoS model (QOSM)

RFC5976.title: Y.1541-QOSM: Model for Networks Using Y.1541 Quality-of-Service Classes
RFC5976.summary: Defines the Y.1541-QOSM, a QoS-NSLP QoS model for NSIS based on ITU-T Y.1541 network QoS classes, adding TMOD extension (peak bucket size) and Restoration Priority QSPEC parameters and processing guidance.

NSIS.why: The document specifies a QOSM for the NSIS QoS-NSLP, extending QSPEC with new parameters and processing rules, so it belongs under NSIS.
NSIS.quote: This document describes a QoS-NSLP Quality-of-Service model (QOSM) based on ITU-T Recommendation Y.1541 Network QoS Classes and related guidance on signaling.

rejected.why: Diffserv PHBs (EF, AF, default) are only mentioned as possible implementations of the Y.1541 classes; the document is not about Diffserv.
RSVP and Intserv TSpec/RSpec are referenced only by analogy to QSPEC; the document does not specify or extend RSVP.
The parent is implied by the NSIS tag, so it is not listed separately.
Y.1541 performance objectives (delay, jitter, loss) are used as QoS class parameters, but the document does not define metrics or measurement methods.
The IANA section only registers QSPEC parameter IDs and a restoration priority registry, which is boilerplate for this document.

RFC5977.title: RMD-QOSM: The NSIS Quality-of-Service Model for Resource Management in Diffserv
RFC5977.summary: RFC 5977 specifies RMD-QOSM, an NSIS QoS model and RMD-specific QSPEC for adding edge-to-edge admission control, preemption and severe-congestion handling to Diffserv domains using QoS-NSLP with stateless or reduced-state interior nodes.

NSIS.quote: This document describes a Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) Quality-of-Service (QoS) Model for networks that use the Resource Management in Diffserv (RMD) concept.

RFC5978.title: Using and Extending the NSIS Protocol Family
RFC5978.summary: Informational overview of the NSIS signaling framework (GIST, QoS NSLP, NAT/firewall NSLP), with guidance on deploying the protocols and on extending GIST, the NSLPs and QSPEC.

NSIS.why: The whole document is about the NSIS protocol family. This is the closest fit, but see the gaps note: NSIS is not in the taxonomy as its own tag.
NSIS.quote: This document gives an overview of the Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) framework and protocol suite created by the NSIS Working Group

RFC5979.title: NSIS Operation over IP Tunnels
RFC5979.summary: Experimental RFC defining how NSIS QoS signaling is extended into IP tunnel segments by mapping end-to-end QoS sessions to preconfigured or dynamically created tunnel QoS sessions, with tunnel Flow IDs and a capability discovery object.

NSIS.why: The whole document specifies NSIS QoS NSLP operation over IP tunnels, including a new NODE_CAPABILITY_TUNNEL object.
NSIS.quote: This document defines a mechanism to extend end-to-end NSIS signaling for QoS reservation into IP tunnels.

tunneling.why: The problem is tunnel encapsulation masking original headers; the document defines tunnel Flow IDs for GRE, IP-in-IP, IPv6 and IPsec tunnels.
tunneling.quote: IP tunneling (Figure 1) is a technique for establishing a "virtual link" between two IP nodes for transmitting data packets as payloads of IP packets.

rejected.why: Only referenced as prior work (RSVP-TUNNEL RFC 2746) that the design learns from; not specified here.
IPsec tunnel mode is one of the tunnel types handled (SPI as Flow ID) and security considerations discuss it, but the document is not about IPsec.
One of several tunneling protocols listed; not the subject.
The parent topic is implied by NSIS, which is a child of QoS, so it is not listed separately.
Mentioned only as how NSIS discovery messages are intercepted.

RFC5980.title: NSIS Protocol Operation in Mobile Environments
RFC5980.summary: Informational RFC analysing how the NSIS protocol suite (GIST, QoS NSLP, NAT/FW NSLP) operates under IP mobility, including crossover node discovery, state update, and interaction with Mobile IPv4/v6 and tunnels.

NSIS.why: The whole document analyses NSIS (GIST, QoS NSLP, NATFW NSLP) behaviour under mobility, including CRN discovery and State Update.
NSIS.quote: discusses the effects mobility can cause to the Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) protocol suite, and shows how the NSIS protocols operate

IP mobility.why: A substantial part covers interaction with Mobile IPv4, Mobile IPv6, tunnelling, HMIP and handover; the document does not specify a mobility protocol itself, so the general IP mobility topic fits.
IP mobility.quote: Interaction with Mobile IPv4/v6

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 is the environment NSIS is analysed against, not specified or extended here; covered by the IP mobility parent.
Same as Mobile IPv6: the document only describes NSIS interaction with it.
RSVP is only mentioned once as a comparison for sender- vs receiver-initiated setup.
IP-in-IP tunnelling is discussed as a Mobile IP challenge, but the tunnel signalling itself is specified in RFC 5979.
NAT/FW NSLP is discussed only as one NSLP, not NAT behaviour in general.

gaps.name: NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling), GIST, QoS NSLP, NAT/FW NSLP
gaps.why: The taxonomy fetched for this document has QoS and NAT/firewall tags, and a NSIS tag exists in the QoS subtree, but I used 'NSIS' as the id; verify it matches exactly the taxonomy id 'NSIS' under QoS. This is flagged because the NSIS tag appears as a [tech] under QoS and should be confirmed.

RFC5981.title: Authorization for NSIS Signaling Layer Protocols
RFC5981.summary: Defines a generic SESSION_AUTH object and attribute formats for per-session authorization in NSIS signaling layer protocols (QoS NSLP and NATFW NSLP), with integrity options (shared key, Kerberos, public key, HMAC) and processing rules.

NSIS.quote: This document presents a generic model and object formats for session authorization within the NSIS signaling layer protocols.

RFC5982.title: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Mediation: Problem Statement
RFC5982.summary: Informational problem statement describing flow-measurement scalability, flexibility and reliability problems and showing how IPFIX Mediation (intermediate devices between Exporters and Collectors) can address them, plus implementation problems of Mediators.

IPFIX.why: The whole document is about IPFIX Mediation, a generalized intermediate-device concept for the IPFIX protocol, including its applicability examples and Template/Transport Session handling problems.
