IPFIX.quote: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Mediation fills the gap between restricted metering capabilities and the requirements of measurement applications by introducing an intermediate device called the IPFIX Mediator.

PSAMP.why: PSAMP packet reports, sampling and filtering are repeatedly covered as inputs to Mediation (correlation, one-way delay, adjusted selection fraction).
PSAMP.quote: IPFIX Mediation can be applied to Flow- or packet-based information.

rejected.why: The document is about flow export mediation; one-way delay computation is only an example use, and the IPFIX tag already covers it.
SCTP is mentioned only as a reliable transport choice for export in the data-retention example.
TLS/DTLS only appear in Security Considerations as protection for transport.
Anonymization is one applicability example, not the document's main subject.
Too general; the IPFIX tag is the specific fit.

RFC5983.title: Mailing Lists and Internationalized Email Addresses
RFC5983.summary: RFC 5983 describes considerations and gives recommendations for how mailing lists should handle internationalized (UTF-8) email addresses in transport, List-* header fields, and operational policy, including downgrading and alt-addresses.

mailing lists.why: The whole document is about how mailing lists should behave, including List-* header fields (List-Id, List-Post, etc.) and list operational policy.
mailing lists.quote: This document describes considerations for mailing lists with the introduction of internationalized email addresses.

EAI.why: It is an EAI working group document dealing with UTF8SMTP, alt-addresses and downgrading for internationalized email addresses as they affect lists.
EAI.quote: The introduction of internationalized email addresses affects mailing lists in three main areas: (1) transport (receiving and sending messages)

rejected.why: SMTP and UTF8SMTP are the substrate; the document makes no new protocol specification, and the SMTP extension is covered by EAI.
List header fields are discussed, but they are defined in other RFCs. Here they are treated only as part of mailing list behaviour.
IRIs and URI encoding are mentioned for List-* URLs, but they are not a main subject.
List-* header fields contain URLs and mailto is mentioned, but the document is not about URI syntax.
Sieve is mentioned only as an example of a filter that compares List-Id values.

RFC5984.title: Increasing Throughput in IP Networks with ESP-Based Forwarding: ESPBasedForwarding
RFC5984.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing "ESP-based" (Extra Sensory Perception) forwarding with precognitive packet generation to achieve zero or negative latency and infinite bandwidth.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical parody with Infinite Improbability Drives, Ouija boards and eel-filled hovercraft; it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: This document proposes an experimental way of reaching infinite bandwidth in IP networks by the use of ESP-based forwarding.

rejected.why: Here ESP means Extra Sensory Perception, not IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload; the document is not about IPsec.
TCP slow-start is only mentioned briefly as a joke in Section 5; the document does not address TCP.
NTP is mentioned in passing as the synchronization of the pre-preemptive scheduler; the document is not about it.
Only a one-line remark that a congestion avoidance mechanism may need further study.
The CFE uses a routing table, but the document does not specify any routing protocol or behaviour.
Title acronym ESP is unrelated to IPsec.

RFC5985.title: HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD)
RFC5985.summary: Defines HELD, an XML-based Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol with HTTP and HTTPS bindings, letting a Device retrieve its location from an access-network LIS by value (PIDF-LO) or by reference (Location URIs).

HELD.why: The document specifies HELD itself: its messages, parameters, error codes, XML schema and HTTP binding.
HELD.quote: This document defines a Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol (L7 LCP) and describes the use of HTTP and HTTP/TLS as transports for the L7 LCP.

geolocation.why: Subject matter is acquiring and conveying location information (PIDF-LO, civic/geodetic, location URIs, privacy of location). HELD is a child of geolocation, so the parent tag is added only because the document also addresses geolocation concerns beyond HELD, such as PIDF-LO construction and location privacy.
geolocation.quote: A Device uses the HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) protocol to retrieve its location either directly in the form of a Presence Information Data Format Location Object

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport binding; the document uses a strict subset and defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
TLS is used as a security mechanism (HTTPS) with no new TLS extension or specification.
XML is the message encoding and schema language, not the subject.
PIDF-LO is the location object returned; the document follows RFC 5491 rather than defining or extending PIDF.
Registers application/held+xml, but this is boilerplate IANA registration for the protocol's own media type.
Emergency routing/dispatch is mentioned as a use case for responseTime, but the document is not about emergency calling.

gaps.name: Location Configuration Protocol / GEOPRIV location acquisition (LIS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has HELD under geolocation, but no broader tag for location configuration protocols or PIDF-LO/GEOPRIV location objects.

RFC5986.title: Discovering the Local Location Information Server (LIS)
RFC5986.summary: Defines how a Device discovers its local Location Information Server (LIS) using new DHCPv4/DHCPv6 access network domain name options as input to U-NAPTR resolution, yielding a HELD URI.

HELD.why: The document specifies LIS discovery for HELD, registering the "HELD" application protocol tag and defining the verification of a LIS via HELD requests. It sits under HELD in the location taxonomy.
HELD.quote: the Device MUST dereference the URI using the process described in HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD)

DHCP.why: The document defines new DHCPv4 option 213 and DHCPv6 option 57 for the access network domain name, which is a substantial extension of DHCP.
DHCP.quote: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) options for IP versions 4 and 6 are defined that specify a domain name.

service discovery.why: The document is a service discovery mechanism that uses U-NAPTR/DDDS and registers a new S-NAPTR service tag. No more specific discovery tag fits, since DNS-SD and SLP are different systems.
service discovery.quote: A method is described for the discovery of a LIS in the access network serving a Device.

rejected.why: DNS NAPTR is the substrate for U-NAPTR resolution. The document registers application tags but defines no new DNS record type or DNS behaviour.
The DHCPv6 option is defined, but the DHCP tag already covers both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 equally. The document is not mainly about DHCPv6.
HELD is the more specific tag under geolocation, so the parent is not needed.
HTTP and HTTPS URIs are only the product of discovery and the transport for HELD. The document does not extend HTTP.
VPNs are mentioned only to say that discovery over a VPN interface should be avoided. They are not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: U-NAPTR / DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service)
gaps.why: The document uses and registers S-NAPTR/U-NAPTR application tags. The taxonomy has no tag for DDDS or NAPTR-based application service location, so service discovery is the closest fit.

RFC5987.title: Character Set and Language Encoding for Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Header Field Parameters
RFC5987.summary: Defines an encoding (a profile of RFC 2231) for carrying non-ASCII characters and language information in HTTP header field parameters, using charset'language'percent-encoded-value syntax, plus guidelines for header field specifications.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP header field parameter syntax with an ext-value encoding and gives guidance for HTTP header field definitions. It is about HTTP semantics and syntax extensions.
HTTP.quote: This document specifies an encoding suitable for use in HTTP header fields that is compatible with a profile of the encoding defined in RFC 2231.

character sets.why: A substantial part of the document concerns which character sets are mandatory and how charset names are used and registered in parameter values.
character sets.quote: recipients implementing this specification MUST support the character sets "ISO-8859-1" [ISO-8859-1] and "UTF-8" [RFC3629].
character sets.section: 3.2. Parameter Value Character Set and Language Information

language tags.why: The encoding carries optional language information in parameter values, as required by the IETF language policy, so readers of language tags would want it.
language tags.quote: language      = <Language-Tag, defined in [RFC5646], Section 2.1>

rejected.why: RFC 2231 is cited only to explain which features were adopted. The document says it is purely informative, and the encoding applies to HTTP, not MIME.
UTF-8 is one of two mandatory charsets, but the document is not about the UTF-8 encoding itself.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the grammar.
Percent-encoding from RFC 3986 is used as the mechanism for encoding octets. The document does not define anything new about URIs.
The document is about internationalized header parameters. The more specific tags, character sets and language tags, cover that.

RFC5988.title: Web Linking
RFC5988.summary: RFC 5988 defines a serialisation-independent framework for typed web links, establishes the IANA Link Relation Type registry, and re-specifies the HTTP Link header field for conveying such links.

web linking.why: The whole document defines typed web links, link relation types, the relation type registry and the Link header, which is the core subject of web linking.
web linking.quote: This document specifies relation types for Web links, and defines a registry for them.  It also defines the use of such links in HTTP headers with the Link header field.

rejected.why: The Link header is an HTTP header field, but HTTP is the substrate. The document is about linking, not HTTP semantics, and the more specific web linking tag covers it.
Atom's link relation registry is redefined and Appendix B gives serialisation notes, but the document is not about Atom itself.
HTML4 link relations are imported into the registry and Appendix A has notes, but the document is not about HTML.
Links are built on IRIs and URIs, but only as building blocks. The document defines no new URI syntax or scheme.
It creates registries, but this is part of the web linking subject and the IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like.
IRIs identify link context and target, but they are only used here, not specified or extended.

RFC5989.title: A SIP Event Package for Subscribing to Changes to an HTTP Resource
RFC5989.summary: Defines a SIP event package, "http-monitor", that lets clients subscribe to changes of an HTTP resource. It also defines the "monitor" and "monitor-group" link relations that let an HTTP server advertise the SIP URI to subscribe to.

SIP.why: The document defines a new SIP event package (http-monitor), a new Event header parameter, and the SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY behaviour for it. This is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines a mechanism, based on the SIP Event Framework [4], for subscribing to changes in the resource referenced by an HTTP server.

web linking.why: A substantial part of the document defines two new link relation types, registered in the Link Relations registry. They are conveyed via the HTTP Link header, HTML link and Atom link.
web linking.quote: This document defines two new link relation types ("monitor" and "monitor-group") for this purpose
web linking.section: 3. Associating Monitoring SIP URIs with HTTP URLs

rejected.why: HTTP is the monitored subject and the channel for discovering the SIP URI. The document does not extend HTTP itself beyond using the Link header.
The package uses SIP event machinery and RLS list subscriptions, but it is not a presence or IM package, and it defines no PIDF or XCAP content.
It uses message/http as the NOTIFY body but registers no new media type.
PROPFIND is discussed only in the appendix as a rejected alternative.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations, as a way to protect the Link header.

RFC5990.title: Use of the RSA-KEM Key Transport Algorithm in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC5990.summary: Specifies conventions for using the RSA-KEM key transport algorithm (random-integer RSA encryption plus symmetric key wrapping) for recipients in CMS enveloped-data, including RecipientInfo, certificate, and SMIMECapabilities conventions and ASN.1.

CMS.why: The document defines how RSA-KEM is used in CMS enveloped-data via KeyTransRecipientInfo, so CMS readers need it.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the RSA-KEM Key Transport Algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

RSA.why: The algorithm is an RSA-based key transport scheme, specified in full in Appendix A, with RSA key usage guidance.
RSA.quote: The RSA-KEM Key Transport Algorithm is a one-pass (store-and-forward) mechanism for transporting keying data to a recipient using the recipient's RSA public key.

rejected.why: Only the SMIMECapabilities attribute is touched; the document is about CMS enveloped-data, not S/MIME messaging.
Certificate conventions are a small section augmenting RFC 5280; not the main subject.
AES Key Wrap is just an underlying component, not what the document is about.
Camellia key wrap is an optional component only.
SHA hashes are used only as KDF building blocks.
ASN.1 is the notation for the module, not the subject.

RFC5991.title: Teredo Security Updates
RFC5991.summary: RFC 5991 updates the Teredo protocol (RFC 4380) by randomizing unused Flags bits in Teredo IPv6 addresses to resist address scanning and by deprecating the cone bit to avoid revealing NAT security posture.

Teredo.why: The document updates the Teredo address Flags field and the qualification procedure.
Teredo.quote: Teredo [RFC4380] defines a set of flags that are embedded in every Teredo IPv6 address.  This document specifies a set of security updates

rejected.why: NAT behaviour is background for Teredo; the document does not specify NAT behaviour.
Only compared against in Appendix B for address-prediction resistance; not the subject.
Requires random bits per RFC 4086 but only references existing guidance.
Teredo is a child of this topic and already tagged, so the parent is implied.

RFC5992.title: Internationalized Domain Names Registration and Administration Guidelines for European Languages Using Cyrillic
RFC5992.summary: Informational guideline for registries and registrars on registering Cyrillic-script IDN labels for European languages (Bosnian, Bulgarian, Belarusian, Kildin Sami, Macedonian, Montenegrin, Russian, Serbian, Ukrainian), listing permitted characters and Latin/Greek confusable variants and registry policy options.

IDN.why: The whole document defines per-language Cyrillic character sets, confusable variants and registration bundle policy for IDN labels under IDNA2008.
IDN.quote: This document is a guideline for registries and registrars on registering internationalized domain names (IDNs) based on (in alphabetical order) Bosnian, Bulgarian, Byelorussian

domain registration.why: It gives registries and registrars guidance on registration policy: allocating or blocking variant labels, and keeping a database linking bundle labels to the input label.
domain registration.quote: A registry has at least three policy options for handling the cases where the registration bundle has more than one label.
domain registration.section: 6. Steps after Registering an Input Label

rejected.why: DNS is only the namespace where the labels are registered. The document does not specify DNS protocol or operations.
The document relies on Unicode code points as the basis for its character tables. It is not about Unicode usage in protocols in general; it is about IDN registration.
The IDN tag already covers the subject, and it is more specific than this parent topic.
The document lists Unicode characters per language for domain labels. It does not register or define a character set.

RFC5993.title: RTP Payload Format for Global System for Mobile Communications Half Rate (GSM-HR)
RFC5993.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for GSM Half Rate (GSM-HR) speech codec frames, including ToC structure, SID frames, GSM-HR-specific redundancy, and the audio/GSM-HR-08 media type with SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document's main purpose is defining an RTP payload format for a specific speech codec, which is exactly what this tag covers.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of GSM Half Rate (GSM-HR) codec [TS46.002] encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

rejected.why: RTP is the carrier protocol; the document defines a payload format, which is covered by the more specific child tag.
SDP mapping and offer/answer are standard payload-format boilerplate for a few parameters, not a substantial subject of the document.
The audio/GSM-HR-08 registration is part of the payload format specification and not about media type registry rules.
The GSM-HR-specific redundancy scheme is a small part of the document; generic FEC is only referenced.
GSM is the origin of the codec, but the document is not about IP over cellular networks.
The codec is defined by 3GPP; this document only packetizes it, so the RTP payload format tag fits better.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended mechanism.

RFC5994.title: Application of Ethernet Pseudowires to MPLS Transport Networks
RFC5994.summary: Informational RFC profiling Ethernet pseudowires (RFC 4448) over statically provisioned MPLS transport LSPs, with BFD-based VCCV OAM, as an interim packet transport solution ahead of MPLS-TP.

pseudowire.why: The document profiles the Ethernet pseudowire (control word, static labels, no LDP signalling, VCCV OAM) for transport networks.
pseudowire.quote: The PWE3 encapsulation used by this specification to satisfy the transport requirement is Ethernet [RFC4448]. This is used in "raw" mode.

MPLS-TP.why: The document is framed around MPLS-TP requirements and serves as a stop-gap and foundation for MPLS-TP work, so MPLS-TP readers would want it.
MPLS-TP.quote: The solution described here does not address all of the MPLS-TP requirements, but it provides a viable form of packet transport service

MPLS.why: A substantial section constrains the MPLS LSP layer: static labels, no PHP, no ECMP, no merging, E-LSP/L-LSP, and pipe models.
MPLS.quote: All MPLS labels used in the server layer (Figure 1) MUST be statically provisioned.

rejected.why: BFD is used as the connectivity verification mechanism through VCCV (RFC 5885), but the document does not specify or extend BFD itself.
Ethernet is the client payload carried by the pseudowire. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
GMPLS is only mentioned as an optional control plane in Section 4.2, so it is not a substantial subject of the document.
RSVP-TE is only mentioned as one option for control plane LSP setup, and the document does not extend or profile it.
ECMP is prohibited on the transport LSPs, but this is a configuration restriction and not the subject of the document.

RFC5995.title: Using POST to Add Members to Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) Collections
RFC5995.summary: RFC 5995 defines a WebDAV discovery mechanism (the DAV:add-member property and an "Add-Member" URI) so servers can advertise that HTTP POST adds a new server-named member to a collection, plus a DAV:allow-client-defined-URI precondition.

WebDAV.why: The document extends WebDAV with a new protected property, DAV:add-member, a new precondition, and POST semantics for collections. Readers of WebDAV material would want it.
WebDAV.quote: This specification defines a discovery mechanism through which servers can advertise support for POST requests with the aforementioned "add collection member" semantics.

rejected.why: POST and the Location header are used as the substrate. The new mechanism is defined at the WebDAV layer (properties and preconditions), not as a new HTTP extension.
AtomPub is cited only as precedent for POST creating members, and the Slug header is reused. The document does not specify or extend AtomPub.
CalDAV is mentioned only as a motivating protocol that could benefit. The document does not extend it.
XML DTD fragments are used only as notation for the property and precondition definitions.
The 'Add-Member' URI is a WebDAV concept. The document does not define URI syntax or schemes.

RFC5996.title: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC5996.summary: RFC 5996 specifies IKEv2, the IPsec key exchange protocol for mutual authentication and creation, rekeying and deletion of IKE and Child SAs, replacing RFC 4306 and incorporating RFC 4718 clarifications.

IKE.why: The whole document specifies the IKEv2 protocol: exchanges, payloads, rekeying, error handling, and key derivation.
IKE.quote: This document describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol.

NAT.why: Sections 2.23 and 2.23.1 cover NAT traversal in detail, including NAT detection payloads and transport mode traffic selector handling.
NAT.quote: IKEv2 will use UDP encapsulation of IKE and ESP packets.

rejected.why: IKE is a child of IPsec in the taxonomy, so the parent is implied. ESP and AH are the SAs IKE sets up, not the subject.
EAP is supported as an authentication option (Section 2.16), but the document defines no new EAP method. It is a minor part of the document.
ESP SAs are negotiated by IKE, but ESP itself is not specified here.
IPComp negotiation is a short section (2.22) and its taxonomy tag is not warranted as a main subject.
Section 2.24 only requires ECN support for tunnel mode and does not define ECN behaviour.
Certificates are carried in CERT payloads, but certificate profiles are not defined here.

RFC5997.title: Use of Status-Server Packets in the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) Protocol
RFC5997.summary: Informational RFC documenting the deployed RADIUS Status-Server (Code 12) extension, which lets clients query a RADIUS server's liveness, with packet format, client/server requirements, failover use, and MIB counter interactions.

RADIUS.why: The whole document specifies a RADIUS extension (Status-Server packets), including packet format, attributes, client and server behaviour and failover.
RADIUS.quote: This document describes a deployed extension to the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) protocol, enabling clients to query the status of a RADIUS server.

rejected.why: Section 4.6 only says how Status-Server interacts with existing RADIUS MIB counters. It defines no MIB module and leaves that out of scope.
UDP is only the transport the extension runs over. The document says it focuses on UDP transport, but it does not specify UDP usage.
MD5 is used only for the Response Authenticator, as in core RADIUS. The document is not about it.
RADIUS is the more specific tag. The document does not address AAA frameworks generally.
Message-Authenticator comes from the RADIUS EAP support RFC, but EAP is not the subject. EAP-Message must not appear in Status-Server packets.

RFC5998.title: An Extension for EAP-Only Authentication in IKEv2
RFC5998.summary: RFC 5998 extends IKEv2 so that mutually authenticating, key-generating EAP methods can authenticate the responder without public-key signatures, using a new EAP_ONLY_AUTHENTICATION notification, and lists safe EAP methods.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new notification and changes the IKE_AUTH exchange so the responder can omit its AUTH and CERT payloads.
IKE.quote: If the initiator does not wish to use public-key-based responder authentication, it includes an EAP_ONLY_AUTHENTICATION notification payload (16417) in message 3.

EAP.why: It defines which EAP methods are safe for EAP-only authentication (mutual authentication, key generation, dictionary-attack resistance). It also discusses channel binding and the EAP key use.
EAP.quote: EAP methods to be used with this extension MUST have the following properties:

rejected.why: The AAA backend (RADIUS/Diameter) appears in the scenarios and security considerations, but only as the place where EAP terminates, not as a subject of the document.
IKEv2 sets up IPsec SAs, but the document is about IKE authentication, and the more specific IKE tag covers it.
It argues that PKI is unrealistic for gateway authentication and avoids it, but it does not specify or profile PKI.
RADIUS is mentioned only as a possible protocol between the gateway and the AAA server.

RFC6001.title: Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Protocol Extensions for Multi-Layer and Multi-Region Networks (MLN/MRN)
RFC6001.summary: RFC 6001 defines GMPLS routing (IACD sub-TLV in OSPF/IS-IS) and RSVP-TE signalling extensions (XRO Switching Capability and Label subobjects, CALL_ATTRIBUTES, Pre-Planned LSP flag) to support multi-layer/multi-region networks under a single GMPLS control plane.

GMPLS.why: The whole document extends GMPLS routing and signalling for MLN/MRN, including IACD, XRO subobjects, virtual TE links and call attributes.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines extensions to GMPLS routing and signaling protocols so as to support the operation of GMPLS Multi-Layer / Multi-Region Networks.

RSVP-TE.why: Defines new RSVP-TE objects and flags (XRO SC and Label subobjects, CALL_ATTRIBUTES object, Pre-Planned LSP flag) as a substantial part of the document.
RSVP-TE.quote: this document defines a new subobject of the eXclude Route Object (XRO), see [RFC4874], called the Switching Capability subobject.

OSPF.why: Defines a new OSPF TE link sub-TLV for advertising interface adjustment capability.
OSPF.quote: In OSPF, the IACD sub-TLV is defined as an optional sub-TLV of the TE Link TLV (Type 2, see [RFC3630]), with Type 25 and variable length.

IS-IS.why: Defines the corresponding IS-IS sub-TLV for the IACD.
IS-IS.quote: In IS-IS, the IACD sub-TLV is an optional sub-TLV of the Extended IS Reachability TLV (see [RFC5305]) with Type 27.

rejected.why: GMPLS is the more specific tag under MPLS and covers the document's subject.
IKE is only mentioned in Security Considerations as the means to secure call setup; boilerplate-level, not the document's subject.
TE links and TE domains are the context, but the document's subject is covered by the GMPLS and RSVP-TE tags.
Only required for securing calls in Security Considerations; not about IKE.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new protocol elements, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Multi-Layer/Multi-Region Networks (MLN/MRN)
gaps.why: The document's central subject, GMPLS control of multiple switching layers and regions, has no dedicated tag. GMPLS is the closest.

RFC6002.title: Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Data Channel Switching Capable (DCSC) and Channel Set Label Extensions
RFC6002.summary: RFC 6002 extends GMPLS signaling with a new Data Channel Switching Capable (DCSC) switching type and a Generalized Channel_Set label (and LABEL_REQUEST C-Type) so one LSP can carry many data-plane labels such as VLAN IDs.

GMPLS.why: The whole document defines new GMPLS switching type and label format, updating RFC 3471, 3473, 3945, 4202. This is GMPLS signaling and label extension work.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes two technology-independent extensions to Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

rejected.why: The new objects are carried in RSVP-TE Path/Resv messages, but RSVP-TE is the signaling substrate; the document is about GMPLS extensions.
The extensions originated for Ethernet services (RFC 6004/6005), but this document is technology-independent and does not specify Ethernet behavior.
The DCSC value is carried in OSPF/IS-IS descriptors, but the document explicitly says those documents are not modified.
The DCSC value is carried in IS-IS descriptors, but the document explicitly says RFC 5307 is not otherwise modified.
GMPLS is the more specific tag, and the document is not about general MPLS.

RFC6003.title: Ethernet Traffic Parameters
RFC6003.summary: Defines Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects and a Bandwidth Profile TLV for GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling, carrying MEF Ethernet traffic parameters (CIR, CBS, EIR, EBS, color mode, coupling flag).

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling (updating RFC 3471 and 3473) with Ethernet-specific traffic specification objects and IANA registries.
GMPLS.quote: support of Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) Ethernet traffic parameters as described in MEF10.1 when using Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Resource ReSerVation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) signaling

Ethernet.why: It specifies how Ethernet LSPs (L2SC, Ethernet encoding) and MEF bandwidth profiles are signaled, so readers of Ethernet topics would want it.
Ethernet.quote: The Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC/FLOWSPEC object includes the Ethernet link type (switching granularity) of the requested LSP and the MTU value for the LSP.

rejected.why: The document does extend RSVP-TE, but GMPLS is the more specific tag for the GMPLS signaling extensions here. I considered RSVP-TE as a separate tag and decided against it.
RSVP objects (SENDER_TSPEC, FLOWSPEC) are the substrate being extended. The document is not about RSVP itself.
The ADSPEC section only mentions IntServ ADSPEC as an option, and the document is not about Intserv.
The bandwidth profile is a traffic parameter set, but the document is not a QoS architecture or signalling framework. The GMPLS tag covers the signalling.

RFC6004.title: Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Support for Metro Ethernet Forum and G.8011 Ethernet Service Switching
RFC6004.summary: Defines GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling extensions (Endpoint ID TLV, L2CP TLV, EVPL label, new switching/encoding types) for controlling Ethernet switching that supports MEF and ITU G.8011 EPL and EVPL services.

GMPLS.why: The document specifies GMPLS signaling extensions: new TLVs, an EVPL generalized label, a new switching type and LSP encoding type, and procedures for Calls and LSPs.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes a method for controlling two specific types of Ethernet switching via Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

Ethernet.why: A substantial part of the document concerns Ethernet services (EPL/EVPL), VLAN IDs and L2 control protocol handling, so readers of Ethernet control and interworking would want it.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet private line and Ethernet virtual private line services are covered.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signaling substrate that GMPLS extends here. The document adds GMPLS-specific objects and TLVs, not new RSVP-TE mechanisms in general.
The document concerns Ethernet service switching over GMPLS, not the MPLS Transport Profile.
EVPL is a 'virtual private line' Ethernet service, but the document does not cover provider-provisioned VPNs such as VPLS or L2VPN.
TE LSPs are used, but traffic engineering itself is not the subject. The traffic parameters come from RFC 6003.

RFC6005.title: Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Support for Metro Ethernet Forum and G.8011 User Network Interface (UNI)
RFC6005.summary: Defines GMPLS RSVP-TE UNI procedures (overlay model) for signalling Ethernet EPL and EVPL service LSPs per MEF and ITU-T G.8011, including egress address resolution via Notify messages and VLAN ID control.

GMPLS.why: The document specifies GMPLS RSVP-TE signalling procedures for the Ethernet UNI, extending GMPLS overlay UNI and call procedures; GMPLS is the core subject.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides a method for GMPLS-based control of Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that support the transport services defined in the above documents at the UNI network reference points.

Ethernet.why: It covers signalling for MEF/G.8011 Ethernet services (EPL, EVPL, VLAN ID handling), so readers of Ethernet service control would want it.
Ethernet.quote: Within this framework, [G.8011.1] defines the Ethernet Private Line (EPL) service and [G.8011.2] defines the Ethernet Virtual Private Line (EVPL) service.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signalling substrate; the document reuses it (and adds an error value) rather than specifying RSVP-TE itself. GMPLS is the more specific fit.
The document is about service UNI signalling, not traffic engineering.
EPL/EVPL are Ethernet transport services, not L2VPN as defined here; MP2MP is explicitly out of scope.
Only a single error value assignment in boilerplate-level IANA section.

RFC6006.title: Extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for Point-to-Multipoint Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths
RFC6006.summary: RFC 6006 extends PCEP with new objects, flags, TLVs, objective functions, metrics and error codes so a PCC can request, and a PCE can compute, paths for point-to-multipoint MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies PCEP extensions (END-POINTS, RP flags, SERO/SRRO, error types) for P2MP path computation, which is squarely the PCE/PCEP subject.
PCE.quote: This document describes extensions to the PCE communication Protocol (PCEP) to handle requests and responses for the computation of paths for P2MP TE LSPs.

rejected.why: The document reuses ERO/RRO encodings and P2MP RSVP-TE (RFC 4875) as background, but defines no RSVP-TE signalling itself.
P2MP TE LSPs are the subject of the computation, but the document specifies PCEP, not MPLS architecture or encapsulation.
GMPLS is mentioned as an applicable environment only; nothing GMPLS-specific is specified.
PCEP runs over TCP and fragmentation assumes reliable delivery, but TCP is only the substrate.
A PCE capability flag is added to OSPF discovery, but this is a minor IANA-level addition, not an OSPF specification.
RBNF is used only as the notation for message formats, not as the subject.

RFC6007.title: Use of the Synchronization VECtor (SVEC) List for Synchronized Dependent Path Computations
RFC6007.summary: Informational RFC clarifying how lists of SVEC objects in PCEP PCReq messages are associated and processed for synchronized dependent path computations (e.g., diverse paths) in single- and multi-domain PCE environments, including disjoint VSPT encoding.

PCE.why: The document is entirely about PCEP's SVEC object use in PCE path computation, including associated SVECs, multi-PCE processing, BRPC-based diverse path computation and disjoint VSPT encoding.
PCE.quote: This informational document clarifies the use of the SVEC list for synchronized path computations when computing dependent requests.

rejected.why: Parent of PCE; PCE is the more specific fit and implies it.
Only referenced for P2MP TE LSPs as secondary paths; not the subject.
TE LSPs are the context for path computation but the document does not address MPLS itself.
Mentioned only via a reference to H-PCE; not a subject of the document.
Manageability section only notes no MIB parameters are defined; boilerplate-like.

RFC6008.title: Authentication-Results Registration for Differentiating among Cryptographic Results
RFC6008.summary: RFC 6008 registers a new "header.b" property in the Authentication-Results registry so results for multiple DKIM signatures on one message can be unambiguously matched to the signature they describe.

DKIM.why: The document defines how DKIM verification results are tied to a specific DKIM signature via the b= tag value. It extends the reporting of DKIM results.
DKIM.quote: This memo adds the "header.b" reporting item to the IANA "Email Authentication Methods" registry

email authentication.why: It extends the Authentication-Results header field, which is the general email authentication reporting mechanism. No child tag covers Authentication-Results itself, so the parent topic applies.
email authentication.quote: presents the results of a message authentication effort in a machine-readable format

rejected.why: Authentication-Results is a message header field, but the document only registers a property value. It does not address the Internet message format.
The document adds one registry entry. The registration is the means of the change and the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
SHA1 and SHA256 appear only in a passing remark about collision likelihood.
RSA is mentioned only in passing, as part of the argument that signature prefixes are unlikely to collide.

RFC6009.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Delivery Status Notifications and Deliver-By Extensions
RFC6009.summary: Defines four Sieve email filtering extensions (envelope-dsn, envelope-deliverby, redirect-dsn, redirect-deliverby) giving Sieve scripts access to SMTP DSN and Deliver-By envelope parameters and control over them in the redirect action.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the Sieve language: new envelope parts, a :zone argument, and new redirect arguments.
Sieve.quote: This document describes the "envelope-dsn", "redirect-dsn", "envelope-deliverby", and "redirect-deliverby" extensions to the Sieve email filtering language.

rejected.why: The document relies on the DSN and Deliver-By SMTP extensions as the source of the envelope parameters. It does not specify or extend SMTP, so SMTP is the substrate and Sieve is the subject.
It uses the RFC 3339 date-time production for bytimeabsolute. That is only a reference to an existing format, not a new definition of one.
ABNF is only the notation used for the argument syntax.
The IANA section only registers the four Sieve capability names, which is boilerplate.
Message headers are not the subject. The document deals with envelope parameters.

RFC6010.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Content Constraints Extension
RFC6010.summary: Defines the CMS content constraints certificate/trust-anchor extension that authorizes a public key to validate only specific CMS content types and attribute values, with path-processing rules and TAMP subordination checks.

CMS.why: The extension governs authorization for validating CMS SignedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData, and defines CMS path processing and attribute collection.
CMS.quote: This extension is used to determine whether a public key is appropriate to use in the processing of a protected content.

X.509.why: It defines a new X.509 certificate extension (id-pe-cmsContentConstraints) and augments path validation with it.
X.509.quote: The processing is presented as an augmentation to the certification path validation algorithm described in Section 6 of [RFC5280]

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the extension; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The X.509 child tag is the more specific fit; the general PKI parent is implied.
Authorization is the document's purpose, but the CMS and X.509 tags already cover it more specifically.

gaps.name: Trust Anchor Management Protocol (TAMP) / Trust Anchor Format
gaps.why: Section 5 defines subordination processing for CCC in TAMP trust anchor updates, but the taxonomy has no tag for trust anchor management.

RFC6011.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) User Agent Configuration
RFC6011.summary: Informational RFC specifying how a SIP User Agent discovers its Configuration Service (via DHCP options, U-NAPTR in DNS), fetches configuration over HTTPS, and tracks changes via SIP subscription (http-monitor event package) or HTTP polling.

SIP.why: The document specifies SIP UA configuration procedures, including SIP SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY change subscriptions for the http-monitor event package.
SIP.quote: This document defines procedures for how a SIP User Agent should locate, retrieve, and maintain current configuration information from a Configuration Service.

DHCP.why: Defines a new DHCPv4 option (141) used to discover the Configuration Service Domain.
DHCP.quote: This specification defines DHCP option code 141, the "SIP UA Configuration Service Domains"

DHCPv6.why: Defines a new DHCPv6 option (58) for the Configuration Service domain list.
DHCPv6.quote: This specification defines DHCPv6 option code 58, OPTION_SIP_UA_CS_LIST

service discovery.why: A substantial part of the document is discovery of the Configuration Service using DHCP options and U-NAPTR with a new SFUA.CFG service tag.
service discovery.quote: The Configuration Service Domain is resolved to one or more URLs using the URI-enabled Naming Authority Pointer (U-NAPTR) DDDS application

rejected.why: HTTPS GET and cache control are used as the substrate for fetching configuration, not specified or extended.
TLS is used for the connection and server_name is required, but nothing new is defined about TLS.
NAPTR lookup is used via existing U-NAPTR; no new DNS record type is defined.
The Link header with rel 'monitor' is used per RFC 5989, but the document does not define link relations.
Cache-Control/ETag metadata are used for validity checks, but this is the mechanism rather than the subject.
Basic and Digest are required to be supported, but are not specified or extended here.

gaps.name: Device configuration/provisioning
gaps.why: The document is about automatic provisioning of endpoint devices, but the taxonomy has no general device-configuration or provisioning tag.

RFC6012.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Transport Mapping for Syslog
RFC6012.summary: Defines how syslog messages are carried over DTLS (over UDP or DCCP), including port assignment, handshake, certificate authentication, framing, message size, closure and congestion control.

syslog.why: The document specifies a syslog transport mapping: framing of syslog messages, port assignment, and behaviour of syslog senders and receivers.
syslog.quote: This document describes the transport of syslog messages over the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

DTLS.why: Substantial parts profile DTLS use for syslog: cookie exchange, mandatory cipher suite, certificate authentication, close_notify, renegotiation guidance.
DTLS.quote: Implementations MUST support DTLS 1.0 [RFC4347] and MUST support the mandatory to implement cipher suite

transport mapping.why: The document is a transport mapping, carrying syslog over DTLS on UDP and DCCP, which is exactly what this topic covers.
transport mapping.quote: This memo defines both options, namely syslog over DTLS over UDP, and syslog over DTLS over DCCP.

rejected.why: DCCP is one of the substrates; the document only recommends it for congestion control and does not specify it.
UDP is a substrate; the document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
Section 6 is brief and merely recommends DCCP and refers to existing guidance; the document is not about congestion control.
Certificates are used for authentication by reference to RFC 5280 and RFC 5425, with no profile defined here.
Syslog over TLS is a sibling mapping referenced for policies; this document is about DTLS, not TLS.

gaps.name: syslog
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the syslog protocol itself or the syslog transport mappings. I chose the nearest fit by id, but the id appears in the taxonomy only as 'syslog' under network management. No gap in that sense.

RFC6013.title: TCP Cookie Transactions (TCPCT)
RFC6013.summary: Experimental spec for TCP Cookie Transactions, a TCP option exchange that makes the server stateless during the handshake, defends against spoofing and SYN floods, extends the TCP header, and allows limited SYN data and accelerated close.

TCP.why: The document defines new TCP options (Cookie, Cookie-Pair, Timestamps extended), header extension, accelerated open/close and reset behaviour, i.e. a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: TCP Cookie Transactions (TCPCT) deter spoofing of connections and prevent resource exhaustion, eliminating Responder (server) state during the initial handshake.

rejected.why: Mitigating SYN-flood DoS is the motivation, but the mechanism is a TCP extension; the TCP tag fits best.
Cookie generation and entropy are discussed only briefly; it is not about randomness requirements.
Photuris is mentioned only as historical inspiration for cookies in the History section.
SCTP and DCCP are mentioned only in the History section as comparison points.
RFC 5681 is referenced only incidentally; no congestion control is specified.
Middleboxes and NAT are compatibility concerns only.

RFC6014.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Identifier Allocation for DNSSEC
RFC6014.summary: RFC 6014 changes the IANA allocation policy for the DNSSEC "DNS Security Algorithm Numbers" registry from Standards Action to RFC Required, reserves values 123-251, and leaves mandatory-to-implement algorithms unchanged.

DNSSEC.why: The document updates RFC 4033/4034/4035 and changes how DNSSEC algorithm numbers are registered, and discusses implementation expectations for DNSSEC algorithms. DNSSEC readers need it.
DNSSEC.quote: This document specifies how DNSSEC cryptographic algorithm identifiers in the IANA registries are allocated.

IANA.why: The core content is a registry allocation policy change, including reserving values and re-evaluation criteria for the registry. This is about IANA registry policy in its own right, not boilerplate.
IANA.quote: The registration procedure for values that are assigned after this document is published is "RFC Required".

rejected.why: The document concerns identifier allocation, not the algorithms themselves, their parameters, or their use; it explicitly does not change which are recommended or required.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag and DNS is only its parent; no general DNS protocol content.
It touches on Standards Track vs. RFC Required, but the subject is the registry policy, which is better captured by IANA.

RFC6015.title: RTP Payload Format for 1-D Interleaved Parity Forward Error Correction (FEC)
RFC6015.summary: Defines a new RTP payload format and media type registrations for FEC repair packets generated by a 1-D interleaved parity (XOR) code, extending the RFC 2733 FEC header and aligned with SMPTE 2022-1 and DVB-IPTV AL-FEC.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is a new RTP payload format for FEC repair packets, including packet format, parameters and SDP mapping.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines a new RTP payload format for the Forward Error Correction (FEC) that is generated by the 1-D interleaved parity code

FEC.why: It specifies an XOR parity erasure code with repair packet construction and source packet recovery procedures, protecting against bursty losses.
FEC.quote: The 1-D interleaved parity code is a systematic code, where a number of repair symbols are generated from a set of source symbols

rejected.why: The WG is fecframe, but the document defines a standalone RTP payload format and does not specify the FEC Framework or a scheme within it.
RTP is the carrier whose header is used, but the specific subject is the payload format, which is tagged more specifically.
SDP is used only for parameter mapping and one example; it is not specified or extended here.
The media type registrations are boilerplate-like registrations that accompany the payload format rather than the document's main subject.
DVB-IPTV is the intended use context, but the document does not specify IPTV service delivery.
Section 8 is a short considerations section, not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC6016.title: Support for the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) in Layer 3 VPNs
RFC6016.summary: Specifies how PE routers in BGP/MPLS L3VPNs handle customer RSVP messages (new VPN-IPv4/VPN-IPv6 RSVP objects, Path/Resv processing, inter-AS options) so admission control can be done on PE-CE links and optionally across the provider backbone via MPLS-TE aggregation.

RSVP.why: The document defines new RSVP object types (VPN-IPv4/VPN-IPv6 SESSION, SENDER_TEMPLATE, FILTER_SPEC, RSVP_HOP) and modified Path/Resv processing, so it extends RSVP.
RSVP.quote: This document specifies procedures by which RSVP messages traveling from CE to CE across an L3VPN may be appropriately handled by PE routers

L3VPN.why: It addresses RSVP handling within BGP/MPLS L3VPNs, including PE/ASBR behaviour and inter-AS Options A, B and C, so L3VPN readers need it.
L3VPN.quote: RFC 4364 and RFC 4659 define an approach to building provider-provisioned Layer 3 VPNs (L3VPNs) for IPv4 and IPv6.

rejected.why: MPLS-TE tunnels are used for optional backbone aggregation and CE-CE RSVP-TE is deferred to future work, so RSVP-TE is not the subject.
BGP is used to advertise VPN-IPv4 addresses and labels, but it is only a mechanism the document relies on. The document defines nothing new in BGP.
MPLS label forwarding is the substrate of the VPN. The document does not specify MPLS itself.
The document works around the Router Alert Option by addressing messages directly to the PE. It does not specify the option.
Intserv is background for RSVP admission control, not something the document specifies.
The RSVP tag already covers admission control signalling, and it sits under QoS.

RFC6017.title: Electronic Data Interchange - Internet Integration (EDIINT) Features Header Field
RFC6017.summary: Defines the EDIINT-Features header field, carried in AS1, AS2 and AS3 messages, which lets trading partners advertise optional EDIINT features without out-of-band agreement, and ties it to the AS2/AS3 version header.

EDI.why: The whole document specifies a header extension for EDIINT (AS1/AS2/AS3) EDI-over-Internet transports, so EDI readers would look for it.
EDI.quote: The EDIINT-Features header indicates the capability of the user agent to support the listed feature with its trading partner without out-of-band communication and agreement.

rejected.why: AS2 runs over HTTP and the header applies to HTTP messages, but HTTP is only the substrate; nothing new is defined about HTTP itself.
AS1 runs over mail, but this is only a transport substrate and the document does not define anything about SMTP.
The header is a MIME/message header, but it is specific to EDIINT and the document does not address Internet message format in general.
ABNF is used only to write the header syntax; the document is not about the notation.
AS3 uses FTP transport, but FTP is only referenced as a substrate.
Compression (RFC 5402) is mentioned only as implied by version 1.2; the document is not about compression.

RFC6018.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Greynets
RFC6018.summary: Informational note describing Greynets, sparse-address-space network sensors for detecting scans, and a router modification that forwards datagrams triggering failed ARP/Neighbor Discovery resolution to a collector for IPv4 and IPv6.

operational security.why: The document's whole subject is a darknet/greynet/honeypot sensing technique for detecting scans and attack traffic, an operational security practice for network infrastructure. The quote is from the Security Considerations section but restates what the main body does.
operational security.quote: This note describes a tool for managing IPv4 and IPv6 network security.

neighbor discovery.why: The core mechanism hooks into IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (and ARP) failures. Section 3 proposes a change to router ND behaviour, so readers of that subject would want it.
neighbor discovery.quote: the router forwards a copy of this datagram over an independent link to the Greynet's analytic equipment.
neighbor discovery.section: 2.2. Deployment Using Sparse Address Space - Greynets

ARP.why: The proposal modifies router behaviour when an ARP Request goes unanswered, using that failure as the Greynet trigger.
ARP.quote: Routers use IPv4 ARP [RFC0826] and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery [RFC4861] to determine the MAC (Media Access Control) address of a neighbor
ARP.section: 2.2. Deployment Using Sparse Address Space - Greynets

rejected.why: The document covers both IPv4 and IPv6 and is not about IPv6 specification or deployment; neighbor discovery is the more specific fit.
Only mentioned as a possible way to summarise collected data; not specified or profiled here.
A single sentence notes DDoS attacks terminate on router subnets; the document is not about DDoS mitigation.
Sparse address use is a premise of the technique, but the document is not about address architecture or allocation.
Backscatter via ICMP is mentioned only in passing in the introduction.

gaps.name: Greynets / darknets / network telescopes / honeypots
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for passive network sensors and attack-traffic observation. The closest fit is operational security, which is broader than this.

RFC6019.title: BinaryTime: An Alternate Format for Representing Date and Time in ASN.1
RFC6019.summary: Defines the ASN.1 BinaryTime type (integer seconds since the Unix epoch) and a binary-signing-time attribute for CMS SignedData and AuthenticatedData as an alternative to signing-time.

CMS.why: The document defines a new CMS signed/authenticated attribute as an alternative to signing-time, so it extends CMS.
CMS.quote: the binary-signing-time attribute uses BinaryTime. CMS and the signing-time attribute are defined in RFC 5652.

ASN.1.why: The main content is a new ASN.1 type and an ASN.1 module, with encoding rules for the INTEGER value.
ASN.1.quote: This document specifies a new ASN.1 [ASN1] type for representing time: BinaryTime.

date-time formats.why: It specifies a new date and time representation (Unix-time integer) and compares it with UTCTime and GeneralizedTime.
date-time formats.quote: The integer value is the number of seconds, excluding leap seconds, after midnight UTC, January 1, 1970.

rejected.why: The document is about time representation, not clock synchronization over networks.
RFC 3161 time-stamping is only mentioned in Security Considerations; the document does not address PKI.

RFC6020.title: YANG - A Data Modeling Language for the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF)
RFC6020.summary: RFC 6020 specifies YANG, a data modeling language for configuration data, state data, RPCs and notifications manipulated by NETCONF, including its syntax, built-in types, XML mapping, YIN, and constraint handling.

YANG.why: The document is the core specification of the YANG language: statements, types, constraints, grammar, and module updating rules.
YANG.quote: YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration and state data manipulated by the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF)

NETCONF.why: A substantial part of the document defines how YANG maps to NETCONF: edit-config operation semantics, hello capability announcement, rpc and notification encoding, and error responses.
NETCONF.quote: This document describes the syntax and semantics of the YANG language, how the data model defined in a YANG module is represented in XML, and how NETCONF operations are used to manipulate the data.

rejected.why: XML is the encoding for data and for YIN, but the document is about the data modeling language, not XML usage generally.
Compatibility with SMIv2 is mentioned only briefly; the document is not about MIBs.
The IANA registration of application/yang and application/yin+xml is boilerplate-level and not the document's subject.
The ABNF grammar is merely the formal syntax of YANG, not about ABNF itself.
SMIv2 is mentioned only as a compatibility note.

RFC6021.title: Common YANG Data Types
RFC6021.summary: RFC 6021 defines two YANG modules, ietf-yang-types and ietf-inet-types, containing common derived data types (counters, gauges, timestamps, MAC/IP addresses, prefixes, domain names, URIs, AS numbers, etc.) with SMIv2 equivalents.

YANG.why: The whole document is a library of YANG modules defining reusable data types for YANG data models.
YANG.quote: This document introduces a collection of common data types derived from the built-in YANG data types.

rejected.why: The document maps YANG types to SMIv2 equivalents, but it defines YANG modules, not MIB modules.
NETCONF is mentioned only as the context in which YANG is used; the document doesn't specify or extend it.
The ipv6-address and ipv6-prefix types model IPv6 addresses, but the document is not about IPv6.
The domain-name type models DNS names, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
The uri type only constrains normalisation of URIs defined elsewhere.
The date-and-time type profiles RFC 3339, but it is one type among many and not a main subject.

RFC6022.title: YANG Module for NETCONF Monitoring
RFC6022.summary: Defines the ietf-netconf-monitoring YANG module exposing NETCONF server capabilities, datastores, locks, schemas, sessions and statistics, and a new <get-schema> operation for retrieving data models.

NETCONF.why: The document extends NETCONF with a monitoring data model and a new <get-schema> operation, so it is about NETCONF.
NETCONF.quote: This document defines a Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) data model to be used to monitor the NETCONF protocol.

YANG.why: The main deliverable is a normative YANG module (ietf-netconf-monitoring). It also covers schema discovery for YANG models.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG [RFC6020] model to be used to monitor the NETCONF protocol.

rejected.why: It is a management data model but is not SNMP-related; it only monitors NETCONF.
BEEP appears only as a transport identity in the module, not as a subject of the document.
SSH appears only as a transport identity and in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
XML is the encoding substrate; the document does not define anything about XML itself.
NETCONF over TLS is only a transport identity entry.
The model is a YANG module, not an SMI MIB module.

RFC6023.title: A Childless Initiation of the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) Security Association (SA)
RFC6023.summary: Experimental extension to IKEv2 that lets an IKEv2 SA be created and authenticated via IKE_AUTH without also negotiating a Child SA, using a new CHILDLESS_IKEV2_SUPPORTED notification.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new notification and a modified IKE_AUTH exchange, so it belongs on the IKE page.
IKE.quote: an extension to the Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) protocol that allows an IKEv2 Security Association (SA) to be created and authenticated without generating a Child SA

rejected.why: IKEv2 is the IPsec key management protocol, but the document specifies only the IKEv2 exchange change, not IPsec architecture, ESP or AH. IKE is the more specific tag.
The modified IKE_AUTH exchange is shown in its EAP variant, and EAP is only used as an example authentication method. The document defines nothing about EAP.
It is another IKEv2 extension, but this document does not cover mobility or multihoming.
The IKEv2 SA can be used for authentication only, but the document's subject is the IKEv2 exchange and the IKE tag covers it.

RFC6024.title: Trust Anchor Management Requirements
RFC6024.summary: RFC 6024 describes problems from the lack of a standard trust anchor management mechanism and sets out requirements for trust anchor data formats and push-based management protocols (which led to RFC 5914 and RFC 5934).

PKI.why: The whole document is about managing trust anchors, which is core PKI infrastructure. It covers trust anchor stores, delegation of management authority, and recovery from key compromise.
PKI.quote: This document describes some of the problems associated with the lack of a standard trust anchor management mechanism and defines requirements for data formats and push-based protocols

rejected.why: X.509 certificates and RFC 5280 path validation are the context the requirements work within. The document specifies no X.509 profile itself.
CMS SignedData is mentioned only as one use of trust anchors and as a possible public key identifier. The document is not about CMS.
OCSP responses are given only as an example of a signed object that a trust anchor may verify.
The document concerns managing trust anchors, not key establishment or provisioning in general. The more specific PKI tag fits better.

gaps.name: Trust anchor management
gaps.why: The document and its companions (RFC 5914 trust anchor format, RFC 5934 TAMP) have no specific tag. PKI is the closest fit, but a trust-anchor-management tag would group them.

RFC6025.title: ASN.1 Translation
RFC6025.summary: RFC 6025 is an informational tutorial that guides authors and implementers in translating ASN.1 modules between the 1988 X.208 syntax and the X.680-series syntax without changing the BER/DER encoding.

ASN.1.why: The whole document is about ASN.1 module syntax: open types, information object classes, constraints, parameterization, extensibility, and translation checklists between X.208 and X.68x.
ASN.1.quote: guidance to specification authors and to implementers converting ASN.1 modules from one version of ASN.1 to another version without causing changes to the "bits on the wire"

rejected.why: ContentInfo and SignerInfo from CMS are used only as examples of ASN.1 constructs; the document does not specify or extend CMS.
RFC 5280 structures (Extension, SubjectPublicKeyInfo, TBSCertificate) are used as illustrative examples only; the document is not about certificate profiles.
The document comes from the PKIX working group and draws on PKI modules, but its subject is ASN.1 syntax translation, not PKI.
The ResponseBytes and BasicOCSPResponse definitions appear only as examples of constraints.

RFC6026.title: Correct Transaction Handling for 2xx Responses to Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) INVITE Requests
RFC6026.summary: RFC 6026 updates RFC 3261 to fix SIP INVITE client and server transaction state machines (new Accepted states, Timers L and M) so 2xx responses and INVITE retransmissions are handled correctly, and forbids proxies from forwarding stray responses.

SIP.why: The document is a normative correction to the SIP core specification, modifying INVITE transaction state machines and proxy behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document normatively updates RFC 3261, the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), to address an error in the specified handling of success (2xx class) responses to INVITE requests.

rejected.why: The stray-response forwarding issue is described as a DoS/anonymizing-forwarder security risk, but only as motivation; the document is not about DDoS mitigation.
Not discussed; INVITE sessions are mentioned only generally.
The security rationale is a side effect of the protocol fix, not operational practice guidance.

RFC6027.title: IPsec Cluster Problem Statement
RFC6027.summary: Problem statement defining terminology and requirements for running IKEv2 and IPsec on gateway clusters, covering state synchronization, counters, SPI allocation and addressing gaps.

IKE.why: The document analyses IKEv2 state, message ID counters, SAs and SPIs problems in clusters, and anticipates IKEv2 mechanisms to simplify them.
IKE.quote: requirements for implementing Internet Key Exchange (IKE) and IPsec on clusters

IPsec.why: Covers IPsec SAs, SPD cache, ESP/AH replay counters and counter-mode IVs in clustered gateways; the IPsec architecture side of the problem.
IPsec.quote: IKE and IPsec have a lot of long-lived state

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one way to build a hot standby cluster; the document is not about VRRP.
Replay counters and counter-mode IVs are discussed only as cluster problems; the document is not about ESP itself.
The VPN tag is for provider-provisioned VPNs over BGP/MPLS; this is about IPsec VPN gateways.
DNS is mentioned only as a way for peers to find a cluster member.

gaps.name: high availability / clustering
gaps.why: The document is about gateway clustering, failover and load sharing for availability. The taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC6028.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Multi-Hop Routing Extension
RFC6028.summary: Experimental RFC defining two HIP parameters, ROUTE_DST (source routing via a signed destination list of HITs) and ROUTE_VIA (recording the nodes a HIP packet traversed), to enable multi-hop routing of HIP signaling.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with new ROUTE_VIA and ROUTE_DST parameters, a new NOTIFY type, and processing rules for HIP packets.
HIP.quote: This document specifies two extensions to the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) to implement multi-hop routing.

rejected.why: RELOAD is referenced only for terminology (destination list, via list) and the overlay context; the document does not specify or extend it.
The routing here is source routing of HIP signaling packets between HIP nodes, not IP routing architecture. The HIP tag covers it.
HIP BONE is mentioned as a motivating use case, but the taxonomy tag covers data-plane virtualization overlays such as VXLAN, which this document does not address.
The IANA section registers parameter types and a flags registry, but that is boilerplate for this document and not its subject.

RFC6029.title: A Survey on Research on the Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Problem
RFC6029.summary: IRTF P2PRG survey of research literature on the ALTO problem, covering application-level topology estimation (GNP, Vivaldi, PIC, Meridian, iPlane, Ono) and ISP-cooperation approaches (P4P, oracles, IDIPS), with open issues.

ALTO.why: The whole document surveys approaches to the ALTO problem and is intended as input to the ALTO working group.
ALTO.quote: presents a survey of existing literature on discovering and using network topology information for Application-Layer Traffic Optimization.

P2P.why: The problem is peer selection in P2P overlays; DHTs, BitTorrent, Skype relay selection and P2P/ISP cooperation are discussed throughout.
P2P.quote: A significant part of today's Internet traffic is generated by peer-to-peer (P2P) applications

rejected.why: Network tomography and distance/latency estimation are covered, but only as means for topology estimation within the ALTO survey.
ISP traffic engineering policy is mentioned only as something that can conflict with overlay routing.
TCP throughput is mentioned only as a performance motivation.
Ono uses CDN redirections as a measurement signal, but the document is not about CDNs.
A DDoS attack by a malicious oracle is raised in a single open-issue paragraph.

RFC6030.title: Portable Symmetric Key Container (PSKC)
RFC6030.summary: Defines PSKC, an XML container format for transporting and provisioning symmetric keys (e.g., OTP shared secrets) to crypto modules, with key policy, encryption/MAC protection, signatures, bulk provisioning, and IANA registries.

key management.why: The document's purpose is key provisioning and transport of symmetric keys, with key policy and protection methods. This is key management, and no more specific tag fits.
key management.quote: This document specifies a symmetric key format for the transport and provisioning of symmetric keys to different types of crypto modules.

OTP.why: Much of the format serves OTP shared secrets, with counter, time, response format and an HOTP algorithm profile. OTP readers would want it.
OTP.quote: The document also specifies the information elements that are required when the symmetric key is utilized for specific purposes, such as the initial counter in the HMAC-Based One-Time Password (HOTP)

XML.why: The container is an XML format with a full schema, namespace and an application/pskc+xml media type, so it is an XML-based format.
XML.quote: This document defines a standardized XML-based key container, called Portable Symmetric Key Container (PSKC), for transporting symmetric keys and key-related metadata.

rejected.why: PSKC uses XML-DSig and XML Encryption as mechanisms for protecting the container. It does not specify or extend them.
Passphrase-based encryption is one supported protection method, but the document only uses PBKDF2 and does not define it.
AES key value encoding and AES-CBC are used or referenced, but the document is not about the cipher.
TLS is only mentioned in Security Considerations as an alternative transport protection.
It registers application/pskc+xml in IANA Considerations, which is boilerplate-level evidence, not the main subject.
The keys serve strong authentication devices, but the document is a key container format and does not specify an authentication protocol.

gaps.name: Symmetric key provisioning (KEYPROV)
gaps.why: The document is about the provisioning and portable container format for symmetric keys. The taxonomy has only the broad 'key management' topic and no tag for key provisioning or portable key containers.

RFC6031.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Symmetric Key Package Content Type
RFC6031.summary: Defines a CMS content type (symmetric key package) for transporting plaintext symmetric keys, with ASN.1 versions of PSKC (RFC 6030) attributes for device, key and key policy metadata, plus AES and Triple-DES key encodings.

CMS.why: The document defines a new CMS content type and its ASN.1 structure, which CMS readers need.
CMS.quote: The symmetric key package content type is used to transfer one or more plaintext symmetric keys from one party to another.

key management.why: The package is for provisioning symmetric keys. It carries key identifiers, usage constraints, policy and validity attributes, and the document also defines AES and Triple-DES key encodings.
key management.quote: The following attributes are defined to assist those using the symmetric key package defined in this document as part of a Dynamic Symmetric Key Provision Protocol (DSKPP)

rejected.why: The document is written in ASN.1 and contains ASN.1 modules, but ASN.1 is only the notation. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Several attributes (counter, time interval, time drift) serve OTP algorithms. The document is about key packaging, not OTP systems.
It converts the XML PSKC elements from RFC 6030 to ASN.1, but it does not specify or use XML.
Section 4.1 only defines how an AES key is encoded in an octet string. The document is not about the AES cipher.
Section 4.2 only defines how a Triple-DES key is encoded in an octet string. The document is not about the cipher.

gaps.name: PSKC (Portable Symmetric Key Container) / DSKPP
gaps.why: The document ASN.1-encodes the PSKC attributes and is meant for DSKPP exchanges. The taxonomy has no tag for symmetric key provisioning (keyprov).

RFC6032.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Encrypted Key Package Content Type
RFC6032.summary: Defines a CMS content type (EncryptedKeyPackage) for encrypting symmetric or asymmetric key packages, plus a Content Decryption Key Identifier attribute, designed to work with the CMS Content Constraints extension.

CMS.why: The document specifies a new CMS content type built on EncryptedData, EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData, along with a new CMS attribute. CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: This document defines the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) encrypted key package content type, which can be used to encrypt a content that includes a key package

ASN.1.why: The normative content is an ASN.1 module defining the content type, OIDs and attribute. This is a substantial part of the document, though ASN.1 is the definition notation rather than the main subject.
ASN.1.quote: This appendix provides the normative ASN.1 [X.680] definitions for the structures described in this specification

rejected.why: The CMS Content Constraints extension in X.509 certificates is used for authorization checks, but the document does not define PKI mechanisms.
Certificate path validation and the CCC extension are referenced from other RFCs, and this document does not profile certificates.
The document is about a container for protected key material, not key establishment or provisioning protocols.
OIDs are registered in the S/MIME arc and the ASN.1 modules are shared, but the document is not about secure email.

RFC6033.title: Algorithms for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Encrypted Key Package Content Type
RFC6033.summary: Specifies mandatory and recommended cryptographic algorithms (AES Key Wrap with Padding, AES-GCM/CCM, RSA, RSA-OAEP, DH, RSASSA-PSS, DSA, SHA-256) for CMS EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthEnvelopedData and SignedData when carrying the CMS encrypted key package content type.

CMS.why: The whole document profiles algorithms for CMS content types (EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthEnvelopedData, SignedData) used with encrypted key packages.
CMS.quote: This document describes the conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) encrypted key package content type

AES.why: AES Key Wrap with Padding and AES-GCM/CCM are the central content-encryption algorithm requirements throughout the document.
AES.quote: implementations MUST support AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding [RFC5649] as the content-encryption algorithm.

RSA.why: RSA, RSAES-OAEP and RSASSA-PSS are mandated or recommended for key transport and signatures, with key size requirements.
RSA.quote: When key transport is used, RSA encryption [RFC3370] MUST be supported and RSA Encryption Scheme - Optimal Asymmetric Encryption

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are mentioned only as the easiest way to implement the algorithms; the document is not about PKI.
SHA-256/SHA-1 are required only in one sentence for SignedData; not a substantial subject.
Key transport/agreement choices are mentioned, but the document specifies algorithms, not key management procedures.
No elliptic curve algorithms are specified; DH and DSA are finite-field here.

RFC6034.title: Unicast-Prefix-Based IPv4 Multicast Addresses
RFC6034.summary: Defines the 234/8 IPv4 multicast range in which a organization's unicast prefix is embedded to give it globally unique multicast addresses without an inter-domain allocation protocol, as an IPv4 analogue of RFC 3306 and an alternative to GLOP.

multicast.why: The document specifies IPv4 multicast address allocation based on unicast prefixes. No child multicast tag fits (MADCAP is only mentioned as an alternative), so the parent topic is used.
multicast.quote: A multicast address with the prefix 234/8 indicates that the address is a Unicast-Based Multicast (UBM) address.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an alternative for intra-AS administration; the document does not specify or extend it.
The document concerns multicast address space in IPv4, but it is about multicast address allocation, not IPv4 as a protocol or its address lifecycle.
It does allocate address space, but the multicast tag is more specific to what the document covers.
Only a single IANA assignment of 234/8 appears in boilerplate; the document is not about IANA registries.
RFC 3306 is referenced only as the model for this mechanism; the document does not cover IPv6.
The 4-byte AS number reference (RFC 4893) only explains GLOP's limitation; the document is not about BGP.

RFC6035.title: Session Initiation Protocol Event Package for Voice Quality Reporting
RFC6035.summary: Defines the SIP event package vq-rtcpxr and the application/vq-rtcpxr media type, letting a SIP UA (reporter) send VoIP quality metrics derived from RTCP XR to a collector via SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY or PUBLISH.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP event package (vq-rtcpxr) with SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and PUBLISH usage, message flows and overload handling.
SIP.quote: This document defines a SIP events package [5] for Voice over IP performance reporting.
SIP.section: 3. SIP Events for VoIP Quality Reporting

RTCP.why: A substantial part of the document maps RTCP XR VoIP metrics block fields to the SIP report parameters, so RTCP XR readers would want it.
RTCP.quote: the data contained in RTCP XR VoIP metrics reports (RFC 3611 [4]) are forwarded to a central collection server systems using SIP.

media types.why: It defines and registers a new media type with its own ABNF-defined body format.
media types.quote: This specification defines a new MIME type, application/vq-rtcpxr, which is a text encoding of the RTCP and RTCP-XR statistics

performance measurement.why: The document is about reporting voice quality metrics (loss, delay, jitter, MOS, R-factor) from endpoints to a collector.
performance measurement.quote: enable the collection and reporting of metrics that measure quality for RTP [3] sessions.

rejected.why: SDP is only referenced for codec parameters mapped into the report; the document does not specify or extend it.
RTP is the media being measured; the document does not extend RTP itself.
ABNF is only the notation used for the report syntax.
Uses the SIP event framework and PUBLISH but is not about presence or IM event packages.
Mentioned only in passing regarding NAT addresses in reports.
Reports quality metrics but does not define QoS architectures or signalling.

gaps.name: VoIP quality reporting / voice quality metrics
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for VoIP call quality monitoring (MOS, R-factor); the closest are the generic performance measurement and RTCP tags.

RFC6036.title: Emerging Service Provider Scenarios for IPv6 Deployment
RFC6036.summary: Informational report of a 2010 survey of 31 ISPs on IPv6 deployment experience, plans and requirements, with a gap analysis of products, protocols and documentation.

IPv6 transition.why: The document records ISP choices among dual-stack, 6to4, Teredo, 6rd, DS-Lite, 6PE and NAT64 for IPv6/IPv4 coexistence. Readers of IPv6 transition would want it.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document focuses on alternative (3), while recognizing that many ISPs may be obliged by circumstances to prolong the life of IPv4

IPv6.why: It covers IPv6 deployment status, prefix allocation sizes, prefix delegation and the gaps in IPv6 support. This is general IPv6 deployment beyond transition mechanisms.
IPv6.quote: 42% of ISPs already offer IPv6 as a regular service, although, in general, it is used by fewer than 1% of customers.
IPv6.section: 2.4. Status and Plans for IPv6 Service

rejected.why: NAT64/DNS64 is mentioned as a planned translator and a product gap, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
Prefix delegation methods and the need for a fully featured DHCPv6 are listed among survey answers and gaps, but only briefly.
DS-Lite is mentioned only as one operator's plan, not as a subject of the document.
6to4 relays are survey answers, not a subject of the document.
CGN is mentioned only as an IPv4 alternative that is out of scope.
Management tools are checked for dual-stack support in the survey, but this is not a main subject.

RFC6037.title: Cisco Systems' Solution for Multicast in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs
RFC6037.summary: Historic document describing Cisco's pre-standard MVPN solution for multicast in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, using PIM-built default and data MDTs, GRE encapsulation, MDT-SAFI BGP auto-discovery, and a PIM MVPN Join Attribute.

MVPN.why: The whole document specifies the MVPN solution: multicast domains, default and data MDTs, MDT-SAFI, and the Connector attribute.
MVPN.quote: This document describes the MVPN (Multicast in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs) solution designed and deployed by Cisco Systems.

PIM.why: Defines a new PIM Join Attribute and runs PIM C-instances and P-instances. This is a substantial PIM extension for inter-AS MDT construction.
PIM.quote: We now define a new Join Attribute, which we call the "MVPN Join Attribute".

L3VPN.why: It extends the RFC 4364 L3VPN with multicast VRFs and BGP extensions. The MVPN tag already sits under VPN, but L3VPN readers would also want this document.
L3VPN.quote: The base specification for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs [RFC4364] does not provide a way for IP multicast data or control traffic to travel from one VPN site to another.
