rejected.why: GRE is only the encapsulation used for MDT tunnels, following existing GRE specs; nothing new is defined about GRE.
The document defines the MDT-SAFI and Connector attribute, but BGP is used as a carrier for the VPN signalling and is not the subject.
SSM is one option for building MDTs and is not the subject of the document.
PIM-SM is presupposed, and this document does not extend the PIM-SM specification itself.
The solution uses IP/GRE multicast tunnels in the core, not MPLS forwarding. It only mentions MPLS P2MP LSPs when comparing with the standard MVPN.

RFC6038.title: Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) Reflect Octets and Symmetrical Size Features
RFC6038.summary: RFC 6038 extends TWAMP with two optional Modes: Reflect Octets, where the reflector returns designated octets and padding, and Symmetrical Size, a new sender test packet format that ensures equal packet sizes in both directions.

TWAMP.why: The document extends and updates TWAMP (RFC 5357) with new Modes, control message fields and test packet formats, so it belongs on the TWAMP page.
TWAMP.quote: This memo describes two closely related features for the core specification of the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)

rejected.why: OWAMP (RFC 4656) is only the base protocol that TWAMP derives from and whose formats are referenced. The document does not extend it.
This parent topic is implied by the TWAMP tag, and the document is specifically about TWAMP rather than measurement in general.
The new registry values are boilerplate-level IANA considerations. The document is not about IANA registries in their own right.
HMAC is only used as defined in RFC 4656 for message authentication. Nothing new is specified about it.

RFC6039.title: Issues with Existing Cryptographic Protection Methods for Routing Protocols
RFC6039.summary: Informational analysis of limitations in cryptographic authentication (hash digests, manual keying, replay protection) of the routing protocols OSPFv2, OSPFv3, IS-IS, BGP-4, RIP and BFD.

routing security.why: The whole document analyses weaknesses in cryptographic protection of routing protocols (replay, spoofing, manual keys), which is routing security in general across several protocols.
routing security.quote: This document outlines some of the limitations of the current mechanism, problems with manual keying of these cryptographic algorithms, and possible vectors for the exploitation of these limitations.

OSPF.why: Dedicated sections analyse OSPFv2 authentication management and technical issues.
OSPF.quote: OSPF [RFC2328] describes the use of an MD5 digest with OSPF packets.

OSPFv3.why: A full section covers OSPFv3 manual keying and replay problems with IPsec.
OSPFv3.quote: OSPFv3 [RFC5340] relies on the IP Authentication Header (AH) [RFC4302] and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) [RFC4303]

IS-IS.why: A dedicated section analyses IS-IS authentication issues such as replay and lack of Key ID.
IS-IS.quote: Integrated IS-IS [RFC1195] uses HMAC-MD5 authentication with manual keying, as described in [RFC5304]

BGP.why: A dedicated section covers BGP session protection with TCP MD5 and its management and technical issues.
BGP.quote: [RFC2385] describes the use of the TCP MD5 digest option for providing packet origin authentication and data integrity protection of BGP packets.

RIP.why: A section analyses RIPv2 authentication weaknesses including replay and source-address attacks.
RIP.quote: RIPv2 Cryptographic Authentication" [RFC4822] does not cover the UDP and the IP headers.

BFD.why: A section analyses BFD authentication weaknesses, including echo mode and sequence number wrap.
BFD.quote: The BFD base specification specifies an optional authentication mechanism that can be used by the receiver of a packet to be able to authenticate the source of the packet.

rejected.why: MD5 and SHA-1 weaknesses are discussed as background to the digests used, but the document is not about the hash algorithms themselves.
HMAC is the construction used by the protocols analysed; it is not specified or analysed in its own right.
AH and ESP are discussed only as the mechanism OSPFv3 uses, with manual keying issues, not as the subject.
TCP MD5 and TCP-AO are touched on as BGP's protection, but the document is about BGP protection, not TCP.
Manual keying problems are a major theme, but the document is about routing protocols' protection and proposes no key management solution.
A generic parent topic; routing security fits more specifically.

RFC6040.title: Tunnelling of Explicit Congestion Notification
RFC6040.summary: RFC 6040 redefines how the ECN field is constructed at encapsulation and decapsulation of IP-in-IP tunnels (IPsec and non-IPsec), updating RFC 3168 and RFC 4301 to support two congestion severity levels (e.g. for PCN) while staying backward compatible.

ECN.why: The whole document specifies ECN field processing at tunnel endpoints and updates RFC 3168, the ECN specification.
ECN.quote: This document redefines how the explicit congestion notification (ECN) field of the IP header should be constructed on entry to and exit from any IP-in-IP tunnel.

IP-in-IP.why: It defines encapsulator and decapsulator behaviour for IP-in-IP tunnels, including ingress modes and egress rules.
IP-in-IP.quote: This document specifies common ECN field processing at encapsulation and decapsulation for any IP-in-IP tunnelling, whether IPsec or non- IPsec tunnels.

PCN.why: PCN motivates the changes, and the document explains how operators can require compliance to support two PCN severity levels. Its motivation sections cover PCN in depth.
PCN.quote: The trigger for the changes in this document was the introduction of pre-congestion notification (PCN [RFC5670]) to the IETF Standards Track.

rejected.why: RFC 4301 IPsec tunnel ECN processing is updated, but only the ECN field handling, not the IPsec architecture. IP-in-IP and ECN cover the subject.
Diffserv PHBs and RFC 2983 tunnel models are discussed as context. The document does not specify Diffserv.
The document says it makes no changes to congestion marking or response algorithms. It only covers wire-protocol processing.
RFC 5129 ECN marking in MPLS is mentioned only as a consistency reference.
IKEv2 is mentioned only as the reason IPsec tunnel endpoints know their peers are compliant.

RFC6041.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Applicability Statement
RFC6041.summary: Applicability statement describing where the ForCES protocol, model and TML are and are not appropriate for separating control and forwarding elements in IP routers and similar devices, including deployment localities and manageability.

ForCES.why: The whole document is about the ForCES protocol: its applicable services, CE/FE link and locality considerations, and manageability.
ForCES.quote: In this document we describe the applicability of the ForCES model and protocol.

rejected.why: SNMP and the ForCES MIB are discussed in the manageability section, but only as a supporting topic; the document is not about SNMP.
Section 6.3 summarises the ForCES MIB defined in RFC 5813, but it does not define MIB modules itself.
AgentX is mentioned once as a way to redirect SNMP to CEs; it is not a subject of the document.
IPsec and TLS appear only as security options offered by the TML, and in the security exchange example. The document is not about them.
ECMP is mentioned in a single sentence as something ForCES can configure.
SCTP appears only in a reference title for the TML.

RFC6042.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authorization Using KeyNote
RFC6042.summary: Specifies two new TLS Authorization Data Format types that carry KeyNote credential assertion lists, or a URL with hash pointing to them, in the TLS supplemental data handshake per RFC 5878.

trust management.why: The document defines how KeyNote credential assertions are conveyed and how the receiver evaluates them, using ACTION_AUTHORIZER set to the sender's public key. KeyNote is the trust-management system tagged here.
trust management.quote: This document specifies the use of the KeyNote trust-management system as an authorization extension in the Transport Layer Security (TLS) Handshake Protocol

TLS.why: It defines new TLS authorization data format types (keynote_assertion_list(64) and keynote_assertion_list_url(65)) and the handshake behaviour around them. This is a TLS extension of the kind the taxonomy says to tag.
TLS.quote: KeyNote credentials are exchanged in the supplemental data handshake message.

rejected.why: The document mentions X.509 key encoding and the certificate used for TLS authentication only as context. It does not specify anything about X.509.
HTTP is only the required scheme for fetching the credential URL. The document adds nothing to HTTP itself.
The authorization subject is covered by the more specific trust management tag and the TLS extension. The generic topic is not needed.
Hash algorithms appear only in the URLandHash structure copied from RFC 5878 in the appendix. The document is not about them.
RFC 3986 is only an informative reference for the URL. The document does not address URIs as a subject.

RFC6043.title: MIKEY-TICKET: Ticket-Based Modes of Key Distribution in Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY)
RFC6043.summary: RFC 6043 defines MIKEY-TICKET, new Kerberos-like ticket-based key distribution modes for MIKEY using a trusted key management service, with key forking, group keys, new payloads and 256-bit algorithms.

MIKEY.why: The document extends MIKEY with new ticket-based modes, new payloads, algorithms and a GENERIC-ID map type.
MIKEY.quote: This document introduces a set of new MIKEY modes that go under the common name MIKEY-TICKET.

rejected.why: The ticket concept is modelled on Kerberos, but the document does not specify or extend Kerberos.
SIP forking is a motivating scenario and SIP INVITE carries the messages, but SIP is not specified here.
SRTP is the protected media protocol and only session data fields reference it, so it is not the subject.
HMAC-SHA-256 is used as a PRF and MAC algorithm in a supporting role. It is not the subject.
AES-CM-256 is added as an encryption algorithm, but this is a minor part of the document.
SDP is only the transport for MIKEY messages (RFC 4567) and is not specified here.

RFC6044.title: Mapping and Interworking of Diversion Information between Diversion and History-Info Headers in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6044.summary: Informational RFC giving guidelines for mapping and interworking call-diversion information between the non-standard SIP Diversion header and the standard History-Info header (including cause-param and Voicemail URI), plus a coexistence policy.

SIP.why: The whole document specifies how two SIP headers (Diversion and History-Info) are translated and kept consistent in INVITE requests and 3xx responses, which is SIP signalling deployment and extension guidance.
SIP.quote: This document describes a recommended interworking guideline between the Diversion header and the History-Info header to handle call diversion information.

rejected.why: Not involved; the document concerns SIP header mapping only.
ABNF is only used to restate header syntax in a reminder section; the document is not about the notation.
SIP URIs, tel URIs and the cause/target URI parameters appear in the mappings, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
Only a note suggests converting a tel URI to a SIP URI with user=phone; this is a minor detail.
ISUP and 3GPP CDIV are referenced as inspiration for the mapping, but the document does not address PSTN interworking.

gaps.name: Call diversion / History-Info header (RFC 4244, Diversion header RFC 5806)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SIP call forwarding or request history information, which is the document's real subject; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC6045.title: Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID)
RFC6045.summary: RFC 6045 specifies Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID), an XML envelope schema and message set (TraceRequest, Investigation, Result, Report, IncidentQuery, RequestAuthorization) extending IODEF so network providers and CSIRTs can exchange incident data and continue traces upstream.

RID.why: The document specifies RID itself: its message types, RIDPolicy/RequestStatus/IncidentSource classes, schema and communication flows.
RID.quote: Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) outlines a proactive inter-network communication method to facilitate sharing incident handling data

IODEF.why: RID is built on IODEF, extending it and carrying IODEF documents in every message. Readers of IODEF would want this extension.
IODEF.quote: The RID schema acts as an XML envelope to support the communication of IODEF documents for exchanging or tracing information regarding security incidents.

rejected.why: XML digital signature and encryption are used to secure RID messages but are not specified or profiled by this document.
PKI and consortium trust are discussed in security considerations as supporting infrastructure, not as the document's subject.
DDoS tracing is a motivating use case, but the document specifies an incident-exchange protocol, not DDoS mitigation signalling.
XML is the encoding and schema language for RID messages; it is a substrate and not the subject.
TLS and HTTPS are transport mechanisms defined in RFC 6046, and are not specified here.
Parent of RID/IODEF; the more specific child tags already cover it.

RFC6046.title: Transport of Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) Messages
RFC6046.summary: RFC 6046 specifies a transport protocol for Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) messages, carrying IODEF-based RID messages in HTTP POST requests and responses over TLS on TCP port 4590, with callback semantics for delayed replies.

RID.why: The whole document defines how RID messages are exchanged between RID systems: request/response pairs, callback, port 4590, and error handling. RID is the specific subject.
RID.quote: This document specifies a transport protocol for RID based upon the passing of RID messages over HTTP/TLS (Transport Layer Security).

rejected.why: IODEF is the XML format that RID extends. The document only mentions it as background and says it defines a message format, not a transport. It specifies nothing new about IODEF.
HTTP is the substrate. The document uses POST, 202 and chunked encoding, but defines no new HTTP semantics or extensions.
TLS only secures the connection. The document uses mutual authentication and non-NULL ciphersuites but defines no new TLS extension or mechanism.
X.509 certificates are mentioned only in the Security Considerations for peer trust, which is boilerplate.
This is a transport binding of RID over HTTP/TLS. However, RID is the more specific tag and the child tag fits better.
PKI is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a recommendation for consortia, so the document is not about it.

RFC6047.title: iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol (iMIP)
RFC6047.summary: RFC 6047 defines iMIP, the binding of iCalendar scheduling (iTIP) onto Internet email using MIME text/calendar body parts, with S/MIME-based security rules and examples; it obsoletes RFC 2447.

iCalendar.why: The document is the iMIP binding of iTIP scheduling to email, a core part of the iCalendar family.
iCalendar.quote: specifies a binding from the iCalendar Transport-independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP) to Internet email-based transports

rejected.why: Email is the transport the binding runs over, though the document does define how to wrap calendar objects in messages; the subject is calendaring.
S/MIME is relied on for authentication and confidentiality but not specified here.
MIME is the encapsulation mechanism; the document only profiles the text/calendar header usage.
SMTP is only the transport.

RFC6048.title: Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) Additions to LIST Command
RFC6048.summary: RFC 6048 extends NNTP's LIST capability with new keywords (COUNTS, DISTRIBUTIONS, MODERATORS, MOTD, SUBSCRIPTIONS) and adds new newsgroup status values (x, j, =group) to LIST ACTIVE.

NNTP.why: The document specifies new NNTP LIST variants and extends LIST ACTIVE, updating RFC 3977 and RFC 2980. It is an NNTP protocol extension.
NNTP.quote: This document defines a set of enhancements to the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) that allow a client to request extended information from NNTP servers

rejected.why: NNTP is a child of Netnews and is the more specific tag. The document deals with the server-reader protocol, not article format or distribution architecture.
The document uses ABNF to define its syntax, but only as a notation. It is not about ABNF.
UTF-8 is required for descriptions and the message of the day, but this is a minor encoding requirement, not the subject of the document.
The IANA section registers the NNTP extension, which is boilerplate. The document is not about IANA registries.
Moderator submission address templates are email addresses, but the document is only about how NNTP servers list and use them.

RFC6049.title: Spatial Composition of Metrics
RFC6049.summary: Defines spatial composition functions for IPPM metrics, combining sub-path one-way delay (mean, minimum), packet loss, and delay variation measurements to estimate complete-path performance, with assumptions and failure cases.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines IP performance metrics (delay, loss, delay variation) and composition functions over sub-paths. This is the performance measurement subject.
performance measurement.quote: defines relationships to compose a complete path metric from the sub-path metrics with some accuracy with regard to the actual metrics

rejected.why: The IANA section registers metrics in an IPPM registry MIB, but that is boilerplate. The document does not define MIB modules.
The metric registrations are only IANA Considerations boilerplate. The document is not about IANA registries.
ECMP is mentioned only as one source of deviation between sub-path and complete-path measurements.
MPLS appears only in a single example of manipulated routing that can cause measurement error.
The document defines composition of one-way metrics. It does not specify TWAMP or any measurement protocol.

gaps.name: IPPM metric composition
gaps.why: The document is about spatial composition of IP performance metrics. The taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic, with no more specific tag for IPPM metric definitions.

RFC6050.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Extension for the Identification of Services
RFC6050.summary: RFC 6050 defines private SIP header fields P-Asserted-Service and P-Preferred-Service for trusted SIP networks to assert service identification, plus an informal urn-7 URN namespace for identifying services and applications.

SIP.why: The document defines new SIP header fields and the proxy/UA procedures for them within a trust domain, so it is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: private extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) that enable a network of trusted SIP servers to assert the service of authenticated users

URN.why: It registers the informal URN namespace urn-7 with syntax and IANA-managed service labels, which URN readers would want to find.
URN.quote: This document labels services by means of an informal URN.

rejected.why: SDP is only examined as input for deriving the service; the document does not define anything about SDP.
The IANA registry for Service-ID labels is boilerplate-style registration, not the document's main subject.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the header syntax.
Network-asserted service is related to asserted identity but is not caller-ID authentication.
User authentication such as digest is mentioned only as how a proxy decides to assert the service.

RFC6051.title: Rapid Synchronisation of RTP Flows
RFC6051.summary: Updates RFC 3550 to speed RTP flow synchronisation: lets SSM senders send an immediate RTCP SR, defines an RTP/AVPF RTCP-SR-REQ feedback message, and defines NTP-timestamp RTP header extensions, applied to decoding order recovery in layered codecs.

RTCP.why: The document updates RTCP timing rules for SR packets and defines a new RTCP feedback message (RTCP-SR-REQ). Its core subject is RTCP-based synchronisation.
RTCP.quote: a new feedback packet is defined for use with the extended RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback (RTP/AVPF), allowing video switching MCUs to rapidly request resynchronisation

RTP.why: It defines two RTP header extensions carrying NTP timestamps in-band, and it updates RFC 3550. Readers of RTP would want it, though RTCP is the more specific tag for most of the content.
RTP.quote: new RTP header extensions are defined to allow rapid synchronisation of late joiners

rejected.why: SSM sessions are used as a scenario for the RTCP timing change, but the document does not specify or analyse SSM itself.
SDP is used only to signal the header extension URIs and dependencies; this is substrate use.
SRTP appears only in the Security Considerations and as a note on interaction with header extensions.
H.264 SVC is only the motivating use case and is cited from a separate draft.
The document defines header extensions, not a codec-specific payload format.
NTP-format timestamps are used as the reference clock, but the document does not specify or extend NTP.

RFC6052.title: IPv6 Addressing of IPv4/IPv6 Translators
RFC6052.summary: Defines the algorithmic mapping between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses for IPv4/IPv6 translators, including the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96, the IPv4-embedded IPv6 address format, and guidance on choosing network-specific prefixes.

IPv6 transition.why: The document specifies the address format and prefix used by IPv4/IPv6 translators for stateless and stateful translation, which is the core of IPv6/IPv4 coexistence mechanisms. No more specific child (NAT64, SIIT) is the sole subject, since it serves translators generally.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document reserves a "Well-Known Prefix" for use in an algorithmic mapping.  The value of this IPv6 prefix is:

addressing.why: It defines an IPv6 address format and a reserved prefix, updates RFC 4291, and gives prefix-length and allocation guidance (Sections 3.3 and 3.4), all of which are IP address architecture matters.
addressing.quote: IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses are composed of a variable-length prefix, the embedded IPv4 address, and a variable-length suffix

rejected.why: The document supplies addressing for stateful translators like NAT64, but it does not specify NAT64 itself. It is also used for stateless translation.
It supports stateless translation, but it does not define the SIIT packet translation algorithm. It covers only the address mapping.
DNS64 is mentioned as an example of an address translator that uses this format. The document does not specify it.
BGP appears only in the guidance on advertising prefixes in Section 3.2, not as a subject of the document.
IPv6 is the general context, but the more specific IPv6 transition and addressing tags cover the content better.

RFC6053.title: Implementation Report for Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES)
RFC6053.summary: Implementation and interoperability report for the ForCES protocol, FE model and SCTP TML, surveying three implementations and a July 2009 interop test.

ForCES.why: The whole document reports on implementations and interoperability of ForCES protocol, LFB model and SCTP TML.
ForCES.quote: This document is an implementation report for the ForCES Protocol, Model, and the Stream Control Transmission Protocol-based Transport Mapping Layer (SCTP TML) documents

rejected.why: SCTP is only the transport used by the ForCES TML; the document does not specify or analyse SCTP itself.
IPsec is the mandated TML security mechanism but was not tested or discussed beyond a survey line.
The SCTP TML is covered, but the ForCES tag already captures it; no separate transport mapping subject is the focus.
Wireshark/tcpdump extensions were used only as verification tools.

RFC6054.title: Using Counter Modes with Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH) to Protect Group Traffic
RFC6054.summary: Specifies how to form IVs from a Sender Identifier plus sender-specific counter so multiple senders can share one IPsec SA using counter-mode ciphers (CTR, GCM, CCM, GMAC) in ESP and AH, and sets conventions for group key managers to allocate SIDs.

ESP.why: The document defines how IVs for counter-mode ESP/AH transforms are constructed for group SAs. ESP is the most specific IPsec tag covering this.
ESP.quote: This memo describes the use of counter modes when applied to the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH) in multiple-sender group applications.

GDOI.why: A substantial section sets requirements on group key management systems for SID allocation and distribution, with GDOI as the main example. This is the multicast-security group key management area.
GDOI.quote: This document RECOMMENDS that the GKMS both allocate unique SIDs to group members and distribute them to group members using a GKM protocol such as GDOI or GSAKMP.

AES.why: The document is about using AES counter-based modes (CTR, GCM, CCM, GMAC) safely with group keys, including nonce/IV uniqueness requirements.
AES.quote: Several new AES encryption modes of operation have been specified for ESP: Counter Mode (CTR) [RFC3686], Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) [RFC4106]

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example group key management protocol, and the document does not specify or extend it.
ESP is the more specific tag, and the document does not address the IPsec architecture as a whole.
Its child GDOI is already tagged, so the parent tag is implied.
IKEv2 is mentioned only for point-to-point keying and is not the subject of the document.
The Camellia counter mode is only cited as one of the modes the restriction applies to.
The GOST counter mode is only cited as one of the modes the restriction applies to.

RFC6055.title: IAB Thoughts on Encodings for Internationalized Domain Names
RFC6055.summary: IAB document exploring problems arising from using different encodings (UTF-8 vs. Punycode A-labels) for Internationalized Domain Names across name resolution APIs, DNS and non-DNS protocols, recommending that A-label conversion be done by the entity that knows which protocol/namespace is used.

IDN.why: The whole document is about IDN encodings (U-labels, A-labels, Punycode) and IDNA handling in applications and resolvers.
IDN.quote: explores issues with Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) that result from the use of various encoding schemes such as UTF-8 and the ASCII-Compatible Encoding produced by the Punycode algorithm

DNS.why: A substantial section covers non-ASCII labels in DNS, private namespaces, suffix search lists and resolver behaviour, with recommendations for resolvers and servers.
DNS.quote: A common misconception is that DNS only supports names that can be expressed using letters, digits, and hyphens.

UTF-8.why: The document argues for UTF-8 versus UTF-16/32 and A-labels as the encoding for names, citing the IETF UTF-8 policy.
UTF-8.quote: UTF-8 is a mechanism for encoding a Unicode code point in a variable number of 8-bit octets, where an ASCII code point is preserved as-is.

rejected.why: Mentioned as an example of a non-DNS protocol that uses UTF-8; the document is not about mDNS itself.
Unicode is background for the encoding discussion; the focus is IDN encoding, and UTF-8 is the more specific fit.
Hostname syntax history is discussed only as the source of the misconception about DNS names.
Mentioned once as an example of a protocol using A-labels; not a subject of the document.
getaddrinfo() and GetAddrInfoW() encoding are discussed, but as part of the IDN resolution problem and not as a sockets API extension.
The parent of UTF-8; the more specific tag is chosen instead.

RFC6056.title: Recommendations for Transport-Protocol Port Randomization
RFC6056.summary: BCP describing algorithms for selecting randomized ephemeral client port numbers in transport protocols (TCP, UDP, SCTP, DCCP) to make off-path blind attacks harder, with guidance on collisions, secret keys and NAPT interaction.

transport.why: The document is about ephemeral port selection across transport protocols generally (TCP, UDP, SCTP, DCCP, RTP), so the general transport topic fits better than any single protocol tag.
transport.quote: This document describes a number of simple and efficient methods for the selection of the client port number, such that the possibility of an attacker guessing the exact value is reduced.

NAT.why: A dedicated section gives NAPT-specific recommendations on port obfuscation, port preservation and parity preservation.
NAT.quote: NAPTs should consider obfuscating the selection of ephemeral ports by means of any of the algorithms discussed in this document.
NAT.section: 4. Interaction with Network Address Port Translation (NAPT)

rejected.why: TCP is the main motivating example but the algorithms apply to all transports; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
UDP is only one of several transports the algorithms apply to.
SCTP is mentioned for specific considerations but is not a focus.
The document uses randomness and references RFC 4086 but is not about randomness requirements.
MD5 is only suggested as a hash for the offset function; the document is not about it.
Security motivates the document, but the more specific transport tag covers it; no specific security mechanism is specified.

gaps.name: Ephemeral port selection / port randomization
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for transport-layer port allocation or port randomization, which is the core subject of this RFC.

RFC6057.title: Comcast's Protocol-Agnostic Congestion Management System
RFC6057.summary: Informational RFC describing Comcast's protocol-agnostic congestion management system for its DOCSIS cable network, which uses CMTS port utilization and per-user consumption thresholds to move heavy users' traffic from Priority Best Effort to Best Effort QoS.

congestion control.why: The whole document describes an ISP's network-level congestion management system: thresholds, near-congestion detection, and deprioritizing heavy users. It is not a specific congestion control algorithm, so the parent topic fits best.
congestion control.quote: The goal of Comcast's new congestion management system is to enable all users of our network resources to access a "fair share" of that bandwidth

DOCSIS.why: The system is implemented on DOCSIS cable access networks using CMTS ports, bonded channels and modem bootfiles. A substantial part of the document describes this environment, so readers of DOCSIS would want it.
DOCSIS.quote: A reference standard developed by CableLabs that specifies how components on cable networks need to be built to enable HSI service over an HFC network
DOCSIS.section: 3.8. Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS)

QoS.why: The mechanism is a two-level QoS scheme (PBE vs BE), signalled by PCMM servers to the CMTS. This is central to how the system works.
QoS.quote: Comcast sent new bootfiles to our HSI customers' cable modems that created two Quality of Service (QoS) levels for Internet traffic

rejected.why: SNMP is only used to poll CMTS port utilization. The document does not specify or extend it.
IPDR is a separate usage-record standard used as a data source, and it is not IPFIX. The taxonomy has no IPDR tag, so this is not a fit.
LEDBAT is mentioned only in a short section on possible future work, and the document is not about it.
ConEx is mentioned only as a possible future IETF effort for signalling congestion.
TCP appears only in Briscoe's loss-rate quote and in the note that TCP reset packets are not used.
P2P applications are the target of the old system, which this document contrasts with. The new system is protocol-agnostic and is not about P2P.

gaps.name: ISP traffic management / network neutrality practices
gaps.why: The document records an operator's network management practice, written in response to FCC complaints. The taxonomy has no tag for ISP traffic-management or net-neutrality policy.

gaps.name: PacketCable Multimedia (PCMM)
gaps.why: PCMM is the signalling used to set QoS gates on the CMTS, and IPDR is the usage-record standard. Neither has a taxonomy tag.

RFC6058.title: Transient Binding for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6058.summary: Experimental extension to Proxy Mobile IPv6 that adds a Transient Binding option to PBU/PBA so the LMA can hold a transient binding cache entry with two forwarding entries, enabling late downlink path switch and optimized single- and dual-radio handover.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends PMIPv6 signaling with a Transient Binding option and defines LMA/MAG behaviour for transient binding cache entries.
PMIPv6.quote: This document specifies an extension to PMIPv6 that utilizes a new mobility option in the Proxy Binding Update (PBU) and the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA)

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) is only referenced for the Mobility Options registry and unknown-option handling; the document is about PMIPv6.
Parent of PMIPv6, which is implied; the document is specific to one child.
Router Solicitation/Advertisement and address resolution appear only in the problem analysis, not as the subject.
Address autoconfiguration delay motivates the problem but the document does not specify or extend SLAAC.
3GPP EPC and GSM/UMTS are used as example use cases only, not specified.

RFC6059.title: Simple Procedures for Detecting Network Attachment in IPv6
RFC6059.summary: RFC 6059 specifies Simple DNA, a host procedure for IPv6 Detecting Network Attachment that uses unicast Neighbor Solicitations to previously seen routers, in parallel with Router Solicitations, to decide whether existing addresses and configuration are still valid.

IPv6.why: The document defines the IPv6 DNA host procedure (the SDAT, probing and response handling), and no more specific tag covers detecting attachment. It is about IPv6 host configuration and movement.
IPv6.quote: This document provides simple procedures for Detecting Network Attachment in IPv6 hosts, and procedures for routers to support such services.

neighbor discovery.why: The core mechanism is built on Neighbor Discovery messages: NS/NA probes, RS/RA exchanges and their contents, and the conflict rules between them. Readers of IPv6 neighbor discovery would want this extension.
neighbor discovery.quote: The host uses a combination of unicast Neighbor Solicitations (NSs) and multicast Router Solicitations (RSs)

rejected.why: The document only has the host initiate a standard DHCPv6 exchange and track DHCPv6 addresses. It states that it does not modify DHCPv6.
SLAAC addresses are tracked in the SDAT and the host configures them as in RFC 4862, but the document does not specify or change SLAAC.
SEND appears only as an optional security flag on SDAT entries and in the Security Considerations. The document does not define anything new about SEND.
DNAv4 is mentioned only in a short comparison section, so the document is not about IPv4.

gaps.name: Detecting Network Attachment (DNA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DNA or link-change detection. This is the main subject of RFC 6059 and of related documents such as RFC 4436 and RFC 4957, so a dedicated tag would suit them.

RFC6060.title: Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Control of Ethernet Provider Backbone Traffic Engineering (PBB-TE)
RFC6060.summary: Specifies GMPLS RSVP-TE extensions (new Ethernet label, switching type 802_1 PBB-TE, Service ID TLV, error handling) to establish P2P and P2MP IEEE 802.1Qay PBB-TE Ethernet Switched Paths.

GMPLS.why: The document defines GMPLS signaling extensions (new label format, switching type, Service ID TLV) for controlling PBB-TE Ethernet LSPs.
GMPLS.quote: The purpose of this document is to specify extensions for a GMPLS-based control plane to manage PBB-TE explicitly routed traffic engineered paths.

Ethernet.why: A substantial part concerns Ethernet PBB-TE connection-oriented forwarding, ESPs, B-VIDs and MAC addressing, and the Ethernet label.
Ethernet.quote: PBB-TE ESPs are created bridge by bridge (or switch by switch) by simple configuration of Ethernet forwarding entries.
Ethernet.section: 3. Creation and Maintenance of PBB-TE Paths Using GMPLS

rejected.why: The document uses RSVP-TE as the signaling substrate and defines extensions specific to GMPLS Ethernet, so GMPLS is the better fit.
Parent topic of RSVP-TE and PCE; the document is about a specific GMPLS technology, not traffic engineering generally.
PCE is mentioned only as an optional tool for pre-selecting shared forwarding paths.
Only the GMPLS child is relevant; this is not about MPLS data plane.
CCM and protection switching are only mentioned in passing.

gaps.name: PBB-TE (IEEE 802.1Qay Provider Backbone Bridge Traffic Engineering)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PBB-TE or Ethernet traffic engineering, which is the data plane being controlled.

RFC6061.title: Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the National Emergency Number Association (NENA)
RFC6061.summary: Registers the "nena" URN Namespace ID for the National Emergency Number Association, defining its NSS structure, registry management by the NENA Registry System, and example URNs for emergency responders.

URN.why: The document registers a new URN namespace per RFC 3406, specifying NSS syntax, uniqueness, persistence and assignment. It belongs on the URN namespaces page.
URN.quote: This document describes the Namespace Identifier (NID) "nena" for Uniform Resource Name (URN) resources published by the National Emergency Number Association (NENA).

rejected.why: The namespace is used for NENA emergency call routing, but the document only defines a URN namespace and registry. It specifies no emergency-calling protocol.
XML namespaces motivate the registration, but the document is not about XML usage.
The IANA registration is boilerplate, and the NENA registry is analogous to IANA but separate.
The example URN is for an emergency call routing function, but LoST is not specified or discussed.

RFC6062.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) Extensions for TCP Allocations
RFC6062.summary: Extends TURN to let a client request TCP allocations, defining Connect, ConnectionBind and ConnectionAttempt STUN methods and a CONNECTION-ID attribute so the server can open and accept TCP connections with peers and relay data.

TURN.why: The whole document specifies a TURN extension for TCP allocations, covering client and server behaviour and new methods, attributes and error codes.
TURN.quote: This specification defines an extension of Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN), a relay protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal.

rejected.why: TURN is built on STUN, and the document only registers new STUN methods, attributes and error codes for the TURN extension. It does not specify STUN itself.
TCP is the transport being relayed, but the document does not extend or specify TCP itself.
TLS is only an optional transport for the control connection, and nothing new is defined for it.
ICE is mentioned as the way peers coordinate out of band, but the document does not specify it.
The TURN tag sits under this topic, and a technology tag already covers it.

RFC6063.title: Dynamic Symmetric Key Provisioning Protocol (DSKPP)
RFC6063.summary: RFC 6063 specifies DSKPP, an XML-based client-server protocol (four-pass key agreement and two-pass key transport variants) for provisioning symmetric keys to cryptographic modules, with user authentication, key packages in PSKC format, and an HTTP binding.

key management.why: The document defines a protocol for key establishment and provisioning of symmetric keys, including key agreement, key transport, key wrap and passphrase-based wrap.
key management.quote: a client-server protocol for provisioning symmetric keys between a cryptographic module (corresponding to DSKPP Client) and a key provisioning server

authentication.why: A substantial part of the document defines user authentication using Authentication Codes and derived Authentication Data (TLV format, PBKDF2-derived MAC), plus server authentication MACs.
authentication.quote: the DSKPP Server MUST authenticate the user to be sure he is authorized for the new key.

XML.why: The protocol messages are defined by an XML schema (Section 8) and a registered application/dskpp+xml type, so XML-based format readers would want it.
XML.quote: The principal syntax is XML [XML] and it is layered on a transport mechanism such as HTTP

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is only the mandatory transport binding; the document does not extend HTTP semantics.
TLS is relied on for transport protection only; nothing new is defined for TLS.
Mentions CMP/CMC only as analogues and the protocol explicitly works without PKI.
XMLDSIG KeyInfo and XMLENC identifiers are reused for key payloads, but the document does not specify signature or encryption mechanisms itself.
One-time-password keys (HOTP, SecurID) are example key types being provisioned, not the subject of the document.
The application/dskpp+xml registration is boilerplate-like IANA content, not the main subject.

gaps.name: Symmetric key provisioning / PSKC
gaps.why: The document is about provisioning symmetric keys to cryptographic modules (DSKPP, PSKC key containers); no specific tag exists, so the generic key management topic is the closest fit.

RFC6064.title: SDP and RTSP Extensions Defined for 3GPP Packet-Switched Streaming Service and Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service
RFC6064.summary: Informational RFC that registers with IANA the 3GPP-defined SDP attributes, SDP proto identifiers for MBMS FEC, and RTSP headers and option tags used by 3GPP PSS and MBMS streaming services.

SDP.why: The document describes and registers many SDP attributes and three new SDP proto identifiers for 3GPP services. This is an extension of SDP.
SDP.quote: The Packet-switched Streaming Service (PSS) and the Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service (MBMS) defined by 3GPP use the Session Description Protocol (SDP)

RTSP.why: The document describes and registers RTSP headers and option tags (3GPP-Link-Char, Switch-Stream, 3gpp-pipelined and others) for PSS.
RTSP.quote: The RTSP extensions for PSS consist of a number of new RTSP headers and option tags

cellular.why: The extensions exist for 3GPP mobile streaming and broadcast services (PSS and MBMS), so readers of 3GPP cellular IP topics would want this RFC.
cellular.quote: Packet-switched Streaming Service, a unicast-based streaming service for delivery of on-demand or live streaming multimedia content to mobile terminals.

rejected.why: SRTP is used only for integrity protection configuration and as a proto identifier variant. The document is not about SRTP itself.
MBMS block-based FEC is signalled through new proto identifiers. The FEC mechanism is defined in 3GPP specs, not here.
RTP is only the payload carried in the proto identifiers, and the NADU APP packet is only mentioned in passing.
The 3GPP-Link-Char header carries QoS parameters, but the document does not address QoS architectures or signalling.
The parent topic is implied by the RTSP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The IANA registrations here are for SDP and RTSP parameters, not MIME media types.

RFC6065.title: Using Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting Services to Dynamically Provision View-Based Access Control Model User-to-Group Mappings
RFC6065.summary: Defines a MIB module and elements of procedure that use AAA (RADIUS Management-Policy-Id) information to dynamically populate VACM user-to-group mappings for SNMP access control.

MIB.why: The document defines the SNMP-VACM-AAA-MIB module with vacmAaaSecurityToGroupTable and its procedures, extending VACM tables.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols.

RADIUS.why: The mapping is driven by RADIUS User-Name and Management-Policy-Id attributes; the document specifies how they are consumed, though it defines no new RADIUS behaviour.
RADIUS.quote: the approach here is to leverage existing RADIUS usage for identifying a principal, documented in [RFC5608], along with the RADIUS Management-Policy-Id Attribute [RFC5607].

rejected.why: MIB is the more specific tag; the document's content is a MIB module, and SNMP is the substrate.
RADIUS is the specific AAA tech used; the AAA framework itself is not the subject.
Secure Shell Transport Model is only mentioned as a motivating example transport.
Access control is the topic, but the MIB and RADIUS tags cover it more specifically.

gaps.name: VACM (View-based Access Control Model)
gaps.why: The document is about dynamically provisioning VACM user-to-group mappings for SNMP, and the taxonomy has no VACM tag.

RFC6066.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions: Extension Definitions
RFC6066.summary: RFC 6066 specifies six TLS extensions (server_name, max_fragment_length, client_certificate_url, trusted_ca_keys, truncated_hmac, status_request), obsoleting RFC 4366, and registers the pkix-pkipath media type.

TLS.why: The whole document defines TLS handshake extensions, new handshake messages and alerts. This is TLS protocol extension work.
TLS.quote: This document provides specifications for existing TLS extensions.

OCSP.why: Section 8 defines the status_request extension and CertificateStatus message for carrying OCSP requests and responses in the handshake. This is a substantial part of the document that OCSP readers would want.
OCSP.quote: Allow TLS clients and servers to negotiate that the server sends the client certificate status information (e.g., an Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) [RFC2560] response)

rejected.why: DTLS is mentioned only briefly, in the record_overflow behaviour. The document is not about DTLS.
X.509 certificates are what the extensions carry, and the pkipath type encodes a chain. The document does not specify or profile X.509.
Section 10.1 registers application/pkix-pkipath. That is an IANA boilerplate-style registration, not the main subject.
truncated_hmac only negotiates truncating the MAC output to 80 bits in the TLS record layer. It does not define HMAC.
HTTP is only the mechanism for fetching client certificates from URLs.
DNS hostnames are the only server name type supported. The document says it implies no dependency of TLS on DNS.

RFC6067.title: BCP 47 Extension U
RFC6067.summary: Registers the 'u' extension to BCP 47 language tags for Unicode CLDR locale attributes, keys and types, maintained by the Unicode Consortium.

language tags.why: The document is a BCP 47 language tag extension registration, defining subtag structure (attributes, keys, types) and canonicalization for locale-based refinements of language tags.
language tags.quote: This document defines an extension for identifying Unicode locale-based variations using language tags.  The "singleton" identifier for this extension is 'u'.

rejected.why: The document only registers a record in the Language Extensions Registry; that is boilerplate-level IANA action, not the subject.
Unicode CLDR/LDML is the source of the definitions, but the document is about language tag extension subtags, not Unicode usage in protocols.
Only mentions that subtags follow the existing language tag ABNF; no notation is defined.
Parent of language tags; the more specific child tag applies.

RFC6068.title: The 'mailto' URI Scheme
RFC6068.summary: RFC 6068 defines the 'mailto' URI scheme for identifying Internet mail resources, with syntax, semantics, header-field handling, safety rules and UTF-8 percent-encoding for internationalization, obsoleting RFC 2368.

URI.why: The document specifies a URI scheme (mailto): its syntax, semantics, encoding and IANA scheme registration, so it belongs on the URI page.
URI.quote: This document defines the format of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) to identify resources that are reached using Internet mail.

email.why: The scheme exists to compose email messages with addresses, header fields and body. It covers mail client behaviour and unsafe header fields, which email readers would want.
email.quote: The 'mailto' URI scheme is used to identify resources that are reached using Internet mail.

rejected.why: The document aims for compatibility with IRIs and cites RFC 3987. It defines no IRI syntax itself and is really a URI scheme definition.
It maps URI header fields onto RFC 5322 headers, but it does not specify the message format. That format is only relied on.
UTF-8-based percent-encoding is used, but the UTF-8 encoding is only the mechanism and is not what the document is about.
IDNA conversion of domain names is mentioned, but only as a processing step. The document defines nothing new about IDN.
The document explicitly says it does not address email address internationalization.
SMTP appears only in a security note about the envelope return path.

RFC6069.title: Making TCP More Robust to Long Connectivity Disruptions (TCP-LCD)
RFC6069.summary: RFC 6069 specifies TCP-LCD, an experimental sender-only TCP modification that uses ICMP unreachable messages during timeout-based loss recovery to undo retransmission timer backoffs, so TCP detects restored connectivity sooner after long disruptions.

TCP.why: The document defines a TCP sender-side modification to retransmission timer backoff and loss recovery. Readers of TCP extensions would want it.
TCP.quote: This document proposes an algorithm to make TCP more robust to long connectivity disruptions (TCP-LCD).

ICMP.why: A substantial part of the document (Section 3) analyses ICMP and ICMPv6 destination unreachable codes and their contents as a connectivity disruption indication.
ICMP.quote: It describes how standard ICMP messages can be exploited during timeout-based loss recovery to disambiguate true congestion loss from non-congestion loss

rejected.why: The algorithm interacts with congestion response, but the document is a TCP retransmission timer change. TCP already sits under transport and is the more specific tag.
ECN is only mentioned as an interoperability issue in Section 7.2, not as a subject of the document.
NewReno is cited only to contrast definitions of timeout-based loss recovery.
IPv6/ICMPv6 is covered only as the counterpart of the ICMPv4 behaviour. The document is not about IPv6.
Section 7.3 briefly discusses IP tunnels' compatibility. It is a minor interoperability note.

RFC6070.title: PKCS #5: Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 (PBKDF2) Test Vectors
RFC6070.summary: RFC 6070 supplies test vectors for PBKDF2 (PKCS #5 v2.0) using HMAC-SHA-1 as the pseudorandom function, to help implementers verify their code.

PBKDF2.why: The whole document is a set of PBKDF2 input/output test vectors; readers of the PBKDF2 subject page would want it.
PBKDF2.quote: Test vectors for the algorithm were not included in the original specification, but are often useful for implementers.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is only the pseudorandom function inside PBKDF2. The document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
SHA-1 is only the underlying hash for the PRF, and the document does not address it.
SCRAM is mentioned once as an example user of PBKDF2, but the document is not about SASL or SCRAM.
The parent is implied by PBKDF2, so I did not list it separately.

RFC6071.title: IP Security (IPsec) and Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Document Roadmap
RFC6071.summary: Informational roadmap that lists and briefly describes the IPsec- and IKE-related RFCs (base documents, extensions, algorithms, multicast, outgrowths and protocols using IPsec/IKE), obsoleting RFC 2411.

IPsec.why: The whole document is a roadmap to IPsec architecture, ESP/AH, algorithms, and extensions.
IPsec.quote: This document is a snapshot of IPsec- and IKE-related RFCs.  It includes a brief description of each RFC

IKE.why: Section 4 and much of Section 5 are devoted to IKEv1 and IKEv2 base documents and extensions.
IKE.quote: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is the key negotiation and management protocol that is most commonly used to provide dynamically negotiated and updated keying material for IPsec.

rejected.why: ESP is covered as a part of IPsec; the document is a roadmap and not about ESP alone, so the parent IPsec tag fits better.
Only one of many RFCs described in the roadmap; not a substantial focus.
Algorithm requirement levels are a substantial section but are about their use within IPsec/IKE, which the IPsec/IKE tags already cover.
Described as one outgrowth among many in a short subsection; not a main subject.
Mentioned in a short subsection of outgrowths; not a main subject.
Section 6 covers multicast IPsec briefly as one part of the roadmap; not a main subject.

RFC6072.title: Certificate Management Service for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6072.summary: Defines SIP "certificate" and "credential" event packages forming a credential service that lets SIP UAs discover other users' certificates and store/retrieve their own certificates and private keys, with an rsa-sha256 Identity algorithm.

SIP.why: Defines two new SIP event packages (certificate, credential) with SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY/PUBLISH behaviour and registers them with IANA, extending SIP.
SIP.quote: This document defines a credential service that allows Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) User Agents (UAs) to use a SIP event package to discover the certificates

PKI.why: The document is a certificate distribution and management service: discovery, revocation, replacement, trust of certificates, and private key storage.
PKI.quote: This specification proposes a way to address discovery, retrieval, and management of certificates for SIP deployments.

rejected.why: TLS is used to protect credential transfer and cipher suites are mandated, but it is only the security substrate.
Certificates are PKIX style, but the document does not profile X.509; it only uses it.
S/MIME is the motivation for certificate distribution but is not specified or extended here.
Uses SIP events and PUBLISH, but does not define presence or SIMPLE extensions.
PBKDF2/HMAC algorithm requirements are minor crypto-profile details.
Only mandated for PKCS #8 key encryption in a brief paragraph; not a subject of the document.

RFC6073.title: Segmented Pseudowire
RFC6073.summary: Specifies how to build multi-segment pseudowires by switching PW segments at S-PEs between LDP and L2TPv3 control planes, including SP-PE TLV, VCCV OAM extensions and status mapping.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines multi-segment pseudowires, S-PE switching, signalling, OAM and status mapping.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes how to connect pseudowires (PWs) between different Packet Switched Network (PSN) domains or between two or more distinct PW control plane domains

LDP.why: Defines a new LDP TLV, status code and FEC 128/129 switching procedures.
LDP.quote: The SP-PE TLV is appended to the PW FEC at each S-PE, and the order of the SP-PE TLVs in the LDP message MUST be preserved.

L2TP.why: Defines L2TPv3 AVP and LDP-to-L2TPv3 control plane interworking for switched PWs.
L2TP.quote: The L2TP "PW Switching Point AVP" is Attribute Type 101.

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate (label swap, TTL); the document is about pseudowires, though pseudowire is the more specific fit.
VCCV operations are a substantial part, but they are specific to pseudowire switching and the main tag covers them.
Not related.

gaps.name: Multi-Segment Pseudowire (MS-PW)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a pseudowire tech tag only under MPLS, and no tag for PWE3 or VCCV.

RFC6074.title: Provisioning, Auto-Discovery, and Signaling in Layer 2 Virtual Private Networks (L2VPNs)
RFC6074.summary: Specifies L2VPN provisioning models (point-to-point, VPLS, colored pools, distributed VPLS), the structure of endpoint identifiers (AGI/AII), BGP-based auto-discovery, and their encoding in LDP and L2TPv3 pseudowire signaling, including inter-AS operation.

L2VPN.why: The whole document defines provisioning, auto-discovery and signaling for Layer 2 VPNs, including VPWS and colored pools.
L2VPN.quote: This document specifies a number of L2VPN provisioning models, and further specifies the semantic structure of the endpoint identifiers required by each model.

VPLS.why: A large part covers VPLS identifiers, BGP auto-discovery, signaling and distributed VPLS.
VPLS.quote: The VPLS service requires that a single pseudowire be created between each pair of VSIs that are in the same VPLS.

pseudowire.why: Defines how pseudowire endpoints are identified and signaled, including splicing of multi-segment PWs.
pseudowire.quote: it is necessary to specify rules for encoding each particular kind of endpoint identifier into the relevant fields of each signaling protocol.

LDP.why: Specifies encoding of AGI/AII into the LDP Generalized ID FEC element and new LDP status codes.
LDP.quote: The AGI field in this case consists of a Type of 1, a length field of value 8, and the 8 bytes of the VPLS-id.

rejected.why: BGP is used for auto-discovery with a new NLRI and communities, but the document is about L2VPN, not BGP itself.
L2TPv3 is one of the signaling protocols, but the taxonomy L2TP tag is for the protocol itself; here only identifier encoding is referenced to RFC 4667.
Referenced only for RT/RD and inter-AS option analogies.
Used as data plane substrate for label replace in splicing; not the subject.

RFC6075.title: The Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) Vendor Subtrees Registry
RFC6075.summary: Updates the IANA ACAP Vendor Subtrees registry definition from RFC 2244, clarifying vendor token syntax, restricting registrations to ASCII, and adding an example registration.

ACAP.why: The document updates part of the ACAP specification (RFC 2244), namely the vendor subtree registry and its syntax, so readers of ACAP would want it.
ACAP.quote: The original Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) specification included a vendor registry now used in other protocols.

IANA.why: The document's whole purpose is to define and update an IANA registry, including its registration procedure (first come, first served) and an example registration.
IANA.quote: This specification updates the IANA registry named the ACAP "Vendor Subtrees" registry.

rejected.why: IMAP ANNOTATE and METADATA reuse the registry, but they appear only as examples and the document does not specify IMAP behaviour.
UTF-8 is the encoding of vendor tokens, and the document restricts registrations to ASCII. It is a substrate, not the subject.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the formal syntax.
The internationalization section only explains why registrations are restricted to ASCII. The document is not about Unicode usage in general.

RFC6076.title: Basic Telephony SIP End-to-End Performance Metrics
RFC6076.summary: Defines a set of end-to-end SIP performance metrics for telephony (registration delay, session request delay, disconnect delay, duration, establishment ratios, ineffective attempts) with time measurement and reporting rules.

performance measurement.why: The document's core purpose is defining performance metrics, measurement points, clock accuracy and reporting for both active and passive measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This document defines a set of metrics and their usage to evaluate the performance of end-to-end Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for telephony services

SIP.why: Metrics are defined over SIP message exchanges (REGISTER, INVITE, BYE, response codes, Timer F), so SIP deployment and operation readers would want it.
SIP.quote: Session Request Delay (SRD) is utilized to detect failures or impairments causing delays in responding to a UA session request.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one possible way to transmit collected data; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only in passing regarding early media.
Clock synchronization requirements are stated only to support measurement accuracy; NTP/PTP are not specified.
Only cited for the SSP term in an informative reference.
Considered, but the metrics are performance measurement rather than OAM mechanisms.

RFC6077.title: Open Research Issues in Internet Congestion Control
RFC6077.summary: An IRTF/ICCRG informational RFC surveying open research problems in Internet congestion control: heterogeneity, stability, fairness, network support (ECN, XCP, RCP), corruption loss, packet size, flow startup, multi-domain issues, precedence, and misbehaving senders.

congestion control.why: The whole document is a survey of open research issues in congestion control across transports and network support.
congestion control.quote: This document describes some of the open problems in Internet congestion control that are known today.

ECN.why: Multi-domain ECN transport, attacks on it, and ECN-nonce are discussed substantially, as one of the main explicit feedback mechanisms.
ECN.quote: ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) marks packets -- set by active queue management techniques -- to convey congestion information

AQM.why: Active queue management (RED, REM, parameter setting difficulties) is a recurring part of the network support challenge.
AQM.quote: Various approaches have been proposed and also deployed, such as different AQM techniques.

TFRC.why: TFRC and TFRC-SP are discussed in the packet size and fairness challenges.
TFRC.quote: TFRC Small Packets (TFRC-SP) [RFC4828], a variant of the TFRC mechanism, has been designed for applications that exchange small packets.

rejected.why: TCP congestion control is the main reference point, but the document is about congestion control generally, not TCP specifically.
DCCP CCIDs are described as examples in the packet size section only; not a main subject.
Only a brief mention of multipath congestion control in Other Challenges.
Multi-domain pseudowires are one subsection, discussed as a congestion problem, not about pseudowire specification.
Precedence and Diffserv are discussed briefly under elastic traffic; not a focus.
LEDBAT is mentioned only in passing as lower-precedence transport.

RFC6078.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Immediate Carriage and Conveyance of Upper-Layer Protocol Signaling (HICCUPS)
RFC6078.summary: Defines the experimental HIP_DATA packet type and its SEQ_DATA, ACK_DATA, PAYLOAD_MIC and TRANSACTION_ID parameters, which carry authenticated, reliable upper-layer messages (e.g. overlay signalling) without running the HIP base exchange.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with a new packet type and four new parameters, including generation and reception rules, so it is squarely about HIP.
HIP.quote: we define the HIP DATA packet, which can be used to convey (in a authenticated and reliable way) protocol messages to a remote host without running the HIP base exchange

rejected.why: ESP is mentioned only as the alternative for continuous or confidential communication; HIP_DATA is explicitly not a replacement for it.
The ESP transport is referenced only as what hosts should use via the base exchange for sustained traffic, not specified here.
HIP-based overlays are the motivating environment, but the document does not specify overlay or P2P mechanisms.
The HIP header is treated as an IPv6 extension header, but this is only structural background.
The IANA section merely registers the new packet and parameter types; it is boilerplate.
The MIC is an unkeyed hash, defined as distinct from a MAC, so this tag does not fit.

RFC6079.title: HIP BONE: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Based Overlay Networking Environment (BONE)
RFC6079.summary: RFC 6079 specifies HIP BONE, a framework for building overlay networks that use HIP for connection management and separate peer protocols for storage and maintenance, and defines the OVERLAY_ID and OVERLAY_TTL HIP parameters.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with new parameters (OVERLAY_ID, OVERLAY_TTL) and a notify type and defines how HIP base exchange and signaling are used across an overlay.
HIP.quote: This document specifies a framework to build HIP-based (Host Identity Protocol) overlay networks.  This framework uses HIP to perform connection management.

P2P.why: The framework is about building peer-to-peer style overlay networks (peer protocols, DHTs, RELOAD instances), a substantial part of the document.
P2P.quote: HIP makes HIP a suitable protocol to build overlay networks that implement identifier-based overlay routing over IP networks

rejected.why: HIP's ICE-based NAT traversal is background and reused, not specified here.
Only used via HIP NAT traversal; not specified or extended.
RELOAD is mentioned only as an example peer protocol with a separate instance specification.
ESP protects HIP data traffic as substrate; not discussed beyond a mention.
Overlay routing tables are discussed by analogy to OSPF but this is not Internet routing architecture.
ORCHIDs look like IPv6 addresses but the document is not about IPv6.

RFC6080.title: A Framework for Session Initiation Protocol User Agent Profile Delivery
RFC6080.summary: RFC 6080 specifies a framework for delivering configuration profiles (local-network, device, user) to SIP user agents, defining the new SIP 'ua-profile' event package for enrollment and change notification, with HTTP/HTTPS content retrieval.

SIP.why: The document defines a SIP configuration framework and a new SIP event package ('ua-profile') using SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, extending SIP for UA deployment.
SIP.quote: The framework specifies a new SIP event package, as allowed by [RFC3265]. The purpose is to allow for devices to subscribe to specific profile types

rejected.why: HTTP/HTTPS is only the mandatory content retrieval substrate; nothing new is defined about HTTP.
DHCP is used to discover domain names and SIP servers but only as a dependency.
TLS/SIPS is relied on for securing delivery, not specified or extended.
The event package mechanism is SIP events generally; the document is not about presence, PIDF or XCAP, which is only mentioned as an option.
UUID URN is used as the device identifier format but only as a reference to RFC 4122.
Digest authentication is required but is used from existing specs; nothing new is defined.

gaps.name: SIP UA configuration / profile delivery
gaps.why: The document's main subject is device auto-configuration (provisioning) of SIP user agents, which has no specific tag in the taxonomy beyond SIP.

RFC6081.title: Teredo Extensions
RFC6081.summary: RFC 6081 specifies extensions to Teredo (IPv6 tunnelling over UDP through NATs) that add support for symmetric NATs, UPnP-enabled NATs, port-preserving and sequential port-symmetric NATs, hairpinning, and reduced server load, using new message trailers.

Teredo.why: The whole document defines extensions, new trailers and processing rules for Teredo, so it belongs on the Teredo page.
Teredo.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Teredo protocol, as specified in [RFC4380].

rejected.why: NAT types and traversal are the problem space, but the document is about Teredo extensions, not NAT behaviour or requirements. Teredo is the more specific tag.
UDP is only the transport that Teredo packets are encapsulated in.
This is the parent of Teredo, so it is implied and not listed separately.
This taxonomy tag is for interactive real-time media traversal (ICE, STUN, TURN). Teredo's traversal is for IPv6 connectivity.
The document only creates a trailer Type registry in its IANA Considerations section. That is boilerplate.
IPv6 is the payload that Teredo carries, not the subject of the document.

RFC6082.title: Deprecating Unicode Language Tag Characters: RFC 2482 is Historic
RFC6082.summary: Informational RFC that deprecates RFC 2482 (Unicode language tag characters for plain-text language identification) and moves it to Historic status, advising protocols not to use that facility.

language tags.why: The document deprecates a mechanism for tagging text with language identity (Unicode language tag characters) and points to Content-language as the replacement. Readers of the language tags subject would want it.
language tags.quote: describes a mechanism for using special Unicode language tag characters to identify languages when needed

rejected.why: The tag characters are Unicode code points, but the document is about language identification, not general Unicode usage in protocols. The language tags tag covers it more specifically.
The document changes an RFC's status to Historic, but that is the vehicle, not the subject. It does not describe or change IETF procedures.
The MIME Content-language header (RFC 3282) is mentioned only as a superseding mechanism, not specified or analysed here.
XML is mentioned only as one more general markup alternative, with no content about it.

RFC6083.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) for Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
RFC6083.summary: Specifies how to run DTLS over SCTP, including record mapping, stream usage, chunk authentication, SCTP-AUTH key handling via TLS exporters, handshake and shutdown procedures, replacing TLS over SCTP.

SCTP.why: The document defines how SCTP carries DTLS: stream usage, PPID, authenticated chunks, PR-SCTP and SCTP-AUTH key handling. SCTP readers need it.
SCTP.quote: This document describes the usage of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol over the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

DTLS.why: It profiles DTLS for SCTP, disabling replay detection, PMTU discovery and retransmission, and specifying handshake, renegotiation and shutdown changes.
DTLS.quote: DTLS over SCTP provides communications privacy for applications that use SCTP as their transport protocol

rejected.why: DTLS is a child of TLS and is the more specific tag. TLS over SCTP (RFC 3436) is only background, and the TLS exporter is just used.
The document is a binding of DTLS over SCTP, but the specific SCTP and DTLS tags cover it better.
DTLS is normally run over UDP, but this document replaces that transport with SCTP.
TCP is mentioned only as the usual transport for TLS.

RFC6084.title: General Internet Signaling Transport (GIST) over Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC6084.summary: Experimental RFC defining how GIST (NSIS signaling transport) uses SCTP (including PR-SCTP, multistreaming, multihoming) as a Messaging Association transport and DTLS for securing it, adding MA-Protocol-IDs 3 and 4.

SCTP.why: The document specifies a new Forwards-SCTP MA-Protocol-ID and how to use SCTP streams, PR-SCTP and multihoming for GIST. Readers of SCTP would want this.
SCTP.quote: This document defines the use of SCTP as the underlying transport protocol for GIST

NSIS.why: GIST is the NSIS signaling transport protocol, and the document extends its Connection mode transport options and its API with NSLPs.
NSIS.quote: GIST over SCTP as described in this document does not require any changes to the high-level operation and structure of GIST.

DTLS.why: A substantial part of the document specifies DTLS as a security mechanism for GIST messaging associations, including version, cipher and renegotiation rules.
DTLS.quote: This section specifies a new MA-Protocol-ID "DTLS" (value 4) for the use of DTLS in GIST

rejected.why: DTLS is a child of TLS and is the tag chosen here. TLS itself is only referenced for analogy.
TCP is the existing GIST transport that the document contrasts with SCTP (head-of-line blocking). The document does not specify or extend it.
The document does carry GIST over SCTP, but SCTP is a more specific tag for that subject.
NSIS is a QoS signaling framework, but this document only concerns the signaling transport. NSIS is also the more specific tag and sits under QoS.
The NAT section only defers to other documents and defines no procedures.
UDP is mentioned only in passing as a datagram transport DTLS could run over.

RFC6085.title: Address Mapping of IPv6 Multicast Packets on Ethernet
RFC6085.summary: Updates RFC 2464 to clarify that an IPv6 packet with a multicast destination address may be mapped to an Ethernet link-layer unicast address when only one receiver is relevant, and that receivers must not drop such packets.

Ethernet.why: The document specifies how IPv6 multicast destination addresses map to Ethernet link-layer addresses, updating RFC 2464 (IPv6 over Ethernet). This is the core subject of the Ethernet tag.
Ethernet.quote: This document extends this mapping to explicitly allow for a mapping of an IPv6 packet with a multicast destination address into an Ethernet link-layer unicast address

rejected.why: IPv6 is the packet type being mapped, but the document is about the Ethernet link-layer address mapping, so the more specific Ethernet tag fits better.
The document concerns link-layer address mapping of multicast-addressed packets, not multicast routing, group membership, or deployment.
The motivating use cases (e.g. unicasting multicast-addressed ND/RA messages) are not discussed in the body; the document is only about address mapping.

RFC6086.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) INFO Method and Package Framework
RFC6086.summary: Defines the SIP INFO method and the Info Package framework (Recv-Info and Info-Package header fields, 469 response, IANA registry), obsoleting RFC 2976 and keeping a legacy usage mode.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP method and two new SIP header fields, along with the dialog procedures and rules for Info Packages. It is a core SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines a method, INFO, for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [RFC3261].

rejected.why: SDP offer/answer is mentioned only as an analogy for Recv-Info rules; the document does not specify anything about SDP.
MRCP is listed only as an alternative media-plane mechanism in Section 8.4.
MSRP is mentioned only as an alternative for bulk data transfer, not specified or extended here.
SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY event packages are discussed only as a comparison to Info Packages.
The document defines the Content-Disposition value info-package and uses MIME bodies, but it does not deal with media type registration rules.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate for a protocol extension, not the subject of the document.

RFC6087.title: Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of YANG Data Model Documents
RFC6087.summary: Informational guidelines for authors and reviewers of IETF documents containing YANG data model modules for NETCONF, covering documentation structure, naming, XPath usage, data types, security and IANA sections, with a review checklist and module template.

YANG.why: The whole document gives usage guidelines, a review checklist and a module template for writing YANG modules, so readers of the YANG subject need it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a set of usage guidelines for Standards Track documents containing YANG [RFC6020] data models.

NETCONF.why: The guidelines aim to improve NETCONF interoperability, covering the NETCONF operations and content layers, and the security template covers NETCONF access to the modules. NETCONF is the stated motivation, though the guidance itself concerns YANG.
NETCONF.quote: intended to increase interoperability and usability of Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) implementations that utilize YANG data model modules.

rejected.why: The IANA Considerations guidance covers only registering YANG namespaces and module names, which is a small part of the document, not IANA registry policy in general.
XPath and XML namespaces are mentioned only as they apply inside YANG modules, so the document is not about XML usage in its own right.
The documentation requirements for Internet-Drafts and RFCs are mostly YANG-specific boilerplate rules, so this tag does not fit.
SSH appears only in the security template as the mandatory-to-implement NETCONF transport. It is substrate, not the document's subject.
RFC 4181 (guidelines for MIB documents) is cited as the model for this document, but the document does not address MIB or SMIv2.

RFC6088.title: Traffic Selectors for Flow Bindings
RFC6088.summary: Defines binary IPv4 and IPv6 traffic selector formats (TS Format values 1 and 2) for the traffic selector sub-option of Mobile IPv6 flow bindings defined in RFC 6089.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 flow bindings by defining the binary traffic selector sub-option formats used by the home agent to match packets to a mobile node's bindings.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document defines binary formats for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic selectors to be used in conjunction with flow bindings for Mobile IPv6.

rejected.why: IPv6 header fields (flow label, traffic class, next header) are matched by the selector, but the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
IPv4 header fields are matched, but IPv4 is only the thing being filtered on, not the subject.
The IPsec SPI is just one matchable field, defined in RFC 4303. The document says nothing new about IPsec.
The DS and TC fields are matched, but the document does not address Diffserv itself.
TCP and UDP ports are referenced only as match fields, so TCP is not the subject.
The document itself does not mention NEMO. Only the title of the normative reference RFC 6089 does.

RFC6089.title: Flow Bindings in Mobile IPv6 and Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support
RFC6089.summary: RFC 6089 defines Mobile IPv6/NEMO extensions (flow identification and flow summary mobility options, sub-options) letting a mobile node bind specific traffic flows to specific care-of addresses at home agents, MAPs and correspondent nodes.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 binding updates with new mobility options and processing rules for flow bindings at HAs, MAPs and CNs.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document introduces extensions to Mobile IPv6 that allow nodes to bind one or more flows to a care-of address.

NEMO.why: The extension applies equally to NEMO Basic Support mobile routers, as the title states, with flow bindings for mobile network prefixes.
NEMO.quote: Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support [RFC3963] allow a mobile node / mobile router to manage its mobility using the binding update

rejected.why: ESP and IKEv2 appear only in Security Considerations about anti-replay and parallel SAs; not the subject.
Parent tag is implied by the more specific Mobile IPv6 and NEMO tags.
Multiple care-of addresses motivate the work, but the document specifies flow bindings in Mobile IPv6, not multihoming architecture.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here, not the document's subject.

RFC6090.title: Fundamental Elliptic Curve Cryptography Algorithms
RFC6090.summary: RFC 6090 describes the fundamental elliptic curve cryptography algorithms over prime fields of characteristic greater than three (group operations, ECDH, and KT-I/KT-IV ElGamal-style signatures equivalent to ECDSA), with interoperability notes and validation guidance.

elliptic curve.why: The whole document specifies elliptic curve group arithmetic, parameters, ECDH and elliptic curve signatures, which is the core of the elliptic curve cryptography subject.
elliptic curve.quote: This note contains a description of the fundamental algorithms of ECC over finite fields with characteristic greater than three, based directly on original references.

ECDSA.why: KT-I signatures, a substantial part of the document, are functionally ECDSA and verifiable with ECDSA algorithms, so ECDSA readers would want this RFC.
