ECDSA.quote: KT-I is mathematically and functionally equivalent to ECDSA, and can interoperate with the IEEE [P1363] and ANSI [X9.62] standards

rejected.why: IKE/IKEv2 is mentioned only for interoperability with ECP groups and test vectors; the document does not specify or extend IKE.
SHA-256/384/512 are only recognized as suitable hash functions in the security considerations; the document is not about the SHA family.
Appendix B on random integer generation is brief supporting material and defers to RFC 4086.
RSA appears only via a PKCS#1 reference for octet-string conversion; not a subject of the document.
ECDH is a key agreement primitive described here, but the document is not about key management as a subject area; the specific elliptic curve tag already covers it.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key exchange / ECDH
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Diffie-Hellman or ECDH key agreement. ECDH is a major part of this document (Section 4), but it is only partially covered by the elliptic curve tag.

RFC6091.title: Using OpenPGP Keys for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authentication
RFC6091.summary: Defines a TLS extension (cert_type) and handshake message changes to negotiate and carry OpenPGP certificates for TLS authentication, obsoletes RFC 5081, and updates the IANA registry for non-X.509 certificate types.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS extension (cert_type) and changes to handshake Certificate messages, which is directly about TLS extensions.
TLS.quote: This memo defines Transport Layer Security (TLS) extensions and associated semantics that allow clients and servers to negotiate the use of OpenPGP certificates for a TLS session

OpenPGP.why: OpenPGP keys, subkey IDs and fingerprints are the credential format carried in TLS; readers of OpenPGP usage would want this document.
OpenPGP.quote: This document specifies a way to negotiate the use of OpenPGP certificates for a TLS session, and specifies how to transport OpenPGP certificates via TLS.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the existing default certificate type that the extension coexists with; the document is not about X.509.
Web of trust and certificate verification procedures are explicitly out of scope.
The registry update for TLS Certificate Types is small boilerplate-like content, not the main subject.
Only TLS is discussed; no DTLS-specific content.

RFC6092.title: Recommended Simple Security Capabilities in Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) for Providing Residential IPv6 Internet Service
RFC6092.summary: Informational RFC recommending stateless and stateful packet-filtering behaviours ("simple security") for residential IPv6 gateway CPE, covering ICMPv6, UDP, TCP, SCTP, DCCP, IPsec/IKE, HIP, Mobile IPv6 and Shim6 traversal.

IPv6.why: The document specifies filtering recommendations for residential IPv6 gateways; the IPv6 deployment/CPE subject is its core.
IPv6.quote: recommendations for the makers of devices and describes how to provide for "simple security" capabilities at the perimeter of local-area IPv6 networks

firewall.why: The whole document is a set of stateful and stateless packet-filter recommendations for gateways, i.e. firewall behaviour.
firewall.quote: Stateful packet filters track the state of individual transport flows and prohibit the forwarding of packets that do not match the state of an active flow

NAT.why: Filtering behaviours (endpoint-independent, address-dependent, timeouts) are modelled on NAT behavioural requirements, and passive-listener port mapping is discussed.
NAT.quote: The stateful packet filtering behavior of NAT set user expectations that persist today with residential IPv6 service.

home networking.why: The document targets home and small-office IPv6 gateway CPE and its default configurations.
home networking.quote: residential Internet gateways are assumed to be fairly simple devices with a limited subset of the full range of possible features.

rejected.why: TCP filtering state handling is specified, but TCP itself is not extended or specified; it is a flow type to be filtered.
Only requires the gateway to pass AH/ESP/IKE traffic; IPsec is not specified or profiled.
One filtering subsection; SCTP is not the document's subject.
One filtering subsection; DCCP is not the document's subject.
ICMPv6 forwarding rules appear, but they are incidental to the filtering recommendations.
One recommendation (REC-47) only to forward Shim6 headers; the protocol is not the subject.

RFC6093.title: On the Implementation of the TCP Urgent Mechanism
RFC6093.summary: RFC 6093 analyzes how TCP implementations and middleboxes process the TCP urgent mechanism, updates RFC 793/1011/1122 so the Urgent Pointer points to the octet following urgent data, and advises applications against using urgent indications.

TCP.why: The whole document concerns the TCP urgent mechanism: its semantics, urgent pointer interpretation, implementation practice, and an update to the TCP specifications.
TCP.quote: new applications SHOULD NOT employ the TCP urgent mechanism. However, TCP implementations MUST still include support for the urgent mechanism

rejected.why: SO_OOBINLINE and MSG_OOB are discussed as how implementations expose urgent data, but the document does not specify or extend the sockets API.
Telnet is mentioned only as an example of an application relying on urgent data in Security Considerations.
FTP is mentioned only as an example application relying on urgent data in Security Considerations.
Middleboxes clearing the URG flag are discussed as a reliability issue, but the document is not about firewall mechanisms.
NIDS evasion is cited as motivation and a security implication, not the subject of the document.

RFC6094.title: Summary of Cryptographic Authentication Algorithm Implementation Requirements for Routing Protocols
RFC6094.summary: Informational summary of which cryptographic authentication algorithms (HMAC-MD5, HMAC-SHA family, IPsec AH/ESP algorithms) routing protocols IS-IS, OSPFv2, OSPFv3, RIPv2 and RIPng should implement for interoperability.

routing security.why: The document's whole purpose is securing routing protocol packets via cryptographic authentication algorithm requirements across several routing protocols.
routing security.quote: This document concerns itself with the selection of cryptographic algorithms for use in the authentication of routing protocol packets being exchanged between adjacent routing processes.

OSPF.why: OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 authentication algorithm requirements get dedicated sections.
OSPF.quote: [RFC5709] adds support for the use of the SHA family of hash algorithms for authentication of OSPFv2 packets.

IS-IS.why: IS-IS authentication scheme and algorithm selection is a dedicated section.
IS-IS.quote: [RFC5310] adds support for the use of any cryptographic hash function for authenticating IS-IS PDUs.

RIP.why: RIPv2 and RIPng authentication algorithm requirements are covered in dedicated sections.
RIP.quote: [RFC4822] obsoleted [RFC2082] and added the SHA family of hash algorithms to the list of cryptographic authentications that can be used to protect RIPv2

HMAC.why: The document is largely about migrating from keyed-MD5/HMAC-MD5 to HMAC-SHA and mandating a common HMAC algorithm.
HMAC.quote: there are proposals to replace HMAC-MD5 with keyed HMAC-SHA [SHS] digests

rejected.why: AH and ESP are relied on by OSPFv3 and RIPng; the document only cites their algorithm requirements from RFC 4835 rather than specifying IPsec.
SHA family is the candidate algorithm set but the document does not specify or analyse SHA itself.
MD5 deprecation is motivation, but the document does not discuss MD5 in its own right.
OSPFv3 section is brief and merely defers to IPsec algorithm requirements; parent OSPF tag covers it.
ESP is only cited as the mechanism used by OSPFv3/RIPng.

RFC6095.title: Extending YANG with Language Abstractions
RFC6095.summary: Experimental RFC defining YANG extension statements (complex types with inheritance, abstract types, recursive instances, and typed instance identifiers) to improve model extensibility and reuse in NETCONF data modeling.

YANG.why: The whole document extends the YANG language with complex-type, instance, extends, abstract and instance-type statements, plus a YANG extension module.
YANG.quote: This document defines extensions for the modeling language YANG as new language statements, which introduce language abstractions to improve the model extensibility and reuse.

rejected.why: NETCONF is the management protocol whose payload encoding is affected, but the document is about the YANG modeling language. Only XML encoding and capability advertisement touch NETCONF.
The IPFIX/PSAMP configuration model is used only as an example in Appendix B. The document does not specify or extend IPFIX.
The Entity MIB is a modeling source and example for physical resources, but the document defines YANG extensions, not a MIB module.
XML encoding rules are given for the new constructs, but XML is only the encoding substrate.

RFC6096.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Chunk Flags Registration
RFC6096.summary: RFC 6096 updates RFC 4960 to define the IANA procedure for registering SCTP chunk flags and creates the initial per-chunk-type chunk flag registries.

SCTP.why: The document extends SCTP's chunk extension procedure (updating Section 14.1 of RFC 4960) and defines chunk flag registries for all existing SCTP chunk types, so SCTP readers need it.
SCTP.quote: This document defines the procedure for registering chunk flags with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

rejected.why: The registry procedure is the document's content, but it concerns the SCTP-specific chunk flags registry rather than IANA registry guidance or stewardship in general. The SCTP tag covers it.
It cites the RFC Required and IETF Review policies from RFC 5226 but does not define or change IETF process.

RFC6097.title: Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) Discovery for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6097.summary: Informational RFC describing dynamic ways for a Proxy Mobile IPv6 Mobile Access Gateway to discover a Local Mobility Anchor (via AAA, DNS lookups of constructed FQDNs, and lower-layer data), with handover considerations and a recommendation for AAA-based discovery.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document is about LMA discovery in Proxy Mobile IPv6 deployments, including handover behaviour between MAGs.
PMIPv6.quote: a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) can dynamically discover a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) for a Mobile Node (MN) attaching to a PMIPv6 domain

rejected.why: AAA infrastructure is the main recommended mechanism for delivering the LMA address or FQDN. The document defines no AAA protocol extensions, so it is only a mechanism it relies on.
DNS is used to resolve constructed or received LMA FQDNs. The document adds nothing new about DNS itself, so it is only a substrate.
IKEv2 IDr is given as an example of lower-layer signalling that carries the LMA identity. It is a passing example, not a subject of the document.
RFC 5779 is referenced for the policy store and AAA interaction, but the document does not specify or extend Diameter.
3GPP identities such as IMSI and APN are used as examples of lower-layer data. The document is not about cellular interworking.

RFC6098.title: Generic Notification Message for Mobile IPv4
RFC6098.summary: Defines the Mobile IPv4 Generic Notification Message and Acknowledgement Message (types 22/23), letting HA, FA and MN send asynchronous notifications with a Message String Extension, plus replay protection, retransmission and extensibility rules.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IPv4 with new message types, a Code space, and HA/FA/MN processing rules for notifications.
Mobile IPv4.quote: this document defines a generic notification message and a notification model that can be used by Mobile IPv4 entities to send various notifications.

rejected.why: Only the NTP timestamp format is borrowed for the Identification field; the document is not about NTP.
NEMO prefix changes are mentioned only as an example use; the document does not specify NEMO behaviour.
UDP is just the transport for the messages, which reuse the registration IP/UDP headers.
RADIUS/Diameter triggers between AAA and the FA are explicitly out of scope.
The more specific Mobile IPv4 tag applies, so the parent is not listed.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA registries.

RFC6101.title: The Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Protocol Version 3.0
RFC6101.summary: Historic republication of the SSL 3.0 specification, defining the record layer, handshake, alert and change cipher spec protocols, cipher suites, key derivation and a security analysis.

TLS.why: SSL 3.0 is the direct predecessor of TLS and the document specifies the full protocol (record layer, handshake, cipher suites). Readers of the TLS subject would want this historic specification.
TLS.quote: This document specifies version 3.0 of the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL 3.0) protocol, a security protocol that provides communications privacy over the Internet.

rejected.why: RSA is used as a key exchange and signature algorithm inside SSL, but the document is not about RSA itself.
X.509 certificates are carried in handshake messages but are only a mechanism the protocol relies on, not defined or profiled here.
RC4 appears among the defined cipher suites but is incidental to the protocol specification.
TCP is only the reliable transport substrate beneath the SSL record layer.
MD5 and SHA are used in MAC and key derivation computations but are not the subject of the document.
DES and 3DES appear only as bulk cipher options within cipher suites.

RFC6104.title: Rogue IPv6 Router Advertisement Problem Statement
RFC6104.summary: Informational problem statement describing how rogue (mostly accidental) IPv6 Router Advertisements arise and surveying mitigations such as RA snooping, ACLs, SEND, router preference, host filters, deprecation daemons and DHCPv6 options.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document concerns Router Advertisements, a Neighbor Discovery message, their misconfiguration and mitigation on links.
neighbor discovery.quote: undesired or "bogus" IPv6 RAs appearing on network links or subnets

SEND.why: SEND is evaluated at length as a mitigation, including deployment issues, and is the recurring comparison point in conclusions.
SEND.quote: The SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) [RFC3971] protocol provides a method for hosts and routers to perform secure Neighbor Discovery.

operational security.why: The document gives operators practical guidance on preventing, detecting and recovering from rogue RAs on network infrastructure.
operational security.quote: rogue RAs are an operational issue for which solution(s) are required, and for which best practice needs to be conveyed.

rejected.why: Discussed as a possible alternative (default gateway/prefix options) and in the threat model comparison, but it is not the main subject.
Autoconfiguration is the context in which rogue RAs cause harm, but the document is about RAs and mitigations, not SLAAC itself.
Windows ICS 6to4 gateways are a cause of rogue RAs, but 6to4 itself is not specified or analysed.
The more specific neighbor discovery tag applies, so the IPv6 parent is implied.
Mentioned only in passing as a host that may believe it is multihomed after a rogue RA.

gaps.name: RA-Guard / RA snooping
gaps.why: A major mitigation discussed (layer 2 RA filtering, RFC 6105), but the taxonomy has no specific tag for it.

RFC6105.title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Guard
RFC6105.summary: RFC 6105 describes RA-Guard, a layer-2 device filtering framework (stateless, stateful, and SEND-based) that blocks rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements as a lightweight complement to SEND.

neighbor discovery.why: The document is about filtering rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements, which are Neighbor Discovery messages, at L2 devices. Neighbor discovery is the most specific fitting tag.
neighbor discovery.quote: there is always the risk of facing operational problems due to rogue Router Advertisements (RAs) generated maliciously or unintentionally by unauthorized or improperly configured routers

SEND.why: RA-Guard is positioned as a complement to SEND. Section 4.2 specifies a SEND-based RA-Guard that verifies CGA and signatures and runs CPS/CPA exchanges on behalf of hosts.
SEND.quote: An RA-Guard implementation that SEND-validates RAs on behalf of hosts would potentially simplify some of these challenges.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the general context. The more specific neighbor discovery tag covers the subject.
The L2 devices are generic switches. The document does not specify IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
NTP is only mentioned as something the L2 device may need for certificate validation, and it is not the subject of the document.
Certificates are used by SEND validation, but the document does not profile or discuss X.509.
This is a possible fit for the rogue-RA mitigation theme, but the neighbor discovery and SEND tags cover it more specifically.
RSA is only mentioned as the signature algorithm used in SEND.

RFC6106.title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Options for DNS Configuration
RFC6106.summary: Standards-track document defining two IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement options (RDNSS and DNSSL) that let routers advertise recursive DNS server addresses and a DNS search list to hosts, obsoleting RFC 5006.

neighbor discovery.why: The document specifies two new ND/RA options, their formats, lifetimes and host processing, which is an extension of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: The IPv6 DNS configuration mechanism in this document needs two new ND options in Neighbor Discovery

DNS.why: The payload is DNS resolver configuration (recursive server addresses, search suffixes) and how it feeds the host resolver, so readers of DNS configuration would want it.
DNS.quote: allow IPv6 routers to advertise a list of DNS recursive server addresses and a DNS Search List to IPv6 hosts

rejected.why: Discussed as an alternative and for coexistence and precedence, but the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
Autoconfiguration is the context in which the options are used, but the document does not define or change SLAAC.
SEND is only recommended in the security considerations as a protection for the options.
The broad IPv6 tag is implied by the more specific neighbor discovery tag and the document is not about IPv6 generally.
The IANA section only registers option type 31 and is boilerplate.

RFC6107.title: Procedures for Dynamically Signaled Hierarchical Label Switched Paths
RFC6107.summary: RFC 6107 extends the RSVP-TE LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object with new C-Types, an Actions field and TLVs so LSP endpoints can signal how a hierarchical or stitched LSP is used (TE link, private link, routing adjacency, link bundle), which IGP instance advertises it, and its numbered or unnumbered interface identifiers.

RSVP-TE.why: The document defines new RSVP-TE object C-Types, flags, TLVs and error codes for Path/Resv signaling of hierarchical LSPs. It updates RFC 3477 and RFC 4206.
RSVP-TE.quote: The LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object [RFC3477] is extended for use for all H-LSPs and S-LSPs whether they form numbered or unnumbered IPv4 or IPv6 links.
RSVP-TE.section: 2.1 Common Approach for Numbered and Unnumbered Links

GMPLS.why: The procedures cover GMPLS LSP hierarchy, forwarding adjacencies and multi-layer networks, and update the GMPLS hierarchy specification RFC 4206. GMPLS readers would want this document.
GMPLS.quote: Label Switched Paths (LSPs) set up in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) or Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) networks can be used to form links

rejected.why: MPLS is the general context, but the work is specific to RSVP-TE signaling and GMPLS hierarchy. MPLS is implied as an ancestor of both chosen tags.
The IGPs advertise the resulting links, but the document only identifies IGP instances and defines no OSPF behaviour.
IS-IS is mentioned as an IGP that advertises the TE links. It is not specified or extended here.
RSVP is the base protocol, but the extensions are to RSVP-TE for LSP signaling, not to RSVP QoS reservation.
The document deals with TE links, but the specific technology tag RSVP-TE already sits under this topic.
The IANA registry sections are boilerplate and do not make the document about IANA.

gaps.name: LSP hierarchy / forwarding adjacencies / link bundling
gaps.why: The document is about hierarchical LSPs, forwarding adjacencies and TE link bundles. The taxonomy has no tag for them, so the closest fits are RSVP-TE and GMPLS.

RFC6108.title: Comcast's Web Notification System Design
RFC6108.summary: Informational description of Comcast's deployed system that uses a Squid proxy, an ICAP server and a messaging service to insert critical notices, such as malware-infection warnings, into users' HTTP responses without deep packet inspection.

OPES.why: The whole design is an intermediary (proxy plus ICAP server) adapting HTTP responses to insert content. ICAP RESPMOD content adaptation is the closest fit in the taxonomy, which has no ICAP tag.
OPES.quote: ICAP, an existing IETF protocol, allows for message transformation or adaptation.

operational security.why: The system's purpose is an ISP operational practice of notifying infected customers. The requirements, security considerations and the walled-garden comparison discuss that practice.
operational security.quote: warn them that their traffic exhibits patterns that are indicative of malware or virus infection

rejected.why: HTTP is the content being proxied and modified. The document defines no HTTP extension or semantics.
Diffserv is only used to steer port 80 traffic to the proxy, as a minor mechanism. It is not the subject.
NAT is mentioned only as an option for the load balancer when it forwards traffic to the proxy.
HTML and JavaScript are used only as the payload of the inserted notice.
The document says web content must not be cached. The only caching is of notification messages in the messaging service.

gaps.name: ICAP (Internet Content Adaptation Protocol)
gaps.why: The system is built on ICAP RESPMOD, but the taxonomy has no ICAP tag. OPES is the nearest match.

gaps.name: ISP end-user notification / walled garden
gaps.why: The document is about how ISPs notify customers of malware infection, and compares web notification with walled gardens. No tag covers this.

RFC6109.title: La Posta Elettronica Certificata - Italian Certified Electronic Mail
RFC6109.summary: Informational RFC describing Italy's Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC), a certified email system in which providers sign envelopes and notifications with S/MIME, with its message types, header fields, XML certification data, and an LDAP providers directory.

email.why: The whole document specifies a certified email service: message flow between providers, notifications, envelopes and new mail header fields.
email.quote: Certified electronic mail: A service based on electronic mail, as defined by the [EMAIL] and [SMTP] standards and extensions

S/MIME.why: S/MIME signing of every notification and envelope is central to PEC, and the document defines an S/MIME certificate profile for providers (Section 5.5).
S/MIME.quote: The message is inserted in an S/MIME v3 structure in CMS format and signed with the PEC provider's private key.

LDAP.why: The document defines new LDAP attribute types and object classes for the providers directory and registers them with IANA, which is a substantial part of its content.
LDAP.quote: The PEC providers directory is created through a centralized LDAP server that contains the providers' data and their corresponding PEC mail domains.

rejected.why: SMTP is the transport between providers, and the document only requires SMTP over TLS. It adds no new SMTP extension.
The document registers new header fields, but they are PEC-specific. The document does not specify the Internet message format itself.
XML is only the encoding for the certification data, and the DTD is part of the PEC definition.
A certificate profile is given, but it supports S/MIME signing of PEC messages and is not a general X.509 profile.
TLS is only the secure channel mechanism, and the document defines nothing new about it.

gaps.name: certified/registered email delivery
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for legally binding certified email with delivery receipts. The closest fit is the email tag.

RFC6110.title: Mapping YANG to Document Schema Definition Languages and Validating NETCONF Content
RFC6110.summary: Specifies the mapping of YANG data models to DSDL schemas (RELAX NG, Schematron, DSRL) via an intermediate annotated "hybrid schema", and how to use them to validate NETCONF content.

YANG.why: The whole document defines how every YANG statement maps to DSDL schemas, so readers of YANG will want it.
YANG.quote: This document specifies the mapping rules for translating YANG data models into Document Schema Definition Languages (DSDL)

NETCONF.why: Section 7 and Section 11 describe validating NETCONF datastore contents, RPC replies and notifications using the generated schemas.
NETCONF.quote: Procedures for schema-based validation of such documents are also discussed.

XML.why: The document specifies the use of XML schema languages (RELAX NG, Schematron, DSRL) and an XML annotation vocabulary, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: it is natural to express the constraints on NETCONF content using standard XML schema languages.

rejected.why: SMI/MIB is mentioned only as historical background in the introduction.
The DHCP data model is used only as a worked example in Appendix C.
IANA section only registers two XML namespace URIs and is boilerplate.

gaps.name: DSDL / RELAX NG / Schematron schema languages
gaps.why: The document is substantially about XML schema languages (ISO/IEC 19757), which have no specific tag in the taxonomy; XML is the closest.

RFC6111.title: Additional Kerberos Naming Constraints
RFC6111.summary: Defines well-known Kerberos principal name and realm name types (KRB_NT_WELLKNOWN, WELLKNOWN realm), reserved-name rules, new error codes, and IANA registries, updating RFC 4120.

Kerberos.why: The document extends and updates the Kerberos V5 protocol (RFC 4120) with new principal and realm name types, error codes, and rejection behaviour for KDCs and servers.
Kerberos.quote: A new name type KRB_NT_WELLKNOWN is defined for well-known principal names.

rejected.why: This is about Kerberos principal/realm names, not general naming or name resolution; the Kerberos tag is the more specific fit.
Authentication is the context, but the document is specifically about Kerberos naming constraints and is covered by the Kerberos tag.
The IANA registries are only boilerplate-like section; the main body is about naming rules.
Not discussed; only Kerberos protocol messages are involved.

RFC6112.title: Anonymity Support for Kerberos
RFC6112.summary: Defines Kerberos extensions (anonymous ticket flag and KDC option, anonymous realm/principal, anonymous PKINIT) letting a client obtain anonymous tickets and communicate with services without revealing its identity.

Kerberos.why: The whole document extends Kerberos AS and TGS exchanges with anonymous tickets, a new ticket flag and KDC option, and updates RFC 4120, 4121 and 4556.
Kerberos.quote: This document defines extensions to the Kerberos protocol to allow a Kerberos client to securely communicate with a Kerberos application service without revealing its identity

GSS-API.why: A dedicated section specifies how the anonymous principal maps to GSS-API anonymity and how initiators must check context attributes.
GSS-API.quote: GSS-API defines the name_type GSS_C_NT_ANONYMOUS [RFC2743] to represent the anonymous identity.

privacy.why: The document's goal is client identity privacy, and its security considerations discuss linkability and traffic analysis. It is a Kerberos-specific mechanism, so this tag is secondary.
privacy.quote: the client may wish to authenticate a server and/or protect communications without revealing the client's own identity

rejected.why: Anonymous PKINIT is covered, but it is a Kerberos extension rather than PKI infrastructure.
X.509 certificates are only referenced as an authentication option, and the anonymous PKINIT request omits certificates.
SignedData is used as the PKINIT container with empty signerInfos; the document does not specify anything about CMS.
ASN.1 is only the encoding of the new structures and the DER encoding of PA-PKINIT-KX.
The Kerberos tag already covers this document's authentication subject matter more specifically.

gaps.name: Kerberos
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Kerberos tag in the form needed here. The only entries are 'Kerberos [tech]' under security, which exists, so no gap in practice; listed to flag PKINIT, which has no dedicated tag.

RFC6113.title: A Generalized Framework for Kerberos Pre-Authentication
RFC6113.summary: RFC 6113 defines a generalized framework for Kerberos pre-authentication, including a state model, facilities, key-combining tools, cookie-based KDC state, authentication sets, and the FAST armored tunnel with the encrypted challenge factor.

Kerberos.why: The whole document extends Kerberos (updates RFC 4120) by specifying a pre-authentication framework, FAST, PA-FX-COOKIE, and the encrypted challenge factor.
Kerberos.quote: This document specifies a framework for Kerberos pre-authentication mechanisms.

rejected.why: Kerberos is the more specific tag that fits; the generic authentication topic is implied as the parent.
ASN.1 is only used to define the message structures, so it is notation and not the subject.
Anonymous PKINIT is mentioned only as one way to obtain an armor ticket; the document does not specify it.
PAKE is cited as an example of mechanisms FAST could support, but the document does not specify one.
Key combination (KRB-FX-CF2) serves reply-key strengthening inside Kerberos and is not a general key management subject.

gaps.name: Kerberos
gaps.why: The document is about the Kerberos authentication system, and the taxonomy lists Kerberos under security. However, a Kerberos tag exists in the taxonomy (security > Kerberos), so the id used above is valid and no gap remains.

RFC6114.title: The 128-Bit Blockcipher CLEFIA
RFC6114.summary: Specifies the CLEFIA 128-bit lightweight blockcipher (128/192/256-bit keys): its generalized Feistel structure, F-functions, S-boxes, key schedule, constants and test vectors.

cryptography.why: The whole document specifies a block cipher algorithm. No child tag fits CLEFIA (not AES, DES, etc.), so the parent topic cryptography is used directly.
cryptography.quote: CLEFIA is a 128-bit blockcipher, with key lengths of 128, 192, and 256 bits, which is compatible with the interface of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).

rejected.why: AES is only referenced for interface compatibility and comparison; the document specifies a different cipher.
Constrained devices are mentioned as motivation, but the document defines no IoT protocol or guidance.

gaps.name: Block cipher CLEFIA (lightweight cryptography)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for individual block ciphers or lightweight cryptography other than the named ones (AES, DES, Camellia, ARIA, etc.), so a CLEFIA-specific tag would be needed.

RFC6115.title: Recommendation for a Routing Architecture
RFC6115.summary: IRTF Routing Research Group document surveying proposals for a scalable Internet routing and addressing architecture (LISP, RANGI, Ivip, ILNP, etc.) with critiques and rebuttals, and the chairs' recommendation to pursue Evolution, ILNP and renumbering.

routing architecture.why: The whole document is about routing architecture scalability and the recommendation for future directions.
routing architecture.quote: the Internet routing and addressing architecture is facing challenges in scalability, multihoming, and inter-domain traffic engineering

LISP.why: LISP gets a full section with critique and rebuttal, and many other proposals (Ivip, EEMDP, CRM) are map-and-encap variants of it.
LISP.quote: Implements a locator/identifier separation mechanism using encapsulation between routers at the "edge" of the Internet.

ILNP.why: ILNP has a detailed section and is one of the three areas the chairs recommend the IETF pursue.
ILNP.quote: Provides crisp separation of Identifiers from Locators.

renumbering.why: Renumbering is one of the three recommended work areas.
renumbering.quote: We recommend further work on automating renumbering because even with ILNP, the ability of a domain to change its locators at minimal cost is fundamentally necessary.

multihoming.why: Multihoming scalability is a central goal assessed for every proposal.
multihoming.quote: The Research Group has consensus that the Internet needs to support multihoming in a manner that scales well and does not have prohibitive costs.

rejected.why: Discussed as a comparison point for RANGI and IRON-RANGER but not the subject of the document.
IPv6 is discussed as the target environment for several proposals, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
BGP is the existing routing substrate and used by TIDR and Evolution, but the document is not about BGP.
DNS serves as a mapping system in several proposals, but the document does not specify or analyse DNS.
Encapsulation is used by the map-and-encap proposals, but it is a mechanism rather than the subject.
Mobility is one gain claimed by the proposals, not a primary subject of the document.

gaps.name: Locator/identifier separation (core-edge separation, map-and-encap)
gaps.why: The central theme of the document, covering many proposals beyond LISP and ILNP, has no general taxonomy tag.

RFC6116.title: The E.164 to Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI) Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Application (ENUM)
RFC6116.summary: RFC 6116 specifies the ENUM DDDS application, which maps E.164 telephone numbers to URIs using NAPTR records in the DNS under e164.arpa. It obsoletes RFC 3761 and adds interoperability clarifications for provisioning systems and clients.

ENUM.why: The whole document specifies the ENUM application: the AUS, the First Well Known Rule, the E2U service field, Enumservices, and client and provisioning behaviour.
ENUM.quote: ENUM is designed as a way to translate from E.164 numbers to URIs using NAPTR records stored in DNS.

rejected.why: DNS is the database ENUM runs on. The document defines no new DNS mechanism beyond how NAPTR records are used by this application, which the ENUM tag covers.
DNSSEC appears only in Security Considerations as a recommended mitigation, which is boilerplate.
SIP appears only as an example URI scheme and in the caching-security discussion. The document is not about SIP.
The tel scheme appears only in an Enumservice example (voice:tel). The document does not specify it.
URIs are the output of the ENUM resolution process, and the document specifies nothing about URI syntax or resolution.
The IANA section only records the e164.arpa delegation. Enumservice registration is handled by RFC 6117.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System)
gaps.why: The document is a DDDS application specification, and the taxonomy has no DDDS or NAPTR tag. ENUM is the closest fit.

RFC6117.title: IANA Registration of Enumservices: Guide, Template, and IANA Considerations
RFC6117.summary: RFC 6117 revises the IANA registration procedures for ENUM Enumservices, defines the registration template, classification of Enumservices, expert review process, and guidelines for writing Enumservice Specifications.

ENUM.why: The whole document defines how Enumservices (the service field of ENUM NAPTR records) are specified, classified, and registered, so ENUM readers need it.
ENUM.quote: This document specifies a revision of the IANA registry for Enumservices, which was originally described in [RFC3761].

IANA.why: A large part of the document defines a registry policy, expert review, registration template and change control for the IANA Enumservice Registrations registry.
IANA.quote: "Specification Required", which implies the use of a Designated Expert, according to "Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs" [RFC5226]

rejected.why: NAPTR records in the DNS are the substrate for ENUM. The DNS considerations section is only guidance for Enumservice authors.
URI schemes are named in Enumservice registrations, but the document does not specify or extend URI syntax or schemes.
The tel URI is mentioned only as an example and in loop-mitigation guidance, not specified or extended.
The Enumservice registry is analogous to media type registration, but this document is not about MIME media types.

RFC6118.title: Update of Legacy IANA Registrations of Enumservices
RFC6118.summary: RFC 6118 converts all legacy IANA ENUM Enumservice registrations (email, sms, mms, ems, fax, voice, pstn, sip, h323, pres, im, xmpp, vcard, vpim, web, ft, ical, unifmsg, voicemsg, videomsg) into the new XML-chunk format required by RFC 6117, without changing their functionality.

ENUM.why: The whole document updates the registry of ENUM Enumservices (E.164 numbers in the DNS) and restates each registration, so ENUM readers would look for it.
ENUM.quote: this document revises all Enumservices that were IANA registered under the now obsolete specification of the Enumservice registry defined in RFC 3761

rejected.why: The sip, pstn:sip, and voicemsg:sip Enumservices are only registrations that return sip URIs. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
Many records use the tel URI scheme, but only as a returned URI. The document defines nothing about tel.
This is a registry update, but the registry is the ENUM Enumservice registry, so the more specific ENUM tag fits. The general IANA guidance topic belongs to RFC 6117.
The mailto Enumservices point at email addresses, but email protocols are not specified or changed here.
The im, pres, and xmpp records are only registrations that return URIs of those schemes. The document does not define or change any of the protocols.
The vcard Enumservice record only names vCard as a data type that the returned URI points to. The vCard format is not specified here.

RFC6119.title: IPv6 Traffic Engineering in IS-IS
RFC6119.summary: RFC 6119 defines new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs (IPv6 TE Router ID, IPv6 Interface/Neighbor Address, IPv6 SRLG, IPv6 Global Interface Address) so IS-IS can carry traffic engineering and GMPLS TE information using IPv6 addresses.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS by defining new TLVs and sub-TLVs and rules for processing them in LSPs and IIH PDUs.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies a method for exchanging IPv6 traffic engineering information using the IS-IS routing protocol.

traffic engineering.why: The subject is carrying TE information (TE router ID, link addresses, SRLGs) for IPv6 networks, which traffic engineering readers would want.
traffic engineering.quote: This information enables routers in an IS-IS network to calculate traffic-engineered routes using IPv6 addresses.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 addressing of TE nodes and links and about handling global, unique-local and link-local IPv6 addresses in IS-IS.
IPv6.quote: there is a need to be able to support traffic engineering in IPv6 networks.

GMPLS.why: It defines the IPv6 SRLG TLV, the IPv6 counterpart of the GMPLS SRLG TLV, so GMPLS LSPs can be routed with IPv6 addressing.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines the TLVs that allow traffic engineering information (including Generalized-MPLS (GMPLS) TE information) to be carried in IPv6 IS-IS networks.

rejected.why: MPLS TE is the motivation, but the document specifies IS-IS routing extensions, not MPLS; GMPLS covers the MPLS-side relevance.
The document doesn't specify signalling. It leaves signalling migration out of scope.
Section 6 says there are no migration issues for this routing information, so the document is not about IPv4/IPv6 coexistence mechanisms.
The Security Considerations only point to IS-IS authentication; this is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC6120.title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Core
RFC6120.summary: RFC 6120 specifies the core of XMPP: XML streams, STARTTLS channel encryption, SASL authentication, resource binding, and the message/presence/IQ stanza primitives with error handling, obsoleting RFC 3920.

XMPP.why: The document is the core specification of XMPP, defining streams, stanzas, negotiation and errors.
XMPP.quote: This document defines XMPP's core protocol methods: setup and teardown of XML streams, channel encryption, authentication, error handling, and communication primitives

SASL.why: A full section defines the XMPP SASL profile (service name, initiation, exchange, errors, mechanism preferences), which SASL readers would want.
SASL.quote: XMPP includes a method for authenticating a stream by means of an XMPP-specific profile of the Simple Authentication and Security Layer protocol

rejected.why: STARTTLS is used as the channel-encryption mechanism for XMPP; the document defines the XMPP negotiation wrapper, not new TLS features, so TLS is substrate.
SRV lookup is used for server resolution, but this is use of DNS, not new DNS work.
Instant messaging and presence semantics are defined in RFC 6121 (XMPP-IM); the XMPP tag covers this core document.
XML is the encoding substrate for streams and stanzas; the document is about XMPP, not XML itself.
TCP is only the transport binding for XML streams.
Certificate generation and validation guidance in the Security Considerations is a supporting part, not the document's subject.

RFC6121.title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Instant Messaging and Presence
RFC6121.summary: RFC 6121 specifies the XMPP extensions for instant messaging and presence: roster management, presence subscriptions, presence exchange, message exchange, and server stanza delivery rules, obsoleting RFC 3921.

XMPP.why: The whole document specifies XMPP IM and presence: rosters, subscriptions, presence, messages, and server delivery rules.
XMPP.quote: This document defines extensions to core features of the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) that provide basic instant messaging (IM) and presence functionality

rejected.why: XMPP is the more specific child tag and the document is about XMPP, so the parent is implied.
XMPP presence uses its own stanza format, not PIDF.
SIP presence is mentioned only in a brief comparison of subscription models.
TLS and SASL are substrate mechanisms defined in XMPP Core, not in this document.
XML is the encoding substrate; the document only defines a roster schema in an appendix.
vCards are mentioned only in Appendix C as out of scope.

RFC6122.title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Address Format
RFC6122.summary: Defines the XMPP address format (JID: localpart@domainpart/resourcepart), including internationalization via the Nodeprep and Resourceprep stringprep profiles and Nameprep/IDNA2003 for domainparts, and updates RFC 3920.

XMPP.why: The document specifies the XMPP address (JID) format, a core part of XMPP, and updates RFC 3920.
XMPP.quote: This document defines the format for addresses used in the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP), including support for non-ASCII characters.

internationalization.why: A large part of the document defines the Nodeprep and Resourceprep stringprep profiles and the handling of Unicode, including confusable characters. This is internationalization of text in protocols. The specific tags for Unicode and PRECIS fit less well because the work is stringprep-based.
internationalization.quote: this enables XMPP addresses to include a wide variety of characters outside the US-ASCII range.

rejected.why: Domainparts follow IDNA2003 and Nameprep, but the document only reuses IDNA as a mechanism. It defines nothing new about IDN.

Unicode is the character repertoire the profiles build on. The document is about stringprep profiles for XMPP addresses, not general Unicode usage, so the broader internationalization tag fits better.
DNS is referenced only for FQDN rules and length limits, and for DNSSEC in the security discussion. The document is not about DNS.
The XMPP URI/IRI is mentioned only to say it is not the native address format. It is specified in a different RFC.
The document says PRECIS will eventually replace stringprep, but it does not specify PRECIS.

gaps.name: stringprep
gaps.why: Stringprep profiles (Nodeprep, Resourceprep) are defined here and registered with IANA. The taxonomy has no stringprep tag. The nearest tags are internationalization and PRECIS.

RFC6123.title: Inclusion of Manageability Sections in Path Computation Element (PCE) Working Group Drafts
RFC6123.summary: Historic RFC giving PCE Working Group authors guidance on what to put in Manageability Considerations sections of Internet-Drafts (FCAPS-based subsections), since superseded by RFC 5706.

network management.why: The document is about manageability and operations considerations for new protocols (FCAPS, configuration, liveness monitoring, verifying operation, network impact), which is the network management/operational practice topic.
network management.quote: this document was developed to define recommendations for the inclusion of Manageability Considerations sections in all Internet-Drafts produced within the PCE Working Group

PCE.why: The guidance is specifically scoped to PCE Working Group drafts, so PCE readers would want to find it, though it specifies nothing about PCE/PCEP itself.
PCE.quote: PCE protocols and associated protocols are designed and extended with manageability in mind.

rejected.why: MIB modules are mentioned only as one example of an information/data model; the document does not define or discuss any MIB module in depth.
YANG/NETCONF only appear as alternative management model options in a passing note.
It concerns the content of Internet-Drafts, but only as working-group guidance for manageability sections, not the IETF process itself.
OAM is touched upon in verifying correct operation, but the document is about manageability considerations sections generally, not OAM mechanisms.
The document is about manageability documentation, not operational security practices.

RFC6124.title: An EAP Authentication Method Based on the Encrypted Key Exchange (EKE) Protocol
RFC6124.summary: Defines EAP-EKE, an EAP method for mutual password-based authentication and key derivation built on the Bellovin-Merritt Encrypted Key Exchange, resistant to dictionary attack and not requiring certificates.

EAP.why: The document specifies a new EAP method (type 53), including message formats, exchanges, MSK/EMSK derivation and IANA registries.
EAP.quote: This document defines an authentication mechanism for EAP called EAP-EKE, based on the Encrypted Key Exchange (EKE) protocol.

PAKE.why: The core protocol is a password-authenticated key exchange based on EKE with password-encrypted Diffie-Hellman values and dictionary-attack resistance. No more specific PAKE child tag fits (not SPAKE2, SRP, Dragonfly, OPAQUE or J-PAKE).
PAKE.quote: EAP-EKE is an EAP method [RFC3748] that addresses the problem of password-based authenticated key exchange, using a possibly weak password

rejected.why: Mentioned only for carrying MSK via RFC 2548 attributes; the document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
HMAC is used as the PRF and MAC building block and HKDF construction, but the document is not about HMAC itself.
AES-128-CBC is a mandatory-to-implement algorithm only; the document does not specify AES.
IKEv2 is referenced only for the Diffie-Hellman group definitions; EAP-EKE is not an IKE extension.
EAP-SRP is only cited as a source of borrowed text; this document does not define SRP.
Key derivation of MSK/EMSK is part of the EAP method and PAKE, so the more specific tags cover it.

RFC6125.title: Representation and Verification of Domain-Based Application Service Identity within Internet Public Key Infrastructure Using X.509 (PKIX) Certificates in the Context of Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC6125.summary: RFC 6125 specifies how application services' domain-based identities are represented in PKIX certificates and verified by clients during TLS/DTLS, covering DNS-ID, SRV-ID, URI-ID, CN-ID, wildcards, IDNs and pinning.

X.509.why: The document defines how server identities are encoded in PKIX certificates (subjectAltName, CN) and how clients match them; certificate content and profiling is the core subject.
X.509.quote: specifies recommended procedures for representing and verifying application service identity in certificates intended for use in application protocols employing TLS

TLS.why: Specifies server identity checking during TLS negotiation that TLS-using protocol designers rely on; it is guidance on TLS deployment authentication, not a TLS extension.
TLS.quote: This document applies only to service identities associated with fully qualified DNS domain names, only to TLS and DTLS

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child and fits the certificate-identity subject; the parent is implied.
DNS domain names are the identifier form, but the document explicitly puts DNS resolution out of scope.
DTLS is mentioned in scope only alongside TLS; nothing DTLS-specific is defined.
IDN handling is a small matching rule (U-label to A-label conversion) rather than a main subject.
Parent of nothing chosen here, but the document is specifically about certificate identity, which the X.509 tag covers better.
HTTP and other protocols appear only as examples and prior art in Appendix B.

gaps.name: Service identity verification / certificate name matching (reference and presented identifiers, wildcard certificates)
gaps.why: The central subject has no dedicated tag; X.509 and TLS cover it only approximately.

RFC6126.title: The Babel Routing Protocol
RFC6126.summary: Specifies the Babel routing protocol, a loop-avoiding distance-vector protocol using feasibility conditions and sequenced routes, suited to wired and wireless mesh networks, with its TLV encoding, operation, and metric computation.

Babel.why: The entire document defines the Babel protocol: its conceptual model, operation, TLV encoding, and appendices on metrics and constants.
Babel.quote: Babel is a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol that is robust and efficient both in ordinary wired networks and in wireless mesh networks.

rejected.why: RIP is only mentioned as the naive distance-vector protocol that Babel improves upon; the document is not about RIP.
Babel is suited to wireless mesh networks, but it is not a MANET-WG protocol and the document does not specify MANET routing as such; Babel is the specific tag.
UDP is only the transport for Babel packets and nothing new is defined about its use.
OSPF, IS-IS and EIGRP are mentioned only as alternatives for large stable networks.
AODV is cited only as a source of the sequenced-route technique, not specified or analysed.
Babel carries IPv4 and IPv6 routes, but IPv6 is not itself the document's subject.

RFC6127.title: IPv4 Run-Out and IPv4-IPv6 Co-Existence Scenarios
RFC6127.summary: Informational overview of five IPv4 run-out and IPv4/IPv6 co-existence deployment scenarios (NAT444, distributed NAT, IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnelling/dual-stack lite, NAT64-style translation) that motivated Behave and Softwire rechartering.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document is about IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and transition scenarios and the tools needed for them.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document provides an overview of deployment scenarios with the goal of helping to understand what types of additional tools the industry needs to assist in IPv4 and IPv6 co-existence and transition.

CGN.why: A substantial part covers NAT444 and distributed NAT using a carrier-grade NAT to cope with insufficient public IPv4 addresses.
CGN.quote: This new address translation node has been termed a "Carrier Grade NAT", or CGN

DS-Lite.why: Section 2.2 describes IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnelling to a CGN, i.e. the dual-stack lite model, which led to Softwire work.
DS-Lite.quote: In [DUAL-STACK-LITE], this is referred to as "dual-stack lite", bowing to the fact that it is dual-stack at the gateway, but not at the network.

NAT64.why: Sections 2.3-2.5 discuss IPv6-to-IPv4 translation with NAT64 and DNS64 as the approach for several scenarios.
NAT64.quote: One approach to implement this is to use NAT64 to translate IPv6 into private IPv4 addresses.

rejected.why: NAT is discussed throughout, but the more specific CGN, DS-Lite and NAT64 tags capture it; CGN is the NAT-specific child chosen.
Softwire WG is mentioned as rechartered, but the document does not specify softwire mechanisms.
DNS64 is only referenced in passing as part of the NAT64 approach.
Tunnels are used as a design element but the document is not about tunnelling in general.
IPv4 address exhaustion is the motivation, but the document's subject is coexistence/transition rather than IPv4 address lifecycle per se.
Mentioned only once as one way for a client to get IPv6 reachability.

RFC6128.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Port for Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) Sessions
RFC6128.summary: Defines a new SDP attribute, 'multicast-rtcp', letting the distribution source of an RTP source-specific multicast session choose the RTCP port freely instead of deriving it from the m= line by the +1 rule, updating RFC 5760.

SDP.why: The document's core contribution is a new SDP attribute with ABNF syntax, an example, and an IANA registration in the SDP attribute registry.
SDP.quote: this document defines a new SDP attribute, called 'multicast-rtcp'.

RTCP.why: It changes how the RTCP port is selected and signalled for multicast RTCP sessions, updating RTCP extensions for SSM (RFC 5760).
RTCP.quote: the distribution source uses a desired port for the SSM RTCP session.

SSM.why: The attribute applies specifically to RTP-based source-specific multicast sessions and updates the SSM RTCP specification, so SSM readers would want it.
SSM.quote: In RTP-based SSM sessions, the distribution source can use different multicast RTP and RTCP ports

rejected.why: RTP is the underlying media transport. The document is about the RTCP port signalling, which is covered by the more specific RTCP tag.
ABNF is only used to write the attribute syntax, so it is not a subject of the document.
S/MIME is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the SDP, which is boilerplate.
The document concerns port selection in multicast sessions and has nothing to do with NAT traversal.

RFC6129.title: The 'application/tei+xml' Media Type
RFC6129.summary: Registers the 'application/tei+xml' media type for Text Encoding and Initiative (TEI) XML documents, describing how to recognize TEI files, their fragment identifiers, and security considerations.

media types.why: The document exists to register a new media type, including recognition rules, fragment identifier handling and the registration template.
media types.quote: This document defines the 'application/tei+xml' media type for markup languages defined in accordance with the Text Encoding and Interchange guidelines.

XML.why: The media type covers an XML-based format and follows the +xml convention of RFC 3023. The document describes TEI namespaces, root elements and XML fragment identifier handling.
XML.quote: TEI files are XML documents or fragments having the root element (as defined in [W3C.REC-xml-20081126]) in a TEI namespace.

rejected.why: URIs and IRIs appear only in the namespace name and in security references. They are not the subject of the document.
The IANA registration is the media type template, which is covered by the media types tag. The document gives no guidance on IANA registries in general.
The IPR discussion appears only in Security Considerations, as an aspect of TEI content. The document is not about IPR provisions.
The document uses UTF-8 in its examples and mentions the charset parameter, but internationalization is not a subject of the document.

RFC6130.title: Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP)
RFC6130.summary: RFC 6130 specifies NHDP, a HELLO-message-based protocol that lets MANET routers discover 1-hop and symmetric 2-hop neighbors, with its information bases, message processing, and link quality handling.

NHDP.why: The whole document specifies NHDP: HELLO messages, Link/2-Hop/Neighbor Sets, processing rules and parameters.
NHDP.quote: This document describes a neighborhood discovery protocol (NHDP) for a mobile ad hoc network (MANET) [RFC2501].

rejected.why: NHDP sits under MANET, so the parent is implied; the child tag is more specific.
NHDP is derived from OLSR's neighborhood discovery but is a separate protocol; OLSR is only background.
Packets may be sent over the manet UDP port, but this is only a transport substrate.
The IANA section registers message and TLV types, which is boilerplate for this document.

RFC6131.title: Sieve Vacation Extension: "Seconds" Parameter
RFC6131.summary: Defines the Sieve "vacation-seconds" extension, adding a ":seconds" parameter to the Sieve Vacation action so auto-replies to the same sender can be limited at sub-day granularity, including zero.

Sieve.why: The document extends the Sieve email filtering language's Vacation extension, specifying the new parameter, its value range, capability string and examples.
Sieve.quote: This extension defines a ":seconds" parameter to provide more granularity for such situations.

rejected.why: Auto-replies are email, but the document specifies only a Sieve extension. Sieve is the more specific tag.
Security considerations mention the volume of auto-replies, but the document is not about spam filtering or reporting.
The only IANA content is the registration of the capability name, which is boilerplate.

RFC6132.title: Sieve Notification Using Presence Information
RFC6132.summary: Extends the Sieve Notification extension by registering presence items (busy, show, status) that can be tested with notify_method_capability, so Sieve scripts can tailor mail notifications to a user's presence.

Sieve.why: The document is a Sieve extension that defines new notification-capability items for the notify_method_capability test. Sieve readers would want it.
Sieve.quote: This is a further extension to the Sieve mail filtering language Notification extension, defining presence information that may be checked through the notify_method_capability feature.

instant messaging.why: The document defines presence items (busy, show, status) modelled on XMPP/PIDF presence and tests them in scripts. Presence is a substantial part of the subject, but the document does not specify a presence protocol.
instant messaging.quote: it is not the intent that this extension be tied to XMPP, nor to any particular source of presence

rejected.why: XMPP only supplies the model for the show and status items and the URIs in the examples. The document does not specify or extend XMPP.
PIDF is cited only as an informative reference for presence data formats. The document does not define or extend it.
Sieve is an email filtering language, but this document is about the Sieve extension, not email architecture or transport. The Sieve tag covers it.

RFC6133.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Use of Presence Information with Auto-Responder Functionality
RFC6133.summary: Informational RFC describing how Sieve and its extensions (Vacation, Notify, Notify-presence, External-lists, Vacation-seconds) can be combined to generate auto-replies based on recipient presence and address book membership, with example scripts.

Sieve.why: The whole document is about using the Sieve filtering language and its extensions (vacation, enotify, extlists) to build auto-responders, with example Sieve scripts.
Sieve.quote: can be used to generate automatic replies to incoming electronic mail messages based on the presence information of the recipient

rejected.why: Presence information is the input to the scripts, but the document does not specify presence or IM. It uses presence via the Sieve notify extension.
The examples use xmpp: URIs as the notification method, but XMPP is only the substrate for presence lookup and is not specified or extended here.
The parent of Sieve, which is implied. The document is about the more specific Sieve filtering language.
The address book is referenced only through Sieve external lists. No contact data format is discussed.
Presence data format is not discussed. Presence is accessed through the Sieve notify capability.

RFC6134.title: Sieve Extension: Externally Stored Lists
RFC6134.summary: RFC 6134 defines the Sieve "extlists" extension, adding a :list match type and a :list argument to redirect for checking membership in or redirecting to externally stored lists, plus the "addrbook" Sieve URN parameter, a valid_ext_list test, and a ManageSieve capability.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies a new Sieve extension (capability "extlists") with a new match type, redirect argument and test.
Sieve.quote: This document defines a Sieve extension for accessing externally stored lists -- lists whose members are stored externally to the script

rejected.why: LDAP is only one example of a backing store for lists; the document does not specify or extend it.
It defines an "addrbook" Sieve URN parameter and registers a sieve sub-namespace, but this is a small supporting part of the Sieve extension, not a general URN namespace specification.
CardDAV and address books are mentioned only as possible list stores; the document does not address vCard or CardDAV.
ACAP is merely named as a possible external list store.
Sieve is the more specific tag, and the document is about the filtering language rather than email in general.
URIs are used for naming lists, but the document only uses existing URI syntax and the tag scheme and does not define a URI scheme.

RFC6135.title: An Alternative Connection Model for the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)
RFC6135.summary: Defines an alternative MSRP connection model using SDP COMEDIA (a=setup) so UAs behind NATs can negotiate which endpoint opens the TCP connection, easing NAT traversal.

MSRP.why: The document specifies a new connection model for MSRP, modifying how MSRP UAs establish transport connections.
MSRP.quote: This document defines how an MSRP UA uses COMEDIA in order to negotiate which UA will create the MSRP transport TCP connection towards the other UA.

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document defines usage of SDP a=setup and a=connection attributes in offers and answers for MSRP.
SDP.quote: An MSRP UA uses the SDP a=setup attribute [RFC4145] in order to negotiate which endpoint will create the MSRP transport connection towards the other UA.

NAT traversal.why: The motivation and much of the guidance (when to use actpass vs active, NAT detection, ICE interplay) concerns NAT traversal for real-time media.
NAT traversal.quote: allows MSRP UAs behind Network Address Translators (NATs) to negotiate which endpoint initiates the establishment of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection

rejected.why: SIP carries the SDP offer/answer and is only used for NAT detection hints; the document does not specify SIP.
TCP is the transport whose connection direction is negotiated; nothing new is defined about TCP itself.
Section 4.3 only says to use TLS as defined in RFC 4975/4976; no new TLS mechanism.
ICE is mentioned as an alternative NAT traversal mechanism, not specified or profiled here.
STUN is mentioned only as one way to determine a reachable address.
MSRP is covered by its own child tag, which is more specific.

RFC6136.title: Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Requirements and Framework
RFC6136.summary: Informational framework and requirements document for OAM (fault and performance management) across L2VPN services (VPLS, VPWS), pseudowires and PSN tunnels, using layered OAM domains with MEPs and MIPs.

OAM.why: The whole document defines the OAM framework (layering, domains, MEPs/MIPs) and OAM requirements for fault and performance management.
OAM.quote: This document provides framework and requirements for Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM).

VPLS.why: Large parts of the document give the OAM framework (Section 5) and requirements (Sections 7 and 9) for VPLS, including (V)LAN emulation.
VPLS.quote: VPLS is a bridged LAN service provided to a set of CEs that are members of a VPN.

L2VPN.why: The document covers OAM for L2VPN services generally, including VPWS and IPLS, and gives its own VPWS framework (Section 6) and requirements (Section 8). L2VPN is the parent that covers VPWS, which has no tag of its own.
L2VPN.quote: VPWS is a point-to-point service where Customer Edges (CEs) are presented with point-to-point virtual circuits.

pseudowire.why: The document identifies PW OAM requirements imposed by L2VPN services, and PWs are central to the VPWS and VPLS reference models.
pseudowire.quote: PW OAM for PWs related to a (V)LAN emulation MUST allow detection of a partial-mesh failure condition.

rejected.why: IEEE 802.1ag and Y.1731 Ethernet OAM are leveraged and referenced as candidate mechanisms, but the document defines requirements and a framework, not Ethernet OAM itself.
MPLS/IP is the underlying network and PSN OAM is explicitly out of scope.
BFD is mentioned only as an example of a native OAM mechanism that could be used for segment monitoring.
Frame loss, delay and delay variation requirements are included, but they sit within the L2VPN OAM requirements rather than being a separate subject.
The more specific VPLS and L2VPN tags fit better than the generic VPN parent.

gaps.name: VPWS (Virtual Private Wire Service)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no VPWS tag, so VPWS OAM is covered only by the L2VPN tag.

RFC6137.title: The Network Trouble Ticket Data Model (NTTDM)
RFC6137.summary: Defines the Network Trouble Ticket Data Model (NTTDM), an XML/UML data model and schema for normalizing and exchanging network trouble tickets among NOCs in a Grid (EGEE).

XML.why: The document's core deliverable is an XML representation and XML Schema (Section 6) of the trouble ticket data model, with its own namespace.
XML.quote: XML is used as the common representation language.

rejected.why: Datetime fields use RFC 3339 only as a data type; the document does not address date-time formats.
Trouble ticketing is an NOC operational topic, but the document is mainly a data model. It is not about network management architecture or protocols, so XML is the better fit.
The IANA section only registers an XML namespace and schema URN. That is boilerplate.
SOAP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible exchange mechanism, and the taxonomy has no SOAP tag.

gaps.name: Trouble ticket / NOC incident data exchange
gaps.why: The document is about trouble ticket normalization across network operation centres. The taxonomy has no tag for trouble ticketing or operational incident data models.

RFC6138.title: LDP IGP Synchronization for Broadcast Networks
RFC6138.summary: RFC 6138 updates RFC 5443 by defining a mechanism for LDP-IGP synchronization on broadcast networks, where a router withholds advertising its pseudonode link in OSPF/IS-IS LSAs until LDP is operational with all peers, unless the interface is a cut-edge.

LDP.why: The document is about LDP-IGP synchronization, specifying when a link is advertised until LDP is operational. It is the LDP-related subject page for this RFC and no more specific tag exists for IGP sync.
LDP.quote: This document complements [LDP-IGP-SYNC] by providing a solution to achieve LDP IGP synchronization for broadcast networks.

OSPF.why: The mechanism specifies concrete OSPF behaviour (Router-LSA link-type 2 updates, SPF cut-edge computation), so OSPF readers would want it.
OSPF.quote: If the IGP is [OSPF], the Router-LSA is not updated with a "Link Type 2" (link to transit network) for that subnet until LDP is operational

IS-IS.why: The document specifies IS-IS LSP/TLV update behaviour for the pseudonode link, so it applies to IS-IS as well.
IS-IS.quote: if the IGP is [IS-IS], the "Link State PDU" is updated with an "IS Reachability TLV" (or an "Extended IS Reachability TLV")

rejected.why: LDP is a child of MPLS and is the more specific tag; the document is about LDP signalling, not general MPLS.
VPN traffic is only the example of what gets black-holed; the document does not address VPNs.
The document deals with specific IGP behaviour rather than general routing architecture.

gaps.name: LDP-IGP synchronization
gaps.why: The document's main subject is a specific LDP/IGP interaction. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag, so the LDP tag is the closest fit.

RFC6139.title: Routing and Addressing in Networks with Global Enterprise Recursion (RANGER) Scenarios
RFC6139.summary: Informational use-case document showing how the RANGER map-and-encapsulate architecture (VET, SEAL) applies to routing scaling, enterprise, SOHO, IPv4/IPv6 transition, mobility/MANET and provider scenarios.

routing architecture.why: The document is about a scalable routing and addressing architecture (EID/RLOC separation, recursive enterprise overlays) and DFZ scaling, illustrated through scenarios.
routing architecture.quote: RANGER presents a core/edge separation architecture within this taxonomy that uniquely shows applicability from the core all the way out to edge networks

IPv6 transition.why: A whole scenario section covers IPv4/IPv6 coexistence, translation and encapsulation, including NAT-PT-equivalent and BIS translation.
IPv6 transition.quote: RANGER (with VET and SEAL) makes it possible to carry packets originated in one protocol across a network infrastructure supporting another protocol or routing system.

tunneling.why: The overlay is built from IP-in-IP automatic tunnelling between enterprise border routers, a core element of every scenario.
tunneling.quote: This enterprise network structure uses border routers that configure tunnel endpoints to connect potentially recursively nested networks.

IP mobility.why: Global mobility for aircraft and MANET scenarios is a substantial part, contrasted with Mobile IP home agents.
IP mobility.quote: mobile nodes or mobile routers (that connect arbitrarily complex edge networks or enterprise networks) can move between different points of attachment while remaining reachable

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a compatible map-and-encap scheme, not specified or analysed.
Used as a possible mapping-system synchronisation mechanism and for DFZ growth context, not the subject.
MANET scenarios are use cases of RANGER, but the document does not address MANET routing protocols themselves.
NAT and CGN appear in scenarios as coexisting mechanisms, not as the subject.
Cited only as historical lineage of the architectural principles.
ATN OSI/CLNP encapsulation is a brief example within one scenario, not a main subject.

gaps.name: RANGER / VET / SEAL (map-and-encapsulate enterprise recursion architecture)
gaps.why: The document's central technology family has no dedicated tag; closest are routing architecture and tunneling.

RFC6140.title: Registration for Multiple Phone Numbers in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6140.summary: RFC 6140 defines a SIP REGISTER extension (the 'gin' option tag and 'bnc' Contact URI parameter) letting a SIP-PBX register in bulk with a service provider for many E.164 phone-number AORs, including GRUU and registration-event interactions.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP REGISTER with a new option tag, URI parameters and Contact parameter, and specifies registrar and proxy behaviour and interactions with GRUU, reg-event, Outbound and Path.
SIP.quote: a SIP server acting as a traditional Private Branch Exchange (PBX) can register with a SIP Service Provider (SSP) to receive phone calls for SIP User Agents

rejected.why: Phone numbers appear only as E.164 user parts of SIP URIs; the tel URI scheme is only referenced in the requirements appendix.
HMAC is used as a building block for temp-GRUU construction, not the subject of the document.
RSA encryption is used inside the temp-GRUU construction only as a mechanism.
The registration event package is discussed for interaction behaviour, but the document is not about SIMPLE event packages as such.
It addresses SIP trunking of phone numbers between a PBX and provider, but there is no PSTN interworking or gateway control.
The mechanism is designed to avoid reliance on DNS entries; it does not specify DNS behaviour.

RFC6141.title: Re-INVITE and Target-Refresh Request Handling in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6141.summary: RFC 6141 updates RFC 3261 by specifying how a SIP UAS should respond (success vs. error) to re-INVITEs, how target-refresh requests update dialog targets, and how UAs recover when they lose their contact during a re-INVITE.

SIP.why: The whole document updates SIP core procedures (RFC 3261) for re-INVITE handling, target refresh and dialog contact loss.
SIP.quote: this document defines in which situations a UAS (User Agent Server) should generate a success response and in which situations a UAS should generate an error response to a re-INVITE.

rejected.why: SDP is used in examples and offer/answer is referenced, but the document does not specify or extend SDP; it is the payload.
ICE is mentioned only in passing as connectivity checks that do not count as media.
RTCP is mentioned only as a reason to use a null IP address rather than inactive streams.
A UA changing IP address is the motivating scenario, but the document addresses SIP dialog target handling, not IP-layer mobility.

RFC6142.title: ANSI C12.22, IEEE 1703, and MC12.22 Transport Over IP
RFC6142.summary: Informational RFC defining how ANSI C12.22/IEEE 1703/MC12.22 smart-metering (AMI) application-layer messages are carried over IP, covering native address encoding, port 1153, UDP/TCP transport modes, and multicast groups.

IoT.why: The document maps a smart-grid metering protocol onto IP. No more specific IoT tag fits, so the IoT parent topic is the best subject for AMI/meter communication.
IoT.quote: framework for transporting ANSI C12.22/IEEE 1703/MC12.22 Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) Application Layer Messages on an IP network

transport mapping.why: The document is a binding of an application protocol onto TCP and UDP. It specifies the port, the active/passive open modes, and how responses choose a transport.
transport mapping.quote: This RFC defines the requirements governing the transmission of ANSI C12.22 Messages via the TCP and UDP transports in IP networks

multicast.why: A substantial part of the document covers multicast: the IANA-assigned groups, IPv6 scoping, IGMP/MLD requirements, and PIM-SM on routers. Readers of multicast deployment would want it.
multicast.quote: all C12.22 IP Relays and Master Relays SHALL support IP multicast

rejected.why: UDP is a substrate here. The document specifies how C12.22 uses it and does not extend UDP itself.
TCP is only the transport used. Connection modes are defined for C12.22 nodes, and TCP itself is not extended or analysed.
It is only a router requirement mentioned in passing in the multicast section.
IPv6 addressing and scoped multicast addresses appear, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The port and multicast address assignments are boilerplate IANA considerations, not guidance about the IANA registries.
BER encoding of the ACSE messages is only referenced as a dependency.

gaps.name: Smart grid / Advanced Metering Infrastructure (ANSI C12.22)
gaps.why: The document is about utility metering protocols over IP. The taxonomy has no smart-metering or smart-grid tag, so the IoT parent is only an approximate fit.

RFC6143.title: The Remote Framebuffer Protocol
RFC6143.summary: Specifies the Remote Framebuffer (RFB) protocol, used by VNC, for remote viewing and control of a graphical desktop, covering handshake, security types, input and display messages, pixel encodings, and IANA registries.

applications.why: The document defines a complete application-layer protocol for remote graphical desktop access. No more specific taxonomy tag fits, so the general applications topic is used.
applications.quote: RFB ("remote framebuffer") is a simple protocol for remote access to graphical user interfaces.

rejected.why: RFB only borrows X11 keysym values for KeyEvent. It is not the X protocol, and it works at the framebuffer level for all windowing systems.
ZRLE encoding uses zlib compression as a substrate. The document defines nothing new about zlib.
RFB usually runs over TCP port 5900, but TCP is only the transport.
IPsec is only mentioned as an optional way to protect sessions.
SSH is only mentioned as an optional way to protect sessions.
VNC Authentication uses DES for its challenge-response, but only as a mechanism within the security type. The document does not address DES itself.

gaps.name: RFB / VNC remote desktop (remote framebuffer access)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for remote desktop or remote display protocols. Readers looking for VNC/RFB would need one.

RFC6144.title: Framework for IPv4/IPv6 Translation
RFC6144.summary: Informational framework document for IPv4/IPv6 translation (replacing NAT-PT), describing eight deployment scenarios, stateless vs stateful translation, and the related document set (address mapping, SIIT, NAT64, DNS64, FTP ALG).

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document frames translation as a coexistence and transition mechanism, with scenarios and a transition plan.
IPv6 transition.quote: This note describes a framework for IPv4/IPv6 translation. This is in the context of replacing NAT-PT

NAT64.why: A substantial part covers stateful translation (NAT64, RFC 6146) and where it applies across the scenarios.
NAT64.quote: For stateful translation, the translation state is maintained between IPv4 address/port pairs and IPv6 address/port pairs

SIIT.why: Stateless translation based on SIIT is one of the two operating modes the framework analyses.
SIIT.quote: The IPv4/IPv6 translator is based on the update to the Stateless IP/ ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT) described in [RFC2765].

DNS64.why: DNS64/DNS46 is a framework component and appears in every scenario figure.
DNS64.quote: DNS64 [RFC6147] and possible future DNS46 documents describe the mechanisms by which a DNS translator is intended to operate.

rejected.why: DNS appears only through DNS64/DNS46 translators, which are tagged more specifically.
FTP is mentioned only as an example application needing an ALG, and the document is not about FTP.
NAT-PT is discussed as the deprecated predecessor, but the document is about translation for transition, which is covered by the IPv6 transition tags.
6to4, Teredo, ISATAP and DS-Lite are cited only as tunnelling alternatives in the motivation.
The IPv6 transition tag fits more specifically than the parent IPv6 tag.

RFC6145.title: IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm
RFC6145.summary: RFC 6145 specifies the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT), defining how IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP messages, are translated by an XLAT, and obsoletes RFC 2765.

SIIT.why: The document is the SIIT specification itself, defining header, ICMP and fragment translation in both directions.
SIIT.quote: the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT), which translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers (including ICMP headers)
