ICMP.why: A large part of the document specifies ICMPv4/ICMPv6 type, code, pointer and error-message translation.
ICMP.quote: ICMPv4 packets require special handling in order to translate the content of ICMPv4 error messages and also to add the ICMPv6 pseudo-header checksum.

PMTUD.why: Path MTU discovery, DF-bit handling, fragmentation and the Packet Too Big special considerations (Section 6) are substantial parts.
PMTUD.quote: handling the maximum packet size is critical for the operation of the IPv4/IPv6 translator.

rejected.why: Stateful translation is defined in RFC 6146; this document covers the stateless algorithm and only references stateful mode.
IPv6 is a protocol being translated, but the more specific IPv6 transition SIIT tag covers it; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
The parent of SIIT is implied by the more specific tag.
TCP checksum handling is mentioned only incidentally; the document does not specify TCP.
Only discussed in Security Considerations as incompatibility with AH/ESP.

RFC6146.title: Stateful NAT64: Network Address and Protocol Translation from IPv6 Clients to IPv4 Servers
RFC6146.summary: Specifies stateful NAT64, which translates IPv6 packets to IPv4 and back for TCP, UDP and ICMP using binding and session tables, so IPv6-only clients can reach IPv4 servers (used together with DNS64).

NAT64.why: The whole document specifies stateful NAT64: BIBs, session tables, TCP state machine, address allocation, hairpinning and filtering.
NAT64.quote: This document specifies stateful NAT64, a mechanism for IPv4-IPv6 transition and IPv4-IPv6 coexistence.

rejected.why: DNS64 is the companion mechanism specified in RFC 6147. This document only refers to it for synthesising AAAA records.
NAT64 is the more specific child tag. The document follows the NAT behavioural requirements (RFC 4787, 5382, 5508), but it specifies NAT64 rather than generic NAT.
The header translation algorithm is in RFC 6145 and is only referenced here.
TCP is the traffic being translated. The state machine tracks TCP connections but does not extend TCP.
ICMP queries and errors are translated, but the document does not specify ICMP itself.
This is the parent of NAT64, so it is implied by the NAT64 tag.

RFC6147.title: DNS64: DNS Extensions for Network Address Translation from IPv6 Clients to IPv4 Servers
RFC6147.summary: RFC 6147 specifies DNS64, a mechanism that synthesizes AAAA records from A records for use with IPv6/IPv4 translators such as NAT64, including DNSSEC interaction, PTR handling, and deployment scenarios.

DNS64.why: The document is the specification of DNS64: synthesis algorithm, PTR handling, resolver modes and deployment.
DNS64.quote: DNS64 is a mechanism for synthesizing AAAA records from A records.

DNSSEC.why: A substantial part (Section 3, 5.5, 6.2) specifies how validating DNS64 resolvers handle DO/CD/AD bits and validation, which DNSSEC readers need.
DNSSEC.quote: DNSSEC is designed to detect changes to DNS answers, and DNS64 may alter answers coming from an authoritative server.

rejected.why: The document works with a NAT64 translator but specifies only the DNS side; NAT64 itself is in RFC 6146.
DNS64 is part of the transition toolbox, but the more specific DNS64 tag covers it, and the parent is implied.
Dynamic DNS updates are mentioned only as a deployment scenario in Section 7.3, not specified.
EDNS0 is mentioned only in passing regarding response handling.
DNS is the substrate; the more specific DNS64 child tag is used.

RFC6148.title: DHCPv4 Lease Query by Relay Agent Remote ID
RFC6148.summary: RFC 6148 extends DHCPv4 Leasequery (RFC 4388) with a new query type, query by Relay Agent Remote ID, so relay agents such as DSLAMs can fetch consolidated lease information for a circuit after a reboot.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 Leasequery with a new query type. It defines how the DHCPLEASEQUERY message is built, answered and processed, and it updates RFC 4388.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a new query type based on the Remote ID sub-option.

rejected.why: A DSLAM is used as the example relay agent, but the document specifies a DHCP mechanism and not DSL access networks.
The document covers DHCPv4 only.

RFC6149.title: MD2 to Historic Status
RFC6149.summary: RFC 6149 retires the MD2 message digest algorithm by moving RFC 1319 to Historic status, explaining the cryptanalytic reasons and the minimal impact on RFCs that reference MD2.

MD5.why: The MD5 tag covers MD5 and the MD2/MD4 message digests. This document is entirely about retiring MD2, its attacks, and its deprecation.
MD5.quote: This document retires MD2.  Specifically, this document moves RFC 1319 [MD2] to Historic status.

rejected.why: SHA-1 and SHA-256 are only named as preferred replacements. The document is not about them.
RFC 3279 is listed as one of the RFCs that reference MD2. The document does not address the certificate profile.
TLS appears only as context for where MD2 support was dropped (TLS 1.1).
HMAC-MD2 is mentioned briefly, as a use of MD2 in RFC 2660 and as a key-leakage concern. It is not a subject of the document.
RFC 2660 is one of the documents that referenced MD2, and the document notes it was supplanted by HTTP over TLS. It is a side mention only.
Moving an RFC to Historic is a status action. The document is about the algorithm's weaknesses, not about process.

RFC6150.title: MD4 to Historic Status
RFC6150.summary: Informational RFC that retires RFC 1320 by moving the MD4 message-digest algorithm to Historic status, explaining the cryptanalytic attacks and the impact on RFCs that reference MD4.

MD5.why: The document is about the MD4 message digest algorithm, which the taxonomy groups under the MD5 tag (MD5 and the MD2/MD4 message digests). It moves RFC 1320 to Historic and discusses collision and pre-image attacks.
MD5.quote: MD4 [MD4] is a message digest algorithm that takes as input a message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit "fingerprint"

rejected.why: HMAC-MD4 attacks are discussed in one subsection, but the document is about retiring MD4, not HMAC.
Kerberos 5 encryption types that use MD4 are listed as an impact. The document does not specify or extend Kerberos.
One-time password systems (S/KEY, RFC 2289) are listed as users of MD4. They are affected documents, not the subject.
RC4-HMAC for Windows is mentioned only as an impact of moving MD4 to Historic.
PKCS #1 appears only as a referencing document that discusses MD4.
The document changes a document's status to Historic, but it does so to retire a cryptographic algorithm, not to describe process.

RFC6151.title: Updated Security Considerations for the MD5 Message-Digest and the HMAC-MD5 Algorithms
RFC6151.summary: RFC 6151 updates the security considerations of MD5 (RFC 1321) and HMAC-MD5 (RFC 2104), summarising collision and HMAC cryptanalysis and advising against MD5 for digital signatures and in new HMAC-MD5 designs.

MD5.why: The whole document revises the security considerations of MD5 and HMAC-MD5, covering collision, pre-image and HMAC attacks and giving guidance on continued use.
MD5.quote: MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required such as digital signatures.

HMAC.why: A substantial section analyses HMAC/NMAC-MD5 cryptanalysis and recommends alternatives such as HMAC-SHA256 for new designs. It updates the security considerations of RFC 2104.
HMAC.quote: The attacks on HMAC-MD5 do not seem to indicate a practical vulnerability when used as a message authentication code.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA256 is only named as a recommended alternative; the document is not about the SHA family.
APOP in POP is mentioned once as an example of a collision attack's reach, but the document is not about POP3.
X.509 certificate collision attacks are cited as evidence only; the document does not address certificates.
The more specific MD5 and HMAC tags apply, so the parent topic is implied.

RFC6152.title: SMTP Service Extension for 8-bit MIME Transport
RFC6152.summary: Defines the SMTP 8BITMIME service extension (EHLO keyword 8BITMIME and the BODY parameter on MAIL) allowing relay of MIME content with 8-bit octets, obsoleting RFC 1652.

SMTP.why: The document specifies an SMTP service extension: EHLO keyword 8BITMIME and the BODY parameter on MAIL, with client and server behaviour.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP service whereby an SMTP content body consisting of text containing octets outside of the US-ASCII octet range

MIME.why: The extension exists to transport 8-bit MIME bodies, and it covers the 8BIT content-transfer-encoding and the downgrade to 7-bit MIME encodings. Readers of MIME transfer encodings would want it.
MIME.quote: a MIME message (in strict compliance with [RFC2046] and [RFC2045]) with arbitrary octet content is being sent
MIME.section: 2. Framework for the 8-bit MIME Transport Extension

rejected.why: The Internet message format (RFC 5322) is only referenced. The document is about transport, not header or format definitions.
The parent tag is implied by SMTP, so it is not listed separately.
ABNF is used only to write one syntax rule, so it is notation, not the subject.
The IANA section only updates the registry entry and is boilerplate.
TCP port 25 appears only in the example dialogue as the substrate.

RFC6153.title: DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 Options for Access Network Discovery and Selection Function (ANDSF) Discovery
RFC6153.summary: Defines DHCPv4 option 142 and DHCPv6 option 143 carrying ANDSF server addresses so a mobile node can discover 3GPP Access Network Discovery and Selection Function servers.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv4 option (142) and its client request behaviour via the Parameter Request List.
DHCP.quote: This document defines new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options called the ANDSF IP Address Options, which allow the MN to locate an ANDSF server.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option carrying ANDSF IPv6 addresses and how clients request it via the Option Request Option.
DHCPv6.quote: OPTION-IPv6_Address-ANDSF (143)
DHCPv6.section: 3. ANDSF IPv6 Address Option for DHCPv6

cellular.why: The options exist to support 3GPP ANDSF discovery for inter-system mobility between 3GPP and non-3GPP access networks.
cellular.quote: ANDSF is being developed in the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) and provides inter-system mobility policies and access-network-specific information

rejected.why: The introduction mentions that ANDSF can also be discovered via DNS, but the document specifies only DHCP options.
The document is about locating ANDSF servers, but the DHCP tags cover it more specifically.
The mobility policies are 3GPP inter-system handover data, not IP-layer mobility protocols like Mobile IP.

RFC6154.title: IMAP LIST Extension for Special-Use Mailboxes
RFC6154.summary: Defines IMAP LIST extension attributes (\Drafts, \Sent, \Trash, etc.), a SPECIAL-USE capability and options, a USE parameter on CREATE, and a METADATA entry to identify special-use mailboxes.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP's LIST and CREATE commands with new attributes, capabilities, return/selection options and a response code.
IMAP.quote: This extension adds new optional mailbox attributes that a server may include in IMAP LIST command responses to identify special-use mailboxes to the client

rejected.why: Formal syntax is given in ABNF but only as notation for extending IMAP grammar; the document is not about ABNF.
IMAP is the more specific child tag; the parent is implied.
The \Junk attribute marks a mailbox for junk mail, but the document is not about spam filtering.

RFC6155.title: Use of Device Identity in HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD)
RFC6155.summary: Extends the HELD location request protocol with a "device" XML element carrying Device identifiers (IP, MAC, port, NAI, URI, FQDN, cellular IDs, DUID), enabling third-party requests and non-IP-based location configuration, with privacy and security rules.

HELD.why: The whole document defines an extension to HELD: new identity elements, a badIdentifier error code, and requiredIdentifiers in responses.
HELD.quote: This document extends the HELD protocol to allow the location request message to carry Device identifiers.

geolocation.why: Substantial parts deal with location privacy, authorization by Rule Makers and third-party access to location. This is not covered by the HELD tag alone. HELD is a child of geolocation, so this is a judgement call and could be dropped.
geolocation.quote: Privacy and security considerations describe the conditions where requests containing identifiers are permitted.

rejected.why: The schema is used to express the identifiers, but XML is only the encoding for the extension.
The WiMAX NAI procedure queries an AAA server over RADIUS or Diameter, but only as a supporting mechanism.
Digest authentication is required for requests, but only as a security mechanism.
The DUID is one of the identifier types, and DHCP is not the subject.
Emergency calling is cited as a motivating use case, but the document does not address it directly.
NAT appears only in the discussion of subjective network views.

RFC6156.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) Extension for IPv6
RFC6156.summary: Extends TURN to support IPv6 by defining the REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY attribute, new error codes, and rules for IPv4/IPv6 relaying and packet header translation.

TURN.why: The document extends TURN with a new attribute, error codes, and modified Allocate, Refresh, CreatePermission and ChannelBind processing.
TURN.quote: This document adds IPv6 support to TURN, which includes IPv4-to-IPv6, IPv6-to-IPv6, and IPv6-to-IPv4 relaying.

IPv6 transition.why: A substantial part of the document concerns IPv4/IPv6 coexistence: cross-family relaying, packet translation rules (section 8) and tunnel amplification issues with Teredo and 6to4.
IPv6 transition.quote: an IPv4-only node may request the TURN server to allocate an IPv6 address

rejected.why: TURN is built on STUN and the document registers a STUN attribute and error codes, but STUN itself is not what is being extended; TURN is the subject.
IPv6 is the address family being supported, but the document is about TURN's IPv6 support and transition, not the IPv6 protocol itself.
Translation rules refer to RFC 6145 for header fields, but the document does not specify SIIT; it only borrows its field mappings.
The relaying between IPv4 and IPv6 resembles translation, but this is a TURN relay function, not NAT64.
UDP is only the transport over which TURN runs.
NAT is the problem context for TURN, but the document does not address NAT behaviour.

RFC6157.title: IPv6 Transition in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6157.summary: RFC 6157 describes how IPv4 and IPv6 SIP user agents and proxies interoperate at the signaling and media layers during IPv6 transition, updating RFC 3264 and using ICE/TURN relays and address selection.

SIP.why: The document specifies SIP proxy and user agent behaviour (Record-Route, dual-stack proxies, server location) for IPv4/IPv6 coexistence.
SIP.quote: This document describes how the IPv4 Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) user agents can communicate with IPv6 SIP user agents (and vice versa) at the signaling layer

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document addresses IPv4/IPv6 coexistence for SIP, including dual-stack and relay approaches.
IPv6 transition.quote: a complete solution for IPv6 transition needs to handle both the signaling layer and the media layer.

SDP.why: It normatively updates the SDP offer/answer model (RFC 3264) for IPv6, including .invalid for the unspecified address.
SDP.quote: Each media description in the SDP answer MUST use the same network type as the corresponding media description in the offer.

ICE.why: The document prescribes how ICE is used to gather IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, including relayed addresses, for transition.
ICE.quote: IPv4/IPv6 user agents SHOULD gather both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses using the ICE procedures to generate all their offers.

rejected.why: TURN relays are recommended for obtaining IPv4 addresses, but the TURN extension itself is specified in RFC 6156, not here.
DNS A/AAAA/SRV records are used for proxy discovery and the appendix gives a sample zone, but the document does not specify DNS itself.
RTP is only mentioned as the typical media transport and the document does not address it.
The DHCP options for SIP servers are only mentioned as an example discovery mechanism.

RFC6158.title: RADIUS Design Guidelines
RFC6158.summary: BCP giving design guidelines for RADIUS attributes (data types, vendor space, operational model, allocation), intended for authors and reviewers of RADIUS attribute specifications.

RADIUS.why: The whole document is about designing RADIUS attributes, including data types, vendor-specific attributes and the operational model, so RADIUS readers would want it.
RADIUS.quote: This document provides guidelines for the design of attributes used by the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) protocol.

rejected.why: RADIUS is a child of AAA, and the document is specifically about RADIUS, so the more specific tag is used.
Standard-space allocation is discussed, but the document has no IANA actions and is not about IANA registries in general.
SNMP is only mentioned as a comparison for the data definition language and enterprise OID space.
MD5 is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, and the document is not about MD5.
EAP-Message is used as an example of an opaque attribute, but EAP is not the subject.

RFC6159.title: Session-Specific Explicit Diameter Request Routing
RFC6159.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC defining a Diameter extension (Explicit-Path AVPs, ER-Originator/Proxy/Destination procedures) that lets proxies stay in the path of all requests in a session, motivated by 3GPP WLAN interworking.

Diameter.why: The whole document extends Diameter request routing, defining new AVPs, error codes and proxy/originator/destination procedures.
Diameter.quote: This document describes a mechanism to enable specific Diameter proxies to remain in the path of all message exchanges constituting a Diameter session.

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Section 6, which says no action is needed for RADIUS/Diameter interaction.
3GPP WLAN architecture is only the motivating example; the mechanism is application-independent.
WLAN access is context for the use case, not the subject of the document.
Diameter is the specific AAA protocol tagged; the generic AAA framework is not the topic.
This is application-layer Diameter request routing, not IP routing.

RFC6160.title: Algorithms for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Protection of Symmetric Key Package Content Types
RFC6160.summary: Specifies which cryptographic algorithms (RSA, DSA, ECDSA, DH/ECDH, AES Key Wrap with Padding, AES-GCM/CCM) implementations must or should support when using CMS SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData and AuthEnvelopedData to protect the symmetric key package content type.

CMS.why: The document is a CMS algorithm profile covering SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData and AuthEnvelopedData; CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [RFC5652] to protect the symmetric key package content type

AES.why: AES Key Wrap with Padding and AES-GCM/CCM are the mandated content-encryption algorithms, a substantial part of the document.
AES.quote: implementations MUST support AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding [RFC5649] as the content-encryption algorithm.

rejected.why: RSA signatures and RSAES-OAEP are listed as required algorithms, but only as one item among many. The document does not define anything new about RSA.
ECDSA and ECDH are mentioned only as optional algorithms (MAY), with no specification of their own.
Public key certificates are mentioned only in passing in the Public Key Sizes section.
The document concerns algorithms for protecting symmetric key packages. It does not define key management mechanisms.
SHA-256 and SHA-1 are mentioned only as the hash functions to use with the signature schemes.

RFC6161.title: Elliptic Curve Algorithms for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Encrypted Key Package Content Type
RFC6161.summary: RFC 6161 specifies that ECDH with EnvelopedData and ECDSA with SignedData MAY be supported for the CMS encrypted key package content type, with P-256 keys required, extending RFC 6033.

CMS.why: The document profiles algorithms for CMS EnvelopedData and SignedData when used with the encrypted key package content type, so CMS readers need it.
CMS.quote: conventions for using Elliptic Curve cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) encrypted key package content type

ECDSA.why: It specifies ECDSA use with SignedData and requires support for P-256 keys.
ECDSA.quote: it MAY support the signature scheme ECDSA [RFC6090][RFC5753].

elliptic curve.why: ECDH key agreement is a general elliptic-curve technique and has no more specific tag, so the generic elliptic curve tag covers it.
elliptic curve.quote: standard (as opposed to cofactor) ECDH [RFC6090][RFC5753] MAY be supported.

rejected.why: Certificates are referenced only as the easiest way to carry keys; the document defines nothing about them.
Public key certificates are mentioned in passing; the document is not about PKI.
The encrypted key package carries keys, but the document only profiles algorithms and does not address key management.

RFC6162.title: Elliptic Curve Algorithms for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Asymmetric Key Package Content Type
RFC6162.summary: Updates RFC 5959 to allow ECDSA with CMS SignedData and ECDH with EnvelopedData when protecting the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type, and requires P-256 support.

CMS.why: The document specifies how CMS SignedData and EnvelopedData are used with EC algorithms to protect a content type, so CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: This document describes conventions for using Elliptic Curve cryptographic algorithms with SignedData and EnvelopedData to protect the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type.

ECDSA.why: Defines ECDSA use with SignedData and requires P-256 keys.
ECDSA.quote: If an implementation supports SignedData, then it MAY support ECDSA [RFC6090][RFC5753].

elliptic curve.why: ECDH key agreement with EnvelopedData and the P-256 requirement are elliptic curve conventions. No ECDH-specific tag exists, so the parent tag is used.
elliptic curve.quote: standard (as opposed to cofactor) ECDH [RFC6090][RFC5753] MAY be supported.

rejected.why: Certificates are mentioned only as the easiest way to implement the key handling, and the document does not profile them.
Public key certificates are only referenced, and the document is not about PKI.
The document covers algorithm choices for protecting key packages, not key establishment or provisioning itself.

gaps.name: Asymmetric Key Package (RFC 5958 / CMS content type)
gaps.why: The document is about protecting the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC6163.title: Framework for GMPLS and Path Computation Element (PCE) Control of Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs)
RFC6163.summary: Informational framework describing how GMPLS and the PCE architecture apply to Wavelength Switched Optical Networks, modelling WSON elements and Routing and Wavelength Assignment and identifying implications for GMPLS signaling, routing and PCE.

GMPLS.why: The document is about GMPLS control of wavelength-switched optical networks, including signaling (Label Set, ERO) and routing implications for lambda switching.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides a framework for applying the GMPLS architecture and protocols [RFC3945] and the PCE architecture [RFC4655] to the control and operation of WSONs.

PCE.why: RWA path computation by a PCE and PCEP/PCE-GCO enhancements for WSON, and RWA-capable PCE discovery, are a substantial part of the framework.
PCE.quote: The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture [RFC4655] defines functional components that can be used to compute and suggest appropriate paths

rejected.why: RSVP-TE signaling (Label Set, ERO) is discussed as a mechanism for distributed wavelength assignment, but the document does not specify or extend it.
OSPF-TE is only mentioned as the routing mechanism that would carry WSON information; no OSPF content is specified.
The parent topic of PCE and RSVP-TE; the PCE tag already covers it, so a separate traffic engineering tag is not needed.
SONET/SDH regenerator overhead is compared in a table, but the document is not about IP or multi-access protocols over SONET/SDH.
NETCONF is named only as one possible way to communicate RWA information.

gaps.name: Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSON) / Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for optical/WDM networks or RWA. GMPLS and PCE only partly cover this subject, which is the document's main focus.

RFC6164.title: Using 127-Bit IPv6 Prefixes on Inter-Router Links
RFC6164.summary: Standards Track RFC recommending that routers support /127 prefixes on inter-router point-to-point IPv6 links, giving the rationale (ping-pong forwarding loops, neighbor cache exhaustion) and address-assignment cautions around anycast.

IPv6.why: The document specifies IPv6 prefix length usage and addressing on inter-router links, including Subnet-Router anycast handling. This is IPv6 addressing specification and deployment practice.
IPv6.quote: Routers MUST support the assignment of /127 prefixes on point-to-point inter-router links.

neighbor discovery.why: A main motivation for /127 is avoiding neighbor cache exhaustion attacks on Neighbor Discovery. A substantial section analyses this.
neighbor discovery.quote: the use of a 64-bit prefix length on an inter-router link that uses Neighbor Discovery (e.g., Ethernet) potentially allows for denial-of-service attacks

rejected.why: The document is about addressing, but IPv6 is the more specific tag and already sits under it. Its parent addressing is implied, so I did not list it separately.
EBGP is mentioned only as an example of why operators assign specific addresses. The document does not address BGP.
ICMPv6 is cited only for its mitigation of the ping-pong issue. The document does not extend or specify it.
SONET is only an example of a link medium that lacks Neighbor Discovery.

RFC6165.title: Extensions to IS-IS for Layer-2 Systems
RFC6165.summary: Defines two generic IS-IS TLVs (Multi-Topology-aware Port Capability, type 143, and MAC-Reachability, type 147) to support link-state routing of Layer-2 addresses for systems like RBridges, SPB and OTV.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies new IS-IS TLVs (MT-PORT-CAP and MAC-RI) carried in IIH and LSP PDUs, so it extends IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) extensions necessary to support link state routing for any protocols running directly over Layer-2.

rejected.why: RBridges is cited as one user of the TLVs, but the document defines only generic IS-IS TLVs and leaves the TRILL-specific use to other documents.
The TLVs carry MAC addresses and VLAN IDs, but the document is about IS-IS encoding and does not cover Ethernet itself.
OTV is mentioned only as an example of a system that could use the TLVs, and the document does not specify any overlay.

RFC6166.title: A Registry for PIM Message Types
RFC6166.summary: Instructs IANA to create a registry of PIM version 2 message types, sets its initial contents from the PIM-DM, PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM RFCs, defines an IETF Review assignment policy, and reserves type 15 for future type-space extension.

PIM.why: The whole document defines the registry of PIM message types, including initial contents (Hello, Register, Join/Prune, etc.) and assignment rules. PIM readers would want it.
PIM.quote: IANA has created a PIM message type registry.  It has been placed in the "Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM)" branch of the tree.

rejected.why: The document creates an IANA registry, but the subject is PIM message types. The IANA topic is for registry guidance and stewardship in general, and this registry is specific to PIM.
The initial registry cites PIM-SM (RFC 4601) as a source of message types. The document does not specify or extend PIM-SM itself, and also draws on PIM-DM and BIDIR-PIM.
IGMP is mentioned only as the basis of PIM version 1 message types, which explains why a separate registry is needed. The document is not about IGMP.

RFC6167.title: URI Scheme for Java(tm) Message Service 1.0
RFC6167.summary: Defines the "jms" URI scheme for identifying Java Message Service connection factories and Destinations, with jndi, queue and topic variants, shared parameters, and an IANA variant registry.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme: its syntax, semantics, encoding, security considerations and registration. This is the core subject.
URI.quote: This document defines the format of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) as defined in RFC 3986, for designating connections and destination addresses used in the Java(tm) Messaging Service

rejected.why: JMS is the thing the URI identifies, but the document defines only a URI scheme. It says it defines no new APIs or protocols and excludes how JMS delivers messages.
The document creates a registry of jms URI variants, but this is boilerplate registration for the scheme. The main body is not about IANA procedures.
IRI conversion is mentioned only briefly in the encoding considerations, so IRIs are not a subject of the document.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the syntax and is not itself a subject of the document.
The ACAP vendor subtree is referenced only for vendor variant name registration, so ACAP is not a subject of the document.
JNDI is used for lookup of Destinations, but the document does not specify directory services. JNDI is a Java API dependency.

gaps.name: Java Message Service (JMS) / JNDI
gaps.why: The document is closely tied to the Java messaging API and its naming interface. The taxonomy has no tag for message-oriented middleware or Java APIs, so only the URI tag fits.

RFC6168.title: Requirements for Management of Name Servers for the DNS
RFC6168.summary: RFC 6168 lists requirements for a standardized management system for DNS name servers, covering control, configuration, monitoring, alarms, security and extensibility.

DNS.why: The document is about managing DNS name servers (authoritative, recursive, master, slave), including zone, TSIG, DNSSEC trust anchor and authorization configuration. It is DNS server operations.
DNS.quote: there is not an interoperable way to manage (monitor, control, and configure) the internal aspects of a name server itself.

network management.why: It sets requirements for a management architecture (control, configuration, monitoring, alarms, data model, security, extensibility) with no specific protocol, so the topic tag fits.
network management.quote: This document discusses the requirements of a management system for name servers and can be used as a shopping list of needed features

rejected.why: Trust anchor and security policy management are only some of the configuration items to be managed. The document does not specify or analyse DNSSEC itself.
The earlier DNS MIB modules are cited only as history. No protocol is chosen, so SNMP is not the subject.
RFC 1611 and RFC 1612 are mentioned as failed prior work. This document defines no MIB.
Dynamic update is listed as an existing zone modification mechanism. The document does not address it.
The document calls for a common data model but names no modelling language.
No management protocol is selected or discussed by name.

RFC6169.title: Security Concerns with IP Tunneling
RFC6169.summary: RFC 6169 is an informational document cataloguing security concerns with IP tunneling (bypass of network security, NAT holes, guessable tunnel addresses, tunnel server changes) and recommending mitigations for administrators and protocol designers.

tunneling.why: The whole document is about security issues of IP tunnels in general, across Teredo, L2TP, 6to4, ISATAP and SSL VPNs, not one specific tunnel protocol.
tunneling.quote: A number of security concerns with IP tunnels are documented in this memo.

NAT.why: Section 4 is devoted to NAT holes created by tunnels, their exposure, and how public tunnels defeat restricted NAT filtering.
NAT.quote: the opening created in a NAT device due to a tunnel client increases its Internet attack surface area.

IPv6 transition.why: Much of the analysis concerns IPv6-over-IPv4 transition tunnels (Teredo, 6to4, ISATAP), with recommendations on their use and tunnel preference.
IPv6 transition.quote: to provide an IPv6 transition solution, the network should provide native IPv6 connectivity or a tunnel solution (e.g., ISATAP or 6over4

rejected.why: Teredo is the main running example, but the document does not specify or extend it. The taxonomy tag for it is under IPv6 transition, and the document is about tunnels generally.
Firewall and filtering bypass are discussed as a consequence of tunneling, but the document does not address firewalls as a subject in its own right.
L2TP is only cited as an example of a tunnel protocol over UDP.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific tags. The document is about tunnel security, not general security guidance.
6to4 is mentioned only as an example, such as identification by IPv4 protocol 41.
ISATAP is mentioned only as an example and as a recommended alternative, and is not analysed in its own right.

RFC6170.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure -- Certificate Image
RFC6170.summary: RFC 6170 defines a new "otherLogos" certificate image type for the RFC 3709 Logotype extension in X.509 certificates, giving a complete visual representation of a certificate, with rules for embedding via data URLs and for PDF, SVG and PNG image formats.

X.509.why: The document defines a new image type carried in the X.509 Logotype certificate extension (RFC 3709), updating RFC 3709 and profiling certificate content.
X.509.quote: This standard specifies how to bind a certificate image to a certificate (defined in [RFC5280]), providing a visual representation of that certificate

rejected.why: It names media types (application/pdf, image/svg+xml, image/png) for use in LogotypeDetails, but registers none and sets no registry rules.
SVG is XML-based, but the document only restricts the SVG profile for images and is not about XML usage.
SVGZ uses gzip compression, but only as a substrate for the image format.
X.509 is the more specific tag, so its parent PKI is implied.
The ASN.1 module only defines an OID, so ASN.1 is not the subject.
The data URL scheme (RFC 2397) is used for embedding images but is not specified or extended here.

RFC6171.title: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Don't Use Copy Control
RFC6171.summary: Defines the LDAP Don't Use Copy control, which lets a client require that a Compare or Search be served from original (master) rather than replicated or cached information, based on the X.511 dontUseCopy option.

LDAP.why: The document specifies a new LDAP control extension, including its OID, criticality, applicable operations and server and client behaviour.
LDAP.quote: This document defines the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Don't Use Copy control extension, which allows a client to specify that copied information should not be used

rejected.why: The control is based on the X.511 dontUseCopy option, but the document specifies only an LDAP extension. X.500 is cited for background.
This parent is implied by the LDAP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The OID and protocol mechanism registrations are boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC6172.title: Deprecation of the Internet Fibre Channel Protocol (iFCP) Address Translation Mode
RFC6172.summary: Deprecates the iFCP address translation mode specified in RFC 4172 because it no longer matches Fibre Channel standards and has no implementations, keeps address transparent mode, and records that IP Protocol Number 133 stays allocated for pre-standard FCIP.

iFCP.why: The document's purpose is to deprecate part of iFCP (address translation mode) while retaining address transparent mode, updating RFC 4172.
iFCP.quote: This document deprecates iFCP address translation mode because the specification has not tracked changes in Fibre Channel and because there are no known implementations.

rejected.why: Address translation mode is only described as analogous to NAT; the document concerns Fibre Channel addresses, not IP NAT.
Parent of iFCP, so implied by the iFCP tag; FCIP and Protocol 133 are mentioned only briefly and no FCIP-specific tag exists.
The IANA section merely adds a supplemental reference for Protocol Number 133; this is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
Deprecating a protocol mode and treating it as Historic is incidental to the technical subject, not a process document.

gaps.name: FCIP (Fibre Channel over TCP/IP) and IP Protocol Number 133
gaps.why: The document records the state of Protocol Number 133 used by pre-standard FCIP, but the taxonomy has no FCIP tag; the closest is the fibre channel parent.

RFC6173.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Internet Fibre Channel Protocol (iFCP)
RFC6173.summary: Defines the IFCP-MGMT-MIB SMIv2 module for monitoring and controlling iFCP gateway instances, their sessions and session statistics, and obsoletes RFC 4369 after the deprecation of iFCP address translation mode.

iFCP.why: The MIB models iFCP gateways, sessions, N_PORTs, IP_TOV and liveness intervals, so it belongs on the iFCP page.
iFCP.quote: This document defines Management Information Base (MIB) objects to monitor and control the Internet Fibre Channel Protocol (iFCP) gateway instances and their associated sessions

MIB.why: The document's main content is an SMIv2 MIB module (IFCP-MGMT-MIB) with tables, textual conventions and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, and the MIB tag is more specific.
iFCP sessions map to TCP connections and the TCP-MIB is referenced, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Fibre Channel objects are imported from FC-MGMT-MIB, but the document is about iFCP specifically, which is the more specific tag.
CRC error counters are just statistics; the document does not address CRC polynomials or error detection.

RFC6174.title: Definition of IETF Working Group Document States
RFC6174.summary: RFC 6174 defines new Datatracker states and annotation tags for tracking IETF Working Group Internet-Draft status, and documents the existing IESG document states and availability states.

IETF process.why: The document defines the WG draft lifecycle states (adoption, WG last call, submission to IESG) and the IESG evaluation states used in the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: This document defines new states and status annotation tags that need to be added to the Datatracker to enable WG Chairs and their Delegates to track the status of Internet-Drafts

rejected.why: It touches I-D to RFC progression, but the focus is the IETF's WG and IESG draft-tracking process, not RFC format or publication.
IANA review appears only as an example of an expert review tag, not as a subject of the document.
It defines state names, but these are process states, not a glossary or requirements language.

gaps.name: IETF Datatracker / Internet-Draft tracking
gaps.why: The document is about the Datatracker tool and I-D state tracking. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it, so it falls under the general IETF process tag.

RFC6175.title: Requirements to Extend the Datatracker for IETF Working Group Chairs and Authors
RFC6175.summary: Specifies requirements for extending the IETF Datatracker so WG Chairs, Delegates and Document Shepherds can input, track and report the WG status of Internet-Drafts, using the states and tags defined in RFC 6174.

IETF process.why: The document is about IETF process tooling: tracking WG draft states, chair/delegate/shepherd roles, WG last call, adoption, and handoff to the IESG. Readers of IETF process material would want it.
IETF process.quote: requirements for new functionality to be added to the IETF Datatracker tool to make it possible for Working Group (WG) Chairs and their Delegates to input and update the status

rejected.why: IANA status is only mentioned as something WG Chairs may not edit; the document is not about IANA registries.
The document concerns I-D status tracking in the Datatracker, not RFC format, style or publication.
Login with a personal user-id and password is only a requirement for write access to the web tool; the document does not address HTTP authentication schemes.
The access-control requirements are specific to Datatracker roles and are part of the process tooling, not a general treatment of authorization.
The Datatracker sends notification e-mails, but the document is not about email protocols or systems.

gaps.name: IETF Datatracker / document status tracking tools
gaps.why: The document is about extending the Datatracker. The taxonomy has no tag for IETF tooling, so only the broader IETF process tag fits.

RFC6176.title: Prohibiting Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Version 2.0
RFC6176.summary: RFC 6176 updates TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 to forbid TLS clients and servers from negotiating SSL 2.0, and sets out SSL 2.0's deficiencies and the required client and server behaviour.

TLS.why: The document updates the backward compatibility sections of TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2. It sets new protocol requirements for TLS clients and servers, so it is about TLS protocol behaviour and deployment guidance.
TLS.quote: TLS clients MUST NOT send the SSL version 2.0 compatible CLIENT- HELLO message format.

rejected.why: MD5 is mentioned only as one of SSL 2.0's weaknesses (message authentication). The document is not about MD5.
TCP FIN injection is cited only as an example of how SSL 2.0 sessions can be terminated. The document does not address TCP.
The document names weak cryptographic practices in SSL 2.0, but its subject is a protocol version prohibition in TLS, not a cryptographic algorithm.
XMPP appears only in the acknowledgements, as the source of the idea for the document.

RFC6177.title: IPv6 Address Assignment to End Sites
RFC6177.summary: RFC 6177 obsoletes RFC 3177 and gives guidance on IPv6 address assignment size to end sites, moving away from a one-size-fits-all /48 default toward flexible assignments (e.g., /56 for homes) while ensuring sites get more than a single /64.

addressing.why: The document is about IP address allocation and assignment policy for end sites, including prefix length boundaries and CIDR applicability. It sits within addressing and is specific to IPv6 assignment guidance.
addressing.quote: This document focuses on the (more narrow) question of what is an appropriate IPv6 address assignment size for end sites.

IPv6.why: It gives IPv6 architectural and operational guidance, including impacts on RFC 3056 and IPv6 multicast addressing, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: The exact choice of how much address space to assign end sites is an issue for the operational community.

rejected.why: Renumbering is one motivation discussed for /48, but the document is about assignment sizing, not renumbering procedures.
CIDR is mentioned as continuing to apply to all prefix bits, but only in passing; the document is not about CIDR itself.
RFC 3056 is discussed only for its impact on subnet numbering; the document does not specify or change 6to4.
Reverse DNS delegation under ip6.arpa gets only a brief mention and is not a substantial subject.
IPv6-to-IPv6 NAT is mentioned only as an outcome to avoid, not as a subject of the document.
Multihoming and GSE are mentioned briefly as an RFC 3177 consideration that no longer applies.

RFC6178.title: Label Edge Router Forwarding of IPv4 Option Packets
RFC6178.summary: Standards-track update to RFC 3031 requiring ingress MPLS Label Edge Routers to decide on MPLS encapsulation and label selection for IPv4 packets without considering IPv4 header options, mitigating option-based DoS attacks on LSRs.

MPLS.why: The document specifies ingress LER behavior for MPLS encapsulation and updates the MPLS architecture (RFC 3031), so MPLS readers need it.
MPLS.quote: When determining whether to push an MPLS label stack onto an IPv4 packet, the determination is made without considering any IPv4 options

rejected.why: IPv4 options are the packets being handled, but the document specifies MPLS LER behavior, not IPv4 itself.
Router Alert option and label are discussed as an example attack vector, but the document is not about the Router Alert option itself.
The security considerations motivate the policy, but the document specifies a forwarding requirement rather than general operational practice.
RSVP is mentioned only as a case where the policy must not alter specific processing rules.
BGP/MPLS VPNs are mentioned only as not subject to the threats described.
Diffserv tunnels are mentioned only as one of the bypass attack scenarios.

RFC6179.title: The Internet Routing Overlay Network (IRON)
RFC6179.summary: IRTF experimental RFC proposing IRON, a global routing overlay of tunnelling Clients, Servers and Relays that uses Virtual Prefixes to reduce routing-table growth and supports mobility, multihoming, traffic engineering and NAT traversal without changing hosts or BGP.

routing architecture.why: The document proposes a routing architecture to address routing scalability, using an overlay with virtual prefixes and mapping.
routing architecture.quote: it is clear that current routing architectures and operational practices must be updated.  This document proposes an Internet Routing Overlay Network (IRON)

overlay networks.why: IRON is a data-plane overlay using encapsulation (VET/SEAL) over the Internet as NBMA links, which is the substance of the architecture.
overlay networks.quote: The IRON is a global routing system comprising virtual overlay networks managed by Virtual Prefix Companies (VPCs)

IP mobility.why: Mobility management is a stated goal and handled via Server hand-off and redirects.
IP mobility.quote: When a Client changes its network point of attachment (e.g., due to a mobility event), it configures one or more new locators.

multihoming.why: Multihoming support is a core stated goal of IRON, with registration of multiple ISP connections.
multihoming.quote: A Client may register multiple locators with its Server.  It can assign metrics with its registrations to inform the Server of preferred locators

rejected.why: IRON relays advertise VPs into BGP but the document does not specify or change BGP; it is the substrate.
Encapsulation is central but defined in VET/SEAL, which are separate documents; the overlay networks tag fits better.
NAT traversal is a short section (6.7) only; not a substantial part.
Anycast is used for discovering Relays/Servers, but only as a mechanism, not the subject.
Only brief subsections on inbound/outbound TE; not a major focus and not MPLS/PCE style TE.
Section 6.6 briefly covers renumbering avoidance; minor part.

gaps.name: Core-edge separation / locator-identifier split (map-and-encap)
gaps.why: IRON is a routing-scalability proposal using EP/locator separation with mapping; the taxonomy only has LISP and ILNP for related work, nothing generic.

RFC6180.title: Guidelines for Using IPv6 Transition Mechanisms during IPv6 Deployment
RFC6180.summary: Informational guidance document recommending four IPv6 deployment models (native dual stack, tunneling across IPv4 islands, IPv6-only core with DS-Lite, IPv6-only with translation) and the IETF transition tools that support them.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document is guidance on choosing IPv6/IPv4 coexistence and transition mechanisms, which is exactly the IPv6 transition topic.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document discusses the IPv6 deployment models and migration tools, and it recommends ones that have been found to work well in operational networks

DS-Lite.why: Section 4.3 is built around DS-Lite as the recommended tool for an IPv6-only core network.
DS-Lite.quote: The recommended tool for this model is Dual Stack Lite [DS-lite].

6rd.why: 6rd is recommended as the ISP tunneling approach for crossing IPv4 islands, with a dedicated discussion.
6rd.quote: The IPv6 Rapid Deployment (6RD) [RFC5969] approach is a newer version of the 6to4 tunneling solution without the above drawbacks.

NAT64.why: Network-layer stateful and stateless translation (NAT64/DNS64 framework) is the core of the fourth deployment model.
NAT64.quote: a broadband ISP may support dual-stack connectivity for customers that require both IPv4 and IPv6, and offer IPv6-only and NAT64 service for others.

rejected.why: Tunneling is discussed as one deployment model, but the specific IPv6 transition tags cover it better and the document does not specify generic tunnelling.
IPv4/IPv4 NAT is discussed as context for dual stack, but the document is not about NAT behaviour itself.
Mentioned as an example with known problems and superseded by 6rd, not a subject of the document.
Only cited as a reference within the translation framework, with no substantive discussion.
Implied parent of IPv6 transition; the more specific transition tag fits.
Listed only among tunneling mechanisms in passing.

RFC6181.title: Threat Analysis for TCP Extensions for Multipath Operation with Multiple Addresses
RFC6181.summary: An informational threat analysis of Multipath TCP using multiple addresses per endpoint, covering flooding and hijacking (including time-shifted) attacks, NAT considerations, and recommending reachability checks and HMAC-protected address additions.

MPTCP.why: The whole document analyses the security threats of Multipath TCP and recommends security mechanisms for its design.
MPTCP.quote: The scope of the analysis included in this note is limited to a particular approach, namely MPTCP, that relies on the usage of multiple IP address per endpoint

rejected.why: MPTCP is the more specific child tag; TCP is only the base protocol being extended.
Discussed only as related work (RFC 5062 analysis); the document is not about SCTP.
MIPv6 route optimization is compared as related work, not the subject.
Shim6 threat analysis is cited only as prior work.
NAT considerations are one section, but the document is about MPTCP security, not NAT behaviour.
Multihoming is mentioned as a side benefit; the focus is attacks on MPTCP.

RFC6182.title: Architectural Guidelines for Multipath TCP Development
RFC6182.summary: Informational architecture document setting goals, a functional decomposition and high-level design decisions (sequence numbering, buffers, signalling, path management, congestion control, security, middlebox interaction) for Multipath TCP (MPTCP).

MPTCP.why: The whole document is the architecture and design rationale for MPTCP: goals, functional decomposition, and design decisions.
MPTCP.quote: This document outlines architectural guidelines for the development of a Multipath Transport Protocol, with references to how these architectural components come together in the development of a Multipath TCP (MPTCP).

rejected.why: MPTCP is the specific child tag; TCP is only the base protocol that subflows run as, and the ancestor is implied.
Coupled congestion control is covered only briefly in Section 5.7 and is delegated to a companion document.
Mentioned only as a related protocol and comparison in Section 2.4, not the subject of the document.
Cited only as a possible way to use ports as path selectors; the document is not about ECMP.
Middleboxes such as NATs are discussed only as compatibility constraints, not specified or analysed in their own right.
Multihomed hosts are the scenario for MPTCP, but multihoming architectures are not the subject.

RFC6183.title: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Mediation: Framework
RFC6183.summary: Informational framework extending the IPFIX reference model (RFC 5470) by defining IPFIX Mediator components, Intermediate Processes (conversion, selection, aggregation, anonymization, correlation), their combinations, message header encoding and security considerations.

IPFIX.why: The whole document defines the IPFIX Mediation architecture, Intermediate Processes and header encoding considerations for IPFIX.
IPFIX.quote: This framework extends the IPFIX reference model specified in RFC 5470 by defining the IPFIX Mediator components.

PSAMP.why: Mediators also handle PSAMP Packet Reports. But the taxonomy has PSAMP only as a child of IPFIX, so it is not separately tagged here.
PSAMP.quote: IPFIX Mediation can be applied to flow-based or packet-based information.

rejected.why: TLS and DTLS are only the transport security mechanism; Security Considerations discuss security level downgrade and upgrade but define nothing new about TLS itself.
SCTP is mentioned only as a transport for protocol conversion; it is not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations regarding exporting certificates.
Considered as a secondary tag, but PSAMP is not a tag id in the taxonomy; PSAMP is only a mention under IPFIX.
Correlation examples such as one-way delay are only illustrations; the document is about flow export mediation.

RFC6184.title: RTP Payload Format for H.264 Video
RFC6184.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for H.264/AVC video, including NAL unit packetization modes, aggregation and fragmentation units, decoding order numbers, and media type/SDP parameters; obsoletes RFC 3984.

H.264.why: The whole document defines how H.264 NAL units are packetized in RTP, plus the video/H264 media type and its parameters.
H.264.quote: This memo describes an RTP Payload format for the ITU-T Recommendation H.264 video codec

RTP payload format.why: It is an RTP payload format specification, defining single NAL unit, aggregation and fragmentation unit packets. This is the RTP payload format category the subject's readers would want.
RTP payload format.quote: The payload format defines three different basic payload structures.

SDP.why: Substantial sections define SDP fmtp parameter mapping, offer/answer rules and declarative usage for H.264.
SDP.quote: The media type video/H264 string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)

rejected.why: Parent of RTP payload format and implied; the document specifies a payload format, not RTP itself.
The media type registration of video/H264 is part of the payload format, not a document about media type registry rules.
FEC (RFC 5109) is only discussed in informative application examples; the document does not specify it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a suggested mechanism.
Only a passing reference to RTCP FIR feedback for decoder refresh.
Parent of H.264, which is the more specific tag.

RFC6185.title: RTP Payload Format for H.264 Reduced-Complexity Decoding Operation (RCDO) Video
RFC6185.summary: Defines the H264-RCDO media subtype and SDP parameters for an RTP payload format carrying H.264 Reduced-Complexity Decoding Operation video, reusing the RFC 6184 H.264 payload format.

H.264.why: The document specifies an H.264 RTP payload format variant (RCDO), with profile-level-id semantics and H.264 parameters. H.264 is the codec tag covering H.264 payload formats.
H.264.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for the Reduced-Complexity Decoding Operation (RCDO) for H.264 Baseline profile bitstreams

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification, registering the H264-RCDO media subtype and its parameters.
RTP payload format.quote: The payload format defined in Section 5 of RFC 6184 [1] SHALL be used.

SDP.why: A substantial part defines SDP fmtp parameters, offer/answer rules and declarative SDP considerations for H264-RCDO.
SDP.quote: The mapping of the above defined payload format media subtype and its parameters SHALL be done according to Section 3 of RFC 4855 [10].

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format runs over; the child tag RTP payload format is more specific.
Registers a media subtype, but this is boilerplate for a payload format registration, not a document about media type registry rules.
The more specific H.264 tag applies.
The congestion control section only refers to RFC 3550 and the RTP profile; it is boilerplate.
Base64/base16 encodings are used only for parameter values.

RFC6186.title: Use of SRV Records for Locating Email Submission/Access Services
RFC6186.summary: Defines new DNS SRV service labels (submission, imap, imaps, pop3, pop3s) so email clients can auto-configure submission and message access servers from a user's email address, with guidance for MUAs and service providers.

DNS-SD.why: The document defines new DNS SRV service labels used to discover email services, which is DNS-based service discovery.
DNS-SD.quote: This specification defines new SRV service types for the message submission, IMAP, and POP3 services, to enable simple auto- configuration of MUAs.

IMAP.why: Defines _imap and _imaps labels and how IMAP servers are located and chosen, a substantial part of the document.
IMAP.quote: This specification adds two SRV service labels for IMAP [RFC3501]:

POP3.why: Defines _pop3 and _pop3s labels and formally updates RFC 1939; readers of POP3 would want it.
POP3.quote: This specification adds two SRV service labels for POP3 [RFC1939]:

SMTP.why: Defines the _submission label for locating mail submission agents, an SMTP profile.
SMTP.quote: This specification adds one SRV service label for message submission [RFC4409]:

rejected.why: SRV records are used as the mechanism; the document does not define new DNS protocol behaviour beyond service labels, which DNS-SD covers.
TLS is only the security mechanism for the connections; no new TLS extension is defined.
A more specific child tags (IMAP, POP3, SMTP) fit, so the parent is implied.
The more specific DNS-SD tag applies.
Certificate verification is just referenced from RFC 6125, not specified here.

RFC6187.title: X.509v3 Certificates for Secure Shell Authentication
RFC6187.summary: Defines new SSH public key algorithms (x509v3-ssh-dss, x509v3-ssh-rsa, x509v3-rsa2048-sha256, x509v3-ecdsa-sha2-*) that convey keys as X.509v3 certificate chains with optional OCSP responses, plus ExtendedKeyUsage OIDs for SSH client/server.

SSH.why: The document extends SSH by defining new public key algorithms, key formats, signature encodings and their use in SSH authentication and key exchange messages.
SSH.quote: This document specifies how to use X.509 version 3 public key certificates in public key algorithms in the Secure Shell protocol.

X.509.why: It profiles X.509v3 certificates for SSH: chain ordering, KeyUsage, new ExtendedKeyUsage OIDs, subjectAltName host name matching and validation per RFC 5280.
X.509.quote: This document defines two ExtendedKeyUsage key purpose IDs that MAY be used to restrict a certificate's use: id-kp-secureShellClient

OCSP.why: OCSP responses are embedded in the SSH key format, with rules on their number, production time and handling when absent or revoked.
OCSP.quote: the key format consists of a sequence of one or more X.509v3 certificates followed by a sequence of 0 or more Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) responses

rejected.why: ECDSA signatures are used and encoded per RFC 5656, but the document only references them; it does not define ECDSA itself.
RSA signing follows RFC 3447 as an existing algorithm; the document only specifies SSH encoding and a 2048-bit constraint.
The specific X.509 and OCSP tags fit better than the general PKI parent.
RFC 4462 is referenced only as a message where the new keys may appear.

RFC6188.title: The Use of AES-192 and AES-256 in Secure RTP
RFC6188.summary: Defines AES-192 and AES-256 counter-mode ciphers, corresponding key derivation functions, and four new crypto suites for SRTP/SRTCP, registered in the SDP Security Descriptions registry.

SRTP.why: The document extends SRTP with new ciphers, key derivation functions and crypto suites, so it belongs on the SRTP page.
SRTP.quote: This memo describes the use of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) with 192- and 256-bit keys within the Secure RTP (SRTP) protocol.

AES.why: It specifies how the larger AES key sizes are used in counter mode and as a PRF, and gives test vectors for them.
AES.quote: AES-192 counter mode and AES-256 counter mode and are denoted as AES_192_CM and AES_256_CM, respectively.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is only reused unchanged from RFC 3711 as the authentication function in the suites; nothing new is defined for it.
SHA-1 appears only as the hash inside HMAC-SHA1 in the crypto suite tables.
RTP is the underlying protocol that SRTP protects, and is not the subject here.
SDP Security Descriptions is only the registry where the suite names are registered, which is IANA boilerplate.
The document defines key derivation functions within SRTP. It does not address key establishment or provisioning, so the broader topic does not fit.

RFC6189.title: ZRTP: Media Path Key Agreement for Unicast Secure RTP
RFC6189.summary: RFC 6189 specifies ZRTP, a media-path Diffie-Hellman key agreement protocol multiplexed on RTP ports that derives keys for SRTP sessions, with SAS-based MiTM detection, key continuity caching, and an SDP zrtp-hash attribute.

SRTP.why: The document defines a key agreement protocol whose purpose is keying SRTP sessions; it is the core subject for readers of secure RTP.
SRTP.quote: ZRTP, a protocol for media path Diffie-Hellman exchange to agree on a session key and parameters for establishing unicast Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) sessions

key management.why: Large parts cover key agreement modes, key derivation, shared-secret caching and key destruction, which is key management for media sessions.
key management.quote: ZRTP is a key agreement protocol that performs a Diffie-Hellman key exchange during call setup in the media path

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute (registered with IANA) and its ABNF, binding the media path to signalling.
SDP.quote: The ZRTP attribute, a=zrtp-hash, is used to indicate support for ZRTP and to convey a hash of the Hello message.

rejected.why: ZRTP is multiplexed on RTP ports but the document is about keying SRTP, not RTP itself; SRTP is the more specific tag.
SIP is the signalling context and interactions are described, but ZRTP is explicitly independent of signalling protocol.
Only mentioned as running before ZRTP and as a packet-format distinction from STUN.
DTLS-SRTP is only compared against in discussion; not the subject.
Optional SAS signatures use ECDSA, but only as an optional mechanism, not the document's subject.
OpenPGP signatures are an optional signature format for the SAS, a minor part.

RFC6190.title: RTP Payload Format for Scalable Video Coding
RFC6190.summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for H.264 Scalable Video Coding (Annex G), with new NAL unit types (PACSI, empty, NI-MTAP), single- and multi-session transmission modes, decoding order recovery, and the H264-SVC media type with SDP parameters.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for a video codec, defining packetization and de-packetization rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes an RTP payload format for Scalable Video Coding (SVC) as defined in Annex G of ITU-T Recommendation H.264

H.264.why: The payload format is for the SVC extension of H.264/AVC and is backward compatible with RFC 6184 for the base layer.
H.264.quote: SVC is specified in Amendment 3 to ISO/IEC 14496 Part 10 [ISO/IEC14496-10] and equivalently in Annex G of ITU-T Rec. H.264

SDP.why: A substantial part defines SDP parameter mapping, offer/answer rules, dependency signalling and examples.
SDP.quote: The media type video/H264-SVC string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) as follows

media types.why: Registers the video/H264-SVC media type with many optional parameters.
media types.quote: Media subtype name:  H264-SVC

rejected.why: The child tag RTP payload format fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
SRTP is mentioned only in passing in connection with MANEs and is not a subject of the document.
RTCP rewriting by MANEs is mentioned but the document does not extend or specify RTCP.
Layered multicast appears only as an application example in the informative appendix.
Section 9 is a short discussion of reducing bitrate by dropping layers and defers to RFC 6184, so it is not a substantial subject.
RTSP is mentioned only as a context for declarative SDP usage.

gaps.name: Scalable Video Coding (SVC)
gaps.why: The codecs subtree has H.264 but no dedicated tag for the SVC extension and layered video coding. H.264 is the closest fit.

RFC6191.title: Reducing the TIME-WAIT State Using TCP Timestamps
RFC6191.summary: BCP describing an algorithm for TCP to accept SYN segments for connections in TIME-WAIT using TCP Timestamps (and ISN) heuristics, enabling higher connection-establishment rates.

TCP.why: The document modifies TCP's handling of SYN segments in the TIME-WAIT state and discusses the Timestamps option, ISNs and PAWS interactions, so it is a TCP implementation and extension document.
TCP.quote: This document describes an algorithm for processing incoming SYN segments that allows higher connection-establishment rates between any two TCP endpoints when a TCP Timestamps option is present

rejected.why: Only TCP-layer behaviour is addressed; IP is not discussed.
Security considerations only point to another document, and ISN predictability is a side discussion.
ISN and timestamp randomization are mentioned only as interacting factors, not as the subject.

RFC6192.title: Protecting the Router Control Plane
RFC6192.summary: Informational RFC describing a method to protect a router's control plane by identifying legitimate control-plane traffic and installing forwarding-plane filters and rate limiters, with Cisco CoPP and Juniper firewall filter examples.

operational security.why: The whole document is an operational practice for hardening network infrastructure (routers) against DoS and unwanted traffic via filters and rate limiters.
operational security.quote: This memo provides a method for protecting a router's control plane from undesired or malicious traffic.

rejected.why: The filters are router control-plane ACLs/policers, not a firewall or middlebox traversal specification; operational security fits better.
DoS protection is the motivation, but the document is a general control-plane filtering practice rather than DDoS mitigation or signalling.
ICMP is rate-limited as one traffic class, but the document does not specify or analyse ICMP.
BGP, OSPF, SSH, SNMP, RADIUS, DNS and NTP appear only as example permitted traffic classes in the filter; the document is not about them.
It touches router control/forwarding plane separation, but the focus is protection filters, not routing architecture or scalability.

gaps.name: Control Plane Policing (CoPP) / router control plane protection
gaps.why: The document's specific subject is protecting router control planes with forwarding-plane filters and rate limiters. The taxonomy has only the general operational security topic for it.

RFC6193.title: Media Description for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE) in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC6193.summary: Informational RFC defining SDP media formats "ike-esp" and "ike-esp-udpencap" and the "ike-setup" and "psk-fingerprint" attributes so SIP endpoints can negotiate IKE/IPsec VPN sessions using self-signed certificate fingerprints, with ICE-based NAT traversal.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with new media formats and attributes (ike-setup, psk-fingerprint) and specifies offer/answer negotiation for IKE.
SDP.quote: this document defines new media formats "ike-esp" and "ike-esp-udpencap", which can be used when the protocol identifier is "udp"

IKE.why: The document is about bootstrapping IKE and generating IPsec SAs via SDP negotiation, using certificate fingerprints for authentication.
IKE.quote: It extends the protocol identifier of the Session Description Protocol (SDP) so that it can negotiate use of the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE)

SIP.why: SIP is used as the signalling mechanism to establish the on-demand VPN media session; this is a deployed use of SIP described by the document.
SIP.quote: This document proposes the use of SIP as a name resolution and authentication mechanism

ICE.why: Sections 5.4 and 5.5 specify port usage and demultiplexing of STUN, IKE and UDP-encapsulated ESP when using ICE.
ICE.quote: this document also covers the method to combine IKE/IPsec NAT-Traversal [RFC3947][RFC3948] with ICE.

rejected.why: IPsec/IKE specifications are not modified; IPsec is the resulting SA, and the IKE tag covers the subject more specifically.
Only the comedia-tls fingerprint approach of RFC 4572 is borrowed; the document defines nothing new for TLS.
STUN is only demultiplexed from IKE/ESP on the shared UDP path; the document does not specify or extend STUN.
Self-signed certificates are used via fingerprints, but certificate formats and profiles are not addressed.
The VPN tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs; this is an on-demand host/home-router IPsec VPN.
NAT traversal is handled through ICE and IPsec NAT-T, so the more specific ICE tag fits.

RFC6194.title: Security Considerations for the SHA-0 and SHA-1 Message-Digest Algorithms
RFC6194.summary: Informational RFC summarizing published collision, pre-image and HMAC attacks on SHA-0 and SHA-1 and advising IETF protocol designers to move away from SHA-1 for signatures and never use SHA-0.

SHA.why: The whole document analyses the security of SHA-0 and SHA-1, members of the SHA hash family, and gives guidance on their use in IETF protocols.
SHA.quote: The published attacks against both algorithms show that it is not prudent to use either algorithm when collision resistance is required.

HMAC.why: Dedicated subsections (2.3, 3.3) assess attacks on HMAC-SHA-0 and HMAC-SHA-1, and the conclusions recommend HMAC-SHA-1, so HMAC readers would want this.
HMAC.quote: HMAC-SHA-1 remains secure and is the preferred keyed-hash algorithm for IETF protocol design.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in passing (signatures assume existing PKIs); the document is not about PKI.
Not discussed; the document covers SHA-0/SHA-1 only, and the related hash-attack survey is merely referenced (RFC 4270).

RFC6195.title: Domain Name System (DNS) IANA Considerations
RFC6195.summary: BCP defining IANA allocation policies for DNS parameters: header bits, OpCodes, RCODEs, RRTYPEs, CLASSes, AFSDB subtypes, with an expert-review process and an RRTYPE allocation template.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies allocation policies and registry contents for core DNS protocol parameters (RRTYPEs, CLASSes, OpCodes, RCODEs, header bits), so DNS readers need it.
DNS.quote: IANA parameter assignment considerations for the allocation of Domain Name System (DNS) resource record types, CLASSes, operation codes, error codes, DNS protocol message header bits

rejected.why: The document is an IANA considerations BCP, but its subject is DNS parameter registries specifically; the general IANA topic covers registry guidance and stewardship, and DNS is the more specific fit.
OPT RR and its RCODE extension are mentioned only as part of RCODE space discussion; EDNS is not specified or extended here.
Security Considerations merely point to DNSSEC RFCs; not about DNSSEC.
Update OpCode and RCODEs are listed in registries, but dynamic update is not the subject.

RFC6196.title: Moving mailserver: URI Scheme to Historic
RFC6196.summary: RFC 6196 re-registers the undocumented, non-interoperable mailserver: URI scheme as Historic in the IANA URI scheme registry and discourages future implementations.

URI.why: The document is entirely about the status of a single URI scheme (mailserver:) and its registration in the URI scheme registry, updating RFC 1738.
URI.quote: this document discourages any future implementations of this URI scheme and asks IANA to mark it as Historic in the URI scheme registry

rejected.why: Email is only the subject area the scheme nominally concerned; the document does not specify or analyse email protocols.
The IANA registry update is the mechanism of the change, not a document about IANA registries or guidance generally.
IMAP, POP and mailto URI schemes are only mentioned as alternatives to use instead of mailserver:.
Not about typed links or link relations; it concerns a URI scheme registration.

RFC6197.title: Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Service List Boundary Extension
RFC6197.summary: Defines an experimental LoST extension that adds a Service List Boundary to listServicesByLocation responses, plus a getServiceListBoundary request, so mobile clients notice changes in available (e.g. emergency) services.

LoST.why: The document extends the LoST protocol with new elements, a new request/response pair and a new namespace, so LoST readers need it.
LoST.quote: this document defines a Service List Boundary that returns a local context along with the list of services returned

rejected.why: XML and Relax NG are only the encoding and schema language for the extension; the document is not about XML usage.
Civic and geodetic locations appear in the examples, but the document does not address location formats or conveyance itself; LoST is the more specific fit.
Emergency calling motivates the extension, but the parent is implied by the LoST tag, and the extension is generic to service lists.
The schema and namespace registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject of the document.

RFC6198.title: Requirements for the Graceful Shutdown of BGP Sessions
RFC6198.summary: Informational requirements document for a mechanism to gracefully shut down (and bring up) BGP sessions during planned maintenance so as to minimize or eliminate traffic loss during BGP convergence.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies requirements for a BGP graceful shutdown (g-shut/g-noshut) mechanism, addressing BGP convergence, route reflection, EBGP/IBGP topologies and operations.
BGP.quote: a solution is required for the graceful shutdown of a (set of) BGP session(s) in order to limit the amount of traffic loss during a planned shutdown

rejected.why: Route reflectors are discussed as a cause of hidden backup paths and in the appendix topologies, but the document is about graceful shutdown generally, not route reflection.
BGP/MPLS VPNs are mentioned as a use case and context, but the requirements are not about the VPN technology itself.
RFC 5714/5715 are only cited as related frameworks for loop-free convergence; the document does not address IP fast reroute.
The BGP tag fits more specifically; the document is not about general routing architecture or scalability principles.

RFC6201.title: Device Reset Characterization
RFC6201.summary: RFC 6201 specifies a benchmarking methodology for characterizing device reset and defining "reset time" for forwarding devices, updating RFC 2544 and RFC 1242.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a BMWG benchmarking methodology defining reset time and test procedures (hardware, software, power interruption), updating RFC 2544 and RFC 1242.
benchmarking.quote: This document specifies a methodology for characterizing reset (and reset time) during benchmarking of forwarding devices

rejected.why: The document is a device benchmarking methodology in a lab, not network performance measurement; benchmarking is the more specific fit.
Only mentioned as one protocol in a reporting parameter list and as a related benchmarking RFC reference.
MPLS appears only as an example protocol in the reporting table and in a cited RFC 5695.
Port media and encapsulation are listed only as reporting parameters.
The document is lab benchmarking of reset recovery, not OAM mechanisms.

RFC6202.title: Known Issues and Best Practices for the Use of Long Polling and Streaming in Bidirectional HTTP
RFC6202.summary: Informational RFC describing known issues and best practices for HTTP long polling and HTTP streaming used to achieve server-push (bidirectional) communication, with overviews of Bayeux, BOSH and Server-Sent Events.

HTTP.why: The whole document analyses how HTTP is used for server-initiated communication, covering pipelining, chunked transfer, connection limits, proxies, timeouts and caching behaviour.
HTTP.quote: This document describes known issues and best practices related to such "bidirectional HTTP" applications, focusing on the two most common mechanisms: HTTP long polling and HTTP streaming.

rejected.why: BOSH is described as an XMPP transport binding, but only as one of three example technologies. The document is not about XMPP itself.
TCP is only the substrate. Connection handling is discussed in the context of HTTP, not as TCP behaviour.
Caching is mentioned only briefly, as a best practice of suppressing it with Cache-Control: no-cache. That is not a substantial part of the document.
Cookies are mentioned in one sentence as a way to detect multiple long poll requests from the same browser.
JSON is only the encoding Bayeux uses for its messages.
WebSocket is not discussed in the body of the document.

gaps.name: Long polling / Comet / HTTP server push
gaps.why: The document is about HTTP-based server-push techniques (long polling, streaming, Comet, Bayeux, BOSH, Server-Sent Events). The taxonomy has no tag for them beyond the generic HTTP tag.

RFC6203.title: IMAP4 Extension for Fuzzy Search
RFC6203.summary: Defines the IMAP SEARCH=FUZZY extension, adding a FUZZY search key, relevancy scores, and RELEVANCY return option and sort criterion for inexact IMAP searches.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP capability (SEARCH=FUZZY) extending SEARCH and SORT, so it belongs under IMAP.
IMAP.quote: This document describes an IMAP protocol extension enabling a server to perform searches with inexact matching and assigning relevancy scores for matched messages.

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag; email is its ancestor and is implied.
Message content is only searched; MIME is not specified or extended.
ABNF is only used to write the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
The IANA section only registers the capability; this is boilerplate.
UTF-8 is mentioned only in Security Considerations and in a SORT example.

RFC6204.title: Basic Requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge Routers
RFC6204.summary: RFC 6204 specifies basic requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge routers, covering WAN-side provisioning (SLAAC, DHCPv6, prefix delegation) and LAN-side configuration (ULA, Router Advertisements, DHCPv6 server, DNS information) for home and small-office networks.

IPv6.why: The whole document is a set of IPv6 deployment requirements for CE routers, covering addressing, router advertisement behaviour and end-user network architecture.
IPv6.quote: This document defines basic IPv6 features for a residential or small-office router, referred to as an IPv6 CE router.

DHCPv6.why: A large share of the requirements concern DHCPv6 client behaviour, prefix delegation (IA_PD), DUID persistence, DHCPv6 options, and the LAN-side DHCPv6 server.
DHCPv6.quote: The router MUST act as a requesting router for the purposes of DHCPv6 prefix delegation ([RFC3633]).
