SLAAC.why: Address assignment requirements cover SLAAC on the WAN side and the A/L flag and RA behaviour for hosts on the LAN side.
SLAAC.quote: The IPv6 CE router MUST support Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) [RFC4862].

neighbor discovery.why: Many requirements specify Router Advertisement and Router Discovery behaviour, such as Router Lifetime handling, Route Information Options, and the M/O/A/L flags.
neighbor discovery.quote: The IPv6 CE router MUST support router behavior according to Neighbor Discovery for IPv6 [RFC4861].

rejected.why: The document concerns a single CE router with its LAN interfaces; automatic provisioning of more complex home topologies is explicitly out of scope.
DNS server information is only distributed to hosts through DHCPv6 and RA options. The document does not specify DNS itself.
ICMPv6 is required through a reference and used for unreachable messages. It is not a subject of the document.
NAT appears only in the description of the IPv4 architecture, for contrast.
Security requirements are brief and defer to RFC 6092, so filtering is not a substantial part of the document.
There is no ULA tag in the taxonomy. ULA handling is covered by the IPv6 and addressing tags.

gaps.name: IPv6 CE router / CPE requirements
gaps.why: The document defines requirements for customer edge routers as a device class. The taxonomy has no tag for CPE or CE router requirements, so IPv6 is the closest fit.

RFC6205.title: Generalized Labels for Lambda-Switch-Capable (LSC) Label Switching Routers
RFC6205.summary: Defines a standard wavelength label format for GMPLS signaling and routing with lambda-switch-capable (LSC) equipment, based on the ITU-T DWDM and CWDM grids, and updates RFC 3471.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS with a standardized wavelength label for LSC LSRs, covering the label format, its use in RSVP-TE Label_Set, ERO and RRO objects, and optical transport network control. It updates RFC 3471.
GMPLS.quote: this document defines a standard lambda label format, which is compliant with both the Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) grid [G.694.1] and the Coarse Wavelength Division Multiplexing (CWDM) grid

rejected.why: GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling carries the label, but the document defines only the label format. It does not specify or extend RSVP-TE itself.
GMPLS is a child of MPLS in the taxonomy and fits more specifically. The parent is implied.
CSPF is mentioned only in passing and is explicitly out of scope.
The new subregistries are boilerplate registrations for the label fields, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Optical/WDM wavelength switching (DWDM/CWDM grids, lambda labels)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for WDM or optical-layer labels. GMPLS is the closest fit, but the DWDM/CWDM grid label encoding is itself a subject.

RFC6206.title: The Trickle Algorithm
RFC6206.summary: Specifies the Trickle algorithm, a timer-based mechanism for lossy shared-medium and low-power networks that adaptively controls message transmission to keep nodes consistent, and gives guidance and requirements for protocols that use it.

IoT.why: The algorithm targets low-power and lossy networks and constrained nodes (4-11 bytes of RAM). No more specific technology tag fits, since RPL is only cited as a user of Trickle. The IoT topic is the best fit.
IoT.quote: The Trickle algorithm allows nodes in a lossy shared medium (e.g., low-power and lossy networks) to exchange information in a highly robust, energy efficient, simple, and scalable manner.

rejected.why: RPL is cited only as one example user of Trickle in Section 6.8. The document does not specify or extend RPL.
Trickle sends to a local multicast or broadcast address, but this is only the substrate. The document is not about multicast routing or group membership.
Routing control traffic is only one of the example uses. The document defines a general timer algorithm, not a routing design.
IPv6 is mentioned only as an example of an address family for the local communication address.

gaps.name: Trickle algorithm / timer-based consistency and suppression
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for generic polite-gossip or suppression timers for lossy networks. This is the document's core subject and it is used by RPL, MPL and others.

RFC6207.title: The Media Types application/mods+xml, application/mads+xml, application/mets+xml, application/marcxml+xml, and application/sru+xml
RFC6207.summary: Registers five XML-based media types (MODS, MADS, METS, MARCXML, SRU response) for Library of Congress metadata and search-result formats.

media types.why: The document exists to register five application/*+xml media types, with a registration template for each.
media types.quote: This document specifies media types for the following formats: MODS (Metadata Object Description Schema), MADS (Metadata Authority Description Schema), METS

XML.why: All registered formats are XML schemas using the +xml suffix convention, and the document's registrations are defined by reference to application/xml. Readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: These are all XML schemas providing representations of various forms of information including metadata and search results.

rejected.why: RFC 3986 is cited only in Security Considerations, and the SRU name is just a protocol's name.
RSS and Atom are mentioned only as possible alternative SRU response formats, not specified here.
MODS, MADS and METS are library metadata schemas, not directory access protocols.
The document is about media type registration, not MIME body structure or encodings; the media types tag is more specific.

gaps.name: Library/bibliographic metadata (MODS, MADS, METS, MARC, SRU)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for digital library or bibliographic metadata formats or the SRU search protocol, which are the actual subjects of these media types.

RFC6208.title: Cloud Data Management Interface (CDMI) Media Types
RFC6208.summary: Registers five CDMI (Cloud Data Management Interface) media types (cdmi-object, -container, -domain, -capability, -queue) with IANA and summarizes their processing.

media types.why: The document's purpose is registering five application/cdmi-* media types with IANA and describing their processing.
media types.quote: This document describes several Internet media types defined for the Cloud Data Management Interface (CDMI) by the Storage Networking Industry Association (SNIA).

storage.why: The media types represent cloud storage objects, containers, domains, capabilities and queues, so readers of storage access protocols would want it.
storage.quote: is the functional interface that applications will use to create, retrieve, update, and delete data elements from the cloud.

rejected.why: CDMI only runs over HTTP; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Representations are JSON, but this is only the encoding substrate.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as the transport confidentiality mechanism.
Only referenced in the encoding considerations of the registration templates.
The text explicitly notes the CDMI 'domain' is not a DNS domain name.
Cited only in a note distinguishing CDMI domains from DNS domain names; the document has nothing to do with HEMS.

gaps.name: Cloud storage / CDMI
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for cloud data management; the storage topic is the closest fit.

RFC6209.title: Addition of the ARIA Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC6209.summary: Informational RFC defining 38 TLS cipher suites (CBC with SHA-2 HMAC, GCM, and PSK variants, including elliptic curve key exchange) that use the Korean ARIA block cipher.

ARIA.why: The document's purpose is to define ARIA cipher suites, including ARIA CBC and GCM modes, for TLS. This is exactly the ARIA tag's scope: its GCM and CCM modes and its use in TLS.
ARIA.quote: This document specifies cipher suites for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) [RFC5246] protocol to support the ARIA [RFC5794] encryption algorithm as a block cipher algorithm.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS cipher suites and code points (including PSK and ECDHE suites) and specifies their PRFs. This is a TLS extension that TLS readers would want to find.
TLS.quote: The RSA, DHE_RSA, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DH_DSS, DH_anon, ECDH, and ECDHE key exchanges are performed as defined in [RFC5246].

rejected.why: AES GCM is referenced only as the model for defining ARIA GCM; the document is about ARIA, not AES.
HMAC with SHA-256/384 is just a component of the cipher suites, not the subject.
SHA-2 hashes are used as MAC and PRF components; the document does not address them in their own right.
ECDH/ECDHE key exchanges are reused unchanged from existing TLS RFCs; only the cipher suite combinations are new.
PSK cipher suites are reused from other RFCs; the document does not specify any key management mechanism.
The IANA section merely registers the cipher suite code points. It is boilerplate, not a subject of the document.

RFC6210.title: Experiment: Hash Functions with Parameters in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and S/MIME
RFC6210.summary: Experimental RFC defining XOR-MD5, a parameterized hash algorithm, and how to use it in CMS (ASN.1 digestAlgorithms handling) and S/MIME multipart/signed micalg, to test whether hash parameters break implementations.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with a parameterized digest algorithm and specifies how SignedData, DigestedData and AuthenticatedData handle it.
CMS.quote: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) has not currently defined any hash algorithms with parameters, but anecdotal evidence suggests that defining one could cause major problems.

S/MIME.why: Defines the micalg encoding for multipart/signed S/MIME messages with hash parameters, and includes S/MIME message examples.
S/MIME.quote: This section defines the string that appears in the micalg parameter.

rejected.why: MD5 is only the building block of the experimental XOR-MD5 algorithm; the document is not about MD5 itself.
ASN.1 is the notation used to define the algorithm identifier and module, not the subject.
MIME multipart/signed micalg handling is covered under S/MIME; the document does not define general MIME body structure.
HMAC-SHA1 appears only in the authenticated-data example.
RSA is used only for signing and key transport in the examples.

RFC6211.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Algorithm Identifier Protection Attribute
RFC6211.summary: Defines a new CMS signed/authenticated attribute (CMSAlgorithmProtection) that copies digest, signature, or MAC algorithm identifiers into the protected attributes to defeat algorithm substitution attacks, with verification rules and an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with a new signed/authenticated attribute for SignerInfo and AuthenticatedData and changes CMS verification procedures.
CMS.quote: This document defines a new attribute that contains a copy of the relevant algorithm identifiers so that they are protected by the signature or authentication process.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the attribute and module, not the subject of the document.
X.509 certificates are mentioned only as a comparison for how signature algorithm protection is done there.
The OID arc is S/MIME, but the document is about CMS structures, not secure email itself.
Concerns algorithm identifier protection within CMS rather than specifying cryptographic algorithms; CMS is the more specific fit.
RSA PKCS#1 and RSA-PSS are mentioned only as examples of implicit algorithm protection.
SHA-1 and SHA-3 are mentioned only as examples of digest algorithms.

RFC6212.title: Authentication-Results Registration for Vouch by Reference Results
RFC6212.summary: Registers the "vbr" method with header.md/header.mv properties and result codes in the Authentication-Results registries so Vouch By Reference query results can be relayed in email headers.

email authentication.why: The document extends the Authentication-Results framework for email authentication by adding a VBR method, properties, and result codes. No specific child (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC, ARF) is the subject, so the parent topic fits.
email authentication.quote: This memo updates the registry of properties in Authentication-Results: message header fields to allow relaying of the results of a Vouch By Reference query.

spam.why: VBR is a domain-level reputation mechanism used to assess mail legitimacy, and the document relays its results to filters. That makes it relevant to readers of spam filtering and reputation.
spam.quote: a mechanism by which a message receiver can query a "vouching" service to determine whether or not a trusted third party is willing to state that mail

rejected.why: DKIM appears only in the example alongside the VBR result. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document defines header-field properties, but only as registry entries for an existing header. It does not define message format itself.
VBR queries use DNS, but only as a substrate. The document adds nothing about DNS.
The IANA registry additions are the mechanism for this document, but the document is about email authentication results, not IANA process.
The gateway receives mail over SMTP, but the document says nothing about SMTP.

gaps.name: Vouch By Reference (VBR)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the VBR domain reputation and vouching mechanism or for Authentication-Results header reporting. The closest matches are the email authentication and spam topics.

RFC6213.title: IS-IS BFD-Enabled TLV
RFC6213.summary: Defines a new IS-IS TLV (type 148) carried in IIHs to advertise BFD enablement per MTID/NLPID, and specifies the adjacency state rules needed so IS-IS reacts correctly to BFD-detected forwarding failures.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new TLV and modifies adjacency establishment and maintenance rules.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes a type-length-value (TLV) for use in the IS-IS routing protocol that allows for the proper use of the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol.

BFD.why: The document specifies how BFD is applied to IS-IS adjacencies, including BFD session state driving adjacency state and BFD admin-down handling.
BFD.quote: One specific application of BFD as described in [RFC5882] is to verify the forwarding ability of an IS-IS [RFC1195] router's adjacencies

rejected.why: Concerns failure detection and adjacency handling, not repair paths or loop-free alternates.
The document is protocol-specific (IS-IS), so the more specific IS-IS tag applies.

RFC6214.title: Adaptation of RFC 1149 for IPv6
RFC6214.summary: An April 1st humor RFC specifying how to carry IPv6 datagrams over the avian-carrier medium of RFC 1149, covering MTU, framing, addressing, multicast, QoS, routing and multihoming.

humor.why: Dated 1 April, it is a parody of RFC 1149 and RFC 2549 with carrier ages, ink colours and H5N1 quarantine. It belongs on the humor page.
humor.quote: This document specifies a method for transmission of IPv6 datagrams over the same medium as specified for IPv4 datagrams in RFC 1149.

IPv6.why: The document adapts IPv6 to a link. It covers the MTU of 1280 octets, address configuration, neighbor discovery, SLAAC and multicast mapping.
IPv6.quote: it is therefore necessary, indeed urgent, to specify a method of transmitting IPv6 datagrams [RFC2460] over the RFC 1149 medium

rejected.why: Section 4 mentions DSCP and per-hop behaviors only as a joke about ink colours. The document does not specify or analyse Diffserv.
It is mentioned only to say that it should not be used. The document is not about it.
It is mentioned only to say that it is impossible on this link. The document is not about it.
Section 6 is a brief joke about homing pigeons. The document does not address multihoming architectures.

RFC6215.title: MPLS Transport Profile User-to-Network and Network-to-Network Interfaces
RFC6215.summary: RFC 6215 updates the MPLS-TP framework (RFC 5921) with detailed reference-point diagrams and functional architecture for the MPLS-TP User-to-Network Interface (UNI-C/UNI-N) and Network-to-Network Interface (NNI).

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines the architecture of the MPLS-TP UNI and NNI reference points, updating the MPLS-TP framework.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document updates those reference models to show detailed reference points for these interfaces, along with further clarification of the functional architecture of MPLS-TP at a UNI and NNI.

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the more specific child tag; the parent is implied.
Only mentioned in a note that the client service control plane may be GMPLS; not what the document is about.
PWE3 is mentioned only in the context of the joint IETF/ITU-T effort; the document does not address pseudowires.
The UNI/NNI service model is not a L2VPN specification.

RFC6216.title: Example Call Flows Using Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Security Mechanisms
RFC6216.summary: Informational document giving example SIP call flows (MESSAGE over TLS, S/MIME signed/encrypted bodies), test certificates and scripts for a mock CA, and observed interoperability issues for SIP security.

SIP.why: The document exists to show SIP security call flows, SIPS URIs, and SIP-specific certificate and interoperability guidance, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document shows example call flows demonstrating the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS), and Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

S/MIME.why: A major part is signed, encrypted, and signed-plus-encrypted S/MIME bodies with ASN.1 dumps of the CMS structures, and S/MIME-specific interoperability notes.
S/MIME.quote: The text from Section 4.1 through Section 4.3 shows some simple SIP call flows using S/MIME to sign and encrypt the body of the message.

TLS.why: It gives a TLS handshake trace for SIP, and lists certificate-name checks and TLS test scenarios, so TLS readers would find it useful.
TLS.quote: The flow below shows the edited SSLDump output of the host example.com forming a TLS [RFC5246] connection to example.net.

X.509.why: It provides CA, host and user test certificates, SIP EKU and subjectAltName usage, scripts for making them, and certificate validation tests.
X.509.quote: This is an X.509v3 ([X.509]) certificate. Note that the X.509v3 Basic Constraints in the certificate allows it to be used as a CA

rejected.why: The SIP MESSAGE request is only the example payload, and the CPIM-related subjectAltName entries are incidental.
CMS structures are shown as ASN.1 dumps, but the document is about S/MIME in SIP, not CMS itself.
OCSP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a pointer, and no revocation flows are shown.
ASN.1 dumps serve only as illustrative output and the document does not address ASN.1 itself.
The X.509 tag is more specific for the test certificates and the mock CA.
MIME is the container for the S/MIME bodies, and S/MIME is the more specific tag.

RFC6217.title: Regional Broadcast Using an Atmospheric Link Layer
RFC6217.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing broadcast of datagrams via skytyping smoke in the atmosphere as a link layer, with a minimal "ADVERT" network-layer format and optional UDP-in-text encapsulation.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st joke RFC describing skywriting-based datagram broadcast as a link layer, so it belongs on the humor page.
humor.quote: The datagram MUST be displayed in the atmosphere, at an altitude of 7000 to 17000 feet (2133 to 5181 meters).

rejected.why: The 'atmospheric link layer' is a parody; the document actually forbids link-layer encapsulation and is not a real link-layer specification.
UDP is only used as an example transport for binary content in the joke encoding, not specified or extended.
Source field representations are mentioned in passing; the document is not about IP address architecture.
Base64 is merely used as the encoding for the example payload.
IPv4 and RFC 919 broadcast are referenced as background and source-address options, not the subject.

RFC6218.title: Cisco Vendor-Specific RADIUS Attributes for the Delivery of Keying Material
RFC6218.summary: Independent-stream RFC defining three Cisco vendor-specific RADIUS attributes (Keying-Material, MAC-Randomizer, Message-Authentication-Code) for AES-key-wrapped delivery of keying material such as the EAP MSK and for strong HMAC/CMAC authentication of any RADIUS message.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS vendor-specific attributes and how they are used in RADIUS messages, including Access-Accept, accounting and CoA.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines a set of vendor-specific RADIUS Attributes, allocated from the Cisco vendor space, that can be used to securely transfer cryptographic keying material

key management.why: A central purpose is delivering keying material (e.g. EAP MSK) from AAA server to access point, wrapped with a KEK and identified by KEK ID and KM ID. Readers of key provisioning would want it.
key management.quote: Many remote access deployments (for example, deployments utilizing wireless LAN technology) require the secure transmission of cryptographic keying material from a RADIUS

rejected.why: The EAP MSK is the keying material delivered, but the document does not specify or extend EAP.
AES Key Wrap (RFC 3394) and CMAC-AES are used as mechanisms; the document does not define AES itself.
HMAC-SHA variants are MAC Type options used for message authentication; HMAC itself is not what the document is about.
RADIUS is the more specific tag; the general AAA framework is not the subject.
SHA is only the hash underlying HMAC options, not a subject of the document.
The MAC-Randomizer only references RFC 4086 for random number requirements, which is a minor dependency.

RFC6219.title: The China Education and Research Network (CERNET) IVI Translation Design and Deployment for the IPv4/IPv6 Coexistence and Transition
RFC6219.summary: Informational RFC describing CERNET's IVI design and deployment, a prefix-specific stateless IPv4/IPv6 address mapping and translation mechanism (early precursor to the IETF stateless translation standards), with DNS, multicast, host operation and implementation notes.

SIIT.why: IVI is a stateless IPv4/IPv6 translation scheme built on SIIT with its own address mapping; the document covers header, transport, ICMP and fragmentation translation, so SIIT readers would want it.
SIIT.quote: the translation of the IPv4 and IPv6 headers MUST be performed according to SIIT [RFC2765], except for the source and destination addresses in the header

IPv6 transition.why: The document is about an IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and transition mechanism deployed between CERNET (IPv4) and CERNET2 (IPv6).
IPv6 transition.quote: This document presents the CERNET IVI translation design and deployment for the IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and transition.

DNS64.why: A dedicated section specifies DNS address synthesis for IPv4-only names, equivalent to DNS64, decoupled from the translator.
DNS64.quote: If the AAAA record does not exist, the IVI DNS will query the A record and map it to IVIG6(i), and return a AAAA record
DNS64.section: 4.2. DNS Service for the IVIG6(i) Addresses

rejected.why: Stateful translation is only mentioned as an IETF standard alongside IVI; IVI is stateless.
DNS is only used as supporting infrastructure; the IVI DNS behaviour is better covered by DNS64.
Multicast mapping is a brief subsection using PIM-SSM; not the main subject of the document.
Only mentioned as a way to assign IVI6 addresses.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag fits better than the parent IPv6.
Traceroute output appears only in an appendix to illustrate address mapping.

RFC6220.title: Defining the Role and Function of IETF Protocol Parameter Registry Operators
RFC6220.summary: IAB informational RFC describing the role, responsibilities and requirements of IETF Protocol Parameter Registry Operators (IANA function) and the roles of the IAB, IESG, IETF Trust and IAOC in relation to them.

IANA.why: The whole document defines the IANA protocol parameter registry function, its operator's duties, and oversight by IAB, IESG and IAOC.
IANA.quote: this document describes the operation and role of a delegated IETF Protocol Parameter Registry Operator, to be selected and administered by the IETF Administrative Support Activity
IANA.section: 2. Roles and Responsibilities Concerning IETF Protocol Parameter Registries

IPR.why: A dedicated subsection and a requirements bullet address who holds IPR in registry contents and the IETF Trust's role, which is substantive in the body.
IPR.quote: Any intellectual property rights of the IETF protocol parameter assignment information, including the IETF protocol parameter registry and its contents, are to be held by the IETF Trust

rejected.why: The document touches IESG and IAB roles but is about the registry operator function, which IANA covers more specifically.
The RFC Editor is mentioned only as an example of structural separation of roles.

RFC6221.title: Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent
RFC6221.summary: Specifies the Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent (LDRA), a Layer 2 access-node function that inserts Interface-ID relay agent options into DHCPv6 exchanges without IPv6 routing, and updates RFC 3315 server handling of zero link-address.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new relay agent variant for DHCPv6, specifying its Relay-Forward/Relay-Reply behaviour and updating RFC 3315 server behaviour.
DHCPv6.quote: A Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent (LDRA) allows Relay Agent Information to be inserted by an access node that performs a link-layer bridging (i.e., non-routing) function.

rejected.why: IPv6 is only the network the DHCPv6 messages run over; the document is about DHCPv6 relaying, not IPv6 itself.
Access nodes are Ethernet switches/DSLAMs but the document specifies no Ethernet-specific mechanism.
DSL access is only a motivating deployment example (TR-101), not the subject.
The more specific DHCPv6 child tag fits better.

RFC6222.title: Guidelines for Choosing RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Canonical Names (CNAMEs)
RFC6222.summary: Updates RFC 3550 guidance for choosing RTCP CNAMEs, replacing FQDN/IPv4-based names with UUID-, MAC-, or hash-derived identifiers to ensure uniqueness, persistent vs per-session.

RTCP.why: The whole document specifies how to choose the RTCP Canonical Name, an RTCP source description item, and updates RFC 3550 Section 6.5.1.
RTCP.quote: This memo updates those guidelines to allow endpoints to choose unique RTCP CNAMEs.

UUID.why: A UUID (version 1, 2 or 4) is the mandated method for long-term persistent CNAMEs, so UUID readers would want this use.
UUID.quote: an RTP endpoint MUST generate and store a Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) [RFC4122] for use as the "host" part of its RTCP CNAME.

rejected.why: RTP is the context, but the document is specifically about the RTCP CNAME; RTCP is the more specific tag.
SHA-256 is used only as a mixing step in the identifier procedure; no security properties are assumed.
Base64 is only the encoding for per-session identifiers.
Mentioned in Security Considerations only regarding correlation and encryption of SRTCP.
NAT is cited as a reason that IPv4 addresses are not unique, not a subject of the document.
Per-session CNAMEs give limited privacy, but this is a side consideration, not the main topic.

RFC6223.title: Indication of Support for Keep-Alive
RFC6223.summary: Defines a new SIP Via header field parameter, "keep", letting adjacent SIP entities negotiate use of the RFC 5626 NAT keep-alive mechanisms for registrations and dialogs, including the recommended keep-alive frequency.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new Via header field parameter and specifies UA and proxy behaviour for registrations and dialogs. It is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This specification defines a new Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [RFC3261] Via header field parameter, "keep", which allows adjacent SIP entities to explicitly negotiate usage

rejected.why: STUN is only the keep-alive message mechanism taken from RFC 5626. The document defines nothing new about STUN.
NAT binding maintenance is the motivation. The document specifies SIP negotiation, not NAT behaviour.
The ABNF is only a small grammar extension for the new parameter.
The only IANA content is a boilerplate registration of the Via parameter.
TLS and DTLS appear only in the Security Considerations as hop-by-hop protection.
The document negotiates keep-alives for SIP. It does not define interactive NAT traversal for real-time media, which is what this tag covers.

RFC6224.title: Base Deployment for Multicast Listener Support in Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Domains
RFC6224.summary: Informational document describing how to deploy multicast listener support in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains using MLD/IGMP proxy functions at MAGs and LMAs as multicast anchors, without changing existing protocol standards.

PMIPv6.why: The document specifies how multicast works within PMIPv6 domains, covering MAG and LMA operations, handover and binding handling.
PMIPv6.quote: deployment options for activating multicast listener functions in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains without modifying mobility and multicast protocol standards

multicast.why: The document is about deploying multicast listener support and forwarding state. This is multicast deployment generally, with no more specific child tag covering it fully.
multicast.quote: Local Mobility Anchors of Proxy Mobile IPv6 serve as multicast subscription anchor points, while Mobile Access Gateways provide Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) proxy functions

MLD.why: MLD proxying, queries, reports and timer tuning at the MAG are central to the deployment. IGMP is covered analogously for IPv4.
MLD.quote: an MLD proxy function [RFC4605] needs to be deployed on the MAG that selects the tunnel interface corresponding to the MN's LMA

rejected.why: IGMP is handled only as the IPv4 analogue of MLD in a short section, so MLD is the better fit.
MIPv6 is referenced only as background and as a comparison (home agent, bidirectional tunneling); the document is about PMIPv6.
AMT is mentioned only as one option for multicast availability in the access network.
GRE keys are discussed briefly to show that multicast needs no special treatment, so GRE is not a subject of the document.
IPv6 is only the context in which MLD operates.
PIM-SM appears only in the appendix on proxy implementations.

RFC6225.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Options for Coordinate-Based Location Configuration Information
RFC6225.summary: Defines DHCPv4 (options 123 and 144) and DHCPv6 (option 63) options that give a client its coordinate-based geodetic location (latitude, longitude, altitude, uncertainty/resolution, datum), obsoleting RFC 3825.

DHCP.why: The document defines new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option formats, client/server support rules and IANA registries for them.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol options (both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) for the coordinate-based geographic location of the client.

DHCPv6.why: It defines the new DHCPv6 GeoLoc Option (code 63), so DHCPv6 readers need it. DHCPv6 is a child of DHCP, so this tag applies alongside DHCP.
DHCPv6.quote: The format of the DHCPv6 [RFC3315] GeoLoc Option is as follows:

geolocation.why: The document is about the format and conveyance of geodetic location information, including datums, uncertainty and conversion to PIDF-LO and GML.
geolocation.quote: The Location Configuration Information (LCI) includes Latitude, Longitude, and Altitude, with resolution or uncertainty indicators for each.

rejected.why: The document describes conversion to PIDF-LO, but PIDF is only the target format and is not specified here.
Emergency calling is cited as motivation, but the document does not address emergency services protocols.
GML templates appear in the appendices, but they are only illustrative mappings.
The document creates registries, but this is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the document's main subject.

RFC6226.title: PIM Group-to-Rendezvous-Point Mapping
RFC6226.summary: RFC 6226 defines a deterministic algorithm for PIM-SM routers to choose a Rendezvous Point among Group-to-RP mappings learned via Embedded-RP, BSR, Auto-RP or static configuration, updating RFC 4601 and clarifying PIM-STD-MIB use.

PIM-SM.why: The document updates the PIM-SM RP selection algorithm of RFC 4601 Section 4.7.1, including BSR hash handling and BIDIR preference, so it belongs under PIM-SM.
PIM-SM.quote: This document defines a standard algorithm to deterministically choose between several Group-to-RP mappings for a specific group.

rejected.why: Sections 7 and 8 clarify how PIM-STD-MIB objects are interpreted, but the document defines no MIB module; this is a minor part.
The more specific child PIM-SM applies, so the parent is implied.
Embedded-RP for IPv6 is mentioned only as the top-priority case in the algorithm, not as a subject of the document.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate mapping protocols.
Implied by the PIM-SM tag, which is more specific.

RFC6227.title: Design Goals for Scalable Internet Routing
RFC6227.summary: An IRTF Routing Research Group document listing prioritized design goals (scalability, traffic engineering, multihoming, loc/id split, mobility, renumbering, security, deployability) for a new scalable Internet routing and addressing architecture.

routing architecture.why: The whole document is a prioritized list of design goals for a new, scalable routing architecture, which is the subject of routing architecture, scalability and design principles.
routing architecture.quote: the Internet routing and addressing architecture is facing challenges in inter-domain scalability, mobility, multi-homing, and inter-domain traffic engineering

multihoming.why: A dedicated design goal covers scalable multihoming, and it is one of the core challenges the document names.
multihoming.quote: Multi-homing is the capability of an organization to be connected to the Internet via more than one other organization.

renumbering.why: A dedicated design goal addresses simplified renumbering, so readers of that subject would want this RFC.
renumbering.quote: It is strongly desired that a new architecture allow end-sites to renumber their network with significantly less disruption

traffic engineering.why: Scalable inter-domain traffic engineering is one of the stated goals, with its own section.
traffic engineering.quote: Inter-domain traffic engineering today is frequently accomplished by injecting more-specific prefixes into the global routing table

IP mobility.why: A dedicated goal covers scalable mobility support, including a discussion of home agents and tunnelling approaches.
IP mobility.quote: Mobility is the capability of a host, network, or organization to change its topological connectivity with respect to the remainder of the Internet

rejected.why: BGP routing table growth is cited as motivation, but the document does not specify, extend or analyse the protocol.
Security is only one short goal, which says the new architecture must be at least as secure as today's. It does not address securing routing protocols in substance.
The loc/id separation goal is discussed in general terms. No specific protocol such as LISP is covered.
RFC 1958 is incorporated by reference. The document is about routing architecture goals specifically, not general Internet architecture principles.
Addressing is discussed only as it relates to routing scalability. The more specific renumbering and multihoming tags cover it.

gaps.name: Locator/identifier separation
gaps.why: The document sets a design goal of separating host location from identification namespaces. The taxonomy has no general tag for this, only the specific LISP, HIP and ILNP protocols.

RFC6228.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Response Code for Indication of Terminated Dialog
RFC6228.summary: RFC 6228 defines the SIP 199 Early Dialog Terminated provisional response code and a "199" option-tag, letting forking proxies and UASs tell upstream entities that an early dialog has ended before a final response is sent.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new response code and option-tag, and specifies UAC, UAS and proxy behaviour for it.
SIP.quote: This specification defines a new Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) response code, 199 Early Dialog Terminated

rejected.why: Section 8 only says a 199 response should not carry an SDP offer/answer except where RFC 3264 requires it. SDP is incidental, not a subject of the document.
SIP, which sits under this topic, is already tagged, so the parent topic is implied.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as a way to mitigate attacks, so it is boilerplate and not a subject of the document.
The IANA section registers the response code and option-tag. That is boilerplate, not a topic the document is about.

RFC6229.title: Test Vectors for the Stream Cipher RC4
RFC6229.summary: Informational RFC providing keystream test vectors for the RC4 stream cipher across several key lengths and stream offsets, for implementers.

RC4.why: The whole document is RC4 keystream test vectors for implementers, so the RC4 page is where readers would look for it.
RC4.quote: This document contains several test vectors for different key lengths and for different offsets in the stream.

rejected.why: SHA-256 is only used to derive Key 2 from a string; the document is not about SHA.
RFC 4345 (SSH Arcfour modes) motivated the document, but SSH is not specified or profiled here.
The RC4 tag is more specific and already covers this parent topic.

RFC6230.title: Media Control Channel Framework
RFC6230.summary: Defines the Media Control Channel Framework: a SIP/SDP (COMEDIA)-negotiated TCP control channel between application servers and media servers, with SYNC, CONTROL, REPORT and K-ALIVE methods, response codes, and a Control Package extension mechanism.

SIP.why: The framework is built around SIP INVITE dialogs to set up and tie the control channel lifetime to the dialog. It defines UAC/UAS behaviour for this and a new 'cfw-id' SDP attribute.
SIP.quote: The framework uses the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) to establish an application-level control mechanism between application servers and associated external servers such as media servers.

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute and the SDP offer/answer format for the application/cfw media line, using COMEDIA. SDP readers would want this.
SDP.quote: This specification defines a new media-level value attribute: 'cfw-id'.

MRCP.why: This is the framework for controlling media servers (speech and IVR services) through Control Packages. It is the closest taxonomy fit for media server control, though it is not MRCP itself.
MRCP.quote: The motivation for this framework comes from a set of requirements for Media Server Control

rejected.why: XCON requirements motivated the work, but the document is a generic control framework and does not specify the XCON framework or data model.
Megaco is mentioned only as the alternative that this framework deliberately does not follow.
TLS is a security mechanism the document requires for the channel. It defines nothing new about it.
The document registers application/cfw, but that is IANA boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
RTP is the media flow the control server handles. The document does not specify RTP.
TCP is only the substrate for the control channel.

gaps.name: Media server control / Media Control Channel Framework (MEDIACTRL)
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers generic media server control frameworks and their Control Packages. MRCP is the nearest, but it is a separate protocol.

RFC6231.title: An Interactive Voice Response (IVR) Control Package for the Media Control Channel Framework
RFC6231.summary: Defines the msc-ivr/1.0 Media Control Channel Framework control package: XML elements for preparing, starting, terminating and auditing IVR dialogs (prompt playback, DTMF collection, recording, runtime controls) on a media server, with VoiceXML usage.

MRCP.why: The document specifies a media server control package for IVR/speech-style dialog services. MRCP is the closest taxonomy fit for media resource control, though it is a different protocol.
MRCP.quote: This document defines a Media Control Channel Framework Package for Interactive Voice Response (IVR) dialog interaction on media connections and conferences.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document is the XML schema and element definitions for the package, so readers of XML-based protocol formats would want it.
XML.quote: The functionality of this package is defined by messages, containing XML [XML] elements, transported using the Media Control Channel Framework.

rejected.why: SIP only sets up the control channel and connections; the package itself does not extend SIP.
Dialogs can run on conferences, but the document is not about conferencing frameworks. The mixer is a separate package.
It registers application/msc-ivr+xml, but this is boilerplate IANA material rather than the subject.
HTTP is only used to fetch and upload media, grammars and dialogs.
SDP labels are only referenced in stream selection.
RTP and DTMF payloads are only mentioned in passing.

gaps.name: Media Control Channel Framework / MEDIACTRL control packages
gaps.why: The document is a control package for the Media Control Channel Framework, and a media server control tag for the framework and its packages is missing. MRCP is only an approximate fit.

gaps.name: IVR / VoiceXML dialog languages
gaps.why: IVR dialogs, DTMF collection and VoiceXML usage have no tag in the taxonomy.

RFC6232.title: Purge Originator Identification TLV for IS-IS
RFC6232.summary: Defines the Purge Originator Identification TLV (code 13) for IS-IS, added to purges to record the system ID of the originating or upstream IS, and extends use of the Dynamic Hostname TLV in purges.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies a new IS-IS TLV and its handling in purge flooding, and updates IS-IS RFCs 5301, 5304 and 5310.
IS-IS.quote: this document defines a TLV to be added to purges to record the system ID of the IS generating the purge.

rejected.why: Only IS-IS is addressed; OSPF is not mentioned.
The authentication interaction is a Security Considerations caveat about legacy systems discarding purges, not the subject of the document.
Locating the purge source aids operators, but the document defines a protocol TLV rather than management practice.

RFC6233.title: IS-IS Registry Extension for Purges
RFC6233.summary: Extends the IANA IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry with a Purge column listing which TLVs may appear in purged LSPs, and updates the rules for generating and accepting purges when IS-IS authentication is used.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies IS-IS purge generation and processing rules and which TLVs are allowed in purged LSPs, updating RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. Readers of IS-IS would want it.
IS-IS.quote: an implementation that implements authentication MUST NOT accept a purge that contains any TLV listed in the registry that is not acceptable in a purge.

rejected.why: The registry extension is IANA-related, but the substance is IS-IS protocol behaviour for purges. The IANA section is boilerplate-like application of that change, not a document about IANA stewardship.

Authentication interaction with purges is covered, but the document is about IS-IS purge rules and the TLV registry, not routing security generally. The cryptographic authentication mechanisms themselves are defined in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310.
Authentication is only the context for the updated purge acceptance rules. The document does not define an authentication mechanism.

RFC6234.title: US Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA and SHA-based HMAC and HKDF)
RFC6234.summary: RFC 6234 specifies the US SHA-224/256/384/512 hash algorithms and supplies reference C code for SHA, SHA-based HMAC and HKDF, with a test driver; it obsoletes RFC 4634.

SHA.why: The document specifies SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 (padding, functions, constants, processing) and provides code, including SHA-1.
SHA.quote: This document makes open source code performing these SHA hash functions conveniently available to the Internet community.

HMAC.why: Section 7.1 and 8.3 provide HMAC code built on every SHA variant, with test vectors; the HMAC specification itself is in RFC 2104.
HMAC.quote: code to perform SHA-based Hashed Message Authentication Codes (HMACs) is also included.

rejected.why: HKDF is a key derivation function and code is provided, but the document is not about key management; it only supplies an implementation of RFC 5869.
RFC 4086 is mentioned only as a general use of hashes for random number generation; not a subject of this document.
The SHA OIDs are listed in passing; no ASN.1 modules or encoding defined.
Different hash family; not discussed.

gaps.name: HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function)
gaps.why: The document adds sample code for HKDF, but the taxonomy has no HKDF or generic KDF tag; the nearest parent, key management, is not a good fit.

RFC6235.title: IP Flow Anonymization Support
RFC6235.summary: Describes anonymization techniques for IP flow data and defines IPFIX Information Elements and an Options Template to export anonymization metadata, plus guidelines for anonymized export and storage over IPFIX.

IPFIX.why: The document extends the IPFIX information model with new Information Elements (285-287) and an Anonymization Options Template, and gives IPFIX-specific guidelines for export and storage.
IPFIX.quote: defines an information model and Options-based method for anonymization metadata export within the IPFIX protocol or storage in IPFIX Files.

privacy.why: A large part of the document categorizes anonymization techniques and their parameters to protect user privacy in flow data. No privacy-technique tag fits better, so the generic privacy topic applies.
privacy.quote: anonymization (i.e., the deletion or transformation of information that is considered sensitive and that could be used to reveal the identity of subjects involved in a communication)

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a way to secure the channel to a Mediator and in Security Considerations. It is not the subject.
Only mentioned as a transport and for per-stream export of anonymization records. Nothing new is defined about it.
Mentioned only as a possible out-of-band information leak.
IPv6 addresses appear only as a field type to anonymize. The document does not address IPv6 itself.
Mentioned only as an example keyed permutation function. The document is not about HMAC.
Flow measurement is the context, but the document is about anonymizing and exporting flow data, not measurement methods.

gaps.name: Traffic data anonymization
gaps.why: Anonymization of network trace and flow data (truncation, permutation, prefix-preserving pseudonymization) is a major subject here. The taxonomy has only the generic privacy topic for it.

RFC6236.title: Negotiation of Generic Image Attributes in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC6236.summary: Defines the SDP 'imageattr' media-level attribute for negotiating image size, sample/picture aspect ratio and preference in offer/answer exchanges, with syntax, rules, codec interactions and examples.

SDP.why: The document specifies a new SDP attribute, its ABNF syntax, offer/answer rules and IANA registration of the attribute.
SDP.quote: This section defines the SDP image attribute 'imageattr', which can be used in an SDP Offer/Answer exchange to indicate various image attribute parameters.

rejected.why: H.264 and its sprop-parameter-sets are discussed only as a codec the attribute must interoperate with, not specified here.
The attribute is deliberately codec agnostic; codecs (H.263, H.264, MPEG-4) are only discussed for interaction, not defined.
SIP UPDATE/REFER are mentioned only as renegotiation triggers; the document is about SDP.
Payload formats such as RFC 6184 are referenced for interaction only; none is defined.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the attribute syntax.

RFC6237.title: IMAP4 Multimailbox SEARCH Extension
RFC6237.summary: Defines the IMAP MULTISEARCH extension, adding an ESEARCH command that searches multiple mailboxes in one command, with MAILBOX/TAG/UIDVALIDITY correlators in ESEARCH responses, and updates RFC 4466.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP4 with a new ESEARCH command, source options and a MULTISEARCH capability. IMAP is the protocol it specifies and extends.
IMAP.quote: This extension allows a client to search multiple mailboxes with one command, and includes MAILBOX and TAG fields in the ESEARCH response

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section. The document is not about ABNF.
IMAP is a child of email, so the parent is implied and is not listed separately.
The only IANA content is the boilerplate registration of the MULTISEARCH capability, which is not the document's subject.

RFC6238.title: TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
RFC6238.summary: RFC 6238 specifies TOTP, a time-based variant of the HOTP one-time password algorithm that replaces the counter with a time-step value, with security guidance, resynchronization, a reference implementation and test vectors.

OTP.why: The document defines the TOTP one-time password algorithm, an extension of HOTP, so it belongs on the One-Time Passwords page.
OTP.quote: TOTP is the time-based variant of this algorithm, where a value T, derived from a time reference and a time step, replaces the counter C

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-1/256/512 is the building block used inside HOTP and TOTP. The document does not specify or extend HMAC.
SHA-256 and SHA-512 are allowed as the hash functions underneath HMAC, but the document is not about the hash family.
Key generation guidance only refers to RFC 4086 in the Security Considerations. This is not a main subject.
Resynchronization covers clock drift between prover and verifier for OTP validation. It is not about network clock synchronization protocols.
OTP is the more specific tag for two-factor authentication tokens, so the broader parent is not needed.

RFC6239.title: Suite B Cryptographic Suites for Secure Shell (SSH)
RFC6239.summary: Informational RFC profiling the SSH transport and user authentication protocols for NSA Suite B compliance, mandating ECDH, ECDSA with X.509v3 certificates, AES-GCM and SHA-256/384, with allowed algorithm name lists and security-level rules.

SSH.why: The document profiles SSH transport, key exchange negotiation (SSH_MSG_KEXINIT) and user authentication for Suite B, so it is about SSH.
SSH.quote: This document describes the architecture of a Suite B compliant implementation of the Secure Shell Transport Layer Protocol and the Secure Shell Authentication Protocol.

ECDSA.why: A substantial part of the document sets rules for ECDSA on P-256/P-384 for host and user authentication.
ECDSA.quote: SecSh-B uses ECDSA-256/384 for server authentication, user authentication, and in X.509 certificates.

X.509.why: The document requires X.509v3 certificates conforming to the Suite B certificate profile for server and user authentication.
X.509.quote: User authentication MUST begin with public key authentication using ECDSA-256/384 with X.509v3 certificates

AES.why: The document mandates AES-GCM (128 and 256) for SSH packet encryption and integrity, with a dedicated section.
AES.quote: AES GCM will both encrypt the packet and form a 16-octet authentication tag to ensure data integrity.
AES.section: 6. Confidentiality and Data Integrity of SSH Binary Packets

rejected.why: ECDSA is the more specific tag for the signature use. The ECDH key exchange is covered by the SSH profile and is not a separate primary subject.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 are only named as components of the suite. The document does not specify or analyse them.
The document only points to the Suite B certificate profile (RFC 5759). X.509 is the more specific tag.
The specific tags AES, ECDSA and X.509 already cover the cryptographic content.

gaps.name: Suite B
gaps.why: The document is about the NSA Suite B cryptographic suite profile. The taxonomy has no tag for Suite B or national cryptographic suites.

RFC6240.title: Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) Circuit Emulation over Packet (CEP) MIB Using SMIv2
RFC6240.summary: Defines the PW-CEP-STD-MIB SMIv2 module for managing and monitoring SONET/SDH circuit emulation pseudowires over a packet network, including configuration, fractional SPE, and performance-history tables.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (PW-CEP-STD-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables, conformance groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

pseudowire.why: The MIB manages CEP pseudowires and works with PW-STD-MIB, so it belongs on the pseudowire emulation page.
pseudowire.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling Synchronous Optical Network/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) circuits over a Packet Switch Network (PSN).

SONET.why: A large part of the module models SONET/SDH paths, VTs, VC-3/VC-4 fractional mappings and pointer adjustments, so SONET/SDH readers would want it.
SONET.quote: CEP is currently specified to carry "structured" SONET/SDH paths, meaning that each SONET/SDH path or Virtual Tributary (VT)

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Performance-history counters (ES/SES/UAS) are part of the MIB but are not a measurement methodology.
RTP header suppression is only a single configuration object.

gaps.name: Circuit Emulation over Packet (CEP) / TDM circuit emulation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TDM circuit emulation services; pseudowire is the closest fit.

RFC6241.title: Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF)
RFC6241.summary: RFC 6241 specifies the NETCONF protocol, an XML/RPC-based mechanism to install, manipulate and delete network device configuration, including its operations, datastores, capabilities, subtree filtering, error model and a YANG module of the operations; it obsoletes RFC 4741.

NETCONF.why: The document is the base NETCONF protocol specification: RPC model, operations, datastores, capabilities and errors.
NETCONF.quote: The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) defined in this document provides mechanisms to install, manipulate, and delete the configuration of network devices.

XML.why: A substantial part covers XML encoding rules, namespaces, an XML schema for the messages layer, and XML subtree filtering and XPath filtering.
XML.quote: XML serves as the encoding format for NETCONF, allowing complex hierarchical data to be expressed in a text format

YANG.why: The document normatively defines the ietf-netconf YANG module for the protocol operations and registers it.
YANG.quote: The syntax and XML encoding of the protocol operations are formally defined in the YANG module in Appendix C.

rejected.why: SSH is the mandatory transport mapping, but it is defined in RFC 6242; here it is only a substrate.
TLS is mentioned only as an example secure transport, so it is not tagged.
The parent topic is implied by the NETCONF tag.
BEEP appears only as an example transport layer in the figure and security text.
The document sets transport requirements, but the actual mappings are in other documents.
RADIUS is mentioned only as an example authentication mechanism.

RFC6242.title: Using the NETCONF Protocol over Secure Shell (SSH)
RFC6242.summary: Defines how NETCONF runs as the "netconf" SSH subsystem (port 830), including capability exchange, chunked and end-of-message framing, and session close; obsoletes RFC 4742.

NETCONF.why: The document specifies a transport mapping for NETCONF, including hello exchange, framing and session termination, so NETCONF readers need it.
NETCONF.quote: This document describes a method for invoking and running the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) within a Secure Shell (SSH) session as an SSH subsystem.

SSH.why: It defines a new SSH subsystem, port usage and username handling, so SSH readers would look for it.
SSH.quote: the NETCONF client will invoke NETCONF as an SSH subsystem called "netconf".

rejected.why: NETCONF messages are XML, but XML is only the payload that is framed, not the subject.
ABNF is only used as notation for the chunked framing rule.
Considered because this is a NETCONF-over-SSH binding. NETCONF and SSH tags already cover it more specifically.
The IANA section only records the port 830 and subsystem name assignments, which is boilerplate.
Not discussed; the document is only about transport.

RFC6243.title: With-defaults Capability for NETCONF
RFC6243.summary: Defines the NETCONF with-defaults capability, which lets a server advertise its default-handling basic mode (report-all, trim, explicit) and lets clients control retrieval of default data via a <with-defaults> parameter and a 'default' XML attribute, with a YANG module and XSD.

NETCONF.why: The document extends NETCONF with a new capability, a new parameter on <get>, <get-config>, <copy-config>, and changes to <edit-config> behaviour.
NETCONF.quote: This document defines a capability-based extension to the NETCONF protocol that allows the NETCONF client to identify how defaults are processed by the server

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document is the normative ietf-netconf-with-defaults YANG module, which augments the NETCONF operations.
YANG.quote: The following YANG module defines the addition of the with-defaults element to the <get>, <get-config>, and <copy-config> operations.

rejected.why: XML and XSD are used only to encode the 'default' attribute and messages; the document is not about XML usage itself.
SNMP is only mentioned in the terminology as one way a management application can reach the device.
The IANA section registers a capability URN, XML namespaces and a module name, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The parent topic is implied by the NETCONF tag, and a more specific tag fits.

RFC6244.title: An Architecture for Network Management Using NETCONF and YANG
RFC6244.summary: Informational architecture document describing how NETCONF and YANG together support network management applications, covering their elements, solution-building roles, and modeling considerations such as defaults, compliance, and config vs. operational state data.

NETCONF.why: The document describes NETCONF operations, datastores, capabilities and transports as a core element of the architecture.
NETCONF.quote: NETCONF defines an XML-based remote procedure call (RPC) mechanism that leverages the simplicity and availability of high-quality XML parsers.

YANG.why: A large part of the document covers YANG statements, constraints, extensibility, YIN/DSDL translations, and modeling considerations.
YANG.quote: YANG is a data modeling language for NETCONF.  It allows the description of hierarchies of data nodes ("nodes") and the constraints that exist among them.

rejected.why: RESTCONF is not mentioned; the document predates it and covers only NETCONF.
SSH is only the mandatory transport for NETCONF, not a subject of the document.
XML is the encoding substrate for NETCONF and YANG content, not the subject.
The parent is implied by the NETCONF and YANG tags, and the document is about those technologies specifically.
Mentioned only in passing (MIB browser analogy); not about SNMP.
Listed only as one of several NETCONF transport mappings.

RFC6245.title: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) Key Extension for Mobile IPv4
RFC6245.summary: Defines a new Mobile IPv4 extension, the GRE Key Extension, letting a Foreign Agent and Home Agent exchange GRE Key values so GRE tunnels can distinguish per-session data streams (e.g., overlapping VPN home addresses).

Mobile IPv4.why: The document defines a new Mobile IPv4 registration extension and the FA/HA/MN procedures for using it.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This document specifies a new extension for use by a Foreign Agent (FA) operating Mobile IP for IPv4.

GRE.why: The extension carries the GRE Key field value and governs GRE tunnel setup and keying between FA and HA, so GRE readers would want it.
GRE.quote: This extension contains the GRE key [RFC2890] required for establishing a GRE tunnel between the FA and the HA.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the default encapsulation and fallback; the document is about GRE as the alternative.
Only cited as the source of the overlapping-home-address use case (3GPP2 X.S0011); the document is not about cdma2000.
VPNs are the motivating use case (overlapping home addresses), but the document does not specify provider-provisioned VPNs.
IANA section only registers type 48 and a sub-type space; boilerplate, not the subject.

RFC6246.title: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Interoperability with Customer Edge (CE) Bridges
RFC6246.summary: Informational RFC describing how a VPLS PE can be modelled with an IEEE 802.1ad bridge module so that interoperability issues with customer-edge IEEE bridges (service mapping, protocol handling, partial PW mesh, multicast, topology changes, redundancy, MAC learning) are delegated to the bridge module.

VPLS.why: The whole document is about VPLS PE architecture and its interoperability with CE bridges and 802.1ad networks.
VPLS.quote: This document extends the PE model described in [RFC4664] based on the IEEE 802.1ad bridge module and illustrates a clear demarcation between IEEE bridge module and IETF LAN emulation module.

rejected.why: The document is about IEEE 802.1ad bridging and Ethernet services, but VPLS is the more specific subject and the Ethernet tag is about IP over Ethernet and Ethernet OAM. It was considered as a secondary tag and rejected.
Pseudowires are the substrate of VPLS here (full mesh, partial mesh failures). The document does not specify or extend pseudowire emulation itself.
IGMP snooping is mentioned only as one possible way to make multicast delivery more efficient. It is not a main subject.
VPLS is a child of L2VPN and the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
802.1AX link aggregation is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that needs peering.
MPLS is the underlying network for VPLS. The document does not address MPLS itself.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.1ad provider bridges / Spanning Tree (RSTP/MSTP) bridging
gaps.why: A large part of the document covers 802.1ad provider bridge behaviour, S-VLAN/C-VLAN components and customer spanning tree handling. The taxonomy has no tag for IEEE bridging.

RFC6247.title: Moving the Undeployed TCP Extensions RFC 1072, RFC 1106, RFC 1110, RFC 1145, RFC 1146, RFC 1379, RFC 1644, and RFC 1693 to Historic Status
RFC6247.summary: Reclassifies eight undeployed TCP extension RFCs (long-delay paths, big window/NAK, alternate checksum, T/TCP, partial order service) as Historic and directs IANA to mark the associated TCP options obsolete.

TCP.why: The whole document concerns the status of TCP extensions and the TCP option registry, so TCP readers would look for it.
TCP.quote: This document reclassifies several TCP extensions that have never seen widespread use to Historic status.

rejected.why: The alternate checksum options RFC 1145/1146 are only listed for status change; the document does not address checksums itself.
The IANA action (marking TCP options obsolete) is a minor boilerplate-like step, not the document's subject.
The status changes are RFC Editor actions, but the document is about TCP extensions rather than RFC series format or policy.

RFC6248.title: RFC 4148 and the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) Registry of Metrics Are Obsolete
RFC6248.summary: Obsoletes RFC 4148 and withdraws the IANA IPPM Metrics Registry because its structure cannot uniquely identify IPPM metrics and it has no users.

performance measurement.why: The document concerns the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) registry of metrics. It explains why the registry cannot uniquely identify metrics given Type P, metric and stream parameter variability. Readers of performance measurement would want it.
performance measurement.quote: the IETF reclassify [RFC4148] as Obsolete.
performance measurement.section: 2. Action to Reclassify RFC 4148 and the Corresponding IANA Registry as Obsolete

IANA.why: The document directs IANA to withdraw a registry and modifies the registry MIB description. It is a registry lifecycle action, so IANA registry readers would want it.
IANA.quote: the IANA withdraw the current IPPM Metrics Registry from further updates and note that it too is Obsolete.
IANA.section: 2. Action to Reclassify RFC 4148 and the Corresponding IANA Registry as Obsolete

rejected.why: The registry is defined as a MIB module and its DESCRIPTION is edited. That is only the registry's encoding, and the document does not define or specify MIB content.
Not discussed. The MIB is mentioned only as the format of the registry.

RFC6249.title: Metalink/HTTP: Mirrors and Hashes
RFC6249.summary: Specifies Metalink/HTTP, which conveys mirror lists, peer-to-peer metainfo, signatures and whole-file digests in HTTP Link and Digest header fields so clients can do robust multi-source downloads.

HTTP.why: The document defines how HTTP header fields (Link, Digest, ETag) carry download metadata. It also specifies client and server behaviour for range requests, If-Match and multi-source downloads.
HTTP.quote: Metalink/HTTP describes multiple download locations (mirrors), Peer-to-Peer, cryptographic hashes, digital signatures, and other information using existing standards for HTTP header fields.

web linking.why: It defines a new Link relation type, "duplicate", and new link attributes (pri, geo, pref, depth, name). Readers of web linking would want this.
web linking.quote: Mirrors are specified with the Link header fields [RFC5988] and a relation type of "duplicate" as defined in Section 8.

rejected.why: Metalink/XML (RFC 5854) is referenced as an alternative representation and for partial hashes. This document does not specify it.
OpenPGP signatures are only advertised via a Link header with a media type. The document defines nothing about OpenPGP itself.
S/MIME signatures are only referenced through a Link relation. The document says nothing new about S/MIME.
FTP is only a possible mirror protocol that clients should support. The document does not specify it.
ETags are used for mirror consistency checks and early mismatch detection, not for caching.
SHA-256 is mandated as the digest algorithm, but the document is not about the hash family.

gaps.name: Metalink download description / mirrors
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for download mirroring or multi-source download metadata (Metalink). It is only partly covered by HTTP and web linking.

RFC6250.title: Evolution of the IP Model
RFC6250.summary: IAB informational RFC documenting the IP service model as seen by upper layers and applications, and how it evolved, organised as a list of common misconceptions (routing, addressing, extensibility, security) with guidance to protocol designers.

internet architecture.why: The document is an IAB architectural discussion of the IP service model, its invariants, and how it should evolve.
internet architecture.quote: The key to maintaining an interoperable Internet is documenting and maintaining invariants that higher layers can depend on, and being very judicious with changes.

internet layer.why: It is about the IP layer's service: datagram delivery, addressing, subnets and links, and multicast/broadcast. No specific child tag covers the service model as a whole.
internet layer.quote: we use the term "IP service model" to refer to the model exposed by IP to higher-layer protocols and applications.

rejected.why: IPv6 is mentioned as one example of changing address assumptions, but the document is not about IPv6.
NATs and firewalls are cited as a cause of broken assumptions, but they are not specified or analysed in their own right.
Section 3.2 covers address misconceptions, but it is only one part of a broader IP service model document. The internet layer tag covers it.
Multicast and broadcast support are discussed as misconceptions, in only two or three subsections. This is not a document about multicast.
Mobile IPv6 and HIP appear as examples that restore address stability, not as subjects of the document.
TCP is mentioned as being affected by reordering and as an example transport. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC6251.title: Using Kerberos Version 5 over the Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol
RFC6251.summary: RFC 6251 defines a STARTTLS extension for Kerberos V5 that upgrades KDC-client TCP exchanges to TLS, with DNS SRV discovery ("kerberos-tls") and server certificate rules.

Kerberos.why: The document extends the Kerberos V5 protocol with a STARTTLS extension, new KDC discovery service, and certificate requirements for KDCs.
Kerberos.quote: describes how a Kerberos V5 implementation may upgrade communication between clients and Key Distribution Centers (KDCs) to use the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol

transport mapping.why: It specifies a binding of Kerberos over TLS/TCP, including framing, negotiation, and shutdown, which is a transport mapping.
transport mapping.quote: the Kerberos V5 authentication protocol is performed within the protected TLS channel, like a normal TCP Kerberos V5 exchange

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate used for protection. The document defines no new TLS extension, only how Kerberos uses TLS.
DNS SRV records are used for discovery, but the only new item is a service name. This is not about DNS itself.
The SAN otherName for the realm is a small certificate-binding detail, not the main subject.
The Kerberos TCP extension mechanism (RFC 5021) is relied on but not extended as a TCP matter.

RFC6252.title: A Framework of Media-Independent Pre-Authentication (MPA) for Inter-Domain Handover Optimization
RFC6252.summary: Informational IRTF MOBOPTS framework describing Media-independent Pre-Authentication (MPA), a mobile-assisted, mobility-protocol-agnostic handover optimization combining pre-authentication, pre-configuration and proactive handover over a tunnel, with experimental results.

IP mobility.why: The document is a handover optimization framework for IP-layer and higher mobility protocols (MIPv4/v6, MOBIKE, HIP, SIP mobility). No specific child mobility tag fits since it is protocol-independent.
IP mobility.quote: MPA is a mobile-assisted, secure handover optimization scheme that works over any link layer and with any mobility management protocol

authentication.why: Pre-authentication with an authentication agent, establishing an MPA-SA and deriving keys, is a core part of the framework, including bootstrapping link-layer security.
authentication.quote: MPA's pre-authentication, pre-configuration, and proactive handover techniques allow many of the handoff-related operations to take place before the mobile node has moved

rejected.why: PANA is used as one possible authentication/tunnel-management protocol, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Mobile IPv6 is one of several mobility protocols MPA is applied to, not the subject.
IKEv2 is an optional mechanism for address acquisition and tunnel management, not the subject.
DHCP is used for proactive address acquisition as a substrate; no new DHCP behaviour is defined.
EAP is only referenced as the kind of authentication protocol that would be suitable, not specified or extended.
HOKEY is cited as related work; MPA is a different approach.

gaps.name: Handover optimization / fast handover
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for generic mobility handover optimization; the closest is the broad IP mobility topic.

RFC6253.title: Host Identity Protocol Certificates
RFC6253.summary: Specifies the HIP CERT parameter for carrying digital certificates in HIP control packets, the HIT representation in X.509 v3 and SPKI certificates, and error signaling for failed certificate verification.

HIP.why: The document defines a new HIP parameter, its grouping rules, certificate types and NOTIFY error types, and updates RFC 5201.
HIP.quote: This document specifies the CERT parameter, which is used to transmit digital certificates in HIP.

X.509.why: A substantial section profiles how HITs are carried in X.509 v3 issuer and subject alternative name extensions, with a full example.
X.509.quote: the respective HIT MUST be placed into the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension using the GeneralName form iPAddress
X.509.section: 3. X.509 v3 Certificate Object and Host Identities

SPKI.why: The document defines how HITs are represented in SPKI certificates and gives a full example.
SPKI.section: 4. SPKI Cert Object and Host Identities

rejected.why: The document uses certificates but the PKI tag is implied by its X.509 and SPKI children, so it is not listed separately.
LDAP URLs and DNs are only referenced as certificate-location encodings, not specified or extended.
HITs are formatted as IPv6 addresses (ORCHID), but the document is not about IPv6.
DER is only cited as the wire format for X.509 and is not something the document defines.
The hash-and-URL encoding is borrowed from the IKEv2 specification, and the document does not address IKE.

RFC6254.title: Request to Move RFC 2754 to Historic Status
RFC6254.summary: Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2754 and recommends moving it to Historic status, because its IANA actions (creating and signing RPSL inetnum and as-block objects) were never carried out and RPKI now fills that role.

RPSL.why: The document concerns the RPSL IANA requests (signed inetnum and as-block objects in the Distributed RPSL system) and retires them. Readers of the RPSL subject would want it.
RPSL.quote: RFC 2754 [RFC2754] requests that the IANA create a repository of Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) objects and digitally sign them.

rejected.why: RPKI and ROAs are mentioned only as the alternative technology that replaced Distributed RPSL. The document does not specify or analyse them.
The document directs IANA not to carry out RFC 2754's actions, but that is an administrative consequence. It does not give guidance on IANA registries or stewardship in general.
The security aspects are only the RPSL object signing that never happened. RPSL covers this more specifically, and RPKI is only mentioned in passing.
It is a request to reclassify an RFC as Historic, but it does not describe or change IETF process.

RFC6255.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking Bundle Protocol IANA Registries
RFC6255.summary: Describes the IANA registries created for the Delay-Tolerant Networking Bundle Protocol (block types, version, control flags, status report flags and reason codes), handed off from the DTNRG ad hoc registries.

DTN.why: The whole document defines registries for fields of the DTN Bundle Protocol, so DTN readers would want it.
DTN.quote: The Bundle Protocol (BP) [RFC5050] has fields requiring a registry managed by IANA.

rejected.why: The document is about registries for one specific protocol, and the DTN tag covers it. The IANA topic is for general registry guidance and stewardship, which this document does not provide.
SDNV encoding is mentioned only as how flag fields are encoded. It is not ASN.1.
The document is an IRTF hand-off of registries. It does not describe IETF procedures.

RFC6256.title: Using Self-Delimiting Numeric Values in Protocols
RFC6256.summary: Informational IRTF DTNRG document explaining the Self-Delimiting Numeric Value (SDNV) variable-length integer encoding, with encode/decode algorithms, comparison to TLV and older formats, and usage guidance.

DTN.why: SDNVs were created by the DTN Research Group for the Bundle Protocol and LTP, and the document explains their motivation in DTN. Readers of the DTN subject would want it.
DTN.quote: Self-Delimiting Numeric Values (SDNVs) have recently been introduced as a field type in proposed Delay-Tolerant Networking protocols.

data formats.why: The document defines a generic numeric encoding format with encoding and decoding algorithms. No more specific data-format tag fits, so the parent topic applies.
data formats.quote: SDNVs encode an arbitrary-length non-negative integer or arbitrary-length bitstring with minimum overhead.

rejected.why: SDNV resembles the ASN.1 BER tag-identifier encoding, but the document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
TCP's receive window is used only as an example of a fixed-width field that proved too small.
The IPv4 address length is used only as a motivating example.
The document says its motivation is extensibility, not data compression, even though the encoding is equivalent to Elias gamma coding.

gaps.name: variable-length integer encoding / protocol field design
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for generic binary field encodings such as SDNV or varints. Only the generic 'data formats' topic fits.

RFC6257.title: Bundle Security Protocol Specification
RFC6257.summary: Defines the Bundle Security Protocol for DTN, providing hop-by-hop authentication, payload integrity and confidentiality, and extension-block protection for the Bundle Protocol through security blocks and mandatory ciphersuites.

DTN.why: The RFC specifies security blocks (BAB, PIB, PCB, ESB) and processing rules for the DTN Bundle Protocol, so it belongs on the DTN page.
DTN.quote: This document defines the bundle security protocol, which provides data integrity and confidentiality services for the Bundle Protocol.

rejected.why: CMS is used only to package keys and signatures inside security blocks; the document does not specify or extend CMS.
AES-GCM is used in the mandatory ciphersuites, but the document is not about AES itself.
RSA is a building block in the ciphersuites; the document defines no new RSA usage beyond that.
HMAC-SHA1 is the primitive inside the BAB-HMAC ciphersuite, not the subject of the document.
X.509 certificates are mentioned only for key distribution in the Key Management section, which defers key management.
This is a general parent topic; the specific DTN tag already covers the subject, and DTN sits under transport.

RFC6258.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking Metadata Extension Block
RFC6258.summary: Defines the Metadata Extension Block for the DTN Bundle Protocol, which carries typed metadata that nodes use for storage and forwarding decisions, and defines a URI metadata type and a metadata type registry.

DTN.why: The whole document specifies an extension block for the DTN Bundle Protocol, including its format and processing rules.
DTN.quote: This document defines an extension block that may be used with the Bundle Protocol [RFC5050] within the context of a Delay-Tolerant Networking architecture

rejected.why: URIs are only the encoding for one metadata type (0x01). The document does not specify or extend the URI syntax itself.
The IANA section registers a metadata type registry and a block type code. This is boilerplate, and the body is not about IANA guidance.
BAB-HMAC appears only in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate and not what the document is about.
The Security Considerations only discuss how the Bundle Security Protocol applies to the new block. The main body is not about security.

RFC6259.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking Previous-Hop Insertion Block
