RFC6259.summary: Defines the Previous-Hop Insertion Block, a one-hop DTN Bundle Protocol extension block carrying the forwarding node's member EID to the next-hop node, with its format and processing rules.

DTN.why: The document specifies a new Bundle Protocol extension block (PHIB), its format and processing, so it is squarely about DTN and the Bundle Protocol.
DTN.quote: This document defines an extension block for use with the Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) Bundle Protocol.

rejected.why: Flood routing is only cited as a use case for the PHIB; the document defines a block, not a routing protocol.
Security blocks (BAB, PIB) are discussed only in relation to the PHIB in the Security Considerations; the document does not specify a security mechanism.
The only IANA action is allocating one block type codepoint, which is boilerplate.
Tunnelling is mentioned as an example where the previous hop cannot be inferred, but the document is not about tunnelling.

RFC6260.title: Compressed Bundle Header Encoding (CBHE)
RFC6260.summary: Defines Compressed Bundle Header Encoding, a convergence-layer convention that compresses DTN Bundle Protocol primary-block endpoint IDs into integer node/service pairs, and registers the "ipn" URI scheme for conformant EIDs.

DTN.why: The whole document specifies a convergence-layer adaptation for the Bundle Protocol, compressing primary block EIDs.
DTN.quote: convention by which Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) Bundle Protocol (BP) "convergence-layer" adapters may represent endpoint identifiers in a compressed form within the primary blocks of bundles

URI.why: Defines and registers the new "ipn" URI scheme (syntax, semantics) that is central to CBHE conformance; URI readers would want it.
URI.quote: this document defines an additional URI scheme named "ipn".

rejected.why: CBHE compresses DTN bundle headers, not protocol headers on constrained links in the sense of ROHC/IPHC; DTN tag fits more specifically.
The IANA section only registers the ipn scheme; boilerplate-like and covered by the URI tag.
ABNF is used only to write the URI syntax, not the subject.
Security considerations are boilerplate here and the document only mentions BSP interactions in passing.

RFC6261.title: Encrypted Signaling Transport Modes for the Host Identity Protocol
RFC6261.summary: Experimental RFC defining two HIP signaling transport modes (ESP and ESP-TCP), negotiated via a new HIP_TRANSPORT_MODE parameter, so HIP control messages travel over the encrypted ESP connection, including failure recovery and mobility handling.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with a new parameter, negotiation procedure, and transport modes for HIP signaling messages.
HIP.quote: This document defines how the encrypted connection can be used also for HIP signaling messages.

ESP.why: A substantial part defines carrying HIP messages directly inside ESP, including next-header values and interaction with ESP SAs.
ESP.quote: The ESP header's next header value for HIP messages sent over ESP MUST be set to HIP (139).

rejected.why: TCP is only used inside the ESP tunnel as a carrier for HIP messages; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Mobility handling is only HIP-specific UPDATE behavior; HIP is the better fit than the generic IP mobility topic.
ESP is used as a substrate; ESP tag is the more specific child, and the document does not address IPsec architecture.
UDP encapsulation for NAT traversal is mentioned only as interacting context, not the subject.
Considered since it carries HIP over ESP/TCP, but HIP is the more specific tag and a topic tag shouldn't be added alongside it.

RFC6262.title: RTP Payload Format for IP-MR Speech Codec
RFC6262.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for the SPIRIT IP-MR wideband scalable speech codec, supporting multiple frames per packet and in-band redundancy, and registers the audio/ip-mr_v2.5 media type.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines an RTP payload format for a specific speech codec: header, TOC, data and redundancy structure. This is the core subject.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of SPIRIT IP-MR encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

rejected.why: The IP-MR codec is described only as background for the payload format. The document does not define the codec itself, and RTP payload format is the more specific tag.
SDP is used only for the media type parameter mapping in Section 7.2. It is not a subject of the document.
The media type registration (audio/ip-mr_v2.5) is boilerplate-like and is incidental to the payload format.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended mechanism.
RTP is the substrate. The more specific RTP payload format tag covers the document.
Section 5 is the standard payload-format congestion considerations note and is not a substantial subject of the document.

gaps.name: IP-MR speech codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the SPIRIT IP-MR codec. The codecs parent is too generic, and no child exists for it.

RFC6263.title: Application Mechanism for Keeping Alive the NAT Mappings Associated with RTP / RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Flows
RFC6263.summary: Lists mechanisms for keeping NAT mappings alive for RTP/RTCP flows (empty packets, comfort noise, multiplexed RTCP, STUN indications, bad-version or unknown-payload RTP), recommends multiplexed RTCP, and specifies timing rules; not applicable to ICE agents.

NAT traversal.why: The document is about keeping NAT mappings alive for real-time media, which is interactive NAT traversal. It covers the non-ICE case, so the NAT traversal topic tag fits better than ICE.
NAT traversal.quote: enable applications using the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) and the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) to keep their RTP Network Address Translator (NAT) mappings alive

RTP.why: It specifies keepalive behaviour for RTP sessions, including packet construction for the unknown payload type and incorrect version options.
RTP.quote: the RTP media stream packets themselves normally fulfill this requirement. However, there exist some cases where RTP does not generate the minimum required flow activity.

RTCP.why: The recommended mechanism is RTCP multiplexed with RTP. A whole section gives RTCP interval and bandwidth calculations (Twc, Tmin, trr-int) needed to keep RTCP flows alive.
RTCP.quote: RTCP packets are sent periodically and can thus normally keep the NAT mappings open as long as they are sent frequently enough.

rejected.why: The document explicitly excludes ICE agents. It only mentions ICE as the alternative full solution.
A STUN Binding Indication is only one of the listed alternatives, and the document does not recommend it. It does not specify or extend STUN.
SDP direction attributes (sendonly, recvonly, inactive) are used to explain why keepalives are needed. The document does not specify SDP.
SIP is mentioned only as an example context where unidirectional media or hold arises.
The document deals with NAT traversal for media, so the more specific NAT traversal tag fits. NAT behaviour itself is only cited from RFC 4787 and RFC 5382.
SAVP and SAVPF profiles come up only in the RTCP timing parameter constraints.

RFC6264.title: An Incremental Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) for IPv6 Transition
RFC6264.summary: Informational document proposing an incremental Carrier-Grade NAT approach that combines v4-v4 CGN with v6-over-v4 tunnelling (e.g., 6rd) in a dual-stack CGN and home gateway, to provide IPv6 service over a legacy IPv4 ISP network and ease transition to dual-stack, DS-Lite or IPv6-only.

CGN.why: The document specifies a deployment model for a dual-stack CGN with v4-v4 NAT plus tunnel endpoint, and a configurable CGN device reusable across transition phases.
CGN.quote: This document proposes an incremental CGN approach for IPv6 transition.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document is about IPv4-to-IPv6 transition strategy for ISPs, including migration towards dual-stack or IPv6-only networks.
IPv6 transition.quote: It can provide IPv6 access services for IPv6-enabled hosts and IPv4 access services for IPv4 hosts while leaving most of legacy IPv4 ISP networks unchanged.

6rd.why: 6rd is the assumed tunnelling mechanism between the home gateway and the CGN, and the transition from 6rd to incremental CGN is discussed.
6rd.quote: 6rd [RFC5569, RFC5969] technology appears suitable to support v6-over-v4 tunneling with low operational cost.

DS-Lite.why: DS-Lite is compared as the inverse approach, and the smooth-transition model has the CGN and HG switch to DS-Lite mode later.
DS-Lite.quote: The approach is similar to DS-Lite but the other way around.

rejected.why: NAT64 integration is mentioned in Section 2.6 for intercommunication, but the document explicitly says its integration is out of scope.
Tunnelling is central, but the more specific 6rd tag captures the chosen mechanism; the document defines no new generic tunnelling.
The more specific CGN tag fits; the document is about carrier-grade NAT rather than NAT in general.
The home gateway is referenced per RFC 6204, but the document is about ISP-side transition rather than home network architecture.
Only mentioned as a signal the HG observes to detect native IPv6; not a subject of the document.
Listed only as an alternative tunnelling mechanism that could be considered, not discussed further.

RFC6265.title: HTTP State Management Mechanism
RFC6265.summary: RFC 6265 specifies the HTTP Cookie and Set-Cookie header fields, covering server and user agent requirements, storage model, and privacy and security considerations, and obsoletes RFC 2965.

cookies.why: The whole document specifies the cookie mechanism: syntax, user agent processing algorithms, storage model, and privacy and security issues.
cookies.quote: This document defines the HTTP Cookie and Set-Cookie header fields.

rejected.why: Cookies are an HTTP extension, but the more specific child tag cookies fits; the parent is implied.
Only Section 6.3 touches IDNA for host canonicalization, which is a minor dependency.
Security considerations discuss CSRF and session fixation, but the document is about the cookie mechanism itself, not a general web security mechanism.
Third-party cookie and tracking privacy are discussed in Section 7, but as a supporting part of the cookie spec rather than a general privacy threat model.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax.
Only mentioned as a reliance in the Security Considerations.

RFC6266.title: Use of the Content-Disposition Header Field in the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
RFC6266.summary: RFC 6266 defines the Content-Disposition header field for HTTP responses (attachment/inline types, filename and filename* parameters), including internationalization of filenames and security guidance for recipients.

HTTP.why: The document specifies an HTTP response header field, its grammar, processing and conformance requirements, and updates RFC 2616.
HTTP.quote: This specification takes over the definition and registration of Content-Disposition, as used in HTTP.

rejected.why: Content-Disposition originates in MIME (RFC 2183) and is profiled here, but the document is about its use in HTTP, not MIME body structure.
Filename internationalization is a substantial part, but it relies on the RFC 5987 encoding defined elsewhere, and the document defines no new internationalization mechanism.
ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8 are mentioned only as encodings for the filename parameter, not as a character-set subject.
The document does not register media types. It registers a header field and relies on an existing disposition registry.
The IANA section only updates a header field registration and is boilerplate.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the grammar.

RFC6267.title: MIKEY-IBAKE: Identity-Based Authenticated Key Exchange (IBAKE) Mode of Key Distribution in Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY)
RFC6267.summary: RFC 6267 defines MIKEY-IBAKE, a new MIKEY key distribution mode using identity-based encryption and an elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman exchange for mutual authentication and session key derivation without key escrow, with new payloads and message exchanges.

MIKEY.why: The document specifies a new MIKEY mode with new message types, payloads (IBAKE, ESK), key derivation and IANA registries. MIKEY readers would want it.
MIKEY.quote: This document describes a key management protocol variant for the Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) protocol that relies on a trusted key management service.

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned only for use cases (forking, retargeting) and as the signalling carrier for MIKEY messages; the document does not specify SIP.
SRTP is the media security protocol keyed by the derived TGK/TEK, but the document does not specify it.
EC Diffie-Hellman and a curve registry are used, but the document is about key exchange in MIKEY rather than elliptic curve cryptography in its own right.
The parent of MIKEY, which is already tagged and implies it.
The document contrasts IBE with PKI as an advantage but does not address PKI.

gaps.name: Identity-Based Encryption (IBE / IBAKE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for identity-based cryptography, which is the core mechanism of this document and of RFC 5091, 5408 and 5409.

RFC6268.title: Additional New ASN.1 Modules for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and the Public Key Infrastructure Using X.509 (PKIX)
RFC6268.summary: RFC 6268 republishes ASN.1 modules from several CMS and PKIX RFCs (compressed data, IP/AS certificate extensions, BinaryTime, content collection, HMAC-SHA2, WLAN extensions, AuthEnvelopedData, CMS, multiple signatures) in 2008 ASN.1 syntax, with no change to bits on the wire.

CMS.why: Most modules are CMS content types and attributes (CMS itself, AuthEnvelopedData, CompressedData, ContentCollection, MultipleSignatures), so the document is chiefly a CMS ASN.1 update.
CMS.quote: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) format, and many associated formats, are expressed using ASN.1.

ASN.1.why: The purpose is converting modules to 2008 ASN.1 syntax, and it includes a section on module identifiers in ASN.1.
ASN.1.quote: This document updates some auxiliary ASN.1 modules to conform to the 2008 version of ASN.1; the 1988 ASN.1 modules remain the normative version.

X.509.why: It updates the PKIX certificate extension modules for IP address and AS identifiers (RFC 3779) and WLAN SSID extensions (RFC 4334).
X.509.quote: We have updated the ASN.1 module associated with RFC 3779 to be ASN.1 2008 compliant

rejected.why: S/MIME capabilities are referenced in the modules, but the document is about CMS and PKIX ASN.1 syntax, not S/MIME message specification.
It includes an HMAC-SHA2 ASN.1 module, but only as one small algorithm identifier module among many.
RFC 3779 extensions are used by RPKI, but the document does not address RPKI.
The CompressedData module is one small piece; the document is not about compression.

RFC6269.title: Issues with IP Address Sharing
RFC6269.summary: Informational memo identifying the issues common to all large-scale IPv4 address sharing approaches (CGN, DS-Lite, NAT64, A+P), such as port allocation, application breakage, geolocation, traceability, security, ICMP/MTU, and transport effects.

CGN.why: The whole document analyses issues arising from carrier-grade/large-scale NAT and port-range address sharing deployments; CGN is the central class of solution.
CGN.quote: Carrier Grade NAT (CGN a.k.a. LSN for Large Scale NAT)

NAT.why: Discusses NAT behaviour, ALGs, NAT traversal, port mapping and state, with comparison to CPE NAT; broader NAT issues are substantial.
NAT.quote: Security issues associated with NAT have long been documented

IPv4.why: The document is motivated by IPv4 address exhaustion and the address lifecycle, and sharing of IPv4 addresses.
IPv4.quote: how they will continue providing IPv4 connectivity service to their subscribers when there are no longer sufficient IPv4 addresses

rejected.why: Mentioned as one example of an address sharing solution; solution-specific discussion is out of scope.
Only listed as one of the sharing approaches; not specified or analysed in its own right.
Mentioned as an in-progress solution for port forwarding; only a brief reference.
Section 17 touches on 6to4/Teredo interactions but it is a minor part; the document says IPv6 deployment is the long-term fix.
Not a taxonomy tag; logging/traceability is covered as an issue within the CGN analysis.
Short section on MTU and PMTUD effects; a minor part of the document.

RFC6270.title: The 'tn3270' URI Scheme
RFC6270.summary: Defines the 'tn3270' URI scheme (syntax, semantics, IANA registration) for designating access to TN3270 and TN3270E Telnet sessions, updating RFCs 1041, 1738 and 2355.

TN3270.why: The document defines the URI scheme for TN3270/TN3270E sessions and updates the RFCs specifying those protocols, so TN3270 readers would want it.
TN3270.quote: specification of the 'tn3270' Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme, which is used to designate the access to the resources available via Telnet 3270 mode (TN3270)

URI.why: It specifies a new URI scheme with ABNF syntax, semantics and registration, so it belongs under URIs.
URI.quote: The 'tn3270' URI takes the following form (the syntax below is non- normative): tn3270://<userinfo>@<host>:<port>/

rejected.why: Telnet is the underlying protocol, and the document defines only the URI scheme. TN3270 is the more specific fit, and the Telnet authentication option is mentioned only for the userinfo part.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the one-line grammar rule.
The IANA registration template is boilerplate for the scheme registration, not the subject of the document.
SSH is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a more secure alternative.
TCP is only the transport, mentioned for the default port 23.

RFC6271.title: Requirements for SIP-Based Session Peering
RFC6271.summary: RFC 6271 is an informational SPEERMINT document capturing protocol requirements for SIP-based session peering between SIP Service Providers, covering border elements, session establishment data, presence/IM peering, and security properties.

SPEERMINT.why: The whole document is the SPEERMINT requirements document for SIP session peering between SIP Service Providers, covering border elements, SED, LUF/LRF and security.
SPEERMINT.quote: This memo captures protocol requirements to enable session peering of voice, presence, instant messaging, and other types of multimedia traffic.

SIP.why: The requirements concern SIP deployment between providers, including SBEs, SIP URIs, DNS-based server location and SIP security, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: we assume that the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is used to establish sessions between SIP Service Providers (SSPs)

SIMPLE.why: A full section sets requirements for inter-domain presence subscriptions, IM exchange, privacy sharing and PIDF use between SSPs.
SIMPLE.quote: Requirements for Session Peering of Presence and Instant Messaging

rejected.why: DNS via RFC 3263 is discussed as a solution space for advertising SBEs, but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
ENUM is mentioned only as a possible LUF protocol whose solution space is undefined.
SRTP and DTLS-SRTP are given as examples of end-to-end media security, not the subject of the document.
TLS is cited as a means of securing SIP transport, only as a substrate.
PIDF is touched on in one requirement about standard presence documents, which is too minor for its own tag; SIMPLE covers the presence peering.
Not related to the document's subject.

RFC6272.title: Internet Protocols for the Smart Grid
RFC6272.summary: Informational survey that guides Smart Grid designers in profiling the Internet Protocol Suite, annotating key IETF protocols by layer (security, network, transport, infrastructure, management, discovery, applications) with an AMI example.

internet architecture.why: The document's core is an overview of the Internet architecture and protocol suite layering and a business architecture view, applied to the Smart Grid.
internet architecture.quote: we discuss the layered architecture of the IPS, the functions of the various layers, and their associated protocols.

IoT.why: Smart Grid devices (meters, HAN sensors) are constrained IoT-type devices; the document gives guidance on IP profiles for them, touching 6LoWPAN, RPL, CoAP.
IoT.quote: Service and resource discovery are among the most important protocols for constrained resource self-organizing networks.

security.why: A substantial section surveys the security toolbox (AAA, IPsec, TLS, CMS, SSH, PKI, Kerberos) at each layer.
security.quote: The following sub-sections outline a few of those commonly used security building blocks.

IPv6 transition.why: Dedicated subsection advises on dual stack, tunneling, and translation for IPv4/IPv6 coexistence.
IPv6 transition.quote: The following sections describe the IETF's coexistence and transition mechanisms for IPv4 and IPv6.

routing.why: Survey of routing protocols (RIP, OSPF, IS-IS, BGP, MANET, RPL, multicast) is a major part; no single protocol dominates.
routing.quote: IETF specified routing protocols include RIP Version 2 [RFC2453], OSI IS-IS for IPv4 [RFC1195], OSPF Version 2 [RFC2328], and BGP-4 [RFC4271].

rejected.why: Only one entry in a survey of transport protocols; not specified or analysed.
Briefly listed among management protocols; the document is not about SNMP.
Short survey of SNMP/NETCONF; minor part of the document.
Mentioned as a work-in-progress for resource discovery in one subsection; not the document's subject.
Described as a tool in the security toolbox, not specified or extended here.
Section 4 summarises NAT documents briefly as middleware context; not the main subject.

gaps.name: Smart Grid / Advanced Metering Infrastructure
gaps.why: The document's application domain (smart meters, HAN/NAN, demand response) has no taxonomy tag; energy management is only loosely related.

RFC6273.title: The Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) Hash Threat Analysis
RFC6273.summary: Informational analysis of how collision and pre-image attacks on SHA-1 and MD5 affect the hash uses in SEND (CGAs, PKIX router certificates, RSA Signature option, Key Hash field), concluding only CGA attacks are a practical concern.

SEND.why: The whole document is a threat analysis of SEND's hash usage, covering its RSA Signature option, Key Hash field, CGAs and router authorization.
SEND.quote: This document analyzes the use of hashes in Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), the possible threats to these hashes and the impact of recent attacks on hash functions used by SEND.

SHA.why: The analysis centres on attacks against SHA-1 (and MD5) collision resistance and their impact, so readers of SHA/hash-attack material would want it.
SHA.quote: SEND [RFC3971] uses the SHA-1 hash algorithm [SHA1] to generate the contents of the Key Hash field and the Digital Signature field

rejected.why: PKIX certificates used for router authorization are analysed only as one hash-use site; the document does not specify or profile X.509.
MD5 collision attacks on certificates are cited as background; the document's focus is SHA-1 use in SEND, and MD5 is not analysed in its own right.
The RSA Signature option is a SEND component; the document is about its hash, not RSA cryptography.
SEND runs on IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 itself; the more specific SEND tag covers it.
SEND is a child tag of neighbor discovery and is the more specific fit, so the parent is not listed.
Router authorization certificates are discussed only as a hash-attack surface, not as PKI design or operations.

gaps.name: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA)
gaps.why: The document analyses attacks on CGAs (RFC 3972/4982), which are central to its conclusion. The taxonomy has no CGA tag.

gaps.name: Cryptographic hash attacks / hash agility
gaps.why: The document is a threat analysis of collision and pre-image attacks and the lack of hash algorithm agility. The taxonomy has no tag for hash-function attacks beyond the algorithm-specific SHA and MD5 tags.

RFC6274.title: Security Assessment of the Internet Protocol Version 4
RFC6274.summary: RFC 6274 is a CPNI-derived security assessment of IPv4 that reviews each IP header field, IP options, fragment reassembly, forwarding and addressing, giving threats, sanity checks and countermeasures.

IPv4.why: The whole document analyses IPv4 header fields, options, reassembly and addressing from a security perspective.
IPv4.quote: This document is the result of an assessment of the IETF specifications of the Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4), from a security point of view.

operational security.why: It gives operators and implementers guidance on filtering, NIDS evasion, firewall bypass, and packet sanity checks and mitigations.
operational security.quote: it provides insights about the security aspects of the Internet Protocol that may be of help to the Internet operations community.

rejected.why: The Router Alert option is only one of many options discussed, in a short subsection.
ICMP appears only incidentally, as error messages sent when packets are dropped.
ECN and the DS field are covered only briefly as one header field.
The more specific IPv4 tag and operational security fit better than the generic security topic.
The CIPSO and DoD security options are covered only in short subsections.
TCP appears only as an example of a connection-oriented transport protocol.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation and reassembly
gaps.why: A large part of the document (Section 4.1) addresses fragment reassembly attacks and countermeasures, and the taxonomy has no fragmentation tag.

RFC6275.title: Mobility Support in IPv6
RFC6275.summary: RFC 6275 specifies Mobile IPv6, which lets IPv6 nodes stay reachable at a home address while moving. It defines the Mobility Header, binding management, the return routability procedure, home agent operation, and Neighbor Discovery changes. It obsoletes RFC 3775.

Mobile IPv6.why: The whole document specifies the Mobile IPv6 protocol: home agents, correspondent nodes, binding updates, route optimization and security.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document specifies Mobile IPv6, a protocol that allows nodes to remain reachable while moving around in the IPv6 Internet.

rejected.why: IPsec ESP is used to protect Binding Updates and home agent tunnels, but the document only relies on it. It does not specify IPsec.
The document modifies Router Advertisements and Prefix Information options and adds new options, but this is in service of Mobile IPv6 rather than being about Neighbor Discovery itself.
IPv6 is the substrate. The document defines a mobility extension, not IPv6 in general.
It defines new ICMP message types for home agent discovery and prefix discovery, but these are components of Mobile IPv6, not a treatment of ICMP.
HMAC_SHA1 is used in return routability but is only a building block.
IKEv2 is only mentioned as an optional key management option for the home agent security associations.

RFC6276.title: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation for Network Mobility (NEMO)
RFC6276.summary: Specifies how DHCPv6 prefix delegation is used between a NEMO mobile router (requesting router, plus co-located relay agent when away) and its home agent (delegating router) to assign mobile network prefixes.

NEMO.why: The document defines how mobile network prefixes are assigned to NEMO mobile routers by the home agent, working with NEMO Basic Support.
NEMO.quote: One aspect of network mobility support is the assignment of a prefix or prefixes to a mobile router for use on the links in the mobile network.

DHCPv6.why: It profiles DHCPv6 prefix delegation: roles, relay agent co-located in the mobile router, message fields, home agent selection, and Rapid Commit use.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies how DHCPv6 prefix delegation can be used for this configuration task.

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 is the substrate (Binding Updates, Home Address option, Routing Header type 2), not what the document specifies.
IPsec is only used to protect the DHCPv6 signaling, with example SPD/SAD entries in Security Considerations. It is not the subject.
IPv6 prefixes are the object of delegation, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC6277.title: Online Certificate Status Protocol Algorithm Agility
RFC6277.summary: RFC 6277 updates OCSP (RFC 2560) by defining rules for responder signature algorithm selection and a client request extension to indicate preferred signature algorithms, plus updated mandatory algorithms.

OCSP.why: The document extends OCSP with a new request extension and specifies responder algorithm selection rules, and it updates RFC 2560's mandatory algorithms.
OCSP.quote: A client MAY declare a preferred set of algorithms in a request by including a preferred signature algorithms extension in requestExtensions of the OCSPRequest
OCSP.section: 4. Client Indication of Preferred Signature Algorithms

rejected.why: X.509 certificates and CRLs are the context for OCSP, but the document doesn't profile them.
ASN.1 modules appear only to define the extension syntax, so ASN.1 is just the encoding.
The SMIMECapability type is reused only as a structure for public key algorithm parameters.
Elliptic curve algorithms appear only as examples of values a client might indicate.
RSA with SHA-1 and SHA-256 appear in the updated mandatory algorithm list, but the document isn't about RSA.

RFC6278.title: Use of Static-Static Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement in Cryptographic Message Syntax
RFC6278.summary: Informational RFC specifying how to use static-static ECDH key agreement (standard and cofactor) with CMS EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData, reusing RFC 5753 algorithm identifiers.

CMS.why: The document specifies conventions for KeyAgreeRecipientInfo fields and sender/receiver actions in CMS EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData.
CMS.quote: This document describes how to use the static-static Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key-agreement scheme

elliptic curve.why: The core subject is ECDH key agreement over elliptic curve groups, including standard and cofactor variants, curve parameter checks and KDF use.
elliptic curve.quote: we specify the conventions for using static-static Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) for both standard and cofactor methods

rejected.why: Certificates hold the static ECDH keys, but the document does not profile or specify certificates; it only references RFC 5480 key identifiers.
AES key wrap and content-encryption algorithms are listed as required or optional, but only in passing; the document is not about AES.
CMS structures are defined in ASN.1, but the document explicitly defines no new ASN.1 structures.
Key agreement is the subject, but the more specific CMS and elliptic curve tags cover it; the document is not a general key management treatment.
CMS is the base of S/MIME, but the document does not address S/MIME or email.
SHA hash functions are only named as KDF and MAC choices, not specified or analysed.

RFC6279.title: Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Localized Routing Problem Statement
RFC6279.summary: Problem statement for localized routing in Proxy Mobile IPv6, analysing use cases, IPv4 and roaming considerations, and functional requirements for direct MAG-to-MAG paths bypassing LMAs.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document analyses localized routing between MAGs in PMIPv6 networks and lists requirements for an extension to RFC 5213.
PMIPv6.quote: This document describes the problem space of localized routing in Proxy Mobile IPv6.

rejected.why: Only referenced for contrast (route optimization and return routability are not applicable); the document is about PMIPv6.
Section 3.3 covers IPv4 home addresses in PMIPv6, but it is a PMIPv6 sub-issue, not about IPv4 itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible protection mechanism.
Referenced only as a pointer to policy/authorization work, not discussed.
The more specific PMIPv6 tag applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC6280.title: An Architecture for Location and Location Privacy in Internet Applications
RFC6280.summary: Describes the Geopriv architecture for privacy-preserving location-based services: roles, Location Objects, privacy rules, and the location life cycle (positioning, distribution, use), with security and privacy requirements and example scenarios.

geolocation.why: The whole document is the Geopriv architecture for conveying location information, with Location Objects, positioning, distribution and location-by-reference. It belongs on the geolocation page.
geolocation.quote: This document describes an architecture for privacy-preserving location-based services in the Internet, focusing on authorization, security, and privacy requirements

privacy.why: A substantial part of the document covers location-specific privacy risks, privacy paradigms and privacy rules (access control and usage rules) bound to location data.
privacy.quote: Geopriv gives data subjects the ability to express their choices with respect to their own location information

rejected.why: HELD is only cited as one of several location configuration protocols. The document does not specify or profile it.
LoST is used in the emergency calling example only. The document is not about it.
Emergency calling is one example scenario in Section 6.3, not a main subject.
SIP appears only as a carrier of location objects in examples.
TLS and IPsec are mentioned only as secure transports in the Security Considerations.
Presence services and PIDF-LO appear as examples, not as the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Geopriv / PIDF-LO location object and privacy rules
gaps.why: The taxonomy has geolocation as a generic topic but no technology tag for the Geopriv Location Object format or the Common Policy rules language.

RFC6281.title: Understanding Apple's Back to My Mac (BTMM) Service
RFC6281.summary: Informational description of Apple's Back to My Mac service, which combines DNS-SD, dynamic DNS update, LLQ, NAT-PMP, IPv6 ULA host identifiers, Kerberos and IPsec to give mobile hosts end-to-end connectivity through NATs.

NAT-PMP.why: A full section covers how BTMM uses NAT-PMP for port mapping, lifetimes, and public address discovery, so readers of NAT-PMP would want this.
NAT-PMP.quote: NAT-PMP is a protocol that is designed specifically to handle the NAT traversal without manual configuration.

DNS update.why: Dynamic DNS updates with update leases and TSIG are central to how BTMM publishes changing reachability.
DNS update.quote: dynamic DNS update [RFC2136] to refresh the DNS resource records (RRs) when a host detects network changes

DNS-SD.why: BTMM publishes host reachability via DNS SRV/AAAA/A/TXT records and DNS-SD style service naming (autotunnel).
DNS-SD.quote: It uses DNS-based Service Discovery [DNS-SD] to announce host reachability information

NAT.why: NAT traversal behind NAPT, including unsupported scenarios like nested NATs, is a main theme of the document.
NAT.quote: BTMM's NAT traversal function requires NAT router devices to support NAT-PMP or the Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) Internet Gateway Device (IGD).

IPsec.why: The document discusses at length how IPsec ESP and IKE are used, with design rationale for end-to-end SAs surviving address changes.
IPsec.quote: BTMM decides to put the IPv6 ULA into the destination field of IPsec Security Associations.

Kerberos.why: Kerberos with PKINIT provides single sign-on authentication between hosts, a stated goal of BTMM.
Kerberos.quote: authentication is performed using the Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos (PKINIT) protocol [RFC4556] with that certificate.
Kerberos.section: 7.1 Authentication for Connecting to Remote Host

rejected.why: IPv6 ULA is used as a host identifier and socket interface, but the document is not about IPv6 specification or deployment.
TLS only protects DNS messages in passing.
HIP is mentioned only as a considered and rejected alternative for host identifiers.
Host mobility is handled via DNS updates and stable identifiers rather than Mobile IP mechanisms.
HMAC-MD5 is mentioned only as the algorithm underlying TSIG.
IKE is described only briefly (aggressive mode with a pre-shared key) as a supporting step. IPsec covers it better.

gaps.name: DNS Long-Lived Queries (LLQ)
gaps.why: BTMM relies on LLQ push notifications of DNS changes, and the document describes the handshake and leases. The taxonomy has no tag for it beyond DNS.

RFC6282.title: Compression Format for IPv6 Datagrams over IEEE 802.15.4-Based Networks
RFC6282.summary: Defines the LOWPAN_IPHC IPv6 header compression and LOWPAN_NHC next-header compression formats (including extension headers and UDP) for 6LoWPAN over IEEE 802.15.4, updating RFC 4944.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document specifies the 6LoWPAN header compression encoding (LOWPAN_IPHC/LOWPAN_NHC) over IEEE 802.15.4, updating RFC 4944.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document specifies an IPv6 header compression format for IPv6 packet delivery in Low Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs).

rejected.why: Relevant, but the document is about the 6LoWPAN-specific format, which is better covered by the 6LoWPAN tag. Header compression is a transport topic for RTP/PPP-style links.
The document compresses IPv6 headers but does not specify IPv6 itself. IPv6 is the payload being compressed.
UDP header compression is defined here, but only as one encoding within LOWPAN_NHC. It does not change UDP.
Multicast address compression is covered, but only as an address encoding in the header format, not as multicast routing or group membership.

RFC6283.title: Extensible Markup Language Evidence Record Syntax (XMLERS)
RFC6283.summary: Specifies an XML syntax and processing rules (XMLERS) for Evidence Records that provide long-term non-repudiation of existence and integrity of archived data using renewed archive time-stamps and hash trees, as an XML alternative to ASN.1 ERS (RFC 4998).

LTANS.why: The document is the LTANS XML Evidence Record Syntax for long-term archive evidence, including time-stamp renewal and hash tree renewal.
LTANS.quote: This document specifies XML syntax and processing rules for creating evidence for long-term non-repudiation of existence and integrity of data.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document defines an XML schema, namespace, and canonicalization rules for the evidence record format.
XML.quote: The syntax of an Evidence Record is defined as an XML schema [XMLSchema], see Section 8.

rejected.why: CMS signatures are mentioned only as motivation; the document does not specify or extend CMS.
XMLDSig is referenced for algorithm URIs and canonicalization, and an example time-stamp format, but the document is not about XML signatures.
ERS in ASN.1 (RFC 4998) is the conceptual basis, but this document provides the XML alternative and does not define ASN.1 modules.
Certificates and CRLs are only stored as supporting cryptographic information; not specified here.
OCSP responses are merely a type of stored cryptographic information.
Base64 is just the encoding for digest values, a substrate.

gaps.name: Time-stamping / Time-Stamp Protocol (RFC 3161)
gaps.why: The document centers on archive time-stamps built on TSA tokens, but the taxonomy has no time-stamping tag; LTANS is the closest.

RFC6284.title: Port Mapping between Unicast and Multicast RTP Sessions
RFC6284.summary: Defines a token-based port mapping mechanism, with new RTCP TOKEN packet types and an SDP 'portmapping-req' attribute, letting RTP clients pick their own ports for auxiliary unicast sessions alongside multicast sessions while protecting against DoS and amplification attacks.

RTCP.why: The core of the document is a new RTCP packet type (TOKEN, 210) with four sub-message types, which extends RTCP. It also registers the packet type with IANA.
RTCP.quote: A new RTCP control packet type is introduced, and four port mapping messages using this control packet are defined

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP media-level attribute, with offer/answer considerations and an example. Readers of SDP would want it.
SDP.quote: The formal description of the 'portmapping-req' attribute is defined by the following ABNF

SSM.why: The unicast and multicast session mixing is motivated by SSM distribution with unicast feedback and retransmission, so the work is relevant to multicast RTP. It is not the main subject.
SSM.quote: An example scenario is where the RTP packets are distributed through source-specific multicast (SSM)

rejected.why: NAT behaviour affects port choice and keepalive, but the document does not specify or extend NAT. It addresses NATs only as a deployment condition.
HMAC-SHA1 is only the recommended way to build the token. The document does not define anything new about HMAC.
SRTCP is mentioned once in the security considerations as an optional protection. It is not what the document is about.
RTP is the substrate and the RTCP extension is the actual subject, so the more specific RTCP tag applies.
There is no DDoS tag matching the taxonomy's DDoS topic well. The attack protection is a feature of the token mechanism, not a DDoS mitigation framework.

RFC6285.title: Unicast-Based Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions
RFC6285.summary: Defines RAMS, a method using RTCP feedback messages (RAMS-R/I/T) and an auxiliary unicast RTP retransmission burst session to reduce acquisition delay when joining SSM multicast RTP sessions, with SDP signaling and IANA registries.

RTCP.why: The document defines new RTCP transport-layer feedback messages (RAMS-R, RAMS-I, RAMS-T) with a new FMT value, which is the core of the specification.
RTCP.quote: This document defines extensions to [RFC4585] for an RTP receiver to request a unicast burst as well as for additional control messaging

RTP.why: The method is built on RTP retransmission packets and a separate unicast RTP session; RTP session behaviour is a substantial part of the design.
RTP.quote: an auxiliary unicast RTP session carrying the Reference Information to the receiver precedes or accompanies the multicast stream

SSM.why: The method targets source-specific multicast sessions, coordinating the unicast burst with the SFGMP join to the SSM group.
SSM.quote: in this specification we address it for the SSM-based applications by describing a method that uses the fundamental tools offered by the existing RTP and RTCP

SDP.why: Section 8 defines a new 'rai' rtcp-fb nack parameter and the 'rams-updates' SDP attribute.
SDP.quote: rtcp-fb-nack-param =/ SP "rai"

IPTV.why: The motivating use case is faster channel change in IPTV multicast video, which IPTV readers would want.
IPTV.quote: A primary use case for this method is to reduce the channel-change times in IPTV networks

rejected.why: This id is not in the taxonomy; the closest tag is RTCP under RTP, which was used above in error and should be treated as the RTCP tech tag.
The SSM tag exists only as source-specific multicast under multicast; the document uses SSM as its operating environment but defines nothing new about it.
IGMP and MLD are only the join/leave mechanism the receiver uses; the document does not specify or extend them.
NAT is covered in a short section that defers to RFC 6284 for the port mapping; it is not a substantial subject of the document.
Burst shaping guidance is informative and explicitly leaves algorithms out of scope.
SRTP and DTLS-SRTP appear only in Security Considerations as mitigations.

gaps.name: Rapid Acquisition of Multicast Sessions (RAMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for rapid channel acquisition or join-latency reduction in multicast RTP; RAMS is the document's core subject.

RFC6286.title: Autonomous-System-Wide Unique BGP Identifier for BGP-4
RFC6286.summary: Updates RFC 4271 to redefine the BGP Identifier as a 4-octet non-zero integer unique only within an AS, with revised OPEN error handling and connection collision resolution.

BGP.why: The document modifies the base BGP-4 specification: the BGP Identifier definition, OPEN message error handling, and connection collision resolution.
BGP.quote: this document relaxes the definition of the BGP Identifier to be a 4-octet, unsigned, non-zero integer

rejected.why: Route reflection is only mentioned in the Remarks as an existing use of the BGP Identifier that is unaffected.
IPv6-only networks motivate the change, but the document does not specify anything about IPv6.
The document is a specific BGP protocol change, so the BGP tag fits better than the broader routing architecture topic.

RFC6287.title: OCRA: OATH Challenge-Response Algorithm
RFC6287.summary: RFC 6287 specifies OCRA, an OATH challenge-response algorithm generalizing HOTP for one-way and mutual authentication and symmetric-key short electronic signatures, using HMAC-based computation with configurable OCRASuite inputs.

OTP.why: OCRA is a one-time-password style algorithm built as an extension of HOTP, defining the computation, suites, and modes. Readers of the one-time password subject would want it.
OTP.quote: The OATH Challenge-Response Algorithm (OCRA) is a generalization of HOTP with variable data inputs not solely based on an incremented counter and secret key values.

rejected.why: HMAC is the underlying primitive used by HOTP/OCRA, not the subject of the document.
Challenge-response authentication is addressed, but the more specific OTP tag covers it; the OTP tag is the better fit.
SHA-1/256/512 are only hash functions selected as parameters.
TLS is only mentioned as a recommended secure channel in implementation considerations.
Key provisioning is explicitly out of scope (PSKC referenced only).
Only used as the encoding for the session information field.

RFC6288.title: URN Namespace for the Defence Geospatial Information Working Group (DGIWG)
RFC6288.summary: Registers the "dgiwg" URN Namespace ID for the Defence Geospatial Information Working Group, defining the NSS structure and the DGIWG Registry System's assignment and persistence rules.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration under RFC 3406, specifying the dgiwg NID, its syntax, uniqueness, persistence and assignment rules.
URN.quote: This document describes the Namespace Identifier (NID) for Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace resources published by the Defence Geospatial Information Working Group (DGIWG).

rejected.why: XML namespaces are mentioned only as motivation for needing persistent names; the document does not specify XML usage.
The IANA registration is boilerplate for the URN namespace registry; the document is not about IANA guidance or stewardship.
URN is the more specific fit; the document does not address general URI syntax or schemes.
The more specific URN tag already covers this; the general naming topic is implied as an ancestor.
The document concerns geospatial standards bodies only as the registrant; it does not address location information formats or conveyance.

RFC6289.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for CableLabs
RFC6289.summary: Registers the 'cablelabs' URN Namespace Identifier for CableLabs, defining its NSS structure ({CLclass}:{CLClassSpecificString}) and assignment and management rules per RFC 3406.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration. It specifies the NID, syntax, uniqueness, persistence and assignment rules for the 'cablelabs' namespace, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: the registration of a specific Uniform Resource Name (URN) [RFC2141] Namespace Identifier (NID) for use by CableLabs is being specified in this document

rejected.why: DOCSIS is only named as one CableLabs project in the introduction. The document does not specify or discuss it.
The only IANA content is the routine registry entry in the IANA Considerations section. That is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA registries.
XML namespaces and schema locations are mentioned only as possible uses of the identifiers. The document does not address XML.
SIP appears only in a hypothetical example, a PacketCable Residential SIP Telephony URN. The document says nothing about SIP itself.

RFC6290.title: A Quick Crash Detection Method for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE)
RFC6290.summary: Defines Quick Crash Detection (QCD), an IKEv2 extension in which a QCD token is exchanged during IKE_AUTH so a rebooted peer can prove the loss of state and trigger immediate deletion of the IKE SA and quick recovery.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new notification (QCD_TOKEN), new exchanges and processing rules for crash recovery, so it is squarely about IKE.
IKE.quote: an extension to the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2) that allows for faster detection of Security Association (SA) desynchronization using a saved token

rejected.why: IPsec tunnels are what is being recovered, but the specification is an IKE protocol extension; IKE is the more specific tag.
Only used as an example exchange in which a replacement token can be piggybacked (Section 4.4); the document does not extend or specify MOBIKE.
Token generation uses a generic HASH, only as example methods, not an HMAC-specific specification.
Tokens must be unpredictable and secrets random, but this is a requirement on the mechanism, not the subject of the document.
Child SAs and ESP packets trigger INVALID_SPI handling, but ESP itself is not specified or extended.

RFC6291.title: Guidelines for the Use of the "OAM" Acronym in the IETF
RFC6291.summary: BCP defining the IETF-recommended expansion of the "OAM" acronym (Operations, Administration, Maintenance), along with "O&M" and "Mgmt", after surveying usage in other SDOs and in earlier RFCs.

OAM.why: The whole document defines and analyses the OAM term and its components, so readers browsing OAM would expect it.
OAM.quote: The main purpose of this document is to provide a definition of the acronym "OAM" (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) for use in all future IETF documents that refer to OAM.

rejected.why: It is a terminology document, but it concerns a single networking term; the more specific OAM tag fits the subject better.
The document distinguishes OAM from Management and explicitly does not define Management, so the OAM tag is the more specific fit.
MPLS RFCs are cited only as examples of how OAM is expanded, and the document is not about MPLS.
IEEE 802.3 and Y.1731 Ethernet OAM are cited only as examples of other SDOs' usage of the acronym.

RFC6292.title: Requirements for a Working Group Charter Tool
RFC6292.summary: Informational RFC listing requirements for a Datatracker tool that Area Directors would use to create, recharter and close IETF working groups, including charter review states, ballots, search and an Atom feed.

IETF process.why: The document specifies requirements for tooling that supports the IETF WG chartering process: review states, IESG ballots, telechats and closing of WGs. Readers of IETF process would want it.
IETF process.quote: The IETF intends to provide a new tool to Area Directors for the creation, re-chartering, and closing of Working Groups.

rejected.why: The tool must offer an Atom feed of charter changes, but Atom is only used as a feed mechanism. The document does not specify or extend it.
The tool is a web application, but the document is about internal IETF process tooling, not web architecture.

gaps.name: IETF tools / Datatracker
gaps.why: The document is about requirements for the IETF Datatracker and Secretariat tooling. The taxonomy has no tag for IETF tools, so only the broader IETF process tag fits.

RFC6293.title: Requirements for Internet-Draft Tracking by the IETF Community in the Datatracker
RFC6293.summary: Informational RFC giving requirements for extending the IETF Datatracker so community members can build lists of Internet-Drafts and RFCs and track their status via web views, Atom feeds, mail streams and file output.

IETF process.why: The document is about IETF Datatracker tooling that tracks I-D and RFC progress through the IETF standards process, including document states, ADs, WGs and streams. This is IETF process administration.
IETF process.quote: requirements for extending the IETF Datatracker to give individual IETF community members, including the IETF leadership, easy methods for tracking the progress of the Internet-Drafts and RFCs

Atom.why: Atom feeds are a core notification mechanism required of the tool, with a dedicated requirement section. The document does not extend Atom itself, so this is secondary.
Atom.quote: The list will have two Atom feeds that are generated from the changes to the list

rejected.why: Mail streams are just a notification channel, with no email protocol content.
Tracking IANA registry changes is only a possible future idea in an appendix, so the document is not about IANA registries.
The document tracks I-Ds and RFCs as items but is not about RFC series format or publication.
URLs and web views are only the substrate for the tool and are not specified by the document.

gaps.name: IETF Datatracker / tools
gaps.why: The document is about the Datatracker, the IETF document-tracking tool, and the taxonomy has no tag for IETF tools or the Datatracker beyond the general IETF process topic.

RFC6294.title: Survey of Proposed Use Cases for the IPv6 Flow Label
RFC6294.summary: An independent-stream survey of published proposals for using the IPv6 Flow Label, which reviews the RFC 3697 flow label standard and its dependency prohibition and assesses how consistent each proposal is with it.

IPv6.why: The whole document is about the IPv6 header's Flow Label field: its specification (RFC 3697), its issues, and its proposed uses. IPv6 is the most specific tag that fits.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 protocol includes a flow label in every packet header, but this field is not used in practice.

QoS.why: Most surveyed proposals use the flow label for QoS signalling, including Diffserv, Intserv and RSVP variants. A substantial part of the document therefore addresses QoS.
QoS.quote: These proposals almost all assume that the flow label's main purpose is to support QoS, and their flow label mechanisms are entangled with QoS mechanisms.

rejected.why: Diffserv is discussed as a comparison point and in a few proposals (Section 3.4), but the document is not about Diffserv itself. The QoS tag covers the QoS discussion.
MPLS is only an analogy for the hop-by-hop switching proposals (CATNIP, 6LSA), and the document does not specify or analyse it.
RSVP is mentioned only as the assumed signalling mechanism in one proposal and as a filter use in Section 3.5.
Load-balancing with the flow label is a brief subsection (3.1.2) that points to a separate draft. It is not a substantial part of this survey.
The document touches on the end-to-end principle and stateless design, but only as a rationale for the flow label rules. It does not address architecture in its own right.

RFC6295.title: RTP Payload Format for MIDI
RFC6295.summary: RFC 6295 defines the RTP payload format for MIDI commands, including the recovery journal for packet-loss resilience, SDP media type parameters, and an mpeg4-generic mode; it obsoletes RFC 4695.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies a new RTP payload format for MIDI, including packet layout, command section and recovery journal.
RTP payload format.quote: this memo defines an RTP payload format and its media type.

SDP.why: A substantial part defines SDP fmtp parameters, session description examples and offer/answer usage for configuring streams.
SDP.quote: Section 6 and Appendices C and D define the media types identifying the payload format, the parameters needed for configuration, and the utilization of the parameters in SDP.

media types.why: Registers audio/rtp-midi, the rtp-midi mode of mpeg4-generic, and audio/asc, along with parameter registries.
media types.quote: In Section 11.1, we request the registration of a new media type: audio/rtp-midi.

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers it.
RTCP feedback is used by the closed-loop policy but the document does not specify RTCP.
SIP is used in interoperability examples only.
RTSP appears as a content-streaming interoperability guideline, not the subject.
MIDI is a command language, not an audio codec; mpeg4-generic is only a mode.
Congestion control section just defers to RFC 3550/3551.

gaps.name: MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface)
gaps.why: The document is about MIDI transport over RTP, and the taxonomy has no MIDI or music-networking tag.

RFC6296.title: IPv6-to-IPv6 Network Prefix Translation
RFC6296.summary: Specifies NPTv6, a stateless, checksum-neutral, algorithmic 1:1 IPv6 prefix translation that gives edge networks address independence, covering its algorithm, deployment topologies and application implications.

NAT.why: The document defines a new address translation function, its behaviour, NAT behavioural requirements (hairpinning, no port mapping) and application implications; this is the NAT subject.
NAT.quote: a stateless, transport-agnostic IPv6-to-IPv6 Network Prefix Translation (NPTv6) function that provides the address-independence benefit associated with IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT (NAPT44)

IPv6.why: The mechanism operates on IPv6 address structure (prefix, subnet field, IID) and addresses IPv6 address independence, multihoming and renumbering.
IPv6.quote: NPTv6 may be implemented in an IPv6 router to map one IPv6 address prefix to another IPv6 prefix as each IPv6 datagram transits the router.

rejected.why: Checksum-neutral mapping is a design property that uses the Internet checksum; the document is not about the checksum itself.
NPTv6 is IPv6-to-IPv6 translation, not IPv4/IPv6 coexistence; the transition mechanisms are only mentioned as related work.
Multihoming is one deployment scenario (Section 2.4), not the main subject, and NAT is the more specific tag for the document.
STUN, TURN and ICE are mentioned only as possible application workarounds, not specified here.
IPsec AH and IKEv2 interactions are noted as limitations, but the document is not about them.
Avoiding renumbering is the motivation, but the document does not address renumbering procedures.

RFC6297.title: A Survey of Lower-than-Best-Effort Transport Protocols
RFC6297.summary: Informational survey of lower-than-best-effort (LBE) transport protocols and mechanisms (delay-based, non-delay-based, upper-layer, network-assisted) that yield to standard TCP, placing the LEDBAT algorithm in context.

LEDBAT.why: The survey is a LEDBAT working group product that contextualizes the LEDBAT algorithm and has a section on LEDBAT considerations; readers of LEDBAT would want it.
LEDBAT.quote: It aims at putting the congestion control algorithm that the working group has specified [Sha11] in the context of the state of the art in LBE transport.

congestion control.why: The bulk of the document surveys congestion control algorithms (TCP Vegas, Nice, TCP-LP, 4CP, MulTFRC, NF-TCP) for LBE service, which does not fit a narrower congestion control child tag.
congestion control.quote: transport protocols that are designed to have a smaller bandwidth and/or delay impact on standard TCP than standard TCP itself

rejected.why: Standard TCP is the baseline competitor and several surveyed schemes are TCP variants, but the document does not specify or extend TCP itself.
MulTFRC is an extension of TFRC discussed in one paragraph; not a substantial subject of the document.
ECN and RED are mentioned only as part of NF-TCP's mechanism.
AQM/RED is mentioned as a network-assisted aid, not the subject of the survey.
The Diffserv Lower-Effort PDB is mentioned only to be declared out of scope.
CONEX is mentioned only as out-of-scope related work.

gaps.name: Lower-than-Best-Effort (LBE) / background transport
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for low-priority or scavenger transport services other than the LEDBAT tech tag, which covers the specific algorithm.

RFC6298.title: Computing TCP's Retransmission Timer
RFC6298.summary: RFC 6298 specifies the standard algorithm TCP senders must use to compute and manage the retransmission timer (RTO), including SRTT/RTTVAR estimation, Karn's algorithm, clock granularity, backoff, and a lowered initial RTO of 1 second.

TCP.why: The whole document specifies TCP sender behaviour for the retransmission timer, updating RFC 1122 and obsoleting RFC 2988.
TCP.quote: This document defines the standard algorithm that Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) senders are required to use to compute and manage their retransmission timer.

rejected.why: RFC 5681 congestion control is referenced and the RTO supports network stability, but this document does not alter congestion control behaviour; it only specifies the timer.
Not discussed; only RFC 5681 loss recovery is referenced.
RTT sampling is internal to the TCP timer algorithm, not a network measurement methodology.

RFC6301.title: A Survey of Mobility Support in the Internet
RFC6301.summary: Informational survey of Internet mobility support protocols (Columbia, VIP, Mobile IP, HMIP, FMIPv6, NEMO, HIP, MOBIKE, PMIP, ILNP, LISP-Mobility, etc.) from 1991-2009, classifying design approaches and identifying open issues.

IP mobility.why: The whole document surveys and compares IP-layer mobility protocols and design directions; the general IP mobility topic is the best fit.
IP mobility.quote: we conducted a systematic survey of the previous efforts to gain an overall understanding on the solution space of mobility support

Mobile IPv6.why: Mobile IPv6 and its extensions (HMIP, FMIPv6) are described in detail and used as the reference design for comparison.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Here we use Mobile IPv6 as an example. Each mobile node has a Home Agent (HA), from which it acquires its Home Address (HoA)

PMIPv6.why: PMIP is the main example of the operator-controlled approach, discussed in 4.16 and 5.3.
PMIPv6.quote: Proxy Mobile IP (PMIP) [RFC5213] was proposed in 2006 to meet the interest of mobile network operators

NEMO.why: Network mobility is surveyed as one of the protocols.
NEMO.quote: Network Mobility (NEMO) [RFC3963], as a backward-compatible extension to Mobile IP, was introduced in 2000

Mobile IPv4.why: Mobile IPv4 and its revisions are covered together with Mobile IPv6.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Later, the IETF developed the Mobile IPv4 [RFC3344] and Mobile IPv6 [RFC3775] standards in 2002 and 2004

rejected.why: Described in one subsection as one of many surveyed protocols; not a substantial focus.
Only one short subsection among 18 surveyed protocols.
Briefly surveyed in one subsection; document is not about ILNP.
LISP-Mobility is a brief subsection only.
DNS is used as a mapping mechanism in several surveyed designs but the document is not about DNS.
Connexion and WINMO use BGP, but only as examples of the routing-based approach.

RFC6302.title: Logging Recommendations for Internet-Facing Servers
RFC6302.summary: BCP recommending that Internet-facing servers log source port, accurate UTC timestamps, and transport protocol/destination port in addition to client IP addresses, because IPv4 address sharing (CGN/NAT) makes IP alone insufficient to identify subscribers.

CGN.why: The document exists to address the effect of address sharing (carrier-grade NAT) on server-side logging and abuse attribution. Its recommendations are driven entirely by CGN/NAT behaviour such as port reuse.
CGN.quote: In the wake of IPv4 exhaustion and deployment of IP address sharing techniques, this document recommends that Internet-facing servers log port number and accurate timestamps

operational security.why: It gives operational logging practice for servers to support abuse mitigation and incident investigation, including protecting the logs from tampering.
operational security.quote: In the absence of the source port number and accurate timestamp information, operators deploying any address sharing techniques will not be able to identify unambiguously customers

rejected.why: CGN is the more specific fit for the carrier-grade address sharing that drives the document. NAT44 is only mentioned as background.
It is only listed as one example of an address sharing technique. The document does not specify or analyse it.
It is only listed as an example of an address sharing technique.
It is only cited as an example of a traceable time source for timestamps. The document does not address NTP itself.
The document asks for accurate timestamps but does not address clock synchronization over networks.
IPv4 exhaustion is the motivation, but the document does not address IPv4 or its address lifecycle in its own right.
The document recommends which fields to log and does not mention or specify the syslog protocol.

gaps.name: Server logging / log content recommendations
gaps.why: The core subject is what fields Internet-facing servers should log, such as source port, timestamp and transport. No tag covers general logging practice outside the syslog protocol.

RFC6303.title: Locally Served DNS Zones
RFC6303.summary: BCP requiring iterative resolvers and recursive nameservers to automatically serve empty local zones for RFC 1918, link-local, loopback, documentation and similar reverse (IN-ADDR.ARPA/IP6.ARPA) zones, to reduce leakage of queries to public servers like AS112 and the root.

DNS.why: The document specifies resolver/nameserver behaviour for serving empty zones, including SOA/NS defaults and name error responses, which is core DNS server and resolver behaviour and operations.
DNS.quote: there are a number of DNS zones that all iterative resolvers and recursive nameservers SHOULD automatically serve, unless intentionally configured otherwise

special-use domain names.why: It defines a registry and list of reserved reverse zones (RFC 1918, link-local, loopback, documentation prefixes) that must be locally served and are not globally resolvable, which readers of special-use names would want.
special-use domain names.quote: IANA has established a registry of zones that require this default behaviour. The initial contents of this registry are defined in Section 4.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a note on insecure delegations and trust anchors; not the subject of the document.
IPv6 reverse zones are listed, but the document is about DNS zone serving, not IPv6 specification or addressing.
Dynamic UPDATE is mentioned only to explain why the NS record is needed in the empty zone.
RFC 1918 and special-use address ranges are the basis for the zone list, but the document is about DNS serving behaviour, not address allocation.
The registry of zones is created, but the document is not about IANA considerations in general; this is boilerplate-level.

RFC6304.title: AS112 Nameserver Operations
RFC6304.summary: Informational guide for installing and operating an AS112 anycast nameserver node that sinks misdirected reverse-DNS queries for private-use IPv4 addresses, including BGP and BIND configuration, testing, and operations.

DNS.why: The document specifies the authoritative zones, zone contents, and nameserver configuration for AS112 DNS service and its operation.
DNS.quote: AS112 nodes operate as fully functional and standards-compliant DNS authoritative servers

anycast.why: The AS112 service is an anycast deployment, and the document covers prefix origination, node placement, and withdrawal practices for anycast operation.
anycast.quote: Each nameserver functions as a single node in an AS112 anycast cloud [RFC4786]

BGP.why: A substantial section gives Quagga BGP configuration, including filters that stop the node becoming a transit router, and route withdrawal during downtime.
BGP.quote: each AS112 node is a BGP speaker and announces the prefix 192.175.48.0/24 to the Internet with origin AS 112

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only to say the AS112 zones are not signed; the document is not about it.
The document concerns serving reverse zones for private-use address space, not the special-use domain name registry.
Private-use IPv4 addresses are the context for the queries, but the document is about the DNS sink service rather than IPv4 addressing.
Security considerations are mostly boilerplate-level and the document is an operations guide for a DNS service, not general operational security practice.
Dynamic update queries are mentioned only in passing as what PRISONER.IANA.ORG receives.

RFC6305.title: I'm Being Attacked by PRISONER.IANA.ORG!
RFC6305.summary: Informational document explaining to firewall/IDS operators that unexpected inbound DNS responses from AS112 nameservers (e.g. PRISONER.IANA.ORG) are replies to misdirected reverse-mapping queries for RFC 1918 addresses, not attacks, and listing corrective measures.

DNS.why: The document is about reverse-mapping (PTR) DNS queries for private-use addresses and the AS112 authoritative servers that answer them, including operational advice on resolver configuration and AS112 nodes.
DNS.quote: Hosts should never normally send DNS reverse-mapping queries for those addresses on the public Internet. However, such queries are frequently observed.

rejected.why: Firewall and IDS alarms are the audience and context, but the document is not about firewall mechanisms or middlebox traversal; it explains DNS traffic.
It gives advice on interpreting traffic, but the subject is DNS AS112 behaviour rather than general operational security practices.
AS112 nodes are anycast-deployed, but the document does not discuss anycast addressing or operation.
RFC 1918 private addresses are background only; the document does not address address architecture or allocation.
Responses are noted as UDP datagrams with source port 53, but only as incidental detail.

gaps.name: AS112 project
gaps.why: The document is about AS112 nameservers and their traffic; the taxonomy has no AS112 tag, so the generic DNS tag is the closest fit.

RFC6306.title: Hierarchical IPv4 Framework
RFC6306.summary: RFC 6306 describes the hierarchical IPv4 (hIPv4) framework, an IRTF Routing Research Group proposal that splits IPv4 addressing into global Area Locators and regional Endpoint Locators, using a locator shim header and Realm Border Routers to reduce DFZ routing state.

routing architecture.why: The document proposes a new hierarchical addressing and routing architecture to improve routing scalability, as an RRG locator/identifier-separation proposal.
routing architecture.quote: a core address space (Area Locators, ALOCs) that is globally unique, and an edge address space (Endpoint Locators, ELOCs) that is regionally unique

addressing.why: A substantial part covers the two-level IPv4 address scheme, the Global Locator Block, and RIR allocation policy changes (Appendix A).
addressing.quote: Therefore, a 32x32 bit addressing scheme and a hierarchical routing architecture are achieved.

multihoming.why: Appendix B and Section 12 detail how hIPv4 replaces classical multi-homing and provides site mobility, with ALOC-switching and multipath transport.
multihoming.quote: Multi-homing becomes multi-pathing.

rejected.why: LISP is the inspiration and a contrasting approach, but the document specifies a different, non-overlay architecture.
The framework extends IPv4 but is mainly about hierarchical locator architecture; the more specific routing architecture and addressing tags fit better.
MPTCP is discussed as a candidate identifier/locator split mechanism, not specified or extended here.
A new ALOC resource record is proposed in a short subsection, but DNS is a supporting extension and not the main subject.
Multicast RBR handling is covered in a subsection, but is a consequence rather than the document's focus.
Mobility is discussed as a consideration, but the document says it will not define a mobility solution.

gaps.name: Locator/identifier separation (loc/id split) architectures
gaps.why: The document is a core-edge locator/identifier separation proposal, and the taxonomy has no general tag for it besides LISP, ILNP and HIP.

RFC6307.title: Encapsulation Methods for Transport of Fibre Channel Traffic over MPLS Networks
RFC6307.summary: Specifies the encapsulation of Fibre Channel frames, login frames, primitive sequences and control frames in an MPLS pseudowire (FC Port Mode PW type), with control word usage, MTU, LDP signaling parameters and timing requirements.

pseudowire.why: The document defines a new pseudowire type and its encapsulation, control word use, signaling parameters and failure mapping, which is the core of pseudowire emulation.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies the encapsulation of FC traffic into an MPLS pseudowire and related PW procedures to transport FC traffic over MPLS PWs.

fibre channel.why: The document is about carrying Fibre Channel traffic across a wide-area network, covering FC frames, primitive sequences, login and timeouts. Readers of the Fibre Channel transports subject would want it.
fibre channel.quote: Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP), as described in [RFC3821] and [FC-BB-6], interconnects otherwise isolated FC SANs over IP Networks.

rejected.why: LDP is used only as the signaling mechanism per RFC 4447. The document just sets FEC and interface parameters and defines nothing new for LDP itself.
MPLS is the transport substrate. The document is about what rides over it, not MPLS operations.
FCIP and iFCP are mentioned only for contrast. The document does not specify or extend them.

RFC6308.title: Overview of the Internet Multicast Addressing Architecture
RFC6308.summary: Informational overview of IP multicast address allocation (to networks) and assignment (to hosts/applications) mechanisms, obsoleting RFC 2908 and reclassifying RFCs 2776 and 2909 to Historic.

multicast.why: The whole document surveys IP multicast addressing: GLOP, unicast-prefix-based, admin-scoped, IANA static, and dynamic allocation/assignment. No narrower multicast child tag covers general multicast address architecture.
multicast.quote: this memo describes the allocation and assignment techniques and mechanisms currently (as of this writing) in use.

MADCAP.why: MADCAP and the MALLOC allocation architecture are analysed as the dynamic assignment approach, with the conclusion that they are not widely deployed. The document also obsoletes RFC 2908, the allocation architecture.
MADCAP.quote: Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol (MADCAP) [RFC2730] as an example.

rejected.why: This is about multicast address allocation, which the multicast tag covers more specifically.
IPv6 multicast address formats are discussed only as part of multicast addressing; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
SSM is mentioned only to say it is out of scope because its addresses have only local significance.
PIM-SM appears only in passing, in the embedded-RP description.
IANA assignment is one of several methods described, but the document is not about IANA registries or policy in general.
DHCPv6 is mentioned only in a terminology note and as a proposed assignment mechanism that gained no traction.

RFC6309.title: IANA Rules for MIKEY (Multimedia Internet KEYing)
RFC6309.summary: RFC 6309 relaxes and clarifies the IANA registration rules (IETF Review or IESG Approval, Specification Required) for the MIKEY registries defined in RFCs 3830, 4563, 5410 and 6043, obsoleting RFC 4909.

MIKEY.why: The whole document concerns the MIKEY protocol's registries and their allocation policies, updating several MIKEY RFCs. MIKEY readers need these rules.
MIKEY.quote: This document relaxes the IANA rules for Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) [RFC3830].

IANA.why: The document's substance is IANA registry allocation policy (IETF Review, IESG Approval, Specification Required) and value ranges, so readers of IANA registry guidance would want it.
IANA.quote: This document changes, for majority of the namespaces, the requirement of "IETF Review" to "IETF Review or IESG Approval" [RFC5226].

rejected.why: SRTP appears only as the name of some MIKEY namespaces (SRTP Type, SRTP encr alg); the document is not about SRTP.
The parent topic is implied by the MIKEY tag, which sits under it, so it is not listed separately.

RFC6310.title: Pseudowire (PW) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Message Mapping
RFC6310.summary: Specifies how PEs map and notify defect states between pseudowires and attachment circuits for ATM, Frame Relay, TDM and SONET/SDH (CEP) PW services over MPLS and L2TPv3/IP PSNs, defining single-emulated-loop and coupled-loop OAM modes.

pseudowire.why: The whole document standardizes PE behavior for PW and AC defects across ATM, FR, TDM and CEP pseudowire services.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies the mapping and notification of defect states between a pseudowire (PW) and the Attachment Circuits (ACs) of the end-to-end emulated service.

OAM.why: It defines OAM defect notification modes, FDI/RDI mapping and defect state entry/exit, which is OAM mechanism specification.
OAM.quote: Its objective is to standardize the behavior of PEs with respect to defects on PWs and ACs

ATM.why: A substantial section maps ATM AIS/RDI/CC OAM cells (F4/F5) to PW defect states.
ATM.quote: The following procedures apply to Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) pseudowires [RFC4717].

frame relay.why: A dedicated section maps Frame Relay PVC status (Q.933) to PW defect states.
frame relay.quote: The following procedures apply to Frame Relay (FR) pseudowires [RFC4619].
frame relay.section: 8. Procedures for Frame Relay PW Service

SONET.why: CEP PW defect handling with AIS-P/V and control word bits is covered in its own section.
SONET.quote: The following procedures apply to SONET/SDH Circuit Emulation [RFC4842].

rejected.why: LDP status TLV is used as the notification mechanism, but the document defines nothing new about LDP.
BFD diagnostic codes are mapped to defect indications for VCCV-BFD, but BFD itself is not specified or extended.
The L2TP Circuit Status AVP is used as a notification mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend L2TP.
MPLS is only the PSN substrate carrying the pseudowires.

gaps.name: TDM circuit emulation (SAToP/CESoPSN/TDMoIP)
gaps.why: The document has a TDM PW section, but the taxonomy has no tag for TDM or circuit emulation. SONET covers only the CEP part.

RFC6311.title: Protocol Support for High Availability of IKEv2/IPsec
RFC6311.summary: Defines an IKEv2 extension (four new Notify types) to synchronize IKEv2 Message ID counters and IPsec replay counters after failover in hot standby IPsec HA clusters, plus implementation advice for other cluster issues.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new notification payloads and processing rules for Message ID synchronization after cluster failover.
IKE.quote: This document defines an extension to the IKEv2 protocol to solve the main issues of IKE Message ID synchronization and IPsec SA replay counter synchronization

IPsec.why: A substantial part addresses IPsec ESP/AH replay counter synchronization, SPI collisions and counter-mode IV issues in HA clusters.
IPsec.quote: the newly active member and the peer both increment their respective counter values, "skipping forward" by a large number, to ensure that no IPsec counters are ever reused.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as one example method of building a hot standby cluster; the document is not about VRRP.
ESP sequence numbers are the counters affected, but ESP itself is not specified or extended; the IPsec tag covers it.
Counter-mode ciphers are mentioned only briefly regarding IV reuse.
Not related; IKEv2 mobility is not addressed.

gaps.name: IPsec high availability clustering
