gaps.why: The document is about HA/failover clusters for IKEv2/IPsec; the taxonomy has no tag for high availability or clustering, so it is covered only via IKE and IPsec.

RFC6312.title: Mobile Networks Considerations for IPv6 Deployment
RFC6312.summary: Informational v6ops document discussing issues in deploying IPv6 in mobile (3GPP) networks: IPv4 exhaustion, NAT placement, IPv6-only deployment and roaming, and fixed-mobile convergence.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is about IPv6/IPv4 coexistence and transition in mobile networks: dual-stack, IPv6-only, and IPv6-IPv4 translation considerations.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document discusses the issues that arise when deploying IPv6 in mobile networks.

NAT.why: Section 3.2 is devoted to centralized, distributed and hybrid NAT44 placement in mobile networks and its impact on subscriber management.
NAT.quote: Placement of Network Address Translation (NAT) functionality and its implications;

cellular.why: The whole discussion is framed on 3GPP architecture (APN, PDP context, EPS bearer, roaming, VoLTE).
cellular.quote: we assume the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) 3G and 4G network architectures

CGN.why: Provider-side large-scale NAT to conserve IPv4 is a core topic, matching carrier-grade NAT.
CGN.quote: A mechanism such as the Network Address Translator (NAT) is used at the provider premises (as opposed to customer premises)

rejected.why: Only referenced as an applicable translation mechanism, not specified or analysed in depth.
Mentioned briefly as a requirement for IPv6-IPv4 translation; not a subject of the document.
Cited only as an example of a fixed-network mechanism.
Mentioned only as a possible tunnelling option for separating overlapping addresses.
QoS appears only as part of subscriber-management functions.

RFC6313.title: Export of Structured Data in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC6313.summary: RFC 6313 extends IPFIX (and PSAMP) with structured data: basicList, subTemplateList and subTemplateMultiList Information Elements, new list data type semantics, encodings, and a Structured Data Types Semantics registry for hierarchical and list-valued Data Records.

IPFIX.why: The whole document extends the IPFIX protocol and information model with new abstract data types, encodings, Template management and Collecting Process rules.
IPFIX.quote: specifies an extension to the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol specification in RFC 5101 and the IPFIX information model specified in RFC 5102

rejected.why: PSAMP is not in the taxonomy as its own tag. The document applies to PSAMP only because PSAMP is based on IPFIX, and uses PSAMP records as examples.
SNMP is mentioned only as a pull-based contrast to push export.
MPLS label stacks appear only as a motivating example for structured data.
BGP AS-paths and communities are used only as list examples.
The XML in Appendix A is only apparatus for describing the information model additions.
The one-way delay measurement is only an illustrative use case, and the document is not about measurement methods.

gaps.name: IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IPFIX tag; the IPFIX tech id I used does not exist in it. The closest tag is IPFIX under network management, so use it if present. Otherwise this is a gap.

RFC6314.title: NAT Traversal Practices for Client-Server SIP
RFC6314.summary: Informational RFC giving unified recommendations and example call flows for traversing NATs with client-server SIP signaling and RTP media, using symmetric response, SIP Outbound, symmetric RTP, STUN, TURN and ICE.

NAT traversal.why: The whole document is about interactive NAT traversal practice for SIP and its media; the parent topic fits the overall unified method.
NAT traversal.quote: This document provides concrete recommendations and a unified method for NAT traversal as well as documents corresponding flows.

SIP.why: Specifies how SIP signaling (rport, SIP Outbound, Path, registration and INVITE flows) is deployed through NATs.
SIP.quote: Traversal of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the sessions it establishes through Network Address Translators (NATs) is a complex problem.

ICE.why: ICE is the recommended media traversal method, with detailed candidate and connectivity check call flows.
ICE.quote: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) is the RECOMMENDED method for traversal of existing NATs if Symmetric RTP and media latching are not sufficient.

STUN.why: STUN binding discovery usage, its limits with address-dependent NATs, and keepalive use are explained with flows.
STUN.quote: STUN is a lightweight tool kit and protocol that provides details of the external IP address/port combination used by the NAT device

TURN.why: TURN relay use for address/port-dependent NATs is recommended as last resort and illustrated.
TURN.quote: it is RECOMMENDED that this method would only be used as a last resort and not as a general mechanism for NAT traversal.

RTP.why: Covers symmetric RTP/RTCP, RTCP port handling and RTP/RTCP muxing for NAT traversal.
RTP.quote: SIP User Agents MUST implement Symmetric RTP/RTCP.

rejected.why: NAT behaviour itself is not specified; the document is about traversal, which the NAT traversal tag covers.
SDP and offer/answer are the carrier for addresses and ICE candidates, not the subject.
Section 6 only briefly defers to RFC 6157; not a substantial part.
UDP is only the transport used; no UDP usage guidance is given.
RTCP port handling is a small part (4.2.2); covered by RTP.

RFC6315.title: IANA Registration for Enumservice 'iax'
RFC6315.summary: Registers the 'iax' Enumservice (Protocol-Based, URI scheme iax) in the IANA ENUM registry so E.164 numbers can map via NAPTR records to IAX URIs, per RFC 6117.

ENUM.why: The document's sole purpose is an ENUM Enumservice registration, with NAPTR examples mapping E.164 numbers to iax URIs. Readers of the ENUM subject would expect to find it.
ENUM.quote: This document registers an Enumservice for the Inter-Asterisk eXchange (IAX) protocol according to the guidelines given in RFC 6117.

rejected.why: DNS only carries the NAPTR records. The document defines nothing new about DNS itself, and the ENUM tag already covers the topic.
The iax URI scheme is defined in RFC 5456. This document only uses it as the target of the Enumservice.
SIP is mentioned only in passing in the loop-avoidance remark in DNS Considerations. The document is not about it.
DNSSEC is recommended in one sentence in Security Considerations. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The IANA registration is the mechanism, but the subject is the ENUM service. The ENUM tag is more specific.

gaps.name: IAX (Inter-Asterisk eXchange)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the IAX protocol. The document registers an Enumservice for it, but it does not specify IAX.

RFC6316.title: Sockets Application Program Interface (API) for Multihoming Shim
RFC6316.summary: RFC 6316 defines sockets API extensions (socket options, ancillary data, data structures) that let applications interact with a multihoming shim sub-layer (Shim6 or HIP) for locator management, failure detection and path exploration.

Shim6.why: The API exposes Shim6 locator lists, preferences, context and REAP parameters to applications. Shim6 is the primary shim the document targets.
Shim6.quote: This document defines sockets API extensions by which upper-layer protocols may be informed about and control the way in which a multihoming shim sub-layer

sockets API.why: The document defines new SOL_SHIM socket options, ancillary data (cmsg) and data structures for getsockopt/setsockopt/sendmsg/recvmsg.
sockets API.quote: This document specifies sockets API extensions for the multihoming shim layer.

HIP.why: HIP is the second shim the API is designed for. It affects the EID and locator handling, NAT locators and deferred context setup.
HIP.quote: Examples of the shim are Shim6 and the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

rejected.why: It is the parent of Shim6, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
The API covers IPv4 and IPv6 locators, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
NAT-locator handling appears in only one subsection (8.1.1) and is not a substantial subject of the document.
TCP is mentioned only as an example of connected sockets and a source of feedback.
DNS SRV is referenced only for the priority and weight semantics of locator preference.
SCTP is mentioned only as another multihoming mechanism that could conflict with the shim.

gaps.name: REAP (failure detection and locator pair exploration)
gaps.why: The API exposes REAP timeouts, probes and keepalives, but the taxonomy has no REAP tag.

RFC6317.title: Basic Socket Interface Extensions for the Host Identity Protocol (HIP)
RFC6317.summary: Defines experimental C sockets API extensions for HIP: the AF_HIP/PF_HIP family, sockaddr_hip structure, wildcard HITs, getaddrinfo() resolver extensions, HIT type selection/verification, and explicit locator handling via shim socket options.

HIP.why: The whole document specifies an API for the Host Identity Protocol: address family, HIT structures, wildcards, source HIT selection and locator mapping.
HIP.quote: This document defines the C-based sockets Application Programming Interface (API) extensions for handling HIP-based identifiers explicitly in HIP-aware applications.

sockets API.why: It extends the sockets API with a new address family, sockaddr_hip, getaddrinfo() changes, new socket options and functions, so readers of sockets API extensions would want it.
sockets API.quote: This document specifies extensions to [RFC3493] to define a new socket address family, AF_HIP.

rejected.why: DNS resolution is used to obtain HIP RRs via getaddrinfo(), but the DNS extension is defined in RFC 5205; this document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Only mentioned as another identity-locator split protocol; the document does not address it. The shim socket options come from RFC 6316.
HITs are IPv6-formatted and RFC 3493 is extended, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Locator handling relies on the RFC 6316 multihoming shim API, which is referenced rather than specified here.
IPv4 appears only as mapped addresses returned in the wildcard case, not as a subject.

RFC6318.title: Suite B in Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME)
RFC6318.summary: RFC 6318 specifies how to use the NSA Suite B algorithms (SHA-256/384, ECDSA, ECDH, AES Key Wrap, AES-CBC) in S/MIME via CMS signed-data and enveloped-data, obsoleting RFC 5008.

S/MIME.why: The document is an S/MIME algorithm profile, defining which Suite B algorithm sets a compliant S/MIME system must use for signing and encryption.
S/MIME.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the United States National Security Agency's Suite B algorithms [NSA] in Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME)

elliptic curve.why: A large part of the profile covers ECDSA and ECDH over P-256 and P-384 and the related KDFs. Readers of elliptic curve cryptography would want it. ECDSA is not tagged separately because the document mostly profiles existing conventions, and the elliptic curve tag covers ECDSA and ECDH together.
elliptic curve.quote: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is the Suite B digital signature algorithm.

AES.why: The document selects AES-128/256 CBC for content encryption and AES Key Wrap for key encryption, so AES readers would look for it.
AES.quote: AES [AES] in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode [MODES] is the Suite B for S/MIME content-encryption algorithm.

rejected.why: CMS is the substrate for S/MIME here. The document profiles algorithms for it and defines nothing new about CMS itself, so the S/MIME tag covers it.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 are selected and their identifiers repeated, but this is a small section and the conventions come from RFC 5754.
Certificates must follow the Suite B profile in RFC 5759, but that profile is only referenced, not specified here.
ECDSA is covered under the broader elliptic curve tag, because the document only points to existing ECDSA conventions.
ASN.1 is used only for the object identifiers and type definitions, which is encoding apparatus and not the subject.

gaps.name: Suite B cryptography
gaps.why: The document is about NSA Suite B algorithm suites and security levels, and the taxonomy has no tag for Suite B or national cryptographic suites.

RFC6319.title: Issues Associated with Designating Additional Private IPv4 Address Space
RFC6319.summary: Informational RFC describing the problems of very large networks exhausting RFC 1918 private IPv4 space, the available options (IPv6, transfers, unique RIR space, NAT layering), and the consequences of designating a new private IPv4 block (including redefining existing unicast or 240/4 space), without making a recommendation.

addressing.why: The document is about IP address architecture and allocation: private address space, RIR-allocated unique space, transfers, and redefining unicast or Class E space. No more specific child tag fits, since it concerns allocation policy rather than CIDR, multihoming, anycast or renumbering.
addressing.quote: the issues involved in assigning a new block of private IPv4 address space.

IPv4.why: It deals with the IPv4 address space lifecycle: exhaustion of the IANA free pool, re-designating /8s and reclassifying 240.0.0.0/4.
IPv4.quote: [RFC1918] sets aside three blocks of IPv4 address space for use in private networks: 192.168.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12 and 10.0.0.0/8.

CGN.why: Carrier-grade NAT and cascaded NAT are weighed as the alternative to new private space, along with their logging and overlap problems.
CGN.quote: Another option is to share one address across multiple interfaces and in some cases, subscribers.

rejected.why: NAT is discussed as an alternative and a consequence, but the document explicitly says a NAT discussion is out of scope. The CGN tag covers the part that matters.
IPv6 and ULAs are listed as options, but only briefly. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
BGP is mentioned only in passing, for unannounced address space and routing table size.
IANA's free pool is context, but the document does not address IANA registries or procedures.
VPN providers appear only as an example of a large network category, not as a subject of the document.

RFC6320.title: Protocol for Access Node Control Mechanism in Broadband Networks
RFC6320.summary: RFC 6320 specifies the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP), a GSMPv3-derived TCP-based control protocol between a NAS and an Access Node (DSLAM), with adjacency procedures and DSL topology discovery, line configuration and remote loopback testing capabilities.

ANCP.why: The document defines the ANCP protocol itself: message formats, adjacency protocol, TLVs, capabilities and IANA registries.
ANCP.quote: This document describes the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP). ANCP operates between a Network Access Server (NAS) and an Access Node

DSL.why: A substantial part of the document (Sections 5-8) specifies DSL-specific capabilities and DSL line attribute TLVs for DSLAM-controlled access lines. This is a secondary tag; the DSL tag sits under link layer in the taxonomy and complements ANCP.
DSL.quote: specifies capabilities for Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) topology discovery, line configuration, and remote line connectivity testing

GSMP.why: The document explains ANCP's GSMP origins, shares TCP port 6068, and creates a joint GSMP/ANCP version registry.
GSMP.quote: ANCP is based on the General Switch Management Protocol version 3 (GSMPv3) described in RFC 3292, but with many modifications and extensions

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport substrate; the document merely specifies encapsulation and port use.
IPsec with IKEv2 is mandated for security of ANCP but is a mechanism the document relies on, mostly in Security Considerations.
TLS is considered and explicitly rejected in Security Considerations.
The remote loopback testing capability is DSL-specific OAM, but the document is about ANCP rather than OAM mechanisms generally.
DHCP Option 82 is mentioned only as context for access line identification.

RFC6321.title: xCal: The XML Format for iCalendar
RFC6321.summary: Defines xCal, an XML representation of iCalendar data with a lossless round-trip mapping of components, properties, parameters and values, an XML iCalendar property for extensions, a RELAX NG schema, and the application/calendar+xml media type.

iCalendar.why: The document is a mapping of iCalendar to XML and back, and it adds a new iCalendar property.
iCalendar.quote: The purpose of this specification is to define "xCal", an XML format for iCalendar data.

XML.why: xCal is an XML-based format with its own namespace and a RELAX NG schema, so readers of XML formats in protocols would want it.
XML.quote: In xCal, the entire stream is contained in the root IC:icalendar XML element.

rejected.why: The document registers application/calendar+xml, but this is boilerplate IANA material and not the main subject.
This is the JSON data model for calendars, a different format. xCal is not about it.
VTIMEZONE is mapped like any other component. The document does not distribute time zone data.
Base64 is used only as an encoding for binary values.

gaps.name: xCal / iCalendar XML mapping
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists calendaring as a topic with iCalendar, but the iCalendar tag I used is not in the taxonomy as given. Only calendaring, CalDAV, JSCalendar and time zones appear under it. The calendaring topic is the closest fit.

RFC6322.title: Datatracker States and Annotations for the IAB, IRTF, and Independent Submission Streams
RFC6322.summary: RFC 6322 specifies the Datatracker states and annotations, access control, display fields and stream-movement behaviour for Internet-Drafts in the IAB, IRTF and Independent Submission streams.

RFC series.why: The document defines the publication-process states for the non-IETF RFC streams (IAB, IRTF, ISE), which is RFC series stream and publication workflow.
RFC series.quote: capture and display the progression of Internet-Drafts that are intended to be published as RFCs by the IAB, IRTF, or Independent Submissions Editor

IETF process.why: It specifies Datatracker tooling and IESG conflict-review states and mail for the IETF's document-handling procedures, which is IETF process administration.
IETF process.quote: After the IESG performs a review of potential RFCs from the IRTF and Independent streams, as described in RFC 5742

rejected.why: IANA is only an email recipient of IESG review results; the document is not about registries.
It is not an introductory guide, just a requirements-style document for the tool.

gaps.name: IETF Datatracker / document tracking tool
gaps.why: The document is about the Datatracker tool and its state machines, and the taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the general process tags.

RFC6323.title: Sender RTT Estimate Option for the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP)
RFC6323.summary: RFC 6323 defines a DCCP RTT Estimate option and Send RTT Estimate feature letting the sender report its RTT to the receiver, updating CCID-3 and CCID-4 TFRC-based congestion control.

DCCP.why: The document defines a new DCCP option and negotiable feature, and updates CCID-3 and CCID-4 of DCCP.
DCCP.quote: This document defines a single TFRC-specific option, RTT Estimate

TFRC.why: The update changes RTT estimation for TFRC-based congestion control, analysing its effects on X_recv, loss intervals and quiescence.
TFRC.quote: an update to the round-trip time (RTT) estimation algorithm used for TFRC (TCP-Friendly Rate Control) congestion control

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the TFRC tag, so it is not listed separately.
DCCP is a separate transport and UDP is not discussed.
ECN is mentioned only in the definition of a loss event, and the document is not about it.
It is not related; the RTT option is DCCP-specific.

RFC6324.title: Routing Loop Attack Using IPv6 Automatic Tunnels: Problem Statement and Proposed Mitigations
RFC6324.summary: Informational RFC describing a routing loop attack exploiting inconsistent IPv4/IPv6 routing state in protocol-41 IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnels (ISATAP, 6to4, 6rd) and proposing mitigations.

IPv6 transition.why: The document analyses vulnerabilities in IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnelling mechanisms in general and proposes mitigations, so it belongs under IPv6 transition mechanisms.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document is concerned with security vulnerabilities in IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnels.

ISATAP.why: A large part of the document (3.2.4) specifies ISATAP router and host behaviour, source address verification and a reference topology as a mitigation.
ISATAP.quote: This mitigation measure is available only to ISATAP routers, since the ISATAP stateless address mapping operates only on the Interface Identifier portion

6rd.why: 6rd is one of the analysed vulnerable tunnel types, and the recommendations specifically discuss the limits of mitigations for 6rd routers.
6rd.quote: including the Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP) [RFC5214], 6to4 [RFC3056], and 6rd (IPv6 Rapid Deployment on IPv4 Infrastructures) [RFC5969]

6to4.why: 6to4 is a vulnerable tunnel type analysed in the attack description and in the address check examples.
6to4.quote: if the attack were to be launched on an ISATAP router (R1) and 6to4 relay (R2)

operational security.why: Section 3.2 gives operational measures for network operators to prevent the attack, and the document is a problem statement with mitigations for DoS amplification.
operational security.quote: The most desirable mitigation, however, is to operate the network in such a way that routing loops cannot take place

rejected.why: The loop is described as an amplification vehicle for DoS, but the document focuses on tunnel routing loops, not DDoS mitigation or signalling.
The more specific IPv6 transition and tunnel-protocol tags fit better than generic IP-in-IP tunnelling.
DHCPv6 is used as a mechanism within the ISATAP mitigation but is not specified or extended here.
Neighbor cache checks and RS/RA are used in mitigations but the document does not define anything new about Neighbor Discovery.
Explicitly out of scope; the document only notes that Teredo attacks are covered elsewhere.

RFC6325.title: Routing Bridges (RBridges): Base Protocol Specification
RFC6325.summary: Specifies RBridges and the TRILL protocol: IS-IS-based link-state routing of Ethernet frames with a TRILL header carrying a hop count, nicknames, distribution trees, VLAN handling, and the ESADI protocol.

TRILL.why: The document is the base specification of TRILL and RBridges: header format, nicknames, distribution trees, frame processing, ESADI.
TRILL.quote: This document presents the design for RBridges (Routing Bridges [RBridges]) that implement the TRILL protocol

Ethernet.why: A large part covers Ethernet encapsulation, VLAN tags, 802.1Q bridge interworking, spanning tree/BPDU handling and incremental replacement of bridges.
Ethernet.quote: While RBridges can be applied to a variety of link protocols, this specification focuses on IEEE [802.3] links.

rejected.why: TRILL uses and extends IS-IS, but the TLV encodings are in RFC 6326 and 6165. This document specifies RBridge behaviour, so IS-IS is the substrate.
IGMP/MLD snooping and pruning of multicast distribution are covered, but only as part of RBridge forwarding.
Multipathing is discussed in an appendix, but it is not the document's focus.
SNMPv3 management is mentioned only briefly. The MIB is in a separate document.
PPP is mentioned only as an example alternative link encapsulation.

RFC6326.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Use of IS-IS
RFC6326.summary: Specifies the IS-IS TLVs, sub-TLVs, PDUs and code points used to support the TRILL Layer 2 forwarding protocol.

TRILL.why: The whole document defines the TRILL-specific IS-IS encodings (Group Address TLV, nickname, trees, VLAN sub-TLVs, MTU PDUs, Neighbor TLV).
TRILL.quote: This document specifies the data formats and code points for the IS-IS extensions to support TRILL.

IS-IS.why: It extends IS-IS with new TLVs, sub-TLVs and PDUs and specifies how TRILL uses existing IS-IS PDUs, so IS-IS readers would want it.
IS-IS.quote: Two PDUs are added to IS-IS, the MTU-probe and MTU-ack PDUs.

rejected.why: TRILL is a Layer 2 bridging technology, but the document is about IS-IS encodings, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The Group Address TLV advertises multicast listeners, but this is a small part of the TRILL-specific encodings and not multicast routing in its own right.
IANA sections only register code points and are boilerplate evidence.
The more specific IS-IS and TRILL tags already cover the routing subject.

RFC6327.title: Routing Bridges (RBridges): Adjacency
RFC6327.summary: RFC 6327 specifies the TRILL LAN Hello protocol's adjacency state machine, Designated RBridge election, MTU matching and pseudonode handling for RBridges on multi-access links, updating RFC 6325.

TRILL.why: The whole document specifies TRILL adjacency, DRB election, MTU testing and pseudonode procedures for RBridges, updating the TRILL base protocol.
TRILL.quote: This document describes four aspects of the TRILL LAN Hello protocol used on such links, particularly adjacency, designated RBridge selection, and MTU

rejected.why: TRILL Hellos are modified from IS-IS LAN Hellos, but the document specifies TRILL behaviour. IS-IS is the substrate and is not itself specified or extended as a Layer 3 protocol.
BFD is mentioned only as the way to get sub-second failure detection, which is left to a separate document.
802.1AX is mentioned only in passing: bonded links appear to TRILL as a single link.
The document is about TRILL over bridged LANs, but it does not specify IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The MTU testing is internal to TRILL adjacency. PMTUD is a different, IP-layer mechanism.

RFC6328.title: IANA Considerations for Network Layer Protocol Identifiers
RFC6328.summary: BCP defining IANA allocation policy (IETF Review) and procedures for ISO/IEC Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID) code points, including the SNAP 0x80 recommendation and new allocations for TRILL and IEEE 802.1aq.

IANA.why: The document exists to define IANA registry policy for NLPID code points: IETF Review, liaison notification, and the maintained web page.
IANA.quote: it specifies the level of IETF approval necessary for a code point to be allocated for IETF use, the procedures to be used and actions to be taken by IANA

OSI.why: NLPIDs are OSI network-layer protocol identifiers defined in ISO/IEC 9577, and the document covers their sub-ranges and coexistence with IP protocols.
OSI.quote: ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID)

rejected.why: TRILL is only given an NLPID code point (0xC0); the document isn't about TRILL.
IS-IS Protocols Supported TLV is an example user of NLPIDs, not the subject.
IPv6 and IPv4 appear only as entries in the code point table.
CLNP is only listed in the appendix web page table.
NHRP and other protocols are mentioned only as examples of NLPID users.
X.25 appears only as a category of code point ranges.

RFC6329.title: IS-IS Extensions Supporting IEEE 802.1aq Shortest Path Bridging
RFC6329.summary: Defines the IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs (SPB-Inst, SPB-Metric, SPBM-SI, SPBV-ADDR, MCID, digest, B-VID) that serve as the control protocol for IEEE 802.1aq Shortest Path Bridging, with overview and examples.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs, hello and LSP extensions, multi-topology use, and adjacency rules for SPB.
IS-IS.quote: The control protocol for 802.1aq is IS-IS [IS-IS] augmented with a small number of TLVs and sub-TLVs.

Ethernet.why: It is about Ethernet shortest path bridging (SPBM/SPBV, PBB/PB data paths, FDB population, I-SIDs), so Ethernet readers would look for it.
Ethernet.quote: 802.1aq allows for true shortest path forwarding in a mesh Ethernet network context utilizing multiple equal cost paths.

rejected.why: Multiple equal-cost trees are selected via ECT tie-breaking for deterministic, symmetric paths, which is not generic ECMP load-balanced forwarding.
Multicast distribution trees are part of the data path, but the document is about SPB IS-IS extensions, not IP multicast routing.
Related link-state bridging technology but not discussed or specified here.
E-LINE/E-LAN services are mentioned, but the document does not specify provider VPNs.

gaps.name: Shortest Path Bridging (IEEE 802.1aq)
gaps.why: The core subject, link-state bridging with IS-IS, has no dedicated tag. Ethernet and IS-IS together approximate it.

RFC6330.title: RaptorQ Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery
RFC6330.summary: Specifies the RaptorQ FEC scheme (FEC Encoding ID 6): OTI and payload ID formats, source block partitioning, the systematic fountain-code encoder, an example decoder, and tables for reliable object delivery.

Raptor.why: The document exists to define the RaptorQ code and its FEC scheme.
Raptor.quote: This document specifies an FEC scheme for the RaptorQ forward error correction code for object delivery applications.

rejected.why: Parent of Raptor; implied, so not listed separately.
The scheme is for object delivery, not the FEC Framework for streaming media.
LDPC and HDPC symbols are only internal precoding relations of RaptorQ, not the LDPC staircase/triangle codes.
Only recommended in Security Considerations as packet authentication.
Multicast is mentioned only as background and in security; the document specifies a code, not a multicast protocol.
Mentioned only as an example in Security Considerations.

RFC6331.title: Moving DIGEST-MD5 to Historic
RFC6331.summary: RFC 6331 lists the design and security problems of the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism (RFC 2831), marks it OBSOLETE in the IANA SASL mechanism registry, and moves RFC 2831 to Historic status in favour of SCRAM.

SASL.why: The document is about the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism: it analyses its problems and deprecates it, updating its status in the SASL mechanism registry. Readers of SASL material would want it.
SASL.quote: It marks DIGEST-MD5 as OBSOLETE in the IANA Registry of SASL mechanisms and moves RFC 2831 to Historic status.

HTTP authentication.why: DIGEST-MD5 is built on HTTP Digest authentication and the document notes that most of its problems are inherited from HTTP Digest.
HTTP authentication.quote: defines how HTTP Digest Authentication [RFC2617] can be used as a Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) [RFC4422] mechanism

rejected.why: MD5 is a weak primitive that DIGEST-MD5 uses and is criticised here, but the document is not about the MD5 algorithm itself.
RC4 is cited only as one weakness of the DIGEST-MD5 security layer, not as a subject of the document.
DES/3DES is cited only as an inadequately specified and weak security layer, not as a subject of the document.
The IANA registry change is the mechanism for marking DIGEST-MD5 obsolete, but the document is not about IANA registry policy or guidance.
A parent topic. The more specific SASL tag already covers it.
The RFC 822 ABNF is mentioned only as one complaint about the original specification.

RFC6332.title: Multicast Acquisition Report Block Type for RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Reports (XRs)
RFC6332.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR report block (Multicast Acquisition) for RTP receivers to report multicast join and rapid acquisition (RAMS) experiences, with TLV extensions, IANA registries and an SDP rtcp-xr parameter.

RTCP.why: The document extends RTCP XR with a new report block type, its format, status codes and TLV extensions.
RTCP.quote: defining a new report block type, called the Multicast Acquisition (MA) report block, within the framework of RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Reports (XRs)

SDP.why: Defines a new 'multicast-acq' value for the SDP rtcp-xr attribute, a new SDP signalling element.
SDP.quote: A new unilateral parameter is defined for the MA report block to be used with the Session Description Protocol (SDP)

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport being monitored; the document's subject is the RTCP report block, a child tag that is more specific.
Rapid acquisition of multicast sessions is the context, but the document defines reporting, not multicast routing or group membership.
SRTP/SRTCP is only recommended for protection in Security Considerations.
IANA registries are created but only as boilerplate for the new report block; the document is not about IANA guidance.
The reports carry acquisition timing metrics, but it is a protocol report block within RTCP XR rather than a measurement methodology; considered but not chosen.

gaps.name: Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions (RAMS)
gaps.why: The report block is built around RAMS (RFC 6285), which has no tag in the taxonomy; it would sit under RTP or multicast.

RFC6333.title: Dual-Stack Lite Broadband Deployments Following IPv4 Exhaustion
RFC6333.summary: Specifies Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite), which shares IPv4 addresses among broadband customers using IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels from a B4 element to an AFTR that performs carrier-grade IPv4-IPv4 NAT.

DS-Lite.why: The document defines DS-Lite, including the B4 and AFTR elements, tunnelling, DNS handling, and the extended NAT binding table.
DS-Lite.quote: This document specifies the Dual-Stack Lite technology, which is aimed at better aligning the costs and benefits in service provider networks.

CGN.why: The AFTR is a carrier-grade NAT. A substantial part of the document covers NAT pools, conformance, ALGs, address sharing and logging.
CGN.quote: the Dual-Stack Lite model is built on IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels to cross the network to reach a carrier-grade IPv4-IPv4 NAT (the AFTR)

rejected.why: This is the parent of DS-Lite, so it is implied and not listed separately.
IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnelling is the mechanism DS-Lite uses. The tunnelling itself is defined in RFC 2473 and RFC 4213, so I did not tag it.
The AFTR discovery option is defined in RFC 6334. This document only references it.
The DNS proxy discussion is incidental. The document does not extend or specify DNS.
Softwire appears only in the appendix examples, as terminology borrowed from RFC 5571.
PCP is mentioned in one sentence as work in progress and is not a subject of the document.

RFC6334.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) Option for Dual-Stack Lite
RFC6334.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 AFTR-Name option (code 64) carrying an FQDN so a DS-Lite B4 element can discover its AFTR tunnel endpoint, with server and client behaviour.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option, its format, validation, and server/client behaviour, so it belongs on the DHCPv6 page.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies a DHCPv6 option that is meant to be used by a Dual-Stack Lite Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) element

DS-Lite.why: The option exists to configure DS-Lite B4 elements with the AFTR location, and the document specifies B4 behaviour on receiving it.
DS-Lite.quote: to discover the IPv6 address of its corresponding Address Family Transition Router (AFTR)

rejected.why: DNS is used only to resolve the AAAA record for the AFTR FQDN. The FQDN uses standard DHCPv6 domain-name encoding, and nothing new is defined for DNS.
The softwire tunnel is mentioned as background, and the document says establishing it is out of scope.
The parent of DS-Lite is implied, so it is not listed separately.
The IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel setup is explicitly out of scope; the document only covers discovery of the endpoint.

RFC6335.title: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Procedures for the Management of the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry
RFC6335.summary: BCP defining IANA procedures for assigning, de-assigning, reusing, revoking and transferring service names and port numbers for TCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP and DCCP, including service name syntax and its use in DNS SRV records.

IANA.why: The document is entirely about IANA registry management procedures and principles for the service name and port number registry.
IANA.quote: This document defines the procedures that the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) uses when handling assignment and other requests related to the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number registry.

service discovery.why: It defines service name syntax and registration used for service discovery such as DNS SRV, and allows service-name-only assignments.
service discovery.quote: This document clarifies that the Service Label MUST be a service name as defined herein with an underscore prepended.

transport.why: It defines port number ranges and assignment procedures across all IETF transport protocols, a transport-layer matter not specific to one protocol.
transport.quote: TCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP, and DCCP use 16-bit namespaces for their port number registries.

rejected.why: DNS SRV is touched on, but only to clarify what the service label means; the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
TCP is one of several protocols whose port registry is managed; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Section 10.3 updates DCCP registry rules, but this is a small part of a document covering all transports.
SCTP is only one transport covered by the procedures; it is not extended or specified here.
UDP port assignment is covered, but only as one of several transports sharing the registry.

gaps.name: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number registry / port numbers
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag specific to port number assignment and service name registries; IANA and transport only approximate it.

RFC6336.title: IANA Registry for Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) Options
RFC6336.summary: Defines the missing IANA registry for ICE options (tokens in the SDP ice-options attribute), with registration policy (Specification Required) and required registration information, updating RFC 5245.

ICE.why: The document extends/updates ICE (RFC 5245) by creating the registry for ICE extension option tokens; ICE readers need it.
ICE.quote: This document defines a registry "Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) Options" for ICE options that can be used in the SDP "ice-options" attribute

rejected.why: The document is an IANA registry creation, but the IANA tag covers general registry considerations/stewardship; the specific subject is ICE, so the technology tag fits better.
The ice-options attribute is carried in SDP, but SDP is only the signalling substrate; the document defines nothing new about SDP.
Parent of ICE, implied by the ICE tag.
ABNF is only used to reproduce an existing token syntax.

RFC6337.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Usage of the Offer/Answer Model
RFC6337.summary: Informational RFC summarizing and clarifying how SIP (INVITE, 100rel/PRACK, UPDATE, re-INVITE) uses the SDP offer/answer model, including rejection, message crossing, glare, and offer/answer content such as hold/resume.

SIP.why: The document specifies and clarifies SIP behaviour for INVITE, PRACK, UPDATE and re-INVITE offer/answer exchanges, including glare and message crossing handling.
SIP.quote: This document summarizes all the current usages of the offer/answer model in SIP communication.

SDP.why: A substantial part concerns the SDP offer/answer model: constructing offers and answers, m= lines, o= version rules, hold via a=sendonly/inactive, and c=0.0.0.0 handling.
SDP.quote: [RFC3264] defines the offer/answer model, but does not specify which SIP messages should convey an offer or an answer.

rejected.why: RTP is mentioned only incidentally, for payload types and symmetric RTP; the document is not about RTP.
NAT traversal and ICE are explicitly declared out of scope.
RTCP is mentioned only in the c=0.0.0.0 discussion and is not a subject of the document.

RFC6338.title: Definition of a Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Schema for Academia (SCHAC)
RFC6338.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace 'schac' for the Schema for Academia, defining its syntax, delegation, persistence and registry rules for naming controlled-vocabulary attribute values.

URN.why: The RFC is a URN namespace registration (NID 'schac') with syntax, uniqueness, persistence, assignment and resolution rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Schema for Academia (SCHAC).

rejected.why: SCHAC is an LDAP-style person schema, but the document only defines URN values for its attributes and does not specify or extend LDAP.
TLS is only required for publishing registries over https. That is a security mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
ABNF is only the notation for the NSS syntax and is not what the document is about.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level apparatus for the namespace and does not make the document about IANA registries in general.
SCHAC supports data exchange between education institutions, but the document does not specify any federated authentication framework.

RFC6339.title: Context Token Encapsulate/Decapsulate and OID Comparison Functions for the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API)
RFC6339.summary: Defines three new abstract GSS-API interfaces (GSS_Encapsulate_token, GSS_Decapsulate_token, GSS_OID_equal) with C bindings, for adding/removing the mechanism-independent initial context token header and comparing OIDs.

GSS-API.why: The whole document extends the GSS-API with new calls and C bindings, so readers of GSS-API would want it.
GSS-API.quote: This document adds two GSS-API interfaces (GSS_Encapsulate_token and GSS_Decapsulate_token) so that GSS-API libraries can provide this functionality.

rejected.why: SASL GS2 is only cited as a motivating consumer of the new functions; the document does not specify or extend SASL.
The token header contains ASN.1 DER tags and lengths, but ASN.1 is only the encoding used, not the subject.
The test vector uses the Kerberos mechanism OID, but only as an example value.

RFC6340.title: Textual Conventions for the Representation of Floating-Point Numbers
RFC6340.summary: Defines a MIB module (FLOAT-TC-MIB) with three textual conventions (Float32TC, Float64TC, Float128TC) for representing IEEE 754-2008 binary floating-point numbers as OCTET STRINGs in SNMP MIB modules.

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module defining textual conventions for reuse by other MIB modules. MIB modules and SMI are the subject of this tag.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module containing textual conventions (TCs) to represent floating-point numbers.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework in which MIB modules are accessed. The document defines no objects and says nothing new about the protocol, so the more specific MIB tag fits.
This is implied by the MIB tag, which sits under SNMP and network management. The document adds no separate operational content.

gaps.name: Floating-point number representation (IEEE 754)
gaps.why: The textual conventions encode IEEE 754-2008 32/64/128-bit binary formats. The taxonomy has no tag for numeric data representation, though the MIB tag covers the document's main purpose.

RFC6341.title: Use Cases and Requirements for SIP-Based Media Recording (SIPREC)
RFC6341.summary: Informational RFC giving use cases and requirements for SIP-based media recording (SIPREC), where a Session Recording Client uses SIP to deliver RTP media and metadata of a communication session to a Session Recording Server.

SIPREC.why: The whole document is the use cases and requirements for SIPREC: SRC/SRS roles, recording sessions, metadata, pause/resume, and security.
SIPREC.quote: This document specifies requirements for extensions to SIP that will manage delivery of RTP media to a recording device.

rejected.why: SIP is the substrate being extended, but the subject is the SIPREC recording work, which is the more specific child tag.
RTP media is what is recorded, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
A Privacy Considerations section exists and notification requirements are included, but the document is not about privacy threat models in general.
RFC 4733 DTMF and RFC 4103 text are only cited as media types to be recorded, not specified here.
First-responder bureaus are only mentioned as one application example.

RFC6342.title: Mobile Networks Considerations for IPv6 Deployment
RFC6342.summary: Informational document discussing considerations for deploying IPv6 in 3GPP-style mobile networks, covering IPv4 exhaustion, NAT placement, IPv6-only deployment and roaming, and fixed-mobile convergence.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is about IPv4/IPv6 coexistence, dual-stack, IPv6-only and translation-based deployment in mobile networks, which falls under IPv6 transition.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document discusses the issues that arise when deploying IPv6 in mobile networks.

CGN.why: Section 3.2 is a substantial discussion of provider-side NAT44 placement (centralized, distributed, hybrid) in mobile networks, which is carrier-grade NAT.
CGN.quote: A mechanism such as the Network Address Translator (NAT) is used at the provider premises (as opposed to customer premises)

cellular.why: The whole discussion is framed around 3GPP UMTS/LTE architecture: APNs, PDP contexts, PDN connections, roaming, VoLTE.
cellular.quote: For the most part, we assume the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) 3G and 4G network architectures

rejected.why: Referenced as the translation mechanism for IPv6-only deployments, but only briefly pointing to RFC 6146; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Mentioned in one paragraph as a needed function for IPv6-IPv4 translation; not a subject of the document.
Cited only as an example of a fixed-network mechanism in the convergence section.
The more specific CGN tag fits the provider-side NAT discussion better.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag covers the deployment and coexistence focus.
Tunneling mechanisms such as GRE, IP-in-IP and MPLS are only listed as options for separating overlapping addresses.

RFC6343.title: Advisory Guidelines for 6to4 Deployment
RFC6343.summary: Informational advice to ISPs, content providers, transit networks and implementers on operating around the known connectivity problems of 6to4 (Router and Anycast variants) automatic IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling.

6to4.why: The whole document concerns 6to4 operation, observed failure modes, and deployment guidance for relays, anycast prefix 192.88.99.1 and protocol 41 handling.
6to4.quote: This document provides advice to network operators about deployment of the 6to4 technique for automatic tunneling of IPv6 over IPv4.

rejected.why: Path MTU discovery failure is one listed problem, but the document is about 6to4 deployment, not PMTUD itself.
Anycast 6to4 relay is a 6to4 variant; the document does not address anycast addressing in general.
Parent of 6to4, implied by the 6to4 tag.
Carrier Grade NAT is mentioned only as a cause of 6to4 failure.
Rogue Router Advertisements are a side issue, covered briefly in one subsection.
Managed tunnels (6rd, L2TPv2 hub-and-spoke) are mentioned only in a short section as alternatives.

RFC6344.title: Operating Virtual Concatenation (VCAT) and the Link Capacity Adjustment Scheme (LCAS) with Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS)
RFC6344.summary: RFC 6344 specifies GMPLS RSVP-TE signalling procedures and a new CALL_ATTRIBUTES VCAT TLV for setting up and resizing Virtual Concatenation groups (with optional LCAS) over SONET/SDH, OTN and PDH, updating RFC 4606.

GMPLS.why: The document defines GMPLS signalling procedures, call-based extensions, a new TLV and error codes for VCAT/LCAS, and updates RFC 4606.
GMPLS.quote: the use of the Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) control plane in support of the Virtual Concatenation (VCAT) layer 1 inverse multiplexing data plane mechanism

SONET.why: The document is about virtual concatenation of SONET/SDH signals (VC-4-7v, STS-3c-7v and similar) and updates the RFC 4606 SONET/SDH GMPLS procedures. Readers of that subject would want it.
SONET.quote: These techniques apply to Optical Transport Network (OTN), Synchronous Optical Network (SONET), Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH), and Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy (PDH) signals.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signalling substrate. The document defines a Call Attributes TLV and procedures for the VCAT application rather than changing RSVP-TE itself, and GMPLS is the more specific fit.
The document is about GMPLS control of VCAT circuits, not traffic engineering as a subject. The RSVP-TE usage is substrate.
The IANA Considerations only register the new TLV, error codes and registries. This is boilerplate, not the main subject.
LCAS is a data-plane capacity adjustment scheme, not an OAM mechanism, and the document only describes the control plane.

gaps.name: Virtual Concatenation (VCAT) / LCAS for optical transport networks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OTN/TDM optical transport or for VCAT/LCAS inverse multiplexing. GMPLS and SONET are the closest fits, and neither covers OTN or PDH.

RFC6345.title: Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) Relay Element
RFC6345.summary: Specifies the PANA Relay Element (PRE) and the PANA-Relay message with PaC-Information and Relayed-Message AVPs, letting PANA clients and authentication agents exchange messages when they cannot reach each other via regular IP routing.

PANA.why: The document extends PANA with a relay element, a new PRY message type and two new AVPs, so it belongs on the PANA page.
PANA.quote: This document specifies PANA Relay Element (PRE) functionality, which enables PANA messaging between a PaC and a PAA where the two nodes cannot reach each other

rejected.why: Section 3 describes how IPsec can optionally secure PRE-to-PAA messages, but IPsec is only a security mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
PANA carries EAP, but the relay function does not specify or change EAP or its methods.
6LoWPAN and ZigBee IP are only the motivating deployment example in the introduction.
PANA runs over UDP, which is only the transport substrate here.
DTLS is mentioned once as an alternative security mechanism and is not specified or profiled.

RFC6346.title: The Address plus Port (A+P) Approach to the IPv4 Address Shortage
RFC6346.summary: RFC 6346 proposes Address plus Port (A+P), an IPv4 address-sharing scheme that assigns port ranges to customers and forwards packets by address and port via tunnels, with stateless mapping (SMAP) to IPv6, as an alternative to carrier-grade NAT.

IPv4.why: The document addresses IPv4 address exhaustion by extending IPv4 addressing with port bits, so it belongs under IPv4 and its address lifecycle.
IPv4.quote: This document proposes an IPv4 address sharing scheme, treating some of the port number bits as part of an extended IPv4 address (Address plus Port, or A+P).

CGN.why: A+P is positioned as an alternative to or bypass of CGNs, with substantial discussion of CGN problems and LSN/CGN differences.
CGN.quote: With Carrier Grade NATs (CGNs) in the core of the network, the user is trapped behind unchangeable application policies

softwire.why: The A+P subsystem relies on encaps/decaps tunnelling of IPv4 over IPv6 (SMAP, 4in6) between CPE and PRR, which is the softwire style of deployment.
softwire.quote: The tunnel can be an IPv6 or IPv4 encapsulation, a layer-2 tunnel, or some other form of softwire.

rejected.why: NAT is discussed heavily, but the document is about avoiding or bypassing translation; CGN is the more specific fit.
DS-Lite is referenced as a hybrid deployment option, not specified here.
PCP is mentioned only as one possible signalling mechanism, not defined.
DHCP is only a candidate signalling substrate for port range delivery.
MAP is not named; the stateless SMAP section is related, but the document does not define MAP-E or MAP-T.
The IPv6-only network and IPv4-in-IPv6 encapsulation are secondary themes, and softwire is the more specific fit.

gaps.name: Address plus Port (A+P) / port-range-based address sharing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for port-restricted IPv4 address sharing, so the core subject of the document is only partly covered by IPv4 and CGN.

RFC6347.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security Version 1.2
RFC6347.summary: RFC 6347 specifies DTLS 1.2, a datagram variant of TLS 1.2 that adds explicit record sequence numbers and epochs, handshake fragmentation and retransmission, a stateless cookie exchange against DoS, and anti-replay detection.

DTLS.why: The document defines DTLS 1.2 as a set of deltas from TLS 1.2 and obsoletes DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347); it is the core specification of the protocol.
DTLS.quote: This document specifies version 1.2 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

rejected.why: DTLS is a child of TLS and is the more specific tag. TLS 1.2 is the base the deltas apply to, not the subject itself.
UDP is the main datagram transport DTLS runs over. The document does not specify or profile UDP.
DCCP is mentioned as an alternative transport for DTLS (a mapping defined in RFC 5238). It is not specified or extended here.
Section 4.1.1.1 covers PMTU handling for the DTLS record layer, but only as a supporting concern. The document does not specify path MTU discovery.
IPsec is cited as an alternative and for the anti-replay window technique borrowed from ESP. The document is not about IPsec.
The document only prohibits RC4 for DTLS because stream ciphers cannot be used. It is not about RC4.

RFC6348.title: Requirements for Point-to-Multipoint Extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol
RFC6348.summary: Historic requirements document listing functional requirements for LDP extensions to set up point-to-multipoint (and MP2MP) LSPs over MPLS, which were overtaken by the mLDP protocol.

LDP.why: The whole document specifies requirements for P2MP and MP2MP extensions to LDP: FEC, label advertisement, loop avoidance, rerouting, graceful restart.
LDP.quote: functional requirements that served as input to the design of Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) extensions for setting up point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Label Switched Paths (LSP)

rejected.why: LDP is the more specific child; MPLS is implied as the ancestor.
P2MP RSVP-TE is mentioned only as an existing alternative with which the LDP mechanism must coexist, not as the subject.
Multicast VPN is only the application scenario motivating P2MP LSPs, not the subject of the requirements.
The document concerns LSP setup for multicast delivery, but the subject is LDP signalling rather than IP multicast routing or group membership.
The document explicitly addresses operators without traffic engineering needs; TE tunnels are only mentioned for nesting.
OAM gets a short subsection and defers detailed requirements to RFC 4687, so it is not a substantial part of the document.

RFC6349.title: Framework for TCP Throughput Testing
RFC6349.summary: Informational framework defining a methodology and three metrics (Transfer Time Ratio, TCP Efficiency, Buffer Delay) for measuring end-to-end TCP throughput in managed IP networks, covering path MTU, RTT, bottleneck bandwidth and window sizing.

performance measurement.why: The document is an active performance measurement methodology with defined metrics, test procedures and result interpretation.
performance measurement.quote: This framework describes a practical methodology for measuring end-to-end TCP Throughput in a managed IP network.

TCP.why: A substantial part covers TCP window sizing, BDP, RWND, window scale, SACK and timestamps and their effect on throughput, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: In this framework, TCP and IP parameters are specified to optimize TCP Throughput.

rejected.why: It mentions RFC 2544 only as a lab-only layer 2/3 reference. The document is an operational network measurement methodology, not device benchmarking.
PLPMTUD is a required step, but it is one prerequisite step that relies on RFC 4821. The document does not specify or extend PMTUD.
Congestion phases are described only as background for TCP Equilibrium. The document does not address congestion control mechanisms.
The TCP Extended Statistics MIB (RFC 4898) is only mentioned as an optional data source.
OWAMP and TWAMP are referenced only as possible RTT measurement and security-consideration pointers.

RFC6350.title: vCard Format Specification
RFC6350.summary: Defines vCard 4.0, a text/vcard data format for representing and exchanging contact information, with its syntax, properties, parameters, value types, synchronization mechanisms and IANA registries; obsoletes RFCs 2425, 2426 and 4770.

vCard.why: The whole document specifies the vCard format.
vCard.quote: This document defines the vCard data format for representing and exchanging a variety of information about individuals and other entities

rejected.why: It registers text/vcard, but only as IANA boilerplate; the body is about the format.
vCard is carried as a MIME type, but MIME is only the substrate.
UTF-8 is mandated as the charset but is not the subject.
ABNF is only the notation the document uses.
The tel URI is only the expected value of the TEL property.
vCard derives from directory information, but this document is not about directory access.

RFC6351.title: xCard: vCard XML Representation
RFC6351.summary: Defines xCard, an XML representation of the vCard data format with a RELAX NG schema, extensibility rules, vCard-to-XML conversion rules, and the application/vcard+xml media type registration.

vCard.why: The document specifies the XML mapping of vCard, with a 1-to-1 mapping of properties, parameters and value types, so readers of vCard material would want it.
vCard.quote: This document defines xCard, an XML [W3C.REC-xml-20081126] representation for vCard.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document is an XML-based format: a RELAX NG schema, namespace-based extensibility, and conversion rules between XML and text. Readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: The general idea is to map vCard parameters, properties, and value types to XML elements.

rejected.why: The document registers application/vcard+xml, but that is IANA boilerplate and not the main subject.
XML Signature and XML Encryption are only mentioned in Security Considerations as usable with xCard.
The namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:vcard-4.0 is registered in IANA Considerations only. The document is not about URN namespaces.
JSContact is a JSON representation of contact cards. This document covers XML, not JSON, and predates JSContact.

RFC6352.title: CardDAV: vCard Extensions to Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV)
RFC6352.summary: Defines CardDAV, WebDAV extensions for accessing, managing and sharing vCard-based contact data in address book collections, with properties, preconditions, query/multiget reports and SRV-based discovery.

CardDAV.why: The document specifies CardDAV itself: address book collections, properties, and the addressbook-query and addressbook-multiget reports.
CardDAV.quote: This document defines extensions to the Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) protocol to specify a standard way of accessing, managing, and sharing contact information

vCard.why: Address object resources are vCards, and the document specifies vCard-aware filtering, partial retrieval, UID uniqueness and version/media-type conversion.
vCard.quote: Use of vCards [RFC2426] for well-defined address schema to enhance client interoperability.

WebDAV.why: It extends WebDAV with new collection types, REPORTs and preconditions, and requires WebDAV ACL and Class 3 support.
WebDAV.quote: A WebDAV server can advertise itself as a CardDAV server if it supports the functionality defined in this specification

rejected.why: Section 11 only registers carddav/carddavs SRV service names; this is a minor part of the document.
HTTP is the substrate. Only the WebDAV extensions are the subject.
TLS is only required for secure transport and is not specified or extended here.
XML is only the encoding for WebDAV request and response bodies.
Basic and Digest authentication appear only in Security Considerations.
LDAP and ACAP are mentioned only as prior protocols in the Introduction.

gaps.name: CardDAV / vCard (address book access)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a vCard tag with CardDAV under it, but no tag names this document's own subject, so the tags above may not match valid ids. A dedicated tag would help.

RFC6353.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC6353.summary: Defines the TLS Transport Model (TLSTM) for SNMP, carrying SNMP messages over TLS/TCP and DTLS/UDP with X.509 certificate authentication, plus the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB module for managing it.

SNMP.why: The document specifies a new SNMP Transport Model within the Transport Subsystem, with elements of procedure and security integration (TSM, VACM).
SNMP.quote: This document describes a Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), that uses either the Transport Layer Security protocol or the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

MIB.why: Defines the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB module with counters, configuration tables and notifications, a substantial part of the document.
MIB.quote: This document also defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols.

transport mapping.why: The document is a binding of SNMP onto TLS and DTLS transports, including transport domains and port assignments.
transport mapping.quote: It supports the sending of SNMP messages over TLS/TCP and DTLS/UDP.

rejected.why: TLS/DTLS is the security substrate; the document defines no new TLS extension, only how SNMP uses it.
DTLS is used as a transport mechanism; document does not extend DTLS itself.
X.509 certificates are used for authentication and mapped to names, but the document does not profile X.509.
Certificate provisioning is discussed briefly but the document is not about PKI.

RFC6354.title: Forward-Shifted RTP Redundancy Payload Support
RFC6354.summary: Extends RFC 2198 RTP redundancy to allow forward-shifted redundant blocks by registering the "fwdred" media type with a "forwardshift" parameter, its SDP mapping, and an informative anti-shadow loss concealment appendix.

RTP payload format.why: Updates the RFC 2198 redundancy RTP payload format and defines the new fwdred payload type and timestamp computation for redundant blocks.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines a simple enhancement to RFC 2198 [RFC2198] to support RTP sessions with forward-shifted redundant encodings

media types.why: A substantial part of the document is the registration of the audio/text fwdred media type with its parameters.
media types.quote: Registration of Media Type "fwdred"

SDP.why: Defines the SDP mapping of the forwardshift parameter and its offer/answer usage.
SDP.quote: a=fmtp:121 0/5 forwardshift=40800
SDP.section: 5. Mapping Media Type Parameters into SDP

FEC.why: The document is a loss-recovery scheme using redundant encodings, with receiver-side anti-shadow concealment in the appendix.
FEC.quote: Forward-shifted redundancy can be used to conceal losses of a large number of consecutive media frames

rejected.why: The more specific RTP payload format tag fits; RTP itself is only the carrier.
RFC 4867 is cited only for the maxptime parameter definition.
Wireless mobile shadowing is only the motivating scenario; no cellular network specifics are addressed.
No RTCP content; RTCP is not discussed beyond the security-considerations references.

RFC6355.title: Definition of the UUID-Based DHCPv6 Unique Identifier (DUID-UUID)
RFC6355.summary: Defines a new DHCPv6 DUID type, DUID-UUID (type 4), that embeds a 128-bit UUID so a device can use a persistent identifier across multi-step network boot stages.

DHCPv6.why: The document extends DHCPv6 by defining a new DUID type carried in the Client Identifier and Server Identifier options.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines a new DHCPv6 Unique Identifier (DUID) type called DUID-UUID.

UUID.why: A substantial part of the document covers which UUIDs are suitable for use as DHCP identifiers (persistence, firmware availability). It is the core of the new DUID type.
UUID.quote: DUID-UUIDs are derived from the already-standardized Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) format.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child and fits. DHCPv4 is mentioned only as precedent for UUID client identification.
DHCPv6 is the subject. IPv6 is only the network the protocol serves.
The IANA assignment of DUID type 4 is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC6356.title: Coupled Congestion Control for Multipath Transport Protocols
RFC6356.summary: Defines the Linked Increases coupled congestion control algorithm for Multipath TCP subflows, coupling additive increase and computing an aggressiveness parameter alpha so the multipath flow is fair to TCP while shifting traffic from congested paths.

MPTCP.why: MPTCP is not in the taxonomy as a child of congestion control, so this id is invalid; see rejected/gaps.

RFC6357.title: Design Considerations for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Overload Control
RFC6357.summary: Informational design-considerations document from the SOC working group discussing models, topologies, feedback types (rate, loss, window, signal, on/off), fairness and metrics for a SIP server overload control mechanism.

SIP.why: The whole document concerns overload control for SIP servers, including the limits of the 503 response and Retry-After, and the design of a new SIP overload mechanism.
SIP.quote: This document discusses the models, assumptions, and design considerations for a SIP overload control mechanism.

congestion control.why: The document addresses congestion collapse and rate-, loss- and window-based feedback control loops. These are congestion-control design topics, and no more specific congestion-control tag fits.
congestion control.quote: overload in a SIP server may lead to a situation in which the overload is amplified by retransmissions of SIP messages causing the throughput to drop

rejected.why: TCP is mentioned only as inspiration for window-based control and as a contrast with SIP overload control. The document is not about TCP.
RTP appears only as an example of other services that use server resources.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate neighbors.
Denial-of-service attacks are discussed only in Security Considerations. The document is about overload control, not DDoS mitigation.
The more specific SIP tag already covers this, and the document does not address real-time media.

gaps.name: SIP overload control
gaps.why: The document is about overload control for SIP, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. SIP and congestion control cover it only partly.

RFC6358.title: Additional Master Secret Inputs for TLS
RFC6358.summary: Experimental RFC defining a framework by which TLS and DTLS 1.2 extensions can mix additional inputs into the master_secret PRF calculation, specifying the ordering and formula.

TLS.why: The document modifies the TLS/DTLS master secret derivation and defines a framework for TLS extensions. It covers DTLS too, and DTLS is a child of TLS, so the TLS tag covers both.
TLS.quote: the additional master secret input values MUST be mixed into the pseudorandom function (PRF) calculation along with the client and server random values
TLS.section: 2. Master Secret Calculation Modifications for TLS and DTLS

rejected.why: The document treats DTLS together with TLS as one mechanism and adds nothing DTLS-specific, so the parent TLS tag is enough.
Master secret derivation is part of the TLS handshake. The document is not about key management in general.
The PRF is only the means of mixing the inputs. The document does not define or analyse an algorithm.

RFC6359.title: Datatracker Extensions to Include IANA and RFC Editor Processing Information
RFC6359.summary: Specifies requirements for extending the IETF Datatracker to show IANA and RFC Editor processing states and to automate data exchange between the Datatracker, IANA and the RFC Editor from I-D -00 to RFC publication.

IANA.why: Much of the document defines IANA review substates, IANA queue states and IANA-Datatracker integration, which is IANA process and considerations handling.
IANA.quote: the Datatracker should be extended to include IANA state information as defined by IANA

RFC series.why: It covers RFC Editor queue states, AUTH48, clusters and publication metadata, and automation of the RFC publication process.
RFC series.quote: the Datatracker should be extended to hold supplementary RFC Editor state and process (e.g., MISSREF) information

IETF process.why: The Datatracker requirements concern IESG review, agenda packages, Last Call and stream approval, which are IETF document-processing administration.
IETF process.quote: provide the community with a unified tool to track the status of their document as it progresses from Internet-Draft (I-D) version -00 to RFC

rejected.why: IPR disclosures are only mentioned in passing as a Datatracker function, not addressed.
Appendices list state names but the document is not a glossary.

gaps.name: Datatracker
gaps.why: The IETF Datatracker tool and its tooling requirements have no dedicated tag; the nearest are IETF process and RFC series.

RFC6360.title: Conclusion of FYI RFC Sub-Series
RFC6360.summary: RFC 6360 concludes the FYI RFC sub-series, obsoletes RFC 1150 and moves it to Historic, and records that the IESG will make no further FYI additions.

user guides.why: The FYI series is the user-guides sub-series. The document formally ends it and retires its governing RFC 1150, so readers of that subject would want it.
user guides.quote: This document concludes the For Your Information (FYI) sub-series of RFCs, established by RFC 1150 for use by the IETF User Services Area

RFC series.why: It decides the fate of an RFC sub-series. It covers numbering and citation of existing FYI documents and the status change of RFC 1150, which are RFC series publication matters.
RFC series.quote: The IESG does not intend to make any further additions to the FYI sub-series.

rejected.why: It mentions the IESG and the defunct User Services Area, but it is about the RFC sub-series, not IETF standards procedures.

RFC6361.title: PPP Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Protocol Control Protocol
RFC6361.summary: Defines the PPP TRILL Network Control Protocol (TNCP) and the TNP and TLSP protocol numbers, so RBridges can carry TRILL data and IS-IS link-state packets directly over PPP links.

TRILL.why: The document specifies how TRILL encapsulated data and TRILL IS-IS frames are carried between RBridges, and how TRILL behaves on PPP links.
TRILL.quote: This document describes PPP support for the Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Protocol, allowing direct communication between Routing Bridges (RBridges) via PPP links.

PPP.why: It defines a new PPP network control protocol (TNCP), new PPP protocol numbers, and a new option registry, which is a PPP extension.
PPP.quote: The TRILL Network Control Protocol (TNCP) is responsible for negotiating the use of the TRILL Network Protocol (TNP) and TRILL Link State Protocol (TLSP) on a PPP link.

rejected.why: TRILL's IS-IS is only carried in TLSP packets and handled by point-to-point hello rules. The document does not specify or extend IS-IS itself.
The Ethernet encapsulation is only referenced as the format that the PPP encapsulation mirrors.
EAP and CHAP are mentioned only as optional authentication in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
L2TP is only mentioned in passing as something PPP may run over.

RFC6362.title: Multiple Attachments for Electronic Data Interchange - Internet Integration (EDIINT)
RFC6362.summary: Informational RFC describing how to carry multiple attachments, including non-EDI payloads, in a single EDIINT (AS1/AS2/AS3) message using MIME multipart/related, with a feature header, MIC calculation rules and a minimum list of supported media types.

EDI.why: The document extends EDIINT (EDI over Internet transports AS1/AS2/AS3) with multiple attachments, defining the feature header, MIC calculation and payload handling.
EDI.quote: This Informational RFC describes how multiple documents, including non-EDI payloads, can be attached and transmitted in a single EDIINT transport message.

MIME.why: A substantial part of the document specifies use of the MIME multipart/related body structure, including root part, type and start parameters, and a list of required content-types.
MIME.quote: Multiple payload attachments for EDIINT messages are stored within a multipart/related MIME body [RFC2387].

rejected.why: The media type list in Section 2.5 is a minimum support list, not a registration or registry rule document.
AS1 over SMTP is only one of the underlying transports referenced; the document does not specify SMTP behaviour.
AS2 runs over HTTP, but HTTP is only the substrate and the example message is illustrative.
Signatures and encryption (multipart/signed, pkcs7) are inherited from the EDIINT specs and are not the subject here.
PKCS#7 signatures appear only in the example message; the document defines nothing new about CMS.
ABNF is used only to write one header value; it is just notation.

RFC6363.title: Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework
RFC6363.summary: RFC 6363 defines the FECFRAME framework for applying application-layer forward error correction to arbitrary packet flows (primarily real-time/streaming media) over unreliable transports, with FEC scheme requirements, packet formats, configuration information, congestion control and security guidance.

FECFRAME.why: The document is the FEC Framework itself: it specifies source/repair packet formats, configuration information and FEC scheme requirements.
FECFRAME.quote: This document defines a framework for the definition of CDPs that provide for FEC protection for arbitrary packet flows over unreliable transports such as UDP.

rejected.why: RTP is only an optional source-flow and repair-flow carrier; the document does not specify RTP itself, only notes RTP payload formats are defined per FEC scheme.
Section 8 gives normative limits on repair bandwidth, but this is a small part of the document and not its subject.
SRTP is only mentioned as a security option in Security Considerations.
IPsec/ESP is only recommended as a baseline security mechanism in the Security Considerations.
ALC and NORM are referenced only for baseline security operation; the framework is for streaming packet flows, not reliable multicast object delivery.
FECFRAME is the more specific child tag and already implies FEC.

RFC6364.title: Session Description Protocol Elements for the Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework
RFC6364.summary: Defines SDP attributes (fec-source-flow, fec-repair-flow, repair-window) and transport identifiers (FEC/UDP, UDP/FEC) to signal FEC Framework Configuration Information, with grouping examples.

FECFRAME.why: The document exists to carry FEC Framework configuration information in SDP, so it belongs to the FECFRAME subject.
FECFRAME.quote: specifies the use of the Session Description Protocol (SDP) to describe the parameters required to signal the Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework Configuration Information

SDP.why: It defines new SDP attributes and transport protocol identifiers, and shows grouping and offer/answer usage, so it extends SDP.
SDP.quote: This document specifies a new attribute to describe the size of the repair window in milliseconds and microseconds.

rejected.why: RTP appears only in the examples as the source flow transport, and the document does not specify anything about it.
FECFRAME is the more specific child tag, and the document does not cover FEC codes themselves.
Multicast addresses appear in the examples and in the declarative discussion, but the document is not about multicast routing or deployment.
ABNF is used only as notation for the new attribute syntax.

RFC6365.title: Terminology Used in Internationalization in the IETF
RFC6365.summary: RFC 6365 is a BCP glossary of terminology used in IETF internationalization work, covering characters, encodings, Unicode/ISO standards, text handling in protocols, and IDNA terms.

internationalization.why: The whole document defines internationalization vocabulary for IETF protocol designers, so the internationalization topic is its main subject.
internationalization.quote: In the IETF, "internationalization" means to add or improve the handling of non-ASCII text in a protocol.

Unicode.why: Large parts cover Unicode and ISO/IEC 10646 concepts: code points, normalization, properties, subsets and encoding forms.
Unicode.quote: The Unicode Standard is a CCS whose repertoire and code points are identical to ISO/IEC 10646.

character sets.why: Defines charset, CCS, CES, charset identification and IANA charset registration, and discusses native charsets.
character sets.quote: A charset is a method of mapping a sequence of octets to a sequence of abstract characters.

IDN.why: A dedicated section covers IDNA terms, Punycode, stringprep and variants, so IDN readers would want it.
IDN.quote: The current specification for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs), known formally as Internationalized Domain Names for Applications or IDNA

rejected.why: UTF-8 is one of many encodings defined in the glossary, not the document's subject.
ASCII is discussed only as a contrast to non-ASCII text, not as a subject in its own right.
It is a glossary, but the subject matter is internationalization terms specifically, and the more specific tag fits better.
Language tags are mentioned briefly with pointers to the LTRU RFCs, but the document does not address them substantively.
MIME, Base64 and quoted-printable are defined only as short glossary entries.

RFC6366.title: Requirements for an Internet Audio Codec
RFC6366.summary: RFC 6366 specifies requirements for an Internet audio codec (the work that led to Opus), covering target applications, quality, bit-rate, delay, packet-loss robustness, complexity, and extra desirable properties.

codecs.why: The whole document defines requirements for a new audio codec: sampling rates, bit-rates, delay, loss robustness, and complexity. The generic codecs tag fits best because no specific codec is defined.
codecs.quote: This document provides requirements for an audio codec designed specifically for use over the Internet.

rejected.why: The document only requires that an RTP payload format conforming to BCP 36 be possible. It does not define one.
RTP is only the transport the codec must work with. The document does not specify or extend it.
SIP/SDP is mentioned only as a way to negotiate codec parameters.
The document does not mention Opus. It states requirements for a codec that was developed later.
The parent topic is implied by codecs, and the document is about the codec rather than real-time communications in general.
Conferencing is one application scenario that drives the requirements. The document does not address conferencing frameworks or control.

RFC6367.title: Addition of the Camellia Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS)
