RFC6367.summary: RFC 6367 defines forty-two TLS cipher suites using the Camellia block cipher in CBC and GCM modes, with SHA-2 HMACs, elliptic curve and PSK key exchange variants.

Camellia.why: The document exists to define Camellia-based cipher suites for TLS, which is exactly the scope of the Camellia tag (its cipher suites in TLS).
Camellia.quote: This document specifies forty-two cipher suites for the Transport Security Layer (TLS) protocol to support the Camellia encryption algorithm as a block cipher.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS with new cipher suites and registers code points in the TLS Cipher Suite Registry, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document proposes the addition of new cipher suites to the Transport Layer Security (TLS) [8] protocol

rejected.why: AES GCM is referenced only as the model for defining Camellia GCM; the document is not about AES.
HMAC with SHA-256/384 is just the MAC used in the suites, not something specified or analysed here.
SHA-2 is used as the hash and PRF hash; it is a building block, not the subject.
ECDH/ECDHE key exchange is used in suite names but defined in other RFCs; nothing new about elliptic curves is specified.
Key exchange methods (RSA, DHE, PSK) are inherited from existing RFCs; the document only combines them with Camellia.
ECDSA appears only in cipher suite names as an authentication algorithm and is not specified here.

RFC6368.title: Internal BGP as the Provider/Customer Edge Protocol for BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
RFC6368.summary: Defines the ATTR_SET BGP path attribute and procedures so iBGP can be used between PE and CE routers in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, making the VPN act as a transparent route server for customer BGP attributes.

L3VPN.why: The document extends BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 4364) with PE-CE iBGP procedures, VRF import/export handling and inter-AS deployment considerations.
L3VPN.quote: This document defines protocol extensions and procedures for BGP Provider/Customer Edge router iteration in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs.

BGP.why: It defines a new BGP optional transitive path attribute, its encoding, malformed-attribute handling and next-hop/AS_PATH rules for iBGP PE-CE sessions.
BGP.quote: this document defines a new BGP path attribute: ATTR_SET (type code 128)

route reflection.why: The route-server model is built on route reflection semantics (split horizon, client-to-client reflection disabled, CE as RR), a substantial part of the design.
route reflection.quote: one can consider the VPN as the equivalent of an Internal BGP Route Server that multiplexes information from _N_ VPN attachment points.
route reflection.section: 3. IP VPN as a Route Server

rejected.why: That tag is for Internet exchange route servers; here the route-server idea is only a conceptual model for the VPN.
MPLS is the VPN substrate; the document concerns BGP attribute handling, not label switching.
Communities are mentioned only as an example of attributes carried transparently.

RFC6369.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Implementation Experience
RFC6369.summary: Informational document capturing implementation experience for the ForCES protocol and FE model, giving strategies for building components, LFBs, TLV handling, and message (de)serialization.

ForCES.why: The whole document is about implementing ForCES: LFB/component class design, TLV hierarchy, message serialization, and TML considerations.
ForCES.quote: This document captures the experience of implementing the ForCES protocol and model.

rejected.why: SCTP is only the mandatory TML transport substrate; the document merely notes platform support and port forwarding.
Mentioned only as the required transport security for the SCTP TML, a boilerplate-level dependency.
The TML is discussed briefly (Section 3.2), but the document is not about defining transport mappings; ForCES covers it.
ForCES is control/forwarding separation, but the document does not discuss SDN as a subject.
NAT is mentioned only in passing regarding port forwarding for remote deployments.

RFC6370.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Identifiers
RFC6370.summary: RFC 6370 defines an initial set of IP/MPLS-compatible identifiers for MPLS-TP (Global_ID, Node_ID, IF_ID, Tunnel, LSP, PW path, MEG/MEP/MIP identifiers) to support configuration, management and OAM without a control plane.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines identifiers for MPLS-TP entities (nodes, interfaces, tunnels, LSPs, PWs, MEGs, MEPs, MIPs), so readers of MPLS-TP need it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document specifies an initial set of identifiers to be used in the Transport Profile of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS-TP).

rejected.why: Pseudowire path identifiers are defined (Section 6), but they reuse the existing RFC 4447 Generalized PWid FEC and RFC 5003 AII; the document does not extend pseudowire signalling itself.
Section 5.3 informatively maps LSP_IDs to the RSVP-TE 5-tuple, but RSVP-TE is not specified or extended here.
The identifiers are designed for compatibility with GMPLS interface IDs, but GMPLS is only referenced as a convention source.
MEG/MEP/MIP identifiers support OAM, but the document defines identifiers, not OAM mechanisms. The MPLS-TP tag covers it.
LDP is only the signalling protocol whose FEC fields the PW identifiers map onto.
AS numbers are used to derive the Global_ID, but the document explicitly says this is unrelated to the use of ASNs in BGP.

RFC6371.title: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance Framework for MPLS-Based Transport Networks
RFC6371.summary: Informational framework describing protocol-neutral OAM functions and architecture (MEPs, MIPs, MEGs, SPMEs) for MPLS-TP transport networks, covering proactive, on-demand and administrative OAM.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines the OAM framework for MPLS-TP: maintenance entities, reference models for sections, LSPs, PWs and SPMEs, and OAM functions. MPLS-TP is the specific technology addressed.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document describes a framework to support a comprehensive set of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) procedures that fulfill the MPLS-TP OAM requirements

OAM.why: The document is a general OAM framework (CC-V, RDI, AIS, LKR, loss and delay measurement, loopback, route tracing). OAM is a topic tag with no technology tag chosen under it, so it is added directly.
OAM.quote: Sections 5, 6, and 7 provide a protocol-neutral description of the OAM functions, defined in RFC 5860 [11]

rejected.why: Pseudowires appear as monitored entities (PW MEGs, MS-PW SPMEs), but the document does not specify pseudowire emulation itself.
MPLS is implied as the parent of MPLS-TP; the more specific MPLS-TP tag fits.
Packet loss and delay measurement are covered, but only as OAM functions within the framework, not as a measurement methodology in their own right.
Route tracing is described as one on-demand OAM function, with only a brief section and no specified mechanism.
PHB, E-LSP and L-LSP handling for OAM packets is mentioned, but the document is not about Diffserv.

RFC6372.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Survivability Framework
RFC6372.summary: Informational framework describing how survivability (protection and restoration of LSPs) is provided in an MPLS Transport Profile network via data-plane, OAM, management-plane and control-plane mechanisms.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines the survivability framework for MPLS-TP: linear, ring and shared mesh protection, recovery domains, SPMEs and recovery in layered networks.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document comprises a framework for the provision of survivability in an MPLS-TP network; it describes recovery elements, types, methods, and topological considerations.

rejected.why: The GMPLS control plane (RSVP-TE recovery extensions, LMP) is described as an optional control-plane mechanism in Section 6.5, but it is not the main subject. The document is about MPLS-TP survivability.
MPLS-TP OAM is used to detect faults and trigger recovery, but the OAM tools themselves are specified in RFC 6371. Here OAM is only a trigger mechanism.
Pseudowire recovery is explicitly out of scope and is only briefly considered in Section 7.
RSVP-TE extensions are referenced as existing mechanisms for establishing protection LSPs. The document does not specify or extend them.
Protection and restoration concepts are discussed, but the subject is MPLS-TP survivability rather than traffic engineering in general.

gaps.name: Network survivability / protection switching and restoration
gaps.why: The document's core subject is recovery (protection and restoration) of transport networks: 1:1, 1+1, 1:n and shared mesh protection, and ring protection. The taxonomy has no survivability or resilience tag, so MPLS-TP is the closest fit.

RFC6373.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Control Plane Framework
RFC6373.summary: Informational framework describing how the MPLS-TP control plane (GMPLS RSVP-TE/OSPF-TE/IS-IS-TE for LSPs, targeted LDP for pseudowires) meets MPLS-TP requirements, and identifying needed extensions.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is the control plane framework for MPLS Transport Profile.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document provides the framework for MPLS-TP dynamic provisioning and covers control-plane addressing, routing, path computation, signaling, traffic engineering, and path recovery.

GMPLS.why: Large parts review GMPLS functions (signaling, routing, recovery, hierarchy) and how they meet MPLS-TP requirements.
GMPLS.quote: MPLS-TP uses Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) signaling and routing, see [RFC3945], as the control plane for LSPs.

pseudowire.why: Section 5 covers the PW control plane for MPLS-TP, its requirements table and needed extensions.
pseudowire.quote: The SS-PW signaling control plane is based on targeted LDP (T-LDP) with specific procedures defined in [RFC4447].

rejected.why: Used as the GMPLS signaling mechanism but the document is not specifying RSVP-TE itself; covered under GMPLS.
Targeted LDP is the PW signaling substrate; the document defines nothing new in LDP, only anticipates extensions.
Routing protocol referenced only as GMPLS routing foundation.
Referenced only as GMPLS routing foundation.
Mentioned briefly; PCE-specific MPLS-TP extensions explicitly out of scope.
OAM configuration requirements are listed, but the document is about control plane, not OAM mechanisms.

RFC6374.title: Packet Loss and Delay Measurement for MPLS Networks
RFC6374.summary: RFC 6374 specifies LM and DM protocols over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel to measure packet loss, delay, delay variation and throughput on LSPs, pseudowires and MPLS sections.

performance measurement.why: The document defines loss and delay measurement protocols, message formats and procedures. No specific measurement-protocol tech tag (OWAMP, TWAMP, STAMP) fits, so the parent topic applies.
performance measurement.quote: This document specifies protocol mechanisms to enable the efficient and accurate measurement of these performance metrics in MPLS networks.

MPLS.why: The protocols are defined for MPLS LSPs, pseudowires and sections, and use new G-ACh channel types. MPLS readers would want this RFC.
MPLS.quote: The LM and DM protocols operate over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) [RFC5586] and support measurement of loss, delay, and related metrics

MPLS-TP.why: The document explicitly targets MPLS-TP and points to a companion profile (RFC 6375). That applicability is a notable part of its scope.
MPLS-TP.quote: The LM and DM protocols are applicable to the LSPs, pseudowires, and sections of networks based on the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP)

OAM.why: LM and DM are OAM tools for monitoring and troubleshooting MPLS channels. The document describes them as infrastructure for diagnostics and monitoring.
OAM.quote: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an IP-network comparison; the document defines a different protocol.
Mentioned only as an IP-network comparison; the document defines a different protocol.
Only its timestamp format is one of the supported options; the document is not about NTP.
IEEE 1588 timestamp format is the default, but PTP itself is not specified or profiled here.
ECMP is discussed only as a measurement consideration in one subsection.
Pseudowires are one kind of channel being measured, not the subject of the document.

RFC6375.title: A Packet Loss and Delay Measurement Profile for MPLS-Based Transport Networks
RFC6375.summary: Informational profile of the RFC 6374 MPLS packet loss and delay measurement procedures, fixing default parameters and message rates to meet MPLS-TP transport network OAM requirements.

MPLS-TP.why: The document profiles RFC 6374 loss and delay measurement specifically for MPLS-TP, so MPLS-TP readers would want it.
MPLS-TP.quote: describes a profile, i.e., a simplified subset, of these procedures that suffices to meet the specific requirements of MPLS-based transport networks

performance measurement.why: The body specifies default parameters and message intervals for packet loss measurement (LM) and delay measurement (DM) sessions.
performance measurement.quote: Procedures for the measurement of packet loss, delay, and throughput in MPLS networks are defined in [RFC6374].

rejected.why: The measurement is OAM-related, but the more specific performance measurement tag covers it. OAM is mentioned only through the requirements reference.
It is implied as the parent of MPLS-TP.
The NMS and configuration are only assumed external, not addressed.
IEEE 1588v2 truncated timestamps are only a default format parameter, not the subject.
Mentioned only as an excluded topology consideration.

RFC6376.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures
RFC6376.summary: RFC 6376 specifies DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), a cryptographic domain-level message signing mechanism for email, including the DKIM-Signature header field, canonicalization, DNS-based key records, and signer and verifier actions; it obsoletes RFC 4871 and RFC 5672.

DKIM.why: The document is the core DKIM specification: signature header field, canonicalization, key records, and signer/verifier procedures.
DKIM.quote: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) permits a person, role, or organization that owns the signing domain to claim some responsibility for a message

rejected.why: DNS TXT records under _domainkey are used only as the key-distribution substrate; DNS itself is not specified or extended.
RSA with SHA-1/SHA-256 is the signing algorithm used, but the document does not specify or analyse RSA.
Relies on RFC 5322 header fields, but does not define message format; it defines a signature header field.
SHA-1 and SHA-256 are used as hash functions only, not specified or analysed.
DMARC is not defined here; this RFC predates it and only mentions Authentication-Results in passing.
SMTP is only the transport that carries signed mail; reply codes are mentioned in passing.

RFC6377.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) and Mailing Lists
RFC6377.summary: BCP giving guidance on how DKIM signing, verification and ADSP should be handled by authors, mailing list managers and receivers when messages transit mailing lists, which commonly break signatures.

DKIM.why: The whole document is best-practice guidance on DKIM signing and verification with MLMs, including MLM signatures and signature removal.
DKIM.quote: this document provides guidance for the use of DKIM with scenarios that include Mailing List Managers (MLMs).

mailing lists.why: It classifies MLM types (aliasing, resending, authoring, digesting) and how their behaviour affects message signatures, so it belongs on the mailing list page.
mailing lists.quote: there are two categories of MLMs in relation to DKIM: participating and non-participating.

ARF.why: The document devotes sections to feedback loops and abuse reports for list mail, which is ARF's domain. ARF itself is only referenced, so this tag is weak.
ARF.quote: FBLs tend to use the [ARF] or the [IODEF] formats.
ARF.section: 1.3. Feedback Loops and Other Bilateral Agreements

rejected.why: The child tag DKIM already covers this parent.
SMTP is the substrate. The document only recommends a 5.7.0 enhanced status code and discard-versus-reject behaviour for policy failures.
Header fields such as Authentication-Results and List-Id are discussed only for how list changes affect signatures. The document does not specify the message format.
DMARC is not mentioned. The policy mechanism discussed is ADSP, which has no tag in the taxonomy.
Spam filtering is mentioned only in passing, as a side effect of broken signatures.
MIME body changes by MLMs are discussed only as ways signatures are broken.

gaps.name: ADSP (Author Domain Signing Practices)
gaps.why: A large part of the document covers ADSP policies, including 'discardable' and MLM handling of them at subscription time. The taxonomy has no ADSP tag, and DKIM is the closest fit.

RFC6378.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Linear Protection
RFC6378.summary: Defines the MPLS-TP Protection State Coordination (PSC) protocol, carried over the G-ACh, and its state machine for linear (1:1 and 1+1) protection switching of LSPs.

MPLS-TP.why: The RFC specifies the PSC protocol and state machine for MPLS-TP linear protection, so it belongs on the MPLS-TP page.
MPLS-TP.quote: The scope of this document is to present a protocol for the Protection State Coordination of Linear Protection.

rejected.why: MPLS is the general substrate. MPLS-TP is the more specific tag that applies.
It is mentioned only for control-plane-triggered recovery, which defers to RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. The document is not about GMPLS.
OAM indications are inputs to the Local Request logic. The document does not define OAM mechanisms.
Pseudowires appear only through the PW associated channel type registry and the architecture references.
The IANA section only registers the PSC channel type and the Request registry. That is boilerplate.
This is MPLS-TP linear protection switching. It is not IP or LDP fast reroute.

gaps.name: Protection switching / network survivability
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for protection switching or survivability. MPLS-TP is the closest fit, but linear protection (1:1, 1+1) is the document's main subject.

RFC6379.title: Suite B Cryptographic Suites for IPsec
RFC6379.summary: Defines four Suite B cryptographic UI suites (Suite-B-GCM-128/256, Suite-B-GMAC-128/256) for IPsec ESP and IKEv2, obsoleting RFC 4869.

IPsec.why: The document defines cryptographic suites that are collections of option values for IPsec ESP and IKEv2, so IPsec readers need it.
IPsec.quote: Each of the following UI suites provides choices for ESP (see [RFC4303]) and for Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2)

AES.why: The suites are named and differentiated by AES mode (GCM, GMAC) and key length, so AES modes are a substantial part of the content.
AES.quote: This suite provides ESP integrity protection and confidentiality using 128-bit AES-GCM (see [RFC4106]).

rejected.why: IKEv2 algorithm choices are part of each suite, but the document does not specify or extend IKE itself; IPsec covers it.
ESP is the protocol the suites configure; the document does not define ESP behaviour, and the IPsec tag fits better.
HMAC-SHA-256/384 are listed as IKEv2 PRF and integrity choices, but the document is not about HMAC.
ECP groups are referenced only as the Diffie-Hellman group selection, not discussed in their own right.
SHA-256/384 appear only inside HMAC algorithm names in the suite tables.

RFC6380.title: Suite B Profile for Internet Protocol Security (IPsec)
RFC6380.summary: RFC 6380 profiles the use of NSA Suite B cryptography (AES, ECDSA, ECDH on P-256/P-384, SHA-256/384) in IPsec, mandating IKEv2 and ESP with four Suite B UI suites, ECDSA authentication and Suite B certificates.

IPsec.why: The document is an IPsec profile constraining ESP, SA negotiation and policy for Suite B compliance.
IPsec.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using NSA Suite B Cryptography [SuiteB] in IP Security (IPsec).

IKE.why: Much of the body specifies IKEv2 behaviour: authentication, KE payload, SA proposals, keying material derivation, CREATE_CHILD_SA rules.
IKE.quote: Suite B compliant implementations for IPsec MUST use IKEv2 [RFC5996].

elliptic curve.why: Requires ECDH and ECDSA on P-256 and P-384 curves, with curve naming and DH group numbers.
elliptic curve.quote: Suite B requires that key establishment and signature algorithms be based upon Elliptic Curve Cryptography and that the encryption algorithm be AES

rejected.why: ECDSA is used for IKEv2 authentication per RFC 4754, but this document only profiles its use; elliptic curve covers the cryptography subject.
AES is mandated as the cipher but the document defines nothing new about it.
Certificates are required to follow RFC 5759, only referenced in one short section.
ESP is used via the UI suites defined in RFC 6379; the document does not specify ESP itself beyond suite selection, so IPsec covers it.
SHA-256/384 are listed as part of Suite B but not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Suite B cryptography
gaps.why: The document is about the NSA Suite B algorithm policy profile; the taxonomy has no Suite B tag, only the general cryptography topic.

RFC6381.title: The 'Codecs' and 'Profiles' Parameters for "Bucket" Media Types
RFC6381.summary: Defines the 'codecs' and 'profiles' optional parameters for container ("bucket") media types such as 3GPP, MP4 and QuickTime, so receivers can tell from Content-Type which codecs and container profiles are needed; obsoletes RFC 4281.

media types.why: The document defines new parameters for existing media types (audio/3gpp, video/mp4, video/quicktime, etc.) and updates their registrations. Readers of media type registration rules would want it.
media types.quote: This document specifies two parameters, 'codecs' and 'profiles', that are used with various MIME types or type/subtype combinations

codecs.why: A large part of the document defines codec naming for ISO base media file format, including mp4a, mp4v and AVC/SVC/MVC (avc1) profile/level encoding. Readers of audio and video codec definitions would want it.
codecs.quote: the first element of a 'codecs' parameter value is a sample description entry four-character code as registered by the MP4 Registration Authority

rejected.why: The parameters are carried in MIME Content-Type headers and use RFC 2045/2231 syntax, but the document does not change MIME body structure or encodings. It is better covered by media types.
Defines how to encode AVC profile_idc, constraint flags and level_idc into the codecs string, but the document is not about the H.264 codec itself.
AMR is mentioned only as an example of a codec found in 3GPP containers.
MMS and email are cited only as motivating use cases.

gaps.name: ISO Base Media File Format / MP4 / 3GPP container formats
gaps.why: The document is about the codecs and profiles parameters for ISO-family file containers (mp4, 3gpp, QuickTime). The taxonomy has no tag for these container formats beyond Matroska.

RFC6382.title: Unique Origin Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) per Node for Globally Anycasted Services
RFC6382.summary: BCP recommending that globally anycasted critical infrastructure services (e.g., root/TLD DNS) use a unique origin ASN per anycast node, giving BGP control-plane discriminators for monitoring, policy and RPKI ROA granularity.

anycast.why: The whole document is operational guidance on anycast deployment: how anycast nodes should be identified in the routing system through per-node origin ASNs.
anycast.quote: globally anycasted critical infrastructure services in order to provide routing system discriminators for a given anycasted prefix

BGP.why: The recommendation concerns BGP origin AS practice, inconsistent-origin reporting, and AS path based policy, so BGP operators would want it.
BGP.quote: anycasting in BGP requires injection of reachability information in the routing system for a common IP address prefix from multiple locations

RPKI.why: A substantive paragraph explains the benefit for ROA issuance and avoiding a single ROA revocation taking down a whole anycast service.
RPKI.quote: Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs), and routing policies that may be derived based on those ROAs, can be employed with per-anycast-node resolution

rejected.why: Root and TLD name servers are the motivating example, but the document specifies nothing about DNS protocol or operations.
Mentioned only as a service-layer authenticity mechanism and in security considerations; not the subject.
RPSLng is cited once as a way to express per-node upstream ASNs; not a subject of the document.
The RPKI tag covers the relevant routing-security content and sits under this topic, so the parent is not tagged.
Considered because of the monitoring and detection motivation, but the document's focus is anycast and origin ASN practice, which is better covered by more specific tags.

RFC6383.title: Advice on When It Is Safe to Start Sending Data on Label Switched Paths Established Using RSVP-TE
RFC6383.summary: Informational RFC clarifying, without new procedures, when RSVP-TE signalling exchanges for MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs mean cross-connects are programmed and it is safe to start sending data, for unidirectional and bidirectional LSPs.

RSVP-TE.why: The whole document analyses RSVP-TE Path/Resv/ResvConf message handling relative to cross-connect programming for TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document clarifies and summarizes the RSVP-TE protocol exchanges with relation to the programming of cross-connects along an LSP

GMPLS.why: A substantial part covers GMPLS-specific behaviour: Suggested_Label, Upstream_Label, bidirectional LSPs, Admin_Status, and optical laser safety.
GMPLS.quote: GMPLS supports unidirectional and bidirectional LSPs.  These are split into separate sections for discussion.

rejected.why: Plain RSVP is only the base that RSVP-TE extends. The document is about the TE extensions, so RSVP-TE is the more specific tag.
MPLS is the setting. The document's subject is signalling behaviour, which RSVP-TE and GMPLS cover more specifically.
Section 4 only notes how the clarifications affect interpreting RFC 5814 metrics. It defines no metrics or methods.

RFC6384.title: An FTP Application Layer Gateway (ALG) for IPv6-to-IPv4 Translation
RFC6384.summary: Specifies an FTP Application Layer Gateway for IPv6-to-IPv4 translators that rewrites EPSV/EPRT commands to PASV/PORT, and defines the new ALGS command to query and control the ALG.

FTP.why: The document specifies FTP control-channel translation behaviour, command translation and a new FTP command (ALGS, registered in the FTP Commands registry).
FTP.quote: this document standardizes an FTP Application Layer Gateway (ALG) that will allow unmodified IPv6 FTP clients to interact with unmodified IPv4 FTP servers

IPv6 transition.why: It is an ALG making FTP work through IPv6-to-IPv4 translators, which is an IPv6/IPv4 coexistence mechanism. No more specific child tag fits, since the document is about the ALG rather than NAT64 or SIIT themselves.
IPv6 transition.quote: The recommendations and specifications in this document apply to all forms of IPv6-to-IPv4 translation, including stateless translation such as [RFC6145] as well as stateful translation such as [RFC6146].

rejected.why: Stateful NAT64 is the translator the ALG works alongside, but the document specifies the FTP ALG, not NAT64.
Stateless translation (RFC 6145) is only referenced as an environment the ALG works with.
The ALG must implement Telnet only to the degree needed to parse the control channel, and the document does not extend or specify Telnet.
TLS appears only as a case where the ALG goes transparent on AUTH, not as a subject of the document.
TCP sequence number adjustment is an implementation detail of the ALG, and the document does not specify TCP.
The ALG is part of IPv6/IPv4 translation, which is covered by the IPv6 transition tag, not general NAT behaviour.

RFC6385.title: General Area Review Team (Gen-ART) Experiences
RFC6385.summary: RFC 6385 describes the IETF General Area Review Team (Gen-ART) review process for Internet-Drafts, including assignment procedures, review form, results and lessons learned over seven years.

IETF process.why: The document describes a volunteer review team that supports IESG review of I-Ds before approval. It covers the process, assignment procedures and lessons learned, so it belongs under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: The General Area Review Team (Gen-ART) has been doing reviews of Internet-Drafts (I-Ds) since 2004.

rejected.why: The reviews cover RFC style and IANA sections, but the document is about I-D review in the IETF process, not RFC format or publication.
IANA considerations are only one item on the reviewers' checklist; the document is not about IANA registries.
Architectural RFCs appear only as review criteria, not as the subject of the document.
The document does not define terms or requirements language as its subject.

RFC6386.title: VP8 Data Format and Decoding Guide
RFC6386.summary: Specifies the VP8 compressed video data format and its decoding procedure, with the reference decoder source code as an attachment.

VP8.why: The whole document defines the VP8 bitstream, boolean entropy decoding, prediction, transforms, loop filter and reference decoder.
VP8.quote: This document describes the VP8 compressed video data format, together with a discussion of the decoding procedure for the format.

rejected.why: VP8 is a child of codecs and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The document does not define an RTP payload format; it covers only the bitstream and decoder.
The boolean entropy coder is part of the VP8 format, not a general lossless compression format the document is about.
No media type registration appears in the body.

RFC6387.title: GMPLS Asymmetric Bandwidth Bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC6387.summary: Standards-track document defining UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC, UPSTREAM_TSPEC and UPSTREAM_ADSPEC RSVP objects so GMPLS RSVP-TE can signal bidirectional LSPs with different bandwidth in each direction; it obsoletes the experimental RFC 5467.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS signalling (RFC 3473) to support asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional LSPs, applicable to any GMPLS switching technology.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines a method for the support of GMPLS asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs).

RSVP-TE.why: It defines new RSVP objects and the Path/Resv message formats and procedures for them, extending RSVP-TE signalling for traffic-engineered LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: The setup of an asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional LSP is signaled using the bidirectional procedures defined in [RFC3473] together with the inclusion of the new UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC

rejected.why: MPLS-TP's requirement for asymmetric bandwidth motivates the document, but the mechanism is generic to any GMPLS technology and is not MPLS-TP specific.
The RSVP objects (TSPEC, FLOWSPEC, ADSPEC) are reused and extended, but the document is about GMPLS LSP signalling, and RSVP-TE is the more specific fit.
Ethernet use cases (RFC 6060, RFC 6003) are only cited as background; the Ethernet-specific approach was removed.
RBNF is only used as the syntax notation for the packet formats; the document is not about it.

RFC6388.title: Label Distribution Protocol Extensions for Point-to-Multipoint and Multipoint-to-Multipoint Label Switched Paths
RFC6388.summary: Specifies multipoint LDP (mLDP) extensions to LDP for receiver-initiated setup of P2MP and MP2MP LSPs, including new FEC elements, capabilities, MP Status TLV, root redundancy, and make-before-break procedures.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with new FEC elements, capability TLVs, status TLV and procedures for multipoint LSPs, so it belongs on the LDP page.
LDP.quote: This document describes extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) for the setup of point-to-multipoint (P2MP) and multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

rejected.why: MPLS is the general setting, but the more specific LDP tag covers the document. The LSPs it builds are MPLS LSPs.
The LSPs can carry multicast traffic, but the document says it works without any multicast protocol and that applications are out of scope.
RFC 4875 (RSVP-TE P2MP) is only mentioned as a related document and as an interface type. This document does not specify it.
Multicast in L3VPNs is named only as a possible application, and the document leaves its specification out of scope.
The Manageability section only notes that existing MIB modules suffice and that any new MIB work is future study.
The document describes tree construction from unicast routing, not traffic engineering.

RFC6389.title: MPLS Upstream Label Assignment for LDP
RFC6389.summary: Defines LDP extensions (capability, TLVs, tunnel identifier sub-TLVs) for distributing MPLS upstream-assigned labels, and applies them to avoid branch-LSR replication for LDP P2MP LSPs on a LAN.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with a new capability parameter, Upstream-Assigned Label and Label Request TLVs, and Interface ID sub-TLVs.
LDP.quote: This document describes procedures for distributing upstream-assigned labels for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

multicast.why: A substantial part (Section 6) applies upstream labels to LDP P2MP LSPs on a LAN so one copy of each multicast packet is sent. No narrower multicast tag fits, since MLDP is not in the taxonomy.
multicast.quote: avoid branch LSR traffic replication on a LAN for LDP point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

rejected.why: LDP is a child of MPLS and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The RSVP-TE P2MP LSP sub-TLV only identifies an outer tunnel. RSVP-TE is not specified or extended here.
The Interface ID TLV is reused from RFC 3472 and IANA registry, but the document is not about GMPLS.
IANA Considerations is boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: MLDP / LDP point-to-multipoint LSPs
gaps.why: The document is largely about P2MP LSPs set up by LDP (RFC 6388). The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS multicast or MLDP.

RFC6390.title: Guidelines for Considering New Performance Metric Development
RFC6390.summary: BCP defining a framework and process for developing Performance Metrics for protocols and applications over IETF protocols, including metric definition template and the Performance Metrics Directorate review process.

performance measurement.why: The whole document is about defining, specifying and reviewing performance metrics for active and passive measurement, which is the performance measurement subject.
performance measurement.quote: This document describes a framework and a process for developing Performance Metrics of protocols and applications transported over IETF-specified protocols.

rejected.why: QoS and QoE are defined as terminology to relate to metrics, but the document is not about QoS architectures or signalling.
IPFIX is mentioned only as an example of where metrics could be exported, not specified or profiled.
RTCP XR LossRate is used as the worked example only; the document does not extend RTCP.
A process for metric review by a directorate is described, but it concerns metric development, not the general IETF process; the subject is performance measurement.
OWAMP is cited only in Security Considerations as a reference for active measurement.
RAQMON/RMON appear only as background in the motivation section.

RFC6391.title: Flow-Aware Transport of Pseudowires over an MPLS Packet Switched Network
RFC6391.summary: Defines an optional flow label (an extra MPLS label stack entry at the bottom of the stack) for pseudowires so LSRs can load-balance flows within a PW over ECMPs, LAGs and multiple TE paths, with LDP signalling via a Flow Label Sub-TLV.

pseudowire.why: The document extends pseudowires with a flow LSE, a new signalling Sub-TLV, static PW, multi-segment PW and VCCV OAM handling.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a method of identifying the flows, or flow groups, within pseudowires such that Label Switching Routers can balance flows at a finer granularity

ECMP.why: The purpose is to give LSRs entropy for ECMP load balancing of flows within a PW; substantial discussion of ECMP applicability.
ECMP.quote: it can be desirable to carry those flows over the Equal Cost Multiple Paths (ECMPs) that exist in the packet switched network

MPLS.why: The mechanism is a new label stack entry in the MPLS encoding, with TTL/TC rules and relation to entropy labels.
MPLS.quote: The mechanism uses an additional label in the MPLS label stack.

rejected.why: LAG is only one of several applicability cases (Section 8.2), not the focus.
LDP signalling per RFC 4447 is used as substrate; the new item is a Sub-TLV for PW signalling, not LDP itself.
Mentioned only as one load-balancing applicability scenario.
Section 8.5 merely says the mechanism must not be deployed in MPLS-TP networks.
VCCV considerations are a short section, not a main subject.

RFC6392.title: A Survey of In-Network Storage Systems
RFC6392.summary: Survey of deployed and experimental in-network storage systems and related storage protocols (S3, CDN, DTN, NDN, web cache, NFS, iSCSI, WebDAV, etc.), evaluating their applicability to the DECADE architecture.

storage.why: The whole document surveys network storage systems and storage access/authorization models, which is the storage subject area.
storage.quote: This document surveys deployed and experimental in-network storage systems and describes their applicability for the DECADE (DECoupled Application Data Enroute) architecture.

CDN.why: A full survey section is devoted to content delivery networks as in-network storage, with infrastructure and access models.
CDN.quote: CDNs offer fast and reliable applications and services by distributing content to cache or edge servers located close to users.

HTTP caching.why: Web caches and P2P/HTTP caching are surveyed as in-network storage, and caching runs through the whole document.
HTTP caching.quote: A Web cache can cache the Web documents (e.g., HTML pages, images) between server and client to reduce bandwidth usage, server load, and perceived lag.

DTN.why: DTN is surveyed as an in-network storage system with its bundle layer persistent storage.
DTN.quote: A key aspect of the DTN is a store-and-forward overlay layer called the "Bundle Protocol" or "Bundle Layer"

ICN.why: NDN and NetInf, both information-centric networking architectures with in-network caching, are surveyed in their own sections.
ICN.quote: Named Data Networking (NDN) [17] is a research initiative that proposes to move to a new model of addressing and routing for the Internet.

NFS.why: NFS is surveyed as a storage protocol and evaluated for DECADE, including its ACL model.
NFS.quote: The Network File System (NFS) is designed to allow users to access files over a network in a manner similar to how local storage is accessed.

iSCSI.why: iSCSI is one of the surveyed storage protocols with its own evaluation section.
iSCSI.quote: Internet SCSI (iSCSI) [32] is a protocol enabling SCSI commands to be sent over TCP.

WebDAV.why: WebDAV is surveyed in depth, including ACL, search, quota and ticketing extensions.
WebDAV.quote: WebDAV [40] is a protocol designed for Web content authoring.

OAuth.why: OAuth's delegation model is evaluated for DECADE access control in its own section.
OAuth.quote: OAuth itself, however, is not a network storage protocol.

P2P.why: P2P applications and P2P caches are the motivating context and a surveyed system.
P2P.quote: DECADE aims to provide a standard protocol allowing P2P applications (including content providers) to make use of in-network storage

rejected.why: HTTP is surveyed briefly as a storage-related protocol, but the document is not about HTTP itself; it is mainly the substrate of several surveyed systems.
DNS is only mentioned as the discovery mechanism for several systems.
Usenet gets a short survey subsection, but only as one example of in-network storage.
The document surveys systems rather than addressing architectural principles.
Only mentioned incidentally in connection with NFS.

gaps.name: DECADE (DECoupled Application Data Enroute) in-network storage for P2P
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no dedicated tag; storage and P2P are the nearest fits.

RFC6393.title: Moving RFC 4693 to Historic
RFC6393.summary: Administrative RFC that moves RFC 4693 (IETF Operational Notes, an IETF process experiment) to Historic status and obsoletes it after the IESG ended the IONs experiment.

IETF process.why: The document closes an IETF process experiment (the IONs series) and changes the status of the RFC that defined it. This is IETF procedure and administration.
IETF process.quote: RFC 4693 [RFC4693] established the IETF Operational Notes (IONs) series of documents on the experimental basis [RFC3933].

rejected.why: The document changes an RFC's status to Historic, but it is about closing a process experiment, not the format, style or publication of the RFC series.
The parent is implied by the more specific IETF process tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC6394.title: Use Cases and Requirements for DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE)
RFC6394.summary: Informational document describing use cases and requirements for DANE: using DNS/DNSSEC to publish CA constraints, certificate constraints, trust anchor assertions and delegated-service arrangements that support TLS server authentication.

DANE.why: The whole document defines the use cases and requirements for DANE, so the DANE page is the right home for it.
DANE.quote: The goal of technologies for DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) is to use the DNS and DNSSEC to provide additional information about the cryptographic credentials

rejected.why: TLS is the handshake whose authentication DANE would supplement. The document does not specify or change TLS, so it is the substrate here.
DNSSEC is a prerequisite that protects the DANE records. The document does not specify DNSSEC signing or validation.
PKIX certificates and CAs are the context for the use cases. The document does not profile certificates.
CA trust is discussed as the problem DANE addresses. The document is about the DNS-based mechanism, not PKI itself.
The DANE tag already covers the DNS aspects. The document has no general DNS protocol content.

RFC6395.title: An Interface Identifier (ID) Hello Option for PIM
RFC6395.summary: Defines a new PIM Hello option (type 31) carrying a 64-bit Interface Identifier (router ID plus local interface ID) so PIM protocols can uniquely identify a neighbor's interface.

PIM.why: The document specifies a new PIM Hello option and its message format. It extends PIM, so readers of PIM should find it.
PIM.quote: This document defines a new PIM Hello option to advertise an Interface Identifier that can be used by PIM protocols to uniquely identify an interface

rejected.why: RFC 4601 is only referenced for the Hello message format. The document extends PIM Hello generally, not the sparse-mode specification.
BGP is mentioned only as an example of another protocol using 32-bit router identifiers.
OSPFv2 is mentioned only as an example of another protocol using 32-bit router identifiers.
ifIndex from the Interfaces Group MIB is cited only as a possible source for the Local Interface Identifier.
The IANA section only records the assignment of Hello option type 31, which is boilerplate.

RFC6396.title: Multi-Threaded Routing Toolkit (MRT) Routing Information Export Format
RFC6396.summary: Defines the MRT binary record format for exporting and archiving routing protocol messages, BGP state changes, and RIB snapshots (BGP4MP, TABLE_DUMP_V2, OSPF, IS-IS types), with IANA registries for type and subtype codes.

BGP.why: The core of the format is encoding BGP messages, FSM state changes and RIB dumps (BGP4MP, TABLE_DUMP, TABLE_DUMP_V2), so BGP readers would want it.
BGP.quote: The BGP routing protocol, in particular, has been the subject of extensive study and analysis, which have been significantly aided by the availability of the MRT format.

OSPF.why: Defines MRT record types for exporting OSPFv2 packets, and OSPFv3 in 4.6, a distinct part of the format.
OSPF.quote: This type supports the OSPFv2 protocol as defined in RFC 2328 [RFC2328].  It is used to encode the exchange of OSPF protocol packets.

IS-IS.why: Defines the ISIS and ISIS_ET record types for exporting IS-IS PDUs.
IS-IS.quote: This type supports the IS-IS routing protocol as defined in RFC 1195 [RFC1195].

rejected.why: RIP and RIPng export types appear only as deprecated types in Appendix B, a minor part of the document.
The OSPFv3 type is a short section that extends the OSPFv2 type. The OSPF tag covers it.
IPv6 addresses are only carried in fields. The document is not about IPv6.
The IANA section registers MRT type and subtype codes, which is boilerplate for this document, not its subject.
A more specific routing protocol tag already applies, so the parent is implied.
UTF-8 is only used to encode the view name and diagnostic strings.

gaps.name: MRT (Multi-Threaded Routing Toolkit) export format
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for routing data export or archive formats, or for routing measurement and collection. BGP, OSPF and IS-IS are the nearest tags.

RFC6397.title: Multi-Threaded Routing Toolkit (MRT) Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Routing Information Export Format with Geo-Location Extensions
RFC6397.summary: Extends the MRT BGP routing information export format with a GEO_PEER_TABLE subtype carrying optional WGS84 latitude/longitude of a BGP collector and its peers.

BGP.why: The document extends the MRT export format for BGP routing data and describes BGP collectors and peers. BGP is the subject of the data and the best fit in the taxonomy.
BGP.quote: extending it to include optional terrestrial coordinates of a BGP collector and its BGP peers

geolocation.why: The document defines how location coordinates are formatted and conveyed. It also has a privacy section based on GEOPRIV defaults.
geolocation.quote: The GEO_PEER_TABLE Subtype updates the TABLE_DUMP_V2 Types to include geo-location information in the form of the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84)

rejected.why: BMP is a different protocol for monitoring BGP. This document covers the MRT archive format, not BMP.
The privacy considerations are specific to location data. They are covered by the geolocation tag, and the document is not a general privacy analysis.
The document says it adds no security risk. It does not secure routing.

gaps.name: MRT (Multi-Threaded Routing Toolkit) export format
gaps.why: The document's main subject is the MRT routing data export format. The taxonomy has no tag for it, and BGP is only the closest fit.

RFC6398.title: IP Router Alert Considerations and Usage
RFC6398.summary: BCP describing security concerns of the IPv4/IPv6 IP Router Alert Option, recommending against end-to-end Internet use, identifying controlled environments where it is safe, and giving protection and implementation guidance for providers and routers.

router alert.why: The whole document analyses the Router Alert Option, its DoS risks, usage guidelines and router implementation recommendations.
router alert.quote: This document discusses security aspects and usage guidelines around the use of the current IP Router Alert Option, thereby updating RFC 2113 and RFC 2711.

operational security.why: A substantial part gives operator protection practices (filtering, rate limiting, tunnelling) against Router Alert DoS attacks.
operational security.quote: a service provider MUST implement strong protection of its network against attacks based on IP Router Alert.

rejected.why: RSVP is used as the main example of a protocol using Router Alert but is not specified or extended here.
IPv6 Router Alert is covered only as one of the two option variants; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
IPv4 option is just the carrier of Router Alert; the IPv4 protocol is not the subject.
DoS is the threat motivating the guidance, but the document is about the option rather than DDoS mitigation in general; operational security covers the practices.
IGMP, MLD, MRD and PGM are mentioned only as users of Router Alert.
Tunnelling of RAO packets (RFC 6178) is cited as a protection mechanism but is not defined here.

RFC6401.title: RSVP Extensions for Admission Priority
RFC6401.summary: Defines two new RSVP policy elements (Admission Priority and Application-Level Resource Priority) so RSVP nodes can give prioritized sessions elevated admission probability without preemption, with bandwidth allocation model examples.

RSVP.why: The document extends RSVP by defining two new policy elements carried in POLICY_DATA objects, with merging rules and default handling.
RSVP.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Resource reSerVation Protocol (RSVP) that can be used to support such an admission priority capability at the network layer.

rejected.why: SIP's Resource-Priority header is the source of the application-level priority, but the document does not specify or extend SIP.
The MAM, RDM and MAR bandwidth models come from Diffserv-aware MPLS TE, but the document only reuses them as informative examples for admission control.
The Router Alert Option is mentioned only in the applicability and security discussion, so it is not a subject of the document.
The IANA section registers P-types and extends registries, which is boilerplate for this document.
Diffserv appears only in the titles of the referenced MPLS TE models, not as a subject of the document.

RFC6402.title: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) Updates
RFC6402.summary: RFC 6402 updates the CMC certificate management protocol (RFCs 5272/5273/5274) with new controls (RA Identity Witness, Response Body), a Change Subject Name attribute, CMC extended key usages, a Subject Information Access type, TCP port 5318 registration, and updated ASN.1 modules.

PKI.why: CMC is a PKI certificate enrollment/management protocol; no CMC-specific tag exists, so PKI is the best fit. The document extends its controls, attributes and server certificate requirements.
PKI.quote: CMC, a Certificate Management protocol using the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

CMS.why: CMC messages are CMS-based and the document updates CMC's CMS-carried syntax and unsigned attributes; CMS is a substantial but supporting aspect.
CMS.quote: CMC, a Certificate Management protocol using the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

X.509.why: Defines new Extended Key Usage values and a Subject Information Access id-ad-cmc for X.509 certificates of CMC servers.
X.509.quote: Certificates for servers used in the CMC protocol SHOULD conform to the profile defined in [RFC5280].

ASN.1.why: Roughly half the document is updated 1988 and 2008 ASN.1 modules.
ASN.1.quote: This section contains the updated ASN.1 module for [RFC5272].

rejected.why: CMC merely gets a registered TCP port; TCP is substrate.
Mentioned as the primary CMC transport but not specified here.
Port registration is boilerplate-like and incidental to the main body.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: No dedicated tag for CMC; it is the main subject and is only approximated by PKI and CMS.

RFC6403.title: Suite B Profile of Certificate Management over CMS
RFC6403.summary: Profiles the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol for enrolling and rekeying NSA Suite B (P-256/P-384 ECDSA, SHA-256/384) X.509 certificates between clients, RAs and CAs.

PKI.why: CMC is a PKI certificate management protocol, and no CMC-specific tag exists. The document profiles enrollment and rekey between client, RA and CA, so PKI is the best fit.
PKI.quote: This document specifies a profile of the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol for managing Suite B X.509 public key certificates.

X.509.why: It constrains the content of Suite B certificate requests (key usage, SubjectAltName, public key format) per RFC 5759, so X.509 certificate profile readers would want it.
X.509.quote: to manage X.509 public key certificates compliant with the United States National Security Agency's Suite B Cryptography

ECDSA.why: A large part of the profile mandates ECDSA on P-256/P-384 with SHA-256/384 for requests, responses and proof-of-possession.
ECDSA.quote: signatureAlgorithm MUST be ecdsa-with-sha256 for P-256 certification requests and MUST be ecdsa-with-sha384 for P-384 certification requests

CMS.why: CMC messages are CMS SignedData objects, and the profile also covers CMS Content Constraints extension handling.
CMS.quote: the Full PKI Request MUST be used; it MUST be encapsulated in a SignedData; and the SignedData MUST be constructed as defined in [RFC6318]

rejected.why: RFC 6318 (Suite B in S/MIME) is only referenced for how SignedData is constructed. The document is not about secure email.
HMAC-SHA256/384 is mandated for identity proof and POP Link Witness, but only as a minor algorithm choice.
SHA-256/384 are named as algorithm choices only. The document is not about the hash functions.
ECDSA is the more specific tag. P-256/P-384 are used only as Suite B parameters.
CMP is a different certificate management protocol and is not discussed here.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CMC, the protocol this document profiles. PKI is the nearest parent.

gaps.name: Suite B Cryptography
gaps.why: The NSA Suite B algorithm policy is the document's organizing theme, and no tag covers it.

RFC6404.title: Session PEERing for Multimedia INTerconnect (SPEERMINT) Security Threats and Suggested Countermeasures
RFC6404.summary: Informational RFC enumerating security threats to SPEERMINT SIP peering functions (LUF, LRF, SF, MF) and suggesting countermeasures such as DNSSEC, TLS/DTLS, SRTP, identity assertion, rate limiting and topology hiding.

SPEERMINT.why: The whole document is the threat analysis for SPEERMINT peering between SIP Service Providers, organised by the SPEERMINT functions.
SPEERMINT.quote: The objective of this document is to identify and enumerate SPEERMINT-specific threat vectors and to give guidance for implementers on selecting appropriate countermeasures.

SIP.why: A large part of the document covers SIP-specific attacks (teardown, forged responses, fuzzing) and SIP countermeasures (identity assertion, privacy, torture tests).
SIP.quote: SIP request spoofing, SIP reply spoofing, and SIP message tampering.

DNSSEC.why: A dedicated countermeasure section explains how to apply DNSSEC (trust anchors, authentication chain) to secure the LRF, which a DNSSEC reader would want.
DNSSEC.quote: In the context of SSP peering, DNSSEC can provide authentication and integrity regarding the location of a Signaling Function (SF) entity retrieved via DNS.

rejected.why: SRTP is recommended as a countermeasure in one short subsection but is not specified or analysed in depth.
TLS/DTLS is the suggested transport protection, but the document only recommends it and defines nothing new about it.
IPsec is briefly compared with TLS in Section 3.2 as an alternative, not the subject of the document.
The generic security topic is implied, and the more specific SPEERMINT tag fits better.
RTP/RTCP attacks are listed in the Media Function threats, but the document is not about RTP itself.
Identity assertion via RFC 4474 is mentioned, but STIR is a later and different mechanism.

RFC6405.title: Voice over IP (VoIP) SIP Peering Use Cases
RFC6405.summary: Informational SPEERMINT document describing common VoIP SIP peering use cases (static direct, static indirect, with assisting LUF/LRF providers, and on-demand) with example call flows between SIP service providers.

SPEERMINT.why: The document exists to describe SIP peering use cases between service providers, which is the SPEERMINT subject, including direct/indirect and static/on-demand peering.
SPEERMINT.quote: These use cases are determined by the Session PEERing for Multimedia INTerconnect (SPEERMINT) working group

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling used in the call flows, but the document is about peering between providers, covered by the more specific SPEERMINT tag.
ENUM is used as an example LUF database in the call flows but is not specified or extended here.
NAPTR/SRV/A lookups are used as the LRF mechanism but only as a substrate.
SDP is mentioned only in passing, when an I-SBE modifies the offer to point to its DBE.
SRTP appears only as an example of why an I-DBE might be used, in one sentence.

RFC6406.title: Session PEERing for Multimedia INTerconnect (SPEERMINT) Architecture
RFC6406.summary: Defines the SPEERMINT reference architecture for Layer 5 SIP peering between SIP Service Providers, describing the LUF, LRF, SBE/SF and DBE functions and the steps to establish an inter-domain session.

SPEERMINT.why: The document is the SPEERMINT peering architecture itself, defining the functional components (LUF, LRF, SBE, DBE) and session establishment between SSP peering domains.
SPEERMINT.quote: This document defines a peering architecture for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and its functional components and interfaces.

ENUM.why: A substantial section describes the ENUM lookup procedure (E2U+sip enumservice, NAPTR responses, public and private roots) as the main example of the Lookup Function.
ENUM.quote: the Originating (or Indirect) SSP consults the public "User ENUM" rooted at e164.arpa, according to the procedures described in [RFC6116].

rejected.why: SIP is the protocol being peered, but the document is about the peering architecture, which has its own SPEERMINT tag; it does not specify or extend SIP itself.
TLS is only the security mechanism recommended between SSPs; the document defines nothing new about TLS.
IPsec is mentioned as an alternative trust mechanism and deferred to a future document.
DNS resolution per RFC 3263 is used as a substrate for locating SIP servers, with nothing new defined.
RTP media flows through the DBE, but the document does not address RTP itself.
PSTN termination is mentioned only briefly as a fallback in routing table handling.

RFC6407.title: The Group Domain of Interpretation
RFC6407.summary: RFC 6407 specifies the Group Domain of Interpretation (GDOI), an ISAKMP-based group key management protocol (GROUPKEY-PULL and GROUPKEY-PUSH) that distributes group security associations and keys for IPsec and other data security protocols, replacing RFC 3547.

GDOI.why: The whole document specifies the GDOI protocol: the GROUPKEY-PULL and GROUPKEY-PUSH exchanges, its payloads, and algorithm requirements.
GDOI.quote: This document describes the Group Domain of Interpretation (GDOI), which is an Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol (ISAMKP) [RFC2408] Domain of Interpretation (DOI), a group key management system.

rejected.why: IPsec AH and ESP are the data security protocols whose SAs GDOI distributes. The document is about the key management protocol, not IPsec itself.
GDOI reuses ISAKMP Phase 1 exchanges from IKEv1 as a substrate and defines nothing new about IKE.
This is the parent of GDOI, which is implied. The document is about the specific GDOI protocol, not group key management in general.
The document uses the Logical Key Hierarchy (LKH) group management method, not the LMS hash-based signatures. LKH has no taxonomy tag, so it appears in gaps.
ESP is a protected data protocol whose SAs and counter modes are distributed. The document does not specify ESP.

gaps.name: Logical Key Hierarchy (LKH)
gaps.why: The document specifies LKH key download and update arrays for group rekeying and for forward and backward access control. The taxonomy has no tag for group key management algorithms such as LKH.

RFC6408.title: Diameter Straightforward-Naming Authority Pointer (S-NAPTR) Usage
RFC6408.summary: Updates RFC 3588 Diameter peer discovery by defining an extended S-NAPTR service tag format (aaa+apN:diameter.transport) so a realm can advertise supported Diameter applications and transports via DNS NAPTR records.

Diameter.why: The document updates Diameter base protocol peer discovery, defines application and transport tags for Diameter agents, and registers tags for Diameter applications.
Diameter.quote: describes an improvement using an extended format for the Straightforward-Naming Authority Pointer (S-NAPTR) application service tag that allows for discovery of the supported applications

service discovery.why: The document is about S-NAPTR/DDDS-based discovery of Diameter peers. No S-NAPTR-specific tag exists, so the general service discovery tag fits.
service discovery.quote: permit the discovery of Diameter peers that support a specific Diameter application and transport protocol

rejected.why: NAPTR and SRV records are the substrate for discovery. The document defines no new DNS record type or resolver behaviour, only service-field values.
ABNF is only used to state the tag syntax.
SCTP, TCP and TLS appear only as transport protocol tag values.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-like tag reservations, not the main subject.
The Diameter tag is more specific. The AAA framework itself is not the subject.

gaps.name: S-NAPTR / DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System)
gaps.why: The document's core mechanism is S-NAPTR application service and protocol tags. The taxonomy has no S-NAPTR or NAPTR tag, so only the generic service discovery tag applies.

RFC6409.title: Message Submission for Mail
RFC6409.summary: RFC 6409 (STD 72) specifies message submission for email: a Message Submission Agent on port 587 that accepts mail from MUAs using ESMTP with required authentication, mandatory/recommended/optional server actions, SMTP extension applicability, and permitted message modifications.

SMTP.why: The document defines the submission variant of SMTP, with the MSA's required behaviours, reply codes and extension usage. It is the standard for mail submission and relaying separation.
SMTP.quote: Port 587 is reserved for email message submission as specified in this document.  Messages received on this port are defined to be submissions.

rejected.why: SMTP AUTH is required, but the document only references it as the authentication mechanism and does not specify SASL.
The MSA adds or fixes Date, Sender and Message-ID headers, but this is a side effect of submission and the document does not define the format.
STARTTLS is mentioned as an optional extension, but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
Spam prevention motivates the split between submission and relay, but the document is not about spam filtering or reputation.
Mentioned only as a signature that message modification can invalidate.
IMAP and POP3 are mentioned only in describing the split-MUA model.

RFC6410.title: Reducing the Standards Track to Two Maturity Levels
RFC6410.summary: BCP updating RFC 2026 to reduce the IETF Standards Track from three maturity levels (Proposed, Draft, Full Standard) to two (Proposed Standard and Internet Standard), with new advancement criteria and transition rules.

IETF process.why: The document changes the IETF standards process: maturity levels, advancement criteria, removal of annual review, and transition rules for existing documents.
IETF process.quote: This document updates the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Standards Process defined in RFC 2026. Primarily, it reduces the Standards Process from three Standards Track maturity levels to two.

rejected.why: Criterion (4) mentions patented or controlled technology and licensing, but this is a minor advancement criterion, not the subject of the document.
Concerns standards-track maturity classification, not RFC format, style or publication.
IANA appears nowhere in the body; the document is about standards maturity, not registries.

RFC6411.title: Applicability of Keying Methods for RSVP Security
RFC6411.summary: Informational comparison of group, per-interface and per-neighbor keying for RSVP hop-by-hop authentication and encryption, covering key provisioning, GDOI group keying, IPsec modes (AH/ESP tunnel, address preservation), and special cases like RSVP-TE/GMPLS.

RSVP.why: The whole document analyses keying and security of RSVP INTEGRITY-object protection and its deployment scenarios.
RSVP.quote: This document compares group keying for RSVP with per-neighbor or per-interface keying, and discusses the associated key provisioning methods as well as applicability and limitations

GDOI.why: GDOI is the main dynamic group key distribution method discussed for RSVP, and GSA policy is used for IPsec protection of RSVP.
GDOI.quote: [GDOI-MAC] describes a mechanism to distribute group keys to a group of RSVP speakers, using GDOI

IPsec.why: A full section analyses applicability of AH/ESP, tunnel mode, transport mode and address-preserving tunnel mode for RSVP.
IPsec.quote: The discussions about the various keying methods in this document are also applicable when using IPsec [RFC4301] to protect RSVP.

RSVP-TE.why: Section discusses group keying for RSVP-TE, Fast Reroute, P2MP and GMPLS signalling.
RSVP-TE.quote: Use of RSVP authentication for RSVP-TE [RFC3209] and for RSVP-TE Fast Reroute [RFC4090] deserves additional considerations.

rejected.why: Considered as a topic, but GDOI is tagged and the RSVP-specific tags capture the keying subject better.
GDOI is a child of this tag and is already tagged; the document is not about multicast itself.
ESP is discussed only as an IPsec mode option for RSVP protection, not specified or extended; IPsec covers it.
Mentioned only as a case where group keying helps, not a subject of the document.
Listed only as one similar deployment model in Section 8.

RFC6412.title: Terminology for Benchmarking Link-State IGP Data-Plane Route Convergence
RFC6412.summary: Defines terminology (convergence types, instants, methods, benchmarks, measurement terms) for black-box data-plane benchmarking of link-state IGP route convergence, companion to the RFC 6413 methodology.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG terminology specification for benchmarking route convergence: methods, benchmarks, instants and measurement terms.
benchmarking.quote: The terminology is to be used for benchmarking IGP convergence time through externally observable (black-box) data-plane measurements.

performance measurement.why: It defines measurement methods and metrics (packet loss, forwarding rate, sampling interval, convergence time) for network performance, so readers of performance measurement would want it.
performance measurement.quote: The method to calculate convergence time benchmarks from observing the Forwarding Rate each Packet Sampling Interval

rejected.why: OSPF is named only as an example IGP to which the terminology applies. The document does not specify or extend it.
IS-IS is named only as an example IGP to which the terminology applies. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document is about measuring convergence from the data plane, not about routing architecture or design principles.
ECMP appears only as a test topology variant, not as a subject of the document.

RFC6413.title: Benchmarking Methodology for Link-State IGP Data-Plane Route Convergence
RFC6413.summary: Defines a black-box, data-plane methodology and test cases for benchmarking convergence time and loss of connectivity of link-state IGPs (IS-IS, OSPF) on routers, with test topologies, measurement methods and reporting formats.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking methodology: test topologies, offered load, measurement methods, accuracy, reporting formats and test cases for a device under test.
benchmarking.quote: This document describes the methodology for benchmarking Link-State Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) Route Convergence.

IS-IS.why: IS-IS is one of the two link-state IGPs whose convergence is benchmarked, so IS-IS readers would want this RFC. It is tested rather than specified.
IS-IS.quote: The methodology can be applied to any link-state IGP, such as IS-IS and OSPF.

OSPF.why: OSPF is the other target IGP, with OSPF-specific considerations such as areas. It is tested rather than specified.
OSPF.quote: The methodology can be applied to any link-state IGP, such as IS-IS and OSPF.

rejected.why: ECMP member failures are test topologies and cases, but the document is not about ECMP itself.
The parent topic of benchmarking in the taxonomy is network management; benchmarking is the more specific fit. The document is device benchmarking, not an IPPM-style network performance metric.
Explicitly out of scope.
Fast reroute is explicitly out of scope.
The document benchmarks IGP convergence, not routing architecture.

RFC6414.title: Benchmarking Terminology for Protection Performance
RFC6414.summary: Defines common terminology and metrics (failover time, packet loss, reversion, additive backup delay, calculation methods) for benchmarking sub-IP protection mechanisms such as APS, VRRP, HA and MPLS-FRR, measured at the IP layer.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking terminology RFC defining test setups, benchmarks (Failover Time, Failover Packet Loss, Additive Backup Delay) and time calculation methods for protection mechanisms.
benchmarking.quote: This document provides common terminology and metrics for benchmarking the performance of sub-IP layer protection mechanisms.

rejected.why: VRRP is only one example protection mechanism the terminology applies to; the document does not specify or analyse VRRP itself.
MPLS-FRR is mentioned as an example mechanism only; the document is not about fast reroute itself.
SONET APS is only cited as an example of local link protection, not a subject of the document.
MPLS Fast Reroute appears only as an example of a protection mechanism the terminology can be applied to.
The document is more specifically benchmarking of devices in a lab, which has its own tag, so the broader performance measurement topic is not needed.
Although a terminology document, it is specific to benchmarking terminology, which is better covered by the benchmarking tag.

gaps.name: Sub-IP protection switching / high availability failover
gaps.why: The document's core subject is protection switching and failover (APS, VRRP, stateful HA, path/node/link protection), which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy apart from specific fast-reroute or VRRP tags.

RFC6415.title: Web Host Metadata
RFC6415.summary: Defines host-meta, a well-known URI (/.well-known/host-meta) and XRD/JRD document format for discovering host-wide and per-resource metadata via link templates and LRDD documents, and registers the "lrdd" link relation.

web linking.why: The document defines link-based metadata for hosts, link templates, and registers the "lrdd" link relation type. Its core content is typed links and link relations.
web linking.quote: Link Templates - links using a URI template instead of a fixed target URI, providing a way to define generic rules for generating resource-specific links

URI.why: It registers well-known URIs and defines a URI template syntax with a "uri" variable and percent-encoding rules. Readers of URI templates and well-known URIs would want it.
URI.quote: This document also registers the well-known URI suffix "host-meta" in the Well-Known URI Registry

rejected.why: HTTP GET, redirects and Accept headers are only the retrieval substrate for the metadata documents.
XRD is the document format used, but the document is not about XML usage generally.
The JRD appendix is a JSON serialisation of XRD, but it is secondary to the host-meta mechanism.
host-meta and LRDD are the basis for WebFinger, but this document does not specify WebFinger.
The document is about metadata discovery, which is a looser fit than web linking, and the taxonomy treats this under naming.
It mentions the application/xrd+xml media type but does not register it.

gaps.name: Well-known URIs / host metadata (host-meta, XRD, LRDD)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the well-known URI mechanism or the XRD resource descriptor format. Those are the central subject of this RFC.

RFC6416.title: RTP Payload Format for MPEG-4 Audio/Visual Streams
RFC6416.summary: Defines RTP payload formats for carrying MPEG-4 Audio (LATM) and MPEG-4 Visual bitstreams directly in RTP without MPEG-4 Systems, including fragmentation rules, media type registrations (MP4V-ES, MP4A-LATM) and SDP mappings; obsoletes RFC 3016.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for MPEG-4 audio and video, covering RTP header field use and fragmentation rules.
RTP payload format.quote: The RTP payload formats described in this document specify how MPEG-4 Audio [14496-3] and MPEG-4 Visual streams [14496-2] are to be fragmented and mapped directly onto RTP packets.

codecs.why: MPEG-4 Audio/Visual codecs are the subject being packetized, with details of AAC, SBR, PS, MPEG Surround and VOP/video packet structure; no more specific codec tag exists for MPEG-4.
codecs.quote: MPEG-4 Visual is a visual coding standard with many features, including: high coding efficiency; high error resiliency; and multiple, arbitrary shape object-based coding

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document defines SDP mappings and a=fmtp parameters (config, cpresent, SBR-enabled, etc.) with many declarative examples.
SDP.quote: The media type video/MP4V-ES string is mapped to fields in SDP [RFC4566], as follows:
SDP.section: 7.2. Mapping to SDP for MPEG-4 Visual

media types.why: The document registers/updates the video/MP4V-ES and audio/MP4A-LATM media types with their parameters.
media types.quote:
Type name: audio

   Subtype name: MP4A-LATM
media types.section: 7.3. Media Type Registration for MPEG-4 Audio

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the RTP payload format tag; the document is about a payload format specifically.
SIP is only mentioned as an example of signalling that uses media type and SDP; the document does not specify SIP.
H.323 is mentioned as an example system using the payload format; not a subject of the document.
SRTP appears only in Security Considerations as a recommended protection mechanism.
Generic FEC and redundant audio are mentioned only in passing as optional protection mechanisms.
The document is about MPEG-4 Visual, not H.264; H.263 is referenced only for the short video header mode.

gaps.name: MPEG-4 Audio/Visual (AAC, LATM, MPEG Surround)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPEG-4 codecs; the generic 'codecs' tag is the closest fit.

RFC6417.title: How to Contribute Research Results to Internet Standardization
RFC6417.summary: Informational guide advising academic researchers how to bring research results into IETF (and IRTF) standardization, covering venue choice, starting work, building community, BoFs and WGs, and examples of MPTCP and Congestion Exposure.

IETF process.why: The whole document explains how to participate in the IETF process: finding WGs, BoFs, Internet-Drafts, rough consensus, and chartering new working groups.
IETF process.quote: The goal of this document is to highlight such differences and provide a rough guideline that will hopefully enable researchers new to the IETF to become successful contributors more quickly.

rejected.why: Multipath TCP is only a case study of a successful research-to-IETF path, described in a short example; the document does not specify or analyse the protocol.
Congestion Exposure is likewise used only as an example of the process and WG chartering compromise, not as the subject.
Intellectual property is mentioned briefly (Note Well, patents) but is a minor point, not a substantial part of the document.
Research origin of Internet architecture is mentioned in the abstract only; the document is about process, not architecture.

gaps.name: IRTF / research-to-standards transfer
gaps.why: The document concerns the relationship between the IRTF/academic research and IETF standardization; the taxonomy has no IRTF or research community tag, though IETF process covers it adequately.

RFC6418.title: Multiple Interfaces and Provisioning Domains Problem Statement
RFC6418.summary: Problem statement describing issues (DNS resolution, routing, address selection, policy conflicts, session management) faced by nodes attached to multiple provisioning domains, mostly multi-interface hosts.

multihoming.why: The whole document is about multihomed nodes attached to multiple provisioning domains and the resulting configuration, routing and selection problems. Multihoming architectures is the closest fitting tag.
multihoming.quote: A multihomed node may have multiple provisioning domains (via physical and/or virtual interfaces).

addressing.why: Source and destination address selection and address-space overlap are a substantial category of the problems.
addressing.quote: Default address selection policies may be specific to their corresponding provisioning domain. However, a MIF node may not be able to manage address selection policies per provisioning domain

DNS.why: Section 4.1 analyses DNS resolution failures (private namespaces, NXDOMAIN, DNS64 synthesised answers) when multiple DNS server sets exist.
DNS.quote: A DNS query could be sent to the wrong interface because DNS server addresses may be node-scoped.

rejected.why: DHCP is only mentioned as one of the ways configuration is received; the document is not about it.
Node routing tables are discussed as a host issue, not as routing protocols or systems.
Captive portals appear as an example of DNS and connectivity-check issues, not as the subject.
Mobility is explicitly out of scope and only referenced.
APIs are discussed briefly as existing work and a gap, not specified.
Mentioned only as one case of a synthesised AAAA answer being valid on just one network.

gaps.name: Multiple interfaces (MIF) / provisioning domains
gaps.why: There is no tag for multi-interface hosts or provisioning domain selection. The nearest fit is multihoming, but that tag is aimed at site multihoming rather than host-level interface management.

RFC6419.title: Current Practices for Multiple-Interface Hosts
RFC6419.summary: Informational survey of how mobile and desktop operating systems handle multiple network interfaces (interface selection, first-hop routing, source address selection, DNS configuration), supporting the MIF problem statement.

multihoming.why: The document surveys host-side multi-interface practice: interface selection, first-hop selection, source address selection and per-interface configuration. Multihoming architectures is the closest fit.
multihoming.quote: Multiple-interface hosts face several challenges not faced by single-interface hosts

addressing.why: A substantial part of the document compares source address selection policy across operating systems, including RFC 3484 support and weak versus strong host models.
addressing.quote: IPv6 specifies a specific source address selection mechanism in [RFC3484], and several systems implement this mechanism with similar support for IPv4.

rejected.why: DNS server list configuration per interface is discussed, but only as a host configuration problem. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
DHCP clients are described for how they overwrite global configuration. DHCP itself is not specified or extended.
IPv6 address selection is mentioned in passing, but the document is not about IPv6.
Cellular devices serve as examples, but the document is not about IP over 3GPP systems.

gaps.name: Multiple interfaces (MIF) / provisioning domains on hosts
