gaps.why: The document's central subject, host behaviour with multiple interfaces and connection managers, has no dedicated tag. Multihoming is only an approximate fit.

RFC6420.title: PIM Multi-Topology ID (MT-ID) Join Attribute
RFC6420.summary: Defines a new PIM Join Attribute (MT-ID) and Hello option letting downstream routers signal which RPF topology to use when building multicast trees, with validation and conflict-resolution rules.

PIM.why: The document extends PIM with a new Join Attribute and Hello Option, and specifies sending, receiving, validation and conflict resolution for PIM Join/Assert messages.
PIM.quote: This document introduces a new type of PIM Join Attribute that extends PIM signaling to identify a topology that should be used when constructing a particular multicast distribution tree.

rejected.why: The attribute applies to PIM SM/SSM/Bidir generally and does not change PIM-SM itself; the parent PIM tag fits better.
OSPF multi-topology routing is only background for the RPF topologies and is used in the example; the document does not specify OSPF.
IS-IS multi-topology is only mentioned as a source of topologies, not specified here.
MBGP appears only in the example topology as the route source for S.
This id isn't in the taxonomy as written; the MVPN draft is only referenced for RPF vector interaction.
SSM is listed only as one mode where the attribute applies; the document is not about SSM.

gaps.name: Multi-topology routing / RPF topology selection
gaps.why: The document's subject is selecting among multiple routing topologies for multicast RPF. The taxonomy has no multi-topology tag, so it is covered only by the general PIM tag.

RFC6421.title: Crypto-Agility Requirements for Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS)
RFC6421.summary: Informational RFC defining requirements for a crypto-agility solution for RADIUS, covering algorithm negotiation, integrity, replay protection, confidentiality, backward compatibility and key management.

RADIUS.why: The whole document specifies requirements for extending RADIUS security (algorithm negotiation, packet protection, attribute hiding, backward compatibility).
RADIUS.quote: This memo describes the requirements for a crypto-agility solution for Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS).

rejected.why: Crypto-agility is the subject, but the document is about the RADIUS protocol's security requirements. It specifies no algorithms or parameters, so the RADIUS tag fits better.
MD5 and HMAC-MD5 appear as the legacy weaknesses motivating the work, but the document is not about them.
RADIUS over IPsec is mentioned only as an existing option. The document expects other techniques.
Section 4.6 discusses whether automated key management is required, but this is a small part of the document.
RADIUS is a more specific tag under AAA, and no general AAA framework is addressed.

RFC6422.title: Relay-Supplied DHCP Options
RFC6422.summary: RFC 6422 defines the DHCPv6 Relay-Supplied Options option (RSOO), letting relay agents hand options to the DHCPv6 server to pass on to clients, and updates RFC 3315 to forbid relays from modifying Relay-Reply payloads.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_RSOO, code 66), specifies relay agent and server behaviour for it, and updates RFC 3315. DHCPv6 is the protocol it extends.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes a mechanism whereby the DHCPv6 relay agent can provide such information to the DHCPv6 server, which can, in turn, pass this information on to the DHCP client.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag and fits. The document is about DHCPv6 only, so the parent is implied.
The ERP local domain name is only the motivating example, and the document does not specify any EAP behaviour.
The IANA registry it creates is boilerplate-like apparatus for the option. The main body is not about IANA stewardship.

RFC6423.title: Using the Generic Associated Channel Label for Pseudowire in the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP)
RFC6423.summary: Updates RFC 5586 to remove the restriction on using the Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) with pseudowires in MPLS-TP, so GAL may be used with PWs in both MPLS and MPLS-TP.

MPLS-TP.why: The document specifies GAL usage in MPLS Transport Profile networks, updating RFC 5586's MPLS-TP rule for PWs.
MPLS-TP.quote: the GAL can be used with packets on a G-ACh on LSPs, Concatenated Segments of LSPs, Sections, and PWs in both MPLS and MPLS-TP environments

pseudowire.why: The change concerns how pseudowires may use the GAL and G-ACh, which is relevant to readers of pseudowire material.
pseudowire.quote: [RFC5586] is updated by removing the restrictions on using GAL for PW as follows

rejected.why: The more specific MPLS-TP tag fits. MPLS is only the underlying architecture.
The G-ACh carries OAM, but the document does not specify any OAM mechanism.

RFC6424.title: Mechanism for Performing Label Switched Path Ping (LSP Ping) over MPLS Tunnels
RFC6424.summary: Defines the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV (deprecating the RFC 4379 Downstream Mapping TLV), new return codes and FEC-stack-change procedures so MPLS LSP ping/traceroute can validate FECs and trace through MPLS tunnels and stitched LSPs.

MPLS.why: The document extends MPLS LSP ping/traceroute (data-plane failure detection) to hierarchical and stitched LSPs, defining new TLVs, sub-TLVs, and return codes. No more specific MPLS child tag covers LSP ping.
MPLS.quote: This documents describes methods for performing LSP ping (specified in [RFC4379]) traceroute over MPLS tunnels.

traceroute.why: A large part of the document specifies ingress and transit procedures for MPLS traceroute and path discovery over tunnels.
traceroute.quote: The techniques outlined in RFC 4379 are insufficient to perform traceroute Forwarding Equivalency Class (FEC) validation and path discovery

rejected.why: LSP ping is an OAM tool, but the MPLS and traceroute tags are more specific, and the topic tag is only to be given when no technology tag under it already fits.
LDP appears only as an example of an LSP type in the figures and is not specified or extended.
RSVP tunnels are used as example outer tunnels only; the document does not extend RSVP-TE.
The multipath data sub-TLV is carried over from RFC 4379 with no new ECMP behaviour defined.
LSP stitching is referenced via RFC 5150 only as background.
The IANA section registers the TLV, sub-TLVs, and return codes, but this is boilerplate and not the main subject.

RFC6425.title: Detecting Data-Plane Failures in Point-to-Multipoint MPLS - Extensions to LSP Ping
RFC6425.summary: RFC 6425 extends MPLS LSP ping (RFC 4379) to point-to-multipoint LSPs, defining new Target FEC sub-TLVs for P2MP RSVP-TE and multicast LDP LSPs, responder-scoping and jitter TLVs, a TTL-expired flag, and ping/traceroute procedures.

MPLS.why: The document extends MPLS LSP ping (data-plane failure detection) to P2MP LSPs, defining new TLVs, sub-TLVs and procedures. No narrower MPLS tag fits OAM for P2MP LSPs.
MPLS.quote: The scope of this document is fault detection and isolation for P2MP MPLS LSPs.

OAM.why: The document is fundamentally an OAM mechanism (connectivity verification and fault isolation via ping and traceroute modes), so OAM readers would want it.
OAM.quote: The procedures in this document provide OAM functions for P2MP MPLS LSPs and may be used to enable bootstrapping of other OAM procedures.

rejected.why: The document only uses RSVP-TE P2MP SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE fields to identify the LSP under test. It does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
Multicast LDP FEC fields are used only to identify the LSP under test. LDP itself is not extended.
The traceroute mode is a part of LSP ping for MPLS LSPs. The document is not about the general traceroute tool or IP path discovery.
P2MP LSPs replicate packets, but the document is about MPLS OAM, not IP multicast routing or group membership.
BFD for LSPs (RFC 5884) is mentioned only as an OAM procedure that LSP ping can bootstrap.
ICMP echo is cited only as the analogy for the ping/traceroute paradigm.

gaps.name: LSP ping / MPLS OAM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no MPLS-specific OAM or LSP ping tag. The document is covered only by the generic MPLS and OAM tags.

RFC6426.title: MPLS On-Demand Connectivity Verification and Route Tracing
RFC6426.summary: RFC 6426 extends MPLS LSP ping (RFC 4379) with a non-IP address type, source/destination identifier TLVs, static LSP/PW FEC sub-TLVs, an ACH channel type and reverse-path validation, so on-demand connectivity verification and route tracing work in MPLS-TP networks.

MPLS-TP.why: The document specifies how LSP ping performs on-demand CV and route tracing for MPLS-TP LSPs and PWs, including static LSP/PW identification and non-IP ACH operation.
MPLS-TP.quote: extensions to LSP ping so that LSP ping can be used for on-demand connectivity verification of MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) LSPs and pseudowires

OAM.why: It is an OAM mechanism specification, meeting the on-demand CV and route tracing requirements from the MPLS-TP OAM framework.
OAM.quote: This document describes how LSP ping can be used for on-demand connectivity verification (Section 3) and route tracing (Section 4) functions

traceroute.why: A full section defines route tracing procedures using TTL expiry and the Downstream Mapping TLV, so path-discovery readers would want it.
traceroute.quote: This section specifies how on-demand CV route tracing can be used in the context of MPLS-TP LSPs.
traceroute.section: 4. Performing On-Demand Route Tracing over MPLS-TP LSPs

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the more specific child tag and fits; the parent is implied.
Pseudowires are objects being verified (static PW FEC sub-TLV), not the subject of the document.
BFD is only mentioned in passing as another OAM packet type using non-IP encapsulation.
ECMP appears only in a short caveat that ACH-based CV should not be used with ECMP.
The IANA section registers code points and creates a registry but is boilerplate relative to the main subject.

gaps.name: LSP ping (MPLS echo request/reply data-plane failure detection)
gaps.why: The document extends LSP ping (RFC 4379), but the taxonomy has no LSP ping tag; MPLS-TP and OAM only partially cover it.

RFC6427.title: MPLS Fault Management Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM)
RFC6427.summary: Defines the MPLS Fault Management OAM channel and AIS and Lock Report messages (with Link Down Indication) that tell MPLS-TP LSP end points about server-layer faults or administrative locks, so client-layer alarms can be suppressed.

MPLS-TP.why: The document specifies fault-management OAM messages and an associated channel for MPLS Transport Profile LSPs. MPLS-TP readers need it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document defines FM capabilities to meet the MPLS-TP requirements as described in RFC 5654 [1]

OAM.why: It is a fault-indication OAM mechanism (AIS, LKR, clearing procedures). The OAM topic is a fitting general home for it, since no tag exists for fault management OAM alone.
OAM.quote: This document specifies Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) messages to indicate service disruptive conditions for MPLS-based transport network Label Switched Paths.

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the more specific child tag and the document is scoped to MPLS-TP LSPs. The parent is implied.
MS-PWs and the PW associated channel type registry are mentioned, but the document is not about pseudowire emulation itself.
The IANA section creates registries, but boilerplate is not evidence of subject.
The Continuity Check/LOC function is mentioned only as context for how the L-Flag is treated, and BFD is not specified or discussed.

RFC6428.title: Proactive Connectivity Verification, Continuity Check, and Remote Defect Indication for the MPLS Transport Profile
RFC6428.summary: Specifies BFD extensions (new ACH code points, Source MEP-ID TLV, BFD profile, state machines, diagnostic code 9) to provide proactive Continuity Check, Connectivity Verification and Remote Defect Indication for MPLS-TP LSPs, pseudowires and Sections.

MPLS-TP.why: The document defines MPLS-TP OAM mechanisms (CC, CV, RDI) with MPLS-TP MEP-IDs, G-ACh code points, and defect handling for MPLS-TP LSPs, PWs and Sections.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document specifies specific extensions to Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) and methods for proactive Continuity Check, Continuity Verification, and Remote Defect Indication for MPLS-TP pseudowires, Label Switched Paths, and Sections

BFD.why: It extends BFD with a new diagnostic code, CV message format, a BFD profile for MPLS-TP, and modified state machines for coordinated and independent sessions.
BFD.quote: This document describes the use of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) [4] for CC, proactive CV, and RDI of a PW, LSP, or Sub-Path Maintenance Entity

rejected.why: PWs are one of the monitored entities (with VCCV and AC_ID/AGI in the PW MEP-ID), but the document does not specify pseudowire emulation itself.
The topic tag is implied by being about MPLS-TP OAM, but the BFD-based specification is better captured by the specific tags; no separate OAM tag is needed.
Not related; MPLS-TP LSPs here are monitored, not signalled via GMPLS.
IANA code point allocations appear only in the IANA Considerations boilerplate section.
MPLS is the parent of MPLS-TP, which is the more specific tag chosen.

RFC6429.title: TCP Sender Clarification for Persist Condition
RFC6429.summary: Informational TCPM clarification that RFC 1122's zero window probe/persist condition requirement does not prevent TCP connections in persist state from being aborted by applications or the OS, motivated by a DoS scenario.

TCP.why: The document clarifies TCP sender behaviour in the persist (zero window probe) condition under RFC 1122, which is core TCP protocol specification.
TCP.quote: a TCP implementation needs to allow connections in the ZWP or persist condition to be closed or aborted by their applications or other resource management routines

rejected.why: HTTP is only used as an example of a server in the DoS scenario; the document is not about HTTP.
Mentioned once as another flow-controlled protocol to which the problem applies; not a subject of the document.
The document describes a DoS attack scenario but is a TCP clarification, not about DDoS mitigation or signalling.
Resource exhaustion is discussed only as motivation for the TCP clarification, not as operational security practice.

RFC6430.title: Email Feedback Report Type Value: not-spam
RFC6430.summary: Defines a new ARF feedback report type value, "not-spam", used to report email messages mistakenly classified as spam, and registers it with IANA.

ARF.why: The document extends the Abuse Reporting Format by defining a new feedback type value, so it belongs on the ARF page.
ARF.quote: This document defines a new feedback report type, "not-spam", which extends the Email Feedback Reports specification [RFC5965].

spam.why: The report type addresses spam filtering feedback: correcting false positives and retraining classifiers. Readers of the spam subject would want it. ARF is a child of email authentication, not spam, so spam is tagged separately.
spam.quote: It can be used to report a message that was mistakenly marked as spam.

rejected.why: Only used to sign the example report; the document does not specify or extend DKIM.
The report is a multipart/report MIME message, but MIME is just the substrate; the document defines nothing new about it.
The parent is implied by ARF and spam, so it is not listed separately.
Not about blocklists; it concerns user feedback on spam classification.

RFC6431.title: Huawei Port Range Configuration Options for PPP IP Control Protocol (IPCP)
RFC6431.summary: Defines two Huawei vendor-specific PPP IPCP options (Port Range mask/value and cryptographically random port range) to convey delegated or forwarded port sets to a client, for port-range (A+P) and CGN-based IPv4 address sharing.

PPP.why: The document specifies new IPCP configuration options (vendor extensions per RFC 2153) negotiated over PPP, with Configure-Request/Nak/Ack/Reject exchanges between host and BRAS.
PPP.quote: This document defines Huawei IPCP options to be used to carry port range information.

CGN.why: Port delegation and forwarding in a Carrier-Grade NAT context is a stated use case, and port forwarded/delegated modes relate to NAT port handling.
CGN.quote: These options can be used in a CGN context to bypass the NAT

rejected.why: NAT is a use-case context; the document defines PPP options, not NAT behaviour. CGN is the more specific fit as the secondary tag.
IPv4 address depletion motivates the work but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
AES is only used as a round function inside an example Feistel construction for port randomization.
Random port selection is used as an attack mitigation, but the document does not address randomness requirements or generation in general.
Port range sharing relates to address sharing, but the document's subject is the IPCP options; CGN/PPP capture it better.

gaps.name: Port range / address-plus-port (A+P) IPv4 address sharing
gaps.why: The document is built around port-range-based IPv4 address sharing, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC6432.title: Carrying Q.850 Codes in Reason Header Fields in SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) Responses
RFC6432.summary: Standards-track document that normatively allows any SIP response except 100 (Trying) to carry a Reason header field with a Q.850 cause code, codifying existing practice for INVITE responses gatewayed from the PSTN.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP by specifying use of the Reason header field in responses to carry Q.850 cause codes. It is a SIP header-field usage specification.
SIP.quote: Any SIP Response message, with the exception of a 100 (Trying), MAY contain a Reason header field with a Q.850 [Q.850] cause code.

rejected.why: The Q.850 codes come from PSTN-gatewayed calls, but the document only specifies the SIP header usage. It does not cover gateway control, ISUP interworking or signalling transport.
No ISUP encapsulation or SIP-I interworking is specified. Only the Reason header usage in responses is defined.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as an optional hop-by-hop integrity mechanism.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible integrity mechanism, so it is boilerplate rather than subject matter.

RFC6433.title: Requirements for a Working Group Milestones Tool
RFC6433.summary: RFC 6433 specifies requirements for a Datatracker tool letting WG chairs, ADs and the Secretariat create, update, approve and track IETF working group charter milestones, updating RFC 6292.

IETF process.why: The document is about the administrative tooling for WG chartering and milestone procedures, including chair/AD approval workflows, which is IETF process administration.
IETF process.quote: The IETF intends to provide a new tool to Working Group chairs and Area Directors for the creation and updating of milestones for Working Group charters.

rejected.why: The Atom feed of milestone changes is only a delivery mechanism cited as a requirement; the document is not about Atom.
Concerns Datatracker tooling for WG milestones, not RFC format or publication.
Email notifications are used by the tool but are not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: IETF Datatracker / tools requirements
gaps.why: The document specifies requirements for an IETF administrative tool (Datatracker milestones); the taxonomy has no tag specific to IETF tooling, so IETF process is the nearest fit.

RFC6434.title: IPv6 Node Requirements
RFC6434.summary: RFC 6434 is an applicability statement that collects and states which IPv6 specifications (IP layer, ND, addressing, DHCPv6, MLD, DNS, transition, mobility, IPsec, MIBs) IPv6 hosts and routers MUST, SHOULD or MAY implement, obsoleting RFC 4294.

IPv6.why: The whole document defines requirements for IPv6 nodes, covering the IPv6 specification, addressing, and deployment guidance.
IPv6.quote: This document defines common functionality required from both IPv6 hosts and routers.

neighbor discovery.why: A substantial section gives detailed ND requirements (router discovery, NUD, redirects, DAD), plus router-side ND requirements.
neighbor discovery.quote: All nodes MUST support the sending and receiving of Neighbor Solicitation (NS) and Neighbor Advertisement (NA) messages.

SLAAC.why: The document sets requirements for SLAAC, DAD, optimistic DAD and privacy extensions.
SLAAC.quote: Hosts MUST support IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration as defined in [RFC4862].

DHCPv6.why: Several sections, including the DHCP versus RA discussion and router relay requirements, address DHCPv6 support.
DHCPv6.quote: all hosts SHOULD implement address configuration via DHCPv6.

MLD.why: A dedicated section sets requirements for MLDv1, MLDv2 and Lightweight MLDv2.
MLD.quote: Nodes that need to join multicast groups MUST support MLDv1 [RFC2710].

IPsec.why: The security section changes the IPsec/IKEv2 recommendation and sets ESP, AH and algorithm requirements.
IPsec.quote: making support of the IPsec Architecture [RFC4301] a SHOULD for all IPv6 nodes.

IPv6 transition.why: A section addresses IPv4 support and transition mechanisms.
IPv6 transition.quote: If an IPv6 node implements dual stack and tunneling, then [RFC4213] MUST be supported.
IPv6 transition.section: 8.1.1. Basic Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 Hosts and Routers - RFC 4213

IP mobility.why: A section sets the requirement level (MAY) for Mobile IPv6 and related specs.
IP mobility.quote: Mobile IPv6 [RFC6275] and associated specifications [RFC3776] [RFC4877] allow a node to change its point of attachment

rejected.why: DNS stub-resolver requirements (AAAA, ip6.arpa, EDNS0) are a short subsection of requirements, not the subject of the document.
ICMPv6 gets a one-line MUST; it is not a substantial part of the document.
SEND is covered in a short subsection and is only optional (MAY); it is not a substantial focus.
Path MTU Discovery is a brief subsection among many requirements.
Only two MIB modules are listed as SHOULD for SNMP-capable nodes.
The router alert option is mentioned in a single short subsection.

RFC6435.title: MPLS Transport Profile Lock Instruct and Loopback Functions
RFC6435.summary: Specifies the MPLS-TP Lock Instruct (LI) OAM message carried in the G-ACh and describes how the loopback function operates, updating RFC 6371.

MPLS-TP.why: Defines the MPLS-TP lock instruct OAM message (new ACH type 0x0026) and loopback operation on LSPs, PWs and sections; it updates the MPLS-TP OAM framework RFC 6371.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document specifies the lock function for MPLS networks and describes how the loopback function operates in MPLS networks.

OAM.why: Lock and loopback are OAM functions, and the document is about OAM mechanisms generally. This is a topic tag kept separate from the MPLS-TP technology tag.
OAM.quote: Two useful Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions in a transport network are "lock" and "loopback".

rejected.why: Pseudowires are one of the transport paths that can be locked, but the document does not specify pseudowire emulation.
The parent of MPLS-TP is implied, so it is not listed separately.
RFC 6428 (CC/CV/RDI) is referenced for the MEP Source ID TLV only. This document does not specify BFD.
Lock and loopback are commanded through management, but the document specifies a data-plane OAM message and not a management architecture.

RFC6436.title: Rationale for Update to the IPv6 Flow Label Specification
RFC6436.summary: Informational background document explaining why the IPv6 flow label specification (RFC 3697) should be updated, motivating changes (companion to RFC 6437) to encourage uniformly distributed labels for stateless load distribution and to relax immutability.

IPv6.why: The whole document concerns the IPv6 header's flow label field and the rules for setting and handling it, so it belongs on the IPv6 page.
IPv6.quote: The flow label field in the IPv6 header was reserved but left Experimental by [RFC2460]

ECMP.why: Stateless load distribution through hashing, including ECMP, is the main motivating use for the proposed changes, so ECMP readers would want this rationale.
ECMP.quote: The expected default usage of the flow label is some form of stateless load distribution, such as the ECMP/LAG usage defined in [RFC6438].

rejected.why: Diffserv is mentioned only as an analogy (DSCP, flow label domain) and in the rejected alternatives. The document is not about it.
QoS semantics in the flow label are discussed only as a proposal that was rejected. The document is not about QoS.
LAG is mentioned only through a reference to RFC 6438, which is a separate document.
RSVP is cited only as the one pre-existing signaling option for the flow label.

RFC6437.title: IPv6 Flow Label Specification
RFC6437.summary: Specifies the IPv6 Flow Label field, minimum requirements for source and forwarding nodes labeling flows statelessly, flow-state establishment constraints, and corrects RSVP's flow label size; obsoletes RFC 3697.

IPv6.why: The document specifies the IPv6 header Flow Label field and replaces Section 6 and Appendix A of RFC 2460, so it belongs in IPv6.
IPv6.quote: The 20-bit Flow Label field in the IPv6 header [RFC2460] is used by a node to label packets of a flow.

rejected.why: ECMP load distribution is a motivating use case, with details in RFC 6438. This document only specifies labeling.
There is only a small correction to RFC 2205 about the 24-bit versus 20-bit field size. The document is not about RSVP.
IPsec interaction is discussed only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-level evidence.
LAG is mentioned only as a load-distribution use case, with no specification of it.
Flow-specific treatment and stateful service models are explicitly out of scope.
Firewall rewriting of labels is discussed only in the covert channel risk subsection of Security Considerations.

RFC6438.title: Using the IPv6 Flow Label for Equal Cost Multipath Routing and Link Aggregation in Tunnels
RFC6438.summary: Standards-track guidelines for setting the IPv6 flow label in outer headers of IP-in-IPv6 tunnels and for including it in ECMP/LAG hash inputs at routers, consistent with the IPv6 flow label specification.

ECMP.why: The document specifies how routers must build ECMP hashes using the flow label and how tunnel endpoints should set the label to avoid polarization.
ECMP.quote: the hash algorithm used to determine the outgoing component-link in an ECMP and/or LAG toward the next hop MUST minimally include the 3-tuple

IPv6.why: The document concerns the use and rules of the IPv6 flow label field, a substantial IPv6 specification matter.
IPv6.quote: The flow label in the outer packet SHOULD be set by the sending TEP to a 20-bit value in accordance with [RFC6437].

link aggregation.why: LAG load balancing using the flow label is a co-equal subject in the title and guidelines.
link aggregation.quote: Two such techniques are known as equal cost multipath (ECMP) routing and link aggregation (LAG) [IEEE802.1AX].

tunneling.why: The guidelines are specifically for IP-in-IPv6 tunnels, where the tunnel endpoint labels outer packets.
tunneling.quote: Inner packets MUST be encapsulated in an outer IPv6 packet whose source and destination addresses are those of the tunnel endpoints (TEPs).

rejected.why: The tunnel is IP-in-IPv6 generally, but the document is about flow label use, not the encapsulation mechanism itself; tunneling is the better fit.
GRE is mentioned only as an example of header-analysis complexity.
MPLS entropy labels and OAM are mentioned only as related issues.
A single bullet notes OAM will need adaptation; not a substantial part of the document.
Only cited as a reference for similar OAM issues.

gaps.name: IPv6 flow label
gaps.why: The document is about the IPv6 flow label, which has no dedicated tag; IPv6 is the closest fit.

RFC6439.title: Routing Bridges (RBridges): Appointed Forwarders
RFC6439.summary: RFC 6439 improves the documentation of the TRILL Appointed Forwarder mechanism, specifying how RBridges are appointed per VLAN on multi-access links and the inhibition timers that prevent loops, updating RFC 6325.

TRILL.why: The document specifies the TRILL Appointed Forwarder mechanism, including DRB appointment and VLAN inhibition timers, for RBridges.
TRILL.quote: The purpose of this document is to improve the documentation of the Appointed Forwarder mechanism; thus, it updates RFC 6325.

rejected.why: TRILL uses IS-IS Hello sub-TLVs to carry appointments, but IS-IS is only the substrate and is not specified or extended here.
The document deals with VLANs and bridged LAN links, but it is about the TRILL forwarder mechanism, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Multiple ports of one RBridge on a link are discussed, but this is not link aggregation (IEEE 802.1AX).
TRILL is sometimes used in data centres, but the document does not address data-centre-scale routing.

gaps.name: TRILL / RBridges
gaps.why: The document is about TRILL (RBridges), and the taxonomy has a tag id 'TRILL' listed as a tech under routing; I used it. If it is not accepted exactly as written, no other tag fits the Appointed Forwarder mechanism.

RFC6440.title: The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) Local Domain Name DHCPv6 Option
RFC6440.summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option (OPTION_ERP_LOCAL_DOMAIN_NAME) that lets a DHCPv6 server give a client the local domain name needed for ERP/DSRK derivation, with client and relay agent behaviour.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option, including its format, client behaviour and relay agent behaviour. It belongs on the DHCPv6 page.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Version 6 (DHCPv6) option designed to allow a DHCPv6 server to inform clients

HOKEY.why: The option exists to support ERP local domain name discovery, which is needed to derive the DSRK. That is the HOKEY/ERP work, and the document came from the hokey WG.
HOKEY.quote: The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) [RFC5296] is designed to allow faster re-authentication of a mobile device

rejected.why: EAP is the context for the option, but the document does not specify or extend an EAP method. ERP is covered by the HOKEY tag, which is a child of EAP.
Only the domain name encoding and the FQDN length limit are referenced. The document does not address DNS itself.
A single note says the encoding allows A-labels. That is incidental and not what the document is about.
AAA is mentioned only as a possible source of the local domain name at a relay agent. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC6441.title: Time to Remove Filters for Previously Unallocated IPv4 /8s
RFC6441.summary: BCP advising network operators to remove packet and BGP prefix filters based on the registration status of formerly unallocated IPv4 /8s now that IANA has none left, and pointing to RFC 5735 for Martian prefixes that should still not be routed.

IPv4.why: The document is about the IPv4 address space after allocation of the last unallocated /8s, and the status of those blocks. It also covers which special-use IPv4 prefixes remain unroutable.
IPv4.quote: Now that there are no longer any unallocated IPv4 /8s, this practise is more complicated, fragile, and expensive.

operational security.why: It gives operational guidance on border-router bogon and packet filtering practice, advising operators to drop filters that would now block legitimate traffic.
operational security.quote: Network operators SHOULD remove both ingress and egress packet filters as well as BGP prefix filters for previously unallocated IPv4 /8s.
operational security.section: 3.1. No Longer Filtering Based on Address Registration Status

rejected.why: BGP prefix filters are mentioned, but the document does not specify or extend BGP. It only advises on filter practice.
The IPv4 tag is more specific for IPv4 address lifecycle, so the parent is not also listed.
IANA's exhaustion of /8s is the background, but the document does not cover IANA registries or their stewardship.
The filters are bogon filters, not RPKI or routing-protocol security mechanisms, so the operational security tag fits better.

RFC6442.title: Location Conveyance for the Session Initiation Protocol
RFC6442.summary: Defines SIP extensions (Geolocation, Geolocation-Routing and Geolocation-Error header fields, 424 response code, location profile option tags) for conveying geographic location by value or reference and for location-based routing.

SIP.why: The document specifies new SIP header fields, a new response code and option tags, so it is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) to convey geographic location information from one SIP entity to another SIP entity.

geolocation.why: The subject is conveying location information in the GEOPRIV architecture, with SIP as the Using Protocol. It covers PIDF-LO bodies, location URIs, privacy rules and dereferencing.
geolocation.quote: This document defines how SIP conveys geographic location information of a Target to a Location Recipient (LR).

rejected.why: PIDF-LO is the location object format that is carried. The document does not define or extend it.
HTTP is only one of the dereferencing mechanisms, named through the geolocation-http option tag. The document does not specify it.
The presence event package is used for dereferencing location URIs, but the document does not define or extend it.
Emergency calling is mentioned as a use case, but the document says specialised emergency deployments are out of scope.
TLS only protects the signalling hop by hop, as a security mechanism the document relies on.
The privacy section is largely a pointer to the GEOPRIV documents, so it is not enough to justify a general privacy tag.

gaps.name: GEOPRIV / location conveyance (PIDF-LO)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the geolocation topic and the HELD tech, but no tag specific to GEOPRIV location objects. The geolocation topic is the closest fit.

RFC6443.title: Framework for Emergency Calling Using Internet Multimedia
RFC6443.summary: Informational framework document describing how IETF-standardized components (SIP, LoST, location configuration and conveyance, service URNs) fit together to support emergency calls from citizens to PSAPs over Internet multimedia.

emergency services.why: The whole document is an architecture framework for emergency calling, covering identification, routing, signalling, callbacks, media and testing.
emergency services.quote: This document describes how all of those component parts are used to support emergency calls from citizens and visitors to authorities.

LoST.why: LoST is the core mechanism for routing calls to PSAPs, obtaining dial strings and validating locations. It is discussed in many sections, including discovery in Section 7.
LoST.quote: The call is routed (Section 8) based on location using the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol [RFC5222], which maps a location to a set of PSAP URIs.
LoST.section: 3. Overview of How Emergency Calls Are Placed

geolocation.why: Section 6 is a large part of the document and covers location types, determination, configuration, conveyance, updates, multiple locations and validation.
geolocation.quote: Location is central to the operation of emergency services.  Location is used for two purposes in emergency call handling: routing of the call and dispatch of responders.
geolocation.section: 6. Location and Its Role in an Emergency Call

HELD.why: HELD is described as one of the location configuration protocols alongside DHCP and LLDP, with notes on NAT/VPN effects and dereference for PSAPs.
HELD.quote: HELD [RFC5985] can deliver a civic or geo location object, by value or by reference, via a Layer 7 protocol.

SIP.why: The framework profiles SIP signalling for emergency calls, including UA and proxy requirements, TLS use, callbacks, transfer and termination.
SIP.quote: This document discusses the use of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [RFC3261] by PSAPs and calling parties.

rejected.why: DHCP location options are mentioned as one location configuration protocol, but the document does not specify or extend DHCP.
TLS is only the hop-by-hop protection mechanism for signalling, with a retry-without-TLS recommendation. It is not the subject.
RTP, SRTP and media codecs appear only as media requirements for PSAPs in a short section.
The service URN urn:service:sos is used but is defined in RFC 5031. This document only uses it, so it is not about URN namespaces.
IM and MSRP are mentioned only as media PSAPs should accept.
VPNs are discussed only as an obstacle to location determination, and the tag refers to provider-provisioned VPNs.

gaps.name: GEOPRIV / PIDF-LO location objects
gaps.why: Location configuration, conveyance and the PIDF-LO format are a substantial part of the document. The taxonomy has only the generic geolocation topic and the PIDF tag under instant messaging, and neither fits cleanly.

RFC6444.title: Location Hiding: Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC6444.summary: Informational problem statement and requirements list for emergency call routing when an ISP/IAP withholds precise location from endpoints and VoIP service providers, within the ECRIT architecture.

emergency services.why: The whole document gives requirements for emergency call routing to PSAPs when location is hidden, within the ECRIT architecture.
emergency services.quote: There MUST be a way for the ISP/IAP to withhold precise location information from the endpoint and from the VSP.

geolocation.why: A substantial part concerns conveying, withholding and referencing location (location by value vs by reference, LIS), which is a location-privacy and conveyance problem.
geolocation.quote: The PSAP MUST receive precise location information (by value) about emergency callers.

LoST.why: Several requirements constrain the solution relative to LoST for PSAP URI resolution, and the document explains that LoST requires location by value.
LoST.quote: The solution MUST NOT interfere with the use of LoST for non-emergency services.

rejected.why: HELD is only mentioned as an instantiation of the LCP that supports location by reference. The document does not specify or extend it.
SIP appears only in Req-9 (no SIP needed at the ISP) and in a reference to location conveyance. The document is not about SIP.
Privacy is one motivation for hiding location, but the document is a requirements list for emergency routing, not a privacy threat-model document.
DHCP is mentioned only once, in Req-20, as something to minimize impact on.

RFC6445.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering Management Information Base for Fast Reroute
RFC6445.summary: Defines three SMIv2 MIB modules (general, one-to-one backup, facility backup) for managing MPLS TE fast reroute per RFC 4090 on LSRs.

MIB.why: The document is a set of MIB modules (MPLS-FRR-GENERAL/ONE2ONE/FACILITY-STD-MIB) defined in SMIv2, so it belongs under MIB.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used to support two fast reroute (FRR) methods for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS)-based traffic engineering (TE)

IP fast reroute.why: The managed objects model MPLS TE fast reroute (detour LSPs, bypass tunnels, PLRs), so readers of fast reroute would want it.
IP fast reroute.quote: The two methods are the one-to-one backup method and the facility backup method.

RSVP-TE.why: The MIB manages RFC 4090 RSVP-TE FRR state (DETOUR object, SESSION_ATTRIBUTE flags, RRO), and it sits alongside the MPLS TE MIB for TE tunnels.
RSVP-TE.quote: Fast Reroute Extensions to RSVP-TE for LSP Tunnels

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the MIB tag covers the subject.
A parent of the more specific tags chosen, so it is implied.
The RSVP-TE tag sits under it and is already chosen.
Section 5 only notes that 32-bit LSR IDs are needed for IPv6 tunnels; it is a minor point.

RFC6446.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Event Notification Extension for Notification Rate Control
RFC6446.summary: Defines SIP Event header parameters (max-rate, min-rate, adaptive-min-rate) letting a subscriber control the rate of event notifications for any SIP event package, updating RFC 3265.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP events framework (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY) with new Event and Subscription-State header field parameters and updates RFC 3265.
SIP.quote: This document specifies mechanisms for adjusting the rate of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) event notifications.

rejected.why: Presence and RLS are used as use cases, but the extension applies to all event packages and is not specific to SIMPLE.
ABNF is only used to define the grammar of the new parameters.
Mentioned only as a complementary bandwidth-saving mechanism.
Rate control here is about notification frequency, not transport congestion control.
Presence data is only referenced for partial-state notification considerations.

RFC6447.title: Filtering Location Notifications in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6447.summary: Defines location-specific filters (movement, speed, region entry/exit, civic element change, location type, rate control) as an extension to the RFC 4661 XML event notification filter format, for SIP presence-event subscriptions carrying PIDF-LO location.

SIMPLE.why: The document extends SIMPLE-family specifications: SIP event notification filters (RFC 4661) over the presence event package, using PIDF-LO. This is the best-fitting tag for SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY filtering.
SIMPLE.quote: These filters are designed as an extension to RFC 4661, an XML-based format for event notification filtering, and based on RFC 3856, the SIP presence event package.

geolocation.why: The subject is conveyance of location information. It covers geodetic and civic location, region entry/exit, movement and speed triggers, and PIDF-LO.
geolocation.quote: This document describes filters that limit asynchronous location notifications to compelling events.

rejected.why: SIP event notification is the substrate. The document defines filters for it rather than extending SIP call signalling, and SIMPLE is the more specific fit.
XML is only the encoding for the filter format and schema. The document is not about XML usage in general.
PIDF-LO is the carrier of the location data. The document does not define or extend it.
HELD is mentioned only in passing, in Security Considerations and informative references.
Emergency call routing is used only as an example use case for rate control.

RFC6448.title: The Unencrypted Form of Kerberos 5 KRB-CRED Message
RFC6448.summary: Specifies the unencrypted form of the Kerberos 5 KRB-CRED message (etype 0, cleartext EncKrbCredPart) for transferring credentials over a secure transport, such as in the SAML Kerberos attribute profile.

Kerberos.why: The document defines a Kerberos 5 message variant and its encoding rules, so readers of the Kerberos subject would want it.
Kerberos.quote: The unencrypted form of the KRB-CRED message contains EncryptedData as defined in Section 5.2.9 of [RFC4120]. The encryption type (etype) MUST be specified as 0.
Kerberos.section: 3. The Unencrypted Form of the KRB-CRED Message

rejected.why: TLS is only named as an example of a secure transport in Security Considerations. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
GSS-API is mentioned only as the legacy context where unencrypted KRB-CRED was already used. The document does not specify a GSS-API mechanism.
SAML is the motivating application, but the document only specifies the KRB-CRED message format. It does not specify a SAML profile.
The only IANA action is updating the reference for Kerberos encryption type 0. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC6449.title: Complaint Feedback Loop Operational Recommendations
RFC6449.summary: Informational RFC codifying MAAWG operational practices for complaint feedback loops, in which mailbox providers send ARF-format spam complaint reports to feedback consumers such as senders, ESPs and ISPs, and how each side should enrol, process and act on them.

spam.why: The whole document concerns spam complaint reporting, feedback handling, complaint rates, suppression and reputation. This is the spam subject area, and no more specific child tag covers feedback loop operations.
spam.quote: The intent of a Complaint Feedback Loop is to provide Feedback Consumers with information necessary to mitigate Spam or the perception of Spam.

ARF.why: ARF is the standard format for feedback messages. It is recommended throughout, and Appendix A describes its history and structure. The RFC is operational guidance rather than the ARF specification, so the role is secondary.
ARF.quote: It is recommended that Feedback Messages be sent using the standard Abuse Reporting Format, to facilitate uniformity and ease of processing

rejected.why: Appendix B explains using the DKIM d= domain to route feedback. This is a minor use of DKIM as an identifier, and the document does not specify or extend DKIM.
SMTP is only the transport for feedback messages and is not specified or changed here.
The document is about spam complaint feedback, which the more specific spam and ARF tags cover. It is not about email architecture generally.
MIME appears only in the description of the ARF multipart/report structure and is not the subject.
Whitelists and reputation come up only in passing. The document does not define DNS-based list conventions.
WHOIS records are mentioned only as one way to cross-check IP ownership during enrolment.

RFC6450.title: Multicast Ping Protocol
RFC6450.summary: Specifies the Multicast Ping Protocol, a UDP-based client/server protocol (port 9903) with TLV options that tests SSM and ASM multicast reception and reports tree setup time, hop count, delay and loss, based on ssmping/asmping.

multicast.why: The protocol exists to test multicast connectivity for SSM and ASM, so it belongs under multicast. No more specific child tag covers a multicast ping/diagnostic protocol.
multicast.quote: allows for checking whether an endpoint can receive multicast -- both Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) and Any-Source Multicast (ASM)

performance measurement.why: The protocol measures RTT, one-way delay, loss and hop counts, so it is an active measurement tool, similar to ping.
performance measurement.quote: the protocol can provide related information, such as multicast tree setup time, the number of hops the packets have traveled, and packet delay and loss

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport; the document doesn't extend or specify UDP itself.
ICMP Echo is only an analogy; the protocol is separate and runs over UDP.
SSM is one of the multicast modes being tested, not the subject of the specification.
Multicast ping is loosely an OAM tool, but performance measurement and multicast fit better.
The registries it creates are boilerplate IANA Considerations for this protocol, not the subject of the document.

RFC6451.title: Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Protocol Extensions
RFC6451.summary: Experimental extension to the LoST protocol adding "N nearest", "within distance X" and "served by" findService query types, with new <region>, <limit> and <serviceLocation> elements for non-emergency location-based services.

LoST.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the LoST protocol: new query types, new XML elements and a schema in the lost-ext namespace.
LoST.quote: We extend LoST with three additional <findService> query types, giving the protocol the ability to find the N nearest instances of a particular service

rejected.why: Shapes and civic/geodetic locations (PIDF-LO) are used as query inputs, but the document extends LoST rather than addressing location formats or privacy.
The protocol is XML-based and a RELAX NG schema is given, but XML is only the encoding.
LoST is a child of emergency services, which is already implied. The document says the extensions SHOULD NOT be used for emergency routing and do not change emergency behaviour.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the transport protection.
Service URNs are used in queries but are not defined or extended here.

RFC6452.title: The Unicode Code Points and Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA) - Unicode 6.0
RFC6452.summary: Documents IETF consensus that the three Unicode 6.0 code point property changes (U+0CF1, U+0CF2, U+19DA) require no update to the IDNA2008 derived property algorithm in RFC 5892.

IDN.why: The document is about IDNA derived property values for code points and concludes that RFC 5892 needs no update, which is squarely IDNA/IDN subject matter.
IDN.quote: derived character properties related to the three code points, existing in Unicode 5.2, that changed property values when version 6.0 was released

rejected.why: The document concerns Unicode character property changes, but only as they affect IDNA derived property values. It is not about Unicode usage in protocols generally, so IDN is the better fit.
The IANA section only records an update to the derived property registry. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
IDN is the more specific tag for this document, and its parent is already implied.

RFC6453.title: A URN Namespace for the Open Grid Forum (OGF)
RFC6453.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "ogf" for the Open Grid Forum, defining its subnamespace-based syntax, assignment, persistence, lexical equivalence and validation rules.

URN.why: The document is a formal URN namespace registration (NID "ogf") following the RFC 3406 template, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document describes a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace that is engineered by the Open Grid Forum (OGF) for naming persistent resources.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the syntax of the OGF-URN; the document is not about the notation.
The IANA Considerations section only records the NID registration, which is boilerplate. The body is about the namespace itself.
RFC 3986 is cited for generic validation, but the document specifies a URN namespace, and URN is the more specific tag.
XML schemata are listed only as an expected use of the namespace.

RFC6454.title: The Web Origin Concept
RFC6454.summary: Defines the web "origin" concept underlying the same-origin policy, including how to compute, compare and serialize the origin of a URI, and registers the HTTP Origin header field.

web security.why: The whole document defines the origin as the unit of isolation for the browser same-origin policy, a web platform security mechanism. No child tag (HSTS, token binding, S-HTTP) fits.
web security.quote: The same-origin policy is one of the cornerstones of security for many user agents, including web browsers.

HTTP.why: Section 7 specifies the syntax, semantics and user agent requirements of a new HTTP header field, and registers it. That is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: It also defines an HTTP header field, named "Origin", that indicates which origins are associated with an HTTP request.

URI.why: A substantial part of the document gives algorithms for deriving an origin from a URI (scheme, host, port), comparing origins, and serializing them.
URI.quote: The origin of a URI is the value computed by the following algorithm:

rejected.why: DNS appears only as a dependency in Security Considerations (reliance on DNS for naming authority). The document does not specify or analyse DNS.
IDNA is mentioned only as an assumption about URI host processing and as a migration risk. The document does not define IDN behaviour.
Cookies are cited only as an example of a technology with a different isolation unit.
TLS is mentioned only to explain why the scheme is part of the origin. The document defines nothing about TLS.
HTML is used for examples and is deferred to for details of the same-origin policy. The document is not about HTML.
WebSocket is only cross-referenced as another specification that applies origin details.

gaps.name: same-origin policy / origin concept
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the same-origin policy or origin model. It is covered here only by the broader 'web security' topic. A dedicated tag would help with CORS-like and origin-related RFCs.

RFC6455.title: The WebSocket Protocol
RFC6455.summary: RFC 6455 specifies the WebSocket Protocol: an HTTP Upgrade-based opening handshake, binary message framing with masking, closing handshake, extension and subprotocol negotiation, ws/wss URI schemes, and related IANA registries.

WebSocket.why: The document is the core specification of the WebSocket protocol: handshake, framing, closing, extensions, and registries.
WebSocket.quote: The WebSocket Protocol enables two-way communication between a client running untrusted code in a controlled environment to a remote host that has opted-in to communications from that code.

rejected.why: HTTP is only used for the Upgrade handshake; the protocol itself is an independent TCP-based protocol, and the document defines new header fields only for the handshake.
WebSocket is layered over TCP as substrate; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
TLS is used for wss as a security mechanism; nothing new about TLS is defined.
The ws/wss URI schemes are defined, but they are part of the WebSocket protocol and a subsidiary aspect, so the WebSocket tag covers them.
The origin-based security model and masking are part of the WebSocket design, not a general web security mechanism document.
SHA-1 is used only in the handshake accept computation, and the document says it doesn't depend on its security properties.

RFC6456.title: Multi-Segment Pseudowires in Passive Optical Networks
RFC6456.summary: Informational RFC describing how to build multi-segment pseudowires whose end segment runs over a G-PON/XG-PON, with the OLT as S-PE and ONU as T-PE, and how to provision PW labels via OMCI instead of static configuration or LDP.

pseudowire.why: The whole document is about constructing and provisioning MS-PWs, with the PON segment as T-PE end segment and the OLT as S-PE.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes the application of MPLS multi-segment pseudowires (MS-PWs) in a dual-technology environment comprising a Passive Optical Network (PON) and an MPLS Packet Switched Network (PSN).

rejected.why: MPLS LSP tunnels with PHP carry the PWs, but they are substrate; the subject is pseudowires, which is the more specific tag.
LDP is mentioned only as the dynamic signalling the document avoids, to keep ONUs simple.
OMCI provisioning is a central theme, but OMCI is an ITU-T protocol and there is no matching tag. Provisioning is part of the PW subject here.
The document is about PON and optical access, not GMPLS control of optical networks.
ATM and TDM appear only as native services emulated by the PWs.

gaps.name: Passive Optical Networks (G-PON/XG-PON) and OMCI
gaps.why: The document is about PON access and its OMCI management protocol, and the taxonomy has no PON or optical access tag. The nearest tags are DSL and DOCSIS under link layer.

RFC6457.title: PCC-PCE Communication and PCE Discovery Requirements for Inter-Layer Traffic Engineering
RFC6457.summary: RFC 6457 sets out requirements for PCEP communication between PCCs and PCEs, and for PCE discovery, to support inter-layer (multi-layer) MPLS/GMPLS traffic engineering path computation.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies PCEP and PCE discovery requirements for inter-layer path computation, which is the PCE architecture and PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document complements the generic requirements and presents detailed sets of PCC-PCE communication protocol requirements and PCE discovery protocol requirements for inter-layer traffic engineering.

GMPLS.why: Multi-layer and multi-region GMPLS networks, with their adaptation and virtual network topology, are the problem setting. Many requirements concern GMPLS layers and models.
GMPLS.quote: MPLS and GMPLS networks may be constructed from layered client/server networks.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is mentioned only as the signaling that uses the EROs the PCE returns. The document does not specify it.
MPLS is the general context. GMPLS and PCE are the more specific subjects.
The PCE tag, which is under traffic engineering, already covers this subject.
The document says PCEP extensions must come with MIB objects. That is a brief manageability requirement and the MIB is not the subject.

RFC6458.title: Sockets API Extensions for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
RFC6458.summary: Informational RFC defining a sockets API mapping for SCTP, including one-to-one and one-to-many socket styles, ancillary data, notifications, socket options, and new library functions.

sockets API.why: The document defines the sockets API for SCTP.
sockets API.quote: This document describes a mapping of the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) into a sockets API.

RFC6459.title: IPv6 in 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Evolved Packet System (EPS)
RFC6459.summary: Informational overview of how IPv6 (and dual-stack IPv4v6) is supported in 3GPP GPRS and EPS networks, covering PDP contexts/PDN connections, address configuration, prefix delegation, neighbor discovery issues, and deployment and roaming issues.

cellular.why: The whole document describes IP connectivity over 3GPP GPRS/EPS/LTE: PDP contexts, PDN connections, bearers, APNs and inter-RAT handovers.
cellular.quote: This document describes the support for IPv6 in 3GPP network architectures.

IPv6.why: It covers IPv6 address configuration, /64 prefix allocation, prefix delegation, IPv6-only and dual-stack bearers, and deployment of IPv6 in 3GPP networks.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), as specified in [RFC4861] and [RFC4862], is the only supported address configuration mechanism.

neighbor discovery.why: A dedicated section discusses Neighbor Discovery behaviour and known problems on 3GPP point-to-point links, including RA handling and address resolution failures.
neighbor discovery.quote: The 3GPP link between the UE and the next-hop router (e.g., the GGSN) resembles a point-to-point (p2p) link, which has no link-layer addresses

rejected.why: Dual-stack deployment and transition are discussed, but the document is mainly a 3GPP IPv6 support overview. It states that 3GPP does not describe translation. IPv6 is the better tag.
SLAAC is described as the only address configuration mechanism, but it is a subsection of the broader IPv6 coverage and the document specifies nothing new about it.
Stateless DHCPv6 and prefix delegation are mentioned. They are referenced as existing mechanisms and are not the subject of the document.
PMIPv6 and GTP are named only as S5/S8 mobility options. The document is not about them.
NAT64/DNS64 are mentioned only as an optional deployment consideration for IPv6-only bearers.
The APN being an FQDN is only a terminology note.

gaps.name: GTP (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol)
gaps.why: The document refers to GTP repeatedly as the 3GPP tunnelling protocol, but the taxonomy has no GTP tag. Cellular is the nearest fit.

RFC6460.title: Suite B Profile for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC6460.summary: RFC 6460 defines a Suite B-compliant profile of TLS 1.2 (and DTLS 1.2) restricting cipher suites, curves, signatures and certificates to NSA Suite B algorithms (AES-GCM, ECDH, ECDSA P-256/P-384), with a transitional profile for TLS 1.0/1.1 in an annex; it obsoletes RFC 5430.

TLS.why: The document profiles TLS 1.2: mandated cipher suites, supported curves extension, signature_algorithms, CertificateRequest, CertificateVerify and ServerKeyExchange requirements. TLS readers need it for deployment guidance.
TLS.quote: This document defines a profile of Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.2 that is fully compliant with Suite B.

elliptic curve.why: A substantial part of the document constrains elliptic curve use (P-256/P-384, ECDH, ECDSA) as required by Suite B.
elliptic curve.quote: Suite B TLS connections MUST use secp256r1(23) or secp384r1(24).

DTLS.why: The profile explicitly covers DTLS 1.2 and a transitional DTLS 1.0 profile, though it is mostly TLS-focused.
DTLS.quote: conventions for using National Security Agency (NSA) Suite B Cryptography [SuiteB] with the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, and the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

rejected.why: Considered since ECDSA is central to the authentication requirements, but the document applies it as a Suite B policy requirement in TLS rather than defining or analysing ECDSA; the parent elliptic curve tag covers the cryptographic content.
AES in GCM mode is mandated by the cipher suites, but the document defines no AES specifics; it relies on existing RFC 5288/5289 suites.
Certificates must comply with the Suite B certificate profile (RFC 5759), but this document only references it and does not profile certificates itself.
SHA-256/384 are used in the PRF and signatures, but only as components of the suites; the document is not about the hash family.
The general topic is implied by the more specific elliptic curve tag, so it is not listed directly.

gaps.name: NSA Suite B Cryptography
gaps.why: The document is about a national cryptographic algorithm policy (Suite B) and its application to TLS. The taxonomy has no tag for algorithm suites or policy profiles.

RFC6461.title: Data for Reachability of Inter-/Intra-NetworK SIP (DRINKS) Use Cases and Protocol Requirements
RFC6461.summary: Informational DRINKS WG document giving use cases and protocol requirements for provisioning session establishment data (SED) into a registry used by SIP service providers for session peering and routing.

SPEERMINT.why: The document covers provisioning SED registries for peering between SIP service providers, building on SPEERMINT terminology (SED, LUF, LRF). The SPEERMINT tag explicitly includes peering provisioning.
SPEERMINT.quote: interfaces that provision session establishment data into Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Service Provider components to assist with session routing

rejected.why: SIP is the context for the routing data, but the document does not specify or extend SIP itself.
Registries may hold DNS NAPTR-based records and the document cites Infrastructure ENUM requirements, but ENUM is not the subject.
DNS records (NS, CNAME, NAPTR) are mentioned only in one example use case.
Routing numbers and TN ranges are used as data objects, but the tel URI scheme is only cited for the RN definition.
Provisioning of registry objects is the topic, but EPP is not mentioned or specified here.

RFC6462.title: Report from the Internet Privacy Workshop
RFC6462.summary: IAB report on the December 2010 Internet Privacy Workshop (with W3C, ISOC, MIT CSAIL), covering privacy design and deployment challenges (fingerprinting, information leakage, first vs third party, usability, incentives) and next steps for IETF and W3C.

workshop reports.why: The document is a report on the proceedings of an IAB-co-hosted workshop, which is exactly what this topic collects.
workshop reports.quote: On December 8-9, 2010, the IAB co-hosted an Internet privacy workshop with the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), the Internet Society (ISOC), and MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory

privacy.why: The whole report is about privacy in Internet protocols: threats, fingerprinting, leakage, and guidance for protocol designers on privacy considerations.
privacy.quote: The workshop revealed some of the fundamental challenges in designing, deploying, and analyzing privacy-protective Internet protocols and systems.

rejected.why: Cookies come up in the first-party/third-party discussion, but only as an example. The document does not specify or analyse the cookie mechanism.
The Referer header and HTTP's generic design are used as examples of information leakage. The document is not about HTTP itself.
The IPv6 privacy extensions (RFC 4941) are cited as an example of a targeted privacy feature, and nothing more.
OAuth is mentioned once, as a cross-site data-sharing example. It is not a subject of the report.
The Geolocation API and GEOPRIV appear as case studies. Geolocation is not the focus of the report.
The report suggests a privacy directorate and privacy considerations sections. These are side outcomes, and the document is mainly about privacy, not IETF process.

gaps.name: Do Not Track / web tracking and fingerprinting
gaps.why: The report discusses DNT, tracking and browser fingerprinting at length, but the taxonomy has no tag for them. The closest fit is the generic privacy topic.

RFC6463.title: Runtime Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) Assignment Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6463.summary: Defines runtime LMA assignment for Proxy Mobile IPv6: new mobility options (Redirect-Capability, Redirect, Load Information, Alternate IPv4 CoA) and MAG/LMA procedures letting an LMA redirect a MAG to another LMA during PBU/PBA exchange, e.g. for load balancing.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends PMIPv6 with new mobility options and MAG/LMA behaviour for assigning an LMA at runtime during the PBU/PBA exchange.
PMIPv6.quote: This document describes a runtime local mobility anchor assignment functionality and corresponding mobility options for Proxy Mobile IPv6.

rejected.why: DNS-based LMA discovery is only discussed as a motivation for why this solution is independent of it.
AAA-based LMA selection is mentioned only as an alternative the spec does not depend on.
Security associations and IKEv2 are assumed and out of scope; only a substrate.
Anycast rfLMA addressing is one deployment option but the document is not about anycast in its own right.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific PMIPv6 tag.
The document uses IPv6 and IPv4 transport but is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC6464.title: A Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) Header Extension for Client-to-Mixer Audio Level Indication
RFC6464.summary: Defines an RTP header extension (using RFC 5285 mechanism) that lets audio senders indicate per-packet audio level and optional voice activity, so conference mixers can pick loudest streams without decoding.

RTP.why: The document specifies a new RTP header extension element, its encoding, and its signalling, so it belongs under RTP.
RTP.quote: this document defines an RTP header extension [RFC5285] through which senders of audio packets can indicate the audio level of the packets' payload

rejected.why: SDP's extmap attribute is used to signal the extension and the document defines a 'vad' extension attribute, but this is a small signalling detail, not the subject.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a confidentiality concern for header extensions.
Conferencing is the motivating use case, but the document defines an RTP header extension and not a conferencing framework or control.
G.711 u-law is cited only as an example for the dBov reference level.

RFC6465.title: A Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) Header Extension for Mixer-to-Client Audio Level Indication
RFC6465.summary: Defines an RTP header extension (via RFC 5285) letting conference mixers report per-contributing-source audio levels in -dBov to clients, with SDP extmap signalling and a reference level calculator.

RTP.why: The document defines a new RTP header extension carrying per-CSRC audio levels in RTP packets, extending RTP itself.
RTP.quote: This document specifies an RTP extension header that allows such mixers to deliver audio level information to conference participants

conferencing.why: The extension addresses audio conferences with mixers and focus entities, so conferencing readers would want it.
conferencing.quote: a mechanism for RTP-level mixers in audio conferences to deliver information about the audio level of individual participants

rejected.why: SDP is used only to signal the extmap URI and offer/answer direction; nothing new is defined for SDP itself.
SIP appears only as the conferencing framework context and in examples; it is not specified or extended.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as not protecting the header extension.
RTCP is mentioned only for CNAME mapping; the document does not extend it.
The IANA section registers one extension URI, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The framework is cited as background (RFC 4353, SIP conferencing); the document does not specify XCON.

RFC6466.title: IANA Registration of the 'image' Media Type for the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC6466.summary: Registers 'image' as a top-level SDP media type in the IANA SDP parameters registry, used mainly to negotiate T.38 fax media streams.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP by adding a new top-level media name ('image') to the SDP media registry, so readers of SDP need it.
SDP.quote: The purpose of this document is to register with IANA the 'image' media type as a top-level SDP media type.

fax.why: The motivation and main use of the registration is establishing T.38 fax-over-IP streams, including an SDP example of a T.38 offer.
fax.quote: is widely used in SDP implementations for setting up T.38 Real-Time Facsimile [T38] media streams.

rejected.why: The 'image' MIME type already exists. This document registers it in the SDP media registry, not in the MIME media type registry.
SIP only carries the SDP offer/answer in the example. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
The IANA registration is the whole substance of the document, but it concerns one SDP registry entry. It is not guidance about IANA registries in general.
UDPTL and TCP appear only as transports in the example and are not the subject of the document.
MIME is background for the shared namespace history. The document does not define anything about MIME itself.

gaps.name: T.38
gaps.why: T.38 real-time fax over IP is the main use case. The taxonomy covers it only through the general 'fax' tag, which is the closest fit.

RFC6467.title: Secure Password Framework for Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC6467.summary: Defines a generic IKEv2 framework for negotiating which symmetric secure password (PAKE) authentication method to use during IKE_SA_INIT and a generic GSPM payload to carry method-specific data in IKE_AUTH.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a Notify payload for method negotiation, a new GSPM payload type and an AUTH method number, so it is about IKE.
IKE.quote: This document defines a generic way for Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) to use any of the symmetric secure password authentication methods.

PAKE.why: It is a framework for plugging multiple password-authenticated key exchange methods into IKEv2, though it defines none itself. PAKE readers would want it.
PAKE.quote: a symmetric secure password authentication protocol that supports the use of low-entropy shared secrets, and to protect against off-line dictionary attacks

rejected.why: IPsec is the context. The document's specific subject is IKEv2 payloads and negotiation, which the IKE tag already covers.
AAA is mentioned only to contrast with EAP-based remote access, not as a subject of the document.
EAP is mentioned only as an alternative that these methods avoid. The document is not about it.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate for this document. The main body is about the IKEv2 framework.

RFC6468.title: Sieve Notification Mechanism: SIP MESSAGE
RFC6468.summary: Defines a Sieve notification mechanism profile that sends email notifications as SIP MESSAGE requests using sip/sips URIs, and registers it with IANA.

Sieve.why: The document extends Sieve's notify action with a new notification method, defining the method parameter, :from, :importance, :message handling and the notify_method_capability test.
Sieve.quote: This document describes a profile of the Sieve extension for notifications, to allow notifications to be sent over SIP MESSAGE.

SIP.why: A substantial part specifies how to form SIP MESSAGE requests: URI parameters, From and Priority headers, body content type, size limits and retry behaviour. Readers of SIP usage would want it.
SIP.quote: This document defines how Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) URIs [RFC3261] are used to generate notifications via SIP MESSAGE [RFC3428].

rejected.why: SIP MESSAGE is the instant-messaging extension, but the document is about delivering email notifications, not instant messaging or presence itself.
The triggering object is an email, but the document specifies only the Sieve notification mechanism. Sieve is the more specific tag.
Presence is only mentioned in passing, in the reference to RFC 3856 for the online capability test.
UTF-8 is only the body encoding. The document defines nothing new about it.

RFC6469.title: RTP Payload Format for DV (IEC 61834) Video
RFC6469.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for DV (IEC 61834, SMPTE 314M/370M) video and bundled audio, including media type registrations and SDP parameters, and obsoletes RFC 3189.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines how DV DIF blocks are packed into RTP packets, with header usage, timestamps and marker bit rules. This is a codec-specific RTP payload format.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the packetization scheme for encapsulating the compressed digital video data streams commonly known as "DV" into a payload format for the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP).

media types.why: A substantial part of the document is the registration of the video/DV and audio/DV media types with the encode and audio parameters.
media types.quote: This registration is done using the template defined in RFC 4288 [RFC4288] and following RFC 4855 [RFC4855].

SDP.why: It defines the SDP mapping of the fmtp parameters, offer/answer usage and grouping of bundled and unbundled streams, with examples.
SDP.quote: The media subtype ("DV") goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name.

rejected.why: DV is a codec, but the document specifies only its RTP packetization. The more specific RTP payload format tag covers this.
RTP is the transport the payload format is built for. The payload format tag sits under it and is the more specific fit.
It is mentioned only in the security considerations and in the list of changes from RFC 3189, as a way to reduce unwanted traffic.
RTCP is mentioned only for lip synchronization via reference timestamps. The document does not specify or extend it.
IEEE 1394 appears only as background on the IEC 61883 digital interface. The document is not about IP over IEEE 1394.

RFC6470.title: Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) Base Notifications
RFC6470.summary: Defines a YANG module of NETCONF base event notifications (config change, capability change, session start/end, confirmed-commit) delivered over the NETCONF notification stream.

NETCONF.why: The document extends NETCONF with standard base event notifications on the 'NETCONF' stream, reporting server state changes such as sessions, capabilities and confirmed-commit.
NETCONF.quote: This document defines a YANG module that allows a NETCONF client to receive notifications for some common system events.

YANG.why: The main body is a YANG module definition with groupings and notifications, so YANG modelling readers would want it.
YANG.quote: module ietf-netconf-notifications {

rejected.why: Only the mandatory-to-implement NETCONF transport named in Security Considerations; the document defines nothing about SSH.
XML namespaces appear only in the IANA registration and as NETCONF's encoding; the document is not about XML.
The notifications resemble management data but the module is YANG, not an SMI MIB.
The events are NETCONF notifications, not syslog messages, though both report system events.

RFC6471.title: Overview of Best Email DNS-Based List (DNSBL) Operational Practices
RFC6471.summary: An IRTF ASRG informational memo summarizing best operational practices for operators of public DNS-based lists (DNSBLs) used in email filtering, and guidance for DNSBL users.

DNSBL.why: The whole document is about operating and using DNSBLs: listing/delisting policy, operational flags, shutdown, and query-root conventions. DNSBL is the most specific tag and sits under spam.
DNSBL.quote: This memo summarizes guidelines of accepted best practice for the management of public DNSBLs by their operators as well as for the proper use of such lists

rejected.why: DNS is only the distribution mechanism. The document gives no new DNS protocol behaviour beyond DNSBL conventions, such as subdomain query roots and a TEST-NET shutdown example.
Parent of DNSBL and implied by that tag. The document is about the list practices, not spam filtering in general.
Mail servers consume DNSBL results, but the document does not specify or discuss SMTP.
The scanning guidance in 3.6 is a small part of the document and concerns DNSBL operator conduct, not infrastructure security practice.
Email filtering is the context, but the document is about the lists rather than email architecture or transport.

RFC6472.title: Recommendation for Not Using AS_SET and AS_CONFED_SET in BGP
RFC6472.summary: A BCP recommending that BGP operators stop generating announcements containing AS_SET and AS_CONFED_SET path segments, to simplify BGP and ease RPKI-based origin validation.

BGP.why: The document is operational guidance on a BGP AS_PATH attribute feature, recommending against AS_SET and AS_CONFED_SET and discussing aggregation policy.
BGP.quote: It is RECOMMENDED that operators not generate any new announcements containing AS_SETs or AS_CONFED_SETs.

RPKI.why: A key motivation is that AS_SETs impede route origin authentication in RPKI-based security technologies, so readers of RPKI origin validation would want it.
RPKI.quote: This future work will also simplify the design and implementation of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) and systems that will rely on it.

rejected.why: AS_CONFED_SET relates to confederations, but the document is about AS_PATH set segments, not confederation or route reflection mechanisms.
Security is a motivation, but RPKI is the more specific tag and the document is mainly BGP operational guidance.
RFC 3779 is cited only as an example of technology affected by AS_SETs; the document does not address certificates.
Route aggregation is discussed, but the document is about AS_SET use in BGP, not CIDR itself.

RFC6473.title: vCard KIND:application
RFC6473.summary: Defines a new "application" value for the vCard KIND property so vCards can represent software applications such as servers, chat rooms and bots.

vCard.why: The whole document extends the vCard format with a new KIND value and describes which vCard properties apply to it.
vCard.quote: This document defines a value of "application" for the vCard KIND property so that vCards can be used to represent software applications.

rejected.why: XMPP is only the example context (XEP-0292 server vCard); the document does not specify or extend XMPP.
applicationProcess object class is cited only as a functional analogy.
xCard XML representation is used only for the example.
The registry entry is boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA practice.
LDAP schema reference is just an analogy, not the subject.

RFC6474.title: vCard Format Extensions: Place of Birth, Place and Date of Death
RFC6474.summary: Extends vCard 4.0 with three new properties, BIRTHPLACE, DEATHPLACE and DEATHDATE, and registers them in the IANA vCard Properties registry.

vCard.why: The document extends the vCard format by defining new properties (BIRTHPLACE, DEATHPLACE, DEATHDATE), so it belongs on the vCard page.
