vCard.quote: This specification adds three new properties to vCard 4.0: place of birth, place of death, and date of death.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the property syntax definitions; the document is not about it.
The IANA section just registers the new properties in the vCard Properties registry. It is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
DEATHDATE reuses the date-and-or-time value type from vCard 4.0 and does not define a new date format.
URI values are allowed for the place properties, but the document says nothing new about URIs.

RFC6475.title: Proxy Mobile IPv6 Management Information Base
RFC6475.summary: Defines the PMIPV6-MIB and PMIPV6-TC-MIB SMIv2 modules for monitoring and controlling Proxy Mobile IPv6 MAG and LMA entities, including binding caches, statistics, configuration and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module specification (SMIv2 objects, textual conventions, conformance groups) for PMIPv6.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Proxy Mobile IPv6 Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

PMIPv6.why: The managed subject is PMIPv6 entities (MAG and LMA), their binding state, tunnels and signalling counters, so PMIPv6 readers would want it.
PMIPv6.quote: the Proxy Mobile IPv6 MIB can be used to monitor and control the mobile access gateway (MAG) and the local mobility anchor (LMA) functions

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the MIB tag already sits under SNMP, and the document does not specify SNMP itself.
PMIPV6-MIB extends the MIPV6-MIB, but the document is about Proxy Mobile IPv6, not base Mobile IPv6.
IPv6 addressing appears only as object syntax; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Security Considerations mention of SNMPv3, USM, AES and TLS is boilerplate, not the document's subject.

RFC6476.title: Using Message Authentication Code (MAC) Encryption in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC6476.summary: Specifies the authEnc pseudo-algorithm for CMS authenticated-enveloped-data, deriving encryption and MAC keys from a master secret via a PRF (PBKDF2) to provide encrypt-and-authenticate protection, with test vectors and SMIMECapabilities usage.

CMS.why: The document defines new CMS algorithm identifiers and processing rules for authenticated-enveloped-data, so it is squarely about CMS.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using MAC-authenticated encryption with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) authenticated-enveloped-data content type.

S/MIME.why: Defines how S/MIME clients advertise authEnc support via SMIMECapabilities, and the OIDs are in the S/MIME arc. This is a smaller part of the document.
S/MIME.quote: An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the set of cryptographic functions that it supports by using the SMIMECapabilities attribute [SMIME].

rejected.why: PBKDF2 is used only as the default PRF to derive keys, with salt empty and iteration count one. The document is not about password hashing.
HMAC-SHA1 is the example MAC algorithm and is not specified here.
AES appears only as an example encryption algorithm in the test vectors.
Triple DES is used only in a test vector.
IPsec, SSH and TLS are cited only as precedents for the encrypt-and-authenticate mechanism.
TLS is cited only as precedent for deriving keys from a master secret.

RFC6477.title: Registration of Military Message Handling System (MMHS) Header Fields for Use in Internet Mail
RFC6477.summary: Registers fourteen MMHS-* Internet message header fields for RFC 5322 mail, giving ABNF syntax and rules for gatewaying between STANAG 4406/ACP 123 (X.400 P772) and Internet email via MIXER.

message format.why: The document defines new Internet message header fields with syntax and semantics, registered in the message header field registry.
message format.quote: This document specifies message header fields and associated processing for RFC 5322 (Internet Message Format) to provide a comparable messaging service.

X.400.why: A substantial part covers MIXER-based gatewaying and mapping of X.400 P772 heading extensions to and from Internet mail.
X.400.quote: This document supports translating most of the Elements of Service defined in ACP 123 [ACP123] to Internet message header fields

rejected.why: Parent of message format; the more specific child is chosen.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax, not the subject.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection option.
Mentioned only as a way to protect messages and in a note about deprecated labels.
The header field registration is routine IANA boilerplate, not a subject in its own right.
SMTP is only the transport for the messages; the document defines header fields rather than SMTP behaviour.

gaps.name: Military Message Handling System (MMHS) / STANAG 4406 / ACP 123
gaps.why: The document is about military messaging elements of service. The taxonomy has no tag for military messaging, so the closest fits are X.400 and message format.

RFC6478.title: Pseudowire Status for Static Pseudowires
RFC6478.summary: Defines a mechanism to carry pseudowire status TLVs in-band in a PW OAM message over the MPLS generic associated channel for static PWs (no LDP control plane), including S-PE bypass mode, and updates RFC 5885 on BFD VCCV status signalling.

pseudowire.why: The whole document specifies PW status signalling for static pseudowires, including S-PE operation, status TLV transport and acknowledgment procedures.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies a mechanism to signal Pseudowire (PW) status messages using a PW associated channel (ACh).

rejected.why: LDP is the default PW control plane referenced; this document is for use where LDP is absent, and only adds an LDP flag bit for S-PE bypass. Not the subject.
MPLS label stack and GAL are used as substrate for the OAM message; the document is about pseudowire status, which sits under a more specific tag.
Document relates to PW OAM message mapping, but it is a specific PW status mechanism; the pseudowire tag covers it better.
RFC 5885 BFD VCCV status signalling is only mentioned as something not to be used together with this mechanism.
Static PW/MPLS-TP segment ID is only referenced for an SP-PE TLV code point; MPLS-TP is not the subject.

gaps.name: Pseudowire (PW) / PWE3 status signalling
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a 'pseudowire' tag under MPLS (id 'pseudowire'), but I used its id as given; no gap in tag id. However, no dedicated tag exists for PW OAM/VCCV and segmented pseudowires, which this document addresses.

RFC6479.title: IPsec Anti-Replay Algorithm without Bit Shifting
RFC6479.summary: RFC 6479 describes an alternate receiver-side anti-replay window algorithm for IPsec AH and ESP that avoids bit shifting by using a ring of blocks, and includes example C code.

IPsec.why: The whole document is an alternate implementation method for the IPsec anti-replay service in AH and ESP. IPsec readers would want it.
IPsec.quote: This document presents an alternate method to do the anti-replay checks and updates for IP Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Protocol (ESP).

rejected.why: ESP is one of two protocols the anti-replay method applies to, alongside AH. The document does not specify or extend ESP itself. The IPsec tag covers both.

RFC6480.title: An Infrastructure to Support Secure Internet Routing
RFC6480.summary: RFC 6480 describes the architecture of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), including resource certificates, ROAs, manifests, and distributed repositories, to support origin validation and more secure BGP routing.

RPKI.why: The document is the RPKI architecture: resource certificates, ROAs, manifests, repositories, trust anchors, and local cache validation for route origin authorization.
RPKI.quote: The foundation of this architecture is a Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) that represents the allocation hierarchy of IP address space and Autonomous System (AS) numbers

rejected.why: BGP is the routing protocol being secured; the document does not specify or extend BGP itself, only uses ROAs to construct route filters.
Resource certificates use the PKIX profile and RFC 3779 extensions, but the profile is defined in RFC 6487; this document only uses it.
CMS is only the wrapper for signed objects, defined elsewhere (RFC 6488).
BGPsec/S-BGP is mentioned only as a possible future consumer of the infrastructure.
The parent of RPKI, implied by it; RPKI is the more specific fit, and RPKI itself sits under routing security.

RFC6481.title: A Profile for Resource Certificate Repository Structure
RFC6481.summary: Defines the structure of the RPKI repository: object file naming and extensions, contents of CA publication points, repository considerations, and relying-party local cache synchronization.

RPKI.why: The whole document specifies how RPKI certificates, CRLs, manifests and ROAs are published and how relying parties synchronize them, which is the core of RPKI.
RPKI.quote: This document defines a profile for the structure of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) distributed repository.

rejected.why: Resource certificates are the objects being stored, but the document profiles repository layout, not the certificate format (that is RFC 6487).
X.509 certificates and CRLs are published, but the subject is repository structure, which is covered by the more specific RPKI tag.
IANA registers two media types, but this is boilerplate-like registration, not the main subject.
URIs in SIA/AIA identify publication points but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
RPKI is implied by the more specific tag, so the parent is not listed.
The registry of filename extensions is a small part of the document, not its subject.

RFC6482.title: A Profile for Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs)
RFC6482.summary: Defines the standard profile for Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs), RPKI signed objects (CMS-wrapped) that authorize an AS to originate routes to IP prefixes, including the content type OID, eContent ASN.1 syntax, and an extra validation step.

RPKI.why: The ROA is a core RPKI object used for route origin validation; the document profiles it and defines its validation rules.
RPKI.quote: A ROA is a digitally signed object that provides a means of verifying that an IP address block holder has authorized an Autonomous System (AS) to originate routes

ASN.1.why: A substantial part of the document is the ASN.1 definition of the ROA eContent, with a normative ASN.1 module in Appendix A.
ASN.1.quote: The ASN.1 syntax for the ROA eContent.  (This is the payload that specifies the AS being authorized to originate routes

rejected.why: CMS is only the wrapper, supplied by the RPKI signed object template (RFC 6488); this document adds no new CMS specification.
The document relies on RFC 3779 extensions and RPKI resource certificates, but defines nothing new about certificates.
ROAs concern BGP route origins, but the document doesn't specify or extend BGP; it defines the authorization object.
The parent of RPKI, which already covers it and is the more specific tag.
An ancestor of the RPKI-related tooling; the routing-specific RPKI tag is more specific and fits better.

RFC6483.title: Validation of Route Origination Using the Resource Certificate Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) and Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs)
RFC6483.summary: Defines the semantics of Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) and the procedure for classifying BGP routes as valid, invalid or unknown using RPKI, including route selection use, AS 0 disavowal and validation lifetime.

RPKI.why: The whole document defines route origin validation semantics using ROAs in the RPKI, which is exactly the RPKI subject.
RPKI.quote: A ROA provides a means of verifying that an IP address block holder has authorized a particular AS to originate routes in the inter-domain routing environment

rejected.why: BGP is the routing protocol whose route origination is validated, but the document does not specify or extend BGP itself; it defines RPKI validation semantics and local policy use.
Resource certificates are X.509, but this is only background substrate; the document is not about the certificate profile.
Parent of RPKI, which is implied by the more specific tag.
Path validation is not addressed; only origin validation.

RFC6484.title: Certificate Policy (CP) for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC6484.summary: RFC 6484 defines the certificate policy (BCP) for the Resource PKI, which issues certificates attesting to holdings of IP addresses and AS numbers, following the RFC 3647 CP template.

RPKI.why: The document is the certificate policy for the RPKI, governing CAs, subscribers, relying parties, repositories and certificate lifecycle for resource certificates.
RPKI.quote: This document describes the certificate policy for a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) used to attest to Internet Number Resource (INR) holdings

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are the substrate; the document is a CP for the RPKI, not a profile of X.509 (that is RFC 6487).
Parent of RPKI is implied; RPKI is the more specific tag.
AS numbers and routing are only the motivating context; BGP is not specified or discussed beyond definitions.
Mentioned only to say it is not used in this PKI.
IANA appears as a CA in the hierarchy, not as registry guidance.

RFC6485.title: The Profile for Algorithms and Key Sizes for Use in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC6485.summary: Profile specifying the signature algorithm (RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256), 2048-bit key size, key and signature formats for RPKI certificates, CRLs and signed objects, for both signers and relying parties.

RPKI.why: The document is an RPKI profile defining the algorithms and key sizes used for RPKI certificates, CRLs and signed objects, so RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: specifies the algorithms, algorithms' parameters, asymmetric key formats, asymmetric key size, and signature format for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) subscribers

RSA.why: The profile mandates RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signatures with specific key size and exponent, a substantial part of the content.
RSA.quote: The RSA key pairs used to compute the signatures MUST have a 2048-bit modulus and a public exponent (e) of 65,537.

SHA.why: The profile mandates SHA-256 as the hash, with SHA-1 for key identifiers, as part of the algorithm suite.
SHA.quote: The hashing algorithm used in certificates, CRLs, and signed objects is SHA-256 [SHS].

rejected.why: Certificates are the objects being signed, but the document only profiles algorithms and keys, not the certificate profile itself (RFC 6487).
CMS SignedData is where the OIDs are placed for signed objects, but the document does not specify CMS; it only references its algorithm fields.
BGPsec is a different profile; this document covers the RPKI object algorithms.
Only mentions future algorithm transition generically, without addressing post-quantum cryptography.

RFC6486.title: Manifests for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC6486.summary: Defines the RPKI manifest, a CMS signed object listing the files and hashes at a CA's repository publication point, and specifies its generation and how relying parties use it to detect stale data and deleted objects.

RPKI.why: The document defines a new RPKI signed object, its generation by CAs and its validation and use by relying parties. RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: Manifests are intended to enable a relying party (RP) to detect certain forms of attacks against a repository.

rejected.why: CRL and EE certificate profiles are relied on but the document does not profile them. Manifest fields are only modelled on CRLs.
The manifest is wrapped in CMS SignedData via the RPKI signed object template (RFC 6488). CMS is the encoding substrate and is not specified here.
The appendix gives an ASN.1 module, but ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the object.
ROAs and route filters are mentioned only as the context for RP use. The document does not address BGP.
Considered as the parent. The more specific RPKI tag fits, so the parent is not listed.
Considered as the parent of RPKI. The RPKI tag is more specific and implies it.

gaps.name: RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) repository and signed objects
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists RPKI only in the text of the routing security and BGP descriptions and has no standalone tag. The tag id "RPKI" appears under routing security, but it is described there as route origin validation. I used it as the closest fit, though manifests and repository structure are a slightly different aspect.

RFC6487.title: A Profile for X.509 PKIX Resource Certificates
RFC6487.summary: Defines the profile for X.509 resource certificates and CRLs in the RPKI (certifying IP address and AS number rights-of-use), including certificate request profiles and relying-party path validation.

RPKI.why: The document is the normative certificate/CRL profile for the RPKI, including validation procedure and profile agility.
RPKI.quote: This document contains the normative specification of Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) syntax in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI).

X.509.why: It profiles X.509/PKIX certificates and CRLs, constraining fields and extensions relative to RFC 5280.
X.509.quote: This document defines a standard profile for X.509 certificates [X.509] for use in the context of certification of Internet Number Resources

rejected.why: CMS signed objects are only mentioned as the container for EE certificates; the specification is in RFC 6488.
Not about BGPsec; router EKU use is only mentioned as future work.
UUIDs appear only as a non-normative example for generating subject names.
Implied by the X.509 tag, which is the more specific child.
ASN.1 types are used for field encoding but the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC6488.title: Signed Object Template for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC6488.summary: Defines a generic profile of CMS signed-data for RPKI signed objects (template for ROAs, manifests, etc.), including syntax constraints and generic validation steps.

RPKI.why: The document specifies the generic signed object template and validation procedure for the RPKI, which readers of RPKI would need.
RPKI.quote: This document standardizes a template for specifying signed objects that can be validated using the RPKI.

CMS.why: A substantial part of the document profiles CMS SignedData and SignerInfo fields (version, sid, signedAttrs, etc.), so CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: The RPKI signed object is a profile of the CMS [RFC5652] signed-data object

rejected.why: X.509 EE certificates are referenced for validation but profiled in RFC 6487, not here.
ASN.1 and DER are just the encoding used for the structures; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Implied as the parent of RPKI; the more specific RPKI tag is chosen.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not the main body.

RFC6489.title: Certification Authority (CA) Key Rollover in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC6489.summary: BCP describing the planned CA key rollover procedure in the RPKI, including staging period, reissuance of certificates and signed objects, and relying party cache synchronization requirements.

RPKI.why: The whole document specifies CA key rollover operations in the RPKI and their effect on relying parties, so RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: This document describes how a Certification Authority (CA) in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) performs a planned rollover of its key pair.

rejected.why: RPKI resource certificates are X.509, but the document only relies on them. It defines a rollover procedure, not a certificate profile.
RPKI signed objects use CMS wrappers, but this is only a substrate and the document does not specify CMS.
Key rollover is a form of key management, but the RPKI tag is more specific and covers this document's subject. The document is not a general key management treatment.
RPKI is the more specific child of PKI, so the parent tag is not needed.

RFC6490.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Trust Anchor Locator
RFC6490.summary: Defines the Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) format, an rsync URI plus a Base64 subjectPublicKeyInfo, used to retrieve and verify RPKI trust anchor certificates, with constraints on the trust anchor and relying party procedures.

RPKI.quote: This document defines a Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)

Base64 only encodes the key in the TAL and is not the subject.

RPKI underpins routing security, but the document does not address BGPsec or route origin validation.

RFC6491.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Objects Issued by IANA
RFC6491.summary: Directs IANA to issue RPKI objects (AS 0 ROAs, ghostbusters record, CA certificates, CRLs, manifests) covering reserved, unallocated, special-purpose and certain multicast IPv4/IPv6 resources.

RPKI.why: The whole document specifies which RPKI objects (ROAs, CA, EE certs, CRLs, manifests, ghostbusters) IANA must issue for number resources it manages.
RPKI.quote: IANA SHOULD issue an AS 0 ROA for all reserved IPv4 and IPv6 resources not intended to be routed.

rejected.why: Although IANA is the actor, the document is not about IANA registry stewardship or considerations guidance; it directs IANA's issuance of RPKI objects, which is RPKI subject matter.
The document explicitly says it does not deal with BGP routing systems; BGP is only context for ROA semantics.
Certificates follow the RFC 6487 profile and RFC 3779 extensions but the document defines nothing new about X.509 itself.
Appendices list reserved address blocks but only to determine which RPKI objects to issue, not to address allocation itself.
Multicast ranges are merely enumerated for AS 0 ROA issuance; the document is not about multicast routing or deployment.

RFC6492.title: A Protocol for Provisioning Resource Certificates
RFC6492.summary: Defines the RPKI up-down provisioning protocol, an HTTP request/response exchange of CMS-signed XML messages by which a resource holder asks an issuing CA to list resource classes and to issue or revoke resource certificates.

RPKI.why: The document specifies the protocol by which RPKI resource certificates are issued and revoked between issuer and subject CAs. This is RPKI operation and its readers would look for it there.
RPKI.quote: This Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) certificate provisioning protocol defines a basic set of interactions that allow a subject to request certificate issuance, revocation, and status

CMS.why: A large part of the document is a CMS profile for the signed message wrapper: SignedData fields, signed attributes and validation rules. It is a profile of CMS, not just a use of it.
CMS.quote: CMS is used as the signing format to sign the message object.

media types.why: The document registers the application/rpki-updown media type for the protocol messages. The registration is of lesser weight than the protocol itself.
media types.quote: IANA has registered the following media type:  application/rpki-updown

rejected.why: HTTP POST is only the transport for the messages. The document defines nothing new about HTTP.
Resource certificates are the objects being managed. The certificate profile is in RFC 6487, not in this document.
The protocol is for RPKI certificate management, and the RPKI tag covers it. The document says it is not a general certificate management framework.
XML is the message encoding, and the RELAX NG schema is part of the protocol definition. The document is not about XML usage in general.
ASN.1 appears only in the CMS profile structures. It is the encoding substrate, not the subject.
The protocol is not CMP. The document says it is not part of a more general certificate management framework.

RFC6493.title: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Ghostbusters Record
RFC6493.summary: Defines the RPKI Ghostbusters Record, a CMS signed object carrying a severely profiled vCard so the maintainer of an RPKI CA certificate can be contacted.

RPKI.why: The document specifies a new RPKI signed object, its packaging as an RPKI signed object, its validation, and its IANA registrations. RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: This document specifies the RPKI Ghostbusters Record, an object verified via an end-entity (EE) certificate, issued under a CA certificate

vCard.why: A substantial part of the document profiles vCard 4.0, selecting which properties are required, allowed and forbidden for the payload.
vCard.quote: The Ghostbusters vCard payload is a minimalist subset of the vCard as described in [RFC6350].

rejected.why: CMS is only the signed-object packaging, taken from RFC 6488. The document does not define anything new about CMS itself.
ROAs and routing quality are the motivation for the record. The document says nothing about BGP itself.
EE and CA certificates are used, with the RFC 3779 'inherit' attribute, but the document does not profile X.509.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate for the new object. The document is not about media type rules.
The document says it is not meant to replace resource registry whois data.

RFC6494.title: Certificate Profile and Certificate Management for SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND)
RFC6494.summary: Specifies an RPKI-based (RFC 6487) X.509 certificate profile for SEND, defining four extended key usage values (router, proxied router, owner, proxied owner), deployment models, trust anchors, revocation and validation rules, updating RFC 3971.

SEND.why: The document profiles certificates for SEND router/proxy/owner authorization and updates RFC 3971, so it is about SEND.
SEND.quote: SEND certificates MUST comply with the RPKI resource profile described in [RFC6487].

X.509.why: It defines an X.509 certificate profile with new extended key usage OIDs and an ASN.1 module.
X.509.quote: This specification defines four KeyPurposeId values: one for authorizing routers (Router Authorization Certificates), two for authorizing proxies

RPKI.why: SEND certificates are based on RPKI resource certificates, and deployment models and trust anchors are tied to the RPKI.
RPKI.quote: SEND will use the RPKI Certificate Profile and certificate validation detailed in [RFC6487].

rejected.why: OCSP is only mentioned briefly as an optional revocation check in one subsection; the document does not specify or extend it.
IPv6 address extensions are used in the certificates, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
An ASN.1 module appears in the appendix, but only to define the OIDs; it is apparatus rather than the subject.
X.509 and RPKI are the more specific tags that fit the PKI content.

RFC6495.title: Subject Key Identifier (SKI) SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) Name Type Fields
RFC6495.summary: Defines new SKI-based Name Type values (SHA-1/224/256/384/512), plus experimental and reserved values, for the SEND ICMPv6 Trust Anchor option, and updates RFC 3971's registry procedures.

SEND.why: The document extends the SEND Trust Anchor option with new Name Types and gives router processing rules for them.
SEND.quote: This document specifies new Name Type fields in the SEND TA option that allows the use of the SKI X.509 extension to identify TA X.509 certificates.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates and their SKI extension are used as the identifier source, but the document does not profile certificates; that is done in RFC 6494 and RFC 6487.
SEND is the more specific child of neighbor discovery, so the parent is implied.
The registry update is boilerplate-like and is not the main subject of the document.
SHA hashes are only used to compute the SKI value; the document says nothing new about the hash family itself.
The PKI concepts, such as trust anchors, are used only as context; the document is not about PKI itself.

RFC6496.title: Secure Proxy ND Support for SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND)
RFC6496.summary: Extends SEND with a Proxy Signature option and proxy-authorizing certificates so that ND proxies (Mobile IPv6 home agents, PMIPv6 MAGs, RFC 4389 ND proxies) can secure Proxy ND messages.

SEND.why: The document defines a new Proxy Signature option and modified processing rules for SEND, so it is an extension of SEND.
SEND.quote: This document extends the current SEND specification with support for Proxy ND.

rejected.why: SEND is the more specific child and already covers this. Ancestors are implied.
Proxy Mobile IPv6 is only one of three application scenarios. The document does not specify or extend it.
Mobile IPv6 is only used as an application scenario, with the home agent acting as proxy. The document does not extend the protocol.
The certificate profile (KeyPurposeId values) is defined in the companion RFC 6494. This document only uses it.
RSA/PKCS#1 signatures and SHA-1 are only the mechanism used for the signature, not the subject.
Certificates and certification paths are relied on but not specified here. The profile is in RFC 6494.

gaps.name: Neighbor Discovery Proxy (RFC 4389 ND proxy)
gaps.why: The document is about securing proxied ND. The taxonomy has no tag for ND proxying itself, so the closest fit is SEND.

RFC6497.title: BCP 47 Extension T - Transformed Content
RFC6497.summary: Defines the BCP 47 language tag extension 't' (transformed content), whose subtags identify the source language or script of transliterated, transcribed or translated content, plus an 'm0' transform-mechanism field maintained by the Unicode Consortium.

language tags.why: The whole document defines a BCP 47 language tag extension, its syntax, canonicalization and registration, so it belongs under language tags.
language tags.quote: This document specifies an Extension to BCP 47 that provides subtags for specifying the source language or script of transformed content

rejected.why: The document only registers the extension in the Language Extensions Registry. That is boilerplate-level IANA action, not a document about IANA registries.
A parent of language tags. The more specific child tag is the better fit.
It depends on Unicode LDML/CLDR as the maintaining authority and data source, but it does not address Unicode usage in protocols.
It gives ABNF for the extension syntax, but ABNF is only the notation used.
It shows the CLDR XML data file structure, but only incidentally as the machine-readable data format.
It defines a numeric date subtag loosely related to RFC 3339, but this is a minor detail and it explicitly differs from RFC 3339.

RFC6498.title: Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) Voiceband Data (VBD) Package and General-Purpose Media Descriptor Parameter Package
RFC6498.summary: Defines two MGCP packages (VBD and GPMD) letting a Call Agent authorize and monitor gateway transitions to voiceband data, with and without redundancy/FEC, and describes using the FM and Fax packages with VBD.

MGCP.why: The document specifies new MGCP packages (VBD, GPMD) with events and a LocalConnectionOption, and extends use of the FM and FXR packages.
MGCP.quote: This document defines Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) packages that enable a Call Agent to authorize and monitor the transition of a connection to and from Voiceband Data (VBD)

rejected.why: SDP is used in examples and the gpmd option parallels an SDP attribute, but the document does not specify SDP.
RFC 2198 redundancy and FEC payloads are used via the FM package, but no payload format is defined here.
The FXR package is used with VBD and extended with a bracketed gw parameter, but it is an MGCP fax package, not fax over Internet mail or IP as the taxonomy tag means.
SIP only connects the Call Agents in the call-flow examples.
RTP is the transport for VBD, not the subject.
SRTP appears only as a security option in Security Considerations.

RFC6501.title: Conference Information Data Model for Centralized Conferencing (XCON)
RFC6501.summary: Defines the XML-based conference information data model (conference object) for XCON centralized conferencing, extending the RFC 4575 SIP conference-state format with floor control, scheduling, media controls and user policy elements, and registers the xcon and xcon-userid URI schemes.

XCON.why: The document specifies the XCON conference object data model, its schema, and the XCON-URI conference identifier, so it belongs on the XCON page.
XCON.quote: This document defines an XML- based conference information data model to be used for conference objects.

BFCP.why: A substantial part of the model is floor-information, with elements mapped to BFCP conference, floor and moderator identifiers. Readers of BFCP would want it, though the document does not define BFCP itself.
BFCP.quote: When BFCP serves as the floor control protocol, the <conference-ID> is a 32-bit BFCP conference identifier

XML.why: The model is an XML format with a normative RELAX NG schema, a non-normative W3C XML Schema, a namespace and an extensibility mechanism, so it is an XML-based format specification.
XML.quote: Conference object documents MUST be based on XML 1.0 and MUST be encoded using UTF-8.

rejected.why: The model extends the RFC 4575 SIP conference event package format. It is deliberately protocol-neutral and SIP is only one supported call signaling protocol, so the document does not specify SIP behavior.
It registers the xcon and xcon-userid URI schemes, but these are conference identifiers within the data model and not general URI work.
This is the parent of XCON, so it is implied by the XCON tag.
The <base> element embeds iCalendar objects, but only as an incorporated component.
SDP appears only in a reference to BFCP subscription offer/answer, which is incidental.

RFC6502.title: Conference Event Package Data Format Extension for Centralized Conferencing (XCON)
RFC6502.summary: Specifies how the SIP conference-state event package carries XCON data model documents as full notifications and adds an XML-patch-based partial notification format for centralized conferencing, with media type and namespace registrations.

XCON.why: The document defines the XCON notification protocol, supporting the XCON data model and partial notifications. It is squarely about XCON.
XCON.quote: This document specifies the notification mechanism for XCON (centralized conferencing).

SIP.why: The notification mechanism is a SIP SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY event package usage, with new content types and Accept/Content-Type handling. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This mechanism reuses the SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) event package for conference state.

media types.why: The document registers two new media types, application/xcon-conference-info+xml and application/xcon-conference-info-diff+xml, as part of its function.
media types.quote: This section registers the 'application/xcon-conference-info+xml' MIME type.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for the notification documents and the patch format. The document is not about XML usage in general.
The more specific XCON tag already applies, so the parent is implied.
The SIP event package for conference state is used here, but this is not SIMPLE presence, PIDF extensions or XCAP.

RFC6503.title: Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol
RFC6503.summary: Specifies CCMP, an XML-over-HTTP client-server protocol for creating, retrieving, updating and deleting XCON conference objects (blueprints, conferences, users, sidebars), with message definitions, response codes, XML schema, DNS-based server discovery and IANA registries.

XCON.why: CCMP is the XCON conference control protocol, operating on the XCON data model and framework; the whole document specifies it.
XCON.quote: The Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP) allows a Centralized Conferencing (XCON) system client to create, retrieve, change, and delete objects that describe a centralized conference.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport for CCMP (POST bodies, a strict subset of features); nothing new is defined about HTTP itself.
XML and XML Schema are the encoding for messages; the document is about the conferencing protocol, not XML usage.
TLS is only the security mechanism required for the HTTP transport.
DNS U-NAPTR is used for server discovery in a short section; it is a substrate, though S-NAPTR tags are registered. Not enough to tag.
The application/ccmp+xml registration is IANA boilerplate-level apparatus, not the subject.
SIP is only mentioned as a call signaling protocol and for notifications in the XCON framework; CCMP does not specify it.

RFC6504.title: Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP) Call Flow Examples
RFC6504.summary: Informational document giving detailed CCMP call-flow examples (conference creation, user manipulation, sidebars, removal/deletion) between a conference control client and server per the XCON framework.

XCON.why: The whole document illustrates CCMP, the XCON conference control protocol, with call flows over the XCON framework and data model; XCON is the fitting tag.
XCON.quote: This document provides detailed call flows for the scenarios documented in the Framework for Centralized Conferencing (XCON) (RFC 5239) and in the XCON scenarios (RFC 4597).

rejected.why: SIP is only used for call signaling and notifications and its details are explicitly not shown.
Floor control is mentioned only in passing; the document says BFCP details are not included.
HTTPS is merely the transport for CCMP messages, shown in one illustrative example.
CCMP messages are XML, but XML is only the encoding substrate.
The XCON event package notifications are mentioned briefly, but SIP messaging details are not included.
The more specific XCON tag applies, so the parent is not listed.

gaps.name: CCMP (Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has XCON for the framework and data model, but no dedicated tag for CCMP itself. XCON covers it adequately.

RFC6505.title: A Mixer Control Package for the Media Control Channel Framework
RFC6505.summary: Defines the MEDIACTRL Mixer Control Package (msc-mixer/1.0), an XML-based package for the Media Control Channel Framework that lets an application server create, modify and destroy conference mixers, join/unjoin media streams, receive notifications, and audit mixers and capabilities on a media server.

conferencing.why: The document specifies conference mixer creation, audio mixing, video layouts, video switching and active talker notification for a media server. This is multiparty conferencing control, and no more specific conferencing tag (XCON, telepresence, BFCP) fits.
conferencing.quote: This document defines a Media Control Channel Framework Package for managing mixers for media conferences and connections.

rejected.why: Only borrows XCON video layout names and the codec element model from RFC 6501. The document does not specify the XCON framework.
SIP is the substrate for setting up the control channel and the media connections. The package defines nothing about SIP itself.
XML is only the encoding for the package's messages and schema. The document is not about XML usage as such.
RTP sessions appear only as the terminations of media connections. The document does not specify RTP.
SDP labels and offer/answer are referenced only in passing for stream identification.
A media type, application/msc-mixer+xml, is registered, but that is IANA boilerplate.

gaps.name: Media Control Channel Framework / MEDIACTRL control packages
gaps.why: The document is a control package for the Media Control Channel Framework (RFC 6230) for media server control. The taxonomy has no tag for media server control or the framework, so only conferencing is close.

RFC6506.title: Supporting Authentication Trailer for OSPFv3
RFC6506.summary: Defines an OSPFv3 Authentication Trailer with an AT-bit option, security associations, a 64-bit sequence number and HMAC-SHA digests, giving OSPFv3 a non-IPsec authentication mechanism with replay protection.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends OSPFv3 with a new AT-bit in the Options field, an Authentication Trailer format, and packet verification procedures.
OSPFv3.quote: This document defines an alternative mechanism to authenticate OSPFv3 protocol packets so that OSPFv3 does not only depend upon IPsec for authentication.

HMAC.why: A substantial part of the document specifies HMAC-SHA-1/256/384/512 computation (Ipad/Opad, Apad, key preparation) for the trailer digest.
HMAC.quote: This specification discusses the computation of OSPFv3 Cryptographic Authentication data when any of the NIST SHS family of algorithms is used in the Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) mode.

rejected.why: IPsec AH/ESP is the existing mechanism that this document provides an alternative to. It is background, not specified or extended here.
The SHA algorithms are only the hash functions used inside HMAC. The document defines nothing new about them.
The topic fits, but the OSPFv3 technology tag is the more specific home. The document is not about routing security in general.
OSPFv3 is the more specific child tag, and the document concerns OSPFv3 only. The OSPFv2 text is a comparison.
Keys are manually configured, and the SA parameters and key lifetimes are only a small supporting part of the document.
The generic topic is covered by the more specific OSPFv3 and HMAC tags.

RFC6507.title: Elliptic Curve-Based Certificateless Signatures for Identity-Based Encryption (ECCSI)
RFC6507.summary: RFC 6507 specifies ECCSI, an elliptic-curve certificateless signature scheme for identity-based cryptography, including key material construction by a KMS, signing and verification algorithms, and test data.

elliptic curve.why: The document specifies an elliptic-curve signature scheme, with curve parameters, point representations and signing/verification algorithms over F_p, so it belongs under elliptic-curve cryptography.
elliptic curve.quote: This document describes an efficient scheme, ECCSI, for elliptic curve-based certificateless signatures, primarily intended for use with Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) schemes

key management.why: A substantial part of the document describes the KMS root of trust (KSAK/KPAK) and how it derives and provisions SSK/PVT key material to devices.
key management.quote: A KMS provisions key material for a set of communicating devices (a "user community").

rejected.why: ECCSI is based on ECDSA and shares its verification step, but it is a different scheme and does not specify ECDSA.
MIKEY-SAKKE (RFC 6509) uses ECCSI, but this document only mentions MIKEY for message formatting and does not specify it.
The scheme is explicitly certificateless and avoids PKI, so it is not about PKI.
SHA-256 is only the hash used in the test data and is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Identity-based cryptography / certificateless signatures
gaps.why: The document is about identity-based signature schemes, and the taxonomy has no tag for identity-based cryptography or digital signatures in general.

RFC6508.title: Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption (SAKKE)
RFC6508.summary: Informational RFC specifying the Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption (SAKKE) identity-based encryption algorithm, using pairings on supersingular elliptic curves, for a Sender to transmit a shared secret value to a Receiver.

elliptic curve.why: The document defines a pairing-based cryptosystem on a specific supersingular elliptic curve, including Tate-Lichtenbaum pairing computation and point representation. Elliptic-curve cryptography is the core subject.
elliptic curve.quote: In this document, we use supersingular curves with equation y^2 = x^3 - 3 * x modulo p.

key management.why: SAKKE is a key exchange/encapsulation scheme with a Key Management Service, secret key extraction, and user provisioning. Readers of key management would expect it.
key management.quote: The aim of the SAKKE scheme is for the Sender to securely transmit a shared secret value to the Receiver.

rejected.why: MIKEY-SAKKE is a separate document (RFC 6509); this RFC only references it and uses its parameters for test data.
Pairing-based on elliptic curves; not post-quantum.
Mentioned only conceptually as traditional public key; not used.
Only a Security Considerations reference to RFC 4086.
SHA-256 is used only for test data; the hash function is a parameter.

gaps.name: Identity-Based Encryption (IBE)
gaps.why: The document is about identity-based, pairing-based encryption, which has no dedicated tag in the cryptography subtree.

RFC6509.title: MIKEY-SAKKE: Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption in Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY)
RFC6509.summary: Defines MIKEY-SAKKE, a new MIKEY key distribution mode using identity-based SAKKE encryption and ECCSI signatures with a KMS as root of trust, including payloads, identifiers, and key periods.

MIKEY.why: The document specifies a new MIKEY mode, with new payloads (SAKKE), data types, S type and ID roles, and processing rules extending RFC 3830.
MIKEY.quote: MIKEY-SAKKE, a method for key exchange and source authentication designed for use in IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) Media Plane Security

tel URI.why: The document defines a constrained profile of the tel URI (global notation, no visual separators, no parameters) used to form SAKKE identifiers.
tel URI.quote: the identifying data MUST take the form of a constrained "tel" URI.

rejected.why: Forking and retargeting are discussed only as scenarios the key exchange must handle; the document does not specify SIP.
ECCSI and SAKKE are specified in RFC 6507 and RFC 6508; this document only uses them and fixes parameters (P-256, SHA-256).
SHA-256 is merely a selected parameter, not the subject.
The keys are for media protection, but SRTP is not specified or profiled here.
The MIKEY tag is the more specific fit and already sits under key management.
US-ASCII is only the encoding of the identifier string.

gaps.name: Identity-based cryptography (SAKKE/ECCSI)
gaps.why: The document's core mechanism is identity-based encryption and certificateless signatures, with no matching tag in the taxonomy.

RFC6510.title: Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Message Formats for Label Switched Path (LSP) Attributes Objects
RFC6510.summary: Specifies the RBNF message formats for RSVP-TE Path and Resv messages carrying LSP_ATTRIBUTES and LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES objects, clarifying per-LSP and per-S2L sub-LSP operational status reporting for P2MP LSPs, updating RFC 4875 and RFC 5420.

RSVP-TE.why: The document defines Path and Resv message formats for RSVP-TE LSP signalling with LSP Attributes objects, updating RFC 4875 and RFC 5420.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document specifies how LSP attributes are to be carried in RSVP Path and Resv messages using the Routing Backus-Naur Form

rejected.why: RBNF is only the notation used to express the message formats; the document does not specify or extend the notation.
MPLS LSPs are the context, but the document is specifically about RSVP-TE signalling, which is the more specific tag.
GMPLS signalling (RFC 3473) is referenced as a base for point-to-point LSPs, but the document does not address GMPLS-specific extensions.
Generic RSVP is the substrate; RSVP-TE for LSP tunnels is the specific subject.

RFC6511.title: Non-Penultimate Hop Popping Behavior and Out-of-Band Mapping for RSVP-TE Label Switched Paths
RFC6511.summary: RFC 6511 defines two new LSP Attributes flags (non-PHP behavior and OOB mapping) plus an RRO counterpart and a Notify error sub-code for RSVP-TE P2P and P2MP LSPs, so egress LSRs allocate non-NULL labels and await out-of-band application/payload bindings.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signaling with new LSP Attributes flags, RRO Attributes subobject flags and a new error sub-code, which is the core of the specification.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines two new flags in the Attributes Flags TLV of the LSP Attributes object defined in [RFC5420]

rejected.why: Penultimate hop popping and label assignment are MPLS concepts, but the document specifies RSVP-TE signaling, which is the more specific tag under traffic engineering.
MVPN is only a motivating application for out-of-band mapping; the document does not specify MVPN procedures.
BGP is only mentioned as an example OOB mechanism. The OOB mechanism itself is explicitly out of scope.
VPLS is cited only as an example application that uses OOB binding.
MPLS-TP is mentioned only as another possible user of non-PHP behavior.
RFC 3473 is referenced only for Notify messages. The document is not about GMPLS.

RFC6512.title: Using Multipoint LDP When the Backbone Has No Route to the Root
RFC6512.summary: Defines Recursive and VPN-Recursive Opaque Value types for mLDP FEC elements so P2MP/MP2MP LSPs can be built across a BGP-free core by temporarily replacing the root with the BGP next hop, with uses in inter-AS MVPN and limited Carrier's Carrier.

LDP.why: The document extends mLDP FEC opaque value encodings and procedures for LDP-signalled multipoint LSPs.
LDP.quote: The document [mLDP] extends LDP [LDP] to support multipoint Label Switched Paths.

MVPN.why: Section 3 specifies the VPN-Recursive Opaque Value for MVPN inter-AS P-tunnels and Carrier's Carrier use.
MVPN.quote: This is applicable when MP LSPs are being used to carry the multicast traffic of a VPN [MVPN].

rejected.why: BGP routes and next hops are the reason for the problem, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
BGP/MPLS VPNs are the context for the VRF and Carrier's Carrier scenarios, not the subject.
Covered by the more specific LDP tag.

RFC6513.title: Multicast in MPLS/BGP IP VPNs
RFC6513.summary: RFC 6513 specifies the framework and procedures (PMSIs, P-tunnels, BGP auto-discovery, PE-PE C-multicast routing, inter-AS, duplicate prevention, BIDIR-PIM support, encapsulations) for carrying IP multicast across BGP/MPLS IP VPNs.

MVPN.why: The whole document specifies multicast VPN service over BGP/MPLS.
MVPN.quote: A BGP/MPLS IP VPN service that supports multicast is known as a "Multicast VPN" or "MVPN".

RFC6514.title: BGP Encodings and Procedures for Multicast in MPLS/BGP IP VPNs
RFC6514.summary: Specifies the BGP MCAST-VPN NLRI, PMSI Tunnel attribute, extended communities and procedures for auto-discovery, tunnel binding and C-multicast route exchange for multicast in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 6513).

MVPN.why: The document exists to define the BGP encodings and procedures for multicast in MPLS/BGP IP VPNs.
MVPN.quote: This document defines a new Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI), MCAST-VPN NLRI.

RFC6515.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Infrastructure Addresses in BGP Updates for Multicast VPN
RFC6515.summary: RFC 6515 updates RFC 6514 to specify that PE (provider) addresses in MCAST-VPN BGP routes and the VRF Route Import extended community are IPv4 or IPv6 according to address length, not the AFI field, and clarifies PMSI Tunnel attribute address-family rules.

MVPN.why: The document specifies encoding of provider addresses in MCAST-VPN BGP routes, I-PMSI A-D routes and PMSI Tunnel attributes, which is Multicast VPN in BGP/MPLS VPNs.
MVPN.quote: whenever a PE address occurs in an MCAST-VPN route (whether in the NLRI or in an attribute), the IP address family of that address is determined by the length of the address

rejected.why: BGP is the substrate carrying MCAST-VPN routes; the document is about MVPN-specific encodings, not BGP generally.
IPv6 addresses appear in the encoding, but the document is not about IPv6 specification or deployment.
Unicast VPN routes are mentioned only for the VRF Route Import extended community carried with MVPN; the subject is multicast VPN.
Mixed IPv4/IPv6 provider and customer spaces are addressed only as an encoding issue, not a transition mechanism.

RFC6516.title: IPv6 Multicast VPN (MVPN) Support Using PIM Control Plane and Selective Provider Multicast Service Interface (S-PMSI) Join Messages
RFC6516.summary: Extends the MVPN specification (RFC 6513) to support customer IPv6 multicast flows when PE-PE PIM and S-PMSI Join messages run over an IPv4 provider infrastructure, defining the Type 4 S-PMSI Join and multi-join UDP encapsulation.

MVPN.why: The document is an extension of the Multicast VPN specification, defining a new S-PMSI Join type and PE-PE PIM/IPv6 handling for IPv6 customer flows.
MVPN.quote: This document extends the MVPN specification (RFC 6513) so that these options can be used when the customer multicast flows are IPv6 flows.

rejected.why: PIM is used as the PE-PE control protocol, but the document specifies no PIM changes beyond source address conventions for MVPN. It is a substrate here.
IPv6 is the customer address family, but the document is about MVPN support, not IPv6 itself.
GRE/IPv4 is the existing P-tunnel encapsulation from RFC 6513 and is only used here, not specified.
S-PMSI Joins are carried in UDP, but UDP is only the substrate. The multi-join packing is part of the MVPN message definition.
MVPN is the more specific tag, and this document is about multicast in BGP/MPLS VPNs.

RFC6517.title: Mandatory Features in a Layer 3 Multicast BGP/MPLS VPN Solution
RFC6517.summary: Informational RFC that compares the optional mechanisms in the multicast BGP/MPLS VPN specification (RFC 6513/6514) and recommends a mandatory-to-implement subset for auto-discovery, S-PMSI signalling, C-multicast routing, P-tunnel encapsulation, inter-AS, BIDIR-PIM, co-located RPs and duplicate avoidance.

MVPN.why: The whole document selects mandatory features for multicast in BGP/MPLS L3VPNs.
MVPN.quote: this document defines a subset of features that is considered mandatory for a multicast BGP/MPLS VPN implementation.

RFC6518.title: Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) Design Guidelines
RFC6518.summary: Informational KARP framework document that categorizes routing protocols by message type and keying model, and lays out a two-phase roadmap (improve existing authentication, then add automated key management) plus gap-analysis guidance for securing routing protocol packets on the wire.

routing security.why: The document exists to guide securing routing protocol exchanges between peers, which is the routing security subject.
routing security.quote: defining a roadmap of protocol specification work for the use of modern cryptographic mechanisms and algorithms for message authentication in routing protocols

key management.why: A large part of the document covers KMP design considerations, key life cycle, peer versus group keying, and the key exchange mechanism.
key management.quote: it defines the framework for a key management protocol that may be used to create and manage session keys for message authentication and integrity

rejected.why: BGP is one of several routing protocols categorized as examples; the document is not about BGP itself.
RSVP-TE is discussed as one protocol in the categorization with authentication notes, but it is not a main subject.
The authentication here is specific to routing protocols, which is covered by the more specific routing security tag.
TCP-AO is mentioned as a shared authentication mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Group keying for PIM-SM is touched on, but only as one of the protocol categories, and MSEC work is noted as not directly applicable.
ISAKMP/IKE is mentioned only as a possible existing KMP that could be extended, not specified or analysed.

gaps.name: KARP (Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols)
gaps.why: The document is the design guideline for the KARP working group, and the taxonomy has no tag for this effort beyond the general routing security and key management tags.

RFC6519.title: RADIUS Extensions for Dual-Stack Lite
RFC6519.summary: Defines a new RADIUS attribute, DS-Lite-Tunnel-Name, carrying the DS-Lite AFTR FQDN from the AAA server to the NAS so the NAS can populate the DHCPv6 OPTION_AFTR_NAME option for the B4 element.

RADIUS.why: The document's main deliverable is a new RADIUS attribute (type 144) with its format, packet usage, CoA and accounting behaviour.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines a new RADIUS attribute to be used for carrying the DS-Lite Tunnel Name

DS-Lite.why: The attribute exists to configure DS-Lite B4 elements with the AFTR tunnel name, so it belongs on the DS-Lite page.
DS-Lite.quote: Dual-Stack Lite [RFC6333] is a solution to offer both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity to customers that are addressed only with an IPv6 prefix

DHCPv6.why: A substantial part of the document describes how RADIUS data feeds DHCPv6 messages (Solicit, Renew, Rebind, Reconfigure) and the option encoding.
DHCPv6.quote: the NAS SHALL use the name returned in the RADIUS DS-Lite-Tunnel-Name attribute to populate the DHCPv6 OPTION_AFTR_NAME option
DHCPv6.section: 3. DS-Lite Configuration with RADIUS and DHCPv6

rejected.why: Used only as one of two session types in the message flow example; the document does not specify or extend PPP.
RADIUS is the more specific child tag and covers the AAA aspect.
The softwire initiator concept is mentioned in passing; the document is not about softwire tunnelling mechanisms.
The FQDN uses DNS label encoding borrowed from DHCPv6, but nothing about DNS itself is specified.

RFC6520.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Heartbeat Extension
RFC6520.summary: Defines the TLS/DTLS Heartbeat Extension, a new record-layer protocol with HeartbeatRequest/Response messages for keep-alive liveness checks and as a basis for DTLS path MTU discovery.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS hello extension and a new protocol running on the TLS record layer. It is a TLS extension specification.
TLS.quote: This document describes the Heartbeat Extension for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocols.

DTLS.why: The extension is specified for DTLS as well as TLS. It covers DTLS retransmission, epochs and PMTU probing, so DTLS readers need it.
DTLS.quote: The Heartbeat protocol is a new protocol running on top of the Record Layer.

PMTUD.why: One of the two stated purposes is to give DTLS a probe message for PMTU discovery. A dedicated use-case section covers it.
PMTUD.quote: DTLS performs path MTU discovery as described in Section 4.1.1.1 of [RFC6347]. A detailed description of how to perform path MTU discovery is given in [RFC4821].

rejected.why: TCP is only a transport the extension can run over. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
SCTP is mentioned as a transport and as an analogy to the PAD-chunk. The document does not specify or extend SCTP.
UDP is only an underlying unreliable transport for DTLS.
The single-request-in-flight rule ensures congestion is handled appropriately. This is a side effect of the design, not the subject of the document.
The document notes that heartbeats refresh NAT state. This is a minor remark, not a subject of the document.
DCCP is mentioned only as an example of an unreliable transport.

RFC6521.title: Home Agent-Assisted Route Optimization between Mobile IPv4 Networks
RFC6521.summary: Experimental RFC defining home agent-assisted route optimization between Mobile IPv4 NEMO mobile routers: prefix advertisement from the HA, return routability, direct inter-MR tunnels, and prefix/realm compression.

NEMO.why: The document extends NEMOv4 so mobile routers can route optimally between their mobile networks via direct tunnels.
NEMO.quote: This document describes a home agent-assisted route optimization functionality for the IPv4 Network Mobility Protocol.

Mobile IPv4.why: It defines new Mobile IPv4 messages and extensions (HoTI/CoTI/HoT/CoT, prefix advertisement) and a return routability procedure for Mobile IPv4 registration.
Mobile IPv4.quote: Traditionally, there has been no method for route optimization in Mobile IPv4 [RFC5944] apart from an early attempt [MIP-RO].

rejected.why: Only referenced as the origin of the return routability design, not specified here.
NAT traversal is handled through RFC 3519 and is a special consideration only.
GRE is just one optional tunnel encapsulation among several.
VPNs appear only as motivating background.
HMAC-SHA1 is used as a mechanism for the keygen tokens and authenticator, not as the subject.
Multihoming is part of the motivation but the document is not about multihoming architectures.

RFC6522.title: The Multipart/Report Media Type for the Reporting of Mail System Administrative Messages
RFC6522.summary: RFC 6522 defines the multipart/report MIME media type as a container for mail system administrative reports (such as delivery status reports) and the text/rfc822-headers type, removing the old outermost-only constraint and obsoleting RFC 3462.

media types.why: The document registers and defines two media types, multipart/report and text/rfc822-headers, with full registration templates and rules for registering new report types.
media types.quote: Per [MIME-REG], the multipart/report media type is defined as follows:

MIME.why: The multipart/report type is a MIME multipart container with specified body-part structure, so MIME body structure readers would want it.
MIME.quote: The syntax of multipart/report is identical to the multipart/mixed content type defined in [MIME].

email.why: The document is about mail system administrative and delivery status reports, and it covers returning original message headers or content in them. No more specific email child fits, so the email tag applies.
email.quote: general "family" or "container" type for electronic mail reports of any kind.

rejected.why: It refers to RFC 5322 headers only as the content returned in text/rfc822-headers. It does not specify the message format.
DSN-SMTP is mentioned only as an informative reference for requesting return of content. The document does not specify SMTP.
Spam detection modules are listed only as applications that use the media type.

RFC6525.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Stream Reconfiguration
RFC6525.summary: RFC 6525 extends SCTP with the RE-CONFIG chunk and six parameters so endpoints can reset stream sequence numbers, reset SSN/TSN, and add streams, with procedures and sockets API considerations.

SCTP.why: The document defines a new SCTP chunk type, parameters and procedures extending the protocol for stream reconfiguration.
SCTP.quote: Many applications that use SCTP as defined in [RFC4960] want the ability to "reset" a stream.

rejected.why: Section 6 describes sockets API events and options for the feature, but it is informational and secondary to the protocol extension itself.
TCP is mentioned only in a comparison about sequence numbers not being exposed via the sockets API.
The IANA section registers a chunk type and parameter types, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC6526.title: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Per Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Stream
RFC6526.summary: Extends IPFIX (RFC 5101) over PR-SCTP so each Template and its Data Records travel in one ordered SCTP stream, adding a dataRecordsReliability Information Element and Options Template to enable per-Template loss calculation and immediate Template withdrawal/reuse.

IPFIX.why: The document extends the IPFIX protocol: new Information Element, Options Template, template management and Template Withdrawal rules, and collector behaviour.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies an extension to the specifications in RFC 5101, IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX), when using the Partial Reliability extension of SCTP

SCTP.why: A substantial part specifies how SCTP streams and PR-SCTP partial reliability are used, with ordered delivery per stream and stream addition per RFC 6525.
SCTP.quote: This document specifies a method for exporting a Template Record and its associated Data Sets in a single SCTP stream

rejected.why: The document refines how IPFIX uses SCTP streams rather than defining a new mapping of a protocol onto a transport; IPFIX and SCTP tags cover it.
No PSAMP tag exists, and PSAMP is mentioned only as inheriting the specification from IPFIX.
The IANA section only records the allocation of one Information Element; it is boilerplate here.
Data Record loss calculation concerns export reliability, not network performance metrics.

RFC6527.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol Version 3 (VRRPv3)
RFC6527.summary: Defines the VRRPv3-MIB SNMP MIB module (obsoleting RFC 2787) for configuring, monitoring and controlling VRRPv3 routers over IPv4 and IPv6, with operations, associated-address and statistics tables plus notifications.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (VRRPV3-MIB) with tables, notifications and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: it defines objects for configuring, monitoring, and controlling routers that employ the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol Version 3 (VRRPv3) for both IPv4 and IPv6

VRRP.why: The MIB models VRRPv3 virtual router state, priority, preemption, advertisement and error statistics, so readers of VRRP would want it.
VRRP.quote: This MIB module contains three tables:

rejected.why: SNMP is the management framework the MIB is carried over. The MIB tag sits under it and is more specific.
The MIB handles both IPv4 and IPv6 virtual routers, but only as an address-type index. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
IPv4 is only an address-type value in the tables, not a subject of the document.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC6528.title: Defending against Sequence Number Attacks
RFC6528.summary: Specifies a standards-track algorithm for generating TCP Initial Sequence Numbers using a keyed pseudorandom function of the connection four-tuple plus a timer, to defend against off-path sequence number guessing; obsoletes RFC 1948 and updates RFC 793.

TCP.why: The document specifies a new TCP ISN generation algorithm and formally updates RFC 793, so it is about TCP protocol behaviour and implementation security.
TCP.quote: TCP SHOULD generate its Initial Sequence Numbers with the expression: ISN = M + F(localip, localport, remoteip, remoteport, secretkey)
TCP.section: 3. Proposed Initial Sequence Number Generation Algorithm

rejected.why: MD5 is only suggested as one possible hash for the PRF, with a brief caveat. The document is not about MD5.
RFC 4086 is cited only for choosing the secret key. This is a passing reference, not a subject of the document.
The topic is covered by the more specific TCP tag. The document is a TCP-specific defence, not general security guidance.
IPsec and TCP-AO are mentioned in Security Considerations as the proper cryptographic alternatives. They are not what the document addresses.
NAT is mentioned only as a side information-leak concern in Security Considerations.
Telnet and the r-commands appear only as historical attack examples in the appendix.

RFC6529.title: Host/Host Protocol for the ARPA Network
RFC6529.summary: RFC 6529 reproduces the January 1972 ARPANET Host/Host Protocol (NCP), which handled connection establishment, termination, flow control, interrupts, echo and reset between hosts, published for the historical record.

NCP.why: The whole document is the specification of the ARPANET Host-Host protocol, commonly called NCP. Its control commands, sockets, links and flow control are all defined here.
NCP.quote: Processes within a Host are envisioned as communicating with the rest of the network through a Network Control Program (NCP), resident in that Host, which implements the second level protocol.

rejected.why: TCP is mentioned only as the protocol that superseded NCP; the document does not specify or extend it.
The document is historical, but it is a protocol specification and not a history or retrospective. The ARPANET/NCP tag fits better.
Telnet appears only in a list of anticipated higher-layer protocols.
The parent of NCP is implied, so it is not listed separately.

RFC6530.title: Overview and Framework for Internationalized Email
RFC6530.summary: Overview and framework document for internationalized email (SMTPUTF8), introducing the SMTP extension, UTF-8 message headers, internationalized DSNs, downgrading issues, and changes from the experimental RFC 4952 set.

EAI.why: The document is the framework for email address internationalization, which is exactly the EAI subject.
EAI.quote: This document introduces a series of specifications that define mechanisms and protocol extensions needed to fully support internationalized email addresses.

SMTP.why: A substantial part describes the SMTPUTF8 extension, relay behaviour, DSN extension interaction and downgrading in SMTP transactions.
SMTP.quote: An SMTP extension, "SMTPUTF8", is specified as follows:

message format.why: Covers extending email header syntax to carry UTF-8, updating RFC 5322 header handling.
message format.quote: Transmission of Email Header Fields in UTF-8 Encoding

rejected.why: IDNA is assumed background for the domain part; the document is about local parts and email, not defining IDN.
UTF-8 is the encoding used, not the subject; the document is about email addressing.
Normalization advice is a small part of one section, not a main subject.
IMAP and POP3 are only mentioned as companion documents' subjects.
MIME encoded words are discussed only as legacy transition context.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a future coordination issue.

RFC6531.title: SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email
RFC6531.summary: RFC 6531 defines the SMTPUTF8 SMTP service extension, which lets SMTP carry internationalized (UTF-8) email addresses and headers. It adds MAIL/VRFY/EXPN parameters, extended mailbox syntax, reply codes and enhanced status codes, and it obsoletes the experimental RFC 5336.

EAI.why: The document is the SMTP transport piece of the Email Address Internationalization work. It specifies SMTPUTF8 and the extended mailbox syntax.
EAI.quote: This document specifies an SMTP extension for transport and delivery of email messages with internationalized email addresses or header information.

SMTP.why: It specifies an SMTP service extension: the EHLO keyword, new MAIL/VRFY/EXPN parameters, reply codes, trace WITH types, and a registry update. SMTP readers need it.
SMTP.quote: One OPTIONAL parameter, SMTPUTF8, is added to the MAIL command.

rejected.why: IDNA is required for domain-name handling (A-labels/U-labels), but the document only relies on it and defines nothing new about it.
The UTF-8 header format is defined in RFC 6532. This document only references it.
UTF-8 is the encoding used. The document is not about the encoding itself.
MIME is mentioned only in passing for body parts and 8BITMIME/BINARYMIME use.
ABNF is used as notation for the syntax rules and is not the subject.
The IANA section registers entries for this extension and is boilerplate.

RFC6532.title: Internationalized Email Headers
RFC6532.summary: RFC 6532 extends the Internet Message Format and MIME so UTF-8 can be used directly in mail addresses and header field values, defines the message/global media type, and relaxes the RFC 2045 rule on content-transfer-encoding for message/ subtypes.

EAI.why: The document is the EAI working group's specification for internationalized email headers and addresses, so it belongs under email address internationalization.
EAI.quote: This document specifies an enhancement to the Internet Message Format and to MIME that allows use of Unicode in mail addresses and most header field content.

message format.why: A large part of the document extends the RFC 5322 ABNF (atext, ctext, qtext, dtext, VCHAR) and changes the header line length limit from characters to octets.
message format.quote: the header definition in [RFC5322] is extended to support the new format.

media types.why: The document defines and registers the new message/global media type, and readers of media type registrations would want to find it.
media types.quote: The registration is as follows: Type name: message Subtype name: global

rejected.why: The document updates Section 6.4 of RFC 2045 on content-transfer-encoding, but it is mainly about header internationalization. The MIME change is a supporting adjustment, and the media type registration is covered by the media types tag.
SMTPUTF8 (RFC 6531) is only referenced as the transport this format needs. This document does not specify it.
UTF-8 is the encoding the document adopts for header fields. The document does not define it or specify it as a subject in its own right.
Unicode and NFC normalization are mentioned as guidance. The document is about email headers, not Unicode usage in general.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the syntax extensions.

RFC6533.title: Internationalized Delivery Status and Disposition Notifications
RFC6533.summary: RFC 6533 defines a UTF-8 address type for DSN/MDN and new message/global-delivery-status, message/global-headers and message/global-disposition-notification media types so internationalized email recipient addresses are preserved in delivery and disposition notifications.

EAI.why: The document is part of the EAI suite, extending delivery status and disposition notifications to handle internationalized addresses and SMTPUTF8 messages.
EAI.quote: This specification adds a new address type for international email addresses so an original recipient address with non-ASCII characters can be correctly preserved even after downgrading.

media types.why: It defines and registers message/global-delivery-status, message/global-headers and message/global-disposition-notification, with full IANA media type templates.
media types.quote: three new media types have been defined.

SMTP.why: It updates the DSN SMTP extension's ORCPT parameter handling and sets requirements on SMTP servers returning undeliverable SMTPUTF8 messages.
SMTP.quote: An SMTP [RFC5321] server that advertises both the SMTPUTF8 extension [RFC6531] and the DSN extension [RFC3461] MUST accept a UTF-8 address type in the ORCPT parameter

rejected.why: The message/global type is defined in RFC 6532. This document only references it and defines notification formats.
MIME is the substrate. The document registers media types but doesn't change MIME structure beyond a Content-Transfer-Encoding allowance.
UTF-8 is used as the encoding of the new types. The document doesn't specify the encoding itself.
ABNF is just the notation used for syntax definitions.
The EAI tag is more specific for this internationalized-email work.

gaps.name: Delivery Status Notifications (DSN) and Message Disposition Notifications (MDN)
gaps.why: The document is centrally about DSN and MDN formats, but the taxonomy has no tag for them; they sit under email only loosely.

RFC6534.title: Loss Episode Metrics for IP Performance Metrics (IPPM)
RFC6534.summary: Defines one-way packet loss episode metrics (frequency and average duration) for IPPM, based on geometric-stream bi-packet probing, with proto-metrics and a relation to the Gilbert loss model.

performance measurement.why: The document defines new IPPM active performance metrics and the probing methodology to measure them, which is exactly the performance measurement topic. No specific technology tag (OWAMP, TWAMP, etc.) applies.
performance measurement.quote: This document defines one-way packet loss episode metrics, specifically, the frequency and average duration of loss episodes and a probing methodology under which the loss episode metrics are to be measured.

rejected.why: RFC 3611 (RTCP XR) is only cited as related work on VoIP burst metrics; this document does not specify or extend RTCP.
Metrics are defined for IPPM but no measurement protocol such as OWAMP is specified or used.
Congestion is mentioned only as background for why loss is bursty; the document does not address congestion control.
The metrics concern active measurement of live paths, not benchmarking methodology for network devices.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metric definitions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic, with no tag for IPPM metrics such as one-way loss or delay.

RFC6535.title: Dual-Stack Hosts Using "Bump-in-the-Host" (BIH)
RFC6535.summary: Specifies Bump-in-the-Host (BIH), a host-based IPv4-to-IPv6 translation mechanism using synthetic IPv4 addresses, a name resolver extension and either socket-API or SIIT-based translation so IPv4-only applications can reach IPv6-only peers; obsoletes RFC 2767 and RFC 3338.

IPv6 transition.why: The document defines a host-based IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanism for transition. No more specific child tag (NAT64, SIIT, etc.) matches BIH itself.
IPv6 transition.quote: Bump-in-the-Host (BIH) is a host-based IPv4 to IPv6 protocol translation mechanism that allows a class of IPv4-only applications

sockets API.why: The recommended implementation is a socket-API-layer translator (function mapper), with an appendix listing the intercepted API functions.
sockets API.quote: the translator intercepts IPv4 socket API function calls and invokes corresponding IPv6 socket API function calls to communicate with IPv6 hosts.

DNS64.why: The Extension Name Resolver synthesizes A records from AAAA records, which is analogous to DNS64 but done on the host. It also covers DNSSEC, reverse lookup and cache interactions. This is a substantial part of the document.
DNS64.quote: The ENR asks the address mapper to assign a synthetic IPv4 address corresponding to each received IPv6 address

rejected.why: BIH uses SIIT (RFC 6145) for network-layer translation but does not specify or extend it.
The document only says that BIH should not be combined with NAT64. Its security text is borrowed from NAT64, but BIH is not NAT64.
DNSSEC interaction is covered in a short subsection and the document does not specify DNSSEC. DNS64 and the transition tag capture the resolver aspects.
BIH relies on applications' NAT traversal and uses RFC 1918 addresses, but it is not a NAT specification.
DNS is the mechanism the ENR works with, but the document does not specify DNS protocol behaviour.

RFC6536.title: Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) Access Control Model
RFC6536.summary: RFC 6536 defines the NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM), including design objectives, enforcement procedures for RPCs, data nodes and notifications, and the ietf-netconf-acm YANG module.

NETCONF.why: The document extends NETCONF with a standard access control model governing operations, datastore access and notifications, so NETCONF readers need it.
NETCONF.quote: There is a need for standard mechanisms to restrict NETCONF protocol access for particular users to a pre-configured subset of all available NETCONF protocol operations and content.

YANG.why: It defines the ietf-netconf-acm YANG module and YANG extensions (default-deny-write, default-deny-all) for security tagging of data models.
YANG.quote: The following YANG module specifies the normative NETCONF content that MUST by supported by the server.

authorization.why: The core subject is authorization: rules, groups and permit/deny enforcement procedures. The NETCONF and YANG tags sit under network management, not under authorization, so this topic tag is added directly.
authorization.quote: access control rule:  The criterion used to determine if a particular NETCONF protocol operation will be permitted or denied.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an optional external source of group names; the document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
The examples use XML and rules refer to XML paths, but XML is only the encoding substrate.
Not related. Access control here is for NETCONF, not SNMP's VACM.
