The model concerns authorization of NETCONF operations on the server, not an AAA framework.

RFC6537.title: Host Identity Protocol Distributed Hash Table Interface
RFC6537.summary: Specifies an interface for using HIP with an OpenDHT-style XML-RPC distributed hash table to provide name-to-HIT and HIT-to-address lookup, defining the HDRR record format.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with DHT-based lookup services, defining a new HIP packet type (HDRR) built from HIP parameters, HITs, and locators.
HIP.quote: specifies a common interface for using the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) with a Distributed Hash Table (DHT) service

P2P.why: The document specifies use of a DHT overlay (OpenDHT/Bamboo) with put/get/rm operations for storing and retrieving records, which is peer-to-peer overlay infrastructure.
P2P.quote: DHTs manage such data well by applying a hash function that distributes data across a number of servers.

naming.why: It defines a name-to-HIT resolution service and HIT-to-address lookup as an alternative to DNS, so it fits general naming and name resolution rather than DNS itself.
naming.quote: The HIT lookup uses a text name to discover a peer's HIT.

rejected.why: DNS is only contrasted as the alternative; the document defines a non-DNS lookup service and a record distinct from the HIP DNS RR.
XML-RPC is only the substrate encoding of the OpenDHT interface, not the subject.
SHA-1 is used for keys and secret hashes only; the document is not about the hash algorithm.
Certificates are an optional parameter taken from RFC 6253; the document does not profile them.
The IANA section merely registers the HDRR packet type, which is boilerplate.
Base64 is just used to encode values in the XML-RPC fields.

gaps.name: Distributed Hash Table (DHT) lookup services
gaps.why: The core subject is a DHT service interface for identifier lookup; the taxonomy only has P2P as a loose fit.

RFC6538.title: The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Experiment Report
RFC6538.summary: IRTF HIP research group report summarizing experiences and lessons learned from HIP implementations, infrastructure, applications, operator concerns and privacy, plus related ID-locator split work.

HIP.why: The whole report is about experience with the Host Identity Protocol: host stack, infrastructure, application, operator and privacy implications.
HIP.quote: documenting the collective experiences and lessons learned from studies, related experimentation, and designs completed by the research group

firewall.why: Substantial discussion of HIP-aware firewalls, HIT-based ACLs and middlebox traversal.
firewall.quote: A HIP-aware firewall operating in the middle identifies flows using HITs of communicating hosts, as well as SPI values and IP addresses.

rejected.why: ESP/BEET mode is the data-plane mechanism HIP relies on; discussed as implementation detail, not the subject.
HIP DNS records and HIT resolution are discussed in sections, but only as infrastructure for HIP, not a DNS-focused document.
Multihoming and mobility are HIP features discussed briefly, with transport-protocol effects; not the document's focus.
Legacy NAT traversal is one subsection among many; the document is not about NAT behavior.
Section 6 covers user privacy, but only as one section of a HIP report; HIP tag covers it.
Mentioned only in related work on ID-locator split.

gaps.name: Identifier-locator split
gaps.why: The report is about decoupling identifiers from locators and related architectures (i3, LISP, ILNP, shim6), but the taxonomy has no tag for this general subject beyond HIP/ILNP/LISP.

RFC6539.title: IBAKE: Identity-Based Authenticated Key Exchange
RFC6539.summary: Specifies IBAKE, a three-message identity-based authenticated key exchange protocol that combines IBE encryption with elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman to give mutual authentication, forward/backward secrecy and no PKG key escrow.

key management.why: The document defines an authenticated key exchange protocol for establishing session keys, which is key establishment. No narrower tag fits, so the parent topic is used.
key management.quote: This document specifies the Identity-Based Authenticated Key Exchange (IBAKE) protocol.

elliptic curve.why: The protocol uses elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and pairing-friendly supersingular curves for IBE, and Section 3.3 discusses curve choice in detail.
elliptic curve.quote: the protocol described in this document relies on the use of elliptic curves.

rejected.why: The document contrasts IBE with PKI and certificates as motivation. It does not specify or profile PKI.
An EAP method based on IBAKE is only mentioned as a separate work in progress, so EAP is not part of this document.
Mutual authentication is a property of the key exchange. It is not a separate subject here, and key management already captures the document.
RFC 5409 (IBE with CMS) is only referenced for the IBE framework, and CMS is not used by IBAKE.
Key escrow immunity is a security property of the protocol and is not about protocol privacy considerations.

gaps.name: Identity-Based Encryption (IBE)
gaps.why: The protocol is built on IBE (RFC 5091/5408/5409) with a Private-Key Generator, and the taxonomy has no tag for identity-based cryptography. Readers of that subject would want this RFC.

RFC6540.title: IPv6 Support Required for All IP-Capable Nodes
RFC6540.summary: BCP stating that IPv6 support is no longer optional: new IP implementations must support IPv6, updates should, and the generic term "IP" in older RFCs may mean IPv4 only.

IPv6.why: The whole document is a best-current-practice recommendation on IPv6 support and deployment in IP nodes. It also clarifies IPv4/IPv6 ambiguity in older specifications.
IPv6.quote: New IP implementations must support IPv6.

rejected.why: IPv4 exhaustion and the ambiguity of 'IP' are the motivation, but the document is about requiring IPv6 rather than specifying or analysing IPv4.
Dual-stack coexistence is mentioned in one recommendation and transition is background, but the document does not specify or analyse transition mechanisms.
Carrier-grade NAT appears only in a cited reference on IPv4 extension trade-offs.
NAT is mentioned only indirectly as one of the IPv4 extension technologies, with no substantive treatment.

RFC6541.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Authorized Third-Party Signatures
RFC6541.summary: Experimental extension to DKIM defining Authorized Third-Party Signatures (ATPS), where an author domain publishes DNS TXT records authorizing third-party DKIM signers whose signatures are treated as equivalent to its own.

DKIM.why: The document extends DKIM with new signature tags (atps, atpsh) and verifier semantics for third-party signers.
DKIM.quote: This experimental specification proposes a modification to DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) allowing advertisement of third-party signature authorizations

rejected.why: DNS TXT records are only the publication substrate for ATPS data; no new DNS RR type or DNS behaviour is defined (Appendix B explicitly reuses TXT).
DMARC is not mentioned; the document relates to ADSP, which has no tag in the taxonomy, and is covered by the DKIM tag.
Parent of DKIM, implied by the DKIM tag.
Hashing is only used to fix the label width of the query name; the document says it is not a security mechanism.
Base32 encoding is used merely to build DNS labels, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: ADSP (Author Domain Signing Practices)
gaps.why: The document specifies how ATPS interacts with ADSP, but the taxonomy has no tag for ADSP.

RFC6542.title: Kerberos Version 5 Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Channel Binding Hash Agility
RFC6542.summary: RFC 6542 updates the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism (RFC 4121) so channel binding verifiers are computed with a negotiated Kerberos checksum (get_mic) instead of MD5, and defines an extensible Exts field with a Channel Binding MIC extension and an IANA registry.

GSS-API.why: The document modifies the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism's 0x8003 checksum and channel binding handling, which is GSS-API mechanism content.
GSS-API.quote: This document updates RFC 4121 to allow channel bindings using algorithms negotiated based on Kerberos crypto framework as defined in RFC 3961.

Kerberos.why: It specifies Kerberos-specific changes: use of the Kerberos crypto framework get_mic, session and sub-session keys, and the KRB_CRED-bearing checksum structure.
Kerberos.quote: The output obtained by applying the Kerberos V get_mic operation [RFC3961] with key usage number 43 to the channel binding data

rejected.why: MD5 is the weak algorithm being replaced; the document is not about MD5 itself, only moves away from it.
Hash agility is the motivation, but the document specifies a protocol field and checksum selection via Kerberos rather than cryptographic algorithms in their own right.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level and secondary to the main body.
Channel binding is typically used with TLS, but TLS is not specified or discussed in this document.

gaps.name: channel binding
gaps.why: The document is about channel bindings in GSS-API, but the taxonomy has no channel binding tag; GSS-API is the closest fit.

RFC6543.title: Reserved IPv6 Interface Identifier for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6543.summary: Reserves an Ethernet unicast address (00-00-5E-00-52-13) and the derived IPv6 interface identifier (0200:5EFF:FE00:5213) for the fixed MAG link-layer and link-local addresses in Proxy Mobile IPv6, updating RFC 5213.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document specifies reserved addresses for use by mobile access gateways in Proxy Mobile IPv6 and updates RFC 5213, so PMIPv6 readers need it.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification reserves an IPv6 interface identifier, 0200:5EFF:FE00:5213.

rejected.why: Neighbor Discovery is only mentioned as the traffic in which the reserved link-local address is used. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document reserves an interface identifier, but it is about PMIPv6 operation and adds nothing to IPv6 addressing in general.
An Ethernet address is reserved, but the document does not cover IP over Ethernet or Ethernet interworking.
The IANA registry reservations are boilerplate-like registrations that support the main subject. The document is not guidance on IANA registries.

RFC6544.title: TCP Candidates with Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)
RFC6544.summary: Extends ICE (RFC 5245) to TCP-based media, defining active, passive and simultaneous-open TCP candidates, their prioritization, SDP encoding (tcptype), connectivity checks over RFC 4571 framing, and connection management.

ICE.why: The whole document defines TCP candidates for ICE: candidate types, pairing, priorities, SDP encoding, checks and restarts.
ICE.quote: This specification extends ICE to TCP-based media, including the ability to offer a mix of TCP and UDP-based candidates for a single stream.

rejected.why: TCP is the transport whose connections ICE manages; the document does not specify or extend TCP itself.
STUN connectivity checks are used as in ICE; no new STUN behaviour is defined.
TURN relayed candidates are mentioned as a candidate source, but the document does not specify TURN.
The a=candidate tcptype attribute is part of ICE's SDP encoding; SDP is the carrier rather than the subject.
Implied by the ICE parent; the ICE tag covers it more specifically.
RTP over TCP is a use case, and RFC 4571 framing is the substrate. The document does not define RTP.

RFC6545.title: Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID)
RFC6545.summary: RFC 6545 specifies Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID), an XML-based protocol and IODEF-RID schema for CSIRTs and service providers to exchange incident reports, trace requests, investigation requests, queries and results with policy, signature and encryption requirements.

RID.why: The document defines RID itself: message types, the RIDPolicy/RequestStatus/IncidentSource schema, communication flows and security requirements.
RID.quote: Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) outlines a proactive inter-network communication method to facilitate sharing incident-handling data

rejected.why: IODEF is not a taxonomy id; RID carries IODEF documents but is defined separately (RFC 5070 is the IODEF spec).
RID mandates XML signatures and encryption for messages, but only as a mechanism it relies on, not something it newly specifies.
Parent of RID, which is the more specific tag and already implied.
Transport over HTTP/TLS is defined in RFC 6546, not here.
Mentioned as transport security only; substrate.
Section 9.3 discusses PKI for trust, but this is supporting guidance, not the document's subject.
Messages are XML, but XML is just the encoding; the document is about the incident exchange protocol.

gaps.name: IODEF (Incident Object Description Exchange Format)
gaps.why: RID is an envelope and extension for IODEF documents, and IODEF-related RFCs would be browsed together, but the taxonomy has no IODEF tag.

RFC6546.title: Transport of Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) Messages over HTTP/TLS
RFC6546.summary: Specifies the application-layer transport of RID (Real-time Inter-network Defense) incident messages over HTTP/TLS, including POST usage, callback token, port 4590, and mutual X.509 TLS authentication.

RID.why: The document defines the RID transport binding: message types, callback mechanism, port, and authentication. RID is the subject, including its transport bindings.
RID.quote: This document specifies an application-layer protocol for RID based upon the passing of RID messages over HTTP/TLS.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is the substrate; the document uses POST and adds a callback token header but does not extend HTTP for general readers.
TLS is the security mechanism relied on; no new TLS extension is defined.
IODEF is the underlying message format, which this document does not specify; only RID transport is covered.
X.509 certificates are used for mutual authentication, but no profile is defined.
The parent is implied by RID, so it is not listed separately.
Considered because the document maps RID onto HTTP/TLS. RID is the more specific tag and already covers this transport binding.

RFC6547.title: RFC 3627 to Historic Status
RFC6547.summary: Moves RFC 3627 (against /127 prefixes on router links) to Historic status, linking it to RFC 6164 which gives updated guidance on 127-bit IPv6 prefixes on inter-router links.

IPv6.why: The document concerns IPv6 prefix length guidance (/127) for inter-router links, an IPv6 addressing matter. IPv6 is the most specific fitting tag.
IPv6.quote: Using 127-Bit IPv6 Prefixes on Inter-Router Links

rejected.why: IPv6 already covers the IPv6 prefix-length guidance; the document is not a general IP address architecture or allocation discussion.
The document uses the process of moving an RFC to Historic status, but its subject is the IPv6 prefix guidance, not the process itself.
Marking an RFC obsolete is an RFC-series housekeeping action, but the content readers want is the IPv6 /127 guidance.

RFC6548.title: Independent Submission Editor Model
RFC6548.summary: Defines the role, qualifications and responsibilities of the Independent Submission Editor (ISE) of the RFC Series and the Independent Submission Editorial Board, obsoleting parts of RFC 5620.

RFC series.why: The document defines the ISE management role in the Independent Submission stream of the RFC Series, including its relations to the RSE, Production Center and Publisher.
RFC series.quote: This document describes the function and responsibilities of the RFC Independent Submission Editor (ISE).

rejected.why: The ISE and Independent Submission stream sit outside the IETF standards process. The topic concerns the RFC Series, not IETF procedures.
Only boilerplate copyright text appears. The body does not address IPR.

RFC6549.title: OSPFv2 Multi-Instance Extensions
RFC6549.summary: Defines an OSPFv2 Instance ID in the packet header (splitting the Authentication Type field) so multiple OSPFv2 protocol instances can run on one interface, with instance ID values, compatibility and IANA registry.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 with a new packet header field and interface data structure element, and updates RFC 2328.
OSPF.quote: This document defines the OSPFv2 Instance ID to enable separate OSPFv2 protocol instances on the same interface.

rejected.why: OSPFv3's instance mechanism is only the inspiration; the document specifies OSPFv2 only.
The OSPF MIB is mentioned only for SNMP notification filtering advice in compatibility considerations.
Only a brief recommendation about notification filtering; not a subject of the document.
IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level for this document; main body is about the OSPF extension.

RFC6550.title: RPL: IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC6550.summary: Specifies RPL, the IPv6 distance-vector routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks, including DODAG construction, upward/downward routes, ICMPv6 control messages, security, and manageability.

RPL.why: The document defines the RPL protocol itself: DODAGs, DIO/DAO/DIS messages, storing and non-storing modes, and loop detection.
RPL.quote: This document specifies the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL)

rejected.why: RPL runs over IPv6 and borrows ND options, but the document is about routing, not IPv6 itself.
It reuses the PIO and RIO formats from ND, but ND is not specified or extended here.
AES-128 CCM is only the cryptographic mechanism for the optional security mode.
The RPL control messages are carried in a new ICMPv6 message type, but this is the substrate, not the subject.
The RPL tag is more specific, and routing architecture as a whole is not the subject.
Only mentioned as a deployment context.

RFC6551.title: Routing Metrics Used for Path Calculation in Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC6551.summary: Defines link and node routing metrics and constraints (node energy, hop count, throughput, latency, LQL, ETX, link color) and their object formats carried in RPL's DAG Metric Container for path calculation in low-power and lossy networks.

RPL.why: The document specifies the metric and constraint objects carried in RPL DIO messages in the DAG Metric Container, extending RPL for path calculation.
RPL.quote: this document specifies a set of link and node routing metrics and constraints suitable to LLNs to be used by the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL)

rejected.why: The document defines specific metric objects for RPL rather than general routing architecture or design principles.
The RPL tag sits under IoT and already covers the subject, so the parent is implied.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as historical contrast for static link metrics.
Mentioned only as an example of an IGP with static metrics, and for the overload bit analogy.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-style sections that merely register this document's own objects.
MPLS TE is mentioned only as a comparison for constraint-based path computation.
The metrics are explicitly not specific to any link layer.

RFC6552.title: Objective Function Zero for the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL)
RFC6552.summary: Specifies Objective Function Zero (OF0), a basic default RPL objective function that computes Rank and selects preferred parent and backup feasible successor using only core RPL objects.

RPL.why: The document defines OF0 for RPL, specifying rank computation, parent selection, constants and the OCP, so it is squarely about RPL.
RPL.quote: This document specifies a basic Objective Function that relies only on the objects that are defined in the RPL and does not use any protocol extensions.

rejected.why: RPL is a child technology tag under IoT here, and the more specific tag RPL fits; the generic routing topic is not needed.
Implied as the parent of RPL; not chosen separately.
OCP 0 registration is boilerplate-like IANA section; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
The Manageability Considerations section is brief and inherited from RFC 6550; not a main subject.
RPL runs over IPv6 but the document does not address IPv6 itself.

RFC6553.title: The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) Option for Carrying RPL Information in Data-Plane Datagrams
RFC6553.summary: Defines the RPL Option, an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option carrying RPL routing information in data packets for data-path inconsistency detection among RPL routers, with IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnelling rules.

RPL.why: The document specifies the RPL Option format and RPL router behaviour for data-plane datagrams, extending the RPL protocol.
RPL.quote: this document defines a new IPv6 option, called the RPL Option, to be carried within the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop header.

IP-in-IP.why: The document specifies when and how IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation must be used to carry the option, which is a substantial part of the router behaviour.
IP-in-IP.quote: routers MUST use IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling [RFC2473] and place the RPL Option in the tunnel header.

rejected.why: IPv6 Hop-by-Hop options are the carrier mechanism; the document is about RPL, though it defines a new IPv6 option. RPL is the more specific subject.
ICMPv6 errors are mentioned only as a reason for using tunnelling.
Path MTU Discovery is mentioned briefly regarding header expansion, not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only as an example of a link with a 1280-octet MTU.
Referenced only as a contrast to RPL's data-path verification.
The IANA section is boilerplate registering the option value and sub-TLV registry.

RFC6554.title: An IPv6 Routing Header for Source Routes with the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL)
RFC6554.summary: Defines the RPL Source Route Header, a new IPv6 Routing header type (type 3) with compressed addresses, for source routing within an RPL routing domain, including generation and processing rules.

RPL.why: The document specifies the source routing header used by RPL and the router behaviour for generating and processing it, so RPL readers need it.
RPL.quote: This document specifies a new IPv6 Routing header type for delivering datagrams within a RPL routing domain.

IPv6.why: It defines a new IPv6 extension header (Routing Type 3), its processing rules and the Hop Limit handling, which is a substantial IPv6 protocol extension.
IPv6.quote: The format of the SRH draws from that of the Type 0 Routing header (RH0) [RFC2460].

rejected.why: IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnelling (RFC 2473) is used to carry the SRH when the route is partial, but it is a mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
ICMPv6 errors and a new Destination Unreachable code 7 are defined, but only as error signalling for the SRH.
6LoWPAN is mentioned only in the MTU discussion as an example of a constrained link.
The security considerations concern RH0 deprecation attacks and are boilerplate. The document is not mainly about securing routing.
The IANA section only registers the routing type and ICMPv6 code, which is boilerplate.

RFC6555.title: Happy Eyeballs: Success with Dual-Stack Hosts
RFC6555.summary: RFC 6555 specifies requirements for Happy Eyeballs algorithms, which let dual-stack clients quickly fall back from broken IPv6 to IPv4 when connecting, and gives an example algorithm.

happy eyeballs.why: The document defines the Happy Eyeballs requirements and example algorithm for racing IPv6 and IPv4 connection attempts, which is exactly this tag's subject.
happy eyeballs.quote: This document specifies requirements for algorithms that reduce this user-visible delay and provides an algorithm.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the context, but the document is about the specific connection racing technique, which has a more specific tag under IPv6 transition.
TCP connection attempts are the mechanism being raced, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
A and AAAA lookups are mentioned (Section 5.4), but only as the source of addresses, not as a DNS subject.
IPv4 address sharing and CGN are cited as motivation for preferring IPv6, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.
Same-origin policy appears in Section 5.6 as a constraint, but only briefly and the document is not about web security mechanisms.
ICE is mentioned as an inspiration and an analogous mechanism for UDP, not a subject of the document.

RFC6556.title: Testing Eyeball Happiness
RFC6556.summary: Defines a black-box lab test and metrics (session setup interval, max/min, attempt pattern) for measuring how quickly applications establish sessions in dual-stack or multi-prefix IPv6 networks, supporting Happy Eyeballs.

happy eyeballs.why: The document is a test methodology for evaluating Happy Eyeballs behaviour of applications and hosts in dual-stack networks.
happy eyeballs.quote: This note describes a test to determine how quickly an application can reliably open sessions in a complex environment, such as dual-stack (IPv4+IPv6) deployment

performance measurement.why: It defines formal metrics (Session Setup Interval, maximum, minimum, attempt pattern) with methodology, units, and timing precision, so it is a measurement methodology.
performance measurement.quote: The measurements taken are the duration of the interval from the initial DNS request until the session is seen to have been established

rejected.why: DNS queries are just the start of the measured interval; the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
TCP handshake is the event timed, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Path MTU black-holing is mentioned only as one failure scenario to configure in the test bed.
Considered since BMWG commented, but this is an end-host behaviour test rather than benchmarking of network devices.
Parent of happy eyeballs; the more specific tag is used instead.
The getaddrinfo sequential-trial behaviour is background motivation, not the subject.

RFC6557.title: Procedures for Maintaining the Time Zone Database
RFC6557.summary: BCP defining procedures for maintaining the Time Zone (TZ) Database: the TZ mailing list, update criteria, selection and replacement of the TZ Coordinator as an IANA designated expert, appeals to the IESG, reference code distribution, database ownership, and IANA's hosting role.

time zones.why: The whole document is about maintaining and releasing the Time Zone Database, including update criteria, signed distribution and the TZ Coordinator role. Readers of the time zone data subject would want it.
time zones.quote: This memo specifies procedures involved with maintenance of the TZ database and associated code, including how to submit proposed updates, how decisions for inclusion of those updates are made

IANA.why: The TZ Coordinator is made an IANA Designated Expert, and IANA hosts the database, the mailing list and the signing key. This is a substantial part of the operational model, not just boilerplate.
IANA.quote: Maintenance of a repository for the TZ database and associated reference code.  The TZ Coordinator SHALL be named by the IESG as described above

rejected.why: iCalendar TZID is only cited as a consumer of the TZ database. The document does not specify or extend iCalendar.
DHCP time zone options are mentioned only as a user of the database. The document does not specify them.
The appeal and expert-selection procedures are specific to the TZ database, not general IETF process.
The database ownership and public-domain section is a small part of the document and specific to the TZ database. It is not a general IPR document.

RFC6558.title: Sieve Extension for Converting Messages before Delivery
RFC6558.summary: Defines a Sieve extension adding a "convert" action/test that uses the IMAP CONVERT framework to transcode message body parts between media types before delivery.

Sieve.why: The document specifies a new Sieve extension (the convert action and test), its interaction with other actions, and examples, so it belongs on the Sieve page.
Sieve.quote: This document defines a similar extension to the Sieve mail filtering language [RFC5228], which reuses the conversion parameters and framework established by IMAP CONVERT.

rejected.why: IMAP CONVERT is only reused for its conversion parameters and framework. The document defines no IMAP behaviour.
Body parts and media types are the objects being converted, and the document does not specify MIME itself. It also uses Sieve MIME part tests only as supporting machinery.
This is implied by Sieve, and the document is specifically about the Sieve extension.
The document does not register or define media types. It only refers to them as conversion inputs and outputs.

RFC6559.title: A Reliable Transport Mechanism for PIM
RFC6559.summary: Defines PORT (PIM Over Reliable Transport), an experimental extension that carries PIM Join/Prune messages over TCP or SCTP connections between neighbors, removing periodic refresh.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM Sparse-Mode (and SSM/BIDIR) Join/Prune processing with reliable transport, new Hello options, and explicit tracking. PIM-SM is the most specific PIM tag in the taxonomy.
PIM-SM.quote: To create a simple incremental mechanism to provide reliable PIM Join/Prune message delivery in PIM version 2 for use with PIM Sparse-Mode (PIM-SM)

TCP.why: The document specifies how PIM uses TCP: connection establishment rules, Connection IDs, avoiding duplicate TCP connections, keep-alives, and TCP congestion and retransmit concerns. It defines more than a substrate.
TCP.quote: The reliable transport mechanism can use either TCP or SCTP as the transport protocol.

SCTP.why: SCTP is a first-class transport choice here. It is preferred over TCP, and multi-streaming is used to avoid head-of-line blocking across address families.
SCTP.quote: If both the router and its neighbor have announced both PIM-over-TCP-Capable and PIM-over-SCTP-Capable Options, SCTP MUST be used.

rejected.why: This fits as a concept, since PIM messages are carried over TCP/SCTP. But the specific TCP and SCTP tags capture it better.
This is the parent of PIM-SM, so it is implied.
The generic PIM tag is the parent of PIM-SM, so it is implied. The document is about the sparse-mode family (SM, SSM, BIDIR).
PIM-SSM is mentioned only as covered by PIM-SM Join/Prune handling. The document does not specify anything about SSM itself.
IPv6 appears only as an address family for Connection IDs and the Join/Prune option. The document is not about IPv6.

RFC6560.title: One-Time Password (OTP) Pre-Authentication
RFC6560.summary: Defines a Kerberos FAST pre-authentication factor that lets clients authenticate with one-time password values (four-pass and two-pass modes, PIN change, resynchronization), including the ASN.1 message types and key derivation.

Kerberos.why: The document specifies a Kerberos V5 pre-authentication mechanism (PA-OTP-CHALLENGE, PA-OTP-REQUEST, PA-OTP-PIN-CHANGE) built on the FAST framework, with KDC/AS-REQ/AS-REP processing.
Kerberos.quote: This document describes the use of this framework to carry out One-Time Password (OTP) authentication.

OTP.why: The document is about carrying OTP values (time-based, counter-based, challenge-response tokens), including PIN handling and resynchronization, in a generic OTP-mechanism-neutral way.
OTP.quote: allows One-Time Password (OTP) values to be used in the Kerberos V5 [RFC4120] pre-authentication in a manner that does not require use of the user's Kerberos password

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only used to define the message encodings in an appendix and section 4; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Generic parent topic; the specific Kerberos and OTP tags cover the subject.
The iterated hashing of the OTP is a custom construction with string-to-key, not PBKDF2.
SASLprep is only cited for PIN string normalization; the document does not use or specify SASL.
Reply and client key derivation is part of the Kerberos pre-auth mechanism, not a key management subject in its own right.

gaps.name: Kerberos pre-authentication / FAST
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a Kerberos tag in the security hierarchy, but the document is specifically about a FAST pre-authentication factor. My tag list uses ids Kerberos and OTP, which I should double-check exist exactly as written.

RFC6561.title: Recommendations for the Remediation of Bots in ISP Networks
RFC6561.summary: Informational guidance for ISPs on detecting malicious bot infections among subscribers, notifying users (email, walled garden, SMS, IM, web), and supporting remediation.

operational security.why: The document is operational guidance for ISPs on detecting, notifying and remediating bot-infected hosts, which is operational security practice for network infrastructure.
operational security.quote: recommendations on how Internet Service Providers can use various remediation techniques to manage the effects of malicious bot infestations on computers used by their subscribers

DDoS.why: Reducing botnet size to limit DDoS capability is a stated motivation, and bot detection through DDoS observation is discussed. It is not DDoS mitigation signalling, so this is secondary.
DDoS.quote: Bots are frequently used as part of coordinated DDoS attacks for criminal, political, or other motivations

rejected.why: Spam is a motivation and a detection signal, but the document is about bot remediation, not spam filtering or reputation.
ARF is only mentioned as a feedback loop format in the detection list; the document does not specify or extend it.
IODEF is only cited as a format for data sharing in a detection method, not specified or profiled here.
Considered because of data sharing and abuse reports, but the document's focus is ISP end-user notification and remediation, not incident exchange coordination.
PII protection is addressed in short passages and a Privacy Considerations section, but it is not a main subject.
Walled garden notification is one method discussed in Section 5.4, but it is not captive portal detection or interaction as a protocol subject.

gaps.name: botnets / malware remediation
gaps.why: The document's core subject is botnet detection and remediation by ISPs. The taxonomy has no botnet or malware tag, so operational security is the closest fit.

RFC6562.title: Guidelines for the Use of Variable Bit Rate Audio with Secure RTP
RFC6562.summary: RFC 6562 gives guidelines on the traffic-analysis risks of using variable bit rate audio codecs and voice activity detection with SRTP, recommending CBR, random overhang periods and RTP padding as mitigations.

SRTP.why: The whole document is about securing RTP audio with SRTP and the information leakage from packet sizes and timing that SRTP does not hide. It gives guidance on padding and on the use of VAD.
SRTP.quote: This memo discusses potential security issues that arise when using variable bit rate (VBR) audio with the secure RTP profile.

codecs.why: Much of the guidance concerns how VBR and CBR speech codecs and VAD should be used, so readers of the codecs subject would want it. It covers no specific codec.
codecs.quote: When using SRTP with voice streams compressed using variable bit rate (VBR) codecs, the length of the compressed packets will depend on the characteristics of the speech signal.

rejected.why: RTP is the underlying protocol. The document is about SRTP, which is the more specific tag, and it adds nothing to RTP itself apart from the use of RTP padding.
The traffic-analysis leakage is a privacy concern. The document treats it as an SRTP security issue and is not a protocol privacy-considerations document.
Speex is cited only as an example in the research results. It is not the subject of the document.
The document defines no payload format. It only gives guidance on packet padding.

RFC6563.title: Moving A6 to Historic Status
RFC6563.summary: Informational IETF document that summarizes the problems with the DNS A6 resource record for IPv6 addresses and moves RFC 2874 from Experimental to Historic, recommending AAAA only.

DNS.why: The document is about the A6 DNS resource record type: its resolution issues, usage in resolvers like BIND, and deprecation, including recommended resolver and server behaviour.
DNS.quote: this document moves RFC 2874 [RFC2874] to Historic status, thereby clarifying that implementers and operators should represent IPv6 addresses in the DNS by using AAAA records only.

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses are what A6 represents, but the document is about the DNS record type, not IPv6 itself.
Renumbering and multihoming are mentioned only as A6's original motivation, not as a subject of the document.
The IANA action (marking A6 Obsolete) is boilerplate-level and not the subject of the document.
The status change to Historic is the vehicle, but the document's subject is the A6 record rather than process.

RFC6564.title: A Uniform Format for IPv6 Extension Headers
RFC6564.summary: Updates RFC 2460 to give guidance on when new IPv6 extension headers may be defined (prefer destination options, no new hop-by-hop headers) and mandates a uniform Next Header/Hdr Ext Len format for any new extension headers.

IPv6.why: The document defines a common format and restrictions for IPv6 extension headers and updates the IPv6 specification (RFC 2460). It is about IPv6 itself.
IPv6.quote: MUST use the consistent format defined in Figure 1. This minimizes breakage in intermediate nodes that examine these extension headers.

rejected.why: Firewalls and middleboxes that parse extension headers motivate the uniform format, but the document specifies neither firewall behaviour nor traversal mechanisms.
The document has nothing to do with IPv4/IPv6 coexistence.
It discusses extensibility of IPv6 but is a protocol-specific format rule, not a general architectural principles document.

gaps.name: IPv6 extension headers
gaps.why: The document is specifically about extension header design and format. IPv6 is the closest tag, but there is no narrower tag for extension headers or options.

RFC6565.title: OSPFv3 as a Provider Edge to Customer Edge (PE-CE) Routing Protocol
RFC6565.summary: Extends the OSPFv2 PE-CE specification for BGP/MPLS VPNs to OSPFv3, covering instances, Domain IDs, LSA type mapping, BGP extended communities, DN-bit loop prevention and sham links.

L3VPN.why: The document specifies PE-CE routing in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 4364/4659), with VRFs, route distinguishers, route targets and MP-BGP interaction. It is an L3VPN WG product.
L3VPN.quote: This document defines the mechanisms required to enable the operation of OSPFv3 as the PE-CE routing protocol.

OSPFv3.why: It extends OSPFv3 for PE-CE use: multiple instances per link, LSA types, DN-bit, sham links, and address families (RFC 5838).
OSPFv3.quote: OSPFv3 operates on a per-link basis as opposed to OSPFv2, which operates on a per-IP-subnet basis.

rejected.why: BGP and MP-BGP carry the VPN-IPv6 routes, but BGP itself is not specified here. The BGP extended communities are defined only to carry OSPF information.
It defines OSPF Domain ID, Router ID and Route Type extended communities, but only as OSPF-specific attributes for L3VPN. The document is not about BGP communities generally.
MPLS is the backbone tunnelling substrate and is not specified or extended here.
IPv6 is the address family in use, not the subject of the document.

RFC6566.title: A Framework for the Control of Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs) with Impairments
RFC6566.summary: Informational framework describing how GMPLS and the PCE architecture can support impairment-aware routing and wavelength assignment (IA-RWA) in wavelength switched optical networks, covering computation scenarios, architectures and protocol implications.

GMPLS.why: The document frames the GMPLS control plane (routing and signaling) for optical WSONs with impairments, and analyses the protocol implications for GMPLS routing and signaling.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides a framework for applying GMPLS protocols and the PCE architecture to the control and operation of IA-RWA for WSONs.

PCE.why: A large part of the document defines PCE roles (RWA-Coord PCE, IV-Candidates PCE, IV-Detailed PCE), their TE database needs, and PCEP request/reply impacts for IA-RWA.

rejected.why: Signaling is discussed only as a mechanism for distributed impairment validation; the document doesn't specify or extend RSVP-TE itself.
OSPF-TE is only mentioned in Security Considerations; routing is discussed generically.
The more specific PCE and GMPLS tags already cover the TE aspects of the document.
The document is about optical-layer control plane computation, not general routing architecture.

gaps.name: Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSON) / optical impairments
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for WDM/optical network control or impairment-aware RWA. GMPLS is the nearest fit, but WSON readers would want a dedicated optical networking subject.

RFC6567.title: Problem Statement and Requirements for Transporting User-to-User Call Control Information in SIP
RFC6567.summary: Informational problem statement and requirements for a SIP mechanism to carry call-control User-to-User Information (UUI) during session setup, including interworking with ISDN UUI, with four use cases and fifteen requirements.

SIP.why: The document defines requirements for a new SIP extension to carry UUI in INVITE, REFER, 3xx and BYE messages, covering proxy, redirect and referral behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document describes the transport of User-to-User Information (UUI) during SIP [RFC3261] session setup.

rejected.why: ISDN is only the interworking counterpart, not specified here; PSTN interop is the better fit.
The document concerns UUI interworking in general, not ISUP encapsulation in SIP-T/SIP-I.

Not used by the document.

RFC6568.title: Design and Application Spaces for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs)
RFC6568.summary: Informational document describing design-space dimensions and use cases (industrial and structural monitoring, connected home, healthcare, vehicle telematics, agricultural monitoring) that motivate 6LoWPAN work.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document is about application scenarios and design dimensions for 6LoWPAN networks, so readers of the 6LoWPAN subject would expect it there.
6LoWPAN.quote: this document provides a list of use cases and market domains that may benefit and motivate the work currently done in the 6LoWPAN Working Group.

rejected.why: IPsec and IKEv2 are discussed only briefly in Security Considerations as too heavy for LoWPANs; the document is not about them.
6LoWPAN ND is referenced as the mechanism for addressing and bootstrapping in use cases, but it is not specified or analysed here.
Considered as the parent topic, but 6LoWPAN is the more specific tag and implies IoT.
QoS is one design-space dimension among many, mentioned only as a requirement per use case.
IPv6 is the underlying protocol carried over LoWPANs, not the subject of the document.

RFC6569.title: Guidelines for Development of an Audio Codec within the IETF
RFC6569.summary: Informational guidelines for the IETF codec WG on how to develop, evaluate, specify, and handle IPR for an interactive Internet audio codec (which led to Opus).

codecs.quote: provides general guidelines for work on developing and specifying an interactive audio codec within the IETF

IPR.quote: Producing an unencumbered codec is desirable for the following reasons

rejected.why: The RTP payload format is mentioned only as work to be done in the PAYLOAD WG. The document does not define one.
RTP is cited only in passing as the transport the codec payload format will target.
The document does describe a WG development process, but it is specific to codec work, and the codecs tag captures that better. It is not general IETF procedure.
AMR-WB is mentioned only as an example of a codec contributed from 3GPP to the ITU-T.
Base64 is mentioned only as an optional encoding for the source code, which is incidental.
Opus is not named. The document is generic guidelines for a codec that was not yet specified.

RFC6570.title: URI Template
RFC6570.summary: RFC 6570 defines the URI Template syntax and the expansion process, in four levels of operators and modifiers, that turns a template into a URI reference.

URI.why: The whole document specifies URI Templates: their syntax, expansion into URI references, and pct-encoding rules. URI templates are named in the URI tag's description.

Section 1.6 covers Unicode normalization and UTF-8 encoding for expansion. That is a small part of the document, not a main subject.
HTTP appears only in example URIs and the security discussion. The document is not about HTTP.
The document mentions computed links and service discovery as uses, but it does not define link relations or typed links.

RFC6571.title: Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) Applicability in Service Provider (SP) Networks
RFC6571.summary: Informational analysis of how well Loop-Free Alternate IP fast reroute applies to SP access topologies (triangle, full mesh, square, extended U) and core networks, with simulation results, capacity planning guidance and comparison with MPLS TE FRR.

IP fast reroute.quote: we analyze the applicability of the Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) [RFC5714] [RFC5286] method of providing IP fast reroute (IPFRR) in both the core and access parts

rejected.why: Used only as the reference IGP for the analysis; the document is not about IS-IS itself.
Mentioned only as equally applicable; not a subject of the document.
MPLS TE FRR is compared as an alternative, but the document is not about it.
Capacity planning is discussed in the LFA context, not as a TE subject in its own right.
The parent of the chosen tag would be implied only if it fit; topology design is addressed specifically for LFA.
MPLS TE FRR is mentioned only for comparison.

gaps.name: IP fast reroute / Loop-Free Alternates

RFC6572.title: RADIUS Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6572.summary: Defines new RADIUS attributes and interface procedures for the MAG and LMA to interact with a RADIUS AAA server for authentication, authorization, policy and accounting in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain.

Only the MIP6-Feature-Vector attribute from Mobile IPv6 AAA work is reused; the document concerns network-based mobility, not host-based Mobile IPv6.
The parent AAA tag is implied by the RADIUS tag and the document addresses a specific protocol, not AAA frameworks in general.

RFC6573.title: The Item and Collection Link Relations
RFC6573.summary: Defines and registers the reciprocal 'item' and 'collection' Web Linking link relation types for expressing the relationship between a collection and its members.

web linking.why: The document defines and registers two new typed link relations under RFC 5988 Web Linking, which is exactly the subject of the web linking tag.

rejected.why: HTML anchors are only used as examples of where the rel values appear; the document is not about HTML.

RFC6574.title: Report from the Smart Object Workshop
RFC6574.summary: IAB workshop report on interconnecting smart objects with the Internet, summarizing discussions on architecture, sleeping nodes, security and routing in constrained environments, with recommendations for IETF/IRTF work.

IoT.why: The whole report is about deploying IETF protocols on constrained smart objects, covering constrained nodes and networks, architecture, energy and security guidance for IoT.
IoT.quote: The term "Internet of Things" denotes a trend where a large number of devices employ communication services offered by the Internet protocols.

workshop reports.why: It is an IAB workshop report that summarizes discussions and gives conclusions and recommendations.
workshop reports.quote: This document provides an overview of a workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) on 'Interconnecting Smart Objects with the Internet'.

rejected.why: RPL and mesh-under versus route-over routing are discussed in one section, but the report is not about RPL itself.
CoAP is mentioned as an example application protocol and for congestion control, but it is not the subject.
Security is one discussion area, but the report is not about a specific security mechanism.
6LoWPAN is only named as a working group, and the report does not specify or analyse it.
Information-centric networking is a brief discussion point and next-step item, not a main subject.
Not relevant; energy and sleeping nodes are the topic, and energy management is only a minor part of the discussion.

RFC6575.title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) Mediation for IP Interworking of Layer 2 VPNs
RFC6575.summary: Specifies ARP Mediation, the PE procedures for resolving IPv4/IPv6 link-layer addresses so VPWS pseudowires can interconnect Attachment Circuits of different technologies carrying IP, including LDP signalling of CE IPv4 addresses and IPv6 stack capability advertisement.

L2VPN.quote: ARP Mediation refers to the process of resolving Layer 2 addresses when different resolution protocols are used on either Attachment Circuit.

ARP.why: The core subject is proxying and mediating ARP and Inverse ARP between PEs and CEs.
ARP.quote: PE1 MUST interpret the meaning of the ARP requests and mediate the necessary information with PE2 before responding.

pseudowire.why: The IP Layer 2 Interworking pseudowire type is central, with new LDP signalling (Address List TLV, Stack Capability sub-TLV, status codes) for it.
pseudowire.quote: The encapsulation for the IP Layer 2 Transport pseudowire is described in [RFC4447].

neighbor discovery.why: A substantial section specifies how PEs intercept and modify IPv6 ND/IND, RS and RA messages.
neighbor discovery.quote: Intercepting ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery [RFC4861] and Inverse Neighbor Discovery [RFC3122] packets received over the AC as well as over the PW

rejected.why: LDP is the signalling substrate for pseudowire setup; the document only adds a TLV and status codes within RFC 4447 procedures.
IPCP/IPv6CP proxy negotiation is one discovery mechanism for PPP-attached CEs, a minor part of the document.
Frame Relay is only an example attachment circuit type using Inverse ARP.
SEND is discussed only in Security Considerations as incompatible with the modifications.
Appendix A gives brief notes on IGPs over these VPNs, not the main subject.
The more specific L2VPN tag applies.

RFC6576.title: IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) Standard Advancement Testing
RFC6576.summary: BCP defining how to test whether independent implementations of IPPM performance-metric RFCs yield statistically equivalent results (Anderson-Darling K-sample tests, tunnelled identical-path test setups) to support Standards Track advancement.

performance measurement.why: The document is about validating IPPM metric implementations via statistical comparison of measurement results, the core of performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: tests to determine if multiple independent instantiations of a performance-metric RFC have implemented the specifications in the same way

IETF process.why: It defines an advancement-testing procedure and implementation report requirements for moving metric RFCs along the Standards Track.

rejected.why: L2TPv3 is only used as the example tunnel for the test setup, not specified or extended.
OWAMP/TWAMP are mentioned as protocols and RTT reference, but the document is not about them.
Tunnels are used as a test-setup tool to avoid ECMP; the document does not specify tunneling.
ECMP is a problem to avoid in test setups, not the subject.
Clock synchronization via NTP is discussed briefly as a measurement accuracy concern only.
Concerns live-network metric implementation equivalence rather than device benchmarking methodology.

RFC6577.title: Authentication-Results Registration Update for Sender Policy Framework (SPF) Results
RFC6577.summary: Updates the IANA registries for Authentication-Results email header result names, replacing the SPF 'hardfail' result with 'fail' and adding a Status column to the registries.

rejected.why: The IANA registry changes are the mechanism for the correction. The document is about email authentication result names, not IANA procedures in general.
Authentication-Results is a message header field, but this document only changes registry values and does not define header syntax.
Only mentioned within the quoted 'fail' definition. It is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Authentication-Results header field
gaps.why: The document updates RFC 5451's Authentication-Results registry. The taxonomy has no tag for that header field or its registries, so the closest fit is the email authentication parent.

RFC6578.title: Collection Synchronization for Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV)
RFC6578.summary: Defines a WebDAV extension, the DAV:sync-collection report and DAV:sync-token property, that lets clients efficiently synchronize the contents of a WebDAV collection using opaque synchronization tokens.

XML request and response bodies are only the encoding for the WebDAV report; nothing new is defined about XML.
CalDAV and CardDAV are only mentioned as protocols that define other report types a client could use for initial sync; this document does not extend them.
Only cited as an example of another source of initial synchronization; not what the document is about.

RFC6579.title: The 'disclosure' Link Relation Type
RFC6579.summary: Specifies and registers the 'disclosure' Web Linking relation type, whose target is a list of patent/IPR disclosures about the context material.

The Link header field is used only in an example. The document does not extend HTTP.
HTML appears only as an example of how the relation can be used. The document does not specify HTML.
The registry entry is boilerplate that follows from defining the relation. The document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
IRIs are the link context and target as defined by RFC 5988, and the document says nothing new about them.

RFC6580.title: IANA Registries for the Remote Direct Data Placement (RDDP) Protocols
RFC6580.summary: Creates IANA registries for RDDP (RDMAP, DDP, MPA) error codes, RDMAP operation codes, and SCTP function codes for DDP session control, populating them from the original RDDP RFCs and setting allocation policy.

RDMA.why: The document is about the RDDP/RDMAP protocol suite's registries (error codes, opcodes). The only fitting taxonomy tag is RDMA under storage.

IANA.why: The document's whole purpose is creating IANA registries and defining allocation policy (Standards Action), which is IANA registry guidance.

rejected.why: SCTP function codes for DDP are registered, but the document is about RDDP registries, not SCTP itself; SCTP is only the substrate for the DDP adaptation.
MPA runs over TCP, but TCP is only the substrate and not specified or changed here.
iSCSI is not mentioned; RDMA/iWARP is related to storage but not to this protocol.

gaps.name: RDDP / iWARP protocol suite (DDP, MPA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has RDMA but no specific tag for the DDP and MPA layers of the RDDP suite. RDMA is the closest available tag.

RFC6581.title: Enhanced Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) Connection Establishment
RFC6581.summary: Updates RFC 5043 and RFC 5044 by extending MPA and SCTP DDP connection establishment with IRD/ORD negotiation, peer-to-peer mode and Ready-to-Receive (RTR) indication options for RDMA connections.

RDMA.why: The whole document extends RDMA (RDDP/MPA/DDP) connection establishment, including IRD/ORD negotiation and RTR indications, so RDMA readers need it.

rejected.why: MPA runs over TCP, but TCP is only the substrate and nothing new is defined about TCP.
The document adds SCTP session control chunk function codes for DDP. SCTP is the substrate and the changes are to RFC 5043's DDP adaptation, not to SCTP itself.
The IANA section only adds registry entries, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The document extends connection setup for RDMA over TCP/SCTP and is not a generic binding of one protocol over a transport.

RFC6582.title: The NewReno Modification to TCP's Fast Recovery Algorithm
RFC6582.summary: Specifies the NewReno modification to TCP fast recovery, which responds to partial acknowledgments to recover from multiple losses in a window for non-SACK connections, obsoleting RFC 3782.

NewReno.quote: This document describes a specific algorithm for responding to partial acknowledgments, referred to as "NewReno".

TCP.quote: This document describes a modification to the fast recovery algorithm in RFC 5681 that incorporates a response to partial acknowledgments received during fast recovery.

rejected.why: This is the parent of NewReno, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.

RFC6583.title: Operational Neighbor Discovery Problems
RFC6583.summary: Informational RFC describing how IPv6 Neighbor Discovery implementations can suffer DoS when scanning of huge /64 subnets triggers address resolution for many unassigned addresses, and giving operational mitigations and implementor recommendations.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document analyses ND implementation weaknesses (NDP queue, neighbor cache) and recommends prioritisation and queue tuning for RFC 4861 implementations.
neighbor discovery.quote: simplistic implementations of Neighbor Discovery may fail to perform as desired when they perform address resolution of large numbers of unassigned addresses

Parent of neighbor discovery, so implied.
Mentioned only as a limitation of some mitigations (prefixes longer than /64), not a subject.
Only mentioned as the IPv4 analogue in passing.

RFC6584.summary: Defines four per-packet authentication schemes (RSA signature, ECDSA signature, group-keyed HMAC, and combined signature+MAC) with anti-replay, carried in the EXT_AUTH header extension of ALC and NORM multicast content delivery protocols.

ALC.why: The document specifies authentication header extensions for ALC sessions and analyses replay impacts on ALC.

HMAC.quote: MUST communicate the Cryptographic MAC Function -- for instance, HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256

rejected.why: Only discussed as a comparison; it is specified in RFC 5776, not here.
The EXT_AUTH header extension of LCT is used, but LCT itself is not specified or extended.
RFC 4303 anti-replay and RFC 4359 are borrowed from, but the document is not about IPsec.
Hash functions are merely parameters of the schemes.
The tagged ALC and NORM children are more specific and cover this.
A child tech (multicast security, ECDSA, etc.) fits better.

RFC6585.summary: RFC 6585 defines four new HTTP status codes (428, 429, 431, 511), including 511 for captive-portal network authentication, and registers them with IANA.

RFC6586.title: Experiences from an IPv6-Only Network
RFC6586.summary: Informational report on experiences running a small office and home network as IPv6-only with a NAT64/DNS64 device for IPv4 access, covering application, OS and web problems, with recommendations.

RFC6589.summary: Informational guidance on how content providers can transition web content to IPv6, covering challenges, migration tactics (IPv6-specific names, DNS resolver whitelisting/blacklisting, direct dual stack), and phases.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document addresses IPv6 deployment/coexistence for content: tactics, phases, dual-stack migration.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document describes considerations for the transition of end-user content on the Internet to IPv6.

DNS.why: A large part of the document analyses DNS resolver whitelisting/blacklisting, selective AAAA responses by authoritative servers, and comparison with DNS load balancing and split DNS.
DNS.quote: a domain's authoritative DNS will selectively return a AAAA resource record to DNS recursive resolvers on a whitelist maintained by the domain

rejected.why: Only discussed briefly in Security Considerations to note whitelisting does not break the chain of trust; not the subject.
CDNs/GSLB are mentioned only as analogies to whitelisting.
RFC 6555 is only cited as out-of-scope solution to impairment.
Large-scale NAT is mentioned as an alternative/side scenario, not a subject.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag fits better.

RFC6590.title: Redaction of Potentially Sensitive Data from Mail Abuse Reports
RFC6590.summary: Specifies a consistent-transformation method (e.g., hashing) for redacting private data such as recipient local-parts in ARF email abuse reports while still letting receivers correlate reports about the same user.

ARF.why: The document extends the Abuse Reporting Format by specifying how generators redact sensitive data in ARF reports, and includes an ARF example.
ARF.quote: This memo presents a practice for conducting redaction in a manner that allows a report receiver to detect that two reports were caused by the same end user

rejected.why: HMAC is only mentioned as one possible transformation; no transformation is mandated.
Base64 is only used to encode transformation output into a valid replacement; it is a supporting mechanism.
Privacy motivates the work, but the document is about a specific ARF redaction practice; ARF is the more specific fit.
SMTP is cited only for local-part syntax constraints.
Abuse reports are the context, but the subject is redaction in the ARF format, already covered by ARF.
SHA1 appears only in the appendix example as one possible choice.

RFC6591.title: Authentication Failure Reporting Using the Abuse Reporting Format
RFC6591.summary: Registers the "auth-failure" ARF feedback type and new header fields so receivers can send detailed reports about messages failing DKIM, ADSP or SPF authentication checks.

ARF.why: The document extends ARF with a new feedback type and header fields for authentication failure reports; this is its sole purpose.
ARF.quote: This memo registers an extension report type for the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF), affecting multiple registries, for use in generating receipt-time reports

DKIM.why: A large part of the extension defines DKIM-specific report fields (domain, selector, canonicalized header/body) and DKIM failure types, so DKIM readers would want it.
DKIM.quote: DKIM-Domain:  The domain that signed the message, taken from the "d=" tag of the signature.

SPF.why: Defines SPF-specific report fields and the spf failure type, so the document substantially addresses reporting SPF failures.
SPF.quote: SPF-DNS:  This field MUST appear once for every SPF record [SPF] used to obtain the SPF result.

rejected.why: Parent of ARF, DKIM and SPF, which are tagged directly, so it is implied.
Internet message format (RFC 5322) is only the substrate for the header fields; the document does not specify it.
The report is a multipart/report MIME message, but MIME is only the container and is not specified here.
DNS records are referenced in SPF-DNS and DKIM-Selector-DNS fields but the document does not define DNS behaviour.
Abuse reporting relates to spam, but the document focuses on authentication failure reports, not spam filtering.
Base64 is only used as an encoding for canonicalized header and body fields.

RFC6592.title: The Null Packet
RFC6592.summary: An April 1st humor RFC that "defines" the Null Packet as a zero-dimensional packet with no protocol ID, leaving its formal definition blank and joking about performance metrics and security.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical parody; the whole document is a joke definition of a nonexistent packet, with an intentionally blank formal-definition section and an IANA request to not create an empty registry.
humor.quote: The Null Packet is a zero-dimensional packet.  The Null Packet exists since it is non-self-contradictorily definable.

rejected.why: RFC 1144 is cited only for an early mention of a 'null packet'; the document is not about header compression.
The Paradoxical Firewall section is a joke in the Security Considerations, not a substantive treatment of firewalls.
Next Header 59 is mentioned in passing only to say it does not create a Null Packet.
Implicit NULL label is mentioned as a joke in Security Considerations; the document does not address MPLS.
Section 3 jokes about metrics for null traffic, but it is a brief aside rather than a real treatment.

RFC6593.title: Service Undiscovery Using Hide-and-Go-Seek for the Domain Pseudonym System (DPS)
RFC6593.summary: An April 1st parody RFC describing "service undiscovery" via hide-and-go-seek over a fictitious Domain Pseudonym System, with hint PDUs, ICMP insult messages and a timeout state for misbehaving clients.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical parody of service discovery, with insults, hide-and-seek and a three-valued evil bit. Humorous RFCs belong on the humor page.
humor.quote: This document is unscoped, as the scoping service cannot be found.

rejected.why: The document parodies service discovery but defines no real discovery mechanism; humor is the proper subject.
The Domain Pseudonym System is fictitious and not the real DNS; no DNS records or resolver behaviour are specified.
ICMP types and codes are used only for the joke 'Insult' messages and the administratively-prohibited replies, not specified in a meaningful way.
TCP is just the stated transport for the parody protocol.
Echo is referenced for a joke hiding technique, but the document is not about the Echo service.

RFC6594.title: Use of the SHA-256 Algorithm with RSA, Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), and Elliptic Curve DSA (ECDSA) in SSHFP Resource Records
RFC6594.summary: Updates the IANA SSHFP RR registries from RFC 4255 to add ECDSA as a public key algorithm (number 3) and SHA-256 as a fingerprint type (number 2), with implementation guidance and examples.

DNS.why: The document defines new field values for the SSHFP DNS resource record type and gives resolver-side/client implementation guidance for them, so it belongs under DNS.
DNS.quote: SHA-256 fingerprints of the public keys are stored in SSHFP Resource Records with the fingerprint type 2.

SSH.why: It sets requirements for SSH implementations verifying host keys via SSHFP, including preferring SHA-256 over SHA-1 and handling ECDSA host keys.
SSH.quote: SSHFP-aware Secure Shell implementations SHOULD support the SHA-256 fingerprints for verification of the public key.

ECDSA.why: Adds ECDSA keys as a supported algorithm in SSHFP and gives an ECDSA example, so readers of ECDSA would want it.
ECDSA.quote: ECDSA public keys are stored in SSHFP Resource Records with the algorithm number 3.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is relied on to authenticate SSHFP lookups but the document defines nothing new about it.
SHA-256 is used as a fingerprint digest, but the document does not specify or analyze the hash. It only assigns a registry value, so SHA is not the subject.
The registry updates are the document's mechanism, but IANA as a topic means registry stewardship and guidance. This is a protocol-specific code point addition.
RSA appears only in an example key and is not the subject of the document.

RFC6595.title: A Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) and GSS-API Mechanism for the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)
RFC6595.summary: Specifies the SAML20 SASL mechanism and corresponding GSS-API (GS2) mechanism that let applications such as XMPP and IMAP authenticate users through existing SAML 2.0 Identity Providers using the Web Browser SSO profile.

SASL.why: The document defines a new SASL mechanism named SAML20, including its message flow, initial response, and IANA registration. SASL readers would want it.
SASL.quote: This memo specifies a SASL mechanism and a GSS-API mechanism for SAML 2.0 that allows the integration of existing SAML Identity Providers with applications using SASL

GSS-API.why: It defines a GSS-API mechanism with an OID, context flag requirements and principal name types, so it belongs on the GSS-API page.
GSS-API.quote: This section specifies a GSS-API mechanism that, when used via the GS2 bridge to SASL, behaves like the SASL mechanism defined in this document.

federated authentication.why: The mechanism lets non-web applications act as SAML relying parties and use IdP assertions. That is cross-domain federated authentication with SAML SSO.
federated authentication.quote: allows the integration of existing SAML Identity Providers with applications using SASL and GSS-API

rejected.why: XMPP appears only as an example application protocol for the mechanism. The document does not specify or extend XMPP.
IMAP is only a second worked example of a protocol that can use the mechanism.
TLS is required as the protecting channel, but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
SAML messages are XML, but XML is only the encoding. The document does not address XML usage itself.
IDN handling for the IdP-Identifier is a minor detail that relies on the existing IDNA specifications.
HTTP redirects carry the SAML flow, but HTTP is substrate and the document adds nothing to it.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SAML. The closest, federated authentication, covers it only partly. SAML 2.0 Web SSO is the subject of the document.

RFC6596.title: The Canonical Link Relation
RFC6596.summary: Registers and defines the "canonical" link relation type under the Web Linking framework (RFC 5988), letting authors designate a preferred IRI among resources with duplicative content for search engines and other applications.

web linking.why: The document defines and registers a new link relation type under RFC 5988 Web Linking, with HTML and HTTP Link header usage examples.
web linking.quote: This document describes a new type of such a relationship, "canonical", to designate an Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI) as preferred over resources with duplicative content.

rejected.why: HTTP status codes and the Link header are used for redirect guidance and examples, but the document defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
HTML link elements are shown as one way to declare the relation; the document does not specify or extend HTML.
IRIs are the targets of the relation, but the document does not address IRI syntax or processing.
URI syntax is only referenced for relative references; the document is not about URIs.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level apparatus for the link relation and not a subject in its own right.

RFC6597.title: RTP Payload Format for Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) ST 336 Encoded Data
RFC6597.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for packetizing SMPTE ST 336 KLV (Key-Length-Value) metadata into KLVunits, specifying RTP header usage, loss handling, and the application/smpte336m media type.

RTP payload format.why: The whole document is an RTP payload format specification for SMPTE ST 336 KLV data, including timestamp and marker bit usage, fragmentation, and damaged-unit handling.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload format for packetization of KLV (Key-Length-Value) Encoded Data, as defined by the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) in SMPTE ST 336, into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

rejected.why: RTP is specified through the more specific RTP payload format tag; the parent is implied.
The application/smpte336m registration is only a section of a payload format document, not a document about media type registration rules.
The SDP mapping section says there are no specific considerations; SDP is only used for signaling.
SRTP is only recommended in Security Considerations as one possible mechanism, which is boilerplate.
KLV is a metadata encoding, not an audio or video codec.
The congestion control section only points to general RTP considerations and does not define anything new.

gaps.name: SMPTE ST 336 KLV (Key-Length-Value) metadata encoding
gaps.why: The document is about carrying KLV-encoded metadata, and the taxonomy has no tag for this data encoding or for streaming metadata associated with video.

RFC6598.title: IANA-Reserved IPv4 Prefix for Shared Address Space
RFC6598.summary: BCP that requests IANA allocation of 100.64.0.0/10 as Shared Address Space for numbering CGN-to-CPE interfaces, updating RFC 5735 special-use IPv4 addresses, with usage, filtering and risk rules.

CGN.why: The whole document exists to provide address space for CGN deployment and specifies how it is used and its risks and impacts.
CGN.quote: This document requests the allocation of an IPv4 /10 address block to be used as Shared Address Space to accommodate the needs of Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) devices.

IPv4.why: It allocates a new special-use IPv4 block (100.64.0.0/10) and updates the special-use IPv4 address registry, which concerns IPv4 address lifecycle and exhaustion.
IPv4.quote: This document details the allocation of an additional special-use IPv4 address block and updates [RFC5735].

rejected.why: CGN is the more specific child under NAT and already covers it.
DNS zone and reverse-query filtering rules are a minor side requirement, not the subject.
6to4 impact is discussed as a risk only; it is not the document's subject.
PCP is only mentioned as a mitigation example in the empirical data.
IPv4 is the more specific tag and addresses the allocation of the block.
The IANA allocation is the request itself, but the document is about the address block, not IANA registry guidance.

RFC6601.title: Generic Connection Admission Control (GCAC) Algorithm Specification for IP/MPLS Networks
RFC6601.summary: Experimental RFC defining a generic connection admission control (GCAC) reference model and algorithm for IP/MPLS networks, using DS-TE bandwidth parameters advertised by the IGP to decide whether links can admit LSPs/flows meeting QoS objectives.

traffic engineering.why: The algorithm is built on Diffserv-aware MPLS TE bandwidth constraints models (MAM, MAR, RDM), CSPF link inclusion and TE tunnel bandwidth management.
traffic engineering.quote: MPLS GCAC bandwidth allocation parameters for each DS-TE CT are as defined within DS-TE [RFC4126], OSPF-TE extensions [RFC4203], and IS-IS-TE extensions [RFC5307].

QoS.why: Admission control to deliver QoS objectives, with CoS inputs, NSIS QSPEC signalling and Diffserv queuing examples.
QoS.quote: MPLS GCAC functions are implemented in a distributed manner to deliver the objective Quality of Service (QoS) for specified QoS constraints.

MPLS.why: Admission control for MPLS LSPs and pseudowires across domains, a core MPLS topic.
MPLS.quote: MPLS GCAC focuses on MPLS and PW-level CAC functions, rather than application-level CAC functions.

rejected.why: Used to signal DS-TE tunnels and for aggregation, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned as an option for path computation, which the document explicitly leaves out of scope as vendor proprietary.
Appendix example of QoS signalling only; not specified or extended here.
Used as the advertisement mechanism for bandwidth parameters; not extended.
Queuing examples in the appendix are illustrative; Diffserv is a supporting mechanism.
RSVP aggregation is a mechanism the model relies on, not the subject.

gaps.name: Connection admission control (CAC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for admission control as a subject; QoS and traffic engineering are the nearest fits.

RFC6602.title: Bulk Binding Update Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6602.summary: Defines bulk binding update and bulk revocation extensions to Proxy Mobile IPv6, adding a B flag, a Mobile Node Group Identifier option and a status code so a MAG and LMA can act on groups of mobility sessions with a single message.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 PBU/PBA and binding revocation signalling between MAG and LMA with group-scoped operations.
PMIPv6.quote: This document defines a new mobility option, the Mobile Node Group Identifier option, and the extensions to procedures related to binding update and binding revocation

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 (RFC 6275) only supplies the mobility header, status-code and option number spaces. The document is about the network-based PMIPv6 extension.
The more specific PMIPv6 tag already covers this subject, so the parent is implied.
The IANA actions are boilerplate registry allocations and do not make the document about IANA guidance.

RFC6603.title: Prefix Exclude Option for DHCPv6-based Prefix Delegation
RFC6603.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option, which lets a delegating router exclude one prefix from a delegated prefix, and updates RFC 3633 prefix delegation procedures.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option and the requesting/delegating router behaviour for DHCPv6 prefix delegation, extending RFC 3633.
DHCPv6.quote: This specification defines a new DHCPv6 option, OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE (67), that is used to exclude exactly one prefix from a delegated prefix.

rejected.why: IPv6 prefixes are the subject matter, but the document specifies a DHCPv6 option, not IPv6 itself; DHCPv6 is the more specific tag.
Mentioned only in the problem background as an address autoconfiguration method used with the uplink prefix; not specified or extended.
A topic tag is not needed since the DHCPv6 technology tag already covers this and the document does not address IP addressing architecture in its own right.

gaps.name: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCPv6-PD)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has DHCPv6 but no specific child for prefix delegation, which is the document's precise subject.

RFC6604.title: xNAME RCODE and Status Bits Clarification
RFC6604.summary: Clarifies how the DNS response RCODE and the AA/AD status bits relate to the query cycles of an xNAME (CNAME/DNAME) redirection chain, requiring RCODE to reflect the final query cycle.

DNS.why: The document updates core DNS specifications (RFC 1035, 2308, 2672) and specifies resolver/server behaviour for RCODE and AA bit handling when CNAME/DNAME redirection occurs.
DNS.quote: The RCODE in the ultimate DNS response MUST BE set based on the final query cycle leading to that response.

rejected.why: The AD bit and DNSSEC protection are discussed, but only as a restatement of RFC 4035 semantics and in Security Considerations; the document is not about DNSSEC itself.

RFC6605.title: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) for DNSSEC
RFC6605.summary: Defines ECDSA (P-256/SHA-256 and P-384/SHA-384) algorithms for DNSKEY and RRSIG records in DNSSEC, plus the SHA-384 DS digest type.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies new DNSSEC signing algorithms, DNSKEY/RRSIG formats, algorithm numbers, and a new DS digest type, plus NSEC3 validation requirements.
DNSSEC.quote: This document defines the DNSKEY and RRSIG resource records (RRs) of two new signing algorithms: ECDSA (Elliptic Curve DSA) with curve P-256 and SHA-256

ECDSA.why: It specifies the ECDSA curves, key encoding and signature encoding (r | s) for use in DNSSEC, so readers of ECDSA would want it.
ECDSA.quote: ECDSA public keys consist of a single value, called "Q" in FIPS 186-3.  In DNSSEC keys, Q is a simple bit string
ECDSA.section: 4. DNSKEY and RRSIG Resource Records for ECDSA

rejected.why: SHA-256 and SHA-384 are used as hash components and SHA-384 DS digest is defined, but the document is not about the SHA family itself; it only references it.
The more specific ECDSA tag fits; the document is not about elliptic curve cryptography generally.
Not a taxonomy tag; NSEC3 is covered under DNSSEC, and the document only requires validators to handle it.
DNS is the underlying system; DNSSEC is the more specific tag and its ancestors are implied.

RFC6606.title: Problem Statement and Requirements for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) Routing
