RFC6606.summary: Informational problem statement and requirements document for routing (route-over and mesh-under) in 6LoWPAN networks over IEEE 802.15.4, listing requirements R01-R18 on device, link, network, security, and management properties.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document is about routing requirements for 6LoWPAN networks, including route-over and mesh-under approaches over IEEE 802.15.4 and the adaptation layer.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document provides the problem statement and design space for 6LoWPAN routing.  It defines the routing requirements for 6LoWPANs

RPL.why: Requirements for routing in low-power lossy networks are explicitly input to ROLL, the home of RPL. Readers of RPL would want this requirements background. RPL itself is not specified here, so this is secondary.
RPL.quote: This document is intended as input to groups working on routing protocols relevant to 6LoWPANs, such as the IETF ROLL WG.

rejected.why: IPsec is discussed in Section 5.4 only as being too heavyweight for 6LoWPAN nodes. It is not specified or profiled.
Ad hoc routing is mentioned as background, but the document is about low-power wireless personal area networks, not MANET protocols.
ND threats are mentioned briefly in the security discussion, but the document is not about ND.
The document covers routing requirements for one network type. The 6LoWPAN and RPL tags are more specific.
IPv6 is the network layer the document works on, but it is not the document's subject. 6LoWPAN is the more specific tag.

RFC6607.title: Virtual Subnet Selection Options for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6
RFC6607.summary: Defines the DHCPv4 Virtual Subnet Selection option, the DHCPv6 VSS option, and the DHCPv4 VSS and VSS-Control Relay Agent Information sub-options, so clients, relays and proxies can tell DHCP servers which VPN to allocate addresses from; also updates RFC 3046 sub-option echoing.

DHCP.why: The document specifies new DHCPv4 options and Relay Agent Information sub-options, including client, relay and server behaviour and the update to RFC 3046. DHCP is the protocol being extended.
DHCP.quote: This memo defines a DHCPv4 Virtual Subnet Selection (VSS) option, a DHCPv6 VSS option, and the DHCPv4 VSS and VSS-Control sub-options

DHCPv6.why: It defines OPTION_VSS (68) for DHCPv6, with relay agent, client and server behaviour, including prefix delegation. This is a substantial part of the document.
DHCPv6.quote: a DHCPv6 VSS option defined in this document should be included in the Relay-forward and Relay-reply messages

rejected.why: The VPN tag covers provider-provisioned VPN technology. VPNs here are only the context that determines the address space, and the document specifies no VPN mechanism.
The IANA section registers option codes and a VSS Type sub-registry. That is boilerplate and not the main subject.
Address allocation is the purpose, but the document is about DHCP options rather than IP address architecture. The DHCP tags cover it.
NVT ASCII is only used as one encoding of the VPN identifier.

RFC6608.title: Subcodes for BGP Finite State Machine Error
RFC6608.summary: Defines subcodes for the BGP Finite State Machine Error NOTIFICATION code (unexpected message in OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established states), updates RFC 4271, and creates an IANA registry for them.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP error signalling by defining FSM Error subcodes and requiring implementations to send them in NOTIFICATION messages, updating RFC 4271.
BGP.quote: This document defines several subcodes for the BGP [RFC4271] Finite State Machine (FSM) Error that could provide more information to help network operators

rejected.why: The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-like support for the BGP subcodes; the document is not about IANA registry guidance itself.
Subcodes aid operator diagnosis, but the document specifies protocol error signalling, not management practice.
Security Considerations only notes fingerprinting; the document is not about securing routing.

RFC6609.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Include Extension
RFC6609.summary: Defines the Sieve "include" extension, which adds include, return and global commands and a global variables namespace so one Sieve script can include another, from personal or site-wide repositories.

Sieve.why: The whole document specifies a new extension to the Sieve email filtering language, including its commands, variable scoping and interaction with other Sieve extensions.
Sieve.quote: The Sieve Email Filtering "include" extension permits users to include one Sieve script inside another.

rejected.why: Email is only the domain where Sieve runs. The document is about the filtering script language, which is already covered by the more specific Sieve tag.
Scripts examine headers such as List-ID, but the document says nothing about the message format itself.
The IANA section only registers the Sieve extension capability. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.

RFC6610.title: DHCP Options for Home Information Discovery in Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6)
RFC6610.summary: Defines new DHCPv6 options that let a Mobile IPv6 mobile node discover its home agent address, home agent FQDN, or home network prefix, with client, relay and server behaviour.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines new DHCPv6 options and specifies client, relay agent and server behaviour for them, so it extends DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies extensions to DHCPv6 [RFC3736] [RFC3315] to deliver the home agent information to the mobile node

Mobile IPv6.why: The purpose is bootstrapping Mobile IPv6 by discovering home agent and home network information, which supplements the RFC 6275 home agent discovery.
Mobile IPv6.quote: New DHCP options are defined that allow a mobile node to request the home agent IP address, Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN), or home network prefix

rejected.why: FQDNs are carried in options and resolved to A/AAAA records, but the document defines nothing new about DNS.
The document refers to the RFC 5447 NAS/AAA interaction, but only briefly in Section 4.4, and it does not define AAA behaviour.
IPv4-Embedded IPv6 addresses (RFC 6052) are used only to reach a home agent over IPv4, and this is incidental.
The DHCPv6 tag is more specific and fits better.

RFC6611.title: Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) Bootstrapping for the Integrated Scenario
RFC6611.summary: Defines how a Mobile IPv6 mobile node discovers its home agent in the integrated scenario (access and mobility authorizer are the same), using DHCPv6 options with AAA-supplied home agent info relayed by the NAS/DHCP relay.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document specifies Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping (home agent address discovery) for the integrated scenario, so it belongs on the Mobile IPv6 page.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document defines the MIPv6 bootstrapping procedures for the integrated scenario.

DHCPv6.why: The core mechanism is DHCPv6 exchange, with relay agent and server behaviour using the RFC 6610 options, specified in the body.
DHCPv6.quote: the mobile node sends a DHCPv6 Information-request message [RFC3315] to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address.
DHCPv6.section: 4.2.1. Home Agent Allocation in the MSP

AAA.why: AAAH assigns the home agent and passes it to the NAS via AAA, and the document specifies the interworking among NAS, DHCP and AAA entities.
AAA.quote: It enables home agent assignment in the integrated scenario by utilizing DHCP and Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) protocols.

rejected.why: Diameter (RFC 5447 AVPs) is only the AAA transport used; the document defines nothing new about it.
IPsec SA setup is mentioned only as a bootstrapping component handled per RFC 5026, not addressed here.
DNS-based home agent discovery is only mentioned as the fallback defined in RFC 5026.
IKEv2 SA bootstrapping is referenced to RFC 5026 in one short section; not the subject.

RFC6612.title: Interactions between Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) and Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6): Scenarios and Related Issues
RFC6612.summary: Informational RFC analysing scenarios where Proxy Mobile IPv6 and Mobile IPv6 are deployed together (hierarchical, inter-domain roaming, mixed node types), identifying binding cache, race-condition and security issues, and recommending HA/LMA handling.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document analyses PMIPv6 interactions with MIPv6, including LMA/MAG behaviour and binding cache handling.
PMIPv6.quote: PMIPv6 and MIPv6 will always create two different BCEs in the HA/LMA, which implies that the HA and LMA are logically separated.

Mobile IPv6.why: MIPv6 home agent behaviour, bootstrapping and binding updates are analysed together with PMIPv6, so MIPv6 is equally a subject.
Mobile IPv6.quote: it is recommended that when the MIPv6 home link is implemented as a PMIPv6 domain, the HA/LMA implementation treat the two protocols as independent.

rejected.why: IPsec SA establishment via IKEv2 is mentioned only as a MIPv6 bootstrapping step, not the subject.
IKEv2 attributes are referenced for HoA assignment but the document defines nothing new about IKE.
Mentioned only as one way to discover the HA/LMA, with details out of scope.
Only the R bit from NEMO is mentioned in passing.
Parent of the specific tags chosen, so it is implied.
DNS is only mentioned as a discovery option for the HA/LMA.

RFC6613.title: RADIUS over TCP
RFC6613.summary: Experimental RFC defining RADIUS carried over TCP (RADIUS/TCP), to be used only under TLS or IPsec, specifying port usage, watchdog/liveness detection, retransmission, connection-closing rules, ID limits and EAP session handling.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies changes to RADIUS for a new transport, including packet handling, ports, Status-Server watchdog and EAP session handling.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines RADIUS over the Transmission Control Protocol (RADIUS/TCP)

transport mapping.why: It is a binding of an application protocol to TCP, with transport-specific issues such as head-of-line blocking, retransmission and connection closure. TCP itself is not specified, so the transport mapping topic fits better than the TCP tag.
transport mapping.quote: RADIUS/TCP involves sending RADIUS application messages over a TCP connection.

rejected.why: TCP is the substrate that RADIUS is carried over. The document does not define or extend TCP.
RADIUS/TLS is defined in RFC 6614. This document only requires a secure layer such as TLS and does not specify TLS.
IPsec is mentioned only as an alternative secure layer under bare TCP.
EAP over RADIUS is discussed for session handling, but the document is not about EAP or its methods.
The MIB section only states that the existing RADIUS MIBs do not cover TCP. No MIB is defined.
Congestion issues for proxies are discussed briefly, but the document does not specify any congestion control mechanism.

RFC6614.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Encryption for RADIUS
RFC6614.summary: RFC 6614 specifies a transport profile for RADIUS over TLS on TCP port 2083 (RadSec), covering connection setup, mutual authentication models, client identity and packet handling, to secure RADIUS between peers.

RADIUS.why: The document defines how RADIUS packets are carried over TLS, including packet type rules, the fixed shared secret and compatibility with other RADIUS transports. It is a RADIUS specification.
RADIUS.quote: This document specifies a transport profile for RADIUS using Transport Layer Security (TLS) over TCP as the transport protocol.

TLS.why: A large part of the document sets TLS requirements for RADIUS: minimum versions, mandatory mutual authentication, ciphersuites, PSK, and certificate validation and trust models. This is deployment profile guidance for TLS readers.
TLS.quote: immediately negotiate TLS sessions according to [RFC5246] or its predecessor TLS 1.1.

transport mapping.why: The document is a binding of RADIUS onto TLS/TCP. It covers port assignment, stream framing by the Length field, and the differences from UDP transport. This fits the transport mapping topic.
transport mapping.quote: The default destination port number for RADIUS over TLS is TCP/2083.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate here. RADIUS over TCP is specified in RFC 6613, and this document defers to it for connection behaviour.
X.509 certificates are used for peer authentication, but the document relies on RFC 5280 validation and defines no new certificate profile.
Diameter is mentioned only in a short compatibility section, and the document is not about it.
RADIUS over DTLS is only referred to as a separate, related proposal.
PKIX trust models are one of the peer authentication options. The document does not specify PKI mechanisms.
RADIUS is a AAA protocol, but the more specific RADIUS tag already covers this.

RFC6615.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IP Flow Information Export
RFC6615.summary: RFC 6615 defines the IPFIX-MIB and IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB SMIv2 modules for monitoring IPFIX Exporters and Collectors (transport sessions, templates, export groups, metering, observation points, selection processes, statistics), obsoleting RFC 5815.

IPFIX.why: The MIB modules model IPFIX Exporters, Collectors, templates, metering and selection processes, so readers of IPFIX would want this RFC.
IPFIX.quote: This document defines managed objects for IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX).

MIB.why: The document's main content is two SMIv2 MIB modules with tables, objects, compliance and groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies MIB modules that are compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific fit.
Sampling and filtering are referenced but explicitly out of scope; only a placeholder selector function (select all) is defined.
Only referenced as a transport via the SCTP association ID object; the document is not about SCTP.
TCP and UDP appear only as transport protocol values in the session table.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC6616.title: A Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) and Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Mechanism for OpenID
RFC6616.summary: Specifies the OPENID20 SASL mechanism and corresponding GS2-based GSS-API mechanism that let SASL/GSS-API applications authenticate users via existing OpenID 2.0 providers, tunnelling OpenID indirect messages through the SASL exchange.

SASL.why: The document defines a new SASL mechanism named OPENID20, including message flow, error handling and IANA registration in the SASL Mechanisms registry.
SASL.quote: This memo specifies a SASL and GSS-API mechanism for OpenID that allows the integration of existing OpenID Identity Providers with applications using SASL and GSS-API.

GSS-API.why: It defines a GSS-API mechanism with an OID, name types, context flags and mechanism attributes, so GSS-API readers need it.
GSS-API.quote: The OpenID SASL mechanism is actually also a GSS-API mechanism.

federated authentication.why: The mechanism integrates a cross-domain web single sign-on/identity provider system (OpenID) with non-web protocols, with relying party and OP roles; readers of federated authentication would want it.
federated authentication.quote: OpenID 2.0 [OpenID] is a web-based three-party protocol that provides a means for a user to offer identity assertions and other attributes

rejected.why: TLS is only required as the protecting channel and for server certificate validation; nothing new is defined about TLS.
IMAP is used only as the example application protocol; the document does not extend or profile it.
OpenID flows over HTTP via the browser, but the document does not specify HTTP itself.
URIs are used to encode the OpenID messages, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
Covered by the more specific SASL, GSS-API and federated authentication tags.

gaps.name: OpenID 2.0
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the OpenID web single sign-on protocol itself, which this document profiles for SASL/GSS-API use.

RFC6617.title: Secure Pre-Shared Key (PSK) Authentication for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE)
RFC6617.summary: RFC 6617 defines an experimental IKEv2 authentication method that uses the Dragonfly password-authenticated key exchange, so weak pre-shared keys resist dictionary attack.

Dragonfly.why: The document specifies the Dragonfly balanced PAKE (hunting-and-pecking SKE, Commit payloads) and its use in IKE.
Dragonfly.quote: The key exchange described in this memo is based on the "Dragonfly" key exchange, which has also been defined for use in 802.11 wireless networks

IKE.why: It extends IKEv2 with a new authentication method. It adds a Commit round trip in IKE_AUTH and changes the AUTH computation.
IKE.quote: This memo describes a secure pre-shared key (PSK) authentication method for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE).

rejected.why: IPsec is the context IKE negotiates for. The document is about IKE authentication, so the IKE tag fits better.
This is the parent of Dragonfly, so it is implied and not listed separately.
ECP groups are used as the discrete-log setting, but the document is not about elliptic curve cryptography itself.
HMAC-SHA256 and the prf are only building blocks used in the exchange.
EAP-pwd (RFC 5931) is only mentioned as another use of Dragonfly.
SASLprep/stringprep preprocessing of passwords is a minor detail, not a main subject.

RFC6618.title: Mobile IPv6 Security Framework Using Transport Layer Security for Communication between the Mobile Node and Home Agent
RFC6618.summary: Experimental RFC defining an alternative Mobile IPv6 security framework in which a Home Agent Controller bootstraps MN-HA security associations, keys and MIPv6 parameters over a TLS session, with UDP-encapsulated protected signaling and data between the MN and HA.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document specifies how Mobile IPv6 MN-HA signaling and data are secured, including new packet formats, a BA status code and bootstrapping parameters.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document proposes an alternate security framework for Mobile IPv6 and Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6

TLS.why: TLS is used as the keying and bootstrapping mechanism, with channel binding (tls-server-endpoint) and a ciphersuite subset mapping. This is a substantive part of the design, though TLS itself is unchanged.
TLS.quote: relies on a secure TLS session established between the MN and the HAC for mutual authentication and MN-HA security association bootstrapping

rejected.why: The document replaces IKE/IPsec for MN-HA security. It only borrows ESP packet field rules and is not about IPsec.
IKEv2 is the alternative being avoided, not something specified or extended here.
EAP messages are carried transparently as one authentication option. No EAP method is defined.
UDP is only the encapsulation substrate for the MN-HA packets.
HAC-to-AAA interworking is explicitly out of scope.
Key bootstrapping is central, but the specific Mobile IPv6 tag is the better fit. A generic key management tag would be redundant.
The document concerns host-based Mobile IPv6, not network-based mobility.

RFC6619.title: Scalable Operation of Address Translators with Per-Interface Bindings
RFC6619.summary: Specifies that a NAT manage its mappings per internal interface so that many point-to-point-connected users can reuse the same private IPv4 addresses, letting large networks scale NAT without needing large private address space.

NAT.why: The document specifies a NAT behaviour variant (per-interface mappings) enabling scalable deployment of address translators.
NAT.quote: a NAT MUST manage its mappings on a per-interface basis, by associating a particular NAT session not only with the five tuples

CGN.why: The problem addressed is large-scale carrier/provider NAT deployment serving millions of subscribers, such as cellular gateways and consumer broadband.
CGN.quote: Networks that serve more than 2^24 (16 million) users cannot assign a unique private IPv4 address to each user

rejected.why: IPv6 coexistence is discussed in one short section as deployment context, but the document is about NAT binding behaviour.
Stateful NAT64 (RFC 6146) is only mentioned as a deployment model where per-interface mappings are generally unnecessary.
RFC 6333 is cited as a tunneling-based alternative; this document explicitly avoids tunneling.
PPP, PPPoE and ATM PVCs are examples of point-to-point links, not subjects of the document.
IPv4 address exhaustion is motivation, but the document is about NAT mapping, not IPv4 itself.

RFC6620.title: FCFS SAVI: First-Come, First-Served Source Address Validation Improvement for Locally Assigned IPv6 Addresses
RFC6620.summary: RFC 6620 specifies FCFS SAVI, a first-come-first-served mechanism in which switches bind IPv6 source addresses to switch-port anchors, using Neighbor Discovery DAD messages to validate local-link traffic and drop spoofed packets.

SAVI.why: The document specifies FCFS SAVI, a Source Address Validation Improvement solution, including binding anchors, protection perimeter, trusted/validating ports and the state machine.
SAVI.quote: a mechanism that provides source address validation for IPv6 networks using the FCFS principle

neighbor discovery.why: The mechanism is built on ND NS/NA, DAD and Router Advertisement processing. It also discusses interaction with SEND. Much of the specification is about how devices handle and generate ND messages.
neighbor discovery.quote: FCFS SAVI uses NS and NA messages to preserve the coherency of the FCFS SAVI binding state distributed among the FCFS SAVI devices

rejected.why: SLAAC and DAD are the address-configuration context the mechanism observes. The document does not specify or extend SLAAC.
SEND is mentioned only in one short section, which recommends using SAVI-SEND instead. The document is not about SEND.
DHCPv6-assigned addresses are only mentioned as being handled by a separate SAVI-DHCP mechanism.
IPv6 is the environment the mechanism operates in. The document does not specify IPv6 itself.
The mechanism runs on L2 switches and uses switch ports as anchors, but it does not specify Ethernet behaviour.
MLD snooping and group joins are minor implementation details. MLD is not a tag in the taxonomy anyway, and the nearest candidate, multicast, is not the subject.

RFC6621.title: Simplified Multicast Forwarding
RFC6621.summary: Specifies Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) for MANETs: duplicate packet detection for IPv4/IPv6 (including an IPv6 SMF_DPD hop-by-hop option), classic flooding and reduced relay set selection (E-CDS, S-MPR, MPR-CDS), NHDP TLVs, and border router considerations.

MANET.why: SMF is a MANET multicast forwarding protocol with relay set selection algorithms (E-CDS, S-MPR, MPR-CDS) for ad hoc networks; no MANET multicast-specific tag exists, so the MANET routing parent fits.
MANET.quote: provides basic Internet Protocol (IP) multicast forwarding suitable for limited wireless mesh and mobile ad hoc network (MANET) use

NHDP.why: The document defines SMF-specific NHDP TLVs and neighborhood discovery requirements for relay set selection, a substantial part of the specification.
NHDP.quote: "SMF_TYPE" and "SMF_NBR_TYPE" Message and Address Block TLV structures (per [RFC5444]) are defined by this document for use with NHDP

multicast.why: The document is about IP multicast forwarding, including border router interaction with PIM, IGMP/MLD proxying and scoping; a general multicast tag fits since no child covers MANET multicast forwarding.
multicast.quote: Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) extends the efficient flooding concept to the data forwarding plane, providing an appropriate multicast forwarding capability

rejected.why: MPR relay selection is borrowed from OLSR, but the document does not specify or extend OLSR.
PIM is only an external multicast protocol that border routers interoperate with; it is not specified here.
The IPv6 SMF_DPD hop-by-hop option is part of DPD, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
IGMP/MLD proxying is mentioned only as out-of-scope future work.
IPsec sequence numbers are only used as DPD identifiers, so IPsec is not the subject.
SHA-1 is used only as a hash for duplicate detection, not as a cryptographic subject.

gaps.name: Duplicate packet detection / flooding for MANET multicast (SMF)
gaps.why: No tag covers MANET multicast forwarding or flooding specifically, and the RFC defines the SMF_DPD IPv6 option and relay set algorithms.

RFC6622.title: Integrity Check Value and Timestamp TLV Definitions for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs)
RFC6622.summary: Defines ICV (digital signature/MAC) and Timestamp TLVs for RFC 5444 packets, messages and address blocks in MANET routing protocols, with a hash-plus-cryptographic-function ICV structure and IANA registries.

MANET.why: The document defines security TLVs for the RFC 5444 format used by MANET routing protocols such as NHDP and OLSRv2, so it belongs under MANET. No more specific child tag (OLSR, NHDP) is specified by it.
MANET.quote: general and flexible TLVs for representing cryptographic Integrity Check Values (ICVs) (i.e., digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs)) as well as timestamps

rejected.why: NHDP is only mentioned as an example of a protocol that can reject messages with invalid ICVs. The document does not specify it.
OLSRv2 is only an informative example of a protocol that could use these TLVs. The document is not about it.
HMAC is only one entry in the cryptographic function registry. The document is not about it.
The SHA family appears only as initial entries in the hash function registry.
The NTP timestamp format is only one of the timestamp type extensions. The document does not specify NTP.
The document supplies a syntax for integrity values and defines no authentication mechanism. MANET is the better fit.

gaps.name: RFC 5444 packet/message format (generalized MANET packet format)
gaps.why: The document extends this TLV-based format, but the taxonomy has no tag for it apart from the general MANET tag.

RFC6623.title: IANA Registry for MEDIACTRL Interactive Voice Response Control Package
RFC6623.summary: Creates the IANA registry of status codes for the MEDIACTRL Interactive Voice Response (IVR) Control Package from RFC 6231, copying the existing codes into a registry with Standards Action policy.

real-time communications.why: The document concerns the MEDIACTRL IVR control package, a media server control mechanism for real-time voice and media. No narrower tag fits, so the topic tag is used directly.
real-time communications.quote: This document creates an IANA registry for the response codes for the MEDIACTRL Interactive Voice Response Control Package

IANA.why: The whole document exists to create a registry and set its assignment policy (Standards Action), so readers of IANA registries would want it.
IANA.quote: IANA has created the "MEDIACTRL Interactive Voice Response Control Package Status Codes" registry per this document.

rejected.why: MRCP is a different speech-services control protocol. The MEDIACTRL IVR package is not MRCP.
Some status codes mention conferences, but the document is about the IVR package's status codes, not conferencing frameworks.
The status codes refer to XML schema elements, but XML is only the encoding of the underlying package and is not what this document is about.
The Media Control Channel Framework is typically set up with SIP, but this document doesn't specify or discuss SIP.

gaps.name: MEDIACTRL (Media Control Channel Framework and IVR control package)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the media server control framework and its packages, so the document can only be placed under the general real-time communications topic.

RFC6624.title: Layer 2 Virtual Private Networks Using BGP for Auto-Discovery and Signaling
RFC6624.summary: RFC 6624 describes how to offer point-to-point Layer 2 VPNs (VPWS) over an IP/MPLS provider network, using BGP for auto-discovery and signaling as in RFC 4761. It adds Encaps Types, a circuit status vector TLV, and IP-only Layer 2 interworking.

L2VPN.why: The whole document specifies L2VPN (VPWS) operation, configuration, PE information exchange and interworking over a shared provider network.
L2VPN.quote: This document presents a new approach to the problem of offering L2VPN services where the L2VPN customer's experience is virtually identical to that offered by traditional L2VPNs

BGP.why: The document extends BGP L2VPN NLRI and the L2-info extended community with new Encaps Types and TLVs, and creates two BGP IANA registries.
BGP.quote: it advertises to other PEs the fact that it is participating in a VPN via BGP messages, as per [RFC4761], Section 3.

rejected.why: VPLS is the multipoint predecessor (RFC 4761) that this document builds on. The document itself covers point-to-point VPWS.
Pseudowires and the RFC 4448/4618/4619/4717 encapsulations are reused for transport but not defined here.
MPLS labels serve as the demultiplexor and the tunnel substrate, but the document is not about MPLS itself.
RFC 4364 L3VPNs appear only as a comparison and as the source of RDs and RTs.
The OAM section is brief and only covers carrying circuit status, so it is not a main subject.
Diffserv is mentioned only as a benefit of IP-only interworking.

RFC6625.title: Wildcards in Multicast VPN Auto-Discovery Routes
RFC6625.summary: RFC 6625 updates RFC 6514 to let MVPN S-PMSI auto-discovery routes carry wildcard (C-*,C-G), (C-S,C-*) and (C-*,C-*) flow identifiers, so one BGP route can bind many customer multicast flows to a single provider tunnel, and it gives the encoding, matching rules and procedures.

MVPN.why: The whole document extends Multicast VPN S-PMSI A-D routes with wildcard encodings and procedures, so it belongs on the MVPN page.
MVPN.quote: This document eliminates these restrictions by specifying the use of "wildcard" elements in the customer flow identifiers.

rejected.why: BGP only carries the MCAST-VPN NLRI. The document defines no new BGP protocol behaviour beyond the MVPN route encoding.
PIM is the customer-side protocol and is referenced for terminology (C-RP, shared trees). The document does not specify or extend it.
BGP/MPLS VPNs are the base for MVPN, but this document is about the multicast extension, which MVPN covers.
P-tunnels can be MPLS LSPs, but the document does not address MPLS itself.
The more specific MVPN tag already covers the subject.

RFC6626.title: Dynamic Prefix Allocation for Network Mobility for Mobile IPv4 (NEMOv4)
RFC6626.summary: RFC 6626 extends NEMOv4 so a Mobile Router can request, and the home agent can dynamically allocate, mobile network prefixes by sending a zero Prefix field in the Mobile Network Request extension.

NEMO.why: The document specifies dynamic mobile prefix allocation for NEMOv4, updating RFC 5177 (NEMO extensions for Mobile IPv4). Network mobility is the subject. NEMO is the most specific tag; Mobile IPv4 is a sibling under IP mobility.
NEMO.quote: the Prefix field of the Mobile Network Request extension MUST be set to zero to indicate that the Mobile Router requests mobile network prefix(es) be assigned to it by the home agent

Mobile IPv4.why: The mechanism is an extension to Mobile IPv4 registration request and reply messages, binding caches, NAI extension and home address allocation. Mobile IPv4 readers would want it.
Mobile IPv4.quote: A home agent receiving a Mobile Network Request extension with the Prefix field set to zero MAY return a Mobile Network Acknowledgement extension

rejected.why: Prefix allocation is done by the home agent in Mobile IPv4 registration. DHCP is not used or specified.
Prefix allocation is part of the mobility protocol extension. The document does not address IP address architecture in general.
IPv4 is only the network layer of Mobile IPv4. The document is not about IPv4 itself.

RFC6627.title: Overview of Pre-Congestion Notification Encoding
RFC6627.summary: Informational overview of the PCN working group's explored approaches for encoding pre-congestion marks (NM, ThM, ETM) in the IP DS and ECN fields, with the constraints (DSCP scarcity, tunneling rules) and a comparison of baseline, 3-in-1, 3-in-2 and PSDM encodings.

PCN.why: The whole document is about Pre-Congestion Notification encoding, its marking schemes (DM, SM, PSDM), and encoding options.
PCN.quote: The PCN working group explored a number of approaches for encoding this pre-congestion information into the IP header.

ECN.why: A substantial part analyses redefining the ECN field for PCN and ECN tunneling rules (RFC 6040) constraints.
ECN.quote: The ECN field may be redefined for other purposes and [RFC4774] gives guidelines for that.

Diffserv.why: PCN operates within a Diffserv domain and the DS field/DSCP constraints and tunneling models are a major section.
Diffserv.quote: PCN encoding should use only one additional DSCP for each DSCP originally used to indicate the PHB

rejected.why: IPsec tunneling is discussed only as one tunneling case affecting encoding, not the subject.
Tunneling rules are constraints on the encoding, not the document's subject in its own right.
Mentioned only as an example signaling protocol for PSDM admission requests.
Mentioned only as a layer with few DSCP bits; not discussed in substance.
Ancestor of PCN/Diffserv, implied by more specific tags.

RFC6628.title: Efficient Augmented Password-Only Authentication and Key Exchange for IKEv2
RFC6628.summary: Specifies AugPAKE, an efficient augmented password-authenticated key exchange protocol, and describes its integration into IKEv2 as a secure password authentication method with a notify payload and GSPM payload.

PAKE.why: The document's core is the AugPAKE augmented PAKE protocol, its specification and security analysis against dictionary attacks and server compromise.
PAKE.quote: This document describes an efficient augmented password-only authentication and key exchange (AugPAKE) protocol where a user remembers a low-entropy password and its verifier is registered

IKE.why: A substantial part defines how AugPAKE plugs into IKEv2: extra round trip, SECURE_PASSWORD_METHODS notify, GSPM payload and AUTH computation.
IKE.quote: The AugPAKE protocol, described in Section 2, can be easily integrated into IKEv2 [RFC5996] as a "weak" pre-shared key authentication method

rejected.why: SRP is only compared against for efficiency; the document does not specify or extend it.
IKEv2 is the specific subject; IPsec is only the surrounding context.
SASLprep is merely used for password preprocessing.
Another PAKE used in IKE, but not discussed here.
Parent of PAKE and IKE; the more specific tags apply.
IANA section only registers a method value; boilerplate.

RFC6629.title: Considerations on the Application of the Level 3 Multihoming Shim Protocol for IPv6 (Shim6)
RFC6629.summary: Informational applicability statement for Shim6 (RFC 5533/5534) site multihoming in IPv6, covering addresses (CGA/HBA), capabilities, application impact, and interactions with MIPv6, SEND, SCTP/MPTCP, NEMO, HIP, firewalls and NPTv6.

Shim6.why: The whole document analyses how and where Shim6 applies: deployment scenarios, capabilities, and interactions with other protocols.
Shim6.quote: This document discusses some considerations on the applicability of the level 3 multihoming Shim protocol for IPv6 (Shim6)

rejected.why: Section 7.1 discusses Shim6 interaction with MIPv6, but MIPv6 is only one of several interacting protocols, not the document's subject.
Section 7.5 compares Shim6 with HIP, but it is a comparison, not a document about HIP.
Only a short subsection on CGA sharing between SEND and Shim6.
Mentioned as an alternative and a recommended non-use alongside Shim6 in one subsection; the document is not about MPTCP.
One short subsection on interaction only.
Shim6 is the more specific child tag and already covers the multihoming subject.

gaps.name: CGA/HBA (Cryptographically Generated Addresses, Hash-Based Addresses)
gaps.why: Section 3 compares CGA and HBA for securing locator sets, but the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC6630.title: EAP Re-authentication Protocol Extensions for Authenticated Anticipatory Keying (ERP/AAK)
RFC6630.summary: RFC 6630 extends the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) with Authenticated Anticipatory Keying, defining a new E flag, TLVs, and a key hierarchy (pRK/pMSK) so a peer can pre-establish keys on candidate attachment points before handover.

HOKEY.why: The document extends ERP (the EAP Re-authentication Protocol) with new flags, TLVs and key derivation. It is a HOKEY working group product, so the HOKEY/ERP tag fits.
HOKEY.quote: This document specifies the extensions necessary to enable AAK support in ERP.

EAP.why: It extends EAP-Initiate/EAP-Finish packets and the EAP keying hierarchy (EMSK/DSRK-derived keys). Readers of EAP would want it, but HOKEY is the more specific child tag.
EAP.quote: ERP/AAK reuses the packet format defined by ERP, but specifies a new flag to differentiate EAP early authentication from EAP re-authentication.

rejected.why: AAA transport of pMSK is mentioned, but only as a substrate and the Diameter application is left to other documents.
The AAA infrastructure is used to transport keys, but the document only says a new AAA message should be specified elsewhere.
HMAC-SHA256 cryptosuites are used for the authentication tag, but only as a mechanism.
The document does define key derivation, but the more specific HOKEY tag covers this.
IDNA is cited only for the realm part of the NAI, a passing reference.

RFC6631.title: Password Authenticated Connection Establishment with the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC6631.summary: Experimental RFC adapting the PACE password-authenticated key exchange to IKEv2 as a new password authentication mode, defining new notifications, a GSPM payload, and optional conversion of the password into a long-term PSK.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new authentication mode, defining new notify types (PSK_PERSIST, PSK_CONFIRM), a payload, and exchange changes.
IKE.quote: This document describes the integration of PACE into IKEv2 [RFC5996] as a new authentication mode, analogous to the existing certificate and Pre-Shared Key (PSK) authentication modes.

PAKE.why: PACE is a password-authenticated key exchange, and the document specifies it for IKEv2. No specific PAKE child tag exists for PACE, so the parent PAKE tag is used.
PAKE.quote: PACE belongs to a family of protocols often referred to as Zero-Knowledge Password Proof (ZKPP) protocols, all of which amplify weak passwords into strong session keys.

rejected.why: IKEv2 sets up IPsec SAs, but the document is about the IKE authentication exchange. The IKE tag already covers it.
EAP is mentioned only as the alternative approach the document compares itself to, not specified here.
The long-term PSK generation is part of the IKE and PAKE material, so the parent topic is not needed.
Password processing uses SASLprep, but only briefly in one subsection. It is not a main subject.
SASLprep is only a string preparation profile that the document references. SASL is not specified or used.
ECDH is one supported variant of the mapping but is not the subject of the document.

RFC6632.title: An Overview of the IETF Network Management Standards
RFC6632.summary: An informational overview of IETF Standards Track network management protocols (SNMP, syslog, IPFIX/PSAMP, NETCONF/YANG, RADIUS, Diameter, CAPWAP, ANCP, ACAP, XCAP) and data models, classified for orientation including an FCAPS view.

network management.why: The document is a cross-protocol survey and classification of network management standards, which is the general topic.
network management.quote: This document gives an overview of the IETF network management standards and summarizes existing and ongoing development of IETF Standards Track network management protocols and data models.

SNMP.why: Substantial section covering SNMP architecture, versions, USM, VACM and transport models.
SNMP.quote: The SNMPv3 Framework [RFC3410], builds upon both the original SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 Frameworks.

MIB.why: SMI and many MIB modules are surveyed in Section 4 by layer and FCAPS task.
MIB.quote: SNMP MIB modules are defined with the notation and grammar specified as the Structure of Managed Information (SMI).

syslog.why: Dedicated section on the syslog protocol, its structured data, transports and signing.
syslog.quote: Syslog is a mechanism for distribution of logging information initially used on Unix systems

IPFIX.why: Dedicated section on IPFIX and PSAMP, including the information model and mediation.
IPFIX.quote: defines a push-based data export mechanism for transferring IP flow information in a compact binary format from an Exporter to a Collector.

NETCONF.why: Core protocol section covering NETCONF, notifications, transports and NACM.
NETCONF.quote: The NETCONF protocol [RFC6241] provides mechanisms to install, manipulate, and delete the configuration of network devices

YANG.why: Dedicated section describing YANG properties and related RFCs.
YANG.quote: the NETMOD working group developed a data modeling language defining the semantics of operational and configuration data, notifications, and operations [RFC6020].

RADIUS.why: A long section surveys RADIUS and its extensions.
RADIUS.quote: describes a client/server protocol for carrying authentication, authorization, and configuration information between a Network Access Server (NAS)

Diameter.why: The longest protocol section surveys Diameter and its applications.
Diameter.quote: Diameter [RFC3588] provides an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) framework for applications such as network access or IP mobility.

performance measurement.why: Covers IPPM metrics, OWAMP and TWAMP, plus performance management models.
performance measurement.quote: The IPPM working group has defined metrics for accurately measuring and reporting the quality, performance, and reliability of Internet data delivery.

CAPWAP.quote: the CAPWAP working group developed the CAPWAP protocol [RFC5415] to facilitate control, management, and provisioning of WTPs

ANCP.quote: The Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) [RFC6320] realizes a control plane between a service-oriented Layer 3 edge device, the NAS and a Layer 2 Access Node

ACAP.quote: The Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) [RFC2244] is designed to support remote storage and access of program option, configuration, and preference information.

DHCP.why: DHCP is covered as an IP address management mechanism.
DHCP.quote: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) [RFC2131] provides a framework for passing configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network

COPS.why: Covers COPS-PR and its non-recommendation.
COPS.quote: COPS-PR [RFC3084] uses the Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol [RFC2748] for the provisioning of policy information.

energy management.quote: Energy management is becoming an additional requirement for network management systems due to several factors including the rising and fluctuating energy costs

rejected.why: The document explicitly excludes data-path OAM and refers to other overview documents.
Policy framework is covered only briefly in one subsection, under COPS.
The V6OPS list in Section 3.2 is a brief pointer list, not a substantial part of the document.
TLS is only a transport and security substrate for SNMP, syslog, RADIUS and NETCONF.
RMON appears within the data model survey but is not a major focus.
SASL is only mentioned as ACAP's authentication mechanism.

gaps.name: XCAP (XML Configuration Access Protocol)
gaps.why: Section 3.10 covers XCAP, but the taxonomy has no XCAP tag. SIMPLE is the closest fit and was not applied because the document treats XCAP as a configuration protocol.

RFC6633.title: Deprecation of ICMP Source Quench Messages
RFC6633.summary: Standards Track document that formally deprecates ICMP Source Quench messages, requiring hosts, routers and transports (TCP, UDP, SCTP, DCCP) to ignore them and updating RFC 792, 1122 and 1812.

ICMP.why: The document is about the ICMP Source Quench message type: it deprecates it, updates the ICMP specification and host/router requirements, and IANA marks ICMP type 4 as Deprecated.
ICMP.quote: This document formally deprecates the use of ICMP Source Quench messages by transport protocols, formally updating RFC 792, RFC 1122, and RFC 1812.

congestion control.why: Source Quench was a congestion control mechanism; the document explains why it is abandoned in favour of transport-level congestion control and ECN. Readers of congestion control history would want it.
congestion control.quote: ICMP Source Quench has been known to be an ineffective (and unfair) antidote for congestion

rejected.why: TCP is one of the transports told to discard Source Quench, but the document does not specify or extend TCP; it updates only how received ICMP messages are handled.
ECN is cited only as the direction the IETF moved toward, not something the document specifies or analyses.
UDP, SCTP and DCCP get a short clarification that they must discard Source Quench, which is incidental to the ICMP deprecation.
SCTP gets only a short clarification that it must discard Source Quench, which is incidental.
DCCP gets only a short clarification that it must discard Source Quench, which is incidental.

RFC6635.title: RFC Editor Model (Version 2)
RFC6635.summary: IAB document defining version 2 of the RFC Editor model: the RFC Series Editor, RFC Production Center and RFC Publisher roles, RSOC oversight, and IAOC administrative and contractual relationships, obsoleting RFC 5620.

RFC series.why: The whole document defines how the RFC Series is edited, produced, published and overseen, which is the RFC series topic.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor model divides the responsibilities for the RFC Series into the following components: RFC Series Editor (RSE) RFC Production Center RFC Publisher

rejected.why: It covers IAB/IAOC governance and the contracting structure of the RFC Editor. It does not cover the IETF standards process, so RFC series is the better fit.
IANA is mentioned only in coordination duties of the Production Center and in the IANA Considerations boilerplate, which says no action is needed.
RFC 3777 is cited only to explain the appointment cycle. The document does not address NomCom procedures.

RFC6636.title: Tuning the Behavior of the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) for Routers in Mobile and Wireless Networks
RFC6636.summary: Informational guideline for tuning IGMPv3/MLDv2 router parameters (query interval, response interval, last member query count, startup interval, robustness variable) and explicit tracking for mobile and wireless networks.

IGMP.why: The whole document recommends settings for IGMPv3 queries, timers and counters on routers, so IGMP readers would want it.
IGMP.quote: This document describes ways to tune IGMPv3 and MLDv2 protocol behavior -- on the multicast router and proxy side

MLD.why: MLDv2 is tuned in parallel with IGMPv3 throughout, with MLD-specific values such as Maximum Response Code and LLQT.
MLD.quote: This document describes ways to tune IGMPv3 and MLDv2 protocol behavior -- on the multicast router and proxy side

rejected.why: Proxy Mobile IPv6 is only a deployment scenario for the tuning advice, not the subject of the document.
Mobile IPv6 appears only as a tunnelled deployment scenario in Section 4.6; the document does not specify or extend it.
Source-Specific Multicast is mentioned only in the interoperability discussion; the document does not address it in its own right.
IEEE 802.11b is cited only as an example of a bursty link; the document is not about IP over 802.11.
The IP mobility parent is implied by the mobile deployment context, but the document is about multicast group management tuning, not mobility protocols.

RFC6637.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) in OpenPGP
RFC6637.summary: Defines ECC extension to OpenPGP: ECDSA and ECDH public key algorithms, NIST P-256/P-384/P-521 curves, KDF, AES key wrap, key and message encodings, and compatibility profiles including Suite B.

OpenPGP.why: The document extends the OpenPGP key and Public-Key Encrypted Session Key packet formats and registers new algorithm IDs, so it belongs on the OpenPGP page.
OpenPGP.quote: This document defines an Elliptic Curve Cryptography extension to the OpenPGP public key format

elliptic curve.why: It specifies ECC curves, point encoding, ECDH and the use of ECDSA. This is the main cryptographic content. ECDSA is a child tag, but the document mainly defines ECDH and curve usage, so the parent tag fits better.
elliptic curve.quote: This document references three named prime field curves, defined in [FIPS-186-3] as "Curve P-256", "Curve P-384", and "Curve P-521".

rejected.why: ECDSA is used as defined in FIPS 186-3. The document adds only an algorithm ID and key encoding, and no new signature format. The new work is mostly ECDH.
AES Key Wrap is used as a building block for wrapping session keys, and the document does not define anything new about AES.
SHA-2 hashes are only selected for the KDF and for signatures. The document is not about the hash family.
The ECDH key derivation and wrapping serve OpenPGP message encryption. The document does not address key management in general.
ASN.1 OIDs and DER truncation are used only to name the curves.

RFC6638.title: Scheduling Extensions to CalDAV
RFC6638.summary: Defines the CalDAV "calendar-auto-schedule" feature, in which a CalDAV server performs implicit iTIP-based scheduling (invitations, replies, cancellations, busy-time requests) when clients create, modify or delete calendar resources. It adds scheduling Inbox/Outbox collections, privileges, properties, iCalendar parameters and HTTP headers.

CalDAV.why: The whole document specifies and extends CalDAV with the calendar-auto-schedule feature.
CalDAV.quote: extensions to the Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV (CalDAV) "calendar-access" feature to specify a standard way of performing scheduling operations

iCalendar.why: It defines new iCalendar parameters (SCHEDULE-AGENT, SCHEDULE-FORCE-SEND, SCHEDULE-STATUS), new REQUEST-STATUS codes and IANA registries, and builds on iTIP scheduling.
iCalendar.quote: This specification defines additional iCalendar property parameters to support the CalDAV scheduling extensions.

rejected.why: WebDAV is the substrate: properties, ACL privileges and preconditions are used, but the document is about CalDAV scheduling, not WebDAV itself.
The document defines three new HTTP headers, but only as plumbing for CalDAV scheduling. HTTP is the carrier, not the subject.
TLS is required only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate evidence.
XML is used only as the encoding for WebDAV properties and elements.
iMIP and email are mentioned only as external-user delivery paths, which this specification does not define.

RFC6639.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) MIB-Based Management Overview
RFC6639.summary: Informational overview of the MIB-based management architecture for MPLS-TP, surveying existing MPLS/GMPLS/PW MIB modules, analysing gaps for MPLS-TP, and identifying new MIB modules needed.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document analyses how MPLS-TP tunnels, pseudowires, sections, OAM and protection are managed and which MIB extensions are needed.
MPLS-TP.quote: The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is a packet transport technology based on a profile of the MPLS functionality specific to the construction of packet-switched transport networks.

MIB.why: It describes existing MIB modules, their interdependencies, gaps, and the new MIB modules required.
MIB.quote: This document describes the MIB-based management architecture for MPLS, as extended for MPLS-TP.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB modules; the document is about MIB content, not SNMP itself.
PW MIB modules are covered, but the subject is MIB management of MPLS-TP, so the MPLS-TP and MIB tags fit better.
New BFD MIB extensions are mentioned briefly as a gap, not a substantial part of the document.
GMPLS MIBs are listed as optional context, not the subject.
OAM MIB gaps are one section; MPLS-TP and MIB tags cover the document better.
The parent of MPLS-TP, which is implied.

RFC6640.title: IETF Meeting Attendees' Frequently Asked (Travel) Questions
RFC6640.summary: An informational RFC listing frequently asked travel and local-information questions from IETF meeting attendees, as a checklist for hosts and the Secretariat to pre-populate meeting wikis or sites.

IETF process.why: The document concerns the administration and logistics of IETF meetings, including what hosts and the Secretariat can provide to attendees. This is the closest fit in the taxonomy, under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: frequently asked questions (FAQs) posed by IETF meeting attendees regarding travel logistics and local information

rejected.why: It is a guide for meeting hosts and organizers, not an introductory FYI guide for Internet users, and it is not part of the FYI series.
Public Wi-Fi availability is only one bullet in the communications checklist. The document is not about IP over 802.11.
GSM, LTE and UMTS are mentioned only as examples of local SIM service types to report to attendees.
The document is an RFC but says nothing about RFC format, style or publication.

gaps.name: IETF meeting logistics and attendee travel information
gaps.why: The document is about meeting logistics such as travel, visas, food and local information. The taxonomy has no tag for IETF meetings, so it is placed under IETF process as the nearest fit.

RFC6641.title: Using DNS SRV to Specify a Global File Namespace with NFS Version 4
RFC6641.summary: Defines a DNS SRV service name (_nfs-domainroot._tcp) that lets NFSv4 clients locate an organization's domain-root file system, enabling a global NFS namespace mounted at /nfs4/{domain}.

NFS.why: The document specifies how NFSv4 clients and servers use domain roots, the /.domainroot export path, fs_locations usage and client automount behaviour to build a global NFS namespace.
NFS.quote: This standard defines a mapping from a DNS name to the NFS file system(s) providing the root of the file system namespace associated with that DNS name
NFS.section: 3. Use of the SRV Resource Record in DNS

DNS.why: It defines a new SRV service label (_nfs-domainroot._tcp) and its record usage and client lookup and caching behaviour, which DNS/SRV readers would want. It is a use of an existing RR type rather than a new one, so this is secondary.
DNS.quote: The DNS SRV RR type [RFC2782] is used to locate domain root file servers.
DNS.section: 3. Use of the SRV Resource Record in DNS

rejected.why: The document does discover a service via SRV, but DNS and NFS already cover this. Its subject is the NFS namespace, not service discovery in general.
Section 4.4 explicitly says mDNS is not defined or used here.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended protection. The document is not about DNSSEC.
Domain-based service names are referenced in Security Considerations only, so this is boilerplate evidence.
AFS is cited only as an analogy for the uniform cross-organizational namespace, and the document does not specify AFS.

RFC6642.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extension for a Third-Party Loss Report
RFC6642.summary: Defines two new RTCP feedback messages (transport-layer TLLEI and payload-specific PSLEI Third-Party Loss Reports) that let intermediaries tell RTP receivers to suppress NACK/FIR/PLI feedback, plus SDP rtcp-fb "nack" parameters to signal them.

RTCP.why: The document specifies new RTCP feedback message types (RTPFB FMT=7, PSFB FMT=8) extending RTP/AVPF feedback, which is the core subject of RTCP.
RTCP.quote: defines a new RTCP Third-Party Loss Report that can be used to inform receivers that the feedback target is aware of some loss event, allowing them to suppress feedback

SDP.why: A whole section defines new SDP rtcp-fb nack parameters (tllei, pslei) with ABNF to negotiate the feature.
SDP.quote: we extend the rtcp-fb attribute to include the commands and indications that are described for Third-Party Loss Reports in the present document.

rejected.why: Source-Specific Multicast is one use case (RFC 5760 unicast feedback), but the document does not specify or extend SSM itself.
SRTP/SAVPF is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to protect the messages; the document is not about it.
RTP is the underlying session context; the new content is specifically RTCP feedback, so the RTCP tag is more specific.
Multicast topologies (SSM, RAMS) are example use cases only; the document does not address multicast routing or group management.
ABNF is only used as notation for the SDP attribute syntax.

RFC6643.title: Translation of Structure of Management Information Version 2 (SMIv2) MIB Modules to YANG Modules
RFC6643.summary: Defines the rules for translating SMIv2 MIB modules into read-only (config false) YANG modules for NETCONF access, plus the ietf-yang-smiv2 extension module.

YANG.why: The document specifies how to generate YANG modules from SMIv2 and defines the ietf-yang-smiv2 YANG extension module, so it is about YANG modelling.
YANG.quote: This document defines a translation of SMIv2 MIB modules into YANG modules, enabling read-only (config false) access to data objects defined in SMIv2 MIB modules via NETCONF.

MIB.why: The document covers the SMIv2 constructs (MODULE-IDENTITY, TEXTUAL-CONVENTION, OBJECT-TYPE, NOTIFICATION-TYPE) and how MIB modules map to YANG, so MIB/SMI readers would want it.
MIB.quote: The SMIv2 uses the OBJECT-TYPE macro to define objects and the structure of conceptual tables.

NETCONF.why: Section 11 discusses NETCONF persistency semantics and how translated nodes can be exposed as configuration data, so NETCONF readers have a reason to look at it.
NETCONF.quote: enabling read-only (config false, as defined in Section 7.19.1 of RFC 6020) access to SMIv2 objects defined in SMIv2 MIB modules via NETCONF

rejected.why: SNMP is the origin of the MIB modules, but the document does not specify or extend the SNMP protocol. The MIB tag covers the SMI aspects.
XML namespaces are used for module naming and IANA registration only, and the document is not about XML.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The DIFFSERV-MIB and RMON2-MIB appear only as translation examples.

RFC6644.title: Rebind Capability in DHCPv6 Reconfigure Messages
RFC6644.summary: Updates RFC 3315 so a DHCPv6 server can send a Reconfigure message whose Reconfigure Message option specifies Rebind, and clarifies client behavior (Renew Server Identifier) when responding to Reconfigure.

DHCPv6.why: The document updates the DHCPv6 specification (RFC 3315), changing server and client behavior for Reconfigure, Renew and Rebind messages.
DHCPv6.quote: It extends the Reconfigure message to allow a DHCPv6 server to cause a DHCPv6 client to send a Rebind message.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag and the document concerns only DHCPv6.
IPv6 is merely the environment for DHCPv6; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Security Considerations mention the Reconfigure Key authentication and Secure DHCPv6, but this is boilerplate-level discussion, not the main body.

RFC6645.title: IP Flow Information Accounting and Export Benchmarking Methodology
RFC6645.summary: RFC 6645 defines a benchmarking methodology and a new metric (Flow Monitoring Throughput / Flow Export Rate) for measuring the performance impact of IPFIX-style IP flow monitoring and export on network devices, alongside RFC 2544 forwarding measurements.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking methodology defining test setups, procedures and report formats for a device under test.
benchmarking.quote: This document provides a methodology and framework for quantifying the performance impact of the monitoring of IP flows on a network device and the export of this information to a Collector.

IPFIX.why: The document is about measuring flow metering and export performance for IPFIX-architecture devices, covering Cache, timeouts, Flow Records and the Exporting Process. Readers of IPFIX would want it.
IPFIX.quote: The metric is only applicable to the devices compliant with RFC 5470, "Architecture for IP Flow Information Export".

rejected.why: Benchmarking is the more specific tag for lab methodology on a DUT; this is not active or passive network performance measurement.
Packet sampling is explicitly out of scope (Section 4.5); PSAMP is only mentioned for MIB retrieval.
MPLS traffic is only a test traffic type, with its flow record specifics. The document does not address MPLS itself.
The IPFIX and PSAMP MIBs are only mentioned in an appendix as a way to retrieve configuration for reports.
IPv6 is only one traffic type that can be tested, with specifics deferred to RFC 5180.

gaps.name: NetFlow
gaps.why: The document mentions NetFlow (RFC 3954) as an alternative export protocol, but the taxonomy has no NetFlow tag. It is only a minor part of the document, so this is a weak gap.

RFC6646.title: DECoupled Application Data Enroute (DECADE) Problem Statement
RFC6646.summary: Problem statement for DECADE: argues that P2P traffic stresses ISP networks, that P2P caches are complex and closed, and that a standard open protocol for accessing in-network storage is needed.

P2P.why: The whole document concerns P2P applications, their traffic stress on networks, and in-network storage and caches for them. P2P is the closest fitting tag.
P2P.quote: This document discusses the introduction of in-network storage for P2P applications and shows the need for a standard protocol for accessing this storage.

rejected.why: CDN/P2P hybrids appear only as a usage scenario; the document is not about content delivery networks.
Web caches are mentioned only as a comparison with P2P caches; the document is not about HTTP caching.
RFC 5693 is cited only as a reference on network-agnostic peering; the document does not specify or analyse ALTO.
The storage tag covers block and file access protocols over IP such as NFS and iSCSI. This document is a P2P in-network storage problem statement, so the P2P tag fits better.

gaps.name: In-network storage / DECADE
gaps.why: The document is about in-network storage for applications, and the taxonomy has no dedicated tag for DECADE or in-network storage. P2P covers it only approximately.

RFC6647.title: Email Greylisting: An Applicability Statement for SMTP
RFC6647.summary: RFC 6647 is an applicability statement describing email greylisting (temporary SMTP 4xx failures for unknown clients) as an anti-spam technique, its variants, costs, unintended consequences, and recommended practices.

spam.why: Greylisting is an anti-spam filtering technique; the whole document describes it, its benefits, costs and effectiveness measurement.
spam.quote: the practice of providing temporarily degraded service to unknown email clients as an anti-abuse mechanism

SMTP.why: The document is an applicability statement for SMTP, analysing greylisting at each SMTP phase (connection, HELO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA), retry behaviour and reply code choice.
SMTP.quote: Greylisting exploits this by rejecting mail from unfamiliar sources with a "transient (soft) fail" (4xx) [SMTP] error code.

rejected.why: DNSBLs are mentioned only as a heuristic input and for exceptions or measurement; the document is not about DNSBL conventions.
Parent of SMTP and spam, which are more specific; ancestors are implied.
CIDR blocks are mentioned only as a grouping option for tracking client addresses.
MX records and PTR are mentioned in passing as context; the document is not about DNS.
Section 7 briefly notes IPv6 applicability, but it is a short caveat, not a substantial subject of the document.

gaps.name: Greylisting
gaps.why: The document's central subject is greylisting, a specific anti-spam technique, and the taxonomy has no dedicated tag for it. The nearest tag is spam.

RFC6648.title: Deprecating the "X-" Prefix and Similar Constructs in Application Protocols
RFC6648.summary: BCP that deprecates the "X-" prefix and similar constructs for naming newly defined textual parameters in application protocols, and gives recommendations for implementers, parameter creators and protocol designers.

IANA.why: Much of the guidance concerns how parameter registries and registration procedures should be designed, which is of interest to readers of IANA registry guidance. The document is not itself an IANA considerations guide, so this is secondary.
IANA.quote: SHOULD establish registries with potentially unlimited value-spaces, defining both permanent and provisional registries if appropriate.

rejected.why: Email headers and RFC 822/2822 are used as historical examples of the X- convention, but the document is not about email.
HTTP headers and x-gzip are cited as examples only.
Media type names such as x-gzip and RFC 4288 registration are cited as an example. The document does not specify media type registration.
It is a BCP on protocol design conventions, not on IETF process or administration.
FTP X-commands appear in the historical background only.
The SIP P- header is mentioned as a parallel precedent only.

gaps.name: protocol extension and parameter naming conventions
gaps.why: The document is about how to name and extend protocol parameters (the X- prefix) across application protocols. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol design or extensibility guidance, and the closest fits are the broad applications topic or IANA.

RFC6649.title: Deprecate DES, RC4-HMAC-EXP, and Other Weak Cryptographic Algorithms in Kerberos
RFC6649.summary: BCP that deprecates single DES, RC4-HMAC-EXP, and weak checksum and GSS-API algorithm types in Kerberos 5, updating RFCs 1964, 4120, 4121 and 4757, and recommends moving RFC 1510 to Historic.

Kerberos.why: The document updates the Kerberos specifications and sets requirement levels for Kerberos encryption and checksum types, and recommends reclassifying RFC 1510 as Historic.
Kerberos.quote: updates RFC 1964, RFC 4120, RFC 4121, and RFC 4757 to deprecate the use of DES, RC4-HMAC-EXP, and other weak cryptographic algorithms in Kerberos

DES.why: The central subject is deprecating DES, with a section on its insecurity (brute-force key search, NIST withdrawal).
DES.quote: Kerberos implementations and deployments SHOULD NOT implement or deploy the following single DES encryption types: DES-CBC-CRC(1), DES-CBC-MD4(2), DES-CBC-MD5(3)

RC4.why: The document deprecates RC4-HMAC-EXP and discusses why RC4-HMAC is retained for interoperability.
RC4.quote: SHOULD NOT implement or deploy the following "export strength" RC4 variant encryption type: RC4-HMAC-EXP(24)

GSS-API.why: It updates RFC 1964 and deprecates the DES-based SGN and SEAL algorithms of the Kerberos GSS-API mechanism.
GSS-API.quote: Kerberos GSS mechanism implementations and deployments SHOULD NOT implement or deploy the following SGN ALG: DES MAC MD5(0000), MD2.5(0100), DES MAC(0200)

rejected.why: RSA-MD5 and MD4 checksum types are discussed only as Kerberos checksum types; the document is not about the MD5 algorithm.
The more specific DES and RC4 tags cover the cryptographic subject.
Kerberos is the specific tag; the generic topic adds nothing.
The recommendation to reclassify RFC 1510 as Historic is incidental to the technical deprecation.

RFC6650.title: Creation and Use of Email Feedback Reports: An Applicability Statement for the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF)
RFC6650.summary: Applicability statement describing how to use the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) for solicited and unsolicited abuse reports and automatic authentication failure reports, updating RFC 5965.

ARF.why: The whole document gives guidance on generating and handling ARF feedback reports for abuse and authentication failure; ARF is the subject.
ARF.quote: This applicability statement provides direction for using ARF in both contexts.

spam.why: Much of the document covers spam/abuse complaint feedback loops: when to report, where to send, and how to handle reports, so spam readers would want it.
spam.quote: The purpose for reporting abusive messages is to stop recurrences.

rejected.why: Only the transport for reports; the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Mentioned for authenticating reports and deciding when to report; SPF itself is not the subject.
Used for signing reports and as context for failure reporting; the document is not about DKIM itself.
Section 6 touches authentication failure reports, but that is covered by ARF; the ARF tag is more specific and no authentication tag is needed.
Only mentioned as a place to find abuse contacts.
RFC 5322 is only the container for ARF reports.

RFC6651.title: Extensions to DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) for Failure Reporting
RFC6651.summary: RFC 6651 extends DKIM and ADSP with an r= signature tag and DNS reporting TXT record/ADSP tags so verifiers send ARF-formatted failure reports on demand.

DKIM.why: The document extends DKIM with a new signature tag, a reporting TXT record at _report._domainkey, and a reporting algorithm, plus ADSP tags.
DKIM.quote: This document presents extensions to the DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) specification to allow for detailed reporting of message authentication failures in an on-demand fashion.

ARF.why: Failure reports are generated in ARF format, and the document defines when and how they are generated and requested, which is of interest to ARF readers.
ARF.quote: All reports generated as a result of requests contained in these extension parameters MUST be generated in compliance with [ARF] and its extension specific to this work

rejected.why: DNS TXT records are used as the substrate for publishing reporting parameters; no new DNS RR type or resolver behaviour is defined.
SMTP is only the transport for reports and the carrier of the optional rs= error string; it is not specified or extended here.
Abuse and spam are context for failure reports, but the document is about authentication failure reporting, not spam filtering.
The IANA section registers tags and creates a registry, which is boilerplate relative to the main body.

RFC6652.title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) Authentication Failure Reporting Using the Abuse Reporting Format
RFC6652.summary: Extends SPF records with ra=, rp= and rr= modifiers so domain owners can request ARF-format authentication failure reports, and creates an IANA registry of SPF modifiers (updating RFC 4408).

SPF.why: The document defines new SPF modifiers (ra, rp, rr), creates the SPF modifier registry, and updates RFC 4408, so it is about SPF.
SPF.quote: This document extends [SPF] to add an optional reporting address and other parameters.

ARF.why: It specifies how SPF failure reports are requested and generated using the Abuse Reporting Format. It covers ARF Incidents usage and report-generation rules.
ARF.quote: allow for detailed reporting of message authentication failures in an on-demand fashion

rejected.why: SPF records are published in DNS, but DNS is only the substrate here. Nothing new is defined about DNS.
SMTP is mentioned only for the return address and HELO choices in the Security Considerations. It is not a subject of the document.
The parent is implied by the SPF and ARF tags, so it is not listed separately.
The SPF modifier registry is a minor part of the document. IANA stewardship and guidance are not its subject.

RFC6653.title: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation in Long-Term Evolution (LTE) Networks
RFC6653.summary: Informational RFC describing how an LTE access router (PDN Gateway) uses DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation to obtain, assign and release per-mobile-node IPv6 prefixes from a DHCP server, including prefix sourcing via RADIUS/Diameter AAA.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies how DHCPv6-PD (IA_PD, Solicit/Request/Release, Rapid Commit) is used between the access router and DHCP server, and for MN-as-requesting-router.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes how to use DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCPv6-PD) in mobile networks

cellular.why: The whole scenario is IPv6 prefix management in 3GPP LTE/EPS networks, covering attach, PDN connection and handover.
cellular.quote: In a Long-Term Evolution (LTE) network, the Access Router (AR) is the Packet Data Network (PDN) Gateway [3GPP-23401].

RADIUS.why: Section 4 describes using RADIUS Framed-IPv6-Prefix and Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attributes for prefix management.
RADIUS.quote: the RADIUS server may send an Access-Accept message with prefix information to the AR using the Framed-IPv6-Prefix attribute.
RADIUS.section: 4. Prefix Delegation Using RADIUS and Diameter

Diameter.why: The same section describes Diameter AA-Request/Answer carrying the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix AVP for prefix delegation.
Diameter.quote: When Diameter is used, the DHCP server as DR, as shown in Figure 2, sends an AA-Request message.
Diameter.section: 4. Prefix Delegation Using RADIUS and Diameter

rejected.why: IPv6 is the context, but the document's subject is more specifically DHCPv6 prefix delegation; the child DHCPv6 tag is chosen instead.
Router Solicitation/Advertisement are used only to advertise the delegated prefix to the MN; not the subject.
Stateless address configuration is mentioned as a scenario, but it is not specified or extended.
MNs are mobile but the document does not address IP-layer mobility protocols such as Mobile IP or PMIPv6.
Prefix management is addressed through DHCPv6-PD; route aggregation in 3.5.2 is a minor part.
RADIUS and Diameter are tagged directly as the more specific children.

RFC6654.title: Gateway-Initiated IPv6 Rapid Deployment on IPv4 Infrastructures (GI 6rd)
RFC6654.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC proposing Gateway-initiated 6rd, in which an operator-owned gateway at the IPv4 network edge, not customer equipment, originates the 6-in-4 tunnels, and defining the delegated prefix structure.

6rd.why: The document defines an alternative 6rd deployment model (GI 6rd), including the prefix format and the differences from basic 6rd of RFC 5969. It is about 6rd.
6rd.quote: The alternative model described in this document initiates the 6-in-4 tunnels from an operator-owned Gateway collocated with the operator's IPv4 network edge rather than from customer equipment

rejected.why: Prefix assignment uses DHCPv6 or SLAAC in the normal way. The document only mentions it, and notes that the 6rd DHCPv6 option does not apply.
Mentioned only as one of the ways prefixes are assigned to customer equipment. The document is not about it.
Cited in the problem statement as an alternative that also needs IPv4 addresses. It is not specified or extended here.
The parent of 6rd, so it is implied by the 6rd tag.
6-in-4 tunnelling is the mechanism, but the specific 6rd tag covers it.

RFC6655.title: AES-CCM Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC6655.summary: Defines sixteen AES-CCM TLS cipher suites (RSA, DHE_RSA, PSK, DHE_PSK; 16- and 8-octet tags) and two new AEAD algorithms, AEAD_AES_128_CCM_8 and AEAD_AES_256_CCM_8, for TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2.

TLS.why: The document specifies new TLS cipher suites, including code points, nonce construction and version rules. TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: describes the use of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in the Counter with Cipher Block Chaining - Message Authentication Code (CBC-MAC) Mode (CCM) of operation within Transport Layer Security (TLS)

AES.why: The document specifies AES-CCM, an AES mode, and defines new AEAD algorithms with 8-octet tags. Readers of the AES page would want it.
AES.quote: AES-CCM provides both authentication and confidentiality and uses as its only primitive the AES encrypt operation

rejected.why: The suites can be used with DTLS 1.2, and the document explains how the sequence number is formed there. DTLS is a minor applicability note, not the document's subject.
IPsec ESP is mentioned only as prior use of AES-CCM (RFC 4309), so the document is not about it.
HMAC appears only as the TLS 1.2 PRF and a truncation note. It is not what the document specifies.
RSA is only the key-exchange mechanism in some suites, as defined in RFC 5246.

RFC6656.title: Description of Cisco Systems' Subnet Allocation Option for DHCPv4
RFC6656.summary: Informational RFC documenting Cisco's pre-existing DHCPv4 Subnet Allocation option (option 220), with suboptions for requesting, describing, renewing, releasing and reporting usage of dynamically allocated subnets.

DHCP.why: The document specifies a DHCPv4 option and its suboptions, plus the client/server message exchanges (DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK, RELEASE, FORCERENEW) that use it.
DHCP.quote: This memo documents a DHCP option [RFC2132], the Subnet Allocation option, that was developed by Cisco and allows a DHCP Client to allocate a subnet

rejected.why: Section 9 only compares the option with DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation; the document specifies DHCPv4 only.
Prefix lengths are used for subnet sizing and RFC 4632 is cited, but the document is not about CIDR.
The IANA section merely records option 220 assignment; it is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
Only the Subnet-Name suboption's encoding is UTF-8; it is a minor detail, not a subject.
Subnet allocation touches addressing, but the DHCP tag is the more specific fit and the document is about a DHCP option.

RFC6657.title: Update to MIME regarding "charset" Parameter Handling in Textual Media Types
RFC6657.summary: Updates RFC 2046 to change default "charset" parameter rules for text/* media types, so new subtypes should not define a default (or use UTF-8) and must specify how charset is determined.

media types.why: The document sets rules for registering text/* media types and their charset parameter handling, which is the media type registration subject.
media types.quote: Each subtype of the "text" media type that uses the "charset" parameter can define its own default value for the "charset" parameter
media types.section: 3. New Rules for Default "charset" Parameter Values

character sets.why: The document is substantially about charset defaults and how charset is determined, including US-ASCII and UTF-8 defaults.
character sets.quote: all new "text/*" registrations MUST clearly specify how the charset is determined
character sets.section: 3. New Rules for Default "charset" Parameter Values

rejected.why: The document updates RFC 2046, but media types is the more specific child that fits its subject.
The HTTP default of ISO-8859-1 is only mentioned as background and the document does not specify HTTP.
text/html is cited only as an example of a type with in-payload charset information.
UTF-8 is only named as the fallback default charset for new subtypes, not specified or analysed.
US-ASCII is mentioned as the legacy default, but the document is about default rules in general rather than ASCII itself.

RFC6658.title: Packet Pseudowire Encapsulation over an MPLS PSN
RFC6658.summary: Defines a packet pseudowire that carries client-layer IP/MPLS and support protocols over an MPLS PSN by using a virtual Ethernet (Ethernet raw mode PW) between co-resident client LSR and server PE, and allocates two Ethernet addresses.

pseudowire.why: The whole document specifies a packet pseudowire encapsulation (Ethernet raw mode PW type 5) and its forwarding model.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a pseudowire mechanism that is used to transport a packet service over an MPLS PSN

rejected.why: MPLS is the server PSN and client network, but the document's subject is the pseudowire encapsulation, which sits under pseudowire.
