Virtual Ethernet is used only as a multiplexing encapsulation; no IP-over-Ethernet or Ethernet OAM is specified, and the document explicitly restricts Ethernet features.
LDP signaling per RFC 4447 is only referenced for address selection; nothing new is defined for LDP.
The two MAC address allocations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the main subject.

RFC6659.title: Considerations for Deploying the Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions (RAMS) Method
RFC6659.summary: Informational document giving deployment scenarios and guidance for using the RAMS (unicast-based rapid acquisition of multicast RTP sessions) method when acquiring multiple associated streams, including feedback targets, SSRC/session multiplexing, and FEC bandwidth allocation.

RTP.why: RAMS is an RTP-based method; the document discusses RTP session and SSRC multiplexing, payload-type multiplexing, and RTP retransmission sessions in depth. No taxonomy tag exists for RAMS itself, so RTP is the closest fit.
RTP.quote: The Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions (RAMS) solution is a method based on RTP and the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP)

SSM.why: The scenarios hinge on how SSM sessions map to feedback targets and RAMS sessions, so Source-Specific Multicast concepts are substantively discussed.
SSM.quote: An SSM session is defined by its (distribution) source address and (destination) multicast group, and there can be only one feedback target per SSM session

FEC.why: A full section analyses deploying FEC streams alongside primary video during rapid acquisition and how to divide bandwidth between them.
FEC.quote: FEC during RAMS and Bandwidth Issues
FEC.section: 5. FEC during RAMS and Bandwidth Issues

rejected.why: SDP descriptions are used to illustrate the scenarios, but the document is not about SDP itself.
RAMS messages use RTCP feedback, but the document does not extend or specify RTCP; it concerns deployment of RAMS.
Multicast is the context, but the document focuses on RTP/RAMS session configuration rather than multicast routing or group membership; SSM is the more specific tag.
The FEC Framework is only referenced as the preferred FEC deployment model, not specified or analysed.
Multicast video delivery is the use case, but the document is about RTP session configuration for RAMS, not streaming operations in general.

gaps.name: RAMS (Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about deploying RAMS, but the taxonomy has no tag for it; RTP is used as the nearest fit.

RFC6660.title: Encoding Three Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) States in the IP Header Using a Single Diffserv Codepoint (DSCP)
RFC6660.summary: Specifies the 3-in-1 PCN encoding, which reuses the ECN field with a single PCN-compatible DSCP to carry not-marked, threshold-marked and excess-traffic-marked states in IP headers, defines ingress/interior/egress node behaviour, and obsoletes RFC 5696.

PCN.why: The document defines the PCN wire encoding and node behaviour.
PCN.quote: This document specifies how PCN-marks are to be encoded into the IP header by reusing the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) codepoints within a PCN-domain.

RFC6661.title: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) Boundary-Node Behavior for the Controlled Load (CL) Mode of Operation
RFC6661.summary: Specifies the experimental Controlled Load (CL) PCN boundary-node behavior: egress-node measurement and reporting, Decision Point flow admission and termination, a Diffserv per-domain behavior specification, and operational/management guidance including syslog events and counters.

PCN.why: The whole document specifies PCN boundary-node behavior for the CL mode: metering of marked traffic, CLE-based admission and flow termination.
PCN.quote: The behavior described here is that for a form of measurement-based load control using three PCN marking states: not-marked, threshold-marked, and excess-traffic-marked.

rejected.why: Diffserv is the substrate. The document includes a RFC 3086 per-domain behavior template, but its subject is PCN edge behavior, and PCN is the more specific tag.
Syslog is used only for event logging, with a few structured-data IDs. That is a minor part of the document, not its subject.
The Diffserv MIB is mentioned only as a provisioning and counter mechanism.
ECN bits are reused for PCN marking, but the encoding is defined in RFC 6660, not here.
ECMP is mentioned only as a reason for reporting excess-traffic-marked flow identifiers.

RFC6662.title: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) Boundary-Node Behavior for the Single Marking (SM) Mode of Operation
RFC6662.summary: Experimental RFC specifying PCN boundary-node (ingress, egress, Decision Point) behavior for the Single Marking mode, using excess-traffic marking for flow admission and termination in a Diffserv domain.

PCN.why: The document specifies PCN boundary-node behaviour for admission control and flow termination based on marking. PCN is a congestion-notification mechanism for QoS.
PCN.quote: This behavior is known informally as the Single Marking (SM) PCN-boundary-node behavior.

Diffserv.why: Section 4 is a Diffserv per-domain behavior specification, covering PHB configuration, classification and service classes.
Diffserv.quote: because PCN uses Diffserv codepoint (DSCP) values to carry its markings, a specification of PCN-boundary-node behavior must include the per-domain behavior (PDB) template

rejected.why: Syslog is used only for event-log formats in the management section; the document is not about the protocol.
The Diffserv MIB is mentioned for provisioning and counters, but the document does not define a MIB module.
ECN bits are reused for PCN marking and coexistence is only mentioned; the document is not about ECN.
PCN is admission control and flow termination rather than transport congestion control. The more specific PCN tag was considered instead.
RSVP-PCN is referenced only as a possible signaling protocol, which is out of scope here.
Tunnelling between ingress and egress nodes is a deployment choice discussed briefly, not the subject.

RFC6663.title: Requirements for Signaling of Pre-Congestion Information in a Diffserv Domain
RFC6663.summary: Informational PCN WG memo specifying requirements for signaling protocols that carry PCN egress reports to Decision Points and ingress sent-rate requests/reports in a Diffserv domain, for the CL and SM edge behaviors.

PCN.why: The whole document defines signaling requirements for Pre-Congestion Notification: report contents for the SM and CL edge behaviors, and the sent-rate request/report between Decision Point and ingress node.
PCN.quote: This memo describes the requirements for the signaling applied within the PCN-domain: (1) PCN-feedback-information is carried from the PCN-egress-node to the Decision Point

rejected.why: The PCN domain is a Diffserv domain, but the document only specifies PCN signaling. Diffserv is the context, not the subject.
PCN protects QoS, but PCN is the more specific tag and the QoS parent is implied.
RFC 3084 (COPS-PR) is cited only as an out-of-scope example solution for Decision Point to ingress signaling.
Generic aggregate RSVP appears only in a Security Considerations reference, so it is not a subject of the document.
RFC 5431 is cited only as an out-of-scope example solution.

RFC6664.title: S/MIME Capabilities for Public Key Definitions
RFC6664.summary: Defines new S/MIME Capability ASN.1 types for PKIX public key types (RSA, RSASSA-PSS, RSAES-OAEP, DSA, DH, EC, ECDH, ECMQV) and an RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm capability, so a requester can specify key and signature algorithm preferences.

S/MIME.why: The document extends S/MIME capabilities with new capability types for public keys and the RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm.
S/MIME.quote: This document defines a set of Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Capability types for ASN.1 encoding for the current set of public keys

ASN.1.why: The document specifies ASN.1 types and provides normative 1988 and informative 2008 ASN.1 modules.
ASN.1.quote: The main body of the text is written using snippets of ASN.1 that are extracted from the ASN.1 2008 module in Appendix A.

RSA.why: A substantial part defines capabilities for RSA, RSASSA-PSS and RSAES-OAEP keys and the PSS signature algorithm.
RSA.quote: There are currently three different public key object identifiers for RSA public keys.

elliptic curve.why: Defines capability types for EC, ECDH and ECMQV public keys.
elliptic curve.quote: There are currently three Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) public key object identifiers.

rejected.why: RFC 6277 OCSP agility is only the motivating use case; this document does not specify OCSP.
Certificate public key OIDs are referenced, but the document does not profile certificates.
Public key types come from PKIX but the document is about S/MIME capabilities, not PKI.
S/MIME capabilities are used in CMS messages but CMS itself is not specified here.

RFC6665.title: SIP-Specific Event Notification
RFC6665.summary: RFC 6665 specifies the SIP SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY event notification framework (event packages, subscription state, Subscription-State and Event headers), obsoleting RFC 3265.

SIP.why: The document defines the SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods, new SIP header fields and response codes, and node behavior as an extension to SIP.
SIP.quote: The purpose of this extension is to provide an extensible framework by which SIP nodes can request notification from remote nodes indicating that certain events have occurred.

rejected.why: Presence and event packages are mentioned only as examples. SIMPLE event packages are defined in other documents, and this is the base framework.
PINT is mentioned only for a small compatibility rule (a SUBSCRIBE with no Event header). The document is not about PINT.
The IANA registries for event packages and reason codes are boilerplate-like support for the framework. The main body is not about IANA.
S/MIME is mentioned only in passing as an optional encryption mechanism.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax definitions.

RFC6666.title: A Discard Prefix for IPv6
RFC6666.summary: Informational RFC recording IANA allocation of the IPv6 discard-only prefix 0100::/64 to support remote triggered black hole (RTBH) filtering and routing against DoS attacks.

addressing.why: The document is about allocating a special-purpose IPv6 address prefix (0100::/64) and how it should be used and scoped, which is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: By assigning a globally unique discard prefix for IPv6, the IETF will introduce good practice for the implementation of IPv6 RTBH configurations

DDoS.why: The purpose of the prefix is to facilitate RTBH black-holing used to mitigate DoS attacks, and the operational guidance addresses its effect on attack traffic.
DDoS.quote: describes a method of mitigating the effects of denial-of-service attacks by selectively discarding traffic based on source or destination address

rejected.why: BGP is only the mechanism used to propagate the discard prefix inside an AS; the document specifies no BGP behaviour beyond not announcing it to third parties.
The prefix is IPv6, but the document is about an address allocation, which is covered by the more specific addressing tag; it does not specify IPv6 itself.
IANA records the allocation, but this is only boilerplate-level registry action; the body is about the prefix's purpose, not IANA registry procedures.
RTBH is related to traffic filtering but the document does not discuss Flow Specification.
Considered since RTBH is an operational practice, but the document's focus is the address assignment and DDoS use, which are covered by tagged subjects.

gaps.name: Remote triggered black hole (RTBH) filtering
gaps.why: The document's central subject is RTBH filtering/routing, and the taxonomy has no specific tag for it; DDoS is the closest fit.

RFC6667.title: LDP 'Typed Wildcard' Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) for PWid and Generalized PWid FEC Elements
RFC6667.summary: Defines the LDP Typed Wildcard FEC Element format for PWid (0x80) and Generalized PWid (0x81) pseudowire FEC element types, with use cases such as consistency check, graceful shutdown, wildcard PW status and VPLS MAC withdrawal.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with a new Typed Wildcard FEC Element format for PW FEC types, covering label request, withdraw, release and notification procedures.
LDP.quote: This document specifies the format of the Typed Wildcard FEC Element for the "PWid FEC Element" and "Generalized PWid FEC Element".

pseudowire.why: The wildcard elements scope to PW FEC types and PW types, and the use cases (consistency check, graceful shutdown, PW status) concern LDP pseudowire signaling per RFC 4447.
pseudowire.quote: The use of Typed Wildcard FEC Elements for PW can be useful under several scenarios.

VPLS.why: A dedicated section specifies wildcard MAC withdrawal in VPLS using Address Withdraw messages with the Typed Wildcard PW FEC.
VPLS.quote: The use of PW Typed Wildcard FEC enhances the scope of MAC withdrawal beyond just a single VPLS instance
VPLS.section: 4.4. Typed Wildcard MAC Withdrawal in VPLS

rejected.why: LDP is the more specific tag and its ancestor MPLS is implied; the document is not about MPLS in general.
L2VPN PW bindings are only the context for the use cases; the document does not specify L2VPN services.
The PW type wildcard value 0x7FFF is cited from the IANA registry but the document does not address IANA registries.

RFC6668.title: SHA-2 Data Integrity Verification for the Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol
RFC6668.summary: Defines two new SSH MAC algorithm names, hmac-sha2-256 (RECOMMENDED) and hmac-sha2-512 (OPTIONAL), for data integrity in the SSH transport layer, updating RFC 4253.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport layer with new MAC algorithm names and updates RFC 4253, so SSH readers need it.
SSH.quote: This memo defines algorithm names and parameters for use in some of the SHA-2 family of secure hash algorithms for data integrity verification in the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol.

HMAC.why: The new algorithms are HMAC constructions with specified digest and key lengths, so HMAC readers would find it relevant.
HMAC.quote: hmac-sha2-256     RECOMMENDED   HMAC-SHA2-256

SHA.why: The MACs are built on SHA-256 and SHA-512 from the SHA-2 family, chosen over SHA-1 and MD5 for security reasons.
SHA.quote: The SHA-2 family of secure hash algorithms is defined in [FIPS-180-3].

rejected.why: MD5 is mentioned only as an existing algorithm with security concerns, not as a subject of the document.
The IANA section merely registers the two MAC names; it is boilerplate and not the main subject.
The more specific HMAC and SHA tags already cover the cryptographic content.

RFC6669.title: An Overview of the Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Toolset for MPLS-Based Transport Networks
RFC6669.summary: Informational overview of the MPLS-TP OAM toolset, recapping requirements and functions (CC-CV, RDI, AIS, LKR, lock instruct, loopback, loss/delay measurement) and mapping each to the RFCs that define the protocols.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is about OAM for the MPLS Transport Profile, its requirements, generic mechanisms (G-ACh, GAL) and tools.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document provides an overview of the MPLS-TP OAM toolset, which consists of tools for MPLS-TP fault management and performance monitoring.

OAM.why: The document is an overview of an OAM toolset covering fault management and performance monitoring, so the general OAM topic fits.
OAM.quote: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) plays a significant role in carrier networks.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part covers MPLS-TP packet loss, delay, and throughput measurement tools (RFC 6374/6375).
performance measurement.quote: The packet loss and delay measurement toolset enables operators to measure the quality of the packet transmission over a PW, LSP, or Section.

rejected.why: BFD is used as the CC-CV/RDI tool, but this overview only references RFC 6428 and does not specify or extend BFD.
The parent of MPLS-TP is implied, and the document is specifically about MPLS-TP.
Pseudowires are one of the monitored entities (and VCCV is mentioned), but the document is not about pseudowire emulation.
Only mentioned in passing as a dynamic control-plane option.
Route tracing is one function summarised via LSP ping, but it is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC6670.title: The Reasons for Selecting a Single Solution for MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM)
RFC6670.summary: Informational RFC arguing why a single MPLS-TP OAM solution should be standardized instead of a parallel second one, covering interworking costs, coexistence models and rebuttals of arguments for two solutions.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document concerns MPLS-TP OAM solution selection, justifying a single OAM toolset for the MPLS Transport Profile.
MPLS-TP.quote: this document sets out the reasons for selecting a single, coherent set of solutions for standardization.

OAM.why: The document is about OAM mechanisms (fault management, performance monitoring, continuity check) and the implications of having two OAM protocols.
OAM.quote: OAM provides a comprehensive set of capabilities that operate in the data plane.

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the more specific tag; MPLS is the parent and is implied.
Ethernet OAM is discussed only as one argument for a second solution, not as a subject of the document.
SONET/SDH appears only in the interworking examples in the appendices and as a look-and-feel comparison.
The IPv4/IPv6 transition is only an appendix example of interworking problems.
RFC 1958 is cited for the 'choose one' principle, but the document is about MPLS-TP OAM, not general architecture.
Packet loss and delay measurement are listed as OAM features, but the document does not address them in its own right.

RFC6671.title: Allocation of a Generic Associated Channel Type for ITU-T MPLS Transport Profile Operation, Maintenance, and Administration (MPLS-TP OAM)
RFC6671.summary: Informational RFC recording IANA's allocation of G-ACh Type 0x8902 for ITU-T G.8113.1 MPLS-TP OAM messages, restricting its use to OAM functions in RFC 5860, with an IESG note not endorsing the alternate OAM.

MPLS-TP.why: The document defines a G-ACh Type for MPLS-TP OAM, scoping its use on MPLS-TP sections, LSPs and PWs. Readers of MPLS-TP would want it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document assigns a Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) Type for carrying ITU-T MPLS Transport Profile Operations, Administration, and Management (MPLS-TP OAM) messages

rejected.why: The OAM topic is implied by the MPLS-TP tag only loosely. The document is about a channel type code point and does not specify OAM mechanisms itself.
The IANA allocation is the document's mechanism, but it is about MPLS-TP G-ACh, not IANA registry guidance or stewardship.
The Pseudowire Associated Channel Types registry is only where the value is allocated. The document does not address pseudowires.
G.8113.1 builds on Y.1731 Ethernet OAM, but this document does not address Ethernet.

RFC6672.title: DNAME Redirection in the DNS
RFC6672.summary: RFC 6672 revises the DNAME resource record specification (obsoleting RFC 2672), defining subtree redirection in the DNS, server and resolver algorithms, CNAME synthesis, DNSSEC and dynamic update interactions, and updating RFC 3363.

DNS.why: The document specifies the DNAME resource record, its substitution rules, and server and resolver processing algorithms, which is core DNS protocol and resource record content.
DNS.quote: The DNAME record provides redirection for a subtree of the domain name tree in the DNS.

DNSSEC.why: Section 5.3 specifies how DNSSEC validators must handle DNAME, including unsigned synthesized CNAMEs, NSEC bitmaps, and validation chains, which is substantial for DNSSEC readers.
DNSSEC.quote: In any negative response, the NSEC or NSEC3 [RFC5155] record type bitmap SHOULD be checked to see that there was no DNAME that could have been applied.

rejected.why: Section 5.2 covers DNAME/CNAME interaction under dynamic update, but it is a short side topic, not a substantial part of the document.
Punycode alternates are mentioned only as a use case for DNAME, and the document is not about IDNA.
Only notes that no EDNS signalling exists for DNAME, which is a clarification of a non-feature.
Updates RFC 3363 on DNAME in the IPv6 reverse tree, but only through a brief paragraph; it is not about IPv6 itself.
Reverse-delegation and renumbering examples are illustrative, and the document does not address address architecture or allocation.

RFC6673.title: Round-Trip Packet Loss Metrics
RFC6673.summary: Defines a round-trip packet loss metric (singleton, sample stream, and loss ratio statistic) within the IPPM framework, building on RFC 2680/2681 and referencing TWAMP as a measurement method.

performance measurement.why: The document defines a new IPPM performance metric (singleton, sample, statistic) for round-trip packet loss, which is squarely the performance measurement subject.
performance measurement.quote: This memo adds round-trip loss to the set of IP Performance Metrics (IPPM).

rejected.why: TWAMP (RFC 5357) is cited as an example measurement method and for responder behaviour, but the document does not specify or extend it; it defines a metric.
Ping/ICMP Echo is mentioned only as an alternative measurement mechanism with caveats; not the subject.
One-way measurement is only discussed as inference from round-trip results; OWAMP is not covered.
The TCP handshake is used only as motivation for two-way connectivity.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metric definitions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic 'performance measurement' topic; there is no tag for IPPM metrics such as one-way delay, loss and reordering, which would group this RFC with its siblings.

RFC6674.title: Gateway-Initiated Dual-Stack Lite Deployment
RFC6674.summary: Defines Gateway-Initiated Dual-Stack Lite (GI-DS-Lite), a DS-Lite variant that extends existing access tunnels from an access gateway to an AFTR (IPv4-IPv4 NAT) over softwires, using a Context Identifier to identify each access device's flows.

DS-Lite.why: The document specifies a variant of DS-Lite, including AFTR NAT binding behaviour extended with CID and SWID.
DS-Lite.quote: Gateway-Initiated Dual-Stack Lite (GI-DS-Lite) is a variant of Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) [RFC6333], applicable to network architectures that use point-to-point tunnels

softwire.why: Softwire identification, management and embodiments (GRE, MPLS VPN, IPv4-in-IPv6, etc.) between access gateway and AFTR make up a substantial part of the document.
softwire.quote: With GI-DS-Lite, the access gateway and AFTR are connected by a softwire [RFC4925]. The softwire is identified by a softwire identifier (SWID).

rejected.why: The AFTR performs IPv4-IPv4 NAT, but the NAT is part of DS-Lite, which is the more specific tag; NAT behaviour is not the document's own subject.
GRE with Key extension is one softwire embodiment used to carry the CID, not the subject of the document.
Proxy Mobile IPv6 and Mobile IPv6 appear only as example access architectures in the appendix.
MPLS VPN and IPv4/IPv6-in-MPLS are only listed as optional softwire embodiments.
Tunnelling is the mechanism used. The softwire tag already covers the document's tunnel-specific content.

RFC6675.title: A Conservative Loss Recovery Algorithm Based on Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) for TCP
RFC6675.summary: RFC 6675 specifies a conservative SACK-based loss recovery algorithm for TCP (scoreboard, pipe, NextSeg, rescue retransmission), obsoleting RFC 3517 and conforming to RFC 5681 congestion control.

TCP.why: The document specifies a TCP sender loss recovery algorithm using SACK, defining fast retransmit entry, scoreboard, pipe and RTO interaction. This is a TCP protocol extension.
TCP.quote: This document presents a conservative loss recovery algorithm for TCP that is based on the use of the selective acknowledgment (SACK) TCP option.

congestion control.why: The algorithm replaces fast recovery, adjusts cwnd/ssthresh and uses a pipe-based sending limit, so congestion control readers would want it. There is no more specific child tag that fits, since NewReno is a different algorithm.
congestion control.quote: The algorithm presented in this document conforms to the spirit of the current congestion control specification (RFC 5681)

rejected.why: NewReno (RFC 6582) is only mentioned as another advanced recovery algorithm; this document specifies a different, SACK-based one.
Not relevant; the document is about loss recovery, not QoS.

RFC6676.title: Multicast Addresses for Documentation
RFC6676.summary: RFC 6676 reserves IPv4 and IPv6 multicast address ranges for use in documentation examples and explains how to derive GLOP, unicast-prefix-based, administratively scoped and Embedded-RP example addresses from documentation AS numbers and unicast prefixes.

multicast.why: The document defines reserved IPv4 and IPv6 multicast address ranges and how to construct example multicast addresses (ASM, SSM, GLOP, scoped, embedded-RP). Multicast addressing is the central subject.
multicast.quote: This document discusses which multicast addresses should be used for documentation purposes and reserves multicast addresses for such use.

addressing.why: It is about reserving address blocks for documentation, parallel to the unicast documentation prefixes. Readers of addressing allocation and reservation would want it.
addressing.quote: For unicast, there are both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses reserved for this purpose; see [RFC5737] and [RFC3849], respectively.

rejected.why: IPv6 multicast documentation addresses are covered, but the document is about multicast address reservation, not the IPv6 protocol or its deployment.
The IANA actions are only the registrations that result from the document. They are boilerplate-level here, and the main body is not about IANA registry stewardship.
SSM is mentioned only to say that the choice of group address matters little and that documentation unicast sources should be used. The document does not specify or extend SSM.
Embedded-RP addresses involve a rendezvous point, but the document only gives example address derivations. It does not address PIM.

RFC6677.title: Channel-Binding Support for Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Methods
RFC6677.summary: Defines EAP channel bindings, where the peer sends its view of authenticator-advertised network information to the EAP server inside an integrity-protected EAP method channel, so the server can detect a "lying NAS" or "lying provider", and defines the message encoding, RADIUS namespace, EAP-Lower-Layer attribute and IANA registries.

EAP.why: The document specifies an extension to EAP methods: a channel-binding data and response format carried within EAP methods, plus requirements on methods and lower layers.
EAP.quote: This document defines how to implement channel bindings for Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) methods to address the "lying Network Access Service (NAS)" problem

RADIUS.why: It defines the new RADIUS EAP-Lower-Layer attribute (code 163), a RADIUS namespace for channel-binding encoding, and which RADIUS attributes the server should validate.
RADIUS.quote: A new RADIUS attribute is defined to carry information on which EAP lower layer is used for this EAP authentication.

rejected.why: AAA infrastructure is the context in which i2 attributes are received, but RADIUS is the more specific protocol tagged and the document does not define an AAA framework.
The EAP tag is more specific and already covers the authentication subject.
The GSS-API EAP mechanism is mentioned only as one example lower layer and use case.
IEEE 802.11 is used for examples and attack scenarios, but the document is not about IP over Wi-Fi.
PANA is listed only as an initial lower-layer registration in the IANA table.
The document creates registries, but IANA considerations are boilerplate here and not the main subject.

gaps.name: EAP channel binding
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no sub-tag under EAP for channel bindings. The subject is distinct from RFC 5056 channel bindings.

RFC6678.title: Requirements for a Tunnel-Based Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Method
RFC6678.summary: RFC 6678 specifies requirements for a TLS-based EAP tunnel method, covering use cases, tunnel establishment, inner password and EAP method carriage, cryptographic binding, and channel binding.

EAP.why: The whole document is a requirements specification for an EAP tunnel method, including inner EAP methods, chaining, cryptographic binding, MSK/EMSK key generation and channel binding.
EAP.quote: This memo defines the requirements for a tunnel-based Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Method.

TLS.why: A substantial part of the document sets requirements on how TLS is used to establish the tunnel: cipher suites, session resumption, extensions and downgrade protection.
TLS.quote: The tunnel-based method MUST support TLS version 1.2 [RFC5246] and may support earlier versions

rejected.why: Carrying NEA/PB-TNC inside the tunnel is only one use case (Section 3.6), so the document is not about NEA.
OCSP is mentioned only as a way to check server certificate revocation. The document does not specify it.
RADIUS appears only in a security consideration about the password attribute, which is peripheral.
The document concerns EAP method requirements. AAA key management is only referenced through RFC 4962 compliance.
UTF-8 is only an encoding requirement for strings and is not what the document is about.

RFC6679.title: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) for RTP over UDP
RFC6679.summary: Specifies how ECN is used with RTP over UDP, defining a new RTCP ECN feedback message, an RTCP XR ECN summary block, SDP signalling (a=ecn-capable-rtp), and a STUN ECN-CHECK attribute for ICE-based initiation, plus failure detection and translator/mixer handling.

ECN.why: The whole document defines how ECN marking, feedback, verification and fallback work for RTP/UDP.
ECN.quote: This memo specifies how Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) can be used with the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) running over UDP

RTCP.why: Defines new RTCP feedback packet (FMT=8) and XR block (BT=13) as the core feedback mechanism.
RTCP.quote: It defines a new RTCP Extended Report (XR) block for periodic ECN feedback, a new RTCP transport feedback message for timely reporting of congestion events

SDP.why: A substantial part defines SDP attributes and offer/answer rules for negotiating ECN capability.
SDP.quote: One new SDP attribute, "a=ecn-capable-rtp:", is defined.

STUN.why: Defines a new STUN attribute for ECN path verification.
STUN.quote: sending the "ECN-CHECK" attribute in a STUN packet that is ECT marked

ICE.why: Defines an ICE option and an ICE-based initiation method for ECN.
ICE.quote: One new ICE [RFC5245] option, "rtp+ecn", is defined.

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate; the document does not define anything new about UDP itself.
RTP is tagged via its child RTCP, which is what the document extends.
ECN tag already sits under it; congestion response algorithms are explicitly out of scope.
The document does not specify an RTP congestion control algorithm; it only supplies the ECN signal.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as protection for RTCP.
Multicast topologies are discussed but only as one deployment case, not the subject.

RFC6680.title: Generic Security Service Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) Naming Extensions
RFC6680.summary: RFC 6680 extends the GSS-API naming model with name attributes and new functions (display, inquire, get/set/delete attribute, composite export) so applications can obtain authenticated or asserted attributes about peers for authorization.

GSS-API.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the GSS-API: new functions, C-bindings, and name attribute semantics.
GSS-API.quote: This document introduces new APIs that extend the GSS-API naming model to support name attribute transfer between GSS-API peers.

rejected.why: Kerberos authorization data and PKINIT are used only as examples of attribute sources; the document does not specify or extend Kerberos.
Attributes are intended for authorization decisions, but the document defines a naming API, not an authorization framework.
X.509 certificate extensions are cited as example attribute sources only.
SAML is mentioned as an example attribute source and trust context, not specified here.
This is GSS-API name attributes, not Internet naming or name resolution generally; the GSS-API tag covers it.

RFC6681.title: Raptor Forward Error Correction (FEC) Schemes for FECFRAME
RFC6681.summary: Defines six fully-specified FEC Schemes (IDs 1-6) applying Raptor (RFC 5053) and RaptorQ (RFC 6330) codes within the FEC Framework to protect arbitrary packet flows, small-block-optimized flows, and single sequenced (e.g. RTP) flows, with payload ID formats and source symbol construction.

FECFRAME.why: The document specifies FEC Schemes for the FEC Framework, including FEC Payload ID formats, source block construction and scheme IDs registered in the FECFRAME registry.
FECFRAME.quote: This document describes six FEC Schemes that make use of the Raptor and RaptorQ FEC codes as defined in [RFC5053] and [RFC6330].

Raptor.why: All six schemes are built on the Raptor and RaptorQ codes, and the document specifies how they are applied to packet flows, including symbol construction and block-size optimizations.
Raptor.quote: The FEC encoder defined in [RFC5053] SHALL be used for FEC Scheme 1 and the FEC encoder defined in [RFC6330] SHALL be used for FEC Scheme 2.

rejected.why: RTP is only a possible source/repair transport; Section 8.2.4 gives only sequence-number and length rules for RTP source flows, which is not enough to make RTP a subject.
The SDP section is a single example of signalling; the SDP syntax is defined elsewhere (RFC 6364).
The parent is implied by FECFRAME and Raptor, so it is not listed separately.
UDP is only the datagram transport for the flows and is not specified or profiled here.
The schemes are based on the RMT FEC Building Block, but the document is about FECFRAME streaming protection, not reliable multicast object delivery.

RFC6682.title: RTP Payload Format for Raptor Forward Error Correction (FEC)
RFC6682.summary: Defines the RTP payload format and media type registrations (application/video/audio/text raptorfec) for carrying Raptor/RaptorQ FEC repair flows in the FEC Framework, with SDP mapping and offer/answer rules.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is an RTP payload format, including RTP header usage and payload data rules for Raptor repair packets.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies an RTP payload format for the Forward Error Correction (FEC) repair data produced by the Raptor FEC Schemes.

Raptor.why: The payload format carries repair data from the Raptor and RaptorQ FEC schemes, and the parameters map to those schemes.
Raptor.quote: The Raptor and RaptorQ codes are efficient block-based fountain codes, meaning that from any group of source packets

FECFRAME.why: The payload format is defined in terms of the FEC Framework (FECFRAME) and carries its repair flows and Configuration Information.
FECFRAME.quote: The FEC Framework [RFC6363] defines a general framework for the use of Forward Error Correction in association with arbitrary packet flows

media types.why: A large part of the document is registration of four raptorfec media types with parameters.
media types.quote: This RTP payload format is identified using the 'application/raptorfec' media type that is registered in accordance with [RFC4855]

SDP.why: Sections 7-9 and 11 specify SDP mapping, offer/answer and declarative considerations, and an example for the payload format.
SDP.quote: The mapping of the above defined payload format media type and its parameters SHALL be done according to Section 3 of [RFC4855]
SDP.section: 7. Mapping to the Session Description Protocol (SDP)

rejected.why: The more specific RTP payload format tag fits, and the parent is implied.
RTCP is only used per RFC 3550, with CNAME association. Nothing new is defined.
SRTP is only recommended in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
Not about LDPC. Only Raptor codes are used.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations.

RFC6683.title: Guidelines for Implementing Digital Video Broadcasting - IPTV (DVB-IPTV) Application-Layer Hybrid Forward Error Correction (FEC) Protection
RFC6683.summary: Informational guidelines describing how to implement the DVB-IPTV two-layer AL-FEC protocol (1-D interleaved parity base layer plus Raptor enhancement layer) using existing RFCs, with RTP exceptions and SDP signaling.

FECFRAME.why: The document is an FEC framework-related guideline for application-layer FEC protecting streaming media, built from FECFRAME-based Raptor schemes and parity FEC, written in the fecframe WG.
FECFRAME.quote: This document describes how one can implement the DVB-IPTV AL-FEC protocol by using the 1-D interleaved parity code and Raptor code that have already been specified

Raptor.why: The enhancement layer uses Raptor code and hybrid decoding combines it with parity; a substantial part of the document addresses it.
Raptor.quote: The FEC scheme for the enhancement layer SHALL be the Raptor FEC scheme for a Single Sequenced Flow with FEC encoding ID 5.

IPTV.why: The document addresses DVB-IPTV service protection and operational use of AL-FEC for IPTV streams.
IPTV.quote: covers several areas related to the transmission of MPEG2 transport stream-based services over IP networks.

rejected.why: RTP is the carrier of source and repair streams; the document notes incompatibilities but does not specify RTP itself.
SDP is used to signal the FEC configuration with an example, but nothing new is defined for SDP.
The payload formats are defined in RFC 6015 and RFC 6682; this document only says how to use them or not use them.
Not used; the document uses XOR parity and Raptor, not LDPC codes.

RFC6684.title: Guidelines and Template for Defining Extensions to the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF)
RFC6684.summary: Informational guidelines and an Internet-Draft template for defining extensions to IODEF (RFC 5070), covering when to extend, the extension mechanisms, and example extensions.

IODEF.why: The whole document is about how to extend IODEF: applicability, extension mechanisms (enumerated attributes, AdditionalData/RecordItem), and a template with examples.
IODEF.quote: This document provides guidelines for extensions to the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) described in RFC 5070 for exchange of incident management data

rejected.why: IODEF extensions are XML schemas, but XML is only the encoding substrate; the document is about IODEF extension, not XML usage generally.
RID is mentioned only as an example of the containment extension mechanism; it is not specified or profiled here.
The template describes registering namespaces and schemas, but this is boilerplate guidance for extension documents, not the main subject.
Covered by the more specific IODEF tag, which sits under it.
The template is for Internet-Drafts about IODEF extensions, but its subject is IODEF, not RFC format or publication.

RFC6685.title: Expert Review for Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) Extensions in IANA XML Registry
RFC6685.summary: RFC 6685 requires an additional IODEF Expert Review, with experts designated by the Security Area Directors, for registrations of IODEF extension schemas in the IANA XML Schema registry, and it updates RFC 5070.

IODEF.why: The whole document is about reviewing extensions to IODEF (AdditionalData and RecordItem extensions) for correctness and compatibility, so IODEF readers would want it.
IODEF.quote: Changes to the XML Schema registry for schema names beginning with "urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:iodef" are subject to an additional IODEF Expert Review
IODEF.section: 2. Expert Review of IODEF-Related XML Registry Entries

IANA.why: The document sets registration policy for part of the IANA XML registry, which is IANA registry guidance in its own right, not mere boilerplate.
IANA.quote: specifies restrictions on additions to the subset of the IANA XML Namespace and Schema registries, to require Expert Review

rejected.why: XML schemas and namespaces are only the registry subject matter. The document defines no XML usage or format.
The IODEF tag already sits under this topic and covers it.
It designates experts, but only for a registry review policy, which the IANA tag covers better.

RFC6686.title: Resolution of the Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and Sender ID Experiments
RFC6686.summary: Informational report concluding the SPF and Sender ID experiments (RFCs 4405-4408) by presenting DNS RRTYPE 99 vs TXT deployment surveys, implementation data, SUBMITTER SMTP extension usage, and conclusions.

SPF.why: The document evaluates SPF deployment and concludes its experiment. SPF's subject readers would want this resolution report.
SPF.quote: SPF has widespread implementation and deployment, comparable to that of many Standards Track protocols.

email authentication.why: The document concludes the experiments on Sender ID (with PRA and SUBMITTER), which have no child tag. The parent topic covers them.

DNS.why: A substantial part covers DNS RRTYPE 99 vs TXT surveys, and Appendix A covers the difficulty of deploying new RRTYPEs.
DNS.quote: There has not been substantial adoption of the RRTYPE 99 (SPF) DNS resource record.

SMTP.why: A full section surveys deployment of the SUBMITTER SMTP extension, which is an SMTP extension.
SMTP.quote: The SUBMITTER extension to SMTP is a mechanism to provide an early hint

rejected.why: It discusses the IESG experiment outcome and an RRTYPE allocation lesson, but the main subject is protocol deployment evidence.
The PRA heuristic extracts an address from message headers, but the document does not specify header formats.

gaps.name: Sender ID
gaps.why: No tag exists for Sender ID, PRA or SUBMITTER specifically. The document concludes their experiments, so they are covered only by the email authentication parent.

RFC6687.title: Performance Evaluation of the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL)
RFC6687.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC presenting simulation-based performance evaluation of RPL (path quality, routing table size, delay, control overhead, loss of connectivity, scaling) on real outdoor sensor and large smart meter network topologies.

RPL.why: The whole document evaluates RPL behaviour (DODAG construction, trickle timers, global/local repair, storing mode) via simulation, so RPL readers would want it.
RPL.quote: This document presents a performance evaluation of the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) for a small outdoor deployment of sensor nodes

rejected.why: The metrics are simulation results for one protocol, not a measurement methodology or active/passive measurement of networks; RPL tag fits better.
802.15.4 framing is only the simulated link layer, not the subject.
Parent of RPL, already implied; document is specifically about RPL.
LLN routing is not MANET routing; no MANET protocol is discussed.
This is a protocol simulation study, not a benchmarking methodology for network devices.

RFC6688.title: Parallel NFS (pNFS) Block Disk Protection
RFC6688.summary: Updates RFC 5663 to define a GPT partition GUID that labels pNFS block storage devices so clients and other hosts can identify and protect them at boot without contacting the NFSv4 metadata server.

NFS.why: The document extends the pNFS block layout (RFC 5663) for NFSv4.1 with a new device identification mechanism, so it belongs on the NFS subject page.
NFS.quote: The pNFS block storage partitions are identified in the GPT with GUID e5b72a69-23e5-4b4d-b176-16532674fc34, which has been generated for this purpose.

rejected.why: The GUID is only a partition type identifier, and RFC 4122 is cited just for the point that GUIDs have no central registry. The document is not about UUID specification or use.
The parent topic is implied by NFS, so it is not listed separately. Block storage is the subject area but NFS is the more specific tag.
SCSI and SAN access control are mentioned only as background. The document does not specify iSCSI.

gaps.name: GUID Partition Table (GPT) labelling of block devices
gaps.why: The core mechanism is a GPT partition type GUID, but the taxonomy has no tag for disk partitioning or block-device labelling.

RFC6689.title: Usage of the RSVP ASSOCIATION Object
RFC6689.summary: Informational CCAMP document clarifying how the RSVP ASSOCIATION object is used to associate GMPLS end-to-end and segment recovery LSPs (and resource sharing), without defining new procedures.

GMPLS.why: The document explains how the ASSOCIATION object associates GMPLS recovery LSPs (end-to-end and segment recovery), which is GMPLS signalling and recovery.
GMPLS.quote: End-to-end and segment recovery are defined for GMPLS-controlled label switched paths (LSPs) in [RFC4872] and [RFC4873], respectively.

RSVP-TE.why: The ASSOCIATION object is an RSVP-TE Path message object. The document analyses its fields, matching rules and Association ID selection.
RSVP-TE.quote: the association of one LSP to another LSP across different RSVP - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) sessions.

rejected.why: Base MPLS LSPs are only mentioned as a point of comparison. The subject is GMPLS recovery association.
RSVP is the base protocol for RSVP-TE. The document concerns the TE extension (ASSOCIATION object), not general RSVP reservations.
RSVP-TE already covers the signalling. The document does not address traffic engineering in general.

RFC6690.title: Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Link Format
RFC6690.summary: Defines the CoRE Link Format, a Web Linking serialization (based on RFC 5988 Link header) for constrained servers to describe hosted resources, with rt/if/sz attributes, the /.well-known/core discovery interface, query filtering, the application/link-format media type, and CoRE parameter registries.

web linking.why: The document specifies a serialization of typed links extending RFC 5988 and a new 'hosts' link relation type, so it belongs under Web Linking.
web linking.quote: This specification defines Web Linking using a link format for use by constrained web servers to describe hosted resources, their attributes, and other relationships between links.

CoAP.why: CoRE Link Format is the CoAP resource discovery mechanism (/.well-known/core), with multicast discovery and CoAP-specific guidance such as multicast response suppression and the 'sz' attribute.
CoAP.quote: This specification is applicable for use with Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) [COAP], HTTP, or any other suitable web transfer protocol.

media types.why: Registers a new media type, application/link-format, as a substantive part of the document.
media types.quote: This specification thus defines the Internet media type 'application/link-format' for the CoRE Link Format (see Section 7.3).

service discovery.why: CoRE Resource Discovery of resources hosted on constrained servers, including unicast and multicast discovery and filtering, is a core purpose.
service discovery.quote: A well-known relative URI "/.well-known/core" is defined as a default entry point for requesting the list of links about resources hosted by a server

rejected.why: The format reuses the HTTP Link header syntax and is applicable to HTTP, but HTTP is only a basis and possible transport, not the subject.
URIs and URI Templates are used for targets and query filtering, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes; the well-known URI registration is minor.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the format.
Targeted at constrained M2M nodes, but IoT is context; the CoAP tag covers the technology readers would look for.
Mentioned only as a way to protect the resource in Security Considerations.
Registries are established, but this is boilerplate-level relative to the main subject.

gaps.name: CoRE resource discovery / resource directory
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a CoAP tag but no CoRE-specific tag for link format or resource directory; CoAP is the closest fit.

RFC6691.title: TCP Options and Maximum Segment Size (MSS)
RFC6691.summary: Informational RFC clarifying that the TCP MSS option value should subtract only the fixed IP and TCP headers, not IP/TCP options, and correcting RFC 879 and RFC 2385 accordingly.

TCP.why: The document specifies how to compute the value of the TCP MSS option and updates RFC 879 and RFC 2385, so it is about TCP protocol behaviour and options.
TCP.quote: the MTU value SHOULD be decreased by only the size of the fixed IP and TCP headers and SHOULD NOT be decreased to account for any possible IP or TCP options

rejected.why: Path MTU Discovery is mentioned only in a short additional-considerations section with references. The document is not about it.
IPv6 header size and jumbograms are mentioned briefly, but the document is not about IPv6.
ROHC appears only as an example of a variable effective MTU in a brief subsection.
RFC 2385 (TCP MD5 for BGP) is corrected, but only its MSS statement. The document is not about BGP.

RFC6692.title: Source Ports in Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) Reports
RFC6692.summary: Defines a new ARF header field, Source-Port, so abuse feedback reports can carry the TCP source port of the connection involved, complementing Source-IP; updates RFC 6591.

ARF.why: The document extends the Abuse Reporting Format with a new report field, its syntax and usage guidance, so it belongs on the ARF page.
ARF.quote: A new ARF header field called "Source-Port" is defined.

rejected.why: RFC 6591 authentication failure reports are mentioned, but the document only recommends the new field for them. ARF is the more specific tag.
The ABNF imports CFWS from RFC 5322, but the document does not address the Internet message format itself.
The field carries a TCP port number, but TCP is only the connection being described. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
IP address sharing is the motivation for the field, but the document does not address NAT behaviour or deployment.
The reports concern email abuse, but the document defines a report field rather than spam filtering or reputation.
The document registers a field in the Feedback Report Header Fields registry. That is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.

RFC6693.title: Probabilistic Routing Protocol for Intermittently Connected Networks
RFC6693.summary: Defines PRoPHET, an experimental probabilistic routing protocol for intermittently connected (delay/disruption-tolerant) networks that uses encounter history and transitivity to prune epidemic forwarding of bundles, with architecture, message formats and state machines.

DTN.why: The document specifies a routing protocol for delay/disruption-tolerant networks that carries bundles. It is built around the DTN architecture and the Bundle Protocol agent.
DTN.quote: PRoPHET is a variant of the epidemic routing protocol for intermittently connected networks that operates by pruning the epidemic distribution tree

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate the PRoPHET signalling runs over. The document defines nothing new about TCP.
The networks are sparse and intermittently connected, with mobile nodes. The protocol is not a MANET routing protocol that assumes connected paths, and it is placed in DTN.
The document defines a specific routing protocol, not general routing architecture principles.

RFC6694.title: The "about" URI Scheme
RFC6694.summary: Defines the "about" URI scheme used by web browsers to designate internal resources, defines the well-known token "about:blank", and creates an IANA registry of well-known about tokens.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme: its syntax, semantics, encoding considerations and registration. Readers browsing URI schemes would expect it.
URI.quote: This document describes the "about" URI scheme, which is widely used by Web browsers and some other applications to designate access to their internal resources

rejected.why: ABNF is used only as the notation for the scheme syntax, so it is substrate rather than subject.
The document creates a small token registry, but this is a minor part of the scheme specification and the document is not about IANA guidance.
Browsers are the context for the scheme, but the document does not specify HTML or hypertext formats.
The document refers only to URIs under RFC 3986 and does not deal with internationalized identifiers.

RFC6695.title: Methods to Convey Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework Configuration Information
RFC6695.summary: Informational RFC describing how existing signaling protocols (SAP for multicast; SIP and RTSP for unicast) can convey FEC Framework Configuration Information between sender and receivers, defining only an RTSP option tag.

FECFRAME.why: The whole document is about conveying FEC Framework (RFC 6363) configuration information between sender and receivers, so it belongs on the FECFRAME page.
FECFRAME.quote: This document describes how to use signaling protocols such as the Session Announcement Protocol (SAP), the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), the Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP)

RTSP.why: Section 5.2.2 extends RTSP with a new option tag used in SETUP Require headers to request FEC protection, and IANA registers it. RTSP readers would want this.
RTSP.quote: This specification defines the 'FEC-protection-needed' option tag

SIP.why: It describes using SIP's SDP offer/answer to exchange FEC configuration for unicast sessions. This is a smaller part of the document.
SIP.quote: This document extends the usage of this model for exchanging the FEC Framework Configuration Information

rejected.why: SDP is only an example encoding format, and its FEC elements are defined in RFC 6364. The document explicitly leaves the encoding choice out of scope.
Multicast is the delivery mechanism for SAP announcements. PIM is mentioned only as out of scope.
UDP is the transport substrate for SAP, not a subject of the document.
SAP announces sessions, but the document is about conveying FEC configuration, not about discovering services in general.
This is not relevant. I considered nothing email-related; the document only uses MIME content types in the SAP Payload Type field, so MIME and media types are not tagged either.

gaps.name: SAP (Session Announcement Protocol)
gaps.why: Section 5.1 specifies in detail how SAP version 2 is used to multicast FEC configuration, including sender and receiver procedures. The taxonomy has no SAP tag.

RFC6696.title: EAP Extensions for the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP)
RFC6696.summary: RFC 6696 specifies the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP): new EAP codes (Initiate/Finish), packet formats, and a re-authentication key hierarchy (rRK, rIK, rMSK) for method-independent fast re-authentication with a home or local ER server, obsoleting RFC 5296.

HOKEY.why: The document is the core ERP specification, which is what the HOKEY tag covers (handover keying and ERP). It defines the ER key hierarchy and the Initiate/Finish exchanges.
HOKEY.quote: This document specifies EAP Re-authentication Extensions (ERXs) for efficient re-authentication using EAP. The protocol that uses these extensions is itself referred to as the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP).

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by HOKEY, and the ERP extensions are covered by the more specific child, so it is not listed separately.
The document relies on AAA to carry ERP messages and rMSK/DSRK. Section 7 delegates transport to other RFCs (RFC 5749 and the Diameter ERP draft), so AAA is not the subject.
Diameter transport is only referenced as a separate document (DIAMETER-ERP) and is not specified here.
IKEv2 is mentioned only as a lower layer that needs updating to carry ERP messages. This document does not specify those changes.
RADIUS attributes are referenced only as examples of channel binding information (Called-Station-Id and similar) and as the AAA User-Name attribute. This is incidental use.
HMAC-SHA256 serves as the integrity cryptosuite, which is a mechanism relied on and not a subject of the document.

RFC6697.title: Handover Keying (HOKEY) Architecture Design
RFC6697.summary: Informational RFC defining the HOKEY architecture for reducing EAP re-authentication delay at handover, covering design goals, functions, components (peer, authenticators, EAP server, ER server) and usage scenarios.

HOKEY.why: The document is the HOKEY architecture: design goals, functions, components and scenarios for EAP re-authentication and early authentication keying.
HOKEY.quote: This document defines the HOKEY architecture.

rejected.why: HOKEY is the more specific child of EAP; the EAP parent is implied.
AAA is used as transport for EAP/ERP messages and keys; section 7 analyses it briefly but the document is not about AAA frameworks.
Only referenced as a possible AAA transport for ERP and key delivery; not specified here.
Mentioned as a candidate protocol for carrying EAP and pre-authentication, not the subject.
Handover is the context, but the document concerns authentication keying, not IP mobility.

RFC6698.title: The DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol: TLSA
RFC6698.summary: Defines the TLSA DNS resource record and the DANE protocol for associating TLS/DTLS server certificates and public keys with domain names, secured by DNSSEC.

DANE.why: The document specifies the DANE TLSA protocol: RR format, certificate usages, selectors, matching types, naming and client processing.
DANE.quote: The TLSA DNS resource record (RR) is used to associate a TLS server certificate or public key with the domain name where the record is found

rejected.why: DNSSEC is relied on to validate TLSA records, but the document does not specify or extend DNSSEC.
TLS is the protocol the associations are used with. The document defines no new TLS extension; it only changes client certificate validation.
A new RR type is defined, but it is the DANE-specific record. DANE is the more specific tag.
PKIX certificates are matched against TLSA data, but the document does not profile or specify X.509.
DTLS is mentioned as also covered, but the document is mostly about TLS generally and does not specify DTLS.

RFC6701.title: Sanctions Available for Application to Violators of IETF IPR Policy
RFC6701.summary: RFC 6701 describes the administrative sanctions available within IETF processes against participants who violate the IETF's IPR disclosure policy, who may initiate them, and how to choose among them fairly.

IPR.why: The whole document concerns enforcement of the IETF IPR policy (BCP 79) and the sanctions for violating its disclosure rules, so IPR is the central subject.
IPR.quote: This document discusses these issues and provides a suite of potential actions that can be taken within the IETF community in cases related to patents.

IETF process.why: It covers IETF administrative procedure: roles of WG chairs and ADs, posting rights actions, editor removal, and appeals under RFC 2026. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: Normally, the working group chairs and area directors assume the responsibility for ensuring the smooth running of the IETF and for the enforcement of IETF policies

rejected.why: Posting rights suspensions concern IETF discussion lists as a governance matter, not the mailing list protocols or headers in the taxonomy.
No NomCom procedure is addressed.
Attribution moves in documents are mentioned as a sanction, but the document is not about RFC series format or publication.

RFC6702.title: Promoting Compliance with Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Disclosure Rules
RFC6702.summary: Informational RFC suggesting strategies for ADs, WG chairs and secretaries to promote timely IPR disclosure by authors and contributors at key points in the IETF document lifecycle, with sample reminder messages.

IPR.why: The whole document is about compliance with IETF IPR disclosure rules (BCP 78/79) and how chairs and ADs can encourage early disclosure.
IPR.quote: This document describes some strategies for promoting compliance with the IPR disclosure rules.

IETF process.why: It covers process steps such as WG adoption, WGLC, AD review and IETF Last Call, and the roles of chairs, ADs and shepherds.
IETF process.quote: identifies opportunities to promote IPR disclosure within the document lifecycle for IETF working group documents.

rejected.why: IANA is not discussed. The document is about IPR disclosure, not registries.
The document touches RFC streams only in passing. It is about the standards process, not the format or publication of RFCs.

RFC6703.title: Reporting IP Network Performance Metrics: Different Points of View
RFC6703.summary: Informational IPPM memo on how the two audiences (network characterization vs application performance) shape parameter selection and long-term reporting of loss, delay, delay variation, reordering, raw and bulk transfer capacity metrics, test streams and sample size.

performance measurement.why: The whole document is about selecting parameters and reporting IP performance metrics (loss, delay, PDV, reordering, capacity), the IPPM subject area.
performance measurement.quote: This memo provides "long-term" reporting considerations (e.g., hours, days, weeks, or months, as opposed to 10 seconds), based on analysis of the points of view of two key audiences.

rejected.why: Bulk transfer capacity is measured with TCP and a Type-C TCP configuration is introduced, but the document is about reporting metrics, not TCP itself.
OWAMP/TWAMP are mentioned only for how Type-P (DSCP) is communicated; they are not specified or profiled here.
Only cited in passing for Type-P and in the Security Considerations; not the subject.
This is about active network performance metrics reporting, not device benchmarking methodology.
DSCP appears only as a Type-P qualifier, in one sentence.
Large-scale measurement platforms are not discussed; only the short-term reporting draft is referenced.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metric definitions and reporting
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic 'performance measurement' topic, with no tag for the IPPM metrics themselves (one-way delay, loss, PDV, reordering, capacity).

RFC6704.title: Forcerenew Nonce Authentication
RFC6704.summary: RFC 6704 defines Forcerenew Nonce Authentication for DHCPv4 FORCERENEW messages: the server sends a nonce in the initial ACK and later authenticates FORCERENEW with an HMAC-MD5 keyed by it, avoiding out-of-band key distribution; it updates RFC 3203.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 with a new option (FORCERENEW_NONCE_CAPABLE) and an authentication protocol for FORCERENEW, updating RFC 3203. DHCP readers would want it.
DHCP.quote: This document defines extensions to Authentication for DHCPv4 Messages [RFC3118] to create a new authentication protocol for DHCPv4 FORCERENEW [RFC3203] messages

rejected.why: The nonce mechanism is borrowed from RFC 3315 (DHCPv6) Reconfigure Key, but this document specifies DHCPv4 only.
HMAC-MD5 is just the mechanism used to compute the digest; the document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
MD5 is used as the fixed algorithm but the document is not about MD5.
The authentication is specific to DHCP FORCERENEW, so the DHCP tag covers it; the generic topic adds nothing.
The nonce must be cryptographically strong random, but this is a one-line requirement, not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC6705.title: Localized Routing for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6705.summary: Specifies a localized routing mechanism for Proxy Mobile IPv6, letting MAGs and LMAs set up direct forwarding or inter-MAG tunnels between mobile nodes, using new LRI and LRA Mobility Header messages and a MAG IPv6 Address option.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document extends PMIPv6 with localized routing between MAGs and LMAs, defining new messages, options and handover behaviour.
PMIPv6.quote: This document proposes initiation, utilization, and termination mechanisms for localized routing between mobile access gateways within a proxy mobile IPv6 domain.

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 is referenced only as the protocol that the MAG proxies. The document extends PMIPv6, not Mobile IPv6 itself.
GRE is listed as one possible inter-MAG encapsulation, taken from RFC 5845. The document defines nothing new about GRE.
IPsec is the security mechanism for protecting LRI and LRA, and it appears only in Security Considerations.
Inter-MAG tunnelling is covered only by reference to existing PMIPv6 encapsulation modes. It is not a generic tunnelling specification.
Section 9 covers IPv4 home address support only as an application of RFC 5844 to localized routing. The document is not about IPv4 itself.

RFC6706.title: Asymmetric Extended Route Optimization (AERO)
RFC6706.summary: Experimental RFC defining AERO, an on-demand route optimization mechanism for large multi-access/NBMA links using Predirect and Redirect messages (UDP-encapsulated ICMPv6-Redirect-like) mediated by a trusted intermediate router.

routing architecture.why: AERO is a new on-demand route optimization/dynamic routing mechanism for multi-access links, motivated against OSPF, AODV, etc. It is about routing design and scalability, with no more specific tag.
routing architecture.quote: This document therefore introduces an Asymmetric Extended Route Optimization (AERO) capability that addresses the issues.

neighbor discovery.why: AERO extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery redirection, using neighbor cache entries, RS/RA, and redirect validation rules. Much of the specification is an ND extension.
neighbor discovery.quote: AERO Redirect/Predirect messages use the same format as for ICMPv6 Redirect messages depicted in Section 4.5 of [RFC4861]

rejected.why: IPv6 is the network layer the mechanism is described over, but the document is about redirection/route optimization; neighbor discovery is the more specific fit.
UDP is only the encapsulation for AERO messages, with a port assignment. It is substrate.
AERO messages are modelled on ICMPv6 Redirect but deliberately distinguished from it by UDP encapsulation.
NBMA tunnel virtual interfaces are a motivating use case, but the document does not specify tunnelling.
Prefix delegation via DHCPv6 is mentioned only as a way edge routers acquire prefixes.
MANETs are one example use case, and the document positions AERO against MANET routing protocols, but it does not specify MANET routing.

gaps.name: Route optimization / redirection on multi-access links
gaps.why: AERO's core subject is on-demand redirection-based route optimization. The taxonomy has only the broad routing architecture tag for it.

RFC6707.title: Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI) Problem Statement
RFC6707.summary: Informational problem statement for the CDNI working group that outlines why standalone CDNs should be interconnected, defines the four CDNI interfaces (control, request routing, metadata, logging), and scopes what is in and out of IETF work.

CDN.why: The whole document is about interconnecting content delivery networks: use cases, the interface model, and scoping. The CDN tag fits exactly.
CDN.quote: The goal of this document is to outline the problem area of CDN Interconnection for the IETF CDNI (CDN Interconnection) working group.

rejected.why: HTTP is only suggested as a possible protocol for the interfaces and for content acquisition. The document does not specify or extend it.
ALTO is discussed as a complementary WG and as a candidate for footprint information. Only a short appendix covers it, and the document is not about ALTO.
XMPP is named only as an example candidate protocol for the metadata interface.
syslog, SNMP and FTP are listed only as candidate protocols for the logging interface.
PPSP and DECADE are covered only in a short appendix on relationships to other working groups.
DNS-based request routing is mentioned only as one redirection scenario. The document does not address DNS itself.

RFC6708.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Requirements
RFC6708.summary: RFC 6708 enumerates requirements for ALTO client protocols, server discovery mechanisms, host-group descriptors, rating criteria, and security/privacy, to guide specification and assessment of ALTO protocols.

ALTO.why: The whole document defines requirements for ALTO protocols, server discovery, and information disclosure, so it belongs on the ALTO page.
ALTO.quote: The goal of Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) is to provide guidance to applications that have to select one or several hosts from a set of candidates

rejected.why: P2P file sharing is the main motivating use case, but the document is about ALTO guidance and not about P2P overlays or applications.
Requirements AR-26 and AR-34 to AR-36 say ALTO must work behind NATs. NAT behaviour is a constraint on ALTO here, not a subject the document addresses.
DNS, DHCP and PPP are named only as examples of existing mechanisms that server discovery could reuse. The document does not specify or analyse them.
ALTO server discovery is covered by the ALTO tag. The document does not address service discovery in general.
AR-13 and AR-14 say ALTO must not replace congestion control. They are limits on ALTO's scope and not a treatment of congestion control.
Privacy and information disclosure are discussed, but only as requirements on ALTO. The document is not a general privacy threat model.

RFC6709.title: Design Considerations for Protocol Extensions
RFC6709.summary: IAB informational document giving architectural design considerations for extensibility of Internet protocols (routine vs major extensions, versioning, parameter spaces, unknown-extension handling, crypto agility), with RADIUS, TLS and L2TP case studies.

internet architecture.why: The document is an IAB statement of architectural principles for protocol extensibility and versioning, applicable across all Internet protocols.
internet architecture.quote: The purpose of this document is to describe the architectural principles of sound extensibility design, in order to minimize such risks.

RADIUS.why: A substantial case study analyses RADIUS extension problems: VSAs, self-allocation, data types, unknown attribute handling.
RADIUS.quote: The RADIUS [RFC2865] protocol was designed to be extensible via addition of Attributes.

TLS.why: A full case study covers TLS/SSL version negotiation and extension interoperability failures, and is cited repeatedly in the main body.
TLS.quote: Extension mechanisms were finally defined in "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions" [RFC4366]

L2TP.why: A dedicated case study discusses L2TP AVP extensions, vendor-specific AVPs and the M-bit.
L2TP.quote: L2TP also provides for a "mandatory" bit in AVPs.

rejected.why: Parameter registration is discussed (Sec 3.6, 4.4) but as part of extension design, not as IANA registry guidance itself.
EAP type-space exhaustion and versioning are used as examples, not a subject of the document.
Procedures are the subject of the companion RFC 4775; this document focuses on design considerations.
Cryptographic agility is a short subsection (4.5), not a main subject.
Mentioned only as examples of critical protocols and extension documents.
Attribute tunneling is a brief example of extending critical protocols.

gaps.name: protocol extensibility / extension design
gaps.why: The document's main subject, the design of protocol extension mechanisms and versioning, has no dedicated tag; only the broad internet architecture tag fits.

RFC6710.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Extension for Message Transfer Priorities
RFC6710.summary: Defines the MT-PRIORITY SMTP service extension, which lets clients label messages with a priority from -9 to 9 for preferential handling by MSAs, MTAs and LMTP servers, and sets up an IANA registry of Priority Assignment Policies.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP extension: the MT-PRIORITY EHLO keyword and MAIL FROM parameter, with relay, submission and LMTP rules.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines an extension to the SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) service whereby messages are given a label to indicate preferential handling

rejected.why: This is the parent of SMTP, which is implied. The document is about an SMTP extension and not email architecture in general.
Mentioned only as network-level priority mechanisms that can complement this extension. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Mentioned only as an example of network priority, together with RFC 6401. The document is not about it.
Network QoS appears only in the introduction and in Appendix D.3's analogy. The document's subject is application-level message priority.
The IANA registry for Priority Assignment Policies is boilerplate-like support for the extension. The document is not about IANA guidance.
The Received header PRIORITY clause is only a minor addition. The header-field tunnelling is in a separate companion document.
The NS/EP policy in Appendix C is one example policy and is not the focus of the document.

RFC6711.title: An IANA Registry for Level of Assurance (LoA) Profiles
RFC6711.summary: RFC 6711 establishes an IANA registry for Level of Assurance (LoA) Profiles, defining the registration template, expert-review policy and semantics so SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect and other protocols can discover LoA definitions.

authentication.why: Levels of assurance categorize authentication methods by strength, and the registry catalogues LoA profiles used across protocols. This is a cross-protocol authentication subject.
authentication.quote: The purpose of this specification is to create an IANA registry where such LoA definitions can be discovered.

IANA.why: The main body defines a new IANA registry, including its template, registration policy and reviewer expectations. These are not boilerplate, because the document exists to create the registry.
IANA.quote: The registry is to be operated under the "Expert Review" policy from RFC 5226 [RFC5226], employing a pool of experts.

rejected.why: The document mentions identity federations and trust frameworks as context, but it defines only a registry of LoA profiles. It does not specify a federation framework.
SAML Authentication Context Class XML schemas are the registered content, but the document does not specify or profile XML itself.
ABNF is used only to define the registry name syntax, so it is notation and not a subject of the document.
Relying parties choose a required LoA for access to resources, but the document does not address authorization.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) authentication context
gaps.why: The registry is built around SAML 2.0 Authentication Context Classes and URIs, but the taxonomy has no SAML tag. Readers of SAML would want this RFC.

RFC6712.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure -- HTTP Transfer for the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP)
RFC6712.summary: Specifies how to transfer CMP (Certificate Management Protocol) PKIMessages over HTTP using POST, including media type, status codes, request URI and pushed announcements; updates RFC 4210.

CMP.why: The document is the CMPtrans specification for CMP, defining how CMP messages and announcements are transported and updating RFC 4210.
CMP.quote: This document describes how to layer the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) over HTTP.

HTTP.why: A substantial part of the document defines how HTTP is used for CMP: versions, persistent connections, status codes, Content-Type and Request-URI. This is a new usage profile of HTTP, which readers of HTTP usage would want.
HTTP.quote: A DER-encoded [ITU.X690.1994] PKIMessage [RFC4210] is sent as the entity-body of an HTTP POST request.

rejected.why: TLS is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a protection option, so it is not tagged.
The document uses application/pkixcmp, which was registered earlier, and registers nothing new.
CMP is the more specific tag in this area, and PKI is its parent, so it is implied.
X.509 appears only in the title as the context of CMP. The document does not define certificate formats or profiles.
DER encoding of PKIMessage is only a substrate. The document defines nothing about ASN.1 itself.
The document is a transport binding of CMP over HTTP, so this topic fits loosely. It is better covered by the specific CMP and HTTP tags.

gaps.name: CMP (Certificate Management Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a CMP tech id under PKI, but I'm using it as given. If the CMP id were missing, the document would need a tag for it.

RFC6713.title: The 'application/zlib' and 'application/gzip' Media Types
RFC6713.summary: Registers the 'application/zlib' and 'application/gzip' media types for data compressed with the zlib and gzip formats, replacing various informal types.

media types.why: The document's purpose is registering two media types, with full registration templates, so it belongs on the media type registrations page.
media types.quote: This document defines the 'application/gzip' and 'application/zlib' media types for compressed data using the gzip and zlib compression formats.

gzip.why: The gzip media type, magic number and file extension are defined here, which readers of gzip would want.
gzip.quote: The 'application/gzip' media type describes a block of data that is compressed using gzip [RFC1952] compression.

zlib.why: Defines the media type for zlib-compressed data, including its magic numbers, so zlib readers would want it.
zlib.quote: The 'application/zlib' media type describes a block of data that is compressed using zlib [RFC1950] compression.

rejected.why: DEFLATE is only the underlying compression scheme mentioned in the introduction. The document does not specify or extend it.
A parent of gzip and zlib, which are already tagged, so it is implied.
The parent of media types. The document is about the registrations, not MIME body structure or encodings.
The IANA section only records the registration, which is boilerplate.

RFC6714.title: Connection Establishment for Media Anchoring (CEMA) for the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)
RFC6714.summary: Defines CEMA, an MSRP extension and SDP 'msrp-cema' attribute letting endpoints use the SDP c/m-line to establish the MSRP connection so middleboxes can anchor media without acting as MSRP B2BUAs, preserving end-to-end TLS.

MSRP.why: The document specifies an extension to MSRP connection establishment, including offerer/answerer procedures and relay interaction.
MSRP.quote: This document defines a Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) extension, Connection Establishment for Media Anchoring (CEMA).

rejected.why: SDP is the signalling substrate; the document only adds one attribute and uses offer/answer, though the attribute is new. Primary subject is MSRP connection behaviour.
SIP carries the SDP and is context only; no SIP behaviour is specified.
TLS is used end-to-end and discussed in security considerations, but nothing new about TLS is defined.
NAT traversal is mentioned as a middlebox function, but the document is about media anchoring for MSRP, not ICE/STUN/TURN.
