Middleboxes are central, but the document does not address firewall/middlebox security traversal as a subject; it assumes middlebox behaviour.

RFC6715.title: vCard Format Extensions: Representing vCard Extensions Defined by the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) Converged Address Book (CAB) Group
RFC6715.summary: Defines vCard extensions (EXPERTISE, HOBBY, INTEREST, ORG-DIRECTORY properties and INDEX, LEVEL parameters) taken from the OMA Converged Address Book specification, for use with vCard 4.0.

vCard.why: The whole document defines new vCard properties and parameters and registers them in the vCard registries, so it belongs on the vCard page.
vCard.quote: This document defines extensions to the vCard data format for representing and exchanging certain contact information.

rejected.why: An ldap URI appears only as an example value for ORG-DIRECTORY. The document does not specify or extend LDAP.
ORG-DIRECTORY holds a URI pointing to an organizational directory, but the document says it specifies no lookup mechanism. The directory is incidental to a vCard property definition.
ABNF is only the notation used for format definitions, so it is a substrate and not the subject.
ORG-DIRECTORY takes a URI value, but the document defines nothing new about URIs.
The IANA section only registers vCard properties and parameters, which is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC6716.title: Definition of the Opus Audio Codec
RFC6716.summary: RFC 6716 defines the Opus interactive speech and audio codec, combining SILK (linear prediction) and CELT (MDCT) layers, with its packet framing, range coder, decoder and encoder descriptions, conformance testing and a normative reference implementation.

Opus.why: The whole document specifies the Opus codec: TOC byte framing, range decoder, SILK and CELT layers, encoder, and conformance.
Opus.quote: This document defines the Opus interactive speech and audio codec.

rejected.why: RTP, UDP and Ogg are only mentioned as lower layers carrying packets. The RTP payload format is defined in a separate document.
Opus is a child of codecs and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
RTP is mentioned only as a transport that supplies packet lengths; the document is not about RTP.
Ogg is mentioned only as one possible lower-layer container.
Matroska is mentioned only as one possible lower-layer container.
The in-band FEC (LBRR) is a codec feature inside Opus. It is not a general loss-recovery scheme for packet transport.

RFC6717.title: kx509 Kerberized Certificate Issuance Protocol in Use in 2012
RFC6717.summary: Informational RFC documenting the kx509 protocol, a UDP request/reply exchange in which a client uses a Kerberos service ticket to obtain an X.509 certificate from a Kerberized Certificate Authority (KCA).

Kerberos.why: The protocol is built on Kerberos AP-REQ and session keys and is a Kerberized service (KCA), so Kerberos readers would want it.
Kerberos.quote: This document describes a protocol, called kx509, for using Kerberos tickets to acquire X.509 certificates.

X.509.why: The protocol's purpose is issuing X.509 certificates, specifying their content (subjectAltName id-pkinit-san, serial numbers, lifetimes) and a grid certificate profile.
X.509.quote: The returned certificate MUST identify the Kerberos client principal from the AP-REQ in the original KX509Request in the subject of the certificate

rejected.why: Certificate issuance is covered, but X.509 is the more specific fit; the document explicitly excludes path construction and verification.
Only uses SRV records to locate the KCA; DNS is a substrate here.
Mentioned only as an example use of the issued certificate in Security Considerations.
HMAC-SHA1 is used for integrity of messages, but the document is not about the algorithm.
Client key type is RSA, but only as an encoding detail.
UDP is merely the transport used by the exchange.

RFC6718.title: Pseudowire Redundancy
RFC6718.summary: Informational framework describing scenarios and requirements for pseudowire redundancy, introducing a Preferential Forwarding Status (active/standby) for redundant PWs between PEs/T-PEs.

pseudowire.why: The whole document is about redundant pseudowires: reference scenarios with SS-PWs and MS-PWs, preferential forwarding status, and protection-switching requirements.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a framework comprised of a number of scenarios and associated requirements for pseudowire (PW) redundancy.

VPLS.why: Three of the six reference scenarios (H-VPLS MTU-s dual-homing, VPLS ring, VPLS n-PE protection) apply PW redundancy to VPLS, including MAC withdraw behaviour and dropping of VPLS packets on standby PWs.
VPLS.quote: PW Redundancy for PE-rs Protection in H-VPLS Using SS-PWs

rejected.why: LDP is only the signalling substrate for PW setup (RFC 4447) and is mentioned in Security Considerations. The document does not specify LDP behaviour.
MPLS LSPs and fast reroute are mentioned as PSN protection that is outside the scope of this document.
MPLS fast reroute is mentioned only as an underlying PSN mechanism that complements PW redundancy.
OAM is mentioned only in the terminology, for the traffic that active and standby PWs may forward. It is not a subject of the document.
A single requirement says the MIB must support monitoring of PW redundancy, which is too minor to count as the subject.

RFC6719.title: The Minimum Rank with Hysteresis Objective Function
RFC6719.summary: Specifies MRHOF, an RPL Objective Function that selects minimum-path-cost parents over additive metrics (default ETX) using hysteresis to limit churn, and defines Rank computation, parameters and manageability.

RPL.why: The document defines an Objective Function for RPL, covering parent selection, Rank computation, DIO metric advertisement and parameters, and registers an RPL OCP. RPL readers would look for it.
RPL.quote: This specification describes the Minimum Rank with Hysteresis Objective Function (MRHOF), an Objective Function that selects routes that minimize a metric

rejected.why: The document is about one RPL Objective Function, so the more specific RPL tag fits better than a general routing design tag.
ETX and latency are routing metrics used for path selection and are not measured or specified here, since RFC 6551 covers them.
The document does not address constrained link layers. RPL is the only relevant protocol here.
The only IANA content is the OCP code point allocation in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate.

RFC6720.title: The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)
RFC6720.summary: Defines how GTSM (TTL=255 verification) is negotiated and applied for single-hop LDP peering sessions, using a new G flag in the LDP Common Hello Parameters TLV, and updates RFC 5036.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP: it defines a new G flag in the Common Hello Parameter TLV and new Hello and Initialization procedures, and it updates RFC 5036.
LDP.quote: This document defines the GTSM use for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

rejected.why: The document is about securing one specific protocol (LDP) with GTSM. It is not general operational security practice.

GTSM protects the LDP control plane from off-link attacks. Routing security is aimed at securing routing protocols and infrastructure such as RPKI and BGPsec, and LDP is a label distribution protocol rather than a routing protocol.
The LDP session runs over TCP and the TTL check applies to that TCP connection. TCP is only the substrate, and the document defines nothing new about TCP.
LDP is the MPLS label distribution protocol and is already covered by the LDP tag. The document says nothing about MPLS architecture or forwarding.
LDP Hello discovery uses UDP, but only as a substrate.
The document improves security, but only through the protocol-specific mechanism, which is the GTSM use for LDP. The tag LDP covers it, and no general security guidance is given.

gaps.name: GTSM (Generalized TTL Security Mechanism)
gaps.why: The document's subject is applying GTSM (RFC 5082) to LDP. The taxonomy has no tag for GTSM or TTL-based protection of the control plane, so readers looking for GTSM usage across protocols have no subject page.

RFC6721.title: The Atom "deleted-entry" Element
RFC6721.summary: Extends the Atom Syndication Format with an at:deleted-entry element (tombstone) and a Deleted Entry Document with media type application/atomdeleted+xml so publishers can signal removed entries.

Atom.why: The document is an extension to the Atom Syndication Format, defining a new element for feeds and a standalone document type.
Atom.quote: This specification adds mechanisms to the Atom Syndication Format that publishers of Atom Feed and Entry documents can use to explicitly identify Atom entries that have been removed.

rejected.why: XML-Signature is only permitted as an optional mechanism on the element; the document defines nothing new about it beyond processor requirements.
XML is the encoding substrate of Atom; the document is about the Atom element, not XML usage generally.
The IANA registration of application/atomdeleted+xml is boilerplate-level apparatus, not the main subject.
RFC 3339 timestamps are only used for the 'when' attribute.
IRI use is simply inherited from RFC 4287 in one sentence.

RFC6722.title: Publishing the "Tao of the IETF" as a Web Page
RFC6722.summary: RFC 6722 obsoletes RFC 4677 and moves the "Tao of the IETF" from an RFC to a web page, and it sets out the procedure by which the IESG and a designated editor publish and revise that page.

IETF process.why: The document defines the IETF's procedure for editing, approving and publishing the Tao, with the IESG having final say. It is an IETF process and administration document.
IETF process.quote: The Tao is edited by one or more people as designated by the IESG.
IETF process.section: 2. Procedure for Publishing and Editing the Tao

RFC series.why: It changes how a long-running document is published, moving it out of the RFC series to a web page and obsoleting RFC 4677. Readers of the RFC series topic would want it.
RFC series.quote: this document formally obsoletes the last version of the Tao that was published as an RFC

rejected.why: The Tao is only published as a web page. The document is about publication procedure, not web architecture or protocols.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the transport for the page, so it is boilerplate and only the substrate.
The page is served over HTTP, but the document says nothing about HTTP itself.
The Tao is a novice's guide, but this document does not contain the guide. It only covers how the guide is published.

RFC6723.title: Update of the Pseudowire Control-Word Negotiation Mechanism
RFC6723.summary: RFC 6723 updates the pseudowire control-word negotiation in RFC 4447 and RFC 6073 by adding an LDP Label Request message procedure so a change from NOT PREFERRED to PREFERRED renegotiates correctly, for single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires.

pseudowire.why: The whole document fixes pseudowire control-word (C-bit) negotiation for single-segment and segmented pseudowires, so it belongs on the pseudowire page.
pseudowire.quote: This document updates RFC 4447 and RFC 6073 by adding the Label Request message to resolve this control-word negotiation issue for single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires.

LDP.why: The fix is a new LDP message exchange: Label Request, Label Release, Label Withdraw and Label Mapping. It also changes how an S-PE processes Label Request messages. That is a substantive extension of LDP usage for pseudowire signalling.
LDP.quote: The local PE MUST send a Label Request message to the peer PE, and then MUST wait until it receives a Label Mapping message

rejected.why: Pseudowires run over MPLS, but the document is about LDP-based PW signalling, not MPLS architecture or encapsulation.
Pseudowires are a building block for L2VPN services, but the document does not address L2VPN services themselves.

RFC6724.title: Default Address Selection for Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6)
RFC6724.summary: RFC 6724 specifies default source and destination address selection algorithms for IPv6 (and dual-stack IPv4/IPv6) nodes, with a policy table for administrative override, obsoleting RFC 3484.

IPv6.why: The document specifies default IPv6 address selection behaviour for all IPv6 nodes, covering scopes, deprecated/temporary addresses and the policy table. It is IPv6 specification and deployment guidance.
IPv6.quote: This document describes two algorithms, one for source address selection and one for destination address selection. The algorithms specify default behavior for all Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) implementations.

rejected.why: It is about address selection, but IPv6 is the more specific tag and already sits under internet layer. The addressing topic is broader than this document's IPv6-specific scope.
The policy table handles 6to4, Teredo and IPv4 preference, but these are only handled as address prefixes. The document does not specify or profile any transition mechanism.
Section 10.5 gives a multi-homed site example, but it is one illustration of policy configuration, not the subject of the document.
Home and care-of addresses appear only as a preference rule (Rule 4) and are not the subject of the document. Mobile IPv6 is not specified or extended here.
DNS results (via getaddrinfo) supply the destination list that gets sorted, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Preferred, deprecated and temporary address states come from RFC 4862 and RFC 4941 and are only used as inputs to the rules.

RFC6725.title: DNS Security (DNSSEC) DNSKEY Algorithm IANA Registry Updates
RFC6725.summary: Updates the IANA "DNS Security (DNSSEC) Algorithm Numbers" registry, changing algorithm numbers 4, 9 and 11 to Reserved and refreshing the references for several entries.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document revises the DNSSEC algorithm number registry, which is core DNSSEC subject matter for signing algorithm identifiers.
DNSSEC.quote: This document updates a set of entries in the IANA registry titled "DNS Security (DNSSEC) Algorithm Numbers".

rejected.why: The document is an IANA registry update, but the registry is DNSSEC-specific. The IANA tag is for general registry guidance and stewardship, not one protocol's registry content.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already implies DNS.
RSA/MD5 and RSA/SHA-1 appear only as rows in the registry table. The document does not address RSA itself.
The algorithms are only listed as registry entries. The document says it is not a discussion of algorithm superiority.

RFC6726.title: FLUTE - File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport
RFC6726.summary: Defines FLUTE version 2, a protocol for unidirectional file delivery built on ALC/LCT, using an XML-based File Delivery Table to signal file properties in-band; obsoletes the experimental RFC 3926.

FLUTE.why: The document specifies FLUTE itself: file delivery sessions, the FDT, EXT_FDT and EXT_CENC header extensions.
FLUTE.quote: This document defines File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport (FLUTE), a protocol for the unidirectional delivery of files over the Internet, which is particularly suited to multicast networks.

rejected.why: ALC is the base protocol FLUTE builds on and is only updated with two header extensions. The document is about FLUTE, not ALC.
LCT is the building block under ALC. It gains two new header extensions but is not the subject of the document.
XML is only the encoding for the FDT Instance, so it is a substrate here.
FEC Object Transmission Information is carried in the FDT, but the FEC schemes themselves are defined elsewhere.
Only a single media type registration (application/fdt+xml) appears in IANA boilerplate.
Security considerations are boilerplate. TESLA, IPsec/ESP and MIKEY are only referenced there.

RFC6727.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Packet Sampling
RFC6727.summary: Defines the PSAMP-MIB module, extending IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB with managed objects that report packet sampling and filtering selector functions (count-based, time-based, random n-out-of-N, uniform probabilistic, property match, hash-based) and their parameters.

PSAMP.why: The document is about packet sampling and filtering functions and their managed objects.
PSAMP.quote: this memo defines the PSAMP- MIB module containing managed objects for providing information on applied packet selection functions and their parameters.

RFC6728.title: Configuration Data Model for the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) and Packet Sampling (PSAMP) Protocols
RFC6728.summary: Defines a YANG/NETCONF configuration and state data model (UML-described, XML-encoded) for IPFIX and PSAMP Monitoring Devices, covering Selection Processes, Caches, Exporting Processes and Collecting Processes.

IPFIX.why: The whole document configures and monitors IPFIX Exporting and Collecting Processes, Caches, templates, and transport sessions.
IPFIX.quote: specifies a data model for the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) and Packet Sampling (PSAMP) protocols

PSAMP.why: Selection Processes, with their Sampling and Filtering methods and Packet Reports, are a major part of the model.
PSAMP.quote: configuring and monitoring Selection Processes, Caches, Exporting Processes, and Collecting Processes of IPFIX- and PSAMP-compliant Monitoring Devices

YANG.why: The document's core normative content is a new YANG module, including features and deviations.
YANG.quote: The data model is defined using UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagrams and formally specified using YANG.

NETCONF.why: The model is intended for NETCONF-based configuration, and the NETCONF hello message announces its features and deviations. The document does not extend NETCONF itself, so this is secondary.
NETCONF.quote: The configuration data model is designed for use with the NETCONF protocol [RFC6241] in order to configure remote Monitoring Devices.

rejected.why: The IPFIX MIB is referenced for correspondence of parameters, but the document is not about SNMP or MIB definitions.
TLS/DTLS configuration is a small class, which only configures certificate restrictions for an existing mechanism.
SCTP is only an export transport option whose parameters are configured. The document defines nothing new about SCTP.
XML is only the encoding of configuration data.
IPFIX is tagged directly, and that tag sits under network management rather than this topic.
Certificates are referenced only for TLS authentication restrictions.

RFC6729.title: Indicating Email Handling States in Trace Fields
RFC6729.summary: RFC 6729 registers a "state" clause for the SMTP Received trace header field, with registered keywords (auth, content, quarantine, moderation, timed, etc.), to show when a message enters special handling queues or states.

SMTP.why: The document extends SMTP trace fields (Received) with a new clause and an IANA sub-registry in the SMTP MAIL Parameters registry, and specifies MTA behaviour for generating it.
SMTP.quote: This specification defines a clause, called "state", which MAY be used when creating a Received header field (see Section 4.4 of [SMTP])

rejected.why: The Received header field is a message header, but the document's focus is the SMTP trace clause and MTA handling, not the Internet message format itself; it only uses CFWS/FWS ABNF from RFC 5322.
Mailing list moderation is only one example state keyword, not the subject of the document.
Spam scanning and quarantine appear only as example causes for states; the document explicitly says it is not for categorizing messages.
The IANA registry creation supports the clause; the subject is not IANA guidance.
ABNF is only used to define the clause syntax, not the subject.

RFC6730.title: Requirements for IETF Nominations Committee Tools
RFC6730.summary: Defines requirements for a web tool supporting the IETF Nominations Committee (NomCom): authentication, encrypted storage, nominations, accept/decline tracking, questionnaires and feedback collection.

NomCom.why: The whole document specifies requirements for tools supporting NomCom operation, so the NomCom procedures page is where readers would look for it.
NomCom.quote: This document defines the requirements for a set of tools for use by the IETF Nominations Committee.

rejected.why: NomCom is a child of IETF process and is the more specific fit, so the parent is implied.
Public/private key encryption of feedback is a requirement, and the appendix uses openssl to generate a key pair. The document is about NomCom tooling, not PKI.
The appendix creates a self-signed certificate only as a way to carry the public key. The document does not profile X.509.
The appendix example uses rsa:2048 only as an illustrative key generation command.
The authentication section just reuses datatracker logins and defines role levels. It is tool access control, not authentication as a subject.
The tool sends and archives email, but email is only the medium and the document specifies no email protocol behaviour.

gaps.name: IETF tools / datatracker
gaps.why: The document is a requirements spec for an IETF administrative web tool integrated with the datatracker. The taxonomy has no tag for IETF tooling, and no NomCom tag exists apart from the NomCom topic.

RFC6731.title: Improved Recursive DNS Server Selection for Multi-Interfaced Nodes
RFC6731.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that deliver per-RDNSS domain/network information and preference so multi-interfaced nodes can choose the right recursive DNS server, plus the selection procedure including DNSSEC handling.

DHCPv6.why: Defines a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_RDNSS_SELECTION, 74) with its format, usage rules and message restrictions.
DHCPv6.quote: OPTION_RDNSS_SELECTION contains one or more domains of which the related RDNSS has particular knowledge.

DHCP.why: Defines the new DHCPv4 RDNSS Selection option (146), so the document specifies a DHCP extension.
DHCP.quote: The DHCPv4 option described below can be used to inform resolvers which RDNSS can be contacted when initiating forward or reverse DNS lookup procedures.

DNS.why: The core subject is recursive DNS server selection and resolver behaviour with private namespaces, including follow-up queries and cache handling.
DNS.quote: the node needs to be able to correctly select the right RDNSS for the DNS resolution
DNS.section: 2.1 Fully Qualified Domain Names with Limited Scopes

DNSSEC.why: The selection procedure has normative DNSSEC validation rules, and an appendix covers multiple trust anchors. DNSSEC is a substantial part of the algorithm.
DNSSEC.quote: it is necessary to prefer data that can be validated under DNSSEC over data that cannot.
DNSSEC.section: 4.1 Procedure for Prioritizing RDNSSes and Handling Responses

rejected.why: DNS64 AAAA synthesis appears only as an example of interface-specific addresses.
RFC 6147 is cited only as an informative example of synthesized AAAA records, and nothing about DNS64 is specified.
VPNs are a deployment scenario for the client, not the provider-provisioned VPN technology the tag covers.
The document uses IPv6 for the DHCPv6 option and examples but is not about IPv6 itself.
Multi-interfaced nodes are the context, but the document addresses DNS server selection rather than multihoming architecture.

gaps.name: Multiple interfaces / provisioning domains (MIF)
gaps.why: The document comes from the MIF working group and addresses host behaviour with multiple simultaneously active interfaces. The taxonomy has no tag for this.

RFC6732.title: 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels
RFC6732.summary: Informational independent-stream RFC defining 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels, which add stateless or stateful IPv6 prefix translation at 6to4 relays so operators get stable forward and return paths, especially behind CGN.

6to4.why: The document is a framework for managing anycast 6to4 tunnels and relays. It extends 6to4 relay operation with prefix translation.
6to4.quote: 6to4-PMT translates the prefix portion of the IPv6 address from the 6to4-generated prefix to a provider-assigned prefix that is used to represent the source.

CGN.why: A central use case is 6to4 breaking behind carrier-grade NAT with shared address space. Section 4.2 is devoted to it.
CGN.quote: One of the key objectives of 6to4-PMT is to also help reverse the negative impacts of 6to4 in CGN environments.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is an interim IPv6 transition option for operators before 6RD or native IPv6, but it is not covered by a more specific tag.
IPv6 transition.quote: Operators that are actively deploying IPv6 networks and operate legacy IPv4 access environments may want to utilize the existing 6to4 behavior

rejected.why: Anycast 6to4 relay operation (RFC 3068) is the context, but the document is not about anycast addressing in its own right.
6RD is mentioned only as a comparison and a preferred alternative. The document does not specify or extend it.
Prefix translation is similar to NPTv6, but the document is not about NAT behaviour or requirements generally. The NAT-related content is CGN.
The Packet Too Big handling in the PMTU section is only a deployment note.
The MTU discussion is one short deployment consideration, not a substantial part of the document.
The tunnelling is 6to4, which has its own more specific tag.

gaps.name: IPv6 Prefix Translation (NPTv6)
gaps.why: Stateless or stateful translation of the 6to4 2002::/16 prefix to a provider prefix is the core mechanism, and the taxonomy has no tag for NPTv6.

RFC6733.title: Diameter Base Protocol
RFC6733.summary: RFC 6733 specifies the Diameter base protocol, an AAA framework covering message format, peer connections, capabilities exchange, routing through agents, error handling, session state machines and accounting, obsoleting RFC 3588 and 5719.

Diameter.why: The whole document defines the Diameter protocol: header, AVPs, peers, routing, errors, sessions and accounting.
Diameter.quote: The Diameter base protocol is intended to provide an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) framework for applications such as network access or IP mobility

rejected.why: Only compared against and translated to/from; the document does not specify RADIUS.
TLS/DTLS is the security substrate for Diameter connections; no new TLS extension is defined.
SCTP is a transport Diameter runs over; only usage guidelines for mapping messages to streams are given.
DNS NAPTR/SRV is used for peer discovery but the document defines nothing new for DNS.
The parent of Diameter is implied by the Diameter tag, so it is not listed separately.
TCP is only the transport substrate.

RFC6734.title: Diameter Attribute-Value Pairs for Cryptographic Key Transport
RFC6734.summary: Defines a set of Diameter AVPs (Key, Key-Type, Key-Name, Keying-Material, Key-Lifetime, Key-SPI) for transporting multiple cryptographic keys such as DSRK, rRK and rMSK in a single Diameter message, mainly for EAP/ERP use.

Diameter.why: The document extends Diameter by defining new AVPs and a Key-Type registry for native key delivery, so readers of the Diameter subject need it.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies a set of AVPs allowing the transport of multiple cryptographic keys in a single Diameter message.

key management.why: The AVPs provision and transport keying material (DSRK, rRK, rMSK) with lifetime, name and SPI, which is key provisioning.
key management.quote: This document specifies a set of Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) providing native Diameter support of cryptographic key delivery.

EAP.why: The AVPs exist to carry keys derived from EAP methods and ERP (DSRK, rRK, rMSK), extending the Diameter EAP application's key transport.
EAP.quote: the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) [RFC6696] specifies new keys that may need to be transported between Diameter nodes.

rejected.why: TLS is only mentioned in the Security Considerations as a way to protect the messages and in an example EAP method; the document is not about it.
Mentioned only as an alternative protection mechanism in Security Considerations.
ERP keys are referenced, but the document only defines Diameter AVPs, not the HOKEY or ERP protocol.
The Diameter tag is more specific than the AAA framework tag.
The registry creation is boilerplate for the AVP definitions, not the main subject.

RFC6735.title: Diameter Priority Attribute-Value Pairs
RFC6735.summary: Defines Diameter AVPs (Dual-Priority, Admission-Priority, SIP-Resource-Priority, Application-Level-Resource-Priority) that carry RSVP and SIP priority parameters for use with the Diameter QoS application.

Diameter.why: The document extends Diameter by defining new AVPs and registering AVP codes, so it belongs on the Diameter page.
Diameter.quote: This document defines a number of Attribute-Value Pairs (AVP) that can be used within the Diameter protocol [RFC6733] to convey a specific set of priority parameters.

QoS.why: The AVPs convey authorized QoS priority values (preemption, admission, resource priority) and extend the Diameter QoS application. Readers interested in QoS signalling and priority would want it.
QoS.quote: This set of priority-related AVPs is for use with the Diameter QoS application [RFC5866]

rejected.why: RSVP priority fields are mapped into AVPs, but RSVP itself is not specified or extended here.
The SIP Resource-Priority header is only the source of values for the SIP-Resource-Priority AVP. SIP is not specified or extended.
Diameter is the more specific tag and is already chosen. The AAA framework is only the general context.
Only RSVP-related priority policy elements are referenced, not the Intserv architecture.

RFC6736.title: Diameter Network Address and Port Translation Control Application
RFC6736.summary: Defines the Diameter NAT Control Application (DNCA), a Diameter application with NCR/NCA commands and AVPs that lets a NAT controller (NAS or AAA server) manage per-endpoint NAT/NAPT bindings, limits and accounting on a NAT device.

Diameter.why: The document specifies a new Diameter application with commands, AVPs, state machines and accounting.
Diameter.quote: This document describes the framework, messages, and procedures for the Diameter Network address and port translation Control Application.

NAT.why: The purpose is controlling NAT/NAPT binding behaviour, limits, pools and reporting on NAT devices.
NAT.quote: This Diameter application allows per-endpoint control of Network Address Translators and Network Address and Port Translators

rejected.why: NAT64 is mentioned as a supported translation scenario, but the document is about controlling NAT devices generally, not specifying NAT64.
Diameter is the child tech under AAA, and the more specific tag was chosen; AAA integration is context.
SNMP is mentioned only as an alternative management protocol.
Mentioned only as an alternative configuration protocol.
Mentioned only as another method that must not conflict with DNCA.
CGN requirements are referenced as motivation, but the document does not specify CGN itself.

gaps.name: MIDCOM (Middlebox Communications)
gaps.why: The document positions DNCA as a MIDCOM protocol for NAT middleboxes, but the taxonomy has no middlebox-communication tag.

RFC6737.title: The Diameter Capabilities Update Application
RFC6737.summary: Defines the Diameter Capabilities Update application (Application-Id 10) and CUR/CUA commands (code 328) so peers can dynamically update capabilities over an open connection.

Diameter.why: The document specifies a new Diameter application with new commands (CUR/CUA), extending the Diameter base protocol.
Diameter.quote: This document defines a new Diameter application intended to allow the dynamic update of a subset of Diameter peer capabilities over an existing connection.

rejected.why: SCTP is mentioned only for Host-IP-Address handling when Diameter runs over it; it is a substrate, not the subject.
Diameter is already tagged as a child of AAA; the parent is implied.
The IANA section only assigns an Application-Id and a Command Code; it is boilerplate here.

RFC6738.title: Diameter IKEv2 SK: Using Shared Keys to Support Interaction between IKEv2 Servers and Diameter Servers
RFC6738.summary: Defines a new Diameter application (IKESK, Application-Id 11) with IKEv2-SK-Request/Answer commands and AVPs so an IKEv2 server can obtain a shared key for IKEv2 peer authentication from a home Diameter (HAAA) server, including a default SK derivation procedure.

Diameter.why: The document specifies a new Diameter application, with new commands, AVPs and session handling between a Diameter client (IKEv2 server) and Diameter server.
Diameter.quote: This specification defines a new Diameter application and its respective Application Identifier:

IKE.why: The Diameter application is built around IKEv2 shared-key authentication: it carries IKEv2 nonces and IDi/IDr and returns the key used to verify IKE_AUTH.
IKE.quote: This document specifies the IKEv2-server-to-Diameter-server communication when the IKEv2 peer authenticates using IKEv2 with SK.

rejected.why: IPsec (ESP/AH) is only the context in which IKEv2 sets up SAs; the document does not specify IPsec itself. IKE is the more specific tag.
Mobile IPv6 is only an example use case (HA as IKEv2 server); the document does not specify Mobile IPv6 behaviour.
EAP is mentioned as the alternative covered by RFC 5778 and as a possible source of the EMSK; this document deals with SK, not EAP.
HMAC-SHA-256 is used only as the KDF borrowed from RFC 5295; nothing new is specified about it.
Key delivery and derivation are involved, but the document is about a Diameter application. Key transport AVPs come from RFC 6734.

RFC6739.title: Synchronizing Service Boundaries and <mapping> Elements Based on the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Protocol
RFC6739.summary: Defines an XML protocol (LoST Sync) for exchanging authoritative LoST <mapping> elements (service boundaries) between two nodes via getMappings and pushMappings exchanges over HTTPS, for emergency-service PSAP routing.

LoST.why: The document extends the LoST ecosystem with a synchronization protocol reusing the LoST <mapping> element and schema, for keeping LoST servers and forest guides in sync.
LoST.quote: This document defines an XML protocol to exchange these mappings between two nodes.

XML signatures.why: The document mandates signing distributed mappings with XML digital signatures to prevent tampering, a notable requirement of the mechanism.
XML signatures.quote: authoritative mapping servers MUST sign mappings they distribute using an XML digital signature

rejected.why: HTTPS POST is only the transport for the protocol messages; nothing new is defined about HTTP.
TLS is required as the security mechanism but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
XML and RELAX NG are the encoding of the messages; the document is not about XML usage in general.
LoST is already the more specific child tag under emergency services; the parent is implied.
The media type registration for application/lostsync+xml is IANA boilerplate, not the document's subject.
Service boundaries use geodetic and civic location data, but the document is about synchronizing mappings, not location formats.

RFC6740.title: Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP) Architectural Description
RFC6740.summary: RFC 6740 gives the architectural description and concept of operations for ILNP, an experimental IRTF protocol that replaces IP addresses with separate Identifier and Locator namespaces to support multihoming, mobility, and IPsec.

ILNP.why: The document exists to describe ILNP architecture: Identifiers, Locators, I-LVs, Locator Updates, and the ILNPv6/ILNPv4 instances.
ILNP.quote: This document provides an architectural description and the concept of operations for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP)

multihoming.why: A whole section covers host and site multihoming using PA locators, a main motivation for ILNP.
multihoming.quote: Essentially, for ILNP, multihoming is implemented by enabling: a) multiple Locator values to be used simultaneously by a node

IP mobility.why: Host and network mobility, handover and rendezvous are described as a core ILNP capability, an alternative to Mobile IP.
IP mobility.quote: ILNP supports mobility directly, rather than relying upon special-purpose mobility extensions

rejected.why: ILNPv6 is built on IPv6, but the document is about ILNP, not about specifying IPv6.
Section 7 adapts IPsec SAs to bind to Identifiers, but this is a short part of the document, not its main subject.
DNS carries the new ILNP records (defined in RFC 6742) and Secure Dynamic Update is used unchanged; DNS is a substrate here.
Routing scalability motivates ILNP, but the document describes an end-system naming change rather than routing architecture.
The document does propose an architectural change to the Internet, but ILNP is the more specific tag and already covers it.

RFC6741.title: Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP) Engineering Considerations
RFC6741.summary: RFC 6741 describes version-independent engineering details of the experimental Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP): identifier/locator encoding, transport changes, the ILNP communication cache, DNS usage, IPsec changes, and incremental deployment.

ILNP.why: The whole document specifies engineering aspects of ILNP: identifier syntax, encodings in IPv6/IPv4, ILCC, locator updates.
ILNP.quote: This document describes common (i.e., version independent) engineering details for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP)

DNS.why: A whole section covers new RR types (NID, L32, L64, LP), TTL values, secure dynamic update and dual A/AAAA operation.
DNS.quote: Unlike IP, ILNP also uses DNS to support features such as mobility and multihoming.

rejected.why: ILNPv6 is encoded into IPv6 address space, but IPv6 is the substrate being enhanced, not the subject.
Section 9 describes IPsec changes for ILNP, but this is a small part of the document; ILNP is the subject.
Secure Dynamic DNS Update is relied on for locator updates, not specified or extended here.
Mobility is a motivation and ILNP replaces Mobile IP, but the document does not address IP mobility protocols in their own right.
The ICMP Locator Update messages are defined in separate RFCs; this document only references them and discusses nonce authentication.
ILNPv4 is encoded over IPv4, but IPv4 is only the substrate.

RFC6742.title: DNS Resource Records for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP)
RFC6742.summary: Defines four new optional DNS resource record types (NID, L32, L64, LP) that publish node identifiers and locators for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP), including wire and presentation formats and additional-section processing.

DNS.why: The document's main body defines new DNS RR types, with RDATA formats, presentation formats, and additional section processing rules for ILNP-aware servers and resolvers.
DNS.quote: This document specifies several new and closely related DNS data resource records (RRs). These new RR types have the mnemonics "NID", "L32", "L64", and "LP".

ILNP.why: The records exist to support ILNP, publishing the identifiers and locators that ILNP nodes use to find and recognise ILNP-capable correspondents. The document is part of the ILNP document set.
ILNP.quote: These optional resource records are for use with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP).

rejected.why: The Security Considerations only say that existing DNS security mechanisms can be used unchanged. The document does not specify anything about DNSSEC.
Secure dynamic update is mentioned only in passing, in the introduction and Security Considerations. Nothing is defined about it.
The document borrows IPv6 interface identifier and prefix syntax for the NID and L64 fields. It is not about IPv6 itself.
Multihoming is a use case for multiple locator records. The document does not address multihoming architectures.
The RRTYPE allocation is boilerplate in the IANA Considerations section.

RFC6743.title: ICMP Locator Update Message for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv6 (ILNPv6)
RFC6743.summary: Defines the experimental ICMPv6 Locator Update message (Type 156) that an ILNPv6 node uses to tell correspondents about changes to its valid Locator set, with advertisement/acknowledgement operation, nonce-based protection and IANA type assignment.

ILNP.why: The whole document specifies an ILNPv6 protocol message, part of the ILNP document set, so readers of the ILNP subject need it.
ILNP.quote: This message is used to dynamically update Identifier/Locator bindings for an existing ILNP session.

ICMP.why: It defines a new ICMPv6 message type with its format, checksum and processing rules, which ICMP readers would want to find.
ICMP.quote: The ICMPv6 message described in this section has ICMP Type 156 and is used ONLY with a current ILNPv6 session.

rejected.why: ILNPv6 is built on IPv6, but the document specifies an ILNP message rather than IPv6 itself.
IPsec is only an optional additional protection for the message and is not the subject of the document.
The L64 record preferences are referenced from RFC 6742, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
Multihoming is mentioned as motivation for handling many Locators, but the document is not about multihoming architecture.
Mobility is mentioned only as a general concern in the introduction, and the document does not specify mobility mechanisms.

RFC6744.title: IPv6 Nonce Destination Option for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv6 (ILNPv6)
RFC6744.summary: Defines the ILNPv6 Nonce Destination Option, an IPv6 Destination Options header option that signals ILNP use and protects ILNP sessions and ICMP Locator Update messages from off-path attacks.

ILNP.why: The whole document specifies an ILNPv6 protocol element: the nonce option, its use for mode signalling, location changes and backwards compatibility.
ILNP.quote: This document describes an experimental Nonce Destination Option used only with ILNP for IPv6 (ILNPv6).

IPv6.why: It defines a new IPv6 Destination Option type (0x8B), with its syntax, header alignment rules and IANA assignment. This is an extension to IPv6 and relevant to IPv6 readers.
IPv6.quote: This document describes a new option for the IPv6 Destination Options header that is used with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv6 (ILNPv6).

rejected.why: IPsec is discussed in relation to the nonce (AH calculations, SAD, ESP encryption of the option). The document does not specify or extend IPsec.
The nonce is carried in ICMP Locator Update messages, but those messages are defined in RFC 6743. This document is not about ICMP.
DNS NID and L64 records are used to detect ILNP support, but they are defined elsewhere in RFC 6742.
Nonce generation cites RFC 4086, but randomness is only a requirement here and not the subject.
CALIPSO is mentioned only for option ordering and MLS considerations in a minor way.

RFC6745.title: ICMP Locator Update Message for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv4 (ILNPv4)
RFC6745.summary: Defines an experimental ICMPv4 Locator Update message (Type 253) that ILNPv4 nodes use to advertise changes to their valid Locator set to correspondent nodes and receive acknowledgements.

ILNP.why: The document is part of the ILNP document set and specifies an ILNPv4 control message for updating Locator bindings.
ILNP.quote: The ICMP message defined herein is used to dynamically update Identifier/Locator bindings for an existing ILNP session.

ICMP.why: It defines a new experimental ICMPv4 message type, with its format, fields, checksum and processing rules, so ICMP readers would want it.
ICMP.quote: The ICMP for IPv4 message described in this section has ICMP Type 253
ICMP.section: 2. ICMP Locator Update Message for ILNPv4

rejected.why: ILNPv4 is built on IPv4, but the document specifies an ICMP message rather than IPv4 itself.
IPsec is only an optional additional protection for the message; the document does not specify or extend it.
The Preference and Lifetime fields mirror the L32 DNS records of RFC 6742, but the document defines no DNS content.
Multihoming is cited as a motivation for supporting many Locators in one message, but it is not the subject.
The checksum is computed the same way as for any other ICMPv4 message, so nothing new is specified.

RFC6746.title: IPv4 Options for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP)
RFC6746.summary: Defines two new IPv4 options (ILNP Identifier and ILNP Nonce, sharing experimental option number 158) used by ILNPv4, the IPv4 instantiation of the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol.

ILNP.why: The whole document specifies ILNPv4 packet format and its Identifier and Nonce options, so it is squarely about ILNP.
ILNP.quote: This document defines two new IPv4 Options that are used only with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv4 (ILNPv4).

rejected.why: IPv4 options are the carrier for ILNPv4 fields, but the document is about ILNP, not IPv4 itself. The more specific ILNP tag fits.
The nonce protects ICMP messages from off-path attacks, but ICMP is not specified here. The ICMP Locator Update is in RFC 6745.
Mentioned only in the security considerations as an additional protection.
Only a reference to RFC 4086 for generating nonces, which is a passing mention.
ILNPv6 is mentioned only for comparison.

RFC6747.title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv4 (ILNPv4)
RFC6747.summary: Defines ARP request and reply extensions (experimental OP codes 24 and 25) that carry 64-bit Node Identifiers alongside 32-bit Locators, so ILNPv4 can resolve addresses on a link.

ARP.why: The document specifies new ARP request and reply packet formats and operation for ILNPv4. It is an extension of ARP.
ARP.quote: ILNPv4 relies upon an extended version of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [RFC826], which is defined here.

ILNP.why: The document is part of the ILNP document set. It defines the ILNPv4 instantiation's link-layer address resolution, carrying Locator (L32) and Node Identifier values.
ILNP.quote: The Identifier Locator Network Protocol (ILNP) is a proposal for evolving the Internet Architecture.

rejected.why: ILNPv4 is based on IPv4, but the document only extends ARP. It does not specify IPv4 itself.
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery is mentioned only as the ILNPv6 counterpart. This document does not cover it.
The DNS resource records for ILNP are defined in RFC 6742 and only cited here.
The document uses the shared experimental ARP OP codes from RFC 5494 and makes no IANA request. It is not about IANA registries.

RFC6748.title: Optional Advanced Deployment Scenarios for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP)
RFC6748.summary: Describes optional advanced ILNP deployment scenarios built on a Site Border Router that rewrites Locators: localised numbering, site multihoming, site mobility, traffic engineering, datacentre VM mobility, and location privacy.

ILNP.why: The whole document describes optional ILNP deployment options using an ILNP-capable SBR.
ILNP.quote: optional advanced deployment scenarios for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP), which is an evolutionary enhancement to IP

multihoming.why: A major section gives an SBR-controlled alternative for site multihoming, including failover, DNS updates and TTLs.
multihoming.quote: it is possible to leave the control of S-MH to an ILNP-enabled SBR

IP mobility.why: Section 4 covers site (network) mobility via the SBR with soft handover, and VM mobility is discussed in Section 6.
IP mobility.quote: it is possible to leave the control of site mobility to an ILNP-enabled SBR

traffic engineering.why: Section 5 covers load balancing and egress path control through Locator rewriting.
traffic engineering.quote: The use of Locator rewriting provides some simple yet useful options for traffic engineering (TE) controlled from the edge-site via the SBR

rejected.why: Locator rewriting is compared to NAT and replaces some NAT functions, but the document is not about NAT itself.
It uses the ILNP L32/L64/LP records, which RFC 6742 defines. Split-horizon DNS and TTL guidance are discussed only as supporting detail.
Location and identity privacy are brief sections (7 and 8) and are not a substantial subject of the document.
It is mentioned in one paragraph, and no mechanism is defined.
ILNPv6 is an instance of ILNP, and IPv6 is only the substrate.
Section 6 is a short, non-prescriptive discussion of VM mobility, so it is not substantial enough to tag.

RFC6749.title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
RFC6749.summary: RFC 6749 specifies the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework, in which a client obtains limited access to HTTP resources via access tokens issued by an authorization server, covering grant types, endpoints, token issuance and refresh, extensibility and security.

OAuth.why: The document defines the OAuth 2.0 framework: roles, grant types, endpoints, tokens, extensibility and security considerations.
OAuth.quote: The OAuth 2.0 authorization framework enables a third-party application to obtain limited access to an HTTP service

rejected.why: OAuth runs over HTTP and uses redirections and headers, but the document does not extend HTTP itself; it is only the substrate.
TLS is required for endpoints but is only a security mechanism relied upon, not specified or extended here.
Client authentication uses HTTP Basic and token types plug into the Authorization header, but the document defines no new HTTP auth scheme (that is RFC 6750).
Token responses are encoded in JSON, which is only an encoding substrate.
It establishes OAuth registries, but that is boilerplate IANA Considerations about OAuth, not about IANA practice.
ABNF is used as notation for parameter syntax in the appendix; it is not the subject.

RFC6750.title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: Bearer Token Usage
RFC6750.summary: Defines how to present OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens in HTTP requests (Authorization header, form body, URI query) and the Bearer WWW-Authenticate challenge with error codes, plus bearer-token security guidance.

OAuth.why: The document is a companion to OAuth 2.0 defining the Bearer access token type and registering OAuth error values. OAuth readers need it.
OAuth.quote: This specification describes how to use bearer tokens in HTTP requests to access OAuth 2.0 protected resources.

HTTP authentication.why: It defines the Bearer HTTP authentication scheme, its Authorization header syntax and WWW-Authenticate challenge parameters.
HTTP authentication.quote: this specification actually defines a general HTTP authorization method that can be used with bearer tokens from any source

rejected.why: TLS is mandated as the protection for tokens but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
Cookies are mentioned only in security advice not to store bearer tokens in clear-sent cookies.
The access_token query parameter is used, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
HTTP is the substrate; the relevant HTTP-specific content is the authentication scheme, covered by HTTP authentication.
Token encoding and contents are explicitly out of scope.
ABNF is only used as notation for the credentials syntax.

RFC6751.title: Native IPv6 behind IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT Customer Premises Equipment (6a44)
RFC6751.summary: Experimental spec of 6a44, an IPv6 transition mechanism giving hosts behind IPv4-only NAT44 CPEs ISP-assigned native IPv6 addresses via UDP/IPv4 tunnels to stateless ISP relays, as a Teredo complement.

IPv6 transition.why: 6a44 is a new IPv6/IPv4 coexistence tunnelling mechanism with its own address format, clients and relays. No child tag (Teredo, 6to4, 6rd) fits, since the document defines a new mechanism.
IPv6 transition.quote: 6a44 is a complementary solution that, being based on ISP cooperation, avoids these limitations.

NAT.why: The design is shaped by NAT44 and CGN behaviour, with NAT mapping maintenance and traversal central to the tunnel maintenance algorithm.
NAT.quote: there is therefore a need for IPv6 connectivity behind NAT44s, including those of the [NAT444] model.

rejected.why: Teredo is the mechanism 6a44 complements and interoperates with, but the document does not specify or extend it. The taxonomy tag would also be a child of IPv6 transition, so it is not chosen here.
6rd is cited as an analogy for replacing the well-known prefix with ISP prefixes. 6a44 does not specify it.
6to4 is mentioned only as a comparison and for sharing the 192.88.99.0/24 prefix for the anycast address.
UDP is only the encapsulation substrate. The document does not define anything about UDP itself.
The tunnelling here is part of the transition mechanism, which is covered by the more specific IPv6 transition tag.
A relay anycast address is used, but the document is not about anycast operation.

RFC6752.title: Issues with Private IP Addressing in the Internet
RFC6752.summary: Informational RFC discussing the technical and operational problems of using RFC 1918 private or non-globally-routable addresses on link and loopback interfaces in an ISP core, including effects on traceroute, PMTUD, NAT, anti-spoofing, DNS and security, and alternatives such as iACLs and IS-IS core hiding.

addressing.why: The whole document is about the consequences of private/non-global IP address use for infrastructure links and loopbacks in provider networks; addressing is the fitting subject.
addressing.quote: potential problems of using private, RFC 1918, or non-globally routable addressing within the core of a Service Provider (SP) network

traceroute.why: A large section with worked examples shows how private addresses break traceroute and troubleshooting.
traceroute.quote: the single biggest effect caused by the use of private addressing [RFC1918] within an Internet core is the fact that it can disrupt the operation of traceroute

PMTUD.why: A dedicated section analyses how private link addresses cause PMTUD failure and black-holing.
PMTUD.quote: If the router's interface address is a private IP address, then this ICMP reply packet may be discarded due to unicast reverse path forwarding (uRPF) or ingress filtering

operational security.why: The security rationale (core hiding), its gaps, and alternatives such as iACLs and IS-IS core hiding are a substantial part of the body and concern operational security of provider infrastructure.
operational security.quote: There are three key security gaps that exist in a privately addressed IP core.

rejected.why: Section 5 covers interactions with NAT/CGN, but only as one effect; the document is not about NAT behaviour itself.
CGN and RFC 6598 shared address space are mentioned briefly as a related scenario, not the subject.
ICMP is the mechanism for traceroute and PMTUD replies; RFC 5837 is only referenced in passing.
Section 8 mentions reverse resolution of infrastructure addresses briefly; the document is not about DNS.
IS-IS core hiding is noted as one alternative approach in a paragraph, not specified or analysed in depth.
Loopback peering for multi-hop BGP is mentioned in one short section only.

RFC6753.title: A Location Dereference Protocol Using HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD)
RFC6753.summary: Specifies how HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery) is used as a location dereference protocol: a Location Recipient holding an http/https location URI retrieves a PIDF-LO via a restricted HELD request or HTTP GET, with authorization-by-possession and access-control models discussed.

HELD.why: The document profiles HELD for dereferencing: only locationRequest allowed, restricted parameters, and GET behaviour equivalent to a HELD request.
HELD.quote: This section describes how HELD can be used to dereference a location URI.

rejected.why: HTTP GET/POST and content negotiation are used as substrate for HELD; the document does not define new HTTP semantics.
TLS is the required security mechanism but nothing new is defined about TLS.
Considered as a topic, but the HELD tech tag sits under it and already covers the document.
PIDF-LO is the returned payload format, defined elsewhere (RFC 4119); this document does not specify or extend it.
SIP is only mentioned as a conveyance protocol for location URIs.
Privacy is a concern addressed via authorization models, but the document is about the dereference protocol, not privacy threat models.

gaps.name: Location dereference / location-by-reference (location URI)
gaps.why: The document is about dereferencing location URIs and their authorization models; the taxonomy has only HELD and the generic geolocation topic, which cover this adequately but not specifically.

RFC6754.title: Protocol Independent Multicast Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) Redirect
RFC6754.summary: Defines the PIM ECMP Redirect message and Hello option, letting upstream PIM routers tell downstream routers which ECMP interface and neighbor to use as RPF neighbor, based on administrative metrics.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM Sparse Mode (RFC 4601) with a new message type and Hello option, modifying RPF neighbor selection and building on Assert-style tiebreaking.
PIM-SM.quote: The use of ECMP Redirect applies to shared trees or source trees built with procedures described in [RFC4601].

rejected.why: ECMP tag covers load-balanced forwarding in general; here ECMP is the setting, but the document specifies a PIM mechanism, and PIM-SM is the more specific fit. ECMP is arguably a secondary candidate, but the work is PIM RPF selection.
Parent of PIM-SM; the more specific child PIM-SM is chosen and the parent is implied.
Interface ID is used for IPv6 link-local addresses, but only incidentally.
Only the NTP timestamp format is referenced for the Metric field; the document is not about NTP.
IANA section only assigns a Hello option type and message type; boilerplate.

RFC6755.title: An IETF URN Sub-Namespace for OAuth
RFC6755.summary: Registers the urn:ietf:params:oauth IETF URN sub-namespace and a corresponding IANA "OAuth URI" registry with a registration template for OAuth-related URNs.

URN.why: The document's whole purpose is to establish a new URN sub-namespace (urn:ietf:params:oauth) and define how URNs under it are registered, so readers of URN namespaces would want it.
URN.quote: This document creates and registers an IETF URN Sub-namespace, as documented in RFC 3553 [RFC3553], for use with such specifications.

rejected.why: OAuth 2.0 is only the context in which the URNs will be used; the document specifies no OAuth protocol behaviour, only a namespace for identifiers.
The IANA registry is created, but only as the mechanism for the URN sub-namespace; the document is not general IANA guidance.
URN is the more specific tag and covers the subject; the document does not address URI syntax or schemes in general.

RFC6756.title: Internet Engineering Task Force and International Telecommunication Union - Telecommunication Standardization Sector Collaboration Guidelines
RFC6756.summary: IAB-approved guidance on how the IETF and ITU-T collaborate on standards development: contact points, liaison statements, mailing lists, document sharing, cross-referencing and preliminary work efforts; obsoletes RFC 3356.

IETF process.why: The document describes IETF procedures for liaison statements, working group and BOF interaction, and document sharing with another standards body. That is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document provides non-normative guidance to aid in the understanding of collaboration on standards development between the Telecommunication Standardization Sector of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)

rejected.why: Copyright and IPR rules are mentioned only briefly, as references for contributions. They are not the subject of the document.
The IETF process tag is more specific. The document is about inter-organization procedure, not governance in general.
It mentions Internet-Draft format and RFC publication only in passing.

gaps.name: Standards development organization liaison and collaboration
gaps.why: The document is about relations with an external standards body (ITU-T) through liaison statements. The taxonomy has no tag for this, and the closest fit is IETF process.

RFC6757.title: Access Network Identifier (ANI) Option for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6757.summary: Defines the Access Network Identifier mobility option and its sub-options (Network-Identifier, Geo-Location, Operator-Identifier) that a Proxy Mobile IPv6 MAG uses to tell the LMA about the access network.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with a new mobility option carried in PBU/PBA messages, plus MAG and LMA processing rules.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification defines a mechanism and a related mobility option for carrying the access network identifier and the access operator identification information from the mobile access gateway to the local mobility anchor over Proxy Mobile IPv6.

rejected.why: Mobility header option space comes from RFC 6275, but the document is about the PMIPv6 extension, not Mobile IPv6 itself.
Includes a Geo-Location sub-option, but it is one field of the option, not a document about geolocation formats or conveyance.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as protection for signalling.
DHCP Option 82 is mentioned only as one possible source of the information at the MAG.
IANA registries are created, but that is boilerplate for the new option and sub-option types.
3GPP policy systems and PLMN identifiers are mentioned as context and as a Network Name value, but the document does not address cellular networks.

RFC6758.title: Tunneling of SMTP Message Transfer Priorities
RFC6758.summary: Defines the MT-Priority message header field to tunnel SMTP Message Transfer Priority values through MTAs that do not support the MT-PRIORITY SMTP extension, and updates RFC 6710 relay and handling rules accordingly.

SMTP.why: The document extends SMTP's MT-PRIORITY extension handling, updating the receiving and relaying rules for MSAs and MTAs.
SMTP.quote: This memo defines a mechanism for tunneling of SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) Message Transfer Priority values through MTAs

message format.why: A substantial part defines a new Internet message header field (MT-Priority) with its ABNF and registers it.
message format.quote: The tunneling is done by adding a new message header field to the Internet Message Format specified in [RFC5322].

rejected.why: DKIM is discussed only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the header field; the document is not about DKIM.
STARTTLS appears only in the example transcript as incidental.
ABNF is only the notation used for the header field syntax.
Covered by the more specific SMTP and message format tags, so the parent is not listed.

RFC6759.title: Cisco Systems Export of Application Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC6759.summary: Informational Cisco RFC that adds IPFIX Information Elements (applicationId, classificationEngineId, applicationName, category/group and technology attributes) and a Classification Engine ID registry for exporting application identification information in IPFIX flow records.

IPFIX.why: The document defines ten new IPFIX Information Elements and Options Template usage for exporting application information, so it extends the IPFIX information model.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies a Cisco Systems extension to the IPFIX information model specified in RFC 5102 to export application information.

rejected.why: It creates a Classification Engine ID registry and new IPFIX IEs, but this is IANA boilerplate for the IPFIX extension, not guidance about IANA itself.
Mentioned only in passing (MIB polling, SNMP port 161 as an example).
Only appears in the port-collision tables in the appendix, not as a subject.
NetFlow v9 is referenced only as a legacy protocol that lacks variable-length IEs; it is not in the taxonomy and not the subject.
The selectorId concept is cited for analogy only.

gaps.name: IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export) information model and Information Elements
gaps.why: The document is about extending the IPFIX information model, but the taxonomy has IPFIX only as a tech tag under network management, so I could not confirm the tag id 'IPFIX' as valid for use; it does appear in the taxonomy as 'IPFIX' under network management, so no gap beyond a lack of a tag specific to application identification or classification.

RFC6760.title: Requirements for a Protocol to Replace the AppleTalk Name Binding Protocol (NBP)
RFC6760.summary: Informational RFC giving background on AppleTalk NBP and listing 15 requirements for an IP-based replacement, motivating mDNS and DNS-SD.

AppleTalk.why: The document describes AppleTalk's Name Binding Protocol in detail and uses it as the basis for the replacement requirements, so readers of AppleTalk material would want it.
AppleTalk.quote: This document presents a brief overview of the capabilities of AppleTalk NBP and outlines the properties required of an IP-based replacement.

service discovery.why: The requirements are for a zeroconf service discovery and naming protocol: browsing, typed names, conflict detection and cache coherency. It is generic and not specific to one system.
service discovery.quote: What remains is the need for Zero Configuration name-to-address translation and Zero Configuration service discovery

rejected.why: mDNS is the solution these requirements motivated. It is specified in RFC 6762, and this document does not specify it.
DNS-SD is specified in RFC 6763. This document only states the requirements that it meets.
SLP is discussed in Section 4 only to explain why it is not a sufficient replacement. The document is not about SLP.
DNS is used for comparison, for example SRV records and service names. The document does not specify or extend DNS.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as the recommended character set for names.

gaps.name: Zeroconf (Zero Configuration Networking)
gaps.why: The document is framed around zero-configuration networking, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC6761.title: Special-Use Domain Names
RFC6761.summary: RFC 6761 defines what it means for a domain name to be reserved for special use, the procedure and seven-category considerations for reserving one, and creates the IANA Special-Use Domain Names registry seeded with private reverse-mapping domains, test, localhost, invalid, and example names.

special-use domain names.why: The whole document defines the special-use domain name concept, the reservation procedure, and the initial registry entries such as localhost, test, invalid and example.
special-use domain names.quote: This document describes what it means to say that a Domain Name (DNS name) is reserved for special use, when reserving such a name is appropriate, and the procedure for doing so.

rejected.why: DNS is the namespace being reserved from, but the document does not specify DNS protocol behaviour. The special-use domain names tag sits under DNS and is the more specific fit.
The document creates an IANA registry, but that is a mechanism for the main subject. It is not a general piece of IANA registry guidance.
Registrar treatment is only one of the seven considerations, and the document does not address registry or registrar operations in their own right.
Special-use IPv4 addresses are mentioned only as an analogy and for the private reverse-mapping domains.

RFC6762.title: Multicast DNS
RFC6762.summary: RFC 6762 specifies Multicast DNS (mDNS), which lets hosts perform DNS-like queries and responses over link-local IP multicast, with probing, conflict resolution, caching rules, and the reserved .local domain.

mDNS.why: The document is the mDNS protocol specification: querying, responding, probing, announcing, conflict resolution and message format.
mDNS.quote: Multicast DNS (mDNS) provides the ability to perform DNS-like operations on the local link in the absence of any conventional Unicast DNS server.

special-use domain names.why: It reserves .local and the link-local reverse-mapping domains, and Section 22.1 gives their special handling. Sections 3, 4 and 12 also define the special semantics of these names.
special-use domain names.quote: IANA has recorded the list of domains below as being Special-Use Domain Names [RFC6761]:

rejected.why: DNS-SD is the companion technology, specified in RFC 6763. This document only mentions it as a use case, so it is not tagged.
NSEC records are reused only to express nonexistence, not for DNSSEC security. DNSSEC is mentioned only as a recommended protection.
Section 16 requires UTF-8 for names, but this is a single design choice and not the subject of the document.
OPT is mentioned only in passing, regarding the top bit of the rrclass field.
A more specific tag, mDNS, fits, so the parent DNS tag is not used.
UDP is only the transport. The document uses port 5353 but does not define anything new about UDP.

RFC6763.title: DNS-Based Service Discovery
RFC6763.summary: Specifies DNS-SD, a convention for naming and structuring DNS PTR, SRV and TXT records so clients can browse and resolve named service instances using standard unicast or multicast DNS queries.

DNS-SD.why: The whole document defines DNS-Based Service Discovery: instance enumeration, resolution, TXT record syntax, service names, subtypes, flagship naming, and domain enumeration.
DNS-SD.quote: This document specifies how DNS resource records are named and structured to facilitate service discovery.

rejected.why: Multicast DNS is specified in RFC 6762; this document is compatible with it and uses it as a transport but does not define it.
Only uses existing DNS record types and queries, and proposes no change to DNS; DNS-SD is the more specific tag.
Dynamic Update is mentioned as a way to register records, but the document defines nothing about it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations and the appendix rationale.
Parent of DNS-SD, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Punycode/IDNA is only a fallback mention for name encoding; the document is not about IDNA.

RFC6764.title: Locating Services for Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV (CalDAV) and vCard Extensions to WebDAV (CardDAV)
RFC6764.summary: Defines how CalDAV and CardDAV clients locate services using DNS SRV and TXT records and well-known URIs, with a client bootstrapping procedure and service provider guidance, and registers the caldav/carddav well-known URIs and service names.

CalDAV.why: The document specifies service discovery and client bootstrapping for CalDAV, and updates RFC 4791. CalDAV readers would want it.
CalDAV.quote: This specification defines new SRV service types for the CalDAV protocol and gives an example of how clients can use this together with other protocol features

CardDAV.why: The document specifies discovery and bootstrapping for CardDAV and updates RFC 6352, including the carddav well-known URI and TXT record use.
CardDAV.quote: [RFC6352] defines the CardDAV address book access protocol based on HTTP [RFC2616], for accessing contact data stored on a server.

DNS-SD.why: It uses DNS SRV and TXT records as DNS-based service discovery and defines a new TXT key. It also adds SRV service labels for CalDAV.
DNS-SD.quote: uses a TXT RR that follows the syntax defined in Section 6 of [RFC6763] and defines a "path" key for use in that record.
DNS-SD.section: 4. CalDAV and CardDAV Service TXT Records

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate: the document uses redirects, PROPFIND and caching headers but defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
WebDAV is relied on for PROPFIND and current-user-principal. The document is about CalDAV/CardDAV discovery, not WebDAV.
TLS is only used for the caldavs/carddavs services and for certificate verification. Nothing new is defined for TLS.
SRV and TXT records are used as is. No new record type or DNS behaviour is defined, so the more specific DNS-SD fits better.
The well-known URI registrations are IANA boilerplate use of RFC 5785 and not a new URI scheme or syntax.

RFC6765.title: xDSL Multi-Pair Bonding (G.Bond) MIB
RFC6765.summary: Defines the GBOND-MIB module (and the IANA-GBOND-TC-MIB) for managing multi-pair bonded xDSL interfaces under ITU-T G.998.1/2/3, as an extension of the IF-MIB with configuration, status, discovery and performance-monitoring objects.

MIB.why: The document's main content is an SMIv2 MIB module (GBOND-MIB) plus an IANA-maintained TC MIB, with objects, tables, notifications and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB module common to all 3 schemes.

DSL.why: The MIB manages bonded xDSL interfaces (G.998.x G.Bond), including BCE line interworking and xDSL line MIBs, so DSL access readers would want it.
DSL.quote: xDSL Multi-pair bonding allows a service provider to provide high-bandwidth services to business and residential customers over multiple xDSL lines

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol used to access the MIB; the document defines objects rather than extending SNMP. The MIB tag covers it.
G.998.1 ATM bonding is covered only by reference to a separate G9981-MIB; ATM itself is not the subject.
G.998.2 Ethernet bonding is handled in a separate MIB (RFC 6767); this document is only common objects.
IANA-maintained TC module is part of the MIB; not about IANA registry guidance in general.
Mentioned only as a clock source for aligning performance intervals.

RFC6766.title: xDSL Multi-Pair Bonding Using Time-Division Inverse Multiplexing (G.Bond/TDIM) MIB
RFC6766.summary: Defines the G9983-MIB SMIv2 module extending GBOND-MIB for managing G.998.3 xDSL multi-pair bonded interfaces using time-division inverse multiplexing, including FEC/interleaver configuration, service configuration, notifications and performance monitoring.

MIB.why: The document's main body is a MIB module (G9983-MIB) with SMIv2 objects, tables, notifications and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: a set of objects for managing multi-pair bonded xDSL interfaces using Time-Division Inverse Multiplexing (TDIM), as defined in ITU-T Recommendation G.998.3

DSL.why: The MIB manages bonded xDSL interfaces (G.Bond/TDIM), so readers of DSL access networks would want it.
DSL.quote: defines a method for bonding (or aggregating) multiple xDSL lines (or individual bearer channels in multiple xDSL lines) into a single bidirectional logical link

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour. The MIB tag sits under SNMP, so the MIB module is covered by that.
ATM appears only as one of the service types carried over the bonded link, not as a subject of the document.
The performance monitoring counters are a minor, standard section of the MIB, not the document's subject.
The FEC and interleaver objects are only configuration knobs for G.998.3 ports, not a loss-recovery scheme for packet transport.

RFC6767.title: Ethernet-Based xDSL Multi-Pair Bonding (G.Bond/Ethernet) MIB
RFC6767.summary: Defines the G9982-MIB SNMP module extending GBOND-MIB for managing Ethernet-based multi-pair bonded xDSL interfaces (ITU-T G.998.2), including BACP objects, PTM-TC types, error counters and performance monitoring.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module (SMIv2) defining managed objects, tables, groups and compliance statements for G.Bond/Ethernet ports.
MIB.quote: This document defines an extension to the GBOND-MIB module with a set of objects for managing Ethernet-based multi-pair bonded Digital Subscriber Line (xDSL) interfaces

DSL.why: The managed subject is xDSL multi-pair bonding (G.998.2), so DSL access networks readers would want it.
DSL.quote: defines a method for bonding (or aggregating) multiple xDSL lines (or individual bearer channels in multiple xDSL lines) into a single bidirectional logical link carrying Ethernet traffic

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through; the document defines a MIB module, not SNMP itself, and the MIB tag is more specific.
Ethernet is the traffic carried over the bonded link, but the document manages xDSL bonding, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Bonding is conceptually similar, but this is xDSL pair bonding per G.998.2, not IEEE 802.1AX LAG.
The data model is SMIv2 MIB, not YANG.

RFC6768.title: ATM-Based xDSL Bonded Interfaces MIB
RFC6768.summary: Defines the G9981-MIB SMIv2 module extending GBOND-MIB with objects for configuring, monitoring and performance-tracking ATM-based multi-pair bonded xDSL interfaces (G.998.1, G.Bond/ATM).

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition (G9981-MIB) with configuration, status, notification and performance monitoring objects.
MIB.quote: The MIB module defined in this document defines a set of managed objects for the management of G.998.1 bonded interfaces

DSL.why: The managed subject is bonded multi-pair xDSL interfaces (G.Bond/ATM, G.998.1), so DSL readers would want it.
DSL.quote: bonding (or aggregating) multiple xDSL lines (or individual bearer channels in multiple xDSL lines) into a single bidirectional logical link carrying an ATM stream

rejected.why: ATM-MIB is only referenced as an optional way to manage ATM aspects; the document is about xDSL bonding management, not IP over ATM.
SNMP is the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the MIB tag, and does not extend SNMP itself.
Performance monitoring counters are part of the MIB, but they are interface counters and not a measurement methodology.

RFC6769.title: Simple Virtual Aggregation (S-VA)
RFC6769.summary: Informational RFC describing Simple Virtual Aggregation (S-VA), a BGP-based technique where routers announce a VA prefix within an AS so edge routers can suppress more-specific routes from their FIB.

BGP.why: The document specifies a BGP-speaker technique: how VA prefixes are announced with specific path attributes and how routes are suppressed from the FIB. It is about BGP operation and policy.
BGP.quote: allows some BGP routers not to install all of those routes into the Forwarding Information Base (FIB)

routing architecture.why: S-VA addresses routing table and FIB scalability within an AS, which is a routing architecture and scalability concern.
routing architecture.quote: All BGP routers in the Default-Free Zone (DFZ) are required to carry all routes in the Default-Free Routing Table (DFRT).

rejected.why: NO_EXPORT community is only attached as a mechanism to keep VA prefixes inside the AS; the document is not about communities.
Not discussed; IBGP multipath is mentioned only briefly.
Aggregation is the concept used, but the document is not about CIDR itself.
Only mentions that S-VA applies to IPv6 address families; not about IPv6.

RFC6770.title: Use Cases for Content Delivery Network Interconnection
RFC6770.summary: Informational document describing use cases (footprint extension, offload, capability, policy enforcement) that motivate CDN Interconnection (CDNI) interfaces, obsoleting RFC 3570.

CDN.why: The whole document is about CDN Interconnection use cases: footprint extension, offload, capability and delivery policy enforcement across interconnected CDNs.
CDN.quote: use cases that correspond to identified industry needs and that are expected to be realized once open interfaces and protocols supporting the interconnection of CDNs are specified

rejected.why: HTTPS and delivery protocols are mentioned only as examples of capabilities a CDN may lack; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
HTTPS appears only as an example delivery requirement, not as a subject of the document.
Caching is mentioned as a CDN benefit but the document does not address HTTP caching mechanisms.
