DNS appears only in the abbreviations list and a passing mention of DNS load-balancing.
IPv6 delivery is one example in the capability use cases, not a subject of the document.
QoE/QoS appears as a motivation for interconnection; no QoS architecture or signalling is addressed.

RFC6771.title: Considerations for Having a Successful "Bar BOF" Side Meeting
RFC6771.summary: RFC 6771 advises organizers of unofficial IETF "bar BOF" side meetings on how to invite, where, how and when to meet, and recommends replacing the term "bar BOF" with "side meeting".

IETF process.why: The document is guidance on how unofficial side meetings relate to the IETF process for developing new work, BOFs and working group consensus. It fits IETF process directly.
IETF process.quote: New work is typically brought to the IETF by a group of interested individuals.

rejected.why: It recommends dropping the term 'bar BOF' in favour of 'side meeting'. That is a minor point, not a glossary or definitions document.
It is an ordinary informational RFC about meeting practice. It is not about RFC format or publication.
It gives guidance on side meetings. It does not report on a workshop.

RFC6772.title: Geolocation Policy: A Document Format for Expressing Privacy Preferences for Location Information
RFC6772.summary: Defines a Common Policy extension (Geolocation Policy) for location-based authorization rules over PIDF-LO location objects, with transformations including two location obfuscation algorithms (civic and geodetic), XCAP usage and an IANA registry of location profiles.

geolocation.why: The whole document specifies privacy rules, conditions and granularity-reducing transformations for location information, so it belongs on the geolocation page.
geolocation.quote: This document defines an authorization policy language for controlling access to location information.

authorization.why: The document defines an authorization policy format extending Common Policy, with conditions, actions and transformations that control who may receive what.
authorization.quote: An authorization policy is a set of rules that regulates an entity's activities with respect to privacy-sensitive information, such as location information.

privacy.why: The document is about expressing privacy preferences, and it includes substantial discussion of obfuscation limits and leakage.
privacy.quote: Location information needs to be protected against unauthorized access to preserve the privacy of humans.

rejected.why: XML is the encoding for the policy documents and the schema. The document is not about XML usage in general.
The document explicitly does not describe the protocol that conveys location from the Location Server to the Location Recipient.
PIDF-LO is the location object the rules apply to and is referenced throughout. The document does not define or extend PIDF.
XCAP is used to carry the rules, and the presence authorization rules are only referenced. The document does not define SIMPLE extensions.

gaps.name: Common Policy / XCAP
gaps.why: The document extends the Common Policy framework and defines an XCAP application usage. The taxonomy has no tag for either.

RFC6773.title: DCCP-UDP: A Datagram Congestion Control Protocol UDP Encapsulation for NAT Traversal
RFC6773.summary: Specifies DCCP-UDP, an encapsulation of DCCP inside UDP so DCCP can traverse legacy NAT/NAPT devices, including checksum, port demultiplexing rules, and SDP signalling updates to RFC 5762.

DCCP.why: The document defines a new encapsulation of DCCP, updating RFC 4340 and RFC 5762, so readers of DCCP would expect it.
DCCP.quote: This document specifies an alternative encapsulation of the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), referred to as DCCP-UDP.

NAT.why: NAT traversal is the stated purpose, and the design covers NAT/NAPT checksum and port-mapping behaviour.
NAT.quote: This encapsulation allows DCCP to be carried through the current generation of Network Address Translation (NAT) middleboxes without modification of those middleboxes.

SDP.why: Section 5 defines new SDP proto values (UDP/DCCP/...) and the dccp-port attribute, so SDP readers need it.
SDP.quote: This document also updates the SDP specification for DCCP [RFC5762] to convey the encapsulation type.

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate carrying DCCP. The document explicitly does not modify UDP.
ICE is mentioned only as a possible future negotiation mechanism, with details left for future study.
RTP is only the example upper-layer protocol whose SDP signalling is updated. The document does not specify RTP.
DTLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations and as an upper-layer protocol, so it is not tagged.
The ECN section only defers to the DCCP-STD procedures in RFC 4340.

RFC6774.title: Distribution of Diverse BGP Paths
RFC6774.summary: Informational RFC proposing distribution of the Nth-best BGP path by adding parallel route-reflector (or route-server) planes with extra IBGP/EBGP sessions, as an alternative to BGP add-paths, without any protocol changes.

route reflection.why: The core mechanism is multi-plane BGP route reflection, with each plane distributing the Nth best path to clients over separate sessions.
route reflection.quote: The proposed solution is based on the use of additional route reflectors or new functionality enabled on the existing route reflectors

route server.why: A dedicated section applies the multi-plane approach to IX route servers so peers get more than one best path.
route server.quote: the proposed multi-plane architecture may be of particular applicability is the EBGP route servers used at many Internet exchange points.
route server.section: 4.3. Multi-Plane Route Servers for Internet Exchanges

rejected.why: A more specific child tag (route reflection) fits, and the document makes no changes to the BGP protocol itself.
Fast connectivity restoration is a motivating application, but the document does not specify fast reroute mechanisms.
MPLS is mentioned only as a possible encapsulation between PE routers and is not a subject of the document.
IPv6 is mentioned only because the solution applies to any address family.

gaps.name: BGP add-paths / multiple path advertisement
gaps.why: The document compares itself against BGP Add-Paths and best-external as alternatives for distributing multiple paths. The taxonomy has no tag for these BGP path-diversity mechanisms.

RFC6775.title: Neighbor Discovery Optimization for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs)
RFC6775.summary: RFC 6775 specifies optimizations to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for 6LoWPANs: host address registration (ARO), 6LoWPAN context and border router options, and multihop duplicate address detection, updating RFC 4944.

6LoWPAN.why: The document defines 6LoWPAN-ND, the neighbor discovery mechanism for 6LoWPANs, updating RFC 4944 and distributing header compression context.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document describes simple optimizations to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, its addressing mechanisms, and duplicate address detection for Low-power Wireless Personal Area Networks

neighbor discovery.why: It extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery with new options (ARO, 6CO, ABRO), DAR/DAC messages, and modified host and router behaviour.
neighbor discovery.quote: specifically aimed at low-power and lossy networks such as LoWPANs

rejected.why: Address autoconfiguration is used and constrained (M flag, DAD), but the document is about ND optimization, not SLAAC itself.
New ICMPv6 message types are defined, but only as part of the ND extension, not as an ICMP specification.
Only mentioned as an alternative address assignment mechanism.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible future use.
A more specific child tag (neighbor discovery) fits better than the parent.
Header compression context is distributed, but the compression format is RFC 6282, not SCHC; also not a taxonomy match.

RFC6776.title: Measurement Identity and Information Reporting Using a Source Description (SDES) Item and an RTCP Extended Report (XR) Block
RFC6776.summary: Defines a new RTCP SDES item (APSI) and an RTCP XR Measurement Information block that identify and describe a measurement period (sequence numbers, interval and cumulative durations) for other RTCP XR metric blocks to reference.

RTCP.why: The document extends RTCP with a new SDES item and a new XR block carrying measurement identity and period information, so RTCP readers would want it.
RTCP.quote: This document defines one new RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Source Description (SDES) [RFC3550] item and one new Extended Report (XR) block

rejected.why: RTP is the underlying protocol whose sequence numbers are referenced; the document specifies RTCP extensions, and the more specific RTCP tag fits.
The document follows the performance metrics framework but defines no metrics itself; the XR block explicitly contains no measurement results.
Only the NTP timestamp format is borrowed for the cumulative duration field; the document is not about NTP.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

RFC6777.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Data Path Delay Metrics in Generalized MPLS and MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) Networks
RFC6777.summary: Defines five IPPM-style performance metrics (RRFD, RSRD, PRFD, PSFD, PSRD) measuring delay between RSVP-TE signaling events and data path readiness for LSPs in GMPLS/MPLS-TE networks, plus sampling and statistics.

performance measurement.why: The document defines singleton and sample delay metrics, methodologies and statistics in the IPPM style, which is the core of performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This document defines a series of performance metrics to evaluate the connectivity of the data path in the signaling process.

GMPLS.why: The metrics characterize LSP setup in GMPLS and MPLS-TE networks, relating RSVP-TE signaling to cross-connect programming across data-plane technologies. GMPLS is the closest specific tag, as it also covers the MPLS-TE signaling context.
GMPLS.quote: we define five performance metrics to characterize the performance of data path provisioning with GMPLS/MPLS-TE signaling.

rejected.why: The metrics are timed against PATH and Resv messages, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE. It only uses its messages as measurement reference points.
MPLS-TE is the network context, but the document is about measuring data path delay, not traffic engineering itself.
GMPLS is the more specific fit, and the document does not address MPLS architecture or encapsulation.
The metrics verify data path connectivity, but they are performance metrics rather than an OAM mechanism.

RFC6778.title: Requirements for Archiving IETF Email Lists and for Providing Web-Based Browsing and Searching
RFC6778.summary: RFC 6778 sets out requirements for an IETF email list archive and search system, covering web browsing and search, archiving, import and export, redundancy, administration and transition from MHonArc.

mailing lists.why: The whole document specifies requirements for archiving, searching and browsing mailing list messages, including list archive import and export and handling of lists from different list managers. That is mailing list management and archive tooling.
mailing lists.quote: The system must provide a web interface for searching and browsing archived messages.

rejected.why: Section 4 only says the archive must anticipate integrating with a separate IMAP access system, which is specified in another document.
Section 3 says the system should anticipate internationalized addresses, with no firm requirement. This is a passing mention.
The Archived-At header and Message-Id threading are mentioned as requirements for the archive. The document does not define or extend message format.
The application/mbox media type is only referenced as an import and export format.
The archive serves IETF work, but the document is about tooling requirements, not IETF procedures.
Mailing lists is the more specific tag, so the parent is not listed.

RFC6779.title: Definition of Managed Objects for the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol
RFC6779.summary: Defines the NHDP-MIB SNMP MIB module for configuring, monitoring, and receiving notifications about the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP, RFC 6130) on routers.

NHDP.why: The MIB module exists to manage NHDP: its configuration parameters, information bases (link sets, 2-hop sets, neighbor sets), performance counters, and notifications.
NHDP.quote: it describes objects for configuring parameters of the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) process on a router.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (NHDP-MIB) with tables, textual conventions, notifications, and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific fit.
MANET routing is the deployment context, but the document is about NHDP, which has its own tag under MANET, so the parent is implied.
The Performance Group contains NHDP counters, but this is part of the MIB rather than a performance measurement methodology.
TLS/DTLS and SSH appear only in the Security Considerations as transport options for SNMP.
AES appears only as the USM cipher recommendation in the Security Considerations.

RFC6780.title: RSVP ASSOCIATION Object Extensions
RFC6780.summary: Generalizes the RSVP ASSOCIATION object beyond GMPLS recovery to non-LSP and Path/Resv usage (e.g., resource sharing) and defines IPv4/IPv6 Extended ASSOCIATION objects for MPLS-TP identification.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends the RSVP-TE ASSOCIATION object (RFC 4872/3209/3473), defining processing in Path and Resv messages and new Extended C-Types.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document expands the possible usage of the ASSOCIATION object to non-GMPLS and non-recovery contexts.

RSVP.why: It updates RFC 2205 and defines association of plain non-LSP RSVP sessions for resource sharing (call waiting, shared line, symmetric NAT).
RSVP.quote: The expanded usage applies equally to GMPLS LSPs [RFC3473], MPLS LSPs [RFC3209], and non-LSP RSVP sessions [RFC2205]

rejected.why: The document extends usage beyond GMPLS and recovery; GMPLS is the original context, not the subject.
Extended objects are usable in MPLS-TP, but the document is not about MPLS-TP itself and only uses its Global_ID identifiers.
RSVP-TE is the more specific tag; the document applies to MPLS LSPs only as one session type.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats.
Mentioned only in a symmetric NAT example.

RFC6781.title: DNSSEC Operational Practices, Version 2
RFC6781.summary: RFC 6781 is an informational guide for zone administrators on operating DNSSEC: key generation and storage, ZSK/KSK/algorithm rollovers, emergency rollover, parent policies, signature timing, and NSEC vs NSEC3 choices.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is operational guidance for DNSSEC: key management, rollovers, signature validity, NSEC/NSEC3 parameters.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes a set of practices for operating the DNS with security extensions (DNSSEC).

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific child tag; ancestors are implied.
Registry/registrar DS exchange and changing DNS operators are discussed, but as part of DNSSEC operations, not as registration protocol content.
EPP is mentioned only briefly as one way to transfer DS records to the registry.
Key generation, storage and rollover are covered, but as DNSSEC-specific operations already captured by the DNSSEC tag.
Mentioned only as a comparison for key strength and for authenticating announcement websites.
RSA key sizes and algorithm choice are discussed in a short subsection within DNSSEC practice, not as the document's subject.

RFC6782.title: Wireline Incremental IPv6
RFC6782.summary: Informational framework guiding wireline operators through phased IPv6 deployment (foundation, 6rd tunneling, native dual stack, CGN, IPv6-only with DS-Lite/NAT64) while maintaining IPv4 connectivity.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document is a phased IPv6 transition/coexistence deployment framework, which is exactly this topic.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document helps provide a framework for wireline providers who are faced with the challenges of introducing IPv6 along with meeting the legacy needs of IPv4 connectivity

6rd.why: 6rd is the Phase 1 technology, with its own deployment considerations section (relays, anycast, provisioning, MTU).
6rd.quote: 6rd provides tunneled connectivity for IPv6 over the existing IPv4 path.

DS-Lite.why: DS-Lite is a Phase 3 technology with dedicated analysis and deployment considerations.
DS-Lite.quote: DS-Lite provides tunneled connectivity for IPv4 over the IPv6 path between the subscriber's network device and a provider-managed gateway

NAT64.why: NAT64/DNS64 is analysed and has its own deployment considerations section for IPv6-only networks.
NAT64.quote: NAT64 provides the ability to connect IPv6-only connected clients and hosts to IPv4 servers without any tunneling.

CGN.why: An intermediate CGN/NAT444 phase with deployment considerations is a substantial part of the framework.
CGN.quote: CGN is often considered undesirable by operators but is required in many cases.

rejected.why: Discussed only briefly as ambient automatic tunneling and breakage with CGN; not a main subject.
Only mentioned in passing alongside 6to4.
Prefix delegation is mentioned as a needed supporting system, but the document is not about DHCPv6.
The more specific IPv6 transition tag fits better.
Cable, DSL and fibre are named only as the scope of the wireline access environments; no access-specific content.
CGN is the more specific tag and already covers the NAT444 material.

RFC6783.title: Mailing Lists and Non-ASCII Addresses
RFC6783.summary: Informational document describing considerations for mailing lists once non-ASCII (SMTPUTF8) email addresses are introduced, covering list scenarios, SMTP envelope/bounce issues and List-* header downgrading, without specifying protocol changes.

mailing lists.why: The whole document is about how mailing list agents, list headers (List-Id, List-Post etc.) and list policies are affected by non-ASCII addresses.
mailing lists.quote: This document describes considerations for mailing lists with the introduction of non-ASCII UTF-8 email addresses.

EAI.why: It is an EAI working group product addressing SMTPUTF8 addresses, mixed lists and downgrading, so readers of email address internationalization need it.
EAI.quote: The introduction of internationalized email addresses affects mailing lists in three main areas

rejected.why: SMTP envelope and bounce handling are discussed, but only as they relate to lists and SMTPUTF8; no SMTP specification or extension is defined.
List-* header fields are discussed, but the document is about list handling, which is covered by the mailing lists tag, and defines no header format changes.
mailto and percent-encoding of URIs in List headers are mentioned as a detail; the document is not about URIs.
MIME header downgrading is mentioned only briefly.
Sieve is only mentioned as an example of filters that compare List-ID values.

RFC6784.title: Kerberos Options for DHCPv6
RFC6784.summary: Defines four DHCPv6 options (principal name, realm name, default realm name, KDC) that carry Kerberos configuration, including KDC addresses and realm names, to clients and servers.

DHCPv6.why: The document's main body specifies new DHCPv6 options, their formats, option codes and client/server operation.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines four new options for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6).

Kerberos.why: The options convey Kerberos realm, principal and KDC information, and define a Kerberos transport type registry. Kerberos readers need this KDC discovery mechanism.
Kerberos.quote: These options are used to carry configuration information for Kerberos.

rejected.why: DNS SRV is referenced as the alternative KDC discovery method and for Priority/Weight semantics, but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
Options carry IPv6 addresses, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
TLS is only listed as a Kerberos transport type value, with no new TLS content.
TCP and UDP are only listed as transport type values for the KDC option.
IANA section registers option codes and a sub-registry, which is boilerplate for this document.

RFC6785.title: Support for Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) Events in Sieve
RFC6785.summary: Defines how Sieve email filter scripts are invoked on IMAP events (APPEND, COPY, flag changes), using IMAP METADATA to associate scripts with mailboxes, specifying action applicability and new environment items, and updating RFC 5228.

Sieve.why: The document is a Sieve extension (imapsieve) specifying action applicability, environment items and updates to RFC 5228.
Sieve.quote: This document defines how Sieve can plug into points in IMAP where messages are created or changed

IMAP.why: Defines a new IMAP capability (IMAPSIEVE=), affects APPEND, COPY, and flag-change handling, and registers METADATA entries.
IMAP.quote: This specification defines extensions to IMAP [RFC3501] to support the invocation of Sieve scripts at times when the IMAP server creates new messages

rejected.why: Message submission is only used by redirect to send out messages; it is not the subject.
Appears only in a notify example URI.
MIME part tests are mentioned only as one interacting Sieve extension.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and do not make the document about IANA.
The more specific Sieve and IMAP tags cover the subject.

RFC6786.title: Encrypting the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) Attribute-Value Pairs
RFC6786.summary: Defines a mechanism for PANA to deliver selected AVPs in encrypted form, adding Encryption-Algorithm and Encryption-Encap AVPs, key derivation, AES128_CTR, and an encryption policy table.

PANA.why: The document extends PANA with new AVPs, keys and an encryption policy for existing PANA AVPs.
PANA.quote: This document specifies a mechanism for delivering the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) in encrypted form.

AES.why: A substantial section specifies AES-128 CTR mode as the mandatory algorithm, with nonce and counter block construction.
AES.quote: The AES128_CTR encryption algorithm uses the AES-CTR (Counter) mode of operation as specified in [NIST_SP800_38A] using the AES-128 block cipher.

rejected.why: EAP only supplies the MSK that PANA uses for key derivation; the document does not specify or extend EAP.
Only the prf+ function from IKEv2 is borrowed for key derivation; nothing about IKE is specified.
Key derivation is a small part of the PANA-specific mechanism, not a general key management subject.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new AVPs and do not make the document about IANA.

RFC6787.title: Media Resource Control Protocol Version 2 (MRCPv2)
RFC6787.summary: RFC 6787 specifies MRCPv2, a protocol for clients to control speech synthesizer, recognizer, recorder, and speaker verification resources on media servers, using SIP/SDP for session setup and TCP/TLS for control messages, with NLSML result formats.

MRCP.quote: MRCPv2 allows client hosts to control media service resources such as speech synthesizers, recognizers, verifiers, and identifiers residing in servers on the network.

rejected.why: SIP is used only as the session establishment substrate; the document does not extend SIP.
SDP is used to negotiate control channels, but SDP itself is not what the document is about, though it registers new attributes.
RTP carries the media; the document does not specify RTP.
TLS is only a transport option for the control channel.
NLSML is XML-based, but XML is only the encoding.

gaps.name: speech services / speech recognition and synthesis control
gaps.why: The taxonomy lacks a general speech-services topic beyond MRCP, and I used the MRCP id for it. NLSML result markup is also not covered.

RFC6788.title: The Line-Identification Option
RFC6788.summary: Defines the IPv6 Line-Identification destination option, which lets a DSL/GPON Access Node tunnel Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements to an Edge Router so it can identify subscriber lines in N:1 VLAN Ethernet aggregation networks.

neighbor discovery.why: The document extends IPv6 Router Solicitation/Advertisement handling by tunnelling ND messages with a new destination option, specifying AN and Edge Router behaviour for RS/RA.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document uses a mechanism that tunnels Neighbor Discovery (ND) packets inside another IPv6 packet that uses a destination option (Line-ID option)

DSL.why: The applicability is DSL/GPON Ethernet aggregation networks with DSLAM Access Nodes (Broadband Forum TR-101 model), which readers of DSL access topics would want.
DSL.quote: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) is a widely deployed access technology for Broadband Access for Next Generation Networks.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 relay options are only the model from which the Line-ID encoding is derived; the document is about RS/RA, not DHCP.
The parent is implied by neighbor discovery; the document is not about IPv6 generally.
RFC 2473 tunnelling is just the mechanism used to carry ND messages; the document does not define new generic tunnelling.
ANCP is only mentioned as an optional out-of-band mechanism for circuit-down notification.
SLAAC is the context in which hosts use RAs, but the document does not specify or extend SLAAC itself.
Ethernet aggregation and VLANs are deployment context, not the subject of the specification.

RFC6789.title: Congestion Exposure (ConEx) Concepts and Use Cases
RFC6789.summary: Informational entry-point document for the ConEx protocol, explaining the motivation for exposing congestion information in IP headers and its core use case of congestion-volume-based traffic management.

ConEx.why: The whole document explains ConEx concepts, congestion-volume, rest-of-path congestion, use cases and deployment, so it belongs on the ConEx page.
ConEx.quote: This document provides the entry point to the set of documentation about the Congestion Exposure (ConEx) protocol.

rejected.why: ECN markings are the congestion signal that ConEx builds on and combines with, but the document is not about ECN itself.
Mentioned as a scavenger transport that ConEx-based management would incentivise. It is not specified or analysed here.
Cited only as an analogy for edge policing architecture.
ConEx is a child of this topic, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The traffic management here is policing of users by congestion-volume, not traffic engineering of paths.
TCP sender modifications are defined in a companion document, and TCP appears here only as context.

RFC6790.title: The Use of Entropy Labels in MPLS Forwarding
RFC6790.summary: Defines entropy labels (with the Entropy Label Indicator, reserved label 7) that MPLS ingress LSRs insert to improve ECMP/LAG load balancing at transit LSRs, with data-plane rules and LDP, BGP and RSVP-TE capability signaling.

MPLS.why: The document specifies the entropy label and ELI in the MPLS label stack and the egress, ingress, transit and penultimate-hop forwarding rules. It updates RFC 3031 and RFC 3209.
MPLS.quote: This memo suggests ways of improving load balancing across MPLS networks using the concept of "entropy labels".

LDP.why: It defines a new LDP TLV (Type 0x0206) and its propagation rules, and updates RFC 5036.
LDP.quote: A new LDP TLV [RFC5036] is defined to signal an egress's ability to process entropy labels.  This is called the ELC TLV

RSVP-TE.why: It defines a new RSVP-TE Attribute Flags bit for entropy label capability, and updates RFC 3209.
RSVP-TE.quote: Entropy label support is signaled in RSVP-TE [RFC3209] using the Entropy Label Capability (ELC) flag in the Attribute Flags TLV

BGP.why: It defines a new BGP path attribute (type 28) for signaling entropy label capability with labeled NLRI, and updates RFC 3107.
BGP.quote: the BGP UPDATE message may include the ELC attribute as part of the Path Attributes.  This is an optional, transitive BGP

ECMP.why: The motivation is load-balanced forwarding across ECMP and LAG paths, and the document specifies how transit LSRs choose keys for it.
ECMP.quote: Load balancing, or multi-pathing, is an attempt to balance traffic across a network by allowing the traffic to use multiple paths.

rejected.why: LAG is only one of two load-balancing contexts mentioned. The document does not specify LAG behaviour.
Section 7 only says entropy labels are not applicable to MPLS-TP.
Pseudowire entropy labels are left to RFC 6391. This document covers tunnels.
BFD is only mentioned in the OAM section, which says to use an EL value from the label range for BFD packets.
The LSP traceroute update is a short subsection of the OAM section, not a main subject.
VPNs appear only as example applications running over the tunnels.

RFC6791.title: Stateless Source Address Mapping for ICMPv6 Packets
RFC6791.summary: Updates RFC 6145 by recommending that a stateless IPv4/IPv6 translator map ICMPv6 messages from non-IPv4-translatable sources to a public IPv4 source address (random from a pool) and carry the original IPv6 address in an RFC 5837 ICMP extension.

ICMP.why: The document specifies how ICMPv6 messages are translated to ICMP and how the ICMP extension is used for the source address, so ICMP behaviour is the core subject.
ICMP.quote: The ICMP message SHOULD include the Interface IP Address Sub-Object and specify the source IPv6 addresses of the original ICMPv6.

SIIT.why: It updates the stateless IP/ICMP translation algorithm (RFC 6145) with a source address mapping for a case that algorithm left open.
SIIT.quote: A stateless IPv4/IPv6 translator may receive ICMPv6 packets containing non-IPv4-translatable addresses as the source.

traceroute.why: Traceroute visibility across the translator drives the design: random pool selection and the extension that exposes the IPv6 hop addresses.
traceroute.quote: Random selection reduces the probability that two ICMP messages elicited by the same TRACEROUTE might specify the same source address

rejected.why: The document concerns stateless translation, and stateful translation is mentioned only as the alternative.
IPv6 is the context, but the document is about translation and ICMP, and the narrower SIIT tag covers it.
The parent is implied by the SIIT tag, so it is not listed separately.
It touches on IPv4 address pool selection and RFC 1918 and 6598 space, but only as a means of choosing a translated source address.

RFC6792.title: Guidelines for Use of the RTP Monitoring Framework
RFC6792.summary: Informational guidelines for an extensible RTP monitoring framework, recommending that new RTCP XR report blocks carry a single metric, include payload type, use SDES for correlation, and reduce measurement information repetition.

RTCP.why: The document gives guidelines for extending RTCP with new XR metrics blocks, which is the core RTCP subject (feedback, reports, extended reports).
RTCP.quote: extending the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) with a new RTCP Extended Reports (XR) block type to report new metrics regarding media transmission or reception quality

performance measurement.why: The framework covers monitors, transport-level, application-level and end-system metrics, and where to measure them, so it is substantially about performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: Standard methods for gathering RTP performance metrics from these applications are needed to manage uncertainties in the behavior and availability of their services.

rejected.why: RTCP is the more specific tag. RTP is the underlying session and transport being monitored.
SDP offer/answer is only mentioned as a way to signal payload format details.
IPFIX and NetFlow are listed only as non-RTP export mechanisms, not specified or profiled.
SIP appears only as an example transport for forwarding RTCP XR data to a collection server.
The RTP MIB is only mentioned in passing as an alternative monitoring mechanism.
ASM and SSM are only brief monitoring scenarios and are not the subject of the document.

RFC6793.title: BGP Support for Four-Octet Autonomous System (AS) Number Space
RFC6793.summary: RFC 6793 extends BGP to carry four-octet AS numbers, defining a capability, the AS4_PATH and AS4_AGGREGATOR attributes, AS_TRANS, and transition and error-handling rules between NEW and OLD speakers.

BGP.why: The document specifies BGP protocol extensions: a new capability, two new path attributes, AS path reconstruction and error handling. It updates RFC 4271.
BGP.quote: this document describes extensions to BGP to carry the AS numbers as four-octet entities

rejected.why: Section 5 only notes that classic communities cannot carry four-octet AS numbers and points to RFC 5668. That is a minor aside.
Confederations are mentioned only for the AS4_PATH segment restrictions and the transition rules. The document is not about confederations.
The IANA section is boilerplate, and it is only about registering code points for this extension.
The manageability section only says the BGP4-MIB needs no changes. Management is not the subject of the document.
IPFIX appears only as a one-line manageability remark about information element lengths.

RFC6794.title: A Framework for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Session Policies
RFC6794.summary: Defines a SIP framework for session policies, covering session-independent policies (delivered via ua-profile subscriptions) and session-specific policies (rendezvous with policy servers via new Policy-Contact and Policy-ID headers and a separate policy channel).

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with new header fields, an option tag, and proxy/UA/UAS behaviour for rendezvousing with policy servers.
SIP.quote: The Policy-Contact header field is a new header field defined in this specification.

rejected.why: SDP session descriptions are the policy subject matter, but the document does not specify or extend SDP.
The policy channel uses SIP event packages, but the event package itself is defined in RFC 6795, not here.
Only recommended as a transport to protect URI integrity; it is a security mechanism, not the subject.
Bandwidth limits are given as an example policy, but the document is not about QoS architectures or signalling.
Policy decision-making is explicitly out of scope; the document covers SIP signalling of policies.
Firewall/NAT pinholes are an example use case only; the document is not about firewall traversal.

RFC6795.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Event Package for Session-Specific Policies
RFC6795.summary: Defines the SIP event package "session-spec-policy" that lets user agents subscribe to session-specific policies from a policy server and receive NOTIFYs when the policy decisions change.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP event package, including SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY rules, parameters and call flows, so it is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This specification defines a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) event package for session-specific policies.

rejected.why: SDP session descriptions are carried inside the Media Policy format, but the document does not define or extend SDP.
TLS is only the security mechanism for protecting the SIP signalling (SIPS); nothing new is defined about it.
The application/media-policy-dataset+xml format is defined in RFC 6796; this document merely uses it as a body format.
The document uses an existing media type and does not register a new one. It registers only an event package name.
The taxonomy ties SIMPLE to presence event packages and XCAP, and this package is about session policy, not presence or IM.
The IANA registration of the event package name is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.

gaps.name: SIP session policy framework
gaps.why: The document and its companions (RFC 6794, RFC 6796) address policies for SIP sessions imposed by network intermediaries. The taxonomy has no tag for this, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC6796.title: A User Agent Profile Data Set for Media Policy
RFC6796.summary: Defines the Media Policy Data Set Format (MPDF), an XML format for session info documents and session policy documents describing and restricting media properties (codecs, media types, bandwidth, DSCP, intermediaries) of SIP sessions, with merging rules and a RELAX NG schema.

SIP.why: The document defines a SIP user agent profile data set for session policy, used with the SIP session policy framework and event package. It is SIP deployment and extension material.
SIP.quote: This specification defines an XML document format to describe the media properties of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) sessions.

XML.why: A new XML-based format is defined, with namespace, media type, extensibility rules and a RELAX NG schema. XML-based formats readers would want this.
XML.quote: The MPDF format is based on XML [W3C.REC-xml-20081126]. An MPDF document MUST be well-formed and MUST be valid according to schemas

SDP.why: A substantial section specifies a mapping between SDP descriptions (including offer/answer) and session info documents.
SDP.quote: A UA MUST create a separate <stream> element for each "m=" line in a session description or SDP offer/answer pair

rejected.why: The <turn-intermediary> element only references TURN as one kind of media intermediary. The document does not specify or extend TURN.
The <msrp-intermediary> element merely refers to MSRP relays. The document does not specify MSRP.
The document registers one media type, but it is not about media type registration rules.
The <qos-dscp> element carries a DSCP value. That is a single policy field, not a Diffserv specification.
Codecs are only named in allow/exclude policy lists. No codec is defined.
IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: SIP session policy / UA profile data sets
gaps.why: The document is a data set for SIP session policy and UA profile delivery (RFC 6080, 6794, 6795). The taxonomy has no tag for it, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC6797.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)
RFC6797.summary: Defines HTTP Strict Transport Security: the Strict-Transport-Security response header field and the server and user-agent processing rules that force web access over secure transport and treat secure-transport errors as fatal.

HSTS.why: The document specifies HSTS: the STS header field, max-age and includeSubDomains directives, and server and UA processing models.
HSTS.quote: This specification defines a mechanism enabling web sites to declare themselves accessible only via secure connections

rejected.why: HSTS is defined as an HTTP response header field, but HTTP is the substrate. The more specific HSTS tag covers the document.
TLS is the underlying secure transport that HSTS relies on. The document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
Cookie leakage motivates the work and includeSubDomains protects domain cookies, but the document does not specify cookies.
IDNA canonicalization of domain names is a dependency of the UA processing model. The document does not define IDN behaviour.
TLSA appears only as a deployment alternative in a non-normative note.
The document rewrites URIs and constructs the Effective Request URI, but it only uses URI syntax and does not define it.

RFC6798.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for Packet Delay Variation Metric Reporting
RFC6798.summary: Defines an RTCP XR block (BT=15) that reports packet delay variation metrics (MAPDV2 and 2-point PDV) for RTP streams, with SDP signalling and a new IANA registry of PDV types.

RTCP.why: The document extends RTCP XR with a new report block carrying PDV metrics, so it belongs on the RTCP subject page.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of packet delay variation metrics

performance measurement.why: The block defines and reports transport performance metrics (MAPDV2, 2-point PDV) and guidance on their use, which is performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: The Performance Metrics Framework [RFC6390] provides guidance on the definition and specification of performance metrics.

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate whose streams are measured. The document only extends RTCP reporting.
The document adds an xr-format value to the rtcp-xr SDP attribute. This is a small signalling piece, not a new SDP subject.
Not a taxonomy tag. Delay variation is covered under performance measurement.

gaps.name: RTCP XR (RTP Control Protocol Extended Reports) blocks
gaps.why: RTCP is a child of RTP in the taxonomy, and the document's main subject is a new RTCP XR block. Tagging RTCP directly would be ideal. The id 'RTCP' is not in the taxonomy as given, which lists it only as an entry under RTP.

RFC6801.title: Pseudo Content Delivery Protocol (CDP) for Protecting Multiple Source Flows in the Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework
RFC6801.summary: Informational RFC giving a pseudo Content Delivery Protocol showing how the FEC Framework and its SDP elements can be combined to protect multiple source flows with one or more repair flows, with worked source block and repair packet examples.

FECFRAME.why: The whole document shows how to use the FEC Framework to build a CDP. It covers source block construction from multiple flows, repair flow generation, and receiver-side recovery.
FECFRAME.quote: This document provides a pseudo Content Delivery Protocol (CDP) to protect multiple source flows with one or more repair flows based on the Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework

rejected.why: SDP is used to describe the flows (fec-source-flow, fec-repair-flow attributes), but those elements are defined in RFC 6364. This document only uses them in examples.
FECFRAME is the more specific child tag and fits better than the parent.
The example source flows are RTP/AVP, but RTP is only the carrier of the protected media and the document says nothing about it.
The examples use multicast addresses, but only as example flow addresses. The document is not about multicast routing.

RFC6802.title: Ericsson Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) Value-Added Octets
RFC6802.summary: Informational RFC describing Ericsson's optional TWAMP-Test extension that embeds value-added octets in packet padding so a Session-Sender and Session-Reflector can send and reflect packet trains to measure capacity metrics (available path capacity, tight section capacity, UDP delivery rate) in both directions.

TWAMP.why: The document extends the TWAMP-Test protocol with new fields in the padding octets and new Session-Sender and Session-Reflector behaviours, so it belongs on the TWAMP page.
TWAMP.quote: This memo describes an optional extension to the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) [RFC5357]. It is called the Ericsson TWAMP Value-Added Octets feature.

rejected.why: It is the parent of TWAMP, so it is implied. The measurement algorithms for capacity metrics are explicitly out of scope.
TWAMP-Test runs over UDP, and UDP delivery rate is only a metric being measured. The document does not specify or analyse UDP.
DSCP-based evaluation is mentioned only in passing as a possible use. The document is not about QoS.
The document only borrows the OWAMP fractional-second timestamp format and references RFC 4656. It does not extend OWAMP.

RFC6803.title: Camellia Encryption for Kerberos 5
RFC6803.summary: Specifies two Kerberos 5 encryption types and two checksum types using the Camellia block cipher in CBC-CTS mode with CMAC integrity, including key derivation, string-to-key, and test vectors.

Camellia.why: The document defines Kerberos enctypes and checksum types built on Camellia, so the Camellia subject page should list it.
Camellia.quote: The new types use the Camellia block cipher in CBC mode with ciphertext stealing and the CMAC algorithm for integrity protection.

Kerberos.why: It extends the Kerberos 5 cryptosystem framework with new encryption and checksum types and registers them with IANA for Kerberos.
Kerberos.quote: This document specifies two encryption types and two corresponding checksum types for the Kerberos cryptosystem framework defined in RFC 3961.

rejected.why: AES enctypes (RFC 3962) are referenced as a model and for salt differentiation, but the document is not about AES.
PBKDF2 is used for string-to-key with a modified salt, but it is a building block and not defined or changed by the document.
HMAC-SHA1 appears only inside the PBKDF2 call; CMAC is the actual MAC used.
Key derivation is part of the Kerberos cryptosystem profile, already covered by the Kerberos tag.
The parent topic is implied by the Camellia tag.

gaps.name: CMAC (Cipher-based MAC) / CBC-CTS mode
gaps.why: The document uses CMAC and CBC ciphertext stealing for integrity and encryption, but the taxonomy has no tag for block cipher modes or CMAC apart from AES and HMAC.

RFC6804.title: DISCOVER: Supporting Multicast DNS Queries
RFC6804.summary: Historic RFC documenting the DISCOVER DNS opcode, an experimental extension from the TBDS project that multicasts DNS queries for resource and service discovery and handles multiple responses.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS opcode with its own processing rules, wildcard semantics, and stub authoritative server behaviour, so it is a DNS protocol extension.
DNS.quote: the DISCOVER opcode, an experimental extension to the Domain Name System (DNS) to use multicast queries for resource discovery

mDNS.why: It specifies multicast DNS queries to an administratively scoped address (239.255.255.251) and handling of multiple responses. It is an early precursor of Multicast DNS.
mDNS.quote: TBDS was the first known use of multicast transport for DNS. A client multicasts a DNS query using the DISCOVER opcode

service discovery.why: A substantial part of the document describes locating servers and services via SRV lookups over multicast DISCOVER.
service discovery.quote: To lookup a service name using DISCOVER, the following steps may be used:

rejected.why: It uses SRV names for service lookup but does not define DNS-SD (PTR/TXT-based browsing); the mechanism is its own DISCOVER opcode.
IP multicast is the transport used; the document does not specify multicast routing or group management. Only an administratively scoped address is used.
Mentioned only in security considerations, which say TBDS did not use DNSSEC.
The IANA section only notes that an opcode value would need assignment, which is boilerplate.

RFC6805.title: The Application of the Path Computation Element Architecture to the Determination of a Sequence of Domains in MPLS and GMPLS
RFC6805.summary: Informational framework describing the hierarchical PCE architecture (parent/child PCEs) for computing optimal multi-domain MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSP paths when the domain sequence is not known in advance, with requirements for PCEP extensions and ASON applicability.

PCE.why: The whole document defines the hierarchical PCE architecture, its procedures, and the PCEP extension requirements it implies.
PCE.quote: In the hierarchical PCE architecture, a parent PCE maintains a domain topology map that contains the child domains

GMPLS.why: Substantial part addresses GMPLS inter-domain path computation and mapping to the ASON routing architecture (G.7715.2).
GMPLS.quote: GMPLS traffic engineering in the ASON architecture

rejected.why: TE LSP signalling is background; the document is about path computation, not RSVP-TE signalling.
BGP-TE is only discussed briefly as an alternative or complement in a short section.
Implied as the parent of PCE, which is the more specific tag chosen.
MPLS-TE is the context for the LSPs, but the document is about PCE architecture rather than MPLS itself; the GMPLS tag covers the technology.
IGP areas are discussed only as one kind of domain; no OSPF specification is involved.

RFC6806.title: Kerberos Principal Name Canonicalization and Cross-Realm Referrals
RFC6806.summary: RFC 6806 specifies how Kerberos KDCs canonicalize principal names and issue client and server referrals (error or cross-realm TGT), plus a negotiation/checksum mechanism to detect request tampering and discover FAST support; it updates RFC 4120.

Kerberos.why: The whole document extends the Kerberos protocol (updates RFC 4120) with name canonicalization, referrals, enterprise principal names, and the PA-REQ-ENC-PA-REP negotiation mechanism.
Kerberos.quote: a method for a Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) to respond to client requests for Kerberos tickets when the client does not have detailed configuration information

rejected.why: DNS host names and insecure DNS lookups are mentioned only as background for how clients currently find realms; the document is not about DNS.
General authentication topic is implied by Kerberos, a specific technology tag that already covers it.
Appears only in Appendix A for PKINIT SAN compatibility with Microsoft; not a substantive subject.
RFC 5322 email names are cited only as an example of a familiar user name style.
ASN.1 structures are used to define the protocol elements but the document is not about ASN.1 itself.

RFC6807.title: Population Count Extensions to Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM)
RFC6807.summary: Experimental RFC defining a PIM Join Attribute (type 3) and a Pop-Count-Supported Hello option that carry multicast distribution-tree accounting data (branch counts, SSM/ASM membership, node/diameter/domain/TZ counts, MTU and link speeds) upstream.

PIM.why: The document extends PIM with a new Hello option and a new Join Attribute type for Join/Prune messages, so it belongs on the PIM page.
PIM.quote: Simple extensions to the Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) protocol allow a rough approximation of tree-based data in a scalable fashion.

rejected.why: The document builds on the PIM-SM specification (RFC 4601) but extends PIM in general via Join Attributes, not the sparse-mode specification itself.
IGMP and MLD reports are only inputs that set the S and A flags and stub-link counts; the document does not specify them.
MLD reports are only inputs that set the S and A flags and stub-link counts; the document does not specify them.
SSM versus ASM membership is reported as one accounting flag; the document is not about SSM itself.
AMT is mentioned only as an example of an auto-tunnel for the 'a' flag.
The document explicitly says that defining a MIB module was not considered.

RFC6808.title: Test Plan and Results Supporting Advancement of RFC 2679 on the Standards Track
RFC6808.summary: Test plan and results comparing two independent implementations (NetProbe and Perfas+) of the IPPM one-way delay metric (RFC 2679) to support advancing it on the Standards Track under the RFC 6576 process.

performance measurement.why: The document tests implementations of the IPPM one-way delay metric: calibration, ADK equivalence, loss threshold, serialization and differential delay. This is active network performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo provides the supporting test plan and results to advance RFC 2679 on one-way delay metrics along the Standards Track

rejected.why: Cited only in Security Considerations. The document does not specify or analyse OWAMP.
Cited only in Security Considerations. The document is not about TWAMP.
L2TPv3 tunnels are only test-bed apparatus, used to hide test flows from hash-based load balancing.
Traceroute is mentioned only for reporting the path, not as a subject of the document.
The document follows the RFC 6576 advancement process, but its body is metric test results, not process definition.
UDP is only the carrier for test packets.

RFC6809.title: Mechanism to Indicate Support of Features and Capabilities in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6809.summary: Defines the SIP Feature-Caps header field and feature-capability indicators, letting proxies, registrars and B2BUAs not represented by the Contact URI indicate supported features, and creates an IANA registry of indicator trees.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field, with procedures for UAs, proxies, registrars and B2BUAs across dialogs, registrations and standalone transactions.
SIP.quote: This specification defines a new SIP header field, Feature-Caps.

rejected.why: The new registry is a part of the SIP extension. The document is not about IANA stewardship or guidance in general.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as hop-by-hop confidentiality.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax.
The document draws on media feature tags only by analogy. It does not register media types.
SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY are mentioned only briefly. The document does not cover presence or event packages.

RFC6810.title: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) to Router Protocol
RFC6810.summary: Specifies the RPKI-to-Router protocol (RTR), a PDU-based protocol by which a router fetches validated ROA prefix-origin data from a trusted cache, including sequences, transports, and error codes.

RPKI.why: The document defines the RPKI-Router protocol that delivers RPKI validated ROA prefix origin data from caches to routers, used for BGP origin validation.
RPKI.quote: This document describes a protocol to deliver validated prefix origin data to routers.

rejected.why: BGP origin validation is the use case, but the document specifies a cache-to-router protocol, not BGP itself.
TCP is only the transport; TCP-AO and MD5 are options for protecting it, not what the document is about.
SSH is one optional transport (subsystem rpki-rtr); substrate only.
TLS is an optional transport with certificate rules, but the document defines no new TLS mechanism.
Only mentioned as an optional transport.
The parent is implied by RPKI, which is the more specific tag.

RFC6811.title: BGP Prefix Origin Validation
RFC6811.summary: Specifies how a BGP speaker assigns a validation state (Valid, Invalid, NotFound) to received routes by comparing prefix and origin AS against a database of Validated ROA Payloads, typically derived from the RPKI, and how that state is used in policy.

RPKI.why: The document defines route origin validation using Validated ROA Payloads from the RPKI. This is the core subject of the RPKI tag (route origin validation).
RPKI.quote: This document describes a simple validation mechanism to partially satisfy this requirement.

BGP.why: It specifies BGP speaker behaviour: validation state as a route attribute, its effect on the decision process, route policy, LOCAL_PREF and IBGP propagation via communities.
BGP.quote: When a BGP speaker receives an UPDATE from a neighbor, it SHOULD perform a lookup as described above for each of the Routes in the UPDATE message.

rejected.why: The document explicitly excludes path validation and covers only origin validation.
RFC 3779 certificates are mentioned only as background for how the RPKI works. The document does not profile them.
This is the parent of RPKI, which is already chosen, so listing it would be redundant.
Communities are mentioned only as a way to carry the validation state to IBGP peers. This is a minor point and not the subject.

RFC6812.title: Cisco Service-Level Assurance Protocol
RFC6812.summary: Describes Cisco's SLA Protocol (UDP-Measurement type), an active performance measurement protocol with a control phase and a measurement phase for measuring latency, jitter and loss, published for vendor interoperability.

performance measurement.why: The whole document specifies an active performance measurement protocol for latency, delay variation and loss. No specific child tag (OWAMP/TWAMP/STAMP) fits since this is a distinct Cisco protocol, so the parent topic is used.
performance measurement.quote: Cisco's Service-Level Assurance Protocol (Cisco's SLA Protocol) is a Performance Measurement protocol that has been widely deployed.

rejected.why: Only cited as a related IETF protocol; this document defines a different protocol.
Only mentioned as related work in the Introduction.
UDP is only the transport for control and measurement messages; nothing new is defined about UDP.
Security Considerations recommend IPsec, but that is boilerplate and the document is not about IPsec.
HMAC-SHA-256 is used for message authentication only, in a supporting role.
NTP timestamp format from RFC 5905 is merely reused for timestamps.
The measurement traffic can simulate RTP voice/video, but the document does not specify RTP.

RFC6813.title: The Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) Asokan Attack Analysis
RFC6813.summary: Informational analysis of the NEA Asokan Attack, a forwarding/man-in-the-middle attack on NEA posture exchanges, and countermeasures (identity binding and cryptographic binding to the TLS tunnel, preferring tls-unique channel binding).

NEA.why: The whole document analyses an attack against the NEA protocols (PA, PB, PT) and the countermeasures NEA transports should use.
NEA.quote: The Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) protocols are subject to a subtle forwarding attack that has become known as the NEA Asokan Attack.

rejected.why: TLS is the tunnel substrate; the document only uses existing exporters and channel bindings (RFC 5705, RFC 5929) and defines nothing new for TLS.
PT-EAP and EAP-TLS are mentioned as transports/examples, but the document is not about EAP or its methods.
The EMA and TCG PTS attestation protocol are discussed only as context for lying endpoints, which is declared out of scope.
The original Asokan attack involves AAA servers, but only as an illustrative analogy.
The parent is implied by the NEA tag, which is the more specific fit.

RFC6814.title: Formally Deprecating Some IPv4 Options
RFC6814.summary: RFC 6814 formally deprecates nine obsolete IPv4 header options in the IANA IP option registry and moves RFCs 1385, 1393, 1475 and 1770 to Historic.

IPv4.why: The document is about IPv4 header options, deprecating several of them and describing why each is obsolete. IPv4 readers would want it.
IPv4.quote: A number of IPv4 options have become obsolete in practice, but have never been formally deprecated.  This document deprecates such IPv4 options

rejected.why: The IANA registry is only updated as a consequence of the deprecation. The document is about the IPv4 options, not IANA policy.
The Traceroute IP option is one of the deprecated options. The document does not specify or analyse traceroute tools.
IPv6 is mentioned only as superseding the Extended Internet Protocol option.
BIDIR-PIM is mentioned only as the origin of the deprecated Upstream Multicast Pkt. option.
The RFC status changes to Historic are administrative follow-ups, not the subject of the document.

RFC6815.title: Applicability Statement for RFC 2544: Use on Production Networks Considered Harmful
RFC6815.summary: An applicability statement clarifying that RFC 2544 benchmarking methods are for isolated laboratory test environments only and must not be used on production networks, pointing to IPPM and other work for production measurement.

benchmarking.why: The document is about the scope and applicability of RFC 2544 and BMWG benchmarking methodology, restricting it to isolated lab testing.
benchmarking.quote: This memo clarifies the scope of RFC 2544 and other IETF BMWG benchmarking work for isolated test environments only

rejected.why: It mentions IPPM and production performance measurement only as the alternative venue; the document itself is about benchmarking, a sibling topic.
The 198.18.0.0/15 test address range is mentioned only in passing as part of containing test traffic.
RFC 5180's IPv6 test address range is a single passing mention.
OAM is cited in one sentence as other standards that may help; not the subject of the document.
CIR/SLA validation is mentioned as an out-of-scope use, not addressed in its own right.

RFC6816.title: Simple Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) Staircase Forward Error Correction (FEC) Scheme for FECFRAME
RFC6816.summary: Specifies a fully specified FEC scheme (FEC Encoding ID 7) using LDPC-Staircase codes to protect arbitrary ADU flows within the FECFRAME framework, defining source block creation, FFCI/FSSI, and FEC payload IDs.

LDPC.why: The document specifies the use of LDPC-Staircase codes, inheriting the core code from RFC 5170, and gives operational guidance on their performance.
LDPC.quote: fully specified simple Forward Error Correction (FEC) scheme for Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) Staircase codes

FECFRAME.why: The scheme is a FECFRAME FEC scheme, defining ADU block and source block creation, FFCI and payload ID formats for the framework.
FECFRAME.quote: protect media streams along the lines defined by FECFRAME

rejected.why: RTP is only a possible encapsulation of ADUs; the document does not specify RTP.
SDP is merely a way to carry the FFCI/FSSI parameters, specified in RFC 6364.
Raptor is mentioned only as a comparison with other FEC schemes in the introduction.
The document is about FECFRAME streaming protection, not reliable multicast; ALC and NORM appear only as background.
IPsec/ESP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a baseline from RFC 6363.
The FEC parent is implied by the FECFRAME and LDPC tags and is not listed separately.

RFC6817.title: Low Extra Delay Background Transport (LEDBAT)
RFC6817.summary: RFC 6817 specifies LEDBAT, an experimental delay-based congestion control algorithm for background bulk transfers that uses one-way delay measurements to yield to standard TCP and limit added queueing delay.

LEDBAT.why: The document defines the LEDBAT algorithm: sender and receiver operation, parameters, and open experimentation areas.
LEDBAT.quote: Low Extra Delay Background Transport (LEDBAT) is an experimental delay-based congestion control algorithm that seeks to utilize the available bandwidth on an end-to-end path

rejected.why: Standard TCP congestion control (RFC 5681) is the baseline LEDBAT is compared to and must not exceed. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
This is the parent topic of LEDBAT, so it is implied by the LEDBAT tag and not listed separately.
ECN is mentioned only briefly: LEDBAT should treat a mark like a loss. The document is not about ECN.
AQM appears only in the applicability discussion of how it interacts with LEDBAT. The document is not about AQM.
NTP is referenced only for the clock offset and skew terminology in Appendix A.

RFC6818.title: Updates to the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
RFC6818.summary: RFC 6818 updates RFC 5280 (the Internet X.509 PKI certificate and CRL profile) by changing allowed explicitText encodings, aligning IDN ToASCII rules for distinguished names, clarifying self-signed certificates and trust anchors, and revising security considerations.

X.509.why: The document is an update to the PKIX X.509 certificate and CRL profile, changing certificate policy qualifier encodings, self-signed certificate guidance, and path validation text.
X.509.quote: This document updates RFC 5280, the "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile".

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child tag and covers the document; the parent is implied.
The IDN ToASCII rule change for domainComponent labels is a small part of a certificate profile update; the document is not about IDNA itself.
NFC normalization of explicitText is mentioned only incidentally within the certificate field encoding rules.
String types such as UTF8String and IA5String are used as certificate field encodings; the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC6819.title: OAuth 2.0 Threat Model and Security Considerations
RFC6819.summary: RFC 6819 gives a comprehensive threat model for the OAuth 2.0 framework, describing attacks on clients, authorization and token endpoints, grant flows and resource access, with countermeasures.

OAuth.why: The whole document is a threat model and set of countermeasures for OAuth 2.0 tokens, grants, endpoints and clients.
OAuth.quote: This document gives additional security considerations for OAuth, beyond those in the OAuth 2.0 specification, based on a comprehensive threat model for the OAuth 2.0 protocol

rejected.why: TLS is only recommended as a transport countermeasure; the document defines nothing new about it.
HTTP is the substrate; Cache-Control and Authorization header remarks are incidental.
JWT and SAML are only mentioned as example assertion formats; token formats are out of scope.
CSRF and clickjacking are covered, but only as OAuth-specific threats; OAuth is the more specific tag.
The parent of OAuth is implied by the OAuth tag and is not chosen separately.
Cookies are mentioned only in passing, in analogies and session-binding remarks.

RFC6820.title: Address Resolution Problems in Large Data Center Networks
RFC6820.summary: Informational ARMD WG document describing ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery scaling "pain points" in large data center networks, including router ARP processing, ND probing and switch MAC table limits.

data center networking.why: The whole document analyses address resolution scaling problems in large data centers, covering data center topologies, virtualization and L2/L3 boundary design.
data center networking.quote: This document examines address resolution issues related to the scaling of data centers with a very large number of hosts.

ARP.why: ARP behaviour, broadcast load, cache handling, gratuitous ARP and router slow-path processing are analysed at length.
ARP.quote: From a scaling perspective, there are a number of problems with ARP. First, it uses broadcast

neighbor discovery.why: ND multicast queries, NUD probing and the failure of gratuitous-update mitigation in IPv6 are a main subject, analysed as scaling problems.
neighbor discovery.quote: Though IPv6's Neighbor Discovery behaves much like ARP, there are several notable differences that result in a different set of potential issues.

rejected.why: L2 switching and MAC tables are discussed only as context for the address resolution scaling problems, not as Ethernet specification or operation.
Overlays are covered briefly in Section 6.4.4 as one design option, not specified or analysed in depth.
Solicited-node multicast is mentioned only as part of how ND works.
ICMP destination unreachable is mentioned only in passing.

RFC6821.title: Improving Peer Selection in Peer-to-peer Applications: Myths vs. Reality
RFC6821.summary: An IRTF P2PRG informational document that evaluates seven "myths" about locality-aware peer selection in P2P applications (cross-domain traffic, performance, uplink use, peering/transit impacts, swarm weakening, caching) by citing studies, to inform IETF ALTO work.

P2P.why: The whole document analyses peer selection and traffic localization in P2P applications such as BitTorrent swarms, so it belongs on the P2P page.
P2P.quote: Peer-to-peer (P2P) traffic optimization techniques that aim at improving locality in the peer selection process have attracted great interest in the research community

ALTO.why: The document is explicitly meant to inform ALTO work and evaluates the locality-aware optimization (P4P, oracle, Ono) that ALTO addresses. It specifies no protocol itself, so this tag is secondary.
ALTO.quote: some of which are now being considered for standardization in the IETF [ALTO]. While this document serves to inform the protocol work going on in the IETF ALTO working group

rejected.why: It reports results from field trials and simulations, but the subject is P2P locality effects, not network performance metrics or methods.
The caching discussed is P2P caching, not HTTP or web caching.
The document concerns ISP economics (peering, transit) and P2P behaviour, not architectural principles of the Internet.
Congestion on inter-domain links is mentioned as motivation, but no congestion control mechanism is discussed.
Peering and transit are discussed as commercial agreements, not as routing protocols or routing architecture.

RFC6822.title: IS-IS Multi-Instance
RFC6822.summary: Defines Multi-Instance IS-IS, an extension letting a router run multiple IS-IS instances on a circuit, each with instance-specific adjacencies and per-topology LSDBs, identified by a new IID-TLV.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the IS-IS protocol: the IID-TLV, instance-specific adjacencies, update process operation and interoperability with legacy routers.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines an extension to IS-IS to remove this restriction.  The extension is referred to as "Multi-Instance IS-IS" (MI-IS-IS).

rejected.why: The document is about a specific protocol extension, which the IS-IS tag covers more precisely than the general routing architecture topic.
RFC 6213 BFD-Enabled TLV is mentioned only in passing, to say the ITID may replace the MTID.
The IANA section only registers the TLV and MAC addresses; it is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
The document does not discuss OSPF; it deals with IS-IS only.

RFC6823.title: Advertising Generic Information in IS-IS
RFC6823.summary: Defines the IS-IS GENINFO TLV (type 251) for advertising generic, non-routing application information in LSPs, along with flooding/leaking procedures, use of non-zero instances, and standardization requirements.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies a new IS-IS TLV and the flooding and leaking procedures for LSPs carrying it, so it is an extension of IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: defines an encoding format for GENINFO that minimizes the consumption of TLV codepoints

rejected.why: The new registry for Application Identifiers is created in the IANA Considerations section. That is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA stewardship.
It is mentioned nowhere in the body. The document is IS-IS-specific.
The document is about IS-IS, which has its own tag. It is not about routing architecture in general.

RFC6824.title: TCP Extensions for Multipath Operation with Multiple Addresses
RFC6824.summary: RFC 6824 specifies Multipath TCP (MPTCP), a set of TCP options and procedures that let one TCP connection use multiple subflows over different paths/addresses, including handshake, data sequencing, address management, fallback and middlebox handling.

MPTCP.why: The document is the core MPTCP protocol specification: MP_CAPABLE, MP_JOIN, DSS, ADD_ADDR, fallback and related options.
MPTCP.quote: Multipath TCP provides the ability to simultaneously use multiple paths between peers. This document presents a set of extensions to traditional TCP to support multipath operation.

rejected.why: MPTCP is the more specific child tag; TCP is implied as its ancestor and not listed separately.
Congestion control is only referenced (coupled algorithm is in RFC 6356); this document just gives considerations.
HMAC-SHA1 is used as a mechanism for subflow authentication, not specified or analysed in its own right.
SHA-1 is only used for token and IDSN derivation; it is a substrate, not the subject.
NAT traversal is a design constraint and a section on middleboxes, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.
ECMP is mentioned only as a context where ports can give disjoint paths.

RFC6825.title: Traffic Engineering Database Management Information Base in Support of MPLS-TE/GMPLS
RFC6825.summary: Defines the TED-MIB SMIv2 module for managing the MPLS-TE/GMPLS Traffic Engineering Database (TE link info from OSPF-TE/IS-IS-TE, including GMPLS switching capability and SRLG) over SNMP.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is a new MIB module (tedTable, tedSwCapTable, etc.) in SMIv2 for the TED.
MIB.quote: This memo defines the MIB objects for managing TED in support of MPLS-TE/GMPLS for use with network management protocols.

GMPLS.why: The MIB exposes GMPLS TE link attributes (switching capability, encoding, protection, SRLG, unnumbered link IDs), so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: The tedSwCapTable is identical to the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor information in a sub-TLV of the Link-TLV.

rejected.why: OSPF-TE is the source of the TE link data but the document does not specify or extend OSPF; it is a separate MIB.
IS-IS TE is only a source of advertised information; the document does not specify IS-IS.
SNMP is the access substrate; the MIB tag already sits under SNMP and covers the document.
The document is about managing TE database information via MIB; the GMPLS tag and MIB tag fit better, with no standalone TE topic needed.
MPLS-TE is covered through GMPLS and the MIB; the document is not about MPLS in general.
The data model is SMIv2/MIB, not YANG.

gaps.name: Traffic Engineering Database (TED)
gaps.why: The document is about managing the TED, but the taxonomy has no tag specifically for TED/TE link-state information.

RFC6826.title: Multipoint LDP In-Band Signaling for Point-to-Multipoint and Multipoint-to-Multipoint Label Switched Paths
RFC6826.summary: Specifies mLDP in-band signaling, where PIM (S,G) or (*,G) state is encoded in the mLDP FEC opaque value so IP multicast trees can be spliced across an MPLS domain via P2MP/MP2MP LSPs, and defines four new transit opaque TLVs.

LDP.why: The document extends mLDP by defining new opaque value TLV types in the P2MP/MP2MP FEC element and the procedures for using them.
LDP.quote: the information needed to establish the mapping between an LSP and the set of multicast packets to be forwarded over it is carried in the "opaque value" field of an mLDP FEC

multicast.why: It is about carrying PIM-built IP multicast trees (source-specific and bidirectional) across an MPLS core, including mapping (S,G)/(*,G) state to LSPs.
multicast.quote: The result is an IP multicast tree consisting of a set of IP multicast sub-trees that are spliced together with a multipoint LSP.

rejected.why: PIM interacts at the domain borders, but the document specifies mLDP encodings and procedures rather than PIM itself.
The MPLS domain is the environment, but the specification is the mLDP extension, which sits under LDP.
ASM shared-tree transit is explicitly out of scope, and PIM-SM is only referenced.
SSM-mode source trees are mentioned as one source of trees, but the document does not specify SSM.
Source and RP addresses in a VPN context are explicitly out of scope.
The registry allocation is boilerplate for the new TLV types.

RFC6827.title: Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) Routing for OSPFv2 Protocols
RFC6827.summary: Defines OSPFv2 TE LSA extensions (new sub-TLVs for Local/Remote TE Router ID and Inter-RA export loop prevention) to meet ASON routing requirements from RFC 4258, obsoleting RFC 5787 and updating RFC 5786.

OSPF.why: The document specifies new OSPFv2 TE LSA sub-TLVs and processing rules, so it is an extension of OSPF.
OSPF.quote: This document defines extensions to the OSPFv2 Link State Routing Protocol to meet the requirements for routing in an ASON.

GMPLS.why: ASON routing is realized as GMPLS routing for optical/TDM networks, using ISCD and GMPLS OSPF extensions. Readers of GMPLS would want this RFC.
GMPLS.quote: The Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) protocol suite is designed to provide a control plane for a range of network technologies.

rejected.why: The TE LSAs are the carrier, but the document is about ASON routing hierarchy and reachability rather than TE as a subject; GMPLS covers the optical control-plane aspect.
SONET/SDH is only mentioned as an example network technology; technology-specific details are explicitly out of scope.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as an OSPF authentication mechanism.
It addresses ASON hierarchical routing areas but through the specific OSPF extension; OSPF and GMPLS are more specific tags.

gaps.name: ASON (Automatically Switched Optical Network) routing
gaps.why: The document's central subject is ITU-T ASON routing requirements and hierarchical routing areas, and the taxonomy has no ASON or optical-network tag.

RFC6828.title: Content Splicing for RTP Sessions
RFC6828.summary: Informational RFC describing use cases and requirements for content splicing (e.g., local ad insertion) in RTP sessions, and guidelines for using an RTP mixer as the splicer, including RTP/RTCP processing and congestion control.

RTP.why: The document specifies how to splice content in RTP sessions using an RTP mixer, covering SSRC/CSRC, sequence number and timestamp handling.
RTP.quote: It provides concrete guidelines for how an RTP mixer can be used to handle content splicing.

RTCP.why: A substantial section covers rewriting and forwarding RTCP reports, XR blocks, SDES/BYE and AVPF feedback through the splicer.
RTCP.quote: the mixer can leave the SSRC identifier in the RTCP report intact

rejected.why: Section 4.4 discusses congestion considerations, but only as a consequence of splicing and via RTCP feedback; the document is not about congestion control itself.
RFC 6679 ECN feedback is mentioned as one report type the mixer must handle, but ECN is not a subject of the document.
SRTP appears only in Security Considerations as a way for the splicer to re-protect packets; this is boilerplate-level mention.
Codec differences cause packet count mismatches, but no codec is defined or profiled.

gaps.name: Content splicing / ad insertion
gaps.why: The document's core subject is media content splicing (RTP mixers as splicers), and the taxonomy has no tag for splicing or RTP middleboxes (mixers/translators).

RFC6829.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping for Pseudowire Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs) Advertised over IPv6
RFC6829.summary: Extends MPLS LSP Ping and traceroute (RFC 4379) to pseudowires signalled over IPv6 LDP sessions by defining new FEC 128 and FEC 129 Pseudowire IPv6 Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs and renaming the existing ones as IPv4.

pseudowire.why: The document defines LSP Ping FEC sub-TLVs specifically for MPLS pseudowires (FEC 128 and FEC 129), so readers of the pseudowire subject need it.
pseudowire.quote: extends the PW LSP Ping and traceroute mechanisms so they can be used with PWs that are set up and maintained using IPv6 LDP sessions

MPLS.why: It updates RFC 4379 MPLS LSP Ping/traceroute data-plane failure detection with new Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs and IANA registry entries.
MPLS.quote: The Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping and traceroute mechanisms are commonly used to detect and isolate data-plane failures

rejected.why: IPv6 LDP sessions signal the PWs, but the document only uses the session addresses in the FEC sub-TLVs and does not specify LDP.
IPv6 addresses are carried in the new sub-TLVs, but the document does not address IPv6 itself.
Traceroute is mentioned as part of RFC 4379 mechanisms, but no new traceroute procedures are defined; the document says it defines no new procedures.
LSP Ping is an OAM tool, but the more specific MPLS and pseudowire tags cover the document.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP Ping / data-plane failure detection
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS LSP Ping (RFC 4379) itself, which is the central subject of the document.

RFC6830.title: The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP)
RFC6830.summary: Specifies LISP, an experimental network-layer protocol separating IP addresses into EIDs and RLOCs, with UDP encapsulation, EID-to-RLOC mapping control messages, reachability, and mobility/multicast considerations.
