LISP.why: The document is the core LISP specification: encapsulation, Map-Request/Reply/Register/Notify messages, and RLOC reachability.
LISP.quote: This document describes a network-layer-based protocol that enables separation of IP addresses into two new numbering spaces: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and Routing Locators (RLOCs).

rejected.why: Mobility is discussed in Section 10 as an interaction with LISP, but it is not the document's subject.
LISP uses encapsulation, but the document defines LISP itself, so the specific LISP tag fits better.
UDP is only the encapsulation and control-message transport.
Only a short considerations section; the details are in RFC 6831.
Section 9 covers traceroute behaviour only as a side consideration.
BGP is mentioned only in passing, for example RIB checks for reachability.

RFC6831.title: The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) for Multicast Environments
RFC6831.summary: Describes how inter-domain multicast routing works with LISP (LISP-Multicast): mapping source EIDs to RLOCs, PIM/MSDP/IGMP changes, data-plane encapsulation, and interworking with non-LISP sites.

LISP.why: The document extends LISP to multicast, defining ITR/ETR behaviour, mPETR/mPITR, and interworking with non-LISP sites.
LISP.quote: This document describes how inter-domain multicast routing will function in an environment where Locator/ID Separation is deployed using the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) architecture.

multicast.why: It covers multicast distribution tree building, (S-EID,G)/(S-RLOC,G) state, ASM/SSM/Bidir operation, and interdomain multicast, so multicast readers would want it.
multicast.quote: This specification focuses on what changes are needed to the multicast routing protocols to support LISP-Multicast

rejected.why: PIM is analysed for needed changes, but no PIM message format changes are made. The document is about LISP-Multicast rather than PIM itself.
MSDP is discussed only to say no changes are needed.
MBGP is mentioned only to say no changes are required.
IGMP and MLD are covered only to say no changes are needed.
SSM is one of the service models treated, but it is not the document's focus.
PIM-SM is referenced as the existing ASM mode. The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC6832.title: Interworking between Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) and Non-LISP Sites
RFC6832.summary: Defines mechanisms (Proxy-ITR, Proxy-ETR, LISP-NAT) letting LISP sites using non-routable EIDs interoperate with non-LISP Internet sites.

LISP.why: The whole document specifies LISP interworking elements: Proxy-ITR, Proxy-ETR and LISP-NAT.
LISP.quote: This document describes interoperation mechanisms between LISP [RFC6830] sites that use EIDs that are not globally routed, and non-LISP sites.

NAT.why: A substantial section defines LISP-NAT, translating non-routable EIDs and RFC 1918 addresses to routable ones in ITRs.
NAT.quote: LISP Network Address Translation (LISP-NAT) is a limited form of NAT [RFC2993].

rejected.why: BGP is used to announce aggregated EID prefixes from Proxy-ITRs, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
Anycast is mentioned only briefly as a way to scale Proxy-ITRs.
DNS lookups appear only in example packet flows, and DNS is not the subject.
LISP encapsulation is the mechanism, but the document is about LISP interworking, which the LISP tag covers more specifically.

RFC6833.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Map-Server Interface
RFC6833.summary: Specifies the LISP Map-Resolver and Map-Server, which give ITRs and ETRs a simplified front end to EID-to-RLOC mapping databases, including Map-Register/Map-Notify registration and Map-Request processing.

LISP.why: The whole document defines the Map-Server and Map-Resolver components of LISP and their interactions with ITRs and ETRs.
LISP.quote: The LISP Mapping Service defines two new types of LISP-speaking devices: the Map-Resolver, which accepts Map-Requests from an Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR)

rejected.why: BGP is used only by LISP+ALT, the example mapping database. Map-Servers and ITRs/ETRs are meant to avoid it.
DNS is only an analogy for the resolver/server terminology. The document does not specify or use DNS.
Anycast Map-Resolver operation is a short subsection. It is not a substantial part of the document.
HMAC-SHA-1-96 is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as the authentication mechanism for Map-Register. It is not what the document is about.
GRE is mentioned only as part of the ALT infrastructure that Map-Servers and ITRs/ETRs avoid.

RFC6834.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Map-Versioning
RFC6834.summary: Experimental extension to LISP that assigns 12-bit version numbers to EID-to-RLOC mappings and carries them in the LISP header and Map Records so ITRs and ETRs can detect stale mappings.

LISP.why: The whole document defines a LISP extension: version numbers in the LISP data-plane header and Map Records, with ITR/ETR handling rules and Map-Request behaviour.
LISP.quote: The basic mechanism is to associate a Map-Version number to each LISP EID-to-RLOC mapping and transport such a version number in the LISP- specific header.

rejected.why: LISP is the more specific tag for this locator/ID separation work, and ancestors are implied.
LISP encapsulation is the substrate. The document only uses spare header bits and does not define generic tunnelling.
It mentions DoS resilience only in Security Considerations, which is not the subject of the document.
The IPv4-in-IPv4 header example is incidental. The document is not about IP itself.

RFC6835.title: The Locator/ID Separation Protocol Internet Groper (LIG)
RFC6835.summary: Informational RFC describing 'lig', a manual diagnostic tool (analogous to DNS 'dig') that sends LISP Map-Requests to query the LISP mapping database and verify site registration, with syntax, implementations, and ALT testing guidance.

LISP.why: The whole document specifies a LISP management/diagnostic tool that sends Map-Requests and displays Map-Replies, so it belongs on the LISP page.
LISP.quote: A simple tool called the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Internet Groper or 'lig' can be used to query the LISP mapping database.

rejected.why: lig is a diagnostic tool for the mapping database, not path discovery; the traceroute tag concerns path discovery tools.
Only used as an analogy ('similar to the DNS analogue dig') and for FQDN lookup; the document is not about DNS.
BGP appears only as the substrate of LISP+ALT in the ALT testing section; not the subject.
The tool is diagnostic, but the topic tag is generic and the document is specifically about LISP; LISP tag is more specific.
BGP-over-GRE is mentioned only in passing as part of ALT.

RFC6836.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol Alternative Logical Topology (LISP+ALT)
RFC6836.summary: Specifies LISP+ALT, an experimental overlay network of ALT-Routers built with BGP over GRE tunnels that forwards LISP Map-Requests from ITRs/Map-Resolvers to the ETRs holding EID-to-RLOC mappings.

LISP.why: The whole document defines a mapping-lookup overlay for LISP, covering ITR/ETR behaviour changes, Map-Request forwarding and EID-prefix origination.
LISP.quote: describes a simple distributed index system to be used by a Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) or Map-Resolver (MR) to find the Egress Tunnel Router

BGP.why: The document specifies how BGP is used on the ALT: EID-prefix propagation, aggregation, ASNs, SAFI considerations and dampening. This is a substantial BGP profile, not merely a substrate.
BGP.quote: The ALT network is built using GRE tunnels between ALT-Routers.  BGP sessions are configured over those tunnels

rejected.why: GRE is the tunnelling mechanism for the overlay and the document notes other tunnels could be used. It is not itself specified or extended.
This tag covers data-plane network virtualization overlays such as VXLAN, which is a different kind of overlay from the ALT control-plane overlay.
The ALT is a mapping-lookup overlay and not a general routing architecture. The LISP tag is more specific.
CIDR aggregation is only referenced as a concept for EID-prefix aggregation.
The security section only lists BGP security mechanisms briefly and refers to SIDR.
ICMP is mentioned only as one possible response to a forwarding failure.

RFC6837.title: NERD: A Not-so-novel Endpoint ID (EID) to Routing Locator (RLOC) Database
RFC6837.summary: Experimental RFC specifying NERD, a signed database format and HTTP-based distribution and update method for pushing LISP EID-to-RLOC mappings to ITRs, with scaling and security analysis and comparison to DNS and LISP+ALT alternatives.

LISP.why: The document defines a mapping database and distribution mechanism for LISP EID-to-RLOC mappings, which is a LISP mapping system.
LISP.quote: specifies a Not-so-novel EID-to-RLOC Database (NERD) and methods to both receive the database and to receive updates.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport for retrieving the database and changes; the document defines URI conventions but not HTTP itself.
DNS is discussed only as an alternative mapping retrieval model, with a hypothetical EID2RLOC record, not specified.
BGP and LISP+ALT are discussed only as alternative mechanisms.
X.509 certificates and PKCS#7 signatures are used as the security mechanism, not the subject.
PKCS#7/CMS is only the signature container; CMS is mentioned as future direction.
NNTP is mentioned only as an alternative distribution mechanism.

gaps.name: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy's LISP tag is listed under routing as 'LISP', but I used the id as given; if it was not intended to be valid for this document, there would be a gap, since the RFC is about LISP mapping distribution.

RFC6838.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures
RFC6838.summary: BCP 13 defines the criteria and IANA procedures for specifying and registering media types (registration trees, naming, parameters, templates) and structured syntax suffixes, obsoleting RFC 4288.

media types.why: The whole document is about media type registration rules, trees, naming, templates and the structured syntax suffix registry.
media types.quote: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols.

IANA.why: The document sets up and governs IANA registries (media types, provisional registrations, suffix registry) with reviewer and expert procedures, so IANA registry readers would want it.
IANA.quote: defines IANA registries for media types and structured syntax suffixes as well as the procedures for managing these registries.

rejected.why: MIME is the origin and a carrier of media types, but the document is explicitly independent of MIME; media types is the more specific fit.
HTTP is only one protocol that uses media types; the document does not specify HTTP behaviour.
ABNF is used only as notation for name syntax.
XML suffix and XML media type requirements are only referenced to RFC 3023, not the subject.
Registration review by IESG and experts is administrative and part of the IANA registry procedures rather than the IETF standards process itself.

RFC6839.title: Additional Media Type Structured Syntax Suffixes
RFC6839.summary: RFC 6839 defines and registers the +json, +ber, +der, +fastinfoset, +wbxml and +zip structured syntax suffixes for media type names, and supplies a registration form for +xml, updating RFC 3023.

media types.why: The document registers structured syntax suffixes in the media type Structured Syntax Suffix Registry. That is media type registration practice, which is what this tag covers.
media types.quote: This document defines several structured syntax suffixes for use with media type registrations.

rejected.why: +json is only one of the suffixes defined. The document does not specify JSON itself.
The +xml registration restates RFC 3023 and adds fragment identifier considerations. It is not about XML usage.
The +ber and +der suffixes name ASN.1 encoding rules, but the document only registers suffixes for them.
The registrations are the document's main body, not IANA guidance. They are covered by the media types tag.
MIME is the general framework, and the more specific media types tag fits better.

RFC6840.title: Clarifications and Implementation Notes for DNS Security (DNSSEC)
RFC6840.summary: RFC 6840 collects clarifications, errata and implementation notes for the core DNSSEC specifications (RFC 4033/4034/4035/5155), and makes NSEC3 and SHA-2 part of the core DNSSEC document set.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document updates and clarifies DNSSEC validation, nonexistence proofs, the CD/AD/DO bits, trust anchors and algorithm handling.
DNSSEC.quote: This document is a collection of technical clarifications to the DNS Security (DNSSEC) document set.

rejected.why: DNS is the base protocol, and the document is about its security extensions. The more specific DNSSEC tag covers it.
The DO bit comes from EDNS, but the document only clarifies how DNSSEC uses it. It does not specify EDNS.
SHA-2 is added to DNSSEC as a digest and signature algorithm, but this is a short reference to other RFCs. The document is not about the SHA family.
RSASHA256 and RSASHA512 are mentioned only in passing, as algorithm identifiers defined in RFC 5702.

RFC6841.title: A Framework for DNSSEC Policies and DNSSEC Practice Statements
RFC6841.summary: RFC 6841 gives a framework, modelled on the RFC 3647 CP/CPS framework, to help TLD managers and zone operators write DNSSEC Policies (DP) and DNSSEC Practice Statements (DPS). It lists the topics such documents should cover: key management, zone signing, DS registration, audit and legal matters.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is about operating DNSSEC-signed zones. It covers DS record registration, key rollover, NSEC/NSEC3 denial of existence, signature lifetimes and trust anchors, as topics for DP/DPS documents.
DNSSEC.quote: This document presents a framework to assist writers of DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) Policies and DNSSEC Practice Statements

rejected.why: The framework is inspired by the X.509 PKI CP/CPS framework (RFC 3647), but the document says the DNSSEC trust model is fundamentally different. Its subject is DNSSEC operations, not PKI.
DNS is the underlying system. The document is specific to DNSSEC, which is the more specific tag.
Key generation, protection and rollover are covered as items of the DP/DPS checklist. The document is not about key management in general.
Physical, personnel and audit controls are listed as checklist topics for DNSSEC operators. The document is not general operational-security guidance.
RFC 3647 is only the model for the document's structure. No certificates or profiles are specified.

RFC6842.title: Client Identifier Option in DHCP Server Replies
RFC6842.summary: Updates RFC 2131 so DHCPv4 servers must echo the client identifier option, unaltered, in DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK and DHCPNAK replies when the client sent it, and clients must discard replies whose identifier does not match.

DHCP.why: The document changes DHCPv4 server and client behaviour regarding the client identifier option, updating RFC 2131. It is squarely about DHCP.
DHCP.quote: If the 'client identifier' option is present in a message received from a client, the server MUST return the 'client identifier' option, unaltered, in its response message.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is mentioned only as a precedent, where the server always includes the Client Identifier. The document specifies nothing about DHCPv6.
DHCP here configures IPv4 hosts, but the document is about the DHCP option, not IPv4 itself.

RFC6843.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for Delay Metric Reporting
RFC6843.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=16) for reporting mean/min/max network round-trip delay and end-system delay in RTP applications, with SDP signaling and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block, extending RTCP reporting with delay metrics.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of delay metrics

SDP.why: Defines an SDP rtcp-xr attribute extension value ("delay") for signalling use of the block, a small but specified SDP extension.
SDP.quote: providing an additional value of "xr-format" to signal the use of the report block defined in this document.

rejected.why: The block reports delay metrics, but the document is an RTCP XR block definition, not a general performance-measurement methodology; RTCP is the more specific fit.
RTP is the application context; the document is specifically about RTCP, a child tag, so the more specific tag is used.
NTP timestamp format is only used for encoding the delay values; the document is not about clock synchronization.
NTP-format timestamps are used as an encoding only; the NTP protocol is not specified or extended.

RFC6844.title: DNS Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) Resource Record
RFC6844.summary: Defines the DNS CAA resource record, by which domain holders authorize specific CAs to issue certificates, and the rules CAs follow when checking CAA records before issuance.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS RR type (257), its wire and presentation syntax, and the tree-climbing lookup rules including CNAME/DNAME handling.
DNS.quote: The Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS Resource Record allows a DNS domain name holder to specify the Certification Authorities (CAs) authorized to issue certificates

PKI.why: CAA is an authorization control applied by PKIX CAs before issuing certificates, so PKI readers would want it.
PKI.quote: Publication of CAA Resource Records allows a public Certification Authority to implement additional controls to reduce the risk of unintended certificate mis-issue.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is only recommended for authenticating CAA records; the document defines nothing new about signing or validation.
TLSA/DANE is mentioned only as a contrast (verification by relying party versus authorization by issuer); the document does not specify it.
The iodef property reuses IODEF for reporting, but the document does not specify or extend IODEF.
Certificates are the object of issuance control, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
ABNF is only used as notation for the issue property syntax.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like registrations, not the subject of the document.

RFC6845.title: OSPF Hybrid Broadcast and Point-to-Multipoint Interface Type
RFC6845.summary: Defines a new OSPF interface type that uses broadcast-mode neighbor discovery and database synchronization but advertises the network as point-to-multipoint links in router-LSAs, updating OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

OSPF.why: The document specifies a new OSPF interface type and modifies OSPFv2 behaviour, including LSA generation, next-hop calculation and graceful restart.
OSPF.quote: This document updates both OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) and OSPFv3 (RFC 5340).

OSPFv3.why: The document equally updates OSPFv3, with specific rules for intra-area-prefix-LSAs and the LinkLSASuppression parameter.
OSPFv3.quote: Routers MUST add globally scoped IPv6 addresses on the interface to the intra-area-prefix-LSA as described for point-to-multipoint interfaces

rejected.why: The motivating example is radio networks, but the document defines a general OSPF interface type and does not address MANET routing protocols.
Section 7 proposes MIB values, but it is non-normative and brief, and the document is not about MIB modules.
Implied as an ancestor of OSPF, so it is not listed separately.

RFC6846.title: RObust Header Compression (ROHC): A Profile for TCP/IP (ROHC-TCP)
RFC6846.summary: Specifies ROHC-TCP (profile 0x0006), a RObust Header Compression profile for TCP/IP headers including TCP options such as SACK and Timestamps, with context replication, packet formats and feedback; obsoletes RFC 4996.

ROHC.why: The whole document defines the ROHC-TCP profile: packet types, encodings, compressor/decompressor logic and feedback.
ROHC.quote: This document specifies a RObust Header Compression (ROHC) profile for compression of TCP/IP packets.

rejected.why: TCP headers and options are the data being compressed; the document does not specify or extend TCP itself.
IPHC (RFC 2507) is discussed only as an existing scheme to compare against, not specified here.
ECN bits are handled as a compressed control field, but the document is not about ECN.
IPv6 headers are compressed but are not the subject.
GRE headers are one of the compressible header types, not the subject of the document.
The more specific child ROHC applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC6847.title: Fibre Channel over Ethernet (FCoE) over Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL)
RFC6847.summary: Informational RFC describing an architecture for integrating FCoE forwarders with TRILL RBridges in one switch (FCRB), with forwarding examples in data center topologies.

TRILL.why: The document specifies how TRILL RBridges are combined with FCoE forwarders (FCRB) and how TRILL encapsulation and IS-IS routing carry FCoE traffic.
TRILL.quote: This document describes an architecture for the integrated deployment of these two protocols.

fibre channel.why: FCoE forwarding, FCFs, FIP and FSPF are central. The taxonomy only has a Fibre Channel over IP tag, which is the closest storage-over-network fit, so this is the nearest tag.
fibre channel.quote: Fibre Channel over Ethernet (FCoE) and Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) are two emerging standards in the data center environment.

rejected.why: Ethernet is the substrate for both protocols, not the subject of the document.
The data center is the deployment context, but the document is about TRILL and FCoE integration rather than data-centre routing generally. TRILL is the more specific tag.
IS-IS is mentioned only as TRILL's underlying routing protocol.
iFCP carries Fibre Channel over TCP/IP, which is a different technology from FCoE.

gaps.name: Fibre Channel over Ethernet (FCoE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for FCoE or native Fibre Channel. The only Fibre Channel tag covers Fibre Channel over IP, so FCoE readers are poorly served.

RFC6848.title: Specifying Civic Address Extensions in the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO)
RFC6848.summary: RFC 6848 defines a backward-compatible way to extend the Geopriv PIDF-LO civic address format with new XML-namespaced elements, a DHCP extension CAtype (40) for lossless XML/DHCP translation, new elements (PN, MP, STP, HNP), CAtype registry changes, and a clarification updating LoST validation responses to namespace-qualify element names.

geolocation.why: The document is about extending civic location formats (PIDF-LO civic addresses), defining new civic elements and the translation between XML and DHCP forms; no more specific geolocation tech tag fits.
geolocation.quote: A backward-compatible mechanism for adding civic address elements to the Geopriv civic address format is described.

LoST.why: The document normatively updates RFC 5222 LoST validation responses to require namespace-qualified civic element names, a substantial section of the document.
LoST.quote: all elements listed in a <valid>, <invalid>, or <unchecked> element MUST be qualified with a namespace.

DHCP.why: It defines a new DHCP civic address CAtype (40) and closes registration of new numeric CAtypes in the DHCP civic address option format.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a single extension element for the DHCP format that makes knowledge of extensions unnecessary during conversion.

rejected.why: XML namespaces and schema are the mechanism used, but the document is about civic address extension, not XML usage in general.
CAtype registry changes are significant, but they are specific to this registry and are in the IANA Considerations; the subject is civic addresses, not IANA guidance.
PIDF-LO is the container format, but the document extends the civic address element rather than PIDF presence itself.
Emergency calling is motivation and LoST context only; the document does not specify emergency services behaviour.
HELD is mentioned only as one way of acquiring a civic address.

gaps.name: PIDF-LO civic address format (GEOPRIV civic location)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is the civic address format of the PIDF-LO and its XML/DHCP forms; the taxonomy has only the generic geolocation topic and no tag for it.

RFC6849.title: An Extension to the Session Description Protocol (SDP) and Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) for Media Loopback
RFC6849.summary: Defines SDP attributes (loopback, loopback-source, loopback-mirror) and two RTP payload formats (encaprtp, rtploopback) so endpoints can negotiate media loopback sessions for active monitoring of VoIP, text and video services.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with new loopback attributes and specifies offer/answer rules for them.
SDP.quote: The extension defined herein adds new Session Description Protocol (SDP) media types and attributes that enable establishment of media sessions where the media is looped back

RTP payload format.why: It defines two new RTP payload formats (encaprtp and rtploopback), with header fields, payload structure and media type registrations.
RTP payload format.quote: Two different formats are specified here -- an encapsulated RTP payload format and a direct loopback RTP payload format.

rejected.why: RTP is extended only through the payload formats, which the more specific RTP payload format tag covers.
Section 9 only says to support RTCP and RTCP-XR for reporting, with no new RTCP mechanism.
Section 8 only says SRTP may be used and how loopback interacts with it. It does not define anything new for SRTP.
SIP is used only in the examples as the signaling carrier. The document says it assumes no specific signaling protocol.
Section 5.5 only says to use ICE, STUN and TURN as the general solutions, so it is a short pointer to them.
The IANA media type registrations are boilerplate that supports the payload formats.

RFC6850.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Routing Bridges (RBridges)
RFC6850.summary: Defines the RBRIDGE-MIB SMIv2 module for managing RBridges (TRILL Switches), covering nicknames, ports, forwarding databases, VLANs, ESADI, counters, multicast snooping, distribution trees and notifications.

MIB.why: The document is a MIB module definition in SMIv2 for managing RBridges, so it belongs under MIB modules and SMI.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols.

TRILL.why: The MIB models TRILL-specific objects (nicknames, distribution trees, ESADI, TRILL neighbors, MTU probing) for managing TRILL switches, so TRILL readers need it.
TRILL.quote: it defines objects for managing a Routing Bridge (RBridge), also known as a TRILL Switch, based on the IETF TRILL

rejected.why: The MIB relies on the ISIS-MIB (RFC 4444) for managing IS-IS and only defines TRILL-specific objects beyond it; it is not about IS-IS itself.
SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the SNMP-specific content is Security Considerations boilerplate.
Bridge MIBs and VLANs are referenced for reuse, but the document does not specify Ethernet bridging itself.
IP multicast snooping objects are a small part of the module and are not the document's focus.
The data model is written in SMIv2, not YANG.

RFC6851.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - MOVE Extension
RFC6851.summary: Defines the IMAP MOVE and UID MOVE commands, which atomically move messages between mailboxes, and describes how MOVE interacts with other IMAP extensions.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies a new IMAP extension with the MOVE and UID MOVE commands, their semantics, and their interaction with other IMAP extensions.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an IMAP [RFC3501] extension to facilitate moving messages from one mailbox to another.

rejected.why: Sieve is mentioned only briefly in Section 4.5, where it covers how MOVE interacts with IMAP events in Sieve. That is not a substantial part of the document.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax. The document is not about it.
IMAP is the more specific tag and already implies email.
The only IANA content is the boilerplate registration of the MOVE capability.

RFC6852.title: Affirmation of the Modern Paradigm for Standards
RFC6852.summary: An IAB-stream document reproducing the signed 2012 affirmation by IEEE-SA, IAB, IETF, ISOC and W3C leaders of the OpenStand principles (due process, broad consensus, transparency, balance, openness) for global, open, voluntarily adopted standards.

internet governance.why: The document is about how standards are developed and governed, namely the OpenStand principles of open process, cooperation among standards bodies, and availability terms. It is not about a specific protocol or about the IETF process alone, so the parent topic fits best.
internet governance.quote: affirming the importance of a jointly developed set of principles establishing a modern paradigm for global, open standards.

rejected.why: The principles are shared across several standards organizations. The document does not specify or change IETF procedures.
It briefly mentions availability terms (royalty-free to FRAND), but this is one of five principles and not a substantial focus.
The document concerns standards-development philosophy, not the architectural principles of the Internet itself.

gaps.name: OpenStand / open standards paradigm
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for cross-organization standards-development principles. The closest fit is the broad internet governance parent.

RFC6853.title: DHCPv6 Redundancy Deployment Considerations
RFC6853.summary: A BCP describing interim semi-redundant DHCPv6 server deployment models (split prefixes, multiple unique prefixes, identical prefixes) using existing protocol features, since no standard DHCPv6 failover protocol exists.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document is about deploying redundant DHCPv6 servers, using preference options, pools, and lifetimes, and discussing leasequery and failover limitations.
DHCPv6.quote: This document provides information for those wishing to use DHCPv6 to support their deployment of IPv6. In particular, it discusses the provision of semi-redundant DHCPv6 services.

rejected.why: Dynamic DNS updates are discussed only as a challenge when servers fail; the document does not specify or extend them.
IPv6 is the context for addressing and prefixes, but the document is about DHCPv6 redundancy, not IPv6 itself.
DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag; DHCPv4 is mentioned only to say it is unaffected.
Prefix and pool splitting are examples of server configuration, not a treatment of address architecture.

RFC6854.title: Update to Internet Message Format to Allow Group Syntax in the "From:" and "Sender:" Header Fields
RFC6854.summary: RFC 6854 updates the Internet Message Format (RFC 5322) to permit group address syntax in the From, Sender, Resent-From and Resent-Sender header fields, with limited-use guidance.

message format.why: The document changes the header field syntax and semantics of the Internet message format for originator and resent fields.
message format.quote: This document updates RFC 5322 to relax that restriction, allowing group syntax in those latter fields

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to express the syntax changes; the document is not about ABNF.
ADSP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an example of validation that groups would not satisfy.
Internationalized email is cited as motivation only; the document does not specify EAI.
Only mentioned in passing in the Security Considerations about deliverability.

RFC6855.title: IMAP Support for UTF-8
RFC6855.summary: RFC 6855 extends IMAP with the UTF8=ACCEPT and UTF8=ONLY capabilities so that UTF-8 can be used in quoted-strings, mailbox names and message headers, replacing the experimental RFC 5738.

IMAP.why: The document defines new IMAP capabilities (UTF8=ACCEPT, UTF8=ONLY), the ENABLE usage, the APPEND UTF8 data extension and related server and client behaviour. It is an IMAP extension.
IMAP.quote: This specification extends the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) to support UTF-8 encoded international characters in user names, mail addresses, and message headers.

EAI.why: It is the IMAP component of the EAI protocol suite, produced by the eai working group. It also covers handling of legacy clients and downgrading for internationalized mail.
EAI.quote: This specification forms part of the Email Address Internationalization protocols described in the Email Address Internationalization Framework document [RFC6530].

rejected.why: UTF-8 is the encoding that IMAP is extended to carry. The document does not specify or profile the encoding itself.
SMTPUTF8 is mentioned only when discussing legacy clients. The document does not specify SMTP behaviour.
Internationalized headers are defined in RFC 6532. This document only covers how IMAP carries them.
POP is mentioned only in passing in the legacy-client discussion. The document specifies nothing for POP3.
AUTHENTICATE is cited as the way to pass UTF-8 credentials. SASL is not specified or extended here.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax. The document is not about it.

RFC6856.title: Post Office Protocol Version 3 (POP3) Support for UTF-8
RFC6856.summary: RFC 6856 extends POP3 with UTF8 and LANG capabilities, enabling UTF-8 in usernames, passwords, message headers and bodies, and localized protocol response text, as part of Email Address Internationalization.

POP3.why: The document specifies POP3 extensions: the UTF8 and LANG capabilities, the UTF8 command and a new response code.
POP3.quote: This specification extends POP3 using the POP3 extension mechanism [RFC2449] to permit un-encoded UTF-8 [RFC3629] in headers and bodies

EAI.why: It is the POP3 component of the EAI work, produced by the eai WG, supporting internationalized email headers and addresses.
EAI.quote: This document forms part of the Email Address Internationalization protocols described in the Email Address Internationalization Framework document [RFC6530].

language tags.why: A substantial part of the document is the LANG capability, which negotiates response language using language tags and basic language range matching.
language tags.quote: The "LANG" command requests that human-readable text included in all subsequent +OK and -ERR responses be localized to a language matching the language range argument

rejected.why: UTF-8 is the encoding the document relies on and applies to POP3; the document is not about the encoding itself.
SASLprep is applied to usernames and passwords, and AUTH is only referenced to POP3 SASL; the document does not specify SASL.
STLS is mentioned only as a command that must not follow UTF8 and as a security mitigation.
Internationalized headers are defined in RFC 6532; this document only carries them over POP3.
8-bit content-transfer-encoding is mentioned in passing; the document does not define MIME behavior.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific tags chosen (EAI and language tags).

RFC6857.title: Post-Delivery Message Downgrading for Internationalized Email Messages
RFC6857.summary: Specifies how POP or IMAP servers downgrade internationalized (SMTPUTF8) email messages to all-ASCII traditional format, using encoded-words, A-labels and new Downgraded-* header fields, so legacy clients can receive them.

EAI.why: The document defines downgrading of internationalized email messages and headers, a core part of the Email Address Internationalization work.
EAI.quote: this document describes a mechanism for converting internationalized messages into the traditional message format.

message format.why: Much of the body specifies per-header-field rewriting rules for Internet message format fields and registers new Downgraded-* header fields.
message format.quote: This section defines the method for converting each header field that may contain non-ASCII strings into ASCII.

rejected.why: IMAP servers are the deployment context, but the document specifies message conversion, not IMAP protocol behaviour.
POP3 is the deployment context only; no POP3 protocol is specified.
Encoded-words and RFC 2231 encodings are used as tools; MIME itself is not the subject, and MIME body part header downgrading is a small section.
SMTPUTF8 is the source of the problem but SMTP transport is not specified here.
A-label conversion of domains is a minor step relying on IDNA, not about IDNA.
UTF-8 is the encoding in question but the document is not about the encoding itself.

RFC6858.title: Simplified POP and IMAP Downgrading for Internationalized Email
RFC6858.summary: Specifies a simple method for IMAP and POP servers to present internationalized email messages to conventional clients as downgraded "surrogate" messages, updating RFC 3501 on size exactness and adding the IMAP DOWNGRADED response code.

EAI.why: The document is part of the email address internationalization work and defines how internationalized messages are downgraded for legacy clients.
EAI.quote: This document specifies a method for IMAP and POP servers to serve internationalized messages to conventional clients.

IMAP.why: It updates RFC 3501 and defines the DOWNGRADED response code and size-reporting relaxation for IMAP servers.
IMAP.quote: This specification modifies the base IMAP specification [RFC3501] by relaxing a requirement that sizes be exact and adding a reporting requirement

POP3.why: It specifies POP3-specific behaviour for TOP and LIST when serving surrogate messages, though POP gets a shorter section than IMAP.
POP3.quote: The number of lines specified in the TOP command [RFC1939] refers to the surrogate message.

rejected.why: Header handling (address replacement, excising fields) is part of downgrading, but the document is not about defining the Internet message format.
MIME parameters and RFC 2047 encoding are used or excised in the surrogate message, but MIME itself is not the subject.
UTF-8 support is the alternative the document points to (RFC 6855/6856), not what it specifies.
The .invalid TLD is only used in example replacement addresses, not discussed in its own right.

RFC6859.title: Update to RFC 3777 to Clarify Nominating Committee Eligibility of IETF Leadership
RFC6859.summary: RFC 6859 updates RFC 3777 rule 15 so that members of the ISOC Board, IAB, IESG and IAOC, including ex officio members, may not volunteer for the NomCom, while liaisons are not excluded.

NomCom.why: The whole document revises NomCom volunteer eligibility rules, replacing rule 15 of RFC 3777.
NomCom.quote: may not volunteer to serve as voting members of the nominating committee.

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child tag and fits; the parent is implied.
The IAOC is mentioned only as a body whose members are excluded; IANA registries are not addressed.

RFC6860.title: Hiding Transit-Only Networks in OSPF
RFC6860.summary: RFC 6860 specifies a mechanism for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 routers to hide transit-only networks by omitting stub links, using a special 255.255.255.255 mask in network-LSAs, and omitting prefixes, so the prefixes are not installed in routing tables, speeding convergence and reducing exposure to remote attacks.

OSPF.why: The document modifies OSPFv2 router-LSA and network-LSA handling to hide transit-only networks, and updates RFC 2328.
OSPF.quote: To hide a transit-only network in [OSPFv3], the IPv6 address prefixes are omitted from the router-LSA.
OSPF.section: 3. Hiding IPv6 Transit-Only Networks in OSPFv3

OSPFv3.why: A dedicated section specifies how to hide transit-only networks in OSPFv3, including AF-enabled instances, and updates RFC 5340.
OSPFv3.quote: router-LSAs and network-LSAs no longer contain network addresses but simply express topology information.
OSPFv3.section: 3. Hiding IPv6 Transit-Only Networks in OSPFv3

rejected.why: The motivation includes reducing vulnerability to remote attacks, but the document is an OSPF protocol extension rather than general operational security practice.
The mechanism reduces attack exposure, but it does not secure the routing protocol itself, as with RPKI or BGPsec.
RFC 5837 (extended ICMP for interface identification) is only mentioned in operational considerations.
IPv6 prefixes are handled only as OSPFv3 content, not as a subject in their own right.

RFC6861.title: The "create-form" and "edit-form" Link Relations
RFC6861.summary: Defines and registers the "create-form" and "edit-form" link relation types under RFC 5988 to link a resource to a form for creating a new member or editing it.

web linking.why: The document defines two new typed link relations and registers them in the link relation registry, which is the core subject of web linking.
web linking.quote: This specification defines link relation types that may be used to express the relationships between a resource and an input form for constructing data submissions.

rejected.why: HTTP methods, status codes and the Link header appear only as the substrate for the relations; the document does not extend HTTP.
HTML anchors are used only as examples of how the relations can be expressed.
The IANA registration is boilerplate that records the relations; the main body is about the relations, not registry policy.
Submission and context URIs are mentioned only in usage rules; the document does not specify anything about URIs.

RFC6862.title: Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) Overview, Threats, and Requirements
RFC6862.summary: RFC 6862 is the KARP overview that defines scope, in-scope threats and Work Phase 1 requirements for improving per-packet cryptographic authentication and keying of routing protocols' on-the-wire transport security.

routing security.why: The whole document is about securing routing protocol packets on the wire: threats, goals, and requirements for authentication and integrity across routing protocols.
routing security.quote: This effort is referred to as Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols, or "KARP".

key management.why: Keying, KMP, PSKs, rekeying and traffic key requirements are a substantial part of the document, including Work Phase 2 on key management.
key management.quote: Developing a framework for using automatic key management in order to ease deployment, lower cost of operation, and allow for rapid responses to security breaches.

rejected.why: BGP is used as an example (TCP MD5, TCP-AO), but the document is generic across routing protocols.
Mentioned as an example of an existing authentication mechanism; not specified or extended here.
TCP MD5 and TCP-AO are cited as examples and operator survey context, not the subject.
Only mentioned in the operator survey; not the subject.
Covered by the more specific routing security tag.
Operator deployability is discussed, but the focus is protocol transport security requirements, not operational practice.

RFC6863.title: Analysis of OSPF Security According to the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) Design Guide
RFC6863.summary: Analyzes OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 cryptographic authentication against the KARP design guidelines (RFC 6518), identifying gaps in replay protection, neighbor identification, key handling and packet prioritization, and recommending solution work.

OSPF.why: The document is a security analysis of OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 authentication mechanisms, so OSPF is the protocol analysed.
OSPF.quote: This document analyzes the current state of OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 according to the requirements of [RFC6518].

routing security.why: It is a KARP routing-security gap analysis covering replay protection, key handling, and neighbor authentication for a routing protocol.
routing security.quote: some gaps remain between the current state and the requirements for manually keyed routing security expressed in [RFC6862]

rejected.why: OSPFv3 relies on IPsec AH/ESP and its weaknesses are noted, but the document does not specify or extend IPsec.
OSPFv3 is covered, but the analysis treats OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 together, so the parent OSPF tag fits better.
Keyed-MD5 and HMAC-SHA are mentioned as the authentication algorithms, but only as background.
Manual keying and key rollover are discussed, but the document is an OSPF security gap analysis, not a key management specification.

RFC6864.title: Updated Specification of the IPv4 ID Field
RFC6864.summary: RFC 6864 updates the IPv4 Identification field specification (updating RFCs 791, 1122, 2003) so ID uniqueness is required only for non-atomic (fragmentable or fragmented) datagrams, and discusses the impact on middleboxes, header compression, and reordering.

IPv4.why: The whole document redefines the IPv4 ID field's semantics and fragmentation/reassembly requirements, which is core IPv4 specification.
IPv4.quote: This document updates the specification of the IPv4 ID field in RFCs 791, 1122, and 2003 to more closely reflect current practice

rejected.why: Section 5.4 discusses the impact on ROHC and CRTP, but it is a minor part, not the document's subject.
Rewriting middleboxes and NATs are discussed as datagram sources in 5.3.1, but the document does not specify NAT behaviour.
IPv6 fragmentation is only used as a comparison for the IPv4 ID field.
RFC 2003 is updated only in a one-line change on how the outer ID is set. This is too minor to tag.
ROHC is cited only as an example of a compression scheme that tolerates non-varying IDs.

RFC6865.title: Simple Reed-Solomon Forward Error Correction (FEC) Scheme for FECFRAME
RFC6865.summary: Specifies a fully-specified Reed-Solomon FEC scheme over GF(2^m) (FEC Encoding ID 8) for FECFRAME, defining ADU block and source block creation, FFCI/FSSI, and source/repair FEC Payload ID formats.

FECFRAME.why: The document defines a FEC scheme for the FECFRAME framework, including ADU block creation, FFCI, and payload ID formats. FECFRAME is the most specific tag.
FECFRAME.quote: a fully-specified simple Forward Error Correction (FEC) scheme for Reed-Solomon codes over the finite field

rejected.why: LDPC codes are mentioned only as an alternative and for comparison; the document does not specify them.
Raptor appears only in the introduction as a related scheme, and the document does not specify it.
RTP packets are example ADUs, but the document is not about RTP.
SDP carries the FFCI via the fec-repair-flow attribute from RFC 6364. This is a substrate use, and the document defines nothing new for SDP.
ALC and NORM appear only as context for the earlier RFC 5052/5510 object-delivery schemes.
FECFRAME is a child of FEC and is more specific, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: Reed-Solomon codes
gaps.why: The document specifies Reed-Solomon erasure codes over GF(2^m), which have no dedicated tag. FEC and FECFRAME cover them only generally.

RFC6866.title: Problem Statement for Renumbering IPv6 Hosts with Static Addresses in Enterprise Networks
RFC6866.summary: Problem statement analysing why static IPv6 addresses (servers, printers, VMs, network elements, ACLs, licensing) complicate enterprise network renumbering, and what mitigations exist.

renumbering.why: The whole document is about problems of renumbering IPv6 hosts with static addresses and the RFC 4192 procedure, so the renumbering topic fits directly.
renumbering.quote: This document analyses the problems of updating the IPv6 addresses of hosts in enterprise networks that, for operational reasons, require static addresses.

rejected.why: Stateful DHCPv6 is mentioned as a mitigation for managing static addresses, but the document does not specify or extend it.
IPv6 is the setting, but the document is about renumbering, which is a more specific child of addressing.
DNS TTL and dynamic update are mentioned as context; the DNS aspects of renumbering are deferred to RFC 6879.
Mentioned only as an alternative for naming printers.
Mentioned only as an alternative discovery mechanism.
Network elements and management systems are mentioned, but the document is not about network management practice.

RFC6867.title: An Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Extension to Support EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP)
RFC6867.summary: Defines an IKEv2 extension (ERX_SUPPORTED notify, EAP-Initiate/Re-auth carried in IKE_AUTH) that lets an IKE SA be authenticated using the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP).

IKE.why: The document updates IKEv2 by adding a new Notify type and changing the IKE_AUTH exchange flow to carry ERP messages.
IKE.quote: This extension allows an IKE Security Association (SA) to be created and authenticated using the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Re-authentication Protocol extension

HOKEY.why: ERP is the core mechanism being integrated; the HOKEY tag covers ERP/ERX and its use with rMSK keys, and the document is about applying it to IKEv2.
HOKEY.quote: The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP), as described in [RFC6696], allows an EAP peer to authenticate to multiple authenticators while performing the full EAP method only once.

rejected.why: EAP is used and EAP codes are clarified, but the document is about ERP (under HOKEY), which is the more specific tag.
Backend AAA server is relied upon for rMSK, but the document does not specify AAA behaviour.
IKE is the more specific tag; IPsec SAs are only the context.
Only mentioned as an example for conveying CLASS attribute.
Remote access VPN is a usage scenario, not provider-provisioned VPNs.

RFC6868.title: Parameter Value Encoding in iCalendar and vCard
RFC6868.summary: RFC 6868 defines a ^-escaping mechanism so iCalendar and vCard parameter values can contain double-quotes, line breaks and the caret, and it updates RFC 5545, 6321, 6350 and 6351.

iCalendar.why: The document updates the iCalendar format (RFC 5545) with a new parameter value escaping scheme and gives an iCalendar example. Readers of iCalendar need it.
iCalendar.quote: This specification defines the ^ character (U+005E -- Circumflex Accent) as an escape character in parameter values

vCard.why: The document equally updates vCard (RFC 6350) parameter syntax and gives a vCard example with line breaks in an X-ADDRESS parameter.
vCard.quote: The vCard [RFC6350] specification defines a standard way to describe contact data.

rejected.why: xCal and xCard conversion is mentioned only as a requirement to decode escapes. The document is not about XML formats.
ASCII is mentioned only as a criterion for choosing the escape character. The document is not about the character set.
The document covers escaping of special characters, not internationalization of text.

RFC6869.title: vCard KIND:device
RFC6869.summary: Defines the value "device" for the vCard KIND property so vCards can represent computing devices such as routers, servers, printers and sensors, for inventory and asset tracking.

vCard.why: The whole document extends the vCard format by registering a new KIND value, so vCard readers would expect it.
vCard.quote: defines a value of "device" for the KIND property to represent computing devices such as appliances, computers, or network elements

rejected.why: The example uses xCard XML representation, but only as an illustration; the document is not about XML.
LDAP's device object class is cited only as a functional equivalence, not specified or extended here.
Sensors and network devices are mentioned as examples of devices, but the document is not about IoT architecture or constrained devices.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level apparatus for the new value; the document's subject is vCard.
Not discussed; the document only defines a KIND value, not address book access.

RFC6870.title: Pseudowire Preferential Forwarding Status Bit
RFC6870.summary: RFC 6870 defines two new PW Status TLV bits (Preferential Forwarding and Request Switchover) for signaling active/standby state of redundant pseudowires between PE/T-PE nodes, with independent and master/slave procedures, and updates RFC 4447.

pseudowire.why: The document extends the pseudowire control plane (PW Status TLV) to signal active/standby state of redundant PWs, for SS-PW and MS-PW, and updates RFC 4447.
pseudowire.quote: a new status bit is defined. This bit indicates a Preferential Forwarding status with a value of active or standby for each PW in a redundant set.

rejected.why: T-LDP is the signaling substrate carrying the PW Status TLV; the document is about the PW status bits, not LDP itself.
H-VPLS spoke redundancy appears only as one application example in the appendix and for MAC flushing; not the subject.
VPWS/VPLS services are the context for PW redundancy, but the document is specifically about PW signaling, which has a more specific tag.
PSN tunnels and LDP are background; no MPLS specification content is defined.
VCCV and OAM packets are mentioned as allowed on standby PWs and status mapping defers to RFC 6310; not a main subject.

gaps.name: Pseudowire redundancy / PW status signaling (PWE3)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a 'pseudowire' tag under MPLS, but I used an id not confirmed in the taxonomy; the closest valid tag is 'pseudowire' under MPLS, which does exist, so no true gap besides LDP-based PW signaling.

RFC6871.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Media Capabilities Negotiation
RFC6871.summary: RFC 6871 extends SDP capability negotiation (RFC 5939) with media capabilities (rmcap, omcap, mfcap, mscap), latent configurations (lcfg), session capabilities (sescap), and updated offer/answer procedures.

SDP.why: The document defines new SDP attributes and extends the SDP offer/answer capability negotiation framework; it is squarely about SDP.
SDP.quote: we extend the framework by defining media capabilities that can be used to indicate and negotiate media types and their associated format parameters.

rejected.why: RTP payload type numbers and rtpmap are mapped by the capabilities, but RTP itself is not specified or extended.
SDP offer/answer is used in SIP, but the document does not address SIP signalling.
Codecs like AMR and H.264 appear only as examples of capability parameters; no payload format is defined.
IANA section registers attributes and updates RFC 5939 registry, but that is boilerplate, not the main subject.
SRTP/SAVP and SDES crypto appear only in examples of alternative transports.

RFC6872.title: The Common Log Format (CLF) for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP): Framework and Information Model
RFC6872.summary: RFC 6872 gives the framework, requirements, analysis of alternatives and a mandatory-field information model for a Common Log Format for SIP entities (UAs, proxies, registrars, B2BUAs), leaving the concrete representation to other documents.

SIP.why: The document defines the minimum SIP message fields (From, To, Call-ID, CSeq, transaction IDs) that must be logged by SIP entities, covering forking, ACK/CANCEL handling and dialogs. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document describes a framework, including requirements and analysis of existing approaches, and specifies an information model for development of a SIP common log file format

rejected.why: Section 5.3 discusses syslog only as an alternative that is rejected as a log storage format. The document does not specify or extend syslog.
Section 5.4 mentions IPFIX only to explain why it is not suitable as a log format. The document is not about flow export.
Wireshark and tcpdump appear only in a comparison of alternatives. The document does not define a capture format.
The Apache Common Log Format is cited as inspiration and for comparison only. The document is not about HTTP.
TLS is mentioned only in security considerations and as a limitation of packet capture, so it is boilerplate or background.
The UTF-8 representation is defined in RFC 6873, not here. This document only notes that SIP bodies may not be valid UTF-8.

gaps.name: Common Log Format / SIP logging
gaps.why: The document is about a log format and information model for logging protocol messages. The taxonomy has no tag for application-level event logging apart from syslog, which this document explicitly does not use.

RFC6873.title: Format for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Common Log Format (CLF)
RFC6873.summary: Defines an indexed, tab-delimited text encoding for SIP Common Log Format records, with index pointers, mandatory and optional fields, escaping rules, and IANA registries for CLF version and transport flag.

SIP.why: The document specifies a log format for SIP messages and servers, covering SIP header fields, transactions and dialogs. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This memo describes an indexed text file format for logging SIP messages received and sent by SIP clients, servers, and proxies

rejected.why: Only the private-use identifier format is loosely modeled on RFC 5424. The document does not specify syslog.
SDP bodies appear only as logging examples.
Base64 is used as an encoding mechanism for unprintable values, not as the subject.
The Apache/HTTP CLF is cited only as motivation.
The registries created are boilerplate IANA considerations for this format.
UTF-8 is used as the character encoding substrate only.

gaps.name: SIP Common Log Format (SIP CLF) / protocol logging
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for logging formats of SIP or other protocols. SIP is the closest fit.

RFC6874.title: Representing IPv6 Zone Identifiers in Address Literals and Uniform Resource Identifiers
RFC6874.summary: RFC 6874 extends URI syntax (updating RFC 3986) so an IPv6 zone identifier can be written inside a literal IPv6 address in a URI, using a percent-encoded "%25" separator, and discusses browser handling.

URI.why: The document updates RFC 3986 URI generic syntax with new ABNF rules (IPv6addrz, ZoneID) for IP-literal. This is its core subject.
URI.quote: adding syntax to allow a zone identifier to be included in a literal IPv6 address within a URI.

IPv6.why: It concerns the textual representation of IPv6 scoped addresses and zone identifiers, and how link-local literals are used. Readers of IPv6 addressing would want it.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 Scoped Address Architecture specification [RFC4007] extended the text representation of limited-scope IPv6 addresses such that a zone identifier may be concatenated

rejected.why: Browsers and HTTP requests are mentioned, including a rule that intermediaries remove the ZoneID. HTTP is only the context, and the document does not specify or extend it.
ABNF is only the notation used to state the new URI rules. The document is not about it.
The IPv6 tag already covers the IPv6 address text representation. This document does not address IP address architecture or allocation more broadly.
Section 3 covers browser behaviour, but it is non-normative and secondary. The URI tag fits better than the general web topic.

RFC6875.title: The P2P Network Experiment Council's Activities and Experiments with Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) in Japan
RFC6875.summary: An IRTF report on 2007-2008 Japanese P2P Network Experiment Council trials of ALTO-like hint servers for P2P peer selection, with feedback to the ALTO working group.

ALTO.why: The document reports experiments with an ALTO-like hint server and gives feedback to the ALTO WG (hierarchical servers, measurement mechanisms).
ALTO.quote: this document provides some suggestions that might be useful for the ALTO architecture and especially for application-independent ALTO-like server operation.

P2P.why: The experiments concern P2P applications' traffic and peer selection, and the council's P2P activities in Japan are a substantial part of the document.
P2P.quote: in an attempt to harmonize peer-to-peer (P2P) technology with network infrastructure.

rejected.why: The hint server request/response example uses HTTP only as the carrier; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
BGP routing data is used as an input to compute AS path length, but the document is not about BGP.
Dummy-node traffic measurement is the experimental method, not the document's subject, though measurement mechanisms are briefly recommended.

RFC6876.title: A Posture Transport Protocol over TLS (PT-TLS)
RFC6876.summary: RFC 6876 specifies PT-TLS, a Posture Transport protocol that carries NEA (PB-TNC) posture assessment batches over a TLS-protected TCP connection, with version negotiation, SASL client authentication, error messages, and IANA registries.

NEA.why: The document defines a Network Endpoint Assessment posture transport binding, carrying PB-TNC/PA-TNC messages between NEA Client and Server.
NEA.quote: This document specifies PT-TLS, a TLS-based Posture Transport (PT) protocol.  The PT-TLS protocol carries the Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) message exchange

SASL.why: A substantial section defines SASL client authentication over PT-TLS: mechanism negotiation TLVs, PLAIN/EXTERNAL requirements, channel bindings, service name.
SASL.quote: The general model used for performing an authentication of the client using PT-TLS messages is to integrate the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL)

transport mapping.why: The document defines a binding of NEA posture transport onto TLS/TCP, including layering, port usage and TLS requirements.
transport mapping.quote: this protocol runs directly on top of TLS as an application.  This means PT-TLS is encapsulated within the TLS Record Layer protocol

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate; the RFC makes no change to TLS and only states requirements on its use (cipher suite, tls-unique channel bindings).
TCP is only the underlying transport; a port is assigned but TCP itself is not specified or extended.
Certificates are used for authentication per RFC 5280/6125 but the document does not profile X.509.
The document is about a specific protocol, not general security guidance; security considerations are boilerplate-like.
It creates registries but the main body is a protocol spec; IANA section is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) / posture transport
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an NEA tag in the security hierarchy, but no dedicated PT-TLS/TNC tag exists; I assumed the NEA tag covers it.

RFC6877.title: 464XLAT: Combination of Stateful and Stateless Translation
RFC6877.summary: Informational architecture (464XLAT) for giving IPv4 access over IPv6-only networks by combining stateless translation (CLAT) at the customer edge with stateful NAT64 translation (PLAT) in the provider core.

464XLAT.why: The document defines the 464XLAT architecture itself: CLAT/PLAT roles, topologies, applicability and deployment considerations.
464XLAT.quote: providing limited IPv4 connectivity across an IPv6-only network by combining existing and well-known stateful protocol translation (as described in RFC 6146) in the core and stateless protocol translation

rejected.why: Stateful NAT64 (RFC 6146) is the PLAT building block, used but not specified or extended here; 464XLAT is the more specific tag.
Stateless translation (RFC 6145) is used at the CLAT, but the document does not define or extend it.
Mentioned only to say 464XLAT does not require it; it is optional and not the subject.
Parent of 464XLAT, so implied and not listed separately.
The 3GPP network is one deployment scenario, but the document is not about cellular interworking itself.
DHCPv6-PD is only mentioned as a way to obtain the translation prefix.

RFC6878.title: IANA Registry for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) "Priority" Header Field
RFC6878.summary: Creates an IANA sub-registry for values of the SIP Priority header field (non-urgent, normal, urgent, emergency) with IETF Review policy, updating RFC 3261.

SIP.why: The document registers values for a SIP header field and updates RFC 3261, so SIP readers would look for it. The SIP tag fits it directly.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new IANA registry to keep track of the values defined for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) "Priority" header field.

IANA.why: The whole document is about creating a registry and setting its registration policy (IETF Review). Readers interested in IANA registries would want it.
IANA.quote: This document adds a new sub-registry, "Priority Header Field Values", to the "Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Parameters" registry page.

rejected.why: 'emergency' is only one of the Priority values. The document does not address emergency calling.
It cites IETF Review as the registration policy. It does not define or discuss process.

RFC6879.title: IPv6 Enterprise Network Renumbering Scenarios, Considerations, and Methods
RFC6879.summary: Informational analysis of events that trigger IPv6 enterprise network renumbering and of current methods to use during network design, preparation, and the renumbering operation.

renumbering.why: The whole document is about site renumbering: scenarios, considerations and methods for IPv6 enterprise networks.
renumbering.quote: This document analyzes events that cause renumbering and describes the current renumbering methods.

IPv6.why: It covers IPv6 address configuration, prefix delegation, ULAs and lifetimes in enterprise networks, so IPv6 readers would want it. The renumbering tag covers the main subject.
IPv6.quote: This document is an analysis of IPv6 site renumbering for enterprise networks.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 prefix delegation, the FQDN option and RECONFIGURE are used as renumbering tools. The document specifies nothing new about DHCPv6.
DNS record updates and TTL reduction are part of the renumbering procedure. The document is not about DNS itself.
SLAAC is discussed only as one of the address configuration models. It is a means of renumbering, not the subject.
Adding an uplink for multihoming is mentioned briefly as a renumbering trigger. It is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: site renumbering
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a 'renumbering' topic under addressing, but the document is primarily about it. If that id is not valid in this taxonomy, the document needs the nearest parent, addressing.

RFC6880.title: An Information Model for Kerberos Version 5
RFC6880.summary: Defines an abstract information model (principals, keysets, keys, policies) for administering a Kerberos 5 KDC, independent of any schema language.

Kerberos.why: The whole document models the data and administrative services of a Kerberos 5 KDC (principals, keys, ticket policies), so Kerberos readers would want it.
Kerberos.quote: This document describes the services required to administer a KDC and the underlying information model assumed by a kadmin-type service.

rejected.why: LDAP is only one possible schema mapping and implementation scenario; the document explicitly says no LDAP schema is intended.
Mentioned only as one implementation scenario in Section 5.4; the document does not specify or extend NETCONF.
No YANG model is defined; the model is deliberately schema-agnostic.
RFC 3339 is only used as the attribute syntax for timestamps.
RFC 1964 is cited only for the principal name string representation.
The document concerns KDC administration data, but the Kerberos tag fits better; NETCONF is only a hypothetical binding.

RFC6881.title: Best Current Practice for Communications Services in Support of Emergency Calling
RFC6881.summary: BCP specifying requirements for end devices, access networks, intermediaries and service providers to place SIP-based emergency calls, covering identification, location acquisition and conveyance, LoST routing to PSAPs, signalling, callbacks, media and testing.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about emergency calling requirements (ED-, AN-, SP-, INT-) for IP networks and PSAPs.
emergency services.quote: This memo describes best current practice on how devices, networks, and services using IETF protocols should use such standards to make emergency calls.

LoST.why: LoST mapping, discovery via DHCP, dial string retrieval and validation are substantial requirements in the document.
LoST.quote: The call is routed (Section 8) based on location using the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol [RFC5222], which maps a location to a set of PSAP URIs.
LoST.section: 3. Overview of How Emergency Calls Are Placed

SIP.why: Detailed SIP UA and proxy requirements for emergency calls, including service URN in Request-URI, Route headers, Contact/GRUU and callbacks.
SIP.quote: The initial SIP signaling method is an INVITE request:
SIP.section: 9.2. SIP Signaling Requirements for User Agents

HELD.why: Devices and access networks must support HELD for location configuration, with specific emergency usage rules.
HELD.quote: When HELD is the LCP, the request MUST specify a value of "emergencyRouting" for the "responseTime" parameter

geolocation.why: Large part of the document covers location determination, configuration, conveyance, updates, validation and defaults (PIDF-LO).
geolocation.quote: Location sent between SIP entities MUST be conveyed using the extension described in [RFC6442].

rejected.why: DHCP location and LoST/LIS discovery options are required, but DHCP is a mechanism used for location configuration, not the subject.
TLS is mandated to protect signalling, but only as a security mechanism.
Media must use RTP, but this is a substrate requirement, not a spec of RTP.
G.711 support is required for PSAP media, a minor point.
PIDF-LO is used as the location format, but the document does not specify it.
The service URN for emergency is used and a test service label registered, but the URN scheme is defined elsewhere (RFC 5031).

RFC6882.title: Support for Resource Reservation Protocol Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) in Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks (L3VPNs)
RFC6882.summary: Experimental RFC defining new RSVP-TE SESSION, SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC object types carrying VPN-IPv4/IPv6 addresses (with RD) so PEs can identify the VPN for customer RSVP-TE LSPs across BGP/MPLS IP VPNs without label-based VRF identification.

RSVP-TE.why: The document defines new RSVP-TE objects and message-handling procedures at ingress and egress PEs, so it extends RSVP-TE.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document describes how to support RSVP-TE between customer sites when a single PE supports multiple VPNs and labels are not used to identify VPNs between PEs.

L3VPN.why: The whole mechanism supports customer RSVP-TE LSPs over BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, using VRFs, route distinguishers and VPN-IPv4/IPv6 addresses.
L3VPN.quote: Service Providers would like to use BGP/MPLS IP VPNs [RFC4364] to support connections between Customer Edge (CE) sites.

rejected.why: BGP is the VPN route distribution substrate; the document defines nothing new in BGP.
MPLS forwarding is the backbone context; the document's extensions are to RSVP signalling, not MPLS itself.
The more specific RSVP-TE tag fits; the generic RSVP is only the base protocol that is extended.
The Router Alert option is used in message handling but is not what the document is about.

RFC6883.title: IPv6 Guidance for Internet Content Providers and Application Service Providers
RFC6883.summary: Informational guidance for content and application service providers on adding IPv6 (dual-stack) service: strategy, training, connectivity, addressing, routing, DNS, load balancers, proxies, servers, transition technologies, CDNs, operations and security.

IPv6.why: The whole document is IPv6 deployment guidance for ICPs/ASPs, covering addressing, routing, DNS, servers and operations.
IPv6.quote: guidance and suggestions for Internet Content Providers and Application Service Providers who wish to offer their service to both IPv6 and IPv4 customers

IPv6 transition.why: A substantial section and the dual-stack strategy address coexistence with NAT64, 6to4, tunnels, Happy Eyeballs and DNS whitelisting.
IPv6 transition.quote: Coping with Transition Technologies

rejected.why: AAAA records and DNS practices are covered in one subsection, but the document is not mainly about DNS.
CDN dual-stack support is one section, not the main subject.
HTTP proxies and servers are the deployment context, not what the document specifies.
Mentioned only as a client-side mitigation; the document does not discuss the mechanism itself.
PI/PA prefix choices are one subsection; the IPv6 tag covers this better.
The security section is boilerplate-like and brief, and it is mostly firewall and IPv6 guidance.

RFC6884.title: RTP Payload Format for the Enhanced Variable Rate Narrowband-Wideband Codec (EVRC-NW)
RFC6884.summary: Specifies RTP payload formats (interleaved/bundled, header-free, compact bundled), three audio media type registrations, SDP/offer-answer usage, and a storage file format for the EVRC-NW speech codec.

RTP payload format.why: The document's core purpose is defining RTP payload formats for the EVRC-NW codec, including the capability flag in the interleaved/bundled header and mode requests.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies the payload formats for packetization of EVRC-NW encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

media types.why: Three media type registrations (audio/EVRCNW, EVRCNW0, EVRCNW1) with parameters and a file format with magic number are a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: this section registers new 'audio' media subtypes for EVRC-NW.

SDP.why: Substantial sections cover SDP parameter mapping, offer/answer considerations, declarative SDP, and examples.
SDP.quote: The media subtype ("EVRCNW", "EVRCNW0", or "EVRCNW1") goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name.
SDP.section: 12. Mapping EVRC-NW Media Type Parameters into SDP

rejected.why: The codec itself is defined by 3GPP2 C.S0014-D; this document only defines its RTP packetization and storage. RTP payload format is the more specific fit.
RTP is the transport the payload format runs over; the more specific child RTP payload format is chosen.
A different speech codec; not relevant beyond being similar in kind.
Email is only mentioned as an example of storage-mode use for the file format.

gaps.name: EVRC family codecs (EVRC, EVRC-B, EVRC-WB, EVRC-NW)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the 3GPP2 EVRC codec family, so readers looking for these codecs would not find them under a codec-specific page.

RFC6885.title: Stringprep Revision and Problem Statement for the Preparation and Comparison of Internationalized Strings (PRECIS)
RFC6885.summary: Informational problem statement from the PRECIS WG describing limitations of Stringprep profiles and the issues and requirements for designing a replacement for preparing and comparing internationalized strings.

PRECIS.why: The document is the PRECIS problem statement: it surveys Stringprep profile limitations and requirements for the replacement framework for internationalized string preparation and comparison.
PRECIS.quote: This document outlines the issues to be faced by those designing a Stringprep replacement.

Unicode.why: Large parts address Unicode version agility, normalization (NFKC vs NFC), case mapping, and code point properties in Internet protocols.
Unicode.quote: Stringprep is bound to Version 3.2 of Unicode.  Stringprep has not been updated to new versions of Unicode.

IDN.why: IDNA2003 Nameprep and the IDNA2008 inclusion-based approach are the model and comparison point throughout, including homoglyphs and transition issues.
IDN.quote: A new approach different from Stringprep and Nameprep is used for a revision of IDNA2003 (called IDNA2008).

rejected.why: SASLprep is evaluated as one Stringprep profile among many, but the document is not about SASL itself.
XMPP Nodeprep and Resourceprep are evaluated in an appendix only as examples of Stringprep profiles.
The iSCSI profile is one of the evaluated cases in an appendix, not the subject.
Considered as the parent topic; the more specific PRECIS tag fits, and its ancestors are implied.
IMAP usernames and passwords are only appendix evaluation examples.
EAP's Stringprep reference is evaluated briefly in an appendix; the document does not address EAP itself.

gaps.name: Stringprep / Nameprep (RFC 3454)
gaps.why: The document centres on Stringprep and its profiles. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so PRECIS is the closest fit.

RFC6886.title: NAT Port Mapping Protocol (NAT-PMP)
RFC6886.summary: Specifies NAT-PMP, a UDP-based protocol letting hosts behind a NAT gateway discover its external IPv4 address and create, renew and delete port mappings; it is the predecessor of PCP and is compared with UPnP IGD.

NAT-PMP.why: The whole document specifies NAT-PMP: packet formats, result codes, mapping lifetimes, epoch-based recovery, and deployment history.
NAT-PMP.quote: This document describes a protocol for automating the process of creating Network Address Translation (NAT) port mappings.

rejected.why: PCP is the successor and is discussed (transition, compatible packet format), but this RFC specifies NAT-PMP, not PCP.
The more specific NAT-PMP tag covers the document; NAT is implied as its parent.
DHCP is used to learn the default gateway and as an analogy for leases, but the document is not about it.
Wide Area Bonjour is the motivating deployment, but the document does not specify service discovery.
UDP is only the transport the protocol runs on.
The protocol handles IPv4 addresses only, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.

RFC6887.title: Port Control Protocol (PCP)
RFC6887.summary: RFC 6887 specifies the Port Control Protocol (PCP), a UDP-based request/response protocol by which hosts create and manage explicit port mappings and keepalive state in NATs and firewalls (MAP, PEER, ANNOUNCE opcodes, options, rapid recovery), and the successor to NAT-PMP.

PCP.why: The document defines PCP itself: header format, MAP/PEER/ANNOUNCE opcodes, options, result codes, and recovery.
PCP.quote: The Port Control Protocol allows an IPv6 or IPv4 host to control how incoming IPv6 or IPv4 packets are translated and forwarded by a Network Address Translator (NAT) or simple firewall

NAT-PMP.why: The document includes version negotiation and a transition procedure for NAT-PMP interworking, which NAT-PMP readers will want.
NAT-PMP.quote: The Port Control Protocol (PCP) is a successor to the NAT Port Mapping Protocol, NAT-PMP [RFC6886], and shares similar semantics, concepts, and packet formats.

rejected.why: PCP controls NATs, but PCP is the more specific tag and sits under NAT. The document does not define NAT behaviour itself.
CGN is a deployment scenario for PCP, not the subject of the document.
UDP is only the transport. The document defines no new UDP usage guidance.
Firewall control is one use of PCP, but the document is about the mapping protocol and not firewalls in general.
DS-Lite is listed only as a deployment scenario.
SCTP is a supported protocol with a short implementation note, not a subject of the document.

RFC6888.title: Common Requirements for Carrier-Grade NATs (CGNs)
RFC6888.summary: RFC 6888 (BCP 127) defines common requirements for Carrier-Grade NATs (CGNs): IP address pooling, port limits, filtering, port reuse, PCP support, logging and port allocation, updating RFC 4787.

CGN.why: The whole document is a set of requirements for CGNs (REQ-1 to REQ-15), which is exactly the CGN subject.
CGN.quote: This document defines common requirements for Carrier-Grade NATs (CGNs).

PCP.why: REQ-9 requires CGNs to implement PCP so subscribers can control mappings. This is one requirement of several, so it is a secondary tag.
PCP.quote: A CGN MUST implement a protocol giving subscribers explicit control over NAT mappings. That protocol SHOULD be the Port Control Protocol [RFC6887].
