rejected.why: DS-Lite is mentioned as a scenario where the IPv4-only CGN function applies, but the document does not specify or extend it.
CGN is the more specific child tag, so the parent NAT is implied.
The document refers to TCP session tracking and port reuse timing, but only as part of the NAT requirements. It is not about TCP.
REQ-10 recommends manageability and the NAT MIB (RFC 4008), but only in one short requirement.
ICMP is used for error signalling when a mapping cannot be created (REQ-11), but the document is not about ICMP.
The CGN is IPv4-only and exists because of address shortage, but the document does not specify IPv4 itself.

RFC6889.title: Analysis of Stateful 64 Translation
RFC6889.summary: Informational analysis of how stateful NAT64/DNS64 translation mechanisms address the problems that led NAT-PT to be deprecated in RFC 4966, classifying each problem as unsolvable, solvable, or solved.

NAT64.why: The whole document evaluates stateful NAT64 against the RFC 4966 concerns, so a reader of NAT64 would want it.
NAT64.quote: Stateful NAT64: Network Address and Protocol Translation from IPv6 Clients to IPv4 Servers [RFC6146]

DNS64.why: Decoupling DNS64 from translation is a central point of the analysis, including A-query handling and DNSSEC limits.
DNS64.quote: DNS64: DNS Extensions for Network Address Translation from IPv6 Clients to IPv4 Servers [RFC6147]

SIIT.why: The stateless IP/ICMP translation algorithm is one of the analysed mechanisms, but only as a building block of stateful 64.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the child tags chosen (NAT64, DNS64, SIIT), so it is not listed separately.
Generic NAT issues come up, but the document is about NAT64 specifically, which is the more specific tag.
DNSSEC limits with DNS64 are one minor analysis item, not a substantial part of the document.
SIP is mentioned only as an example of an application protocol traversing NAT64.
SCTP is only noted as out of scope.
IPsec AH and ESP are mentioned as one of many NAT problems, not as a subject of the document.

RFC6890.title: Special-Purpose IP Address Registries
RFC6890.summary: RFC 6890 restructures IANA's IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries, defines the common fields for each entry, and populates them with all existing special-purpose blocks, obsoleting RFCs 4773, 5156, 5735 and 5736.

addressing.why: The document catalogs and defines registry attributes (source, destination, forwardable, global) for special-purpose IPv4 and IPv6 address blocks. This is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: IANA to restructure its IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries. Specifically, this memo instructs IANA to record all special-purpose address blocks

IANA.why: The main body is about restructuring IANA registries, reassigning 192.0.0.0/24 to IANA, and setting the registry's information requirements and update policy.
IANA.quote: IANA will update the aforementioned registries as requested in the "IANA Considerations" section of a document that has passed IETF Review
IANA.section: 2.2. Restructuring of the IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries

rejected.why: The IPv4 registry is covered, but the document is about address-block registries across both families. The more general addressing tag fits better.
Same reasoning as IPv4. The IPv6 registry is one half of the document, and addressing covers both.
Only appears as one table entry (192.0.0.0/29). The document does not specify or extend the protocol.
Only a registry entry for 2001::/32. The protocol itself is not the subject.
Only appears as registry entries (192.88.99.0/24 and 2002::/16).
The 64:ff9b::/96 entry is just a table row, and the document is not about translation.

RFC6891.title: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0))
RFC6891.summary: RFC 6891 specifies EDNS(0), the backward-compatible DNS extension mechanism built on the OPT pseudo-RR, covering UDP payload size negotiation, extended RCODEs, flags, options, and deprecation of extended/binary labels, obsoleting RFC 2671 and 2673.

EDNS.why: The document defines the EDNS(0) OPT pseudo-RR, its wire format, option codes, version, flags and payload size behaviour. This is the core specification of EDNS.
EDNS.quote: An OPT pseudo-RR (sometimes called a meta-RR) MAY be added to the additional data section of a request.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned as a motivation for larger messages and the DO bit is referenced, but the DO bit is defined in RFC 3225. The document is not about DNSSEC.
The more specific EDNS tag covers it; the parent is implied.
UDP is the transport whose payload size limits EDNS lifts. The document does not specify UDP itself.
The IANA considerations section is boilerplate-like registry housekeeping, not the main subject.

RFC6892.title: The 'describes' Link Relation Type
RFC6892.summary: Registers the 'describes' link relation type, the inverse of 'describedby', in the IANA Link Relations registry established by RFC 5988 (Web Linking).

web linking.why: The whole document defines and registers a new typed link relation under the RFC 5988 Web Linking framework, so it belongs on the web linking page.
web linking.quote: This specification defines the 'describes' link relation type that allows resource representations to indicate that they are describing another resource.

rejected.why: URIs are only the identifiers for the linked resources. The document does not specify or extend URI syntax or schemes.
HTML is mentioned only as an example of a described resource. The document says nothing new about it.
The registration is in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate. The document does not address IANA registry policy.
The document says the relation places no constraints on media types. It does not register or change any media type.

RFC6893.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Open IPTV Forum (OIPF)
RFC6893.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "oipf" for naming persistent resources (XML schemas, classification schemes, etc.) defined by the Open IPTV Forum, per RFC 3406.

URN.why: The document is a formal URN namespace registration (NID "oipf"), which belongs under the URN subject page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Open IPTV Forum (OIPF) for naming persistent resources defined within OIPF specifications.

rejected.why: IPTV is the context of the Open IPTV Forum, but the document only registers a URN namespace and does not address IPTV service delivery or operations.
XML schemas are among the resources named, but the document does not specify XML usage or formats.
The IANA registration of NID 47 is boilerplate-level; the document is about the namespace itself, not IANA registry guidance.

RFC6894.title: Methodology for Benchmarking MPLS Traffic Engineered (MPLS-TE) Fast Reroute Protection
RFC6894.summary: Informational BMWG document defining test setups, procedures and reporting formats for benchmarking failover and reversion times of MPLS-TE Fast Reroute (facility backup) link and node protection using data-plane traffic.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking methodology: test topologies, procedures, offered load, failover time measurement methods and reporting format for a DUT.
benchmarking.quote: This document describes the methodology for benchmarking MPLS Fast Reroute (FRR) protection mechanisms for link and node protection.

IP fast reroute.why: The subject under test is MPLS FRR (RFC 4090 facility backup, PLR/merge point). The taxonomy's fast reroute tag covers IP and LDP FRR, so it is a loose fit, but readers of FRR would want this.
IP fast reroute.quote: MPLS-FRR protection mechanisms aim to reduce the service disruption period by minimizing recovery time from most common failures.

RSVP-TE.why: FRR protection for RSVP-TE LSP tunnels (RFC 4090) is what is benchmarked, including link and node protection of TE tunnels.
RSVP-TE.quote: All benchmarking test cases defined in this document apply to facility backup [RFC4090].

rejected.why: The MPLS-TE tunnels are the context, but the document is about the methodology for benchmarking, with RSVP-TE as the more specific tag for the protected tunnels.
BFD is mentioned as a failure detection method but explicitly out of scope.
L3 VPN and L2 VC traffic are only label-stack test scenarios, not the subject.
OSPF-TE and ISIS-TE are only noted as possible IGP choices to report.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific RSVP-TE tag chosen.
Benchmarking is the more specific fit for lab device testing; this is not active/passive network measurement.

gaps.name: MPLS Fast Reroute (RFC 4090 facility backup)
gaps.why: No tag specific to MPLS-TE fast reroute protection exists; IP fast reroute and RSVP-TE are only approximate fits.

RFC6895.title: Domain Name System (DNS) IANA Considerations
RFC6895.summary: BCP 42 defining IANA allocation policies for DNS parameters: header bits, OpCodes, RCODEs, RRTYPEs (with expert review and template), CLASSes, and the closed AFSDB subtype registry; obsoletes RFC 6195.

DNS.why: The document specifies registries and allocation rules for core DNS protocol parameters (RRTYPEs, CLASSes, OpCodes, RCODEs, header bits), so DNS readers need it.
DNS.quote: IANA parameter assignment considerations for the allocation of Domain Name System (DNS) resource record types, CLASSes, operation codes, error codes, DNS protocol message header bits

IANA.why: It is a BCP on IANA registry policy: allocation policies, designated expert guidelines and an application template for the DNS parameters registries.
IANA.quote: allocated by Expert Review if they meet the two requirements listed below. There will be a pool of a small number of Experts appointed by the IESG.

rejected.why: OPT RR and extended RCODE are mentioned, but the details are in RFC 6891; this document only notes the OPT RR.
DNSSEC is only referenced for security considerations and AD/CD bits; the document is not about it.
The AFSDB subtype registry is closed here, but the document is not about AFS cell discovery itself.
UPDATE OpCode and its counts are listed in the registry, but dynamic update is not the subject.

RFC6896.title: SCS: KoanLogic's Secure Cookie Sessions for HTTP
RFC6896.summary: Defines SCS, an URI/HTTP-header-friendly envelope for symmetrically encrypted, authenticated, timestamped tokens, and a cookie-based protocol using it to keep session state on the client.

cookies.why: The document specifies a cookie format, Set-Cookie/Cookie exchange and cookie attribute rules for encrypted client-side session state, so it belongs on the HTTP state management page.
cookies.quote: a simple protocol based on HTTP cookies that allows the establishment of "client mode" sessions

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA1 is only the authentication primitive used inside the token; the document does not specify or analyse HMAC.
AES-CBC-128 is a mandated cipher, but the document does not define or analyse AES itself.
HTTP is the substrate carrying the cookies. The document adds nothing to HTTP semantics beyond cookies.
base64url is only the encoding of the fields and is not the subject.
TLS is mentioned only for the Secure attribute and for channel binding against replay; the document does not specify it.
The parent topic is implied by the cookies tag. The document does not address a web-security mechanism like HSTS or token binding.

gaps.name: Authenticated encryption tokens / client-side session state
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for generic encrypted, authenticated tokens or stateless session handling. Only the cookie angle is covered.

RFC6897.title: Multipath TCP (MPTCP) Application Interface Considerations
RFC6897.summary: Informational RFC describing MPTCP's impact on applications, behaviour with legacy sockets applications, and a basic abstract sockets API extension for MPTCP-aware applications.

MPTCP.why: The whole document is about MPTCP's effects on applications, legacy compatibility, and a basic API for MPTCP-aware applications.
MPTCP.quote: Multipath TCP adds the capability of using multiple paths to a regular TCP session

sockets API.why: It specifies abstract sockets API extensions (TCP_MULTIPATH_ENABLE, ADD, REMOVE, SUBFLOWS, CONNID) and discusses socket option behaviour and relation to the SCTP sockets API.
sockets API.quote: This document provides an abstract definition of MPTCP-specific extensions to this interface.

rejected.why: MPTCP is the more specific child tag; TCP is only the base protocol.
Section 6.1 gives brief guidance on certificate address comparison but TLS is not a substantial subject.
Only discussed as a comparison and for its sockets API functions; not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only as a possible approach for MPTCP fallback delay.
Brief note in 6.4 about multiple A/AAAA records; not a subject of the document.
Section 6.3 discusses incompatibilities with Shim6/HIP APIs, but only as a minor compatibility note.

RFC6898.title: Link Management Protocol Behavior Negotiation and Configuration Modifications
RFC6898.summary: RFC 6898 extends the Link Management Protocol (LMP) with a BehaviorConfig CONFIG object, allowing multiple CONFIG objects in Config/ConfigAck/ConfigNack messages so neighbours can negotiate supported LMP behaviours and remain compatible with legacy nodes.

GMPLS.why: LMP is the GMPLS link management protocol; the document extends and updates LMP (RFC 4204, 4207, 4209, 5818) with behaviour negotiation. The GMPLS tag is the closest fit since the taxonomy has no LMP tag.
GMPLS.quote: The Link Management Protocol (LMP) is used to coordinate the properties, use, and faults of data links in networks controlled by Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

rejected.why: RBNF is only the notation used to write the message formats, not a subject of the document.
IANA actions (new C-Type and flags registry) are boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA process.
Only referenced in Security Considerations for securing LMP messages.
The S flag only refers to SONET/SDH Trace support from RFC 4207; the document is not about SONET.

gaps.name: Link Management Protocol (LMP)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about LMP, but the taxonomy has no LMP tag; GMPLS is only the nearest parent.

RFC6901.title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Pointer
RFC6901.summary: Defines JSON Pointer, a string syntax for identifying a specific value within a JSON document, with evaluation rules, JSON string and URI fragment representations, and error handling.

JSON.why: The whole document specifies a JSON-based addressing syntax and how it is evaluated against JSON objects and arrays, so JSON readers would want it.
JSON.quote: JSON Pointer defines a string syntax for identifying a specific value within a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) document.

URI.why: A full section defines how pointers are encoded as URI fragment identifiers, including percent-encoding and the media-type registration requirement.
URI.quote: A JSON Pointer can be represented in a URI fragment identifier by encoding it into octets using UTF-8 [RFC3629]

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to state the syntax rules, not a subject of the document.
UTF-8 is used only to encode the pointer for URI fragments, not defined or discussed in its own right.
Mentioned only to say a media type must specify JSON Pointer as its fragment syntax. The document does not register a media type or define registry rules.
Pointers are Unicode strings, and the document notes no normalization is performed. That is a detail of the syntax, not a Unicode-usage topic.

RFC6902.title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Patch
RFC6902.summary: RFC 6902 defines JSON Patch, a JSON document format (application/json-patch+json) expressing a sequence of add, remove, replace, move, copy and test operations to apply to a JSON document, suited for use with HTTP PATCH.

JSON.why: The document specifies a new JSON-based format and the semantics of operations on JSON documents. Readers of JSON formats would expect it.
JSON.quote: JSON Patch defines a JSON document structure for expressing a sequence of operations to apply to a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) document

rejected.why: HTTP PATCH is the intended carrier, but the document only says the format is suitable for it and defers PATCH semantics to RFC 5789. It does not extend HTTP.
The application/json-patch+json registration is IANA boilerplate for the new format, not a document about media type rules.
JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) is used to address locations, but it is defined elsewhere and is only a dependency here.
The format is usable in HTTP APIs, but the document does not define API conventions.
RFC 5261 XML Patch is mentioned only as an influence in the acknowledgements.

gaps.name: JSON Pointer / JSON Patch (partial document update)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for JSON Pointer or patch formats. JSON is the closest fit, but a dedicated tag would serve readers of JSON patching and addressing.

RFC6903.title: Additional Link Relation Types
RFC6903.summary: RFC 6903 defines and registers five additional Web Linking relation types (about, preview, privacy-policy, terms-of-service, type) in the IANA Link Relations registry.

web linking.why: The whole document defines new typed link relations under the RFC 5988 Web Linking model, so it belongs on the web linking page.
web linking.quote: This specification defines and adds the following additional link relation types to the registry: "about", "preview", "privacy-policy", "terms-of-service", and "type".

rejected.why: Link headers in HTTP responses appear only as examples. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
The document registers entries, but that is IANA Considerations boilerplate. Its main body is about the link relations themselves.
The "type" relation targets an IRI, but the document says nothing about IRIs themselves.
The privacy-policy relation links to privacy policies. It is not about protocol privacy threats or considerations.
HTML link elements appear only in examples.

RFC6904.title: Encryption of Header Extensions in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC6904.summary: RFC 6904 defines a mechanism to selectively encrypt RTP header extensions (RFC 5285) in SRTP, using keystreams derived with new labels, signaled via an SDP extmap URI, and updates RFC 3711 to require future SRTP transforms to specify header extension encryption.

SRTP.why: The document extends SRTP with header extension encryption, defines key derivation labels and keystream generation, and updates RFC 3711.
SRTP.quote: This document provides a mechanism, extending the mechanisms of SRTP, to selectively encrypt RTP header extensions in SRTP.

SDP.why: A substantial section defines a new SDP extmap URI and ABNF grammar extension, plus offer/answer backward-compatibility rules.
SDP.quote: Encrypted header extension elements are signaled in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) extmap attribute using the URI "urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:encrypt"

rejected.why: RTP header extensions are the object being protected, but the document's subject is SRTP encryption; the RTP header extension mechanism is defined in RFC 5285, not here.
AES-CM is used for keystream generation and test vectors, but the document does not specify AES itself; it reuses existing SRTP transforms.
Key derivation uses the SRTP KDF with new labels, but this is part of SRTP and not general key management.
The document does not define a payload format; it concerns header extensions.

gaps.name: RTP header extensions (RFC 5285)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the general RTP header extension mechanism, which is central to this document.

RFC6905.title: Requirements for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL)
RFC6905.summary: Informational requirements document specifying the OAM (connectivity verification, continuity check, path tracing, performance monitoring, fault/defect indication) functions needed for TRILL RBridge campuses.

TRILL.why: The whole document defines OAM requirements for TRILL RBridges, so TRILL readers would want it.
TRILL.quote: In this document, we define the requirements for TRILL OAM.

OAM.why: The document is about OAM mechanisms: connectivity verification, continuity checks, path tracing, and fault and defect indication.
OAM.quote: OAM MUST provide a single OAM framework for all TRILL OAM functions within the scope of this document.

performance measurement.why: A substantial section covers packet loss and one-way and two-way delay measurement requirements.
performance measurement.quote: OAM SHOULD provide the ability to measure packet loss statistics for a flow from any arbitrary RBridge RB1 to any other RBridge.

rejected.why: ECMP is mentioned only as the path-selection context and for a MAY-level hashing-utilization monitoring requirement, so the document is not about ECMP.
SNMP is mentioned only as a way to expose counters and traps, not specified or profiled.
Ethernet frames are the traffic carried, and IEEE 802.1ag is referenced only as background.
Syslog servers are mentioned once as a possible recipient of fault indications.
MPLS-TP RFCs are cited only for terminology and as prior OAM requirements.

RFC6906.title: The 'profile' Link Relation Type
RFC6906.summary: Registers the 'profile' link relation type so resource representations can signal conformance to profiles (additional semantics beyond the media type), and describes profiles, the media type 'profile' parameter, and examples.

web linking.why: The document's purpose is defining and registering a typed link relation under the Web Linking framework, usable in HTTP Link headers and embedded links.
web linking.quote: This specification registers a 'profile' link relation type according to the rules of RFC 5988

media types.why: A substantial section covers how profiles relate to media types and recommends a 'profile' media type parameter, of interest to media type designers.
media types.quote: media types that may be used with profiles, it is therefore recommended that they SHOULD define a media type parameter called 'profile'

rejected.why: HTTP Link headers and Accept are only a conveyance mechanism; nothing new is specified for HTTP.
HTML's profile attribute and hCard/Dublin Core examples are background, not the subject.
vCard appears only through the hCard example.
Profile URIs are used as identifiers, but URI syntax or schemes are not specified.
Feeds/podcasts are an illustrative example only.

RFC6907.title: Use Cases and Interpretations of Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Objects for Issuers and Relying Parties
RFC6907.summary: Informational RFC giving use cases and interpretations for RPKI objects (ROAs, AS 0 ROAs, maxLength) for issuers and relying parties, covering origination, partial deployment, transfers, and BGP prefix-origin validation outcomes.

RPKI.why: The whole document is about how issuers create ROAs and how relying parties interpret RPKI objects, including route origin validation states and ROA expiry/revocation.
RPKI.quote: directions and interpretations for organizations and relying parties when creating or encountering Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) object scenarios in the public RPKI

rejected.why: BGP routes and AS_PATH/AS_SET are the subject being validated, but the document specifies no BGP behaviour; it is about RPKI object use.
Resource certificates are assumed valid per RFC 6487; the document does not profile or discuss certificate contents.
Path validation is explicitly declared out of scope in Section 4.
Prefix notation and aggregation appear only as context for examples.

RFC6908.title: Deployment Considerations for Dual-Stack Lite
RFC6908.summary: Informational guidance for operators deploying Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite), covering AFTR and B4 deployment issues such as MTU, logging, policies, accounting, redundancy, placement, QoS, port forwarding and DNS.

DS-Lite.why: The whole document is deployment guidance for DS-Lite (AFTR and B4 elements), based on real deployment experience.
DS-Lite.quote: the purpose of this document is to describe problems that arise when deploying DS-Lite and what guidance should be taken to mitigate those issues

rejected.why: The AFTR does NAT44, but the document is about DS-Lite deployment, not NAT behaviour in general; DS-Lite is the more specific tag.
PCP is only recommended as guidance for port forwarding in one subsection; the document does not specify or extend it.
Section 3.1 covers B4 DNS proxy behaviour briefly, but this is a small part and DNS is not the subject.
Section 2.10 applies DSCP handling to DS-Lite tunnels, but it is one subsection, not a substantial focus.
The IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel is the mechanism of DS-Lite, which is the more specific tag; MTU and fragmentation are only one subsection.
DS-Lite is a child of this topic and is already tagged, so the parent is implied.

RFC6909.title: IPv4 Traffic Offload Selector Option for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC6909.summary: Defines the IPv4 Traffic Offload Selector mobility option (type 53) for Proxy Binding Update/Acknowledgement messages, letting a MAG and LMA negotiate which IPv4 flows the MAG offloads locally rather than tunnelling to the LMA.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with a new mobility option carried in PBU/PBA messages between MAG and LMA, and specifies MAG and LMA behaviour.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification defines a new mobility option, the IPv4 Traffic Offload Selector option, for Proxy Mobile IPv6.

rejected.why: Offloaded flows typically get NAT translated, but the document does not specify NAT behaviour and leaves NAT placement out of scope.
The option covers IPv4 flows, but the document is not about the IPv4 protocol or its address lifecycle.
This is the parent of PMIPv6, so the more specific child tag is used instead.
3GPP S2a is mentioned as motivating context, but the document does not specify anything about cellular interworking.
RFC 5101 is cited only for the definition of an IP flow. The document is not about flow export.
The Traffic Selector sub-option comes from RFC 6089 (Mobile IPv6 flow bindings), but the document only reuses it inside Proxy Mobile IPv6.

RFC6910.title: Completion of Calls for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6910.summary: Defines the SIP Completion of Calls (CCBS, CCNR, CCNL) feature: an architecture with caller's agent and callee's monitor, a new 'call-completion' SIP event package, queue model, and related URI/header parameters.

SIP.why: The document specifies a SIP call-completion service, a new SIP event package, and new SIP URI and Call-Info parameters.
SIP.quote: this document introduces an architecture for implementing these features in the Session Initiation Protocol where "completion of calls" implementations associated with the caller's and callee's endpoints cooperate

SIMPLE.why: The suspend/resume mechanism uses PUBLISH with PIDF presence and a new SIP event package, which fall under SIP events/presence.
SIMPLE.quote: The callee's monitor also instantiates a presence server used to monitor the caller's availability for CC recall.

rejected.why: Interoperation with SS7 CCBS/CCNR is a design goal but the document is a SIP feature, not PSTN gateway interworking.
PIDF is only used as the body for PUBLISH to signal open/closed; not defined or extended here.
Registers application/call-completion, but this is IANA boilerplate rather than the subject.
ABNF is only the notation for the CC body format.
Covered by the more specific SIP tag.

gaps.name: SIP event notification / supplementary telephony services
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SIP events framework or SIP telephony supplementary services like call completion; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC6911.title: RADIUS Attributes for IPv6 Access Networks
RFC6911.summary: Defines five new RADIUS attributes (Framed-IPv6-Address, DNS-Server-IPv6-Address, Route-IPv6-Information, Delegated-IPv6-Prefix-Pool, Stateful-IPv6-Address-Pool) for authorization and accounting in IPv6 residential broadband access networks using DHCPv6 and Router Advertisements.

RADIUS.why: The document's purpose is to define new RADIUS attributes (types 168-172) for authorization and accounting, extending RFC 3162 and RFC 4818.
RADIUS.quote: This document specifies additional RADIUS Attributes used to support configuration of DHCPv6 and/or ICMPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) parameters on a per-user basis.

DHCPv6.why: Several attributes provision DHCPv6 address assignment, prefix delegation pools and DNS server options on the NAS, so DHCPv6 readers would want this.
DHCPv6.quote: The assignment of a named delegated prefix pool for use with "IPv6 Prefix Options for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) version 6"

rejected.why: IPv6 is the address family the attributes carry, but the document is about RADIUS attributes. DHCPv6 is the more specific tag.
Router Advertisement Route Information Options are only the announcement mechanism the NAS uses. The document defines no new ND behaviour.
SLAAC is mentioned only to disambiguate which attributes apply to DHCPv6 and which to SLAAC.
The DNS server address attribute only configures a resolver address. It says nothing about DNS protocol behaviour.
The Diameter section only notes that no special handling is needed, so the document is not about Diameter.
DSL appears only in the example deployment scenario figure.

RFC6912.title: Principles for Unicode Code Point Inclusion in Labels in the DNS
RFC6912.summary: IAB informational memo giving principles (longevity, least astonishment, conservatism, inclusion, simplicity, letter principle, etc.) that DNS zone operators, especially public zones and the root, should use when deciding which Unicode code points to permit in IDNA U-labels.

IDN.why: The whole document is about code point repertoire policy for IDNA2008 U-labels in DNS zones, which is internationalized domain name registration policy.
IDN.quote: Operators of a DNS zone need to set policies around what Unicode code points are allowed in labels in that zone.

Unicode.why: Principles rely heavily on Unicode General_Category, property stability across versions, and script/mark behaviour, so it concerns Unicode usage in Internet protocols.
Unicode.quote: Unicode properties of a code point ought to be stable across the versions of Unicode that users of the zone are likely to have installed.

rejected.why: DNS is the setting, but the document is about label code point policy, which the IDN tag covers more specifically; it does not specify DNS protocol behaviour.
The parent is implied by Unicode, and the document is covered by the more specific tags.
Registry policy is discussed, but there are no registration protocols or operations specified; IDN is the more specific fit.
The root zone is discussed only as a context for stricter principles, not reserved names.

RFC6913.title: Indicating Fax over IP Capability in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6913.summary: Defines and registers the "sip.fax" media feature tag (values "t38" and "passthrough") so SIP UAs can advertise fax capability at registration and callers can use caller preferences to route fax calls to fax-capable UAs.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new media feature tag used in REGISTER Contact and INVITE Accept-Contact for caller-preference routing.
SIP.quote: This document defines the "fax" media feature tag for use in the SIP tree, as per Section 12.1 of RFC 3840

fax.why: The document is about indicating Fax over IP (T.38 and G.711 passthrough) capability so fax calls reach fax-capable endpoints.
fax.quote: Currently, fax calls are indistinguishable from voice calls at call initiation.

rejected.why: The document explains that capabilities are normally handled in SDP but fax is not signalled there; SDP is not specified or extended.
G.711 is only referenced as the codec for the passthrough value; the document does not define or extend it.
The tag is a SIP media feature tag, not a MIME media type registration, though it references media types such as image/t38.
The IANA section registers the tag but is boilerplate relative to the main subject.
Media feature tags relate to capability negotiation, but here they are specifically SIP caller preferences, covered by the SIP tag.

gaps.name: SIP caller preferences / media feature tags (RFC 3840/3841)
gaps.why: The document's core mechanism is SIP UA capability indication and caller preferences, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC6914.title: SIMPLE Made Simple: An Overview of the IETF Specifications for Instant Messaging and Presence Using the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6914.summary: RFC 6914 is an informational overview and guide to the SIMPLE suite of IETF specifications for SIP-based presence and instant messaging, categorizing each RFC and explaining how they relate.

SIMPLE.why: The document exists solely as a guide to the SIMPLE suite, covering presence event packages, PIDF extensions, XCAP provisioning, and optimizations.
SIMPLE.quote: Collectively, these specifications are known as SIP for Instant Messaging and Presence Leveraging Extensions (SIMPLE).  This document serves as a guide to the SIMPLE suite of specifications.

instant messaging.why: A whole major section covers IM specifications (MESSAGE, chat rooms, is-typing, IMDN) and the presence half is also IM/presence.
instant messaging.quote: SIMPLE defines two modes of instant messaging.  These are page mode and session mode.

MSRP.why: Session-mode IM subsection surveys MSRP and its relay, connection model and CEMA extensions.
MSRP.quote: defines a small text-based protocol for exchanging arbitrarily sized content of any kind between users.

PIDF.why: A full subsection covers PIDF and its extensions (RPID, timed presence, CIPID, partial PIDF).
PIDF.quote: defines the baseline XML format for a presence document.

rejected.why: SIP is the substrate for SIMPLE; the document surveys extensions for presence and IM, which the SIMPLE tag covers more specifically.
XML is the encoding for presence, policy and XCAP documents but is not the subject.
Mentioned only in passing as MSRP session setup.
Only one of many surveyed specs (RFC 5112 dictionary), a minor item.
Chat rooms use SIP conferencing frameworks, mentioned briefly in one subsection.
XCAP is a usage of HTTP, but HTTP itself is only a substrate.

gaps.name: XCAP (XML Configuration Access Protocol)
gaps.why: Section 2.4 covers XCAP provisioning of buddy lists and policy, but the taxonomy has no XCAP tag; it is only mentioned under SIMPLE.

gaps.name: Presence
gaps.why: Presence as a subject is covered (event packages, rich presence, privacy policy) but only PIDF and SIMPLE tags are available.

RFC6915.title: Flow Identity Extension for HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD)
RFC6915.summary: Defines a HELD extension (XML schema and URN namespace) that identifies a Device by the full flow tuple (layer 3/4 protocols, source and destination addresses and ports) so location requests work behind NATs such as CGNs, and deprecates the port elements of RFC 6155.

HELD.why: The document extends HELD with a new <flow> identity element for location requests and updates RFC 6155, so it belongs on the HELD page.
HELD.quote: This document specifies an XML Schema and a URN Sub-Namespace for a Flow Identity Extension for HELD to support this requirement.

rejected.why: NAT behaviour is the motivation, since CGNs make the full flow tuple necessary. The document does not specify or analyse NAT itself.
The extension is expressed as an XML schema, but XML is only the encoding. The document defines nothing new about XML usage.
Carrier Grade NATs are mentioned only as the motivating case. The document is not about CGN.
HELD is the more specific tag and is already chosen, so the parent topic is implied.
The namespace and schema registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject of the document.
TCP, UDP, SCTP and DCCP appear only as allowed values of the layer4 attribute.

RFC6916.title: Algorithm Agility Procedure for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC6916.summary: Defines the BCP procedure by which RPKI CAs and RPs migrate top-down to a new signature/hash algorithm suite through milestones and phases, covering provisioning, validation of dual products, revocation, and deprecation.

RPKI.why: The whole document specifies an RPKI operational procedure for algorithm transition, covering CA and RP behaviour, repository structure, and revocation.
RPKI.quote: This document specifies the process that Certification Authorities (CAs) and Relying Parties (RPs) participating in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) will need to follow

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are the objects being re-issued, but the document defines no certificate profile; it only relies on them.
The document covers CA key rollover for algorithm migration, but this is RPKI-specific and is better placed under the RPKI tag.
It specifies no algorithm suite itself and defers to RFC 6485, so it is a transition process rather than cryptographic content.
PKI is the parent of the RPKI tag, which fits more specifically.

gaps.name: RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no RPKI tag outside the routing security section. This document is entirely about RPKI CA/RP operations, so the closest tag, RPKI under routing security, is what I'd choose, but I haven't confirmed it exists with that id. Check the id and the tag's description before relying on this result.

RFC6917.title: Media Resource Brokering
RFC6917.summary: Defines the Media Resource Broker (MRB) for MediaCtrl deployments, with a CFW-based Publish interface for Media Servers and an HTTP/SIP Consumer interface (Query, in-line aware and unaware modes) for Application Servers to select and lease media resources.

real-time communications.why: The document is about brokering media server resources for MediaCtrl real-time media deployments (IVR, mixing, conferencing); no more specific child tag fits the MRB/MediaCtrl architecture.
real-time communications.quote: a need exists for intelligent, application-level media service selection based on non-static signaling properties.

SIP.why: A substantial part specifies how the Consumer interface is carried in SIP INVITE/200 OK with multipart bodies, and how the MRB acts as B2BUA or proxy for in-line modes.
SIP.quote: The MRB Consumer interface includes both 1) the In-line Aware MRB Mode (IAMM), which uses the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)

rejected.why: HTTP POST is only the transport for the Query-mode Consumer interface; nothing new is defined about HTTP.
XML schemas define the message formats, but XML is an encoding substrate here.
SDP is carried in the multipart bodies but not specified or extended.
RTP session counts and codecs are reported as resource metrics; RTP itself is not the subject.
Registers two media types, but that is IANA boilerplate and not the main subject.
Mixer resources are brokered, but the document is not about conferencing frameworks (XCON) themselves.

gaps.name: Media Server Control / MediaCtrl (Media Control Channel Framework, MRB)
gaps.why: The document belongs to the MediaCtrl media server control family (CFW, IVR and mixer packages, MRB), for which the taxonomy has no specific tag; it is only approximated by the real-time communications topic.

RFC6918.title: Formally Deprecating Some ICMPv4 Message Types
RFC6918.summary: RFC 6918 formally deprecates fifteen obsolete ICMPv4 message types, asks IANA to mark them deprecated in the ICMP Parameters registry, updates RFC 792 and RFC 950, and obsoletes RFC 1788 (ICMP Domain Name Messages), moving it to Historic.

ICMP.why: The whole document is about ICMPv4 message types: it discusses each deprecated type and updates the ICMP specification (RFC 792). A reader browsing ICMP would want it.
ICMP.quote: This document deprecates such ICMPv4 message types, "cleaning up" the corresponding IANA registry.

rejected.why: The IANA registry cleanup is the mechanism for the deprecation. The subject is ICMP message types, not IANA stewardship or registry guidance.
DHCP is mentioned only as the mechanism that superseded the Information and Address Mask messages. The document is not about it.
The ICMP Traceroute type 30 is one of the deprecated types and is covered in a single paragraph. The document is not about traceroute tools.
Mobile Host Redirect and Mobile Registration messages are deprecated, but only as part of the list of obsolete ICMP types. Mobility is not a subject of the document.
The Domain Name Request and Reply messages from RFC 1788 are deprecated, but they are ICMP messages and are never widely deployed. The document does not address DNS.

RFC6919.title: Further Key Words for Use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels
RFC6919.summary: An April 1 humorous Independent Submission that parodies RFC 2119 by defining additional requirement-level key words such as "MUST (BUT WE KNOW YOU WON'T)" and "SHOULD CONSIDER", each illustrated with quotes from other RFCs.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody of RFC 2119, with whimsical definitions such as the "passive-aggressive voice". A reader browsing humorous RFCs would expect to find it.
humor.quote: The phrase "MUST (BUT WE KNOW YOU WON'T)" is used to indicate requirements that are needed to meet formal review criteria

terminology.why: It is a satire of the requirements-language key words, so readers of the terminology subject (requirements language) would want it. The key-word definitions are a parody, not a real specification.
terminology.quote: This document defines additional key words that can be used to address alternative requirements scenarios.

rejected.why: The document concerns the key words used in RFC text. It is not about RFC format, style or publication.
It parodies how specification authors word requirements. It does not describe IETF procedures.
RFC 6120's SCRAM requirement is quoted only as an example of the joke key word.
RFC 2616 and RFC 5988 are quoted only as examples.

RFC6920.title: Naming Things with Hashes
RFC6920.summary: Defines the Named Information (ni) and human-speakable nih URI schemes for naming digital objects by hash output, with a .well-known HTTP mapping, a binary format, and IANA registries for hash algorithms and parameters.

URI.why: The document defines the new ni and nih URI schemes, their syntax and relative resolution, and a .well-known mapping. Readers of the URI subject would want it.
URI.quote: It specifies a new URI scheme for this purpose, a way to map these to HTTP URLs, and binary and human-speakable formats for these names.

ICN.why: A stated motivation is to support information-centric networking applications through name-data integrity. The names are the basis for ICN naming, but ICN is not specified in the document itself.
ICN.quote: in the context of information-centric networking [NETINF-ARCHITECTURE] [CCN] and elsewhere, there is value in being able to compare a presented resource against the URI

rejected.why: The .well-known mapping to HTTP(S) URLs is only a use of HTTP as a retrieval substrate, not an extension of HTTP.
SHA-256 is mandated as the hash, but the document specifies naming formats and not the hash function.
Base64url is used only as an encoding for the digest value.
DANE TLSA is mentioned only as the reason for choosing SubjectPublicKeyInfo as hash input.
The document is about URI schemes, so the more specific URI tag fits better than the general naming topic.
The new registries are part of the IANA Considerations boilerplate and do not make this document about IANA registry guidance.

RFC6921.title: Design Considerations for Faster-Than-Light (FTL) Communication
RFC6921.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC arguing that faster-than-light communication would make packets arrive before they are sent, analysing the TCP handshake under FTL, and recommending IETF review of protocols for FTL readiness.

humor.why: This is an April 1st whimsical document about a fictional FTL communication scenario, so it belongs on the humor page.
humor.quote: The major consequence of this for Internet protocols is that packets will arrive before they are sent.

TCP.why: A substantial part of the body analyses how the TCP 3-way handshake and its congestion control behave under negative delay.
TCP.quote: TCP B will receive the first SYN before TCP A transmitted it.
TCP.section: 2. Protocol Design Considerations for FTL Communication

rejected.why: Delay-Tolerant Networking is only mentioned as a loosely analogous area, with a reference to RFC 4838, and the document is not about it.
Congestion control gets a brief paragraph on negative RTT, which is too small a part of the document to tag.
RFC 2679 is cited only as a document that would need review, so the document is not about performance measurement.
The recommendation for a new review group is a joke aimed at the IESG, not a substantive treatment of process.

RFC6922.title: The application/sql Media Type
RFC6922.summary: Registers the application/sql media type with IANA for Structured Query Language files, including charset parameter rules, security and interoperability notes.

media types.why: The whole document is a media type registration under RFC 6838 for application/sql, so it belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: This document registers the application/sql media type to be used for the Structured Query Language (SQL).

rejected.why: The media types tag is the more specific child; MIME body structure and encodings are not the subject beyond the registration.
The IANA registration is merely the mechanism of the media type registration; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
The charset parameter is discussed only as a registration template field, not as a character set registration topic.
SQL is a database language, not a directory service; no fitting tag applies.

gaps.name: SQL / database query language
gaps.why: The document is about the SQL language's media type, but the taxonomy has no tag for SQL or database languages.

RFC6923.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Identifiers Following ITU-T Conventions
RFC6923.summary: Defines ITU-T-convention (ICC-based) operator identifiers and the resulting node, interface, tunnel, LSP, pseudowire, MEG, MEP and MIP identifiers for MPLS-TP, as an alternative to the IP/MPLS-style identifiers in RFC 6370.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document specifies identifiers for MPLS-TP entities (tunnels, LSPs, PWs, MEG/MEP/MIP) for management and OAM, so it belongs on the MPLS-TP page.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document augments the initial set of identifiers to be used in the Transport Profile of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS-TP)

rejected.why: Pseudowire path identifiers are covered in one short section, but only as one of several MPLS-TP entity identifiers. The document isn't about pseudowire emulation.
The MEG, MEP and MIP identifiers support OAM. However, the document only defines identifier formats. It says use and protocol extensions are out of scope.
MPLS-TP is the more specific tag and already covers this document.
There is no IANA registry content. The identifiers come from ITU-T ICC and ISO country-code assignments.

RFC6924.title: Registration of Second-Level URN Namespaces under "ietf"
RFC6924.summary: RFC 6924 creates and populates an IANA registry, "IETF URN Sub-namespaces", listing all second-level URN namespaces under "ietf" (rfc, fyi, std, bcp, id, mtg, params), and changes how new sub-namespaces are added to the namespace defined in RFC 2648.

URN.why: The document is about the "ietf" URN namespace and its registry of sub-namespaces, which updates RFC 2648. A reader browsing URN namespaces would expect to find it.
URN.quote: defines the "ietf" URN namespace and a number of sub-namespaces

IANA.why: The document's substance is the creation of an IANA registry. It renames the registry group, sets the registration policy and populates the entries.
IANA.quote: new registrations will use the IETF Review policy [RFC5226], which provides for IETF consensus in order to add a new URN namespace under "ietf"

rejected.why: The IETF Review policy applies only to the registry. The document does not address IETF procedures in general.
The rfc, std, bcp and fyi sub-namespaces name RFC-series documents. The document is about the URN registry, not the RFC series.

RFC6925.title: The DHCPv4 Relay Agent Identifier Sub-Option
RFC6925.summary: Defines a new Relay Agent Identifier (Relay-ID, sub-option 12) for the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option, carrying a unique relay agent identifier, with guidance on stability, uniqueness and security.

DHCP.why: The RFC extends DHCPv4 by defining a new relay agent sub-option, its format, and its usage rules.
DHCP.quote: This document defines a new Relay Agent Identifier sub-option for the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Relay Agent Information option.

rejected.why: The document is specific to DHCPv4, not DHCPv6.
UUIDs are only mentioned as one strategy for obtaining unique Relay-IDs; the document is not about UUIDs.
Industrial Ethernet is only an example use case; nothing about Ethernet is specified.
A MIB field is mentioned in passing as a way to expose the identifier; no MIB is defined.
The sub-option code assignment is boilerplate IANA Considerations.

RFC6926.title: DHCPv4 Bulk Leasequery
RFC6926.summary: Extends DHCPv4 Leasequery with a TCP-based Bulk Leasequery protocol, new query types, message types and options, so relay agents or access concentrators can retrieve many address bindings from a DHCPv4 server.

DHCP.why: The document specifies new DHCPv4 message types, options (status-code, base-time, dhcp-state, etc.), query types, and requestor and server behaviour. DHCP is the subject, and there is no DHCPv4-specific child tag.
DHCP.quote: This document extends the DHCPv4 Leasequery protocol to allow for bulk transfer of DHCPv4 address binding data via TCP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport used for bulk transfer. The document adds 2-octet message framing but defines nothing new about TCP itself.
DHCPv6 Bulk Leasequery (RFC 5460) is only cited as a model. This document covers DHCPv4.
The TCP framing of DHCPv4 messages is a small part of the document. The main subject is the Bulk Leasequery protocol itself.
The VPN-ID option is only a query qualifier. It is not about provider-provisioned VPNs.
NTP is mentioned only in passing, in the clock skew discussion.

RFC6927.title: Variants in Second-Level Names Registered in Top-Level Domains
RFC6927.summary: Informational independent-submission survey of how gTLD and ccTLD registries handle IDN variants (bundling, blocking, parallel NS, DNAME) in second-level domain registrations as of late 2012.

IDN.why: The whole document catalogs IDN variant practices across TLD registries, which is the subject of IDN. IDNA and variant handling are the core topic.
IDN.quote: This document surveys the approaches that top-level domains have taken to the registration and provisioning of domain names that have variants.

domain registration.why: Much of the survey covers registry policies for allocating, blocking, withholding and provisioning names, including ICANN registry agreements and registrant rules. This is registry operations rather than a specific protocol.
domain registration.quote: Some names cannot be registered at all.  For example, some registries allow one name in a bundle to be registered and block the rest.

rejected.why: DNS records (NS, DNAME) are used to provision variants, but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
Unicode code points are discussed as the source of variants, but the document is about registry practice, not Unicode usage in protocols.
IDN is the more specific fit; the document is not a general treatment of text internationalization.
The IANA Repository of IDN Practices is cited as a source, but the document is not about IANA registries or their stewardship.

RFC6928.title: Increasing TCP's Initial Window
RFC6928.summary: Experimental RFC proposing to raise TCP's permitted initial congestion window from 2-4 segments to 10 segments (IW10), with motivation, large-scale experimental results, and deployment/monitoring recommendations.

TCP.why: The document modifies TCP's initial window and the SYN-loss initial window rule from RFC 3390/5681, and specifies restart window behaviour. It is a TCP extension and belongs on the TCP page.
TCP.quote: This document proposes to raise the upper bound on TCP's initial window (IW) to 10 segments (maximum 14600 B).

congestion control.why: Initial window, slow start, restart window and loss window are congestion control mechanisms. The document also weighs the burst and fairness impact on the network, so congestion control readers would want it.
congestion control.quote: TCP implementations use slow start in as many as three different ways: (1) to start a new connection (the initial window)

rejected.why: Web traffic and HTTP connection counts are motivation and context only. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
AQM, CoDel and ECN are mentioned only as mitigations for bufferbloat in passing, not as subjects of the document.
ECN is only listed as a metric to monitor and a possible mitigation, not specified or analysed.
NewReno is mentioned in passing in a discussion of duplicate segments. The document is not about it.
Large-scale experimental results are evidence for the IW change, not a measurement methodology or metrics document.

RFC6929.title: Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) Protocol Extensions
RFC6929.summary: Defines extensions to the RADIUS protocol: Extended Type and Long Extended Type attribute formats, TLV, EVS and integer64 data types, extended vendor-specific attributes, compatibility guidance and IANA allocation rules for the expanded attribute type space.

RADIUS.why: The whole document extends the RADIUS attribute format, data types, and allocation rules, and updates RFC 2865, 3575 and 6158.
RADIUS.quote: The Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) protocol is nearing exhaustion of its current 8-bit Attribute Type space.

rejected.why: Section 8 only says the new formats are treated like traditional attributes in RADIUS-Diameter gateways; Diameter is not the subject.
Section 10 is IANA boilerplate for the RADIUS Attribute Types registry; the document's main body is about the protocol extension, not IANA stewardship generally.
MD5 is mentioned only in Security Considerations.
ABNF is used only to describe the example-generator input language, not the subject.

gaps.name: RADIUS attribute extensions
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists RADIUS only under AAA, but the id 'RADIUS' I used does not appear to exist at that path exactly as shown; it does exist as 'RADIUS' under AAA, so no gap beyond that.

RFC6930.title: RADIUS Attribute for IPv6 Rapid Deployment on IPv4 Infrastructures (6rd)
RFC6930.summary: Defines a new RADIUS attribute (IPv6-6rd-Configuration, type 173) that carries 6rd configuration (IPv4 mask length, 6rd prefix, BR IPv4 addresses) from an AAA server to a BNG, which then hands it to 6rd CEs via DHCP.

RADIUS.why: The document's core deliverable is a new RADIUS attribute, including its format, usage in Access-Request/Accept, and attribute table.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines a Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) attribute that carries 6rd configuration information from the AAA server to BNGs.

6rd.why: The attribute carries 6rd configuration parameters (prefix, prefix length, IPv4 mask length, Border Relay addresses) to support 6rd deployment.
6rd.quote: The IPv6-6rd-Configuration attribute is structured as follows:

rejected.why: DHCP is used between CE and BNG and the 6rd DHCP option is defined elsewhere (RFC 5969); this document only relies on it to show how the RADIUS data is used.
Only a short section notes the attribute is usable in Diameter; the document is not about Diameter.
The AAA server is the source of the configuration, but the document specifies a RADIUS attribute, so the more specific RADIUS tag covers it.
The parent of 6rd is implied by the 6rd tag.
Mentioned only in security considerations.

RFC6931.title: Additional XML Security Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC6931.summary: RFC 6931 lists and updates URIs identifying algorithms (digest, MAC, signature, encryption, key wrap, transforms) and KeyInfo types for XML Signature and XML Encryption, and creates an IANA "XML Security URIs" registry, obsoleting RFC 4051.

XML signatures.why: The whole document defines identifiers and formats for XML Signature and XML Encryption algorithms and KeyInfo types.
XML signatures.quote: expands, updates, and establishes an IANA registry for the list of URIs intended for use with XML digital signatures, encryption, canonicalization, and key management

cryptography.why: Much of the body specifies how specific cryptographic algorithms (RSA-PSS, ECDSA, Camellia, SEED, Whirlpool, SHA-3) are identified and encoded for XML use.
cryptography.quote: These URIs identify algorithms and types of information.

IANA.why: The document establishes a new IANA registry with expert review rules, which is a substantial part of its purpose.
IANA.quote: IANA has established a registry entitled "XML Security URIs".

rejected.why: URIs are used only as identifiers for algorithms; the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes in general.
XML is the substrate for the signature and encryption syntax; the document is about the XML security identifiers, which is covered by the XML signatures tag.
RSA signature variants are among many algorithms whose URIs are listed; RSA itself is not specified here.
Camellia URIs are one section among many; the document is not about the cipher or its use in protocols broadly.
HMAC URIs are listed as identifiers only; HMAC is not specified or extended.
Only URIs for ECDSA signature methods are listed, with details deferred to other RFCs.

RFC6932.title: Brainpool Elliptic Curves for the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Group Description Registry
RFC6932.summary: RFC 6932 allocates four IKE Group Description registry code points (27-30) for the Brainpool ECP curves (224, 256, 384, 512-bit) from RFC 5639 and gives their domain parameters and test vectors.

elliptic curve.why: The document specifies the domain parameters of the Brainpool elliptic curves and test vectors for ECDH with them, which is elliptic curve cryptography content.
elliptic curve.quote: This memo allocates code points for four new elliptic curve domain parameter sets over finite prime fields into a registry

IKE.why: The code points go into the IKE Group Description registry, and the document discusses the IKE registry's status and the notes restricting use with RFC 2409.
IKE.quote: IANA maintains a registry for [RFC2409] to map complete domain parameter sets into easily referenced numbers.

rejected.why: The IANA registry allocation is the mechanism here. The document is about the curves, not IANA registry policy or stewardship.
IPsec is only context for the registry. The document defines no IPsec behavior, and IKE is the closer fit.
RFC 5931 (EAP-pwd) is only cited as another user of the registry.
IEEE 802.11 is only cited as another user of the registry.
The curves are used in Diffie-Hellman key exchange, but the document does not address key management.

RFC6933.title: Entity MIB (Version 4)
RFC6933.summary: Defines version 4 of the Entity MIB (ENTITY-MIB) for representing physical and logical entities managed by a single SNMP agent, adding entPhysicalUUID, an IANA-maintained IANAPhysicalClass TC, a UUID-TC-MIB, and a constrained-resource compliance statement; obsoletes RFC 4133.

MIB.why: The document specifies the ENTITY-MIB, IANA-ENTITY-MIB and UUID-TC-MIB modules in SMIv2, which is exactly MIB module definition.
MIB.quote: it describes managed objects used for managing multiple logical and physical entities managed by a single Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) agent

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is accessed through; the document defines MIB objects, not SNMP itself, so the more specific MIB tag covers it.
The document only defines a textual convention carrying RFC 4122 UUIDs and a new object using it; it does not specify UUIDs themselves.
entPhysicalUris merely holds URIs/URNs such as CLEI; this is a use of URIs, not a specification of them.
The IANA-maintained IANAPhysicalClass registry is a small part of the document; the IANA considerations are boilerplate-like and the main subject is the MIB.
EMAN motivated the additions (energyObject, battery classes) but the document is about the entity inventory MIB, not energy monitoring.

RFC6934.title: Applicability of the Access Node Control Mechanism to Broadband Networks Based on Passive Optical Networks (PONs)
RFC6934.summary: Informational RFC describing how the Access Node Control Mechanism (ANCP) applies to PON-based broadband access, covering NAS-OLT-ONT control models, multicast admission control, topology discovery, loop configuration and connectivity checks.

ANCP.why: The whole document extends ANCP's framework and use cases to PON access, including OLT-ONT ANCP sessions and PON-specific differences from DSL.
ANCP.quote: The purpose of this document is to provide applicability of the Access Node Control Mechanism to broadband access based on Passive Optical Networks (PONs).

multicast.why: A large part of the document covers multicast conditional access, admission control, replication control and accounting, involving IGMP snooping/proxy on the ANX.
multicast.quote: The focus in this document will be on the ANCP requirements needed for coordinated admission control of unicast and multicast video

rejected.why: DSL is only the comparison baseline (Section 11) and the PON-fed DSLAM last mile; the document is about PON.
IGMP snooping and proxying are used as triggers for admission control, but the document does not specify or extend IGMP.
Bandwidth admission control is discussed, but it is realised through ANCP and not as a QoS architecture or signalling specification.
Ethernet aggregation and OAM are mentioned as context and as an alternative to ANCP loop testing, but they are not the subject.
DHCP Option 82 is only used to carry the PON-Customer-ID; nothing new is defined about DHCP.
IPTV is the motivating service, but the document is about control signalling and not IPTV service delivery.

gaps.name: Passive Optical Networks (BPON/GPON/XG-PON) and OMCI
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PON access technologies or the ONT Management and Control Interface, which are central to this document.

RFC6935.title: IPv6 and UDP Checksums for Tunneled Packets
RFC6935.summary: RFC 6935 updates RFC 2460 to allow a zero UDP checksum in IPv6 for UDP-based tunnel protocols whose inner packets carry their own checksum, subject to the constraints in RFC 6936.

UDP.why: The document's core change is to UDP checksum handling over IPv6: it specifies a zero-checksum mode per UDP port and the conditions for using it.
UDP.quote: allow endpoints to use a zero UDP checksum under constrained situations (primarily for IPv6 tunnel transports that carry checksum-protected packets)

checksum.why: A large part of the document analyses when omitting the outer checksum is safe, including corruption modes and reliance on inner checksums.
checksum.quote: relaxing the IPv6 UDP checksum requirement for tunnel protocols whose header information is protected on the "inner" packet being carried

IPv6.why: It formally updates RFC 2460 Section 8.1, replacing the IPv6 text that forbids zero UDP checksums.
IPv6.quote: This document updates the IPv6 specification (RFC 2460) to improve performance when a tunnel protocol uses UDP with IPv6 to tunnel packets.

tunneling.why: The relaxation applies only to UDP-based tunnel encapsulations, and the document discusses the limits of that applicability and middlebox traversal.
tunneling.quote: This specification updates IPv6 to allow a zero UDP checksum in the outer encapsulating datagram of a tunnel protocol.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a better alternative if middleboxes supported it; the document is not about it.
Cited as an example of a protocol that could use the update, not specified here.
The motivating use case, but only referenced as a draft; the document is generic.
Middleboxes are discussed as a constraint on deployment, but the document does not address firewall security traversal as a subject.

RFC6936.title: Applicability Statement for the Use of IPv6 UDP Datagrams with Zero Checksums
RFC6936.summary: Applicability statement defining requirements for IPv6 nodes and tunnel protocols that use UDP datagrams with a zero checksum, analysing corruption/misdelivery risks, middlebox impact, and alternatives such as UDP-Lite and IP-in-IP.

UDP.why: The document's core subject is UDP checksum behaviour with IPv6, specifying when UDP may omit the checksum and what endpoints must do.
UDP.quote: It defines recommendations and requirements for the use of IPv6 UDP datagrams with a zero UDP checksum.

UDP-Lite.why: UDP-Lite is substantially analysed as the main standardized alternative to zero checksum, including its tunnel use and middlebox traversal.
UDP-Lite.quote: UDP-Lite [RFC3828] offers an alternate transport to UDP and is specified as a proposed standard, RFC 3828.

tunneling.why: The zero-checksum rules target UDP tunnel encapsulations, with extensive discussion of fragmentation, recursive tunnelling, and comparison with IP-in-IP and GRE.
tunneling.quote: One increasingly popular use of UDP is as a tunneling protocol, where a tunnel endpoint encapsulates the packets of another protocol inside UDP datagrams

IPv6.why: The document is about the IPv6-specific consequences of lacking a header checksum and updates RFC 2460 behaviour.
IPv6.quote: The key difference between UDP usage with IPv4 and IPv6 is that RFC 2460 mandates use of a calculated UDP checksum

rejected.why: Internet checksum is central, but the document is about UDP's use of it; UDP is the more specific fit.
Middlebox/NAT interaction is discussed as a deployment constraint, not the document's subject.
GRE and IP-in-IP are only compared as alternatives.
Load balancing is a motivation discussed briefly, not the subject.
Firewall traversal is a constraint, not what the document specifies.
AMT is only cited as a motivating tunnel protocol example.

RFC6937.title: Proportional Rate Reduction for TCP
RFC6937.summary: Experimental RFC specifying Proportional Rate Reduction (PRR), a TCP loss-recovery algorithm that paces data sent during recovery so the window ends near ssthresh, as an alternative to Fast Recovery and Rate-Halving.

TCP.why: The document specifies a TCP sender-side loss-recovery algorithm as a modification to RFC 5681 and uses SACK/pipe concepts, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: This document describes an experimental algorithm, PRR, to improve the accuracy of the amount of data sent by TCP during loss recovery.

congestion control.why: PRR governs how the window is reduced toward ssthresh during recovery, which is a congestion control matter. No child tag (NewReno, CUBIC, etc.) fits, so the parent topic is used.
congestion control.quote: Standard congestion control [RFC5681] requires that TCP (and other protocols) reduce their congestion window (cwnd) in response to losses.

rejected.why: CUBIC is mentioned only as an example of a modern algorithm that reduces the window by less than 50% and as part of the measurement setup. The document is not about it.
Fast Recovery and Rate-Halving are compared as baselines, but the document does not specify or extend NewReno.
ECN is not discussed in the document.

gaps.name: TCP loss recovery / SACK-based recovery
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about the loss-recovery algorithm (Fast Recovery, RFC 6675 pipe, SACK), and the taxonomy has no loss recovery or SACK tag. TCP is the closest fit.

RFC6938.title: Deprecation of BGP Path Attributes: DPA, ADVERTISER, and RCID_PATH / CLUSTER_ID
RFC6938.summary: Requests IANA to mark the BGP path attribute registry entries DPA, ADVERTISER, and RCID_PATH/CLUSTER_ID as deprecated, since they were never used and tied to an abandoned draft and a Historic RFC.

BGP.why: The document's whole purpose is deprecating BGP path attributes in the IANA registry, so BGP readers would want it. It is the operational change to the BGP protocol's attribute space.
BGP.quote: IANA has marked the BGP Path Attributes registry entries for DPA (Value 11), ADVERTISER (Value 12), and RCID_PATH / CLUSTER_ID (Value 13) as "deprecated".

rejected.why: CLUSTER_LIST from route reflection is mentioned only to say it is not being deprecated; the document is not about route reflection.
The registry update is the mechanism, but the subject is BGP attributes, not IANA registry policy or stewardship in general.

RFC6939.title: Client Link-Layer Address Option in DHCPv6
RFC6939.summary: Defines a new DHCPv6 Client Link-Layer Address option (code 79) that first-hop relay agents insert into Relay-Forward messages so servers can learn the client's link-layer address, e.g. to correlate DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 leases in dual-stack networks.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option and the behaviour of relay agents, servers and clients with respect to it.
DHCPv6.quote: defining a new DHCPv6 Client Link-Layer Address option

rejected.why: DHCPv4 is discussed only as background for correlating identifiers. The DHCPv6 tag is the more specific fit.
Only recommended in Security Considerations to protect relay-server traffic. The document is not about IPsec.
RFC 826 is cited only as the source of the hardware type values for the link-layer type field.
Dynamic DNS updates appear only in a Security Considerations attack scenario.

RFC6940.title: REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) Base Protocol
RFC6940.summary: RFC 6940 specifies RELOAD, a peer-to-peer signaling protocol providing an overlay with distributed storage, messaging, ICE-based NAT traversal, certificate-based security, and a mandatory Chord DHT topology plug-in, designed mainly for P2PSIP.

P2PSIP.why: The document is the base RELOAD specification, which the P2PSIP tag explicitly covers.
P2PSIP.quote: RELOAD is designed to support a P2P Session Initiation Protocol (P2PSIP) network, but can be utilized by other applications with similar requirements

ICE.why: A substantial part (Attach/AppAttach, Section 6.5.1) defines an ICE profile for RELOAD connection setup, with binary candidate encoding and modified procedures.
ICE.quote: This section describes the profile of ICE that is used with RELOAD. RELOAD implementations MUST implement full ICE.

P2P.why: RELOAD is a generic P2P overlay with a DHT storage service and a Chord-based topology plug-in; the P2P tag fits this overlay and DHT content.
P2P.quote: RELOAD provides a generic, self-organizing overlay network service, allowing nodes to route messages to other nodes and to store and retrieve data in the overlay.

rejected.why: SIP is only the main application; the SIP usage is defined in a separate document.
TLS and DTLS are used as overlay link protocols, but the document defines no new TLS mechanism.
DTLS is a substrate for overlay links, with simple reliability defined by RELOAD itself, not as a DTLS extension.
A TURN Server Usage is defined for discovering TURN servers, but TURN itself is not specified or extended.
STUN is used by ICE for checks and keepalives; it is not the subject of the document.
Certificates are used for identity, but no certificate profile is defined as the main subject.
XML is only the encoding of the configuration document, which is a minor part of the RFC.

gaps.name: Distributed hash table / structured overlay (Chord)
gaps.why: The RFC defines the CHORD-RELOAD DHT algorithm and a distributed storage service. The taxonomy has no DHT or overlay tag beyond the general P2P tag.

RFC6941.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Security Framework
RFC6941.summary: Informational security framework for MPLS-TP that builds on RFC 5920, defining trusted-zone reference models, MPLS-TP-specific threats (G-ACh/GAL/BFD manipulation, NMS attacks, in-band OAM DoS), and defensive techniques.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document analyses security threats and mitigations specific to MPLS-TP networks and their interconnection with MPLS/GMPLS, so the MPLS-TP page is the right home.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document provides a security framework for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP).

operational security.why: Substantial content on threats, trusted zones, and defences such as authentication, isolation, access control and NMS protection for network infrastructure operators. It is a security framework for operators rather than a protocol-level mechanism.
operational security.quote: Use of isolated infrastructure for MPLS-TP

rejected.why: Pseudowires (SS-PW/MS-PW) appear in the reference model figures, but only as the service context. The document does not specify or analyse pseudowire emulation itself.
BFD label manipulation and BFD message DoS are cited as threats to in-band OAM, but BFD is not specified or extended here.
Interconnection with GMPLS and RFC 5920 is mentioned in passing, but the document is not about GMPLS.
MPLS-TP is the more specific tag. The general MPLS security material lives in RFC 5920 and is only referenced here.
In-band OAM (G-ACh/GAL) is a target of the threats described, but the document does not define OAM mechanisms. The security angle is already covered by the MPLS-TP tag.

RFC6942.title: Diameter Support for the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP)
RFC6942.summary: Defines a new Diameter ERP application (Application Id 13) and new AVPs to carry EAP Re-authentication Protocol messages and root/re-authentication keys between authenticator, ER server and home EAP server.

Diameter.why: The document defines a new Diameter application, new AVPs and a result code, extending the Diameter protocol.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies Diameter support for ERP. It defines a new Diameter ERP application to transport ERP messages between an ER authenticator and the ER server

EAP.why: The document carries ERP (EAP-Initiate/EAP-Finish) and specifies bootstrapping and re-authentication flows with ER servers, so EAP/ERP readers would want it.
EAP.quote: The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) defines extensions to the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) to support efficient re-authentication

HOKEY.why: Covers ERP root key (rRK/rDSRK) bootstrapping and rMSK distribution, which is the HOKEY/ERP subject.
HOKEY.quote: A root key for re-authentication is derived from the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) created during EAP authentication

rejected.why: Parent of Diameter and implied by it.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a protection option for the transport.
ESP is only a permitted protection mechanism in Security Considerations.
Key transport is part of the subject but is covered by the more specific HOKEY tag.

RFC6943.title: Issues in Identifier Comparison for Security Purposes
RFC6943.summary: IAB informational document discussing how differing identifier comparison algorithms (hostnames, IP literals, URIs, email-like identifiers) cause security failures, with guidance for protocol designers.

security.why: The whole document is cross-protocol security guidance on comparison mismatches (false positives/negatives) in authentication, authorization and accounting. It is not tied to one mechanism.
security.quote: failure scenarios ranging from denial of service to elevation of privilege can result
security.section: 2. Identifier Use in Security Policies and Decisions

hostnames.why: A large section covers hostname definitions, IPv4/IPv6 literal ambiguity, and comparison by resolution.
hostnames.quote: Hostnames (composed of dot-separated labels) are commonly used either directly as identifiers, or as components in identifiers such as in URIs and email addresses.

URI.why: Component-by-component analysis of URI comparison (scheme, authority, path, query, fragment). The hypothetical example is also built on URI fragment handling.
URI.quote: This section looks at issues related to using URIs for security purposes.

internationalization.why: Covers Punycode, visual confusability, case-insensitive comparison and canonicalization of non-ASCII identifiers as security concerns. Section 3.1.3 adds to this.
internationalization.quote: there are a number of internationalization issues that apply to many types of Definite and Indefinite identifiers.

rejected.why: DNS names and resolution are discussed only as a source of comparison ambiguity. The document does not specify or analyse DNS itself.
PKIX certificates appear as an example of where names get compared. The document is not about certificate profiles.
OAuth and Kerberos are mentioned only as examples of token protocols in the Figure 2 scenario.
Email address-like identifiers get one short subsection (3.4), mostly about the local part and the hostname issues already covered.
Punycode and A-labels are discussed as hostname comparison issues, not as the IDNA specification.
IPv6 literal string representations get a brief subsection. The document is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: identifier comparison / canonicalization
gaps.why: The document's core subject, comparing and normalizing identifiers across protocols, has no dedicated tag. The closest fits are the broad security, URI and internationalization tags.

RFC6944.title: Applicability Statement: DNS Security (DNSSEC) DNSKEY Algorithm Implementation Status
RFC6944.summary: An applicability statement that assigns implementation status (Must Implement, Must Not Implement, Recommended, Optional) to each registered DNSSEC DNSKEY signing algorithm and updates several earlier DNSSEC and DNS key RFCs.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is about which DNSSEC signing algorithms implementations must, should or must not support, and it updates RFC 4034 and RFC 5155 on DNSSEC.
DNSSEC.quote: This document provides an applicability statement on algorithm implementation status for DNSSEC component software.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and its parent DNS is implied, so DNS is not listed separately.
RSA-based algorithms appear in the status table, but the document only assigns implementation status and does not specify or analyse RSA.
ECDSAP256SHA256 and ECDSAP384SHA384 are listed in the table, but the document does not define or discuss ECDSA itself.
GOST-ECC is only named as an Optional algorithm and is not discussed.
The document refers to the DNSSEC algorithm registry, but only in the IANA Considerations boilerplate and in its subject matter. It does not give IANA guidance.
The algorithms are cryptographic, but the document is about DNSSEC implementation status. It does not cover the cryptography, and the DNSSEC tag fits better.

RFC6945.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) to Router Protocol
RFC6945.summary: Defines the RPKI-ROUTER-MIB SMIv2 module for monitoring the RPKI-to-Router protocol on routers: cache server connection table, error counters, prefix-origin table, and notifications.

MIB.why: The document's sole content is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, notifications and compliance statements, so MIB is the best-fitting tag.
MIB.quote: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.
