RPKI.why: The MIB monitors the RPKI-to-Router protocol: cache server connections, serials, session IDs, and validated prefix/origin-AS data. Readers of RPKI would want it.
RPKI.quote: The objects defined in this document are used to monitor the RPKI-Router Protocol [RFC6810].

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the MIB tag covers SNMP-related content and the document doesn't extend SNMP itself.
TLS appears only as a connection type enumerated in a textual convention and in security references; not the subject.
SSH is only listed as one of the transport options for the router-to-cache connection.
Origin AS and prefix data relate to BGP origin validation, but the document does not address BGP itself.
Parent of RPKI, which is already tagged more specifically.
Only listed as a connection type enumeration value.

RFC6946.title: Processing of IPv6 "Atomic" Fragments
RFC6946.summary: Updates RFC 2460 and RFC 5722 so that IPv6 atomic fragments (Fragment Header with offset 0 and M=0) are processed in isolation from other fragments, removing a fragmentation-based attack vector.

IPv6.why: The document updates the core IPv6 specification's fragment reassembly rules, specifying how atomic fragments must be handled.
IPv6.quote: A host that receives an IPv6 packet that includes a Fragment Header with the "Fragment Offset" equal to 0 and the "M" flag equal to 0 MUST process that packet in isolation

rejected.why: ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages trigger atomic fragments, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP; it is only the trigger.
Path MTU handling is the context for generating atomic fragments, but the document does not change PMTUD behaviour.
IPv6/IPv4 translators are mentioned as the reason for the Fragment Header, but the document is not about translation mechanisms.
The document has a security motivation, but the general security topic is not needed beyond the specific IPv6 tag.

gaps.name: IPv6 fragmentation
gaps.why: The document is about IPv6 fragment handling and reassembly, and the taxonomy has no specific tag for fragmentation. The IPv6 tag is the closest fit.

RFC6947.title: The Session Description Protocol (SDP) Alternate Connectivity (ALTC) Attribute
RFC6947.summary: Defines the SDP "altc" media-level attribute letting an SDP offer carry alternative IPv4/IPv6 connection addresses and ports in a backward-compatible way, as a replacement for ANAT where ICE connectivity checks are not needed.

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute, its syntax and offer/answer usage, and registers it. This is the core subject.
SDP.quote: The basic concept is to use a new SDP attribute, "altc", to indicate the IP addresses for potential alternative connection addresses.

IPv6 transition.why: The motivation and use cases are IPv4/IPv6 coexistence. They include avoiding NAT64 and CGN/DS-Lite traversal and avoiding IPv4/IPv6 interworking, so readers of IPv6 transition would want it.
IPv6 transition.quote: SIP-based services using an IPv4-only core service platform to an IPv6-enabled UA
IPv6 transition.section: A.3.2 Basic Scenario for IPv6 SIP Service Delivery

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling context in which the SDP offer is carried. The document defines nothing new in SIP itself and says SIP-layer interworking is out of scope.
ICE is discussed only as an alternative mechanism and for how ALTC interacts with it. The document does not specify or extend ICE.
NAT64 is mentioned only as a function that ALTC lets deployments avoid.
DS-Lite appears only as a use-case scenario that ALTC is meant to help with.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the attribute syntax.
RTP and RTCP ports are mentioned only as details of the attribute's port fields and its interaction with a=rtcp and rtcp-mux. The document is not about RTP.

RFC6948.title: Some Measurements on World IPv6 Day from an End-User Perspective
RFC6948.summary: Reports end-user measurements of AAAA record availability, TCP connection failure rates and setup delay differences between IPv4 and IPv6 for the top Alexa sites before, during and after World IPv6 Day (June 2011).

IPv6.why: The whole document analyses IPv6 deployment on World IPv6 Day, comparing IPv6 and IPv4 reachability and delay. IPv6 deployment is within the IPv6 tag's scope.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 [RFC2460] was enabled by default for 24 hours on numerous networks and sites that previously supported only IPv4.

performance measurement.why: The document describes an active measurement methodology and reports delay and failure statistics, so readers of performance measurement would want it.
performance measurement.quote: The connection setup delay was measured by recording the time immediately before and after the connect system call.

rejected.why: AAAA record presence is counted, but only as an indicator of IPv6 adoption. The document says nothing new about DNS protocol or operations.
TCP connection setup is the probe used for reachability and delay. The document does not specify or analyse TCP itself.
RFC 6555 is cited only as background on fallback delays. The document does not discuss the mechanism.
It covers dual-stack deployment results only in passing. It does not address transition mechanisms, and 6to4 and tunnelling are mentioned only as causes of problems.

RFC6949.title: RFC Series Format Requirements and Future Development
RFC6949.summary: IAB document capturing the requirements and requested enhancements for the canonical format of RFCs (ASCII, pagination, reflowable text, metadata, graphics), updating RFC 2223 and guiding future RFC format changes.

RFC series.why: The whole document defines requirements for RFC format, publication stages and RFC Editor goals, which is the RFC series' format and publication.
RFC series.quote: This document describes the current requirements and requests for enhancements for the format of the canonical version of RFCs.

character sets.why: A substantial part debates ASCII versus UTF-8 for RFC text and sets the rule for non-ASCII characters.
character sets.quote: ASCII is required for all text that must be read to understand or implement the technology described in the RFC.

rejected.why: Accessibility for visual disabilities is one requirement among many, and the tag is for accessibility of Internet communications, so it doesn't fit.
XML is discussed as a possible revisable format, but the document does not specify the RFCXML vocabulary.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as an option in the encoding debate. The document is not about the encoding itself.
HTML is named only as a possible publication or revisable format, not specified or analysed.

RFC6950.title: Architectural Considerations on Application Features in the DNS
RFC6950.summary: IAB guidance document examining the architectural consequences and limits of using the DNS as an application platform (service location, NAPTR/DDDS, arbitrary data, compound queries, split horizon), advising when to use other protocols instead.

DNS.why: The whole document is about what the DNS should and should not be used for by applications, covering resolver, server, caching behaviour, large data, split horizon, and EDNS limits.
DNS.quote: This document explores the architectural consequences of using the DNS to implement certain application features, and it provides guidance to future application designers as to the limitations of the DNS

ENUM.why: ENUM and DDDS/NAPTR are the running example throughout (compound queries, number portability zones, send-n metadata), so ENUM readers would want this analysis.
ENUM.quote: Since many of these new requirements have emerged from the ENUM space, the following sections use ENUM as an illustrative example

rejected.why: Mentioned as a security aid for redirection and DKIM keys, but not the subject of the document.
Discussed as a way to carry compound queries and its size and amplification limits, but the document only argues against such uses and does not specify or extend EDNS.
Used only as an example of storing keys in TXT records.
Cited as an alternative protocol for features the DNS handles badly, not the subject.
Only mentioned briefly as an example of service naming conventions.
Section 2.1 covers locating services via MX and SRV, but only as background to the DNS-as-platform argument.

review: model chose 'architecture', which is not a tag

notes: model chose 'architecture', which is not a tag

RFC6951.title: UDP Encapsulation of Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) Packets for End-Host to End-Host Communication
RFC6951.summary: Specifies how to encapsulate SCTP packets in UDP for end-host to end-host communication, enabling SCTP through legacy NATs and user-space SCTP implementations, with procedures, PMTU/ICMP handling and a socket option.

SCTP.why: The document specifies an extension to SCTP stacks (encapsulation/decapsulation, per-destination remote UDP port, address handling via ASCONF, socket option), so it belongs on the SCTP page.
SCTP.quote: This document describes a simple method of encapsulating SCTP packets into UDP packets.

UDP.why: Defines a usage of UDP as the encapsulation layer, including port 9899, checksum rules and UDP header handling, which UDP usage readers would want.
UDP.quote: a UDP header as defined in [RFC0768] is inserted between the IP header as defined in [RFC0791] and the SCTP common header

NAT.why: Legacy NAT traversal is a main motivation and drives address-handling rules (wildcard addresses, no embedded IPs) and UNSAF considerations.
NAT.quote: This allows the usage of SCTP in networks with legacy NATs that do not support SCTP.

rejected.why: The document explicitly excludes tunneling endpoints and covers only end-hosts; it is transport-layer encapsulation, not generic tunneling.
Only a short section adjusts the path MTU for the UDP header; PMTUD is not the subject.
The socket option is a small informational section extending the SCTP sockets API, not the main subject.
ICMP handling is a brief mapping consideration, not the subject.
IPv6 is just one of the IP versions carried, not a subject of the document.

RFC6952.title: Analysis of BGP, LDP, PCEP, and MSDP Issues According to the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) Design Guide
RFC6952.summary: KARP analysis of the security state (authentication, keying, TCP-AO/MD5, gaps) of the TCP-based routing protocols BGP, LDP, PCEP and MSDP against RFC 6518 design guidelines.

routing security.why: The document is a KARP analysis of authentication, keying and integrity protection for routing protocols; this is the routing security subject.
routing security.quote: In order to secure the routing protocols, this document performs an initial analysis of the current state of four TCP-based protocols

BGP.why: BGP's session security is one of the four protocols analysed.
BGP.quote: All BGP communications take place over TCP. Therefore, all security vulnerabilities for BGP can be categorized as relating to the security of the transport protocol itself

LDP.why: LDP gets the most detailed treatment: spoofing and DoS threats, Hello authentication gaps, and its own subsections in the gap analysis.
LDP.quote: Spoofing a Hello packet for an existing adjacency can cause the adjacency to time out and result in termination of the associated session.

PCE.why: PCEP security threats, PCE discovery and keying gaps are analysed in their own subsections.
PCE.quote: Attacks on PCEP [RFC5440] may result in damage to active networks.

MSDP.why: MSDP's authentication weakness and state-limit mitigation are analysed as one of the four protocols.
MSDP.quote: the Multicast Source Distribution Protocol (MSDP) uses TCP MD5 [RFC2385] to protect TCP sessions via the TCP MD5 option.

key management.why: Keying mechanisms, key rollover and a key management protocol for routers are central themes of the analysis and gap section.
key management.quote: the KMP for the routing sessions should help negotiate unique, pair-wise random keys without administrator involvement.
key management.section: 3. Optimal State for BGP, LDP, PCEP, and MSDP

rejected.why: TCP-AO and TCP MD5 are discussed as the protection mechanisms, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
IKEv2 is only mentioned as a possible key management option, not analysed in its own right.
OSPF is referenced only as a companion KARP analysis (RFC 6863).
The weakness of MD5 is cited as a reason to move to TCP-AO, but the document is not about MD5 itself.
Securing routing data is explicitly out of scope and left to SIDR.
A more specific routing security tag applies, so this general authentication topic is not needed.

gaps.name: KARP (Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the KARP effort, which covers authentication and keying across routing protocols. Routing security is the closest fit.

RFC6953.title: Protocol to Access White-Space (PAWS) Databases: Use Cases and Requirements
RFC6953.summary: Informational RFC giving the problem statement, use cases and requirements for PAWS, a protocol by which white-space devices query a spectrum-availability database based on geolocation.

PAWS.why: The whole document defines the problem, use cases and requirements for the PAWS protocol, which is exactly what this tag covers.
PAWS.quote: This document covers the requirements for a protocol to allow a device to access a database to obtain spectrum availability information.

rejected.why: Device location is an input to database queries (D.1), but the document is about spectrum database access, not location formats or conveyance.
Database discovery is one requirement (P.1, Section 3.2), but only a minor part of the document.
Wi-Fi appears only in use cases as a non-white-space link or backhaul; the document is not about IP over 802.11.
Privacy appears in one requirement (P.7) and a threat; it is not a main subject.

RFC6954.title: Using the Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool Curves for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC6954.summary: Registers IKEv2 Diffie-Hellman group transform IDs for four ECC Brainpool curves and specifies key exchange payload encoding and shared secret derivation, with test vectors.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new Diffie-Hellman group transform IDs and defines KE payload encoding and shared secret derivation for them.
IKE.quote: This document specifies use of the Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool elliptic curve groups for key exchange in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2).

elliptic curve.why: It is about using the Brainpool elliptic curve groups, including twisted curves, point encoding, and public value validation, which is elliptic-curve cryptography in IKEv2.
elliptic curve.quote: the Diffie-Hellman public value passed in a key establishment (KE) payload consists of two components, x and y, corresponding to the coordinates of an elliptic curve point.

rejected.why: IKEv2 is the protocol extended here; the IPsec architecture itself (ESP, AH, policy) is not addressed, and IKE is the more specific tag.
The document concerns key exchange, not signatures; ECDSA is mentioned only in a reference.
Certificates are mentioned only to contrast with RFC 5639's OIDs; the document does not address them.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level here; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

RFC6955.title: Diffie-Hellman Proof-of-Possession Algorithms
RFC6955.summary: RFC 6955 specifies two Diffie-Hellman and one ECDH-based Proof-of-Possession algorithms (static DH/ECDH MAC-based and a discrete-log signature) for PKCS #10 and CRMF certification requests, with ASN.1 OIDs, obsoleting RFC 2875.

PKI.why: The document defines POP algorithms for certification requests (PKCS #10, CRMF) so CAs can verify key possession for DH/ECDH keys, a PKI certificate-enrollment matter.
PKI.quote: The process of validating that the private key is held by the requester of the certificate is called Proof-of-Possession (POP).

elliptic curve.why: A full section specifies the static ECDH POP algorithm over elliptic-curve groups.
elliptic curve.quote: The Static ECDH POP algorithm is set up to use a KDF and a MAC.

ASN.1.why: The document defines ASN.1 structures, OIDs and two ASN.1 modules (2008 and 1988) for the algorithms.
ASN.1.quote: The ASN.1 structures associated with the Static DH POP algorithm are:

rejected.why: Certificates are the context, but the document defines POP signature algorithms for requests, not certificate profiles.
HMAC is used as the MAC building block, not specified here.
SHA hashes are parameters of the algorithms, not the subject.
The document explicitly chose not to create an ECDSA-parallel algorithm.
IssuerAndSerialNumber and MessageDigest are only imported from CMS modules.
The algorithms provide proof of possession, not key establishment, though DH shared secrets are used.

RFC6956.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Logical Function Block (LFB) Library
RFC6956.summary: Defines the base ForCES LFB class library (Ethernet processing, IP validation, IPv4/IPv6 forwarding, redirect, metadata dispatch, scheduler) with XML definitions conforming to the ForCES FE model, plus IANA registries for LFB class, metadata, exception and validate-error IDs.

ForCES.why: The whole document specifies the base LFB library for ForCES, defining LFB classes in XML per the FE model and protocol.
ForCES.quote: This document defines basic classes of Logical Function Blocks (LFBs) used in Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES).

rejected.why: IPv6 validation and forwarding LFBs are modelled, but the document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself.
Ethernet LFBs abstract ports for a router model; the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
ARP appears only as a use case where the CE handles ARP via redirect LFBs.
XML is merely the definition format for LFBs, not the subject.
ECMP is only a flag and output port supported by the LPM LFB; the document says it does not provide ECMP itself.
IANA registries are created, but that is boilerplate-type content secondary to the library.

gaps.name: ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lacks a ForCES tag, but the ForCES entry in the routing area is the closest fit; I used it. If it were absent the RFC would be a gap.

RFC6957.title: Duplicate Address Detection Proxy
RFC6957.summary: Specifies a DAD proxy function on the first-hop router (BNG) that keeps a Binding Table of IPv6 addresses and defends them, so Duplicate Address Detection works in split-horizon DSL/Fiber point-to-multipoint access networks.

neighbor discovery.why: The document specifies a proxy mechanism built on IPv6 Neighbor Discovery NS/NA messages, DAD and NUD, defining how the router defends addresses.
neighbor discovery.quote: Based on the DAD signaling, the first-hop router stores in a Binding Table all known IPv6 addresses used on a point-to-multipoint domain

SLAAC.why: DAD is defined in the stateless address autoconfiguration spec (RFC 4862), and the document adapts DAD for hosts that autoconfigure addresses in split-horizon networks.
SLAAC.quote: it is not completely reliable, and the goal of this document is not to fix DAD.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a complementary mechanism for source address spoofing protection in Security Considerations.
Only discussed as an interoperability limitation in Security Considerations.
DSL/Fiber access is the deployment context, but the document specifies an IPv6 ND mechanism rather than DSL technology.
RFC 6775 is discussed only as an existing solution that is insufficient.
Ethernet/VLAN is the underlying link layer; the document isn't about Ethernet itself.

RFC6958.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for Burst/Gap Loss Metric Reporting
RFC6958.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=20) that reports burst/gap packet loss metrics (burst durations, packets lost in bursts, number of bursts) for RTP streams, with SDP signaling and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block extending RFC 3611, with its field layout and semantics, so it belongs under RTCP.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block that allows the reporting of burst and gap loss metrics

rejected.why: SDP is only used to signal the new XR block via a small rtcp-xr attribute value; this is a minor part of the document, not its subject.
The block reports performance metrics and follows the RFC 6390 template, but the document is chiefly an RTCP block definition. The RTCP tag is the more specific fit.
RTP is the stream being measured. The document extends RTCP, which is already a child tag, so the parent is implied.
The IANA section only registers a block type and an SDP parameter. This is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The document does not define a payload format for any codec or media type. It only defines an RTCP report block.

RFC6959.title: Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) Threat Scope
RFC6959.summary: Informational threat-scope document for the SAVI effort, describing spoofed-source-address attack vectors, existing anti-spoofing tools and topological enforcement points, and the challenges for host-granularity source address validation.

SAVI.why: The whole document is the threat scope and starting-point analysis for SAVI: attacks enabled by source spoofing, current solutions, topological challenges, and host-granularity analysis.
SAVI.quote: The Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) effort aims to complement ingress filtering with finer-grained, standardized IP source address validation.

rejected.why: Flood and reflective DoS attacks are described as spoofing attack vectors, but the document is about source address validation, not DDoS mitigation or signalling.
DHCP snooping is mentioned as a way to build bindings, but DHCP is not specified or analysed in its own right.
ND and SLAAC are discussed as address-assignment mechanisms and poisoning targets; the document is not about them.
ARP spoofing is given as an example attack, but ARP is not the subject.
BCP 38 ingress filtering is referenced, but CIDR itself is not addressed.
The document is a threat analysis for SAVI. SAVI is the more specific tag and already covers it.

gaps.name: Ingress filtering / IP source address spoofing (BCP 38, uRPF)
gaps.why: The document is largely about source address spoofing and filtering (BCP 38, uRPF). The taxonomy has no tag for them apart from SAVI, which covers the in-scope subject.

RFC6960.title: X.509 Internet Public Key Infrastructure Online Certificate Status Protocol - OCSP
RFC6960.summary: RFC 6960 specifies the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP), which lets clients query a responder for the revocation status of X.509 certificates without using CRLs. It obsoletes RFC 2560 and 6277, and adds extensions such as preferred signature algorithms and extended revoked.

OCSP.why: The whole document specifies OCSP: request and response syntax, response statuses, extensions, authorized responders and ASN.1 modules.
OCSP.quote: The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) enables applications to determine the (revocation) state of identified certificates.

rejected.why: OCSP checks X.509 certificates and imports their syntax from RFC 5280. The document does not profile certificates, so the OCSP tag covers it.
Appendix A only describes carrying OCSP over HTTP GET and POST. HTTP is the transport here and nothing new is defined for it.
The ASN.1 modules are the protocol's own encoding. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Appendix C registers the ocsp-request and ocsp-response media types, but this is a small appendix and the document is not about registry rules.
TLS is mentioned only as an optional way to protect OCSP over HTTP.

RFC6961.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Multiple Certificate Status Request Extension
RFC6961.summary: Defines the TLS status_request_v2 extension (OCSP stapling v2) letting clients offer multiple certificate status methods and servers return OCSP responses for the whole certificate chain via a new ocsp_multi type.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension, status_request_v2, with new handshake message formats and a new IANA registry, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document defines the Transport Layer Security (TLS) Certificate Status Version 2 Extension to allow clients to specify and support several certificate status methods.

OCSP.why: It defines the ocsp_multi status type that carries OCSP responses for every certificate in the chain, and covers OCSP request extensions, nonce encoding and client handling of responses.
OCSP.quote: a new method based on the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) that servers can use to provide status information about not only the server's own certificate

rejected.why: Certificates and CRLs are the objects whose status is checked, but the document does not specify or profile X.509.
The PKI is the context. The document extends a TLS mechanism, not PKI itself. OCSP is the more specific tag.
DER-encoded ASN.1 types are used only as the encoding of OCSP structures.
EAP-TLS is mentioned only as an example of an application that might continue after an inconclusive response.

RFC6962.title: Certificate Transparency
RFC6962.summary: Defines the experimental Certificate Transparency protocol: public append-only Merkle-tree logs of TLS certificates, Signed Certificate Timestamps, a TLS extension for delivering SCTs, an HTTPS/JSON log API, and monitor/auditor roles.

certificate transparency.why: The whole document specifies certificate transparency logs, SCTs, Merkle trees, log client messages, monitors and auditors.
certificate transparency.quote: providing publicly auditable, append-only, untrusted logs of all issued certificates

TLS.why: Defines a new TLS extension, and rules for TLS servers and clients about requiring SCTs. TLS readers need this.
TLS.quote: The SCT can be sent during the TLS handshake using a TLS extension with type "signed_certificate_timestamp".

rejected.why: Precertificates and an X.509 extension are defined, but the document is about logging, not profiling certificates.
OCSP stapling is only one of three ways to carry SCTs, not the document's subject.
HTTPS GET/POST is just the transport for the log API.
JSON is only the encoding for log API messages.
SHA-256 is merely the hash used in the Merkle tree.

RFC6963.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for Examples
RFC6963.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace identifier "example" so authors and developers can mint URNs for documentation, testing and experimentation without conflicting with real URNs.

URN.why: The document defines and registers a new URN namespace (urn:example:{NSS}) with a completed namespace definition template, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: this document registers a formal namespace identifier of "example", similar to "example.com" and other domain names

rejected.why: It is compared to example.com and RFC 2606, but the document registers a URN NID, not a domain name.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level for this document. It adds one entry to the Formal URN Namespaces registry and does not give guidance on IANA registries.
URNs are a child of URI and the more specific URN tag is already chosen. The document only mentions URI processing in passing.
The NSS is specified as ASCII characters, but this is incidental to the syntax declaration.

RFC6964.title: Operational Guidance for IPv6 Deployment in IPv4 Sites Using the Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP)
RFC6964.summary: Informational operational guidance for deploying IPv6 inside predominantly IPv4 sites using ISATAP, covering SLAAC with shared and individual prefix models, loop avoidance, scaling, renumbering and path MTU.

ISATAP.why: The whole document is operational guidance for deploying ISATAP: advertising routers, hosts, PRL, prefix models, and administration.
ISATAP.quote: This document therefore provides operational guidance for deployment of IPv6 within predominantly IPv4 sites using the Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP).

rejected.why: SLAAC is the autoconfiguration mechanism ISATAP hosts use; the document is about ISATAP deployment, not SLAAC itself.
ISATAP is a child of this topic and is the more specific tag; the parent is implied.
Renumbering is a short section (Section 6) within the ISATAP guidance, not a main subject.
Path MTU is only briefly discussed for tunnels, deferring to RFC 4213.
6rd is mentioned only as a prefix source and an alternative approach.
IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation is the mechanism of ISATAP, covered by the ISATAP tag.

RFC6965.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Applicability: Use Cases and Design
RFC6965.summary: Informational RFC describing MPLS-TP applicability through use cases (metro access/aggregation, packet optical transport, mobile backhaul) and network design considerations such as provisioning mode, PW design and OAM tools.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is about where and how MPLS-TP is deployed and designed, so it belongs on the MPLS-TP page.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document describes the applicability of the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) with use case studies and network design considerations.

pseudowire.why: A full design section covers SS-PW vs MS-PW choice and PW protection in MPLS-TP networks.
pseudowire.quote: In general, PWs in MPLS-TP work the same as in IP/MPLS networks.  Both Single-Segment PW (SS-PW) and Multi-Segment PW (MS-PW) are supported.
pseudowire.section: 3.5. PW Design Considerations in MPLS-TP Networks

OAM.why: OAM tools (BFD CC, LDI, AIS) and end-to-end OAM consistency are a substantial design topic in the document.
OAM.quote: MPLS-TP provides both proactive and on-demand OAM tools.  As a proactive OAM fault management tool, BFD Connectivity Check (CC) can be sent at regular intervals
OAM.section: 3.6. Proactive and On-Demand MPLS-TP OAM Tools

rejected.why: The GMPLS control plane is mentioned as an optional dynamic provisioning mode, but the document does not specify or analyse GMPLS itself.
BFD is used as the proactive CC tool and discussed only as a design choice of interval; the document is not about BFD.
Mobile backhaul (2G/3G/LTE) is a use case, but the document concerns MPLS-TP transport, not IP over 3GPP systems.
L2VPN and L3VPN are only services listed as needing support; not the subject.
TE properties are mentioned in passing; not a focus of the document.
SONET/SDH is the legacy technology being replaced, not the subject.

RFC6967.title: Analysis of Potential Solutions for Revealing a Host Identifier (HOST_ID) in Shared Address Deployments
RFC6967.summary: Informational analysis of nine candidate mechanisms (IP-ID, IP option, TCP option, HTTP Forwarded header, PROXY protocol, port sets, HIP, ICMP notification, Ident) for revealing a HOST_ID to remote servers when CGN or proxies share an IP address, with privacy discussion and no recommendation.

NAT.why: The whole document addresses a problem caused by address sharing via NAT/CGN and analyses solutions for it. NAT is the broader subject here; CGN is a child tag but the document covers general address sharing, CGN and A+P.
NAT.quote: revealing a host identifier (denoted as HOST_ID) when a Carrier Grade NAT (CGN) or application proxies are involved in the path

privacy.why: Section 3 is a dedicated discussion of the privacy implications (fingerprinting, tracking, persistence) common to all the HOST_ID proposals.
privacy.quote: HOST_ID specification document(s) should explain the privacy impact of the solutions they specify

Ident.why: One of the nine analysed solutions is repurposing Ident to return a host identifier. The document analyses it in its own section.
Ident.quote: An implementation example may rely on the Identification Protocol (Ident) [RFC1413].

HIP.why: HIP is analysed as a candidate solution and found not viable. This gives it a section of its own, though a short one.
HIP.quote: [RFC5201] specifies an architecture that introduces a new namespace to convey identity information.

TCP.why: The TCP option approach is analysed in the most detail of all the candidates, covering option space, SYN versus ACK placement and Fast Open.
TCP.quote: The HOST_ID may be conveyed in a dedicated TCP option.

rejected.why: CGN is the main deployment context. The document is about address sharing generally (proxies, A+P), so the parent NAT tag fits better.
The Forwarded/XFF header is one of the nine options, but it is a minor part and the document specifies nothing about HTTP.
The IP-ID and IP option approaches touch the IPv4 header. IPv4 is not the subject, and RFC 6864 is only cited.
An ICMP Echo Request is used as a notification channel in one candidate. It is a substrate and nothing new about ICMP is defined.
A+P and port sets are mentioned, but the focus is host identification, not address architecture.
TLS appears only as the meaning of 'encrypted traffic' in the summary table.

RFC6968.title: FCAST: Object Delivery for the Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) and NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) Protocols
RFC6968.summary: RFC 6968 defines FCAST, an object (file) delivery application with Compound Object and Carousel Instance Descriptor formats, running over ALC/LCT or NORM reliable multicast transports.

reliable multicast.why: FCAST is a reliable multicast object delivery application defined over ALC/LCT and NORM. No child tag fits FCAST itself, so the parent topic is used.
reliable multicast.quote: FCAST reliable object (e.g., file) delivery application. It is designed to operate either on top of the underlying Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC)

ALC.why: FCAST/ALC is one of the two variants. The document specifies how to use ALC, including TOI handling and ALC-specific security guidance.
ALC.quote: FCAST/ALC, which relies on the Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) [RFC5775] and Layered Coding Transport (LCT) [RFC5651]

NORM.why: FCAST/NORM is the second variant. The document gives NORM-specific handling, including NormTransportId and NORM_INFO metadata carriage in Appendix B.
NORM.quote: FCAST/NORM, which relies on the NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) [RFC5740] transport protocol.

rejected.why: FLUTE is only mentioned as an alternative that FCAST differs from. FCAST is not an extension or profile of it.
ESP is recommended only in the security sections, which is boilerplate-level evidence.
TESLA is discussed only as one authentication option in the security considerations.
FCAST borrows the HTTP/1.1 metainformation format for its metadata but does not specify or extend HTTP.
FCAST reuses the Internet checksum in its header, but the document is not about the checksum.
FEC is transparent to FCAST and is mentioned only in passing.

RFC6969.title: OSPFv3 Instance ID Registry Update
RFC6969.summary: Updates the IANA OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values registry (from RFC 5838) by splitting the unassigned range 128-255 into Standards Action (128-191) and Private Use (192-255).

OSPFv3.why: The document changes the OSPFv3 Instance ID registry defined for OSPFv3 address families, so OSPFv3 readers would want it.
OSPFv3.quote: modifies the "Unassigned" number space in the IANA "OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values" registry by dividing it in two halves

IANA.why: The substance is a registry policy change: allocation procedures for ranges within an IANA registry.
IANA.quote: Instance IDs from 192-255 are Reserved for Private Use [RFC5226]. For the remaining unassigned values (128-191), the registration procedure is Standards Action.

rejected.why: IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses are mentioned only as an example motivating Private Use Instance IDs; the document is not about IPv6.
The parent is implied by OSPFv3, which is the more specific tag.

RFC6970.title: Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) Internet Gateway Device - Port Control Protocol Interworking Function (IGD-PCP IWF)
RFC6970.summary: Specifies the UPnP IGD-PCP Interworking Function embedded in CP routers, translating UPnP IGD WANIPConnection actions into PCP MAP requests to control an upstream provider NAT, with or without a NAT in the IGD.

PCP.why: The document specifies how UPnP IGD requests are mapped to PCP MAP requests, errors and lifetimes, with the IWF acting as a PCP client. It is a PCP interworking specification.
PCP.quote: A UPnP IGD-PCP IWF is required to be embedded in Customer Premises (CP) routers to allow for transparent NAT control

rejected.why: NAT is the context, including cascaded NAT, but the NAT port-mapping control protocol is PCP, which is the more specific tag.
The provider NAT is the PCP server being controlled. The document does not specify CGN behaviour.
Mentioned only as a deployment example where no NAT is in the IGD.
Mentioned only as a deployment example where no NAT is in the IGD.
Only mentioned as a PCP server discovery method and for state tie-in. The document is not about DHCP.

gaps.name: UPnP IGD (Universal Plug and Play Internet Gateway Device)
gaps.why: The document specifies behaviour of the UPnP IGD WANIPConnection service, but the taxonomy has no UPnP tag.

RFC6971.title: Depth-First Forwarding (DFF) in Unreliable Networks
RFC6971.summary: Specifies Depth-First Forwarding (DFF), an experimental forwarding-plane mechanism for IPv6 route-over and 6LoWPAN mesh-under networks that tries alternate next hops via depth-first search, with loop detection, to improve delivery in lossy, dynamic networks.

6LoWPAN.why: DFF is specified for mesh-under LoWPAN forwarding, defining a new LOWPAN_DFF dispatch header and mapping terms to RFC 4944. Constrained low-power wireless networks are its target.
6LoWPAN.quote: for "mesh-under" forwarding using the LoWPAN adaptation layer [RFC4944]

IPv6.why: The route-over mode defines a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option (IP_DFF) and modifies IPv6 forwarding behaviour.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies the Depth-First Forwarding (DFF) protocol for IPv6 networks, both for IPv6 forwarding [RFC2460]

routing architecture.why: DFF is a forwarding mechanism that complements routing protocols, interacting with the RIB and loop detection. It is not a routing protocol itself, so the general routing topic fits best.
routing architecture.quote: The protocol operates entirely on the forwarding plane but may interact with the routing plane.

rejected.why: Cited only as an example of the external neighborhood discovery that DFF depends on. It is not specified or extended here.
The networks are lossy and mesh-like, but DFF is a forwarding mechanism and not a MANET routing protocol.
IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation is used only to limit DFF scope at the domain boundary.
RPL is not mentioned. DFF works with unspecified routing protocols, and the deployments use a distance-vector protocol.
The ICMP Packet Too Big message is used only in MTU handling and is not the subject.

gaps.name: Packet forwarding / data-plane reliability
gaps.why: DFF is a forwarding-plane mechanism for reliable delivery over lossy links. The taxonomy has no forwarding tag, so it is covered only loosely by routing architecture.

RFC6972.title: Problem Statement and Requirements of the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol (PPSP)
RFC6972.summary: Informational problem statement and requirements document for the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol (PPSP), covering the tracker and peer protocols, use cases, and operational, management and security requirements.

PPSP.why: The whole document is the PPSP problem statement, scope, use cases and requirements for the tracker and peer protocols.
PPSP.quote: This document identifies problems associated with proprietary protocols; proposes the development of the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol (PPSP), which includes the tracker and peer protocols

rejected.why: CDN deployment and CDN/P2P collaboration appear as problems and use cases, but the document is about PPSP, not CDN technology or interconnection.
ALTO is mentioned once as a possible aid for the tracker's peer-list generation. It is not a subject of the document.
The document is about P2P streaming, and PPSP is the more specific tag under streaming. The generic P2P overlay tag is not needed.
P2P caches are discussed, but only as a contrast to HTTP caching and as a deployment use case, not as HTTP caching itself.
Section 6.2 lists operational and management requirements for PPSP, but these are a small part of a PPSP requirements document.

RFC6973.title: Privacy Considerations for Internet Protocols
RFC6973.summary: IAB informational guidance for protocol designers on analysing and documenting privacy considerations: terminology, communications model, threats, mitigations, a questionnaire, and a presence-protocol worked example.

privacy.why: The whole document is a privacy threat model, mitigation set and guideline questionnaire for protocol designers, which is the privacy topic.
privacy.quote: This document offers guidance for developing privacy considerations for inclusion in protocol specifications.

rejected.why: Presence is only the worked example in Section 8; the document is not about instant messaging or presence protocols.
SIP and P-Asserted-Identity appear only as illustrative examples of anonymity.
GEOPRIV and PIDF-LO are discussed only within the presence example.
EAP identity confidentiality is cited as an example only, not specified or analysed in its own right.
TLS session resumption is mentioned briefly as a correlation example.
The document is about privacy, not general security; privacy is the more specific tag.

RFC6974.title: Applicability of MPLS Transport Profile for Ring Topologies
RFC6974.summary: Informational RFC describing how MPLS-TP linear protection (RFC 6378) using SPMEs can provide wrapping and steering protection for P2P and P2MP paths traversing ring topologies, with no new protocols.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is about applying MPLS-TP linear protection, SPMEs and OAM to ring topologies, so it belongs on the MPLS-TP page.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document presents an applicability of existing MPLS protection mechanisms, both local and end-to-end, to the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) in ring topologies.

rejected.why: Fast Reroute (RFC 4090) is mentioned only as an analogy to wrapping. The document does not specify or analyse RSVP-TE.
Protection switching is the subject, not traffic engineering. MPLS-TP is the more specific tag.
OAM is used as the fault-detection trigger and defined in RFC 6371, but this document is not about OAM mechanisms.
MPLS-TP is the more specific tag and already implies its parent MPLS.
RSVP is cited only in passing for shared-explicit bandwidth reservation (RFC 2205).

gaps.name: Network protection and survivability (ring protection, linear protection switching)
gaps.why: The document is about protection switching, wrapping and steering for ring topologies. The taxonomy has no survivability or protection topic outside the MPLS-TP tag.

RFC6975.title: Signaling Cryptographic Algorithm Understanding in DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC)
RFC6975.summary: Defines three new EDNS0 options (DAU, DHU, N3U) by which validating DNS resolvers signal supported DNSSEC signing and hash algorithms to servers, so zone administrators can judge when to complete an algorithm rollover.

EDNS.why: The document's core content is the specification of new EDNS0 options, their wire format, and how resolvers and servers handle them.
EDNS.quote: This document defines three new EDNS0 options for a client to signal which digital signature and/or hash algorithms the client supports.
EDNS.section: 3. Signaling DNSSEC Algorithm Understood (DAU), DS Hash Understood (DHU), and NSEC3 Hash Understood (N3U) Using EDNS

DNSSEC.why: The options signal DNSSEC algorithm support for validators and support algorithm rollover, so the document is about DNSSEC operations and validation behaviour.
DNSSEC.quote: allow zone administrators to know when it is possible to complete an algorithm rollover in a DNSSEC-signed zone.

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen tags; implied, and the document is specifically about EDNS and DNSSEC rather than general DNS.
The IANA section only registers option codes 5, 6 and 7; this is boilerplate and not the subject.
Algorithms are only identified by code numbers for signalling; the document does not specify or analyse any algorithm.

RFC6976.title: Framework for Loop-Free Convergence Using the Ordered Forwarding Information Base (oFIB) Approach
RFC6976.summary: Informational framework describing the ordered FIB (oFIB) approach, which sequences FIB updates on link-state routers after non-urgent topology changes to prevent transient loops, with completion messages, state machine, and fallback (AAH) mechanisms.

IP fast reroute.why: The document describes loop-free convergence by ordered FIB updates, which is a method in the IP fast reroute family and is meant to be combined with FRR repair paths. The taxonomy's IP fast reroute tag is the closest fit for this subject.
IP fast reroute.quote: Additional work is needed to specify the necessary routing protocol extensions necessary to support this IP fast reroute (FRR) method before implementation or deployment.

routing architecture.why: The document covers general link-state convergence design, including rank computation, timers, state machines and fallback to conventional convergence. This is routing design that is not tied to one protocol.
routing architecture.quote: prevents the transient loops that would otherwise occur during topology changes. It does this by correctly sequencing the forwarding information base (FIB) updates on the routers.

rejected.why: OSPF is cited only as an example link-state protocol. The mechanism is protocol-independent and nothing in OSPF is specified or extended.
IS-IS is cited only as an example link-state protocol. The mechanism is protocol-independent and nothing in IS-IS is specified or extended.
RSVP-TE FRR is mentioned only as one repair mechanism. The document does not address traffic engineering.
Appendix B covers synchronizing convergence timer values across routers. That is about agreeing on a configuration value, not synchronizing clocks.

gaps.name: Loop-free convergence / ordered FIB (oFIB)
gaps.why: The core subject is loop-free convergence of link-state routing protocols by ordering FIB updates. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so IP fast reroute and routing architecture are only approximate.

RFC6977.title: Triggering DHCPv6 Reconfiguration from Relay Agents
RFC6977.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 Reconfigure-Request and Reconfigure-Reply messages and the Link Address Option so a relay agent can prompt a server to send a Reconfigure message to clients when relay-supplied configuration changes.

DHCPv6.why: The document extends DHCPv6 with new message types, a new option, and relay and server behaviour for triggering Reconfigure.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines two new DHCPv6 messages: Reconfigure-Request and Reconfigure-Reply.

rejected.why: RADIUS CoA is only used as an example trigger for the configuration change in the problem statement. The document does not specify or extend it.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection option.
DS-Lite AFTR name is only an example of relay-supplied configuration data.
DHCPv6 is the more specific tag and the document concerns only DHCPv6.

RFC6978.title: A TCP Authentication Option Extension for NAT Traversal
RFC6978.summary: Experimental extension to TCP-AO (TCP-AO-NAT) that adds localNAT/remoteNAT flags to the MKT so addresses and ports are zeroed when computing traffic keys and MACs, allowing TCP-AO connections to traverse NATs/NAPTs.

TCP.why: The document extends TCP-AO, a TCP option for segment authentication, changing how traffic keys and MACs are computed. No narrower TCP tag fits.
TCP.quote: an extension to the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) [RFC5925] called TCP-AO-NAT to support its use in the presence of Network Address Translators

NAT.why: The whole purpose is making TCP-AO work through NATs/NAPTs, including client and server flag usage, symmetric NATs, and ALG caveats.
NAT.quote: TCP-AO without TCP-AO-NAT extensions would be sensitive to these modifications and would discard authenticated segments.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one potential application; the document does not specify anything about Multipath TCP.
TCP-AO is segment authentication, but the TCP tag is more specific and the topic would be redundant.
Cited only for the term 'symmetric NATs'; the document is not about STUN.
The document changes the inputs to traffic key derivation but leaves the KDF and key generation algorithms unchanged, so key management is not its subject.

RFC6979.title: Deterministic Usage of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)
RFC6979.summary: RFC 6979 specifies a deterministic procedure, based on HMAC_DRBG, for generating the per-signature nonce k in DSA and ECDSA. The signatures stay compatible with unmodified verifiers. The RFC includes test vectors and sample code.

ECDSA.why: The document defines deterministic signature generation for ECDSA. It gives ECDSA test vectors for many NIST curves.
ECDSA.quote: Such signatures are compatible with standard Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) digital signatures

randomness.why: The document's purpose is to remove the need for a random source at signing time. It does this by deriving k deterministically, and it discusses the entropy requirements involved.
randomness.quote: they do not need access to a source of high-quality randomness

rejected.why: HMAC is only the building block used inside the HMAC_DRBG construction. The document does not specify or extend HMAC.
ECDSA is the more specific tag. The curves appear only as parameters in the test vectors.
The SHA hash functions are only used as inputs to the procedure and in the test vectors.
DER encoding of the signature is mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm)
gaps.why: The document covers DSA equally with ECDSA, but the taxonomy has no DSA tag.

gaps.name: Digital signatures / deterministic signature generation
gaps.why: There is no general tag for digital signature schemes. The nearest are the RSA and ECDSA technology tags.

RFC6980.title: Security Implications of IPv6 Fragmentation with IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
RFC6980.summary: RFC 6980 analyses security problems of IPv6 fragmentation with Neighbor Discovery and SEND, updates RFC 4861 to forbid the Fragment Header in ND messages, and updates RFC 3971 with advice on fragmented Certification Path Advertisements.

neighbor discovery.why: The document updates RFC 4861 to forbid fragmentation in NS, NA, RS, RA and Redirect messages, and to ignore fragmented ones.
neighbor discovery.quote: Nodes MUST NOT employ IPv6 fragmentation for sending any of the following Neighbor Discovery and SEcure Neighbor Discovery messages

SEND.why: A substantial part covers SEND and its Certification Path Advertisement messages, updating RFC 3971 with SHOULD NOT advice on fragmented CPAs.
SEND.quote: formally updates RFC 3971 by providing advice on the use of IPv6 fragmentation with SEND

rejected.why: IPv6 fragmentation is the subject, but the more specific neighbor discovery tag covers the document; the parent is implied.
ND messages are ICMPv6, but the document is not about ICMP itself.
Mentions RA-Guard and monitoring tools, but only as context for the ND fragmentation rule.
Security motivates the document, but the specific ND and SEND tags cover it better.
Certificates appear only in message size estimates in the appendix.
Certificate sizes are discussed only to estimate message length; nothing about the certificate format.

RFC6981.title: A Framework for IP and MPLS Fast Reroute Using Not-Via Addresses
RFC6981.summary: An informational framework describing IP and MPLS fast reroute using not-via addresses and single-level encapsulation to repair link, node and SRLG failures, published as a document of record.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document specifies the not-via IPFRR approach, including repair computation, SRLG and LAN failures, and interaction with LFAs.
IP fast reroute.quote: presents an illustrative framework for providing fast reroute in an IP or MPLS network through encapsulation and forwarding to "not-via" addresses

rejected.why: Section 9 only notes that LDP distributes labels for not-via addresses; LDP is a substrate, not the subject.
MPLS fast reroute is covered in one short section; the document is about IP fast reroute generally.
Link-state IGPs are assumed for computation but no specific protocol is specified.
Encapsulation types (IP-in-IP, GRE, L2TPv3) are only listed as usable options in a short section.
BFD is mentioned only as a failure-detection or diagnostic aid.
The more specific IP fast reroute tag fits; the parent is implied.

RFC6982.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section
RFC6982.summary: RFC 6982 defines an experimental process in which Internet-Draft authors add an Implementation Status section recording known implementations, so reviewers and working groups can weigh running code in the IETF standards process.

IETF process.why: The document defines an optional step in IETF document development, including how working groups use implementation information, and runs it as a process experiment. It is about IETF standards process and procedures.
IETF process.quote: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section.

rejected.why: The Implementation Status section is meant to be removed before RFC publication. The document is about Internet-Draft practice, not RFC format or publication.
It quotes 'rough consensus and running code' but does not define terms or serve as a glossary.
There is no IANA content. The Security Considerations is boilerplate and nothing here concerns registries.

RFC6983.title: Models for HTTP-Adaptive-Streaming-Aware Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI)
RFC6983.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC analysing how HTTP Adaptive Streaming affects CDN Interconnection (CDNI) interfaces, presenting options and recommendations for file management, acquisition, request routing, logging, URL signing and purge.

CDN.why: The whole document analyses CDN interconnection (CDNI metadata, logging, request routing, control interfaces) in the presence of HAS, so it belongs on the CDN page.
CDN.quote: This document presents thoughts on the potential impact of supporting HTTP Adaptive Streaming (HAS) technologies in Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI) scenarios.

streaming.why: HAS (HLS, Smooth Streaming, DASH) chunking, manifest files and live vs VoD delivery are a substantial subject of the document, so readers of media streaming delivery would want it.
streaming.quote: HTTP Adaptive Streaming is an umbrella term for various HTTP-based streaming technologies that allow a client to adaptively switch between multiple bitrates

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate for HAS delivery and redirection; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Cookies are discussed as one URL-signing authorization option (Option 5.4/5.5), but not a main subject.
Relative and absolute URLs in manifests and URL signing are discussed, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
Cacheability of manifests is mentioned incidentally; the document focuses on CDNI, not HTTP caching semantics.
RTSP is mentioned only as a traditional streaming method contrasted with HAS.
URL signing is a substantial section, but it is one of six problem areas about CDNI/HAS rather than a general authorization treatment.

gaps.name: HTTP Adaptive Streaming (HAS) / DASH / HLS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for HTTP adaptive streaming technologies; the generic 'streaming' topic is the closest fit.

RFC6984.title: Interoperability Report for Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES)
RFC6984.summary: Reports results of the second ForCES interoperability test (Feb 2011) among three implementations covering LFB operations, TML over IPsec, CE high availability and OSPF packet forwarding, updating RFC 6053.

ForCES.why: The whole document reports interoperability testing of the ForCES protocol, FE model, TML, LFB library and CE high availability.
ForCES.quote: This document captures the results of the second interoperability test of the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES)

rejected.why: IPsec (via Racoon/IKEv2) secured the TML channel in one scenario, but it is a substrate and nothing new is specified about IPsec.
OSPF was run only as a test application to exercise forwarding LFBs; the document is not about OSPF.
SCTP is the transport of the ForCES TML and is not itself examined.
The FE model is defined in XML but the document does not address XML.
Wireshark and tcpdump were used only as verification tools.

gaps.name: ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a ForCES tag in the routing subtree, but I'm unsure it matches exactly. The ForCES tag I used must be verified against the taxonomy, where it appears as 'ForCES' under routing.

RFC6985.title: IMIX Genome: Specification of Variable Packet Sizes for Additional Testing
RFC6985.summary: Defines the IMIX Genome, a compact notation for specifying the exact repeating sequence of packet sizes used in mixed-size benchmarking load tests, plus custom IMIX and alternatives for long or pseudorandom sequences.

benchmarking.why: The document extends RFC 2544-style benchmarking methodology by specifying repeatable mixed packet-size test conditions for network devices.
benchmarking.quote: This memo defines a method to unambiguously specify the sequence of packet sizes used in a load test.

rejected.why: The subject is test-stimulus specification for lab device benchmarking, which falls under benchmarking rather than general performance measurement.
RFC 5470 is only mentioned as one way to gather packet-size information; the document is not about IPFIX.
Ethernet frame sizes and jumbo frame CRC are mentioned in passing only as packet-size context.

RFC6986.title: GOST R 34.11-2012: Hash Function
RFC6986.summary: Informational RFC describing the Russian GOST R 34.11-2012 (Streebog) cryptographic hash function with 256- and 512-bit outputs, including parameters, round functions, procedure and test examples; updates RFC 5831.

GOST.why: The whole document specifies the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function, one of the Russian GOST cryptographic algorithms, with parameters, transformations and test vectors.
GOST.quote: The Russian Federal standard hash function (GOST R 34.11-2012) establishes the hash-function algorithm and the hash-function calculation procedure

rejected.why: Only a different hash family; the document is not about SHA.
GOST R 34.10-2012 signatures are mentioned as a use of the hash, but the document does not specify them or elliptic curves.
Parent of GOST, which is implied and more specific.

RFC6987.title: OSPF Stub Router Advertisement
RFC6987.summary: Informational RFC (obsoleting RFC 3137) describing how an OSPF router can advertise itself as a stub router by setting non-stub link costs to MaxLinkMetric (0xffff), or via the OSPFv3 R-bit, so it is not used for transit traffic.

OSPF.why: The whole document specifies an OSPF technique (stub router advertisement via MaxLinkMetric in router-LSAs) applicable to OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
OSPF.quote: router X announces its router-LSA to the neighbors with the cost of all non-stub links (links of the types other than 3) being set to MaxLinkMetric

OSPFv3.why: The document covers the OSPFv3 R-bit as an alternative technique and discusses its behaviour compared to MaxLinkMetric in deployment considerations.
OSPFv3.quote: OSPFv3 [RFC5340] introduces additional options to provide similar control of the forwarding topology; the R-bit provides an indication of whether a router is active

rejected.why: Traffic engineering is only mentioned as one possible administrative reason for using stub router advertisement; the document is not about TE.
The document defines a single OSPF mechanism, not routing architecture or design principles; the OSPF tag fits more specifically.
Security Considerations is boilerplate saying no new issues; the document is about routing operations, not security.

RFC6988.title: Requirements for Energy Management
RFC6988.summary: RFC 6988 lists requirements that future Energy Management standards (monitoring and control of power, energy, Power States, batteries, and reporting on or controlling other entities) must meet.

energy management.why: The whole document is a requirements list for monitoring and controlling energy use, Power States, power supply and batteries of networked devices.
energy management.quote: This document defines requirements for standards specifications for Energy Management, both monitoring functions and control functions.

rejected.why: SNMP is cited only as an example of a pull-based protocol and for its security requirements. The document does not specify or extend it.
MIB modules such as the Entity MIB and Power Ethernet MIB are referenced only for reusing identifiers. No MIB is defined here.
IPFIX is mentioned once as an example of push-based reporting. It is not the subject of the document.
NTP is mentioned only as a way to synchronize time between entities.
The document mentions ecological motivation, but it is about management requirements for devices, not the environmental impact of Internet infrastructure.

RFC6989.title: Additional Diffie-Hellman Tests for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC6989.summary: RFC 6989 updates IKEv2 (RFC 5996) by adding mandatory recipient tests on received Diffie-Hellman public values for MODP, small-subgroup and elliptic curve groups, specifying error behaviour, and describing timing side-channel countermeasures when DH keys are reused.

IKE.why: The document updates IKEv2 (RFC 5996), defining required checks on KE payloads and the protocol behaviour on test failure. IKE is the most specific tag for this.
IKE.quote: This document adds a small number of mandatory tests required for the secure operation of the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2) with elliptic curve groups.

elliptic curve.why: A substantial part of the document defines public-value validation for elliptic curve DH groups, which is the main motivation for the update.
elliptic curve.quote: A receiving peer MUST check that its peer's public value is valid; that is, the x and y parameters from the peer's public value satisfy the curve equation

rejected.why: IKE is the more specific tag and IPsec is implied as its ancestor. The document does not address ESP or AH.
The document covers DH key exchange validation, but the specific IKE tag already captures it.
Unrelated. The document concerns classical DH and ECDH.
The IANA section only adds a column to the IKEv2 DH group registry. This is boilerplate-level and is not the main subject.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key exchange / DH group validation
gaps.why: The document is about DH public value tests, small-subgroup and timing attacks, but the taxonomy has no Diffie-Hellman tag. The nearest ones are IKE, elliptic curve and key management.

RFC6990.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for MPEG-2 Transport Stream (TS) Program Specific Information (PSI) Independent Decodability Statistics Metrics Reporting
RFC6990.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=22) that reports counts of ETSI TR 101 290 PSI-independent MPEG-2 TS decodability errors for MPEG-2 TS carried over RTP, plus its SDP signalling parameter.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block, extending RTCP as defined in RFC 3611, with its format and fields.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of MPEG-2 TS decodability statistics metrics

rejected.why: The document adds only a small rtcp-xr attribute value for signalling. SDP is a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
RTP is the transport the metrics describe. The document extends RTCP, which sits under RTP, so the more specific RTCP tag covers it.
IPTV is mentioned only as the motivating deployment. The document does not specify IPTV service delivery.
The block does report metrics, but it is a specific RTCP XR block. The RTCP tag fits it better, and the document only follows the metrics framework guidelines.
SRTP/SAVPF appears only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the block.
The document uses the ETSI DVB measurement guidelines as a source of metrics. It does not cover IP over DVB links.

gaps.name: MPEG-2 Transport Stream
gaps.why: The document is about reporting MPEG-2 TS decodability errors, but the taxonomy has no tag for the MPEG-2 TS container or for ETSI TR 101 290 monitoring.

RFC6991.title: Common YANG Data Types
RFC6991.summary: RFC 6991 defines the ietf-yang-types and ietf-inet-types YANG modules, a collection of common derived data types (counters, gauges, timestamps, MAC/IP addresses, domain names, URIs) for use in YANG models, obsoleting RFC 6021.

YANG.why: The whole document is YANG modules of reusable derived types; readers of the YANG subject would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document introduces a collection of common data types to be used with the YANG data modeling language.

MIB.why: Each type is mapped to an equivalent SMIv2 type or textual convention, bridging MIB modules and YANG; useful to MIB/SMI readers.
MIB.quote: the types defined in the ietf-yang-types YANG module and the corresponding SMIv2 types

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the context that YANG models; the document defines no NETCONF behaviour.
ipv6-address and prefix types are defined, but only as data types, not about IPv6 itself.
domain-name type represents DNS names but the document does not specify DNS.
A uuid typedef is included, but it is one minor type referencing RFC 4122.
The uri typedef is one type among many; the document does not define URI syntax.
date-and-time profiles RFC 3339, but it is a single typedef, not the document's subject.

RFC6992.title: Routing for IPv4-Embedded IPv6 Packets
RFC6992.summary: Informational RFC describing how to route IPv4 packets across an IPv6-only network by translating to IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses (RFC 6145/6052) and advertising them via a separate OSPFv3 instance (RFC 5838) with its own routing table.

OSPFv3.why: The core of the document is using a dedicated OSPFv3 instance (Instance ID, AF-bit, AS-External-LSAs, DN bit) to route IPv4-embedded IPv6 prefixes.
OSPFv3.quote: a separate OSPFv3 instance is configured in the IPv6 network [RFC5838]

IPv6 transition.why: It addresses IPv4/IPv6 coexistence by interconnecting IPv4 client networks across an IPv6-only core using stateless header translation and IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document describes a routing scenario where IPv4 packets are transported over an IPv6 network

rejected.why: RFC 5565 softwire mesh is discussed only as the alternative tunnel-based solution, not what this document specifies.
Stateless translation per RFC 6145 is used as a building block, but the document is about routing, not the translation algorithm.
IBGP is mentioned only as the RFC 5565 alternative.
Uses the RFC 6052 addressing but the translation is stateless and no NAT64 is specified.
Covered more specifically by OSPFv3 and IPv6 transition tags.
MTU handling is a brief section that only recommends path discovery; not a main subject.

RFC6993.title: Instant Messaging and Presence Purpose for the Call-Info Header Field in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC6993.summary: Defines and registers the "impp" value for the "purpose" parameter of the SIP Call-Info header field, so SIP endpoints can advertise their XMPP (or other IM/presence) URIs for CUSAX interoperability.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP by registering a new Call-Info purpose value; SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: defines and registers a value of "impp" ("instant messaging and presence protocol") for the "purpose" header field parameter of the Call-Info header field

XMPP.why: The use case is advertising XMPP addresses in SIP for combined SIP/XMPP (CUSAX) endpoints, so XMPP readers would want it.
XMPP.quote: advertise each endpoint's SIP address over XMPP and each endpoint's XMPP address over SIP

rejected.why: The parent is implied by XMPP, so it is not listed separately.
URIs are only carried in the header value; the document defines nothing about URI syntax.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection mechanism.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection mechanism.
The registration is boilerplate-level; the document is about the SIP header parameter value, not IANA policy.
The document is not about SIMPLE presence event packages or PIDF; it only advertises IM/presence URIs.

RFC6994.title: Shared Use of Experimental TCP Options
RFC6994.summary: RFC 6994 defines an experiment identifier (ExID) field for the TCP experimental option codepoints 253 and 254 so multiple TCP extensions can share them, and creates an IANA ExID registry.

TCP.why: The document specifies a change to the TCP option structure and option processing rules (ExID in SYN segments, ignoring unmatched ExIDs). It is a TCP extension, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: This document extends the option structure for experimental codepoints (253, 254) with an experiment identifier (ExID), which is either 2 or 4 bytes in length.

rejected.why: The IANA registry for ExIDs is created here, but it is a TCP-specific registry. The document is not about IANA registry practice in general, and the IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like.
Mentioned only as an example of an option that squats on unassigned codepoints. The document is not about it.
Mentioned only as an example of a protocol that uses magic numbers.
Mentioned only in the rationale section, which discusses Private Enterprise Numbers as an alternative ID space.

RFC6996.title: Autonomous System (AS) Reservation for Private Use
RFC6996.summary: BCP that documents the IANA reservation of two Private Use AS number ranges (16-bit and 32-bit) and gives operational guidance on removing them from AS paths before advertising to the global Internet, updating RFC 1930 Section 10.

BGP.why: The document's operational guidance concerns BGP AS_PATH handling, EBGP speakers and four-octet AS support for Private Use ASNs, so readers of BGP operations would want it.
BGP.quote: Private Use ASNs MUST be removed from AS path attributes (including AS4_PATH if utilizing a four-octet AS number space) before being advertised to the global Internet.

rejected.why: The IANA registry reservation is the mechanism for the ASN ranges, but the document is about the BGP operational use of Private Use ASNs, not IANA registry stewardship or guidance. It is also covered only in the IANA Considerations boilerplate.
ASNs are not IP address architecture, so the addressing topic does not fit.
The document is about a BGP resource reservation and its operational handling, not routing architecture or scalability.
The security section says Private Use ASNs raise no unique concerns, and that section is boilerplate in any case.

gaps.name: Autonomous System numbers
gaps.why: The document is about AS number reservation and registration, and the taxonomy has no tag for AS numbers or number resources. BGP is the closest fit.

RFC6997.title: Reactive Discovery of Point-to-Point Routes in Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC6997.summary: Experimental RFC defining P2P-RPL, a reactive on-demand point-to-point route discovery mechanism for RPL in low-power and lossy networks, using temporary DAGs, a new P2P mode of operation, the P2P-RDO option, and P2P-DRO/DRO-ACK messages.

RPL.why: The document extends RPL with a new Mode of Operation, new control message option and messages, and security rules, so it is squarely about RPL.
RPL.quote: This document specifies a point-to-point route discovery mechanism, complementary to the Routing Protocol for Low-power and Lossy Networks (RPL) core functionality.

rejected.why: IPv6 routers and addresses are the substrate; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
The more specific RPL tag fits; this is not general routing architecture.
LLN context only; the RPL tag is the more specific subject and no IoT-general guidance is given.
Cost measurement of existing routes is only referenced to RFC 6998, not specified here.
Secure operation is a section, but it is RPL's own security framework rather than a routing security topic in its own right.

gaps.name: RPL (IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no RPL tag under IoT (it lists 6LoWPAN, RPL as 'RPL' under IoT in the hierarchy), so the id used must match; if absent, this RFC's main subject is unrepresented.

RFC6998.title: A Mechanism to Measure the Routing Metrics along a Point-to-Point Route in a Low-Power and Lossy Network
RFC6998.summary: Experimental RFC defining the RPL Measurement Object control message, which lets an RPL router measure aggregated routing metrics along an existing point-to-point route in a low-power lossy network so it can decide whether to run P2P-RPL discovery.

RPL.why: The document extends RPL with new control messages (Measurement Object and Secure MO), defines their processing at start, intermediate and end points, and registers new RPL control codes.
RPL.quote: This document specifies a mechanism that enables a Routing Protocol for Low-power and Lossy Networks (RPL) router to measure the aggregated values of given routing metrics

rejected.why: It measures routing metrics (ETX, hop count) along a route using RPL control messages. It is not a general active or passive network performance measurement method.
RPL runs over IPv6 and the document uses IPv6 addresses and source routes, but it does not specify IPv6 itself.
ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable is only mentioned as an optional error message, so ICMP is not a subject of the document.
Secure MO is a small part of the document and just reuses the existing RPL security framework. The document does not secure routing in general.

gaps.name: RPL (IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks) / LLN routing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RPL tag only under IoT as 'RPL'. I used that id because it exists, but there is no tag for the P2P-RPL route discovery and metrics work in ROLL.

RFC7001.title: Message Header Field for Indicating Message Authentication Status
RFC7001.summary: Defines the Authentication-Results email header field, which conveys the results of message authentication checks (DKIM, SPF, Sender ID, iprev, SMTP AUTH) from border MTAs to MUAs and downstream filters, along with its trust model, header removal rules, and IANA registries.

email authentication.why: The whole document defines a common framework for reporting email authentication results across methods (DKIM, SPF, etc.) and the trust handling around it. No single method child fits, so the parent is used.
email authentication.quote: specifies a message header field called Authentication-Results for use with electronic mail messages to indicate the results of message authentication efforts

message format.why: The document specifies a new trace header field with ABNF syntax, placement rules and IANA header registration, which is Internet message header format work.
message format.quote: It is a Structured Header Field as defined in Internet Message Format ([MAIL]), and thus all of the related definitions in that document apply.

rejected.why: DKIM is one of several methods whose results are reported; the document does not specify or extend DKIM itself.
SPF results are referenced and carried in the header field, but SPF is not specified or extended here.
SMTP is the substrate for mail transfer and SMTP AUTH is one reported method; the document does not extend SMTP.
DNS is used by the iprev method, but the document defines nothing new about DNS itself.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like registrations supporting the header field, not the main subject.
Spam is mentioned only as motivation and in security considerations; the document is not about spam filtering.

RFC7002.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for Discard Count Metric Reporting
RFC7002.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=24) that reports a count of RTP packets discarded at the receiver (duplicate, too early, or too late), with SDP signaling and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block, its fields and semantics, which is an extension of RTCP extended reports.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of a simple discard count metric

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport being monitored; the document extends RTCP rather than RTP itself, and RTCP is the more specific tag.
SDP is used only to signal the new block via an rtcp-xr attribute value; this is a small part of the document and not the subject.
The metric follows the RFC 6390 performance metric guidelines, but the document is about the RTCP XR block format, and the RTCP tag already covers it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection option.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here, not the main body.

RFC7003.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for Burst/Gap Discard Metric Reporting
RFC7003.summary: Defines an RTCP XR block (BT=20) reporting burst/gap packet discard metrics from receiver jitter buffers, with SDP signaling via rtcp-xr and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block type, extending RTCP reporting.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of burst and gap discard metrics

performance measurement.why: The block defines transport-related end-system performance metrics (burst/gap discard rates), with an appendix using the RFC 6390 metric template.
performance measurement.quote: The Performance Metrics Framework [RFC6390] provides guidance on the definition and specification of performance metrics.

rejected.why: RTCP is a child of RTP in the taxonomy, so RTP is implied. The RTCP tag is more specific.
The SDP rtcp-xr attribute extension is a small signaling piece. The document does not centre on SDP.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new block type and SDP parameter.
The document defines no media payload format.
FEC and retransmission are mentioned only to say when the metrics apply.

RFC7004.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Blocks for Summary Statistics Metrics Reporting
RFC7004.summary: Defines three RTCP XR block types (burst/gap loss summary, burst/gap discard summary, and frame impairment statistics summary) for reporting summary statistics metrics in RTP applications, plus SDP rtcp-xr signalling values.

RTCP.why: The document specifies new RTCP XR report blocks extending RFC 3611, which is the core subject of the RTCP tag.
RTCP.quote: This document defines three RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) blocks that allow the reporting of loss, duplication, and discard summary statistics metrics
