SDP.why: The document extends the SDP rtcp-xr attribute with new xr-format values and describes offer/answer usage, a modest but real SDP extension.
SDP.quote: This section augments the SDP [RFC4566] attribute "rtcp-xr" defined in Section 5.1 of [RFC3611] by providing three additional values of "xr-format"

rejected.why: RTP is the stream being measured, but the document is about RTCP reporting blocks, so the more specific RTCP tag fits.
The blocks report performance metrics, but this is RTCP-specific metric reporting under the RTP monitoring framework, not general network performance measurement methodology.
Video frame types (key/derived frames) are discussed only to define what is counted. The document does not define any codec.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: RTCP XR (RTCP Extended Reports) / RTP monitoring framework
gaps.why: The taxonomy has RTCP, with parent RTP, but I used 'RTCP' as the tag id. Wait: the taxonomy lists RTCP as a tech under RTP, so it is valid. No real gap exists beyond a lack of a dedicated tag for RTCP XR metric blocks.

RFC7005.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for De-Jitter Buffer Metric Reporting
RFC7005.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=23) that reports de-jitter buffer metrics (nominal, maximum, high-water and low-water delay) from RTP receivers, with SDP signalling and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document extends RTCP by defining a new XR report block, including its format and field semantics. RTCP is the most specific tag for XR block definitions.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of de-jitter buffer metrics for a range of RTP applications.

performance measurement.why: The block defines performance metrics, written using the RFC 6390 metric template (Appendix A). Readers of performance metrics for RTP would want it.
performance measurement.quote: The new block type provides information on de-jitter buffer configuration and performance.

rejected.why: SDP is used only to signal the XR block via a new rtcp-xr attribute value. That is a small addition and SDP is not the subject of the document.
RTP is the media transport being monitored. The document specifies an RTCP report block, which is tagged under RTCP.
The IANA section registers a block type and an SDP parameter. This is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.

RFC7006.title: Miscellaneous Capabilities Negotiation in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC7006.summary: RFC 7006 extends the SDP Capability Negotiation framework with new capability attributes (bcap, ccap, icap), configuration parameters and option tags to negotiate bandwidth, connection data and title lines within SDP offer/answer.

SDP.why: The document defines new SDP attributes and extends SDP capability negotiation within the offer/answer model, so it is about SDP.
SDP.quote: this memo provides a mechanism to negotiate bandwidth ("b="), connection data ("c="), and session or media titles ("i=")

rejected.why: RTP appears only in examples and as a motivating use of capability negotiation; the document is not about it.
ICE is mentioned only to say it remains the Standards Track mechanism for negotiating IP addresses; the document does not specify it.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the syntax, not a subject of the document.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the main body of the document.
SIP is not discussed. SDP offer/answer is the context here, and SIP is not specified or profiled.

RFC7007.title: Update to Remove DVI4 from the Recommended Codecs for the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences with Minimal Control (RTP/AVP)
RFC7007.summary: Updates RFC 3551 to remove the SHOULD for DVI4 support in the RTP/AVP profile, leaving PCMU as the sole recommended minimum audio codec.

RTP.why: The document amends the RTP/AVP profile (RFC 3551) and by extension the SAVP, AVPF and SAVPF profiles, so it is about RTP profile specification.
RTP.quote: Audio applications operating under this profile SHOULD, at a minimum, be able to send and/or receive payload type 0 (PCMU).

G.711.why: PCMU is G.711 mu-law. The document makes it the sole recommended minimum codec and notes that some environments necessitate support for it.

rejected.why: RTP/SAVP is only mentioned as a profile built on RTP/AVP that is affected by extension. The document says nothing specific about secure RTP.
RTP/AVPF is mentioned only as a dependent profile. The document does not address RTCP feedback.
The document is about a codec recommendation within an RTP profile, and G.711 is the more specific tag. It does not define any codec.
No payload format is defined or changed. Only the recommended minimum codec set is altered.

RFC7008.title: A Description of the KCipher-2 Encryption Algorithm
RFC7008.summary: RFC 7008 describes the KCipher-2 stream cipher (128-bit key, 128-bit IV), giving its internal state, init/next/stream operations, S-box and GF(2^32) multiplication tables, a C reference implementation and test vectors.

cryptography.why: The document specifies a symmetric stream cipher algorithm in full. No narrower taxonomy tag fits KCipher-2, so the cryptography topic is applied directly.
cryptography.quote: KCipher-2 is a stream cipher with a 128-bit key and a 128-bit initialization vector.

rejected.why: sub_K2 reuses the AES S-box and MixColumn operations as components, but the document specifies a different cipher, not AES or its modes.
The document defines a keystream generator for encryption. It does not address randomness requirements or generation.
Key expansion is part of the cipher's own initialization. The document does not address key establishment or provisioning.

gaps.name: stream cipher
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for stream ciphers. Only the generic cryptography topic is available, so the document cannot be indexed more specifically.

RFC7009.title: OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation
RFC7009.summary: RFC 7009 defines an OAuth 2.0 token revocation endpoint that lets clients tell the authorization server a refresh or access token is no longer needed, with request/response formats, an error code, and a token type hints registry.

OAuth.why: The whole document extends OAuth 2.0 with a token revocation endpoint, including request parameters, responses, errors and implementation notes on token styles.
OAuth.quote: This document proposes an additional endpoint for OAuth authorization servers, which allows clients to notify the authorization server that a previously obtained refresh or access token is no longer needed.

rejected.why: The revocation request is an HTTP POST, but HTTP is only the substrate; nothing new is defined about HTTP itself.
TLS is required for the endpoint but only as a security mechanism, with no new TLS definitions.
Access tokens may be self-contained, but JWT is not mentioned or specified.
The IANA registry sections are boilerplate-like and the document is not about IANA process in its own right.
The CORS/JSONP section is a small side note and not the subject of the document.

RFC7010.title: IPv6 Site Renumbering Gap Analysis
RFC7010.summary: A 6renum gap analysis of existing mechanisms for planned IPv6 site renumbering, organized by renumbering steps (prefix management, address configuration, updating address-relevant entries, event management, multicast and mobility) and listing solvable and unsolvable gaps.

renumbering.why: The whole document is a gap analysis of site renumbering procedures, which is exactly the renumbering topic.
renumbering.quote: This document briefly introduces the existing mechanisms that could be utilized for IPv6 site renumbering and tries to cover most of the explicit issues and requirements

SLAAC.why: A substantial section analyses SLAAC/DHCPv6 interaction and RA M/O flag ambiguity for renumbering hosts.
SLAAC.quote: SLAAC-configured hosts might not be able to add a DHCPv6 address(es)

DHCPv6.why: DHCPv6 and prefix delegation, reconfiguration and renewal are central to the renumbering steps analysed.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv6-PD (Prefix Delegation) [RFC3633] enables automated delegation of IPv6 prefixes using the DHCPv6.

multicast.why: A dedicated section covers the impact of renumbering on multicast sources, RPs and group addresses (SSM, PIM-SM).
multicast.quote: Renumbering of Multicast Sources

rejected.why: Secure dynamic DNS update is discussed as one renumbering step, but only as a gap within a broader analysis, not as the document's subject.
IPv6 is the context, but the more specific renumbering, SLAAC and DHCPv6 tags cover the content.
Mentioned only as a possible alternative for pushing configuration updates.
RA is used as a renumbering mechanism, but ND itself is not specified or extended; the SLAAC tag covers it.
Mobility gets only a short subsection about home agent address change.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations.

RFC7011.title: Specification of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol for the Exchange of Flow Information
RFC7011.summary: RFC 7011 specifies the IPFIX protocol (obsoleting RFC 5101): message, set, template and data record formats, template management, and transport over SCTP, UDP and TCP, with TLS/DTLS security for exporting flow information from Exporting to Collecting Processes.

IPFIX.why: The whole document defines the IPFIX protocol: message format, templates, options templates, data encoding, template management and transport.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol, which serves as a means for transmitting Traffic Flow information over the network.

rejected.why: SCTP (with PR-SCTP) is a transport IPFIX runs over; the document only specifies how IPFIX uses it, not SCTP itself.
TLS/DTLS is the security mechanism relied on in Security Considerations; no new TLS extension is defined.
UDP is a transport substrate for IPFIX, not the subject.
TCP is a transport substrate for IPFIX, not the subject.
PSAMP is only mentioned as a related framework that uses IPFIX; not specified here. The taxonomy tag PSAMP is a child of IPFIX anyway and the document is not about it.
The IPFIX MIB modules (RFC 6615, RFC 6727) are only referenced in Management Considerations; they are not defined here.

RFC7012.title: Information Model for IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC7012.summary: RFC 7012 defines the data types, type semantics, naming conventions and registry management policy for the IPFIX information model (the IANA IPFIX Information Elements registry), obsoleting RFC 5102.

IPFIX.why: The whole document specifies the IPFIX information model: Information Element properties, abstract data types, semantics, identifiers and registry extension rules.
IPFIX.quote: This document defines the data types and management policy for the information model for the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol.

rejected.why: The IANA registry management is part of the IPFIX information model itself; the IANA Considerations are boilerplate-like and the document is not about IANA stewardship generally.
SNMP counters and the SMI enterprise numbers are only referenced for analogy and for private enterprise IDs; the document is not a MIB.
XML schema for the registry is mentioned only as a machine-readable syntax of the registry; the document is not about XML usage.
Traffic measurement is the context, but the document is about the IPFIX data model, which is covered by the IPFIX tag.
The MPLS label type subregistry is a minor registry detail, not a document about MPLS.

RFC7013.title: Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Elements
RFC7013.summary: BCP giving guidelines for authors and IE-DOCTORS expert reviewers on defining, revising, and deprecating IPFIX Information Elements in the IANA registry, plus a textual IESpec notation for IEs and Templates.

IPFIX.why: The whole document concerns IPFIX Information Elements, their registry, review process, and a notation for templates.
IPFIX.quote: This document provides guidelines for how to write definitions of new Information Elements for the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol.

IANA.why: Substantial part defines Expert Review procedures, revision and deprecation policy for the IANA IPFIX Information Element registry.
IANA.quote: provides guidelines for expert reviewers to evaluate new registrations.

rejected.why: IPFIX has its own tag and this is a child of network management; IPFIX is the specific fit.
SIP appears only as an example (sipResponseStatus); the document is not about SIP.
SMI Private Enterprise Numbers mentioned only incidentally.
PSAMP is referenced as an example application, not the subject.
Expert review process is specific to the IANA registry, better covered by IANA tag.

RFC7014.title: Flow Selection Techniques
RFC7014.summary: RFC 7014 describes Intermediate Flow Selection Process techniques (filtering, sampling, flow-state dependent selection) for IPFIX Exporters, Collectors and Mediators, with configuration parameters and new IPFIX Information Elements for reporting.

IPFIX.why: The document defines flow selection within the IPFIX architecture and registers new IPFIX Information Elements for configuring and reporting selection.
IPFIX.quote: The Intermediate Flow Selection Process is the process of selecting a subset of Flows from all observed Flows.

PSAMP.why: It extends PSAMP packet selection work, covering flow-state dependent packet selection configuration and hash-based and sampling techniques. It also builds on RFC 5475 and RFC 5476.
PSAMP.quote: This document also addresses configuration and reporting parameters for Flow-state dependent packet selection as described in [RFC5475]

rejected.why: The subject is measurement, but the IPFIX and PSAMP tags are more specific, and the taxonomy lists them under the broader measurement area.
It registers an OID in the IPFIX-SELECTOR-MIB registry, but only as an IANA action. The document does not define a MIB.
It registers Information Elements, but these are boilerplate IANA actions and not the subject of the document.

RFC7015.title: Flow Aggregation for the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol
RFC7015.summary: RFC 7015 defines terminology, an Intermediate Aggregation Process architecture, counter distribution and Original Flow counting methods, and new IPFIX Information Elements for exporting Aggregated Flows.

IPFIX.why: The document specifies flow aggregation for IPFIX, including new Information Elements and an Options Template for exporting aggregated flows.
IPFIX.quote: This document provides a common implementation-independent basis for the interoperable application of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol to the handling of Aggregated Flows

rejected.why: Flow aggregation is a data reduction technique, not a performance measurement metric or method.
Not related; no MIB or SNMP content.
Mentioned only as an entropy example for anomaly detection.
Anonymizing effect is mentioned briefly, but the document is not about privacy considerations.

gaps.name: IPFIX Mediation / flow aggregation
gaps.why: IPFIX is a technology under network management in the taxonomy, but IPFIX is listed there as IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export); I tagged it by that id. The taxonomy has IPFIX as a tech under network management, so there is no real gap, but there is no finer tag for Mediators or Intermediate Aggregation Process.

RFC7016.title: Adobe's Secure Real-Time Media Flow Protocol
RFC7016.summary: Specifies Adobe's RTMFP, a secure UDP-based endpoint-to-endpoint transport for parallel real-time media and bulk data flows, with session handshake, NAT traversal via redirector/forwarder, flow and congestion control.

transport.why: RTMFP is a new general-purpose transport protocol with sessions, flows, reliability, acknowledgements and flow control. No specific transport protocol tag fits, so the parent topic is used.
transport.quote: an endpoint-to-endpoint communication protocol designed to securely transport parallel flows of real-time video, audio, and data messages, as well as bulk data, over IP networks

congestion control.why: A substantial part of the document covers session-wide congestion control, time-critical reverse notification, burst avoidance and an example algorithm in Appendix A.
congestion control.quote: An RTMFP MUST implement congestion control and avoidance algorithms that are "TCP compatible"

NAT traversal.why: The startup handshake with Redirector and Forwarder introduction services is designed for P2P connectivity through NATs.
NAT traversal.quote: Session multiplexing and facilities to support UDP hole-punching simplify Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal in peer-to-peer systems.

rejected.why: UDP is only the usual encapsulation for RTMFP packets, not the subject of the document.
RTMFP carries real-time media but is a separate transport, not RTP or an RTP extension.
P2P is a use case supported by the protocol, but the document specifies a transport and not a peer-to-peer overlay or application.
TCP congestion control is referenced as a baseline for RTMFP's algorithms. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
The Redirector/Forwarder hole-punching mechanism is similar in purpose, but it is not ICE and does not use it.
The security framework is a pluggable Cryptography Profile that is not defined here, and it is a feature of the transport rather than the document's subject.

RFC7017.title: IMAP Access to IETF Email List Archives
RFC7017.summary: Informational memo capturing requirements for a service giving standard IMAP client access to browse and search archived IETF email lists, as input to later design work.

IMAP.why: The whole document specifies requirements for an IMAP server interface to list archives, including IMAP extensions (ANNOTATE, METADATA, SORT/THREAD, multimailbox and fuzzy search) to consider.
IMAP.quote: The system should expose the archive using an IMAP interface, with each list represented as a mailbox.
IMAP.section: 2. Requirements for IMAP Access to Archived IETF Lists

mailing lists.why: The subject is archiving and access to IETF mailing list archives, including restricted versus open archives, which readers of mailing list topics would want.
mailing lists.quote: The IETF makes heavy use of email lists to conduct its work.  This often involves accessing the archived history of those email lists.

rejected.why: The ANONYMOUS SASL mechanism is mentioned only as one option for anonymous access, not a subject of the document.
Internationalized addresses get a brief non-binding consideration with no firm requirement; not a substantial part of the document.
Covered by the more specific IMAP and mailing lists tags.
The document is about a tooling requirement for list archives, not about IETF process or procedures.

RFC7018.title: Auto-Discovery VPN Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC7018.summary: Informational problem statement and requirements for Auto-Discovery VPN (ADVPN), a solution for dynamically establishing direct IPsec tunnels between many gateways and endpoints with minimal configuration.

IPsec.why: The whole document is about large-scale IPsec deployments, dynamic SA establishment, and impacts on SPD/PAD databases from RFC 4301. It states requirements for an IPsec-based VPN solution.
IPsec.quote: enabling a large number of systems to communicate directly using IPsec to protect the traffic between them

VPN.why: Covers star, full-mesh and dynamic full-mesh VPN topologies, hubs and spokes, and requires L3VPNs to run over the tunnels. It is a customer-built IPsec VPN rather than a provider-provisioned one, but VPN readers would want it.
VPN.quote: A VPN solution that enables a large number of systems to communicate directly, with minimal configuration and operator intervention

rejected.why: IKE is mentioned as needing peer configuration, but the document sets no IKE protocol requirements.
L3VPN is only a requirement that ADVPN carry L3VPNs as an application, not the subject.
NAT traversal is one requirement among sixteen, not a substantial part of the document.
OSPF and GRE are only protocols that may run over the tunnels.
GRE is only an example of a protocol run over the IPsec tunnels, not something the document specifies or analyses.
Multicast scaling is a single SHOULD requirement.

gaps.name: Auto-Discovery VPN (ADVPN)
gaps.why: The document defines ADVPN as a distinct topic: dynamic spoke-to-spoke IPsec tunnels. The taxonomy has no tag for it, and the VPN tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs.

RFC7019.title: Application-Layer Multicast Extensions to REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD)
RFC7019.summary: Defines a RELOAD Usage and experimental message mapping for Application-Layer Multicast, with a pluggable algorithm architecture and example Scribe and P2PCast algorithm mappings.

P2PSIP.why: The document extends RELOAD (the P2PSIP overlay protocol) with a new Usage, Kind, and message types. P2PSIP is the tag covering RELOAD.
P2PSIP.quote: We define a REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) Usage for Application-Layer Multicast (ALM) as well as a mapping to the RELOAD experimental message type to support ALM.

multicast.why: The subject is overlay/application-layer multicast tree creation, join, leave, and data push, including Scribe and P2PCast tree algorithms. It is not native IP multicast, but readers of the multicast subject would want it.
multicast.quote: Application-Layer Multicast (ALM) has been demonstrated to be a viable multicast technology where native multicast isn't available.

rejected.why: The overlay is peer-to-peer, but RELOAD is only the substrate. The document defines multicast over it, and the P2PSIP tag already covers RELOAD.
RELOAD comes from the P2PSIP work, but this document has no SIP signalling content.
NAT traversal is only mentioned as a RELOAD mechanism that is reused.
The registries for algorithm, message and error codes are boilerplate IANA sections and do not make the document about IANA.
The multicast is overlay-based tree forwarding, not a reliable multicast transport.

gaps.name: Application-Layer Multicast / overlay multicast
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ALM or overlay multicast trees, so the multicast topic tag is the closest available fit.

RFC7020.title: The Internet Numbers Registry System
RFC7020.summary: RFC 7020 describes the current Internet Numbers Registry System (IANA, RIRs, LIRs) for distributing IP address space and AS numbers, its goals, and how it evolves, replacing RFC 2050.

addressing.why: The document describes how IP address space and AS numbers are allocated through the IANA/RIR/LIR hierarchy, which is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: the current Internet Numbers Registry System used in the distribution of globally unique Internet Protocol (IP) address space and autonomous system (AS) numbers

IANA.why: A substantial part covers the IANA role at the top of the number allocation hierarchy and its relationship to ICANN, the IETF and the RIRs.
IANA.quote: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) is a role, not an organization.

rejected.why: WHOIS is only mentioned as a technical consideration for registry policy; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Reverse DNS zone delegation is mentioned briefly as a consideration, not a subject of the document.
The document touches on governance of the registry system, but the more specific addressing tag fits better, and IANA already covers the governance-related role.
Aggregation is mentioned as a goal, but CIDR itself is not discussed.

gaps.name: Regional Internet Registries / Internet Numbers Registry System
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RIR and LIR structure and number resource registry administration beyond the generic addressing topic.

RFC7021.title: Assessing the Impact of Carrier-Grade NAT on Network Applications
RFC7021.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC reporting lab testing by CableLabs, Time Warner Cable and Rogers of how NAT444 and DS-Lite Carrier-Grade NAT break or degrade common Internet applications, with brief mitigation pointers.

CGN.why: The whole document assesses the application impacts of Carrier-Grade NAT (NAT444) through test cases, results and mitigations.
CGN.quote: This document identifies areas where adding a second layer of NAT disrupts the communication channel for common Internet applications.

DS-Lite.why: DS-Lite was tested alongside NAT444, with its own results table in Section 4.2 and DS-Lite-specific observations such as the suspected MTU-related slowdown.
DS-Lite.quote: This document was updated to include the Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) impacts also.

rejected.why: The more specific child CGN fits, and ancestors are implied, so NAT is not listed separately.
PCP (RFC 6887) is only cited as a possible workaround in the mitigation table, not specified or analysed.
6to4 failure is mentioned briefly in test results, but the document is not about 6to4.
Teredo failure is a brief test-result entry, not a subject of the document.
The document frames NAT444 and DS-Lite as transition mechanisms, but its content is application impact of CGN, which CGN and DS-Lite cover more specifically.
STUN is mentioned only as a uTorrent workaround, with a timeout tweak noted in passing.

RFC7022.title: Guidelines for Choosing RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Canonical Names (CNAMEs)
RFC7022.summary: Replaces RFC 6222 with simpler guidelines for choosing unique RTCP CNAMEs (UUID-based persistent or CSPRNG-generated per-session identifiers), updating RFC 3550.

RTCP.why: The document specifies how to choose the RTCP CNAME item, updating RFC 3550's RTCP guidance; RTCP readers need it.
RTCP.quote: The RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Canonical Name (CNAME) is a persistent transport-level identifier for an RTP endpoint.

UUID.why: One of the two persistent CNAME methods mandates using a version 1, 2 or 4 UUID, so UUID readers may want it.
UUID.quote: an RTP endpoint MUST generate and store a Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) [RFC4122] for use as the "host" part of its RTCP CNAME.

rejected.why: RTP is the parent of RTCP, which is implied; the content is specific to RTCP CNAMEs.
The procedure just says to use a CSPRNG per RFC 4086; it relies on randomness rather than being about it.
Base64 is only used as an encoding of the identifier.
Linkability is discussed in Security Considerations, but the document is not mainly about privacy.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations.
NAT-caused address non-uniqueness is only motivation for the change.

RFC7023.title: MPLS and Ethernet Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Interworking
RFC7023.summary: Specifies how PEs map defect states and OAM notifications between Ethernet attachment circuits (CFM/Y.1731 CCM and AIS, Link OAM, E-LMI) and Ethernet pseudowires (LDP status, VCCV-BFD), augmenting RFC 6310.

pseudowire.why: The document defines PE behaviour for Ethernet pseudowire and attachment circuit defects, including PW status notification and receive/transmit defect states.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies the mapping of defect states between ACs and associated Ethernet PWs connected in accordance with the PWE3 architecture

Ethernet.why: It covers Ethernet OAM (Link OAM, E-LMI, CCM, AIS, RDI) and its interworking with PW OAM, which the Ethernet tag explicitly includes.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet Continuity Check (CC) [CFM] [Y.1731]

OAM.why: The document is about OAM mechanism interworking and defect notification; this is the general OAM topic, which no chosen technology tag sits under.
OAM.quote: There are a number of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) technologies defined for Ethernet, providing various functionalities.

rejected.why: VCCV-BFD diagnostic codes are used as a signalling mechanism defined elsewhere (RFC 5885); the document does not specify or extend BFD.
LDP status notification is only the signalling substrate for PW status, defined in RFC 4447.
MPLS PSN is just the underlying network; the document is about Ethernet/PW OAM mapping, not MPLS itself.
The service is point-to-point emulated Ethernet via PWs, not a L2VPN service specification.
The document does not address MPLS-TP; it covers PW OAM mapping only.

RFC7024.title: Virtual Hub-and-Spoke in BGP/MPLS VPNs
RFC7024.summary: Defines Virtual Hub-and-Spoke for BGP/MPLS VPNs, where only V-hub PEs hold all VPN routes and V-spokes import default routes, with Internet connectivity, forwarding and multicast (MVPN) procedures.

L3VPN.why: The document extends BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 4364) with V-hub and V-spoke PE roles, VPN-IP default routes and RT-based import/export policies.
L3VPN.quote: allows the VPN service provider to reduce the number of PE routers that have to maintain all these routes by requiring only a subset of these routers

MVPN.why: A substantial part specifies I-PMSI/S-PMSI A-D route handling by V-hubs and V-spokes and changes to ingress replication procedures in RFC 6514.
MVPN.quote: This section describes procedures for supporting Multicast VPN (MVPN) in the presence of Virtual Hub-and-Spoke.

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier of VPN routes and RTs, but the document is about VPN hub-and-spoke design, not BGP protocol or policy itself.
MPLS labels and NHLFE are used as substrate; no new MPLS mechanism is defined.
Route Target extended communities are used for import/export policy but not specified or extended.
The L3VPN tag fits more specifically; hierarchy of PEs is VPN-specific.

RFC7025.title: Requirements for GMPLS Applications of PCE
RFC7025.summary: Informational requirements document describing what PCEP and PCE path computation must support for GMPLS networks (TDM/SDH, WDM label constraints, unnumbered interfaces, asymmetric bandwidth, protection), covering PCReq/PCRep extensions.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies requirements on PCE path computation requests and replies and PCEP extensions for GMPLS.
PCE.quote: this document describes functional requirements for GMPLS applications of PCE.

GMPLS.why: The requirements concern GMPLS TE attributes: switching capability, encoding, signal and concatenation types, labels, protection, unnumbered links, asymmetric bandwidth. Readers of GMPLS would want it.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides requirements for GMPLS applications of PCE in support of GMPLS path computation

rejected.why: RSVP-TE procedures (ERO, XRO, ASSOCIATION) are referenced as the signalling that consumes the computed paths. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
MPLS is background, since the original PCE work targeted MPLS. The document focuses on GMPLS.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering. Inter-layer and inter-area TE are explicitly out of scope.
SDH/SONET/OTN serve only as an example TDM scenario and are not the subject of the document.
Section 3.3 only briefly says PCEP MIB modules should be extended. This is a minor point and not a substantial part of the document.

RFC7026.title: Retiring TLVs from the Associated Channel Header of the MPLS Generic Associated Channel
RFC7026.summary: RFC 7026 updates RFC 5586 by retiring ACH TLVs from the MPLS Generic Associated Channel header, forbidding TLVs before G-ACh messages and deleting the related IANA registry and column.

MPLS.why: The document changes the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (RFC 5586) header format by removing ACH TLVs. MPLS has no more specific tag for G-ACh, so readers of MPLS would want this.
MPLS.quote: A G-ACh message MUST NOT be preceded by an ACH TLV.

rejected.why: The ACH originates in pseudowire control words (RFC 4385) and the PWE3 registry is touched, but the document is about the generic G-ACh for Sections, LSPs and PWs, not pseudowire emulation itself.
The IANA changes (deleting a registry and a column) only implement the main change and are boilerplate-like. The document is not about IANA guidance.
OAM is mentioned only in Manageability Considerations as a possible use of TLVs. The document does not address OAM.
G-ACh is used by MPLS-TP, but the document does not mention or profile MPLS-TP.

gaps.name: MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about the G-ACh and ACH header. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so it falls under the general MPLS tag.

RFC7027.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool Curves for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC7027.summary: Defines TLS NamedCurve values (26-28) for the ECC Brainpool curves brainpoolP256r1, P384r1 and P512r1 so they can be negotiated for key exchange, updating RFC 4492, with test vectors.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS ECC negotiation with new NamedCurve code points and updates RFC 4492; TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document adds new NamedCurve types to three elliptic curves defined in [RFC5639] as follows:

elliptic curve.why: It concerns the Brainpool elliptic curves and their use in ECDH, including Diffie-Hellman test vectors for each curve.
elliptic curve.quote: This document specifies the use of several Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool curves for authentication and key exchange

rejected.why: DTLS is mentioned only in passing as suitable for these curves; the document is not about DTLS.
X.509 certificates are mentioned only as an existing way to use the curves for authentication; nothing new is defined.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate that simply records the new values.
Signatures are not specified; the document covers curve negotiation for key exchange.

RFC7028.title: Multicast Mobility Routing Optimizations for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC7028.summary: Experimental RFC defining multicast mobility optimizations for Proxy Mobile IPv6: a Multicast Tree Mobility Anchor (MTMA) and a direct routing mode in which MAGs act as MLD proxies, plus a new Dynamic IP Multicast Selector mobility option.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document extends PMIPv6 with an MTMA, a direct routing option and a new mobility option carried in PBA messages.
PMIPv6.quote: This document proposes some experimental enhancements to the base solution to support IP multicasting in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) domain.

multicast.why: It addresses multicast delivery and tunnel convergence, with the MAG acting as an MLD/IGMP proxy and the MTMA as multicast router or proxy. A substantial part of the document is about multicast routing and group membership.
multicast.quote: allowing a mobile access gateway to connect directly to a multicast router for simple access to local content.

rejected.why: MLD is used and proxied per RFC 4605, but the document does not specify or extend MLD itself. The option only reuses its Multicast Address Record format.
IGMP is covered only as an IPv4 compatibility note in Section 8, not as a subject of the document.
A more specific child tag, PMIPv6, fits, so the parent is not listed.
Mentioned only as one way to connect a MAG to a multicast router.
Mentioned only as one way to connect a MAG to a multicast router.
IPsec is mentioned only as the security mechanism in the Security Considerations.

RFC7029.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Mutual Cryptographic Binding
RFC7029.summary: Informational memo analysing server insertion and man-in-the-middle attacks on EAP tunnel methods and recommending EMSK-based mutual cryptographic binding, state tracking of mutual authentication, and other mitigations.

EAP.why: The whole document is about EAP tunnel methods (TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS), their cryptographic binding, MSK/EMSK use and mutual authentication.
EAP.quote: recommends cryptographic binding based on an Extended Master Session Key, a new form of cryptographic binding that protects both peer and server

rejected.why: Tunnel methods use TLS as a substrate, and the document only touches on certificate validation of tunnel servers.
Certificate naming and validation for tunnel servers are discussed briefly as a mitigation and a recommendation, not as the document's subject.
AAA transport of the MSK is part of the attack scenario, but the document is not about AAA protocols.
GSS-EAP is used only as an example motivating channel binding.
It is not mentioned. AAA is only the generic backend in the attack diagrams.
Posture transport is mentioned only as an example of a peer service that relies on the EAP server.

RFC7030.title: Enrollment over Secure Transport
RFC7030.summary: RFC 7030 specifies Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST), a profile for certificate enrollment, CA certificate distribution, re-enrollment, server-side key generation and CSR attribute retrieval using CMC messages over HTTPS.

EST.why: The document defines the EST protocol itself: its operations, URIs, message types and authentication/authorization rules.
EST.quote: This profile, called Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST), describes a simple, yet functional, certificate management protocol targeting Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) clients

rejected.why: TLS is the transport security substrate; the document relies on it (and on channel binding and TLS-SRP) but defines no new TLS extension.
HTTP is the transfer mechanism for EST messages; EST is not an extension of HTTP semantics, only a well-known URI and media types usage.
CMC and CMS are the message formats profiled and used; the document is about the enrollment profile, not CMS itself.
Certificates are the objects enrolled, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates; EST is already the more specific PKI tag.
Registers application/csrattrs and an smime-type value, but this is IANA boilerplate rather than the main subject.
TLS-SRP cipher suites are suggested for certificate-less authentication, but only as a referenced mechanism.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The document profiles CMC messages (Simple/Full PKI Request) but the taxonomy has no CMC tag; CMP and EST exist, but CMC does not.

RFC7031.title: DHCPv6 Failover Requirements
RFC7031.summary: Informational requirements document for a DHCPv6 failover protocol, covering scenarios, failure modes, synchronization approaches, and the core requirements and out-of-scope features; it defines no protocol.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document concerns failover for DHCPv6 servers: lease database sharing, prefix delegation support, and recovery from server failure and network partition.
DHCPv6.quote: This document outlines requirements for DHCPv6 failover, enumerates related problems, and discusses the proposed scope of work to be conducted.

rejected.why: Dynamic DNS updates are mentioned only as a feature that failover should remain compatible with, not as a subject of the document.
The document concerns IPv6 address and prefix leasing only through DHCPv6, so the more specific DHCPv6 tag is the right one.
DHCPv6 is the more specific tag, and the DHCPv4 failover comparison is background only.
The security requirement is a short boilerplate-level statement about peer authentication, not a substantial topic.

gaps.name: DHCP failover / high availability
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for server redundancy and failover of DHCP services. DHCPv6 is the closest fit, but readers looking for failover would find nothing specific.

RFC7032.title: LDP Downstream-on-Demand in Seamless MPLS
RFC7032.summary: Describes LDP Downstream-on-Demand label distribution use cases and procedures for access nodes in Seamless MPLS, and defines a new Queue Request TLV in the LDP Label Request message for fast-up convergence.

LDP.why: The document specifies LDP DoD use cases and procedures and defines a new LDP TLV (Queue Request), so it is about LDP.
LDP.quote: A new optional TLV type in the LDP Label Request message is defined for fast-up convergence.

MPLS.why: The document works within the Seamless MPLS architecture, covering MPLS label state on access nodes, LSPs, and failure handling across the MPLS network.
MPLS.quote: Seamless MPLS design enables a single IP/MPLS network to scale over core, metro, and access parts of a large packet network

rejected.why: Labeled BGP (RFC 3107) is only used on the network side of the AGN. The document does not specify or extend it.
PWE3 and tLDP are used only as an example service. The document says LDP DoD operations are service agnostic.
BGP/MPLS IP VPN is only a second example service, and the document is not about it.
IPFRR LFA is used as a motivation for liberal label retention, but the document does not specify it.
ECMP is only mentioned as a forwarding feature that LDP DoD must support, so it is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Seamless MPLS
gaps.why: The document is built around the Seamless MPLS architecture for access networks. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so MPLS is the closest fit.

RFC7033.title: WebFinger
RFC7033.summary: RFC 7033 specifies the WebFinger protocol, which discovers information about people or other entities identified by URIs through HTTPS queries to /.well-known/webfinger returning a JSON Resource Descriptor (JRD).

WebFinger.why: The document defines the WebFinger protocol, its query syntax, JRD format, hosted services, and the process for defining applications.
WebFinger.quote: This specification defines the WebFinger protocol, which can be used to discover information about people or other entities on the Internet using standard HTTP methods.

rejected.why: HTTP and HTTPS are only the substrate for WebFinger queries. The document does not extend HTTP semantics.
The JRD is a JSON object, but JSON is only the encoding. The document does not define a generic JSON format.
WebFinger reuses link relations and the IANA link relation registry, but it does not extend Web Linking itself.
URIs are the query target and the subject of lookups. The document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
It registers application/jrd+json only in IANA boilerplate. The main body is not about media type rules.
HTTPS is required, but TLS is only the security mechanism the document relies on.
CORS is used to let browsers query the resource. This is a supporting mechanism and not the subject of the document.

RFC7034.title: HTTP Header Field X-Frame-Options
RFC7034.summary: Informational RFC documenting the non-standard X-Frame-Options HTTP response header field (DENY, SAMEORIGIN, ALLOW-FROM) that lets servers tell browsers not to render content in frames, as a defence against clickjacking.

web security.why: The document specifies a browser-enforced web platform security mechanism against clickjacking, so it belongs on the web security page.
web security.quote: To improve the protection of web applications against clickjacking, this document describes the X-Frame-Options HTTP header field

HTTP.why: It defines a new HTTP response header field, with its syntax, ABNF, and registration in the message header registry. Readers of HTTP extensions would want it.
HTTP.quote: The X-Frame-Options HTTP header field indicates a policy that specifies whether the browser should render the transmitted resource within a <frame> or an <iframe>.

rejected.why: Frames and iframes are the subject of the policy, but the document does not specify HTML itself.
Section 2.3.2.4 advises against caching the header, but this is a minor point and not the document's subject.
The document only uses ABNF to define the header syntax. It is not about ABNF.
Serialized origins are used in ALLOW-FROM, but the document does not address URIs as a subject.
HSTS is another web security header, but this document does not relate to it.
The Privacy Considerations section is short boilerplate-like content and not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: Clickjacking / framing protection (Content Security Policy, same-origin policy)
gaps.why: The document is about browser anti-clickjacking policy and the web origin concept. The taxonomy has no specific tag for CSP or origin-based web security, so the generic web security tag is the closest fit.

RFC7035.title: Relative Location Representation
RFC7035.summary: Defines a PIDF-LO extension (XML and binary TLV) for expressing location as an offset relative to a civic or geodetic reference point, with shapes and optional map metadata.

geolocation.why: The document defines a location representation (relative location with reference, offset shapes, and map metadata), which is the geolocation formats subject.
geolocation.quote: an extension to the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) (RFC 4119) for the expression of location information that is defined relative to a reference point

PIDF.why: The document extends PIDF-LO by adding a <relative-location> element to <location-info>, so readers of PIDF would want it.
PIDF.quote: Two formats are included: an XML form that is intended for use in PIDF-LO [RFC4119]

rejected.why: XML and GML are only the encoding used for the extension. The document is about location, not XML usage in general.
The binary TLV format reuses the DHCP civic and coordinate location encodings (RFC 4776, RFC 6225), but the document does not specify DHCP.
Media types are used to describe the map document type, but the document does not register or define media types.
The document registers URNs for coordinate reference systems in an IANA registry, but this is boilerplate IANA material and not a URN namespace in its own right.
The new registries are IANA Considerations boilerplate and are not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: PIDF-LO / GEOPRIV location object formats
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no PIDF-LO tag. The PIDF tag does not exist either, so I had to leave it out; geolocation covers the subject.

RFC7036.title: Object Identifier Registry for the Long-Term Archive and Notary Services (LTANS) Working Group
RFC7036.summary: Informational RFC that documents the object identifiers assigned under the LTANS working group's OID arc (module identifiers, CMS content types, ERS encryption methods) and sets IANA Expert Review policy for future assignments.

LTANS.why: The whole document is the OID registry for the Long-Term Archive and Notary Services work (ERS, LTAP, DSSC), so readers of LTANS would want it.
LTANS.quote: an object identifier arc was set aside for use by that working group. This document describes the object identifiers that were assigned

IANA.why: The document creates new IANA registries under SMI Security Codes and sets their allocation policy, which is a substantial part of its purpose.
IANA.quote: Updates to the four new tables require Expert Review, as defined in [RFC5226].

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation in which the OIDs and modules are written. The document does not specify ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
CMS content type OIDs are listed, but the document does not specify or extend CMS. It only records identifiers.
Not related. SCVP and certificate validation appear only as a referenced module name.
Certificate validation (SCVP) is only mentioned in passing as a referenced module, not addressed by this document.

gaps.name: Object identifier (OID) registries / SMI Security Codes
gaps.why: The document is about OID arc allocation and the SMI Security Codes registry. The taxonomy has no OID tag, so only the IANA topic fits partially.

RFC7037.title: RADIUS Option for the DHCPv6 Relay Agent
RFC7037.summary: Defines a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_RADIUS) that lets a NAS acting as relay agent and RADIUS client pass RADIUS Access-Accept authorization attributes to a central DHCPv6 server, and creates an IANA registry of permitted attributes.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option and specifies relay agent, server and client behaviour for it.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies a new DHCPv6 option for the DHCPv6 Relay Agent to transfer the authorization information of RADIUS attributes

RADIUS.why: A substantial part concerns how RADIUS attributes from Access-Accept are carried and which are permitted, including the NAS/RADIUS client interplay; readers of RADIUS would want it.
RADIUS.quote: The OPTION_RADIUS is a DHCPv6 option used by the DHCPv6 relay agent to carry the authorization information of RADIUS attributes

rejected.why: PPPoE is only one of two access scenarios in the figures, not specified or extended.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a recommended protection.
The more specific DHCPv6 child tag fits.
IPv6 is context; the document is about DHCPv6/RADIUS interaction.
RADIUS tag is more specific; no general AAA framework is addressed.

RFC7038.title: Use of OSPF-MDR in Single-Hop Broadcast Networks
RFC7038.summary: Experimental RFC describing how to use OSPF-MDR (the MANET interface type of RFC 5614) in single-hop broadcast networks, with recommended parameter settings and simplified router-LSA origination and MDR selection procedures.

OSPF.why: The document profiles and simplifies OSPF-MDR, an OSPF extension, giving configuration recommendations, router-LSA origination and MDR selection changes. OSPF is the most specific fitting tag.
OSPF.quote: This document describes the use of OSPF-MDR in a single-hop broadcast network, which is a special case of a MANET

MANET.why: The document treats a single-hop broadcast network as a special case of a MANET and uses the OSPF MANET interface type, so MANET routing readers would want it.
MANET.quote: OSPF-MDR [RFC5614] specifies an extension of OSPF [RFC2328, RFC5340] to support mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs)

rejected.why: RFC 5340 is only referenced. The document concerns OSPF-MDR generally and does not specify OSPFv3 behaviour.
The document is about a specific protocol's interface-type usage, not routing architecture in general.

gaps.name: OSPF-MDR (MANET Designated Router)
gaps.why: The document is about OSPF-MDR specifically. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so OSPF and MANET are the closest fits.

RFC7039.title: Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) Framework
RFC7039.summary: Informational framework document describing and motivating the design of SAVI methods, which validate IP source addresses at fine granularity by binding addresses to link-layer anchors on a shared link.

SAVI.why: The whole document is the SAVI framework: model, binding anchors, deployment options, scalability and reliability optimizations, and prefix configuration.
SAVI.quote: SAVI method was developed to complement ingress filtering with standardized IP source address validation at the maximally fine granularity of individual IP addresses.

rejected.why: DHCP is one of the address assignment methods SAVI traces, not the subject of the document.
SLAAC is only one address assignment method that SAVI variants handle.
SEND is only mentioned as an address configuration variant to be accommodated.
Ingress filtering and source validation relate to it, but the document addresses link-level SAVI, which has its own tag.
Spoofing prevention reduces DoS attacks as a motivation, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation.
Privacy is only referenced to RFC 6959 in one note and is not a substantial part of the document.

RFC7040.title: Public IPv4-over-IPv6 Access Network
RFC7040.summary: Describes Public 4over6, a hub-and-spoke softwire mechanism providing IPv4 connectivity over an IPv6-only access network using IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels, global non-shared IPv4 addresses and per-subscriber bindings on the border relay; informational and not recommended for new deployments.

softwire.why: The document specifies Public 4over6, an IPv4-over-IPv6 hub-and-spoke softwire mechanism (CE and BR behaviour, address binding), developed in the softwire WG.
softwire.quote: The mechanism follows the Hub and Spoke softwire model [RFC4925] and uses IPv4-in-IPv6 tunneling as the basic data-plane method.

rejected.why: Referenced for fallback, fragmentation and DNS procedures and as a complementary deployment, but the document is about Public 4over6, not DS-Lite.
DHCPv4 over IPv6 is used for address provisioning but is specified in another document; it is only a mechanism relied on here.
IPv4-in-IPv6 encapsulation per RFC 2473 is the data-plane substrate; the softwire tag covers the mechanism.
CE NAPT is mentioned only incidentally; the design aims to avoid carrier NAT.
Parent of softwire, so it is implied by the softwire tag.
Used only to provision the IPv6 address and the BR address; the AFTR-Name option is referenced but not defined here.

RFC7041.title: Extensions to the Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Provider Edge (PE) Model for Provider Backbone Bridging
RFC7041.summary: Informational RFC describing how IEEE 802.1ah Provider Backbone Bridging is integrated into the VPLS PE reference model (PBB-VPLS), covering the PE model, packet walkthrough, control plane reuse, replication and OAM.

VPLS.why: The document extends the VPLS PE reference model with PBB components, which is the core subject.
VPLS.quote: This document discusses extensions to the VPLS Provider Edge (PE) model required to incorporate desirable PBB components

rejected.why: PBB is an IEEE Ethernet bridging technology, but the document is about its integration into VPLS rather than IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Pseudowires and the PW Forwarder are used as building blocks, but the document does not specify pseudowire emulation itself.
VPLS is the more specific tag and covers the document's L2VPN subject, so the parent is not listed.
MPLS is the substrate for the backbone and is not specified or extended here.
BGP auto-discovery is mentioned only as reusable existing control-plane procedure.
OAM gets only a short section that points to existing VPLS, PW and Ethernet CFM tools, not a substantial treatment.

gaps.name: Provider Backbone Bridging (IEEE 802.1ah, PBB)
gaps.why: The document is largely about PBB, I-SID and B-component concepts. The taxonomy has no tag for IEEE bridging, PBB or Provider Bridges.

RFC7042.title: IANA Considerations and IETF Protocol and Documentation Usage for IEEE 802 Parameters
RFC7042.summary: BCP defining IANA assignment procedures (Expert Review and IESG Ratification) for EUI-48/EUI-64 MAC identifiers, SNAP protocol numbers and other parameters under the IANA OUI (00-00-5E), plus documentation values, IETF use of IEEE 802 code points, and new MAC-address AFNs/RRTYPEs.

IANA.why: The document's main purpose is the IANA registration policy for code points under the IANA OUI, including expert review procedures, templates and documentation values.
IANA.quote: This document specifies IANA considerations for the assignment of code points under the IANA OUI.

Ethernet.why: A substantial part covers Ethernet MAC identifiers, Ethertypes, LSAPs and SNAP protocol identifiers and how the IETF uses them, so Ethernet readers would want it.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet protocol parameters provide a means of indicating the contents of a frame -- for example, that its contents are IPv4 or IPv6.

rejected.why: Modified EUI-64 interface identifiers for IPv6 are discussed in one subsection, but the document is not about IPv6 addressing itself.
It mentions the EUI48/EUI64 RRTYPEs, but those are defined in RFC 7043; here they only appear as IANA assignments.
VRRP MAC address blocks are listed only as assignments in a table, and the protocol is not specified or extended.
The CF Series of OUIs from RFC 2153 is mentioned only as a deprecated assignment, not a PPP specification.
This concerns link-layer MAC identifier allocation, not IP address architecture.
ARP appears only in a list of Ethertypes in the appendix.

gaps.name: IEEE 802 parameters / MAC address (EUI-48/EUI-64) and Ethertype registries
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MAC identifier or OUI assignment, so readers looking for it find only the generic IANA and Ethernet tags.

RFC7043.title: Resource Records for EUI-48 and EUI-64 Addresses in the DNS
RFC7043.summary: Defines two new DNS resource record types, EUI48 and EUI64, for encoding IEEE link-layer addresses in DNS, with a recommendation against publishing them in the public DNS because of privacy risks.

DNS.why: The document specifies new DNS RR types, including their wire and presentation formats. This is a direct extension of DNS.
DNS.quote: This document describes two new DNS resource record types, EUI48 and EUI64, for encoding Ethernet addresses in the DNS.

rejected.why: The document discusses privacy risks of publishing link-layer addresses, but mainly in its Security Considerations and as a caveat. It is not a privacy threat-model document.
EUI-48 and EUI-64 are the address formats being encoded. The document does not address IP over Ethernet, interworking or OAM.
DOCSIS address tracking is only an example use case in Section 5. The document is not about DOCSIS networks.
DHCP is mentioned only as the source of the address mapping in the example use case.
The IANA section only records the RR type assignments. It is boilerplate and not a subject of the document.

RFC7044.title: An Extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for Request History Information
RFC7044.summary: RFC 7044 defines the SIP History-Info header field, the rc/mp/np parameters for History-Info and Contact, the "history" Privacy priv-value, and the "histinfo" option tag for capturing request retargeting history, obsoleting RFC 4244.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field, header field parameters, a Privacy priv-value and an option tag, and specifies UA, proxy and redirect server behavior for them.
SIP.quote: This document defines a standard mechanism for capturing the history information associated with a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) request.

rejected.why: The Privacy header handling (anonymizing hi-entries) is a SIP-specific mechanism within the extension, not a general treatment of privacy threat models.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations to protect the header; the document does not specify anything new about TLS.
ABNF is used only to define the header syntax, not the subject of the document.
Tel-URIs are mentioned only as a case where Reason and Privacy cannot be carried; the document is not about the tel URI scheme.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here, not the main subject.

RFC7045.title: Transmission and Processing of IPv6 Extension Headers
RFC7045.summary: Updates RFC 2460 to require IPv6 forwarding nodes and middleboxes to pass packets with any standard extension headers by default, relaxes Hop-by-Hop processing, and creates an IANA IPv6 Extension Header Types registry.

IPv6.why: The document specifies how forwarding nodes must handle IPv6 extension headers, updating the IPv6 specification.
IPv6.quote: This document updates RFC 2460 to clarify how intermediate nodes should deal with such extension headers and with any that are defined in the future.

firewall.why: A substantial part of the document sets requirements for firewalls and other middleboxes, including configurable discard policy and defaults.
firewall.quote: if a forwarding node is designed to examine extension headers for any reason, such as firewalling, it MUST recognise and deal appropriately with all standard IPv6 extension header types

IANA.why: The document creates a new IANA registry for extension headers and updates RFC 2780 guidance, which is a substantial part of its content.
IANA.quote: IANA has closed the existing empty "Next Header Types" registry to new entries and is redirecting its users to a new "IPv6 Extension Header Types" registry.

rejected.why: ICMPv6 is mentioned only in passing as a possible upper-layer header.
ESP and AH appear only as entries in the extension header registry list, not as subjects of the document.
HIP is listed only as one registry entry (protocol 139).
Shim6 is listed only as one registry entry (protocol 140).
The Mobility Header and Routing Header Type 2 are mentioned only as registry entries and examples.
The security discussion is boilerplate in the Security Considerations section and does not make the document about operational security practices.

RFC7046.title: A Common API for Transparent Hybrid Multicast
RFC7046.summary: An IRTF experimental RFC defining a common, technology-agnostic multicast API with a "ham" URI scheme for group names, name-to-address mapping, and use of the API to build inter-domain multicast gateways between IP multicast and overlay multicast.

multicast.why: The whole document is about a multicast group communication API and hybrid multicast gateways bridging ASM/SSM IP multicast and overlay multicast. No specific multicast protocol child tag fits as the main subject.
multicast.quote: This document describes a common multicast API that is suitable for transparent communication in underlay and overlay and that grants access to the different flavors of multicast.

URI.why: The document defines and registers the new provisional "ham" URI scheme with syntax, semantics and namespaces for multicast group names. This is a substantial part of the document.
URI.quote: ham-URI   = ham-scheme ":" namespace ":" group [ "@" instantiation ] [ ":" port ] [ "/" sec-credentials ]

sockets API.why: The document specifies an abstract multicast socket API (create, join, send, receive, socket options) with C signatures, as an alternative to the standard sockets API.
sockets API.quote: The standard multicast socket options [RFC3493] [RFC3678] are bound to an IP version by not distinguishing between the naming and addressing of multicast identifiers.

rejected.why: PIM-SM is discussed only in an appendix as a gateway deployment case, and the document does not specify or extend it.
SIP is only one of the namespaces that can be mapped to groups and is used as an example name source. The document does not specify or extend SIP.
IGMP and MLD reports are only mentioned as possible effects of a join call. The document does not specify or analyse them.
Overlay multicast and RELOAD are used as underlying technologies behind the API. The document is not about peer-to-peer overlays themselves.
Group Names and name-to-address mapping are central, but the naming is for multicast groups and is covered by the URI scheme tag. It is not general name resolution.
SSM is one flavor the API supports and a deployment case in the appendix. The document does not specify SSM.

gaps.name: Hybrid/overlay (application-layer) multicast
gaps.why: The core subject is bridging native IP multicast and overlay or application-layer multicast through gateways. The taxonomy has no tag for application-layer or overlay multicast, so the general multicast tag is used.

RFC7047.title: The Open vSwitch Database Management Protocol
RFC7047.summary: Defines the OVSDB management protocol, a JSON-RPC 1.0 based protocol over TCP for managing and configuring Open vSwitch instances through a schema-driven database with transactions, monitoring and locks.

OVSDB.why: The whole document specifies the OVSDB protocol: schema format, RPC methods, and database operations.
OVSDB.quote: This document defines the OVSDB management protocol.

rejected.why: JSON and JSON-RPC are only the wire encoding; the document defines no new JSON format.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations to secure connections.
TCP is only the transport; the IANA port assignment is boilerplate.
UUIDs are used as row identifiers, but the document does not define or extend UUIDs.
OpenFlow and OVS are in an SDN context, but the document specifies a database management protocol, not SDN architecture.
I2RS is mentioned only as a pointer for future routing-related schema extensions.

gaps.name: Open vSwitch / virtual switch management
gaps.why: The document covers virtual switch (vswitch) configuration, which the taxonomy has no tag for apart from the OVSDB tag.

RFC7048.title: Neighbor Unreachability Detection Is Too Impatient
RFC7048.summary: Updates RFC 4861 to relax IPv6 Neighbor Unreachability Detection retransmission rules by adding an UNREACHABLE neighbor cache state with multicast NS and exponential backoff when no alternative neighbor exists.

neighbor discovery.why: The document modifies IPv6 Neighbor Discovery's NUD state machine and retransmission behaviour, updating RFC 4861.
neighbor discovery.quote: this document introduces a new UNREACHABLE state in the conceptual model described in [RFC4861].

rejected.why: Neighbor discovery is the more specific child tag; the parent is implied.
ARP is mentioned only as a comparison for robustness; the document does not specify or change it.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as being unaffected.
Referenced only to justify the 60-second maximum retransmit timer.

RFC7049.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
RFC7049.summary: RFC 7049 specifies CBOR, a compact binary data format based on an extended JSON data model, with its encoding, tags, canonicalization and strict-mode guidance, JSON conversion, diagnostic notation and IANA registries.

CBOR.why: The document defines the CBOR format: major types, tags, canonical form, strict mode and registries. It is the core CBOR specification.
CBOR.quote: The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size

JSON.why: Section 4 gives CBOR-to-JSON and JSON-to-CBOR conversion rules, and JSON compatibility is a design objective. Readers on JSON would want it.
JSON.quote: The underlying data model is an extended version of the JSON data model [RFC4627].

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only compared against CBOR in Appendix E; the document does not specify or extend it.
The application/cbor registration and +cbor suffix are IANA boilerplate; the body is not about media type rules.
CoAP is only mentioned as a Content-Format registration and as an inspiration for length encoding.
Constrained nodes are a motivation, but the document is a general data format specification.
Base64 appears only in tag definitions and conversion hints; the document does not define it.
The registries are created in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate for this document.

RFC7050.title: Discovery of the IPv6 Prefix Used for IPv6 Address Synthesis
RFC7050.summary: Specifies a DNS-based heuristic using the well-known name "ipv4only.arpa." by which nodes detect DNS64/NAT64 and learn the IPv6 prefix (Pref64::/n) for local address synthesis, with optional DNSSEC validation and connectivity checks.

DNS64.why: The whole method is about detecting DNS64 synthesis and learning the prefix from synthesized AAAA records. It also sets requirements on DNS64 operators.
DNS64.quote: This document describes a method for detecting the presence of DNS64 and for learning the IPv6 prefix used for protocol translation on an access network.

special-use domain names.why: It reserves the special-use name ipv4only.arpa and answers the RFC 6761 questions, and the name is central to the method.
special-use domain names.quote: IANA has delegated a new second-level domain in the .ARPA zone for the well-known domain name "ipv4only.arpa."

DNSSEC.why: A substantial part of the document covers DNSSEC validation of discovered prefixes, with requirements on both the network and the node.
DNSSEC.quote: The domain serving the well-known name MUST be signed with DNSSEC.

NAT64.why: The document works within NAT64 deployments, covering prefix discovery, connectivity checks to the translator and operator considerations. It does not specify NAT64 itself.
NAT64.quote: The information learned enables nodes to perform local IPv6 address synthesis and to potentially avoid NAT64

rejected.why: The more specific tags DNS64 and NAT64 already cover this parent.
ICMPv6 Echo is only used as a simple connectivity check and nothing new is defined about it.
DNS is the substrate. The document uses ordinary AAAA, PTR and A queries and defines no new DNS behaviour beyond DNS64 and the special name.
Captive portals are mentioned only as a source of false positives.
The IANA section is boilerplate for the registrations, so it is not a subject of its own.

RFC7051.title: Analysis of Solution Proposals for Hosts to Learn NAT64 Prefix
RFC7051.summary: Informational analysis of proposed solutions (DNS well-known name, EDNS0 options, A64 RR, U-NAPTR/TXT, DHCPv6, RA, STUN, access-specific) for hosts to learn whether NAT64/DNS64 address synthesis occurs and which NAT64 prefix is used, recommending the heuristic DNS-based discovery.

NAT64.why: The document is about how hosts discover the presence and prefix of NAT64 for synthesis or avoidance. NAT64 is in the taxonomy as a tag under IPv6 transition.
NAT64.quote: learning the Network-Specific Prefix (NSP) [RFC6052] used by the NAT64 [RFC6146] and the DNS64 [RFC6147] devices

DNS64.why: Detecting DNS64 synthesis and its prefix is the core subject. Most proposals analyzed are DNS64-based signalling.
DNS64.quote: A network entity that synthesizes IPv6 addresses and AAAA records out of IPv4 addresses and A records

EDNS.why: Two analyzed proposals are EDNS0 options or flags for signalling synthesis.
EDNS.quote: defined a new Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS0) option [RFC2671] that contained 3 flag bits (called SY-bits)

DHCPv6.why: A full section analyzes DHCPv6 options for delivering the NAT64 prefix.
DHCPv6.quote: described a new DHCPv6 [RFC3315] option (OPTION_AFT_PREFIX_DHCP)

STUN.why: A section analyzes a proposed STUN extension for NSP discovery.
STUN.quote: the STUN client sends a request to the STUN server containing a new 'SENDING-TO' attribute

rejected.why: Router Advertisement option is one analyzed proposal, but only one section; not the focus.
Covered more specifically by DNS64 and EDNS tags.
Mentioned only as a use case and in security considerations.
Parent of NAT64; implied.
Mentioned only as an example application using IPv4 literals in SDP.

RFC7052.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) MIB
RFC7052.summary: Defines the read-only LISP-MIB SNMP module for monitoring LISP devices (ITR, ETR, PITR, PETR, Map-Server, Map-Resolver): feature status, mapping tables, and counters.

LISP.why: The MIB models LISP devices, roles, map-cache, mapping database and map-server registrations, so LISP readers would want it.
LISP.quote: Specifically, the MIB for managing devices that support the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) is described.

MIB.why: The document's main content is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, objects, and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This document defines the MIB module that contains managed objects to support the monitoring devices of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP).

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; nothing new is specified about SNMP itself.
Only imports MplsL3VpnName from RFC 4382 to map Instance IDs to VRFs; not about L3VPN.
Mentioned only in boilerplate Security Considerations.
The counters are device statistics within the MIB, not a measurement methodology; covered by MIB.

RFC7053.title: SACK-IMMEDIATELY Extension for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC7053.summary: RFC 7053 updates SCTP (RFC 4960) by defining an I (Immediate) bit in the DATA chunk header so a sender can ask the receiver to send the SACK without delay.

SCTP.why: The document extends the SCTP DATA chunk format and the sender and receiver SACK procedures. It updates RFC 4960, so SCTP is its main subject.
SCTP.quote: defining a method for the sender of a DATA chunk to indicate that the corresponding Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) chunk should be sent back immediately

rejected.why: Section 7 is informational only and just describes an SCTP_SACK_IMMEDIATELY send flag. The document is not about the sockets API.
The IANA section only registers one DATA chunk flag bit. That is boilerplate, not the subject.
The I bit can help throughput when windows fill, but the document does not define congestion control.

RFC7054.title: Addressing Requirements and Design Considerations for Per-Interface Maintenance Entity Group Intermediate Points (MIPs)
RFC7054.summary: Informational RFC setting out requirements and design considerations for addressing OAM messages to per-interface (incoming and outgoing) MIPs within MPLS-TP nodes, including nodes with minimal outgoing interfaces and P2MP branch points.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document concerns OAM MIP addressing in MPLS-TP nodes for LSPs and PWs, so MPLS-TP readers would want it.
MPLS-TP.quote: The framework for Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) within the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) describes how the Maintenance Entity Group Intermediate Points (MIPs) may be situated

rejected.why: OAM is a topic tag, but it is not given directly because the MPLS-TP tech tag is the more specific fit. Note, however, that the document is mainly about OAM, and OAM is not a child of MPLS-TP, so it could be added as secondary.
PWs are mentioned as carriers of OAM messages, but the document does not specify or extend pseudowire emulation.
Parent of MPLS-TP; implied by the child tag.
Traceroute is listed as one OAM function that needs MIP addressing, but it is not the subject of the document.

RFC7055.title: A GSS-API Mechanism for the Extensible Authentication Protocol
RFC7055.summary: Defines the GSS-EAP GSS-API mechanism that encapsulates an EAP conversation (with RADIUS/AAA backend), including naming, channel binding, token formats, key derivation, and the SASL EAP-AES128 mechanism registration, for ABFAB federated access.

GSS-API.why: The document defines a new GSS-API mechanism: its names, context tokens, per-message services, channel binding and PRF.
GSS-API.quote: This mechanism is a GSS-API mechanism that encapsulates an EAP conversation.

EAP.why: It defines a new EAP lower layer, EAP method selection and EAP channel binding use, with EAP key derivation feeding the mechanism.
EAP.quote: From the perspective of RFC 3748, this specification defines a new lower-layer protocol for EAP.

SASL.why: Registers the EAP-AES128 and EAP-AES128-PLUS SASL mechanisms via GS2, so SASL readers need it.
SASL.quote: these protocols also define how Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) applications use the Extensible Authentication Protocol.

RADIUS.why: Defines new RADIUS attributes (164-167) carrying the acceptor name to the EAP server.
RADIUS.quote: See Section 7.4 for registrations of RADIUS attribute types to carry the acceptor service name.

rejected.why: Only borrows RFC 3961 crypto framework and RFC 4121 per-message tokens; the document is not about Kerberos itself.
Mentioned only as a discovery/negotiation alternative.
Mentioned only as an alternative AAA transport; no Diameter definitions.
Only referenced for tunnel EAP methods and as an analogy to SNI.
Provides motivating architecture context (ABFAB), but the document specifies a mechanism, not a federation framework.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like considerations for this mechanism, not the main subject.

RFC7056.title: Name Attributes for the GSS-API Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Mechanism
RFC7056.summary: Defines how GSS-API naming extensions expose RADIUS attributes, SAML assertions, SAML attributes and NameIDs from the GSS-EAP mechanism, via URN-named attributes in the federated context, and registers the GSS URN namespace.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies GSS-API name attributes (naming extensions) for the GSS-EAP mechanism, including how GSS_Get_name_attribute returns values and authenticated flags.
GSS-API.quote: This document describes how to use the Naming Extensions API to access that information.

EAP.why: The document is specific to the EAP GSS-API mechanism (GSS-EAP) and names the attributes it receives.
EAP.quote: The Extensible Authentication Protocol GSS-API mechanism [RFC7055] allows an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) peer to provide authorization attributes alongside an authentication response.

RADIUS.why: A full section defines the naming and value encoding of RADIUS attributes as GSS name attributes.
RADIUS.quote: This section describes how RADIUS attributes received in an access-accept message by the GSS-EAP [RFC7055] mechanism are named.

federated authentication.why: Defines the federated trust context and SAML IdP assertions, attributes and name identifiers exposed to services.
federated authentication.quote: In the federated context, the trusted source of the peer credential is typically some identity provider.

rejected.why: SAML elements are serialized as UTF-8 XML, but XML is only an encoding substrate here.
It registers a GSS URN sub-namespace in IANA, but this is incidental; the document is about name attributes, not URN namespace design.
AAA is the transport of the attributes, covered more specifically by RADIUS.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level; the main body is about name attributes.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
gaps.why: The document is substantially about naming SAML assertions, attributes and NameIDs, but the taxonomy has no SAML tag.

RFC7057.title: Update to the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Applicability Statement for Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond Web (ABFAB)
RFC7057.summary: Updates the EAP applicability statement in RFC 3748 to allow EAP for application-layer authentication (as in ABFAB), requiring channel bindings, MSK possession proof, and addressing retransmission and re-authentication.

EAP.why: The document revises EAP's applicability statement and sets channel binding, MSK, retransmission and re-authentication requirements for EAP use beyond network access.
EAP.quote: This document updates the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) applicability statement from RFC 3748

GSS-API.why: The motivating use case is the EAP GSS-API mechanism for application access; the document discusses requirements for applications carrying EAP, though it does not specify GSS-API itself.
GSS-API.quote: the use of EAP over Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) for generic application layer access
GSS-API.section: 2. Uses of EAP for Application-Layer Access

rejected.why: ABFAB's federated environment is the motivation, but the document only changes EAP's applicability and does not define a federation framework.
RADIUS/AAA is not discussed beyond a NAI reference; the document is not about AAA frameworks.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that may not need re-authentication.
SMTP is mentioned only as an example in the re-authentication discussion.

gaps.name: EAP channel binding
gaps.why: The core of the document is channel binding for EAP; no taxonomy tag covers it specifically, so it falls under EAP.

RFC7058.title: Media Control Channel Framework (CFW) Call Flow Examples
RFC7058.summary: Informational collection of call flow examples showing how an Application Server uses the MEDIACTRL Media Control Channel Framework (SYNC, K-ALIVE, IVR and Mixer packages, and Media Resource Broker interfaces) to control a Media Server for echo tests, phone calls, conferencing, voice mail and similar scenarios.

real-time communications.why: The document is about controlling media servers that mix, play, record and bridge real-time audio and video, which sits under real-time communications. No more specific technology tag fits the MEDIACTRL framework.
real-time communications.quote: This document provides a list of typical MEDIACTRL Media Control Channel Framework [RFC6230] call flows.

rejected.why: SIP carries the control dialogs and 3PCC call setup, but the document focuses on CFW transactions and does not specify or extend SIP.
SDP is used for COMEDIA negotiation and the cfw-id attribute, but only as a substrate. The document does not define anything new about SDP.
Conferencing is a large part of the examples. The document covers media server control more broadly (echo test, voice mail, IVR, MRB), so I tagged the parent. XCON is not specified here.
