BFCP appears only in a short floor-control scenario where the AS acts as the floor control server. The document is not about BFCP.
RTP is only the media transport between the UACs and the Media Server and is not itself addressed.
The control packages are encoded in XML, which is only an encoding substrate here.

gaps.name: MEDIACTRL (Media Control Channel Framework, Media Server control)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the MEDIACTRL framework, its IVR and Mixer control packages, or the Media Resource Broker. Readers looking for media server control have no specific subject page.

RFC7059.title: A Comparison of IPv6-over-IPv4 Tunnel Mechanisms
RFC7059.summary: Informational overview and comparison of IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnel mechanisms (configured, 6to4, 6rd, ISATAP, Teredo, AYIYA, LISP, SEAL, 6bed4, etc.) to help readers select one, with evaluation of NAT, MTU, robustness, state and performance.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document compares IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling mechanisms, one of the three IPv4-to-IPv6 transition tools. No single child tech covers it, so the parent topic fits.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document provides an overview of various ways to tunnel IPv6 packets over IPv4 networks.

tunneling.why: Encapsulation, protocol 41, GRE, MTU and overhead aspects of tunnels are central to the comparison.
tunneling.quote: Tunnels work by encapsulating IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets

6to4.why: 6to4 and its relay and provider-managed variants get a dedicated section and are compared throughout.
6to4.quote: 6to4 is specified in "Connection of IPv6 Domains via IPv4 Clouds"

Teredo.why: Teredo is described and evaluated, including its robustness and failure rate.
Teredo.quote: Teredo is specified in [RFC4380] and a few updates; it is designed as an automatic tunnel mechanism of last resort.

6rd.why: 6rd is one of the main mechanisms compared.
6rd.quote: 6rd [RFC5969] is used by service providers to connect customer networks behind a CPE

ISATAP.why: ISATAP is described and compared with 6over4.
ISATAP.quote: ISATAP [RFC5214] uses protocol 41 encapsulation to provide connectivity between isolated IPv6-capable nodes

GRE.why: GRE is covered as one of the compared tunnel mechanisms.
GRE.quote: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) [RFC2784] is a generic point-to-point tunnel mechanism

LISP.why: LISP is described, including its terminology and deployment, as a tunnelling option.
LISP.quote: It is possible to use IPv6 EIDs with IPv4 RLOCs and thereby use LISP for tunneling IPv6 over IPv4.

rejected.why: NAT traversal is an evaluation criterion, but the document is about tunnel mechanisms, not NAT behaviour.
MTU issues are discussed in one subsection, but the document is not about PMTUD.
CGN is mentioned only as a context that breaks some mechanisms.
IPsec is explicitly out of scope.
The document covers IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels. It mentions DS-Lite and MAP only to exclude them as IPv4-in-IPv6.
The document is about transition tunnelling, which is covered by the more specific IPv6 transition tag.

gaps.name: Tunnel brokers and tunnel setup protocols (TSP, TIC, SixXS Heartbeat)
gaps.why: The document covers tunnel broker services and setup protocols, and the taxonomy has no tag for them.

gaps.name: AYIYA, 6a44, 6bed4, SEAL
gaps.why: These tunnel mechanisms are discussed substantively, but the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC7060.title: Using LDP Multipoint Extensions on Targeted LDP Sessions
RFC7060.summary: RFC 7060 specifies how to use mLDP (P2MP/MP2MP LSP extensions to LDP) over Targeted LDP sessions, covering upstream LSR selection, unicast replication, and multicast tunneling with upstream-assigned labels.

LDP.why: The document extends/profiles LDP multipoint procedures (mLDP) for Targeted LDP sessions, including label mapping/request procedures and capabilities. LDP is the most specific tag fitting mLDP.
LDP.quote: This document provides the specification for using the LDP Multipoint Extensions over a Targeted LDP session.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE P2P tunnels and P2MP LSPs are only mentioned as upstream selection criteria and possible multicast tunnel types, not specified here.
MPLS label stacks and upstream-assigned labels are used, but LDP is the more specific subject; the parent is implied.
Multicast tunnels are used for data delivery, but the document is about LDP multipoint LSP signalling, not IP multicast routing.
BGP next hop is only one criterion for choosing the upstream LSR; BGP is not specified or extended.

RFC7061.title: eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML) XML Media Type
RFC7061.summary: Registers the application/xacml+xml media type for XACML requests, responses and policies, with parameters, interoperability notes on XACML versions and namespaces, and security considerations.

XACML.why: The document exists to register a media type for XACML, covering its versions, namespaces and usage. Readers of the XACML subject would want it.
XACML.quote: The XACML media type represents an XACML request, response, or policy in the XML-based format defined by the core XACML specification

media types.why: The main body is a media type registration template (application/xacml+xml) following RFC 6838.
media types.quote: This specification details the registration of an XML-based media type for the eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML).

rejected.why: XML is the underlying format of the media type. The document defines nothing new about XML itself.
Signed XACML is mentioned only in the security considerations and interoperability notes. It is not the subject of the document.
XACML is the more specific tag under authorization, so the parent is implied.
HTTPS and REST are mentioned only in passing as publication protocols.

RFC7062.title: Framework for GMPLS and PCE Control of G.709 Optical Transport Networks
RFC7062.summary: Informational framework describing how G.709 (2012) OTN features (ODU0, ODU2e, ODU4, ODUflex, 1.25G tributary slots) affect GMPLS signalling, routing, LMP and PCE, to guide protocol extensions beyond RFC 4328.

GMPLS.why: The document is a GMPLS control framework for OTN, covering signalling, routing and link management implications.
GMPLS.quote: framework to allow the development of protocol extensions to support Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) and Path Computation Element (PCE) control of Optical Transport Networks

PCE.why: A dedicated section and the title cover PCE/PCEP implications for OTN path computation.
PCE.quote: PCE Communication Protocol (PCECP) also has a desire to be extended to carry the new signal type and related variable bandwidth information

rejected.why: Signalling extensions are discussed as requirements, but the document is a framework, not an RSVP-TE specification.
Routing extensions are discussed generically; OSPF is not the subject.
GMPLS is the relevant child; the document is not about MPLS in general.
TE is implied through GMPLS/PCE; no standalone focus.
OAM is only briefly mentioned in the management section.

gaps.name: Optical Transport Network (G.709 OTN) / optical transport control
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OTN or optical transport networks. GMPLS is the closest fit, but it does not cover OTN-specific topics such as ODU, tributary slots and ODUflex.

RFC7063.title: Survey Report on Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) Implementations and Deployments
RFC7063.summary: Survey report compiling operator and vendor responses on PIM-SM implementations and deployments, supporting advancement of PIM-SM (RFC 4601) to Internet Standard and removal of unimplemented features such as (*,*,RP) and PMBR.

PIM-SM.why: The whole document analyses PIM-SM implementations and deployments, including RP discovery, Anycast-RP, and which RFC 4601 features are implemented.
PIM-SM.quote: This document provides supporting documentation to advance the IETF stream's Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) protocol from Proposed Standard to Internet Standard.

rejected.why: MSDP is mentioned only as one way operators deploy Anycast-RP; the document is not about it.
SSM appears only as one item in a list of RFC 4601 features vendors implemented.
Only a single deployment alongside PIM-SM is mentioned, in passing.
The document serves the standards-maturity advancement process, but its subject is PIM-SM implementation and deployment experience, not the process itself.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect PIM messages.

RFC7064.title: URI Scheme for the Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) Protocol
RFC7064.summary: Defines and registers the "stun" and "stuns" URI schemes for identifying a STUN server, including syntax, semantics, default ports and SRV transport implications.

STUN.why: The document specifies a URI scheme for naming STUN servers, extending how STUN servers are identified and configured, so STUN readers would want it.
STUN.quote: The "stun" and "stuns" URI schemes are used to designate a stand-alone STUN server or any Internet host performing the operations of a STUN server

URI.why: It defines and registers new URI schemes with ABNF syntax, semantics and IANA registration, which is core URI scheme work.
URI.quote: This document specifies the syntax and semantics of the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme for the Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) protocol.

rejected.why: STUN is the more specific child tag; the parent is implied.
TLS is only the secure transport selected by the "stuns" scheme; nothing new is defined about TLS.
SRV lookup transport selection is mentioned briefly, but the document is not about DNS.
WebRTC is cited as motivation only; the document does not specify WebRTC.
ABNF is only used as notation for the syntax definition.
Only mentioned in a design note for symmetry with the TURN URI; not the subject.

RFC7065.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) Uniform Resource Identifiers
RFC7065.summary: Defines the "turn" and "turns" URI schemes for identifying a TURN relay server, providing the inputs (secure flag, host, port, transport) to the TURN resolution mechanism of RFC 5928.

TURN.why: The document specifies URI schemes for provisioning and identifying TURN servers, so readers of the TURN subject would expect it.
TURN.quote: The "turn" and "turns" URI schemes are used to designate a TURN server (also known as a relay) on Internet hosts accessible using the TURN protocol.

URI.why: It defines new URI schemes with ABNF syntax, semantics, and IANA registrations, and notes they are opaque, non-hierarchical URIs.
URI.quote: This document specifies the syntax and semantics of the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme for the Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) protocol.

rejected.why: The TURN tag sits under it and already covers the subject; the parent is implied.
The 'turns' scheme signals TURN over TLS, but TLS is only the secure transport and nothing new is defined for it.
WebRTC is cited only as motivation for consistent TURN server provisioning, and the document does not address it.
STUN is mentioned only for URI symmetry in the design notes, and the document does not specify it.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax.
The RFC 5928 resolution mechanism is referenced, but this document does not specify DNS behaviour.

RFC7066.title: IPv6 for Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Cellular Hosts
RFC7066.summary: Informational guidance (obsoleting RFC 3316) on which IPv6 features cellular hosts attached to 3GPP GPRS/UMTS/EPS networks should implement beyond the IPv6 Node Requirements, and how they behave on the 3GPP point-to-point link model.

cellular.why: The whole document profiles IPv6 host behaviour over 3GPP cellular links (GPRS/UMTS/EPS), which is the cellular tag's subject.
cellular.quote: This document considers IPv6 for cellular hosts that attach to the General Packet Radio Service (GPRS), Universal Mobile Telecommunications System (UMTS), or Evolved Packet System (EPS) networks

IPv6.why: It is a host-requirements profile for IPv6, covering extension headers, fragmentation, prefix handling and other IPv6 features.
IPv6.quote: This document also lists specific IPv6 functionalities that need to be implemented in addition to what is already prescribed in the IPv6 Node Requirements document (RFC 6434).

neighbor discovery.why: A substantial section explains how Neighbor Discovery and NUD apply on the 3GPP point-to-point link without link-layer addresses, with MTU and RA option handling.
neighbor discovery.quote: A cellular host must support Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages [RFC4861].

SLAAC.why: SLAAC is the sole address configuration method in 3GPP. The document covers DAD omission, the single /64 prefix and infinite lifetimes, and Appendix A expands on this.
SLAAC.quote: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration is defined in [RFC4862]. This specification is a mandatory part of IPv6 and also the only mandatory method

DHCPv6.why: The document covers DHCPv6 use on cellular hosts, including stateless DHCPv6 and Prefix Delegation with the Prefix Exclude Option.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation was added as an optional feature to the 3GPP system architecture [RFC3633].

rejected.why: IPV6CP over PPP between the MT and TE is covered in only one short section, so it is not a main subject.
Section 4 says IP mobility is not relevant to this document and mentions DSMIPv6 only in passing.
Transition mechanisms are explicitly out of scope, and dual-stack is mentioned only in passing.
SIP appears only as an example of an upper-layer protocol that supplies reachability confirmation.
IPsec is referred to the Node Requirements document and not discussed in its own right.
CDMA2000 is only named in the introduction, while the document's scope is 3GPP networks.

RFC7067.title: Directory Assistance Problem and High-Level Design Proposal
RFC7067.summary: Informational TRILL WG framework describing how directory services (push and pull models) can assist edge RBridges in reducing unknown-unicast flooding and ARP/ND broadcast in data centers, improving scalability and anti-spoofing security.

TRILL.why: The document is entirely about extending TRILL edge switch (RBridge) behaviour with directory assistance for MAC&Label to egress RBridge mapping.
TRILL.quote: This document describes a framework for using directory services in environments where such services are available, such as typical data centers, to assist edge TRILL switches.

data center networking.why: The scaling problem, VM migration, ToR/EoR topology examples and motivation are all data-center specific; large parts of the document analyse them.
data center networking.quote: Data centers, especially Internet and/or multi-tenant data centers, tend to have a large number of end stations with a wide variety of applications.

rejected.why: ARP/ND interception is one benefit, but the document does not specify or extend ARP.
ND flooding reduction is mentioned, but ND itself is not specified or changed.
Directory here is a generic database fed by VM management systems, not the LDAP/X.500 directory services subject.
TRILL uses IS-IS as substrate; the document only mentions it in scaling discussion.
Considered since the work concerns MAC learning, but the document is about TRILL specifically.

RFC7068.title: Diameter Overload Control Requirements
RFC7068.summary: Informational requirements document describing limitations of existing Diameter overload mechanisms (DIAMETER_TOO_BUSY, DPR BUSY, watchdog) and specifying requirements for a new Diameter overload control mechanism.

Diameter.why: The whole document analyses Diameter's existing overload handling and sets requirements for extending the Diameter protocol with an overload control mechanism.
Diameter.quote: The existing mechanisms provided by Diameter are not sufficient for managing overload conditions.  This document describes the limitations of the existing mechanisms

rejected.why: The document explicitly distinguishes application-layer overload from network congestion and puts transport congestion out of scope.
SIP overload work is cited only as background; the document is not about SIP.
DoS attacks appear as one cause of overload and in security discussion, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation.
3GPP mobile networks are used as a case study but the document is not about IP over cellular systems.
TLS/IPsec are mentioned only in passing in the security considerations.
Diameter is tagged via its own entry, but there is no Diameter tag in the taxonomy; the closest is the Diameter tech under AAA.

gaps.name: Overload control
gaps.why: The document is about application-layer overload control for signalling protocols, which the taxonomy has no tag for.

RFC7069.title: DECoupled Application Data Enroute (DECADE)
RFC7069.summary: Informational document describing the DECADE architecture for in-network storage that content distribution (e.g., P2P) applications can use, including principles, components, token-based authorization, and abstract DRP/SDT protocols.

P2P.why: DECADE is designed to let P2P and similar content distribution applications use in-network storage; the P2P tag is the closest fit for the document's subject area.
P2P.quote: Content distribution applications, such as peer-to-peer (P2P) applications, are widely used on the Internet to distribute data objects

authorization.why: Token-based delegated authorization and resource control is a core architectural feature, covered in several sections (4.5, 5.5, 6.2.1).
authorization.quote: an Application Endpoint can authorize other Application Endpoints to store or retrieve data objects from its in-network storage via tokens

rejected.why: HTTP is evaluated only as a candidate SDT/DRP in Appendix A; the document is not about HTTP.
OAuth is evaluated as a possible token mechanism in the appendix, but the document does not specify or extend it.

The taxonomy's storage topic covers storage access protocols over IP, such as NFS and iSCSI. DECADE is in-network storage for content distribution, which is a looser fit, and P2P/authorization describe it better.
CDNs are mentioned only as a possible additional use; the primary focus is P2P.
Naming of data objects uses RFC 6920 hash names, but the document does not define URI syntax; naming here is just a discussion of object identifiers.

gaps.name: In-network storage / DECADE
gaps.why: The document is about an in-network storage architecture for content distribution. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so it only partly fits P2P and storage.

RFC7070.title: An Architecture for Reputation Reporting
RFC7070.summary: RFC 7070 describes a general architecture for reputation services: a client queries a provider for ratings and assertions about an identifier such as a domain name. It defines the vocabulary (Application, Response Set, Assertion, Rating, reputon) and leaves the media type, HTTP query protocol and email application to companion RFCs.

rejected.why: Email is the motivating example (DKIM identifiers, MSA/MDA/MTA figure). The architecture is generic and its email application is specified in RFC 7073, so email is context, not the subject.
DKIM only supplies validated identifiers in the worked example. The document does not specify or extend it.
Spam and phishing are cited as motivation, but the document does not address spam filtering, reporting or reputation lists in their own right.
DNSBL is mentioned only as an example of DNS as a query transport. The document does not define DNS-based list conventions.
DNS is named only as one possible transport for queries. Nothing new is specified for it.
HTTP is only referenced as the transport defined in RFC 7072. This document does not specify it.
The document is an application-level query architecture, but the tag covers application protocols in general and gives readers no useful grouping for reputation services.
The Privacy Considerations section is a considerable part of the document, but it is a considerations section for this architecture. The document is not about privacy threat models in general.

gaps.name: reputation services / reputation reporting (Repute)
gaps.why: The whole document is about a generic reputation query architecture (ratings, assertions, response sets). The taxonomy has no reputation or trust-assessment tag, so readers looking for the Repute family (RFC 7070-7073) have no subject page.

RFC7071.title: A Media Type for Reputation Interchange
RFC7071.summary: Defines the "reputon" JSON data object and the application/reputon+json media type for carrying reputation query responses, plus an IANA registry of reputation application names and response sets.

media types.why: The document's core deliverable is the registration of a new media type and a registry of application names used with it, so media type readers would want it.
media types.quote: a new media type, "application/reputon+json", is defined for the JSON representation of reputational data

JSON.why: Section 6 gives a formal JSON structure for the reputon object and its members, defining a JSON-based format.
JSON.quote: The meta-format selected for the representation of a reputon is JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)

rejected.why: The HTTP query method is defined in RFC 7072; this document only defines the payload and media type.
Only mentioned in an example as one identity type; not the subject.
Only mentioned in an example; not the subject.
Spam appears only in the email-id example; the document is generic to reputation, not spam handling.
The IANA registry is created here, but it is boilerplate-like registration of the document's own content, and the document is about the media type and data format rather than IANA guidance.
MIME is referenced only for registration and token syntax; media types tag covers the substance.

gaps.name: reputation services / reputation interchange
gaps.why: The document's main subject is reputation data exchange (reputons, reputation applications), and the taxonomy has no tag for reputation services.

RFC7072.title: A Reputation Query Protocol
RFC7072.summary: Defines a reputation query protocol in which a client fetches a URI template from a well-known URI over HTTP, expands it, and issues an HTTP GET to retrieve reputation data in JSON.

HTTP APIs.why: The document defines a convention for building a query API on HTTP: well-known template retrieval, URI template expansion, GET queries and Expires handling. It is not a general HTTP extension, so the API-conventions tag fits.
HTTP APIs.quote: The template file is retrieved by requesting the [WELL-KNOWN-URI] "repute-template" from the host providing reputation service, using HTTP.

URI.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how URI templates are expanded, including empty-variable handling and unambiguous URI construction. It also registers a well-known URI.
URI.quote: The syntax for the [URI] of the query is constructed using a template as per [URI-TEMPLATE].

rejected.why: HTTP is the transport. The document uses GET and Expires but defines no new HTTP semantics, so the more specific HTTP APIs tag applies.
JSON is only the payload meta-format. The media type that carries it is defined in RFC 7071, not here.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an optional way to conceal queries.
Spam appears only as an example assertion name. The protocol is not about spam filtering.
The reputon media type is defined in RFC 7071. This document only references it and registers a well-known URI.

gaps.name: Reputation services
gaps.why: The document is about querying reputation data services, and the taxonomy has no reputation tag. Readers looking for reputation services would not find it by subject.

RFC7073.title: A Reputation Response Set for Email Identifiers
RFC7073.summary: Defines the "email-id" reputation application for the reputon framework, with assertions (abusive, fraud, invalid-recipients, malware, spam), an identity extension and query parameter for email identifiers.

spam.why: The document defines reputation assertions about email sources (spam, fraud, malware, abuse) for filtering decisions, so it belongs under spam: reputation and filtering of unwanted email.
spam.quote: spam:  The subject identifier is associated with the sending or handling of unwanted bulk email

email authentication.why: The identity extension distinguishes authenticated identifiers (DKIM, SPF) from unvalidated ones and discusses how that affects the value of reputation, which is relevant to email authentication readers.
email authentication.quote: The signing domain, i.e., the value of the "d=" tag, found on a valid DomainKeys Identified Mail [DKIM] signature in the message

rejected.why: DKIM signing domains are only one possible identifier source; the document doesn't specify or extend DKIM.
SPF is only referenced as a source of a verified domain identity; nothing about SPF is defined.
RFC5321 HELO and MailFrom values are merely identifier sources, not the subject of the document.
The reputon media type is defined in RFC 7071; this document only registers a reputation application.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-like for the reputation application registry; the document's body is about the response set.
The document concerns a JSON-based reputon reputation framework, not DNS query conventions for blocklists.

gaps.name: reputation services / reputons (REPUTE)
gaps.why: The whole document is about a reputation response set within the REPUTE reputation-reporting framework (RFC 7070/7071), and the taxonomy has no tag for reputation services.

RFC7074.title: Revised Definition of the GMPLS Switching Capability and Type Fields
RFC7074.summary: RFC 7074 revises the definition of the GMPLS Switching Capability (routing) and Switching Type (signaling) fields, narrowing them to identify a per-technology SCSI format and deprecating PSC-2, PSC-3 and PSC-4.

GMPLS.why: The document redefines GMPLS Switching Capability and Switching Type fields used in GMPLS routing and signaling. Readers of GMPLS would expect it.
GMPLS.quote: This document is intended to resolve the inconsistent definition and use of the Switching Capability and Type fields by narrowly scoping the meaning and use of the fields.

rejected.why: The OSPF extensions (RFC 4203) carry the field, but the document only redefines the field's meaning, not OSPF itself.
IS-IS (RFC 5307) is only one of the protocols carrying the field. The document does not specify IS-IS behaviour.
RSVP-TE signaling (RFC 3473) carries the Switching Type field, but the document does not extend or specify RSVP-TE.
The IANA registry update is boilerplate-level apparatus. The main body is about the field definitions.
GMPLS is a child of MPLS in the taxonomy and fits more specifically.

gaps.name: GMPLS
gaps.why: The document is about GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) switching types. The taxonomy lacks a GMPLS-specific routing/signaling tag; the closest available is the GMPLS tag under MPLS, which I used above.

RFC7075.title: Realm-Based Redirection In Diameter
RFC7075.summary: RFC 7075 extends the Diameter base protocol with realm-based redirection, adding a new result code (DIAMETER_REALM_REDIRECT_INDICATION) and a Redirect-Realm AVP, so a server or proxy can redirect requests to a whole realm instead of individual hosts.

Diameter.why: The document extends and updates the Diameter base protocol (RFC 6733) with a new result code, a new AVP, and redirect behavior for servers, proxies and clients.
Diameter.quote: a new result code, DIAMETER_REALM_REDIRECT_INDICATION (3011); a new attribute-value pair (AVP), Redirect-Realm (620)

rejected.why: S-NAPTR/DNS-based peer discovery is mentioned only as an alternative that this document does not use; the document does not specify any DNS behaviour.
Diameter is the specific AAA protocol and its tag sits under AAA, so the ancestor is implied and not listed separately.
TLS, DTLS and IPsec appear only in Security Considerations as ways to secure Diameter peer connections.

RFC7076.title: P6R's Secure Shell Public Key Subsystem
RFC7076.summary: Informational independent-submission RFC defining P6R's SSH Public Key Subsystem, which extends RFC 4819 with namespaces and operations to add, remove and list certificates and namespaces, and namespace-aware public key operations.

SSH.why: The document specifies a new SSH subsystem (publickey@p6r.com) extending the RFC 4819 SSH Public Key Subsystem, so it is a protocol extension within SSH.
SSH.quote: P6R's Secure Shell Public Key Subsystem has been designed to run on top of the Secure Shell transport layer [3] and user authentication protocols [4].

key management.why: The protocol is a key and certificate provisioning mechanism, organizing keys by namespace on a server. No technology tag under key management fits, so the topic is tagged directly.
key management.quote: allow the provisioning of keys and certificates to a server using the SSH transport.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are only one example certificate format carried as DER blobs. The document does not profile or specify X.509.
The protocol uploads keys and certificates to a server but does not define PKI infrastructure or certificate management.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the namespace string, which is substrate usage.
Access control is left to server implementations and is mentioned only in Security Considerations and error codes.
SNMP is named only as an example application that namespaces could configure.
DER is only referenced for encoding certificates and is not the subject of the document.

RFC7077.title: Update Notifications for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC7077.summary: Defines Update Notification (UPN) and Update Notification Acknowledgement (UPA) Mobility Header messages (types 19/20) so a Proxy Mobile IPv6 LMA can asynchronously notify a MAG about mobility session changes or request re-registration.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with new LMA-to-MAG notification messages, their processing rules, and IANA registries.
PMIPv6.quote: allowing the local mobility anchor in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain to asynchronously notify the mobile access gateway about changes related to a mobility session

rejected.why: IPsec ESP is only the mechanism protecting the signaling; the document merely requires the existing security association be reused.
Mobility Header and RFC 6275 checks are the substrate; the document is specifically about the Proxy Mobile IPv6 extension, which is the more specific tag.
IANA registries are created but that is boilerplate for the protocol extension, not the main subject.
QoS policy updates are only a motivating example of what UPN can carry; the QoS option is not specified here.
UDP encapsulation on port 5436 for IPv4 transport is just substrate.

RFC7078.title: Distributing Address Selection Policy Using DHCPv6
RFC7078.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 options OPTION_ADDRSEL and OPTION_ADDRSEL_TABLE that let a site administrator distribute the RFC 6724 IPv6 default address selection policy table and the A and P flags to clients.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 options (84 and 85), their formats and client processing, so it belongs under DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines a new DHCPv6 option for such configuration, allowing a site administrator to distribute address selection policy

addressing.why: The options configure IPv6 source and destination address selection policy (precedence and label table), which is a subject for readers of addressing.
addressing.quote: allow nodes to select an appropriate address when faced with multiple source and/or destination addresses to choose between

rejected.why: The document is about IPv6 address selection only through the DHCPv6 option. The more specific tags cover it, so the IPv6 parent is not needed.
IPv4/IPv6 prioritization appears only as an example policy and a security note. The document does not address transition mechanisms.
The document discusses handling multiple interfaces, but only as a processing detail. It does not address multihoming architecture.
The option code assignment is boilerplate IANA Considerations.
RFC 4941 temporary addresses are referenced through the P flag only. The document does not address address autoconfiguration.

gaps.name: Default address selection policy (RFC 6724)
gaps.why: The document is largely about IPv6 source and destination address selection policy tables. The taxonomy has no specific tag for address selection, so addressing is the closest fit.

RFC7079.title: The Pseudowire (PW) and Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV) Implementation Survey Results
RFC7079.summary: Informational report presenting results of a user-community survey on pseudowire encapsulation deployment, Control Word optionality, and VCCV control channel and connectivity verification types, showing CW-less PWs remain widely deployed.

pseudowire.why: The whole survey concerns pseudowire encapsulations (Ethernet, PPP, HDLC, Frame Relay, ATM, TDM), Control Word use and VCCV deployment, so readers of the pseudowire subject would want it.
pseudowire.quote: The Pseudowire (PW) and Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV) Implementation Survey Results

rejected.why: PWs run over MPLS, but the survey is about PW encapsulation and VCCV rather than MPLS architecture; pseudowire is the more specific fit.
VCCV is an OAM mechanism, but the document surveys PW/VCCV deployment rather than defining OAM mechanisms; pseudowire covers it.
BFD is mentioned only as an option missing from the survey choices and in respondent comments.
ECMP inhibition is mentioned as a reason for the Control Word, but it is not a subject of the document.
Respondents mention L2VPN services, but the document does not address them.

RFC7080.title: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Interoperability with Provider Backbone Bridges
RFC7080.summary: Informational RFC describing how IEEE 802.1ah Provider Backbone Bridge functionality can be integrated with H-VPLS (Ethernet and MPLS access) to improve MAC address and service instance scalability, including mixed-access and migration scenarios.

VPLS.why: The whole document is about H-VPLS interoperating with PBB, covering U-PE/N-PE roles, PW mapping and VPLS instances.
VPLS.quote: This document describes interoperability scenarios where IEEE 802.1ah functionality is used in H-VPLS with Ethernet or MPLS access network

rejected.why: 802.1ah/802.1ad bridging is central, but the tag is for IP over Ethernet and Ethernet OAM, and the document's subject is VPLS interworking.
Ethernet PW raw and tagged modes (RFC 4447/4448) are used as existing mechanisms, not specified or extended.
The tag is too general. VPLS is the more specific child and the document is about VPLS.
MPLS is the core and access substrate. The document does not define anything new about MPLS.
LDP signaling is referenced only for existing PW setup. The document does not specify or extend it.

gaps.name: Provider Backbone Bridging (IEEE 802.1ah) / 802.1ad QinQ
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IEEE Ethernet bridging, such as PBB, I-SID or B-VLAN. The document is largely about it.

RFC7081.title: CUSAX: Combined Use of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)
RFC7081.summary: Informational RFC suggesting client and server configuration strategies for combining SIP (telephony/media) and XMPP (IM/presence) into one service (CUSAX), without defining new protocols.

SIP.why: The document is about combined use of SIP for audio/video/telephony with XMPP, covering SIP account handling, Call-Info headers, and conferencing. SIP is a co-subject.
SIP.quote: SIP remains the protocol of choice for telephony-like services

XMPP.why: XMPP is the other half of CUSAX: rosters, JIDs, MUC rooms and Jingle. The document gives guidance on its combined use with SIP.
XMPP.quote: XMPP remains the protocol of choice for IM and presence services

rejected.why: vCard 'tel' fields are used to link XMPP contacts to SIP URIs, but the document does not specify or extend vCard.
Section 4 covers linking SIP conferences with XMPP MUC rooms, but only briefly and as a lightweight suggestion.
TLS is mentioned only in the security considerations as a source of mismatch between the SIP and XMPP sides.
SIMPLE is cited as background. The document deliberately disables SIP IM and presence.
WebFinger is mentioned once, as a possible future basis for provisioning.
SASL appears only in the security considerations, as the XMPP authentication framework.

RFC7082.title: Indication of Conference Focus Support for the Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP)
RFC7082.summary: Informational RFC defining two SIP-based mechanisms (a new Call-Info "purpose" value 'ccmp' and a new <service-uris> purpose 'ccmp' in the conference event package) for a client to learn that a conference focus supports CCMP.

XCON.why: The document is about indicating that a conference focus supports CCMP and the XCON conference event package, extending the XCON centralized conferencing framework.
XCON.quote: The Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP) [RFC6503] allows authenticated and authorized users to create, manipulate, and delete conference objects.

SIP.why: A substantial part of the document defines a new Call-Info purpose value and uses INVITE/OPTIONS and the SIP conference event package, extending SIP.
SIP.quote: The first option uses the Call-Info [RFC3261] header, which is suitable for application servers that need to discover if a UA supports CCMP.

rejected.why: XCON is a more specific child tag that fits, so the parent is not also listed.
DNS-based CCMP server discovery is mentioned only in Security Considerations as existing background.
XML is merely the format of the conference event package elements; the document defines nothing about XML itself.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA registries.
The document does not specify or use SDP.

RFC7083.title: Modification to Default Values of SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT
RFC7083.summary: Updates RFC 3315 to raise the default DHCPv6 SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT from 120 to 3600 seconds and defines two DHCPv6 options letting a server override those client retransmission values.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines new DHCPv6 options and changes DHCPv6 client/server retransmission behaviour, updating RFC 3315.
DHCPv6.quote: A DHCPv6 server sends the SOL_MAX_RT option to a client to override the default value of SOL_MAX_RT.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag and fits; the parent is implied.
The IANA section only records option code assignments; the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC7084.title: Basic Requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge Routers
RFC7084.summary: RFC 7084 specifies basic requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge routers: WAN and LAN provisioning (SLAAC, DHCPv6, prefix delegation, ULA), plus 6rd and DS-Lite transition support, and obsoletes RFC 6204.

IPv6.why: The document is a requirements baseline for IPv6 CE routers, covering addressing, router advertisements, ULA and deployment behaviour.
IPv6.quote: This document defines basic IPv6 features for a residential or small-office router, referred to as an "IPv6 CE router"

DHCPv6.why: A large share of the requirements concern DHCPv6 client and server behaviour, prefix delegation, and DHCPv6 options.
DHCPv6.quote: The router MUST act as a requesting router for the purposes of DHCPv6 prefix delegation ([RFC3633]).

6rd.why: A dedicated section sets 6rd requirements for the CE router, including DHCPv4 option 212 and hub-and-spoke mode.
6rd.quote: The CE router SHOULD support 6rd functionality.  If 6rd is supported, it MUST be implemented according to [RFC5969].

DS-Lite.why: A dedicated section sets DS-Lite requirements for the CE router, including DHCPv6 option configuration and no NAT on encapsulated traffic.
DS-Lite.quote: The IPv6 CE router SHOULD implement DS-Lite functionality.  If DS-Lite is supported, it MUST be implemented according to [RFC6333].

rejected.why: Router Advertisements and Router Discovery are used heavily, but the document only requires conformance to RFC 4861 and does not specify neighbor discovery.
SLAAC support is one requirement among many, and the document does not specify SLAAC itself.
Only one SHOULD requirement (W-6) mentions a PCP client, which is too minor for a tag.
NTP is mentioned only as an optional client requirement (WAA-5), which is too minor for a tag.
The parent is implied by the specific 6rd and DS-Lite tags.
NAT appears only as background on IPv4 CE behaviour and in the DS-Lite no-NAT requirement.

RFC7085.title: Top-Level Domains That Are Already Dotless
RFC7085.summary: Informational RFC listing the TLDs in the root zone that had A, AAAA or MX records at the apex ("dotless domains") as of September 2013, with a shell script for finding them.

DNS.why: The document surveys DNS root zone TLDs for address and MX records at the apex and supplies a DNS-querying script. It is about DNS operations and data, with no more specific DNS tag that fits.
DNS.quote: we consider any TLD with an A, AAAA, and/or MX record at the apex to be dotless.

rejected.why: Dotless TLDs are ordinary delegated ccTLDs that happen to carry apex records. They are not special-use or reserved names.
The document concerns DNS data in the root zone, not registry or registrar operations or protocols. ICANN policy is mentioned only in passing.
MX records at TLD apexes are listed, but only as DNS data. Mail transport is not specified or analysed.
The document concerns apex address records of TLDs, not host naming conventions or host tables.

RFC7086.title: Host Identity Protocol-Based Overlay Networking Environment (HIP BONE) Instance Specification for REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD)
RFC7086.summary: Specifies how to build a RELOAD-based overlay using HIP as the forwarding/link layer (HIP BONE instance), covering Node ID generation, message mapping to HIP DATA, routing, enrollment, NAT traversal and a configuration document extension.

HIP.why: The document is a HIP BONE instance specification: it defines how HIP base exchange, DATA messages, ORCHIDs, and multi-hop routing replace RELOAD's forwarding and link management layer.
HIP.quote: The document provides the details needed to build a RELOAD-based overlay that uses HIP.

P2PSIP.why: It profiles RELOAD, the P2PSIP peer protocol, with HIP as the link layer, including Node ID modes, enrollment, bootstrapping and overlay configuration document extensions.
P2PSIP.quote: The peer protocol to be used is REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) [RFC6940].

rejected.why: NAT traversal is delegated to existing HIP extensions (RFC 5770); the document only requires implementing it.
TLS is only what RELOAD normally uses; this document replaces it with HIP encrypted connections.
The IPsec/ESP connections are the HIP data transport substrate, not something the document specifies.
This taxonomy tag covers data-plane virtualization overlays such as VXLAN, not P2P overlays like HIP BONE.
P2PSIP is the more specific fit for RELOAD-based overlays.
Certificates are used with HITs but are not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: RELOAD (REsource LOcation And Discovery)
gaps.why: No dedicated tag for RELOAD itself; P2PSIP is the closest fit, which covers RELOAD in the taxonomy.

RFC7087.title: A Thesaurus for the Interpretation of Terminology Used in MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Internet-Drafts and RFCs in the Context of the ITU-T's Transport Network Recommendations
RFC7087.summary: RFC 7087 is an informational thesaurus mapping MPLS-TP terminology (MEs, MEPs, MIPs, SPMEs, transport paths, layer networks, etc.) to ITU-T Transport Network terms.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines and interprets MPLS-TP terms, so readers of the MPLS-TP subject would expect it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document provides a thesaurus for the interpretation of MPLS-TP terminology within the context of the ITU-T Transport Network Recommendations.

terminology.why: The document is a glossary of terms and definitions, which fits the terminology topic. MPLS-TP is the main subject, but a glossary is a substantial part of what the document is.
terminology.quote: This document provides a thesaurus (the analogy to the Rosetta Stone has been used within the working groups) for the interpretation of MPLS-TP terminology

rejected.why: OAM terms such as ME, MEG, MEP and MIP are defined here. The document does not specify OAM mechanisms, so OAM is not its subject.
MPLS-TP is the more specific tag, and the MPLS architecture is only the source of the terms.
It is mentioned only in passing, in the SCC definition and the reference to RFC 4397.
PWs and MS-PWs appear in the definitions but are not the subject.

RFC7088.title: Session Initiation Protocol Service Example -- Music on Hold
RFC7088.summary: Informational RFC describing a SIP-based music-on-hold technique using an offerless re-INVITE and a separate dialog to an external media source that sends RTP directly to the remote UA, with SDP handling details and caveats.

SIP.why: The document specifies a SIP call-handling service (music on hold) using re-INVITE, UPDATE, REFER, INVITE with Replaces and the sip.rendering feature parameter, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: Within systems based on SIP [RFC3261], it is desirable to be able to provide features that are similar to those provided by traditional telephony systems.

SDP.why: A substantial part of the document covers SDP offer/answer manipulation: o= line rewriting, directionality attributes, payload type number handling and multiple m= lines.
SDP.quote: it provides no Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] offer [RFC3264] [RFC6337], thus compelling the remote UA to provide an SDP offer.

rejected.why: RTP is only the media carried from the music source; the document does not specify or extend RTP beyond noting source-port conventions.
ICE is mentioned only as a reason to pass through re-INVITEs from the MOH source; it is not the subject.
SIP and SDP tags already sit under this topic and cover the document.
Payload type number assignment in SDP is discussed, but no payload format for a codec is defined.
TLS appears only in example message Via headers and sips URIs as the substrate.

RFC7089.title: HTTP Framework for Time-Based Access to Resource States -- Memento
RFC7089.summary: Defines the Memento framework, an HTTP extension adding datetime negotiation (Accept-Datetime, Memento-Datetime headers), TimeGates and TimeMaps, and new link relation types (original, timegate, timemap, memento) for accessing prior states of web resources.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with new request/response headers and defines detailed HTTP interaction patterns, status code behaviour and redirects for time-based access.
HTTP.quote: It introduces two new headers ("Accept-Datetime" and "Memento-Datetime") and introduces new values for two existing headers ("Vary" and "Link").

web linking.why: A substantial part defines and registers four new link relation types and their use in Link headers and TimeMap link-format serialisations.
web linking.quote: The Memento framework defines the "original", "timegate", "timemap", and "memento" Relation Types to convey typed links

content negotiation.why: Datetime negotiation is a new negotiation dimension using Accept-Datetime and Vary, and is a core mechanism of the document.
content negotiation.quote: Datetime negotiation is a variation on content negotiation by which a user agent expresses a datetime preference

rejected.why: Concerns archived resource versions, not cache validation or freshness; Vary is used only to signal datetime negotiation.
URIs (URI-R, URI-M, etc.) are used as identifiers, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes; the Dated URI scheme is only referenced informatively.
Uses RFC 1123 date format for the headers but defines no new timestamp format of its own.
IANA registrations of headers and relation types are boilerplate here, not the main subject.

gaps.name: Web archiving / resource versioning (Memento)
gaps.why: The document is fundamentally about accessing archived and prior versions of web resources; the taxonomy has no web archiving or versioning tag.

RFC7090.title: Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) Callback
RFC7090.summary: Defines a new "psap-callback" value for the SIP Priority header field so that PSAP callbacks after an emergency call can be recognised and given preferential treatment, with scenarios where the existing domain-matching approach fails and security rules for trusting the marking.

emergency services.why: The whole document addresses PSAP callbacks in the IETF emergency calling architecture: scenarios where callbacks fail and a mechanism to mark them.
emergency services.quote: A call taker may trigger a callback to the emergency caller using the contact information provided with the initial emergency call.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP by defining a new Priority header field value and its usage by proxies and UAs, and registers it with IANA.
SIP.quote: This section defines a new header field value, called "psap-callback", for the SIP Priority header field defined in [RFC3261].

rejected.why: LoST appears only in a routing scenario (multi-stage routing and network-based URN resolution) as background; the document does not specify or extend it.
STIR is mentioned only as ongoing work that will improve calling-party identity; the document does not address it.
The document only registers one value in the SIP Priority registry, which is boilerplate-level IANA action, not a document about IANA.
The security section discusses white-list-based trust for preferential treatment, but this serves the SIP marking mechanism and is not a general authorization subject.
PSTN interworking is described as a scenario but explicitly declared out of scope and unsupported.

RFC7091.title: GOST R 34.10-2012: Digital Signature Algorithm
RFC7091.summary: RFC 7091 is an English translation of the Russian GOST R 34.10-2012 elliptic-curve digital signature standard, specifying signature generation and verification, parameters, and test vectors, and updating RFC 5832.

GOST.why: The document is the specification of a Russian national GOST digital signature algorithm, so readers of the GOST subject would expect it.
GOST.quote: GOST R 34.10-2012 describes the generation and verification processes for digital signatures, based on operations with an elliptic curve points group, defined over a prime finite field.

rejected.why: The algorithm uses elliptic curve groups, but GOST is the more specific fit for this document, which is about the GOST signature scheme rather than elliptic curve cryptography in general.
GOST R 34.10 is a different signature scheme from ECDSA; the document does not specify or discuss ECDSA.
The hash function is GOST R 34.11-2012, defined elsewhere (RFC 6986), not the SHA family.

gaps.name: Digital signature algorithms
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no general tag for digital signature schemes, which this document defines.

RFC7092.title: A Taxonomy of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Back-to-Back User Agents
RFC7092.summary: Informational RFC giving a taxonomy of SIP Back-to-Back User Agent roles (signaling-plane and signaling/media-plane) and mapping device types such as PBXs, SBCs, application servers and transcoders to those roles.

SIP.why: The whole document classifies SIP B2BUA behaviours relative to proxies and UAs per RFC 3261, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document identifies several common B2BUA roles in order to provide taxonomy other documents can use and reference.

rejected.why: RTP/RTCP handling is mentioned as part of media-plane roles but the document does not specify or analyse RTP.
SDP modification is a distinguishing criterion for roles, but SDP itself is not the subject.
Only mentioned as an example of a media-aware terminator and in security considerations.
Mentioned in passing as a back-to-back MSRP agent example; not about MSRP.
Transcoders are discussed as a B2BUA role, but codecs themselves are not the subject.
Conference servers are covered briefly only to say whether they are B2BUAs.

gaps.name: Session Border Controller (SBC) / B2BUA
gaps.why: The document is about B2BUAs and SBC-type middleboxes, which has no dedicated tag; SIP is the closest fit.

RFC7093.title: Additional Methods for Generating Key Identifiers Values
RFC7093.summary: Defines four additional example methods for generating Key Identifier values for the X.509 AKI and SKI certificate extensions, using truncated SHA-256/384/512 hashes of the public key and a hash of the DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo.

X.509.why: The document extends X.509 certificate profile guidance (RFC 5280) by defining new ways to compute the AKI and SKI certificate extension values, which is directly about X.509 certificates.
X.509.quote: This document specifies additional example methods for generating Key Identifier values for use in the AKI (Authority Key Identifier) and SKI (Subject Key Identifier) certificate extensions.

rejected.why: SHA-256/384/512 are only the hash primitives used to compute identifiers; the document does not specify or analyse the hash algorithms, and notes hash security properties are not needed.
A P-256 ECDSA key appears only as the example input in Section 3; the document is not about ECDSA.
X.509 is the more specific tag that fits; the document concerns certificate extensions rather than PKI broadly.
DER encoding of SubjectPublicKeyInfo is referenced only as the input to hashing, not as a subject of the document.

RFC7094.title: Architectural Considerations of IP Anycast
RFC7094.summary: An IAB informational memo analysing the architectural implications of IP anycast, including its history in IETF protocols, principles for using anycast addresses as destinations and sources, transport and middlebox implications, security, and deployment trade-offs.

anycast.why: The whole document analyses anycast addressing architecture, its safe uses as source and destination, and its operational and security implications.
anycast.quote: IP anycast is a technique with a long legacy and interesting engineering challenges.

DNS.why: A substantial part (Section 2.3 on DNS anycast, RFC 3258, NSID, and withdrawal trade-offs in 4.5) covers anycast deployment of DNS servers and resolvers.
DNS.quote: IP anycast is used for at least one critical Internet service: that of the Domain Name System [RFC1035] root servers.

rejected.why: TCP's problems with anycast are discussed (4.2), but only as one transport implication, not a specification or extension of TCP.
Route injection and withdrawal in BGP are discussed, but BGP itself is not the subject.
Anycast in IPv6 is covered (2.2), but the document is about anycast generally, not IPv6.
RPKI is mentioned only briefly in security considerations about per-node origin ASNs.
It is an IAB architectural document, but the specific subject is covered by the anycast tag, which is more precise.
Anycast as DDoS mitigation is mentioned in a security subsection, not a main subject.

RFC7095.title: jCard: The JSON Format for vCard
RFC7095.summary: Defines jCard, a JSON representation of vCard data, with conversion rules between vCard and JSON for properties, parameters, value types, and unknown/extension handling, plus the application/vcard+json media type registration.

vCard.why: The document exists to map vCard to JSON.
vCard.quote: The purpose of this specification is to define "jCard", a JSON format for vCard data.

RFC7096.title: Evaluation of Existing GMPLS Encoding against G.709v3 Optical Transport Networks (OTNs)
RFC7096.summary: Informational evaluation of how well existing GMPLS routing (OSPF/IS-IS TE) and RSVP-TE signaling extensions support the new ITU-T G.709-2012 OTN features (ODUflex, new tributary slot granularity, multi-stage multiplexing, labels), identifying gaps to be addressed by other documents.

GMPLS.why: The document analyses GMPLS routing and signaling (ISCD, IACD, labels, RSVP-TE) against OTN requirements and identifies needed extensions.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides an evaluation of existing Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) routing and signaling protocols against the G.709 OTNs.

rejected.why: OSPF GMPLS TE extensions are evaluated for ISCD advertisement, but the document does not specify OSPF itself; it is covered under GMPLS.
RFC 5307 is cited as part of existing routing evaluated, but only in passing.
RSVP-TE signaling gaps are discussed, but they are evaluated as part of GMPLS, and the document specifies no RSVP-TE extensions.
TE information is considered, but GMPLS is the more specific tag.
PCE is only mentioned in passing regarding ERO and path computation.
SDH/SONET is mentioned only as a contrast to OTN's hierarchy.

gaps.name: OTN (Optical Transport Networks, G.709)
gaps.why: The document is about ODU/OTU containers, tributary slots and ODUflex in OTN, and the taxonomy has no OTN tag; the nearest is GMPLS, which mentions optical transport network control.

RFC7097.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) for RLE of Discarded Packets
RFC7097.summary: Defines a new RTCP Extended Report block (BT=25) using run-length encoding to report which individual RTP packets were discarded from the de-jitter buffer, with an SDP 'discard-rle' signaling parameter.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block, its format, and receiver/sender behaviour. This is an extension to RTCP reporting.
RTCP.quote: This document specifies a per-packet report metric capturing individual packets discarded from the de-jitter buffer after successful reception.

SDP.why: The document augments the SDP 'rtcp-xr' attribute with a new xr-format parameter and describes its use in offer/answer.
SDP.quote: The parameter 'discard-rle' is used to indicate support for the Discard RLE report block defined in Section 3.

rejected.why: RTP is the underlying protocol being reported on. The document's subject is the RTCP report block, which has its own more specific tag.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the report block.
The block does carry a per-packet metric. It is a protocol report format, and RTCP is the more specific fit.

RFC7098.title: Using the IPv6 Flow Label for Load Balancing in Server Farms
RFC7098.summary: Informational RFC describing how the IPv6 flow label can be used by layer 3/4 load balancers in server farms to identify flows, including with fragmented traffic and extension headers.

IPv6.why: The document is about a use of the IPv6 flow label field and how load balancers use it instead of transport headers behind IPv6 extension headers. No narrower IPv6 child tag fits.
IPv6.quote: This document describes how the currently specified IPv6 flow label can be used to enhance layer 3/4 (L3/4) load distribution and balancing for large server farms.

ECMP.why: Layer 3/4 load balancing by hashing flow identifiers is closely related to ECMP load-balanced forwarding. The document treats ECMP as one implementation of the balancer, and the flow label hashing follows RFC 6438.
ECMP.quote: a standard function of some network switches or routers (e.g. using Equal-Cost Multipath Routing (ECMP) [RFC2991])
ECMP.section: 3. Summary of Server Farm Load-Balancing Techniques

rejected.why: HTTP is only the example workload for the server farm. The document is about layer 3/4 balancing and says the proxies are not its focus.
Balancers track TCP sessions, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
DNS-based load splitting is mentioned and explicitly declared out of scope.
Anycast addressing is only listed as one way to redirect traffic to servers, and the document says the choice is unaffected by the flow label.
Path MTU Discovery handling is noted as unaffected by the flow label and out of scope.
NAPT is mentioned only as a redirection method where the flow label gives no benefit.

gaps.name: Server load balancing
gaps.why: The document's central subject is L3/4 server farm load balancing. The taxonomy has no tag for load balancing as such, only ECMP for routers.

RFC7100.title: Retirement of the "Internet Official Protocol Standards" Summary Document
RFC7100.summary: This BCP updates RFC 2026 to drop the requirement for the periodic "Internet Official Protocol Standards" summary (STD 1), obsoletes RFC 5000, and asks the IESG to move it to Historic.

IETF process.why: The document changes the IETF standards process (RFC 2026) by removing the requirement for a standards summary RFC and the ISOC newsletter standards-actions summary.
IETF process.quote: This document updates RFC 2026 to no longer use STD 1 as a summary of "Internet Official Protocol Standards".

rejected.why: STD 1 is an RFC, but the document is about retiring a standards-status summary under the standards process, not RFC format, style or publication.
It mentions requirement-level nomenclature only in a quoted paragraph being removed.

RFC7101.title: List of Internet Official Protocol Standards: Replaced by a Web Page
RFC7101.summary: RFC 7101 announces that the RFC Editor's periodic "Internet Official Protocol Standards" snapshot RFCs (the xx00 documents) are replaced by an online web page, retires STD 1, and frees RFC numbers ending in 00 for assignment.

RFC series.why: The document concerns RFC series publication practice: discontinuing the xx00 snapshot RFCs, the STD 1 subseries identifier, and RFC number assignment.
RFC series.quote: the RFC Editor will classify unpublished RFC xx00 numbers through 7000 as never issued. Starting with the RFC number 7100, xx00 numbers will be available for assignment.

rejected.why: It touches on the IETF decision to retire the snapshot document and RFC 2026, but the focus is RFC Editor publication and numbering, not the standards process.
RFC number assignment is an RFC Editor matter, not an IANA registry matter.

RFC7102.title: Terms Used in Routing for Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC7102.summary: A glossary defining common terminology (LLN, LBR, DAG, sleepy node, upstream/downstream, etc.) for ROLL working group documents on routing in Low-Power and Lossy Networks.

IoT.why: The glossary defines terms for constrained embedded devices and Low-Power and Lossy Networks, which is the IoT subject area. No more specific technology tag fits since the document is terminology, not a protocol spec.
IoT.quote: this document specifies the common terminology to be used in all ROLL working group documents.

terminology.why: The document is a glossary of definitions, so readers browsing terminology would expect to find it.
terminology.quote: This document provides a glossary of terminology used in routing requirements and solutions for networks referred to as Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs).

rejected.why: RPL is only defined as one glossary entry. The document does not specify, extend or analyse the protocol.
The document defines routing-related terms but discusses no routing architecture or design principles.
Link technologies such as IEEE 802.15.4 are mentioned only in passing, and the document does not cover IPv6 adaptation over them.
MPLS TE is cited only as an analogy for the P2MP definition.

gaps.name: Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLN) routing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ROLL or LLN routing in general, apart from the RPL protocol tag under IoT.

RFC7103.title: Advice for Safe Handling of Malformed Messages
RFC7103.summary: Informational guidance for email handlers on safely mitigating common malformed Internet messages (headers, MIME, line termination, charsets, oversized lines), with a security focus.

message format.why: Most of the document is about handling anomalies in Internet Message Format headers: address syntax, folding, repeated or missing fields, spacing. It is guidance for RFC 5322 parsing.
message format.quote: Some messages contain a line of text in the header that is not a valid message header field of any kind.

MIME.why: A substantial part covers MIME anomalies: missing MIME-Version, faulty base64 encodings, missing or incorrect charset labels, and 8-bit data in MIME entities.
MIME.quote: Any message that uses [MIME] constructs is required to have a MIME-Version header field.

rejected.why: SMTP is only the transport. Line termination and 8-bit data touch on it, but the document does not specify or extend it.
DKIM is mentioned as an example of a system sensitive to message alterations, but the document is not about it.
Malicious and abusive content is the motivation for the advice, but the document does not address spam filtering or reputation as such.
The parent is implied by the more specific message format tag, and the document is not about email architecture generally.
EAI is mentioned only briefly for 8-bit addresses in headers.
Charset heuristics appear in one subsection, within a MIME context, and the document does not cover charset registration or use as a subject.

RFC7104.title: Duplication Grouping Semantics in the Session Description Protocol
RFC7104.summary: Defines the "DUP" grouping semantics for the SDP group and ssrc-group attributes so that redundant (duplicated) RTP streams can be associated in session descriptions, with offer/answer considerations and examples.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP by defining new grouping semantics (DUP) for the group and ssrc-group attributes, including offer/answer behaviour and SDP examples.
SDP.quote: This document defines the semantics for grouping redundant streams in the Session Description Protocol (SDP).

RTP.why: A substantial part covers duplicated RTP streams, including ssrc-group DUP for SSRC-multiplexed streams in one RTP session, for loss recovery.
RTP.quote: Grouping semantics at the Synchronization Source (SSRC) level are also defined in this document for RTP streams using SSRC multiplexing.

rejected.why: Source-specific multicast appears only in the examples as the delivery context, not as a subject of the document.
Packet duplication is a loss-recovery technique, but this document only defines SDP grouping semantics, not the FEC/ARQ mechanism itself, which is in RTP-DUP.
IP multicast is the motivating deployment environment, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
IPTV is mentioned as a use case in the introduction, but the document does not address IPTV service delivery.
UDP/IP is only the substrate carrying the streams and is not addressed by the document.

RFC7105.title: Using Device-Provided Location-Related Measurements in Location Configuration Protocols
RFC7105.summary: Defines an XML container and measurement schemas (LLDP, DHCP relay agent info, WiFi, cellular, GNSS, DSL) letting a Device send location-related measurements to a LIS in HELD location requests, plus a PIDF-LO source extension and privacy/security analysis.

geolocation.why: The whole document is about conveying location-related measurement data to improve location estimates, including the PIDF-LO source extension and location privacy.
geolocation.quote: This document describes a protocol for a Device to provide location-related measurement data to a Location Information Server (LIS) within a request for location information.

HELD.why: It extends HELD with measurement data in requests and measurementRequest elements in locationUnknown error responses; HELD is the primary example LCP.
HELD.quote: This shows a HELD location request message with an Ethernet switch and port measurement taken using the Link-Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding and schema language for the container; the document is not about XML usage generally.
Only the relay agent information option is reported as measurement data; DHCP itself is not specified or extended.
802.11 parameters are one measurement type reported, not IP over 802.11.
Cell identifiers are one measurement type; the document does not address IP over cellular networks.
DSL attachment identifiers are one measurement type, not the DSL access network itself.
TLS is only mandated for protecting the transport; nothing new is defined about it.
Privacy considerations are a section of the document, but the document is not about privacy in general; geolocation covers it.

gaps.name: GNSS / location measurements (GEOPRIV, PIDF-LO)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the GEOPRIV location object format (PIDF-LO) or for GNSS measurement data; the geolocation tag only partly covers them.

RFC7106.title: A Group Text Chat Purpose for Conference and Service URIs in the SIP Event Package for Conference State
RFC7106.summary: Registers the "grouptextchat" value in the SIP Conference Event Package's URI Purposes registry so conference focus agents can advertise an associated multi-user chat room URI.

conferencing.why: The document extends the SIP conference event package's service-URI entries so conferences can advertise an associated group chat. It concerns conference state and auxiliary services, which fits the conferencing topic. No conferencing technology tag (XCON etc.) fits, since RFC 4575 is the SIP event package.
conferencing.quote: The new value allows conference mixers or focus agents to advertise a multi-user chat location (i.e., a chat room) associated with the current conference.

SIP.why: It extends SIP's Conference Event Package (RFC 4575) and the SIP Parameters URI Purposes registry, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document defines and registers a value of "grouptextchat" ("Group Text Chat") for the URI <purpose> element of SIP's Conference Event Package.

rejected.why: XMPP MUC is only one example of a URI scheme that the chat entry may carry; the document does not specify or extend XMPP.
MSRP is mentioned only as an example of a chat service reachable through a sip: URI; nothing new is defined about it.
The chat rooms are the target of the advertised URI, but the document defines no instant messaging behaviour itself.
irc: is only listed as a possible URI scheme in an example.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-like in effect; the document is about the SIP-specific purpose value, not IANA registry practice.
XML is just the encoding of the conference event package; the document adds no XML-specific content.

RFC7107.title: Object Identifier Registry for the S/MIME Mail Security Working Group
RFC7107.summary: Informational RFC that documents the object identifiers assigned in the S/MIME working group's donated OID arc (id-smime), transfers the arc to IANA, and creates the IANA registries and allocation policy for it.

S/MIME.why: The whole document is a registry of S/MIME and CMS object identifiers under id-smime, so readers of the S/MIME subject would want it.
S/MIME.quote: an object identifier arc was donated by RSA Data Security for use by that working group

CMS.why: Several of the registries list CMS content types, attributes and algorithm identifiers, so CMS readers would use it.
CMS.quote: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types

IANA.why: The document creates IANA registries and sets their allocation policy. Here this is the main body, not boilerplate.
IANA.quote: Updates to the new tables require both Specification Required and Expert Review as defined in [RFC5226].

rejected.why: OIDs are mostly used with ASN.1, but the document only lists identifier values. It does not specify ASN.1 modules or encodings.
Some registered values come from PKIX documents, but the document is not about PKI.
A few RPKI-related OIDs appear in the tables, but only as entries.
X.509 is only a source of a few referenced identifiers and is not the subject.

gaps.name: Object identifier (OID) registries / SMI numbers
gaps.why: The document is about an OID arc and the SMI-numbers registry. The taxonomy has no tag for OID allocation, so the IANA tag is only an approximate fit.

RFC7108.title: A Summary of Various Mechanisms Deployed at L-Root for the Identification of Anycast Nodes
RFC7108.summary: Informational document describing the DNS-based mechanisms (NSID, HOSTNAME.BIND, ID.SERVER, IDENTITY/NODES TXT and A records) deployed at L-Root to identify which anycast node answers a query.

anycast.why: The document is about identifying and mapping nodes of an anycast-deployed service, and covers operational troubleshooting issues such as re-routing between successive queries.
anycast.quote: Anycast is a deployment technique commonly employed for authoritative-only servers in the Domain Name System (DNS). L-Root, one of the thirteen root servers, is deployed in this fashion.

DNS.why: It specifies DNS operational conventions: CH-class TXT queries, IN-class identity zones, caching effects, and single-server delegation of the identity zone. All of this concerns root server operations.
DNS.quote: The fully qualified DNS name IDENTITY.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG (note the use of ORG, not NET) has associated TXT and A RR Sets that are unique to the responding node.

EDNS.why: A whole section covers use of the NSID EDNS(0) option as one of the node identification mechanisms, with dig examples.
EDNS.quote: L-Root supports the use of the Name Server Identifier (NSID) option [RFC5001] to return the identity of an L-Root node along with the response to a DNS query.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only in Section 5, to say the zone is unsigned and secure responses for the identity zone are unlikely. The document is not about DNSSEC.
Section 3 gives a naming scheme for nodes using IATA codes. It is a brief node naming convention, not host naming conventions or host tables.
The document is motivated by measurement and mapping. It defines identification facilities, not metrics or measurement methods.

RFC7109.title: Flow Bindings Initiated by Home Agents for Mobile IPv6
RFC7109.summary: Experimental RFC defining Flow Binding Indication/Acknowledgement Mobility Header messages and sub-options so a Mobile IPv6 home agent can initiate add, delete, modify, refresh, move and revoke of flow bindings at a mobile node, including dual-stack support.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends Mobile IPv6 flow bindings (RFC 6089) with new Mobility Header messages (FBI/FBA), sub-options and IANA registries so the home agent can initiate flow binding operations.
Mobile IPv6.quote: this document defines new signaling messages and sub-options for Mobile IPv6

rejected.why: RFC 6089 covers NEMO too, but this document addresses only mobile node flow bindings with the home agent.
Only cited informatively for QoS attributes; not the subject.
Mentioned briefly as a deployment scenario in Section 5; not specified or analysed here.
QoS provisioning is a use case motivating the work, not the subject of the document.
Mobile IPv6 is the more specific tag; dual-stack handling relies on RFC 5555 and is a minor part.

RFC7110.title: Return Path Specified Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping
RFC7110.summary: Extends MPLS LSP ping (RFC 4379) with a new "Reply via Specified Path" reply mode, a Reply Path TLV, new RSVP/static tunnel sub-TLVs and a Reply TC TLV so the initiator can control the echo reply return path and test both directions of an LSP in one operation.

MPLS.why: The document extends MPLS LSP ping, an MPLS data-plane OAM/failure-detection mechanism, with new TLVs, reply mode and procedures for MPLS LSPs (including MPLS-TP). No narrower MPLS child tag covers LSP ping.
MPLS.quote: extensions to the data-plane failure-detection protocol for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) known as "LSP ping"

OAM.why: LSP ping is an OAM connectivity-verification tool; the document's goal is verifying bidirectional connectivity and making the failure detection more robust.
OAM.quote: This document defines extensions to the data-plane failure-detection protocol for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

rejected.why: MPLS-TP scenarios are mentioned and a non-IP encapsulation note is included, but the document is about LSP ping for both IP/MPLS and MPLS-TP generally, not the MPLS-TP profile.
The new IPv4/IPv6 RSVP Tunnel sub-TLVs only reuse RSVP tunnel identifiers as FEC descriptors in ping; no RSVP-TE signalling is specified.
BFD for LSPs (RFC 5884) is cited only as one use case for the generic tunnel sub-TLVs; the document does not specify BFD.
GMPLS appears only as a reference for the co-routed bidirectional LSP definition and primary/secondary LSP terms.
Traceroute mode is explicitly out of scope; only ping mode is covered.
Echo replies are UDP packets per RFC 4379, but UDP is only the substrate.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP ping / MPLS data-plane failure detection
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for LSP ping (RFC 4379) under MPLS; the closest are the MPLS parent and the generic OAM topic.

RFC7111.title: URI Fragment Identifiers for the text/csv Media Type
RFC7111.summary: Defines URI fragment identifiers (row, col, cell selections with ranges and multi-selections) for the text/csv media type, updating the RFC 4180 registration.

CSV.why: The document specifies fragment identifiers into text/csv documents and updates the text/csv registration, which is exactly the CSV tag's scope (the media type and fragment identifiers into it).
CSV.quote: This memo defines URI fragment identifiers for text/csv MIME entities.

URI.why: A substantial part of the document defines URI fragment identifier syntax and processing semantics for a media type, which URI readers would want.
URI.quote: The semantics of a fragment identifier is a property of the media type resulting from a retrieval action

media types.why: The document amends the text/csv media type registration with fragment identifier considerations, relevant to media type registration readers.
media types.quote: IANA has added a reference to this specification in the text/csv media type registration.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used as the notation for the fragment syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
MIME is background for the media type; the document does not extend MIME body structure or encodings.
RFC 3987 is only referenced in security considerations boilerplate.
The IANA section merely adds a reference to the registration; the document is not about IANA registry policy.
Web architecture is general context; the more specific URI and CSV tags fit better.

RFC7112.title: Implications of Oversized IPv6 Header Chains
RFC7112.summary: RFC 7112 updates RFC 2460 to require that the first IPv6 fragment contain the entire IPv6 header chain, to prevent stateless firewall evasion, and defines ICMPv6 Parameter Problem Code 3 for discards.

IPv6.why: The document amends the core IPv6 specification (RFC 2460) with new requirements on fragmentation and extension header chains.
IPv6.quote: it updates RFC 2460 such that the First Fragment of a fragmented datagram is required to contain the entire IPv6 Header Chain.

ICMP.why: Defines a new ICMPv6 Parameter Problem code and its use when discarding offending first fragments.
ICMP.quote: the ICMPv6 error message MUST be Type 4 ("Parameter Problem") and MUST use Code 3 ("First Fragment has incomplete IPv6 Header Chain")

firewall.why: The motivation is that header chains spanning fragments let packets evade stateless firewall filtering; the rule is meant to restore enforceability.
firewall.quote: Many forwarding devices implement stateless firewalls. A stateless firewall enforces a forwarding policy on a packet-by-packet basis.

rejected.why: Path MTU discovery is referenced only to bound the header chain length; the document is not about it.
ESP is mentioned only in the definition of the header chain terminator.
TCP is only an example of an upper-layer header.
