The security aspect is fragment-based filter evasion, which is covered by the IPv6 and firewall tags rather than general operational practice.

RFC7113.title: Implementation Advice for IPv6 Router Advertisement Guard (RA-Guard)
RFC7113.summary: RFC 7113 describes how IPv6 extension headers and fragmentation can evade RA-Guard implementations and updates RFC 6105 with filtering rules (parse the full header chain, drop undeterminable first fragments) to close those evasion vectors.

neighbor discovery.why: RA-Guard is a Layer-2 filtering mechanism protecting against rogue Router Advertisements, a Neighbor Discovery message. The document specifies implementation rules for it, so the neighbor discovery page is the closest fit.
neighbor discovery.quote: RA-Guard must parse the entire IPv6 header chain present in the packet, to identify whether the packet is a Router Advertisement message.

IPv6.why: A substantial part of the document analyses IPv6 extension headers, header chains and fragmentation as evasion vectors, which is relevant to readers of IPv6 specifics.
IPv6.quote: the L2 device implementing RA-Guard would be unable to identify the attack packet and would thus fail to block it.
IPv6.section: 2.2. Attack Vector Based on IPv6 Fragmentation

rejected.why: ICMPv6 Router Advertisements are the object being filtered, but the document does not specify or extend ICMPv6 itself.
Mentioned only as a similar attack target in Other Implications; the DHCPv6 shield is a separate document.
Mentioned only in a note that ESP is treated as an upper-layer header; not a subject of the document.
The document is a protocol security implementation advice, more specifically about ND/RA-Guard; a generic operational security tag is less specific.

gaps.name: RA-Guard / Layer-2 first-hop IPv6 security
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RA-Guard or first-hop IPv6 security (rogue RA mitigation, RFC 6105/6104), which is the main subject of the document.

RFC7114.title: Creation of a Registry for smime-type Parameter Values
RFC7114.summary: Creates an IANA registry for S/MIME smime-type Content-Type parameter values, populates it with existing values from several RFCs, and sets Specification Required as the registration policy.

S/MIME.why: The registry documents the smime-type parameter of application/pkcs7-mime, an S/MIME mechanism. Readers of S/MIME would want to find it.
S/MIME.quote: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) defined the Content-Type parameter "smime-type".

media types.why: The document creates a media type parameter sub-registry and sets its registration policy, and it updates the application/pkcs7-mime registration reference.
media types.quote: IANA has created a new sub-registry under the "MIME Media Type Sub-Parameter Registries" top-level registry.

rejected.why: The document is an IANA registry creation, but the tag covers registries and stewardship in general. The specific media type and S/MIME tags fit better.
CMS-related types such as CMC and enveloped-data appear only as registry entries. The document does not specify CMS.
EST contributes only the server-generated-key value to the initial registry. The document is not about EST.
The media types tag is more specific and already covers the MIME media type registry work.

RFC7115.title: Origin Validation Operation Based on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC7115.summary: BCP describing operational considerations for deploying RPKI-based BGP origin validation: cache placement and distribution, ROA issuance practices, and local routing policy for Valid/NotFound/Invalid announcements.

RPKI.why: The whole document gives operational guidance on RPKI-based origin validation: caches, TALs, ROA issuance, max length, Ghostbusters records and validation states.
RPKI.quote: Deployment of BGP origin validation that is based on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) has many operational considerations.

BGP.why: A substantial part covers BGP routing policy: Local-Preference mapping, AS_PATH ordering, handling Invalid announcements, and four-octet AS support in border routers.
BGP.quote: Origin validation based on the RPKI marks a received announcement as having an origin that is Valid, NotFound, or Invalid

rejected.why: NTPv4 is mentioned only as a recommended time service for routers; the document is not about it.
Considered since it is operational guidance, but the RPKI tag is more specific and the topic is covered by it.
Only mentioned implicitly in the Security Considerations, which note origin validation does not address AS_PATH validation. BGPsec is not specified here.
Certificate validation is referenced only through the RPKI profile RFCs; the document does not profile certificates.

RFC7116.title: Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP), Compressed Bundle Header Encoding (CBHE), and Bundle Protocol IANA Registries
RFC7116.summary: Informational IRTF document that asks IANA to create and manage registries for LTP cancel reason codes, LTP engine and client service IDs, CBHE node and service numbers, and Bundle Protocol administrative record types.

DTN.why: All registries concern DTN protocols: LTP, CBHE and the Bundle Protocol. Readers of DTN would want these code-point registries.
DTN.quote: IANA has set up a registry to manage CBHE Node Numbers. This registry, titled "CBHE Node Numbers", has been added to the list of registries associated with the Bundle Protocol.

IANA.why: The document's whole body defines new IANA registries, with their registration policies and initial values, handed off from the research group.
IANA.quote: This document describes the necessary IANA actions.

rejected.why: The 'ipn' URI scheme is mentioned only as the context for CBHE node and service numbers. The document does not define or change the scheme.
SDNVs are mentioned only as the encoding of the registered values. The document does not specify or discuss that encoding.

RFC7117.title: Multicast in Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS)
RFC7117.summary: Specifies VPLS multicast procedures using P2MP LSP trees (RSVP-TE and mLDP) in the provider network, with inclusive/selective/aggregate trees, BGP A-D routes, the new MCAST-VPLS NLRI, and inter-AS options.

VPLS.why: The whole document extends VPLS (RFC 4761/4762) with multicast tree procedures, auto-discovery, data forwarding and MAC learning.
VPLS.quote: This document describes solutions for overcoming a subset of the limitations of the existing VPLS multicast solution.

MVPN.why: Inclusive/selective P-multicast trees, PMSI Tunnel attribute and S-PMSI/leaf A-D routes follow MVPN procedures. Readers of multicast-in-VPN would want it.
MVPN.quote: Multicast trees used for VPLS can be of two types: + Inclusive trees.

RSVP-TE.why: Specifies how RSVP-TE P2MP LSPs are used as P-multicast trees, including the egress behaviour and PHP-off requirement.
RSVP-TE.quote: Procedures in [RFC4875] are used to signal the P2MP LSP.

BGP.why: Defines a new BGP NLRI/SAFI and route types, and uses the PMSI_TUNNEL attribute and inter-AS BGP A-D procedures.
BGP.quote: This document defines a new BGP NLRI, called the "MCAST-VPLS NLRI".

LDP.why: mLDP P2MP LSPs are a mandatory tree-building mechanism specified in use for VPLS.
LDP.quote: Each egress PE SHOULD "join" the P2MP MPLS tree by sending LDP label mapping messages for the LDP P2MP FEC

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific MVPN tag; the subject is multicast in VPN service.
IGMP/MLD snooping is only the source of membership state for selective trees, not specified here.
Mentioned only as a possible CE-CE protocol; PIM procedures are not defined.
VPLS is the more specific child tag for this document.
Pseudowires are the underlying VPLS mechanism and ingress replication baseline, not specified here.

gaps.name: P2MP LSPs (point-to-multipoint MPLS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for P2MP/mLDP LSPs as such; only MPLS, LDP and RSVP-TE are available.

RFC7118.title: The WebSocket Protocol as a Transport for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC7118.summary: Defines the WebSocket SIP subprotocol, making WebSocket a reliable SIP transport, with new Via/URI transport values, NAPTR service values, a relaxed Via "received" rule, keep-alive and authentication guidance.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new transport (WS/WSS), new Via and URI transport parameter values, NAPTR service values, and updates RFC 3261 on the Via received parameter.
SIP.quote: This document specifies a WebSocket subprotocol as a reliable transport mechanism between Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) entities to enable use of SIP in web-oriented deployments.

WebSocket.why: It specifies a new WebSocket subprotocol ("sip"), including handshake negotiation, message encoding in text/binary frames and ping keep-alive, registered in the WebSocket Subprotocol Name registry.
WebSocket.quote: This specification defines a WebSocket subprotocol (as defined in Section 1.9 of [RFC6455]) for transporting SIP messages between a WebSocket client and server

rejected.why: This is a transport-mapping document in spirit, but the SIP and WebSocket technology tags already cover it more specifically.
The WebSocket handshake uses HTTP Upgrade only as substrate; the document defines nothing new about HTTP.
Secure WebSocket uses TLS only as a security mechanism; no new TLS extension or guidance is defined.
Cookies are one of the authentication options mentioned, but the document doesn't extend or analyse them.
Basic/Digest challenge at handshake is referenced as an option only, not specified.
NAPTR service values SIP+D2W/SIPS+D2W are defined for SIP server location, but this is a small part and is covered by SIP.

RFC7119.title: Operation of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol on IPFIX Mediators
RFC7119.summary: Specifies how the IPFIX protocol operates on IPFIX Mediators, covering message headers, Template mapping and management, preserving original Observation Point/Domain information, timing, and Intermediate Process reporting, and defines five new Information Elements.

IPFIX.why: The whole document adapts and extends IPFIX for Mediators: Template Mapping, header handling, new Information Elements and Options Templates.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol in the context of the implementation and deployment of IPFIX Mediators.

rejected.why: Only named as the required transport for Mediators in the transport section; the document adds nothing new about SCTP.
Only mentioned as an optional transport; the document defines nothing about TCP itself.
Only mentioned as an optional transport; the document defines nothing about UDP itself.
The document notes its rules also apply to PSAMP, but this is incidental and PSAMP is not its subject.
This is flow export and mediation, not performance measurement methods, and the IPFIX tag already covers it.
MIB modules are cited only as an out-of-band way to check configuration consistency.

RFC7120.title: Early IANA Allocation of Standards Track Code Points
RFC7120.summary: BCP 100 defines the process by which IANA may make temporary early allocations of code points from Specification Required, RFC Required, IETF Review, and Standards Action registries before an RFC is published, obsoleting RFC 4020.

IANA.why: The whole document defines IANA procedures for early, temporary code point allocation, including request, follow-up, expiry, and deprecation. It belongs on the IANA registries and considerations page.
IANA.quote: This memo describes the process for early allocation of code points by IANA from registries for which "Specification Required", "RFC Required", "IETF Review", or "Standards Action" policies apply.

IETF process.why: The process assigns roles to WG chairs, Area Directors, and the IESG, and ties allocation to the standards-track document lifecycle. It is an IETF procedure BCP.
IETF process.quote: The Working Group chairs and Area Directors (ADs) judge that there is sufficient interest in the community for early (pre-RFC) implementation and deployment

rejected.why: The document concerns code point allocation for IETF Stream drafts, not the format, style, or publication of RFCs.
It uses allocation-policy terms from RFC 5226 but does not define terminology.

RFC7121.title: High Availability within a Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Network Element
RFC7121.summary: RFC 7121 describes control element high availability in a ForCES network element, clarifies the cold standby mechanism of RFC 5810, and specifies hot standby via a new FEPO LFB version 1.1 with new components, datatypes, and events.

ForCES.why: The whole document specifies CE failover and hot standby behaviour in ForCES, updating RFC 5810 and defining FEPO LFB v1.1.
ForCES.quote: This document discusses Control Element (CE) High Availability (HA) within a Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Network Element (NE).

rejected.why: ForCES has its own tag, which is more specific. The document is not about general routing architecture.
HA is a control/forwarding plane redundancy matter, not network operations or management.
The FEPO LFB definition is in XML, but that is only the model encoding and not the subject.
Mentioned only as an example TML transport and not used or specified here.

RFC7122.title: Datagram Convergence Layers for the Delay- and Disruption-Tolerant Networking (DTN) Bundle Protocol and Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP)
RFC7122.summary: Specifies how to carry DTN Bundle Protocol bundles and LTP segments over UDP and DCCP datagrams, with recommendations on congestion control, fragmentation, keep-alives, checksums, and port/service code use.

DTN.why: The document defines convergence layers for the Bundle Protocol and LTP, which is core DTN subject matter.
DTN.quote: This document specifies the preferred method for transporting Delay- and Disruption-Tolerant Networking (DTN) protocol data over the Internet using datagrams.

DCCP.why: DCCP is a main candidate transport, with specific guidance on ports, service codes, checksum coverage, and CCID2 as the default congestion control.
DCCP.quote: DCCP addresses the congestion control problem, and its use is recommended whenever possible.

UDP.why: The document gives UDP-specific rules for congestion control, checksums, fragmentation, and port use when carrying DTN data.
UDP.quote: UDP can only be used on a local network or in cases where the DTN node implements explicit congestion control.

rejected.why: Congestion control is discussed, but DCCP and UDP are tagged and the document is about transport mappings, not congestion control in general.
The TCP convergence layer is only referenced as the default alternative and is defined in another document.
It fits in spirit, but the DTN, DCCP and UDP technology tags already capture the subject.
Path MTU Discovery appears only as background to fragmentation avoidance, and no mechanism is recommended.
CCID3/TFRC is mentioned only to explain why CCID2 is preferred.
Checksum rules are a small subsection that applies only to the UDP and DCCP bindings.

RFC7123.title: Security Implications of IPv6 on IPv4 Networks
RFC7123.summary: Informational opsec RFC describing security implications of native IPv6 and IPv6 transition/tunneling mechanisms on enterprise IPv4-only networks, with filtering mitigations for each mechanism.

IPv6 transition.why: The document covers security exposure from transition mechanisms (6in4, 6over4, 6to4, ISATAP, Teredo, TSP, AYIYA) and how to filter them. Several are children of this topic, but the document treats the set as a whole.
IPv6 transition.quote: discusses the security implications of native IPv6 support and IPv6 transition/coexistence technologies on "IPv4-only" networks

operational security.why: It is an opsec operational guidance document with filtering policies and mitigations such as RA-Guard and default-deny rules for network operators.
operational security.quote: This document describes operational practices to prevent security exposure in enterprise networks resulting from unplanned use of IPv6 on such networks.

6to4.why: A full section gives 6to4-specific filtering rules, including the 192.88.99.0/24 anycast prefix and 2002::/16.
6to4.quote: 6to4 traffic could be filtered by applying filtering rules such as: Filter outgoing IPv4 packets that have the Destination Address set

Teredo.why: A substantial section covers Teredo-specific filtering, since Teredo traverses NATs and exposes internal hosts.
Teredo.quote: an organizational firewall could filter outgoing UDP packets with a Destination Port of 3544.

ISATAP.why: It has its own section on ISATAP filtering, including the difficulty of blocking its DNS and LLMNR-based router discovery.
ISATAP.quote: ISATAP can be easily blocked by blocking IPv4 packets with a Protocol field of 41.

6rd.why: It has a dedicated section on 6rd filtering, though a short one.
6rd.quote: 6rd can be blocked by blocking IPv4 packets with the Protocol field set to 41.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the subject matter, but the document is about coexistence and transition security, which the more specific transition tag covers.

gaps.name: AYIYA / tunnel broker (TSP)
gaps.why: The document covers AYIYA and the Tunnel Broker with TSP as tunnelling mechanisms, and the taxonomy has no tag for either.

RFC7124.title: Ethernet in the First Mile Copper (EFMCu) Interfaces MIB
RFC7124.summary: RFC 7124 updates RFC 5066 to record that maintenance of the EFM-CU-MIB (managing 2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS copper Ethernet interfaces) moved to IEEE 802.3, and adds a security considerations section for the IF-CAP-STACK-MIB that stays with the IETF.

MIB.why: The document concerns the EFM-CU-MIB and IF-CAP-STACK-MIB modules: their maintenance, their coexistence with the IEEE MIB, and the IF-CAP-STACK-MIB security considerations.
MIB.quote: RFC 5066 [RFC5066] defines two MIB modules:

Ethernet.why: The MIB modules manage Ethernet in the First Mile copper interfaces, and the document covers the transition of that work to IEEE 802.3.
Ethernet.quote: managing 10PASS-TS and 2BASE-TL Ethernet in the First Mile Copper (EFMCu) interfaces

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol the MIB is used with. The document defines nothing new for SNMP itself, and its security text is boilerplate.
2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS run over copper, but the document is about MIB maintenance and does not address DSL access networks.
The document does not deal with IANA registries.

RFC7125.title: Revision of the tcpControlBits IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Element
RFC7125.summary: Revises the IPFIX tcpControlBits Information Element from RFC 5102 to cover the 16-bit TCP flags field, including the ECN-related CWR, ECE and NS bits.

IPFIX.why: The document redefines an IPFIX Information Element, including its data type, encoding and export rules. Readers of IPFIX would want it.
IPFIX.quote: This document revises the tcpControlBits IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Element as originally defined in RFC 5102

rejected.why: The TCP header flags are only the thing being measured. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
ECN flags (CWR, ECE, NS) are included in the bit field so IPFIX can measure ECN use. The document does not define or change ECN.
The IANA registry update is boilerplate-level. The document is about the element definition, not IANA guidance.
The document defines an IPFIX Information Element, not an SNMP MIB module.

RFC7126.title: Recommendations on Filtering of IPv4 Packets Containing IPv4 Options
RFC7126.summary: BCP giving per-option advice for operators and implementers on whether routers, firewalls and security gateways should drop, ignore or process IPv4 packets carrying each IPv4 option, with operational impact and threats.

IPv4.why: The document is about IPv4 options (formats, uses, threats) and how to handle packets carrying them, which is IPv4 protocol operation.
IPv4.quote: This document discusses the filtering of IPv4 packets based on the IPv4 options they contain.

operational security.why: It is operational security advice for routers, firewalls and gateways on filtering policy, DoS risks to the control plane, and defaults for configuration knobs.
operational security.quote: Dropping such packets can help to mitigate the security issues that arise from use of different IP options.

router alert.why: A dedicated section covers filtering advice for the Router Alert option, its DoS threat and the impact on RSVP.
router alert.quote: The Router Alert option has the semantic "routers should examine this packet more closely

security labels.why: Sections 4.12-4.14 discuss IPSO BSO/ESO and CIPSO sensitivity-label options and why they should not be dropped by default.
security labels.quote: transmit from source to destination in a network standard representation the common security labels required by computer security models

rejected.why: Firewalls are the audience of the advice, but the document is about IPv4 options filtering rather than firewall technology itself.
CPU-exhaustion DDoS risk is mentioned as motivation, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation signalling.
Probe MTU and Reply MTU options are obsolete and mentioned only briefly.
The obsolete Traceroute option is one short subsection; the document is not about traceroute tooling.
RSVP is only mentioned as an application that uses Router Alert.
ICMP is only mentioned in passing, for example in PMTUD and traceroute context.

gaps.name: IP options
gaps.why: IPv4 option handling is the core subject but has no dedicated tag, so IPv4 is the closest fit.

RFC7127.title: Characterization of Proposed Standards
RFC7127.summary: BCP that updates RFC 2026 Section 4.1.1 with a revised, more accurate characterization of IETF Proposed Standard maturity and review.

IETF process.why: The document revises the IETF standards-track process description (maturity levels and IESG review) from RFC 2026, so it is about IETF process.
IETF process.quote: A Proposed Standard specification is stable, has resolved known design choices, has received significant community review, and appears to enjoy enough community interest

rejected.why: It characterizes maturity levels but is not a glossary or requirements-language document.
It concerns standards-track status, not RFC format, style or publication.

RFC7128.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Router Implementation Report
RFC7128.summary: Implementation report summarizing which features of the RPKI-to-Router protocol (RFC 6810) are supported by eight router and cache implementations, based on respondent questionnaires.

RPKI.why: The whole document reports on implementations of the RPKI-to-Router protocol, which delivers validated RPKI prefix origin data to routers for origin validation. The RPKI subject page is where readers would look for it.
RPKI.quote: This document is an implementation report for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Router protocol as defined in RFC 6810.

rejected.why: BGP origin validation is the motivation for the protocol, but the document reports on RTR protocol implementations, not BGP itself.
SSH appears only as one of the transports in the transport support table; the document does not specify or analyse SSH.
TLS appears only as a row in the transport table, where every implementation answers NO. The document is not about TLS.
IPsec is only a row in the transport support table, with NO for every implementation.
TCP is only listed as a transport option in the table; the document says nothing new about it.
The RPKI tag already covers this, since RPKI sits under routing security. The document is about a specific technology and not about routing security in general.

gaps.name: RPKI-to-Router protocol (RTR, RFC 6810)
gaps.why: The document is about this protocol, but the taxonomy has no RTR tag. The nearest tag is RPKI, which is where it was placed.

RFC7129.title: Authenticated Denial of Existence in the DNS
RFC7129.summary: Informational explainer of how DNSSEC authenticated denial of existence works, covering NXDOMAIN/NODATA, NSEC, NSEC3, opt-out, wildcards, closest encloser proofs, and online signing techniques.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document explains NSEC and NSEC3 denial of existence in DNSSEC, including opt-out, wildcards, closest encloser proofs and online signing.
DNSSEC.quote: This document provides additional background commentary and some context for the NSEC and NSEC3 mechanisms used by DNSSEC to provide authenticated denial-of-existence responses.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag; the basic NXDOMAIN/NODATA and wildcard discussion supports the DNSSEC explanation and is covered by the ancestor.
SHA-1 is only the hash used for NSEC3 owner names, not the subject of the document.
Base32 encoding of hashes is mentioned incidentally via RFC 4648; the document is not about it.

RFC7130.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) on Link Aggregation Group (LAG) Interfaces
RFC7130.summary: Defines running independent Asynchronous-mode BFD sessions (micro-BFD) on each LAG member link, with a new UDP port 6784 and dedicated multicast MAC, to control whether a member link is used in load balancing.

BFD.why: The document specifies how BFD sessions are established and demultiplexed per member link, including a new UDP port and amended receive procedures.
BFD.quote: This document defines a mechanism to run Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) on Link Aggregation Group (LAG) interfaces.

link aggregation.why: It specifies the interaction of BFD with LAG member link state, LACP, and load-balancing tables, so link aggregation readers would want it.
link aggregation.quote: make BFD control whether the LAG member link should be part of the L2 load-balancing table of the LAG interface

rejected.why: It specifies Ethernet MAC details for micro-BFD packets, but the subject is BFD on LAG, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
BFD control packets are carried over UDP with a new port, but UDP is only the substrate.
Mentioned only as an example of an L3 protocol that treats the LAG as one interface.
IPv4 and IPv6 address families are mentioned for micro-BFD sessions, but the document is not about IPv6.

RFC7131.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) History-Info Header Call Flow Examples
RFC7131.summary: Informational document giving SIP call-flow examples and message details for the History-Info header field (RFC 7044), covering forking, privacy, ACD, aliases, voicemail, GRUU, limited-use addresses, service invocation and toll-free numbers.

SIP.why: The whole document is SIP call flows illustrating the History-Info extension, with full SIP message details. This is SIP extension deployment and usage.
SIP.quote: describes use cases and documents call flows that require the History-Info header field to capture the Request-URIs as a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Request is retargeted

rejected.why: SDP bodies appear in the messages but are never shown or discussed; they are only payload.
ENUM is mentioned only in passing in the toll-free number use case, as a possible translation mechanism.
The toll-free section touches PSTN numbers, but the document is about SIP History-Info and not PSTN interworking.
Sections 3.2 and 3.3 show the Privacy header with History-Info, but this is a SIP header feature illustrated in two examples. It is not a general privacy treatment.
UUIDs and urn:uuid appear in the GRUU examples only as instance identifiers.
urn:uuid appears only as a +sip.instance value in the GRUU examples. The document is not about UUIDs.

RFC7132.title: Threat Model for BGP Path Security
RFC7132.summary: Informational threat model for BGP path security (PATHSEC) built on the RPKI, characterizing adversary classes, attacks on routers, operator management computers, repository publication points and RPKI CAs, and residual vulnerabilities.

routing security.why: The document is a threat model for securing BGP routing, covering adversaries, attacks and residual vulnerabilities.
routing security.quote: This document describes a threat model for the context in which External Border Gateway Protocol (EBGP) path security mechanisms will be developed.

RPKI.why: A substantial part (Sections 4.3-4.5, 5) analyses attacks on RPKI repositories, CAs and relying parties.
RPKI.quote: Because PATHSEC will rely on the RPKI, threats and attacks against the RPKI are included.

BGP.why: The attacks analysed are on BGP AS_PATH and update messages and BGP routers (Section 4.2); readers of BGP security would want it.
BGP.quote: refers to any design used to preserve the integrity and authenticity of the AS_PATH attribute carried in a BGP update message

rejected.why: The document deliberately avoids BGPSEC, using the generic term PATHSEC for any design; it does not specify or analyse BGPSEC itself.
Mentioned only as a possible way to protect router-to-router sessions, which is declared out of scope.
BGP sessions run over TCP and TCP-AO is mentioned, but the document is not about TCP.
RPKI certificates are discussed as threat targets, not profiled or specified.
The focus is on protocol threat modelling rather than operational practices.

RFC7133.title: Information Elements for Data Link Layer Traffic Measurement
RFC7133.summary: Defines new and updated IPFIX Information Elements (and IANA registry changes) for exporting data link layer (Ethernet, VLAN, Provider Backbone Bridge) traffic measurements, including layer 2 counters, frame sections, and I-TAG fields.

IPFIX.why: The whole document specifies IPFIX Information Elements for layer 2 measurement and modifies existing IPFIX registry entries. A reader of IPFIX would want it.
IPFIX.quote: They are used by the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol for encoding measured data link layer traffic information.

rejected.why: Ethernet/VLAN/PBB frame formats are the thing being measured, not specified or extended. The document defines IPFIX elements, not Ethernet behaviour.
This id is not in the taxonomy as a standalone tag. Only the PSAMP packet sampling tag under IPFIX exists, and the document reuses PSAMP packet-section elements rather than defining sampling.
MPLS label stack section elements are only edited to add sectionOffset. The document is not about MPLS.
Not relevant; no data models are defined.
The parent topic is implied by IPFIX and this is flow export, not performance metrics methodology.
Document concerns measurement of link-layer traffic, but it is about IPFIX encoding, not link-layer protocols.

RFC7134.title: The Management Policy of the Resource Priority Header (RPH) Registry Changed to "IETF Review"
RFC7134.summary: Updates RFC 4412 to change the IANA registration policy of the Resource-Priority Namespaces and Priority-values registries from Standards Action to IETF Review.

SIP.why: The document updates RFC 4412, the SIP Resource-Priority header specification, by changing the policy of its registries. SIP readers need it to know how to register new namespaces and priority values.
SIP.quote: RFC 4412 defines the "Resource-Priority Namespaces" and "Resource-Priority Priority-values" registries.

IANA.why: The whole document is about the registration policy of two IANA registries, which is a registry-management matter.
IANA.quote: IANA has changed the management policy of the "Resource-Priority Namespaces" and "Resource-Priority Priority-values" registries to "IETF Review"

rejected.why: The change is to an IANA registry policy, not to the IETF standards process itself.
Not relevant; the document does not touch SDP.

RFC7135.title: Registering a SIP Resource Priority Header Field Namespace for Local Emergency Communications
RFC7135.summary: Defines and registers the new SIP Resource-Priority header field namespace 'esnet' (five priority levels, queue-based) for emergency communications to PSAPs, between PSAPs, and with first responders within ESInets.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP by defining a new Resource-Priority namespace under RFC 4412, specifying its priority values and usage rules.
SIP.quote: creates the new Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Resource Priority header (RPH) field namespace 'esnet' for local emergency usage and registers this namespace with IANA

emergency services.why: The namespace exists to support emergency session establishment and priority within emergency services networks (ESInets), so it belongs on the emergency services page.

rejected.why: The IANA registration is boilerplate-like for this document; the document is about the namespace itself, not IANA registry guidance.
Resource priority gives preferential treatment, but the document defines a SIP namespace, not a QoS architecture or signalling mechanism.
RFC 5031 service URN is only referenced to contrast with RPH marking; the document does not specify URNs.
Not related to location-to-service translation; emergency calling is addressed only through priority marking.

RFC7136.title: Significance of IPv6 Interface Identifiers
RFC7136.summary: RFC 7136 clarifies that IPv6 interface identifier bits (including the u and g bits) carry no generic meaning and that the whole IID is an opaque value, updating RFC 4291's Modified EUI-64 requirement.

addressing.why: The document is about IPv6 address architecture, specifically the significance of interface identifier bits, and it updates RFC 4291. No more specific technology tag covers IPv6 addressing architecture, so the addressing topic fits.
addressing.quote: This document clarifies that the bits in an interface identifier have no meaning and that the entire identifier should be treated as an opaque value.

rejected.why: The document is about IPv6, but its subject is the narrower matter of IID semantics within addressing, so the more specific addressing tag was chosen.

ILNP is mentioned in one paragraph as an example that does not rely on universally unique IIDs. The document is not about ILNP.
The reserved IID registry is only noted in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate and not the main subject.

RFC7137.title: Use of the OSPF-MANET Interface in Single-Hop Broadcast Networks
RFC7137.summary: Experimental RFC updating RFC 5820 to describe using the OSPF-MANET interface on single-hop broadcast networks, with a Router Priority-based smart peering heuristic and dynamic single-hop detection.

OSPF.why: The document extends and profiles OSPF's MANET interface (RFC 5820), defining smart peering heuristics, a SingleHop flag, and a ModeChange timer.
OSPF.quote: This document describes the use of the OSPF-MANET interface in single-hop broadcast networks.

OSPFv3 is mentioned only for the Router Priority definition; the document is not about it.
Ethernet is only an example of a single-hop broadcast medium.

RFC7138.title: Traffic Engineering Extensions to OSPF for GMPLS Control of Evolving G.709 Optical Transport Networks
RFC7138.summary: Defines OSPF-TE (OSPFv2 opaque LSA) extensions for GMPLS to advertise G.709-2012 OTN switching capabilities, adding the OTN-TDM switching type and Bandwidth sub-TLVs in the ISCD, with examples.

GMPLS.quote: OSPF-TE) routing protocol extensions to support GMPLS control of Optical Transport Networks (OTNs) specified in ITU-T Recommendation G.709 as published in 2012

OSPF.quote: OSPF-TE must be extended to be able to advertise the termination and Switching Capabilities of each different ODUj and ODUk/OTUk

rejected.why: OSPF-TE is the vehicle, but the document is about GMPLS/OTN routing encodings; GMPLS and OSPF tags cover it.

RSVP-TE.quote: to provide Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) extensions to support control for [G709-2012].

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by RSVP-TE, so I did not list it separately.

RFC7140.title: LDP Extensions for Hub and Spoke Multipoint Label Switched Path
RFC7140.summary: Defines the hub and spoke multipoint (HSMP) LSP, an mLDP extension in which root-to-leaf traffic follows a P2MP tree and leaf traffic goes upstream only to the root, with new FEC elements, a capability TLV, procedures, and LSP ping support.

RFC7141.title: Byte and Packet Congestion Notification
RFC7141.summary: BCP that recommends AQM algorithms (RED, PCN, CoDel, PIE) not take packet size into account when dropping or marking, while transports should scale their congestion response by packet size; deprecates RED byte-mode drop and updates RFC 2309.

AQM.why: The document's core subject is how AQM algorithms such as RED should measure queues and encode drop/mark probability with respect to packet size.
AQM.quote: recommendations of best current practice for dropping or marking packets using any active queue management (AQM) algorithm, including Random Early Detection (RED), BLUE, Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN)

congestion control.why: A major part of the document is transport-side recommendations on scaling congestion response by packet size, and it adds to the congestion control principles of BCP 41.
congestion control.quote: packet size should be taken into account when transports detect and respond to congestion indications

rejected.why: ECN marking is mentioned as one way to signal congestion, but the document is about packet-size treatment in any notification, not about ECN itself.
PCN is named as one AQM scheme the advice applies to, but it is not specified or analysed in its own right.
TCP is the main example of a transport whose response is discussed, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
CoDel is only listed as an algorithm the advice applies to; the document does not define or analyse it.
TFRC-SP is discussed in the survey of past advice, but only as a related transport example, not as the subject.

RFC7142.title: Reclassification of RFC 1142 to Historic
RFC7142.summary: Reclassifies RFC 1142 (the republication of the draft-proposal OSI IS-IS specification, ISO DP 10589) to Historic and obsoletes it, directing readers to ISO/IEC 10589 instead.

IS-IS.why: The whole document concerns the status of the RFC that republished the IS-IS specification and says which IS-IS specification should be referenced. Readers of the IS-IS subject would want it.
IS-IS.quote: This memo reclassifies RFC 1142, "OSI IS-IS Intra-domain Routing Protocol", to Historic status.

rejected.why: The document mentions OSI and ISO 8473 only as the context of IS-IS. It does not address OSI network-layer protocols or their coexistence with IP.
ISO 8473 (CLNP) appears only in the formal title of ISO/IEC 10589, not as a subject of the document.
This is a status change for a single RFC, not a document about the format, style or publication of the RFC series. The IS-IS tag fits its subject better.
The reclassification is a status action on one document. It does not describe or change IETF procedures.

RFC7143.title: Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) Protocol (Consolidated)
RFC7143.summary: Consolidated specification of iSCSI, the transport mapping of SCSI over TCP: sessions, login and negotiation, task management, error recovery, naming, PDU formats, and authentication/security keys.

iSCSI.why: The entire document specifies iSCSI: PDUs, login, sessions, error recovery, and text keys.
iSCSI.quote: This document describes a transport protocol for SCSI that works on top of TCP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate over which iSCSI runs.
IPsec is a security mechanism iSCSI relies on (Section 9.3); the document does not define it.
SRP is one of the in-band authentication methods listed in Sections 9.2 and 12; it is not the subject of the document.
Kerberos is one of the authentication methods listed in Sections 9.2 and 12; the document is not about it.
iSER and RDMA are mentioned only in passing (e.g. STags for iSER); the document does not specify them.
The CRC digests are a minor part of the PDU format and error handling.

gaps.name: iSCSI
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no iSCSI tag at all, and the only iSCSI entry I found is not an id I can use here. 'iSCSI' appears under storage in the taxonomy, so the right id is probably 'iSCSI'. If that id is valid, the tag above is correct. If it is not, storage would be the fallback.

RFC7144.title: Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) SCSI Features Update
RFC7144.summary: RFC 7144 is a companion to RFC 7143 that extends iSCSI to support SAM-3/4/5 SCSI features: command priority, status qualifier, new task management functions, and the iSCSIProtocolLevel negotiation key.

iSCSI.why: The whole document specifies new iSCSI PDU fields, task management functions, and a negotiation key, so it is about iSCSI.
iSCSI.quote: This document defines enhancements to the iSCSI protocol to support certain additional features of the SCSI protocol that were defined in SAM-3, SAM-4, and SAM-5.

rejected.why: iSCSI runs over TCP, but the document says nothing new about TCP; it is only the substrate.
The IANA section creates and modifies iSCSI registries, but that is boilerplate and not the main subject.
The iSCSI tag sits under storage, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
This is a sibling subject (Fibre Channel over IP) and the document does not address it.

RFC7145.title: Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) Extensions for the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) Specification
RFC7145.summary: RFC 7145 specifies iSER, the extensions that let iSCSI run over RDMA-capable protocols (iWARP, InfiniBand), covering the datamover interface, login keys, PDU mapping to RDMA operations, flow control, STag management and error handling, and it obsoletes RFC 5046.

iSCSI.why: The document defines iSER as an extension of iSCSI, including new login/text keys and handling of every iSCSI PDU type.
iSCSI.quote: This document describes the extensions to the iSCSI protocol to support RDMA services as provided by an RDMA-Capable Protocol.

RDMA.why: The document specifies how RDMA Write, RDMA Read and Send operations and STags are used for SCSI data transfer.
RDMA.quote: An RDMA-Capable Protocol provides RDMA Read and Write services, which enable data to be transferred directly into SCSI I/O Buffers without intermediate data copies.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport under iWARP and traditional iSCSI; nothing about TCP is specified.
InfiniBand is one RCaP and has only an informative appendix; it is not the subject.
IPsec appears only in Security Considerations as a requirement inherited from iSCSI.
The parent topic is implied by the specific iSCSI and RDMA tags.
The IANA section only registers keys and opcodes, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: iSCSI/SCSI block storage
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no iSCSI tag. iSCSI is not a listed tag, so the ids I used need checking; the nearest valid tags are the parent storage and RDMA.

RFC7146.title: Securing Block Storage Protocols over IP: RFC 3723 Requirements Update for IPsec v3
RFC7146.summary: RFC 7146 updates RFC 3723's IPsec requirements for block storage protocols (iSCSI, FCIP, iFCP, RDMA/DDP, etc.) to IPsec v3, specifying ESP, IKEv2 and cryptographic algorithm requirements such as AES CBC, GCM and GMAC and the demotion of 3DES.

IPsec.why: The document's main purpose is to set IPsec v2/v3 implementation requirements (ESP, extended sequence numbers, transforms) for block storage protocols.
IPsec.quote: This document updates RFC 3723's IPsec requirements to IPsec v3 (RFC 4301 and related RFCs)

IKE.why: A whole section specifies IKEv1 and IKEv2 requirements, including authentication, identification types, DH group size and PFS.
IKE.quote: This document adds a requirement that IKEv2 [RFC5996] SHOULD be supported for peer authentication, negotiation of security associations, and key management.

storage.why: The subject is securing block storage protocols over IP (iSCSI, FCIP, iFCP, RDMA), and it updates many storage RFCs. No child tag fits as well, since the document covers the group of protocols rather than one.
storage.quote: RFC 3723 specifies IPsec requirements for block storage protocols over IP (e.g., iSCSI [RFC3720])

rejected.why: AES CBC, GCM and GMAC are mandated as IPsec transforms, but the document is about IPsec requirements, not the cipher itself.
iSCSI is not a tag in the taxonomy as a standalone; I considered it, but the document only updates its IPsec requirements.
RDMAP and DDP are among the updated protocols, but only their IPsec requirements change, so the document is not about RDMA.
ESP requirements are covered, but they sit inside the IPsec requirements and the broader IPsec tag suffices.
3DES CBC is demoted to MAY, but this is one algorithm change within a broader requirements update.
OCSP is mentioned only as an allowed alternative to CRLs for certificate checking.

RFC7147.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI)
RFC7147.summary: Defines the SMIv2 MIB module (ISCSI-MIB) for managing iSCSI instances, portals, nodes, targets, initiators, sessions and connections, obsoleting RFC 4544 to track the consolidated iSCSI spec (RFC 7143).

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, counters, notifications and conformance groups for iSCSI.
MIB.quote: This document defines a MIB module for iSCSI [RFC7143], used to manage devices that implement the iSCSI protocol.

iSCSI.why: The subject is managing iSCSI: targets, initiators, sessions, connections, login and logout statistics and failure notifications.
iSCSI.quote: This MIB module structure supplies configuration, fault, and statistics information for iSCSI devices [RFC7143].

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the Security Considerations mention of SNMPv3 is boilerplate, and the document defines no SNMP-framework feature.
The MIB cross-references the TCP MIB and records TCP ports and addresses, but it does not specify or extend TCP.
This parent topic is implied by the iSCSI tag, so it is not listed separately.
Authorization lists point to the IPS-AUTH MIB (RFC 4545), which is a separate module. This document defines no authentication mechanism.
IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are represented through InetAddress textual conventions. That is incidental, not the subject.

RFC7148.title: Prefix Delegation Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC7148.summary: Extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with a Delegated Mobile Network Prefix option and status codes so a mobile router can obtain prefixes via DHCPv6 prefix delegation (or static configuration) and have network-based mobility for them.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends PMIPv6 with a new mobility option, status codes, and MAG/LMA procedures for delegated prefixes.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification defines extensions to the Proxy Mobile IPv6 protocol for allowing mobility support to the mobile networks attached to a mobile router.

DHCPv6.why: A substantial part describes DHCPv6 prefix delegation interworking between the MAG/LMA and DHCPv6 DR/relay/RR functions in two deployment models.
DHCPv6.quote: the DHCPv6 requesting router function running on the mobile router sends a Solicit message requesting a prefix.
DHCPv6.section: 3.2.1. Delegating Router Co-located with Mobile Access Gateway

rejected.why: Mobile networks behind a mobile router are the topic, but the document extends PMIPv6 (network-based mobility), not NEMO basic support; NEMO is referenced only for DHCP PD terms.
Section 5.3 gives example SPD/SAD entries, but IPsec is only the security mechanism relied on for signalling.
The document uses IPv6 prefixes but is not about IPv6 specification or addressing in itself.
IANA registrations (option type 55, status codes) are boilerplate in this context.

RFC7149.title: Software-Defined Networking: A Perspective from within a Service Provider Environment
RFC7149.summary: An informational perspective on Software-Defined Networking from a service provider viewpoint, proposing a functional taxonomy of SDN techniques (metadomains) and discussing automation, bootstrapping, operations, PDP-centred intelligence, scalability and risks.

SDN.why: The whole document is about what SDN is, its taxonomy, and issues for service providers.
SDN.quote: This document aims to clarify the SDN landscape by providing a perspective on requirements, issues, and other considerations about SDN

policy management.why: The document frames SDN around PDP/PEP policy-based management and devotes a section to the PDP as the locus of intelligence.
policy management.quote: SDN techniques as a whole are an instantiation of the policy-based management framework.

rejected.why: PCE/PCEP is only cited as one example of an existing or candidate protocol, not discussed in its own right.
NETCONF is just listed among candidate configuration protocols.
ForCES is mentioned once as a prior example of control/forwarding separation; not the subject.
COPS-PR appears only in a list of candidate protocols.
Operations issues are discussed, but the more specific SDN and policy management tags cover them; parent not needed.
BGP and IGPs are mentioned only as possible discovery/bootstrap means.

RFC7150.title: Conveying Vendor-Specific Constraints in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol
RFC7150.summary: RFC 7150 defines a Vendor Information object and a VENDOR-INFORMATION TLV for PCEP so that PCCs and PCEs can carry vendor-specific constraints and other proprietary information in path computation messages.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with a new object and a new TLV, including the procedures, message encodings and backward compatibility handling. That puts it squarely under the PCE and PCEP tag.
PCE.quote: This document defines a facility to carry vendor-specific information in PCEP using a dedicated object and a new Type-Length-Variable that can be carried in any existing PCEP object.

rejected.why: PCE is the more specific tag under traffic engineering, and its ancestors are implied.
The RBNF notation is only used to write the message encodings. The document is not about RBNF.
The Management Considerations section only mentions the PCEP MIB, which is outside the main body of the document.
The IANA Considerations section only records the new object and TLV code point allocations. It is boilerplate.
TCP is only the transport PCEP runs over, and it is mentioned only in the Security Considerations.

RFC7151.title: File Transfer Protocol HOST Command for Virtual Hosts
RFC7151.summary: RFC 7151 defines a new FTP HOST command, with syntax, semantics, error handling and FEAT advertisement, letting clients name the virtual host they want on an FTP server that shares one IP address among several DNS names.

FTP.why: The document extends FTP (updates RFC 959) with the HOST command, its syntax, reply codes, REIN interaction, and FEAT response. FTP readers need it.
FTP.quote: This document defines a new FTP command that provides a mechanism for FTP clients and servers to identify individual virtual hosts on an FTP server.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.0 and 1.1 and the Host header are cited only as an analogy for the problem and its solution. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
The server_name extension and FTP-over-TLS are discussed for how HOST interacts with the handshake, but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
DNS names are the reason virtual hosts exist, but the document only references names and does not specify or operate DNS.
The HOST command carries a hostname, but the document is about FTP virtual host selection, not host naming conventions or host tables.
IDNA A-labels are mentioned in one sentence as the permitted internationalized form. That is incidental to the command.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the command syntax.

RFC7152.title: Requirements for Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) Support in Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN)
RFC7152.summary: Informational requirements document specifying functional requirements for supporting MEF E-Tree (rooted-multipoint, leaf-to-leaf restricted) services in multipoint L2VPN solutions such as VPLS and E-VPN.

L2VPN.why: The whole document defines requirements for L2VPN solutions to support E-Tree, with Leaf-to-Leaf restriction and Root/Leaf ACs on PEs.
L2VPN.quote: This document provides functional requirements for the support of Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) Ethernet Tree (E-Tree) in multipoint Layer 2 Virtual Private Network solutions

VPLS.why: VPLS is used to illustrate the problem and the backward-compatibility requirements; its limitations motivate the requirements.
VPLS.quote: VPLS does not include any mechanism for communication restriction between specific ACs. Therefore, it is insufficient for emulating generic E-Tree service

EVPN.why: E-VPN is a target technology for E-Tree support and is covered by the applicability and backward-compatibility requirements.
EVPN.quote: A solution MUST identify the L2VPN technology ([RFC4761], [RFC4762], [EVPN]) to which the solution is applicable.

rejected.why: The Ethernet tag covers IP over Ethernet and Ethernet OAM; MEF E-Tree is an Ethernet service emulated over L2VPN, which the L2VPN tags cover better.
The IP/MPLS PSN is only the substrate for the emulated service; the document does not specify MPLS.
Pseudowires appear in the problem-scenario figure but are not what the document is about.
Broadcast/multicast traffic flows and the VPMS comparison are mentioned in passing; the document is not about IP multicast routing.
IEEE 1588 PTPv2 is just one E-Tree use case in a table.

gaps.name: MEF E-Tree / Ethernet services (Metro Ethernet Forum)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MEF carrier Ethernet service definitions such as E-LAN, E-Tree and ENNI. This is the document's central subject, so it is covered only indirectly through the L2VPN tags.

RFC7153.title: IANA Registries for BGP Extended Communities
RFC7153.summary: Reorganizes the IANA registries for BGP Extended Communities type and sub-type values (and the IPv6-Address-Specific variant), and clarifies how to request codepoints, updating RFC 4360 and RFC 5701.

BGP communities.why: The whole document restructures the registries for BGP Extended Communities and explains how to request Type and Sub-Type codepoints. It updates RFC 4360 and RFC 5701, so readers of the BGP communities subject need it.
BGP communities.quote: This document reorganizes the IANA registries for the type values and sub-type values of the BGP Extended Communities attribute

rejected.why: The document is IANA-registry work, but it concerns one specific family of BGP registries. The BGP communities tag covers it more precisely, and the IANA topic is for general IANA guidance and stewardship.
BGP is the protocol context, but the document defines no BGP protocol behaviour. It only reorganizes the codepoint registries, so the more specific communities tag is used.
The IPv6-Address-Specific Extended Community registries are covered, but they are part of the BGP communities subject, not IPv6 addressing.
Flow spec codepoints appear in the registry listings only. The document does not specify or extend flow spec.
EVPN sub-types are listed in a registry table only. The document does not specify EVPN.

RFC7154.title: IETF Guidelines for Conduct
RFC7154.summary: RFC 7154 updates the IETF guidelines for conduct (obsoleting RFC 3184), setting out expectations for respectful, impersonal, technically focused personal interaction among IETF participants.

IETF process.why: The document is a BCP defining participant conduct norms within the IETF, which is part of IETF procedures and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document provides a set of guidelines for personal interaction in the Internet Engineering Task Force.

rejected.why: It only refers to BCP 79 in one guideline; the document is not about intellectual property.
It is itself an RFC but is not about RFC format, style or publication.
Not related; no nominating committee procedures are discussed.

RFC7155.title: Diameter Network Access Server Application
RFC7155.summary: Specifies the Diameter NAS application (AAR/AAA, RAR/RAA, STR/STA, ASR/ASA, ACR/ACA commands and NAS-specific AVPs) for authentication, authorization and accounting of network access, obsoleting RFC 4005.

Diameter.why: The whole document defines a Diameter application: command codes, message formats, and NAS AVPs, so Diameter readers would look for it.
Diameter.quote: This document describes the Diameter protocol application used for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting in the Network Access Server (NAS) environment.

rejected.why: AVPs derive from RADIUS attributes and the document points to RADIUS registries, but RADIUS/Diameter interaction text was removed; RADIUS is background, not the subject.
PPP, CHAP and PAP are carried or referenced as access methods, but the document does not specify or extend PPP.
Tunneling AVPs describe L2TP/PPTP tunnel attributes, but the document only conveys tunnel parameters and does not define L2TP.
The EAP application is a companion specification (RFC 4072) and is only referenced.
The more specific Diameter tag fits better, and AAA is its ancestor.
IPsec and TLS appear only as transport protection, mentioned in Security Considerations and the User-Password text.

RFC7156.title: Diameter Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6 Localized Routing
RFC7156.summary: Specifies how Diameter (via the MIP6-Feature-Vector AVP and a new INTER_MAG_ROUTING_SUPPORTED flag) lets MAGs and LMAs obtain AAA server authorization for Proxy Mobile IPv6 localized routing.

PMIPv6.why: The document supports authorizing PMIPv6 localized routing between MAGs and LMAs, extending the PMIPv6 localized routing protocol (RFC 6705) with AAA authorization.
PMIPv6.quote: Localized Routing Service Authorization can happen during the network access authentication procedure [RFC5779] before localized routing is initialized.
PMIPv6.section: 5. Example Signaling Flows for Localized Routing Service Authorization

Diameter.why: It extends Diameter usage by defining a new capability flag in the MIP6-Feature-Vector AVP and reusing AVPs in AA-Request/Answer exchanges between MAG/LMA and the AAA server.
Diameter.quote: This document describes Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) support using Diameter [RFC6733] for the authorization procedure between the PMIPv6 mobility entities

rejected.why: Diameter is the more specific child tag and already covers the AAA framework use here; the parent is implied.
PMIPv6 is a more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
Authorization is the purpose, but the Diameter tag already covers the mechanism, and the topic tag should only be added directly when no technology tag under it applies.
The only IANA content is boilerplate registration of one flag bit; the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC7157.title: IPv6 Multihoming without Network Address Translation
RFC7157.summary: Informational analysis of IPv6 multihoming without NAT/NPTv6 for hosts and small networks, covering source address selection, next hop selection and DNS server selection problems and DHCPv6-based solutions.

multihoming.why: The whole document analyses multi-prefix multihoming scenarios and requirements for hosts and small networks, so the multihoming topic fits directly.
multihoming.quote: In this document, we analyze the use cases of multihoming, describe functional requirements, and describe the problems with IPv6 multihoming.

DHCPv6.why: The proposed solutions rest on DHCPv6 policy distribution (address selection policy RFC 7078, DNS selection RFC 6731). The document evaluates these options but does not specify them.
DHCPv6.quote: We conclude that DHCPv6-based solutions are suitable to solve the multihoming issues described in this document

NAT.why: A central theme is avoiding NAPT and NPTv6 as multihoming mechanisms. The document compares them with IPv6 alternatives and discusses NPTv6 as an intermediate fallback.
NAT.quote: NAT and NPTv6 should be avoided, if at all possible, to permit transparent end-to-end connectivity.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the setting. The specific subject is multihoming, which has its own tag.
Router Advertisements are mentioned as a next-hop mechanism, but the document is not about ND.
Mentioned only as an alternative with too little operational experience for a recommendation.
DNS recursive server selection is one of three problems, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour itself.
The document covers multihoming rather than IPv4/IPv6 coexistence mechanisms.
Only mentioned in passing as another possible approach.

RFC7158.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
RFC7158.summary: RFC 7158 is a revised specification of the JSON text-based data interchange format, defining its grammar, values, numbers, strings, encoding, parser/generator behaviour and the application/json media type, obsoleting RFC 4627.

JSON.why: The whole document specifies the JSON format: grammar, values, numbers, strings, parsers and generators, plus interoperability guidance.
JSON.quote: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a text format for the serialization of structured data.

rejected.why: The document registers application/json, but that is only IANA boilerplate. The body is about the JSON format itself, not media type registration rules.
JSON strings are Unicode and the document discusses encodings and surrogates. That is a dependency of the format rather than the subject.
UTF-8 is the default JSON encoding, but the document does not define or extend it.
The grammar is written in ABNF, which is only the notation used, not the subject.
The IANA section is a routine media type registration and is not evidence for this subject.

RFC7159.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
RFC7159.summary: RFC 7159 is the revised JSON specification: it defines the JSON grammar, value types, string and number handling, parser and generator requirements, and the application/json media type, and it obsoletes RFC 4627.

JSON.why: The whole document specifies the JSON format: its grammar, values, objects, arrays, numbers, strings, parsers and generators, and interoperability guidance.
JSON.quote: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a text format for the serialization of structured data.

rejected.why: The IANA section registers application/json, but this is boilerplate-like registration apparatus. The document is about the format, not media type registry rules.
JSON strings are Unicode and the document discusses encoding and string comparison. That is a dependency of the format, not the document's subject.
Section 8.1 sets UTF-8 as the default encoding for JSON text. This is a requirement on the format and not a specification of UTF-8 itself.
The grammar is written in ABNF, which is only the notation used to define JSON.

RFC7160.title: Support for Multiple Clock Rates in an RTP Session
RFC7160.summary: RFC 7160 updates RFC 3550 to specify how RTP senders and receivers handle multiple clock rates in one RTP session, recommending a distinct SSRC per clock rate, multiple SR packets in compound RTCP, and a corrected jitter calculation.

RTP.why: The document updates RFC 3550 and defines RTP sender/receiver behaviour for timestamp calculation and SSRC use when clock rates change.
RTP.quote: This document clarifies the RTP specification regarding the use of different clock rates in an RTP session.

RTCP.why: A substantial part concerns RTCP SR packets, BYE, and the receiver jitter calculation in RR reports, affected by clock rate changes.
RTCP.quote: the next compound RTCP packet sent by the RTP sender MUST contain multiple SR packets, the first one containing the mapping for the current clock rate

rejected.why: Clock rate is a payload-format parameter, but the document does not define any specific payload format.
RFC 3556 bandwidth modifiers are mentioned only to describe turning RTCP off; the document is not about SDP.
G722 and MPA are cited only as examples of clock rate differing from sampling rate.

RFC7161.title: Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Multicast Handover Optimization by the Subscription Information Acquisition through the LMA (SIAL)
RFC7161.summary: Experimental RFC defining SIAL, a PMIPv6 extension (new mobility option, S flag, Subscription Query/Response messages) that lets the LMA hand a mobile node's multicast subscription context to the new MAG during handover.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends PMIPv6 signalling (PBU/PBA flag, new mobility option, new Mobility Header messages) for multicast handover.
PMIPv6.quote: This document specifies an experimental multicast handover optimization mechanism for Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) to accelerate the delivery of multicast traffic to mobile nodes after handovers.

multicast.why: It addresses multicast delivery and subscription context (MLD/IGMP state) transfer for mobile nodes, though it is a mobility extension, not a multicast protocol change.
multicast.quote: No extension is required in any of the multicast-related protocols in use (IGMP/MLD or PIM protocols).

rejected.why: MLD report formats are carried inside the new option, but MLD itself is not extended or specified.
IGMP formats are reused for the IPv4 option only; IGMP is not modified.
Mobility Header and RFC 6275 constants are reused as substrate; the document is about PMIPv6.
Only used to protect signalling in Security Considerations (boilerplate).
Registrations for mobility parameters are in the IANA section only.

RFC7162.title: IMAP Extensions: Quick Flag Changes Resynchronization (CONDSTORE) and Quick Mailbox Resynchronization (QRESYNC)
RFC7162.summary: RFC 7162 specifies the IMAP CONDSTORE and QRESYNC extensions for mod-sequence based conditional STORE and quick flag/expunge resynchronization of mailboxes, obsoleting RFC 4551 and RFC 5162.

IMAP.why: The document defines two IMAP extensions (new response codes, FETCH/STORE/SELECT modifiers, VANISHED response), so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: The Quick Mailbox Resynchronization (QRESYNC) IMAP extension is an extension to CONDSTORE that allows a reconnecting client to perform full resynchronization

rejected.why: IMAP is the specific child tag; the parent is implied.
ABNF is used only to write the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
NTP is mentioned only as an example of why the system clock cannot be used as a mod-sequence.
Not relevant to the document body.

RFC7163.title: URN for Country-Specific Emergency Services
RFC7163.summary: Updates the RFC 5031 registration guidance for 'sos' service URN sub-services so that emergency services offered in only one country can be registered.

emergency services.why: The document changes expert-review rules for registering emergency service URN sub-services, so it belongs on the emergency services page. No more specific child fits: LoST and eCall are not the subject.
emergency services.quote: allow the registration of service URNs with the 'sos' service type for emergency services that, at the time of registration, are offered in one country only

URN.why: It updates the registration policy for a URN namespace (service URNs), so URN readers would want it.
URN.quote: This document updates the registration guidance provided in Section 4.2 of RFC 5031, which allows the registration of service URNs with the 'sos' service type

IANA.why: The substance is revised designated-expert guidance for an IANA registry. This is the main body of the update, not boilerplate.
IANA.quote: This document updates the advice to the expert of the "'sos' Sub-Services" registry.

rejected.why: LoST uses service URNs, but this document does not specify or extend it.
Service URNs are used in SIP emergency calling, but the document says nothing about SIP itself.
The change is to registry expert-review guidance, not to IETF procedures generally.

RFC7164.title: RTP and Leap Seconds
RFC7164.summary: RFC 7164 updates RFC 3550 by specifying how RTP senders and receivers should handle UTC leap seconds when RTP streams are referenced to wall-clock (NTP) time, notably around RTCP sender reports and playout.

RTCP.why: The core normative recommendations concern RTCP sender reports and receiver reports and their NTP timestamps near a leap second. This is RTCP behaviour, a child of RTP.
RTCP.quote: RTP Senders using a leap-second-bearing reference for timestamps SHOULD NOT generate sender reports containing an originating NTP timestamp in the vicinity of a positive leap second.

RTP.why: The document updates the RTP specification, covering RTP timestamp mapping and packet playout (Section 5.2). RTCP is the more specific tag, but the playout guidance is RTP-level.
RTP.quote: This document updates RFC 3550 [1] by providing recommendations for smoothly rendering streamed media referenced to common wall clocks

time synchronization.why: A substantial part of the document compares how UTC, NTP, POSIX and TAI-based clocks (IEEE 1588, GPS) behave during leap seconds. This is a clock and time-scale subject. NTP and PTP are not specified here, so I tagged the topic rather than those technologies.
time synchronization.quote: Under NTP [8], a leap second is inserted at the beginning of the last second of the day.

rejected.why: The document relies on the NTP timestamp field and describes NTP leap-second behaviour, but it does not specify or extend NTP.
IEEE 1588 appears only as an example of a non-leap-second-bearing reference clock.
No codec or payload format is defined. The 8 kHz audio stream appears only in an example.
The document is about leap-second behaviour of clocks, not about the representation of timestamps in text formats.

gaps.name: Leap seconds / UTC timescale
gaps.why: The central subject is how leap seconds in UTC, TAI, POSIX and NTP affect timestamping. The taxonomy has no leap-second or timescale tag, so it is covered only approximately by the time synchronization topic.

RFC7165.title: Use Cases and Requirements for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE)
RFC7165.summary: Informational RFC defining use cases (tokens, OAuth, OpenID Connect, XMPP, ALTO, alerting, WebCrypto, constrained devices) and requirements for the JSON-based JOSE signed/encrypted object and key formats.

JOSE.why: The whole document gathers use cases and requirements for the JOSE signed object, encrypted object and key formats (JWS, JWE, JWK).
JOSE.quote: the IETF JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) working group has been chartered to develop a secure object format based on JSON

JWT.why: Security tokens and JWT drive the compact, URL-safe requirement, and the OAuth and OpenID Connect use cases are built around JWT.
JWT.quote: JSON Web Token [JWT] is a security token format based on JSON and JOSE.

OAuth.why: A substantial use-case section analyses OAuth token integrity, authentication and size constraints for JOSE.
OAuth.quote: The OAuth protocol defines a mechanism for distributing and using authorization tokens using HTTP

rejected.why: XMPP is only one use case; the document is not about XMPP itself.
ALTO is one use case among several, not the subject of the document.
CMS is the analogy and baseline for JOSE, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
Constrained-device object security over CoAP is a brief use case only.
JSON is the encoding substrate for the JOSE formats, not the subject.
TLS is mentioned only as the channel-based security alternative.

RFC7166.title: Supporting Authentication Trailer for OSPFv3
RFC7166.summary: Defines the OSPFv3 Authentication Trailer, a non-IPsec HMAC-SHA cryptographic authentication mechanism for OSPFv3 packets with SA IDs, 64-bit replay-protecting sequence numbers and migration guidance; obsoletes RFC 6506.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends OSPFv3 with an AT-bit option, Authentication Trailer format, and packet processing rules.
OSPFv3.quote: This document defines an alternative mechanism to authenticate OSPFv3 protocol packets so that OSPFv3 does not depend only upon IPsec for authentication.

rejected.why: IPsec AH/ESP is the existing mechanism the document provides an alternative to; it is not specified or extended here.
HMAC-SHA is used as the algorithm for the trailer digest but the document does not define or analyse HMAC itself.
SHA-family hashes are only used as primitives inside the HMAC computation.
The topic is relevant, but the more specific OSPFv3 tag covers it; no RPKI/BGPsec-like content.
The parent is implied by OSPFv3; the document concerns only OSPFv3 (OSPFv2 is referenced for comparison).
Keys are manually configured with SA lifetimes; no key management mechanism is defined.

RFC7167.title: A Framework for Point-to-Multipoint MPLS in Transport Networks
RFC7167.summary: Informational framework defining the elements and functions of the MPLS Transport Profile architecture specific to point-to-multipoint LSPs and pseudowires, covering requirements, forwarding, OAM, control plane, survivability and management.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document is an MPLS-TP framework extension for P2MP transport paths, covering OAM, survivability, control plane and management.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document defines the elements and functions of the MPLS-TP architecture applicable specifically to supporting point-to-multipoint transport paths.

GMPLS.why: The control plane section identifies GMPLS as the control plane for P2MP LSPs and discusses GMPLS recovery, a substantial part of the document.
GMPLS.quote: The MPLS-TP control plane for P2MP LSPs uses GMPLS and is based on RSVP-TE for P2MP LSPs as defined in [RFC4875].

pseudowire.why: Unidirectional P2MP pseudowires are an architectural element, with control plane, encapsulation and survivability discussed.
pseudowire.quote: The MPLS-TP control plane for P2MP PWs should be based on the LDP control protocol used for point-to-point PWs [RFC4447]

rejected.why: RSVP-TE for P2MP LSPs (RFC 4875) is relied on as the GMPLS control plane but the document does not specify or extend it.
Targeted LDP is only referenced as the PW control plane, with details left for further study.
P2MP transport paths resemble multicast, but the document concerns transport profile paths, not IP multicast routing.
OAM is covered in one short section that defers to RFC 6371 and a separate P2MP OAM draft, so it is not a main subject.
MIB-based management is only mentioned briefly in the Network Management section, which defers to other RFCs.

RFC7168.title: The Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol for Tea Efflux Appliances (HTCPCP-TEA)
RFC7168.summary: April Fools' RFC extending HTCPCP (the coffee pot control protocol) to support tea brewing, adding the message/teapot media type, Alternates-based variety selection, new Accept-Additions options and status code usage.

humor.why: A 1 April whimsical RFC specifying a protocol for networked teapots; the humor topic is the fitting home.
humor.quote: This paper outlines an extension to HTCPCP to allow for pots to provide networked tea-brewing facilities.

HTTP.why: The HTTP-derived protocol is extended with BREW/POST methods, Alternates header, Accept-Additions changes and status codes 300, 403, 418, 503.
HTTP.quote: HTCPCP-TEA makes use of normal HTTP error codes and those defined in the base HTCPCP specification.

rejected.why: It defines a new message/teapot MIME type, but only as a minor part of the joke protocol, with no registry rules.
It uses the Alternates header from RFC 2295 to list tea varieties, but only as a mechanism, not as a subject of the document.

RFC7169.title: The NSA (No Secrecy Afforded) Certificate Extension
RFC7169.summary: An April 1st joke RFC defining the "NSA (No Secrecy Afforded)" X.509 certificate extension, a boolean flag indicating a certificate's private key has been shared with a third party.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical document with a parody extension and tongue-in-cheek security considerations ("Secrecy is hard").
humor.quote: Knowledge is power, after all.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 certificate extension with an OID under id-pe, extending the RFC 5280 profile.
X.509.quote: This document defines the NSA (No Secrecy Afforded) certificate extension appropriate for use in certain PKIX (X.509 Pubic Key Certificates) digital certificates.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only used to write the extension's syntax; the document is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
Parent of X.509, which is the more specific fit, so it is implied.
Key sharing is mentioned, but the document does not address protocol privacy threat models.

RFC7170.title: Tunnel Extensible Authentication Protocol (TEAP) Version 1
RFC7170.summary: Defines TEAP version 1, a standards-track tunnel-based EAP method that uses a TLS tunnel for mutual authentication and carries inner EAP methods, password authentication, PAC and certificate provisioning, and channel binding as TLVs, with crypto-binding and key derivation.

EAP.why: The document specifies the TEAP EAP method: its phases, TLVs, inner method sequencing, crypto-binding and MSK/EMSK derivation.
EAP.quote: TEAP is a tunnel-based EAP method that enables secure communication between a peer and a server by using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate used to build the tunnel. TEAP defines no new TLS extension, though it uses session tickets as PAC and registers an exporter label.
RADIUS is only mentioned as a possible carrier of EAP between the authenticator and the server.
Certificate validation and Peer-Id derivation are mentioned, but the document is not about certificate profiles.
PKCS#7 is used only as a container for delivering certificates in TLVs, so the document is not about CMS.
In-tunnel certificate provisioning is a minor feature, not the main subject.
The AAA servers that carry EAP are context only. Channel binding mentions AAA but is not about AAA frameworks.

gaps.name: EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) and methods
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists an EAP tag in the security hierarchy in its description of 'EAP [tech]', but the id I used in tags must exist. If the exact id 'EAP' is not valid in the taxonomy, no fitting tag is available.

RFC7171.title: PT-EAP: Posture Transport (PT) Protocol for Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Tunnel Methods
RFC7171.summary: RFC 7171 specifies PT-EAP, an EAP inner method that transports NEA PB-TNC posture batches before network access, designed to run only inside TLS-based EAP tunnel methods such as TEAP.

NEA.why: The document defines the NEA Posture Transport protocol for pre-admission assessment, carrying PB-TNC batches and PA-TNC attributes between NEA Client and Server.
NEA.quote: PT-EAP, a Posture Transport (PT) protocol based on the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)

EAP.why: PT-EAP is itself a new EAP method (Type 54), with EAP message format, tunnel method requirements (TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS) and RFC 3748 security claims.
EAP.quote: PT-EAP is an inner EAP [RFC3748] method designed to be used inside a protected tunnel

rejected.why: TLS protects the outer EAP tunnel; PT-EAP defines nothing new about TLS beyond using tls-unique channel bindings.
The method type and version registry are boilerplate-level IANA actions, not the subject of the document.
X.509 server authentication is only mentioned as a feature of the tunnel methods.

RFC7172.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Fine-Grained Labeling
RFC7172.summary: RFC 7172 updates the TRILL base protocol with optional fine-grained labeling (24-bit FGL labels) for large data centers, specifying packet format, ingress/transit/egress processing, and safe coexistence with VLAN-labeled RBridges.

TRILL.why: The document specifies extensions to the TRILL base protocol (fine-grained labels, processing, IS-IS advertisement), so TRILL readers need it.
