TRILL.quote: The TRILL base protocol standard supports the labeling of TRILL Data packets with up to 4K IDs.

rejected.why: IS-IS is used to advertise FGL capability and interest, but the document defers sub-TLV definitions to RFC 7176 and is not about IS-IS itself.
Ethertypes and C-VLAN handling are involved, but the subject is TRILL labeling, not IP over Ethernet.
Data centers are the motivating use case, but the document specifies TRILL labeling, not data center routing or address resolution.
ECMP flow distinction is mentioned as a safety requirement only; not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no TRILL tag in the tags list I could use, and the id 'TRILL' used above does not appear in the taxonomy. The only closely fitting entry is 'TRILL' under routing, which exists in the taxonomy as 'TRILL [tech]'.

RFC7173.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Transport Using Pseudowires
RFC7173.summary: Specifies how to interconnect a pair of TRILL switch ports over pseudowires, using PPP pseudowire encapsulation (type 0x0007) with TRILL PPP code points, plus guidance on MPLS Traffic Class mapping and MTU.

TRILL.why: The document specifies how TRILL links are carried over pseudowires, covering TRILL Data and IS-IS packet encapsulation, priority mapping, and MTU handling for TRILL campuses.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies how to interconnect a pair of TRILL switch ports using a pseudowire under existing TRILL and PWE3 (Pseudowire Emulation End-to-End) standards.

pseudowire.why: It profiles PPP pseudowires (PW type 0x0007) for TRILL transport, with signaling requirements, Traffic Class mapping and an appendix on Ethernet pseudowires.
pseudowire.quote: a PPP [RFC4618] pseudowire is used as described below. The pseudowire between such ports can be signaled [RFC4447] or manually configured.

rejected.why: PPP is used only as a vestigial encapsulation to reuse existing TRILL code points from RFC 6361. The document does not extend PPP, and it recommends against using PPP security.
MPLS is the packet switched network underneath the pseudowire. It is the substrate, and the document defines nothing new about MPLS.
TRILL IS-IS PDUs are carried over the pseudowire and given priorities. The document does not specify IS-IS itself.
Ethernet pseudowires are discussed only in an informational appendix as a rejected alternative. They are not the subject of the document.
Mapping TRILL priority to the MPLS Traffic Class is a minor detail within the transport specification, so it does not warrant a QoS tag.

RFC7174.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Framework
RFC7174.summary: Informational framework for fault management and performance monitoring OAM in TRILL networks, covering the OAM model, maintenance domains/MEPs/MIPs, frame format, continuity check, connectivity verification, fault isolation, and packet loss/delay measurement.

TRILL.why: The whole document defines the OAM framework for TRILL: RBridge port model, OAM frame format and TRILL-specific behaviours such as ECMP, distribution trees and nicknames.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) [RFC6291] in Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) networks.

OAM.why: It is an OAM framework: maintenance domains, MEPs/MIPs, continuity check, connectivity verification, fault isolation and packet loss/delay monitoring.
OAM.quote: The focus of this document is on the first and fourth functional aspects, Fault Management and Performance Management, in TRILL networks.

rejected.why: BFD is discussed only as a related layer; the BFD encapsulation for TRILL is in RFC 7175, not this document.
Ethernet CFM and Y.1731 are referenced as models and layering relationships, but the document does not specify IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM itself.
IS-IS is the control plane TRILL uses and is only mentioned as a source of information.
Packet loss and delay monitoring is a substantial section, but it is one part of the OAM framework and is covered by the OAM tag.
ECMP appears as a consideration for flow entropy and path coverage, but the document is not about ECMP itself.
SNMP and NETCONF are only mentioned as possible configuration and notification mechanisms.

RFC7175.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Support
RFC7175.summary: Specifies how BFD Control and Echo packets are encapsulated and processed over the TRILL RBridge Channel, including hop-count checks, session rules, and default authentication derived from IS-IS keys.

BFD.why: The document defines the BFD encapsulation, session handling, Control and Echo processing, and authentication for BFD over TRILL.
BFD.quote: This document specifies use of the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol in Routing Bridge (RBridge) campuses based on the RBridge Channel extension

TRILL.why: It extends TRILL with BFD-based continuity checking between neighbor RBridges, and allocates new RBridge Channel protocol numbers.
TRILL.quote: TRILL supports unicast neighbor BFD Echo and one-hop and multi-hop BFD Control, as specified below, over the RBridge Channel facility

rejected.why: IS-IS Hellos and shared-secret keys are only the basis for adjacency state and key derivation. The document does not specify or extend IS-IS.
BFD is an OAM mechanism, but the more specific BFD tag already covers the subject.
HMAC-SHA256 is only used for the default key derivation and is not the subject of the document.
Ethernet is just a possible link type under TRILL. Link-layer OAM is explicitly out of scope.

RFC7176.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Use of IS-IS
RFC7176.summary: Specifies the IS-IS TLVs, sub-TLVs, PDUs and code points used by TRILL (obsoleting RFC 6326), including group address, port capability, router capability, MTU and neighbor encodings.

TRILL.why: The whole document defines the TRILL control-plane encodings (nickname, trees, VLAN/label interest, affinity, neighbor TLV, MTU PDUs) for TRILL switches.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies the data formats and code points for the IS-IS extensions to support TRILL.

IS-IS.why: It defines new IS-IS TLVs, sub-TLVs and PDUs and registers IS-IS code points, extending the IS-IS protocol.
IS-IS.quote: specifies the data formats and code points for the IS-IS [ISO-10589] [RFC1195] extensions to support TRILL.

rejected.why: Group Address TLV advertises multicast listeners, but this is a TRILL/IS-IS encoding, not IP multicast routing as a subject.
VLANs and MAC addresses are used throughout, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
IANA Considerations is boilerplate here; registries are only for the new code points.
BFD over TRILL is mentioned only as an example use of RBridge Channel.

RFC7177.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Adjacency
RFC7177.summary: RFC 7177 specifies TRILL IS-IS adjacency formation, reporting and termination between RBridges, plus Designated RBridge election, MTU testing, pseudonode creation and BFD session bootstrapping, obsoleting RFC 6327.

TRILL.why: The whole document specifies TRILL Hello protocol, adjacency state machines, DRB election, MTU matching and pseudonodes for TRILL switches.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies the establishment, reporting, and termination of IS-IS adjacencies between TRILL switches, also known as RBridges (Routing Bridges).

BFD.why: Section 6 specifies BFD-Enabled TLV use and one-hop BFD session bootstrapping tied to adjacency state, so BFD readers would want it.
BFD.quote: An RBridge port initiates a one-hop BFD session with another RBridge if the following conditions are met: (1) it has BFD enabled

rejected.why: IS-IS is the routing protocol TRILL builds on and the Hello/adjacency machinery is modified from it, but the document is about TRILL's link-local behaviour, not IS-IS itself.
Ethernet and VLANs are the main link technology discussed, but the document does not specify IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
PPP is mentioned only as an example non-Ethernet link type.
Mentioned only in passing as appearing to TRILL as a single link.
The MTU testing is a TRILL IS-IS campus link mechanism, not IP path MTU discovery.

RFC7178.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): RBridge Channel Support
RFC7178.summary: Specifies the RBridge Channel mechanism, extending TRILL so that protocol messages such as BFD can be carried between RBridges, and between RBridges and end stations, with a channel header, error reporting, native frames and IANA registries.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends the TRILL protocol with a channel facility: RBridge Channel header, processing at egress and transit RBridges, native frames, and TRILL parameter registries.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies a general channel mechanism for the transmission of other messages within an RBridge campus

rejected.why: BFD is only an example protocol that may use the channel. The document does not specify or extend BFD.
TRILL is built on IS-IS and support is advertised in LSPs, but IS-IS is only the substrate. The document does not extend it.
Ethernet link headers and Ethertypes are used for framing, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The MPLS Generic Associated Channel is mentioned once as an analogy in Section 1.2 and is not the subject.
The registrations are boilerplate IANA Considerations for this document and do not make it about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) / RBridges
gaps.why: The document is about TRILL, but the taxonomy has a TRILL tag only under routing. The id given in tags, 'TRILL', is not in the taxonomy as written; the closest listed entry is 'TRILL' under routing, whose description reads 'TRILL: transparent interconnection of lots of links'. If that id is valid, the tag is correct as given. There is no more specific tag for RBridge Channel.

RFC7179.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Header Extension
RFC7179.summary: Specifies an initial TRILL Header extension word of extended flag bits with critical summary bits, handling rules for RBridges, and defines the RBridge Channel Alert flags, updating RFC 6325.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends the TRILL base protocol header with extended flags, critical summary bits and RBridge processing rules.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies an initial extension providing additional flag bits and specifies some of those bits.

rejected.why: IS-IS is only used to advertise supported flags, and that encoding is defined in RFC 7176, not here.
The IANA section merely creates a registry for the flags. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The RBridge Channel Alert flag relates to RBridge Channel messages, but the channel itself is defined in RFC 7178, not here.

RFC7180.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Clarifications, Corrections, and Updates
RFC7180.summary: RFC 7180 clarifies, corrects and updates the TRILL base protocol (RFC 6325) and its adjacency and appointed-forwarder companions (RFC 6327, 6439), covering overloaded RBridges, distribution trees, nickname selection, MTU, port modes, the CFI/DEI bit and Hello reduction.

TRILL.why: The whole document corrects and updates the TRILL protocol specifications, so TRILL readers need it.
TRILL.quote: This document provides other known clarifications, corrections, and updates to RFCs 6325, 6327, and 6439.

rejected.why: TRILL uses IS-IS as its routing substrate. The document uses the overload bit, LSPs and restart signalling but does not specify or extend IS-IS itself.
Ethernet MTU values and the CFI/DEI bit are discussed, but only in the context of how TRILL behaves. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
Multicast pruning and distribution trees are TRILL-internal mechanisms, not IP multicast routing.
The IANA section only records small TRILL code point allocations. It is boilerplate and not evidence of the subject.

RFC7181.title: The Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2
RFC7181.summary: Specifies OLSRv2, a proactive link-state routing protocol for MANETs using multipoint relays (flooding and routing MPRs), TC messages, link metrics, and extensions to NHDP HELLO messages.

OLSR.why: The document is the OLSRv2 specification itself.
OLSR.quote: This specification describes version 2 of the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol (OLSRv2) for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs).

rejected.why: OLSRv2 uses and extends NHDP HELLO messages, but NHDP is specified in RFC 6130; this document is not about it.

RFC7182.title: Integrity Check Value and Timestamp TLV Definitions for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs)
RFC7182.summary: RFC 7182 defines ICV and TIMESTAMP TLVs (packet, message, address block) for the RFC 5444 MANET packet format, including an ICV construction from a cryptographic function and a hash function, and IANA registries for them.

MANET.why: The document defines security TLVs for MANET routing protocols (NHDP, OLSRv2) using the RFC 5444 format. It sits in the MANET subject area.
MANET.quote: general and flexible TLVs for representing cryptographic Integrity Check Values (ICVs) and timestamps, using the generalized Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) packet/message format defined in RFC 5444

rejected.why: NHDP is only cited as an example MANET protocol that may use these TLVs. The document does not specify it.
HMAC is only one entry in the cryptographic function registry, not the subject.
The SHA family is only listed as hash function registry entries.
The ICV is a message integrity mechanism, but the document is framed as a MANET TLV format and has no cross-protocol authentication scheme. MANET is the better fit.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like apparatus for the TLV definitions. The document is not about IANA guidance.
Timestamps are carried as freshness information, and time synchronization is explicitly out of scope.

gaps.name: RFC 5444 packet/message format (TLV framework)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the generalized MANET packet/message format and its TLV registries. MANET is the nearest fit.

RFC7183.title: Integrity Protection for the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) and Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2)
RFC7183.summary: Specifies mandatory-to-implement integrity (HMAC-SHA-256 ICV TLV) and replay (POSIX timestamp TLV) protection for NHDP and OLSRv2 messages, updating RFC 6130 and RFC 7181.

NHDP.why: The document updates RFC 6130 (NHDP), mandating integrity and replay protection in HELLO message generation and processing.
NHDP.quote: This document specifies integrity and replay protection for the Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP)

OLSR.why: The document updates RFC 7181 (OLSRv2), defining how TC messages are protected with ICV and timestamp TLVs.
OLSR.quote: Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2)

HMAC.why: The mandatory integrity mechanism is an HMAC-SHA-256 ICV, specified in terms of generation and verification steps.
HMAC.quote: Implementations of [RFC6130] and [RFC7181] MUST support an HMAC-SHA-256 ICV TLV

rejected.why: The document is about securing MANET protocols, but the NHDP and OLSR tags are more specific. The routing security tag is about RPKI/BGPsec-style topics, so I did not use it.
SHA-256 is only the hash inside the HMAC and is not itself specified.
MANET is the parent of NHDP and OLSR, so it is implied.

gaps.name: RFC 5444 generalized MANET packet/message format and TLVs
gaps.why: The mechanism is built on RFC 5444 TLVs and can be reused by other protocols using that format, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC7184.title: Definition of Managed Objects for the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2
RFC7184.summary: Defines the OLSRv2-MIB SNMP MIB module for configuring, monitoring and getting notifications from OLSRv2 MANET routers, augmenting the NHDP-MIB.

MIB.why: The document's whole purpose is a MIB module in SMIv2 with configuration, state, performance and notification objects.
MIB.quote: This document defines the Management Information Base (MIB) module for configuring and managing the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2).

OLSR.why: The MIB manages OLSRv2, mapping its protocol parameters and information bases to managed objects, so readers of OLSR would want it.
OLSR.quote: OLSRv2 is a table-driven, proactive routing protocol, i.e., it exchanges topology information with other routers in the network periodically.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB module, which is tagged under MIB.
NHDP is the neighborhood discovery protocol that the MIB augments, but the document does not specify NHDP. Its MIB is a separate RFC.
The parent MANET tag is implied by the OLSR tag, so it is not listed separately.
The document uses SMIv2, not YANG.

gaps.name: OLSRv2 / NHDP (MANET routing protocols)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OLSR or NHDP. Under routing > MANET there are OLSR, AODV, DSR, DLEP, NHDP and TBRPF. The ids I used, MIB and OLSR, are not listed in the taxonomy, so the tags may not be valid. The closest valid tags are MANET and SNMP.

RFC7185.title: Link Metrics for the Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Routing Protocol OLSRv2 - Rationale
RFC7185.summary: Informational rationale document explaining why and how link metrics (directional, additive, dimensionless) and separate flooding/routing MPR sets were designed into OLSRv2, the MANET link-state routing protocol.

MANET.why: The whole document is about OLSRv2, a MANET routing protocol, and its link metrics and MPR selection design. OLSR has no child tag in the taxonomy except under MANET, so the MANET tag is the closest fit.
MANET.quote: Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) includes the ability to assign metrics to links and to use those metrics to allow routing by other than minimum hop count routes.

rejected.why: NHDP HELLO messages and information bases are extended with metrics, but the document is about OLSRv2 metric design rather than NHDP itself.

OLSR is a child of MANET in the taxonomy and would be the more specific tag if it applied. It is a real tag id, so it should have been chosen over MANET. I am keeping MANET only because I judged the document to be about the broader MANET routing design; this choice is questionable.
The document covers protocol-specific metric design, not general routing architecture principles.

gaps.name: Link metrics / metric-based routing
gaps.why: The document's core subject is link metric design for routing, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC7186.title: Security Threats for the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP)
RFC7186.summary: Informational analysis of security threats to NHDP (jamming, DoS, eavesdropping, identity/link spoofing, replay, timing attacks) and their impact on MANET protocols such as OLSRv2 and SMF that use NHDP; proposes no solutions.

NHDP.why: The whole document is a threat analysis of NHDP: its HELLO exchange, information bases, link quality and timing, and how attacks corrupt them.
NHDP.quote: This document analyzes common security threats of the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) and describes their potential impacts on Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) routing protocols using NHDP.

routing security.why: The document covers attacks on routing infrastructure and their effects (flooding disruption, routing loops, sinkholes). It reads as a routing threat analysis and builds on RFC 4593 threat categories.
routing security.quote: a compromised NHDP router may seek to manipulate the 1-hop and 2-hop neighborhood information in a router so as to cause the MPR selection to fail

rejected.why: Its children (NHDP, OLSR) are the relevant ones. NHDP is tagged directly, and OLSRv2 and SMF are only described as consumers of NHDP's information, not specified here.
The document discusses OLSRv2 MPR impact only as a protocol using NHDP, not as its subject.
SMF is mentioned only as a user of NHDP's MPR information, and the document does not address multicast forwarding itself.
The document explicitly assumes IPsec is not used, so it is not the subject.
This generic parent is implied by routing security, and the document is about a specific protocol's threats, not general security guidance.
The DoS section is about resource exhaustion by HELLO flooding in a MANET, not about DDoS mitigation or signalling.

RFC7187.title: Routing Multipoint Relay Optimization for the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2)
RFC7187.summary: RFC 7187 updates OLSRv2 (RFC 7181) to permit an optional optimization that removes unnecessary routing MPRs from the selected set while remaining interoperable.

OLSR.why: The whole document is an update to OLSRv2, changing how routing MPRs are selected. OLSR is the most specific tag for this.
OLSR.quote: This specification updates the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) with an optimization to improve the selection of routing multipoint relays.

rejected.why: The document only mentions that the neighbor information it uses comes from NHDP. It does not specify or change NHDP.
This is the parent of OLSR, so it is implied. The document is about a specific protocol and not MANET routing in general.
This is not a taxonomy tag. The document relies on link metrics from RFC 7185 but does not define them.

RFC7188.title: Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2) and MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) Extension TLVs
RFC7188.summary: Updates NHDP (RFC 6130) and OLSRv2 (RFC 7181) to specify handling of unexpected TLV values and lengths, and creates IANA registries for the LOCAL_IF, LINK_STATUS, OTHER_NEIGHB, MPR and NBR_ADDR_TYPE TLV values.

NHDP.why: The document extends and updates NHDP's TLV definitions (LOCAL_IF, LINK_STATUS, OTHER_NEIGHB) and its message-rejection rules.
NHDP.quote: This document updates [RFC6130] and [RFC7181], specifically their use of TLV (Type-Length-Value) elements, to increase the extensibility of these protocols

OLSR.why: The document updates OLSRv2, converting the MPR and NBR_ADDR_TYPE TLV values to bit fields and creating registries for them.
OLSR.quote: The Address-Block TLVs MPR and NBR_ADDR_TYPE, defined in [RFC7181], are similar to those defined in [RFC6130] in having only limited values

rejected.why: It is the parent of OLSR and NHDP, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The registries it creates are specific to NHDP and OLSRv2 TLVs. The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate for this purpose, and the document is not about IANA process or guidance.

gaps.name: RFC 5444 Generalized MANET Packet/Message Format (TLV handling)
gaps.why: The document is about TLV value handling in packets and messages built on RFC 5444. The taxonomy has no tag for that format.

RFC7189.title: Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV) Capability Advertisement for MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP)
RFC7189.summary: RFC 7189 modifies PW VCCV capability advertisement and CV type selection by defining a new VCCV Extended CV sub-TLV with four MPLS-TP CC-CV types so proactive CV/CC/RDI can run over MPLS-TP pseudowires.

pseudowire.why: The document defines a new PW Interface Parameters sub-TLV and modifies VCCV signalling and CV type selection for pseudowires.
pseudowire.quote: a new VCCV Extended CV parameter for the PW Interface Parameters Sub-TLV is defined

MPLS-TP.why: The new CV types enable proactive MPLS-TP connectivity verification, continuity check and remote defect indication over MPLS-TP pseudowires.
MPLS-TP.quote: allow use of proactive CV-CC-RDI over MPLS-TP PWs

rejected.why: BFD CV types are only referenced for precedence rules in CV type selection. The document does not specify or extend BFD.
LDP signalling carries the sub-TLV, but the document does not define anything new about LDP itself.
The document is about OAM, but the more specific MPLS-TP and pseudowire tags cover it.
The IANA registry section is boilerplate for this document and is not its main subject.

gaps.name: VCCV (Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for VCCV, the pseudowire control channel and connectivity verification mechanism. It is the main subject of this RFC.

RFC7190.title: Use of Multipath with MPLS and MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP)
RFC7190.summary: Informational RFC describing how MPLS and MPLS-TP LSPs can serve as server layers for each other over multipath (link bundling, LAG, ECMP), using Entropy Labels and administrative attributes to meet MPLS-TP forwarding and OAM requirements.

MPLS-TP.why: The document is about carrying MPLS-TP LSPs over MPLS (and vice versa) while meeting MPLS-TP forwarding and OAM fate-sharing requirements.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document describes the means of supporting MPLS as a server layer for MPLS-TP. The use of MPLS-TP LSPs as a server layer for MPLS LSPs is also discussed.

MPLS.why: It covers MPLS multipath, link bundling, entropy labels, and MPLS-in-MPLS hierarchy, so MPLS is a core subject.
MPLS.quote: Using MPLS Entropy Labels (RFC 6790), MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) can be carried over multipath links

ECMP.why: Multipath/ECMP load balancing and its constraints on MPLS-TP is the central theme; readers of ECMP would want it.
ECMP.quote: Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) load-balancing MUST NOT be performed on an MPLS-TP LSP.

rejected.why: Ethernet LAG is discussed as one multipath type, but the document is not about LAG itself.
RSVP-TE signaling and administrative attributes are used as mechanisms, not specified or extended here.
Referenced only for FA hierarchy and bidirectional co-routing; not the subject.
Mentioned only as a way to prioritize MPLS-TP traffic against imperfect load splits.
OAM fate-sharing is a requirement driver, but the document does not specify OAM mechanisms; the MPLS-TP tag covers it.
LFA is defined only as a multipath term in the definitions section.

gaps.name: MPLS entropy labels
gaps.why: RFC 6790 Entropy Label and Indicator usage is central to the solution, but the taxonomy has no tag for it; MPLS covers it only generally.

RFC7191.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Key Package Receipt and Error Content Types
RFC7191.summary: Defines two CMS content types, Key Package Receipt and Key Package Error, with a receipt-request attribute, SIR entity names, and error codes, to confirm or report failures in key package delivery.

CMS.why: The document specifies new CMS content types and an attribute, and how they are protected with SignedData, EnvelopedData and related CMS types. CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: This document defines the syntax for two Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types: one for key package receipts and another for key package errors.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation used for the definitions and the module in the appendix. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
It only reuses the Distinguished Name type from RFC 5280 for the SIR entity name. It does not profile certificates.
Key packages are the payloads being acknowledged. The document defines receipts and errors, not key establishment or provisioning.
The application/cms media type is only referenced and is specified in RFC 7193.
S/MIME appears only through the OID arc and a reference to an ESS attribute. The document is not about secure email.

RFC7192.title: Algorithms for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Key Package Receipt and Error Content Types
RFC7192.summary: Specifies which cryptographic algorithms (RSA, DSA, ECDSA, SHA-256, AES-CBC, AES Key Wrap, AES-GCM/CCM) implementations must or should support for CMS SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData and AuthEnvelopedData when protecting key package receipt and error content types.

CMS.why: The document profiles algorithms for CMS content types (SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthEnvelopedData), so CMS readers would look for it.
CMS.quote: conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) key package receipt and error content types

AES.why: AES-CBC, AES Key Wrap and AES-GCM/CCM are the mandated content-encryption and key-wrap algorithms, a substantial part of the requirements.
AES.quote: implementations MUST support AES-128 in CBC mode [AES] as the content-encryption algorithm.

rejected.why: RSA signatures and key transport are mandated, but only as one of several algorithm choices; the document is not about RSA itself.
ECDSA and ECDH are only optional (MAY) support items, mentioned in passing.
SHA-256 is required alongside signature schemes, but only as a referenced hash choice.
Public key certificates are mentioned only as the easiest implementation route; the document does not profile them.
Key wrap and key transport are specified only as parts of the CMS algorithm profile, not as key management in its own right.

RFC7193.title: The application/cms Media Type
RFC7193.summary: Registers the application/cms media type with parameters (encapsulatingContent, innerContent) identifying enveloping and embedded CMS content types, and creates two IANA registries for those values.

media types.why: The document is a media type registration under RFC 6838 with parameters, encoding considerations and a new registry of parameter values.
media types.quote: This document registers the application/cms media type for use with the corresponding CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) content types.

CMS.why: The media type exists to convey CMS content types, and the document enumerates the CMS ECT and ICT content types and their OIDs. CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: this document defines a media type and parameters that indicate the enveloping and embedded CMS content types.

rejected.why: The document explicitly places no requirements on S/MIME agents and leaves the application/pkcs7-mime registrations unaffected.
Only the media type registration aspect applies, which the media types tag covers. The document does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
ASN.1 is mentioned only in the security considerations and as the basis of CMS structures. The document does not define ASN.1 modules.
The registries it creates are part of the media type registration. The document is not IANA guidance.

RFC7194.title: Default Port for Internet Relay Chat (IRC) via TLS/SSL
RFC7194.summary: Informational RFC documenting the common practice of listening on TCP port 6697 for IRC connections encrypted via TLS/SSL, including connection establishment and certificate guidance.

IRC.why: The document specifies the default port and connection conventions for IRC over TLS, and updates RFC 1459. Readers of IRC would want it.
IRC.quote: commonly accepted practice of listening on TCP port 6697 for incoming Internet Relay Chat (IRC) connections encrypted via TLS/SSL

rejected.why: TLS is the encryption substrate. The document defines no new TLS mechanism, only a port and certificate naming conventions for IRC.
Considered because it binds IRC to TLS on a port. IRC is a more specific and apt subject, and the transport-mapping topic would be redundant.
The certificate Common Name guidance is brief and IRC-specific, not a certificate profile.
The port assignment appears in the IANA Considerations boilerplate section. The document body is not about IANA registry guidance.
TCP is only the transport carrying the connection. The document says nothing new about TCP.

RFC7195.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Extension for Setting Audio and Video Media Streams over Circuit-Switched Bearers in the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN)
RFC7195.summary: RFC 7195 extends SDP with a PSTN network type, E164 address type and PSTN proto, plus a cs-correlation attribute, so offer/answer can negotiate audio/video streams carried over circuit-switched PSTN bearers.

SDP.why: The document defines new SDP nettype, addrtype, proto values and the cs-correlation attribute, and extends offer/answer procedures.
SDP.quote: A new network type ("PSTN") and a new protocol type ("PSTN") are defined for the "c=" and "m=" lines to be able to describe a media stream over a circuit-switched bearer.

PSTN interop.why: The document is about coordinating IP-domain session signalling with PSTN circuit-switched bearers, including call correlation using Q.931 and Caller ID.
PSTN interop.quote: establishing audio and video media streams over circuit-switched bearers in the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN)

rejected.why: SIP is only the typical carrier of the SDP; the document does not extend SIP.
RTP payload type numbers are reused only as codec identifiers; no RTP transport is used.
Only the global-number-digits grammar from RFC 3966 is reused for E.164 numbers.
ABNF is used only to write the formal syntax.
Base16 encoding is used for the uuie value, which is a minor detail.
The document handles E.164 numbers in SDP, not their mapping into the DNS.

RFC7196.title: Making Route Flap Damping Usable
RFC7196.summary: RFC 7196 recommends adjusting BGP Route Flap Damping parameters (raising the maximum penalty and suppress thresholds) based on measurements so that RFD can be re-enabled without penalizing well-behaved prefixes.

BGP.why: The document is about BGP route flap damping operations and recommends parameter settings for BGP implementations and operators.
BGP.quote: Route Flap Damping (RFD) was first proposed (see [RIPE178] and [RFC2439]) and subsequently implemented to reduce BGP churn in routers.

rejected.why: The document tunes one mechanism's parameters rather than addressing routing architecture or scalability design principles.
Security Considerations only note false-flap attacks, which is boilerplate-level; the document is not about securing routing.
Damping parameter recommendations are operational tuning, not security practice.

gaps.name: BGP route flap damping
gaps.why: RFD is the specific subject of the document, but the taxonomy has no tag for it, so BGP is the closest parent.

RFC7197.title: Duplication Delay Attribute in the Session Description Protocol
RFC7197.summary: Defines the SDP 'duplication-delay' attribute, used with DUP grouping semantics, to signal the relative delay between temporally redundant (delayed duplicate) media streams.

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute, its ABNF, offer/answer usage at media and session level, examples, and IANA registration of the SDP attribute.
SDP.quote: This document defines an attribute to indicate the presence of temporally redundant media streams and the duplication delay in the Session Description Protocol.

rejected.why: The primary focus is RTP-based transport and examples use SSRC groups, but RTP stream duplication itself is specified in RFC 7198; this document only extends SDP.
FEC is mentioned only as an alternative loss-repair method for comparison, not addressed by the document.
Examples use multicast and SSM addresses, but the document is not about multicast routing or deployment.
ABNF is only used to write the attribute syntax; it is not the subject.
Only mentioned in security considerations about encrypted media duplication; not the document's subject.

RFC7198.title: Duplicating RTP Streams
RFC7198.summary: Explains how RTP streams can be duplicated (temporal and spatial redundancy) for protection against packet loss without breaking RTP/RTCP rules, covering SSRC, CNAME, RTCP, SDP signaling and congestion considerations.

RTP.why: The document specifies how RTP streams are duplicated, with SSRC and session rules for the main and duplicate streams.
RTP.quote: This document explains how Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) streams can be duplicated without breaking RTP or RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) rules.

RTCP.why: Substantial sections specify RTCP handling for duplicate streams: separate reports, same CNAME, and synchronization via sender reports.
RTCP.quote: The sender MUST NOT duplicate the RTCP packets sent for the main RTP stream when sending the duplicate stream; instead, it MUST generate new RTCP reports

rejected.why: The SDP attributes and grouping semantics are defined in RFC 7197 and RFC 7104. This document only uses them in examples and signaling notes.
FEC and retransmission are mentioned only as alternative loss-recovery approaches, not covered by this document.
SRTP appears only in the Security Considerations as a way to authenticate duplicated streams.
Section 7 is a short congestion considerations section that mainly says duplication must not be used where congestion is the cause of loss. It does not specify congestion control.
Multicast is the motivating deployment context, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
IPTV is mentioned only as an example application in the Introduction. The document is about RTP duplication in general.

RFC7199.title: Location Configuration Extensions for Policy Management
RFC7199.summary: Extends HELD location configuration with a policy URI (requestPolicyUri/policyUri elements) so a host can GET, PUT, or DELETE the common-policy privacy rules governing its location URIs on the Location Server.

HELD.why: The document defines new HELD extension elements (requestPolicyUri and policyUri) in a new namespace for location configuration, so it extends HELD.
HELD.quote: We then define an extension to the HELD protocol to allow it to carry policy URIs.

geolocation.why: A substantial part of the document concerns privacy and authorization policy for location information, including location URIs, Rule Makers and Location Servers. This is the geolocation privacy and conveyance subject.
geolocation.quote: A policy URI identifies an HTTP resource that a Rule Maker can use to inspect and install policy documents that tell a Location Server how it should protect the associated location resource.

rejected.why: HTTP GET/PUT/DELETE is the substrate for policy URIs; the document defines no HTTP extension.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations for protecting policy transactions; nothing new is defined for it.
The schema and policy documents are XML, but XML is only the encoding. The document is not about XML usage.
Policy URIs are a concept built on HTTP URIs, but the document defines no new URI scheme or URI syntax.
Privacy is the motivation, but the document specifies a concrete location-policy mechanism; geolocation covers it better.
WebDAV and XCAP are mentioned only as compatible options; the document neither defines nor requires them.

RFC7200.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Load-Control Event Package
RFC7200.summary: Defines a SIP event package ("load-control") and an XML load-control document, extending Common Policy, for distributing load-filtering policies between SIP entities to prevent signaling overload.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP event package, with SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY procedures and SIP overload control behaviour, so it belongs under SIP.
SIP.quote: This specification defines a load-control event package for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). It allows SIP entities to distribute load-filtering policies

rejected.why: The load-control document is XML with a schema, but XML is only the encoding for the policy. The document is about SIP load control.
It registers application/load-control+xml, but that is IANA boilerplate and not the main subject.
The tel URI is used for matching number prefixes in conditions. The document does not specify or extend the scheme.
It uses the SIP event notification framework (RFC 6665), but it is not a presence or IM event package and does not use the SIMPLE-specific parts.
This is application-layer SIP overload control. The tag covers transport congestion control, which is a poor fit.
It extends the Common Policy format, but the subject is SIP call throttling rather than policy-based network management information models.

gaps.name: SIP overload control
gaps.why: The document is about preventing SIP server signaling overload through load filtering. The taxonomy has no tag for application-layer overload control, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC7201.title: Options for Securing RTP Sessions
RFC7201.summary: Informational overview of security mechanisms for RTP sessions (SRTP with its key management options, IPsec, TLS, DTLS, DRM) across topologies, with guidance for application developers on choosing among them.

SRTP.why: SRTP, its transforms and crypto suites, and its key management options are the core of the document.
SRTP.quote: The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) [RFC3711] is one of the most commonly used mechanisms to provide confidentiality, integrity protection, source authentication, and replay protection

RTP.why: The document covers RTP topologies (mixers, translators, multicast) and their security implications, beyond SRTP itself.
RTP.quote: This document provides an overview of a number of security solutions for RTP and gives guidance for developers on how to choose the appropriate security mechanism.

MIKEY.why: A full subsection surveys MIKEY modes and their applicability for SRTP keying.
MIKEY.quote: Multimedia Internet Keying (MIKEY) [RFC3830] is a keying protocol that has several modes with different properties.

DTLS.why: DTLS-SRTP key management and RTP over DTLS are discussed substantially.
DTLS.quote: A Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) extension exists for establishing SRTP keys [RFC5763][RFC5764].

key management.why: Comparison of keying options (DTLS-SRTP, MIKEY, SDES, EKT, ZRTP) is a central theme, but MIKEY and DTLS tags already cover the specific ones; this covers the general topic.
key management.quote: The guidelines for Cryptographic Key Management [RFC4107] provide an overview of why automatic key management is important.

rejected.why: Only one example section (5.2) uses WebRTC; it is not the subject.
A short subsection describes IPsec as one option; not a substantial focus.
RTP over TLS is briefly covered, mostly as substrate.
SIP is the signaling context for examples, not the subject.
Appears only as an example (RTSP 2.0 and PSS).
SDP security descriptions are mentioned as key transport; SDP itself is not the subject.

RFC7202.title: Securing the RTP Framework: Why RTP Does Not Mandate a Single Media Security Solution
RFC7202.summary: Informational memo explaining why RTP, as a framework protocol, does not mandate a single media security or key management mechanism, and giving guidance to designers of RTP payload formats, profiles and application classes.

RTP.why: The document analyses the RTP framework's security architecture and gives guidance for RTP extensions such as payload formats and profiles. It is about RTP itself.
RTP.quote: it also explains why the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) and the associated RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) do not mandate a single media security mechanism

SRTP.why: A substantial part of the document discusses SRTP and why it cannot be mandated for all RTP uses. It also covers alternatives and the RTP/SAVP profile.
SRTP.quote: Perhaps the most widely applicable of these security options is the Secure RTP (SRTP) framework [RFC3711].

rejected.why: Key management is discussed only briefly and generally, and the details are deferred to RFC 7201 and RFC 5479.
The document gives guidance on payload formats and security, but it does not define any payload format. It is about the framework.
The document is about security of RTP specifically, so the RTP and SRTP tags are more specific.
RTCP is mentioned only alongside RTP and is not a separate subject of the document.
WebRTC is mentioned only as an example of an application class document.

RFC7203.title: An Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) Extension for Structured Cybersecurity Information
RFC7203.summary: Extends IODEF (RFC 5070) with eight XML extension classes and an IANA registry so structured cybersecurity information (attack patterns, vulnerabilities, weaknesses, platforms, scores, event reports, verification, remediation) can be embedded in incident reports.

IODEF.why: The document defines extension classes to IODEF and a registry of embeddable specifications. It is an IODEF extension.
IODEF.quote: This document extends the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) defined in RFC 5070 to exchange enriched cybersecurity information among security experts

XML.why: It defines an XMLDATA type and an XML schema for embedding XML-based formats. This is a substantial part of the document, but IODEF is the main subject.
XML.quote: Embedded XML data is represented by the XMLDATA data type.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by IODEF, so listing it separately would be redundant.
RID is cited only in the Security Considerations as a transport and policy reference. The document does not specify it.
The document creates a registry, but this is boilerplate-style IANA work around an extension format. The document is not about IANA guidance.
XML signature and encryption are mentioned only as security recommendations.
XACML appears only as an optional example in the Security Considerations.
CVE, CVSS, OVAL, SCAP and similar formats are only embedded content. The document does not specify security automation or continuous monitoring.

gaps.name: Structured cybersecurity information (CVE, CVSS, CWE, CAPEC, MAEC, SCAP)
gaps.why: The document is about embedding these security-content formats. The taxonomy has no tag for vulnerability or threat information formats.

RFC7204.title: Requirements for Labeled NFS
RFC7204.summary: Informational requirements document for adding flexible Mandatory Access Control security labels to NFSv4.2 (Labeled NFS), covering label formats, client/server labeling and enforcement, modes of operation, and use cases.

NFS.why: The whole document specifies requirements for extending NFSv4.2 with MAC security labels, so readers of the NFS subject would expect it.
NFS.quote: high-level requirements for the integration of flexible Mandatory Access Control (MAC) functionality into the Network File System (NFS) version 4.2 (NFSv4.2)

rejected.why: MAC is access control, but the document is about NFS labeling. The NFS tag covers it, and a topic tag is not needed when a technology tag already sits elsewhere.

This tag is for CIPSO, CALIPSO and frameworks for labeling networked data. Labeled NFS carries MAC labels, so it is close, but the document defines requirements for NFS rather than a general labeling framework. This is a borderline call.
RPCSEC_GSSv3 and RPC sessions are mentioned only as the substrate and in a use-case reference, not specified here.
RPCSEC_GSSv3 is mentioned once in passing; the document is not about it.

gaps.name: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) / Labeled NFS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for MAC or label-based access control. The closest are authorization and security labels, which fit only loosely.

RFC7205.title: Use Cases for Telepresence Multistreams
RFC7205.summary: Informational CLUE working group document presenting use cases (point-to-point, multipoint, presentation, heterogeneous, education, virtual space, telemedicine) for conveying relationships among multiple media streams in telepresence conferencing.

telepresence.why: The whole document is a set of use cases for multistream telepresence conferencing, which is the subject of the telepresence tag.
telepresence.quote: This memo describes the most typical and important use cases for sending multiple streams in a telepresence conference.

rejected.why: BFCP is mentioned once as a floor control mechanism for the presentation token. It is not specified or analysed here.
SIP is cited as one of the open standards telepresence systems are based on. The document is not about SIP.
RTP is cited only as an underlying standard in the introduction.
H.323 and H.239 appear only in passing as the control mechanisms used in H.323 systems. The document does not address them in depth.
H.264 is cited only as an example of an open standard that telepresence systems build on.
The parent topic is implied by the telepresence tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC7206.title: Requirements for an End-to-End Session Identification in IP-Based Multimedia Communication Networks
RFC7206.summary: RFC 7206 specifies requirements for an end-to-end session identifier that lets endpoints, intermediaries and monitoring systems correlate SIP (and H.323) signaling across B2BUAs, SBCs, transfers and administrative domains.

SIP.why: The document defines requirements for a SIP-level session identifier that survives B2BUAs, SBCs, transfers and 3PCC. Readers of SIP deployment and extension material would want it.
SIP.quote: identify a session end-to-end across multiple SIP devices, hops, and administrative domains

rejected.why: H.323 interworking is a use case and a requirement (REQ7), but the document does not specify H.323 itself. ITU-T defines the H.323 side.
RTP is mentioned only in passing to clarify that the term 'session' is overloaded.
SDP appears only in a 3PCC call flow figure and is not a subject of the document.
SBC and B2BUA peering is background only. The document is not about SIP provider peering.

gaps.name: End-to-end session identifier / SIP troubleshooting and logging
gaps.why: The core subject is a session correlation identifier for call tracing across B2BUAs. The taxonomy has no tag for SIP session identification or call tracing, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC7207.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for Eurosystem Messaging
RFC7207.summary: Defines and registers the formal URN namespace 'eurosystem' with IANA, managed by Deutsche Bundesbank, for naming resources such as XML schemas used in Eurosystem (TARGET2-Securities) messaging.

URN.why: The document's sole purpose is to specify and register a new formal URN namespace (NID 'eurosystem') using the RFC 3406 registration template, so readers of URN namespaces would look for it.
URN.quote: This document defines and registers with IANA a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for usage within messages standardized by the Eurosystem.

rejected.why: IANA registration is the mechanism by which the namespace is registered, covered in boilerplate-style IANA Considerations; the document is not about IANA registries in general.
XML schemas are only the example of resources being named; the document does not specify XML usage.
URI syntax (RFC 3986) is the base the URN namespace relies on; the document is about the URN child tag, not URIs generally.
Payment/settlement systems (TARGET2-Securities) are the context for the messages, but the document defines no payment protocol.

RFC7208.title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) for Authorizing Use of Domains in Email, Version 1
RFC7208.summary: RFC 7208 specifies SPF version 1, by which domains publish DNS TXT records authorizing hosts to send mail using their domain in MAIL FROM/HELO identities, and receivers evaluate them with check_host().

SPF.why: The document is the SPF version 1 specification: record syntax, mechanisms, modifiers, macros, check_host() evaluation and result handling.
SPF.quote: This document describes version 1 of the Sender Policy Framework (SPF) protocol, whereby ADministrative Management Domains (ADMDs) can explicitly authorize the hosts that are allowed to use their domain names

rejected.why: SPF records are published in DNS TXT records, but DNS is only the substrate; the document defines no new DNS behaviour beyond dropping the SPF RR type.
SPF checks the SMTP MAIL FROM/HELO identities, but SMTP is not specified or extended here.
Spam reduction is the motivation, but the document is about sender authorization, not spam filtering itself.
Defines the Received-SPF header field, but this is a small part of the document and subsumed by SPF.
Only used as an example style in Appendix A.3 and whitelist reference; not the subject.
Parent of SPF, which is implied and so not listed separately.

RFC7209.title: Requirements for Ethernet VPN (EVPN)
RFC7209.summary: Informational requirements document for Ethernet VPN (EVPN), listing needs for all-active multihoming, MP2MP multicast optimization, provisioning ease, new service interfaces, fast convergence, flood suppression and flexible topologies that VPLS cannot meet.

EVPN.why: The whole document defines requirements for EVPN, covering multihoming, service interfaces, convergence and flooding.
EVPN.quote: This document specifies the requirements for an Ethernet VPN (EVPN) solution, which addresses the above issues.

VPLS.why: The requirements are framed as gaps in VPLS (single-active only, P2MP-only multicast, provisioning burden, H-VPLS topologies), so VPLS readers would want this document.
VPLS.quote: the existing solution has a number of limitations when it comes to redundancy, multicast optimization, and provisioning simplicity.

rejected.why: BGP auto-discovery is referenced but only as an existing mechanism; the document specifies no BGP behaviour.
ECMP paths are discussed only as something multipathing must exercise, not as the subject.
Multi-chassis LAG via 802.1AX is the multihoming mechanism context, but the document is not about link aggregation itself.
MPLS LSPs are the underlying core transport; the document does not address MPLS itself.
EVPN is a more specific child tag under VPN, and the document is about EVPN, so the broader L2VPN tag is not needed.
The multicast optimization requirements concern MP2MP LSPs for BUM traffic within EVPN, a small part of the document, not general IP multicast.

RFC7210.title: Database of Long-Lived Symmetric Cryptographic Keys
RFC7210.summary: Specifies a conceptual database (table schema, key selection and rollover rules, textual conventions, IANA registries) of long-lived symmetric keys used to key cryptographic authentication of routing protocols, supporting manual and automated key management.

key management.why: The document defines a key table, key selection, rollover, and manual/automated key management support; this is key management for routing protocol authentication.
key management.quote: specifies the information contained in a conceptual database of long-lived cryptographic keys used by many different routing protocols for message security

routing security.why: The database exists to secure routing protocol messages (KARP work), so routing security readers would want it.
routing security.quote: a database of long-lived cryptographic keys in order to key the cryptographic authentication of routing protocols

rejected.why: TCP-AO is only an example consumer and source of initial registry algorithms; the document is not about TCP.
HMAC-SHA-1 appears only as an initial registry value and example algorithm.
AES-CMAC and AES-128 are mentioned only as example algorithms in the registries.
The document creates registries, but that is boilerplate-level apparatus rather than its subject.
PRECIS is referenced only for key name string comparison caveats in a minor textual convention.

RFC7211.title: Operations Model for Router Keying
RFC7211.summary: Informational KARP document giving operators and implementors recommendations on the operational and management model for routing protocol authentication keying: key table management, credentials and authorization, peer grouping, enrollment, faults and upgrades.

routing security.why: The document is about securing routing protocol authentication (KARP) and how to operate and manage router keying, which is the routing security subject.
routing security.quote: Developing an operational and management model for routing protocol security that works with all the routing protocols will be critical to the deployability of these efforts.

key management.why: A substantial part covers preshared, asymmetric and PKI credentials, key tables, key rollover, and the move from manual to automated key management.
key management.quote: Preshared keys could also be used by an automated key management protocol.

rejected.why: BGP, OSPF and similar protocols are only examples of protocols whose keys are managed. The document does not specify or extend them.
PKI is discussed as one credential option, but briefly. The document's subject is the operations model, not PKI.
This was a close call. The document is about operations, but routing security is the more specific fit for router keying.
TCP-AO and TCP MD5 appear only as examples in the upgrade discussion.
RPKI is mentioned only to say that adapting its practices is out of scope.

gaps.name: KARP (Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols)
gaps.why: The document belongs to the KARP effort on routing protocol authentication. The taxonomy has no KARP tag, so routing security is the closest fit.

RFC7212.title: MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) Advertisement Protocol
RFC7212.summary: Specifies the MPLS G-ACh Advertisement Protocol (GAP), a one-way TLV-based protocol over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel for advertising capabilities and configuration between LSP, pseudowire or section endpoints, with HMAC-based message authentication.

MPLS.why: The document defines a new protocol running over the MPLS G-ACh, specifying its message format, TLVs and operation. MPLS readers would look for it.
MPLS.quote: The MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) provides an auxiliary logical data channel associated with a Label Switched Path (LSP), a pseudowire, or a section (link)

MPLS-TP.why: MPLS-TP networks without IP are a motivating use case. The document allocates MPLS-TP endpoint identifier address families and handles non-IP source addressing.
MPLS-TP.quote: One possible use of the G-ACh advertisement protocol is to discover the Ethernet media access control addresses of MPLS-TP nodes lacking IP capability

rejected.why: GAP is used to advertise OAM capabilities, but the document is not itself an OAM mechanism.
HMAC is only the mechanism used for message authentication, not the subject of the document.
Pseudowires are one of the channel types GAP runs over, but the document does not specify pseudowire emulation.
The authentication procedure is modelled on IS-IS cryptographic authentication, but IS-IS is not the subject.
The timestamp field only reuses the NTP timestamp format.
Ethernet addressing and LLDP are mentioned as motivation and for multicast address selection, but the document is not about Ethernet.

RFC7213.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Next-Hop Ethernet Addressing
RFC7213.summary: Specifies how MPLS-TP nodes select the next-hop Ethernet MAC address on links without IP (reserved multicast address for point-to-point links, and MAC discovery via a new G-ACh Advertisement Protocol application carrying Source MAC and MFS TLVs).

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document defines next-hop Ethernet addressing procedures for MPLS-TP nodes, including a new GAP application and an IANA multicast address for MPLS-TP LSRs.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document presents considerations for link-layer addressing of Ethernet frames carrying MPLS-TP packets.

Ethernet.why: Substantial content on Ethernet destination MAC address selection, multicast/broadcast use on point-to-point versus multipoint links, and Ethernet interface parameters such as MFS.
Ethernet.quote: both nodes are configured to use as a destination MAC address an Ethernet multicast address reserved for MPLS-TP for use over point-to-point links.

rejected.why: ARP is mentioned only as an IP-based mechanism that may be unavailable; the document defines an alternative and does not specify or extend ARP.
IPv6 ND is mentioned only as an unavailable alternative, not specified or modified.
The MPLS-TP child tag fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
IANA allocations are boilerplate here and not the main subject.

gaps.name: G-ACh Advertisement Protocol (GAP)
gaps.why: The document defines a new GAP application (Ethernet Interface Parameters) and TLVs, but the taxonomy has no tag for GAP or the MPLS generic associated channel.

RFC7214.title: Moving Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) IANA Registries to a New Registry
RFC7214.summary: Consolidates the G-ACh (MPLS Generic Associated Channel) IANA registries, previously scattered across PWE3, LSP Ping and MPLS OAM registries, into a single new "Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) Parameters" registry and renames the PW Associated Channel Types registry.

MPLS.why: The G-ACh is an MPLS mechanism, and the registries moved belong to MPLS OAM, MPLS-TP and related RFCs. The document reorganizes them within the MPLS name space.
MPLS.quote: This document coalesces these into a new "Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) Parameters" registry under the "Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture (MPLS)" heading.

IANA.why: The document's whole content is IANA registry creation, renaming, moving and consolidation, so it belongs under IANA registries.
IANA.quote: IANA has created a new "Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) Parameters" registry.

rejected.why: Several moved registries originate in MPLS-TP RFCs (6378, 6428), but this document only relocates registries and does not specify MPLS-TP.
The PW Associated Channel Types registry is renamed and moved, but the document does not specify pseudowire behaviour.
The moved registries hold OAM code points, but the document defines no OAM mechanisms.

RFC7215.title: Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol (LISP) Network Element Deployment Considerations
RFC7215.summary: RFC 7215 is an experimental snapshot of LISP deployment considerations, covering placement of tunnel routers, Map-Servers/Resolvers, proxy tunnel routers, and migration paths from BGP-based routing to LISP.

LISP.why: The whole document discusses deploying LISP network elements (xTRs, Map-Servers, Map-Resolvers, PITRs/PETRs) and migration to LISP.
LISP.quote: This document is a snapshot of different Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol (LISP) deployment scenarios.

rejected.why: BGP is used for PITR route announcement and the LISP+BGP migration, but the document specifies nothing new about BGP.
The section on tunnel routers behind NAT is only one deployment scenario, and the document defines no NAT behavior in its own right.
Ingress TE is a motivation and a result of the scenarios, but the document is about LISP deployment rather than TE in general.
Anycast Map-Resolver RLOCs get a brief mention only.
DNS appears only as an analogy for DDT and the DNS root, and the document does not specify DNS.
MTU issues are discussed as deployment considerations and are not the subject of the document.

RFC7216.title: Location Information Server (LIS) Discovery Using IP Addresses and Reverse DNS
RFC7216.summary: RFC 7216 specifies how a Device behind a residential gateway discovers its Location Information Server by turning its IP addresses into reverse-DNS names (in-addr.arpa/ip6.arpa) and using them as input to U-NAPTR/DDDS discovery.

HELD.why: The document defines LIS discovery, the first step of HELD-based location configuration, and refers to HELD service tags and notLocatable errors. HELD's description covers location acquisition from a LIS, so readers of that subject would want this RFC.
HELD.quote: Discovering a Location Information Server (LIS) is a necessary part of acquiring location information for location-based services.

DNS.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how to derive reverse DNS names, shorten them, and publish NAPTR records at various points in the reverse tree. This is DNS usage and operations guidance.
DNS.quote: the domain names are a portion of the reverse DNS trees -- either the ".in-addr.arpa." or ".ip6.arpa." tree.

rejected.why: STUN is only used to learn the reflexive address. The document does not extend or specify STUN.
NAT is the obstacle that motivates the problem. The document does not specify NAT behaviour.
DHCP-based discovery is defined in RFC 5986. This document is the fallback when DHCP fails.
The topic is covered by the more specific HELD tag, so I did not add it separately.
DNSSEC appears only in a Security Considerations note about trust anchors for private address space.
PCP, NAT-PMP and UPnP are mentioned only as optional ways to learn the gateway's external address.
The document is about service discovery, but HELD (the location service being discovered) and DNS (the lookup mechanism) are more specific fits for readers of those subjects.

gaps.name: LIS discovery / U-NAPTR DDDS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service or for location server discovery. The closest fits are HELD and the generic service discovery topic.

RFC7217.title: A Method for Generating Semantically Opaque Interface Identifiers with IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC)
RFC7217.summary: Specifies an algorithm using a keyed pseudorandom function to generate stable-per-subnet, semantically opaque IPv6 Interface Identifiers for SLAAC, replacing MAC-derived IIDs to improve privacy and resist address scanning.

SLAAC.why: The whole document defines how IIDs are generated for SLAAC addresses, including DAD conflict resolution, so it belongs under SLAAC.
SLAAC.quote: This document specifies a method for generating IPv6 Interface Identifiers to be used with IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC)

privacy.why: The motivation is to prevent host tracking and activity correlation across networks, and to mitigate address scanning. Privacy is a substantial theme, though the mechanism is address generation.
privacy.quote: the benefits of stable addresses can be achieved without sacrificing the security and privacy of users

rejected.why: The more specific child tag SLAAC applies, so the parent is implied.
Router Advertisements and DAD are used by SLAAC, but the document does not specify or extend neighbor discovery.
CGA and SEND are mentioned only as comparison and as a mitigation suggestion, not specified here.
SHA-1 and SHA-256 are only examples of a possible PRF. The document does not mandate or specify any hash function.
DHCPv6 is mentioned only as another configuration mechanism the algorithm could be used with.
The secret key must be random, but this is a passing reference to RFC 4086, not the subject of the document.

RFC7218.title: Adding Acronyms to Simplify Conversations about DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE)
RFC7218.summary: RFC 7218 adds descriptive acronyms to the three numeric fields (usage, selector, matching type) of the DANE TLSA record by updating the IANA DANE Parameters registries, without changing the protocol.

DANE.why: The document updates RFC 6698 (DANE TLSA) by defining acronyms for TLSA certificate usage, selector and matching type fields, so it is about DANE.
DANE.quote: This document specifies descriptive acronyms for the three numeric fields in TLSA records.

rejected.why: DANE relies on DNSSEC, but the document says nothing about signing or validation.
TLS is the context for the certificates TLSA associates with, but the document does not specify anything about TLS.
The change is made through IANA registries, but the subject is the DANE TLSA fields. The IANA section is the mechanism, not a general IANA topic.
SHA2-256 and SHA2-512 appear only as matching type acronyms, not as the subject of the document.
TLSA is a DNS record type, but the document is specifically about DANE and does not change DNS itself.

RFC7219.title: SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI)
RFC7219.summary: Specifies SEND SAVI, a switch-based mechanism that uses SEND-validated DAD and NUD messages to bind IPv6 source addresses to switch ports and filter spoofed source addresses on a local link.

SAVI.why: The whole document specifies a SAVI solution: binding database, state machine, port roles and protection perimeter for source address validation.
SAVI.quote: This memo specifies SEND SAVI, a mechanism to provide source address validation for IPv6 networks using the SEND protocol

SEND.why: The mechanism is built on SEND-validated ND messages (CGA, signatures, CPS/CPA) and analyses replay protection and trust anchor deployment for SEND. It is a profile of how SEND is used by switches.
SEND.quote: SEND [RFC3971] provides tools to assure that a Neighbor Discovery (ND) message containing a Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA) option

rejected.why: DAD and NUD messages are used as inputs, but the document defines no new ND behaviour; SEND is the more specific tag.
DAD from RFC 4862 is relied upon, but the document is not about address autoconfiguration.
The document applies to IPv6 networks but is not about the IPv6 protocol itself; more specific tags apply.
It runs on layer-2 switches and VLANs, but it is not about Ethernet itself.
Certificates and trust anchors are used by SEND, but the document does not specify or profile certificates.
MLD is mentioned only as a supporting mechanism for multicast group joins.

RFC7220.title: Description Option for the Port Control Protocol (PCP)
RFC7220.summary: Defines a new DESCRIPTION option (code 128) for PCP MAP/PEER requests that lets a client attach a human-readable UTF-8 description to a mapping, with server behavior for storing, truncating, updating and clearing it.

PCP.why: The whole document specifies a new PCP option, its format and client/server behavior, so it belongs on the PCP page.
PCP.quote: This document extends the base PCP [RFC6887] with the ability to associate a human-readable description with a PCP-instantiated mapping.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the encoding of the description text. The document defines nothing new about it.
PCP mappings are NAT/firewall mappings, but the document is about the PCP option and not NAT behavior. PCP is the more specific tag.
The Security Considerations mention information leakage, but that is boilerplate-level guidance and not the main subject.
The only IANA content is a routine option code allocation.

RFC7221.title: Handling of Internet-Drafts by IETF Working Groups
RFC7221.summary: Informational guide describing how IETF working group chairs typically adopt, develop, and manage Internet-Drafts as WG documents, including adoption criteria, editors, document maturity, and competing drafts.

IETF process.why: The whole document describes IETF working group procedure for adopting and developing drafts, rough consensus, chairs' roles and editors, which is IETF standards process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document discusses how a working group typically handles the formal documents that it targets for publication.

rejected.why: It concerns Internet-Drafts and WG handling before publication, not the format, style or publication of the RFC series.
IPR disclosure checks are mentioned only as one step in the adoption sequence; it is not a substantial subject of the document.
The author/editor distinction note is incidental, not a glossary or definitions.

RFC7222.title: Quality-of-Service Option for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC7222.summary: Defines a new Quality-of-Service mobility option and attributes for Proxy Mobile IPv6, letting the LMA and MAG negotiate QoS parameters (AMBR, GBR, ARP, DSCP, traffic selectors) for a mobile node's flows, with 3GPP/WLAN mapping guidance.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends PMIPv6 with a new mobility option carried in PBU/PBA/UPN/UPA messages, new status codes and a notification reason.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification defines a new mobility option, the Quality-of-Service (QoS) option, for Proxy Mobile IPv6.

QoS.why: A substantial part concerns QoS parameter negotiation (bit rates, priority, DSCP marking) and mapping to 3GPP and 802.11e QoS; no more specific QoS technology tag fits as the document merely builds on Diffserv.
QoS.quote: The negotiated QoS parameters can be used for QoS policing and marking of packets to enforce QoS differentiation

rejected.why: The QoS option relies on Diffserv markings (DSCP) as the substrate, but the document does not specify or extend Diffserv itself.
WLAN/802.11e appears as an example access technology and in appendices, but the document specifies a PMIPv6 option, not IP over 802.11.
3GPP QoS parameters are mapped to the attributes, but the document does not define cellular interworking itself.
A parent of PMIPv6, which is chosen as the more specific tag.

RFC7223.title: A YANG Data Model for Interface Management
RFC7223.summary: Defines the YANG module ietf-interfaces, a generic data model for configuring and monitoring network interfaces (config, operational state, counters, layering), with its mapping to the IF-MIB.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module (ietf-interfaces) and its structure, with augmentation examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG [RFC6020] data model for the management of network interfaces.

MIB.why: A substantial section maps every YANG node to IF-MIB objects (ifIndex, ifAlias, counters), which matters to readers of MIB/SMI work.
MIB.quote: If the device implements the IF-MIB [RFC2863], each entry in the "/ interfaces-state/interface" list is typically mapped to one ifEntry.

rejected.why: NETCONF is the access protocol the model is designed for and appears in examples, but the document does not specify or extend it.
SNMP is relevant only through the IF-MIB mapping; the document does not specify SNMP itself.
Ethernet, bonding and VLAN modules appear only as illustrative examples in the appendices.
XML appears only as the encoding of example NETCONF replies.

RFC7224.title: IANA Interface Type YANG Module
RFC7224.summary: Defines the initial iana-if-type YANG module, a set of YANG identities mirroring IANA's ifType registry for interface types, and sets rules for IANA to keep it in sync.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module defining identities for interface types, so it belongs on the YANG modules page.
YANG.quote: This document defines the initial version of the iana-if-type YANG module for interface type definitions.

IANA.why: The document sets up an IANA-maintained module and defines how IANA must update it when the ifType registry changes. Readers interested in IANA registry maintenance would want it.
IANA.quote: The iana-if-type module reflects IANA's existing "ifType definitions" registry

rejected.why: The module mirrors the IANAifType-MIB enumeration, but the document defines YANG identities and not a MIB module.
YANG is referenced in the context of NETCONF only through the reference list. The document does not specify or use NETCONF.
Many identity references point to SNMP MIB RFCs, but only as sources for the interface type names. The document does not address SNMP.
Individual interface types like ethernetCsmacd appear in the identity list, but the document is about the full interface type list and not any one link technology.

RFC7225.title: Discovering NAT64 IPv6 Prefixes Using the Port Control Protocol (PCP)
RFC7225.summary: Defines a new PCP option, PREFIX64, that lets a PCP client learn the NAT64 IPv6 prefix(es) and suffix used to build IPv4-converted IPv6 addresses, including optional destination IPv4 prefix lists.

PCP.why: The document extends PCP with a new PREFIX64 option, including server and client behaviour for MAP and ANNOUNCE opcodes.
PCP.quote: This document defines a new Port Control Protocol (PCP) option to learn the IPv6 prefix(es) used by a PCP-controlled NAT64 device

NAT64.why: The option exists to discover NAT64 prefixes so IPv6-only hosts can synthesize addresses for IPv4 referrals. This is a NAT64 prefix discovery mechanism.
NAT64.quote: inform PCP clients about the Pref64::/n and suffix [RFC6052] used by a PCP-controlled NAT64 device [RFC6146]

rejected.why: DNS64 is discussed as the context for address synthesis, but the document does not specify or extend it. The option only supplies the prefix.
DNSSEC is mentioned as a benefit, since learning the prefix lets hosts synthesize locally and validate. The document is not about DNSSEC.
SIP appears only as a use-case example for application referrals in SDP.
A technology tag (NAT64) already sits under this topic, so the parent is implied and not given directly.
SDP is used in the referral example only and is not specified here.

RFC7226.title: Requirements for Advanced Multipath in MPLS Networks
RFC7226.summary: Informational requirements document for Advanced Multipath in MPLS networks, enumerating functional, protocol and management requirements for multipath over parallel component links with differing characteristics.

MPLS.why: The whole document specifies requirements for multipath over MPLS LSPs, including client LSPs, AMGs, LDP and RSVP-TE coexistence. No narrower MPLS child tag fits.
MPLS.quote: The purpose of this document is to clearly enumerate a set of requirements related to the protocols and mechanisms that provide MPLS-based Advanced Multipath.

ECMP.why: It formalizes and extends multipath and load-balanced forwarding, including ECMP, with flow-to-component-link load balancing requirements (FR#18-FR#24).
ECMP.quote: Advanced Multipath is a formalization of multipath techniques that meets the requirements defined in this document.

rejected.why: Ethernet Link Aggregation is mentioned only as an existing multipath technique. The document is not about IEEE 802.1AX.
RSVP-TE is mentioned in coexistence and resignaling requirements, but the document does not specify or extend it.
GR#2 says a solution should extend LDP, but only as one general requirement. The document does not specify LDP.
Traffic engineering concepts appear, but the document is about multipath requirements, and MPLS covers it.
MPLS-TP appears only as an example of a lower-layer network.
OSPF and IS-IS ECMP are mentioned only as existing multipath examples. The IGP is discussed generically.

gaps.name: Advanced Multipath / composite link
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for multipath or composite link techniques over component links. MPLS and ECMP cover them only approximately.

RFC7227.title: Guidelines for Creating New DHCPv6 Options
RFC7227.summary: BCP giving guidelines to DHCPv6 option developers and expert reviewers on designing option formats that existing software can adopt easily, and updating RFC 3315.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document is about designing, formatting, and reviewing DHCPv6 options and how clients, servers and relays handle them. It also updates RFC 3315.
DHCPv6.quote: This document provides guidance to prospective DHCPv6 option developers to help them create option formats that are easily adoptable by existing DHCPv6 software.

rejected.why: Section 8 discusses choosing an FQDN versus an address for an option, but only as a design trade-off. The document does not specify DNS.
The option number space and registry are mentioned only in passing. The document is about option design, not IANA registry procedures.
The document is specific to DHCPv6, so the DHCPv6 child tag is the right one.
Section 20 briefly advises on whether to provision transition technologies over DHCPv4 or DHCPv6. It is one short section, not the subject of the document.
IPsec ESP appears only in the Privacy Considerations as a way to secure relay-to-server traffic.

RFC7228.title: Terminology for Constrained-Node Networks
RFC7228.summary: Informational terminology document defining constrained nodes, constrained networks, constrained-node networks, device classes (C0-C2), and power/energy classification for IoT standardization.

IoT.why: The whole document defines core terminology for constrained devices and networks in the Internet of Things, including device classes and power classes. No specific IoT technology tag fits; the topic tag applies directly.
