IoT.quote: The Internet Protocol Suite is increasingly used on small devices with severe constraints on power, memory, and processing resources, creating constrained-node networks.

terminology.why: It is a glossary-style terminology document, so readers browsing terminology would expect it.
terminology.quote: This document provides a number of basic terms that have been useful in the standardization work for constrained-node networks.

rejected.why: 6LoWPAN and LoWPAN are only briefly explained as related terms, and the document says it does not intend to define them.
RPL and LLN are mentioned as related terms from the ROLL work, but RPL is not specified or analysed here.
CoAP is cited only as an example protocol stack suited to Class 1 devices.
DTN is mentioned in one sentence to distinguish challenged networks from constrained networks.
The power and energy classes describe device limitations, not monitoring or managing the energy of networked devices.
TLS appears only as an example of a protocol stack that Class 1 devices cannot easily support.

RFC7229.title: Object Identifiers for Test Certificate Policies
RFC7229.summary: RFC 7229 defines a set of ASN.1 object identifiers under the PKIX arc for use as test certificate policy identifiers when testing certificate path processing software.

X.509.why: The document defines certificate policy OIDs consistent with the RFC 5280 X.509 profile, used to test certificate policy, policy constraints and policy mapping extension handling. Readers of X.509 certificate profiles would want it.
X.509.quote: They are appropriate for testing the certificate policy processing, especially the handling of the certificate policy extension, the policy constraints extension, and the policy mapping extension.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the OIDs and the module. The document does not specify ASN.1 encoding rules or ASN.1 itself.
The parent of X.509 is implied. The document is specific to certificate policy extension profiling and testing, so the more specific tag is used.
The IANA section only notes that the arc was already delegated to PKIX. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC7230.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Message Syntax and Routing
RFC7230.summary: RFC 7230 specifies HTTP/1.1 message syntax, parsing, routing and connection management, and defines the http and https URI schemes, the transfer codings, and related security considerations.

HTTP.why: The document is the core HTTP/1.1 specification covering message framing, intermediaries, routing, connection management and the Upgrade mechanism.
HTTP.quote: This document provides an overview of HTTP architecture and its associated terminology, defines the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes, defines the HTTP/1.1 message syntax

URI.why: It defines the http and https URI schemes, including their normalization and comparison, and registers them. A substantial part of the document addresses this, so readers of URI schemes would want it.
URI.quote: The "http" URI scheme is hereby defined for the purpose of minting identifiers according to their association with the hierarchical namespace

rejected.why: Caching is only summarized in the architecture section and delegated to RFC 7234. It is not a main subject here.
TLS is the substrate that the https scheme uses. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
TCP is the default transport for the http scheme. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document defines a #rule list extension to ABNF in Section 7, but this is a minor supporting notation, not the subject of the document.
The gzip, deflate and compress codings are listed as HTTP transfer codings. They are referenced, not specified.
Set-Cookie is mentioned only as an exception to the rule on multiple header fields.

RFC7231.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Semantics and Content
RFC7231.summary: RFC 7231 specifies HTTP/1.1 semantics: representations, request methods, request and response header fields, status codes, and content negotiation. It obsoletes RFC 2616 and sets up the HTTP method, status code and content coding registries.

HTTP.why: The whole document specifies HTTP semantics: methods, status codes, header fields and registries.
HTTP.quote: This document defines the semantics of HTTP/1.1 messages, as expressed by request methods, request header fields, response status codes, and response header fields

content negotiation.why: Section 3.4 and the Accept* fields in Section 5.3 define proactive and reactive negotiation, which is a substantial part of the document.
content negotiation.quote: This specification defines two patterns of content negotiation that can be made visible within the protocol: "proactive"

rejected.why: Media types are used in Content-Type and Accept, but the document does not define registration rules. It only points to BCP13.
Language tags are used in Accept-Language and Content-Language, but the tag syntax and matching come from RFC 5646 and RFC 4647.
Caching is specified in RFC 7234. This document only notes which methods and status codes are cacheable.
Authentication is defined in RFC 7235. This document only lists the credential and challenge header fields.
URIs are the identifiers used for resources and in Location. The document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammar and is not what the document is about.

RFC7232.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Conditional Requests
RFC7232.summary: RFC 7232 specifies HTTP/1.1 conditional requests: the ETag and Last-Modified validators, the If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Unmodified-Since preconditions, the 304 and 412 status codes, and the rules for evaluating and ordering preconditions.

HTTP.why: The document specifies HTTP header fields, status codes (304, 412) and evaluation semantics. It is a core part of the HTTP/1.1 specification.
HTTP.quote: This document defines HTTP/1.1 conditional requests, including metadata header fields for indicating state changes, request header fields for making preconditions on such state

HTTP caching.why: Validators, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since and 304 handling exist chiefly for cache validation, so readers of the HTTP caching subject would want this RFC. The caching rules themselves are defined in RFC 7234.
HTTP caching.quote: Conditional GET requests are the most efficient mechanism for HTTP cache updates [RFC7234].

rejected.why: WebDAV is mentioned only as an example of extensions defining other validators and conditional fields (the If header). The document does not specify it.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammar and is not the subject of the document.
Content negotiation appears only in an ETag example and in the discussion of validators. It is not specified here.
HTTP-date is imported by reference from RFC 7231. This document does not define date formats.
The more specific HTTP tag already covers this document.

RFC7233.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Range Requests
RFC7233.summary: Defines HTTP/1.1 range requests: Range, If-Range, Accept-Ranges and Content-Range header fields, 206 and 416 status codes, rules for combining partial responses, and the multipart/byteranges media type.

HTTP.why: The whole document specifies HTTP semantics extensions: range request header fields, 206 and 416 status codes, and the rules for combining partial responses. HTTP readers need it.
HTTP.quote: This document defines HTTP/1.1 range requests, partial responses, and the multipart/byteranges media type.

media types.why: It defines and registers the multipart/byteranges media type (Appendix A), a substantial normative part of the document.
media types.quote: This document serves as the specification for the Internet media type "multipart/byteranges".

rejected.why: It says how 206 responses are cached and how partial responses are combined, but caching is defined in RFC 7234. This document is about range requests, not caching.
multipart/byteranges uses MIME multipart framing, but the document does not extend MIME body structure itself. It only registers a media type, which the media types tag covers.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar, not the subject.
The registrations (range unit registry, status codes, header fields) are boilerplate-style IANA sections. The body is about range requests.

RFC7234.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Caching
RFC7234.summary: RFC 7234 specifies HTTP/1.1 caching: how caches store, reuse, validate, and invalidate responses, and defines the Age, Cache-Control, Expires, Pragma, and Warning header fields plus cache directive and warn code registries.

HTTP caching.why: The whole document specifies HTTP cache behavior: storage, freshness, validation, invalidation, and Cache-Control and related header fields.
HTTP caching.quote: This document defines HTTP caches and the associated header fields that control cache behavior or indicate cacheable response messages.

rejected.why: The more specific child HTTP caching fits; the parent is implied and the document is not about HTTP broadly.
The cache directive and warn code registries are boilerplate-like sections secondary to the main body.
ABNF is only the notation used to define syntax, not a subject of the document.
NTP is mentioned only as a recommendation for clock synchronization, not the subject.
Set-Cookie is mentioned only briefly in Security Considerations.

RFC7235.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Authentication
RFC7235.summary: RFC 7235 defines the HTTP/1.1 authentication framework: challenge/response model, realms, 401 and 407 status codes, the WWW-Authenticate, Authorization, Proxy-Authenticate and Proxy-Authorization header fields, and the authentication scheme registry.

HTTP authentication.why: The whole document specifies the HTTP authentication framework, including challenges, credentials, realms, status codes, header fields and the scheme registry.
HTTP authentication.quote: HTTP provides a general framework for access control and authentication, via an extensible set of challenge-response authentication schemes

rejected.why: The more specific child HTTP authentication fits; the parent is implied.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as the means to protect credentials; the document defines nothing about TLS.
Caching interactions of Authorization are mentioned briefly and refer to RFC 7234; not a substantial part of this document.
ABNF is only the notation used for the grammar, not the subject.
The registry sections are boilerplate-like IANA considerations for the authentication scheme registry; the main body is about HTTP authentication.
The child tag HTTP authentication is more specific and already chosen.

RFC7236.title: Initial Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Authentication Scheme Registrations
RFC7236.summary: Registers the Basic, Bearer, Digest, Negotiate and OAuth HTTP authentication schemes, defined in earlier RFCs, in the IANA HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry.

HTTP authentication.why: The whole document is a registration of HTTP authentication schemes (Basic, Digest, Bearer, Negotiate, OAuth) in the HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry, so readers of HTTP authentication would want it.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document registers Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) authentication schemes that have been defined in RFCs before the IANA HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry was established.

rejected.why: The document does add registry entries, but it is about the HTTP-specific authentication scheme registry. It does not address IANA registry practice or stewardship in general.
OAuth 1.0 and Bearer are listed in the table, but the document does not specify or analyse OAuth. They are only registered names.
Negotiate is registered with a note about how it violates HTTP semantics and syntax. SPNEGO itself is not specified or discussed.
The document is narrower than HTTP in general. The more specific HTTP authentication tag covers it.

RFC7237.title: Initial Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Method Registrations
RFC7237.summary: Registers in the IANA HTTP Method Registry the HTTP methods (mostly WebDAV and extensions, plus PATCH, LINK, UNLINK) defined in RFCs before the registry existed, with safe and idempotent properties.

HTTP.why: The document is about HTTP methods: registering names with safe and idempotent properties in the HTTP Method Registry. Readers of HTTP extensions would want it.
HTTP.quote: This document registers those Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) methods that have been defined in RFCs other than [RFC7231] before the IANA HTTP Method Registry was established.

WebDAV.why: Most of the registered methods come from WebDAV and its extensions (versioning, ACL, bindings, ordered collections, SEARCH), so WebDAV readers would look for this.
WebDAV.quote: | PROPFIND          | yes  | yes        | [RFC4918], Section 9.1    |

rejected.why: The document is an IANA registration, but it concerns a specific HTTP registry. It is not about IANA registries or guidance in general.
Only MKCALENDAR is registered, as one row in a table. The document is not about CalDAV.
LINK and UNLINK are registered, but they are methods in the table, not about link relations.

RFC7238.title: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 308 (Permanent Redirect)
RFC7238.summary: Defines the new HTTP status code 308 (Permanent Redirect), the permanent counterpart to 307 that disallows changing POST to GET, with deployment guidance and IANA registration.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP semantics by specifying a new status code, its caching behaviour, Location header use, and deployment considerations.
HTTP.quote: this specification adds the status code 308, defining this missing variant

rejected.why: Only notes that a 308 response is cacheable by default and refers to RFC 7234; caching is not a substantial subject of the document.
Redirects point to new URIs, but the document does not specify anything about URI syntax or schemes; RFC 3986 is only a reference.
The HTML meta refresh appears only as a fallback example in deployment considerations, not as a subject of the document.
The status code registration is boilerplate-level IANA action, not the document's subject.

RFC7239.title: Forwarded HTTP Extension
RFC7239.summary: Defines the HTTP "Forwarded" header field, with by/for/host/proto parameters and node identifiers, letting proxies disclose information lost in proxying, plus privacy guidance and an IANA registry of parameters.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a new HTTP header field, its syntax, parameters and proxy handling rules, so it is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: This document defines an HTTP extension header field that allows proxy components to disclose information lost in the proxying process

rejected.why: Privacy considerations and obfuscated identifiers are present, but they are a secondary aspect of an HTTP header definition; the document is not a privacy threat model.
Proxies are discussed only as forwarding or reverse proxies; caching is mentioned in passing, not specified.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax.
IPv6 addresses appear only as a node identifier format, not as the subject.
NAT is mentioned only as a related issue, referring to RFC 6269.
The registry creation is boilerplate-like IANA considerations, not the main body.

RFC7240.title: Prefer Header for HTTP
RFC7240.summary: Defines the HTTP Prefer request header and Preference-Applied response header, lets clients express optional processing preferences to servers, defines initial preferences (respond-async, return, wait, handling), and creates an IANA registry of preferences.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with new Prefer and Preference-Applied header fields and a registry of preferences.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines an HTTP header field that can be used by a client to request that certain behaviors be employed by a server while processing a request.

rejected.why: Caching and Vary are mentioned only as a caution for preferences that affect responses, not as the document's subject.
The Atom Publishing Protocol is cited only as an example in the introduction.
ABNF is used only as the syntax notation.
The document says Prefer SHOULD NOT be used for content negotiation.
The registry is created for this document's own preferences, and IANA Considerations is boilerplate-like evidence.
The header is a protocol-level extension, not a set of conventions for building APIs, though it is useful to API designers.

RFC7241.title: The IEEE 802/IETF Relationship
RFC7241.summary: IAB informational RFC (obsoleting RFC 4441) describing how IEEE 802 and the IETF organise themselves, cooperate, exchange information on new work, review each other's documents, use liaisons, and coordinate protocol parameter registries.

IETF process.why: The document describes IETF structure, culture, review and approval processes, liaison handling and cooperation with another SDO. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document contains a set of principles and guidelines that serve as the basis for coordination between Project 802 of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers

IANA.why: Section 6 covers IANA and IEEE Registration Authority parameter allocation, Ethertypes and joint-use registries. This is a substantial part of the document.
IANA.quote: Both IEEE 802 and IETF maintain registries of assigned protocol parameters, and some protocol parameters assigned in one organization are of interest to the other organization.

rejected.why: Ethertype allocation and IEEE 802.3 are mentioned only in the context of registries and process, not Ethernet technology.
Appendix A.3 describes EAP security review as an example of cooperation. The document is not about EAP itself.
Appendix A.2 gives RADIUS/Diameter attribute review guidance as an example of cooperation, in a minor appendix.
Appendix A.1 mentions MIB review as a cooperation example. The document does not define MIB content.
The comparison of IETF and IEEE terms is incidental to the cooperation guidance and does not make this a glossary.

gaps.name: Standards body liaison and cooperation (IEEE 802/IETF)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is inter-SDO liaison and coordination. The taxonomy has no tag for liaison relationships with other standards bodies, so IETF process is the closest fit.

RFC7242.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking TCP Convergence-Layer Protocol
RFC7242.summary: Specifies TCPCL version 3, the TCP-based convergence-layer protocol that carries Delay-Tolerant Networking bundles over TCP, covering the contact header, segment/ack/refusal/keepalive/shutdown messages and negotiation.

DTN.why: The whole document defines a DTN convergence-layer adapter for carrying Bundle Protocol bundles, so it belongs on the DTN page.
DTN.quote: This document describes the TCP-based convergence-layer protocol for Delay-Tolerant Networking.

rejected.why: TCP is only the bearer transport the convergence layer runs over. The document defines nothing new about TCP itself.
This fits loosely, since it carries bundles over TCP. But DTN is the more specific subject, and the document is a convergence-layer protocol rather than a generic transport binding.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as something that is not prevented.

gaps.name: Bundle Protocol convergence layers
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the broad DTN tag. It has no tag for the Bundle Protocol or its convergence-layer adapters.

RFC7243.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for the Bytes Discarded Metric
RFC7243.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=26) that reports the number of RTP payload bytes discarded from the de-jitter buffer, per interval or cumulatively, plus its SDP 'discard-bytes' signalling parameter.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP Extended Report block and its operation by receivers and senders, so it belongs under RTCP.
RTCP.quote: An XR block is defined in this document to indicate the number of RTP payload bytes discarded, per interval or for the duration of the session

rejected.why: RTP is the parent of RTCP and is implied. The document extends RTCP reporting, not RTP itself.
The document only adds an 'xr-format' parameter to the existing rtcp-xr attribute. That is signalling apparatus, not a subject of the document.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the report.
The block reports a metric, but it is an RTCP report block following the RFC 6390 template. The RTCP tag fits better and no measurement-framework subject is addressed.

RFC7244.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Blocks for Synchronization Delay and Offset Metrics Reporting
RFC7244.summary: Defines two RTCP XR report blocks (RTP Flow Initial Synchronization Delay and Synchronization Offset) for reporting media synchronization metrics, with SDP signaling parameters and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies new RTCP XR block types extending RFC 3611, so it belongs under RTCP.
RTCP.quote: This document defines two RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) blocks that allow the reporting of initial synchronization delay and synchronization offset metrics

performance measurement.why: The blocks define performance metrics per the RFC 6390/6792 metric framework, with an appendix using the metric template.
performance measurement.quote: The metrics defined in the RTP Flow Synchronization Offset Metrics Block can be used by the network manager for troubleshooting

rejected.why: RTCP is the more specific tag; RTP is the parent and implied.
SDP is used only to signal the XR blocks via rtcp-xr parameters; no new SDP mechanism beyond two parameter names.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations.
NTP timestamp format is only used for the offset value representation.
RFC 6190 is only cited for layered video context; no payload format defined.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here, not the document's subject.

RFC7245.title: An Architecture for Media Recording Using the Session Initiation Protocol
RFC7245.summary: Informational SIPREC architecture document describing how a Session Recording Client and Session Recording Server establish SIP recording sessions, carry replicated media and metadata, and where the SRC can be located.

SIPREC.why: The whole document is the SIPREC architecture: SRC/SRS roles, recording session establishment, metadata and notifications.
SIPREC.quote: This document describes architectures for deploying session recording solutions in an environment that is based on the Session Initiation Protocol.

rejected.why: SIP is the substrate for the recording session; the specific subject is SIPREC, the more specific child tag.
SDP direction attributes (sendonly/recvonly/inactive) are used for the recording session but only as existing mechanisms, not specified or extended here.
Replicated media is carried over RTP, but the document does not address RTP itself.
The conference focus acting as an SRC is covered in one subsection only; the document is not about conferencing.
Media encryption is mentioned only in security considerations in passing.

RFC7246.title: Multipoint Label Distribution Protocol In-Band Signaling in a Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) Table Context
RFC7246.summary: Extends mLDP in-band signaling (RFC 6826) for PIM-to-mLDP conversion to work when the interface between non-MPLS and MPLS regions is in a VRF, defining four new opaque value TLVs carrying source/RP, group and Route Distinguisher.

LDP.why: The document extends mLDP, the multipoint LDP extensions, by defining new opaque value types for P2MP/MP2MP FECs and the procedures for using them.
LDP.quote: an mLDP Label Mapping message is sent by PE1. This message will contain either a P2MP FEC or an MP2MP FEC
LDP.section: 2. VRF In-Band Signaling for MP LSPs

PIM.why: The procedures map PIM source-specific and bidirectional trees onto mLDP LSPs and back at the region boundary, so PIM users would want this.
PIM.quote: Suppose that a PE router, PE1, receives a PIM Join(S,G) message over one of its interfaces that is associated with a VRF.
PIM.section: 2. VRF In-Band Signaling for MP LSPs

L3VPN.why: The VRF context from BGP/MPLS IP VPNs is central. The RD in the opaque value selects the VRF, though the document targets non-MVPN uses.
L3VPN.quote: extends the procedures from [RFC6826] to handle the case where the link connecting the two regions is a Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) table link

rejected.why: The document explicitly says it is primarily aimed at multicast applications other than multicast VPN, and does not use the MVPN procedures.
BGP/MPLS VPN is only referenced for VRF definitions. The document specifies no BGP behaviour.
MPLS is the general setting, but the specific LDP tag fits better.

RFC7247.title: Interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Architecture, Addresses, and Error Handling
RFC7247.summary: Defines the architectural assumptions for SIP-XMPP gateway interworking and specifies mappings of addresses (sip/im/pres URIs to JIDs, GRUUs to resourceparts) and of error conditions between the two protocols.

SIP.why: The document specifies how SIP addresses, GRUUs and response codes map to XMPP, so SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: this document specifies the architectural assumptions underlying such mappings as well as the mapping of addresses and error conditions.

XMPP.why: It specifies XMPP JID mapping and XMPP error conditions mapped to SIP codes, so it is about XMPP interworking.
XMPP.quote: The XMPP address format is specified in [RFC6122]

rejected.why: SIMPLE is mentioned as the source of SIP IM/presence extensions, but the document does not specify or extend it. Presence and messaging mappings are left to other documents.
The address mapping works on sip/im/pres URIs and uses percent-encoding. It specifies a protocol-to-protocol mapping, not URI syntax or schemes.
DNS SRV lookups are used to decide whether a domain speaks SIP or XMPP. They are a mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
TLS and DTLS appear only in the Security Considerations as protection for gateways.
The document is the foundation for IM and presence interworking, but the mappings for those are in companion documents.

RFC7248.title: Interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Presence
RFC7248.summary: Defines a bidirectional mapping between SIP (SIMPLE) presence and XMPP presence, covering subscription establishment, refresh and cancellation, presence notifications, and presence requests/probes via gateways.

SIMPLE.why: The SIP side of the mapping is SIP presence via the SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY presence event package and PIDF, which is SIMPLE territory. Subscriptions, notifications and PIDF bodies are mapped in detail.
SIMPLE.quote: Various extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol ([RFC3261]) for presence, in particular [RFC3856]

XMPP.why: The document maps XMPP presence stanzas, subscription states and probes to SIP, so it is substantially about XMPP presence behaviour at gateways.
XMPP.quote: XMPP presence subscriptions are managed using XMPP <presence/> stanzas of type "subscribe", "subscribed", "unsubscribe", and "unsubscribed".

PIDF.why: The presence mapping tables translate to and from PIDF data (basic status, tuple id, note, priority) and describe embedding the jabber:client <show/> element in PIDF.
PIDF.quote: The mapping of XMPP syntax elements to SIP syntax elements SHOULD be as shown in the following table.

rejected.why: SIP is used as one side of the mapping, but the document specifies presence interworking and the presence-specific SIMPLE tag fits better. It defines nothing new for SIP itself.
It is the parent of XMPP, PIDF and MSRP and is implied by the child tags. The document covers presence only, not instant messages.
XML is only the encoding for XMPP stanzas and PIDF documents.
This is unrelated ISUP/SIP interworking; the document concerns SIP-XMPP presence gateways.

gaps.name: SIP-XMPP interworking / protocol gateway mapping
gaps.why: The document is part of a series on direct SIP-to-XMPP protocol mapping (gateways), and the taxonomy has no tag for this cross-protocol interworking subject.

RFC7249.title: Internet Numbers Registries
RFC7249.summary: RFC 7249 identifies the IANA registries that make up the Internet Numbers Registry System (AS numbers, IPv4 and IPv6 address space) and creates the Special-Purpose AS Numbers registry.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is to identify IANA registries for number resources and to create the Special-Purpose AS Numbers registry with its IETF Review policy.
IANA.quote: This companion document identifies the IANA registries that are part of the Internet Numbers Registry System at this time.

addressing.why: A substantial part covers allocation and reservation of IPv4 and IPv6 address space and AS numbers through RIRs and special-purpose registries.
addressing.quote: The allocation and registration functions for all non-reserved, globally unique unicast IPv4 addresses are handled by the Internet Numbers Registry System

rejected.why: AS numbers are mentioned and RFC 6793 is cited, but the document does not specify or analyse BGP.
IPv6 address space registries are mentioned, but the document does not address the IPv6 protocol or its deployment.
IPv4 special-purpose address registry is referenced only as part of the registry system, not the protocol or its address lifecycle in depth.
The IANA tag is the more specific fit under this parent.

gaps.name: Internet Numbers Registry System / Regional Internet Registries
gaps.why: The document is about number resource registries and RIR allocation, which the taxonomy covers only partly through IANA and addressing.

RFC7250.title: Using Raw Public Keys in Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC7250.summary: Defines a new TLS/DTLS certificate type (RawPublicKey) and the client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type extensions so peers can authenticate with bare SubjectPublicKeyInfo structures instead of X.509 certificates.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS extensions and a certificate type, and specifies client and server handshake behaviour. It applies equally to DTLS, which is a child of TLS, so TLS is the right tag.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a new certificate type and two TLS extensions for exchanging raw public keys in Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS).

rejected.why: The extensions apply to DTLS, but the text specifies the mechanism in TLS 1.2 handshake terms and has no DTLS-specific content. I tagged the parent TLS instead.
The document uses the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure from PKIX and contrasts raw keys with X.509 certificates. It does not profile or extend X.509.
DANE is mentioned only as an example out-of-band way to bind a key to an identity. The document does not specify or extend it.
The SubjectPublicKeyInfo is DER-encoded ASN.1 and Appendix A shows an example encoding. This is incidental encoding, not a document about ASN.1.
CoAP is cited only as a motivating use case for smart objects using DTLS.
The document is about avoiding the PKIX certificate machinery by using raw keys, not about PKI itself.

RFC7251.title: AES-CCM Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for TLS
RFC7251.summary: Defines four TLS 1.2 ECDHE_ECDSA cipher suites using AES-CCM (16- and 8-octet tags) AEAD, with curve and hash guidance, for constrained environments and DTLS.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS cipher suites, their version requirements (TLS 1.2 only), extension usage and IANA registry values, so TLS readers need it. It also covers DTLS use, but DTLS is only mentioned as supported.
TLS.quote: This document describes the use of Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) [AES] in Counter with CBC-MAC Mode (CCM) [CCM] in several TLS cipher suites.

AES.why: The suites are built on AES-CCM AEAD algorithms (AES-128/256, CCM and CCM_8), so readers of AES and its modes would want this RFC.
AES.quote: AES-CCM provides both authentication and confidentiality (encryption and decryption) and uses as its only primitive the AES encrypt block cipher operation.

elliptic curve.why: The suites use ECDHE/ECDSA, and the document sets requirements on curves, point formats and hash/curve pairing (Section 2.2 and Appendix A).
elliptic curve.quote: Curves with a cofactor equal to one SHOULD be used; this simplifies their use.

rejected.why: The suites can be used with DTLS and are marked DTLS-OK, but the document defines nothing DTLS-specific beyond the sequence number note.
ECDSA is only the authentication method in the cipher suite names, with requirements inherited from RFC 4492. The document does not specify ECDSA itself.
Constrained environments are the motivation, but the document is not about IoT architecture or guidance.
HMAC is mentioned only for the PRF and for the truncated_hmac extension having no effect.
The IANA section only assigns cipher suite values, which is boilerplate.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 appear only as hash choices for the PRF and signatures.

RFC7252.title: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC7252.summary: RFC 7252 specifies CoAP, a UDP-based RESTful web transfer protocol for constrained nodes and networks, covering message format, reliability, request/response semantics, options, caching, proxying, URIs, discovery, multicast, DTLS security and HTTP mapping.

CoAP.why: The document is the core CoAP specification, defining the protocol, its messages, options, codes and registries.
CoAP.quote: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) is a specialized web transfer protocol for use with constrained nodes and constrained (e.g., low-power, lossy) networks.

rejected.why: DTLS is only the security binding for CoAP; the document defines how CoAP uses it but nothing new about DTLS itself.
HTTP is the model and the cross-proxy mapping target; the document specifies CoAP, not HTTP, so HTTP readers don't need it.
6LoWPAN is the motivating constrained network, mentioned for context and port compression only.
UDP is the transport substrate; CoAP does not define new UDP usage beyond binding to it.
The coap and coaps URI schemes are defined, but they are part of CoAP and covered by the CoAP tag.
Multicast CoAP is a section of the protocol, not IP multicast routing or group membership.

RFC7253.title: The OCB Authenticated-Encryption Algorithm
RFC7253.summary: Specifies OCB, a blockcipher-based authenticated-encryption with associated data (AEAD) algorithm, with AES-based parameter sets, pseudocode, and test vectors, as a CFRG product.

cryptography.why: The document defines a new cryptographic algorithm (an AEAD mode of operation) with its parameters and security analysis. No child technology tag fits an OCB/AEAD mode, so the topic tag is given directly.
cryptography.quote: OCB, a shared-key blockcipher-based encryption scheme that provides confidentiality and authenticity for plaintexts and authenticity for associated data

rejected.why: AES is only the blockcipher used to instantiate OCB parameter sets. The document is about the OCB mode, not about AES itself.
The IANA section merely registers AEAD identifiers. It is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
Key management is mentioned only as a recommendation in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: Authenticated encryption (AEAD) modes
gaps.why: OCB and RFC 5116 style AEAD algorithms have no dedicated tag; they sit under the general cryptography topic. A tag for AEAD or block cipher modes would collect RFCs like this one, as well as GCM, CCM and SIV.

RFC7254.title: A Uniform Resource Name Namespace for the Global System for Mobile Communications Association (GSMA) and the International Mobile station Equipment Identity (IMEI)
RFC7254.summary: Registers the 'gsma' URN namespace with an 'imei' NSS (and 'svn' parameter for IMEISV) so mobile device identifiers can be used as URNs, with privacy and security guidance.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration (gsma NID, imei NSS) with syntax, equivalence and persistence rules per RFC 3406.
URN.quote: This specification defines a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Global System for Mobile Communications Association (GSMA)

rejected.why: IMEI comes from GSM/3GPP, but the document only defines a URN representation, not IP over cellular networks.
GSM is the origin of the identifier; the document does not cover SIM authentication or GSM interworking.
Privacy considerations are discussed in Security section, but it is boilerplate-position and not the main subject.
SIP is mentioned only by reference to RFC 7255 and an analogy; not the subject.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax.
UUID is cited only as an analogy for why a URN was chosen.

RFC7255.title: Using the International Mobile station Equipment Identity (IMEI) Uniform Resource Name (URN) as an Instance ID
RFC7255.summary: Specifies how the GSMA IMEI URN is used as the SIP '+sip.instance' instance-id in Contact headers for 3GPP IMS registrations and emergency requests, with UAC, UAS and registrar procedures.

SIP.why: The document defines SIP UAC, UAS and registrar behaviour for the sip.instance Contact parameter (outbound, GRUU) using the IMEI URN.
SIP.quote: MUST include in the "sip.instance" media feature tag the GSMA IMEI URN according to the syntax specified in RFC 7254

URN.why: It concerns the use of a specific URN namespace (GSMA IMEI) as an instance identifier, so URN readers would want it.
URN.quote: how the Uniform Resource Name (URN) reserved for the Global System for Mobile Communications Association (GSMA) identities and its sub-namespace for the International Mobile station Equipment Identity (IMEI) can be used as an instance-id

rejected.why: UUID URN is mentioned only as the default instance-id that the IMEI URN is an alternative to.
The document mentions GSM/UMTS/LTE and IMS as context, but it specifies SIP header usage rather than cellular networking.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as a protection mechanism for REGISTER requests.
Emergency sessions and the PSAP appear as use cases for including the IMEI, but the document is not about emergency calling.
Privacy is discussed in the Security Considerations as a constraint on exposing the IMEI, but it is not the main subject.

RFC7256.title: Multicast Control Extensions for the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP)
RFC7256.summary: Specifies ANCP extensions (new messages, TLVs, capabilities) for multicast control between a NAS and an Access Node: NAS-initiated replication, white/black/grey-list conditional access and admission control, bandwidth delegation, and committed bandwidth reporting.

ANCP.why: The document extends ANCP with new messages, TLVs and capabilities and updates RFC 6320.
ANCP.quote: This document specifies the extensions to the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) (RFC 6320) required for support of the multicast use cases

multicast.why: The extensions control IP multicast replication and admission (IGMP/MLD joins, flows, SSM/ASM) at the access node, so multicast readers would want it.
multicast.quote: multicast replication initiated by the Network Access Server (NAS); conditional access and admission control with white and black lists

rejected.why: IGMP/MLD joins are the triggers the AN snoops, but the document does not specify or extend IGMP.
MLD is only the signaling the AN handles, not something the document specifies or extends.
IPTV is the motivating application, but the document defines ANCP protocol extensions, not IPTV service delivery.
The capabilities are stated to be independent of access technology, and DSL appears only as an example.
Bandwidth delegation and committed bandwidth reporting touch admission control, but the document is about ANCP messaging, not a QoS architecture.
AAA/policy servers are mentioned only as external peers and in the privacy discussion.

RFC7257.title: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Management Information Base
RFC7257.summary: Defines three SMIv2 MIB modules (VPLS-GENERIC-MIB, VPLS-LDP-MIB, VPLS-BGP-MIB) for configuring and monitoring LDP- and BGP-signalled Virtual Private LAN Services, used together with the PW-STD-MIB.

VPLS.why: The whole document is the management model for VPLS services, including LDP and BGP signalling specifics and pseudowire bindings.
VPLS.quote: it describes managed objects to configure and/or monitor Virtual Private LAN services.

MIB.why: It specifies three SMIv2 MIB modules with tables, notifications and conformance groups, so MIB readers will want it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific tag.
Pseudowires are consumed via PW-STD-MIB (RFC 5601) and linked by the binding table, but the document does not define pseudowire emulation.
BGP signalling and auto-discovery are managed through objects, but the BGP protocol is not specified or extended here.
LDP signalling parameters are managed via the MIB, but LDP itself is not defined or changed.
VPLS is the more specific tag under L2VPN; the document is about VPLS rather than L2VPN services in general.
No YANG is used; the data model is SMIv2.

RFC7258.title: Pervasive Monitoring Is an Attack
RFC7258.summary: BCP statement that pervasive monitoring is a technical attack on Internet privacy and that the IETF will work to mitigate it in protocol design.

privacy.why: The whole document is about pervasive monitoring as a privacy threat and the need to mitigate it in protocol design. This fits the privacy topic of threat models and privacy considerations.
privacy.quote: The IETF community's technical assessment is that PM is an attack on the privacy of Internet users and organisations.
privacy.section: 1. Pervasive Monitoring Is a Widespread Attack on Privacy

rejected.why: It is mentioned only as an example of monitoring that can help mitigate pervasive monitoring. The document is not about it.
The document says it is entirely about privacy. The more specific privacy tag fits, so the general security tag is not needed.
The process note only explains why this is published in the IETF stream. The document's subject is the technical stance on pervasive monitoring, not IETF procedure.
It touches on architectural decisions affecting vulnerability to pervasive monitoring. Its focus is the threat and the IETF stance, not architectural principles.

RFC7259.title: The Jabber-ID Header Field
RFC7259.summary: Defines the Jabber-ID header field for email and netnews messages, letting an author associate a message with an XMPP address, including syntax, encoding, usage and IANA registration.

message format.why: The document defines a new internet message header field, its syntax, generation, processing and registration in the provisional header field registry.
message format.quote: This document defines a header field that enables the author of an email or netnews message to include a Jabber ID in the message header block

XMPP.why: The header carries XMPP addresses (Jabber IDs) and uses XMPP URI encoding rules, and the document shows how user agents can offer presence and chat. It does not extend XMPP itself, so this is secondary.
XMPP.quote: associating the author with a particular Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) address

rejected.why: Netnews messages are a second applicable protocol, but the document does not define or extend the Netnews format. It only registers the header for use there.
DKIM is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the header from forging.
The document relies on the XMPP URI path rule and percent-encoding but defines nothing new about URIs.
The more specific tag message format fits better, because the document is about a header field rather than mail transport or access.
The provisional header registration is routine boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC7260.title: GMPLS RSVP-TE Extensions for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Configuration
RFC7260.summary: Specifies RSVP-TE extensions (LSP attribute flags, OAM Configuration TLV, Admin_Status bits, error codes) so GMPLS LSP signaling can establish, adjust and delete OAM entities and functions along with the LSP.

RSVP-TE.why: The document defines new RSVP-TE objects, TLVs, flags and error codes and the procedures for using them in Path/Resv exchanges.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document specifies extensions to Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) to support the establishment and configuration of OAM entities along with Label Switched Path signaling.

GMPLS.why: The extensions are GMPLS signaling extensions that use the GMPLS Admin_Status object, and the title names GMPLS.
GMPLS.quote: if the GMPLS control plane is employed, it is desirable to bind OAM setup and configuration to connection establishment signaling

OAM.why: The subject is configuring OAM entities (MEPs/MIPs) and functions (CC, CV, PM, alarms), and OAM readers would want this RFC.
OAM.quote: OAM is an integral part of transport connections; hence, it is required that OAM functions be activated/deactivated in sync with connection commissioning/decommissioning

rejected.why: MPLS-TP OAM requirements are summarised as background, but the document is technology-agnostic and does not specify MPLS-TP.
MPLS is one of several data planes cited, and LSP ping is only mentioned as an alternative bootstrap method.
PBB-TE and CFM are mentioned as motivating examples only, and no Ethernet-specific OAM is defined.
SONET/SDH is listed only as one data-plane technology GMPLS can control.

RFC7261.title: Offer/Answer Considerations for G723 Annex A and G729 Annex B
RFC7261.summary: Specifies how SDP offer/answer should interpret mismatched annexa (G723) and annexb (G729, G729D, G729E) voice activity detection parameters, with examples.

G.729.why: Most of the document defines how the G729, G729D and G729E annexb parameter is interpreted in offer/answer, with all examples using G729.
G.729.quote: offer/answer considerations for the annexa parameter of G723 and the annexb parameter of G729, G729D, and G729E

SDP.why: The document is an offer/answer specification for SDP fmtp parameters, with SDP offer and answer examples.
SDP.quote: [RFC3264] requires SDP extensions that define new fmtp parameters to specify their proper interpretation in offer/answer.

rejected.why: It concerns SDP parameter negotiation for codecs, not the RTP payload format definitions.
RTP is only the context of the codecs; the document does not specify RTP.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The more specific G.729 tag applies. G723 has no taxonomy tag.
RFC 4856 registrations are referenced, but the document does not register or change media types.

gaps.name: G.723.1 speech codec
gaps.why: The document covers G723 annexa negotiation, but the taxonomy has no G.723.1 tag, only G.711, G.729 and G.722.

RFC7262.title: Requirements for Telepresence Multistreams
RFC7262.summary: Informational CLUE WG document that states the problem of telepresence interoperability and lists 18 requirements for a future specification that exchanges media-capture and endpoint information between SIP-based telepresence systems.

telepresence.why: The whole document is the CLUE telepresence multistream requirements, so it belongs on the telepresence (CLUE) page.
telepresence.quote: The purpose of this document is to describe the requirements for a specification that enables interworking between different SIP-based [RFC3261] telepresence systems

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling substrate the requirements assume (REQ-10 on interoperability with plain SIP endpoints). The document does not specify or extend SIP.
SDP is only mentioned as existing technology that might meet some requirements. The document does not define SDP work.
The multipoint requirements (REQ-12, REQ-13) and the XCON/CCMP references are secondary. The document is about telepresence streams, and telepresence is the more specific tag.
RTP appears only in the definition of media. Nothing in the body is about RTP itself.

RFC7263.title: An Extension to the REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) Protocol to Support Direct Response Routing
RFC7263.summary: Defines an optional RELOAD extension (a new forwarding option, state-keeping flag and overlay configuration element) letting responses go directly from destination peer to requester instead of following the reverse path, with fallback to symmetric recursive routing.

P2PSIP.why: The document extends RELOAD, the P2PSIP peer-to-peer overlay protocol, with a new routing mode, forwarding option and configuration element.
P2PSIP.quote: This document defines an optional extension to the REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) protocol to support the direct response routing mode.

rejected.why: STUN and RFC 5780 NAT behavior discovery appear only in the informative appendix as ways to find reflexive addresses. The document is not about STUN.
NAT affects when DRR works, and the appendix covers reachability tests. The document does not specify or analyse NAT behaviour.
It is mentioned only in an appendix as one way to learn a mapped address.
(D)TLS appears only in the cost comparison as handshake overhead. The document defines nothing about it.
The general P2P tag is superseded by the more specific P2PSIP tag, which already covers RELOAD.
The document is about overlay response routing in RELOAD, not Internet routing architecture.

gaps.name: RELOAD peer-to-peer overlay routing
gaps.why: RELOAD is covered only through the P2PSIP tag. Overlay response-routing modes (SRR, DRR, RPR) have no dedicated tag.

RFC7264.title: An Extension to the REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) Protocol to Support Relay Peer Routing
RFC7264.summary: Defines an optional RELOAD extension adding Relay Peer Routing (RPR), where responses go via a publicly reachable relay peer to shorten the response path versus symmetric recursive routing, with a new forwarding option, overlay configuration element and relay discovery.

P2PSIP.why: The document extends RELOAD (the P2PSIP overlay protocol) with a new routing mode, new ForwardingOption and message-processing rules.
P2PSIP.quote: This document defines an optional extension to the REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) protocol to support the relay peer routing mode.

rejected.why: NATs motivate relay peers, but the document is about overlay response routing, not interactive NAT traversal for media.
TURN server discovery is mentioned only as an analogy for discovering relay peers.
This is overlay (P2P) message routing within RELOAD, not IP routing architecture.
DTLS appears only in the cost comparison tables as a connection setup cost, so it is not a subject of the document.
The IANA section registers one forwarding option code, which is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
P2PSIP is the working group context, but the document specifies no SIP signalling.

gaps.name: RELOAD / overlay routing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a P2PSIP tag under SIP, which fits only loosely. There is no tag for RELOAD overlay routing modes, such as RPR, DRR and SRR.

RFC7265.title: jCal: The JSON Format for iCalendar
RFC7265.summary: Defines jCal, a JSON mapping for iCalendar data (components, properties, parameters, value types, unknown-type handling) that round-trips with iCalendar, and registers the application/calendar+json media type.

iCalendar.why: The document is about the iCalendar data format's JSON representation; the iCalendar tag is the subject readers would browse.
iCalendar.quote: This specification defines "jCal", a JSON format for iCalendar data.

JSON.why: Defines a JSON-based format with arrays and objects structure, type mappings and escaping rules; a JSON-based format readers of JSON would want.
JSON.quote: jCal is defined as a straightforward mapping into JSON from iCalendar, so that iCalendar data can be converted to JSON

rejected.why: Registers application/calendar+json, but this is boilerplate IANA section; the main body is about the mapping.
xCal (RFC 6321) is only cited as the design analogue; not about XML.
Uses ISO 8601 extended formats for jCal values but only as part of the mapping, not defining Internet timestamps.
Mentions vCard only in a typo in the Integer section; not about vCard.
Base64 is just an encoding preserved for binary values, not the subject.

gaps.name: iCalendar
gaps.why: The document is about the iCalendar format. The taxonomy has an iCalendar tag under calendaring, so it is used above, but the output must reflect that no JSON-calendar specific tag exists besides JSCalendar, which is a different format.

RFC7266.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Blocks for Mean Opinion Score (MOS) Metric Reporting
RFC7266.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=29) for reporting MOS media-quality metrics with single-channel and multi-channel audio segment types, plus SDP signalling (rtcp-xr "mos-metric", "calgextmap") and a registry of calculation algorithms.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP Extended Report block for MOS reporting, extending RTCP XR (RFC 3611).
RTCP.quote: This document defines a new block type to augment those defined in [RFC3611], for use in a range of RTP applications.

SDP.why: A substantial part defines SDP parameters (mos-metric, calgextmap) and offer/answer rules for negotiating calculation algorithm IDs.
SDP.quote: This section augments the SDP [RFC4566] attribute "rtcp-xr" defined in [RFC3611] by providing an additional value of "xr-format"

rejected.why: RTP is the protocol being monitored; the specification is about RTCP reporting, which is the more specific tag.
The block reports performance metrics, but the RTCP tag is the more specific fit and the document defines a report format, not measurement methodology.
Payload types are referenced only to identify the reported stream; no payload format is defined.
IANA registrations are boilerplate-like and only support the block definition.
ABNF is only used to write the SDP syntax.

RFC7267.title: Dynamic Placement of Multi-Segment Pseudowires
RFC7267.summary: Specifies LDP signaling and BGP-based PW routing extensions to dynamically place segments and select S-PEs for multi-segment pseudowires, and corrects the PW Switching Point PE sub-TLV length to 14 (updating RFC 6073).

pseudowire.why: The whole document concerns multi-segment pseudowires: addressing, PW routing, LDP signaling, failure handling and OAM of MS-PWs.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes extensions to the PW control protocol to dynamically place the segments of the multi-segment pseudowire among a set of Provider Edge (PE) routers.

rejected.why: LDP is the signaling protocol the extensions are carried in (new Bandwidth TLV and status codes), but the document is about pseudowire placement, not LDP itself. The new TLV and codes are PW-specific.
BGP with a new SAFI is used to advertise PW reachability, but this is a single subsection and BGP is used as a substrate for distributing PW routes.
MPLS is the PSN over which the PWs run. The document does not specify MPLS itself.
Only the SENDER_TSPEC format from RFC 2210 is reused for the Bandwidth TLV, so the document is not about RSVP.
The OAM section only fixes the switching point sub-TLV length, which is a small part of the document.

gaps.name: pseudowire (PWE3) / multi-segment pseudowires
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for pseudowires. The `pseudowire` tag I used above does not exist as written, and the only related entry is `pseudowire` under MPLS. Please verify that id; if it is not valid, this subject has no fitting tag and the document is best described as a gap.

RFC7268.title: RADIUS Attributes for IEEE 802 Networks
RFC7268.summary: Defines 17 new RADIUS attributes for IEEE 802.1X and 802.11 authenticators acting as AAA clients, and clarifies EAP-Key-Name and Called-Station-Id usage, updating RFCs 3580 and 4072.

RADIUS.why: The whole document specifies new RADIUS attributes, their packet types and formats, and updates RFC 3580 RADIUS usage guidelines.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines additional attributes suitable for usage by IEEE 802 authenticators acting as AAA clients.

WiFi.why: Many attributes (WLAN-HESSID, venue, cipher, AKM suite, RF band, reason code) carry IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN information. Readers of Wi-Fi would want it.
WiFi.quote: The WLAN-Reason-Code Attribute contains information on the reason why a Station has been refused network access and has been disassociated or de-authenticated.

EAP.why: Defines EAP-Peer-Id and EAP-Server-Id attributes and clarifies EAP-Key-Name, which carries the EAP Session-Id used to derive MACsec keys.
EAP.quote: The EAP-Peer-Id Attribute contains a Peer-Id generated by the EAP method.

rejected.why: EAP-Key-Name originates in the Diameter EAP application (RFC 4072). This document only reuses it in RADIUS and the Diameter protocol is not its subject.
The AAA framework is the context, but the RADIUS tag is the more specific fit.
IEEE 802.1X wired networks are mentioned (NID-Name, EAPoL-Announcement), but the document does not address IP over Ethernet.
UTF-8 is only the string encoding of one attribute (WLAN-Venue-Name).
The IANA section only records attribute type assignments and is boilerplate.

RFC7269.title: NAT64 Deployment Options and Experience
RFC7269.summary: Informational RFC summarizing NAT64 deployment scenarios (carrier-grade NAT and server front end) and operational experience, covering DNS64, high availability, traceability, geolocation, application testing, MTU and ULA use.

NAT64.why: The whole document is about deploying and operating stateful and stateless NAT64 in CGN and front-end scenarios.
NAT64.quote: This document summarizes NAT64 function deployment scenarios and operational experience.

DNS64.why: A dedicated subsection covers DNS64 deployment, DNSSEC interaction and use of DNS64 for load balancing, which readers of DNS64 would want.
DNS64.quote: DNS64 [RFC6147] is recommended for use in combination with stateful NAT64, and it will likely be an essential part of an IPv6 single- stack network

IPv6 transition.why: The document covers IPv6/IPv4 coexistence and transition deployment, including NAT44 coexistence, 464XLAT and Happy Eyeballs.
IPv6 transition.quote: A translation mechanism based on a NAT64 function [RFC6145] [RFC6146] is likely to be a key element of Internet connectivity for IPv6-IPv4 interoperability.

rejected.why: NAT64-CGN is a central term, but the document is about NAT64 placement, not carrier-grade NAT44 as such. NAT64 is the more specific tag.
It is mentioned as a way to help IPv4-only applications. It is not the subject of the document.
The SIP voice call test result is only one row of the application test table.
Syslog is only the mechanism used to transport NAT64 logs.
VRRP and BFD are used for failover in the HA testing. The document is not about them.
It is mentioned briefly in the NAT64/NAT44 coexistence discussion only.

RFC7270.title: Cisco-Specific Information Elements Reused in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC7270.summary: Defines additional IPFIX Information Elements in the 1-127 range (NetFlow v9-compatible), mostly deprecated sampler/class/engine fields plus forwardingStatus and BGP policy accounting traffic indexes, and registers them with IANA.

IPFIX.why: The document extends the IPFIX Information Model with new Information Elements, so it belongs on the IPFIX page.
IPFIX.quote: This document describes some additional IPFIX Information Elements in the range of 1-127, which is the range compatible with field types used by NetFlow version 9

rejected.why: BGP policy accounting traffic index elements are mentioned, but the document is not about BGP itself.
Sampling-related elements reference PSAMP selectorAlgorithm only as the replacement for deprecated elements; the document does not specify PSAMP.
The appendix uses XML to specify the elements, which is only the encoding of the registry definitions.
The IANA section only registers the elements, which is boilerplate here.

gaps.name: NetFlow
gaps.why: The document is about Cisco NetFlow v9 compatibility, but the taxonomy has no NetFlow tag. IPFIX is the closest fit.

RFC7271.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Linear Protection to Match the Operational Expectations of Synchronous Digital Hierarchy, Optical Transport Network, and Ethernet Transport Network Operators
RFC7271.summary: Defines alternate and additional MPLS-TP linear protection capabilities (priority modification, non-revertive changes, MS-W, SD protection, EXER), a capability-advertisement TLV, and PSC/APS modes with priority logic and state tables, updating RFC 6378.

MPLS-TP.why: The document extends and updates the MPLS-TP linear protection protocol (PSC), defining new capabilities, modes, priority logic and state machine.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document describes alternate mechanisms to perform some of the functions of MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) linear protection defined in RFC 6378

rejected.why: Protection switching is survivability for MPLS-TP, not traffic engineering; MPLS-TP is the more specific fit.
RFC 4427 recovery terminology is referenced only for non-revertive and manual switch semantics; GMPLS is not the subject.
Document concerns protection-switching coordination, with EXER as a protocol-test command only; it is not about OAM mechanisms generally.
The more specific child MPLS-TP applies, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: Linear protection switching / survivability
gaps.why: The document is about protection switching (1:1, 1+1, APS) in transport networks, and the taxonomy has no tag for protection or resilience beyond MPLS-TP.

RFC7272.title: Inter-Destination Media Synchronization (IDMS) Using the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP)
RFC7272.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR IDMS Report Block, an RTCP IDMS Settings packet type (PT=211) and an SDP rtcp-idms attribute so receivers can report arrival/playout times and synchronize playout across multiple destinations.

RTCP.why: The document extends RTCP with a new packet type and XR block type for IDMS reporting and settings distribution.
RTCP.quote: This document defines a new RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Packet Type and an RTCP Extended Report (XR) Block Type to be used for achieving Inter-Destination Media Synchronization (IDMS).

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP attribute with offer/answer and declarative rules, a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: The SDP attribute rtcp-idms is used to signal the use of the RTCP IDMS Settings Packet and the associated RTCP XR IDMS Report Block.
SDP.section: 10. SDP Signaling for RTCP IDMS Settings Packet

rejected.why: NTP is only relied on for wallclock synchronization and timestamp format; the document does not specify or extend it.
Clock sync is a prerequisite discussed in Section 8, but the document is about media playout synchronization, not clock synchronization.
RTP is the underlying transport; the document's new definitions are in RTCP, which is the more specific tag.
Media streaming is the application context, but the document specifies RTCP signalling rather than streaming delivery.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Inter-destination media synchronization (IDMS)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is synchronizing playout across multiple receivers, and the taxonomy has no tag for media synchronization.

RFC7273.title: RTP Clock Source Signalling
RFC7273.summary: RFC 7273 defines two SDP attributes, ts-refclk and mediaclk, that signal the timestamp reference clock sources (NTP, PTP, GPS and others) and the media clock sources for RTP streams, and it covers their use in offer/answer.

SDP.why: The document defines new SDP attributes (ts-refclk, mediaclk) with ABNF, source/media/session-level semantics, offer/answer usage and IANA registries. This is an extension of SDP.
SDP.quote: This memo specifies Session Description Protocol (SDP) signalling that identifies timestamp reference clock sources and SDP signalling that identifies the media clock sources

RTP.why: The signalling concerns RTP timestamps, NTP-format timestamps in RTCP sender reports and RTP media clocks. It is about RTP synchronisation, and the document extends no other RTP-specific mechanism.
RTP.quote: The media clock source for a stream determines the timebase used to advance the RTP timestamps included in RTP packets.

rejected.why: NTP and PTP are only named as possible reference clock sources in the SDP syntax. The document does not specify or extend them.
PTP (IEEE 1588) is identified as a clock source in SDP, but the document does not specify PTP. It only defines how to signal it.
RTCP sender reports are referenced for the NTP/RTP timestamp mapping, but the document defines nothing new in RTCP.
The subject is signalling which clocks are used, not clock synchronisation methods. SDP and RTP tags fit better.
SIP is mentioned only as one protocol that can carry updated SDP.
Only SDP attribute registries are created. No MIME media types are registered.

RFC7274.title: Allocating and Retiring Special-Purpose MPLS Labels
RFC7274.summary: Defines new IANA allocation and retirement procedures for special-purpose (formerly "reserved") MPLS labels 0-15, designates label 15 as the Extension Label, and creates an Extended Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values registry with data-plane handling rules.

MPLS.why: The document specifies MPLS label stack semantics: the Extension Label, extended special-purpose labels, and LSR forwarding behaviour. It updates many MPLS RFCs and is squarely about MPLS label encoding and operations.
MPLS.quote: A special-purpose label (the "Extension Label", XL, value 15) is set aside for the purpose of extending the space of special-purpose labels.

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document sets allocation policy, early allocation, retirement and registry renaming/creation for MPLS label registries, which is IANA registry guidance.
IANA.quote: Allocation of special-purpose MPLS labels is via "Standards Action".

rejected.why: Load balancing is addressed only briefly (ESPLs MUST NOT be used for load balancing); the document is not about ECMP.
RFC 5960 and 5921 are merely updated for terminology; the document is not about the transport profile.
RFC 6391 and 6478 are only in the list of updated RFCs for the term change.
RFC 3209 is only in the list of updated RFCs for the term change.

RFC7275.title: Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol for Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) Provider Edge (PE) Redundancy
RFC7275.summary: Specifies ICCP, an LDP-based protocol that lets L2VPN PEs in a Redundancy Group synchronize state and configuration for pseudowire redundancy and multi-chassis LACP attachment circuit redundancy.

LDP.why: The document defines new LDP message types, TLVs, a capability advertisement and status codes, so it extends LDP.
LDP.quote: ICCP is built as a secondary protocol running within LDP and taking advantage of the LDP session mechanisms

pseudowire.why: It defines the PW-RED application, with TLVs and procedures for pseudowire redundancy and status synchronization between PEs.
pseudowire.quote: enables Provider Edge (PE) device redundancy for Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) and Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) applications

L2VPN.why: The whole protocol provides PE redundancy for L2VPN services, VPWS and VPLS.
L2VPN.quote: The PE devices may be offering any type of L2VPN service, i.e., Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) or Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS).

link aggregation.why: A large part of the document defines mLACP TLVs and procedures for multi-chassis link aggregation over ICCP.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as one optional way to detect PE failure; the document does not specify or extend BFD.
Used only as the transport that LDP already runs over, along with TCP-AO for security; nothing new is defined for TCP.
The mLACP procedures apply to Ethernet attachment circuits, but the document is about link aggregation redundancy rather than IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
VPLS is a service the protocol supports, not something the document specifies or extends.
The document runs over an MPLS core, but LDP and pseudowire tags cover its subject better.

RFC7276.title: An Overview of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Tools
RFC7276.summary: Informational overview and index of IETF OAM tools (ping, traceroute, BFD, MPLS/MPLS-TP OAM, pseudowire OAM, OWAMP/TWAMP, TRILL OAM) for fault detection, isolation and performance monitoring.

OAM.why: The whole document surveys OAM functions, terminology and tools, so the OAM topic is its core subject.
OAM.quote: OAM" is a general term that refers to a toolset for detecting, isolating, and reporting failures, and for monitoring network performance.

BFD.why: BFD has its own section covering Control and Echo modes, and it is reused across MPLS, MPLS-TP and pseudowire OAM.
BFD.quote: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection [BFD], defined by the IETF BFD working group, is a generic OAM tool that can be deployed over various encapsulating protocols

MPLS-TP.why: A large section covers the MPLS-TP OAM toolset, including G-ACh, CC-V, lock, alarm reporting, LM and DM.
MPLS-TP.quote: The MPLS working group has defined the OAM toolset that fulfills the requirements for MPLS-TP OAM.

OWAMP.why: OWAMP is described in its own section, including its roles and its control and test protocols.
OWAMP.quote: OWAMP [OWAMP] enables measurement of one-way characteristics of IP networks, such as one-way packet loss and one-way delay.

TWAMP.why: TWAMP has its own subsection covering its roles and sessions.
TWAMP.quote: TWAMP [TWAMP] is a similar protocol that enables measurement of both one-way and two-way (round-trip) characteristics.

traceroute.why: Traceroute and path discovery are covered in a dedicated section and in the functions summary.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute ([TCPIP-Tools], [NetTools]) is an application that allows users to discover a path between an IP source and an IP destination.

pseudowire.why: Pseudowire OAM (VCCV, G-ACh, AC-PW mapping) is a full section.
pseudowire.quote: VCCV, as defined in [VCCV], provides a means for end-to-end fault detection and diagnostic tools to be used for PWs

MPLS.why: MPLS OAM (LSP Ping, BFD for MPLS) is one of the main toolsets covered.
MPLS.quote: The IETF MPLS working group has defined OAM for MPLS LSPs.

TRILL.why: TRILL OAM requirements get their own section and a row in the summary tables.
TRILL.quote: The requirements of OAM in TRILL are defined in [TRILL-OAM].

ICMP.why: IP Ping, based on ICMP Echo, is a covered toolset.
ICMP.quote: The ICMP Echo request/reply exchange in Ping is used as a Continuity Check function for the Internet Protocol.

rejected.why: Covered more specifically by the OWAMP and TWAMP tags. The performance monitoring (LM/DM) discussion sits under those tools.
Only mentioned as a pointer to the L2VPN OAM framework document, not a substantive part.
OWAMP/TWAMP control runs over TCP, but TCP is just the substrate.
Mentioned as a challenge for tracing multipath, not a subject of the document.
Used as probe and test transport only.

RFC7277.title: A YANG Data Model for IP Management
RFC7277.summary: Defines the YANG module ietf-ip, augmenting the interface data model with IPv4/IPv6 per-interface configuration and operational state (addresses, neighbor caches, MTU, forwarding, autoconf), with a mapping to the IP-MIB.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module (ietf-ip) with tree diagrams and module source, so YANG readers would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG [RFC6020] data model for management of IP implementations.

IPv6.why: A substantial part of the model manages IPv6: enablement, forwarding, MTU, addresses, neighbor cache, DAD, and SLAAC and privacy-address autoconfiguration parameters.
IPv6.quote: The data model covers configuration of per-interface IPv4 and IPv6 parameters, and mappings of IP addresses to link-layer addresses.

IPv4.why: Manages IPv4 per-interface parameters: addresses, netmasks, MTU, forwarding and the ARP cache.
IPv4.quote: The data model defines two configuration containers per interface -- "ipv4" and "ipv6", representing the IPv4 and IPv6 address families.

MIB.why: A dedicated section maps the YANG nodes to IP-MIB objects, which is relevant to readers of MIB modules.
MIB.quote: The following tables list the YANG data nodes with corresponding objects in the IP-MIB.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the access protocol the module is designed to be used with. It appears in the example and Security Considerations, but the document defines nothing new about it.
The neighbor cache is modelled, but the document does not specify or extend neighbor discovery. It only references it.
Autoconf parameters are configured, but SLAAC is referenced rather than specified or extended here.
The ARP cache is modelled as the IPv4 neighbor list, but ARP itself is not specified or extended.
XML appears only as the encoding of the example reply, so it is substrate.

RFC7278.title: Extending an IPv6 /64 Prefix from a Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Mobile Interface to a LAN Link
RFC7278.summary: Informational RFC giving requirements and two example methods for a 3GPP UE acting as an IPv6 router to extend its cellular-assigned /64 prefix to a LAN link via Router Advertisements, as an interim before DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation.

cellular.why: The document is about IPv6 over 3GPP cellular networks: how a UE shares its 3GPP-assigned /64 prefix with a LAN, so cellular readers would want it.
cellular.quote: this document describes requirements and provides examples on how the 3GPP UE radio interface assigned global /64 prefix may be extended from the 3GPP radio interface to a LAN link.

neighbor discovery.why: The mechanism relies on RA re-origination, DAD defence of addresses on the LAN, and a comparison with ND Proxy, so a substantial part concerns neighbor discovery behaviour.
neighbor discovery.quote: receiving the Router Advertisement (RA) [RFC4861] announced globally unique /64 IPv6 prefix from the 3GPP radio interface by the UE and then advertising the same IPv6 prefix to the LAN link with RA.

addressing.why: The document specifies how a single /64 prefix and a /128 anycast address are assigned and shared across two interfaces, which is IPv6 address allocation and use.
addressing.quote: The 3GPP UE maintains the same consistent 128-bit global-scope IPv6 anycast address [RFC4291] on the 3GPP radio interface and the LAN link.

rejected.why: Prefix Delegation is mentioned only as the preferred alternative that this document works around; the document does not specify it.
SLAAC is used by LAN hosts and disabled on the 3GPP interface, but it is not what the document specifies or extends.
The more specific tags (neighbor discovery, addressing, cellular) cover the content. IPv6 is the general setting.
An IEEE 802.11 SSID is mentioned only as an example of a LAN. The document does not address Wi-Fi.
The scenario is a single-link tethering or CPE router setup, not a home network architecture with prefix assignment and routing.
The document does not cover IPv4/IPv6 coexistence or transition.

RFC7279.title: An Acceptable Use Policy for New ICMP Types and Codes
RFC7279.summary: BCP defining an acceptable use policy for adding new ICMPv4/ICMPv6 message types and codes, limiting them to forwarding-plane anomaly reporting and node/router/network discovery, and discouraging use of ICMP as a routing or transport protocol.

ICMP.why: The whole document is a policy on what new ICMP types and codes may be added, with a classification of existing types and guidance on extensions.
ICMP.quote: we describe an acceptable use policy for new ICMP message types and codes, and provide some background about the policy.

rejected.why: Discussed only as an anomalous example of a protocol using ICMP as transport; the document is not about RPL.
Mentions RFC 2780 allocation guidelines but explicitly does not supersede them; the focus is on policy for ICMP, not registry procedures.
ICMPv6 is covered as part of ICMP, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Only listed as an application that uses existing ICMP messages.
Mentioned only as an example application using ICMP error messages.
Neighbor Discovery messages appear in the message type list but are not discussed in their own right.

RFC7280.title: IANA Guidance for Managing the Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) Next-Header Registry
RFC7280.summary: RFC 7280 updates RFC 4326 to set IANA allocation rules (Specification Required with Designated Expert guidelines), reserve a private-use range, and add explanatory notes for the ULE Next-Header registry used by ULE and GSE.

IANA.why: The document exists to define registry allocation policy, expert review guidelines, and a private-use reservation for the ULE Next-Header registry.
IANA.quote: Allocations in the ULE Next-Header registry are to be assigned by IANA using the "Specification Required" policy defined in [RFC5226].
IANA.section: 3. Updated IANA Guidance on Allocation in the ULE Next-Header Registry

DVB.why: ULE and GSE are encapsulations for IP over MPEG-2/DVB links; the document clarifies the registry that records their Extension Header and Type code points, so readers of that subject would want it.
DVB.quote: The Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) [RFC4326] specifies an encapsulation for links that employ the MPEG-2 Transport Stream

rejected.why: ULE carries IP datagrams but the document only concerns a registry of Next-Header values, not IP itself.
ULE is an encapsulation, but the document is about registry management, not generic tunnelling.
The Designated Expert and Specification Required rules are IANA registry policy, covered better by the IANA tag.

gaps.name: Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) / Generic Stream Encapsulation (GSE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ULE or GSE specifically. The nearest is DVB (IP over MPEG-2/DVB), so a ULE-specific tag would help readers.

RFC7281.title: Authentication-Results Registration for S/MIME Signature Verification
RFC7281.summary: Defines a new "smime" authentication method, with result codes and body.smime-* properties, for the Authentication-Results header field so that S/MIME signature verification status can be conveyed to MUAs and downstream filters.

S/MIME.why: The document defines how S/MIME signature verification results are reported, including result codes and parameters tied to S/MIME signatures and certificates. S/MIME readers would want it.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME signature and countersignature verification is represented by the "smime" method and is defined in [RFC5751].

email authentication.why: It extends the Authentication-Results framework with a new email authentication method and registers it in the Email Authentication Parameters registry. No specific child (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC) fits.
email authentication.quote: This document defines a new authentication method to be used in the Authentication- Results header field for S/MIME-related signature checks.
