rejected.why: Authentication-Results is a message header field, but the document only registers a method for it and does not specify the message format itself.
X.509 certificate fields (serial, issuer) are referenced as parameter values, but the document does not profile certificates.
CMS content types are mentioned only to describe how nested signatures are referenced; the document is not about CMS.
The IMAP section syntax is borrowed only to reference MIME body parts.
MIME part references are used as a parameter value, but the document does not specify MIME structure or encodings.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-style registrations that follow from the main body, which is not about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: Authentication-Results header field
gaps.why: RFC 7001 and its method registrations have no dedicated tag. The nearest fit is email authentication, which is used here.

RFC7282.title: On Consensus and Humming in the IETF
RFC7282.summary: An informational essay explaining the IETF's rough consensus decision-making principle, why humming is not voting, and how chairs should judge consensus by addressing objections rather than counting heads.

IETF process.why: The whole document is about how the IETF makes decisions: rough consensus, humming, consensus calls by chairs, and appeals. This is IETF process, though it deliberately proposes no procedural change.
IETF process.quote: This document explains some features of rough consensus, what is not rough consensus, how we have gotten away from it

rejected.why: The parent is implied by IETF process. The document fits that child better than the broader governance topic.
NomCom is another IETF procedure and is not mentioned in the document.
The document explains terms such as 'rough consensus', 'hum' and 'consensus call'. It is not a glossary, though, and its subject is the decision-making practice.

RFC7283.title: Handling Unknown DHCPv6 Messages
RFC7283.summary: Updates RFC 3315 to specify that DHCPv6 relay agents must forward unknown message types toward the server, and that clients and servers must silently discard unknown message types.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies and updates DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) behavior for relay agents, clients and servers on unknown message types.
DHCPv6.quote: A client or server MUST silently discard any received DHCPv6 message with an unknown message type.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag; the parent is implied.
DHCPv6 runs over IPv6 but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Security Considerations is boilerplate-like and the document does not address a security mechanism.

RFC7284.title: The Profile URI Registry
RFC7284.summary: Establishes an IANA "Profile URIs" registry (First Come First Served) for URIs identifying profiles as defined by the 'profile' link relation type, with a registration template and initial entries.

IANA.why: The document's whole purpose is to create a new IANA registry with a registration template, procedure and initial contents.
IANA.quote: This document establishes the "Profile URIs" registry. The registration procedure for new entries requires a request in the form of the following template

URI.why: The registry centrally manages URIs that identify profiles, so readers of URI topics would find the registry relevant.
URI.quote: Profiles are identified by a URI and can thus be created without central coordination.

rejected.why: Builds on the 'profile' link relation (RFC 6906) but the document defines only a URI registry, not link relation behaviour.
Profiles are compared to media types for central management, but no media type registration rules are defined.
JSON-LD profile URIs appear as initial registry entries only; the document is not about JSON.
The Dublin Core HTML profile is just one initial entry.

RFC7285.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Protocol
RFC7285.summary: Specifies the ALTO Protocol, a REST/JSON-over-HTTP interface by which networks publish network maps, cost maps, endpoint properties and endpoint costs to applications such as P2P and CDNs for traffic optimization.

ALTO.why: The whole document defines the ALTO Protocol: Map, Map-Filtering, Endpoint Property and Endpoint Cost services, the IRD, data types and registries.
ALTO.quote: This document describes a protocol implementing the ALTO services.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate; the document uses GET/POST and caching but does not extend HTTP itself.
JSON is only the encoding used for messages.
TLS/HTTPS is required for security but is just the mechanism relied on; nothing new is defined about it.
It registers application/alto-* media types, but this is IANA boilerplate secondary to the protocol itself.
P2P applications are use cases for ALTO, but the document does not specify P2P protocols.
STUN is mentioned only as a way for a client to learn its public address.

RFC7286.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Server Discovery
RFC7286.summary: Specifies a two-step ALTO server discovery procedure for resource-consumer-embedded ALTO clients: obtain a domain name via local configuration or DHCP, then perform a U-NAPTR lookup in DNS to get the HTTP(S) URI of the ALTO server's Information Resource Directory.

ALTO.why: The whole document defines how ALTO clients discover ALTO servers, and registers the ALTO U-NAPTR service tag.
ALTO.quote: This document specifies a procedure for resource-consumer-initiated ALTO server discovery, which can be used if the ALTO client is embedded in the resource consumer.

service discovery.why: It is a service discovery procedure using U-NAPTR/DDDS, so readers of service discovery would want it.
service discovery.quote: Before an ALTO client can ask for guidance it needs to discover one or more ALTO servers that can provide guidance to this specific client.

DHCP.why: A main step of the procedure retrieves the access network domain name through specific DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options.
DHCP.quote: the ALTO server discovery procedure MUST try to retrieve DHCP option 213 (OPTION_V4_ACCESS_DOMAIN)

rejected.why: DNS, including NAPTR records, is the lookup mechanism. The document defines no new record type, only a U-NAPTR application service tag.
HTTP(S) URIs are only the result of discovery. The document does not specify HTTP behaviour.
DNSSEC is only recommended in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate evidence.
The ALTO tag registration is routine IANA Considerations, not the subject of the document.
Multihoming is discussed only briefly in the deployment considerations.
DHCPv6 is only a substrate for retrieving the domain name, and the document defines no new option for it. The DHCP tag already covers it.

gaps.name: U-NAPTR / DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service)
gaps.why: The core mechanism is a U-NAPTR lookup with a newly registered ALTO application service tag. The taxonomy has no tag for DDDS or NAPTR-based service location.

RFC7287.title: Mobile Multicast Sender Support in Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Domains
RFC7287.summary: Experimental RFC specifying support for mobile multicast senders in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains via MLD proxies at MAGs, direct PIM/BIDIR-PIM routing at MAGs, and an MLD proxy peering function.

PMIPv6.why: The document defines how multicast sources work across handovers in PMIPv6 domains, specifying MAG and LMA operations.
PMIPv6.quote: This document describes the support of mobile multicast senders in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains for the base deployment scenario

multicast.why: IP multicast routing and group membership proxying are central, including the MLD proxy peering function and source/listener handling.
multicast.quote: Multicast communication can be enabled in Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) domains via the Local Mobility Anchors by deploying Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) proxy functions

PIM-SM.why: Substantial sections describe PIM-SM phases, register handling and handover optimizations for mobile sources at LMAs and MAGs.
PIM-SM.quote: Local Mobility Anchors that operate the Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) routing protocol [RFC4601] will require sources to be directly connected

MLD.why: The document defines a new MLD proxy peering function and multiple-upstream-interface proxy extensions.
MLD.quote: an optimized approach to multicast source mobility based on extended peering functions among proxies is defined in this section

rejected.why: Only referenced as the base that PMIPv6 extends; the document is about PMIPv6, not MIPv6.
IGMP is mentioned for IPv4 analogy, but the focus is MLD proxying.
SSM considerations are brief subsections, not a main subject.
Mentioned only in a note that GRE keys are not used for multicast.
The document runs over IPv6 but is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC7288.title: Reflections on Host Firewalls
RFC7288.summary: An IAB informational document examining the architectural effects of host firewalls, why applications are run then blocked, and recommending policy be expressed via applications or explicit library/services (like PCP) rather than opaque firewall rules.

firewall.why: The whole document analyses host and network firewalls, their rule sources, and approaches to attack surface reduction and security policy.
firewall.quote: Unlike traditional firewalls that protect network links, host firewalls run in end-user systems.

rejected.why: Mentioned as an example of the explicit application-to-firewall model, but not specified or extended here.
Only noted briefly as often mistaken for a firewall.
Blocking ICMP and its effect on path MTU discovery is cited only as an example.
The document has architectural themes, but its subject is firewalls, which the more specific firewall tag covers.
The document is an architectural reflection on firewalls, not guidance on operational security practice.

RFC7289.title: Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) Deployment with BGP/MPLS IP VPNs
RFC7289.summary: Informational framework for deploying Carrier-Grade NAT (NAT444) in operator networks by using BGP/MPLS IP VPNs to separate CGN-mediated flows from traditional IPv4 and IPv6 flows, with deployment requirements and bypass models.

CGN.why: The whole document defines architectural requirements and an integration model for CGN deployments, including bypass, logging, and overlap space.
CGN.quote: This document specifies a framework to integrate a Network Address Translation (NAT) layer into an operator's network to function as a Carrier-Grade NAT

L3VPN.why: The proposed integration model is built on BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, using VRFs, RD/RT, and extranet Services VRFs to provide routing separation; a substantial part of the document applies L3VPN to this use.
L3VPN.quote: The BGP/MPLS IP VPN [RFC4364] framework for CGN segregates the internal realms within the service-provider space into Layer 3 MPLS-based VPNs.

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are used as the forwarding substrate for the VPN model; the document is not about MPLS itself, and L3VPN is the more specific fit.
Dual-stack operation is discussed briefly (4.2.1) and DS-Lite/NAT64 are only mentioned as possible future steps; the focus is IPv4 CGN, not transition mechanisms.
Mentioned only as an alternative translation environment to which operators may later transition.
Referenced only as a possible future translation environment, not specified or analysed.
MPLS-TE and PBR are discussed only as alternatives the VPN model avoids (4.4).
Multicast gets one short section pointing to other RFCs; not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC7290.title: Test Plan and Results for Advancing RFC 2680 on the Standards Track
RFC7290.summary: Test plan and results comparing two independent implementations (NetProbe, Perfas+) of the RFC 2680 one-way packet loss metric, supporting its advancement on the Standards Track.

performance measurement.why: The document tests implementations of the IPPM one-way packet loss metric (RFC 2680) using active measurement, loss thresholds, Poisson sampling and statistical equivalence comparisons.
performance measurement.quote: a performance metric RFC defining one-way packet loss metrics, along the Standards Track

rejected.why: L2TPv3 is only the tunnel used in the test setup to hide addresses from hashing; the document defines nothing about it.
OWAMP and TWAMP are referenced only in Security Considerations; the tested implementations are NetProbe and Perfas+.
Traceroute output is shown only as path reporting in the test setup; the document is not about traceroute.
UDP is only the carrier of the test packets.
The document touches on Standards Track advancement but is an interoperability-style test report for a metric, not about process itself.
The tests are of live-network metric definitions and implementations, not device benchmarking methodology.

RFC7291.title: DHCP Options for the Port Control Protocol (PCP)
RFC7291.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that deliver PCP server IP addresses to hosts, with client behaviour and server configuration guidelines.

PCP.why: The document extends PCP deployment by defining how clients discover PCP servers. Readers of the PCP subject would want it.
PCP.quote: This document defines DHCPv4 [RFC2131] and DHCPv6 [RFC3315] options that can be used to configure hosts with PCP server [RFC6887] IP addresses.

DHCPv6.why: Defines the new DHCPv6 option OPTION_V6_PCP_SERVER, its format and client behaviour.
DHCPv6.quote: The DHCPv6 PCP server option can be used to configure a list of IPv6 addresses of a PCP server.

DHCP.why: Defines the new DHCPv4 option OPTION_V4_PCP_SERVER and its client and server behaviour. DHCP is the parent of DHCPv6, and the DHCPv4 option is a primary subject.
DHCP.quote: The DHCPv4 PCP server option can be used to configure a list of IPv4 addresses of a PCP server.

rejected.why: PCP controls NAT and firewall devices, but this document only covers server address discovery.
Mentioned only as an example deployment context for IPv4-mapped addresses in DHCPv6.
IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses are used in the option, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
FQDN resolution by the DHCP server is mentioned in passing and is out of scope.

RFC7292.title: PKCS #12: Personal Information Exchange Syntax v1.1
RFC7292.summary: Republication of PKCS #12 v1.1, defining the PFX transfer syntax for personal identity information (private keys, certificates, CRLs, secrets) with password- or public-key-based privacy and integrity modes, plus password-based key derivation.

PKI.why: The document specifies a container format for exchanging private keys, certificates and CRLs between platforms. This is PKI key and certificate material handling, and no more specific PKI child tag fits.
PKI.quote: describes a transfer syntax for personal identity information, including private keys, certificates, miscellaneous secrets, and extensions.

ASN.1.why: The document defines the PFX, SafeBag and related types and includes a full ASN.1 module (Appendix D). Readers of ASN.1 modules would want it.
ASN.1.quote: ASN.1 and BER-encoding ensure platform independence.

password hashing.why: Appendices B and C specify a password-based key and IV derivation method with salt and iteration count. They also give guidance on moving to PKCS #5 PBKDF2.
password hashing.quote: We present here a general method for using a hash function to produce various types of pseudorandom bits from a password and a string of salt bits.

rejected.why: The document uses PKCS #7 ContentInfo, EnvelopedData and SignedData as wrappers. It does not specify or extend CMS.
HMAC is only the MAC used in password integrity mode. The document does not define anything new about it.
X.509 certificates and CRLs are carried in bags as opaque DER-encoded OCTET STRINGs. The document does not profile them.
PBKDF2 is only recommended as a replacement for the method in Appendix B. The document does not specify it.
SHA hashes are the underlying algorithms for HMAC and key derivation. The document is not about the SHA family.
RC4 object identifiers appear in the PBE list in Appendix C. That is a minor part of the document, not its subject.

gaps.name: PKCS #12 / PFX personal information exchange
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for key and certificate bundle or keystore formats, so the document is placed under the generic PKI tag.

RFC7293.title: The Require-Recipient-Valid-Since Header Field and SMTP Service Extension
RFC7293.summary: Defines the RRVS SMTP extension and the Require-Recipient-Valid-Since header field, letting senders state when a mailbox's ownership was known so mail isn't delivered to a new owner of a reassigned address.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension (EHLO keyword, RCPT parameter, relay behaviour, enhanced status codes), so it belongs under SMTP.
SMTP.quote: This document defines an extension for the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) called "RRVS" to provide a method for senders to indicate to receivers a point in time

message format.why: A substantial part defines a new Internet message header field, its syntax, handling, removal and conversion to and from the SMTP extension.
message format.quote: This document also defines a header field called "Require-Recipient-Valid-Since" that can be used to tunnel the request through servers that do not support the extension.

rejected.why: It registers an Authentication-Results method (rrvs) but the topic is mailbox ownership continuity, not sender domain authentication or anti-spoofing.
NTP is only cited as the clock synchronization protocol implementations must use; the document is not about it.
It reuses RFC 3339 timestamps with a restriction, but defines no new date-time format.
The more specific SMTP and message format tags cover the subject, and their ancestor email is implied.
Privacy considerations are discussed, but mainly in boilerplate-style sections; the document is not about privacy threat models.

RFC7294.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Blocks for Concealment Metrics Reporting on Audio Applications
RFC7294.summary: Defines two RTCP XR report blocks (Loss Concealment Metrics and Concealed Seconds Metrics) for reporting receiver-side packet loss concealment on audio RTP streams, with SDP signaling and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies new RTCP XR block types (BT=30 and BT=31), extending RTCP reporting per RFC 3611.
RTCP.quote: This document defines two RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) blocks that allow the reporting of concealment metrics for audio applications of RTP.

rejected.why: SDP is used only to signal XR block use via a small rtcp-xr attribute extension; it is not the subject of the document.
RTP is the media transport being monitored; the document is about RTCP reporting, which is tagged more specifically.
Considered because it defines performance metrics under the RFC 6390 framework. RTCP is the more specific fit, so I did not add this.
G.711 is only cited as an informative reference for PLC quality; the document is not about the codec.
The IANA section is boilerplate registrations and does not make the document about IANA.

gaps.name: RTCP XR (RTP Control Protocol Extended Reports) blocks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an RTCP tag only as a child of RTP. A tag for 'RTCP XR' would suit this document and the other xrblock metrics-block RFCs better, but the tag 'RTCP' I used does not appear in the taxonomy as written (the listed id is 'RTCP' under RTP, so it fits).

RFC7295.title: Report from the IAB/IRTF Workshop on Congestion Control for Interactive Real-Time Communication
RFC7295.summary: IAB/IRTF workshop report summarizing discussions on congestion control for interactive real-time (RTP/WebRTC) media, bufferbloat, AQM, ECN, and recommendations to the IETF.

RTP congestion control.why: The whole report is about congestion control for interactive real-time media over RTP, leading to the RMCAT work.
RTP congestion control.quote: The main goal of the workshop was to foster a discussion on congestion control mechanisms for interactive real-time communication.

AQM.why: Bufferbloat and AQM (RED, CoDel) are a substantial discussion and a recommended solution track, leading to the AQM WG.
AQM.quote: Active queue management (AQM) aims to prevent queues from growing too large.

ECN.why: ECN deployment and its benefit to real-time media is a recurring recommendation.
ECN.quote: ECN allows routers along the end-to-end path to signal the onset of congestion and allows applications to respond early

workshop reports.why: The document is an IAB/IRTF workshop report.
workshop reports.quote: This document provides a summary of the IAB/IRTF Workshop on 'Congestion Control for Interactive Real-Time Communication'

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport context; the document concerns congestion control, not the RTP protocol itself.
TFRC is discussed as a past attempt, but only as one example within the broader congestion control discussion.
RTCWEB is the motivating use case but the document is not about WebRTC architecture.
Mentioned only briefly in passing.
Discussed briefly as one traffic segregation mechanism, not a main subject.
Mentioned only in passing as an explanation of why networks work well.

gaps.name: Bufferbloat
gaps.why: A major theme of the workshop; no taxonomy tag exists specifically for bufferbloat, though AQM covers the main solution.

RFC7296.title: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC7296.summary: RFC 7296 specifies IKEv2, the IPsec key exchange and SA management protocol, obsoleting RFC 5996 and advancing IKEv2 to Internet Standard.

IKE.why: The document is the IKEv2 specification: exchanges, payloads, rekeying, authentication and error handling.
IKE.quote: This document describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol.

NAT.why: A substantial section defines NAT traversal for IKE and ESP, including UDP encapsulation on port 4500 and transport-mode traffic selector handling.
NAT.quote: Opening an IPsec connection through a NAT introduces special problems.

rejected.why: IKE is a child of IPsec in the taxonomy and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
EAP is used as an optional authentication method in Section 2.16, but the document does not specify EAP itself.
ESP and AH are the Child SAs that IKE negotiates, not the subject of this document.
MOBIKE is only referenced as an alternative for address-change recovery.
IPComp negotiation is a short section, not a substantial part of the document. The taxonomy tag is for IPComp, but the section is minor.
UDP is the transport for IKE and not the subject of the document.

RFC7297.title: IP Connectivity Provisioning Profile (CPP)
RFC7297.summary: Informational RFC defining the Connectivity Provisioning Profile (CPP), a technology-agnostic template (in RBNF) capturing IP/MPLS connectivity requirements such as scope, QoS guarantees, availability, capacity, isolation, flow identification and notifications between customers and network providers.

QoS.why: The CPP centres on negotiating IP transfer guarantees (delay, loss, jitter, capacity, conformance traffic, DSCP re-marking, classes of service), which is QoS provisioning at the architecture level.
QoS.quote: QoS guarantees denote a set of IP transfer performance metrics that characterize the quality of the IP transfer treatment to be experienced

performance measurement.why: The profile expresses guarantees in terms of IPPM metrics (one-way delay, loss, delay variation) and measurement intervals, so performance-metrics readers would find it relevant.
performance measurement.quote: Appropriate performance metrics, such as one-way delay or one-way delay variation, are used to characterize an IP transfer service.

traffic engineering.why: CPP is meant to drive TE objectives and be translated into MPLS-TE and routing actions, and it specifies dedicated paths for TE or resilience.
traffic engineering.quote: set (traffic) objectives of Traffic Engineering functions and service management functions

rejected.why: MPLS is the network context and a target for translating CPP clauses, but the document does not specify or extend MPLS.
VPN services and BGP/MPLS VPN are mentioned only as example translations of the traffic isolation clause, not as a subject of the document.
RBNF is used only as notation for the template, not something the document is about.
BFD, VRRP, IP fast reroute and LSP ping are given as example availability mechanisms in a list, not addressed in their own right.
CPP is a service-level requirements template, not a policy information model, though it is loosely related.
RFC 7149 and ABNO are cited as usage examples only; the document is not about SDN.

gaps.name: Service-level connectivity provisioning / service negotiation templates

RFC7298.title: Babel Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) Cryptographic Authentication
RFC7298.summary: RFC 7298 specifies an optional, backward-compatible HMAC-based cryptographic authentication extension for the Babel routing protocol, adding TS/PC and HMAC TLVs, replay protection state, and key/security-association handling.

Babel.why: The document extends and updates the Babel protocol (RFC 6126) with new TLV types, data structures and sending/receiving procedures.
Babel.quote: This document describes a cryptographic authentication mechanism for the Babel routing protocol.

HMAC.quote: Description of the algorithm: 1. Preparation of the Key ... First-Hash = H(Ko XOR Ipad || Text)

RFC7299.title: Object Identifier Registry for the PKIX Working Group
RFC7299.summary: RFC 7299 documents the object identifiers assigned under the PKIX arc (1.3.6.1.5.5.7), returns the arc to IANA, and creates IANA registries with a Specification Required policy for future PKIX-related OIDs.

PKI.why: The document is a registry of OIDs for PKIX (modules, certificate extensions, CMP/CMC/SCVP/OCSP identifiers, etc.), so PKI readers would look for it.

RFC7300.title: Reservation of Last Autonomous System (AS) Numbers

RFC7301.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation Extension
RFC7301.summary: Defines the TLS ALPN extension, letting client and server negotiate the application-layer protocol (e.g., HTTP/2) within the TLS handshake, and creates an IANA registry of ALPN protocol IDs.

RFC7303.title: XML Media Types

RFC7305.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Internet Technology Adoption and Transition (ITAT)
