RFC7321.summary: Updates the mandatory-to-implement cryptographic algorithm requirements for IPsec ESP and AH (obsoleting RFC 4835) and gives guidance on choosing among them.

ESP.why: The document sets algorithm requirements and usage guidance for ESP and AH. ESP is the most specific IPsec tag that fits.
ESP.quote: This document specifies the current set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms for ESP and AH

IPsec.why: AH is covered alongside ESP, and AH has no child tag. The IPsec parent covers AH and the guidance on combining ESP and AH.
IPsec.quote: ESP can provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, or the combination of both of those security services. AH provides only data origin authentication.

cryptography.why: The document chooses among algorithms (AES-GCM, AES-CBC, 3DES, DES, HMAC and others) and gives the rationale for each choice. No single algorithm tag covers the whole document, so the topic tag is used.
cryptography.quote: The nature of cryptography is that new algorithms surface continuously and existing algorithms are continuously attacked.

rejected.why: AES modes are among the algorithms listed, but the document is about requirement levels across many algorithms, not about AES itself.
DES and 3DES are moved to MUST NOT and MAY, but this is one row in a larger table and not the subject of the document.
HMAC-SHA1-96 is a listed algorithm, but the document is not about HMAC.
Key exchange is not discussed. The scope is ESP and AH algorithms only.
MD5 appears only in a rationale paragraph about HMAC-MD5, which is not recommended.

RFC7322.title: RFC Style Guide
RFC7322.summary: RFC 7322 is the RFC Style Guide, which sets out the editorial conventions, document structure and related procedures for publishing RFCs, and obsoletes RFC 2223.

RFC series.why: The whole document defines RFC format, style, structure and the RFC Editor's editorial process. That is the core subject of the RFC series page.
RFC series.quote: describes the fundamental and unique style conventions and editorial policies currently in use for the RFC Series

rejected.why: The IANA Considerations section is only described as a required part of an RFC. The document does not address IANA registries themselves.
Copyright and IPR boilerplate is mentioned only as a structural element of an RFC and is not discussed in substance.
It touches on requirements-language use and term consistency, but only as style rules and not as a glossary or definitions document.
It gives conventions for writing URIs in RFCs and references, which is a style matter and not about URI syntax or schemes.
The document is about RFC publication and editing and not about how the IETF develops standards.

RFC7323.title: TCP Extensions for High Performance
RFC7323.summary: RFC 7323 specifies the TCP Window Scale and Timestamps options, plus the RTTM and PAWS mechanisms, for high bandwidth-delay-product and high-speed paths, and obsoletes RFC 1323.

TCP.why: The document defines the TCP Window Scale and Timestamps options, RTTM and PAWS. It is a core TCP extension specification.
TCP.quote: This document specifies a set of TCP extensions to improve performance over paths with a large bandwidth * delay product and to provide reliable operation over very high-speed paths.

rejected.why: Section 5.7 requires PAWS implementations to also implement Path MTU Discovery. This is a dependency, not the subject of the document.
The document touches on the congestion window and RTO estimation, but only incidentally. The subject is window scaling and timestamps.
There is no SACK tag in the taxonomy. SACK is explicitly out of scope here and is only referenced.
The TCP checksum is mentioned only in passing, in the header prediction and security discussions.
IPv6 Jumbograms are mentioned only in the Security Considerations and in Appendix A.

RFC7324.title: Updates to MPLS Transport Profile Linear Protection
RFC7324.summary: RFC 7324 updates the MPLS-TP linear protection Protection State Coordination (PSC) logic of RFC 6378. It adds TLV error-handling rules, fixes incorrect status after a failure, specifies behaviour on capability mismatches, fixes a reversion deadlock, and clarifies handling of multiple inputs.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document corrects and clarifies PSC, the linear protection mechanism for MPLS-TP, and it updates RFC 6378. Readers of the MPLS-TP subject would want it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document contains a number of updates to the Protection State Coordination (PSC) logic defined in RFC 6378, "MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Linear Protection".

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the more specific child tag, and the document is about MPLS-TP protection, not general MPLS.
PSC is a protection-switching mechanism, not an OAM mechanism. The document says nothing about OAM beyond operator alerts.
Syslog is mentioned only as one possible way to alert operators, and the document does not specify it.
The document is about protection switching state machines, not traffic engineering of paths.

RFC7325.title: MPLS Forwarding Compliance and Performance Requirements
RFC7325.summary: Informational guidance for implementers and deployers on MPLS forwarding compliance and performance: label stacks, special-purpose labels, Diffserv, FRR, pseudowire CW/flow/entropy labels, multipath hashing, packet rates, DoS protection, OAM, with supplier questions and tests.

MPLS.why: The whole document is about MPLS forwarding behaviour, label stack handling, entropy labels, FRR and related requirements.
MPLS.quote: This document provides guidelines for implementers regarding MPLS forwarding and a basis for evaluations of forwarding implementations.

MPLS-TP.why: Substantial coverage of MPLS-TP UHP forwarding, OAM toolset, LM/DM and protection state coordination hardware requirements.
MPLS-TP.quote: MPLS-TP introduces forwarding demands that will be extremely difficult to meet in a core network.

pseudowire.why: Covers pseudowire control word, sequence number, flow label and their impact on forwarding.
pseudowire.quote: A pseudowire encapsulated at a network edge must have a means to prevent reordering within the core

ECMP.why: Extensive guidance on which MPLS and IP fields to hash for multipath load balancing, including entropy labels.
ECMP.quote: hash-based multipath techniques are used in the core and in the edge.

performance measurement.why: Section 4 gives forwarding compliance and performance tests, benchmark-style, though the benchmarking tag is more apt.
performance measurement.quote: Performance testing is the domain of the IETF Benchmark Methodology Working Group (BMWG).

rejected.why: BFD is discussed as an OAM mechanism but only as part of the broader OAM hardware-support discussion.
Referenced for FRR and signalling but the document focuses on forwarding, not signalling.
Considered; tests are provided but they are checklists rather than a formal benchmarking methodology, so rejected in favour of MPLS-focused tags.
Only a short subsection on hardware support for IPFIX.
Section 2.1.2 covers DSCP-to-TC mapping but it is one of many forwarding topics.
DoS protection of control plane is a subsection, not the main subject.

RFC7326.title: Energy Management Framework
RFC7326.summary: Defines the EMAN framework for energy management of network-attached devices: a physical reference model and an information model of Energy Objects with identity, context, power/energy/demand measurements, Power State control, and power-source, metering and aggregation relationships.

energy management.why: The whole document is the Energy Management framework: Energy Objects, measurements, Power States, relationships, and IANA Power State Set registries.
energy management.quote: This document defines a framework for Energy Management (EMAN) for devices and device components within, or connected to, communication networks.

rejected.why: MIB modules implementing the model are in other EMAN documents; this one only gives an abstract information model and SNMP security notes in boilerplate.
The framework mentions MIB modules but does not define one; the information model is protocol-independent.
UUIDs are only used to identify Energy Objects; nothing new is specified about UUIDs.
The IANA Power State Set registries are a small part, boilerplate-like, and not the subject of the document.
Not used; the information model uses a UML-like notation, not YANG.

gaps.name: Energy Management (EMAN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists 'energy management' only in the network management hierarchy, but I used the id as given; if that id doesn't exist exactly as written, this framework would need a dedicated tag.

RFC7328.title: Writing I-Ds and RFCs Using Pandoc and a Bit of XML
RFC7328.summary: RFC 7328 describes Pandoc2rfc, a toolchain that lets authors write Internet-Drafts and RFCs in Pandoc Markdown plus a little XML, converting via DocBook and XSLT to xml2rfc input.

RFC series.why: The document is about authoring tooling and source formats for producing I-Ds and RFCs, which is RFC series format and publication tooling.
RFC series.quote: a source format for documents that are Internet-Drafts (I-Ds) or RFCs

Markdown.why: Pandoc Markdown syntax is the authoring format; the document details its constructs for lists, figures, tables and references.
Markdown.quote: a Markdown [Markdown] syntax variant, called Pandoc [Pandoc]

rejected.why: The document uses xml2rfc XML (RFC 2629) as the target format but does not specify or extend the vocabulary; it is about writing in Pandoc that is converted to it.
XML and XSLT are the intermediate conversion substrate, not the subject.

gaps.name: Pandoc2rfc / document authoring tools
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RFC/I-D authoring toolchains; the 'Markdown text formats' tag is the nearest fit, but it is missing a tag for Pandoc and xml2rfc tooling.

RFC7329.title: A Session Identifier for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC7329.summary: Defines a new SIP header field, Session-ID, a globally unique identifier that survives B2BUAs and proxies so administrators can troubleshoot and correlate related SIP dialogs.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field and specifies UAC, UAS, proxy and B2BUA behaviour, transfer handling (REFER, Replaces) and migration.
SIP.quote: this document proposes a new SIP header to carry such a value: Session-ID.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-1 is only used as the mechanism to generate the identifier value; the document is not about HMAC.
SHA-1 is merely the hash inside the HMAC used to generate the value.
The Session-ID is a 128-bit hex value but is not a UUID and does not use the UUID format.
The IANA section registers the header field, which is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
ABNF is used only to define the header's syntax.

RFC7330.title: Definitions of Textual Conventions (TCs) for Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Management
RFC7330.summary: RFC 7330 defines two SMIv2 MIB modules (BFD-TC-STD-MIB and IANA-BFD-TC-STD-MIB) containing Textual Conventions for BFD session index, interval, multiplier, ports, diagnostics, session type, state, and authentication, for reuse by BFD MIB modules.

BFD.why: The textual conventions model BFD management information: session state, diagnostic codes, session types, authentication types, and control port numbers, so BFD readers would want this RFC.
BFD.quote: This document defines two MIB modules that contain Textual Conventions for Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocols.

MIB.why: The document's content is two SMIv2 MIB modules defining TEXTUAL-CONVENTIONs, which fits the MIB modules and SMI subject.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is only the framework through which MIB objects are accessed. The document defines no SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
The UDP port numbers appear only as value ranges in the BFD port textual conventions. The document is not about UDP.
The IANA-maintained MIB module is part of the content, but the document is not about IANA registry guidance or stewardship in general.
RFC 6428 is referenced only for a couple of diagnostic codes. The document is not about MPLS-TP.
The BFD-on-LAG port 6784 is mentioned only in passing as one allowed value.

RFC7331.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Management Information Base
RFC7331.summary: Defines the BFD-STD-MIB SMIv2 module with managed objects for configuring and monitoring BFD sessions, performance counters, mapping tables and notifications.

BFD.why: The MIB models BFD sessions, parameters, authentication, echo mode and counters, so BFD readers would want it.
BFD.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition (BFD-STD-MIB), with tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and MIB is the more specific tag.
UDP ports appear as BFD session objects, but the document is not about UDP.
The only IANA content is the boilerplate OID assignment; the IANA-BFD-TC MIB is defined elsewhere.
This parent topic is implied by the more specific MIB tag.

RFC7332.title: Loop Detection Mechanisms for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs)
RFC7332.summary: Defines normative requirements for SIP B2BUAs to copy and decrement Max-Forwards and copy Max-Breadth from the UAS side to the UAC side, and recommends Via-based loop detection, so request loops and forking amplification are bounded.

SIP.why: The document specifies required SIP behavior for B2BUAs regarding Max-Forwards, Max-Breadth and Via loop detection, so it belongs on the SIP page.
SIP.quote: All B2BUA types MUST copy the received Max-Forwards header field from the received SIP request on their UAS side, to any request(s) they generate on their UAC side

rejected.why: Not about session recording; B2BUAs are only the subject of loop behavior.
No SIP peering between providers is discussed.
Loops here are SIP request loops handled by SIP header fields, not general routing architecture.

RFC7333.title: Requirements for Distributed Mobility Management
RFC7333.summary: Defines requirements for network-layer Distributed Mobility Management (DMM), contrasting it with centralized mobility anchors (Mobile IPv6/PMIPv6, 3GPP), stating problems and eight requirements.

IP mobility.why: The whole document is about requirements for network-layer IP mobility management with distributed anchors, replacing centralized anchors such as HA/LMA.
IP mobility.quote: This document defines the requirements for Distributed Mobility Management (DMM) at the network layer.

rejected.why: PMIPv6 is used as background and terminology and as an example of centralized anchoring; the document does not specify or extend it.
Mobile IPv6 is likewise referenced as an existing centralized protocol for terminology and comparison, not specified here.
3GPP GPRS/EPS are mentioned as examples of centralized mobility, but the document is about IP-layer mobility generally.
SNMP, NETCONF, YANG, syslog and IPFIX are listed as example management protocols in REQ6 without being the document's subject.
Multicast appears in one problem (PS8) and one requirement (REQ8) but is a minor part of the document.
REQ6 covers operations and management considerations, but it is one requirement among eight.

gaps.name: Distributed Mobility Management (DMM)
gaps.why: The document is about DMM specifically; the taxonomy only has the general IP mobility topic and no DMM tag.

RFC7334.title: PCE-Based Computation Procedure to Compute Shortest Constrained Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Inter-Domain Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths
RFC7334.summary: Experimental RFC defining a PCE-based "core-tree" procedure and a new RP object C-bit in PCEP for computing shortest constrained inter-domain P2MP TE LSPs, extending BRPC.

PCE.why: The document specifies PCE procedures and a PCEP extension (C-bit in the RP object) for inter-domain P2MP path computation, using an extended BRPC procedure.
PCE.quote: This document describes an experiment to provide procedures and extensions to the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) for the computation of inter-domain paths for P2MP TE LSPs.

rejected.why: P2MP TE LSPs are the object of computation, but the document is about PCE path computation, not MPLS encoding or operation.
RFC 4875 signalling is referenced only as the way the computed LSPs are set up; the document does not extend it.
GMPLS networks are mentioned as an applicable environment, but nothing GMPLS-specific is defined.
P2MP LSPs serve multicast services, but the document does not address IP multicast routing.
The PCE tag is a child of this topic and already covers it.

RFC7335.title: IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix
RFC7335.summary: Generalizes the IANA reservation of 192.0.0.0/29 from DS-Lite's B4 element to an "IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix" usable by any IPv6 transition solution (e.g., 464XLAT) needing a non-routed IPv4 interface address.

464XLAT.why: The document's motivating new use case is the 464XLAT CLAT needing an IPv4 address on the host, and it has a whole section on it.
464XLAT.quote: 464XLAT has the same need for a non-routed IPv4 prefix, and this same need may be common for other similar solutions.

DS-Lite.why: The document updates RFC 6333's reservation for DS-Lite and generalizes it while preserving DS-Lite use.
DS-Lite.quote: DS-Lite [RFC6333] directs IANA to reserve 192.0.0.0/29 for the Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) element.

IPv4.why: The document is about an IPv4 special-purpose address block, its naming and its allocation, which IPv4 address readers would want.
IPv4.quote: IANA has updated the IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry

rejected.why: A more specific child tags (464XLAT, DS-Lite) already cover it, so the parent is implied.
The IANA registry update is the mechanism, not the subject. The subject is the address-prefix use for transition technologies.
Considered since it concerns address allocation, but the IPv4 tag fits the special-purpose block more precisely.

RFC7336.title: Framework for Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI)
RFC7336.summary: Informational framework RFC describing the components, interfaces (control, request routing, metadata, logging), message-flow examples, deployment models and trust model for interconnecting content delivery networks (CDNI).

CDN.why: The whole document is about CDN interconnection: request routing, metadata, logging and control interfaces between CDNs, deployment models and trust.
CDN.quote: This document presents a framework for Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI).

rejected.why: HTTP redirects and conditional GETs are used as mechanisms in examples, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
DNS-based redirection (CNAME/NS) is a building block and example, but the document does not define DNS behavior; it is substrate for request routing.
Section 3.4.1 only briefly notes signing considerations for on-the-fly CNAMEs; a minor note, not a main subject.
Caching is the CDN's function, but the document is about interconnection, not HTTP cache semantics.
HTTP Adaptive Streaming is discussed in one section, with detail deferred to RFC 6983.

RFC7337.title: Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI) Requirements
RFC7337.summary: Informational RFC listing the requirements (generic, control, request routing redirection, footprint/capabilities, metadata, logging, security) for the CDNI solution and interfaces to be specified by the CDNI working group.

CDN.why: The whole document specifies requirements for interconnecting content delivery networks, which is exactly the CDN/CDNI subject.
CDN.quote: The goal of the present document is to outline the requirements for the solution and interfaces to be specified by the CDNI working group.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the delivery and acquisition data-plane protocol the CDNI solution must support; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Purge, revalidation and cache behaviour metadata appear as CDNI interface requirements, but the document is not about HTTP caching mechanisms.
DNS-based request routing is mentioned only as an example redirection mode.
HTTP Adaptive Streaming support is a handful of requirements, not a streaming specification.

RFC7338.title: Requirements and Framework for Point-to-Multipoint Pseudowires over MPLS Packet Switched Networks
RFC7338.summary: Informational requirements and framework document for point-to-multipoint pseudowires over MPLS PSNs, covering reference model, P2MP LSP underlay, signalling, OAM/failure detection, protection and scalability.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines requirements for P2MP pseudowires, an extension of the PWE3 architecture. The pseudowire tag is the best fit.
pseudowire.quote: This document presents a set of requirements and a framework for providing a point-to-multipoint pseudowire (PW) over MPLS Packet Switched Networks.

rejected.why: VPLS is named only as a potential application of P2MP PWs. The document does not specify or analyse it.
MPLS is the substrate and P2MP LSPs are the underlay. The document does not define anything new about MPLS itself.
P2MP RSVP-TE is mentioned only as one possible tunnel setup protocol.
mLDP and LDP status notification are mentioned only in passing as existing mechanisms.
The document is about P2MP PW emulation. Multicast is only a motivating use case and the source of encapsulation terminology.
Failure detection and OAM requirements are one subsection. They are not enough for a topic tag, and the document's main subject is the pseudowire.

RFC7339.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Overload Control
RFC7339.summary: Defines SIP overload control: four new Via header parameters (oc, oc-algo, oc-validity, oc-seq) for hop-by-hop feedback from overloaded servers to upstream clients, general client/server behavior, and a mandatory-to-implement loss-based scheme with a default algorithm.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with new Via header parameters and specifies SIP client/server overload behavior. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document defines four new parameters for the SIP Via header for overload control.

congestion control.why: It specifies an application-layer overload and congestion control mechanism, including a loss-based throttling algorithm, which fits congestion control in general. No more specific congestion child fits SIP overload.
congestion control.quote: so that clients can reduce the volume of traffic sent to overloaded servers, avoiding congestion collapse and increasing useful throughput.

rejected.why: A DDoS attack is discussed only as a security threat to the mechanism. The document is about overload feedback, not DDoS mitigation.
TLS is only recommended as a protection for overload feedback on the link, and the document defines nothing new about it.
RFC 3263 server location uses DNS, but only as a substrate for next-hop selection.
The SIP event package alternative is discussed only as a rejected design option in Section 10.1.2.
Emergency calls (SOS URN) are mentioned only as a message prioritization policy example.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax section.

gaps.name: SIP overload control
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers SIP-specific overload or load control (the SOC working group). SIP and congestion control are the closest fits.

RFC7340.title: Secure Telephone Identity Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC7340.summary: Problem statement and high-level requirements for secure caller-origin (telephone number) identity in SIP/VoIP and PSTN interworking, reviewing PAI, SIP Identity and VIPR and why they failed; it launched the STIR effort.

STIR.why: The document is the STIR problem statement and requirements, covering caller-ID authentication for telephone numbers in SIP.
STIR.quote: This document examines the reasons why providing identity for telephone numbers on the Internet has proven so difficult

SIP.why: Substantial analysis of SIP identity mechanisms (P-Asserted-Identity, SIP Identity) and their limits with B2BUAs.
SIP.quote: The SIP Identity mechanism [RFC4474] provides two header fields for securing identity information in SIP requests

PSTN interop.why: Use cases cover VoIP-PSTN call flows and gateways, and how identity survives PSTN interworking.
PSTN interop.quote: Interworking with non-SIP networks makes end-to-end identity problematic.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the failure of public ENUM in environmental changes; not the subject.
Cited briefly as a possible improvement for certificate binding.
Robocalls are a motivating problem, but the spam tag concerns unsolicited email.
Telephone numbers appear as identifiers, but the tel URI scheme itself is not specified or extended.
Certificate authority delegation for numbers is discussed only as an environmental consideration.

RFC7341.title: DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 (DHCP 4o6) Transport
RFC7341.summary: Defines a mechanism to carry DHCPv4 messages inside DHCPv6 using two new messages (DHCPv4-query, DHCPv4-response) and two new options, so clients on IPv6-only networks can obtain IPv4 configuration.

DHCPv6.why: The document extends DHCPv6 with new message types and options (DHCPV4-QUERY, DHCPV4-RESPONSE, OPTION_DHCPV4_MSG, OPTION_DHCP4_O_DHCP6_SERVER) and specifies client, relay and server behaviour.
DHCPv6.quote: Two new DHCPv6 messages and two new DHCPv6 options are defined for this purpose.

DHCP.why: DHCPv4 messages and state machine (RFC 2131) are encapsulated and processed by the server; the unicast flag and retransmission rules are defined in terms of DHCPv4 behaviour.
DHCP.quote: This document describes a transport mechanism to carry DHCPv4 messages using the DHCPv6 protocol

IPv6 transition.why: The mechanism provisions IPv4 configuration across IPv6-only networks, supporting dual-stack transition mechanisms such as lightweight 4over6.
IPv6 transition.quote: IPv4 connectivity is still needed as networks migrate towards IPv6.

rejected.why: Lightweight 4over6 is only mentioned as an informative example of a mechanism that might enable 4o6; it is out of scope.
The document does carry one protocol over another, but the subject is DHCP provisioning; the more specific DHCP tags fit better.
DHCPv6 runs over UDP; this is only a substrate and nothing new is defined about UDP.
IPv6 is the underlying network, not the subject; the document is about DHCP configuration delivery.

RFC7342.title: Practices for Scaling ARP and Neighbor Discovery (ND) in Large Data Centers
RFC7342.summary: Informational independent-stream RFC documenting operational practices (gratuitous ARP, rate limiting, snooping, static entries, proxies, overlays) for scaling ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery in large data center networks.

data center networking.why: The whole document addresses address resolution scaling at data-centre scale, covering L3-to-access, large L2 and overlay designs.
data center networking.quote: This memo documents some operational practices that allow ARP/ND to scale in data center environments.

ARP.why: ARP behaviour, caching, snooping, static entries and proxy ARP variants are analysed throughout.
ARP.quote: For IPv4 networks, a practice to alleviate this problem is to have the L2/L3 boundary router send periodic gratuitous ARP

neighbor discovery.why: IPv6 ND scaling, its bidirectional validation requirement and ND proxy are discussed alongside ARP.
neighbor discovery.quote: IPv6 end stations are still required to send unicast ND messages to their default gateway router

rejected.why: Overlays (VXLAN, TRILL) are discussed in one short section as a design option, not specified or analysed in depth.
IGMP/MLD snooping is touched on in Section 5.4 as a related scaling issue, but it is not the document's subject.
SEND is mentioned only as a security constraint on proxying and relaxing bidirectionality.
Mentioned only as a possible mechanism for updating static entries.
The document covers both IPv4 and IPv6, and the specific IPv6 subject is covered by the neighbor discovery tag.

RFC7343.title: An IPv6 Prefix for Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers Version 2 (ORCHIDv2)
RFC7343.summary: RFC 7343 defines ORCHIDv2, a new IPv6 prefix (2001:20::/28) and hash-based construction for non-routable, overlay-routable cryptographic identifiers (e.g., HIP HITs) with an algorithm-agility identifier, obsoleting RFC 4843.

addressing.why: The document's core is an IPv6 prefix allocation and the format of identifiers that look like IPv6 addresses but are non-routable at the IP layer. This is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: IANA has allocated a new 28-bit prefix out of the IANA IPv6 Special Purpose Address Block, namely 2001:0000::/23

HIP.why: ORCHIDs are produced in the HIP working group and are the format of HITs. HIP readers need this, though the document defines no HIP protocol behaviour.
HIP.quote: Examples of these include Host Identity Tags (HITs) in the Host Identity Protocol (HIPv2)

rejected.why: IPv6 is the address format ORCHIDs imitate, and the prefix comes from IPv6 special-purpose space. The document is about the prefix and identifiers, so the more specific addressing tag fits better.
SHA1 is mentioned only as an example hash for HIPv2. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Public keys are inputs to the hash, but the document defines no key establishment or provisioning.
The prefix allocation is part of the subject. The document is not about IANA registry guidance in general.
RFC 1918 is cited only as an analogy for address hijacking.

gaps.name: Cryptographic hash identifiers / cryptographic agility
gaps.why: The OGA ID field provides hash-algorithm agility for identifiers. There is no specific tag for cryptographic identifiers or agility, though the cryptography parent might partly cover it.

RFC7344.title: Automating DNSSEC Delegation Trust Maintenance
RFC7344.summary: Defines the CDS and CDNSKEY DNS resource records, which a child zone publishes so its parent can automatically poll and update the DS records, automating DNSSEC delegation trust maintenance and KSK rollover.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies CDS/CDNSKEY records and processing rules for maintaining DS records and rolling Key Signing Keys, so it is about DNSSEC operations and delegation trust.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes a method to automate publication of subsequent DS records after the initial one has been published.

rejected.why: The new RR types are DNSSEC-specific, and DNSSEC is the more specific tag, so the parent DNS tag is implied and not listed separately.
EPP is mentioned only as an example of a parent-child communication path and in the RRR background appendix. The document does not specify or extend it.
Registry/registrar relationships are background for the problem. The mechanism itself is DNS-based and does not define registration protocols.
Dynamic DNS UPDATE appears only as a prior proposal that failed to reach consensus. The adopted mechanism is polling.

RFC7345.title: UDP Transport Layer (UDPTL) over Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC7345.summary: Specifies carrying T.38 fax's UDPTL over DTLS, with a new SDP proto value UDP/TLS/UDPTL and SIP/SDP offer/answer negotiation of DTLS roles and certificate fingerprints.

DTLS.why: The document defines how UDPTL is carried in DTLS application_data records, including cipher suite requirements, rekeying, and demultiplexing with STUN.
DTLS.quote: This document specifies fax transport using UDPTL over DTLS [RFC6347], which enables integrity and confidentiality protection of fax in IP networks.

SDP.why: It defines the UDP/TLS/UDPTL proto value and the offer/answer procedures using the setup and fingerprint attributes, and registers the value with IANA.
SDP.quote: this document specifies a new <proto> value [RFC4566] for the SDP media description ("m=" line)

fax.why: The purpose is secure T.38 fax transport over IP, so readers of fax topics would want this RFC.
fax.quote: the UDP Transport Layer (UDPTL) protocol, the predominant transport protocol for T.38 fax

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling used to negotiate the stream. The document does not extend SIP, and its SIP messages appear only in examples.
ICE and STUN interaction are covered in one short subsection of miscellaneous considerations. The document does not specify or extend them.
UDP is only the underlying substrate. The document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
The document uses DTLS and needs no TLS extensions. DTLS is the more specific tag.
RTP/SAVP is mentioned only as a background alternative for fax security and is not specified here.

gaps.name: UDPTL / T.38 fax transport
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for UDPTL or T.38 specifically. The fax tag is the closest fit, but it is described as fax over Internet mail and IP.

RFC7346.title: IPv6 Multicast Address Scopes
RFC7346.summary: Updates the IPv6 multicast scope definitions in RFC 4291 and RFC 4007, defining scop 3 as Realm-Local (automatically configured), establishing an IANA registry of scopes, and defining Realm-Local for IEEE 802.15.4.

multicast.why: The document is about IPv6 multicast address scopes and their boundaries, which fits the multicast topic. No child technology tag such as PIM or MLD fits.
multicast.quote: This document updates the definitions of IPv6 multicast scopes and therefore updates RFCs 4007 and 4291.

IPv6.why: It amends the IPv6 addressing architecture (RFC 4291) and the scoped address architecture (RFC 4007), so it belongs on the IPv6 page.
IPv6.quote: The following table updates the definitions in [RFC4291]:

IANA.why: The document creates a new registry and sets its policy and reference rules for Realm-Local scope definitions. This is a substantial part of the document.
IANA.quote: IANA has established a sub-registry titled "IPv6 Multicast Address Scopes" in the existing "IPv6 Multicast Address Space Registry".

rejected.why: The document defines scop 3 for IEEE 802.15.4 and was motivated by MPL, but it does not specify 6LoWPAN or any constrained link layer itself.
This was considered because the document concerns IPv6 address scopes. The IPv6 tag is more specific, since it covers the IPv6 addressing architecture.

RFC7347.title: Pre-standard Linear Protection Switching in MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP)
RFC7347.summary: Describes the pre-standard, deployed MPLS-TP linear protection switching (1+1 and 1:1) and its APS protocol carried over the G-ACh, published for the record and interworking.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document specifies linear protection switching, the APS PDU, timers and state machines for MPLS-TP LSPs and pseudowires.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document describes the pre-standard implementation of MPLS-TP Linear Protection that has been deployed by several network operators using equipment from multiple vendors.

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
Pseudowires are only named as one kind of protected transport entity. They are not the subject.
OAM only supplies the SF/SD fault triggers. The document does not specify OAM mechanisms.
SONET/SDH APS is cited only as the model the protocol follows. It is not what the document covers.
Protection switching is resilience, not traffic engineering, and no TE tag fits.

gaps.name: Linear protection switching / network resilience
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for protection switching or recovery in general. MPLS-TP is the closest fit.

RFC7348.title: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN): A Framework for Overlaying Virtualized Layer 2 Networks over Layer 3 Networks
RFC7348.summary: Informational RFC documenting the deployed VXLAN protocol, a MAC-in-UDP encapsulation with a 24-bit VNI that overlays virtualized Layer 2 segments on Layer 3 networks for multi-tenant data centers.

VXLAN.why: The whole document specifies the VXLAN encapsulation, its frame format, VTEP behaviour, gateways and deployment scenarios.
VXLAN.quote: VXLAN is a Layer 2 overlay scheme on a Layer 3 network. Each overlay is termed a VXLAN segment.

rejected.why: UDP is only the outer transport for the encapsulation. The port assignment and checksum rules are details of VXLAN itself, not a usage guideline for UDP.
Ethernet frames are the payload being tunnelled. The document does not address IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Multicast carries broadcast and unknown-destination traffic, but IGMP and PIM are only relied on and not specified or profiled.
ECMP is a motivation, and the UDP source-port entropy serves it, but the document is not about ECMP forwarding.
IPsec is only suggested in Security Considerations as a way to protect tunnelled traffic.
Data centres are the context, but VXLAN is the more specific tag for what the document defines.
VXLAN is a tunnelling scheme, but the more specific overlay networks tag covers it.

RFC7349.title: LDP Hello Cryptographic Authentication
RFC7349.summary: Defines a new optional Cryptographic Authentication TLV for LDP Hello messages, using HMAC with SHA-family hashes, security associations and a 64-bit sequence number to protect against spoofing and replay.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP by defining a new optional Hello parameter (TLV 0x0405) and the procedures for sending and receiving it.
LDP.quote: This document introduces a new optional Cryptographic Authentication TLV that LDP can use to secure its Hello messages.

HMAC.why: A substantial part of the document specifies HMAC-SHA-1/256/384/512 key preparation and hash computation for the TLV, so readers of HMAC would want it.
HMAC.quote: The HMAC authentication mode defined in [RFC2104] is used.

routing security.why: The document secures a routing/label-distribution protocol, following the KARP approach, with a cross-protocol attack mitigation and replay protection.
routing security.quote: It secures the Hello messages against spoofing attacks and some well-known attacks against the IP header.

rejected.why: The SHA hashes are only the algorithms plugged into HMAC. The document defines nothing new about them.
LDP is the protocol under change, and the document is not about MPLS architecture generally. The more specific LDP tag fits.
UDP is only the transport the Hello messages use. The document does not specify anything about UDP itself.
This is a generic topic tag, and the more specific routing security and HMAC tags already cover the subject.

RFC7350.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) as Transport for Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC7350.summary: Specifies DTLS over UDP as a transport for STUN and TURN, giving guidance per STUN usage, and updating the STUN/TURN URI handling and the TURN S-NAPTR resolution mechanism (new "turn.dtls" tag, "stuns"/"turns" UDP service names).

STUN.why: The document extends STUN with a new transport and discusses each STUN usage with DTLS, updating RFC 5389.
STUN.quote: This document adds DTLS as a valid transport for STUN.

TURN.why: It adds DTLS/UDP as a TURN transport and modifies TURN URIs and the TURN resolution mechanism (updates RFC 5928).
TURN.quote: TURN [RFC5766] defines three combinations of transports/allocations: UDP/UDP, TCP/UDP, and TLS/UDP.  This document adds DTLS/UDP as a valid combination.

DTLS.why: The document specifies how DTLS is used, including mandatory cipher suites, MTU handling and DoS countermeasures, for STUN/TURN.
DTLS.quote: DTLS-over-UDP (referred to in this document as simply DTLS [RFC6347]) offers the same security advantages as TLS-over-TCP

ICE.why: Analyses DTLS applicability to ICE connectivity checks and keep-alives, which are STUN usages.
ICE.quote: Adding DTLS on top of the connectivity check would delay, and consequently impair, the ICE process.

rejected.why: This is a transport-binding topic, but the specific STUN/TURN/DTLS technology tags already sit elsewhere; the topic tag adds nothing more specific.
S-NAPTR/SRV resolution is used and a new S-NAPTR tag is defined, but only as part of TURN server resolution, not as DNS itself.
The document says it makes no changes to the syntax of STUN/TURN URIs; it only specifies how the schemes are used with DTLS.
SIP keep-alive is mentioned only briefly as one STUN usage.
UDP is just the substrate under DTLS; nothing new is defined about UDP.
TLS is referenced for comparison and cipher-suite rules, but the document is about DTLS, not TLS.

gaps.name: STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only NAT traversal and ICE/STUN/TURN under real-time communications; I used STUN and TURN ids as listed, and the STUN and TURN ids exist under NAT traversal, so no real gap.

RFC7351.title: A Media Type for XML Patch Operations
RFC7351.summary: Defines the XML patch document format (application/xml-patch+xml) built on RFC 5261 patch operations, for use with HTTP PATCH, and registers the media type.

XML.why: The document specifies an XML-based patch format with a schema, namespace and XPath-selector handling, including namespace patching issues.
XML.quote: The XML patch document format defines an XML document structure for expressing a sequence of patch operations to be applied to an XML document.

media types.why: It registers the application/xml-patch+xml media type, a substantial part of the document's purpose.
media types.quote: The Internet media type [RFC6838] for an XML patch document is application/xml-patch+xml.

rejected.why: HTTP PATCH is only the intended usage context; the document defines no HTTP protocol behaviour.
Appendix B provides an ABNF grammar, but only as an implementation aid for the XPath subset, not as the subject.
HTTP PATCH is the use context only; the document is about the patch format and media type, not the web in general.

gaps.name: XML patch / XPath selectors
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for XML patching or XPath; XML is the closest fit.

RFC7352.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Detecting Duplicate Deliveries
RFC7352.summary: Defines the Sieve "duplicate" test extension, which detects previously seen messages (by Message-ID, header, or arbitrary unique ID) across script executions, with :handle, :seconds and :last arguments.

Sieve.why: The RFC specifies a new Sieve extension (test, arguments, capability string), so it belongs on the Sieve page.
Sieve.quote: This document defines a new test command, "duplicate", for the Sieve email filtering language.

mailing lists.why: Handling duplicates from list subscriptions and crossposting is the main motivating application, but the document does not define list protocols or headers.
mailing lists.quote: Duplicate deliveries are a common side effect of being subscribed to a mailing list.

rejected.why: Message-ID and header unfolding are used as inputs, but the document does not specify message format.
Only mentioned for imapsieve exclusion and the seen flag; not the subject.
Appears only in an example notification target.
Sieve is the more specific tag; the document is not about email architecture generally.
Duplicate detection is not spam filtering.

RFC7353.title: Security Requirements for BGP Path Validation
RFC7353.summary: Informational requirements document for a BGP security protocol (BGPsec) that gives cryptographic assurance of origin AS authority to announce a prefix and of the AS path in BGP UPDATEs.

BGPsec.why: The whole document lists requirements for BGPsec path validation, so the BGPsec tag fits directly.
BGPsec.quote: requirements for a BGP security protocol design to provide cryptographic assurance that the origin Autonomous System (AS) has the right to announce the prefix and to provide assurance of the AS Path

RPKI.why: RPKI origin validation is the starting point and the gap BGPsec fills. The document assumes ROAs and RPKI deployment and sets requirements on the security infrastructure, but it does not specify RPKI itself.
RPKI.quote: Origin validation based on Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) [RFC6811] provides a measure of resilience to accidental mis-origination of prefixes

rejected.why: BGPsec is a more specific child tag, and the document is about securing BGP rather than BGP operations or policy.
This is the parent of BGPsec and RPKI, so it is implied by those tags.
TLS is only named as one mechanism that could protect the link layer (3.8), and the document defines nothing new about it.
IPsec is only mentioned as an option for protecting the session, not addressed in its own right.
TCP-AO is only listed as an example mechanism for authenticating sessions.
SNMP is mentioned only as an example of how to signal security exceptions.

RFC7354.title: Update to the Registrant Information for the Digital Video Broadcasting Project (DVB) Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace
RFC7354.summary: Updates the registrant contact information for the "dvb" URN namespace originally registered in RFC 5328 for the Digital Video Broadcasting Project.

URN.why: The document updates the registration of a formal URN namespace (dvb), so it belongs on the URN page alongside other namespace registrations.
URN.quote: RFC 5328 registered the Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace "dvb" for the Digital Video Broadcasting Project.

rejected.why: The IANA section only adds a reference to the Formal URN Namespaces registry entry. That is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registry policy.
URN is the more specific tag, so the URI parent is implied and not listed.

RFC7355.title: Indicating WebSocket Protocol as a Transport in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Common Log Format (CLF)
RFC7355.summary: RFC 7355 updates the SIP Common Log Format (RFC 6873) by defining and registering a new 'W' Transport Flag value for SIP messages carried over WebSocket (plain and secure), with example log records.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP Common Log Format, a SIP logging specification, with a new transport flag for SIP over WebSocket. Readers of SIP topics would want it.
SIP.quote: This document updates RFC 6873 [RFC6873] by defining a new SIP CLF "Transport Flag" value for WebSocket.

WebSocket.why: The document defines how WebSocket transport (plain and secure) of SIP is indicated in logs. It adds nothing to the WebSocket protocol itself but is about its use as a SIP transport.
WebSocket.quote: SIP CLF records of messages transported over a plain WebSocket connection (WS) MUST set the "Transport Flag" to this new 'W' value
WebSocket.section: 4. Usage of the WebSocket Transport Flag

rejected.why: Secure WebSocket runs over TLS, but TLS is only the substrate. The document only maps it to the Encryption Flag 'E'.
The document concerns SIP CLF logging, but CLF is not the syslog protocol.
Base64 is used only to encode the example log records.
SDP bodies are mentioned in the examples but omitted, so the document is not about SDP.
The IANA registration of the new flag value is boilerplate. The document is not about IANA registries in general.
HTTP is mentioned only as the WebSocket handshake basis in the introduction.

gaps.name: SIP Common Log Format (CLF)
gaps.why: The document is about SIP message logging formats. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol logging formats within SIP, so the SIP tag is the closest fit.

RFC7356.title: IS-IS Flooding Scope Link State PDUs (LSPs)
RFC7356.summary: Defines new IS-IS PDUs (FS-LSP, FS-CSNP, FS-PSNP) for new flooding scopes (circuit, domain, extended LSP set capacity), plus extended TLVs with 16-bit type/length fields and a scope support announcement TLV.

IS-IS.why: The whole document extends the IS-IS protocol: new PDUs, Update Process operation per scope, extended TLVs, and a new IIH TLV.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines new Protocol Data Units (PDUs) that provide support for new flooding scopes as well as additional space for advertising information

rejected.why: Appointed Forwarder information from TRILL is only cited as a motivating use case; the document is not about TRILL.
IS-IS tag is the specific fit; no broader architecture discussion.
IANA registries are created but that is boilerplate for this protocol extension, not the subject.

RFC7357.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): End Station Address Distribution Information (ESADI) Protocol
RFC7357.summary: RFC 7357 specifies the TRILL ESADI protocol, an optional per-Data-Label IS-IS-style flooding protocol by which TRILL switches distribute end station MAC reachability, replacing the ESADI description in RFC 6325.

TRILL.why: The whole document specifies ESADI, a TRILL protocol, and updates the TRILL base protocol RFC 6325. It covers ESADI PDU processing, DRB election, duplicate MAC handling and the ESADI-LSP contents.
TRILL.quote: ESADI (End Station Address Distribution Information) is an optional protocol by which a TRILL switch can communicate, in a Data Label

rejected.why: ESADI reuses IS-IS reliable flooding and the E-L1CS PDU formats, but the document specifies a separate TRILL protocol and does not extend IS-IS itself.
Ethernet is only the link framing for ESADI packets and the medium whose MAC addresses are being distributed. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
EAP and 802.1X are mentioned only as a possible source of authenticated enrollment for the addresses ESADI carries.
HMAC-SHA256 is used once, to derive the default authentication key. That is a minor mechanism and not what the document is about.
ECMP appears only as one permitted strategy for handling duplicate MAC addresses, within a small subsection.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tag in the routing hierarchy only as 'TRILL' under routing, and I used that id. If it is not actually present in the taxonomy, this RFC would have no fitting tag and a dedicated TRILL tag would be needed.

RFC7358.title: Label Advertisement Discipline for LDP Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs)
RFC7358.summary: Updates RFC 5036 and several FEC-defining RFCs to clarify that an LDP FEC type, not the session's negotiated label advertisement mode, governs label advertisement, and specifies the discipline (DU, DoD, etc.) for every defined LDP FEC type.

LDP.why: The whole document clarifies LDP label advertisement behaviour per FEC type and updates RFC 5036 (LDP specification) and other LDP extension RFCs.
LDP.quote: The label advertising behavior of an LDP speaker for a given Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) is governed by the FEC type and not necessarily by the LDP session's negotiated label advertisement mode.

rejected.why: The CR-LSP FEC is one row in the table (DoD), but the document is not about CR-LDP signalling itself.
PWid FEC elements are listed with their discipline, but pseudowire setup is not the subject.
LDP is the specific subject; MPLS in general is only the surrounding context, and LDP is the more specific tag.
The IANA registry is extended with a new column, but that is a consequence of the update, not the document's subject.

RFC7359.title: Layer 3 Virtual Private Network (VPN) Tunnel Traffic Leakages in Dual-Stack Hosts/Networks
RFC7359.summary: RFC 7359 describes how IPv6-unaware Layer 3 VPN clients (IPsec or SSL/TLS) on dual-stack hosts can leak traffic in the clear, covers both inadvertent and attacker-triggered cases, and recommends mitigations.

IPv6.why: The problem arises from IPv4/IPv6 coexistence on dual-stack hosts and networks. The document analyses it and recommends IPv6-aware VPN clients, so IPv6 deployment readers need it.
IPv6.quote: the lack of proper IPv6 support in popular Virtual Private Network (VPN) tunnel products, may inadvertently result in VPN tunnel traffic leakages

IPsec.why: IPsec tunnel-mode VPNs are one of the two VPN types in scope. The leakage analysis applies to them, though the document does not specify or extend IPsec.
IPsec.quote: IPsec-based VPN tunnels simply employ IPsec in tunnel mode to encapsulate and transfer Layer 3 packets over the VPN tunnel.

operational security.why: The document gives operational mitigations and a client-side hardening guide against traffic leakage. These are operational security practice.
operational security.quote: an administrator may want to disable IPv6 connectivity on all network interfaces of the node employing the IPv6-unaware VPN client.

rejected.why: The VPN tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs (L3VPN over BGP/MPLS and similar). This document is about client-based remote-access VPNs, so it does not fit.
SSL/TLS is only the encryption substrate of one VPN type. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
Forged Router Advertisements are the attack vector. The document does not specify or analyse neighbor discovery itself.
DNS A/AAAA records are background for how IPv4 and IPv6 are glued together, and RDNSS spoofing is an attack step. The document is not about DNS.
The document is about dual-stack coexistence side effects, not a transition mechanism.

RFC7360.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) as a Transport Layer for RADIUS
RFC7360.summary: Experimental RFC specifying DTLS as a transport for RADIUS (RADIUS/DTLS over UDP/2083), including coexistence with RADIUS/UDP, session management, and security considerations.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies a new transport for the RADIUS protocol, its behaviour changes, and its coexistence with RADIUS/UDP.
RADIUS.quote: We define a method for using DTLS [RFC6347] as a RADIUS transport protocol.

DTLS.why: A substantial part covers how DTLS sessions are used, tracked, resumed and closed for RADIUS, with DTLS-specific guidance such as cookies, heartbeats, and ciphersuites.
DTLS.quote: RADIUS/DTLS servers SHOULD use the stateless cookie tracking technique described in [RFC6347], Section 4.2.1.

rejected.why: Only the substrate for RADIUS/TLS comparison; DTLS is the relevant child and RFC 6614 is the TLS spec.
UDP is the underlying transport; the document does not define UDP usage guidance.
Mentioned only as the prior approach for securing RADIUS.
Mentioned only as the weakness motivating the change.
Considered since this is RADIUS carried over DTLS, but the RADIUS and DTLS tags cover it more specifically.
Certificates are used for authentication but are not specified or profiled here.

RFC7361.title: LDP Extensions for Optimized MAC Address Withdrawal in a Hierarchical Virtual Private LAN Service (H-VPLS)
RFC7361.summary: Defines an LDP MAC Flush Parameters TLV enabling optimized "negative" MAC address withdrawal in H-VPLS, plus PBB-VPLS extensions (B-MAC and I-SID list sub-TLVs) to flush only the MACs needing relearning.

VPLS.why: The document extends VPLS/H-VPLS MAC withdrawal procedures, including PBB-VPLS.
VPLS.quote: This document defines an enhancement to the MAC address withdraw procedure with an empty MAC list (RFC 4762); this enhancement enables a Provider Edge (PE) device to remove only the MAC addresses that need to be relearned.

rejected.why: LDP is the signalling substrate; the document adds a TLV but is about VPLS MAC flushing, so VPLS readers are the target.
Spoke/mesh PWs are used as context, but the document is not about pseudowire emulation itself.
Parent of VPLS, implied by the more specific tag.
MAC learning and PBB are discussed only as context for VPLS behaviour.

RFC7362.title: Latching: Hosted NAT Traversal (HNT) for Media in Real-Time Communication
RFC7362.summary: Informational RFC describing Hosted NAT Traversal (HNT) as performed by SBCs and other signaling intermediaries, focusing on media relaying and latching for SIP and XMPP, its limitations, and its security issues, and advising ICE/TURN instead.

NAT traversal.why: The whole document describes how SBCs traverse NATs for real-time media via latching and relaying, which is the NAT traversal subject in real-time communications.
NAT traversal.quote: HNT is a set of mechanisms, such as media relaying and latching, that such intermediaries use to enable other RTC devices behind NATs to communicate with each other.

SIP.why: The SBC behaviour, SDP rewriting in INVITE/200 and the latching call flow are described for SIP deployments, and SBC behaviour is a SIP deployment matter.
SIP.quote: The rest of this document focuses primarily on the use of HNT for SIP.

NAT.why: The document analyses NAT behaviour (endpoint-dependent filtering, CGNs) and how deployed intermediaries work around it, and its security section discusses CGN implications.
NAT.quote: this document uses the term "NAT" for devices that map any IPv4 or IPv6 address and transport port number to another IPv4 or IPv6 address and transport port number.

rejected.why: ICE is recommended as the alternative and its ice-mismatch interaction is discussed, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Only mentioned as an alternative relay mechanism, not described or specified.
SDP is the carrier of rewritten addresses and offer/answer is the substrate, not the subject.
RTP media is what gets latched, but the document is not about RTP itself.
SRTP is only mentioned in security considerations as a mitigation.
The XMPP/Jingle example is a secondary illustration of latching, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Session Border Controllers (SBC) / Hosted NAT Traversal
gaps.why: The document is about SBC behaviour and HNT/latching, for which the taxonomy has no specific tag. NAT traversal is the closest fit.

RFC7363.title: Self-Tuning Distributed Hash Table (DHT) for REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD)
RFC7363.summary: Extends RELOAD's mandatory chord-reload DHT algorithm with self-tuning, estimating overlay size, failure and join rates to adapt stabilization interval and routing table size, plus a new message extension and config element.

P2PSIP.why: The document specifies an extension to the RELOAD chord-reload topology plugin, with new Probe message extension and overlay configuration element. P2PSIP covers RELOAD.
P2PSIP.quote: This document describes how the default topology plugin of RELOAD can be extended to support self-tuning, that is, to adapt to changing operating conditions

rejected.why: Generic P2P overlays tag is broader; the more specific P2PSIP (RELOAD) tag fits, and ancestors are implied only within its own hierarchy.
Only referenced for the inactivity timer Tr used in failure detection.
STUN keepalives are used only as a substrate for failure detection.
SHA-1 is mentioned only in passing as Chord's base hash for identifiers.
The RELAX NG config element is minor apparatus, not the subject.
RELOAD is a SIP-related overlay, but this document does not deal with SIP itself.

gaps.name: Distributed Hash Table (DHT) / structured overlay algorithms (Chord)
gaps.why: The core subject is DHT stabilization and self-tuning of Chord; the taxonomy has only the generic P2P tag and P2PSIP, with no DHT-specific tag.

RFC7364.title: Problem Statement: Overlays for Network Virtualization
RFC7364.summary: Problem statement for the NVO3 WG describing multi-tenant data center network virtualization issues and making the case for overlay-based virtual networks, with NVE/NVA control-plane work areas.

overlay networks.why: The document is the problem statement for data-plane network virtualization overlays (NVO3), covering map-and-encap, NVE/NVA, and overlay design characteristics.
overlay networks.quote: Each virtual network instance is implemented as an overlay. The original packet is encapsulated by the first-hop network device, called a Network Virtualization Edge (NVE)

data center networking.why: The problems addressed (VM mobility, forwarding table sizes, address separation, cross-pod expansion) are data-center-scale networking issues.
data center networking.quote: This document describes issues associated with providing multi-tenancy in large data center networks

rejected.why: BGP/MPLS IP VPNs are only reviewed as related work in Section 5.1, not specified or analysed in depth.
E-VPN is mentioned briefly as related work only.
TRILL is only a short related-work subsection and not the subject.
LISP is cited as an example overlay and related work, not the subject.
No specific encapsulation is defined or discussed; the document says no new encapsulation is needed.
Mentioned only as the basis of SPB and as a possible NVA protocol.

gaps.name: Network virtualization / multi-tenancy (NVO3 architecture)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no general network virtualization tag; overlay networks and data center networking cover it only partly.

RFC7365.title: Framework for Data Center (DC) Network Virtualization
RFC7365.summary: Informational NVO3 framework defining a reference model (NVE, NVA, VNI, VAP, VN Context) and functional components for data center network virtualization overlays over an L3 underlay.

data center networking.why: The whole document is a framework for data center network virtualization, with DC architecture, reference models, NVE/NVA components, multihoming and VM mobility.
data center networking.quote: This document provides a framework for Data Center (DC) Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) tunnels.

overlay networks.why: Defines the data-plane network virtualization overlay model, tunnel encapsulation options, VN Context, and overlay/underlay issues. It does not specify a particular encapsulation such as VXLAN, so the parent tag fits.
overlay networks.quote: An overlay network is a layer of virtual network topology on top of the physical network.

rejected.why: L2/L3 VPN services (VPLS, EVPN, BGP/MPLS IP VPN) are only cited as analogues for L2 and L3 NVE service types, not specified or profiled.
GRE, L2TP and IPsec are listed only as possible encapsulation options; the document is not about generic tunneling.
Path MTU is discussed in one subsection as an overlay issue, with existing mechanisms referenced; not a main subject.
BUM handling with ingress replication versus underlay multicast trees is a trade-off discussion within the overlay topic, not multicast routing itself.
No specific encapsulation is defined or mentioned; the framework is encapsulation-agnostic.
Mentioned only as a possible tunneling option and for security considerations.

gaps.name: Network virtualization / NVO3 framework
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only an overlay-encapsulation tag and a data center tag, with no dedicated tag for NVO3 architecture or the NVE/NVA control-plane reference model.

RFC7366.title: Encrypt-then-MAC for Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC7366.summary: RFC 7366 defines a TLS/DTLS extension (encrypt_then_mac, type 22) that negotiates switching record protection from MAC-then-encrypt to encrypt-then-MAC, with processing rules and renegotiation handling.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS extension and the record-protection changes it triggers, including rehandshake rules. It covers both TLS and DTLS, so it belongs on the TLS page.
TLS.quote: The use of encrypt-then-MAC is negotiated via TLS/DTLS extensions as defined in TLS [2].

DTLS.why: The extension applies equally to DTLS. The document gives the DTLS record layout and DTLS-specific handling of a bad MAC.
DTLS.quote: The equivalent DTLS packet [4] is then:

RFC7367.title: Definition of Managed Objects for the Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Simplified Multicast Framework Relay Set Process
RFC7367.summary: Defines the SMF-MIB (and IANA-SMF-MIB) SNMP modules for configuring, monitoring and getting notifications from the Simplified Multicast Forwarding relay set process in MANET routers.

MIB.why: The document's main content is the SMF-MIB and IANA-SMF-MIB modules, with conformance groups, tables, and notifications.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

MANET.why: The managed process is SMF, the MANET multicast forwarding mechanism with relay set selection, DPD, and NHDP interaction.
MANET.quote: it describes objects for configuring aspects of the Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) process for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs).

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines a MIB module, which is covered by the MIB tag.
NHDP supplies neighbor information to SMF, and the MIB only configures TLV inclusion in NHDP messages; the document is not about NHDP itself.
The multicast forwarding here is MANET-specific SMF, already covered by the MANET tag; the document does not address general IP multicast routing.
OLSR is mentioned only as a user of the sMPR relay algorithm in a textual convention; the document is not about OLSR.

gaps.name: SMF (Simplified Multicast Forwarding)
gaps.why: There is no taxonomy tag for SMF itself, the MANET flooding and relay-set protocol that this MIB manages. The MANET tag is the closest fit.

RFC7368.title: IPv6 Home Networking Architecture Principles
RFC7368.summary: Informational architecture document defining principles for IPv6 home networks (homenet): multiple subnets, ULAs, prefix delegation, routing, security borders, naming and service discovery.

home networking.why: The whole document is the homenet IPv6 architecture, which is exactly what this tag covers.
home networking.quote: The goal of this document is to define a general architecture for IPv6-based home networking, describing the associated principles, considerations, and requirements.

multihoming.why: Multihoming topologies, source-based routing and source address selection are a substantial part of the architecture, including topology models B and C.
multihoming.quote: A homenet may be multihomed to multiple providers, as the network models above illustrate.

renumbering.why: The document discusses flash versus planned renumbering and requires that homenet protocols support rapid renumbering.
renumbering.quote: When an ISP does need to restructure, and in doing so renumber its customer homenets, 'flash' renumbering is likely to be imposed.

service discovery.why: Section 3.7 sets principles for naming and for zero-configuration service discovery across multiple subnets.
service discovery.quote: Thus, naming and service discovery must be supported in the homenet, and given the nature of typical home network users

rejected.why: The document is about IPv6 but its subject is home networking. The more specific home networking tag fits, and IPv6 is the substrate.
Naming is a section of the architecture, but the document does not define naming mechanisms. The service discovery tag covers that part.
DNS is mentioned as the likely homenet name service, but the document specifies no DNS behaviour.
NAT is discussed as something to avoid, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.
Border filtering and the 'Simple Security' model are covered in a subsection but are not the document's main subject.
mDNS is mentioned only in passing as one example of a zero-configuration protocol.

RFC7369.title: GMPLS RSVP-TE Extensions for Ethernet Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Configuration
RFC7369.summary: Defines Ethernet-specific OAM Configuration sub-TLVs and error codes for GMPLS RSVP-TE so that CFM/Y.1731 MEPs and MIPs are set up automatically when Ethernet LSPs (PBB-TE) are signalled.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signalling with new Ethernet OAM Configuration TLVs for Ethernet LSPs, so it belongs under GMPLS.
GMPLS.quote: specifies extensions of the GMPLS RSVP-TE protocol to support the setup of the associated Ethernet OAM entities of Ethernet LSPs

Ethernet.why: A substantial part covers Ethernet OAM (CFM, MEPs, MAID, CCM intervals, Y.1731 performance monitoring) and how to configure it, which suits the Ethernet OAM tag.
Ethernet.quote: Ethernet Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) defines an adjunct connectivity-monitoring OAM flow to check the liveliness of Ethernet networks

rejected.why: Signalling is done with RSVP-TE, but the document's focus is the GMPLS extension carrying OAM configuration, which GMPLS covers more specifically. RSVP-TE is the substrate.
OAM is the general subject, but the Ethernet tag is the more specific child and already covers Ethernet OAM, so the parent is implied.
PBB-TE and explicitly routed LSPs are background. The document does not address traffic engineering itself.
Proactive PM is only briefly discussed, in one short section on dual-ended loss measurement. It is not a substantial focus.

RFC7370.title: Updates to the IS-IS TLV Codepoints Registry
RFC7370.summary: RFC 7370 recommends editorial changes to the IANA IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry (merging sub-TLV registries for neighbor and prefix reachability TLVs) and sets guidance for Designated Experts on early codepoint allocation under Expert Review.

IS-IS.why: The document restructures and governs the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry, documenting the state of the IS-IS protocol's TLVs and sub-TLVs, so IS-IS readers would want it.
IS-IS.quote: the existing separate sub-TLV registries have been combined into a single registry entitled "Sub-TLVs for TLVs 135, 235, 236, and 237"

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document is guidance for Designated Experts on Expert Review allocations and early allocation, which is IANA registry policy.
IANA.quote: it also sets out new guidelines for Designated Experts to apply when reviewing allocations from the registry.

rejected.why: IS-IS is the more specific tag, so the general routing parent is implied and not listed.
The Designated Expert guidance concerns registry allocation, which IANA covers. It is not a general IETF process document.

RFC7371.title: Updates to the IPv6 Multicast Addressing Architecture
RFC7371.summary: RFC 7371 updates the IPv6 multicast addressing architecture by redefining reserved bits 17-20 as generic flag bits (ff2), requiring implementations to treat flags as separate bits, and amending RFC 3306 (unicast-prefix-based/SSM) and RFC 3956 (Embedded-RP) accordingly.

IPv6.why: The document amends the IPv6 multicast address format and updates RFC 4291, the IPv6 addressing architecture.
IPv6.quote: This document updates the IPv6 addressing architecture [RFC4291] by redefining reserved bits as generic flag bits

multicast.why: The whole document concerns the IPv6 multicast address flag/scope structure and Embedded-RP and SSM prefix handling; no more specific multicast child tag fits it as a whole.
multicast.quote: Bits 17-20 of a multicast address, where bit 1 is the most significant bit, are defined in [RFC3956] and [RFC3306] as reserved bits.

SSM.why: Update #2 to RFC 3306 clarifies that the SSM prefix range is not limited to ff3x::/32 once flags are treated as separate bits.
SSM.quote: ff3x::/32 is not the only allowed SSM prefix range.  For example, if the most significant flag bit in ff1 is set, then we would get the SSM range ffbx::/32.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the more specific tag for this IPv6 address-format change, and multicast covers the multicast addressing subject.
Embedded-RP is used with PIM-SM, but the document only changes address-format flag rules, not the PIM-SM protocol.

gaps.name: Embedded-RP (IPv6 multicast address with embedded rendezvous point)
gaps.why: RFC 3956 Embedded-RP is substantially amended (Updates #1-#4) but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC7372.title: Email Authentication Status Codes
RFC7372.summary: Registers new SMTP enhanced status codes (X.7.20–X.7.26) for rejecting or deferring mail due to DKIM, SPF, reverse-DNS, or multiple email authentication failures, and updates RFC 7208's recommended codes.

email authentication.why: The document defines status codes for reporting email authentication failures across DKIM, SPF, reverse DNS and multiple-mechanism cases, so it is about the general topic rather than one mechanism.
email authentication.quote: allow status codes to be returned to an email client to indicate that a message is being rejected or deferred specifically because of email authentication failures

SMTP.why: It registers new SMTP enhanced status codes and gives guidance on how servers should return them. Readers of SMTP would want it.
SMTP.quote: By the nature of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), only one enhanced status code can be returned for a given exchange between client and server.

rejected.why: The document only references DKIM verification outcomes to define failure codes. It does not specify or extend DKIM.
Two codes relate to SPF results and the document updates RFC 7208's recommended codes. Even so, SPF is one of several mechanisms covered, and the document does not specify SPF itself.
Reverse DNS checks appear only as one failure condition to be reported. The document says nothing about DNS protocol behaviour.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level apparatus for the status code registry. The document is not about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: SMTP Enhanced Status Codes
gaps.why: The document is mostly about registering enhanced mail system status codes (RFC 3463 and RFC 5248 registry). The taxonomy has no specific tag for them, and SMTP is the closest fit.

RFC7373.title: Textual Representation of IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Abstract Data Types
RFC7373.summary: Defines canonical UTF-8 textual encodings (with ABNF) for each IPFIX abstract data type so IPFIX Information Elements can be used in text-based protocols such as JSON or XML.

IPFIX.why: The whole document specifies how IPFIX Information Model abstract data types are represented in text, extending the IPFIX information model usage.
IPFIX.quote: defines UTF-8 representations for IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) abstract data types (ADTs) to support interoperable usage of the IPFIX Information Elements

rejected.why: JSON is only an example enclosing context (Appendix A); the document does not define a JSON format.
XML is mentioned only as an example enclosing context.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the encodings.
Timestamp encoding is based on RFC 3339 with modifications, but it is one small section of the document.
The string section defers to the Enclosing Context's Unicode rules and adds no Unicode-specific specification.
The ipv6Address encoding reuses existing RFC 4291/5952 text representation; it is not about IPv6.

RFC7374.title: Service Discovery Usage for REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD)
RFC7374.summary: Defines how the ReDiR service discovery mechanism is applied to RELOAD peer-to-peer overlays, including the REDIR Kind, data structure, registration and lookup procedures, a NODE-ID-MATCH access control policy and a configuration extension.

P2PSIP.why: The document is a RELOAD usage defining a new Kind, access control policy and configuration extension, so it belongs with P2PSIP/RELOAD.
P2PSIP.quote: This document defines how the Recursive Distributed Rendezvous (ReDiR) service discovery mechanism specified in [Redir] can be applied to RELOAD overlays.

service discovery.why: The core subject is a generic service discovery mechanism (ReDiR) with registration and lookup of service providers, so readers of service discovery would want it.
service discovery.quote: ReDiR implements service discovery by building a tree structure of the service providers that provide a particular service.

rejected.why: TURN server discovery is only one example namespace; the document is not about TURN.
The overlay is peer-to-peer, but the more specific P2PSIP tag covers RELOAD.
Different service discovery system; not related to this document.
The configuration extension uses XML/RELAX NG only as a mechanism, not as the subject.
SHA-1 is only mentioned as an example hash function.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and not the main subject.

gaps.name: Distributed hash tables / RELOAD overlay storage
gaps.why: The document is about a DHT-based tree structure stored via Store and Fetch, but the taxonomy has no DHT tag beyond P2PSIP.

RFC7375.title: Secure Telephone Identity Threat Model
RFC7375.summary: Informational threat model for the STIR working group that analyses actors, attacker capabilities and attack scenarios involving impersonation of calling party numbers in telephony (robocalling, voicemail hacking, TDoS).

STIR.why: This is the STIR working group's threat model for caller-ID authentication. It describes the attacks that STIR solutions must counter.
STIR.quote: the primary enabler of robocalling, vishing, swatting, and related attacks is the capability to impersonate a calling party number.

rejected.why: SIP is used in the attack scenarios, for example the From header in an INVITE. The document does not specify or extend it.
The scenarios cross IP-PSTN gateways, but the document is about calling-number impersonation. It does not cover interworking or gateway control.
WebRTC appears only as an example service from which an attacker can place a call.
Text-message spam is mentioned briefly as a related attack, but it is not a substantial focus.
The document is a security threat model and does not treat privacy threats.
H.323 appears only in one attack scenario as the network behind a gateway.

RFC7376.title: Problems with Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) Long-Term Authentication for Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN)
RFC7376.summary: Informational RFC listing security and practical problems with STUN long-term credential authentication as used for TURN, intended as input for designing stronger authentication mechanisms.

TURN.why: The document analyses the authentication of TURN messages and the problems of its long-term credential mechanism, so it belongs on the TURN page.
TURN.quote: This document discusses some of the security problems and practical problems with the current Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) authentication for Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) messages.

STUN.why: The problems analysed are in the STUN long-term credential mechanism (USERNAME, REALM, MESSAGE-INTEGRITY, HMAC-SHA1), so STUN readers would want this document.
STUN.quote: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) [RFC5389] specifies an authentication mechanism called the long-term credential mechanism.

rejected.why: ICE is mentioned only as the context in which TURN candidates are gathered. The document does not address it.
WebRTC appears as a use case and in the JavaScript credential-exposure problem, but the document is not about WebRTC.
HMAC-SHA1 is mentioned only as part of the STUN authentication being criticised, and the document does not address HMAC itself.
MD5 is cited as a weakness of the credential storage, but the document is not about MD5.
The generic authentication topic is implied by the more specific STUN and TURN tags and by the document's focus on those protocols.
Privacy leakage is one of several problems listed, but the document is not a privacy-considerations document.

RFC7377.title: IMAP4 Multimailbox SEARCH Extension
RFC7377.summary: Specifies the IMAP MULTISEARCH extension (ESEARCH command) allowing one command to search multiple mailboxes, with MAILBOX/TAG/UIDVALIDITY correlators in ESEARCH responses; moves RFC 6237 to Standards Track and updates RFC 4466.

IMAP.why: The document defines a new IMAP command (ESEARCH) and the MULTISEARCH capability, extending IMAP4 searching across mailboxes and updating the search-correlator in RFC 4466.
IMAP.quote: This extension allows a client to search multiple mailboxes with one command and includes MAILBOX and TAG fields in the ESEARCH response

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific child tag; the email parent is implied.
The document gives formal syntax in ABNF but is not about the notation; it is only used to specify the extension.
The only IANA action is updating a capability registry reference; boilerplate, not the subject.
