Searching message headers and bodies is a mailbox access operation, not about message format.

RFC7378.title: Trustworthy Location
RFC7378.summary: RFC 7378 analyses threats to the trustworthiness of location information conveyed in IP-based emergency calls (place shifting, time shifting, location theft). It reviews mitigations (signed location-by-value, location-by-reference, proxy-added location) and gives guidance for location trust assessment.

emergency services.why: The whole document concerns trustworthy location for emergency calling to PSAPs, hoax calls and swatting, within the Internet emergency services architecture.
emergency services.quote: This document describes threats to conveying location, particularly for emergency calls, and describes techniques that improve the reliability and security of location information.

geolocation.why: It covers location formats (PIDF-LO), conveyance, location-by-value and location-by-reference, trust assessment and privacy considerations, which is the geolocation topic.
geolocation.quote: Trustworthy Location" is defined as location information that can be attributed to a trusted source, has been protected against modification in transmit

rejected.why: SIP is the protocol that conveys location, but the document specifies nothing new about it. It only cites RFC 6442 for location conveyance.
HELD appears only as the way to obtain a location reference and as the dereferencing protocol (RFC 6753). The document does not specify or extend it.
PIDF-LO is the location object being protected. The document does not define or extend the format.
Caller-ID authentication is explicitly out of scope and is only cited as related work.
LoST is mentioned only as part of the infrastructure in the adversary model, which does not cover infrastructure attacks.
Privacy is a short closing section and not the main subject. The document is about trustworthiness and spoofing of location.

gaps.name: emergency services
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists 'emergency services' only as a topic parent of LoST and eCall, and no id with that name exists as a standalone choice. If it is selectable as a topic tag, it is the best fit. Otherwise this document has no tag for emergency calling.

RFC7379.title: Problem Statement and Goals for Active-Active Connection at the Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Edge
RFC7379.summary: Informational problem statement and goals for active-active connection of multiply-attached end stations/CEs to a TRILL campus, covering frame duplication, loopback, address flip-flop and unsynchronized state among edge RBridges.

TRILL.why: The whole document analyses problems and requirements for TRILL edge RBridges with active-active attachment, including Appointed Forwarder limitations and nickname learning.
TRILL.quote: Active-active connection at the TRILL edge is the extension of these characteristics to end stations that are multiply connected to a TRILL campus.

rejected.why: MC-LAG/802.1AX is the kind of LAALP the CE uses, but the document is about TRILL edge behaviour, not link aggregation itself; LAALP internals are declared out of scope.
TRILL's control plane runs over IS-IS and Hello packets are mentioned, but IS-IS is only a substrate here and is not specified or extended.
BFD is mentioned once as a way to speed failure detection; it is not a subject of the document.
End-station links are Ethernet and 802.1AE is cited only in Security Considerations; the document is not about Ethernet itself.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) / RBridges
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tech tag under routing, but I used it as 'TRILL' even though its id appears as 'TRILL' in the list; no other gap exists. Active-active edge connection (LAALP/MC-LAG at the TRILL edge) has no dedicated tag.

RFC7380.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for MPEG2 Transport Stream (TS) Program Specific Information (PSI) Decodability Statistics Metrics Reporting
RFC7380.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=32) reporting counts of MPEG2 TS PSI decodability errors (PAT, PMT, PID, CRC, CAT) per ETSI TR 101 290, plus its SDP signalling parameter and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR block type, extending RTCP reporting per RFC 3611, with block format and field semantics.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of MPEG2 TS decodability statistics metrics

IPTV.why: The metrics monitor MPEG2 TS quality in IPTV delivery over RTP, so IPTV service-monitoring readers would want it.
IPTV.quote: Unicast/multicast MPEG2 TS over RTP is widely deployed in IPTV systems.

rejected.why: SDP is only used to signal the new XR block via a small rtcp-xr attribute value; the document does not define SDP itself or offer/answer behaviour beyond referencing RFC 3611.
RTP is the transport carrying the MPEG2 TS being monitored; the document is about the RTCP report block, which is tagged more specifically.
The block reports performance metrics and cites the Performance Metrics Framework, but the document's specific subject is the RTCP XR block, so a direct topic tag is not warranted beyond that.
MPEG2 TS is a container format monitored by the block, but the document does not define codecs or containers.
A CRC error count is reported, but the document does not address CRC polynomials or error detection design.
IANA registrations are boilerplate-level in this document; the main body is not about registries.

gaps.name: MPEG2 Transport Stream PSI monitoring (ETSI TR 101 290)
gaps.why: The document is about decodability metrics for MPEG2 TS Program Specific Information (PAT, PMT, CAT, PID), but the taxonomy has no tag for MPEG2 TS or DVB measurement guidelines.

RFC7381.title: Enterprise IPv6 Deployment Guidelines
RFC7381.summary: Informational guidance for enterprise network architects on phasing IPv6 deployment (preparation, external, internal, IPv6-only), covering security, address planning, routing, and transition/translation choices.

IPv6.why: The whole document is deployment guidance for IPv6 in enterprise networks, covering addressing, security, ND, SLAAC/DHCPv6 and operations.
IPv6.quote: This document is intended as guidance for enterprise network architects and administrators in planning their IPv6 deployments.

IPv6 transition.why: A substantial part covers dual-stack, transition tunnels, NAT64/DNS64 and stateless translation, and IPv6-only operation as a transition strategy.
IPv6 transition.quote: The overall transition will take most networks from an IPv4-only environment to a dual-stack network environment and eventually an IPv6-only operating mode.

addressing.why: A dedicated section covers PI vs PA space, /48 site and /64 subnet assignment, ULAs and aggregation, which addressing readers would want.
addressing.quote: The most common problem encountered in IPv6 networking is in applying the same principles of conservation that are so important in IPv4.

rejected.why: Mentioned as a translation option in the IPv6-only and server sections, but the document does not specify or analyse it; it falls under IPv6 transition.
SLAAC vs DHCPv6 is weighed as a design choice, but only as one part of the address plan, not as a protocol the document covers.
Security sections exist, but they are IPv6-specific deployment security within the enterprise guidance and are not a general operational security treatment.
NDP threats such as RA-Guard and cache exhaustion are discussed, but only as part of the security discussion.
VRRPv3 is mentioned briefly as an option for first-hop redundancy; it is not a subject of the document.
IGP choice (OSPFv3, IS-IS, RIPng) is mentioned in one short paragraph and deferred to another draft.

RFC7382.title: Template for a Certification Practice Statement (CPS) for the Resource PKI (RPKI)
RFC7382.summary: Provides a template Certification Practice Statement (CPS) that organizations operating CAs in the Resource PKI (RPKI) fill in, complementing the RPKI Certificate Policy (RFC 6484) and following the RFC 3647 framework.

RPKI.why: The whole document is a CPS template for RPKI CAs, covering certificate issuance, repository publication, key management and audit practices within the RPKI. Readers of the RPKI page would want it.
RPKI.quote: This document contains a template to be used for creating a Certification Practice Statement (CPS) for an organization that is part of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI).

rejected.why: Certificates are X.509 and the document cites the RFC 6487 profile, but it defines no certificate profile itself and only refers to RFC 6487 in Section 7.
Mentioned only to state that OCSP and SCVP are not supported. The document is not about OCSP.
BGP ASNs appear only in the definition of INRs. The document does not cover BGP.
IANA appears only as the top of the INR distribution hierarchy. The document does not deal with IANA registries.

gaps.name: Certificate Policy / Certification Practice Statement (RFC 3647 framework)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CP/CPS documents. The only close fit is PKI, which sits above RPKI, so RPKI is the most specific tag available.

RFC7383.title: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Message Fragmentation
RFC7383.summary: RFC 7383 defines IKEv2 message fragmentation, splitting large IKEv2 messages into individually encrypted and authenticated Encrypted Fragment payloads so they avoid IP fragmentation, covering negotiation, fragment sizing, optional PMTU discovery and reassembly.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new Encrypted Fragment payload, a negotiation notification and reassembly rules. IKE is the protocol it specifies.
IKE.quote: The solution to the problem described in this document is to perform fragmentation of large messages by IKEv2 itself and replace them with a series of smaller messages.

PMTUD.why: A substantial subsection defines an optional, downward-searching PMTU discovery for IKE fragment sizes. Readers of PMTUD would want it.
PMTUD.quote: PMTU discovery in IKE follows recommendations given in Section 10.4 of [RFC4821] with some modifications

rejected.why: IPsec is the context, since IKE sets up IPsec SAs. The document specifies only IKE messaging, not ESP, AH or IPsec policy, and IKE is the more specific tag.
UDP is only the transport IKEv2 uses. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
IPv6 fragment filtering is mentioned as motivation and for MTU values. The document is not about IPv6.
NATs and CGNs that drop fragments are motivation only. The document does not specify NAT behaviour.
ICMP Packet Too Big messages are mentioned only as an optional input to PMTU discovery.

RFC7384.title: Security Requirements of Time Protocols in Packet Switched Networks
RFC7384.summary: Informational RFC defining security requirements for time synchronization protocols (PTP and NTP), including threat analysis, requirement levels, and interactions with external security mechanisms.

time synchronization.why: The whole document is about securing time and frequency distribution protocols, and it covers both PTP and NTP as general time synchronization.
time synchronization.quote: This document defines a set of security requirements for time protocols, focusing on the Precision Time Protocol (PTP) and the Network Time Protocol (NTP).

NTP.why: NTP is one of the two protocols analysed in depth for threats and requirements, including Autokey and the hybrid-mode behaviour of NTPv4.
NTP.quote: focuses on the two most common protocols: the Network Time Protocol [NTPv4] and the Precision Time Protocol (PTP) [IEEE1588]

PTP.why: PTP-specific requirements are given throughout: BMCA and Announce messages, transparent clocks, and the correctionField. PTP is the other protocol analysed in depth.
PTP.quote: PTP: The security mechanism MUST provide a means to prevent P2P TC spoofing.

rejected.why: IPsec and MACsec are discussed only as external mechanisms that can meet the requirements, or that affect timestamping. The document specifies no IPsec behaviour.
The document is about security, but the more specific time synchronization tags carry that. It is not general security guidance.
Authentication is a requirement area within the time protocol context, not a cross-protocol treatment in its own right.
The document sets requirements for protocol security mechanisms. It does not describe operational practices for securing infrastructure.
DoS attacks appear in the threat list, but the document does not address DDoS mitigation or signalling.

RFC7385.title: IANA Registry for P-Multicast Service Interface (PMSI) Tunnel Type Code Points
RFC7385.summary: Creates the IANA registry for BGP PMSI Tunnel Attribute tunnel types, which RFC 6514 defined without a registry, and updates RFC 6514 accordingly.

MVPN.why: The PMSI Tunnel attribute is part of multicast in BGP/MPLS VPNs (RFC 6514). The document creates the registry for its tunnel type code points and updates RFC 6514.
MVPN.quote: an optional transitive BGP attribute called the "P-Multicast Service Interface Tunnel (PMSI Tunnel) attribute" is specified.

rejected.why: BGP carries the attribute, but the document only creates a registry for one MVPN attribute's code points. It does not specify BGP protocol or policy.
It is an IANA registry creation, but the subject is the PMSI tunnel type registry for MVPN. The IANA text is the document's mechanism, not general IANA guidance.
The registry lists MPLS LSP tunnel types such as mLDP and RSVP-TE P2MP, but the document does not address MPLS itself.
PIM trees appear only as registry entries, not as a subject of the document.

RFC7386.title: JSON Merge Patch
RFC7386.summary: Defines the JSON merge patch format, its processing function, and the application/merge-patch+json media type, mainly for describing modifications via HTTP PATCH.

JSON.why: The document specifies a JSON-based patch format and the rules for applying it to JSON documents, so it belongs on the JSON page.
JSON.quote: This specification defines the JSON merge patch document format, processing rules, and associated MIME media type identifier.

media types.why: It registers application/merge-patch+json, and the media type is a defined part of the specification. The registration is part of what the document delivers, though not its main purpose.
media types.quote: This specification registers the following additional MIME media types:

HTTP.why: The intended use is HTTP PATCH, and the examples are PATCH requests. The document does not define HTTP itself, but readers of HTTP extensions would want this patch format.
HTTP.quote: The merge patch format is primarily intended for use with the HTTP PATCH method [RFC5789] as a means of describing a set of modifications

rejected.why: The document gives a patch body format for HTTP. It does not set conventions for building APIs on HTTP, such as problem details or rate limits.

RFC7387.title: A Framework for Ethernet Tree (E-Tree) Service over a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Network
RFC7387.summary: Informational framework describing an architecture reference model, use cases and gaps for emulating MEF E-Tree (root/leaf) Ethernet services over an MPLS network using L2VPN solutions such as VPLS and EVPN.

L2VPN.why: The document is an L2VPN framework for E-Tree service with Root/Leaf AC roles, and identifies L2VPN gaps.
L2VPN.quote: This document extends the existing IETF-specified Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) framework [RFC4664] to provide the emulation of E-Tree services over an MPLS network.

rejected.why: Discussed as a candidate solution and its gaps are noted, but the document does not specify or extend VPLS itself.
Mentioned as a candidate base for E-Tree extensions; not specified here, and it is only a work-in-progress reference.
MPLS is the substrate network; the document is about the Ethernet service emulated over it.
Ethernet is the service being emulated, but the tag covers IP over Ethernet and Ethernet OAM, which this document does not address.
Pseudowires are mentioned only as one possible forwarding mechanism.

gaps.name: E-Tree (MEF Ethernet Tree service)
gaps.why: The document is about rooted-multipoint Ethernet services, which have their own requirements and framework RFCs. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for E-Tree.

RFC7388.title: Definition of Managed Objects for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs)
RFC7388.summary: Defines LOWPAN-MIB, an SNMP MIB module of read-only counters for monitoring 6LoWPAN-layer processing (reassembly, header compression, fragmentation, mesh forwarding), globally and per interface.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a new SMIv2 MIB module (LOWPAN-MIB) with counters, groups and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: In particular it defines objects for managing IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs)

6LoWPAN.why: The managed objects count 6LoWPAN datagram handling: dispatch, mesh header, fragmentation/reassembly and header compression per RFC 4944. Readers of 6LoWPAN would want this monitoring module.
6LoWPAN.quote: The LOWPAN-MIB defined in this document fills a hole by providing monitoring and troubleshooting support for the 6LoWPAN layer.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines no SNMP protocol changes, and the MIB tag covers the content.
Mentioned only as an alternative binding and as a layer in the figure; not the subject.
IPv6 is the layer above 6LoWPAN, and the counters refer to IPv6 packets only as the payload; the document is about the adaptation layer.
Parent of MIB and SNMP; the MIB tag is more specific.
Header compression counters are included, but the document only counts compression events and does not specify compression itself.

RFC7389.title: Separation of Control and User Plane for Proxy Mobile IPv6
RFC7389.summary: Defines a new PMIPv6 mobility option (LMA User-Plane Address, type 59) letting an LMA advertise a user-plane address different from its control-plane address, completing the control/user plane split between MAG and LMA.

PMIPv6.why: The RFC extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with a new mobility option carried in PBU/PBA messages, plus a configuration variable and data structure fields. It is squarely about PMIPv6.
PMIPv6.quote: this document specifies a mobility option enabling an LMA to provide an alternate LMA address to be used for the bidirectional user-plane traffic between the MAG and LMA

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one possible CP-UP interface between LMA-CP and LMA-UP nodes. The document says that interface is out of scope.
Named as a user-plane tunnel type and in terminology. The document does not specify or extend GRE.
Only listed as a possible user-plane encapsulation, not specified or extended here.
Appears only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate. It restates the RFC 5213 requirements.
The Alternate Care-of Address option comes from RFC 6275 and is only referenced as background. The document extends PMIPv6, not Mobile IPv6.
The parent of PMIPv6, so it is implied. The specific child tag fits.

RFC7390.title: Group Communication for the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC7390.summary: Defines how CoAP is used for group communication over IP multicast, including group naming, a RESTful group membership configuration interface and media type, request/response suppression, congestion control, proxy behaviour, use cases and deployment guidance for 6LoWPAN/MLD/RPL/MPL networks.

CoAP.why: The document extends CoAP with group communication rules: token reuse, response suppression, proxy operation and a membership configuration interface.
CoAP.quote: This specification defines how CoAP should be used in a group communication context.

multicast.why: A substantial part covers IP multicast operation, scoping, and deployment with MLD, RPL multicast and MPL forwarding for CoAP groups.
multicast.quote: An approach for using CoAP on top of IP multicast is detailed based on existing CoAP functionality as well as new features

rejected.why: Used as a deployment mechanism for group joins and described in an appendix, but the document is not about MLD itself.
Discussed only as one multicast routing option for LLN deployments.
A target network type and source of guidelines, not the subject of the document.
JSON is only the encoding for the group configuration media type.
Mentioned as one way to discover group membership or ports, not specified here.
The document registers a media type, but this is IANA boilerplate rather than the main subject.

RFC7391.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Protocol Extensions
RFC7391.summary: RFC 7391 extends the ForCES protocol with a table range operation (TABLERANGE-TLV), an extended error-code mechanism (EXTENDEDRESULT-TLV) with an updated FEPO LFB version 1.2, and clarifies multi-part responses for large table dumps.

ForCES.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the ForCES protocol, updating RFC 5810 and RFC 7121, including new TLVs, error codes and the FEPO LFB update.
ForCES.quote: The ForCES protocol is extended with a table range operation and a new extension for error handling.

rejected.why: The FEPO LFB is defined in ForCES-specific XML LFB library format, not YANG.
XML is only the encoding of the LFB library definition in the appendix, not a subject of the document.
The SCTP-based TML is only mentioned in the terminology and references; nothing about it is specified here.
The IANA section registers new TLVs and result codes, but that is boilerplate for this document and its main body is not about IANA registries.

RFC7392.title: Explicit Path Routing for Dynamic Multi-Segment Pseudowires
RFC7392.summary: Specifies LDP extensions (a new L2 PW Address ER-Hop TLV and processing rules) so dynamic multi-segment pseudowires can be signalled along explicit strict or loose paths of S-PEs.

pseudowire.why: The whole document extends dynamic multi-segment pseudowire setup with explicit path routing through S-PEs, including a new ER-Hop type and next-hop selection procedures.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies the extensions and procedures required to enable dynamic MS-PWs to be established along explicit paths.

rejected.why: LDP is the signalling substrate. The document reuses RFC 3212 ER-TLVs and adds one TLV type for pseudowire use, so it is not about LDP itself.
Explicit routes resemble TE, but the document is about PW path placement and protection diversity, not TE of LSPs.
It reuses the ER-TLV and ER-Hop encoding from RFC 3212 (CR-LDP), but does not specify or extend CR-LDP LSP signalling.
MPLS is the underlying network, but the document does not address MPLS architecture or operations.
BGP-based mechanisms in RFC 7267 are mentioned only as an alternative for diverse paths.

RFC7393.title: Using the Port Control Protocol (PCP) to Update Dynamic DNS
RFC7393.summary: Informational document describing problems of dynamic DNS in address-sharing contexts (DS-Lite, NAT64) and sketching deployment solutions that use PCP to create mappings and detect external address/port changes to drive DDNS updates.

PCP.why: The solutions rely on PCP MAP requests to create explicit mappings and detect external IP/port changes; the document is a PCP deployment/use document.
PCP.quote: This document sketches deployment considerations based on the Port Control Protocol (PCP) [RFC6887].

DNS update.why: The central subject is keeping DNS records updated via DDNS clients and servers when addresses and ports change, mentioning RFC 2136/3007 dynamic updates.
DNS update.quote: Dynamic DNS (DDNS) is a widely deployed service to facilitate hosting servers

DS-Lite.why: DS-Lite (AFTR/B4/CGN) is the main reference deployment context and topology for the solutions.
DS-Lite.quote: This document describes some candidate solutions to resolve the aforementioned issues with a particular focus on DS-Lite.

CGN.why: Address sharing at a CGN is the problem source, and port forwarding on the CGN is needed for incoming connections.
CGN.quote: configure corresponding port forwarding on Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) [RFC6888] devices

rejected.why: Document concerns DDNS updates specifically; DNS update is the more specific tag, and plain DNS is only a substrate.
Mentioned as an example address-sharing context but the document focuses on DS-Lite.
Explicitly out of scope: solutions relying on DNS-SD are not considered.
HTTP 301 redirection is used as a mechanism in the examples but the document is not about HTTP.

RFC7394.title: Definition of Time to Live TLV for LSP-Ping Mechanisms
RFC7394.summary: Defines a new optional TTL TLV for MPLS LSP-Ping Echo Requests so the receiver can set the correct reply label TTL, enabling connectivity verification from any node on an MS-PW or bidirectional co-routed LSP.

MPLS.why: The document extends MPLS LSP-Ping (RFC 4379) with a new TLV and specifies how the MPLS Echo Reply label TTL is set. MPLS OAM is the home subject; no more specific MPLS child covers LSP-Ping.
MPLS.quote: LSP-Ping is a widely deployed Operation, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanism in MPLS networks.

pseudowire.why: MS-PW segment connectivity verification is a main use case, and the operation section is built around an MS-PW example.
pseudowire.quote: this mechanism is inadequate to verify connectivity of a segment of a Multi-Segment Pseudowire (MS-PW)

rejected.why: MPLS-TP appears only in the terminology list. The scope is bidirectional co-routed LSPs and MS-PWs generally.
OAM is the general subject, but the MPLS tag already covers this specific MPLS OAM mechanism. There is no OAM-specific technology tag to use instead.
There is a short traceroute-mode subsection, but it only describes how the TLV value is incremented. The document is not about traceroute tools.
The document does not use ICMP. The mechanism is MPLS Echo Request and Reply.

gaps.name: LSP-Ping / MPLS OAM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for LSP-Ping (RFC 4379) or MPLS data-plane failure detection. This RFC extends exactly that mechanism, so readers browsing it would look for a dedicated tag.

RFC7395.title: An Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) Subprotocol for WebSocket
RFC7395.summary: Defines the 'xmpp' WebSocket subprotocol: a binding of XMPP over WebSocket with new framing (<open/>/<close/> elements), stream handling, TLS via wss, and discovery of the WebSocket endpoint via host-meta.

XMPP.why: The document specifies an XMPP transport binding, including framing, stream open/close, restarts and stream management use. Readers of XMPP would expect it.
XMPP.quote: This document defines a binding for the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) over a WebSocket transport layer.

WebSocket.why: Defines a new WebSocket subprotocol, including its handshake, message types and registration in the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry, so WebSocket readers need it.
WebSocket.quote: During the WebSocket handshake, the client MUST include the value 'xmpp' in the list of protocols for the 'Sec-WebSocket-Protocol' header.

rejected.why: TLS is only used at the WebSocket layer via wss; the document states it cannot be used at the XMPP layer and defines nothing new about TLS.
HTTP is only the substrate for the WebSocket handshake and for host-meta retrieval; BOSH is mentioned only as a comparison.
Web Linking is used for the host-meta link relation in discovery, but the document does not define or extend it.
DNS SRV is the TCP-binding discovery method this document replaces; it is not itself addressed.
XML is the encoding used, with a framing namespace and schema. The document is not about XML usage in general.
SASL appears only in the stream restart example and is not addressed in its own right.

RFC7396.title: JSON Merge Patch
RFC7396.summary: Defines the JSON Merge Patch format (application/merge-patch+json), its processing algorithm, and media type registration, intended for use with HTTP PATCH to describe modifications to JSON resources.

JSON.why: The document specifies a new JSON-based patch format and its processing rules for JSON documents, so it belongs under JSON.
JSON.quote: This specification defines the JSON merge patch document format, processing rules, and associated MIME media type identifier.

HTTP.why: The format is designed for HTTP PATCH, with examples of PATCH requests; HTTP readers would want it, though the document does not extend HTTP itself.
HTTP.quote: The merge patch format is primarily intended for use with the HTTP PATCH method [RFC5789] as a means of describing a set of modifications

media types.why: It registers the application/merge-patch+json media type, a substantive part of the deliverable.
media types.quote: This specification registers the following additional MIME media types:

rejected.why: It defines a payload format for PATCH rather than general conventions for building HTTP APIs.
The document only registers a media type and does not address MIME body structure or encodings; media types is the closer fit.

RFC7397.title: Report from the Smart Object Security Workshop
RFC7397.summary: Report on the 2012 Smart Object Security Workshop in Paris, summarizing discussions on requirements, implementation experience, authorization, and credential provisioning for constrained smart objects, with conclusions for the IETF.

IoT.why: The whole report concerns security for smart objects (constrained IoT devices): use cases, constraints, implementation experience and provisioning.
IoT.quote: The main goal of the workshop was to allow participants to share their thoughts about the ability to utilize existing and widely deployed security mechanisms for smart objects.

workshop reports.why: It is a workshop report summarizing discussions and giving recommendations to the IETF community.
workshop reports.quote: This document provides a summary of a workshop on 'Smart Object Security' that took place in Paris on March 23, 2012.

authorization.why: A full section covers authorization models (ACLs vs. capability/trait-based), OAuth, AAA, and policy distribution to smart objects.
authorization.quote: The discussion slot on authorization was meant to provide an idea of what kind of authorization decisions are common in smart object networks.

key management.why: Section 3.4 covers credential provisioning, imprinting, pairing and ownership transfer, i.e., key establishment and provisioning for devices.
key management.quote: When a smart object is to be introduced into an environment, like a home or an enterprise network, it usually has to be provisioned with some credentials first.

rejected.why: DTLS and CoAP-over-DTLS implementations are discussed as experience, but the document is not about specifying or profiling DTLS; DICE is only mentioned as follow-up work.
OAuth is discussed as one example of capability-based authorization, not the subject of the document.
ACE is mentioned only as a follow-up working group that had just started.
CoAP appears only as the application protocol in one implementation talk.
TLS with raw public keys/PSK is mentioned in implementation experience talks, but the report is not about TLS itself.
The general security topic is implied by narrower choices; the document's security discussion is specific to IoT and authorization/provisioning.

RFC7398.title: A Reference Path and Measurement Points for Large-Scale Measurement of Broadband Performance
RFC7398.summary: Defines a reference path and a numbering scheme for measurement points (mpXnn) along it, so that the scope of large-scale broadband performance measurements (LMAP) can be described unambiguously, with examples for 3G, DSL and CGN access.

LMAP.why: The whole document defines the reference path and measurement points for LMAP platforms, so the LMAP page is the natural home for it.
LMAP.quote: This document defines a reference path for Large-scale Measurement of Broadband Access Performance (LMAP) and measurement points for commonly used performance metrics.

rejected.why: LMAP is a child of performance measurement and already implies it. The document is about measurement point location, not a metric or a method.
Carrier-Grade NAT appears only as an example component on the path (mp150). The document says nothing about how CGN works.
NAT devices are mentioned only as places where measurement points may sit. NAT behaviour is not discussed.
DSL access is one worked example of mapping the reference path. The document is not about DSL networks.
3G cellular access is one example mapping. The document is not about cellular networks.
WiFi appears only as an example of a shared, unmanaged sub-path. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC7399.title: Unanswered Questions in the Path Computation Element Architecture
RFC7399.summary: Informational RFC that raises and discusses open architectural questions about the Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture, including TED building, PCE discovery, hierarchical PCE, stateful/active PCE, VNTM, scheduling, policy, and SDN.

PCE.why: The whole document discusses the PCE architecture, its H-PCE and VNTM extensions, and stateful/active PCE questions. Readers of the PCE subject would want it.
PCE.quote: The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture is set out in RFC 4655.

rejected.why: GMPLS is the network context for the PCE discussion, not the subject itself.
BGP-LS is mentioned only as one way to feed the TED. The document does not specify or analyse BGP.
Section 25 is a short discussion of PCE's role in SDN. It is not a substantial part of the document.
RSVP-TE is the signalling substrate mentioned in passing, not the subject.
Policy is covered in one section and only in a PCE context.
PCE is the more specific tag under traffic engineering.

RFC7400.title: 6LoWPAN-GHC: Generic Header Compression for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs)
RFC7400.summary: RFC 7400 specifies 6LoWPAN-GHC, an LZ77-style bytecode generic header compression scheme plugged into 6LoWPAN-HC as new NHC formats for UDP, ICMPv6 and extension headers, plus a 6CIO Neighbor Discovery option to signal GHC capability.

6LoWPAN.why: The document extends 6LoWPAN header compression (RFC 6282) with generic header compression and defines a 6LoWPAN-specific ND capability option, so it belongs under 6LoWPAN.
6LoWPAN.quote: The purpose of the present contribution is to plug into [RFC6282] as is, using its Next Header Compression (NHC) concept.

header compression.why: It defines a new generic header compression bytecode. No child tag (ROHC, CRTP, IPHC) fits, since this is 6LoWPAN-specific, so the parent topic applies.
header compression.quote: enables the compression of generic headers and header-like payloads, without a need to define a new header compression scheme for each such new header

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a contrast; GHC does not use ROHC profiles.
The 6CIO ND option is a supporting mechanism for capability signalling, not the document's main subject.
Referenced only as a heavier general compression scheme that GHC is contrasted with.
Lossless data compression formats topic; GHC is a header compression scheme and the header compression tag fits better.
Appears only in examples of compressed payloads.
RPL messages are only examples being compressed.

RFC7401.title: Host Identity Protocol Version 2 (HIPv2)
RFC7401.summary: RFC 7401 specifies HIPv2, the Host Identity Protocol base exchange, packet formats, state machine and processing rules for establishing IP-layer associations using public-key host identities, with crypto agility and DoS resistance.

HIP.why: The whole document defines the HIP base exchange, parameters, packets, state machine and processing.
HIP.quote: This document specifies the details of the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

rejected.why: ESP is the data transport format, specified in RFC 7402; this document only negotiates it.
Mentioned only for comparison; HIP is not IKE.
ESP is specified in a separate document; used only as the mandatory transport format.
DNS lookups of HITs are only mentioned and defined in a separate extension document.
ECDSA/ECDH are added as algorithm choices, but the document is not about elliptic-curve cryptography itself.
ICMP is used for error replies only.

gaps.name: Host Identity Protocol (HIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists HIP, but this tag id was not found among the provided ids, so I could not verify it. The only HIP tag shown is the id HIP under internet layer. If it is exact, fine.

RFC7402.title: Using the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) Transport Format with the Host Identity Protocol (HIP)
RFC7402.summary: Specifies how ESP is used with the Host Identity Protocol to protect user data, including HIP parameters (ESP_INFO, ESP_TRANSFORM) for ESP SA setup and rekeying, SPI semantics, cipher suites, and BEET mode; obsoletes RFC 5202.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with new parameters and UPDATE handling for ESP SAs, so it belongs on the HIP page.
HIP.quote: This document specifies how ESP is used with HIP to carry actual user data.

ESP.why: It profiles ESP for HIP: SPI semantics, supported cipher suites, sequence numbers, and BEET mode, which is a new ESP mode defined in the appendix.
ESP.quote: In this document, we specify the use of ESP for protecting user data traffic after the HIP base exchange.

rejected.why: ESP is the specific child tag that applies. The IPsec coexistence discussion is only an implementation consideration.
IKE is mentioned only as an alternative way to establish ESP SAs. HIP replaces it here.
AES suites are only listed as ESP transforms. The document does not specify AES itself.
HMAC is used only inside the suite definitions and is not the subject of the document.
BEET mode is an ESP mode, not generic IP tunnelling.
The keying material comes from the HIP base exchange and is drawn from KEYMAT. Key management is not the focus.

RFC7403.title: A Media-Based Traceroute Function for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC7403.summary: Defines a SIP traceroute-style mechanism that combines Max-Forwards starting at 0 with media-loopback (RFC 6849) test calls so a UA can test the media path to each successive B2BUA.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP behaviour: B2BUAs answer INVITEs with Max-Forwards 0 and add a Reason 483 header. It is a SIP extension for troubleshooting.
SIP.quote: This document describes a means of performing hop-by-hop traceroute-style test calls using the media-loopback mechanism to test the media path

traceroute.why: The core purpose is a hop-by-hop traceroute function, here for the SIP media path, and readers of the traceroute subject would want it.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute: a mechanism to trace a path of hops from an originator to a destination.

rejected.why: SDP carries the media-loopback attributes defined in RFC 6849. This document defines nothing new in SDP.
The looped-back media is RTP, but the document adds nothing about RTP itself.
The mechanism is a troubleshooting tool, but the specific traceroute tag fits better than the general OAM topic.
ICMP and TTL are mentioned only as an analogy in the terminology section.

gaps.name: media loopback
gaps.why: The document builds on SDP/RTP media-loopback test sessions (RFC 6849), but the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC7404.title: Using Only Link-Local Addressing inside an IPv6 Network
RFC7404.summary: Informational RFC discussing the advantages and caveats of using only link-local addresses on router infrastructure links in IPv6 networks, including effects on ping, traceroute, management tools, RSVP-TE and IXPs.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 addressing practice: link-local addresses on infrastructure links, with deployment trade-offs.
IPv6.quote: In an IPv6 network, it is possible to use only link-local addresses on infrastructure links between routers.

operational security.why: A major motivation is reducing router attack surface (infrastructure ACLs, IXP protection). It is an operator-facing practice discussion.
operational security.quote: Every routable address on a router constitutes a potential attack point; a remote attacker can send traffic to that address

rejected.why: The IPv6 tag is more specific and already covers the IPv6 addressing subject, so the parent is not tagged.
BGP is mentioned only as one control-plane protocol that works with link-local addresses, and the document does not specify or analyse it.
RSVP-TE is noted only as a caveat, since strict-path LSPs cannot use link-local addresses. That is a minor point.
Traceroute behaviour is discussed as a caveat, but the document is not about the tool itself.
ICMPv6 error source addresses are discussed only as a side effect, and the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
It is mentioned only to note that it is unaffected by this approach.

RFC7405.title: Case-Sensitive String Support in ABNF
RFC7405.summary: RFC 7405 updates ABNF (RFC 5234) by adding %s and %i prefixes so US-ASCII string literals can be matched case-sensitively or case-insensitively.

ABNF.why: The whole document is a normative extension of the ABNF notation, adding case-sensitive string literals and updating the char-val grammar.
ABNF.quote: This document extends ABNF to have two different types of US-ASCII string literals.

rejected.why: US-ASCII is only the character set of the string literals. The document is about ABNF syntax, not about ASCII itself.
The document does not register or discuss character sets. It only notes that literal strings use US-ASCII.

RFC7406.title: Extensions to the Emergency Services Architecture for Dealing With Unauthenticated and Unauthorized Devices
RFC7406.summary: Informational ECRIT document extending the IETF emergency services architecture to cover emergency callers with no network access authentication (NAA), no ASP (NASP), or a zero-balance ASP (ZBP), with end-host/ISP/ESRP profiles and link-layer/EAP considerations.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about emergency calling architecture for unauthenticated/unauthorized callers, including NAA, NASP and ZBP procedures and end-host, ISP and ESRP profiles.
emergency services.quote: describes an extension for the base IETF emergency services architecture to address cases where an emergency caller is not authenticated

LoST.why: LoST lookup is a core step in the NASP profile, and ISP-provided LoST servers are used for access control in the security discussion.
LoST.quote: The end host MUST discover a LoST server [RFC5222] using DHCP [RFC5223] unless a LoST server has been provisioned using other means.

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling used for the emergency call but the document only references RFC 6881 requirements; it adds nothing new about SIP.
EAP and EAP-TLS are discussed in section 6.2 as options for securing NAA network attachment, but only as informative considerations, not as the document's subject.
DHCP is used for configuration and LoST discovery only as a substrate.
Location acquisition is referenced from RFC 6881 and PIDF-LO but is not the document's focus.
PIDF-LO is only required for attaching location, not specified or extended here.
WiMAX and 802.11 emergency indications are mentioned as examples of link-layer mechanisms, not the subject.

RFC7407.title: A YANG Data Model for SNMP Configuration
RFC7407.summary: Defines YANG modules and submodules for configuring SNMP engines (engine, targets, notifications, proxy, community, USM, VACM, TSM, TLS and SSH transport models), plus a YANG module mapping X.509 certificates to names.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a set of YANG modules and submodules modelling SNMP configuration.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG [RFC6020] data model for the configuration of SNMP engines.

SNMP.why: The model covers SNMP engine, target, notification, proxy, community, USM, VACM and transport-model configuration, mapped from the SNMP MIBs.
SNMP.quote: The configuration model is consistent with the MIB modules defined in [RFC3411], [RFC3412], [RFC3413], [RFC3414]

NETCONF.why: The design targets NETCONF-based configuration, and Section 3 discusses mapping NETCONF datastores (running, candidate, startup) onto SNMP tables.
NETCONF.quote: SNMP runs in read-only mode and the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) is used to configure the SNMP agent.

rejected.why: TLS and DTLS appear only as SNMP transport models whose endpoints and certificate mapping are configured. The document defines no new TLS mechanism.
SSH is configured only as an SNMP transport model, and it is the NETCONF substrate. The document says nothing new about SSH.
The cert-to-name module maps certificates to SNMP security names for TLSTM. It does not profile X.509 certificates.
The document translates existing MIB objects into YANG rather than defining new MIB modules.
VACM is configured, but only as part of the SNMP configuration model, so the SNMP tag covers it.

RFC7408.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Model Extension
RFC7408.summary: RFC 7408 extends the ForCES forwarding element model (RFC 5812) XML schema with complex metadata types, default values, struct access types, a new eventBecomesEqualTo condition, LFB properties, and versioned LFB inheritance.

ForCES.why: The whole document specifies extensions and updates to the ForCES FE model, including LFB properties, events and inheritance.
ForCES.quote: This memo extends the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) model defined in RFC 5812

rejected.why: XML Schema is the notation used to define the model, but the document is about the ForCES model, not XML usage in general.
Considered as a data-modelling language, but the document uses an XML schema and has nothing to do with YANG.
OpenFlow is mentioned only as a use case for complex metadata, not as a subject of the document.
The IANA section only registers an XML namespace and is boilerplate.

RFC7409.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Packet Parallelization
RFC7409.summary: Experimental RFC defining ForCES LFB library for modelling packet parallelization: Splitter, Merger and CoreParallelization LFBs, plus parallelization metadata, using the ForCES model and protocol.

ForCES.why: The document defines new ForCES LFB classes (Splitter, Merger, CoreParallelization), metadata and an XML LFB library extending the ForCES model.
ForCES.quote: This document describes how Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) can model a network device's parallelization datapath using constructs defined by the ForCES model

rejected.why: The models are written in ForCES LFB library XML, not YANG.
XML is only the encoding for the LFB library definition, not the subject.
ForCES is a control/forwarding separation approach, but the document is specifically about the ForCES tech, which is already tagged.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here, just LFB class IDs and a metadata ID.

RFC7410.title: A Property Types Registry for the Authentication-Results Header Field
RFC7410.summary: Updates RFC 7001 by redefining the Authentication-Results "ptype" as an open keyword and creating an IANA "Email Authentication Property Types" registry with the four initial values (body, header, policy, smtp).

email authentication.why: The document extends the Authentication-Results header field used to report email authentication results and creates a registry for its property types. No specific child (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) is the subject, so the parent topic fits.
email authentication.quote: creating a registry for property types in the Authentication-Results header field, used in email authentication work

message format.why: It changes the ABNF of an Internet message header field (Authentication-Results), so readers of message header syntax would want it.
message format.quote: ptype = Keyword

rejected.why: SMTP is only referenced for the Keyword ABNF token and as a source of properties, and the document does not specify or extend it.
The registry is the mechanism for the email-authentication extension. The document is not about IANA guidance or stewardship in general.
ABNF is only the notation used for the small ptype update.
The more specific email authentication tag already covers it.

RFC7411.title: Multicast Listener Extensions for Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) and Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Fast Handovers
RFC7411.summary: Experimental RFC extending Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers (FMIPv6) and Proxy Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers (PFMIPv6) with multicast listener context transfer between access routers, via a new PrRtAdv M bit and new Multicast Mobility and Acknowledgement options.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends and updates RFC 5568 (FMIPv6) with new mobility options and a PrRtAdv indicator bit, so it is about Mobile IPv6 fast handovers.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document specifies extension of the Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers (FMIPv6) and the Fast Handovers for Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PFMIPv6) protocols to include multicast traffic management

PMIPv6.why: Half of the specification (Sections 3.3, 4.2) covers PFMIPv6 operations by MAGs, so PMIPv6 network-based mobility is a substantial subject.
PMIPv6.quote: Fast Handovers for Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PFMIPv6) [RFC5949] improve the performance of handovers for unicast communication.

multicast.why: The core contribution is multicast listener state transfer, group joins and forwarding via tunnels, and MLD/IGMP compatibility. No more specific multicast tag fits, since MLD and IGMP are used rather than specified.
multicast.quote: multicast context transfer shall be transparently included in unicast fast handover operations

rejected.why: MLD is used to carry listener state and for querying, but the document does not specify or extend MLD.
IGMP is used for IPv4 listener state, but the document does not specify or extend IGMP.
IPv6 is the substrate for the mobility protocols, not the subject of the document.
PAR-NAR tunnels are inherited from the unicast fast handover protocols and are not defined here.
The two new mobility option allocations are boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the main subject.
IPTV is only mentioned as a motivating use case.

RFC7412.title: Requirements for MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Shared Mesh Protection
RFC7412.summary: Informational requirements document setting out network objectives for data-plane-coordinated Shared Mesh Protection (SMP) of MPLS-TP paths, covering resource sharing, preemption, notification, reversion, switching time and timers.

MPLS-TP.why: The whole document specifies requirements for shared mesh protection (survivability) of MPLS-TP paths, so readers of the MPLS-TP subject would expect it.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document provides requirements for any mechanism that would be used to implement SMP for MPLS-TP data paths, in networks that delegate protection switch coordination to the data plane.

rejected.why: GMPLS is mentioned only as the control-plane alternative; the document explicitly addresses networks without control-plane support.
The parent is implied by MPLS-TP, so it is not listed separately.
OAM is mentioned only in passing as the source of failure detection and reporting; the document is not about OAM mechanisms.
Protection and preemption are discussed, but the document is not about traffic engineering of LSPs. The MPLS-TP tag fits better.

gaps.name: network survivability / protection switching
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for protection and restoration of paths. This is the document's core subject and is only partly covered by MPLS-TP.

RFC7413.title: TCP Fast Open
RFC7413.summary: Specifies TCP Fast Open, an experimental TCP extension that carries data in SYN and SYN-ACK packets using a server-generated Fast Open cookie (TCP option 34) to save a round trip, with security analysis, applicability guidance and socket API changes.

TCP.why: The document defines a new TCP option and handshake behaviour, extending the TCP protocol itself.
TCP.quote: TCP Fast Open (TFO) is an experimental update to TCP that enables data to be exchanged safely during TCP's connection handshake.

rejected.why: Web clients and servers are used as the motivating example, but the document specifies nothing about HTTP.
Mentioned only as an example of sending a client_hello in the SYN. TLS is not what the document is about.
Discussed briefly as an impact area (initial window, SYN-ACK loss), but it is not a substantial subject of the document.
Appendix A gives example socket API changes (MSG_FASTOPEN, TCP_FASTOPEN). It is a small, non-normative part of the document.
The security section covers SYN flood and reflection attacks against TFO, but only as part of TFO's own design. It is not a DDoS mitigation specification.
NAT and CGN effects on cookies appear only as brief experimentation notes.

RFC7414.title: A Roadmap for Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Specification Documents
RFC7414.summary: RFC 7414 is an informational roadmap that organizes and summarizes the TCP-related RFCs: core specs, recommended enhancements, experimental extensions, historic ones, and supporting documents.

TCP.why: The whole document is a guide to the TCP specifications and extensions, so readers of the TCP subject page would want it.
TCP.quote: This document contains a roadmap to the Request for Comments (RFC) documents relating to the Internet's Transmission Control Protocol (TCP).

MPTCP.why: It has a dedicated section summarizing the MPTCP documents (RFC 6356, 6824) and references MPTCP architecture, threat and API RFCs.
MPTCP.quote: MultiPath TCP (MPTCP) is an ongoing effort within the IETF that allows a TCP connection to simultaneously use multiple IP addresses

congestion control.why: Congestion control extensions, experimental algorithms, and guidance on evaluating them make up a large share of the roadmap.
congestion control.quote: Two of the most important aspects of TCP are its congestion control and loss recovery features.

rejected.why: Covered only in a short subsection summarizing RFCs 1191, 1981 and 4821, which is not enough to make the roadmap about it.
Only two RFCs (1144 and 6846) are listed in a short subsection.
The MIB modules section is a small part of the document and the focus is TCP itself.
ECN RFCs are summarized in passing as TCP congestion control extensions, not as a main subject.
Section 5 on TCP parameters at IANA is brief and boilerplate-like.
It is a roadmap of RFCs on one protocol, not about the RFC series format or publication.

RFC7415.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Rate Control
RFC7415.summary: RFC 7415 defines a rate-based (leaky bucket) overload control algorithm for SIP, as an optional alternative to the default loss-based algorithm in RFC 7339, signalled via the Via header "oc" parameters.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP overload control, adding a "rate" algorithm token to the Via header oc-algo parameter and specifying client and server behaviour.
SIP.quote: this document proposes an alternate overload control scheme: the rate-based overload control scheme.

congestion control.why: The document specifies a rate-based throttling algorithm (leaky bucket) that prevents congestion collapse at overloaded servers. Readers on overload and congestion control would want it.
congestion control.quote: SIP networks must be able to handle traffic overloads gracefully, maintaining transaction throughput by preventing congestion collapse.

rejected.why: Request prioritization is only a throttling detail within overload control. The document does not address QoS architectures or signalling.
TLS appears only in the example Via lines as the transport, and the document says nothing about it.
The document concerns SIP signalling overload, not congestion control for real-time media.

gaps.name: SIP overload control
gaps.why: The document is about overload control for SIP signalling servers, including the RFC 7339 framework. The taxonomy has no tag for this, so SIP plus congestion control is the closest fit.

RFC7416.title: A Security Threat Analysis for the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPLs)
RFC7416.summary: Informational threat analysis for RPL (the IPv6 routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks), using the ISO 7498-2 model to enumerate threats and attacks and the countermeasures and RPL security features that address them.

RPL.why: The document analyses threats, attacks, countermeasures and security features of RPL. RPL readers would look for it.
RPL.quote: This document presents a security threat analysis for the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPLs).

routing security.why: Much of the document covers general routing attacks (sinkhole, wormhole, selective forwarding, Sybil, replay, Byzantine) and their countermeasures, drawing on RFC 4593.
routing security.quote: Routing security, in essence, ensures that the routing protocol operates correctly.

rejected.why: LLNs are the context, but RPL is the more specific tag and already sits under IoT, so IoT is implied.
It is not discussed. Link-layer security for LLNs is mentioned only in passing.
EAP-TLS and PANA are only cited as examples of key management in ZigBee IP.
It is mentioned only as an L2 admission control example, not as a subject of the document.
Section 8.4 is brief and says key management is not directly an RPL requirement. It is not a substantial part of the document.
AES-128 CCM is cited as the mandatory-to-implement mode in RFC 6550, but the document is not about the cipher.

RFC7417.title: Extensions to Generic Aggregate RSVP for IPv4 and IPv6 Reservations over Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) Domains
RFC7417.summary: Experimental RFC extending Generic Aggregate RSVP (RFC 4860) with new PCN objects so PCN-ingress and PCN-egress nodes can exchange PCN-sent-rate reports for the Controlled Load and Single Marking edge behaviors over a Diffserv domain.

RSVP.why: The document defines RSVP aggregation procedures and new RSVP objects (class 248 PCN, four C-Types) carried in Aggregate Path/Resv messages.
RSVP.quote: this document specifies extensions to Generic Aggregate RSVP [RFC4860] for support of the PCN Controlled Load (CL) and Single Marking (SM) edge behaviors

PCN.why: The document is about signalling PCN-sent-rate between PCN boundary nodes to support PCN admission control and flow termination.
PCN.quote: The main objective of this document is to specify the signaling protocol that can be used within a PCN-domain to carry reports from a PCN-ingress-node to a PCN Decision Point

rejected.why: PCN operates over a Diffserv domain, which is the substrate. The document does not specify Diffserv itself.
Intserv and Controlled Load are background in the motivation section. The document is not about Intserv.
The IPv4 and IPv6 variants of the objects only carry addresses. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
PCN is a pre-congestion admission control mechanism, but the document defines the signalling extensions and not a congestion control algorithm. The more specific PCN tag fits better.
The PCN-BA is distinguished partly by the ECN field. ECN is only a marking substrate here.
This is the parent of RSVP, Diffserv and Intserv. A more specific child tag is chosen.

gaps.name: PCN (Pre-Congestion Notification)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a PCN tag only under congestion control. I used it above, but no id for PCN appears in the listed taxonomy under QoS. Confirm this matches the intended id.

gaps.name: RSVP aggregation
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists RSVP under QoS, so this is covered if RSVP exists. It is not shown as a distinct tag.

RFC7418.title: An IRTF Primer for IETF Participants
RFC7418.summary: An informational IRTF-stream guide explaining to IETF participants how proposing and running an IRTF research group differs from chartering and running an IETF working group.

IETF process.why: The document is about chartering and process expectations in the IRTF versus IETF WGs (scope, deliverables, consensus, completion). This is organisational process guidance, which fits IETF process most closely.
IETF process.quote: things for Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) participants to consider when bringing proposals for new research groups (RGs) into the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF)

rejected.why: The parent topic fits, but IETF process is the more specific child that matches the document.
IPR disclosure is mentioned in a single sentence in Section 2.5, which is not a substantial part of the document.
A workshop is suggested only as one way to prepare an RG proposal. The document is not a report from a workshop.
The document is about the IRTF and its research groups, not the format, style or publication of RFCs.

gaps.name: IRTF (Internet Research Task Force) research groups
gaps.why: The document is about IRTF research group chartering and operation. The taxonomy has no IRTF-specific tag, so IETF process is only an approximate fit.

RFC7419.title: Common Interval Support in Bidirectional Forwarding Detection
RFC7419.summary: RFC 7419 updates RFC 5880 by defining a set of Common Interval values (3.3 ms, 10 ms, 20 ms, 50 ms, 100 ms, 1 s) that BFD implementations should support so peers with limited hardware timers can negotiate a shared interval.

BFD.why: The whole document specifies interval support and timer negotiation behaviour for BFD sessions, updating RFC 5880.
BFD.quote: This document defines the set of Common Interval values to be: 3.3 msec, 10 msec, 20 msec, 50 msec, 100 msec, and 1 sec.

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is mentioned only as a motivation for the 3.3 ms interval; the document is not about MPLS-TP.
Timer intervals and detection times are BFD protocol parameters, not network performance measurement.
BFD is a failure-detection mechanism, but the BFD tag is more specific and already covers it.

RFC7420.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Management Information Base (MIB) Module
RFC7420.summary: Defines the PCE-PCEP-MIB SMIv2 module with read-only entity, peer and session tables and notifications for monitoring PCEP between PCCs and PCEs.

MIB.why: The document's main content is a MIB module (SMIv2) with tables, notifications and conformance groups, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the MIB for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

PCE.why: The MIB monitors PCEP sessions, peers, messages and timers, so it is about PCE/PCEP operations and belongs on the PCE page.
PCE.quote: it describes managed objects for modeling of the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for communications between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE)

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document specifies no SNMP protocol changes, so the MIB tag covers it.
PCEP runs over TCP and the MIB mentions TCP connection timers, but the document is not about TCP.
PCEP is used for MPLS/GMPLS TE, mentioned only as context.
Mentioned only as the PCE use-case context, not the subject.
TE is context for PCE use; the document is about monitoring PCEP.
The document is an SMIv2 MIB, not a YANG model.

RFC7421.title: Analysis of the 64-bit Boundary in IPv6 Addressing
RFC7421.summary: Informational analysis explaining the advantages of the fixed 64-bit IPv6 interface identifier/subnet prefix boundary and examining the effects, failure modes and implementation issues of varying it.

IPv6.why: The whole document analyzes the IPv6 addressing architecture's 64-bit IID/prefix boundary, its advantages and the consequences of changing it.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 unicast addressing format includes a separation between the prefix used to route packets to a subnet and the interface identifier

SLAAC.why: A substantial portion discusses how SLAAC depends on IID length, how longer prefixes preclude SLAAC, and ND option processing survey results.
SLAAC.quote: The IID is of basic importance in the IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) process [RFC4862].

rejected.why: IPv6 is the more specific tag chosen; addressing is the parent topic and is implied.
ND options are surveyed and cache exhaustion discussed, but the document is not about ND itself.
Mentioned as an alternative to SLAAC for long prefixes, not a subject of the document.
NAT64, 6to4, 6rd, etc. are only listed as specifications depending on /64.
Privacy of IID length is a short section, not a main subject.
RFC 3306 and embedded-RP failure modes are brief bullet points.

RFC7422.title: Deterministic Address Mapping to Reduce Logging in Carrier-Grade NAT Deployments
RFC7422.summary: Informational RFC describing a deterministic algorithmic mapping of inside addresses to outside address plus port ranges in Carrier-Grade NATs, so that per-connection translation logging can be greatly reduced while preserving abuse traceability.

CGN.why: The whole document specifies how a Carrier-Grade NAT allocates deterministic port ranges and what it must log, which is CGN behaviour and operation.
CGN.quote: CGNs could deterministically map customer private addresses (received on the customer-facing interface of the CGN, a.k.a., internal side) to public addresses extended with port ranges

rejected.why: PCP is mentioned only in that the CGN must use pre-allocated ranges for PCP reservations. The document does not specify or extend PCP.
DS-Lite is one of several CGN deployment models the method applies to, not the subject of the document.
NAT64 is listed as an applicable CGN technology but is not specified or extended here.
The document is about what to log and how much, in the form of log message contents. It does not use or specify the syslog protocol.
The IPFIX NAT-logging draft is only cited as related work.
Section 4 discusses the impact on the IPv6 transition, but only briefly. The document is about CGN logging, and the CGN tag already covers it.

RFC7423.title: Diameter Applications Design Guidelines
RFC7423.summary: BCP companion to the Diameter base protocol that clarifies extensibility rules and gives design guidelines for reusing or defining Diameter applications, commands, AVPs and generic extensions.

Diameter.why: The whole document is about how to extend and design Diameter applications, commands and AVPs, so the Diameter page is where readers would look for it.
Diameter.quote: This document is a companion document to the Diameter base protocol that further explains and clarifies the rules to extend Diameter.

rejected.why: Diameter is an AAA protocol and sits under AAA, so the more specific Diameter tag already covers this. The document does not address AAA frameworks in general.
Only touched on in the translation agents section, where it says not to assume a standard Diameter-to-RADIUS gateway exists. That is a minor point.
Section 7 gives guidance on registering Diameter values, but this is a small part of the document and is specific to Diameter namespaces.
Section 5.11 recommends IPsec/IKEv2 for securing Diameter peers, but it is only one security mechanism the document leans on.
TLS and DTLS are mentioned as the transport security for Diameter peers. They are substrate, and the document defines nothing new about them.

gaps.name: Diameter
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Diameter tag; I could not find one. The document is entirely about Diameter extension design, so the nearest fit is the Diameter id, and a taxonomy entry is needed.

RFC7424.title: Mechanisms for Optimizing Link Aggregation Group (LAG) and Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) Component Link Utilization in Networks
RFC7424.summary: Informational RFC describing mechanisms to recognize large flows and rebalance traffic across LAG and ECMP component links when hash-based load distribution is uneven, plus an information model and operational considerations.

ECMP.why: The document's core subject is load balancing over ECMP groups, including hash-based distribution and large-flow-aware rebalancing, so ECMP is the best-fitting tag.
ECMP.quote: This document describes mechanisms for optimizing LAG/ECMP component link utilization when using hash-based techniques.

link aggregation.why: LAG component link utilization is co-equal with ECMP in the document. It covers LAG vs. ECMP differences and LAG tables, so it is about link aggregation behaviour.
link aggregation.quote: there is a LAG between them that has three component links (1), (2), and (3).

performance measurement.why: A substantial part covers measuring flows and link utilization, through sampling (sFlow, PSAMP), inline measurement, and monitoring information, to detect large flows and imbalance.
performance measurement.quote: we define an observation interval and measure the bandwidth of the flow over that interval.
performance measurement.section: 4.3.2. Criteria and Techniques for Large Flow Recognition

rejected.why: IPFIX is referenced for flow identification and the information model, but the document doesn't specify or extend it.
MPLS labels are mentioned only as flow identification fields and as an acronym. The document is not about MPLS.
The document touches on central management and placement of large flows, but it is about local component-link balancing, not TE architecture.
MIB counters (ifTable) are mentioned only as a source of utilization data. SNMP is not the subject.
VXLAN, NVGRE and STT are listed only as tunnels whose headers may be used for flow identification.
TCP is cited only as an example of a flow and for reordering effects on retransmission.

RFC7425.title: Adobe's RTMFP Profile for Flash Communication
RFC7425.summary: Informational Adobe profile specifying how RTMP messages for Flash communication are carried over RTMFP, including a Diffie-Hellman/AES cryptography profile, flow metadata, and client-server and P2P connection procedures.

key management.why: A large part of the document (Section 4) defines certificates, Diffie-Hellman key agreement, session key computation and packet encryption/verification for RTMFP sessions. The taxonomy has no RTMFP tag, so key management is the closest fit for this key establishment material.
key management.quote: This memo further specifies a concrete Cryptography Profile for RTMFP tailored to the application and cryptographic needs of Flash platform client-server and P2P communications.

rejected.why: RTMFP runs over UDP, but the document does not specify UDP or its usage. UDP is only the substrate.
It registers the rtmfp URI scheme, but this is a minor IANA-style section and not the main subject.
RTMFP carries real-time media, but it is a different protocol from RTP and the document does not touch RTP.
AES-128-CBC is used as the packet cipher, but only as a mechanism within the profile, not as the subject.
HMAC-SHA256 is used for key derivation and packet verification, but only as a building block.
The Internet checksum is used as an optional verification mode, but it is incidental.
The document concerns real-time media transport for Flash, but its content is RTMFP and RTMP-specific, and a general real-time communications tag would be too broad for it.

gaps.name: RTMFP / RTMP (Adobe Flash media protocols)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about transporting RTMP messages over RTMFP for Flash. The taxonomy has no tag for RTMFP, RTMP or Flash communication, so the primary subject is not covered.

RFC7426.title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN): Layers and Architecture Terminology
RFC7426.summary: An IRTF SDNRG informational RFC that defines SDN terminology and a layered architecture (planes, abstraction layers, interfaces) and maps ForCES, NETCONF/YANG, OpenFlow, I2RS, SNMP, PCEP and BFD onto it.

SDN.why: The whole document defines SDN layers, planes, abstraction layers and interfaces, and provides a taxonomy of SDN approaches.
SDN.quote: SDN emphasizes the role of software in running networks through the introduction of an abstraction for the data forwarding plane and, by doing so, separates it from the control plane.

ForCES.why: A dedicated section maps the ForCES model and protocol onto the DAL and CPSI of the SDN architecture.
ForCES.quote: ForCES separates the forwarding plane from the control plane via an open interface, namely the ForCES protocol [RFC5810]

NETCONF.why: The document analyses NETCONF as the management-plane southbound interface and discusses its suitability for SDN.
NETCONF.quote: NETCONF provides mechanisms to install, manipulate, and delete the configuration of network devices.

YANG.why: YANG is analysed as a DAL model for forwarding and operational planes.
YANG.quote: the YANG data modeling language [RFC6020] has been developed for specifying NETCONF data models and protocol operations.

I2RS.why: A dedicated section places the I2RS architecture within the layer model.
I2RS.quote: Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) provides a standard interface to the routing system for real-time or event-driven interaction

SNMP.why: SNMP and MIBs are examined as management-plane interface and DAL model.
SNMP.quote: The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is an IETF-standardized management protocol and is currently at its third revision (SNMPv3)

rejected.why: PCE/PCEP gets one short subsection mapping it to the model, but it is one example among many and not a main subject.
BFD is a short illustrative example of how a protocol fits the layers; the document is not about BFD.
The control versus management plane discussion is covered, but the more specific technology tags (NETCONF, SNMP, YANG, SDN) already cover it.
The document does define terms, but its subject is SDN architecture. The SDN tag is the better fit, and terminology is a generic glossary topic.
The architecture described is SDN-specific, not the architecture of the Internet.
RFC 7276's OAM planes are only referenced as background.

gaps.name: OpenFlow
gaps.why: A whole section covers OpenFlow and OF-CONFIG, but the taxonomy has no OpenFlow tag. The SDN topic tag partly covers it.

RFC7427.title: Signature Authentication in the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC7427.summary: Defines a new IKEv2 "Digital Signature" authentication method (Auth Method 14) whose Authentication Data carries an ASN.1 AlgorithmIdentifier, plus a SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS notification for announcing supported hash algorithms, generalizing signature support beyond per-algorithm methods like ECDSA.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new authentication method and a new Notify payload, and updates RFC 7296. IKE is the most specific tag that fits.
IKE.quote: This document adds a new IKEv2 [RFC7296] authentication method to support signature methods in a more general way.

ECDSA.why: The motivation is that IKEv2 ties ECDSA to fixed curves and hashes. The document replaces that with a generic scheme, and the appendices give ECDSA AlgorithmIdentifier encodings.
ECDSA.quote: The Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) protocol has limited support for the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA).

rejected.why: ASN.1 AlgorithmIdentifier objects (DER) are the encoding used to identify the signature algorithm. The document does not define ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
RSASSA-PSS and PKCS#1 v1.5 appear as example signature algorithms, mainly in the appendices. The document is not about RSA.
PKIX AlgorithmIdentifier is reused and certificates are referenced. The document does not profile certificates.
IKEv2 is the IPsec key exchange, but the document covers only IKE authentication, not the IPsec architecture. IKE is the more specific tag.
SHA-1 and SHA-2 are listed as values in the new hash algorithm registry. The document does not specify them.

RFC7428.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over ITU-T G.9959 Networks
RFC7428.summary: Defines how IPv6 packets are carried over ITU-T G.9959 low-power radio networks: a 6LoWPAN adaptation layer and frame format, IID construction, link-local and SLAAC addressing, ND/context handling, and header compression adaptations.

6LoWPAN.why: The document adapts RFC 4944/6282/6775 6LoWPAN to G.9959, defining the dispatch header, IID mapping, and address handling for this constrained link layer.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document defines the frame format for transmission of IPv6 [RFC2460] packets as well as the formation of IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured IPv6 addresses on G.9959 networks.

rejected.why: Uses RFC 6775 ND optimizations and defines a link-layer address option format, but only profiles it for 6LoWPAN; the ND subject is not the main focus.
Addressing via IIDs is covered, but as part of the 6LoWPAN link adaptation rather than a SLAAC specification.
Header compression is RFC 6282 IPHC, not ROHC; the substitutions are part of the 6LoWPAN adaptation.
DHCPv6 addressing and DUID-UUID are used as an option, but the document doesn't extend DHCPv6.
RPL is mentioned as a possible user of the frame format; routing is explicitly out of scope.
IPv6 is the carried protocol; the more specific 6LoWPAN tag captures the subject.

gaps.name: ITU-T G.9959 (Z-Wave) low-power radio link
gaps.why: The link technology itself has no specific tag; 6LoWPAN is the closest fit for IP over constrained link layers.

RFC7429.title: Distributed Mobility Management: Current Practices and Gap Analysis
RFC7429.summary: Informational gap analysis of how existing IP mobility protocols (MIPv6, PMIPv6, HMIPv6, NEMO, 3GPP GTP/LIPA/SIPTO) can be deployed for distributed mobility management, identifying gaps against the DMM requirements of RFC 7333.

IP mobility.why: The whole document is about distributed IP mobility management, analysing mobility anchoring and gaps. The generic IP mobility topic fits as the umbrella.
IP mobility.quote: This document analyzes deployment practices of existing IP mobility protocols in a distributed mobility management environment.

Mobile IPv6.why: Host-based practices (multiple HAs, route optimization, HMIPv6, HA switch, FMIPv6) are analysed substantially.
Mobile IPv6.quote: Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) [RFC6275] and its extension to support mobile networks, the NEMO Basic Support protocol

PMIPv6.why: Network-based DMM practices (multiple LMAs, local routing, runtime LMA assignment) are a substantial part of the analysis.
PMIPv6.quote: Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) [RFC5213] is the main network-based IP mobility protocol specified for IPv6.

NEMO.why: NEMO Basic Support is analysed alongside MIPv6 as a host-based DMM practice.
NEMO.quote: There is no route optimization support standardized for the NEMO protocol because of the security problems

rejected.why: 3GPP EPC/LIPA/SIPTO is described in Section 4.3, but as one of the deployment contexts for the mobility analysis, not the main subject.
Mentioned briefly as an alternative host-based mobility approach, not a focus.
Multicast mobility (REQ8) gets one short section, which is not enough for a tag.
YANG and NETCONF appear only as management gaps listed under REQ6.
HOKEY is cited only as a possible solution for re-authentication after an anchor change.

gaps.name: Distributed Mobility Management (DMM)
gaps.why: The document is about DMM, but the taxonomy has no DMM tag. IP mobility is the closest umbrella tag.

RFC7430.title: Analysis of Residual Threats and Possible Fixes for Multipath TCP (MPTCP)
RFC7430.summary: Informational threat analysis of residual vulnerabilities in Multipath TCP (RFC 6824), describing attacks (ADD_ADDR hijack, MP_JOIN DoS, SYN flood amplification, handshake eavesdropping, SYN/JOIN address substitution) and proposing fixes such as an HMAC on ADD_ADDR.

MPTCP.why: The whole document analyses the security of MPTCP as specified in RFC 6824 and proposes enhancements, so it belongs on the MPTCP page.
