MPTCP.quote: This document analyzes the residual threats for Multipath TCP (MPTCP) and explores possible solutions to address them.

rejected.why: MPTCP is the more specific child tag. The TCP attack details (sequence numbers, RFC 5961) are background for the MPTCP analysis.
It is only cited as a possible mitigation and is not specified or analysed in the document.
The SYN flooding amplification section is about MPTCP-specific DoS, not DDoS mitigation or signalling in general.
The document is about security, but the MPTCP tag is more specific and the document has no generic security guidance.
HMAC is only used as the proposed protection for ADD_ADDR and is not the subject of the document.
SCTP is mentioned only as a comparison point for the security level (RFC 5061).

RFC7431.title: Multicast-Only Fast Reroute
RFC7431.summary: Informational RFC describing Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR), which has merge-point routers join a multicast tree via primary and secondary upstream paths (PIM or mLDP) and switch quickly on failure, with LFA-based secondary selection and dual-plane topology applicability.

multicast.why: The document is about fast-reroute for IP multicast trees, joining primary and secondary upstream paths for PIM and mLDP trees. No more specific multicast child tag captures MoFRR itself, so the parent topic fits.
multicast.quote: Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) works by making simple enhancements to multicast routing protocols such as Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) and Multipoint LDP (mLDP).

IP fast reroute.why: MoFRR is a fast-reroute mechanism that uses LFAs and has applicability tied to LFA FRR. The tag covers IP and LDP fast reroute and loop-free alternates.
IP fast reroute.quote: The secondary UMH is a Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) as per [RFC5286].

PIM.why: A substantial section covers how MoFRR selects primary and secondary UMH and does RPF checks for PIM trees. The RFC does not change PIM itself.
PIM.quote: The UMH selection in PIM is also known as the Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) procedure.

LDP.why: The document covers MoFRR operation for mLDP P2MP and MP2MP LSPs, including label-based acceptance of packets from the primary upstream LSR.
LDP.quote: The UMH selection in mLDP also depends on unicast routing, but the difference from PIM is that the acceptance of multicast packets is based on MPLS labels

ECMP.why: ECMP-mode MoFRR is one of the two main modes and relies on equal-cost paths in dual-plane topologies for the secondary path.
ECMP.quote: If the IGP installs two ECMP paths to the source, then as per [RFC5286] the LFA is a primary next-hop.

rejected.why: BFD is only mentioned as one example of failure detection in Section 5, so it is not a subject of the document.
MVPN is only mentioned in one sentence saying the principle may be applied to it.
IPTV is the motivating use case, but the document specifies a general multicast protection mechanism and not IPTV service delivery.
PIM-SM is referenced for RPF and RP behaviour, but the document makes no changes to it and is not about its specification.
MPLS labels only matter for the mLDP case, which is covered by the LDP tag.
The dual-plane topology discussion is applicability guidance for MoFRR and does not address routing architecture in general.

RFC7432.title: BGP MPLS-Based Ethernet VPN
RFC7432.summary: RFC 7432 specifies BGP MPLS-based Ethernet VPN (EVPN): a new BGP EVPN NLRI with route types, extended communities, multihoming (ESI, DF election, split horizon, aliasing), MAC learning/mobility, and BUM traffic handling over MPLS.

EVPN.why: The document is the base EVPN specification, defining route types, multihoming, MAC advertisement, mobility and forwarding procedures.
EVPN.quote: This document describes procedures for a BGP MPLS-based solution called Ethernet VPN (EVPN) to address the requirements specified in [RFC7209].

BGP.why: It extends BGP with a new NLRI (AFI 25/SAFI 70), new extended communities and route-type procedures, which BGP readers need.
BGP.quote: This document defines a new BGP Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) called the EVPN NLRI.

rejected.why: VPLS is the technology EVPN improves upon and is referenced for comparison and multicast procedures, but the document does not specify or extend it.
MPLS LSPs and labels are the data-plane substrate; the document defines EVPN label usage, not MPLS itself.
EVPN is the more specific child tag under VPN; L2VPN is an ancestor-adjacent sibling and EVPN fits better.
RFC 4364 mechanisms (RDs, RTs) are reused but the document is not about L3VPN.
ARP/ND proxying and suppression is a minor section; the document does not specify ARP.
LAG/LACP is used by CEs for all-active multihoming and for ESI Type 1 derivation, but the document does not specify link aggregation.

RFC7433.title: A Mechanism for Transporting User-to-User Call Control Information in SIP
RFC7433.summary: Defines the SIP User-to-User header field (with purpose, content and encoding parameters, a "uui" option tag, IANA registries and package guidelines) for carrying opaque call control UUI data during session setup.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new header field, option tag, and parameters, plus package guidelines and redirection/History-Info behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new SIP header field, User-to-User, to transport UUI data, along with an extension mechanism.

rejected.why: ISDN UUI interworking is defined in the separate RFC 7434; this document only defines the SIP-native mechanism and mentions interworking.
SIP-T is only mentioned in an appendix as the model for the rejected MIME body approach.
The IANA registries are boilerplate for the SIP header and package registrations, not the subject of the document.
TLS is only mentioned as hop-by-hop security in the requirements discussion.
Hex (base16) encoding is referenced from RFC 4648 as a small encoding detail, not the subject.
A MIME body approach is discussed only as a rejected alternative in the appendix.

RFC7434.title: Interworking ISDN Call Control User Information with SIP
RFC7434.summary: Defines the "isdn-uui" package of the SIP User-to-User header field for interworking ISDN (DSS1/Q.931 UUS1 implicit, and QSIG) user-to-user information with SIP, including UAC/UAS/gateway requirements and a media feature tag.

PSTN interop.why: The document specifies how ISDN UUS1 user-to-user data is interworked with SIP at ISDN gateways, which is PSTN/Internet interworking. No narrower child tag (SIP-T, SIGTRAN, etc.) fits the interworking being defined.
PSTN interop.quote: This document defines a usage (a new package called the ISDN UUI package) of the User-to-User header field to enable interworking with this ISDN service.

SIP.why: It extends SIP by defining a User-to-User header field package, new purpose/content parameter values, a media feature tag, and UAC/UAS behaviour.
SIP.quote: The UAC MUST only use this UUI mechanism extension package in association with the initial INVITE method and the BYE method relating to an INVITE dialog.

rejected.why: Section 4 discusses SIP-T only to explain that this document takes a different approach (native header field rather than MIME encapsulation of ISUP).
The document registers a media feature tag and UUI registry values, not MIME media types.
This tag covers IP over ISDN access; the document is about SIP/ISDN signalling interworking rather than IP carried over ISDN.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and the body is not about registry guidance.
The sip.uui-isdn media feature tag is defined per RFC 3840 with no further provisions, so it is a minor part of the document.

RFC7435.title: Opportunistic Security: Some Protection Most of the Time
RFC7435.summary: Defines the concept of Opportunistic Security: cleartext as baseline, with encryption and authentication negotiated whenever peers support them, along with design principles and an SMTP STARTTLS example.

security.why: The document is a general security-policy concept and design-principles document, not tied to one mechanism, so the general security topic fits.
security.quote: "Opportunistic Security" (OS) is defined as the use of cleartext as the baseline communication security policy, with encryption and authentication negotiated and applied

privacy.why: Motivation is countering pervasive monitoring by making encryption widespread, which readers of privacy and pervasive monitoring topics would want.
privacy.quote: The use of encryption defends against pervasive monitoring and other passive attacks.

rejected.why: TLS is only the example mechanism; the document defines no TLS protocol behaviour.
STARTTLS in SMTP is one illustrative example section, not the subject of the document.
DANE is mentioned as an out-of-band authentication source, not specified or extended here.
Only mentioned as a dependency of DANE and its limited deployment.
Authentication is discussed as an opportunistic component, but the overall subject is better covered by security.
Email appears only as the example application.

gaps.name: Opportunistic Security
gaps.why: The document defines this concept; no taxonomy tag exists for opportunistic/unauthenticated encryption, so the general security tag is used.

RFC7436.title: IP-Only LAN Service (IPLS)
RFC7436.summary: RFC 7436 specifies IPLS, a simplified VPLS variant for IP-only CEs that uses LDP signaling of MAC/IP addresses and unicast and multicast pseudowires instead of data-plane MAC learning, and is published as Historic.

VPLS.why: The document defines IPLS, a VPLS-like service, with its own signaling and forwarding procedures. VPLS readers would want it.
VPLS.quote: We call this simplified type of VPLS an "IP-only LAN Service" (IPLS).

pseudowire.why: A substantial part of the document specifies unicast and multicast MP2P pseudowires, their encapsulations and PW FEC signaling extensions (MAC Address TLV, Stack Capability sub-TLV).
pseudowire.quote: a PE device sets up a pseudowire (PW) to each of the other PEs that supports the same IPLS instance.

rejected.why: LDP is the signaling substrate (RFC 4447), though new TLVs and status codes are defined. The extensions are PW-specific, so LDP itself is not the subject.
ARP is snooped and proxied as part of CE discovery, but the document does not specify or extend ARP.
IPv6 ND is intercepted for CE discovery, but the document does not extend ND.
EVPN is only mentioned as later work that adopted these concepts.
VPLS is the more specific tag and already covers this.
MPLS is only the underlying tunnel network.

RFC7437.title: IAB, IESG, and IAOC Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Operation of the Nominating and Recall Committees
RFC7437.summary: RFC 7437 consolidates BCP 10, specifying how the IETF Nominating Committee is selected and operates to choose IAB, IESG and IAOC members, how they are confirmed, and how members are recalled.

NomCom.why: The whole document specifies NomCom selection, operation, confirmation and the related recall committee procedures, so it belongs on the NomCom subject page.
NomCom.quote: The nominating committee comprises at least a Chair, 10 voting volunteers, two liaisons, and an advisor.

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child tag that fits, and its ancestors are implied, so the parent is not listed separately.
Only boilerplate copyright text mentions IPR. The body is not about intellectual property.
There is no IANA considerations content. The document is about leadership selection, not registries.

RFC7438.title: Multipoint LDP (mLDP) In-Band Signaling with Wildcards
RFC7438.summary: Specifies wildcard encodings (for source and/or group) in mLDP in-band signaling Opaque Value TLVs so that ASM shared trees and aggregated (S,G) trees can be attached to a single MP-LSP, updating RFC 6826 and RFC 7246.

LDP.why: The document extends mLDP (multipoint LDP) FEC Opaque Value TLV encodings and procedures at Ingress and Egress LSRs. mLDP is an LDP extension, and LDP is the most specific fitting tag.
LDP.quote: This document specifies a way to encode an mLDP "Opaque Value" in which either the "S" or the "G" or both are replaced by a "wildcard"

multicast.why: The core subject is attaching IP multicast trees (ASM shared trees, aggregated SSM trees) to MP-LSPs. It covers PIM shared-tree forwarding, IGMP/MLD proxying and Anycast RP, which are IP multicast deployment matters.
multicast.quote: Procedures are described for using the wildcard encoding to map non-bidirectional ASM shared trees to MP-LSPs and for mapping multiple (S,G) trees

rejected.why: PIM-SM shared trees, threshold infinity and the RP are discussed, but only as the multicast side being mapped onto MP-LSPs. The document does not specify or extend PIM-SM.
MP-LSPs are the substrate, but the specific protocol being extended is mLDP, which falls under LDP.
IGMP/MLD proxying is a use case that follows RFC 4605. The document does not define or extend IGMP.
MSDP is mentioned only as one way to learn sources and is not specified or extended here.
SSM address ranges appear in the wildcard semantics, but the document is not about SSM itself.
VPN context is mentioned only briefly (RD in FEC), and the document points to the MVPN RFCs for cases needing source discovery.

RFC7439.title: Gap Analysis for Operating IPv6-Only MPLS Networks
RFC7439.summary: Gap analysis of the MPLS protocol suite (data plane, LDP/mLDP, RSVP-TE, PCE, BGP, VPNs, OAM, MIBs) for IPv6-only operation, identifying major and minor gaps and work in progress to fix them.

MPLS.why: The whole document reviews MPLS protocols and applications for IPv6-only operation.
MPLS.quote: this document reviews the MPLS protocol suite in the context of IPv6 and identifies gaps that must be addressed

IPv6.why: The document concerns IPv6-only and IPv6-primary operation and the gaps in IPv4 dependence.
IPv6.quote: allow MPLS-related protocols and applications to be used with IPv6-only networks and networks that are primarily IPv6

LDP.why: LDP and mLDP have the major control-plane gaps, and they drive the EVPN and mLDP findings.
LDP.quote: While LDP was designed to use an IPv4 or dual-stack IP network, it has a number of deficiencies that prevent it from working in an IPv6-only network.

L3VPN.why: A substantial section covers L3VPN, 6PE/4PE and 6VPE/4VPE gaps, including the major 4PE gap.
L3VPN.quote: RFC 4659 does not formally update RFC 4364, and thus an implementer may miss this additional set of standards

OAM.why: MPLS OAM (LSP Ping, extended ICMP, BFD, VCCV) is analysed with major gaps for IPv6-only.
OAM.quote: RFC 4379 needs to be updated to better support multipath IPv6.

rejected.why: Covered in one subsection with a minor gap in RFC 6074. It is not a main focus.
Found to have no gap, so it is only a brief part of the analysis.
Reviewed briefly and found to have no gap.
BGP label distribution (RFC 3107) is mentioned with no gap, and BGP is mostly the substrate for the VPN material.
Declared out of scope, since MPLS-TP does not require IP.
MIB modules are a short subsection and the MIB tag does not exist as a specific fit. Taxonomy has only SNMP, MIB under SNMP, which is only marginal here.

RFC7440.title: TFTP Windowsize Option
RFC7440.summary: Defines a TFTP option, negotiated via the RFC 2347 option mechanism, that lets client and server use a window of multiple consecutive data blocks before an ACK, improving throughput over lockstep TFTP.

TFTP.why: The document specifies a new extension option to TFTP, including request format, OACK negotiation, traffic flow and error handling.
TFTP.quote: this document presents a negotiated extension, under the terms of the "TFTP Option Extension" [RFC2347], that produces TFTP transfer rates comparable to those achieved by modern file transfer protocols

rejected.why: TFTP runs over UDP and the document cites UDP congestion guidelines, but it is only the substrate and nothing new is defined about UDP.
Section 6 briefly refers to RFC 5405 congestion control guidance and a circuit breaker, but this is a minor part of the document, not its subject.
TFTP is a distinct protocol with its own tag; the generic FTP tag is not about it.

gaps.name: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TFTP tech tag in the applications section, but I used an id 'TFTP' that is listed as 'TFTP' in the taxonomy, so no gap exists; noted only for verification.

RFC7441.title: Encoding Multipoint LDP (mLDP) Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs) in the NLRI of BGP MCAST-VPN Routes
RFC7441.summary: Updates RFC 6514 to define three new BGP MCAST-VPN route types whose NLRI carries an mLDP FEC Element, so BGP/MPLS VPN customers using mLDP for MPLS multicast are supported without restrictive assumptions.

MVPN.why: Defines new MCAST-VPN route types and NLRI encodings for multicast in BGP/MPLS VPNs.
MVPN.quote: This document defines three new route types: C-Multicast Source Tree Join route for C-multicast mLDP, S-PMSI A-D route for C-multicast mLDP

RFC7442.title: Carrying Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) in Any-Source Multicast (ASM) Mode Trees over Multipoint LDP (mLDP)
RFC7442.summary: Specifies two mechanisms for mapping PIM-SM ASM multicast trees (shared and source trees) onto mLDP P2MP LSPs across an MPLS domain, defining new Transit IPv4/IPv6 Shared Tree TLVs and use of BGP Source Active A-D routes.

PIM-SM.why: The document specifies how PIM-SM ASM (*,G) and (S,G,RPT-bit) state is handled at LSRs and carried over MPLS, including pruning sources off the shared tree.
PIM-SM.quote: This document describes how to map mLDP P2MP trees to multicast trees created by PIM-SM in Any-Source Multicast (ASM) mode.

LDP.why: It extends mLDP in-band signaling with new TLVs for shared trees, with IANA allocations in the LDP registry. mLDP is the sole LDP-family tag here since no mLDP-specific tag exists.
LDP.quote: this document defines two new mLDP TLVs: the Transit IPv4 Shared Tree TLV and the Transit IPv6 Shared Tree TLV.
LDP.section: 3.1. In-Band Signaling for IP Multicast Shared Trees

MVPN.why: The document originates and consumes MCAST-VPN NLRI Source Active A-D routes, borrowed from the BGP MVPN procedures, as a core part of both mechanisms.
MVPN.quote: This document uses BGP Source Active auto-discovery routes, as defined in [RFC6514].

rejected.why: SSM-mode mapping is covered by RFC 6826; this document only builds on it for ASM.
BGP is used only to carry Source Active A-D routes via RFC 6514 encodings; the document does not specify BGP itself.
MPLS is the domain traversed, but the document is about multicast mapping over mLDP, not MPLS architecture.
MSDP is mentioned only as one way an RP learns sources; nothing is specified about it.
NO_EXPORT is merely applied to the routes; the document does not address communities.

gaps.name: mLDP in-band signaling (multipoint LDP P2MP/MP2MP LSPs)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has LDP but no specific tag for multipoint LDP and its in-band signaling, which is central to this document and to RFC 6826 and RFC 7438.

RFC7443.title: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Labels for Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) Usages
RFC7443.summary: Defines and registers two ALPN protocol labels, 'stun.turn' and 'stun.nat-discovery', so STUN usages can be negotiated within TLS/DTLS handshakes.

STUN.why: The document defines ALPN labels identifying STUN usages (TURN and NAT discovery) over (D)TLS, extending how STUN is used and identified.
STUN.quote: This document proposes the following ALPN labels to identify STUN protocol [RFC5389] usages.

TURN.why: One of the two labels, 'stun.turn', identifies TURN usage, so TURN readers would want it.
TURN.quote: Label to identify the specific use of STUN over (D)TLS for TURN (Section 4.6 of [RFC7350]).

TLS.why: The document registers ALPN protocol IDs for use in the TLS/DTLS handshake, which is new TLS extension usage readers of TLS would need.
TLS.quote: ALPN [RFC7301] enables an endpoint to positively identify an application protocol in TLS/DTLS and distinguish it from other TLS/ DTLS protocols.

rejected.why: Labels apply to DTLS as well, but this is covered by the TLS tag; the document does not specify DTLS itself.
The registry entries are the document's purpose but are a registration of labels for TLS ALPN, not IANA policy or guidance.
Parent of STUN and TURN, implied by those tags.

gaps.name: ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation)
gaps.why: The document is about ALPN labels, but the taxonomy has no ALPN tag; TLS is the closest fit.

RFC7444.title: Security Labels in Internet Email
RFC7444.summary: Defines the SIO-Label email header field carrying a security label and display marking for message sensitivity, and the SIO-Label-History trace header recording label changes.

security labels.why: The document specifies a protocol for conveying security labels and display markings on email messages, which is the subject of security labels for networked data.
security labels.quote: a header field, SIO-Label, for use in Internet email to convey the sensitivity of the message

message format.why: It defines new Internet message header fields with ABNF syntax, extending the RFC 5322 message format; readers of email header fields would want it.
message format.quote: The SIO-Label-History header field is considered to be a trace field as defined in Section 3.6.7 of [RFC5322].

rejected.why: ESS for S/MIME is discussed only as a related alternative; this protocol does no signing.
Covered by the more specific message format tag; the document does not address mail transport or access.
Uses RFC 2231 parameter syntax but is not about MIME body structure.
XML is only one encoding option for the label value.
Base64 is only the encoding of label values, a substrate.
BER-encoded ESS/X.411 labels are referenced, not defined here.

RFC7445.title: Analysis of Failure Cases in IPv6 Roaming Scenarios
RFC7445.summary: Informational analysis of failure cases faced by IPv6-enabled mobile users roaming between 3GPP networks (attachment, PDP/PDN creation, service requests), with causes and mitigations such as roaming APN settings, DAF, and HLR/HSS profile configuration.

cellular.why: The document is about IPv6 over 3GPP networks (SGSN/MME, GGSN/PGW, HLR/HSS, PDP/PDN types) in roaming, which is cellular interworking.
cellular.quote: identifies a set of failure cases that may be encountered by IPv6-enabled mobile customers in roaming scenarios

IPv6 transition.why: Dual-stack vs IPv6-only deployment inconsistencies and use of translation (464XLAT, NAT64, DNS64) are a substantial part of the analysis.
IPv6 transition.quote: Translation-based methods, for example, 464XLAT [RFC6877] or Bump-in-the-Host (BIH) [RFC6535], may help to address the issue

rejected.why: Section 5.2 discusses 464XLAT failures in roaming, but the document does not specify or extend it; covered under IPv6 transition.
IPv6 is the subject context, but the more specific cellular and transition tags capture the content better.
RADIUS/Diameter are mentioned only as a way for the GGSN/PGW to query a AAA server; not the subject.
Only mentioned as a component 464XLAT relies on; the document does not analyse NAT64 itself.
Mentioned once as possibly missing in the visited network; not a subject of the document.

RFC7446.title: Routing and Wavelength Assignment Information Model for Wavelength Switched Optical Networks
RFC7446.summary: RFC 7446 defines an information model of node and link information (connectivity matrices, resource pools, port label restrictions, dynamic wavelength availability) needed for Routing and Wavelength Assignment path computation in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks under a GMPLS control plane.

GMPLS.why: The model describes WSON/WDM routing and wavelength assignment information for GMPLS-controlled optical networks, including port label restrictions and link information from GMPLS routing extensions.
GMPLS.quote: The purpose of the WSON information model described in this document is to facilitate constrained optical path computation

rejected.why: The model supports path computation and references the PCE framework, but the document defines no PCE architecture or PCEP content.
OSPF and IS-IS extensions are referenced as sources of link information, but the document does not specify or extend them.
RBNF syntax is merely used as a notation to write the model, not the subject.
TE metric and administrative group are summarized from existing RFCs; the document is not about traffic engineering as such.
Only cited as an existing source of link information.

gaps.name: WSON (Wavelength Switched Optical Networks) / Routing and Wavelength Assignment
gaps.why: The document is primarily about optical WDM networks and RWA, for which the taxonomy has no tag; GMPLS is the nearest fit.

RFC7447.title: Deprecation of BGP Entropy Label Capability Attribute
RFC7447.summary: Deprecates the BGP Entropy Label Capability attribute (ELCA, path attribute 28) defined in RFC 6790 because its optional-transitive nature means incapable routers cannot be relied on to strip it.

BGP.why: The document deprecates a BGP path attribute and specifies how BGP speakers must treat it, so it is about BGP protocol behaviour.
BGP.quote: This document deprecates the ELCA path attribute.  This means that implementations MUST NOT generate the attribute.

MPLS.why: The attribute advertises MPLS entropy label capability. The document updates RFC 6790, an MPLS entropy label specification, but only the BGP attribute is changed, so this is a weaker fit.
MPLS.quote: The Use of Entropy Labels in MPLS Forwarding

rejected.why: Entropy labels support load balancing, but the document never discusses load-balanced forwarding.
The IANA action is only a registry marking, which is boilerplate here.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate and the document does not concern securing routing.

RFC7448.title: MIB Transfer from the IETF to the IEEE 802.3 WG
RFC7448.summary: Informational RFC recording the transfer of responsibility for eight Ethernet-related MIB modules (DOT3-OAM-MIB, MAU-MIB, EtherLike-MIB, etc.) from the IETF to the IEEE 802.3 WG, with the procedural aspects of the transfer.

MIB.why: The document is entirely about the change of ownership of specific MIB modules and the procedures (OID registration, MIB Doctor reviews, ASCII MIB location) for that transfer.
MIB.quote: transfer of responsibility for the Ethernet-related MIB modules DOT3-OAM-MIB, SNMP-REPEATER-MIB, POWER-ETHERNET-MIB, DOT3-EPON-MIB, EtherLike-MIB, EFM-CU-MIB, ETHER-WIS, and MAU-MIB

Ethernet.why: All the transferred modules cover Ethernet interfaces, repeaters, OAM, power over Ethernet and MAUs, so Ethernet readers would want this record.
Ethernet.quote: Clause 10, Ethernet-like interface MIB module

rejected.why: SNMP is the management protocol context of the MIB modules, but the document does not specify or discuss the protocol itself.
The document records a handover of work between standards bodies, which touches on process, but it is a narrow administrative record rather than a description of IETF standards procedures.
DOT3-OAM-MIB is one of the eight modules listed, but the document is not about OAM mechanisms.
EFM-CU-MIB (Ethernet in the First Mile copper) is only listed in a table and is not a subject of the document.

RFC7449.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Requirements for Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON) Routing and Wavelength Assignment
RFC7449.summary: Informational document listing application-specific requirements for PCEP to support Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA) path computation in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs).

PCE.why: The document specifies requirements for PCEP extensions (request types, bulk requests, reoptimization, constraints) for RWA, so it is about PCE/PCEP.
PCE.quote: This memo provides application-specific requirements for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for the support of Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs).

GMPLS.why: WSON lightpath computation and wavelength label assignment is GMPLS optical/transport network control, which a reader of GMPLS would want to find.
GMPLS.quote: WSON refers to WDM-based optical networks in which switching is performed selectively based on the wavelength of an optical signal.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as the signalling used for distributed wavelength assignment, which the document explicitly declares out of scope.
PCE is the more specific tag under it; the document is not about TE in general.
Section 4.2 says no MIB module is defined; it only refers to the PCE MIB.
RFC 5088 is mentioned only as a PCE discovery reference in manageability considerations.

gaps.name: Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSON) / RWA
gaps.why: The document is about optical-network routing and wavelength assignment, and the taxonomy has no WSON or optical-networking tag. GMPLS is the closest fit.

RFC7450.title: Automatic Multicast Tunneling
RFC7450.summary: Specifies Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT), a UDP-encapsulation protocol in which gateways use relays (found via anycast discovery) to receive multicast traffic from networks without native multicast connectivity.

AMT.why: The document defines the AMT protocol: its messages, gateway and relay operation, and tunnelling.
AMT.quote: Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT), a protocol for delivering multicast traffic from sources in a multicast-enabled network to receivers that lack multicast connectivity

rejected.why: AMT encapsulates and relies on IGMP, and specifies only minimal host and router subset requirements. IGMP itself is not specified or extended.
Same as IGMP: it is carried inside AMT messages, and the document does not specify it.
SSM is mentioned as a supported service, but the document is not about SSM.
UDP is only the encapsulation substrate. The zero-checksum discussion is a minor point.
Anycast is used for relay discovery. It is a mechanism within AMT, not the subject of the document.
It is only mentioned as an example upstream multicast protocol.
NAT traversal is handled as a consideration. The document does not specify NAT behaviour.

RFC7451.title: Extension Registry for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol
RFC7451.summary: Defines the procedure and registration form for an IANA registry of Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extensions, including designated-expert review criteria and initial entries.

EPP.why: The whole document is about managing and registering extensions to EPP, the domain registry provisioning protocol.
EPP.quote: This document describes a procedure for the registration and management of extensions to EPP, and it specifies a format for an IANA registry to record those extensions.

IANA.why: The document creates a new IANA registry with Specification Required policy and designated expert guidance, which is central to its content and of interest to readers of IANA registry matters.
IANA.quote: IANA has created the "Extensions for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)" registry to manage EPP extensions.

rejected.why: EPP is a child tag under domain registration and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
The DNSSEC mapping for EPP appears only as an initial registry entry, not as subject matter.
The ENUM-related EPP mappings are only listed as initial registry entries.
Designated expert appointment is part of the registry procedure, which the IANA tag covers better.

RFC7452.title: Architectural Considerations in Smart Object Networking
RFC7452.summary: IAB informational document giving architectural guidance to engineers designing Internet-connected smart objects (IoT): communication patterns, reuse of Internet protocols, deployed-Internet constraints, design for change, and security/privacy considerations.

IoT.why: The whole document is IoT architectural guidance: communication patterns, reuse of protocols, and design for change for smart objects.
IoT.quote: This document offers guidance to engineers designing Internet-connected smart objects.

internet architecture.why: Substantial parts discuss architectural principles: end-to-end, transparency, middleboxes, tussle, evolvability and incremental deployability.
internet architecture.quote: the community believes that the goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end rather than hidden in the network.

rejected.why: Mentioned as an example application protocol in the patterns; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Security Considerations is a general list of smart-object security concerns, but it is boilerplate-position and the document is not mainly about security.
Short privacy section pointing to RFC 6973; not a main subject.
Only cited as an example of a reusable building block in the back-end sharing pattern.
Appears only in protocol stack figures as a substrate.
Software update is mentioned as a need in Design for Change, but briefly and without specifying any mechanism.

RFC7453.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Traffic Engineering (TE) Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC7453.summary: Defines four SMIv2 MIB modules (MPLS-TC-EXT, MPLS-ID, MPLS-LSR-EXT, MPLS-TE-EXT) extending the MPLS TE and LSR MIBs to manage MPLS-TP bidirectional tunnels, non-IP node identifiers and cross-connects.

MIB.why: The document's whole content is MIB modules, textual conventions, tables and compliance statements in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

MPLS-TP.why: The MIBs manage MPLS-TP tunnels, identifiers (Global_ID, ICC) and LSPs, so MPLS-TP readers would look for it.
MPLS-TP.quote: The MPLS-TP TE MIB defined in this document extends the MIB modules defined in [RFC3812] to cover all six combinations

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines MIB content, not SNMP itself, so the MIB tag fits better.
The GMPLS TE MIB (RFC 4802) is referenced and extended only in passing; the document is not about GMPLS.
MPLS-TP is the more specific tag and is already chosen; the parent is implied.
Tunnels are TE tunnels, but the document is a management data model, not about TE practice; MPLS-TP covers it.
The identifiers support OAM, but OAM mechanisms are not specified here.

RFC7454.title: BGP Operations and Security
RFC7454.summary: BCP describing operational security practices for BGP: protecting the speaker and sessions (ACLs, TCP-AO, GTSM), prefix/AS-path/next-hop filtering, max-prefix, route flap damping, and community scrubbing.

BGP.why: The whole document is operational best practice for BGP peerings, covering session protection and route filtering, damping and max-prefix.
BGP.quote: This document describes measures to protect the BGP sessions itself such as Time to Live (TTL), the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO), and control-plane filtering.

routing security.why: The document is about securing inter-domain routing, including prefix filtering, IRR-based filters and RPKI origin validation, so the routing security topic fits directly.
routing security.quote: The main aspect of securing BGP resides in controlling the prefixes that are received and advertised on the BGP peerings.

RPKI.why: It gives recommendations for route origin validation with ROAs and advises signing routing objects.
RPKI.quote: each external route received on a router SHOULD be checked against the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) data set

RPSL.why: A substantial subsection covers building and refreshing prefix filters from IRR data, including AS-SETs and IRRToolSet.
RPSL.quote: An Internet Routing Registry (IRR) is a database containing Internet routing information, described using Routing Policy Specification Language objects
RPSL.section: 6.1.2.2.1 Prefix Filters Created from Internet Routing Registries (IRRs)

BGP communities.why: It has a dedicated section with recommendations on community scrubbing, and it also covers black-hole communities.
BGP communities.quote: Network administrators SHOULD scrub inbound communities with their number in the high-order bits

route server.why: Route server behaviour comes up in the AS-path, next-hop and IXP LAN guidance, with specific exceptions for route-server peerings.
route server.quote: This is a desirable property for BGP route-server setups [17], where the route server will relay routing information

rejected.why: TCP is the substrate for BGP sessions. The document recommends TCP-AO and MD5 for protecting those sessions but does not specify or extend TCP.
This is a plausible fit, but BGP and routing security already cover the subject more specifically.
It is mentioned only to say there is not enough experience to give guidelines.
Special-purpose and unallocated prefix filtering touches on addressing. The document is about filtering routes, not addressing architecture.
It is mentioned only as ongoing work that cannot yet be implemented.
It appears only in the IXP LAN loose uRPF discussion, which is a minor point.

RFC7455.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Fault Management
RFC7455.summary: Specifies TRILL OAM fault management: CFM-based Loopback, Path Trace, Multi-destination Tree Verification and Continuity Check messages, new TLVs, an Alert flag in the TRILL header, and capability announcement, updating RFC 6325.

TRILL.why: The document extends TRILL with an OAM Alert flag, OAM capability flags, new OpCodes and TLVs, and updates RFC 6325.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) fault management.

OAM.why: It defines OAM fault-management mechanisms (CCM, loopback, path trace, tree verification) for TRILL.
OAM.quote: Methods in this document follow the CFM (Connectivity Fault Management) framework defined in IEEE 802.1 and reuse OAM tools where possible.

Ethernet.why: It reuses IEEE 802.1Q CFM (Ethernet OAM) formats and the MEP/MIP/MA model, layered within IEEE 802.1 sublayers.
Ethernet.quote: The TRILL OAM Message Channel is formatted as specified in IEEE Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) [8021Q].

rejected.why: IS-IS is used only for capability announcement (TRILL-VER sub-TLV) and the authentication TLV/keying; it is not what the document is about.
The TRILL OAM MIB is deferred to a separate document; only a brief augmentation sketch appears here.
SNMP traps are mentioned for CCM error notification but are not the subject.
Multipath is the reason for flow entropy, but the document is about OAM, not ECMP.
The Path Trace is analogous to traceroute and uses hop-count expiry, but it is a TRILL OAM message, not the traceroute tool.
Performance monitoring is in RFC 7456, explicitly out of scope here.

gaps.name: TRILL
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tag (listed under routing) that applies here as a technology tag; if it is not actually available in the taxonomy, no other tag fits TRILL itself.

RFC7456.title: Loss and Delay Measurement in Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL)
RFC7456.summary: RFC 7456 specifies Loss Measurement (1SL, SLM/SLR) and Delay Measurement (1DM, DMM/DMR) OAM protocols for TRILL networks, based on ITU-T Y.1731 performance monitoring.

TRILL.why: The document extends TRILL with performance-monitoring OAM messages exchanged between RBridges, including packet formats and procedures, so it belongs on the TRILL page.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies mechanisms for Loss Measurement and Delay Measurement in Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) networks.

performance measurement.why: The core content is active loss and delay measurement methods and metrics (packet loss, delay, delay variation), which is performance measurement. No specific child tag such as OWAMP or TWAMP applies.
performance measurement.quote: PM consists of two main building blocks: Loss Measurement and Delay Measurement.

OAM.why: The protocols are OAM tools built on TRILL OAM encapsulation, MEPs and Maintenance Domains, so OAM readers would want this document.
OAM.quote: Performance Monitoring (PM) is a key aspect of OAM.

rejected.why: Only the IEEE 1588 timestamp format is reused, and clock synchronization is explicitly out of scope.
Y.1731 is an Ethernet OAM standard and is the basis for the OpCodes and procedures, but the document defines TRILL OAM rather than Ethernet OAM.
One-way delay measurement needs synchronized clocks, but the document says the synchronization method is outside its scope.
RFC 6374 is cited only as a precedent for the timestamp format, and the document does not address MPLS.

RFC7457.title: Summarizing Known Attacks on Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram TLS (DTLS)
RFC7457.summary: Informational RFC summarizing known attacks on TLS and DTLS (BEAST, CRIME, POODLE, RC4 biases, Triple Handshake, Heartbleed, etc.) to motivate the UTA working group's usage recommendations.

TLS.why: The whole document catalogues attacks on TLS and DTLS and their mitigations, so TLS readers would want it. DTLS is a child of TLS, but the document treats DTLS only as equivalent to TLS, so TLS is the right tag.
TLS.quote: This document summarizes these attacks, with the goal of motivating generic and protocol-specific recommendations on the usage of TLS and Datagram TLS (DTLS).

RC4.why: A dedicated section covers RC4 keystream-bias attacks and concludes RC4 is unsuitable for TLS, which is relevant to readers of the RC4 subject.
RC4.quote: RC4 can no longer be seen as providing a sufficient level of security for TLS sessions.

rejected.why: Section 3 only says DTLS 1.0 and 1.2 are equivalent to TLS 1.1 and 1.2 for these attacks. DTLS is not the focus, so TLS covers it.
HSTS is only mentioned as a mitigation for SSL stripping and for downgrade attacks.
HTTP appears only as the protocol carried over TLS in the BEAST, CRIME and BREACH attacks. The document is not about HTTP.
Compression attacks (CRIME, BREACH) are described only as TLS attacks. The document does not address compression formats.
Section 2.7 and 2.8 cover RSA-related attacks on TLS only briefly, in the context of certificates and key theft.
The document summarizes attacks and does not give operational practices. Those are in the companion BCP.

RFC7458.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Attributes for Wi-Fi Integration with the Evolved Packet Core
RFC7458.summary: Defines six new EAP-AKA/AKA'/SIM attributes enabling APN selection, multiple PDN connectivity and Wi-Fi to UTRAN/E-UTRAN handover for trusted Wi-Fi access to the Evolved Packet Core, as triggers for Proxy Mobile IPv6 operations.

EAP.why: The document extends EAP-AKA/AKA'/SIM with new skippable attributes, their formats and registry, so it is about EAP methods.
EAP.quote: This document defines a few new EAP attributes to enable the above-mentioned functions in such networks.

cellular.why: Concerns 3GPP EPC integration: APN selection, PDN connections, and handover between Wi-Fi and UTRAN/E-UTRAN.
cellular.quote: it has become important to provide functions commonly available in 3G and 4G networks in Wi-Fi access networks as well.

WiFi.why: Targets trusted Wi-Fi access networks and describes the 802.11 EAP flow for attaching to the EPC.
WiFi.quote: In a Wi-Fi network, EAP is carried over the IEEE 802.1X Authentication protocol.

rejected.why: Attributes only trigger PMIPv6 MAG/LMA operations; PMIPv6 itself is not specified or extended.
The AAA server is merely the EAP server endpoint; no AAA protocol is defined.
Mentioned only in passing as a way to split the WAN functions.
IANA section registers attributes and a new registry, but that is boilerplate relative to the document's subject.
Mentioned only as how the MN gets its first IP address.

RFC7459.title: Representation of Uncertainty and Confidence in the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO)
RFC7459.summary: Defines uncertainty and confidence concepts for location estimates, adds a PIDF-LO "confidence" XML element and schema, and gives methods for manipulating location estimates with uncertainty (centroids, conversions, scaling, region overlap).

geolocation.why: The whole document is about expressing and manipulating uncertainty and confidence in location information, and defines a PIDF-LO confidence element. No more specific geolocation child (HELD) applies.
geolocation.quote: This document defines key concepts of uncertainty and confidence as they pertain to location information.

PIDF.why: Section 4 and the schema in Section 7 extend PIDF-LO with a new confidence element, and the document updates RFCs 4119 and 5491. The PIDF-LO format is central.
PIDF.quote: A confidence extension for the Presence Information Data Format - Location Object (PIDF-LO) [RFC4119] is described.

rejected.why: The XML schema is only the vehicle for the new element. The document is not about XML usage in general.
RFC 6225 DHCP location options are mentioned only briefly in Section 3.4 for their uncertainty interpretation.
RFC 5222 is cited only as an example of a decision process choosing among regions.
Privacy appears only in the Security Considerations and in passing remarks on obfuscation. It is not a main subject.

gaps.name: PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format Location Object)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a PIDF tag under instant messaging for presence, but no tag for the geopriv location object format. I used the closest tag, which is not ideal.

RFC7460.title: Monitoring and Control MIB for Power and Energy
RFC7460.summary: Defines the ENERGY-OBJECT-MIB, POWER-ATTRIBUTES-MIB and IANAPowerStateSet-MIB modules for monitoring power, Power States, energy and AC power quality of networked devices via SNMP.

MIB.why: The document's main content is SMIv2 MIB modules, which is exactly what the MIB tag covers.
MIB.quote: The Energy Monitoring MIB has two independent MIB modules: ENERGY-OBJECT-MIB and POWER-ATTRIBUTES-MIB.
MIB.section: 5. Architecture Concepts Applied to the MIB Modules

energy management.why: The MIB's purpose is monitoring and controlling power and energy of devices. This is the Energy Management Framework's subject area.
energy management.quote: The MIB modules in this document are designed to provide a model for energy management, which includes monitoring for Power State and energy consumption of networked elements.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB objects. The document defines MIB modules, not new protocol behaviour, so MIB is the better tag.
It creates an IANA-maintained PowerStateSet MIB module and registry, but this is a small part of the document and sits in boilerplate-like IANA sections.
The document uses SMIv2, not YANG.
The Power-over-Ethernet and LLDP-MED MIBs are only discussed as related MIBs for linkage, not specified here.

RFC7461.title: Energy Object Context MIB
RFC7461.summary: Defines the ENERGY-OBJECT-CONTEXT-MIB and IANA-ENERGY-RELATION-MIB SNMP MIB modules for identifying Energy Objects, reporting their context, and describing metering, power-source and aggregation relationships between them, as part of the EMAN work.

MIB.why: The document's main content is SMIv2 MIB modules (eoTable, eoRelationTable, textual conventions, IANA-maintained module). Readers browsing MIB modules would expect it.
MIB.quote: This document defines a subset of a Management Information Base (MIB) for energy management of devices.

energy management.why: It is an EMAN standard covering energy object identification, context and relationships. The taxonomy has no 'energy management' tag, so the closest fit is the topic 'energy management'.
energy management.quote: The focus of the MIB module specified in this document is on the identification of Energy Objects and reporting the context and relationships of Energy Objects

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself.
UUIDs are used as identifiers for relationships, but the document defines nothing new about UUIDs.
eoMgmtDNSName only reuses the DNS name encoding.
Power over Ethernet and LLDP are only linked to via index objects, not specified.
The data model is SMIv2 MIB, not YANG.
The IANA-maintained module is a small part and the IANA considerations are boilerplate; the subject is the MIB itself.

RFC7462.title: URNs for the Alert-Info Header Field of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC7462.summary: Defines a new "alert" URN namespace and IANA registries for use in the SIP Alert-Info header field, and updates RFC 3261 to allow Alert-Info in non-100 provisional responses and proxy modification.

SIP.why: The document updates RFC 3261 and specifies Alert-Info header behaviour for UAs and proxies in SIP, so SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: This specification changes the usage of the Alert-Info header field defined in [RFC3261] by additionally allowing its use in any non-100 provisional response to INVITE.

URN.why: It registers a new URN namespace with syntax, registry, extension and private-name rules, making it a URN namespace definition.
URN.quote: this specification defines the new URN namespace "alert" for the SIP Alert-Info header field

rejected.why: IANA registries are created, but this is boilerplate-like registration for the namespace itself, not a document about IANA guidance.
Accessibility for deaf and hard-of-hearing users is a motivation, not the main subject.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommendation.
ABNF is only the notation used for the URN syntax.
PSTN country ringback tones are a use case, but the document is not about gateway interworking.

RFC7463.title: Shared Appearances of a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Address of Record (AOR)
RFC7463.summary: Specifies the shared appearances (BLA/SCA) telephony feature for a SIP AOR, defining dialog event package extensions (appearance, exclusive, joined-dialog, replaced-dialog), an Alert-Info appearance parameter, and Appearance Agent and UA behaviour.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP (updates RFC 3261 and 4235) with a new Alert-Info parameter, an Event header parameter and dialog package extensions to implement shared line appearances.
SIP.quote: This document discusses use cases, lists requirements, and defines extensions to implement this feature.

SIMPLE.why: A large part of the document extends the SIP dialog event package using SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY/PUBLISH with a State Agent and Event State Compositor, which is SIP event-package work.
SIMPLE.quote: This specification defines four new elements as extensions to the SIP Dialog Event package [RFC4235].

rejected.why: The XML schema only encodes the dialog package extensions; XML is the encoding substrate, not the subject.
TLS is mentioned only as a hop-by-hop confidentiality option in Security Considerations.
SDP appears only inside example INVITE messages.
The IANA section registers parameters and a namespace but the document is not about IANA practice.
SIP is the more specific tag that fits.

gaps.name: SIP event packages / dialog event package
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SIP event notification or the dialog event package. SIMPLE is the closest fit, but it is oriented to presence and instant messaging.

RFC7464.title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Text Sequences
RFC7464.summary: Defines the JSON text sequence format (RS-prefixed, LF-terminated UTF-8 JSON texts) with parsing and encoding rules and registers the application/json-seq media type.

JSON.why: The document specifies a new JSON-based format for sequences of JSON texts, including parsing and truncation handling, so readers of JSON formats would want it.
JSON.quote: This document describes the concept and format of "JSON text sequences", which are specifically not JSON texts themselves but are composed of (possible) JSON texts.

rejected.why: It registers application/json-seq, but that is in IANA Considerations boilerplate. The body is about the format itself.
UTF-8 is required as the encoding, but the document only relies on it and defines nothing new about it.
ABNF is used as the notation for the grammar, not as the subject of the document.
ASCII RS and LF are used as delimiters, but the document is not about ASCII.

RFC7465.title: Prohibiting RC4 Cipher Suites
RFC7465.summary: RFC 7465 prohibits TLS clients and servers from offering or negotiating RC4 cipher suites in any TLS version, updating RFCs 5246, 4346 and 2246, and lists the affected suites.

RC4.why: The whole document deprecates RC4 cipher suites in TLS and cites the keystream biases that make RC4 insecure, which is the RC4 tag's stated scope (its cipher suites in TLS and their deprecation).
RC4.quote: TLS clients MUST NOT include RC4 cipher suites in the ClientHello message.

TLS.why: It changes TLS negotiation behaviour for clients and servers and updates the TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 specifications, so it belongs on the TLS page.
TLS.quote: TLS servers MUST NOT select an RC4 cipher suite when a TLS client sends such a cipher suite in the ClientHello message.

rejected.why: The RC4 tag already sits under cryptography and covers the cipher, so the parent is implied.
Some listed suites use MD5 as a MAC, but the document is not about MD5.
The KRB5 cipher suites appear only in the Appendix A list of RC4 suites. The document is not about Kerberos.
RSA key exchange appears only in the names of the listed suites.

RFC7466.title: An Optimization for the Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP)
RFC7466.summary: RFC 7466 optionally updates NHDP (RFC 6130) and OLSRv2 (RFC 7181) so that symmetric 2-hop neighbor tuples are retained but ignored when link quality drops below threshold, via a new N2_lost flag.

NHDP.why: The document modifies NHDP's 2-Hop Tuples, HELLO processing and information base rules, so it is directly about NHDP.
NHDP.quote: This specification updates RFC 6130 "Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP)"

OLSR.why: Section 5 specifies changes to OLSRv2 (RFC 7181) so it ignores 2-hop tuples with N2_lost = true. The only OLSR tag in the taxonomy is OLSR, and the document formally updates RFC 7181.
OLSR.quote: For [RFC7181], given that this protocol uses 2-hop information for Multipoint Relay (MPR) Set and Routing Set calculation

rejected.why: It is the parent of NHDP and OLSR, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The NHDP-MIB is mentioned only as an informative reference that reflects the new state. The document does not define MIB objects.

RFC7467.title: URN Namespace for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)
RFC7467.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace identifier "nato" under RFC 3406, used to name XML artefacts for NATO message text formats and service specifications.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration, defining the NID, syntax, assignment, persistence and resolution rules for urn:nato.
URN.quote: This document allocates a formal Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for assignment by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), as specified in RFC 3406.

rejected.why: XML artefacts are what the URNs will name, but the document specifies no XML format or usage; it only defines a URN namespace.
The IANA registration of the NID is boilerplate for a namespace registration. The document is not about IANA registries in general.
The document cites the generic URI syntax only as a normative reference. It is about a URN namespace, which the more specific URN tag covers.

RFC7468.title: Textual Encodings of PKIX, PKCS, and CMS Structures
RFC7468.summary: Standards-track document specifying the de facto PEM-style textual (base64 with BEGIN/END boundary) encodings and labels for PKIX certificates, CRLs, PKCS #10/#7/#8, CMS, attribute certificates, and public keys.

PKI.why: The whole document defines text encodings and labels for PKI objects (certificates, CRLs, certification requests, keys, attribute certificates), so PKI readers would want it.
PKI.quote: This document describes and discusses the textual encodings of the Public-Key Infrastructure X.509 (PKIX), Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS), and Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

X.509.why: Substantial parts cover textual encoding of X.509 certificates, CRLs and SubjectPublicKeyInfo from RFC 5280.
X.509.quote: Public-key certificates are encoded using the "CERTIFICATE" label.  The encoded data MUST be a BER (DER strongly preferred; see Appendix B) encoded ASN.1 Certificate structure

CMS.why: Defines the CMS and PKCS #7 textual encodings and labels, with guidance to prefer CMS.
CMS.quote: Cryptographic Message Syntax structures are encoded using the "CMS" label.  The encoded data MUST be a BER-encoded ASN.1 ContentInfo structure

Base64.why: The document defines the framing, line wrapping, and ABNF of base64-based textual encoding, which Base64 readers would find relevant.
Base64.quote: Between these lines, or "encapsulation boundaries", are base64-encoded data according to Section 4 of [RFC4648].

rejected.why: ASN.1 BER/DER structures are the payload being encoded; the document defines text armor, not ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
PEM is historic background and the origin of the format, but the document defines a distinct textual encoding rather than specifying PEM.
ABNF is used only as a notation for the grammar.
OpenPGP ASCII armor is mentioned only as a related variation.

gaps.name: PEM-style textual encoding / ASCII armor
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PEM-style textual encapsulation of binary data, which is the main subject of this document.

RFC7469.title: Public Key Pinning Extension for HTTP
RFC7469.summary: Defines the HTTP Public-Key-Pins and Public-Key-Pins-Report-Only header fields (HPKP) by which hosts tell user agents to pin SPKI fingerprints in their TLS certificate chains, with UA processing, validation, and JSON failure reporting.

web security.why: HPKP is a web platform security mechanism like HSTS. No narrower web-security child tag fits it, so the parent topic applies.
web security.quote: This document defines a new HTTP header that allows web host operators to instruct user agents to remember ("pin") the hosts' cryptographic identities

HTTP.why: The document specifies new HTTP response header fields, their syntax and processing, so it extends HTTP.
HTTP.quote: The "Public-Key-Pins" and "Public-Key-Pins-Report-Only" header fields, also referred to within this specification as the PKP and PKP-RO header fields

rejected.why: HPKP is meant to be used alongside HSTS and refers to it, but the document does not specify or extend HSTS.
Pin validation happens during TLS connection setup, but TLS is the substrate. No TLS extension or protocol change is defined.
Pins are SPKI hashes of X.509 certificates, but the document defines no certificate profile or format; X.509 is only the thing being pinned.
Cookies are mentioned only in a security-considerations note on cookie scoping.
Certificate transparency is only cited as a way to detect misissuance.
JSON is only the encoding of the failure report.

gaps.name: Public key pinning (HPKP)
gaps.why: No tag covers certificate or public-key pinning. The closest match, 'web security', is a broad parent.

RFC7470.title: Conveying Vendor-Specific Constraints in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol
RFC7470.summary: RFC 7470 defines a Vendor Information object and a VENDOR-INFORMATION TLV for PCEP so vendor-specific constraints and metrics can be carried in path computation messages. It obsoletes RFC 7150 by clarifying TLV use and changing the object's code point.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP, the PCE communication protocol, with a new object and TLV and specifies the procedures for PCCs and PCEs that handle them.
PCE.quote: This document defines a facility to carry vendor-specific information in PCEP using a dedicated object and a new Type-Length-Value (TLV)

rejected.why: RBNF is only the notation used to write the PCReq and PCRep message encodings. The document is not about it.
The IANA section only records the object and TLV code point assignments. That is boilerplate, not the subject.
The MIB is mentioned only in the management considerations, which advise against extending it. It is not the subject.
The parent topic is implied by the PCE tag. The document is specifically about PCEP.
PCEP runs over TCP, but the document says nothing new about TCP.

RFC7471.title: OSPF Traffic Engineering (TE) Metric Extensions
RFC7471.summary: Defines new OSPFv2/OSPFv3 TE Link TLV sub-TLVs (types 27-33) to advertise link delay, delay variation, loss, and residual/available/utilized bandwidth, plus rules for thresholds, suppression and stability.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 TE (RFC 3630) and OSPFv3 TE (RFC 5329) with new sub-TLVs in the Link TLV, so it is about OSPF.
OSPF.quote: This document defines new OSPF TE sub-TLVs that are used to distribute network performance information.
OSPF.section: 3. TE Metric Extensions to OSPF TE

traffic engineering.why: The extensions distribute TE link metrics for constrained path computation (CSPF, RSVP-TE, PCE), so TE readers would want it.
traffic engineering.quote: The information distributed using OSPF TE Metric Extensions can then be used to make path selection decisions based on network performance.

rejected.why: The document covers both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 in common, not OSPFv3 specifically, so the parent OSPF fits better.
RSVP-TE is only mentioned as a consumer of the distributed data and in the bandwidth definitions. The document does not specify it.
A PCE is mentioned only as a possible user of the data. The document does not cover it.
The document explicitly places measurement methods out of scope and only covers how the values are distributed.
ALTO is mentioned only as a possible consumer of the data.
MPLS appears as background context for LSP use cases. The document is not about MPLS.

RFC7472.title: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) over HTTPS Transport Binding and the 'ipps' URI Scheme
RFC7472.summary: Defines the IPP over HTTPS transport binding and the 'ipps' URI scheme for secure Internet Printing Protocol services, updating RFC 2910 and RFC 2911.

IPP.why: The document specifies a new IPP transport binding and updates RFC 2910/2911, so IPP readers need it.
IPP.quote: This document defines the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) over HTTPS transport binding and the corresponding 'ipps' URI scheme

URI.why: A substantial part defines and registers a new URI scheme: syntax, default port, encoding, comparison rules.
URI.quote: The 'ipps' URI scheme syntax in ABNF [STD68] is defined as follows:

rejected.why: HTTP/HTTPS is only the substrate the binding runs over; no new HTTP semantics are defined.
TLS 1.2 is required as the security mechanism but nothing new is defined about TLS.
The security is transport-level for printing, not a web platform mechanism.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.
TCP is only mentioned as the underlying connection and port 631 usage; not the subject.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has IPP under applications, with the id 'IPP'; no gap. However, printing as a general topic has no separate tag, which is fine since IPP covers it.

RFC7473.title: Controlling State Advertisements of Non-negotiated LDP Applications
RFC7473.summary: RFC 7473 defines an LDP State Advertisement Control capability TLV that lets an LDP speaker tell its peer it is not interested in IP prefix LSP and L2VPN P2P PW state, avoiding unnecessary advertisements, at session setup or dynamically.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with a new Capability Parameter TLV (SAC, 0x050D) and procedures for Initialization and Capability messages.
LDP.quote: a new capability TLV is defined as follows

rejected.why: P2P PW FEC 128/129 state is one of the applications whose advertisement is controlled, but the document does not specify pseudowire signalling itself.
LDP is under MPLS, but the more specific LDP tag fits the document.
L2VPN PW signalling is only an affected application, not the subject.
IPv4/IPv6 prefix LSP distinction is just an application type selector, not about IPv6.

gaps.name: LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) capabilities
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an LDP tag only as a child of MPLS in the form 'LDP'; checked below. No gap beyond that.

RFC7474.title: Security Extension for OSPFv2 When Using Manual Key Management
RFC7474.summary: Defines a new OSPFv2 authentication type (3) with 64-bit extended sequence numbers (boot count plus counter), key selection from a key table, and inclusion of the IP source address in the HMAC computation, to stop replay and IP-header attacks under manual keying.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication: a new AuType, packet format change, extended sequence numbers, and a modified Apad. It updates RFC 2328 and RFC 5709.
OSPF.quote: This document defines changes to the authentication sequence number mechanism that will protect OSPFv2 from both inter-session and intra-session replay attacks

routing security.why: It secures a routing protocol against replay and source-address spoofing attacks as part of the KARP effort. Readers of routing security would want it.
routing security.quote: This document rectifies the manual key management procedure that currently exists within OSPFv2, as part of Phase 1 of the KARP Working Group.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA is used as the underlying mechanism per RFC 5709. The document only changes the Apad constant and key preparation, so it is not about HMAC itself.
The SNMPv3 snmpEngineBoots variable is mentioned only as an analogy for the boot count and as an optional source for it.
The document covers key selection from the key table for manual keying. It defines no key establishment or provisioning, so the topic is not a good fit.
The document applies only to OSPFv2.

RFC7475.title: Increasing the Number of Area Directors in an IETF Area
RFC7475.summary: A BCP that updates RFC 2026 and RFC 2418 to change the definition of an IETF Area so it may be managed by one or more Area Directors instead of one or two.

IETF process.why: The document changes IETF process definitions in RFC 2026 and RFC 2418 about how IETF Areas are managed by the IESG.
IETF process.quote: An Area is managed by one or more Area Directors.

rejected.why: NomCom is mentioned only to note that its review of half the IESG positions each year is unchanged; the document is not about NomCom procedures.

RFC7476.title: Information-Centric Networking: Baseline Scenarios
RFC7476.summary: IRTF ICNRG informational document that surveys ICN literature and defines baseline evaluation scenarios (social networking, real-time, mobile, vehicular, DTN, IoT, smart city, etc.) for comparing information-centric networking approaches.

ICN.why: The whole document is about ICN architectures (CCN, NDN, NetInf, PSI, DONA) and the scenarios used to evaluate and compare them.
ICN.quote: establishing a common understanding about a set of scenarios that can be used as a base for the evaluation of different information-centric networking (ICN) approaches

DTN.why: Section 2.7 and its subsections cover integrating ICN with delay- and disruption-tolerant networking (ICDTN) and the Bundle Protocol, a substantial part of the document.
DTN.quote: The DTN architecture [RFC4838] is based on a "store, carry, and forward" paradigm

rejected.why: Section 2.6 covers VANETs, but only as an ICN evaluation scenario, not IP in vehicular environments.
Section 2.8 treats IoT as one ICN scenario; the document is not about IoT constrained-device guidance.
Mobile networking is discussed as an ICN scenario, with Mobile IP only as the host-centric comparison.
CDNs appear as a comparison baseline, not as a subject of the document.
Evaluation metrics are mentioned, but methodology is deferred to a separate document.
Energy efficiency is a cross-scenario consideration (Section 3.2) of ICN, not monitoring or management of devices.

RFC7477.title: Child-to-Parent Synchronization in DNS
RFC7477.summary: Defines the CSYNC DNS resource record by which a child zone signals a parental agent to copy NS and glue A/AAAA delegation records into the parent zone, with DNSSEC validation and processing rules.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS RR type, its wire and presentation formats, and the processing of delegation records between child and parent zones.
DNS.quote: This document introduces a new Resource Record Type (RRType) named "CSYNC" that indicates which delegation records published by a child DNS operator should be processed

rejected.why: DNSSEC validation is required as the trust mechanism, but the document does not specify DNSSEC itself; it explicitly does not synchronize DS/DNSKEY records.
Parental agents may be registries or registrars, but the document defines a DNS-based polling mechanism, not registry/registrar protocols.
The parent is updated by the parental agent polling the child, not by dynamic DNS update messages.
IANA registrations (CSYNC type and flags registry) are boilerplate here, not the subject.

RFC7478.title: Web Real-Time Communication Use Cases and Requirements
RFC7478.summary: Informational RFC from the rtcweb WG describing web-based real-time communication use cases (video calls, screen sharing, multiparty, PSTN calls) and deriving browser and API requirements from them.

WebRTC.why: The whole document is the WebRTC use cases and requirements for browser functionality and the web API, so WebRTC is the subject.
WebRTC.quote: This document describes web-based real-time communication use cases. Requirements on the browser functionality are derived from the use cases.

rejected.why: ICE, STUN and TURN are assumed in a few use cases (global provider, enterprise), but the document only sets requirements such as using several servers. It does not specify or extend them.
NAT and firewall traversal appears in several requirements (F2, F18, F21), but it is one part of the WebRTC requirements and not a subject the document addresses on its own.
SIP is mentioned only in a legacy interop requirement (F33) and as a possible non-browser client type. The document does not address it.
A single requirement (F22) and one use case touch QoS differentiation. This is too minor for a tag.
The document never discusses RTP. Its media transport requirements are generic.
Per-packet encryption and integrity are stated as generic requirements (F13) with no mention of SRTP or any specific mechanism.

RFC7479.title: Using Ed25519 in SSHFP Resource Records
RFC7479.summary: Informational RFC that adds SSHFP algorithm number 4 for Ed25519 host keys to the IANA registry and gives an example SSHFP record with a SHA-256 fingerprint.

DNS.why: The document extends the SSHFP DNS resource record with a new algorithm number and gives an example RR. Readers of DNS resource record topics would want it.
DNS.quote: defines a DNS resource record, "SSHFP", which can be used to publish a fingerprint of the SSH server public key in the DNS

SSH.why: The SSHFP record publishes SSH host key fingerprints, and the document covers the Ed25519 SSH host key encoding. SSH readers would want it, though it is mainly a DNS registry update.
SSH.quote: The Ed25519 signature algorithm, specifically Ed25519-SHA-512, has been implemented in OpenSSH.

EdDSA.why: The document is about using Ed25519 public keys in SSHFP records and describes their encoding. This is a use of EdDSA in an Internet protocol.
EdDSA.quote: an Ed25519 public key is a 32-octet value representing a 255-bit y-coordinate of an elliptic curve point
EdDSA.section: 2. Ed25519 Public Key with SHA-256 Fingerprint

rejected.why: DNSSEC is not specified here. The Security Considerations only mention accessing DNS securely.
SHA-256 is only the fingerprint hash used in the example, not the subject of the document.
The registry update is the vehicle for the change. The document is about SSHFP and Ed25519, not IANA policy.
The more specific EdDSA tag covers the Ed25519 content.

RFC7480.title: HTTP Usage in the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP)
RFC7480.summary: RFC 7480 specifies how the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) uses HTTP: methods, Accept headers, response codes, redirects, rate limits, CORS, and an extension registry.

RDAP.why: The document profiles RDAP's HTTP transport behaviour and defines the RDAP Extensions registry, so RDAP readers need it.
RDAP.quote: This document describes the usage of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) [RFC7230] for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP).

HTTP APIs.why: It sets conventions for building a REST-style API on HTTP: method use, status codes, 429 rate limiting, redirects, CORS and extensibility.
HTTP APIs.quote: tie together usage patterns of HTTP into a common profile applicable to the various types of directory services serving registration data

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate. The document profiles its use for RDAP and does not extend HTTP itself, so HTTP APIs is the better fit.
WHOIS is only the predecessor that RDAP replaces, and it is mentioned for context and in Appendix C.
JSON is only the response encoding. The format is defined elsewhere (RFC 7483).
Section 9.1 only mentions the IRI-to-URI transformation as an internationalization point.
IRIs are mentioned only briefly in the internationalization section.
Cache busting appears only in an informational appendix.

RFC7481.title: Security Services for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP)
RFC7481.summary: RFC 7481 describes how RDAP achieves access control, authentication, authorization, availability, confidentiality and integrity by relying on HTTP and TLS features, including federated authentication options and registration-data privacy threats.

RDAP.why: The whole document specifies the security services of RDAP, so readers of the RDAP subject page need it.
RDAP.quote: This document describes information security services, including access control, authentication, authorization, availability, data confidentiality, and data integrity for RDAP.

federated authentication.why: A dedicated subsection discusses federated authentication for RDAP (OAuth, OpenID, SAML, CA-based certificates).
federated authentication.quote: Federated authentication mechanisms allow clients to use one credential to access multiple RDAP servers and reduce client credential management complexity.

HTTP authentication.why: The document sets requirements for Basic and Digest authentication support by RDAP clients and servers.
HTTP authentication.quote: RDAP clients and servers MUST implement the authentication framework specified in "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Authentication" [RFC7235].

rejected.why: TLS is the mechanism used for confidentiality and integrity, but the document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
WHOIS is only the legacy protocol RDAP is compared against; the document is not about it.
OAuth is mentioned as one possible federation approach and no OAuth profile is defined.
Section 4 covers privacy threats, but it is a short part of a document whose main subject is security services. RDAP and federated authentication cover the focus.
The authorization section is brief and specific to RDAP, and RDAP already covers it.
HTTP is only the substrate RDAP runs over; the document uses its status codes and authentication but does not extend HTTP.

RFC7482.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Query Format
RFC7482.summary: Defines the RDAP query format: uniform HTTP URL path patterns for looking up and searching IP network, AS number, domain, nameserver and entity registration data at RIRs and DNRs, as a replacement for WHOIS.

RDAP.why: The whole document specifies the RDAP query syntax (lookup and search path segments, query processing).
RDAP.quote: These uniform patterns define the query syntax for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP).

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate; the document defines URL patterns for RDAP, not HTTP semantics or extensions.
WHOIS is mentioned as the legacy protocol RDAP replaces, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
IDN label handling (A-labels/U-labels) is applied in queries but the document does not define IDNA itself.
URLs are constructed per RFC 3986, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
JSON response formats are defined in RFC 7483, not here.
EPP is only cited as an example of contact identifier syntax.

RFC7483.title: JSON Responses for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP)
RFC7483.summary: Defines the JSON data structures (object classes for entities, nameservers, domains, IP networks, autnums, plus errors, help, search and truncation) used in RDAP query responses from RIRs and DNRs.

RDAP.why: The document specifies the response format of RDAP, so it belongs on the RDAP page.
RDAP.quote: This document describes JSON data structures representing registration information maintained by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and Domain Name Registries (DNRs).

JSON.why: A substantial part of the document defines JSON data structures, naming and extension rules for members, and a media type registration for application/rdap+json.
JSON.quote: This document describes responses in the JSON [RFC7159] format for the queries as defined by the Registration Data Access Protocol Query Format

rejected.why: The secureDNS member carries DS/DNSKEY data, but it is only a small part of the response model and the document does not specify DNSSEC.
Mentioned only via the port43 member pointing to a WHOIS server; the document is about RDAP, its replacement.
jCard is reused for contact information in entities but is not defined here.
Referenced only for status mapping and motivation; not specified or extended.
HTTP usage is in RFC 7480; this document only defines the JSON bodies.
Variants and LDH/Unicode names appear, but the document does not specify IDN itself.

RFC7484.title: Finding the Authoritative Registration Data (RDAP) Service
RFC7484.summary: Specifies how RDAP clients find the authoritative RDAP server for domains, IP addresses and AS numbers using JSON bootstrap registries created and maintained by IANA.

RDAP.why: The whole document defines RDAP bootstrap: registry structure, matching rules for domains, IPs and AS numbers, and client behaviour. It is an extension to RDAP.
RDAP.quote: This document specifies a method to find which Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) server is authoritative to answer queries for a requested scope

rejected.why: IANA registries are the data source and Section 12 creates them, but the document is about RDAP discovery, not IANA registry guidance.
JSON is only the encoding of the bootstrap registries.
HTTP is only the transport for fetching the registries and RDAP queries. Caching is mentioned briefly, but nothing new is defined for HTTP.
DNS is mentioned only as an optional check for whether a TLD has been delegated.
CIDR prefix notation is used for the IP entries but is not the subject.
RDAP is the specific child tag that fits, so the parent is not needed.

RFC7485.title: Inventory and Analysis of WHOIS Registration Objects
RFC7485.summary: Informational WEIRDS document that inventories and statistically analyses WHOIS response objects from the five RIRs and 124 DNRs (ccTLDs and gTLDs) to serve as input for RDAP data model discussions.

WHOIS.why: The whole document is an inventory and analysis of existing WHOIS output objects and labels across registries, so it belongs on the WHOIS subject page.
WHOIS.quote: WHOIS output objects from registries, including both Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and Domain Name Registries (DNRs), were collected and analyzed.
