RDAP.why: The inventory was created as input for RDAP's data model (RFC 7483) and proposes reference extension objects for RDAP, so RDAP readers would want it.
RDAP.quote: The purpose of this document is to build an object inventory to facilitate discussions of data objects included in Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) responses.

rejected.why: EPP mappings are only used as a reference to classify which objects are public; the document does not specify or analyse EPP.
RPSL is mentioned only as an example of other data structures; the document explicitly excludes analysing RPSL objects.
The more specific WHOIS and RDAP tags already cover the registration data subject.
IDNs are mentioned only as a WHOIS shortcoming in the introduction; the document is not about them.
JSON is mentioned only in passing in connection with RDAP names; the document does not address JSON itself.

RFC7486.title: HTTP Origin-Bound Authentication (HOBA)
RFC7486.summary: Defines HOBA, an experimental HTTP authentication scheme (and JavaScript design pattern) using per-origin client key pairs and digital signatures over a server challenge instead of passwords, plus registration, logout, and challenge-fetch services.

HOBA.why: The document specifies HOBA itself: the auth-scheme, HOBA-TBS and client-result formats, registration, logout and challenge fetching.
HOBA.quote: HTTP Origin-Bound Authentication (HOBA) is a digital-signature-based design for an HTTP authentication method.

rejected.why: Session cookies are the way HOBA hands off to applications (Section 1.1), but the document does not specify or extend cookies.
TLS is required as the secure substrate, and the document defines no TLS extension.
Implied as the parent of HOBA, so it is not listed separately.
RSA-SHA256 is the mandatory-to-implement signature algorithm, but the document only selects it and does not define RSA.
It is referenced only for the hashed public key identifier format in the registry.
RFC 6750 bearer-token security considerations are cited only for replay, and the document is not about OAuth.
HTTP is the substrate, and the document only adds an auth scheme and a header field, which fall under the HOBA child tag.

RFC7487.title: Configuration of Proactive Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Functions for MPLS-Based Transport Networks Using RSVP-TE
RFC7487.summary: Defines RSVP-TE sub-TLVs for configuring proactive MPLS-TP OAM functions (BFD CC/CV, loss/delay performance monitoring, fault management signals) on an LSP, plus new error codes and IANA registries.

MPLS-TP.why: The document specifies how to configure proactive OAM for MPLS Transport Profile LSPs, which is MPLS-TP subject matter.
MPLS-TP.quote: describes the configuration of proactive MPLS-TP OAM functions for a given LSP using TLVs that use GMPLS RSVP-TE

GMPLS.why: It extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signalling with new OAM Configuration sub-TLVs, new OAM type and error codes.
GMPLS.quote: using a set of TLVs that are carried by the GMPLS RSVP-TE protocol based on the OAM Configuration Framework for GMPLS RSVP-TE

BFD.why: A substantial part defines BFD session configuration (identifiers, timers, authentication, encapsulation) for MPLS-TP CC/CV.
BFD.quote: the BFD Configuration Sub-TLV has an Integrity flag that, when set, enables BFD Authentication using Keyed SHA1

performance measurement.why: Defines configuration of loss, delay, jitter and throughput measurement parameters per RFC 6374.
performance measurement.quote: Performance Monitoring Sub-TLV provides the configuration information mentioned in Section 7 of [RFC6374]

rejected.why: Considered as the signalling carrier, but the taxonomy's RSVP-TE tag concerns TE LSP signalling; here it is mainly the substrate, and GMPLS covers the extension.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific tags chosen; no direct topic tag needed.
Not involved; configuration is via signalling TLVs, not data models.
IANA registries are boilerplate-like here and not the document's main subject.
Parent of MPLS-TP, implied by the more specific tag.

gaps.name: MPLS-TP OAM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an OAM topic under network management but no tag specifically for MPLS-TP OAM configuration; MPLS-TP and GMPLS cover it approximately.

RFC7488.title: Port Control Protocol (PCP) Server Selection
RFC7488.summary: RFC 7488 updates PCP (RFC 6887) by specifying how a PCP client selects and contacts PCP servers when configured with one or more server IP addresses, using RFC 6724 address sorting, retransmission limits, and fallback, with multihoming examples.

PCP.why: The whole document specifies PCP client behaviour for server selection and updates the PCP specification RFC 6887.
PCP.quote: This document specifies the behavior to be followed by a Port Control Protocol (PCP) client to contact its PCP server(s) when one or several PCP server IP addresses are configured.

rejected.why: NAT is the function PCP servers control, but the document is about PCP client server selection, not NAT behaviour. PCP is the more specific tag.
Multihoming appears only as an example deployment in the appendix and is not the document's subject.
DHCP is only mentioned as a way to configure server addresses (RFC 7291); the document does not define DHCP options.
RFC 6724 address sorting is reused as a mechanism; the document does not address IP address architecture.
IPv6 appears only in the examples and RFC 6724 sorting, not as a subject.

RFC7489.title: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)
RFC7489.summary: RFC 7489 specifies DMARC, a DNS-published policy and reporting mechanism that lets domain owners tell mail receivers how to handle messages failing SPF/DKIM identifier alignment with the RFC5322.From domain, and defines aggregate and failure reporting.

DMARC.why: The document defines DMARC itself: policy records, identifier alignment, receiver actions, and feedback reporting.
DMARC.quote: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC), a mechanism by which email operators leverage existing authentication and policy advertisement technologies

rejected.why: SPF is one of two underlying authentication inputs DMARC consumes; the document does not specify or extend SPF.
DKIM is an input mechanism that DMARC relies on; only alignment against its d= domain is defined here, not DKIM itself.
DNS is just the substrate for publishing the policy TXT record at _dmarc; no new DNS record type or DNS behaviour is defined.
The AFRF/ARF format is used and slightly augmented (Identity-Alignment field) for failure reports, but this is a minor part of the document and DMARC is the subject.
SMTP is the context for rejection and processing, not something the document specifies or extends.
XML is only the encoding of the aggregate report schema in Appendix C, a substrate rather than the subject.

RFC7490.title: Remote Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) Fast Reroute (FRR)
RFC7490.summary: RFC 7490 extends basic LFA IP fast reroute by tunneling repair traffic to a PQ node (remote LFA) when no local loop-free alternate exists, covering computation, tunnel endpoint selection, LDP operation and topology analysis.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document specifies Remote LFA, an extension of LFA IP fast reroute, including P-space/Q-space computation and repair path selection.
IP fast reroute.quote: an extension to the basic IP fast reroute mechanism, described in RFC 5286, that provides additional backup connectivity for point-to-point link failures

rejected.why: Targeted LDP is used to learn labels at the PQ node, but LDP is only the substrate for the repair tunnel; no new LDP behaviour is defined.
The label-stack repair tunnel in MPLS networks is one deployment option, not the subject.
Repair tunnels are central, but the choice of tunnel mechanism is explicitly out of scope.
OSPF and IS-IS overload behaviour is mentioned only for interaction with repair path computation.
The IS-IS overload bit is only mentioned in the interaction section, not specified or extended.
Mentioned only as an out-of-scope alternative for extended repair.

gaps.name: IP Fast Reroute / Loop-Free Alternates (LFA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IP fast reroute. I used the tag id 'IP fast reroute' and it does not appear in the taxonomy, so it is invalid. The closest tag, 'IP fast reroute', is the one the taxonomy lists as 'IP and LDP fast reroute, loop-free alternates', so check the id spelling against the taxonomy before accepting this result.

RFC7491.title: A PCE-Based Architecture for Application-Based Network Operations
RFC7491.summary: RFC 7491 describes the ABNO architecture, a PCE-centred framework of existing components (ABNO Controller, PCE, TED, VNTM, ALTO Server, I2RS client, OAM handler, Provisioning Manager) for application-driven network operations, with use cases.

PCE.why: The architecture is PCE-based. PCE, stateful/active PCE, hierarchical PCE and PCEP are central to the components, interfaces and use cases.
PCE.quote: The Path Computation Element (PCE) [RFC4655] was developed to provide path computation services for GMPLS- and MPLS-controlled networks.

traffic engineering.why: Use cases cover GCO, make-before-break reoptimization, multi-layer inter-layer TE, and a TED/LSP-DB. These are traffic engineering subjects beyond PCE itself.
traffic engineering.quote: Global Concurrent Optimization (GCO) is defined in [RFC5557] and represents a key technology for maximizing network efficiency by computing a set of traffic-engineered paths concurrently.

ALTO.why: The ALTO Server is an architectural component with its own use case (Section 3.8) on abstract topology, network maps and cost maps.
ALTO.quote: The ALTO Server provides network information to the application layer based on abstract maps of a network region.

SDN.why: The document is an architecture for application-driven programmatic control of networks, using controllers, OpenFlow and I2RS, so it fits the SDN topic.
SDN.quote: ABNO is compatible with pre-existing Network Management System (NMS) and Operations Support System (OSS) deployments as well as with more recent developments in programmatic networks such as Software-Defined Networking (SDN).

I2RS.why: The I2RS client is an architectural component, and I2RS is repeatedly proposed as the protocol for several undefined interfaces.
I2RS.quote: The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) is described in [I2RS-Arch].
I2RS.section: 2.3.1.5. Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) Client

rejected.why: Used in the multi-layer and optical use cases, but the document is not about GMPLS itself.
Section 3.6 is one use case among many. Pseudowires are not the document's subject.
Listed as one candidate configuration protocol among many; not specified or analysed here.
Mentioned as the signalling used for LSP setup and make-before-break; it is substrate, not subject.
Named as one of several provisioning mechanisms; not the subject.
The OAM Handler is a component, but OAM mechanisms themselves are not the subject.

gaps.name: Application-Based Network Operations (ABNO)
gaps.why: The document defines this architecture, but the taxonomy has no tag for it. Closest are PCE, SDN and traffic engineering.

RFC7492.title: Analysis of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Security According to the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) Design Guidelines
RFC7492.summary: Informational gap analysis of BFD's authentication and replay protection against the KARP design guidelines (RFC 6518), covering weak MD5/SHA-1, replay exposure, echo mode, and CPU cost, with suggested improvements such as GMAC.

BFD.why: The whole document analyses BFD's security: its authentication mechanisms, sequence numbers, discriminators and echo mode, and where they fall short.
BFD.quote: This document performs a gap analysis of the current state of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection [RFC5880] according to the requirements of KARP Design Guidelines [RFC6518].

routing security.why: This is a KARP analysis of securing routing infrastructure. It covers authentication strength, replay protection and DoS resistance for a protocol that routing protocols depend on.
routing security.quote: BFD therefore needs to match the routing protocols in its strength of algorithm.

rejected.why: MD5 is discussed only as a weak algorithm used in BFD keyed authentication. The document is not about MD5 itself.
SHA-1 and SHA-2 are mentioned as BFD authentication algorithms. The document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
HMAC-SHA-2 for BFD is referenced as a solution proposed in other drafts. This document does not define or analyse it.
GMAC as used in IPsec is cited only as a candidate MAC function, so IPsec is not a subject of the document.
The broader authentication topic is covered by routing security and BFD, which are more specific fits.

gaps.name: KARP (Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols)
gaps.why: The document is part of the KARP series, and the taxonomy has no KARP tag. The routing security tag is the closest fit.

RFC7493.title: The I-JSON Message Format
RFC7493.summary: RFC 7493 defines I-JSON, a restricted profile of JSON with constraints on encoding, numbers, and object members, plus protocol design recommendations for interoperable JSON use.

JSON.why: The document specifies a JSON-based message format profile, with constraints on UTF-8 encoding, numbers and duplicate member names, so it belongs on the JSON page.
JSON.quote: I-JSON (short for "Internet JSON") is a restricted profile of JSON designed to maximize interoperability

rejected.why: UTF-8 is required as the encoding, but the document does not define or specify it; it is relied on as a substrate.
Section 4.3 recommends RFC 3339 timestamps, but this is a brief recommendation, not a substantial part of the document.
Section 4.4 recommends base64url for binary data in one sentence; it is only a use of the encoding.
The surrogate and noncharacter restrictions are part of the JSON profile and do not make the document about Unicode usage in general.

RFC7494.title: IEEE 802.11 Medium Access Control (MAC) Profile for Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP)
RFC7494.summary: Defines CAPWAP IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile message elements (Supported MAC Profiles and MAC Profile) so the AC and WTP unambiguously agree whether Split MAC encryption is at the WTP or AC.

CAPWAP.why: The document extends the CAPWAP IEEE 802.11 binding with new message elements (types 1060, 1061) and a profile negotiation exchange between WTP and AC.
CAPWAP.quote: this specification defines an IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile message element in which each profile specifies an unambiguous division of encryption functionality between the WTP and AC

rejected.why: The IEEE 802.11 MAC is the subject of the CAPWAP binding, but the document is about CAPWAP WTP/AC functional split, not IP over 802.11; CAPWAP is the more specific tag.
IEEE 802.1X/EAP appears only as a row in the function-split tables, with no change to it.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here, not the main subject.
802.11 QoS functions are only table rows in the split description.

RFC7495.title: Enumeration Reference Format for the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF)
RFC7495.summary: Defines a stand-alone XML ReferenceName format (specIndex plus ID) for referencing external enumerations such as CVE within IODEF, and creates an IANA registry of external enumeration specifications.

IODEF.why: The document extends IODEF's Reference class with a structured ReferenceName format for enumeration references, used in IODEF v2.
IODEF.quote: This document establishes a stand-alone data format to include both the external specification and specific enumeration identification value

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document defines a new registry with fields, allocation policy and expert review guidance for external enumeration specifications.
IANA.quote: IANA has created and maintains the following registry: Name of the Registry: "Security External Enumeration Registry"

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for the schema; the document is about the IODEF enumeration reference format, not XML usage in general.
ABNF is used only to define registry field syntax; it is not a subject of the document.
Parent of IODEF, which is the more specific tag and already implied.
URIs appear only as registry fields pointing to specifications; the document does not address URI matters.

gaps.name: Security automation enumerations (CVE, CCE, CPE)
gaps.why: The document concerns referencing security enumeration identifiers such as CVE, but the taxonomy has no tag for vulnerability or security enumeration formats.

RFC7496.title: Additional Policies for the Partially Reliable Stream Control Transmission Protocol Extension
RFC7496.summary: Defines two new PR-SCTP policies (Limited Retransmissions and Priority) extending RFC 3758, plus informational sockets API extensions for them and for PR-SCTP status and support.

SCTP.why: The document extends the SCTP Partial Reliability extension with new policies governing message abandonment, which is SCTP protocol behaviour.
SCTP.quote: This document specifies the following two additional PR-SCTP policies:

sockets API.why: A substantial section defines new socket options (SCTP_PR_STREAM_STATUS, SCTP_PR_ASSOC_STATUS, SCTP_PR_SUPPORTED) and policy constants for the SCTP sockets API.
sockets API.quote: This section describes how the socket API defined in [RFC6458] is extended to support the newly defined PR-SCTP policies

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an example of where the Priority Policy could be used; the document is not about IPFIX.
WebRTC data channels are cited only as an example user of the Limited Retransmissions Policy.
DTLS over SCTP appears only in Security Considerations as an alternative for securing PR-SCTP.
The text only notes that the sender still adapts the congestion window on retransmission events. It does not address congestion control itself.

RFC7497.title: Rate Measurement Test Protocol Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC7497.summary: Problem statement and requirements for test protocols (e.g., OWAMP/TWAMP) to perform active access-rate measurement, including asymmetric rate and packet-size control and stream-generation categories.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines requirements for active network rate/capacity measurement in the IPPM framework, so performance measurement is the subject.
performance measurement.quote: This memo presents a problem statement for access rate measurement for test protocols to measure IP Performance Metrics (IPPM).

TWAMP.why: The requirements target two-way test protocols like TWAMP, including a new asymmetric packet-size capability that TWAMP lacks.
TWAMP.quote: the scale and complexity aspects of end-user or aggregated access measurement clearly favor two-way (with a low-complexity user-end device and round-trip results collection, as found in [RFC5357])

OWAMP.why: OWAMP is a named one-way test protocol for which the requirements apply, including results collection in a one-way architecture.

rejected.why: TCP open-loop sender requirements are discussed, but TCP is only one transport option for test streams, not the subject.
UDP is only the transport of test packets.
Mentioned only as a reason test traffic must resemble user traffic.
LMAP is cited only for privacy considerations in the security section.
Traffic management of user vs test traffic is mentioned in passing; the document is about rate measurement, not QoS.

RFC7498.title: Problem Statement for Service Function Chaining
RFC7498.summary: Problem statement for service function chaining (SFC), describing the topology-coupled deployment problems of service functions such as firewalls and load balancers and identifying service overlay, classification and SFC encapsulation as areas for the SFC working group.

SFC.why: The whole document is the SFC problem statement, covering the problem space and key areas (service overlay, classification, SFC encapsulation) for the SFC working group.
SFC.quote: The term "service function chaining" is used to describe the definition and instantiation of an ordered list of instances of such service functions

rejected.why: Service overlays are discussed, but only as an SFC concept built on whatever overlay or underlay the operator prefers; VXLAN and similar are named as transports, not specified.
NAT44 and NAT64 appear only as examples of service functions.
Firewalls are an example service function whose deployment is problematic. The document does not address firewall security.
VXLAN is mentioned only as one possible transport for the service overlay.
OAM status is mentioned only briefly as information the SFC encapsulation can carry.

RFC7499.title: Support of Fragmentation of RADIUS Packets
RFC7499.summary: Experimental RFC specifying how RADIUS clients and servers fragment large authorization data across multiple Access-Request/Access-Accept exchanges using new Frag-Status and Proxy-State-Length attributes, a T flag for Long Extended attributes, and State/Service-Type handling, transparent to legacy proxies.

RADIUS.why: The document extends RADIUS with new attributes, a new Service-Type value, and a chunking procedure for packets, so it belongs on the RADIUS page.
RADIUS.quote: This document provides a mechanism to allow RADIUS peers to exchange large amounts of authorization data exceeding the 4096-byte limit by fragmenting it across several exchanges.

rejected.why: EAP-over-RADIUS fragmentation is mentioned only as an existing mechanism that this document does not modify. The document is not about EAP.
RADIUS/UDP is the substrate. The document only notes that it keeps the existing lock-step behaviour and does not specify anything new about UDP.
RADIUS is the more specific tag for this document, so the AAA parent is implied and not listed separately.
PMTU is mentioned only as a factor in chunk size. The document does not address Path MTU Discovery itself.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate registration of attributes and values, so it is not evidence for this tag.
RADIUS/TCP and the bigger-packets draft are mentioned only as alternatives. The document does not specify or analyse them.

RFC7500.title: Principles for Operation of Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Registries
RFC7500.summary: IAB informational RFC setting out principles (uniqueness, stability, predictability, public, open, transparent, accountable) for the operation of IANA protocol parameter registries.

IANA.why: The whole document is about how IANA registries should be operated and overseen, including stewardship and accountability.
IANA.quote: This document provides principles for the operation of Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) registries.

rejected.why: The IANA tag is more specific and fits; the parent is implied.
IAOC/IAB oversight and Nomcom are mentioned only as accountability mechanisms, not the subject.
Nomcom is only cited as how IAB/IAOC are held accountable.
Number registries and RIRs are mentioned only as an example of a delegated registry oversight model.

RFC7501.title: Terminology for Benchmarking Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Devices: Basic Session Setup and Registration
RFC7501.summary: RFC 7501 defines terminology, test components, setup parameters and benchmarks (Session Establishment Rate, Registration Rate) for black-box benchmarking of SIP signaling performance on devices such as proxies, registrars and SBCs.

SIP.why: The DUTs are SIP proxies, registrars, B2BUAs and SBCs, and the benchmarks measure SIP INVITE and REGISTER signaling capacity. Readers of SIP would want this document.
SIP.quote: This document provides a terminology for benchmarking the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) performance of devices.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking terminology following the RFC 1242 template. It defines Device Under Test, test setup parameters and benchmarks, and no technology tag covers benchmarking.
benchmarking.quote: The intent of the two documents is to provide a normalized set of tests that will enable an objective comparison of the capacity of SIP devices.

rejected.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking terminology for devices in a lab; the benchmarking tag fits more specifically.
Media is only used to observe its effect on signaling; media performance is explicitly out of scope.
SDP is mentioned only as part of the signaling plane and to define Associated Media; it is not specified or extended.
Presence and subscribe-notify benchmarking are explicitly out of scope.
SCTP is only one of the SIP transports to be recorded as a test condition.
TLS is listed only as a possible transport value to record.

RFC7502.title: Methodology for Benchmarking Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Devices: Basic Session Setup and Registration
RFC7502.summary: RFC 7502 specifies a methodology for benchmarking SIP devices (proxies, registrars, SBCs) for session establishment rate and registration rate, including test topologies, parameters, a rate-finding algorithm, and reporting formats.

SIP.why: The document defines test cases for SIP session setup and registration on SIP proxies, registrars and SBCs, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document provides a methodology for benchmarking the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) performance of devices.

benchmarking.why: It is a benchmarking methodology document with a DUT, test topologies, a rate-finding algorithm and reporting formats.
benchmarking.quote: The intent of the two documents is to provide a normalized set of tests that will enable an objective comparison of the capacity of SIP devices.

rejected.why: TLS is only one transport configuration under test; the document defines nothing new about TLS.
IPsec-encrypted SIP is a single test case. The document is not about IPsec itself.
RTP/SRTP appear only as optional associated media, and the media itself is out of scope.
The more specific benchmarking tag fits better than this parent topic.
SDP is not discussed in the document.

RFC7503.title: OSPFv3 Autoconfiguration
RFC7503.summary: RFC 7503 specifies mechanisms for OSPFv3 to self-configure (defaults, relaxed Hello/RouterDead interval checking, router ID selection, duplicate Router ID detection via a new Autoconfiguration LSA, and hysteresis for self-originated LSAs), updating RFC 5340 for use in IPv6 home networks.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends and updates OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) with autoconfiguration, a new AC LSA and TLVs, relaxed timer checks and LSA hysteresis.
OSPFv3.quote: This document describes the necessary mechanisms for OSPFv3 to be self-configuring.

home networking.why: The motivating use case is home networks (HOMENET origin, CPE guidance, back-to-back Ethernet), so readers of home networking would want it.
home networking.quote: One such environment is the IPv6 home network where users expect to simply plug in a router and have it automatically use OSPFv3

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is the more specific child tag; the OSPFv2 content is referenced only as the base specification.
IPv6 is the environment OSPFv3 runs in; SLAAC DAD and link-local addresses are only referenced, not specified.
Only referenced for duplicate address detection before adjacency formation; not the subject.
Although about self-configuration, it concerns OSPFv3-specific autoconfiguration, not the autonomic networking framework.
OSPFv3 IPsec and Authentication Trailer are mentioned as authentication options, but are out of scope.
IANA section registers an LSA function code and a TLV registry; this is boilerplate, not the main subject.

RFC7504.title: SMTP 521 and 556 Reply Codes
RFC7504.summary: Defines two new SMTP reply codes, 521 (host does not accept mail, at connection time) and 556 (domain does not accept mail, e.g. via null MX), updating RFC 5321 and ending the RFC 1846 experiment.

SMTP.why: The document extends SMTP by adding two reply codes and amending RFC 5321's reply code lists and command-reply sequences.
SMTP.quote: This specification adds the 521 reply code to the repertoire specified in SMTP, reserving it for use at connection-opening time

rejected.why: The null MX record is only mentioned as one way a relay can learn a domain accepts no mail; the DNS record itself is defined in RFC 7505.
The parent of SMTP, which is implied by the SMTP tag.
The IANA section only updates an existing enhanced status codes registry entry, which is boilerplate.

RFC7505.title: A "Null MX" No Service Resource Record for Domains That Accept No Mail
RFC7505.summary: Defines the "null MX" record (MX preference 0 with root label ".") by which a domain declares it accepts no email, with SMTP rejection behaviour and new enhanced status codes.

SMTP.why: Specifies how SMTP clients and servers treat null MX, including the reply codes and enhanced status codes. This changes mail relaying behaviour.
SMTP.quote: When a submission or SMTP relay server rejects an envelope recipient due to a domain's null MX record, it SHOULD use a 556 reply code

DNS.why: Defines a new usage convention for the MX resource record in the DNS. It is the core of the document.
DNS.quote: a single MX RR (see Section 3.3.9 of [RFC1035]) with an RDATA section consisting of preference number 0 and a zero-length label

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as an optional way to secure the record.
SPF is mentioned in one sentence as a way to declare that a domain sends no mail. The document is not about it.
SMTP is the more specific tag and is already chosen.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate. They only add two enhanced status codes.

RFC7506.title: IPv6 Router Alert Option for MPLS Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM)
RFC7506.summary: Allocates IPv6 Router Alert Option value 69 for MPLS OAM (e.g., LSP Ping/Traceroute) and updates RFC 4379 to require it for IPv6 headers.

router alert.why: The document's sole purpose is defining a new IPv6 Router Alert Option value, so it belongs on the router alert page.
router alert.quote: This document defines a new Option Value (69) for the IPv6 RAO to alert transit routers to examine the packet more closely for MPLS OAM purposes.
router alert.section: 3. IPv6 RAO Value for MPLS OAM

MPLS.why: It updates RFC 4379 (MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute) for MPLS in IPv6 environments, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: A commonly deployed MPLS OAM tool is specified in [RFC4379], "Detecting Multi-Protocol Label Switched (MPLS) Data Plane Failures"

OAM.why: The value is a generic code point for any MPLS OAM tool, so the OAM topic applies.
OAM.quote: this value is applicable to all MPLS OAM and not limited to MPLS LSP Ping/ Traceroute.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the environment, but the document only allocates one Router Alert value. The router alert tag covers that more specifically.
The code point assignment is IANA boilerplate here and is not the subject of the main body.
MPLS echo messages are UDP-based and are not ICMP.

RFC7507.title: TLS Fallback Signaling Cipher Suite Value (SCSV) for Preventing Protocol Downgrade Attacks
RFC7507.summary: Defines the TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV signalling cipher suite value and inappropriate_fallback alert so TLS/DTLS servers can detect and reject unnecessary client protocol version downgrades.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS with a new cipher suite value and alert, and specifies client and server behaviour for version fallback. It updates the TLS RFCs.
TLS.quote: This document defines a Signaling Cipher Suite Value (SCSV) that prevents protocol downgrade attacks on the Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocols.

rejected.why: DTLS 1.0 and 1.2 are covered, but only as a variant to which the same SCSV applies. The document is about TLS fallback, so TLS is the right tag.
The IANA section registers a cipher suite value and an alert. This is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC7508.title: Securing Header Fields with S/MIME
RFC7508.summary: Experimental RFC defining "Secure Headers", an S/MIME extension that embeds RFC 5322 header fields in a CMS signed attribute (with duplicated/deleted/modified statuses and DCA-based encryption handling) to provide header integrity, non-repudiation and confidentiality.

S/MIME.why: The whole document specifies an extension to S/MIME for protecting header fields, including signing, encryption/decryption processes, and triple wrapping.
S/MIME.quote: This document describes how the S/MIME protocol can be extended in order to secure message header fields defined in RFC 5322.

CMS.why: The mechanism defines a new CMS signed attribute (OID registered) and builds on CMS signature generation and verification, so CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: The message header fields to be secured are integrated in a structure (SecureHeaderFields structure) that is encapsulated in the signed attributes structure of the SignerInfo object.
CMS.section: 4. Mechanisms to Secure Message Header Fields

rejected.why: Discussed as an alternative that does not meet the requirements, and its canonicalization algorithms are reused, but the document is not about DKIM.
The headers being protected are RFC 5322 fields, but the document does not specify or extend the message format itself.
ASN.1 is only used to define the new attribute structure and module; the document is not about ASN.1.
Implied parent of S/MIME's context; the more specific S/MIME tag fits better.
Mentioned only as a recommended channel protection between MUAs and DCAs in Security Considerations.
Mentioned only as a limitation motivating the use of a DCA for encryption and decryption.

RFC7509.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) for Post-Repair Loss Count Metrics
RFC7509.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=33) reporting post-repair loss count and repaired loss count metrics for RTP streams, with SDP signaling and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block with its format, semantics and usage, extending RTCP reporting.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows reporting of a post-repair loss count metric

SDP.why: A dedicated section defines a new SDP rtcp-xr attribute value and offer/answer usage for signaling the block.
SDP.quote: This session augments the SDP attribute "rtcp-xr" defined in Section 5.1 of [RFC3611] by providing an additional value of "xr-format"

rejected.why: RTCP is a child of RTP and is the more specific tag; RTP itself is the substrate.
FEC and retransmission are repair mechanisms whose effectiveness is measured, but the document does not specify or extend them.
The metrics are performance metrics, but the RTCP tag is the more specific fit and the document defines a report block, not measurement methodology generally.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to secure the reports.
IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: RTCP XR (RTP Control Protocol Extended Reports)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no RTCP tag. RTCP is only listed as the parent of nothing but is mentioned in RTP's children; I used RTCP above but it does not appear in the taxonomy, so the nearest fit is RTCP under RTP.

RFC7510.title: Encapsulating MPLS in UDP
RFC7510.summary: RFC 7510 specifies MPLS-in-UDP, a data-plane encapsulation of MPLS packets in UDP (port 6635, with 6636 for DTLS) that uses the UDP source port as entropy for ECMP and LAG load balancing. It also sets congestion and IPv6 zero-checksum usage restrictions.

MPLS.why: The document defines how MPLS label-stack packets are carried over UDP/IP tunnels between LSRs, so it is about MPLS encapsulation.
MPLS.quote: This document specifies an IP-based encapsulation for MPLS, i.e., MPLS-in-UDP

UDP.why: A large part of the document covers UDP usage: the source port as entropy, the allocated destination ports, UDP checksum rules including IPv6 zero-checksum mode, and UDP tunnel congestion considerations.
UDP.quote: By encapsulating the MPLS packets into a UDP tunnel and using the source port of the UDP header as an entropy field

ECMP.why: The main motivation for the encapsulation is to let existing routers load-balance MPLS traffic using the UDP five-tuple hash for ECMP.
ECMP.quote: fine-grained load balancing of MPLS packets over IP networks over Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) and/or Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs) is required

rejected.why: The document is about tunneling, but MPLS and UDP are more specific tags and cover it. No GRE or IP-in-IP tag fits, since GRE is only mentioned for comparison.
DTLS is only an optional security mechanism, with port 6636 allocated for it. The document defines no DTLS extension of its own.
IPsec is mentioned only as a way to secure the tunnel, and the document notes it hides the UDP header.
MPLS-in-GRE is cited only as an existing encapsulation that this document is compared against.
IPv6 matters here only through UDP zero-checksum rules for tunnels. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
The congestion section sets usage restrictions for the tunnel. It does not specify any congestion control mechanism.

RFC7511.title: Scenic Routing for IPv6
RFC7511.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC defining a "Scenic Routing Option" IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option that steers packets over avian carriers and wireless links for maximum fresh-air time.

humor.why: An April 1st parody RFC with whimsical content (pigeons, packets seeing culture), so the humor page is the right home.
humor.quote: in the spirit of "Green IT", whereby packets will be routed to get as much fresh-air time as possible

IPv6.why: The document specifies a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option with its layout and type, so it is about extending IPv6.
IPv6.quote: The Scenic Routing Option (SRO) is placed in the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options Header that must be examined by every node

rejected.why: It is parody path selection through a header option, not a real routing architecture; BGP and OSPF are mentioned only as future work.
Only mentioned in Related Work as a possible extension target; not specified.
Backbone operators are told to keep separate MPLS paths, but this is a passing mention, not the subject.
The 'Green IT' framing is satirical; the document does not address real energy efficiency.
The IANA section is boilerplate and asks for no actions.

RFC7512.title: The PKCS #11 URI Scheme
RFC7512.summary: Defines the pkcs11 URI scheme for identifying PKCS #11 objects, tokens, slots and Cryptoki libraries, including syntax, query attributes, matching, comparison and IANA registration as a permanent scheme.

URI.why: The document defines a new URI scheme (syntax, semantics, comparison, generation, registration), so it belongs under URI.
URI.quote: This memo specifies a PKCS #11 Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Scheme for identifying PKCS #11 objects stored in PKCS #11 tokens

rejected.why: PKCS #11 tokens hold keys, but the document only defines identifiers for them, not key management.
Certificates and keys can be identified by the URI, but the document does not specify or profile PKI.
The scheme refers to cryptographic tokens but defines no algorithms or crypto usage.
ABNF is only used as the notation for the syntax.
UTF-8 encoding is used for attribute values, but it is a supporting mechanism rather than the subject.
The scheme uses UTF-8 percent-encoding in a URI; it does not define IRIs.

gaps.name: PKCS #11 (Cryptoki) cryptographic token interface
gaps.why: The document is closely tied to the PKCS #11 API for cryptographic tokens, and the taxonomy has no tag for it or for hardware security tokens.

RFC7513.title: Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) Solution for DHCP
RFC7513.summary: RFC 7513 specifies SAVI-DHCP, which snoops DHCPv4/DHCPv6 address assignments (and optionally data packets) to build binding-anchor/IP address bindings on a switch and filter packets with spoofed source addresses.

SAVI.why: The whole document defines the SAVI-DHCP solution: binding state table, snooping state machines, perimeter and filtering rules for source address validation.
SAVI.quote: This document specifies the procedure for creating a binding between a DHCPv4/DHCPv6-assigned IP address and a binding anchor on a Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) device.

DHCP.why: Substantial parts cover DHCPv4/DHCPv6 message snooping, trust attributes for servers/relays and Leasequery use. DHCPv6 is a child but the document covers both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, so the parent DHCP is the fitting tag.
DHCP.quote: SAVI-DHCP snoops DHCP address assignments to set up bindings between IP addresses assigned by DHCP and corresponding binding anchors.

rejected.why: The document covers DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 equally, so the parent DHCP tag fits better.
ARP is used only for duplicate detection and verification probes within the Data Snooping Process, not specified or extended.
NS/NA are used as probes and filtered, but the document is not about neighbor discovery itself.
The mechanism applies to both IPv4 and IPv6 and does not define IPv6 behaviour as such.
Mentioned only as a recommendation for securing Leasequery in the Security Considerations.

RFC7514.title: Really Explicit Congestion Notification (RECN)
RFC7514.summary: An April 1st Independent Submission defining a new ICMP message (RECN) that routers send to hosts that ignore packet loss and ECN signals, carrying a 4-byte ASCII word to be shown or spoken to the user.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a parody protocol that delivers escalating ASCII words to users, with text-to-speech and a security flag from RFC 3514. Readers of humorous RFCs would expect it.
humor.quote: A router may escalate the content in the Explicit Notification field if it determines that a sender has not adjusted its transmission rate

ICMP.why: The document defines a new ICMP message type for IPv4 and IPv6, including its format, type values and checksum.
ICMP.quote: This document proposes a new ICMP message that a router or host may use to advise a host to reduce the rate at which it sends

ECN.why: The message is meant to supplement ECN, and the document motivates it by stalled ECN deployment. It does not extend ECN itself, so this is secondary.
ECN.quote: in cases where the host ignores other signals such as packet loss and ECN

rejected.why: The document is about a congestion signal, but the ECN tag already sits under congestion control, so the parent is implied.
The Explicit Notification field uses ASCII from RFC 20, but only as an encoding for the payload. The document is not about ASCII.
The message has an IPv6 type value and checksum pseudo-header, but IPv6 is only a carrier here. ICMP covers both IP versions.
RFC 5927 on ICMP attacks against TCP is cited only in Security Considerations. The document does not address TCP.

RFC7515.title: JSON Web Signature (JWS)
RFC7515.summary: Specifies JSON Web Signature (JWS), a JSON-based data structure with compact and JSON serializations for content protected by digital signatures or MACs, including the JOSE header parameters and processing rules.

JOSE.why: The document defines JWS, a core JOSE specification, including header parameters, serializations, and signing/validation procedures.
JOSE.quote: JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs) using JSON-based data structures.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding substrate for the structures; the document is about signing, not JSON itself.
JWT is only referenced as an example payload type, not specified here.
TLS is required only for fetching jku/x5u resources; nothing new is defined about it.
X.509 certificates appear only as key-identification header parameters (x5c, x5u, x5t); the document does not profile certificates.
base64url is the encoding used, with implementation notes in an appendix, but it is not the subject.
The application/jose and jose+json registrations are IANA boilerplate, not the main subject.

RFC7516.title: JSON Web Encryption (JWE)
RFC7516.summary: Defines JSON Web Encryption (JWE), a JSON-based representation of encrypted and integrity-protected content with Compact and JSON serializations, header parameters, and encryption/decryption procedures.

JOSE.why: The document specifies JWE, a core JOSE specification, including the JOSE header, serializations and processing rules.
JOSE.quote: JSON Web Encryption (JWE) represents encrypted content using JSON-based data structures

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding substrate for the structures; the document is about JWE itself.
AES GCM and AES key wrap are used in examples; algorithms are defined in JWA, not here.
CMS is only cited as a conceptual influence in the acknowledgements.
base64url is used as an encoding mechanism, not the subject.
Only referenced as the 'zip' parameter value DEF; incidental.
X.509 header parameters just reference certificates; not about X.509 itself.

RFC7517.title: JSON Web Key (JWK)
RFC7517.summary: RFC 7517 defines the JSON Web Key (JWK) JSON representation of cryptographic keys and the JWK Set structure, with their parameters, IANA registries, media types, and encrypted-JWK conventions.

JOSE.why: The document is a core JOSE specification defining JWK and JWK Set, used by JWS and JWE. JOSE is the specific technology tag covering JWK.
JOSE.quote: A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data structure that represents a cryptographic key.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding substrate for the key structure; the document does not extend or profile JSON itself.
X.509 certificates are referenced through x5u/x5c/x5t parameters, but the document does not specify or profile X.509.
The document is a key representation format, not about key establishment, provisioning or storage; JOSE is the more specific fit.
It registers application/jwk+json and jwk-set+json, but that is IANA boilerplate-level registration, not the subject of the document.
The document represents keys but does not define algorithms; algorithms are in JWA.
The registries it establishes are part of the format specification, not a document about IANA guidance.

RFC7518.title: JSON Web Algorithms (JWA)
RFC7518.summary: RFC 7518 (JWA) registers the cryptographic algorithms, key types, curves and header parameters used with JWS, JWE and JWK, and defines the IANA registries for them.

JOSE.why: JWA is a core JOSE specification. It defines the alg/enc identifiers, key types and header parameters used by JWS, JWE and JWK.
JOSE.quote: This specification registers cryptographic algorithms and identifiers to be used with the JSON Web Signature (JWS), JSON Web Encryption (JWE), and JSON Web Key (JWK) specifications.

elliptic curve.why: The document specifies EC key representation (P-256/384/521), ECDH-ES key agreement and the Concat KDF. ECDSA signing is also covered, but the ECDSA tag is not used because the document is not about ECDSA in its own right.
elliptic curve.quote: JWKs can represent Elliptic Curve [DSS] keys.  In this case, the "kty" member value is "EC".

RSA.why: The document defines RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, RSASSA-PSS, RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 and RSA-OAEP usage, plus the RSA key parameters.
RSA.quote: JWKs can represent RSA [RFC3447] keys.  In this case, the "kty" member value is "RSA".

AES.why: The document defines AES Key Wrap, AES GCM key encryption, AES GCM content encryption and the AES_CBC_HMAC_SHA2 composite algorithms, with test cases.
AES.quote: This section defines a family of authenticated encryption algorithms built using a composition of AES [AES] in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode

HMAC.why: HS256/384/512 are defined for JWS, and HMAC is also used inside AES_CBC_HMAC_SHA2 and PBES2.
HMAC.quote: Hash-based Message Authentication Codes (HMACs) enable one to use a secret plus a cryptographic hash function to generate a MAC.

PBKDF2.why: The document defines PBES2-HS*+A*KW algorithms with the p2s/p2c header parameters, built on PBKDF2.
PBKDF2.quote: performing password-based encryption of a JWE CEK, by first deriving a key encryption key from a user-supplied password using PBES2 schemes

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for JOSE structures. The document does not specify anything about JSON itself.
The document creates registries, but its subject is the algorithms. IANA guidance is boilerplate-like, so the IANA topic is not tagged.
SHA-2 hashes are used as building blocks but are not specified or profiled here.
ECDSA with P-curves is used for JWS signatures, but the document only profiles its use inside JOSE. The elliptic curve tag covers it.
JWT is not mentioned in the body. This is a JOSE algorithms document only.
base64url is only the encoding of values here, so it is substrate.

gaps.name: JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) / JWS / JWE / JWK
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists JOSE only inside the JOSE tag's description, but I used the id from the taxonomy. If the id is not in the taxonomy exactly as written, readers need a dedicated JOSE tag. The taxonomy does have JOSE under security, so this is fine.

RFC7519.title: JSON Web Token (JWT)
RFC7519.summary: Defines JSON Web Token (JWT), a compact URL-safe claims format carried as a JWS or JWE payload, with registered claims, creation and validation rules, nesting, and IANA registrations.

JWT.why: The document specifies the JWT format, its claims, and creation and validation procedures.
JWT.quote: JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties.

rejected.why: JWT is built on JWS and JWE, but those are defined in other RFCs. This document only profiles their use, so JOSE is substrate.
JSON is the encoding of the claims set. It is not what the document is about.
The document came from the OAuth WG and registers an OAuth URN, but it is a general token format and does not specify OAuth.
It registers application/jwt, but this is only IANA boilerplate and the document is not about media type rules.
Base64url is used for encoding the parts, and it is defined by JWS.
It registers one URN in the OAuth sub-namespace, a minor IANA item. The document does not define a URN namespace.

RFC7520.title: Examples of Protecting Content Using JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE)
RFC7520.summary: RFC 7520 is an informational cookbook of worked examples showing JWK objects and JWS/JWE signing and encryption results (all serializations, multiple algorithms, nesting) for checking JOSE implementations.

JOSE.why: The whole document provides JWK, JWS and JWE examples; this is the JOSE subject page material.
JOSE.quote: This document contains a set of examples using JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) technology to protect data.

JWT.why: The nested signing/encryption example uses a JWT payload with typ JWT and cty JWT, but JWT is only a small part.
JWT.quote: this example uses the JSON Web Token [JWT] content from Figure 222

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding of the objects; the document is not about JSON itself.
AES modes (GCM, CBC-HMAC, key wrap) are used as algorithms in examples, not specified or analysed.
RSA algorithms are used as inputs to examples; the document is not about RSA.
ECDSA ES512 is one example signature among many; not the subject.
base64url is just the encoding used for octet strings.
Only one example uses zip DEF compression; incidental.

RFC7521.title: Assertion Framework for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication and Authorization Grants
RFC7521.summary: Defines an abstract framework for using assertions with OAuth 2.0 as a client authentication mechanism and as an authorization grant type, with token endpoint parameters and general processing rules; SAML and JWT profiles are in companion RFCs.

OAuth.why: The document extends OAuth 2.0 with new token endpoint parameters (assertion, client_assertion, client_assertion_type) and processing rules for grants and client authentication.
OAuth.quote: This specification provides a framework for the use of assertions with OAuth 2.0 in the form of a new client authentication mechanism and a new authorization grant type.

rejected.why: JWT is only mentioned as a concrete profile defined in RFC 7523; this document is the abstract framework.
HTTP request parameters are only the transport for the token endpoint; no new HTTP semantics are defined.
TLS is only mandated as the secure channel; nothing new about TLS is defined.
Client authentication is covered, but the OAuth tag is more specific and already captures it.
Assertions interwork with other identity systems, but the document is specifically OAuth parameters and not a federation framework.
The IANA section only registers three OAuth parameters, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) assertions
gaps.why: Assertions are the central concept and SAML is the main example format, but the taxonomy has no SAML tag; this RFC is only the abstract framework anyway.

RFC7522.title: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) 2.0 Profile for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication and Authorization Grants
RFC7522.summary: Profiles the OAuth 2.0 Assertion Framework to define how a SAML 2.0 Bearer Assertion is used as an authorization grant and for client authentication at the token endpoint, with assertion validation rules.

OAuth.why: The document defines a new OAuth extension grant type and client authentication method using SAML bearer assertions, so OAuth readers need it.
OAuth.quote: This specification defines the use of a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) 2.0 Bearer Assertion as a means for requesting an OAuth 2.0 access token

federated authentication.why: It carries SAML identity assertions issued by an identity provider across security domains into OAuth. It specifies SAML assertion format and processing requirements, so it fits cross-domain federated authentication.
federated authentication.quote: provide a bridge between OAuth and other trust frameworks

rejected.why: The assertion must be signed, but the document only mandates RSA-SHA256 by reference. It does not specify XML signature mechanics.
SAML is XML-based, but XML is only the assertion's encoding and the document does not address XML usage in its own right.
The document uses HTTP POST parameters to the token endpoint but does not extend HTTP.
It requires base64url encoding of the assertion, but this is only a substrate detail.
The companion JWT profile is a different document. This one covers SAML only.
Client authentication is covered, but the more specific OAuth and federated authentication tags fit better.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SAML itself. This profile and other SAML-related RFCs would be found under it.

RFC7523.title: JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication and Authorization Grants
RFC7523.summary: RFC 7523 profiles the OAuth 2.0 Assertion Framework to define using a JWT bearer token as an authorization grant and as a client authentication mechanism at the token endpoint, with JWT validation rules and URN registrations.

OAuth.why: The document defines an OAuth 2.0 extension grant type and client authentication method, so it belongs on the OAuth page.
OAuth.quote: This specification defines the use of a JSON Web Token (JWT) Bearer Token as a means for requesting an OAuth 2.0 access token as well as for client authentication.

JWT.why: A large part of the document specifies the claims and validation rules a JWT must meet (iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti) when used as an assertion, which is a profile of JWT usage.
JWT.quote: The JWT MUST contain an "iss" (issuer) claim that contains a unique identifier for the entity that issued the JWT.

rejected.why: The signature and MAC requirements are only referenced from JWT/JWA; the document does not specify JWS, JWE or JWK.
HTTP is only the transport of token requests; the document defines OAuth parameter bindings, not HTTP semantics.
The document registers two URNs in the OAuth URN sub-namespace, but this is IANA boilerplate for the grant and assertion types, not about URN namespaces.
Client authentication is covered, but it is specific to OAuth, so the OAuth tag already covers it.
JSON is only the encoding of JWT claims and error responses.

RFC7524.title: Inter-Area Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Segmented Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC7524.summary: Specifies procedures for building inter-area P2MP segmented service LSPs for BGP MVPN, VPLS multicast and global table multicast, partitioning them into intra-area segments (P2MP RSVP-TE, mLDP, or ingress replication) stitched at ABRs using BGP Leaf A-D routes and a new Inter-Area P2MP Next-Hop extended community.

MVPN.why: The document extends BGP MVPN I-PMSI/S-PMSI A-D and Leaf A-D route procedures from RFC 6514 to inter-area segmented P2MP LSPs. MVPN is a main application, with a section on virtual hub-and-spoke.
MVPN.quote: The applications/services that use such inter-area service LSPs may be BGP Multicast VPN (BGP MVPN), VPLS multicast, or global table multicast over MPLS.

MPLS.why: The core subject is building segmented P2MP LSPs over MPLS, including ABR label-stack switching, upstream-assigned labels and P2MP LSP hierarchy.
MPLS.quote: describes procedures for building inter-area point-to-multipoint (P2MP) segmented service LSPs by partitioning such LSPs into intra-area segments

VPLS.why: VPLS multicast is a named application, and the document gives VPLS-specific A-D route procedures and data-plane MAC-learning notes.
VPLS.quote: Egress PEs discover the P2MP FEC of the service LSPs used by VPLS, using the VPLS A-D routes that are originated by the ingress PEs
VPLS.section: 5.2. LDP VPLS with BGP Auto-discovery or BGP VPLS

route reflection.why: ABRs act as route reflectors re-advertising A-D routes across areas, with specific BGP next-hop handling rules (next-hop-self and next-hop-unchanged).
route reflection.quote: The procedures in this document require that at least one ABR in a given IGP area act as a Route Reflector for MVPN A-D routes.

multicast.why: Substantial parts cover global table multicast over MPLS, including PIM-SM ASM handling and Source Active A-D routes.
multicast.quote: This document specifies a particular way of supporting the global table multicast service.

rejected.why: P2MP RSVP-TE is only one of the intra-area signalling options used. The document defines nothing new in RSVP-TE itself.
mLDP and LDP LSPs are intra-area substrates. The document specifies no LDP extensions.

BGP is the inter-area signalling vehicle, but the document defines MVPN-specific routes and extended communities, not general BGP protocol behaviour. The BGP route-reflection tag covers the RR procedures.
PIM-SM in ASM mode is handled only as it interacts with Leaf and Source Active A-D routes for global table multicast. The document does not specify PIM-SM.
VPLS is the specific tag that fits. L2VPN is the broader parent and is implied by it.

gaps.name: Seamless MPLS / inter-area P2MP segmented LSPs
gaps.why: The document is about multicast for seamless MPLS across IGP areas, and the taxonomy has no tag for inter-area or segmented LSP architecture. MPLS is the closest fit.

RFC7525.title: Recommendations for Secure Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC7525.summary: BCP giving recommendations for secure deployment and implementation of TLS and DTLS: protocol versions, compression, resumption, renegotiation, SNI, cipher suites, key lengths, and certificate revocation.

TLS.why: The whole document is deployment guidance for TLS and DTLS, including versions, cipher suites, resumption, renegotiation and SNI. DTLS is a child of TLS, and DTLS 1.0/1.2 versions are covered in only one subsection, so TLS is the tag.
TLS.quote: This document provides recommendations for improving the security of deployed services that use TLS and DTLS.

DTLS.why: The recommendations apply to both TLS and DTLS, and there are explicit DTLS version recommendations, so DTLS readers would want this RFC.
DTLS.quote: Implementations MUST support and MUST prefer to negotiate DTLS version 1.2 [RFC6347].

rejected.why: Certificate revocation, OCSP and stapling are discussed only in one Security Considerations subsection as supporting practice. The document is not about OCSP itself.
HSTS is recommended as a strict-TLS measure but only briefly. The document does not specify or extend it.
AES-GCM cipher suites are recommended, but the document concerns TLS cipher suite selection rather than the AES algorithm.
HTTP is only one of the application protocols that run over TLS, and the document does not address it.
Certificate validation and key-length points are brief and incidental to TLS configuration.
RC4 is only forbidden in one bullet, by reference to RFC 7465. The document is not about RC4.

RFC7526.title: Deprecating the Anycast Prefix for 6to4 Relay Routers
RFC7526.summary: BCP that deprecates the 6to4 anycast relay prefix (192.88.99.0/24) from RFC 3068, obsoletes RFC 3068 and RFC 6732, and gives implementation and operational recommendations for residual 6to4 use.

6to4.why: The whole document concerns the 6to4 transition mechanism: it deprecates its anycast mode, advises that 6to4 be disabled by default, and gives operational guidance for relays.
6to4.quote: This document formally deprecates the anycast 6to4 transition mechanism defined in [RFC3068] and the associated anycast IPv4 address 192.88.99.1.

rejected.why: The anycast here is just the 6to4 relay address mechanism. The document does not address anycast addressing or operation in general, so the 6to4 tag fits better.
6rd is mentioned only briefly as related work that avoids the anycast problems. It is not the subject of the document.
It is cited only as the reason 6to4 failures are hidden from users. The document does not address it.
It appears only in a single remark that IPv6-only providers need a route to a return relay.
The IANA section only marks 192.88.99.0/24 as deprecated in the special-purpose registry. That is boilerplate, not the main subject.
The 6to4 tag is more specific and sits under this topic, so the parent is implied.

RFC7527.title: Enhanced Duplicate Address Detection
RFC7527.summary: RFC 7527 specifies the Enhanced DAD algorithm, which uses the SEND Nonce option to detect looped-back Neighbor Solicitation messages during IPv6 Duplicate Address Detection, and updates RFCs 4429, 4861 and 4862.

neighbor discovery.why: The document defines new sender and receiver processing for NS(DAD) messages using the ND Nonce option and amends RFC 4861 text. DAD is part of IPv6 neighbor discovery and address autoconfiguration.
neighbor discovery.quote: The Enhanced DAD algorithm specified in this document focuses on detecting an NS looped back to the transmitting interface during the DAD operation.

SLAAC.why: It updates RFC 4862 (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) and RFC 4429 (Optimistic DAD), changing how DAD failure is determined for tentative and optimistic addresses.
SLAAC.quote: It updates RFCs 4429 and 4862 to use the Enhanced DAD algorithm to detect looped back DAD probes

rejected.why: Only the SEND Nonce option is reused. The document does not specify or extend SEND, and mentions it for security recommendations.
Random nonces are needed, but the document just points to RFC 4086 for pseudorandom function guidance.
PPP magic number loopback detection is given as one example of a Layer 2 mitigation only.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection against on-link rogues.
The more specific neighbor discovery and SLAAC tags cover the subject, so the parent tag is implied.

RFC7528.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Hybrid Broadcast Broadband TV (HbbTV) Association
RFC7528.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace "hbbtv" for the HbbTV Association, specifying its structure, assignment, persistence and resolution properties per RFC 3406.

URN.why: The document is a formal URN namespace registration (NID "hbbtv") under RFC 3406, so it belongs on the URN namespaces page.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Hybrid Broadcast Broadband TV (HbbTV) Association for naming persistent resources

rejected.why: HbbTV is a hybrid broadcast/broadband TV platform, but the document only registers a URN namespace for naming its resources. It does not specify IPTV service delivery.
XML schemas are among the resources that will be named, but the document does not address XML usage.
The IANA section only records the NID registration. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
URN is the more specific child tag and already covers the URI aspect.

RFC7529.title: Non-Gregorian Recurrence Rules in the Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
RFC7529.summary: Extends iCalendar's RRULE with RSCALE and SKIP elements to support non-Gregorian recurrence rules, updates xCal and jCal representations, clarifies iTIP handling, and defines CalDAV server advertisement of supported calendar scales.

iCalendar.why: The document's main purpose is extending the iCalendar RRULE property with RSCALE and SKIP, updating RFC 5545.
iCalendar.quote: This document defines extensions to the Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar) (RFC 5545) to support use of non-Gregorian recurrence rules.

RFC7530.title: Network File System (NFS) Version 4 Protocol
RFC7530.summary: RFC 7530 is the Standards Track definition of the NFS version 4 (NFSv4.0) distributed file system protocol, covering filehandles, attributes, ACLs, namespaces, locking and state, client caching with delegations, internationalization, and operations; it obsoletes RFC 3530.

NFS.why: The whole document specifies NFSv4.
NFS.quote: The Network File System (NFS) version 4 protocol is a distributed file system protocol that builds on the heritage of NFS protocol version 2 (RFC 1094) and version 3 (RFC 1813).

rejected.why: NFSv4 runs over ONC RPC and XDR, but they are the substrate, not what the document specifies.
RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos are used for security. The document does not define them.
Kerberos V5 is a mandatory-to-implement mechanism that the document relies on. It is not the subject.
TCP is the transport NFSv4 must support. Only brief guidance on connection use is given.
DNS names appear in owner strings and fs_locations. The document does not address DNS itself.
The internationalization section covers UTF-8 handling for file names, but it is a minor part of the document.

gaps.name: NFS (Network File System)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an NFS tag only under storage and it is written as 'NFS'. I used the id 'NFS' as it appears in the taxonomy, but the listed id is 'NFS' under storage; no other fitting tag exists.

RFC7531.title: Network File System (NFS) Version 4 External Data Representation Standard (XDR) Description
RFC7531.summary: RFC 7531 supplies the machine-extractable XDR (nfs4_prot.x) description of the NFSv4.0 protocol defined in RFC 7530, covering types, attributes, operations, COMPOUND and callback procedures.

NFS.why: The whole document is the normative XDR definition of the NFSv4.0 protocol: operations, attributes, errors, and callbacks. Readers of NFS would want it.
NFS.quote: This document contains the External Data Representation (XDR) [RFC4506] description of the NFSv4.0 protocol [RFC7530].

rejected.why: XDR and ONC RPC program definitions are the encoding substrate for NFSv4; the document defines NFS content, not a new XDR or RPC specification.
Not relevant; the data description language is XDR, not ASN.1.
RPCSEC_GSS appears only in the secinfo4 structure as a flavor; the document is not about GSS-API.
utf8string typedefs appear only as field types; internationalization is not addressed in its own right.

gaps.name: XDR (External Data Representation)
gaps.why: The document is a body of XDR source, but the taxonomy only has ONC RPC and XDR combined under ONC RPC, which describes the RPC substrate rather than this NFS description.

RFC7532.title: Namespace Database (NSDB) Protocol for Federated File Systems
RFC7532.summary: Specifies the NSDB protocol for federated file systems: an LDAP-based namespace database schema (FSNs, FSLs, NFS URI locations) and operations by which administrators and fileservers define and resolve filesets for NFSv4 referrals.

NFS.why: The taxonomy has no NFS child tag listed under that id; see rejected. Placeholder not valid.
NFS.quote: The federated file system protocols in this document define how to construct a namespace accessible by a Network File System (NFS) version 4.0

RFC7533.title: Administration Protocol for Federated File Systems
RFC7533.summary: Specifies the FedFS administration protocol, an ONC RPC program by which administrators create, delete and look up junctions and replication info and configure NSDB connection parameters on fileservers in a federated NFS namespace.

ONC RPC.why: The document defines a new ONC RPC program (100418) in XDR with its procedures. The ONC RPC and XDR tag is the closest taxonomy fit for this new RPC program.
ONC RPC.quote: The Remote Procedure Call (RPC) protocol used to convey administration operations is the Open Network Computing (ONC) RPC protocol

NFS.why: The protocol administers junctions and replication that produce NFSv4 referrals and fs_locations. It is a companion to NFS federated namespaces.
NFS.quote: subsequent references via NFSv4.0 [RFC7530] or NFSv4.1 [RFC5661] clients to the directory that has been replaced by the junction will result in a referral

storage.why: The document concerns federated file system namespace administration, which is a storage subject area.
storage.quote: enables file access and namespace traversal across collections of independently administered fileservers

rejected.why: LDAP is used between fileserver and NSDB and appears only in error codes and connection parameters. The NSDB protocol itself is in RFC 7532.
StartTLS and a trust-anchor certificate are carried as parameters. TLS is the security mechanism only, with nothing new defined about it.
RPCSEC_GSS is mentioned only in Security Considerations.
UUIDs are used as identifiers for FSNs and FSLs but the document does not define UUIDs.
A root certificate is carried in secData, which is incidental.

gaps.name: Federated File Systems (FedFS)
gaps.why: The document is about FedFS namespace administration, junctions, and NSDB, and the taxonomy has no FedFS or NFS-federation tag.

RFC7534.title: AS112 Nameserver Operations
RFC7534.summary: RFC 7534 describes how to install and operate an AS112 anycast DNS nameserver node that sinks misdirected reverse-lookup queries for private-use addresses, including BGP and BIND configuration, and obsoletes RFC 6304.

DNS.why: The document is about operating authoritative DNS servers for reverse zones (IN-ADDR.ARPA), with zone files, delegation, DNAME redirection and testing.
DNS.quote: AS112 nodes operate as fully functional and standards-compliant DNS authoritative servers

anycast.why: The AS112 service is an anycast deployment. The document covers topology, prefix advertisement, and withdrawing routes when the DNS software is down.
anycast.quote: Each nameserver functions as a single node in an AS112 anycast cloud

BGP.why: A substantial section gives BGP configuration for originating the service prefixes and preventing transit. It is operational use of BGP, not a protocol extension.
BGP.quote: each AS112 node is a BGP speaker and announces the prefixes 192.175.48.0/24 and 2620:4f:8000::/48 to the Internet with origin AS 112

rejected.why: The document only notes that the AS112 zones are not signed. It is not about DNSSEC.
EDNS0 and NSID are mentioned in passing, as a size constraint on TXT responses and an optional identification mechanism.
The private-use addresses of RFC 1918 are the source of the queries, but NAT is not discussed.
The document uses reserved zones such as EMPTY.AS112.ARPA, but it is about operating the nodes, not about defining special-use names.
Private-use addresses and the special-purpose registry entries are context and IANA actions, not the main subject.

RFC7535.title: AS112 Redirection Using DNAME
RFC7535.summary: Describes using DNAME redirection to the new EMPTY.AS112.ARPA zone so any zone owner can sink queries to AS112 anycast infrastructure without coordinating with AS112 operators, and records the related IANA address and zone assignments.

DNS.why: The document specifies a DNS deployment technique: DNAME redirection to a new AS112.ARPA zone, with resolver behaviour, CNAME synthesis, negative caching and nameserver operations. This is DNS operations.
DNS.quote: Each part of the DNS namespace for which it is desirable to sink queries at AS112 nameservers should be redirected to the EMPTY.AS112.ARPA zone using DNAME

anycast.why: The design depends on anycast service prefixes, and the document assigns a /24 and a /48 for anycast distribution of the AS112 nameserver. Anycast is a substantial part of the operational design, but not the main subject.
anycast.quote: This addressing plan accommodates the anycast distribution of the BLACKHOLE.AS112.ARPA service using a single IPv4 service prefix and a single IPv6 service prefix.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is only mentioned as a way to sign the DNAME records and the AS112.ARPA zone. The document is not about DNSSEC.
AS112.ARPA is a new infrastructure zone, not a special-use domain name in the sense of that tag. The document concerns the redirection mechanism.
The IPv4 and IPv6 address assignments are IANA considerations boilerplate for the DNS service.
The IANA actions are boilerplate for this document. The main body is about DNS redirection.

gaps.name: AS112
gaps.why: The AS112 sink service for non-unique reverse lookups has no dedicated tag. It is covered here only by the general DNS tag.

RFC7536.title: Large-Scale Broadband Measurement Use Cases
RFC7536.summary: Informational RFC describing two use cases (ISP and regulator) for large-scale measurement of broadband performance, to guide development of the LMAP framework, information model and protocol.

LMAP.why: The whole document is the LMAP use cases document, covering ISP and regulator scenarios for large-scale broadband measurement platforms.
LMAP.quote: This document describes two use cases for the Large-scale Measurement of Broadband Performance (LMAP).

performance measurement.why: It discusses active versus passive measurement, probes, panels and metrics such as latency, loss and jitter, but defines no metrics itself. It fits the performance measurement topic, though LMAP is the more specific tag.
performance measurement.quote: Active measurements are the most obvious approach, i.e., special measurement traffic is sent by -- and to -- the probe.
performance measurement.section: 3.1. Understanding the Quality Experienced by Customers

rejected.why: Privacy concerns appear only in the Security Considerations and in passing. They are not the document's main subject.
IPv6 is mentioned only as one example of a new technology to measure before rollout.
It is mentioned once, as an example of a QoS mechanism whose markings could be checked.
TCP options appear only as an example experiment, citing Extend-TCP.

RFC7537.title: IANA Registries for LSP Ping Code Points
RFC7537.summary: RFC 7537 creates IANA registries for MPLS LSP Ping code points (DS Flags, Multipath Types, Pad Types, Interface and Label Stack Address Types), updating RFC 4379 and RFC 6424.

MPLS.why: The document extends the MPLS LSP Ping specifications (RFC 4379/6424) by creating registries for their code points. MPLS is the most specific fitting tag for LSP Ping and its OAM.
MPLS.quote: RFCs 4379 and 6424 created name spaces for Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping.

IANA.why: The main body creates IANA registries with registration policies and initial assignments, so readers of IANA registry matters would want it.
IANA.quote: IANA has created and now maintains a registry entitled "Multipath Types".

rejected.why: LSP Ping is an OAM mechanism, but the document only creates registries and defines no OAM behaviour. The MPLS tag already covers its subject.
LSP Ping/Trace is related, but the document is about registries rather than the path-discovery tool.
The document does not address MPLS Transport Profile.

RFC7538.title: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 308 (Permanent Redirect)
RFC7538.summary: Defines HTTP status code 308 (Permanent Redirect), the permanent counterpart of 307 that forbids changing the request method from POST to GET, and obsoletes experimental RFC 7238.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a new HTTP status code, its semantics, header use, cacheability and deployment considerations, so it belongs under HTTP.
HTTP.quote: this specification adds the status code 308, defining this missing variant

rejected.why: Cacheability by default of 308 is mentioned in one sentence, but the document is not about caching.
URIs are the redirect targets, but the document does not define or extend URI syntax or schemes.
The HTML meta refresh is shown only as a fallback in an example, not as a subject of the document.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a mitigation.
The registry update is boilerplate registering the status code, not the subject of the document.

RFC7539.title: ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols
RFC7539.summary: Defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher, the Poly1305 authenticator, and the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 combined construction as a stable reference and implementation guide, with test vectors.

ChaCha20.why: The whole document specifies ChaCha20, Poly1305 and their AEAD combination, which is exactly what this tag covers.
ChaCha20.quote: This document defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher as well as the use of the Poly1305 authenticator

rejected.why: AES is discussed only as the motivation and performance comparison; the document specifies an alternative cipher.
IKEv2, ESP and IPsec are mentioned as example consumers of the algorithms, not specified here.
TLS is cited as a use case and in the performance comparison only; no TLS cipher suite is defined.
HMAC appears only in the discussion of why Poly1305 is not suitable as a PRF.
Parent of ChaCha20, so it is implied and not listed separately.

gaps.name: Poly1305 / AEAD constructions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for message authentication codes or AEAD algorithms generally. Poly1305 and AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 are core subjects of the document, and the ChaCha20 tag only partly covers them.

RFC7540.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)
RFC7540.summary: RFC 7540 specifies HTTP/2, a binary-framed, multiplexed mapping of HTTP semantics onto a connection with stream flow control, prioritization, header compression, server push, and TLS usage requirements.

HTTP/2.why: The document is the core HTTP/2 specification: framing, streams, flow control, priority, server push and HTTP mappings.
HTTP/2.quote: This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2).

rejected.why: TLS is the security substrate; Section 9.2 restricts TLS 1.2 features and cipher suites for HTTP/2, but the document does not define TLS extensions or the protocol itself.
HTTP/2 runs over TCP as transport; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
The more specific child HTTP/2 applies, so the parent is implied.
Cookie header splitting for compression is a minor detail (Section 8.1.2.5), not a substantial subject of the document.
