Cacheability of pushed responses is addressed only briefly and is not a main subject.
Stream priority is an HTTP/2 internal prioritization mechanism, not a QoS architecture.

gaps.name: HPACK header compression
gaps.why: HTTP/2 relies on HPACK (RFC 7541), which is a separate document, so it is not a gap for this RFC.

RFC7541.title: HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2
RFC7541.summary: RFC 7541 defines HPACK, a header compression format for HTTP/2 that uses static and dynamic indexing tables and a static Huffman code, and addresses compression-related security risks such as CRIME-style attacks.

HTTP/2.why: HPACK is the header compression component of HTTP/2, specified for use by that protocol. Readers of the HTTP/2 subject need it.
HTTP/2.quote: This specification defines HPACK, a compression format for efficiently representing HTTP header fields, to be used in HTTP/2.

rejected.why: HTTP/2 is the more specific child tag, and the document is about HTTP/2 header compression, so the parent is implied.

The document defines a lossless compression format for header fields, but it is specific to HTTP/2. The listed compression children are different formats (DEFLATE, gzip and others). A general compression tag would not help readers of that subject.
DEFLATE is mentioned only as the SPDY approach that enabled the CRIME attack. HPACK replaces it rather than specifying or using it.
TLS is mentioned only in the security discussion, which notes that it does not hide compressed lengths. The document is not about TLS.
Cookie headers appear as examples of sensitive fields not to be indexed. The document does not address cookie state management.

gaps.name: Header compression for HTTP (HPACK) / Huffman coding
gaps.why: The header compression subtopic has no HTTP-specific tag. The taxonomy's header compression tags cover IP/UDP/RTP/PPP only. HTTP/2 is the closest fit.

RFC7542.title: The Network Access Identifier
RFC7542.summary: RFC 7542 defines the syntax and handling of the Network Access Identifier (user@realm), an internationalized UTF-8 user identifier used for inter-domain authentication and AAA routing, obsoleting RFC 4282.

AAA.why: The NAI is the user identifier for roaming/inter-domain AAA, and the document covers routing inside AAA systems by realm, proxy behaviour and RADIUS/Diameter length limits. No more specific AAA child (RADIUS, Diameter) is specified here, so the AAA framework tag fits.
AAA.quote: In order to provide inter-domain authentication services, it is necessary to have a standardized method that domains can use to identify each other's users.

internationalization.why: A major purpose of the revision is fixing internationalization: UTF-8 usernames and realms, NFC normalization, IDNA-valid labels, and Punycode handling.
internationalization.quote: This specification allows both international usernames and realms. International usernames are based on the use of Unicode characters, encoded as UTF-8.

rejected.why: RADIUS is the main carrier of NAIs (User-Name attribute), but the document does not specify or extend RADIUS. It only notes length limits.
Mentioned for User-Name length and routing, but the document does not specify or profile Diameter.
The realm must be IDNA-valid and Punycode is discussed, but the document defines no IDN mechanism. It relies on IDNA and the DNS.
EAP identity and TTLS inner/outer identifiers are discussed, but EAP is a context for the NAI, not the subject.
The ABNF reproduces UTF-8 octet rules from RFC 3629, but this is substrate. The document is not about the UTF-8 encoding.
Realms are DNS names, and name administration piggybacks on DNS, but DNS protocol behaviour is not specified or extended.

RFC7543.title: Covering Prefixes Outbound Route Filter for BGP-4
RFC7543.summary: Defines the Covering Prefixes Outbound Route Filter (CP-ORF), a new BGP ORF type letting a speaker pull covering routes for a host address, applied to Virtual Hub-and-Spoke VPNs and EVPN.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new ORF type carried in ROUTE-REFRESH, with encoding and processing rules for Outbound Filter and Adj-RIB-Out.
BGP.quote: This document defines a new ORF-type, called the Covering Prefixes ORF (CP-ORF).  A BGP speaker sends a CP-ORF to a peer in order to pull routes

L3VPN.why: A substantial section describes CP-ORF operation in Virtual Hub-and-Spoke BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, using IPv4-VPN/IPv6-VPN routes and route targets.
L3VPN.quote: CP-ORF is applicable in Virtual Hub-and-Spoke VPNs [RFC7024] [RFC4364].

EVPN.why: Defines CP-ORF encoding and matching for EVPN route types, with UMR/DMG procedures in a dedicated section.
EVPN.quote: It also is applicable BGP/MPLS Ethernet VPN (EVPN) [RFC7432] networks.

rejected.why: Only a short note on not using CP-ORF routes for UMH selection; not a main subject.
The Transitive Opaque Extended Community is used as a marker, but the document is not about communities.
Not related; only considered for routing-security context and the Security Considerations are boilerplate-like.
IANA code point assignments are boilerplate here.

RFC7544.title: Mapping and Interworking of Diversion Information between Diversion and History-Info Header Fields in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC7544.summary: Informational RFC (obsoleting RFC 6044) giving guidelines for mapping and interworking call-diversion information between the historic SIP Diversion header field and the standard History-Info header field, including privacy handling and a voicemail URI appendix.

SIP.why: The whole document specifies mapping between two SIP header fields (Diversion and History-Info) for call diversion in SIP signaling, so it belongs under SIP.
SIP.quote: This document describes a recommended interworking guideline between the Diversion header field and the History-Info header field to handle call diversion information.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to restate header syntax; the document is not about the notation.
SIP/tel URIs and the cause parameter appear in mappings, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
The tel URI is only mentioned in a note on converting it to a SIP URI; not a subject of the document.
Privacy mapping (Privacy header, anonymization) is a section of the interworking, but the document is not a privacy threat model or general privacy considerations document.
3GPP CDIV and ISUP-inspired mapping are referenced as context, but the document does not address PSTN interworking.

RFC7545.title: Protocol to Access White-Space (PAWS) Databases
RFC7545.summary: RFC 7545 specifies PAWS, a JSON-RPC-over-HTTPS protocol by which radio devices query geolocation databases for available white-space spectrum, including initialization, registration, spectrum query, use notification, device validation, and IANA registries for rulesets, parameters and errors.

PAWS.why: The document is the core specification of PAWS, defining its messages, parameters, errors, encoding and registries.
PAWS.quote: This document defines such a protocol, the "Protocol to Access White-Space (PAWS) Databases".

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport (POST bodies, redirects); the document defines no new HTTP semantics.
TLS is used for security via HTTPS and BCP guidance is referenced, but nothing new about TLS is defined.
JSON-RPC and JSON are just the message encoding substrate.
vCard/jCard is used for DeviceOwner contact info only as an embedded format.
GeoLocation reuses PIDF-LO shapes for device location, but the document is about spectrum database access, not location formats or conveyance.
IANA registries are created but this is boilerplate-level registry setup for the protocol, not guidance about IANA itself.

gaps.name: White-space spectrum database access (PAWS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists PAWS only as a child of link layer. I assumed the id "PAWS" is valid, but it isn't in the taxonomy. The closest valid id is "PAWS" under "link layer", which is what I used. The id is a listed tech: "PAWS [tech]: PAWS (Protocol to Access White-Space databases)".

RFC7546.title: Structure of the Generic Security Service (GSS) Negotiation Loop
RFC7546.summary: RFC 7546 describes the generic structure of the GSS-API security context negotiation loop for initiators and acceptors, including control flow, error handling, post-negotiation checks and sample C code, so application protocols can reference it.

GSS-API.why: The whole document is about how applications correctly use GSS_Init_sec_context and GSS_Accept_sec_context in a negotiation loop, including error tokens, flags checks and sample code.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies the generic structure of the negotiation loop to establish a Generic Security Service (GSS) security context between initiator and acceptor.

rejected.why: Only mentioned in a reference and author affiliation; the document is mechanism-agnostic.
RFC 4752 and RFC 5801 are cited only as examples of protocols that each specified their own loop.
SSH is only an example of an application protocol that uses GSS-API, and its username parameter is mentioned in passing.
The GSS-API tag covers the subject more specifically; no cross-protocol authentication topic is addressed in its own right.
RPCSEC_GSS is only cited as an example of a protocol with its own loop description.

RFC7547.title: Management of Networks with Constrained Devices: Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC7547.summary: Informational problem statement and requirements document for managing networks that include constrained (IoT) devices, covering management topology, architecture, protocols/data models, configuration, monitoring, energy, security and transport requirements.

IoT.why: The whole document concerns constrained-device networks and the Internet of Things, focusing on their constraints and classes. No more specific IoT technology tag fits as the primary subject.
IoT.quote: Constrained devices (also known as sensors, smart objects, or smart devices) with limited CPU, memory, and power resources can be connected to a network.

network management.why: It is a network management requirements document. It covers management architecture, configuration, monitoring, self-management and topology options, and it is not specific to one protocol such as SNMP or NETCONF.
network management.quote: This document provides a problem statement and lists requirements for the different use cases of management of a network with constrained devices.

energy management.why: Section 3.7 and monitoring requirement 4.002 address energy monitoring and management of devices, including the EMAN MIBs. This is a substantial part of the requirements.
energy management.quote: Enable managing power resources in the network, e.g., reduce the sampling rate of nodes with critical battery and reduce node transmission power, put nodes to sleep

rejected.why: CoAP is cited as an example application-layer protocol and as a RESTful approach, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
The document says current management protocols are too heavyweight and does not define or profile any specific protocol. It mentions EMAN MIBs only in passing.
6LoWPAN and RPL appear only as network-type examples in section 1.3, not as subjects of the document.
MANET is one of the network types discussed, but the document is not about MANET routing.
Only one requirement (8.001, group-based provisioning) touches firmware update, which is too minor to tag.
TLS/DTLS is named once as a possible secure transport in requirement 10.004. It is a substrate and is not specified here.

RFC7548.title: Management of Networks with Constrained Devices: Use Cases
RFC7548.summary: Informational document describing use cases (environmental monitoring, industrial, energy, medical, building/home automation, transport, community networks, field operations) for managing networks of constrained devices, with access technologies and device life cycle considerations.

IoT.why: The whole document concerns constrained devices and constrained-node networks (IoT) and their management use cases; IoT is the best fit topic.
IoT.quote: This document aims to understand use cases for the management of a network in which constrained devices are involved.

network management.why: The document is about NMS requirements and management responsibilities across use cases and device life cycle, so network management is a primary subject.
network management.quote: Network management is characterized by monitoring network status, detecting faults (and inferring their causes), setting network parameters

energy management.why: A dedicated use case section covers energy management, Smart Grid, smart metering and AMI.
energy management.quote: The EMAN working group developed an energy-management framework [RFC7326] for devices and device components within or connected to communication networks.

rejected.why: Community networks section mentions NHDP and OLSRv2 only as examples of routing used in the use case; the document does not specify or analyse them.
SNMP and NETCONF are mentioned only as existing protocols that may be too heavy for constrained routers; not the subject.
Mentioned only in passing and by reference to RFC 6568; not discussed in its own right.
Section 2.2 discusses cellular access for M2M gateways, but only as a brief access-technology consideration.
DNS is mentioned once as a place where building network parameters are stored; not about DNS.

RFC7549.title: 3GPP SIP URI Inter-Operator Traffic Leg Parameter
RFC7549.summary: Defines the SIP URI parameter 'iotl' (Inter-Operator Traffic Leg) used in 3GPP IMS networks to indicate the end of a specific traffic leg, with values, usage in Route/Path/Service-Route, ABNF, and IANA registration.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP by defining a new SIP URI parameter and its use in Request-URI, Route, Path and Service-Route header fields, with call flows.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new SIP URI parameter, 'iotl' (an abbreviation for Inter-Operator Traffic Leg).

rejected.why: The parameter is a SIP URI parameter, but the document is about SIP signalling semantics in 3GPP rather than URI syntax or scheme generally.
Targets 3GPP IMS networks, but the specification is a SIP extension, not IP over 3GPP link systems.
ABNF is only used to express the syntax; the document is not about it.
IANA registration is boilerplate-level; it registers one SIP URI parameter value.
Concerns inter-operator signalling, but not SIP service provider peering as specified by SPEERMINT.

gaps.name: 3GPP IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) roaming
gaps.why: The document is about IMS roaming roles and traffic legs between home/visited networks, which the taxonomy has no specific tag for.

RFC7550.title: Issues and Recommendations with Multiple Stateful DHCPv6 Options
RFC7550.summary: Updates RFC 3315 and 3633 to specify how DHCPv6 clients and servers handle multiple stateful IA option types (IA_NA and IA_PD) in one session, covering Advertise status codes, T1/T2 timers, Renew/Rebind, Confirm and Decline behaviour.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document modifies the DHCPv6 protocol specification (RFC 3315 and RFC 3633 prefix delegation) for coexistence of stateful options in a single session.
DHCPv6.quote: Applications that use IA_NA and IA_PD together have revealed issues that need to be addressed.  This document updates RFCs 3315 and 3633 to address these issues.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag; the document concerns only DHCPv6, so the parent is implied.
DHCPv6 runs in IPv6 and delegates IPv6 prefixes, but the document is about the DHCPv6 protocol, not IPv6 itself.
Address and prefix assignment is the function of the options, but the document specifies DHCPv6 protocol behaviour, not address architecture.
Not discussed; the document concerns stateful DHCPv6 assignment.

RFC7551.title: RSVP-TE Extensions for Associated Bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC7551.summary: Defines RSVP-TE extensions (new Association Types and a REVERSE_LSP object) to bind two unidirectional LSPs into an associated bidirectional LSP, with single-sided and double-sided provisioning, motivated by MPLS-TP requirements.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling with new ASSOCIATION Association Types, the REVERSE_LSP object, processing rules and a new PathErr sub-code for traffic-engineered LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document describes Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) extensions to bind two point-to-point unidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs) into an associated bidirectional LSP.

MPLS-TP.why: The work is driven by MPLS-TP requirements for associated bidirectional LSPs and asymmetric bandwidth, so MPLS-TP readers would want it.
MPLS-TP.quote: The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) requirements document [RFC5654] specifies that MPLS-TP MUST support associated bidirectional point-to-point Label Switched Paths (LSPs).

rejected.why: IANA registries and RFC 4872 recovery objects are GMPLS-related, but the document is framed as RSVP-TE extensions for MPLS-TP; it only builds on GMPLS ASSOCIATION objects.
RSVP is the base protocol, but the document is about RSVP-TE for LSPs, not the QoS reservation use of RSVP.
RBNF is only used as the notation for message formats; the document is not about it.
PCE-based path computation is explicitly stated to be outside the scope of the document.
The more specific RSVP-TE and MPLS-TP tags already cover the subject.

RFC7552.title: Updates to LDP for IPv6
RFC7552.summary: RFC 7552 updates LDP (RFC 5036) and its GTSM extension (RFC 6720) to specify LDP behaviour in IPv6-only and dual-stack networks, covering discovery, transport connection selection via a new Dual-Stack capability TLV, address and label distribution, and TTL security.

LDP.why: The whole document specifies updates to LDP procedures: LSP mapping, identifiers, discovery, session establishment, binding distribution and a new Dual-Stack capability TLV.
LDP.quote: This document corrects and clarifies the LDP behavior when an IPv6 network is used (with or without IPv4).

IPv6.why: A substantial part of the document concerns IPv6 deployment: IPv6 multicast groups, link-local and global addresses, IPv4-mapped address prohibition, and dual-stack coexistence. The main subject remains LDP, so this tag is secondary.
IPv6.quote: This document addresses the above deficiencies by specifying the desired behavior/rules/details for using LDP in IPv6-enabled networks (IPv6-only or Dual-stack networks).

rejected.why: LDP is the specific subject, and its tag already sits under MPLS, so the parent is implied.
Dual-stack LDP operation is covered, but the document does not specify a transition mechanism such as tunnelling or translation.
TCP is only the transport for LDP sessions. The document defines active/passive role selection at the LDP level and nothing new about TCP.
'Neighbor Discovery' here means LDP Hello discovery, not IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
The IANA section only registers a TLV type and two status codes, which is boilerplate.

RFC7553.title: The Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) DNS Resource Record
RFC7553.summary: Describes the URI DNS resource record (RRTYPE 256), its presentation and wire format, owner-name service labels, and its relation to NAPTR, S-NAPTR, U-NAPTR and SRV for mapping hostnames to URIs.

DNS.why: The document specifies a DNS resource record type, including its format, owner name conventions, RDATA wire format and relation to NAPTR/SRV.
DNS.quote: This document describes the already registered DNS resource record (RR) type, called the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) RR, that is used for publishing mappings from hostnames to URIs.

rejected.why: URIs are only the data stored in the record; the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
Security Considerations recommend signing the record, but DNSSEC is not the subject of the document.
The record is used for looking up a URI for a known service, and the document explicitly says it is not a replacement for NAPTR discovery. DNS is the more specific fit.
Enumservice registrations are only used as a source of service labels in the owner name.
TLS is mentioned only as a security mechanism in Security Considerations.
The IANA registration of RRTYPE 256 is boilerplate-level here and not the main subject.

RFC7554.title: Using IEEE 802.15.4e Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) in the Internet of Things (IoT): Problem Statement
RFC7554.summary: Informational problem statement describing the environment, issues and goals for using the IEEE 802.15.4e TSCH MAC in IPv6-based low-power lossy networks, including what a scheduling entity (LLC/6top) must do, with an appendix summarizing TSCH.

6TiSCH.why: The RFC is the 6TiSCH working group's problem statement for running IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4e, covering scheduling, join, synchronization and security goals.
6TiSCH.quote: This document describes the environment, problem statement, and goals for using the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) Medium Access Control (MAC) protocol of IEEE 802.14.4e

rejected.why: RPL is discussed as the routing layer that the TSCH schedule must match, but the document does not specify or extend it.
6LoWPAN is background for the adaptation layer sitting above TSCH; the document is not about it.
CoAP is mentioned only as part of the expected protocol stack.
Synchronization is described as a TSCH feature (Appendix A.8), but it is part of the MAC and not a general time-sync subject.
PCE is cited only as one possible external scheduler, which is a passing mention.
RSVP is cited only as an analogy for multi-hop cell allocation.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.15.4 / 802.15.4e TSCH MAC
gaps.why: The RFC is about this link-layer MAC, which has no specific link-layer tag. 6TiSCH is the closest fit.

RFC7555.title: Proxy MPLS Echo Request
RFC7555.summary: Defines MPLS Proxy Ping Request/Reply messages and TLVs that extend LSP Ping (RFC 4379) so a third-party LSR can ask another LSR to send MPLS Echo Requests, mainly for scalable tracing of P2MP/MP2MP LSPs.

MPLS.why: The RFC extends MPLS LSP Ping (data-plane OAM) with new messages, TLVs, return codes and IANA registries for MPLS LSPs, including P2MP and MP2MP LSPs. MPLS is the most specific fitting tag.
MPLS.quote: This document defines protocol extensions to MPLS ping [RFC4379] to allow a third party to remotely cause an MPLS Echo Request message to be sent down an LSP

rejected.why: mLDP P2MP/MP2MP LSPs motivate the tracing use case, but the document specifies LSP Ping extensions, not LDP.
RSVP-TE P2MP LSPs are only mentioned as another case where the root knows the tree. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
The document is MPLS OAM, but the technology tag MPLS is more specific. No OAM-specific tag fits better under MPLS, so I did not add the topic tag.
The document supports leaf-to-root tracing of LSPs, but it is about proxying LSP Ping messages. It does not specify a general traceroute tool.
Nothing in the document concerns the MPLS Transport Profile.

gaps.name: LSP Ping / MPLS data plane failure detection (OAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for MPLS LSP Ping, and the closest options are generic MPLS and OAM. Readers looking for LSP Ping documents would benefit from a dedicated tag.

RFC7556.title: Multiple Provisioning Domain Architecture
RFC7556.summary: Informational architecture RFC defining Provisioning Domains (PvDs), consistent sets of network configuration, and a reference model for multi-homed/multi-interface nodes to keep configuration separate and consistently used across name resolution, address selection, and connections.

multihoming.why: The document is an architecture for nodes attached to multiple networks/interfaces, keeping configuration separate and consistent. Multihoming architectures is the closest fit.
multihoming.quote: outlines a solution framework for some of the issues experienced by nodes that can be attached to multiple networks simultaneously

DHCPv6.why: Section 3 discusses how DHCPv6 would need extending to convey PvD information, including separate vs. combined messages, securing, and updating.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv6 and Router Advertisements (RAs) are the two most common methods of configuring hosts.

neighbor discovery.why: Router Advertisements/Router Discovery options are a main proposed vehicle for PvD identity and association with prefixes.
neighbor discovery.quote: these protocols would need to be extended to convey explicit PvD information

rejected.why: IKEv2 is mentioned only as one delivery mechanism for configuration in a short subsection.
Name resolution per PvD is an example use; the document does not specify DNS behavior.
Document is not IPv6-specific; IPv6 address selection and RAs are used as examples.
Mentioned only as an example of a transport aggregating connections.
Referenced only as an analogy for parallel lookups across PvDs.
Source address selection within a PvD is one example; not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Provisioning Domains (PvD) / multiple interfaces
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for provisioning domains or multi-interface host configuration management; multihoming is only an approximate fit.

RFC7557.title: Extension Mechanism for the Babel Routing Protocol
RFC7557.summary: Defines the rules for extending the Babel routing protocol (RFC 6126): new versions, new TLVs, sub-TLVs (with Pad1/PadN), Flags bits and the packet trailer, and creates the Babel IANA registries.

Babel.why: The whole document specifies the extension encoding mechanism (TLVs, sub-TLVs, flags, trailer) for the Babel routing protocol, so Babel readers need it.
Babel.quote: This document formalises a set of rules for extending the Babel protocol that are designed to ensure that no such incompatibilities arise

rejected.why: The registries it creates are Babel-specific and described only in the IANA Considerations boilerplate; the document is not about IANA guidance.
Babel packets are carried in UDP datagrams, which is only substrate; the trailer discussion is about Babel's packet format.
The more specific Babel tag already covers it.

RFC7558.title: Requirements for Scalable DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) / Multicast DNS (mDNS) Extensions
RFC7558.summary: RFC 7558 gives a problem statement, use cases and 15 requirements for extending DNS-SD/mDNS so service discovery scales beyond a single link, including multi-link, 802.11 and low-power mesh networks.

DNS-SD.why: The whole document gathers requirements for scalable extensions to DNS-based Service Discovery, so readers of DNS-SD would want it.
DNS-SD.quote: This document provides a problem statement and a list of requirements for scalable DNS-SD.

mDNS.why: The document analyses mDNS limitations (multi-link, Wi-Fi multicast cost, LLN meshes) and sets requirements for extending it.
mDNS.quote: mDNS (by design) does not work across routers.

rejected.why: The more specific DNS-SD tag applies, and ancestors are implied.
Dynamic DNS Update is only mentioned as one existing, onerous way to populate DNS-SD records, not the subject.
The 802.11 multicast problems are a motivating section, but the document is not about IP over Wi-Fi.
6LoWPAN and RPL meshes appear as a use case and challenge, but the document does not specify or analyse those protocols.
DNSSEC is mentioned only briefly in the authorization security discussion.

RFC7559.title: Packet-Loss Resiliency for Router Solicitations
RFC7559.summary: RFC 7559 updates IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) so hosts keep retransmitting Router Solicitations with exponential backoff (as in DHCPv6) until a Router Advertisement is received, making them resilient to loss of the initial RSs.

neighbor discovery.why: The document modifies the Router Solicitation retransmission behaviour of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (updates RFC 4861), so it belongs under neighbor discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: the host needs to continue retransmitting the Router Solicitations until it receives a Router Advertisement, or until it is willing to accept that no router exists

rejected.why: Only borrows the DHCPv6 exponential backoff algorithm and timing values (RFC 3315/7083); the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
Mentioned only as an example of a non-multicast link with special RS mechanisms; not about ISATAP.
The more specific child neighbor discovery fits, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
RAs enable autoconfiguration, but the document addresses Router Solicitation retransmission, not address autoconfiguration.

RFC7560.title: Problem Statement and Requirements for Increased Accuracy in Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Feedback
RFC7560.summary: Informational problem statement and requirements for a more accurate TCP ECN feedback scheme than classic RFC 3168 ECN, motivated by ConEx and DCTCP, with sketches of design approaches.

ECN.why: The whole document is about ECN feedback accuracy: requirements, classic ECN recap, and design approaches for encoding CE marks in TCP.
ECN.quote: This document specifies requirements for an update to the TCP protocol to provide more accurate ECN feedback.

TCP.why: The requirements target an update to TCP header flags, options and handshake negotiation, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: Given more accurate ECN feedback will involve a change to the TCP protocol, it should be negotiated between the two TCP endpoints.

ConEx.why: ConEx is one of the two principal use cases motivating the requirements, discussed in the use-cases section.
ConEx.quote: ConEx is an experimental approach that allows a sender to relay congestion feedback provided by the receiver into the network along the forward data path.

DCTCP.why: DCTCP is the other main use case, and Appendix A analyses the ambiguity of its feedback scheme.
DCTCP.quote: DCTCP offers very low and predictable queuing delay.  DCTCP changes the reaction to congestion of a TCP sender

rejected.why: The document covers only the feedback signal, not sender reaction. ECN, ConEx and DCTCP are more specific tags under it.
SCTP ECN is mentioned only as a comparison for feedback richness, not specified or analysed.
ECN for RTP/UDP (RFC 6679) is cited only as an example of detailed feedback.
The IP header ECN codepoints are described only as background for the TCP feedback.

RFC7561.title: Mapping Quality of Service (QoS) Procedures of Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) and WLAN
RFC7561.summary: Informational companion to RFC 7222 that maps QoS signalling procedures and parameters (TSPEC, TCLAS, access categories, data rates) between IEEE 802.11/WMM-AC and Proxy Mobile IPv6 QoS options to enable end-to-end QoS in a Wi-Fi access PMIPv6 domain.

PMIPv6.why: The document profiles PMIPv6 QoS procedures (PBU/PBA, UPN/UPA, QoS options) and maps them onto the Wi-Fi segment; PMIPv6 is a core subject.
PMIPv6.quote: PMIPv6 QoS signaling between the Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) and Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) provisions the per-MN QoS policies in the MAG.

WiFi.why: Covers IEEE 802.11 QoS (EDCA, ADDTS/DELTS, TSPEC, TCLAS, 802.11aa) and its mapping to PMIPv6; the IP over 802.11 access is central.
WiFi.quote: IEEE 802.11, Wi-Fi Multimedia (WMM), and Wi-Fi Multimedia - Admission Control (WMM-AC) describe ways to provide QoS for Wi-Fi traffic

QoS.why: The document is about end-to-end QoS signalling and parameter mapping (DSCP, QCI, access categories, bandwidth), a QoS architecture topic with no more specific child tag fitting.
QoS.quote: This document provides a mapping between the above two sets of QoS procedures and the associated QoS parameters.

rejected.why: DSCP values are mapped to access categories, but Diffserv itself is not specified or extended.
SIP is mentioned only as an example upper-layer trigger for QoS requests.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as the way PMIPv6 messages are secured.
3GPP QCI and EPC concepts are referenced for parameters, but the document concerns WLAN access, not cellular networks.

RFC7562.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authorization Using Digital Transmission Content Protection (DTCP) Certificates
RFC7562.summary: Defines a new TLS authorization data type (dtcp_authorization) so clients and servers can exchange DTCP device certificates in the TLS SupplementalData handshake message, per the RFC 5878 authorization extensions framework.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS authorization data format, hello extension usage, handshake message flow and alert usage. This is a TLS extension, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document specifies the use of Digital Transmission Content Protection (DTCP) certificates as an authorization data type in the authorization extension for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are only tied to the DTCP certificate via a signature. The DTCP certificate is explicitly not X.509, and the document does not profile X.509.
DTLS compatibility is mentioned only in the IANA Considerations as a DTLS-OK flag. The document is not about DTLS.
Authorization is the purpose of the data type, but the document is a TLS extension and leaves the authorization semantics out of scope. The TLS tag covers it.
DTCP certificates come from DTLA's own certificate system. The document does not address Internet PKI.
ECDSA is only the signature algorithm DTCP uses, and it is referenced from the DTCP spec. The document does not define or profile it.

gaps.name: DTCP (Digital Transmission Content Protection)
gaps.why: The document is about carrying DTCP certificates from DTLA-licensed consumer devices. The taxonomy has no tag for DTCP or content protection.

RFC7563.title: Extensions to the Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Access Network Identifier Option
RFC7563.summary: RFC 7563 extends the Proxy Mobile IPv6 Access Network Identifier option with Civic-Location, MAG-Group-Identifier and ANI Update-Timer sub-options, and specifies MAG and LMA handling of them.

PMIPv6.why: The document defines new sub-options of the PMIPv6 ANI mobility option and the MAG/LMA behaviour for PBU/PBA exchanges. It updates RFC 6757, so it is squarely about Proxy Mobile IPv6.

RFC7564.title: PRECIS Framework: Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings in Application Protocols
RFC7564.summary: RFC 7564 defines the PRECIS framework, which replaces Stringprep, for preparing, enforcing and comparing internationalized Unicode strings in application protocols. RFC7565.summary: Defines the 'acct' URI scheme for generically identifying a user's account at a service provider, independent of interaction protocol, and registers it with IANA.

RFC7566.summary: Registers the 'acct' Enumservice in the IANA ENUM services registry so E.164 telephone numbers can be mapped via NAPTR records to 'acct' URIs, with use cases, examples and DNS loop-avoidance guidance.

RFC7567.title: IETF Recommendations Regarding Active Queue Management

RFC7569.title: Registry Specification for Mandatory Access Control (MAC) Security Label Formats
RFC7569.summary: Creates an IANA registry of security label format specifiers (CIPSO, CALIPSO, FLASK, IPSO) so multiple MAC label formats can coexist, initially for Labeled NFS, with registration procedures.

RFC7570.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Attribute in the Explicit Route Object (ERO)
RFC7570.summary: Defines a new Hop Attributes subobject for the RSVP-TE Explicit Route Object and Record Route Object so per-hop LSP attributes (building on RFC 5420 TLVs) can be specified and reported in MPLS/GMPLS signalling.

RFC7571.title: GMPLS RSVP-TE Extensions for Lock Instruct and Loopback
RFC7571.summary: Specifies GMPLS RSVP-TE extensions (ADMIN_STATUS A bit use, a new Loopback attribute flag, new OAM Problem error sub-codes) to provision Lock Instruct and Loopback OAM functions on LSPs.

RFC7572.title: Interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Instant Messaging
RFC7572.summary: Defines a bidirectional mapping between SIP MESSAGE requests (pager-mode instant messages) and XMPP message stanzas, for gateways interworking SIP/SIMPLE and XMPP.

RFC7573.title: Interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): One-to-One Text Chat Sessions
RFC7573.summary: Defines a bidirectional mapping between XMPP one-to-one chat messages and SIP/MSRP session-mode chat, including session state, composing events, delivery reports, and message size handling.

XMPP.quote: this document specifies mappings between XMPP messages of type "chat" and the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)

RFC7575.title: Autonomic Networking: Definitions and Design Goals
RFC7575.summary: An IRTF NMRG informational RFC defining common terminology (autonomic, intent, autonomic domain, etc.), design goals and non-goals, and a high-level reference model for autonomic networking.

RFC7576.title: General Gap Analysis for Autonomic Networking
RFC7576.summary: An IRTF NMRG informational document that gives a problem statement and gap analysis for Autonomic Networking, reviewing automatic aspects of current IP networks and non-autonomic behaviours, and outlining missing features such as reusable discovery, synchronization and negotiation components and a secure control plane.

autonomic networking.why: The whole document is a gap analysis for Autonomic Networking: self-management, missing coordination, reusable components, secure control plane.

Mentioned briefly as a complicating factor for configuration management.

RFC7577.title: Definition of Managed Objects for Battery Monitoring
RFC7577.summary: Defines the BATTERY-MIB SMIv2 module for monitoring battery status (charge, capacity, cycles, temperature, charging state control, and notifications) in managed devices, plus an IANA battery technology registry.

RFC7581.summary: Defines protocol-agnostic binary encodings for WSON-specific routing and wavelength assignment information fields (resource block sets, accessibility, wavelength constraints, pool state, resource block info with ITU optical interface class mappings) for use in GMPLS routing and PCE protocols.

RFC7582.title: Multicast Virtual Private Network (MVPN): Using Bidirectional P-Tunnels
RFC7582.summary: RFC 7582 specifies procedures for using bidirectional (MP2MP LSP and BIDIR-PIM) P-tunnels to carry customer multicast in BGP/MPLS multicast VPNs, including assigning C-flows to tunnels, advertising via PMSI Tunnel attributes, and matching flows for transmission and reception.

RFC7583.summary: Informational document describing timelines and timing relationships (intervals, delays, TTLs) for ZSK and KSK rollover methods in DNSSEC-signed zones, including RFC 5011 trust anchor interactions and standby keys.

RFC7586.summary: Experimental independent-stream RFC defining SARP, a proxy-gateway architecture that rewrites MACs and proxies ARP/ND between access segments to shrink switch FDB tables and reduce ARP/ND load in large multi-site data centers with VM mobility.

data center networking.why: The document specifies a scaling architecture for address resolution and forwarding at data-centre scale, including VM migration, HA and overlay interaction.
data center networking.quote: SARP is based on fast proxies that significantly reduce switches' Filtering Database (FDB) table sizes and reduce impact of ARP and Neighbor Discovery

ARP.why: A substantial part of the spec is proxying ARP requests/replies and gratuitous ARP, rewriting MAC addresses and caching mappings.
ARP.quote: SARP proxies maintain a cache of the IP-to-MAC mapping.  This cache is based on ARP/ND messages that are sent by hosts and traverse the SARP proxies.

neighbor discovery.why: IPv6 ND (NS/NA/UNA) is proxied in the same way as ARP, so the proxy behaviour extends IPv6 neighbor discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: the ARP/NS request is propagated to all access segments that might have VMs in the same virtual network as the originating VM

rejected.why: SARP is designed to run over overlays (VXLAN, NVGRE, VPLS, TRILL) but only discusses interaction briefly; it does not define overlay encapsulation.
RFC 4664 and ARP mediation are cited only as existing alternatives in the comparison and IESG note.
Mentioned only as an example overlay in one section.
Master/backup proxy with keepalive is described informally, not using VRRP.
IPv6 ND is handled, but the document is not about IPv6 specifically; it is covered by neighbor discovery.

RFC7587.title: RTP Payload Format for the Opus Speech and Audio Codec
RFC7587.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for Opus-encoded speech and audio, including the audio/opus media type registration, SDP parameters and offer/answer rules, and an applicability statement.

Opus.why: The whole document concerns using the Opus codec over RTP: bitrate, DTX, FEC, stereo and framing. Opus readers would want it.
Opus.quote: This document defines the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format for packetization of Opus-encoded speech and audio data

RTP payload format.why: It specifies RTP header usage, timestamp clock rate and payload structure for a codec, which is an RTP payload format definition.
RTP payload format.quote: An RTP payload MUST contain exactly one Opus packet as defined by that document.

SDP.why: Substantial sections give the SDP mapping of the media type parameters, examples, offer/answer rules and declarative SDP use.
SDP.quote: The media subtype ("opus") goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name. The RTP clock rate in "a=rtpmap" MUST be 48000

media types.why: The document registers the audio/opus media type with its full parameter definitions. This registration is a core deliverable and part of the main body.
media types.quote: One media subtype (audio/opus) has been defined and registered as described in the following section.

rejected.why: The child tag RTP payload format fits more specifically, and the ancestor is implied.
The Opus child tag is more specific.
Section 5 is brief and only points to RMCAT and general UDP guidance. It is not a substantial part of the document.
SRTP appears only in security references and in the VBR guidance pointer to RFC 6562. The document is not about it.
The in-band FEC is a feature of the Opus codec, not a packet-level loss recovery scheme specified here.
SIP is not discussed. The document uses SDP offer/answer, which is generic.

RFC7588.title: A Widely Deployed Solution to the Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) Fragmentation Problem
RFC7588.summary: Informational memo describing the widely deployed, configurable vendor solution to GRE tunnel fragmentation: fragment the payload by default, drop non-fragmentable packets and send ICMP PTB, with optional delivery-packet fragmentation and reassembly at egress.

GRE.why: The whole document specifies GRE ingress and egress fragmentation behaviour, MTU estimation and DF-bit handling for GRE tunnels.
GRE.quote: This memo describes how many vendors have solved the Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) fragmentation problem.

PMTUD.why: A substantial part covers GRE MTU estimation and discovery, PMTUD use and disabling it for GRE tunnels, and PTB generation.
PMTUD.quote: Typically, GRE ingress nodes further refine their GMTU estimate by executing PMTUD procedures.

rejected.why: ICMP PTB messages are sent as part of the procedure, but ICMP itself is not specified or extended here.
IPv6 payloads and delivery are covered only as GRE cases; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
MPLS appears only as one possible GRE payload type.
IPv4 fragmentation and DF behaviour are used as mechanisms, but the document is not about IPv4 itself.
GRE is the more specific tag under tunneling, so the parent is implied.

RFC7589.title: Using the NETCONF Protocol over Transport Layer Security (TLS) with Mutual X.509 Authentication
RFC7589.summary: Specifies how NETCONF runs over TLS with mutual X.509 authentication (port 6513), including connection setup, NETCONF 1.1 message framing, certificate validation, and derivation of NETCONF usernames from client certificates; obsoletes RFC 5539.

NETCONF.why: The document defines the NETCONF transport mapping over TLS, including framing, connection closure and username derivation, so NETCONF readers need it.
NETCONF.quote: This document describes how to use the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol with mutual X.509 authentication to secure the exchange of NETCONF messages.

TLS.why: The document specifies how TLS is used (client/server roles, mutual authentication, cipher suites, closure), which is a substantial part of its content and useful to TLS deployment readers.
TLS.quote: Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] and are REQUIRED to support the mandatory-to-implement cipher suite.

X.509.why: A significant part of the document covers certificate validation and the mapping of certificate fields (subjectAltName, CommonName, fingerprint) to NETCONF usernames.
X.509.quote: Both peers MUST use X.509 certificate path validation [RFC5280] to verify the integrity of the certificate presented by the peer.

rejected.why: Topic tag not chosen directly: the NETCONF and TLS tech tags already cover this subject.
Only mentioned as the alternative transport (RFC 6242) whose framing is reused; the document is not about SSH.
The SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB is cited only because the username derivation algorithm matches it.
The ietf-x509-cert-to-name YANG module and the server model are referenced but not defined here.
The port 6513 registration is boilerplate-level IANA considerations and not the subject of the document.

RFC7590.title: Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) in the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)
RFC7590.summary: Updates RFC 6120 to require XMPP implementations to follow BCP 195 (RFC 7525) TLS recommendations, and gives XMPP-specific guidance on STARTTLS, compression, session resumption, authenticated connections, SNI and human factors.

XMPP.why: The document updates the XMPP core specification with requirements for how XMPP uses TLS, so readers of XMPP want it.
XMPP.quote: this document updates [RFC6120] by specifying that XMPP implementations and deployments MUST follow the best current practices documented in the "Recommendations for Secure Use of TLS and DTLS"

TLS.why: It gives TLS deployment guidance for XMPP: session resumption, compression, SNI, certificate authentication and cipher choices via RFC 7525.
TLS.quote: This document provides recommendations for the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) in the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP).

rejected.why: DANE is only mentioned as one server authentication method in the DNA framework, not specified or profiled here.
PKIX certificate validation is deferred to RFC 6120 and RFC 6125, and this document does not modify it.
SASL is mentioned only in passing as the authentication layer alongside TLS.
DNSSEC appears in a single parenthetical about strengthening Server Dialback keys.
XMPP is tagged directly, which is the more specific tag under instant messaging.
DTLS is only named in the title of RFC 7525, and this document does not address datagram TLS.

RFC7591.title: OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Protocol
RFC7591.summary: Defines the OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Protocol, in which clients or developers register with an authorization server through a JSON/HTTP registration endpoint, with common client metadata, software statements (JWTs), and two new IANA registries.

OAuth.why: The whole document specifies an OAuth 2.0 extension: the client registration endpoint, client metadata, and the registries for token endpoint authentication methods.
OAuth.quote: This specification defines mechanisms for dynamically registering OAuth 2.0 clients with authorization servers.

rejected.why: Software statements are JWTs, but JWT is only the container for the signed metadata. The document defines no new JWT mechanism.
JWS and JWK are used for signing software statements and for the jwks/jwks_uri fields. They are relied on, not specified or extended.
JSON is the encoding of requests and responses, so it is substrate only.
The registration endpoint uses HTTP POST and status codes, but HTTP is only the transport here.
TLS is required in Security Considerations only, which is boilerplate evidence.
The document creates two IANA registries, but they are part of the OAuth extension and not a general IANA guidance topic.
Section 2.2 uses BCP 47 tags on metadata member names. This is a small feature of the document, not a main subject.

RFC7592.title: OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Protocol
RFC7592.summary: Defines an experimental OAuth 2.0 protocol extension for reading, updating, and deleting dynamic client registrations via a client configuration endpoint authenticated by a registration access token.

OAuth.why: The document extends OAuth 2.0 dynamic client registration with read, update and delete management methods, so it belongs under OAuth.
OAuth.quote: This specification defines methods for management of OAuth 2.0 dynamic client registrations for use cases in which the properties of a registered client may need to be changed

rejected.why: HTTP GET, PUT and DELETE are only the substrate for the management operations. The document defines nothing new about HTTP.
JSON is only the payload encoding for requests and responses.
TLS is required for transport protection, but the requirement appears only in Security Considerations, and the document specifies nothing new about TLS.
The examples mention jwks_uri and software statements, but the document does not specify JWT.
Bearer tokens are used for authentication, but they are defined by the OAuth bearer token specification. This document only uses them.

RFC7593.title: The eduroam Architecture for Network Roaming
RFC7593.summary: Describes the eduroam federated Wi-Fi roaming architecture (802.1X, EAP, RADIUS hierarchy), its operational problems, and the move to RADIUS/TLS with DNS-based dynamic peer discovery, plus abuse handling and privacy.

RADIUS.why: The trust fabric is a RADIUS proxy hierarchy; the document analyses its failure handling, UDP issues, RADIUS/TLS replacement, and attributes like Operator-Name and CUI.
RADIUS.quote: The eduroam trust fabric consists of a proxy hierarchy of RADIUS servers (organizational, national, global)

EAP.why: EAP methods, tunneled EAP, supplicant validation and error signalling are central to the architecture and its security discussion.
EAP.quote: The use of the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) [RFC4372] serves two purposes.

federated authentication.why: The document is about a cross-domain federation with IdP/SP trust relations, and relates to ABFAB.
federated authentication.quote: This document describes the architecture of the eduroam service for federated (wireless) network access in academia.

WiFi.why: Covers IEEE 802.1X on 802.11 networks, SSID conventions and WPA2 requirements for roaming wireless access.
WiFi.quote: an SP that offers wireless network access MUST broadcast the Service Set Identifier (SSID) 'eduroam'

TLS.why: Substantial section on moving RADIUS to TLS transport, with TLS-PSK vs X.509 trade-offs.
TLS.quote: RADIUS/TLS [RFC6614] allows any given RADIUS link in eduroam to be upgraded without the need of a "flag day".

DNS-SD.why: Dynamic discovery of RADIUS servers uses NAPTR/SRV records; this is a service discovery mechanism.
DNS-SD.quote: eduroam-specific service discovery information into the global DNS tree. In eduroam, this is done by using NAPTR records as per the S-NAPTR specification

rejected.why: DNSSEC+DANE only mentioned as a possible alternative.
Briefly discussed as alternative for discovery, not a main subject.
Separate eduroam PKI is mentioned but only briefly.
Privacy section exists but is a modest part; the document is about the architecture.
Considered and rejected as a candidate, not the subject.
RADIUS is the more specific tag and already chosen.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.1X port-based network access control
gaps.why: The architecture is built on 802.1X, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC7594.title: A Framework for Large-Scale Measurement of Broadband Performance (LMAP)
RFC7594.summary: Informational RFC defining the LMAP framework and terminology for large-scale broadband performance measurement: Measurement Agents, Controllers, Collectors, the Control and Report protocol models, deployment considerations, and privacy/security analysis.

LMAP.why: The document is the LMAP framework itself, defining its components, terminology, protocol model and deployment.
LMAP.quote: This document presents an overall framework for large-scale measurements.  It also defines terminology for LMAP (Large-Scale Measurement of Broadband Performance).

privacy.why: A substantial section applies RFC 6973 to LMAP: sensitive information, threats, and mitigations such as anonymity sets and data minimisation.
privacy.quote: The LMAP work considers privacy a core requirement and will ensure that by default the Control and Report Protocols operate in a privacy-sensitive manner

rejected.why: Only cited as an example Measurement Peer protocol; not specified or extended here.
Only used as a deployment example of a Measurement Peer; not the subject.
Mentioned as a possible Report Protocol and for the Flow definition; not specified or extended here.
Named as a possible Control Protocol or bootstrap option; the document does not specify it.
Considered as the parent topic of LMAP. LMAP is a more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate-like and is not the document's main subject.

RFC7595.title: Guidelines and Registration Procedures for URI Schemes
RFC7595.summary: BCP 35 updating RFC 4395: sets guidelines for defining new URI schemes and the IANA registration procedures (permanent, provisional, historical) for the URI Schemes registry, and registers the "example" scheme.

URI.why: The whole document concerns URI scheme definition requirements, scheme naming, and registration in the IANA URI Schemes registry.
URI.quote: This document updates the guidelines and recommendations, as well as the IANA registration processes, for the definition of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.

IANA.why: A substantial part defines the registry policy (First Come First Served, Expert Review), Designated Expert role, and registry restructuring.
IANA.quote: IANA checks the submission for completeness; if required sections of the scheme registration request are missing or any citations are not correct, IANA will reject the registration request.

rejected.why: IRIs are discussed only briefly as sharing the same scheme registry; the document is not about IRIs themselves.
URN namespaces are explicitly excluded from scope.
HTTP methods are cited only as a model example for defining operations.
Section 3.6 on character encoding is a minor guideline, not a main subject.

RFC7596.title: Lightweight 4over6: An Extension to the Dual-Stack Lite Architecture
RFC7596.summary: Specifies Lightweight 4over6, an extension to DS-Lite that moves NAPT44 from the AFTR to the CPE-based B4 and gives each B4 a port-restricted IPv4 address, with provisioning via DHCPv6 and lwB4/lwAFTR behaviour.

DS-Lite.why: The document defines lw4o6, a direct extension of DS-Lite, specifying lwB4 and lwAFTR behaviour, binding tables and ICMP handling.
DS-Lite.quote: This document specifies an extension to DS-Lite called "Lightweight 4over6", which moves the Network Address and Port Translation (NAPT) function from the centralized DS-Lite tunnel concentrator

rejected.why: NAPT44 is used and its behaviour is referenced, but the document is about the DS-Lite extension; DS-Lite is the more specific fit, and NAT is a mechanism it relies on.
Provisioning uses OPTION_S46_CONT_LW defined in RFC 7598. This document only uses DHCPv6 and defines no new options.
lw4o6 is a softwire mechanism, but DS-Lite is the more specific tag for this document.
MAP-E is mentioned only for comparison and for the address construction and port-set algorithm it reuses.
PCP is listed only as an alternative provisioning mechanism.
The ICMP handling section is a minor part of the document, specific to lw4o6.

RFC7597.title: Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E)
RFC7597.summary: Specifies MAP-E, a stateless mechanism for carrying IPv4 packets across an IPv6 network via IP-in-IPv6 encapsulation, with algorithmic mapping between IPv6 prefixes and IPv4 addresses plus transport ports (port sets/PSIDs).

MAP.why: The document defines MAP-E: Basic and Forwarding Mapping Rules, CE and BR behaviour, and the port-mapping algorithm.
MAP.quote: This document describes a mechanism for transporting IPv4 packets across an IPv6 network using IP encapsulation.

NAT.why: MAP CE uses NAPT restricted to a port set for IPv4 address sharing, with NAT44 and ICMP behaviour requirements.
NAT.quote: The NAT44 implemented in the MAP CE SHOULD conform to the behavior and best current practices documented in [RFC4787], [RFC5508], and [RFC5382].

rejected.why: Parent of MAP, which is implied by the MAP tag.
Encapsulation follows RFC 2473, but the document specifies MAP rather than a generic tunnelling mechanism.
Provisioning options are defined in RFC 7598, not in this document.
Mentioned only as the stateful counterpart; this document is not about it.
Fragmentation and MTU handling is a short section within MAP, not the document's subject.
Cited only as prior art in the introduction.

RFC7598.title: DHCPv6 Options for Configuration of Softwire Address and Port-Mapped Clients
RFC7598.summary: Defines DHCPv6 options (Softwire46 container, rule, BR, DMR, binding, port parameters) for provisioning MAP-E, MAP-T and Lightweight 4over6 CE devices.

DHCPv6.why: The document's main content is a set of new DHCPv6 options, with client and server behaviour for them.
DHCPv6.quote: This memo specifies a set of DHCPv6 [RFC3315] options to provision Softwire46 configuration information to CE routers.

MAP.why: The options provision MAP-E and MAP-T CEs, including the Basic, Forwarding and Default Mapping Rules and the port-set parameters, so MAP readers need it.
MAP.quote: configuring the Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E) [RFC7597], Mapping of Address and Port using Translation (MAP-T) [RFC7599]

softwire.why: It provisions Softwire46 CEs, including Lightweight 4over6, which has no separate tag, for IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnelling softwires.
softwire.quote: Softwire46 is a collective term used to refer to architectures based on the notion of IPv4 Address plus Port (A+P)

rejected.why: Lightweight 4over6 is an extension of DS-Lite, but this document only provisions it and does not specify DS-Lite.
Parent of the chosen MAP and softwire tags, so it is implied and not listed.
DHCPv6 is the more specific tag. DHCPv4 is mentioned only as the way other IPv4 configuration is provisioned.
Encapsulation and translation are what the provisioned mechanisms do. The document only conveys parameters.

gaps.name: Lightweight 4over6
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for it. It is covered only loosely by softwire and DS-Lite, and the document provisions it via OPTION_S46_CONT_LW.

RFC7599.title: Mapping of Address and Port using Translation (MAP-T)
RFC7599.summary: Specifies MAP-T, a stateless double NAT64 translation architecture for providing shared or unshared IPv4 connectivity across an IPv6 network, with CE and BR forwarding, mapping rules, ICMP and fragmentation handling.

MAP.why: The document specifies MAP-T, the translation mode of MAP. The MAP tag covers MAP-E and MAP-T.
MAP.quote: The Mapping of Address and Port using Translation (MAP-T) architecture specified in this document is such a double stateless NAT64-based solution.

rejected.why: MAP-T builds on stateless NAT64 translation (RFC 6145) but does not specify NAT64 itself. It extends it with the MAP algorithm, which MAP covers.
The IP/ICMP header translation is referenced from RFC 6145 and is not defined here.
DHCPv6 options (RFC 7598) are only recommended for provisioning. They are specified elsewhere.
The CE NAPT44 behaviour is only referenced, and the main subject is MAP address and port mapping, which is covered by MAP.
MAP is under this parent, so the more specific MAP tag is used instead.
It is mentioned only in usage considerations as needed in some cases. It is not the subject of the document.

RFC7600.title: IPv4 Residual Deployment via IPv6 - A Stateless Solution (4rd)
RFC7600.summary: Experimental specification of 4rd, a stateless IPv4-over-IPv6 transition mechanism that reversibly translates IPv4 headers to IPv6 across an IPv6-only domain, with mapping rules, shared addresses via port sets, fragmentation handling and DHCPv6 provisioning.

softwire.why: 4rd is a softwire-WG IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnelling/translation mechanism between CEs and Border Relays, in mesh or hub-and-spoke topologies.
softwire.quote: This document specifies a stateless solution for service providers to progressively deploy IPv6-only network domains while still offering IPv4 service to customers.

rejected.why: Only used to provision 4rd parameters; the new options are part of 4rd, not a DHCPv6 subject in their own right.
NAT64+ is mentioned as an optional upgraded element, but the document is not about NAT64 itself.
MAP is a related prior work (stateless A+P) but this document specifies a different mechanism, 4rd.
Parent of softwire, which is chosen and implies it.
CE NAT44 and port sets are used, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.
Referenced as the reverse mechanism and in an appendix example only.

gaps.name: A+P / stateless IPv4-over-IPv6 address sharing (4rd)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for 4rd or address-plus-port sharing, so softwire is the closest fit.

RFC7601.title: Message Header Field for Indicating Message Authentication Status
RFC7601.summary: Defines the Authentication-Results email header field, which carries results of message authentication checks (DKIM, SPF, iprev, SMTP AUTH, etc.) from border MTAs to MUAs and filters, and describes the related IANA registries.

email authentication.why: The whole document defines a common framework for conveying email authentication results across methods (DKIM, SPF, DMARC, iprev, etc.), so it fits the parent email authentication topic rather than any one method.
email authentication.quote: a message header field called Authentication-Results for use with electronic mail messages to indicate the results of message authentication efforts

message format.why: Specifies a new trace header field with ABNF, placement and prepending rules, and header registration, which is substantive Internet message header work.
message format.quote: It is a Structured Header Field as defined in Internet Message Format ([MAIL]), and thus all of the related definitions in that document apply.

rejected.why: DKIM results are reported by the header field, but the document does not specify or extend DKIM; it is one of several methods.
SPF results are mapped into the header field but SPF itself is only referenced, not defined or changed.
SMTP is the substrate where checks occur and AUTH results are reported, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
DMARC is only listed as one method with registry entries; not the subject.
The registry updates are boilerplate-like IANA actions supporting the header field; the main body is about the header field itself.
The iprev method uses PTR/A lookups, but DNS is just a mechanism used; nothing new about DNS is defined.

RFC7602.title: IS-IS Extended Sequence Number TLV
RFC7602.summary: Defines the IS-IS Extended Sequence Number TLV (type 11) carried in IIH and SNP PDUs to protect IS-IS from replay attacks, with deployment (send/verify modes) and ESSN encoding guidance.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new TLV for IIH and SNP PDUs, specifying its encoding, processing rules and deployment.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines the Extended Sequence Number TLV to protect Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) PDUs from replay attacks.

routing security.why: The purpose is securing a routing protocol against replay attacks, complementing IS-IS cryptographic authentication; no more specific child (RPKI/BGPsec) applies.
routing security.quote: A replayed IS-IS PDU can potentially cause many problems in IS-IS networks, including bouncing adjacencies, blackholing, and even some form of Denial-of-Service

rejected.why: Group key management is mentioned only as complementary background; the document defines no key management.
NTP timestamp format is only one optional ESSN encoding suggestion in the appendix.
NTP is referenced only for its 64-bit timestamp format in Appendix A.1, not specified or extended.
RFC 5304/5310 authentication is referenced as the context, but this document defines anti-replay sequence numbers rather than authentication.

RFC7603.title: Energy Management (EMAN) Applicability Statement
RFC7603.summary: Applicability statement for the IETF EMAN energy management framework, describing use-case scenarios and target devices, use case patterns, limitations, and the relationship of EMAN to other energy standards.

energy management.why: The whole document is about applying the EMAN energy monitoring and control framework to devices and scenarios, and relating it to other energy standards.
energy management.quote: The objective of Energy Management (EMAN) is to provide an energy management framework for networked devices.

rejected.why: SNMP and MIB modules are the mechanism EMAN uses to report; this document does not specify or extend SNMP or any MIB.
The EMAN MIBs are defined in other RFCs (7460, 7461, 7577); this document only summarizes them and discusses applicability.
YANG and NETCONF are mentioned only in passing as alternative mechanisms.
The document concerns energy monitoring and control of devices, not environmental impact of Internet infrastructure in general, though energy efficiency is a motivation.
Data centers are one use-case scenario among many, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Energy Management (EMAN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an 'energy management' topic under network management with the id 'energy management', but I must use only ids from the taxonomy as written; the listed id is 'energy management' and is used here. No further gap, though smart grid and building automation standards are not represented.

RFC7604.title: Comparison of Different NAT Traversal Techniques for Media Controlled by the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP)
RFC7604.summary: Informational RFC comparing NAT traversal techniques (STUN, embedded STUN, ICE, Latching variants, ALGs, TCP tunneling, TURN) for RTP media controlled by RTSP, with firewall discussion, used to select the RTSP 2.0 NAT traversal approach.

RTSP.why: The whole evaluation is about how RTSP-controlled media can traverse NATs, including the RTSP extensions each technique needs and the selection for RTSP 2.0.
RTSP.quote: This document describes several Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal techniques that were considered to be used for establishing the RTP media flows controlled by the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP).

NAT traversal.why: The document compares NAT traversal techniques against requirements. NAT traversal is the central subject, and it also covers firewall interaction.
NAT traversal.quote: This document describes several NAT traversal mechanisms for RTSP-controlled media streaming.

ICE.why: ICE gets a full section on how it would be used in RTSP, its implementation burden and its security. It is the technique the WG chose.
ICE.quote: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) [RFC5245] is a methodology for NAT traversal that has been developed for SIP using SDP offer/answer.

STUN.why: Stand-alone STUN and server-embedded STUN are two of the evaluated techniques, including deviations from RFC 5389 for embedding.
STUN.quote: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) [RFC5389] is a standardized protocol that allows a client to use secure means to discover the presence of a NAT

TURN.why: TURN relaying is evaluated as one technique, with usage steps for RTSP, deployment drawbacks and DoS risks.
TURN.quote: TURN [RFC5766] is a protocol for setting up traffic relays that allow clients behind NATs and firewalls to receive incoming traffic for both UDP and TCP.

rejected.why: RTP is the media flow being traversed through NATs. The document does not specify or extend RTP, apart from discussing keep-alives and SSRC use in latching.
The NAT tag covers NAT behaviour and requirements. This document is about traversing NATs for RTSP, so the more specific NAT traversal tag fits better.
There is a short firewall section, but firewalls are discussed mainly as a comparison to NATs and as ALG interaction. They are not a main subject.
SDP only carries the ICE support indication and the media descriptions. The document does not define anything new about it.
TCP tunneling of RTP is one evaluated technique, but the document only reviews how RTSP already does it. It specifies nothing about TCP.
TLS is only suggested as a way to stop ALGs from modifying RTSP signalling. It is a security mechanism the document leans on, not a subject of the document.

RFC7605.title: Recommendations on Using Assigned Transport Port Numbers
RFC7605.summary: BCP guidance for protocol designers on when and how to request IANA transport port number assignments (System/User/Dynamic ranges), complementing RFC 6335, covering conservation, security, versioning, transport choice and squatting.

IANA.why: The document is guidance on interacting with the IANA port number registry and its RFC 6335 processes, so the IANA subject page is where readers would look.
IANA.quote: how to use the transport protocol port number space and when to request a port assignment from IANA

transport.why: It explains the transport-layer port concept, its history and use across TCP, UDP, SCTP and DCCP. No specific transport protocol is specified, so the general transport topic fits.
transport.quote: A port number is a 16-bit number used for two distinct purposes: Demultiplexing transport endpoint associations within an end host

rejected.why: TCP and UDP are mentioned as transports that ports apply to, but the document does not specify or extend them.
Firewall and NAT considerations get a short subsection, but the document is not about firewall traversal.
DNS SRV records and mDNS/DNS-SD are cited only as alternatives to assigning a port, not discussed in their own right.
TLS and DTLS are named only as security mechanisms for new services.
The history section traces port numbers back to NCP and the ARPANET, but it is background and not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry
gaps.why: The document is about this registry and its port number ranges. The taxonomy has IANA but no specific tag for port number or service name assignment.

RFC7606.title: Revised Error Handling for BGP UPDATE Messages
RFC7606.summary: RFC 7606 revises BGP UPDATE error handling, replacing session reset with treat-as-withdraw or attribute discard for malformed path attributes, specifying per-attribute procedures and guidance for authors of new attributes.

BGP.why: The document revises BGP UPDATE message error handling and updates several BGP RFCs, including RFC 4271, so it belongs on the BGP page.
BGP.quote: a BGP speaker that receives an UPDATE message containing a malformed attribute is required to reset the session over which the offending attribute was received

rejected.why: Community and Extended Community attributes get error-handling revisions, but only as two of many attributes. The document is not about communities.
ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_ID error handling is revised, but this is a minor part of the document.
The security motivation is resilience against malformed optional transitive attributes. The document does not specify a routing-security mechanism.
ATTR_SET from RFC 6368 and typed NLRI of VPN address families are mentioned in passing only.
The Operational Considerations section is brief and applies to BGP error handling, not to general operational security practice.

RFC7607.title: Codification of AS 0 Processing
RFC7607.summary: Updates RFC 4271 to forbid AS 0 in BGP OPEN, AS_PATH, AS4_PATH, AGGREGATOR and AS4_AGGREGATOR, specifying error handling for UPDATEs and OPEN messages containing it, motivated by RPKI ROAs that use AS 0 to mark prefixes as not to be routed.

BGP.why: The document updates BGP-4 (RFC 4271) error handling and speaker behaviour for AS 0 in OPEN and UPDATE messages.
BGP.quote: A BGP speaker MUST NOT originate or propagate a route with an AS number of zero in the AS_PATH, AS4_PATH, AGGREGATOR, or AS4_AGGREGATOR attributes.

rejected.why: RPKI ROAs with AS 0 are the motivation, but the document only specifies BGP message processing, not RPKI objects or validation.
Security rationale is stated (preventing hijack via AS 0), but the normative content is BGP protocol processing, so the BGP tag covers it.
The only IANA action is a minor registry entry wording change; boilerplate.

RFC7608.title: IPv6 Prefix Length Recommendation for Forwarding
RFC7608.summary: BCP requiring IPv6 forwarding to apply longest-match-first on prefixes of any length from /0 to /128, with no design restriction on prefix length, in line with CIDR rules.

IPv6.why: The document sets IPv6 forwarding and prefix-length requirements and clarifies the /64 boundary in IPv6 addressing. It is about IPv6 specifically.
IPv6.quote: forwarding processes MUST be designed to process prefixes of any length up to /128, by increments of 1.

CIDR.why: The recommendation is grounded in the CIDR architecture and longest-match forwarding. It applies CIDR rules to IPv6 prefixes of arbitrary length.
CIDR.quote: IPv6 implementations MUST conform to the rules specified in Section 5.1 of [RFC4632].

rejected.why: SLAAC is mentioned only to explain the conventional /64 for subnets. The document is not about it.
The IPv6 tag already covers the addressing subject here, and the document is about forwarding rather than address allocation.
It is cited only as one example of how longer prefixes get configured.
The document makes a forwarding recommendation. It does not discuss routing architecture or scalability.

RFC7609.title: IBM's Shared Memory Communications over RDMA (SMC-R) Protocol
RFC7609.summary: Specifies IBM's SMC-R protocol, which transparently moves TCP socket traffic onto RDMA over RoCE, with TCP-option-based rendezvous, link groups for failover and load balancing, and RMB-based data flow and termination.

RDMA.why: The whole document defines an RDMA-based protocol (RMBs, RKeys, queue pairs, RoCE, link groups) for carrying TCP socket data. RDMA protocols are the subject area readers would look under.
RDMA.quote: SMC-R is a protocol for Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) communication between TCP socket endpoints.

TCP.why: The document defines a new experimental TCP option (ExID SMCR) and specifies how keepalive, termination, urgent data and window updates interact with TCP, so it extends TCP behaviour rather than only using it.
TCP.quote: SMC-R Rendezvous starts with the TCP/IP three-way handshake, during which connection peers use TCP options to announce their SMC-R capabilities.

rejected.why: RoCE runs over Ethernet, but this is only the substrate. The document does not specify IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
TLS/SSL is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as working unchanged above SMC-R.
IPsec is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as incompatible with SMC-R.
InfiniBand is mentioned only as a possible future fabric. The document targets RoCE, not IP over InfiniBand.
Appendix B covers socket API considerations, but it only says no application changes are needed. It does not define socket API extensions.
The only IANA content is a TCP ExID registration, which is boilerplate here.

gaps.name: RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet)
gaps.why: The protocol is built specifically on RoCE fabrics, queue pairs and SendMsg. The taxonomy has no RoCE tag, so RDMA is the closest fit.

RFC7610.title: DHCPv6-Shield: Protecting against Rogue DHCPv6 Servers
RFC7610.summary: RFC 7610 specifies DHCPv6-Shield, a BCP for layer 2 devices to filter DHCPv6 server messages on non-permitted ports, protecting hosts from rogue DHCPv6 servers (analogous to RA-Guard and IPv4 DHCP snooping).

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies filtering of DHCPv6-server messages at layer 2 to defend DHCPv6 clients against rogue servers. It is operational and security guidance about DHCPv6 deployment, so DHCPv6 readers would want it.
DHCPv6.quote: a mechanism for protecting hosts connected to a switched network against rogue DHCPv6 servers

rejected.why: The document parses IPv6 header chains and extension headers, but IPv6 is only the packet format being inspected. The subject is DHCPv6 protection.
RA-Guard and Router Advertisements are mentioned only as an analogy and explicitly out of scope.
This is a plausible topic tag, but the DHCPv6 technology tag is the more specific fit.
ESP is mentioned only for how to treat it in header chain parsing.
RFC 7513 is mentioned only as a complementary mitigation.
The document concerns generic layer 2 switches and does not specify Ethernet behaviour.

RFC7611.title: BGP ACCEPT_OWN Community Attribute
RFC7611.summary: Defines the BGP ACCEPT_OWN well-known community, letting a route reflector re-advertise a VPN route back to its originating PE so it can be imported into a different VRF on that PE, plus the related decision-process step.

BGP communities.why: The document's core is a new well-known BGP community and its processing rules, so it belongs on the BGP communities page.
BGP communities.quote: This memo defines ACCEPT_OWN, a new well-known BGP community in the First Come First Served [RFC5226] range, whose value as assigned by IANA is 0xFFFF0001.

L3VPN.why: The mechanism concerns RT/RD handling and import between VRFs in BGP/MPLS VPNs, including an extranet application, so L3VPN readers need it.
L3VPN.quote: it is desirable for a route reflector to be able to modify the RT list of a VPN route that the route reflector distributes

route reflection.why: The route reflector re-advertising routes back to the originator, and the ORIGINATOR_ID handling that this requires, are central to the document, so route reflection readers would want it.
route reflection.quote: the route reflector attaches the ORIGINATOR_ID attribute to the UPDATE messages so that if such prefix advertisements reach the originator, the originator can reject them

rejected.why: BGP is the parent of BGP communities, which is the more specific tag chosen, so the ancestor is implied.
MPLS is only the underlying VPN substrate; the document does not specify anything about MPLS itself.
L3VPN is the more specific child that fits, so the parent is not listed.

RFC7612.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): Schema for Printer Services
RFC7612.summary: RFC 7612 defines an LDAP schema (object classes and attribute types) for describing printers and print services in directories, based on IPP/1.1, Printer MIB v2 and PWG specs, obsoleting RFC 3712.

LDAP.why: The document specifies an LDAP schema (object classes, attribute types, OIDs, matching rules) for printers; LDAP directory schema readers would look for it.
LDAP.quote: This document defines a schema, object classes, and attributes, for Printers and print services, for use with directories that support the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol
