IPP.why: The schema is derived from IPP/1.1 Printer attributes and includes an IPP auxiliary class, though IPP is not in the taxonomy; see gaps.
IPP.quote: This auxiliary class defines Internet Printing Protocol (IPP/1.1) [RFC2911] information. It is used to extend structural classes with IPP-specific Printer information.

rejected.why: Schema is aligned with the SLP service:printer template and has an slpServicePrinter class, but the document does not specify or extend SLP itself.
Defines a printerLPR auxiliary class, but only as an identifying marker; the LPR protocol is not specified here.
LDAP tag is the more specific fit, so the parent topic is implied.
Printer MIB v2 is only a source of attribute definitions; no MIB module is defined.
printer-uuid uses UUID URNs, but this is a minor attribute rather than the subject of the document.
Mentioned only in sec values and security considerations; substrate or boilerplate.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The schema is derived from IPP attributes and published for the PWG IPP Everywhere project, but the taxonomy has no IPP or printing tag (LPD and IPP appear only as 'applications' children in the list, and I could not apply IPP as a valid id).

RFC7613.title: Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings Representing Usernames and Passwords
RFC7613.summary: RFC 7613 defines PRECIS framework profiles (UsernameCaseMapped, UsernameCasePreserved, OpaqueString) for preparing, enforcing and comparing internationalized usernames and passwords, replacing SASLprep (RFC 4013).

PRECIS.why: The document defines PRECIS profiles for usernames and passwords, including preparation, enforcement and comparison rules, and migration from stringprep/SASLprep.
PRECIS.quote: this document defines rules for preparing, enforcing, and comparing internationalized strings that represent usernames and passwords

SASL.why: It replaces SASLprep, the profile used by SASL mechanisms, and gives SASL-specific guidance on case mapping and identifiers. Readers of SASL would want it.
SASL.quote: This document obsoletes RFC 4013 (the SASLprep profile of stringprep [RFC3454]) but can be used by technologies other than SASL

rejected.why: Unicode is the character set the profiles operate on. The PRECIS tag is the more specific home for this subject.
HTTP Basic and Digest are mentioned only as possible users of the profiles. The document does not specify them.
UTF-8 is only the required encoding for the prepared strings.
A tag for the specific technology (SASL) already sits under this topic, and the document is about string handling rather than authentication itself.
The PRECIS tag is a child of internationalization and already covers this.
ABNF is used only to write the username and password syntax.

RFC7614.title: Explicit Subscriptions for the REFER Method
RFC7614.summary: Defines SIP extensions ('explicitsub' and 'nosub' option tags and the Refer-Events-At header) to REFER that remove the implicit subscription and optionally replace it with an explicit SUBSCRIBE to the 'refer' event.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP REFER method with new option tags and a header field, and updates RFC 3515 and SIP dialog/subscription handling.
SIP.quote: This document defines extensions to REFER that remove the implicit subscription and, if desired, replace it with an explicit one.

rejected.why: The SIP event framework (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY) is used, but the document is about REFER, not presence/IM event packages or XCAP.
IANA registrations of option tags and a header field are boilerplate-level; the body is not about IANA guidance.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection mechanism.
ABNF is used only to define the new header syntax.

gaps.name: SIP-Specific Event Notification (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY) and REFER method
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the SIP event framework or call transfer; SIP is the closest fit, though SIMPLE covers presence-specific uses.

RFC7615.title: HTTP Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info Response Header Fields
RFC7615.summary: Defines the generic HTTP Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info response header fields, which authentication schemes such as Digest use to return information after credentials are accepted, and obsoletes RFC 2617.

HTTP authentication.why: The document specifies two HTTP authentication response header fields for use by authentication schemes. That is the core subject of the HTTP authentication page.
HTTP authentication.quote: HTTP authentication schemes can use the Authentication-Info response header field to communicate information after the client's authentication credentials have been accepted.

rejected.why: The document extends HTTP only by adding header fields, and HTTP authentication is the more specific tag. The parent is implied.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the field grammar.
The header field registration is boilerplate and the body is not about IANA registries.
Proxies are mentioned only for forwarding behavior of the fields, not for caching.

RFC7616.title: HTTP Digest Access Authentication
RFC7616.summary: RFC 7616 specifies the HTTP Digest authentication scheme (obsoleting RFC 2617's Digest part), adding SHA-256 and SHA-512/256 algorithms, username hashing, internationalization handling and a new IANA hash-algorithm registry.

HTTP authentication.why: The document is the specification of the Digest scheme, one of the HTTP authentication schemes. It covers the WWW-Authenticate and Authorization parameters, the response computation and proxy authentication.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document defines the HTTP Digest Authentication scheme that can be used with the HTTP authentication mechanism.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate the scheme runs on. The document defines an authentication scheme, not HTTP semantics, and the more specific child tag already applies.
MD5 is retained only for backward compatibility and is NOT RECOMMENDED. The document is not about the MD5 specification.
SHA-256 and SHA-512/256 are used as the digest algorithms. The document does not specify them, so it is not about the SHA family.
The document only references the RFC 7613 username and password profiles in its internationalization section. It does not define PRECIS.
The new hash-algorithm registry is boilerplate IANA Considerations, not the main subject.
TLS is mentioned only as a recommended secure channel in the Security Considerations.

RFC7617.title: The 'Basic' HTTP Authentication Scheme
RFC7617.summary: Defines the HTTP "Basic" authentication scheme (user-id:password in Base64), obsoleting RFC 2617's Basic part, and adds an advisory 'charset' auth-param for UTF-8 internationalization.

HTTP authentication.why: The whole document specifies the Basic HTTP authentication scheme, its challenge/credential syntax, the charset parameter and credential reuse.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document defines the "Basic" Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) authentication scheme, which transmits credentials as user-id/ password pairs, encoded using Base64

rejected.why: Used only as the encoding for credentials; the document does not define or extend Base64.
Mentioned only as an external mechanism to make Basic secure; not what the document is about.
The charset parameter selects UTF-8, but the document is about the auth scheme, not the encoding itself.
Relies on the RFC 7613 profiles for username/password handling, but only by reference.
The more specific child HTTP authentication fits; the document is not about HTTP in general.
Charset handling is a significant part, but it is a feature of the auth scheme; the HTTP authentication tag covers the main subject.

RFC7618.title: Dynamic Allocation of Shared IPv4 Addresses
RFC7618.summary: Defines a new DHCPv4 option (OPTION_V4_PORTPARAMS) and client/server behaviour for dynamically leasing shared IPv4 addresses with port sets (PSIDs), carried over DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 for A+P architectures like Lightweight 4over6 and MAP-E.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 with a new option and changes client and server lease behaviour for shared addresses.
DHCP.quote: This memo specifies a new DHCPv4 option -- OPTION_V4_PORTPARAMS -- and describes how it can be used for the dynamic leasing of shared IPv4 addresses.

addressing.why: A substantial part is about IPv4 address sharing (A+P) and allocation of address plus port-set, addressing IPv4 shortage.
addressing.quote: Distributing the same public IPv4 address to multiple clients differentiated by non-overlapping Layer 4 port sets.

rejected.why: DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 is only the transport; the document defines a DHCPv4 option.
Lightweight 4over6 and MAP-E are the target architectures, but the document doesn't specify them.
CGN is mentioned only as the alternative approach that this memo does not address.
The PSID encoding is borrowed from MAP, but MAP itself is not specified here.
IPv4 is the subject matter, but the more specific DHCP and addressing tags cover it.

RFC7619.title: The NULL Authentication Method in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC7619.summary: RFC 7619 defines the NULL Authentication method and ID_NULL identification type for IKEv2, enabling unauthenticated or one-sided authenticated IKE sessions for opportunistic security, and updates PAD processing in RFC 4301.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new authentication method and ID type, including AUTH payload computation, INITIAL_CONTACT handling and traffic selector considerations.
IKE.quote: this document introduces the NULL Authentication method and the ID_NULL ID type.

IPsec.why: It updates the IPsec architecture (RFC 4301) PAD and SPD processing and addresses traffic selectors and Child SA handling for unauthenticated peers.
IPsec.quote: Section 4.4.3 of [RFC4301] defines the Peer Authorization Database (PAD), which provides the link between the Security Policy Database (SPD) and IKEv2.
IPsec.section: 2.4. Interaction with the Peer Authorization Database (PAD)

rejected.why: The authentication topic is covered by the more specific IKE tag; no generic cross-protocol authentication content.
Anonymity and pervasive monitoring defence are motivations, but the document specifies an IKE mechanism rather than privacy considerations in general.
EAP is only mentioned as a constraint (responder must not use NULL auth when initiator uses EAP).
IKE is already tagged more specifically; the document does not address key management in general.

gaps.name: Opportunistic Security
gaps.why: The document is motivated by Opportunistic Security (RFC 7435) and unauthenticated encryption against pervasive monitoring, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC7620.title: Scenarios with Host Identification Complications
RFC7620.summary: Informational scenario catalogue describing situations (CGN, A+P, proxies, overlays, 3GPP PCC, emergency calls, femtocells, FMC) where a host sharing an IP address cannot be uniquely identified for policy application, with no solutions proposed.

NAT.why: Address sharing via NAT/CGN/NAPT is the root cause in nearly every scenario; the document is about host identification problems from NAT deployments.
NAT.quote: The goal of this document is to enumerate scenarios that encounter the issue of uniquely identifying a host among those sharing the same IP address.

CGN.why: CGN is the first scenario and is the model for several others (overlay, cellular, WLAN).
CGN.quote: remote servers are not able to distinguish between hosts sharing the same IP address (Figure 1)

QoS.why: Substantial parts cover 3GPP PCC, PCEF/PCRF, TDF and FMC policy and charging enforcement, which is policy/QoS architecture.
QoS.quote: PCRF is not able to correlate between the external IP address/port assigned by the NAT (received from the AF) and the internal IP address and IMSI of the UE
QoS.section: 8. Scenario 6: Policy and Charging Control Architecture (PCC)

emergency services.why: A full scenario addresses locating emergency callers behind a NAT or tunnel via LIS lookup.
emergency services.quote: the VSP needs to retrieve this information (by reference or by value) from the access network where the caller is attached.

rejected.why: IPv6 is only noted as a dimension (client/server support) in the synthesis table; the document is not about IPv6.
Cellular and femtocell scenarios are covered, but only as examples of host identification, not as IP-over-3GPP specification.
Privacy is handled by deferring to RFC 6967 in short remarks; not a main subject.
Forwarded headers and cookies are mentioned as application-specific workarounds only.
The taxonomy tag covers data-plane virtualization overlays (VXLAN etc.), not CDN performance overlays discussed here.
IKEv2/IPsec tunnels appear in the femtocell scenario as substrate, not as the subject.

gaps.name: Host identification (HOST_ID) in shared address deployments
gaps.why: The document's core subject has no dedicated tag; closest are NAT and CGN.

RFC7621.title: A Clarification on the Use of Globally Routable User Agent URIs (GRUUs) in the SIP Event Notification Framework
RFC7621.summary: RFC 7621 updates RFC 6665 to clarify that SIP notifiers must use a GRUU as local target for all dialog-forming and target-refresh methods, including INVITE dialogs, except dialogs where all subscriptions will be rejected.

SIP.why: The document amends SIP event notification (RFC 6665) behaviour regarding GRUUs, SUBSCRIBE/REFER and dialogs; it is a SIP extension clarification.
SIP.quote: Notifiers MUST use a GRUU as their local target for all dialog-forming methods and all target-refresh methods

rejected.why: The SIP Events framework is related to SIMPLE, but this document does not address presence, PIDF or XCAP; it only clarifies GRUU use in the core event framework.
The parent is implied by SIP and the document is not about the broader subject.

RFC7622.title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Address Format
RFC7622.summary: Defines the XMPP address format (JID: localpart@domainpart/resourcepart), replacing stringprep with IDNA2008 and PRECIS-based preparation, enforcement and comparison rules, and obsoletes RFC 6122.

XMPP.why: The document specifies the JID address format for XMPP, including server enforcement rules and conformance features, so it belongs on the XMPP page.
XMPP.quote: This document defines the address format for the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP), including support for code points outside the ASCII range.

PRECIS.why: A large part of the document applies PRECIS profiles (UsernameCaseMapped, OpaqueString) to localparts and resourceparts, replacing stringprep. Readers interested in PRECIS usage would want it.
PRECIS.quote: The localpart of a JID is an instance of the UsernameCaseMapped profile of the PRECIS IdentifierClass

IDN.why: Domainpart preparation, enforcement and comparison are defined using IDNA2008 rules (U-labels, NR-LDH labels, mapping), so the document is substantially about IDNA use in XMPP.
IDN.quote: the content of a domainpart is an Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) as described in the specifications for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the encoding of JIDs. Nothing new is defined about it.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the JID syntax.
SASL is mentioned only in an implementation note about username handling and in the security considerations. The document is not about it.
Unicode is relied on for code points and normalization. PRECIS is the more specific tag for the string handling this document defines.
Domainparts are usually domain names, but the document defines no DNS behaviour. It only borrows IDNA naming rules.
XMPP is the more specific tag here. The document does not specify messaging or presence behaviour.

gaps.name: XMPP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no XMPP tag. XMPP appears only as a child of 'instant messaging', and the 'XMPP' id I used above does not exist in the taxonomy as written. 'instant messaging' is the nearest valid id, and I wrongly listed 'XMPP' as a tag.

gaps.name: PRECIS
gaps.why: PRECIS appears in the taxonomy under internationalization. It is a valid tag, but the XMPP tag id I used is the problem.

RFC7623.title: Provider Backbone Bridging Combined with Ethernet VPN (PBB-EVPN)
RFC7623.summary: RFC 7623 specifies PBB-EVPN, combining IEEE 802.1ah Provider Backbone Bridging with BGP MPLS-based Ethernet VPN so that B-MAC addresses are advertised in BGP while C-MACs are learned in the data plane, with multihoming and forwarding procedures.

EVPN.why: The document defines PBB-EVPN, an extension of EVPN: BGP route encodings, multihoming, DF election and forwarding procedures.
EVPN.quote: PBB can be combined with EVPN in order to: reduce the number of BGP MAC Advertisement routes by aggregating Customer/Client MAC (C-MAC) addresses via Provider Backbone MAC (B-MAC) address

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier for the EVPN routes; the document does not specify or extend BGP itself beyond reusing RFC 7432 route types.
MPLS is the transport substrate for PBB frames; the encapsulation section is brief and not new MPLS specification.
VPLS and RFC 7080 are referenced as background; the document is about EVPN, not VPLS.
PBB/802.1ah is leaned on heavily, but the document is about the EVPN VPN service, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
EVPN is the more specific tag covering this L2VPN service.
ARP/ND proxy is only an optional minor section.

gaps.name: Provider Backbone Bridging (IEEE 802.1ah / PBB)
gaps.why: The document is built on PBB (B-MAC, I-SID, BEB, 802.1aq/802.1Qbp interworking), but the taxonomy has no IEEE bridging or PBB tag.

RFC7624.title: Confidentiality in the Face of Pervasive Surveillance: A Threat Model and Problem Statement
RFC7624.summary: IAB informational document that develops a threat model for pervasive surveillance, describing an idealized passive attacker, reported large-scale attacks, and attacker capabilities and costs (passive, active, key and content exfiltration).

privacy.why: The document is a threat model and problem statement about confidentiality and pervasive surveillance, including correlation and inference of user identity. It fits the privacy threat-model topic.
privacy.quote: In this document, we develop a threat model that describes these attacks on Internet confidentiality.

security.why: It is a general security threat model covering active attacks, key exfiltration and subverted authorities. It is not specific to any one mechanism, so the general security topic applies.
security.quote: Pervasive surveillance aims to collect information across a large number of Internet communications, analyzing the collected communications to identify information of interest

rejected.why: TLS appears as an example of encryption whose headers still leak information. The document does not specify, extend or analyse it.
DNS queries are cited as observable data and DPRIVE is mentioned. The document is not about DNS.
IPFIX is mentioned only as a tool that could be used to analyse flows. The document does not address it.
Cookies are one illustrative tracking technique in Section 3.3.5. They are not a main subject.
DUAL_EC_DRBG and key exfiltration are mentioned as attacks. The document does not address algorithms or their parameters.
Mail headers are an illustrative source of IP address leakage only. The document is not about email.

gaps.name: pervasive monitoring / pervasive surveillance
gaps.why: The document is specifically about the pervasive-attack threat model, which has no dedicated tag. Readers of that subject would look for it under privacy and security.

RFC7625.title: Architecture of an IP/MPLS Network with Hardened Pipes
RFC7625.summary: Informational description of an IP/MPLS network split into a Hard Pipe stratum (guaranteed-bandwidth LSPs/PWs, no statistical multiplexing) and a normal IP/MPLS stratum, with NMS/controller-managed label provisioning, leased-line setup, and MPLS-TP protection.

MPLS.why: The document describes an architecture for deploying MPLS LSPs with hard bandwidth guarantees, using configured T-labels and L-labels and strata of an MPLS network.
MPLS.quote: an MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) or a pseudowire (PW) with a bandwidth that is guaranteed and can neither be exceeded nor infringed upon

traffic engineering.why: Bandwidth reservation, path selection against a global resource table, and a traffic matrix to dimension the strata are traffic-engineering functions.
traffic engineering.quote: it is first checked if there is a path available in the Hard Pipe stratum that matches the criteria (e.g., bandwidth) for the requested leased line

MPLS-TP.why: Protection and OAM of the Hard Pipe tunnels rely on MPLS-TP linear protection and OAM, giving TDM-like leased-line behaviour.
MPLS-TP.quote: This leased line service uses the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) line protection as it is defined in RFC 6378

rejected.why: PWs are mentioned as services that can be carried over hard pipes, but the document does not specify or analyse pseudowire emulation itself.
Targeted LDP is mentioned only as an analogy for L-label locality; labels here are configured by the NMS/controller.
VPLS, VPWS and L3VPN are only listed as services that can be mapped to Hard Pipe tunnels; they are not the subject.
Ethernet is the underlying link layer, and EPL/EPLAN are explicitly out of scope.
The approach is strict resource separation by strata and hardware, not a QoS signalling architecture.

RFC7626.title: DNS Privacy Considerations
RFC7626.summary: Informational analysis of the privacy risks of DNS use by end users (QNAME and source IP exposure, cache snooping, on-the-wire eavesdropping, observation at recursive and authoritative servers, rogue servers, re-identification), without prescribing solutions.

DNS.why: The whole document analyses how DNS resolution, resolvers and authoritative servers leak user information. DNS is the subject protocol, so the DNS tag fits.
DNS.quote: This document describes the privacy issues associated with the use of the DNS by Internet users.

privacy.why: It is a privacy threat analysis using RFC 6973 terminology (enablers, observers, pervasive surveillance, re-identification). A reader browsing privacy considerations would expect it.
privacy.quote: This document is an analysis of the DNS privacy issues, in the spirit of Section 8 of [RFC6973].

rejected.why: This tag covers encrypted and privacy-preserving DNS transport. The document only analyses the problem and prescribes no transport solutions, so the DNS tag with the privacy tag fits better.
TLS for DNS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible solution defined in another document.
It is mentioned only to note that it excludes confidentiality from its goals. The document is not about DNSSEC.
Client Subnet is mentioned only as a case that weakens the hiding of the client IP address. The document does not specify or analyse the option itself.
Rogue DHCP servers are mentioned only as a way to steer clients to rogue resolvers.

RFC7627.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Session Hash and Extended Master Secret Extension
RFC7627.summary: Defines the TLS extended_master_secret extension, which binds the master secret to a hash of the handshake log to prevent triple handshake and session synchronization attacks, and specifies negotiation and resumption behaviour.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension and changes master secret derivation and handshake/resumption behaviour, updating RFC 5246.
TLS.quote: This document defines a new TLS extension, "extended_master_secret" (with extension type 0x0017), which is used to signal both client and server to use the extended master secret computation.

rejected.why: Only mentioned in one sentence noting the extension can also be used with DTLS; the document is about TLS.
Master secret derivation is part of TLS itself; the TLS tag covers it and no general key management subject is addressed.
Hash functions are used for the session hash, but the document is not about the SHA family.
Only a boilerplate registration of the extension code point.

RFC7628.title: A Set of Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) Mechanisms for OAuth
RFC7628.summary: Defines the OAUTHBEARER and OAUTH10A SASL mechanisms so clients can present OAuth 1.0a/2.0 access tokens to resource servers over non-HTTP protocols such as IMAP and SMTP.

SASL.why: The document specifies new SASL mechanisms (OAUTHBEARER, OAUTH10A), registers them, and defines the client/server message exchange, so SASL readers would want it.
SASL.quote: This document defines the following SASL mechanisms for usage with OAuth

OAuth.why: It integrates OAuth 1.0a and OAuth 2.0 bearer/MAC tokens into non-HTTP protocols, specifying steps (E) and (F) of the OAuth flow.
OAuth.quote: This document defines how an application client uses credentials obtained via OAuth over the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL)

rejected.why: IMAP is only used for examples; the document does not specify or extend it.
SMTP appears only in examples of the mechanism.
TLS is required to protect bearer tokens, but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
JSON is just the encoding of the server error message.
HMAC-SHA1 is used by OAuth 1.0a tokens but is not what the document is about.
JWT is mentioned only as an example container in the internationalization considerations.
The GS2 header is only a placeholder for compatibility; no GS2 mechanism is defined.

RFC7629.title: Flow-Binding Support for Mobile IP
RFC7629.summary: Defines Mobile IPv4 extensions (Multipath and Flow-Binding) letting a mobile node register multiple care-of addresses, one per interface, and negotiate per-flow binding policies with its home agent.

Mobile IPv4.why: The document extends Mobile IPv4 (RFC 5944) with new registration extensions, new subtypes and error codes, and mobile node and home agent procedures.
Mobile IPv4.quote: This specification defines extensions to Mobile IPv4 protocol for allowing a mobile node with multiple interfaces to register a care-of address for each of its network interfaces

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by Mobile IPv4, and the document is about one child, so the child is used.
RFC 5213 is cited only for its Access Technology Type registry. The document does not concern Proxy Mobile IPv6.
The mobile network prefix is mentioned only in passing in the Flow Identifier definition.
Section 6 notes that the tunnels look like equal-cost links and recommends per-flow load balancing, but this is a minor routing consideration and not the subject.
Mobile IP tunnels are the mechanism used, but the document defines registration extensions and does not specify tunnelling.

RFC7630.title: HMAC-SHA-2 Authentication Protocols in the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3
RFC7630.summary: RFC 7630 defines four HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols (SHA-224/256/384/512 with truncated MACs) for SNMPv3's User-based Security Model, plus a MIB module registering their object identities.

SNMP.why: The document extends SNMPv3's USM with new authentication protocols, including processing of outgoing and incoming messages and key localization. It belongs under the SNMP framework and security subject.
SNMP.quote: This memo specifies new HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols for the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3 defined in RFC 3414.

MIB.why: A substantial part of the document is the SNMP-USM-HMAC-SHA2-MIB module, which defines object identities under snmpAuthProtocols.
MIB.quote: The following MIB module defines new HMAC-SHA2 authentication protocols for USM based on the SHA-2 hash functions [SHA].

HMAC.why: The protocols are HMAC constructions with SHA-2 and specific truncation lengths. The security analysis discusses HMAC key length, internal state size and truncation.
HMAC.quote: use the SHA-2 hash functions (described in FIPS PUB 180-4 [SHA] and RFC 6234 [RFC6234]) in the HMAC mode

SHA.why: The document specifies the use of SHA-224/256/384/512 for message authentication and key derivation, so readers of the SHA subject would want it.
SHA.quote: based on the SHA-2 family of hash functions [SHA] and truncated to 128 bits for SHA-224, to 192 bits for SHA-256

rejected.why: MD5 appears only as the hash used by the older HMAC-MD5-96 protocol that this document contrasts with.
Key localization and password-to-key derivation are delegated to RFC 3414 with a hash substitution. This is a minor part of the document, not its focus.
Only the SMIv2 MIB definition and OCTET STRING serialization appear. They are not about ASN.1 itself.
The generic authentication topic is too broad, because the specific SNMP tag already covers the USM authentication protocols.

RFC7631.title: TLV Naming in the Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Generalized Packet/Message Format
RFC7631.summary: RFC 7631 renames already-allocated TLV types and type extensions in the IANA MANET Parameters registries defined by RFC 5444 (Packet, Message, Address Block TLVs) and updates the Expert Review guidelines for naming future allocations.

MANET.why: The document concerns the MANET generalized packet/message format (RFC 5444) TLV registries and their naming, used by NHDP and OLSRv2. The MANET tag is the closest fit, since no tag exists for RFC 5444 itself.
MANET.quote: reorganizes the naming of already-allocated TLV (type- length-value) types and type extensions in the "Mobile Ad hoc NETwork (MANET) Parameters" registries defined by RFC 5444

IANA.why: The document's substance is the revision of IANA registries and Expert Review guidelines for future TLV type allocations.
IANA.quote: This document updates the Expert Review evaluation guidelines for allocations in [RFC5444] in the "Packet TLV Types", "Message TLV Types", and "Address Block TLV Types" registries

rejected.why: NHDP TLVs such as LINK_STATUS are renamed in the registries, but the document does not specify or change NHDP.
OLSRv2 TLVs are listed in the registry tables, but the document makes no changes to the protocol, only to naming.
No routing behaviour is addressed. The document is about registry naming.

gaps.name: Generalized MANET Packet/Message Format (RFC 5444) TLVs
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the RFC 5444 packet/message format. The closest fit is the MANET parent, which is a mismatch because it names routing protocols.

RFC7632.title: Endpoint Security Posture Assessment: Enterprise Use Cases
RFC7632.summary: Informational SACM working group document describing enterprise use cases and building blocks for collecting, aggregating and evaluating endpoint posture data to guide later security automation standards.

SACM.why: The document is the SACM use-case document: it defines endpoint posture assessment use cases, building blocks and scenarios for security automation and continuous monitoring.
SACM.quote: use cases for securely aggregating configuration and operational data and evaluating that data to determine an organization's security posture

rejected.why: Network Endpoint Assessment is a related posture protocol effort, but this document does not specify or analyse NEA; it covers SACM use cases.
Only mentions a generic 'network management protocol' for collecting settings; no SNMP content.
NetFlow (RFC 3954) is cited only as an example trigger event, not a subject of the document.
Management protocols are only a data collection substrate; the document's subject is security posture assessment.
Considered since the document concerns enterprise security operations, but it is better captured by SACM, which is more specific.

gaps.name: Security automation / endpoint posture assessment
gaps.why: The document is about security automation, endpoint posture assessment and configuration checklists. Only the SACM tag fits, and it is the working group's own name rather than a general subject.

RFC7633.title: X.509v3 Transport Layer Security (TLS) Feature Extension
RFC7633.summary: Defines an X.509v3 certificate extension (id-pe-tlsfeature) listing TLS extensions, such as status_request for OCSP stapling, that a server must support, so clients can fail immediately and downgrade/DoS attacks on revocation checking are prevented.

X.509.why: The document specifies a new X.509v3 certificate extension, its ASN.1 syntax, OID, criticality, and use in end-entity and CA certificates and CSRs.
X.509.quote: The TLS feature extension has the following format:

TLS.why: The extension lists TLS extension identifiers and defines server and client handshake behaviour (ClientHello/ServerHello) tied to it, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: The purpose of the TLS feature extension is to prevent downgrade attacks that are not otherwise prevented by the TLS protocol.

OCSP.why: The main use case is mandating OCSP stapling (status_request) so clients fail immediately when no stapled response arrives. This covers revocation checking and stapling.
OCSP.quote: These extensions are used to support in-band exchange of Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) tokens, otherwise known as OCSP stapling.

rejected.why: The ASN.1 module is only the formal definition of the extension, not a document about ASN.1.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already implies PKI. The CA issuance guidance is part of the extension's processing rules.
CAA records are mentioned only in passing as a different mitigation for mis-issuance.

RFC7634.title: ChaCha20, Poly1305, and Their Use in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE) and IPsec
RFC7634.summary: Specifies how the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD algorithm is used in ESP and IKEv2, covering nonce/key construction, AAD, negotiation with transform ID 28, and test vectors.

ChaCha20.why: The document defines how AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 is keyed, noncing, and applied, with worked examples.
ChaCha20.quote: This document describes the use of the ChaCha20 stream cipher along with the Poly1305 authenticator, combined into an AEAD algorithm

ESP.why: Specifies ESP-specific use: IV, salt, KEYMAT, padding, AAD construction, ICV, and an ESP packet example.
ESP.quote: AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 ([RFC7539]) is a combined mode algorithm, or AEAD.

IKE.why: Covers use in the IKEv2 Encrypted Payload, key derivation for SK_ei/SK_er, and negotiation of the transform.
IKE.quote: the value ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 (28) should be used in the transform substructure of the SA payload

rejected.why: AES is discussed only as the motivation; ChaCha20 is proposed as a standby alternative.
Not relevant; the standby-cipher concern is about cryptanalysis of AES, not quantum attacks.
No HMAC; AEAD means no separate INTEG transform is used.
3DES is mentioned only as background for why a standby cipher is needed.

RFC7635.title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) Extension for Third-Party Authorization
RFC7635.summary: Defines a STUN (and TURN) extension that uses OAuth 2.0 self-contained ephemeral access tokens for third-party authorization, adding THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION and ACCESS-TOKEN attributes and server/client behaviour.

STUN.why: The document extends STUN with new attributes (THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION, ACCESS-TOKEN) and specifies STUN server and client behaviour for token validation.
STUN.quote: this document proposes the use of third-party authorization using OAuth 2.0 [RFC6749] for STUN.

TURN.why: A full section and a usage subsection specify TURN-specific behaviour for the token mechanism, including Allocate/Refresh handling and lifetime limits.
TURN.quote: The TURN client MUST include the ACCESS-TOKEN attribute only in Allocate and Refresh requests.

OAuth.why: The document profiles OAuth 2.0 for STUN: it defines the 'stun' scope, uses the implicit grant and self-contained tokens, and maps the OAuth roles onto the STUN/TURN deployment.
OAuth.quote: This specification uses the OAuth 2.0 grant type 'Implicit' as explained in Section 1.3.2 of [RFC6749]

rejected.why: WebRTC is used only as an illustrative deployment scenario; the document says it is for illustrative purpose only.
JWA/JWE/JWS parameter names are borrowed for key distribution, but the document is not about JOSE.
HTTP is only the substrate for key retrieval and token requests.
The 'exp' claim is referenced from the JWT specification, but the document does not define JWT usage.
The parent topic is implied by the chosen STUN and TURN tags.

RFC7636.title: Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients
RFC7636.summary: Defines PKCE, an OAuth 2.0 extension using a per-request code verifier and derived code challenge (plain or S256) to mitigate authorization code interception attacks against public clients.

OAuth.why: The document extends the OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant with new authorization and token request parameters (code_challenge, code_verifier) and registers them in the OAuth Parameters registry.
OAuth.quote: OAuth 2.0 public clients utilizing the Authorization Code Grant are susceptible to the authorization code interception attack.

rejected.why: SHA-256 is only used as the S256 transformation; the document is not about the hash family.
TLS is the substrate that protects the authorization server communication; nothing new is specified about TLS.
Base64url encoding is used and explained in an appendix, but it is a supporting encoding, not the subject.
Custom URI schemes and unreserved characters are mentioned only as context for the attack and the verifier syntax.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level in this document; the main body is about the protocol.
The proof-of-possession check is a part of OAuth authorization code redemption, so the OAuth tag covers it better.

RFC7637.title: NVGRE: Network Virtualization Using Generic Routing Encapsulation
RFC7637.summary: Informational RFC specifying NVGRE, which uses the GRE header's Key field to carry a 24-bit Virtual Subnet ID for tunnelling Ethernet frames over IP to virtualize multi-tenant data center networks.

NVGRE.why: The document defines the NVGRE encapsulation, frame format, VSID and FlowID semantics, and deployment considerations.
NVGRE.quote: This document describes the usage of the Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) header for Network Virtualization (NVGRE) in multi-tenant data centers.

GRE.why: The document profiles GRE header use (C and S bits zero, K bit set, protocol type 0x6558), so GRE readers would want it.
GRE.quote: NVGRE leverages the Key extension specified in RFC 2890 [4] to carry the VSID.

rejected.why: ECMP is discussed only briefly as a deployment consideration, with a hash recommendation. The document is not about ECMP itself.
Data centers are the context, but the document specifies an overlay encapsulation. The overlay networks child (NVGRE) is the more specific fit.
The site-to-site VPN gateway appears only in a cross-premise example and is not provider-provisioned VPN content.
IPsec is mentioned only for security mitigation and NIC offload, and is not the subject of the document.
Ethernet frames are the payload being tunnelled, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
TRILL is mentioned only in the introduction as an alternative approach.

RFC7638.title: JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint
RFC7638.summary: Defines a method for computing a canonical hash (thumbprint) over the required members of a JSON Web Key so it can identify or select the key, e.g. as a "kid".

JOSE.why: The document extends the JOSE JWK specification with a thumbprint computation, and adds IANA Designated Expert instructions to the JOSE registries. It is squarely about JWK.
JOSE.quote: This specification defines a method for computing a hash value (a.k.a. digest) over a JSON Web Key (JWK) [JWK].

JSON.why: A substantial part covers canonical JSON serialization: member ordering, no escaping, integer number representation, and practical JSON/Unicode considerations.
JSON.quote: Construct a JSON object [RFC7159] containing only the required members of a JWK representing the key and with no whitespace or line breaks

rejected.why: SHA-256 is only an example hash function. The hash choice is left to the application, and the document does not specify SHA.
Section 5 only compares thumbprints to X.509 SPKI digests. The document does not profile X.509.
Unicode ordering and normalization concerns are practical considerations for the canonical form, not the subject of the document.
base64url encoding of the thumbprint is mentioned in passing and is not specified here.
The hash is a building block. The document defines key identification and does not address algorithms or parameters.
IANA instructions are boilerplate-like registry guidance for Designated Experts and are not the main subject.

RFC7639.title: The ALPN HTTP Header Field
RFC7639.summary: Defines the ALPN HTTP header field, which lets a client's HTTP CONNECT request tell a proxy which application protocol(s) it intends to use inside the tunnel, using ALPN identifiers.

HTTP.why: The document defines a new HTTP header field for CONNECT requests, including its syntax, usage and header registration. That is an extension of HTTP.
HTTP.quote: This specification allows HTTP CONNECT requests to indicate what protocol is intended to be used within the tunnel once established, using the ALPN header field.

rejected.why: ALPN identifiers come from the TLS ALPN extension, but this document only reuses the identifier registry. It defines nothing new for TLS.
TURN is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as an example use of CONNECT, so the document is not about it.
The document defines a header field, not link relations.
ABNF is only the notation used for the header syntax.
Percent-encoding from RFC 3986 is only borrowed for encoding protocol identifiers.
Proxy policy decisions are mentioned, but the document is not about firewall or middlebox security traversal.

RFC7640.title: Traffic Management Benchmarking
RFC7640.summary: RFC 7640 is a BMWG framework defining lab benchmarking methodology, metrics, and TCP test patterns for traffic management functions (classification, policing, queuing/scheduling, shaping) in network devices.

benchmarking.why: The whole document defines repeatable benchmarking tests, metrics and reporting formats for network device traffic management.
benchmarking.quote: a practical methodology for benchmarking the traffic management capabilities of networking devices (i.e., policing, shaping, etc.)

QoS.why: Policing, shaping, queuing and scheduling are QoS mechanisms, and the framework benchmarks their capacity and accuracy.
QoS.quote: Traffic management (i.e., policing, shaping, etc.) is an increasingly important component when implementing network Quality of Service (QoS).

rejected.why: AQM benchmarking is explicitly out of scope; CoDel and PIE are mentioned only as possible later uses of the TCP metrics.
TCP is used to build test patterns and metrics (from RFC 6349), but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
DSCP and the three-color markers appear only as classification and marking examples.
SCTP is mentioned only as a protocol the test patterns could be applied to in future.
The benchmarking tag is more specific. The document is about lab benchmarking of devices, not general network performance measurement.
The document benchmarks devices' queues and shapers. It does not define congestion control.

RFC7641.title: Observing Resources in the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC7641.summary: RFC 7641 specifies the CoAP Observe option, letting clients register on a resource and receive server-pushed notifications with reordering detection, caching, congestion control and proxy behaviour.

CoAP.why: The document defines the Observe Option extension to CoAP, including client and server requirements, notifications, and intermediary behaviour.
CoAP.quote: This document specifies a simple protocol extension for CoAP that enables CoAP clients to "observe" resources

rejected.why: CoAP caching (freshness and validation via Max-Age and ETag) is discussed, but it is CoAP's own cache model, not HTTP caching.
Section 6 defines an 'obs' link attribute, but it is a minor part of the document; the document is about CoAP observation.
DTLS appears only as a security mode in Security Considerations, as a substrate.
Section 4.5.1 applies CoAP congestion control limits to notifications, but it is a subsection and the CoAP tag covers it.
HTTP is only mentioned as background for comparison (polling, long polling).
The CoAP tag is the more specific fit, and constrained-node context is only background.

RFC7642.title: System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Definitions, Overview, Concepts, and Requirements
RFC7642.summary: Informational overview of SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) giving definitions, actors, flows, user scenarios, use cases and requirements for identity provisioning across cloud providers.

SCIM.why: The whole document defines and explains SCIM concepts, actors, flows and use cases, so it belongs on the SCIM page.
SCIM.quote: This document provides the SCIM definitions, overview, concepts, flows, scenarios, and use cases.

rejected.why: SSO and federation appear as use cases, but SCIM here is explicitly provisioning separate from authentication; federation is not the subject.
OAuth and SAML are only mentioned as example authorization protocols in one use case.
Authentication appears only as a requirement in use cases, not as the document's subject.
Privacy and regulatory points are brief requirements and security considerations, not the main body.
Directory service A appears only in generic use-case descriptions; no directory protocol is covered.

RFC7643.title: System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Core Schema
RFC7643.summary: RFC 7643 defines the SCIM core schema and extension model, in JSON, for representing Users, Groups, enterprise user extensions, service provider configuration, resource types and schema definitions, and registers the SCIM URN sub-namespace.

SCIM.why: The document is the SCIM core schema specification: User, Group, EnterpriseUser, ServiceProviderConfig, ResourceType and Schema definitions.
SCIM.quote: This document provides a platform-neutral schema and extension model for representing users and groups and other resource types in JSON format.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for the schema representation. The document defines no new JSON format in its own right.
HTTP is the substrate that the SCIM protocol (RFC 7644) uses. This document references ETag and Content-Location but does not specify HTTP.
The document registers the urn:ietf:params:scim sub-namespace, but this is IANA boilerplate for the schema URIs and is not the main subject.
LDAP and vCard are only design inputs, and the schema is not a directory access protocol.
The x509Certificates attribute only carries DER-encoded certificates. No certificate profile is defined.
The registry creation and schema registration procedure is a minor part of the document, not its main subject.

gaps.name: SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about SCIM, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. The SCIM tag I used is the nearest fit I could name, but it does not appear in the taxonomy; the closest existing tag is `SCIM` under security, which must be verified.

RFC7644.title: System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Protocol
RFC7644.summary: RFC 7644 specifies the SCIM protocol, an HTTP/JSON REST-style protocol for creating, retrieving, querying, patching, deleting and bulk-managing identity resources (Users, Groups) across domains, including filtering, versioning, discovery endpoints and multi-tenancy.

SCIM.why: The document is the normative SCIM protocol specification, defining endpoints, operations, filters, PATCH, bulk and error handling.
SCIM.quote: The SCIM protocol is an application-level HTTP-based protocol for provisioning and managing identity data on the web and in cross-domain environments

rejected.why: SCIM is built on HTTP and uses its methods, status codes and ETags, but it defines an application protocol over HTTP rather than specifying or extending HTTP.
JSON is the payload encoding; the document does not define JSON itself. It does register application/scim+json, but that does not make JSON the subject.
Bearer tokens and OAuth 2.0 are only mentioned as example authentication mechanisms; the document explicitly leaves authentication out of scope.
Section 2 lists HTTP auth schemes (Basic, HOBA) as options only. SCIM does not define any scheme.
Section 5 requires PRECIS rules for usernames and passwords, but this is a short normative reference, not the document's subject.
TLS is only the required transport security (Security Considerations); the document defines nothing new about its use.

RFC7645.title: The Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocol (KARP) IS-IS Security Analysis
RFC7645.summary: Informational KARP analysis of IS-IS authentication and key usage, identifying replay, spoofing and DoS gaps and requirements for manual keying and group key management such as GDOI.

IS-IS.why: The document analyses IS-IS cryptographic authentication, key usage, and threats, and gives security requirements for IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: This document analyzes the current state of the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol according to the requirements set forth in

routing security.why: It is a KARP routing protocol security analysis covering replay, spoofing and DoS threats and key management for routing.
routing security.quote: lists security gaps, and provides specific recommendations to thwart the threats for both manual keying and automated key management mechanisms

GDOI.why: The automated key management requirement section recommends GDOI for distributing group keys to IS-IS routers.
GDOI.quote: A mechanism is needed to distribute group keys to a group of ISes in a Level-1 area or Level-2 domain, using the Group Domain of Interpretation (GDOI)

rejected.why: HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA are discussed only as the algorithms used by existing IS-IS authentication, not as the subject.
Key management is a substantial theme, but the more specific GDOI tag and routing security cover it.
HMAC-MD5 is only mentioned as the weaker existing mechanism to move away from.
The HMAC-SHA family is mentioned as the algorithm family in RFC 5310, not as a subject of this document.

gaps.name: KARP (Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols)
gaps.why: The KARP framework is the document's organising context, but the taxonomy has no tag for it; routing security is the closest fit.

RFC7646.title: Definition and Use of DNSSEC Negative Trust Anchors
RFC7646.summary: Defines Negative Trust Anchors, a local resolver configuration that temporarily disables DNSSEC validation for a misconfigured domain, and gives guidance on their use, expiry, removal and diagnosing broken domains.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is about a validating-resolver mechanism for DNSSEC: trust anchors, validation failures, key rollover errors and operational handling.
DNSSEC.quote: This document defines Negative Trust Anchors (NTAs), which can be used to mitigate DNSSEC validation failures by disabling DNSSEC validation at specified domains.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; the subject is DNSSEC validation behaviour, so the child tag DNSSEC covers it.
The document explicitly says NTAs pertain only to DNSSEC and not to PKIs such as X.509.
EDNS client subnet is mentioned only in passing as a cause of differing answers.
The document is DNSSEC-specific operational guidance, so the DNSSEC tag fits better than the generic operational security topic.

RFC7647.title: Clarifications for the Use of REFER with RFC 6665
RFC7647.summary: Updates RFC 3515 (SIP REFER) to align with RFC 6665: GRUU mandatory for REFER-accepting UAs, no dialog reuse for REFER that may create implicit subscriptions, and 202 response code deprecated in favour of 200.

SIP.why: The document specifies updated behaviour of the SIP REFER method, including GRUU use, dialog handling and response codes. A reader of SIP would want it.
SIP.quote: A user agent constructing a REFER request that could result in an implicit subscription in a dialog MUST build it as an out-of-dialog message

rejected.why: The SIP event notification framework (RFC 6665) is the basis for REFER's implicit subscription, but the document is about REFER behaviour, not event packages, presence or XCAP.
Not discussed in the document.
The document has no IANA considerations of substance and is not about registries.

RFC7648.title: Port Control Protocol (PCP) Proxy Function
RFC7648.summary: Defines the PCP proxy, a functional element that relays PCP requests from downstream clients to upstream PCP servers, covering NAT cascades, relay use, recursion termination, unknown opcodes/options, mapping repair, and multiple servers.

PCP.why: The whole document specifies a new PCP functional element and its behaviour, including request/reply relaying, epoch handling, ANNOUNCE handling and THIRD_PARTY option use.
PCP.quote: This document defines a new Port Control Protocol (PCP) [RFC6887] functional element: the PCP proxy.

rejected.why: NAT cascades are the motivating use case and the proxy may be co-located with a NAT, but the document specifies PCP behaviour, not NAT behaviour. PCP is the more specific tag.
Carrier-Grade NAT is mentioned only as a context for load-balancing among PCP servers, so it is not a subject of the document.
The PCP anycast address draft is only mentioned as an alternative way to reach a server.
DHCP is cited only as one way to provision PCP server addresses.
Firewalls are mentioned as a kind of PCP-controlled device, but the document is not about firewall traversal in its own right.

RFC7649.title: The Jabber Scribe Role at IETF Meetings
RFC7649.summary: An informational guide to the volunteer "Jabber scribe" role at IETF meetings, in which a person relays comments, hums and speaker names between the physical session room and its textual chatroom.

IETF process.why: The document describes a procedural role in how IETF meeting sessions run and how remote attendees take part. That is IETF meeting practice and administration, not a protocol.
IETF process.quote: individual volunteers often help sessions run more smoothly by relaying information back and forth between the physical meeting room and an associated textual chatroom

rejected.why: Jabber/XMPP is only the chatroom substrate. The document does not specify, extend or analyse XMPP, and it says another technology could replace it.
The chatrooms are used as a tool, but the document is about the human scribe role, not about instant messaging technology.
Section 10 briefly says chatroom comments count as contributions under BCP 78 and BCP 79. It is a minor point in a document about the scribe role.
Meetecho and audio streaming are mentioned in passing as context. The document does not address real-time media technology.

gaps.name: Remote participation at IETF meetings
gaps.why: The document is about how remote attendees take part in IETF sessions, but the taxonomy has no tag for meeting logistics or remote participation. IETF process is the closest fit.

RFC7650.title: A Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Usage for REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD)
RFC7650.summary: Defines a CoAP Usage for RELOAD that lets CoAP nodes register URIs, look up resources, and cache sensor data in a RELOAD P2P overlay, with two new data Kinds and two access control policies.

P2PSIP.why: The document is a RELOAD Usage: it defines new RELOAD Kinds (CoAP-REGISTRATION, CoAP-CACHING), access control policies, and use of AppAttach, so P2PSIP/RELOAD readers would want it.
P2PSIP.quote: This document defines a Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Usage for REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD).

CoAP.why: It specifies how CoAP nodes and resources are registered, discovered, and cached via the overlay, extending CoAP deployment, including a CoAP-related caching mechanism.
CoAP.quote: The CoAP Usage provides the functionality to federate Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) in a peer-to-peer fashion.

rejected.why: The P2P aspect is covered by the more specific RELOAD/P2PSIP tag; the document is not about generic P2P applications.
Context is constrained sensor networks, but CoAP tag already captures the IoT subject; no general IoT guidance is given.
Caching is of sensor data in the overlay, not HTTP caching; CoAP caching is only referenced.
ICE is used only for connectivity checks after AppAttach; not specified here.
Lookup is a function, but it is specific to RELOAD/CoAP resources and covered by the chosen tags.
TLS/DTLS is only the overlay link security substrate; the document defines nothing new about it.

RFC7651.title: 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystems (IMS) Option for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC7651.summary: Defines two new IKEv2 configuration payload attributes (P_CSCF_IP4_ADDRESS and P_CSCF_IP6_ADDRESS) that let an IPsec gateway such as a 3GPP ePDG deliver the P-CSCF address of the IMS network to a client.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new configuration payload attributes and registers them in the IKEv2 Configuration Payload Attribute Types registry.
IKE.quote: This document defines two new configuration attributes for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2).

cellular.why: The attributes serve 3GPP S2b/ePDG interworking and IMS access, so readers of 3GPP/cellular interworking would want this RFC.
cellular.quote: allowing a mobile node (MN) attached in an untrusted, non-3GPP IP access network to securely connect to a 3GPP network and access IP services

rejected.why: The P-CSCF is a SIP proxy, but the document only conveys its address in IKEv2 and does not specify SIP.
ESP tunnels are the context, but the document only extends IKEv2 configuration attributes; IKE is the more specific tag.
PMIPv6 is used between the ePDG and PGW as background only.
DHCP is mentioned only as an alternative discovery approach that was rejected.
The IPv6 address attribute is just one of two attributes; the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC7652.title: Port Control Protocol (PCP) Authentication Mechanism
RFC7652.summary: Defines an in-band authentication mechanism for the Port Control Protocol (PCP) that carries EAP exchanges inside PCP messages, derives transport keys from the EAP MSK, and adds a new AUTHENTICATION opcode, result codes and options to protect PCP messages.

PCP.why: The document extends PCP with a new AUTHENTICATION opcode, options, result codes and session handling, and it updates RFC 6887.
PCP.quote: This document defines a PCP security extension that enables PCP servers to authenticate their clients with the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP).

EAP.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how EAP is carried in PCP. This covers EAP method requirements (EAP-TTLS MUST, TEAP SHOULD), MSK-based key derivation, fragmentation and re-authentication.
EAP.quote: In a PA session, an EAP request message is transported within a PA-Server message and an EAP response message is transported within a PA-Client message.

rejected.why: NATs and firewalls are the devices PCP controls, but the document is about authenticating PCP clients, not NAT behaviour.
It only borrows the IKEv2 transform type identifiers for the PRF and MAC algorithm values. It does not specify or extend IKE.
HMAC-SHA2-256 is used as the mandatory PRF and MAC algorithm, but the document does not specify or analyse HMAC.
UDP is only the transport PCP runs over. The document adds sequence numbers and retransmission on top of it and defines nothing new about UDP.
The ID_INDICATOR field uses the PRECIS UsernameCaseMapped profile, but PRECIS is only a dependency for one field.
AAA servers are mentioned only in the MTU discussion. The document does not specify a AAA framework.

RFC7653.title: DHCPv6 Active Leasequery
RFC7653.summary: Defines DHCPv6 Active Leasequery, an extension of Bulk Leasequery over TCP that streams real-time DHCPv6 binding changes to a requestor, adding the ACTIVELEASEQUERY and STARTTLS messages and new time options.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 messages (ACTIVELEASEQUERY, STARTTLS) and options and updates RFC 5460, so it belongs under DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: This document expands on the DHCPv6 Leasequery protocol and allows for active transfer of real-time DHCPv6 binding information data via TCP.

rejected.why: TLS is only the security mechanism used for the connection. The STARTTLS message is a DHCPv6 message, not a new TLS extension.
TCP is the transport for the long-lived connection. The document does not define or extend TCP.
The document uses TCP framing borrowed from Bulk Leasequery, but it is about the leasequery protocol and not primarily a transport binding.
The parent tag is implied by DHCPv6, and the document is specific to DHCPv6.
NTP is mentioned only in passing, as a way to synchronize clocks and avoid clock skew.

RFC7654.title: Benchmarking Methodology for In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU)
RFC7654.summary: RFC 7654 specifies a benchmarking methodology for characterizing a forwarding device's control- and data-plane disruption, and timing, during an In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU).

benchmarking.why: This is a BMWG benchmarking methodology: test topology, load model, measured frame loss and impact times, and a reporting format for a DUT undergoing ISSU.
benchmarking.quote: This document specifies a set of common methodologies and procedures designed to characterize the overall behavior of a Device Under Test (DUT), subject to an ISSU event.

rejected.why: BFD is mentioned only as an example of a feature that may not support ISSU. The document does not specify or analyse it.
BGP route flapping is only an example of a stress stimulus in the optional negative-stimuli test. The document is not about BGP.
NTP is only suggested as a time source for timing accuracy. It is not a subject of the document.
The benchmarking tag is the more specific fit. The measurements here are lab benchmarking, not active or passive network performance metrics.
The document covers software upgrade procedures and outage characterization, not security practices. Its Security Considerations are boilerplate.

gaps.name: In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU) / device software upgrade and redundancy
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is ISSU behaviour of redundant routers (RP switchover, non-stop operation). The taxonomy has no tag for it, so only the benchmarking aspect can be captured.

RFC7655.title: RTP Payload Format for G.711.0
RFC7655.summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for ITU-T G.711.0 lossless G.711 compression, including multi-channel payloads, the audio/G711-0 media type with SDP mapping, and a storage mode file format.

G.711.why: The document defines the RTP payload format, media type, and storage mode for G.711.0, which the taxonomy covers under G.711 (extensions and payload formats).
G.711.quote: This document specifies the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) RFC 3550 [RFC3550] payload format and storage modes for this compression.

rejected.why: This is the generic RTP payload-format tag, but the more specific G.711 tag covers it and already implies its ancestors.
SDP is only used for parameter mapping and offer/answer. The document does not extend SDP itself.
Registering audio/G711-0 is a routine part of any payload format, not the main subject.
RTP is the substrate the payload format runs over. Nothing new is defined for RTP itself.
The more specific G.711 tag already covers this.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as an applicable profile.

RFC7656.title: A Taxonomy of Semantics and Mechanisms for Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP) Sources
RFC7656.summary: Informational RFC defining a common taxonomy and terminology for RTP sources: the media chain of streams and transformations, communication entities (endpoints, RTP sessions, participants), and relationships such as simulcast, layered streams, redundancy, retransmission and FEC.

RTP.why: The whole document is a taxonomy of RTP concepts: RTP streams, SSRC, RTP sessions, media transport and the related terminology.
RTP.quote: This document describes a number of existing and proposed properties and relationships among RTP sources and defines common terminology for discussing protocol entities

rejected.why: CNAME is discussed only as an identification and synchronization mechanism. The document does not specify or extend RTCP.
RTP-based security is a single transformation in the media chain, and SRTP is cited as an example. The document is not about SRTP.
FEC and retransmission appear as example relationships among RTP streams. The document does not specify or analyse them.
SDP grouping and attributes are mentioned for signalling stream relations. They are not the subject of the document.
CLUE terms are mapped to the RTP taxonomy in Section 4.1, but the document is not about telepresence itself.
RtcMediaStream terms are mapped to RTP concepts, but WebRTC is only a source of terminology here.

RFC7657.title: Differentiated Services (Diffserv) and Real-Time Communication
RFC7657.summary: Informational memo describing how Diffserv per-hop behaviors and DSCP marking/remarking interact with real-time communication (RTP, RTCP, WebRTC bundled on one 5-tuple), especially reordering and congestion control, and giving guidelines.

Diffserv.why: The document is about DSCP usage, PHBs (DF, AF, EF, CS, LE), remarking, and guidelines for using Diffserv with real-time traffic.
Diffserv.quote: This memo describes the interaction between Differentiated Services (Diffserv) network quality-of-service (QoS) functionality and real-time network communication

RTP.why: Substantial parts cover RTP multiplexing, streams, jitter buffers and reordering effects, with guidelines for DSCP use within RTP streams.
RTP.quote: including communication based on the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

RTCP.why: A dedicated section gives DSCP marking guidance for RTCP packets and receiver reports.
RTCP.quote: A sender of RTCP packets that also sends RTP packets (i.e., originates an RTP stream) should use the same DSCP marking for both types of packets.

WebRTC.why: WebRTC's use of SDP bundle to multiplex streams on one 5-tuple is the motivating scenario, and guidance is explicitly applied to it.
WebRTC.quote: This memo covers the implications of these Diffserv aspects for real-time network communication, including WebRTC.

rejected.why: Reordering's impact on congestion control is discussed, but as a consequence of DSCP use, not the document's subject.
SDP bundle negotiation is the context that causes shared 5-tuples, but the document doesn't specify or extend SDP.
SCTP is covered only for the recommendation to use a single DSCP per association; it is not the subject.
Only discussed as a transport sensitive to reordering, with a single-DSCP recommendation.
UDP is the encapsulation substrate; the document doesn't address UDP usage itself.
Mentioned only as background on reordering sensitivity.

RFC7658.title: Deprecation of MIB Module NAT-MIB: Managed Objects for Network Address Translators (NATs)
RFC7658.summary: Deprecates the NAT-MIB module from RFC 4008 by republishing all its objects with STATUS deprecated, explaining the lessons learned and pointing to NATV2-MIB (RFC 7659) as replacement.

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module definition (NAT-MIB) with all objects marked deprecated, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This memo deprecates MIB module NAT-MIB, a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) previously defined in RFC 4008

NAT.why: The MIB models NAT bindings, sessions, address maps and NAPT, and Section 3 critiques how NAT implementations vary; NAT readers would want the management objects.
NAT.quote: NAT types and their characteristics are defined in [RFC2663]. Traditional NAT function, in particular, is defined in [RFC3022].

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document specifies no SNMP protocol behavior, and MIB sits under SNMP as the more specific tag.
ICMP identifiers appear in object descriptions for ICMP query sessions, but the document is not about ICMP.
The objects support IPv4 and IPv6 address types, but only incidentally.
The MIB covers traditional NAT; carrier-grade NAT is not addressed.

RFC7659.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Network Address Translators (NATs)
RFC7659.summary: Defines NATV2-MIB, a new SNMP MIB module for monitoring NAT instances (basic, pooled and carrier-grade NAT), replacing NAT-MIB (RFC 4008).

MIB.why: The document's core is the NATV2-MIB module: SMIv2 tables, notifications, and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for devices implementing the Network Address Translator (NAT) function.

NAT.why: The managed subject is NAT: mappings, pools, behaviors per RFC 4787, fragments, and hairpinning. NAT readers would want this.
NAT.quote: NATV2-MIB can be used for the monitoring of NAT instances on a device capable of NAT function.

CGN.why: CGN is one of three conformance scenarios, with a subscriber table and DS-Lite-specific mapping objects.
CGN.quote: support for the carrier-grade NAT (CGN) application, including subscriber-awareness, support for an arbitrary number of address realms

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the MIB tag already sits under it and covers the document's subject.
DS-Lite is handled only as a special case for address representation in mapping tables, not specified or extended.
DS-Lite support is incidental to the NAT MIB.
Implied by the MIB tag, which is more specific.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as SNMPv3 USM boilerplate.
Mentioned only when mapping RFC 3489 NAT types to RFC 4787 behaviors.

RFC7660.title: Diameter Congestion and Filter Attributes
RFC7660.summary: Defines four optional Diameter AVPs (ECN-IP-Codepoint, Congestion-Treatment, Flow-Count, Packet-Count) extending RFC 5777 filter rules to match ECN-marked traffic, specify congestion actions, and report flow/packet counts.

Diameter.why: The document specifies new Diameter AVPs extending RFC 5777 and the Diameter credit-control usage, so it is a Diameter extension.
Diameter.quote: This document also defines two optional AVPs, Flow-Count and Packet-Count, used for conveying flow information within the Diameter protocol [RFC6733].

ECN.why: A substantial part adds ECN codepoint classification and congestion-triggered treatment to Diameter filters, which ECN readers would want.
ECN.quote: The ECN-IP-Codepoint AVP (AVP Code 628) is of type Enumerated and specifies the ECN codepoint values to match in the IP header.

rejected.why: QoS-Profile-Template and QoS-Parameters are reused from RFC 5777 only; the document does not define a QoS architecture.
The document is about ECN-related filter and reporting AVPs, not congestion control algorithms; the ECN tag is more specific.
Diameter is the more specific tag under AAA, and the credit-control example is just an illustration.
ABNF is only the notation used to describe the AVPs, not the subject.

RFC7661.title: Updating TCP to Support Rate-Limited Traffic
RFC7661.summary: RFC 7661 specifies an experimental TCP congestion window validation update (New CWV) that lets rate-limited or idle senders preserve cwnd for a bounded non-validated period using pipeACK measurement, and obsoletes/reclassifies RFC 2861 as Historic.

TCP.why: The document updates TCP sender congestion control behaviour and obsoletes RFC 2861 (TCP-CWV); it is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: It provides an experimental update to TCP that allows a TCP sender to restart quickly following a rate-limited interval.

congestion control.why: The core content is congestion window validation: pipeACK estimation, non-validated phase, congestion response and cwnd/ssthresh adjustments. TCP's child tag does not cover the general congestion-control subject, but TCP is the only protocol addressed, so this topic is added as secondary-level coverage of the CC subject itself.
congestion control.quote: This update allows an application to preserve a recently used cwnd while in the non-validated phase and then to resume transmission at a previous rate

rejected.why: Only references RFC 5681 standard congestion control; the document is not about NewReno's fast recovery.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example application using persistent connections.
Mentioned only as an alternative some applications use instead of TCP.
Not about QoS architectures or signalling.

RFC7662.title: OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection
RFC7662.summary: Defines an OAuth 2.0 token introspection endpoint by which a protected resource queries an authorization server for the active state and metadata of a token, and creates an IANA registry for introspection response members.

OAuth.why: The document extends the OAuth 2.0 framework with a new introspection endpoint, request and response format, so readers of OAuth materials need it.
OAuth.quote: a method for a protected resource to query an OAuth 2.0 authorization server to determine the active state of an OAuth 2.0 token

rejected.why: JWT claim names are reused for response members, but the document does not specify or extend JWT.
JSON is only the response encoding.
HTTP POST is only the transport for the endpoint.
TLS is required as a security mechanism but nothing new is defined about it.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not the main subject.
Bearer and Basic are used to authorize calls, but authentication methods are out of scope.

RFC7663.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Stack Evolution in a Middlebox Internet (SEMI)
RFC7663.summary: IAB workshop report on stack evolution in a middlebox Internet, summarizing discussions on transport ossification, middlebox impairments, UDP encapsulation (SPUD), and middlebox measurement and design guidelines.

transport.why: The report is about evolving the transport layer in the face of ossification caused by middleboxes. It covers UDP encapsulation, TCP extensibility and the transport interface, and no specific transport protocol is its subject.
transport.quote: The transport layer of the Internet has become ossified, squeezed between narrow interfaces (from BSD sockets to pseudo-transport over HTTPS)

internet architecture.why: The workshop aims to give architectural guidance on the end-to-end principle, middlebox roles, and the balance of power between endpoints and the network.
internet architecture.quote: Recognizing that the end-to-end principle has long been compromised, we start with the fundamental question of matching paths through the Internet

workshop reports.why: This is an IAB workshop report summarizing contributions, discussion and outcomes.
workshop reports.quote: The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) holds occasional workshops designed to consider long-term issues and strategies for the Internet

rejected.why: NAT and middlebox traversal are discussed as background to middlebox interference, but the report is about middleboxes and ossification generally, not NAT behaviour.
UDP encapsulation is a central proposal (SPUD), but the report does not specify or analyse UDP itself. It is the substrate for new transports.
TCP extensibility is discussed as one of two camps in the evolution debate, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
DTLS is mentioned as something SPUD should cooperate with, not as the subject of the report.
TAPS is mentioned only briefly as related work on decoupling applications from transport protocols.
Middlebox measurement is one outcome area, but it concerns measuring impairment prevalence from logs, not performance metrics.

gaps.name: middleboxes / stack ossification
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about middleboxes and protocol-stack ossification. The taxonomy has no tag for middleboxes, so the general transport tag is the closest fit.

RFC7664.title: Dragonfly Key Exchange
RFC7664.summary: RFC 7664 specifies the Dragonfly password-authenticated key exchange, using discrete logarithm groups (ECC and MODP) with a hunting-and-pecking password element derivation, commit and confirm exchanges, resistant to offline dictionary attack.

Dragonfly.why: The whole document defines the Dragonfly balanced password-authenticated key exchange, including password element derivation and the commit and confirm exchanges.
Dragonfly.quote: This document specifies a key exchange using discrete logarithm cryptography that is authenticated using a password or passphrase.

rejected.why: ECC groups are used as one of two group types, but the document is about the password-authenticated key exchange, not elliptic curve cryptography itself.
IKEv2 is mentioned only as an example of a protocol exposed to offline dictionary attack, and mk could be exported to IPsec. The document does not specify IKE.
EAP-GPSK is cited only as an example of a protocol that is vulnerable to offline dictionary attack.
The exchange does yield a shared key, but Dragonfly is a more specific tag for this subject, so the parent is not needed.

RFC7665.title: Service Function Chaining (SFC) Architecture
RFC7665.summary: RFC 7665 defines the Service Function Chaining architecture: service function chains and paths, classifiers, service function forwarders, SFC proxies, the SFC encapsulation and metadata, and related control-plane, OAM, MTU and resilience concepts.

SFC.why: The whole document specifies the SFC architecture, including SFFs, SFPs, classifiers, proxies and encapsulation. The SFC tag covers it directly.
SFC.quote: This document describes an architecture for the specification, creation, and ongoing maintenance of Service Function Chains (SFCs) in a network.

rejected.why: Overlay transport is only the substrate under the SFF. The document does not specify any overlay encapsulation.
NATs appear only as examples of service functions that can be chained. The document is not about NAT behaviour.
Firewalls are mentioned as example service functions, but the document does not address them.
VRRP is mentioned once as a possible redundancy mechanism. It is not a subject of the document.
Section 5.7 on SFC OAM is brief and sits inside the SFC architecture. It is not a substantial separate subject.
GRE, L2TPv3, VXLAN and IP-in-IP are listed only as examples of local attachment circuits for the SFC proxy.

RFC7666.title: Management Information Base for Virtual Machines Controlled by a Hypervisor
RFC7666.summary: Defines the VM-MIB (and an IANA storage media type MIB) for managing hypervisors and the virtual machines, virtual CPUs, memory, storage and network interfaces they control, including state notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a new SMIv2 MIB module (VM-MIB) plus an IANA-maintained MIB module, and to relate it to HOST-RESOURCES-MIB and IF-MIB.
MIB.quote: this specifies objects for managing virtual machines controlled by a hypervisor (a.k.a. virtual machine monitor)

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB objects; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself, so MIB is the more specific fit.
vmUUID merely uses the UUID textual convention for identifying VMs; the document is not about UUIDs.
The IANA-maintained media type MIB is a small part of the work; IANA considerations are boilerplate.
Data centers are mentioned only as motivation for bulk notifications; no routing or addressing at data-centre scale is specified.

gaps.name: Virtualization / hypervisor management
gaps.why: The document is about managing hypervisors and virtual machines, but the taxonomy has no virtualization tag; MIB captures only the specification vehicle.
