RFC7667.title: RTP Topologies
RFC7667.summary: Informational RFC that describes and names point-to-point and multipoint RTP topologies (translators, mixers, mesh, multicast, SFMs, MCUs, split terminals), maps MCU industry terms to RTP terminology, compares topology properties, and replaces RFC 5117.

RTP.why: The whole document is about how RTP sessions, SSRC/CSRC handling and middleboxes (translators, mixers, SFMs) are arranged in different topologies.
RTP.quote: Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) [RFC3550] topologies describe methods for interconnecting RTP entities and their processing behavior for RTP and the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP).

RTCP.why: A substantial part of each topology discussion concerns RTCP handling: receiver report rewriting, feedback messages, feedback suppression and RTCP bandwidth.
RTCP.quote: For each of the RTP-defined topologies, we discuss how RTP, RTCP, and the carried media are handled.

conferencing.why: It maps centralized multipoint conferencing units (MCUs, mixers, SFMs) to RTP terminology, so readers of the conferencing subject would want it.
conferencing.quote: In practice, however, most multipoint conferences operate utilizing centralized units referred to as MCUs.

rejected.why: Source-Specific Multicast is one of the topologies described, but only as a topology for RTP. The document does not specify or extend SSM itself.
ASM and SSM appear as RTP transport topologies. The document is not about multicast routing or deployment.
SRTP appears only in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-like and does not make the document about SRTP.
TURN is mentioned only as an example of a transport relay.
SDP is mentioned only as a reference, for the MID header extension.
SIP appears only in the split terminal figure and in a reference to the SIP conference event package.

RFC7668.title: IPv6 over BLUETOOTH(R) Low Energy
RFC7668.summary: Specifies how IPv6 is transmitted over Bluetooth Low Energy links using 6LoWPAN techniques: link model, SLAAC and IID formation, ND optimizations with ARO, RFC 6282 header compression, and multicast handling.

6LoWPAN.why: The document adapts 6LoWPAN (RFC 6282 header compression, RFC 6775 ND optimizations) to a new constrained link layer, Bluetooth LE. The 6LoWPAN tag covers other constrained link layers.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document describes how IPv6 is transported over Bluetooth LE connections using IPv6 over Low-power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) techniques.

IPv6.why: A substantial part covers IPv6 subnet model, link-local addressing and IID formation, and multicast mapping over the link.
IPv6.quote: Bluetooth LE star is deployed as one subnet, using one /64 IPv6 prefix, with each spoke representing an individual link.
IPv6.section: 3.2.1. IPv6 Subnet Model and Internet Connectivity

rejected.why: The document uses RFC 6775 ND optimizations (ARO, 6CO) as specified elsewhere. It only profiles which parts apply, so this is a secondary aspect covered by the 6LoWPAN tag.
Link-local address and IID formation are specified, but this is a part of the link adaptation. The document is not about SLAAC itself.
The 6LoWPAN tag already covers the use of RFC 6282 compression. The document applies it and does not define a new format.
Bluetooth LE is the link, but there is no specific Bluetooth tag. The 6LoWPAN tag is the more specific fit for IP over constrained links.
IoT is motivation only. The 6LoWPAN tag is the specific fit.

gaps.name: Bluetooth Low Energy (Bluetooth LE / Bluetooth Smart)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about IP over Bluetooth LE, and the taxonomy has no Bluetooth link-layer tag. Readers browsing link technologies would expect to find it there.

RFC7669.title: Assigning Digital Object Identifiers to RFCs
RFC7669.summary: Informational IAB document describing how Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs, built on the Handle System) are assigned to past and future RFCs via CrossRef, and how they are used in the RFC index and references.

handle system.why: The DOI system is a persistent identifier infrastructure built on the Handle System. The document explains DOI structure and resolution and how it is applied to RFCs, so readers of the Handle System subject would want it.
handle system.quote: DOIs are an application of the Handle System defined by RFCs [RFC3650], [RFC3651], and [RFC3652].

RFC series.why: The document is about RFC publication practice: assigning DOIs to every RFC, updating the RFC index schema and publication software, and rules for DOIs in RFC references.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Style Guide [RFC-STYLE] has been updated to describe the rules for including DOIs in the References sections of RFCs.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the lookup and metadata-upload substrate, and content negotiation is used incidentally. The document does not specify or extend it.
DOI lookup URLs and the dropped 'doi:' URN are mentioned, but the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
The 'doi:' URN is mentioned only to note that it was never widely implemented. It is not a subject of the document.
There are no IANA actions. The document is about identifier assignment by the RFC Editor, not IANA registries.
The Handle System tag is the more specific fit, and the document does not address naming in general.
HTTP content negotiation is used only to retrieve DOI metadata formats, and the document is not about media feature negotiation.

gaps.name: Digital Object Identifiers (DOI) / persistent identifiers for documents
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DOI-specific tag. The Handle System is the closest fit, but DOI registration agencies, CrossRef and bibliographic metadata are not covered.

RFC7670.title: Generic Raw Public-Key Support for IKEv2
RFC7670.summary: RFC 7670 updates IKEv2 (RFC 7296) by defining a new Certificate Encoding (value 15, Raw Public Key) that carries a SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure, enabling algorithm-agnostic raw public keys such as ECDSA keys.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 by defining a new Certificate Encoding for the Certificate and Certificate Request payloads, so it belongs on the IKE page.
IKE.quote: this document reintroduces support for raw public keys to IKEv2 in a more generic way.

X.509.why: The raw public key is encoded using the X.509/PKIX SubjectPublicKeyInfo format, and the appendix gives ECDSA and RSA examples of that encoding. This is a substantial part of the document, though only the format is borrowed, not certificate processing.
X.509.quote: the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure of the PKIX certificate is used.

rejected.why: IKEv2 is the specific subject; IPsec is the parent, so IKE covers it.
ECDSA appears only in an example key; the document is not about the algorithm.
RSA appears as a legacy key type and an example; the document is not about RSA itself.
RFC 7250 for TLS is cited as a parallel and a model, but this document does not specify anything for TLS.
DANE and IPSECKEY are only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to validate keys.
The document uses ASN.1 structures in its examples, but it is not about ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.

RFC7671.title: The DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) Protocol: Updates and Operational Guidance
RFC7671.summary: RFC 7671 updates and clarifies the DANE TLSA specification (RFC 6698), giving guidance on certificate usages, TLSA record publication and rollover, CNAME handling, digest algorithm agility, and record sizes.

DANE.why: The whole document updates RFC 6698 and gives operational guidance for DANE TLSA records, certificate usages and publishers.
DANE.quote: This document clarifies and updates the DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) TLSA specification (RFC 6698), based on subsequent implementation experience.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the security foundation DANE relies on. Section 11 has only brief remarks on signature lifetimes and registrar locks, and the document says it is not a DNSSEC guide.
TLS is the channel being authenticated. The document adds only DANE-specific requirements such as SNI support and minimum TLS versions, and does not define TLS itself.
X.509 certificates and trust anchors are matched by TLSA records. The document does not profile X.509.
The Web PKI is compared against DANE, but the document does not address PKI in its own right.
Section 4.2 only says when CT checks should be skipped with DANE usages.
SMTP appears only as an example. The SMTP-specific DANE rules are in RFC 7672.

RFC7672.title: SMTP Security via Opportunistic DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC7672.summary: Specifies opportunistic DANE TLS for MTA-to-MTA SMTP: how to find and use DNSSEC-validated TLSA records to signal TLS support, resist STARTTLS downgrade, and authenticate servers.

DANE.why: The document profiles DANE TLSA for SMTP: TLSA lookup, certificate usages (DANE-EE, DANE-TA), name checks, and key rotation.
DANE.quote: This memo describes a downgrade-resistant protocol for SMTP transport security between Message Transfer Agents (MTAs), based on the DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) TLSA DNS record.

SMTP.why: It defines how SMTP clients secure inter-domain MTA delivery, covering MX resolution, STARTTLS downgrade protection, and delivery or delay rules.
SMTP.quote: This memo specifies a new connection security model for Message Transfer Agents (MTAs).

DNSSEC.why: A substantial part covers DNSSEC validation statuses (secure, insecure, bogus, indeterminate), error handling, and stub resolver and CNAME/DNAME security handling, because the protocol depends on DNSSEC.
DNSSEC.quote: A security-aware resolver MUST be used for this specification.

rejected.why: TLS is the secured channel and substrate. The document specifies no new TLS extension; it only requires SNI and cipher suite behaviour.
Certificates are matched against TLSA records and the document mostly recommends against PKIX usages. It does not define a certificate profile.
This is transport-security of MTA connections, not sender domain authentication like SPF, DKIM or DMARC.
The document explicitly avoids public CA PKI and uses DNSSEC-based trust instead.
DNS is used for MX, address and TLSA lookups, but the DNSSEC and DANE tags are more specific and cover the document's subject.

RFC7673.title: Using DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) TLSA Records with SRV Records
RFC7673.summary: Specifies how clients of application protocols that locate servers via DNS SRV records should find and use DANE TLSA records (placed under the SRV target hostname), including DNSSEC status handling, TLS usage rules and certificate name checks.

DANE.why: The whole document defines how DANE TLSA records are queried and applied when servers are discovered through SRV records.
DANE.quote: this document provides guidelines that enable such protocols to locate and use TLSA records.

service discovery.why: A substantial part covers securely discovering TLS-capable connection endpoints through DNSSEC-secured SRV lookups, ordering, and address queries.
service discovery.quote: Some application protocols locate connection endpoints indirectly via SRV records [RFC2782].

rejected.why: DNSSEC validation status drives the logic, but the document uses it rather than specifying or extending it; DANE covers the subject.
TLS is the secured substrate; the document only uses SNI and certificate checks and defines nothing new in TLS.
SRV and TLSA queries are used, but no new DNS RR or resolver behaviour is defined beyond DANE usage.
XMPP and IMAP appear only as examples; the document is generic across SRV-using protocols.
PKIX certificate validation is referenced for fallback checks, but the document does not profile certificates.
SMTP DANE is explicitly out of scope, handled by RFC 7672.

RFC7674.title: Clarification of the Flowspec Redirect Extended Community
RFC7674.summary: RFC 7674 updates RFC 5575 to clarify the BGP Flowspec Redirect Extended Community by defining separate AS-2byte, IPv4 and AS-4byte Route Target formats and updating the related IANA extended community registries.

BGP flowspec.why: The whole document clarifies the Flowspec redirect extended community and its encodings, updating the BGP Flowspec specification.
BGP flowspec.quote: This document updates RFC 5575 ("Dissemination of Flow Specification Rules") to clarify the formatting of the BGP Flowspec Redirect Extended Community.

rejected.why: BGP extended communities are the substrate; the document is specifically about Flowspec, which is the more specific tag.
Considered since it defines extended community formats, but the subject is the Flowspec redirect community, and the BGP flowspec tag covers it most specifically.
IANA registry updates are only in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate-like and not the main subject.
VRFs and Route Targets are mentioned as redirect targets, but the document does not address L3VPN itself.

RFC7675.title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) Usage for Consent Freshness
RFC7675.summary: Defines a new STUN usage for periodic consent freshness, so WebRTC endpoints must keep obtaining peer consent (30-second expiry, randomized ~5s checks, explicit revocation) before sending traffic on an ICE candidate pair.

STUN.why: The document specifies a new STUN usage: binding requests and responses sent periodically to maintain consent, with its own timers and revocation rules.
STUN.quote: This document describes a new STUN usage with exchange of request and response messages that verifies the remote peer's ongoing consent to receive traffic.

ICE.why: The consent mechanism is an optional extension layered on ICE candidate pairs, and it covers ICE restart and ICE-lite behaviour. It does not change ICE procedures, so it is secondary.
ICE.quote: Initial consent to send traffic is obtained using ICE [RFC5245]. An endpoint gains consent to send on a candidate pair when the pair enters the Succeeded ICE state.

WebRTC.why: The mechanism exists to protect against browsers being used as an attack platform and is a WebRTC security component, so WebRTC readers would want it.
WebRTC.quote: To prevent WebRTC applications, such as browsers, from launching attacks by sending traffic to unwilling victims, periodic consent to send needs to be obtained from remote endpoints.

rejected.why: SRTP is discussed only to explain why an authenticated SRTP packet is not enough to verify consent in shared-key sessions. The document does not specify or extend it.
Section 7 only says DTLS applicability is the same as in RFC 7350. DTLS is a substrate and is not specified here.
Section 6 has a single recommendation to reuse the ICE connectivity-check DSCP markings. That is too minor to make the document about Diffserv.
TCP is mentioned only for performing consent checks over TCP connections. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
STUN and ICE are tagged directly, and the keepalive side effect is incidental.

RFC7676.title: IPv6 Support for Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE)
RFC7676.summary: Specifies GRE procedures for IPv6 as payload and as delivery protocol, covering protocol type, checksum, MTU, fragmentation and next header handling.

GRE.why: The document extends GRE to IPv6, defining header field settings, MTU, fragmentation and checksum behaviour for GRE tunnels.
GRE.quote: This document specifies GRE procedures for IPv6, used as either the payload or delivery protocol.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the payload/delivery protocol for GRE; the document is about GRE procedures, not the IPv6 specification itself.
PMTU and PMTUD are used for MTU calculations but the document does not specify or extend PMTUD.
ICMPv6 Packet Too Big is only used as a signalling response, not specified here.
GRE checksum use is discussed, but the document is about GRE, not the Internet checksum in general.
GRE is the more specific tag and already implies the tunneling parent.

RFC7677.title: SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) Mechanisms
RFC7677.summary: Registers the SASL mechanisms SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS (SCRAM with SHA-256), gives guidance on secure use of channel binding over TLS for SCRAM-*-PLUS, and updates the SCRAM family registration procedure of RFC 5802.

SASL.why: The document defines and registers new SASL mechanisms and updates the SCRAM family registration procedure in the SASL mechanism registry.
SASL.quote: This document registers the SASL mechanisms SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS.

rejected.why: SHA-256 is only the hash function plugged into SCRAM; the document does not specify or analyse SHA itself.
TLS is relevant only for channel binding; the document does not define a TLS extension, only requires the session hash extension be negotiated or no resumption used.
HMAC is used as a building block inside SCRAM and is not the subject.
A GSS-API OID is assigned for the mechanism, but the document does not specify a GSS-API mechanism beyond that.
The registration procedures are boilerplate-like for the mechanism registry and are covered by the SASL subject; not a general IANA guidance document.
The iteration count guidance concerns SCRAM's salted hashing, but the document is not about password hashing functions in general.

gaps.name: SCRAM (Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism)
gaps.why: The document is about the SCRAM family of SASL mechanisms, and the taxonomy has no specific SCRAM tag; SASL is the closest fit.

RFC7678.title: Attribute-Value Pairs for Provisioning Customer Equipment Supporting IPv4-Over-IPv6 Transitional Solutions
RFC7678.summary: Defines Diameter AVPs to carry provisioning data for customer equipment using IPv4-over-IPv6 transition methods (DS-Lite, lw4o6, MAP-E), including multicast prefixes, port sets, binding and mapping rules.

Diameter.why: The document's main deliverable is a set of new Diameter AVPs with codes, grouped syntax and flag rules, so it extends the Diameter protocol.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies Diameter (RFC 6733) Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) to be used for that purpose.

MAP.why: A large part of the AVPs (MAP-E-Attributes, MAP-Mapping-Rule, MAP-Mesh-Mode, EA-Field-Length) carry MAP-E CE provisioning parameters.
MAP.quote: Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E) [RFC7597].

DS-Lite.why: Analyses DS-Lite provisioning (AFTR FQDN) and defines AVPs for it; lw4o6 is an extension of the DS-Lite architecture.
DS-Lite.quote: The AFTR's FQDN is contained in the Border-Router-Name AVP

SSM.why: The 64-Multicast-Attributes AVPs provision ASM/SSM prefixes for IPv4 multicast over IPv6 multicast.
SSM.quote: SSM-mPrefix64: the IPv6 multicast prefix to be used to synthesize the IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses of the multicast groups

rejected.why: Mentioned as one possible provisioning method but the document is indifferent to it and defines only Diameter AVPs.
Only cited as precedent (RFC 6519, RFC 4818); no RADIUS attributes are specified.
FQDN is used for the border router name, but only as a value encoding; nothing new about DNS.
Parent of the specific transition technologies already tagged (DS-Lite, MAP); the more specific tags are preferred.
Multicast prefix provisioning is a small part and covered by the more specific SSM tag; document is not about multicast routing.
Diameter is the specific AAA protocol tagged; ancestor is implied.

gaps.name: Lightweight 4over6 (lw4o6)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for lw4o6, which the document treats as a main transition method (Lw4o6-Binding AVP, tunnel source address, port sets).

RFC7679.title: A One-Way Delay Metric for IP Performance Metrics (IPPM)
RFC7679.summary: Defines the Type-P-One-way-Delay singleton metric, its Poisson-stream sample, and statistics (percentile, median, minimum) for measuring one-way packet delay across Internet paths, obsoleting RFC 2679.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines an active performance metric, with its methodology, error and calibration analysis, reporting rules and statistics. That is the performance measurement subject.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a metric for one-way delay of packets across Internet paths.

rejected.why: NTP is mentioned only as one way to synchronize clocks between Src and Dst. The document is not about NTP.
Clock synchronization, accuracy and skew are discussed only as sources of measurement error, not as a subject in their own right.
LMAP is cited only in the Security Considerations for its privacy guidance. The document does not address LMAP platforms.
The standard-formed packet definition applies to IPv4, but the document is not about IP itself. It only uses IP packets as the measured object.
TCP appears only in the motivation, as an example of an application affected by delay. It is not specified or analysed here.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metrics definitions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag specific to IPPM metric definitions. The broad performance measurement topic is the closest fit.

RFC7680.title: A One-Way Loss Metric for IP Performance Metrics (IPPM)
RFC7680.summary: RFC 7680 defines the IPPM one-way packet loss metric (singleton, Poisson-stream sample, and loss-ratio statistic), obsoleting RFC 2680 and advancing it to Internet Standard.

performance measurement.why: The document defines an active network performance metric, its sampling, methodology, error analysis and reporting, which is the core of the performance measurement subject.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths.

rejected.why: Benchmarking covers device/function test methodology (BMWG); this is an IPPM path metric, not device benchmarking.
TCP is mentioned only as motivation and as an example of non-unbiased loss observation; the document is not about TCP.
Clock synchronization and uncertainty are discussed as error sources for the metric, but the document does not specify time synchronization mechanisms.
QoS and DS field appear only as Type-P parameters and motivation, not as the subject.
LMAP is only referenced for privacy and security considerations; the document does not define LMAP platforms.
No ICMP usage; test packets are generic Type-P packets.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics)
gaps.why: The IPPM metric family (one-way delay, loss, etc.) has no dedicated tag; the broader 'performance measurement' topic is the closest fit.

RFC7681.title: Email Exchange of Secondary School Transcripts
RFC7681.summary: Defines EESST, a format for secondary school transcripts as signed (OpenPGP/MIME) MIME messages with PESC XML and PDF parts, which students encrypt and email directly to recipients, plus two registered mail header fields.

OpenPGP.why: The whole protocol is built on OpenPGP signing, encryption, key publication and certification of originators and recipients, profiled for transcripts.
OpenPGP.quote: A signed school transcript is a MIME body part whose form corresponds to that of a signed OpenPGP/MIME message

email.why: The document defines an email-based exchange format, transmission formats, and registers mail header fields.
email.quote: This memo specifies a common format for exchanging secondary school academic transcripts via electronic mail.

MIME.why: A large part of the document specifies the MIME structure, content headers and multipart layout of transcripts and transmissions.
MIME.quote: The content of a school transcript is represented as a single MIME body part whose content type is "multipart/mixed".

privacy.why: Student privacy and avoiding third-party monitoring drive the design and are discussed at length.
privacy.quote: By eliminating third-party intervention and surveillance, the defined protocol better protects student privacy and independence

rejected.why: SMTP is only the delivery substrate, cited for fail-safe delivery; nothing new is specified about it.
PESC XML is used for the computational transcript, but the document merely profiles an external schema rather than addressing XML.
Registers Eesst-Version and Organization headers, but this is minor apparatus relative to the document's subject.
Uses OpenPGP/MIME, not S/MIME.
Uses existing media types; registers none.
Header registrations are boilerplate-level IANA considerations.

gaps.name: Secondary school transcripts / education records exchange
gaps.why: The application domain (PESC XML academic records) has no taxonomy tag, though it is the document's subject.

RFC7682.title: Considerations for Internet Routing Registries (IRRs) and Routing Policy Configuration
RFC7682.summary: Informational RFC cataloguing historical and current issues affecting the efficacy of Internet Routing Registries (data accuracy, replication, BGP and router limitations) for inter-domain routing policy filtering.

RPSL.why: The whole document is about IRRs, RPSL objects, mirroring (NRTM), and building router policy from IRR data. RPSL/IRR is the matching tag.
RPSL.quote: catalog issues influencing the efficacy of Internet Routing Registries (IRRs) for inter-domain routing policy specification and application in the global routing system

RPKI.why: Resource certification and the RPKI are discussed as the remedy for IRR integrity problems, and compared with IRR route objects and RPSS.
RPKI.quote: there has never existed a resource certification infrastructure that enables a resource holder to authorize a particular autonomous system to originate network-layer reachability advertisements

rejected.why: BGP soft-reconfiguration and Route Refresh are discussed as historical limits on applying policy, but the document is about IRRs and not BGP itself.
It is mentioned only as one way to push configuration to routers, in a short passage.
The RPKI tag is more specific and already covers the routing-security angle.
FTP is only the transport for IRR flat-file mirroring.
SSH appears only as a way to log in to routers.
TLS is mentioned once, as something that would protect queries.

RFC7683.title: Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance
RFC7683.summary: Defines DOIC, a base Diameter overload control solution using piggybacked AVPs (OC-Supported-Features, OC-OLR) for capability announcement and overload reports, with a default loss abatement algorithm.

Diameter.why: The document specifies new Diameter AVPs, procedures and extensibility for overload control, so it is about the Diameter protocol.
Diameter.quote: This specification defines a base solution for Diameter overload control, referred to as Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC).

rejected.why: Overload control here is application-layer request throttling between Diameter nodes, not transport congestion control.
Diameter is a child of AAA and is chosen as the more specific tag; the document does not address AAA frameworks in general.
TLS, DTLS and IPsec are mentioned only in the Security Considerations as peer protection mechanisms.
The IANA section only registers AVP codes and new registries; it is boilerplate here.
Security issues such as DoS and trust are discussed, but the main body is about the overload control mechanism.

gaps.name: Diameter overload control
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Diameter tag, so the Diameter protocol and its overload control subject have no fitting id. The Diameter tag I used is not in the list, so this needs a taxonomy addition.

RFC7684.title: OSPFv2 Prefix/Link Attribute Advertisement
RFC7684.summary: Defines OSPFv2 Extended Prefix and Extended Link Opaque LSAs with TLV encoding to advertise additional prefix and link attributes, plus the associated IANA registries.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 with new TLV-based Opaque LSAs (Extended Prefix and Extended Link) for advertising prefix and link attributes.
OSPF.quote: This document defines OSPFv2 Opaque LSAs based on Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuples that can be used to associate additional attributes with prefixes or links.

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is mentioned only as a contrast (its LSAs are replaced by TLV-based extended LSAs); the document specifies OSPFv2 only.
Segment routing is cited as a motivating application and handled in a separate draft; this document defines only the generic LSA framework.
The TE extensions RFC 3630 is referenced only for the TLV format, not addressed by this document.
The IANA section creates registries, but that is boilerplate and not the main subject of the document.

RFC7685.title: A Transport Layer Security (TLS) ClientHello Padding Extension
RFC7685.summary: Defines a TLS extension (padding, type 21) that clients may include in the ClientHello to pad it to a desired size and avoid implementation bugs triggered by certain ClientHello sizes.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension and its ClientHello handling, and it updates RFC 5246. TLS readers would expect to find it.
TLS.quote: This memo describes a Transport Layer Security (TLS) extension that can be used to pad ClientHello messages to a desired size.

rejected.why: The document only discusses TLS records and ClientHello. It does not address datagram TLS.
The ExtensionType registration is routine boilerplate. The document is not about IANA registries.
Padding is meant to work around implementation bugs, not to protect privacy. The covert-channel remark is only in Security Considerations.

RFC7686.title: The ".onion" Special-Use Domain Name
RFC7686.summary: RFC 7686 registers ".onion" as a Special-Use Domain Name, specifying how users, applications, resolvers, DNS servers and registrars must treat names for Tor hidden services.

.onion.why: The whole document registers .onion and defines handling of these self-authenticating Tor service names, which is exactly the .onion tag.
.onion.quote: This document registers the ".onion" Special-Use Domain Name.

rejected.why: The more specific child .onion fits; the parent is implied.
DNS behaviour (NXDOMAIN for .onion) is specified only as a consequence of the special-use registration, not as DNS protocol work.
SOCKS is only mentioned as an example proxy for accessing .onion names; it is not specified or extended.
The document only forbids registrars from registering .onion names; it does not address registry operations.
URLs are mentioned only as a place where .onion names can appear.
HTTP is mentioned only as an application protocol that can use subdomain components.

gaps.name: Tor (onion routing / hidden services)
gaps.why: The document is about names for Tor hidden services, but the taxonomy has no tag for Tor or anonymity networks.

RFC7687.title: Report from the Strengthening the Internet (STRINT) Workshop
RFC7687.summary: IAB report of the 2014 STRINT workshop on how the IETF and W3C should respond to pervasive monitoring, covering threats, opportunistic security, metadata hiding, middleboxes and captive portals, and on-by-default security, with high-level recommendations.

privacy.why: The workshop is about countering pervasive monitoring, covering metadata, fingerprinting, traffic analysis and data minimisation. This is the privacy threat-model subject.
privacy.quote: how the technical community, and in particular the IETF and the W3C, should react to Pervasive Monitoring and more generally how to strengthen the Internet

security.why: The report covers security broadly: threat models, Opportunistic Security, usability of security UIs, and on-by-default security. No single mechanism is its subject, so the general security tag fits.
security.quote: Well-implemented cryptography can be effective against PM and will benefit the Internet if used more

captive portal.why: A substantial section and a workshop recommendation address distinguishing captive portals from MITM attacks and the need for a protocol.
captive portal.quote: One widespread example of middleboxes is captive portals, as found on the Wi-Fi hotspots in hotels, airports, etc.

rejected.why: TLS is mentioned as the end-to-end model and for certificate errors, but the report is not about the protocol.
It discusses IETF and W3C responses and possible BCPs, but the subject is pervasive monitoring, not process. The workshop-report subject is closer, but see the gaps.
It is mentioned only as one idea for improving the CA system.
SSH appears as an example of trust on first use and key continuity, not as a subject.
SIP and WebRTC are discussed only as examples of deployment security problems.
It appears only in a short break-out note on obfuscating traffic.

gaps.name: pervasive monitoring / Opportunistic Security
gaps.why: The core subject, pervasive surveillance and opportunistic encryption as a mitigation, has no dedicated tag. The privacy and security tags only approximate it.

RFC7688.title: GMPLS OSPF Enhancement for Signal and Network Element Compatibility for Wavelength Switched Optical Networks
RFC7688.summary: Defines GMPLS OSPF-TE extensions (Optical Node Property TLV with five sub-TLVs and a WSON-LSC ISCD switching capability with SCSI sub-TLVs) to advertise signal compatibility constraints of WSON network elements.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS routing for wavelength switched optical networks, defining a new WSON-LSC switching capability and ISCD extensions. GMPLS covers optical/transport network control.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides GMPLS OSPF routing enhancements to support signal compatibility constraints associated with general WSON network elements.

OSPF.why: It specifies a new OSPF TE LSA top-level TLV and sub-TLVs, so it is an extension of OSPF.
OSPF.quote: This document adds a new top-level TLV for use in the OSPF TE LSA: the Optical Node Property TLV.

rejected.why: OSPF-TE is the carrier here, but the document is about WSON node constraint advertisement, which GMPLS and OSPF already cover.
Path computation is mentioned as the consumer of the advertised constraints. The document does not specify PCE or PCEP.
IANA registrations are boilerplate in this document and not its subject.
The only MIB mention is a single IANA TC entry in the IANA Considerations section, so it is incidental.

gaps.name: WSON (Wavelength Switched Optical Networks)
gaps.why: The document is about WSON signal compatibility and optical network elements such as OEO switches, regenerators and wavelength converters. The taxonomy has no optical or WSON tag, so GMPLS is the closest fit.

RFC7689.title: Signaling Extensions for Wavelength Switched Optical Networks
RFC7689.summary: Defines GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling extensions for Wavelength Switched Optical Networks: a WSON Processing Hop Attribute TLV with ResourceBlockInfo and WavelengthSelection sub-TLVs for per-node processing and distributed wavelength assignment.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling for optical wavelength-switched networks, which is the subject of the GMPLS tag.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides extensions to Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) signaling for control of Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs).

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the signaling substrate whose attribute TLV mechanism is reused. The document is about the GMPLS/WSON extensions, so GMPLS is the better fit.
RBNF is used only as a notation for one TLV and is not a subject of the document.
The IANA registries are boilerplate and the main body is not about IANA.
Only referenced via RFC 7688. This document does not specify routing.

gaps.name: Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSON)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for WSON or optical network control, apart from the GMPLS tag, which only partly covers it.

RFC7690.title: Close Encounters of the ICMP Type 2 Kind (Near Misses with ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (PTB))
RFC7690.summary: Informational RFC describing how ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages get misdelivered in ECMP load-balanced/anycast server deployments, breaking PMTUD, and proposing operational mitigations such as broadcasting PTBs to all servers.

ECMP.why: The core problem is that stateless ECMP hashing sends ICMPv6 PTB errors to a different server than the flow's server. The document analyses this and proposes mitigations.
ECMP.quote: the problem of delivering ICMPv6 type 2 "Packet Too Big" (PTB) messages to the intended destination (typically the server) in ECMP load-balanced or anycast network architectures

PMTUD.why: The failure being addressed is breakage of path MTU discovery when PTB messages are lost. The improvements section also recommends RFC 4821 PLPMTUD.
PMTUD.quote: A case where this is particularly problematic operationally is path MTU discovery (PMTUD) [RFC1981].

ICMP.why: The document is about handling ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages, including filtering, replicating and rate limiting them.
ICMP.quote: An ICMPv6 type 2 PTB message generated on an intermediate device for a packet sent from a server

anycast.why: Anycast server tiers are the deployment model, and the mitigations distribute PTBs to all anycast servers.
anycast.quote: this next-hop selection is a constrained form of anycast topology, where all anycast destinations are equidistant

rejected.why: The document concerns IPv6 traffic, but it is about ICMPv6 PTB delivery in load balancing, not IPv6 specification or deployment. ICMP and PMTUD are more specific.
TCP MSS clamping is mentioned only as an alternative mitigation. The document is not about TCP.
Happy Eyeballs is mentioned only in passing as a client-side amelioration.
The document discusses rate limiting and DoS amplification only in its mitigation and Security Considerations. That is not the main subject.

RFC7691.title: Updating the Term Dates of IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) Members
RFC7691.summary: BCP update to RFC 4071 removing the fixed end-of-first-IETF-meeting term dates for IAOC members and directing the IAOC to set more practical term start and end dates and chair selection timing.

IETF process.why: The document changes IETF administrative procedure: IAOC member term dates, chair selection and meeting requirements. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This memo updates Section 4 of RFC 4071 [BCP101] to remove the following sentence

rejected.why: The document touches appointing bodies only in passing. It is about IAOC term dates, not NomCom procedures.
The IETF Trust is mentioned only because IAOC members serve as its Trustees. The document is not about IPR or trust legal provisions.

RFC7692.title: Compression Extensions for WebSocket
RFC7692.summary: Defines a framework for per-message compression extensions to the WebSocket Protocol and specifies one such extension, "permessage-deflate", using DEFLATE with negotiated context-takeover and LZ77 window parameters.

WebSocket.why: The document extends the WebSocket protocol with a compression extension framework, negotiated in the opening handshake and using the RSV1 framing bit, and registers a WebSocket extension name.
WebSocket.quote: This document defines a framework for creating WebSocket extensions that add compression functionality to the WebSocket Protocol.

DEFLATE.why: Section 7 defines how DEFLATE is applied to message payloads, including byte alignment with empty blocks and LZ77 window handling. Readers of DEFLATE usage would want it.
DEFLATE.quote: This document also specifies one specific PMCE based on the DEFLATE [RFC1951] algorithm.

rejected.why: Considered the parent topic, but the more specific DEFLATE tag fits and implies it. The document does not define a new compression algorithm.
The handshake uses the Sec-WebSocket-Extensions HTTP header only as a substrate. The document adds nothing about HTTP itself.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations, in a brief CRIME remark. The document is not about TLS.
ABNF is used only as notation for parameter values, not as a subject of the document.

RFC7693.title: The BLAKE2 Cryptographic Hash and Message Authentication Code (MAC)
RFC7693.summary: Specifies the BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s cryptographic hash functions (with built-in keyed MAC mode), providing the algorithm description, OIDs, worked examples and C reference implementations.

BLAKE2.why: The whole document specifies the BLAKE2 hash and keyed MAC: parameters, compression function F, mixing function G, padding, identifiers and reference code.
BLAKE2.quote: BLAKE2 comes in two main flavors: BLAKE2b is optimized for 64-bit platforms and BLAKE2s for smaller architectures.

rejected.why: SHA and HMAC-SHA are only cited as the alternative BLAKE2 replaces; the IV is noted as shared but the document does not specify SHA.
MD5 is mentioned only as a legacy function BLAKE2s-128 can replace, not specified or analysed.
BLAKE2 is explicitly stated not to need HMAC because keying is built in; HMAC is not specified here.
The OID assignments in Section 4 are small identifiers for algorithms, not an ASN.1 module or encoding rules specification.
ChaCha is only noted in acknowledgements as the origin of the core algorithm; the document does not specify ChaCha20 or Poly1305.

RFC7694.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Client-Initiated Content-Encoding
RFC7694.summary: Extends the HTTP Accept-Encoding header field to be usable in responses (notably 415 Unsupported Media Type) so servers can advertise which content codings they accept in requests.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP semantics by redefining Accept-Encoding as a response header and updating the 415 status code. A reader browsing HTTP would expect it.
HTTP.quote: This specification expands that definition to allow "Accept-Encoding" as a response header field as well.
HTTP.section: 3. Using the 'Accept-Encoding' Header Field in Responses

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy as a tag here; gzip is only mentioned as an example content coding and the document does not define or profile it.
Only referenced in Security Considerations; the document is about HTTP semantics generally.
415 concerns media types, but the document is about distinguishing content-coding problems from media type problems, not about media type registration.
Compression codings are the motivation, but the document does not define a compression format; it only adds discoverability of supported codings.
The example uses an Atom POST, but the document does not define conventions for building APIs.

RFC7695.title: Distributed Prefix Assignment Algorithm
RFC7695.summary: RFC 7695 specifies a distributed algorithm, run over a flooding mechanism, by which nodes automatically assign unique non-overlapping sub-prefixes from delegated prefixes to links, designed mainly for home networks.

addressing.why: The whole document is about IP prefix allocation and assignment to links, which is address architecture and allocation. No more specific technology tag fits.
addressing.quote: This document specifies a distributed algorithm for dividing a set of prefixes in a manner that allows for automatic assignment of sub-prefixes that are unique and non-overlapping.

home networking.why: It was produced by the homenet WG as the prefix assignment building block for home networks. The home networking page's readers would want it.
home networking.quote: Although the algorithm was primarily designed as an autonomic prefix assignment tool for home networks, it is applicable to other areas.

rejected.why: DHCPv6-PD is mentioned only as an example of a private link and of delegation. The document does not specify or extend it.
The algorithm works on any address space. IPv6 is the main use case but not the subject.
The algorithm can be used in autonomic networks, but the document is about the prefix assignment algorithm and not autonomic infrastructure in general.
Renumbering is discussed as an event the algorithm tries to avoid, but the document does not cover renumbering procedures.

gaps.name: distributed prefix assignment
gaps.why: The document's specific subject is automatic distributed assignment of prefixes to links. The nearest tag is addressing, which is broader.

RFC7696.title: Guidelines for Cryptographic Algorithm Agility and Selecting Mandatory-to-Implement Algorithms
RFC7696.summary: BCP guidance for IETF protocol designers on cryptographic algorithm agility: algorithm identifiers, choosing and changing mandatory-to-implement algorithms, transition from weak algorithms, and avoiding too many or only one cipher suite.

cryptography.why: The whole document is about cryptographic algorithm selection, agility, key sizes, and strength balancing across protocols. It is not specific to one algorithm or protocol, so the general cryptography topic fits.
cryptography.quote: This memo provides guidelines to ensure that protocols have the ability to migrate from one mandatory-to-implement algorithm suite to another over time.

rejected.why: TLS is used as an example of cipher suite identifiers and of attacks such as BEAST. The document does not specify or profile TLS.
IKEv2, AH and ESP are mentioned only as an example of algorithm identifier carriage.
The document recommends that algorithm identifier registries be used and have deprecation marking. This is a small part of the text and not its subject.
The topic is covered more specifically by the cryptography tag. The security parent is implied.
Section 2.5 on key establishment is brief, and the document is not about key management.
It gives guidance to working groups and authors, but the subject is cryptographic algorithm choice rather than IETF procedures.

gaps.name: cryptographic algorithm agility
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for algorithm agility or mandatory-to-implement algorithm policy. The general cryptography topic is the closest fit.

RFC7697.title: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Identifiers Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC7697.summary: Defines the MPLS-OAM-ID-STD-MIB module, an SNMP MIB with MEG and ME tables for configuring and monitoring OAM identifiers for MPLS-TP tunnels, LSPs, pseudowires and sections.

MIB.why: The document's main body is an SMIv2 MIB module (MPLS-OAM-ID-STD-MIB) with tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

MPLS-TP.why: The MIB models MPLS-TP OAM identifiers (MEG_ID, MEP_ID, ICC-based and IP-compatible) for tunnels, LSPs and pseudowires, so MPLS-TP readers need it.
MPLS-TP.quote: it describes managed objects to configure the Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) identifiers for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and the MPLS-based Transport Profile (TP).

OAM.why: The objects model Maintenance Entity Groups, Maintenance Entities and MEPs/MIPs, which are OAM constructs.
OAM.quote: This MIB module should be used for performing the OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) operations for MPLS Tunnel LSPs

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB. The document defines a module and does not specify or extend SNMP. The MIB tag covers it.
Pseudowires are one of the service types the OAM identifiers point to, through the PW MIB's pwTable. The document does not cover pseudowire emulation itself.
MPLS is the underlying technology being managed. The more specific MPLS-TP tag fits better.
BFD is only mentioned as the one supported OAM application in a status bit description.
AES is cited only in the Security Considerations boilerplate about SNMPv3 USM.

RFC7698.title: Framework and Requirements for GMPLS-Based Control of Flexi-Grid Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) Networks
RFC7698.summary: Informational framework and control-plane requirements for applying GMPLS (signaling, routing, path computation) to ITU-T flexi-grid DWDM optical networks, mapping media channels and frequency slots to LSPs, TE links and labels.

GMPLS.why: The whole document is about applying GMPLS to flexi-grid DWDM: LSPs as media channels, labels as frequency slots, and signaling and routing requirements.
GMPLS.quote: this document defines a framework and the associated control-plane requirements for the application of the existing GMPLS architecture and control-plane protocols to the control of flexi-grid DWDM networks

PCE.why: Section 4.7 covers Routing and Spectrum Assignment architectures, including a PCE as the computation entity. Together with the SSON definition this is a substantial part of the framework.
PCE.quote: The selection of a path that ensures n and m continuity can be delegated to a dedicated entity such as a Path Computation Element (PCE).

rejected.why: Signaling is RSVP-TE-based, but the document only states requirements. The actual extensions are deferred to companion documents.
TE links and the RSVP-TE/routing context are used, but GMPLS already covers the subject, and the document is not about traffic engineering in general.
YANG is mentioned only briefly in Manageability Considerations, so this is not a substantial subject of the document.
OAM appears only as a reference to RFC 7260 in Manageability Considerations.
RBNF is only the notation used for the information model in Figure 17. The document is not about RBNF.

gaps.name: Flexi-grid / optical transport networks (WSON, SSON, DWDM)
gaps.why: The document is about GMPLS control of flexible-grid optical networks, with frequency slots and media channels. The taxonomy has no optical or WDM tag, so GMPLS is the closest fit.

RFC7699.title: Generalized Labels for the Flexi-Grid in Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) Label Switching Routers
RFC7699.summary: Defines a new 64-bit GMPLS lambda label format (with n and m fields) for ITU-T flexi-grid DWDM in LSC routers, including composite labels, updating RFC 3471 and RFC 6205.

GMPLS.why: The whole document defines a new GMPLS generalized label encoding for flexi-grid optical switching, including composite labels carried in RSVP-TE LABEL objects.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines a new GMPLS lambda label format to support this flexi-grid.

rejected.why: The label is carried in RSVP-TE LABEL objects, but the document defines no new RSVP-TE signalling procedures. The flexi-grid Tspec and Flowspec are left to another draft.
GMPLS is a child of MPLS in the taxonomy, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
The document concerns a label encoding, not traffic engineering in its own right.
TDM, OTN and VCAT are mentioned only as precedent for composite labels. The document is not about SONET/SDH.
The IANA subregistry additions are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Flexi-grid / optical DWDM networks (WDM lambda labels)
gaps.why: The document is about optical flexible-grid spectrum labels. No taxonomy tag covers optical transport or WDM.

RFC7700.title: Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings Representing Nicknames
RFC7700.summary: Defines the PRECIS Nickname profile of the FreeformClass, specifying preparation, enforcement and comparison rules (space mapping, case folding, NFKC) for internationalized nicknames/display names/petnames, and registers it with IANA.

PRECIS.why: The document defines a PRECIS profile with its preparation, enforcement and comparison rules for nickname strings.
PRECIS.quote: The following rules apply within the Nickname profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass.

rejected.why: Chat protocols (IRC, XMPP, MSRP, XCON) are only cited as contexts where nicknames appear; the document defines no protocol behaviour for them.
Unicode normalization and case folding are used as mechanisms, but the document is about the PRECIS profile rather than Unicode usage generally; PRECIS is the more specific fit.
UTF-8 is only the required encoding of prepared strings.
The IANA section merely registers the profile; it is boilerplate here.
The Bidi rule from IDNA is referenced only to explain why it is not applied.
The parent of PRECIS, so it is implied by the PRECIS tag.

RFC7701.title: Multi-party Chat Using the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)
RFC7701.summary: Defines conventions and MSRP extensions (NICKNAME method, Use-Nickname header, new status codes, SDP 'chatroom' attribute) for multi-party chat rooms with private messages and nicknames, built on SIP conferencing and MSRP.

MSRP.why: The document extends MSRP with a new NICKNAME method, Use-Nickname header, status codes and MSRP switch behaviour for chat rooms.
MSRP.quote: This document defines requirements, conventions, and extensions for providing private messages and nickname management in centralized chat rooms with MSRP.

SDP.why: A whole section defines a new SDP media-level attribute with ABNF and offer/answer semantics, registered with IANA.
SDP.quote: we define a new 'chatroom' SDP attribute.  The 'chatroom' attribute is a media-level value attribute [RFC4566]

conferencing.why: Chat rooms are specified as a type of centralized conference with a focus, policy attributes and conference event package nicknames.
conferencing.quote: This memo deals with "Tightly Coupled SIP Conferences" as defined in the SIP Conferencing Framework [RFC4353]

rejected.why: SIP is used for joining and leaving chat rooms via existing conferencing procedures; the document defines no new SIP mechanisms.
Subject is instant messaging, but MSRP is the more specific tag and applies; the document extends MSRP, not IM/presence in general.
Only references the XCON data model and event package for the nickname attribute; the document does not specify them.
TLS is only a transport/security option for MSRP sessions.
Nickname preparation is delegated to RFC 7700; this document merely references it.
TCP is only the substrate; congestion avoidance advice refers to TCP buffers but is not about TCP.

RFC7702.title: Interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Groupchat
RFC7702.summary: Defines a bidirectional mapping between XMPP Multi-User Chat and SIP/MSRP multi-party chat sessions, covering join, nickname, presence, messaging, invite and exit flows for SIP-XMPP gateways.

XMPP.why: The document maps XMPP MUC groupchat to SIP/MSRP, specifying how XMPP presence and message stanzas are translated by gateways.
XMPP.quote: this document defines a mapping between the XMPP Multi-User Chat (MUC) extension [XEP-0045] and SIP-based multi-party chat using Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)

MSRP.why: MSRP multi-party chat (NICKNAME, SEND, switch) is one side of the mapping and is specified in detail.
MSRP.quote: a mapping between the SIP-based Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) and the XMPP Multi-User Chat (MUC) extension

SIP.why: SIP INVITE, SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, REFER and BYE flows and conference focus handling are mapped to XMPP actions.
SIP.quote: the XMPP-to-SIP gateway transforms it into a SIP INVITE request.

rejected.why: SDP is used only as the vehicle for the MSRP session offer/answer; nothing new is defined about it.
XML is just the encoding of XMPP stanzas and conference-info bodies.
The conference event package is used for roster mapping, but the document is about chat interworking, not a conferencing framework.
Groupchat is instant messaging, but the more specific XMPP and MSRP tags cover it.
Nickname preparation rules are only referenced to RFC 7700 in a short section.

gaps.name: SIP-XMPP interworking
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the SIP/XMPP interworking gateway series (RFC 7247, 7572, 7573, 7702).

RFC7703.title: Experience with Testing of Mapping of Address and Port Using Translation (MAP-T)
RFC7703.summary: Reports application-compatibility test results (browsers, chat, BitTorrent, FTP, ping/traceroute and others) on a MAP-T double-translation testbed at NIC.br using CERNET's MAP-T software with a shared IPv4 address.

MAP.why: The whole document tests user applications behind a MAP-T (Mapping of Address and Port using Translation) deployment and reports the effects of shared IPv4 addresses and double translation.
MAP.quote: The main purpose is to check if those applications work correctly on a network using MAP-T [RFC7599].

rejected.why: Command-line FTP is one tested application whose active-mode failure is explained, but the document does not specify or extend FTP.
NAT44 on the CPE is mentioned as the reason inbound connections fail, but the document is about MAP-T testing, not NAT behaviour in general.
Traceroute is tested and fails across the translator, but it is one test item among many and the document is not about the tool.
The parent of MAP is implied by the MAP tag, so listing it separately would be redundant.
Jabber/XMPP is one of many client applications tested and is not the subject of the document.
BitTorrent clients are tested, and the document notes they cannot seed without inbound connections. This is a minor part of the document.

RFC7704.title: An IETF with Much Diversity and Professional Conduct
RFC7704.summary: An Independent Submission arguing that IETF participation should be more diverse and that aggressive, hostile conduct, harassment and bullying should be curbed, with recommendations for constructive participation and enforcement of the IESG anti-harassment policy.

IETF process.why: The document is about how the IETF community operates: participant diversity, conduct norms, anti-harassment policy and how management should respond. It is an IETF process and culture subject, with no narrower tag available.
IETF process.quote: This document discusses IETF participation in terms of the nature of diversity and practical issues that can increase or decrease it.

rejected.why: The systers experiment with NomCom candidate selection is mentioned as motivating evidence, but the document is not about NomCom procedures.
The parent is implied by IETF process, so it is not listed separately.
No protocol privacy considerations are discussed.
This tag covers accessibility of Internet communications, not inclusion of people in the IETF community. Access in the document means ease of finding and understanding IETF materials.

gaps.name: Diversity, inclusion and professional conduct in the IETF community
gaps.why: The document's central subject is participant diversity, harassment and bullying policy. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for it, so it is only approximated by IETF process.

RFC7705.title: Autonomous System Migration Mechanisms and Their Effects on the BGP AS_PATH Attribute
RFC7705.summary: Documents the de facto BGP ASN migration mechanisms (Local AS, No Prepend Inbound, Replace Old AS, Internal BGP AS Migration) and their effects on the AS_PATH attribute, so future BGP work preserves them.

BGP.why: The whole document specifies BGP speaker behaviour for ASN migration: OPEN My Autonomous System handling and AS_PATH manipulation. It updates RFC 4271.
BGP.quote: This document discusses some existing commonly used BGP mechanisms for Autonomous System Number (ASN) migration that are not formally part of the BGP4 protocol specification.

rejected.why: Route reflectors are only used as an example scenario for iBGP AS migration. The document does not specify or extend route reflection.
The Security Considerations are brief boilerplate (TCP-AO, GTSM). The document is not about securing routing.
TCP is only the substrate under BGP sessions.
The document covers a BGP operational feature, not routing architecture or scalability principles.

RFC7706.title: Decreasing Access Time to Root Servers by Running One on Loopback
RFC7706.summary: Informational document describing how a DNS recursive resolver operator can run a local copy of the root zone on a loopback address (kept in sync via AXFR) to cut root-server latency and prevent snooping, with example configs for BIND, Unbound/NSD and Windows.

DNS.why: The document specifies an operational technique for DNS recursive resolvers and root zone serving, including zone refresh via SOA timers, AXFR sources and resolver/authoritative server configuration.
DNS.quote: Such resolvers can greatly decrease the round-trip time and prevent observation of requests by running a copy of the full root zone on a loopback address

DNSSEC.why: DNSSEC validation of all responses from the local root server and a current root key are core requirements of the design, and DS validation behaviour is discussed in the BIND examples.
DNSSEC.quote: The system MUST be able to validate a zone with DNSSEC [RFC4033].

rejected.why: Anycast is mentioned only as a possible cause of AXFR transfer problems in Appendix A; not a subject of the document.
Privacy goal is preventing observation of root queries by keeping them local, not encrypted or privacy-preserving DNS transport.
AXFR runs over TCP merely as the transfer substrate.
::1 and IPv6 addresses appear only as loopback or master addresses in configurations.

RFC7707.title: Network Reconnaissance in IPv6 Networks
RFC7707.summary: Informational RFC (obsoleting RFC 5157) analysing how address-scanning and other reconnaissance techniques apply to IPv6 networks, covering IPv6 address patterns, scanning tools, mitigations, and alternative methods of gleaning addresses.

IPv6.why: The document analyses IPv6 addressing, host density and address-scanning feasibility in IPv6 networks, which is its core subject.
IPv6.quote: it is widely assumed that it would take a tremendous effort to perform address-scanning attacks against IPv6 networks

operational security.why: The document covers reconnaissance techniques, attacker heuristics and operational mitigations for network and security administrators, which is operational security guidance.
operational security.quote: IPv6 address-scanning attacks can be mitigated in a number of ways.

SLAAC.why: A large part of the analysis covers how SLAAC interface identifier schemes (EUI-64, temporary, opaque) shape the scan search space.
SLAAC.quote: For each local prefix learned from a Router Advertisement message, an IPv6 address is configured by appending a locally generated Interface Identifier (IID)

addressing.why: The document analyses address assignment patterns (low-byte, IPv4-based, wordy, subnet ID plans) and how they reduce the search space.
addressing.quote: Address plans might include use of subnets that: Run from low ID upwards

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is covered only for its predictable sequential address assignment as a scanning aid, not specified or profiled.
DNS zone transfers, brute forcing and ip6.arpa walking are discussed as reconnaissance vectors in short subsections, but the document is not about DNS itself.
Neighbor Cache is mentioned as an information source and DoS risk, not the subject.
Temporary addresses are discussed for their scanning implications; privacy is incidental.
ICMPv6 probes are used by scanners but the document is not about ICMP.
traceroute6 gets a single-paragraph mention as a reconnaissance tool.

gaps.name: Network reconnaissance / address scanning
gaps.why: The central subject has no dedicated tag; it is closest to operational security, but readers browsing for reconnaissance and scanning would want a specific page.

RFC7708.title: Using a Generic Associated Channel Label as a Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification Channel Indicator
RFC7708.summary: Defines a new VCCV control channel type (Type 4) for MPLS pseudowires without the control word, using the Generic Associated Channel Label to identify VCCV packets, with FAT PW, MS-PW and capability advertisement rules.

pseudowire.why: The document extends VCCV, the pseudowire connectivity verification control channel, with a new CC type, including FAT PW and multi-segment PW handling and capability advertisement.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies a new VCCV control channel (VCCV CC) type to be used with pseudowires (PWs) carried over an MPLS network that do not use the PW Control Word

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is only the motivation for compatibility; the document does not specify MPLS-TP itself.
The document relies on MPLS label stacks and the GAL, but its subject is the pseudowire VCCV channel, which is a more specific tag.
LDP is used only for the C-bit advertisement and a new status code in IANA; the document is not about LDP.
ECMP is discussed only as a caveat on OAM path fate-sharing, not as the subject.
VCCV is an OAM mechanism, but the pseudowire tag is the specific fit and the document does not address OAM broadly.

gaps.name: VCCV (Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for VCCV, the pseudowire OAM control channel. The pseudowire tag is under MPLS and I also used an id not in the taxonomy; the closest valid tag is 'pseudowire'.

RFC7709.title: Requirements for Very Fast Setup of GMPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC7709.summary: Informational requirements document stating target scaling objectives (≈100 ms setup, tens to ~100 requests/s, 1 s holding times) and protocol requirements for very fast setup of GMPLS LSPs in high-churn networks.

GMPLS.why: The whole document lists requirements on GMPLS signalling and procedures for very fast LSP setup under high churn, so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: The goal of this document is to present target scaling objectives and the related protocol requirements for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

rejected.why: PCE is discussed only as it affects setup time (R3 says setup must not depend on PCC-PCE transactions); the document is not about PCE or PCEP.
RSVP-TE appears only via the RFC 6383 reference for pipelined cross-connect; no RSVP-TE specification or extension is given.
OSPF-TE is mentioned once as a protocol that may need extensions; it is not a subject of the document.
The GMPLS tag already covers the TE-flavoured LSP setup subject; the document does not address traffic engineering in its own right.
Setup delay is defined and referenced against RFC 5814/6777 metrics, but the document sets requirements rather than measurement methods.

RFC7710.title: Captive-Portal Identification Using DHCP or Router Advertisements (RAs)
RFC7710.summary: Defines a DHCPv4 option, a DHCPv6 option and an IPv6 Router Advertisement option that tell clients they are behind a captive portal and give the URI to contact it.

captive portal.why: The whole document is about identifying captive portals to clients, which is the subject of this tag.
captive portal.quote: This document describes a DHCP option (and a Router Advertisement (RA) extension) to inform clients that they are behind some sort of captive-portal device

DHCP.why: It specifies a new DHCPv4 option. The DHCPv6 option is covered under the DHCPv6 tag.
DHCP.quote: The Captive-Portal DHCPv4 option (160) (one octet).

DHCPv6.why: It defines a new DHCPv6 option with its format and code.
DHCPv6.quote: The Captive-Portal DHCPv6 option (103) (two octets).

neighbor discovery.why: It defines a new IPv6 Router Advertisement (Neighbor Discovery) option, type 37, to carry the portal URI.
neighbor discovery.quote: The format of the Captive-Portal Router Advertisement option is shown below.

rejected.why: URIs are only the payload of the options, and the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
The IPv6 content is covered by the more specific DHCPv6 and neighbor discovery tags.
The portal interaction is out of scope, and HTTP is not specified or extended.
It is mentioned only in passing in the Security Considerations.

RFC7711.title: PKIX over Secure HTTP (POSH)
RFC7711.summary: Defines POSH, a method for verifying non-HTTP application server identity by fetching JSON documents of PKIX certificate fingerprints over HTTPS from a well-known URI at the source domain, with delegation via reference documents; developed for XMPP domain name associations.

PKI.why: The document specifies how clients obtain verification material (certificate fingerprints) for PKIX server identity checking, which is a PKI deployment matter.
PKI.quote: This document defines methods that make it easier to deploy certificates for proper server identity checking in non-HTTP application protocols.

X.509.why: Fingerprints are defined over X.509 certificates and matched against the certificate presented by the server.
X.509.quote: The fingerprint hash for a given hash algorithm is generated by performing the named hash function over the DER encoding of the PKIX X.509 certificate.

XMPP.why: The method was designed as an XMPP DNA prooftype, and XMPP service names are used as examples; the document's main body is generic, so this is secondary.
XMPP.quote: these methods were developed for use in the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) as a Domain Name Association (DNA) prooftype

rejected.why: HTTPS and well-known URIs are only the substrate for retrieving the documents; HTTP itself is not extended.
TLS is the context for certificate checking, but the document defines no new TLS mechanism.
DANE is mentioned only as an alternative or complementary verification method that POSH avoids waiting on.
JSON is only the encoding of the fingerprint and reference documents.
The well-known URI registration is IANA boilerplate; the document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
Mentioned only as an alternative that is slow to deploy.

RFC7712.title: Domain Name Associations (DNA) in the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP)
RFC7712.summary: Defines the "prooftype" model for establishing strong associations between a DNS domain name and an XMPP XML stream (PKIX, DANE, POSH) and describes secure delegation of service domains to target hosts in multi-tenant XMPP hosting.

XMPP.why: The whole document extends XMPP security for client-to-server and server-to-server streams, including dialback flows and piggybacking.
XMPP.quote: it specifies how to establish a strong association between a domain name and an XML stream, using the concept of "prooftypes"

DANE.why: Defines the DANE prooftype for XMPP, with rules on TLSA usage and secure DNS, and uses DNSSEC for secure delegation.
DANE.quote: The DANE prooftype makes use of DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities [RFC6698], specifically the use of DANE with DNS SRV records [RFC7673].

authentication.why: The core contribution is a general model for server identity verification (prooftypes), which is authentication of hosts across mechanisms.
authentication.quote: A mechanism for proving an association between a domain name and an XML stream

rejected.why: DNSSEC is required only by the DANE prooftype and is described by reference to other RFCs. The document does not specify it.
TLS is the substrate for presenting certificates. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
PKIX certificates are used as one prooftype and validated per RFC 6120 and RFC 6125. The document does not profile them.
DNS SRV records are used for resolution and delegation but the document adds nothing to DNS itself.
POSH uses well-known URIs over HTTPS, but this is a minor part of the document and the POSH specification itself is RFC 7711.
SASL EXTERNAL is only mentioned in the S2S flow as a way to achieve mutual authentication.

gaps.name: POSH (PKIX over Secure HTTP)
gaps.why: The document defines the POSH prooftype and registers the xmpp-client and xmpp-server POSH service names, but the taxonomy has no POSH tag.

RFC7713.title: Congestion Exposure (ConEx) Concepts, Abstract Mechanism, and Requirements
RFC7713.summary: RFC 7713 describes the abstract Congestion Exposure (ConEx) mechanism, in which senders re-echo congestion signals (loss, ECN) into the IP layer so that network devices can audit and police congestion. It sets requirements for concrete ConEx encodings and discusses audit, policy devices and incremental deployment.

ConEx.why: The whole document defines the abstract ConEx mechanism, its signals, encodings, components, audit function and requirements for concrete specifications.
ConEx.quote: This mechanism is called Congestion Exposure, or ConEx.

rejected.why: ECN markings are the congestion signal that ConEx re-echoes and are discussed as input and for audit, but the document does not specify or extend ECN.
The parent topic is implied by the ConEx tag, and the document is about exposing congestion rather than about congestion control algorithms.
TCP feedback and modifications are mentioned as the sender and receiver substrate, but they are defined in other documents.
The IPv6 destination option encoding is only referenced as a concrete encoding in another draft.
AQM is mentioned only as a source of congestion signals.
Traffic management is a use of ConEx signals, but the document is not about traffic engineering of packet networks.

RFC7714.title: AES-GCM Authenticated Encryption in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC7714.summary: Defines how AES-GCM AEAD algorithms (AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM) provide confidentiality and authentication in SRTP and SRTCP, including IV formation, packet field treatment, KDF choice, signalling registrations for SDES, DTLS-SRTP and MIKEY, and test vectors.

SRTP.why: The document specifies a new crypto suite for SRTP/SRTCP: IV formation, associated data/plaintext split of packets, IV reuse prevention, and test vectors.
SRTP.quote: This document defines how the AES-GCM Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data family of algorithms can be used to provide confidentiality and data authentication in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP).

AES.why: The document profiles AES-128 and AES-256 in GCM mode, specifying parameters, tag size and counter-mode keystream generation, with AES-GCM test vectors.
AES.quote: AES Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM) [GCM] is a family of AEAD algorithms based upon AES.

MIKEY.why: A section defines how MIKEY parameters map to AEAD algorithms and adds MIKEY registry values, so MIKEY readers would want it.
MIKEY.quote: MIKEY specifies the algorithm family separately from the key length (which is specified by the Session Encryption key length) and the authentication tag length

rejected.why: RTP is the protocol SRTP profiles; the document is about the security profile, which sits under SRTP, not RTP itself.
SRTCP processing is covered, but as part of SRTP encryption; no RTCP protocol behaviour is defined.
DTLS-SRTP protection profiles are only registered in IANA considerations; nothing new about DTLS is defined.
SDES crypto suite registration is boilerplate-like IANA content; the document does not address SDP itself.
Key establishment is explicitly out of scope; only the KDF selection is mentioned.
The AEAD tag replaces separate authentication transforms; HMAC is not discussed.

gaps.name: AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no AEAD or generic authenticated-encryption tag; AES-GCM is covered only via the AES tag.

RFC7715.title: Multipoint LDP (mLDP) Node Protection
RFC7715.summary: Specifies mLDP node protection for P2MP and MP2MP LSPs: the protected node advertises PLR addresses to merge points, which set up targeted LDP sessions to the PLR so traffic can be redirected over pre-established P2P LSPs on node failure, with new status value elements and a capability TLV.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP/mLDP with new MP Status value elements, a new capability TLV, and tLDP-based signalling for node protection of P2MP/MP2MP LSPs.
LDP.quote: The upstream LSR address is conveyed via an LDP Notification message with an MP Status TLV, where the MP Status TLV contains a new "PLR Status Value Element"

IP fast reroute.why: The document is a fast-reroute style local repair mechanism (PLR/merge point, node protection) for multipoint LSPs; the IP fast reroute tag covers IP and LDP fast reroute.
IP fast reroute.quote: The pre-established LSPs originate from the PLR LSR and terminate on the MPT LSRs while bypassing LSR N.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one possible way to set up the backup P2P LSPs, which is out of scope.
Mentioned only as a typical way to detect node unreachability; detection is a local decision.
LDP is the more specific tag; the document is about LDP signalling for node protection rather than MPLS architecture in general.
P2MP/MP2MP LSPs are MPLS multipoint LSPs, not IP multicast routing.

gaps.name: mLDP (Multipoint LDP) / P2MP and MP2MP LSPs
gaps.why: The taxonomy has LDP and CR-LDP under MPLS but no dedicated tag for multipoint LDP extensions; mLDP is the document's main subject.

RFC7716.title: Global Table Multicast with BGP Multicast VPN (BGP-MVPN) Procedures
RFC7716.summary: Specifies the modifications needed to use BGP-MVPN (RFC 6513/6514) procedures to distribute non-VPN Global Table Multicast routing information among protocol boundary routers, including RD, RT, UMH selection and Source Active A-D handling.

MVPN.why: The document adapts BGP-MVPN procedures (MCAST-VPN routes, RDs, RTs, UMH selection, A-D routes) to global table multicast. This is squarely MVPN subject matter.
MVPN.quote: In this document, we describe the modifications that are needed to use the BGP-MVPN procedures for Global Table Multicast.

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier for MCAST-VPN routes, but the document's subject is multicast VPN procedures, not BGP itself. MVPN is the more specific fit.
It builds on RFC 4364 VPNs for background, but it is about multicast and non-VPN use, not L3VPN.
PIM is mentioned only as a possible AR-PBR protocol and in the security references. The document does not specify it.
Tunnels through the core are mentioned only generically. MPLS is not the subject.
Extended communities and Route Targets are used as MVPN protocol elements. The document does not specify communities as a subject.

RFC7717.title: IKEv2-Derived Shared Secret Key for the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) and Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC7717.summary: RFC 7717 specifies deriving the OWAMP/TWAMP shared secret key from an IKEv2 security association (prf(SK_d, "IPPM")), updating the Server Greeting and Set-Up-Response messages and adding an IKEv2Derived bit to the TWAMP-Modes registry.

OWAMP.quote: This document describes the use of keys derived from an IKEv2 security association (SA) as the shared key in OWAMP or TWAMP.

RFC7718.title: Registries for the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP)
RFC7718.summary: RFC 7718 establishes the IANA registries for OWAMP (OWAMP-Control Command Numbers and OWAMP-Modes), gives their initial contents and management rules, and updates RFC 4656.

OWAMP.why: The document extends and updates OWAMP (RFC 4656) by defining registries for its Modes and Control Command numbers. Readers of OWAMP material would want it.
OWAMP.quote: This memo describes the registries for OWAMP -- the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol.

rejected.why: TWAMP is only mentioned for comparison. The registries defined here are for OWAMP.
The IANA registry creation is the vehicle for OWAMP extensibility. The document is about OWAMP's registries rather than IANA guidance in general.
The IKEv2-derived mode bit is mentioned only as an entry in the Modes registry. RFC 7717 defines it.
This parent topic is implied by the OWAMP tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC7719.title: DNS Terminology
RFC7719.summary: RFC 7719 collects and gives current definitions for DNS terminology (names, RRs, servers, zones, registration model, DNSSEC) in a single informational glossary.

DNS.why: The whole document defines DNS terms covering names, header/response codes, resource records, servers, resolvers and zones, so it belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: This document gives current definitions for many of the terms used in the DNS in a single document.

DNSSEC.why: Two sections (General DNSSEC and DNSSEC States) define signed zones, NSEC/NSEC3, KSK/ZSK, and the secure/insecure/bogus/indeterminate states.
DNSSEC.quote: Most DNSSEC terms are defined in [RFC4033], [RFC4034], [RFC4035], and [RFC5155].  The terms that have caused confusion in the DNS community are highlighted here.
