terminology.why: The document is a glossary of definitions, which is what readers of the terminology subject look for.
terminology.quote: This document collects a wide variety of DNS-related terms.

rejected.why: The Registration Model section briefly defines registry, registrar and registrant. It is a small part of a DNS glossary, so it is not tagged.
EPP is only defined as a term in one short entry; the document does not specify or discuss the protocol.
RDAP appears only as a glossary entry pointing to other RFCs.
WHOIS appears only as a glossary entry pointing to RFC 3912.
EDNS and OPT get brief glossary entries only, and the document does not extend or specify them.
IDN has a single glossary entry that points to the IDNA RFCs.
Anycast has a single glossary entry quoted from RFC 4786.

RFC7720.title: DNS Root Name Service Protocol and Deployment Requirements
RFC7720.summary: BCP defining protocol and deployment requirements for the DNS root name service (obsoleting RFC 2870), requiring core DNS, IPv4/IPv6, UDP/TCP, DNSSEC and EDNS(0) support and serving the unique root zone.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies requirements on root name servers, which are authoritative DNS servers. It is about DNS server behaviour and operations.
DNS.quote: The protocol and deployment requirements for the DNS root name service are defined in this document.

DNSSEC.why: Requires root servers to implement DNSSEC. This is one of a few protocol requirements, so it is a minor but real part.
DNSSEC.quote: MUST implement DNSSEC [RFC4035] as an authoritative name service.

EDNS.why: Mandates EDNS(0) support in the root service. It is a listed requirement, not a specification of EDNS.
EDNS.quote: MUST implement extension mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0)) [RFC6891].

rejected.why: UDP and TCP are only required as transports for DNS queries; the document does not specify or analyse them.
IPv4/IPv6 transport support is a one-line requirement; the document is not about IPv6.
Mentioned only as a required transport for DNS, not as a subject.
Security Considerations calls the root service a key architectural component, but the body is a DNS requirements list and not about architecture principles.
Operational requirements are explicitly out of scope and deferred to RSSAC-001.

gaps.name: DNS root name service / root server system
gaps.why: The document is specifically about root server requirements; the taxonomy has no root-server tag, so it is covered only by the general DNS tag.

RFC7721.title: Security and Privacy Considerations for IPv6 Address Generation Mechanisms
RFC7721.summary: Informational analysis of privacy and security properties (correlation, location tracking, address scanning, device exploits) of IPv6 interface identifier generation mechanisms such as EUI-64, CGA, temporary, stable opaque, and DHCPv6 addresses.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 addressing and interface identifier generation, evaluating how each mechanism fares against privacy and security threats.
IPv6.quote: This document discusses privacy and security considerations for several IPv6 address generation mechanisms, both standardized and non-standardized.

SLAAC.why: Most analysed mechanisms are SLAAC IID generation methods (EUI-64, temporary, stable opaque, CGA), so SLAAC readers would want this analysis.
SLAAC.quote: With stateless autoconfiguration, routers advertise on-link prefixes and hosts generate their own Interface Identifiers (IIDs) to complete their addresses.

privacy.why: A substantial part of the document is a privacy threat analysis (correlation, location tracking) of address generation.
privacy.quote: A host using a CGA can be correlated for as long as the lifetime of the combination of the public key and the chosen modifier block

rejected.why: DHCPv6-based address generation is one of several mechanisms compared in a single section, not a subject the document specifies or extends.
CGA and SEND are discussed only as one compared mechanism, not specified or analysed in depth.
Teredo is mentioned as an example of an embedded-IPv4 address scanning weakness, not a subject of the document.
Neighbor discovery appears only through the SEND/CGA reference and probing attacks; it is not the document's subject.
IPv6 is the more specific tag that fits, and addressing is a sibling-level subject already covered by IPv6.
Transition technologies are covered only briefly in Section 4.8 as examples of inherited address properties.

RFC7722.title: Multi-Topology Extension for the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2)
RFC7722.summary: Experimental extension to OLSRv2 that lets MANET routers maintain multiple routing topologies, one per link metric type, while interoperating with unextended OLSRv2 routers; it adds the MPR_TYPES TLV and extends the MPR_WILLING, MPR, GATEWAY and LINK_METRIC TLVs.

OLSR.why: The whole document extends OLSRv2: information bases, HELLO and TC processing, MPR and routing set calculation for multiple metric types.
OLSR.quote: This specification describes an extension to the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) to support multiple routing topologies

rejected.why: OLSRv2 is built on NHDP, but this document explicitly does not modify NHDP. It only changes OLSRv2-specific sets and TLVs.
DSCP is only suggested as a way to choose the topology per packet, and that selection is outside the scope of this document.
OSPF multi-topology routing is mentioned only as a motivating analogy.
OLSR is the more specific tag and already sits under MANET, so the parent is implied.
The TLV registry changes are boilerplate-like updates that serve the protocol extension. The document is not about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: Multi-topology routing
gaps.why: The document is about routing with multiple topologies keyed by link metric type. The taxonomy has no general multi-topology routing tag, so only the OLSR protocol tag fits.

RFC7723.title: Port Control Protocol (PCP) Anycast Addresses
RFC7723.summary: Defines well-known IPv4 (192.0.0.9) and IPv6 (2001:1::1) anycast addresses that PCP clients can use to discover and reach their closest on-path PCP server (NAT/firewall), with client/server behaviour, deployment and security notes.

PCP.why: The document extends PCP with well-known server discovery addresses and specifies client and server behaviour for them.
PCP.quote: The Port Control Protocol (PCP) anycast addresses enable PCP clients to transmit signaling messages to their closest PCP-aware on-path NAT, firewall, or other middlebox

anycast.why: The core mechanism is anycast addressing, with deployment limitations (asymmetric routing, parallel firewalls) and anycast-specific security issues discussed.
anycast.quote: it establishes two well-known anycast addresses for the PCP server, one IPv4 address and one IPv6 address.

rejected.why: NATs and firewalls are the devices PCP controls, not the subject; PCP is the more specific tag.
DHCP option is only mentioned as an alternative discovery method.
Mentioned only as an example of dynamic routing affecting anycast.
The special-purpose address registrations are boilerplate-style IANA considerations, not the main subject.
Carrier-Grade NAT is only an example deployment scenario.
The IPv6 address is one of two registered, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC7724.title: Active DHCPv4 Lease Query
RFC7724.summary: RFC 7724 specifies Active DHCPv4 Leasequery, an extension of DHCPv4 Bulk Leasequery over TCP (optionally TLS) that streams near real-time binding updates to a requestor, and updates RFC 6926.

DHCP.why: The document defines new DHCPv4 message types, status codes, and requestor/server behaviour for Active Leasequery, extending RFC 4388 and RFC 6926.
DHCP.quote: allows for active transfer of near real-time DHCPv4 binding information data via TCP

rejected.why: TLS is only the security mechanism for the secure mode of the TCP connection; no new TLS extension is defined.
TCP is the transport substrate for the long-lived connection; the document defines nothing new about TCP itself.
It does carry DHCPv4 over TCP, but this is incidental to the Leasequery protocol, which reuses RFC 6926 framing.
DHCPv6 Active Leasequery is only mentioned in the acknowledgments; this document covers DHCPv4 only.

RFC7725.title: An HTTP Status Code to Report Legal Obstacles
RFC7725.summary: Defines HTTP status code 451 (Unavailable For Legal Reasons) for responses when access is denied due to a legal demand, and registers the "blocked-by" link relation to identify the blocking entity.

HTTP.why: The document's core is a new HTTP status code, 451, extending HTTP semantics, including its cacheability and response content.
HTTP.quote: This document specifies a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) status code for use when a server operator has received a legal demand to deny access

web linking.why: Defines and registers a new link relation type, "blocked-by", used with the Link header to identify the blocking entity. Readers of web linking would want it.
web linking.quote: the "Link" header field MUST have a "rel" parameter whose value is "blocked-by"

rejected.why: It only notes that 451 is cacheable by default per RFC 7234; caching is not a substantial topic.
The Link header value is a URI reference per RFC 3986, but this is only a dependency.
This is a general status code for web resource access, not a convention for building APIs.
DNS servers are mentioned only as one possible blocking entity.
The IANA registry updates are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC7726.title: Clarifying Procedures for Establishing BFD Sessions for MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC7726.summary: Clarifies RFC 5884 procedures for establishing, maintaining, and removing multiple concurrent BFD sessions per <MPLS LSP, FEC>, bootstrapped via LSP ping.

BFD.why: The document updates RFC 5884 and specifies BFD session establishment, demultiplexing by discriminators, removal and discriminator changes for BFD over MPLS LSPs.
BFD.quote: clarifies the procedures for establishing, maintaining, and removing multiple, concurrent BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) sessions for a given <MPLS LSP, FEC>

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs and LSP ping are the substrate on which BFD sessions run. The document specifies BFD session handling, not MPLS itself.
ECMP is only mentioned as a motivating scenario for multiple sessions. The document is not about it.
Segment Routing is cited once as an example use case, in an informative reference. It is not a subject of the document.
LSP ping is used only to bootstrap the sessions, and the document does not specify or extend it.

RFC7727.title: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) Application of the Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol (ICCP)
RFC7727.summary: Defines the STP application of ICCP: new ICCP TLVs and procedures that let a PE redundancy group act as a single virtual root bridge when multihoming a customer STP/MSTP network, synchronizing STP configuration and state among PEs.

L2VPN.why: The document extends ICCP, the L2VPN PE redundancy protocol, with an STP application (TLVs, procedures) for multihomed Layer 2 attachment circuits to a VPLS/L2VPN service. No ICCP tag exists, so L2VPN is the closest fit.
L2VPN.quote: Provider Edge (PE) devices in a Redundancy Group (RG) running ICCP are used to offer multihomed connectivity to Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) networks

Ethernet.why: A large part of the document concerns Ethernet bridging: STP/MSTP, BPDUs, bridge identifiers, topology changes, MAC flushing, and CIST/MSTI parameters from IEEE 802.1Q.
Ethernet.quote: This document introduces support of STP as a new application of ICCP.  When a bridged STP network is connected to an RG

rejected.why: VPLS is the service context and is cited for MAC withdrawal and split horizon. The document specifies nothing new about VPLS and says its specification remains unchanged.
LDP is only mentioned for sending Address Withdraw messages. It is not what the document is about.
Pseudowires appear only in the topology figure and as the existing VPLS core. They are not addressed in the document.
ICCP runs over TCP, but TCP is only the substrate.
The MPLS core is background. The document does not specify MPLS behaviour.

gaps.name: ICCP (Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is an application of ICCP, and the taxonomy has no ICCP tag. Readers browsing PE redundancy or ICCP would expect to find it.

gaps.name: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP/MSTP)
gaps.why: The document is about STP/MSTP interworking, and the taxonomy has no spanning tree tag. Ethernet is only an approximate fit.

RFC7728.title: RTP Stream Pause and Resume
RFC7728.summary: Defines new RTCP transport-layer feedback messages (PAUSE, RESUME, PAUSED, REFUSED) and TMMBR/TMMBN usage so an RTP receiver can pause and resume an incoming stream, with SDP signalling via the ccm "pause" parameter; updates RFC 5104.

RTCP.why: The document's core is a new RTCP feedback message type (FMT 9, RTPFB) extending the Codec Control Message feedback package, so it belongs under RTCP feedback.
RTCP.quote: This document defines a new transport-layer feedback message, which is further subtyped into either a PAUSE request, a RESUME request, a PAUSED indication, or a REFUSED notification.

SDP.why: A substantial part defines the SDP rtcp-fb ccm pause parameter with config/nowait attributes and offer/answer rules.
SDP.quote: This specification defines a new parameter "pause" to the "ccm" feedback value defined in CCM [RFC5104]

rejected.why: RTP is the stream being controlled, but the specification is about RTCP feedback; RTCP is the more specific tag.
SIP/SDP signalling is only contrasted as an alternative in design considerations; not specified here.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a protection option.
Only mentioned in passing in the declarative-use discussion as having its own PAUSE.
No payload format is defined; the codecs and SVC are only context.

RFC7729.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Logical Functional Block (LFB) Subsidiary Management
RFC7729.summary: Defines the ForCES Subsidiary Management (SM) LFB class, letting a Control Element configure a Forwarding Element's LFB class loading, CE associations, debug log levels and generic attributes.

ForCES.why: The document specifies a new ForCES LFB class (SM LFB) with components, capabilities and events for managing FEs.
ForCES.quote: This document introduces the SM LFB class, an LFB class that specifies the configuration parameters of an FE.

rejected.why: Only the syslog severity levels are borrowed for the debug log-level enumeration; the syslog protocol is not specified or used.
The LFB library is written in XML per the ForCES model, but XML is just the definition format, not the subject.
Not used; the data model is the ForCES LFB XML library, not YANG.
The SM LFB is a management-style function, but the specific subject is the ForCES LFB. It was considered as a broader parent tag and not chosen.

gaps.name: ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about ForCES LFB definitions, and the taxonomy has a ForCES-related tag only as ForCES under routing; the id I used does not appear in the taxonomy, so no exact tag fits.

RFC7730.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Trust Anchor Locator
RFC7730.summary: Defines the RPKI Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) format, a file of rsync URIs plus a public key used by relying parties to retrieve and verify RPKI trust anchor certificates, and obsoletes RFC 6490 by allowing multiple URIs.

RPKI.why: The whole document specifies the RPKI TAL and how relying parties use it to retrieve and validate RPKI trust anchors. This is core RPKI material.
RPKI.quote: This document defines a Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) [RFC6480].

rejected.why: The trust anchor is an X.509 CA certificate, but the document defines no new certificate profile. It relies on RFC 6487 and RFC 5280 for that.
It is a generic parent of RPKI, which is the more specific tag. The trust-anchor-format discussion is covered by RPKI.
RPKI supports secure routing, but this document says nothing about BGP itself.
Base64 is only the encoding of the key in the TAL, so it is substrate.
The TAL uses rsync URIs defined in RFC 5781 and defines no new URI scheme.
RPKI is the more specific child tag and already covers this.

RFC7731.title: Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (MPL)
RFC7731.summary: Specifies MPL, an IPv6 multicast forwarding protocol for low-power and lossy networks that disseminates messages to all forwarders in a domain using Trickle-based proactive/reactive forwarding or classic flooding, without maintaining a multicast topology.

multicast.why: The document defines a new IPv6 multicast forwarding protocol, MPL, with domains, data messages and control messages. No more specific multicast child tag covers a Trickle-based forwarding protocol, so the parent topic fits.
multicast.quote: MPL avoids the need to construct or maintain any multicast routing topology, disseminating multicast messages to all MPL Forwarders in an MPL Domain.

IoT.why: MPL is designed for constrained, low-power and lossy networks and is produced by the ROLL working group. IoT readers would want it. No more specific IoT tag fits.
IoT.quote: MPL is an IPv6 multicast forwarding protocol designed for the communication characteristics and resource constraints of LLNs.

rejected.why: RPL is mentioned as context and as one way to configure MPL Domains, but the document does not specify or extend it.
PIM is cited only as a traditional topology-maintaining approach that MPL avoids.
MPL defines an ICMPv6 message type for its control messages, but ICMPv6 is only the carrier, not the subject.
MPL runs over IPv6 and defines a Hop-by-Hop option, but the document is about multicast forwarding and not IPv6 itself.
IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation is used as a mechanism for MPL Data Messages, but it is not the subject.
6LoWPAN compression is mentioned only in the IANA multicast address allocation.

gaps.name: Trickle algorithm
gaps.why: MPL is built on Trickle (RFC 6206) and defines how its timers are used for data and control messages. The taxonomy has no tag for Trickle or for gossip or flooding dissemination.

RFC7732.title: Forwarder Policy for Multicast with Admin-Local Scope in the Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (MPL)
RFC7732.summary: Specifies an automated forwarding policy for a border router (the "MPL4 router") that forwards MPL multicast messages with Admin-Local (scope 4) across interfaces and meshes, including zone determination, network identifiers, and layer-2 protection rules.

multicast.why: The document defines multicast forwarding policy for MPL messages across scopes and zones in a border router. MPL has no specific tag, so the multicast topic fits directly.
multicast.quote: specify an automated policy for the routing of Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (MPL) multicast messages with Admin-Local scope in a border router

6LoWPAN.why: It targets low-power lossy mesh networks and maps network identifiers for IEEE 802.15.4, G.9959 and BTLE constrained links. Readers of constrained-link IPv6 topics would want it.
6LoWPAN.quote: a Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (LoWPAN) is defined by an IEEE 802.15.4 Layer 2 mesh network, composed of all connected nodes sharing the same Personal Area Network (PAN) ID

rejected.why: PIM-DM and PIM-SM are mentioned only as ways non-MPL multicast messages may arrive; the document does not specify them.
IGMP and MLD are cited only for legality of received messages, not specified or extended.
RPL is a routing protocol for LLNs but is not discussed; the document concerns MPL multicast forwarding.
The document relies on IPv6 multicast scopes but does not specify IPv6 itself.
RFC 7576 is referenced only as a motivating idea; the document is not about autonomic networking.
IEEE 802.11 appears only as one network identifier mapping (SSID), not as a subject of the document.

gaps.name: MPL (Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPL or its Trickle-based forwarding, though it is the central subject of the document.

RFC7733.title: Applicability Statement: The Use of the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) Protocol Suite in Home Automation and Building Control
RFC7733.summary: Applicability statement profiling RPL, P2P-RPL and MPL (with security via PANA/EAP-TLS and link-layer keys) for home automation and building control networks.

RPL.why: The document profiles RPL and P2P-RPL (modes, objective function, DAO policy, Trickle parameters) for home and building automation.
RPL.quote: guidance in the selection and use of protocols from the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) protocol suite

PANA.why: A substantial part of the document specifies the PANA/PANA relay, EAP-TLS key distribution mechanism for the network-wide key.
PANA.quote: the Authentication Server sends the network security material to the joining node through the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA)

rejected.why: TLS with PSK/ECC cipher suites is only a layer inside the authentication stack, not the subject.
EAP and EAP-TLS are used as part of the PANA authentication stack, not defined or changed here.
CoAP is only mentioned as the expected application protocol and for multicast configuration.
The adaptation layers are cited as assumptions; Section 4.2.3 says not applicable.
MPL multicast profile is a part of the document, but MPL is most specifically a Trickle-based LLN multicast, and no matching child tag exists; the general multicast tag is for IP multicast routing.
The document is about RPL for low-power networks; the RPL tag under IoT is more specific.

gaps.name: MPL (Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks)
gaps.why: Section 5 gives an MPL profile with Trickle parameters, but the taxonomy has no MPL tag.

gaps.name: Home and building automation
gaps.why: The application domain is the document's main subject, but no tag covers building or home control.

RFC7734.title: Support for Shortest Path Bridging MAC Mode over Ethernet VPN (EVPN)
RFC7734.summary: Specifies how Shortest Path Bridging MAC mode (SPBM) islands interwork with PBB PEs over an EVPN core, mapping IS-IS SPB information to and from EVPN BGP routes with per-B-VID designated forwarder election.

EVPN.why: The document extends EVPN (PBB-EVPN) with SPBM interworking: control-plane mapping to EVPN NLRI, DF election and data-plane procedures at the PE.
EVPN.quote: This document describes how Ethernet Shortest Path Bridging MAC mode (SPBM) can be combined with Ethernet VPN (EVPN) to interwork with Provider Backbone Bridging Provider Edges

IS-IS.why: Substantial part of the procedures is processing IS-IS SPB TLVs and advertising into the IS-IS SPB routing system, so IS-IS readers would want it.
IS-IS.quote: incorporates control-plane interworking in the PE to map ISIS-SPB [RFC6329] information elements into the EVPN Next Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) and vice versa

rejected.why: BGP carries the EVPN routes, but the document defines EVPN procedures, not new BGP protocol behavior.
The IP/MPLS network is the EVPN core substrate; nothing new is specified about MPLS.
The subject is Ethernet bridging (SPBM/PBB) but the tag is about IP over Ethernet and Ethernet OAM; EVPN is the more specific fit.
EVPN is the more specific child under VPN; no separate L2VPN service is defined.

gaps.name: Shortest Path Bridging (SPB / IEEE 802.1aq) and Provider Backbone Bridging
gaps.why: The document is about SPBM and PBB interworking, but the taxonomy has no tag for IEEE 802.1 bridging technologies such as SPB or PBB.

RFC7735.title: Tracking Reviews of Documents
RFC7735.summary: Informational RFC setting out requirements for a reimplemented review-tracking tool integrated with the IETF Datatracker, supporting review team secretaries, reviewers, requesters and statistics for IETF document reviews.

IETF process.why: The document covers how IETF review teams (Gen-ART, SecDir, etc.) assign and track reviews of Internet-Drafts during Last Call and Telechat. This is IETF process administration and tooling.
IETF process.quote: Several review teams ensure specific types of review are performed on Internet-Drafts as they progress towards becoming RFCs.

rejected.why: The reviews concern Internet-Drafts in the IETF process, not RFC format, style or publication.
Email is used in the workflows (assignments, notifications) but is not specified or analysed by the document.
It is a requirements document for a tool, not a workshop report.

gaps.name: Datatracker / IETF tools
gaps.why: The document is mainly about requirements for the IETF Datatracker review tool. The taxonomy has no tag for IETF tooling.

RFC7736.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Media Type Registration
RFC7736.summary: Registers the application/cdni media type with a required ptype parameter and creates the IANA CDNI Payload Types registry for the CDNI protocol suite.

media types.why: The document's main content is the registration of application/cdni and the rules for its ptype registry, which is media type registration.
media types.quote: this document defines a single new media type for CDNI that includes a required payload-type parameter.

CDN.why: The media type is defined for the CDNI protocol suite, so readers of CDN interconnection would expect to find it.
CDN.quote: developing a set of protocols to enable the interconnection of multiple content delivery networks (CDNs)

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for some CDNI payloads. The document defines nothing about JSON.
The CDNI interfaces run over HTTP, but HTTP is only the substrate here.
ABNF is used only to define the ptype syntax. The document is not about the notation.
The IANA registry creation is the mechanism for the media type and payload types. The document is not general IANA guidance, and the media types tag fits better.

RFC7737.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping and Traceroute Reply Mode Simplification
RFC7737.summary: Updates RFC 7110 so MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute "Reply via Specified Path" (mode 5) can omit the Reply Path TLV to mean the reverse LSP, and adds an optional Reply Mode Order TLV carrying a preferred-order list of reply modes.

MPLS.why: The document specifies changes to MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute (RFC 4379/7110 data-plane failure detection), including a new TLV and reply-mode procedures. No dedicated LSP ping tag exists, so MPLS is the closest fit.
MPLS.quote: This document updates the procedures for the "Reply via Specified Path" Reply Mode.

OAM.why: LSP Ping and Traceroute are OAM diagnostic mechanisms, and the document addresses their operational reliability and manageability.
OAM.quote: This results in a false failure of MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute operations.

rejected.why: That tag is for traceroute tools generally. Here MPLS LSP Traceroute is only one of two operations affected by the MPLS echo reply-mode change.
MPLS-TP LSPs are only mentioned as an example of LSP types that have a reverse LSP; the document is not about MPLS-TP.
Bidirectional RSVP-TE LSPs are cited only as an example of LSPs with a reverse path.
Reply mode 2 (reply via IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet) is just one of the listed reply options.
The TLV type assignment is boilerplate IANA Considerations.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP Ping / LSP Traceroute (MPLS echo request/reply, RFC 4379)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about the MPLS data-plane failure detection protocol, and the taxonomy has no dedicated tag for it.

RFC7738.title: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS)
RFC7738.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace identifier "ccsds" for persistently naming documents, XML schemas and registries published by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems, defining its subnamespace syntax and assignment via SANA.

URN.why: The document defines a new formal URN namespace (NID "ccsds") per RFC 3406, with syntax, uniqueness, persistence and assignment rules. This is exactly what the URN subject page covers.
URN.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace intended for persistently and uniquely naming resources published by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS).

rejected.why: XML schemas are only one of the things the namespace will name. The document does not specify or profile any XML usage.
The only IANA action is the routine registration of the NID. The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax definition, so it is not a subject of the document.
The document is about a URN namespace, which is covered by the more specific URN tag. RFC 3986 is cited only for reserved characters.

RFC7739.title: Security Implications of Predictable Fragment Identification Values
RFC7739.summary: Informational RFC analysing security implications of predictable IPv6 Fragment Header Identification values and giving algorithms (per-destination counter, random, hash-based) for selecting them.

IPv6.why: The document is about the IPv6 Fragment Header Identification field: its attacks and how implementations should choose values. IPv6 is the most specific fitting tag; no taxonomy tag exists for fragmentation.
IPv6.quote: This document analyzes the security implications of predictable Identification values, and provides implementation guidance for setting the Identification field of the Fragment Header

rejected.why: Forged ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages are used in the attack scenarios, but ICMP is only the trigger mechanism, not the subject.
Path MTU discovery is discussed as an enabler of the attacks, not as the subject.
PRNG choice is explicitly declared out of scope; RFC 4086 is only referenced.
The document is a security analysis, but it is specific to IPv6 fragmentation, so IPv6 is the more specific tag and a general security tag adds nothing.
RFC 6145 translators are mentioned only to justify the 16-bit effective ID length.
The Destination Cache is referenced for storing per-destination state, but the document is not about neighbor discovery.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation and reassembly
gaps.why: The document is about fragment identification and fragmentation-based attacks, and the taxonomy has no tag for fragmentation. It is covered only loosely by the IPv6 tag.

RFC7740.title: Simulating Partial Mesh of Multipoint-to-Multipoint (MP2MP) Provider Tunnels with Ingress Replication
RFC7740.summary: Specifies how a partial mesh of MP2MP provider tunnels for bidirectional customer multicast (BIDIR-PIM) in BGP/MPLS MVPNs can be simulated using Ingress Replication, via S-PMSI and Leaf A-D route procedures.

MVPN.why: The document defines S-PMSI A-D and Leaf A-D route procedures and forwarding state for bidirectional C-flows in BGP/MPLS multicast VPNs, extending RFC 6513/6514/7582.
MVPN.quote: This document specifies how a partial mesh of MP2MP tunnels can be simulated using Ingress Replication.

rejected.why: BIDIR-PIM is the customer-side protocol whose flows are carried, but the document does not specify or extend PIM itself.
BGP A-D routes are the signalling mechanism, but the document is about MVPN procedures, not BGP itself.
The VPN context is L3VPN, but the document's subject is multicast within it, which MVPN covers more specifically.
mLDP is mentioned only as an alternative way to realize MP2MP tunnels that this document avoids.
MPLS labels are used for the data plane, but MPLS is not the subject of the document.

RFC7741.title: RTP Payload Format for VP8 Video
RFC7741.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for VP8 video: payload descriptor, partition packetization, RPSI/SLI feedback use, and the video/VP8 media type with SDP parameters.

VP8.why: The document specifies how VP8 video is packetized in RTP, including partitions, temporal scalability and reference-frame handling. VP8 readers would want it.
VP8.quote: This memo describes an RTP payload specification applicable to the transmission of video streams encoded using the VP8 video codec [RFC6386].

RTP payload format.why: It is an RTP payload format specification: payload descriptor, header usage, marker bit, fragmentation and aggregation rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This section describes how the encoded VP8 bitstream is encapsulated in RTP.

RTCP.why: A substantial section defines how the RTCP feedback messages RPSI and SLI are used with VP8 PictureIDs, including an example exchange.
RTCP.quote: Using VP8 with RPSI and SLI Feedback
RTCP.section: 5. Using VP8 with RPSI and SLI Feedback

SDP.why: It defines the SDP mapping and offer/answer rules for the max-fr and max-fs parameters.
SDP.quote: The media type video/VP8 string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] as follows:
SDP.section: 6.2.1. Mapping of Media Subtype Parameters to SDP

rejected.why: It registers video/VP8, but the registration is a routine part of a payload format. The document is not about media type rules.
VP8 is a child of codecs and is the more specific tag.
SRTP appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate, as RTP profiles that may be used.
The section is brief and defers to RFC 3550. It only notes that non-reference frames can be discarded.
RTP is the substrate. The more specific RTP payload format tag already covers it.

RFC7742.title: WebRTC Video Processing and Codec Requirements
RFC7742.summary: Specifies WebRTC video requirements: pre/post-processing, stream orientation (CVO), mandatory-to-implement codecs (VP8 and H.264 Constrained Baseline), and codec-specific SDP parameters.

WebRTC.why: The whole document defines video handling requirements for WebRTC endpoints, including processing, orientation and mandatory codecs.
WebRTC.quote: This specification provides the requirements and considerations for WebRTC applications to send and receive video across a network.

VP8.why: VP8 is a mandatory codec, with its own section on payload formats and max-fr/max-fs handling.
VP8.quote: WebRTC Browsers MUST implement the VP8 video codec as described in [RFC6386]

H.264.why: H.264 is a mandatory codec, and the document specifies its profiles, SDP parameters and SEI message handling.
H.264.quote: they MUST support Constrained Baseline Profile Level 1.2 and SHOULD support H.264 Constrained High Profile Level 1.3.

rejected.why: SDP attributes such as imageattr and H.264 fmtp parameters are used, but SDP is only the signalling substrate here.
The document references the VP8 and H.264 payload formats (RFC 7741, RFC 6184) but defines none itself.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the protection mechanism, which is boilerplate.
The specific child tags VP8 and H.264 fit better than the parent.
H.265 appears only as an example of codec-specific orientation SEI signalling.

RFC7743.title: Relayed Echo Reply Mechanism for Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping
RFC7743.summary: RFC 7743 extends MPLS LSP Ping (RFC 4379) with a Relayed Echo Reply message and a Relay Node Address Stack TLV so replying LSRs without a route to the initiator can return Echo Replies via relay nodes such as ASBRs in inter-AS and inter-area deployments.

MPLS.why: The document extends and updates MPLS LSP Ping and traceroute, defining a new message type, TLV and return code for MPLS data-plane failure detection. No narrower MPLS tag fits (OAM is a topic, and LSP Ping has no dedicated tag).
MPLS.quote: This document describes extensions to the Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping specified in [RFC4379] by adding a Relayed Echo Reply mechanism

OAM.why: LSP Ping and traceroute are OAM mechanisms for fault detection and localization, and the document fixes failures of that mechanism across AS and area boundaries.
OAM.quote: LSP Ping [RFC4379] defines a mechanism to detect data-plane failures and localize faults.

rejected.why: The document affects LSP traceroute (Section 4.7) but is about the MPLS LSP Ping relay mechanism, not the general traceroute tool.
Relayed Echo Reply messages are carried in UDP on port 3503, but UDP is only the substrate.
Inter-AS scenarios and ASBRs are the setting, but BGP is not specified or extended.
Seamless MPLS and inter-AS/inter-area topologies are used as motivating examples; the document does not address routing architecture.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP Ping / LSP traceroute (RFC 4379 data-plane failure detection)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for MPLS LSP Ping, so the document falls back to the MPLS parent tag and the generic OAM topic.

RFC7744.title: Use Cases for Authentication and Authorization in Constrained Environments
RFC7744.summary: Informational ACE working group document collecting use cases (container monitoring, home automation, health monitoring, building automation, smart metering, sports, industrial control) that identify authentication and authorization problems for constrained devices.

ACE.why: The document is the ACE working group use-case document. It lists authorization problems to guide a solution for authentication and authorization in constrained environments.
ACE.quote: This document includes a collection of representative use cases for authentication and authorization in constrained environments.

IoT.why: The use cases cover IoT domains such as smart homes, smart metering, building automation and eHealth, and they set out the constraints of the devices involved.
IoT.quote: Constrained devices [RFC7228] are nodes with limited processing power, storage space, and transmission capacities.

rejected.why: CoAP is assumed only where specific detail is needed. The document does not specify or extend it.
The ACE tag is more specific and fits the document's scope. The generic authorization topic is implied by it.
Privacy appears in individual use cases and in a short Privacy Considerations section. It is not a main subject of the document.
DTLS is mentioned once, as an example of end-to-end security that proxies could break.

RFC7745.title: XML Schemas for Reverse DNS Management
RFC7745.summary: Defines RelaxNG XML schemas used by ICANN's RESTful HTTPS service for registries to update NS and DS records for reverse DNS delegations under IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA, and to query queued updates.

domain registration.why: The document specifies a registry-facing provisioning interface for reverse DNS delegations (NS/DS updates) operated by ICANN and RIRs, which is registry operations. No more specific child (EPP, RDAP, WHOIS) fits.

XML.why: The core deliverable is a pair of XML schemas (RelaxNG Compact) for zone updates and queue entries, an XML-based format.
XML.quote: The following Schema, used for PUT, GET, and DELETE operations, is an XML document using the RelaxNG Compact [RELAXNG] specification.
XML.section: Appendix A. Schema Definition for rDNS Updates

DNSSEC.why: The motivation and schema content include DS record management in parent zones for DNSSEC key rollover, so DNSSEC readers would find it relevant.
DNSSEC.quote: updates to DS records in the parent zone for child delegations follow the key rollover and expiry of the child zone.

rejected.why: HTTP GET/PUT/DELETE is only the transport for the REST service; the document defines no HTTP extension.
Client and server certificates are used for authentication, but only as a mechanism; nothing new is specified about X.509.

The schemas carry NS and DS data, but the document specifies no DNS protocol or resource record behaviour; it concerns registry management.
It describes a specific REST service, but not general conventions for building HTTP APIs.

RFC7746.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Self-Ping
RFC7746.summary: Defines LSP Self-ping, a lightweight UDP-based data-plane mechanism by which an RSVP-TE ingress LSR verifies that forwarding state is installed on all downstream LSRs before sending traffic onto an LSP.

RSVP-TE.quote: When an ingress LSR receives an RESV message, it can invoke LSP Self-ping procedures to ensure that forwarding state has been installed on all downstream nodes.

MPLS.why: It specifies a new MPLS data-plane verification protocol for LSPs, with PHP behaviour and MPLS OAM comparison. It fits the MPLS page alongside the RSVP-TE tag.
MPLS.quote: LSP Self-ping is a new protocol.  It is not an extension of LSP Ping.

rejected.why: The document states LSP Self-ping is not a general-purpose MPLS OAM mechanism, though it is compared with LSP Ping and S-BFD.
S-BFD is mentioned only as a comparison and a rejected alternative, not specified here.
UDP is only the substrate carrying the Self-ping message; nothing new is defined about UDP itself.
The document covers point-to-point and bidirectional LSPs but is not about GMPLS.
The CSPRNG recommendation for Session-IDs appears only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The UDP port assignment is only IANA Considerations boilerplate.

RFC7747.title: Basic BGP Convergence Benchmarking Methodology for Data-Plane Convergence
RFC7747.summary: Defines a methodology for benchmarking BGP data-plane (FIB) convergence on a device under test using three- or four-node topologies, with test cases for route advertisement, link failure, resets, withdrawals, attribute changes and graceful restart, plus a reporting format.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking methodology from the BMWG, with test setups, procedures and a reporting format for measuring device convergence.
benchmarking.quote: This document defines the methodology for benchmarking data-plane Forwarding Information Base (FIB) convergence performance of BGP in routers and switches

BGP.why: All test cases measure BGP convergence behaviour (eBGP, iBGP, route refresh, graceful restart, withdrawals), so BGP readers would want this RFC.
BGP.quote: BGP is widely deployed and used by several service providers as the default inter-AS (Autonomous System) routing protocol.

rejected.why: An ECMP link failure test appears (5.2.3), but it is one minor test case and the document is not about ECMP forwarding.
RPKI origin validation and SIDR features are mentioned only as a parameter to document in tests, not as a subject of the document.
BGPsec is cited only as a feature to record in the reporting table, so the document is not about it.

TCP parameters and TCP-AO are listed as configurable timers or settings, not specified or analysed.

RFC7748.title: Elliptic Curves for Security
RFC7748.summary: RFC 7748 specifies the Curve25519 and Curve448 elliptic curves, the X25519 and X448 scalar-multiplication functions, and their use in Diffie-Hellman key agreement, with deterministic curve generation and test vectors.

Curve25519.why: The document defines curve25519 and curve448, the X25519/X448 functions, their parameters, encodings and test vectors. That is the content of the Curve25519 and Curve448 tag.
Curve25519.quote: This memo specifies two elliptic curves ("curve25519" and "curve448") that lend themselves to constant-time implementation

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by Curve25519, so it is not listed separately.
The edwards25519 and edwards448 curves are given with birational maps, but no signature scheme is specified here.
TLS is mentioned only as an intended application in the abstract. The document specifies no TLS extension or cipher suite.
Diffie-Hellman key agreement is specified only as a use of the X25519/X448 functions. The document does not address key management in its own right.
Quantum attacks are mentioned in a single sentence of the Security Considerations, and the document is not about post-quantum cryptography.

RFC7749.title: The "xml2rfc" Version 2 Vocabulary
RFC7749.summary: RFC 7749 defines version 2 of the xml2rfc XML vocabulary used to write RFCs and Internet-Drafts, describing each element and attribute, boilerplate generation, the RELAX NG schema, and the application/rfc+xml media type, and obsoletes RFC 2629.

RFCXML.why: The whole document specifies the xml2rfc vocabulary, which is the RFC XML vocabulary processed by xml2rfc. The RFCXML tag fits it exactly.
RFCXML.quote: This document defines the "xml2rfc" version 2 vocabulary: an XML-based language used for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts.

media types.why: The document registers the application/rfc+xml media type. Readers of media type registrations would want it, though this is a smaller part of the document.
media types.quote: This document serves as the specification for the Internet Media Type "application/rfc+xml".

rejected.why: XML is the substrate for the vocabulary. The document defines an XML-based format rather than being about XML usage generally, and RFCXML is the more specific tag.
RFCXML already sits under RFC series. The document is about the vocabulary, not series format or style policy.
Appendix A describes how the ipr attribute selects boilerplate text. This is an implementation detail of the vocabulary, not a discussion of IPR policy.
ABNF is only mentioned as one use of the artwork element. The schema is written in RELAX NG, not ABNF.
URIs appear only as attribute value types and in references. The document defines nothing about URIs.
The phone and facsimile elements point to the tel URI syntax. This is only a value convention and not a subject of the document.

RFC7750.title: Differentiated Service Code Point and Explicit Congestion Notification Monitoring in the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC7750.summary: RFC 7750 defines an optional TWAMP extension (a new Modes flag and a changed Session-Reflector test packet format) that lets the Session-Sender learn the DSCP and ECN values received at the Session-Reflector.

TWAMP.why: The document extends TWAMP (updates RFC 5357) with a new Modes-field capability bit and a modified reflector packet format, so it belongs on the TWAMP page.
TWAMP.quote: This document describes an optional extension for Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) allowing the monitoring of the Differentiated Service Code Point and Explicit Congestion Notification fields

rejected.why: DSCP is the field being monitored, but the document defines no Diffserv behaviour; Diffserv is only the subject of the measurement.
ECN is observed and reported by the extension, but the document does not specify or change ECN; the reflector ignores congestion indications.
Implied by TWAMP, which is the more specific tag chosen.
Cited only as the source of the Type-P Descriptor. The taxonomy has no separate OWAMP tag in play for this document's subject, which is TWAMP.

RFC7751.title: Kerberos Authorization Data Container Authenticated by Multiple Message Authentication Codes (MACs)
RFC7751.summary: Specifies the Kerberos AD-CAMMAC authorization data container, superseding AD-KDC-ISSUED, with kdc, service and other MAC verifiers so KDCs and services can authenticate the contained authorization data, and updates RFC 4120.

Kerberos.why: The document extends the Kerberos V5 protocol with a new authorization data type and updates RFC 4120, assigning an ad-type and a key usage number.
Kerberos.quote: This document specifies a new authorization data container for Kerberos, called the CAMMAC (Container Authenticated by Multiple MACs).

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only used to define the AD-CAMMAC type, so it is the notation and not the subject.
The topic is general, and the document is about Kerberos authorization data specifically. Kerberos is already tagged.
The MACs are RFC 3961 checksums. The document does not specify or discuss HMAC.
The document does not mention GSS-API, and it is not the subject.

RFC7752.title: North-Bound Distribution of Link-State and Traffic Engineering (TE) Information Using BGP
RFC7752.summary: RFC 7752 defines BGP-LS: a new BGP NLRI (AFI 16388, SAFI 71/72) and BGP-LS path attribute that carry IGP link-state and TE information (nodes, links, prefixes) from networks to external consumers such as PCEs and ALTO servers.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new NLRI format, path attribute, capability negotiation and error handling, so it belongs on the BGP page.
BGP.quote: a mechanism by which link-state and TE information can be collected from networks and shared with external components using the BGP routing protocol

PCE.why: A PCE obtaining its TED is a main use case, which motivates the design. PCE readers would want this document.
PCE.quote: The following figure shows how a PCE can get its TED information using the mechanism described in this document.

ALTO.why: ALTO servers are a stated application, with a dedicated motivation section. The document does not define the ALTO protocol itself.
ALTO.quote: The mechanism defined in this document provides a single interface through which an ALTO server can retrieve all the necessary prefix and network topology data

rejected.why: OSPF is only a source of the link-state data, and its fields are mapped into BGP-LS TLVs. The document does not specify or extend OSPF.
IS-IS is likewise only an information source, and its sub-TLV encodings are reused. The document does not extend IS-IS.
TE information is the payload being distributed, but the document is about the BGP encoding. The PCE tag already covers the TE use case.
MPLS-TE is only context for the PCE use case and for the MPLS Protocol Mask TLV. The document does not specify MPLS.
Dedicated route reflectors are only suggested as an operational deployment option, not specified.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link-State)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for BGP-LS itself. It has BGP-SPF, which uses BGP-LS, but nothing for this base link-state NLRI specification. The BGP tag is the closest fit.

RFC7753.title: Port Control Protocol (PCP) Extension for Port-Set Allocation
RFC7753.summary: RFC 7753 extends the Port Control Protocol with a PORT_SET option on MAP requests so a client can request, renew and delete a set of ports in a single exchange. Motivating uses include Lightweight 4over6, firewall control and stateless mapping discovery.

PCP.why: The whole document specifies a new PCP MAP option (PORT_SET), including client and server behaviour, renewal, overlap handling and operational guidance.
PCP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Port Control Protocol (PCP) that allows clients to manipulate a set of ports as a whole.

rejected.why: Carrier-Grade NAT is mentioned as a use case and as a server that may allocate bulk ports. The document does not specify or analyse CGN.
Lightweight 4over6 is cited as a motivating use case with a short description. The document does not extend or define that architecture, and the taxonomy has no lw4o6 tag.
PCP controls NAT devices, and the examples use NAT44. The NAT itself is not the subject, and the PCP tag already covers the document's specific topic.
Firewall control is one of the use cases listed, but only briefly. The document is about port-set allocation in PCP, not about firewalls.
A SIP UAS is used only as an example of an application that needs many ports.
RTP is mentioned for port parity and port ranges only. The document does not address RTP itself.

RFC7754.title: Technical Considerations for Internet Service Blocking and Filtering
RFC7754.summary: IAB informational document analysing network-based, rendezvous-based and endpoint-based Internet blocking and filtering approaches by scope, granularity, efficacy and security, concluding that endpoint-based filtering fits the Internet architecture best.

internet architecture.why: The document evaluates blocking design patterns against architectural principles such as end-to-end security, layering and collateral damage.
internet architecture.quote: examines several technical approaches to Internet blocking and filtering in terms of their alignment with the overall Internet architecture

firewall.why: Firewalls, packet filtering, deep packet inspection and TLS-intercepting enterprise proxies are the central network-based blocking mechanisms analysed.
firewall.quote: Firewalls of various sorts are very commonly employed at many points in today's Internet

operational security.why: The document considers operator and enterprise blocking practices, including ingress filtering, spam filtering and safe browsing, and their consequences.
operational security.quote: Preventing or responding to security threats.  Network operators, enterprises, application providers, and end users often block communications

rejected.why: DNS-based blocking and domain seizure are discussed as examples of rendezvous blocking, but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
TLS is mentioned as a mechanism that blocking systems break through interception, and the document defines nothing new about it.
Spam filtering and DNS blacklists appear as one example among many, not as a main subject.
Privacy is raised only as a side effect of TLS interception, not as a subject in its own right.
Route leaks (Pakistan/YouTube) and RPKI manipulation are cited as examples, not as the topic.
DNSSEC is mentioned only as a factor limiting the workarounds for DNS blocking.

gaps.name: Internet blocking and filtering / censorship
gaps.why: The whole document is about blocking and filtering of Internet content and services. The taxonomy has no tag for censorship or content filtering, and the nearest tags (firewall, internet architecture) only partly cover it.

RFC7755.title: SIIT-DC: Stateless IP/ICMP Translation for IPv6 Data Center Environments
RFC7755.summary: RFC 7755 describes deploying stateless IP/ICMP translation (SIIT) with Border Relays in IPv6-only Internet data centers so legacy IPv4 clients can reach IPv6 services, with guidance on prefixes, routing, MTU and fragmentation.

SIIT.why: The whole document specifies a deployment model built on SIIT, with BRs, EAMs and translation prefixes.
SIIT.quote: This document describes the use of the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT) in an IPv6 Internet Data Center (IDC).

data center networking.why: It targets Internet data center operators and covers topology, BR placement, ECMP and routing within the IDC.
data center networking.quote: The primary audience is IDC operators who are deploying IPv6, running out of available IPv4 addresses, and/or feeling that dual stack

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a contrasting stateful technology; SIIT-DC is stateless.
Mentioned as an optional combination for outbound traffic, not a subject of the document.
MTU and fragmentation handling is a section of the document but the subject is SIIT translation behaviour, not PMTUD itself.
Parent of SIIT, implied by the SIIT tag.
Used for load balancing across BRs but only as a supporting mechanism.
Appears only in the example topology as the routing substrate.

RFC7756.title: Stateless IP/ICMP Translation for IPv6 Internet Data Center Environments (SIIT-DC): Dual Translation Mode
RFC7756.summary: RFC 7756 extends SIIT-DC with an Edge Relay component that reverses Border Relay stateless IPv4/IPv6 translation, giving IPv4-only nodes and applications native-looking IPv4 connectivity in an IPv6-only data center.

SIIT.why: The document specifies the SIIT-DC Edge Relay, a stateless IP/ICMP translator used in dual translation with the Border Relay, so it belongs on the SIIT page.
SIIT.quote: An ER is at its core an implementation of the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm [RFC6145] that supports Explicit Address Mappings [RFC7757].

rejected.why: The document acknowledges 464XLAT as the inspiration, but it specifies a stateless-only SIIT-DC extension, not 464XLAT.
The translation is stateless SIIT with explicit address mappings, not stateful NAT64.
The topic is relevant, but the more specific SIIT tag already sits beneath it.
It is only mentioned as the way the ER attracts traffic to its IPv6 Service Addresses. The document does not specify or extend it.
DHCPv4 appears only in deployment examples for assigning addresses and the MTU.
The MTU sections are deployment advice about configuring values. They are not about path MTU discovery.

gaps.name: SIIT-DC (Stateless IP/ICMP Translation for IPv6 Data Center Environments)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the SIIT-DC architecture. SIIT is the closest fit, but the data-center-specific Border Relay and Edge Relay design has no tag of its own.

RFC7757.title: Explicit Address Mappings for Stateless IP/ICMP Translation
RFC7757.summary: RFC 7757 extends SIIT (RFC 6145) with an Explicit Address Mapping Table algorithm so stateless IPv4/IPv6 translators can map arbitrary non-IPv4-translatable IPv6 addresses, including hairpinning and overlap handling.

SIIT.why: The document defines the EAM algorithm as an extension to SIIT and updates RFC 6145 sections on address translation, so it belongs on the SIIT page.

rejected.why: Only presented as a use case in Appendix A.1; the document is not about 464XLAT itself.
The parent of SIIT; SIIT is the more specific tag and the ancestor is implied.
Stateful translation is not the subject; this document is about stateless translation.
IPv6 addressing is the context, but the document is about the translation algorithm rather than IPv6 itself.

RFC7758.title: Time Capability in NETCONF
RFC7758.summary: Defines an experimental NETCONF capability (:time) that lets clients schedule RPCs for execution at a given time and lets servers report execution timestamps, with a YANG module, a cancel-schedule RPC and a notification.

rejected.why: Clock synchronization is assumed and explicitly out of scope; NTP and PTP are only referenced.

Only the mandatory-to-implement transport for NETCONF, mentioned in the security considerations.

RFC7759.summary: Defines the MPLS OAM Functions TLV and sub-TLVs carried in LSP Ping (MPLS Echo Request/Reply) to configure proactive MPLS-TP OAM (BFD CC/CV, loss/delay measurement, fault management signals) on an LSP, plus new return codes.

MPLS-TP.quote: This specification describes the configuration of proactive MPLS-TP Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions for a given Label Switched Path (LSP)

BFD.why: A large part of the document defines BFD configuration sub-TLVs (discriminator, timers, authentication) to bootstrap and tune BFD sessions.
BFD.quote: the BFD Configuration sub-TLV (refer to Section 2.2.1) has an Integrity flag that, when set, enables BFD Authentication

performance measurement.why: Defines PM, Loss and Delay sub-TLVs for configuring packet loss and delay measurement.
performance measurement.quote: it is possible to configure Performance Monitoring functionalities such as Loss, Delay, Delay/Interpacket Delay variation (jitter), and throughput

OAM.why: The document is about configuring OAM functions generally, including fault management signals (AIS/LKR).
OAM.quote: The MPLS OAM Functions TLV presented in Figure 1 is carried as a TLV of the MPLS Echo Request/Reply messages

rejected.why: The more specific MPLS-TP tag fits better, so the parent is implied.
Only mentioned as an alternative configuration method, which is covered by RFC 7487.
Targeted LDP is mentioned only as another option, not specified here.
LSP Ping is the carrier of the TLVs but the document does not extend ping as a diagnostic tool. No taxonomy tag exists for LSP Ping.
The IANA section is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: LSP Ping (MPLS data plane failure detection)
gaps.why: The document extends LSP Ping (RFC 4379) with a new TLV and return codes. The taxonomy has no tag for LSP Ping or MPLS OAM.

RFC7760.title: Statement of Work for Extensions to the IETF Datatracker for Author Statistics
RFC7760.summary: A statement of work for extending the IETF Datatracker to produce statistics and graphs about RFCs, Internet-Drafts, their authors (affiliation, country, continent) and IETF meeting attendees.

IETF process.why: The document specifies work on IETF administrative tooling (the Datatracker) to report on document authorship and meeting participation, which is IETF process and administration. It is not about any protocol.
IETF process.quote: ensure that the software is maintained as part of the IETF information services

rejected.why: The statistics cover RFCs and their authors, but the document is about Datatracker tooling and IETF participation, not RFC format, style or publication.
Section 7 only suggests that a future XML schema could carry author continent. This is a passing remark, not the subject.
XML is mentioned as a possible future data source and as one specification technique to count. The document is not about XML.
ABNF is named only as one of the specification techniques whose usage the statistics should count.
ASN.1 is named only as one of the specification techniques whose usage the statistics should count.
JSON is named only as one of the specification techniques whose usage the statistics should count.

RFC7761.title: Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM): Protocol Specification (Revised)
RFC7761.summary: RFC 7761 is the Internet Standard specification of PIM-SM, a multicast routing protocol using RP-rooted shared trees and optional source-specific shortest-path trees, replacing RFC 4601 and removing (*,*,RP), PMBR and IPsec authentication.

PIM-SM.why: The whole document is the PIM-SM protocol specification: state, forwarding, Register, Join/Prune, Assert, RP discovery, packet formats and timers.
PIM-SM.quote: This document specifies Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM).

SSM.why: Section 4.8 defines PIM-SSM behaviour, modifications for SSM addresses and PIM-SSM-only routers, which SSM readers would want.
SSM.quote: The Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) service model [6] can be implemented with a strict subset of the PIM-SM protocol mechanisms.

rejected.why: IGMP/MLD are only used as the local membership mechanism; the document does not specify them.
MBGP is mentioned only as a possible source for the MRIB.
Authentication using IPsec was removed; it is mentioned only in Security Considerations and Appendix A.
IPv6 is supported in the formats but the document is not about IPv6.
Parent of PIM-SM, so it is implied and not listed separately.
The PIM checksum is a standard Internet checksum applied to the protocol, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Bootstrap Router (BSR) RP discovery
gaps.why: Section 4.7 covers group-to-RP mapping and the hash function, but BSR itself is specified in RFC 5059 and the taxonomy has no BSR tag.

RFC7762.title: Initial Assignment for the Content Security Policy Directives Registry
RFC7762.summary: Establishes an IANA registry for Content Security Policy directives, defines its Specification Required registration policy, and populates it with the CSP Level 2 directives.

web security.why: Content Security Policy is a web platform security mechanism, and the registry covers its directives, so readers of web security would look for this RFC.
web security.quote: This document establishes an Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA) registry for Content Security Policy directives

IANA.why: The main body creates a registry and defines its registration policy (Specification Required, designated expert criteria), which is IANA registry guidance.
IANA.quote: This specification creates a new top-level IANA registry named "Content Security Policy Directives".

rejected.why: CSP is delivered via HTTP headers, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
ABNF is used only to give the directive-name syntax, so the document is not about it.
CSP controls resources fetched by pages, but the document does not define HTML or hypertext formats.

gaps.name: Content Security Policy (CSP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CSP itself. The nearest fit is the web security topic, which only broadly covers it.

RFC7763.title: The text/markdown Media Type
RFC7763.summary: Registers the text/markdown media type with charset and variant parameters, fragment identifiers, a preview-type Content-Disposition parameter, and a Markdown Variants IANA registry.

Markdown.why: The whole document defines the media type for Markdown, its variants, fragment identifiers and variant registry. Readers of the Markdown subject would want it.
Markdown.quote: This document registers the text/markdown media type for use with Markdown, a family of plain-text formatting syntaxes

media types.why: A substantial part is a formal media type registration template, with parameters such as charset and variant.
media types.quote: This section provides the media type registration application for the text/markdown media type (see Section 5.6 of [RFC6838]).

rejected.why: HTML is only a common output target of Markdown processing. The document does not specify it.
MIME is the substrate. The Content-Disposition preview-type parameter is minor, and media type registration is covered by the media types tag.
Fragment identifiers are defined (the line parameter), but that is a small part of the document and relies on existing URI syntax.
The new Markdown Variants registry is boilerplate-level IANA work, not the document's main subject.
Email attachment appears only in an example.

gaps.name: Markdown
gaps.why: The taxonomy's data formats branch has a 'Markdown text formats' tag. The id I used appears in the taxonomy as 'Markdown', so no gap exists. This entry is noted only for completeness.

RFC7764.title: Guidance on Markdown: Design Philosophies, Stability Strategies, and Select Registrations
RFC7764.summary: Informational companion to RFC 7763 that explains Markdown's design philosophy, gives strategies for preserving the text/markdown media type and variant parameters in local storage and version control, and registers several Markdown variants (MultiMarkdown, GFM, Pandoc, Fountain, CommonMark, kramdown-rfc2629, Pandoc2rfc, Markdown Extra).

media types.why: The document elaborates on the text/markdown media type, its variant and charset parameters, and how to preserve them. It also registers syntaxes in the Markdown Variants registry.
media types.quote: This document serves as an informational companion to [RFC7763], the text/markdown media type registration.

Markdown.why: The document covers Markdown's design philosophy, uses and variants. The taxonomy's Markdown tag ('Markdown text formats') fits it directly.
Markdown.quote: Markdown, the subject of this document, is an /informal/ plain-text formatting syntax

rejected.why: HTML is only mentioned as a formal markup language that Markdown can be converted to. The document is not about it.
XML appears as a contrast to Markdown and as the output of the kramdown-rfc2629 and Pandoc2rfc converters, so it is not a subject of the document.
The MIME headers and message/global-headers are used as storage strategies, but the document is not about MIME itself.
The kramdown-rfc2629 and Pandoc2rfc registrations produce xml2rfc input, but this document does not describe the RFC XML vocabulary.
The IANA section only records registrations in the Markdown Variants registry. The main body is not about IANA registries in general.

RFC7765.title: TCP and Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) RTO Restart
RFC7765.summary: Experimental RFC specifying RTO Restart (RTOR), a sender-side modification to TCP and SCTP retransmission timer management that restarts the timer with a reduced timeout for faster loss recovery when little data is outstanding, plus an SCTP socket option to control it.

TCP.why: The document modifies TCP's retransmission timer management (updating RFC 6298) and describes its implementation for TCP, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: This document specifies an OPTIONAL sender-only modification to TCP and SCTP, which updates step 5.3 in Section 5 of [RFC6298]

SCTP.why: The algorithm applies equally to SCTP, and the document defines an SCTP socket option (SCTP_RTO_RESTART) to control it.
SCTP.quote: a similar update in Section 6.3.2 of [RFC4960] for SCTP

sockets API.why: Section 7 defines a new SCTP socket option, extending the sockets API.
sockets API.quote: This section describes how the socket API for SCTP defined in [RFC6458] is extended to control the usage of RTO restart for SCTP.

rejected.why: The document touches on congestion window effects of timeouts, but its subject is loss detection and recovery timers, not congestion control.
Web applications are cited only as motivating traffic examples, not as something the document addresses.
Related loss-recovery mechanisms such as early retransmit and TLP are only discussed as related work.

gaps.name: TCP loss recovery / retransmission timer
gaps.why: The document is about TCP and SCTP loss detection and RTO timer management, which has no specific taxonomy tag. The closest fits are the TCP and SCTP tags.

RFC7766.title: DNS Transport over TCP - Implementation Requirements
RFC7766.summary: RFC 7766 makes TCP support mandatory for general-purpose DNS implementations and gives guidance on DNS-over-TCP connection reuse, pipelining, idle timeouts, response reordering, and message length handling.

DNS.why: The document updates core DNS specifications (RFC 1035, RFC 1123) to require TCP for resolvers and servers, and gives DNS implementation and operational guidance.
DNS.quote: All general-purpose DNS implementations MUST support both UDP and TCP transport.

TCP.why: A large part of the document covers TCP connection management for DNS: concurrent connections, idle timeouts, teardown, the length field, and TCP Fast Open. Readers interested in TCP usage by applications would want it.
TCP.quote: To amortise connection setup costs, both clients and servers SHOULD support connection reuse by sending multiple queries and responses over a single persistent TCP connection.

rejected.why: This is a close fit, since the document is about carrying DNS over TCP. But the DNS tag already covers it, and the document is about requirements and operational behaviour rather than defining a new binding.
DNS over TLS is only mentioned as motivation and in the TFO discussion. The document does not specify it.
EDNS0 and edns-tcp-keepalive are referenced as background and for idle-timeout signalling, but the document does not specify them.
DNSSEC is cited only as a cause of larger responses that drive TCP use.
UDP is the comparison transport, not the subject of the document.
DoS mitigation for TCP-enabled servers appears only briefly in the Security Considerations and in the server-practices discussion.

RFC7767.title: Application-Initiated Check-Pointing via the Port Control Protocol (PCP)
RFC7767.summary: Defines a new PCP option, CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED, that lets a PCP client tell a PCP-controlled device which MAP/PEER mappings should be check-pointed to a backup system for high availability.

PCP.why: The document defines a new PCP option (code 192) for MAP and PEER messages and specifies client and server behaviour for it.
PCP.quote: This document specifies how PCP [RFC6887] can be extended to indicate which connection should be check-pointed for high availability

rejected.why: PCP-controlled devices are often NATs or firewalls, but the document makes no assumptions about the device and does not address NAT behaviour.
The option code allocation is boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the subject of the document.
Not rejected; listed as primary tag.
HA and check-pointing are mentioned, but the document specifies a PCP signalling option and not a management architecture.
RFC 7149 is cited only as an alignment with open network APIs; the document is not about SDN.

gaps.name: high availability / state check-pointing
gaps.why: The document is about signalling which connection state should be replicated to a backup device for failover, and the taxonomy has no tag for high availability or stateful failover.

RFC7768.title: Port Management to Reduce Logging in Large-Scale NATs
RFC7768.summary: Informational RFC proposing that large-scale NATs (AFTR/DS-Lite, NAT64) allocate ports to subscribers in blocks and log only block allocation/deallocation, reducing log volume while preserving traceability, with discussion of port-guessing security tradeoffs.

CGN.why: The document specifies a port-block allocation and logging policy for large-scale/carrier-grade NATs, responding to RFC 6888 requirements REQ-13 and REQ-14.
CGN.quote: ports are allocated to the user in blocks. Logs are generated only when blocks are allocated or deallocated.

rejected.why: DS-Lite/AFTR is named as an example of a large-scale NAT, but the document does not specify or extend DS-Lite itself.
NAT64 is mentioned as an example deployment; the document is generic to large-scale NATs, not about NAT64 mechanics.
Logging is discussed in the abstract, and syslog is only mentioned incidentally in the appendix config examples; the document is not about the syslog protocol.
The Security Considerations discuss port-guessing attacks, but this is a secondary aspect and the CGN tag covers the main subject.
Transition motivates the work, but the document is about port allocation and logging in the NAT, which the CGN tag covers.

RFC7769.title: Media Access Control (MAC) Address Withdrawal over Static Pseudowire
RFC7769.summary: Defines a PW OAM message carried in the pseudowire Associated Channel that signals MAC address withdrawal over statically provisioned pseudowires in VPLS/H-VPLS, with sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission.

VPLS.why: The document extends VPLS/H-VPLS MAC withdrawal (RFC 4762, RFC 7361) to static PWs, defining a new OAM message, sequence number TLV and sender/receiver procedures.
VPLS.quote: This document specifies a mechanism to signal Media Access Control (MAC) address withdrawal notification using a pseudowire (PW) Associated Channel (ACH).

pseudowire.why: The mechanism is built on static pseudowire in-band OAM signalling and the PW Associated Channel, with a new G-ACh channel type, so pseudowire readers would want it.
pseudowire.quote: In this document, we use a PW OAM message to withdraw MAC address(es) learned via a static PW.

rejected.why: LDP-based MAC withdrawal is the mechanism this document replaces for static PWs; LDP is only referenced as background and for the TLV registry.
MPLS is the substrate for the PWs; the document does not specify MPLS itself.
The message is PW OAM, but the document is about MAC withdrawal signalling, not OAM mechanisms in general; the pseudowire and VPLS tags cover it.
VPLS is the more specific child fitting this document.

RFC7770.title: Extensions to OSPF for Advertising Optional Router Capabilities
RFC7770.summary: Defines the OSPF Router Information (RI) LSA for OSPFv2 (Opaque LSA type 4) and OSPFv3 (function code 12), with informational and functional capability TLVs, multiple instances and flooding scopes, obsoleting RFC 4970.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with a new LSA and TLVs for advertising router capabilities.
OSPF.quote: This document proposes extensions to OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 for advertising optional router capabilities.

OSPFv3.why: A substantial part specifies the OSPFv3 RI LSA, with its function code, flooding bits and Instance ID usage.
OSPFv3.quote: The OSPFv3 Router Information LSA has a function code of 12 while the S1/S2 bits are dependent on the desired flooding scope

rejected.why: IANA registry updates are boilerplate-like and not the main subject.
TE support is only one capability bit referencing RFC 3630; the document is not about TE.
Not related; graceful restart and stub router are only listed capability bits.

RFC7771.title: Switching Provider Edge (S-PE) Protection for MPLS and MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Static Multi-Segment Pseudowires
RFC7771.summary: Updates RFC 6870 so redundant static MS-PWs, using RFC 6478 PW OAM status signaling instead of LDP, protect against S-PE failure, with an optional MPLS-TP Linear Protection (PSC) approach for PWs.

pseudowire.why: The document specifies redundancy and protection procedures for static single- and multi-segment pseudowires against S-PE failure.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes how to achieve this protection via redundant MS-PWs by updating the existing procedures in RFC 6870.

MPLS-TP.why: The optional approach extends MPLS-TP Linear Protection and the PSC protocol to protect PWs, and the document targets MPLS-TP environments.
MPLS-TP.quote: This appendix extends these RFCs to be applicable for PWs (SS-PW and MS-PW) as well.

rejected.why: LDP is explicitly not used for static PWs; the document only contrasts against it and notes LDP-based procedures are replaced.
MPLS LSPs are only the tunnels carrying PWs; tunnel protection is mentioned as existing and insufficient.
L2TPv3-based PWs are explicitly out of scope.
Protection switching here is PW-level redundancy, not traffic engineering.

RFC7772.title: Reducing Energy Consumption of Router Advertisements
RFC7772.summary: BCP recommending operational practices for routers and hosts (unicast solicited RAs, limiting multicast RA frequency, sleeping-host behaviour) to reduce the battery power cost of IPv6 Router Advertisements.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document is about the operation of IPv6 Router Advertisements and Router Solicitations from Neighbor Discovery: how often to send them, unicast versus multicast responses, and how hosts handle them while asleep.
neighbor discovery.quote: Routing information is communicated to IPv6 hosts by Router Advertisement (RA) messages [RFC4861].

energy management.why: The document's motivation and analysis concern the energy and battery cost of receiving RAs on battery-powered devices, including a power budget calculation. This fits energy management of networked devices.
energy management.quote: If these messages are sent too frequently, they can severely impact power consumption on battery-powered hosts.

rejected.why: IPv6 is implied as the parent of neighbor discovery. The document does not address IPv6 in general.
Renumbering is mentioned only as a reason some networks send frequent RAs. The document is not about renumbering procedures.
The Security Considerations section briefly mentions rogue RAs. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The concern is per-device battery life, not environmental impact of Internet infrastructure.

RFC7773.title: Authentication Context Certificate Extension
RFC7773.summary: Defines an X.509 certificate extension carrying authentication context about how the subject was authenticated to the CA, plus a SAML-based context information type mapping SAML attributes to certificate subject attributes.

X.509.why: The RFC defines a new X.509 certificate extension (AuthenticationContexts) with ASN.1 modules, extending the PKIX certificate profile.
X.509.quote: This document defines an extension to X.509 certificates.

federated authentication.why: A substantial part defines how SAML federation authentication context (IdP, level of assurance, attribute mappings) is carried into certificates.
federated authentication.quote: In a SAML federation, the subject presents a SAML assertion in exchange for a certificate that can be uniquely linked to information provided in the original SAML assertion

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding of the contextInfo payload and schema; the document is not about XML usage generally.
ASN.1 modules are just the formal syntax for the extension, not the subject.
Implied as the parent of X.509; not chosen separately.
Considered as a topic, but the federated authentication tag already fits more specifically.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
gaps.why: The document profiles SAML assertion information into certificates, but the taxonomy has no SAML tag; federated authentication is the closest.
