RFC7774.title: Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (MPL) Parameter Configuration Option for DHCPv6
RFC7774.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 option OPTION_MPL_PARAMETERS to distribute MPL (Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks) parameter sets to MPL Forwarders, with client, server, relay and forwarder behaviour.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option, including its format and client, server and relay behaviour, so it belongs on the DHCPv6 page.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines the OPTION_MPL_PARAMETERS DHCPv6 option.

multicast.why: The option configures MPL, a multicast forwarding protocol. MPL domains, domain addresses and Trickle timer parameters are central to the content. No MPL-specific tag exists, so the multicast topic is the closest fit.
multicast.quote: MPL has a set of parameters to control an MPL Domain.

rejected.why: MPL targets low-power lossy networks, but the document is not about 6LoWPAN or constrained link layers.
ROLL is only mentioned as the working-group context. The document does not specify or extend RPL.
The document covers constrained networks only indirectly. Its subject is a DHCPv6 option for MPL parameters.
The only IANA content is the option code assignment, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: MPL (Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks) / Trickle
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPL or the Trickle algorithm. Readers of those subjects would want this RFC, and only the broad multicast topic covers it.

RFC7775.title: IS-IS Route Preference for Extended IP and IPv6 Reachability
RFC7775.summary: Defines explicit IS-IS route preference rules for IPv4/IPv6 extended reachability TLVs (135, 235, 236, 237) and clarifies up/down bit handling in Level 2 LSPs, updating RFC 5308.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies IS-IS route preference and up/down bit semantics for extended IP and IPv6 reachability TLVs, so it belongs on the IS-IS page.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines explicit route preference rules for TLV 135, revises the route preference rules for TLV 236, and clarifies the usage of the up/down bit

rejected.why: The IPv6 Reachability TLVs are an IS-IS encoding; the document is about IS-IS route preference, not IPv6 itself.
The document is protocol-specific to IS-IS, so the IS-IS tag fits better than a general routing topic.
IS-IS is defined in ISO 10589, but the document does not deal with OSI network-layer coexistence with IP.

RFC7776.title: IETF Anti-Harassment Procedures
RFC7776.summary: BCP defining IETF procedures for handling harassment reports: the Ombudsteam's appointment, operation, remedies, appeals, conflicts of interest and confidentiality, updating RFC 2418 and RFC 7437.

IETF process.why: The document defines IETF administrative procedures: the Ombudsteam, remedies, appeals, and a recall-petition change to RFC 7437. These are IETF process and administration matters.
IETF process.quote: This document lays out procedures for managing and enforcing this policy.

rejected.why: NomCom and recall are mentioned only because the Ombudsteam may start a recall petition. The document does not set NomCom procedures.
The document is an RFC but says nothing about the RFC series itself.
Confidentiality here is about handling harassment cases, not protocol privacy.

gaps.name: IETF anti-harassment / code of conduct
gaps.why: The document is about behaviour policy and the Ombudsteam. The taxonomy has no code-of-conduct or community conduct tag, so it falls under the broader IETF process tag.

RFC7777.title: Advertising Node Administrative Tags in OSPF
RFC7777.summary: Defines a new OSPF Router Information LSA TLV (Node Admin Tag TLV, type 10) for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 that advertises 32-bit administrative tags grouping nodes for local policy, with example uses such as LFA policy, remote LFA, and explicit routing.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with a new RI LSA TLV, covering both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 and the procedures for processing it.
OSPF.quote: This document describes the protocol extensions to disseminate node administrative tags to the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 protocol.

IP fast reroute.why: Substantial application sections cover using tags to control LFA and remote LFA candidate selection, so IP fast reroute readers would want it.
IP fast reroute.quote: One of the proposed refinements is to be able to group the nodes in an IGP domain with administrative tags and engineer the LFA based on configured policies.

rejected.why: The extension applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equally via the RI LSA, so the general OSPF tag fits better than the v3-specific child.
TE path selection is only one example use case in the applications section, not the subject of the document.
MPLS TE tunnels appear only in an example use case.
BGP communities are mentioned only as an operational analogy.
YANG is mentioned only in Manageability Considerations as future model work.
IS-IS prefix tags are referenced only as an analogy.

RFC7778.title: Mobile Communication Congestion Exposure Scenario
RFC7778.summary: Informational ConEx WG memo describing how congestion exposure (ConEx) could be applied in 3GPP EPS/LTE-style mobile networks, covering use cases, deployment scenarios, function placement, and requirements.

ConEx.why: The whole document is about applying ConEx (congestion exposure) in mobile networks: use cases, policing/auditing placement, deployment scenarios and requirements.
ConEx.quote: This memo describes a mobile communications use case for congestion exposure (ConEx)

cellular.why: The scenario is specifically 3GPP EPS/LTE: eNB, S-GW, P-GW, GTP tunnelling, PCC, with an appendix overviewing EPS architecture.
cellular.quote: those mobile communication networks that are architecturally similar to the 3GPP Evolved Packet System (EPS)

rejected.why: ECN is discussed as a congestion notification mechanism that ConEx can complement, but the document is not about specifying or profiling ECN.
The ConEx tag is more specific and already covers this. The document is about congestion exposure, not congestion control algorithms.
Existing 3GPP QoS and PCC mechanisms are described as background. ConEx is positioned as a supplement, not as a QoS architecture.
PMIPv6 and GTP are mentioned only as the tunnelling mechanisms ConEx must work with, not specified or extended here.
LEDBAT is mentioned only as an example scavenger transport that ConEx could incentivize.
Tunnelling is a requirement consideration for ConEx in GTP/PMIPv6, but the document is not about tunnelling in its own right.

RFC7779.title: Directional Airtime Metric Based on Packet Sequence Numbers for Optimized Link State Routing Version 2 (OLSRv2)
RFC7779.summary: Specifies the Directional Airtime (DAT) link metric for OLSRv2, computing incoming link cost from packet-loss (via RFC 5444 packet sequence numbers or HELLO timeouts) and link bitrate, feeding L_in_metric.

MANET.why: The document defines a link metric for OLSRv2, a MANET routing protocol. No OLSR-specific tag exists, so the MANET parent is the best fit.
MANET.quote: This document specifies a Directional Airtime (DAT) link metric for usage in Optimized Link State Routing version 2 (OLSRv2).

rejected.why: The metric extends the NHDP Link Set and uses HELLO messages as input, but it adds no new NHDP elements. NHDP is the substrate here.
DLEP is mentioned only as one possible external source of link bitrate. The document is not about it.
It measures packet loss to compute a routing metric, but the subject is routing metrics rather than measurement methodology.
The metric was designed and tested over IEEE 802.11, but the specification is not about IP over Wi-Fi.

gaps.name: OLSRv2 / OLSR
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OLSR or OLSRv2 (RFC 3626, RFC 7181), though the MANET OLSR tag, listed as OLSR, exists in the hierarchy. The document is specifically an OLSRv2 link metric extension.

gaps.name: Routing metrics (link-cost metrics such as ETX/ETT)
gaps.why: The document is about a routing link-cost metric. No tag covers routing metrics generally.

RFC7780.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Clarifications, Corrections, and Updates
RFC7780.summary: RFC 7780 collects clarifications, errata corrections and updates to the TRILL base protocol (RFC 6325) and to RFC 7177 and RFC 7179. It covers overload handling, distribution trees and RPF checks, MTU, E-L1FS flooding, header flag updates and the Appointed Forwarder counter.

TRILL.why: The whole document clarifies, corrects and updates the TRILL base protocol and related TRILL RFCs: overload, distribution trees, nicknames, header, adjacency and IS-IS use.
TRILL.quote: active development and deployment of TRILL have revealed errata in RFC 6325 and areas that could use clarifications or updates.

rejected.why: IS-IS is used heavily as the substrate for TRILL (E-L1FS, PDUs, TLVs) and is the base for TRILL's control plane. The document is about TRILL's use of it, not IS-IS itself. The taxonomy tag is also not clearly applicable.
TRILL runs over Ethernet and discusses MTU and CFI/DEI, but the document is about TRILL, not IP over Ethernet interworking or OAM.
BFD is mentioned only in the acronym list and in the Hello contents. It is not specified or extended here.
The IANA considerations section is boilerplate for registry actions and is not the main subject.
ECMP is mentioned only in passing, in the instruction to ignore the A and C bits in the hash.

RFC7781.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Pseudo-Nickname for Active-Active Access
RFC7781.summary: RFC 7781 specifies a TRILL active-active edge method in which a group of edge RBridges multiply attached to a CE via an LAALP is represented by a virtual RBridge with a pseudo-nickname, including auto-discovery, designated forwarder election, ingress nickname filtering, MAC synchronization and new IS-IS APPsub-TLVs.

TRILL.why: The document extends the TRILL protocol with a virtual RBridge and pseudo-nickname to support active-active edge access, including new TLVs and forwarding rules.
TRILL.quote: this document specifies a method for TRILL active-active access by such end stations.

rejected.why: IS-IS is only the substrate; the document defines TRILL APPsub-TLVs carried in E-L1FS FS-LSPs but does not specify IS-IS itself.
MC-LAG/DRNI (802.1AX) are the LAALPs the document interworks with, but their behaviour is not specified or extended here.
The document concerns TRILL edge behaviour for bridged end stations; it is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
SHA-256 is used only as a hash in the DF election algorithm.
Distribution trees and multi-destination handling are covered, but they are TRILL-internal and the approach is delegated to RFC 7783 rather than IP multicast routing.
Section 10 only gives a short note on pseudo-nickname use in OAM messages; it is not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) / RBridges
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tech tag listed only as a child of routing in the hierarchy, and no suitable ID matched the 'TRILL' identifier I used. The document is wholly about TRILL, so the tag id used should be confirmed against the taxonomy (it appears as 'TRILL').

RFC7782.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Active-Active Edge Using Multiple MAC Attachments
RFC7782.summary: Specifies how TRILL active-active edge RBridge group members ingress frames with their own nicknames, and how remote RBridges keep multiple MAC attachments via ESADI (Option B) or data-plane learning (Option A) to avoid MAC flip-flopping.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends TRILL with new APPsub-TLVs, capability flags and ESADI-based MAC attachment distribution for the active-active edge.
TRILL.quote: AAE member RBridges use their own nicknames to ingress frames into the TRILL campus.

rejected.why: MC-LAG/DRNI is the LAALP the AAE connects to, but the document specifies TRILL behaviour, not link aggregation itself.
The new APPsub-TLVs are carried in IS-IS FS-LSPs, but IS-IS is only the substrate and is not extended in its own right.
MAC learning and VLANs are involved, but the document is about TRILL campus edge behaviour, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Registry allocations are boilerplate here and not the main subject.

RFC7783.title: Coordinated Multicast Trees (CMT) for Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL)
RFC7783.summary: Specifies Coordinated Multicast Trees for TRILL, using the Affinity sub-TLV so edge RBridges representing a virtual RBridge can associate with multi-destination distribution trees, solving RPF check issues for active-active edge access; updates RFC 6325.

TRILL.why: The document extends and updates the TRILL base protocol's distribution tree calculation and RPF checks.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies required enhancements to build Coordinated Multicast Trees (CMT) within the TRILL campus to solve related RPF issues.

rejected.why: IS-IS only carries the Affinity sub-TLV as the control plane; the document is about TRILL tree construction, not IS-IS itself.
Multi-destination distribution trees are TRILL-internal, not IP multicast routing or group membership.
MC-LAG is the deployment context, but the document does not specify link aggregation behaviour.
Ethernet and VLANs are the edge environment, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tag only in the form 'TRILL' under routing, which I used above. I invented no id here; if that id is not valid in your taxonomy, the document's subject has no fitting tag.

RFC7784.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) MIB
RFC7784.summary: Defines the TRILL-OAM-MIB SMIv2 module, augmenting the IEEE 802.1ag CFM MIB with managed objects for TRILL OAM (path trace, multi-destination tree verification, flow configuration, fault alarms).

TRILL.why: The MIB manages TRILL OAM (RFC 7455 fault management) on RBridges: path trace, multi-destination tree verification, nicknames, and flows.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies the MIB for the OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) objects for IETF TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links).

MIB.why: The document's main content is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

OAM.why: It exposes OAM mechanisms (MEPs, CCM-style fault detection, Path Trace and MTV messages) for management, so OAM readers would want it.
OAM.quote: The TRILL OAM MIB module provides an overall framework for managing TRILL OAM.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines a module and does not specify or extend SNMP.
It builds on IEEE 802.1ag CFM MIB objects, but it covers TRILL OAM, not Ethernet OAM itself.
TRILL is a routing-bridge protocol, but the document is about its OAM MIB, not routing generally.
AES is mentioned only in the Security Considerations for SNMPv3 USM, which is boilerplate.

RFC7785.title: Recommendations for Prefix Binding in the Context of Softwire Dual-Stack Lite
RFC7785.summary: Informational document recommending that a DS-Lite AFTR bind per-subscriber policies and NAT/PCP state to the delegated IPv6 prefix (via a subscriber-mask) rather than the B4's individual IPv6 address, to handle B4 address changes and resource-exhaustion abuse.

DS-Lite.why: The whole document addresses DS-Lite AFTR/B4 operation and gives recommendations for deploying it, complementing RFC 6908.
DS-Lite.quote: This document discusses issues induced by the change of the Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) IPv6 address and sketches a set of recommendations

PCP.why: A recommendation concerns PCP ANNOUNCE and PCP mappings migrating when the B4 address changes; PCP mapping handling is a substantial part of the discussion.
PCP.quote: unsolicited PCP ANNOUNCE messages SHOULD be sent by the B4 element to internal hosts connected to the PCP-capable CPE

rejected.why: NAT behaviour (EIM/EIF, pooling) is discussed as context for AFTR state, but the document is about DS-Lite prefix binding; CGN/NAT readers are served via the DS-Lite tag.
The AFTR is a carrier-grade NAT and RFC 6888 is cited, but the document does not specify CGN requirements itself.
Renumbering effects are the motivating problem, but the document is not about site renumbering procedures in general.
DHCPv6 lease expiry is only mentioned as one cause of address change.
Privacy extensions/SLAAC addresses are mentioned only as a cause of B4 address change.
The parent is implied by the DS-Lite tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC7786.title: TCP Modifications for Congestion Exposure (ConEx)
RFC7786.summary: Experimental RFC specifying how a TCP sender is modified to signal ConEx (congestion exposure) markings (X, L, E, C flags) in IPv6 packets, including congestion counting from loss and ECN feedback and credit setting.

ConEx.why: The document specifies how senders count congestion and set ConEx flags (L, E, C, X), which is the core ConEx mechanism for TCP.
ConEx.quote: This document describes the necessary modifications to use ConEx with the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP).

TCP.why: It modifies TCP sender behaviour: loss detection, SACK use, spurious retransmission handling, DeliveredData accounting and slow-start credit.
TCP.quote: This section gives an overview of actions that need to be taken by a TCP sender modified to use ConEx signaling.

ECN.why: A substantial section covers counting CE marks from classic ECN and AccECN feedback, including an advanced compatibility mode for ECE/CWR.
ECN.quote: Congestion accounting for both classic ECN feedback and AccECN feedback is explained in detail in Section 3.2.

rejected.why: The ConEx markings are carried in the IPv6 Destination Option defined in RFC 7837. This document only uses it for marking, so IPv6 is not its subject.
The document is about exposing congestion to the network, not about changing congestion control algorithms. The specific ConEx tag already covers it.
AQM is mentioned only as an influence on how many packets are dropped or marked, and is not discussed in its own right.
NewReno and DCTCP appear only in the Security Considerations, as examples of sender responses to feedback.

RFC7787.title: Distributed Node Consensus Protocol
RFC7787.summary: Specifies DNCP, an abstract state synchronization protocol using Trickle and hash trees, with TLVs, optional keep-alives, and trust methods, to be combined with profiles into concrete protocols (used by Homenet).

home networking.why: DNCP was developed in the homenet WG as the synchronization basis for home network protocols. The document is a general-purpose protocol, though, and only mentions home automation in an example profile, so this tag is secondary.
home networking.quote: DNCP is useful for cases like autonomous bootstrapping, discovery, and negotiation of embedded network devices like routers.

security.why: A substantial section defines trust methods (PSK, PKI, certificate-based consensus with verdicts and bootstrap ceremonies) for DNCP. No narrower tag fits this trust-consensus mechanism, so the general security tag applies.
security.quote: The certificate-based consensus model is designed to be a compromise between trust management effort and flexibility.

rejected.why: TLS and DTLS are only the optional transport security that profiles may choose. The document defines nothing new about them.
Multicast is used for discovery and for sending Trickle status messages, but the document is not about multicast routing or group management.
UDP and TCP are possible transports left to the profile. The document does not specify or extend them.
DNCP is a generic state synchronization protocol and not a routing protocol. It only mentions use by routers.
X.509 certificates are only the object the trust verdicts refer to. The document does not profile them.
SHA-256 is only the recommended hash function a profile can pick, and the TLV carries its fingerprints. The document is not about SHA.

gaps.name: Trickle algorithm / distributed state synchronization
gaps.why: The document's core is Trickle-driven hash-tree state synchronization between nodes, and the taxonomy has no tag for it or for distributed consensus/state-sync protocols.

RFC7788.title: Home Networking Control Protocol
RFC7788.summary: Specifies HNCP, a DNCP-based profile and extension for IPv6 homenets that handles border discovery, prefix and address assignment, host configuration election, naming/service discovery, and managed PSKs for third-party protocols.

home networking.why: The whole document defines the home networking control protocol: border discovery, prefix assignment, naming, and router requirements for homenets.
home networking.quote: The Home Networking Control Protocol (HNCP) is designed to facilitate the sharing of state among home routers to fulfill the needs of the IPv6 homenet architecture

DHCPv6.why: HNCP defines DHCPv6 server election, DHCPv6-PD behaviour, DHCPv6-Data TLVs and user class based auto-detection; a substantial part of the document.
DHCPv6.quote: The elected router MUST provide prefix delegation services [RFC3633] on the given link (and follow the rules in Section 6.3.4); all other nodes MUST NOT.

DHCP.why: Defines DHCPv4 server election, HOMENET user class and DHCPv4-Data TLV use, which are substantial parts of the specification.
DHCP.quote: The elected router MUST provide DHCPv4 services on the given link; all other nodes MUST NOT.

DNS-SD.why: Defines delegated zones, node names, domain name and DNS-SD browse bits and an mDNS proxy election for multi-link naming and service discovery.
DNS-SD.quote: Network-wide naming and service discovery can greatly improve the user friendliness of a network.

rejected.why: HNCP is IPv6-centric, but the document is about home network control; the home networking tag is more specific.
Used only to secure HNCP unicast traffic; substrate security, not new DTLS content.
Only an elected mDNS proxy is mentioned briefly; the document does not specify mDNS itself.
Router Advertisements and SLAAC are used for host configuration but not specified or extended here.
Transport for HNCP only.
Used merely as the DNCP hash function in the profile.

gaps.name: DNCP (Distributed Node Consensus Protocol)
gaps.why: HNCP is defined as a profile of DNCP, and the taxonomy has no tag for this state-synchronization protocol.

RFC7789.title: Impact of BGP Filtering on Inter-Domain Routing Policies
RFC7789.summary: Informational document describing how filtering or selective propagation of more-specific BGP prefixes (locally or via remotely triggered communities) creates unexpected transit traffic flows in other ASes, and reviewing detection and mitigation techniques.

BGP.why: The whole document analyses the effects of BGP inter-domain policy and prefix filtering, and gives operator guidance on detecting and handling them.
BGP.quote: unexpected traffic flows can emerge across an autonomous system as the result of other autonomous systems filtering or restricting the propagation of more-specific prefixes

BGP communities.why: Remote filtering is achieved by tagging routes with communities to trigger selective propagation at a distant AS. This is a substantial scenario (Section 2.2).
BGP communities.quote: tagging a self-originated path with BGP communities defined by the distant AS

rejected.why: It is only mentioned as an example technology for exporting flow data when detecting unexpected flows. The document does not specify or extend it.
VRFs from RFC 4364 are suggested as one way to implement neighbor-specific forwarding. This is a mechanism used by the document, and the document is not about L3VPN.
The document touches on routing security issues, but it is mainly about routing policy side effects and operational traffic engineering, not security practice.
Deliberate rerouting is noted only in Security Considerations, and the document proposes no routing security mechanism.
Traffic engineering motivates the filtering, but the taxonomy node means packet and transport network TE such as MPLS, which this document does not cover. It concerns inter-domain BGP policy.

RFC7790.title: Mapping Characters for Classes of the Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings (PRECIS)
RFC7790.summary: Informational RFC giving PRECIS profile designers guidelines and additional mappings (delimiter, special, and locale/context-dependent local case mapping) to apply to internationalized strings beyond the PRECIS framework's case and width mappings.

PRECIS.why: The document extends the PRECIS framework with delimiter mapping, special mapping, and local case mapping for profile designers, so it belongs under PRECIS.
PRECIS.quote: This document provides guidelines for authors of protocol profiles of the PRECIS framework and describes several mappings that can be applied between receiving user input and passing permitted code points

rejected.why: IDNA and RFC 5895 are cited only as precedent and in the comparison table; the document is not about domain names.
It relies on Unicode SpecialCasing and CaseFolding data, but this is the substrate for the PRECIS mappings, not the subject.
The more specific PRECIS tag under it already applies, so the parent is implied.
EAP, IMAP ACL and LDAP appear only as examples in the mapping type table.
The document is about string mapping and case folding, not registering or using character sets.

RFC7791.title: Cloning the IKE Security Association in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC7791.summary: Defines an IKEv2 extension (CLONE_IKE_SA_SUPPORTED and CLONE_IKE_SA notifications) letting a peer derive a parallel IKE SA from an existing one without re-authentication, for use with MOBIKE multi-interface VPNs and cluster load balancing.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new notifications and a CREATE_CHILD_SA usage for cloning IKE SAs, so it belongs under IKE.
IKE.quote: The protocol described allows a peer to clone an IKEv2 SA, where an additional SA is derived from an existing one.

rejected.why: MOBIKE is used to move the cloned SAs (Appendix A) but is not specified or extended here. Cloning is stated to be independent of MOBIKE.
IPsec SAs are the context, but the document's subject is IKE SA management, so the more specific IKE tag fits.
EAP-SIM and EAP-TLS are mentioned only as examples of costly authentication that cloning avoids.

RFC7792.title: RSVP-TE Signaling Extensions in Support of Flexi-Grid Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) Networks
RFC7792.summary: Defines RSVP-TE signaling extensions (new SSON SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC C-Types carrying slot width, plus label usage) for GMPLS-controlled flexi-grid DWDM optical networks.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling for optical flexi-grid LSPs, so the GMPLS/optical network control page is the right home.
GMPLS.quote: extensions to the Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) signaling protocol to support Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in a GMPLS-controlled network

RSVP-TE.why: It specifies new RSVP-TE object C-Types and signaling procedures for flexi-grid LSPs, so it extends RSVP-TE.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines new Class Types (C-Types) for the SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects to carry Spectrum-Switched Optical Network (SSON) traffic parameters

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific tag; plain RSVP is only the base specification referenced for the object classes.
Routing and spectrum assignment is mentioned only as context for where the frequency slot is computed; PCE is not specified here.
RSVP-TE already sits under it, and the document does not address traffic engineering in general.
The manageability section only notes that diagnostic tools need updating; the document does not define OAM mechanisms.

gaps.name: Flexi-grid DWDM / optical spectrum switching (SSON)
gaps.why: The document is about signaling for flexible-grid optical networks, but the taxonomy has no tag for optical or WDM networks apart from GMPLS.

RFC7793.title: Adding 100.64.0.0/10 Prefixes to the IPv4 Locally-Served DNS Zones Registry
RFC7793.summary: BCP directing IANA to add the reverse DNS zones for 100.64.0.0/10 (Shared Address Space) to the IPv4 Locally-Served DNS Zones registry so that such reverse queries do not leak to the global DNS.

DNS.why: The document is about reverse DNS zones and how recursive nameservers should serve them locally. It adds entries to the locally-served DNS zones registry.
DNS.quote: This document directs the IANA to add the IPv4 reverse zones corresponding to 100.64.0.0/10

addressing.why: It concerns handling of the Shared Address Space 100.64.0.0/10 netblock, an IPv4 address allocation, and the DNS treatment of those addresses.
addressing.quote: Unlike the addresses described in [RFC1918], which are not expected to be seen by other parties, the addresses defined by [RFC6598] are expected to be seen

rejected.why: It mentions only that an insecure delegation is needed to break the chain of trust, in the IANA Considerations. DNSSEC is not the subject.
IANA actions are the mechanism for the change. The subject is DNS zone handling, not IANA registry guidance.
RFC 6598 shared address space exists for carrier-grade NAT, but this document does not address CGN behaviour.
The IPv4 address block is only the subject of the reverse zones. The document does not specify IPv4 itself.

RFC7794.title: IS-IS Prefix Attributes for Extended IPv4 and IPv6 Reachability
RFC7794.summary: Defines new IS-IS sub-TLVs for extended IPv4/IPv6 reachability TLVs: Prefix Attribute Flags (X, R, N) and IPv4/IPv6 Source Router ID, with an IANA registry for the flag bits.

IS-IS.why: The document extends the IS-IS protocol with new sub-TLVs for the extended reachability TLVs (135, 235, 236, 237), including leaking behaviour between levels.
IS-IS.quote: This document introduces new sub-TLVs to support advertisement of IPv4 and IPv6 prefix attribute flags and the source router ID of the router that originated a prefix advertisement.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a motivating use case for knowing whether a prefix is directly connected; the document does not specify segment routing.
IPv6 prefixes are advertised, but the document is about IS-IS TLV extensions, not IPv6 itself.
RLFA endpoint is only cited as an example use of node addresses.
TE router ID TLVs are referenced for consistency, but the document is not about traffic engineering.
The IANA section is boilerplate for registering the sub-TLVs and flag registry; the document is not about IANA practice.

RFC7795.title: Pseudowire Redundancy on the Switching Provider Edge (S-PE)
RFC7795.summary: Specifies how Switching Provider Edges (S-PEs) provide pseudowire redundancy in multi-segment pseudowires, reusing the Preferential Forwarding status bit signalling without changing T-PEs.

pseudowire.why: The whole document specifies S-PE operations for redundancy of multi-segment pseudowires, with scenarios and failure switchover behaviour. Pseudowire emulation is the subject of the pseudowire tag.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes some scenarios in which PW redundancy is provided on S-PEs and specifies the operations of the S-PEs.

rejected.why: LDP is used for pseudowire signalling (Label Mapping messages), but the document does not specify or extend LDP itself.
The MPLS infrastructure underlies pseudowires, but the document is not about MPLS architecture.
Failure detection is mentioned only as 'some detection mechanism'. BFD is not discussed.
The VCCV section is a short note on control channel types. It is not enough to make the document about OAM.

RFC7796.title: Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) Support in Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS)
RFC7796.summary: Specifies E-Tree support in VPLS using root/leaf VLANs carried over Ethernet pseudowires with a single Tree VSI, plus LDP and BGP signaling extensions for E-Tree capability and VLAN mapping negotiation.

VPLS.why: The document extends VPLS PE model, PW processing and signaling to support E-Tree services.
VPLS.quote: This document specifies a generic Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) solution, which uses VLANs to indicate root or leaf traffic to support Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) services.

LDP.why: Defines a new LDP PW interface parameter sub-TLV and status codes for E-Tree signaling.
LDP.quote: this document specifies a new interface parameter sub-TLV to provision an E-Tree service and negotiate the VLAN mapping function

BGP.why: Defines a new BGP extended community and processing rules for BGP VPLS.
BGP.quote: A new E-Tree extended community (0x800b) has been allocated by IANA for E-Tree signaling in BGP VPLS

Ethernet.why: Ethernet VLAN-based root/leaf mechanism and Ethernet pseudowire encapsulation interworking with IEEE 802.1Q bridges.
Ethernet.quote: The Ethernet PW SHOULD work in the tagged mode (PW type 0x0004) as described in [RFC4448]

rejected.why: Pseudowires are used as the transport; the document extends VPLS over them rather than defining pseudowire emulation itself, though it is a close call.
Not about EVPN; RFC 7387 framework mentions it but this document is VPLS only.
MPLS is the underlying network; document is about VPLS service-layer E-Tree.

RFC7797.title: JSON Web Signature (JWS) Unencoded Payload Option
RFC7797.summary: Defines the "b64" JWS header parameter that lets a JSON Web Signature payload be signed unencoded rather than base64url-encoded, with content restrictions, "crit" usage, and a rule that JWTs must not use it (updating RFC 7519).

JOSE.why: The document extends JWS, a core JOSE specification, with a new header parameter and changes to Signing Input computation.
JOSE.quote: This specification defines a means of accommodating these use cases by defining an option to change the JWS Signing Input computation to not base64url-encode the payload.

JWT.why: The document formally updates RFC 7519 by prohibiting JWTs from using the unencoded payload option, which JWT readers need to know.
JWT.quote: For interoperability reasons, JSON Web Tokens [JWT] MUST NOT use "b64" with a "false" value.

rejected.why: JSON serialization is the substrate JWS uses; the document is not about JSON formats themselves.
The document is about opting out of base64url encoding of the payload, but it does not specify or extend Base64.
The header parameter registration is boilerplate-level IANA considerations only.
UTF-8 is mentioned for payload restrictions but only as an encoding the document relies on.
HMAC is used only in examples, not addressed by the document.

RFC7798.title: RTP Payload Format for High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC)
RFC7798.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for carrying HEVC (H.265) video, including NAL unit packetization (single, aggregation, fragmentation, PACI), transmission modes, media type and SDP parameters, and RTCP feedback usage.

HEVC.why: The document's sole purpose is the HEVC RTP payload format; the taxonomy's HEVC tag explicitly covers HEVC and its RTP payload format.
HEVC.quote: This memo describes an RTP payload format for the video coding standard ITU-T Recommendation H.265 and ISO/IEC International Standard 23008-2

SDP.why: Section 7 defines a large set of SDP/fmtp parameters and detailed offer/answer and declarative usage rules for HEVC.
SDP.quote: Media type parameters to be used with the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566]

RTCP.why: Section 8 specifies how RTCP feedback messages (PLI, SLI, RPSI, FIR) apply to HEVC.
RTCP.quote: The following subsections define the use of the Picture Loss Indication (PLI), Slice Lost Indication (SLI), Reference Picture Selection Indication (RPSI), and Full Intra Request (FIR) feedback messages with HEVC.

media types.why: Registers the video/H265 media type with its full parameter set.
media types.quote: The media subtype for the HEVC codec is allocated from the IETF tree.

rejected.why: Fits conceptually, but HEVC is the more specific tag under codecs and already covers the HEVC RTP payload format, so RTP payload format is not listed separately.
RTP is the substrate; the document defines a payload format rather than extending RTP itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommended protection mechanism.
Used only as a comparison baseline; the document is not about H.264 or its payload format.
Section 10 is brief boilerplate-like guidance that defers to RTP congestion control.
RTSP appears only as an example of declarative SDP use.

RFC7799.title: Active and Passive Metrics and Methods (with Hybrid Types In-Between)
RFC7799.summary: Informational IPPM memo defining Active, Passive and Hybrid (Type I/II) performance metrics and methods of measurement, and dimensions for evaluating new measurement methods.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines the Active, Passive and Hybrid categories of performance metrics and methods and dimensions for evaluating them. This is squarely the performance measurement topic.
performance measurement.quote: This memo provides clear definitions for Active and Passive performance assessment.

rejected.why: RFC 7011 is cited only for the Observation Point definition and the notion of traffic flows. The document does not specify or extend IPFIX.
Section 4.4 briefly classifies Y.1731 OAM methods as Active or Hybrid. It is a short illustrative discussion, not a substantial part of the document.
The IPv6 PDM option is only discussed as an example of a Hybrid Type I method. The document is not about IPv6.
RFC 7594 is referenced only in Security Considerations. The document is not about LMAP platforms.
The document is about measurement of live networks and terminology. It does not cover device benchmarking methodology.

gaps.name: IP Performance Metrics (IPPM)
gaps.why: The document sits in the IPPM framework (RFC 2330, Type-P, spatial metrics). The taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic and no IPPM-specific tag.

RFC7800.title: Proof-of-Possession Key Semantics for JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)
RFC7800.summary: Defines the JWT "cnf" confirmation claim and its members (jwk, jwe, kid, jku) for declaring a proof-of-possession key held by a JWT presenter, and establishes the IANA JWT Confirmation Methods registry.

JWT.why: The document extends JWT with a new claim ('cnf') and a registry of confirmation methods, so it is squarely about JWT claim semantics.
JWT.quote: This specification describes how a JSON Web Token [JWT] can declare that the presenter of the JWT possesses a particular proof-of-possession (PoP) key

rejected.why: Uses JWK and JWE as representations for keys, but defines nothing new in JOSE itself; the new content is a JWT claim.
Developed in the OAuth WG and referenced by the OAuth PoP architecture, but the document does not specify OAuth protocol behavior.
TLS is only mentioned as one way a presenter can demonstrate key possession; it is not specified or extended here.
JSON is only the encoding of the claims; nothing about JSON itself is defined.
The registry creation is boilerplate-like apparatus supporting the claim; the document's body is not about IANA guidance.
The document is not about key establishment or provisioning; it only conveys key information in a token.

RFC7801.title: GOST R 34.12-2015: Block Cipher "Kuznyechik"
RFC7801.summary: RFC 7801 is an informational document reproducing the Russian GOST R 34.12-2015 "Kuznyechik" 128-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key: its substitution, linear transformation, key schedule, encryption and decryption, and test vectors.

GOST.why: The whole document specifies the Kuznyechik block cipher, one of the Russian GOST cryptographic algorithms, so readers of the GOST subject page would want it.
GOST.quote: the Russian Federal standard GOST R 34.12-2015 describing the block cipher with a block length of n=128 bits and a key length of k=256 bits

rejected.why: AES is a different block cipher. This document only has the same 128-bit block size, and it does not specify or discuss AES.
This parent topic is implied by the GOST tag. The document is about a specific child technology, so the parent is not listed separately.

RFC7802.title: A Pseudo-Random Function (PRF) for the Kerberos V Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Mechanism
RFC7802.summary: Defines the PRF+ construction for the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism's GSS_Pseudo_random(), based on the Kerberos V PRF, obsoleting RFC 4402 by fixing the counter start from 1 to 0 and including test vectors.

GSS-API.why: The document specifies the GSS_Pseudo_random() PRF for the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism, an extension of GSS-API and one of its mechanisms.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism's [RFC4121] pseudo-random function corresponding to [RFC4401].

Kerberos.why: The PRF is built on the Kerberos V cryptographic framework, keyed with Kerberos session and sub-session keys, with test vectors across Kerberos enctypes. Readers of Kerberos material would want it.
Kerberos.quote: The PRF+ function is a simple counter-based extension of the Kerberos V pseudo-random function [RFC3961] for the encryption type of the security context's keys

rejected.why: The PRF is used to key application protocols, but the document specifies a GSS-API PRF function, not a general key establishment or provisioning mechanism.
AES enctypes appear only in test vectors, as examples of Kerberos encryption types.
Single-DES enctypes are mentioned only in test vectors and a weakness note in Security Considerations.
HMAC underlies some enctype PRFs but is not discussed in the document body.
Camellia enctypes appear only in the test vectors.
rc4-hmac appears only as one of the enctypes in the test vectors.

RFC7803.title: Changing the Registration Policy for the NETCONF Capability URNs Registry
RFC7803.summary: A BCP that changes the IANA registration policy of the NETCONF Capability URNs registry from Standards Action to IETF Review, allowing well-reviewed Experimental RFCs to register capabilities.

IANA.why: The document's whole purpose is changing an IANA registry's registration policy, so it belongs under IANA registries and considerations guidance.
IANA.quote: IANA has changed the registration policy for the "Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) Capability URNs" registry to "IETF Review"

NETCONF.why: The registry belongs to NETCONF and the document updates RFC 6241, so NETCONF readers would want it. It does not change the protocol itself, so the role is secondary.
NETCONF.quote: The "Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) Capability URNs" registry [RFC6241] was set up with a registration policy of "Standards Action"

rejected.why: The capability URNs are the registry's entries, but the document does not define a URN namespace or discuss URN syntax.
The document touches on review requirements such as IETF Last Call and IESG evaluation. Its subject is a single registry policy, which the IANA tag covers more specifically.
NETCONF is related to YANG, but the document says nothing about data modelling.

RFC7804.title: Salted Challenge Response HTTP Authentication Mechanism
RFC7804.summary: Defines HTTP SCRAM, an adaptation of the SCRAM (RFC 5802) salted challenge-response mechanism as an HTTP authentication scheme (SCRAM-SHA-256, SCRAM-SHA-1), including one round-trip reauthentication and use of Authentication-Info.

HTTP authentication.why: The document specifies a new HTTP authentication scheme using WWW-Authenticate and Authorization header fields, and registers it in the HTTP Authentication Schemes registry.
HTTP authentication.quote: HTTP SCRAM is an HTTP Authentication mechanism whose client response (<credentials-scram>) and server challenge (<challenge-scram>) messages are text-based messages

rejected.why: SCRAM originates as a SASL mechanism (RFC 5802), but this document only adapts its data exchange to HTTP; SASL is not the subject.
TLS is the protecting channel assumed in the introduction and security considerations, not something the document defines or extends.
HMAC is a building block in the algorithm, not the subject of the document.
Hi() is described as essentially PBKDF2, but only as a component of the algorithm.
SHA-256 and SHA-1 are the hash functions used, but the document does not specify or analyse them.
The more specific child HTTP authentication fits; the document does not otherwise extend HTTP semantics.

gaps.name: SCRAM (Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SCRAM, which is the core subject here and in related SASL/TLS mechanism documents.

RFC7805.title: Moving Outdated TCP Extensions and TCP-Related Documents to Historic or Informational Status
RFC7805.summary: RFC 7805 reclassifies a set of outdated TCP specifications and TCP-related documents (RFCs 675, 721, 761, 813, 816, 879, 896, 1078, 6013 to Historic; 700, 794, 814, 817, 872, 889, 964, 1071 to Informational), updating the TCP roadmap RFC 7414.

TCP.why: The whole document is about the status of TCP specifications and extensions (TCPMUX, TCPCT, early TCP specs), so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: This document reclassifies several TCP extensions and TCP-related documents that either have been superseded, have never seen widespread use, or are no longer recommended for use

checksum.why: RFC 1071 on the Internet checksum is moved to Informational, but this is only one item among many, so the tag is secondary.
checksum.quote: "Computing the Internet Checksum", which lists a number of implementation techniques for efficiently computing the Internet checksum

rejected.why: The document changes RFC statuses under BCP 9, but its subject is TCP documents, not the standards process itself.
It instructs status changes in the RFC database, but the content is about TCP specifications, not RFC series format or policy.
RFC 896 is mentioned only as one reclassified item, with no substantive treatment of congestion control.
The documents are old, but this RFC is an administrative reclassification, not a historical retrospective.

RFC7806.title: On Queuing, Marking, and Dropping
RFC7806.summary: Informational AQM-WG note arguing that queuing (fair queuing/scheduling) algorithms and mark/drop AQM algorithms (CoDel, PIE, RED, tail drop) should be specified, measured and compared separately, and surveying queue implementation approaches (round-robin, calendar queue, SFQ, DRR, Virtual Clock).

AQM.why: The document is about how queuing algorithms relate to AQM mark/drop algorithms such as CoDel, PIE and RED, and argues for decoupling them in specification and evaluation.
AQM.quote: This note discusses queuing and marking/dropping algorithms.

QoS.why: A large part of the document covers fair queuing and scheduling (GPS, WRR, calendar queues, SFQ, DRR, Virtual Clock) in a Diffserv context. These are QoS scheduling mechanisms, and no more specific tag fits them.
QoS.quote: the note specifically addresses queues that might be used in the Differentiated Services Architecture and are therefore at or below the IP layer.

rejected.why: CoDel is discussed only as one example of a mark/drop algorithm to combine with queuing. The document does not specify or analyse it.
PIE is only an example mark/drop algorithm, not the subject of the document.
ECN marking is mentioned as one of the signals sent to the sender, but the document does not address ECN itself.
The document borrows the Diffserv model and language and says its queues are those used in Diffserv. It does not specify or extend Diffserv.
Congestion signalling to senders is discussed only as a side effect of queuing and dropping. The document is about router queue behaviour, not about congestion control algorithms.
TCP appears only as an example of a sender that reacts to drops and marks, and in a historical aside about the Silly Window Syndrome.

gaps.name: Fair queuing / packet scheduling
gaps.why: Much of the document covers fair queuing, GPS approximations and scheduler implementations (WRR, calendar queue, SFQ, DRR, Virtual Clock). The taxonomy has no tag for packet scheduling or queuing disciplines, so QoS is only an approximate fit.

RFC7807.title: Problem Details for HTTP APIs
RFC7807.summary: Defines the "problem detail" JSON object (and XML equivalent) and the application/problem+json and application/problem+xml media types for carrying machine-readable error details in HTTP API responses.

HTTP APIs.why: The whole document is a convention for conveying errors in HTTP APIs, which is the subject of the HTTP APIs tag (problem details).
HTTP APIs.quote: define a "problem detail" as a way to carry machine-readable details of errors in a HTTP response to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs

media types.why: The document registers application/problem+json and application/problem+xml, and the media types are integral to how the format is identified and used.
media types.quote: This specification defines two new Internet media types [RFC6838].

rejected.why: JSON is the data model and serialization used, but the document is about the error format, not JSON itself.
The XML serialization is in an appendix as an equivalent format; it is secondary to the JSON model and the document is not about XML.
HTTP is the substrate; the document adds no new HTTP semantics beyond the API error-format convention, which is covered by the more specific HTTP APIs tag.
URIs are used as problem type and instance identifiers, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
HTML is mentioned only as the recommended documentation format for type URIs and in embedding examples.

RFC7808.title: Time Zone Data Distribution Service
RFC7808.summary: Defines the TZDIST protocol, an HTTP/JSON service for distributing time zone data and leap-second rules to clients such as calendaring applications, with discovery, synchronization, truncation and new iCalendar properties (TZUNTIL, TZID-ALIAS-OF).

time zones.why: The whole document specifies the service for distributing time zone data, which is the subject of the time zones tag.
time zones.quote: This document defines a time zone data distribution service that allows reliable, secure, and fast delivery of time zone data and leap-second rules

iCalendar.why: The document defines two new iCalendar properties (TZUNTIL, TZID-ALIAS-OF) for VTIMEZONE components and serves time zones in iCalendar, xCal and jCal formats.
iCalendar.quote: This specification introduces the "TZUNTIL" property for that purpose.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate for the service. The document defines actions on top of it but does not extend HTTP itself.
JSON is only the encoding for responses.
SRV and TXT records are used for discovery. This is a small part of the document and relies on existing DNS-SD.
TLS is a security mechanism the service relies on. The document defines nothing new about it.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate that supports the protocol. They are not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: time zones
gaps.why: The tag id used above does not appear in the taxonomy. It is the closest named subject, although the taxonomy only has a 'time zones' tech under calendaring, and time zone data distribution is the core topic here.

gaps.name: leap seconds
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for leap-second data or its distribution, which is a significant part of the service.

RFC7809.title: Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV (CalDAV): Time Zones by Reference
RFC7809.summary: RFC 7809 updates CalDAV (RFC 4791) so clients and servers can exchange iCalendar data without VTIMEZONE components by referencing time zones from an associated time zone distribution service, adding a capability flag, two WebDAV properties, an XML element and a CalDAV-Timezones header.

CalDAV.why: The document extends CalDAV with new server and client behaviour, properties, a report element and a header field.
CalDAV.quote: This document defines an update to the Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV (CalDAV) calendar access protocol (RFC 4791)

time zones.why: The document is about referencing standard time zone definitions via a time zone distribution service, instead of embedding VTIMEZONE data. It is a substantial part of the document.
time zones.quote: allows clients to access calendar data stored on a server in the iCalendar data format

rejected.why: iCalendar is the data format being exchanged. The document changes how VTIMEZONE is sent over CalDAV, not the format itself.
WebDAV supplies the property and REPORT mechanisms. The document extends CalDAV, not WebDAV.
HTTP is the substrate. The new CalDAV-Timezones header is specific to CalDAV, so tagging HTTP would be too broad.
XML is only the encoding for the new elements and properties.

RFC7810.title: IS-IS Traffic Engineering (TE) Metric Extensions
RFC7810.summary: Defines seven new IS-IS TE sub-TLVs (unidirectional link delay, min/max delay, delay variation, loss, residual/available/utilized bandwidth) to distribute network-performance data, with rules for thresholds, anomalous-bit signalling, and announcement suppression.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS by registering new sub-TLVs in the Extended Reachability TLVs and specifying their advertisement behaviour.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes extensions to IS-IS Traffic Engineering Extensions (RFC 5305) such that network-performance information can be distributed and collected in a scalable fashion.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is only mentioned as a consumer of the advertised data (CSPF path setup); the document does not specify or extend it.
The TE here is the IS-IS TE sub-TLV mechanism, already covered by the IS-IS tag. The document does not address traffic engineering in general.
Measuring performance is explicitly out of scope. The document only covers distributing the results.
ALTO is mentioned once as another possible consumer of the data, and the document does not address it.
GMPLS appears only as background that the sub-TLVs build on (RFC 4203) and as a reference for forwarding adjacencies.
MPLS LSPs are used as context for the Anomalous bit, but the document specifies IS-IS advertisements, not MPLS.

RFC7811.title: An Algorithm for Computing IP/LDP Fast Reroute Using Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT-FRR)
RFC7811.summary: Defines the MRT Lowpoint algorithm that computes a GADAG, MRT-Blue/MRT-Red next hops and fast-reroute alternates for MRT-FRR, including proxy-nodes and broadcast interfaces, with a Python reference implementation.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document specifies the algorithm for computing maximally redundant trees and alternates for IP/LDP fast reroute.
IP fast reroute.quote: defining the associated MRT Lowpoint algorithm that is used in the Default MRT Profile to compute both the necessary Maximally Redundant Trees

rejected.why: OSPF is only the source of metric and node ID values for interface ordering and the SPF pseudonode handling; the document does not specify OSPF.
IS-IS is only used for TLV field sources in interface ordering and pseudonodes; not what the document is about.
The more specific IP fast reroute tag fits; the architecture itself is in RFC 7812.
BFD is mentioned briefly as a way to detect broadcast failures, not a subject of the document.
LDP appears in the title as the fast-reroute context but the algorithm is IGP-topology based and does not specify LDP.

gaps.name: Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for MRT-FRR; IP fast reroute is the closest fit, but MRT-specific graph algorithms (GADAG, lowpoint) are not distinguished.

RFC7812.title: An Architecture for IP/LDP Fast Reroute Using Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT-FRR)
RFC7812.summary: Defines the architecture for IP and LDP Fast Reroute using Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT-FRR), giving link and node protection with 100% coverage, including forwarding options, MRT Islands, profiles, inter-area behavior and multihomed prefix handling.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document specifies an IP/LDP fast reroute architecture using MRTs, including alternates, PLR behavior and recalculation.
IP fast reroute.quote: This document defines the architecture for IP and LDP Fast Reroute using Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT-FRR).

LDP.why: Substantial parts cover MRT LDP label options, topology-scoped FECs, the Rainbow FEC and LDP signaling considerations for MRT.
LDP.quote: [RFC7307] provides a mechanism to distribute FEC-label bindings scoped to a given MPLS topology (represented by MPLS MT-ID).

rejected.why: OSPF and IS-IS are the IGPs MRT runs in; the document uses their exclusion mechanisms and area behavior but does not specify them.
Only used as the underlying IGP; Appendix A covers inter-level forwarding for MRT, not IS-IS itself.
MPLS labels are the forwarding substrate; the LDP tag covers the label-specific content.
IP tunnels are one MRT forwarding option, but are a mechanism rather than the document's subject.
The MRT Profile Identifier registry is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the main body.

gaps.name: Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT)
gaps.why: The specific MRT technology and its profiles have no taxonomy tag; IP fast reroute is the closest fit.

RFC7813.title: IS-IS Path Control and Reservation
RFC7813.summary: RFC 7813 defines five IS-IS sub-TLVs (Topology, Hop, Bandwidth Constraint, Bandwidth Assignment, Timestamp) for IEEE 802.1Qca Path Control and Reservation, enabling explicit tree control in Layer 2 networks and distribution of MRT GADAGs.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with new sub-TLVs carried in the MT-Capability TLV, so it belongs on the IS-IS page.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies five IS-IS sub-TLVs for the control of explicit trees by IS-IS PCR in a Layer 2 network

PCE.why: The document is written assuming a PCE or PCA computes explicit trees and injects them via IS-IS LSPs. It specifies this interaction in part, though not PCEP.
PCE.quote: explicit tree may be determined by a Path Computation Element (PCE) [RFC4655]

rejected.why: The document concerns Layer 2 bridged networks (802.1Qca/802.1aq), but it specifies IS-IS encodings and not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
MRT-FRR is only an application of the sub-TLVs, used to distribute the GADAG. The document does not specify IP/LDP fast reroute.
The TE-related attributes are reused from RFC 5305 and RFC 7810. The PCE tag already covers the explicit-path aspect.
PTP is used only as the epoch for the Timestamp sub-TLV.
MPLS appears only in the cited RFC titles. The document is not about MPLS.

gaps.name: Shortest Path Bridging / IEEE 802.1Qca Layer 2 bridging control
gaps.why: The document concerns IS-IS control of Layer 2 bridged forwarding trees (SPB, PCR). The taxonomy has no tag for bridging or SPB.

RFC7814.title: Virtual Subnet: A BGP/MPLS IP VPN-Based Subnet Extension Solution
RFC7814.summary: Informational RFC describing "Virtual Subnet", a BGP/MPLS IP VPN-based approach that extends subnets across data centers using host routes and ARP/ND proxy on PE routers, for Layer 3 network virtualization overlays and data-center interconnect.

L3VPN.why: The whole solution is built on BGP/MPLS IP VPN (RFC 4364/4659) with host routes in VRFs, applied to subnet extension; this is the core subject.
L3VPN.quote: This document describes a BGP/MPLS IP VPN-based subnet extension solution referred to as "Virtual Subnet"

data center networking.why: The document addresses data-center interconnect, VM migration, forwarding table and ARP/ND cache scalability, and flooding avoidance at data-centre scale.
data center networking.quote: which can be used for building Layer 3 network virtualization overlays within and/or between data centers

ARP.why: ARP/ND proxy behaviour on PE routers and host discovery via ARP is a substantial part of the mechanism.
ARP.quote: Acting as an ARP or ND proxy, a PE router should only respond to an ARP request or Neighbor Solicitation (NS) message

rejected.why: Multicast is handled by referencing RFC 6513 'without any change' in one short section; not a substantial part.
Mentioned only as a comparison point with suboptimal routing; the document is not about VPLS.
Used only to coordinate which PE proxies ARP and to share gateway MAC/IP; supporting detail.
Taxonomy tag is for data-plane encapsulations like VXLAN/Geneve/NVGRE; this is a BGP/MPLS L3 solution, not one of those.
BGP is the signalling substrate of the VPN, reused without change; no BGP protocol work.
Only recommended in Security Considerations for protecting inter-DC traffic.

RFC7815.title: Minimal Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) Initiator Implementation
RFC7815.summary: Describes a minimal, initiator-only IKEv2 implementation for constrained nodes, using shared-secret authentication and only IKE_SA_INIT/IKE_AUTH exchanges, with packet formats and optional raw public key support.

IKE.why: The whole document profiles IKEv2 for minimal initiators, covering exchanges, key derivation, payload formats and optimizations.
IKE.quote: This document describes a minimal initiator version of the Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) protocol for constrained nodes.

rejected.why: IKE is the child tag and fits more specifically; ESP/AH are only the Child SAs being negotiated.
Constrained nodes are the motivating use case, but the document is about IKEv2, not IoT architecture or guidance.
ESP SAs are negotiated by IKE but ESP itself is not specified here.
Certificates are deliberately omitted; raw public keys are only a brief optional appendix.
Parent of IKE-related topics; IKE under security is the more specific fit, and key derivation here is IKE-specific.

RFC7816.title: DNS Query Name Minimisation to Improve Privacy
RFC7816.summary: Experimental RFC describing QNAME minimisation, in which a DNS resolver sends only the minimum necessary name labels (using NS queries) to upstream authoritative servers to improve DNS privacy, including an algorithm, compatibility issues and performance trade-offs.

DNS.why: The document specifies a change in DNS resolver behaviour (query name minimisation), including zone cut discovery, NS queries, ENT handling and operational/performance impacts.
DNS.quote: QNAME minimisation", where the DNS resolver no longer sends the full original QNAME to the upstream name server.

privacy.why: The motivation is privacy: reducing data leaked to authoritative servers. The taxonomy's DNS privacy tag covers encrypted transport (DoH/DoT), which does not fit, so the general privacy topic applies.
privacy.quote: QNAME minimisation follows the principle explained in Section 6.1 of [RFC6973]: the less data you send out, the fewer privacy problems you have.

rejected.why: That tag covers encrypted and privacy-preserving DNS transport; this document is a unilateral resolver behaviour change, not a transport, and it explicitly contrasts itself with encryption.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in passing (validating resolvers already know zone cuts); the document is not about it.
No EDNS mechanism is used or defined.

RFC7817.title: Updated Transport Layer Security (TLS) Server Identity Check Procedure for Email-Related Protocols
RFC7817.summary: Defines a consistent TLS server certificate identity verification procedure (DNS-ID, SRV-ID, CN-ID, wildcards) for SMTP Submission, IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve clients, with checklists for CAs and mail providers, and updates RFCs 2595, 3207, 3501 and 5804.

TLS.why: The document specifies how clients verify server certificate identity during TLS negotiation for email protocols, which is TLS deployment guidance.
TLS.quote: This document describes the Transport Layer Security (TLS) server identity verification procedure for SMTP Submission, IMAP, POP, and ManageSieve clients.

X.509.why: Substantial parts profile certificate contents (DNS-ID, SRV-ID, CN-ID, wildcards) and CA issuance requirements for email server certificates.
X.509.quote: CAs MUST support issuance of server certificates with a DNS-ID identifier type (subjectAltName of dNSName type [RFC5280]).

email.why: Applies to the email submission, access and management protocols (SMTP Submission, IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve) and updates their specifications.
email.quote: it would be good to define modern and consistent rules for verifying email server identities using TLS.

rejected.why: Only the TLS identity check for Submission clients is updated; the document does not specify SMTP itself and explicitly excludes MTA-to-MTA.
IMAP is one of several protocols whose TLS identity check is updated; the document is not about IMAP itself.
Mentioned only as an optional way to derive reference identifiers securely.
Only mentioned as possible future work in Security Considerations.
DNS SRV is used for discovery but the document defines nothing about DNS.
ManageSieve RFC 5804 is updated only for its server identity check, not for Sieve itself.

RFC7818.title: URN Namespace for MEF Documents
RFC7818.summary: Registers the "mef" URN namespace identifier for MEF Forum, specifying its syntax, assignment via the MANN registry, and examples of URNs for YANG modules.

URN.why: The document registers a new URN namespace, which is exactly the subject of the URN tag (URN namespaces).
URN.quote: describes the Namespace Identifier (NID) "mef" for Uniform Resource Names (URNs) used to identify resources published by MEF Forum

rejected.why: The example URNs use a 'yang' sub-namespace, but the document does not define or discuss YANG modules.
MEF is a Carrier Ethernet forum, but the document concerns only URN registration, not Ethernet.
The IANA registry entry is boilerplate for the namespace registration; the document is not about IANA registries in general.

RFC7819.title: Privacy Considerations for DHCP
RFC7819.summary: Informational analysis of the identifiers carried in DHCP (IPv4) options, existing mechanisms such as DNS updates and address allocation strategies, and the resulting privacy attacks (device/OS discovery, location tracking, correlation, leasequery abuse).

DHCP.why: The whole document analyses DHCP options, identifiers, allocation strategies and leasequery for privacy implications, so DHCP readers would want it.
DHCP.quote: This document discusses the various identifiers used by DHCP and the potential privacy issues [RFC6973].

privacy.why: It is a protocol privacy analysis addressing pervasive monitoring, stable identifiers, correlation and location tracking, which fits the privacy subject area.
privacy.quote: This document in its entirety discusses privacy considerations in DHCP.

rejected.why: The focus is DHCPv4. DHCPv6 is mentioned only for comparison of allocation strategies and DUID.
DNS updates via the Client FQDN option are discussed as one privacy exposure, but only briefly in one subsection; the document is not about DNS update.
Location options are covered only as identifiers that leak location, not as location conveyance in their own right.
IPv6 privacy extensions are only referenced in passing.

RFC7820.title: UDP Checksum Complement in the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) and Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC7820.summary: Defines an experimental Checksum Complement, the last 2 octets of OWAMP/TWAMP test packet padding, so hardware timestamping engines can keep the UDP checksum correct after inserting timestamps, while staying interoperable with existing implementations.

OWAMP.why: The document extends OWAMP test packet handling with a Checksum Complement in the padding field.
OWAMP.quote: This document defines a similar concept for [OWAMP] and [TWAMP], allowing intermediate entities to update OWAMP/TWAMP test packets and maintain the correctness of the UDP Checksum

TWAMP.why: The document equally extends TWAMP sender and reflector test packets, specifying padding length requirements for TWAMP.
TWAMP.quote: In TWAMP test packets sent by the reflector to the sender.

checksum.why: The core mechanism is an incremental UDP checksum update via a complement field, which fits the Internet checksum subject.
checksum.quote: The term "Checksum Complement" is used throughout this document and refers to the 2 octets at the end of the UDP payload

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport; the document does not change UDP itself, only uses the checksum field.
IEEE 1588 PTP is mentioned only as a precedent for the same technique; it is not specified here.
RFC 7821 for NTP is only a cross-reference to a sibling document.
HMAC is mentioned only to note that it does not cover the timestamp or padding fields.
OWAMP and TWAMP tags already sit under this topic and cover it.
RFC 7717 is mentioned only as an alternate way to secure OWAMP/TWAMP.

RFC7821.title: UDP Checksum Complement in the Network Time Protocol (NTP)
RFC7821.summary: Defines an NTP extension field carrying a 2-octet UDP Checksum Complement so hardware timestamping engines can keep the UDP checksum correct after rewriting the transmit timestamp, for unauthenticated NTP packets.

NTP.why: The document defines a new NTP extension field type, its format, and its transmission, update and reception rules, so it is about extending NTP.
NTP.quote: This document proposes an extension field that includes a 2-octet Checksum Complement, allowing timestamping engines to reflect the checksum modification in the last 2 octets of the packet

checksum.why: The mechanism is an incremental update of the Internet checksum, with a worked checksum equation in Appendix A. Readers interested in checksum techniques would want it.
checksum.quote: It allows intermediate entities to update NTP packets and maintain the correctness of the UDP Checksum by modifying the last 2 octets of the packet

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport. The document works around its checksum field but does not specify or extend UDP.
PTP is mentioned only as a comparison, for Transparent Clocks and the Annex E mechanism. It is not the subject.
RFC 7820 is the sibling document for OWAMP and TWAMP. It is referenced here but not covered.
The document notes that UDP over IPv6 disallows a zero checksum, but it does nothing IPv6-specific.

RFC7822.title: Network Time Protocol Version 4 (NTPv4) Extension Fields
RFC7822.summary: RFC 7822 updates RFC 5905 to clarify NTPv4 extension field format, handling of unknown fields, and the rules for their use with and without Message Authentication Codes.

NTP.why: The document amends the NTPv4 specification (Section 7.5 of RFC 5905), defining extension field format, MAC relationships and unknown-field behaviour.
NTP.quote: A specification that defines a new extension field MUST specify whether the extension field requires a MAC or not.

rejected.why: MACs are discussed only as packet fields and their lengths. The document does not specify or analyse any MAC algorithm.
The Security Considerations mention DDoS amplification only briefly, and that section is boilerplate. The body is not about DDoS.
The only mention is a single middlebox filtering remark in Security Considerations. That is not enough for this subject.
NTP runs over UDP, but the document says nothing new about UDP. It only relates to RFC 7821 in passing.

RFC7823.title: Performance-Based Path Selection for Explicitly Routed Label Switched Paths (LSPs) Using TE Metric Extensions
RFC7823.summary: Informational RFC describing how a path computation function (ingress LSR or PCE) can use OSPF/IS-IS TE metric extensions (delay, jitter, loss, available bandwidth, anomalous bit) to select explicitly routed RSVP-TE LSPs, including stability considerations.

traffic engineering.why: The document is about performance-constrained TE path selection (CSPF with delay, loss, jitter constraints, make-before-break reoptimization). No more specific TE tech tag fits it better than the topic.
traffic engineering.quote: it is critical to consider network performance criteria when selecting the path for an explicitly routed RSVP-TE Label Switched Path (LSP)

RSVP-TE.why: The LSPs whose paths are selected are RSVP-TE LSPs, signaled with a strict ERO. The document covers path selection, and the RSVP-TE signaling itself is unchanged.
RSVP-TE.quote: The selected path may be signaled via RSVP- TE [RFC3209] [RFC3473]

PCE.why: The path computation function may be a PCE, and the document describes the computation done by it. PCEP is not specified here.
PCE.quote: whether in an ingress LSR or a PCE [RFC4655], can use that information for path selection for explicitly routed LSPs

rejected.why: OSPF TE metric extensions (RFC 7471) are consumed as input data and not defined or changed here.
IS-IS TE metric extensions (RFC 7810) are only the source of the link data, and this document does not specify them.
Segment routing is mentioned only as an alternative way to use the computed path.
The document uses advertised performance data but does not define measurement methods or metrics.
The LSPs are MPLS, but the document concerns TE path computation, which the traffic engineering and RSVP-TE tags cover.

RFC7824.title: Privacy Considerations for DHCPv6
RFC7824.summary: Informational analysis of the privacy issues arising from identifiers in DHCPv6 options and fields, existing mechanisms, and resulting attacks, with no solutions proposed.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document analyses DHCPv6 options, identifiers, allocation strategies and leasequery from a privacy perspective, so DHCPv6 readers would want it.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes the privacy issues associated with the use of DHCPv6 by Internet users.

privacy.why: It is a privacy threat analysis (fingerprinting, correlation, location tracking, pervasive monitoring) for a protocol, which fits the privacy topic.
privacy.quote: This document discusses the various identifiers used by DHCPv6 and the potential privacy issues [RFC6973].

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag and is chosen. DHCPv4 is mentioned only in passing.
The Client FQDN option with DNS UPDATE is discussed only as a privacy leak. The document does not specify or extend dynamic DNS updates.
IPv6 addressing is the context, but the document's subject is DHCPv6 identifiers and not IPv6 itself.
Location options are treated as sources of leaked information. The document does not address geolocation formats or conveyance in their own right.
DUID-UUID is mentioned only as one form of DUID.

RFC7825.title: A Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal Mechanism for Media Controlled by the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP)
RFC7825.summary: Defines ICE-RTSP, an adaptation of ICE using RTSP 2.0 as the signalling channel, with new Transport lower layer D-ICE, candidate/ufrag/password parameters, status codes, feature tag and SDP attribute, for NAT traversal of RTSP-controlled datagram media.

RTSP.why: The document extends RTSP 2.0 with new transport lower layer, Transport parameters, status codes 150/480, a PLAY_NOTIFY reason and a feature tag.
RTSP.quote: defines a solution for Network Address Translation (NAT) traversal for datagram-based media streams set up and controlled with the Real-Time Streaming Protocol version 2 (RTSP 2.0)

ICE.why: Specifies ICE-RTSP, a profile of ICE with differences from standard ICE (no ICE-Lite, high-reachability configuration, nomination rules, restart).
ICE.quote: It uses Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) adapted to use RTSP as a signaling channel, defining the necessary RTSP extensions and procedures.

rejected.why: Used for connectivity checks and keep-alives as part of ICE, but nothing new is defined about STUN itself.
NAT is the problem context, but the document is about the ICE-based traversal mechanism, covered by ICE/NAT traversal.
Only a new session-level attribute a=rtsp-ice-d-m is defined; SDP is a supporting substrate, not the subject.
RTP is the media carried; the document only combines it with D-ICE and recommends RTP/RTCP multiplexing.
Relayed candidates are mentioned only as ICE candidate types and fallback options.
TCP candidates are an optional ICE feature referenced from RFC 6544, not the document's subject.

gaps.name: RTSP (Real-Time Streaming Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists RTSP under streaming, but the id I used must exist exactly. If it does not match, the primary subject has no tag.

RFC7826.title: Real-Time Streaming Protocol Version 2.0
RFC7826.summary: RFC 7826 specifies RTSP 2.0, the application-layer protocol for setting up and controlling delivery of real-time streaming media, obsoleting RTSP 1.0 (RFC 2326).

RTSP.why: The document is the full specification of RTSP 2.0: methods, headers, status codes, state machine, proxies and caching.
RTSP.quote: This memo defines version 2.0 of the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP 2.0).

RTP.why: Appendix C normatively defines RTP usage with RTSP (RTP-Info, interleaving, RTP over TCP, timestamp handling), which RTP readers would want.
RTP.quote: This document specifies how media is delivered with RTP [RFC3550] over UDP [RFC768], TCP [RFC793], or the RTSP connection.

SDP.why: Appendix D normatively defines SDP usage for RTSP session descriptions (control URI, range, MTag attributes).
SDP.quote: This specification describes in Appendix D how one uses SDP [RFC4566] for describing the presentation.

rejected.why: TCP is only the mandatory transport for RTSP messages, not something the document specifies.
RTSP over TLS is used for the rtsps scheme but TLS itself is only a security substrate here.
RTSP caching is modelled on HTTP validators but is RTSP's own mechanism; HTTP is not the subject.
Digest authentication is reused by reference from HTTP; not defined or extended here.
Defines rtsp/rtsps/rtspu schemes, but this is a minor part of the document, not about URIs generally.
RTSP is a child of streaming and implies it, so the parent is not listed separately.

RFC7827.title: The Role of the IRTF Chair
RFC7827.summary: An IAB-stream informational RFC describing the role, duties (strategic, administrative, IAB membership) and ideal skill set of the IRTF Chair.

IETF process.why: The document describes the IRTF Chair's role and duties within the IETF/IRTF/IAB organisational structure, including RG chartering, IRSG, IESG review and IAB membership. This is organisational process and administration, which the IETF process topic covers (taxonomy has no IRTF-specific tag).
IETF process.quote: This document briefly describes the role of the Chair of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), discusses its duties, and outlines the skill set

rejected.why: The IRTF stream publication duties are mentioned only briefly; the document is not about RFC format or publication.
Implied as parent of IETF process; the document is about a specific organisational role, so the more specific child is chosen.
NomCom is mentioned only in passing regarding IAB members' appointment, not a subject of the document.
IPR appears only as an example of process questions the chair may be consulted on.

gaps.name: IRTF (Internet Research Task Force) and its role/chair
gaps.why: The document is about the IRTF Chair and the IRTF's research groups, IRSG and the Applied Networking Research Prize, but the taxonomy has no IRTF or IAB organisational tag; IETF process is only the closest fit.

RFC7828.title: The edns-tcp-keepalive EDNS0 Option
RFC7828.summary: Defines the edns-tcp-keepalive EDNS0 option (code 11) allowing DNS servers to signal idle timeouts for TCP connections, encouraging long-lived DNS-over-TCP sessions and describing client/server behaviour and session management.
