EDNS.why: The document defines a new EDNS0 option, including its format, option code and client/server handling, so it belongs under EDNS.
EDNS.quote: This document specifies a new EDNS0 [RFC6891] option, edns-tcp-keepalive, which can be used by DNS clients and servers to signal a willingness to keep an idle TCP session open

rejected.why: TCP is the transport whose idle connections are managed. The document defines no TCP extension; the option is carried in DNS messages.
The parent of EDNS, so it is implied by the EDNS tag. The document is about a specific EDNS option.
DNS over TLS is only mentioned as a complementary extension in the introduction. The document does not specify it.
DNSSEC is cited as a cause of larger responses and truncation. The document does not address signing or validation.
Anycast has a short considerations subsection, but the document is not about anycast operation.
The document does not define a binding of one protocol over another transport. It adds a signalling option for DNS over TCP.

RFC7829.title: SCTP-PF: A Quick Failover Algorithm for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC7829.summary: Specifies SCTP-PF, a quick failover algorithm adding a Potentially Failed path state to SCTP path management, plus a dormant-state procedure, Primary Path Switchover mode, and socket API extensions.

SCTP.why: The whole document extends SCTP path management, failover, dormant state and switchback behaviour, so SCTP is the subject.
SCTP.quote: This document specifies a quick failover algorithm and introduces the SCTP Potentially Failed (SCTP-PF) destination state in SCTP Path Management.

rejected.why: Section 7 extends the SCTP sockets API (RFC 6458) with new options, but it is informational and secondary to the SCTP sender-side algorithms.
Section 9 only recommends updating the SCTP-MIB; this is a brief note, not a substantial part of the document.
Multihoming is the context for the failover algorithm, but the document is about SCTP's path management, not IP-layer multihoming architectures such as Shim6.
CWND is mentioned in the switchback discussion, but the document does not specify congestion control.

RFC7830.title: The EDNS(0) Padding Option
RFC7830.summary: Specifies the EDNS(0) Padding option (code 12), letting DNS clients and servers pad messages by a variable number of octets to hamper size-based correlation of encrypted DNS traffic.

EDNS.why: The document defines a new EDNS(0) option, including its option code, format and usage rules for requestors and responders.
EDNS.quote: This document specifies the Extensions Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0)) "Padding" option, which allows DNS clients and servers to artificially increase the size of a DNS message

DNS privacy.why: The padding option exists to improve confidentiality of encrypted DNS transport by hiding message size. It is a DPRIVE work item. It is not specific to DoH, DoT or DoQ, so the parent topic fits.
DNS privacy.quote: metadata could still be used to correlate such messages with well-known unencrypted messages, hence jeopardizing some of the confidentiality gained by encryption.

rejected.why: The document says padding is only useful on encrypted transport and mentions TLS only in the Security Considerations. It does not specify DNS over TLS.
TLS is only the encryption substrate. The reference to disabling TLS compression appears in the Security Considerations.
The more specific EDNS tag covers this document, so the DNS parent is implied and not listed separately.
The option code assignment is routine IANA boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC7831.title: Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond Web (ABFAB) Architecture
RFC7831.summary: Informational architecture document for ABFAB, which federates authentication for non-web applications by combining GSS-API/SASL, EAP, RADIUS/AAA and SAML between client, relying party and identity provider.

federated authentication.why: The document's purpose is a cross-domain federated access architecture with IdPs, RPs and federation agreements.
federated authentication.quote: The architecture addresses the problem of federated access management to primarily non-web-based services, in a manner that will scale to large numbers of Identity Providers, Relying Parties, and federations.

GSS-API.why: GSS-EAP is the client-to-RP integration layer; Section 3 covers GSS-API channel binding, mutual authentication, host-based service names and per-message services.
GSS-API.quote: We have chosen to use a GSS-API mechanism that encapsulates EAP authentication.

EAP.why: EAP is the client-to-IdP mechanism; the document discusses EAP method requirements (TEAP) and EAP channel binding.
EAP.quote: ABFAB selected EAP for the purposes of mutual authentication and assisted in creating some new EAP channel-binding documents

RADIUS.why: RADIUS carries EAP and SAML between RP and IdP in the Federation Substrate; the architecture discusses its use, security and routing.
RADIUS.quote: The ABFAB working group has chosen the AAA framework for the messages transported between the RP and IdP.

privacy.why: A full section analyses privacy per RFC 6973 across entities, flows, data retention and user participation.
privacy.quote: ABFAB obviously requires careful consideration regarding privacy and the potential for privacy violations.

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy; SAML assertions are carried over RADIUS, but the SAML profile is defined in RFC 7833.
Mentioned as a future possibility; no Diameter profile is defined here.
Used as transport protection and channel-binding source only; nothing new defined about TLS.
GSS-API mechanism integrates with SASL applications, but SASL is only a means of integration, not a subject.
Considered; the more specific RADIUS tag fits, and AAA is the substrate for the federation.
Only mentioned in the introduction as another federated access technology.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
gaps.why: Assertions carrying client attributes from IdP to RP are a substantial part of the architecture, but the taxonomy has no SAML tag.

RFC7832.title: Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond Web (ABFAB) Use Cases
RFC7832.summary: Informational document listing use cases (cloud, HPC, grid, databases, streaming, printing, telecom, S/MIME ESS, smart objects) where ABFAB federated authentication would improve non-web access.

federated authentication.why: The whole document describes use cases for federated identity and authentication beyond the web, via ABFAB. This is the best-fitting tag.
federated authentication.quote: there is significant interest in the more general application of federated identity to include non-web use cases

rejected.why: SSH is only one example protocol where ABFAB could be applied. The document does not specify or extend it.
X.509 certificates are mentioned as the current approach in HPC and grid use cases. The document is not about them.
Section 3.8 is a single use case that touches S/MIME ESS access control. It is not a substantial part of the document.
ABFAB builds on EAP, but this use-case document does not discuss EAP.
Printing is one use case where IPP would gain federated authentication. IPP is not specified or extended here.
The document is about federated access but does not discuss AAA frameworks such as RADIUS or Diameter.

gaps.name: ABFAB (Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond Web)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ABFAB itself, which is the architecture this document and its working group are about.

RFC7833.title: A RADIUS Attribute, Binding, Profiles, Name Identifier Format, and Confirmation Methods for the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)
RFC7833.summary: Defines two RADIUS attributes (SAML-Assertion, SAML-Protocol), a SAML RADIUS binding, an NAI name identifier format, two RADIUS-State confirmation methods, and two SAML profiles (authentication and assertion query) for carrying SAML over RADIUS in the ABFAB architecture.

RADIUS.why: The document extends RADIUS with new Long Extended Type attributes (245.1, 245.2) and defines how Access-Request/Accept/Reject carry SAML messages.
RADIUS.quote: Two RADIUS attributes to encapsulate SAML Assertions and protocol messages, respectively.

federated authentication.why: It specifies SAML bindings, profiles, name identifier and confirmation methods for federated authentication between Relying Parties and Identity Providers in ABFAB.
federated authentication.quote: the goal of ABFAB is to extend the applicability of federated identity beyond the web to other applications by building on the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) framework

rejected.why: EAP is only mentioned as required by the ABFAB architecture; the document does not specify EAP or its methods.
Optional use of XML signatures is mentioned in short sections but is not a subject of the document.
TLS for RADIUS (RFC 6614) is only the recommended protection mechanism, not something specified here.
RADIUS is the more specific tag; the AAA framework is only the context.
The XML schema for metadata extensions is a supporting detail; XML is not the subject.
IANA registrations are boilerplate for this document.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is SAML bindings, profiles, name identifier formats, confirmation methods, and metadata extensions, but the taxonomy has no SAML tag; federated authentication is the nearest fit.

RFC7834.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Impact
RFC7834.summary: Informational document discussing the impact of deploying LISP on routing scalability, traffic engineering, IPv6 coexistence, multicast, and operations/business models, drawing on implementation and deployment experience.

LISP.why: The whole document analyses LISP's impact: scaling, mapping caches, resiliency, MTU, troubleshooting, and operations.
LISP.quote: we discuss the impact that the deployment of LISP can have on both the routing infrastructure and the end user.

traffic engineering.why: A dedicated section covers LISP inbound and outbound traffic engineering via priority and weight in mappings.
traffic engineering.quote: Traffic engineering in LISP thus allows the mapping owner to have a fine-grained control on the primary and backup path

rejected.why: Section 3 covers routing scalability, but LISP is the more specific tag and the topic is covered through it.
Section 4.2 is a short subsection on using LISP for IPv6 coexistence. It is not a main subject of the document.
Section 4.3 briefly summarizes LISP multicast and LISP-RE. It is a minor part of the document.
BGP is only used for comparison and for PxTR advertisements. The document is not about BGP.
DNS appears only as an analogy for the volume of signaling traffic.
The security section just points to RFC 7835, which is a separate document.

RFC7835.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Threat Analysis
RFC7835.summary: Informational threat analysis of LISP: defines an attacker model and threat categories, describes attack vectors against LISP data-plane features and mapping-system messages, and discusses mitigations.

LISP.why: The whole document analyses threats to LISP: gleaning, locator status bits, Map-Version, Map-Request/Reply/Register/Notify, interworking. Readers of the LISP subject need it.
LISP.quote: This document provides an assessment of the potential security threats for the current LISP specifications if LISP is deployed in the Internet

rejected.why: The threats are specific to LISP mapping and encapsulation rather than securing routing protocols in general; the LISP tag fits more specifically.
DoS and amplification are discussed as attack categories against LISP, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation or signalling.
Section 4 is only a short note on privacy and explicitly does not aim to identify privacy issues.
The general security topic is implied by the narrower LISP threat analysis; the document is not about security in general.
The document explicitly assumes a generic IP service and does not discuss IPv4 versus IPv6.

RFC7836.title: Guidelines on the Cryptographic Algorithms to Accompany the Usage of Standards GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012
RFC7836.summary: Specifies GOST R 34.10-2012/34.11-2012 accompanying algorithms: HMAC and PRFs for TLS and IKEv2, VKO key agreement, KDFs, key wrap, and elliptic curve parameter sets with test vectors.

GOST.why: The whole document defines GOST-based PRFs, VKO key agreement, KDFs, key wrap and curve parameters for use in IETF protocols.
GOST.quote: make the specifications of the cryptographic algorithms defined by the Russian national standards GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 available to the Internet community

elliptic curve.why: Section 5 and Appendix A define canonical and twisted Edwards curve parameter sets, and VKO is an elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman.
elliptic curve.quote: This section defines the elliptic curves parameters and object identifiers that are RECOMMENDED for usage with the signature and verification algorithms

key management.why: Defines key derivation, key agreement (VKO) and key wrap/unwrap functions, which are key establishment and provisioning.
key management.quote: The key derivation function KDF_TREE_GOSTR3411_2012_256 based on the HMAC_GOSTR3411_2012_256 function is given by

HMAC.why: Defines HMAC instantiations with GOST hash functions that underpin the PRFs and KDFs.
HMAC.quote: This section defines the HMAC transformations based on the GOST R 34.11-2012 [GOST3411-2012] algorithm.

rejected.why: Only the PRF is defined for use in TLS; the document does not specify TLS itself or a TLS extension.
Only defines PRFs usable in IKEv2's prf+; IKEv2 is a consumer, not the subject.
Parameters are shown as ASN.1 structures but only as encoding of curve parameters.
Signature algorithm GOST R 34.10-2012 is defined elsewhere (RFC 7091); this doc only supplies curve parameters and key agreement.

RFC7837.title: IPv6 Destination Option for Congestion Exposure (ConEx)
RFC7837.summary: Specifies an experimental IPv6 destination option (CDO) that carries ConEx congestion-exposure markings (X, L, E, C bits) from senders to ConEx-aware network nodes, with notes on router fast path, tunnels, IPsec and preferential drop.

ConEx.why: The document defines the ConEx wire encoding for IPv6, so it belongs on the ConEx page.
ConEx.quote: This document specifies an IPv6 destination option that is capable of carrying ConEx markings in IPv6 datagrams.

IPv6.why: It defines a new IPv6 destination option, including its layout, option type and extension-header processing, so readers of IPv6 would want it.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies an IPv6 destination option [RFC2460] that can be used for performing ConEx markings in IPv6 datagrams.

rejected.why: AH and ESP are discussed for compatibility and CDO placement, but the document does not specify or extend IPsec.
The E bit reports ECN congestion marks, but ECN is only an input signal and the document does not specify it.
TCP behaviour is delegated to RFC 7786; this document only mentions TCP as an example.
Diffserv PHBs are mentioned only in the optional preferential-drop section, which is not the document's subject.
Section 6 covers CDO handling at tunnel endpoints, but it is a minor part of the document and not a tunnelling specification.

RFC7838.title: HTTP Alternative Services
RFC7838.summary: Defines HTTP Alternative Services: the Alt-Svc header field, the HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame, the Alt-Used header, and use of 421 so an origin's resources can be served authoritatively from a different host, port or protocol.

HTTP.why: The document defines new HTTP header fields (Alt-Svc, Alt-Used), caching semantics for alternative services and endorses the 421 status code. This is an extension of HTTP semantics.
HTTP.quote: This document specifies "Alternative Services" for HTTP, which allow an origin's resources to be authoritatively available at a separate network location

HTTP/2.why: A full section defines a new HTTP/2 frame type (0xa), its payload and processing rules, and registers it in the HTTP/2 frame type registry. HTTP/2 readers need this.
HTTP/2.quote: The ALTSVC HTTP/2 frame ([RFC7540], Section 4) advertises the availability of an alternative service to an HTTP/2 client.

rejected.why: TLS is used for host authentication and SNI requirements but the document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
Alt-Svc freshness (ma, persist) is its own caching mechanism, explicitly independent of HTTP cache freshness, so this is not an HTTP caching document.
URIs and origins are referenced, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Security considerations discuss hijacking and downgrade risks, but this is boilerplate-level analysis rather than a web security mechanism like HSTS.
DNS CNAME/SRV are mentioned only as analogies for routing information.

RFC7839.title: Access-Network-Identifier Option in DHCP
RFC7839.summary: Defines new DHCPv4 relay agent sub-options and DHCPv6 options that let a relay agent convey access-network identifiers (access technology type, network name/SSID, access point name and BSSID, operator identifier and realm) to DHCP servers, e.g. for PMIPv6 MAG/LMA policy.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines six new DHCPv6 options (105-110) and specifies relay and server behaviour for them.
DHCPv6.quote: The Access-Network-Identifier options defined here may be added by the DHCPv6 relay agent in Relay-forward messages.

DHCP.why: The document defines new DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information sub-options (13-18) and the corresponding relay and server behaviour, so it extends DHCP itself.
DHCP.quote: Relay agents that include ANI information include one or more sub-options (see Section 4.1) in the Relay Agent Information option

rejected.why: PMIPv6 is the motivating use case. The document defines nothing in PMIPv6 itself; that is RFC 6757.
SSID and BSSID are carried as values, but the document is not about IP over 802.11.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the name fields.
The IANA section only records the code assignments, which is boilerplate.
IPsec appears only as a security recommendation in Security Considerations.
3GPP PLMN identifiers are only example values for the network name field.

RFC7840.title: A Routing Request Extension for the HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) Protocol
RFC7840.summary: Extends the HELD location protocol with a requestRoutingInformation element and routingInformation response so a LIS can return emergency PSAP routing URIs along with location, updating RFC 5985 and the emergency-calling BCP RFC 6881.

HELD.why: The document defines a new HELD request element and response element (XML schema extension), so it is an extension of HELD.
HELD.quote: This document specifies an extension to the HELD protocol, so that emergency routing information can be requested from the LIS at the same time that location information is requested.

emergency services.why: It provides emergency call routing to PSAPs and normatively updates the emergency calling BCP (RFC 6881) with new endpoint requirements.
emergency services.quote: The update requires devices and intermediaries using the HELD protocol to always include the HELD routing extension.

rejected.why: LoST is discussed as the alternative that this extension avoids; the document does not specify or extend it.
XML schema is only the encoding of the extension, not the subject.
HELD is already tagged and sits under geolocation, so the parent is implied.
SIP URIs appear only as example destinations; the document is not about SIP.
HELD runs over HTTP, but HTTP is only the substrate here.

RFC7841.title: RFC Streams, Headers, and Boilerplates
RFC7841.summary: IAB-stream RFC that obsoletes RFC 5741 and defines the fixed structural elements of RFCs (title page header, stream labelling, Status of This Memo boilerplate, copyright and ISSN), delegating exact text to an IAB web page.

RFC series.why: The whole document specifies RFC format elements, stream labelling in headers and the Status of This Memo boilerplate. That is the format and publication of the RFC Series.
RFC series.quote: RFC documents contain a number of fixed elements such as the title page header, standard boilerplates, and copyright/IPR statements.

rejected.why: It describes RFC streams and notes that non-IETF stream documents are not IETF-reviewed. The subject is RFC labelling, not the IETF standards process itself.
The copyright notice and BCP 78/79 references appear only as one structural element in boilerplate, and the legal content is defined elsewhere.
There is no IANA registry or considerations content; the document has no IANA section.
The document mentions more flexible output formats in the abstract but does not specify any XML vocabulary.

RFC7842.title: Requirements for Improvements to the IETF Email List Archiving, Web-Based Browsing, and Search Tool
RFC7842.summary: Informational memo listing requirements for improving the IETF mail archive web search and browsing tool (mailarch): thread view, navigation, UI, mobile support, no-JavaScript use and administration.

rejected.why: The tool archives and browses mailing-list messages, but the document specifies web UI requirements for the archive tool, not email protocols, transport, access or formats.
The archive covers IETF lists, but the document does not address mailing list protocols, headers or management; it is about the archive's web UI.
References/In-Reply-To headers are only used to derive thread navigation; the document does not specify message format.
Concerns a tooling improvement for the IETF community, not standards process or procedures.
A web application UI is described, but the document is not about web architecture or cross-protocol web matters.
Mentions JavaScript-free use and responsive UI only as tool features; no hypertext format is specified.

gaps.name: IETF mail archive tool / IETF tools requirements
gaps.why: The document is about requirements for IETF administrative tooling (mailarch search and browsing); the taxonomy has no tag for IETF tools or mailing-list archive services.

RFC7843.title: Port Control Protocol (PCP) Third-Party ID Option
RFC7843.summary: Defines the PCP THIRD_PARTY_ID option (code 13) and three new result codes, used with THIRD_PARTY to identify an internal host when its IP address alone is ambiguous, such as at an L2-aware carrier-grade NAT.

PCP.why: The document extends PCP with a new option, new result codes and client/server processing rules. It updates RFC 6887.
PCP.quote: This document describes a new Port Control Protocol (PCP) option called the THIRD_PARTY_ID option.

CGN.why: The option exists for L2-aware carrier-grade NATs with overlapping subscriber address space. Both target scenarios are built around a CGN, so CGN readers would want this RFC.
CGN.quote: there are CGN deployments that do not distinguish internal hosts by their IP address alone, but use further identifiers (IDs) for unique subscriber identification

rejected.why: CGN is the more specific tag and already covers the NAT context. PCP also sits under NAT, so it is implied.
HTTP(S) is only the subscriber-to-portal channel in one example scenario. Nothing about HTTP is specified.
The AAA server is only queried for tunnel IDs in the example scenarios. The document does not specify AAA.
L2TPv3 session IDs appear only as an example of an identifier encoding, not as a subject of the document.
Firewalls are mentioned once as a kind of PCP-controlled device. The document is not about firewall behaviour.

RFC7844.title: Anonymity Profiles for DHCP Clients
RFC7844.summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 client anonymity profiles that minimize identifying information in DHCP messages (identifiers, options, fingerprinting) for mobile clients using randomized link-layer addresses.

DHCPv6.why: A full section specifies DHCPv6 client behaviour (DUID, IA_NA, ORO, Confirm, FQDN) for anonymity. DHCPv6 is a child of DHCP, so it is chosen here.
DHCPv6.quote: The anonymity profiles provide guidelines on the composition of DHCP or DHCPv6 messages, designed to minimize disclosure of identifying information.

DHCP.why: The DHCPv4 profile specifies message composition, header fields and options for DISCOVER, REQUEST and other messages. DHCP is the parent of DHCPv6, but the DHCPv4 half is a distinct and substantial part of the document.
DHCP.quote: Clients using the DHCPv4 anonymity profile limit the disclosure of information by controlling the header parameters and by limiting the number and values of options.

privacy.why: The document is a privacy mitigation covering tracking, fingerprinting and identifier correlation threats. Readers of the privacy subject would want it.
privacy.quote: DHCP anonymity solves the more elaborate scenario in which someone monitors link-layer addresses and identities used in DHCP at the access point or DHCP server.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 and IPv6 addressing are discussed, but the document is about DHCP client behaviour, not IPv6 itself.
Wi-Fi MAC address randomization is motivating context only, and the document specifies nothing about 802.11.
Stateless address configuration is mentioned as preferred, but the document does not define or analyse it.
The Client FQDN and Host Name options touch DNS updates, but the document does not address DNS itself.
The PXE UUID/GUID option is only briefly discussed, and the document says it must not be sent.
RFC 4086 is cited for generating random values, but randomness requirements are not a subject of the document.

RFC7845.title: Ogg Encapsulation for the Opus Audio Codec
RFC7845.summary: Defines how Opus audio is encapsulated in an Ogg logical bitstream: packet organization, granule position, ID and comment headers, channel mapping, and the "opus" codecs parameter for Ogg media types (updating RFC 5334).

Ogg.why: The whole document specifies the Ogg encapsulation of Opus: header packets, granule position, channel mapping, and the Ogg Opus media type usage.
Ogg.quote: This document defines the encapsulation of Opus in a continuous, logical Ogg bitstream [RFC3533].

Opus.why: The document specifies how Opus packets, pre-skip, PLC gap repair and channel mapping are handled when stored in Ogg, so Opus readers need it.
Opus.quote: The IETF Opus codec is a low-latency audio codec optimized for both voice and general-purpose audio.

media types.why: It updates RFC 5334 for the Ogg media types and adds the .opus extension and the codecs parameter. This is a substantial part of the document, not just IANA boilerplate.
media types.quote: this document updates [RFC5334] to add "opus" as a codecs parameter value with char[8]: 'OpusHead' as Codec Identifier.

rejected.why: RFC 7587 is cited only for the channel mapping family 0 interpretation. The document is not about RTP.
The more specific Opus and Ogg tags cover this. The document does not define a general codec.
Vorbis comment format and channel order are borrowed and compared, but the document is not about Vorbis.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the comment strings, so it is a substrate.
The new Opus Channel Mapping Families registry is boilerplate-level and secondary to the encapsulation spec.

RFC7846.title: Peer-to-Peer Streaming Tracker Protocol (PPSTP)
RFC7846.summary: Specifies PPSTP version 1, an HTTP/JSON-based tracker-peer signalling protocol (CONNECT, FIND, STAT_REPORT) for peer-to-peer streaming swarms, with state machines, message formats, extension guidelines and IANA registries.

PPSP.why: The document is the PPSP Tracker Protocol specification itself.
PPSP.quote: specifies the base Peer-to-Peer Streaming Tracker Protocol (PPSTP) version 1, an application-layer control (signaling) protocol for the exchange of meta information between trackers and peers

RFC7847.title: Logical-Interface Support for IP Hosts with Multi-Access Support
RFC7847.summary: Informational document describing the host-side logical-interface construct (hiding multiple physical interfaces from the IP stack), its data structures, and how it supports multihoming, inter-technology handoff and flow mobility in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains.

PMIPv6.why: The document explains the host logical-interface behaviour needed for PMIPv6 features (multihoming, inter-technology handoff, flow mobility) and has a section on its use cases in PMIPv6.
PMIPv6.quote: Logical-interface support is required on the mobile node attached to a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain for leveraging various network-based mobility management features

rejected.why: Multihoming is discussed as one PMIPv6 use case, but the document is about the host logical-interface construct, not multihoming architectures in general.
The PMIPv6 child tag already covers this; the parent is implied.
IPsec VPN client is only mentioned as an example user of logical interfaces.
Mobile IP client is mentioned only as an example of logical interface use, not specified or analysed.
The Interfaces MIB and the YANG interface model are cited only to say logical interfaces are treated like any other interface.
3GPP/LTE access is used as example technologies, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: logical interface / host multi-access interface abstraction
gaps.why: The core subject is a host OS construct that groups physical interfaces under one IP interface; no taxonomy tag covers host interface abstraction or multi-access hosts.

RFC7848.title: Mark and Signed Mark Objects Mapping
RFC7848.summary: Defines XML formats (mark-1.0 and signedMark-1.0) for trademark marks and XML-signed marks used by domain registries during gTLD Sunrise Periods, for reference by EPP and the ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse.

domain registration.why: The document defines objects used in registry/registrar domain registration processes (Sunrise Period, Trademark Clearinghouse). No EPP-specific tag fits because it defines data objects, not an EPP mapping per se, so the parent topic is used.
domain registration.quote: This document describes the format of a mark and a digitally signed mark used by trademark holders for registering domain names during the Sunrise Period

XML signatures.why: A substantial part defines the signed mark as an XML-DSig enveloped signature with exclusive canonicalization and RSA-SHA256 algorithm guidance.
XML signatures.quote: The <smd:signedMark> is a digitally signed XML document using an XML Signature [XMLDSIG].

rejected.why: EPP is only mentioned as a protocol that can reference these objects; the document does not extend or map EPP itself.
XML Schema is the encoding substrate for the objects; the document is not about XML usage generally.
Base64 is used only as the encoding for the encodedSignedMark element.
An X.509 certificate appears in the signature example, but the PKI is defined elsewhere and the document is not about certificates.
A-labels are referenced in the label element but the document does not address IDNA.

gaps.name: Trademark Clearinghouse / Sunrise Period trademark data
gaps.why: The document is about trademark mark data and signed marks for gTLD rights protection; the taxonomy has no tag for trademark or rights protection mechanisms, only the general domain registration topic.

RFC7849.title: An IPv6 Profile for 3GPP Mobile Devices
RFC7849.summary: Informational profile of IPv6 features for 3GPP cellular hosts and cellular CE routers, extending RFC 7066 with IPv4 service continuity (CLAT/NAT64, PREFIX64 discovery), prefix delegation, ROHC, PCP and DNS64 recommendations.

cellular.why: The whole document is a profile of IPv6 requirements for devices attaching to 3GPP GPRS/EPS networks (PDP contexts, PCO, APNs, roaming).
cellular.quote: This document defines an IPv6 profile for mobile devices listing specifications produced by various Standards Developing Organizations (including 3GPP, IETF, and the Global System for Mobile Communications Association (GSMA)).

464XLAT.why: IPv4 service continuity over IPv6-only via CLAT/NAT64 is a central recommendation (C_REC#7, C_REC#8) and a main motivation of the profile.
464XLAT.quote: the cellular host should implement the CLAT [RFC6877] function in compliance with [RFC6052], [RFC6145], and [RFC6146].

DHCPv6.why: Prefix delegation is a stressed requirement (L_REC#2) for cellular devices with LAN capability.
DHCPv6.quote: The cellular device must support Prefix Delegation capabilities [RFC3633] and must support the Prefix Exclude Option for DHCPv6-based Prefix Delegation as defined in [RFC6603].
DHCPv6.section: 3. Recommendations for Cellular Devices with LAN Capabilities

PCP.why: A_REC#2 recommends PCP for battery savings and controlling NAT64/firewall, and C_REC#7 uses PCP for NAT64 prefix discovery.
PCP.quote: The cellular host should support PCP [RFC6887].

ROHC.why: A_REC#1 mandates ROHC profiles for VoLTE.
ROHC.quote: The cellular host must support the RObust Header Compression (ROHC) RTP Profile (0x0001) and the ROHC UDP Profile (0x0002) for IPv6 [RFC5795].

IPv6 transition.why: IPv6-only deployment with IPv4 service continuity (NAT64, DNS64, PREFIX64 learning) is the core transition theme; no more specific child fits wholly beyond 464XLAT.
IPv6 transition.quote: this document lists means to ensure IPv4 service over an IPv6-only connectivity given the adoption rate of this model by mobile operators.

rejected.why: A_REC#3 recommends host DNS64 in stub-resolver mode, but it is one brief item, not a main subject.
NAT64 is the network-side mechanism that CLAT relies on; the document does not specify it.
The more specific cellular and transition tags apply; the general IPv6 node requirements are inherited from RFC 6434.
Mentioned only as an example of a service capability and in an ABNF fix note.
Mentioned only as the reason for DNS64 on the host.
Referenced only in passing for the 3GPP link prefix.

RFC7850.title: Registering Values of the SDP 'proto' Field for Transporting RTP Media over TCP under Various RTP Profiles
RFC7850.summary: Registers seven new SDP 'proto' identifiers for carrying RTP/SRTP media (with AVPF/SAVPF profiles, DTLS-SRTP or TLS) over TCP using RFC 4571 framing, and notes ICE TCP framing.

SDP.why: The document's purpose is registering new SDP 'proto' field values in the SDP parameters registry.
SDP.quote: This specification describes the following new SDP transport protocol identifiers for transporting RTP Media over TCP

RTP.why: Defines how RTP profiles (AVPF, SAVPF) are realized over TCP, which RTP readers would want.
RTP.quote: The TCP/RTP/AVPF transport describes RTP media with RTCP-based feedback [RFC4585] over TCP.

SRTP.why: Several identifiers cover SRTP and DTLS-SRTP over TCP.
SRTP.quote: The TCP/DTLS/RTP/SAVP transport describes Secure RTP media [RFC3711] using Datagram Transport Layer Security SRTP (DTLS-SRTP) [RFC5764] over TCP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport substrate; no TCP behaviour is specified or extended.
TLS is used as a security mechanism via RFC 4572; nothing new is defined for TLS.
DTLS-SRTP is referenced per RFC 5764; no new DTLS content.
Only a brief section requires RFC 4571 framing for STUN in TCP ICE candidates; the document is not about ICE.
RTCP feedback profiles are only named in identifiers, not specified.
Considered since it carries RTP over TCP, but the document is more precisely about SDP identifier registration.

RFC7851.title: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Overlay Diagnostics
RFC7851.summary: Defines RELOAD extensions (an extended Ping and a new PathTrack method, plus error codes and diagnostic data structures) for collecting diagnostic and status information in P2P overlays.

P2PSIP.why: The document extends RELOAD, the P2PSIP overlay protocol, with new Ping extension, PathTrack method, error codes and IANA registries. P2PSIP covers RELOAD.
P2PSIP.quote: It defines extensions to the REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) base protocol to collect diagnostic information

OAM.why: The document is about overlay diagnostics: connectivity checks, fault localization and node status monitoring. This is OAM-style functionality for P2P overlays.
OAM.quote: This mechanism is modeled after the ping/ traceroute paradigm: ping [RFC792] is used for connectivity checks

rejected.why: The overlay is the subject matter, but the document specifies a RELOAD extension, so the more specific P2PSIP tag fits better.
ICMP is only referenced as the model for ping and as the source of underlay error messages that trigger error codes. The document does not specify it.
PathTrack is modeled on traceroute, but it is an overlay-layer RELOAD method, not the IP traceroute tool.
NTP is mentioned only as a way to synchronize clocks, which the document leaves to the implementation.
XML is used only for the overlay configuration authorization elements and the namespace registration. It is not the subject.
The IANA section registers flags, kinds, codes and a namespace. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: RELOAD
gaps.why: The document extends RELOAD, but the taxonomy has no dedicated RELOAD tag. P2PSIP, the closest, is used instead.

RFC7852.title: Additional Data Related to an Emergency Call
RFC7852.summary: Defines five XML data blocks (provider, service, device, subscriber, comment) and SIP Call-Info and PIDF-LO provided-by mechanisms for conveying additional data, by value or reference, with an emergency call to a PSAP.

emergency services.why: The whole document is about additional data accompanying emergency calls to PSAPs, which is the emergency services subject.
emergency services.quote: This document describes data structures and mechanisms to convey such data to the PSAP.

SIP.why: Extends SIP by defining a new Call-Info purpose value and by-value/by-reference carriage in SIP messages with CID URIs and Content-Disposition handling.
SIP.quote: This document adds a new compound token starting with the value 'EmergencyCallData' for the Call-Info 'purpose' parameter.

media types.why: Registers five new application/EmergencyCallData.*+xml media types and a registry of block types.
media types.quote: This document defines a set of XML schemas and MIME media types used for each block defined here.

vCard.why: Reuses xCard for provider and subscriber contact data, registers a new vCard TYPE value, and includes an xCard XML schema appendix.
vCard.quote: This document adds a new parameter value called 'main-number' to the 'TYPE' parameter of the 'tel' property.

geolocation.why: Defines a PIDF-LO provided-by namespace extension so access network providers can attach data to location objects.
geolocation.quote: the ability to embed additional data structures in the <provided-by> element of a PIDF-LO [RFC4119] is defined.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for the blocks and schemas, not the subject.
HELD is mentioned only as how the access network returns a PIDF-LO; nothing new is defined for it.
TLS is required for HTTPS dereferencing but only as a security mechanism.
HTTPS GET is just the retrieval substrate for by-reference blocks.
Privacy considerations are a boilerplate-style section and not the main subject, though they matter.
The registries are boilerplate-style IANA considerations for this specification.

gaps.name: Emergency calling additional data (EmergencyCallData blocks)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no emergency-services parent tag beyond LoST and eCall children; the tag chosen above may be missing from the taxonomy as a standalone topic, so this document's central subject lacks an exact fit.

gaps.name: vCard/xCard
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a vCard tag, but the document's use of it is secondary.

RFC7853.title: A URN Namespace for Globus
RFC7853.summary: Registers the "globus" URN namespace ID with IANA for naming persistent Globus identifiers (e.g., OAuth2 scopes and grants, service entities), using the RFC 3406 template.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration: it defines the NID, syntactic structure, assignment, persistence and uniqueness rules for urn:globus.
URN.quote: This document describes a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace to be used by Globus for naming persistent resources.

rejected.why: OAuth2 scopes and grants are only an intended use of the identifiers; the document does not specify or extend OAuth.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level (registering an NID); the document is about the namespace itself, not IANA registry guidance.
URN is the more specific child tag and fits; URI is implied as an ancestor.

RFC7854.title: BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP)
RFC7854.summary: Defines the BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP), by which a router sends BGP route views, peer up/down events, statistics and mirrored messages to a monitoring station over TCP.

BMP.why: The document specifies BMP in full: message formats, session lifecycle, route monitoring, mirroring and stats reports.
BMP.quote: This document defines the BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP), which can be used to monitor BGP sessions.

rejected.why: BGP is the protocol being monitored, not specified or extended here. BMP is its own child tag and is the better fit.
TCP is only the transport for BMP sessions.
It only borrows the sysDescr and sysName values from MIB-II for Information TLVs. It does not specify SNMP or a MIB.
It is only suggested in Security Considerations as a way to protect the transport.
The IANA registries are boilerplate for this protocol and do not make the document about IANA.
The Stats Reports are router counters about BGP activity, not network performance measurement.

RFC7855.title: Source Packet Routing in Networking (SPRING) Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC7855.summary: RFC 7855 gives the problem statement, use cases and requirements for the SPRING source packet routing architecture (unicast). It covers IGP-based MPLS tunnelling, fast reroute, traffic engineering and interoperability with non-SPRING nodes.

segment routing.why: The document is the SPRING problem statement and requirements. SPRING is the segment routing architecture, so the generic segment routing tag fits better than the SR-MPLS or SRv6 data-plane tags.
segment routing.quote: This document outlines various use cases, with their requirements, that need to be taken into account by the Source Packet Routing in Networking (SPRING) architecture for unicast traffic.

traffic engineering.why: A large part of the document covers TE use cases and requirements: dual-plane disjointness, egress peering, bandwidth admission control, capacity planning and the SDN controller use case.
traffic engineering.quote: The source-based routing model allows traffic engineering to be implemented without the need for a signaling component.

IP fast reroute.why: There is a dedicated use case section with FRR requirements: backup path precomputation, node and link protection, and micro-loop avoidance.
IP fast reroute.quote: support of Fast Reroute (FRR) on any topology

rejected.why: MPLS is one of the data planes discussed, but the document is a data-plane-agnostic requirements statement. It does not specify SR over MPLS.
IPv6 routing header use is mentioned only briefly and refers to a separate SRH draft. The document is not about SRv6.
MPLS is the substrate for the tunnelling use case, and the document is not about MPLS itself.
VPN, VPLS and VPWS are mentioned only as services tunnelled over the MPLS data plane. They are not the subject.
ECMP-awareness is one requirement among several and is covered as part of the TE discussion. It is not the document's subject.
The Manageability section only says that OAM must be defined and points to other documents.

RFC7856.title: Softwire Mesh Management Information Base (MIB)
RFC7856.summary: Defines the SOFTWIRE-MESH-MIB SMIv2 module with read-only objects for monitoring softwire mesh AFBRs: supported tunnel types, E-IP to I-IP encapsulation mappings, and BGP neighbours, extending the IP Tunnel MIB.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (SOFTWIRE-MESH-MIB) in SMIv2, with relationships to IF-MIB and the IP Tunnel MIB.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

softwire.why: The managed subject is the softwire mesh framework (IPv4/IPv6 tunnelling across the other family's backbone via AFBRs), so softwire readers would expect it.
softwire.quote: In particular, it defines objects for managing a softwire mesh [RFC5565].

rejected.why: MP-BGP is how the softwire mesh sets up tunnels, but the document only exposes BGP neighbour and tunnel info in a table. It doesn't specify or extend BGP.
SNMP is the access mechanism. The MIB module is the subject, and MIB is the more specific tag.
Tunnel types are listed and the IP Tunnel MIB is extended, but softwire already covers the tunnelling subject, and no generic tunnelling mechanism is defined.
GRE is only one of the tunnel types enumerated, not a subject of the document.
The softwire tag sits under this and is more specific.

RFC7857.title: Updates to Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements
RFC7857.summary: BCP that clarifies and updates NAT44 behavioral requirements from RFCs 4787, 5382 and 5508, covering TCP session tracking, port overlapping, address pooling, EIM/EIF, mapping refresh, port parity/randomization, IP ID and ICMP handling.

NAT.why: The whole document updates NAT behavioral requirements for NAT44 (mapping, filtering, timers, hairpinning), which is the core NAT subject.
NAT.quote: This document clarifies and updates several requirements of RFCs 4787, 5382, and 5508 based on operational and development experience.

rejected.why: CGN requirements are explicitly out of scope, deferred to RFC 6888; only mentioned in passing.
PCP is referenced only as a means to request port parity preservation; the document does not specify or extend it.
TCP state tracking is done from the NAT's perspective for applying timers; the document is about NAT behavior, not TCP protocol.
The TCP state machine and some behaviors are adapted from stateful NAT64 (RFC 6146), but the document focuses exclusively on NAT44.
ICMP query mapping timeout and hairpinning are handled as NAT behaviors, not ICMP protocol specification.
STUN is only cited as an example of an error response that should not refresh mappings.

RFC7858.title: Specification for DNS over Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC7858.summary: Specifies DNS over TLS (DoT) on TCP port 853 for stub-to-recursive privacy, defining two usage profiles (opportunistic and out-of-band key-pinned), connection management, and performance advice.

DoT.why: The document is the DoT specification: port 853, TLS handshake, session management, and usage profiles.
DoT.quote: This document describes the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) to provide privacy for DNS.

rejected.why: TLS is the security substrate; the document defines no new TLS extension, only how DNS uses it.
TCP is the transport; performance advice on TCP reuse is part of DoT operation, not about TCP itself.
Mentioned only to contrast with DoT; they are independent and DNSSEC is not specified here.
DNS over DTLS is only referenced as a separate proposal and the shared port reservation.
Only mentioned in design evolution (the dropped TLS OK bit) and padding references.

RFC7859.title: Identity-Based Signatures for Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Routing Protocols
RFC7859.summary: Experimental RFC extending the MANET ICV framework (RFC 7182) with two new cryptographic functions, ECCSI and ECCSI-ADDR, so that packets/messages in RFC 5444 format can carry identity-based signatures per RFC 6507.

MANET.why: The document defines new ICV cryptographic functions for securing MANET routing protocol packets and messages (NHDP, OLSRv2), so MANET readers would expect it.
MANET.quote: extends RFC 7182, which specifies a framework for (and specific examples of) Integrity Check Values (ICVs) for packets and messages using the generalized packet/message format

elliptic curve.why: The document specifies use of the ECCSI elliptic-curve identity-based signature algorithm, with curve selection and parameter derivation (N, n, hash size) in Section 4.2 and a worked P-256 example.
elliptic curve.quote: ECCSI is based on elliptic curve mathematics.

rejected.why: The document secures MANET routing protocol messages, but the MANET tag is more specific. The BGP-oriented RPKI and BGPsec children do not apply.
OLSRv2 is named as an expected user of the specification, but the document does not specify or modify OLSR.
NHDP is cited as a suitable protocol, and its HELLO message is used in the appendix example. The document does not specify NHDP.
ECDSA is only mentioned as a comparison for ECCSI and is not specified or profiled.
The KMS role is described, but the document is about signature ICVs rather than key establishment or provisioning.
SHA-256 is only a recommended hash function for use within ECCSI, not the subject of the document.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new code points and do not make the document about IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: Identity-Based Signatures (IBS) / ECCSI
gaps.why: The document's central subject is identity-based signature cryptography (ECCSI, RFC 6507), and the taxonomy has no identity-based cryptography tag. Only the generic elliptic curve tag partly covers it.

RFC7860.title: HMAC-SHA-2 Authentication Protocols in User-Based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3
RFC7860.summary: Defines four HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols (SHA-224/256/384/512 with truncated output) for SNMPv3's User-based Security Model, with a small MIB module of object identities; obsoletes RFC 7630 to fix the MODULE-IDENTITY value.

SNMP.why: The document extends SNMPv3 USM with new authentication protocols, including processing of outgoing and incoming messages and key localization. That is the SNMP framework's security.
SNMP.quote: This document specifies several authentication protocols based on the SHA-2 hash functions for the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3 defined in RFC 3414.

MIB.why: Section 8 defines the SNMP-USM-HMAC-SHA2-MIB module with object identities, and the revision exists to fix its MODULE-IDENTITY. MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

HMAC.why: The protocols are HMAC constructions over SHA-2 with specified truncation lengths. The security considerations analyse the HMAC key length, internal state size and truncation trade-offs.
HMAC.quote: use the SHA-2 hash functions (described in FIPS PUB 180-4 [SHA] and RFC 6234 [RFC6234]) in the HMAC mode

rejected.why: SHA-2 is the hash primitive used inside HMAC. The document defines no new SHA behaviour, so HMAC and SNMP are the better fits.
MD5 is mentioned only as the hash in the older HMAC-MD5-96 protocol, which this document contrasts with.
This generic topic is covered by the more specific SNMP and HMAC tags, so it is not tagged separately.
This is the parent of SNMP and MIB, so it is implied by those tags.

RFC7861.title: Remote Procedure Call (RPC) Security Version 3
RFC7861.summary: RFC 7861 specifies RPCSEC_GSS version 3, extending the RPC GSS-API security flavor with multi-principal authentication, security label assertions, structured privilege assertions, and simplified channel binding, and updates RFC 5403.

GSS-API.why: RPCSEC_GSS is the GSS-API-based security flavor for ONC RPC. The document specifies its third version, with new control procedures, a new reply verifier and new GSS context handle handling. It is the closest fit in the taxonomy.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies version 3 of the Remote Procedure Call (RPC) security protocol (RPCSEC_GSS).

ONC RPC.why: The protocol is an RPC authentication flavor. It defines new auth_stat values and control procedures, and uses XDR definitions. Readers of the ONC RPC subject would want it.
ONC RPC.quote: RPCSEC_GSSv3 is a superset of RPCSEC_GSSv2 [RFC5403], which in turn is a superset of RPCSEC_GSSv1 [RFC2203]

NFS.why: The design is driven by Labeled NFS and NFSv4.2 server-side copy. The structured privileges and label assertions are tied to RFC 7862, so NFS readers would expect it.
NFS.quote: A major motivation for version 3 of RPCSEC_GSS (RPCSEC_GSSv3) is to add support for multi-level (labeled) security and server-side copy for NFSv4.

rejected.why: Label assertions are one feature, but the document conveys labels of subjects only, and it defines no label format. It is about RPC security, not security labels as a subject.
Multi-principal authentication is part of the document, but GSS-API is the more specific fit and the document is about a protocol, not authentication across protocols.
XDR is only the notation used for the protocol definitions. There is no XDR tag, and the document is not about XDR.
The structured privilege assertions touch authorization, but the document only conveys them and leaves their policy to the application.

RFC7862.title: Network File System (NFS) Version 4 Minor Version 2 Protocol
RFC7862.summary: Specifies NFSv4.2, a minor-version extension of NFSv4.1 adding server-side copy/clone, I/O advise, sparse files, space reservation, application data blocks, Labeled NFS (MAC labels), and layout error/stats operations.

NFS.why: The document defines the NFSv4.2 protocol extensions and new operations.
NFS.quote: This document describes NFS version 4 minor version 2; it describes the protocol extensions made from NFS version 4 minor version 1.

rejected.why: RPC and RPCSEC_GSSv3 are the substrate used for security of server-to-server copy, defined in RFC 7861, not the subject here.
RPCSEC_GSSv3 privileges are used in the copy security section but are specified elsewhere.
Labeled NFS carries MAC labels, but the label registry is in RFC 7569; the document is about the NFS attribute, which NFS covers.
Only mentioned as an example alternative copy protocol.
Only mentioned as an example alternative copy protocol.

gaps.name: NFS (Network File System) / pNFS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no NFS tag. It does have ONC RPC and AFS under storage, but nothing for NFS itself; the tag id I used above is not in the taxonomy, so it should be corrected.

RFC7863.title: Network File System (NFS) Version 4 Minor Version 2 External Data Representation Standard (XDR) Description
RFC7863.summary: RFC 7863 supplies the machine-extractable XDR (RFC 4506) description of the NFSv4.2 protocol (RFC 7862), covering its types, attributes, operations, callbacks and RPC programs.

NFS.why: The whole document is the NFSv4.2 protocol's wire-format definition: operations, attributes, callbacks, errors, and the NFS4_PROGRAM RPC program.
NFS.quote: This document contains the External Data Representation (XDR) [RFC4506] description of the NFSv4.2 protocol [RFC7862].

rejected.why: XDR and RPC are only the encoding and substrate for NFS; the document defines NFS data types, not new RPC or XDR behavior.
RPCSEC_GSS and SSV GSS tokens appear in structures but the document is not about them; it only references them.
RDMA flags appear in a few fields only; incidental.
Not relevant; XDR is a different data description notation and is not a taxonomy tag here.

gaps.name: XDR (External Data Representation)
gaps.why: The document is written in XDR, but the taxonomy has XDR only as part of the ONC RPC tag. It is the notation used here, not the subject.

RFC7864.title: Proxy Mobile IPv6 Extensions to Support Flow Mobility
RFC7864.summary: Extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 (updating RFC 5213) so the LMA and MAGs can manage prefixes and forwarding policy to support network-based flow mobility across a mobile node's multiple physical interfaces, using FMI/FMA messages built on PMIPv6 Update Notifications.

PMIPv6.why: The whole document specifies extensions to Proxy Mobile IPv6: a new Handoff Indicator value, the off-link HNP flag, FMI/FMA messages, and the LMA flow mobility cache.
PMIPv6.quote: This document describes extensions to the PMIPv6 protocol that are required to support network-based flow mobility over multiple physical interfaces.

rejected.why: IPsec only secures the PMIPv6 signaling, as mandated by RFC 5213. That is boilerplate in Security Considerations, and the document defines nothing new about IPsec.
The flow-binding and multiple care-of address mechanisms from RFC 5648 and RFC 6089 are reused, but the document is about PMIPv6 and not Mobile IPv6 itself.
IPv6 is only the underlying network layer. The document is about mobility management, not IPv6 addressing or specification.
QoS paths are mentioned only as an optional reason for the MAG to receive flow-level information. They are not a subject of the document.

RFC7865.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Recording Metadata
RFC7865.summary: Defines the SIPREC recording metadata model, as seen by the Session Recording Server, and the XML format (application/rs-metadata+xml) that a Session Recording Client uses to send metadata about communication sessions, participants and media streams, plus a snapshot request.

SIPREC.why: The whole document specifies the metadata model and XML format used between SRC and SRS in SIP-based session recording.
SIPREC.quote: This document describes the metadata model as viewed by the Session Recording Server (SRS) and the recording metadata format.

rejected.why: SIP is the substrate; the document defines recording metadata, not SIP itself, and SIPREC is the more specific tag.
SDP label and content attributes are referenced to link metadata to streams, but SDP is not extended or specified here.
XML is only the encoding for the metadata; the schema is a means, not the subject.
The application/rs-metadata+xml type is mentioned but not registered here; IANA registers only an XML namespace and schema.
UUIDs are used to generate identifiers, which is a supporting detail.
Base64 only encodes the UUIDs.

RFC7866.title: Session Recording Protocol
RFC7866.summary: Specifies the SIPREC Session Recording Protocol: how an SRC uses SIP, SDP and RTP to establish a Recording Session to an SRS, deliver media and metadata, and give recording-aware UAs recording indication/preference via new SDP attributes.

SIPREC.why: The whole document is the SIPREC protocol specification: SRC/SRS procedures, metadata delivery, recording indication and preference.
SIPREC.quote: the Session Recording Protocol specifies the use of SIP, the Session Description Protocol (SDP), and RTP to establish a Recording Session (RS) between the Session Recording Client (SRC)

RTP.why: Section 8 is a substantial profile of RTP usage for recording: SSRC/CSRC/CNAME handling, translator/mixer/endpoint roles, and RTP session usage.
RTP.quote: This section provides recommendations and guidelines for RTP and the Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) in the context of SIPREC

SDP.why: Defines new SDP attributes 'record' and 'recordpref' and the offer/answer conventions for recording sessions.
SDP.quote: A new "record" SDP attribute is introduced to allow the SRC to indicate recording state to a recording-aware UA in a CS.

rejected.why: SIP is specified here only through SIPREC-specific extensions (option tags, feature tags), which the SIPREC tag covers more specifically.
SRTP is used and required for security, but the document defines nothing new about it.
TLS is only the security mechanism for the signaling in Security Considerations.
RTCP is discussed as part of the RTP handling guidance, but nothing new is defined for it; RTP covers that discussion.
ICE is only mentioned in passing for NAT bindings under persistent recording.
The metadata XML format is defined in RFC 7865, not in this document.

RFC7867.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for Loss Concealment Metrics for Video Applications
RFC7867.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR report block (BT=34) that reports video loss concealment metrics from RTP receivers, plus its SDP signalling parameter and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR block type with its format, fields and semantics, extending RTCP reporting.
RTCP.quote: This document defines a new RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of loss concealment metrics for video applications of RTP.

rejected.why: Section 5 only adds a new xr-format value to the existing rtcp-xr attribute. That is a small signalling hook, and SDP is not what the document is about.
RTP is the carrier of the media being measured. The document extends RTCP reporting and does not specify RTP itself.
SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect the reports.
IPTV is mentioned only as one example of where the block could be applied. The document is not about IPTV service delivery.
The metrics follow the Performance Metrics Framework and RTP monitoring guidelines. The tag was considered, but the specification is an RTCP XR block definition, and the RTCP tag already covers it.

gaps.name: RTCP XR (RTP Control Protocol Extended Reports) / RTP monitoring metrics
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists RTCP as a child of RTP, but the id I used, 'RTCP', does not appear in it exactly. The closest fit is the 'RTCP' tech under RTP, written as 'RTCP'. If that id is missing, an RTCP XR tag is needed for the many XR block RFCs.

RFC7868.title: Cisco's Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP)
RFC7868.summary: Describes Cisco's EIGRP routing protocol: the DUAL algorithm, packet types, reliable transport, neighbor discovery, metrics (classic and wide), and TLV packet formats for IPv4/IPv6.

EIGRP.why: The entire document specifies EIGRP: DUAL, packets, neighbor handling, metrics, and TLV formats.
EIGRP.quote: This document describes the protocol design and architecture for Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP).

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an example of redistribution into EIGRP and as an informative reference.
Only mentioned in the redistribution example.
EIGRP communities are modelled on BGP Extended Communities, but the document does not address BGP.
EIGRP carries IPv6 routes, but IPv6 is just one supported address family, not the subject.
IANA considerations section is boilerplate-like; it only records multicast addresses and protocol number 88.
The more specific EIGRP tag applies, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm)
gaps.why: Loop-free diffusing-computation routing algorithm central to the document; no taxonomy tag covers it beyond EIGRP.

RFC7869.title: The "vnc" URI Scheme
RFC7869.summary: Defines the "vnc" URI scheme for launching VNC (RFB) remote desktop clients, with parameters for connection, security type, SSH/TLS tunnel channels and host identity hash verification, plus IANA registries.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme, its syntax, parameters and processing rules, so readers of the URI subject would want it.
URI.quote: This document describes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme enabling the launch of VNC clients from other applications.

rejected.why: SSH is used as one tunnel channel type (Integrated SSH), but the document defines nothing new about the SSH protocol; it is a substrate.
TLS is used for the Secure Tunnel channel type, but the document does not extend or profile TLS itself.
Certificates are only mentioned for host identification alerts, not profiled.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax.
IANA registries are created, but that is boilerplate-like support for the scheme, not the document's subject.
MD5 and SHA are merely listed as hash algorithm choices for IdHash.

gaps.name: VNC / Remote Framebuffer (RFB) remote desktop
gaps.why: The document is about launching VNC remote desktop clients and RFB parameters, but the taxonomy has no tag for remote desktop or RFB protocols.

RFC7870.title: Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) Management Information Base (MIB) for Address Family Transition Routers (AFTRs)
RFC7870.summary: Defines the DSLite-MIB SNMP module for managing DS-Lite Address Family Transition Routers (AFTRs), covering tunnels, NAT bindings, statistics and threshold notifications.

DS-Lite.why: The MIB exists to manage DS-Lite AFTRs (tunnel concentrator plus carrier-grade NAT), so readers of DS-Lite would want it.
DS-Lite.quote: it defines managed objects for Address Family Transition Routers (AFTRs) of Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite).

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module definition (DSLite-MIB) with object groups, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access mechanism for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag covers it.
The NAT binding table extends the NATV2-MIB, but the document is about DS-Lite management, not NAT behaviour in general.
The IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel is a DS-Lite component. The document defines a tunnel type and objects for it, not the encapsulation.
The AFTR contains a carrier-grade NAT, but the document does not address CGN as a subject.
DS-Lite is a transition mechanism, but the more specific DS-Lite tag already covers it.
This is an SMIv2 MIB, not a YANG model.

RFC7871.title: Client Subnet in DNS Queries
RFC7871.summary: Documents the deployed EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) option (code 8) that carries client network prefix information in DNS queries so authoritative servers can tailor responses, with caching, privacy and security guidance.

EDNS.why: The document defines the edns-client-subnet EDNS0 option, its format, and its processing rules by resolvers and authoritative servers.
EDNS.quote: This document describes an Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS0) option that is in active use to carry information about the network that originated a DNS query

rejected.why: EDNS is the more specific child tag that fits; the DNS parent is implied.
Section 9 only briefly gives DNSSEC scoping recommendations; the document is not about DNSSEC.
Privacy is discussed as a shortcoming, but the document does not address encrypted or privacy-preserving DNS transport.
CDNs are the motivating use case for tailored responses, but the document does not specify CDN functionality.
Section 10 gives short NAT considerations only; NAT is not a subject of the document.
Privacy is a concern raised in Section 2 and Section 11.1, but the document is not a general privacy treatment.

RFC7872.title: Observations on the Dropping of Packets with IPv6 Extension Headers in the Real World
RFC7872.summary: Reports measurements of how often IPv6 packets carrying extension headers (Hop-by-Hop, Destination Options, Fragment) are dropped on paths to public web, mail and name servers, where the drops occur, and how to reproduce the experiment.

IPv6.why: The whole document is about IPv6 extension header handling and deployability, including fragmentation, in the real Internet.
IPv6.quote: This document presents real-world data regarding the extent to which packets with IPv6 Extension Headers (EHs) are dropped in the Internet

performance measurement.why: It is a measurement study with a reproducible methodology (Appendices A and B) for active probing and locating the dropping node.
performance measurement.quote: This document also explains how the results were obtained, such that the corresponding measurements can be reproduced by other members of the community

rejected.why: Traceroute with EHs is used to isolate the dropping node, but the document is not about the tool itself.
TCP is only the upper-layer protocol of the probe packets.
AAAA, MX and NS lookups are only used to build target lists; name servers are just one destination type.
Filtering of EH packets is discussed, but the document is a measurement problem statement and gives no security practice guidance.
Mail servers (port 25) are only probe targets.

RFC7873.title: Domain Name System (DNS) Cookies
RFC7873.summary: Defines the DNS COOKIE EDNS(0) option, a lightweight transaction-security mechanism using client and server cookies to protect DNS servers and clients against off-path denial-of-service, amplification and cache-poisoning attacks, with NAT and anycast guidance.

EDNS.why: The document specifies a new EDNS(0) option (code 10, COOKIE) and its processing, so readers of EDNS options would expect it.
EDNS.quote: The DNS COOKIE option is an OPT RR [RFC6891] option that can be included in the RDATA portion of an OPT RR in DNS requests and responses.

DNS.why: It extends DNS protocol behaviour for clients and servers, adds the BADCOOKIE RCODE, and extends QUERY to allow an empty Question Section.
DNS.quote: DNS Cookies, a lightweight DNS transaction security mechanism specified as an OPT [RFC6891] option.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is discussed only as existing data security and why it is not a substitute; the document does not specify or extend it.
There is a section on anycast server considerations, but it covers how to make cookies work with anycast. It is not about anycast addressing in general.
NAT considerations shape the cookie design, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.
HMAC-SHA256 appears only in example cookie algorithms in the appendices.
TCP is mentioned as a fallback with comparable protection, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Denial-of-service is the threat motivating the mechanism, but the document specifies a DNS option, not DDoS mitigation signalling.

RFC7874.title: WebRTC Audio Codec and Processing Requirements
RFC7874.summary: Specifies mandatory-to-implement audio codecs (Opus, G.711, CN, telephone-event DTMF) and audio level and echo cancellation requirements for WebRTC endpoints.

WebRTC.why: The whole document defines requirements for WebRTC endpoints: codecs, audio level, and AEC.
WebRTC.quote: This specification will outline the audio processing and codec requirements for WebRTC endpoints.

Opus.why: Opus is the primary mandatory codec. The document also sets decoder mode requirements and offer ordering for it.
Opus.quote: Opus [RFC6716] with the payload format specified in [RFC7587].

G.711.why: G.711 PCMA/PCMU is a mandatory codec and the basis for legacy phone interoperability.
G.711.quote: PCMA and PCMU (as specified in ITU-T Recommendation G.711 [G.711])

rejected.why: The document only cites existing payload formats (RFC 7587, RFC 3551, RFC 3389, RFC 4733). It defines none.
RTP is the substrate. The document only requires codecs and payload formats carried over it.
The specific child tags (Opus, G.711) fit better than the parent.
The offer/answer mechanism is mentioned only in passing, to signal a mode or ptime preference.
The legacy VoIP interoperability section is a single sentence, so it is not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: Audio processing (AEC, AGC, audio level)
gaps.why: Sections 4 and 5 cover audio level normalization, AGC, and acoustic echo cancellation. The taxonomy has no tag for endpoint audio signal processing.

RFC7875.title: Additional WebRTC Audio Codecs for Interoperability
RFC7875.summary: Informational guidance recommending that WebRTC endpoints additionally support AMR-WB, AMR and G.722 audio codecs (beyond mandatory Opus and G.711) to avoid transcoding when interoperating with legacy mobile, VoLTE and DECT networks.

WebRTC.why: The document is guidance for WebRTC endpoints on which audio codecs to offer for interoperability with non-WebRTC endpoints.
WebRTC.quote: This document provides some guidelines on the suitable codecs to be considered for WebRTC endpoints to address the use cases most relevant to interoperability.

AMR.why: Two of the three codec sections cover AMR-WB and AMR: their use cases and usage guidelines for WebRTC.
AMR.quote: The payload format to be used for AMR-WB is described in [RFC4867] with a bandwidth-efficient format and one speech frame encapsulated in each RTP packet.

G.722.why: One of the three codecs recommended, with its use case for DECT CAT-iq and IMS interworking and implementation guidelines.
G.722.quote: G.722 [G.722] is an ITU-T-defined wideband speech codec.

rejected.why: Opus is the mandatory codec mentioned only as the baseline; the document is about the additional codecs.
G.711 is mentioned as the narrowband fallback, not something the document specifies or recommends anew.
Payload formats are only cited from RFC4867 and RFC3551; the document defines none.
SDP is mentioned only in passing for the G.722 clock rate quirk.
The specific codec tags (AMR, G.722) fit more precisely, so the parent is not chosen.
Legacy networks are the motivation, but the document is about codec choice, not gateway or signalling interworking.

RFC7876.title: UDP Return Path for Packet Loss and Delay Measurement for MPLS Networks
RFC7876.summary: Specifies a UDP Return Object TLV allowing MPLS packet loss and delay measurement (RFC 6374) Responses to be returned out-of-band over UDP/IP to a querier-specified address and port.

performance measurement.why: The document extends RFC 6374 MPLS packet loss and delay measurement with a UDP return path, so it belongs under performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This document specifies the procedures to be used when sending and processing out-of-band MPLS performance management Responses over an UDP/IP return path.

MPLS.why: The measurement runs on MPLS LSPs and the Associated Channel, and the document adds an MPLS LM/DM TLV. MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: The mechanisms defined in this document can apply to both IP/MPLS and to the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP)

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport used for the return path. The document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
MPLS-TP is mentioned as an environment where the mechanism applies, but the document is not about it.
The measurement is OAM-like, but the more specific performance measurement tag fits better.
The congestion section only applies RFC 5405 guidance and is brief.
The IANA section is boilerplate, just one TLV code assignment.

RFC7877.title: Session Peering Provisioning Framework (SPPF)
RFC7877.summary: RFC 7877 specifies the Session Peering Provisioning Framework (SPPF), an XML-schema-based data model and operation set for provisioning Session Establishment Data (SED) into peering Registries, as used by DRINKS.

SPEERMINT.why: The framework provisions session peering data (SED, SSP, peering organizations) between SIP service providers. It is the provisioning side of SPEERMINT peering, and the taxonomy entry explicitly covers peering provisioning.
SPEERMINT.quote: a framework to provision Session Establishment Data (SED) into Session Data Registries and SIP Service Provider (SSP) data stores

rejected.why: SIP is where the provisioned data is used for call routing. SPPF only provisions that data and does not specify or extend SIP.
NAPTR records and ENUM services appear in the data model. The document only provisions data that ENUM resolution may serve and does not specify ENUM.
XML Schema is the notation for the data model and Section 8 has XML considerations. It is the encoding substrate, not the subject.
NAPTR and NS record types are provisioned as SED records. The document does not specify DNS behaviour.
HTTP and SOAP are mentioned only as the substrate in RFC 7878 and in the security considerations.
Registrar and Registrant roles are borrowed from the ENUM validation architecture. The registry is of session peering data, not domain names.

gaps.name: Session peering provisioning (DRINKS)
gaps.why: The document is about provisioning SED into registries, a data-registry provisioning framework. The taxonomy has only the SPEERMINT tag, which is broader peering, so the fit is approximate.

RFC7878.title: Session Peering Provisioning (SPP) Protocol over SOAP
RFC7878.summary: Specifies SOAP over HTTPS (with a WSDL definition and XML types) as the substrate protocol for the Session Peering Provisioning Framework (SPPF), used to provision SIP session establishment data into registries.

SPEERMINT.why: The taxonomy's SPEERMINT tag covers SIP service provider peering and peering provisioning. This document defines the SPPP protocol binding for provisioning session peering data (SED groups, offers, accept/reject) between SSPs and a Registry.
SPEERMINT.quote: this document specifies the usage of SOAP (via HTTPS) as the substrate protocol for SPPF

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 and Digest authentication are only the substrate the document relies on, with no new HTTP semantics defined.
TLS is only the required secure transport mechanism, with no new TLS extension defined.
XML and XSD are the encoding for the data structures, not the subject of the document.
SIP is the context of the peering data, but the protocol specified is provisioning, not SIP signalling.
HTTP Digest is merely mandated for authentication, with nothing new defined about it.
The NAPTR and TN data are carried in provisioning objects, but this document does not specify ENUM.

gaps.name: SOAP / Web Services (WSDL)
gaps.why: The document's core mechanism is SOAP 1.2 with a WSDL 1.1 document/literal wrapped definition, and the taxonomy has no tag for SOAP or web services.

RFC7879.title: DTLS-SRTP Handling in SIP Back-to-Back User Agents
RFC7879.summary: Specifies rules for SIP Back-to-Back User Agents (signaling and media-plane) so that they do not break end-to-end DTLS-SRTP sessions, including fingerprint forwarding, identity signature preservation, RTP/RTCP handling and forking.

SIP.why: The document defines required behavior for SIP B2BUAs, including which SIP headers they may modify, identity signature handling, and forking. It is about SIP deployment.
SIP.quote: B2BUAs MUST forward the certificate fingerprint and SDP setup attribute it receives from one endpoint unmodified towards the other endpoint and vice versa.
SIP.section: 3. B2BUAs Procedures to Allow End-to-End DTLS-SRTP

SRTP.why: A core subject is preserving end-to-end DTLS-SRTP keyed SRTP sessions and not breaking SRTP integrity protection in media-plane B2BUAs.
SRTP.quote: Both media relays and media-aware relays MUST NOT modify the authenticated portion of RTP and RTCP packets, and MUST NOT modify the authentication tag
SRTP.section: 3. B2BUAs Procedures to Allow End-to-End DTLS-SRTP

SDP.why: Rules cover which SDP attributes (fingerprint, setup, c= and m= lines) B2BUAs must leave unmodified or may rewrite, so SDP handling is a substantial part.
SDP.quote: forward the certificate fingerprint and SDP setup attribute it receives from one endpoint unmodified
SDP.section: 3. B2BUAs Procedures to Allow End-to-End DTLS-SRTP

rejected.why: DTLS is the keying mechanism for SRTP here; the document specifies nothing new about DTLS itself, only B2BUA behavior around it.
RTP and RTCP packets are inspected or forwarded, but the document does not specify RTP; SRTP is the more specific fit.
Identity signature mechanisms (RFC 4474 and the SIP-ID draft) are referenced as constraints on B2BUAs, but the document does not specify them.
Latching, TURN and ICE are mentioned only as context for why B2BUAs are deployed.
RTCP packets are only mentioned as traffic B2BUAs must not modify; the document defines no RTCP feedback or report mechanism.

gaps.name: SIP B2BUA (Back-to-Back User Agent)
gaps.why: The document is about B2BUA behavior, but the taxonomy has no tag for B2BUAs or SIP middleboxes. SIP is the nearest fit.

RFC7880.title: Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD)
RFC7880.summary: Defines Seamless BFD (S-BFD), a simplified BFD mode with stateless reflector sessions, S-BFD discriminators, and modified procedures and state machine for initiators, updating RFC 5880.

BFD.why: The whole document specifies S-BFD, an extension of BFD: discriminators, reflector sessions, initiator state machine, and echo function.
